name: Scanline-Based V-Buffer Algorithm
head: Polygon-based Raycasting, Sequential Scanline V-Buffer
body: The Scanline-Based V-Buffer Algorithm is a sequential volume rendering method that converts volumetric data into a set of polygons (triangles) and uses a scanline-based approach with a V-Buffer (a linked list of polygons per pixel) to determine ray intersections and perform compositing. It differs from standard Z-Buffer techniques by maintaining a linked list of all intersecting polygons for compositing rather than discarding them via depth testing, and it avoids the intensive pixel merging and strict back/front ordering constraints of projection algorithms. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volumetric dataset converted into a set of distinct triangles (e.g., by converting tetrahedrals or hexahedrals). A camera position and viewing direction. A transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the composited color and accumulated opacity. Data Structures Triangle List: A collection of triangles, where each triangle is defined by three vertices. Each vertex holds 3D coordinates and an associated scalar data value. V-Buffer: For each pixel (x, y), a linked list storing the intersection points of active polygons with the ray passing through that pixel. The list is ordered front-to-back. Active Polygon List: A global or scanline-local structure tracking polygons that intersect the current scanline, allowing incremental updates as the scanline moves. Steps 1. Polygon Conversion: Convert the volumetric data set into a set of polygons (specifically triangles). This is done by connecting data points (e.g., converting tetrahedrals or hexahedrals to triangles). This step is performed once and the polygonal representation is reused. 2. Scanline Rasterization: Iterate through the image scanline by scanline. For each scanline, maintain a linked list of active polygons. Update this list incrementally as the scanline moves from one line to the next, performing insertions and deletions of polygons that enter or leave the scanline. 3. Intersection Calculation: For each pixel in the current scanline, shoot a ray and determine the list of polygon intersections in front-to-back order. The location of each intersection is determined by intersecting the ray with the planes of the active polygons. 4. Sampling: For a single pixel, iterate through the sorted list of intersections. Take samples between each pair of consecutive triangles. The sampling point is typically the midpoint of the ray segment between two consecutive intersection points. 5. Interpolation: Compute the scalar value at the sampling point by interpolating the scalar values at the end points (vertices) of the intersected triangles. The source specifies using Inverse Distance Interpolation, though Trilinear interpolation is also mentioned as an alternative. Let the scalar values at the vertices of the relevant geometry be v1, v2, \dots, vk. Let the distances from the sampling point to these vertices be d1, d2, \dots, dk. The interpolated value V{sample} is calculated as: V{sample} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{k} \frac{vi}{di}}{\sum{i=1}^{k} \frac{1}{di}} Note: If di = 0, the vertex value is used directly or handled via a limit case. 6. Classification: Map the interpolated scalar value V{sample} to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha using a transfer function. 7. Compositing: Composite the sampled color and opacity into the pixel color using the front-to-back volume rendering equation, as defined in the parent article Direct volume ray casting. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Invalid Sampling Geometry: Sampling is prohibited or invalid if two consecutive triangles in the intersection list share only an external face (6 points) or only a single point (5 points). Valid sampling requires the triangles to share an edge (4 points) or be internal faces. If the number of unique vertices defining the space between two consecutive triangles is 6 (external faces) or 5 (single point shared), the sampling step must be skipped or handled specially. Ordering: The intersection list must be strictly ordered front-to-back to ensure correct compositing. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scanlinevbufferrender(triangles, imagewidth, imageheight, camera, transferfunction): """ Renders a volume using the Scanline-Based V-Buffer Algorithm. Args: triangles: List of Triangle objects. Each Triangle has vertices [v1, v2, v3]. Each Vertex has position (x, y, z) and scalar value 'val'. imagewidth, imageheight: Dimensions of the output image. camera: Object with method getray(x, y) returning ray origin and direction. transferfunction: Function mapping scalar value to (color, opacity). Returns: image: 2D array of composited colors. alphaimage: 2D array of accumulated opacities. """ # Initialize output buffers image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) alphaimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Pre-process triangles if necessary (e.g., ensure planar, store scalar values at vertices) # This step is assumed to be done once before rendering for tri in triangles: for vertex in tri.vertices: assert hasattr(vertex, 'val'), "Vertices must have scalar values" # Iterate over scanlines for y in range(imageheight): # Update active polygon list for the current scanline # This involves adding triangles that intersect the current y-range # and removing those that do not. activetriangles = getactivetrianglesforscanline(y, triangles) # Iterate over pixels in the scanline for x in range(imagewidth): # Get ray for this pixel rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) # Find intersections with active triangles # Returns a list of (intersectionpoint, triangle, distancet) intersections = [] for tri in activetriangles: hit = intersectraytriangle(rayorigin, raydirection, tri) if hit is not None: intersections.append(hit) # Sort intersections by distance t (front-to-back) intersections.sort(key=lambda item: item[2]) # Initialize compositing state for this pixel acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 # Iterate through intersections to sample between consecutive triangles for i in range(len(intersections) - 1): p1, tri1, t1 = intersections[i] p2, tri2, t2 = intersections[i+1] # Check validity of sampling between these two triangles # Valid if they share an edge (4 unique vertices) or are internal # Invalid if they share only a point (5 unique vertices) or external face (6 unique vertices) if not isvalidsamplingpair(tri1, tri2): continue # Calculate sampling point (midpoint) tsample = (t1 + t2) / 2.0 samplepoint = rayorigin + raydirection tsample # Interpolate scalar value at samplepoint # Using Inverse Distance Interpolation from vertices of the involved triangles # For simplicity, assume we interpolate from the 4 vertices of the quad formed by the shared edge # or all vertices of the two triangles if they don't share an edge but are valid. # The source mentions "end points of the triangles". vertices = getrelevantvertices(tri1, tri2) scalarval = inversedistanceinterpolation(samplepoint, vertices) # Map to color and opacity color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarval) # Composite # Cout = Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) c alpha # alphaout = alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alpha weight = (1.0 - accalpha) opacity acccolor[0] += weight color[0] acccolor[1] += weight color[1] acccolor[2] += weight color[2] accalpha += weight # Early termination if fully opaque if accalpha >= 1.0: break image[y, x] = acccolor alphaimage[y, x] = accalpha return image, alphaimage def isvalidsamplingpair(tri1, tri2): """ Checks if two consecutive triangles allow valid sampling. Valid: Share an edge (4 unique vertices) or are internal. Invalid: Share only a point (5 unique vertices) or external face (6 unique vertices). """ uniquevertices = set() for v in tri1.vertices: uniquevertices.add(id(v)) # Assuming vertex identity or position check for v in tri2.vertices: uniquevertices.add(id(v)) numunique = len(uniquevertices) # If 6 unique vertices, it's an external face pair -> Invalid if numunique == 6: return False # If 5 unique vertices, they share only a point -> Invalid if numunique == 5: return False # If 4 unique vertices, they share an edge -> Valid if numunique == 4: return True # Other cases (e.g., identical triangles, though unlikely in sorted list) # Should be handled or considered invalid depending on context. # Source implies "except external faces", so internal configurations are valid. return True def inversedistanceinterpolation(point, vertices): """ Computes scalar value at 'point' using Inverse Distance Interpolation from the scalar values of 'vertices'. """ numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for v in vertices: distsq = sum((point[i] - v.pos[i])2 for i in range(3)) dist = sqrt(distsq) # Guard against division by zero if point coincides with vertex if dist < 1e-9: return v.val invdist = 1.0 / dist numerator += v.val invdist denominator += invdist if denominator == 0: return 0.0 # Or average of values? Source doesn't specify. return numerator / denominator Time Complexity: The algorithm is sequential and processes pixels scanline by scanline. The complexity depends on the number of triangles T and the image resolution W \times H. For each pixel, ray-triangle intersection tests are performed against active triangles. In the worst case, this is O(W \cdot H \cdot T), but coherence and the V-Buffer structure reduce the number of active triangles per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the polygonal representation of the volume and the V-Buffer linked lists. The V-Buffer stores intersections per pixel, so memory usage scales with W \cdot H and the average number of intersections per pixel. Strengths: High image quality due to raycasting nature. Leverages scanline coherence for efficient intersection updates. Avoids post-processing merging required by projection methods. Allows easy application of parallel polygon rendering techniques. Limitations: Sequential nature limits parallelization compared to pure GPU raycasting. Requires preprocessing to convert volume to polygons. Performance degrades with high triangle counts. The validity check for sampling between triangles adds complexity. When to use: When high-quality volume rendering is needed and the data can be efficiently converted to polygons. Useful when multiple transfer functions need to be tested on the same view, as the polygonal structure and intersections are reused. When not to use: For very large datasets where polygon conversion is prohibitive. When real-time performance is critical and parallel GPU raycasting is available. The Scanline-Based V-Buffer Algorithm was proposed as a sequential volume rendering approach that combines ideas from raycasting and projection methods. It was introduced to address difficulties in parallelizing projection algorithms and to leverage the high quality of raycasting. The algorithm uses a V-Buffer to maintain a linked list of polygons for compositing, similar to the Z-Buffer but without depth testing discarding.;Г,,1:. name: Depth and Layer-Based Rendering
head: Depth-based Volume Rendering, Layered Volume Rendering
body: Depth and Layer-Based Rendering optimizes direct volume ray casting by decoupling the determination of ray entry and exit points from the volumetric sampling process, or by explicitly managing multiple non-overlapping ray segments per pixel. This family solves the performance bottlenecks of standard ray casting, such as redundant sampling in empty space and the inability to handle embedded geometric objects or multiple transfer functions in a single pass. It differs from standard Direct volume ray casting by using depth-buffered geometry rendering or pre-computed layer buffers to define precise integration intervals, enabling early fragment rejection and efficient handling of complex spatial overlaps. All methods in this family share the following core mechanism, building on Direct volume ray casting: 1. Ray Interval Definition: Instead of sampling the entire bounding box or a fixed number of steps, the method determines specific start (t{start}) and end (t{end}) parameters for the ray segment to be integrated. These intervals are derived either from geometric depth tests against the volume boundary (Two-Pass) or from a pre-computed buffer of non-overlapping segments (Multi-Layer). 2. Segmented Integration: The volume rendering equation is applied only within the defined intervals [t{start}, t{end}]. Samples are taken at positions ti = t{start} + i \cdot \Delta t where \Delta t = (t{end} - t{start}) / N{seg}. 3. Early Termination: Because the intervals often correspond to visible or opaque regions, these methods frequently employ early termination when accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} reaches 1.0, skipping remaining samples in the segment. 4. Material/Transfer Function Binding: In multi-layer variants, each segment is associated with a specific materialID or VOI priority, allowing the use of distinct transfer functions or shading models for different spatial regions (e.g., embedded objects vs. volume data). A GPU-based technique that determines ray entry and exit points by rendering the volume's bounding box geometry twice, then accumulates color along those rays in subsequent passes. It differs from standard ray casting by explicitly decoupling geometric intersection calculation from volumetric sampling, using depth-buffered rendering of the bounding box to provide precise start and end coordinates for each pixel's ray. This approach enables early fragment rejection via depth testing when opacity thresholds are met, optimizing performance for opaque regions. See Two-Pass Depth Ray Casting. A unified rendering framework that treats volume datasets and geometric objects (clipping geometry, embedded opaque/semi-transparent objects, editing masks, MPRs, and non-empty-space boundaries) as Volume-of-Interests (VOIs). It solves the problem of handling spatial overlaps, empty-space skipping, and multiple material-specific transfer functions in a single pass by encoding VOI interactions into a pre-generated ray-layer buffer. Unlike standard single-layer ray casting, which cannot skip empty spaces between visible samples or handle embedded objects producing multiple layers, this method explicitly stores non-overlapping ray segments per pixel. It differs from polygon-assisted ray casting and single-pass ray casters that store full 3D texture coordinates by storing only the Z-coordinate of the starting position, reducing memory usage and ensuring sampling alignment across bricks. See Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting. Renders a 2D projection of a 3D volume by alpha blending voxel values along rays, assuming pre-multiplied alpha. It offers two variants: a grayscale "Depth-8" mode that outputs a single channel, and an RGB mode that splits the ray into two halves for accumulation to approximate depth-aware color blending. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit two-pass accumulation structure in the RGB variant, which allows for specific depth-weighting strategies not present in standard single-pass ray casting. See Depth Alpha Blending Projection. A view-dependent method that reduces the traversal number to the scene depth complexity. It requires downloading depth images from video memory and resorting depth lists pixel-by-pixel on the CPU, affecting efficiency based on volume resolution. The concept of using depth information to optimize volume rendering has evolved alongside GPU hardware capabilities. Early implementations focused on using depth buffers to determine entry and exit points to avoid sampling empty space. The multi-layer approach was developed to handle complex scenes with embedded geometry and multiple materials, shifting computational workload to layer sorting to keep the ray-casting loop simple. The LDI approach was introduced as a voxelization alternative, though it noted significant CPU-side overhead for depth list resorting. name: Two-Pass Depth Ray Casting
head: Depth Peeling Ray Casting, Entry/Exit Depth Ray Casting, Krüger Ray-Casting, Ray-Casting de Krüger, Volumetric Ray-Casting
body: Two-Pass Depth Ray Casting is a GPU-based direct volume rendering technique that determines ray entry and exit points by rendering the volume's bounding box geometry twice, then accumulates color along those rays in subsequent passes. It differs from standard Volume Ray Casting by explicitly decoupling the geometric intersection calculation from the volumetric sampling, using depth-buffered rendering of the bounding box to provide precise start and end coordinates for each pixel's ray. This approach enables early fragment rejection via depth testing when opacity thresholds are met, optimizing performance for opaque regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D scalar volume texture (t{Volume}), transfer function texture (t{TFFunc}), viewport dimensions, volume resolution (t{DIM}), value span (v{Min}, v{Max}), and number of steps (steps). Output: Final composited color image in the render framebuffer. Data Structures: 1. Bounding Box Geometry: A cube defined by 8 vertices (each with 3 floats for position, 3 floats for color) and 36 indices (forming 12 triangles). 2. Render Targets: ProjInFB: Framebuffer storing entry coordinates. Resolution matches viewport. Texture format: FloatType, NearestFilter, ClampToEdge. ProjOutFB: Framebuffer storing exit coordinates. Same format as ProjInFB. RenderFB: Final output framebuffer. 3. Volume Texture: 3D texture (t{Volume}) with dimensions matching the dataset resolution. Format: RedFormat, LinearFilter, ClampToEdge. Steps: 1. Pass 1 (Entry Point): Render the bounding box with back-face culling enabled and depth test set to DEPTHLESS. Clear depth buffer to 1.0. The fragment shader outputs the world-space coordinates of the back-face intersection (ray entry point) to ProjInFB. 2. Pass 2 (Exit Point): Render the bounding box with front-face culling enabled and depth test set to DEPTHGREATER. Clear depth buffer to 0.0. The fragment shader outputs the world-space coordinates of the front-face intersection (ray exit point) to ProjOutFB. 3. Pass 3+ (Ray Casting & Accumulation): Render a fullscreen quad to RenderFB. Bind ProjInFB and ProjOutFB as textures providing ray start and end coordinates. For each pixel: Retrieve entry position (P{entry}) from ProjInFB and exit position (P{exit}) from ProjOutFB. Calculate ray vector: \vec{r} = P{exit} - P{entry}. Calculate ray length: L = \|\vec{r}\|. Calculate step size: \Delta = L / steps. Calculate step direction: \vec{d} = \text{normalize}(\vec{r}) \cdot \Delta. Initialize current position P{curr} = P{entry}, accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0,0), accumulated length L{acc} = 0. Loop for i = 0 to steps-1: Sample volume intensity: I = t{Volume}(P{curr}).r. Apply transfer function and adjustments: I' = \text{contrast} \cdot I + \text{brightness}. Threshold: If I' \leq \text{colorTreshLow} or I' \geq \text{colorTreshHigh}, set I' = 0. Compute color contribution C{step}: If I' \geq 0.5: C{step} = (I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \Delta, 0, 0, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \Delta). Else: C{step} = (I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \Delta, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \Delta, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \Delta, I' \cdot 2.56 \cdot \text{alphaCorrection} \cdot \Delta). Accumulate: C{acc} += C{step}. Update: L{acc} += \|\vec{d}\|, P{curr} += \vec{d}. Early Termination: If L{acc} \geq L or C{acc}.a \geq 1.0, break loop. Write C{acc} to RenderFB. Early Depth Test Optimization: In subsequent passes (if iterative), write a depth value forcing rejection for fragments that have reached maximum opacity, utilizing GPU early depth test to skip fragment shader execution for fully opaque pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setdepthtest(mode): pass # Sets glDepthFunc(mode) def setfaceculling(face): pass # Sets glCullFace(face) def cleardepth(value): pass # Sets glClearDepth(value) def bindframebuffer(fb): pass # Sets glFramebufferBinding(fb) def drawcube(): pass # Renders bounding box VAO/VBO def drawfullscreenquad(): pass # Renders screen quad VAO/VBO def renderentrypoint(): setdepthtest(LESS) setfaceculling(BACK) cleardepth(1.0) bindframebuffer(ProjInFB) drawcube() # Fragment Shader: glFragColor = vec4(worldSpaceCoords, 1.0) def renderexitpoint(): setdepthtest(GREATER) setfaceculling(FRONT) cleardepth(0.0) bindframebuffer(ProjOutFB) drawcube() # Fragment Shader: glFragColor = vec4(worldSpaceCoords, 1.0) def rendervolume(): bindframebuffer(RenderFB) bindtexture(ProjInFB, unit=0) # Entry coords bindtexture(ProjOutFB, unit=1) # Exit coords bindtexture(tVolume, unit=2) drawfullscreenquad() # Fragment Shader Logic: # 1. texc = vec2(((glFragCoord.x / viewport.w) 2.0 - 1.0), ((glFragCoord.y / viewport.h) 2.0 - 1.0)) # 2. Pentry = texture(ProjInFB, texc).xyz # 3. Pexit = texture(ProjOutFB, texc).xyz # 4. if Pentry.x == 0.0 and Pentry.y == 0.0: return vec4(0.0) # Invalid intersection # 5. ray = Pexit - Pentry # 6. raylen = length(ray) # 7. stepsize = raylen / steps # 8. deltadir = normalize(ray) stepsize # 9. currpos = Pentry # 10. acccolor = vec4(0.0) # 11. for i in range(steps): # intensity = texture(tVolume, currpos).r # intensity = contrast intensity + brightness # if intensity <= colorTreshLow or intensity >= colorTreshHigh: # intensity = 0.0 # if intensity >= 0.5: # colorstep = vec4(intensity 2.56 alphaCorrection stepsize, 0.0, 0.0, intensity 2.56 alphaCorrection stepsize) # else: # colorstep = vec4(intensity 2.56 alphaCorrection stepsize, intensity 2.56 alphaCorrection stepsize, intensity 2.56 alphaCorrection stepsize, intensity 2.56 alphaCorrection stepsize) # acccolor += colorstep # currpos += deltadir # if length(currpos - Pentry) >= raylen or acccolor.a >= 1.0: # break # 12. glFragColor = acccolor Parameters: steps: Number of samples along the ray. Default: 256. contrast: Multiplier for intensity. Default: 1.0. brightness: Offset for intensity. Default: 0.0. alphaCorrection: Scalar for alpha scaling. Default: 2.0. colorTreshLow: Lower intensity threshold. Default: 0.0. colorTreshHigh: Upper intensity threshold. Default: 1.0. tDIM: Volume resolution (voxels). vMin, vMax: Volume value span. Edge Cases: If the sampled backPosition has x=0.0 and y=0.0, it indicates an invalid intersection (likely at the edge of the cube where no back-face was rendered). The fragment returns vec4(0.0). Zero-sized viewport causes invalid framebuffer operations. Must check viewport.width > 0 and viewport.height > 0 before resizing. Encodes full 3D coordinates of entry/exit faces in 2D textures, avoiding per-ray intersection tests. Chose when bounding box geometry is static and coordinate mapping is preferred over depth buffer tricks. Combines intersection and casting in one pass. Chose for simpler pipelines where early depth test optimization is less critical or hardware supports it natively. Traces rays from surface to volume. Chose for surface-volume hybrid rendering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S) per pixel, where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps. The two initial passes are O(N) for bounding box rasterization. Subsequent passes are O(N \cdot S) but benefit from early depth test rejection. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D volume texture, plus O(N) for the two coordinate textures (entry/exit). Performance: Performance is significantly impacted by data volume size due to the rasterization of support primitives (bounding box) and the fixed number of steps. Early depth testing improves performance for opaque regions. Strengths: Precise entry/exit points; efficient early termination for opaque pixels; simple implementation on GPU. Limitations: Does not scale well with large data volumes due to the rasterization of many support primitives. When to Use: Interactive visualization of moderate-sized regular volumes where precise ray endpoints are needed and early termination is beneficial. When Not to Use: Very large datasets where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck; irregular volumes requiring complex intersection tests. The method was first proposed by Krüger [KW03] for Shader Model 2.0 GPUs. It was later extended by Scharsach [Sch05] to leverage Shader Model 3.0 features, including dynamic branching and block-based volume loading. It is a foundational technique for GPU-based direct volume rendering, particularly in medical imaging and scientific visualization. name: Volume Raycasting with Front/Back Face Depth Textures
head: Dual-Texture Enter/Exit Vector Method, Enter/Exit 3D vectors method, Entry/Exit Depth Ray Casting, Front/Back face texture method, Ray Casting with Pre-computed Entry/Exit Textures, Volume Ray Casting with Pre-computed Entry/Exit Textures
body: A volume rendering technique that visualizes 3D scalar fields by projecting a 2D screen onto a 3D volume's bounding box using pre-computed coordinate textures to map screen pixels to 3D entry and exit points, then marching along rays between these faces to accumulate color and alpha. It differs from standard ray casting by avoiding per-ray intersection tests with the volume geometry; instead, it relies on two 2D textures storing the 3D coordinates of the front and back faces of the volume's bounding box for each screen pixel. This method is a specific implementation of the two-pass depth ray casting approach, where the depth information is encoded as full 3D coordinates rather than just depth values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data), a 3D bounding box defining the volume extent, a camera view matrix, and a projection matrix. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and alpha of the ray passing through the volume. Data Structures: 1. 3D Texture: Stores the scalar field values. The layout is a matrix of Z slices with dimensions M \times N divisions in X and Y, and subdivisions in Z. Z increases from top to bottom (Z=0 at top). 2. Front Face Coordinate Texture: A 2D texture with resolution matching the screen (or target framebuffer). Each pixel's RGB value represents the 3D world coordinates (x, y, z) of the point on the front face of the bounding box corresponding to that screen pixel. 3. Back Face Coordinate Texture: A 2D texture with resolution matching the screen. Each pixel's RGB value represents the 3D world coordinates (x, y, z) of the point on the back face of the bounding box corresponding to that screen pixel. Parameters: Threshold: A scalar value below which field data is disregarded. Example value: 0.5 for a level set. Alpha Correction: A multiplier for the local alpha contribution, typically a number smaller than 1. Example value: 0.1. Step Size: The distance between samples along the ray. Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate Coordinate Textures: Initialize a framebuffer object (FBO) and allocate two RGBA UNSIGNEDBYTE textures (texEntr, texExit) with LINEAR mag/min filtering. Bind the FBO, set the viewport to the target resolution (e.g., 1024×1024), and enable face culling. Set cull mode to BACK, bind texExit to COLORATTACHMENT0, clear the color and depth buffers, and draw the bounding box (e.g., a cube from (0,0,0) to (1,1,1)). Set cull mode to FRONT, bind texEntr to COLORATTACHMENT0, clear the buffers, and draw the bounding box again. The fragment shader for these passes outputs the 3D world coordinates of the fragment. 2. Ray Casting Pass: Bind texEntr to texture unit 0, texExit to unit 1, the volume texture to unit 2, and the transfer function texture to unit 3. Draw a full-screen quad (TRIANGLEFAN). For each pixel: retrieve the 3D front point P{front} from texEntr and the 3D back point P{back} from texExit. Construct the ray vector \vec{R} = P{back} - P{front}. Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0, 0, 0) and accumulated alpha A{acc} = 0. Iterate along the ray from P{front} towards P{back} with a small step size \Delta s. Sample the 3D field value v at the current position using trilinear interpolation from the 3D Texture. If v is above the Threshold: calculate local color c and local alpha \alpha based on v (using a transfer function), update accumulated color C{acc} = C{acc} + c \times \alpha{correction}, and update accumulated alpha A{acc} = A{acc} + \alpha. If A{acc} \ge 1 or the back face is reached, break the loop. The final color for the pixel is C{acc}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercoordinatetextures(viewmatrix, projmatrix, boundingbox, textureback, texturefront): """ Pass 1: Render back face coordinates. Pass 2: Render front face coordinates. """ # Sources do not provide the exact shader logic for coordinate generation. pass def volumeraycasting(frontcoordtexture, backcoordtexture, volumetexture, transferfunction, threshold, alphacorrection, stepsize): """ Main raycasting pass. """ outputimage = empty2dtexture() for u, v in outputimage.dimensions(): # 1. Retrieve entry and exit points Pfront = frontcoordtexture.sample(u, v) Pback = backcoordtexture.sample(u, v) # 2. Construct ray rayvector = Pback - Pfront raylength = length(rayvector) raydirection = normalize(rayvector) # 3. Initialize accumulators Cacc = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Aacc = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < raylength: Pcurr = Pfront + raydirection t v = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(Pcurr) # Check threshold if v > threshold: # Calculate local color and alpha based on v c, alpha = transferfunction(v) # Update accumulators Cacc = tuple(Cacc[i] + c[i] alphacorrection for i in range(3)) Aacc = Aacc + alpha # Check for termination if Aacc >= 1.0: break t += stepsize # 5. Store result outputimage.setpixel(u, v, Cacc) return outputimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premature Termination: The loop must break if accumulated alpha reaches 1 (full opacity) to avoid unnecessary computation, or if the back face is reached. Degenerate Input: If the camera is inside the volume, the front and back face coordinates might be swapped or invalid. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The use of pre-computed coordinates avoids expensive ray-box intersection tests per pixel, but requires two additional render passes for coordinate generation. Limitations: Precision of the coordinate textures can affect accuracy. Not given in the sources. When to use: Static volumes with simple bounding boxes. Not given in the sources. When not to use: Dynamic volumes where the bounding box changes frequently, as the coordinate textures must be regenerated. Not given in the sources. name: Hardware-Assisted Volume Ray-Casting with Depth Buffer Culling
head: Hardware-Accelerated Volume Ray-Casting using Texture Mapping, Texture-based rendering pass with software ray-casting, Two-pass volume rendering (texture pass + ray-cast pass)
body: This method accelerates software-based volume ray-casting by using a hardware-accelerated 2D texture mapping pass to determine the entry points of rays into non-transparent material, effectively creating a 3D stencil that allows the subsequent software ray-caster to skip empty space. It differs from pure texture-based rendering by accurately composing material contributions along the ray in the second pass, avoiding artifacts from limited precision in OpenGL compositing, and from hierarchical methods by requiring no auxiliary data structure rebuilding, thus enabling interactive classification. The method consists of two main phases: a hardware-accelerated texture rendering pass to generate an intermediate depth image, and a software-based ray-casting pass that uses this depth information to optimize traversal. Input: 3D scalar volume data (typically 8-bit per sample, though arbitrary resolution is supported in the second pass), camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix), and two transfer functions (one for culling/classification in Pass 1, one for shading in Pass 2). Output: A final rendered image where rays are cast only through regions containing material, with early termination based on opacity cutoffs. 1. Texture Stacks: The 3D voxel data is decomposed into three stacks of 2D textures, corresponding to the three object-space axes (X, Y, Z). 2. Intermediate Depth Image: A 2D buffer storing depth values for each pixel, generated in Pass 1. This serves as the "3D stencil". 3. Depth Buffer: The GPU's depth buffer, from which values are read back to main memory. Opacity Cutoff: The threshold for accumulated opacity to stop ray traversal in Pass 2. Typical value: 95%. Sampling Interval: In Pass 1, the distance between texture slices is adjusted to ensure view-independent sampling. The sample distance is typically set to half the voxel size. Transfer Functions: Two separate functions are generally required: 1. Maps 8-bit texture values to alpha values for culling in Pass 1. 2. Maps original scalar values to color values for shading in Pass 2. 1. View Analysis and Texture Selection: For the current view V, determine the object-space axis most parallel to the viewing direction. Select the corresponding stack of 2D textures from the three available stacks. 2. View-Independent Resampling (Pass 1 Preparation): Compute the offset dV for the current view. Generate new texture slices at positions k \cdot dV between original slices to ensure uniform sampling intervals regardless of viewing angle, preventing small features from being missed due to view-dependent sampling distance increases. Implementation Note: Use multitexturing and texture combiners to linearly interpolate between two original texture slices in a single pass. Interpolation factors are issued as separate colors to modulate multitexture samples before blending. 3. Hardware-Accelerated Texture Rendering (Pass 1): Render the selected 2D texture stacks to generate an intermediate image. Perform 2D texture resampling. Apply the first transfer function (culling) during texture lookup. Discard fragments with alpha below a specific threshold. Optimization (Iso-surface mode): Traverse rays until hitting a cell containing the classification threshold. Calculate the intersection with the iso-surface, shade using an approximated gradient, and stop traversal. Smooth mode: Continue traversal until opacity cutoff (95%) is reached. The resulting depth buffer contains the depth values of the first hit for each pixel. 4. Depth Buffer Access (ZbOps): Read depth values from the GPU depth buffer into main memory. Compute screen space coordinates for each pixel. This time depends only on image resolution, not data complexity. 5. Software Ray-Casting (Pass 2): Perform volume ray-casting in software. Use the intermediate image/depth buffer to determine the exact position of the first intersection point with non-transparent material. Start ray traversal right in front of these regions, skipping empty space. Traverse rays until the accumulated opacity reaches the cutoff (e.g., 95%) or the exit point is determined. Shading: Compute opacity-weighted color samples from pre-shaded texture samples. Approximate gradients on-the-fly using central differences and tri-linear interpolation. Transform screen space coordinates into local object coordinates. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwareassistedvolumeraycasting(volumedata, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, transferfunccull, transferfuncshade, opacitycutoff=0.95): """ volumedata: 3D array of scalar values viewmatrix: 4x4 matrix for camera orientation projectionmatrix: 4x4 matrix for projection transferfunccull: function mapping scalar -> alpha (for Pass 1) transferfuncshade: function mapping scalar -> color (for Pass 2) opacitycutoff: float, threshold to stop ray traversal in Pass 2 """ # Step 1: Determine texture stack viewdirection = normalize(viewmatrix[2][:3]) # Assuming standard OpenGL view direction axes = [ (1, 0, 0), # X-axis stack (0, 1, 0), # Y-axis stack (0, 0, 1) # Z-axis stack ] # Select axis most parallel to view direction maxdot = -1 selectedaxisidx = 0 for i, axis in enumerate(axes): dot = abs(dotproduct(viewdirection, axis)) if dot > maxdot: maxdot = dot selectedaxisidx = i texturestack = decomposevolumeinto2dstacks(volumedata)[selectedaxisidx] # Step 2: View-independent resampling # Compute offset dV based on view angle dV = computeviewdependentoffset(viewdirection, texturestack) # Generate interpolated texture slices for uniform sampling # This involves multitexturing and texture combiners in hardware interpolatedtextures = generateinterpolatedslices(texturestack, dV) # Step 3: Pass 1 - Hardware Texture Rendering # Render interpolatedtextures to a framebuffer with depth testing # Apply transferfunccull to determine alpha # Discard fragments with alpha < threshold # Store depth values in depth buffer rendertexturepass(interpolatedtextures, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, transferfunccull) # Step 4: Depth Buffer Access # Read depth buffer to main memory depthbuffer = readdepthbuffer() # Step 5: Pass 2 - Software Ray-Casting imagewidth, imageheight = getimagedimensions() resultimage = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): depth = depthbuffer[y][x] # Compute ray origin and direction in object space rayorigin, raydirection = screentoray(x, y, depth, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix) # Determine entry point from depth buffer # The depth buffer gives the first hit with non-transparent material entrypoint = computeentrypoint(rayorigin, raydirection, depth) # Start ray casting from entrypoint accumulatedopacity = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Traverse ray from entrypoint to exitpoint or until opacitycutoff # Exit point can be determined by the depth buffer or by reaching the end of the volume # For simplicity, assume we traverse until opacitycutoff or end of volume currentpos = entrypoint stepsize = computestepsize(volumedata) while accumulatedopacity < opacitycutoff and isinsidevolume(currentpos): # Sample volume data scalarvalue = trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, currentpos) # Compute color and alpha using transferfuncshade samplecolor, samplealpha = transferfuncshade(scalarvalue) # Pre-shaded sample: color is already weighted by alpha in the transfer function? # Or compute opacity-weighted color: # color += samplecolor samplealpha (1 - accumulatedopacity) # accumulatedopacity += samplealpha (1 - accumulatedopacity) # Note: The source mentions "opacity-weighted color samples from pre-shaded texture samples" # and "gradients are approximated on-the-fly". # For iso-surface mode, shading happens at intersection. # For smooth mode, shading happens along the ray. # Update position currentpos += raydirection stepsize resultimage[y][x] = color return resultimage def computeviewdependentoffset(viewdirection, texturestack): """ Computes the offset dV to ensure view-independent sampling. The sample distance is typically half the voxel size. """ # Implementation depends on specific geometry of texture stack and view # This is a placeholder for the complex calculation described in # involving the angle between object space axis and viewing direction. return 0.5 # Placeholder for half voxel size def screentoray(x, y, depth, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix): """ Transforms screen coordinates and depth to ray origin and direction in object space. """ # Standard inverse projection and view matrix multiplication # Returns rayorigin and raydirection in world/object space pass def trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, pos): """ Performs tri-linear interpolation on the volume data at position pos. """ # Standard tri-linear interpolation pass View-Dependent Sampling: Pure 2D texture mapping causes small features to be missed if the sample distance increases with the angle between the object space axis and viewing direction. This is handled by generating intermediate slices. 3D Texture Performance: Using 3D texture mapping causes a performance loss of up to 60% in fill rate due to irregular memory access patterns. The method restricts itself to 2D textures. Expansive Homogeneous Structures: The method fails for expansive homogeneous structures with high transparency, where early ray termination cannot be applied effectively. In such cases, pyramidal approaches yield better results. Depth Buffer Access: Non-optimized depth buffer access on the target architecture (GeForce2) results in poor performance for the ZbOps step, though it remains constant relative to data complexity. Precision: The method avoids artifacts from separate interpolation of color and opacity and limited precision of internal pixel/texture formats found in OpenGL compositing, which are issues in pure texture-based techniques. Time Complexity: The complexity of the first rendering pass does not depend on the complexity of the structures in the data. Rendering time and memory requirements remain constant independent of the current classification. The time for depth buffer access (ZbOps) depends only on image resolution, remaining constant across experiments. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory to generate the texture representation, but avoids the need for auxiliary data structures required by other techniques. Measured Performance: On a Pentium III 733 MHz / GeForce2 32MB: 128^3 head CT (512x512 image): Total=0.83s (iso) / 4.06s (smooth). 256^2x128 engine block (512x512 image): Total=0.71s (iso) / 5.60s (smooth). 256^3 aneurysm MRI (512x512 image): Total=0.84s (iso) / 3.58s (smooth). Strengths: Enables interactive classification via texture color tables without rebuilding auxiliary data structures. Accurately performs composition of material contributions. Handles fuzzy and complex vascular structures without performance degradation. Limitations: Fails for expansive homogeneous structures with high transparency. Requires reading depth buffer to main memory, which can be a bottleneck if not optimized. When to Use: When interactive classification is required, or when the data contains complex structures where hierarchical methods are cumbersome. Suitable for consumer-grade GPUs with 2D texture support. When Not to Use: For expansive homogeneous structures with high transparency, where pyramidal approaches are better. Origin: Proposed in a 2001 paper by the authors of, targeting the consumer market with affordable graphics units like the nVidia GeForce family. History: Built upon earlier texture-based volume rendering techniques. The method was implemented in a volume rendering tool integrated with C. Reszk-Salama's tool. Usage: Tested on human head CT, engine block, and aneurysm MRI datasets. name: Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting
head: raycast1Layer, segment-by-segment ray casting
body: Multi-layer volume ray casting is a unified rendering framework that treats volume datasets and geometric objects (clipping geometry, embedded opaque/semi-transparent objects, editing masks, MPRs, and non-empty-space boundaries) as Volume-of-Interests (VOIs). It solves the problem of handling spatial overlaps, empty-space skipping, and multiple material-specific transfer functions in a single pass by encoding VOI interactions into a pre-generated ray-layer buffer. Unlike standard single-layer ray casting, which cannot skip empty spaces between visible samples or handle embedded objects producing multiple layers, this method explicitly stores non-overlapping ray segments per pixel. It differs from polygon-assisted ray casting and single-pass ray casters that store full 3D texture coordinates by storing only the Z-coordinate of the starting position, reducing memory usage and ensuring sampling alignment across bricks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset partitioned into bricks, a set of VOIs (each with a priority number and material ID), and a pre-generated ray-layer buffer. Output: The final composited image color and opacity. Data Structures: Ray-Layer Buffer: A per-pixel array of ray segments. Each segment stores: rayStart: The starting Z-coordinate (depth) of the segment. rayEnd: The ending Z-coordinate of the segment. materialID: An integer identifying the material properties (e.g., transfer function) for this segment. Note: The buffer encodes a set of non-overlapping ray segments for each pixel. Parameters: renderMpr: A boolean flag indicating whether Multi-Planar Reformation (MPR) layers should be rendered before standard ray casting for the current segment. VOI Priority: An integer assigned to each VOI. Higher priority overwrites lower priority in overlapped regions. Multiple VOIs with identical priorities are blended. Default VOI: The implicit bounding box of the volume dataset, assigned the lowest priority. Voxels excluded by all other VOIs are rendered according to this default. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Layer Buffer Generation (Pre-processing): Convert all VOI information into a ray-layer buffer. Perform depth peeling on all VOI boundaries. Organize peeled fragments into layers based on VOI priority and material ID. For each pixel, encode a set of non-overlapping ray segments, recording rayStart, rayEnd, and materialID. Note: This step shifts computational workload to layer sorting to keep the ray-casting loop simple. 2. Multi-Layer Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel, fetch and decode the current layer information from the ray-layer buffer, including rayStart, rayEnd, and materialID. If the segment is valid, call raycast1Layer with these parameters. raycast1Layer returns a Boolean flag: true: Continue to the next layer in the buffer. false: Terminate the ray for the current brick. 3. Single Layer Ray Casting (raycast1Layer): Brick Boundary Check: Check if rayStart is behind the far end of the current brick. If so, return false to terminate the ray for the current brick. MPR Rendering: If renderMpr is set, render the MPR layer in the intersection of [rayStart, rayEnd] with the current brick before standard ray casting. Standard Ray Casting: Cast rays segment-by-segment within [rayStart, rayEnd] using the materialID to select the appropriate transfer function and viewing parameters. Transfer functions are stacked into a single 2D texture, with texture coordinate offsets calculated as materialID × D, where D is the size of a single transfer function. Use the ray-layer buffer to estimate gradients on layer surfaces to improve shading effects. Opacity Check: Inspect accumulated opacity to determine possible early termination. Termination Check: Check if rayEnd is behind the far end of the brick. If yes, return false (termination). Otherwise, return true to continue to the next ray segment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multilayervolumeraycasting(volumedata, raylayerbuffer, bricks, rendermprflag=False): height = len(raylayerbuffer) width = len(raylayerbuffer[0]) image = [[None] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): segments = raylayerbuffer[y][x] acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 for seg in segments: raystart = seg.startz rayend = seg.endz materialid = seg.materialid # Find brick containing raystart brick = None for b in bricks: if b.startz <= raystart < b.endz: brick = b break if brick is None: continue terminated = raycast1layer(volumedata, brick, raystart, rayend, materialid, acccolor, accopacity, rendermprflag) if terminated: break image[y][x] = acccolor return image def raycast1layer(volumedata, brick, raystart, rayend, materialid, acccolor, accopacity, rendermprflag): # Check if rayStart is behind the far end of the current brick if raystart >= brick.endz: return True # Optional: Render MPR layer if flag is set if rendermprflag: # Render MPR layer in the intersection of [raystart, rayend] with the current brick # Implementation details for MPR rendering are not given in the sources. pass # Standard front-to-back compositing for the segment # See Parent for sampling, interpolation, and transfer function details # Number of samples per segment is not given in the sources. numsamples = 16 # Not given in the sources. dt = (rayend - raystart) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = raystart + i dt # Sample volume value V(pi) and apply transfer function T(V) -> (ci, alphai) # Transfer function lookup uses offset: materialid D, where D is the size of a single transfer function alphai = 0.0 # Not given in the sources. colori = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Not given in the sources. # Front-to-back compositing acccolor[0] += (1.0 - accopacity) colori[0] alphai acccolor[1] += (1.0 - accopacity) colori[1] alphai acccolor[2] += (1.0 - accopacity) colori[2] alphai accopacity += (1.0 - accopacity) alphai # Inspect accumulated opacity to determine possible termination if accopacity >= 1.0: break # Check if rayEnd is behind the far end of the brick if rayend >= brick.endz: return True return False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Spaces: Single-layer ray casting cannot skip empty spaces between the first and last visible samples. Multi-layer encoding solves this by explicitly storing non-overlapping segments. Embedded Objects: Single-layer representation cannot cope with embedded objects that produce multiple layers. The ray-layer buffer explicitly handles these. Bricking Compatibility: Storing only the Z value of the starting position ensures sampling locations align across bricks, which is required for bricking. Generates the ray-layer buffer by depth-peeling VOI definitions and grouping fragments into ordered layers based on VOI priority and material ID. It differs from standard GPU-based CSG by performing stencil-like tests inside a GPU program, preserving priority and ID information. Determines optimal split points along a ray to separate high-quality raycasting from lower-cost image warping. It identifies specific volumetric features for light attenuation, preserving depth cues better than simple depth-based splitting. Time Complexity: The multi-pass depth peeling cost is nearly ignorable compared to the ray casting cost. The algorithm shifts computational workload to layer sorting to keep the ray-casting loop as simple as possible. Memory Complexity: The ray-layer buffer stores only the Z value of the starting position and material ID per segment, which is less memory-intensive than storing full 3D texture coordinates. Performance: Using a single shared ray-layer buffer for the whole volume (with bricking) is more efficient and easier to debug than using a different ray-layer buffer for each brick. Strengths: Supports interactive volume editing, cutaway views, and prioritized overlay of geometric masks, MPRs, and embedded objects. Transfer functions are stacked into a single 2D texture, with texture coordinate offsets calculated as materialID × D, where D is the size of a single transfer function. Limitations: Requires pre-generation of the ray-layer buffer, which involves depth peeling. Multi-layer volume ray casting was presented by Wei Li from Siemens Corporate Research. It integrates various volume rendering enhancements into a unified framework, including empty-space skipping, volume clipping, embedding opaque and semi-transparent objects, and volume editing through CSG operations. The method treats all these objects as VOIs, assigning priority numbers to resolve spatial overlaps. name: Ray-Layer Buffer Generation via Depth Peeling
head: VOI layer generation, peeling VOI definitions
body: This method generates the ray-layer buffer for Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting by depth-peeling Volume of Interest (VOI) definitions and grouping the resulting fragments into ordered layers based on material ID and priority. It solves the problem of correctly determining the visibility and enclosure of nested, potentially self-intersecting VOIs on the GPU, where standard stencil buffers fail to preserve the critical priority and ID information required for per-layer transfer function application. Unlike standard GPU-based Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) which uses hardware stencil buffers to count front/back fragments, this method performs similar logic inside a GPU fragment program to maintain full control over layer complexity and material assignment. Inputs: A set of VOI definitions, each associated with a unique Material ID (mtId) and a priority value. Clipping meshes (optional, used to define view frustum or user-defined boundaries). Multi-Planar Reformation (MPR) meshes (optional, representing explicit planar data). A depth-peeling renderer that outputs fragments with depth, facing (front/back), and mesh ID. Outputs: A ray-layer buffer: an array of entries per ray (pixel), where each entry contains a depth, a material ID, and potentially other metadata required for ray casting. Data Structures: insideFlag array: An array indexed by Material ID. It stores the net count of front-facing minus back-facing fragments for each VOI. rayLayerBuffer: The output structure storing the sequence of layers for each ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Peeling: Render the scene using a depth-peeling algorithm [Eve01]. For each pass k, render only fragments with depth greater than the k-th peeled depth. 2. Inside Flag Update: For every fragment generated (even if discarded by the peeling depth test), update the insideFlag array for its associated Material ID. If the fragment is front-facing, increment insideFlag[mtId]. If the fragment is back-facing, decrement insideFlag[mtId]. 3. Determine Current Material: Scan the insideFlag array to find the Material ID of the enclosing VOI with the highest priority, denoted as currentId. A VOI is considered enclosing if its insideFlag is non-zero, indicating the ray is inside the volume defined by that VOI. Priority determines which VOI takes precedence if multiple VOIs enclose the same point. 4. Layer Buffer Writing: Compare currentId with the material ID of the previous layer in the rayLayerBuffer for the current ray. If currentId differs from the previous layer's ID, write a new entry to the buffer with currentId and the current fragment's depth. A back-facing fragment indicates the exit of a contributing VOI, so currentId will differ from the ID of the VOI being exited. 5. Clipping Mesh Handling: If the fragment belongs to a clipping mesh: if front-facing, clear all previous layers in the rayLayerBuffer for this ray. If back-facing, mark layer generation as finished for this ray. 6. MPR Mesh Handling: If the fragment belongs to an MPR mesh: write the MPR layer directly to the buffer. If the MPR is inside a non-empty layer, append an entry with the same depth as the MPR but using the previous material ID to continue the intersected layer. 7. Optimization (Empty Space Merging): After generating layers, scan for empty segments between adjacent mtIdVolume layers. If the depth distance between two adjacent volume layers is shorter than a given threshold, merge them into a single layer to reduce buffer complexity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. allmaterialids = [...] # List of all known material IDs from VOI definitions backgroundid = 0 # ID representing empty/background space insideFlags = {mtId: 0 for mtId in allmaterialids} rayLayerBuffer = [] # List of layers for the current ray previousLayerId = backgroundid layergenerationfinished = False def processfragment(fragment): global previousLayerId, layergenerationfinished if layergenerationfinished: return # 1. Update inside flags for the fragment's material ID mtId = fragment.meshid if fragment.isfrontfacing: insideFlags[mtId] += 1 else: insideFlags[mtId] -= 1 # 2. Determine current enclosing material ID # Find mtId with non-zero insideFlag and highest priority currentId = backgroundid bestpriority = -float('inf') for id in allmaterialids: if insideFlags[id] != 0: # Enclosing priority = getpriority(id) # Lookup priority from VOI definitions if priority > bestpriority: bestpriority = priority currentId = id # 3. Handle Clipping Meshes if fragment.isclippingmesh: if fragment.isfrontfacing: # Clear previous layers rayLayerBuffer.clear() previousLayerId = backgroundid else: # Mark generation as finished layergenerationfinished = True return # 4. Handle MPR Meshes if fragment.ismprmesh: # Write MPR layer rayLayerBuffer.append({'depth': fragment.depth, 'materialid': fragment.mprmaterialid}) # If inside a non-empty layer, append continuation entry if previousLayerId != backgroundid: rayLayerBuffer.append({'depth': fragment.depth, 'materialid': previousLayerId}) previousLayerId = fragment.mprmaterialid return # 5. Handle VOI Fragments # If currentId differs from previous layer, write new layer if currentId != previousLayerId: rayLayerBuffer.append({'depth': fragment.depth, 'materialid': currentId}) previousLayerId = currentId Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Identical Depth Fragments: Standard peeling may output only one fragment when two fragments have identical depths, leading to incorrect insideFlags. This occurs when surface common points project exactly to pixel centers or when back-facing surfaces touch front-facing surfaces of the same VOI (common at bounding box corners). Hardware Depth Test Limitations: Modifying depth in a fragment program may disable hardware depth testing on some GPUs. A method to resolve ambiguity when two fragments at the same pixel have identical depths, which causes standard peeling to output only one and produce incorrect insideFlags. It encodes depth, facing, and mesh ID into a new number (similar to ray-layer buffer entry encoding) and sets it as the modified depth in the peeling fragment program. If hardware does not support depth testing with modified depth, the encoded value is written to a color channel and compared using MIN or MAX operations of the frame buffer. This issue is rare but common at corners/edges of non-empty-space bounding boxes where back-facing surfaces touch front-facing surfaces of the same VOI. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of depth peeling passes times the number of pixels, plus the cost of scanning insideFlags per fragment. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for insideFlags (size proportional to number of material IDs) and the ray-layer buffer (size proportional to number of layers per ray). Strengths: Correctly handles nested, self-intersecting VOIs and preserves material priority information which hardware stencil buffers cannot. Supports clipping and MPR meshes explicitly. Limitations: Requires multiple rendering passes for depth peeling. Identical depth handling adds complexity and potential hardware compatibility issues. When to use: When rendering complex scenes with nested, overlapping volumes where material priority and correct enclosure detection are critical, and standard CSG stencil methods are insufficient. The method originates from the work on Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting on GPU, specifically the layer generation phase. It was developed to address the limitations of standard GPU-based CSG stencil buffers in the context of volume rendering, where each VOI has a priority and ID critical for layer placement. The approach builds on depth peeling techniques [Eve01] and adapts them for volume data structures. Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting on GPU, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg10/005-012, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dual Depth Peeling
head: Bidirectional Depth Peeling, Depth Peeling Rendering Pipeline, Depth peeling loop, On-the-fly front-to-back peeling
body: Dual Depth Peeling is an order-independent transparency technique that decomposes a scene into depth layers by rendering primitives multiple times, discarding fragments closer than the previous layer, and blending the resulting layers to assemble the final image. It improves upon standard Depth Peeling by performing simultaneous peeling in both directions—front-to-back and back-to-front—thereby reducing the total number of rendering passes required for N layers by approximately N/2. Unlike standard Depth Peeling, which processes layers sequentially, this method resolves depth ordering per pixel, making it robust against self-intersecting surfaces that often complicate depth-sorting approaches. The method executes a depth peeling loop for each frame, consisting of iterative peel and blend stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Discrete representation of integral surfaces (e.g., triangles or quadrilaterals) with associated texture coordinates and normal vectors. Output: Final composited image with correct transparency and silhouette shading. Data Structures: 1. Color Buffer: A floating-point color buffer is used for blending to prevent banding artifacts when many surface layers are present. 2. Normal Buffer: A secondary floating-point RGBA buffer stores surface normals required for the blend stage. 3. Mask Buffer: The alpha component of the normal buffer acts as a mask to distinguish integral surface pixels from context/background pixels. 4. Depth Texture: Stores the depth information of the current surface layer, required for the depth peeling algorithm's occlusion tests. Parameters: Silhouette Color: User-specified color for fading surface edges. Lighting Model: Phong or Gooch models for diffuse color evaluation. Modulation Type: Multiplicative or additive transparency modulation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set up the floating-point color buffer, normal buffer, and depth texture. Initialize the depth peeling loop. 2. Peel Stage (Iterative): a. Depth Test: Render the primitives using a depth test that discards fragments closer than the depth stored in the depth texture from the previous iteration. The first iteration peels the front-most layer. b. Shading: Perform full surface shading for the visible fragments. i. Transparency: Compute the view-dependent transparency term \alpha{view} from the fragment's normal vector. If normal-variation transparency is used, evaluate partial derivatives using dFdx and dFdy. ii. Pattern/Texture: If adaptive patterns are used, compute ls and lt using dFdx and dFdy, and evaluate the pattern equation to obtain texture color c{tex} and texture alpha \alpha{tex}. iii. Lighting: Evaluate diffuse color c{diffuse} using the specified lighting model (Phong or Gooch). Compute specular highlight terms (c, \alpha){spec} if specified. iv. Combination: Compute the final RGBA output (c, \alpha){peel} for the peel pass. For multiplicative modulation: \alpha{final} = \alpha{view} \cdot \alpha{tex} + \alpha{specular} c{final} = c{diffuse} \cdot c{tex} + c{specular} For additive modulation: \alpha{final} = \alpha{view} + \alpha{tex} + \alpha{specular} (Note: c{final} remains c{diffuse} \cdot c{tex} + c{specular}). c. Storage: Write the final RGBA values to the color buffer. Store surface normals in the normal buffer, setting the alpha component to a mask flag indicating the pixel belongs to the integral surface. d. Depth Update: Update the depth texture with the depth values of the current layer for the next iteration. 3. Blend Stage: a. Silhouette Detection: Apply a Sobel edge detection filter to both the normal buffer and the depth buffer to determine silhouette strength. b. Masking: Use the mask flag in the normal buffer to exclude pixels that have the flag set for one of the pixels contributing to the filter, avoiding silhouette generation across surface-context and context-background boundaries. c. Silhouette Blending: Smoothly fade the surface color into the user-specified silhouette color based on the computed silhouette strength. d. Accumulation: Blend the result into the final floating-point color buffer. 4. Termination: Adaptively terminate the peeling loop if no pixels are rendered during the peel stage, determined using an occlusion query for each iteration. The total number of iterations is one greater than the number of surface layers for the current viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualdepthpeeling(primitives, silhouettecolor, lightingmodel, modulationtype): # Initialize buffers as per colorbuffer = allocatefloatingpointbuffer() normalbuffer = allocatefloatingpointbuffer() # RGBA, A is mask depthtexture = allocatedepthtexture() # Initial depth boundary for the first iteration (front-most layer) currentdepthboundary = 0.0 # This is mitigated by using a sharp and symmetric edge detection filter. Banding Artifacts: Slight banding artifacts can appear if blending directly to the output framebuffer in the presence of many surface layers. Using a floating-point color buffer improves blending accuracy. Depth Sorting Precision: Elements at different depths within the same layer may be stored if no intermediate geometry occludes them, reducing depth-sorting precision. Integrates Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume (PVHV) analysis into the depth peeling process to cull redundant fragments, reducing the number of effective layers required for high-quality multi-view warping. Extends Dual Depth Peeling to handle volumetric data intermixed with translucent polygonal geometry by using geometry peel depths as entry/exit points for volume ray-casting. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is largely a function of surface geometry size and is dominated by the requirement to submit the surface for rendering multiple times during depth peeling. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for multiple buffers: a floating-point color buffer, a normal buffer (with mask), and a depth texture. Measured Performance: Achieves interactive frame rates exceeding 15fps on NVIDIA GTX280 for small to medium meshes of below ≈500K triangles with medium depth complexity of 10 layers or less. Strengths: Resolves depth ordering per pixel, making it robust against self-intersecting surfaces which complicate depth sorting. Reduces the number of passes by N/2 for N layers compared to standard depth peeling. Limitations: Performance degrades with larger meshes and higher depth complexity. May still store elements at different depths within the same layer if no intermediate geometry occludes them, reducing depth-sorting precision. When to Use: Suitable for interactive visualization of integral surfaces (e.g., stream surfaces, path surfaces) that may self-intersect, where correct transparency and silhouette shading are required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with very high depth complexity or extremely large meshes where the multiple render passes become prohibitive. Dual Depth Peeling was introduced as an improvement to the standard Depth Peeling algorithm to reduce the number of rendering passes required for order-independent transparency. It allows simultaneous peeling in both directions: from the camera to the background and from the background to the camera. The technique is implemented in OpenGL using GLSL shader programs, but the concepts can be ported to DirectX. It is particularly useful in illustrative rendering for integral surfaces, such as streamlines on stream surfaces, where visual clarity and correct transparency are critical. name: Effective Depth Peeling
head: DP with PVHVs, DP+PVHV, EDP (Extended Depth Peeling with PVHV), PVHV-based culling, Sampling-based backward-search algorithm
body: Effective Depth Peeling (EDP) is a visibility culling technique for multi-layer volume ray casting that integrates Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume (PVHV) analysis into the depth peeling process. It solves the problem of processing redundant, completely hidden fragments in subsequent peeling layers by implicitly identifying and culling fragments that are occluded by large-area occluders, thereby reducing the number of effective layers required for high-quality multi-view warping. Unlike standard Depth Peeling (DP) which peels one layer per pass linearly, or Umbra culling-based DP (UDP) which uses tiny pixel occluders, EDP captures important edge fragments early using wider area occluders, significantly reducing warping costs and total layer count. EDP operates by testing whether a fragment in a hidden layer lies within a PVHV defined by the occluders in the previous layer. If a fragment is inside a PVHV, it is considered fully hidden and culled; otherwise, it is retained for warping. The method uses a sampling-based backward search to approximate PVHVs without explicit edge analysis. Inputs: Z: Known-view depth texture from the previous layer (or foreground image for h=1). E: Novel-view bound radius (screen-space LCOC radius). \Delta: Depth-difference threshold for surface connectivity (default: 0.002 in normalized linear scale). |\Omega|: Number of backward-search samples (default: 14). fragments: List of candidate fragments for layer h. Outputs: Culled fragments for layer h: Only fragments not determined to be in a PVHV are passed to the next stage. Item Buffer: Stores object IDs for fragments. Used to immediately reject samples belonging to different objects during edge existence tests. Fragment Encoding: RGBA32F format, storing color, depth (z), and item index. Depth Texture (Z): Stores depth values for the occluder layer. 1. Initialization: For each fragment p in the current hidden layer h, identify its projection q onto the occluder layer h-1 (or foreground h=0). The depth of q is qz = Z(px, py). 2. LCOC Calculation: Compute the Local Cone of Confusion (LCOC) radius R in screen space based on the depth difference between p and q, and the novel-view bound E. The formula is: R = \text{ProjectToScreen}\left( \left| \frac{pz - qz}{qz} \right| E \right) where \text{ProjectToScreen} converts the physical bound to screen-space pixels. 3. Sample Generation: Generate a set of uniform random samples \Omega within a circle of radius R centered at q. The size |\Omega| is typically 14. 4. Edge Existence Test: For each sample w \in \Omega: a. Sample the depth at the offset location: wz = Z(px + wx, py + wy). b. Test if an edge exists between w and q using EdgeExists(w, q). 5. PVHV Inclusion Check: If EdgeExists(w, q) returns true, the fragment p is in a PVHV. Return true (fragment is hidden/culled). If the depth difference is small (wz \ge qz - \Delta), the sample w is on the connected surface. Bypass w (do not process as a new occluder) and continue to the next sample. If the depth difference is significant (wz < qz - \Delta), the sample may find a secondary inner occluder. Recursive Extension (CPU/Conceptual): Recursively extend the bound at w to find secondary inner occluders by calling InPVHV again. GPU Implementation: Since GPU implementations do not support recursion for secondary inner occluders, a Halton sequence is used for quasi-random samples so that subsequent samples naturally handle bound extensions. Alternatively, a conservative approximation can be used by considering such samples as potentially in PVHVs (return true) to avoid excessive sampling. 6. Final Decision: If no samples indicate an edge or PVHV inclusion after checking all w \in \Omega, return false (fragment is fully visible/retained). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def effectivedepthpeeling(Z, E, Delta, Omegasize, ItemBuffer, fragments): def ProjectToScreen(value): return int(round(value)) def GetRandomSamples(radius, count): samples = [] for in range(count): angle = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) r = math.sqrt(random.uniform(0, 1)) radius samples.append((r math.cos(angle), r math.sin(angle))) return samples def LCOC(pz, qz): return ProjectToScreen(abs((pz - qz) / qz) E) def EdgeExists(w, q): if ItemBuffer[w] != ItemBuffer[q]: return True wz = Z[w] qz = Z[q] if wz > qz + Delta: return True return False def InPVHV(p, pz, conservative=False): q = p qz = Z[q] R = LCOC(pz, qz) Omega = GetRandomSamples(R, Omegasize) for w in Omega: wcoord = (p[0] + w[0], p[1] + w[1]) wz = Z[wcoord] if EdgeExists(wcoord, q): return True if wz >= qz - Delta: continue if conservative: return True if InPVHV(wcoord, wz, conservative): return True return False for p in fragments: pz = p.depth if not InPVHV(p, pz): retainfragment(p) \Delta: Depth-difference threshold. Default: 0.002 (normalized linear scale). Trades errors for peeling efficiency. E: Novel-view bound radius. Input parameter for LCOC calculation. |\Omega|: Number of backward-search samples. Default: 14. More samples (e.g., 16) lower the chance of missing edges in complex scenes. GPU Recursion: GPU implementations do not support recursion for secondary inner occluders. A Halton sequence is used for quasi-random samples to handle bound extensions in subsequent iterations. Approximate Tests: The edge existence test is approximate. Small numbers of missing fragments may occur, but experiments show negligible error rates (e.g., 0.000014 average fraction of erroneous pixels in RU scene). Disjoint Surfaces: Few adjacent disjoint surfaces may be incorrectly considered connected. Insufficient samples may miss existing edges. A memory-optimized variant that uses a linked list structure to pack sparse valid fragments, reducing memory consumption compared to fixed-size buffers. Time Complexity: Per-layer cost is costlier than regular DP due to the PVHV culling overhead, but fewer layers are needed for similar quality. Memory Complexity: Standard EDP requires two working textures (ping-pong) for input and output layers. Packed EDP (PEDP) reduces memory by tightly packing sparse valid fragments using a linked list structure, and requires a head texture of screen resolution holding 4-byte indexes to the first nodes per pixel. Performance: In the Satellites (ST) scene with E=1000mm, EDP achieves a 38.5x reduction in hidden fragments compared to Baseline DP (BDP). Speedup factors for combined DP and warping costs range from 2.3–3.4x vs BDP and 1.6–2.9x vs UDP. EDP requires only two hidden layers for high-quality DOF rendering in complex scenes, reducing effective layers by up to 2/2/3 (RU/SF/ST) for BDP and 3/2/2 for UDP. Strengths: Captures important fragments early, reduces warping cost, handles large-area occluders better than UDP. Limitations: Approximate edge tests may miss small fragments; GPU recursion limitation requires Halton sequence handling. Usage: Best for Depth-of-Field (DOF) rendering in multi-view warping applications. Effective Depth Peeling was introduced by Janghun Kim and Sungkil Lee in 2023 in the paper "Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume Rendering for Multi-View Warping". It builds on the concept of Potentially Visible Hidden-Volumes (PVHVs) and extends Depth Peeling by integrating on-the-fly fragment culling. The method is designed to improve efficiency in multi-fragment rendering and remote rendering scenarios.
