name: Packed Effective Depth Peeling
head: Packed EDP
body: Packed Effective Depth Peeling (PEDP) is a memory-optimized variant of Effective Depth Peeling (EDP) that reduces memory consumption by tightly packing sparse valid fragments using a linked list structure on the GPU. It solves the problem of fixed-size memory scaling in conventional Depth Peeling by removing empty pixels, causing memory consumption to scale directly with peeling efficiency. Unlike standard EDP, which retains fixed-size buffers for all potential fragment slots, PEDP dynamically allocates storage only for valid fragments, offering significant memory efficiency improvements at the cost of slightly increased warping latency due to pointer dereferencing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of fragments generated by the previous peeling layer h-1 (or the initial ray casting for h=0). Output: A packed linked list of fragments for layer h, stored in a node buffer, and a head texture pointing to the first node of each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Node Buffer: A dynamic array of linked list nodes. Each node consumes 16 bytes in RGBA32F format: 8 bytes: Color (RGBA32F). 4 bytes: Depth. 4 bytes: Indexed pointer to the next node (an integer index into the node buffer). 2. Head Texture: A texture of screen resolution holding 4-byte indexes to the first node of the linked list for each pixel. If a pixel has no fragments, the index is null/zero. Memory consumption: W \times H \times 4 bytes, where W and H are screen width and height. For the tested resolutions, this consumes approximately 7.9 MB. Algorithm Steps: 1. Peel Layer h: Perform the standard EDP peeling pass for layer h, generating a set of valid fragments. 2. Post-Peeling Packing: Immediately after peeling layer h, perform fragment packing to convert the sparse fragment buffer into the linked list structure. This is a per-layer process. It avoids keeping the entire layer in a fixed-size buffer. Use two working textures (input h-1 and output h) alternating in a ping-pong fashion to avoid keeping entire layers in memory. Iterate through the valid fragments generated in step 1. For each fragment, allocate a new node in the node buffer. Store the fragment's color and depth in the node. Set the node's "next" pointer to the current head of the linked list for that pixel's coordinate. Update the head texture for that pixel to point to the newly allocated node index. 3. Warping: Use the head texture and node buffer to traverse the linked lists during the warping phase. For each pixel, read the head index. Dereference the index to get the first node. Traverse the linked list using the "next" pointers until the end or a stopping condition is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. nodebuffer = [] # List of Node objects pingponga = [0] (width height) # 4-byte indexes per pixel pingpongb = [0] (width height) currenthead = pingponga class Node: color: list # RGBA32F depth: float nextindex: int def packlayerfragments(fragments, width, height): """ Pack sparse fragments into a linked list structure. fragments: List of (x, y, color, depth) tuples generated by peeling. """ # Initialize output head texture for this layer nexthead = pingpongb if currenthead is pingponga else pingponga nexthead[:] = [0] (width height) nextnodeidx = len(nodebuffer) for x, y, color, depth in fragments: node = Node() node.color = color node.depth = depth node.nextindex = nexthead[y width + x] nodebuffer.append(node) nexthead[y width + x] = nextnodeidx nextnodeidx += 1 currenthead = nexthead return currenthead def warplayer(head, width, height): """ Traverse linked lists to warp fragments. """ for y in range(height): for x in range(width): idx = head[y width + x] while idx != 0: # Assuming 0 is null node = nodebuffer[idx] # Warping computation uses node.color and node.depth idx = node.nextindex Parameters and Typical Values: Node Size: 16 bytes. Head Texture Size: 4 bytes per pixel. Packing Time: For two hidden layers (L=2), packing takes 0.6–0.8 ms. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Unfriendliness: Random memory access during node traversal can be cache-unfriendly, making PEDP likely slightly slower than EDP in terms of warping speed. Dereferencing Overhead: Additional dereferencing to the first pointer in the head texture is required during warping. Memory Scaling: Memory consumption scales directly with the number of valid fragments, not the screen resolution or maximum layer count. The parent method that uses PVHVs for fragment culling. PEDP is EDP with fragment packing. EDP A depth peeling technique that renders front and back faces in separate passes. PEDP is an alternative to DDP in the context of volume ray casting. DDP The general process of generating layers. PEDP optimizes the storage of these layers. RLB Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Scales directly with the number of valid fragments and screen resolution (for the head texture). It avoids fixed-size memory scaling with the number of layers. Time: Peeling time is similar to EDP. Packing adds 0.6–0.8 ms for two hidden layers. Warping is slightly slower than EDP due to cache-unfriendly random memory access during node traversal. Measured Performance: Memory Efficiency: PEDP consumes significantly less memory than standard EDP and BDP. In the Ruins (RU) scene with E=50mm, PEDP consumes 17.7 MB compared to 316.4 MB for BDP, a 37.5× memory efficiency improvement. Overall memory efficiency ranges from 25.1× to 166.1× relative to BDP. Speedup: The average speedup factors of PEDP against BDP and UDP are 2.2× and 1.8× respectively for all combinations of E and scenes. Hardware: Tested on Intel Core i9-10900 2.8 GHz and NVIDIA GPU (specific model not given in notes). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant memory reduction, making it suitable for resource-limited environments. Removes empty fragments, reducing warping workload. Limitations: Slightly slower warping than EDP due to pointer dereferencing and cache misses. Implementation complexity is higher due to linked list management on GPU. When to Use: Use PEDP when memory is a critical constraint and the scene has sparse valid fragments (high peeling efficiency). Use when the slight increase in warping latency is acceptable for the memory savings. When Not to Use: Use standard EDP if warping speed is more critical than memory usage and the scene has dense fragments. Use BDP or UDP if memory is not a constraint and simpler implementation is preferred. PEDP was developed for Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume Rendering (PVHVR) for Multi-View Warping. It builds on the concept of Effective Depth Peeling (EDP) by adding a fragment packing step to reduce the memory footprint of the depth peeling pipeline. The method was evaluated in the context of Depth-of-Field (DOF) rendering, where it demonstrated significant memory efficiency improvements over Baseline Depth Peeling (BDP) and Unordered Depth Peeling (UDP). name: Volume-peeling
body: Volume-peeling is a technique to correctly order translucent geometry and volumes in rasterized scenes by using geometry peel depths as entry/exit points for volume ray-casting. It extends Dual Depth Peeling to handle volumetric data intermixed with translucent polygonal geometry, ensuring that volumes are composited in the correct depth order relative to the geometry layers. It sets itself apart from standard Dual Depth Peeling by adding a specific ray-casting pass that utilizes the depth buffers generated by the geometry peeling process. Volume-peeling operates in a multi-pass pipeline that interleaves geometry peeling with volumetric ray-casting. The method requires a renderer capable of dual depth peeling and a volume mapper. Inputs: Scene containing translucent polygonal geometry and volumetric data. Renderer configuration with SetUseDepthPeelingForVolumes enabled. Ray-sampling distance and volume mapper settings. Outputs: A final composited image where translucent geometry and volumes are correctly ordered. Data Structures: Front and Back Accumulation Buffers: Separate color buffers used to accumulate fragment colors from front-to-back and back-to-front ray-casting, respectively. Depth Buffers: Updated depth values from each geometry peel pass, which define the entry and exit points for the subsequent volume ray-casting. Steps: 1. Initialization Pass: Render sections of the volume that are not enclosed within any translucent geometry. This pass initializes the front and back accumulation buffers with the colors of the volume parts visible outside the geometry. 2. Geometry Peeling Pass: Perform a dual depth peeling pass on the translucent geometry. This computes the color and depth of the front and back layers (peels) of the geometry in a single render pass. The computed colors are accumulated in separate geometry buffers, and the updated depths are stored to feed the next pair of peels. 3. Volumetric Peel Pass: Invoke the volume mapper in an additional render pass. Use the entry and exit depth points obtained from the most recent geometry peel as the boundaries for ray-casting through the volume. This renders the peels of volume contained within the current peels of geometry. 4. Simultaneous Ray-Casting: Accommodate both front and back ray-casting of the current volume peel in a single render pass. Write the fragment colors from the front ray-casting directly to the front accumulation buffer. Accumulate the fragment colors from the back ray-casting in a following pass (or buffer). 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for subsequent layers of geometry peels until all layers are processed or the maximum number of peels is reached. 6. Final Composition: Composite the front and back accumulation buffers to produce the final image. Parameters: SetUseDepthPeelingForVolumes: A boolean parameter exposed through the renderer to explicitly enable volume-peeling. It is off by default. MaxPeels: The maximum number of geometry layers to peel. Limiting this reduces the overhead of repeatedly initializing ray-casting code. Pitfalls: Overhead: There is significant overhead from repeatedly initializing ray-casting code when switching between volumetric and translucent geometry rendering passes. Performance Sensitivity: Performance is highly dependent on geometry complexity (higher complexity requires more passes) and ray-sampling distance. Time Complexity: Performance depends on geometry complexity and ray-sampling distance. The time spent rendering volume peels is far greater than the time spent drawing the translucent geometry. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for front and back accumulation of both geometry and volume layers, plus depth buffers for peeling. Measured Performance: Initial benchmarks suggest that the accumulated time spent peeling volumes is around 75% greater than the time required to render them without peeling. Strengths: Correctly orders translucent geometry and volumes in rasterized scenes, solving a long-standing issue in VTK. Limitations: High computational cost due to ray-casting overhead; performance degrades with high geometry complexity and large ray-sampling distances. When to Use: When correct depth ordering between translucent polygons and volumetric data is required in a rasterized rendering pipeline. Volume-peeling was introduced as an extension to Dual Depth Peeling to address the issue of rendering translucent geometry intermixed with volumes in VTK (Visualization Toolkit). It was implemented in vtkDualDepthPeelingPass and exposed via vtkRenderer::SetUseDepthPeelingForVolumes. The technique was discussed in a Kitware blog post in June 2017 by Alvaro Sanchez and Allison Vacanti. Rendering translucent geometry intermixed with volumes, https://www.kitware.com/rendering-translucent-geometry-intermixed-with-volumes/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Polygon Embedding via Dual Depth Buffers
head: Dual Depth Buffer Polygon Embedding
body: Polygon Embedding via Dual Depth Buffers is a technique for integrating opaque or translucent polygonal geometry into volume rendering by inserting polygon images pixel-by-pixel between volume samples along rays. It solves the problem of correctly ordering hybrid scene elements (volumes and polygons) without requiring complex scene graph traversal or separate rendering passes for each object type. Unlike Dual Depth Peeling, which peels layers from both camera and background simultaneously to handle transparency, this method uses two depth buffers to define a specific depth interval D0, D1) for [volume sampling, effectively "slicing" the volume ray to leave gaps for polygon layers. Inputs: Volume dataset. Sequence of polygon layers, each represented by a color buffer and a depth buffer. Initial foreground depth D{fg} (typically 0 or near-plane). Outputs: Final composite image with polygons embedded within the volume. Data Structures: Two depth buffers, D0 and D1, of size matching the screen resolution. Color buffers for storing polygon images and the accumulating volume result. Parameters: Depth range D0, D1): D0 is the back depth (start of volume sampling), D1 is the front depth (end of volume sampling). Steps: 1. Initialization: Set D0 to the depth of the foreground (e.g., near [clipping plane). Load the depth buffer of the first polygon layer into D1. 2. Volume Rendering: Render the volume for the current depth range [D0, D1). Samples (xs, ys, zs) are included if they satisfy the depth test: D0[xs, ys] \leq D(xs, ys, zs) < D1[xs, ys] where D0[xs, ys] and D1[xs, ys] are the values in the depth buffers at pixel (xs, ys), and D(xs, ys, zs) is the depth of the volume sample. Note: The source formula (9) uses D[xs, ys] for both bounds, which is interpreted here as D0 and D1 respectively based on the context of the range D0, D1). 3. Blending: Blend the color buffer of the current polygon layer behind the image produced by the volume-rendering pass. 4. Iteration: For subsequent layers, replace D0 with the contents of D1. Load the depth buffer of the next polygon layer into D1. Initialize the rays for the next volume pass to the blended image from the previous pass. 5. Repeat: Steps 2–4 are repeated for each polygon layer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. D0 = createdepthbuffer(screenwidth, screenheight) D1 = createdepthbuffer(screenwidth, screenheight) D0.fill(foregrounddepth) polygonlayers = getpolygonlayers() # List of (colorbuffer, depthbuffer) currentimage = createcolorbuffer(screenwidth, screenheight) currentimage.fill(0) # Or clear color for i, (polycolor, polydepth) in enumerate(polygonlayers): # Load next polygon depth into D1 D1.copyfrom(polydepth) # Render volume for range [D0, D1) # The volume renderer must support depth-based sample culling volumeimage = rendervolume(currentimage, D0, D1) # Blend polygon color behind the volume result # Assuming standard alpha blending where polygon is in front of volume # But the description says "blend the first color buffer behind the image produced by the volume-rendering pass" # This implies: Result = Volume + Polygon (1 - VolumeAlpha) ? # Or simply: Result = Blend(Polygon, Volume) # The text says: "blend the first color buffer behind the image produced by the volume-rendering pass" # This phrasing is ambiguous. Usually, "blend behind" means the new element is further back. # However, the goal is to insert polygons between volume samples. # If we render volume for [D0, D1), and D1 is the polygon depth, # the volume samples are behind the polygon (assuming D increases with depth). # So the polygon is in front of the volume segment. # "Blend A behind B" usually means B is in front of A. # Let's assume standard compositing: Final = Polygon + Volume (1 - PolygonAlpha) # But the text says "blend the first color buffer behind the image produced by the volume-rendering pass" # This might mean: Volume is rendered, then Polygon is blended on top? # No, "behind" suggests order. # Let's look at the next step: "rays are initialized to the blended image". # This implies the blended image is the input to the next volume pass. # If the polygon is in front, the volume samples behind it should be occluded. # The depth test D(x) < D1 ensures volume samples are behind the polygon. # So the polygon is visually in front of the volume segment. # Standard blending: Out = Src Alpha + Dst (1 - Alpha) # If Polygon is Src and Volume is Dst, and Polygon is in front: # Result = Poly Alpha + Vol (1 - Alpha) blendedimage = blendbehind(polycolor, volumeimage) # Update current image for next pass currentimage = blendedimage # Update D0 for next iteration D0.copyfrom(D1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The process must be repeated for every change in view direction, model transformation, or other parameters affecting depth. Precision issues may arise if depth buffers do not have sufficient resolution to distinguish between volume samples and polygon depths. The method assumes polygon layers are sorted by depth. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of polygon layers N, as each layer requires a separate volume rendering pass and blending step. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two depth buffers and color buffers for intermediate results. Strengths: Simple to implement if the volume renderer supports depth-based sample culling; allows arbitrary polygon geometry to be embedded. Limitations: Requires N passes for N layers; sensitive to depth precision; must be re-executed for every view change. When to use: When integrating a small number of polygonal objects into a volume render, and the volume renderer supports efficient depth-based skipping. When not to use: When there are many polygon layers, or when dynamic view changes are frequent and performance is critical. The technique is described in the context of the VolumePro 1000 hardware renderer, which supports dual depth buffers and flexible depth tests. It is part of the [shear-image order ray casting approach. Shear-image order ray casting volume rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/641480.641510, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Layer Separation Heuristic
head: Feature Peeling
body: The Layer Separation Heuristic determines optimal split points along a ray in multi-layer volume rendering to separate high-quality raycasting from lower-cost image warping. It solves the problem of identifying the main visual effect of light attenuation, which frequently occurs in the middle of a ray interval rather than at entry or exit. Unlike simple depth-based splitting, this heuristic identifies main visual effects along the ray, preserving depth cues and providing better visual approximation for transparent volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray sampled at discrete steps through the volume, where each sample provides voxel opacity \alphai and accumulated transmittance Ti. Output: A set of depth values defining layer separation points along the ray. Data Structures: The method operates on a 1D array of sample values along the ray, requiring no complex spatial data structures beyond the standard ray marching buffer. Steps: 1. Evaluate Criteria: For each sample point i along the ray, calculate a score using either the maximum opacity criterion (\alphai) or the maximum color impact criterion (Ci = \alphai \times Ti). 2. Identify Local Maxima: Find local maxima in the score sequence, where a point i is a local maximum if its score is greater than or equal to its immediate neighbors. 3. Resolve Discrete Spans: If a local maximum spans several consecutive sample points, select the median index of these points as the separation depth. 4. Select Layers: Choose the top N separation points based on their scores, with the Maximum Color Impact method generally preferred for slight visual quality advantages. Formulas: Color Impact: Ci = \alphai \cdot Ti Where: \alphai is the opacity of the voxel at sample i. Ti is the transmittance (remaining opacity along the ray segment) from the camera to sample i. Parameters: Number of Layers (N): A fixed integer determined in advance. Evaluations tested layer counts from 2 to 9. Criterion Selection: Binary choice between "Max Opacity" and "Max Color Impact". Pitfalls: Fixed Layer Count: Layers must be allocated in advance. If the heuristic is overly sensitive, it may allocate too many layers to features close to the camera, leaving distant features underrepresented. Heuristic Failure: The heuristic is fixed and cannot adapt to dynamic scene complexity; insufficient layers or poor distribution lead to visual artifacts. Depth Cues: Simple entry or exit depth choices fail to capture main light attenuation effects occurring in the middle of the ray interval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findlayerseparation(rays, numlayers, criterion="colorimpact"): """ Finds layer separation points for a batch of rays. rays: List of Ray objects, each containing a list of sample points. numlayers: Integer, number of layers to separate. criterion: String, "opacity" or "colorimpact". Returns: List of lists, where each inner list contains depth values for that ray. """ separationpoints = [] for ray in rays: points = ray.samples if not points: separationpoints.append([]) continue scores = [] for i, point in enumerate(points): alpha = point.opacity Ti = point.accumulatedtransmittance # Transmittance from camera to this point if criterion == "colorimpact": score = alpha Ti else: # maximumopacity score = alpha scores.append((score, point.depth, i)) # Find local maxima with proper boundary handling localmaxima = [] for i in range(len(scores)): ismax = True if i > 0 and scores[i][0] < scores[i-1][0]: ismax = False if i < len(scores) - 1 and scores[i][0] < scores[i+1][0]: ismax = False if ismax: localmaxima.append(scores[i]) # Resolve plateaus: if consecutive points share the max score, pick median index resolvedmaxima = [] if localmaxima: currentgroup = [localmaxima[0]] for j in range(1, len(localmaxima)): if localmaxima[j][2] == currentgroup[-1][2] + 1: currentgroup.append(localmaxima[j]) else: medianidx = currentgroup[len(currentgroup)//2][2] resolvedmaxima.append((max(currentgroup, key=lambda x: x[0])[0], next(p.depth for p in points if p.index == medianidx), medianidx)) currentgroup = [localmaxima[j]] medianidx = currentgroup[len(currentgroup)//2][2] resolvedmaxima.append((max(currentgroup, key=lambda x: x[0])[0], next(p.depth for p in points if p.index == medianidx), medianidx)) # Select top N layers based on score resolvedmaxima.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) selected = resolvedmaxima[:numlayers] depths = [m[1] for m in selected] separationpoints.append(depths) return separationpoints Groups volume elements by distance and opacity to ensure consistent shading, overcoming single-image warping limitations. Assigns high-quality raycasting to close layers and warping to distant ones, exploiting depth proximity for quality allocation. Performance: Enables multi-frame rate rendering by allowing high-quality raycasting for a subset of layers while warping the rest. Layer images can be transferred separately to the fast node as soon as completed, reducing latency. Strengths: Preserves depth cues better than single surface approaches; outperforms single layered image warps for transparent transfer functions (e.g., MANIX dataset). Limitations: Visual quality suffers if layers are not distributed well (e.g., too many close to camera); fixed number of layers limits adaptability; quality gain is less significant for opaque transfer functions revealing bones (e.g., VIX dataset). When to Use: Transparent volumes where depth cues are critical and view-dependent lighting is needed. When Not to Use: Opaque volumes with simple structures where the quality difference is negligible. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the context of Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering by S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg. It addresses the limitations of single-layer image warping by separating volume layers based on visual impact rather than uniform depth intervals. The approach was evaluated on datasets such as MANIX (head CT) and VIX (foot). Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/egpgv.egpgv10.019-026, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Layered Image Warping
head: Feature Peeling-based Layered Warping
body: Layered Image Warping is a technique for transparent volume rendering that overcomes the limitations of single-image warping by representing the inner structure of an object as multiple partial images, called layers. It solves the problem of preserving depth cues and handling view-dependent lighting in transparent volumes, which cannot be shaded correctly using a single map of normal vectors. Unlike sibling methods that use uniform or heuristic-based splitting, this method groups volume elements by distance from the camera and similar opacity to ensure consistent shading. Inputs: A volume dataset, a ray path through the volume, and a smoothing kernel for opacity. Outputs: A set of layer images, each associated with a depth value for warping. Data Structures: Layer: A 2D image buffer storing color and depth values for a specific subset of the volume. Ray Profile: A 1D array of opacity values sampled along the ray, smoothed to detect features. Algorithm Steps: 1. Smoothing: Smooth the opacity values along the ray to reduce noise. Let oi be the opacity at sample i. The smoothed opacity \hat{o}i is computed using a smoothing kernel. 2. Feature Detection: Detect local minima and maxima of the smoothed opacity \hat{o}i along the ray. 3. Layer Separation (Feature Peeling): Use the detected extrema to separate the ray into segments (layers). Noise Suppression: Suppress layers that have a total opacity of less than 10%. This threshold prevents the creation of layers from noise. Feature Preservation: Avoid separating connected, highly opaque regions, as they likely belong to the same feature. 4. Depth Value Selection: For each pixel in a layer image, determine a depth value representing the ray interval. Two methods are evaluated to locate the "main effect" of light attenuation within the layer's interval: Method A (Max Opacity): Select the point with the maximum opacity after classification within the layer's segment. Method B (Max Color Impact): Select the point with the maximum impact on color, calculated as the voxel's opacity multiplied by the remaining opacity along the ray segment. Method B is preferred for slight advantages. 5. Rendering: Render each layer independently. The depth value associated with each pixel allows for correct warping and compositing of the layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def layeredimagewarping(raysamples, smoothingkernel, minopacitythreshold=0.1): """ raysamples: list of tuples (depth, opacity, color) along the ray. smoothingkernel: function returning smoothed list of opacities. minopacitythreshold: minimum opacity for a layer to be valid (default 0.1). """ # Step 1: Smooth opacity opacities = [s[1] for s in raysamples] smoothedopacities = smoothingkernel(opacities) # Step 2: Detect local minima and maxima extremaindices = findlocalextrema(smoothedopacities) # Step 3: Separate layers using extrema layers = [] currentstart = 0 for idx in extremaindices: segment = raysamples[currentstart:idx + 1] segmentopacity = sum(s[1] for s in segment) # Noise suppression: require at least 10% opacity if segmentopacity < minopacitythreshold: currentstart = idx + 1 continue # Feature preservation: avoid splitting connected, highly opaque regions # The sources do not specify the exact heuristic for connected opaque regions. # A typical implementation would check if segmentopacity > 0.9 and merge with the next segment. # Step 4: Depth Value Selection (Method B: Max Color Impact) # Calculate transmittance (remaining opacity) before each sample in segment transmittance = 1.0 maximpact = -1.0 bestdepth = segment[0][0] for s in segment: impact = s[1] transmittance if impact > maximpact: maximpact = impact bestdepth = s[0] transmittance = (1.0 - s[1]) # Step 5: Compositing (Standard front-to-back alpha blending) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 for s in segment: c, o = s[2], s[1] color = [color[j] + c[j] o (1.0 - alpha) for j in range(3)] alpha = alpha + o (1.0 - alpha) layers.append({ 'segment': segment, 'depth': bestdepth, 'color': color }) currentstart = idx + 1 # Handle last segment if currentstart < len(raysamples): segment = raysamples[currentstart:] segmentopacity = sum(s[1] for s in segment) if segmentopacity >= minopacitythreshold: transmittance = 1.0 maximpact = -1.0 bestdepth = segment[0][0] for s in segment: impact = s[1] transmittance if impact > maximpact: maximpact = impact bestdepth = s[0] transmittance = (1.0 - s[1]) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 for s in segment: c, o = s[2], s[1] color = [color[j] + c[j] o (1.0 - alpha) for j in range(3)] alpha = alpha + o (1.0 - alpha) layers.append({ 'segment': segment, 'depth': bestdepth, 'color': color }) return layers def findlocalextrema(values): """Returns indices of local minima and maxima.""" indices = [] for i in range(1, len(values) - 1): if (values[i] > values[i - 1] and values[i] > values[i + 1]) or \ (values[i] < values[i - 1] and values[i] < values[i + 1]): indices.append(i) return indices Parameters: Minimum Opacity Threshold: 10% (0.1). Layers with less than this opacity are suppressed to reduce noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Without smoothing and the 10% threshold, noise can create spurious layers. Connected Opaque Regions: Highly opaque connected regions should not be split, as they belong to the same feature. Depth Selection: Using entrance or exit depth can fail to capture the main effect of light attenuation, which may occur in the middle of the ray interval. Performance: On a volumetric foot dataset (VIX), increasing the number of layers from 2 to 9 increases the average absolute pixel error (visual quality degradation) from ~0.2 to ~0.6, but also increases the framerate from ~6 fps to ~9 fps. Strengths: Provides efficient cues about the inner structure of an object and handles view-dependent lighting better than single-image warping. Limitations: Increasing layers degrades visual quality (higher pixel error). Requires deferred shading for correct view-dependent lighting. Origin: The method is based on the idea of feature peeling [MMG07] and was introduced in the context of Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering. History: It was developed to address the limitations of single image warping for transparent volumes. Usage: Used in multi-frame rate volume rendering to improve performance while maintaining visual quality. name: Distribution by Depth Layer
head: Adaptive Layer Distribution, Quality/Performance Tradeoff via Layer Count
body: Distribution by Depth Layer is a workload distribution method that assigns high-quality raycasting to the first n depth layers (representing close structures) and multi-frame rate image warping to the remaining layers. It exploits the observation that close structures contribute more to the final image than distant ones. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using depth proximity as the primary heuristic for quality allocation, whereas Layered Image Warping focuses on the warping mechanism itself. Inputs: Volume dataset. Camera position and orientation. Target minimum frame rate (FPS{min}). Hardware configuration: a fast GPU and a slow GPU. Outputs: Final rendered image. Dynamic number of raycasted layers (n). Data Structures: Depth layers extracted from the volume dataset, ordered by distance from the camera. Parameters: n: The number of front layers to raycast. FPS{min}: The desired minimum frame rate. Steps: 1. Initial Setup: Determine the total number of layers N in the volume dataset. Initialize n to a starting value. 2. Layer Assignment: Assign layers 0 to n-1 (the closest n layers) to be rendered via raycasting on the fast GPU. Assign layers n to N-1 (the remaining back layers) to be rendered via multi-frame rate image warping on the slow GPU. 3. Rendering: Perform raycasting for the front n layers. Perform image warping for the back N-n layers. Composite the results into the final image. 4. Performance Monitoring: Measure the current frame rate FPS{curr}. 5. Adaptive Adjustment: If FPS{curr} < FPS{min}, immediately decrease n by 1. Periodically attempt to render with n+1 layers to check if improved quality is possible. 6. Repeat: Return to Step 2 for the next frame or update cycle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distributionbydepthlayer(volume, camera, fpsmin): # Extract depth layers and sort by distance from camera (closest first) layers = sorted(volume.getdepthlayers(), key=lambda layer: layer.distancefrom(camera)) totallayers = len(layers) # Initial guess for n (number of raycasted layers) n = max(1, totallayers // 2) # Standard initialization framecount = 0 while True: # 1. Assign layers raycastlayers = layers[:n] warplayers = layers[n:] # 2. Render # Raycast close layers frontimage = raycast(raycastlayers, camera) # Warp back layers backimage = imagewarp(warplayers, camera, frontimage) # Composite finalimage = composite(frontimage, backimage) # 3. Monitor Frame Rate currentfps = 1.0 / getframetime() # 4. Adaptive Adjustment if currentfps < fpsmin: # Decrease n immediately to improve performance if n > 0: n -= 1 else: # Periodically check if higher quality is possible # Using a simple frame counter for periodicity if framecount % 30 == 0 and n + 1 <= totallayers: # Try rendering with n+1 layers testfront = raycast(layers[:n+1], camera) testback = imagewarp(layers[n+1:], camera, testfront) testfps = 1.0 / getframetime() if testfps >= fpsmin: n += 1 # Else: keep n as is yield finalimage framecount += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If n=0, all layers are warped, potentially losing all high-frequency detail from close structures. If n=N, all layers are raycasted, potentially missing the performance benefit of warping. Precision: The transition between raycasting and warping at layer n may introduce visible seams if the warping accuracy is insufficient for the depth discontinuity. Boundary: The number of raycasted layers cannot exceed the total number of layers N. Extends this concept by distributing workload between GPUs to replace some image warping with raycasting for higher quality beyond strict node assignment. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of raycasted layers n. Performance (FPS) degrades linearly as n increases. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the volume dataset and intermediate buffers for raycasting and warping. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluation on a scene rotated 90 degrees showed that reconstruction error converges to the reference image as more layers are raycasted. Performance (FPS) degrades linearly as more layers are raycasted. The benefit of warping more than 6 layers vanishes. Strengths: Automatically adjusts quality/performance tradeoff based on current frame rate. Exploits the perceptual importance of close structures. Limitations: Requires two GPUs (fast and slow) for optimal implementation as described. The "vanishing benefit" after 6 layers suggests diminishing returns for high layer counts. Originated in the paper "Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering" by S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg (2010). The method is part of a broader framework for multi-frame rate rendering, aiming to provide the best quality for a given maximum latency by dynamically adjusting the rendering workload. Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/egpgv.egpgv10.019-026, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes
head: Adaptive GPU Workload Distribution, Flexible Workload Distribution
body: Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes are methods that distribute rendering workload between a fast GPU (performing raycasting or image warping) and a slow GPU (performing raycasting) to improve visual quality beyond strict node assignment by replacing some image warping with raycasting. Unlike separation planes which create perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading approximation and poor adaptation to scene interest, flexible schemes adapt to focus regions, segmentations, or depth importance. The core principle is the relaxation of strict workload assignment between fast and slow nodes. When viewport resolution and sampling rate are small enough, raycasting on modern GPUs can be acceptably fast, allowing visual quality to be improved by replacing some of the image warping with raycasting. This approach requires special attention to the amount of workload shifted, as it reduces the frame rate of the fast node. The latency compensation step of the system is extended by raycasting to handle these dynamic assignments. Distribution by Quality Maps is a workload distribution method that uses a quality map to identify badly reconstructed pixels (mostly from disocclusions or undersampling during image warping) and replaces them with high-quality raycasting. Step: On the fast node: 1. Use image warping to reconstruct m layers. 2. Project the volume’s bounding geometry to the screen. 3. Iterate through the closest m layers for each pixel covered by the projection. 4. If layers are empty, raycast this pixel. Parameter: m: The number of empty layers required per pixel to classify the pixel as disoccluded. A lower m switches to raycasting more frequently. Pitfall: In layered image warping, completely empty pixels are rare, but holes in foremost layers commonly happen and disocclude content from back layers, resulting in unsatisfying reconstructions. The parameter m helps steer the quality vs. performance tradeoff. Comparison: Performance scales with frame-to-frame coherence: large viewpoint motion induces more raycasting (lower performance), while slow motion allows more warped fragments. Unlike fixed layer counts, this is user-input dependent. Origin: S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg, "Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering" (2010). The method addresses the limitations of traditional parallel raycasting algorithms that divide workload by separation planes in screen space or object space (sort-first or sort-last), which often lead to perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading from warped images being only an approximation to per-sample phong shading. These regions do not adapt well to what is really interesting in a scene, such as focus regions, segmentations, or magic lenses. The authors propose a more flexible workload distribution to account for the fact that features close to the current viewpoint are more important and better perceivable than distant features. Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/egpgv.egpgv10.019-026, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Depth Alpha Blending Projection
head: Depth-8 Alpha Blending Projection, Depth-aware RGB projection, Two-half alpha blending
body: Depth Alpha Blending Projection renders a 2D projection of a 3D volume by alpha blending voxel values along rays, assuming pre-multiplied alpha. It offers two variants: a grayscale "Depth-8" mode that outputs a single channel, and an RGB mode that splits the ray into two halves for accumulation to approximate depth-aware color blending. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit two-pass accumulation structure in the RGB variant, which allows for specific depth-weighting strategies not present in standard single-pass ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture (grayscale or RGB), a transformation matrix T defining the ray origin and direction, and image dimensions Nx \times Ny. Output: A 2D image buffer (8-bit grayscale or 32-bit RGBA). Data Structures: Volume: Accessed via trilinear interpolation. For RGB, the source data is assumed to be stored in a format where the alpha channel is the 4th component (e.g., lut[index] returns RGBA). Transform Matrix T: A 4 \times 4 matrix. The relevant components are T.m[i][j] (row-major or column-major as per implementation, but indices are explicit in steps). Parameters: Nz: The depth dimension of the volume. Nx, Ny: The width and height of the output image. Algorithm Steps: The method consists of two distinct modes. Both iterate over the image pixels (x, y). 1. Initialize Ray: For each pixel y in 0 \dots Ny-1: Calculate start point p0 at (0, y, (Nz-1)/2.0) using transform T. Extract initial coordinates x0, y0, z0 from p0. Extract forward step vector (dx, dy, dz) from T.m[0][0], T.m[1][0], T.m[2][0]. Extract backward step vector (dxd, dyd, dzd) from -T.m[0][2], -T.m[1][2], -T.m[2][2]. 2. Accumulate Backwards: Initialize alpha = 1.0, gray = 0.0. Set current position x1 = x0, y1 = y0, z1 = z0. Loop iz from 0 to Nz-1: Get voxel value here = trilinear interpolation at (x1, y1, z1). Normalize: here = here / 255.0. Compute effective alpha: h{alpha} = \sqrt{here}. Update gray value: gray = here \cdot h{alpha} + gray \cdot (1 - h{alpha}). Increment position: x1 \leftarrow x1 + dxd, y1 \leftarrow y1 + dyd, z1 \leftarrow z1 + dzd. 3. Write Output: Compute final intensity: val = 255.99 \cdot gray / alpha. Write uint8t(val) to dest[y Nx + x]. Increment ray start: x0 \leftarrow x0 + dx, y0 \leftarrow y0 + dy, z0 \leftarrow z0 + dz. 1. Initialize Ray: Same as Depth-8 mode. 2. Accumulate First Half (Front): Initialize a=0, r=0, g=0, b=0. Set current position x1 = x0, y1 = y0, z1 = z0. Loop iz from 0 to \lfloor Nz/2 \rfloor - 1 (first half): Get herergb from volume lookup. Extract normalized RGB channels rh, gh, bh (and alpha ah, though bh is used as alpha proxy in source). Compute effective alpha: ah = bh \cdot bh. Update color and alpha: r = rh \cdot ah + r \cdot (1 - ah) g = gh \cdot ah + g \cdot (1 - ah) b = bh \cdot ah + b \cdot (1 - ah) a = ah + a \cdot (1 - ah) Increment position: x1 \leftarrow x1 + dxd, etc. 3. Accumulate Second Half (Back): Loop iz from \lfloor Nz/2 \rfloor to Nz-1 (second half): Get herergb. Extract rh, gh, bh. Compute effective alpha: ah = bh \cdot bh. Update color and alpha using the standard front-to-back blending formula with the accumulated front alpha: r = r + rh \cdot ah \cdot (1 - a) g = g + gh \cdot ah \cdot (1 - a) b = b + bh \cdot ah \cdot (1 - a) a = a + ah \cdot (1 - a) Increment position: x1 \leftarrow x1 + dxd, etc. 4. Write Output: Convert accumulated r, g, b to 8-bit integers: r1 = \lfloor 255.99 \cdot r \rfloor, etc. Write result as 32-bit integer: 0xff000000u + b1 + 256ug1 + 65536ur1 to dest. Increment ray start: x0 \leftarrow x0 + dx, etc. Formulas: The core blending equation for the RGB mode's second half is: outA = frontA + backA \cdot (1 - frontA) outRGB = frontRGB + backRGB \cdot (1 - frontA) where frontA is the accumulated alpha from the first half, and backA, backRGB are the contributions from the current voxel in the second half. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha Definition: The method assumes the volume's alpha channel (or the 4th component in RGB lookup) represents density/transmittance. The square root operation (\sqrt{here}) implies that the raw voxel value is squared density or requires gamma correction. Half-Split Boundary: The split at Nz/2 is arbitrary. If Nz is odd, the middle voxel is included in the second half (loop starts at Nz/2). This asymmetry should be noted. Precision: Accumulation is done in floating point. Final conversion uses 255.99 to handle rounding correctly for 8-bit output. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthalphablendinggrayscale(volume, transform, nx, ny, nz): dest = [0] (nx ny) # Extract steps from transform matrix T # Assuming T is a flat list or accessible via T.m[row][col] dx = transform.m[0][0] dy = transform.m[1][0] dz = transform.m[2][0] dxd = -transform.m[0][2] dyd = -transform.m[1][2] dzd = -transform.m[2][2] for y in range(ny): # Calculate start point p0 at (0, y, (nz-1)/2.0) using transform # This implies a specific ray origin calculation. # We assume p0 is the result of applying transform to (0, y, (nz-1)/2.0) p0 = transform.apply(0, y, (nz - 1) / 2.0) x0, y0, z0 = p0.x, p0.y, p0.z alpha = 1.0 gray = 0.0 x1, y1, z1 = x0, y0, z0 for iz in range(nz): # Trilinear interpolation here = volume.trilinear(x1, y1, z1) herenorm = here / 255.0 halpha = math.sqrt(herenorm) gray = herenorm halpha + gray (1.0 - halpha) x1 += dxd y1 += dyd z1 += dzd val = int(255.99 gray / alpha) dest[y nx + x0] = val # Note: x0 is not updated in loop, but dest index needs current x # Increment for next pixel x0 += dx y0 += dy z0 += dz return dest def depthalphablendingrgb(volume, transform, nx, ny, nz): dest = [0] (nx ny) dx = transform.m[0][0] dy = transform.m[1][0] dz = transform.m[2][0] dxd = -transform.m[0][2] dyd = -transform.m[1][2] dzd = -transform.m[2][2] for y in range(ny): p0 = transform.apply(0, y, (nz - 1) / 2.0) x0, y0, z0 = p0.x, p0.y, p0.z a = 0.0 r = 0.0 g = 0.0 b = 0.0 x1, y1, z1 = x0, y0, z0 # First half halfnz = nz // 2 for iz in range(halfnz): herergb = volume.lookup(iz, x1, y1, z1) # Assuming lookup handles trilinear rh, gh, bh = herergb.r, herergb.g, herergb.b ah = bh bh r = rh ah + r (1.0 - ah) g = gh ah + g (1.0 - ah) b = bh ah + b (1.0 - ah) a = ah + a (1.0 - ah) x1 += dxd y1 += dyd z1 += dzd # Second half for iz in range(halfnz, nz): herergb = volume.lookup(iz, x1, y1, z1) rh, gh, bh = herergb.r, herergb.g, herergb.b ah = bh bh r = r + rh ah (1.0 - a) g = g + gh ah (1.0 - a) b = b + bh ah (1.0 - a) a = a + ah (1.0 - a) x1 += dxd y1 += dyd z1 += dzd r1 = int(255.99 r) g1 = int(255.99 g) b1 = int(255.99 b) # Write as 0xff000000 | B | G | R pixel = 0xff000000 | b1 | (g1 << 8) | (r1 << 16) dest[y nx + x0] = pixel x0 += dx y0 += dy z0 += dz return dest Time Complexity: O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) for both variants, as every voxel along every ray is visited. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per pixel, excluding the volume storage. Performance: The RGB variant performs two passes over the depth axis (conceptually), but in practice iterates once, splitting the accumulation logic. This adds negligible overhead compared to the grayscale version but requires more register state (R, G, B, A). Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a depth-aware projection without full ray marching; the two-half split allows for different weighting of front vs. back surfaces. Limitations: The square root alpha assumption is non-standard and may require pre-processing of volume data; the hard split at Nz/2 is arbitrary and may not align with semantic object boundaries; no shadowing or lighting calculations. The method is described in the gvox library documentation, which provides an unofficial implementation of volume rendering techniques. It is a specific instance of layer-based rendering, building on the principles of Depth and Layer-Based Rendering. wagenadl/gvox, https://github.com/wagenadl/gvox, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Layered Depth Image (LDI) extraction
head: LDI extraction
body: LDI extraction is a view-dependent method that reduces the ray traversal count to the scene's depth complexity by generating a buffer of depth layers per pixel. Unlike Two-Pass Depth Ray Casting which uses geometric bounding boxes, or Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting which uses pre-computed static layers, LDI extraction derives intervals dynamically from rendered depth images, making it sensitive to the specific model and view. Inputs: 3D volume data; camera parameters (position, orientation, projection). Outputs: A Layered Depth Image (LDI) buffer, typically structured as a list of depth values (and optionally color/opacity) for each pixel. Data Structures: The LDI buffer is an array of lists, one per pixel (u, v). Each list contains entries sorted by depth t. An entry typically contains: t: depth value along the ray. color: RGBA or density value (optional, depending on implementation). opacity: \alpha value (optional). Steps: 1. Render Depth Pass: Render the volume's bounding geometry or a simplified representation to a depth buffer (Z-buffer) to obtain the visible surface depths. 2. Extract Depths: For each pixel (u, v), read the depth values from the depth buffer. If multiple layers are required (e.g., for internal structures), this step may involve multiple render passes or specialized hardware queries to extract all front-to-back depth intersections. 3. Sort Depths: The extracted depth values for each pixel must be sorted in front-to-back order (t1 < t2 < \dots < tn). This sorting is performed on the CPU. 4. Construct LDI: Populate the LDI buffer with the sorted depth lists. Each list represents the non-overlapping ray segments for that pixel. 5. Ray Casting (Downstream): Use the LDI buffer to define integration intervals [t{start}, t{end}] for the volume rendering equation, as described in Depth and Layer-Based Rendering. Pitfalls: CPU Bottleneck: The method requires downloading depth images from video memory and resorting depth lists pixel-by-pixel on the CPU, which significantly impacts efficiency, especially at high volume resolutions. View Dependence: The LDI must be regenerated for every new view, making it unsuitable for static scenes with camera movement unless caching strategies are employed. Extends LDI by storing depth values in a 3D texture for fast point-in-volume tests, optimized for volumetric parity rather than just rendering. Time Complexity: Dominated by the depth extraction and CPU sorting steps. Efficiency is heavily affected by volume resolution and the number of depth layers per pixel. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of pixels times the average depth complexity (number of layers per pixel). Strengths: Reduces traversal to actual depth complexity; simple and robust implementation. Limitations: High CPU overhead due to data transfer and sorting; view-dependent; not suitable for real-time if depth complexity is high or resolution is very large. LDI extraction was presented as part of a scheme for real-time voxelization of complex models, aiming to represent resultant volumes as 2D textures for efficient implementation on PC graphics hardware.
