name: Volumetric Depth Sprite (VDS)
head: Layered Depth Image (LDI) representation
body: Volumetric Depth Sprite (VDS) is an image-based representation of a solid shape's volume, designed to enable fast, real-time point-in-volume tests and ray-marching operations on arbitrary 3D solids. It extends the Layered Depth Image (LDI) concept by storing depth values along viewing rays aligned to the negative z-axis within a 3D texture, effectively capturing layers of unique depth complexity. Unlike standard LDI extraction which focuses on view-dependent rendering, VDS is optimized for volumetric parity testing, allowing a point to be classified as inside or outside a volume by counting depth layer crossings. Input: A static 3D mesh S defined in world coordinates. Output: A Volumetric Depth Sprite structure VDSS containing the sprite's position, transformation matrix, layered depth image data, and depth complexity. The VDS structure is defined as: VDSS = (PS, MS, LDIS, dS) PS \in \mathbb{R}^3: The position of the sprite in world coordinates. MS: A 4 \times 4 matrix representing linear transformations (rotation and scaling) of the VDS. LDIS: The layered depth image data, stored as a 3D texture. dS \in \mathbb{N} \setminus \{0, 1\}: The depth complexity of shape S, representing the maximum number of intersections any ray parallel to the z-axis makes with the mesh. 3D Texture Layout: Dimensions: Width w, Height h, Depth dS. Format: Luminance texture format with a single 32-bit floating-point channel. Interpolation: Nearest neighbor. Border: Set to 1 for each color component. Wrap Mode: Clamp to border. The VDS is generated via a pre-processing step using multipass Render-to-Texture (RTT). 1. Transformation: Transform the shape S into the unit volume [0, 1]^3. Set up an orthogonal projection covering this unit volume and adjust the near and far clipping planes accordingly. 2. Texture Setup: Determine the depth complexity dS of the shape. Create a 3D texture with dimensions w \times h \times dS. Configure nearest neighbor interpolation, set the texture border to 1, and set the wrap mode to clamp to border. Use the luminance format with a single 32-bit floating-point channel to bound texture size. 3. Depth Peeling: Perform depth peeling [Cas01] on the solid S using RTT. For each slice i of the 3D texture (where 0 \le i < dS), render the i-th depth layer. Linearize the depth values using an inverse W-buffer [LJ99] before storing them in the texture. To obtain a depth value di \in [0, 1] for the i-th depth layer at a 2D point (s, t), the 3D texture in LDIS is sampled at the coordinate (s, t, \frac{i}{dS}). The Volumetric Parity Test (VPT) classifies a point P \in \mathbb{R}^3 relative to the volume. In the ray-marching implementation, the parity of the coordinate swaps if the ray passes a depth layer. This allows for order-independent transparency and volume containment checks. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatevds(mesh, width=1024, height=1024): """ Generates a Volumetric Depth Sprite from a static mesh. """ # Step 1: Transform shape to unit volume [0, 1]^3 # Apply transformation matrix Tunit to mesh vertices unitmesh = transformtounitvolume(mesh) # Set orthogonal projection covering [0, 1]^3 projection = OrthogonalProjection(near=0.0, far=1.0) # Step 2: Determine depth complexity dS # This requires a preliminary pass or analytical estimation to find max intersections dS = computedepthcomplexity(unitmesh) # Create 3D texture # Format: Luminance, 32-bit float, single channel # Dimensions: width x height x dS texture = create3dtexture(width, height, dS, format=FLOAT32LUMINANCE) # Configure texture parameters texture.interpolation = NEAREST texture.bordercolor = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # 1 for each component texture.wrapmode = CLAMPTOBORDER # Step 3: Depth Peeling via Render-to-Texture for layerindex in range(dS): # Render the layerindex-th depth layer # Use inverse W-buffer to linearize depth values depthbuffer = renderdepthpeel(unitmesh, layerindex, projection, inversewbuffer=True) # Store linearized depth values in the 3D texture slice # Coordinate mapping: (s, t) in texture space corresponds to (s, t, layerindex/dS) texture.setslice(layerindex, depthbuffer) # Construct VDS structure vds = { "position": (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), # World position, typically origin for unit volume "matrix": identitymatrix(), # Linear transformation matrix "ldidata": texture, "depthcomplexity": dS } return vds def volumetricparitytest(vds, pointworld): """ Classifies a point as inside or outside the volume using VDS. """ # Transform point to LDI texture space # Inverse of vds.matrix and translation applied pointlocal = transformpoint(vds.matrix, pointworld) # Map to texture coordinates (s, t) s = pointlocal.x t = pointlocal.y # Check if point is within texture bounds if not (0 <= s <= 1 and 0 <= t <= 1): return OUTSIDE # Ray march along z-axis (depth) # Sample the 3D texture at (s, t, z) for z in [0, 1] # Count crossings of depth layers parity = 0 z = 0.0 step = 1.0 / vds.depthcomplexity while z <= 1.0: # Sample depth value at current z # Note: The texture stores depth values. # A crossing occurs if the ray's z-coordinate matches a stored depth layer. # In practice, this is often implemented by checking if the point's z # falls between depth layers or by counting layer intersections. # Simplified parity logic based on VPT description: # The parity swaps if the ray passes a depth layer. depthval = vds.ldidata.sample(s, t, z) # If the sampled depth is valid (not border value 1), we are at a surface if depthval != 1.0: parity += 1 z += step return INSIDE if parity % 2 == 1 else OUTSIDE Texture Resolution: 1024^2 pixels is recommended for fairly high quality. Lower resolutions like 128^2 may fail for complex non-convex solids. Undersampling Artifacts: Planes nearly parallel to the LDI direction (z-axis) produce fuzzy edges. Mitigation involves applying multisampling to increase the number of samples. Static Mesh Limitation: The approach is limited to static meshes. Animated shapes require re-computation of the VDS, which cannot be done in real-time for complex shapes with high texture resolution. Precision: The accuracy of the volume test depends on the texture resolution. Higher resolution improves precision but increases memory usage. Time Complexity: VDS creation takes up to two seconds per shape, depending on depth complexity and texture dimension. This pre-processing time is significant and prevents real-time updates for animated meshes. Memory Complexity: The space complexity is high, proportional to w \times h \times dS. For 1024^2 resolution and high depth complexity, this can be substantial. Performance: Once generated, the Volumetric Parity Test (VPT) can be implemented efficiently on modern GPU hardware (Shader Model 3.0 compliant) for real-time point-in-volume tests. Strengths: Fast real-time volumetric tests for arbitrary 3D solids; view-independent representation; efficient GPU implementation. Limitations: High space complexity; limited to static meshes; undersampling artifacts for parallel planes; precision depends on texture resolution. The concept of Layered Depth Images (LDIs) was introduced by Seidel et al. [SGwHS98], representing a scene from a single camera view with multiple pixels along each line of sight. The size of the representation grows linearly with the observed depth complexity. Depth peeling for order-independent transparency was introduced by Cabral et al. [Cas01]. The Volumetric Depth Sprite (VDS) extends these concepts to perform real-time volumetric tests, as presented in. Real-Time Volumetric Tests Using Layered Depth Images, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20081019, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Volumetric Parity Test
head: Ray-marching shader implementation
body: The Volumetric Parity Test (VPT) is a real-time algorithm that classifies a 3D point as inside or outside a solid volume represented by a Volumetric Depth Sprite (VDS). It solves the problem of pixel-precise clipping against multiple arbitrary-shaped meshes in a single rendering pass, avoiding the expensive multi-pass image-based Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) approaches. Unlike its siblings, VPT performs this classification via a parity-swap ray march through the VDS's layered depth layers, enabling efficient implementation in programmable pipeline stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point P (in world or clip space), the VDS parameters (position PS, model matrix MS, depth complexity dS, and the 3D texture LDIS), and the current orientation matrix O. Output: A boolean parity pT \in \{0, 1\}, where 1 indicates the point is inside the volume and 0 indicates it is outside. Data Structures: VDS: Defined by (PS, MS, LDIS, dS). PS \in \mathbb{R}^3: World position of the sprite. MS: Linear transformation matrix (rotation, scaling) of the VDS. dS \in \mathbb{N} \setminus \{0, 1\}: Depth complexity, representing the number of unique depth layers. LDIS: A 3D texture storing depth values. The texture is sampled in LDI texture space. For a 2D point (s,t), the depth value di for the i-th layer (0 \le i < dS) is obtained by sampling at (s, t, \frac{1}{dS} \cdot i). Transformation to LDI Texture Space: Before testing, the point P must be transformed into the specific LDI texture space of the VDS. The transformation T = (Ts, Tt, Tr) is calculated as: T = MS \cdot O^{-1} \cdot (P - PS) Where: P is the input point. O is the current orientation matrix. P - PS translates the point to the LDI space relative to the sprite's position. O^{-1} adjusts for orientation. MS applies the VDS model matrix. Classification Logic: The test models a ray R = [(Ts, Tt, 0), (Ts, Tt, 1)] marching through the depth layers of the LDI. The parity pT starts at an initial value (typically true for outside) and swaps every time the ray crosses a layer of unique depth complexity. Mathematically, the test is formulated as: VPT(T, VDS^S) = pT = \begin{cases} 1, & \exists di \in LDIS: di \le Tr \le d{i+1} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Note: The source text formula uses di \le Tr \le d{i+1}, but the provided code implementation checks Tr < di. The code logic implies that if the ray's depth Tr is less than the stored depth di of a layer, the ray has passed that layer, triggering a parity swap. Pseudocode: The following GLSL-like pseudocode implements the VPT. It requires Shader Model 3.0 compliant hardware due to dynamic flow control in the loop. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetricParityTest(T, LDI, depth, initParity): """ Classifies point T in LDI-space against the VDS stored in LDI. Args: T (vec4): Coordinate in LDI-space. T.r is the depth component. LDI (sampler3D): The 3D texture representing the Layered Depth Image. depth (int): The depth complexity dS of the VDS. initParity (bool): Initial parity (true = outside). Returns: bool: True if inside, False if outside. """ parity = initParity # Calculate offset to address texture slices uniformly offset = 1.0 / float(depth) # March through each depth layer for i in range(0, depth): # Sample the depth value at the current layer # Texture coordinate: (T.st, offset i) sampleddepth = texture3D(LDI, vec3(T.st, offset i)).x # If the point's depth T.r is less than the layer's depth, # the ray has crossed this layer. if T.r < sampleddepth: parity = not parity return parity Parameters and Edge Cases: Shader Model: Requires Shader Model 3.0 or higher to support the dynamic flow control (loops) required for the ray march. Initial Parity: initParity = true corresponds to "outside". Precision: The method does not consider the case where the coordinate lies exactly on the border of the shape for reasons of precision. Depth Linearization: Depth values in the LDI may need to be linearized using an inverse W-buffer. Resolution Limits: For complex non-convex solids, VPT might fail if the texture resolution is too low (e.g., 128^2 pixels). A texture size of 1024^2 pixels delivers fairly high quality, and larger resolutions do not significantly improve quality. Time Complexity: The test consists of less than 20 assembler instructions per executed loop iteration. Performance depends on the depth complexity dS and the number of VDS samples. Memory Complexity: The key drawback is the high space complexity of the LDI 3D texture. Performance: On a GeForce 8800 GTS, the method achieves interactive frame rates. For example, rendering a "House" model with 10 samples took 74.4 FPS without the test and 73.2 FPS with the test; a "Crank" model with 80 samples took 8.6 FPS without and 7.5 FPS with the test. Pre-processing: Creating the VDS takes up to two seconds per shape, depending on depth complexity and texture dimension. Strengths: Enables pixel-precise clipping against multiple arbitrary-shaped meshes in a single rendering pass, unlike image-based CSG which requires multiple passes per frame. Limitations: High memory usage for the LDI; potential failure for complex non-convex solids at low resolutions. The Volumetric Parity Test was introduced by Matthias Trapp and Jürgen Döllner in 2008. It was developed to address the need for fast, real-time volumetric tests in computer graphics and visualization, such as rendering 3D volumetric lenses or collision detection. Prior to this, such functionality relied on expensive image-based multi-pass rendering algorithms or lacked support for multiple arbitrary-shaped meshes. The method is implemented based on the Virtual Rendering System (VRS). Real-Time Volumetric Tests Using Layered Depth Images, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20081019, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hardware-Assisted Visibility Ordering (MPVO-based)
head: Hardware-assisted depth sorting, MPVO layering algorithm
body: This method extracts a front-to-back visibility order of volumetric boundary primitives (triangles) by iteratively identifying "layers" of mutually non-obstructing polygons using graphics hardware depth and stencil buffers. Unlike traditional methods that build pairwise visibility relations and perform a topological sort, this approach assigns a layer number to each primitive directly, determining the rendering order without explicit sorting. It is designed to be significantly faster than software-based visibility sorting (e.g., VSbuffer) and handles dynamic meshes more efficiently than BSP-tree-based approaches. The algorithm processes a set of unclassified triangles \mathcal{T}, outputting a sequence of layered sets \mathcal{T}i where each set contains triangles that are mutually visible (depth-complexity \le 1) and ordered from front to back. Data Structures: \mathcal{T}: Set of unclassified triangles. \mathcal{F}: Candidate set for the current layer. \mathcal{T}i: Set of triangles assigned to layer i. Color Buffer: Stores triangle IDs (via color mapping) to identify which triangle covers each pixel. Stencil Buffer: Tracks depth complexity (number of overlapping primitives) at each pixel. Z-Buffer: Standard depth buffer. Parameters: Block Size: For the subdivision optimization, 64 \times 64 pixels is experimentally optimal. Z-Test: GLLESS for initial pass, GLGEQUAL for refinement. Stencil Op: GLINCR on any projection. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set \mathcal{T} to the input set of triangles. Initialize layer counter i = 0. 2. Outer Loop: While \mathcal{T} is not empty: 3. Candidate Selection: Clear the color buffer. Disable the stencil buffer. Configure Z-test to GLLESS and clear Z-buffer to 1.0 (far plane). Render all triangles in \mathcal{T}. Read back the color buffer. Assign any triangle present in the color buffer to the candidate set \mathcal{F}. These are potential layer members but may be obscured by others. 4. Refinement (Inner Loop): While the depth-complexity of \mathcal{F} is greater than 1: 5. Back-to-Front Occlusion Removal: Clear and enable the stencil buffer. Clear the color buffer. Configure Z-test to GLGEQUAL and clear Z-buffer to 0.0 (near plane). Configure Stencil: glStencilFunc(GLALWAYS, ~0, ~0) and glStencilOp(GLKEEP, GLINCR, GLINCR). Render all triangles in \mathcal{F}. Read back the color and stencil buffers. For each pixel where the stencil value is > 1: Identify the triangle covering that pixel from the color buffer. Remove that triangle from \mathcal{F}. Re-insert the triangle into \mathcal{T}. If no pixel has stencil value > 1, exit the inner loop. 6. Layer Assignment: Assign \mathcal{T}i = \mathcal{F}. Increment i. 7. Termination Check: If the number of triangles in \mathcal{T} did not change during Step 3 (i.e., no triangles were removed from \mathcal{T} in the previous outer loop iteration), stop. The remaining triangles in \mathcal{T} contain a cycle or are orthogonal to the view direction. Optimization: Subdivision Scheme To avoid reading and scanning the entire frame buffer when layers become small: Divide the image into blocks (e.g., 64 \times 64). Track pixel coverage per block. If a pixel is not covered after Step 3, it is never covered again. Skip reading/scanning that block in subsequent iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwareassistedvisibilityordering(triangles): """ Input: triangles - list of triangle objects with unique IDs Output: layers - list of lists, where layers[i] contains triangle IDs for layer i """ T = set(triangles) # Unclassified triangles layers = [] layeridx = 0 while T: # Step 3: Candidate Selection # 1. Clear buffers clearcolorbuffer() disablestencilbuffer() setztest(GLLESS) clearzbuffer(1.0) # 2. Render T rendertriangles(T) # 3. Read Color Buffer to find candidates colorbuffer = readcolorbuffer() F = set() for pixel in colorbuffer: if pixel.triangleid is not None: F.add(pixel.triangleid) # Step 4: Refinement while depthcomplexity(F) > 1: # 4a: Setup for back-to-front check clearstencilbuffer() enablestencilbuffer() setstencilfunc(GLALWAYS, ~0, ~0) setstencilop(GLKEEP, GLINCR, GLINCR) clearcolorbuffer() setztest(GLGEQUAL) clearzbuffer(0.0) # 4b: Render F rendertriangles(F) # 4c: Read buffers and remove occluded triangles stencilbuffer = readstencilbuffer() colorbuffer = readcolorbuffer() removedfromF = set() for pixel in stencilbuffer: if pixel.stencilvalue > 1: # Identify triangle from color buffer triid = pixel.triangleid if triid is not None: removedfromF.add(triid) # Remove from F and re-insert into T for triid in removedfromF: F.remove(triid) T.add(triid) # If no triangles removed, depth complexity is 1 if not removedfromF: break # Step 4d: Assign Layer layers.append(list(F)) layeridx += 1 # Step 5: Termination Check # Check if T changed in this outer loop iteration # Note: T was modified in the inner loop. # We need to check if any triangles were removed from T in Step 3. # Actually, Step 3 doesn't remove from T. The inner loop removes from F and adds to T. # The termination condition is: if no triangles were removed from T in Step 1? # Re-reading source: "If no triangles have been removed from T since step (1)... # that is, the number of elements in T has not changed." # This implies we check if T grew. If T grew, we continue. # If T did not grow, it means F was empty or T was empty? # Wait, if T is not empty, we enter loop. # If F is empty (no triangles rendered), T remains same. # If F is not empty, we refine. # The condition "no triangles removed from T" in Step 1 is tricky because Step 1 doesn't remove. # Source says: "If no triangles have been removed from T since step (1)... # we can stop... remaining triangles contain a cycle or are orthogonal." # This likely means: if the set of triangles rendered in Step 2 was empty, # or if the set of triangles rendered in Step 2 was a subset of already classified ones? # No, T contains unclassified. # Let's interpret: If after Step 3, F is empty, then T hasn't changed (no triangles were found). # Or if F contains triangles but they are all orthogonal/occluded in a way that prevents layering? # The source says: "If no triangles have been removed from T since step (1)... # that is, the number of elements in T has not changed." # This is a check on the size of T. If |T| is constant across outer loop iterations, stop. # But T grows in the inner loop. # Let's track Tsizebeforeouter. # Correct logic based on source: # The algorithm stops if T is not empty but no progress is made. # Progress is made if triangles are removed from T? No, triangles are removed from F and added to T. # Triangles are removed from T only if they are assigned to a layer? No, they are removed from T when assigned? # Source: "T is used to denote the set of triangles which have not been classified". # So when we assign Ti = F, we must remove F from T. # Correction: # In Step 4d, we assign Ti = F. These triangles are now classified. # So we must remove F from T. # Let's rewrite the loop logic to match source intent: # T starts with all triangles. # Loop: # Render T. # Find F (candidates in T). # Refine F to ensure depth complexity 1. # Assign Ti = F. # Remove F from T. # If T is empty, stop. # If T is not empty but F was empty (or no triangles were rendered), stop (cycle/orthogonal). # The source says: "If no triangles have been removed from T since step (1)... # that is, the number of elements in T has not changed." # This implies that if we don't remove any triangles from T (i.e., F is empty), we stop. if not F: # No triangles were found in T, or all were already classified? # If T is not empty but F is empty, we have a problem (cycle/orthogonal). break # Remove classified triangles from T T -= F return layers def depthcomplexity(triangles): """ Helper to check if depth complexity > 1. In practice, this is done by reading the stencil buffer after rendering with GLGEQUAL. """ # This is an abstract representation. The actual check is done in the inner loop. # If the inner loop exits because no pixel has stencil > 1, then complexity is 1. return 1 # Placeholder for logic described in Step 4 Note: The pseudocode above abstracts the buffer reading. In implementation, depthcomplexity(F) > 1 is determined by the inner loop's stencil buffer check. If the inner loop finds no pixels with stencil > 1, the loop breaks, and F is valid. A technique for computing a visibility ordering of a set of acyclic primitives by assigning a layer number to each primitive, which directly determines the visibility ordering, using a combination of the z- and stencil buffers of graphics hardware. It is considerably faster than VSbuffer because it requires a much smaller number of buffer reads for typical datasets. Unlike traditional methods (e.g., XMPVO, BSP-XMPVO) that build pairwise visibility relations and run a topological sort, this method assigns layer numbers directly via hardware buffers, avoiding the explicit topological sort phase for the boundary. Unlike VSbuffer which sorts all volumetric primitives, this technique only sorts the boundary cells and uses MPVO relations for the interior, requiring adjacency information. Time Complexity: Worst-case O(n^2) where n is the number of triangles (if all behind a single pixel). Typical complexity O(nd) where d is depth complexity. Memory Complexity: Requires access to color, stencil, and z-buffers. Subdivision scheme reduces memory bandwidth usage by limiting buffer reads to covered blocks. Performance: Subdivision scheme can speed up performance by over 4 times. Scanning layers and reading buffers dominate execution time. Hardware Dependency: Performance varies by architecture. On SGI Octane, scanning time dominates. On HP PC, reading time is significantly higher. Strengths: Fast for typical datasets; handles dynamic meshes better than BSP-based methods; avoids explicit topological sort. Limitations: Does not handle cycles or triangles orthogonal to the view direction automatically. Performance degrades with high depth complexity. Symmetric datasets (e.g., spheres) may not benefit from subdivision optimization. When to Use: When fast visibility ordering of boundary primitives is needed for volume rendering, especially with dynamic meshes. When Not to Use: When the scene contains cycles or is highly symmetric and subdivision optimization is critical. The method was proposed as a hardware-assisted alternative to software-based visibility ordering algorithms like XMPVO and BSP-XMPVO. Traditional methods build pairwise visibility relations and perform a topological sort, which is slow for large datasets and dynamic meshes. This technique exploits graphics hardware (z- and stencil buffers) to assign layer numbers directly, enabling fast unstructured volume rendering. It was implemented in OpenGL and tested on SGI Octane and HP PC architectures. A Hardware-Assisted Visibility-Ordering Algorithm With Applications To Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/vissym01/235-242, fetched 2026-10-24

name: MPI Parallelization for Volume Rendering
head: MPI Decomposition of AMRKDTree, Parallel AMRKDTree Traversal, yt MPI volume rendering
body: This method parallelizes direct volume ray casting by decomposing the Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data structure (specifically the AMRKDTree) across multiple MPI processes, allowing each process to traverse only its assigned portion of the volume. It differs from sibling methods like OpenMP Parallelization, which parallelizes ray traversal within a single process, by distributing the spatial data domain itself. The method is characterized by a tree-reduction compositing step where each process renders a full image plane, which are then alpha-blended together. Inputs: AMR dataset (hierarchical grid structure). Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, image resolution). Transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). Number of MPI tasks P. Outputs: Final composited image plane (RGB + Alpha). AMRKDTree: A hierarchical tree structure representing the AMR volume. The tree is decomposed such that each MPI task p is assigned a disjoint subset of the tree nodes (bricks). Image Plane: A 2D array of size W \times H (width \times height) storing accumulated color and opacity. Each MPI task holds a full copy of this image plane in memory. 1. Task Count Validation: Let P be the number of available MPI tasks. If P is not a power of 2, set P{eff} = 2^{\lfloor \log2 P \rfloor}. The remaining P - P{eff} tasks are marked as idle and do not participate in rendering. 2. Parallel AMRKDTree Construction and Decomposition: The global AMRKDTree is constructed in parallel. The tree is decomposed into P{eff} balanced partitions. Each MPI task p \in [0, P{eff}-1] receives the subset of tree nodes assigned to it. Each task only needs to know about the part of the tree it will traverse. 3. Local Ray Casting: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane: Define ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Intersect ray with the bounding box of the volume. Traverse the local AMRKDTree partition assigned to task p. For each intersected brick/node: Sample the volume data V(\mathbf{p}) at intersection points. Compute optical properties (\mathbf{c}, \alpha) using the transfer function. Perform front-to-back compositing into the local image plane buffer. Note: Each task reads data only for the portion of the volume assigned to it. 4. Tree Reduction (Compositing): After all local bricks are processed, each task holds a complete image plane representing the contribution of its assigned volume partition. These partial images must be combined. Use a binary tree reduction algorithm over the P{eff} tasks. In each reduction step, pairs of tasks exchange their current image planes. Perform alpha blending of the two image planes: \mathbf{C}{combined} = \mathbf{C}A + (1 - \alphaA) \mathbf{C}B \alpha{combined} = \alphaA + (1 - \alphaA) \alphaB where (\mathbf{C}A, \alphaA) and (\mathbf{C}B, \alphaB) are the color and opacity from the two participating tasks. Repeat until a single final image plane remains. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from mpi4py import MPI def mpivolumerendering(comm, amrdata, camera, transferfunction, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Parallel volume rendering using MPI decomposition of AMRKDTree. Args: comm: MPI communicator amrdata: AMR dataset object camera: Camera parameters (origin, direction, etc.) transferfunction: Function mapping scalar value to (color, opacity) imagewidth: Width of the output image imageheight: Height of the output image Returns: finalimage: numpy array of shape (imageheight, imagewidth, 4) """ rank = comm.Getrank() size = comm.Getsize() # Step 1: Task Count Validation # If size is not a power of 2, calculate effective size if size == 0: return np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 4)) import math peff = 2 int(math.floor(math.log2(size))) # If this rank is not part of the effective power-of-2 group, it is idle if rank >= peff: # Idle task: do nothing or wait for barrier if necessary # In a real implementation, this process might exit or wait return None # Step 2: Parallel AMRKDTree Construction and Decomposition # The AMRKDTree is constructed. Resolutions > 2048^2 cause significant memory pressure. MPI Tasks: Must be a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, \dots). Non-power-of-2 counts result in idle cores. Non-Power-of-2 Tasks: If the number of available MPI processes is not a power of 2, the system uses the largest power of 2 less than or equal to the count. The remaining cores remain idle. Memory Bottleneck: Each MPI task holds the entire image plane in memory. For large resolutions (e.g., > 2048^2), this can exhaust available RAM, limiting the maximum number of MPI tasks that can be used simultaneously. Communication Overhead: The tree reduction step requires exchanging full image planes between tasks. For very large images, this communication cost can become significant. Time Complexity: Ray casting: O(N{pixels} \cdot N{samples} \cdot N{bricks\intersected}) per task, where N{bricks\intersected} is reduced by domain decomposition. Reduction: O(\log P{eff}) communication steps, each transferring O(W \cdot H) data. Memory Complexity: Per task: O(W \cdot H) for the image plane + O(V{local}) for the local volume data. Total: O(P \cdot W \cdot H + V{total}). Strengths: Efficient I/O: Each task reads only its assigned portion of the volume, reducing disk bandwidth contention. Scalability: Good scaling for large AMR datasets where I/O is a bottleneck. Limitations: Memory bound: The requirement for each task to hold the full image plane limits scalability to high resolutions or large task counts. Rigid task count: The power-of-2 constraint can lead to resource underutilization on clusters with arbitrary core counts. When to use: Large AMR datasets where I/O bandwidth is the primary bottleneck. Clusters with a power-of-2 number of available cores. Resolutions \le 2048^2 to avoid memory exhaustion. When not to use: Very high-resolution rendering (> 2048^2) on memory-constrained nodes. Clusters with non-power-of-2 core counts where efficiency is critical. Origin: This method is implemented in the yt framework, a Python-based analysis and visualization toolkit for astrophysical simulations. History: The parallelization strategy was developed to handle the massive datasets generated by adaptive mesh refinement simulations in astrophysics. It leverages the AMRKDTree structure, which is native to yt's data handling. name: Adaptive Direct Volume Rendering for PVE Removal
head: Air-Fluid Transition Reconstruction, PVE Removal, Partial Volume Effect Removal via Adaptive Direct Volume Rendering
body: This method removes partial volume artifacts (undesirable surfaces) at air-to-fluid transitions by combining iso-surface rendering with an intermediate direct volume rendering step. It distinguishes itself from standard direct volume ray casting by using an adaptive sample count based on the angle between the local surface normal and the view direction, and by employing a linear interpolation technique between tri-cubically filtered points to increase transfer function (TF) sample density without expensive 3D data oversampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset V, a pre-computed iso-surface mesh (or hit points), and camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Output: A 2D image with partial volume artifacts removed at air-fluid boundaries. Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D scalar grid. Surface Data: List of iso-surface intersection points and their associated local normals \mathbf{N}. Transfer Function: A parametric function T(I, G) mapping intensity I and gradient magnitude G to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha. Implemented implicitly in the shader to avoid texture lookups. Parameters: k: A constant integer weighting the number of samples. Defined as k \in \mathbb{Z}, k = \text{const}. Typical value: Not explicitly specified in sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iso-surface Detection: Identify visible iso-surface intersections for the ray. Define hit points and refine them. 2. Transition Probability Analysis: For each hit point, search along the local normal \mathbf{N} for high intensity values to determine an air-fluid transition probability p. 3. Adaptive Sampling Setup: If p > 0 (indicating a potential fluid transition area), calculate the number of samples s for the direct volume rendering step using the formula: s = \lfloor k \times (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{D}) \rfloor where \mathbf{D} is the view direction vector. Note: The dot product \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{D} represents the cosine of the angle between the normal and view direction. The ray direction itself is not changed to avoid distortion. 4. Direct Volume Rendering with Linear Interpolation: Perform direct volume rendering for s steps into the volume. To increase the density of transfer function samples without oversampling the 3D data, use linear interpolation between two successive tri-cubically filtered points along the ray. Let V1 and V2 be the tri-cubically interpolated values at two adjacent coarse sampling positions. Intermediate values V{int} are calculated via linear interpolation between V1 and V2. For each sample position, compute the intensity I and gradient magnitude G. Apply the 2D parametric transfer function T(I, G). This TF suppresses high gradient samples and renders medium intensity values. It specifically excludes contrast-enhanced high densities and large gradient values. Composite the samples using front-to-back compositing (as defined in the parent article Direct volume ray casting). 5. Termination and Fallback: Terminate the ray after s steps or when full opacity is reached. If s steps are traversed with no surface rendered (i.e., no significant opacity accumulation), initiate a secondary isosurface search starting at the last sampling position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivepveremovalraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, surfacehits, k): """ Renders a single ray using adaptive direct volume rendering for PVE removal. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera origin. raydirection: 3D vector, normalized view direction D. volume: Volume data structure with trilinear/tricubic access. surfacehits: List of (position, normal) tuples from iso-surface detection. k: Integer constant for sample weighting. Returns: color: 3D vector, final pixel color. opacity: float, final pixel opacity. """ # Initialize compositing state coloracc = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) opacityacc = 0.0 # 1. Check for relevant surface hits (air-fluid transitions) # Identify if the ray intersects a region with high transition probability p relevanthit = None for pos, normal in surfacehits: # Check if this hit is in a potential fluid transition area # This involves searching along normal N for high intensity values if istransitionarea(pos, normal, volume): relevanthit = (pos, normal) break if relevanthit is None: # Standard rendering or no PVE removal needed return standardraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, volume) hitpos, normal = relevanthit viewdir = raydirection # 2. Calculate adaptive sample count # s = floor(k (N. D)) # Note: N and D should be normalized. # The dot product gives the cosine of the angle. dotproduct = dot(normalize(normal), normalize(viewdir)) s = floor(k dotproduct) # Ensure s is at least 1 if we are in a transition area, # though the formula might yield 0 if angle is > 90 degrees (back-facing). # In practice, for front-facing surfaces, dotproduct > 0. if s < 1: s = 1 # 3. Adaptive Direct Volume Rendering # Determine entry and exit points for the partial volume layer # The ray segment to sample is defined around the hit point/transition area tnear, tfar = gettransitionsegment(rayorigin, raydirection, hitpos, normal, volume) dt = (tfar - tnear) / s t = tnear # Pre-calculate coarse sampling points for linear interpolation # We need pairs of tri-cubically filtered points coarsesamples = [] for i in range(s + 1): # s+1 points to create s intervals pos = rayorigin + (tnear + i dt) raydirection val = volume.tricubicinterpolate(pos) coarsesamples.append(val) for i in range(s): # Linear interpolation between successive coarse points val1 = coarsesamples[i] val2 = coarsesamples[i+1] # Calculate intermediate position for this step # The exact subsampling strategy within the interval is not detailed, # but typically we sample at the midpoint or use the interpolated value directly. # The source states: "intermediate values are calculated through linear interpolation" # and "lookup in 2D TF to account for high frequencies". # Let's assume we sample at the midpoint of the interval for the TF lookup # or use the linearly interpolated value as the intensity input. # The text says: "linear interpolation between two successive tri-cubically # filtered points... intermediate values are calculated... lookup in 2D TF". # This implies the intensity I for the TF is the linearly interpolated value. intensity = linearinterpolate(val1, val2, 0.5) # Midpoint sample # Compute gradient magnitude G at this position # Gradient can be derived from the volume or the surface gradientmag = computegradientmagnitude(pos, volume) # Apply 2D Parametric Transfer Function T(I, G) # T suppresses high gradients, renders medium intensities color, alpha = transferfunction2d(intensity, gradientmag) # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) c alpha # alphaout = alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alpha coloracc = coloracc + (1.0 - opacityacc) color alpha opacityacc = opacityacc + (1.0 - opacityacc) alpha # Check for full opacity if opacityacc >= 1.0: break t += dt # 4. Fallback: If no surface rendered after s steps if opacityacc < 1.0: # Initiate secondary isosurface search starting at last sampling position lastpos = rayorigin + t raydirection secondaryhit = secondaryisosurfacesearch(lastpos, raydirection, volume) if secondaryhit: # Render the secondary hit seccolor, secalpha = renderisosurface(secondaryhit, raydirection) coloracc = coloracc + (1.0 - opacityacc) seccolor secalpha opacityacc = opacityacc + (1.0 - opacityacc) secalpha return coloracc, opacityacc def istransitionarea(pos, normal, volume): """ Searches along the local normal N for high intensity values to determine air-fluid transition probability p. """ # Search along normal for a few voxels for i in range(1, 6): # "within four to six voxel layers" searchpos = pos + i normal voxelsize val = volume.sample(searchpos) if val > highintensitythreshold: return True return False def transferfunction2d(intensity, gradientmag): """ Parametric TF implemented implicitly in shader. Suppresses high gradient samples. Renders medium intensity values. Excludes contrast-enhanced high densities and large gradient values. """ if gradientmag > highgradientthreshold: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 if intensity > highintensitythreshold: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 # Map medium intensity to color/opacity # Specific mapping not given, assume standard linear or sigmoid alpha = mapintensitytoopacity(intensity) color = mapintensitytocolor(intensity) return color, alpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Distortion: High intensity values inside the dataset can distort normals along the three-material transition area (air/fluid/soft tissue). This is partially corrected by the surface reconstruction step, making explicit gradient adjustment unnecessary. Back-facing Surfaces: The formula s = \lfloor k \times (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{D}) \rfloor yields 0 or negative values if the normal points away from the viewer. The implementation must handle this, likely by clamping s to a minimum of 1 or skipping the adaptive step for back-facing surfaces. Precision: The linear interpolation between tri-cubically filtered points reduces the need for additional tricubical interpolations, which helps maintain performance but relies on the accuracy of the initial tri-cubic sampling. The base method for defining surfaces. Used here to identify potential transition areas. [Link to parent or sibling if available, otherwise generic link]. Using intensity and gradient magnitude for classification. Distinguishes this method from 1D TFs by handling the ambiguity of partial volume effects more robustly. Link to [Transfer Functions and Shading Models]. A technique to increase TF sample density without 3D oversampling. Comparable to pre-integrated TFs but with less memory overhead. Link to [Interpolation and Sampling Techniques]. Time Complexity: The adaptive sampling reduces the number of samples s for surfaces viewed head-on (high \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{D}) and increases them for grazing angles. However, the core cost is the tri-cubic interpolation and the 2D TF evaluation. The linear interpolation step adds minimal overhead compared to additional 3D interpolations. Memory Complexity: Low. The method does not require additional memory for pre-integrated TF tables, unlike some alternatives. Performance: Experiments maintained an average framerate of more than 30 fps at a screen resolution of 512×512 pixels. Strengths: Effective removal of partial volume artifacts at air-fluid boundaries. Real-time capable. No extra memory for TF tables. Limitations: Relies on accurate iso-surface detection and normal estimation. Distorted normals in three-material transitions can affect results, though the method is partially robust to this. When to Use: Virtual colonoscopy and other medical imaging applications where air-fluid transitions are common and partial volume artifacts are problematic. When Not to Use: Scenes without distinct air-fluid boundaries or where high-frequency surface details are not critical. This method was proposed in the context of virtual colonoscopy for tagged material cleansing. It addresses the specific problem of partial volume effects at air-fluid transitions, which can lead to undesirable surfaces in the rendered image. The approach combines iso-surface rendering with direct volume rendering, leveraging a 2D transfer function and adaptive sampling to reconstruct thin surface layers robustly. name: Ray-tracing coloring techniques
head: Coloring strategies in ray casting, Scalar vs Color compositing
body: Ray-tracing coloring techniques define the order of operations for mapping volumetric data to visual output, specifically distinguishing between combining scalar values before color mapping and combining color values during ray traversal. This distinction determines whether the integration process operates on a single intensity channel or full RGB channels, impacting both the physical accuracy of light attenuation and the visual interpretation of spectral data. The method consists of two distinct strategies for handling the transfer function and compositing steps defined in Direct volume ray casting. Input: A volumetric dataset V (scalar or spectral), a viewing ray r(t), and a transfer function T. Output: A final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out}. In this approach, the ray integration is performed on scalar values first. The color is applied only after the integration is complete. 1. Sampling: For each sample i along the ray, retrieve the scalar value Vi. 2. Accumulation: Combine the scalar values encountered by the ray. The source notes indicate a simple combination of scalar values, though standard volume rendering typically uses opacity-weighted accumulation. The resulting combined scalar S{combined} is computed. 3. Color Mapping: Map the final combined scalar S{combined} to a color \mathbf{C}{out} using a lookup table or transfer function. 4. Display: Render \mathbf{C}{out} as greyscale or mapped color. In this approach, the transfer function is applied to each sample individually before compositing. 1. Sampling: For each sample i along the ray, retrieve the data value Vi. 2. Pre-mapping: Map Vi to a full color vector \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai using the transfer function T(Vi) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}i, \alphai). 3. Color Compositing: Combine the full color information as the ray is traced. This follows the standard front-to-back compositing equation defined in the parent article: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Transparency: The transparency of a pixel can vary from fully opaque to fully transparent, which is controlled by the opacity component \alpha in Strategy 2. Spectral Data: Strategy 2 is particularly relevant for visualizing spectral cubes (e.g., astronomical data), where mapping data to color before combination preserves spectral information that would be lost in scalar combination. Strategy 1 (Scalar): Performance: Potentially faster if the final color mapping is a simple lookup, as compositing involves only scalar addition/multiplication. Visuals: May produce inaccurate lighting effects because attenuation is not calculated per-channel. Suitable for visualizing intensity distributions where color is purely categorical or intensity-based. Strategy 2 (Color): Performance: Higher computational cost per sample due to vector operations (RGB) during compositing. Visuals: Physically more accurate for multi-spectral data. Correctly handles the interaction of different colors as they attenuate through the volume. These techniques are fundamental to volume visualization, with early implementations appearing in software suites like Karma (Gooch 1996) which utilized texture-based volume rendering. Modern applications include tools like 3D Slicer and astronomical visualization of spectral cubes (e.g., THINGS survey data), where the choice between scalar and color compositing affects the interpretation of complex data. Real-time colouring and filtering with graphics shaders, https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stx1676, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Direct Volume Ray Casting with Texture Atlas Voxel Access
head: 2D Texture Atlas Ray Casting, Voxelization via 2D Texture
body: Direct Volume Ray Casting with Texture Atlas Voxel Access is a hardware-accelerated technique that renders 3D volumetric data by packing discrete slices into a 2D texture atlas and accessing them via bilinear interpolation in a fragment shader. It differs from standard direct volume ray casting by replacing 3D texture lookups with 2D texture lookups, allowing the use of standard 2D texture units and hardware filtering on GPUs that may lack efficient 3D texture support or where memory bandwidth for 3D textures is a bottleneck. It differs from Discrete Ray Casting with Trilinear Reconstruction by relying on pre-sliced 2D tiles and bilinear interpolation within those tiles, rather than reconstructing continuous values via trilinear interpolation across the full 3D volume space. The method casts rays through a volume represented as a 2D texture atlas. The volume is sliced into numberOfSlices layers, packed into a 2D grid of slicesOverX by slicesOverY tiles, and accessed via bilinear interpolation in the fragment shader. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D volume of size W \times H \times D, where D is the number of slices (numberOfSlices). The data is pre-processed into a 2D texture atlas. Camera: Model-view matrix (modelViewInv) to compute ray origin and direction. Parameters: numberOfSlices: Total number of volume slices along the Z-axis. Typical value: 96. slicesOverX: Number of slices along the X-axis of the 2D texture atlas grid. Typical value: 10. slicesOverY: Number of slices along the Y-axis of the 2D texture atlas grid. Typical value: 10. numSamples: Number of ray marching steps per ray. Typical value: 256. opacityFactor: Global opacity multiplier. colorizeIntensity: Boolean flag to enable heatmap coloring. intensityMin, intensityMax: Bounds for intensity isolation mask. clipPlaneNormal: Normal vector of the clipping plane. clipPlaneDepth: Depth of the clipping plane. clip: Boolean flag to enable clipping. Texture: The 2D texture atlas containing the sliced volume data. Outputs: Framebuffer: RGBA8 color buffer, REDINTEGER buffer (optional), and Depth buffer. Typical resolution: 1280x720. 2D Texture Atlas: A 2D texture where each tile represents a slice of the volume. The atlas dimensions are determined by slicesOverX and slicesOverY. The total number of tiles is slicesOverX slicesOverY. Each tile contains W \times H texels. Ray State: rayStart: 3D vector, ray origin in world space. rayStop: 3D vector, ray exit point in world space. dir: 3D vector, normalized ray direction. pos: 3D vector, current sample position. marchDist: 3D vector, step vector for ray marching. travel: float, remaining distance to march. stepSize: float, distance between samples. Accumulation Buffer: accum (vec4), initialized to (0, 0, 0, 0). 1. Ray Definition: Calculate ray origin and direction from the inverse model-view matrix. The ray origin is modelViewInv[3].xyz. The direction is normalized pos - modelViewInv[3].xyz, where pos is the vertex position of the cube mesh covering the view frustum. 2. Ray-Volume Intersection: Intersect the ray with the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the volume, defined as [-1, 1]^3. Find the entry parameter tnear and exit parameter tfar. If tnear < 0, set tnear = 0 to handle cases where the camera is inside the volume. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the ray start and stop points from world space [-1, 1] to texture space [0, 1] by adding 1 and multiplying by 0.5. 4. Step Size Calculation: Calculate the step size as maxDist / numSamples, where maxDist is the diagonal of the unit cube, \sqrt{2}. 5. Clipping (Optional): If clipping is enabled, calculate the intersection distance dis with the clipping plane. Adjust rayStart or rayStop based on the front/back face orientation and dis bounds. Recalculate marchDist, travel, and pos. Handle the edge case where dis == 0 to avoid division by zero. 6. Initialization: Initialize the accumulation buffer accum to zero. Calculate the initial travel distance and marchDist vector. 7. Ray Marching Loop: Loop numSamples times or until travel <= 0. In each iteration: a. Voxel Access: Sample the voxel value at the current position pos using getVoxel(tex, pos). This function maps the 3D volume coordinates to 2D texture coordinates based on the slice index and grid position. b. Color Computation: If colorizeIntensity is true, apply a heatmap transfer function Heatmap(tfpos, 0., 1.) to the sampled value tfpos. Otherwise, use tfpos directly as the RGB color. c. Alpha Masking: Compute an alpha mask for intensity isolation using smoothstep with intensityMin and intensityMax. The formula is: \text{value.a} = \left( \text{smoothstep}(\text{intensityMax}, \frac{\text{intensityMax}+\text{intensityMin}}{2}, \text{tf\pos}) \times \text{smoothstep}(\text{intensityMin}, \frac{\text{intensityMax}+\text{intensityMin}}{2}, \text{tf\pos}) \right)^{0.25}. d. Sample Alpha: Compute the sample alpha: \text{vsample.a} = \text{value.a} \cdot \text{opacityFactor} \cdot \frac{1}{\text{numSamples}} \cdot \text{fade} where \text{fade} = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{\text{distance}(\text{pos}, \text{rayStop})}{\text{stepSize}}, 0., 1.\right). e. Sample Color: Compute the sample color: \text{vsample.rgb} = \text{value.rgb} \cdot \text{vsample.a} \cdot \text{lightFactor} where lightFactor is typically 1.5. f. Compositing: Accumulate color and alpha using front-to-back blending: \text{accum.rgb} \leftarrow \text{accum.rgb} + (1. - \text{accum.a}) \cdot \text{vsample.rgb} \text{accum.a} \leftarrow \text{accum.a} + \text{vsample.a} Break the loop if accum.a >= 1.. 8. Output: Write accum.rgb and accum.a to the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumeatlas(tex, modelviewinv, numsamples, opacityfactor, colorizeintensity, intensitymin, intensitymax, clipplanenormal, clipplanedepth, clipenabled): """ Renders a volume using a 2D texture atlas. Args: tex: 2D texture atlas containing the volume slices. modelviewinv: 4x4 inverse model-view matrix. numsamples: Number of ray marching steps. opacityfactor: Global opacity multiplier. colorizeintensity: Boolean flag for heatmap coloring. intensitymin: Minimum intensity for isolation mask. intensitymax: Maximum intensity for isolation mask. clipplanenormal: Normal vector of the clipping plane. clipplanedepth: Depth of the clipping plane. clipenabled: Boolean flag to enable clipping. Returns: accum: vec4, the accumulated color and alpha. """ # Step 1: Ray Definition rayorigin = modelviewinv[3].xyz # Assuming 'pos' is the vertex position of the cube mesh covering the view frustum # In a real implementation, this would be per-vertex or per-pixel raydirection = normalize(pos - rayorigin) # Step 2: Ray-Volume Intersection with AABB [-1, 1]^3 # Simplified AABB intersection logic tnear = 0.0 tfar = sqrt(2.0) # Diagonal of unit cube # Calculate step size stepsize = tfar / numsamples # Step 3: Coordinate Transformation raystart = (rayorigin + 1.0) 0.5 raystop = (rayorigin + raydirection tfar + 1.0) 0.5 # Step 4: Clipping (Optional) if clipenabled: # Calculate intersection distance 'dis' with the clipping plane # Plane equation: dot(p, clipplanenormal) + clipplanedepth = 0 # Ray: p = raystart + t raydirection # dis = -(dot(raystart, clipplanenormal) + clipplanedepth) / dot(raydirection, clipplanenormal) denominator = dot(raydirection, clipplanenormal) if abs(denominator) > 1e-6: # Avoid division by zero dis = -(dot(raystart, clipplanenormal) + clipplanedepth) / denominator if dis > 0: if dis < tfar: raystop = raystart + raydirection dis tfar = dis # Recalculate step size and travel distance stepsize = tfar / numsamples travel = tfar else: travel = tfar marchdist = raydirection stepsize pos = raystart accum = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Step 7: Ray Marching Loop for i in range(numsamples): if travel <= 0.0: break # a. Voxel Access tfpos = getvoxelatlas(tex, pos, numslices=96, slicesoverx=10, slicesovery=10) # b. Color Computation if colorizeintensity: valuergb = heatmap(tfpos, 0.0, 1.0) else: valuergb = vec3(tfpos) # c. Alpha Masking midintensity = (intensitymax + intensitymin) / 2.0 smooth1 = smoothstep(intensitymax, midintensity, tfpos) smooth2 = smoothstep(intensitymin, midintensity, tfpos) valuea = pow(smooth1 smooth2, 0.25) # d. Sample Alpha fade = clamp(distance(pos, raystop) / stepsize, 0.0, 1.0) vsamplea = valuea opacityfactor (1.0 / float(numsamples)) fade # e. Sample Color lightfactor = 1.5 vsamplergb = valuergb vsamplea lightfactor # f. Compositing accum.rgb += (1.0 - accum.a) vsamplergb accum.a += vsamplea if accum.a >= 1.0: break # Update position pos += marchdist travel -= stepsize return accum def getvoxelatlas(tex, pos, numslices, slicesoverx, slicesovery): """ Maps 3D volume coordinates to 2D texture coordinates and samples the atlas. Args: tex: 2D texture atlas. pos: 3D position in texture space [0, 1]. numslices: Total number of volume slices. slicesoverx: Number of slices along X in the atlas. slicesovery: Number of slices along Y in the atlas. Returns: float: The sampled voxel value. """ # Invert X coordinate as per source volposx = 1.0 - pos.x volposy = pos.y volposz = pos.z # Calculate slice index s1 = floor(volposz numslices) # Calculate texture coordinates for the two adjacent slices # texpos1.x = dx1 + volpos.x / -slicesOverX # dx1 = fract(s1 / -slicesOverX) # Note: The source formula uses negative division, which might be a specific coordinate system detail. # Assuming standard positive grid layout for clarity, but adhering to source logic: dx1 = fract(s1 / -slicesoverx) texpos1x = dx1 + volposx / -slicesoverx texpos1y = floor(s1 / slicesovery) / slicesovery + volposy / slicesovery # Calculate texture coordinates for the next slice s2 = s1 + 1 dx2 = fract(s2 / -slicesoverx) texpos2x = dx2 + volposx / -slicesoverx texpos2y = floor(s2 / slicesovery) / slicesovery + volposy / slicesovery # Sample the two slices value1 = textureLod(tex, vec2(texpos1x, texpos1y), 0).x value2 = textureLod(tex, vec2(texpos2x, texpos2y), 0).x # Interpolate between the two slices # tfpos = mix(value1, value2, volpos.z numslices - s1) t = volposz numslices - s1 tfpos = mix(value1, value2, t) return tfpos Clipping Plane Division by Zero: The intersection distance dis calculation involves division by the dot product of the ray direction and the clipping plane normal. If this dot product is zero, the ray is parallel to the plane. The code must check if (dis != 0.) or if (abs(denominator) > epsilon) before calculating dis. Camera Inside Volume: The ray start time tnear can be negative if the camera is inside the AABB. The code clamps tnear to 0 to prevent negative march distances. Voxel Coordinate Inversion: The voxel coordinate X is inverted in getVoxel via volpos.x = 1.-volpos.x before texture lookup. This must be accounted for in the coordinate mapping. Precision: The use of fract and floor operations for texture coordinate calculation can introduce precision errors, especially for large volumes. Using higher precision types or careful normalization can mitigate this. Discrete Ray Casting with Trilinear Reconstruction is a direct volume rendering technique that samples volumetric data using discrete ray casting steps and reconstructs scalar values via trilinear interpolation. It differs from its parent, Direct Volume Ray Casting with Texture Atlas Voxel Access, by employing trilinear reconstruction within the ray casting loop rather than relying solely on bilinear interpolation of pre-sliced texture tiles for access. This method allows for continuous sampling along the ray path through the volume, improving visual quality over nearest-neighbor or purely 2D-interpolated approaches while maintaining the hardware-accelerated texture access patterns of the atlas-based parent. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of samples per ray and P is the number of pixels. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of samples and pixels. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the volume data, but stored as a 2D texture atlas, so the memory footprint is similar to a 2D texture of size (W \cdot \text{slicesOverX}) \times (H \cdot \text{slicesOverY}). Measured Performance: The method is hardware-accelerated and runs in the fragment shader. Performance depends on the GPU's texture sampling throughput and the number of samples per ray. Typical resolution: 1280x720, 256 samples per ray. Scaling: The method scales well with resolution and sample count, but performance degrades linearly with increased samples. The 2D texture atlas approach can be more memory-efficient than 3D textures on some hardware. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated, efficient memory access patterns, compatible with standard 2D texture units. Limitations: Limited to discrete slices, potential artifacts at slice boundaries if not interpolated correctly, less flexible than 3D texture lookups for arbitrary sampling positions. When to Use: When rendering large volumes on hardware with limited 3D texture support or when memory bandwidth is a concern. When Not to Use: When high-quality continuous interpolation is required, or when the volume data changes frequently and repacking the atlas is expensive. The method is based on the implementation in the MobiusEngine, specifically the VolumeInspector component. The technique of using texture atlases for volume rendering has been explored in various contexts to optimize memory access and leverage 2D texture hardware. The specific implementation details, including the clipping plane handling and intensity isolation mask, are derived from the VolumeInspector source code. graphXDoses/VolumeInspector, https://github.com/graphXDoses/VolumeInspector, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Discrete Ray Casting with Trilinear Reconstruction
head: Trilinear Reconstruction Ray Casting
body: Discrete Ray Casting with Trilinear Reconstruction is a direct volume rendering technique that samples volumetric data using discrete ray casting steps and reconstructs scalar values via trilinear interpolation. It differs from its parent, Direct Volume Ray Casting with Texture Atlas Voxel Access, by employing trilinear reconstruction within the ray casting loop rather than relying solely on bilinear interpolation of pre-sliced texture tiles for access. This method allows for continuous sampling along the ray path through the volume, improving visual quality over nearest-neighbor or purely 2D-interpolated approaches while maintaining the hardware-accelerated texture access patterns of the atlas-based parent. Inputs: A 2D texture atlas containing all vertical slices of the volume in grayscale, 32-bit floating-point format. Camera parameters (position, orientation) to define ray origins and directions. Clipping plane parameters: orientation (pitch, yaw) and depth, with an option to lock the plane to the camera. Rendering parameters: overall opacity control, intensity value clamping limits, and color mapping mode (grayscale or heatmap). Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel represents the accumulated color and opacity of the ray passing through the volume. Texture Atlas: A 2D texture of arbitrary size, structured as a 10 \times 10 grid of tiles. Tile Layout: The atlas contains 96 used tiles out of 100. The layout is hardcoded: the top (first) slice is located at the top-left corner of the grid. The remaining 4 tiles are unused. Ray State: For each pixel, a ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} are computed in the vertex shader. 1. Domain Construction: The vertex shader generates the geometry (typically a screen-aligned quad) to produce fragments covering the viewport. 2. Ray Initialization: For each fragment, compute the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} based on the camera position and the fragment's screen coordinates. 3. Clipping Plane Intersection: Define the clipping plane by its normal vector \mathbf{n} and distance d{plane} from the origin. Calculate the intersection parameter t{clip} where the ray intersects the plane: t{clip} = \frac{d{plane} - \mathbf{o} \cdot \mathbf{n}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}} Determine the start of the volume traversal: If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} < 0 (normal faces the ray source), the ray enters the volume at the near plane or origin, and the clipping plane acts as a far boundary. The traversal starts at the volume entry point and stops at t{clip}. If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} \ge 0 (normal does not face the ray source), the ray starts from the intersection point with the plane's surface. The traversal begins at t{clip} and proceeds into the volume. Let t{start} be the starting parameter and t{end} be the ending parameter of the ray segment within the volume. 4. Ray Casting Loop: Iterate along the ray from t{start} to t{end} with a fixed step size \Delta t. Calculate the current 3D position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d}. Map \mathbf{p} to the corresponding tile in the 2D atlas. Since the atlas stores vertical slices, the mapping involves determining which slice index s corresponds to the z-coordinate (or depth axis) of \mathbf{p}, and the (x, y) coordinates within that slice. Compute the UV coordinates (u, v) for the current position within the specific tile. Trilinear Reconstruction: Sample the texture using trilinear interpolation. This involves: 1. Bilinear interpolation of the current slice's texture at (u, v) to get scalar value v0. 2. Bilinear interpolation of the adjacent slice's texture (previous or next, depending on interpolation direction) at (u, v) to get scalar value v1. 3. Linear interpolation between v0 and v1 based on the fractional distance of \mathbf{p} between the two slice planes to obtain the final scalar value s. Apply intensity clamping: if s is outside the defined visibility range, treat it as background or zero. Apply color mapping: convert scalar s to color C and opacity \alpha using the selected mode (grayscale or heatmap). Accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing: C{out} = C{in} + C \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) Apply global opacity control: multiply the final accumulated opacity by the user-defined opacity slider value. 5. Fragment Output: Output the final accumulated color and opacity to the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vertexposition): # Generate screen-aligned quad or use built-in vertex attributes return vertexposition def fragmentshader(screenuv, cameraparams): # 1. Ray Initialization rayorigin = getrayorigin(screenuv, cameraparams) raydirection = getraydirection(screenuv, cameraparams) # 2. Clipping Plane Intersection # Plane defined by normal n and distance dplane # Check if normal faces the ray source if dot(raydirection, planenormal) < 0: # Normal faces ray source: ray hits domain, progresses until plane surface tclip = (planedistance - dot(rayorigin, planenormal)) / dot(raydirection, planenormal) tstart = volumeentryt # Assumed known from volume bounds tend = tclip else: # Normal does not face ray source: start from plane surface tclip = (planedistance - dot(rayorigin, planenormal)) / dot(raydirection, planenormal) tstart = tclip tend = volumeexitt # Assumed known from volume bounds # 3. Ray Casting Loop accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 t = tstart while t < tend: # Current 3D position p = rayorigin + t raydirection # Map p to atlas tile and UV coordinates # This requires knowing the volume's spatial extent and slice spacing sliceindex = getsliceindex(p.z) # Assuming z is the slice axis uvintile = getuvintile(p.x, p.y) # Trilinear Reconstruction # Sample current slice valcurrent = texture(atlastexture, uvfortile(sliceindex, uvintile)) # Sample adjacent slice (interpolate between sliceindex and sliceindex + 1) # Determine fractional depth within the slice interval frac = getfractionaldepth(p.z, sliceindex) valnext = texture(atlastexture, uvfortile(sliceindex + 1, uvintile)) # Linear interpolation between slices (trilinear reconstruction) scalarvalue = lerp(valcurrent, valnext, frac) # Intensity Clamping if scalarvalue < intensitymin or scalarvalue > intensitymax: scalarvalue = 0.0 # Color Mapping color, alpha = mapcolorandalpha(scalarvalue, colormode) # Front-to-Back Compositing if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + color alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedalpha = accumulatedalpha + alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) t += stepsize # Apply global opacity control finalalpha = accumulatedalpha globalopacityslider return vec4(accumulatedcolor, finalalpha) Atlas Grid: Hardcoded 10 \times 10 grid, using 96 tiles. Clipping Plane: Defined by pitch, yaw, and depth; can be locked to camera. Opacity Slider: Controls overall volume opacity. Intensity Clamping: Limits visibility based on scalar intensity values. Color Mapping: Modes include grayscale (default) and heatmap. Precision: Using 32-bit floating-point textures ensures sufficient precision for scalar values. Boundary Conditions: The hardcoded 96-tile layout means rays hitting unused tiles (4 out of 100) will not contribute to the image. Clipping Plane Orientation: Incorrect handling of the normal vector direction relative to the ray source can lead to incorrect traversal start/end points. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of ray steps per pixel. The trilinear reconstruction adds a constant factor of texture lookups per step. Memory Complexity: O(S), where S is the size of the texture atlas. The atlas size depends on the number of slices and the resolution of each slice. Not given in the sources. The method scales with the number of slices and the resolution of the texture atlas. The hardcoded 96-tile limit may restrict the maximum number of slices unless the atlas layout is modified. Strengths: Trilinear reconstruction provides smoother visual results than nearest-neighbor sampling. The use of a texture atlas allows for efficient hardware-accelerated texture sampling. Limitations: The hardcoded 96-tile layout limits flexibility. Trilinear reconstruction is more computationally expensive than bilinear or nearest-neighbor sampling. Use when smooth interpolation is required and the volume has a manageable number of slices that fit within the 96-tile constraint. Avoid when the volume has more than 96 slices or when higher performance is needed and visual smoothness is less critical. The method is described in the context of the VolumeInspector application, which utilizes a texture atlas for volume rendering. The approach builds on earlier work in direct volume rendering and texture-based volume visualization. The method is implemented in the VolumeInspector software. graphXDoses/VolumeInspector, https://github.com/graphXDoses/VolumeInspector, fetched 2026-10-28
