name: Intensity-isolated Front-to-back Ray Marching
head: Front-to-back volume ray marching with intensity isolation mask, Intensity-masked Volume Ray Marching
body: Intensity-isolated Front-to-back Ray Marching is a direct volume rendering technique that restricts the visual contribution of a ray to a specific scalar intensity range, defined by intensityMin and intensityMax. It solves the problem of visual clutter in dense volumes by masking out voxels outside this range using a smoothstep-based opacity mask, while maintaining the standard front-to-back compositing order. It differs from standard ray casting by the explicit intensity gating and from Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) by preserving depth-based occlusion and alpha accumulation rather than selecting only the highest value. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume texture tex, camera ray parameters (origin, direction, rayStop), and shader uniforms: intensityMin, intensityMax, opacityFactor, numSamples, colorizeIntensity, and lightFactor. Output: A final pixel color accum.rgb and accumulated opacity accum.a. Data Structures: accum: A structure containing rgb (vec3) and a (float), initialized to (0, 0). vsample: A structure containing rgb (vec3) and a (float), representing the weighted contribution of the current sample. value: A temporary structure containing rgb (vec3) and a (float), representing the raw transfer function output before masking and weighting. Parameters: intensityMin: Lower bound of the isolated intensity range. intensityMax: Upper bound of the isolated intensity range. opacityFactor: Global multiplier for sample alpha. numSamples: Total number of samples per ray, used to normalize opacity. colorizeIntensity: Interpolation factor between raw intensity color and a heatmap color. lightFactor: Multiplier for sample color contribution. marchDist: Step increment for ray position per iteration. rayStop: Endpoint of the ray segment being marched. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize pos to the ray origin, accum to (0, 0), and travel to the distance from pos to rayStop. 2. Loop while travel > 0: a. Calculate fade: \text{fade} = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{\text{distance}(\text{pos}, \text{rayStop})}{\text{stepSize}}, 0., 1.\right) where stepSize is derived from the total ray length divided by numSamples. b. Sample the voxel at pos: \text{tf\pos} = \text{getVoxel}(\text{tex}, \text{pos}) This retrieves the scalar intensity value V(\mathbf{p}). c. Compute the base color value.rgb: \text{value.rgb} = \text{mix}(\text{vec3}(\text{tf\pos}), \text{Heatmap}(\text{tf\pos}, 0., 1.), \text{float}(\text{colorizeIntensity})) This mixes the raw scalar value (cast to RGB) with a heatmap color based on colorizeIntensity. d. Compute the opacity mask value.a using a smoothstep function centered on the isolated range: \text{value.a} = \text{pow}\left( \text{smoothstep}(\text{intensityMax}, \frac{\text{intensityMax}+\text{intensityMin}}{2}, \text{tf\pos}) \times \text{smoothstep}(\text{intensityMin}, \frac{\text{intensityMax}+\text{intensityMin}}{2}, \text{tf\pos}), 0.25 \right) The smoothstep function creates a bell-shaped mask that is 1.0 at the midpoint of the range and 0.0 outside the bounds, raised to the power of 0.25 to soften the transition. e. Compute the final sample alpha vsample.a: \text{vsample.a} = \text{value.a} \times \text{opacityFactor} \times \left(\frac{1.0}{\text{numSamples}}\right) \times \text{fade} This normalizes the opacity by the number of samples and applies the fade factor. f. Compute the final sample color vsample.rgb: \text{vsample.rgb} = \text{value.rgb} \times \text{vsample.a} \times \text{lightFactor} This weights the color by the computed alpha and a lighting factor. g. Accumulate the color: \text{accum.rgb} \leftarrow \text{accum.rgb} + (1.0 - \text{accum.a}) \times \text{vsample.rgb} h. Accumulate the alpha: \text{accum.a} \leftarrow \text{accum.a} + \text{vsample.a} i. Check for early termination: If accum.a >= 1.0, break the loop. j. Update position: \text{pos} \leftarrow \text{pos} + \text{marchDist} \text{travel} \leftarrow \text{travel} - \text{stepSize} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intensityisolatedraymarch(tex, rayorigin, raydirection, raystop, intensitymin, intensitymax, opacityfactor, numsamples, colorizeintensity, lightfactor): # Calculate step size and initial parameters raylength = distance(rayorigin, raystop) stepsize = raylength / numsamples pos = rayorigin travel = raylength accumrgb = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accuma = 0.0 # Pre-calculate midpoint for smoothstep midpoint = (intensitymax + intensitymin) 0.5 while travel > 0.0: # 1. Calculate fade factor disttostop = distance(pos, raystop) fade = clamp(disttostop / stepsize, 0.0, 1.0) # 2. Sample voxel intensity tfpos = getvoxel(tex, pos) # 3. Compute color # Assuming vec3(tfpos) casts scalar to RGB (e.g., grayscale) rawcolor = vec3(tfpos) heatmapcolor = computeheatmap(tfpos, 0.0, 1.0) valuergb = mix(rawcolor, heatmapcolor, float(colorizeintensity)) # 4. Compute opacity mask using smoothstep # smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) returns 0 if x <= edge0, 1 if x >= edge1 # First term: 1 when tfpos <= midpoint, decreasing to 0 at intensityMax term1 = smoothstep(intensitymax, midpoint, tfpos) # Second term: 0 when tfpos <= intensityMin, increasing to 1 at midpoint term2 = smoothstep(intensitymin, midpoint, tfpos) valuea = pow(term1 term2, 0.25) # 5. Compute sample alpha vsamplea = valuea opacityfactor (1.0 / numsamples) fade # 6. Compute sample color vsamplergb = valuergb vsamplea lightfactor # 7. Accumulate color accumrgb += (1.0 - accuma) vsamplergb # 8. Accumulate alpha accuma += vsamplea # 9. Early termination check if accuma >= 1.0: break # 10. Update position pos += raydirection stepsize # marchDist is effectively stepsize along direction travel -= stepsize return accumrgb, accuma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Termination: The loop breaks when accum.a >= 1.0 to avoid overdraw and wasted computation. Intensity Range: If intensityMin >= intensityMax, the smoothstep mask will likely result in zero opacity for all samples, rendering the volume invisible. Precision: The fade calculation uses distance(pos, rayStop). If pos exceeds rayStop due to floating-point error, fade may become negative before clamping, though clamp handles this. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is numSamples. The loop runs until full opacity is reached or all samples are processed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, storing only the accumulator and current sample values. Strengths: Effectively isolates specific tissue types or data ranges in medical or scientific visualization by suppressing background noise. Simple to implement as a shader modification. Limitations: The smoothstep mask is not a hard cutoff, which may lead to subtle leakage of adjacent intensities. Performance is identical to standard ray casting, but visual utility is restricted to the specified range. When to use: When the user needs to inspect a specific density range within a complex volume without removing other structures entirely (which might require multiple passes or segmentation). When not to use: When global context is required, or when the intensity range is unknown and requires interactive adjustment. This method is derived from the implementation details of the VolumeInspector tool within the graphXDoses project. It represents a practical application of intensity masking in real-time volume rendering, utilizing GLSL-style operations (smoothstep, mix, clamp) typical of GPU-based ray marching. graphXDoses/VolumeInspector, https://github.com/graphXDoses/VolumeInspector, fetched 2026-10-28

name: V-Buffer image order ray casting
head: V-Buffer, V-Buffer cell-by-cell processing
body: V-Buffer image order ray casting is a volume rendering technique that generates an interpretable representation of volumetric data for scientific and engineering analysis rather than a photorealistic image. It distinguishes itself from standard ray casting by processing volume cells in a strict front-to-back, plane-by-plane order, determining which pixels are affected by each cell before compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset defined on a grid of cells; camera parameters (viewpoint, projection); transfer functions for scalar-to-color/opacity mapping; shading and depth cuing parameters. Output: A 2D image where each pixel stores accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Volume: A grid of cells. The method processes these cells in a specific order: front-to-back, plane-by-plane, and within each plane, by increasing distance from the viewpoint. Pixel Buffer: Stores the accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} and opacity \alpha{acc} for each pixel. Initialized to (0, 0). Ray State: For each pixel, the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} are defined. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0, 0, 0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0 for all pixels. 2. Iterate Cells: Process each cell in the volume in front-to-back order. a. Identify Affected Pixels: For the current cell, determine which pixels in the image plane are intersected by the cell's projection. b. Ray Intersection: For each affected pixel, determine the entry point of the ray into the current cell. c. Step Through Cell: Step the ray along the segment inside the current cell. d. Sample and Compute: At each stepping point within the cell: i. Determine the scalar value V at the sample position. ii. Map V to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha using transfer functions. iii. Apply shading and depth cuing calculations. e. Composite: Update the pixel's accumulated color and opacity using the front-to-back compositing equation: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c} \cdot \alpha \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alpha f. Termination Check: If \alpha{acc} reaches unity (1.0), stop processing further cells for this pixel. 3. Store Result: After all cells are processed or opacity reaches unity, store the final \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} for the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vbufferimageorderraycasting(volume, camera, transferfunction, shadingmodel): # Initialize pixel buffers numpixels = camera.imagewidth camera.imageheight pixelcolors = [Vector3(0, 0, 0) for in range(numpixels)] pixelopacities = [0.0 for in range(numpixels)] # Get cells sorted in front-to-back, plane-by-plane order sortedcells = volume.getcellssortedbydistance(camera.eyepoint) for cell in sortedcells: # Determine which pixels are affected by this cell affectedpixels = cell.getintersectedpixels(camera) for pixelidx in affectedpixels: # If pixel is already fully opaque, skip if pixelopacities[pixelidx] >= 1.0: continue # Define ray for this pixel rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(pixelidx) # Find intersection of ray with current cell tentry, texit = cell.intersectray(rayorigin, raydirection) if tentry is None: continue # Step through the cell stepsize = cell.getstepsize() t = tentry while t < texit: # Sample position samplepos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Get scalar value scalarval = volume.sampleat(samplepos) # Transfer function color, alpha = transferfunction(scalarval) # Shading and depth cuing color = shadingmodel(color, samplepos, scalarval) # Composite pixelcolors[pixelidx] += (1.0 - pixelopacities[pixelidx]) color alpha pixelopacities[pixelidx] += (1.0 - pixelopacities[pixelidx]) alpha # Advance step t += stepsize # Early termination if fully opaque if pixelopacities[pixelidx] >= 1.0: break return pixelcolors, pixelopacities Parameters: Step Size: The distance between sampling points within a cell. Not given in the sources. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity. Defined by the user. Shading Model: Computes base color based on local gradients. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Unity: If accumulated opacity reaches 1.0, further cells do not contribute to the pixel color. This optimization must be checked per pixel. Cell Order: Processing order is critical for correct front-to-back compositing. Cells must be processed from closest to furthest relative to the viewpoint. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of cells times the average number of pixels affected per cell, times the number of steps per cell. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of pixels for the color and opacity buffers. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides interpretable representations for scientific analysis. Explicit cell-by-cell processing allows for detailed control over shading and depth cuing. Limitations: Not designed for photorealism. Performance may be impacted by the overhead of determining affected pixels for each cell. When to Use: When interpretability for scientists/engineers is the primary goal. When Not to Use: When photorealistic rendering is required. The V-Buffer image order ray casting method was introduced as an alternative to standard ray casting techniques, focusing on interpretability rather than photorealism. It builds on the principles of ray casting where rays are traversed from the eye point through each pixel into the volume. The method processes cells in a front-to-back order, beginning on the plane closest to the viewpoint and progressing plane-by-plane. name: Image-order volume rendering
head: Levoy's Image-order Volume Rendering
body: Image-order volume rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that precomputes optical properties for every voxel before rendering. Unlike on-the-fly methods, it shifts shading and classification to a preprocessing phase, allowing the rendering pass to sample and composite pre-calculated arrays. It is distinguished by this explicit separation of property generation from integration, enabling higher-order interpolation on the precomputed data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset V on a 3D grid, a transfer function T mapping scalar values to optical properties, and a shading model for computing color from gradients. Output: Two precomputed 3D arrays: a color array \mathbf{C}{pre} and an opacity array \alpha{pre}, aligned with the voxel grid. The final image is generated by ray casting through these arrays. Data Structures: 1. Volume Grid: V[x, y, z] stores scalar values. 2. Precomputed Color Array: \mathbf{C}{pre}[x, y, z] stores RGB vectors. 3. Precomputed Opacity Array: \alpha{pre}[x, y, z] stores scalar opacity values. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: For each voxel (x, y, z), generate the color and opacity arrays using preprocessing techniques. This involves performing a shading operation to compute the color array and applying transfer functions to define the opacity array. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel, traverse a viewing ray from the eye point into the volume. Evaluate the volume rendering integral using equidistant sampling along the ray. Composite samples front-to-back from the eye into the volume. Formulas: The front-to-back compositing for samples i=1 \dots N with color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai is: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) Iteratively, initialized to (\mathbf{C}{acc}, \alpha{acc}) = (\mathbf{0}, 0): \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def intersectbox(origin, direction, bounds): tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < bounds[2i] or origin[i] > bounds[2i+1]: return None, None else: t1 = (bounds[2i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[2i+1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - Step Size: Equidistant sampling is used along the viewing rays. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory: Requires storing the original volume plus two additional arrays of identical dimensions. Data Updates: If the volume data or transfer function changes, the preprocessing phase must be repeated. Processes volume cells individually during ray traversal, combining image-order precomputation with cell-based optimization. Time Complexity: Preprocessing scales as O(V) where V is the voxel count, covering shading and classification for every voxel. Rendering scales as O(P \cdot N) where P is pixel count and N is samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires 3 \times the base memory footprint of the scalar volume (original data, color array, opacity array). Strengths: Reduces per-pixel runtime computation by moving shading and classification to a single preprocessing pass. Enables higher-order interpolation on precomputed data. Limitations: High memory consumption. Requires full preprocessing regeneration for dynamic data or transfer function changes. When to Use: Static volumes where high-quality rendering with higher-order interpolation is prioritized and memory is sufficient. When Not to Use: Dynamic volumes, interactive transfer function adjustment, or memory-constrained environments. The image-order volume rendering algorithm was developed by Harold W. Levoy. name: Projection and Ray Geometry
head: Ray Definition, Camera Model, Projection Types
body: Projection and Ray Geometry defines the mathematical relationship between the 3D volume data and the 2D image plane by establishing the origin, direction, and traversal parameters of the rays used in direct volume ray casting. It solves the problem of mapping pixel coordinates to volumetric space, determining which voxels contribute to which pixels. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its foundational role: while Standard Ray Casting implements the sampling loop, this family defines the coordinate systems (perspective vs. parallel) and ray generation logic that precede sampling. All direct volume ray casting methods share the following core mechanism: 1. Ray Definition: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane, a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. The ray is intersected with the volume bounding box to determine the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far}. 2. Sampling: The ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] is discretized into N samples at positions ti = t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N. At each sample position \mathbf{p}i = r(ti), the scalar volume value V(\mathbf{p}i) is retrieved, typically via trilinear interpolation of the surrounding voxels. 3. Classification (Transfer Function): The scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) is mapped to optical properties: a color vector \mathbf{c}i (RGB) and an opacity scalar \alphai (A). This mapping is defined by a transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). The opacity is often corrected for the step size \Delta t to approximate continuous attenuation, using models such as Beer-Lambert: \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta t}, where \sigmai is the extinction coefficient derived from V(\mathbf{p}i). 4. Compositing (Integration): The samples are composited into the final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out} using the front-to-back volume rendering equation: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) In iterative form, for each sample i: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} are initialized to (0, 0). 5. Shading: At each sample, a shading model (e.g., Phong, Blinn-Phong) may be applied to compute the base color \mathbf{c}i based on the local gradient \nabla V(\mathbf{p}i), which serves as the surface normal. A composition scheme where interpolated samples are summed to mimic X-ray attenuation, losing depth cues. An object-order technique projecting voxels directly to the image plane via splatting, relying on traversal order for hidden surface removal. Definition: A ray-tracing projection where every ray follows a trajectory parallel to all other rays, maintaining constant direction and spacing throughout the volume. Step: Rays are shot through the spectral cube, and pixel values are calculated based on voxel values encountered along each ray's path. A transfer function combines the sampled voxel values into the final pixel's color and transparency values. The distinction between parallel (orthographic) and perspective projection is fundamental to ray-tracing volume rendering. For a parallel projection, each ray has a trajectory that is parallel to other rays, while for a perspective projection, all ray trajectories diverge from a focal point that corresponds to the observer's eye. The geometric setup determines how ray origins and directions are computed from camera parameters. name: Forward Projection (aTx)
head: Fan Beam Projection, Parallel Beam Projection, X-ray projection, aTx
body: X-ray projection (also called Forward Projection or aTx) is a volume rendering composition scheme where interpolated samples along a ray are simply summed to produce an image. It mimics the physical process of X-ray attenuation, where the total signal is the integral of density along the ray path. Unlike alpha blending, which preserves depth cues through opacity accumulation, this method loses depth information, making it suitable for visualizing high-density structures like bones or vessels where relative depth is less critical than total integrated intensity. Inputs: A 3D volume V (scalar field, e.g., density or attenuation coefficient). Ray parameters defining the projection geometry (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, sampling interval \Delta s). Outputs: A 2D projection image P where each pixel value P{ij} is the sum of interpolated volume values along the corresponding ray. Data Structures: The volume V is stored as a 3D array or grid. The accumulator for each ray is a scalar initialized to 0. Steps: 1. For each pixel (i, j) in the output image, define the ray \mathbf{r}(s) = \mathbf{o}{ij} + s \cdot \mathbf{d}{ij}, where s ranges from the near to the far clipping plane. 2. Initialize the accumulator A = 0. 3. Iterate through samples k along the ray at positions sk: a. Compute the 3D world position \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{r}(sk). b. Sample the volume value vk = V(\mathbf{p}k) using interpolation (e.g., trilinear). c. Update the accumulator: A \leftarrow A + \Delta s \cdot vk. 4. Assign the final accumulator value to the pixel: P{ij} = A. Formula: The discrete approximation of the line integral is: P{ij} = \sum{k=1}^{N} vk \cdot \Delta s where vk is the interpolated volume value at sample k, and \Delta s is the step size along the ray. Parameters: \Delta s: Sampling interval. Typical values depend on the volume resolution and desired accuracy; often set to the voxel size or a fraction thereof. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Loss of Depth Information: Since only the sum is stored, occlusion and depth ordering are not represented. Aliasing: If \Delta s is too large relative to the frequency content of the volume, artifacts may appear. Boundary Conditions: Rays that do not intersect the volume should return 0. It exploits rotational invariance to reduce 3D line integrals to a 1D radial problem, distinguishing it from general 3D projectors that handle arbitrary distributions. Choose it when the target volume exhibits axisymmetry and computational efficiency is prioritized over arbitrary geometry support. A method that replaces local affine approximations with exact ray tracing to compute line integrals through 3D Gaussian primitives analytically. It directly computes ray-primitive intersections, avoiding the non-overlapping Gaussian assumption and addressing nonlinear corrections like arc-correction in PET scanners. Choose it when quantitative accuracy and geometric flexibility are required over screen-space splatting pipelines. A variant that initializes CT reconstruction by computing a reference image via Fan beam ray transform and filtered back projection (FBP), then creates a sparse sinogram by subsampling and resizing. It is used when preparing initialization data for tomographic pipelines that require sparse or resized projection inputs. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast computation, good for visualizing dense structures. Limitations: No depth information, no transparency effects, sensitive to sampling density. When to use: When depth cues are not required, and the goal is to visualize the total integrated density (e.g., bone visualization in CT). When not to use: When transparency, occlusion, or depth perception is important. Not given in the sources. name: CT Initialization via Fan Beam Ray Transform and FBP
head: MFG (Multiplicative First Guess), Multiplicative First Guess
body: This method initializes the intensity distribution of a 3D volume from pre-processed projection images to reduce calculation time and accelerate the convergence of iterative reconstruction algorithms. It differs from sibling methods by combining a Fan beam ray transform with Filtered Back Projection (FBP) to generate a reference image, followed by a multiplicative update rule based on voxel visibility across all cameras. Unlike Cylindrical Symmetry Projector which assumes symmetry, or Analytic 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomography which models point spread functions, this method relies on geometric visibility and multiplicative updates. Inputs: Pre-processed projection images (one per camera/view). Outputs: Initialized 3D volume intensity distribution. Data Structures: sinogram: Array of shape [batch, 720, 720], dtype float32. sparsesinogram: Array of shape [batch, 720, 720], dtype float32. oriimg: Array of shape [batch, 720, 720], dtype float32. sinogrammax: Array of shape [batch, 1], dtype float32. volume: 3D grid of voxels with intensity values. Parameters: r: Subsampling stride for the sinogram along the first axis (angular/detector axis). Value not given in the sources. N: Number of cameras/views. Steps: 1. Identify Visible Regions: Determine regions inside the volume such that their intensity values are non-zero for all cameras. 2. Zero Out Non-Visible Voxels: Set the intensity value of any voxel outside these identified regions to zero. 3. Compute Reference Image (FBP): a. Convert input image to CPU numpy array. b. Initialize sinogram, sparsesinogram, and oriimg arrays with shape [batch, 720, 720]. c. For each batch element i: i. Compute sinogram[i] via Fan beam ray transform of the input image: sinogram[i] = Fanraytrafo(img[i]). ii. Compute reference image oriimg[i] via Filtered Back Projection (FBP) of the sinogram: oriimg[i] = FanFBP(sinogram[i]). iii. Store the maximum value of the sinogram: sinogrammax[i] = max(sinogram[i]). d. Subsample sinogram[i] along the first axis with stride r: t = np.copy(sinogram[i,::r,:]). e. Resize t to [720, 720] using bilinear interpolation (cv2.resize) and store in sparsesinogram. 4. Multiplicative Update: For each voxel v in the visible regions: a. Identify the corresponding pixel Pi on the projection for each camera i. b. Let Rij be the weight of voxel v for camera i. c. Update voxel intensity: V{new} = V{old} \times \prod{i=1}^{N} (R{ij} \times Pi). d. Normalize the voxel by raising the new value to the power of 1/N: V{final} = V{new}^{1/N}. This ensures continuity of the relative field amplitude. Pseudocode: Unverified code. When Not to Use: When high precision is critical and computational time is not a constraint. The MFG (Multiplicative First Guess) method was introduced by Worth and Nickels in 2008. It is used in tomographic reconstruction, particularly in particle image velocimetry (PIV) and 3D particle tracking, to estimate the initial intensity distribution of a volume from pre-processed projection images. name: Cylindrical Symmetry Projector
head: Abel Transform, Abel Transform Discretization
body: The Cylindrical Symmetry Projector is a forward and back projector pair designed for objects with cylindrical symmetry. It solves the problem of computing line integrals through axisymmetric volumes by reducing the 3D integration to a 1D radial problem, specifically implementing the Abel Transform for parallel-beam geometries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A radial extinction coefficient profile \alpha(r) defined for r \in [0, r{max}]. Output: The total optical depth \delta{max}(x) for a set of projection rays at impact parameter x. Data Structures: Radial Profile: A vector A of size Nr, representing \alpha(rj) at discrete radii rj. Projection Vector: A vector \Delta of size Nx, representing \delta{max}(xi) at discrete impact parameters xi. Kernel Matrix: A matrix K of size Nx \times Nr, where element K{ij} represents the geometric path length of the i-th ray passing through the j-th concentric ring. Radial Boundaries: An array of size Nr + 1 defining the inner and outer radii of each concentric ring. Steps: 1. Discretization: Discretize the cross-section into Nr concentric rings to approximate the continuous integral as a finite sum. 2. Kernel Construction: Compute the geometric kernel matrix K, where K{ij} corresponds to the path length of the i-th ray through the j-th ring. 3. Forward Projection: Compute the total optical depth vector \Delta using the linear algebraic form \Delta = KA. 4. Back Projection: Reconstruct \alpha(r) from measured \delta{max}(x) by solving the linear system KA = \Delta for A. Formulas: Under axisymmetry, the total optical depth \delta{max}(x) is the Abel transform of the local extinction-coefficient profile \alpha(r): \delta{max}(x) = 2 \int{x}^{r{max}} \frac{\alpha(r) r}{\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}} dr This integral is approximated by the discrete sum: \Deltai = \sum{j=0}^{Nr-1} K{ij} Aj where K{ij} encodes the integral of the geometric factor over the j-th ring for the i-th ray. Parameters: r{max}: Maximum radius of the object. x: Impact parameter (distance from the axis of symmetry to the ray). Nr, Nx: Number of radial bins and projection samples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: The kernel has a singularity at r=x, requiring careful numerical evaluation or analytic integration over ring widths. Ill-Conditioning: The Abel transform is an ill-posed inverse problem, making the back projection sensitive to noise. Out-of-Bounds Rays: Rays with x > r{max} yield zero optical depth and must be clamped to avoid negative square roots. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cylindricalsymmetryprojector(alpha, rboundaries, xgrid): """ Forward projection using Cylindrical Symmetry (Abel Transform). alpha: vector A of size Nr, extinction coefficients per ring. rboundaries: array of size Nr + 1 defining ring inner/outer radii. xgrid: array of impact parameters xi. """ Nr = len(alpha) Nx = len(xgrid) deltamax = [0.0] Nx K = [[0.0] Nr for in range(Nx)] for i in range(Nx): xi = xgrid[i] for j in range(Nr): rinner = rboundaries[j] router = rboundaries[j + 1] # Analytic integral of Abel kernel 2r/sqrt(r^2-x^2) over ring [rinner, router] termouter = math.sqrt(max(router2 - xi2, 0.0)) terminner = math.sqrt(max(rinner2 - xi2, 0.0)) K[i][j] = 2.0 (termouter - terminner) for i in range(Nx): s = 0.0 for j in range(Nr): s += K[i][j] alpha[j] deltamax[i] = s return deltamax The specific mathematical operation applied in parallel-beam geometries for cylindrical symmetry. Choose it when the object is strictly axisymmetric and the projection geometry is parallel. Link: Abel Transform. The method of dividing the radial profile into concentric rings to approximate the continuous integral. Choose finer discretization for higher accuracy but increased computational cost. Link: Radial Discretization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces a 3D integration problem to a 1D radial problem for axisymmetric objects. Limitations: Only applicable to objects with cylindrical symmetry; the back projection involves solving an ill-posed linear system. When to use: When the object is known to be axisymmetric. When not to use: For arbitrary 3D objects or objects with significant asymmetry. The method was implemented as a forward/back projector pair for objects with cylindrical symmetry by Champley & Maddox (2021). It is applied in tomographic reconstruction of axisymmetric sprays and combustion diagnostics. name: Analytic 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomography
head: 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomographic Reconstruction, 3D Gaussian ray tracing, Analytic forward projection for 3D Gaussians
body: This method replaces the local affine approximation of splatting with exact ray tracing to compute line integrals through 3D Gaussian primitives analytically. It solves the problem of quantitative accuracy degradation and geometric inflexibility in tomographic reconstruction, specifically addressing nonlinear corrections like arc-correction in PET scanners. Unlike splatting-based pipelines which project into 2D screen space, this approach directly computes ray-primitive intersections, avoiding the assumption of non-overlapping Gaussians. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by a mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Scanner geometry defining ray origins \mathbf{o}j and directions \mathbf{d}j for each detector element or pixel j. A Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) structure built over the Gaussian primitives for spatial acceleration. Outputs: A set of projected values (line integrals) for each ray, used to optimize Gaussian parameters or form the final reconstruction. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitive: Defined by \boldsymbol{\mu} (position) and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (shape/orientation). The density function is G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right). BVH: A hierarchical spatial partitioning structure storing bounding volumes for subsets of Gaussians to accelerate intersection tests. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Setup: Define ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d} based on the specific scanner geometry (e.g., PET Line of Response or CT cone/parallel beams). 2. Intersection Search: For each ray, use the BVH to efficiently identify all 3D Gaussian primitives intersected by the ray. 3. Analytic Integration: Compute the pixel value by analytically integrating the contribution of each encountered Gaussian along the ray segment. 4. Optimization: Adjust the Gaussian parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) so that the rendered projections match the measured projection data. 5. Reconstruction: Voxelize the optimized Gaussians to obtain the final tomographic reconstruction. Analytic Line Integral Formula: For a single anisotropic 3D Gaussian G(\mathbf{x}) and a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, the line integral I is computed analytically. The core operation is: I = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} G(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) \, dt This avoids the affine collapse inherent in splatting methods. Parameters: Acceleration Structure: BVH is used to limit the number of primitives requiring intersection checks. Kernel: Primarily uses 3D Gaussian kernels, but compact kernels like the Epanechnikov kernel are also supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Sorting: Unlike standard rendering where depth sorting is required for correct alpha blending, sorting of depth-ordered intersections can be waived in tomographic reconstruction because the method computes line integrals rather than pixel colors. Geometric Flexibility: The method requires explicit definition of ray origins and directions to handle non-uniform bin spacing and cylindrical detector arrangements (e.g., PET arc correction). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticforwardprojection(gaussians, bvh, rays): """ Computes the forward projection of 3D Gaussians using analytic ray tracing. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives, each with.mu (3D vector) and.Sigma (3x3 matrix). bvh: Bounding Volume Hierarchy structure built from gaussians. rays: List of rays, each with.origin (3D vector) and.direction (3D vector). Returns: projections: List of scalar line integral values for each ray. """ projections = [] for ray in rays: intersectinggaussians = bvhquery(bvh, ray.origin, ray.direction) totalintegral = 0.0 for gaussian in intersectinggaussians: totalintegral += computeanalyticlineintegral( gaussian.mu, gaussian.Sigma, ray.origin, ray.direction) projections.append(totalintegral) return projections def bvhquery(node, origin, direction): """Standard recursive BVH traversal to find intersecting primitives.""" if not rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, node.bbox): return [] if node.isleaf: return [g for g in node.gaussians if gaussianrayintersect(g, origin, direction)] return bvhquery(node.left, origin, direction) + bvhquery(node.right, origin, direction) def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, bbox): """Slab method for ray-AABB intersection.""" tmin = (bbox.min - origin) / direction tmax = (bbox.max - origin) / direction t1 = min(tmin); t2 = max(tmin) t3 = min(tmax); t4 = max(tmax) return max(t1, t3) <= min(t2, t4) def gaussianrayintersect(g, origin, direction): """Bounding sphere check for pruning non-intersecting Gaussians.""" distsq = sum((o - m)2 for o, m in zip(origin, g.mu)) return distsq <= g.radiussq def computeanalyticlineintegral(mu, Sigma, origin, direction): """ Computes the analytic line integral of a 3D Gaussian along a ray. Integral: int{-inf}^{inf} exp(-0.5 (r(t) - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (r(t) - mu)) dt where r(t) = origin + t direction. """ d = direction / math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in direction)) diff = [o - m for o, m in zip(origin, mu)] Sigmainv = invertmatrix(Sigma) a = dot(d, matvecmul(Sigmainv, d)) b = 2.0 dot(diff, matvecmul(Sigmainv, d)) c = dot(diff, matvecmul(Sigmainv, diff)) if a <= 0: return 0.0 return math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi / a) math.exp(-0.5 (c - b2 / (4.0 a))) def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(row[j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for row in M] def invertmatrix(M): """Standard 3x3 matrix inversion.""" det = (M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])) invdet = 1.0 / det return [ [(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])invdet], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])invdet], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])invdet] ] Projects Gaussians into 2D screen space using local affine approximations. It suffers from affine collapse and cannot easily handle nonlinear geometric corrections. Computes line integrals analytically along rays. It provides higher quantitative accuracy and supports complex scanner geometries (e.g., PET arc correction). Time Complexity: Depends on the BVH traversal and the number of intersecting primitives per ray. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids affine collapse, yielding more physically consistent forward projections. Explicit control over ray origins and directions facilitates precise application of nonlinear geometric corrections (e.g., arc-correction in PET). Naturally handles overlapping Gaussians without the non-overlapping assumption. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than splatting due to analytic integration per primitive. Requires efficient acceleration structures (BVH) to be practical for large scenes. When to use: PET and CT modalities, especially those with cylindrical detector arrangements requiring arc correction. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed in "Radioactive 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomographic Reconstruction". It addresses limitations of splatting-based pipelines, such as degraded reconstruction quantitative accuracy and difficulty in incorporating nonlinear geometric corrections. The framework was evaluated on both PET and CT modalities, including NEMA phantom simulations and realistic PET data. It builds on Forward Projection (aTx) by replacing splatting with analytic ray tracing. name: Analytical Line Integrals of 3D Anisotropic Gabor Kernel
head: Analytical Gabor Kernel Integration, Closed-form definite line integrals for Gabor kernel, Closed-form definite line integrals for projected 3D anisotropic Gabor kernel, Finite-domain Gabor line integral
body: This method computes the exact line integral of a 3D anisotropic Gabor kernel along an arbitrary ray segment, avoiding the numerical sampling errors inherent in discrete voxel-based approaches. It enables distance sampling for multiple scattering by providing a closed-form cumulative distribution function, distinguishing it from splatting-based methods that rely on local affine approximations. It builds on Analytic 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomography by extending the analytical integration to include the oscillatory cosine modulation of the Gabor kernel. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray segment defined by origin \mathbf{x}0 and direction \tilde{\mathbf{v}} (normalized), Gabor kernel parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \Sigma, and modulation vector \vec{\omega}. Output: The definite line integral value I over the segment [t0, t1]. Data Structures: The Gabor kernel is defined by: g(x; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma, \vec{\omega}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi^3|\Sigma|}} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \Sigma^{-1}(x-\boldsymbol{\mu})} \cos\left(\vec{\omega}^T(x-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right) where \vec{\omega} is the effective modulation vector. Steps: 1. Parameterize the Ray: Define the ray line as x(t) = \mathbf{x}0 + \tilde{\mathbf{v}}t for t \in [t0, t1]. Define the offset vector d = \mathbf{x}0 - \boldsymbol{\mu}. 2. Compute Partial Whitening Scalars: Calculate scalar quantities resulting from partial whitening (translation and rotation to local coordinates): a = \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^T \Sigma^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{v}} \beta = \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^T \Sigma^{-1} d \gamma = d^T \Sigma^{-1} d B = \vec{\omega}^T \tilde{\mathbf{v}} \delta = \vec{\omega}^T d These reduce the exponent and cosine argument to quadratic and linear forms in t: (d+t\tilde{\mathbf{v}})^T \Sigma^{-1}(d+t\tilde{\mathbf{v}}) = at^2 + 2\beta t + \gamma \vec{\omega}^T(d+t\tilde{\mathbf{v}}) = Bt + \delta 3. Formulate Complex Exponential Integral: Use Euler's formula \cos \theta = \Re(e^{i\theta}) to rewrite the integral I: I = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi^3|\Sigma|}} \Re\left\{e^{i\delta} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\gamma} \int{t0}^{t1} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}at^2 - \beta t + iBt\right) dt\right\} 4. Complete the Square: Transform the exponent: -\frac{1}{2}at^2 - \beta t + iBt = -\frac{1}{2}a\left(t - \frac{-\beta + iB}{a}\right)^2 + \frac{(-\beta + iB)^2}{2a} 5. Evaluate Finite-Domain Integral: Define auxiliary variables: \alpha = \sqrt{\frac{a}{2}}, \quad \zeta = \frac{-\beta + iB}{\sqrt{2a}} The closed-form solution is: I = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi^3|\Sigma|}} \Re\left\{e^{i\delta} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\gamma} \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2a}} \exp\left(\frac{(-\beta + iB)^2}{2a}\right) \times [\operatorname{erf}(\alpha t1 - \zeta) - \operatorname{erf}(\alpha t0 - \zeta)]\right\} Alternative Whitened Formulation: In a fully whitened space (including scale), the covariance becomes identity, simplifying a=1. The integral is expressed using whitened ray parameters \mathbf{p}W, \vec{v}W and frequency \vec{k}W: W = R^T S^{-1}, \quad \mathbf{p}W = W(\mathbf{x}0 - \boldsymbol{\mu}), \quad \tilde{\mathbf{v}}W = \frac{W \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{v}}}{\|W \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{v}}\|}, \quad \tilde{\mathbf{k}}W = W \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{\sigma}} where \Sigma = R S R^T. The integral becomes: I = \frac{\mathcal{K}}{2} e^{-\frac{1}{2} (c - b^2 + \Omega^2)} \times \text{Re} \left\{ e^{i(d - \Omega b)} \left[ \text{erf} \left( \frac{t1 + b - i\Omega}{\sqrt{2}} \right) - \text{erf} \left( \frac{t0 + b - i\Omega}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \right] \right\} where b = \mathbf{p}W \cdot \vec{v}W, c = \mathbf{p}W \cdot \mathbf{p}W, \Omega = \vec{k}W \cdot \vec{v}W, d = \vec{k}W \cdot \mathbf{p}W, and \mathcal{K} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|} \cdot \|\mathbf{W} \cdot \vec{v}\|}. 6. Infinite-Domain Limit: If t0 \rightarrow -\infty and t1 \rightarrow +\infty, use \operatorname{erf}(\pm\infty) = \pm 1 to simplify: I\infty = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8\pi^3|\Sigma|}} \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{a}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma - \frac{\beta^2}{a}\right)\right) \exp\left(-\frac{B^2}{2a}\right) \cos\left(\delta - \frac{\beta B}{a}\right) Parameters: Segment Size Threshold: \approx 10^{-4} in whitened, local space units. Segments smaller than this use the midpoint rule instead of the error function series. Max Taylor Terms: 16 terms for the complex error function approximation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Segments: For segments below the threshold, the midpoint rule approximation I \approx \Delta t \cdot g(x(t{mid})) is used to avoid numerical instability of the erf series. Complex Error Function: The computation of \operatorname{erf}(z) for complex z requires careful handling. A truncated Taylor expansion is used to avoid branching between multiple algorithms. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def computegaborlineintegral(x0, v, t0, t1, mu, Sigma, omega): """ Computes the line integral of a 3D anisotropic Gabor kernel along a ray segment. Args: x0: Ray origin (3D vector) v: Ray direction (3D vector, assumed normalized) t0, t1: Segment bounds mu: Kernel mean (3D vector) Sigma: Kernel covariance (3x3 matrix) omega: Effective modulation vector (3D vector) Returns: Integral value I """ # 1. Offset d = x0 - mu # 2. Partial whitening scalars # Note: Sigmainv is the inverse of Sigma Sigmainv = inverse(Sigma) a = dot(v, dot(Sigmainv, v)) beta = dot(v, dot(Sigmainv, d)) gamma = dot(d, dot(Sigmainv, d)) B = dot(omega, v) delta = dot(omega, d) # 3. Constants prefactor = 1.0 / math.sqrt(8 math.pi3 determinant(Sigma)) # Handle small segment size optimization segmentlength = t1 - t0 threshold = 1e-4 # Whitened space units approximation if segmentlength < threshold: # Midpoint rule approximation tmid = (t0 + t1) / 2.0 xmid = x0 + v tmid # Evaluate Gabor kernel at midpoint diff = xmid - mu expterm = math.exp(-0.5 dot(diff, dot(Sigmainv, diff))) costerm = math.cos(dot(omega, diff)) kernelval = prefactor expterm costerm return kernelval segmentlength # 4. Complex error function arguments # alpha = sqrt(a/2) # zeta = (-beta + iB) / sqrt(2a) # erfarg(t) = alpha t - zeta sqrta2 = math.sqrt(a / 2.0) sqrt2a = math.sqrt(2.0 a) # Complex number for zeta zetareal = -beta / sqrt2a zetaimag = B / sqrt2a # Helper for erf term def erfterm(t): # z = alpha t - zeta zreal = sqrta2 t - zetareal zimag = -zetaimag return complexerrorfunctionreal(zreal, zimag) # 5. Compute the exponential part outside the erf # exppart = exp( (-beta + iB)^2 / (2a)) # (-beta + iB)^2 = beta^2 - B^2 - 2ibetaB # Divide by 2a numreal = beta2 - B2 numimag = -2.0 beta B expargreal = numreal / (2.0 a) expargimag = numimag / (2.0 a) expouter = math.exp(-0.5 gamma) math.exp(expargreal) expouterimag = math.exp(-0.5 gamma) math.exp(expargreal) math.sin(expargimag) # Not needed for Re{...} directly, but good for debugging # The term inside Re{...} # e^(idelta) expouter sqrt(pi/(2a)) [erf(t1) - erf(t0)] sqrtpi2a = math.sqrt(math.pi / (2.0 a)) # Calculate erf differences erft1 = erfterm(t1) erft0 = erfterm(t0) erfdiff = erft1 - erft0 # Complex multiplication: e^(idelta) (erfdiff) # e^(idelta) = cos(delta) + isin(delta) cosdelta = math.cos(delta) sindelta = math.sin(delta) # (cosdelta + isindelta) (erfdiffreal + ierfdiffimag) # Real part = cosdelta erfdiffreal - sindelta erfdiffimag realpart = cosdelta erfdiff.real - sindelta erfdiff.imag # Combine with expouter and sqrtpi2a # Result = prefactor Re{ expouter sqrtpi2a (complex product) } # Note: expouter is real in the derivation above? # Wait, exp( (-beta + iB)^2 / 2a) is complex. # Let's re-evaluate the complex exponential factor carefully. # Term: exp( (-beta + iB)^2 / 2a) # Let Z = (-beta + iB)^2 / 2a # Z = (beta^2 - B^2 - 2i beta B) / 2a # exp(Z) = exp(Re(Z)) (cos(Im(Z)) + i sin(Im(Z))) Zreal = (beta2 - B2) / (2.0 a) Zimag = (-2.0 beta B) / (2.0 a) expZreal = math.exp(Zreal) math.cos(Zimag) expZimag = math.exp(Zreal) math.sin(Zimag) # Now multiply expZ (complex) by (erfdiff) (complex) # P = expZ erfdiff Preal = expZreal erfdiff.real - expZimag erfdiff.imag Pimag = expZreal erfdiff.imag + expZimag erfdiff.real # Now multiply by e^(idelta) # Q = e^(idelta) P # Qreal = cos(delta)Preal - sin(delta)Pimag Qreal = cosdelta Preal - sindelta Pimag # Final result # I = prefactor Re{ e^(-gamma/2) sqrt(pi/2a) Q } # e^(-gamma/2) and sqrt(pi/2a) are real scalars scalar = math.exp(-0.5 gamma) sqrtpi2a I = prefactor scalar Qreal return I def complexerrorfunctionreal(zreal, zimag): """ Approximates Re[erf(z)] using truncated Taylor expansion. z = zreal + izimag """ # z = (t + b - iOmega)/sqrt(2) in the whitened derivation, # but here we pass the general complex argument for erf(alphat - zeta) # Taylor series: Re[erf(z)] approx (2/sqrt(pi)) sum{n=0}^{N} ((-1)^n Re(z^(2n+1))) / (n! (2n+1)) sumval = 0.0 term = complex(zreal, zimag) # z^1 factorial = 1.0 # Max 16 terms for n in range(16): # Term is (-1)^n Re(z^(2n+1)) / (n! (2n+1)) # We maintain term = z^(2n+1) # Add to sum sumval += ((-1.0)n term.real) / (factorial (2n + 1)) # Prepare next term: z^(2(n+1)+1) = z^(2n+3) = z^(2n+1) z^2 # But we need to update factorial and check convergence if n < 15: # Update factorial for n+1 factorial = (n + 1) # Update term to z^(2n+3) zsq = complex(zreal2 - zimag2, 2.0 zreal zimag) term = term zsq # Early exit check (relative size) # This is a simplified check; in practice, compare magnitude of added term to sum currenttermval = ((-1.0)(n+1) term.real) / (factorial (2(n+1) + 1)) if abs(sumval) > 1e-15 and abs(currenttermval / sumval) < 1e-15: break return (2.0 / math.sqrt(math.pi)) sumval Approximates the real part of the complex error function (Faddeeva function) required for finite segment integration of Gabor kernels, avoiding branching between multiple algorithms. It uses a truncated Taylor expansion of 16 terms maximum, with early exits based on relative term size, ensuring convergence for the expected value range. Time Complexity: The closed-form solution is O(1) per kernel per ray segment, dominated by the evaluation of the complex error function. The Taylor expansion for the error function is bounded by a constant number of terms (16), making it effectively constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary storage for scalar intermediates. Performance: The method avoids numerical sampling errors and enables distance sampling. However, the complex error function computation is relatively expensive. Optimization is achieved by using the midpoint rule for very small segments (< 10^{-4}) and computing paired erf terms jointly. Strengths: Exact integration, supports distance sampling for multiple scattering, handles arbitrary ray orientations and anisotropic kernels without local affine approximations. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than simple midpoint sampling for large segments. Requires careful implementation of the complex error function to avoid numerical instability. This method is derived from the work on "Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering". It extends the analytical integration of 3D anisotropic Gaussians to include the Gabor modulation, enabling physically-based rendering with orientation-selective primitives. The derivation utilizes the continuous Fourier Transform of the Gabor kernel and the shift theorem. Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05081, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Forward Mapping
head: Direct projection volume rendering, object-order algorithms
body: Forward mapping is a direct volume ray casting technique that projects each voxel directly onto the image plane, relying on the traversal order of the data to ensure proper hidden surface removal. Unlike image-order methods that cast rays from pixels into the volume, forward mapping iterates over the volume data and determines the contribution of each reconstruction kernel to the screen pixels. It is distinguished by its object-order nature, where the data drives the rendering process rather than the image plane. Inputs: Volume data (typically a cuberille), viewing parameters (camera origin, direction, right/up vectors, field of view, resolution), transfer function. Outputs: 2D image (color and opacity per pixel). Data Structures: The volume is stored as a 3D grid. A "cuberille" is the subset of voxels belonging to an object. Each voxel contains a scalar value and potentially other attributes. Steps: 1. Determine Traversal Order: For any viewing direction, determine the foremost corner voxel. Establish a traversal order by stepping through rows, columns, and slices such that the foremost voxel is visited last. This requires determining the traversal direction along each of the major axes. 2. Iterate and Project: Iterate over the volume data in the established order. For each voxel, determine its contribution to the image plane. 3. Kernel Convolution (Splatting): The traditional forward mapping algorithm is splatting. It convolves every voxel in object space with a reconstruction kernel and accumulates their contributions on the image plane. 4. Accumulation: Contributions are accumulated on the image plane. Because the traversal order ensures the foremost voxel is visited last, standard alpha compositing (or additive accumulation for specific kernels) can be used without explicit sorting of fragments per pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardmapping(volume, camorigin, camdir, camright, camup, camvoxelsize, camwidth, camheight, camfovx, transferfunction, kernelradius): # Initialize accumulation buffers with zeros acccolor = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(camwidth)] for in range(camheight)] accalpha = [[0.0 for in range(camwidth)] for in range(camheight)] # Back-to-front traversal: step direction matches viewing direction so foremost voxel is visited last stepx = 1 if camdir[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if camdir[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if camdir[2] > 0 else -1 dimx, dimy, dimz = len(volume[0][0]), len(volume[0]), len(volume) startx = 0 if stepx == 1 else dimx - 1 stopx = dimx if stepx == 1 else -1 starty = 0 if stepy == 1 else dimy - 1 stopy = dimy if stepy == 1 else -1 startz = 0 if stepz == 1 else dimz - 1 stopz = dimz if stepz == 1 else -1 for z in range(startz, stopz, stepz): for y in range(starty, stopy, stepy): for x in range(startx, stopx, stepx): val = volume[z][y][x] color, alpha = transferfunction(val) if alpha <= 0.0: continue # Project voxel center to screen space voxelcenter = (x camvoxelsize, y camvoxelsize, z camvoxelsize) rel = (voxelcenter[0] - camorigin[0], voxelcenter[1] - camorigin[1], voxelcenter[2] - camorigin[2]) depth = rel[0]camdir[0] + rel[1]camdir[1] + rel[2]camdir[2] if depth <= 0.0: continue # Standard perspective projection to screen coordinates scale = camwidth / (2.0 camfovx) sx = (rel[0]camright[0] + rel[1]camright[1] + rel[2]camright[2]) / depth scale + camwidth / 2.0 sy = (rel[0]camup[0] + rel[1]camup[1] + rel[2]camup[2]) / depth scale + camheight / 2.0 footprint = int(kernelradius camvoxelsize / depth scale) + 1 # Accumulate splat contribution to covered pixels for dy in range(-footprint, footprint + 1): for dx in range(-footprint, footprint + 1): px, py = int(sx + dx), int(sy + dy) if 0 <= px < camwidth and 0 <= py < camheight: dist = (dxdx + dydy) / (footprintfootprint) weight = max(0.0, 1.0 - dist) r, g, b = acccolor[py][px] a = accalpha[py][px] contrib = alpha weight acccolor[py][px] = (r + (1.0 - a) color[0] contrib, g + (1.0 - a) color[1] contrib, b + (1.0 - a) color[2] contrib) accalpha[py][px] = a + (1.0 - a) contrib return acccolor, accalpha Parameters: Kernel size: Determines the footprint of the splat. Transfer function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity. Edge Cases: Precision issues in projection calculations require careful handling of floating-point arithmetic. Boundary conditions for voxels near the edge of the volume must be clamped or padded to avoid out-of-bounds access. The traditional forward mapping algorithm that convolves every voxel with a reconstruction kernel. It is chosen for its simplicity and hardware acceleration potential. The subset of voxels in the data volume that belong to an object. It is used to optimize forward mapping by only processing relevant voxels. Time Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels. Each voxel is processed once. Memory Complexity: O(I), where I is the number of image pixels, for the accumulation buffer. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient for sparse data (using cuberilles), naturally handles hidden surface removal via traversal order. Limitations: Can suffer from overdraw and blending artifacts if not carefully implemented. Performance depends on the number of voxels rather than the number of pixels. When to use: When the volume is sparse or when hardware acceleration for splatting is available. When not to use: When high-quality anti-aliasing is required without additional filtering, or when the volume is dense and most voxels contribute to the final image. Forward mapping was introduced as an alternative to backward mapping (ray casting) methods. The term "splatting" was introduced by Westover in 1991. The concept relies on the intrinsic spatial presorting of volumetric data sets. name: Hybrid Volume Rendering with Space Leaping
head: Hardware-accelerated Culling with Software Raycasting, Hybrid Texture/Software Raycasting
body: Hybrid Volume Rendering with Space Leaping is a direct volume ray casting method that combines hardware-accelerated 2D texture mapping for material culling with software-based ray casting for high-quality illumination and compositing. It solves the memory overhead and image quality limitations of pure texture-based rendering (such as quantization artifacts and the need for gradient maps) while avoiding the performance costs of ray casting through empty space. Unlike pure texture mapping, which suffers from limited internal texture resolution and color bleeding when interpolating pre-shaded values separately, this method performs ray casting on the original high-resolution data set, allowing for accurate gradient computation and opacity-weighted compositing. The method consists of two distinct phases: a hardware-accelerated culling pass to determine the visible bounds of the volume, and a software-based ray casting pass to render the illuminated structures within those bounds. Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V, camera parameters (projection matrix P, modelview matrix M, viewport V{port}), object-space transformation S, transfer function T, and lighting parameters. Output: A 2D image with accumulated color \mathbf{C}{out} and opacity \alpha{out} per pixel. 1. Depth Buffer: Stores the distance to the closest non-transparent fragment for each pixel. Initialized to infinity (or maximum depth) before the culling pass. 2. Volume Data: The original scalar grid. No gradient maps or pre-computed texture stacks are required for the ray casting phase. 3. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha. In the culling pass, values outside the visible range are assigned \alpha=0. Sampling Distance (s): The step size for ray traversal. Chosen to be equal to half of the voxel size to satisfy the sampling theorem. Opacity Threshold: The threshold at which ray traversal stops (early ray termination). Not given in the sources. 1. Hardware Culling Pass (Space Leaping): 1. Enable OpenGL alpha testing and depth testing. 2. Render the volume using 2D texture maps with texture color tables. The transfer function is applied such that culled materials have \alpha=0. 3. The alpha test discards transparent fragments. The depth test then stores the distance to the closest fragment with \alpha > 0 in the depth buffer. 4. (Optional) To determine the exit position, render the texture stack again in front-to-back order with a reversed depth comparison function to store the farthest non-transparent fragment. This requires a second pass and depth buffer read. 2. Coordinate Transformation: 1. Read the depth value zs for each pixel from the depth buffer. 2. Transform the screen space coordinate (xs, ys, zs) to world space (x, y, z, w) using the inverse of the combined projection, modelview, viewport, and object-space transformation matrices: \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ w \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{PM})^{-1} \mathbf{V} \begin{bmatrix} xs \\ ys \\ zs \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where P is the projection matrix, M is the modelview matrix, \mathbf{V} is the viewport transformation, and \mathbf{S} maps world space to local object coordinates. 3. Compute the parametric ray equation in object coordinates. The object-space transformation matrix \mathbf{S} for an axis-aligned object centered at the origin is: \mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} (sx - vx)/sx & 0 & 0 & sx - vx \\ 0 & (sy - vy)/sy & 0 & sy - vy \\ 0 & 0 & (sz - vz)/sz & sz - vz \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} where components of \vec{s} are half the length of the volume and components of \vec{v} are half the length of a voxel in each direction. 3. Determine Ray Bounds: 1. Calculate the position on the ray where non-transparent media is hit for the first time (start position) using the depth value obtained from the depth buffer. 2. (Optional) If the exit position was determined in Step 1.4, use it as the end position. Otherwise, the ray traverses until it leaves the volume or reaches the opacity threshold. 4. Software Ray Casting: 1. Initialize the ray traversal at the determined first hit position. 2. Compute the distance t from this position to the entry point \vec{e} of the ray into the volume. 3. Position the first sample at: \vec{p}{first} = \vec{e} + (\lfloor d/s \rfloor \cdot s)\vec{d} where s is the sampling distance and \vec{d} is the normalized ray direction. This shift reduces sampling pattern artifacts. 4. For each sample along the ray: a. Interpolation: Reconstruct the material value from adjacent grid points using tri-linear interpolation. Interpolate pre-shaded scalar values. Approximate the gradient using central differences at each grid point, then interpolate the gradient tri-linearly. This avoids storing gradient maps. b. Classification: Map the interpolated scalar value to color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai using the transfer function. c. Compositing: Composite the sample using opacity-weighted colors in front-to-back order to prevent color bleeding artifacts: C{new} = (1 - \alpha{front})\tilde{C}{back} + \tilde{C}{front} \alpha{new} = (1 - \alpha{front})\alpha{back} + \alpha{front} where \tilde{C} is the opacity-weighted color (sample color multiplied by opacity before interpolation). 5. Stop ray traversal when an opacity threshold is reached. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridvolumerendering(volume, camera, transferfunction, lightingmodel): # 1. Hardware Culling Pass # Render volume with texture mapping, alpha test enabled, depth test enabled # Culled materials have alpha=0. Depth buffer stores closest non-transparent depth. rendertexturepass(volume, camera, transferfunction, alphatest=True, depthtest=True) # Optional: Determine exit position by rendering with reversed depth test # rendertexturepass(volume, camera, transferfunction, alphatest=True, depthtest=True, depthfunc=GREATER) # 2. Retrieve Depth and Transform depthbuffer = readdepthbuffer() # Precompute transformation matrices # P: Projection, M: Modelview, V: Viewport, S: Object-space transform # S is computed based on volume dimensions and voxel sizes invPM = inverse(camera.projectionmatrix @ camera.modelviewmatrix) invS = inverse(computeobjectspacetransform(volume)) # 3. Software Ray Casting for each pixel (xs, ys): zs = depthbuffer[xs, ys] # Transform screen space to world space # Homogeneous coordinates screencoord = [xs, ys, zs, 1] worldcoord = invS @ invPM @ camera.viewporttransform @ screencoord # Normalize homogeneous coordinates x, y, z = worldcoord[0]/worldcoord[3], worldcoord[1]/worldcoord[3], worldcoord[2]/worldcoord[3] # Compute ray origin and direction in object space # Ray origin is camera position transformed to object space rayoriginobj = transformtoobjectspace(camera.origin) raydirobj = normalize(transformvectortoobjectspace(camera.direction)) # Calculate entry point into volume (if not already known from depth) # For simplicity, assume rayoriginobj is outside and we intersect with volume bounds entryt, entrypoint = intersectrayvolume(rayoriginobj, raydirobj, volume.bounds) # Start position from depth buffer (closest non-transparent hit) # Convert world space hit point to object space hitpointobj = transformtoobjectspace([x, y, z]) # Compute distance from entry to hit point tstart = distance(entrypoint, hitpointobj) # Determine sampling distance s = volume.voxelsize / 2.0 # First sample position # d is normalized ray direction firstsamplepos = entrypoint + floor(tstart / s) s raydirobj # Initialize compositing variables acccolor = [0, 0, 0] accalpha = 0.0 # Ray traversal currentpos = firstsamplepos while currentpos is inside volume and accalpha < opacitythreshold: # Tri-linear interpolation of scalar value scalarval = trilinearinterpolate(volume, currentpos) # Compute gradient using central differences at grid points gradient = computegradient(volume, currentpos) # Classification color, alpha = transferfunction(scalarval) # Shading (e.g., Phong) shadedcolor = lightingmodel(color, gradient, raydirobj) # Opacity-weighted color weightedcolor = shadedcolor alpha # Front-to-back compositing # Cnew = (1 - alphafront) Cback + Cfront # alphanew = (1 - alphafront) alphaback + alphafront # Here, 'front' is the new sample, 'back' is the accumulator acccolor = (1 - accalpha) acccolor + weightedcolor accalpha = (1 - accalpha) accalpha + alpha # Advance ray currentpos += s raydirobj # Write to image buffer image[xs, ys] = acccolor Color Bleeding: Interpolating pre-shaded color and opacity samples separately during texturing causes color bleeding artifacts. This is avoided in the software ray-casting step by interpolating pre-shaded scalar values and using opacity-weighted compositing. Sampling Pattern Artifacts: If the first sample position is always located in one of the axis-aligned slices, sampling patterns may arise. The shift formula \vec{e} + (\lfloor d/s \rfloor \cdot s)\vec{d} mitigates this. Memory Usage: Pure texture-based rendering requires gradient maps, increasing memory usage. This hybrid approach avoids gradient map storage by computing gradients on the fly in software. Quantization: Low-cost graphics units restrict internal texture resolution to 8 bits, causing quantization artifacts. Software ray casting on the original data set avoids this. Time Complexity: The culling pass is O(N{tex}) where N{tex} is the number of texture slices. The ray casting pass is O(N{samples}) per pixel, where N{samples} is reduced by space leaping. Overall, it is faster than full software ray casting due to skipped empty regions. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data. No additional gradient maps or large texture stacks are required for the ray casting phase, unlike pure texture-based methods. Performance: Provides impressive frame rates due to hardware-accelerated culling. The intermediate image from the texture pass allows for interactive classification and navigation by skipping the ray-casting module when the texture color table is modified or during motion. Strengths: Avoids memory overhead of gradient maps, prevents quantization artifacts, enables accurate lighting models (e.g., Phong) in software, and reduces sampling time via space leaping. Limitations: Requires two depth buffer reads (optional for exit position). The software ray casting step is computationally intensive per sample due to gradient computation and interpolation. The method was proposed in "Accelerated Volume Ray-Casting using Texture Mapping" (2001). It addresses the limitations of early hardware-accelerated volume rendering, which suffered from memory constraints and image quality issues due to 8-bit texture resolution and the need for gradient maps. The approach leverages OpenGL's alpha and depth testing to efficiently cull empty space, allowing software ray casting to focus only on visible regions. name: Function-based Volume Ray Casting
head: Analytic Volume Ray Casting, Procedural Volume Ray Casting, Textureless Volume Rendering
body: Function-based Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique where the volume density field is defined by a continuous mathematical function f(\mathbf{p}) rather than a discrete voxel grid or 3D texture. This method eliminates the need for 3D texture storage and interpolation, allowing for the direct evaluation of continuous data such as analytical probability fields or wave functions. It is distinct from standard ray casting by bypassing the discretization step, thereby avoiding aliasing artifacts associated with voxel sampling and the memory overhead of texture atlases. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a continuous scalar function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow [0, 1] representing density or probability, and a transfer function T mapping density to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha. Output: The accumulated color \mathbf{C}{out} and opacity \alpha{out} for the pixel. Data Structures: No volumetric data structures (e.g., voxel grids, octrees) are required. The only state maintained per ray is the accumulated color and opacity. Steps: 1. Ray Intersection: Determine the entry t{near} and exit t{far} parameters of the ray with the volume bounding box. 2. Discretization: Divide the segment [t{near}, t{far}] into N steps of size \Delta t. 3. Evaluation Loop: For each step i from 0 to N-1: a. Calculate the 3D coordinate \mathbf{p}i at distance ti = t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t from the camera origin. b. Evaluate the function f(\mathbf{p}i) to obtain the local density/probability value di. c. Map di to optical properties (\mathbf{c}i, \alphai) using the transfer function. d. Composite the sample into the accumulator using front-to-back blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def functionbasedvolumeraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, volumefunction, transferfunction, tnear, tfar, numsamples): """ Renders a volume defined by a continuous function f(p). Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (o) raydirection: 3D vector (d), assumed normalized volumefunction: Callable f(p) -> float in [0, 1] transferfunction: Callable T(density) -> (color, opacity) tnear: float, entry parameter tfar: float, exit parameter numsamples: int, number of integration steps Returns: (accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity) """ # Initialize accumulators acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 # Step size deltat = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples # Iterate along the ray for i in range(numsamples): # 1. Calculate 3D coordinates at distance delta from camera # Note: Sources specify iterating distance delta along the ray currentt = tnear + i deltat p = rayorigin + raydirection currentt # 2. Evaluate probability/density at those coordinates using the function density = volumefunction(p) # 3. Map density to color and opacity # Standard transfer function application color, opacity = transferfunction(density) # 4. Add the probability to the ray's accumulated color # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = sum(ci alphai product(1 - alphaj)) # alphaout = 1 - product(1 - alphai) # Iterative update: # Cacc <- Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) ci alphai # alphaacc <- alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alphai weight = (1.0 - accopacity) opacity acccolor = acccolor + weight color accopacity = accopacity + weight # Early exit optimization if fully opaque if accopacity >= 1.0: break return acccolor, accopacity Parameters: numsamples: Determines integration accuracy. Higher values reduce banding but increase cost. Not given in the sources. volumefunction: The specific mathematical definition (e.g., Gaussian, wave function). Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Function Domain: The function must be defined for all coordinates within the bounding box. If the function is undefined or returns NaN, the result is invalid. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in coordinate calculation may cause artifacts in highly oscillatory functions. Performance: Evaluating complex mathematical functions per sample is computationally expensive compared to texture lookups. Uses mathematical expressions for the transfer function rather than lookup tables. Chosen when smooth, differentiable opacity transitions are required. Link to Transfer Functions and Shading Models Uses noise functions (e.g., Perlin, Simplex) as the density function. Chosen for synthetic textures like clouds or marble. Link to Interpolation and Sampling Techniques Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Each sample requires a function evaluation, which can be more expensive than a texture lookup. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No 3D texture storage is required, making it suitable for high-resolution or infinite domains. Strengths: No discretization artifacts (aliasing from voxel grid); infinite resolution; low memory footprint; supports analytical data directly. Limitations: High computational cost for complex functions; no spatial acceleration structures (like BVH) can be easily applied to the function itself without additional bounding volume hierarchies. When to use: When the volume data is naturally defined by a mathematical formula (e.g., scientific simulations, procedural generation) and memory is constrained. When not to use: When the data is discrete (e.g., medical CT scans) or the function evaluation is prohibitively slow. This technique is a direct application of ray casting principles to procedural/analytic volumes. It was discussed in the context of implementing volume ray tracing without 3D textures in WebGL/Three.js environments. It addresses the limitation of texture-based rendering where 3D textures are either unavailable or too large to fit in GPU memory.
