name: Polyhedron Compositing
head: Cell Compositing, Tetrahedral subdivision compositing, Tetrahedron Compositing, Volume cell compositing
body: Polyhedron Compositing is a direct volume ray casting method that combines contour surface rendering with ray integration by subdividing volume cells at contour surfaces into polyhedral pieces (typically tetrahedra), which are then composited in back-to-front order. Unlike standard ray casting that samples a continuous scalar field, this method allows color and opacity to change discontinuously across surfaces and correctly sorts multiple transparent surfaces. It sets itself apart from its siblings by replacing per-pixel ray marching with closed-form analytic integration over geometric primitives, leveraging graphics hardware scan conversion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume defined on a grid of cells. Each cell vertex has associated quantities: emission coefficient c (RGB vector) and absorption fraction per unit density-length \alpha (scalar). A transfer function maps these to physical properties, or they are provided directly. The viewer position and projection matrix (orthographic or perspective) are required. Output: The final frame buffer color F{out} and accumulated opacity. Data Structures: 1. Subdivided Cells: The volume is decomposed into convex polyhedra (tetrahedra). If a contour surface crosses a cell, the cell is split. If a tetrahedron is crossed by a discontinuity surface, it is sliced into two parts. 2. Face Graph: A directed graph where edges correspond to cell faces. Edges are directed from the cell on the viewpoint side to the cell on the side facing away. 3. Temporary Buffers: Face Sorting Variant: Two sets of temporary arrays sized for the whole image: one for front-facing polygons, one for back-facing. Stores interpolated values for z, C, and a. Cell Sorting Variant: Buffers sized for one scan line (using incremental methods). Numbered Steps: 1. Subdivision: Divide any volume cell crossed by a contour surface into tetrahedra. Slice each tetrahedron crossed by a contour surface into two parts to handle discontinuous color/opacity. 2. Sorting: Global Cell Sort: Perform a topological sort of the directed face graph to determine a back-to-front order of cells. This is possible if the data volume is convex with no holes or concavities. Face Sort: Sort the resulting polyhedral pieces and surface polygons in back-to-front order relative to the viewer. If a face has a discontinuity, create two copies (one marked front, one unmarked) with distinct C and a values. 3. Scan Conversion (Projection): Divide the screen projection of a cell into polygons bounded by projected cell edges. Each polygon represents a prismatic region bounded by a single front-facing and a single back-facing cell face. 4. Interpolation: For each polygon, interpolate quantities linearly across the screen space. For orthographic projection, interpolate depth z directly. For perspective projection, interpolate 1/z and derive z. Interpolate C (emission/color) and a (absorption density product) at polygon vertices. 5. Compositing: Calculate the contribution of each polygon to the frame buffer using the closed-form integral. Formulas: The basic compositing equation for a segment with transparency T and added colored intensity I is: F{new} = T \cdot F{old} + I For a volume cell segment of length L, with average absorption density product a and average emission color C (where C = c/\alpha): T = \exp(-L \cdot a) I = C \cdot (1 - T) The accumulated values for a pixel (i, j) within a cell's projection are computed as the average of the front and back face values: L = z{back}(i, j) - z{front}(i, j) a = \frac{a{back}(i, j) + a{front}(i, j)}{2} C = \frac{C{back}(i, j) + C{front}(i, j)}{2} Perspective Projection Adjustment: For perspective projection, the length L and interpolation must account for depth. The quantity to interpolate is 1/z. The effective length L is calculated as: L = \left( \frac{1}{z{front}(i, j)} - \frac{1}{z{back}(i, j)} \right) \cdot \sqrt{1 + x^2 + y^2} where x and y are the coordinates where the ray from the eye through pixel (i, j) intersects the plane z=1. Pseudocode (Face Sorting Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. sortedpolygons = sortbacktofront(polygons) for polygon in sortedpolygons: # Determine if this polygon is a front-facing surface of a volume cell isfront = polygon.isfrontface # Scan convert the polygon to screen pixels for each pixel (i, j) inside polygon: # Interpolate values at (i, j) znew = interpolate(polygon, i, j, field='z') Cnew = interpolate(polygon, i, j, field='C') anew = interpolate(polygon, i, j, field='a') if isfront: # Calculate segment length and average properties # L is depth difference (orthographic) or derived from 1/z (perspective) L = ztemp[i, j] - znew # Average absorption and color between previous front face and current aavg = (atemp[i, j] + anew) / 2.0 Cavg = (Ctemp[i, j] + Cnew) / 2.0 # Compute transparency and intensity T = exp(-L aavg) I = Cavg (1.0 - T) # Composite into frame buffer F[i, j] = T F[i, j] + I # Update temporary buffers for next front face ztemp[i, j] = znew Ctemp[i, j] = Cnew atemp[i, j] = anew Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convexity: The method requires each ray to intersect the volume cell in a single segment (single front and back entry). This is guaranteed if the cell is convex. Sorting Validity: The face sorting variant requires a valid sort order for polygons, which is not always possible for arbitrary non-convex geometries. Discontinuities: If a face has a discontinuity in opacity or color, it must be split into two copies (one marked front, one unmarked) with their own C and a values. Perspective Distortion: Using linear interpolation of z in perspective projection leads to errors. One must interpolate 1/z and compute L using the derived formula. Time Complexity: The method eliminates the need for per-pixel sampling along the ray by using closed-form analytic integration. It relies on scan conversion and sorting. Sorting is O(N \log N) where N is the number of polygons. Scan conversion is linear in the number of pixels covered by the polygons. Memory Complexity: The face sorting variant requires temporary buffers sized for the whole image (O(W \times H)) for z, C, and a. The cell sorting variant can use incremental methods requiring only O(W) memory per scan line. Strengths: Correctly handles discontinuous opacity and color changes across contour surfaces. Allows multiple transparent surfaces to be composited in the correct order. Leverages hardware scan conversion and texture mapping for efficiency. Limitations: Requires subdivision of cells, which can increase the number of primitives. Sorting can be complex or impossible for non-convex shapes. The assumption of linear variation of density/color within cells may introduce approximation errors. When to use: When accurate rendering of discontinuous features (e.g., isosurfaces) within a volume is required, and the volume can be decomposed into convex polyhedra. When not to use: For highly non-convex volumes where sorting is intractable, or when continuous smooth shading is preferred over discrete cell-based compositing. Polyhedron Compositing was introduced by Max, Hanrahan, and Crawfis as a technique to combine contour surface rendering with ray integration. It builds on the idea of compositing polyhedra joining data points, where the integral is integrated separately along viewing ray segments within each polyhedron. The method utilizes topological information for cell sorting (Garrity [11]) and directed graphs for back-to-front sorting (Edelsbrunner [14]). It is particularly relevant in flow visualization and scientific visualization where discontinuous data boundaries are common. Applications of texture mapping to volume and flow visualization, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc626633/?q=volume splatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) New techniques in 3D scalar and vector field visualization, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1384657/?q=volume splatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) Rendering
head: Raycasting of Volumetric Depth Images, VDI raycasting
body: Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) rendering is an image-order method that decouples expensive volume integration from interactive viewpoint changes by compositing pre-computed segments (supersegments) stored in a VDI, rather than integrating the volume rendering integral directly. It differs from standard direct volume ray casting by replacing per-pixel sample accumulation with geometric intersection tests against view-dependent supersegments, and from object-order methods by achieving frame rates an order of magnitude higher near the generation viewpoint while maintaining quality. Inputs and Outputs Input: A Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) generated from a source viewpoint V0, a new target viewpoint VN (defined by camera origin \mathbf{o}N and direction \mathbf{d}N), and a transfer function T (used during VDI generation, not rendering). Output: A 2D image where each pixel (x, y) contains the accumulated color \mathbf{C}{out} and opacity \alpha{out}. Data Structures The VDI consists of NL lists, one for each ray in the generation viewport. NL: Number of lists, determined by the viewport resolution (number of rays). Typically NL \gg NS. Li: The list of supersegments for ray i. NS: The maximum number of supersegments allowed in each list Li. This is a pre-set limit during VDI generation. Sj^i: The j-th supersegment in list Li. It stores: f(Sj^i): Distance from the near-plane to the front face of the supersegment. b(Sj^i): Distance from the near-plane to the back face of the supersegment. \mathbf{C}j^i: Accumulated color between f(Sj^i) and b(Sj^i). \alphaj^i: Accumulated opacity between f(Sj^i) and b(Sj^i). Fully transparent regions are excluded from supersegments. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Definition: For each pixel (x, y) in the target image, define a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o}N + t\mathbf{d}N. 2. NDC Conversion: Convert the ray's start point \mathbf{o}N and a point far along the direction \mathbf{o}N + \mathbf{d}N \cdot D{max} (where D{max} is sufficiently large to cover the volume) from world space to the Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space of the generation viewpoint V0. Let these be \mathbf{p}{start}^{NDC} and \mathbf{p}{end}^{NDC}. 3. NDC Intersection: Step through the list Li (corresponding to the pixel's ray in the generation viewport) in NDC space to determine intersection points S. In NDC space, the supersegments form simplified geometric shapes (rectangular frustums aligned with axes), allowing for efficient intersection calculation compared to irregular pyramidal frustums in world space. 4. World Space Conversion: Convert the intersection points S determined in NDC space back to world space. 5. Length Calculation: Determine the length of the intersection segment in world space using the converted points. This length corresponds to the physical distance the ray travels through the supersegment. 6. Compositing: Composite the supersegments along the ray using the front-to-back volume rendering equation. For each intersected supersegment Sj^i with accumulated color \mathbf{C}j^i and opacity \alphaj^i, and assuming the ray traverses the full extent of the supersegment (or a fraction thereof if the ray exits the volume bounding box early), update the accumulator: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{C}j^i \cdot \alphaj^i \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphaj^i Initialize \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0,0,0) and \alpha{acc} = 0. 7. Output: Store \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} in the pixel buffer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervdi(vdi, cameraorigin, cameradirection, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Renders an image using Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) raycasting. Args: vdi: A list of lists, where vdi[i] is the list Li of supersegments for ray i. Each supersegment S is a tuple (f, b, Cacc, alphaacc). f: distance from near-plane to front face. b: distance from near-plane to back face. Cacc: accumulated color (vec3). alphaacc: accumulated opacity (float). cameraorigin: vec3, origin of the new viewpoint VN. cameradirection: vec3, viewing direction of VN. imagewidth: int, width of the output image. imageheight: int, height of the output image. Returns: image: 2D array of vec3, the rendered color image. """ image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) # Pre-calculate NDC projection matrices for V0 (generation viewpoint) # This assumes V0's projection matrix P0 is known from VDI generation. # NDC coordinates are in range [-1, 1] or [0, 1] depending on convention. # We assume standard OpenGL NDC [-1, 1]. for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # 1. Define ray in world space # Convert pixel (x, y) to camera space direction # This requires the inverse projection matrix of VN or standard perspective projection math # For simplicity, assume we have a function to get ray from pixel rayo, rayd = getrayfrompixel(x, y, cameraorigin, cameradirection, imagewidth, imageheight) # 2. Convert ray endpoints to NDC space of V0 # We need a point at t=0 (rayo) and a point far away (rayo + rayd largevalue) largevalue = 1000.0 # Sufficiently large to cover volume pstartworld = rayo pendworld = rayo + rayd largevalue # Project these points to NDC space of V0 # P0 is the projection matrix of the generation viewpoint pstartndc = projecttondc(pstartworld, P0) pendndc = projecttondc(pendworld, P0) # 3. Determine which ray index i in VDI corresponds to this pixel # This mapping depends on how the VDI was generated relative to the viewport. # Typically, if the new viewpoint is close to V0, the ray indices align. # If not, a more complex mapping is needed. The source implies a direct mapping # for the "generation viewpoint" context, but for arbitrary VN, we assume # the VDI covers the entire volume and we map the ray to the closest VDI ray. # For this implementation, we assume a direct mapping for simplicity, # or that the VDI is dense enough that we can interpolate. # However, the source describes intersecting the list Li. # Let's assume we find the closest ray index i in the VDI. i = findclosestvdirayindex(pstartndc, vdi) Li = vdi[i] # 4. Step through Li in NDC space to find intersections # In NDC space, the supersegments are axis-aligned frustums. # We check if the ray segment (pstartndc to pendndc) intersects each supersegment. intersections = [] for S in Li: fndc = S.f # Distance in NDC? No, f and b are distances from near-plane in world space during generation. # Wait, the source says: "Each ray i generates a list Li of supersegments Sj^i that store the distances # between the near-plane and their front and back faces, f(Sj^i) and b(Sj^i)". # And: "Compute ray-segment intersections in Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space... # as segments form pyramidal frustums in world space but have simplified intersections in NDC." # This implies that during rendering, we convert the ray to NDC, and the supersegments are also represented # in NDC? Or we convert the ray to NDC and intersect with the NDC representation of the supersegments. # The source says: "Once Sj^i intersection points are determined in NDC space, they are converted back to world space". # So we need the NDC bounds of each supersegment. # Let's assume the VDI stores NDC bounds for each supersegment, or we can compute them from f and b. # Since f and b are world-space distances from the near plane, and the near plane is at z=-1 (or 0) in NDC, # we can map f and b to NDC z-coordinates. # However, the source explicitly mentions converting the ray to NDC and intersecting there. # Let's assume the VDI stores the NDC bounds for each supersegment for efficiency. # If not, we must compute them. Given the source's emphasis on NDC intersection, we assume NDC bounds are available. # For the sake of a complete implementation, let's assume the VDI stores NDC bounds. # If the VDI only stores f and b (world space), we need to project the front and back planes of the supersegment to NDC. # This is complex. Convert intersection points back to world space and calculate lengths # 6. If the ray doesn't traverse the full segment, # we need to adjust alphai. # The source doesn't explicitly detail partial traversal compositing. # Assuming the ray traverses the full segment for simplicity, or that the VDI segments are small enough. # If partial traversal is needed, alphai should be scaled by (length / segmentlength). # But the VDI stores f and b, which are the full extent. # Let's assume the ray traverses the full segment for now, as the source focuses on intersection simplification. # Update accumulator # Cacc = Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) Cj^i alphaj^i # alphaacc = alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alphaj^i # If partial traversal, we need to compute the effective alpha for the traversed length. # This requires knowing the extinction coefficient or assuming uniform opacity. # The source does not provide this detail. We assume full traversal for the basic algorithm. Pinv = inverse(P) pointcam = vec4(ndcpoint, 1.0) pointworldhom = Pinv pointcam if pointworldhom.w == 0: return None return pointworldhom.xyz / pointworldhom.w def getndcbounds(supersegment, P): """Returns the NDC bounds (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) of a supersegment.""" # This requires knowing the geometry of the supersegment in world space. # The source says supersegments are irregular pyramidal frustums in world space. # In NDC, they become axis-aligned boxes. # We need to project the 8 corners of the frustum to NDC and find the min/max. # This is computationally expensive. The source implies this is done efficiently. # For the purpose of this article, we assume this function exists and is efficient. pass def intersectrayndcsegment(raystartndc, rayendndc, ndcbounds): """Intersects a ray segment with an axis-aligned box in NDC space.""" # Standard slab method for ray-box intersection pass def findclosestvdirayindex(ndcpoint, vdi): """Finds the index i in the VDI closest to the given NDC point.""" # This depends on the VDI generation. If the VDI is generated for a specific viewport, # the NDC coordinates map directly to pixel indices. # If the new viewpoint is different, the mapping is not direct. # The source mentions "decoupling viewpoint changes", implying the VDI is view-dependent. # For a general implementation, this step is complex. # We assume a simple mapping for the sake of the algorithm description. pass Parameters NS: Maximum number of supersegments per list. Pre-set during VDI generation. NL: Number of lists, equal to the viewport resolution during VDI generation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Irregular Geometry: VDI segments are irregular pyramidal frustums in world space due to perspective projection, making direct intersection calculations complex. This is mitigated by performing intersections in NDC space. Viewpoint Dependency: The VDI is view-dependent. Rendering quality degrades as the new viewpoint moves away from the generation viewpoint V0. Memory Access: The method minimizes memory accesses by exploiting spatial homogeneity in the data. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by the intersection tests in NDC space and the compositing of supersegments. It is generally faster than standard ray casting because it avoids per-sample volume texture lookups and transfer function evaluations. Memory Complexity: The VDI size is proportional to NL \times NS. Since NL \gg NS, the memory footprint is significantly smaller than storing the full volume for high-resolution rendering. Performance: Achieves frame rates an order of magnitude higher than previous object-order rendering algorithms near the generation viewpoint, while maintaining quality comparable to ground-truth volume rendering. Strengths: Efficient for remote visualization, interactive frame rates for high-resolution displays, reduced calculations and memory accesses compared to previous raycasting approaches. Limitations: Quality degrades with viewpoint distance from V0. Requires pre-computation and streaming of VDIs. VDI rendering was introduced by Frey et al. [10] as a compact view-dependent volume representation. The method was further optimized for efficient raycasting by Brady et al. [5] and Lochmann et al. [21]. The specific algorithm described here, which simplifies intersections in NDC space, was proposed in 2023. It is used in remote visualization settings to enable interactive visualization of large volumes at high frame rates. name: VRVRVive Raycasting
head: VRVRVive, Virtual Reality Volume Rendering with the HTC Vive
body: VRVRVive is a two-pass, image-order direct volume raycasting algorithm implemented in a fragment shader, designed specifically for Virtual Reality (VR) rendering on the HTC Vive platform. It solves the performance constraints of real-time VR by integrating Level of Detail (LoD) management, Early Ray Termination (ERT), and Ambient Occlusion (AO) into a single rendering pipeline. Unlike standard raycasting methods, it decouples the ray traversal logic into a normalization pass and a compositing pass, allowing for dynamic step-size adjustment based on depth and explicit culling planes to optimize fragment shader execution. The method operates as a two-pass fragment shader program. It requires a 3D volume texture, a 1D transfer function texture, and 2D UVW map textures for the front and back faces of the volume bounding box. Inputs: volumetexture: sampler3D, the scalar volume data. transferFunctionTex: sampler1D, maps scalar values to RGBA. backuvwmap: sampler2D, stores the UVW coordinates of the ray entry point on the back face of the volume. frontuvwmap: sampler2D, stores the UVW coordinates of the ray exit point on the front face of the volume. Uniforms: uWindowingMinVal, uWindowingRange, uStepSize, uLodMaxLevel, uLodBegin, uLodRange, ALPHASCALE, EMISSIONSCALE, ABSORPTIONSCALE, AMBIENTOCCLUSIONSCALE, AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS, ERTTHRESHOLD. Outputs (FBO Attachments): fragDepth (location 0): Depth buffer. fragColor1 to fragColor4 (locations 1-4): Layered color/depth buffers for compositing. fragColorDebug (location 5): Debug visualization. The method uses a layered compositing structure in Pass 2. It maintains a fixed-size array of 4 layers: layerColor[4]: Stores the accumulated color for each layer. layerDepth[4]: Stores the depth threshold for each layer. ALPHASCALE: Default 20.0. Multiplies the alpha output from the transfer function. ERTTHRESHOLD: Default 0.99. Accumulated opacity threshold to terminate ray marching early. EMISSIONSCALE: Default 1.0. Scales the emission component of the transfer function. ABSORPTIONSCALE: Default 10.0. Scales the absorption coefficient. AMBIENTOCCLUSIONSCALE: Default 2.0. AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS: Default 2.0. Radius for AO sampling in texture space units. uWindowingMinVal: Lower bound for transfer function windowing. uWindowingRange: Range for transfer function windowing. uStepSize: Base ray sampling step size. uLodMaxLevel: Factor controlling LoD degradation intensity. uLodBegin: Depth at which LoD begins. uLodRange: Depth range over which LoD degrades. This pass computes the normalized ray parameters and prepares the UVW coordinates for the volume. 1. Initialize t = 0.0. 2. If RANDOMOFFSET is defined, add 0.002 2.0 rand(passUV) to t. 3. Loop while t < 1.0 + (0.5 parameterStepSize): a. Calculate current UVW: curUVW = mix(startUVW, endUVW, t). b. Calculate current distance: curDistance = mix(startDistance, endDistance, t). c. Level of Detail (LoD): If LEVELOFDETAIL is defined: i. Calculate curLod = max(0.0, min(1.0, ((curDistance - uLodBegin) / uLodRange))) uLodMaxLevel. ii. Update parameterStepSize and distanceStepSize based on curLod. iii. Sample volume: curSample = textureLod(volumetexture, curUVW, curLod).r. d. Else: i. Sample volume: curSample = texture(volumetexture, curUVW).r. e. Store results for Pass 2. This pass performs the actual ray marching, transfer function application, and compositing. 1. Initialize segmentColor = (0,0,0,0), curAlpha = 0.0, curColor = (0,0,0,0). 2. Declare layerColor[4] and layerDepth[4]. 3. Set layerDepth[0..3] based on endDistance and parameterStepSize. 4. Initialize state variables: lastDistance = result.firstHit.a lastAlpha = 0.0 lastNonZero = 0.0 currentLayer = 1 numLayers = 4 currentLayerThreshold = float(currentLayer) / float(numLayers) 5. Initialize t = 0.0. 6. If RANDOMOFFSET is defined, add offset to t. 7. Loop while t < 1.0 + (0.5 parameterStepSize): a. Calculate curUVW = mix(startUVW, endUVW, t) and curDistance. b. Cull Planes: If CULLPLANES is defined, skip if curUVW is outside uCullMin/uCullMax. c. Sampling: i. If LEVELOFDETAIL is defined, calculate curLod and sample using textureLod. Else, sample using texture. ii. Let curSample.value be the sampled scalar. d. Transfer Function & Color Calculation: i. If EMISSIONABSORPTIONRAW is defined: 1. sampleEmissionAbsorption = transferFunctionRaw(curSample.value). 2. Scale RGB by EMISSIONSCALE. 3. Scale A by pow(sampleEmissionAbsorption.a ABSORPTIONSCALE, 2.0). 4. Calculate sampleAlpha = 1.0 - exp(-sampleEmissionAbsorption.a distanceStepSize). 5. sampleColor = vec4(sampleEmissionAbsorption.rgb sampleAlpha, sampleAlpha). ii. Else: 1. Calculate relative value: rel = (value - uWindowingMinVal) / uWindowingRange. 2. Clamp: clamped = \max(0.0, \min(1.0, rel)). 3. Get color from 1D texture: color = texture(transferFunctionTex, clamped). 4. Adjust Alpha: color.a = ALPHASCALE stepSize. 5. Adjust RGB: color.rgb = color.a. 6. sampleColor = color. e. Ambient Occlusion (AO): If AMBIENTOCCLUSION is defined: i. Sample 8 neighbors (±1 in x, y, z) using radius AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS/1.414 curStepSize. Sum occlusion. ii. Sample 6 face neighbors (±1 in x, y, z) using radius AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS curStepSize. Sum occlusion. iii. Apply occlusion to sampleColor (implementation detail implied: modulate alpha or color by occlusion factor). f. Increment t += parameterStepSize. g. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If sampleColor.a < 0.00001, continue to next iteration. h. Compositing: i. Update accumulated color and alpha using front-to-back blending: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai ii. If alphaacc >= ERTTHRESHOLD, break loop. i. Layer Management: Update layerColor and layerDepth arrays based on curDistance and currentLayerThreshold. Transfer Function Mapping: rel = \frac{value - uWindowingMinVal}{uWindowingRange} clamped = \max(0.0, \min(1.0, rel)) color = texture(transferFunctionTex, clamped) color.a = color.a \cdot ALPHA\SCALE \cdot stepSize color.rgb = color.rgb \cdot color.a Beer-Lambert Inversion (for EMISSIONABSORPTIONRAW mode): T = \exp(-A \cdot z) C = E \cdot (1.0 - T) Where A is the absorption coefficient, z is the distance, T is transmission, E is emission, and C is the resulting color contribution. Alpha Correction: sampleAlpha = 1.0 - \exp(-sampleEmissionAbsorption.a \cdot distanceStepSize) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vrviveraycasting(passuv, startuvw, enduvw, startdistance, enddistance, volumetexture, transferfunctiontex, uwindowingminval, uwindowingrange, ustepsize, ulodmaxlevel, ulodbegin, ulodrange, alphascale, emissionscale, absorptionscale, ambientocclusionscale, ambientocclusionradius, ertthreshold, randomoffset): # Pass 1: Normalization (Simplified for context, actual implementation stores intermediates) # This pass calculates curUVW and curDistance for each t # It also determines curLod if LEVELOFDETAIL is active # Pass 2: Compositing segmentcolor = vec4(0.0) curalpha = 0.0 curcolor = vec4(0.0) layercolor = [vec4(0.0) for in range(4)] layerdepth = [0.0 for in range(4)] # Initialize layer depths based on endDistance and parameterStepSize # Implementation detail: specific distribution logic not fully specified in source for i in range(4): layerdepth[i] = enddistance - (i parameterstepsize) lastdistance = 0.0 # result.firstHit.a placeholder lastalpha = 0.0 lastnonzero = 0.0 currentlayer = 1 numlayers = 4 currentlayerthreshold = float(currentlayer) / float(numlayers) t = 0.0 if randomoffset: t += 0.002 2.0 rand(passuv) while t < 1.0 + (0.5 parameterstepsize): curuvw = mix(startuvw, enduvw, t) curdistance = mix(startdistance, enddistance, t) # Cull Planes Check # if cullplanesdefined: # if any(lessthan(curuvw, ucullmin)) or any(greaterthan(curuvw, ucullmax)): # t += parameterstepsize # continue # Sampling if levelofdetaildefined: curlod = max(0.0, min(1.0, (curdistance - ulodbegin) / ulodrange)) ulodmaxlevel # Update step sizes based on curlod cursample = texturelod(volumetexture, curuvw, curlod).r else: cursample = texture(volumetexture, curuvw).r # Transfer Function if emissionabsorptionrawdefined: sampleemabs = transferfunctionraw(cursample) sampleemabs.rgb = emissionscale sampleemabs.a = pow(sampleemabs.a absorptionscale, 2.0) samplealpha = 1.0 - exp(-sampleemabs.a distancestepsize) samplecolor = vec4(sampleemabs.rgb samplealpha, samplealpha) else: rel = (cursample - uwindowingminval) / uwindowingrange clamped = max(0.0, min(1.0, rel)) color = texture(transferfunctiontex, clamped) color.a = alphascale stepsize color.rgb = color.a samplecolor = color # Ambient Occlusion if ambientocclusiondefined: # Sample 8 neighbors aosum = 0.0 radiussmall = ambientocclusionradius / 1.414 curstepsize for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue neighboruvw = curuvw + vec3(dx, dy, dz) radiussmall neighborval = texture(volumetexture, neighboruvw).r # Logic for occlusion calculation implied but not fully detailed aosum += neighborval # Sample 6 face neighbors radiuslarge = ambientocclusionradius curstepsize for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if abs(dx) + abs(dy) + abs(dz) != 1: continue neighboruvw = curuvw + vec3(dx, dy, dz) radiuslarge neighborval = texture(volumetexture, neighboruvw).r # Logic for occlusion calculation implied but not fully detailed aosum += neighborval # Apply AO to samplecolor samplecolor.a = (1.0 - aosum ambientocclusionscale) t += parameterstepsize # Early Ray Termination if samplecolor.a < 0.00001: continue # Compositing # Front-to-back blending curcolor = curcolor + (1.0 - curalpha) samplecolor.rgb samplecolor.a curalpha = curalpha + (1.0 - curalpha) samplecolor.a if curalpha >= ertthreshold: break # Layer Management # Update layercolor and layerdepth based on curdistance and currentlayerthreshold # Specific logic for layer assignment not fully detailed in source return curcolor, curalpha, layercolor, layerdepth LoD Approximation: The Level of Detail calculation is noted as a "bad approximation" in the source comments, potentially leading to visual artifacts or inconsistent sampling rates. Cull Planes Performance: The cull planes check uses any(lessThan(...)), which is described as "lazy" and may have performance implications or logic quirks depending on vectorization. AO Sampling: The source code for Ambient Occlusion cuts off, leaving the exact application of the occlusion sum to sampleColor implied but not explicitly defined. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray, which is determined by the volume depth and the step size. The step size is dynamically adjusted by LoD, potentially reducing complexity for distant samples. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storage for the volume texture, transfer function, and a small fixed-size array for layer compositing (4 layers). Performance: Optimized for VR hardware (HTC Vive) using fragment shaders. The two-pass approach allows for efficient UVW map generation and compositing. Strengths: Integrates LoD, ERT, and AO directly into the raycasting loop. Supports culling planes. Limitations: LoD is a "bad approximation". AO implementation details are incomplete in the source. Relies on specific texture maps (front/back UVW). VRVRVive is an unofficial implementation of virtual reality volume rendering for the HTC Vive headset. It was developed by Secumfex and hosted on GitHub. The project depends on libraries such as Assimp, OpenVR, SDL2, GLFW3, GLEW, and GLM. It is designed to render volumetric data (e.g., from.pvm or binary slice formats) in real-time within a VR environment. name: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting
body: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting renders a specific internal structure within a volume by finding the first point along a viewing ray where the scalar field value equals or crosses a user-defined isovalue \tau. Unlike standard volume rendering which composites all samples along the ray to visualize the entire density distribution, this method treats the volume as an opaque surface defined by the threshold, discarding all subsequent samples after the first valid hit. It sets itself apart from siblings like Direct volume ray casting by focusing on geometric structure and surface shading rather than volumetric transparency, and from Distance-field ray marching by operating directly on scalar field thresholds rather than signed distance functions. All methods in this family share the fundamental mechanism of image-order rendering: for each pixel, a ray is defined in world space, intersected with the volume domain, and sampled along its path to detect the first intersection with the isosurface. The ray is parameterized as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. The traversal order is determined by the pixel's position in the image plane. The core detection logic relies on the isosurface condition. For a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}), the surface is defined by f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau. In discrete voxel data, this is typically detected by a sign change or threshold crossing between consecutive samples: f(\mathbf{p}1) \cdot f(\mathbf{p}2) < 0 relative to \tau, or f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau. Upon detection, the intersection position is often refined (e.g., via linear interpolation or binary search) to reduce discretization artifacts. The surface normal is computed from the gradient \nabla f at the hit point, usually via finite differences or tri-cubic filtering, to enable Phong-like shading. The final color is computed using local lighting models (ambient, diffuse, specular) and potentially ambient occlusion or shadows, with no contribution from voxels behind the surface. A technique that renders an implicit surface defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau directly from voxel data without extracting an explicit polygon mesh. It solves the problem of visualizing specific structures by finding the first intersection along a ray where the scalar value equals or crosses a user-defined isovalue \tau. Unlike standard volume rendering which composites all samples, this method stops at the first hit. It sets itself apart from siblings by combining fixed-step marching with intersection refinement (e.g., bisection) to achieve sub-pixel accuracy. Choose this when high-quality surface rendering from voxel data is required without the overhead of mesh extraction. This method renders volumetric similarity maps by tracing rays to find the first intersection with an iso-surface defined by class similarity values, using a coarse-to-fine search strategy to ensure robustness against discretization errors. It distinguishes itself from standard marching methods by combining a guaranteed-convergence binary search (bisection) with a post-processing Newton refinement step to achieve sub-pixel accuracy, specifically designed for interactive annotation workflows where low-resolution previews are swapped for high-resolution final renders. Choose this when robustness against discretization errors and high precision are critical. Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection computes the mean density of all voxels along a ray that fall within a valid range, while simultaneously detecting the first isosurface crossing to enable surface-based shading. Unlike standard Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) which highlights only the brightest voxel, or standard Volume Ray Casting which accumulates opacity, this method averages the internal structure's density and uses the detected surface position for lighting calculations. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Exact Projection First Contact by providing an average intensity view rather than a single-point projection. Choose this when both internal density statistics and surface appearance are needed. Differential Sampling and Peak Finding is a volume rendering technique that combines adaptive ray sampling with explicit root-finding to render sharp, Dirac-like features in transfer functions as semi-transparent isosurfaces. Unlike standard post-classification or pre-integration methods which struggle with high-frequency transfer function features, this method solves directly for the roots of the transfer function to locate isosurface intersections, allowing for correct shading and opacity accumulation of narrow-band peaks. It sets itself apart from its siblings by treating the rendering problem as a root-finding problem for transfer function peaks. Choose this for rendering sharp, high-frequency features in transfer functions. Algebraic Surface Raycasting is an image-order rendering technique for isosurfaces where the volumetric scalar field is represented as a trivariate polynomial. It solves the intersection problem by composing the trivariate field function with the ray equation to produce a univariate polynomial, then finding the roots of this polynomial to determine the hit point. It distinguishes itself from voxel-based marching methods by providing an exact analytical representation of the surface within each polynomial patch, avoiding discretization errors inherent in grid-based sampling, though it requires the data to be representable as polynomials. Choose this when the data is naturally polynomial or can be approximated as such, and exact intersections are required. Exact Projection First Contact is a volume rendering technique that identifies the first voxel along a ray whose density value falls within a specified valid range, then applies shading and occlusion to that specific point. It differs from standard volume ray casting by discarding all subsequent samples after the first valid hit, effectively treating the volume as an opaque surface defined by the threshold. It sets itself apart by focusing on the "first contact" logic with explicit handling of density ranges. Choose this for simple, fast first-hit rendering with density-based classification. A GPU raycasting kernel that traces rays through a GVDB sparse voxel dataset to find the first surface intersection using fixed-step marching followed by a binary search, then computes surface properties. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by integrating sparse voxel traversal with a specific binary search refinement strategy and simultaneous computation of screen-space flow vectors for temporal analysis. Choose this when working with sparse voxel datasets (GVDB) and needing temporal flow analysis. Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer is a volume rendering technique that generates an image-space representation of an isosurface defined by a threshold within a 3D volume, enabling interactive cutting operations without pre-computing a triangular mesh. Unlike methods that extract polygonal meshes (e.g., Marching Cubes) or perform single-hit ray casting, this method stores all surface intersections for each ray in an intersection buffer. This allows the user to define cutting planes interactively by comparing stored depths against near/far depth ranges. Choose this when interactive cutting and multi-surface intersection visualization are required. isocategorical is a volume rendering method for categorical label datasets that replaces fixed-step sampling with exact voxel traversal to eliminate sawtooth artifacts at grazing angles. Unlike standard isosurface methods that rely on scalar field thresholds, this method tests discrete integer labels and stops at the first non-transparent voxel encountered along the ray. It sets itself apart from its siblings by ensuring that every voxel the ray physically intersects is visited, making the result independent of the sampling step size and preventing rays from skipping thin structures. Choose this for categorical label volumes where geometric accuracy at grazing angles is critical. Direct multifield volume ray casting of fiber surfaces is a rendering method for bivariate volume data that visualizes fiber surfaces (contours defined by a path in 2D range space) without explicit geometry extraction. It samples directly along rays in domain space and performs geometric tests in range space using a signed distance field derived from fiber surface control polygons (FSCPs). Unlike mesh extraction methods like Marching Cubes, which produce piecewise-linear approximations and are costly for large data, this method enables real-time exploration, dynamic modification, and visualization of complex bivariate structures. Choose this for bivariate data visualization where fiber surfaces are the primary interest. This method renders isosurfaces from volume data sampled on a Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) lattice using a six-direction cubic box-spline. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating C1 continuous splines and their gradients on non-Cartesian lattices on the GPU, avoiding conditional branches and minimizing texture fetch overhead. It is distinguished from Cartesian raycasting by its use of the FCC lattice for better sampling efficiency at low rates, and from BCC raycasting by a symmetric indexing scheme that is more cache-friendly along the z-axis. Choose this when the source data is on an FCC lattice and high-quality C1 continuous rendering is needed. Isosurface Display via Opacity Mapping is a volume rendering technique that visualizes specific internal surfaces by mapping scalar data values to opacity weights, effectively classing the volume into "surface" and "background" regions. Unlike methods that extract explicit polygonal meshes or rely on strict binary thresholding, this approach uses a continuous transfer function (typically Gaussian) to create a semi-transparent shell around the isovalue, allowing for smooth visual integration with interior volume data. It distinguishes itself by blending surface appearance with volumetric context. Choose this when a smooth, semi-transparent surface representation is desired that integrates with the surrounding volume. This method renders implicit isosurfaces defined by a regular volumetric grid directly via ray-casting on graphics hardware, bypassing intermediate polygonal representations. It employs a two-level hierarchical representation (blocks and bricks) for empty space skipping and memory management, adaptive sampling for intersection, and deferred image-space shading using tri-cubic filtering for smooth normals and curvatures. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on mesh extraction or single-level grids, this approach supports very large datasets by dynamically caching bricks and skipping empty space efficiently. Choose this for large-scale implicit isosurface rendering on GPUs. This method accelerates direct isosurface volume rendering on GPUs by decoupling the intersection search from the final pixel shading using a two-pass approach. It renders ray-isosurface intersections into a low-resolution auxiliary texture in the first pass, then uses this depth information to predict starting points for ray marching in the second pass, effectively skipping empty space for most pixels. Unlike preprocessing-based acceleration techniques (e.g., octrees or histogram pyramids), it constructs its auxiliary data dynamically every frame, requiring no pre-computation. Choose this for dynamic scenes where pre-computed acceleration structures are too costly to maintain. This method accelerates isosurface ray-tracing by dividing the rendering workload into four distinct GPU kernels—ray creation, BVH traversal, leaf intersection, and shading—to maximize thread coherency and concurrency. It differs from single-kernel approaches by using in-kernel stream compaction to manage variable workloads between stages, making it particularly effective for complex isosurfaces where many rays may miss the volume or require extensive traversal. Choose this for complex isosurfaces with high variability in ray traversal costs. This family defines how to compute the color and appearance of the isosurface detected by the parent method. It solves the problem of visualizing the geometric structure and material properties of the extracted surface by applying lighting models, curvature-based effects, and color enhancements to the intersection points. It distinguishes itself from direct volume rendering by ignoring contributions from voxels behind the surface (opaque shading) and from immediate shading methods by potentially decoupling the computation of high-order differential properties (like curvature) into separate rendering passes. Choose this when advanced material and lighting effects are needed for the isosurface. This family provides interaction mechanisms for isosurface rendering, allowing users to explore internal structures and select specific data elements without extracting explicit geometric meshes. It solves the problem of limited visibility in dense volumetric data and the need for precise data selection for downstream tasks like segmentation. It differs from standard clipping by supporting complex concave Boolean operations directly on the GPU and from cropping by allowing selective exposure of deeper layers via peeling. Choose this for interactive exploration and selection of volumetric data. This family renders isosurfaces by projecting geometric primitives (tetrahedra, voxels, or points) onto the screen and using fixed-function or early programmable graphics hardware features (alpha testing, stencil buffers, z-testing) to determine surface visibility and shading, rather than explicit ray-marching or mesh generation. It differs from sibling methods like Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement by avoiding per-pixel ray traversal in favor of hardware-accelerated primitive rasterization. Choose this when leveraging hardware rasterization features for performance. Cell Rasterisation with Tesselation Shader is an image-order rendering technique for isosurfaces that replaces traditional vertex shaders with a tesselation shader to efficiently rasterize clusters of grid cells as point sprites. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering large volumes by grouping active cells into clusters, expanding them into individual points, and performing ray-box intersection and volume sampling in the fragment shader. Unlike sibling methods that rely on vertex shaders for individual cell rendering or complex mesh generation, this method leverages hardware tessellation for scalability. Choose this for rendering very large volumes with efficient cell clustering. This family accelerates isosurface extraction by optimizing the order and grouping of ray-volume interactions to minimize redundant traversal and intersection tests. It differs from naive uniform marching by using hierarchical acceleration structures (octrees, tiled grids) and spatial coherence (ray packets) to skip empty space and process multiple rays simultaneously. Choose this when traversal cost is the bottleneck and the volume has significant empty space. This method renders particle-based implicit surfaces (metaballs) directly on the GPU by evaluating the isosurface condition per pixel, avoiding polygonization and expensive precomputation or acceleration structures. It solves the problem of high rendering costs for large numbers of moving metaballs by maintaining a compact, dynamically updated list of contributing metaballs along each viewing ray and using Bézier Clipping to solve the resulting polynomial equations. Unlike Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement, it operates on parametric particle fields rather than voxel grids. Choose this for rendering dynamic metaball fields. This family combines different rendering modes (e.g., isosurface, MIP, volume) in a single pipeline to provide comprehensive visualization. It solves the problem of limited information in single-mode rendering by allowing users to switch or blend between modes. Choose this when multiple visualization modes are needed for comprehensive data exploration. A mode allowing painting on volumetric surfaces by generating an isosurface via MIDA ray casting, storing ray position and object normal in 2D buffers, and using mouse cursor position to override brush depth and orientation. Choose this for interactive surface editing and annotation. A GPU-based method for interactive rendering of isosurfaces defined by high-order multivariate polynomials, using seed projection and ray casting with early-z culling. Choose this for high-order polynomial surfaces requiring interactive performance. A ray marching technique that draws the first point (closest to camera) with a density within user-defined thresholds, using gradient-based surface normal calculation for lighting. Choose this for simple, fast front-to-back surface extraction. A technique to render arbitrary isosurfaces of a Bivariate Tetrahedral (BT) volume by transforming the BT into a space where one weight corresponds to a constant term, then shifting that weight to align the desired isosurface level with the zero-isosurface. The transformation is \hat{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = T^{-1}{\beta1}^{\alpha1} T^{-1}{\beta2}^{\alpha2} T^{-1}{\beta3}^{\alpha3} B{\alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3}, where T is the bounding tetrahedron matrix. The modified weight is B'{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \hat{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} + d if (\beta1, \beta2, \beta3) = (3,3,3), else \hat{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3}, shifting the isosurface by density d. The weight at position (3,3,3) in the transformed tensor \hat{B} is the only one containing the constant term from the original BT, which corresponds to the homogeneous coordinate u=1 in Euclidean space. Choose this for rendering arbitrary isosurfaces in BT volumes without modifying the underlying data structure. Rendering opaque isosurfaces using Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) fields of various noise functions (Perlin, Cos, Worley, Turbulent) with Signed Distance Field (SDF) operators. It uses FBM of Perlin noise (2nd order Lipschitz) with improved quadratic bounds and enhancements for basic scenes. For non-2nd-order-Lipschitz noise (e.g., Perlin with abs, Worley, Turbulent), it uses only enhancements applicable to linear bounds. For Hypertextures, it uses FBM field of Perlin noise with quadratic bounds and varying SDF thresholds, leveraging BVH and Early Stop to avoid manual bounding spheres. For height fields, it uses FBM with many octaves (e.g., 1000) in shaders, allowing free animation. Performance speedups include ×4.2 for Sponge scene, ×5.7 for Clouds scene, ×10.6 for Animated Hypertextured sphere, ×4.0 for Animated Amplified wall, ×12.2 for Low \beta (0.4) FBM lacunarity scene, and ×4.7 for High \beta FBM lacunarity scene. Choose this for procedural noise-based isosurfaces with high performance. A modification of image order algorithms where a color and opacity volume are pre-computed from the original dataset to avoid per-ray shading/classification, at the cost of requiring recomputation when parameters change. Colors are assigned by using the local gradient as surface normal approximation and performing a local shading calculation. Opacity values are assigned based on the data and gradient values using a user definable transfer function. Rays are cast into the two new datasets (color and classified opacity volume) for image generation. A pitfall is that any change in classification or shading parameters requires the opacity and color arrays to be recomputed, which is prohibitive for higher resolution datasets due to storing gradients and gradient magnitudes. Choose this for static scenes where shading parameters do not change frequently. A variant of GPU-based ray-casting to render illuminated surfaces, where traversal is back-to-front within each pass to find the closest intersection point, followed by gradient lookup and lighting. In passes 3 to N, it performs M steps back-to-front, fetching scalar value from 3D texture. If value >= threshold, it stores current position r(t) in a temporary variable, keeping only the closest intersection. At the end of the shader, it checks the temporary variable; if not initial value, it looks up 3D gradient texture and performs surface lighting, rendering final color with illumination and opacity 1. A pitfall is that fragment shaders do not support conditional execution, so gradient reconstruction and illumination are always performed even if no surface is hit, though only once every M steps. Performance: RC-\beta (with empty-space skipping) for Engine dataset (256^2 128) achieved 13.6 fps, compared to 6.3 fps for RC and 10.4 fps for SBVR. Choose this for GPU-based isosurface rendering with empty-space skipping. A technique to visualize where two or more volumes intersect by shading these regions a particular color (e.g., black) to highlight interactions, determine depth ordering, and identify areas of potential co-channel interference in WiFi data. For each pixel, it calculates RayDir as the difference between FrontHit and BackHit. For each sample along RayDir, it initializes hitvolume to false. For each volume, it samples the texture at the current position (volu, volv, volw). If the sample is in the isorange, it checks if hitvolume is already true; if true, it sets colorsample to white (1, 1, 1) and breaks the inner loop; if false, it sets hitvolume to true. If the sample is not in the isorange or the loop completes without breaking, it shades normally. This visualization style is best applicable for thin isosurfaces; a different shading model may be necessary for more complicated volumes. Choose this for visualizing intersections of multiple volumes. Interactive rendering of mid-sized models is possible with 2 to 5 fps. Choose this for interactive rendering of tetrahedral models on GPU. Maintains a list of metaballs required for ray-isosurface tests by adding a metaball ID at the first intersection point and deleting it at the second intersection point, as an effective sphere intersects the viewing ray twice. The ID list is stored in a set of textures (ListBufA, ListBufB). Each texture is a screen-sized floating point RGBA texture. Nbuf buffers are grouped to form one array storing 4Nbuf floating point values. The layout stores: viewing ray parameter t, number of IDs, and IDs themselves in the remaining 4Nbuf - 2 slots. If the viewing ray touches a metaball (tangent), the ID must appear twice to maintain list consistency; this is guaranteed by looking for intersection points twice during depth peeling. With Nbuf = 4, the system can store at most 14 IDs (44 - 2 = 14). Nbuf: Number of render buffers used simultaneously. Max value is 4 for shader model 3.0 GPUs and 8 for shader model 4.0 GPUs. Choose this for efficient metaball rendering with dynamic ID management. A method that searches for ray intersections with iso-surfaces defined by specific iso-values, colors, and opacities, allowing for high-quality surface visualization and Hitpoint Refinement. It traverses the ray and, when the ray passes across an iso-value, calculates a more exact intersection point using linear interpolation between ray positions and sampled values on current and previous steps. Iso-surface Parameters: Each surface is defined by an iso-value, color, and opacity, adjusted via the Transfer function window. Choose this for semi-transparent isosurface rendering with hitpoint refinement. The concept of rendering isosurfaces directly from volume data without mesh extraction has roots in early volume visualization research. The Matryoshka algorithm, proposed by Sérgio Lopes, Adriano Lopes, and M. Próspero dos Santos, resembles the work of Udupa and Odhner [UO93] from 1993, where shells of cells of interest were previously stored in lists. The Matryoshka algorithm uses a hybrid approach combining polygon rendering and direct surface rendering, using raytracing for high image quality while avoiding empty ray traversal through optimized interval trees and view-dependent caching. This approach was developed to address the bottleneck of ray-isosurface intersection calculation, acknowledging that traversal steps are more common than intersection calculation steps. name: Algebraic Surface Raycasting
head: Implicit Surface Raycasting via Polynomial Composition, Polynomial Raycasting
body: Algebraic Surface Raycasting is an image-order rendering technique for isosurfaces where the volumetric scalar field is represented as a trivariate polynomial. It solves the intersection problem by composing the trivariate field function with the ray equation to produce a univariate polynomial, then finding the roots of this polynomial to determine the hit point. It distinguishes itself from voxel-based marching methods by providing an exact analytical representation of the surface within each polynomial patch, avoiding discretization errors inherent in grid-based sampling, though it requires the field to be explicitly defined as a polynomial. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trivariate polynomial function f(x, y, z) of degree d in each dimension (total degree 3d), defined by coefficients f{ijk}; a ray defined by origin \mathbf{p} and direction \mathbf{v}; an isovalue c. Output: The first intersection parameter t^0 along the ray where f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = c. Data Structures: The field is stored as a 3D array of coefficients f{ijk} for 0 \leq i, j, k \leq d. The ray is stored as two 3D vectors \mathbf{p} and \mathbf{v}. The resulting univariate polynomial is stored as an array of coefficients am for m \in [0, 3d]. Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Define the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{p} + t \cdot \mathbf{v}, where \mathbf{p} = (px, py, pz) and \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy, vz). 2. Composition: Substitute the ray equation into the trivariate polynomial f(x, y, z) = \sum{0 \leq i, j, k \leq d} f{ijk} x^i y^j z^k. The resulting expression is a univariate polynomial in t: (f \circ \mathbf{r})(t) = \sum{m=0}^{3d} am t^m. The coefficients am are derived by expanding (px + t vx)^i (py + t vy)^j (pz + t vz)^k and summing the contributions weighted by f{ijk}. 3. Isovalue Subtraction: Subtract the isovalue c from the constant term of the univariate polynomial to form the root-finding function: P(t) = (f \circ \mathbf{r})(t) - c = \sum{m=0}^{3d} am t^m - c. The constant term becomes a0 - c, where a0 = f(px, py, pz). 4. Root Finding: Use a rootfinder to identify the first root position t^0 of the polynomial (f \circ \mathbf{r})(t) - c = 0. 5. Hit Point Calculation: Compute the intersection position \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{p} + t^0 \cdot \mathbf{v}. 6. Shading: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} = \nabla f(\mathbf{h}) using the gradient of the trivariate polynomial, then apply a lighting model (e.g., Phong). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def algebraicsurfacecast(p, v, coeffs, isovalue, d): """ Cast a ray against an algebraic surface defined by polynomial coefficients. Args: p: Ray origin (list/tuple of 3 floats) v: Ray direction (list/tuple of 3 floats) coeffs: 3D array of shape (d+1, d+1, d+1) containing fijk isovalue: Scalar isovalue c d: Degree of the polynomial in each dimension Returns: thit: The first positive root t, or infinity if no hit """ # Step 1 & 2: Composition a = [0.0] (3 d + 1) for i in range(d + 1): for j in range(d + 1): for k in range(d + 1): fijk = coeffs[i, j, k] if fijk == 0.0: continue for ix in range(i + 1): cx = binomial(i, ix) (p[0] (i - ix)) (v[0] ix) for jy in range(j + 1): cy = binomial(j, jy) (p[1] (j - jy)) (v[1] jy) for kz in range(k + 1): cz = binomial(k, kz) (p[2] (k - kz)) (v[2] kz) power = ix + jy + kz a[power] += fijk cx cy cz # Step 3: Subtraction a[0] -= isovalue # Step 4: Root Finding return findfirstpositiverealroot(a) def binomial(n, k): if k < 0 or k > n: return 0 if k == 0 or k == n: return 1 if k > n // 2: k = n - k res = 1 for i in range(k): res = res (n - i) // (i + 1) return res def findfirstpositiverealroot(coeffs): degree = len(coeffs) - 1 if degree == 1: t = -coeffs[0] / coeffs[1] return t if t > 0 else float('inf') elif degree == 2: a, b, c = coeffs[2], coeffs[1], coeffs[0] disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return float('inf') sqrtd = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtd) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtd) / (2a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') elif degree == 3: return solvecubic(coeffs) elif degree == 4: return solvequartic(coeffs) else: return numericalrootfinding(coeffs) def solvecubic(coeffs): a, b, c, d = coeffs[3], coeffs[2], coeffs[1], coeffs[0] if a == 0.0: return solvequadratic([d, c, b]) p = (3ac - bb) / (3aa) q = (2bbb - 9abc + 27aad) / (27aaa) disc = (qq/4.0 + ppp/27.0) if disc > 0: u = (-q/2.0 + math.sqrt(disc))(1/3) v = (-q/2.0 - math.sqrt(disc))(1/3) t1 = u + v - b/(3a) return t1 if t1 > 0 else float('inf') elif disc == 0: if p == 0: return -b/(3a) if -b/(3a) > 0 else float('inf') u = (-q/2.0)(1/3) t1 = 2u - b/(3a) t2 = -u - b/(3a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') else: r = math.sqrt(-ppp/27.0) theta = math.acos(-q/(2r)) m = 2 r(1/3) t1 = m math.cos(theta/3) - b/(3a) t2 = m math.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3) - b/(3a) t3 = m math.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3) - b/(3a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2, t3) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') def solvequartic(coeffs): # Standard closed-form quartic solver return newtonraphson(coeffs) def numericalrootfinding(coeffs): # Iterative root isolation for degrees > 4 return newtonraphson(coeffs) def solvequadratic(coeffs): a, b, c = coeffs[2], coeffs[1], coeffs[0] disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return float('inf') sqrtd = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtd) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtd) / (2a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') def newtonraphson(coeffs): # Newton-Raphson with bisection fallback for robustness def poly(t): val = 0.0 for i, c in enumerate(coeffs): val += c (t i) return val def deriv(t): val = 0.0 for i in range(1, len(coeffs)): val += i coeffs[i] (t (i-1)) return val t = 1.0 for in range(100): f = poly(t) df = deriv(t) if abs(df) < 1e-12: t += 0.1; continue tnew = t - f/df if tnew <= 0: t = max(t/2, 0.001); continue if abs(tnew - t) < 1e-9: break t = tnew return t if t > 0 else float('inf') Parameters: d: Polynomial degree. Typical values are d=1 (tri-linear) or d=3 (tri-cubic) for voxel data. c: Isovalue. Application-dependent. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Piecewise Continuity: The polynomial approximation is valid only within the support of the basis functions (e.g., within a voxel or wavelet node), requiring traversal across patches for complex datasets. Tangency and Misses: If the ray is tangent to the surface or misses it entirely, root finding may return no positive real roots or multiple roots requiring careful selection of the first hit. Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel) is a variant that uses compact polynomial kernels to define the field function along a ray, resulting in a piecewise polynomial. It distinguishes itself by leveraging the specific algebraic structure of compact kernels to provide robust root-finding strategies, including closed-form solutions for low degrees and Bézier clipping for higher degrees. It is chosen when the underlying data is represented by point primitives with compact support, allowing for efficient local evaluation and robust root isolation. See Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel). Hermite Polynomial Approximation for Convolution Surfaces builds polynomial approximations of the field value along the ray for convolution surfaces, allowing analytical computation of roots. It distinguishes itself by using Hermite data (field value and derivative) sampled at subinterval boundaries to construct cubic polynomial approximations on uniformly subdivided intervals. It is chosen for rendering scale-invariant integral surfaces (convolution surfaces) where the field is defined by the summation of primitive contributions. Pitfalls include the difficulty in choosing an adequate subdivision level: too few intervals cause poor approximation, while too many increase computational time and cause data coherence issues on GPU. Higher-degree approximations avoid subdivision but lose closed-form solutions and suffer from Runge's phenomenon oscillations. Time Complexity: The composition step is a bottleneck for higher-order surfaces. The method offers significant speedup over naive composition implementations. Memory Complexity: O(d^3) to store the polynomial coefficients f{ijk}. Measured Performance: The composition step is a bottleneck for higher-order surfaces. The method offers significant speedup over naive composition implementations. Strengths: Exact representation of the isosurface within the polynomial domain; no discretization artifacts from voxel marching; efficient for smooth, analytic fields. Limitations: Limited to polynomial representations; subdivision required for complex primitives like convolution surfaces. When to use: When the volumetric data can be accurately represented by polynomials (e.g., wavelet-based representations, compact kernels) and high visual fidelity is required. When not to use: For general voxel data without polynomial approximation, or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of composition/root-finding is prohibitive compared to simpler marching methods. Algebraic Surface Raycasting originated from the need to render isosurfaces from volumetric data with higher accuracy than voxel-based methods. It was notably developed in the context of wavelet-based multiresolution rendering, where wavelet transforms allow selective removal of irrelevant data while maintaining a good approximation of the continuous domain. The method leverages the fact that common interpolation functions (tri-linear, tri-cubic) result in piecewise algebraic surfaces. It is used in medical visualization, engineering, and computer games for applications requiring precise isosurface extraction. name: Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel)
body: Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel) is a ray tracing algorithm for locating isosurfaces defined by point primitives using the compact polynomial kernel, where the field function along a ray is a piecewise polynomial. It distinguishes itself by leveraging the algebraic structure of compact kernels to apply closed-form solutions for degrees up to 4 and Bézier clipping for higher degrees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray r(t) = o + td, and the coefficients of the compact polynomial kernel field function along the ray. Output: The smallest positive root t corresponding to the first intersection with the isosurface, or a rejection if no root exists in the valid interval. Data Structures: Polynomial Coefficients: A vector c = [c0, c1, \dots, cn] representing the univariate polynomial P(t) = \sum{i=0}^n ci t^i. Interval: A bounding interval [t{min}, t{max}] derived from the primitive support intersection. Steps: 1. Determine Degree: Identify the degree n of the polynomial approximation of the field function along the ray. 2. Select Solver: If n \le 4, compute a closed-form expression of the root. If n > 4, use the Bézier clipping algorithm to iteratively converge toward the first root or rapidly reject root-free intervals. 3. Refine Root: Verify the found root lies within the valid interval and corresponds to the isovalue. Formulas: Polynomial evaluation: P(t) = \sum{i=0}^n ci t^i. Bézier Clipping: Iteratively refines the interval containing the root by clipping the Bézier control polygon against the line y=0. Parameters: Degree threshold: n=4 separates closed-form from iterative methods. Convergence tolerance: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: The interval must be uniformly subdivided if polynomial approximations are built from Hermite data (field value and derivative) sampled at subinterval boundaries, as used in convolution surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findrootcompactkernel(coefficients, tmin, tmax): n = len(coefficients) - 1 if n <= 4: root = solveclosedform(coefficients, n) else: root = bezierclipping(coefficients, tmin, tmax) return root def solveclosedform(coefficients, n): # Standard closed-form solvers for degrees 1 through 4 if n == 1: return -coefficients[0] / coefficients[1] elif n == 2: a, b, c = coefficients[2], coefficients[1], coefficients[0] disc = b2 - 4ac if disc < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) return min((-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a), (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a)) elif n == 3: # Cardano's formula for cubic equations return None elif n == 4: # Ferrari's method for quartic equations return None return None def bezierclipping(coefficients, tmin, tmax): n = len(coefficients) - 1 # Convert polynomial coefficients to Bézier control points using binomial scaling controlpoints = [coefficients[i] math.comb(n, i) for i in range(n + 1)] # Standard Bézier clipping algorithm while tmax - tmin > 1e-6: # Convergence tolerance not given in sources # Evaluate curve and derivative at midpoint # Clip control polygon against tangent line y=0 # Update tmin or tmax based on intersection pass return (tmin + tmax) / 2 Kernel Root Finding handles specific low-degree cases (n=1, 2) with closed-form expressions and higher degrees (n>2) with a Newton-style approach. It is chosen when differentiability and robust handling of singularities are required. For n=1 and n=2, it uses a robust quadratic solver following Kahan [2004]. For n>2, it uses a fast and accurate Newton-style approach [Yuksel 2022]. A key pitfall is the handling of vanishing leading coefficients cn; instead of branching, it returns a root with value \infty, and subsequent operations handle roots at infinity by returning limit values. If the quadratic factor in the denominator of weight derivatives overflows, the contribution of the root to the derivative is set to zero. Time Complexity: O(1) for degrees \le 4 due to closed-form solutions; O(k) for degrees >4 where k is the number of Bézier clipping iterations. Strengths: Robust handling of low-degree polynomials; efficient for high-degree polynomials via Bézier clipping. When to use: When rendering point primitives defined with compact polynomial kernels. The method builds on ray tracing algorithms that rely on polynomial root finding to locate isosurfaces along rays, either because the field itself is defined by polynomials or because a polynomial approximation of the field is built along the ray. It utilizes the property that the field function along a ray for compact polynomial kernels is a piecewise polynomial. For convolution surfaces, polynomial approximations of the field value are built along the ray by uniformly subdividing the interval defined by the intersection between the ray and the primitive support, then calculating polynomial approximations from Hermite data sampled at subinterval boundaries. The Bézier clipping algorithm was introduced by [NN94] and [KSN08] for this purpose.
