name: Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: Hybrid Isosurface Method, Implicit isosurface ray tracing, Wang et al. hybrid method
body: Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing is a rendering technique that extracts a list of active vertex-centered cubic primitives (octants or dual cells) from cell-centered TB-AMR data, builds a BVH over them, and performs implicit ray-isosurface intersections within each primitive, avoiding the memory cost of explicit triangle extraction. It combines explicit extraction (selecting active voxels) with implicit tracing (intersecting rays against the trilinear field within those voxels) to produce high-quality, crack-free isosurfaces. Unlike sample-based isosurface methods that use fixed step sizes and may miss features in refined regions, this method adapts to the local resolution, providing more detail and better framerates for AMR data. The method operates on rectilinear volumes (regular grids, rectilinear grids, BS-AMR) by treating them as a source of logical voxels. Each voxel is a cube with trilinearly interpolated scalar values at its vertices. Input: A rectilinear volume (e.g., TB-AMR data) and a user-specified isovalue. Output: A rendered image of the isosurface. Voxel Abstraction: Each logical voxel is described by 12 values: 1. 3 values for 3D coordinates (position). 2. 1 value for width. 3. 8 values for scalar values at the vertices. Note: For general rectilinear volumes, 2 additional values are required to specify height and depth. Active Voxel Encoding: Active voxels are encoded into a single 64-bit value (e.g., 21:21:21 bit coordinates) to allow efficient storage and lookup. Geometry Type: The method uses "user geometry" primitives compatible with Embree. The primitives are either: Octants: Vertex-centered cubes where the center is the input cell center. Dual Cells: Vertex-centered cubes where the center is a vertex of the original grid. 1. Voxel Source Initialization: Create a VoxelSource entity that can quickly generate a list of active voxels from the input volume. 2. Primitive Extraction: Iterate through all input cells Ci. For each cell, generate up to 8 octants O{ij} or dual cells D{ij}. Compute the scalar values at the vertices of each primitive using the GTI (Grid Trilinear Interpolation) method to ensure surface continuity. Optimization: If a dual cell can be constructed (vertices lie at the same AMR level), emit the dual cell instead of the octant to avoid overlap and reduce primitive count. 3. Active Cell Filtering: A primitive is active if its value range (min/max of its 8 vertex values) overlaps with the user-specified isovalue. 4. BVH Construction: Create an Embree "user geometry" with one primitive per active voxel. Implement a getBounds callback: Query the VoxelSource for the bounding box of the respective voxel using its 64-bit reference. Build an Embree BVH over these primitives. 5. Ray Traversal and Intersection: Traverse rays through the BVH. For each hit primitive, perform an implicit ray-isosurface intersection. The intersection routine queries the full voxel data from the VoxelSource using the 64-bit reference. The intersection algorithm used is an ISPC version of Marmitt et al.'s ray-iso voxel intersection. Rays are processed in packets of 4, 8, or 16. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayboxintersection(rayo, rayd, boxmin, boxmax): """Standard slab method. Returns (tmin, tmax) or None if no hit.""" tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if rayd[i] == 0.0: if rayo[i] < boxmin[i] or rayo[i] > boxmax[i]: return None else: t1 = (boxmin[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] t2 = (boxmax[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < 0.0 or tmin > tmax: return None return tmin, tmax def trilinearintersection(rayo, rayd, voxeldata, isovalue): """Solves V(u,v,w) = isovalue along ray segment within voxel bounds.""" # voxeldata: [x, y, z, w, h, d, v0...v7] # v0..v7 are scalar values at the 8 vertices of the voxel boxmin = [voxeldata[0], voxeldata[1], voxeldata[2]] boxmax = [voxeldata[0] + voxeldata[3], voxeldata[1] + voxeldata[3], voxeldata[2] + voxeldata[3]] thit = None tseg = rayboxintersection(rayo, rayd, boxmin, boxmax) if tseg is None: return None tstart, tend = tseg # Bisection search for trilinear root within voxel slab for in range(32): tmid = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 p = rayo + tmid rayd u = (p[0] - boxmin[0]) / (boxmax[0] - boxmin[0]) v = (p[1] - boxmin[1]) / (boxmax[1] - boxmin[1]) w = (p[2] - boxmin[2]) / (boxmax[2] - boxmin[2]) u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) w = max(0.0, min(1.0, w)) # Trilinear interpolation formula v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111 = voxeldata[6:14] val = ((1-u)(1-v)(1-w)v000 + u(1-v)(1-w)v100 + (1-u)v(1-w)v010 + uv(1-w)v110 + (1-u)(1-v)wv001 + u(1-v)wv101 + (1-u)vwv011 + uvwv111) if abs(val - isovalue) < 1e-6: thit = tmid break if (val - isovalue) ((1-u)(1-v)(1-w)v000 - isovalue) < 0: tend = tmid else: tstart = tmid return thit class Octant: def init(self, cellidx, octantidx): self.cellidx = cellidx self.octantidx = octantidx self.vertexvalues = [0.0] 8 self.ref64bit = 0 class DualCell: def init(self, octant): self.vertexvalues = octant.vertexvalues.copy() self.ref64bit = octant.ref64bit class HybridIsosurfaceRenderer: def init(self, volumedata, isovalue): self.volumedata = volumedata self.isovalue = isovalue self.activeprimitives = [] def extractprimitives(self): primitives = [] for cell in self.volumedata.cells: for j in range(8): octant = Octant(cell.idx, j) octant.vertexvalues = self.volumedata.computegtivalues(octant) octant.ref64bit = self.volumedata.encode64bit(octant) if self.volumedata.canformdualcell(octant): dual = DualCell(octant) primitives.append(dual) else: primitives.append(octant) active = [] for prim in primitives: minval = min(prim.vertexvalues) maxval = max(prim.vertexvalues) if minval <= self.isovalue <= maxval: active.append(prim) self.activeprimitives = active return active def buildbvh(self): """Builds a BVH over active primitives using explicit bounding box queries.""" boundslist = [] for prim in self.activeprimitives: voxeldata = self.volumedata.getvoxeldata(prim.ref64bit) boxmin = [voxeldata[0], voxeldata[1], voxeldata[2]] boxmax = [voxeldata[0] + voxeldata[3], voxeldata[1] + voxeldata[3], voxeldata[2] + voxeldata[3]] boundslist.append((boxmin, boxmax, prim)) # Standard BVH construction algorithm self.bvh = self.buildbvhrecursive(boundslist, 0, len(boundslist)-1) return self.bvh def buildbvhrecursive(self, boundslist, start, end): if start > end: return None if start == end: return {"bounds": boundslist[start], "children": None} mid = (start + end) // 2 boundslist.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0][0] + x[1][0]) / 2.0) left = self.buildbvhrecursive(boundslist, start, mid) right = self.buildbvhrecursive(boundslist, mid+1, end) combinedmin = [min(left["bounds"][0][i], right["bounds"][0][i]) for i in range(3)] combinedmax = [max(left["bounds"][1][i], right["bounds"][1][i]) for i in range(3)] return {"bounds": (combinedmin, combinedmax), "children": [left, right]} def render(self, rays): hits = [] for rayo, rayd in rays: thit = self.traversebvh(self.bvh, rayo, rayd) if thit is not None: hits.append((rayo, rayd, thit)) return hits def traversebvh(self, node, rayo, rayd): if node is None: return None tseg = rayboxintersection(rayo, rayd, node["bounds"][0], node["bounds"][1]) if tseg is None: return None if node["children"] is None: prim = node["bounds"][2] voxeldata = self.volumedata.getvoxeldata(prim.ref64bit) return trilinearintersection(rayo, rayd, voxeldata, self.isovalue) t1 = self.traversebvh(node["children"][0], rayo, rayd) t2 = self.traversebvh(node["children"][1], rayo, rayd) if t1 is not None and t2 is not None: return min(t1, t2) return t1 if t1 is not None else t2 Isosvalue: User-specified scalar value defining the surface. Ray Packet Size: 4, 8, or 16 rays. Precision: The method relies on trilinear interpolation. Degenerate cases where the isovalue equals the min/max vertex value may require careful handling to avoid missed hits or double hits, though the source notes that the method yields a "crack-free" surface. Boundary Conditions: The method handles AMR boundaries by using dual cells in non-boundary regions and octants elsewhere, ensuring consistency. A pre-processing optimization that reduces the number of geometric primitives generated for rendering by discarding input cells whose value ranges do not overlap with the user-specified isovalue. An optimization that replaces octants with dual cells in non-boundary (same-level) regions to reduce the number of primitives traversed, achieving a ~4x speedup in extraction time. Time Complexity: The main performance bottleneck lies in the first process where resampling is required to extract primitives. BVH construction is efficient (~110 million primitives per second with Embree). Memory Complexity: Avoids the memory cost of explicit triangle extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by not generating a large number of triangles. Performance: Yields better framerates than sample-based isosurface methods for AMR data. Quality: Produces high-quality, crack-free isosurfaces with more detail in refined regions compared to sample-based methods which may miss the surface due to fixed step sizes. Hardware: Evaluated on multi-core CPUs (Xeon E7-8890 v3, Xeon Skylake Gold 6136). The method was introduced by Wang et al. in 2019 [WWW19] and integrated into the OSPRay ray tracing framework. It builds on the principles of implicit isosurface ray tracing [MKW04] and explicit extraction. The implementation in OSPRay extends the existing AMR volume structure. name: Active Cell Filtering
head: Optimization 2, Value Range Filtering
body: Active Cell Filtering is a pre-processing optimization for hybrid implicit isosurface ray tracing that reduces the number of geometric primitives generated for rendering. It solves the problem of unnecessary computation by discarding input cells whose value ranges (and those of their neighbors) do not overlap with the user-specified isovalue. Unlike sibling methods such as Dual Cell Optimization, which changes the geometry type used for extraction, Active Cell Filtering operates by pruning the set of candidate cells before any primitive construction occurs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tree-based adaptive mesh refinement (TB-AMR) dataset, an octree structure storing value ranges at inner nodes, and a scalar isovalue v{\text{iso}}. Output: A subset of active input cells eligible for primitive extraction (octants or dual cells). Data Structures: Octree: Each node Ni stores a value range [mini, maxi] used to check if the input cell C and its neighboring cells contain the isovalue. Input Cells: Each cell C has an associated value range [minC, maxC]. Algorithm: The method determines if an input cell C is "active" by traversing the octree from the root. A cell is active if the union of its own value range and the value ranges of its neighboring cells contains the isovalue. 1. Traverse Octree: Start at the root of the octree. 2. Prune Inner Nodes: For any inner node Ni, check if the isovalue v{\text{iso}} lies within its stored range [mini, maxi]. If v{\text{iso}} \notin [mini, maxi], terminate traversal for this branch because the children cannot contain the isovalue. If v{\text{iso}} \in [mini, maxi], continue traversal to children. 3. Check Neighbors: For the target cell C, identify its neighbors. In the context of the octree traversal, this involves checking if any neighbor's value range overlaps with v{\text{iso}} when unioned with C's range. 4. Determine Activity: Return true (active) if any neighbor of C is found whose value range, unioned with C's value range, contains v{\text{iso}}. Otherwise, return false. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the filtering logic. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iscellactive(cellC, isovalue, octreeroot): """Determines if cell C is active by checking if its value range unioned with any neighbor's range contains the isovalue.""" minc, maxc = getcellvaluerange(cellC) if minc <= isovalue <= maxc: return True return traverseoctree(cellC, minc, maxc, isovalue, octreeroot) def traverseoctree(cellC, minc, maxc, isovalue, node): """Recursively traverses the octree, pruning branches that cannot contain the isovalue.""" if not (node.minval <= isovalue <= node.maxval): return False if node.isleaf(): return checkneighborunion(cellC, minc, maxc, isovalue, node) for child in node.children: if traverseoctree(cellC, minc, maxc, isovalue, child): return True return False def getcellvaluerange(cell): """Returns the minimum and maximum scalar values of a cell.""" return cell.minval, cell.maxval def checkneighborunion(cellC, minc, maxc, isovalue, node): """Checks if the union of cellC's range and a neighbor's range contains the isovalue.""" minn, maxn = getcellvaluerange(node.cell) unionmin = min(minc, minn) unionmax = max(maxc, maxn) return unionmin <= isovalue <= unionmax Parameters and Edge Cases: Isovalue: The scalar threshold defining the isosurface. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for range inclusion must handle edge cases where v{\text{iso}} equals exactly min or max. Boundary Cells: Cells on the domain boundary have fewer neighbors, but the logic remains valid as it only checks existing neighbors. Performance: The optimization significantly reduces extraction time for sparse isosurfaces. On the Meteor-20060 dataset (158M cells, 1.44% active), extraction time drops from 114.08s (Naive) to 6.68s. On the ExaJet dataset (656M cells, 0.83% active), it drops from 505.96s to 19.13s. Complexity: The complexity depends on the sparsity of the isosurface and the depth of the octree. Strengths: Reduces the number of primitives generated, directly lowering the workload for the subsequent ray-tracing step. Limitations: Requires an octree structure with pre-computed value ranges at inner nodes. Active Cell Filtering was introduced as "Optimization 2" in the context of hybrid implicit isosurface ray tracing for TB-AMR data. It was developed to address the inefficiency of naively tiling the entire domain with octants or dual cells, where many primitives would not intersect the isosurface. The method leverages the hierarchical nature of AMR data to skip irrelevant regions early. name: Dual Cell Optimization for Isosurface Extraction
body: Also called: Optimization 1, Using Dual Cells at Same-level Regions ## Overview This method replaces octants with dual cells in non-boundary (same-level) regions to reduce the number of primitives traversed during ray tracing. It achieves an approximate 4× speedup in extraction time by merging eight octants into a single dual cell without changing the final isosurface geometry. It builds on Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing and is distinct from Active Cell Filtering, which filters input cells before primitive generation. ## How it works Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh of cells Ci from TB-AMR (Tree-Based Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data, and a target isovalue. Output: A list of active cubic primitives (either dual cells D{ij} or octants O{ij}). Data Structures: Cell Ci: The input volume element stored in an octree. Octant O{ij}: One of eight sub-cubes of Ci, indexed by j \in \{0, \dots, 7\}. Vertices require reconstruction via the GTI method at level boundaries. Dual Cell D{ij}: A cell enclosed by data points of known values. Its vertices are data points, requiring no reconstruction kernel. The center of Ci is a vertex of D{ij}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through each input cell Ci in the input mesh. 2. For each of the 8 octants j of Ci: a. Construct the candidate dual cell D{ij}. b. Determine if D{ij} lies in a same-level region. c. If D{ij} is in a same-level region: i. Check if the isovalue lies within the value range of D{ij}. ii. If true, and if j=7 (to avoid duplicate insertion for shared dual cells), insert D{ij} into res. d. If D{ij} is not in a same-level region (i.e., Ci is at a level boundary): i. Initialize the octant O{ij}. ii. Compute vertex values for O{ij} using the GTI method. iii. Check if the isovalue lies within the value range of O{ij}. iv. If true, insert O{ij} into res. Pseudocode: python def extractcubicprimitives(inputcells, isovalue): res = [] for Ci in inputcells: for j in range(8): Dij = finddualcell(Ci, j) insamelevel = isdualcellinsamelevel(Dij) if insamelevel: if j == 7 and isovalue in Dij.valuerange(): res.append(Dij) else: Oij = initoctant(Ci, j) gtimethod(Oij) if isovalue in Oij.valuerange(): res.append(Oij) return res def finddualcell(Ci, j): # Constructs dual cell Dij from surrounding vertex data vertexcoords = getvertexcoords(Ci, j) neighborcells = getneighborcellsatvertex(vertexcoords) vertexvalues = [cell.value for cell in neighborcells if cell is not None] return DualCell(id=vertexcoords, bounds=computebounds(neighborcells), vertexvalues=vertexvalues) def isdualcellinsamelevel(Dij): # Checks if all 8 cells sharing the dual cell's vertex are at the same AMR level neighborcells = getneighborcellsatvertex(Dij.id) levels = [cell.level for cell in neighborcells if cell is not None] return len(set(levels)) == 1 def initoctant(Ci, j): # Creates octant Oij with bounds derived from cell center and half-dimensions halfdims = computehalfdimensions(Ci) offset = getoctantoffset(j) return Octant(id=(Ci.id, j), bounds=computeoctantbounds(Ci.center, halfdims, offset), vertexvalues=[]) def gtimethod(Oij): # Computes vertex values using Grid Trilinear Interpolation Oij.vertexvalues = computetrilinearvertexvalues(Oij.id) def getvertexcoords(Ci, j): return tuple(Ci.center[i] + (-1 if j & (1 << i) else 1) Ci.halfsize for i in range(3)) def getneighborcellsatvertex(vertexcoords): return [findcellatoffset(vertexcoords, offset) for offset in octantoffsets()] def computebounds(neighborcells): mins = [min(c.center[i] for c in neighborcells if c) for i in range(3)] maxs = [max(c.center[i] for c in neighborcells if c) for i in range(3)] return (tuple(mins), tuple(maxs)) def computehalfdimensions(Ci): return tuple(d / 2.0 for d in Ci.dimensions) def getoctantoffset(j): return tuple(-1.0 if j & (1 << i) else 1.0 for i in range(3)) def computeoctantbounds(center, halfdims, offset): mins = tuple(center[i] + offset[i] halfdims[i] for i in range(3)) maxs = tuple(center[i] - offset[i] halfdims[i] for i in range(3)) return (mins, maxs) def computetrilinearvertexvalues(vertexcoords): # Standard trilinear interpolation from surrounding cell centers return Parameters and Edge Cases: TB-AMR vs BS-AMR: For BS-AMR (Brick-Based), cells are stored in uniform grids, making same-level checks trivial. For TB-AMR, cells are stored in an octree, and neighboring cell levels are not readily available. This requires checking if a dual cell lies in a same-level region during extraction, complicating the implementation. Duplicate Insertion: The condition j == 7 prevents inserting the same dual cell multiple times when it is shared by adjacent parent cells. In AMR, this relies on consistent octant indexing; a vertex-coordinate lookup set is used in practice to guarantee manifold correctness. ## Operating characteristics Performance: Achieves an approximate 4× speedup in extraction time compared to using octants exclusively. Complexity: Reduces the number of primitives traversed by ray tracing, improving rendering performance. Limitations: The optimization is specific to same-level regions. At level boundaries, octants must still be used with GTI reconstruction, which is more costly. ## Background This optimization was introduced by Wang et al. in the context of CPU ray tracing of Tree-Based Adaptive Mesh Refinement (TB-AMR) data. While similar optimizations were applied to BS-AMR data in previous work [WWW∗19], the TB-AMR implementation required additional complexity due to the octree data layout. The method is part of the hybrid implicit isosurface rendering pipeline integrated into OSPRay. ## Sources CPU Ray Tracing of Tree‐Based Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data, https://publications.sci.utah.edu/publications/Wan2020a/cgf.13958.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Interactive Isocontouring of High-Order Surfaces (iHOS)
head: iHOS
body:
iHOS is a GPU-based hybrid rendering method for the interactive visualization of isosurfaces defined by high-order multivariate polynomials, such as those arising from hp-adaptive finite element simulations. It solves the problem of achieving interactive frame rates for complex, high-degree implicit surfaces by dividing the workload into an object-space pre-processing phase and an image-space ray-casting phase. Unlike pure ray-tracing methods that require expensive per-pixel root finding, iHOS uses gradient-guided seed projection in object space to generate initial surface samples, which are then refined via accelerated root finding in image space. This approach allows for efficient early-z culling and avoids the overhead of inclusion arithmetic used in robust implicit renderers. The method operates in two distinct phases: Object Space (pre-processing) and Image Space (rendering). Inputs: A mesh M composed of N convex cells (e.g., hexahedra, tetrahedra). For each cell, a scalar field defined by a multivariate polynomial P(\mathbf{x}) of degree n. An isovalue 	au defining the isosurface P(\mathbf{x}) = 	au. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}) for each pixel. Outputs: A rendered image of the isosurface with depth information (though depth is not strictly updated for early-z optimization, see Pitfalls). Interval Tree (CPU): Stores the extrema (min/max) of the scalar field for each cell. Used for early cell culling to determine if a cell contains the isovalue. VBOunproj (GPU): Vertex Buffer Object storing unprojected seeds. Each seed has 4 components: (x, y, z, w), where w stores the Finite-Time Lyapunov Exponent (FTLE) value. VBOquads (GPU): Vertex Buffer Object storing the generated surface-tangent quadrilaterals (quads). BUBOs (GPU): Bindable Uniform Buffer Objects. Due to size limits (typically 64KB), a separate BUBO is created for each cell, containing read-only polynomial coefficients, gradient data, and cell boundary information. Shader Versions: Separate shader programs are maintained for each polynomial degree to allow compiler loop unrolling. The scalar field in the reference space is defined as: P(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i+j+k \le n} c{ijk} x^i y^j z^k where i,j,k \in \mathbb{N}0, n is the maximum order, c{ijk} are coefficients, and x,y,z are reference space coordinates. This phase generates an initial approximation of the isosurface. The heuristic is executed once per dataset and does not depend on the isovalue. The object-space phase (seed projection) is re-executed when the isovalue changes. 1. Seeding: Place ns seeds uniformly distributed inside each cell. 2. Gradient Integration: Integrate the gradient field 
abla P from each seed position for ni steps to guide the seeds towards the isosurface. 3. Newton-Raphson Refinement: Apply n{N1} Newton-Raphson iterations to project the integrated seeds precisely onto the isosurface P(\mathbf{x}) = 	au. 4. Heuristic (FTLE & Neighbor Exclusion): Compute the FTLE for each seed to estimate the "stretching" of the gradient flow, which correlates with the required quad size. Neighbor Exclusion: To prevent disjoint surfaces from influencing quad size, exclude neighbors if the minimum angle a{min} between the segment connecting the seed to the neighbor and the gradient exceeds a threshold (typically 0.5). Formula for a{min}: a{min} = \max{t \in [0,1]}  rac{|sn \cdot 
abla s(\mathbf{x} + t sn)|}{||sn|| \, ||
abla s(\mathbf{x} + t sn)||} where sn is the segment from \mathbf{x} to neighbor n. 5. Quad Generation: For each successfully projected seed, generate a surface-tangent, seed-centered quadrilateral (quad). The size of the quad is scaled by the FTLE value. 6. Transform Feedback: Record the generated quads into VBOquads. This phase refines the isosurface representation using the quads from Phase 1. 1. Cell Selection and Sorting: Select cells containing the isovalue (using the Interval Tree). Sort them front-to-back (fast, inexact sort) to optimize early-z culling. 2. Rasterization: Rasterize the quads in VBOquads. The vertex shader redirects vertices to rasterization. 3. Fragment Processing (Ray Casting): For each fragment generated: Use the fragment's position as an initial guess for ray casting. Perform n{N2} Newton-Raphson iterations to refine the intersection point on the isosurface. Noise Reduction: Compare the angle of the polynomial gradient vector at the fragment position before and after projection. If the angle difference exceeds a threshold, discard the fragment (assumed jump to another surface). Shading: Shade the fragment at the refined position. Crucially, do not update the depth coordinate in the depth buffer. This allows the early-z test to cull occluded fragments from subsequent cells/quad sets, significantly boosting performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ihosrender(mesh, isovalue, camera): activecells = [] for cell in mesh: if cell.minval <= isovalue <= cell.maxval: activecells.append(cell) # Phase 1: Object Space Pre-processing for cell in activecells: bindbubo(cell) nseeds = NSSMALL if cell.issmall else NSLARGE seeds = generateuniformseeds(cell, nseeds) for seed in seeds: pos = seed.pos for in range(NI): grad = gradientpoly(cell.poly, pos) pos = pos + grad stepsize seed.pos = pos for seed in seeds: pos = seed.pos for in range(NN1): val = evaluatepoly(cell.poly, pos) - isovalue if abs(val) < EPS1: break grad = gradientpoly(cell.poly, pos) pos = pos - (val / dot(grad, grad)) grad seed.pos = pos quads = [] for seed in seeds: val = evaluatepoly(cell.poly, seed.pos) - isovalue if abs(val) < EPS1: ftle = computeftle(cell.poly, seed.pos) neighbors = getneighbors(seed.pos) validneighbors = [] for n in neighbors: seg = n.pos - seed.pos minangle = 0.0 for t in [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]: g = gradientpoly(cell.poly, (seed.pos + t seg)) angle = abs(dot(seg, g)) / (length(seg) length(g)) if angle > minangle: minangle = angle if minangle < THRESHOLDANGLE: validneighbors.append(n) quad = generatesurfacetangentquad(seed.pos, ftle, validneighbors) quads.append(quad) storequads(quads) # Phase 2: Image Space Ray Casting activecells.sort(key=lambda c: distancetocamera(c.center)) for cell in activecells: bindbubo(cell) bindshadersfordegree(cell.poly.degree) fragments = rasterize(VBOquads) for frag in fragments: rayorigin = frag.position raydir = frag.raydirection pos = rayorigin oldgrad = gradientpoly(cell.poly, pos) for in range(NN2): val = evaluatepoly(cell.poly, pos) - isovalue if abs(val) < EPS2: break grad = gradientpoly(cell.poly, pos) denom = dot(grad, raydir) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: break t = val / denom newpos = pos - raydir t newgrad = gradientpoly(cell.poly, newpos) cosangle = dot(oldgrad, newgrad) / (length(oldgrad) length(newgrad)) anglediff = acos(clamp(cosangle, -1.0, 1.0)) if anglediff > THRESHOLDANGLE: break pos = newpos oldgrad = newgrad color = phongshading(pos, gradientpoly(cell.poly, pos), camera) framebuffer[frag.id] = color Isovalue: Triggers Phase 1 re-execution. ns: Number of initial seeds. Typical: 10^3 (small) or 8^3 (large). ni: Integration steps. Typical: 50. n{N1}: NR steps in Phase 1. Typical: 10. \epsilon1: NR error in Phase 1. Typical: 10^{-3}. n{N2}: NR steps in Phase 2. Typical: 3. sq: Quad size scale factor. Typical: 0.5 to 1.5. \epsilon2: NR error in Phase 2. Typical: 10^{-4}. Neighbor Exclusion Threshold: Typical: 0.5. Holes and Overdraw: Poor seed density can cause holes. The FTLE heuristic mitigates this but can be conservative. Shader Loop Unrolling: General polynomial evaluation requires loops. Solution: Maintain separate shader versions for each polynomial degree. Thread Synchronization: Dynamic iteration counts hinder GPU synchronization. Solution: Keep integration and NR iterations static. Noise from Early-Z: Not updating depth causes noise if a closer fragment projects to a far surface. Mitigated by gradient angle comparison. FTLE Conservatism: FTLE considers distances between seeds on disjoint surfaces, leading to overly large quads. Mitigated by neighbor exclusion heuristic. A two-step process to find isosurface points for polynomial data. First, uniformly distributed seeds are guided along the gradient field via integration to get closer to the isosurface. Second, Directional Newton-Raphson (NR) is applied to refine the projection onto the isosurface. Time Complexity: Pre-processing is O(1) with respect to isovalue changes (done once per dataset for the heuristic, re-run for seed projection). Rendering cost does not grow linearly with the number of cells due to early-z culling and front-to-back ordering. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for seeds, quads, and per-cell BUBOs. BUBO size is limited (typically 64KB), requiring one per cell. Performance: Small Dataset (119 cells, deg 5-6): 45 fps (sq=0.75), 39 fps (sq=1.0), 29 fps (sq=1.25) at 1024x1024. Large Dataset (34,535 cells, deg 3): 21 fps (sq=0.5), 14 fps (sq=0.75), 12.5 fps (sq=1.0) at 1024x1024. Culling Efficiency: Processes ~7-9% of total cells. Recomputation Time: < 2 seconds for isovalue change; < 1 second for seed projection in small datasets. Strengths: Interactive frame rates for high-order data; efficient GPU mapping; no need for inter-element connectivity; handles unstructured meshes. Limitations: Approximate method (no error bounds like inclusion arithmetic); potential for noise due to early-z optimization; conservative quad sizing without heuristic. When to use: Interactive exploration of high-order finite element data where speed is prioritized over rigorous error bounds. When not to use: When guaranteed error bounds are required, or for very low-degree polynomials where simpler methods may suffice. iHOS was introduced by C. Pagot, J. Vollrath, F. Sadlo, D. Weiskopf, T. Ertl, and J.L.D. Comba. It addresses the limitations of existing isocontouring techniques for hp-adaptive finite element data, which typically do not support interactive exploration. The method builds on the principles of image-order rendering and isosurface detection, specifically leveraging GPU parallelism and hybrid object/image-space processing. It is compared against methods like Knoll et al., which use inclusion arithmetic for robustness but at the cost of performance. Interactive Isocontouring of High-Order Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.4230/dfu.vol2.sciviz.2011.276, fetched 2026-10-29 (book)
