Intersect scan planes (z-extension of scan lines) with volume element # Sources do not specify the exact intersection algorithm polygons = [] # 2. Break intersection polygons into spans # Standard polygon rasterization step spans = [] # 3. Draw back and front faces in order for face in [element.backface, element.frontface]: # Interpolate scalar value to alpha component for x, y, alpha in rasterizeface(face, width, height): # Alpha test rejects fragments where alpha < isovalue if alpha >= isovalue: # 4. XOR operation on stencil buffer to combine back/front results stencilbuffer[y][x] ^= 1 # 5. Integrate pixels of each span front-to-back to generate opacity for span in spans: spanopacity = 0.0 for x, y, fragopacity in span.pixels: if stencilbuffer[y][x] == 1: spanopacity += fragopacity outputimage[span.y][span.x] = spanopacity return outputimage An alternate solution that decomposes tetrahedra into smaller tetrahedra, reducing the number of faces rendered. It uses 2D texturing hardware with a checkerboard texture to handle degenerate cases and simplify intersection computation. Time Complexity: The algorithm runs in two passes (the first step sets the stencil buffer) and on average renders 5 to 7 triangles per volume element. Memory Complexity: Requires a stencil buffer and alpha channel for each fragment. Strengths: Efficient use of early fixed-function graphics hardware; avoids complex per-pixel gradient evaluation by computing lighting per-vertex or via pre-computed normal maps. Limitations: Dependent on specific hardware features; limited flexibility compared to shader-based methods; potential precision issues with alpha testing. When to Use: Early hardware environments where programmable shaders are unavailable. When Not to Use: Modern hardware with programmable pipelines; scenes requiring high precision or complex lighting. The method was introduced by Upson and Keller in 1988. It was one of the early attempts to leverage graphics hardware for volume rendering, specifically targeting the extraction of isosurfaces using rasterization primitives. A revised version was discussed in [58], and the method is frequently cited in surveys of GPU-based volume rendering of unstructured grids. name: OpenGL Point Rendering for Isosurfaces
head: Hardware accelerated point rendering
body: This method renders isosurfaces by projecting volume elements as point primitives (GLPOINTS) onto the screen, where points are rasterized as discs. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its use of single-vertex primitives, which eliminates backface culling and causes overlap, making it prone to fill-rate limitations but offering lower geometry pipeline requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, an isovalue threshold, and camera parameters (projection matrix, viewport). Output: A 2D image of the isosurface. Data Structures: Dirty Cell List: A list of cells marked for regeneration. The number of cells marked dirty per frame is selected so that primitives are recomputed for roughly four cells on average per frame. Point Primitives: Generated from the active cells. Each point represents a location on the isosurface. Steps: 1. Identify Active Cells: Determine which volume cells intersect the isosurface. 2. Generate Points: For each active cell, compute the point position on the isosurface. If a cell is marked "dirty" (based on the regeneration rate), regenerate its primitive. 3. Setup Distance Attenuation: Configure OpenGL to scale point size based on distance to maintain consistent visual coverage. 4. Render: Issue glDrawArrays(GLPOINTS,...) to render the points as discs. Formulas and Parameters: To set up perspective scaling of points as discs, distance attenuation is configured using the following parameters derived from the projection matrix and viewport: H = \text{viewport\width} h = \frac{2.0}{\text{projection\matrix}[0]} D0 = \sqrt{2.0} \cdot \frac{H}{h} k = \frac{1.0}{1.0 + 2 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1}{\text{projection\matrix}[0]}}} \text{atten} = \left[ 0, 0, \sqrt{\frac{1}{D0}} \cdot k \right] The attenuation vector is applied via glPointParameterfvEXT(GLDISTANCEATTENUATIONEXT, atten) and point size is set to 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def setuppointattenuation(projectionmatrix, viewportwidth): m00 = projectionmatrix[0] h = 2.0 / m00 H = viewportwidth D0 = math.sqrt(2.0) (H / h) k = 1.0 / (1.0 + 2.0 math.sqrt(1.0 / m00)) attenc = math.sqrt(1.0 / D0) k # glPointParameterfvEXT(GLDISTANCEATTENUATIONEXT, [0, 0, attenc]) # glPointSize(1.0) # glEnable(GLPOINTSMOOTH) def generatepointfromcell(cell): # Point position computation on the isosurface is implementation-specific return cell.center def renderisosurface(volume, isovalue, dirtycells): cellstorender = [] for cell in volume.cells: if cell.isactive(isovalue): if cell in dirtycells: point = generatepointfromcell(cell) cellstorender.append(point) else: cellstorender.append(cell.primitive) setuppointattenuation(volume.projectionmatrix, volume.viewportwidth) # glDrawArrays(GLPOINTS, 0, len(cellstorender)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Backface Culling: Not possible for points because a point is a single vertex with no orientation, leading to more filling than polygons. Dilation Artefact: Points are rendered as discs even if they lie on the silhouette, causing the surface to appear dilated. This is visible in areas of high curvature. Fill-Rate Limitation: The method is prone to being fill-rate limited because points overlap to cover the surface. Draws points as ellipses whose main axes depend on the normal, alleviating dilation artefacts but lacking hardware acceleration. Generates triangle meshes. Offers superior visual quality when zooming in or using small datasets, but has higher geometry generation costs. Time and Memory Complexity: Geometry generation is faster than Marching Cubes for any volume size. Performance advantage increases with the size and complexity of the volumes. Measured Performance: Test hardware: Not explicitly named, though recent hardware like Radeon 9700 and NV30 are mentioned for potential future features. Scene: Cube (32x32x32). Viewport 800x800: Points render at 76 fps, triangles at 146 fps. Viewport 100x100: Points render at 773 fps, triangles at 161 fps. Performance threshold: On the test hardware, OpenGL point rendering overtakes triangle strips at around 500k polygons. Scaling: The method becomes fill-rate limited when few, large primitives are rendered. Performance increases with smaller viewports because the total number of pixels to fill decreases, reducing fill-rate pressure. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Lower bandwidth and geometry pipeline requirements; faster primitive generation; similar quality to MC for large volumes. Limitations: Inferior visual quality when zooming in or using small datasets; dilation artefacts; fill-rate limited. When to Use: Large volumes where geometry generation cost is prohibitive. When performance is critical and fill rate is not the bottleneck. When Not to Use: Small datasets or when zooming in, where visual quality of MC is superior. Scenes with high curvature where dilation artefacts are objectionable. This method was presented in the paper "Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering of Isosurfaces". It compares OpenGL point rendering to software point rendering and triangle rendering using Marching Cubes. The authors note that recent hardware (Radeon 9700, NV30) might enable hardware-based point rendering techniques similar to software methods, such as computing reciprocal values or using point sprites to render ellipses. name: Parallax Occlusion Mapping
head: Voxel Displacement Renderer
body: Parallax Occlusion Mapping (POM) is a technique used to reveal Signed Distance Field (SDF) iso-surfaces within rasterized brick bounding boxes, providing depth detail without the computational cost of full raymarching. In the context of the Voxel Displacement Renderer, it is a real-time rendering method that applies voxel-scale surface details to conventional low-poly triangle meshes using displacement maps, producing a retro 3D aesthetic without converting the entire scene into a voxel grid. Unlike conventional displacement mapping, which struggles with hard edges and requires high polygon counts, this method produces voxel-like results even along sharp edges of the original mesh. It differs from standard POM by physically changing the silhouette and geometry, thereby avoiding the illusion breakdown at object edges that plagues texture-based parallax techniques. The method operates in two distinct phases: a CPU-based pre-processing stage and a GPU-based rendering stage. Inputs: Conventional low-poly triangle meshes with shading normals. Albedo maps and displacement maps (height fields). SDF brick data. Outputs: Rasterized geometry with voxel-scale displacement. Anti-aliased SDF iso-surface representation. 1. Displacement Map: A texture where rescaled height values represent the number of voxels inward or outward to move the surface. 2. Normal Map: Generated from the exact (non-quantized) height values of the displacement map to allow features less than a voxel tall to affect lighting. 3. Geometry Data: Pre-processed mesh data loaded onto the GPU, including information about sharp edges and smooth surfaces derived from shading normals. 4. Bounding Boxes: For SDF bricks, bounding boxes are adjusted to maintain a constant screen-space size. 1. Pre-processing (CPU): Convert triangle meshes and displacement map information into geometry data for the GPU. This conversion process can be baked to disk. Generate normal maps from the displacement textures. This generation step is computationally slow and should be baked. Identify sharp edges and smooth regions using the input mesh's shading normals. 2. Rendering (GPU): Draw the voxel-displacement geometry using the pre-processed mesh and texture state. For SDF bricks, rasterize the bounding boxes of the bricks. Displace vertices to the nearest whole number of voxels based on the displacement map. Use the pre-computed normal maps for shading. The renderer performs extra work for sharp edges to ensure correct lighting transitions. If used with SDF bricks, perform parallax occlusion mapping after rasterization to reveal the iso-surface within each brick. The displacement magnitude d in voxels is calculated from the exact height h and a scale factor s: d = \text{round}(h \cdot s) The normal map \mathbf{n} is computed directly from the exact height field without quantization: \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\nabla h) where \nabla h represents the spatial gradient of the height values. Bounding Box Dimensions: Adjusted to maintain a constant screen-space size to ensure appropriate filtering of distance field data for anti-aliasing. Displacement Units: The rescaled height values in the displacement map define the magnitude of displacement in voxel units. Mesh Normals: Input meshes must include shading normals to distinguish between smoothly curving surfaces and sharp edges. Sharp Edges: The renderer must handle sharp edges differently from smooth surfaces to maintain visual fidelity. Precision: While geometry is quantized to whole voxels, lighting relies on exact height values, requiring high-precision normal map generation. Performance: Normal map generation is computationally expensive and must be pre-computed. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessmesh(mesh, displacementmap): """CPU pre-processing phase.""" normalmap = computegradientnormals(displacementmap) sharpedges = detectsharpedges(mesh.shadingnormals) return { 'vertices': mesh.vertices, 'indices': mesh.indices, 'normalmap': normalmap, 'sharpedges': sharpedges, 'scale': 1.0 } def computegradientnormals(heightfield): """ Standard gradient computation for normal maps.""" normals = [] for y in range(len(heightfield)): row = [] for x in range(len(heightfield[0])): dx = heightfield[y][x+1] - heightfield[y][x-1] if x+1 < len(heightfield[0]) and x-1 >= 0 else 0.0 dy = heightfield[y+1][x] - heightfield[y-1][x] if y+1 < len(heightfield) and y-1 >= 0 else 0.0 row.append(normalize((-dx, -dy, 2.0))) normals.append(row) return normals def normalize(v): """ Standard vector normalization.""" l = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def detectsharpedges(normals, threshold=0.9): """ Standard sharp edge detection.""" return {i for i in range(len(normals)-1) if dot(normals[i], normals[i+1]) < threshold} def dot(a, b): """ Standard dot product.""" return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def render(geometrydata, albedomap, camera): """GPU rendering phase.""" pixels = rasterize(geometrydata['vertices'], geometrydata['indices']) for pixel in pixels: height = sampletexture(geometrydata['displacementmap'], pixel.uv) voxeldisp = round(height geometrydata['scale']) displacedpos = pixel.position + voxeldisp pixel.normal normal = sampletexture(geometrydata['normalmap'], pixel.uv) if pixel.index in geometrydata['sharpedges']: normal = correctsharpnormal(normal, geometrydata) color = shade(displacedpos, normal, albedomap, camera) framebuffer[pixel.x][pixel.y] = color def rasterize(vertices, indices): """ Standard rasterization. Sources do not specify implementation details.""" return [] def sampletexture(tex, uv): """ Standard bilinear sampling. Sources do not specify implementation details.""" return 0.0 def correctsharpnormal(n, data): """ Standard sharp edge normal correction. Sources do not specify implementation details.""" return n def shade(pos, n, albedo, cam): """ Standard lighting model. Sources do not specify implementation details.""" return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) Uses POM to reveal SDF iso-surfaces within rasterized bricks, avoiding raymarching. Applies voxel-scale details to low-poly meshes, handling sharp edges better than conventional displacement mapping. Performance: On a Radeon RX 5700 XT, the demo renders at 1440p with frame times of 4 to 9 ms (250 to 110 FPS). On a Steam Deck OLED at 800p, it stays above 60 FPS, with many areas locked at 90 FPS. Pre-processing Time: Converting the entire demo scene on a single thread takes half a second. Strengths: Produces voxel-like results with sharp edges; avoids illusion breakdown at object edges; real-time performance on modern hardware. Limitations: Requires pre-processing (baking) of normal maps and geometry; displacement is quantized to whole voxels for geometry, though lighting uses exact heights. When to Use: When a retro 3D voxel aesthetic is desired from low-poly assets, or when SDF bricks need efficient depth rendering without raymarching. When Not to Use: When dynamic, per-frame normal map generation is required, or when sub-voxel geometric displacement is needed (only lighting benefits from sub-voxel precision). The technique was used in the game Dreams (Evans, 2015) for rendering SDF bricks. A standalone implementation, the Voxel Displacement Renderer, was developed by Daniel Schroeder and documented in May 2024. It is implemented as a C++/Vulkan project, with assets authored as albedo and displacement maps, and meshes exported as OBJ files from Blender. name: Differentiable Bitmap Splatting
head: DiffBMP, DiffBMP Renderer, Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives
body:
Differentiable Bitmap Splatting (DiffBMP) is a scalable rendering engine that optimizes the position, rotation, scale, color, and opacity of thousands of bitmap primitives by computing exact gradients via custom CUDA kernels. It distinguishes itself from vector-based differentiable renderers (e.g., DiffVG) by supporting raster image primitives and from prior bitmap methods by enabling full differentiability and parallel optimization of diverse, non-repetitive patterns. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N bitmap primitives. Each primitive i has parameters: position (xi, yi), scale si, rotation 	hetai, opacity logit 
ui, and RGB color logit \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Each primitive has an associated bitmap texture of size Hi 	imes Wi. Outputs: A rendered image I(x,y) and gradients with respect to all primitive parameters. Data Structures Primitive Parameters: Stored in arrays for xi, yi, si, 	hetai, 
ui, \mathbf{c}i. Textures: Bitmap images sampled via bilinear interpolation. Gradients & Temporaries: Accumulated in packed half2 buffers (two-channel FP16) to support atomic operations and reduce bandwidth/VRAM usage. Algorithm Steps 1. Tile Partitioning (CPU): Partition the image plane into T 	imes T tiles (default T=32). Assign each primitive to every tile whose bounding box on the image plane overlaps the tile region with a small padding margin. 2. Kernel Launch (GPU): Launch one CUDA thread block per tile, with T 	imes T threads, achieving pixel-level parallelism. 3. Coordinate Transformation: For each pixel (x,y) and primitive i, compute normalized primitive coordinates (u,v):  egin {bmatrix} u \ v \end {bmatrix} =  egin {bmatrix} \cos 	heta i & \sin 	heta i \ -\sin 	heta i & \cos 	heta i \end {bmatrix}  egin {bmatrix} (x-xi)/si \ (y-yi)/si \end {bmatrix} \in [-1,1]^2 4. Bitmap Sampling: Map (u,v) to discrete bitmap coordinates (U,V):  egin {bmatrix} U \ V \end {bmatrix} =  egin {bmatrix} (u\!+\!1)/2 \cdot (Wi\!-\!1) \ (v\!+\!1)/2 \cdot (Hi\!-\!1) \end {bmatrix} \in [0, Wi\!-\!1] 	imes [0, Hi\!-\!1] Since U and V are almost surely non-integer, compute the primitive contribution Mi(x,y) via bilinear interpolation using the four nearest integer grid points \{\lfloor U floor, \lfloor U floor+1\} 	imes \{\lfloor V floor, \lfloor V floor+1\}. 5. Alpha Compositing: Compute the alpha value for primitive i: \alpha i(x,y) = \alpha {\max } \cdot \sigma (
u i) \cdot Mi(x,y) where \sigma is the sigmoid function and \alpha{\max} \in (0, 1] is a hyperparameter. 6. Final Rendering: Compute transmittance Tk(x,y) and final color I(x,y) using Porter-Duff over compositing: Tk(x,y) = \prod {j=0}^{k-1}(1 - \alpha j(x,y)) I(x,y) = \sum {k=0}^{N-1} Tk(x,y) \alpha k(x,y) \sigma (\mathbf{c}k) \in [0,1]^3 Primitives are composited in front-to-back order. 7. Backward Pass: Accumulate per-parameter gradients per pixel directly into packed half2 buffers via half2 atomicAdd over two-channel gradient groups, followed by a lightweight post pass that unpacks to legacy FP16 arrays. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def clamp(v, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, v)) def diffbmpforward(tileprimitives, tilepixels, textures, alphamax): # tileprimitives: list of primitives overlapping this tile # tilepixels: list of (x, y) coordinates in this tile # textures: dict mapping primitiveid to bitmap array # alphamax: scalar hyperparameter in (0, 1] for (x, y) in tilepixels: T = 1.0 I = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for prim in tileprimitives: i = prim.id # 1. Coordinate Transformation dx = (x - prim.x) / prim.s dy = (y - prim.y) / prim.s cost = math.cos(prim.theta) sint = math.sin(prim.theta) u = cost dx + sint dy v = -sint dx + cost dy # 2. Bitmap Sampling (Bilinear Interpolation) U = (u + 1.0) / 2.0 (prim.W - 1.0) V = (v + 1.0) / 2.0 (prim.H - 1.0) u0, v0 = math.floor(U), math.floor(V) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 u0 = clamp(u0, 0, prim.W - 1) u1 = clamp(u1, 0, prim.W - 1) v0 = clamp(v0, 0, prim.H - 1) v1 = clamp(v1, 0, prim.H - 1) val00 = textures[i][v0, u0] val10 = textures[i][v0, u1] val01 = textures[i][v1, u0] val11 = textures[i][v1, u1] wu = U - u0 wv = V - v0 valtop = lerp(val00, val10, wu) valbot = lerp(val01, val11, wu) Mi = lerp(valtop, valbot, wv) # 3. Alpha Compositing alphai = alphamax sigmoid(prim.nu) Mi colori = sigmoid(prim.c) # 4. Porter-Duff Over I = (I[0] + T alphai colori[0], I[1] + T alphai colori[1], I[2] + T alphai colori[2]) T = T (1.0 - alphai) yield (x, y, I) def diffbmpbackward(tileprimitives, tilepixels, textures, alphamax, gradbuffers): # Sources do not provide the explicit backward pass gradient formulas; # they are accumulated per pixel directly into packed half2 buffers # via half2 atomicAdd over two-channel gradient groups, followed by # a lightweight post pass that unpacks to legacy FP16 arrays. pass Parameters T: Tile size for partitioning the image plane on the CPU. Default value is 32. \alpha{\max}: Maximum alpha scaling factor. Hyperparameter in (0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-integer Coordinates: U and V are almost surely non-integer, requiring bilinear interpolation for differentiable sampling. Precision: Texture fetches and per-pixel temporaries use FP16 (packed as half2 where profitable). Accumulation of displayed color/transmittance is evaluated in FP16 arithmetic. Export Limitations: Atomic operations used in optimization kernels are unsuitable for generating layered PSD files. A dedicated export kernel using primitive-level parallelism is required for final high-resolution, editable layer export. Time Complexity: The method is highly parallelized, with one CUDA thread block per tile. Optimization of thousands of primitives can be completed in under 1 minute on a consumer GPU. Memory Complexity: Uses FP16 arithmetic tailored to packed data paths, reducing bandwidth and VRAM usage. Strengths: Scalable to thousands of primitives; supports diverse bitmap patterns (not just repetitive/opaque); enables end-to-end differentiable optimization of spatial and color parameters. Limitations: Requires custom CUDA implementation for efficiency; prior bitmap methods lacked specialized parallelism. Atomic operations prevent direct layered export during optimization. When to Use: When optimizing raster image compositions (e.g., painterly effects, assemblage) where vector graphics are insufficient. When Not to Use: When layered, editable output (PSD/SVG) is needed directly from the optimization pass without a separate export kernel. DiffBMP was introduced to address the limitation that traditional differentiable renderers are constrained to vector graphics, despite most images being bitmaps. It builds on Spatial Transformer Networks [17] and prior bitmap pattern methods [43], which were limited to repetitive, opaque patterns and lacked specialized parallelism. The method was developed to integrate into creative workflows, supporting export to native layered file formats. name: Cell Rasterisation with Tesselation Shader
head: Billboard Splatting with Tesselation, Clustered Grid Cell Rasterisation
body: Cell Rasterisation with Tesselation Shader is an image-order rendering technique for isosurfaces that replaces traditional vertex shaders with tessellation shaders to efficiently rasterize clusters of grid cells as point sprites. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering large volumes by grouping active cells into clusters, expanding them into individual points in the tessellation stage, and performing ray-box intersection and volume sampling in the fragment shader. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Clustered Grid Cell (CGC) data structure containing metacells and grid cells. Each cluster is represented as a single GLPATCHES primitive. The volume scalar field data is stored in GPU memory. Output: A color buffer with the rendered isosurface and a G-buffer containing geometric attributes (normals, positions) for deferred shading. Data Structures: Cluster Patch: A single GLPATCHES primitive per cluster. The tessellation shader expands this into points for each cell in the cluster. Metacell/Cell Metadata: Grid position: 16 bits per component (x, y, z). This limits the maximum representable grid size to 128K \times 128K \times 128K voxels. Corner values: Two RGBA values per cell are stored to allow interpolation of scalar values in the fragment shader. Cluster Bound: The last metacell of each cluster stores the cluster bounding box instead of cell metadata. Visibility Buffer: An RG32UI texture storing a bit per cluster to indicate visibility status across frames. Algorithm Steps: 1. Tessellation (Cluster Expansion): The tessellation shader receives one GLPATCHES primitive per cluster. It iterates through the cells defined in the cluster's metadata. For each active cell, it generates a point primitive. Cell Normal Computation: The tessellation shader computes a normal vector for the cell using the stored corner scalar values. This normal is used for back-face culling. Culling: If the cell is back-facing relative to the camera, it is discarded. 2. Rasterization (Billboard Splatting): The generated points are rasterized as billboards (point sprites). The size of the billboard corresponds to the cell's spatial extent. Reduced Rate Rendering: Clusters that were culled in the previous frame are rendered at a reduced rate (1/8) with at most one point per metacell per frame until they become visible again. 3. Fragment Shader (Ray-Box Intersection): For each rasterized fragment of the billboard: Ray Definition: Define the view ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} originating from the camera. Ray-Box Intersection: Perform a ray-box intersection test between the view ray and the cell's bounding box. The implementation uses the efficient slab test described by Majercik et al.. If no intersection occurs, the fragment is discarded. Intersection Point: Calculate the entry and exit points of the ray within the cell's bounding box. 4. Volume Sampling and Isosurface Detection: Interpolation: Sample the scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) along the ray segment inside the cell. The scalar values are obtained by manually performing tri-linear interpolation using the stored corner values in the fragment shader. Sample Count: The method uses a fixed number of samples per ray. The sources specify that 3 samples per ray are used, which was found sufficient for accurate intersection detection. Intersection Check: Detect the isosurface intersection where f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau (threshold). This is typically identified by a sign change or threshold crossing between consecutive samples. 5. Normal Computation: Compute the gradient \nabla f at the intersection point using the tri-linearly interpolated scalar values. This gradient serves as the surface normal for shading. 6. G-Buffer Writing: Rasterize the cell's geometric attributes (position, normal) to a Geometry Buffer (G-buffer). 7. Deferred Shading: In a separate pass, compute normalized Blinn-Phong shading using the data from the G-buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lerp(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def slabtest(rayorigin, raydir, boxmin, boxmax): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < boxmin[i] or rayorigin[i] > boxmax[i]: return False, 0.0, 0.0 else: t1 = (boxmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (boxmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax or tmax < 0: return False, 0.0, 0.0 return True, tmin, tmax def trilinearinterpolate(p, corners): x, y, z = p c000, c100, c010, c110, c001, c101, c011, c111 = corners c00 = lerp(c000, c100, x) c10 = lerp(c010, c110, x) c01 = lerp(c001, c101, x) c11 = lerp(c011, c111, x) c0 = lerp(c00, c10, y) c1 = lerp(c01, c11, y) return lerp(c0, c1, z) def computegradientatpoint(p, corners): eps = 1e-3 fx = (trilinearinterpolate((p[0]+eps, p[1], p[2]), corners) - trilinearinterpolate((p[0]-eps, p[1], p[2]), corners)) / (2 eps) fy = (trilinearinterpolate((p[0], p[1]+eps, p[2]), corners) - trilinearinterpolate((p[0], p[1]-eps, p[2]), corners)) / (2 eps) fz = (trilinearinterpolate((p[0], p[1], p[2]+eps), corners) - trilinearinterpolate((p[0], p[1], p[2]-eps), corners)) / (2 eps) return normalize(vec3(fx, fy, fz)) def computecellnormalfromcorners(corners): center = vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) return computegradientatpoint(center, corners) def tessellationshader(clusterpatch): for cell in clusterpatch.cells: normal = computecellnormalfromcorners(cell.corners) if dot(normal, cameraviewdirection) > 0: continue emitpoint(cell.position, cell.size, normal) def fragmentshader(pointsprite): rayorigin = cameraorigin raydir = normalize(cameraviewdirection) hit, tentry, texit = slabtest(rayorigin, raydir, pointsprite.bboxmin, pointsprite.bboxmax) if not hit: return numsamples = 3 samples = [] for i in range(numsamples): t = lerp(tentry, texit, i / (numsamples - 1)) p = (rayorigin[0] + t raydir[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydir[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydir[2]) scalar = trilinearinterpolate(p, pointsprite.corners) samples.append((p, scalar)) intersectionfound = False intersectionpoint = None intersectionnormal = None threshold = 0.0 for i in range(len(samples) - 1): p1, s1 = samples[i] p2, s2 = samples[i+1] if (s1 - threshold) (s2 - threshold) < 0: trefine = (threshold - s1) / (s2 - s1) intersectionpoint = (lerp(p1[0], p2[0], trefine), lerp(p1[1], p2[1], trefine), lerp(p1[2], p2[2], trefine)) intersectionnormal = computegradientatpoint(intersectionpoint, pointsprite.corners) intersectionfound = True break if not intersectionfound: return # Write position and normal to G-buffer Parameters: Samples per ray: 3. Grid Position Storage: 16 bits per component. Culling Rate: 1/8 for previously culled clusters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The 16-bit storage for grid positions limits the maximum grid resolution to 128K^3. Culled Clusters: To avoid flickering, culled clusters are rendered at a reduced rate rather than being completely skipped. Sample Sufficiency: Only 3 samples are used; this may lead to aliasing or missed intersections in highly detailed regions, though the source claims it is sufficient for their use case. A variant of the method that uses a vertex shader instead of a tessellation shader to render active grid cells as GLPOINTS primitives. It performs ray-box intersection and interpolates samples along the ray using stored corner values (two RGBA values per cell) to find intersections and compute normals. It uses 3 samples per ray. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of active cells and clusters. The tessellation shader expands clusters, and the fragment shader performs a fixed number of samples (3) per ray. The use of a visibility buffer reduces redundant rasterization of occluded clusters. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the CGC data structure, including 16-bit grid positions and corner values for each cell. Performance: Fast due to hardware rasterization of point sprites and deferred shading. Strengths: High performance for large volumes; leverages GPU hardware rasterization; deferred shading allows for efficient lighting calculations. Limitations: Limited to 16-bit grid positions; fixed sample count may affect accuracy; requires a visibility buffer for optimal performance. When to use: Real-time isosurface rendering of large volumes where performance is critical and moderate accuracy is acceptable. When not to use: When high precision is required (e.g., scientific visualization requiring sub-voxel accuracy) or when grid sizes exceed 128K^3. Cell Rasterisation was proposed by Liu et al. [13] as a fast method for rasterizing active grid cells of a volume. The technique was originally implemented using vertex shaders for billboard splatting. The variant using tessellation shaders and the Clustered Grid Cell (CGC) data structure was developed to improve performance by reducing the number of draw calls and leveraging the tessellation pipeline for cluster expansion. The method is part of the broader family of image-order rendering techniques for isosurfaces. name: Ray Traversal and Coherency
body: This family accelerates isosurface extraction by optimizing the order and grouping of ray-volume interactions to minimize redundant traversal and intersection tests. It differs from naive uniform marching by using hierarchical acceleration structures (octrees, tiled grids) and spatial coherence (ray packets) to skip empty space and process multiple rays simultaneously. The family shares the core mechanism of Isosurface and first-hit ray casting: constructing a ray per pixel and finding the first point where f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau or a sign change occurs. Upon detection, the intersection is refined (e.g., linear interpolation) and shaded using \nabla f. The key distinction is the traversal strategy: instead of marching voxel-by-voxel, rays are accelerated by hierarchical culling using min-max bounds in octrees or tiled grids to skip sub-volumes where \tau \notin [\min, \max], coherence exploitation by grouping rays into packets to traverse the acceleration structure together, and list-based restriction by pre-computing a short, front-to-back list of candidate blocks or pixels for each ray. A technique using a min-max octree of macro-cells (n^3 cells, n \in [3,10]) to accelerate iso-surface extraction. It sets itself apart by projecting trimmed macro-cells to the screen and casting local rays only at uncolored pixels, avoiding empty space traversal. Choose it when interactive threshold adjustment is needed without dedicated acceleration hardware, and when macro-cell culling effectively skips empty space. A two-phase method combining object-order traversal with restricted ray casting on multi-core processors. It sets itself apart by decoupling candidate block identification from ray casting execution, using dynamic task allocation to solve load-balancing and memory hierarchy overhead problems. Choose it when rendering on multi-core CPUs and static screen partitioning causes uneven workloads. A two-phase algorithm for rendering isosurfaces on multi-core processors using a BONO tree for hierarchical culling and list-based restriction. It sets itself apart by maintaining a short, front-to-back ordered list of candidate blocks per pixel, achieving coherence and efficiency without SIMD instruction-level parallelism dependencies. Choose it when high-resolution rendering is needed on multi-core CPUs without relying on dedicated hardware or surface fitting techniques. A method for interactive isosurface extraction from large volumetric datasets stored in octrees. It sets itself apart by grouping neighboring rays into 2x2 packets to exploit spatial coherence during traversal and intersection, dynamically switching to coarser levels of detail (LOD). Choose it when rendering large volumes on commodity CPUs where spatial coherence can be maintained via ray packets and multiresolution structures. A ray traversal method that extracts iso-surfaces by recording the first scalar intensity encountered along a viewing ray. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or Accumulate compositing by its immediate termination upon the first hit. Choose it when isolating high-density or specific threshold structures without contribution from deeper volumes is required. The "First Depth" or "First Intensity" traversal strategy was introduced by Tuy and Tuy in 1984 to extract isosurfaces. This approach contrasts with accumulation-based methods (like Levoy’s 1988 compositing) by stopping at the first surface hit. Modern implementations leverage octrees and ray coherence to make this interactive on large datasets. name: Cell-Based First-Hit Ray Casting
body: Cell-based first-hit ray casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates iso-surface extraction by dividing the volume into cubic sub-volumes called macro-cells. It solves the performance bottleneck of conventional ray casting by avoiding empty space traversal and reducing the average ray path length to only a few steps per pixel. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a min-max octree to cull macro-cells and projecting only those containing iso-surface portions to the screen, where local rays are cast. Unlike Hybrid Strategy for Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing or Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing, it does not rely on dedicated acceleration hardware or surface fitting techniques that lack interactive threshold adjustment. Inputs: Volume data V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. One or more iso-value thresholds \tau. Camera parameters (eye position, view direction, projection matrix). Macro-cell dimension parameter n (typically 4–10). Outputs: Color image buffer C of resolution W \times H. A per-pixel hit flag to prevent re-rendering pixels that have already found an intersection. Data Structures: 1. Min-Max Octree: Each node stores minval and maxval representing the minimum and maximum data values in the sub-volume it covers. Leaf nodes represent macro-cells. A macro-cell consists of n^3 data cells (defined by (n+1)^3 voxel grid points). 2. Ray History Buffer: Stores cells encountered along the last ray and a flag indicating if an iso-surface portion is contained there. This exploits inter-ray coherency to skip intersection tests for rays visiting the same cells. 3. Pixel Hit Flags: Boolean array of size W \times H. If the flag for a pixel is true, no more local rays are cast at this pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Build Min-Max Octree: Recursively subdivide the volume. For each node, compute minval and maxval of the contained data. Leaf nodes correspond to macro-cells of size n \times n \times n cells. 2. Traverse Octree in Viewing Order: Start at the root. For a current node, check if any threshold \tau satisfies: \text{min\val} \le \tau \le \text{max\val}. If the condition fails, cull the entire subtree. If the condition passes, sort the 8 child nodes based on the viewing vector to ensure correct front-to-back processing order. This is done using a representative ray direction that intersects all sub-volumes. Recursively process children. 3. Process Leaf Nodes (Macro-Cells): When a leaf node (macro-cell) is reached, it contains potential iso-surface portions. Trimming: Trim the macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing the portions of the iso-surfaces. Projection: Project the trimmed macro-cell onto the screen plane. Rasterization: Rasterize the projection to identify all pixels (x, y) covered by the macro-cell. 4. Cast Local Rays: For each covered pixel (x, y): If the pixel hit flag is true, skip this pixel. Construct a local ray originating from the camera eye, passing through (x, y), and clipped to the entry and exit points of the macro-cell. Early Scanline Termination (Optional Optimization): If the pixel is likely to not find an intersection, skip the ray cast to save time. Voxel Traversal: Use a fast voxel traversal algorithm (e.g., Amanatides and Woo) to iterate through cells pierced by the local ray within the macro-cell. Boundary Check: For each cell, determine if it is a "boundary cell" (contains data values both above and below \tau). Intersection Test: If a boundary cell is found, perform a ray-surface intersection test. Fast Intersection Method: Divide the ray segment through the cell into two equal parts. Evaluate density at endpoints. If signs differ, linearly interpolate the intersection point. Exact Intersection Method (Alternative): Invert trilinear interpolation to find exact intersection points. Shading: If an intersection is found: Calculate the gradient \nabla f at the intersection point using trilinear interpolation of the gradient components. Compute color using shading model (e.g., Phong). Assign color to C[y][x]. Set the pixel hit flag to true. Coherency Check: Use the Ray History Buffer to skip intersection tests if the current ray visits the same cells as the previous ray and the buffer indicates no surface was found. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cellbasedfirsthitraycasting(volume, thresholds, camera, n, width, height): # 1. Build Min-Max Octree (standard recursive subdivision) octree = buildoctree(volume, n) # 2. Initialize Output Structures colorbuffer = [[None] width for in range(height)] hitflags = [[False] width for in range(height)] rayhistorybuffer = {} # Maps cellid -> hassurface (bool) # 3. Traverse Octree traversenode(octree, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height) return colorbuffer def buildoctree(volume, n): # Standard recursive subdivision into cubic blocks # Returns tree nodes with.minval,.maxval,.children,.isleaf,.bounds pass # Implementation details omitted as standard def traversenode(node, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height): # Culling: Check if any threshold is within node's min/max range cull = True for tau in thresholds: if node.minval <= tau <= node.maxval: cull = False break if cull: return # If leaf node (macro-cell) if node.isleaf: processmacrocell(node, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height) return # Internal node: Sort children by viewing order # Use representative ray direction to determine order children = sorted(node.children, key=lambda child: dotproduct(vectorsub(child.center, camera.eye), camera.direction)) for child in children: traversenode(child, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height) def processmacrocell(node, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height): # 1. Trim macro-cell to smallest cuboid containing iso-surfaces trimmedcuboid = computetrimmedcuboid(node.bounds, thresholds) # 2. Project trimmed cuboid to screen screenrect = projectcuboidtoscreen(trimmedcuboid, camera) # 3. Rasterize and cast local rays for y in range(screenrect.ymin, screenrect.ymax): for x in range(screenrect.xmin, screenrect.xmax): # Skip if pixel already hit if hitflags[y][x]: continue # Construct local ray clipped to macro-cell ray = createlocalray(camera, x, y, node.bounds) # 4. Voxel Traversal within macro-cell (Amanatides & Woo) cells = amanatideswootraversal(ray, node.bounds, n) intersectionfound = False for cell in cells: # Check coherency cellid = getcellid(cell, node.bounds) if cellid in rayhistorybuffer and not rayhistorybuffer[cellid]: continue # Skip intersection test based on history # Check if boundary cell if isboundarycell(cell, thresholds): # Perform intersection test hitpoint, hitnormal = fastraysurfaceintersection(ray, cell, thresholds) if hitpoint is not None: # Shading gradient = trilineargradient(cell, hitpoint) color = phongshading(hitpoint, hitnormal, gradient, camera) # Update output colorbuffer[y][x] = color hitflags[y][x] = True intersectionfound = True # Update history buffer for this cell rayhistorybuffer[cellid] = True break # First hit wins if not intersectionfound: # Mark cells visited in this ray as 'no surface' for coherency for cell in cells: cellid = getcellid(cell, node.bounds) if cellid not in rayhistorybuffer: rayhistorybuffer[cellid] = False def fastraysurfaceintersection(ray, cell, thresholds): # Fast intersection method: divide segment into two, check signs, interpolate p1 = ray.origin + ray.direction cell.entryt p2 = ray.origin + ray.direction cell.exitt d1 = trilinearsample(p1) d2 = trilinearsample(p2) for tau in thresholds: if (d1 - tau) (d2 - tau) < 0: # Linear interpolation t = cell.entryt + (tau - d1) / (d2 - d1) (cell.exitt - cell.entryt) hitpoint = ray.origin + ray.direction t hitnormal = trilineargradient(cell, hitpoint) return hitpoint, hitnormal return None, None def dotproduct(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def vectorsub(a, b): return (a.x-b.x, a.y-b.y, a.z-b.z) def computetrimmedcuboid(bounds, thresholds): return bounds # Exact cuboid logic def projectcuboidtoscreen(cuboid, camera): return {'ymin':0, 'ymax':1, 'xmin':0, 'xmax':1} # Standard projection def createlocalray(camera, x, y, bounds): return {'origin': camera.eye, 'direction': camera.direction, 'entryt': 0.0, 'exitt': 1.0} # Ray clipping def amanatideswootraversal(ray, bounds, n): return [{'entryt': 0.0, 'exitt': 1.0, 'coords': (0,0,0)}] # Standard traversal def getcellid(cell, bounds): return str(cell.coords) def isboundarycell(cell, thresholds): return True # Standard boundary check def trilinearsample(point): return 0.5 # Standard interpolation def trilineargradient(cell, point): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Standard gradient def phongshading(point, normal, gradient, camera): return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Standard shading Parameters: n: Macro-cell dimension. Typical values: 3–10. Thresholds: Iso-values. Example: 0 HU (soft tissue) to 1100 HU (stent). Image Resolution: 512x512 in reported experiments. Pitfalls: Macro-cell Size: Small n increases octree traversal and projection overhead, splits rays into more segments, and increases expensive ray initialization steps for rays traveling along iso-surfaces without intersecting. Large n reduces early termination effectiveness because small critical regions are less likely to be detected. Viewing Order: Ray segments must be processed in correct viewing order to ensure the first intersection determines the final pixel color. Failure to sort child nodes by viewing vector causes visibility artifacts. Distance Coding: Not used because it would require recomputation for each new iso-value. Soft Tissue Occlusion: When low thresholds hide the surface of interest (e.g., soft tissue hiding a stent), conventional ray casting may be faster because ray-surface distances are short. Cell-based method suffers as almost all macro-cells must be processed and "peep holes" delay termination. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of macro-cells intersecting the iso-surface and the local ray path length. Significantly faster than conventional ray casting when higher thresholds hide soft tissue and reduce macro-cell processing. Measured Performance: Virtual angioscopy (stented aorta): Average frame time 1.291s vs 2.119s for conventional. 450 HU threshold (bones/stent): 1.953s vs 8.563s (4.38x speedup). 1100 HU threshold (stent only): 0.609s vs 12.781s (20.98x speedup). Ray Path Reduction: Reduces average steps per pixel from ~35.5 (conventional) to ~15.6 (cell-based), and further to ~3.9 with optimizations (trimming, early termination). Strengths: Short average ray path lengths; cache-coherent access (each macro-cell processed once); supports interactive threshold adjustment; no dedicated hardware required. Limitations: Performance degrades when low thresholds cause extensive macro-cell processing due to fine-structured tissue ("peep holes"); small macro-cells increase overhead; large macro-cells reduce culling efficiency. When to Use: Fast perspective iso-surfacing, virtual endoscopy, interactive threshold adjustment. When Not to Use: Low-resolution previews (use conventional ray casting or progressive rendering); scenarios with very low thresholds where soft tissue occludes the surface of interest. Origin: Proposed by André Neubauer, Lukas Mroz, H. Hauser, and R. Wegenkittl in 2002. Development: Developed as part of the AlVis project for visualization of high-resolution industrial CT data (aluminum foam) and tested for virtual angioscopy (stent placement assessment). Comparison: Contrasted with Surface Fitting techniques (e.g., Hietala et al.) which require dedicated hardware and lack interactive threshold adjustment. Contrasted with exact ray-surface intersection methods (Lin et al., Parker et al.) which are more accurate but computationally expensive; this method uses a faster, slightly less accurate approximation. name: Hybrid Strategy for Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: Novel Hybrid Strategy, Object-order projection with restricted ray tracing
body: This method enables interactive isosurface rendering on multi-core processors by combining object-order traversal with restricted ray casting. It solves the load-balancing and memory hierarchy overhead problems inherent in static screen partitioning by dynamically allocating ray casting tasks to threads while maintaining spatial locality. Unlike sibling methods that may use static grids or purely image-order traversal, this approach explicitly decouples the identification of candidate data blocks from the ray casting execution, using a two-phase process to restrict the search space to a small, front-to-back list of blocks per pixel. The method operates in two distinct phases: an object-order identification phase and an image-order restricted ray casting phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset V partitioned into 3D tiles (data blocks). A viewing frustum defined by the camera position and orientation. An isosurface threshold \tau. Output: A rendered image where each pixel contains the color of the first isosurface intersection. Data Structures: 1. 3D-Tiled Dataset: The volume is divided into fixed-size 3D blocks. 2. Candidate Lists: For each pixel (or packet of pixels), a list of data blocks that are both visible and intersect the isosurface (\min(block) \le \tau \le \max(block)), ordered front-to-back relative to the viewpoint. Numbered Steps: 1. Phase I: Object-Order Identification 1. Partition the image screen into initial groups (e.g., packets of adjacent pixels). 2. Traverse the 3D-tiled dataset using the compact indexing structure. 3. Project the 3D blocks from object space onto the image space to determine visibility. 4. For each pixel/packet, identify blocks that intersect the isosurface. 5. Sort these blocks in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. 6. Store the resulting limited-size lists of candidate blocks for each pixel. 2. Phase II: Restricted Ray Casting 1. Dynamically allocate groups of ray casting tasks (pixels/packets) to available processor cores. This dynamic allocation ensures load balancing while preserving spatial locality by assigning adjacent pixels to the same thread when possible. 2. For each assigned pixel, retrieve its ordered list of candidate blocks. 3. Cast the primary ray through the candidate blocks in order. 4. Within each block, perform the standard isosurface ray casting (marching or traversal) to find the first intersection point where f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau. 5. Refine the intersection and shade the pixel. 6. If an intersection is found, terminate ray casting for that pixel; otherwise, continue to the next block in the list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading def getray(camera, pixel): return camera.project(pixel) def renderpixel(pixel, color): image[pixel] = color def raycastblock(ray, block, threshold): # Standard isosurface traversal within a single block # Returns intersection point or None return None class TaskQueue: def init(self, tasks): self.tasks = list(tasks) self.lock = threading.Lock() def pop(self): with self.lock: if self.tasks: return self.tasks.pop() return None def worker(queue, candidatelists, threshold, image): while True: pixel = queue.pop() if pixel is None: break blocks = candidatelists[pixel] ray = getray(camera, pixel) hit = False for block in blocks: intersection = raycastblock(ray, block, threshold) if intersection is not None: renderpixel(pixel, intersection.color) hit = True break if not hit: renderpixel(pixel, backgroundcolor) def hybridisosurfacerendering(volumeblocks, camera, threshold, numthreads, image, backgroundcolor): # Phase I: Object-Order Identification candidatelists = {} pixels = [(x, y) for x in range(camera.width) for y in range(camera.height)] for pixel in pixels: ray = getray(camera, pixel) visibleblocks = [] for block in volumeblocks: if block.isvisible(ray) and block.intersectsisosurface(threshold): visibleblocks.append(block) visibleblocks.sort(key=lambda b: b.distancefromviewpoint(ray.origin)) candidatelists[pixel] = visibleblocks # Phase II: Restricted Ray Casting with Dynamic Allocation taskqueue = TaskQueue(pixels) threads = [] for in range(numthreads): t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(taskqueue, candidatelists, threshold, image)) t.start() threads.append(t) for t in threads: t.join() Parameters: Screen Resolution: Tested at 1024 \times 1024. Hardware: Two-processor Clovertown platform, each with a Quad-Core 1.86 GHz Intel Xeon Processor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Hierarchy Overhead: The method explicitly addresses the cost of moving data across memory levels. Failure to manage cache locality during the dynamic allocation or block access can negate performance gains. Load Imbalance: Static screen partitioning can lead to uneven workloads if some regions of the volume are denser. Dynamic allocation mitigates this. Performance: Achieves interactive rendering at 1024^2 resolution for datasets up to the maximum size fitting in main memory on the tested hardware. Strengths: Excellent load balancing via dynamic allocation; high cache performance due to spatial locality and restricted search spaces; scalability on multi-core systems. Limitations: Requires two-pass processing (identification then casting); overhead of managing dynamic tasks and candidate lists. When to use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets on multi-core CPUs where load balancing and memory efficiency are critical. The method was introduced by Qin Wang and Joseph JaJa. It addresses the limitations of static screen partitioning, which is widely used in literature but suffers from load imbalance and poor cache performance on multi-core processors. The approach leverages the spatial coherence of rays and the hierarchical structure of volumetric data to optimize performance on multi-core architectures. Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing on Multi-Core Processors, https://www.umiacs.umd.edu/~joseph/isosurface-paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: BONO-based ray tracing, Two-phase isosurface ray tracing
body: Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing is a two-phase algorithm for rendering isosurfaces in volumetric data on multi-core processors. It solves the performance bottleneck of high-resolution ray casting by decoupling the search for the isosurface into a coarse, projection-based culling phase and a fine, ray-intersection phase. Unlike standard packet ray casting which relies on SIMD instructions for parallelism, this method uses high-level algorithmic techniques—specifically, maintaining a short, front-to-back ordered list of candidate blocks per pixel—to achieve coherence and efficiency without instruction-level parallelism dependencies. It builds on Ray Traversal and Coherency by using a BONO tree for hierarchical culling and list-based restriction to limit the search space. The method operates in two distinct phases. Phase I traverses a coarse BONO tree to build a short, front-to-back ordered list of visible, isosurface-intersecting data blocks for each pixel (or packet). Phase II shoots rays through these lists to find the first isosurface intersection, performing trilinear interpolation and shading. Inputs: Volumetric scalar field data f(\mathbf{p}). Isovalue \tau. Camera parameters (viewpoint, projection matrix). Maximum list size k (typically k \le 20). Adaptive block size configuration (e.g., 8\times8\times8 for far views, 4\times4\times4 for close views). Outputs: For each pixel, the 3D intersection point \mathbf{p} on the isosurface and its normal \mathbf{n}, used for shading. Block Organization: The volumetric data is organized into a coarse grid of equal-sized blocks. Scalar field values within each block are stored contiguously. Each block is identified by the coordinates of a pre-specified corner. The data within a block is indexed by an octree where leaves correspond to 2\times2\times2 cells, containing a pointer to such a cell. Each octree node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of voxels in its region. BONO Tree: A BONO (Branch-On-Need Octree) tree indexes the coarse grid of blocks. It is augmented with value ranges (min/max) at each node. Unlike a standard octree, BONO avoids allocating nodes for empty subtrees when data resolution is not a power of two, making it more space-efficient. Pixel Lists: For each pixel (or packet), a list of pointers to data blocks is maintained. The list is organized in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. The list size is capped at k. Each list also stores a "resume point" indicating where the BONO tree traversal stopped if the list reached size k. Phase I: List Generation 1. Traverse the BONO tree starting from the root. 2. For a node v, check if its stored value range [minv, maxv] contains the isovalue \tau (i.e., minv \le \tau \le maxv). 3. If the range contains \tau, project the minimum axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of node v onto the screen. The 3D AABB is computed from the coordinates of a pre-specified corner and the level of v. 4. Identify all pixels falling within the projected area of node v. 5. For each such pixel: If the size of the pixel's block list is less than k, traverse v's children in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. Otherwise, skip the subtree rooted at v. 6. When a leaf is reached, augment the list of each pixel falling within the projection of the leaf's block with a pointer to this block, unless the list already has k blocks. The lists remain in front-to-back order due to the traversal order. 7. Adaptive Block Size (Close Views): For close views, after traversing the BONO tree, continue traversing the octree of the BONO leaves until the desired block size is reached. Then compute the minimum bounding box and construct lists for the resulting blocks. Phase II: Ray Casting and Shading 1. For each pixel with a non-empty list, shoot a ray from the pixel through the list of blocks in order. 2. If the list is empty, the ray does not intersect the isosurface. 3. For each block in the list: Compute the ray-voxel intersection using the method from [10] (not detailed in sources). If the ray intersects a voxel on the isosurface within the block: Perform trilinear interpolation using the unit cell containing the voxel to refine the intersection point. Compute the normal using forward difference. Apply diffuse shading. Stop further processing for this ray. 4. If the ray reaches the end of the list without finding an intersection: If the list size is k, resume the traversal of the BONO tree from the resume point indicated at the end of the list. Continue searching for intersections in the remaining subtrees. If the list size is less than k, the ray does not intersect the isosurface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interactiveisosurfaceraytracing(data, isovalue, camera, k, blocksizeconfig): """ Main entry point for the two-phase isosurface ray tracing algorithm. """ bonotree = buildbonotree(data, blocksizeconfig) numpixels = camera.resolution[0] camera.resolution[1] pixellists = [[] for in range(numpixels)] resumepoints = [None for in range(numpixels)] traversebonoforlists(bonotree.root, camera, isovalue, k, pixellists, resumepoints) image = [[None for in range(camera.resolution[0])] for in range(camera.resolution[1])] for y in range(camera.resolution[1]): for x in range(camera.resolution[0]): pixelidx = y camera.resolution[0] + x ray = camera.getray(x, y) blocklist = pixellists[pixelidx] if not blocklist: continue intersectionfound = False for block in blocklist: if rayintersectsblock(ray, block): voxelintersection = rayvoxelintersection(ray, block, isovalue) if voxelintersection is not None: point = trilinearinterpolate(voxelintersection, block) normal = computenormalforwarddiff(point, block) color = diffuseshading(point, normal, data) image[y][x] = (color, point, normal) intersectionfound = True break if not intersectionfound and len(blocklist) == k: resumenode = resumepoints[pixelidx] if resumenode is not None: continuetraversalandcast(ray, resumenode, isovalue, image, pixelidx, camera) return image def traversebonoforlists(node, camera, isovalue, k, pixellists, resumepoints): if not (node.minval <= isovalue <= node.maxval): return projectedarea = projectaabbtoscreen(node.aabb, camera) pixelsinarea = getpixelsinarea(projectedarea) needstraversal = False for pidx in pixelsinarea: if len(pixellists[pidx]) < k: needstraversal = True break if not needstraversal: for pidx in pixelsinarea: if len(pixellists[pidx]) == k: resumepoints[pidx] = node return children = getchildrenfronttoback(node, camera.viewpoint) for child in children: traversebonoforlists(child, camera, isovalue, k, pixellists, resumepoints) if node.isleaf(): for pidx in pixelsinarea: if len(pixellists[pidx]) < k: pixellists[pidx].append(node.block) else: resumepoints[pidx] = node def buildbonotree(data, blocksizeconfig): # Constructs the BONO tree indexing the coarse grid of blocks. # Each node stores min/max scalar values. Leaves point to 2x2x2 cells. # Not given in the sources. pass def projectaabbtoscreen(aabb, camera): # Projects the 3D AABB of a node onto the 2D screen. # The 3D AABB is computed from the coordinates of a pre-specified corner and the level of the node. # Not given in the sources. pass def getpixelsinarea(projectedarea): # Returns list of pixel indices falling within the projected area. # Not given in the sources. pass def getchildrenfronttoback(node, viewpoint): # Returns children of the node sorted by distance from viewpoint. # Not given in the sources. pass def rayintersectsblock(ray, block): # Tests if ray intersects the block's bounding box. # Not given in the sources. pass def rayvoxelintersection(ray, block, isovalue): # Computes ray-voxel intersection using the method from [10]. # Not given in the sources. pass def trilinearinterpolate(point, block): # Performs trilinear interpolation using the unit cell containing the voxel. # Not given in the sources. pass def computenormalforwarddiff(point, block): # Computes normal using forward difference. # Not given in the sources. pass def diffuseshading(point, normal, data): # Applies diffuse shading. # Not given in the sources. pass def continuetraversalandcast(ray, resumenode, isovalue, image, pixelidx, camera): # Resumes BONO traversal from the saved point and continues ray casting. # Not given in the sources. pass k: The maximum size of the list of data blocks associated with each pixel. Typical value: k \le 20 gives the most efficient implementation. The algorithm remains correct for any k. Block Size: Adaptive based on view distance. For far views, large blocks (e.g., 8\times8\times8) are used. For close views, smaller blocks (e.g., 4\times4\times4) are used to reduce the number of BONO nodes visited and projected blocks. Precision: Ray-voxel intersection and trilinear interpolation require careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid gaps or overlaps in the isosurface. Boundaries: The BONO tree structure handles non-power-of-two resolutions by avoiding empty subtree nodes, but care must be taken in computing the AABB for nodes near the data boundaries. List Fullness: If a pixel's list reaches size k before the isosurface is found, the algorithm must correctly resume traversal. Failure to store and use the resume point correctly will result in missed intersections. Time Complexity: Phase I is efficient due to the compact BONO tree and projection-based culling. Phase II is efficient due to the limited number of blocks per ray. Memory Complexity: The BONO tree is more space-efficient than a standard octree for non-power-of-two resolutions. Pixel lists are small (k \le 20), keeping memory overhead low. Measured Performance: On a Clovertown platform (two Quad-Core Intel Xeon Processors 5320, 1.86 GHz, 8MB L2 cache per dual-core, 8GB main memory) with a 1024x1024 screen: Far view, k=3 (single pixel lists): List generation time is 273 msec. Far view, k=6 (2x2 pixel packets): List generation time is 110 msec (2.48x speedup). Close view, k=3 (single pixel lists): List generation time is 228 msec. Close view, k=6 (2x2 pixel packets): List generation time is 68 msec (3.35x speedup). Strengths: High performance on multi-core processors due to efficient memory hierarchy usage and algorithmic coherence. Adaptive block size optimizes for different view distances. Limitations: The method avoids performance drops on highly incoherent scenes by not relying on SIMD instructions, but may trade off peak performance on highly coherent scenes where SIMD-based packet ray casting could be more effective. When to Use: Interactive rendering of high-resolution volumetric data on multi-core CPUs where coherence can be exploited. When Not to Use: Hardware without multi-core capabilities, or scenarios where SIMD-based packet ray casting is preferred for highly coherent scenes. The method was introduced in a paper by researchers at the University of Maryland (UMD). It was designed to leverage multi-core processor architectures and their memory hierarchies for efficient isosurface rendering. The BONO (Branch-On-Need Octree) structure is a key component, providing a compact indexing structure for the volumetric data. The approach differs from standard packet ray casting by avoiding SIMD instructions, instead relying on list merging and projection-based culling to handle coherence. name: Coherent Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: Coherent Octree Volume Ray Tracing, Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing with Ray Packets, Multiresolution isosurface ray tracing using ray packets, Packet Ray Tracing with Octree LOD
body: Coherent Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing is a method for interactive isosurface extraction from large volumetric datasets stored in octrees. It solves the performance bottleneck of single-ray isosurface tracing on commodity CPUs by grouping neighboring rays into 2x2 packets to exploit spatial coherence during traversal and intersection. Unlike single-ray approaches, it performs traversal and intersection computations per packet rather than per ray, leveraging the multiresolution nature of the octree to maintain coherence even in complex or distant scenes by dynamically switching to coarser levels of detail (LOD). The method adapts coherent grid traversal techniques to hierarchical octree structures, combining ray packet processing with multiresolution LOD selection. Input: A large volumetric dataset V, an isovalue threshold \tau, a camera configuration (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} per pixel), and an optional LOD cut depth D{cut}. Output: A rendered image where each pixel contains the color of the first isosurface intersection or background. The core data structure is a multiresolution octree stored in CPU main memory. Octree Node: Each node represents a voxel or a block of voxels. Min/Max Bounds: Each node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values (v{min}, v{max}) of the data contained within its subtree. This forms the min/max acceleration structure. Children: Pointers to up to 8 child nodes (if not a leaf). Data: If a leaf, stores the scalar value(s) for the voxel(s). For multiresolution support, interior nodes may store aggregated or representative values if the octree is constructed to allow LOD traversal. Ray Packet: A group of 4 rays (2x2 pixel block). Ray Data: Each ray has origin \mathbf{o}i and direction \mathbf{d}i for i \in \{0,1,2,3\}. SSE Representation: Rays are packed into SIMD registers for parallel processing. 1. Offline Construction: Losslessly compress the original large dataset into a multiresolution octree structure. Compute min/max bounds for each node bottom-up. Store the octree in CPU main memory. 2. Rendering Setup: Generate rays for each pixel in the frame buffer. Group rays into 2x2 packets. Distribute ray packets to worker threads for parallel processing. 3. Per-Packet Traversal: For each packet, perform coherent traversal of the octree. Start at the root node. For each node in the packet's traversal path: Check if the isovalue \tau lies within the node's min/max bounds: \tau \in [v{min}, v{max}]. If \tau \notin [v{min}, v{max}], cull the node (no intersection possible). If \tau \in [v{min}, v{max}], determine which children to visit. LOD Handling: If the current node depth is \ge D{cut} (or if the system decides to switch to LOD due to low coherence/complexity), treat the current node as a leaf for intersection purposes. LOD Intersection: Intersect the rays with the coarser cell represented by the current node instead of traversing deeper. If an intersection is found, refine the intersection point (e.g., linear interpolation within the cell) and shade. If no intersection is found at this LOD level, continue traversal or mark as background depending on implementation details. If not at LOD cut depth, push children to the traversal stack/list. Use coherence: Rays in a packet likely traverse similar nodes. Process children for all rays in the packet together. 4. SSE Intersection: Perform isosurface intersection tests for the rays in the packet using SIMD (SSE) instructions. For a leaf node (fine voxel or LOD cell), compute the intersection of each ray with the isosurface defined within that cell. The intersection test typically involves checking for sign changes of f(\mathbf{p}) - \tau at the cell corners and interpolating. 5. Shading: For the closest intersection found across all rays in the packet, compute the surface normal \nabla f and shade the pixel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpacket(packet, octreeroot, tau, dcut): """ Render a 2x2 ray packet through an octree. packet: list of 4 rays, each with origin o and direction d octreeroot: root of the min/max octree tau: isovalue threshold dcut: depth at which to switch to LOD (coarser intersection) """ # Stack for traversal: stores (node, rayindicesinpacket) # rayindicesinpacket: subset of {0,1,2,3} that are still active in this node stack = [(octreeroot, [0, 1, 2, 3])] closesthit = None # Stores (distance, rayindex, intersectionpoint, normal) while stack: node, activerays = stack.pop() # Check culling condition if not (node.vmin <= tau <= node.vmax): continue # Determine if we should use LOD uselod = (node.depth >= dcut) if uselod: # Intersect rays with the coarser cell represented by this node for i in activerays: hit = intersectraywithcell(packet[i], node) if hit is not None and (closesthit is None or hit.distance < closesthit.distance): closesthit = hit else: # Traverse children if node.isleaf(): # Fine voxel intersection for i in activerays: hit = intersectraywithvoxel(packet[i], node) if hit is not None and (closesthit is None or hit.distance < closesthit.distance): closesthit = hit else: # Push children to stack children = node.children for child in children: # Determine which rays in activerays enter this child childrays = getraysenteringchild(packet, activerays, child) if childrays: stack.append((child, childrays)) return closesthit def intersectraywithcell(ray, node): """ Intersect a ray with the isosurface within a coarse cell. Returns hit object or None. """ # Standard sign-change detection and linear interpolation within the cell bounds pass def intersectraywithvoxel(ray, node): """ Intersect a ray with the isosurface within a fine voxel. Returns hit object or None. """ # Standard sign-change detection and linear interpolation within the voxel bounds pass def getraysenteringchild(packet, activerays, child): """ Determine which rays in activerays intersect the bounding box of child. """ # Ray-AABB intersection test to cull rays that miss the child node pass Packet Size: 2x2 rays. LOD Cut Depth (D{cut}): A specified depth in the octree. Rays do not traverse below this depth; instead, they intersect the coarser cell at this depth. Isovalue (\tau): The threshold for isosurface extraction. Scalability: Coherent grid traversal on hierarchical structures may have scalability issues. Performance Degradation: Coherent traversal may induce more intersection tests than single-ray traversal and can perform worse without optimizations like LOD. Low Coherence: Large volume data exhibits low spatial coherence, particularly from far-away camera positions, which hampers packet performance. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues may arise in intersection tests, though not explicitly detailed in sources. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of nodes visited per packet. With LOD, the depth of traversal is limited, reducing complexity. Without LOD, it can be higher than single-ray due to packet overhead. Memory Complexity: The octree structure is stored in CPU main memory. The multiresolution representation allows for a smaller footprint than uncompressed data. Measured Performance: The system outperforms ray tracing the same large data on a distributed cluster on a multicore workstation. It achieves interactive performance on laptops and commodity desktops. Strengths: Interactive performance on commodity hardware, smooth gradients due to LOD smoothing, lower memory footprint. Limitations: Scalability issues with coherent traversal, potential performance loss without LOD, low coherence in distant views. When to Use: Interactive visualization of large volumes on commodity CPUs where smoothness is acceptable and hardware is limited. When Not to Use: When maximum precision is required at all scales, or when the scene has very high coherence without LOD (single-ray might be simpler). The method was presented in the paper "Coherent Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing" [60], part of a thesis by Knoll. It builds on the coherent kd-tree isosurface ray tracer of Wald et al. [129, 130], adapting it to octree volumes with multiresolution LODs. The work appeared in Chapter 4 of the thesis. name: First Depth Ray Traversal
head: First Depth, First Intensity Ray Traversal, Tuy & Tuy traversal
body: First Depth Ray Traversal is a ray traversal method that extracts iso-surfaces by recording the first scalar intensity encountered along a viewing ray. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or Accumulate compositing by its immediate termination upon the first hit, making it specifically suited for isolating high-density or specific threshold structures without contribution from deeper volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume V, a viewing ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a threshold \tau, and a step size \Delta t. Output: The color and depth of the first voxel where the scalar value meets the selection criteria. Data Structures: The volume is typically stored as a 3D array of scalar values. Ray traversal uses a step size \Delta t corresponding to the voxel grid spacing. Steps: 1. Initialize ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for the pixel. 2. Iterate along the ray from t=0 to the volume exit. 3. At each step, sample the scalar value s = V(\mathbf{r}(t)). 4. Check if s satisfies the condition (e.g., s \ge \tau or first non-background value). 5. If the condition is met: record the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}(t) and value s, then terminate the ray traversal immediately. 6. If the loop completes without a hit, assign background color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def firstdepthtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, threshold, voxelspacing): t = 0.0 maxt = volume.maxdistance backgroundcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while t <= maxt: pos = rayorigin + raydirection t if not volume.boundscheck(pos): t += voxelspacing continue scalarvalue = volume.sample(pos) if scalarvalue >= threshold: color = volume.transferfunction(scalarvalue) return color + [1.0] t += voxelspacing return backgroundcolor Parameters: Threshold \tau: Defines the iso-surface or minimum intensity. Typical values depend on the data normalization (e.g., 0.5 for normalized [0,1] data). Step size \Delta t: Often equal to voxel spacing for exact voxel traversal, or smaller for sub-voxel precision. Edge Cases: If no voxel exceeds the threshold, the ray returns background. Precision errors at boundaries may cause missed hits if step size is not aligned with voxel centers. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of voxels traversed until the first hit. In sparse volumes, this is significantly faster than full compositing. In dense volumes, it may still require traversing the entire ray length if the hit is deep or absent. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, as it does not accumulate opacity/color buffers. Strengths: Fast extraction of specific structures; no need for transfer function tuning for opacity accumulation; ideal for high-contrast features. Limitations: Loses depth information for structures behind the first hit; sensitive to noise (first noisy voxel may be selected); does not show internal structure. First Depth Ray Traversal was introduced by Tuy and Tuy in 1984. It is one of the earliest methods for ray-casting based volume rendering, specifically designed for iso-surface extraction via ray traversal.
