name: Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Size
head: Adaptive Ray Marching, Adaptive Step Ray Casting
body: Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Size is an image-order rendering technique that traverses a volume along rays to detect isosurface intersections, dynamically adjusting the sampling interval based on local signal frequency or feature complexity. It sets itself apart from fixed-step methods by reducing computational waste in smooth regions while maintaining precision near sharp features, and differs from algebraic raycasting by relying on discrete voxel sampling rather than closed-form surface evaluation. All methods in this family share the fundamental mechanism of image-order rendering: for each pixel, a ray is defined in world space, intersected with the volume domain, and sampled along its path to detect the first intersection with the isosurface. The ray is parameterized as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. The traversal order is determined by the pixel's position in the image plane. The core detection logic relies on the isosurface condition. For a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}), the surface is defined by f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau. In discrete voxel data, this is typically detected by a sign change or threshold crossing between consecutive samples: f(\mathbf{p}1) \cdot f(\mathbf{p}2) < 0 relative to \tau, or f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau. Upon detection, the intersection position is often refined (e.g., via linear interpolation or binary search) to reduce discretization artifacts. The surface normal is computed from the gradient \nabla f at the hit point, usually via finite differences or tri-cubic filtering, to enable Phong-like shading. The final color is computed using local lighting models (ambient, diffuse, specular) and potentially ambient occlusion or shadows, with no contribution from voxels behind the surface. A technique that combines adaptive ray sampling with explicit root-finding to render sharp, Dirac-like features in transfer functions as semi-transparent isosurfaces. Unlike standard postclassification or preintegration methods, which struggle with high-frequency transfer function features due to undersampling or incorrect integration assumptions, this method solves directly for the roots of the transfer function to locate isosurface intersections. It sets itself apart by using a 2D lookup table to query potential peak isovales within a ray segment and employing a secant method for precise intersection detection, allowing for correct shading and opacity handling of narrow-band features. An image-order rendering technique that identifies the first voxel along a ray whose scalar value falls within a user-defined density threshold range, treating this point as the visible surface. It discards all data behind the first hit. It differs from Differential Sampling and Peak Finding by using a fixed-step march with binary-refinement rather than derivative-based peak detection, and from Isosurface Ray Marching with Blinn-Phong Shading by stopping at the first hit rather than accumulating transmittance. An image-order rendering technique that casts rays from the camera through each pixel, intersects them with the volume's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB), and marches along the ray to find the first voxel exceeding a specific intensity threshold. It differs from its sibling Differential Sampling and Peak Finding by using a fixed-step march with binary-refinement rather than derivative-based peak detection, and from Front-to-Back Surface Extraction by stopping at the first hit rather than accumulating transmittance. The method computes surface shading using a Blinn-Phong model, providing specular highlights that define the visual appearance of the extracted isosurface. Extends ray integration to include the contribution of external light, combining the object’s own color with the color of external light. C(t) = \int{t{\text{near}}}^{t{\text{far}}} T(t) \cdot \sigma(t) \cdot \left[c(t) + L{\text{ext}}(t)\right] \, dt. L{\text{ext}} is the external light contribution. L{\text{ext}}(t) \approx \Delta s \cdot \sum{k=0}^{M-1} T(sk) \cdot \sigma(sk) \cdot I(\omegad) \cdot p(\omegad, sk). M is the number of samples. \Delta s is the sample interval. sk is the sampling point. T(sk) is the transmittance. \sigma(sk) is the sum of absorption and scattering. I(\omegad) is the intensity of the light coming from direction \omegad. p(\omegad, sk) is the phase function, representing the probability that light scatters toward \omegad at the sample point sk. This approximation considers just a single direction (\omega) instead of every direction to reduce cost. Ray marching is a foundational technique in volume rendering, originating from the need to efficiently traverse voxel grids without explicit mesh generation. Early implementations used fixed step sizes, which were computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes or resulted in aliasing for thin structures. Adaptive step sizing was introduced to optimize the trade-off between accuracy and performance, particularly in scientific visualization where features vary in density. The specific integration of external lighting models into ray marching allows for more physically plausible rendering of participating media, moving beyond self-illumination to include environmental interactions. name: Differential Sampling and Peak Finding
head: Adaptive Surface Detection, Peak Finding, Surface Ray Marching, Surface Raycasting with Adaptive Step Size
body: Differential Sampling and Peak Finding is a volume rendering technique that combines adaptive ray sampling with explicit root-finding to render sharp, Dirac-like features in transfer functions as semi-transparent isosurfaces. Unlike standard postclassification or preintegration methods, which struggle with high-frequency transfer function features due to undersampling or incorrect integration assumptions, this method solves directly for the roots of the transfer function to locate isosurface intersections. It sets itself apart by using a 2D lookup table to query potential peak isovales within a ray segment and employing a secant method for precise intersection detection, allowing for correct shading and opacity handling of narrow-band features. The method operates on a per-pixel ray basis, traversing the volume domain and detecting intersections with specific isovalue peaks defined by the transfer function's opacity component. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in world space. Scalar volume data V. Transfer function \rho\alpha(f), mapping scalar values to opacity. Isosurface threshold (peak isovalue) \upsilon. Lookup table peakTable mapping field value ranges to peak isovales. Parameters: terminationalpha, invalidflag, initial step size b, adaptive step increment a. Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity. Globals: ps0, ps1: vec4 representing position (x, y, z, t) at the start and end of the current ray segment. fs0, fs1: float representing the scalar field values f(\mathbf{p}) at ps0 and ps1. dt: float representing the step size parameter. iso: float representing the isovalue retrieved from the lookup table. Lookup Table (peakTable): A 2D texture (or array) indexed by float2(fs0, fs1). Each entry stores an isovalue \upsilon (or a set of up to four sequential isovales \upsiloni) that corresponds to a local maximum in the opacity component of the transfer function within the range [fi, fo]. Entries are sorted from first to last peak value encountered on the segment. If no peak exists, the entry contains invalidflag. Discretization resolution: Typically 128 bins per dimension. 1. Initialization: Set dt = b. Set ps1.w = 0 (time/parameter t). Set ps1.xyz = ray.origin. Compute fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz). 2. Main Ray Casting Loop: Copy ps1 to ps0 and fs1 to fs0. Advance position: ps1.xyz += dt ray.direction. Update time: ps1.w += dt. Differential Sampling: If DIFFERENTIALSAMPLING is enabled, increment dt by a (adaptive step size adjustment based on image plane frequency). Compute current sample: fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz). 3. Peak Lookup: If !DVRONLY, sample peakTable using float2(fs0, fs1). Let the result be iso. If iso != invalidflag, a potential peak exists in this segment. 4. Root Solving (Peak Finding): If a peak is found, perform root finding to locate the exact intersection. Define the implicit function g(t) = f(\mathbf{R}(t)) - \upsilon. Evaluate endpoints: f0 = fs0 - \upsilon, f1 = fs1 - \upsilon. Descartes' Rule of Signs: Check if the segment contains a root. The source pseudocode uses a sign change check f0 f1 < 0 as a proxy for root existence in the bisection context, but the text describes using Descartes' rule for robustness. Secant/Bisection Iteration: Initialize bounds: p0 = ps0, p1 = ps1, f0 = fs0 - \upsilon, f1 = fs1 - \upsilon. Iterate k from 0 to 1 (2 iterations): Compute intermediate point using secant formula: \mathbf{p}{rt} = \mathbf{p}0 - (\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \frac{f0}{f1 - f0} Evaluate field at intermediate point: f{rt} = \text{volume\filter}(\mathbf{p}{rt}.xyz) - \upsilon. Update bounds: If f{rt} \cdot f0 < 0: Set \mathbf{p}1 = \mathbf{p}{rt}, f1 = f{rt}. Else: Set \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{p}{rt}, f0 = f{rt}. Recompute \mathbf{p}{rt} using the updated bounds. Final Sample: Set f{rt} = 0 (assume the value is exactly the isovalue to avoid Moiré patterns). Set dt = 1.0 (constant opacity scaling). Call dvrsample(prt, frt, dt). 5. Volume Rendering Sample (DVR): If !PEAKONLY (or if PEAKXORDVR is set and no peak was found), call dvrsample(ps1, fs1, dt). This performs standard front-to-back compositing for the segment. 6. Termination: If accumulated color.a > terminationalpha, break loop. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ps0: vec4 # Position at start of segment (x, y, z, t) ps1: vec4 # Position at end of segment (x, y, z, t) fs0: float # Field value at ps0 fs1: float # Field value at ps1 dt: float # Step size parameter iso: float # Isosurface value from lookup table color: vec4 # Accumulated color/opacity def volumefilter(pos: vec3) -> float: # Trilinear or tri-cubic interpolation of volume data at pos return texture(volumetexture, pos) def dvrsample(pos: vec4, fieldval: float, stepsize: float): # Standard front-to-back volume rendering compositing # Uses transfer function to get color and opacity # Opacity is scaled by stepsize (or constant 1.0 for peaks) pass def peakfind(ps0: vec4, ps1: vec4, fs0: float, fs1: float, iso: float): f0 = fs0 - iso f1 = fs1 - iso # Check for sign change (root existence) if f0 f1 < 0: p0 = ps0 p1 = ps1 # Secant method iterations (2 iterations as per source) for k in range(2): # Secant formula for root estimation deltap = p1 - p0 ratio = f0 / (f1 - f0) prt = p0 - deltap ratio # Evaluate field at new point frt = volumefilter(prt.xyz) - iso # Update bounds if frt f0 < 0: p1 = prt f1 = frt else: p0 = prt f0 = frt # Recompute prt for final sample deltap = p1 - p0 ratio = f0 / (f1 - f0) prt = p0 - deltap ratio # Final sample at root # Assume field value is exactly iso to avoid Moire frtfinal = 0.0 dtfinal = 1.0 # Constant opacity scaling for peaks dvrsample(prt, frtfinal, dtfinal) def raycast(rayorigin: vec3, raydirection: vec3, b: float, a: float, terminationalpha: float, invalidflag: float): dt = b ps1 = vec4(rayorigin, 0.0) fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz) color = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) while True: ps0 = ps1 fs0 = fs1 # Advance ray ps1.xyz += dt raydirection ps1.w += dt # Differential Sampling: Adaptive step size if DIFFERENTIALSAMPLING: dt += a fs1 = volumefilter(ps1.xyz) # Peak Finding if not DVRONLY: iso = texture2D(peakTable, float2(fs0, fs1)) if iso != invalidflag: peakfind(ps0, ps1, fs0, fs1, iso) # Standard DVR sampling if not PEAKONLY if not PEAKONLY: if PEAKXORDVR and iso != invalidflag: pass # Skip DVR if peak was found and XOR mode is active else: dvrsample(ps1, fs1, dt) # Termination check if color.a > terminationalpha: break def texture2D(tex: texture, coords: vec2) -> float: # Sample 2D texture with (fs0, fs1) # Returns isovalue or invalidflag return tex.sample(coords) b: Initial step size. Not given in the sources. a: Adaptive step increment for differential sampling. Not given in the sources. terminationalpha: Alpha threshold for ray termination. invalidflag: Value indicating no peak found. Lookup Table Resolution: 128 bins per dimension is sufficient for peak finding. Moire Patterns: Evaluating the field f(\mathbf{R}(t)) at the root estimate can cause Moire patterns with sharp transfer functions. The method assumes the value is exactly the isovalue (\upsilon) at the hit point to avoid this. Opacity Scaling: Standard DVR scales opacity by segment distance \Delta t. Peak finding uses a constant \Delta t = 1.0 to ensure correct opacity regardless of sampling rate. Multiple Peaks: If multiple peaks exist in a segment, the lookup table stores up to four sequential peaks. The algorithm must sequentially perform peak finding for each value. Sign Change Detection: The pseudocode uses a simple sign change check (f0 f1 < 0). The text mentions Descartes' rule of signs for robustness. Implementers should be aware that simple sign changes may miss roots if the function touches the axis without crossing, though for transfer function peaks, crossing is typical. A two-stage search algorithm to find the approximate location of the minimum value in a volume along a ray. The first stage performs a coarse linear scan, and the second stage refines the position using a divide-by-two approach. Note: despite the title, the source implementation searches for the minimum value. Time Complexity: Building the lookup table is O(N^2), where N is the number of bins in the transfer function discretization. Memory Complexity: Requires a 2D lookup table. A coarser resolution (128 bins) is often sufficient, reducing memory compared to preintegration tables which require larger resolutions for comparable quality. Performance: Building the peak-finding table is roughly twice as fast as building a preintegrated table at the same resolution. Heptane fire scene (1024x900): Peak finding renders at 7.1 fps, postclassification at 11.6 fps, preintegration at 8.8 fps. Zebrafish optic tract (1600x512): Peak finding at 2.1 fps, Preintegration at 2.0 fps, Semi-transparent isosurfacing at 4.3 fps. Finding multiple peaks costs roughly 20% more performance. Strengths: Correctly renders sharp, Dirac-like features in transfer functions as semi-transparent isosurfaces. Avoids Moire patterns and incorrect opacity integration associated with preintegration and postclassification for high-frequency features. Supports different rendering modalities (PEAKONLY, DVRONLY, PEAKXORDVR) with no code overhead. Limitations: Introduces bias by assuming discrete impulses for the integral, which may not be ideal for smooth transfer functions where preintegration excels. Requires construction of a 2D lookup table, which adds preprocessing time (though faster than preintegration). When to Use: Use when rendering data with sharp, narrow-band transfer function features (e.g., noisy medical data, entropic data) that standard DVR or preintegration fails to reproduce correctly. When Not to Use: Use standard DVR or preintegration for smooth transfer functions where high-frequency features are not critical, or when performance is paramount and sharp features are not present. The method was introduced by Knoll et al. in "Volume Ray Casting with Peak Finding and Differential Sampling". It addresses the limitations of postclassification and preintegration volume rendering when dealing with transfer functions containing sharp features approaching Dirac impulses. The technique combines concepts from isosurface ray casting (root solving) and volume rendering (compositing), using a 2D lookup table similar to preintegration but storing peak isovales instead of integrated radiance. It also incorporates differential sampling based on Igehy's ray differentials to respect the Nyquist frequency of the image plane. name: Coarse-to-Fine Volume Maximum Search
body: A two-stage search algorithm to find the approximate location of the minimum value in a volume along a ray. The first stage performs a coarse linear scan, and the second stage refines the position using a divide-by-two approach. Note: despite the title, the source implementation searches for the minimum value. Inputs: startcoord (3D coordinate), stepcoord (step vector), nsteps (integer step count), sizef (volume dimensions), and samplevol(coord, sizef) (sampling function returning vec4<f32>). Outputs: thecoord (3D coordinate of the found extremum), theref (scalar extremum value extracted from the r component), and thevalue (full vec4<f32> at thecoord). Data Structures: theref (f32, initialized to 999999.0), thecoord (vec3<f32>, initialized to startcoord), thevalue (vec4<f32>, initialized to zero), and substepcoord (vec3<f32>, initialized to stepcoord). Steps: 1. Coarse Linear Scan: Initialize theref = 999999.0, thecoord = startcoord, and thevalue = vec4<f32>(0.0). Loop iter from 0.0 to nstepsf (exclusive), where nstepsf = f32(nsteps). In each iteration, calculate coord = startcoord + iter stepcoord. Sample value = samplevol(coord, sizef). Extract reff = value.r. If reff < theref, update theref = reff, thecoord = coord, and thevalue = value. 2. Fine Refinement: Initialize substepcoord = stepcoord. Loop iter2 from 0 to 3 (4 iterations). In each iteration, halve the step: substepcoord = substepcoord 0.5. Calculate neighbors: coord1 = thecoord - substepcoord and coord2 = thecoord + substepcoord. Sample neighbors: value1 = samplevol(coord1, sizef) and value2 = samplevol(coord2, sizef). Extract values: ref1 = value1.r and ref2 = value2.r. If ref1 <= theref (deliberate less-equal), update theref = ref1, thecoord = coord1, and thevalue = value1. Else if ref2 < theref, update theref = ref2, thecoord = coord2, and thevalue = value2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofinesearch(startcoord, stepcoord, nsteps, sizef, samplevol): # Stage 1: Coarse Linear Scan theref = 999999.0 thecoord = startcoord thevalue = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) nstepsf = float(nsteps) for iter in range(nsteps): coord = startcoord + iter stepcoord value = samplevol(coord, sizef) reff = value.r if reff < theref: theref = reff thecoord = coord thevalue = value # Stage 2: Fine Refinement substepcoord = stepcoord for iter2 in range(4): substepcoord = substepcoord 0.5 coord1 = thecoord - substepcoord coord2 = thecoord + substepcoord value1 = samplevol(coord1, sizef) value2 = samplevol(coord2, sizef) ref1 = value1.r ref2 = value2.r if ref1 <= theref: # Deliberate less-equal theref = ref1 thecoord = coord1 thevalue = value1 elif ref2 < theref: theref = ref2 thecoord = coord2 thevalue = value2 return thecoord, theref, thevalue Parameters: nstepsf is the number of steps in the coarse linear scan loop. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Refinement iterations: Fixed at 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The refinement loop uses a deliberate less-equal (<=) comparison for the first neighbor (coord1) to handle ties or specific boundary conditions, while using strict less-than (<) for the second neighbor (coord2). Boundary checks for coord1 and coord2 are not explicitly detailed in the source snippet; implementation must ensure samplevol handles out-of-bounds coordinates gracefully or clamps them. Not given in the sources. Originating from implementations in the pygfx library (WGPU renderer), this method is used in image-order volume rendering to efficiently locate peaks along rays for isosurface extraction or maximum intensity projection. It builds on Differential Sampling and Peak Finding. volumeray.wgsl, https://github.com/pygfx/pygfx/blob/main/pygfx/renderers/wgpu/wgsl/volumeray.wgsl, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Front-to-Back Surface Extraction
body: Front-to-Back Surface Extraction is an image-order rendering technique that identifies the first voxel along a ray whose scalar value falls within a user-defined density threshold range, treating this point as the visible surface. It discards all data behind the first hit. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V, a transfer function T(d) mapping density to color, a threshold range [\tau{min}, \tau{max}], a minimum gradient magnitude \tau{grad}, camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), and rendering parameters (step size, jitter factor, flags). Output: A single pixel color C and opacity \alpha. Data Structures: Ray: Struct containing startPos (vec3), endPos (vec3), direction (vec3). RaymarchInfo: Struct containing stepSize (float), numSteps (int), numStepsRecip (float). Volume: 3D texture or array supporting getDensity(pos), getGradient(pos), and optional secondary density/color functions. Parameters: MAXNUMSTEPS: 1024. JITTERFACTOR: Random offset scaling factor. CROSSSECTIONON: Boolean flag for cutout geometry. MULTIVOLUMEISOLATE / MULTIVOLUMEOVERLAY: Boolean flags for multi-volume handling. MinVal, MaxVal: Density threshold bounds. MinGradient: Minimum gradient magnitude for surface detection. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Compute the ray from the camera origin through the pixel center to the volume bounds. Calculate stepSize, numSteps, and numStepsRecip based on the ray length and sampling rate. 2. Jittering: Add a random offset to the ray start position to reduce aliasing: \mathbf{p}{start} = \mathbf{p}{start} + \text{JITTER\FACTOR} \cdot \text{stepSize} \cdot \mathbf{d} \cdot \text{noise}(u, v), where \text{noise}(u, v) is a pseudo-random value derived from pixel coordinates. 3. Iteration: Loop i from 0 to \text{numSteps} - 1: a. Position: Compute current position \mathbf{p} by linear interpolation between start and end: \mathbf{p} = \text{lerp}(\mathbf{p}{start}, \mathbf{p}{end}, i \cdot \text{numStepsRecip}). b. Cutout Check: If CROSSSECTIONON is true, evaluate IsCutout(p). If the point is inside a cutout region, skip to the next step. c. Density Sampling: Retrieve density d = \text{getDensity}(\mathbf{p}). d. Multi-Volume Handling: If MULTIVOLUMEISOLATE is active, retrieve secondary density d{sec}. If d{sec} \le 0, skip to the next step. If MULTIVOLUMEOVERLAY is active, retrieve d{sec}. If d{sec} > 0 and the secondary transfer function yields non-zero alpha, compute the secondary color, normal, and lighting. Set the pixel color to this secondary result, set opacity to 1.0, and terminate the ray march. e. Threshold Check: If \tau{min} < d < \tau{max}: i. Compute gradient \mathbf{g} = \nabla V(\mathbf{p}). ii. Compute gradient magnitude g{mag} = \|\mathbf{g}\|. iii. If g{mag} > \tau{grad}: Compute normal \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{g} / g{mag}. Sample transfer function C{surf} = T(d). Apply lighting model using \mathbf{n}, light direction, and view direction to produce final color. Return C{surf} and terminate. f. Termination: If the loop completes without a hit, return transparent/black. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision loss occurs when numSteps is very large, causing numStepsRecip to underflow or t to lose resolution. Rays parallel to volume faces may yield tmin == tmax; the intersection logic must handle this degenerate case. Unnormalized direction vectors scale the step size incorrectly; the direction must be normalized before jittering or step calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobacksurfaceextraction(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, tf, params): # 1. Initialize Ray # Intersect ray with volume AABB tmin, tmax = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, volume.bounds) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return 0.0, 0.0 raystart = rayorigin + raydirection tmin rayend = rayorigin + raydirection tmax raylength = max(0.0, length(rayend - raystart)) numsteps = int(raylength / params.stepsize) numsteps = max(1, min(numsteps, params.MAXNUMSTEPS)) numstepsrecip = 1.0 / numsteps # 2. Jitter jitterval = params.JITTERFACTOR params.stepsize hashnoise(rayorigin.xy) raystart = raystart + jitterval normalize(raydirection) # 3. Loop for i in range(numsteps): t = i numstepsrecip currpos = raystart + t (rayend - raystart) # Cutout check if params.CROSSSECTIONON and iscutout(currpos): continue density = volume.getdensity(currpos) # Multi-volume overlay if params.MULTIVOLUMEOVERLAY: secdensity = volume.getsecondarydensity(currpos) if secdensity > 0.0: seccolor = volume.getsecondarytfcolor(secdensity) if seccolor.a > 0.0: grad = volume.getgradient(currpos) gradmag = length(grad) if gradmag > 0.0: normal = grad / gradmag lightdir = normalize(-raydirection) color = calculatelighting(seccolor.rgb, normal, lightdir, raydirection) return color, 1.0 # Threshold check if params.MinVal < density < params.MaxVal: grad = volume.getgradient(currpos) gradmag = length(grad) if gradmag > params.MinGradient: normal = grad / gradmag color = tf.getcolor(density) lightdir = normalize(-raydirection) finalcolor = calculatelighting(color.rgb, normal, lightdir, raydirection) return finalcolor, 1.0 return 0.0, 0.0 def intersectaabb(origin, direction, bounds): # Standard ray-AABB intersection tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) < 1e-8: if origin[i] < bounds.min[i] or origin[i] > bounds.max[i]: return -1.0, -1.0 else: t1 = (bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax def hashnoise(coord): # Simple pseudo-random hash x, y = coord n = int(x 12.9898 + y 78.233) return (n 43758.5453) % 1 def iscutout(pos): # Placeholder for cutout geometry check return False def calculatelighting(color, normal, lightdir, viewdir): # Simple diffuse lighting diff = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) return color (0.5 + 0.5 diff) Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of steps along the ray. Typically bounded by MAXNUMSTEPS. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, plus storage for the volume dataset. Strengths: Simple implementation; fast convergence if the surface is near the front; low memory overhead. Limitations: Sensitive to sampling rate (aliasing); no sub-voxel precision without interpolation; fails if the surface is thinner than the step size or if the gradient is too weak. When to use: Real-time visualization of thick, well-defined surfaces; simple cutout effects. When not to use: Thin structures; high-precision medical imaging requiring sub-voxel accuracy; scenes with complex internal structures behind the surface. This method is implemented in the UnityVolumeRendering project by M. Lavik. GitHub - mlavik1/UnityVolumeRendering: Volume rendering, implemented in..., https://github.com/mlavik1/UnityVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Isosurface Ray Marching with Blinn-Phong Shading
head: Ray Marching with Slab Intersection and Blinn-Phong Shading, isosurface rendering via ray marching
body: Isosurface Ray Marching with Blinn-Phong Shading is an image-order rendering technique that casts rays from the camera through each pixel, intersects them with the volume's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB), and marches along the ray to find the first voxel exceeding a specific intensity threshold. It differs from its sibling Differential Sampling and Peak Finding by using a fixed-step march with binary-refinement rather than derivative-based peak detection, and from Front-to-Back Surface Extraction by stopping at the first hit rather than accumulating transmittance. The method computes surface shading using a Blinn-Phong model, providing specular highlights that define the visual appearance of the extracted isosurface. Inputs: Camera parameters: viewport size, aspect ratio, focal length, view matrix, background color, gamma. Volume parameters: AABB defined by bottom and top vectors, volume texture (sampled for intensity), threshold value, step length. Shading parameters: light position, material color, ambient coefficient (Ia), diffuse coefficient (Id), specular exponent, specular coefficient. Outputs: Final pixel color with gamma correction applied. Data Structures: rayorigin: vec3, camera position. raydirection: vec3, normalized direction vector. box.top, box.bottom: vec3, corners of the AABB. volume: Texture object supporting texture(volume, position) returning a vec4 (intensity in.r). Steps: 1. Compute Ray Direction: Calculate the ray direction from fragment coordinates. Let u, v be the fragment coordinates, W, H be the viewport width and height, and A be the aspect ratio. \begin{aligned} ray\direction.xy &= 2.0 \cdot \frac{[u, v]}{[W, H]} - 1.0 \\ ray\direction.x &= A \\ ray\direction.z &= -focal\length \\ ray\direction &= \text{normalize}((\text{ViewMatrix} \cdot [ray\direction, 0]).xyz) \end{aligned} 2. Slab Intersection (Ray-AABB): Find the entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances of the ray with the AABB. \begin{aligned} direction\inv &= 1.0 / ray\direction \\ t\top &= direction\inv \cdot (box.top - ray\origin) \\ t\bottom &= direction\inv \cdot (box.bottom - ray\origin) \\ t\min &= \min(t\top, t\bottom) \\ t0 &= \max(0.0, \max(t\min.x, t\min.y)) \\ t\max &= \max(t\top, t\bottom) \\ t1 &= \min(t\max.x, t\max.y) \end{aligned} If t0 > t1, the ray misses the box. 3. Transform to Texture Coordinates: Map the entry and exit points in world space to volume texture coordinates (normalized [0, 1]). \begin{aligned} ray\start &= \frac{ray\origin + ray\direction \cdot t0 - box.bottom}{box.top - box.bottom} \\ ray\stop &= \frac{ray\origin + ray\direction \cdot t1 - box.bottom}{box.top - box.bottom} \end{aligned} 4. Initialize Marching: Calculate the step vector in texture space. Let L be the length of the ray in texture space (|ray\stop - ray\start|) and s be the steplength. \begin{aligned} ray &= ray\stop - ray\start \\ L &= |ray| \\ step\vector &= s \cdot \frac{ray}{L} \end{aligned} Initialize position and accumulated color. \begin{aligned} position &= ray\start + step\vector \\ colour &= \text{pow}(background\colour, \gamma) \end{aligned} 5. March and Detect Isosurface: Loop while L > 0: a. Sample intensity: I = \text{texture}(volume, position).r. b. If I > threshold: i. Refine position to approximate the exact isosurface intersection: \begin{aligned} position &-= step\vector \cdot 0.5 \\ I &= \text{texture}(volume, position).r \\ position &-= step\vector \cdot (I > threshold ? 0.25: -0.25) \\ I &= \text{texture}(volume, position).r \end{aligned} ii. Compute Blinn-Phong shading (see Step 6) and break loop. c. Else (threshold not reached): \begin{aligned} L &-= s \\ position &+= step\vector \end{aligned} 6. Blinn-Phong Shading: Compute the final color contribution at the hit position. \begin{aligned} L{vec} &= \text{normalize}(light\position - position) \\ V{vec} &= -\text{normalize}(ray\direction) \\ N &= \text{normal}(position, I) \\ H &= \text{normalize}(L{vec} + V{vec}) \\ Ia &= 0.1 \\ Id &= 1.0 \cdot \max(0, N \cdot L{vec}) \\ Is &= 8.0 \cdot \max(0, N \cdot H)^{600} \\ colour &= (Ia + Id) \cdot material\colour + Is \cdot [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] \end{aligned} 7. Gamma Correction: Apply inverse gamma to the final color. colour{final} = \text{pow}(colour, 1.0 / \gamma) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpixel(fragcoord, viewportsize, aspectratio, focallength, viewmatrix, rayorigin, boxbottom, boxtop, volume, threshold, steplength, lightposition, materialcolor, backgroundcolor, gamma): # 1. Compute Ray Direction u, v = fragcoord W, H = viewportsize raydirxy = vec2(2.0 u / W - 1.0, 2.0 v / H - 1.0) raydirxy.x = aspectratio raydirz = -focallength raydirhomogeneous = vec4(raydirxy.x, raydirxy.y, raydirz, 0.0) raydir = normalize((viewmatrix raydirhomogeneous).xyz) # 2. Slab Intersection dirinv = vec3(1.0) / raydir ttop = dirinv (boxtop - rayorigin) tbottom = dirinv (boxbottom - rayorigin) tmin = min(ttop, tbottom) t0 = max(0.0, max(tmin.x, tmin.y)) tmax = max(ttop, tbottom) t1 = min(tmax.x, tmax.y) if t0 > t1: return backgroundcolor # Miss # 3. Transform to Texture Coordinates raystart = (rayorigin + raydir t0 - boxbottom) / (boxtop - boxbottom) raystop = (rayorigin + raydir t1 - boxbottom) / (boxtop - boxbottom) # 4. Initialize Marching rayvec = raystop - raystart raylength = length(rayvec) stepvector = steplength rayvec / raylength position = raystart + stepvector colour = pow(backgroundcolor, vec3(gamma)) # 5. March and Detect Isosurface while raylength > 0: intensity = texture(volume, position).r if intensity > threshold: # Refine position position -= stepvector 0.5 intensity = texture(volume, position).r if intensity > threshold: position -= stepvector 0.25 else: position -= stepvector -0.25 intensity = texture(volume, position).r # 6. Blinn-Phong Shading Lvec = normalize(lightposition - position) Vvec = -normalize(raydir) N = computenormal(position, intensity) # Implementation of normal computation not provided in source Hvec = normalize(Lvec + Vvec) Ia = 0.1 Id = 1.0 max(0.0, dot(N, Lvec)) Is = 8.0 pow(max(0.0, dot(N, Hvec)), 600.0) colour = (Ia + Id) materialcolor + Is vec3(1.0) break else: raylength -= steplength position += stepvector # 7. Gamma Correction finalcolour = pow(colour, vec3(1.0 / gamma)) return finalcolour Parameters: steplength: Not given in the sources. threshold: Not given in the sources. focallength: Not given in the sources. gamma: Not given in the sources. lightposition: Not given in the sources. materialcolor: Not given in the sources. backgroundcolor: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The refinement step uses fixed offsets (0.5 and 0.25 of step vector). If the step size is large relative to the isosurface curvature, the hit position may be inaccurate. Boundaries: The slab intersection handles ray-box clipping, but texture sampling at raystart and raystop assumes valid texture coordinates. If t0 or t1 are negative or out of bounds, behavior is undefined in the source. Degenerate Input: If raydirection has zero components, dirinv becomes infinite. The source does not specify handling for this. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of steps until the isosurface is found or the ray exits the volume. In the worst case (no hit), N is proportional to the ray length divided by steplength. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, excluding the volume texture storage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides specular shading for visual clarity; efficient single-hit extraction. Limitations: Fixed step size may be inefficient in empty regions or miss thin structures; refinement is heuristic and not mathematically exact; no transparency/translucency effects. When to use: Real-time visualization of dense isosurfaces where specular highlights are desired. When not: When accurate surface normals are critical (use gradient-based normals from the volume directly) or when transparency is required. The method originates from the subvol project by jimpelton. It combines standard ray-box intersection techniques with a simple marching algorithm and Blinn-Phong shading to visualize volumetric data. The approach is typical of early GPU-based volume visualization techniques that prioritized speed and visual appeal over physical accuracy. jimpelton/subvol, https://github.com/jimpelton/subvol, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multiple Scattering via Spatial Spreading and Ray Marching
head: Path Integral Based Multiple Scattering, Practical Multiple Scattering
body: This method renders multiple scattering effects in volumetric media by approximating the spatial spreading of light using a point spread function (PSF) derived from path integral analysis, rather than simulating individual photon paths. It distinguishes itself from Monte Carlo methods by capturing qualitative features like spatial blurring and shadowing significantly faster, at the cost of higher memory usage and reduced quantitative accuracy regarding phase function shape. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume grid storing density \rho(\mathbf{x}); absorption cross-section C{abs}; scattering cross-section C{sca}; precomputed light attenuation volumes (light volume pyramid) for each light source; camera parameters. Output: Final image color for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Density Grid: Stores \rho(\mathbf{x}). For a 128^3 voxel grid, this requires 8 Mb. 2. Light Volume Pyramid: Stores reduced intensity/light attenuation for each light source. Requires 32 Mb. 3. Precomputed \ell2 Volume: Stores precomputed values for the light path component. Requires 8 Mb. Total Memory: Approximately 48 Mb for the described setup. Scattering Coefficients: The extinction coefficient a(\mathbf{x}) and scattering coefficient b(\mathbf{x}) are computed from density: a(\mathbf{x}) = C{abs}\rho(\mathbf{x}) b(\mathbf{x}) = C{sca}\rho(\mathbf{x}) where \rho(\mathbf{x}) is the density at point \mathbf{x}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Construct the light volume pyramid and precompute \ell2 values for all light sources. This step is performed once per light source. 2. Ray Marching Setup: For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera into the volume. Initialize the camera path length s1 = 0 and the associated light transport term \ell1 = 1.0. 3. Adaptive Step Sizing: Determine the step size for the current sample. Single Scattering Component: Use a small, fixed step size to resolve fine features of the participating media. Multiple Scattering Component: Use a progressively larger step size as the ray moves further from the camera. This is valid because the blur size (spatial spreading) monotonically increases with distance. 4. Sample Integration: At each step along the ray: Sample the density \rho(\mathbf{x}) and compute a(\mathbf{x}) and b(\mathbf{x}). Camera Path (\ell1): Update \ell1 based on the transmittance along the camera path segment s1. Light Path (\ell2): Retrieve the precomputed \ell2 value from the light volume pyramid for the current position. Multiple Scattering Contribution: Apply the spatial spreading (blurring) approximation using the PSF derived from path integral analysis to the incident radiance. This approximates the effect of light scattering multiple times before reaching the camera. Accumulation: Accumulate the color contribution using front-to-back compositing, combining single scattering (computed with fine steps) and multiple scattering (computed with adaptive, coarser steps). 5. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the volume or the accumulated transmittance falls below a threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermultiplescattering(volumegrid, lightvolumes, cameraray): # Precomputed constants Cabs = 1.0 # Example value Csca = 1.0 # Example value # Initialize camera path variables s1 = 0.0 l1 = 1.0 # Output color color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Step through the volume # Note: Step size logic differs for single vs multiple scattering components # Single scattering requires small steps; multiple scattering uses adaptive larger steps while s1 < volumegrid.maxdistance: # Get current position pos = cameraray.origin + cameraray.direction s1 # Sample density rho = volumegrid.sample(pos) # Compute coefficients a = Cabs rho b = Csca rho # 1. Single Scattering Contribution (Fine Steps) # Requires small step size to resolve fine features # Compute transmittance and single scatter term #... (Standard single scattering integration)... # 2. Multiple Scattering Contribution (Adaptive Steps) # Step size increases as s1 increases (blur size increases) # Retrieve precomputed light path term # l2 is precomputed for each light source and stored in lightvolumes l2total = 0.0 for light in lights: l2 = lightvolumes[light].sample(pos) l2total += l2 # Apply spatial spreading (PSF blur) # The method approximates multiple scattering by blurring incident radiance # based on distance from camera. blurwidth = calculateblurwidth(s1, a, b) # Derived from path integral analysis blurredradiance = applypsfblur(l2total, blurwidth) # Accumulate multiple scattering # Note: Exact weighting of single vs multiple scattering is not detailed in sources # Assuming a standard front-to-back accumulation where multiple scattering # is added to the single scattering term, weighted by the scattering coefficient. multiplescatterterm = b blurredradiance l1 color += multiplescatterterm stepsize # Update camera path transmittance transmittance = exp(-a stepsize) l1 = transmittance # Adaptive step size for multiple scattering # Step size grows with distance s1 stepsize = calculateadaptivestepsize(s1) s1 += stepsize return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Phase Function Approximation: The method considers only the overall statistics of the phase function, not its particular shape. This results in quantitative differences compared to Monte Carlo simulations. Attenuation Calculation: The computation of multiply scattered light attenuation is not straightforward and may require further investigation for high accuracy. Light Source Count: Precomputing light attenuation volumes for each light source becomes expensive in terms of time and space if there are many light sources. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than Monte Carlo methods. For a complex inhomogeneous scene (800x800 resolution, 9 samples per pixel), rendering took approximately 30 minutes on a 1 GHz Powerbook G4. For a rising smoke example, it took ~10 minutes compared to ~3 hours for Monte Carlo. Memory Complexity: Higher than Monte Carlo. The described implementation uses ~48 Mb (8 Mb density, 32 Mb light volume pyramid, 8 Mb precomputed \ell2) compared to ~8 Mb for Monte Carlo. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of light sources due to the precomputation of light volumes. Strengths: Captures qualitative features like spatial blurring and shadowing efficiently; much faster than Monte Carlo for qualitative results. Limitations: Less quantitative accuracy than Monte Carlo; high memory usage; precomputation cost for many lights. When to Use: When qualitative multiple scattering effects (glow, blurring) are desired and computational time is a constraint, and memory is available. When Not to Use: When quantitative accuracy of phase function effects is critical, or when memory is severely constrained. The method was presented by Preim et al. in "Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media". It addresses the high computational cost of direct numerical simulation of multiple scattering (e.g., via Monte Carlo ray marching) by leveraging spatial spreading. The core innovation is the derivation of a point spread function (PSF) from path integral analysis, which allows for the approximation of multiple scattering effects through blurring rather than explicit path tracing. This approach was shown to be effective for both homogeneous and inhomogeneous media, such as clouds and smoke. PDF Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in ParticipatingMedia, https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs667/2005sp/readings/premoze04.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Intersection Refinement and Search
head: Bisection Refinement, Newton Refinement, Binary Search Surface Tracing
body: This family of methods renders implicit isosurfaces directly from volumetric data by detecting the first ray-surface intersection and refining its position to sub-voxel accuracy, thereby eliminating the "staircasing" artifacts inherent in fixed-step ray marching. It differs from Algebraic Surface Raycasting by relying on numerical root-finding rather than analytic polynomial solving, and from Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer by computing the intersection per-pixel in image order rather than via a global buffer. All methods in this family follow a two-phase traversal strategy: 1. Coarse Detection: The ray is marched with a fixed step size h (or brick-aligned steps) until a sign change in the scalar field g(t) = f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) - \tau is detected, or the field value crosses the threshold \tau. 2. Refinement: The interval [ta, tb] bracketing the intersection is refined to reduce discretization error. The hit position is computed as \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t{hit}\mathbf{d}. 3. Shading: Surface normals are computed via gradients \nabla f (analytic, finite differences, or SDF-specific) and used in local lighting models (Phong/Blinn-Phong). Uses bisection or linear interpolation to refine the hit position after coarse ray marching. Choose this for general scalar volumes where analytic gradients are unavailable. It is the standard approach for basic isosurface raycasting. Combines bisection with Newton's method for sub-pixel accuracy, using Lipschitz constants for robustness. Choose this when high precision is required or when the scalar field is defined by a function with known derivatives. Integrates binary search with GVDB sparse voxel traversal, using SDF gradients for shading. Choose this for sparse datasets where brick-based traversal is necessary to maintain performance. The technique originated as a solution to the aliasing artifacts of early ray marching. It is widely used in medical visualization and scientific rendering where explicit mesh extraction is undesirable.

name: Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement
head: 1st ray of raytracing, First Hit Compositing, First Hit Shader, First-Hit Rendering, Isosurface Ray Marching (VPT), Volumetric Isosurface Rendering, iso surface/volume rendering by volume raycasting
body: Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement is an image-order technique that renders an implicit surface defined by a scalar threshold \tau directly from volumetric data, avoiding explicit polygon mesh extraction. It differs from full volume integration (e.g., Direct Volume Rendering) by stopping the ray traversal at the first detected isosurface intersection, and from Marching Cubes by performing surface detection and shading in a single pass without generating geometry. The method distinguishes itself from basic ray marching by applying intersection refinement (typically bisection) to the detected crossing point, reducing discretization artifacts caused by fixed step sizes. Inputs: Scalar volume data f(\mathbf{p}) stored in a 3D texture. Camera parameters: origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, view/projection matrices. Volume domain bounds [\mathbf{u}{min}, \mathbf{u}{max}]. Parameters: isovalue \tau, ray step size h, refinement iteration count N{ref}. Outputs: Pixel color \mathbf{C} and hit status. Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture sampling f(\mathbf{p}). Typically sampler3D with linear filtering. Uniform Buffer Object (UBO): Contains domain bounds, step size, isovalue, and flags. vec3 uDomainMin, vec3 uDomainMax float uStepSize float uIsovalue int uRefinementIterations int uEnableShadows Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) parameters of the ray with the volume bounding box. If t{max} \le t{min}, the ray misses the volume. t{start} = \max(t{min}, 0.0) t{end} = t{max} 2. Ray Marching (Coarse Detection): Iterate t from t{start} to t{end} with step size h. Sample the scalar field g(t) = f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) - \tau. Detect the first interval [ta, tb] where the sign of g(t) changes, indicating a crossing of the isosurface. \text{Sign Change} \iff g(t{prev}) \cdot g(t{curr}) < 0 Note: Some implementations check for f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau directly, but sign change is more robust for general scalar fields. 3. Intersection Refinement: If a sign change is detected at [ta, tb], refine the hit position using bisection for N{ref} iterations. Set t{mid} = (ta + tb) / 2. Evaluate g(t{mid}). If g(ta) \cdot g(t{mid}) \le 0, set tb = t{mid}. Else, set ta = t{mid}. Final hit parameter: t{hit} = (ta + tb) / 2. Alternative Linear Refinement: Some sources use linear interpolation between the previous and next points to estimate the new intersection X{new}: X{new} = X{prev} + (X{next} - X{prev}) \frac{\tau - f{prev}}{f{next} - f{prev}} This is repeated until convergence or a fixed iteration count. 4. Hit Position: Compute the 3D position of the intersection: \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t{hit} \mathbf{d} 5. Normal Computation: Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n} using central differences with step size h (or a dedicated gradient step). nx = f(\mathbf{p}{hit} + h\mathbf{e}x) - f(\mathbf{p}{hit} - h\mathbf{e}x) ny = f(\mathbf{p}{hit} + h\mathbf{e}y) - f(\mathbf{p}{hit} - h\mathbf{e}y) nz = f(\mathbf{p}{hit} + h\mathbf{e}z) - f(\mathbf{p}{hit} - h\mathbf{e}z) \mathbf{n} = -\frac{\nabla f}{\|\nabla f\|} The negative gradient is used so the normal points outward toward the viewer/light. 6. Shading: Compute the color using a local lighting model (e.g., Blinn-Phong or Lambertian). Lambertian: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}{base} \cdot \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \cdot \mathbf{S}, where \mathbf{l} is the light direction and \mathbf{S} is the shadow factor. Blinn-Phong: Includes ambient, diffuse, and specular components using half-vector \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}). 7. Shadow Ray Traversal (Optional): If enabled, cast a shadow ray from \mathbf{p}{hit} in direction \mathbf{l}. Start at t = 2h to avoid self-intersection artifacts. If the isosurface is encountered before leaving the volume, \mathbf{S} = 0; otherwise \mathbf{S} = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderisosurfaceray(o, d, domainmin, domainmax, volumetex, tau, stepsize, numrefinements, enableshadows): # 1. Ray-Box Intersection tmin, tmax = intersectbox(o, d, domainmin, domainmax) if tmin is None or tmax <= tmin: return None, False tstart = max(tmin, 0.0) tend = tmax # 2. Ray Marching (Coarse Detection) tprev = tstart gprev = samplevolume(o + tprev d, volumetex) - tau tcurr = tprev + stepsize while tcurr <= tend: pcurr = o + tcurr d gcurr = samplevolume(pcurr, volumetex) - tau # Check for sign change if gprev gcurr < 0: # 3. Intersection Refinement (Bisection) ta = tprev tb = tcurr ga = gprev gb = gcurr for in range(numrefinements): tmid = (ta + tb) / 2.0 pmid = o + tmid d gmid = samplevolume(pmid, volumetex) - tau if ga gmid <= 0: tb = tmid gb = gmid else: ta = tmid ga = gmid thit = (ta + tb) / 2.0 phit = o + thit d break else: tprev = tcurr gprev = gcurr tcurr += stepsize else: # No intersection found return None, False # 4. Normal Computation h = stepsize nx = samplevolume(phit + vec3(h, 0, 0), volumetex) - samplevolume(phit - vec3(h, 0, 0), volumetex) ny = samplevolume(phit + vec3(0, h, 0), volumetex) - samplevolume(phit - vec3(0, h, 0), volumetex) nz = samplevolume(phit + vec3(0, 0, h), volumetex) - samplevolume(phit - vec3(0, 0, h), volumetex) normal = normalize(vec3(-nx, -ny, -nz)) # Negative gradient # 5. Shading lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, -1.0)) # Example light direction shadow = 1.0 if enableshadows: # 6. Shadow Ray Traversal shadow = traceshadow(phit, lightdir, domainmin, domainmax, volumetex, tau, stepsize) # Lambertian Shading diffuse = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) color = vec3(1.0) diffuse shadow # Base color white return phit, True def intersectbox(o, d, minb, maxb): tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if d[i] == 0: if o[i] < minb[i] or o[i] > maxb[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (minb[i] - o[i]) / d[i] t2 = (maxb[i] - o[i]) / d[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def samplevolume(p, tex): # Standard 3D texture lookup with linear filtering return tex[p] def traceshadow(origin, lightdir, domainmin, domainmax, volumetex, tau, stepsize): t = 2.0 stepsize # Avoid self-intersection while True: p = origin + t lightdir if p.x < domainmin.x or p.x > domainmax.x or \ p.y < domainmin.y or p.y > domainmax.y or \ p.z < domainmin.z or p.z > domainmax.z: return 1.0 if samplevolume(p, volumetex) >= tau: return 0.0 t += stepsize return 1.0 Parameters: tau (Isovalue): User-defined threshold. Typical values depend on data normalization (e.g., 0.333 for normalized [0,1] data). stepsize: Controls sampling density. Smaller steps increase accuracy but cost more. Typical range: 0.001 to 0.01 in normalized domain. numrefinements: Number of bisection iterations. Typical value: 5-10. enableshadows: Boolean flag for shadow ray computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: Shadow rays must start at t > 0 (e.g., 2h) to prevent the shadow ray from immediately hitting the surface it originated from due to numerical precision. Missed Intersections: If stepsize is too large, the ray may jump over thin structures or sign changes. Discretization Artifacts: Without refinement, the hit position is quantized to the grid, causing "staircasing" or aliasing. Normal Accuracy: Central differences require sampling outside the hit point, which may be expensive or invalid at boundaries. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot N{ref}) per pixel, where N is the number of marching steps to the surface and N{ref} is the refinement count. Shadow rays add a secondary traversal cost. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, plus the volume texture storage. Performance: Faster than full volume rendering because it terminates early. Performance scales with volume resolution and isovalue density. Empty-space skipping (using acceleration structures like uniform grids) can significantly reduce N by skipping regions where the isovalue cannot exist. Strengths: Real-time capable on GPUs; no preprocessing (mesh extraction) required; dynamic isovalue adjustment. Limitations: Sensitive to step size; may miss thin features; normals are approximate. Origin: The method is a fundamental technique in volume visualization, often referred to as "first-hit" rendering. It renders implicit surfaces directly from volumetric data by finding a specific scalar value along a ray. Development: Early implementations used simple thresholding. Refinement techniques (bisection, Newton) were added to improve geometric accuracy. Modern implementations leverage GPU shaders for real-time performance. Usage: Commonly used in medical imaging (virtual endoscopy, bone rendering) and scientific visualization where explicit mesh extraction is undesirable or too slow. What it is: Uses Newton's method in addition to bisection for faster convergence of the intersection point. Difference: Newton's method converges quadratically but requires derivative evaluation and can be unstable; bisection is slower but robust. When to choose: When high precision is needed and the scalar field is smooth and differentiable. name: Robust Iso-surface Rendering via Bisection and Newton Refinement
head: Isosurface Raycasting with Binary Search, Similarity Map Rendering, bisection trace with Newton refinement, isoray rendering pipeline
body:
This method renders volumetric similarity maps by tracing rays to find the first intersection with an isosurface defined by class similarity values, followed by Phong shading. It employs a bisection search for intersection detection after a coarse traversal, optionally refined by Newton's method to achieve sub-pixel accuracy. Unlike methods relying solely on linear interpolation, this approach guarantees robustness through interval arithmetic or Lipschitz-based inclusion functions. Inputs: Scalar field function f(\mathbf{p}) returning value and optionally gradient. Camera parameters: origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, field of view, projection type. Iso-value threshold 	au for the specific class C. Bounding box bounds (\mathbf{lo}, \mathbf{hi}). Parameters: newtoniter (default 3), margin (default 0.01), lipschitz (constant or 'auto'), safety (default 1.5), nsamples (default 10000). Outputs: Color buffer with forward-composited surface colors. Depth buffer. Hit masks and surface normals. Data Structures: TraceResult: Contains position (N, 3), normal (N, 3), t (N,), hit (N, bool). AffineForm (for inclusion functions): x0 (N,), xi (N, K), delta (N,). GradientInclusion: Wraps f and a Lipschitz constant L. Steps: 1. Camera Setup: Compute ray origins and directions for each pixel. For perspective projection, use FOV; for parallel, use extent. 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Compute ray-AABB intersection to get t{min} and t{max}. The AABB is expanded by a margin: 	ext{margin} = (\mathbf{hi} - \mathbf{lo}) 	imes 0.01 \mathbf{aabb\lo} = \mathbf{lo} - 	ext{margin} \mathbf{aabb\hi} = \mathbf{hi} + 	ext{margin} 3. Lipschitz Estimation (if lipschitz='auto'): Estimate L by sampling N points in the bounds, computing gradient norms, and taking the maximum multiplied by a safety factor (default 1.5). L = \max{i} \|
abla f(\mathbf{p}i)\| 	imes 1.5 4. Coarse Traversal: Step along the ray from t{min} until f(\mathbf{p}(t)) \ge 	au. 5. Bisection Search: Perform binary search within the interval [t{start}, t{end}] where the threshold crossing was detected. t{mid} =  rac{t{start} + t{end}}{2} Evaluate f(\mathbf{p}(t{mid})). If f \ge 	au, set t{end} = t{mid}; else t{start} = t{mid}. 6. Newton Refinement (Optional): Apply Newton's method to refine t for sub-pixel accuracy. t{new} = t{old} -  rac{f(\mathbf{p}(t{old})) - 	au}{
abla f(\mathbf{p}(t{old})) \cdot \mathbf{d}} Repeat for newtoniter iterations. 7. Normal Computation: Compute surface normal \mathbf{n} at the hit position \mathbf{p}{hit}. If f provides analytic gradient: \mathbf{n} = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}{hit}). Else, use centered finite differences with step h=10^{-5}: \mathbf{n} =  rac{1}{2h}  egin{bmatrix} f(\mathbf{p}+h\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{p}-h\mathbf{x}) \ f(\mathbf{p}+h\mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{p}-h\mathbf{y}) \ f(\mathbf{p}+h\mathbf{z}) - f(\mathbf{p}-h\mathbf{z}) \end{bmatrix} Normalize \mathbf{n}, clamping norm to \ge 10^{-12} to prevent division by zero. 8. Shading: Compute color using Phong model with ambient, diffuse, and specular components. Cast shadow ray to light source. 9. Compositing: Blend surface color onto output buffer using forward compositing. Continue raycasting until early ray termination threshold is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rayaabbintersect(origins, directions, aabblo, aabbhi): """Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection.""" directions = np.where(directions == 0, 1e-12, directions) t1 = (aabblo - origins) / directions t2 = (aabbhi - origins) / directions tenter = np.maximum(t1, t2).min(axis=1) texit = np.minimum(t1, t2).max(axis=1) tmin = np.maximum(tenter, 0.0) tmax = np.minimum(texit, np.inf) hitmask = tmin <= tmax return tmin, tmax, hitmask def centereddifferencenormals(f, pos, h=1e-5): """Compute surface normals via centered difference.""" N = pos.shape[0] offsets = np.array([[h, 0, 0], [-h, 0, 0], [0, h, 0], [0, -h, 0], [0, 0, h], [0, 0, -h]], dtype=pos.dtype) allpoints = (pos[None,:,:] + offsets[:, None,:]).reshape(6 N, 3) allvals, = f(allpoints) v = allvals.reshape(6, N) gradx = (v[0] - v[1]) / (2.0 h) grady = (v[2] - v[3]) / (2.0 h) gradz = (v[4] - v[5]) / (2.0 h) normals = np.stack([gradx, grady, gradz], axis=1) norms = np.linalg.norm(normals, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-12) return normals / norms def estimatelipschitz(f, bounds, nsamples=10000, safety=1.5, h=1e-5): """Estimate Lipschitz constant over bounding box.""" lo, hi = bounds rng = np.random.defaultrng() pts = rng.uniform(lo, hi, (nsamples, 3)) vals, grads = f(pts) if grads is not None: gradnorms = np.linalg.norm(grads, axis=1) else: offsets = np.array([[h, 0, 0], [-h, 0, 0], [0, h, 0], [0, -h, 0], [0, 0, h], [0, 0, -h]], dtype=np.float64) allpoints = (pts[None,:,:] + offsets[:, None,:]).reshape(6 nsamples, 3) allvals, = f(allpoints) v = allvals.reshape(6, nsamples) gx = (v[0] - v[1]) / (2.0 h) gy = (v[2] - v[3]) / (2.0 h) gz = (v[4] - v[5]) / (2.0 h) gradnorms = np.sqrt(gx2 + gy2 + gz2) return float(gradnorms.max() safety) def bisecttrace(f, origins, directions, tmin, tmax, tau, coarsestep=0.01, maxiter=30): """Coarse traversal followed by bisection search for isosurface intersection.""" # Coarse traversal t = tmin.copy() positions = origins + t[:, None] directions vals, = f(positions) while np.any(vals < tau) & np.any(t < tmax): t = np.minimum(t + coarsestep, tmax) positions = origins + t[:, None] directions vals, = f(positions) # Bisection search on the interval where crossing occurred tstart = tmin.copy() tend = t.copy() for in range(maxiter): tmid = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 positions = origins + tmid[:, None] directions vals, = f(positions) inside = vals >= tau tstart[inside] = tmid[inside] tend[~inside] = tmid[~inside] return tmid def newtonrefine(f, origins, directions, t, tau, iterations): """Refine intersection parameter t using Newton's method.""" for in range(iterations): positions = origins + t[:, None] directions vals, grads = f(positions) dvaldt = np.sum(grads directions, axis=1) dvaldt = np.maximum(np.abs(dvaldt), 1e-12) np.sign(dvaldt) t = t - (vals - tau) / dvaldt return t def shadephong(normals, hit, lightdir, viewdir, ambient, diffusecolor, specularcolor, shininess): """Simple Phong shading.""" color = np.zeroslike(ambient) if not hit.any(): return color n = normals[hit] l = lightdir[hit] v = viewdir[hit] r = 2.0 np.sum(n l, axis=1, keepdims=True) n - l diff = np.maximum(np.sum(n l, axis=1), 0.0) spec = np.maximum(np.sum(r v, axis=1), 0.0) shininess color[hit] = ambient + diff diffusecolor + spec specularcolor return np.clip(color, 0.0, 1.0) def robustisosurfacerender( f, bounds, origins, directions, tau, newtoniter=3, margin=0.01, lipschitz='auto', safety=1.5, nsamples=10000, ambient=0.2, diffusecolor=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), specularcolor=np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]), shininess=32.0): lo, hi = bounds marginvec = (hi - lo) margin aabblo = lo - marginvec aabbhi = hi + marginvec tmin, tmax, hitmask = rayaabbintersect(origins, directions, aabblo, aabbhi) if lipschitz == 'auto': L = estimatelipschitz(f, bounds, nsamples, safety) else: L = lipschitz thit = bisecttrace(f, origins, directions, tmin, tmax, tau) if newtoniter > 0: thit = newtonrefine(f, origins, directions, thit, tau, newtoniter) normals = np.zeroslike(origins) validhits = np.isfinite(thit) & hitmask if validhits.any(): hitpositions = origins[validhits] + thit[validhits, None] directions[validhits] vals, grads = f(hitpositions) if grads is None: grads = centereddifferencenormals(f, hitpositions) norms = np.linalg.norm(grads, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-12) normals[validhits] = grads / norms lightdir = np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) viewdir = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) color = shadephong(normals, validhits, lightdir, viewdir, ambient, diffusecolor, specularcolor, shininess) return thit, normals, validhits, color An optional post-processing step applied after the bisection phase to achieve sub-pixel hit-point accuracy by iteratively correcting the position using directional derivatives. Time Complexity: Bisection is O(\log(1/\epsilon)) per ray for precision \epsilon. Newton refinement adds O(k) where k is the number of iterations. Lipschitz estimation is O(N) where N is sample count. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing ray data and results. Affine arithmetic variants may require O(K) per point for noise symbols. Performance: Post-processing (bilateral solver) takes ~0.4s for 256^3 and ~5.3s for 512^3 on Intel i7-8700K. Rendering speed depends on ray count and refinement steps. Strengths: Robust intersection detection; sub-pixel accuracy; handles complex implicit surfaces well. Limitations: Requires differentiable or gradient-accessible functions for Newton refinement; Lipschitz estimation can be costly if done per-frame. When to use: High-quality offline rendering or interactive annotation where precision is critical. This method originates from work on segmentation-based transfer function design, leveraging self-supervised vision transformers to generate similarity maps that are subsequently rendered using robust isosurface raycasting. The implementation details, including the bisection and Newton refinement pipeline, are documented in the isoray package. Leveraging Self-Supervised Vision Transformers for Segmentation-Based Transfer Function Design., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2024.3401755, fetched 2026-10-26 GitHub - narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering: Robust iso-surface..., https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Newton Refinement
head: Post-bisection refinement
body:
Newton Refinement is an optional post-processing step applied after the bisection phase of robust iso-surface rendering to achieve sub-pixel hit-point accuracy. It improves the precision of the intersection point t found by the bisection tracer by iteratively applying Newton's method using directional derivatives. Unlike the bisection method, which guarantees convergence within a bounded interval but may leave a residual error proportional to the voxel size or iteration limit, Newton Refinement converges quadratically near the root, reducing the error significantly with few iterations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The approximate hit position t{approx} (scalar) and position p{approx} (3D vector) from the bisection step, the ray origin o, the ray direction d, the implicit function f(x), its gradient 
abla f(x), and the bisection interval bounds [t{lo}, t{hi}]. Output: Refined hit position t{new} and p{new}. Data Structures: t: Scalar float64 representing the ray parameter. p: Vector (x, y, z) float64 representing the 3D position. f: Function evaluating the implicit field value at a point. 
abla f: Function evaluating the gradient vector at a point. Parameters: newtoniter: Number of Newton refinement iterations to perform. Default value is 3. Set to 0 to disable. tol: Convergence tolerance for the function value or step size. Default 10^{-6}. Steps: 1. Initialize t = t{approx} and compute p = o + t \cdot d. 2. For i from 0 to newtoniter - 1: a. Evaluate the implicit function value at the current position: val = f(p). b. Evaluate the gradient at the current position: grad = 
abla f(p). c. Compute the directional derivative along the ray: f' = grad \cdot d. d. If |f'| < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold, e.g., 10^{-12}), break the loop to avoid division by zero or divergence. e. Compute the Newton step: \Delta t = -val / f'. f. Update t = t + \Delta t and clamp t to [t{lo}, t{hi}] to prevent jumping outside the bisection interval. g. Update p = o + t \cdot d. h. If |val| < tol or |\Delta t| < tol, break the loop. 3. Return t and p. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def newtonrefine(t, origin, direction, f, gradf, tlo, thi, maxiter=3, eps=1e-12, tol=1e-6): """ Refine hit point t using Newton's method. Args: t: Initial ray parameter from bisection. origin: Ray origin (3D vector). direction: Ray direction (3D vector, assumed normalized). f: Function returning scalar field value at 3D point. gradf: Function returning gradient vector at 3D point. tlo, thi: Bisection interval bounds. maxiter: Number of iterations. eps: Minimum absolute directional derivative to avoid division by zero. tol: Convergence tolerance. Returns: Refined t and position p. """ p = [origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], origin[2] + t direction[2]] for in range(maxiter): val = f(p) g = gradf(p) # Directional derivative fdot = g[0] direction[0] + g[1] direction[1] + g[2] direction[2] # Guard against zero or near-zero derivative if abs(fdot) < eps: break # Newton step dt = -val / fdot t = t + dt # Clamp to bisection interval to prevent divergence if t < tlo: t = tlo elif t > thi: t = thi # Update position p = [origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], origin[2] + t direction[2]] # Convergence check if abs(val) < tol or abs(dt) < tol: break return t, p Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the gradient is not available or is zero, Newton's method may fail or diverge. The method assumes the implicit function is differentiable at the hit point. The method is optional and not implemented in all core loops; it must be explicitly called after bisection. Without clamping to the bisection interval [t{lo}, t{hi}] or a convergence threshold, Newton steps can overshoot, diverge, or produce inf values on degenerate inputs. Predictive Newton Termination is a Newton iteration mode that terminates a vertex step if the predicted next error falls below a tenth of the tolerance, avoiding a confirming function evaluation. It differs from Newton Refinement by using a heuristic error prediction instead of a direct convergence check, and from Guaranteed Interval-Based Refinement Test by relying on local derivative estimates rather than interval arithmetic. The method trades a slight increase in residual error for fewer evaluations per vertex. Ray Marching with Newton Localization is a ray tracing approach to find the first parameter along a ray where the field value equals the isovalue c, by isolating the root via sign change detection and localizing it precisely. The behavior is highly correlated to the chosen step size: small steps make the method computationally expensive, while larger step sizes can miss isosurface crossings. Newton Marching is a new method designed for this project, based on the Newton method to intersect flat surfaces more quickly. Forward Newton Marching is a new method designed for this project, based on the Newton method to intersect flat surfaces more quickly. The Newton Projection Step for Mesh Refinement is a technique used in Primal Adaptive Meshing to collapse points to the 0.5-isosurface of the vacancy function v. It defines an auxiliary function f(x) = (0.5 - v(x))^2, linearizes it around xi, and restricts updates to the gradient direction. The update rule is x{i+1} = xi +  rac{0.5 - v(xi)}{2} \mathcal{N}(xi), where \mathcal{N}(x) = 
abla v(x)/\|
abla v(x)\|^2. The scalar step is t =  rac{0.5 - v(xi)}{2\|
abla v(xi)\|^2}. The target isosurface value is 0.5. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of Newton iterations (typically 3). Each iteration requires one function evaluation and one gradient evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays and iterations. Strengths: Provides sub-pixel accuracy, fast convergence near the root. Limitations: Requires differentiable implicit functions, may diverge if gradients are zero or unavailable. When to use: When high precision is required and the implicit function is smooth and differentiable. When not to use: When the gradient is unavailable or the surface is non-differentiable. Newton Refinement was introduced as part of the isoray library for robust iso-surface rendering. It is an optional feature that can be enabled by setting newtoniter to a positive value. The method builds on the standard Newton-Raphson root-finding algorithm, adapted for ray tracing by using the directional derivative along the ray. name: Predictive Newton Termination
head: iso_newton mode 2
body: Predictive Newton Termination is a Newton iteration mode that terminates a vertex step if the predicted next error falls below a tenth of the tolerance, avoiding a confirming function evaluation. It differs from Newton Refinement by using a heuristic error prediction instead of a direct convergence check, and from Guaranteed Interval-Based Refinement Test by relying on local derivative estimates rather than interval arithmetic. The method trades a slight increase in residual error for fewer evaluations per vertex. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current position x, function value f, gradient magnitude |f'|, step size s from the previous iteration, and convergence tolerance \tau. Outputs: Boolean termination flag, and if terminated, the surface normal computed from the gradient of the previous evaluation. Data Structures: Vertex status flags: 1 for converged (confirmed), 2 for predicted termination. Steps: 1. Compute the predicted error for the next Newton step using the formula below. 2. Compare the predicted error against \tau / 10. 3. If the predicted error is below the threshold, mark the vertex for termination with flag 2 and skip the next function evaluation. 4. If the vertex is marked for termination, compute the surface normal using the gradient from the previous evaluation (the one that produced f and |f'|). Formula: For exponentially decaying fields, the predicted error E{pred} is calculated as: E{pred} = \frac{|f'|}{2 |f|} s^2 where |f'| is the gradient magnitude, |f| is the absolute function value, and s is the step size taken in the previous iteration. Parameters: Convergence tolerance \tau: typical value 10^{-4} h. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flag Mixing Bug: In GPU implementations using group-based execution, evaluators originally skipped a group of 64 vertices when the bitwise AND of their vdone flags was set. A mix of flag 1 (converged) and flag 2 (predicted) cleared the AND to 0, causing the group to run in full after convergence. The fix treats any nonzero flag as a termination signal. Normal Accuracy: Since the normal is taken from the previous evaluation, it is not updated for the final predicted position. Field Assumption: The error formula assumes exponentially decaying fields. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictivetermination(fval, gradmag, stepsize, tolerance): """Predictive Newton Termination check. Returns True if the vertex should terminate early.""" if abs(fval) < 1e-15: # Guard against division by zero return True predictederror = (gradmag / (2.0 abs(fval))) (stepsize 2) return predictederror < (tolerance / 10.0) A method using interval arithmetic and Krawczyk's formulation to guarantee the existence and uniqueness of a solution within an interval \mathbf{X}, or to prune intervals that cannot contain a solution. It differs from Predictive Newton Termination by providing rigorous mathematical guarantees rather than heuristic predictions. It is chosen when robustness is critical and computational overhead is acceptable. Definition: Uses interval extensions of Newton-Raphson iteration. Steps: 1. Prune interval \mathbf{X} if \emptyset \notin \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) OR \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{X}) \cap \mathbf{X} = \emptyset. 2. Switch to ordinary 2D Newton iteration if \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{X}) \subseteq \mathbf{X} AND \|I - \mathbf{M}^+ \mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X})\| < 1. This guarantees exactly one unique solution in \mathbf{X} and convergence. 3. If neither condition is met, recursively subdivide the triangle and keep searching. Formula: \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{X}) = m0 - \mathbf{M}^+ f(m0) + I - \mathbf{M}^+ \mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X}) where m0 = m(\mathbf{X}) is the midpoint of interval \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{M} = m(\mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X})) is the midpoint of the interval Jacobian, \mathbf{M}^+ is its pseudoinverse, \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) is the interval representation of f, and \mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X}) is the interval Jacobian. Performance: Reduces evaluations per vertex from 2.0–2.6 to 1.3–2.0 on test datasets (amide/mol) at grid spacings h=0.2 and h=0.12. Accuracy: Largest vertex residual was 1.4 \times 10^{-4} h with a tolerance of 10^{-4} h. Complexity: Time complexity is reduced by avoiding one function evaluation per vertex in predicted cases, while memory complexity remains unchanged. Strengths: Significant speedup in GPU implementations where function evaluation is expensive. Limitations: Provides no guarantee of convergence to the exact root, and residual error may exceed tolerance slightly. Relies on the validity of the error prediction model for exponentially decaying fields. Predictive Newton Termination was introduced in the context of optimized GPU isosurface extraction, specifically in the mdgtoisogpu implementation. It is part of the isonewton mode 2. The method addresses the cost of redundant function evaluations in Newton refinement loops. The associated bug fix regarding vertex group flags was also part of this optimization effort. mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Single Scattering in Refractive Media with Triangle Mesh Boundaries, https://doi.org/10.1145/1531326.1531398, fetched 2026-10-26
