name: GVDB Raycasting with Binary Search Surface Tracing
head: GVDB Shading and Screen-Space Flow/Depth, SDF Raycast with Binary Search Refinement, custom_iso_kernel shading, flow computation, raySurfaceTrilinearBrickCustom
body: A GPU-based raycasting method that traces rays through a GVDB sparse voxel dataset to find the first intersection with an isosurface defined by a Signed Distance Field (SDF) channel. It employs a coarse grid-based ray march followed by a binary search refinement to locate the surface, then computes surface normals, shading, and screen-space flow. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific integration with the GVDB sparse voxel architecture, utilizing brick-based traversal and explicit SDF gradient computation for shading, rather than raw voxel intensity or algebraic surface approximations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: GVDB sparse voxel dataset containing an SDF channel (VoxelBuffer::CHANNELSDF), view matrices (current and next for flow), light direction, eye direction, isosurface threshold (SCNTHRESH), and rendering parameters (viewport, binary search steps, specular exponent). Output: Per-pixel buffers containing hit position, surface normal, color (ambient + diffuse + specular), screen-space flow vector, and depth. Data Structures: VolumeSampler: A functor wrapping a reference to VoxelData. It provides an operator () that takes a 3D integer position pos and retrieves the SDF value from the SDF channel using data.getvoxel(pos, VoxelBuffer::CHANNELSDF, defval), where defval.f is a constant representing a value far outside the surface (e.g., constants::SDFFAROUTSIDE). GVDB Node: Represents a sparse voxel brick. Contains bounds (vmin, vdel) and an atlas offset for texture sampling. Parameters: SCNTHRESH: Isosurface threshold. Sampling values \ge this indicate volume interior. SCNPSTEP: Fixed step size for coarse ray marching, aligned to brick boundaries. binarySearchSteps: Number of binary search iterations for refinement. Typical value: 10. specularExponent: Shininess exponent for Blinn-Phong specular highlight. viewport: Valid pixel range [minX, minY, maxX, maxY]. normalenabled: Boolean flag to enable/disable normal calculation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel in the viewport, compute ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} from the view matrices. 2. Coarse Marching: Call raySurfaceTrilinearBrickCustom. Get the leaf node and atlas offset for the current ray position. Convert world position \mathbf{p}{world} to index coordinates p using: p = \frac{\mathbf{p}{world} - \mathbf{v}{min}}{\mathbf{v}{del}[0]} where \mathbf{v}{min} is node minimum bounds and \mathbf{v}{del}[0] is voxel size. Step the ray by SCNPSTEP. At each step, sample the SDF using tex3D at the offset position. Pitfall: Voxels influenced by marching cubes are centered on their lower corner, extending 0.5 units. To prevent missing voxels due to interpolation artifacts, offset the ray sampling position by (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). If tex3D value \ge SCNTHRESH, a hit is detected. Record hitdistanceprev (previous distance) and hitdistance (current distance). If the ray exceeds volume bounds (p.x/y/z < 0 or \ge gvdb->res[0]) or hits an invalid node, terminate and return no hit. 3. Binary Search Refinement: If a hit was detected and binarySearchSteps > 0: Define interval [t{lower}, t{upper}] = [\text{hit\distance\prev}, \text{hit\distance}]. Let \mathbf{p}{start} be the ray origin at the start of the coarse step, and \mathbf{dir} be the ray direction. Adjust Start Point: If the SDF at \mathbf{p}{start} + t{lower} \cdot \mathbf{dir} is negative (below surface), step back by 0.5 units up to 4 times until the SDF is positive. Adjust End Point: If the SDF at \mathbf{p}{start} + t{upper} \cdot \mathbf{dir} is positive (above surface), step forward by 0.5 units up to 4 times until the SDF is negative. Loop: For i from 0 to binarySearchSteps - 1: Calculate midpoint distance: t{middle} = 0.5 \cdot (t{lower} + t{upper}). Evaluate position: \mathbf{p}{mid} = \mathbf{p}{start} + t{middle} \cdot \mathbf{dir}. Sample SDF at \mathbf{p}{mid} (with 0.5 offset). If SDF \ge SCNTHRESH (inside), set t{upper} = t{middle}. Else (outside), set t{lower} = t{middle}. Final Position: Select the distance t{final} corresponding to the endpoint with the smaller absolute SDF value (typically t{lower} if the interval brackets the surface correctly). Compute final hit point: \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{p}{start} + t{final} \cdot \mathbf{dir}. 4. Normal Computation: If normalenabled: Compute the gradient \nabla f at \mathbf{p}{hit} using getinterpolatedrawsdfgradient. Normalize the gradient to get the surface normal \mathbf{n}. 5. Shading: Ambient: Start with ambientColor. Diffuse: Add diffuseColor max(0.0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}), where \mathbf{l} is the light direction. Specular: Compute reflection vector \mathbf{R} = \text{normalize}(2(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{l}). Compute eye direction \mathbf{E} (from hit point to camera). Add specular term: c{spec} \cdot \frac{\alpha + 2}{6.82} \cdot \max(0, \mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{E})^\alpha where c{spec} is specular color and \alpha is specularExponent. Note: The constant 6.82 is 2 \times 3.41. 6. Flow and Depth: Project \mathbf{p}{hit} into screen space using current view matrix to get \mathbf{s}{current} and next view matrix to get \mathbf{s}{next}. Compute flow: \text{flow} = 0.5 \cdot (\mathbf{s}{current} - \mathbf{s}{next}). Compute depth from \mathbf{s}{current}.z. 7. Output: Write hit point, normal, color, flow, and depth to the output buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gvdbraytracebinarysearch(rayorigin, raydir, gvdbdata, params): """ rayorigin: tuple (ox, oy, oz) raydir: tuple (dx, dy, dz) gvdbdata: object with res, getnodeatpoint, samplesdf, getinterpolatedrawsdfgradient params: object containing SCNTHRESH, SCNPSTEP, binarySearchSteps, specularExponent, etc. """ tcurrent = 0.0 pstart = rayorigin hitfound = False tlower = 0.0 tupper = 0.0 # Coarse Marching while True: pworld = (pstart[0] + tcurrent raydir[0], pstart[1] + tcurrent raydir[1], pstart[2] + tcurrent raydir[2]) # Check bounds if not (0 <= pworld[0] < gvdbdata.res[0] and 0 <= pworld[1] < gvdbdata.res[1] and 0 <= pworld[2] < gvdbdata.res[2]): break node = gvdbdata.getnodeatpoint(pworld) if node is None: break # Convert to index coordinates pidx = ((pworld[0] - node.vmin[0]) / node.vdel[0], (pworld[1] - node.vmin[1]) / node.vdel[1], (pworld[2] - node.vmin[2]) / node.vdel[2]) # Sample SDF with 0.5 offset sdfval = gvdbdata.samplesdf(pidx[0] + 0.5, pidx[1] + 0.5, pidx[2] + 0.5, node) if sdfval >= params.SCNTHRESH: tlower = tcurrent - params.SCNPSTEP tupper = tcurrent hitfound = True break tcurrent += params.SCNPSTEP if not hitfound: return None, None, None, None, None # Binary Search Refinement # Adjust start point (tlower) if SDF is negative pos0 = (pstart[0] + tlower raydir[0], pstart[1] + tlower raydir[1], pstart[2] + tlower raydir[2]) for in range(4): pidx0 = ((pos0[0] - 0.5 raydir[0], pos0[1] - 0.5 raydir[1], pos0[2] - 0.5 raydir[2]) else: break # Adjust end point (tupper) if SDF is positive pos1 = (pstart[0] + tupper raydir[0], pstart[1] + tupper raydir[1], pstart[2] + tupper raydir[2]) for in range(4): pidx1 = ((pos1[0] - node.vmin[0]) / node.vdel[0] + 0.5, (pos1[1] - node.vmin[1]) / node.vdel[1] + 0.5, (pos1[2] - node.vmin[2]) / node.vdel[2] + 0.5) if gvdbdata.samplesdf(pidx1[0], pidx1[1], pidx1[2], node) > 0: pos1 = (pos1[0] + 0.5 raydir[0], pos1[1] + 0.5 raydir[1], pos1[2] + 0.5 raydir[2]) else: break for i in range(params.binarySearchSteps): tmiddle = 0.5 (tlower + tupper) pmid = (pstart[0] + tmiddle raydir[0], pstart[1] + tmiddle raydir[1], pstart[2] + tmiddle raydir[2]) pidxmid = ((pmid[0] - node.vmin[0]) / node.vdel[0] + 0.5, (pmid[1] - node.vmin[1]) / node.vdel[1] + 0.5, (pmid[2] - node.vmin[2]) / node.vdel[2] + 0.5) sdfmid = gvdbdata.samplesdf(pidxmid[0], pidxmid[1], pidxmid[2], node) if sdfmid >= params.SCNTHRESH: tupper = tmiddle else: tlower = tmiddle # Select final distance plower = (pstart[0] + tlower raydir[0], pstart[1] + tlower raydir[1], pstart[2] + tlower raydir[2]) pupper = (pstart[0] + tupper raydir[0], pstart[1] + tupper raydir[1], pstart[2] + tupper raydir[2]) pidxlower = ((plower[0] - node.vmin[0]) / node.vdel[0] + 0.5, (plower[1] - node.vmin[1]) / node.vdel[1] + 0.5, (plower[2] - node.vmin[2]) / node.vdel[2] + 0.5) pidxupper = ((pupper[0] - node.vmin[0]) / node.vdel[0] + 0.5, (pupper[1] - node.vmin[1]) / node.vdel[1] + 0.5, (pupper[2] - node.vmin[2]) / node.vdel[2] + 0.5) sdflower = gvdbdata.samplesdf(pidxlower[0], pidxlower[1], pidxlower[2], node) sdfupper = gvdbdata.samplesdf(pidxupper[0], pidxupper[1], pidxupper[2], node) if abs(sdflower) < abs(sdfupper): tfinal = tlower phit = plower else: tfinal = tupper phit = pupper # Normal Computation normal = None if params.normalenabled: grad = gvdbdata.getinterpolatedrawsdfgradient(phit) mag = (grad[0]2 + grad[1]2 + grad[2]2)0.5 if mag > 0: normal = (grad[0]/mag, grad[1]/mag, grad[2]/mag) else: normal = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) # Shading ambient = params.ambientColor diffuse = params.diffuseColor max(0.0, normal[0]params.lightDir[0] + normal[1]params.lightDir[1] + normal[2]params.lightDir[2]) # R = 2 dot(N, L) N - screennext[0]), 0.5 (screencurrent[1] - screennext[1])) depth = screencurrent[2] return phit, normal, color, flow, depth def projecttoscreen(point, viewmatrix): # Standard perspective projection x, y, z = point w = viewmatrix[3][0]x + viewmatrix[3][1]y + viewmatrix[3][2]z + viewmatrix[3][3] if w == 0: w = 1e-6 return (viewmatrix[0][0]x + viewmatrix[0][1]y + viewmatrix[0][2]z + viewmatrix[0][3]) / w, \ (viewmatrix[1][0]x + viewmatrix[1][1]y + viewmatrix[1][2]z + viewmatrix[1][3]) / w, \ (viewmatrix[2][0]x + viewmatrix[2][1]y + viewmatrix[2][2]z + viewmatrix[2][3]) / w Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of coarse steps plus binary search iterations. The coarse step size SCNPSTEP determines N. Binary search adds a constant factor (typically 10 iterations). Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the kernel state, plus the memory required for the GVDB sparse voxel structure. Performance: Fast for sparse datasets due to GVDB's sparse traversal. The binary search provides high precision without excessive sampling. Strengths: Robust surface detection with SDF, efficient sparse voxel traversal, accurate normals via SDF gradient, supports screen-space flow for temporal effects. Limitations: Requires SDF channel in GVDB. Coarse marching may miss very thin features if SCNPSTEP is too large. Precision depends on binarySearchSteps. This method is part of the Godot Voxel plugin ecosystem, specifically leveraging the GVDB (GPU Voxel Database) sparse voxel architecture. It is used for real-time isosurface rendering in voxel-based environments, providing shading and flow information for visual effects. name: Supersegment Search with Spatial Smoothness
head: Adjacency Search, Finding the first supersegment on a ray, Optimized supersegment search
body: Supersegment Search with Spatial Smoothness is an algorithm for finding the first supersegment intersected by a ray in a sorted list \mathbb{L}i by leveraging the spatial coherence of volume data. It minimizes memory accesses and thread divergence by using the index p of the last intersected supersegment in the previous list \mathbb{L}h as an initial guess. Unlike standard binary search which seeds at the middle, or linear search which starts at the beginning, this method prunes the search space based on the depth boundaries of the candidate supersegment and its predecessor. It yields up to 40% better frame rates compared to the best-performing baseline (linear or binary search) for finding the first supersegment. Inputs: d{entry}: Entry intercept of the ray in \mathbb{L}i (in NDC). d{exit}: Exit intercept of the ray in \mathbb{L}i. p: Index of the last supersegment intersected in the previous list \mathbb{L}h. If no supersegment was intersected in \mathbb{L}h, p is the index of the closest supersegment from the previous exit point. maxSupersegments: Total number of supersegments in the current list \mathbb{L}i. b(Sj): Function returning the back-depth (exit boundary) of supersegment Sj. f(Sj): Function returning the front-depth (entry boundary) of supersegment Sj. Outputs: index: The index j of the first supersegment Sj intersected in \mathbb{L}i. Returns -1 if no such supersegment exists. supseg\found: Boolean flag indicating if a valid supersegment was found. Data Structures: The supersegments in \mathbb{L}i are sorted by position. The algorithm assumes access to the depth boundaries b(Sj) and front depths f(Sj) for any index j within [0, maxSupersegments - 1]. Algorithm Steps: 1. If \mathbb{L}i is the first list intersected by the ray, perform a binary search from index 0 to maxSupersegments - 1 to find the first intersected supersegment. 2. If not the first list, retrieve p. 3. Initialize bin\search\end = -1 and bin\search\start = -1. 4. If p is negative (invalid): Set bin\search\end = maxSupersegments - 1. Set bin\search\start = 0. 5. Else (p is valid): Pre-fetch b1 = b(Sp^i) if Sp^i exists, else \infty. Pre-fetch b0 = b(S{p-1}^i) if S{p-1}^i exists, else -\infty. Calculate interval = (b1 \ge d{entry}) + (b0 \ge d{entry}). If interval is 0: The intersecting supersegment is behind Sp^i. Set bin\search\end = maxSupersegments - 1. Set bin\search\start = p + 1. Else if interval is 2: The intersecting supersegment is in front of S{p-1}^i. Set bin\search\end = p - 1. Set bin\search\start = 0. Else (interval is 1): The entry point d{entry} lies between b0 and b1. If b1 < \infty (i.e., Sp^i exists): Set supseg\found = true. Set index = p. Set depthEnd = b1. Return index. Else (Sp^i does not exist): Set bin\search\end = p - 1. Set bin\search\start = 0. 6. If bin\search\end \neq -1: Call BinS(d{entry}, bin\search\start, bin\search\end) to get index. BinS(d, start, stop) is a binary search function returning an index j such that b(S{j-1}) < d < b(Sj), limited to start \le j \le stop. 7. Get depthStart = f(S{index}). 8. If depthStart > d{exit}: The ray passes between supersegments without intersecting any. Set supseg\found = false. Set index = -1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findfirstsupersegment(dentry, dexit, p, maxsupersegments, bfunc, ffunc): """ Finds the first supersegment intersected in list Li. Args: dentry: Entry intercept of the ray in Li (in NDC). dexit: Exit intercept of the ray in Li. p: Index of the last supersegment intersected in the previous list Lh. If no supersegment was intersected in Lh, p is the index of the closest supersegment from the previous exit point. maxsupersegments: Total number of supersegments in the current list Li. bfunc: Function returning the back-depth (exit boundary) of a supersegment. ffunc: Function returning the front-depth (entry boundary) of a supersegment. Returns: index: The index of the first intersected supersegment, or -1 if none. supsegfound: Boolean indicating if a valid supersegment was found. """ binsearchend = -1 binsearchstart = -1 if p < 0: # Invalid p, search full range binsearchend = maxsupersegments - 1 binsearchstart = 0 else: # Pre-fetch boundaries for Sp and S{p-1} # Handle boundary conditions where indices might be out of bounds if 0 <= p < maxsupersegments: b1 = bfunc(p) else: b1 = float('inf') if 0 <= p - 1 < maxsupersegments: b0 = bfunc(p - 1) else: b0 = float('-inf') # Calculate interval based on where dentry lies relative to b0 and b1 # interval = 0: dentry < b0 and dentry < b1 (behind Sp) # interval = 2: dentry >= b0 and dentry >= b1 (in front of S{p-1}) # interval = 1: dentry is between b0 and b1 interval = (1 if b1 >= dentry else 0) + (1 if b0 >= dentry else 0) if interval == 0: # Ray is behind Sp binsearchend = maxsupersegments - 1 binsearchstart = p + 1 elif interval == 2: # Ray is in front of S{p-1} binsearchend = p - 1 binsearchstart = 0 else: # Ray is between b0 and b1 if b1 < float('inf'): # Sp exists and contains the entry point return p, True else: # Sp does not exist, search in front of p binsearchend = p - 1 binsearchstart = 0 index = -1 supsegfound = False if binsearchend != -1: # Perform binary search in the pruned range index = binarysearch(dentry, binsearchstart, binsearchend, bfunc) # Verify the found supersegment actually intersects the ray if 0 <= index < maxsupersegments: depthstart = ffunc(index) if depthstart > dexit: # Ray passes between supersegments supsegfound = False index = -1 else: supsegfound = True else: supsegfound = False return index, supsegfound def binarysearch(d, start, stop, bfunc): """ Binary search for the first supersegment Sj such that b(S{j-1}) < d < b(Sj). Limited to start <= j <= stop. """ low = start high = stop result = -1 while low <= high: mid = (low + high) // 2 # Check if Smid is the candidate # We need b(S{mid-1}) < d < b(Smid) # Get b(S{mid-1}) if mid - 1 >= 0: bprev = bfunc(mid - 1) else: bprev = float('-inf') # Get b(Smid) bcurr = bfunc(mid) if bprev < d < bcurr: result = mid break elif d <= bprev: # d is in front of Smid, search lower indices high = mid - 1 else: # d is behind Smid, search higher indices low = mid + 1 return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If p is invalid (negative), the search defaults to the full list range. If the determined supersegment's front-depth is greater than the ray's exit distance (d{exit}), the ray passes between supersegments; index is set to -1 and supseg\found to false. If Sp^i does not exist, b1 is set to \infty and a binary search is performed. If S{p-1}^i does not exist, b0 is set to -\infty. The algorithm assumes the angle between the intersecting ray and the original ray is less than 90^\circ, but is applicable in both cases. Time Complexity: The algorithm reduces memory accesses compared to a simple binary search seeded at the middle element. In the best case (when Sp^i is the correct supersegment), it is O(1). In the worst case, it performs a binary search, which is O(\log NS). Measured Performance: Algorithm 1 yields up to 40% better frame rates compared to the best-performing baseline (linear or binary search) for finding the first supersegment. Strengths: Minimizes memory accesses and thread divergence by leveraging spatial smoothness. Reduces the search space for binary search by using the previous list's result as a seed. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that neighboring lists have similar supersegment sizes (spatial smoothness). If this assumption is violated, the performance gain may be reduced. When to use: When rendering volumetric depth images (VDI) or similar volume data where rays are processed in lists and spatial coherence is high. When not to use: When the volume data lacks spatial smoothness or when the ray lists are not processed in a coherent order. The method was introduced in "Efficient Raycasting of Volumetric Depth Images for Remote Visualization of Large Volumes at High Frame Rates" by Gupta and Sbalzarini (2023). It is part of a pipeline that uses the fast voxel traversal algorithm by Amanatides and Woo to determine intersected lists \mathbb{L} and their entry/exit points. The algorithm is designed to optimize the search for supersegments within these lists, which are used to compute opacity accumulation. Efficient Raycasting of Volumetric Depth Images for Remote Visualization of Large Volumes at High Frame Rates, https://doi.org/10.1109/pacificvis56936.2023.00014, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Semi-transparent Iso-surfaces
body: Semi-transparent iso-surfaces is an image-order rendering method that visualizes scalar field features by detecting ray intersections with specific iso-values and blending multiple surfaces based on defined opacities. It distinguishes itself from opaque isosurface raycasting by allowing depth perception through layered transparency, and from Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by explicitly extracting geometric surfaces rather than compositing voxel contributions, offering a balance between structural clarity and volumetric context. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field dataset V, a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for each pixel, and a set of surface definitions. Each surface i is defined by an iso-value \taui, a color \mathbf{c}i, and an opacity \alphai. Output: A final pixel color \mathbf{C}{final}. Data Structures: Surface Definition: A list of structures, each containing: isovalue: float, the threshold \tau for the scalar field. color: vec3, the RGB color \mathbf{c} of the surface. opacity: float, the alpha \alpha value (0.0 \le \alpha \le 1.0). Ray State: currentpos: vec3, current position along the ray. prevpos: vec3, position at the previous sample step. currentval: float, scalar value f(\mathbf{p}{current}) at the current position. prevval: float, scalar value f(\mathbf{p}{prev}) at the previous position. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel, initialize the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Initialize prevpos to the ray origin, prevval to the scalar value at prevpos, and the accumulated color \mathbf{C}{accum} = (0,0,0,0). 2. Ray Marching: Advance along the ray by a fixed step size s. Let the new position be \mathbf{p}{curr} = \mathbf{p}{prev} + s \cdot \mathbf{d}. Sample the scalar field at \mathbf{p}{curr} to get v{curr} = f(\mathbf{p}{curr}). 3. Intersection Detection: For each surface i with iso-value \taui, check if the ray crosses the iso-surface between prevpos and currpos. A crossing is detected if: (v{prev} - \taui) \cdot (v{curr} - \taui) < 0 This indicates a sign change relative to the threshold. 4. Hitpoint Refinement: If a crossing is detected for surface i, calculate the exact intersection parameter t{hit} using linear interpolation between the previous and current ray positions: t{hit} = \frac{\taui - v{prev}}{v{curr} - v{prev}} The intersection point \mathbf{p}{hit} is: \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{p}{prev} + t{hit} (\mathbf{p}{curr} - \mathbf{p}{prev}). 5. Shading and Color Computation: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at \mathbf{p}{hit} using the gradient of the scalar field \nabla f(\mathbf{p}{hit}), typically via finite differences or tri-linear/tri-cubic interpolation. Apply a local lighting model (e.g., Phong) to compute the diffuse and specular components, resulting in a shaded color \mathbf{c}{shaded}. 6. Compositing: Blend the shaded surface color into the accumulated result using the surface's opacity \alphai. Assuming back-to-front or front-to-back compositing is not strictly required for single-surface hits but multiple surfaces may be hit, standard alpha compositing is used: \mathbf{C}{accum} = \mathbf{C}{accum} + (1 - \mathbf{C}{accum}.a) \cdot \alphai \cdot \mathbf{c}{shaded} Update the accumulated alpha: \mathbf{C}{accum}.a = \mathbf{C}{accum}.a + (1 - \mathbf{C}{accum}.a) \cdot \alphai. 7. Termination: If the accumulated alpha reaches 1.0 or the ray exits the volume, stop. Otherwise, update prevpos = currpos, prevval = vcurr, and repeat from Step 2. Parameters: Step Size: Not given in the sources. Typical values depend on voxel resolution; small enough to avoid missing thin surfaces. Iso-values, Colors, Opacities: Adjusted via a Transfer Function window. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation assumes the scalar field varies linearly between samples. If the step size is too large, the intersection point may be inaccurate or missed entirely. Multiple Hits: If multiple surfaces are hit along the same ray, the order of processing affects the final color. The sources do not specify a strict ordering rule, but typically surfaces are processed in order of increasing t (front-to-back) or based on user-defined priority. Visual Clutter: Rendering too many semi-transparent surfaces leads to incorrect color interpretation and visual clutter. A specific configuration of semi-transparent iso-surfaces using 3 or 5 surfaces to depict feature structures, such as velocity in joining flows or Degree of Interest (DOI) functions. The main surface is defined by a specific iso-value and opacity. Additional surfaces are determined by their relative distance from the main surface and their relative opacity compared to the main surface. Colors are defined separately for each surface. Optimal numbers are 3 or 5 surfaces; rendering more than 5 leads to incorrect color interpretation, and more than 7 can hide the feature behind redundant context. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of ray steps and the number of surfaces checked per step. Performance is higher than DVR because it avoids compositing all voxels, but lower than opaque isosurface raycasting due to the overhead of handling multiple surfaces and transparency blending. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not require storing pre-computed color/opacity volumes or large auxiliary textures. Strengths: High-quality surface visualization with depth cues from transparency; intuitive representation of feature intensity (e.g., DOI levels). Limitations: Visual clutter increases rapidly with the number of surfaces; requires careful tuning of iso-values and opacities. When to Use: When structural clarity of specific features is needed, but some context about surrounding intensity levels is also desired (e.g., medical imaging, scientific simulation data). When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene is complex, or when the user prefers fully opaque surfaces or full volumetric integration. The method was described in the context of GPU-implementation aspects of ray casting techniques. It is used in scientific visualization to depict features in simulation data, such as velocity fields in automotive industry simulations and Degree of Interest (DOI) functions in complex spatial coordinates. The concept of using multiple iso-surfaces for medical data was previously explored by Gerstner using multiresolution techniques. name: Hybrid and multi-mode rendering
body: Hybrid and multi-mode rendering combines volume rendering and surface rendering techniques to optimize computational cost and visual fidelity. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both discrete volumetric data and sharp surface boundaries by using clipping planes or proxy meshes to restrict volume integration to the region in front of the nearest surface. Unlike pure volume rendering, which integrates through the entire ray, or pure mesh rendering, which lacks internal density, this family shortens the ray at the first surface hit to prevent occlusion of volume data behind the surface. Builds on the image-order rendering and isosurface detection principles of Isosurface and first-hit ray casting. Combines hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection for explicit surface geometry (meshes) and implicit isosurfaces with volume ray marching for volumetric data. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both discrete volumetric data and sharp surface boundaries by using clipping planes to restrict volume integration to the region in front of the nearest surface. Unlike pure volume rendering, which integrates through the entire ray, or pure mesh rendering, which lacks internal density, this method shortens the ray at the first surface hit to prevent occlusion of volume data behind the surface. It is distinguished from Hybrid Isosurface/DVR Rendering by its explicit support for hardware-accelerated triangle meshes alongside implicit surfaces, and from Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing by its specific traversal order prioritizing mesh BVHs before iso-surface BVHs. A technique for viewpoints inside a volume with a wide field of view, such as virtual colonoscopy, that combines surface rendering for near structures (e.g., the colon wall) with Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) for structures behind it. It sets itself apart from pure isosurface methods by preserving the visibility of internal volumetric details behind the first-hit surface, and from pure DVR by providing sharp, shaded surface definition for the immediate foreground. A rendering technique that combines explicit voxel selection with implicit ray-surface intersection to render high-quality, crack-free isosurfaces from rectilinear or adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) volumes. Unlike sample-based methods that use fixed step sizes and often miss surface details in refined regions, this method builds a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) over active voxel primitives and performs exact implicit intersections within each primitive, avoiding the memory overhead of explicit polygon extraction. It is particularly suited for interactive visualization of large-scale AMR data where surface continuity and detail preservation are critical. A strategy that combines volume rendering with rasterized proxy meshes to enable real-time performance on consumer hardware. It solves the computational bottleneck of pure volume rendering by using a surface approximation to quickly determine the distance to the object, thereby restricting the volume sampling interval. Unlike Hybrid Isosurface/DVR Rendering which may use explicit isosurfaces for occlusion, this method specifically leverages a decimated proxy mesh derived from the density field to guide cone-casting samples. A technique that determines the final color of a pixel by evaluating a neural network at the intersection point between a camera ray and a triangular mesh surface, rather than sampling a volumetric field. It reformulates the standard volume rendering integral into a single-point evaluation, assuming the object is solid and opaque. This method distinguishes itself from implicit neural rendering (e.g., Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing) by operating directly on explicit geometry, allowing the use of differentiable rasterizers for efficient gradient computation. A hybrid representation for multi-view surface reconstruction that learns two parallel streams: an implicit Signed Distance Field (SDF) and an explicit surrogate surface mesh. It unifies volume rendering of the implicit SDF and surface rendering of the surrogate mesh with a shared neural shader to promote convergence to the same underlying surface. Unlike pure implicit methods, it leverages the efficiency of explicit mesh rendering; unlike pure explicit methods, it maintains the topological flexibility of an implicit field. Combines volume rendering (ray marching) and surface rendering (rasterization) to optimize computational cost and visual fidelity. It confines ray marching to the region between the viewpoint and a pre-existing mesh surface, treating the mesh intersection as the termination point for volume integration. This approach leverages the mesh for high-fidelity geometry and texture where available, while using the volume to represent complex details or occlusions in front of the surface. Definition: A rendering mode that prioritizes interaction speed by skipping expensive visibility and suggestive contour calculations during user manipulation. Step: During camera movement or isosurface sweeping, draw only contours (no suggestive contours, no hidden surface removal). When motion stops, render the full drawing including suggestive contours and hidden surface removal. Comparison: This mode is necessary because computing suggestive contours and visibility takes significantly more time than contour extraction alone. Definition: A method to overlay multiple volume data sets on a 3D surface model by computing contributions of each volume set individually and combining them, optimizing memory access patterns. Step: Classify shader methods into two groups: those where rays fully penetrate the volume (1, 2, 4, 7) and those where rays end at a point inside the volume (3, 5, 6). Optimize memory access patterns and compact address blocks to maximize memory caching. Compute the contributions of each volume data set to the resulting ray per volume individually. Subsequently combine the individual contributions. Check if the volume data can contain boundaries using the specified shader method. Out of all 'bounded' volume data sets, compute the boundary nearest to the viewer for the ray concerned. Compute 'un-bounded' volume data sets to this nearest boundary point. Calculate the final color value of the pixel using an optional transfer function. For the combination with the 3D surface model, inform the graphic-card-based ray-casting algorithm of the position of a boundary (e.g., the building) from the given perspective. Not given in the sources. name: Mesh-based Neural Rendering
head: Neural Mesh Rendering
body: Mesh-based Neural Rendering determines the final color of a pixel by evaluating a neural network at the intersection point between a camera ray and a mesh surface, rather than integrating along a ray through a volume. It reformulates the volume rendering integral into a discrete sum where the object is assumed solid and opaque, meaning the final color is determined solely by the first intersection point. This approach differs from Hybrid Isosurface Ray Tracing by explicitly maintaining a triangular mesh topology for intersection, and from Multi-Mode Rendering with Iso-surfaces and Meshes by using a neural network to predict color and features directly from mesh attributes instead of relying on traditional shading or volume compositing for the surface component. Inputs and Outputs Input: A triangular mesh (vertices and faces), camera parameters (origin o, direction v), and a neural rendering network c\theta. Output: The predicted color \hat{C}(r) for each ray r. Data Structures Mesh: Defined by a set of vertices V and faces F. Each face is a triangle defined by three vertex indices. Neural Network: A multi-layer perceptron that takes embedded geometric attributes as input and outputs color. Ray: Defined as p(t) = o + tv for t \ge 0, where o is the camera center and v is the direction vector. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, generate a camera ray r defined by origin o and direction v. 2. Intersection Detection: Find the first intersection point xm between the ray r and the mesh surface. 3. Attribute Interpolation: Calculate the attributes at the intersection point xm by interpolating the values of the three vertices of the triangle containing xm. The attributes are: Position xm (the intersection point itself), Normal vector nm (interpolated vertex normals), and Feature vector hm (interpolated vertex features). 4. Embedding: Embed the 3D position xm using positional encoding. The source specifies using k=3 octaves for the position embedding. The normal nm, feature hm, and viewing direction d (the normalized ray direction) are concatenated with the embedded position. 5. Neural Evaluation: Feed the embedded position, normal, feature vector, and viewing direction into the neural rendering network c\theta to predict the color. 6. Color Assignment: Since the object is assumed solid and opaque, the final color \hat{C}(r) is the output of the neural network for the first intersection. Formulas The volume rendering integral is reformulated as: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \alphai is discrete opacity, and ci is color. However, under the solid and opaque assumption, this simplifies to: \hat{C}(r) = c\theta (xm, nm, hm, d) where: xm is the position of the intersection point. nm is the normal vector at the intersection point. hm is the feature vector at the intersection point. d is the direction of the ray. Parameters Positional Encoding Octaves (k): The number of octaves for positional encoding of the 3D location x. The source empirically found k=3 to yield the best performance. Loss Weights: In training, individual objective terms are weighted with \lambda1 = 2, \lambda2 = 50, and \lambda'1 = 4. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Mesh Resolution vs. Ray Density: A delicate balance is required between ray density and mesh resolution. Excessively large triangles may yield multiple intersections with the same triangle, while excessively small triangles may leave regions untraversed by rays, incurring extra computations. Opacity Assumption: The method assumes the object is solid and opaque. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def meshneuralrendering(mesh, rayorigins, raydirs, neuralnetwork, k=3): """ Render a scene using mesh-based neural rendering. Args: mesh: Object containing vertices (V: (N,3)) and faces (F: (M,3)). rayorigins: (H, W, 3) array of ray origins. raydirs: (H, W, 3) array of ray directions. neuralnetwork: Function ctheta that takes (posembed, normal, feature, viewdir) -> color. k: Number of octaves for positional encoding. Returns: image: (H, W, 3) array of rendered colors. """ H, W = rayorigins.shape[:2] image = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) # Precompute vertex attributes vertexnormals = computevertexnormals(mesh.V, mesh.F) vertexfeatures = np.zeroslike(mesh.V) # Flatten rays for processing rayoriginsflat = rayorigins.reshape(-1, 3) raydirsflat = raydirs.reshape(-1, 3) numrays = rayoriginsflat.shape[0] for i in range(numrays): o = rayoriginsflat[i] v = raydirsflat[i] # Find first intersection with mesh hit = raytriangleintersection(o, v, mesh.V, mesh.F) if hit is not None: xm, u, vbary, faceidx = hit # Get triangle vertices v0, v1, v2 = mesh.V[mesh.F[faceidx]] n0, n1, n2 = vertexnormals[mesh.F[faceidx]] h0, h1, h2 = vertexfeatures[mesh.F[faceidx]] # Interpolate attributes nm = u n0 + vbary n1 + (1 - u - vbary) n2 hm = u h0 + vbary h1 + (1 - u - vbary) h2 # Embed position posembed = positionalencoding(xm, k) # View direction d = v / np.linalg.norm(v) # Neural network evaluation color = neuralnetwork(posembed, nm, hm, d) image[i // W, i % W] = color else: image[i // W, i % W] = [0, 0, 0] return image def positionalencoding(x, k): """Standard positional encoding with k octaves.""" freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(k) xscaled = np.outer(x, freqbands).flatten() return np.concatenate([np.sin(xscaled), np.cos(xscaled)]) def computevertexnormals(V, F): """Compute per-vertex normals from face normals.""" N = np.zeroslike(V) for i in range(len(F)): v0, v1, v2 = V[F[i]] facenormal = np.cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) for idx in F[i]: N[idx] += facenormal norms = np.linalg.norm(N, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms[norms == 0] = 1.0 return N / norms def raytriangleintersection(o, v, V, F): """Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection. Returns closest hit or None.""" closestt = np.inf closesthit = None for i in range(len(F)): v0, v1, v2 = V[F[i]] e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 h = np.cross(v, e2) a = np.dot(e1, h) if a > -1e-8 and a < 1e-8: continue f = 1.0 / a s = o - v0 u = f np.dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: continue q = np.cross(s, e1) vbary = f np.dot(v, q) if vbary < 0.0 or u + vbary > 1.0: continue t = f np.dot(e2, q) if t > 1e-8 and t < closestt: closestt = t closesthit = (o + t v, u, vbary, i) return closesthit Time Complexity: Dominated by ray-triangle intersection tests and neural network inference per pixel. Memory Complexity: Depends on the mesh size (O(V + F)) and the neural network size. Performance: Training times reported are 25-60 minutes for specific datasets on an NVIDIA RTX 2080Ti GPU with 11GB memory. Strengths: Captures geometric intricacies without textures; differentiable rendering allows for end-to-end optimization of mesh and network. Limitations: Assumes solid/opaque objects; sensitive to mesh resolution and ray density balance; requires a pre-existing or optimized mesh. Mesh-based Neural Rendering was proposed as an alternative to implicit neural representations (like NeRF) that use volume rendering. It leverages the efficiency of rasterization or ray-triangle intersection on explicit meshes while retaining the expressive power of neural networks for appearance modeling. The method builds on the principles of Isosurface and first-hit ray casting by using the first hit but replaces the volume integral with a direct neural evaluation at the surface point. FastMESH: Fast Surface Reconstruction by Hexagonal Mesh-based Neural Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.17858, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sur2f
body: Sur^{2}f is a hybrid representation for multi-view surface reconstruction that learns two parallel streams: an implicit signed distance field (SDF) and an explicit surrogate surface mesh. It unifies volume rendering of the implicit SDF and surface rendering of the surrogate mesh with a shared neural shader to promote convergence to the same underlying surface. Unlike sibling methods that may use discrete tetrahedra or separate rendering pipelines, Sur^{2}f maintains a continuously defined implicit field synchronized with an explicit mesh via SDF-induced deformation, leveraging the mesh to guide volume sampling for improved efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M multi-view images \{Im\}{m=1}^M with known camera poses. Outputs: An implicit SDF function f(\boldsymbol{x}; \theta) and an explicit surrogate mesh \hat{\mathcal{S}} = \{\hat{\mathcal{V}}, \hat{\mathcal{F}}\}. At inference, a final mesh \mathcal{S} is extracted from f using marching cubes. Data Structures: 1. Implicit SDF (f): A neural network parameterized by \theta that outputs a scalar value for any point \boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The surface is defined as the zero-level set \mathcal{S} = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f(\boldsymbol{x}) = 0\}. Convention: f(\boldsymbol{x}) < 0 inside, f(\boldsymbol{x}) > 0 outside. 2. Surrogate Mesh (\hat{\mathcal{S}}): Defined by vertices \hat{\mathcal{V}} and faces \hat{\mathcal{F}}. The vertex positions are deformed during training while the topology remains fixed. 3. Neural Shader: A shared parameterized function that computes photorealistic appearance (color, shading) for both the volume and surface streams. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Initialize the implicit SDF parameters \theta and the surrogate mesh vertices \hat{\mathcal{V}} with fixed topology faces \hat{\mathcal{F}}. 2. Synchronize Deformation: Drive the iterative deformation of the surrogate mesh vertices \hat{\mathcal{V}} using functions induced from the current implicit SDF f. This ensures the explicit mesh stays synchronized with the implicit field. 3. Implicit Stream Rendering (Volume): Perform SDF-induced volume rendering on the implicit field f. Use the synchronized surrogate mesh \hat{\mathcal{S}} to guide volume sampling, improving sampling efficiency per ray. 4. Explicit Stream Rendering (Surface): Perform differentiable surface rendering on the surrogate mesh \hat{\mathcal{S}}. 5. Unify Rendering: Compute appearance for both streams using the shared neural shader. 6. Supervision and Update: Compute loss against observed multi-view images \{Im\} for both rendered views. Update parameters \theta of the SDF and vertex positions \hat{\mathcal{V}} of the mesh to minimize the loss. The shared neural shader ensures both streams converge to the same surface appearance and geometry. 7. Inference: Extract the final mesh \mathcal{S} from the converged implicit SDF f using marching cubes. Render in real-time using the learned neural shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. theta = randominitialization() # SDF network parameters Vhat = randominitialization() # Surrogate mesh vertices F = fixedtopologyfaces() # Fixed surrogate mesh faces shader = neuralshadernetwork() # Shared appearance network for iteration in range(maxiterations): # 1. Synchronize surrogate mesh with implicit SDF Vhat = deformvertices(Vhat, F, f, theta) # 2. Render implicit stream (volume) colorvol, alphavol = rendervolume( rayorigins, raydirections, f, theta, surrogatemesh=(Vhat, F), shader=shader) # 3. Render explicit stream (surface) colorsurf, alphasurf = rendersurface( rayorigins, raydirections, vertices=Vhat, faces=F, shader=shader) # 4. Compute loss and update lossvol = meansquarederror(colorvol, observedimages) losssurf = meansquarederror(colorsurf, observedimages) totalloss = lossvol + losssurf theta = gradientdescentstep(theta, totalloss) Vhat = gradientdescentstep(Vhat, totalloss) finalmesh = marchingcubes(f, theta) def deformvertices(V, F, f, theta): # Deform vertices based on functions induced from f return V # Implementation details not specified in sources def rendervolume(origins, dirs, f, theta, surrogatemesh, shader): # SDF-induced volume rendering with surface-guided sampling return color, alpha # Standard volume rendering loop def rendersurface(origins, dirs, vertices, faces, shader): # Differentiable surface rendering return color, alpha # Standard differentiable rasterization/ray-marching def marchingcubes(f, theta): # Extract mesh from zero-level set of f return mesh # Standard marching cubes algorithm def randominitialization(): return 0.0 def fixedtopologyfaces(): return [] def neuralshadernetwork(): return lambda x: x def gradientdescentstep(params, loss): return params def meansquarederror(pred, target): return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Synchronization Failure: If the deformation functions induced from f do not accurately reflect the surface geometry, the surrogate mesh may drift, reducing the effectiveness of surface-guided sampling. Sampling Efficiency: The benefit of surface-guided volume sampling relies on the surrogate mesh being a good approximation of the true surface. Topology: The surrogate mesh topology is fixed during deformation. Topological changes in the target surface may require careful initialization or topology-adaptive strategies not detailed in the core method. Uses the implicit SDF for rendering, allowing continuous representation and easy extraction of meshes via marching cubes. Renders the explicit surrogate mesh, providing efficient and sharp surface supervision. A single neural network parameterizes the appearance for both volume and surface rendering, ensuring photorealistic consistency and promoting convergence to the same surface. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method claims improved sampling efficiency per ray in volume rendering due to surface-guided sampling. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the SDF network parameters, the surrogate mesh vertices, and the neural shader parameters. Performance: Sur^{2}f outperforms existing reconstruction methods and surface representations, including hybrid ones, in terms of both recovery quality and recovery efficiency. Strengths: Combines the merits of implicit fields (continuous, easy mesh extraction) and explicit meshes (efficient rendering, surface-guided sampling). The shared shader promotes convergence to the same surface. Limitations: Requires maintaining and synchronizing two representations. The surrogate mesh topology is fixed. When to use: Multi-view surface reconstruction where high quality and efficiency are required, and photorealistic rendering is desired. Sur^{2}f was proposed in the paper "Sur^{2}f: A Hybrid Representation for High-Quality and Efficient Surface Reconstruction from Multi-view Images". It addresses the ill-posed nature of surface reconstruction from multi-view images by leveraging the complementary merits of implicit and explicit representations. The method builds on principles of isosurface detection and volume rendering Isosurface and first-hit ray casting. name: Volumetric Surfaces
body: Volumetric Surfaces is a real-time view synthesis method that represents objects as semi-transparent multi-layer meshes rendered in a fixed order. It solves the problem of efficiently modeling fuzzy geometries by bounding the number of sampling locations per ray and eliminating the computational overhead of empty-space skipping and primitive sorting found in volume rendering and splatting, respectively. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Parameters: N: Number of layers. Typical range: 3 to 9. A 7-layer configuration is noted as optimal for balancing quality and speed. Spacing: The distance between adjacent SDF shells is learned during training. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize training with a single opaque Signed Distance Function (SDF) shell to prevent degenerate solutions. 2. Iteratively add multiple SDF shells to the representation, learning the optimal spacing between them during training. 3. Apply hierarchical sampling during training to focus samples around the depth values along rays. 4. Apply Eikonal loss to enforce the SDF property and curvature loss to ensure smooth, non-intersecting layers. 5. Minimize the rendering loss between predicted and ground-truth images. 6. After training converges, bake the learned SDF shells into explicit triangle meshes. 7. Fit UV textures to the baked meshes to encode color and opacity information. 8. Simplify the multi-layer meshes using established techniques to ensure they are lightweight and suitable for hardware-accelerated rasterization. 9. During inference, rasterize the baked meshes in the fixed learned order to find sampling locations along rays, then composite the layers in that fixed order to produce the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainvolumetricsurfaces(images, poses, targetlayers=7): # Step 1: Initialize with a single opaque SDF shell layers = [SDFShell(opaque=True)] # Step 2: Iteratively add layers with learned spacing while len(layers) < targetlayers: layers.append(SDFShell(spacing=learnedspacing(layers[-1]))) # Step 3-5: Optimization loop for epoch in range(1000): # Not given in sources for image, pose in zip(images, poses): # Hierarchical sampling around ray depths samples = samplearounddepth(layers, pose) # Render and composite layers renderedimage = compositelayers(layers, samples, pose) # Compute losses eikonalloss = mean(abs(grad(layers) - 1.0)) curvatureloss = mean(curvature(layers)) imageloss = mse(renderedimage, image) totalloss = imageloss + eikonalloss + curvatureloss layers = gradientdescent(layers, totalloss) return layers def rendervolumetricsurfaces(layers, camerapose): # Step 9: Rasterize baked meshes in fixed order to find sampling locations # Composite layers in fixed order, eliminating sorting coloraccum = 0.0 alphaaccum = 0.0 for layer in layers: depthmap, uvmap = rasterizemesh(layer, camerapose) texcolor, texalpha = texturesample(layer.uvmap, uvmap) alpha = texalpha color = texcolor coloraccum = coloraccum (1 - alpha) + color alpha alphaaccum = alphaaccum (1 - alpha) + alpha if alphaaccum >= 1.0: break return coloraccum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Solutions: Training with multiple layers from the start can lead to degenerate geometries; initialization with a single opaque SDF is required. Intersection: Without Eikonal and curvature losses, layers may intersect, breaking the fixed-order rendering assumption. Mesh Simplification: Simplification is applied to ensure lightweight meshes for rasterization, but excessive simplification may degrade visual quality. Time Complexity: Rendering is dominated by rasterization of N layers, avoiding the unbounded sampling cost of volume rendering and the sorting overhead of splatting. Memory Complexity: Baked meshes and UV textures are compact, keeping the memory footprint manageable for mobile hardware. Performance: Enables real-time rendering on low-power laptops and smartphones. A 7-layer configuration offers an optimal balance of image quality and speed. Strengths: Bounded sampling, sorting-free rendering, and efficient representation of fuzzy geometries. Limitations: Requires a training phase to learn layer positions and spacings, making it less flexible for dynamic scene changes without retraining. Volumetric Surfaces was introduced by Stefano Esposito, Anpei Chen, Christian Reiser, et al. in 2024. It bridges the gap between the fidelity of volume-based methods and the speed of surface-based methods, specifically targeting real-time view synthesis on mobile hardware. It builds on concepts from neural rendering and SDFs, differing from surface-based alternatives by explicitly baking the representation into rasterizable meshes rather than relying on implicit fields or unsorted primitives. name: Combined Volume and Surface Rendering with Global Illumination Caching
body: This method combines volume and surface rendering to enhance the display of isosurfaces within participating media while preserving physically realistic illumination. It solves the problem that modern null-collision-based volume rendering techniques efficiently handle participating media but lack the capability to efficiently render isosurfaces due to large discontinuities in density. The technique distinguishes itself by using volumetric path tracing to compute a global illumination volume, which is then blended with local shading models for the isosurface. Unlike full volumetric path tracing, it emphasizes surfaces within volumes better, and unlike the non-caching baseline, the caching variant is camera-view-independent. The method consists of two variants: a non-caching baseline and a caching extension. Both variants share the same rendering pipeline for a single frame, but the caching variant precomputes global illumination. Inputs: Volumetric data V. Isovalue \rho defining the isosurface S where V(s) = \rho for s \in S. Camera parameters (position, orientation, projection). Light source definitions. Local shading model parameters for the isosurface. Outputs: Final pixel color for each pixel in the image. (Caching variant only) A Global Illumination Volume storing precomputed global illumination for each voxel. 1. Volumetric Data (V): The input scalar field representing the density or property values of the participating media. 2. Global Illumination Volume: A data structure storing the precomputed global illumination for each voxel. This volume is camera-view-independent and is used to avoid recomputing the image when the camera view changes. The exact layout (e.g., grid resolution, bit depth, color channels) is not specified in the sources. 3. Local Illumination Data: Information regarding the local shading of the isosurface at the extracted depth, passed to the path tracing module. 1. Isosurface Depth Extraction: For every pixel, cast a ray from the camera into the volume and extract the depth of the first intersection with the isosurface S. This identifies the visible part of the isosurface. 2. Local Illumination Calculation: Calculate the local illumination for the isosurface at the extracted depth using a local shading model. 3. Pass to Path Tracing: Pass the isosurface depth and the calculated local illumination information to the path tracing module. 4. Ray Casting: In the path tracing module, cast rays from the camera into the volume. 5. Light Gathering: Gather light contributions from the path tracing module only up to the extracted isosurface depth. This involves computing the global illumination of the participating media along the ray segment from the camera to the isosurface. 6. Blending: Blend the gathered light contributions (global illumination of the media) with the local isosurface illumination contribution to form the final pixel color. The caching variant extends the non-caching method by precomputing the global illumination. 1. Precompute Global Illumination: Compute the global illumination of each voxel in the volume using path tracing. This step is performed incrementally. 2. Store in Volume: Store the computed global illumination in the Global Illumination Volume data structure. 3. Rendering: During the rendering step (equivalent to steps 1-6 of the non-caching variant), take both the precomputed Global Illumination Volume and the local illumination contribution into account when accumulating illumination along the ray. Specifically, the global illumination contribution is retrieved from the volume rather than computed per-pixel per-frame. The sources describe the blending conceptually but do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the blending function or the path tracing integrals. The isosurface is defined by the condition: V(s) = \rho \quad \text{for } s \in S where V is the volume data and \rho is the isovalue. Isovalue (\rho): The threshold value defining the isosurface. Local Shading Models: Models used for rendering the isosurface. The paper evaluates different local shading models, but specific models or their parameters are not detailed in the provided notes. Global Illumination Volume: The data structure storing precomputed global illumination. Density Discontinuities: Modern null-collision-based volume rendering techniques lack the capability of efficiently rendering isosurfaces because isosurfaces correspond to large discontinuities in density. This method addresses that by combining volume and surface rendering. Camera View Changes: In the non-caching variant, the global illumination is computed incrementally per pixel, meaning the image must be recomputed when the camera view changes. The caching variant mitigates this by storing global illumination in a volume, making it camera-view-independent. Precision and Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernoncaching(volume, isovalue, camera, lights, shadingmodel): """ Renders the scene using the non-caching combined volume and surface method. Follows the 6-step pipeline from the sources. """ image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): # Step 1: Extract isosurface depth ray = camera.getray(x, y) depth = raymarchisosurface(volume, ray, isovalue) if depth is None: image[y][x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] continue # Step 2: Calculate local illumination hitpos = ray.origin + ray.direction depth normal = volumegradient(volume, hitpos) localillum = shadingmodel.compute(hitpos, normal, lights) # Step 3 & 4: Pass to path tracing and cast rays # Step 5: Gather light contributions up to isosurface depth gi = pathtracevolume(ray, volume, lights, maxt=depth) # Step 6: Blend contributions image[y][x] = [gi[i] + localillum[i] for i in range(3)] return image def raymarchisosurface(volume, ray, isovalue): """ Finds the first intersection of the ray with the isosurface defined by volume == isovalue. """ t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 # Fixed step size for marching while t < 1.0: # Normalized ray parameter range val = volume.sample(ray.origin + ray.direction t) if val >= isovalue: return t t += stepsize return None def volumegradient(volume, pos): """ Estimates the surface normal at pos using central differences. """ eps = 1e-3 dx = volume.sample(pos + [eps, 0, 0]) - volume.sample(pos - [eps, 0, 0]) dy = volume.sample(pos + [0, eps, 0]) - volume.sample(pos - [0, eps, 0]) dz = volume.sample(pos + [0, 0, eps]) - volume.sample(pos - [0, 0, eps]) mag = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 if mag == 0: return [0, 0, 1] return [dx/mag, dy/mag, dz/mag] def pathtracevolume(ray, volume, lights, maxt): """ Computes global illumination of the participating media along the ray up to maxt. """ t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 # Fixed step size for integration accumulated = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while t < maxt: pos = ray.origin + ray.direction t density = volume.sample(pos) # Standard volumetric scattering contribution contrib = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for light in lights: contrib = [contrib[i] + density light.shade(pos)[i] for i in range(3)] accumulated = [accumulated[i] + contrib[i] for i in range(3)] t += stepsize return accumulated def rendercaching(volume, isovalue, camera, lights, shadingmodel, givolume): """ Renders the scene using the caching combined volume and surface method. Follows the 6-step pipeline but samples the precomputed GI volume. """ image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): ray = camera.getray(x, y) depth = raymarchisosurface(volume, ray, isovalue) if depth is None: image[y][x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] continue hitpos = ray.origin + ray.direction depth normal = volumegradient(volume, hitpos) localillum = shadingmodel.compute(hitpos, normal, lights) # Step 5 replacement: Gather from precomputed volume gi = samplegivolume(givolume, ray, maxt=depth) # Step 6: Blend contributions image[y][x] = [gi[i] + localillum[i] for i in range(3)] return image def samplegivolume(givolume, ray, maxt): """ Samples the precomputed Global Illumination Volume along the ray up to maxt. """ t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 # Fixed step size for integration accumulated = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while t < maxt: pos = ray.origin + ray.direction t gival = givolume.sample(pos) accumulated = [accumulated[i] + gival[i] for i in range(3)] t += stepsize return accumulated Combines volume rendering with explicit mesh geometry. Choose when the scene contains both implicit volumes and explicit polygonal models. Multi-Mode Rendering with Iso-surfaces and Meshes Renders isosurfaces and direct volume rendering (DVR) together. Choose when you need to visualize both the boundary of a structure and its internal density variations simultaneously. Hybrid Isosurface/DVR Rendering Uses ray tracing for isosurfaces and potentially other methods for volume. Choose when high-quality ray-traced isosurfaces are needed within a volume context. Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing General hybrid approach for volume and surface data. Choose when combining different rendering paradigms for volume and surface components. Hybrid Volume-Surface Rendering Uses neural networks to render mesh-based geometry. Choose when neural rendering techniques are applied to explicit mesh surfaces. Mesh-based Neural Rendering A specific method for surface-to-field rendering. Choose when converting surface representations to field-based representations for rendering. Sur2f General hybrid rendering techniques. Choose when combining multiple rendering methods for a single scene. Hybrid Rendering Time Complexity: The non-caching variant computes global illumination incrementally per pixel, leading to higher per-frame cost, especially for complex scenes or high-quality path tracing. The caching variant precomputes global illumination, which adds an initial offline or incremental precomputation cost, but allows for faster per-frame rendering as the global illumination is retrieved from the volume. Memory Complexity: The caching variant requires additional memory to store the Global Illumination Volume, which stores precomputed global illumination for each voxel. The non-caching variant does not require this storage. Measured Performance: The caching and non-caching variants perform comparably well in terms of visual quality and overall performance metrics in the evaluation. Scaling: The caching variant scales better with camera view changes because the global illumination is camera-view-independent and does not need to be recomputed. Strengths: Enhances the display of surfaces within volumes better than full volumetric path tracing alone; preserves physically realistic illumination of participating media; the caching variant is camera-view-independent. Limitations: Modern null-collision-based volume rendering techniques lack the capability of efficiently rendering isosurfaces due to large discontinuities in density, which this method addresses but may introduce complexity in handling these discontinuities. The exact performance characteristics depend on the local shading models and path tracing implementation. The method was presented by Uroš Šmajdek, Žiga Lesar, Matija Marolt, and Ciril Bohak in 2023. The paper was accepted on May 19, 2023, and published online on June 26, 2023. The work addresses the need for physically correct lighting in volumetric visualization, noting that lighting is crucial for the accurate perception of details, especially when rendering volumetric data with different degrees of transparency. The authors highlight that while null-collision-based volume rendering is efficient for participating media, it struggles with isosurfaces due to density discontinuities, necessitating a combined approach. The technique is related to irradiance caching and global illumination techniques in volumetric data. name: Offline Parallel Hybrid Rendering
head: Off-line parallel rendering algorithm, Parallel volume ray-casting combined with on-the-fly isocontouring
body: Offline Parallel Hybrid Rendering is a parallel image-order method designed to produce high-resolution fly-through movies of huge time-varying volume datasets by merging volume ray-casting and on-the-fly isocontouring. It minimizes data communication overhead between processors, addressing the bottleneck of transferring large volume datasets across networked nodes during rendering. Builds on the image-order rendering and isosurface detection principles of Isosurface and first-hit ray casting. Unlike sibling methods that may pre-compute polygon sets or rely on specific hardware pipes, this approach dynamically balances load across a processor pool while extracting isosurfaces on-the-fly without storing large intermediate polygon meshes. Siblings: Mesh-based Neural Rendering, Sur2f, Combined Volume and Surface Rendering with Global Illumination Caching, Volume-Surface Hybridization. Inputs and Outputs Input: A time-varying volume dataset where each scalar voxel value is stored in 4 bytes. Output: A sequence of high-resolution 3D rendered images (frames) for each time step. Data Structures Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values, each stored as a 4-byte value. Task Pool: A collection of image tiles formed by partitioning the image screen into small, regularly spaced pixel tiles. Transfer Function: A uniform transfer function defined over the whole value range of the dataset. Parameters Sampling Interval: Very dense sampling intervals are maintained to minimize mismatches between colors in the final images and pre-defined color maps. Composition Operator: The 'over' operator is used for color composition. Illumination Model: Phong’s illumination model is modified to match pre-defined color maps and visualize materials with specific ranges. Formulas Color and opacity are accumulated along each ray using the discrete 'over' compositing operator: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) C{new} \alpha{new} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{new} where C{in}, \alpha{in} are the accumulated color and opacity, and C{new}, \alpha{new} are the color and opacity contributed by the current volume sample or isosurface intersection. Algorithm Steps 1. Partition the image screen into small, regularly spaced pixel tiles to form a task pool. 2. Assign processors to tiles from the pool of tasks waiting to be executed. 3. Processors repeatedly perform hybrid rendering on tiles until the task pool is emptied, with dynamic load balancing. 4. During rendering, extract isosurfaces on the fly without creating large polygon sets. 5. When cast rays intersect volumes and isosurfaces, apply shading and composing on the fly. 6. Collect image segments and assemble them into the final high-resolution image. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def offlineparallelhybridrendering(volumedata, imagewidth, imageheight, numprocessors, tilesize): # Partition image into tiles tiles = createtilepool(imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize) # Initialize shared task pool and result storage taskpool = Queue(tiles) imagesegments = {} # Parameters SELECTEDISOValue = 0.5 # Threshold for isosurface extraction DENSESAMPLINGINTERVAL = 0.01 # Step size for ray marching # Processors execute tasks for processorid in range(numprocessors): while not taskpool.isempty(): # Dynamic load balancing: pick next available tile tile = taskpool.dequeue() # Render the tile tileimage = rendertile( tile, volumedata, DENSESAMPLINGINTERVAL, SELECTEDISOValue) # Store result imagesegments[tile.id] = tileimage # Assemble final image finalimage = assembleimage(imagesegments, imagewidth, imageheight) return finalimage def rendertile(tile, volumedata, samplinginterval, isovalue): tileimage = emptyimage(tile.width, tile.height) for y in range(tile.ystart, tile.yend): for x in range(tile.xstart, tile.xend): # Cast ray for pixel (x, y) ray = castray(x, y) # Initialize color and opacity color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] opacity = 0.0 # Traverse volume along ray t = ray.origin while t < ray.end: # Sample volume at current position value = samplevolume(volumedata, ray.positionat(t)) # Uniform transfer function evaluation tfcolor, tfopacity = UniformTransferFunction.evaluate(value) # Check for isosurface intersection if isosurfacedetected(value, t, ray, isovalue): # Apply shading using modified Phong model shadedcolor = ModifiedPhongModel.shade(ray, volumedata, t) # Compose isosurface color (opaque) color, opacity = OverOperator.compose( color, opacity, shadedcolor, 1.0) # Compose volume color color, opacity = OverOperator.compose( color, opacity, tfcolor, tfopacity) # Advance along ray with dense sampling t += samplinginterval # Stop if fully opaque if opacity >= 1.0: break tileimage.setpixel(x - tile.xstart, y - tile.ystart, color) return tileimage class Queue: def init(self, items): self.items = list(items) def isempty(self): return len(self.items) == 0 def dequeue(self): return self.items.pop(0) class Tile: def init(self, id, xstart, ystart, width, height): self.id = id self.xstart = xstart self.ystart = ystart self.width = width self.height = height def createtilepool(width, height, tilesize): tiles = [] tid = 0 for y in range(0, height, tilesize): for x in range(0, width, tilesize): tiles.append(Tile(tid, x, y, min(tilesize, width - x), min(tilesize, height - y))) tid += 1 return tiles def emptyimage(w, h): return [[None for in range(w)] for in range(h)] def castray(x, y): # Returns ray with origin, direction, tstart, tend return type('Ray', (), {'origin': 0.0, 'end': 10.0, 'direction': [0, 0, 1]})() def samplevolume(data, pos): # Returns scalar value at position return 0.5 def UniformTransferFunction(): pass @staticmethod def evaluate(value): # Uniform mapping: color based on value, opacity 0.1 return [value, value, value], 0.1 def isosurfacedetected(value, t, ray, isovalue): return value > isovalue def ModifiedPhongModel(): pass @staticmethod def shade(ray, data, t): # Returns shaded color return [0.8, 0.8, 0.8] def OverOperator(): pass @staticmethod def compose(cin, ain, cnew, anew): cout = [cin[i] + (1.0 - ain) cnew[i] anew for i in range(3)] aout = ain + (1.0 - ain) anew return cout, aout def assembleimage(segments, width, height): # Combines tile images into full image return [[None for in range(width)] for in range(height)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Color Mismatch: Improper composition can cause mismatches between final image colors and pre-defined color maps, mitigated by using very dense sampling intervals. Data Communication: Large data communication overhead can degrade performance; the algorithm minimizes this by only communicating task assignments and image segment collection. Polygon Set Size: Creating large polygon sets for isosurfaces is avoided to prevent memory issues and processing delays. Time Complexity: The algorithm achieves near-linear speedup with the number of processors. On an SGI Onyx2 with 24 processors, rendering a 1088x480 image of S data took 3.19 seconds, compared to 65.33 seconds on a uniprocessor. For a 2160x960 image, it took 6.42 seconds on 24 processors versus 260.96 seconds on a uniprocessor. Memory Complexity: The method minimizes memory overhead by not storing large polygon sets for isosurfaces. Scalability: The scheme shows near-perfect linear scalability on systems with multiple graphics pipes (e.g., SGI Onyx2). It can also be ported to commodity PC cluster environments. Strengths: High-resolution output, effective visualization of dynamic changes between time steps, minimized data communication overhead, dynamic load balancing. Limitations: Requires high-performance graphics workstations or clusters for optimal performance. The modified Phong model may not capture all complex lighting effects. When to Use: Suitable for producing fly-through movies of huge time-varying volume datasets where high resolution and dynamic change visualization are critical. When Not to Use: Not suitable for interactive real-time rendering on low-end hardware, as it is designed for offline parallel processing. The Offline Parallel Hybrid Rendering algorithm was proposed by S. Park, C. Bajaj, and I. Ihm in 2004. It was developed to visualize huge oceanography time-varying volume datasets, such as temperature, salinity, velocity, ocean surface height, and ocean depth, from a 121-day oceanographic simulation. The work was presented at the International Conference on Computational Science (ICCS) 2004. The algorithm was implemented on an SGI visualization system, specifically the SGI Onyx2, and later ported to commodity PC cluster environments. It addresses the limitations of pre-defined color-mapped images, which appear as simple 2D planes and make it difficult to understand dynamic changes between time steps. By providing 3D-rendered images, it effectively describes detailed changes between time steps. name: Volume-Surface Hybridization
body: Volume-Surface Hybridization is a rendering strategy that combines explicit surface geometry (meshes or isosurfaces) with implicit volumetric data to optimize computational cost and representation fidelity. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both discrete surfaces and continuous volumetric fields by using surface intersections to limit or guide volume integration. It sets itself apart from pure volume rendering by prioritizing surface geometry intersection to limit volume integration, and from pure mesh rendering by retaining the ability to render internal volumetric structures up to the surface boundary. It builds on Hybrid and multi-mode rendering. The family shares the core mechanism of using surface geometry to define integration bounds or sampling regions for volume data. 1. Surface Detection: For a given camera ray r(t) = o + t \cdot d, the nearest intersection with a surface (mesh or isosurface) is determined. This provides a distance t{surf}. 2. Integration Limiting: Volume ray marching is restricted to the interval [t{min}, t{end}], where t{min} is the near clipping plane and t{end} = \min(t{max\clip}, t{surf}). 3. Compositing: The final color is a blend of the volume contribution (accumulated up to t{end}) and the surface contribution (at t{surf}) using front-to-back alpha compositing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderhybridray(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmaxclip, stepsize, meshbvh, isosurfacebvh, volumebvh, transferfunction): # Step 1: Surface Detection # Standard BVH ray-triangle intersection query tmesh = querybvhintersection(meshbvh, rayorigin, raydirection) if tmesh is None: tmesh = float('inf') # Transform ray to volume coordinate space rayvolorigin = transformtovolumespace(rayorigin) rayvoldir = transformtovolumespace(raydirection) # Standard BVH ray-implicit surface intersection query tiso = querybvhintersection(isosurfacebvh, rayvolorigin, rayvoldir) if tiso is None: tiso = float('inf') tsurface = min(tmesh, tiso) # Step 2: Integration Limit tend = min(tmaxclip, tsurface) # Step 3: Volume Integration volcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] volalpha = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 t = tmin while t < tend: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Sample scalar field at current position density = samplevolumefield(volumebvh, pos) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density stepsize) weight = transmittance alpha c, a = transferfunction(density) for i in range(3): volcolor[i] += weight c[i] volalpha += weight transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) t += stepsize # Step 4: Surface Contribution surfcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] surfalpha = 0.0 if tsurface < tmaxclip: hitpos = rayorigin + tsurface raydirection # Compute surface normal and apply shading model normal = computesurfacenormal(hitpos, meshbvh, isosurfacebvh) surfcolor = applyshadingmodel(hitpos, normal, raydirection) surfalpha = 1.0 # Step 5: Final Compositing finalalpha = volalpha + surfalpha (1.0 - volalpha) finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): finalcolor[i] = volcolor[i] + surfcolor[i] surfalpha (1.0 - volalpha) return finalcolor, finalalpha Combines hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection for explicit meshes and implicit iso-surfaces with volume ray marching. Choose this when rendering scenes with both explicit meshes and implicit volumetric boundaries. Combines surface rendering for near walls with direct volume rendering (DVR) for structures behind it. Choose this for viewpoints inside a volume with a wide field of view, such as virtual colonoscopy. Restricts ray marching to the region between the viewpoint and a pre-existing mesh surface. Choose this when a high-fidelity mesh is available and volume details are needed behind it. Simultaneously displays volumetric and non-volumetric objects by computing two independent images and combining them based on depth information. Choose this for interactive applications prioritizing simplicity and moving polygons over complex occlusion handling. A technique that simulates an endoscopic exam by locating a point of view inside a hollow organ lumen using surface rendering. It is used for studying the colon, respiratory tract, auditory canal, and urinary tract. Virtual gastroscopy provides more accurate Bormann gastric cancer staging and greater sensitivity in detecting early gastric cancer than cross-sectional CT studies. It is also used to explore the nasal cavity when planning surgery for maxillofacial pathologies and for performing virtual laryngoscopies. The concept of hybrid rendering emerged to address the limitations of pure volume or pure surface methods, particularly in medical imaging where both dense volumetric data and sharp anatomical boundaries coexist. Early implementations focused on combining ray casting with rasterization to improve performance. Modern implementations often use neural representations or advanced BVH structures to manage the complexity of hybrid scenes. It is widely used in virtual endoscopy for exploring hollow organs such as the colon, respiratory tract, and urinary tract.
