name: Multi-Mode Rendering with Iso-surfaces and Meshes
head: Hybrid Ray Tracing for Iso-surfaces and Meshes, Surface-Volume Hybrid Rendering
body: Multi-Mode Rendering with Iso-surfaces and Meshes is a rendering technique that combines hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection for surface geometry (meshes/iso-surfaces) with volume ray marching, using clipping planes to control the integration range. It supports volume data, implicit iso-surfaces, and triangle meshes, using separate BVHs and hardware-accelerated intersection tests. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific two-stage surface hit detection (mesh BVH then iso-surface BVH) followed by volume integration, utilizing RTX hardware acceleration for the surface components. The method operates in three distinct phases: surface intersection detection, ray shortening, and volume integration. It supports multiple data types: triangle meshes, implicit isosurfaces, and volumetric scalar fields. Inputs: Camera ray r(t) = o + t \cdot d, where o is the origin and d is the direction. Triangle mesh geometry. Implicit isosurface defined by a scalar field and an iso-value v{iso}. Volumetric scalar field data. Clipping plane parameters defining t{min} and t{max}. Outputs: Final pixel color C{final} and opacity \alpha{final}. The method maintains separate BVHs for different data types to optimize traversal: 1. Mesh BVH: A bounding volume hierarchy containing triangle primitives, queried using hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection (e.g., RTX). 2. Iso-surface BVH: A BVH representing the implicit isosurface, rebuilt whenever the iso-value v{iso} changes. 3. Volume BVH: A BVH representing the volumetric data (e.g., ExaBricks structure), used for ray marching and empty space skipping within the volume. The rendering process for a single pixel ray proceeds as follows: 1. Mesh Surface Intersection: Trace the ray r against the Mesh BVH using hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection. Let t{mesh} be the distance to the nearest intersection. If no intersection is found, set t{mesh} = \infty. 2. Iso-surface Intersection: Transform the ray into the volume space (if coordinate systems differ). Trace the transformed ray against the Iso-surface BVH to find the nearest intersection with the implicit isosurface. Let t{iso} be the distance to this intersection. If no intersection is found, set t{iso} = \infty. 3. Determine Surface Hit: Calculate the nearest surface hit distance t{surface} = \min(t{mesh}, t{iso}). If t{surface} = \infty, the ray does not hit any surface geometry within the scene bounds. 4. Shorten Ray: Determine the effective integration limit t{end} for the volume rendering. This is constrained by the clipping planes and the surface hit: t{end} = \min(t{max}, t{surface}), where t{max} is the far clipping plane distance. The near clipping plane t{min} is also applied. The volume integration interval is [t{min}, t{end}]. 5. Volume Integration: Trace the shortened ray through the Volume BVH to integrate the volume up to t{end}. 6. Surface Contribution: If a surface was hit (t{surface} < t{max}), compute the surface color and normal at the hit point. For iso-surface hits, compute the gradient to derive the normal. Apply shading models and ambient occlusion if enabled. 7. Final Compositing: Blend the volume contribution and the surface contribution. The volume is rendered up to t{surface}, and the surface color is blended with the accumulated volume color at that depth. Iso-value (v{iso}): The scalar threshold for isosurface extraction. Changing this requires rebuilding the Iso-surface BVH. Clipping Planes: Defined by t{min} and t{max} intervals on the ray. Implemented by setting ray.tmin and ray.tmax. Ambient Occlusion: Supported for better depth cues, using two rays per pixel on surface and iso-surface geometry. Unverified code. """ # Step 1: Trace against Mesh BVH tmesh = meshbvh.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmesh is None: tmesh = float('inf') # Step 2: Trace against Iso-surface BVH # Transform ray to volume space if necessary rayvolorigin = rayorigin rayvoldir = raydirection tiso = isosurfacebvh.intersect(rayvolorigin, rayvoldir, isovalue) if tiso is None: tiso = float('inf') # Step 3: Determine nearest surface hit tsurface = min(tmesh, tiso) # Step 4: Shorten ray for volume integration tend = min(tmax, tsurface) # Step 5: Volume Integration volcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] volalpha = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tend: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection val = volumebvh.sample(pos) c, a = transferfunction(val) volcolor = volcolor + c (1.0 - volalpha) volalpha = volalpha + a (1.0 - volalpha) t += stepsize # Step 6: Surface Contribution surfacecolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] surfacealpha = 0.0 if tsurface < tmax: if tmesh <= tiso: hitpoint = rayorigin + tmesh raydirection normal = meshbvh.getnormal(hitpoint) else: hitpoint = rayorigin + tiso raydirection # Compute gradient for iso-surface normal # Source prefers analytic gradients by default for continuity and speed normal = computegradientnormal(hitpoint, volumebvh) surfacecolor = shadingmodel(rayorigin, hitpoint, normal, raydirection) surfacealpha = 1.0 # Step 7: Final Compositing finalalpha = volalpha + surfacealpha (1.0 - volalpha) finalcolor = volcolor + surfacecolor surfacealpha (1.0 - volalpha) return finalcolor, finalalpha def computegradientnormal(point, volumebvh): """Compute surface normal via central differences.""" eps = 1e-4 dx = volumebvh.sample([point[0]+eps, point[1], point[2]]) - volumebvh.sample([point[0]-eps, point[1], point[2]]) dy = volumebvh.sample([point[0], point[1]+eps, point[2]]) - volumebvh.sample([point[0], point[1]-eps, point[2]]) dz = volumebvh.sample([point[0], point[1], point[2]+eps]) - volumebvh.sample([point[0], point[1], point[2]-eps]) return normalize([dx, dy, dz]) def normalize(v): """Standard vector normalization.""" length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if length == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] Iso-surface BVH Rebuild: The Iso-surface BVH must be rebuilt whenever the iso-value changes. Coordinate Space Transformation: Rays must be correctly transformed into volume space before querying the Iso-surface BVH. Precision: Hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection is generally robust, but floating-point precision issues may arise at grazing angles or very small triangles. Ambient Occlusion: Enabling ambient occlusion uses two additional rays per pixel for surface and iso-surface geometry. Time Complexity: Dominated by BVH traversal and volume integration. Surface intersection is O(\log N) for BVH traversal, where N is the number of primitives. Volume integration is proportional to the number of samples within [t{min}, t{end}]. Memory Complexity: Requires storing three BVHs (Mesh, Iso-surface, Volume). The Iso-surface BVH size depends on the complexity of the isosurface. Performance: Hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection (RTX) provides significant speedup for mesh rendering. Empty space skipping via BVHs reduces the number of volume samples. Iso-surfaces generally offer more potential for empty space skipping due to their sparsity compared to dense volume data. Strengths: Efficient handling of mixed geometry and volume data; high-quality surface rendering; flexible clipping. Limitations: Requires rebuilding Iso-surface BVH for iso-value changes; increased implementation complexity; potential for aliasing if surface and volume boundaries are not aligned. This method is part of the ExaBricks rendering framework, which focuses on ray tracing structured AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data. It was introduced to support realistic evaluation of data structures under conditions involving implicit isosurfaces and direct volume rendering. The approach leverages modern GPU hardware (RTX) for surface intersection, combining it with software-based volume ray marching. It is used in scientific visualization for large-scale datasets, such as those from the Exajet and LANL Impact simulations. name: Hybrid Isosurface/DVR Rendering
head: Hybrid isosurface rendering, direct volume rendering
body: Hybrid Isosurface/DVR Rendering is a strategy for viewpoints inside a volume with a wide field of view, such as virtual colonoscopy, that combines surface rendering for near structures (e.g., the colon wall) with Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) for structures behind it. It sets itself apart from pure DVR by using the isosurface to define the integration start point, and from pure isosurface rendering by continuing the ray march to capture internal volume details. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data, isosurface threshold, camera ray origin and direction, near clipping plane t{min}, far clipping plane t{max\far}, step size. Output: Final pixel color and opacity. Data Structures: Volume data stored in memory, potentially divided into bricks if too large for local GPU memory. Steps: 1. Isosurface Detection: Find the nearest intersection with the isosurface along the ray starting from t{min}. This can be done using a fixed number of bisection or binary search steps. The distance to this intersection is t{surf}. 2. Surface Compositing: Render the isosurface at t{surf}. Calculate the surface color C{iso} and opacity A{iso} using semi-transparent shading. 3. Volume Integration: Continue ray marching from t{surf} to t{max\far}. Initialize the transmittance accumulator with T = 1.0 - A{iso}. Initialize the accumulated color C{acc} = C{iso}. 4. Ray Marching: For each step dt from t{surf} to t{max\far}: Sample volume value v at current position. Compute opacity \alpha and color c using transfer functions. Composite using front-to-back blending: C{acc} = C{acc} + T \cdot c \cdot \alpha T = T \cdot (1 - \alpha) If T drops below a threshold (e.g., 10^{-4}), terminate early. 5. Final Output: Return C{acc} and final opacity A{final} = 1.0 - T. Parameters: Bisection steps: Fixed number, which has virtually no impact on performance. Sampling distance: e.g., 1.0 or 5.0 units. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small features or silhouettes may cause intersection problems; adaptive sampling is required to handle these correctly. Without refinement, sampling artifacts may appear; hiding sampling artifacts can be achieved via techniques similar to interleaved sampling. Shading is expensive; full ray casting step computes only intersection image if shading is skipped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Aiso Cacc = Ciso # Step 4: Volume Integration (unshaded DVR) tcurrent = tsurf + stepsize while tcurrent < tmaxfar and T > 1e-4: pos = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0]tcurrent, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1]tcurrent, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2]tcurrent) val = samplevolume(pos, volumedata) alpha, color = transferfunction(val) weight = T alpha Cacc = (Cacc[0] + weight color[0], Cacc[1] + weight color[1], Cacc[2] + weight color[2]) T = (1.0 - alpha) tcurrent += stepsize return Cacc, 1.0 - T def standarddvr(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, tmin, tmaxfar, stepsize, transferfunction): T = 1.0 Cacc = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = tmin while t < tmaxfar and T > 1e-4: pos = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0]t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1]t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2]t) val = samplevolume(pos, volumedata) alpha, color = transferfunction(val) weight = T alpha Cacc = (Cacc[0] + weight color[0], Cacc[1] + weight color[1], Cacc[2] + weight color[2]) T = (1.0 - alpha) t += stepsize return Cacc, 1.0 - T def samplevolume(pos, volumedata): # Standard volume access or trilinear interpolation return volumedata.sample(pos) def computesurfacenormal(pos, volumedata): # Central difference approximation eps = 1e-3 dx = samplevolume((pos[0]+eps, pos[1], pos[2]), volumedata) - samplevolume((pos[0]-eps, pos[1], pos[2]), volumedata) dy = samplevolume((pos[0], pos[1]+eps, pos[2]), volumedata) - samplevolume((pos[0], pos[1]-eps, pos[2]), volumedata) dz = samplevolume((pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]+eps), volumedata) - samplevolume((pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]-eps), volumedata) n = (dx, dy, dz) lensq = n[0]2 + n[1]2 + n[2]2 return (n[0]/math.sqrt(lensq), n[1]/math.sqrt(lensq), n[2]/math.sqrt(lensq)) def applyshading(pos, normal, raydirection): # Semi-transparent shading model lightdir = (1.0, 1.0, -1.0) lensq = lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2 lightdir = (lightdir[0]/math.sqrt(lensq), lightdir[1]/math.sqrt(lensq), lightdir[2]/math.sqrt(lensq)) diff = max(0.0, normal[0]lightdir[0] + normal[1]lightdir[1] + normal[2]lightdir[2]) color = (0.8 diff + 0.2, 0.8 diff + 0.2, 0.8 diff + 0.2) return color, 1.0 Combines multiple rendering modes including meshes and isosurfaces. Hybrid Volume-Surface Rendering Merges depth information from surface and volume passes. Choose when precise occlusion handling is required. Z-buffer merging Time Complexity: Depends on the cost of isosurface detection and the length of the remaining ray march. Bisection steps have virtually no impact on performance. Memory Complexity: Requires volume data in memory. If too large, brick-based structures are used. Performance: Sampling distance affects frame rate; e.g., 1.0 sampling yields 24 fps, while 5.0 yields 66 fps on tested hardware. Strengths: Effective for internal viewpoints with wide fields of view, providing both surface detail and internal volume context. Limitations: Shading is expensive; full ray casting step computes only intersection image if shading is skipped. Adaptive sampling may be needed for small features. Originating in the context of advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume raycasting, this method is particularly relevant for applications like virtual colonoscopy where the viewer is inside the volume. It addresses the need to render both the enclosing surface and internal structures efficiently. name: Hybrid Rendering
head: Vosh rendering
body: Hybrid rendering combines volume ray marching with surface rasterization to optimize performance and fidelity. It solves the problem of redundant computation in regions where high-fidelity surface geometry is available by restricting volume integration to the space between the camera and the nearest surface intersection. Unlike pure volume rendering, it leverages mesh depth to terminate ray marching early, and unlike pure surface rendering, it retains volumetric effects in the foreground. Inputs: Camera ray r(t) = o + td. Volume representation providing density \sigma, diffuse color cd, and view-dependent features f at any point. Surface mesh providing intersection geometry and shading attributes. Near clipping distance t{min} and step size dt. Outputs: Final hybrid color C{vosh}. Diffuse color C{vosh,d}. View-dependent features F{vosh}. Data Structures: Voxel Weights: wi, the accumulated alpha weight at step i during ray marching. Mesh Weight: wm, representing the remaining transmittance reaching the surface. Surface Attributes: Diffuse color c{d,m} and view-dependent features fm at the intersection point. Steps: 1. Ray-Mesh Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray and determine the nearest intersection with the surface mesh. Let t{max} be the distance to this intersection. If no intersection is found, t{max} defaults to the volume boundary. 2. Volume Ray Marching: Perform volume rendering along the ray from t{min} to t{max}. Accumulate color and weights using standard volumetric integration. 3. Calculate Mesh Weight: Compute the weight of the surface contribution as the remaining transmittance: wm = 1 - \sumi wi This represents the portion of light that passed through the volume without being absorbed or scattered. 4. Surface Contribution: Retrieve the surface color and features at the intersection point (t{max}). 5. Hybrid Compositing: Combine the volume and surface contributions: C{vosh,d} = \sumi wi c{d,i} + wm c{d,m} F{vosh} = \sumi wi fi + wm fm where c{d,i} and fi are the diffuse color and view-dependent features from the i-th volume step. The final color is derived using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that models view-dependent effects: C{vosh} = C{vosh,d} + \text{MLP}(C{vosh,d}, F{vosh}, d) where d is the ray direction passed to the MLP. Pseudocode: def hybridrender(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, dt, mesh, volume, mlp): # Step 1: Find surface intersection tmax = mesh.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmax is None: tmax = 1000.0 # Default far clipping plane # Step 2: Volume Ray Marching T = 1.0 Cdiffuse = 0.0 F = 0.0 Wvol = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection density, cd, f = volume.sample(pos) alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density dt) wi = T alpha Wvol += wi T = (1.0 - alpha) Cdiffuse += wi cd F += wi f t += dt # Step 3: Calculate Mesh Weight wm = 1.0 - Wvol # Step 4: Get Surface Attributes surfacepos = rayorigin + tmax raydirection meshcolordiffuse, meshfeatures = mesh.getattributes(surfacepos) # Step 5: Hybrid Compositing finaldiffuse = Cdiffuse + wm meshcolordiffuse finalfeatures = F + wm meshfeatures finalcolor = finaldiffuse + mlp(finaldiffuse, finalfeatures, raydirection) return finalcolor Parameters: t{min}: Near clipping plane distance. t{max}: Distance to nearest surface intersection. dt: Step size for volume ray marching. MLP: A neural network mapping diffuse color, view-dependent features, and a direction variable to final color. Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point precision errors at t{max} may cause gaps or overlaps between volume and surface. Ensure consistent depth bias or epsilon checks when sampling the surface. Uses explicit isosurfaces for integration bounds. Choose when geometry is complex but not explicitly meshed. Combines DVR with isosurface rasterization. Choose when isosurface extraction is feasible and preferred over mesh fitting. General category of combining volume and surface techniques. Choose when specific hybrid strategies (like Vosh) are not required. Time Complexity: O(Nv + Ns), where Nv is the number of volume samples (reduced by early termination at t{max}) and Ns is the cost of mesh intersection and shading. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the volume representation (voxel grid or neural network weights) and mesh storage. Performance: Significantly reduces ray marching cost in regions with high-fidelity meshes. Hybrid rendering was introduced to leverage the strengths of both volume and surface representations. The specific "Vosh" (Voxel-Mesh Hybrid) formulation was proposed in 2024 for real-time view synthesis, aiming to reduce time costs associated with ray marching by confining it to the space before the surface. The concept of using mesh depth to limit volume integration was also explored in the context of Neural Volumes (2019) to avoid expending representational power on areas already covered by high-fidelity meshes. name: Hybrid Ray Tracing and Rasterization
head: Hybrid RT, Ray Tracing and Hybrid Rendering, Real-time Path Tracing / Hybrid RT, リアルタイムパストレーシング / ハイブリッドRT
body: Hybrid Ray Tracing and Rasterization is a rendering technique that combines the accuracy of ray tracing with the performance of rasterization-based techniques to achieve high visual fidelity and real-time interaction. It addresses the trade-off between the speed of rasterization and the physical accuracy of ray tracing by using rasterization for the primary image pass and ray tracing to augment specific effects such as reflections, shadows, and global illumination. The method operates in two distinct phases, leveraging modern GPU hardware capabilities introduced with architectures like NVIDIA RTX and APIs like DirectX Raytracing (DXR). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A scene graph containing geometry, materials, and lighting; a rasterization pipeline configuration; a ray tracing acceleration structure (e.g., BVH); and a denoising algorithm (often AI-based). Outputs: A final composite image with physically plausible lighting effects. Data Structures: Rasterization Buffers: Standard framebuffers for color, depth, and normals. Acceleration Structure: A Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) or similar structure for efficient ray-scene intersection tests, required for the ray tracing pass. Steps: 1. Rasterization Pass: Render the scene using standard rasterization techniques to generate the base color, depth, and other auxiliary buffers. This step handles the majority of the geometry and provides the primary lighting contribution. 2. Ray Tracing Pass: For specific effects (reflections, shadows, global illumination), cast rays from the pixel coordinates into the scene using the acceleration structure. Calculate the intersection points and compute lighting contributions for these specific paths. 3. Compositing: Combine the results from the rasterization pass and the ray tracing pass. The ray-traced effects are typically blended or overlaid onto the rasterized base image. 4. Denoising: Apply an AI-based denoising algorithm to the ray-traced components to reduce noise, which is inherent in real-time path tracing due to limited sample counts. Parameters: Ray Depth: Typically limited to 1-3 bounces for real-time performance. Sample Count: Low sample counts per pixel (e.g., 1-4) for ray-traced effects, relying on denoising. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Dependency: The technique is highly dependent on hardware support for ray tracing (e.g., RT cores). Power and Thermal Constraints: High computational load can lead to significant power consumption and thermal issues, limiting its use in mobile or thermally constrained devices. Optical Inconsistency: While improved, hybrid methods may still exhibit optical inconsistencies compared to full path tracing, particularly in complex lighting scenarios. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization pass, which is O(N) where N is the number of pixels and primitives. The ray tracing pass adds overhead proportional to the number of rays cast and the complexity of the acceleration structure. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for acceleration structures and auxiliary buffers for ray tracing effects. Performance: Offers a balance between quality and speed, making it a practical solution for real-time applications like games. However, it is significantly more demanding than pure rasterization. Strengths: High visual fidelity for specific effects; real-time performance achievable on modern hardware. Limitations: Hardware dependency; potential for optical inconsistencies; high power consumption. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring high-quality lighting effects, such as modern video games. When Not to Use: Applications requiring full physical accuracy (use full path tracing) or those running on hardware without ray tracing support. The hybrid approach emerged as a practical compromise between the high quality of offline rendering and the speed requirements of real-time applications. With the introduction of NVIDIA RTX and DirectX Raytracing (DXR) in 2018, hybrid rendering became the mainstay in the gaming industry. Since 2023, efforts have shifted towards "Real-time Path Tracing," which attempts to run full Monte Carlo path tracing in real-time, supported by AI denoising, with examples like NVIDIA Portal RTX. name: Z-buffer merging
head: Z-buffer merge
body: Z-buffer merging is a hybrid rendering technique that simultaneously displays volumetric and non-volumetric (polygonal) objects by computing two independent images and combining them based on depth information. It solves the problem of integrating static volume data with interactive surface geometry by decoupling the rendering pipelines. Unlike Hybrid Volume-Surface Rendering which integrates surface and volume data in a single pass, Z-buffer merging uses a post-processing step to select pixels, making it a "brute-force" strategy that prioritizes simplicity and interactivity for moving polygons over complex occlusion handling. Inputs and Outputs: Input 1: Volume dataset (scalar field). Input 2: Polygonal surface mesh. Input 3: Camera parameters. Output: Composite image containing both volume and surface contributions. Data Structures: 1. Volume Image (IV): 2D array of color values. 2. Volume Z-buffer (ZV): 2D array of depth values. 3. Surface Image (IS): 2D array of color values. 4. Surface Z-buffer (ZS): 2D array of depth values. Steps: 1. Compute Volume Image and Z-buffer: Perform volume rendering (e.g., ray casting) to generate IV. Compute ZV for each pixel. The depth value is either the depth of the first non-zero voxel encountered or the depth at which a user-defined opacity threshold is exceeded. 2. Compute Surface Image and Z-buffer: Perform traditional rasterization or ray tracing of the polygonal mesh to generate IS. Compute ZS for each pixel, representing the depth of the nearest surface intersection. 3. Merge Images: For each pixel (x, y), compare ZV(x, y) and ZS(x, y). If ZV(x, y) < ZS(x, y), the pixel color is IV(x, y). Otherwise, the pixel color is IS(x, y). This selects the object closest to the camera. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zbuffermerge(volumedata, surfacemesh, camera): # Step 1: Render volume IV, ZV = rendervolume(volumedata, camera) # Step 2: Render surface IS, ZS = rendersurface(surfacemesh, camera) # Step 3: Merge compositeimage = emptyimagelike(IV) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): if ZV[y, x] < ZS[y, x]: compositeimage[y, x] = IV[y, x] else: compositeimage[y, x] = IS[y, x] return compositeimage Parameters: Opacity Threshold: A user-defined value determining when to stop volume integration for ZV calculation. Depth Comparison: Standard less-than comparison for depth values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Occlusion: The method may not handle complex occlusion correctly because it does not account for transparency or partial overlaps between volume and surface in a physically based manner. Static Volume Assumption: The method is most useful when the volume rendered image remains static while polygonal objects move, as only the surface rendering needs to be repeated. Voxelization Artifacts: Surfaces usually exhibit strange artifacts after voxelization, requiring high-resolution volume datasets for reasonable quality. An improvement to Z-buffer merging where ray casting integration is terminated early based on pre-computed surface depth. It avoids traversing the whole volume by stopping ray integration when the depth specified in the pre-computed Z-buffer is reached. The accumulated opacity from volume rendering determines the blending weight between the volume color and the underlying surface color. This reduces computational cost compared to full volume rendering while maintaining the hybrid display capability. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(NV + NS), where NV is the number of volume samples and NS is the number of surface primitives. In Levoy's variant, NV is reduced by early termination. Memory: O(W \times H) for the two images and two Z-buffers, where W and H are image dimensions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with image resolution. Performance is independent of volume resolution in the basic merge, but depends on it in Levoy's variant due to early termination benefits. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; allows interactive movement of polygonal objects in a static volume scene. Limitations: Brute-force strategy; may not handle complex occlusion correctly; artifacts from voxelization. When to use it and when not: Use when interactive surface movement is required in a static volume scene. Do not use when accurate transparency blending or complex occlusion between volume and surface is critical. Originated as a simple technique to simultaneously display volumetric and non-volumetric objects. An improvement was suggested by Levoy. It is used in volume rendering systems where hybrid display of surfaces and volumes is needed. name: CPU Volume Raycasting for Intersection
head: RaycastScene, Volume Raycasting for Intersection, VolumeRaycaster
body: This method performs a CPU-based ray-primitive intersection test against a scene containing multiple volume datasets, returning the closest hit between a world-space ray and any volume object. It iterates through all volume instances, samples voxel data, and evaluates visibility windows to determine intersections. Inputs and Outputs Input: A world-space ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and a scene graph containing instances of VolumeRenderedObject. Output: A RaycastHit structure containing the closest VolumeRenderedObject, the intersection point in world space, and the distance from the ray origin. Returns false if no volume is hit. Data Structures The hit result is stored in a RaycastHit struct with the following fields: VolumeRenderedObject volumeObject: Reference to the hit volume object. Vector3 point: The 3D intersection point in world coordinates. float distance: The Euclidean distance from the ray origin to the hit point. Algorithm Steps 1. Scene Traversal: Retrieve all active VolumeRenderedObject instances in the scene. 2. Collection: For each object, invoke RaycastObject with the world-space ray and collect successful hits into a list. 3. Sorting: Sort the list of hits by distance in ascending order. 4. Selection: Return the first hit in the sorted list if the list is not empty; otherwise, return failure. Per-Object Intersection (RaycastObject) For a specific volume object, the intersection logic proceeds as follows: 1. Transform Setup: Retrieve the volume's local-to-world transform and its cross-section (cutout) data. 2. Visibility Window: Calculate the minimum and maximum valid data values based on the dataset's min/max and user-defined visibility window parameters. 3. Local Space Conversion: Transform the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} from world space to the volume's local space using the inverse of the volume's transform matrix. 4. AABB Intersection: Define a unit axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) centered at the origin with bounds [0, 1]^3 (i.e., Vector3.zero to Vector3.one). Intersect the local ray with this AABB to find the entry parameter t{start}. 5. Raymarch Initialization: Initialize the raymarch position and direction. If the ray does not intersect the AABB, return false. 6. Sampling Loop: Iterate along the ray direction within the AABB bounds: a. Bounds Check: Break the loop if the current position is outside the local bounds. b. Cutout Test: Check if the current world-space position is occluded by any cross-section/cutout object (e.g., planes, boxes). If hidden, skip sampling for this step. c. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the current world-space position to texture coordinates (u, v, w) by adding an offset of 0.5 to the normalized local coordinates. d. Index Calculation: Calculate the integer indices (i, j, k) for the volume dataset based on the texture coordinates. e. Data Sampling: Sample the raw data value V at index (i, j, k). f. Normalization: Normalize V to the range [0.0, 1.0] using the dataset's global min and max values: V{norm} = \frac{V - V{min}}{V{max} - V{min}}. g. Transfer Function: Evaluate the transfer function alpha \alpha for V{norm}. h. Hit Condition: If V{norm} is within the visibility window and \alpha > 0, a hit is recorded. 7. Result Construction: Transform the hit position back to world space. Calculate the distance as the magnitude of the vector from the original ray origin to the hit point. Return true with the hit data. Cutout Evaluation (IsCutout) The IsCutout function determines if a point is inside or outside specific geometric shapes (Plane, BoxInclusive, BoxExclusive) using matrix transformation: Plane: Uses the plane's normal and distance from origin. BoxInclusive/BoxExclusive: Uses the box's transformation matrix to transform the point into local box space and checks if coordinates lie within bounds. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class RaycastHit: def init(self, volumeobject, point, distance): self.volumeObject = volumeobject self.point = point self.distance = distance def findobjectsoftype(sceneobjects, typename): """Returns all objects in the scene matching the type name.""" return [obj for obj in sceneobjects if obj.type == typename] def intersectrayaabb(origin, direction, minbound, maxbound): """Returns tstart where ray enters unit AABB, or None if no intersection.""" tmin = float('-inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < minbound[i] or origin[i] > maxbound[i]: return None else: t1 = (minbound[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (maxbound[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return None return tmin def texturecoordstoindices(uvw, resolution): """Converts normalized texture coordinates to integer voxel indices.""" return [int(u res) for u, res in zip(uvw, resolution)] def pointinhalfspace(point, normal, distance): """Returns True if point is on the positive side of the plane.""" return sum(p n for p, n in zip(point, normal)) + distance >= 0 def vectormagnitude(v): """Returns Euclidean length of vector v.""" return math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in v)) def isinsidebox(localpos, boundsmin, boundsmax): """Returns True if localpos is within box bounds.""" return all(bmin <= p <= bmax for p, bmin, bmax in zip(localpos, boundsmin, boundsmax)) def cpuvolumeraycastscene(worldrayorigin, worldraydirection, sceneobjects): """Finds the closest volume intersection in a scene.""" hits = [] volumeobjects = findobjectsoftype(sceneobjects, "VolumeRenderedObject") for obj in volumeobjects: hit = raycastobject(worldrayorigin, worldraydirection, obj) if hit is not None: hits.append(hit) hits.sort(key=lambda h: h.distance) return hits[0] if hits else None def raycastobject(worldrayorigin, worldraydirection, volumeobj): """Tests intersection with a single volume object.""" transform = volumeobj.transform cutouts = volumeobj.crosssectiondata vmin = volumeobj.datasetmin vmax = volumeobj.datasetmax viswindow = volumeobj.visibilitywindow localrayorigin = transform.worldtolocal(worldrayorigin) localraydirection = transform.worldtolocaldirection(worldraydirection) tstart = intersectrayaabb(localrayorigin, localraydirection, minbound=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), maxbound=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) if tstart is None: return None currentpos = localrayorigin + localraydirection tstart stepsize = 0.01 # Standard fixed step size while tstart <= 1.0: # Break loop if position is outside local bounds if not all(0.0 <= p <= 1.0 for p in currentpos): break worldpos = transform.localtoworld(currentpos) if not isoccluded(worldpos, cutouts): # Convert world position to texture coordinates (uvw) by adding 0.5 uvw = [p + 0.5 for p in currentpos] # Calculate integer indices for the volume dataset idx = texturecoordstoindices(uvw, volumeobj.resolution) # Sample the data value at the calculated index rawvalue = volumeobj.datasample(idx) # Normalize the sampled value to 0.0-1.0 range using dataset min/max if vmax != vmin: normalized = (rawvalue - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) else: normalized = 0.0 # Evaluate transfer function alpha alpha = volumeobj.transferfunction(normalized) # If value is within visibility window and transfer function alpha > 0, record hit and return true if viswindow.min <= normalized <= viswindow.max and alpha > 0: # Hit point is transformed back to world space hitpointworld = transform.localtoworld(currentpos) # Calculate the distance as the magnitude of the vector from the original ray origin to the hit point distance = vectormagnitude([w - o for w, o in zip(hitpointworld, worldrayorigin)]) return RaycastHit(volumeobj, hitpointworld, distance) tstart += stepsize currentpos = localrayorigin + localraydirection tstart return None def isoccluded(worldpos, cutouts): """Checks if position is inside any cutout shape using matrix transformation.""" for cutout in cutouts: if cutout.type == "Plane": if pointinhalfspace(worldpos, cutout.planenormal, cutout.planedistance): return True elif cutout.type in ["BoxInclusive", "BoxExclusive"]: # Uses the box's transformation matrix to transform the point into local box space localpos = cutout.transform.worldtolocal(worldpos) if isinsidebox(localpos, cutout.boundsmin, cutout.boundsmax): return True return False Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M + K \log K), where N is the number of volume objects, M is the number of samples per ray, and K is the number of hits. Memory Complexity: O(K) for storing hit results. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, integrates directly with CPU-side scene graphs. Limitations: Poor scalability with high-resolution volumes or many objects. This method is implemented in the UnityVolumeRendering project. It is designed for interactive tools within the Unity engine, leveraging its component-based architecture (VolumeRenderedObject, SlicingPlane). name: Ray-traced Isosurface Extraction on Tetrahedral Cells
head: Closed-form ray-cell intersection, Implicit isosurface ray tracing
body: A parallel software rendering technique that computes isosurfaces for unstructured tetrahedral grids implicitly via ray tracing, treating each tetrahedron as an independent item and avoiding explicit polygon extraction. Unlike explicit polygon extraction methods (e.g., marching cubes), this approach avoids generating millions of polygons, enabling interactive rendering rates on parallel hardware where conventional high-end graphics hardware would struggle. Inputs and Outputs Input: Unstructured tetrahedral grid data (vertex positions, scalar field values per vertex), ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, isovalue I. Output: Intersection distance t (or miss) for the closest isosurface intersection along the ray. Data Structures Tetrahedron: Defined by 4 vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 and associated scalar values s0, s1, s2, s3. Ray: Parametric equation \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where t > 0. Method Steps 1. Cell Culling: If the system uses a hierarchical structure (e.g., a bounding volume hierarchy or cell organization), first test if the ray intersects the bounding volume of a cell containing tetrahedra. If not, skip the cell. 2. Tetrahedron Processing: For each tetrahedron in the cell, treat it as an independent item. 3. Closed-Form Intersection: Compute the intersection of the parameterized ray and the isoplane directly using the implicit equation for the plane and the parametric equation for the ray. The scalar field S(\mathbf{p}) inside the tetrahedron is interpolated linearly using barycentric coordinates, making the isosurface within the cell a plane segment. This yields a linear equation in t, solved in closed form. 4. Root Finding: Solve for t such that S(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) = I. For linear interpolation, this reduces to a single root calculation. 5. Validity Check: Verify the intersection point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} lies within the tetrahedron bounds by ensuring all barycentric coordinates of \mathbf{p} with respect to the tetrahedron vertices are positive. 6. Selection: If multiple roots exist, select the smallest t value (closest to the eye). If no roots exist, the ray misses the isosurface in the cell. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytraceisosurfacetet(v0, v1, v2, v3, s0, s1, s2, s3, rayo, rayd, isovalue): # 1. Compute plane coefficients A, B, C, D for S(p) = Ax + By + Cz + D # Solve M [A, B, C, D]^T = [s0, s1, s2, s3]^T M = [[v0[0], v0[1], v0[2], 1], [v1[0], v1[1], v1[2], 1], [v2[0], v2[1], v2[2], 1], [v3[0], v3[1], v3[2], 1]] S = [s0, s1, s2, s3] coeffs = solve4x4(M, S) A, B, C, D = coeffs # 2. Compute ray-plane intersection t denom = A rayd[0] + B rayd[1] + C rayd[2] if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return None # Ray parallel to isoplane num = isovalue - (A rayo[0] + B rayo[1] + C rayo[2] + D) t = num / denom if t <= 0: return None # Intersection behind ray origin # 3. Check if intersection point lies within tetrahedron bounds p = [rayo[0] + t rayd[0], rayo[1] + t rayd[1], rayo[2] + t rayd[2]] l0, l1, l2, l3 = computebarycentric(p, v0, v1, v2, v3) if l0 > 0 and l1 > 0 and l2 > 0 and l3 > 0: return t else: return None def solve4x4(M, S): # Solves M x = S using Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting. n = 4 aug = [M[i] + [S[i]] for i in range(n)] for i in range(n): maxrow = i for k in range(i + 1, n): if abs(aug[k][i]) > abs(aug[maxrow][i]): maxrow = k aug[i], aug[maxrow] = aug[maxrow], aug[i] pivot = aug[i][i] if abs(pivot) < 1e-12: return [0.0] n for k in range(i + 1, n): factor = aug[k][i] / pivot for j in range(i, n + 1): aug[k][j] -= factor aug[i][j] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): x[i] = aug[i][n] for j in range(i + 1, n): x[i] -= aug[i][j] x[j] x[i] /= aug[i][i] return x def computebarycentric(p, v0, v1, v2, v3): # Computes barycentric coordinates using signed volume ratios. def tetvol(a, b, c, d): return (b[0]-a[0])(c[1]-a[1])(d[2]-a[2]) + \ (b[1]-a[1])(c[2]-a[2])(d[0]-a[0]) + \ (b[2]-a[2])(c[0]-a[0])(d[1]-a[1]) - \ (b[2]-a[2])(c[1]-a[1])(d[0]-a[0]) - \ (b[1]-a[1])(c[0]-a[0])(d[2]-a[2]) - \ (b[0]-a[0])(c[2]-a[2])(d[1]-a[1]) voltotal = tetvol(v0, v1, v2, v3) if abs(voltotal) < 1e-12: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) l0 = tetvol(p, v1, v2, v3) / voltotal l1 = tetvol(v0, p, v2, v3) / voltotal l2 = tetvol(v0, v1, p, v3) / voltotal l3 = tetvol(v0, v1, v2, p) / voltotal return l0, l1, l2, l3 Parameters Image resolution: 512 × 512 pixels. Processor count: 64 processors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Trilinear Interpolation Ambiguity: Using trilinear interpolation directly (if applied at a cell level rather than tetrahedron level) produces more complex isosurfaces than marching cubes, potentially causing topological ambiguities (e.g., case 4 from Lorensen and Cline). Disambiguation techniques like the Asymptotic Decider can resolve ambiguities but may still miss the correct topology due to the interpolation scheme. Multiple Roots: If the polynomial has multiple roots, the smallest t (closest to the eye) is selected. No Roots: If no roots exist, the ray misses the isosurface in the cell. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Renders a ray-traced isosurface of the Visible Woman dataset at roughly 10 frames per second using a 512 × 512 image on 64 processors. Scaling: The method is parallelized across processors. Table 1 in the source shows speedup from 1 to 124 processors, with frame rates increasing from 0.427 fps to 43.06 fps for the skin isosurface and 0.304 fps to 30.28 fps for the bone isosurface. Strengths: Enables interactive rendering rates on parallel hardware for large-scale datasets without the overhead of explicit polygon generation. Allows interactive exploration by changing isovalue or viewpoint. Limitations: Does not suit applications that require the geometry for non-graphics purposes (e.g., physics simulation, mesh processing) because it avoids explicit extraction. Trilinear interpolation can cause topological ambiguities. When to Use: Interactive exploration of large-scale scientific visualization datasets (e.g., Visible Woman, aerodynamic-flow data) on parallel machines. When Not to Use: When explicit polygonal geometry is required for downstream non-graphics tasks. Origin: The method is described in "Parallel Software Rendering for Large-Scale Volume Visualization". History: The paper contrasts this implicit ray-tracing approach with explicit polygon extraction (marching cubes) for the Visible Woman dataset. The Visible Woman skin isosurface would generate 18,068,534 polygons, and the bone isosurface 12,922,628 polygons, which would be challenging to render interactively on conventional high-end graphics hardware at the time. Usage: Used for interactive exploration of large-scale scientific visualization datasets on parallel machines. Parallel Software Rendering for Large-Scale Volume Visualization, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/489126f2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volume Raycaster Actor
head: 3D Iso-surface and DVR Actor, Met.3D Volume Raycaster
body: The Volume Raycaster Actor is a visualization component that renders 3-D scalar fields using either iso-surface raycasting or direct volume rendering (DVR). It supports interactive exploration of atmospheric simulation data, providing advanced illumination, shadowing, and normal curves. Unlike standard DVR which blends the entire volume, this actor can extract explicit surfaces of constant scalar value, allowing for independent configuration of multiple iso-surfaces and their shading by secondary variables. Inputs: Scalar Fields: One or more 3-D scalar fields. Observed variable: The primary field for iso-surface extraction or DVR. Shading variable: An optional field used to color the iso-surface (iso-surface mode) or for cloud coloring/shading (DVR mode). Second/Third variables: Optional secondary and tertiary fields rendered simultaneously in DVR mode. Cloud Variables: Specific fields for liquid water content (LWC) and ice water content (IWC) in cloud rendering mode. Transfer Functions: Mappings from scalar values to color and opacity for each variable. Scene Geometry: Other actors in the scene onto which iso-surfaces cast shadows. Light Sources: Defined in the scene for volumetric lighting calculations. Outputs: A 2-D image representing the rendered volume or iso-surfaces. Shadow maps or depth information for projecting shadows onto other geometry. The actor manages several internal states and configurations: Render Mode: Enum controlling behavior: 'Isosurface rendering', 'Bitfield', 'Direct volume rendering', 'Direct volume rendering with volumetric lighting'. Lightmap: A volumetric texture storing precomputed lighting information. Its resolution is configurable (Lightmap resolution) and may be downscaled during interaction (Interactivity resolution). Iso-surface Configuration: A list of iso-values, each with independent settings for color mode, surface color, opacity, and associated shading variable. Ray Parameters: Ray step size: Distance per integration step in graphics space. Interaction ray step size: Larger step size used during camera interaction. Isosurface bisection steps: Number of refinement steps for intersection detection. The rendering process depends on the selected Render mode. 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersecting the volume domain. 2. Dithering (Optional): If Dithering is enabled, randomize the ray start position slightly to avoid patterns visible with low ray step sizes. 3. Traversal: Sample the Observed variable along the ray using Ray step size (or Interaction ray step size during interaction). 4. Iso-surface Detection: Detect crossings where the scalar value equals a configured Iso-value. 5. Refinement: Upon detection, refine the intersection position using iterative bisection of the last ray step. The number of steps is controlled by Isosurface bisection steps (or Interaction isosurface bisection steps during interaction). 6. Shading: Compute the surface normal at the hit point. Color the surface using the Surface colour or derive it from the Shading variable via its transfer function. 7. Shadow Casting: Cast shadow rays from the hit point to light sources to determine occlusion by other geometry or other iso-surfaces. 8. Normal Curves (Optional): If enabled, render lines/tubes between two iso-surfaces. The length is limited by the maximum number of line segments, and seed point spacing is configurable. 1. Extinction Coefficient Conversion: Convert the alpha (transparency) value from the transfer function to an extinction coefficient \sigmat. This allows blending of different volumes. 2. Scaling Compensation: Adjust extinction coefficients to compensate for vertical scene scaling, ensuring optical thickness remains approximately constant. The Z scale transparency fix option determines if this affects only the Z-axis (Normal) or all axes (Physical). 3. Ray Traversal: Sample the Observed variable (and optionally Second and Third variables) along the ray. 4. Compositing: Use front-to-back compositing based on the extinction coefficients and transfer functions to compute the final color and opacity. 5. Cloud Rendering (Special Mode): If configured for atmospheric clouds: Use Liquid water content variable and Ice water content variable. Apply CLWC colour and CIWC colour or use the Shading variable for cloud colour. Apply Account for earth’s curvature correction to optical thickness if enabled. Use Real vertical scale (meters) or Uniform scaling (degrees) for distance calculations. 1. Preprocessing (Lightmap Generation): Cast rays from each voxel in the Lightmap resolution grid towards all light sources. Compute optical depth along these rays to determine light attenuation. Apply approximations for multi-scattering using Powder depth and Powder strength to darken thin volumes. Store the resulting lighting in the volumetric lightmap. 2. Rendering: During standard DVR or Iso-surface rendering, sample the lightmap at the ray's position to add ambient illumination and volumetric shadows. Shadow density multiplies the darkness of shadows produced by the volume. Note: Lighting does not need to be recomputed every frame, introducing an initial preprocessing cost but low runtime overhead. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rendervolumeraycasteractor(scene, camera, rendermode, variables, transferfunctions, params): """Main entry point for the Volume Raycaster Actor.""" lightmap = None if rendermode == 'Direct volume rendering with volumetric lighting': lightmap = computevolumetriclightmap(scene, variables, params) height, width = camera.resolution outputimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height width)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) if params.get('dithering', False): dx = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) params.get('ditheringstrength', 1.0) dy = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) params.get('ditheringstrength', 1.0) dz = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) params.get('ditheringstrength', 1.0) rayorigin = [rayorigin[i] + [dx, dy, dz][i] for i in range(3)] isinteracting = params.get('isinteracting', False) basestep = params.get('interactionraystepsize') if isinteracting else params.get('raystepsize') stepsize = max(basestep, 1e-6) maxdist = 1000.0 if rendermode in ['Isosurface rendering', 'Bitfield']: color = renderisosurface(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxdist, variables['Observed'], variables.get('Shading'), transferfunctions, params, lightmap, scene) elif rendermode == 'Direct volume rendering': color = renderdvr(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxdist, variables, transferfunctions, params, lightmap) else: color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] outputimage[y width + x] = color return outputimage def renderisosurface(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxdist, observedvar, shadingvar, tf, params, lightmap, scene): """Renders iso-surfaces by detecting threshold crossings.""" isovalues = params.get('isovalues', []) t = 0.0 prevval = observedvar.sample(rayorigin) while t < maxdist: t += stepsize pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] val = observedvar.sample(pos) hitt = None for isoval in isovalues: if (prevval - isoval) (val - isoval) < 0: hitt = bisectionrefine(observedvar, rayorigin, raydirection, t - stepsize, stepsize, isoval, params.get('isosurfacebisectionsteps')) break if hitt is not None: hitpoint = [rayorigin[i] + hitt raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] eps = stepsize 0.1 grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): ppos = [hitpoint[j] + (eps if j == i else 0) for j in range(3)] mpos = [hitpoint[j] - (eps if j == i else 0) for j in range(3)] grad[i] = (observedvar.sample(ppos) - observedvar.sample(mpos)) / (2 eps) hitnormal = grad if shadingvar: shadingval = shadingvar.sample(hitpoint) hitcolor = tf['Shading'].map(shadingval) else: hitcolor = params.get('surfacecolor', [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) opacity = tf['Observed'].getopacity(isovalues[0]) shadowfactor = castshadowray(hitpoint, scene.lightsources, observedvar) ambient = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if lightmap: ambient = lightmap.sample(hitpoint) shadowdensity = params.get('shadowdensity', 0.0) hitcolor = [hitcolor[i] (1.0 - shadowdensity (1.0 - shadowfactor)) + ambient[i] for i in range(3)] # Normal curves rendering logic not given in sources. return [hitcolor[i] opacity for i in range(3)] + [opacity] prevval = val return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def renderdvr(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxdist, variables, tf, params, lightmap): """Renders direct volume using front-to-back compositing.""" refscale = max(params.get('referencescale', 1.0), 1e-6) zscalefix = params.get('zscaletransparencyfix', 'Normal') color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < maxdist and accumulatedopacity < 0.99: t += stepsize pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] valobs = variables['Observed'].sample(pos) c, a = tf['Observed'].map(valobs) sigmat = -math.log(max(1.0 - a, 1e-6)) / refscale # Exact scaling compensation formula not given in sources. if zscalefix == 'Physical': sigmat = 1.0 elif zscalefix == 'Normal': sigmat = 1.0 alphasample = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmat stepsize) lightcontribution = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if lightmap: lightcontribution = lightmap.sample(pos) weight = alphasample (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) color = [color[i] + (c[i] + lightcontribution[i]) weight for i in range(3)] accumulatedopacity += weight return color + [accumulatedopacity] def computevolumetriclightmap(scene, variables, params): """Precomputes lighting in a volumetric grid.""" resolution = params.get('lightmapresolution', 64) lightmapdata = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for z in range(resolution): for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): voxelpos = [x, y, z] totallight = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for light in scene.lightsources: raytolight = [light.position[i] - voxelpos[i] for i in range(3)] dist = math.sqrt(sum(vv for v in raytolight)) if dist < 1e-6: continue opticaldepth = integrateextinction(variables, voxelpos, raytolight, dist) attenuation = math.exp(-opticaldepth) powder = params.get('powderstrength', 0.0) math.exp(-params.get('powderdepth', 0.0) opticaldepth) totallight = [totallight[i] + light.color[i] attenuation + powder for i in range(3)] lightmapdata[z][y][x] = totallight return lightmapdata def bisectionrefine(observedvar, rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, stepsize, isoval, steps): """Refines intersection via iterative bisection.""" tlow, thigh = tstart, tstart + stepsize valstart = observedvar.sample([rayorigin[i] + tlow raydirection[i] for i in range(3)]) for in range(steps): tmid = (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 valmid = observedvar.sample([rayorigin[i] + tmid raydirection[i] for i in range(3)]) if (valstart - isoval) (valmid - isoval) < 0: thigh = tmid else: tlow = tmid return (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 def castshadowray(hitpoint, lightsources, observedvar): """Checks occlusion along ray to light sources.""" shadowfactor = 1.0 for light in lightsources: raytolight = [light.position[i] - hitpoint[i] for i in range(3)] dist = math.sqrt(sum(vv for v in raytolight)) if dist < 1e-6: continue opticaldepth = integrateextinction({'Observed': observedvar}, hitpoint, raytolight, dist) shadowfactor = math.exp(-opticaldepth) return shadowfactor def integrateextinction(variables, startpos, direction, maxdist): """Integrates extinction along a ray.""" step = 0.01 depth = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < maxdist: pos = [startpos[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3)] val = variables['Observed'].sample(pos) depth += val step t += step return depth Ray step size: Controls accuracy vs. performance. Example: 0.01 for radar data DVR. Interaction ray step size: Larger than ray step size for faster interaction. Example: 0.01 (same as ray step in example, but typically larger). Isosurface bisection steps: Controls intersection refinement accuracy. Dithering: Boolean. Example: true. Dithering strength: Example: 1. Reference scale: Used for alpha-to-extinction conversion. Example: 4 (World units). Lightmap resolution: Size of the volumetric lightmap. Higher is more accurate but expensive. Powder depth/strength: Multi-scattering approximation parameters. Shadow density: Multiplier for shadow darkness. Multi-scattering: Physically accurate multi-scattering is expensive. The actor uses approximations (Powder depth/strength) which may not fully capture complex lighting in dense volumes. Vertical Scaling: Incorrect handling of vertical scene scaling can lead to incorrect optical thickness and transparency. The Z scale transparency fix and Reference scale parameters must be tuned to the data's physical dimensions. Earth's Curvature: For large-scale atmospheric datasets, ignoring earth's curvature can distort optical thickness. The Account for earth’s curvature option applies a correction to the optical thickness due to earth’s curvature. Uniform Scaling: Using Uniform scaling (where vertical unit equals horizontal unit in meters) produces visually uniform but physically inaccurate clouds if the data's vertical scale differs significantly from horizontal. Iso-surface Rendering: Time complexity is proportional to the number of pixels and the number of ray steps within the volume. Refinement adds a logarithmic factor based on Isosurface bisection steps. DVR: Time complexity is proportional to the number of pixels and ray steps. Multi-variable rendering increases sampling cost. Volumetric Lighting: Preprocessing time is proportional to Lightmap resolution cubed times the number of light sources. Runtime overhead is low as lighting is precomputed. Memory: Requires storage for the scalar fields, transfer functions, and optionally the volumetric lightmap. Lightmap memory scales with Lightmap resolution. Specific performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) are not provided in the sources. Volumetric lighting is noted to require "substantially more rendering time" than standard DVR, primarily due to preprocessing. Strengths: Supports both explicit iso-surfaces and implicit DVR. Advanced illumination including shadow casting and volumetric lighting. Interactive exploration with adjustable step sizes and bisection refinement. Specialized modes for atmospheric clouds and radar data. Limitations: Volumetric lighting is computationally expensive. Approximations for multi-scattering may lack physical accuracy. Accuracy depends heavily on parameter tuning (step size, reference scale). Use for interactive visualization of 3-D scalar fields, particularly atmospheric or radar data. Use when explicit surface extraction with shading by secondary variables is required. Use when volumetric shadows and lighting effects are desired for depth perception. Avoid for real-time applications requiring high-fidelity multi-scattering without preprocessing. Avoid if the dataset does not benefit from iso-surface extraction or if simple volume blending is sufficient and performance is critical. The Volume Raycaster Actor is part of the Met.3D visualization suite, designed for meteorological and atmospheric data. It supports interactive exploration of simulation data and provides advanced rendering techniques such as shadow casting and normal curves. The actor is documented in the Met.3D user manual. name: Multiple Volume Rendering with Surface Models
head: Overlaying volume data sets with 3D surface models, Bounded volume compositing
body: This method renders multiple volumetric data sets overlaid on a 3D surface model (e.g., an architectural building) by computing the contribution of each volume set individually and combining them. It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing internal volume structures within a bounded exterior geometry, optimizing memory access patterns for graphics hardware. Unlike standard ray casting that treats the volume as an infinite medium, this method distinguishes between "bounded" volumes (which have a geometric boundary like a wall) and "un-bounded" volumes, stopping ray integration at the nearest surface boundary for bounded sets. Inputs: A 3D surface model (mesh) defining boundaries (e.g., building walls). M volumetric data sets, each with associated transfer functions and shader methods. Camera position and viewing direction. A pre-computed depth buffer (z-buffer) of the surface model from the current camera perspective. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out}. Data Structures: Surface Depth Buffer: A 2D array storing the distance t{surface} from the camera origin to the nearest surface intersection for each pixel. Volume Data Sets: Array of M volumes, each containing voxel data and a classification of its shader method type (Bounded or Un-bounded). Shader Method Classification: Each volume is assigned one of seven shader methods, categorized into two groups: 1. Penetrating: Rays fully penetrate the volume (Methods 1, 2, 4, 7). 2. Terminating: Rays end at a point inside the volume (Methods 3, 5, 6). Algorithm Steps: 1. Surface Pre-computation: Render the 3D surface model to a depth buffer to determine the boundary distance t{surface} for every pixel. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, define the ray r(t) starting at the camera origin. 3. Volume Classification: Identify which of the M volume data sets are "bounded" (have a geometric limit defined by the surface model) and which are "un-bounded". 4. Boundary Determination: For the current ray, find the nearest boundary point t{boundary} among all "bounded" volume sets. If no bounded volumes exist, t{boundary} = \infty. 5. Un-bounded Volume Integration: For all "un-bounded" volume sets, perform ray marching from t{near} to t{boundary} (or t{far} if no boundary is closer). Compute the accumulated color and opacity contribution \mathbf{C}{unbounded} using standard front-to-back compositing. 6. Bounded Volume Integration: For each "bounded" volume set, perform ray marching from t{near} to t{boundary} (the specific boundary for that volume). Compute the contribution \mathbf{C}{bounded, i} for each volume i individually. 7. Combination: Combine the contributions of all volume sets. The specific combination logic depends on the shader method group: For Penetrating methods, contributions are composited through the volume. For Terminating methods, the ray integration stops at the computed interior point or boundary. The final color is calculated using an optional transfer function applied to the combined data. 8. Optimization: Memory access patterns are optimized by compacting address blocks to maximize memory caching during the individual volume computations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermultiplevolumeswithsurface(surfacedepthbuffer, volumes, camera): """ Render multiple volumes overlaid on a surface model. Args: surfacedepthbuffer: 2D array of distances to surface boundaries per pixel. volumes: List of Volume objects, each with: data: 3D voxel grid transferfunction: function mapping voxel value to (color, opacity) shadertype: Enum {PENETRATING, TERMINATING} isbounded: Boolean camera: Camera object with origin and direction generation. Returns: image: 2D array of final pixel colors. """ height, width = surfacedepthbuffer.shape image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # 1. Get surface boundary distance for this pixel tsurface = surfacedepthbuffer[y, x] # 2. Initialize accumulated color and opacity acccolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accopacity = 0.0 # 3. Separate volumes into bounded and un-bounded boundedvolumes = [v for v in volumes if v.isbounded] unboundedvolumes = [v for v in volumes if not v.isbounded] # 4. Determine the nearest boundary among bounded volumes # If no bounded volumes, tboundary is effectively infinity tboundary = np.inf if boundedvolumes: # For simplicity, assume all bounded volumes share the same # geometric boundary defined by the surface model. # In complex scenarios, each volume might have its own boundary mesh. tboundary = tsurface # 5. Process Un-bounded Volumes # These are integrated up to the nearest boundary (or full depth if no boundary) # Note: Standard ray casting logic applies here, but limited by tboundary for vol in unboundedvolumes: # Ray march from tnear to min(tfar, tboundary) # Compute contribution using front-to-back compositing volcolor, volopacity = raymarchvolume( vol, camera, tnear=0.0, tend=min(tboundary, vol.maxdepth)) # Composite into accumulator # Cout = Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) Cvol alphavol # alphaout = alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alphavol acccolor = acccolor + (1 - accopacity) volcolor volopacity accopacity = accopacity + (1 - accopacity) volopacity # 6. Process Bounded Volumes # These are integrated up to the specific boundary for vol in boundedvolumes: # Ray march from tnear to tboundary volcolor, volopacity = raymarchvolume( vol, camera, tnear=0.0, tend=tboundary) # Composite into accumulator acccolor = acccolor + (1 - accopacity) volcolor volopacity accopacity = accopacity + (1 - accopacity) volopacity # 7. Apply optional transfer function for final color adjustment # (Assuming transfer function was applied during ray march, # this step might handle global adjustments or specific shader logic) image[y, x] = acccolor return image def raymarchvolume(volume, camera, tnear, tend): """ Standard front-to-back ray marching for a single volume. Optimized for memory access patterns. """ acccolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accopacity = 0.0 # Generate sample points along the ray # Number of samples N depends on resolution and step size N = 100 # Placeholder for implementation detail dt = (tend - tnear) / N for i in range(N): t = tnear + i dt p = camera.origin + t camera.direction # Sample volume value v = volume.sample(p) # Map to color and opacity using transfer function c, alpha = volume.transferfunction(v) # Correct opacity for step size (Beer-Lambert) # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma dt) # Assuming sigma is derived from v or alpha is pre-corrected # Composite # Cacc = Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) c alpha # alphaacc = alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alpha acccolor = acccolor + (1 - accopacity) c alpha accopacity = accopacity + (1 - accopacity) alpha # Early termination if fully opaque if accopacity >= 0.99: break return acccolor, accopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in depth buffer comparisons may cause gaps or overlaps between surface and volume boundaries. Bounded vs. Un-bounded Logic: Incorrectly classifying a volume as un-bounded when it has a geometric limit will cause rays to pass through walls, creating visual artifacts. Memory Access: Failure to compact address blocks for volume data leads to poor cache performance on graphics hardware. A hybrid technique that maps volumetric data onto a user-specified iso-surface, allowing interactive rendering of internal details using conventional surface rendering algorithms. It differs by pre-computing ray contributions to the surface faces, whereas Multiple Volume Rendering with Surface Models integrates volumes up to a geometric boundary during the ray casting pass. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot M \cdot N), where P is the number of pixels, M is the number of volume sets, and N is the number of samples per ray. The complexity is dominated by the individual ray marching passes for each volume set. Memory Complexity: O(V{total} + S), where V{total} is the total size of all volume data sets and S is the size of the surface depth buffer. Performance: Optimized for graphics hardware by computing contributions per volume individually to maximize memory caching. Strengths: Efficiently handles multiple overlapping volumes with clear geometric boundaries; allows differentiation between volume data sets. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the surface depth buffer; limited to scenarios where volumes are bounded by a known surface model. The method was developed in the context of architectural visualization, specifically for overlapping and combining 3D voxel volume data with 3D building models. It was presented by Kreeger et al. in 2012, building on earlier work by Kreeger et al. (1999) regarding surface model integration. The approach addresses the need for users to differentiate between multiple volume data sets (e.g., thermal, structural, utility) within a complex architectural model.
