name: Volume on Surface (VoS)
head: VoS (Volume on Surface)
body: Volume on Surface (VoS) is a hybrid rendering technique that integrates surface and volume rendering to visualize internal volume structures using conventional surface rendering algorithms. It solves the problem of efficiently displaying internal volume details without the high computational cost of full volume ray casting by mapping volumetric data onto a user-specified iso-surface extracted from the volume grid. Unlike image-based hybrid approaches that use external bounding surfaces or texture mapping, VoS casts rays directly from the faces of the boundary surface during a pre-visualization step, storing results to allow interactive rendering on commodity graphics hardware. VoS is a two-step method: (i) Pre-visualization, which maps volume information onto an extracted iso-surface, and (ii) Surface rendering, which renders the surface using the pre-computed data. Inputs: A regular volume grid of voxels. An iso-surface S extracted from the volume grid. User-defined transfer functions for color and opacity. Rendering parameters: number of cones per vertex, number of observation lines per cone, high-pass filter threshold, and opacity function type. Outputs: A rendered image of the iso-surface with internal volume structures visible. Pre-computed color values stored at each surface vertex for each observation line. Iso-surface Geometry: Iso-surface geometry and other information required by the mapping process are stored in a topological data structure. High-Pass Filtered Volume: The volume grid is filtered to identify material transitions; values are stored for ray sampling. Vertex Data: Each vertex v on the iso-surface stores a list of pre-computed colors; for each observation line ri originating from v, a color Ci is stored. Ray Samples: Each ray is associated with a list of samples, where a sample is a voxel along the ray trajectory whose high-pass filtered value is within a user-specified threshold. Cones: Virtual cones are defined centered at each vertex, aligned with the vertex normal vector. Cones have equally spaced opening angles. Typical values: 3, 6, or 8 cones per vertex. Example angles: 15°, 45°, 75°. Observation Lines: Uniformly distributed over the surface of each cone. Typical values: 8 lines per cone. If 4 lines are used, the angle between them is 90°. High-Pass Filter Threshold: User-specified threshold to determine which voxels are stored as samples. Opacity Function: Can be intensity-based or position-based. Position-based functions assign opacity based on sample position along the ray to highlight internal or external structures. 1. Extract Iso-surface: Extract the iso-surface S from the volume grid. Store geometry and topology in a topological data structure. 2. Filter Volume: Apply a high-pass filter to the volume grid to identify material transitions. 3. Define Observation Lines: For each vertex v on S: Define k virtual cones centered at v with normal-aligned axes and equally spaced opening angles. For each cone, generate observation lines by uniformly distributing directions over the cone's surface. Let R = \{r1,..., rk\} be the set of all unit vectors pointing outwards from S, where k equals the number of cones multiplied by the number of rays cast per cone. 4. Cast Rays and Store Samples: For each observation line ri \in R starting at vertex v: Compute the discrete ray trajectory through the volume using a 3D scanline algorithm. For each voxel along the trajectory, check if its high-pass filtered value is within the user-specified threshold. If yes, store the voxel as a sample in the ray's list. 5. Compute Colors: For each ray (observation line) with its list of samples: Apply the user-defined color and opacity transfer functions to each sample to get c(i) and \alpha(i). Compute the final color C using Levoy's optical model: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} c(i)\alpha(i) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(j)) where N is the number of samples, c(i) is the color of sample i, and \alpha(i) is the opacity of sample i. Store C at vertex v associated with observation line ri. 1. Determine Viewer Direction: For each visible face vertex v: Let O be the viewer position. Compute the unit vector ro from O to v (pointing towards the viewer). 2. Select Observation Line: Find the observation line ri \in R such that the dot product ri \cdot ro is the largest positive value. This ri best approximates the viewer's line of sight. 3. Assign Color: Attribute the pre-computed color Ci (associated with ri) to vertex v. 4. Render Faces: For each face, compute its color as the average of the colors assigned to its vertices. Render all visible faces using standard surface rendering techniques (e.g., hidden element removal, lighting). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) if mag > 0 else (0, 0, 0) def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def dotproduct(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def applyhighpassfilter(volumegrid): # Standard high-pass filter implementation not provided in sources. return volumegrid def uniformdistributiononcone(position, normal, coneangledeg, numlines): lines = [] coneanglerad = math.radians(coneangledeg) sintheta = math.sin(coneanglerad) costheta = math.cos(coneanglerad) up = (0, 1, 0) if abs(normal[1]) < 0.9 else (1, 0, 0) u = normalize(cross(normal, up)) v = cross(normal, u) for i in range(numlines): phi = 2 math.pi i / numlines dirvec = (sintheta math.cos(phi) u[0] + sintheta math.sin(phi) v[0] + costheta normal[0], sintheta math.cos(phi) u[1] + sintheta math.sin(phi) v[1] + costheta normal[1], sintheta math.cos(phi) u[2] + sintheta math.sin(phi) v[2] + costheta normal[2]) lines.append(normalize(dirvec)) return lines def raytraversegrid(origin, direction, griddims, cellsize=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)): dx, dy, dz = cellsize x, y, z = int(math.floor(origin[0] / dx)), int(math.floor(origin[1] / dy)), int(math.floor(origin[2] / dz)) stepx = 1 if direction[0] > 0 else (-1 if direction[0] < 0 else 0) stepy = 1 if direction[1] > 0 else (-1 if direction[1] < 0 else 0) stepz = 1 if direction[2] > 0 else (-1 if direction[2] < 0 else 0) if direction[0] != 0: boundaryx = (x + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) dx tmaxx = abs(boundaryx - origin[0]) / abs(direction[0]) tdeltax = dx / abs(direction[0]) else: tmaxx = float('inf') tdeltax = float('inf') if direction[1] != 0: boundaryy = (y + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) dy tmaxy = abs(boundaryy - origin[1]) / abs(direction[1]) tdeltay = dy / abs(direction[1]) else: tmaxy = float('inf') tdeltay = float('inf') if direction[2] != 0: boundaryz = (z + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) dz tmaxz = abs(boundaryz - origin[2]) / abs(direction[2]) tdeltaz = dz / abs(direction[2]) else: tmaxz = float('inf') tdeltaz = float('inf') visited = [] maxsteps = griddims[0] griddims[1] griddims[2] steps = 0 while 0 <= x < griddims[0] and 0 <= y < griddims[1] and 0 <= z < griddims[2] and steps < maxsteps: visited.append((x, y, z)) steps += 1 if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: x += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax else: z += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: y += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay else: z += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz return visited def computeraycolor(samples, colorfunc, opacityfunc): if not samples: return (0, 0, 0) finalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for sample in samples: c = colorfunc(sample.value) alpha = opacityfunc(sample.positionalongray, sample.value) contribution = (c[0]alpha, c[1]alpha, c[2]alpha) finalcolor = (finalcolor[0] + contribution[0](1-accumulatedopacity), finalcolor[1] + contribution[1](1-accumulatedopacity), finalcolor[2] + contribution[2](1-accumulatedopacity)) accumulatedopacity += alpha (1 - accumulatedopacity) return finalcolor def previsualization(volumegrid, isosurface, numcones, linespercone, threshold, colorfunc, opacityfunc): filteredvolume = applyhighpassfilter(volumegrid) vertexcolors = {} coneangles = [15, 45, 75] for vertex in isosurface.vertices: normal = vertex.normal lines = [] for i in range(numcones): angle = coneangles[i] if i < len(coneangles) else (i 30) lines.extend(uniformdistributiononcone(vertex.position, normal, angle, linespercone)) for lineindex, linedirection in enumerate(lines): samples = [] raytrajectory = raytraversegrid(vertex.position, linedirection, volumegrid.griddims) for voxel in raytrajectory: if abs(filteredvolume[voxel]) <= threshold: samples.append(voxel) color = computeraycolor(samples, colorfunc, opacityfunc) vertexcolors[(vertex, lineindex)] = color return vertexcolors, lines def rendersurface(isosurface, vertexcolors, lines, viewerposition): for face in isosurface.faces: facecolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for vertex in face.vertices: viewertovertex = normalize((viewerposition[0]-vertex.position[0], viewerposition[1]-vertex.position[1], viewerposition[2]-vertex.position[2])) bestlineindex = -1 maxdot = -float('inf') for lineindex, linedirection in enumerate(lines): d = dotproduct(linedirection, viewertovertex) if d > maxdot: maxdot = d bestlineindex = lineindex color = vertexcolors[(vertex, bestlineindex)] facecolor = (facecolor[0] + color[0], facecolor[1] + color[1], facecolor[2] + color[2]) facecolor = (facecolor[0]/len(face.vertices), facecolor[1]/len(face.vertices), facecolor[2]/len(face.vertices)) # Standard rendering call # renderface(face, facecolor) Precision: Dot product computations for line selection should be performed in hardware for efficiency and precision. Boundaries: Rays are cast from the surface into the volume; the ray trajectory algorithm must handle volume boundaries and zero direction components correctly. Degenerate Input: If the iso-surface is empty or the volume grid is invalid, the method fails; valid input data is required. Transfer Function Changes: If color or opacity functions are modified, the pre-computed colors must be recomputed, but ray casting does not need to be repeated. Time Complexity: Pre-visualization time is proportional to the number of surface vertices, the number of observation lines per vertex, and the number of samples per ray. It is slightly greater than conventional DVR visualization time for small cone counts (e.g., 3 cones, 8 lines) but increases with more cones. Rendering time is fast, comparable to conventional surface rendering, as it involves only dot products and face averaging. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of surface vertices and the number of observation lines. For a dataset with 8 cones per vertex and 8 lines per cone, memory usage was close to 32 MB for a small dataset (86x42x59). Measured Performance: On a Pentium 4, 3.2 GHz, 1 GB RAM with a chest dataset (120x120x241): Conventional ray casting (VolView): ~20 seconds. Isosurface rendering (VTK): ~2 fps. VoS (3 cones, 8 lines): Pre-vis 41s, Best Case 0.25s, Worst Case 2.3s, 1.9 fps. VoS (6 cones, 8 lines): Pre-vis 1min 36s, Best Case 0.49s, Worst Case 3.85s, 1.3 fps. VoS (8 cones, 8 lines): Pre-vis 2min 10s, Best Case 0.64s, Worst Case 4.88s, 1.1 fps. Strengths: Interactive rendering rates on commodity hardware; no camera position issues (unlike keyview-based methods); flexible transfer function updates without re-casting rays. Limitations: Pre-visualization time can be significant; quality depends on the number of observation lines; only shows internal structures of the extracted iso-surface. When to Use: When interactive visualization of internal volume structures is required and conventional ray casting is too slow, but full volume rendering is not necessary. Suitable for scenarios where the iso-surface is well-defined and internal details are of interest. When Not to Use: When the iso-surface is not appropriate for the data, or when external structures are more important than internal ones. Also not suitable if real-time ray casting is required without pre-processing. VoS was introduced in 2006 by researchers presenting at GRAPP 2006. It builds on the idea of enhancing surface rendering with volume information, similar to image-based approaches like Chen et al. (2001), but differs by using an internal iso-surface and direct ray casting from faces. The method leverages Levoy's optical model for volume rendering. Volume on Surface, https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2006/13565/pdf/index.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Projection and Compositing Techniques
head: Isosurface Projection, Surface Compositing
body: This family extends first-hit ray casting by either accumulating statistical properties along the ray segment or correctly handling multiple surface intersections per pixel. It solves the limitation of single-hit methods which discard volumetric context or fail to render overlapping structures. It differs from Algebraic Surface Raycasting by relying on discrete voxel traversal rather than implicit function evaluation, and from Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer by using image-order accumulation rather than a global depth buffer. All methods in this family share the fundamental mechanism of image-order rendering: for each pixel, a ray is defined in world space, intersected with the volume domain, and sampled along its path to detect the first intersection with the isosurface. The ray is parameterized as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. The traversal order is determined by the pixel's position in the image plane. The core detection logic relies on the isosurface condition. For a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}), the surface is defined by f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau. In discrete voxel data, this is typically detected by a sign change or threshold crossing between consecutive samples: f(\mathbf{p}1) \cdot f(\mathbf{p}2) < 0 relative to \tau, or f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau. Upon detection, the intersection position is often refined (e.g., via linear interpolation or binary search) to reduce discretization artifacts. The surface normal is computed from the gradient \nabla f at the hit point, usually via finite differences or tri-cubic filtering, to enable Phong-like shading. The final color is computed using local lighting models (ambient, diffuse, specular) and potentially ambient occlusion or shadows, with no contribution from voxels behind the surface. A hybrid technique that computes the mean density of voxels along a ray within a valid range, rendering this average value with lighting based on the mean position. It differs from standard first-hit ray casting by accumulating statistics over the entire ray segment rather than stopping at the first surface, and from pure volume rendering by restricting accumulation to voxels that satisfy an isosurface crossing condition. This method is chosen when the goal is to visualize the average material properties of a structure while retaining surface-like shading cues derived from the centroid of the sampled volume. Terminates ray marching at the first voxel whose scalar value exceeds a specified threshold, rendering only the surface intersection. It discards all data behind the first hit, providing a clean isosurface visualization with local shading. Correctly renders multiple isosurfaces detected along a single ray by sorting them by depth before compositing. It solves the problem of incorrect visual occlusion when isosurfaces are detected in arbitrary order during ray traversal, ensuring that the closest surface occludes those behind it. It differs from Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection by explicitly handling discrete surface occlusion rather than intensity blending, and from Exact Projection First Contact by supporting multiple visible surfaces per ray rather than only the first hit. Originating from the need to visualize complex volumetric data where single-surface approximations are insufficient, these techniques evolved to support multi-material analysis and statistical visualization. They are widely used in medical imaging for dose visualization and anatomical overlay, and in scientific visualization for fiber tractography and material property averaging.

name: Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection
head: Exact Projection Mean Density
body: Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection is a hybrid volume rendering technique that computes the mean density of voxels along a ray within a valid range, rendering this average value with lighting based on the mean position. It differs from standard first-hit ray casting by accumulating statistics over the entire ray segment rather than stopping at the first surface, and from pure volume rendering by restricting accumulation to voxels that satisfy an isosurface crossing condition. This method is chosen when the goal is to visualize the average material properties of a structure while retaining surface-like shading cues derived from the centroid of the sampled volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, near/far clipping planes t{near}, t{far}, isosurface threshold \tau (called iso in sources), number of steps N=256. Input: 3D scalar texture V (density), 1D color map C. Output: Fragment color \mathbf{c}{out}. Data Structures: meanSum: Float accumulator for density values. meanPos: Vector accumulator for surface positions. color: Vector accumulator for color values. cnt: Integer counter initialized to 1, decremented when no crossing is detected, serving as the denominator for the average. Steps: 1. Initialize meanSum = 0.0, meanPos = (0,0,0), color = (0,0,0,0), and cnt = 1. 2. Iterate i from 0 to N-1: a. Calculate current position \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. b. Transform \mathbf{p}i to texture coordinates \mathbf{u}i using the source's specific layout assumption: \mathbf{tmp} = (px, py, pz \times 2.3486238532110093) \mathbf{u}i = \frac{1 + \mathbf{tmp}}{2} u{i,y} = 1 - u{i,y}. This implies a non-uniform aspect ratio or specific data layout. c. Sample scalar values vi = V(\mathbf{u}i) and v{i+1} = V(\mathbf{u}{i+1}). d. Check for isosurface crossing: if vi < \tau and v{i+1} > \tau, a crossing is detected. e. If crossing detected: i. Refine intersection position \mathbf{p}{surf} using binary search between \mathbf{p}i and \mathbf{p}{i+1}. ii. Sample value at surface: v{surf} = V(\mathbf{p}{surf}). iii. Accumulate color: \mathbf{color} += C(v{surf}). iv. Accumulate position: meanPos += \mathbf{p}{surf}. v. Accumulate density: meanSum += v{surf}. vi. Do not decrement cnt (it remains the denominator). f. If no crossing detected: decrement cnt. 3. After loop, if cnt > 0: a. Calculate mean density: v{mean} = \text{meanSum} / \text{cnt}. b. Calculate mean position: \mathbf{p}{mean} = \text{meanPos} / \text{cnt}. c. Apply compensation factor: \mathbf{color} \times= 1/(\tau + 0.5). d. Map mean density to base color: \mathbf{c}{base} = C(v{mean}). e. If lighting is enabled: i. Compute normal \mathbf{n} = \nabla V(\mathbf{p}{mean}). ii. Compute lit color: \mathbf{c}{lit} = \text{Lighting}(\mathbf{n}, -\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{p}{mean}, \mathbf{c}{base}). iii. Output \mathbf{c}{out} = \mathbf{c}{lit}. f. If lighting is disabled: i. Output \mathbf{c}{out} = \mathbf{c}{base}. 4. If cnt == 0, output black \mathbf{c}{out} = (0,0,0,0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. tnear) / numsteps meansum = 0.0 cnt = 1 # Initialize to 1 to avoid division by zero meanpos = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) coloracc = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(numsteps): t = tnear + i dt pos = rayorigin + t raydir # Transform to texture coordinates tmp = vec3(pos.x, pos.y, pos.z 2.3486238532110093) texpos = (1.0 + tmp) / 2.0 texpos.y = 1.0 - texpos.y # Sample current and next values val = volumetexture.sample(texpos).r tnext = t + dt posnext = rayorigin + tnext raydir tmpnext = vec3(posnext.x, posnext.y, posnext.z 2.3486238532110093) texposnext = (1.0 + tmpnext) / 2.0 texposnext.y = 1.0 - texposnext.y valnext = volumetexture.sample(texposnext).r # Check for isosurface crossing if val < isothreshold and valnext > isothreshold: # Binary search for exact surface position surfpos = binarysearchsurface(texpos, texposnext, isothreshold, volumetexture) surfval = volumetexture.sample(surfpos).r # Accumulate coloracc += colormap.sample(surfval) meanpos += surfpos meansum += surfval # cnt remains unchanged, acting as the denominator else: cnt -= 1 # Exclude non-crossing steps from average denominator if cnt > 0: meanval = meansum / cnt meanp = meanpos / cnt # Apply compensation factor coloracc = 1.0 / (isothreshold + 0.5) basecolor = colormap.sample(meanval) if enablelighting: normal = calculatenormal(meanp, volumetexture) litcolor = calculatelighting(normal, -raydir, meanp, basecolor.rgb) return vec4(litcolor, 1.0) else: return vec4(basecolor.rgb, 1.0) else: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def binarysearchsurface(texposstart, texposend, isothreshold, volumetexture, iterations=10): # Bisection to find t where texture value equals isothreshold tlow, thigh = 0.0, 1.0 for in range(iterations): tmid = (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 texposmid = mix(texposstart, texposend, tmid) valmid = volumetexture.sample(texposmid).r if valmid < isothreshold: tlow = tmid else: thigh = tmid return mix(texposstart, texposend, tlow) def calculatenormal(pos, volumetexture, epsilon=0.001): # Central finite differences dx = volumetexture.sample(pos + vec3(epsilon, 0.0, 0.0)).r - volumetexture.sample(pos - vec3(epsilon, 0.0, 0.0)).r dy = volumetexture.sample(pos + vec3(0.0, epsilon, 0.0)).r - volumetexture.sample(pos - vec3(0.0, epsilon, 0.0)).r dz = volumetexture.sample(pos + vec3(0.0, 0.0, epsilon)).r - volumetexture.sample(pos - vec3(0.0, 0.0, epsilon)).r return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) def calculatelighting(normal, viewdir, pos, basecolor, ambient=0.2, diffuse=0.8, specular=0.5, shininess=32.0): # Phong shading model lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, -1.0)) diff = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) diffuse reflectdir = reflect(-lightdir, normal) spec = pow(max(dot(viewdir, reflectdir), 0.0), shininess) specular return basecolor (ambient + diff + spec) Parameters: numsteps: Fixed at 256. isothreshold: Passed as a uniform; fractional part used for comparison. compensate: A factor 1/(\text{iso} + 0.5) applied to the color accumulator. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The hardcoded multiplier 2.3486238532110093 for the Z-axis assumes a specific non-uniform aspect ratio or data layout. Y-axis inversion is required for image orientation. Division by zero is avoided by initializing cnt to 1 and checking cnt > 0 before averaging. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N=256 is the fixed number of steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for accumulators. Strengths: Provides a smoothed representation of internal structure density while maintaining surface shading cues. Limitations: The fixed step count and specific texture coordinate transformations limit generalizability. The method may produce artifacts if the isosurface is not well-defined or if the density range is not normalized. When to use: When visualizing the average density of a volumetric object with surface-like shading is desired. The method is described in the context of a ray casting implementation using OpenGL and GLSL. It is also referenced in the context of "VisualNifty" as "Exact Projection Mean Density". The technique combines elements of mean density projection with isosurface detection to create a hybrid rendering effect. name: Exact Projection First Contact
head: FHC, First Hit, First-Hit Compositing, FirstHitShader
body: Exact Projection First Contact is a volume rendering technique that terminates ray marching at the first voxel whose scalar value exceeds a specified threshold, rendering only the surface intersection. It discards all data behind the first hit, providing a clean isosurface visualization with local shading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume texture (typically FloatType with RedFormat), camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), a density threshold \tau (iso-value), and optional lighting parameters. Output: A fragment color (RGB) and alpha (1.0) representing the shaded surface at the first contact point. Data Structures: Volume Texture: A 3D texture object storing voxel values, often implemented as a Data3DTexture with linear filtering enabled to support interpolation. Ray Parameters: The ray is defined as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where t is the distance along the ray. The intersection with the volume bounding box (often normalized to [0,1]^3) is calculated using the slab method to determine entry (t{entry}) and exit (t{exit}) distances. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Volume Intersection: Calculate the intersection of the view ray with the unit cube [0,1]^3. If t{entry} > t{exit}, the ray misses the volume; discard the pixel. Clamp t{entry} to \max(0.0, t{entry}) to ensure the start point is in front of the camera. 2. Initialization: Set the current position p0 = \mathbf{o} + t{entry}\mathbf{d} and sample the volume value v0 = \text{sample}(p0). Initialize firstContactVal to 0.0 and firstContactPos to p0. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate along the ray from t{entry} to t{exit} with a step size dt. The step size is determined by the inverse of the volume dimensions and the ray direction components to ensure consistent voxel traversal: dt = \min \left( \frac{\Delta x}{|dx|}, \frac{\Delta y}{|dy|}, \frac{\Delta z}{|dz|} \right) where \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z are the voxel sizes (or inverse dimensions if normalized). 4. Sampling and Detection: At each step, advance to p1 = p0 + \mathbf{d} \cdot dt and sample v1 = \text{sample}(p1). Check if the isosurface condition is met: v1 \ge \tau. 5. Refinement: If the condition is met, compute the linear interpolation factor \alpha to find the exact intersection point: \alpha = \frac{\tau - v0}{v1 - v0} p{hit} = \text{mix}(p0, p1, \alpha) v{hit} = \text{mix}(v0, v1, \alpha) Store p{hit} as firstContactPos and v{hit} as firstContactVal. Break the loop. 6. Fallback: If the loop completes without finding a hit (or if firstContactVal remains \le 0.0), output black color vec4(0.0) and terminate. 7. Shading: Color Mapping: Map firstContactVal to a base color using a color map texture: c{base} = \text{texture}(\text{colorMap}, \text{firstContactVal}). Normal Calculation: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} using the gradient of the scalar field at p{hit}, typically via finite differences or tri-linear filtering of the volume texture. Lighting: Apply a lighting model (e.g., Blinn-Phong, Phong, or Lambert) using \mathbf{n}, the view direction, and the light direction. Occlusion/Shadows: Optionally calculate ambient occlusion and shadows at p{hit}. 8. Output: The final fragment color is c{final} = c{shaded} \cdot c{occlusion} \cdot c{shadow} with alpha 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exactprojectionfirstcontact(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, colormap, threshold, enablelighting, enableao, enableshadow): # 1. Ray-Volume Intersection (Slab Method for unit cube [0,1]^3) invdir = 1.0 / raydirection t0 = (0.0 - rayorigin) invdir t1 = (1.0 - rayorigin) invdir tentry = max(min(t0.x, t1.x), min(t0.y, t1.y), min(t0.z, t1.z)) texit = min(max(t0.x, t1.x), max(t0.y, t1.y), max(t0.z, t1.z)) if tentry > texit: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) tentry = max(tentry, 0.0) # 2. Initialization currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection tentry currentval = samplevolume(volumetexture, currentpos) firstcontactval = 0.0 firstcontactpos = currentpos # 3. Marching Loop dt = calculatestepsize(raydirection, volumedimensions) t = tentry maxiterations = 2000 iterations = 0 while t < texit and iterations < maxiterations: nextpos = currentpos + raydirection dt nextval = samplevolume(volumetexture, nextpos) if nextval >= threshold: alpha = (threshold - currentval) / (nextval - currentval) firstcontactpos = mix(currentpos, nextpos, alpha) firstcontactval = mix(currentval, nextval, alpha) break currentpos = nextpos currentval = nextval t += dt iterations += 1 if firstcontactval <= 0.0: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) basecolor = samplecolormap(colormap, firstcontactval) normal = calculategradient(volumetexture, firstcontactpos) normal = normalize(normal) if enablelighting: shadedcolor = calculatelighting(normal, -raydirection, firstcontactpos, basecolor.rgb) else: shadedcolor = basecolor.rgb occlusion = calculateao(firstcontactpos) if enableao else 1.0 shadow = calculateshadow(firstcontactpos) if enableshadow else 1.0 finalcolor = shadedcolor occlusion shadow return vec4(finalcolor, 1.0) def samplevolume(texture, pos): # Trilinear interpolation of 3D texture at normalized position pos return texture.sample(pos) def calculatestepsize(direction, dimensions): # Compute step size to cross one voxel along the ray dtvec = vec3(1.0 / abs(direction.x), 1.0 / abs(direction.y), 1.0 / abs(direction.z)) return min(dtvec.x, dtvec.y, dtvec.z) def samplecolormap(maptexture, value): # Sample 1D color map texture at normalized value return maptexture.sample(value) def calculategradient(texture, pos): # Compute gradient via central finite differences eps = 0.001 dx = texture.sample(pos + vec3(eps, 0, 0)) - texture.sample(pos - vec3(eps, 0, 0)) dy = texture.sample(pos + vec3(0, eps, 0)) - texture.sample(pos - vec3(0, eps, 0)) dz = texture.sample(pos + vec3(0, 0, eps)) - texture.sample(pos - vec3(0, 0, eps)) return vec3(dx, dy, dz) def calculatelighting(normal, viewdir, pos, basecolor): # Simple Blinn-Phong shading lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, -1.0)) halfdir = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) diff = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) spec = pow(max(dot(normal, halfdir), 0.0), 32.0) return basecolor (0.5 + 0.5 diff) + vec3(0.3) spec def calculateao(pos): # Simple ambient occlusion approximation return 0.8 def calculateshadow(pos): # Placeholder for shadow calculation return 1.0 Parameters: threshold (\tau): The density/isovalue threshold. Default values vary by dataset; e.g., 0.5 for normalized data. steps: Number of ray marching steps. Default 200, can be overridden to 500. MAXLAYERS: Maximum number of iso-surface layers supported (e.g., 3). rendermode: Integer flag where 0 selects First-Hit Compositing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Direction Normalization: The ray direction interpolated from the vertex shader may not be normalized; it must be explicitly normalized before use. No Hit: If no voxel exceeds the threshold, the pixel is typically rendered black or transparent. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps along the ray until the first hit. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the raycasting logic, plus the memory for the volume texture and color map. Performance: Fast for surfaces that are close to the camera or have high contrast, as it terminates early. Strengths: Provides clean surface visualization with shading; computationally cheaper than full volume compositing if hits are frequent and early. Limitations: No internal structure is visible; sensitive to threshold selection; artifacts if step size is too large relative to surface curvature. When to use: When the primary interest is the outer surface of a volume (e.g., bone rendering in CT, skin rendering in MRI) and internal details are not required. Exact Projection First Contact is a fundamental technique in direct volume rendering, often implemented as a shader in interactive visualization tools. It is closely related to the concept of "first-hit" rendering used in medical imaging viewers for isolating specific tissue types (e.g., bones, skin). The method is implemented in various open-source projects such as volumevis (using Three.js) and VisualNifty. It is also featured in educational implementations of direct volume rendering, such as those found in computer graphics lecture notes. niklasgruener/volumevis, https://github.com/niklasgruener/volumevis, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) viljanvr/VisualNifty, https://github.com/viljanvr/VisualNifty, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) KaanAres10/Volume-Rendering, https://github.com/KaanAres10/Volume-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Masdaofdisasda/Vis1DirectVolumeRendering2022W, https://github.com/Masdaofdisasda/Vis1DirectVolumeRendering2022W, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Isosurface Depth Sorting and Compositing
head: Isosurface Compositing Order Correction
body: Isosurface Depth Sorting and Compositing is a method for correctly rendering multiple isosurfaces detected along a single ray by sorting them by depth before compositing. It solves the problem of incorrect visual occlusion when isosurfaces are detected in arbitrary order during ray traversal, ensuring that the closest surface occludes those behind it. It differs from Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection by explicitly handling discrete surface occlusion rather than intensity blending, and from Exact Projection First Contact by supporting multiple visible surfaces per ray rather than only the first hit. Inputs: A ray defined by origin and direction; a volume dataset containing scalar values; isosurface threshold values for one or more materials (e.g., anatomy and dose); sample spacing along the ray. Outputs: A final pixel color and opacity representing the correctly ordered composite of all detected isosurfaces. Data Structures: Surface: A struct containing: depth: Float, distance from ray origin to the intersection point. color: Vector3, RGB color of the surface material. opacity: Float, alpha value of the surface. id: Integer, unique identifier for tracking detection order (optional, for debugging). SurfaceList: A dynamic list of Surface objects. Steps: 1. Ray Traversal and Detection: Cast the ray through the volume. For each slab or sample interval, check if the scalar values cross the isosurface threshold(s). If a crossing is detected, calculate the precise intersection depth d using linear interpolation between sample points v1 at t1 and v2 at t2 with threshold T: t = t1 + \frac{T - v1}{v2 - v1} (t2 - t1) d = | \text{origin} + t \cdot \text{direction} | Create a Surface object with this depth and material properties, and add it to SurfaceList. 2. Sorting: Sort SurfaceList in ascending order of depth. This ensures the surface closest to the viewpoint is first. 3. Compositing: Iterate through the sorted SurfaceList. For each surface, apply front-to-back compositing: C{out} = C{in} + C{surf} \cdot \alpha{surf} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{surf} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) where C{in}, \alpha{in} are the accumulated color and opacity before the current surface, and C{surf}, \alpha{surf} are the current surface's color and opacity. 4. Final Output: The resulting C{out} and \alpha{out} are written to the pixel buffer. Parameters: Isosurface thresholds: Specific to the data (e.g., Hounsfield units for CT, arbitrary units for dose). Not given in the sources. Sample spacing: Determined by volume resolution and ray length. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Arbitrary Detection Order: Surfaces may be detected in any order (e.g., <1,2,3>) depending on traversal direction or data layout. They must be sorted by depth before compositing (e.g., to <2,1,3> if 2 is closest). Multiple Surfaces Between Voxels: If multiple surfaces lie between voxels, they must all be detected and sorted. Precision: Depth calculation must be precise to avoid sorting errors in dense volumes. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isosurfacedepthsortingcompositing(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, thresholds): surfaces = [] # Step 1: Detect isosurfaces # Iterate through volume along ray, detecting crossings # For each crossing, calculate depth and create Surface object # Add to surfaces list # Implementation details for ray-volume traversal omitted; assume standard slab traversal # Step 2: Sort by depth surfaces.sort(key=lambda s: s.depth) # Step 3: Composite in depth order accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for surface in surfaces: # Front-to-back compositing weight = surface.opacity (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = [ accumulatedcolor[i] + surface.color[i] weight for i in range(3) ] accumulatedalpha += weight return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha A variant for merging anatomy and radiation dose volumes where dose isosurfaces are computed on-the-fly and composited with anatomy surfaces. It is chosen when dynamic dose volumes require real-time gradient computation for shading. The key distinction is the on-the-fly gradient calculation for dose, as precomputed gradients are unavailable. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) per ray, where N is the number of detected isosurfaces, due to sorting. Detection is O(M) where M is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray to store detected surfaces. Measured Performance: Rendering high-resolution images on Pixel-Planes 5 took several seconds, requiring adaptive-progressive refinement to balance quality and speed. Strengths: Correctly handles complex occlusion scenarios with multiple surfaces; supports multimodal data fusion. Limitations: Sorting overhead increases with the number of surfaces; on-the-fly gradient computation for dose is expensive. When to Use: When accurate occlusion of multiple isosurfaces is critical, especially in multimodal contexts like radiotherapy planning. When Not to Use: When performance is paramount and approximate occlusion is acceptable, or when only the first surface is needed. Originated in the VISTA system for interactive multimodal volume visualization, specifically for radiotherapy planning (RTP) applications. Developed at UNC in the mid-1990s (tech report 94-040) to handle the dynamic nature of dose volumes where precomputed gradients were unavailable. It was incorporated into the system to ensure proper compositing of anatomy and dose isosurfaces, especially when multiple surfaces lay between voxels. name: Speculative Progressive Raycasting
head: Progressive Wavefront Isosurface Raycasting, implicit isosurface rendering algorithm, progressive algorithm for implicit isosurface raycasting, progressive wavefront traversal with ray-block speculation
body: Speculative Progressive Raycasting is a GPU-based algorithm for interactive, memory-constrained visualization of massive implicit isosurfaces. It solves the problem of rendering large volumes on lightweight devices (e.g., web browsers) by progressively traversing a wavefront of rays through a block-compressed volume, decompressing data on-demand to minimize memory footprint. It differs from static block-caching methods like BCMC by eliminating explicit triangle mesh storage and processing blocks in a view-dependent wavefront, tying compute costs primarily to image size rather than dataset size. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data compressed using ZFP's fixed-rate compression mode. Camera position and isovalue \tau. Output: Progressive image of the isosurface. Rendering completes when all rays have terminated. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains several image-sized buffers (width W, height H) and a GPU-driven LRU cache for decompressed blocks. 1. Ray Data Buffer: Size 16 bytes per-ray. Fields: Ray direction \mathbf{d} (3 floats), entry t value t{entry} (1 float). 2. Iterator State Buffer: Size 32 bytes per-ray. Fields: t{max} (1 float), current coarse cell ID (1 uint), current fine cell ID (1 uint), padding (1 float). 3. RBID Buffer: Image-sized buffer. Type: UINT. Value: Block ID each ray intersects, or UINTMAX if none. 4. Macrocell Grid: Two-level grid constructed on the GPU. Fine Grid: Uses ZFP's 4^3 block decomposition. Coarse Grid: Groups 4^3 regions of ZFP blocks to form coarse cells containing 16^3 voxels. Value Range: Each cell stores the value range [v{min}, v{max}]. This range is computed by combining the range of the cell's voxels/blocks with those of its neighbors in the +x, +y, +z directions to prevent cracks from missing values in the dual grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Upload ZFP-compressed volume data to the GPU. Construct the two-level macrocell grid on the GPU. Compute value ranges for all fine and coarse cells, incorporating neighbor ranges in +x, +y, +z to ensure no isovalue is missed due to dual grid boundaries. Initialize the LRU cache for decompressed blocks. 2. Ray Setup (per camera/isovalue change): Rasterize the backfaces of the volume's bounding box. In the fragment shader, compute ray directions \mathbf{d} and entry t values t{entry} for each pixel. Write \mathbf{d} and t{entry} to the Ray Data Buffer (16 bytes/ray). Mark rays that miss the volume as terminated. 3. Progressive Wavefront Loop: Repeat the following steps until all rays are terminated: 3.1. Macrocell Grid Traversal: For each active ray, traverse the coarse grid using the Amanatides and Woo algorithm. Skip coarse cells where \tau \notin [v{min}, v{max}]. Upon entering a coarse cell containing \tau, traverse the 4^3 fine grid blocks within it. Skip fine blocks where \tau \notin [v{min}, v{max}]. If a block containing \tau is found: Save the current coarse and fine grid iterator states (t{max} and cell IDs) to the Iterator State Buffer. This prevents precision issues from skipping cells between passes. Write the block ID to the RBID buffer for this ray. Mark the ray as having found a block (or terminated if it exits the volume). 3.2. Mark Visible and Active Blocks: Identify all blocks referenced in the RBID buffer as visible. Identify all +x, +y, +z neighbors of visible blocks as active. Active blocks are required to provide data for the visible block's dual grid to avoid cracks. Mark all visible and active blocks for decompression. 3.3. On-Demand Decompression and Caching: For each marked block: If the block is not in the LRU cache, decompress it using a WebGPU port of ZFP's CUDA decompressor. Insert the decompressed block into the LRU cache. If the cache exceeds capacity, evict the least recently used block. 3.4. Block Raycasting Kernel Setup: Perform stream compaction and parallel sorts to construct arrays of: Visible block IDs. Number of rays intersecting each block. Ray IDs sorted by their block ID. 3.5. Block Raycasting and Speculation: Launch the block raycasting kernel. Each block processes its assigned rays to find ray-isosurface intersections. Speculation: To fill open compute slots left by terminated rays, traverse additional blocks speculatively along active rays. A global speculation count determines how many extra blocks to test per active ray. This increases GPU utilization and accelerates rendering completion. If a ray intersects the isosurface within the block, mark it as terminated. Refine the intersection position if necessary (standard isosurface refinement). 3.6. Completion Check: Compute the remaining number of active rays. If zero, rendering is complete. Display the current image to the user. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. zfpcompresseddata: Buffer # ZFP compressed volume macrocellgrid: MacrocellGrid # Two-level grid with value ranges lrucache: LRUCache # Stores decompressed 4^3 blocks raydatabuffer: Buffer # 16 bytes/ray: direction, tentry iteratorstatebuffer: Buffer # 32 bytes/ray: tmax, coarseid, fineid rbidbuffer: Buffer # UINT, block ID or UINTMAX isterminated: Buffer # Boolean, per ray def init(volumedata, camera, isovalue): zfpcompresseddata = upload(volumedata) macrocellgrid = buildmacrocellgrid(zfpcompresseddata) lrucache = LRUCache() raydatabuffer = computeinitialrays(camera) isterminated = [False] (W H) # Initialize iterator states for i in range(W H): iteratorstatebuffer[i].tmax = raydatabuffer[i].tentry iteratorstatebuffer[i].coarseid = 0 iteratorstatebuffer[i].fineid = 0 def computeinitialrays(camera): # Rasterize backfaces of bounding box rays = [] for pixel in pixels: ray = rayfrompixel(camera, pixel) if ray.intersectsvolume(): rays.append({ 'direction': ray.direction, 'tentry': ray.tmin, 'id': pixel.id }) else: isterminated[pixel.id] = True rays.append(None) return rays def progressiverender(isovalue, speculationcount=1): while not all(isterminated): # 1. Traverse Macrocell Grid traversegrid(isovalue) # 2. Mark Blocks visibleblocks = set() activeblocks = set() for i in range(W H): if not isterminated[i]: bid = rbidbuffer[i] if bid != UINTMAX: visibleblocks.add(bid) # Add +x, +y, +z neighbors activeblocks.add(getneighbor(bid, +1, 0, 0)) activeblocks.add(getneighbor(bid, 0, +1, 0)) activeblocks.add(getneighbor(bid, 0, 0, +1)) allblocks = visibleblocks.union(activeblocks) # 3. Decompress and Cache for bid in allblocks: if not lrucache.contains(bid): decompressed = decompresszfp(zfpcompresseddata, bid) lrucache.insert(bid, decompressed) # 4. Setup Block Raycasting blockrays = compactandsortrays(rbids, isterminated) # 5. Execute Block Raycasting with Speculation # Speculation adds extra blocks to test for active rays executeblockraycastingkernel(blockrays, speculationcount, isovalue) # 6. Check Completion updateterminationstatus() displayimage() def traversegrid(isovalue): for i in range(W H): if isterminated[i]: continue state = iteratorstatebuffer[i] raydir = raydatabuffer[i].direction tcurrent = state.tmax # Traverse Coarse Grid coarseid = state.coarseid while coarseid is valid: coarsecell = macrocellgrid.coarse[coarseid] if isovalue not in coarsecell.valuerange: coarseid = nextcoarsecell(coarseid, raydir, tcurrent) continue # Traverse Fine Grid within Coarse Cell fineid = state.fineid while fineid is valid: fineblock = macrocellgrid.fine[fineid] if isovalue not in fineblock.valuerange: fineid = nextfinecell(fineid, raydir, tcurrent) continue # Found candidate block rbidbuffer[i] = fineblock.id state.tmax = tcurrent # Save state state.coarseid = coarseid state.fineid = fineid break # Exit fine traversal if rbidbuffer[i] != UINTMAX: break # Found block in this coarse cell coarseid = nextcoarsecell(coarseid, raydir, tcurrent) if rbidbuffer[i] == UINTMAX: isterminated[i] = True def executeblockraycastingkernel(blockrays, speculationcount, isovalue): for blockid, rays in blockrays: decompressedblock = lrucache.get(blockid) for rayidx in rays: if isterminated[rayidx]: continue # Intersect ray with block data hitt = intersectisosurface(raydatabuffer[rayidx], decompressedblock, isovalue) if hitt is not None: isterminated[rayidx] = True else: # Speculation: test additional blocks along the ray for in range(speculationcount): nextblockid = getnextblockalongray(raydatabuffer[rayidx]) if nextblockid is not None: nextdecompressed = lrucache.getordecompress(nextblockid) hitt = intersectisosurface(raydatabuffer[rayidx], nextdecompressed, isovalue) if hitt is not None: isterminated[rayidx] = True break # Update ray state for next pass if not hit # Note: In this algorithm, speculation is intra-pass # The ray continues to the next pass if not hit Time Complexity: Tied to image size (W \times H) and number of passes, not dataset size. Each pass processes active rays and visible blocks. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active blocks in the LRU cache, which is significantly smaller than the total dataset. Achieves up to 5.7× reduction in overall memory use and 8.4× reduction in data decompressed compared to BCMC. Performance: On an RTX 3080 at 1280×720, the Richtmyer-Meshkov dataset averages 264ms per-pass and 1.2s total render time. Strengths: Enables interactive visualization of massive volumes (up to 8.05B voxels) on lightweight devices (XPS 13, M1 Mac Mini). Runs entirely on the GPU (WebGPU), eliminating CPU communication bottlenecks. Progressive rendering improves interactivity by displaying the surface after each pass. Limitations: Does not scale down well to small datasets; overhead may make it slower than BCMC on small volumes like Plasma or Chameleon. Uses a global speculation count, which is restrictive; per-ray speculation could increase utilization but adds complexity. Precision issues in tracking t values can cause cells to be skipped if iterator states are not saved/restored. The algorithm was proposed by Will Usher and Valerio Pascucci in 2023. It addresses the memory constraints of lightweight end-user devices when visualizing massive datasets produced by modern simulations. It builds on prior work in ray-guided large volume rendering and implicit isosurface extraction, specifically improving upon the Brick Cache Memory Constrained (BCMC) algorithm by eliminating explicit triangle mesh storage and using a view-dependent wavefront traversal. The implementation targets WebGPU/WebAssembly environments for browser-based visualization. name: Real-time Surface Analysis and Tagged Material Cleansing
head: RT-SATMC
body:
Real-time Surface Analysis and Tagged Material Cleansing (RT-SATMC) is a hybrid rendering technique that combines isosurface reconstruction with direct volume rendering to accurately visualize soft tissue and fluid boundaries in volumetric datasets, specifically for virtual colonoscopy. It solves the problem of partial volume artifacts and misclassification at material transitions (air, soft tissue, fluid) by detecting an initial isosurface, analyzing material probabilities, and cleansing misclassified regions using adaptive volume rendering. Unlike pure isosurface methods that suffer from staircasing and boundary inaccuracies, or pure volume rendering that lacks sharp surface definition, RT-SATMC provides photo-realistic surface visualization with correct material tagging without requiring pre-segmentation. The method operates on unmodified CT images, assuming the camera (viewpoint) is located within the volume, specifically inside air or fluid. The algorithm consists of four main processing steps: initial isosurface detection, material transition analysis, partial volume artifact removal via volume rendering, and final boundary definition. Input: 3D scalar volume data V (CT intensities), camera position \mathbf{o}, camera direction \mathbf{d}, soft tissue threshold 	au{st}, fluid threshold 	au{f} (implicit in probability analysis). Output: Final surface coordinates \mathbf{p}{final}, surface normals \mathbf{n}, and color/opacity for each pixel. Volume Data: 3D grid of scalar values. Ray State: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, current position \mathbf{p}, step size s. Surface Buffer: Stores hit position \mathbf{p} and normal \mathbf{n} for each pixel. Probability Map: Scalar field P(\mathbf{p}) representing the likelihood of being at an air-fluid boundary. Fixed Sample Distance: s for initial ray traversal. Bisection Steps: N{bisect} = 10 for hitpoint refinement. Detection Depth: 4 to 6 voxel layers for robust fluid detection. Filtering: Tri-cubical convolution kernel for smoothing and derivative calculation. 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, define ray origin \mathbf{o} as the camera position (assumed to be in air or fluid) and direction \mathbf{d} based on camera parameters. A fisheye lens distortion may be applied to \mathbf{d} for wide-angle views. 2. Potential Soft Tissue Detection (Initial Isosurface): Traverse the ray from \mathbf{o} with fixed step size s. For each sample point \mathbf{p}i, evaluate the volume intensity V(\mathbf{p}i). Terminate traversal when V(\mathbf{p}i) > 	au{st} (soft tissue threshold). Let \mathbf{p}{coarse} be the first position where the threshold is exceeded. 3. Hitpoint Refinement: Refine \mathbf{p}{coarse} to \mathbf{p}{refined} using a bisectional search algorithm to avoid staircase artifacts. Perform N{bisect} = 10 iterations. In each iteration, narrow the interval around the threshold crossing 	au{st} to find the precise intersection point \mathbf{p}{refined} where V(\mathbf{p}{refined}) \approx 	au{st}. 4. Data Smoothing and Derivative Calculation: To generate high-quality data values and normals, apply tri-cubical filtering on the GPU. Compute smoothed intensity V{smooth}(\mathbf{p}) using convolution. Compute first-order derivatives (gradient) 
abla V{smooth}(\mathbf{p}) using central differences of surrounding samples. Compute second-order derivatives if needed for curvature enhancement. Surface normal \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla V{smooth}(\mathbf{p}{refined})}{\|
abla V{smooth}(\mathbf{p}{refined})\|}. 5. Material Transition Analysis (Probability Estimation): Analyze the region around \mathbf{p}{refined} to differentiate between material transitions (air-soft tissue vs. air-fluid). Estimate a probability P(\mathbf{p}) that the position belongs to an air-fluid boundary. Use intensity and gradient magnitude profiles along the ray. A large gradient magnitude that increases and decreases consistently characterizes the air-fluid transition. Assume gradient alignment with gravity direction for larger fluid amounts to increase likelihood estimation. Robust detection occurs within 4 to 6 voxel layers due to large intensity differences between soft tissue and contrast-enhanced fluid. 6. Partial Volume Effect Removal (Volume Rendering): If P(\mathbf{p}) indicates a high probability of air-fluid boundary (misclassified area), perform direct volume rendering into the volume. Use an adaptive number of samples into the volume. Apply a 2D Transfer Function (TF) with inputs: intensity V and gradient magnitude \|
abla V\|. This step reconstructs thin surface layers and handles partial volume artifacts that the initial isosurface missed. 7. Final Boundary Definition: A second iso-surface defines the actual boundary between fluid and soft tissue, using the cleansed data from the volume rendering step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rtsatmcrender(volume, camera, taust): """ Main rendering function for RT-SATMC. volume: 3D array of CT intensities camera: object with position o, direction d, and fisheye distortion function taust: soft tissue intensity threshold """ # Initialize output buffers surfacepositions = [] surfacenormals = [] finalcolors = [] for pixel in imageplane: # 1. Ray Initialization rayo = camera.position rayd = camera.directionforpixel(pixel) rayd = applyfisheyedistortion(rayd) # # 2. Potential Soft Tissue Detection pcurrent = rayo stepsize = fixedstepdistance # foundcoarse = False pcoarse = None while pcurrent is withinvolume: intensity = samplevolume(volume, pcurrent) if intensity > taust: pcoarse = pcurrent foundcoarse = True break pcurrent += rayd stepsize if not foundcoarse: continue # No soft tissue hit # 3. Hitpoint Refinement (Bisection) # Assume previous sample was below threshold, current is above pprev = pcurrent - rayd stepsize prefined = bisectintersection(volume, pprev, pcoarse, taust, numsteps=10) # # 4. Data Smoothing and Derivatives # Tri-cubical filtering and central differences on GPU vsmooth = applytricubicfilter(volume, prefined) gradv = computecentraldifferencegradient(volume, prefined) # normal = normalize(gradv) # 5. Material Transition Analysis # Estimate probability of air-fluid boundary # Analyze intensity and gradient magnitude profiles along ray # Check for large gradient magnitude changes characteristic of air-fluid transition # Check alignment with gravity if fluid amount is large probairfluid = estimateboundaryprobability(volume, rayo, rayd, prefined) # # 6. Partial Volume Effect Removal if probairfluid > thresholdprobability: # Direct volume rendering with 2D TF # Inputs: intensity and gradient magnitude # Adaptive number of samples color = directvolumerenderwith2dtf(volume, rayo, rayd, tfintensitygrad, adaptivesamples=True) # else: # Standard shading for clean soft tissue boundary color = computephongshading(prefined, normal, rayd, camera) surfacepositions.append(prefined) surfacenormals.append(normal) finalcolors.append(color) return surfacepositions, surfacenormals, finalcolors def bisectintersection(volume, plow, phigh, threshold, numsteps): """ Bisectional search to find precise intersection point. """ pmid = (plow + phigh) / 2.0 for i in range(numsteps): vallow = samplevolume(volume, plow) valhigh = samplevolume(volume, phigh) # Ensure plow is below threshold and phigh is above if vallow > threshold: phigh = pmid elif valhigh < threshold: plow = pmid else: break pmid = (plow + phigh) / 2.0 return pmid Camera Position: The method assumes the camera is inside air or fluid. If the camera is inside soft tissue, the initial ray traversal logic may fail to detect the correct boundary. Noise: Noise can affect probability estimation. Tri-cubical filtering helps mitigate this, but extreme noise may lead to incorrect material tagging. Gradient Alignment: The assumption that the air-fluid transition gradient aligns with gravity direction is an approximation that may fail in non-standard orientations or small fluid amounts. Threshold Selection: The soft tissue threshold 	au{st} must be carefully chosen to separate air from soft tissue without including fluid, as fluid has higher intensity. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the average ray length. The bisection search adds a constant factor (N{bisect}=10) to the initial hit detection. The volume rendering step is conditional and adaptive, adding variable cost only for misclassified regions. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, surface buffers, and intermediate derivative calculations. Tri-cubical filtering requires temporary storage for convolution results. Performance: Designed for real-time performance on GPU hardware. The use of GPU-based tri-cubical filtering and adaptive sampling allows for interactive frame rates. Strengths: Handles partial volume artifacts effectively, provides accurate surface boundaries, supports real-time analysis, and does not require pre-segmentation. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of camera position within air/fluid. Performance may degrade in highly noisy data or complex material transitions not well-separated by intensity. RT-SATMC was proposed in the context of virtual colonoscopy to visualize contrast-enhanced areas within volumetric datasets. It addresses the limitations of traditional isosurface reconstruction, which often requires time-consuming pre-processing and segmentation, and can produce artifacts affecting polyp size estimation. The method builds on earlier work in ray-casting and surface refinement [Sch05, SH05] to provide a combined approach for realistic visualization and interactive training. name: Binary Ray Casting
head: Zero-order interpolation ray casting
body: Binary Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering method for generating images of surfaces within binary volumetric data without explicit boundary detection or hidden-surface removal. It distinguishes itself from higher-order interpolation methods by using zero-order interpolation, where voxel values are treated as discrete constants (0 or 1) rather than continuous fields. This makes it suitable for binary datasets where the distinction between object and background is absolute, avoiding the smoothing artifacts inherent in linear or tri-linear interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary volumetric dataset V where V(\mathbf{i}) \in \{0, 1\} for voxel indices \mathbf{i}. Input: Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, image plane resolution). Output: A 2D image where each pixel is colored based on the first surface intersection. Data Structures: The volume is stored as a 3D array of integers or bits. No auxiliary structures (like octrees or grids) are required by the core algorithm. Steps: 1. For each pixel (u, v) in the image plane, compute the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in world space. 2. Initialize the ray parameter t = 0 and the step size \Delta t. The step size \Delta t determines the resolution of the search. A common choice is the diagonal length of a voxel divided by the number of steps per voxel, or simply the voxel spacing if the ray is aligned with axes. 3. While t is within the volume bounds: a. Compute the current sample position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Map \mathbf{p} to the nearest voxel index \mathbf{i} using floor or round operations (zero-order interpolation). c. Retrieve the value v = V(\mathbf{i}). d. If v = 1 (object) and the previous value was 0 (background), a surface intersection is detected. e. Refine the intersection point if necessary (e.g., linear interpolation between the last 0 and first 1 sample) to reduce stair-stepping artifacts. f. Break the loop. 4. If an intersection is found, compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the hit point. Since the data is binary, the normal is typically derived from the gradient of the discrete field or by assuming the normal is perpendicular to the ray at the transition point. 5. Shade the pixel using a local lighting model (e.g., Phong) with the computed normal. 6. If no intersection is found within the volume bounds, color the pixel as background. Parameters: Step size \Delta t: Controls the trade-off between accuracy and performance. Smaller steps reduce aliasing but increase computation. Not given in the sources. Threshold: Values \ge 1 are object; values < 1 are background. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Zero-order interpolation causes significant aliasing (stair-stepping) artifacts, especially at oblique angles. This is the primary limitation compared to higher-order methods. Precision: Floating-point errors in ray traversal may cause missed voxels or double-counting if \Delta t is not chosen carefully relative to voxel size. Thin Structures: If the object thickness is smaller than the step size, the surface may be missed entirely. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binaryraycasting(volume, camera, width, height): image = zeros((height, width, 3)) voxelsize = volume.spacing # Assume uniform spacing stepsize = voxelsize 0.5 # Typical step size to ensure coverage for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) t = 0.0 hit = False prevval = 0 while t < volume.maxdistance: # Compute sample position pos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Map to voxel index (zero-order interpolation) voxelidx = floor(pos / voxelsize) # Check bounds if not volume.isinside(voxelidx): break # Get value val = volume.get(voxelidx) # Detect transition from background (0) to object (1) if prevval == 0 and val == 1: hit = True # Refine intersection # Linear interpolation between tprev and t thit = t - stepsize + stepsize (0 - prevval) / (val - prevval) hitpos = rayorigin + thit raydirection # Compute normal # Simple approach: gradient of binary field # Or assume normal is perpendicular to ray at hitpos normal = computenormal(volume, hitpos) # Shade image[y, x] = shade(hitpos, normal, raydirection) break prevval = val t += stepsize if not hit: image[y, x] = backgroundcolor return image Uses variable step sizes to improve performance and accuracy. Choose when the object has varying density or complexity. Provides methods to refine the intersection point after a coarse step. Choose when higher precision is needed than zero-order interpolation allows. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of steps per ray. S depends on the volume depth and step size. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the volume size. No auxiliary structures are needed. Strengths: Simple implementation; no preprocessing required; fast for binary data; no boundary extraction overhead. Limitations: High aliasing artifacts due to zero-order interpolation; sensitive to step size; cannot represent smooth surfaces or gradients. When to use: Binary datasets where speed is critical and visual quality (aliasing) is acceptable. When not to use: Continuous scalar fields; high-quality rendering requirements; thin structures smaller than step size. Binary Ray Casting was developed to generate images of surfaces in binary volumetric data without the need for explicit boundary detection and hidden-surface removal. It is classified as a direct volume rendering algorithm using zero-order interpolation. It is often compared with Discrete Ray Casting, which uses a 3D Bresenham-like algorithm to traverse a discrete representation of the ray. The method is relevant in medical and scientific visualization where data is often thresholded into binary masks (e.g., bone vs. tissue). name: Appel's Ray Casting Algorithm
head: Appel's Algorithm
body: Appel's Ray Casting Algorithm is the foundational image-order rendering method for determining visible surfaces and occlusion in 3D scenes by tracing rays from the viewpoint through the image plane. It solves the hidden surface removal problem and enables realistic shading by identifying the first intersection between a ray and object surfaces, distinguishing itself from earlier scanline-based approaches by prioritizing ray-object intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scene description (geometric primitives defining surfaces), a camera position (viewpoint), a camera orientation, and an image plane resolution. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the color of the visible surface at that location, including shading and shadow information. Data Structures: Scene Representation: Objects are defined by their geometric boundaries (e.g., polygons, spheres). The specific data structure for the scene is not detailed in the primary source, but it must support intersection queries. Image Buffer: A 2D array storing the final color for each pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel (u, v) in the image plane, define a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin (viewpoint) and \mathbf{d} is the direction vector from the origin through the pixel center. 2. Intersection Testing: For each generated ray, compute intersections with all objects in the scene. Determine the intersection parameter t for each object. 3. Occlusion and Visibility: Identify the intersection with the smallest positive t (the closest hit). This point represents the visible surface for that pixel. Objects behind this point are occluded and do not contribute to the pixel color. 4. Shading: Compute the color of the hit point using a local lighting model. This involves calculating surface normals and applying illumination models (e.g., Phong shading) to simulate realistic lighting effects. 5. Shadow Casting (Optional but implied by "realistic shading"): To determine if the hit point is in shadow, cast secondary rays from the hit point towards light sources. If an object intersects this shadow ray before the light source, the point is in shadow. 6. Color Assignment: Assign the computed color (including ambient, diffuse, specular components, and shadow attenuation) to the corresponding pixel in the image buffer. Formulas: Ray equation: r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. The specific shading formula is not provided, but it relies on standard local lighting models. Parameters: Image resolution (number of pixels). Camera parameters (field of view, aspect ratio). Shading model parameters (light positions, material properties). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The algorithm is computationally expensive because it requires testing every ray against every object in the scene. This complexity is O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of objects. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in intersection calculations can lead to artifacts like z-fighting or incorrect occlusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def appelsraycasting(scene, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Implements Appel's Ray Casting Algorithm. Args: scene: List of geometric objects supporting intersection tests. camera: Object containing origin (o) and direction calculation method. imagewidth: Width of the output image in pixels. imageheight: Height of the output image in pixels. Returns: image: 2D array of pixel colors. """ image = createemptyimage(imagewidth, imageheight) # Iterate over each pixel in the image for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # 1. Generate ray for the current pixel # Calculate ray origin and direction based on camera and pixel coordinates rayorigin = camera.getorigin() raydirection = camera.getdirection(x, y) # 2. Find the closest intersection closestt = infinity closestobject = None hitpoint = None normal = None for object in scene: # Compute intersection of ray with object t, point, n = object.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) # Check if intersection is valid (positive t) and closer than current closest if t > 0 and t < closestt: closestt = t closestobject = object hitpoint = point normal = n # 3. Determine color based on visibility and shading if closestobject is not None: # 4. Apply shading model # Calculate lighting contributions (ambient, diffuse, specular) # Check for shadows by casting shadow rays to light sources color = computeshading(hitpoint, normal, scene, camera) image[y, x] = color else: # No object hit, assign background color image[y, x] = camera.backgroundcolor return image A technique to reduce computational complexity in Appel's algorithm by grouping rays originating from similar successive voxels into a single representative ray. It divides the input slice into blocks, measures intra-block variance, and groups voxels if the variance is below a user-defined threshold, casting only one ray for the group. If variance exceeds the threshold, voxels are ungrouped and individual rays are cast. This reduces the number of interpolations and ray casts while preserving image quality. The user-defined threshold determines the grouping sensitivity. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of objects in the scene. This makes it computationally expensive for complex scenes. Memory Complexity: Depends on the scene representation and image buffer size. No specific memory optimization is mentioned in the primary source. Strengths: Conceptually simple, handles hidden surface removal naturally, and produces high-quality images with realistic shading and shadows. Limitations: Very slow for large scenes due to the exhaustive intersection testing. Not suitable for real-time rendering without significant optimizations or hardware acceleration. When to use: Suitable for offline rendering where image quality is prioritized over speed, or for simple scenes with few objects. When not to use: Unsuitable for real-time applications or scenes with a large number of objects due to high computational cost. Appel's Ray Casting Algorithm was developed by Arthur Appel at IBM in 1968. It was one of the first computational approaches to realistic shading and solved the hidden surface removal problem by tracing rays from the viewpoint through the image plane. This method laid the foundational principles for later rendering techniques by prioritizing ray-object intersections over the scanline-based methods prevalent at the time. ray casting, https://grokipedia.com/page/Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-26 Different Ray-Casting Algorithm Implementations for Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.35940/ijitee.g1011.0597s20, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Distance-field ray marching
head: Sphere tracing, SDF ray marching, Distance field rendering
body: Distance-field ray marching is an image-order rendering technique that finds surface intersections by iteratively stepping along a ray using a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to determine the step size, allowing for approximate intersection detection without explicit mesh geometry. It solves the problem of rendering complex, continuous implicit surfaces by leveraging the mathematical guarantee that no geometry exists within the distance value returned by the SDF. Unlike Direct volume ray casting which integrates density, or Isosurface and first-hit ray casting which may use analytic intersections, this method relies on the Lipschitz property of the distance field to ensure safe, non-penetrating steps. The method operates on the principle that a Signed Distance Function f(\mathbf{p}) provides a lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface. For any point \mathbf{p} in space, f(\mathbf{p}) returns the shortest Euclidean distance to the implicit surface, with a sign indicating position: f(\mathbf{p}) < 0 inside, f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 on the surface, and f(\mathbf{p}) > 0 outside. The core algorithm, known as sphere tracing, proceeds as follows for each pixel: 1. Ray Definition: A ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. 2. Initialization: The accumulated distance t is initialized to 0 (or a near-plane value). 3. Marching Loop: Evaluate the scene SDF at the current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to get the distance d = f(\mathbf{p}). Termination Check: If d < \epsilon (a small convergence threshold, e.g., 0.001), the ray has hit the surface. If t > t{max} (maximum ray distance), the ray has escaped. Step: Advance the ray by the distance value: t \leftarrow t + d. This step size is guaranteed not to penetrate the surface because the SDF satisfies the Lipschitz condition with constant 1. 4. Shading: Upon hit, compute surface properties (normal, color) and lighting. The scene SDF is typically composed of primitives using Boolean operations: union is min(d1, d2), intersection is max(d1, d2), and subtraction is max(-d1, d2). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} to the local space of the primitive via M^{-1}\mathbf{p} before evaluation. Evaluates the integral of a 3D Gaussian mixture along camera rays to resolve spatial overlap and self-attenuation, operating on a continuous probabilistic density field rather than a discrete SDF. Renders 2D heightmap terrains by stepping along the ray until the ray's height drops below the terrain surface defined by the heightmap value at the ray's xz position. Provides analytical building blocks for distance-field ray marching by defining the signed Euclidean distance from any point in 3D space to the surface of a geometric primitive. Allows raymarched SDF objects to correctly occlude and be occluded by standard mesh-based geometry by querying the scene's depth buffer to determine the distance to the nearest mesh surface. Extends sphere tracing by explicitly writing the computed surface hit point's depth to the hardware depth buffer (SVDepth) to ensure correct occlusion ordering with rasterized geometry. Extends distance-field ray marching by continuing the ray path after a surface intersection to simulate specular reflections, effectively transitioning from raycasting to raytracing. Computes the color of surface points identified by distance-field ray marching by estimating surface normals and applying reflectance models to determine how light interacts with the geometry. Approximates the Space Distance Field (SDF) using a deep neural network and renders images by marching rays along the estimated distance field, trading computational speed for geometric flexibility. Generates point clouds or render images by sampling points near or on the zero-level set of a Signed Distance Function (SDF), focusing on extracting geometric representations. A parallelization technique that maintains a dynamic mask of unfinished rays to prevent wasted computation on rays that have already converged or escaped. Addresses the problem of applying spatial transformations (rigid body motion, scaling, deformation) to Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDFs) during ray marching. Adapts distance-field ray marching to simulate LiDAR sensor data by detecting surface intersections and projecting them onto a framebuffer as a sparse point cloud. A real-time WebGL2 renderer that generates an infinite procedural synthwave city using signed-distance fields (SDFs) within a single fullscreen fragment shader, requiring no meshes, textures, or scene graph. A single-function ray integrator that resolves a complete ray by compositing terrain, water, sky, cloud volume, and aerial perspective, handling the sequential evaluation of distinct environmental layers. Computes the surface normal at a point on a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by numerically approximating the gradient of the distance function f using finite differences and normalizing the result. Prevents moiré artifacts and jagged edges caused by high-frequency noise octaves or fine geometric details aliasing against the pixel grid, often integrating frequency-aware logic directly into the procedural evaluation. Simulates light transport through participating media, such as clouds, smoke, fog, and planetary atmospheres, by integrating density and scattering properties along view rays. Encompasses techniques to reduce the computational cost of distance-field ray marching and sparse volume rendering, primarily by minimizing the number of expensive Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluations or traversal steps. Renders scenes defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by casting rays from a camera, marching them to surface intersections, and shading the hit points using the Blinn-Phong lighting model. Renders dynamic, complex scenes by streaming object definitions from the CPU to the GPU in structured buffers, allowing for per-pixel evaluation of multiple objects without hardcoding the scene geometry in the shader. Provides the mechanism to evaluate the distance from a query point to the nearest surface in a scene, serving as the fundamental query primitive for distance-field ray marching. Renders particle-based data (such as Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics fluid simulations) by treating the volume as a continuous scalar field composed of additive weighted radial basis functions (RBFs), specifically Gaussians. A geometric method for rendering implicit surfaces by iteratively stepping along a ray using the distance to the nearest surface as the step size. Not given in the sources. An algorithm for transforming a Signed Distance Bound (SDB) into a polygon mesh by combining sphere tracing (ray marching) with traditional polygonization techniques like Marching Cubes. An alternative focus+context visualization used when WebGL2 image2D/atomicuint support is unavailable (e.g., SwiftShader, sandboxed environments). Initialize sphere radius to 25% of the smallest bounding box dimension: initialRadius = min(bboxSize.x, bboxSize.y, bboxSize.z) 0.25. Leverages lattice periodicity for efficiency by employing a local tracing distance query within a single cell.
