Optimizer: Adam with initial learning rate 0.0005 and cosine annealing scheduler with 5000 warm-up steps. Hardware: Single Nvidia RTX3090-24G GPU. Training time: Approximately 16 hours for each model. Model Architecture: Geometry Code lg(x) (dim 32), Texture Code lt(x) (dim 32), Sign Distance h(x) (dim 1). Interpolated Items include lt(x) (dim 32), gradient of SDF |\text{grad}x s| (dim 256), s (dim 256), \gamma (dim 256), h(x) (dim 1), d (dim 160), \gamma (dim 32). Geometry Decoder outputs (256, 256, 256). Radiance Decoder outputs (3). Calculate the back plate position first. Calculate the front plate position. Perform the marching algorithm along the ray from the observer's point of view through the cube, potentially starting this in the same shader as the front plate calculation to avoid launching the process twice. Update the controller and view matrix based on the old one, applying rescaling if necessary. Draw the frame around the volume and generate the color maps. A raymarching debug overlay that color-codes each pixel based on the number of sphere tracing iterations required to reach the surface, visualized with a Turbo/Viridis colormap. Map step count 1–12 to cobalt/emerald colors. Map step count 13–30 to cyan/yellow colors. Map step count 31–64 to orange/magenta colors, typically occurring at grazing silhouettes. Render a chain of 5 translucent Marching Spheres along a demonstration ray converging toward the target geometry. Distance-field ray marching, often referred to as sphere tracing, was popularized by John C. Hart in 1992 with his paper "Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces". The method gained significant traction in the demoscene and real-time graphics community in the early 2000s, particularly through the work of Inigo Quilez, who detailed distance estimators and procedural modeling techniques. It has since become a standard technique for rendering implicit surfaces, fractals, and procedural geometry in shaders and real-time applications. name: Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion
head: Depth-buffered Raymarching, Raymarching with Mesh Interaction, Z-Buffer Occlusion
body: Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion is a technique that allows raymarched Signed Distance Field (SDF) objects to correctly occlude and be occluded by standard mesh-based geometry in a scene. It solves the problem where raymarched objects typically float on top of all other geometry because the raymarching loop ignores the depth of existing meshes. By sampling the scene's depth buffer to determine the distance to the nearest mesh surface, the raymarcher can terminate early if it passes that distance, ensuring proper layering. The method integrates the scene's depth buffer into the sphere tracing loop defined in Distance-field ray marching. It requires access to the camera's view matrix, inverse view matrix, and the rendered depth texture. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (camera position in world space). Ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized direction in world space). Depth buffer texture \mathcal{D} (e.g., CameraDepthTexture). View matrix V and Inverse View Matrix V^{-1}. SDF function f(\mathbf{p}). Outputs: Final color C for the pixel, blending the raymarched SDF result with the background mesh color. 1. Depth Buffer: A 2D texture storing depth values, accessed via CameraDepthTexture. The values are typically non-linear and must be converted to linear eyespace depth. 2. Vertex Shader Output: A structure containing the world-space ray direction, normalized in the Z-axis. 1. Ray Direction Normalization (Vertex Shader): The ray direction \mathbf{r}d is computed in eyespace (view space). In eyespace, z < 0 is forward. To calculate the true distance from the depth buffer, the ray direction is normalized such that its Z-component magnitude is 1.0. Let \mathbf{r}n be the Z-normalized ray direction in eyespace: \mathbf{r}n = \frac{\mathbf{r}d}{|rd.z|} The absolute value |rd.z| is used to prevent flipping the ray direction if rd.z is negative. Transform \mathbf{r}n from eyespace to worldspace using the inverse view matrix V^{-1}: \mathbf{r}{world} = V^{-1} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{r}n \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} (Treating \mathbf{r}n as a direction vector, the w-component is 0). 2. Depth Sampling (Fragment Shader): Sample the depth buffer at the current pixel's UV coordinates to get the non-linear depth value d{nl}. Convert this to linear eyespace depth d{eye}. Calculate the true Euclidean distance s from the camera origin to the mesh surface along the ray. Using similar triangles, the ratio of the true distance |r| to the eyespace depth d{eye} is equal to the ratio of the length of the Z-normalized ray |\mathbf{r}n| to 1: s = d{eye} \times |\mathbf{r}n| where |\mathbf{r}n| = \sqrt{r{n,x}^2 + r{n,y}^2 + r{n,z}^2}. 3. Raymarching Loop: Perform standard sphere tracing starting from the camera origin \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{r}{world}. For each step i: Current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{r}{world}. Evaluate SDF: dist = f(\mathbf{p}). Occlusion Check: If the accumulated distance t \ge s, the ray has passed the mesh surface. Terminate the loop and return a transparent color to allow the mesh to show through. Surface Hit Check: If dist < \epsilon (convergence threshold), the ray hit the SDF surface. Compute shading and return the color. Step: Advance t \leftarrow t + dist. Max Steps: If i exceeds a maximum step count, terminate. 4. Blending: The final pixel color is a blend of the background mesh color and the raymarched SDF color. If the raymarcher returns transparent (due to occlusion), the background mesh color is used. If it returns an opaque SDF color, it is composited over the background. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vertexpos, invviewmatrix): # Ray direction in eyespace (view space) rdeyespace = normalize(vertexpos) # Normalize Z-component magnitude to 1.0 to prevent flip rneyespace = rdeyespace / abs(rdeyespace.z) # Transform to worldspace (direction vector, w=0) rayworld = invviewmatrix @ vec4(rneyespace, 0.0) return rayworld.xyz def fragmentshader(uv, roworld, rdworld, rayworld, depthtexture, colortexture, nearplane): # Sample depth buffer depthnl = depthtexture.sample(uv).r # Convert to linear eyespace depth (standard projection math) deptheye = 1.0 / (depthnl (1.0 - nearplane) + nearplane) # Calculate true distance to mesh surface scalefactor = length(rayworld) s = deptheye scalefactor # Sample background mesh color bgcolor = colortexture.sample(uv).rgb # Raymarch loop t = 0.0 maxsteps = 64 hitcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(maxsteps): if t >= s: break p = roworld + t rdworld dist = f(p) # Scene SDF evaluation if dist < 0.001: normal = computesdfnormal(f, p) hitcolor = vec4(shadesurface(p, normal), 1.0) break t += dist # Alpha blend with background finalcolor = bgcolor (1.0 - hitcolor.a) + hitcolor.rgb hitcolor.a return finalcolor Max Steps: Typically 64. Convergence Threshold (\epsilon): Typically 0.001. Near Plane: Standard camera parameter. Depth Texture: Platform-specific sampler (e.g., CameraDepthTexture). Ray Direction Flip: In eyespace, z < 0 is forward. Dividing the ray direction by rd.z without taking the absolute value will flip the ray direction if rd.z is negative, causing the raymarched scene to appear inverted. Depth Precision: The depth buffer may have limited precision. Using linear conversion is crucial to convert non-linear depth values to linear distances for accurate comparison. Near Plane Clipping: The depth buffer only contains information for pixels within the view frustum and beyond the near plane. Transparency: If the mesh in the depth buffer is transparent, the depth value may not represent the true front-most surface. This method assumes the depth buffer contains the front-most opaque geometry. This variant addresses the occlusion of scale-invariant integral surfaces (like skeleton-based sphere-cones) in the depth buffer. It computes a scaling factor for the radii of sphere-cone primitives to guarantee correct occlusion. The worst-case configuration for this scaling is two segment primitives aligned with the viewing direction -\mathbf{v}, both having radius \tau at point q. Due to surface scale invariance, the scaling factor is computed numerically for a unit radius case, representing the distance from q to the isosurface in direction \mathbf{v}. This worst-case configuration is independent of the actual skeleton layout, requiring no additional skeleton processing. This variant extends the Holistic UOI pipeline to support 3D object intersections and LOD management by using multipass rendering instead of single-pass. Each scene SDF component is defined as an independent virtual scene equation and rendered in a separate pass. A custom floating-point depth buffer stores the minimum distance values from previous passes. During subsequent passes, the depth buffer acts as another SDF component, and an additional check terminates the raymarch if the traveled distance is smaller than the stored depth buffer value. This solves the original single-pass limitation where occlusion algorithms could not handle intersections between SDF components. Time Complexity: Adds O(1) overhead per pixel for depth sampling and distance calculation. The raymarching loop may terminate earlier, potentially reducing the number of SDF evaluations if the mesh is closer than the SDF surface. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth buffer texture, which is typically already present in the rendering pipeline. Performance: The method is efficient as it leverages existing hardware depth buffers. The primary cost is the additional arithmetic for depth conversion and the early exit check. Strengths: Enables seamless integration of raymarched SDF objects with traditional mesh-based geometry, allowing for correct occlusion and interaction. Limitations: Only works with opaque mesh geometry in the depth buffer. Transparent meshes or SDF objects rendered after the depth pass may not occlude correctly. Requires access to the depth buffer, which may not be available in all rendering contexts (e.g., deferred rendering without depth pre-pass). The technique was popularized by Adrian Booth in a blog post detailing the implementation of raymarched distance fields in Unity. It addresses a common issue in hybrid rendering pipelines where raymarched objects fail to interact with rasterized geometry. The method relies on standard graphics API features (depth buffers, view matrices) and does not require specialized hardware beyond standard GPU capabilities. name: SDF Depth Buffer Integration
head: Depth Writing with Hit Detection, Raymarching with Depth Buffer Output, Sphere Tracing for Depth Output, Sphere Tracing with Depth Buffer Output
body: SDF Depth Buffer Integration is a technique that extends sphere tracing by explicitly writing the computed surface hit point's depth to the hardware depth buffer (SVDepth). This allows ray-marched SDF geometry to participate in standard depth testing, ensuring correct occlusion between sphere-traced objects and rasterized geometry. Without this integration, the depth buffer records the depth of the proxy mesh face (e.g., a bounding cube) rather than the actual ray-marched surface, leading to incorrect occlusion where rasterized objects behind the SDF surface appear in front, or vice versa. It builds on Distance-field ray marching. The method operates in the fragment shader, extending the standard sphere tracing loop to output both color and depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Vertex shader output struct v2f containing clip-space position, object-space local position (ray origin), and object-space view direction (ray direction). Output: SVTARGET (color) and SVDepth (depth value). Data Structures: The vertex-to-fragment struct v2f layout is: position (SVPOSITION): Clip-space vertex position. localPosition (TEXCOORD0): Object-space vertex position, used as the ray origin. viewDirection (TEXCOORD1): Object-space vector from camera to vertex, un-normalized. Parameters: MAXSTEPS: Maximum ray march iterations. Typical value: 32. THICKNESS: SDF value threshold for hit detection. Typical value: 0.001. NORMALEPSILON: Offset for finite difference normal estimation. Typical value: 0.01. Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Setup: Calculate localPosition as the vertex position in object space. Calculate viewDirection as vertex - objectSpaceCameraPos in object space. Calculate position using UnityObjectToClipPos(vertex). 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Extract pos from localPosition. Normalize viewDirection to get dir. Initialize progress (accumulated distance) to 0. Initialize hitsurface flag to false. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate up to MAXSTEPS. Calculate sample point: samplePoint = pos + dir progress. Evaluate SDF: distance = scene(samplePoint). Hit Check: If distance < THICKNESS, set hitsurface = true and break. Step: Advance ray: progress = progress + distance. 4. Miss Handling: If !hitsurface, execute discard. This prevents writing to SVTARGET or SVDepth and avoids driver differences associated with clip(-1). 5. Color Calculation: Compute surface color using samplePoint (normal estimation, lighting) and write to SVTARGET. 6. Depth Calculation: Transform samplePoint to clip space: tracedClipPos = UnityObjectToClipPos(float4(samplePoint, 1.0)). Compute NDC depth: depth = tracedClipPos.z / tracedClipPos.w. Write depth to SVDepth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vert(vertex, worldtoobject, worldspacecamerapos): # Clip-space position for rasterization position = modelviewprojectionmatrix float4(vertex, 1.0) # Ray origin in object space localposition = vertex # Ray direction in object space (un-normalized to preserve interpolation precision) objectspacecamerapos = worldtoobject float4(worldspacecamerapos, 1.0) viewdirection = vertex - objectspacecamerapos return v2f(position, localposition, viewdirection) def frag(i): pos = i.localPosition dir = normalize(i.viewdirection) progress = 0.0 samplepoint = vec3(0.0) hitsurface = False for in range(MAXSTEPS): samplepoint = pos + dir progress distance = scene(samplepoint) if distance < THICKNESS: hitsurface = True break progress += distance if not hitsurface: return # discard pixel # Compute surface color via normal estimation and diffuse lighting color = rendersurface(samplepoint) # Transform hit point to clip space tracedclippos = modelviewprojectionmatrix float4(samplepoint, 1.0) # Perspective divide for NDC depth depth = tracedclippos.z / tracedclippos.w return color, depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Proxy Mesh Depth: Without explicit depth output, the GPU records the proxy mesh depth, causing incorrect occlusion. Early-Z Optimization: Writing SVDepth disables the GPU's early-Z optimization for affected pixels because the hardware cannot know the depth before the fragment shader runs. Discard vs Clip: Using clip(-1) can cause issues with depth buffering or sorting; discard is preferred. Unnormalized View Direction: The view direction is stored un-normalized in TEXCOORD1 to avoid precision loss in interpolation, but must be normalized in the fragment shader. Render Queue: The shader should use Queue=Geometry+1 to render after standard opaque geometry, ensuring rasterized meshes write depth first. DisableBatching=True is required as batching breaks the object-to-world transform used for ray setup. IgnoreProjector=True avoids projector interference. A pixel shader technique to extract the near and far depth values of active cells for ray marching. It uses alpha blending to simultaneously store the smallest depth in the RGB channels and the largest depth in the Alpha channel. The view space Z component (input.projPos.w) is output to the Red channel for the smallest depth and to the Alpha channel for the largest depth. The hardware's output merger keeps the smallest value for color components (RGB) and the largest value for the alpha component when blending, allowing extraction of both near and far depths in a single pass. Clips the ray segment to the viewport boundaries to avoid accessing out-of-bounds depth buffer texels. Viewport bounds are defined as xMax=csZBufferSize.x-0.5, xMin=0.5, yMax=csZBufferSize.y-0.5, yMin=0.5. Alpha for Y clipping is calculated as (P1.y - ((P1.y > yMax) ? yMax: yMin)) / (P1.y - P0.y) if P1.y is out of bounds. Alpha for X clipping is calculated similarly, taking the maximum alpha. Endpoints are interpolated to the clipped position: P1 = lerp(P1, P0, alpha), k1 = lerp(k1, k0, alpha), Q1 = lerp(Q1, Q0, alpha). P0 is assumed to be in the viewport, and P1-P0 is never zero when clipping is required, avoiding division by zero. Integration of KRS ray-casting into incrementally rendered scenes using the depth buffer. The depth buffer is used for early termination of rays. Depth is output from the ray casting shader if necessary, e.g., for transparent geometry rendering or deferred shading. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of ray march steps (MAXSTEPS) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Constant per pixel for the depth buffer write. Performance: Writing SVDepth disables early-Z optimization, which can impact performance on fill-rate limited hardware. Strengths: Ensures correct occlusion between SDF geometry and rasterized geometry. Limitations: Disables early-Z; requires careful render queue management (Geometry+1). When to Use: When SDF geometry needs to occlude or be occluded by rasterized geometry. When Not to Use: When SDF geometry is rendered last and does not need to interact with depth from other geometry, or when early-Z performance is critical and occlusion is not required. The method was introduced in Tutorial 045 of the Ronja Tutorials series, extending previous sphere tracing tutorials (043, 044) to address the depth buffer problem. It is implemented in Unity using HLSL/CG. The technique is part of the broader field of signed distance field rendering and ray marching. name: Deferred SDF Rendering
head: Deferred Signed Distance Field rendering, SDF G-buffer pre-pass
body: Deferred SDF Rendering is a technique that decouples Signed Distance Field (SDF) geometry generation from lighting calculations by rendering SDFs to a G-buffer during a pre-pass. This approach allows SDF geometry to participate in standard deferred post-processing effects such as screen-space reflections, ambient occlusion, and bloom, while reducing shader cost and register pressure compared to integrated forward rendering. It differs from integrated SDF rendering by sacrificing high-quality, SDF-specific reflections and shadows in exchange for compatibility with the existing deferred lighting pipeline. The method renders SDFs using a full-screen triangle pass during the G-buffer pre-pass, utilizing a modified standard shader. The core challenge is generating correct ray directions for ray marching and outputting depth values that correctly sort against existing polygonal geometry in the depth buffer. Inputs: Vertex position and texture coordinates from a full-screen triangle. Camera parameters including WorldSpaceCameraPos (eye position), InverseViewProjectionMatrix (inverse view-projection matrix), and UNITYMATRIXVP (view-projection matrix). Outputs: G-buffer data (albedo, normal, roughness, etc.) as defined by the modified standard shader. Depth value (outDepth) written to the depth buffer. Vertex Input: Standard vertex structure containing position and UVs. Vertex Output: Structure containing clip-space position (pos) and texture coordinates (tex). Ray Data: eye (float3 world-space camera position), worldPos (float3 world-space position on the far plane), worldDir (float3 normalized ray direction). 1. Vertex Shader (Pass-through): The vertex shader passes the input vertex position and texture coordinates to the fragment shader without modification. o.pos = v.vertex o.tex = v.texcoord 2. Fragment Shader: Ray Origin and Direction: Calculate the ray origin as the world-space camera position. eye = \text{WorldSpaceCameraPos} Transform the screen-space texture coordinates (ranging from [0, 1]) to clip-space coordinates (ranging from [-1, 1]), setting z=1.0 (far plane) and w=1.0. The y-component must be flipped to match the coordinate system convention. clipPos = (2.0 \cdot i.tex.xy - 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) clipPos.y = -clipPos.y Transform the clip-space position to world space using the inverse view-projection matrix, then apply a perspective divide to obtain the world position on the far plane. worldPos = \text{InverseViewProjectionMatrix} \times clipPos worldPos.xyz = \frac{worldPos.xyz}{worldPos.w} Compute the ray direction by normalizing the vector from the eye to the world position. worldDir = \text{normalize}(worldPos.xyz - eye) 3. Ray Marching: Perform standard SDF ray marching using eye and worldDir to find the hit position (hitPos) on the SDF surface. 4. Depth Output: To ensure the SDF geometry correctly occludes other geometry and is occluded by it, project the hitPos to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) using the view-projection matrix and output the depth. clipPos = UNITY\MATRIX\VP \times (hitPos, 1.0) outDepth = \frac{clipPos.z}{clipPos.w} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def matmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] def normalize(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def vertSDFDeferred(vvertex, vtexcoord): return vvertex, vtexcoord def fragSDFDeferred(itex): eye = WorldSpaceCameraPos clipPos = [itex[0] 2.0 - 1.0, -(itex[1] 2.0 - 1.0), 1.0, 1.0] worldPos = matmul(InverseViewProjectionMatrix, clipPos) worldPos = [worldPos[0]/worldPos[3], worldPos[1]/worldPos[3], worldPos[2]/worldPos[3]] worldDir = normalize([worldPos[0] - eye[0], worldPos[1] - eye[1], worldPos[2] - eye[2]]) # Sources do not provide the SDF ray marching algorithm; assume hitPos is computed. hitPos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Computed by SDF ray march clipHitPos = matmul(UNITYMATRIXVP, [hitPos[0], hitPos[1], hitPos[2], 1.0]) outDepth = clipHitPos[2] / clipHitPos[3] return outDepth, gbufferdata Far Plane: The ray direction calculation assumes a far plane depth of 1.0 in clip space. Coordinate System: The y-flip in clip space is critical. Depth Precision: Writing depth for ray-marched surfaces requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially for thin SDF features or very close/far distances. Lighting Quality: Decoupling lighting from SDF rendering prevents the production of high-quality reflections and shadows specific to the SDF geometry. Shadow Cost: Rendering SDFs into shadowmaps is possible but significantly increases shadow cost. Material Control: Using the standard material system applies settings (roughness, emissive) uniformly to all SDFs rendered with that material, lacking fine-grained control per SDF instance. Time Complexity: The pre-pass adds a full-screen triangle draw call. The fragment shader cost is dominated by the SDF ray marching loops and branches. Decoupling lighting reduces overall register pressure and shader complexity. Memory Complexity: Requires standard G-buffer storage. No additional memory for SDF-specific lighting data is needed in the deferred pipeline. Strengths: Integrates SDFs into existing deferred post-processing effects (SSR, SSAO, Bloom). Reduces shader register pressure by separating geometry generation from lighting. Correctly sorts SDFs against polygonal geometry via depth buffer integration. Limitations: Lacks high-quality, SDF-specific reflections and shadows. Shadow map rendering for SDFs is expensive and non-trivial. Limited material control granularity when using standard shaders. When to Use: When SDFs are used for environmental geometry or effects that benefit from screen-space post-processing, and high-fidelity SDF-specific lighting is not required. When Not to Use: When high-quality reflections or shadows on SDF geometry are critical, or when fine-grained material control per SDF instance is needed. This technique was demonstrated in December 2017 using Unity 2017.2. It was developed as an experiment to integrate SDFs into an actual rendering engine context, leveraging Unity's material system and deferred rendering pipeline. The approach was described as a "fun exercise" and "hacky" but functional for integrating SDFs with post-processing effects. name: Depth Buffering Setup
head: Depth State Setup, Depth Write Configuration
body: This method configures the graphics pipeline depth state so that ray-marched surfaces in a Signed Distance Field (SDF) volume rendering pass correctly participate in the depth buffer. By writing the correct depth value to SVDepth, the rendered volume occludes geometry behind it and is itself occluded by geometry in front, solving incorrect depth ordering in hybrid pipelines. It differs from Deferred SDF Rendering by focusing specifically on immediate depth state configuration rather than deferring lighting computation. Inputs: Current render target and depth stencil view, depth comparison function, depth write flag. Outputs: Configured depth stencil state. Data Structures: None created by this step; relies on an existing depth buffer populated by prior passes. Steps: 1. Set the depth comparison function to Less. 2. Enable the depth write mask. 3. Apply the configured depth stencil state to the current render pass or pipeline descriptor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupdepthbuffering(comparefunc: str = "less", writeenabled: bool = True): class DepthStencilState: def init(self, comparefunc, writeenabled): self.comparefunc = comparefunc self.writeenabled = writeenabled self.stencilfront = {"fail": "keep", "depthfail": "keep", "pass": "keep"} self.stencilback = {"fail": "keep", "depthfail": "keep", "pass": "keep"} self.mask = 0xFF self.writemask = 0xFF if writeenabled else 0x00 depthstate = DepthStencilState(comparefunc=comparefunc, writeenabled=writeenabled) pipelinedescriptor = {"depthstencil": depthstate} return pipelinedescriptor Parameters: comparefunc: Less. writeenabled: True. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Opaque geometry must be rendered before the volume pass to ensure correct occlusion. Clamping: Depth values written by the ray marcher must be within the valid API range (e.g., [0, 1] for OpenGL/Vulkan, [-1, 1] for DirectX) to avoid undefined behavior. Precision: Depth buffer bit depth affects occlusion accuracy for large scenes or thin geometry; 24-bit or 32-bit buffers are recommended for high precision. This variant reuses the depth buffer from a preliminary object rendering pass to discard volume fragments lying behind opaque geometry. Unlike Extended Depth Peeling, which uses wider area occluders for higher accuracy at greater computational cost, this method treats a single back-projected pixel as the occluder, offering a lighter-weight alternative for deep layers where visibility gains from complex culling diminish. Time Complexity: O(1) for state setup; per-fragment occlusion checks add negligible overhead to ray marching. Memory Complexity: O(1) for state setup; no additional memory allocated. Performance: Culls volume fragments occluded by opaque geometry, reducing ray marching steps. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for immediate occlusion culling, integrates with standard pipelines. Limitations: Requires correct pass ordering; does not handle transparent geometry or complex lighting directly. name: Depth Buffer Integration for Occlusion
head: Objects and Shadows Rendering, Occlusion Culling via Depth Buffer, UDP (Umbra DP), Umbra DP
body: Depth Buffer Integration for Occlusion is a pixel-based culling technique used within hybrid Extended Depth Peeling (EDP) schemes to handle deeper volume layers. It reuses the depth buffer from a preliminary object rendering pass to discard volume fragments that lie behind opaque geometry. Unlike Extended Depth Peeling, which uses wider area occluders for higher accuracy at greater computational cost, this method treats a single back-projected pixel as the occluder, offering a lighter-weight alternative for deep layers where visibility gains from complex culling diminish. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene containing opaque objects and a participating medium; a pre-computed depth buffer from an object rendering pass. Output: A volume rendering result where fragments occluded by opaque objects are discarded. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: A floating-point buffer storing the depth values of opaque surfaces. LightImage: A mipmap pyramid structure used for blurring light data, though primarily associated with shadow computation in the setup pass. Steps: 1. Object Rendering Pass: Render all opaque objects and the background into a floating-point pixel buffer (pbuffer). 2. Color Computation: Use a vertex program to compute the diffuse surface color of the objects. 3. Clamping Prevention: Store the computed diffuse color in a texture coordinate rather than the standard color output to avoid clamping artifacts. 4. Shadow and Final Color: Use a fragment program to output the final color for the objects, applying a standard shadow map for object self-shadows and a light data structure for projected shadows cast by the objects onto the participating medium. 5. Depth Buffer Capture: The depth buffer generated in Step 1 is preserved and reused. 6. Volume Rendering with Occlusion: During the volume rendering pass (specifically for deeper layers in a hybrid EDP scheme), compare the depth of each volume fragment against the stored depth buffer. 7. Culling: If a volume fragment's depth is greater than the depth stored in the buffer (indicating it is behind an opaque object), discard the fragment. 8. Occluder Model: The technique considers the back-projected pixel extent as the occluder, culling fragments in its umbrae. Parameters and Edge Cases: Hybrid Scheme: This method is typically applied only to deeper layers (e.g., layer index h > 2) in a hybrid scheme, while Extended Depth Peeling (EDP) handles the frontmost layers (h \le 2). Propagation: The culling effect from earlier layers propagates to deeper layers, making this simple technique effective even if less precise than EDP. Precision: The use of a floating-point pbuffer ensures accurate depth storage for the comparison. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthbufferintegrationocclusion(volumefragments, objectdepthbuffer): """ Discards volume fragments that are occluded by opaque objects. Args: volumefragments: List of volume fragment objects, each having 'depth', 'screenx', and 'screeny' attributes. objectdepthbuffer: 2D array (rows=y, cols=x) containing depth values of opaque objects from the rendering pass. Returns: List of volume fragments that are not occluded. """ visiblefragments = [] for frag in volumefragments: # Standard depth buffer convention: smaller values are closer to the camera. # Directly sample the depth at the fragment's screen coordinates. occluderdepth = objectdepthbuffer[frag.screeny][frag.screenx] # Fragment is visible if it lies in front of the opaque occluder. if frag.depth < occluderdepth: visiblefragments.append(frag) return visiblefragments Uses wider area occluders for higher culling efficiency in frontmost layers but is more computationally expensive. Choose EDP for h \le 2 where fragment reduction is most critical for warping. Extended Depth Peeling Unaware of scene information and inefficient compared to both EDP and UDP. Generally not recommended for modern hybrid schemes. Basic Depth Peeling Time Complexity: Low overhead per fragment compared to EDP, as it involves a simple depth comparison per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the depth buffer from the object pass. Performance: EDP reduces hidden fragments significantly more than UDP (up to 38.5× vs BDP, and 3.4× more than UDP on average in the first hidden layer). However, UDP adds non-trivial overhead for visibility tests in deeper layers where gains are smaller. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective when combined with EDP for front layers; reduces unnecessary shading for deep volume parts behind objects. Limitations: Less effective than EDP at reducing fragments due to the "tiny pixel" occluder assumption; may leave some fragments near object edges that EDP would catch. When to use: For deeper volume layers (h > 2) in a hybrid rendering pipeline where the marginal benefit of EDP does not justify its cost. The technique is rooted in the work of Lee et al. (2010) on "Umbra culling"-based Depth Peeling (UDP). It was integrated into hybrid schemes by Kim and Lee (2023) to optimize multi-view warping by handling deep layers efficiently after front layers are processed by EDP. The concept of reusing depth buffers for volume occlusion was also explored in earlier lighting models for participating media, such as those by Jensen et al. (2005), which utilized depth buffers to occlude volume portions behind objects. name: Surface Point Sampling for SDFs
head: Forplane Rendering Procedure, Sphere Tracing Surface Sampling
body: Surface Point Sampling for SDFs generates training data or rendering samples by querying a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to locate points near the implicit surface, rather than sampling uniformly throughout the volume. It solves the problem of inefficient volumetric coverage, where most uniform samples fall in empty space or deep inside geometry, providing critical gradient information for the signed distance field values off the zero-level set. It differs from uniform volume sampling by focusing density on the surface transition region, and from pure surface sampling by providing gradient information for the signed distance field (SDF) values off the zero-level set. The method encompasses several strategies for generating points near the SDF surface, primarily categorized by their application in training (Neural Geometric Level of Detail) or rendering (Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction). Inputs: Bounding volume B (typically [-1, 1]^3). SDF function f(\mathbf{p}). Ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Indicator grid Go (in deformable tissue context). Static and dynamic fields \{V^s{3d}, V^d{3d}\}4. Tiny MLP \theta. Outputs: Point set P distributed around the surface. Expected color \hat{C} and depth \hat{D}. Point: Coordinates (x, y, z) and optionally time \tau. Feature Vector: v(x, y, z, \tau) initialized to 1, updated via interpolation. Encoded Features: Concatenation of coordinate-time encoding b(x, y, z, \tau) and interpolated features v(x, y, z, \tau). This variant, used in Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLOD), generates surface points for training implicit shapes. 1. Uniform Initialization: Sample points uniformly distributed in the bounding volume B = [-1, 1]^3. 2. Ray Casting: Choose random points on a sphere to form a ray direction \mathbf{d}. Define ray r(t). 3. Sphere Tracing: Test if the ray hits the surface using sphere tracing (as defined in Distance-field ray marching). Evaluate d = f(\mathbf{p}) at current position. Advance t \leftarrow t + d. Terminate if d < \epsilon (hit) or t > t{max} (miss). 4. Collection: Continue sampling rays until enough rays hit the surface. The hit points constitute the surface samples. 5. Near-Surface Perturbation (Optional): To improve training convergence, perturb surface samples with Gaussian noise \sigma = 0.01 to generate near-surface points. This variant, used in Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction, samples points along a ray filtered by an indicator grid to focus on the surface region. 1. Uniform Ray Sampling: Uniformly sample points Pu along the ray r(t). 2. Indicator Filtering: Pass Pu through the indicator grid Go to obtain sample points P distributed around the surface. 3. Feature Interpolation: For each point P(x, y, z, \tau) in P: Initialize feature vector v(x, y, z, \tau) = 1. Iterate over 4 levels of static and dynamic fields \{V^s{3d}, V^d{3d}\}4 and dimension pairs (xy, xz, x\tau, yz, y\tau, z\tau). For each grid G and dimension pair ij, perform bi-linear interpolation B(G, i, j). Update v via element-wise multiplication: v \leftarrow v \odot B(G, i, j). 4. Encoding and Prediction: Concatenate coordinate-time encoding b(x, y, z, \tau) with features v(x, y, z, \tau). Pass through tiny MLP \theta to predict color ci and density \sigmai. 5. Volume Rendering: Render expected color \hat{C} and depth \hat{D} by integrating radiance and density along the ray: \hat{C} = \int{tn}^{tf} w(t) \cdot c(r(t), d) \, dt \hat{D} = \int{tn}^{tf} w(t) \cdot t \, dt w(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s)) \, ds\right) \sigma(r(t)) Return \hat{C}, \hat{D}. This variant extracts a point cloud from a Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) by projecting random points onto the shape surface S. It does not guarantee uniform sampling over S. 1. Uniform Sampling: Sample a point p uniformly from the bounding box B: p \sim U[B]. 2. Direction Sampling: For each p, sample nv directions vi uniformly from the unit sphere S^2: V(p) = \{vi(p) \sim U[S^2]\}{i=1}^{nv}. 3. Visibility Avoidance: Compose these directions to estimate the best direction vb^(p) to avoid visibility \xi(p, v) = 0. 4. Projection: Compute the surface point q(p, vb^(p)) using the PDDF depth and direction. The condition for q being on S is \xi(p, v) = 1 and q(p, v) = p + d(p, v)v. 5. Iterative Refinement: Repeat the process NH times, starting from the newly found point q (i.e., p \leftarrow q), to improve accuracy for depths far from S. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def samplesurfacepointssdf(sdffunction, boundingboxsize=2.0, numrays=100000, epsilon=0.001, maxsteps=100): """ Generates surface points by casting rays and sphere tracing. Returns a list of 3D points on the surface. """ surfacepoints = [] halfbox = boundingboxsize / 2.0 for in range(numrays): # 1. Choose random point on sphere for ray origin/direction # Using spherical coordinates for uniform distribution on sphere theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) phi = math.acos(random.uniform(-1, 1)) # Ray direction d = [ math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi) ] # Ray origin: random point in bounding box o = [ random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox) ] # 2. Sphere Tracing t = 0.0 hit = False for in range(maxsteps): p = [o[i] + t d[i] for i in range(3)] dist = sdffunction(p) if dist < epsilon: hit = True surfacepoints.append(p) break if t > boundingboxsize 2: # Escape condition break t += dist return surfacepoints Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def samplepddfsurface(pddffunction, boundingboxsize=2.0, nv=128, nh=3): """ Extracts points from PDDF by projecting random points. nv: Number of directions sampled per point. nh: Number of iterative refinements. """ points = [] halfbox = boundingboxsize / 2.0 for in range(10000): # Fixed number of initial samples # 1. Uniform sample in bounding box p = [ random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox) ] currentp = p for in range(nh): # 2. Sample nv directions bestv = None bestdist = float('inf') for in range(nv): # Uniform direction on sphere theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) phi = math.acos(random.uniform(-1, 1)) v = [ math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi) ] # 3. Estimate best direction to avoid visibility issues # Compose directions to estimate vb without optimization depth = pddffunction.getdepth(currentp, v) if depth is not None and depth > 0: q = [currentp[i] + depth v[i] for i in range(3)] # Check if q is on surface (xi=1) if pddffunction.isonsurface(q): currentp = q break points.append(currentp) return points Near-Surface Point Sampling generates training data points in the immediate vicinity of a mesh surface by perturbing existing surface samples with Gaussian noise. It solves the problem of insufficient volumetric coverage near the geometry boundary, which is critical for training neural implicit representations to converge on the correct surface location. It differs from uniform volume sampling by focusing density on the surface transition region, and from pure surface sampling by providing gradient information for the signed distance field (SDF) values off the zero-level set. This method estimates the full parameter set (position, normal, tangent vectors, and scales) for a surfel representation starting from a triangle mesh. It solves the problem of defining local tangent frames and anisotropic kernel shapes for point clouds sampled from meshes, where positions and normals are known but geometric extent is not. It differs from sibling methods by deriving tangent scales from the local point cloud neighborhood structure rather than mesh connectivity or fixed heuristics, offering two variants: isotropic scaling for performance and anisotropic scaling for quality. SDF-guided Sampling is a surface-aware sampling strategy that uses a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to estimate ray-surface intersections, followed by fine-grained sampling around the intersection point to accelerate rendering and emphasize the relationship between surface and radiance fields. It differs from standard NeRF sampling by reducing the number of required sampling points through early surface localization, and from pure mesh-based methods by retaining the flexibility of implicit field evaluation without requiring explicit mesh vertex interpolation. Bidirectional Projective Sampling is a boundary sampling method for physics-based differentiable rendering that generates seed rays from both sensors and emitters to initialize a guiding structure, addressing inefficiencies when scenes contain small-area lights at a distance. It improves upon Zhang et al.'s projective sampling by incorporating rays emitted directly from small-area emitters into the seed ray set during the projection operation, ensuring all successfully projected rays contribute to the guiding structure regardless of emitter size. Unlike previous methods that rely solely on sensor-spawned rays, which have a near-zero probability of intersecting small-area emitters, this method guarantees intersection by explicitly sampling from the emitter, thereby maximizing contribution to the boundary integral. This method extracts a differentiable surface point from volume rendering samples by linearly interpolating SDF zero-crossings, enabling the enforcement of multi-view feature consistency constraints. It differs from sibling methods by relying on the hierarchical sampling density near the surface to approximate the zero-crossing with a single secant step, rather than recursive root-finding or mesh-based parameterization. Definition: The incorporation of projection points derived from gradient information into the power diagram computation to accurately capture the underlying surface, particularly in regions with complex topology or fine details. Steps: Projection points are especially valuable for reconstructing thin structures, sharp edges, and regions with high curvature variation that might otherwise be inadequately captured by discrete SDF sampling points alone. Comparison: The baseline method using only sampling points without projections exhibits substantial topological defects and missing features, whereas the projection-enhanced approach preserves topological integrity. Definition: Constructs a SurfaceInteraction3f structure from a ray and intersection time, computing normal, frame, and other interaction properties without SDF autodiff support. Steps: Set si.t = t, si.p = ray(t), si.shframe.n = normalize(gradient(si.p)), initialize sh frame, set si.n = si.shframe.n, si.wi = tolocal(-ray.d), si.wavelengths = ray.wavelengths, si.dpdu = shframe.s, si.dpdv = shframe.t. Definition: A method to extract a point cloud (PC) from a Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) by projecting random points onto the shape surface S. It does not guarantee uniform sampling over S. Steps: Sample a point p uniformly from the bounding box B: p ~ U[B]. For each p, sample nv directions vi uniformly from the unit sphere S^2: V(p) = {vi(p) ~ U[S^2]}{i=1}^{nv}. Compose these directions to estimate the best direction vb(p) (as in §V-A2 and §V-A3, but without optimization) to avoid visibility ξ(p, v) = 0. Compute the surface point q(p, vb(p)) using the PDDF depth and direction. The condition for q being on S is ξ(p, v) = 1 and q(p, v) = p + d(p, v)v. Repeat the process NH times, starting from the newly found point q (i.e., p <- q), to improve accuracy for depths far from S. Parameters: nv: Number of directions sampled per point. Typical value: 128. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and steps in sphere tracing. Sphere tracing is O(N \cdot S) where N is the number of rays and S is the average number of steps to convergence. Indicator grid sampling adds overhead for grid lookups and MLP inference. Memory Complexity: Low for sphere tracing (only storing points). Indicator grid sampling requires storing the indicator grid and field levels. Strengths: Efficiently targets the surface region, reducing wasted samples in empty space. Provides necessary gradients for training implicit fields. Limitations: Sphere tracing can be slow for complex SDFs with many steps. Explicit PDDF sampling does not guarantee uniform distribution. When to Use: Training neural implicit representations (NGLOD), rendering dynamic deformable tissues, extracting point clouds from PDDFs. The method is used in Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLOD) to generate surface and near-surface training points. It was further developed in Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction using indicator grids for dynamic scenes. Explicit sampling methods were introduced for Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDF) to extract point clouds. Power diagram enhancements with projection points were proposed for adaptive isosurface extraction. name: Near-Surface Point Sampling
head: DeepSDF sampling, Non-Uniform Surface Sampling
body: Near-Surface Point Sampling generates a non-uniform distribution of query points for training implicit surface representations, specifically Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). It samples points non-uniformly near the surface, where most points are close to the surface and some are sampled uniformly. Inputs: A watertight mesh M with correct face normals. Number of points N (default 500,000). Standard deviation for noise \sigma (default 0.01). Bounding radius R (default 1.0, unit sphere). Outputs: A set of N 3D points P = \{p1, \dots, pN\}. Corresponding SDF values D = \{d1, \dots, dN\} and signs S = \{s1, \dots, sN\}. Data Structures: Surface Point Cloud: A set of points on the mesh surface, stored in a kd-tree for nearest-neighbor queries. Steps: 1. Mesh Normalization: Transform the mesh M so that it fits inside a unit sphere centered at the origin. 2. Surface Sampling: Generate a set of points P{surf} uniformly distributed on the surface of M. The number of surface points is determined by the desired split ratio. According to the DeepSDF paper, a 2:2:1 split is used for surface, near, and uniform samples, meaning N{surf} = N{near} = \frac{2}{5}N and N{uniform} = \frac{1}{5}N. 3. Near-Surface Perturbation: For each point p \in P{surf}, generate a perturbed point p' by adding Gaussian noise: p' = p + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) where \sigma = 0.01. These points form the set P{near}. 4. Uniform Volume Sampling: Generate N{uniform} points uniformly distributed within the bounding volume B. These points form the set P{uniform}. 5. SDF Calculation: For all points in P{near} \cup P{uniform}, calculate the SDF value and sign: Value: Find the closest point q on the surface point cloud using a kd-tree. The distance is d = \|p' - q\|. Sign: Determine if the point is inside or outside the surface. Normal Method: Compute the dot product of the vector (p' - q) and the normal nq at q. Depth Method: Project the point into the camera frame of each scan. If the point's depth is greater than the depth buffer value for any camera, it is outside (positive sign). 6. Validation: Check the fraction of points inside the shape (negative SDF). If this fraction is less than minsize (default 0), throw an exception. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def normalizetounitsphere(vertices): scale = np.max(np.linalg.norm(vertices, axis=1)) return vertices / scale def samplemeshsurface(vertices, faces, count): areas = np.linalg.norm(np.cross( vertices[faces[:, 1]] - vertices[faces[:, 0]], vertices[faces[:, 2]] - vertices[faces[:, 0]]), axis=1) / 2.0 probs = areas / np.sum(areas) faceindices = np.random.choice(len(faces), size=count, p=probs) u = np.random.random(count) v = np.random.random(count) sqrtu = np.sqrt(u) b1 = 1.0 - sqrtu b2 = sqrtu (1.0 - v) b3 = sqrtu v p0 = vertices[faces[faceindices, 0]] p1 = vertices[faces[faceindices, 1]] p2 = vertices[faces[faceindices, 2]] return p0 b1[:, None] + p1 b2[:, None] + p2 b3[:, None] def sampleuniforminsphere(R, count): points = [] while len(points) < count: extra = np.random.uniform(-R, R, size=(count 2, 3)) valid = np.sum(extra2, axis=1) <= R2 points.append(extra[valid]) return np.vstack(points)[:count] def getsurfacepointcloud(vertices, faces, count=1000000): areas = np.linalg.norm(np.cross( vertices[faces[:, 1]] - vertices[faces[:, 0]], vertices[faces[:, 2]] - vertices[faces[:, 0]]), axis=1) / 2.0 facenormals = np.cross(vertices[faces[:, 1]] - vertices[faces[:, 0]], vertices[faces[:, 2]] - vertices[faces[:, 0]]) facenormals /= np.linalg.norm(facenormals, axis=1, keepdims=True) faceindices = np.random.choice(len(faces), size=count, p=areas/np.sum(areas)) pts = samplemeshsurface(vertices, faces, count) normals = facenormals[faceindices] return pts, normals def nearsurfacepointsampling(vertices, faces, N=500000, sigma=0.01, R=1.0, minsize=0.0): vertices = normalizetounitsphere(vertices) Nsurf = int(2/5 N) Nnear = int(2/5 N) Nuniform = N - Nsurf - Nnear Psurf = samplemeshsurface(vertices, faces, Nsurf) noise = np.random.normal(0, sigma, (Nnear, 3)) Pnear = Psurf[:Nnear] + noise Puniform = sampleuniforminsphere(R, Nuniform) Pall = np.vstack([Pnear, Puniform]) cloudpts, normals = getsurfacepointcloud(vertices, faces, count=1000000) dists = np.linalg.norm(Pall[:, None,:] - cloudpts[None,:,:], axis=2) idx = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) D = np.min(dists, axis=1) q = cloudpts[idx] n = normals[idx] vec = Pall - q S = np.sign((vec n).sum(axis=1)) uniformmask = slice(Nsurf + Nnear, None) fractioninside = np.sum(S[uniformmask] == -1.0) / Nuniform if fractioninside < minsize: raise Exception(f"Too few points inside shape: {fractioninside} < {minsize}") return Pall, D, S Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight meshes: The sampling method requires watertight meshes with correct face normals. Sign determination: The normal method can produce "bubble" artifacts in concave regions or near holes. The depth method avoids these artifacts but is less accurate. Generates surface points (foot points) from a clamped signed distance field volume by projecting grid voxels onto the isosurface along the gradient direction. It differs by relying on the unit-length gradient property for single-step projection without iterative refinement. Choose it when working with discrete grid volumes rather than explicit meshes. Generates sample points on the primary boundary curve of an implicit surface, defined as the intersection of the surface function and the orientation function. It differs by explicitly targeting visibility discontinuities (silhouettes) where the surface normal is perpendicular to the view vector. Choose it for differentiable rendering of silhouette edges. Distributes training positions for neural implicit surface reconstruction by combining uniform volume samples, uniform surface samples, and perturbed surface samples. It differs by using explicit mixing strategies and area-weighted triangle selection to ensure coverage of the object and its immediate vicinity. Choose it when balanced surface and volume coverage is required for training. Visualizes 3D velocity fields in a thickened region around a contour surface by rendering motion-blurred ellipsoidal particles. It differs by operating on contour surfaces of scalar functions generally unrelated to the velocity vectors, without requiring surface parameterization. Choose it for interactive visualization of volumetric flows near implicit boundaries. Generates random points on the surface of a 3D object (specifically on triangles) for neural network reflectance models. It differs by focusing on uniform spatial distribution over mesh geometry for training data generation. Choose it for NeRF training pipelines requiring explicit surface point clouds. A training strategy that minimizes an L1 loss integrated over \mathbb{R}^3 using importance sampling. It differs by concentrating samples near the zero-level set of the SDF to avoid empty space, and by avoiding bias toward dense vertex regions. Choose it when uniform box sampling proves inefficient for implicit surface training. A set of points E is a loose \mu-sample of a surface S if: 1) For all x \in S \cap V(E), the ball B(x, \mu \times \text{lfs}(x)) contains a point from E (radius of all surface Delaunay balls is less than \mu). 2) The Delaunay triangulation of E restricted to S has vertices on all connected components of S. It differs by providing a formal geometric sampling criterion for mesh generation refinement. Choose it when constructing isotopic surface meshes via Delaunay refinement. Parameter: \mu (scaling factor for local feature size). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Training is performed on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs using PyTorch with a batch size of 512. Strengths: Provides high-density samples near the surface, which improves the accuracy of the learned SDF. Limitations: Requires a watertight mesh and correct normals for the sampling method. The normal sign method can produce "bubble" artifacts in concave regions or near holes. The method was proposed in the DeepSDF paper. It is used in neural implicit surface reconstruction to provide training data that emphasizes the surface boundary. The implementation is available in the meshtosdf repository. name: Distance Field Foot Point Generation
head: Foot point extraction, Point Engine for Distance Fields (hgridf), Point generation from DFV, hgridf point generation
body:
A method to generate surface points (foot points) from a clamped, signed distance field volume (DFV) by projecting grid voxels onto the isosurface along the gradient direction. It differs from general scalar field foot point estimation by relying on the specific property that the gradient of a distance field is unit length, allowing for a single-step projection without iterative refinement. It builds on Near-Surface Point Sampling. Inputs: A hierarchical grid of distance field values (hgridf) representing a signed distance field volume (DFV). Outputs: A set of 3D points lying on the isosurface (typically d=0) and their corresponding gradient vectors, stored for rendering. Data Structures: HGridf Cell: Contains a flag indicating if the cell is "dirty" (needs regeneration) or "clean" (cached). Vertex Array: Stores generated foot points pf and gradients \mathbf{g}. Display List: Cached rendering primitive generated from the vertex array. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through all cells in the hierarchical grid. 2. Skip cells that are empty. 3. For each non-empty cell: a. If the cell is "dirty": i. Traverse all voxels within the cell. ii. For each voxel at position p with distance value d: 1. Check if d \in [0, \sqrt{3}). If not, skip this voxel. 2. Compute the gradient \mathbf{g}{raw} using central differences on the distance field values surrounding p. 3. Normalize the gradient: \mathbf{g} =  rac{\mathbf{g}{raw}}{\|\mathbf{g}{raw}\|}. 4. Calculate the foot point position: pf = p - d \mathbf{g}. 5. Store pf and \mathbf{g} in the vertex array. iii. Generate a display list from the vertex array. iv. Mark the cell as "clean". b. If the cell is "clean": i. Render the associated display list. 4. Move to the next cell. Formulas: Foot Point Calculation: pf = p - d \mathbf{g} Where: pf: The foot point (closest point on the isosurface). p: The position of the current voxel in the grid. d: The signed distance value at voxel p. \mathbf{g}: The normalized gradient vector of the distance field at p. Gradient Normalization: \mathbf{g} =  rac{
abla d}{\|
abla d\|} Where 
abla d is the gradient computed via central differences. Parameters: Interval Threshold: \sqrt{3}. The interval [0, \sqrt{3}) is used to select voxels. This value ensures that all voxels on the positive side of the isosurface are included if they belong to cells intersected by the isosurface, preventing holes in the generated point cloud. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Medial Surface: The gradient \mathbf{g} is undefined at points belonging to the medial surface (where there is an equal shortest distance to two or more surface points). The method assumes \mathbf{g} is well-defined. Gradient Accuracy: Central differences do not yield an exact unit gradient for non-trivial distance fields. Normalization is required to correct this. Holes: Using an interval smaller than [0, \sqrt{3}) may cause holes to appear in the rendered surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computecentralgradient(grid, p): """Compute gradient at p using central differences.""" dx = (grid[p.x + 1, p.y, p.z] - grid[p.x - 1, p.y, p.z]) / 2.0 dy = (grid[p.x, p.y + 1, p.z] - grid[p.x, p.y - 1, p.z]) / 2.0 dz = (grid[p.x, p.y, p.z + 1] - grid[p.x, p.y, p.z - 1]) / 2.0 return (dx, dy, dz) def vectorlength(v): """Compute Euclidean norm of a 3D vector.""" return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def createdisplaylist(vertexarray): """Cache vertex array for rendering.""" return list(vertexarray) def renderdisplaylist(displaylist): """Render cached points.""" for pt, grad in displaylist: # Render point at pt (implementation-specific) pass def generatefootpoints(hgridf): """ Generates foot points for a distance field volume using hgridf. """ for cell in hgridf.cells: if cell.isempty: continue if cell.isdirty: vertexarray = [] for voxel in cell.voxels: p = voxel.position d = voxel.distancevalue # Check interval [0, sqrt(3)) if d < 0 or d >= math.sqrt(3): continue # Compute gradient using central differences graw = computecentralgradient(hgridf.grid, p) # Normalize gradient gnorm = vectorlength(graw) if gnorm == 0: continue # Avoid division by zero; gradient undefined at medial surface g = (graw[0] / gnorm, graw[1] / gnorm, graw[2] / gnorm) # Calculate foot point pf = (p.x - d g[0], p.y - d g[1], p.z - d g[2]) vertexarray.append((pf, g)) # Generate display list from vertex array cell.displaylist = createdisplaylist(vertexarray) cell.isdirty = False cell.isclean = True if cell.isclean: renderdisplaylist(cell.displaylist) An algorithm to detect the medial axis (MA) of a general implicit surface by analyzing characteristic lines (normals) and detecting changes in foot points, providing subgrid accuracy without thinning or post-processing. It differs from its parent Distance Field Foot Point Generation by not just generating surface points, but by identifying the locus of centers of maximal inscribed spheres (the medial axis) to compute the Local Feature Size (LFS) field. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The cost is dominated by gradient computation and normalization for voxels in the 0, \sqrt{3}) band. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Caching via display lists reduces repeated computation for static scenes. Performance: Extremely fast for distance fields compared to iterative methods or Marching Cubes, as it requires only a single projection step per voxel. Strengths: Simple implementation; no iterative convergence required; suitable for interactive applications where latency is critical. Limitations: Only applicable to [signed distance fields (DFVs); fails or produces artifacts at the medial surface where the gradient is undefined. When to use: When rendering isosurfaces from pre-computed distance fields in interactive applications. When not to use: For general scalar fields (requires iterative refinement or Marching Cubes) or when medial axis accuracy is required without post-processing. The method originates from the work on hardware-accelerated point rendering of isosurfaces, specifically within the context of the "point engine for synthetic volume". It leverages the mathematical properties of signed distance fields to simplify surface point generation. The approach was detailed in the paper "Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering of Isosurfaces". It is part of a broader family of near-surface point sampling techniques used in volume rendering.
