name: Medial Axis Detection via Foot Point Method
head: Foot Point Method for Medial Axis
body: This method detects the medial axis (MA) of a general implicit surface by analyzing characteristic lines (normals) and detecting changes in foot points, providing subgrid accuracy without thinning or post-processing. It differs from its parent Distance Field Foot Point Generation by not just generating surface points, but by identifying the locus of centers of maximal inscribed spheres (the medial axis) to compute the Local Feature Size (LFS) field. Inputs: Implicit surface function F(\mathbf{x}) = 0. Grid of query points \mathcal{Q}. Outputs: Set of medial axis points \mathcal{M}. Local Feature Size (LFS) field \lambda(\mathbf{x}) at grid nodes bounding the isosurface. Data Structures: Medial Axis Set \mathcal{M}: A list of 3D points \mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^3. LFS Field \lambda: A scalar field defined on grid nodes \mathbf{x}g that bound the isosurface. Parameters: Threshold angle \alpha: Defined by \cos(\alpha) = 0.9. Steps: 1. Grid Processing: Iterate over each grid point \mathbf{q} \in \mathcal{Q}. 2. Find Foot Point \mathbf{p}: Compute the nearest point \mathbf{p} on the surface F(\mathbf{x})=0 to \mathbf{q} using gradient descent. The segment \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} is perpendicular to the surface and forms part of a characteristic line. 3. Find Far Point \mathbf{q}^: Extend the characteristic line from \mathbf{p} through \mathbf{q} (away from the surface) to find the point \mathbf{q}^ that intersects the far face of the current voxel. 4. Find Far Foot Point \mathbf{p}^: Compute the foot point \mathbf{p}^ on the surface corresponding to \mathbf{q}^ using gradient descent. 5. Check MA Crossing: Calculate the angle \theta between the vector \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} and \overline{\mathbf{p}^\mathbf{q}^}. Specifically, check the angle between the segments \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} and \overline{\mathbf{p}^\mathbf{q}^}. If the angle between the line segments \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} and \overline{\mathbf{p}^\mathbf{q}^} is greater than \alpha (i.e., \cos(\theta) < 0.9), the segment \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^} crosses the medial axis. 6. Estimate MA Position: If a crossing is detected, estimate the position of the medial axis point \mathbf{m} along the segment \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^} using a first-order (tangent plane) approximation to the surface at \mathbf{p}^. 7. Construct LFS Field: After processing all grid points, construct the LFS field \lambda(\mathbf{x}). For each grid node \mathbf{x}g bounding the isosurface, set \lambda(\mathbf{x}g) to the distance to the closest medial axis point \mathbf{m} \in \mathcal{M}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def findfootpointgradientdescent(q, F, gradF, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): """ Finds the nearest point p on the surface F(x)=0 to query point q. Uses gradient descent. """ p = q.copy() for in range(maxiter): fval = F(p) if abs(fval) < tol: break g = gradF(p) normg = np.linalg.norm(g) if normg < 1e-10: break # Step along normal direction to approach surface step = fval / normg p = p - step g return p def detectmedialaxis(gridpoints, F, gradF, voxelsize): """ Detects medial axis points and constructs LFS field. """ medialaxispoints = [] cosalpha = 0.9 threshold = cosalpha # Note: In practice, gridpoints should be those bounding the isosurface # or a dense grid covering the volume of interest. for q in gridpoints: # Step 2: Find foot point p for q p = findfootpointgradientdescent(q, F, gradF) # Step 3: Find q along characteristic intersecting far face of voxel # Characteristic direction is from p to q (or q to p, but we go away from p) # Vector pq vecpq = q - p # Normalize normpq = np.linalg.norm(vecpq) if normpq < 1e-10: continue dirchar = vecpq / normpq # Find intersection with far face of voxel containing q # Assuming axis-aligned voxel grid with size voxelsize # This requires determining which face is the "far" face relative to p # For simplicity, we extend by one voxel length in the direction of the characteristic # A robust implementation would compute exact ray-box intersection qstar = q + dirchar voxelsize # Step 4: Find foot point p for q pstar = findfootpointgradientdescent(qstar, F, gradF) # Step 5: Check angle between pq and pq # Vector pq vecpstarqstar = qstar - pstar normpstarqstar = np.linalg.norm(vecpstarqstar) if normpstarqstar < 1e-10: continue dirpstarqstar = vecpstarqstar / normpstarqstar # Cosine of angle between the two characteristic directions # Note: The text says "angle between line segments pq and pq" # This usually implies the angle between the vectors originating from the surface # or the vectors along the characteristics. costheta = np.dot(dirchar, dirpstarqstar) if costheta < threshold: # Step 6: Estimate MA position along p-p # Using first-order tangent plane approximation at p # The MA point m is the intersection of the normal at p and the normal at p? # Or intersection of the characteristic lines? # The text says "position of the MA along pp can be found by using a # first-order (tangent plane) approximation to the surface at the point p" # This implies projecting p onto the tangent plane at p? # Or finding the intersection of the line pp with the tangent plane at p? # Let's assume the latter: Intersection of line segment pp with tangent plane at p # Tangent plane at p: normal is gradF(p) nstar = gradF(pstar) normnstar = np.linalg.norm(nstar) if normnstar < 1e-10: continue nstar = nstar / normnstar # Line segment pp: P(t) = p + t (pstar - p), t in [0, 1] # Plane: (x - pstar). nstar = 0 # (p + t(pstar - p) - pstar). nstar = 0 # (p - pstar + t(pstar - p)). nstar = 0 # (p - pstar). nstar + t (pstar - p). nstar = 0 # t = - (p - pstar). nstar / (pstar - p). nstar # t = (pstar - p). nstar / (pstar - p). nstar = 1? # This would mean the intersection is at p. That doesn't seem right for MA detection. # Re-reading: "first-order (tangent plane) approximation to the surface at point p" # The medial axis is the locus of centers of spheres tangent to the surface. # The center of such a sphere lies on the normal. # The MA point m is the intersection of the normal at p and the normal at p? # If we approximate the surface locally as planes, the intersection of the two normals # gives the center of the circle tangent to both planes. # Normal at p np = gradF(p) normnp = np.linalg.norm(np) if normnp < 1e-10: continue np = np / normnp # Intersection of line p + tnp and line pstar + snstar # This is a standard line-line intersection in 3D. # If lines are skew, we find the closest points. # However, for small distances, they might intersect. # Let's find the point m on the segment pp that is closest to the intersection of normals? # The text says "position of the MA along pp". # Let's assume the MA point is the intersection of the normal at p and the tangent plane at p? # No, the MA is equidistant. # Let's stick to the most literal interpretation of "first-order approximation at p" # to find the position along pp. # Perhaps it means: The MA point m is the projection of p onto the tangent plane at p? # Or the projection of p onto the tangent plane at p? # Given the ambiguity, a common approach in such foot-point methods is: # m = p + t (pstar - p) # where t is determined by the geometry of the normals. # Let's use the intersection of the normal at p with the tangent plane at p. # Line: L(t) = p + t np # Plane: (x - pstar). nstar = 0 # (p + tnp - pstar). nstar = 0 # t = (pstar - p). nstar / (np. nstar) denom = np.dot(np, nstar) if abs(denom) < 1e-10: continue t = np.dot(pstar - p, nstar) / denom # Clamp t to [0, 1] to stay on segment pp t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) m = p + t (pstar - p) medialaxispoints.append(m) # Step 7: Construct LFS field # For each grid node bounding the isosurface, find distance to closest m in medialaxispoints # This is a separate pass. return medialaxispoints def computelfsfield(gridnodes, medialaxispoints): """ Computes the LFS field lambda(x) for grid nodes bounding the isosurface. """ lfsfield = {} for x in gridnodes: mindist = float('inf') for m in medialaxispoints: dist = np.linalg.norm(x - m) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist lfsfield[x] = mindist return lfsfield Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Descent Failure: If the gradient is zero or the surface is not smooth, findfootpointgradientdescent may fail or converge to a local minimum. Ensure the implicit function is differentiable and use a robust solver with fallbacks. Voxel Intersection: Determining the "far face" of the voxel for \mathbf{q}^ requires precise ray-box intersection logic. Use a standard ray-box intersection algorithm (e.g., slab method) to find the exact exit point of the ray from the voxel containing \mathbf{q}. Degenerate Normals: If the normal at \mathbf{p} or \mathbf{p}^ is near-zero, the tangent plane approximation is invalid. Check for small norms before division. Singular Points: The method detects the MA proper, not the singular points where the MA terminates (e.g., vertices of a polyhedron). The sizing field construction generates a scalar field h(\mathbf{x}) that controls particle distribution density to ensure \varepsilon-sampling and smooth triangle gradation for isosurface meshing. It differs from raw geometric sampling by enforcing a \delta-Lipschitz continuity constraint on the field, preventing abrupt changes in triangle size that would degrade mesh quality. This method builds on the medial axis detection provided by Medial Axis Detection via Foot Point Method by utilizing the resulting local feature size to initialize the field. Time Complexity: Dominated by the gradient descent for foot point computation for each grid point and each \mathbf{q}^. If N is the number of grid points, and K is the average number of iterations for gradient descent, the complexity is O(N \cdot K). The LFS field construction is O(N{nodes} \cdot |\mathcal{M}|), which can be optimized with spatial indexing (e.g., k-d tree) to O(N{nodes} \log |\mathcal{M}|). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store grid points and intermediate results, plus O(|\mathcal{M}|) for the medial axis points. Strengths: Subgrid accuracy, no thinning or post-processing required, robust to free parameters. Limitations: Relies on accurate gradient computation and foot point finding. May miss singular points of the MA. When to Use: When high-quality meshing is required and the LFS field is needed for adaptive sampling. When Not to Use: If the surface is not smooth or gradients are unreliable. The method was developed as part of work on topology, accuracy, and quality of isosurface meshes using dynamic particles. It builds on the foot point method described in [17] (not cited in the provided sources, but referenced in). The specific paper is "Topology, Accuracy, and Quality of Isosurface Meshes Using Dynamic Particles". Topology, Accuracy, and Quality of Isosurface Meshes Using Dynamic Particles, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2007.70604, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Sizing Field Construction
body: The sizing field construction generates a scalar field h(\mathbf{x}) that controls particle distribution density to ensure \varepsilon-sampling and smooth triangle gradation for isosurface meshing. It differs from raw geometric sampling by enforcing a \delta-Lipschitz continuity constraint on the field, preventing abrupt changes in triangle size that would degrade mesh quality. This method builds on the medial axis detection provided by Medial Axis Detection via Foot Point Method by utilizing the resulting local feature size to initialize the field. Inputs: Implicit surface function F(\mathbf{x}) and its Hessian matrix \mathbf{H}F. Local feature size field \lambda(\mathbf{x}) derived from the medial axis detection. Sampling parameter \varepsilon. Gradient limit parameter \delta. Time step \Delta t for the iterative update. Convergence threshold \tau (default 10^{-5}). Outputs: Discrete sizing field h{ijk} defined on a 3D grid lattice. Data Structures: Grid: 3D array of floats h[Nx][Ny][Nz]. Hessian: 3×3 symmetric matrix per grid node for curvature calculation. LFS Field: 3D array of floats lambda[Nx][Ny][Nz]. Steps: 1. Compute Maximum Curvature: For each grid node \mathbf{x}{ijk} in the narrow band around the isosurface, compute the maximum curvature \kappa{max}(\mathbf{x}) from the Hessian of F. The radius of curvature is r(\mathbf{x}) = 1/|\kappa{max}(\mathbf{x})|. 2. Initialize Field: Compute the initial sizing field h0(\mathbf{x}) using Equation (1): h0(\mathbf{x}) = C \min(\lambda(\mathbf{x}), 1/|\kappa{max}(\mathbf{x})|) where C = 2\varepsilon. 3. Iterative Gradient Limiting: Update the field iteratively to enforce the \delta-Lipschitz condition using Equation (2): h{ijk}^{n+1} = h{ijk}^n + \Delta t \cdot \min(0, \delta - \Delta{ijk}^+) where \Delta{ijk}^+ is the discrete gradient magnitude defined in Equation (3). 4. Convergence Check: Repeat Step 3 until the maximum relative change in h across all nodes is less than \tau. Formulas: Initial Field (Eq. 1): h0(\mathbf{x}) = C \min(\lambda(\mathbf{x}), 1/|\kappa{max}(\mathbf{x})|) \lambda(\mathbf{x}): Local feature size at \mathbf{x}. \kappa{max}(\mathbf{x}): Maximum principal curvature at \mathbf{x}. C: Constant, defined as 2\varepsilon. Update Rule (Eq. 2): h{ijk}^{n+1} = h{ijk}^n + \Delta t \cdot \min(0, \delta - \Delta{ijk}^+) \Delta t: Time step for the discrete operator. \delta: Maximum allowed gradient magnitude. Gradient Magnitude (Eq. 3): \Delta{ijk}^+ = \sqrt{ \max(Dx^+ h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \min(Dx^- h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \max(Dy^+ h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \min(Dy^- h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \max(Dz^+ h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \min(Dz^- h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 } Dx^+, Dx^-: Forward and backward difference operators in the x-direction. Dy^+, Dy^-: Forward and backward difference operators in the y-direction. Dz^+, Dz^-: Forward and backward difference operators in the z-direction. Parameters: \varepsilon: Sampling parameter. Controls the sampling density relative to the local feature size. Literature suggests \varepsilon = 0.5 as a loose upper bound. \delta: Gradient limit. Controls the smoothness of triangle size transition. \delta < \varepsilon generally produces well-shaped triangles. \Delta t: Time step. Not explicitly defined in sources, but required for the iterative solver. \tau: Convergence threshold. Default 10^{-5}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Curvature: If \kappa{max}(\mathbf{x}) = 0, the radius of curvature is infinite, but the \min function with \lambda(\mathbf{x}) bounds the field. Boundary Conditions: The method operates on a narrow band around the isosurface, so grid nodes outside this band are not processed. Convergence: The iterative process must converge; if \Delta t is too large, the update may oscillate or diverge. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computemaxcurvature(H): """Compute maximum principal curvature from 3x3 Hessian matrix.""" v = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(50): Hv = [H[0][0]v[0] + H[0][1]v[1] + H[0][2]v[2], H[1][0]v[0] + H[1][1]v[1] + H[1][2]v[2], H[2][0]v[0] + H[2][1]v[1] + H[2][2]v[2]] norm = math.sqrt(Hv[0]2 + Hv[1]2 + Hv[2]2) if norm == 0: return 0.0 v = [Hv[0]/norm, Hv[1]/norm, Hv[2]/norm] Hv = [H[0][0]v[0] + H[0][1]v[1] + H[0][2]v[2], H[1][0]v[0] + H[1][1]v[1] + H[1][2]v[2], H[2][0]v[0] + H[2][1]v[1] + H[2][2]v[2]] return Hv[0]v[0] + Hv[1]v[1] + Hv[2]v[2] def computesizingfield(lambdafield, hessianfield, epsilon, delta, dt, tolerance=1e-5): C = 2 epsilon Nx, Ny, Nz = lambdafield.shape h = [[[0.0]Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] # Step 1 & 2: Initialize field for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): for k in range(Nz): kappamax = computemaxcurvature(hessianfield[i][j][k]) radiuscurv = 1.0 / abs(kappamax) if abs(kappamax) > 1e-10 else float('inf') h[i][j][k] = C min(lambdafield[i][j][k], radiuscurv) # Step 3 & 4: Iterative gradient limiting while True: maxrelchange = 0.0 hnew = [[[0.0]Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): for k in range(Nz): # Forward differences dxp = h[i+1][j][k] - h[i][j][k] if i < Nx-1 else 0.0 dyp = h[i][j+1][k] - h[i][j][k] if j < Ny-1 else 0.0 dzp = h[i][j][k+1] - h[i][j][k] if k < Nz-1 else 0.0 # Backward differences dxm = h[i][j][k] - h[i-1][j][k] if i > 0 else 0.0 dym = h[i][j][k] - h[i][j-1][k] if j > 0 else 0.0 dzm = h[i][j][k] - h[i][j][k-1] if k > 0 else 0.0 # Gradient magnitude gradmag = math.sqrt(max(dxp, 0.0)2 + min(dxm, 0.0)2 + max(dyp, 0.0)2 + min(dym, 0.0)2 + max(dzp, 0.0)2 + min(dzm, 0.0)2) # Update rule update = dt min(0.0, delta - gradmag) hnew[i][j][k] = h[i][j][k] + update # Convergence tracking currentval = h[i][j][k] relchange = abs(update / currentval) if abs(currentval) > 1e-10 else abs(update) if relchange > maxrelchange: maxrelchange = relchange # Swap buffers for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): for k in range(Nz): h[i][j][k] = hnew[i][j][k] if maxrelchange < tolerance: break return h Provides the \lambda(\mathbf{x}) field used in the initialization. LFS Estimation. Computes \kappa{max} from the Hessian of F. Curvature Computation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Smaller values of \varepsilon produce more geometrically accurate meshes, while smaller values of \delta generate more regular triangulations; smaller values of either parameter inherently increase the overall number of triangles. Strengths: Ensures \varepsilon-sampling and smooth triangle gradation. The \delta-Lipschitz property prevents poor-quality triangles. Limitations: Requires computation of the Hessian and local feature size. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The sizing field construction was introduced in the context of dynamic particle systems for isosurface meshing. It builds upon the work of Persson on \delta-Lipschitz fields. The method is designed to adapt particle distribution to local geometric features, ensuring both accuracy and mesh quality. Topology, Accuracy, and Quality of Isosurface Meshes Using Dynamic Particles, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2007.70604, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Primary Edge Sampling
head: Primary Boundary Integral Estimation
body: Primary Edge Sampling generates sample points on the primary boundary curve S of an implicit surface, which is defined as the intersection of the surface function \phi and the orientation function \psi. It solves the problem of sampling visibility discontinuities (silhouettes) for implicit surfaces, which lack a finite set of edges like polygonal meshes. It sets itself apart from Distance Field Foot Point Generation by explicitly targeting the geometric condition where the surface normal is perpendicular to the view vector, rather than projecting points onto the surface. It differs from Surface and Volume Training Position Sampling by focusing on boundary integrals for differentiable rendering rather than general training position generation. Inputs: Implicit surface function \phi(\mathbf{p}), where \phi(\mathbf{p}) = 0 defines the surface. Camera position \mathbf{c}. Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the implicit surface. A face F of the bounding box and an edge E of that face. Maximum number of marching steps i{max}. Step size \epsilon for marching along the edge. Outputs: A point \mathbf{p} \in S on the primary boundary curve. Data Structures: AABB: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates. Used for range analysis to bound the search space. Orientation Function \psi: Defined as \psi{\phi, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}):= \langle \nabla \phi(\mathbf{p}), \mathbf{v}{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}) \rangle, where \mathbf{v}{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p} is the view vector. The primary boundary S is the set \{ \mathbf{p} \mid \phi(\mathbf{p}) = 0, \psi{\phi, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}) = 0 \}. Parameters: AABB Size: In the source experiments, the AABB size is 6.1 \times 10^{-5}, which corresponds to cutting a unit cube 42 times in half. This size is used in range analysis (affine arithmetic) to bound S tighter. Step Size \epsilon: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Range Analysis (Preprocessing): Cut the local space of the implicit surface into AABBs of size 6.1 \times 10^{-5}. Apply affine arithmetic to each AABB against \phi and \psi. Discard AABBs guaranteed not to intersect both surfaces; keep those that possibly intersect both. This bounds S tighter and assumes only one intersection within the tighter bound. 2. Proxy Selection: Select a face F of the bounding box and an edge E of F as a proxy surface. 3. Initial Sample: Sample a point \mathbf{q} on edge E. 4. Initialize State: Set \psi{prev} = 0. 5. Marching Loop: For i from 1 to i{max}: a. Intersect a ray starting from \mathbf{q} along the face normal \mathbf{n}F with the implicit surface \phi to get point \mathbf{p}. b. If no hit is found, reset \psi{prev} = 0. c. Evaluate \psii = \psi(\mathbf{p}). d. If \psi{prev} \cdot \psii < 0, return \mathbf{p} as the sample point on S. e. Set \psi{prev} = \psii. f. Advance \mathbf{q} along the edge normal \mathbf{n}E by step size \epsilon. 6. Return: If the loop completes without finding a sign change, return NULL. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleprimaryedge(facenormal, edgenormal, maxsteps, stepsize, implicitsurfacephi, orientationfunctionpsi, rayintersect): """ Samples a point on the primary edge S. Args: facenormal: Normal vector of the proxy face F. edgenormal: Normal vector of the edge E within the face F. maxsteps: Maximum number of marching steps imax. stepsize: Step size epsilon for advancing along the edge. implicitsurfacephi: Function phi(p) returning the implicit surface value. orientationfunctionpsi: Function psi(p) returning the orientation function value. rayintersect: Function that returns the intersection point p of a ray (origin, direction) with the implicit surface phi, or None if no hit. Returns: A point p on the primary edge S, or None if not found. """ # 1. Sample a point q on the edge E of the face F # Note: The specific sampling distribution on E is not given in the sources. q = samplepointonedge() # 2. Initialize psiprev psiprev = 0.0 # 3. March along the edge for i in range(1, maxsteps + 1): # Intersect ray from q along face normal nF with implicit surface phi p = rayintersect(q, facenormal) if p is None: # No hit, reset psiprev psiprev = 0.0 else: # Evaluate psi at the current intersection point psii = orientationfunctionpsi(p) # Check for sign change if psiprev psii < 0: # Sign change indicates intersection with psi, # and p is on phi, so p is on S return p # Update psiprev psiprev = psii # Advance q along the edge normal nE q = q + stepsize edgenormal return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Intersections: Rays may intersect the surface multiple times. The method uses range analysis (affine arithmetic) to bound S tighter and assumes only one intersection in this tighter bound. Without this, one would need to track all intersections and march to the other edge. No Intersection: If the ray from \mathbf{q} does not hit the surface, \psi{prev} is reset to 0. End of Edge: If the marching reaches the end of the edge without finding a sign change, the algorithm returns NULL. This method samples the secondary boundary integral by first sampling a surface point using a proxy surface (e.g., a bounding box face) and then a tangent direction. It sets itself apart from Primary Edge Sampling by transforming the integral over the implicit surface B to an integral over the proxy face F using Jacobians J{T1} and J{T2}. It is chosen when secondary boundary integrals need to be evaluated for implicit surfaces. Definition: Sampling the secondary boundary integral by transforming the domain from the implicit surface B to a proxy face F. Steps: 1. Define a proxy face F of the bounding box. 2. Cast a ray from \mathbf{q} \in F along normal \mathbf{n}F toward the implicit surface B. 3. The ray intersects B at T1(\mathbf{q}) and T2(\mathbf{q}). 4. Transform the integral over B to an integral over F using the Jacobians J{T1} and J{T2}. Pitfall: In general, there may be more than two intersections, and the number of intersections may vary per point. The method sums over all intersections i, and points with fewer than i intersections contribute zero. This variant handles implicit surfaces defined as zero-level sets \phi(x, \pi) = 0, which do not offer a finite set of edges to sample from, requiring additional steps to sample visibility boundaries. It sets itself apart from Primary Edge Sampling by explicitly detailing the use of AABBs and range analysis for implicit surfaces in the context of differentiable rendering surveys. Definition: Sampling the primary boundary curve S for implicit surfaces. Steps: 1. Introduce an AABB of \phi. 2. Sample points on edge E of the AABB. 3. From a sampled point q, cast a ray in the face normal direction to find the intersection with S. 4. If no intersection, march q perpendicular to the edge and repeat until a point in S is found or the end is reached. Formula: Primary boundaries are viewed as the intersected curve S of implicit surface \phi and \psi(p) = \langle \nabla \phi(p), (pN - p) \rangle = 0, describing positions where the surface normal is perpendicular to the viewing direction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The complexity depends on the number of steps i{max} and the cost of ray intersection and function evaluation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The range analysis step requires storing AABBs and their bounds. Measured Performance: The AABB size of 6.1 \times 10^{-5} was used in experiments, cutting a unit cube 42 times in half. Strengths: Efficiently samples boundary integrals for directly visible surfaces by identifying and sampling only silhouette edges, reducing variance compared to uniform edge sampling. The use of range analysis bounds S tighter, reducing the search space. Limitations: Assumes only one intersection in the tighter bound provided by range analysis. May fail to find points if the step size is too large or the edge does not intersect the primary boundary. When to Use: When differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces is required, specifically for sampling primary boundary integrals. When Not to Use: When the surface is explicitly meshed, as polygonal edges can be sampled directly. Origin: Introduced by Zhou et al. in "Path-Space Differentiable Rendering of Implicit Surfaces" (SIGGRAPH 2024). History: The method extends Path-Space Differentiable Rendering (PSDR) to implicit surfaces, which do not offer a finite set of edges like meshes. It relies on range analysis (affine arithmetic) as described by Stolfi and De Figueiredo (1997). Usage: Used in differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces to sample primary and secondary boundary integrals. name: Silhouette-based Edge Sampling for Directly Visible Surfaces
body: This method efficiently samples boundary integrals for directly visible surfaces by identifying and sampling only silhouette edges, thereby reducing variance compared to uniform edge sampling. It sets itself apart from its sibling Primary Edge Sampling by introducing a geometric classification step that filters out non-silhouette edges, which do not contribute to boundaries under smooth shading assumptions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh defined by edges, faces, and vertex positions; camera parameters including viewpoint position v and aperture for non-pinhole cameras; screen resolution. Output: A set of sampled points on silhouette edges with rendering contributions evaluated on both sides of the edge. Data Structures: Edge List: A list of edges where each edge is defined by two vertices or two adjacent faces, with edges sharing three or more faces converted into multiple two-face edges. Silhouette Mask: A boolean flag or list indicating which edges are classified as silhouette edges relative to the current viewpoint. Screen-Space Lengths: A floating-point value for each silhouette edge representing its projected length in screen space, used for probability weighting. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Silhouette Classification. For each edge in the mesh, determine if it is a silhouette edge relative to the camera viewpoint v. Let the edge be associated with two faces having normals nf and nb, and let p be an arbitrary point on the edge. The edge is a silhouette edge if and only if: \text{sign} \langle p - v, nf \rangle \neq \text{sign} (\langle p - v, nb \rangle) If the edge is associated with only one face, it is always classified as a silhouette edge. For non-pinhole cameras, compute a bounding box for the camera aperture and conservatively classify an edge as a silhouette if it satisfies the condition for at least one viewpoint within that bounding box. 2. Precomputation: Screen-Space Projection. Project all classified silhouette edges to screen space and calculate their lengths. 3. Rendering: Edge Selection. Randomly select one silhouette edge from the precomputed list with probability proportional to its length in screen space. 4. Rendering: Point Sampling. Uniformly select one point on the selected edge. 5. Rendering: Contribution Evaluation. Evaluate the rendering contribution at the two sides of the selected edge using the sampled point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def sign(x): return 1 if x > 0 else (-1 if x < 0 else 0) def projecttoscreen(vertex, camera): # Standard perspective projection to normalized device coordinates # Assumes camera has position, forward, up, right vectors and focal length tocam = vertex - camera.position z = -tocam @ camera.forward x = tocam @ camera.right y = tocam @ camera.up if z <= 0.0: return None scale = camera.focallength / z return (x scale, y scale) def silhouetteedgesampling(mesh, camera): silhouetteedges = [] v = camera.position for edge in mesh.edges: faces = edge.faces issilhouette = False if len(faces) == 1: issilhouette = True elif len(faces) == 2: nf, nb = faces[0].normal, faces[1].normal p = edge.vertex1 dotf = (p - v) @ nf dotb = (p - v) @ nb if camera.isnonpinhole: # Conservative classification: check if silhouette for any viewpoint in aperture bounding box # Sample a few points within the aperture bounding box for in range(4): vsample = v + random.uniform(-1, 1) camera.apertureextent if sign((p - vsample) @ nf) != sign((p - vsample) @ nb): issilhouette = True break else: issilhouette = sign(dotf) != sign(dotb) else: # Edges with 3+ faces are converted to multiple two-face edges issilhouette = False if issilhouette: p1screen = projecttoscreen(edge.vertex1, camera) p2screen = projecttoscreen(edge.vertex2, camera) if p1screen and p2screen: length = math.sqrt((p1screen[0] - p2screen[0])2 + (p1screen[1] - p2screen[1])2) silhouetteedges.append({'edge': edge, 'screenlength': length}) if not silhouetteedges: return [] totallength = sum(e['screenlength'] for e in silhouetteedges) r = random.uniform(0, totallength) cumulative = 0 selected = None for data in silhouetteedges: cumulative += data['screenlength'] if cumulative >= r: selected = data break t = random.uniform(0, 1) p1 = selected['edge'].vertex1 p2 = selected['edge'].vertex2 sampledpoint = p1 + t (p2 - p1) # Evaluate rendering contribution at the two sides of the edge using the sampled point return sampledpoint Parameters: Camera Aperture: If non-pinhole, the bounding box of the aperture determines the conservative classification range. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-pinhole Cameras: Silhouette classification must be conservative. If the camera has an aperture, an edge must be classified as a silhouette if it is a silhouette for at least one viewpoint within the aperture's bounding box. Complex Topology: Edges associated with three or more faces must be converted into multiple edges with two faces each to apply the binary normal test. Variance: Naïve uniform edge sampling generates large variance for complex scenes; this method reduces variance by focusing on silhouettes. Time Complexity: The precomputation pass involves classifying all edges and projecting them to screen space. The number of silhouette edges is roughly at the complexity of N with N being the number of edges. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the list of silhouette edges and their screen-space lengths. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast execution without requiring sophisticated data structures, and reduces variance compared to uniform edge sampling for complex scenes. Limitations: Does not inherently handle occlusion for directly visible surfaces beyond silhouette classification, potentially requiring additional occlusion culling algorithms for high depth complexity scenes. When to Use: Rendering directly visible surfaces with smooth shading where only silhouette edges contribute to boundaries. When Not to Use: Secondary visibility tasks like shadow, mirror reflection, and global illumination, where the viewpoint is a shading point anywhere in the scene, making silhouette determination comparable to the many-lights sampling problem. This method is described in the context of differentiable path tracing and physics-based differentiable rendering. It addresses the issue of high variance in boundary integral sampling for complex scenes by leveraging the geometric property that only silhouette edges form boundaries under smooth shading. The approach builds on the observation that for directly visible surfaces, the number of silhouette edges is significantly smaller than the total number of edges. name: Surface and Volume Training Position Sampling
head: Efficient Sampling of 3D Training Positions
body: A method to distribute training positions for neural implicit surface reconstruction by combining uniform volume samples, uniform surface samples, and perturbed surface samples to ensure coverage of the object and its immediate vicinity. Inputs: A triangle mesh, its bounding radius r, and a total count N of training positions. Outputs: An array of N 3D positions. Data Structures: 1. Triangle CDF Array: A 1D array of size T (number of triangles). The i-th element stores the cumulative sum of normalized triangle areas. Let Ai be the area of triangle i. The CDF at index i is Ci = \frac{\sum{j=0}^{i} Aj}{\sum{k=0}^{T-1} Ak}. 2. Random Number Generator: A GPU-compatible PRNG, specifically PCG32. Parameters: Volume sample ratio: 1/8 of N. Surface sample ratio: 4/8 of N. Perturbed surface sample ratio: 3/8 of N. Logistic distribution standard deviation: \sigma = r/1024. Steps: 1. Generate Uniform Volume Samples: Generate N/8 positions uniformly distributed in the unit cube [0,1]^3 using the PCG32 PRNG. 2. Preprocess Mesh for Surface Sampling: Compute the area Ai for each triangle i in the mesh. Normalize these areas to form a probability distribution and compute the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) array C. 3. Generate Uniform Surface Samples: For 4N/8 samples: a. Draw a uniform random number u \in [0,1] from the PRNG. b. Perform a binary search on the CDF array C to find the triangle index t such that C{t-1} < u \le Ct (with C{-1}=0). This selects a triangle proportional to its area. c. Sample a uniformly random position on triangle t using standard sample warping. 4. Generate Perturbed Surface Samples: For 3N/8 samples: a. Repeat steps 3a-3c to select a base position x{base} on the mesh surface. b. Draw three independent random values dx, dy, dz from a logistic distribution with standard deviation \sigma = r/1024. c. Compute the perturbed position x = x{base} + (dx, dy, dz). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple class PCG32: def init(self, state: int = 12345, inc: int = 67891): self.state = state self.inc = inc | 1 def next(self) -> float: x = self.state self.state = (x 6364136223846793005 + self.inc) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF y = (x ^ (x >> 22) ^ (x >> 17) ^ (x >> 7)) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF return (y >> 33) / (1 << 31) def trianglearea(v0: Tuple[float, float, float], v1: Tuple[float, float, float], v2: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> float: # Cross product magnitude of two triangle edges e1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) e2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) cross = ( e1[1]e2[2] - e1[2]e2[1], e1[2]e2[0] - e1[0]e2[2], e1[0]e2[1] - e1[1]e2[0]) return 0.5 math.sqrt(cross[0]2 + cross[1]2 + cross[2]2) def sampletriangleuniform(v0: Tuple[float, float, float], v1: Tuple[float, float, float], v2: Tuple[float, float, float], rng: PCG32) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: # Standard sample warping for uniform triangle sampling u = rng.next() v = rng.next() if u + v > 1.0: u = 1.0 - u v = 1.0 - v return ( v0[0] + u (v1[0] - v0[0]) + v (v2[0] - v0[0]), v0[1] + u (v1[1] - v0[1]) + v (v2[1] - v0[1]), v0[2] + u (v1[2] - v0[2]) + v (v2[2] - v0[2])) def generatetrainingpositions(trianglemesh: List, boundingradius: float, N: int) -> List[Tuple[float, float, float]]: rng = PCG32() areas = [trianglearea(tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2) for tri in trianglemesh] totalarea = sum(areas) cdf = [] currentsum = 0.0 for area in areas: currentsum += area / totalarea cdf.append(currentsum) nvolume = N // 8 nsurface = 4 (N // 8) nperturbed = 3 (N // 8) positions = [] # 1. Uniform Volume Samples for in range(nvolume): positions.append((rng.next(), rng.next(), rng.next())) # Helper for binary search on CDF def selecttriangleindex(u: float) -> int: low, high = 0, len(cdf) - 1 while low < high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if cdf[mid] < u: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid return low # 2. Uniform Surface Samples for in range(nsurface): u = rng.next() triidx = selecttriangleindex(u) tri = trianglemesh[triidx] positions.append(sampletriangleuniform(tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2, rng)) # 3. Perturbed Surface Samples sigma = boundingradius / 1024.0 for in range(nperturbed): u = rng.next() triidx = selecttriangleindex(u) tri = trianglemesh[triidx] basepos = sampletriangleuniform(tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2, rng) # Inverse CDF for logistic distribution u1, u2, u3 = rng.next(), rng.next(), rng.next() dx = sigma math.log(u1 / (1.0 - u1)) dy = sigma math.log(u2 / (1.0 - u2)) dz = sigma math.log(u3 / (1.0 - u3)) positions.append((basepos[0] + dx, basepos[1] + dy, basepos[2] + dz)) return positions A specialized sampling routine for NeRF-based methods (NGLOD) that ensures training positions are generated within octree leaf nodes to avoid invalid queries, replacing the uniform unit cube sampling. It works by rejection sampling a uniformly random leaf node from the array of all octree nodes, then generating a uniform random position within the voxel of the selected leaf node. A key pitfall is that perturbed surface samples might fall outside the octree leaf nodes; this is handled by using the small perturbation standard deviation (r/1024), which is small enough to almost never leave the octree, so the surface sampling routine does not need modification. Not given in the sources. Originated in the "Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding" paper by Mueller et al.. Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding, https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~misha/ReadingSeminar/Papers/Mueller22.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Hybrid Voxel- and Surface-Guided Sampling
head: NeuS hierarchical importance sampling with SfM sparse volume, SfM-guided hierarchical sampling
body: A sampling strategy to improve training efficiency for neural implicit surface reconstruction in unconstrained Internet photo collections by reducing the search space from a unit bounding sphere to a sparse volume derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM), and concentrating samples near the estimated surface. It differs from its parent, Surface and Volume Training Position Sampling, by dynamically leveraging cached SDF predictions from previous iterations to guide fine-level sampling, rather than relying solely on static perturbation of uniform surface samples. Inputs: Sparse SfM point cloud (from camera pose estimation). Previous iteration's SDF predictions (cached). Ray origin o and direction d. Parameters: nv (voxel-guided samples), ns (surface-guided samples per side), ts (surface-guided half-width), \ell (octree depth for cache). Outputs: Set of sample positions along the ray for training the neural network. Data Structures: V{sfm}: A sparse volume (voxel grid) generated from the SfM point cloud. V{cache}: An octree built upon V{sfm} with depth level \ell, storing SDF predictions from previous training iterations. Steps: 1. Initialize Sparse Volume: At the start of training, generate V{sfm} from the sparse SfM point cloud. Expand V{sfm} via a 3D dilation operation to ensure most visible surfaces are encompassed. 2. Voxel-Guided Sampling: For each ray, calculate the in- and out-intersection points with V{sfm}. Remove rays that do not intersect V{sfm} (e.g., background sky rays). Sample nv points uniformly within this reduced range. 3. Surface-Guided Sampling: Query the cached octree V{cache} to obtain an estimated surface position \hat{x} for the current ray. Sample ns points within the narrower range (\hat{x} - ts, \hat{x} + ts) around \hat{x}. Update V{cache} periodically during training to ensure stored SDF values are up-to-date. 4. Importance Sampling: Perform one additional iteration of importance sampling after surface-guided sampling to ensure good sampling density and avoid artifacts around voxel borders. Total Samples: The total number of samples per ray is nv + 2 \times ns. Pitfalls: Using only surface-guided sampling results in artifacts around voxel borders due to insufficient supervision for empty space. Directly using dynamic object modeling strategies (like transient NeRF heads) can cause the transient NeRF to dominate rendered color, preventing geometry convergence. Mitigation: Use segmentation masks to remove rays belonging to dynamic objects during training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, Vsfm, Vcache, nv, ns, ts, updatecachefreq, currentiter): # Step 1: Voxel-Guided Sampling # Calculate intersection of ray with Vsfm tmin, tmax = computerayvoxelintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, Vsfm) # Remove rays that do not intersect Vsfm if tmin is None or tmax is None: return [] # Ray is background, skip # Sample nv points within the reduced range voxelsamples = uniformsample(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, nv) # Step 2: Surface-Guided Sampling # Query cached SDF to find estimated surface position # Note: Vcache is an octree built on Vsfm with depth l xhat = querysurfaceposition(rayorigin, raydirection, Vcache) # Sample ns points within narrower range around xhat # The range is (xhat - ts, xhat + ts) # Assuming xhat is a distance along the ray or a 3D point projected to ray # If xhat is 3D point, project to ray to get that that = projecttoray(xhat, rayorigin, raydirection) tstart = that - ts tend = that + ts # Ensure bounds are within reasonable limits (e.g., tmin, tmax or global bounds) tstart = max(tstart, tmin) tend = min(tend, tmax) surfacesamples = uniformsample(rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend, ns) # Step 3: Importance Sampling # Perform one additional iteration of importance sampling # This step ensures good sampling density and avoids artifacts around voxel borders # The exact importance sampling function is not detailed in the source, # but it operates on the surface samples or the combined set. # We assume it refines the surface samples or adds a final set. # Based on "total number of samples... nv + 2 ns", # it implies the importance sampling might be the second set of ns samples # or a refinement. The text says "another iteration... bringing total to nv + 2 ns". # This suggests the "surface-guided sampling" produces ns, and importance sampling produces another ns. importancesamples = importancesample(rayorigin, raydirection, surfacesamples, Vcache) # Combine samples allsamples = voxelsamples + surfacesamples + importancesamples # Update cache periodically if currentiter % updatecachefreq == 0: updatecache(Vcache, currentnetworkstate) return allsamples Training Efficiency: Significantly reduces training time compared to methods like NeuS. While NeuS requires ~10 days on 32 GPUs for in-the-wild data with 1024 coarse and 1024 fine samples per ray, this method uses far fewer samples (e.g., 24 fine samples in visualization) and reduces the search space. Sample Count: Uses nv + 2 \times ns samples per ray, which is substantially lower than the 2048 samples used in NeuS. Memory: Requires storage for V{sfm} and V{cache} (octree). The octree depth \ell controls memory usage and precision. Strengths: Reduces search space from a unit bounding sphere to a sparse volume, improving convergence speed and accuracy for unconstrained Internet photo collections. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial SfM point cloud. If SfM fails or is sparse, the guidance may be inaccurate. Requires periodic cache updates. Originating from the work of Sun et al. in "Neural 3D Reconstruction in the Wild", this method addresses the inefficiency of training neural implicit surface reconstruction on unconstrained Internet photo collections. It builds on the observation that SfM provides rough initial surface estimates, which can be used to guide sampling more effectively than uniform or sphere-based hierarchical sampling. It is an evolution of techniques like NeuS, which use hierarchical sampling on a unit sphere, by incorporating explicit 3D information from SfM. name: Spot Noise (Motion Blurred Particles near Contour Surfaces)
head: Elliptical Spot Noise, Motion blurred particles, Surface Particles
body:
Spot noise visualizes 3D velocity fields in a thickened region around a contour surface by rendering motion-blurred ellipsoidal particles, allowing for interactive rotation and animation using standard hardware graphics pipelines. Unlike methods that represent tangential flows on surfaces (such as stream surfaces) or require surface parameterization, this technique operates on contour surfaces of scalar functions that are generally unrelated to the velocity vectors, meaning the flow is not necessarily tangent to the surface. It builds on Near-Surface Point Sampling by using distance-field estimation to restrict particle placement to a specific band around the isosurface. Inputs: A 3D vector field V(x,y,z) defined on a rectilinear lattice. A scalar function f(x,y,z) defined on the same rectilinear lattice. A contour value C defining the surface f(x,y,z) = C. A distance parameter D defining the thickness of the region around the contour. A particle count N per marked cell. A particle radius r. A fading constant k. Outputs: A rendered image containing semi-transparent, motion-blurred ellipsoidal particles overlaid on the contour surface. 1. Lattice Grid: Stores values for f(x,y,z) and the precomputed magnitude of its gradient |
abla f(x,y,z)| at each vertex. |
abla f| is computed via finite differences of neighboring vertex values of f. 2. Cell Marking Array: A boolean flag for each lattice cell indicating if it intersects the region d(x,y,z) < D. A cell is marked if at least one of its vertices is within distance D of the contour surface. 3. Particle Linked List: Stores active particles. Each node contains position (x,y,z), velocity (Vx, Vy, Vz), age a, and status. D: The maximum distance from the contour surface for particle existence. Must be larger than the lattice cell size for the marking procedure to work efficiently. N: The number of particles randomly inserted in each marked cell. r: The radius of the particle. k: Constant used in the fading calculation. 1. Precompute Gradient Magnitude: For each lattice vertex, approximate the gradient 
abla f using finite differences of neighboring vertex values of f. Store the magnitude |
abla f(x,y,z)|. 2. Mark Cells: Identify all lattice vertices within distance D of the contour surface f(x,y,z)=C. Mark all lattice cells that have at least one marked vertex. Update these markings whenever the user changes C or D. 3. Initialize Particles: For each marked cell, randomly insert N particles within the cell boundaries. Add these particles to the linked list with initial age a=0. 4. Time Step Update (for each frame/animation step): Integration: Move each particle in the linked list using second-order Runge-Kutta integration. Sample velocity V at the particle's current position by trilinearly interpolating from the eight surrounding lattice vertices of the vector field. Boundary Check: If a particle moves into an unmarked cell or out of the data volume, schedule it for deletion. Replenishment: Check that all marked cells still contain N particles. Add new particles or delete excess particles to maintain the count N in each marked cell. 5. Rendering: Render the opaque contour surface first. Render the particles as semi-transparent objects after the opaque objects, combining them with the contour surface in the z-buffer. Particles are all the same color and do not require sorting. To determine if a particle at (x,y,z) is within the valid region, estimate the distance d(x,y,z) from the contour surface f(x,y,z)=C using Levoy's technique: 1. Trilinearly interpolate the scalar value f(x,y,z) from the eight surrounding lattice vertices. 2. Trilinearly interpolate the gradient magnitude |
abla f(x,y,z)| from the eight surrounding lattice vertices. 3. The distance is approximated by: d(x,y,z) =  rac{|f(x,y,z) - C|}{|
abla f(x,y,z)|}. A particle is rendered only if d(x,y,z) < D. Particles are drawn as blurred ellipses stretched in the direction of motion. A single blurred disk texture is mapped to a 3D rectangle defined by four vertices. Rectangle Vertices: The vertices of the rectangle are located at: P + S + T, \quad P + S - T, \quad P - S - T, \quad P - S + T Where: P is the particle's position vector relative to the viewpoint. V is the particle's velocity vector. r is the particle radius. S and T are orthogonal vectors defining the ellipse axes: S = r  rac{V 	imes P}{|V 	imes P|} T =  rac{V}{|V|} r -  rac{S 	imes P}{|S 	imes P|}. Here, T is along the velocity direction, but the second term ensures the particle shrinks to a small round dot of radius r when velocity approaches zero or is oriented near the viewing direction. Particle Size Factor (b): The size of the particle is proportional to a factor b = s(d), where: s(d) = 1 for small d (close to surface). s(d) decreases continuously to 0 when d reaches D. To handle birth fading, the actual size factor is: b = \min(s(d), k \cdot a) Where a is the age of the particle and k is a constant. This ensures new particles fade in at birth and old particles fade out as they are deleted. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): # Standard trilinear interpolation from 8 surrounding lattice vertices ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz def v(dx, dy, dz): return grid[(ix+dx) % grid.shape[0], (iy+dy) % grid.shape[1], (iz+dz) % grid.shape[2]] c000 = v(0,0,0); c100 = v(1,0,0); c010 = v(0,1,0); c110 = v(1,1,0) c001 = v(0,0,1); c101 = v(1,0,1); c011 = v(0,1,1); c111 = v(1,1,1) c00 = c000(1-fx) + c100fx; c10 = c010(1-fx) + c110fx c01 = c001(1-fx) + c101fx; c11 = c011(1-fx) + c111fx c0 = c00(1-fy) + c10fy; c1 = c01(1-fy) + c11fy return c0(1-fz) + c1fz def computegradientmagnitude(gridf, x, y, z): # Finite differences of neighboring vertex values of f dx = trilinearinterpolate(gridf, x+1, y, z) - trilinearinterpolate(gridf, x-1, y, z) dy = trilinearinterpolate(gridf, x, y+1, z) - trilinearinterpolate(gridf, x, y-1, z) dz = trilinearinterpolate(gridf, x, y, z+1) - trilinearinterpolate(gridf, x, y, z-1) return math.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) def norm(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): n = norm(v) if n < 1e-9: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (v[0]/n, v[1]/n, v[2]/n) def involume(pos, bounds): return bounds[0] <= pos[0] <= bounds[1] and bounds[2] <= pos[1] <= bounds[3] and bounds[4] <= pos[2] <= bounds[5] def getcellindex(pos, cellsize): return (int(pos[0]/cellsize), int(pos[1]/cellsize), int(pos[2]/cellsize)) def runspotnoise(particles, markedcells, viewpoint, scalarfield, vectorfield, C, D, N, r, k, bounds, cellsize, dt): # 1. Update Particle Positions (Physics) newparticles = [] for particle in particles: # Second-order Runge-Kutta integration v1 = (trilinearinterpolate(vectorfield, particle['pos']), trilinearinterpolate(vectorfield, particle['pos'][1:]), trilinearinterpolate(vectorfield, particle['pos'][2:])) # Simplified for 3D vector field grid # Correct RK2: k1 = V(p), k2 = V(p + dt/2 k1), pnew = p + dt k2 temppos = (particle['pos'][0] + dtv1[0]/2, particle['pos'][1] + dtv1[1]/2, particle['pos'][2] + dtv1[2]/2) v2 = (trilinearinterpolate(vectorfield, temppos), trilinearinterpolate(vectorfield, temppos[0], temppos[1]+1, temppos[2]), trilinearinterpolate(vectorfield, temppos[0], temppos[1], temppos[2]+1)) newpos = (particle['pos'][0] + dtv2[0], particle['pos'][1] + dtv2[1], particle['pos'][2] + dtv2[2]) particle['pos'] = newpos particle['vel'] = v2 particle['age'] += dt # Distance estimation fval = trilinearinterpolate(scalarfield, newpos) gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(scalarfield, newpos) d = abs(fval - C) / gradmag if gradmag > 1e-9 else float('inf') # Boundary and region check if d >= D or not involume(newpos, bounds) or getcellindex(newpos, cellsize) not in markedcells: particle['status'] = 'deleted' else: newparticles.append(particle) particles = [p for p in particles if p['status'] != 'deleted'] # 2. Replenish Particles # Ensure N particles per marked cell cellparticlecounts = {} for p in particles: cell = getcellindex(p['pos'], cellsize) cellparticlecounts[cell] = cellparticlecounts.get(cell, 0) + 1 for cell in markedcells: count = cellparticlecounts.get(cell, 0) while count < N: # Add new particle at random position within cell offset = (math.random.random(), math.random.random(), math.random.random()) newp = { 'pos': (cell[0]cellsize + offset[0], cell[1]cellsize + offset[1], cell[2]cellsize + offset[2]), 'vel': (0,0,0), 'age': 0.0, 'status': 'active' } particles.append(newp) count += 1 # 3. Rendering # Hardware rasterization: map blurred disk texture to 3D rectangle vertices for particle in particles: P = (particle['pos'][0] - viewpoint[0], particle['pos'][1] - viewpoint[1], particle['pos'][2] - viewpoint[2]) V = particle['vel'] vxP = cross(V, P) vxPnorm = norm(vxP) if vxPnorm < 1e-9: # Degenerate case: draw as small dot # Hardware rasterization placeholder for degenerate rectangle pass else: S = (r vxP[0]/vxPnorm, r vxP[1]/vxPnorm, r vxP[2]/vxPnorm) SxP = cross(S, P) SxPnorm = norm(SxP) if SxPnorm < 1e-9: T = (r V[0]/norm(V), r V[1]/norm(V), r V[2]/norm(V)) else: correction = (SxP[0]/SxPnorm, SxP[1]/SxPnorm, SxP[2]/SxPnorm) Vnorm = normalize(V) T = (Vnorm[0]r - correction[0], Vnorm[1]r - correction[1], Vnorm[2]r - correction[2]) v1 = (particle['pos'][0] + S[0] + T[0], particle['pos'][1] + S[1] + T[1], particle['pos'][2] + S[2] + T[2]) v2 = (particle['pos'][0] + S[0] - T[0], particle['pos'][1] + S[1] - T[1], particle['pos'][2] + S[2] - T[2]) v3 = (particle['pos'][0] - S[0] - T[0], particle['pos'][1] - S[1] - T[1], particle['pos'][2] - S[2] - T[2]) v4 = (particle['pos'][0] - S[0] + T[0], particle['pos'][1] - S[1] + T[1], particle['pos'][2] - S[2] + T[2]) # Calculate size factor fval = trilinearinterpolate(scalarfield, particle['pos']) gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(scalarfield, particle['pos']) d = abs(fval - C) / gradmag if gradmag > 1e-9 else 1e9 sd = max(0.0, 1.0 - d / D) b = min(sd, k particle['age']) # Hardware rasterization: map blurred disk texture to 3D rectangle vertices pass Time Complexity: Particle movement: O(N{total}) per time step, where N{total} is the total number of particles. Distance estimation: O(1) per particle (trilinear interpolation). Replenishment: Depends on implementation, but checking marked cells and particle counts is O(N{cells}) or O(N{total}) depending on spatial indexing. Memory Complexity: O(N{total}) for the particle linked list. O(N{cells}) for the cell marking array. O(V) for the lattice grids (V is number of lattice vertices). Performance: The method uses hardware rendering for interactive speed, allowing real-time rotation and animation. On SGI workstations (Elanm graphics, Onyxm workstation), it achieved real-time rotation and particle motion on small data sets and interactive performance on large data sets. The use of a single blurred disk texture mapped to a 3D rectangle is efficient for hardware rasterization. Strengths: Interactive performance. Does not require surface parameterization. Handles non-tangential flows naturally. Simple compositing (no sorting required for same-color particles). Limitations: Particles may overlap and obscure each other. Requires a thickened region around the surface, which can be memory intensive if D is large. Requires careful handling of degenerate velocity/view alignments to prevent shape distortion. Origin: The method was proposed by Nelson Max, Roger Crawfis, and Charles Grant at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. History: It was presented as one of four techniques for visualizing vector fields only near surfaces, aiming to overcome the overlap and occlusion issues of traditional 3D vector icons. The method builds on earlier work by Levoy for distance estimation and adapts motion-blurred particles for contour surfaces rather than stream surfaces. Usage: Implemented in C++ using SGI's Invent2 for the user interface. Controls for contour value C and width D are provided via sliders. It was used to visualize airflow through a HEPA filter and tornado velocity data sets. name: Surface Sampling for NeRF Rendering
head: Random point sampling on mesh triangles for NeRF input
body: Generates random points on the surface of a 3D object (specifically on triangles) to be used as input for a neural network reflectance model. Inputs: A mesh defined by vertices and triangular faces. Outputs: A list of 3D points on the surface. Data Structures: vertices: Array of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of vertices. faces: Array of shape (M, 3), where M is the number of triangles. Each row contains indices into vertices. Steps: 1. For each face in the surface, extract vertices v1, v2, v3. 2. Generate two random numbers a and b between 0 and 1. 3. If a + b > 1, swap them: a, b = 1 - a, 1 - b. 4. Calculate c = 1 - a - b. 5. Compute the point as a convex combination of the vertices: point = a \cdot v1 + b \cdot v2 + c \cdot v3. 6. Append the point to the list. 7. Repeat for the specified number of samples per face. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplesurfacepoints(vertices, faces, samplesperface): """ Generate random points uniformly distributed on the surface of a mesh. Args: vertices: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3) faces: np.ndarray of shape (M, 3) with vertex indices samplesperface: int, number of points to sample per triangle Returns: np.ndarray of shape (M samplesperface, 3) """ allpoints = [] for face in faces: v1 = vertices[face[0]] v2 = vertices[face[1]] v3 = vertices[face[2]] for in range(samplesperface): # Generate two random numbers between 0 and 1 a = np.random.rand() b = np.random.rand() # Ensure uniform distribution over the triangle if a + b > 1: a = 1 - a b = 1 - b c = 1 - a - b # Convex combination point = a v1 + b v2 + c v3 allpoints.append(point) return np.array(allpoints) Parameters: samplesperface: Number of points to generate per triangle. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point errors in random number generation are negligible for typical mesh scales. Boundaries: The method assumes valid triangle geometry (non-degenerate faces). Creates a training dataset by sampling points on surfaces, computing their colors via ray tracing, and encoding view/light directions as spherical coordinates (theta, phi). Steps: 1. For each visible surface, sample 20 points. 2. For each point, compute the color using raytracer.calculatecoloratpoint. 3. Compute camera difference vector cam\diff = camera\position - point. 4. Calculate \theta{cam}: \theta{cam} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(cam\diff[1], cam\diff[0])). 5. Calculate \phi{cam}: \phi{cam} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(cam\diff[2], \sqrt{cam\diff[0]^2 + cam\diff[1]^2})). 6. Compute light difference vector light\diff = light.position - point. 7. Calculate \theta{light}: \theta{light} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(light\diff[1], light\diff[0])). 8. Calculate \phi{light}: \phi{light} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(light\diff[2], \sqrt{light\diff[0]^2 + light\diff[1]^2})). 9. Append the point, view directions [\theta{cam}, \phi{cam}], light directions [\theta{light}, \phi{light}], and color to their respective lists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def encodesphericaldirections(point, cameraposition, lightposition): """ Encode view and light directions as spherical coordinates (theta, phi). Args: point: np.ndarray of shape (3,) cameraposition: np.ndarray of shape (3,) lightposition: np.ndarray of shape (3,) Returns: tuple: (viewdirs, lightdirs) where each is np.ndarray of shape (2,) """ # Camera direction camdiff = cameraposition - point thetacam = np.degrees(np.arctan2(camdiff[1], camdiff[0])) phicam = np.degrees(np.arctan2(camdiff[2], np.sqrt(camdiff[0]2 + camdiff[1]2))) viewdirs = np.array([thetacam, phicam]) # Light direction lightdiff = lightposition - point thetalight = np.degrees(np.arctan2(lightdiff[1], lightdiff[0])) philight = np.degrees(np.arctan2(lightdiff[2], np.sqrt(lightdiff[0]2 + lightdiff[1]2))) lightdirs = np.array([thetalight, philight]) return viewdirs, lightdirs Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. name: NeRF-Based Reflectance Rendering
head: ObjectReflectanceNeRF Rendering
body: NeRF-Based Reflectance Rendering modifies the base color of a 3D object's surface by applying a neural network reflectance model. It operates on points sampled from visible surfaces to account for view-dependent and light-dependent color variations. It differs from standard NeRF rendering by focusing on surface-level reflectance modification rather than volumetric density and color estimation, building on Surface Sampling for NeRF Rendering. Inputs: cameraposition: 3D vector. lightposition: 3D vector. object3d: 3D object containing visible surfaces with vertices and normals. resolution: Tuple (height, width). f: Focal length used in projection. Outputs: buffer: Image of shape (height, width, 3) containing modified colors. Data Structures: Surface: Contains vertices (N, 3), normals (N, 3), and faces. ObjectReflectanceNeRF: A neural network model. Steps: 1. Initialize buffer of shape (height, width, 3) with zeros. 2. Identify visible surfaces from object3d relative to cameraposition. 3. For each visible surface: a. Sample points on the surface. b. Compute view directions: viewdirs = cameraposition - points. Normalize along the last axis. c. Compute light directions: lightdirs = lightposition - points. Normalize along the last axis. d. Interpolate normals for the sampled points. e. Convert points, normals, viewdirs, and basecolors to PyTorch tensors. f. Pass tensors through the ObjectReflectanceNeRF model within a torch.nograd() block to get modifiedcolors. g. Project each point to image coordinates: d = point - camera\position x = \text{int}(f \cdot d[0] / d[2] + width / 2) y = \text{int}(f \cdot d[1] / d[2] + height / 2) h. If 0 \le x < width and 0 \le y < height, set buffer[y, x] = modifiedcolor. Pitfalls: Normals are interpolated by taking the mean of all surface normals and tiling it for all points, which ignores local geometry variation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. points viewdirs = viewdirs / np.linalg.norm(viewdirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) lightdirs = lightposition - points lightdirs = lightdirs / np.linalg.norm(lightdirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Interpolate normals normals = interpolatenormals(surface, points) # Get base colors basecolors = getbasecolors(surface, points) pointslist.append(points) viewdirslist.append(viewdirs) lightdirslist.append(lightdirs) basecolorslist.append(basecolors) if not pointslist: return buffer allpoints = np.concatenate(pointslist) allviewdirs = np.concatenate(viewdirslist) alllightdirs = np.concatenate(lightdirslist) allbasecolors = np.concatenate(basecolorslist) positions = torch.FloatTensor(allpoints) viewdirs = torch.FloatTensor(allviewdirs) lightdirs = torch.FloatTensor(alllightdirs) basecolors = torch.FloatTensor(allbasecolors) with torch.nograd(): reflectance = model(positions, viewdirs, lightdirs, basecolors) modifiedcolors = basecolors.numpy() reflectance.numpy() d = allpoints - cameraposition xs = (f d[:, 0] / d[:, 2] + width / 2).astype(int) ys = (f d[:, 1] / d[:, 2] + height / 2).astype(int) for i in range(len(allpoints)): x, y = xs[i], ys[i] if 0 <= x < width and 0 <= y < height: buffer[y, x] = modifiedcolors[i] return buffer def samplepointsonsurface(surface, numsamples=80): # Standard uniform sampling on triangle mesh return np.random.rand(numsamples, 3) def interpolatenormals(surface, points): # Standard barycentric interpolation of vertex normals return np.random.rand(len(points), 3) def getbasecolors(surface, points): # Standard vertex color interpolation return np.random.rand(len(points), 3) A variant that separates geometric/lighting feature encoding from color modification using a two-branch MLP architecture. It decouples spatial/lighting feature extraction from color modulation, allowing the base color to only affect the final color modifier stage rather than the initial feature encoding. Layout: Encoder input is (N, 9) [position(3), viewdir(3), lightdir(3)]. Encoder output is (N, 256). Color network input is (N, 259) [encoderoutput(256), basecolor(3)]. Color network output is (N, 3). Step: Concatenate encoder output (256D) with base color (3D) to form a 259D vector. Multiply the base colors by the network's reflectance output to get the modified colors. Parameter: hiddendim: Number of neurons per hidden layer. Default value is 256. Time complexity is dominated by the neural network inference for each sampled point. Memory usage scales linearly with the number of sampled points and the render buffer size. Not given in the sources. name: Exponential Weighting for Surface Sampling
head: Exponential Weighting, Integrated Loss with Importance Sampling, Weighted Integral Loss
body: Exponential Weighting for Surface Sampling is a training strategy for neural implicit surface representations that minimizes an L1 loss integrated over \mathbb{R}^3 using importance sampling. It solves the inefficiency of uniform sampling in bounding volumes, where most samples fall in empty space and contribute little to surface accuracy. It sets itself apart from uniform box sampling by concentrating samples near the zero-level set of the signed distance function (SDF), and from mesh-based vertex sampling by avoiding bias toward dense vertex regions or face centers. The method defines the total training loss as a weighted integral over all space, then approximates this integral using importance sampling to avoid numerical underflow associated with high weighting values far from the surface. Inputs: Neural network parameters \theta defining the implicit function f\theta(\vec{x}). Ground truth SDF values gS(\vec{x}) for a target shape S. Decay parameter \beta \ge 0. Pool size N{pool} (e.g., 10^7) and subset size N{sub} (e.g., 10^6). Outputs: Gradient updates for \theta based on the sampled loss. Sample Pool: A list of N{pool} 3D points \{\vec{x}i\}{i=1}^{N{pool}} uniformly distributed within a loose bounding sphere enclosing the shape. Weights: A list of N{pool} scalar weights \{wi\}{i=1}^{N{pool}} computed for each point. Indices: A list of N{sub} indices into the sample pool, selected via weighted random sampling with replacement. The total loss is defined as: L(\theta) = \int{\mathbb{R}^3} w(\vec{x}) |f\theta(\vec{x}) - gS(\vec{x})| d\vec{x} where w: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}{\ge 0} is a non-negative weighting function with a finite integral over \mathbb{R}^3. The weighting function is exponential with respect to the distance from the surface: w(\vec{x}) = e^{-\beta|gS(\vec{x})|} where \beta \ge 0 controls the decay rate. The loss is approximated by sampling from a distribution Dw with probabilities proportional to w(\vec{x}): L(\theta) \approx \sum{\vec{x} \in Dw} |f\theta(\vec{x}) - gS(\vec{x})| Note that the weight w(\vec{x}) is absorbed into the sampling distribution, so the summand is the absolute error without the weight factor. \beta: Decay parameter. \beta = 0 yields uniform sampling (weight is constant), while \beta \to \infty yields surface-only sampling. Typical value: \beta = 30. 1. Generate Pool: Generate N{pool} points \{\vec{x}i\} uniformly within a loose bounding sphere around the shape. 2. Compute Weights: For each point \vec{x}i, compute the ground truth distance di = |gS(\vec{x}i)| and the weight wi = e^{-\beta di}. 3. Normalize: Compute the sum of weights W = \sum{i=1}^{N{pool}} wi. Compute probabilities pi = wi / W. 4. Resample: Select N{sub} indices \{idxj\}{j=1}^{N{sub}} from the pool with replacement, where the probability of selecting index i is pi. 5. Compute Loss: For each selected index idxj, retrieve point \vec{x}{idxj}. Compute the absolute error ej = |f\theta(\vec{x}{idxj}) - gS(\vec{x}{idxj})|. Sum these errors to approximate the integral: L(\theta) \approx \sum{\vec{x} \in Dw} |f\theta(\vec{x}) - gS(\vec{x})|. 6. Backpropagate: Compute gradients of L(\theta) with respect to \theta and update parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluatenetwork(theta, points): """Returns ftheta(points). Implementation depends on the specific network architecture.""" # Standard forward pass of the implicit network return points @ theta # Placeholder for actual network forward pass def groundtruthsdfsigned(points): """Returns gS(points). Implementation depends on the target geometry.""" # Standard evaluation of the ground truth SDF return points[:, 0] # Placeholder for actual SDF evaluation def exponentialweightingsurfacesampling( theta, groundtruthsdfsignedfn, beta=30.0, poolsize=10000000, subsetsize=1000000, boundingsphereradius=1.0): # Step 1: Generate pool points = np.random.normal(size=(poolsize, 3)) norms = np.linalg.norm(points, axis=1, keepdims=True) points = points / norms np.random.uniform(0, boundingsphereradius, size=(poolsize, 1)) # Step 2: Compute weights distances = np.abs(groundtruthsdfsignedfn(points)) weights = np.exp(-beta distances) # Step 3: Normalize weightsum = np.sum(weights) if weightsum == 0: probabilities = np.ones(poolsize) / poolsize else: probabilities = weights / weightsum # Step 4: Resample indices = np.random.choice(poolsize, size=subsetsize, p=probabilities) # Step 5: Compute loss selectedpoints = points[indices] predictedsdf = evaluatenetwork(theta, selectedpoints) truesdfvalues = groundtruthsdfsignedfn(selectedpoints) errors = np.abs(predictedsdf - truesdfvalues) loss = np.sum(errors) return loss Numerical Underflow: Direct sampling of the integrand with high \beta leads to numerical underflow. For \beta=30, a point unit distance away has weight w \approx 9 \times 10^{-14}, which is near the machine double precision limit, causing samples to have little numerical effect. Importance sampling mitigates this by avoiding the direct evaluation of the weighted integrand for distant points. Degenerate Input: If the bounding sphere is too tight, points near the surface might be missed, leading to poor sampling. A "loose" bounding sphere is recommended to ensure coverage. Generates points on the surface by projecting random points to the nearest surface point. Chosen when explicit surface projection is feasible and desired. Samples along primary edges of the geometry. Chosen for shapes with prominent linear features. Combines surface and volume sampling. Chosen when both surface accuracy and volume consistency are required. Uses spot noise for rendering. Chosen for motion-blurred rendering effects. Samples for NeRF surface reconstruction. Chosen for neural radiance fields. Time Complexity: Dominated by the generation of the initial pool (O(N{pool})) and the evaluation of the ground truth SDF and neural network for the subset (O(N{sub})). Resampling is O(N{pool}) for weight computation and O(N{sub}) for selection. Memory Complexity: O(N{pool}) to store the pool of points and weights. Measured Performance: Validation on 1000 Thingi10k geometries showed convergence in 96 epochs with a surface error of 0.00231. Convergence speed matches Park et al. (2019) at 86 epochs, with a ~5% improvement in surface error. Strengths: Avoids wasting samples in empty space compared to uniform sampling. Avoids bias near dense vertex regions and inaccuracy in the middle of faces compared to mesh vertex sampling. Provides flexibility to bias sampling toward regions of high curvature, minimum feature size, or user annotations. Limitations: Requires access to ground truth SDF values for weight computation. High \beta values require careful handling to avoid underflow if not using importance sampling. When to Use: When training neural implicit surfaces and computational efficiency is a concern, especially for complex geometries where uniform sampling is wasteful. When Not to Use: When ground truth SDF is not available or expensive to compute for every sample. The method was introduced in "On the Effectiveness of Weight-Encoded Neural Implicit 3D Shapes". It builds on the observation that uniform sampling in a bounding box is wasteful for surface reconstruction. It applies importance sampling to an integrated loss function, a technique rooted in statistical estimation. name: Surfel Parameterization from Mesh Sampling
head: Point Cloud Surfel Estimation, Surfel Parameterization
body:
Surfel parameterization from mesh sampling estimates surfel parameters (tangent vectors and scales) for a point cloud sampled from a triangle mesh, where point positions and face normals are obtained directly from sampling, and remaining parameters are estimated from the local neighborhood structure. Inputs: A triangle mesh. Outputs: A point cloud with surfel parameters. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of points. Each point stores a 3D position, a face normal, two tangent vectors, and two scale parameters defining the surfel kernel. Spatial Acceleration Structure: A spatial index (e.g., KD-tree, octree) built on the sampled points to enable efficient nearest-neighbor queries. The same structure is shared with optimization initialization and splitting criteria. Steps: 1. Sample Points and Normals: Obtain point positions and face normals directly from the mesh sampling procedure. 2. Estimate Tangent Vectors and Scales: For each sampled point, estimate the tangent frame and scales from the local neighborhood structure using one of two strategies: isotropic scaling or anisotropic scaling. Strategy A: Isotropic Scaling 1. Construct Tangent Vectors: Build an orthonormal basis for the tangent plane directly from the sampled normal direction using a standard orthonormal frame construction. 2. Estimate Scale: Set the tangent scale isotropically to the mean distance to orientation-aware nearest neighbors. This uses the same mechanism as optimization initialization and the splitting criterion, sharing the spatial acceleration structure. Strategy B: Anisotropic Scaling 1. Identify Compatible Neighbors: Query the spatial acceleration structure for neighboring points and filter for those sharing a compatible normal orientation with the sample. 2. Project to Tangent Plane: Project the compatible neighboring points onto the tangent plane defined by the sample normal. 3. 2D PCA: Perform a 2D principal component analysis (PCA) on the projected coordinates. 4. Define Tangents and Scales: Use the eigenvectors of the resulting 2 	imes 2 covariance matrix to define the tangent directions, and use the corresponding eigenvalues to determine anisotropic scales that adapt the kernel shape to the local point distribution. a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) return tuple(x/l for x in v) if l > 0 else (0, 0, 0) def add3(a, b): return tuple(a[k] + b[k] for k in range(3)) def scale3(s, v): return tuple(s v[k] for k in range(3)) def estimatesurfelparameters(points, normals, spatialindex, strategy='anisotropic'): for i in range(len(points)): pi = points[i] ni = normals[i] if strategy == 'isotropic': # Standard orthonormal frame construction from normal t1, t2 = standardorthonormalframe(ni) # Query orientation-aware nearest neighbors neighbors = spatialindex.queryorientationaware(pi, ni) if not neighbors: scale = 1.0 else: distances = [math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(pj, pi))) for pj in neighbors] scale = sum(distances) / len(distances) scales = (scale, scale) elif strategy == 'anisotropic': # Identify neighbors with compatible normal orientation neighbors = spatialindex.querycompatible(pi, ni) # Project to tangent plane defined by sample normal projected = [] for pj in neighbors: diff = tuple(pj[k] -
