dot(a, n)n[k] for k in range(3))) t2 = cross(n, t1) return t1, t2 def compute2x2covariance(coords): n = len(coords) if n == 0: return [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]] meanx = sum(c[0] for c in coords) / n meany = sum(c[1] for c in coords) / n varx = sum((c[0] - meanx)2 for c in coords) / n vary = sum((c[1] - meany)2 for c in coords) / n covxy = sum((c[0] - meanx) (c[1] - meany) for c in coords) / n return [[varx, covxy], [covxy, vary]] def eig2x2(M): # Closed-form eigendecomposition for 2x2 symmetric matrix tr = M[0][0] + M[1][1] det = M[0][0] M[1][1] - M[0][1] M[1][0] disc = math.sqrt(max(0, (tr/2)2 - det)) l1 = tr/2 + disc l2 = tr/2 - disc # Eigenvectors for symmetric 2x2 if abs(M[0][1]) > 1e-8: e1 = normalize((M[0][1], l1 - M[0][0])) e2 = normalize((M[0][1], l2 - M[0][0])) else: e1 = (1, 0) e2 = (0, 1) return (l1, l2), (e1, e2) Parameters: The sources do not specify the neighbor count for spatial queries, the normal compatibility threshold, or a scale multiplier for eigenvalues. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Edges: Isotropic scaling can produce minor visual artifacts at sharp geometric edges where an isotropic kernel does not conform well to the local surface curvature. Computational Cost: Anisotropic scaling has higher computational overhead and memory consumption due to the eigendecomposition and neighbor filtering. A method to compute curvatures (Gaussian and Mean) and local differential geometry for a visible oriented point (p, v) using only the directional distance field d(p, v) and its derivatives with respect to p. It constructs a local coordinate system at the surface point q = p + d(p, v)v by choosing two tangent vectors tx, ty \in Tq(S) such that ||t\alpha||2 = 1 and tx^T ty = 0. In practice, this is done by sampling Gaussian vectors and extracting an orthogonal tangent basis. The surface is reparameterized near q0 via S(x, y) = q0 + x tx + y ty + fS(x, y)n0, where x and y control position on the tangent plane, or equivalently p(u) = p0 + x tx + y ty where u = (x, y). The first-order derivatives of the surface at u=0 are \partiali S|{u=0} = ti + (
ablap d(p, v0) ti) v0, where i \in \{x, y\}. The metric tensor (first fundamental form) is g{ij} = \partiali S^T \partialj S = \delta{ij} + ci cj + ci v0^T tj + cj v0^T ti, where ck = 
ablap d tk. In theory, since 
ablap d is parallel to normal n and orthogonal to tangents, cx = cy = 0, so g{ij} = \delta{ij}. In practice, use the theoretical value g = I2. The shape tensor (second fundamental form) is \Pi{ij} = (tj^T Hp[d] ti) n0^T v0, where Hp[d] is the Hessian of d with respect to p at u=0, and n0 is the surface normal at q0. Gaussian curvature is CK = \det(\Pi) / \det(g) and Mean curvature is CH = 	ext{tr}(\Pi g^{-1}). Performance: The isotropic variant is computationally efficient and available as a drop-in replacement when performance is critical. The anisotropic variant is used for quality in experiments but incurs higher overhead. Strengths: Anisotropic scaling eliminates edge artifacts observed with isotropic kernels by adapting the kernel shape to the local point distribution. Limitations: Isotropic scaling produces artifacts at sharp edges. Anisotropic scaling is slower and uses more memory due to eigendecomposition. The method originates from the 3DSS (3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering) paper. It is used in inverse rendering pipelines to prepare point clouds for splatting-based rendering and relighting. The local differential geometry computation is described in the context of Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3594225, fetched 2026-10-29

name: SDF-guided Sampling
head: Shao et al. SDF-guided Sampling, Surface-guided Sampling Strategy
body: SDF-guided Sampling is a surface-aware sampling strategy that uses a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to estimate ray-surface intersections, followed by fine-grained sampling around the intersection point to accelerate rendering and emphasize the relationship between surface and radiance fields. It differs from standard NeRF sampling by reducing the number of required sampling points through early surface localization, and from pure mesh-based methods by retaining the flexibility of implicit field evaluation without requiring explicit mesh vertex interpolation. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Depth bounds [tn, tf] defining the integration interval along the ray. Surface field function s(x), which outputs a scalar value for any point x. Parameters: Ns: Number of uniform sampling points for initial coarse sampling. Nr: Number of sampling points for fine-grained sampling around the surface. \delta: Interval size for fine-grained sampling around the intersection. Threshold T = 0.5 for determining intersection. Outputs: A set of sample points concentrated around the estimated surface intersection, used to evaluate the radiance field. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the ray parameters and the implicit field function s(x); the method relies on querying the field at discrete points. Steps: 1. Coarse Uniform Sampling: Generate Ns points uniformly distributed along the ray within the depth bounds [tn, tf]. The i-th point xi is calculated as: xi = o + ti d where ti are uniformly spaced values in [tn, tf]. 2. Intersection Estimation: Query the surface field value s(xi) for each coarse sample point. Identify the first intersection position t{int} by finding the smallest ti such that the surface field value exceeds the threshold: t{int} = \min \{ ti \mid s(o + ti d) \ge 0.5 \}. 3. Fine-Grained Sampling: Perform fine-grained sampling around the intersection in an interval of \delta with Nr sampling points to consider the radiance field surrounding the real surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linspace(start, stop, num): """Generate num evenly spaced values over [start, stop].""" step = (stop - start) / (num - 1) if num > 1 else 0 return [start + i step for i in range(num)] def sdfguidedsampling(o, d, tn, tf, sfield, Ns, Nr, delta, threshold=0.5): """ Perform SDF-guided sampling along a ray. Args: o: Ray origin (3D vector) d: Ray direction (3D vector, assumed normalized) tn: Near depth bound (float) tf: Far depth bound (float) sfield: Function that returns surface field value s(x) for point x Ns: Number of coarse sampling points Nr: Number of fine sampling points delta: Interval size for fine sampling around intersection threshold: Threshold for surface intersection detection (default 0.5) Returns: List of sample points (3D vectors) concentrated around the surface """ # Assumes standard vector addition and scalar multiplication # Step 1: Coarse uniform sampling tcoarse = linspace(tn, tf, Ns) pointscoarse = [o + t d for t in tcoarse] # Step 2: Find first intersection tint = None for i in range(Ns): ti = tcoarse[i] xi = pointscoarse[i] sval = sfield(xi) if sval >= threshold: tint = ti break if tint is None: return [] # Step 3: Fine-grained sampling around intersection tfine = linspace(tint - delta, tint + delta, Nr) pointsfine = [o + t d for t in tfine] return pointsfine Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Intersection: If the ray does not intersect the surface within [tn, tf] (i.e., no s(xi) \ge 0.5), the method yields no fine samples. Threshold Sensitivity: The threshold of 0.5 is specific to the DoubleField formulation. Other SDF representations might use 0.0 (zero-level set). The implementer must ensure the threshold matches the normalization of the provided SDF field. Discrete Sampling: The intersection detection relies on discrete coarse samples. If the surface is thin or the coarse sampling is too sparse, the intersection might be missed or inaccurately located. Time Complexity: Dominated by Ns queries to the SDF field for coarse sampling, plus Nr queries for fine sampling, totaling Ns + Nr field evaluations. Memory Complexity: Auxiliary memory scales linearly with the number of sample points, O(Ns + Nr), as it only stores the generated coordinates. Performance: Reported to be much faster than standard NeRF sampling due to fewer sampling points needed for integration. Strengths: Accelerates rendering by focusing samples on the surface; emphasizes the relationship between surface and radiance fields, facilitating training and fine-tuning. Limitations: Requires a well-defined SDF field; performance depends on the accuracy of the SDF; may fail if the surface is not well-represented by the SDF threshold. When to Use: When a high-quality SDF is available and rendering speed is a priority, particularly for human reconstruction and rendering where surface detail is critical. The method was proposed by Shao et al. in the context of the DoubleField network, which bridges neural surface and radiance fields for high-fidelity human reconstruction and rendering. It was introduced to accelerate the rendering process and strengthen the learned relationship between the surface and radiance fields. The approach is part of a broader trend of using implicit representations (SDFs) to guide sampling in neural rendering, as noted in recent surveys of learning-based 3D representations. Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26 DoubleField: Bridging the Neural Surface and Radiance Fields for High-fidelity Human Reconstruction and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01541, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Adaptive Binoctree Sampling
head: Adaptive fine voxel sampling, Sphere + coarse + fine voxel sampling
body: Adaptive Binoctree Sampling is a ray sampling strategy for optimizing neural implicit Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) from omnidirectional video. It solves the problem of inefficient surface localization in large unbounded scenes by replacing standard importance sampling with a hierarchical guide derived from a pre-built spherical binoctree. Unlike SDF-guided Sampling which may rely on generic distance estimates, this method uses coarse and fine sphoxels to conservatively bound the search space, offering superior accuracy over direct depth supervision methods like NeuS-facto-D. Inputs: Input depth maps from omnidirectional video. Camera poses and intrinsics. Neural SDF network. Outputs: Set of sample points along a ray for SDF evaluation. Data Structures: Spherical Binoctree: A hierarchical structure representing spherical space. Nodes are classified as "coarse" or "fine" based on subdivision criteria. Sphoxels: The leaf nodes or active regions of the binoctree, representing volumetric elements in spherical coordinates. Steps: 1. Pre-build Binoctree: Construct a spherical binoctree from the input depth maps to establish coarse spatial bounds for the scene. 2. Subdivision: Subdivide the spherical space based on solid angle measurement and distance from the camera. This creates a spatially variant tree depth, densifying samples near the surface. 3. Baseline Sampling: Initialize ray sampling using sphere sampling as a baseline. 4. Coarse Guidance: Sample points between coarse sphoxels rather than relying solely on sphere bounds. This guides the ray into the relevant geometric region. 5. Fine Sampling: Sample fine sphoxels to locate the surface precisely, replacing the standard importance sampling step. Parameters: Total samples per ray: 128 (kept constant for fairness in ablation studies). Importance sampling samples per step: 64 (in baseline comparisons). Pitfalls: If the initial depth map estimation for coarse voxels is incorrect, it leads to inaccurate guidance for coarse geometry and errors in background regions with nearer initial depths. Mitigation involves dilating and pruning voxels before optimization, but postprocessing may still be required to remove spurious artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivebinoctreesampling(rayorigin, raydirection, binoctree, depthmaps): # Step 1 & 2: Pre-build and Subdivide (Done offline) # binoctree is constructed from depthmaps and subdivided by solid angle/distance # Step 3: Baseline Sphere Sampling # Generate initial samples along the ray within sphere bounds spheresamples = generatespheresamples(rayorigin, raydirection, count=32) # Step 4: Coarse Voxel Sampling # Identify coarse sphoxels intersected by the ray coarsesphoxels = binoctree.getintersectedcoarsesphoxels(rayorigin, raydirection) # Sample more points between coarse sphoxels coarsesamples = [] for sphoxel in coarsesphoxels: # Sample within the bounds of the coarse sphoxel samples = samplesphoxel(sphoxel, count=32) coarsesamples.extend(samples) # Step 5: Fine Voxel Sampling # Identify fine sphoxels near the estimated surface finesphoxels = binoctree.getintersectedfinesphoxels(rayorigin, raydirection) finesamples = [] for sphoxel in finesphoxels: # Sample within the bounds of the fine sphoxel samples = samplesphoxel(sphoxel, count=32) finesamples.extend(samples) # Combine samples # Note: Total samples must be managed to equal 128 as per ablation settings allsamples = spheresamples + coarsesamples + finesamples # If total exceeds 128, subsample or adjust counts # If total is less, pad or adjust return allsamples[:128] Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the binoctree and the number of intersected sphoxels. Pre-building the tree is an offline cost. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of nodes in the binoctree. Performance: Yields more significant improvements in surface reconstruction accuracy compared to direct depth supervision (NeuS-facto-D). Strengths: Conservatively sets bounds upon depth, relying on other losses to optimize surface location, reducing inaccuracies from noisy depth inputs. Effective for small-baseline omnidirectional data. Limitations: Sensitive to initial depth map errors; concave region reconstruction may be challenging due to optimization landscape minima. Requires postprocessing to remove artifacts from incorrect coarse voxel initialization. Adaptive Binoctree Sampling was introduced in the OmniSDF paper (2024) for scene reconstruction using omnidirectional signed distance functions. It addresses the challenges of optimizing neural implicit representations for large unbounded scenes from omnidirectional video. name: Bidirectional Projective Sampling
head: Bidirectional projection, Projective sampling with emitter-emitted seed rays
body: Bidirectional Projective Sampling is a boundary sampling method for physics-based differentiable rendering that generates seed rays from both sensors and emitters to initialize a guiding structure, addressing inefficiencies when scenes contain small-area lights at a distance. It improves upon Zhang et al.'s projective sampling by incorporating rays emitted directly from small-area emitters into the seed ray set during the projection operation, ensuring all successfully projected rays contribute to the guiding structure regardless of emitter size. Unlike previous methods that rely solely on sensor-spawned rays, which have a near-zero probability of intersecting small-area emitters, this method guarantees intersection by explicitly sampling from the emitter, thereby maximizing contribution to the boundary integral. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry (triangular meshes), emitter definitions (triangular meshes with intensity/distance properties), sensor/camera parameters, differentiating geometry (the shape being optimized or differentiated), and a target number of seed rays N. Outputs: An initialized guiding structure containing contributions to the boundary integral, ready for importance sampling. Data Structures: Guiding Structure: A data structure storing accumulated contributions from projected rays to support importance sampling of path segments. Seed Rays: Defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, and source type ('sensor' or 'emitter'). Origins remain fixed during projection; directions are determined by the projection result. Formulas: The method estimates the local formulation of the boundary integral derivative: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int{\partial \mathcal{A}} \int{S^2} Li(\mathbf{x}b, \boldsymbol{\omega}) Wi(\mathbf{x}b, \boldsymbol{\omega}) \sin \phi \left(\frac{\partial \pi \mathbf{x}b}{\partial \pi} \cdot \mathbf{n}b\right) d\boldsymbol{\omega} dl(\mathbf{x}b) + \int{\mathcal{A}} \int{S^1} Li(\mathbf{x}b, \phi) Wi(\mathbf{x}b, \phi) \kappa(\phi) \left(\frac{\partial \pi \mathbf{x}b}{\partial \pi} \cdot \mathbf{n}b\right) d\phi dA(\mathbf{x}b) Where: \pi: Geometric parameters being differentiated. \mathcal{A}: The differentiating geometry surface. \partial \mathcal{A}: The boundary of the differentiating geometry. \mathbf{x}b: A point on the boundary. \boldsymbol{\omega}: Direction in S^2. Li: Incident radiance. Wi: Weight function. \phi: Angle. \mathbf{n}b: Normal at \mathbf{x}b. \kappa(\phi): Curvature-related term. Parameters: Ray Split Ratio: 30% of seed rays are emitted by emitters, 70% are spawned from the sensor. Inverse Rendering Remeshing Interval: Geometry is intermittently remeshed every 20 iterations. Inverse Rendering Sample Doubling Interval: The number of samples per pixel is doubled every 200 iterations. Numbered Steps: 1. Assign Rays to Emitters: Determine the number of rays each emitter must generate based on its intensity and distance from the differentiating shape. Closer and stronger emitters receive more rays. 2. Sample Emitter Points: For each emitter ray, sample a triangle on the emitter proportional to its area, then uniformly sample a point within that triangle to serve as the starting point (origin) for the seed ray. 3. Sample Geometry Points: Determine the endpoint of the seed ray by selecting a triangle on the shape being differentiated based on its area and uniformly sampling a point within that triangle. 4. Generate Emitter Rays: Create seed rays connecting the sampled emitter point to the sampled geometry point. 5. Generate Sensor Rays: Generate seed rays from the sensor side. These rays must directly hit the background plane without intersecting any other geometries as the first ray segment. 6. Combine Rays: Combine the emitter-emitted rays and sensor-spawned rays. Use the specified split ratio (30% emitter, 70% sensor). 7. Reflect Sensor Rays: For sensor rays that hit the background plane, reflect them. These reflected rays affect the geometry being differentiated as the second ray segment. 8. Project Rays: Project the adjusted seed rays onto the geometric boundaries. Use JUMP and WALK strategies for triangular meshes to ensure tangency. Origins remain fixed; directions are determined by the projection results. Filter contributions: Only projected rays that intersect the scene emitter (small-area light) are kept to contribute to the guiding structure. For emitter-emitted rays, all successfully projected rays contribute. 9. Initialize Guiding Structure: Compute the locations of the projected rays within the guiding structure and evaluate their contributions using the integrand in eq. (7) to initialize the guiding structure. 10. Importance Sampling: Perform importance sampling of path segments from the initialized guiding structure, complete the segments into full paths, and evaluate their contributions to the boundary integral. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Parameterization Artifacts: Current state-of-the-art boundary sampling methods parameterize the 3D boundary sample space with the first dimension representing mesh edges and the remaining two dimensions representing unit directions. This 1D edge parameterization breaks the continuous connectivity of silhouette edges, causing sparse and high-frequency features in the guiding structure despite the underlying sample space being intrinsically smooth. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction, source): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.source = source # 'sensor' or 'emitter' def bidirectionalprojectivesampling(sceneemitters, differentiatinggeometry, camera, numseedrays): # Step 1: Assign rays to emitters based on intensity and distance emitterweights = {} totalweight = 0.0 for emitter in sceneemitters: dist = min(math.sqrt(sum((emitter.center[i] - v[i])2 for i in range(3))) for v in differentiatinggeometry.vertices) weight = emitter.intensity / (dist dist) emitterweights[emitter] = weight totalweight += weight targetemitterrays = int(numseedrays 0.3) emitterassignments = {} remaining = targetemitterrays for emitter, weight in emitterweights.items(): count = int(targetemitterrays (weight / totalweight)) emitterassignments[emitter] = count remaining -= count for i, emitter in enumerate(emitterweights.keys()): if remaining > 0: emitterassignments[emitter] += 1 remaining -= 1 emitterrays = [] # Steps 2, 3, 4: Generate emitter-emitted seed rays for emitter, count in emitterassignments.items(): for in range(count): emittertriangle = sampletrianglebyarea(emitter.triangles) origin = uniformsampletriangle(emittertriangle) geotriangle = sampletrianglebyarea(differentiatinggeometry.triangles) endpoint = uniformsampletriangle(geotriangle) direction = normalize(endpoint - origin) emitterrays.append(Ray(origin, direction, 'emitter')) # Step 5: Generate sensor-spawned seed rays sensorraycount = int(numseedrays 0.7) sensorrays = [] for in range(sensorraycount): ray = generateprimaryrayfromcamera(camera) if ray.intersectsbackgroundplane() and not ray.intersectsgeometry(differentiatinggeometry): sensorrays.append(ray) # Step 6: Combine rays allseedrays = emitterrays + sensorrays # Step 7: Reflect sensor rays that hit background for i, ray in enumerate(allseedrays): if ray.source == 'sensor' and ray.intersectsbackgroundplane(): allseedrays[i] = reflectray(ray, backgroundplane) # Step 8: Project rays onto geometric boundaries guidingstructure = {} for ray in allseedrays: # Project using JUMP and WALK strategies for tangency projectedray = projectrayontoboundary(ray, differentiatinggeometry) # Filter contributions: Only projected rays that intersect the scene emitter are kept # For emitter-emitted rays, all successfully projected rays contribute if ray.source == 'emitter' or projectedray.intersectsemitter(sceneemitters): # Step 9: Compute location and evaluate contribution contribution = evaluateboundaryintegralcontribution(projectedray, differentiatinggeometry) guidingstructure[projectedray.location] = contribution # Step 10: Importance sampling is performed later using the structure return guidingstructure def sampletrianglebyarea(triangles): areas = [computetrianglearea(t) for t in triangles] totalarea = sum(areas) r = random.uniform(0, totalarea) cumulative = 0.0 for t, area in zip(triangles, areas): cumulative += area if r <= cumulative: return t return triangles[-1] def uniformsampletriangle(triangle): u, v = random.uniform(0, 1), random.uniform(0, 1) if u + v > 1: u = 1 - u v = 1 - v return triangle.v0 + u (triangle.v1 - triangle.v0) + v (triangle.v2 - triangle.v0) def computetrianglearea(triangle): return 0.5 length(cross(triangle.v1 - triangle.v0, triangle.v2 - triangle.v0)) def projectrayontoboundary(ray, geometry): # JUMP and WALK strategies for triangular meshes to ensure tangency # Source does not specify implementation details. pass def evaluateboundaryintegralcontribution(projectedray, geometry): # Evaluates contribution using the integrand from the boundary integral formula # Source does not specify implementation details. pass def generateprimaryrayfromcamera(camera): # Standard camera ray generation pass def reflectray(ray, plane): # Standard reflection calculation pass def normalize(v): return [x / math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) for x in v] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def length(v): return math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method achieves lower variance gradients in the forward differentiable rendering process and better geometry reconstruction quality in the inverse-rendering results compared to state-of-the-art projective-sampling-based methods. Hardware: Experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 graphics card. Intersection Queries: Performed using OptiX. Scaling: The number of samples per pixel is doubled every 200 iterations during optimization. Strengths: Improves efficiency in scenes with small-area emitters (e.g., mobile phone flashlights) by ensuring rays intersect the emitter, which previous methods struggled with. Limitations: The underlying guiding structures for triangle meshes can still suffer from sparse and high-frequency features due to the 1D edge parameterization of the boundary sample space. When to Use: Use for differentiable rendering of geometry with small-area lights to improve guiding structure quality for importance sampling. When Not to Use: Not explicitly stated, but less beneficial for scenes with large-area emitters where sensor rays are sufficient. Origin: The method was proposed as an augmentation of previous projective-sampling-based boundary-sampling methods, specifically improving upon Zhang et al.'s method. History: It was developed to address the inefficiency of previous methods in scenes with small-area emitters, where the probability of sensor-spawned rays intersecting the emitter approaches zero as the emitter size approaches a point light. Usage: Implemented on the cudaadrgb backend from Mitsuba 3 using the Dr. Jit framework for forward/reverse-mode AD and GPU kernel compilation. name: Explicit Sampling for Point Cloud Extraction
head: PC extraction from DDF, SI3DR evaluation sampling
body: Explicit Sampling is a method to extract a point cloud (PC) from a Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) or Directed Distance Field (DDF) by projecting uniformly sampled points from a bounding box onto the shape surface S. It solves the problem of converting implicit field representations into explicit geometric primitives for evaluation metrics like Chamfer distance. Unlike its siblings, it relies on a simple shoot-and-cast strategy using weighted direction composition to find valid surface intersections, without guaranteeing uniform sampling density over the shape. Inputs: A PDDF or DDF representation providing depth d(p, v) and visibility \xi(p, v) for any point p and direction v. A bounding box B enclosing the shape. Parameters: nv (number of directions per point, typically 128) and NH (number of refinement iterations, typically 3). Outputs: A set of 3D points representing the surface S. Data Structures: Point p \in \mathbb{R}^3: Current sample position. Direction v \in \mathbb{R}^3: Unit vector on the sphere S^2. Set V(p) = \{vi(p)\}{i=1}^{nv}: Collection of sampled directions. Weighted direction v^b(p) \in \mathbb{R}^3: The composed best direction. Steps: 1. Initial Sampling: Sample a point p uniformly from the bounding box B: p \sim U[B]. 2. Direction Sampling: For the current point p, sample nv directions uniformly from the unit sphere S^2: V(p) = \{vi(p) \mid vi(p) \sim U[S^2], i=1 \dots nv\}. 3. Direction Composition: Estimate the best direction v^b(p) that avoids occlusion (\xi(p, v) = 0) by computing a weighted average over the sampled directions V(p). The sources specify a weighted average but do not provide the exact weighting formula. Note that arbitrary directions may not be visible (\xi(p, v) \neq 1), and at certain positions, multiple valid values of v^ may exist. 4. Surface Projection: Compute the projected point q on the shape using the estimated direction and the field's depth: q(p, v^b(p)) = p + d(p, v^b(p)) \cdot v^b(p) The condition for q being on S is \xi(p, v^b(p)) = 1. 5. Refinement (Optional): If depths are less accurate far from the shape, repeat the process NH times, updating the starting point p \leftarrow q for each iteration. 6. Collection: Add q to the point cloud and repeat steps 1-5 for the desired number of points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def extractpointcloud(pddf, boundingbox, nv=128, nh=3, numinitialsamples=10000): """ Extracts a point cloud from a PDDF/DDF using explicit sampling. Args: pddf: Object providing query(p, v) -> (depth, visibility) boundingbox: Bounding box for uniform sampling nv: Number of directions to sample per point nh: Number of refinement iterations numinitialsamples: Total number of points to generate Returns: list of points on the surface """ points = [] for in range(numinitialsamples): # Step 1: Sample initial point p = sampleuniform(boundingbox) currentp = p for h in range(nh): # Step 2: Sample directions directions = [sampleuniformsphere() for in range(nv)] # Step 3: Compose directions to find best vb weightedsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] weighttotal = 0.0 for v in directions: depth, visibility = pddf.query(currentp, v) # Guard: skip invisible directions if visibility <= 0: continue # Simple visibility weighting. Exact formula not provided in sources. w = visibility weightedsum[0] += w v[0] weightedsum[1] += w v[1] weightedsum[2] += w v[2] weighttotal += w if weighttotal == 0: # No visible directions found; skip this sample break # Normalize to get unit vector vb vstar = normalize(weightedsum) # Step 4: Project to surface depth, = pddf.query(currentp, vstar) # Guard: invalid depth if depth is None or depth < 0: break q = currentp[0] + depth vstar[0], currentp[1] + depth vstar[1], currentp[2] + depth vstar[2] # Step 5: Update for next iteration currentp = q # Step 6: Collection points.append(currentp) return points def sampleuniform(box): """Returns a random point uniformly distributed in box [min, max].""" return [random.uniform(box.min[i], box.max[i]) for i in range(3)] def sampleuniformsphere(): """Returns a random unit vector uniformly distributed on S^2.""" u = random.random() v = random.random() theta = 2 math.pi u phi = math.acos(2 v - 1) x = math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = math.cos(phi) return [x, y, z] def normalize(v): """Returns the unit vector in the direction of v.""" mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if mag == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] Parameters: nv: Number of directions sampled per point. Typical value: 128. NH: Number of refinement iterations. Typical value: 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-uniformity: The method does not guarantee uniform sampling over the shape S. Visibility: Arbitrary directions v may not be visible (\xi(p, v) \neq 1), necessitating the composition technique. Ambiguity: At certain positions, there may be multiple valid values of v^. Depth Accuracy: Depths are less accurate far from the shape, which is why refinement (NH > 1) is recommended. It shares the same pitfalls: no guarantee of uniform sampling, visibility issues requiring weighted averages, and potential ambiguity in v^. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; works with generic DDF/PDDF representations; refinement improves accuracy for points far from the surface. Limitations: Does not guarantee uniform sampling; sensitive to visibility estimation errors; multiple valid directions can cause ambiguity. name: Multi-view Feature Consistency via Linear Interpolation
head: differentiable surface point extraction
body: This method extracts a differentiable surface point from volume rendering samples by linearly interpolating SDF zero-crossings, enabling the enforcement of multi-view feature consistency constraints. It differs from sibling methods by relying on the hierarchical sampling density near the surface to approximate the zero-crossing with a single secant step, rather than recursive root-finding or mesh-based parameterization. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Hierarchical sampling points \mathbf{x}(ti) = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d} for i=1, \dots, N, where ti are the sampled distances. SDF values f(\mathbf{x}(ti)) computed by the geometry network at each sample point. Reference pixel \mathbf{p}0 and its associated feature \mathbf{F}0(\mathbf{p}0) from a pre-trained CNN. Camera parameters \{\mathbf{K}i, \mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{t}i\} for Nv neighboring source views. Outputs: Extracted surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}}. Multi-view feature consistency loss \mathcal{L}{feat.}. Data Structures: Array of distances t of size N. Array of SDF values f of size N. Array of 3D points \mathbf{x} of size N (implicitly defined by t). Steps: 1. Search for sign change: Find the first index s such that the SDF value is positive at ts and negative at t{s+1}. s = \arg \mini \{ ti \mid f(\mathbf{x}(ti)) > 0 \text{ and } f(\mathbf{x}(t{i+1})) < 0 \} If no such s exists (no sign change in the sampled range), skip constraints for this ray. 2. Linear Interpolation: Approximate the zero-crossing parameter \hat{t} using linear interpolation between ts and t{s+1}: \hat{t} = \frac{f(\mathbf{x}(ts))t{s+1} - f(\mathbf{x}(t{s+1}))ts}{f(\mathbf{x}(ts)) - f(\mathbf{x}(t{s+1}))} Compute the surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}(\hat{t}). 3. Feature Consistency Loss: Compute the loss by comparing the reference feature with features from neighboring views projected to the extracted surface point: \mathcal{L}{feat.} = \frac{1}{Nc Nv} \sum{i=1}^{Nv} |\mathbf{F}0(\mathbf{p}0) - \mathbf{F}i(\mathbf{K}i(\mathbf{R}i\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{t}i))| where Nc is the number of feature channels, \mathbf{F}i is the feature map from view i, and \mathbf{K}i, \mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{t}i are the intrinsic, rotation, and translation parameters of view i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractsurfacepointandloss(t, f, x, p0, F0, cameraparams, Fextractor): """ t: array of shape (N,), distances along ray f: array of shape (N,), SDF values at t x: array of shape (N, 3), 3D points at t p0: reference pixel coordinates F0: reference feature vector cameraparams: list of dicts with keys 'K', 'R', 't' for Nv views Fextractor: function to extract features from image and pixel """ N = len(t) s = -1 # Step 1: Find first sign change from positive to negative for i in range(N - 1): if f[i] > 0 and f[i+1] < 0: s = i break if s == -1: # No sign change found, skip constraints return None, 0.0 # Step 2: Linear interpolation for zero-crossing fs = f[s] fs1 = f[s+1] ts = t[s] ts1 = t[s+1] # Avoid division by zero if SDF values are identical (unlikely with sign change) denom = fs - fs1 if abs(denom) < 1e-8: # Fallback to midpoint if denominator is near zero that = (ts + ts1) / 2.0 else: that = (fs ts1 - fs1 ts) / denom xhat = x[s] + (x[s+1] - x[s]) ((that - ts) / (ts1 - ts)) # Step 3: Compute multi-view feature consistency loss loss = 0.0 Nv = len(cameraparams) Nc = len(F0) # Assuming feature vector length for i, cam in enumerate(cameraparams): # Project surface point to view i # Xworld = Ri xhat + ti Xworld = cam['R'] @ xhat + cam['t'] Xcam = cam['K'] @ Xworld # Normalize to get pixel coordinates (assuming homogeneous division) u = Xcam[0] / Xcam[2] v = Xcam[1] / Xcam[2] # Extract feature from view i at projected pixel # Note: Fextractor should handle boundary checks Fi = Fextractor(imagei, (u, v)) # Compute L1 difference diff = abs(F0 - Fi) loss += sum(diff) loss = loss / (Nc Nv) return xhat, loss Parameters: N: Number of hierarchical samples. Typical values depend on the scene scale and desired precision; hierarchical sampling concentrates points near the surface. \alpha, \beta: Weights for other loss terms (eikonal, color) in the total loss function. Not given in the sources for this specific method's internal parameters. Edge Cases: No sign change: If the ray does not intersect the surface within the sampled range, or if the SDF does not change sign between consecutive samples, the constraints are skipped for that ray. Degenerate interpolation: If f(\mathbf{x}(ts)) \approx f(\mathbf{x}(t{s+1})), the denominator in the interpolation formula approaches zero. A fallback to the midpoint is recommended. Precision: The accuracy depends on the density of samples near the surface. Hierarchical sampling helps mitigate this by placing more samples near the expected surface location. Focuses on sampling strategies near the surface without explicit feature consistency. Uses mesh-based parameterization for feature consistency. Uses bidirectional projection for feature consistency. Time Complexity: O(N) for finding the sign change and O(Nv) for computing the feature loss, where N is the number of samples per ray and Nv is the number of neighboring views. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sample points and SDF values. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradient-based optimization. Leverages existing hierarchical sampling for efficiency. Limitations: Accuracy depends on sample density. May fail if the surface is not well-sampled. When to use: When multi-view feature consistency is required for neural implicit surface reconstruction. When not to use: When high precision is needed without sufficient sampling, or when computational resources are extremely limited. This method was introduced in "Recovering Fine Details for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction" (WACV 2023) by Chen et al.. It builds on the idea of using SDF values for surface extraction, contrasting with IDR's recursive secant method by using a single interpolation step enabled by hierarchical sampling. name: NeuS Sampler
head: Fixed Variance SDF Sampling, NeuS SDF Sampling
body: The NeuS Sampler is an iterative importance sampling method for Neural Surface Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) that refines sample distributions along rays by merging new high-probability points with existing ones. It distinguishes itself from static sampling strategies by dynamically adjusting the "softness" of the SDF-to-alpha conversion via a fixed variance parameter that scales exponentially with iteration count, ensuring robust convergence near the surface. Inputs and Outputs Input: raysamples (initial uniform samples along rays), sdffn (neural SDF network), numupsamplesteps (integer), numsamplesimportance (integer), basevariance (float). Output: Refined raysamples containing merged uniform and importance samples, sorted by distance. Data Structures raysamples: A structure containing sample positions and distances. Specifically, raysamples.deltas is a tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples-1, 1) representing the distance between adjacent sample points. sdf: Tensor of SDF values evaluated at sample points. weights: Tensor of rendering weights derived from alphas. sortedindex: Indices used to maintain spatial order when merging old and new samples. Parameters numsamples: Number of initial uniform samples. Default: 64. numsamplesimportance: Number of importance samples to draw per upsample step. numupsamplesteps: Number of iterative upsampling steps. Default: 4. basevariance: Base value for the inverse softness parameter invs. Default: 64. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Set totaliters = 0. Initialize sortedindex = None, sdf = None. Set newsamples to the initial raysamples. 2. Iteration Loop: While totaliters < numupsamplesteps: a. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF network on newsamples using sdffn in a no-gradient context (torch.nograd()). b. Merge SDF Values: If sortedindex is not None, concatenate the existing sdf and the newly computed newsdf, then gather using sortedindex to maintain order. Otherwise, set sdf = newsdf. c. Compute Alphas: Calculate rendering alphas using the fixed variance method. The inverse softness parameter is computed as invs = basevariance 2^{totaliters}. Pass raysamples, the reshaped sdf tensor, and invs to the alpha computation function. d. Compute Weights: Calculate weights from the alphas. Concatenate a zero tensor of shape (..., 1) to the end of the weights tensor along dimension 1. e. Draw Importance Samples: Use a PDF sampler to draw numsamplesimportance // numupsamplesteps new importance samples based on the current weights. f. Merge Ray Samples: Merge the current raysamples with the newly drawn newsamples using a merge function. This function returns the updated raysamples and the sortedindex required for the next SDF merging step. g. Increment: Increment totaliters by 1. 3. Return: The final merged raysamples. Alpha Computation Details The core of the sampling lies in converting SDF values to alpha values robustly. Given SDF values at sample points, the algorithm estimates the derivative (cosine) of the SDF to determine the probability of intersection: 1. Compute the cosine of the angle between adjacent SDF values: cos\val = \frac{next\sdf - prev\sdf}{deltas + 10^{-5}} where deltas are the distances between samples. 2. Estimate the previous cosine value by shifting the current cosine array: prev\cos\val = [0, cos\val[:,:-1]] concatenated along the last dimension. 3. Compute the robust cosine by taking the element-wise minimum of the forward and backward estimates, then clipping to [-1e3, 0.0]: cos\val = \min(prev\cos\val, cos\val) cos\val = \text{clip}(cos\val, -1000, 0.0) This step makes sampling robust against non-monotonic SDFs or noise. 4. Estimate the SDF at the midpoints between samples: prev\esti\sdf = mid\sdf - cos\val \times dist \times 0.5 next\esti\sdf = mid\sdf + cos\val \times dist \times 0.5 where dist is the distance between samples. 5. Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) values using the sigmoid function with the current invs: prev\cdf = \sigma(prev\esti\sdf \times inv\s) next\cdf = \sigma(next\esti\sdf \times inv\s) 6. Compute the alpha value: alpha = \frac{prev\cdf - next\cdf + 10^{-5}}{prev\cdf + 10^{-5}}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def neussampler(raysamples, sdffn, numupsamplesteps=4, numsamplesimportance=64, basevariance=64.0): """ Iteratively upsample ray samples using NeuS fixed variance SDF sampling. Args: raysamples: Initial ray samples structure containing positions and deltas. sdffn: Neural SDF function. numupsamplesteps: Number of upsampling iterations. numsamplesimportance: Total importance samples to draw across all steps. basevariance: Base inverse softness parameter. Returns: Refined raysamples. """ totaliters = 0 sortedindex = None sdf = None newsamples = raysamples # Pre-calculate number of importance samples per step numsamplesperstep = numsamplesimportance // numupsamplesteps while totaliters < numupsamplesteps: # 1. Evaluate SDF on new samples with torch.nograd(): newsdf = sdffn(newsamples) # 2. Merge SDF values if sortedindex is not None: # Concatenate old and new SDFs allsdf = torch.cat([sdf, newsdf], dim=-1) # Gather to maintain order sdf = torch.gather(allsdf, -1, sortedindex) else: sdf = newsdf # 3. Compute alphas using fixed variance invs = basevariance (2 totaliters) # Extract deltas from raysamples # Assuming raysamples.deltas has shape (numrays, numsamples-1, 1) deltas = raysamples.deltas[..., 0] # Shape: (numrays, numsamples-1) # Compute cosval # nextsdf and prevsdf are derived from sdf tensor # sdf shape: (numrays, numsamples) prevsdf = sdf[...,:-1] nextsdf = sdf[..., 1:] cosval = (nextsdf - prevsdf) / (deltas + 1e-5) # Compute prevcosval zeros = torch.zeroslike(cosval[...,:1]) prevcosval = torch.cat([zeros, cosval[...,:-1]], dim=-1) # Robust cosine estimation cosvalstack = torch.stack([prevcosval, cosval], dim=-1) cosval, = torch.min(cosvalstack, dim=-1) cosval = torch.clamp(cosval, min=-1e3, max=0.0) # Estimate midpoints # midsdf is the average of prev and next sdf midsdf = (prevsdf + nextsdf) / 2.0 # dist is the delta distance dist = deltas prevestisdf = midsdf - cosval dist 0.5 nextestisdf = midsdf + cosval dist 0.5 # Compute CDFs prevcdf = torch.sigmoid(prevestisdf invs) nextcdf = torch.sigmoid(nextestisdf invs) # Compute alphas alpha = (prevcdf - nextcdf + 1e-5) / (prevcdf + 1e-5) # 4. Compute weights # Alpha is probability of intersection in the interval. # Weight is typically product of (1-alpha) up to that interval. trans = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-5, dim=-1) weights = alpha torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[...,:1]), trans[...,:-1]], dim=-1) # Concatenate zero tensor to weights along dim=1 weights = torch.cat([weights, torch.zeroslike(weights[...,:1])], dim=-1) # 5. Draw new importance samples newsamples = drawimportancesamples(raysamples, weights, numsamplesperstep) # 6. Merge ray samples raysamples, sortedindex = mergeraysamples(raysamples, newsamples) # 7. Increment totaliters += 1 return raysamples def drawimportancesamples(raysamples, weights, numsamples): """ Helper function to draw importance samples. Implementation detail: """ # Normalize weights to form a PDF pdf = weights / (weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-5) cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) # Add boundary conditions cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Draw uniform random numbers u = torch.randlike(cdf) # Inverse CDF sampling indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') # Interpolate positions based on indices # Standard linear interpolation between sample positions pos = raysamples.positions idx = indices.clamp(0, pos.shape[-1] - 2) idxnext = idx + 1 t = (u - cdf[..., idx]) / (cdf[..., idxnext] - cdf[..., idx] + 1e-5) t = t.clamp(0.0, 1.0) newpos = pos[..., idx] + t (pos[..., idxnext] - pos[..., idx]) return raysamples.copywithpositions(newpos) def mergeraysamples(oldsamples, newsamples): """ Helper function to merge and sort ray samples. Implementation detail: """ # Concatenate positions allpositions = torch.cat([oldsamples.positions, newsamples.positions], dim=-1) # Sort positions and get indices sortedpositions, sortedindices = torch.sort(allpositions, dim=-1) # Reconstruct raysamples structure from sortedpositions mergedsamples = oldsamples.copy() mergedsamples.positions = sortedpositions return mergedsamples, sortedindices Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. The method requires multiple forward passes through the SDF network per ray. It is ideal for neural surface reconstruction where the SDF is learned and may exhibit noise or non-ideal properties near the surface. The NeuS Sampler was introduced in the context of Neural Surface SDFs, specifically within the Nerfstudio framework. It builds upon the NeuS (Neural Surface SDF) method, which uses a neural network to represent a signed distance function for implicit surface reconstruction. The method addresses the challenge of efficiently sampling along rays to render high-quality images from noisy or imperfect SDFs. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Relaxed Boundary Integral Method
head: Differentiable SDF Rendering via Boundary Relaxation
body:
The Relaxed Boundary Integral Method computes the gradient of rendered images with respect to scene parameters by approximating the boundary integral term in the differentiable rendering equation. It solves the problem of accurately estimating derivatives for rays that graze the surface (silhouette rays), where standard ray marching fails due to discontinuous visibility changes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by relaxing the strict surface intersection condition (SDF=0) to a band (0 < SDF < \epsilon), yielding more uniform samples around the silhouette compared to relaxing the directional derivative condition, which produces tangential intersections sensitive to curvature. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction  oldsymbol{\omega}, Signed Distance Field (SDF) function S(\mathbf{x}), SDF threshold \epsilon, maximum ray depth. Outputs: Radiance contribution L, gradient of radiance w.r.t. scene parameters  rac{\partial L}{\partial 	heta}. Data Structures: Ray State: \mathbf{x} (current position, \mathbb{R}^3), t (distance along ray, float), S{val} (SDF value at \mathbf{x}, float), S'{val} (directional derivative at \mathbf{x}, float). Boundary Normal: \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}) =  rac{
abla S(\mathbf{x})}{\|
abla S(\mathbf{x})\|} (outward-pointing unit normal). Scalar Normal Velocity: v\perp(\mathbf{x}) = \langle \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}) angle, where \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) =  rac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial 	heta} is the velocity of the point with respect to the parameter 	heta. Parameters: \epsilon: SDF threshold defining the width of the relaxed boundary band. Typical value: 0.002. N{iter}: Number of bisection iterations. Typical value: 12. Steps: 1. Sphere Tracing with Derivative Tracking: Perform sphere tracing along the ray. At each step i, compute S(\mathbf{x}i) and the directional derivative S'(\mathbf{x}i) = \langle 
abla S(\mathbf{x}i),  oldsymbol{\omega} angle. 2. Local Minimum Detection: Check if the directional derivative changes sign from negative to positive between step i-1 and i (S'{i-1} < 0 and S'i > 0). This indicates a local minimum of the SDF along the ray has been passed. 3. Initial Guess Selection: Among all steps where a local minimum was detected, select the step with the smallest SDF value S(\mathbf{x}i) as the initial guess \mathbf{x}{init} for the relaxed silhouette point. 4. Refinement via Bisection: Refine \mathbf{x}{init} to find the relaxed silhouette point \mathbf{x}^ such that S(\mathbf{x}^) = \epsilon (or the specific boundary condition defined by the relaxation). Use the bisection method for N{iter} iterations. The bisection interval is defined by the previous step (where S < \epsilon) and the current step (where S > \epsilon or vice versa, depending on the specific relaxation logic, but typically targeting the band 0 < S < \epsilon). 5. Boundary Integral Approximation: If a valid relaxed silhouette point \mathbf{x}^ exists on the ray segment, compute the boundary term contribution. The approximation is given by: IA =  rac{1}{\epsilon} \int{S^2} v\perp(\mathbf{x}^) \Delta f( oldsymbol{\omega}) \mathbb{1}A( oldsymbol{\omega}) d\sigma( oldsymbol{\omega}) where \Delta f( oldsymbol{\omega}) is the change in radiance and \mathbb{1}A is an indicator function for the area of interest. In practice, this is evaluated analytically after sphere tracing for the ray intersection process, while the interior integral is estimated using automatic differentiation. 6. Gradient Estimation: Add the boundary term to the gradient estimate if \mathbf{x}^ exists. For shadow rays, only one side of the visibility boundary is occluded, so the shading evaluation at \mathbf{x}^ is not required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def relaxedboundaryintegral(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, gradsdffunc, theta, epsilon=0.002, maxsteps=128, bisectioniters=12): """ Computes the boundary integral contribution for a ray using the Relaxed Boundary Integral Method. Args: rayorigin: (3,) float array, origin of the ray. raydirection: (3,) float array, normalized direction of the ray. sdffunc: function(x) -> float, returns SDF value at x. gradsdffunc: function(x) -> (3,) float array, returns gradient of SDF at x. theta: scalar, scene parameter to differentiate w.r.t. epsilon: float, SDF threshold for relaxation. maxsteps: int, maximum number of sphere tracing steps. bisectioniters: int, number of bisection iterations for refinement. Returns: boundaryterm: float, the computed boundary integral contribution. xstar: (3,) float array or None, the relaxed silhouette point. """ x = rayorigin t = 0.0 prevsdfprime = None bestxinit = None bestsdfval = float('inf') # Step 1 & 2: Sphere tracing with derivative tracking for i in range(maxsteps): sdfval = sdffunc(x) grad = gradsdffunc(x) sdfprime = dot(grad, raydirection) # Check for local minimum (derivative changes from negative to positive) if prevsdfprime is not None and prevsdfprime < 0 and sdfprime > 0: # We passed a local minimum. Check if it's within the relaxed band. # The sources indicate selecting the step with the smallest SDF value # among those where a minimum was detected. if sdfval < bestsdfval: bestsdfval = sdfval bestxinit = x # Move along the ray stepsize = max(sdfval, 1e-4) # Avoid zero division t += stepsize x = rayorigin + t raydirection prevsdfprime = sdfprime if sdfval < 1e-4: # Standard intersection, handle separately or break break # Step 3 & 4: Refine the relaxed silhouette point xstar = None if bestxinit is not None: # Bisection method to find x such that SDF(x) = epsilon (or within band) # The interval is roughly around bestxinit. # We need a lower bound where SDF < epsilon and upper bound where SDF > epsilon. # For simplicity, assume bestxinit is close. We refine based on the condition 0 < SDF < epsilon. # The source says "pinpoint the relaxed silhouette point" using bisection for 12 iterations. # We assume the bisection is performed on the distance t along the ray. tlow = t - stepsize thigh = t sdflow = sdffunc(rayorigin + tlow raydirection) sdfhigh = sdffunc(rayorigin + thigh raydirection) # Ensure the interval brackets the target value epsilon # Note: The source implies relaxing SDF condition to 0 < SDF < epsilon. # We target SDF(x) = epsilon for the boundary of the band. for in range(bisectioniters): tmid = (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 xmid = rayorigin + tmid raydirection sdfmid = sdffunc(xmid) if sdfmid > epsilon: thigh = tmid sdfhigh = sdfmid else: tlow = tmid sdflow = sdfmid xstar = rayorigin + ((tlow + thigh) / 2.0) raydirection # Step 5: Compute boundary term boundaryterm = 0.0 if xstar is not None: # Compute normal velocity vperp gradstar = gradsdffunc(xstar) nstar = gradstar / norm(gradstar) # v(x) is the derivative of x w.r.t theta. # If x depends on theta, v = dx/dtheta. # In many differentiable rendering contexts, this is computed via auto-diff. # Here we assume vtheta is available or computed. # For a translation parameter theta in x-direction, v = (1, 0, 0). # This is a placeholder for the actual velocity computation which depends on the scene graph. vtheta = computevelocity(xstar, theta) # Helper to get dx/dtheta vperp = dot(vtheta, nstar) # The integral approximation involves vperp and the change in radiance. # The source formula: IA = (1/epsilon) integral... # In implementation, this is often a discrete term added to the gradient. # We assume deltaf is the radiance difference or visibility change. # For a simple visibility boundary, deltaf might be the radiance of the occluded side. # This part requires context from the specific renderer's radiance calculation. # The source states: "adds a boundary term if a relaxed silhouette point y exists". # Placeholder for the actual boundary term calculation logic which depends on # the specific radiance estimator (e.g., direct lighting vs path tracing). # The source mentions "estimate the interior integral... using automatic differentiation # except for the ray intersection process, whose derivatives are computed analytically". # So the boundary term is the analytical derivative of the intersection. boundaryterm = vperp # Simplified representation of the boundary term contribution return boundaryterm, xstar Subtopics: Near-Surface Point Sampling: Samples points near the surface without relying on SDF gradients. Choose when SDF is unavailable or noisy. Surfel Parameterization from Mesh Sampling: Uses mesh geometry for sampling. Choose for explicit mesh representations. SDF-guided Sampling: Uses SDF values to guide sampling density. Choose for adaptive sampling strategies. Bidirectional Projective Sampling: Samples from both camera and light. Choose for complex lighting scenarios. Explicit Sampling for Point Cloud Extraction: Extracts points directly from SDF. Choose for point cloud generation. Multi-view Feature Consistency via Linear Interpolation: Ensures consistency across views. Choose for multi-view reconstruction. NeuS Sampler: Specific sampler for NeuS networks. Choose when using NeuS. Time Complexity: Dominated by sphere tracing and the bisection refinement. The bisection adds a constant overhead (12 iterations) per ray that grazes the surface. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring only storage for the ray state and a few temporary variables. Measured Performance: Achieves higher PSNR than SDF Convolution, SDF Reparameterization, and Mesh Projective Sampling under different area light sizes, using a 512x512 resolution and 1024 spp direct integrator on an NVIDIA RTX 3090. Strengths: More uniform samples around the silhouette compared to relaxing the directional derivative condition. Less sensitive to curvature. Limitations: Requires computing the directional derivative during sphere tracing. The choice of \epsilon affects the accuracy and stability. When to use: When differentiable rendering of SDFs is required, especially for silhouette derivatives. When not to use: When SDF gradients are expensive to compute or unavailable. The method was introduced in "A Simple Approach to Differentiable Rendering of SDFs". It is implemented in the Mitsuba3 Python package with CUDA and LLVM backends. It is used for forward derivatives of rendered images w.r.t. translation parameters and inverse rendering tasks. The method addresses the difficulty of sampling silhouette points by relaxing the SDF condition to a band 0 < SDF < \epsilon, which produces rays that graze the surface with no intersection, leading to more uniform samples. name: Chamfer-L1 Distance Computation
head: Distance-Aided Ray Marching
body: Chamfer-L1 Distance Computation estimates the Chamfer distance between a predicted SDF surface and a ground-truth mesh by using sphere tracing to sample points on the SDF surface. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by repurposing the ray-marching process to generate surface samples for metric evaluation rather than direct rendering. The method combines sphere tracing with a sampling strategy to generate points on the surface of an SDF-defined object. These points are then used to compute the Chamfer distance, a metric measuring the similarity between two sets of points. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A bounding volume B, a predicted SDF function f(\mathbf{p}), a ground-truth mesh M{gt}, and a target number of samples N. Output: A set of sampled points P{pred} on the predicted surface and the computed Chamfer distance D{Chamfer} between P{pred} and points sampled from M{gt}. Data Structures: Bounding Volume B: A 3D box or sphere enclosing the object. Sample Points: A list of 3D coordinates \mathbf{p}i. Ray Data: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} (unit vector), current distance t. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Define the bounding volume B and initialize an empty list P{pred} for sampled points. 2. Ray Generation: Uniformly sample 2^{17} = 131,072 points in the bounding volume B, and assign each point a random spherical direction \mathbf{d}. 3. Sphere Tracing: For each ray (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}): Initialize t = 0. Loop while t < t{max} and steps < max\steps: Evaluate \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Compute d = f(\mathbf{p}). If d < \epsilon, the ray has hit the surface. Advance t \leftarrow t + \max(d, 10^{-6}) to prevent zero or negative steps that break sphere tracing. If a hit occurred, record \mathbf{p} in P{pred}. 4. Sampling Refinement: If |P{pred}| is less than the minimum required number of points, repeat steps 2-3 with new random rays until the threshold is met. 5. Ground Truth Sampling: Uniformly sample points P{gt} from the ground-truth mesh M{gt} (exact sampling method not specified in sources). 6. Chamfer Distance Calculation: Compute the Chamfer distance between P{pred} and P{gt} using squared Euclidean distance as implemented in PyTorch3D. Formulas: Ray Marching Step: t{new} = t{old} + f(\mathbf{o} + t{old}\mathbf{d}). Chamfer Distance: D{Chamfer} = \frac{1}{|P{pred}|} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in P{pred}} \min{\mathbf{q} \in P{gt}} \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|^2 + \frac{1}{|P{gt}|} \sum{\mathbf{q} \in P{gt}} \min{\mathbf{p} \in P{pred}} \|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}\|^2. Parameters: Initial Samples: 2^{17} = 131,072 rays. Convergence Threshold \epsilon: Not given in the sources. Max Distance t{max}: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Bias: Random spherical directions may miss thin structures or concavities if the bounding volume is large relative to the object. Precision: Floating-point errors in SDF evaluation can cause rays to miss the surface or oscillate near it. Mesh Extraction Error: If ground truth is obtained via Marching Cubes from an SDF, additional error is introduced. Pseudocode: import math import random def chamferl1distancecomputation(sdf, meshgtpoints, numinitialrays=131072, epsilon=1e-4, maxsteps=100, tmax=10.0): """ Compute Chamfer distance between SDF surface and ground truth mesh using sphere tracing. Args: sdf: Callable SDF function f(p) meshgtpoints: List of 3D coordinates sampled from ground truth mesh numinitialrays: Number of initial rays to cast epsilon: Convergence threshold for surface hit maxsteps: Maximum sphere tracing steps per ray tmax: Maximum ray distance Returns: chamferdistance: Scalar Chamfer distance """ # 1. Initialize predpoints = [] # 2. Ray Generation: Uniformly sample points in bounding volume B (assumed unit cube [-0.5, 0.5]^3) # Assign each a random spherical direction origins = [(random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5)) for in range(numinitialrays)] directions = [(random.gauss(0, 1), random.gauss(0, 1), random.gauss(0, 1)) for in range(numinitialrays)] # Normalize directions to unit vectors directions = [(d[0]/math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in d)), d[1]/math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in d)), d[2]/math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in d))) for d in directions] # 3. Sphere Tracing for i in range(numinitialrays): o = origins[i] d = directions[i] t = 0.0 hit = False for in range(maxsteps): p = (o[0] + td[0], o[1] + td[1], o[2] + td[2]) dist = sdf(p) if dist < epsilon: predpoints.append(p) hit = True break # Prevent zero or negative steps that break sphere tracing stepsize = max(dist, 1e-6) t += stepsize if t > tmax: break if hit: continue # 4. Refinement: Repeat ray generation/marching until minimum points obtained # (Implementation omitted as loop condition depends on external target count) # 5. Ground Truth Sampling: Sample points Pgt from meshgt # (Method not specified in sources) # 6. Chamfer Distance Calculation def euclideandistsq(a, b): return sum((x - y)2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) def mindistsq(point, pointslist): return min(euclideandistsq(point, q) for q in pointslist) if not predpoints or not meshgtpoints: return float('inf') forwardsum = sum(mindistsq(p, meshgtpoints) for p in predpoints) backwardsum = sum(mindistsq(q, predpoints) for q in meshgtpoints) chamfer = (forwardsum / len(predpoints)) + (backwardsum / len(meshgtpoints)) return chamfer Stores the radius of the largest empty sphere centered at each voxel in a separate shape texture to take large steps through empty space. It sets itself apart by utilizing the exact Euclidean distance to the nearest solid voxel rather than the L1 distance, providing optimal step sizes in empty regions at the cost of higher preprocessing complexity. Computes the oriented normal vector of a 4D simplex defined by four space-time events for relativistic heavy-ion collision simulations. It distinguishes itself by handling the mixed spatial-temporal signature of Minkowski space. Estimates wall thickness by computing the distance transform of a part relative to the die. The wall thickness is approximated as twice the maximum distance value found in the part voxels. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S + M \log M + P \log P), where N is the number of rays, S is the average number of sphere tracing steps, M is the number of ground truth samples, and P is the number of predicted samples. The nearest neighbor search dominates if M, P are large. Memory Complexity: O(M + P) to store the sampled points. Performance: The method is computationally expensive due to the large number of ray casts (2^{17}) and SDF evaluations. Strengths: Provides a robust metric for training implicit neural representations against mesh ground truth. Limitations: Sensitive to SDF quality and sampling bias. When to use: When evaluating or training implicit neural fields (like NGLOD) against mesh ground truth. When not to use: For real-time rendering where speed is critical; use standard sphere tracing for visualization instead. The technique is described in the context of the "Neural Geometric Level of Detail" (NGLOD) paper. The visualization of sphere tracing, where the distance between steps is pictured as the radius of a sphere touching at least one object, originates from ray casting literature. The specific application to Chamfer distance computation for neural implicit shapes is a modern development in 3D deep learning. name: Sphere Assisted Raymarching
head: Shape Assisted Raymarching, Shape Marching, Sphere Assisted
body: Sphere Assisted Raymarching is a distance-field ray marching technique that stores the radius of the largest empty sphere centered at each voxel in a separate shape texture. This allows rays to take large steps through empty space by using the stored radius as a lower bound for the step size, significantly reducing the number of voxel lookups compared to standard plane-based marching. It sets itself apart from its parent Chamfer-L1 Distance Computation by storing the radius of the largest empty sphere centered at each voxel, providing optimal step sizes in empty regions at the cost of higher preprocessing complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin p0, ray direction d (normalized), maximum check distance maxDistToCheck, voxel grid size voxelGridSize. Textures: voxels: A 3D texture storing normalized float color values. The alpha channel indicates solidity. shape: A 3D texture storing integer values. The red channel stores the distance to the nearest solid voxel as a non-negative integer. Output: A vec4 color value if a solid voxel is hit, or vec4(0) if the ray exits the volume or exceeds maxDistToCheck. Data Structures: The shape texture uses an integer format (e.g., uint) to store the sphere radius. The value 255 is reserved to represent a solid voxel. Empty voxels store the radius of the largest empty sphere centered at that voxel. Parameters: 255: Constant representing a solid voxel in the shape texture. epsilon: A small positive constant added to the step size to guarantee progress and avoid infinite loops due to precision errors. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize ray parameter t = 0. 2. Loop while t \le maxDistToCheck: a. Calculate current position p = p0 + d \cdot t. b. Sample the shape texture at p / voxelGridSize to get shapeValue (integer). c. If shapeValue == 255: i. Sample the voxels texture at p / voxelGridSize. ii. Return the sampled color. d. Calculate deltas to the next plane boundaries along the ray direction: deltas = \frac{(step(0, d) - fract(p / voxelGridSize)) \cdot voxelGridSize}{d} Where step(0, d) is a vector where each component is 0 if di < 0 else 1, and fract(p / voxelGridSize) is the fractional part of the voxel coordinates. e. Calculate the minimum distance to the next voxel boundary: minDelta = \min(deltas) f. Update t: t \leftarrow t + \max(minDelta + shapeValue \cdot voxelGridSize, epsilon) 3. Return vec4(0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphereassistedraymarching(p0, d, maxDistToCheck, voxelGridSize, shapetexture, voxelstexture): t = 0.0 epsilon = 1e-6 # Small constant to prevent zero-step loops while t <= maxDistToCheck: p = p0 + d t # Convert to voxel coordinates for traversal and texture lookup v = p / voxelGridSize fv = v - floor(v) # fract(v) # Sample shape texture shapevalue = shapetexture.samplelevel(v, 0).r # Check for solid voxel if shapevalue == 255: return voxelstexture.samplelevel(v, 0) # Calculate deltas to next plane boundaries in world units # step(0, d) returns 0 if d < 0 else 1 stepvector = vec3(1.0 if d.x >= 0 else 0.0, 1.0 if d.y >= 0 else 0.0, 1.0 if d.z >= 0 else 0.0) # Avoid division by zero if d is exactly 0 (though d is normalized) deltas = (stepvector - fv) voxelGridSize / d # Find minimum delta mindelta = min(deltas.x, min(deltas.y, deltas.z)) # Update t: add distance to next voxel boundary + sphere radius (converted to world units) t += max(mindelta + shapevalue voxelGridSize, epsilon) return vec4(0.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Preprocessing Cost: Generating the shape data (distance field) has a significant upfront computational cost. Precision: Using integer textures for shape data avoids precision issues with normalized floats for color, but limits the maximum representable distance to the texture's bit depth (e.g., 255 for 8-bit). Boundary Conditions: The epsilon is crucial to prevent the ray from getting stuck if minDelta + shapeValue evaluates to 0 due to floating-point inaccuracies. Cube Assisted Raymarching is a distance-field ray marching technique that stores the size of the largest empty cube centered at each voxel instead of the largest empty sphere. It solves the problem of slow shape data generation in Sphere Assisted Raymarching by trading some step optimality for significantly faster preprocessing. While Sphere Assisted Raymarching provides optimal step sizes, Cube Assisted Raymarching is an order of magnitude faster to compute the shape data, making it suitable for larger voxel grids where preprocessing time is a bottleneck. A technique that places a sphere at every empty voxel position, where the sphere radius indicates the distance to the closest non-empty voxel, used for navigation inside hollow volumetric objects. It reduces a ray's space traversal to just a few hops until a boundary wall is reached. Unlike standard sphere tracing which uses the global maximum empty sphere radius, this method is view-sensitive and specifically optimized for hollow structures like those in virtual colonoscopy. Time Complexity: The ray marching loop itself is efficient in empty space, taking large steps. However, the preprocessing cost to generate the shape texture is O(n^2) for a simple implementation, where n is the number of voxels. Memory Complexity: Requires two 3D textures: one for color (voxels) and one for shape (shape). This increases memory usage compared to single-texture approaches. Performance: Reduces the number of voxel lookups in empty space compared to plane marching. However, it is not always a performance win due to the high preprocessing cost and memory bandwidth usage. Strengths: Optimal step sizes in empty space, reducing traversal steps significantly for large empty volumes. Limitations: High preprocessing time for shape data generation and higher memory footprint. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Sphere Assisted Raymarching was introduced by Caleb Leak in his blog post "Raymarching Voxel Rendering". The technique is part of a series of optimizations for voxel rendering, following plane-based marching and preceding cube-assisted variants. It addresses the inefficiency of small steps in empty space by leveraging distance field information. name: Cube Assisted Raymarching
head: Cube Assisted
body: Cube Assisted Raymarching is a distance-field ray marching technique that stores the size of the largest empty cube centered at each voxel instead of the largest empty sphere. It solves the problem of slow shape data generation in Sphere Assisted Raymarching by trading some step optimality for significantly faster preprocessing. While Sphere Assisted Raymarching provides optimal step sizes, Cube Assisted Raymarching is an order of magnitude faster to compute the shape data, making it suitable for larger voxel grids where preprocessing time is a bottleneck. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid indicating occupancy. Output: A shape texture where each voxel stores the side length of the largest empty cube centered at that voxel. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D array of occupancy values (e.g., 0 for empty, 1 for solid). 2. Summed Area Table (SAT): A 3D array of the same dimensions as the voxel grid, storing the cumulative sum of occupancy values from the origin to each coordinate. 3. Shape Texture: A 3D array storing the computed cube side lengths. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Summed Area Table: Iterate through the voxel grid and compute the SAT. 2. Binary Search for Cube Size: For each empty voxel, perform a binary search to find the maximum side length s such that a cube of side s centered at that voxel contains no solid voxels. 3. Store Result: Store the maximum valid s in the shape texture for each voxel. Formulas: SAT Computation: The 3D prefix sum is computed as: SAT[x][y][z] = V[x][y][z] + SAT[x-1][y][z] + SAT[x][y-1][z] + SAT[x][y][z-1] - SAT[x-1][y-1][z] - SAT[x-1][y][z-1] - SAT[x][y-1][z-1] + SAT[x-1][y-1][z-1] where V[x][y][z] is the occupancy value and out-of-bounds indices return 0. Cube Area Check using SAT: The number of solid voxels in a box defined by corners (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) is computed in O(1) time: Count = SAT[x2][y2][z2] - SAT[x1-1][y2][z2] - SAT[x2][y1-1][z2] - SAT[x2][y2][z1-1] + SAT[x1-1][y1-1][z2] + SAT[x1-1][y2][z1-1] + SAT[x2][y1-1][z1-1] - SAT[x1-1][y1-1][z1-1] The cube is empty if Count == 0. Cube Boundaries: For a cube of side s centered at (cx, cy, cz), the inclusive integer boundaries are: x1 = cx - \lfloor s/2 \rfloor, \quad x2 = cx + \lfloor (s-1)/2 \rfloor y1 = cy - \lfloor s/2 \rfloor, \quad y2 = cy + \lfloor (s-1)/2 \rfloor z1 = cz - \lfloor s/2 \rfloor, \quad z2 = cz + \lfloor (s-1)/2 \rfloor Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesat(voxelgrid, dims): Dx, Dy, Dz = dims sat = [[[0] Dz for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): val = voxelgrid[x][y][z] sat[x][y][z] = val if x > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x-1][y][z] if y > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x][y-1][z] if z > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x][y][z-1] if x > 0 and y > 0: sat[x][y][z] -= sat[x-1][y-1][z] if x > 0 and z > 0: sat[x][y][z] -= sat[x-1][y][z-1] if y > 0 and z > 0: sat[x][y][z] -= sat[x][y-1][z-1] if x > 0 and y > 0 and z > 0: sat[x][y][z] += sat[x-1][y-1][z-1] return sat def getboxsolidcount(sat, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, dims): Dx, Dy, Dz = dims def getsat(x, y, z): if x < 0 or y < 0 or z < 0: return 0 if x >= Dx or y >= Dy or z >= Dz: return 0 return sat[x][y][z] return (getsat(x2, y2, z2) getsat(x1-1, y2, z2) getsat(x2, y1-1, z2) getsat(x2, y2, z1-1) + getsat(x1-1, y1-1, z2) + getsat(x1-1, y2, z1-1) + getsat(x2, y1-1, z1-1) getsat(x1-1, y1-1, z1-1)) def computecubeassistedshape(voxelgrid, dims): Dx, Dy, Dz = dims sat = computesat(voxelgrid, dims) shape = [[[0] Dz for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] maxdim = max(Dx, Dy, Dz) for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): if voxelgrid[x][y][z] == 1: shape[x][y][z] = 0 continue low, high, bests = 1, maxdim, 0 while low <= high: s = (low + high) // 2 x1, x2 = x - (s // 2), x + ((s - 1) // 2) y1, y2 = y - (s // 2), y + ((s - 1) // 2) z1, z2 = z - (s // 2), z + ((s - 1) // 2) if x1 < 0 or x2 >= Dx or y1 < 0 or y2 >= Dy or z1 < 0 or z2 >= Dz: high = s - 1 continue if getboxsolidcount(sat, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, dims) == 0: bests = s low = s + 1 else: high = s - 1 shape[x][y][z] = bests return shape Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Cubes extending beyond the voxel grid boundaries are invalid and must be rejected during the binary search. Degenerate Input: A single solid voxel in a large empty grid is used as a test case to demonstrate algorithm behavior. Precision: The SAT uses integer sums, providing exact empty-space checks for binary voxel grids. Time Complexity: Upfront shape data generation is O(n \log n), where n is the number of voxels. This improves upon the O(n^2) complexity of a simple sphere-assisted implementation. Measured Performance: On a 32x32x32 voxel test set, Cube Assisted Raymarching computed shape data an order of magnitude faster than Sphere Assisted Raymarching. Render times were close on smaller sets, but Plane Marching showed a moderate lead as set size increased. Strengths: Significantly faster preprocessing than Sphere Assisted Raymarching while still providing large steps through empty space. Limitations: Slightly suboptimal step sizes compared to Sphere Assisted Raymarching. When to Use: When preprocessing time is a bottleneck and the slight loss in step optimality is acceptable. When Not to Use: When optimal step sizes are critical and preprocessing time is not a concern. Cube Assisted Raymarching was introduced by Caleb Leak in his blog post "Raymarching Voxel Rendering". It was developed as an optimization to Sphere Assisted Raymarching, which suffered from high upfront computational cost. The technique leverages Summed Area Tables, a data structure common in computer vision, to enable fast empty space queries.
