name: Sphere-based Empty Space Leaping
head: Sphere at empty voxel, Sphere-based Empty Voxel Navigation
body: A technique that places a sphere at every empty voxel position, where the sphere radius indicates the distance to the closest non-empty voxel, used for navigation inside hollow volumetric objects. It reduces a ray's space traversal to just a few hops until a boundary wall is reached. Proposed by Wan as a view-sensitive extension of proximity clouds, it specifically targets hollow structures like those encountered in virtual colonoscopy. Inputs: Ray origin O and normalized direction D. Empty Voxel Map: a 3D grid storing the radius r of the largest empty sphere centered at each voxel. Volume bounds and voxel size. Outputs: The ray position where it intersects a non-empty voxel or exits the volume. Data Structures: Empty Voxel Map: A 3D array where each entry corresponds to a voxel. If the voxel is empty, the value is r, the radius to the nearest non-empty voxel. If the voxel is non-empty, the value is 0 or a negative sentinel. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start the ray at origin O. Determine the initial voxel index containing O. 2. Sphere Query: Retrieve the sphere radius r from the Empty Voxel Map at the current voxel index. 3. Step Calculation: The step size is exactly r. This guarantees the ray advances at least to the sphere boundary without intersecting the current empty region. 4. Ray Advance: Update the ray origin: O{new} = O + r \cdot D. 5. Boundary Check: Determine the voxel index of O{new}. If the index is outside volume bounds, terminate. If the radius at the new index is 0 (non-empty), terminate the leap and switch to standard sampling. Otherwise, repeat from Step 2. Parameters: Sphere radius r: Precomputed for each empty voxel. Edge Cases: Non-empty voxels: The technique only applies to empty voxels. Rays hitting non-empty voxels must switch to standard sampling or other traversal methods. Precision: Floating-point precision errors may cause the ray to slightly overshoot or undershoot the boundary. A small epsilon should be used for boundary checks. Degenerate Input: If the volume has no empty voxels, the technique is not applicable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spherebasedemptyspaceleaping(rayorigin, raydirection, emptyvoxelmap, voxelsize, volumemin, volumemax): currentpos = list(rayorigin) dimx = len(emptyvoxelmap) dimy = len(emptyvoxelmap[0]) dimz = len(emptyvoxelmap[0][0]) while True: # Convert world position to integer voxel indices using floor voxelcoords = [math.floor((currentpos[i] - volumemin[i]) / voxelsize) for i in range(3)] # Check bounds if not (0 <= voxelcoords[0] < dimx and 0 <= voxelcoords[1] < dimy and 0 <= voxelcoords[2] < dimz): break # Exited volume # Get sphere radius for current voxel r = emptyvoxelmap[voxelcoords[0]][voxelcoords[1]][voxelcoords[2]] # If non-empty (radius is 0 or negative), stop leaping if r <= 0.0: break # Advance ray by sphere radius currentpos[0] += raydirection[0] r currentpos[1] += raydirection[1] r currentpos[2] += raydirection[2] r return currentpos Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of leaping hops, which is significantly lower than single-voxel traversal in large empty regions. Memory Complexity: Requires one floating-point value per empty voxel for the radius map. Strengths: Efficient for hollow objects with large empty interiors. Reduces traversal steps to a few hops. Limitations: Only applicable to empty voxels. Requires precomputation. Not effective for dense or complex internal structures. When to use: Virtual colonoscopy, navigation inside hollow volumetric objects. When not to use: Dense volumes, volumes with no empty space, or when memory is constrained. Proposed by Wan as a view-sensitive extension of proximity clouds. It addresses the shortcoming of proximity clouds being insensitive to viewing direction, where rays missing the object are still slowed down. It is used for navigation inside hollow volumetric objects, such as in virtual colonoscopy. Meissner suggested an algorithm to quickly re-compute the proximity cloud when the transfer function changes. name: STEVE 4D Normal Vector Computation
head: 4D Space-Time Normal Formulation, STEVE 4D Extension, STEVE 4D Normal Vector Computation & Subspace Orientation
body:
Computes the oriented normal vector of a 4D simplex defined by four space-time events, providing the geometric foundation for the 4D extension of the STEVE algorithm. It handles the mixed spatial-temporal signature of Minkowski space to ensure consistent orientation for higher-dimensional polytope construction in relativistic heavy-ion collision simulations. Inputs: Four 4D events x^\mu1, x^\mu2, x^\mu3, x^\mu4, where each event is a tuple (x, y, z, t) representing spatial coordinates and time. Outputs: A covariant 4-normal vector d\sigma\mu and a contravariant 4-normal vector d\sigma^\mu. Data Structures: The method operates on difference vectors derived from the input events. Let the basis vectors be \mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z, \mathbf{e}t. The contravariant event is defined as x^\mu = x \mathbf{e}x + y \mathbf{e}y + z \mathbf{e}z + t \mathbf{e}t. Parameters: The metric tensor g{\mu
u} is assumed diagonal: g{\mu
u} = 	ext{diag}(g{11}, g{22}, g{33}, g{44}). Relativistic case: g{\mu
u} = 	ext{diag}(-1, -1, -1, +1). Non-relativistic case: g{\mu
u} = 	ext{diag}(+1, +1, +1, +1). Steps: 1. Compute Edge Differences: Calculate the differences between the second, third, and fourth events relative to the first event for each dimension. Let indices 1, 2, 3, 4 correspond to x, y, z, t respectively.  egin{aligned} dx1 &= x2 - x1, & dx2 &= x3 - x1, & dx3 &= x4 - x1 \ dy1 &= y2 - y1, & dy2 &= y3 - y1, & dy3 &= y4 - y1 \ dz1 &= z2 - z1, & dz2 &= z3 - z1, & dz3 &= z4 - z1 \ dt1 &= t2 - t1, & dt2 &= t3 - t1, & dt3 &= t4 - t1 \end{aligned} Define the component mapping: dxm^1 = dxm, dxm^2 = dym, dxm^3 = dzm, dxm^4 = dtm for m \in \{1, 2, 3\}. 2. Compute 3D Determinants of Differences: Calculate the determinant dS^{ikl} for all unique combinations of indices i, k, l \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}. dS^{ikl} = \det  egin{pmatrix} dx1^i & dx2^i & dx3^i \ dx1^k & dx2^k & dx3^k \ dx1^l & dx2^l & dx3^l \end{pmatrix} This determinant represents the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the difference vectors restricted to the subspace defined by indices i, k, l. 3. Compute Contravariant 4-Normal: The contravariant normal d\sigma^\mu is computed by scaling the determinants with the inverse metric components. d\sigma^\mu =  rac{1}{6} \left(  rac{dS^{234}}{g{11}},  rac{dS^{143}}{g{22}},  rac{dS^{124}}{g{33}},  rac{dS^{132}}{g{44}} ight) The \mu-th component uses the determinant of the subspace excluding \mu. 4. Compute Covariant 4-Normal: The covariant normal d\sigma\mu is obtained by lowering the index with the metric tensor g{\mu
u}. d\sigma\mu = g{\mu
u} d\sigma^
u =  rac{1}{6} (dS^{234}, dS^{143}, dS^{124}, dS^{132}) The source notation dS^{2344} etc. denotes the metric-contracted component, but the diagonal metric factors cancel exactly with the contravariant scaling, making the covariant form independent of the 4D metric choice. 5. Subspace Orientation (for VESTA N-cycles): When applying the marching variant of VESTA to the eight 3D bounding subspaces of a 4D cell (tesseract), inverse orientations must be chosen for the generated VESTA N-cycles in the x0, y1, z0, and t1 subspaces. This ensures consistent, orientation-preserving construction of higher-dimensional polytopes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def steve4dnormal(x1, x2, x3, x4, metricdiag): """ Computes the covariant and contravariant 4-normal vectors for a 4D simplex. Args: x1, x2, x3, x4: Tuples (x, y, z, t) representing the 4 events. metricdiag: List/Tuple of 4 floats [g11, g22, g33, g44]. Returns: covariantnormal: Tuple (dsigma1, dsigma2, dsigma3, dsigma4) contravariantnormal: Tuple (dsigma^1, dsigma^2, dsigma^3, dsigma^4) """ # Step 1: Compute differences relative to event 1 # diffs[m][i] stores the i-th component of the m-th edge vector # i=0:x, 1:y, 2:z, 3:t diffs = [[0]4 for in range(3)] for m in range(3): ecurr = [x1, x2, x3, x4][m+1] eref = x1 for i in range(4): diffs[m][i] = ecurr[i] - eref[i] # Step 2: Compute required 3x3 determinants def det3(v1, v2, v3): return (v1[0] (v2[1]v3[2] - v2[2]v3[1]) - v1[1] (v2[0]v3[2] - v2[2]v3[0]) + v1[2] (v2[0]v3[1] - v2[1]v3[0])) # Extract columns for indices 0,1,2,3 (x,y,z,t) col = [[diffs[m][i] for m in range(3)] for i in range(4)] # Compute specific determinants per source formula dS234 = det3(col[1], col[2], col[3]) # y, z, t dS143 = det3(col[0], col[3], col[2]) # x, t, z dS124 = det3(col[0], col[1], col[3]) # x, y, t dS132 = det3(col[0], col[2], col[1]) # x, z, y g11, g22, g33, g44 = metricdiag # Step 3: Contravariant Normal dsigmacontravariant = ( dS234 / g11, dS143 / g22, dS124 / g33, dS132 / g44) # Step 4: Covariant Normal (metric factors cancel) dsigmacovariant = ( dS234, dS143, dS124, dS132) # Scale by 1/6 dsigmacontravariant = tuple(c / 6.0 for c in dsigmacontravariant) dsigmacovariant = tuple(c / 6.0 for c in dsigmacovariant) return dsigmacovariant, dsigmacontravariant Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Isochronous Hypersurface: If dt1=dt2=dt3=0 (all events lie on the same time slice), the covariant normal simplifies to d\sigma\mu =  rac{1}{6} (0, 0, 0, dS^{132}). Here dS^{132} equals the negative volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the spatial difference vectors. Metric Dependence: In the non-relativistic limit (g{\mu
u} = 	ext{diag}(+1, +1, +1, +1)), the covariant and contravariant normals are identical (d\sigma\mu \equiv d\sigma^\mu). In the relativistic case, they differ due to metric scaling. Orientation Consistency: The choice of edge differences (x2-x1, etc.) and the specific determinant permutations are critical for the \oplus/\ominus naming convention and consistent orientation in 4D. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a rigorous geometric foundation for 4D volume extraction in relativistic simulations. Limitations: Requires careful handling of the metric signature. When to use: When processing space-time data in relativistic heavy-ion collision simulations or any application requiring consistent 4D normal vectors for STEVE-based volume extraction. The method originates from the STEVE (Space-Time-Enclosing Volume Extraction) algorithm, specifically its extension to 4D space-time for relativistic applications. It was developed by B. R. Schlei at GSI Helmholtzzentrum für Schwerionenforschung. The work builds upon lower-dimensional (2D, 3D) contour vector orientation principles, extending them to 4D using geometric algebra and multilinear basis concepts. It is used in the context of relativistic heavy-ion collision simulations to extract 4D volumes from event data. name: 2-Pass Distance Transformation
head: Borgefors 2-pass Distance Transformation, Borgefors distance transform, DT-based Wall Thickness, DT-based reasoning, Quantitative Wall Thickness Evaluation
body: The 2-Pass Distance Transformation computes the shortest distance from every voxel in a volume to the nearest object boundary, enabling quantitative wall thickness evaluation in manufacturing contexts such as die casting. It distinguishes itself from standard distance transforms by simultaneously processing both the part and the die within a single voxel volume, using bit-level tagging to distinguish ownership. Unlike Sphere Assisted Raymarching which uses geometric primitives for acceleration, or STEVE 4D Normal Vector Computation which focuses on normal estimation, this method relies on discrete grid propagation to derive scalar field values for thickness analysis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the part and the die. Output: A distance field where each voxel contains the shortest distance to the boundary between the part and the die. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of integers. Voxel Value Layout: The least significant bit (LSB) indicates ownership: 1 (odd) for part voxels, 0 (even) for die voxels. The remaining bits store the distance value. Memory usage is typically 2-3 bytes per voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Identify all boundary voxels during the scan-conversion of the CAD model into voxels. Assign a value of 0 to all boundary voxels. Initialize all non-boundary voxels to the largest possible distance value representable in the voxel type (e.g., 255 for 8-bit, or max integer for larger types). Set the LSB of each voxel to indicate its material (part or die). 2. Forward Pass: Traverse the volume in a specific order (e.g., x, y, z increasing). For each voxel, compare its current value with the values of its neighbors defined by the forward mask. Update the voxel value to the minimum of its current value and the neighbor's value plus the mask constant. 3. Backward Pass: Traverse the volume in the reverse order (e.g., x, y, z decreasing). For each voxel, compare its current value with the values of its neighbors defined by the backward mask. Update the voxel value to the minimum of its current value and the neighbor's value plus the mask constant. 4. Result Extraction: The distance value for a voxel is derived from the propagated values. The wall thickness is approximated as twice the maximum distance value found in the part voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedistancetransform(volume, shape, metricmask): """ Computes the 2-pass distance transform for a part/die volume. Args: volume: 3D numpy array or list of lists of lists. shape: Tuple (D, H, W) dimensions of the volume. metricmask: Dictionary containing 'forward' and 'backward' masks. Each mask is a list of (dx, dy, dz, weight) tuples. Returns: distancevolume: 3D array with distance values. """ D, H, W = shape # Initialize distance volume # Use a large number for non-boundary voxels MAXDIST = 231 - 1 distancevolume = [[[MAXDIST for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(D)] # Identify boundary voxels and initialize # Note: In practice, boundary identification happens during scan-conversion. # Here we assume a function getboundaryvoxels exists or is pre-computed. boundaryvoxels = getboundaryvoxels(volume) # Helper to identify boundaries for (d, h, w) in boundaryvoxels: distancevolume[d][h][w] = 0 # Set ownership bit (LSB) # 1 for part, 0 for die. This is stored in the lower bits. # For simplicity, we assume the input 'volume' has material info. # We will store distance in the upper bits and ownership in LSB. # However, the algorithm updates the distance value. # The LSB must be preserved or re-applied after updates if it's part of the value. # The source says "use the last bit... to distinguish". # This implies the value stored is (distance << 1) | ownership. # But the initialization says "assign 0" to boundary. # If boundary is 0, LSB is 0. # If part voxel is initialized to MAX, LSB is 1 (if MAX is odd). # Let's assume the value stored is the distance, and ownership is tracked separately # or via parity of the distance value itself as per source. # Source: "odd = part, even = die". # So, if a voxel is part, its distance value should be odd? # Or is the ownership bit separate? # "use the last bit of the voxel value to distinguish... odd vs even". # This implies the distance value itself carries the parity. # But distance 0 is even. Boundary voxels are 0. # If boundary is part, it should be odd? # The source says: "all voxels which belong to the die have initial value 0... rest (part)... 255". # 0 is even (die). 255 is odd (part). # So, initialization: # Die boundary: 0 # Part boundary: 1? Or is boundary always 0? # "boundary voxels are assigned the value 0". # If a boundary voxel is part, it is 0. 0 is even. This contradicts "odd=part". # Re-reading: "use the last bit... to distinguish the voxels of the part from ones of the die". # Maybe the ownership is stored in a separate flag, or the distance is shifted? # "In this way, after 2 traversals... voxels of both die and part will have a distance value". # If the value is just distance, how is ownership preserved if distance changes? # Perhaps the ownership is determined by the initial state, or the distance calculation # doesn't overwrite the LSB? # Let's assume the standard Borgefors algorithm updates the distance. # The ownership bit might be a separate channel or the source implies that # the distance value plus the ownership bit is the stored integer. # Given the ambiguity, we store distance in upper bits and ownership in LSB. # Re-initialization with combined value combinedvolume = [[[0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(D)] for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): ispart = volume[d][h][w] == PARTMATERIAL # Assuming material map isboundary = (d,h,w) in boundaryvoxels if isboundary: dist = 0 else: dist = MAXDIST ownershipbit = 1 if ispart else 0 # Store as (dist << 1) | ownershipbit to preserve ownership # However, source says "odd=part". # If dist=0, val=0 (even). If part boundary, should be odd? # Source says "boundary voxels assigned 0". # This suggests the ownership bit might not be strictly LSB of the distance # if distance 0 is used for both. # Let's stick to the source's explicit instruction: # "use the last bit... odd=part, even=die". # And "boundary voxels assigned 0". # This is a contradiction if a part boundary voxel is 0. # Perhaps "boundary" refers to the interface, and one side is 0, # the other is 1? # "all voxels which belong to the die have initial value 0 while the rest... 255". # This implies Die=0, Part=255. # So Part boundary is 255? No, "boundary voxels assigned 0". # Maybe only Die boundary is 0? # "distance from each voxel in the part to its closest voxel(s) in the die". # If we only care about Part-to-Die distance, we only need Part voxels to have values. # But source says "voxels of both die and part will have a distance value". # Implementation Strategy based on "odd=part, even=die": # If a voxel is Part, ensure its value is odd. # If a voxel is Die, ensure its value is even. # Boundary voxels are 0. # If a boundary voxel is Part, set to 1? # Source says "assigned 0". # We will follow the "odd/even" rule for non-boundary, # and assume boundary 0 is Die. Part boundaries might be handled differently # or the source implies the distance is calculated relative to the other object. # Let's assume the standard approach: # Value = Distance. # Ownership is tracked separately or via parity of the initial seed. # For the purpose of the algorithm, we propagate distances. combinedvolume[d][h][w] = dist << 1 | ownershipbit # Forward Pass for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): currentval = combinedvolume[d][h][w] currentdist = currentval >> 1 currentown = currentval & 1 for (dx, dy, dz, weight) in metricmask['forward']: nd, nh, nw = d + dz, h + dy, w + dx # Note: z is depth, y is height, x is width? # Standard 3D: z=depth, y=row, x=col. # Let's assume indices are (z, y, x) or (d, h, w). # Mask offsets are usually (dx, dy, dz). # Let's assume mask is (x, y, z) offsets. # Volume is [z][y][x]. # So neighbor is [d+dz][h+dy][w+dx]. if 0 <= nd < D and 0 <= nh < H and 0 <= nw < W: neighborval = combinedvolume[nd][nh][nw] neighbordist = neighborval >> 1 # Update distance newdist = min(currentdist, neighbordist + weight) # Preserve ownership combinedvolume[d][h][w] = (newdist << 1) | currentown # Backward Pass for d in range(D - 1, -1, -1): for h in range(H - 1, -1, -1): for w in range(W - 1, -1, -1): currentval = combinedvolume[d][h][w] currentdist = currentval >> 1 currentown = currentval & 1 for (dx, dy, dz, weight) in metricmask['backward']: nd, nh, nw = d + dz, h + dy, w + dx if 0 <= nd < D and 0 <= nh < H and 0 <= nw < W: neighborval = combinedvolume[nd][nh][nw] neighbordist = neighborval >> 1 newdist = min(currentdist, neighbordist + weight) combinedvolume[d][h][w] = (newdist << 1) | currentown # Extract distances distancevolume = [[[0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(D)] for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): distancevolume[d][h][w] = combinedvolume[d][h][w] >> 1 return distancevolume Parameters: Metric: A 3x3x3 integer-based chamfer metric is recommended to better approximate Euclidean distance than city-block or chess-board metrics. Initial Value (Non-boundary): Largest possible distance value (e.g., 255 for 8-bit). Initial Value (Boundary): 0. Memory: 2-3 bytes per voxel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Error Type 1: The distance is computed only at voxel grid points. The actual maximum inscribed sphere may not be centered at a voxel, so the local maximum in DT may not represent the true radius. Resolution Error Type 2: Voxelization approximates the boundary. The error from binary voxel approximation can be up to \sqrt{3}/2 times voxel size. Total Error Bounds: Actual wall thickness can be up to \sqrt{3} times voxel size larger than DT-based thickness, or up to \sqrt{3}/2 times voxel size smaller. Thin Region Detection: Applying heavy-mass extraction to thin regions incorrectly selects all boundary voxels as thin. This is solved by restricting thin-region detection to medial surface voxels with small inscribed sphere radii. Memory Efficiency: For elongated objects, use non-cubic volumes to avoid empty voxels. Use coarse resolution as a filter for regions of interest, then apply fine resolution locally. A visualization technique using animation of thresholded distance transforms to identify heavy mass (thick) and thin sections in die casting parts. It highlights regions in red based on a threshold; as the threshold varies, red regions appear to shrink or erode, indicating thick sections. Breaks in the red core pattern indicate non-uniformity in wall thickness. Places where red regions vanish and turn completely gray are thin regions. If 3-D thinning analysis is performed, skeletal voxels (thin sections) stand out explicitly with a green color once the shrinking core reaches the medial surface. The threshold value is dynamically adjusted based on the average distance value of all voxels in the part or the average DT of skeletal points only. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as it requires two full traversals of the volume. Memory Complexity: O(N), requiring 2-3 bytes per voxel. For a 300^3 volume, memory demand is at least 54 M-Bytes. Strengths: Efficient for quantitative wall thickness evaluation; handles both part and die in a single pass; allows for dynamic thresholding and animation for defect visualization. Limitations: Accuracy is limited by voxel resolution; errors can be up to \sqrt{3} times voxel size; not suitable for arbitrarily high precision without adaptive refinement. When to Use: When quantitative wall thickness analysis is needed for die casting parts and computational efficiency is prioritized over sub-voxel accuracy. When Not to Use: When sub-voxel precision is required without adaptive refinement, or for objects with complex geometries where voxelization errors are unacceptable. The method is based on the Borgefors 2-pass distance transformation algorithm, extended to handle both part and die volumes simultaneously. It was developed for die casting part and die design analysis to quantitatively identify thick and thin sections. The approach addresses the limitations of city-block and chess-board metrics by using chamfer metrics to better approximate Euclidean distance. Simple visualization techniques for die casting part and die design. name: Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching
head: Depth Rendering Pipeline, trivial
body: Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching is a multi-scale acceleration technique for Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching that initializes depth estimates at low resolution and recursively refines them at higher resolutions. It distinguishes itself from standard aggressive ray marching by decoupling the coarse initialization phase from the fine-grained recursive refinement, allowing for larger initial steps in empty space while maintaining precision near surfaces. Inputs: Latent code vector z \in \mathbb{R}^d. Camera pose (intrinsic matrix K, extrinsic matrix RT). Image resolution (H, W). Parameters: marchstep (total steps), raymarchingratio (step scaling factor), threshold (SDF surface threshold), clampdist (distance clamping, default 0.1), splittype ('depth' or 'raydepth'), sampleindextype ('minabs', default). Outputs: Rendered depth map Z \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}. Valid mask M \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W}. Minimum SDF sample per ray for differentiability. Points and SDF values along the ray. Data Structures: scalelist: List of resolutions from lowest to highest. rayslist: List of ray origins and directions for each scale. gridmaps: List of SDF values sampled at each scale. indexmaps: Mapping indices for upsampling from lower to higher resolution. recalibmaps: Recalibration factors for ray direction/origin adjustments. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute camera rays for the target resolution (H, W). Calculate initial intersection with unit spheres to determine initzdepth and a preliminary validmask. Initialize minsdfsamplenew tensor with zeros and enable gradients. 2. Scale Pyramid Construction: Generate a list of downscaled grid maps, rays, index maps, recalib maps, and valid masks for each scale in scalelist (reversed order, from coarsest to finest). For scales other than the original (index idx > 0), compute downscaled grid maps and rays using getdownscaledcamerarays. Calculate the valid mask for the current scale by max-pooling the previous scale's valid mask using maxpoolvalidmaskwithindex. 3. Coarse-to-Fine Marching Loop: Iterate through scales from largest (lowest resolution) to smallest (original resolution). For non-final scales (idx > 0): Perform single-scale ray marching using raymarchingtrivial. Unmap the results from the valid mask indices to full image dimensions using unmaptensorwithvalidmask. Upsample the SDF, points, and z-depth to the next higher resolution using the indexmap and recalibmap. For the final scale (idx == 0, original resolution): Perform recursive ray marching using raymarchingrecursive. Concatenate the final scale results with the upsampled results from previous scales, filtering by the valid mask. 4. Differentiable Sample Selection: Identify the minimum SDF sample along the marching path. Copy minsdfsample values to minsdfsamplenew at valid mask indices. For invalid mask indices, set minsdfsamplenew to dist + threshold - radius to handle camera gradients. 5. Depth Computation: Compute source z-depth as initzdepth at valid mask plus marchingzdepth. Copy srczdepth to Z at valid mask indices and reshape to (H, W). Update validmask using validmaskrender. If nograddepth is true, detach Z from the computation graph. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pyramidrecursiveraymarching(latentcode, camera, resolution, marchstep, threshold, clampdist=0.1, splittype='depth', sampleindextype='minabs'): """ Implements Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching. """ # 1. Initialization H, W = resolution rays = getcamerarays(camera, H, W) initzdepth, validmask = computeinitialsphereintersection(rays) # Initialize differentiable min SDF tensor minsdfsamplenew = torch.zeros((H, W), requiresgrad=True) # 2. Build Pyramid # Determine scale list based on resolution and marchstep scalelist = generatescalelist(H, W, marchstep) rayslist = [] gridmaps = [] indexmaps = [] recalibmaps = [] validmasks = [] # Generate lists for all scales (reversed order: coarsest first) for i, scale in enumerate(reversed(scalelist)): if i == 0: # Coarsest scale currentrays = getdownscaledcamerarays(rays, scale) currentgrid = samplesdfgrid(latentcode, currentrays, scale) currentvalid = computevalidmask(currentrays) else: # Intermediate scales prevscale = scalelist[-(i-1)] # Logic simplified for description currentrays = getdownscaledcamerarays(rays, scale) currentgrid = samplesdfgrid(latentcode, currentrays, scale) # Max-pool previous valid mask currentvalid = maxpoolvalidmaskwithindex(validmasks[-1], indexmaps[-1]) rayslist.append(currentrays) gridmaps.append(currentgrid) validmasks.append(currentvalid) # Index and recalib maps generated for upsampling indexmaps.append(generateindexmap(scale, prevscale if i > 0 else None)) recalibmaps.append(generaterecalibmap(splittype, currentrays)) # 3. Coarse-to-Fine Iteration upsampledsdf = None upsampledzdepth = None upsampledpoints = None # Iterate from coarsest (index 0 in reversed list) to finest for idx in range(len(scalelist)): # Note: rayslist[0] is coarsest, rayslist[-1] is finest (original) currentrays = rayslist[idx] currentgrid = gridmaps[idx] currentvalid = validmasks[idx] if idx < len(scalelist) - 1: # Non-final scale: Trivial marching sdflist, zdepthlist, pointslist = raymarchingtrivial( currentrays, currentgrid, marchstep, threshold, clampdist) # Unmap to full resolution sdffull = unmaptensorwithvalidmask(sdflist, currentvalid, H, W) zdepthfull = unmaptensorwithvalidmask(zdepthlist, currentvalid, H, W) pointsfull = unmaptensorwithvalidmask(pointslist, currentvalid, H, W) # Upsample to next scale nextidx = idx + 1 upsampledsdf = upsampletensor(sdffull, indexmaps[nextidx], recalibmaps[nextidx]) upsampledzdepth = upsampletensor(zdepthfull, indexmaps[nextidx], recalibmaps[nextidx]) upsampledpoints = upsampletensor(pointsfull, indexmaps[nextidx], recalibmaps[nextidx]) else: # Final scale: Recursive marching sdflist, zdepthlist, pointslist = raymarchingrecursive( currentrays, currentgrid, marchstep, threshold, clampdist, initzdepth=upsampledzdepth, sdfinit=upsampledsdf) # Concatenate final results with upsampled history finalsdf = concatenatewithupsampled(sdflist, upsampledsdf, currentvalid) finalzdepth = concatenatewithupsampled(zdepthlist, upsampledzdepth, currentvalid) finalpoints = concatenatewithupsampled(pointslist, upsampledpoints, currentvalid) # 4. Differentiable Sample Selection # Find min SDF sample minsdf = findminsdf(finalsdf) # Copy to new tensor at valid indices minsdfsamplenew[currentvalid == 1] = minsdf[currentvalid == 1] # Handle invalid indices for gradient flow invalidmask = currentvalid == 0 if invalidmask.any(): # dist is distance to camera, radius is object radius minsdfsamplenew[invalidmask] = dist + threshold - radius # 5. Depth Computation srczdepth = initzdepth + finalzdepth Z = torch.zeros((H, W)) Z[currentvalid == 1] = srczdepth[currentvalid == 1] # Update valid mask validmask = validmaskrender(finalsdf, threshold) # Detach if necessary if nograddepth: Z = Z.detach() return Z, validmask, minsdfsamplenew, finalpoints Parameters: raymarchingtype: String specifying the marching algorithm. Valid values are 'trivialnonparallel', 'trivial', 'recursive', and 'pyramidrecursive'. splittype: String specifying the splitting strategy for pyramid recursive marching. Valid values are 'depth' and 'raydepth'. If 'raydepth', recalibmapnow is set to ones. clampdist: Float parameter for distance clamping, default 0.1. sampleindextype: String for selecting the sample index, default 'minabs'. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Upsampling artifacts may occur if index maps are not accurately computed. Boundaries: Invalid mask indices must be handled explicitly to prevent NaN gradients during backpropagation. Degenerate Input: If marchsteplist[-1] == -1, it must be set to marchstep - sum(marchsteplist[:-1]) to ensure total steps are preserved. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) where N is the number of pixels, due to the multi-scale approach reducing the number of samples needed at high resolution. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the pyramid levels and intermediate results. Performance: Significantly faster than single-scale recursive marching for high-resolution images, as coarse scales quickly eliminate empty space. Strengths: Efficient initialization of depth, robust handling of large empty spaces, differentiable rendering. Limitations: Complexity of implementation due to multiple upsampling and recalibration steps. Potential for aliasing if downsampling is not handled carefully. Pyramid Recursive Ray Marching is part of the DIST-Renderer project, an unofficial implementation of DeepSDF rendering techniques. It was developed to address the computational cost of high-resolution SDF rendering by leveraging multi-scale processing. The method is used in the context of neural implicit surface representation and differentiable rendering. name: Deformation and Transformation Handling
body: This family addresses the problem of applying spatial transformations (rigid body motion, scaling, deformation) to Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDFs) during ray marching or voxel processing. It enables the rendering of animated, deforming, or dynamically positioned geometry without recomputing the underlying distance field data structures from scratch. It differs from static SDF definitions by introducing time-varying coordinate mappings, and from explicit mesh transformation by operating directly on the implicit field representation (or its voxel approximation) to preserve the analytical or volumetric nature of the distance query. All methods in this family rely on the principle of coordinate space transformation. The core mechanism involves mapping a query point from the rendering space (world space or camera space) into the local space of the primitive or the reference frame of the data before evaluating the distance function or sampling the voxel grid. For rigid transformations, the mapping is defined by a transformation matrix M. If the scene geometry is transformed by M in world space, the SDF evaluation at a world-space point \mathbf{p} requires evaluating the base SDF f{base} at the corresponding local-space point \mathbf{q}: \mathbf{q} = M^{-1} \mathbf{p} f{transformed}(\mathbf{p}) = f{base}(M^{-1} \mathbf{p}) This ensures that the distance value corresponds to the transformed geometry while keeping the primitive definition static in its local frame. For non-rigid or temporal transformations (such as motion compensation in TSDF compression), the mapping is often estimated per-block or per-voxel. The goal is to predict the current state st from a previous state s{t-1} using an estimated rigid transform (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) link to [Motion-Compensated Block Warping]. The prediction error is minimized to find the optimal transform: \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}:= \arg \min{\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}} \sum{i \in \Omega} \left( \hat{s}{t-1}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})) - st(\mathbf{p}i) \right)^2 where \mathbf{T} is the rigid transform and \Omega is the set of sample positions link to [Motion-Compensated Block Warping]. Scaling introduces a change in the metric of the distance field. For uniform scaling by factor s, the distance value must be scaled to preserve the Euclidean distance property: f'(\mathbf{p}) = s \cdot f(\mathbf{p}/s). Non-uniform scaling distorts the distance field unless the metric is adjusted, which is often handled by including scale in the transformation matrix and inverting it, or by post-scaling the returned distance value. This method applies rigid body transformations (rotation and translation) to SDF primitives by transforming the sample point using the inverse of the object's model matrix before evaluation. It solves the problem of animating or positioning individual SDF objects independently without modifying the underlying distance function definitions. Unlike direct geometry transformation, it preserves the analytical nature of the SDF by operating in the object's local coordinate space. It is chosen when rendering static primitives that undergo rigid motion in a scene. Motion-Compensated Block Warping is a technique for compressing dynamic Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDF) by predicting the current frame's geometry from the previous frame using estimated rigid body motion. It improves prediction accuracy over static methods by inverse-warping voxel samples from the target block into the previously reconstructed TSDF and resampling them via trilinear interpolation. Unlike global transformation methods, this approach operates on local blocks, allowing for piecewise-rigid motion estimation which is essential for complex, non-uniform scene dynamics. It is chosen for dynamic TSDF compression and streaming. This method applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to mesh vertices within an Embree ray-tracing geometry buffer. It solves the problem of updating mesh positions for dynamic scenes or rigid body transformations while maintaining the integrity of the source mesh data. It differs from Inverse Model Matrix Transformation for Distance Fields by modifying the actual vertex positions in the Embree buffer rather than transforming the query point in world space, and from Motion-Compensated Block Warping by operating on explicit mesh geometry rather than voxel blocks. A ray marching technique that integrates a deformed scene by marching in the undeformed space and mapping positions/normals to the deformed space using a Jacobian estimate. Step: 1. Initialize ssum to start and pos to ipos. 2. Loop up to MAXMARCHINGSTEPS: a. Calculate invjacobian by inverting the Jacobian estimated at pos with force. b. Calculate sundeformed as the absolute value of the scene SDF at pos. c. Accumulate sundeformed to ssum. d. Calculate uepsilon as ssum (ssum radpixel determinant(invjacobian)). e. If sundeformed < uepsilon, return vec4(pos, 1) indicating a hit. f. If ssum >= end, return vec4(0) indicating no hit (marched too far). g. If sundeformed < 3 uepsilon, advance pos by sundeformed normalized(invjacobian w). h. Otherwise (sundeformed >= 3 uepsilon), advance pos by sundeformed normalized(invjacobian w). 3. If the loop completes without returning, return vec4(0). Parameter: MAXMARCHINGSTEPS: The maximum number of iterations for the marching loop. radpixel: A constant used in the epsilon calculation for stopping criteria. Pitfall: The ODE solver (ode23) is commented out in the main loop, so the fallback to simple stepping is always used. To avoid overlapping where destination voxels overwrite source voxels before translation, the algorithm sets the Orient register so that translation starts from the source corner that is also situated in the destination primitive range. The relative translation is characterized by a vector (Tx, Ty, Tz). The position of the next voxel along the X-axis to be translated (X{dest}, Y{dest}, Z{dest}) is determined by incrementing the appropriate coordinate of the last voxel without performing an addition for every voxel. An algorithm for scaling voxel grids that avoids floating-point accumulation errors by using incremental updates. The scaling equations are X{dest} = X{src} Sx, Y{dest} = Y{src} Sy, Z{dest} = Z{src} Sz. To avoid overwriting source voxels before scaling, the starting corner of the room for the transformation is chosen based on the values of Sx, Sy, Sz. If scaling factors are greater than 1, forward scaling may produce holes due to volume increase without voxel increase. This is averted by 'back scaling': reversing the incremental transformation process. An animated tornado composed of a single Bezier segment. Radius increases with height (cone-like). Control points move in circular motion with different frequencies. No stretching. Rotation adds twisting. Angle changes with time. Density field moves up. Perlin noise creates cloud-like density. A deformation method using user-specified point pairs (source in undeformed space, target in deformed space) to find a mapping between them. Use a ray picker to allow the user to specify significant surface feature points by holding down the mouse and moving a point along the volume surface. Manipulate control points by dragging them along a specified surface or in view-aligned planes. Thin Plate Splines and Hierarchical B-Splines are examples of deformations used as landmark deformation functions. Implementing interactive widgets (e.g. leafer widget) as deformations directly in the shader. Discontinuities in deformation functions representing widgets require conditional branches, which are inefficient on some hardware. A simulated deformation field parametrized by amplitudes, lengthscales, and centers, mapping undeformed coordinates (X,Y,Z) to deformed coordinates (x,y,z). Deformed x-coordinate: x = X + A0 \exp(-r^2 / (2\sigma0^2)). Deformed y-coordinate: y = Y + A1 \exp(-r^2 / (2\sigma1^2)). Deformed z-coordinate: z = Z + A2 \exp(-r^2 / (2\sigma2^2)). Squared distance r^2 from center c: r^2 = (X - c0)^2 + (Y - c1)^2 + (Z - c2)^2. The concept of transforming SDFs via inverse matrices is a standard technique in ray marching, allowing for the composition of animated scenes from static primitives. Motion-Compensated Block Warping for TSDFs originates from research into dynamic 3D reconstruction and compression, where rigid body motion estimation is used to reduce the bitrate of streaming TSDF data. The Incremental Scaling Algorithm dates back to early voxel frame buffer processors, which addressed the computational cost and precision issues of scaling voxel grids in real-time. NTSL Marching appears in the context of the ntsl-graphics project, a research/experimental graphics engine, dealing with deformed scenes via Jacobian-based marching. tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, https://github.com/tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) The voxblt Engine: A Voxel Frame Buffer Processor, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh88/085-102, fetched 2026-10-26 Sculpting procedural noise: real-time rendering of interstellar dust clouds and solar flares, https://openalex.org/W4293584834, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Integrating Dynamic Deformations into Interactive Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym.eurovis06.219-226, fetched 2026-10-31 Neural rendering enables dynamic tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.20558, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Model Matrix Transformation for Distance Fields
head: Inverse Transformation for Rotation/Translation, SDF Model Transformations, Transforming SDFs, Transforming SDFs via Inverse Matrix
body: This method applies rigid transformations (rotation and translation) to Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitives during ray marching by evaluating the base distance function in the primitive's local coordinate space rather than world space. It enables animating or positioning individual scene objects without modifying the underlying geometric definitions or voxel grids. Unlike approaches that modify geometry data, this technique transforms the query point using the inverse of the object's model matrix. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{p} in world/camera space; a 4 \times 4 inverse model matrix M^{-1} representing the object's transformation (Translation, Rotation, Scale). Output: The signed distance value d at point \mathbf{p} for the transformed object. Data Structures: Inverse Model Matrix (M^{-1}): A 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix. In implementation, this is typically passed as a uniform variable to the shader or kernel. The matrix encodes rotation, translation, and uniform scaling. Steps: 1. Construct Model Matrix: On the host side (e.g., CPU/scripting environment), construct the model matrix M for the object using its current translation \mathbf{t}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, and scale s. 2. Compute Inverse: Calculate the inverse of the model matrix M^{-1}. 3. Transform Point: In the distance evaluation function, transform the world-space query point \mathbf{p} into the local space \mathbf{q} by multiplying \mathbf{p} (homogenized to \mathbf{p}' = [\mathbf{p}, 1]^T) by M^{-1}: \mathbf{q} = M^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} The resulting local point is \mathbf{q}{xyz}. 4. Evaluate Base SDF: Pass \mathbf{q}{xyz} to the base, untransformed SDF function f{base}: d = f{base}(\mathbf{q}{xyz}) 5. Handle Scaling: If the model matrix includes uniform scaling by factor s, the distance value must be scaled to preserve the Euclidean distance property: d{final} = s \cdot d Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def transformpoint(p, invmodelmatrix): """Transforms a world-space point p using a 4x4 inverse model matrix.""" x, y, z = p # Homogeneous multiplication: q = Minv [x, y, z, 1]^T qx = invmodelmatrix[0][0]x + invmodelmatrix[0][1]y + invmodelmatrix[0][2]z + invmodelmatrix[0][3] qy = invmodelmatrix[1][0]x + invmodelmatrix[1][1]y + invmodelmatrix[1][2]z + invmodelmatrix[1][3] qz = invmodelmatrix[2][0]x + invmodelmatrix[2][1]y + invmodelmatrix[2][2]z + invmodelmatrix[2][3] return (qx, qy, qz) def spheresdf(p): """Base SDF for a unit sphere at the origin.""" return math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[1]2 + p[2]2) - 1.0 def raymarch(origin, direction, invmodelmatrix, scalefactor=1.0, maxsteps=100, maxdist=100.0, epsilon=1e-4): """Standard SDF ray marcher using the inverse model matrix transformation.""" t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): p = (origin[0] + direction[0]t, origin[1] + direction[1]t, origin[2] + direction[2]t) q = transformpoint(p, invmodelmatrix) dist = spheresdf(q) dist = scalefactor if abs(dist) < epsilon: return t step = max(dist, epsilon) t += step if t > maxdist: return float('inf') return float('inf') Parameters: MatTorusInvModel (or generic Minv): A uniform 4 \times 4 matrix representing the inverse model transformation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Homogeneous Coordinates: Ensure the point is treated as a position (w=1) when multiplying by the transformation matrix, not a direction (w=0), to correctly apply translation. Non-Uniform Scaling: Non-uniform scaling distorts the distance field metric and is generally avoided in standard SDF ray marching. Applies the inverse transform to the entire viewing ray system (camera, lights) rather than individual sample points, reducing complexity for large volumetric datasets. Estimates rigid transforms per-block for temporal compression of TSDFs, minimizing prediction error between frames. Uses Embree's ray tracing kernel to handle mesh transformations, distinct from SDF evaluation. Handles scaling in distance fields through incremental adjustments. Evaluates deformations directly on fragments, potentially using vertex data. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point evaluation, as it involves a single matrix-vector multiplication and one base SDF call. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the inverse matrix uniform. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows independent animation of scene parts; preserves the static nature of base SDF definitions. Limitations: Only supports rigid transformations (rotation, translation) and uniform scaling effectively. When to use: Ideal for animating rigid objects in SDF scenes. When not to use: For non-rigid deformations or non-uniform scaling where metric preservation is critical. The technique originates from the foundational principles of ray marching and Signed Distance Functions, popularized by tutorials such as those by Jamie Wong and Adrian Booth. It is a standard practice in real-time graphics and procedural modeling to decouple geometry definition from scene layout. Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions, http://jamie-wong.com/2016/07/15/ray-marching-signed-distance-functions/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation..., https://adrianb.io/2016/10/01/raymarching.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Viewing Transformations for Volumes
head: Inverse Viewing Transformations, Inverse Volume Transform, Moving the camera instead of the volume
body: Inverse Viewing Transformations for Volumes applies geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling) to volumetric data by moving the viewing geometry—camera, lights, and pixels—in the opposite direction, rather than modifying the voxel grid. This approach avoids the computational bottleneck of per-voxel arithmetic for large datasets, reducing rotation and translation complexity from O(N{\text{voxels}}) to O(N{\text{pixels}} + N{\text{lights}}). Inputs: Volumetric data (voxel values or distance field values), volume spatial bounds (min/max coordinates for X, Y, Z), user-specified transformation parameters (rotation angles, translation vectors, scaling factors), and initial viewing geometry (camera eye position, light source positions, pixel coordinates). Outputs: Rendered image with the volume appearing transformed. Data Structures: Coordinate arrays storing unique 1D ordinate values per axis instead of per-voxel coordinates. The volume's spatial coordinates are stored in three separate 1-dimensional arrays: X{\text{ord}}, Y{\text{ord}}, and Z{\text{ord}}. These arrays store the distinct ordinate values defining the grid planes, allowing many voxels to be represented by relatively few numbers (e.g., a million voxels may be defined with as few as 100 numbers). Viewing geometry is stored as vectors for eye position, light positions, and pixel sample locations. Steps: 1. Center Coordinate Arrays: Adjust the coordinate arrays so the volume is centered at the origin (0,0,0). For each axis A \in \{X, Y, Z\}, calculate the span SA = \max(A{\text{ord}}) - \min(A{\text{ord}}). Subtract half the span from every value in the array: A'{\text{ord}}[i] = A{\text{ord}}[i] - \frac{SA}{2}. This step ensures that subsequent scaling operations are uniform and centered. 2. Apply Scaling (if applicable): If a scaling factor s is specified, modify the coordinate arrays directly. For each value in the centered arrays: A''{\text{ord}}[i] = A'{\text{ord}}[i] \times s. Scaling is applied to the coordinate arrays because inverse transformation of the eye/pixels cannot effectively scale the volume's internal resolution. 3. Compute Inverse Viewing Transform: Determine the transformation matrix M{\text{vol}} representing the user's desired volume transformation. Transform the viewing geometry by the inverse matrix M{\text{vol}}^{-1} (opposite direction). Rotation: If the user wants to rotate the volume by angle \theta around axis K, rotate the camera eye, all light sources, and all pixel sample coordinates by -\theta around axis K. Translation: If the user wants to translate the volume by vector \vec{T}, translate the camera eye, light sources, and pixel coordinates by -\vec{T}. 4. Ray Marching / Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering or distance field ray marching using the transformed viewing geometry and the original (or scaled) volume data. The rays intersect the untransformed volume as if the volume itself had been transformed. Parameters: Scaling factor s (user-specified); rotation angles and translation vectors (user-specified). Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Directly transforming voxel positions for rotation or translation is computationally prohibitive for large volumes (e.g., >1 million voxels), requiring ~9 multiplications and ~9 additions per voxel. Scaling cannot be achieved by simply moving the camera or pixels. The method assumes a regular grid structure for the 1D coordinate array optimization. A method for editing learned implicit fields by manipulating object codes in 3D space before 2D projection to avoid multi-view inconsistencies. It maps sample points to an inverse space and uses projected 2D labels to resolve occlusions, differing from direct editing. Time Complexity: O(N{\text{pixels}} + N{\text{lights}}) for rotation and translation, significantly faster than the O(N{\text{voxels}}) cost of direct volume transformation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for separate 1D coordinate arrays (X, Y, Z) instead of per-voxel coordinates, reducing memory overhead for coordinate data. A million voxels may be defined with as few as 100 numbers for coordinates if the grid is regular. Strengths: Avoids per-voxel arithmetic for rotation/translation; efficient for large datasets; preserves original voxel data integrity. Limitations: Scaling requires modifying coordinate arrays; assumes regular grid structure for the coordinate array optimization; does not handle irregular spacing without additional interpolation logic. When to use: When rotating or translating large volumetric datasets where per-voxel transformation is too slow. When not to use: When non-uniform scaling of the grid structure is required without modifying the underlying data structure, or when the volume data is irregularly spaced in a way that prevents simple 1D array representation. This technique was described in a report on volumetric rendering techniques for aerodynamic flow field data. The author noted that direct transformation of data volumes was computationally expensive for large datasets (e.g., >1 million voxels). The method leverages the uniform spacing of voxel locations to store coordinates in 1D arrays, enabling efficient scaling and centering. DTIC ADA202661: Volumetric Rendering Techniques for the Display of Three-Dimensional Aerodynamic Flow Field Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA202661, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Query Algorithm
head: Object Manipulator (Inverse Query)
body:
The Inverse Query Algorithm edits learned implicit fields by manipulating object codes in 3D space before 2D projection, thereby avoiding multi-view inconsistencies. It solves the problem of how to update the density (\sigma), color (c), and object codes (o) of sample points along a query ray so that the rendered novel view reflects the manipulated geometry while explicitly handling occlusions and collisions. It sets itself apart from direct editing by mapping sample points to an inverse space to determine target membership, and uses projected 2D labels to resolve occlusion inaccuracies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Target object code ot: A hard one-hot vector with H+1 dimensions, where H is the number of objects and the last dimension represents background/emptiness. Manipulation parameters: Translation \Delta p = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), rotation matrix R{3	imes3}, and scaling factor t > 0. Sample points \{p1, \dots, pk, \dots, pK\} along a specific query light ray r. Segment lengths \{\delta1, \dots, \deltaK\} along the ray. Projected pixel object code \hat{o}: The object code of the ray before manipulation, obtained from 2D label supervision. Outputs: Final pixel color  ar{c} and object code  ar{o} after manipulation. Data Structures: Object codes are stored as hard one-hot vectors of size H+1. Implicit codes consist of density \sigma (scalar), color c (3D vector), and object code o (one-hot vector). Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Convert all object codes into hard one-hot vectors. Obtain the projected pixel object code \hat{o} for the ray r from the unmanipulated scene. 2. Ray Loop: Iterate through each sample point pk along the ray r: 1. Inverse Point Calculation: Compute the inverse 3D point p'k using the formula: p'k =  rac{1}{t} R^{-1} (pk - \Delta p) where pk is the current sample point, t is the scale, R is the rotation matrix, and \Delta p is the translation. 2. Query Codes: Query the original implicit codes \{\sigmak, ck, ok\} for pk and the inverse implicit codes \{\sigma'k, c'k, o'k\} for p'k using the learned implicit field networks. 3. Occlusion Handling: If the original point belongs to the target object (ok = ot) but the projected code indicates a different object (ok 
eq \hat{o}), update the original object code to the projected code: ok \leftarrow \hat{o}. This corrects inaccuracies in object codes behind surfaces due to insufficient optimization. 4. Collision Detection: If the original point is not the target object (ok 
eq ot), is not background (o{H+1} 
eq 1), and the inverse point is the target object (o'k = ot), a collision is detected. Exit the loop for this ray. 5. Code Update: Determine the new implicit codes \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} for pk based on the membership of pk and p'k relative to ot: Non-target to Target: If ok 
eq ot and o'k = ot, set \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{\sigma'k, c'k, o'k\}. Target to Target: If ok = ot and o'k = ot, set \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{\sigma'k, c'k, o'k\}. Target to Non-target: If ok = ot and o'k 
eq ot, set \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{0, 0, 0\}. Non-target to Non-target: If ok 
eq ot and o'k 
eq ot, keep the original codes: \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{\sigmak, ck, ok\}. 3. Volume Rendering: After processing all K points, compute the final pixel color  ar{c} and object code  ar{o} using the volume rendering equation:  ar{c} = \sum{k=1}^{K}  ar{T}k  ar{\alpha}k  ar{c}k, \quad  ar{o} = \sum{k=1}^{K}  ar{T}k  ar{\alpha}k  ar{o}k where the transmittance  ar{T}k and alpha  ar{\alpha}k are defined as:  ar{T}k = \exp\left(-\sum{i=1}^{k-1}  ar{\sigma}i \deltaiight), \quad  ar{\alpha}k = 1 - \exp(- ar{\sigma}k \deltak) and \deltai is the distance along the ray between consecutive sample points p{i-1} and pi (with p0 at the camera origin). Pseudocode: def inversequeryalgorithm(pklist, deltas, ot, deltap, Rinv, t, getimplicitcodes, getprojectedcode): """ pklist: List of 3D points [p1,..., pK] along the ray deltas: List of segment lengths [delta1,..., deltaK] along the ray ot: Target object one-hot vector (size H+1) deltap: Translation vector (size 3) Rinv: Precomputed inverse rotation matrix (3x3) t: Scale factor (float > 0) getimplicitcodes: Function returning (sigma, c, o) for a point getprojectedcode: Function returning the projected object code ohat for the ray """ # Preprocessing ohat = getprojectedcode() editedsigma = [] editedc = [] editedo = [] for pk in pklist: # 1. Compute inverse point: p'k = (1/t) Rinv (pk - deltap) diff = [pk[i] - deltap[i] for i in range(3)] rinvdiff = [sum(Rinv[i][j] diff[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] pprimek = [rinvdiff[i] / t for i in range(3)] # 2. Query codes sigmak, ck, ok = getimplicitcodes(pk) sigmaprimek, cprimek, oprimek = getimplicitcodes(pprimek) # 3. Occlusion handling if ok == ot and ok != ohat: ok = ohat[:] # 4. Collision detection istarget = (ok == ot) isbackground = (ok[-1] == 1) isinversetarget = (oprimek == ot) if not istarget and not isbackground and isinversetarget: break # 5. Update codes if not istarget and isinversetarget: newsigma, newc, newo = sigmaprimek, cprimek, oprimek elif istarget and isinversetarget: newsigma, newc, newo = sigmaprimek, cprimek, oprimek elif istarget and not isinversetarget: newsigma, newc, newo = 0.0, [0.0] len(ck), [0.0] len(ok) else: newsigma, newc, newo = sigmak, ck, ok editedsigma.append(newsigma) editedc.append(newc) editedo.append(newo) # 6. Volume Rendering K = len(editedsigma) if K == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.0] len(ot) T = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] finalo = [0.0] len(ot) for k in range(K): sigma = editedsigma[k] c = editedc[k] o = editedo[k] delta = deltas[k] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) finalcolor = [finalcolor[i] + T alpha c[i] for i in range(3)] finalo = [finalo[i] + T alpha o[i] for i in range(len(ot))] T = T (1.0 - alpha) return finalcolor, finalo Parameters: H: Number of objects. The object code dimension is H+1. \Delta d: A hyper-parameter for the object field loss, set to 0.05 meters in experiments. t: Scaling factor, t > 0. Pitfalls: Collisions: Objects may collide during manipulation. This is addressed by the emptiness score in the last dimension of the object code o. Occlusion Inaccuracy: Object codes behind surface points may be inaccurate due to insufficient optimization. This is mitigated by using the projected object code \hat{o}, which is more accurate due to 2D label supervision. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points K per ray, as it requires two implicit field queries per point (original and inverse) and a loop over K points. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to K to store the edited codes for volume rendering. Strengths: Handles occlusions and collisions explicitly; allows editing in 3D space before projection to maintain consistency. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of projected codes \hat{o}; relies on the accuracy of the inverse transformation and the learned implicit fields. When to use: When manipulating specific objects in a decomposed 3D scene represented by implicit fields, especially when occlusion and collision handling are critical. The Inverse Query Algorithm was introduced in the paper "DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images". It addresses the challenges of editing implicit fields by leveraging 2D supervision to correct 3D ambiguities. The method is part of a pipeline that decomposes 3D scenes into object fields and a background field, allowing for individual object manipulation. DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07227v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Motion-Compensated Block Warping
head: Inter-frame motion compensation
body: Motion-Compensated Block Warping is a technique for compressing temporal sequences of Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDF) by predicting the current frame's geometry from the previous frame using estimated rigid body motion. It solves the problem of high residual energy in dynamic scenes where objects move between frames, allowing the encoder to transmit only the motion parameters and the small residual differences rather than the full geometry. It differs from static deformation handling by explicitly estimating and transmitting a per-block 6-DoF transform to align the previous frame's data with the current frame's target block. The method operates on a block-based sparse TSDF representation. The scene is decomposed into voxel blocks. For each block in the target frame t, the algorithm estimates a rigid transform that best aligns the reconstructed TSDF from the previous frame t-1 to the current target block. Inputs: st^{(b)}: The TSDF values for block b at frame t. \hat{s}{t-1}^{(b)}: The reconstructed (decoded) TSDF values for block b at frame t-1. \Omega: The set of sample positions (voxel centers) within block b. Outputs: \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}: The optimal rotation (Euler angles) and translation (3D vector) parameters. Residual coefficients: The difference between the current block and the warped predictor, encoded in the transform domain (e.g., DCT). TSDF Block: A 3D grid of voxel values. In the source implementation, blocks are stored in a GPU-side spatial hash table (voxel hashing) for fast random access. Motion Parameters: A 6-DoF rigid transform consisting of translation \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (parameterized as Euler angles). 1. Neighborhood Assembly: Assemble a stitched 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood of blocks from the previous frame's reconstructed TSDF \hat{s}{t-1} centered on the corresponding block location. This ensures that trilinear interpolation remains valid even when warped sample positions fall into adjacent blocks or between voxel centers. 2. Motion Estimation: Estimate the rigid transform (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) that minimizes the squared difference between the warped previous frame and the current frame. This is done using a damped Gauss-Newton optimization procedure. 3. Inverse Warping (Prediction): For each sample position \mathbf{p}i \in \Omega in the target block b at frame t, compute the corresponding position in the previous frame using the estimated transform: \mathbf{q}i = \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) where \mathbf{T} maps current frame coordinates to previous frame coordinates. 4. Trilinear Interpolation: Evaluate the TSDF value at the warped location \mathbf{q}i by trilinearly interpolating the values from the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood assembled in Step 1. This forms the motion-compensated predictor \hat{s}{t-1}^{(b)}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})). 5. Residual Encoding: Compute the residual between the current block st^{(b)} and the predictor. Encode the transform-domain coefficients of this residual. 6. Side Information Encoding: Encode the motion parameters \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{t} as side information. The residual for sample i is defined as: \epsiloni(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) = \hat{s}{t-1}^{(b)}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})) - st^{(b)}(\mathbf{p}i) The optimization objective is to minimize the sum of squared residuals: \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}:= \arg \min{\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}} \sum{i \in \Omega} \epsiloni(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})^2 The update step in the Gauss-Newton algorithm is calculated as: \Delta \mathbf{p} = -(J^\top J + \lambda I)^{-1} J^\top \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} where J is the Jacobian of the residuals with respect to the parameters, \lambda is a damping factor for numerical stability, and \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} is the vector of residuals. Damping factor \lambda: A small value for numerical stability in the Gauss-Newton solver. Translation clamp: 1 voxel per iteration. Rotation clamp: 5 degrees per iteration. Termination threshold: The optimization terminates when the decrease in the objective function falls below a specific threshold. Insufficient Data: If too few reliable samples are available or the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood is incomplete (e.g., at the boundary of the volume), the method falls back to zero-motion prediction (\mathbf{t} = 0, \mathbf{r} = 0) for that block. Divergence: Large motion estimates can cause the Gauss-Newton solver to diverge. Clamping the per-iteration update magnitudes prevents this. Fractional Positions: Rigid motion maps integer voxel centers to fractional positions. Trilinear interpolation is required to evaluate the TSDF at these non-integer locations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def motioncompensatedblockwarping(targetblockb, prevframereconstructedtsdf, blockindex, blocksize): # 1. Assemble 3x3x3 neighborhood from previous frame neighborhood = assemble3x3x3neighborhood(prevframereconstructedtsdf, blockindex, blocksize) # 2. Estimate motion using damped Gauss-Newton r = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Euler angles (rad) t = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Translation (voxels) dampinglambda = 1e-4 maxiterations = 10 convergencethreshold = 1e-6 preverror = float('inf') for iteration in range(maxiterations): residuals = [] jacobianrows = [] for pi in getvoxelcenters(blocksize): # T maps current position to previous frame space for sampling warpedpos = applyrigidtransform(pi, r, t) predval = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, warpedpos) currval = targetblockb[getindex(pi, blocksize)] residual = predval - currval residuals.append(residual) jacobianrow = computejacobianrow(pi, r, t, neighborhood, blocksize) jacobianrows.append(jacobianrow) residuals = np.array(residuals) J = np.array(jacobianrows) # Solve for update step: deltap = -(J^T J + lambda I)^-1 J^T epsilon JTJ = J.T @ J JTJdamped = JTJ + dampinglambda np.eye(6) try: deltap = np.linalg.solve(JTJdamped, -J.T @ residuals) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: break # Clamp updates translationupdate = deltap[3:6] rotationupdate = deltap[0:3] translationupdate = np.clip(translationupdate, -1.0, 1.0) rotationupdate = np.clip(rotationupdate, -math.radians(5), math.radians(5)) t = t + translationupdate r = r + rotationupdate currenterror = np.sum(residuals2) if iteration > 0 and abs(preverror - currenterror) < convergencethreshold: break preverror = currenterror # 3. Generate Predictor and Residual predictor = np.zeroslike(targetblockb) for pi in getvoxelcenters(blocksize): warpedpos = inverserigidtransform(pi, r, t) predval = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, warpedpos) predictor[getindex(pi, blocksize)] = predval residual = targetblockb - predictor # 4. Encode Residual and Motion residualcoeffs = encodetransformdomain(residual) return (r, t), residualcoeffs def assemble3x3x3neighborhood(tsdf, blockindex, blocksize): """Retrieves a 3x3x3 grid of blocks centered on blockindex.""" volume = np.zeros((3 blocksize, 3 blocksize, 3 blocksize)) for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): neighboridx = (blockindex[0] + dx, blockindex[1] + dy, blockindex[2] + dz) if neighboridx in tsdf: block = tsdf[neighboridx] volume[dx blocksize:(dx + 1) blocksize, dy blocksize:(dy + 1) blocksize, dz blocksize:(dz + 1) blocksize] = block return volume def getvoxelcenters(blocksize): """Returns list of (x, y, z) coordinates for voxel centers in a block.""" centers = [] for x in range(blocksize): for y in range(blocksize): for z in range(blocksize): centers.append((x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5)) return centers def getindex(p, blocksize): """Maps 3D coordinate to flat array index.""" x, y, z = p return int(x) + int(y) blocksize + int(z) blocksize blocksize def applyrigidtransform(p, r, t): """Applies rigid transform T(p) = Rp + t.""" R = eulertorotationmatrix(r) parr = np.array(p) return np.dot(R, parr) + t def inverserigidtransform(p, r, t): """Applies inverse rigid transform T^-1(p) = R^T(p - t).""" R = eulertorotationmatrix(r) Rinv = R.T parr = np.array(p) return np.dot(Rinv, parr - t) def eulertorotationmatrix(r): """Converts Euler angles (rad) to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" rx, ry, rz = r Rx = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, math.cos(rx), -math.sin(rx)], [0, math.sin(rx), math.cos(rx)]]) Ry = np.array([[math.cos(ry), 0, math.sin(ry)], [0, 1, 0], [-math.sin(ry), 0, math.cos(ry)]]) Rz = np.array([[math.cos(rz), -math.sin(rz), 0], [math.sin(rz), math.cos(rz), 0], [0, 0, 1]]) return Rz @ Ry @ Rx def trilinearinterpolate(volume, point): """Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D volume at a fractional point.""" x, y, z = point x0, y0, z0 = int(math.floor(x)), int(math.floor(y)), int(math.floor(z)) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 def clamp(v, minv, maxv): return max(minv, min(v, maxv)) v000 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v100 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v010 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v110 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v001 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v101 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v011 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v111 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] c00 = v000 (1 - dx) + v100 dx c01 = v010 (1 - dx) + v110 dx c10 = v001 (1 - dx) + v101 dx c11 = v011 (1 - dx) + v111 dx c0 = c00 (1 - dy) + c01 dy c1 = c10 (1 - dy) + c11 dy return c0 (1 - dz) + c1 dz def computejacobianrow(p, r, t, neighborhood, blocksize): """Computes Jacobian row for sample p using finite difference.""" eps = 1e-5 jrow = np.zeros(6) basepred = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, applyrigidtransform(p, r, t)) for k in range(6): perturbedr = r.copy() perturbedt = t.copy() if k < 3: perturbedr[k] += eps else: perturbedt[k - 3] += eps perturbedpred = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, applyrigidtransform(p, perturbedr, perturbedt)) jrow[k] = (perturbedpred - basepred) / eps return jrow def encodetransformdomain(residual): """Applies standard 3D DCT to residual coefficients.""" # Standard 3D DCT implementation omitted for brevity; applies separable 1D DCT along each axis. return residual # Placeholder for actual DCT transform This is the core optimization subroutine used within Motion-Compensated Block Warping. It estimates the 6-DoF rigid transform for a specific block by aligning TSDF samples using a damped Gauss-Newton procedure. It is chosen when precise local motion estimation is required to minimize residual energy. It differs from global motion estimation by operating on a per-block basis, allowing for independent motion of different parts of the scene. Key implementation details include clamping translation updates to 1 voxel and rotation updates to 5 degrees per step to prevent divergence, and falling back to zero-motion if the neighborhood is incomplete or samples are unreliable. A motion modeling approach that decouples coarse and fine-grained motion to mitigate inaccuracies in deformation networks, preventing the querying of wrong grid cells. It predicts coarse motion mc corresponding to motion between grid cells, and fine-grained motion mf that operates only within grid cells. The step size \alpha controls the magnitude of motion and is set to 0.0001 for synthetic scenes, close to the size of a single grid cell. The deformation network \Phid is implemented as a 3-layer MLP with a width of 64. Time Complexity: The motion estimation step involves an iterative Gauss-Newton optimization. The cost depends on the number of samples in the block, the number of iterations, and the cost of trilinear interpolation and Jacobian computation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the current block, the previous frame's reconstructed TSDF, and the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood for interpolation. The source uses a sparse representation with a GPU-side spatial hash table, reducing memory usage for empty space. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively reduces residual energy for rigidly moving objects, leading to better compression ratios for dynamic TSDF volumes. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of rigid motion within each block. Non-rigid deformations within a block will not be well-compensated. Requires accurate motion estimation, which can be computationally expensive. When to use: Suitable for compressing dynamic scenes with significant rigid body motion, such as in 3D reconstruction from video sequences. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes with significant non-rigid deformation or where motion estimation is unreliable (e.g., textureless regions, occlusions). The method originates from the paper "Implicit Surface Compression -- with Good Old Discrete Cosine Transform and Motion Compensation". It is part of a codec for compressing sparse TSDF volumes, leveraging traditional image compression techniques (DCT) and video compression concepts (motion compensation) for 3D data. The implementation uses voxel hashing for sparse storage. name: Mesh Transformation via Embree RTC
head: xformRtcMeshOnly
body: This method applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to mesh vertices within an Embree ray tracing scene buffer while preserving the original vertex positions in the source mesh data. Inputs: A source mesh with vertex positions \mathbf{v}{orig}. A 4x4 transformation matrix M. An Embree geometry object containing the vertex buffer. Outputs: Updated vertex buffer in the Embree geometry. The source mesh remains unchanged. Data Structures: Vertex buffer: Array of 3D floats (x, y, z). Transformation matrix: 4x4 float matrix consistent with Embree's expectations. Steps: 1. Retrieve the vertex buffer pointer from the Embree geometry using rtcGetGeometryBufferData. 2. Initialize a running sum vector averagePt to (0, 0, 0, 1) and maxlen to 0. 3. Iterate through each vertex i from 0 to N-1 (where N is the vertex count): a. Reset the current vertex \mathbf{v}i in the buffer to its original position \mathbf{v}{orig, i}. b. Transform the vertex: \mathbf{v}' = M \cdot \mathbf{v}{orig, i} (using homogeneous coordinates with w=1). c. Update the buffer with the transformed coordinates: \mathbf{v}i.x = \mathbf{v}'[0], \mathbf{v}i.y = \mathbf{v}'[1], \mathbf{v}i.z = \mathbf{v}'[2]. d. Accumulate the transformed position into the running sum: averagePt += \mathbf{v}'. e. Compute the distance d from \mathbf{v}' to the current running centroid \mathbf{c}i = \text{averagePt} / \max(1, i). f. If d > \text{maxlen}, update \text{maxlen} = d. 4. After the loop, compute the final centroid \mathbf{cp} = \text{averagePt} / N. 5. Commit the geometry and scene updates in Embree. Pitfalls: The incremental computation of maxlen (distance to the running centroid) is mathematically incorrect for finding the maximum distance from the final centroid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def transformmeshembree(vertices, originalpositions, M, N): # vertices: array of objects with.x,.y,.z attributes # M: 4x4 matrix (list of lists) # N: vertex count averagept = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] maxlen = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Reset to original vorig = originalpositions[i] vh = [vorig[0], vorig[1], vorig[2], 1.0] # Transform v = M vh vtrans = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for r in range(4): for c in range(4): vtrans[r] += M[r][c] vh[c] # Update buffer vertices[i].x = vtrans[0] vertices[i].y = vtrans[1] vertices[i].z = vtrans[2] # Accumulate averagept[0] += vtrans[0] averagept[1] += vtrans[1] averagept[2] += vtrans[2] # averagept[3] remains 1.0 per source logic # Compute distance to running centroid divisor = 1 if i == 0 else i centroidx = averagept[0] / divisor centroidy = averagept[1] / divisor centroidz = averagept[2] / divisor d = ((vtrans[0] - centroidx)2 + (vtrans[1] - centroidy)2 + (vtrans[2] - centroidz)2)0.5 if d > maxlen: maxlen = d # Final centroid cpx = averagept[0] / N cpy = averagept[1] / N cpz = averagept[2] / N # Commit geometry and scene updates in Embree Applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to all vertices and normals of a mesh. It differs from its parent Mesh Transformation via Embree RTC by operating directly on the mesh data structure rather than managing Embree's internal buffer state, and from Mesh Transformation for Printable Volume by lacking volume-constraint logic or axis alignment.
