name: Mesh Transformation
body: Applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to all vertices and normals of a mesh, typically to move geometry from a local object frame to a world frame or to apply kinematic transforms to robot links. Inputs: mesh: Mesh object containing vertex positions and optional normals. xf: 4x4 transformation matrix. Outputs: Updated mesh with transformed vertices and normals. Data Structures: mesh->vertices: Array of 3D vectors. mesh->normals: Array of 3D vectors, optional. xf: 4x4 matrix. Steps: 1. Transform Vertices: Iterate over vertices i from 0 to nv-1. Compute the transformed vertex v'i = xf \cdot vi. Update mesh->vertices[i] = v'i. 2. Transform Normals (if present): Compute the normal transformation matrix nxf from xf. Iterate over normals i from 0 to nv-1. Compute n'i = nxf \cdot ni. Renormalize ni \leftarrow n'i / \|n'i\|. 3. Update Bounding Volumes: If the mesh has valid bounding boxes or spheres, invalidate them and recompute them based on the new vertex positions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyxform(mesh, xf): nv = len(mesh.vertices) # 1. Transform vertices for i in range(nv): v = mesh.vertices[i] x = xf[0][0]v[0] + xf[0][1]v[1] + xf[0][2]v[2] + xf[0][3] y = xf[1][0]v[0] + xf[1][1]v[1] + xf[1][2]v[2] + xf[1][3] z = xf[2][0]v[0] + xf[2][1]v[1] + xf[2][2]v[2] + xf[2][3] mesh.vertices[i] = (x, y, z) # 2. Transform normals if mesh.normals is not None: # Compute normal transformation matrix: inverse transpose of upper-left 3x3 of xf M = [[xf[r][c] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] Minv = invert3x3(M) nxf = [[Minv[c][r] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] for i in range(nv): n = mesh.normals[i] nx = nxf[0][0]n[0] + nxf[0][1]n[1] + nxf[0][2]n[2] ny = nxf[1][0]n[0] + nxf[1][1]n[1] + nxf[1][2]n[2] nz = nxf[2][0]n[0] + nxf[2][1]n[1] + nxf[2][2]n[2] length = (nxnx + nyny + nznz)0.5 if length > 0: mesh.normals[i] = (nx/length, ny/length, nz/length) else: mesh.normals[i] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 3. Update bounding volumes if mesh.boundingbox is not None: minval = (float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')) maxval = (float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')) for v in mesh.vertices: minval = tuple(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(minval, v)) maxval = tuple(max(a, b) for a, b in zip(maxval, v)) mesh.boundingbox.min = minval mesh.boundingbox.max = maxval mesh.boundingbox.valid = True def invert3x3(m): a, b, c = m[0] d, e, f = m[1] g, h, i = m[2] det = a(ei - fh) - b(di - fg) + c(dh - eg) if det == 0: raise ValueError("Matrix is singular") invdet = 1.0 / det return [ [(ei - fh)invdet, (ch - bi)invdet, (bf - ce)invdet], [(fg - di)invdet, (ai - cg)invdet, (cd - af)invdet], [(dh - eg)invdet, (bg - ah)invdet, (ae - bd)invdet] ] Parameters: xf: 4x4 transformation matrix. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Matrices: If the 3x3 linear part of xf is singular, the inverse transpose cannot be computed. Bounding Volume Recomputation: Failing to update bounding volumes after transformation leads to incorrect culling or intersection tests. Computes a 4x4 transformation matrix to scale, rotate, and translate a mesh so it fits within a specified printable volume, typically aligning the largest dimension with the z-axis. It differs from generic mesh transformations by incorporating volume constraints and automatic axis alignment. Time Complexity: O(n) for vertices and normals, where n is the number of vertices. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory if done in-place. Strengths: Simple, efficient, and standard approach for applying rigid or affine transforms to mesh geometry. Limitations: Does not handle dynamic topology changes. Requires careful handling of normals for non-uniform scaling. When to Use: When moving mesh data between coordinate frames (e.g., object to world, link to base). When Not to Use: When the transformation involves non-linear deformations. Not given in the sources. Used in sparse voxel DAGs and robotic SDF visualization. prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, https://github.com/prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - UM-ARM-Lab/pytorchvolumetric: Volumetric structures such as..., https://github.com/UM-ARM-Lab/pytorchvolumetric, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Mesh Transformation for Printable Volume
body: Computes a 4x4 transformation matrix to scale, rotate, and translate a mesh so it fits within a specified printable volume, typically aligning the largest dimension with the z-axis. It differs from generic mesh transformations by incorporating volume constraints and automatic axis alignment. Inputs: mesh: A mesh object with vertex positions and an axis-aligned bounding box (bbox). printsize: A 3D vector [x, y, z] defining the maximum printable dimensions. size (optional): A 3D vector specifying a target size. Outputs: toworld: A 4x4 transformation matrix mapping local mesh coordinates to world/printable coordinates. Data Structures: bbox: Axis-aligned bounding box with fields min (3D vector) and max (3D vector). extents: 3D vector where extents[i] = bbox.max[i] - bbox.min[i]. Steps and Formulas: 1. Compute Extents: Calculate extmax = max(bbox.extents()). 2. Determine Rotation Axis: Identify the axis of maximum extent: axismax = select(bbox.extents() == extmax, 1.0, 0.0). If axismax is not (0, 0, 1), compute rotaxis = cross(axismax, (0, 0, 1)) and rotation matrix R as a 90° rotation around rotaxis. 3. Center in XY Plane: Extract vertex positions, mask non-z dimensions to find the 2D footprint, compute the minimum enclosing circle center Cxy and radius r, and compute translation Txy to center the object at the origin in the XY plane. 4. Compute Scale Factors (default): Calculate sz = printsize.z / extmax and sxy = 0.5 printsize.xy / r. Take s = min(sz, sxy). 5. Assemble Transform (default): toworld = S(s) @ R @ Txy, where S(s) is a uniform scale matrix. 6. Assemble Transform (size provided): If size is provided, check if any component of size exceeds printsize. If so, raise an error. Compute mesh center c = 0.5 (bbox.min + bbox.max). Compute scale factors s' = size / extmax (element-wise division of the size vector by the scalar extmax). Compute toworld = S(s') @ T(-c), where S(s') is a non-uniform scale matrix and T(-c) is a translation by -c. This branch skips rotation and XY centering. Parameters: printsize: Maximum printable dimensions. size: Optional target dimensions. Edge Cases: If extmax is 0, division by zero occurs; guard against empty meshes. If axismax equals (0, 0, 1), no rotation is needed. If size exceeds printsize, an error is raised. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemeshtransform(mesh, printsize, size=None): bbox = mesh.bbox extents = bbox.max - bbox.min extmax = max(extents) if extmax == 0: raise ValueError("Empty mesh") # Rotation axismax = [1.0 if extents[i] == extmax else 0.0 for i in range(3)] if axismax != [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]: rotaxis = cross(axismax, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) rotmat = rotatematrix(rotaxis, 90.0) else: rotmat = identitymatrix() # XY Centering vertices2d = [(v.x, v.y) for v in mesh.vertices] cxy, r = minenclosingcircle(vertices2d) tr = translatematrix([-cxy[0], -cxy[1], 0.0]) if size is None: sz = printsize.z / extmax sxy = 0.5 printsize.xy / r s = min(sz, sxy) scalemat = scalematrix([s, s, s]) toworld = scalemat @ rotmat @ tr else: if any(size[i] > printsize[i] for i in range(3)): raise ValueError("size exceeds printsize") c = 0.5 (bbox.min + bbox.max) scalefactors = [size[i] / extmax for i in range(3)] scalemat = scalematrix(scalefactors) tc = translatematrix([-c.x, -c.y, -c.z]) toworld = scalemat @ tc return toworld Calculates scale and translation factors to align a surface mesh in micron coordinates with a volume defined by voxel size and volume size. It initializes default surfaceScale to 0.00161 and surfaceTranslation to [-313.7, -147.5, -86.5]. If units is 'micron', it calculates micronSize as volSize mapped to e \times \text{voxelSize}[i]. If sizeMax (max of micronSize) > 0, surfaceScale is set to 1 / \text{sizeMax}; otherwise, it is 1. surfaceTranslation is set to micronSize mapped to -e / 2 for each element. It returns an object { surfaceScale: number, surfaceTranslation: [number, number, number] }. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of vertices, due to bounding box and miniball computation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store vertex positions for miniball calculation. Strengths: Automatically orients the object for optimal printing; handles volume constraints. Limitations: The size branch ignores rotation and XY centering, which may lead to suboptimal orientation if the mesh is not already aligned. Originated in the context of inverse rendering for tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing. It is used to prepare meshes for 3D printing by ensuring they fit within the printer's build volume and are oriented correctly. The surface alignment variant is used in web-based volume viewers for scientific visualization. name: Incremental Scaling Algorithm
body: The Incremental Scaling Algorithm applies uniform or non-uniform scaling transformations to voxel grids by computing destination coordinates through iterative addition rather than full matrix multiplication. It solves the computational bottleneck of per-voxel scaling in large volumes by exploiting spatial coherence between neighboring voxels, reducing the arithmetic cost of coordinate transformation to simple additions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Source voxel grid defined by bounds (X{src}, Y{src}, Z{src}) to (X{src\end}, Y{src\end}, Z{src\end}). Input: Scaling factors Sx, Sy, Sz. Input: Destination grid bounds (Xs, Ys, Zs) to (XE, YE, ZE). Output: Destination voxel grid with scaled geometry. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on integer voxel coordinates. Intermediate floating-point coordinates are used for the incremental stepping to maintain precision before rounding to the nearest integer voxel index. Method: The standard scaling relationship maps a source coordinate to a destination coordinate: X{dest} = X{src} Sx Y{dest} = Y{src} Sy Z{dest} = Z{src} Sz Direct computation requires a multiplication for every voxel. The incremental algorithm derives the next coordinate from the previous one by observing that incrementing the source index by 1 scales to an increment of Sx in the destination: X{next} = X{prev} + Sx Y{next} = Y{prev} + Sy Z{next} = Z{prev} + Sz Thus, the next transformed coordinate is obtained by adding the respective scaling factor to the predecessor's coordinate and rounding the results to integer coordinates. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: 1. Holes in Forward Scaling: If any scaling factor is greater than 1, the destination volume expands without a proportional increase in voxels, producing holes in the scaled primitive. 2. Back Scaling: To avert holes, the algorithm reverses the transformation process. It transforms two opposite corners of the source room to find two opposite corners in the destination room, then steps through the destination room. At each destination point, coordinates are reverse-transformed by multiplying by (1/Sx, 1/Sy, 1/Sz) to determine the source voxel value. 3. Parallel Stepping: A more efficient back-scaling variant steps through the source and destination rooms in parallel. The increments for stepping through the source room are (X{incr}/Sx, Y{incr}/Sy, Z{incr}/Sz), where X{incr}, Y{incr}, Z{incr} are the steps used in the destination room. 4. Overwriting: If the source and destination grids share memory, voxels may be overwritten before they are read. Precautions are taken by properly choosing the starting corner of the transformation loop based on the signs of Sx, Sy, Sz. Pseudocode: The following implements back-scaling to prevent holes when S > 1. It assumes the destination bounds are known and the source bounds are derived or known. The direct back-mapping is mathematically equivalent to the parallel stepping variant where the destination steps by 1 and the source steps by 1/S. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalscaling(sourcegrid, destbounds, scalefactors): """ sourcegrid: 3D array of voxel values indexed as [z][y][x] destbounds: tuple (Xs, Ys, Zs, XE, YE, ZE) defining destination voxel range scalefactors: tuple (Sx, Sy, Sz) """ Sx, Sy, Sz = scalefactors Xs, Ys, Zs, XE, YE, ZE = destbounds invSx, invSy, invSz = 1.0 / Sx, 1.0 / Sy, 1.0 / Sz # Initialize destination grid with background value 0 destwidth = XE - Xs + 1 destdepth = ZE - Zs + 1 destheight = YE - Ys + 1 destgrid = [[[0 for in range(destwidth)] for in range(destdepth)] for in range(destheight)] srcwidth = len(sourcegrid[0][0]) srcdepth = len(sourcegrid[0]) srcheight = len(sourcegrid) # Choose starting corner based on scale factors to avoid overwriting # (Exact traversal direction logic depends on Sx, Sy, Sz signs) for y in range(Ys, YE + 1): for z in range(Zs, ZE + 1): for x in range(Xs, XE + 1): # Reverse transform: map destination integer coordinate to source space srcx = x invSx srcy = y invSy srcz = z invSz # Round to nearest integer voxel index in source srcix = int(srcx + 0.5) if srcx >= 0 else int(srcx - 0.5) srciy = int(srcy + 0.5) if srcy >= 0 else int(srcy - 0.5) srciz = int(srcz + 0.5) if srcz >= 0 else int(srcz - 0.5) # Check source bounds to avoid out-of-bounds access if 0 <= srcix < srcwidth and 0 <= srciy < srcdepth and 0 <= srciz < srcheight: destgrid[y - Ys][z - Zs][x - Xs] = sourcegrid[srciz][srciy][srcix] # Else leaves as 0 (background) return destgrid Applies affine transformations (translation, scaling, rotation) by computing new positions from the immediate predecessor's position using a maximum of three additions per coordinate. It reduces arithmetic operations compared to matrix multiplication but requires processing all voxels, including empty ones, making it suitable for parallel architectures. Deforms volumes using 2D user-guided control points and Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) to generate a 3D displacement map. It differs by relying on global smooth interpolation from sparse handles rather than local voxel-wise transformations. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the output grid. The cost per voxel is reduced to a few additions and a rounding operation, compared to multiplications in standard scaling. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output grid. In-place modification is possible if traversal order is managed correctly to prevent overwriting. Strengths: Significantly reduces computational complexity for large rooms/volumes by eliminating multiplications. Limitations: Requires careful handling of scaling factors >1 (back scaling) to avoid holes. Requires processing all voxels in the destination volume, even if empty, unlike sparse voxel approaches. When to use: When scaling voxel primitives in a voxel frame buffer processor and computational efficiency is critical. The algorithm was developed to handle large rooms efficiently by reducing the complexity of geometric transformations. The voxblt Engine: A Voxel Frame Buffer Processor, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh88/085-102, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Incremental Geometric Transformation
head: Incremental Transformation
body: Incremental Geometric Transformation is a method for applying affine transformations (translation, scaling, rotation) to voxel primitives by computing the new position of each voxel based on the already-transformed position of its immediate predecessor, using a maximum of three additions per voxel instead of full matrix multiplication. It sets itself apart from direct matrix multiplication by exploiting spatial coherence between neighboring voxels, significantly reducing arithmetic operations at the cost of requiring all volume elements (including empty ones) to be processed, making it particularly suitable for parallel architectures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid defined by source coordinates (x, y, z), and an affine transformation matrix M. Output: A transformed voxel grid where each voxel's position is updated according to M. Data Structures: Source Grid: A regular 3D array where neighbors are accessible via simple index increments. Transformation Matrix: A 4 \times 4 matrix M representing the affine transform. Intermediate Position: A 4D homogeneous vector storing the transformed position of the current voxel. Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Transformation: Compute the transformed position of the first grid point using one matrix-vector multiplication. 2. Incremental Update: Compute the transformed position of subsequent voxels by adding precomputed incremental deltas derived from the transformation matrix to the transformed position of their immediate predecessor, exploiting inter- and intra-scan-line coherency. 3. Overlap Resolution: If source and destination primitives overlap, perform the transformation in a predefined sequence determined by an orientation algorithm to prevent source voxels from being overwritten before they are translated. This is necessary because no scratch memory is available to hold old voxel information. Formulas: Let \vec{p}{i,j,k} be the source position of voxel (i,j,k), and \vec{p}{i,j,k}' be its transformed position. For the first voxel (0,0,0): \vec{p}{0,0,0}' = M \cdot \vec{p}{0,0,0} For subsequent voxels, the algorithm uses fixed increments corresponding to the transformed basis vectors: \Deltax = M \cdot [1,0,0,0]^T, \quad \Deltay = M \cdot [0,1,0,0]^T, \quad \Deltaz = M \cdot [0,0,1,0]^T The position updates as \vec{p}{i,j,k}' = \vec{p}{i-1,j,k}' + \Deltax (and similarly for y and z). The sources state the method requires "three additions/increments" per voxel, though one source notes "three additions per coordinate"; this refers to updating the three spatial components using the precomputed deltas. Parameters: Transformation Matrix M: Defined by the specific geometric operation (translation, rotation, scaling). Grid Dimensions: Nx, Ny, Nz. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlap: Overlapping source and destination primitives can cause data corruption if voxels are overwritten before being read, resolved by a predefined processing order. Empty Voxels: The method requires transforming all volume elements, including empty ones, increasing computation if not parallelized. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalgeometrictransformation(voxelgrid, transformationmatrix): """ Applies an affine transformation to a voxel grid using incremental updates. Args: voxelgrid: 3D array of voxels with source coordinates. transformationmatrix: 4x4 affine transformation matrix. Returns: Transformed voxel grid (list of lists of lists of 4D homogeneous vectors). """ Nx, Ny, Nz = voxelgrid.shape # Initialize output grid with homogeneous coordinates transformedpositions = [[[[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] for in range(Nz)] for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)]] # Step 1: Transform the first voxel (origin) using matrix multiplication p0src = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] transformedpositions[0][0][0] = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, p0src) # Precompute incremental deltas (transformed basis vectors) dx = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) dy = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) dz = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Step 2: Incrementally update the remaining voxels # Iterate in a predefined sequence to handle overlaps if necessary for z in range(Nz): for y in range(Ny): for x in range(Nx): if x == 0 and y == 0 and z == 0: continue # Already computed elif x > 0: # Update along X-axis using predecessor in X transformedpositions[x][y][z] = vectoradd(transformedpositions[x-1][y][z], dx) elif y > 0: # Update along Y-axis using predecessor in Y transformedpositions[x][y][z] = vectoradd(transformedpositions[x][y-1][z], dy) elif z > 0: # Update along Z-axis using predecessor in Z transformedpositions[x][y][z] = vectoradd(transformedpositions[x][y][z-1], dz) return transformedpositions def matrixvectormultiply(matrix, vector): """Standard 4x4 matrix by 4-vector multiplication.""" result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(4): s = 0.0 for j in range(4): s += matrix[i][j] vector[j] result[i] = s return result def vectoradd(v1, v2): """Component-wise addition of two 4D vectors.""" return [v1[0] + v2[0], v1[1] + v2[1], v1[2] + v2[2], v1[3] + v2[3]] Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels, with a very low constant factor (3 additions per voxel) compared to O(N) with a higher constant for matrix multiplication. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the voxel grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of voxels; performance is highly dependent on parallelization, as all voxels (including empty ones) must be processed. Strengths: Reduces arithmetic operations significantly; exploits spatial coherence; suitable for parallel architectures. Limitations: Requires processing all voxels, including empty ones; potential for overlap issues if not handled with a specific ordering algorithm. When to use: When hardware supports parallel processing and arithmetic operations are expensive; when the transformation is affine and the grid is dense or parallelization is feasible. When not to use: When the grid is sparse and most voxels are empty (wastes computation). The Incremental Geometric Transformation technique was developed as part of the Voxblt Engine, a voxel frame buffer processor, in the late 1980s. It was designed to perform geometric operations (translation, scaling, rotation) efficiently by exploiting inter- and intra-scan-line coherency. The method was implemented in hardware, utilizing parallel memory and barrel shifters to accelerate the incremental updates. It is also discussed in the context of volume visualization and rendering techniques, where it is noted for its suitability to parallel architectures. name: Volume Deformation via Scattered Data Interpolation
head: RBF-based Volume Deformation, Scattered Data Interpolation for Volume Deformation
body: This method deforms volumetric objects by reducing the complexity of 3D manipulation to a 2D user-guided illustration. The user defines control points on a 2D projection (slice, MIP, or composite) and displaces them; scattered data interpolation using Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) generates a 2D displacement map, which is then extruded into a 3D displacement map and applied to the volume. It differs from Incremental Scaling Algorithm and Incremental Geometric Transformation by relying on global smooth interpolation from sparse 2D handles rather than local voxel-wise or mesh-element-wise transformations, allowing for complex, plausible deformations with minimal user input. Input: A volumetric representation (e.g., signed distance field for surface models, or CT/MR voxel grid). A 2D image derived from the volume (slice, MIP, or composite). A set of N control points X = \{x1, \dots, xN\} in \mathbb{R}^2 and their corresponding target displacements D = \{d1, \dots, dN\} in \mathbb{R}^2. Output: A deformed volumetric dataset. Control Points: Array of N 2D coordinates (xi, yi) and 2D displacement vectors (dxi, dyi). RBF Coefficients: Computed on CPU. For each component (x-displacement, y-displacement), a system of linear equations is solved. Matrix \Phi: N \times N matrix where \Phi{ij} = \phi(\|xi - xj\|). Matrix P: N \times 3 matrix where row i is (1, xi, yi). Coefficients \alpha (size N) and \gamma (size 3) for x-displacement; \beta (size N) and \lambda (size 3) for y-displacement. Displacement Map: 2D texture/grid of size W \times H (typically 256 \times 256) storing 2D vectors (u, v). 3D Displacement Map: 3D texture/grid storing 3D vectors (u, v, w) derived from the 2D map. Radial Basis Function: Wendland’s polynomial \psi{3,1}(r) = (1 - r)+^4 (4r + 1), where (1 - r)+^4 = (1 - r)^4 for 0 \le r \le 1 and 0 otherwise. This provides C^2 continuity and compact support. Polynomial Degree: k=1 to ensure the deformation is as-affine-as-possible. Polynomials are pk(x) = \gamma0 x + \gamma1 y + \gamma2 and qk(x) = \lambda0 x + \lambda1 y + \lambda2. Control Points Count: N ranges from <8 to 32. Limited by GPU architecture constraints in the source implementation. Resolution: 256 \times 256 for the 2D displacement map generation. 1. User Interaction: The user views a 2D projection of the volume (slice, MIP, or composite). The user places N control points xi on the image and drags them to new positions, defining displacements di = [dxi, dyi]^T. 2. Solve RBF Coefficients (CPU): Construct and solve the linear systems for the x and y components of the displacement field independently. For x-displacement: \begin{pmatrix} \Phi & P \\ P^T & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha \\ \gamma \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} dx \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} For y-displacement: \begin{pmatrix} \Phi & P \\ P^T & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta \\ \lambda \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} dy \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} Here, \Phi{ij} = \psi{3,1}(\|xi - xj\|) and P{i} = (1, xi, yi). Use a linear algebra solver (e.g., LAPACK). 3. Generate 2D Displacement Map (GPU): Evaluate the RBF interpolant for every pixel (x, y) in the 256 \times 256 grid. u(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^N \alphai \psi{3,1}(\|x - xi\|) + \gamma0 x + \gamma1 y + \gamma2 v(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^N \betai \psi{3,1}(\|x - xi\|) + \lambda0 x + \lambda1 y + \lambda2 Store (u, v) in the 2D displacement map texture. 4. Extrude to 3D Displacement Map: Apply a user-defined rule to extend the 2D displacement (u, v) into the z-dimension to create D{3D}(x, y, z) = (u{3D}, v{3D}, w{3D}). Replication: D{3D}(x, y, z) = (u(x, y), v(x, y), 0). The 2D displacement is replicated along the z-axis. Modulation: D{3D}(x, y, z) = (f(z)u(x, y), f(z)v(x, y), 0). A function f(z) modulates the displacement. For example, f(z)=z creates a smooth transition from zero. Interpolation: Interpolate between multiple 2D displacement maps using tri-linear interpolation provided by graphics hardware to create progressive deformations. 5. Apply Deformation: Use inverse warping to apply the 3D displacement map to the volume. For each sample point p in the deformed volume, compute the source position p{src} = p - D{3D}(p) and sample the original volume at p{src}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def solverbfcoefficients(controlpoints, displacements): """ Solve for RBF coefficients on CPU. controlpoints: Nx2 array of (x, y) displacements: Nx2 array of (dx, dy) Returns: alpha, gamma (for x), beta, lambda (for y) """ N = controlpoints.shape[0] def psi(r): return np.where(r <= 1.0, (1.0 - r)4 (4.0 r + 1.0), 0.0) dists = np.sqrt(np.sum((controlpoints[:, np.newaxis,:] - controlpoints[np.newaxis,:,:])2, axis=2)) Phi = psi(dists) P = np.ones((N, 3)) P[:, 1] = controlpoints[:, 0] P[:, 2] = controlpoints[:, 1] A = np.zeros((N + 3, N + 3)) A[:N,:N] = Phi A[:N, N:] = P A[N:,:N] = P.T rhsx = np.zeros(N + 3) rhsx[:N] = displacements[:, 0] coeffsx = np.linalg.solve(A, rhsx) alpha = coeffsx[:N] gamma = coeffsx[N:] rhsy = np.zeros(N + 3) rhsy[:N] = displacements[:, 1] coeffsy = np.linalg.solve(A, rhsy) beta = coeffsy[:N] lambda = coeffsy[N:] return alpha, gamma, beta, lambda def generate2ddisplacementmap(alpha, gamma, beta, lambda, controlpoints, resolution=256): """ Generate 2D displacement map on GPU (simulated here). Evaluates RBF interpolant at each pixel. """ y, x = np.mgrid[0:resolution, 0:resolution] coords = np.stack((x, y), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 2) dists = np.sqrt(np.sum((coords[:, np.newaxis,:] - controlpoints[np.newaxis,:,:])2, axis=2)) def psi(r): return np.where(r <= 1.0, (1.0 - r)4 (4.0 r + 1.0), 0.0) Phipixels = psi(dists) polyx = gamma[0] x.flatten() + gamma[1] y.flatten() + gamma[2] polyy = lambda[0] x.flatten() + lambda[1] y.flatten() + lambda[2] u = np.dot(Phipixels, alpha) + polyx v = np.dot(Phipixels, beta) + polyy return np.stack((u.reshape(resolution, resolution), v.reshape(resolution, resolution)), axis=-1) def extrude3ddisplacement(2dmap, rule='replication', zfunc=None, depth=256): """ Extrude 2D displacement map to 3D. 2dmap: HxWx2 array rule: 'replication', 'modulation', or 'interpolation' zfunc: function f(z) for modulation """ H, W, = 2dmap.shape z = np.arange(depth) if rule == 'replication': return np.repeat(2dmap[np.newaxis,:,:,:], depth, axis=0) elif rule == 'modulation': if zfunc is None: zfunc = lambda z: z mod = zfunc(z) return np.stack([2dmap mod[i] for i in range(depth)], axis=0) elif rule == 'interpolation': # Tri-linear interpolation between multiple 2D maps is handled by graphics hardware return 2dmap def applydeformation(volume, displacementmap3d): """ Apply 3D displacement to volume using inverse warping. """ deformedvolume = np.zeroslike(volume) for z in range(displacementmap3d.shape[0]): for y in range(displacementmap3d.shape[1]): for x in range(displacementmap3d.shape[2]): src = np.array([x, y, z]) - displacementmap3d[z, y, x] deformedvolume[z, y, x] = volume[src[0], src[1], src[2]] return deformedvolume GPU Limitations: Current GPU architectures (as per source) limit the maximum number of control points to 32 due to texture/register constraints. Rigidity Constraints: To keep parts of the object fixed (e.g., legs of a horse), a rigidity constraint can be added as the distance to the horizontal plane where the object stands, modifying the linear system (Eq. 6 in source). Discontinuities (Cuts): To support cuts, RBFs can be decoupled by dividing control points into sets (e.g., red and green) and moving them in opposite directions. Precision: The use of compactly supported RBFs (Wendland) ensures that only nearby control points affect a given voxel, improving computational efficiency and numerical stability for large N. Time Complexity: CPU (Coefficient Solving): Solving the linear system is O(N^3) for dense matrix inversion, but N is small (<32). Measured time: 0.25 to 2.4 ms for 8 to 32 control points on a Pentium M 1.6 GHz. GPU (Displacement Map Generation): O(W \cdot H \cdot N) for evaluating the RBF at each pixel. Measured time: ~20 ms for a 256 \times 256 image on a Quadro FX Go1400. CPU displacement map generation takes 633 ms (8 points) to 2200 ms (32 points) for a 256x256 image. Memory Complexity: Storage for \Phi (N \times N), P (N \times 3), and coefficients is negligible for small N. Displacement maps: 256 \times 256 \times 2 floats for 2D map; 256 \times 256 \times D \times 3 floats for 3D map (where D is volume depth). Performance: The GPU-based displacement map generation is essential for real-time interaction, being significantly faster than CPU-based evaluation. Strengths: Reduces 3D deformation complexity to 2D; allows for smooth, plausible deformations with few control points; supports various extrusion rules for 3D context. Limitations: Limited to 32 control points on older GPU architectures; 2D input limits the types of deformations that can be intuitively specified (e.g., complex 3D twisting might be hard to guide from a 2D slice). When to Use: Interactive deformation of CT/MR images, surface models (via SDFs), and scientific illustration where user-guided, smooth deformation is desired. When Not to Use: When precise, local, non-smooth deformations are required without interpolation artifacts, or when the number of control points exceeds GPU limits. Origin: Proposed by C. Correa, D. Silver, and M. Chen in 2007. History: The method builds on earlier work in inverse warping for volume rendering [CSC06b, CSC06a] and scattered data interpolation techniques [RM95]. It addresses the need for intuitive, user-guided deformation of large volumetric datasets, which are computationally expensive to manipulate directly. Usage: Applied to deforming CT/MR images, surface models (represented as signed distance fields), and for generating scientific illustrations and animations. Examples include horse models, CT knee/abdomen/head datasets, and lobster datasets. Volume Deformation via Scattered Data Interpolation, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg07/091-098, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Per-fragment Deformation Evaluation
head: Fragment shader deformation, Shader Shift, Shader Sine
body: Per-fragment deformation evaluation is a volume rendering technique that applies deformation functions directly within the fragment shader for every sample point along a ray, rather than deforming proxy geometry on a per-vertex basis. It solves the problem of rendering dynamically deforming volumes, such as those driven by interactive volume widgets, without the retessellation overhead required by per-vertex approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (3D texture), deformation parameters (uniforms for analytical functions or 3D textures for HBSpline), ray origin, ray direction, and view/projection matrices. Output: Color and opacity for the fragment. Data Structures: Deformation Parameters: Uniform variables for analytical deformations (e.g., amplitude, frequency for sine waves) or 3D texture handles for complex deformations (e.g., Hierarchical B-Splines). Volume Texture: Standard 3D texture storing density/opacity values. Steps: 1. Ray Marching Loop: For each fragment, iterate along the ray. 2. Sample Position: Calculate the world-space position \mathbf{p} of the current sample point. 3. Deformation Evaluation: Apply the deformation function to \mathbf{p} using uniform parameters or texture lookups. For analytical deformations (Shader Shift, Shader Sine), compute the offset directly in the shader. For complex deformations (HBSpline), sample a deformation texture to retrieve the offset or transformed coordinate. 4. Volume Sampling: Evaluate the volume density at the deformed position. 5. Shading: Compute color and opacity using transfer functions and potentially gradients (Case 2). 6. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray. Formulas: Shader Shift (Trivial Translation): \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{t}, where \mathbf{t} is a translation vector uniform. Shader Sine: \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} + A \sin(\omega \mathbf{p} + \phi), where A is amplitude, \omega is frequency, and \phi is phase, all uniforms. Hierarchical B-Spline (HBSpline): The deformation is precomputed and stored in a 3D texture T{def}. The offset is retrieved via \mathbf{d} = T{def}(\mathbf{p}), and the deformed position is \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d}. Parameters: Texture Size for HBSpline: 16^3 is used in the primary performance tests. Sample Planes per Voxel: Tested at 0.5 and 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: Volume widgets (e.g., leafer widget) introduce discontinuities in deformation functions, requiring conditional branches in the shader that are inefficient on some hardware. Performance Optimization: Direct texture coordinate feeding (no deformation) is faster than trivial computation (Shader Shift) due to hardware optimizations for direct lookups; the shift operation reduces performance from 39 fps to 29.2 fps in Case 1. Memory Coherence: Texture-based deformations suffer from poor memory coherence and high bandwidth costs for updating deformation textures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perfragmentdeformation(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetex, deformtype, uniforms, deformtex=None): color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 maxdist = 10.0 t = 0.0 while t < maxdist and alpha < 1.0: p = rayorigin + raydirection t if deformtype == "shift": pdeformed = p + uniforms.translation elif deformtype == "sine": pdeformed = p + uniforms.amplitude sin(uniforms.frequency p + uniforms.phase) elif deformtype == "hbspline": d = deformtex.sample(p) pdeformed = p + d else: pdeformed = p density = volumetex.sample(pdeformed).r # Standard transfer function mapping density to color and alpha c = [density, density, density] a = density color[0] = color[0] + c[0] a (1.0 - alpha) color[1] = color[1] + c[1] a (1.0 - alpha) color[2] = color[2] + c[2] a (1.0 - alpha) color[3] = color[3] + a (1.0 - alpha) alpha = alpha + a (1.0 - alpha) t += stepsize return color Deformation Texture is a technique for evaluating complex, computationally expensive deformation functions during volume rendering by encoding the inverse deformation mapping into a 3D texture. It solves the problem of "inverse parameterization," where a shader needs to map a fragment's screen-space or ray-space coordinate back to the deformed object space, a task that is often analytically intractable or too costly for real-time fragment programs. Unlike direct shader evaluation, which is suitable for simple bends and twists, this method is chosen for complex functions like Hierarchical B-Splines and Thin-Plate Splines, trading memory bandwidth for computational simplicity. Time and Memory Complexity: Performance is bound by texture access and memory bandwidth when using texture-based deformations (HBSpline) due to poor memory coherence and the cost of writing/updating deformation textures. Analytical deformations (Shift, Sine) have lower computational overhead but still incur a performance penalty compared to no deformation due to the loss of hardware optimizations for direct texture lookups. Measured Performance: Hardware/Scene: 512x512x106 CT Head. Shader Shift: 29.2 fps (Case 1), 8.5 fps (Case 2). Shader Sine: 29 fps (Case 1), 7.1 fps (Case 2). Texture (HBSpline): 21.7 fps (Case 1), 5.7 fps (Case 2). Baseline (Direct Texture): 39 fps (Case 1). Mouse Torso (256x256x192): HBSpline 16^3 Texture, 1 sample/voxel: 3.96 fps. HBSpline 16^3 Texture, 0.5 samples/voxel: 6.19 fps. Control (no deformation), 1 sample/voxel: 5.15 fps. Control (no deformation), 0.5 samples/voxel: 9.56 fps. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Flexible proxy geometry, avoids retessellation, supports interactive volume widgets. Limitations: Conditional branches for discontinuities are inefficient; texture-based methods suffer from memory bandwidth and coherence issues; analytical methods still lose hardware optimization benefits. When to Use: Use for real-time interactive visualization of deforming volumes, especially when deformations are driven by user interaction (widgets) or simple analytical functions. Avoid for very complex deformations requiring high-frequency detail if memory bandwidth is a bottleneck, unless texture-based methods are optimized. Originating from the work on integrating dynamic deformations into interactive volume visualization, this method addresses the third hurdle of deformation rendering: performance. It contrasts with per-vertex methods that rely on proxy geometry tessellation, which must be retessilated for view-dependent deformations. The approach was implemented to support volume widgets, such as the leafer widget, directly in the shader. Integrating Dynamic Deformations into Interactive Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym.eurovis06.219-226, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Deformation Texture
head: Hardware-Accelerated Deformation via Texture Interpolation, Inverse Deformation Texture, Sampled Deformation Function
body: Deformation Texture is a technique for evaluating complex, computationally expensive deformation functions during volume rendering by encoding the inverse deformation mapping into a 3D texture. It solves the problem of "inverse parameterization," where a shader needs to map a fragment's screen-space or ray-space coordinate back to the deformed object space, a task that is often analytically intractable or too costly for real-time fragment programs. Unlike direct shader evaluation, which is suitable for simple bends and twists, this method is chosen for complex functions like Hierarchical B-Splines and Thin-Plate Splines, trading memory bandwidth for computational simplicity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A deformation function D: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3 (mapping object space to deformed space) or its inverse D^{-1} (mapping deformed space to object space). Output: A 3D texture containing samples of the inverse deformation function, used to retrieve deformed coordinates during rendering. Data Structures: Deformation Texture: A 3D texture with resolution Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Texture Coordinates: Unit volume coordinates (u, v, w) \in [0, 1]^3 representing positions in the deformed space. Stored Values: Each texel stores a 3D vector \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) representing the corresponding position in the original object space. The deformation texture need not have the same resolution as the volume data. Steps: 1. Grid Definition: Define a regular 3D grid of points covering the unit volume of the deformed space. The resolution is determined by the Nyquist theorem, requiring at least two lattice sections per pixel, though practical resolution depends on curvature, pixel coverage, and fire length, ranging from a single section to several hundred sections. 2. Inverse Evaluation: Evaluate the inverse deformation function D^{-1}(\mathbf{u}) for every point \mathbf{u} on the regular 3D grid. If only the forward deformation D(\mathbf{p}) is available, compute the inverse using scattered data interpolation on the CPU. 3. Texture Population: Store the resulting object-space coordinates \mathbf{p} into the 3D texture at the corresponding texture coordinates \mathbf{u}. 4. Fragment Shader Evaluation: In the fragment shader, use the current fragment's position in deformed space (or ray origin) as texture coordinates to perform a single 3D texture lookup. The graphics hardware's trilinear interpolation implicitly evaluates the piecewise-linear approximation of D^{-1}(\mathbf{u}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createdeformationtexture(forwarddeformfunc, resolution): """ Creates a 3D texture storing the inverse deformation. forwarddeformfunc: Function D(p) mapping object space to deformed space. resolution: Integer N, defining NxNxN grid. """ # Initialize 3D array for texture data texturedata = [[[None for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] # If inverse is not known analytically, use scattered data interpolation # to approximate Dinv from samples of D. This step is performed on the CPU. # Standard scattered data interpolation routine inversedeform = computeinversescattereddata(forwarddeformfunc, resolution) for i in range(resolution): for j in range(resolution): for k in range(resolution): # Normalize to [0, 1] u = i / (resolution - 1) v = j / (resolution - 1) w = k / (resolution - 1) # Evaluate inverse deformation p = inversedeform(u, v, w) texturedata[i][j][k] = p return texturedata def fragmentshaderdeformation(texture, rayorigindeformedspace): """ Retrieves the object-space coordinate for a given deformed-space coordinate. """ u, v, w = rayorigindeformedspace # Perform trilinear interpolation on the 3D texture # Hardware typically handles this, but here we define it for completeness objectspacecoord = trilinearinterpolate(texture, u, v, w) return objectspacecoord def computeinversescattereddata(forwardfunc, res): # Standard scattered data interpolation to find p such that D(p) ≈ (u,v,w) pass def trilinearinterpolate(tex, u, v, w): # Standard trilinear interpolation pass Gradient Computation: Because the gradient of the volume data depends on the deformation, it cannot be precomputed. It is computed "on the fly" in the fragment shader using forward finite differences: \nabla v(\mathbf{u}(O)) \approx \left( v(\mathbf{u}(Ox + \Delta Ox, Oy, Oz)) - v(\mathbf{u}(O)), \dots \right) where \mathbf{u} is the inverse deformation function and O is the ray origin. Parameters: Lattice Resolution: Ranges from a single section to several hundred sections. Hardware Interpolation: Relies on linear (trilinear) interpolation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Derivative Discontinuities: Hardware linear interpolation creates discontinuities in the first derivative of the curve at the borders of each lattice section. Smoothness Loss: Piecewise linear approximation may fail to capture high frequencies or desired smoothness unless a large number of samples is used. Performance Bound: Fragment programs often become texture-lookup bound. Inverse Computation: If only the forward deformation is available, the inverse must be computed via scattered data interpolation, which is expensive. Time Complexity: Rendering time is O(1) per fragment for deformation evaluation, as it requires only a single 3D texture lookup. Pre-processing requires dense evaluation of the entire table, which may be expensive. Memory Complexity: Memory scales with the 3D grid resolution required to store the deformation samples. Performance: On circa 2005 hardware (NVIDIA GeForce 6800GT), simple deformations (bends, twists) are faster in shaders, while complex deformations (Hierarchical B-Splines, Thin-Plate Splines) benefit from this method. The method is texture-lookup bound. Strengths: Decouples complex deformation logic from the fragment shader, allowing real-time evaluation of functions that are otherwise intractable. Limitations: Requires pre-computation on the CPU; piecewise linear approximation may fail to capture desired smoothness or high frequencies unless large numbers of samples are used. When to Use: For complex deformation functions (e.g., splines) that are too expensive to evaluate per-fragment. When Not to Use: For simple deformations (bends, twists) which are better handled directly in shaders. The method was employed in the movie "Shrek" and is based on the model described by Lamorlette and Foster. The idea of storing a sampled representation of a function in a 3D texture was suggested in [RSSSG01]. The technique addresses the "inverse parameterization" problem, where the shader operates on the deformed point P' to return the original point P, rather than the forward mapping D(P). Real-time procedural volumetric fire, https://doi.org/10.1145/1230100.1230131, fetched 2026-11-05 Integrating Dynamic Deformations into Interactive Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym.eurovis06.219-226, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Inverse Deformation Texture
head: Inverse Free-Form Volumetric Deformation, Inverse Parameterization, Inverse Parameterization for Volumetric Deformation
body: Inverse Parameterization (also known as Inverse Deformation Texture) is a technique used when forward free-form volumetric deformation is impossible to solve analytically or efficiently in real-time. It constructs a lattice grid around the deformed volume in world space and associates each lattice point with texture coordinates in the unit fire volume, allowing efficient evaluation of the deformation via implicit interpolation in fragment shaders. It sets itself apart from forward deformation methods by avoiding the need to invert the deformation function at runtime, which is computationally prohibitive for infinite-detail volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A deformed volume (e.g., fire) defined by forces or a simulation in world space. Output: A 3D texture mapping world-space positions to unit-volume texture coordinates. Data Structures: Lattice Grid: A 3D regular grid defined in world space coordinates surrounding the deformed volume. Inverse Deformation Texture: A 3D texture where each texel stores the texture coordinates (u, v, w) in the unit fire volume corresponding to the world-space position of the lattice point. Steps: 1. Construct Lattice: Build a lattice grid around the deformed volume in world space coordinates. 2. Associate Coordinates: For each point in the lattice, determine its corresponding texture coordinates in the unit fire volume. This effectively pre-computes the inverse mapping from world space to the reference parameter space. 3. Interpolate: Use a 3D shader flame texture (the reference volume) to implicitly interpolate all points of the fire surfaces by sampling the Inverse Deformation Texture at the fragment's world-space position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildinversedeformationtexture(latticemin, latticemax, resolution): step = (latticemax - latticemin) / resolution texture = [[[] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for i in range(resolution): for j in range(resolution): for k in range(resolution): worldpos = (latticemin.x + i step.x, latticemin.y + j step.y, latticemin.z + k step.z) # The sources do not provide the exact inverse mapping function; it is pre-computed from the fire simulation forces texcoords = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) texture[i][j][k] = texcoords return texture def renderfragment(worldpos, texture, flametexture, resolution, latticemin, step): i = int((worldpos[0] - latticemin.x) / step.x) j = int((worldpos[1] - latticemin.y) / step.y) k = int((worldpos[2] - latticemin.z) / step.z) i = max(0, min(i, resolution - 1)) j = max(0, min(j, resolution - 1)) k = max(0, min(k, resolution - 1)) texcoords = texture[i][j][k] return flametexture.sample(texcoords) Parameters: Lattice resolution: Not given in the sources. Reference volume size: Unit volume (1x1x1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Forward deformation cannot be solved analytically. Numerical solutions for forward deformation require significant computation and exhibit robustness problems. Real-time deformation of the entire infinite-detail volume is impossible. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids real-time inversion of complex deformation functions. Efficient evaluation in fragment shaders. Limitations: Requires pre-computation or setup. Accuracy depends on lattice resolution. Origin: Developed by Y. Vanzine for real-time volumetric rendering of fire in production systems. The method is based on the lattice method described in [13] (referenced in) and [9] (referenced in). Real-Time Volumetric Rendering of Fire in a Production System, https://clas.iusb.edu/math-compsci/prior-thesis/YVanzinethesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Realistic Real-Time Rendering of Fire in a Production System, https://clas.iusb.edu/math-compsci/prior-proposals/YVanzineProposal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Sphere Tracing with Composite SDF and Adaptive Sampling
head: Ray Marching with Character SDFs, SDF Sphere Tracing with Letter/Arc Geometry, SDF-Sphere-Tracing
body: This method extends standard sphere tracing to render scenes composed of primitive shapes, character segments (letters), and arcs using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It integrates a path tracer with up to 3 bounces, handling distinct hit types (DIFFUSE, LETTER, ARC, SUN) with specific shading and reflection logic. The rendering employs adaptive sampling with variance-based convergence to determine when sufficient samples have been collected for each pixel. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit handling of non-primitive character geometry via segment projection and its specific adaptive convergence criteria based on luminance variance. Inputs: Camera parameters: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction vectors, width, height, Field of View (FOV = 32 degrees). Scene data: shapes: List of primitive SDF objects (e.g., boxes) with a Distance(p) method. characters: List of vec3 pairs representing line segments (letters). Index j is start, j+1 is end. arcs: List of arc objects with a distance(p) method. surrondingbbox: A bounding box SDF used for acceleration culling. mats: List of materials with bsdfsample and isSpecular methods. Parameters: thicc = 0.6f, bboxthreshold = 5.5f, smallStep = 0.001f, maximumhitdistance = 1000.0f, minimumhitdistance = 0.0001f, maximumstep = 1024. Outputs: Final image buffer with tone-mapped RGB values. Ray: Struct with vec3 o (origin) and vec3 d (direction). Shape: Abstract base class with virtual float Distance(vec3 p) and material pointer. Arc: Object with float distance(vec3 p) method. Material: Abstract base class with virtual vec3 bsdfsample(const vec3& dirin, const vec3& n) and bool isSpecular(). ONB: Orthonormal Basis constructed from a normal vector, providing u, v, w axes. 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel (i, j), generate a ray \mathbf{r} using a pinhole camera model with 32-degree FOV. 2. Adaptive Sampling Loop: Initialize sum (color accumulator) to \mathbf{0}, sumsquare (luminance squared sum) to 0, sumsofar (luminance sum) to 0, and numsampleused to 0. Loop with step size step = 16 up to ns = 16 total samples: For num from 0 to step-1: Generate a jittered ray \mathbf{r} for the pixel. Compute radiance \mathbf{C} = \text{PathTrace}(\mathbf{r}). Add \mathbf{C} to sum. Compute luminance L = 0.2126 Cx + 0.7152 Cy + 0.0722 Cz. Update sumsquare += L^2 and sumsofar += L. Update numsampleused += step. Compute mean \mu = \frac{\text{sum\so\far}}{\text{num\sample\used}} and variance \sigma^2 = \frac{\text{sum\square}}{\text{num\sample\used}} - \mu^2. Check convergence: If \sigma^2 < 0.0001 and \min(Cx, Cy, Cz) > 0.2 for the current sample average, stop sampling for this pixel. 3. Path Tracing (for a single ray \mathbf{r}): Initialize radiance \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{0} and throughput \mathbf{T} = (1, 1, 1). Loop bounce from 0 to 2: Call SphereTrace with current ray \mathbf{r} to find hit distance t, hit point \mathbf{p}, and hit type. If no hit (miss): Add \mathbf{T} \times (50, 80, 100) to \mathbf{L}. Return \mathbf{L}. Update throughput: \mathbf{T} \leftarrow \mathbf{T} \times 0.2. If HITTYPE == DIFFUSE: Compute normal \mathbf{n} from the shape's SDF gradient. Sample BSDF to get new direction \mathbf{d}{new} using ONB. Create shadow ray towards light direction (0.6, 0.6, 1.0) normalized. If shadow ray hits SUN: Compute incident factor (cosine of angle). Add \mathbf{T} \times (500, 400, 100) \times \text{incident} to \mathbf{L}. Update \mathbf{r} origin to \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \times 0.1 and direction to \mathbf{d}{new}. If HITTYPE == LETTER or ARC: Compute normal \mathbf{n} using central finite differences with smallStep = 0.001f: \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}\left( \frac{f(\mathbf{p} + \Delta x) - f(\mathbf{p} - \Delta x)}{2\Delta x}, \frac{f(\mathbf{p} + \Delta y) - f(\mathbf{p} - \Delta y)}{2\Delta y}, \frac{f(\mathbf{p} + \Delta z) - f(\mathbf{p} - \Delta z)}{2\Delta z} \right) Compute reflected direction \mathbf{d}{refl} = \mathbf{r}.d - 2(\mathbf{r}.d \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n}. Offset hit point: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \times 0.2. Update \mathbf{r} origin to \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \times 0.1 and direction to normalized \mathbf{d}{refl}. If HITTYPE == SUN: Add \mathbf{T} \times (50, 80, 100) to \mathbf{L}. Return \mathbf{L}. 4. Sphere Tracing (finding closest hit): Initialize t = 0, mint = \infty, hittype = UNKNOWN. Loop i from 0 to maximumstep (1024): If t > 1000.0, return MISS. Current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}.o + \mathbf{r}.d \times t. Check Primitives: For each shape j, compute d = \text{shapes}[j].\text{Distance}(\mathbf{p}). If d < \text{mint}, update mint = d, hittype = DIFFUSE, shapeid = j. Check Acceleration: Compute d{bbox} = \text{surronding\bbox}.\text{Distance}(\mathbf{p}). If d{bbox} < 5.5: Check Letters: Iterate characters in pairs (j, j+1): \mathbf{begin} = \text{characters}[j], \mathbf{end} = \text{characters}[j+1]. \mathbf{seg} = \mathbf{end} - \mathbf{begin}. Project \mathbf{p} onto segment: u = -\min\left(\frac{(\mathbf{begin} - \mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{seg}}{\|\mathbf{seg}\|^2}, 0\right). Clamp u = \min(u, 1.0). Closest point \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{begin} + u \times \mathbf{seg}. Distance d = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\| - 0.6. If d < \text{mint}, update mint = d, hittype = LETTER, characterid = j. Check Arcs: For each arc j, compute d = \text{arcs}[j].\text{Distance}(\mathbf{p}). If d < \text{mint}, update mint = d, hittype = ARC, arcid = j. Advance ray: t \leftarrow t + \text{mint}. If mint < 0.0001: Check for SUN: If 19.9 - \mathbf{p}.y < 0, hittype = SUN. Return HIT with t, \mathbf{p}, hittype. 5. Tone Mapping: For each pixel color \mathbf{C}: Add bias: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + \frac{14}{241}. Reinhard tone mapping: \mathbf{C}{final} = \frac{\mathbf{C}}{\mathbf{C} + 1} \times 255. Convert to 8-bit integer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class vec3: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return vec3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return vec3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def mul(self, s): return vec3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def rmul(self, s): return self.mul(s) def truediv(self, s): return vec3(self.x/s, self.y/s, self.z/s) def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y + self.zo.z def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.dot(self)) def length2(self): return self.dot(self) def normalize(self): l = self.length() return self / l if l > 1e-8 else vec3(0,0,0) class ONB: def init(self, n): a = abs(n.x) if a < 0.9999: self.u = (vec3(1,0,0) - n n.x).normalize() else: self.u = (vec3(0,1,0) - n n.y).normalize() self.v = vec3(n.yself.u.z - n.zself.u.y, n.zself.u.x - n.xself.u.z, n.xself.u.y - n.yself.u.x) self.w = n class Shape: def distance(self, p): return 0.0 def gradient(self, p): return vec3(0,0,0) def bsdfsample(self, dirin, n): return vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) class Arc: def distance(self, p): return 0.0 class Material: def bsdfsample(self, dirin, n): return vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) def isSpecular(self): return False class Box(Shape): def init(self, minp, maxp, mat): self.minp, self.maxp, self.mat = minp, maxp, mat def distance(self, p): diff = vec3(max(p.x - self.maxp.x, self.minp.x - p.x, 0.0), max(p.y - self.maxp.y, self.minp.y - p.y, 0.0), max(p.z - self.maxp.z, self.minp.z - p.z, 0.0)) return diff.length() def gradient(self, p): eps = 0.001 dx = self.distance(p + vec3(eps,0,0)) - self.distance(p - vec3(eps,0,0)) dy = self.distance(p + vec3(0,eps,0)) - self.distance(p - vec3(0,eps,0)) dz = self.distance(p + vec3(0,0,eps)) - self.distance(p - vec3(0,0,eps)) return vec3(dx, dy, dz).normalize() class Camera: def init(self, origin, up, width, height, fovdeg=32.0): self.o = origin self.width, self.height = width, height self.tanhalffov = math.tan(math.radians(fovdeg) / 2.0) self.aspect = width / height def generateray(self, u, v): px = (2.0 (u + random.random()) - 1.0) self.tanhalffov self.aspect py = (2.0 (v + random.random()) - 1.0) self.tanhalffov d = vec3(px, py, 1.0).normalize() return Ray(self.o, d) class Ray: def init(self, o, d): self.o = o self.d = d def spheretracing(rayo, rayd, shapes, characters, arcs, surroundingbbox, maxsteps=1024, maxdist=1000.0, mindist=0.0001): t = 0.0 mint = float('inf') hittype = None shapeid = None charid = None arcid = None for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return False, None, None, None, None, None, None p = rayo + t rayd for j, shape in enumerate(shapes): d = shape.distance(p) if d < mint: mint = d hittype = 'DIFFUSE' shapeid = j distbbox = surroundingbbox.distance(p) if distbbox < 5.5: for j in range(0, len(characters), 2): begin = characters[j] end = characters[j+1] seg = end - begin seglensq = seg.dot(seg) if seglensq == 0: continue dotval = (begin - p).dot(seg) / seglensq beginx = -min(dotval, 0.0) beginx = min(beginx, 1.0) hitpointletter = begin + beginx seg d = (p - hitpointletter).length() - 0.6 if d < mint: mint = d hittype = 'LETTER' charid = j for j, arc in enumerate(arcs): d = arc.distance(p) if d < mint: mint = d hittype = 'ARC' arcid = j t += mint if mint < mindist: suncheck = 19.9 - p.y if suncheck < 0.0: hittype = 'SUN' hitpoint = rayo + t rayd return True, t, hitpoint, hittype, shapeid, charid, arcid return False, None, None, None, None, None, None def pathtrace(rayo, rayd, shapes, characters, arcs, mats, surroundingbbox): L = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) T = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) lightdir = vec3(0.6, 0.6, 1.0).normalize() bgcolor = vec3(50.0, 80.0, 100.0) suncolor = vec3(500.0, 400.0, 100.0) for bounce in range(3): hit, t, hitpoint, hittype, shapeid, charid, arcid = spheretracing(rayo, rayd, shapes, characters, arcs, surroundingbbox) if not hit: L += T bgcolor return L T = 0.2 if hittype == 'DIFFUSE': normal = shapes[shapeid].gradient(hitpoint) mat = mats[shapeid] coord = mat.bsdfsample(rayd, normal) onb = ONB(normal) newdir = coord.x onb.u + coord.y onb.v + coord.z onb.w shadowhit,,, shadowtype,,, = spheretracing(hitpoint, lightdir, shapes, characters, arcs, surroundingbbox) if shadowhit and shadowtype == 'SUN': incident = max(0.0, newdir.dot(lightdir)) L += T suncolor incident rayo = hitpoint + normal 0.1 rayd = newdir.normalize() elif hittype in ('LETTER', 'ARC'): smallstep = 0.001 if hittype == 'LETTER': dx = computedistanceletteroptimize(hitpoint + vec3(smallstep, 0, 0), characters, charid) - \ computedistanceletteroptimize(hitpoint - vec3(smallstep, 0, 0), characters, charid) dy = computedistanceletteroptimize(hitpoint + vec3(0, smallstep, 0), characters, charid) - \ computedistanceletteroptimize(hitpoint - vec3(0, smallstep, 0), characters, charid) dz = computedistanceletteroptimize(hitpoint + vec3(0, 0, smallstep), characters, charid) - \ computedistanceletteroptimize(hitpoint - vec3(0, 0, smallstep), characters, charid) else: dx = arcs[arcid].distance(hitpoint + vec3(smallstep, 0, 0)) - arcs[arcid].distance(hitpoint - vec3(smallstep, 0, 0)) dy = arcs[arcid].distance(hitpoint + vec3(0, smallstep, 0)) - arcs[arcid].distance(hitpoint - vec3(0, smallstep, 0)) dz = arcs[arcid].distance(hitpoint + vec3(0, 0, smallstep)) - arcs[arcid].distance(hitpoint - vec3(0, 0, smallstep)) normal = vec3(dx, dy, dz).normalize() reflecteddir = rayd - 2.0 rayd.dot(normal) normal hitpoint += normal 0.2 rayo = hitpoint + normal 0.1 rayd = reflecteddir.normalize() elif hittype == 'SUN': L += T bgcolor return L return L def computedistanceletteroptimize(position, characters, charid): begin = characters[charid] end = characters[charid + 1] seg = end - begin seglensq = seg.dot(seg) if seglensq == 0: return position.length() dotval = (begin - position).dot(seg) / seglensq beginx = -min(dotval, 0.0) beginx = min(beginx, 1.0) hitpointletter = begin + beginx seg d = (position - hitpointletter).length() - 0.6 return d def mainrender(width, height): shapes = [Box(vec3(-40.0, -0.6, -30.0), vec3(40.0, 18.0, 30.0), Material())] characters = [] arcs = [] surroundingbbox = Box(vec3(-50,-50,-50), vec3(50,50,50), Material()) mats = [Material()] ns = 16 step = 16 convergencerate = 0.0001 image = [] cam = Camera(vec3(0, 1.0, 18.0), vec3(0, 1.0, 0), width, height) for j in range(height): for i in range(width): sumcolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sumlumsq = 0.0 sumlum = 0.0 numsamples = 0 converged = False for s in range(0, ns, step): for in range(step): p = ((i + random.random()) / width) q = ((j + random.random()) / height) ray = cam.generateray(p, q) color = pathtrace(ray.o, ray.d, shapes, characters, arcs, mats, surroundingbbox) sumcolor += color lum = 0.2126 color.x + 0.7152 color.y + 0.0722 color.z sumlumsq += lum lum sumlum += lum numsamples += step meanlum = sumlum / numsamples varlum = (sumlumsq / numsamples) - (meanlum 2) avgcolor = sumcolor / numsamples if varlum < convergencerate and min(avgcolor.x, avgcolor.y, avgcolor.z) > 0.2: converged = True break if not converged: avgcolor = sumcolor / ns finalcolor = avgcolor + vec3(14.0/241.0, 14.0/241.0, 14.0/241.0) finalcolor = vec3( finalcolor.x / (finalcolor.x + 1.0) 255.0, finalcolor.y / (finalcolor.y + 1.0) 255.0, finalcolor.z / (finalcolor.z + 1.0) 255.0) image.append(finalcolor) return image thicc: 0.6f (thickness offset for letters). bboxthreshold: 5.5f (distance to surrounding box to trigger letter/arc checks). smallStep: 0.001f (step size for finite difference normal estimation). ns: 16 (total samples per pixel). step: 16 (batch size for adaptive sampling check). convergencerate: 0.0001f (variance threshold to stop sampling). maximumhitdistance: 1000.0f. minimumhitdistance: 0.0001f. maximumstep: 1024 (max sphere trace iterations). FOV: 32 degrees. Max Bounces: 3. Light Color: (500, 400, 100). Background Color: (50, 80, 100). Bias: 14.0/241.0. Normal Estimation: Finite differences for SDFs require a small step size (0.001f) to balance precision and noise. Self-Intersection: Ray origins are offset by normal 0.1 after a hit to prevent self-intersection. Letter Projection: The projection parameter u must be clamped to [0, 1] to ensure the closest point lies on the segment. SUN Detection: The SUN is detected based on the Y-coordinate of the hit point (19.9 - y < 0), which is a scene-specific heuristic. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot B), where N is the number of pixels, M is the number of shapes/letters/arcs, and B is the number of bounces (3). Adaptive sampling may reduce effective N if convergence is reached early. Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing scene geometry. Performance: The method uses a simple bounding box acceleration for letters/arcs, which is less efficient than a BVH but sufficient for small scenes. The use of step = 16 for adaptive sampling reduces variance checks overhead. Strengths: Simple implementation, handles complex character geometry via SDFs, adaptive sampling reduces noise in uniform areas. Limitations: No global illumination beyond direct lighting and simple reflections (no indirect diffuse bounces for letters/arcs, only specular-like reflection), limited to 3 bounces, SUN detection is hardcoded. This method originates from an unofficial GitHub repository by AlerianEmperor, implementing a path tracer with SDF sphere tracing for a scene containing letters and arcs. It is based on the principles of ray marching and signed distance functions, adapted for a specific educational or artistic rendering task. AlerianEmperor/SDF-Sphere-Tracing, https://github.com/AlerianEmperor/SDF-Sphere-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26. (unofficial)

name: Spherical Volume Voxel Traversal
head: walkSphericalVolume
body: A spherical coordinate voxel traversal algorithm that traces a ray with unit direction over a spherical voxel grid, returning a vector of the spherical coordinate voxels traversed. It computes intersections with spherical shells, polar cones, and azimuthal wedges directly, handling the singularity at the origin by starting traversal at the first non-zero radial shell. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Ray (origin, direction, inverse direction), a SphericalVoxelGrid (center, dimensions, precomputed bounds), and maxt (unitized time limit). Output: A std::vector<SphericalVoxel> containing the ordered list of voxels traversed, where each voxel stores its radial, polar, and azimuthal indices and its entry/exit times along the ray. Data Structures: The grid and ray are represented by the following structures: SphereBound: double radial, double polar, double azimuthal. Ray: const BoundVec3 origin, const UnitVec3 direction, const FreeVec3 inversedirection, const enum DirectionIndex NZDindex. RaySegment: const BoundVec3 P2, const DirectionIndex NZDI, BoundVec3 P1, FreeVec3 raysegment. TrigonometricValues: double cosine, double sine. Algorithm Steps: 1. Early Exit: If maxt <= 0.0, return an empty vector. 2. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Compute vector from ray origin to sphere center: rsv = \text{grid.center} - \text{ray.origin}. Compute squared length rsvd = \|rsv\|^2 and dot product v = rsv \cdot \text{ray.direction}. Find radialentrancevoxel such that rsvd < \text{grid.deltaRadiiSquared}(\text{radial\entrance\voxel}). Determine rayoriginisoutsidegrid = (radialentrancevoxel == 0). Compute vectorindex = radialentrancevoxel - !rayoriginisoutsidegrid and entryradiussquared = grid.deltaRadiiSquared(vectorindex). Check miss: If entry\radius\squared \le rsvd - v^2, return empty. Compute d = \sqrt{entry\radius\squared - (rsvd - v^2)}. Reserve output vector capacity: grid.numRadialSections() + grid.numPolarSections() + grid.numAzimuthalSections(). Push initial voxel {radial: currentradialvoxel, polar: 0, azimuthal: 0}. Update maxt = min(trayexit, unitizedraytime) if outside, else unitizedraytime. Initialize collineartimes = {0.0, ray.timeOfIntersectionAt(t)}. 4. Traversal Loop: While t < max\t: Compute next intersection parameters for radial, polar, and azimuthal boundaries using radialHit, polarHit, and azimuthalHit. Check termination: If currentradialvoxel + radial.tStep == 0 or all tMax values are infinite, set voxels.back().exitt = trayexit and return. Determine voxelintersection = minimumIntersection(radial, polar, azimuthal). Update t and voxel indices based on intersection type, applying modulo arithmetic for angular coordinates and checking bounds via inBoundsPolar/inBoundsAzimuthal. If out of bounds, set voxels.back().exitt = trayexit and return. Duplicate Check: If new coordinates match the last voxel, continue. Add Voxel: Set voxels.back().exitt = t and push {radial, polar, azimuthal, entert: t}. 5. Finalization: Loop terminates when t \ge max\t; the final voxel's exit time is implicitly handled by the loop condition or explicit boundary checks. Pseudocode: Unverified code. grid.numazimuthalsections elif intersectiontype == IntersectionType.RADIALPOLARAZIMUTHAL: t = radial.tmax if not inboundspolar(grid, polar.tstep, currentpolarvoxel) or not inboundsazimuthal(grid, currentazimuthalvoxel = (currentazimuthalvoxel + azimuthal.tstep) % grid.numazimuthalsections if (voxels[-1].radial == currentradialvoxel and voxels[-1].polar == currentpolarvoxel and voxels[-1].azimuthal == currentazimuthalvoxel): continue voxels[-1].exitt = t voxels.append(SphericalVoxel(currentradialvoxel, currentpolarvoxel, currentazimuthalvoxel, entert=t)) return voxels Parameters: maxt: Unitized time for ray travel. Expected range [0.0, 1.0]. If maxt <= 0.0, no voxels are traversed. If maxt >= 1.0, the entire sphere is traversed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Voxels: If the computed next voxel coordinates are identical to the current voxel, the loop continues without adding a new entry to prevent duplicates. Boundary Conditions: Angular bounds checks (inBoundsPolar, inBoundsAzimuthal) are critical. If a traversal step would move outside the valid angular range, the traversal terminates, and the last voxel's exit time is set to trayexit. Singularity at Origin: The algorithm handles the origin singularity by starting traversal at the first non-zero radial shell (radialentrancevoxel) and checking if the ray origin is outside the grid.
