name: Quadratic Regression for Distance Fields
head: Quadratic Regression Filtering, Quadratic Regression Normal Estimation
body:
Quadratic Regression for Distance Fields is a method to approximate the zero level surface of a noisy 3D distance field F by fitting a quadratic function f(x,y,z) to neighboring grid points within an Axis Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). It simultaneously solves for filtering (extracting the constant term p{000}) and normal vector estimation (extracting the gradient coefficients). It sets itself apart from linear regression variants by providing a second-order approximation that captures curvature, allowing for smoother gradient estimation and better handling of local surface geometry, while exploiting symmetry to avoid solving large linear systems. It builds on Normal Estimation based on 4D Linear Regression by extending the polynomial basis to include quadratic terms. Inputs: Distance field F(U, V, W) defined on a grid. Grid spacings \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z. Neighborhood size N (number of voxels along one dimension of the cubic domain). Weighting function wi (or kernel W(X,Y,Z)) which is symmetric with respect to coordinate planes and depends only on the distance from these planes. Outputs: Filtered distance value at the center grid point: p{000}. Gradient vector 
abla f at any local coordinate (x,y,z) within the neighborhood. Data Structures: Constants A, B, C, D: Pre-computed scalars. Dependent parameters f{ijk}: Nine scalars computed per grid point via convolution. Coefficients p{ijk}: Nine scalars computed per grid point. Pre-computation: Calculate constants A, B, C, D once based on the weighting function w and integer offsets Xi, Yi, Zi. These are independent of the distance field data. Due to axis symmetry, the following equalities hold: \sumi wi Xi^4 = \sumi wi Yi^4 = \sumi wi Zi^4 = A \sumi wi Xi^2 Yi^2 = \sumi wi Xi^2 Zi^2 = \sumi wi Yi^2 Zi^2 = B \sumi wi Xi^2 = \sumi wi Yi^2 = \sumi wi Zi^2 = C \sumi wi = D Convolution: Compute dependent parameters by convolving the distance field F with weighted kernels. For a grid point (U, V, W), the indices i correspond to relative offsets (Xi, Yi, Zi) within the neighborhood. The coordinates of sample points are xi = Xi \Delta x, yi = Yi \Delta y, zi = Zi \Delta z. The nine dependent sums are: f{200} = \sumi wi Xi^2 fi = \sumX \sumY \sumZ W(X, Y, Z) F(U - X, V - Y, W - Z) f{020} = \sumi wi Yi^2 fi f{002} = \sumi wi Zi^2 fi f{000} = \sumi wi fi f{110} = \sumi wi Xi Yi fi f{011} = \sumi wi Yi Zi fi f{101} = \sumi wi Xi Zi fi f{100} = \sumi wi Xi fi f{010} = \sumi wi Yi fi f{001} = \sumi wi Zi fi Filtering: Replace the distance value at the center grid point with p{000}, calculated as: p{000} =  rac{(A + 2B) f{000} - C(f{200} + f{020} + f{002})}{(A + 2B) D - 3C^2} If the distance field were exact, p{000} represents the distance between the current grid point and the zero level surface. Normal Estimation: Compute the quadratic regression coefficients p{ijk} using the dependent parameters and constants: Quadratic diagonal terms: p{200} =  rac{f{200} - f{000} - (C - BD / C) p{000}}{(A - B)(\Delta x)^2} p{020} =  rac{f{020} - f{000} - (C - BD / C) p{000}}{(A - B)(\Delta y)^2} p{002} =  rac{f{002} - f{000} - (C - BD / C) p{000}}{(A - B)(\Delta z)^2} Mixed quadratic terms: p{110} =  rac{f{110}}{B \Delta x \Delta y} p{011} =  rac{f{011}}{B \Delta y \Delta z} p{101} =  rac{f{101}}{B \Delta x \Delta z} Linear terms: p{100} =  rac{f{100}}{C \Delta x} p{010} =  rac{f{010}}{C \Delta y} p{001} =  rac{f{001}}{C \Delta z} The approximating quadratic function is: f(x, y, z) = p{200}x^2 + p{020}y^2 + p{002}z^2 + p{110}xy + p{101}xz + p{011}yz + p{100}x + p{010}y + p{001}z + p{000} The gradient vector at local coordinates (x,y,z) is: (
abla f)x = 2 p{200} x + p{110} y + p{101} z + p{100} (
abla f)y = 2 p{020} y + p{110} x + p{011} z + p{010} (
abla f)z = 2 p{002} z + p{101} x + p{011} y + p{001} Note: The source text contains a typo in the gradient formula for y and z components in the provided notes ("2 p{020} x" and "2 p{002} x"). Based on the derivative of the quadratic function f(x,y,z), the correct terms are 2 p{020} y and 2 p{002} z respectively. The implementation must use the correct partial derivatives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputeconstants(weights, offsets, numsamples): """ Pre-compute A, B, C, D from weights and integer offsets. weights: list of wi offsets: list of (Xi, Yi, Zi) numsamples: number of sample points """ A = 0.0 B = 0.0 C = 0.0 D = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): w = weights[i] X = offsets[i][0] Y = offsets[i][1] Z = offsets[i][2] A += w (X4) B += w (X2 Y2) C += w (X2) D += w return A, B, C, D def computedependentparams(distancefield, centeru, centerv, centerw, kernelweights, kerneloffsets, dx, dy, dz): """ Compute f200, f020, f002, f000, f110, f011, f101, f100, f010, f001 """ f200 = 0.0 f020 = 0.0 f002 = 0.0 f000 = 0.0 f110 = 0.0 f011 = 0.0 f101 = 0.0 f100 = 0.0 f010 = 0.0 f001 = 0.0 for i in range(len(kernelweights)): w = kernelweights[i] X = kerneloffsets[i][0] Y = kerneloffsets[i][1] Z = kerneloffsets[i][2] # Get distance field value at neighbor # Note: Source uses F(U-X, V-Y, W-Z) uidx = centeru - X vidx = centerv - Y widx = centerw - Z # Boundary check required in implementation fval = distancefield[uidx, vidx, widx] f200 += w (X2) fval f020 += w (Y2) fval f002 += w (Z2) fval f000 += w fval f110 += w X Y fval f011 += w Y Z fval f101 += w X Z fval f100 += w X fval f010 += w Y fval f001 += w Z fval return { 'f200': f200, 'f020': f020, 'f002': f002, 'f000': f000, 'f110': f110, 'f011': f011, 'f101': f101, 'f100': f100, 'f010': f010, 'f001': f001 } def solvequadraticregression(fparams, A, B, C, D, dx, dy, dz): """ Solve for p000 and other coefficients. """ f200 = fparams['f200'] f020 = fparams['f020'] f002 = fparams['f002'] f000 = fparams['f000'] f110 = fparams['f110'] f011 = fparams['f011'] f101 = fparams['f101'] f100 = fparams['f100'] f010 = fparams['f010'] f001 = fparams['f001'] # Solve for p000 numeratorp000 = (A + 2B) f000 - C (f200 + f020 + f002) denominatorp000 = (A + 2B) D - 3 C2 if denominatorp000 == 0: p000 = 0.0 # Guard against division by zero else: p000 = numeratorp000 / denominatorp000 # Common term for quadratic coefficients commonterm = (C - (B D / C)) p000 # Quadratic diagonal coefficients denomquad = (A - B) if denomquad == 0: p200 = 0.0; p020 = 0.0; p002 = 0.0 # Guard else: p200 = (f200 - f000 - commonterm) / (denomquad dx2) p020 = (f020 - f000 - commonterm) / (denomquad dy2) p002 = (f002 - f000 - commonterm) / (denomquad dz2) # Mixed quadratic coefficients denommixed = B if denommixed == 0: p110 = 0.0; p011 = 0.0; p101 = 0.0 # Guard else: p110 = f110 / (denommixed dx dy) p011 = f011 / (denommixed dy dz) p101 = f101 / (denommixed dx dz) # Linear coefficients denomlinear = C if denomlinear == 0: p100 = 0.0; p010 = 0.0; p001 = 0.0 # Guard else: p100 = f100 / (denomlinear dx) p010 = f010 / (denomlinear dy) p001 = f001 / (denomlinear dz) return { 'p000': p000, 'p200': p200, 'p020': p020, 'p002': p002, 'p110': p110, 'p011': p011, 'p101': p101, 'p100': p100, 'p010': p010, 'p001': p001 } def estimategradient(coeffs, x, y, z): """ Estimate gradient at local coordinates (x,y,z). """ p200 = coeffs['p200'] p020 = coeffs['p020'] p002 = coeffs['p002'] p110 = coeffs['p110'] p011 = coeffs['p011'] p101 = coeffs['p101'] p100 = coeffs['p100'] p010 = coeffs['p010'] p001 = coeffs['p001'] gradx = 2 p200 x + p110 y + p101 z + p100 grady = 2 p020 y + p110 x + p011 z + p010 gradz = 2 p002 z + p101 x + p011 y + p001 return (gradx, grady, gradz) Parameters: Symmetry Assumption: The domain of sample points is symmetric onto the coordinate planes, and the weighting scheme wi depends only on the distance from the coordinate planes (i.e., wi is even with respect to x, y, z). This causes all cross-terms with odd exponents in the error minimization sums to vanish. N: The number of voxels along one dimension of the cubic domain. The full domain contains N^3 voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If A=B, B=0, or C=0, the denominators in the coefficient calculations become zero. This may occur if the weighting function or neighborhood is degenerate. Implementers should add guards. Boundary Conditions: The convolution requires accessing grid points outside the domain. Boundary handling (clamping, reflection, or zero-padding) must be defined by the implementer. Gradient Formula Typo: The source text contains a typo in the gradient formula for y and z components (2 p{020} x instead of 2 p{020} y). The correct partial derivatives must be used. A technique to compute dependent parameters (e.g., f{200}) for quadratic regression on a distance field F with cubic complexity O(N^3) by reducing it to linear O(N) complexity using separable filters. It relies on the separability condition W(X, Y, Z) = WX(X)WY(Y)WZ(Z), where W is the filter kernel derived from weights w and coordinates. N is the number of voxels along one dimension of the cubic domain. Time Complexity: The full 3D convolution has cubic complexity O(N^3) with respect to the filter size N. If the filter kernel is separable, the complexity reduces to linear O(N) per dimension, resulting in O(N) total complexity for the convolution step. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the distance field, the pre-computed constants (A, B, C, D), and the dependent parameters (f{ijk}) for the current neighborhood. The constants are global; dependent parameters are per-voxel if pre-filtered, or computed on-the-fly. Performance: The method is designed for real-time volumetric fusion applications running on GPUs. Pre-computation of A, B, C, D reduces runtime overhead. Strengths: Provides smooth surface rendering by allowing gradient estimation at any point within the neighborhood, not just grid points. Exploits symmetry to avoid solving large linear systems. Limitations: Requires a symmetric neighborhood and weighting function. Noise sensitivity is reduced but not eliminated; filtering is still needed before isoparametric surface extraction. Quadratic Regression for Distance Fields was introduced in the paper "Filtering and Gradient Estimation for Distance Fields by Quadratic Regression". It is part of a real-time volumetric fusion application running on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). The method addresses the need for filtering and robust normal vector estimation in inherently noisy distance fields, where differentiation is especially sensitive to noise. name: Scene-Space Normal Estimation
head: Höhne and Bernstein Normal Estimation
body: Scene-Space Normal Estimation is a surface rendering method that uses ray-casting and binary segmentation to determine object boundary locations and estimate normals in scene space. It is characterized by the expression R{bs}(S{bl}, Is). Volume-rendering methods that utilize scene space normals can be described by similar composite expressions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene D (volume or surface data). Output: A rendered image with surface normals estimated in scene space. Data Structures: The method relies on the composition of basic imaging transforms where the order of operation is right-to-left. The scene D is transformed via filtering Fs and interpolation Is. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Optional): The input scene D may be preprocessed to produce D1 or D2. D1 = Is(Fs(D)): Apply filtering Fs then interpolation Is. D2 = Fs(Is(D)): Apply interpolation Is then filtering Fs. 2. Ray-Casting and Binary Segmentation: The method uses ray-casting to traverse the scene. Binary segmentation (Bs) is applied to determine object boundary locations. 3. Normal Estimation: The normal estimation is performed in scene space using the boundary locator S{bl} and interpolation Is. 4. Rendering: The final rendering combines the segmented surface information with the interpolated scene data, expressed as R{bs}(S{bl}, Is)(D) = R{bs}(S{bl}(D), Is(D)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scenespacenormalestimation(sceneD, Fs, Is, Bs, Sbl): # Preprocessing variants (optional) D1 = Is(Fs(sceneD)) D2 = Fs(Is(sceneD)) # Select processed scene (D1, D2, or original D) processedD = D1 # Apply boundary locator and interpolation surfaceinfo = Sbl(processedD) interpscene = Is(processedD) # Render using binary segmentation image = Bs(surfaceinfo, interpscene) return image Parameters: Fs: Scene filtering operator (e.g., smoothing). Is: Scene interpolation operator. Bs: Binary segmentation/surface detector. S{bl}: Surface boundary locator. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If Fs is a smoothing filter, the threshold for binary segmentation must be determined from knowledge of the low (L) and high (H) bounds of the data. The right-to-left composition order of transforms must be strictly maintained to match the defined imaging pipeline. This variant involves creating composite operators by combining basic imaging transforms. Specifically, it refers to the generation of D1 = Is(Fs(D)) or D2 = Fs(Is(D)) to preprocess the scene before normal estimation. This allows for the application of object/surface filtering where the filtered object Q' is determined from the filtered scene Fs(Go(Q)) using a threshold operator, or the filtered surface S' is determined from the filtered scene using a surface detector Bs. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: It is a foundational method used in later surface rendering techniques and has been improved upon in subsequent research. It integrates naturally with volume-rendering methods that use scene space normals. Limitations: The source does not provide specific performance metrics or limitations compared to sibling methods. Scene-space normal estimation was introduced by Höhne and Bernstein for surface rendering. It is characterized by expression (7) R{bs}(S{bl}, Is). The method has been used in later surface rendering techniques (expression 8) and has also been improved further. It is part of a broader framework of imaging transforms used in visualization, manipulation, and analysis of 3D structures. name: Weighted Normal Accumulation
head: Normals Rendering, NormalsRenderer, Transmittance-Weighted Normal Estimation
body: Weighted Normal Accumulation estimates surface normals for volume rendering by aggregating per-sample gradient normals along a ray, weighted by their transmittance contributions. Inputs: normals: A tensor of shape (numsamples, 3) containing the estimated normal vector for each sample along the ray. weights: A tensor of shape (numsamples,) containing the transmittance-based weight for each sample. Outputs: n: A tensor of shape (3,) representing the accumulated normal vector. Data Structures: normals: Float32 array, 3 components per sample. weights: Float32 array, 1 component per sample. Steps: 1. Initialize the accumulated normal vector n to zero. 2. Compute n = \sum (weights \times normals). 3. If normalize is True, normalize the resulting vector n. Formula: The accumulated normal n is computed as: n = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi \mathbf{n}i Where: wi is the transmittance weight for sample i. \mathbf{n}i is the normal vector for sample i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def weightednormalaccumulation(normals, weights, normalize=True): acc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for w, n in zip(weights, normals): acc[0] += w n[0] acc[1] += w n[1] acc[2] += w n[2] if normalize: length = (acc[0]2 + acc[1]2 + acc[2]2)0.5 if length > 1e-8: acc[0] /= length acc[1] /= length acc[2] /= length return acc Parameters: normalize: Boolean, default True. Determines if the result is unit-length. Edge Cases: If all weights are zero, the accumulated normal is zero. Normalization should handle this by returning a default or leaving it as zero. Precision issues may arise if weights vary significantly in magnitude; using higher precision for accumulation is recommended. This variant computes the rendered normal map N{rendered}(u) for a pixel u by summing transmittance-weighted opacity and normals along the ray: N{rendered}(u) = \sum{i=1}^{N{ray}} Ti \alphai ni, where Ti is transmittance, \alphai is opacity, and ni is the normal at sample i. name: Antialiasing (AA)
head: Aliasing Prevention, Procedural Texture Anti-Aliasing, Subpixel Sampling
body: Antialiasing (AA) in distance-field ray marching prevents moiré artifacts and jagged edges caused by high-frequency noise octaves or fine geometric details aliasing against the pixel grid. It differs from standard supersampling by often integrating frequency-aware logic directly into the procedural evaluation or ray differential calculation, rather than relying solely on brute-force pixel subdivision. The method builds on Distance-field ray marching. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, pixel coordinates, scene SDF, procedural noise parameters (octaves, frequency), and AA configuration (samples, mode). Outputs: Final pixel color, free of high-frequency aliasing artifacts. Ray Offsets: A 2D array or vector of (xx, yy) offsets representing subpixel jitter positions within the pixel footprint. LOD State: Integer count of active noise octaves, derived from pixel size or ray differentials. 1. Procedural Frequency Capping (LOD): Calculate the pixel size in world units, s{pixel}. Determine the maximum octave count: n{oct} = \min(N{max}, \lfloor \log2(s{pixel}) \rfloor) where N{max} is the global maximum octaves. Evaluate the noise function using only n{oct} octaves. This skips frequencies finer than the pixel resolution, preventing moiré patterns. Alternative Analytical Filtering: For simple patterns, apply a smoothstep filter based on the derivative of the pattern coordinate u: f{filtered} = \text{smoothstep}(-fw, fw, f(u)) where fw = fwidth(uv) is the rate of change of u across the pixel. 2. Subpixel Jittering: Define a grid of jitter offsets. A standard configuration uses 2 samples in x and 4 samples in y, totaling 8 samples per pixel. The offsets xx and yy are distributed within the pixel space: xx \in \{-0.25, 0.25\} and yy \in \{-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75\}. For each sample (i, j): a. Adjust the ray direction \mathbf{d}' by adding the offset (xxi, yyj) to the ray's origin or direction vector, effectively shifting the ray's entry point into the pixel footprint. b. Perform standard sphere tracing using the adjusted ray. c. Store the resulting color C{ij}. 3. Aggregation: Average the colors from all samples: C{final} = \frac{1}{N{samples}} \sum{i,j} C{ij} For 8 samples, multiply the sum by 0.125 (1/8). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderpixelaa(rayo, rayd, pixelsize, maxoctaves, noisefunc, useaa=True): # 1. Procedural LOD Calculation if pixelsize > 0: lodoctaves = min(maxoctaves, int(math.log2(pixelsize))) else: lodoctaves = maxoctaves if not useaa: return spheretraceinline(rayo, rayd, lodoctaves, noisefunc) # 2. Subpixel Sampling Configuration xoffsets = [-0.25, 0.25] yoffsets = [-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75] accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) # 3. Loop over samples for xx in xoffsets: for yy in yoffsets: jitteredd = normalize(rayd + vec3(xx, yy, 0.0)) accumulatedcolor += spheretraceinline(rayo, jitteredd, lodoctaves, noisefunc) # 4. Average results return accumulatedcolor 0.125 def spheretraceinline(rayo, rayd, lodoctaves, noisefunc): t = 0.0 maxdist = 100.0 epsilon = 0.001 while t < maxdist: p = rayo + t rayd dist = noisefunc(p, lodoctaves) if dist < epsilon: return vec3(1.0) if dist < 0: return vec3(0.0) t += dist return vec3(0.0) AA Samples: 8 samples per pixel (2x4 grid) is a typical configuration. LOD Octaves: Determined dynamically by int(log2(pixelsize)). Jitter Range: xx \in \{-0.25, 0.25\} and yy \in \{-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75\} with step 0.5. Zero Pixel Size: If pixelsize is 0 or negative, log2 is undefined. Guard against this by clamping lodoctaves to maxoctaves. Derivative Calculation: Analytical filtering requires accurate fwidth (derivative) computation. In ray marching, this requires computing ray differentials \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v} manually, as standard texture derivatives may not apply to procedural SDFs. Performance: Subpixel sampling increases cost linearly with sample count. 8 samples is a balance; higher counts (e.g., 16+) may be needed for high-frequency scenes but significantly reduce frame rate. SSAA renders the entire scene at a higher resolution and downsamples to the target resolution. It reduces aliasing by averaging multiple subpixel samples via interpolation. When to choose: When rendering complex scenes with multiple buffers (albedo, depth, normal) and hardware acceleration for interpolation is available. It operates on the final image buffer rather than per-pixel jittering. Implementation: Compute high-res dimensions h = \text{make\divisible}(h0 \cdot ssaa, 8) and w = \text{make\divisible}(w0 \cdot ssaa, 8). Render all buffers at (h, w), then downsample using torch.nn.functional.interpolate with mode='min' (bilinear/bicubic minification). Parameters: ssaa integer multiplier, default 1. Must be >1 to trigger. Time Complexity: Scales linearly with the number of AA samples. LOD capping reduces evaluation cost for distant objects by skipping noise octaves. Memory Complexity: Scales with the render resolution for SSAA. Strengths: Effectively eliminates moiré from procedural noise via LOD capping and jagged edges from geometry via subpixel sampling. Limitations: Subpixel sampling increases computational cost linearly with sample count. Procedural LOD requires careful derivative management for analytical filtering. When to use: Use LOD capping for procedural noise. Use subpixel jittering for geometric AA when performance allows. Use SSAA when post-processing downsampling is feasible and high-quality anti-aliasing is required for all buffers. Antialiasing in ray marching evolved alongside procedural rendering. Early implementations used simple supersampling. The integration of LOD-based octave capping for procedural noise was developed to address specific moiré artifacts in ridged noise and Voronoi patterns, which are particularly visible on axis-aligned surfaces. SSAA in the context of neural and implicit rendering adapts traditional rasterization downsampling techniques to volume rendering pipelines. a1k0n/asciitracing, https://github.com/a1k0n/asciitracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skills/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md at main..., https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/skills/blob/main/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md, fetched 2026-10-27 dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, https://github.com/dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volume Ray Marching with Temporal Accumulation
head: HZL Fluid Effects Volume Rendering
body: Volume Ray Marching with Temporal Accumulation is a real-time rendering technique that integrates the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) through a 3D density field using fixed-step ray marching, stabilized by blending the current frame's result with a history texture. It distinguishes itself from standard ray marching by reducing temporal noise and flickering in animated sequences, making it suitable for fluid simulations where density fields change rapidly. Unlike SDF Cloud Rendering which relies on analytic distance fields, this method operates directly on sampled scalar textures, and unlike Atmospheric Ray Marching which models global atmospheric layers, it targets localized volumetric effects like smoke and fire within a bounded box. The method renders a full-screen quad, computing a ray for each fragment that intersects a unit cube [-1, 1]^3. It samples a density texture, computes lighting (including optional self-shadowing), and accumulates color. The final output is temporally blended with a previous frame's result to smooth noise. Inputs: densityTexture: 3D texture storing density values. sceneDepthTexture: Depth buffer of the scene geometry to clip rays. historyTexture: RGBA texture storing the accumulated color from the previous frame. cameraPosition: World-space camera origin. inverseViewProjection: Inverse of the combined view-projection matrix. lightDirection: Normalized direction vector of the light source. Parameters: stepSize, maximumSteps, densityScale, absorption, emissionStrength, lightIntensity, historyWeight. Outputs: mcolorTexture: Final rendered frame (GLRGBA8). The implementation uses OpenGL textures with specific formats and filtering: mcolorTexture: GLRGBA8, filter GLLINEAR, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. mdepthTexture: GLDEPTHCOMPONENT24, filter GLNEAREST, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. msceneDepthTexture: GLDEPTHCOMPONENT24, filter GLNEAREST, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. mhistoryTexture: GLRGBA8, filter GLLINEAR, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. Cleared to zero at initialization. 1. Initialize Textures: Allocate the four textures described above. Set filtering modes as specified. Clear mhistoryTexture to (0, 0, 0, 0). 2. Compute Ray Origin and Direction: Convert fragment texture coordinate to clip space. Unproject the far plane point using inverseViewProjection to get farWorld. Calculate rayDirection = normalize(farWorld - cameraPosition). 3. Intersect Ray with Unit Cube: Compute intersection of ray origin and inverse ray direction with box [-1, 1]. Return interval [t{min}, t{max}]. Initialize distanceAlongRay = max(t{min}, 0.0). 4. Clip Ray Against Scene Geometry: Sample sceneDepthTexture at fragment coordinates. If sceneDepth < 1.0, unproject the scene point to world space, calculate sceneDistance along rayDirection, and update t{exit} = min(t{exit}, sceneDistance). 5. Discard if No Intersection: If t{exit} <= distanceAlongRay, discard the fragment. 6. Apply Jitter: If jitterEnabled, add a random offset to distanceAlongRay using random(glFragCoord.xy) stepSize. 7. Initialize Accumulation: Set accumulated = vec4(0.0). 8. Ray Marching Loop: Loop index from 0 to maximumSteps-1. Break if index >= maximumSteps or distanceAlongRay >= t{exit}. Calculate position = cameraPosition + rayDirection distanceAlongRay. Sample densityTexture at position 0.5 + 0.5. Get fieldValue (r channel). Set density = fieldValue. 9. Detect Volume Entry: If !foundVolume and density > 0.01, set representativePosition = position and foundVolume = true. 10. Compute Color: Determine smokeColor and emittedLight based on fieldMode: Mode 0 samples temperature/fire textures, computes ambient (0.12, 0.15, 0.20) and direct light (1.0, 0.88, 0.72) \times \text{lightIntensity} \times \text{transmittance}, mixes smoke by position.y, and computes flame emission. Mode 1 mixes smoke color (0.3, 0.04, 0.01) to (1.0, 0.65, 0.08) by density. Modes 2/3 remap density to |density - 0.5| \times 2.0 and color red/blue. 11. Accumulate Color and Opacity: Compute step alpha \alpha = 1.0 - e^{-\text{density} \times \text{stepSize}}. Blend color into accumulated using standard alpha compositing. 12. Temporal Accumulation: If temporalEnabled, blend the current frame's result with historyTexture using historyWeight. 13. Light Transmittance (Self-Shadowing): If selfShadowingEnabled, march 20 steps in direction -normalize(lightDirection + vec3(0.0001)) with step size 0.08. Accumulate opticalDepth = texture(densityTexture, position 0.5 + 0.5).r 0.08. Break if abs(position) > 1.0. Return transmittance T = e^{-\text{opticalDepth} \times \text{absorption} \times \text{densityScale} \times 3.0}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumeraymarchingwithtemporalaccumulation( u, v, cameraposition, inverseviewprojection, scenedepthtexture, densitytexture, historytexture, lightdirection, stepsize, maximumsteps, densityscale, absorption, emissionstrength, lightintensity, historyweight, jitterenabled, frameindex, fieldmode, selfshadowingenabled): def matvecmul(M, v): return vec4( dot(M[0], v), dot(M[1], v), dot(M[2], v), dot(M[3], v)) def jitterrandom(coordinate, frameindex): value = fract(vec3(coordinate.xyx) 0.1031) value += dot(value, value.yzx + 33.33 + float(frameindex) 0.01) return fract((value.x + value.y) value.z) # 1. Compute Ray clippos = vec4(u 2.0 - 1.0, v 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) farworld = matvecmul(inverseviewprojection, clippos) farworld = vec3(farworld) / farworld.w rayorigin = cameraposition raydirection = normalize(farworld - rayorigin) # 2. Intersect with Unit Cube [-1, 1] inversedirection = 1.0 / raydirection first = (-1.0 - rayorigin) inversedirection second = (1.0 - rayorigin) inversedirection minimum = min(first, second) maximum = max(first, second) tentry = max(minimum.x, minimum.y, minimum.z) texit = min(maximum.x, maximum.y, maximum.z) tentry = max(tentry, 0.0) # 3. Clip against Scene Geometry scenedepth = scenedepthtexture.sample(u, v) if scenedepth < 1.0: clipscene = vec4(u 2.0 - 1.0, v 2.0 - 1.0, scenedepth 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0) worldscene = matvecmul(inverseviewprojection, clipscene) worldscene = vec3(worldscene) / worldscene.w tscene = dot(worldscene - rayorigin, raydirection) texit = min(texit, tscene) if texit <= tentry: return vec4(0.0) # 4. Jitter t = tentry if jitterenabled: t = t + jitterrandom(vec2(u, v), frameindex) stepsize # 5. Initialize Accumulation accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) foundvolume = False # 6. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(maximumsteps): if t >= texit: break position = rayorigin + raydirection t texcoord = clamp(position 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) density = densitytexture.sample(texcoord).r if not foundvolume and density > 0.01: foundvolume = True # Compute Lighting lighttransmittance = 1.0 if selfshadowingenabled: opticaldepth = 0.0 lightdir = -normalize(lightdirection + vec3(0.0001)) for in range(20): shadowpos = position + lightdir 0.08 if abs(shadowpos.x) > 1.0 or abs(shadowpos.y) > 1.0 or abs(shadowpos.z) > 1.0: break shadowdensity = densitytexture.sample(shadowpos 0.5 + 0.5).r opticaldepth += shadowdensity 0.08 lighttransmittance = exp(-opticaldepth absorption densityscale 3.0) smokecolor = vec3(0.0) emittedlight = vec3(0.0) if fieldmode == 0: ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.15, 0.20) direct = vec3(1.0, 0.88, 0.72) lightintensity lighttransmittance smokecolor = mix(vec3(0.1), vec3(0.5), position.y) density emittedlight = vec3(1.0, 0.5, 0.1) density emissionstrength elif fieldmode == 1: smokecolor = mix(vec3(0.3, 0.04, 0.01), vec3(1.0, 0.65, 0.08), density) else: density = abs(density - 0.5) 2.0 smokecolor = vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) if density > 0.5 else vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Accumulate alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) colorstep = (ambient + direct + emittedlight) alpha accumulatedcolor.rgb += colorstep (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) accumulatedcolor.a += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) t += stepsize # 7. Temporal Accumulation if historyweight > 0.0: historycolor = historytexture.sample(u, v) finalcolor = historyweight historycolor + (1.0 - historyweight) accumulatedcolor else: finalcolor = accumulatedcolor return finalcolor gridSpacing: float, default 0.5. Used for debug visualization of the grid, not the rendering itself. densityScale: float. Multiplier for density values in light transmittance calculation. stepSize: float. Distance advanced per ray march step. maximumSteps: int. Maximum number of ray march steps per ray. frameIndex: int. Current frame number, used for jitter randomization. jitterEnabled: bool. Adds random offset to starting distance. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: bool. Uniform present, but logic not explicitly shown in the core loop snippet. fieldMode: int. 0: Smoke/Fire, 1: Simple Smoke, 2/3: Abstract/Color-coded. lightDirection: vec3. Light source direction. lightIntensity: float. Light intensity multiplier. absorption: float. Absorption coefficient for Beer-Lambert law. emissionStrength: float. Multiplier for emitted light. selfShadowingEnabled: bool. Enables shadow ray marching. temporalEnabled: bool. Enables temporal blending. historyWeight: float. Weight for previous frame's color. Division by Zero: intersectBox computes 1.0 / rayDirection. If rayDirection is zero, this results in infinity/NaN. The implementation relies on the caller providing normalized directions. Light Direction Normalization: A small epsilon (0.0001) is added to lightDirection before normalization to prevent issues if the light direction is exactly zero. Texture Coordinate Mapping: Density texture is sampled at position 0.5 + 0.5. Texture wrap mode is set to GLCLAMPTOEDGE during initialization to handle out-of-bounds coordinates. Precision: Accumulation of alpha and color can suffer from precision loss if stepSize is very small or maximumSteps is very large. Standard float precision is used. Time Complexity: O(N \times M), where N is the number of pixels and M is maximumSteps. Self-shadowing adds a constant factor (20 steps) per ray if enabled. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output and history textures. The density texture size depends on the simulation resolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces temporal noise, stable for animated fluids, relatively simple to implement. Limitations: Ghosting artifacts if historyWeight is too high or camera moves too fast. Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in sparse regions. Self-shadowing is expensive. When to Use: Real-time fluid simulations, smoke, fire, clouds where temporal stability is important. When Not to Use: Static scenes where offline rendering is acceptable, or scenes requiring high-frequency spatial detail without temporal smoothing. This method is derived from the HZL Fluid Effects Studio, an open-source fluid simulation and rendering tool. It implements a standard volume ray marching algorithm with the specific addition of temporal accumulation to handle the noise inherent in real-time volumetric rendering. The technique builds on the principles of Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering, specifically the discretization of the RTE along a ray. pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, https://github.com/pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Acceleration and Optimization
body: This family encompasses techniques to reduce the computational cost of distance-field ray marching and sparse volume rendering, primarily by minimizing the number of expensive Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluations or traversal steps. Unlike Beam Optimization, which exploits spatial coherence by grouping rays, or Block Culling, which skips empty volume hierarchies, these methods focus on geometric culling, resolution scaling, and step-size adjustments to accelerate the rendering pipeline. Groups adjacent rays into beams and marches them together, reducing redundant computations for rays far from geometry by treating a group as a single entity until local detail requires splitting. Unlike Block Culling which skips entire blocks, or Bounding Shape Optimization which tightens bounds, beam optimization adapts the granularity of ray evaluation based on proximity to surfaces. Choose when rays exhibit high spatial coherence. Details specific algorithmic and hardware-level optimizations to reduce the computational cost of SDF ray marching, focusing on reducing redundant evaluations, minimizing arithmetic intensity, and leveraging spatial coherence. It complements Acceleration and Optimization by providing concrete implementation techniques for bounding volumes, level-of-detail management, and instruction-level parallelism. Unlike Beam Optimization which focuses on ray coherence, or Block Culling which uses hierarchical structures, these methods primarily target the efficiency of the per-pixel ray march loop and SDF evaluation itself. Choose for real-time applications where frame rate is critical. Reduces rendering time by skipping traversal of empty or irrelevant blocks within RGBA volumes. It is particularly effective when sparsity in the volume is induced by runtime parameters, such as narrowing the allowed density range, rather than inherent data sparsity. Unlike Beam Optimization which focuses on ray coherence, or Bounding Shape Optimization which refines geometry bounds, block culling operates on a hierarchical block structure to prune entire regions of the volume tree. Choose when rendering sparse volumes with significant empty space. Reduces redundant density evaluations in volumetric rendering by skipping steps in empty space using pre-defined geometric boundaries. Unlike Beam Optimization which restricts rays to narrow paths, or Block Culling which uses grid-based structures, this method relies on explicit closed geometry (e.g., spheres, boxes) to define the volume extent. It is most effective for scenes with mostly empty density fields where the non-zero density is confined to specific, well-defined regions. Choose when the volume has a well-defined, compact boundary. A parallelization technique for sphere tracing that maintains a dynamic mask of unfinished rays to prevent wasted computation on rays that have already converged or exited the scene. It differs from naive synchronous batching by selectively processing only active rays at each step, and from Adaptive Ray Marching with Dynamic Step Count by focusing on the binary active/inactive state of rays rather than adjusting step counts based on global ray density. Choose when rendering with neural SDFs or batched ray processing where early termination improves throughput. An optimization algorithm that prevents duplicate ray-marching inside overlapping volumetric primitives by discarding overlapping parts of spheres, reducing loop iterations and cutting computing times by half. A CPU-side pre-computation algorithm avoids duplicate or void tracing when spheres or ellipsoids overlap by pre-computing transmittance from the light source to the target voxel. During ray-marching, it detects when a ray enters an overlapping volume region, discards the overlapping parts of the spheres from the marching path, and continues only through non-overlapping regions to reduce total loop iterations. Unlike complex space-partitioning algorithms (K-D trees, Octrees), this method uses bounding boxes and simple overlap checks to eliminate the need for complex structures. Used in real-time GPU volumetric cloud rendering to maximize performance during the pre-computing phase. name: Beam Optimization
head: Beam Optimization for Primary Rays, Ray Batching, Ray Grouping Optimization
body: Beam optimization is a technique to improve the performance of primary rays in distance-field ray marching by grouping adjacent rays and marching them together in a single step. It reduces computations for rays far from geometry by treating a block of pixels as a single unit, splitting only when necessary. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Performance Optimizations for SDF Ray Marching by focusing on spatial coherence of ray bundles rather than per-ray acceleration structures or early stopping logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of primary rays covering a pixel region (typically a beam). Output: Hit distances or intersection points for the rays in the beam. Data Structures: Beam Group: A rectangular block of pixels. Fields: origins (list of ray origins), directions (list of ray directions), centerorigin, centerdirection, size (width/height in pixels). The group is defined by its center pixel's ray for marching purposes. Steps: 1. Initialize Group: Start with a beam of size B \times B pixels (typically 8 \times 8). Calculate the center ray (oc, dc) for the group. 2. March Center Ray: Perform standard Sphere Tracing along the center ray dc from origin oc. 3. Check Collision Potential: Let d{min} be the smallest distance to the scene geometry found during the march step. Let R{group} be the maximum distance from the center ray to any corner of the beam group at the current step position. If d{min} > R{group}, the entire group is safe from collision at this step. 4. Split Decision: If d{min} \le R{group}, there is a potential collision for at least one ray in the group. Split the group into four sub-groups (quadrants). 5. Recursive Marching: Each new sub-group repeats steps 2-4 using its own center ray. 6. Termination: If a group steps far enough into the scene to be discarded entirely, stop processing that group. If a group contains only one ray and it has hit an object, record the hit and stop. The closer the groups are to a target, the more likely it is for a higher amount of sub-groups to be created due to the decreased distance to the geometry, making less pixels fit inside the group. Parameters: Beam size: 8 \times 8 pixels is a common setting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Comparing d{min} with R{group} requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially when rays are nearly parallel or the group is large. Degenerate Input: If the scene has no geometry, the entire beam may be discarded early, which is efficient. If geometry is dense, the beam may split frequently, approaching per-ray performance. Pseudocode: def beamoptimization(rayorigins, raydirections, sceneeval, beamsize=8, maxsteps=1000, epsilon=1e-4): # Standard sphere tracing helper def spheretrace(origin, direction, maxsteps, epsilon): t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): dmin = sceneeval(origin + t direction) if dmin < epsilon: return t if dmin <= 0: return t t += dmin return float('inf') # Initialize beams from ray origins and directions beams = [] n = len(rayorigins) for i in range(0, n, beamsize beamsize): chunko = rayorigins[i:i+beamsizebeamsize] chunkd = raydirections[i:i+beamsizebeamsize] if len(chunko) < beamsize beamsize: break centeridx = beamsize beamsize // 2 beams.append({ 'origins': chunko, 'directions': chunkd, 'centerorigin': chunko[centeridx], 'centerdirection': chunkd[centeridx], 'size': beamsize }) results = {} while beams: currentbeam = beams.pop() centero = currentbeam['centerorigin'] centerd = currentbeam['centerdirection'] bsize = currentbeam['size'] # March center ray hitdist = spheretrace(centero, centerd, maxsteps, epsilon) # Rgroup is the spatial extent of the beam at the hit distance # Approximated using unit pixel spacing and small-angle assumption Rgroup = hitdist (bsize - 1) / 2.0 if hitdist != float('inf') else float('inf') if hitdist == float('inf') or hitdist > Rgroup: # No collision possible for any ray in this beam for flatidx in range(len(currentbeam['origins'])): results[flatidx] = hitdist else: # Potential collision, split beam if bsize == 1: # Single ray hit results[0] = hitdist else: newsize = bsize // 2 half = newsize for q in range(4): qy = (q // 2) half qx = (q % 2) half suborigins = [] subdirs = [] for y in range(half): for x in range(half): flatidx = (qy + y) bsize + (qx + x) if flatidx < len(currentbeam['origins']): suborigins.append(currentbeam['origins'][flatidx]) subdirs.append(currentbeam['directions'][flatidx]) if suborigins: centeridx = len(suborigins) // 2 beams.append({ 'origins': suborigins, 'directions': subdirs, 'centerorigin': suborigins[centeridx], 'centerdirection': subdirs[centeridx], 'size': newsize }) return results An extension of beam optimization to soft shadows by shooting a beam of rays from the view-sample position to the area light to find conservative furthest distances. Definition: Uses a beam of four rays per pixel from the view-sample position to the area light. Steps: 1. Shoot a beam of four rays per pixel from the view-sample position to the area light. 2. Find the conservative furthest distance along these rays where no geometry is intersected. 3. Shorten all shadow rays accordingly based on the conservative furthest distance. 4. Trace the same beam rays in the reverse direction (from the light source) to find a conservative interval where geometry may be intersected. Pitfall: Pixels whose entire beams have no intersection with geometry require no additional shadow rays, which is an optimization opportunity. Time Complexity: Depends on the scene density. In empty space, beams are discarded early, leading to near-constant time per beam. In dense scenes, beams split frequently, approaching O(N) where N is the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Low, as it processes beams iteratively using a stack or queue. The broader rendering system uses a DAG data structure, but beam optimization itself requires minimal auxiliary memory. Measured Performance: Improves performance of primary rays by reducing redundant intersection tests for rays far from geometry. Strengths: Reduces computation for rays in empty space; simple to implement with existing sphere tracing logic. Limitations: May not provide significant benefits in highly complex scenes where beams split often; requires careful calculation of beam offsets. When to Use: When primary rays cover large areas of empty space; when hardware supports efficient parallel processing of ray bundles. When Not to Use: When the scene is extremely dense and beams rarely stay intact; when per-ray precision is critical and beam approximation introduces errors. Beam optimization was described by Laine and Karras. It is used in high-resolution sparse voxel DAG rendering to improve performance. The technique leverages the spatial coherence of primary rays to reduce the number of intersection tests. name: Performance Optimizations for SDF Ray Marching
head: Optimisations, SDF Ray Marching Optimizations
body: This method applies computational and rendering optimizations to Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching to improve frame rates and reduce GPU/CPU load without significantly degrading visual quality. It addresses the high cost of iterative SDF evaluations and texture lookups in real-time rendering. Unlike sibling methods that focus on acceleration structures like Beam Optimization or Block Culling, these optimizations primarily target the efficiency of the ray marching loop itself, the SDF evaluation logic, and the final image resolution. The method applies several independent optimization techniques to the ray marching pipeline. Inputs: Scene SDF definition (primitives, transformations), camera parameters, resolution, and rendering budget (target frame time). Outputs: Rendered image with maintained visual fidelity at higher frame rates. Bounding Volumes: Simple geometric primitives (e.g., spheres) used to enclose complex sub-scenes. Level of Detail (LOD) Parameters: MAXSTEPS and EPSILON values adjusted based on distance. Ray Differentials: Vectors \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}}{\partial u} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}}{\partial v} representing the change in ray origin/position with respect to screen coordinates, used for texture filtering and antialiasing. Surround expensive or distant sub-scenes with a fast, simple SDF check (e.g., a sphere). 1. Define a bounding volume SDF d{bound}(\mathbf{p}) for a group of primitives. 2. During ray marching, evaluate d{bound}(\mathbf{p}) at the current ray position \mathbf{p}. 3. If d{bound}(\mathbf{p}) > \text{current\step\size}, skip the evaluation of the detailed primitives within that volume. Note: This assumes the bounding volume is conservative (i.e., the detailed geometry is entirely contained within the distance field of the bound). Reduce computational effort for objects far from the camera. 1. Calculate the distance dist from the camera to the current ray position or bounding volume. 2. If dist > \text{threshold} (e.g., 10 scene units): Reduce MAXSTEPS for the ray marching loop. Increase EPSILON (the hit threshold). Rationale: The visual difference between high-precision and low-precision marching is imperceptible at large distances. Multiply the step size by a constant factor to skip more empty space per iteration. 1. In the ray marching loop, after calculating the distance d = \text{sdf}(\mathbf{p}): Apply over-relaxation: d{relaxed} = d \times \alpha, where \alpha \in [1.1, 1.6]. Advance the ray: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + d{relaxed} \cdot \mathbf{r}, where \mathbf{r} is the ray direction. 2. Pitfall: This risks artifacts (overshooting) near concave edges or thin geometry, as the guaranteed safe step size of standard sphere tracing is violated. Use only in open scenes or where visual artifacts are acceptable. Render at a lower resolution and upscale. 1. Render the scene to a framebuffer at half the target resolution (e.g., 50% width and height). 2. Upscale the result to the final resolution using a simple bilinear or nearest-neighbor filter. 3. Rationale: This is described as the most effective single optimization for real-time SDF rendering at larger resolutions. Reduce the number of SDF primitive evaluations by exploiting geometric symmetry. 1. Identify symmetries in the scene (e.g., rotational symmetry of gears). 2. Evaluate only a subset of primitives. For example, if an object has 18-fold rotational symmetry, evaluate only 4 representative pieces. 3. Within each primitive, if further symmetry exists (e.g., 12-fold tooth symmetry), evaluate only 1 representative part. 4. Transform the ray position into the local symmetric coordinate system to perform the evaluation. Use ray differentials to improve texture sampling and reduce aliasing. 1. Texture Filtering: Compute ray differentials \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}}{\partial u} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}}{\partial v} to estimate the footprint of the pixel on the texture. Use these to perform proper mipmapping or filtering during texture lookups in the ray march. 2. Antialiasing: Estimate the coverage of the pixel frustum intersecting the geometry. At each step, calculate the distance to the surface d. Use ray differentials to estimate the partial coverage of the pixel by the surface. Composite these partial coverages front-to-back to produce a smooth, anti-aliased edge without pixelization. Use MMX instruction set extensions to accelerate tri-linear interpolation of voxel data. 1. Replace floating-point arithmetic with integer arithmetic for voxel sampling. 2. Use four MMX instructions: PMULHW, PMULLW, PMADDWD, and PSUBW to perform tri-linear interpolation in 37 instructions. 3. Optimize address generation for the eight samples involved in tri-linear interpolation by exploiting their fixed offset relationships. 4. Pitfall: On Pentium-II, this may not improve performance and can worsen it compared to non-MMX versions. On older Pentium processors, it provides 60-80% faster performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchoptimized(rayorigin, raydirection, scenesdf, cameraposition, maxt=100.0, maxsteps=1000, epsilon=0.001, lodthreshold=10.0, overrelaxationfactor=1.0): p = rayorigin i = 0 currentmaxsteps = maxsteps currentepsilon = epsilon currentrelaxation = overrelaxationfactor while i < currentmaxsteps: d = scenesdf(p) if d < currentepsilon: return {"status": "hit", "position": p, "distance": d, "steps": i} distfromcamera = norm(p - rayorigin) if distfromcamera > maxt: return {"status": "miss", "position": p, "distance": d, "steps": i} if distfromcamera > lodthreshold: currentmaxsteps = 50 currentepsilon = 0.01 currentrelaxation = 1.2 stepsize = d currentrelaxation p = p + stepsize raydirection i += 1 return {"status": "miss", "position": p, "distance": d, "steps": i} This method approximates subsurface scattering by computing the local thickness of a surface along random inward hemispherical directions, then using the thickness to modulate a simplified subsurface scattering lighting term. It differs from sibling methods like Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF and SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching by performing a per-pixel thickness probe rather than global acceleration or volumetric integration. Coverage Search is a distance-field ray marching algorithm designed to determine ray hit or miss status in fewer iterations than standard sphere tracing by using a stack to manage coverage spans along the ray. SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching is a technique to accelerate volumetric ray marching by using a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to skip large empty spaces. The SDF stores the distance to the nearest surface of the volume, allowing the ray to advance by that distance in empty space without missing intersections. Unlike uniform sampling, this method spends samples only where clouds exist, avoiding expensive calculations for empty space. It solves the problem of wasting GPU cycles calculating zero-value samples in sparse cloud volumes, which previously led to 'soft, undefined volumes' or 'horrible banding/noisy output' if sample counts were low. This method renders signed distance field (SDF) scenes by marching a ray through the field using an acceleration structure to skip empty space, adaptive step sizing, and sign-change detection for surface refinement. It differs from standard sphere tracing by integrating a spatial acceleration structure that provides lower bounds on distance, allowing larger steps in empty regions while maintaining precision near surfaces. This method marches a ray through a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to find surface intersections while applying a correction factor to counteract distance elongation along non-cardinal directions caused by the Eikonal equation. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by explicitly scaling step sizes based on ray direction to prevent overshooting and jitter. A rendering technique for hair-thin geometry (such as jellyfish tentacles) that prevents flickering by replacing hard surface intersection with soft accumulation. Instead of stopping at the first hit, each ray march step adds a contribution based on the distance to the surface, fading in smoothly via an exponential falloff. This sets it apart from standard SDF ray marching, which typically terminates on hard intersection, and from Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF, which focuses on step size optimization rather than anti-aliasing thin strands. This method improves visual fidelity and performance in static volumetric rendering by pre-calculating shadow and ambient occlusion data into the volume texture. It leverages the static nature of the cloud volume to bake directional shadow rays and ambient attenuation, allowing for dynamic lighting changes (e.g., time-of-day) without runtime ray-marching costs for shadows. It sets itself apart from runtime shadow calculation by using a single texture lookup to match cloud geometry perfectly, and from static lighting by preserving volumetric shadow depth. This method optimizes cloud raymarching by baking a low-resolution 3D Signed Distance Field (SDF) texture that acts as a conservative proxy for the analytical cloud SDF. It allows the marching loop to skip empty space conservatively before falling back to analytical evaluations inside active cells. Unlike sibling methods that modify the ray step size or accumulation logic directly, this approach offloads the distance estimation to a pre-computed texture lookup, reducing the computational cost of the analytical SDF evaluation during the main rendering pass. Squared Distance Field Optimization is a technique to avoid the computational cost of square root operations in Signed Distance Field (SDF) raymarching by using squared distances for sphere comparisons, leveraging the monotonicity of the squaring function. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by replacing Euclidean distance metrics with squared Euclidean metrics for specific primitives (typically spheres) to eliminate sqrt calls, which are often expensive on GPU architectures. Using MMX instruction set extensions to exploit instruction-level parallelism for tri-linear interpolation, executing multiple low-resolution fixed-point operations in parallel. Use four MMX instructions: PMULHW, PMULLW, PMADDWD, and PSUBW to create a tri-linear interpolation version taking only 37 instructions. Performance on Pentium-II does not improve and may worsen compared to non-MMX version. On Pentium-II, MMX provides 0% performance improvement over non-MMX integer version; on Pentium, it provides 60-80% faster performance. Evaluate only a subset of primitives based on object symmetry to reduce computational cost. For example, evaluate only 4 gear pieces instead of 18, and within each gear, evaluate only a single tooth/dent instead of 12. Used in the 'Sphere Gears' Shadertoy example (2019) as an optimization exercise. A technique using ray differentials to do proper texture filtering in a raymarching context. Used in the 'Arlo' Shadertoy example (2015) for procedural modeling. A technique to antialias screen-space edges of raymarched distance fields by estimating how much of the pixel footprint (pixel frustum) intersects the geometry using ray differentials. Compute partial coverage per near-intersection and composite them front to back to give a correct smooth image without edge pixelization. Used in the 'Antialias, sort of' Shadertoy example (2014). Time Complexity: Varies by optimization. Standard sphere tracing is O(N) where N is the number of steps. Bounding volume early-outs and LOD reduce the average N for distant or complex scenes. MMX interpolation reduces instruction count per voxel sample. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory for bounding volumes and ray differentials. SDF texture baking requires storing a 3D texture. Measured Performance: On a 300-MHz Pentium-II, replacing floating-point with integer arithmetic provided 4-6x speedup, while MMX provided 0% improvement on Pentium-II but 60-80% on Pentium. Hand-coded address generation improved performance by up to 15%. Strengths: Significant frame rate improvements in real-time rendering, especially at high resolutions or with complex scenes. Simple to implement for bounding volumes and LOD. Limitations: Over-relaxation can cause visual artifacts. MMX optimization is hardware-specific and obsolete. When to Use: Real-time rendering where frame rate is critical. Use bounding volumes for complex sub-scenes. Use LOD for distant objects. Use resolution scaling for high-resolution displays. When Not to Use: When visual precision is paramount (avoid over-relaxation). When targeting modern GPUs where MMX is irrelevant. When the scene is uniformly complex with no distant parts (LOD benefits are minimal). The techniques described originate from various sources in the real-time rendering community, including Shadertoy examples and academic papers on volume rendering. Sphere tracing was introduced by John C. Hart in 1996. The specific optimizations like bounding volume early-outs, LOD, and over-relaxation are commonly cited in online tutorials and unofficial guides. MMX optimizations were explored in the early 2000s for CPU-based volume rendering. Ray differentials for antialiasing and filtering were demonstrated in Shadertoy examples from 2014-2015. name: Subsurface Scattering Approximation via Local Thickness
head: SSS thickness approximation, local thickness SSS
body: This method approximates subsurface scattering by computing the local thickness of a surface along random inward hemispherical directions, then using the thickness to modulate a simplified subsurface scattering lighting term. It differs from sibling methods like Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF and SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching by performing a per-pixel thickness probe rather than global acceleration or volumetric integration. Inputs: Surface position pos, surface normal norm, and a signed distance field query function sceneSDF(p) that returns a signed distance (negative inside, positive outside). Outputs: A scalar thickness value in the range [0.0, 1.0] used to modulate lighting. Data Structures: Scalar accumulators and hash-based random number generators. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize thickness accumulator to 0.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to SSSThicknessSamples - 1: a. Generate a random scalar sampleLength using a hash function: sampleLength = Hash11(i) SSSSampleDepth. b. Generate a random direction sampleDir in the hemisphere defined by the inward normal -norm using a hash function: sampleDir = GenerateSampleVector(-norm, i). c. Query the scene SDF at the probe endpoint: dist = sceneSDF(pos + sampleDir sampleLength).dist. d. Add the probe length and the SDF distance to the accumulator: thickness += sampleLength + dist. 3. Average the accumulated thickness by multiplying by SSSThicknessSamplesI. 4. Clamp the result to [0.0, 1.0] and return. Formulas: sampleLength = Hash11(i) SSSSampleDepth where Hash11 is a 1D hash, i is the loop index, and SSSSampleDepth is the maximum probe length. sampleDir = GenerateSampleVector(-norm, i) where norm is the outward surface normal and GenerateSampleVector produces a unit vector in the inward hemisphere. thickness += sampleLength + sceneSDF(pos + sampleDir sampleLength).dist where the SDF distance is added to the probe length to ensure positive contributions. result = clamp(thickness SSSThicknessSamplesI, 0.0, 1.0) where SSSThicknessSamplesI averages the accumulation. Parameters: SSSSampleDepth (float): Maximum length of the random hemispherical sampling vector into the object; default 1.0. SSSThicknessSamples (int): Number of samples to perform when calculating local thickness; default 32. SSSThicknessSamplesI (float): Inverse of SSSThicknessSamples (1.0 / 32.0 = 0.03125), used to average the accumulated thickness; default 0.03125. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Internal SDF values are negative, so the formula sampleLength + dist is critical; adding the sample length ensures the thickness contribution remains positive and prevents incorrect darkening. If the probe exits the object, sceneSDF returns a positive distance, which increases the thickness value and is handled by clamping to [0.0, 1.0]. Floating-point accumulation may introduce precision errors for very large scenes, though 32 samples is typically stable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatelocalthickness(pos, norm, sceneSDF, SSSSampleDepth=1.0, SSSThicknessSamples=32): thickness = 0.0 invsamples = 1.0 / SSSThicknessSamples for i in range(SSSThicknessSamples): samplelength = hash11(i) SSSSampleDepth sampledir = generatesamplevector(-norm, i) probepos = pos + (sampledir samplelength) sdfdist = sceneSDF(probepos).dist thickness += samplelength + sdfdist return clamp(thickness invsamples, 0.0, 1.0) def hash11(p): p3 = fract(vec3(p) 443.897) p3 += dot(p3, p3.yzx + 19.19) return fract((p3.x + p3.y) p3.z) def hash33(p3): p3 = fract(p3 vec3(443.897, 441.423, 437.195)) p3 += dot(p3, p3.yxz + 19.19) return fract((p3.xxy + p3.yxx) p3.zyx) def reflectvector(v, n): return v - 2.0 n min(0.0, dot(v, n)) def generatesamplevector(norm, i): randdir = normalize(hash33(norm + i) - vec3(0.5)) return reflectvector(randdir, norm) def clamp(x, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(x, maxval)) def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def fract(v): return v - floor(v) def floor(v): return int(v) if isinstance(v, float) else [int(x) for x in v] def normalize(v): length = sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def sqrt(x): return x 0.5 The thickness value is typically used as a factor in a diffuse or subsurface scattering lighting equation, such as multiplying albedo or scattering color. The quality of the hash functions (Hash11, Hash33) affects the visual noise of the approximation, and the source uses Dave Hoskins' hash functions. Time complexity is O(N) where N is SSSThicknessSamples, as each sample requires one SDF query and arithmetic operations. Memory complexity is O(1) auxiliary space, as the algorithm only uses local scalars. Performance with N=32 is relatively expensive per pixel compared to simple diffuse shading but cheaper than full volumetric ray marching, making it suitable for real-time rendering if optimized. Strengths include simple implementation, compatibility with any SDF, and a plausible approximation of translucency. Limitations include approximation quality depending on sample count, noise with low samples, and lack of multiple scattering or wavelength-dependent effects. Use this method when a cheap approximation of subsurface scattering is needed for SDF-rendered objects and full volumetric methods are too expensive. Do not use it when high-fidelity SSS is required or when the object is very thin, as thickness may saturate. name: Coverage Search
head: SDF Raymarching Algorithm: Coverage Search
body: Coverage Search is a distance-field ray marching algorithm designed to determine ray hit or miss status in fewer iterations than standard sphere tracing by using a stack to manage coverage spans along the ray. Inputs and Outputs: RayOrigin: The starting position of the ray. RayDirection: The normalized direction vector of the ray. TravelStart: Estimated start travel distance, typically from ray intersection with a simple bounding volume. TravelEnd: Estimated end travel distance, typically from ray intersection with a simple bounding volume. SignedDistanceFunction(p): A scene-dependent function returning the signed distance from point p to the nearest surface. Position (output): The 3D position of the hit or the end of the ray. Return value: true if a hit occurred, false otherwise. Data Structures: Coverage: A struct containing: Low: Float, the start of the coverage span along the ray parameter. High: Float, the end of the coverage span along the ray parameter. Sign: Integer, 1 if the span is outside (positive distance), -1 if inside (negative distance), 0 for neutral/initial states. Stack: A dynamic array or fixed-size buffer of Coverage structs. The source notes a required size of approximately 10 for GLSL implementations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the stack with a neutral span at TravelEnd and an initial pivot span. 2. Calculate the initial pivot point in the middle of the travel bounds. 3. Evaluate the SDF at the pivot and determine its coverage span. 4. Iterate through the stack, merging or subdividing spans until the ray start is subsumed by a known coverage span. 5. Determine the final hit position based on the sign of the final cursor span. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def SignedDistanceFunction(p): # Scene-dependent SDF. Defined here as a unit sphere at origin for completeness. return math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[1]2 + p[2]2) - 1.0 def sign(x): if x > 0: return 1 elif x < 0: return -1 else: return 0 class Coverage: def init(self, Low, High, Sign): self.Low = Low self.High = High self.Sign = Sign def CoverageSearch(RayOrigin, RayDirection, TravelStart, TravelEnd): Stack = [] # Push neutral span at TravelEnd Stack.append(Coverage(Low=TravelEnd, High=TravelEnd, Sign=0)) # Initial pivot calculation PivotTravel = (TravelStart + TravelEnd) 0.5 PivotPoint = [RayOrigin[i] + RayDirection[i] PivotTravel for i in range(3)] PivotRadius = SignedDistanceFunction(PivotPoint) # Push initial coverage span SpanLow = PivotTravel - abs(PivotRadius) SpanHigh = PivotTravel + abs(PivotRadius) InitialSign = sign(PivotRadius) Stack.append(Coverage(Low=SpanLow, High=SpanHigh, Sign=InitialSign)) # Initialize Cursor Cursor = Coverage(Low=TravelStart, High=TravelStart, Sign=0) while len(Stack) > 0: Top = Stack[-1] # Check if stack span overlaps with cursor's known high point if Top.Low <= Cursor.High: popped = Stack.pop() # Merge popped span into cursor if popped.High > Cursor.High: Cursor.High = popped.High if popped.Sign == -1: Cursor.Sign = -1 else: # Subdivide between cursor high and stack low PivotTravel = (Top.Low + Cursor.High) 0.5 PivotPoint = [RayOrigin[i] + RayDirection[i] PivotTravel for i in range(3)] PivotRadius = SignedDistanceFunction(PivotPoint) NextSign = sign(PivotRadius) NextLow = PivotTravel - abs(PivotRadius) NextHigh = PivotTravel + abs(PivotRadius) Next = Coverage(Low=NextLow, High=NextHigh, Sign=NextSign) # Check merge condition: signs are not opposite (abs(sum) > 0) and spans overlap if abs(Top.Sign + Next.Sign) > 0 and Top.Low <= Next.High: Top.Low = Next.Low else: Stack.append(Next) # Determine result if Cursor.Sign == -1: HitTravel = max(TravelStart, Cursor.Low) Position = [RayOrigin[i] + RayDirection[i] HitTravel for i in range(3)] return True, Position else: Position = [RayOrigin[i] + RayDirection[i] TravelEnd for i in range(3)] return False, Position Parameters: TravelStart: Typically derived from the intersection of the ray with a simple bounding volume (e.g., AABB or sphere). TravelEnd: Typically derived from the intersection of the ray with a simple bounding volume. Stack Size: Experimentally, a stack size of approximately 10 was required for the GLSL implementation to work correctly, whereas an initial non-shader implementation required only a size of 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shader Occupancy: The stack consumes shader registers/occupancy, which can reduce performance on hardware with limited resources. Branching: The algorithm is branchier than standard sphere tracing, which may impact performance on GPUs. SDF Cost: The approach is only worthwhile if the SignedDistanceFunction is sufficiently expensive to justify the overhead of stack management and branching. Discrepancy in Stack Size: There is an unexplained discrepancy between the required stack size in the GLSL implementation (10) and the initial analysis implementation (4), potentially due to a bug in the GLSL version. Performance: In the ideal case, Coverage Search performs approximately the same number of SignedDistanceFunction calls as sphere tracing. However, it results in half as many calls when the average signed distance approaches zero without hitting zero. Suitability: The method is best suited for environments suitable for recursive algorithms and where the SDF is expensive to evaluate. It is less suitable for scenes with simple, cheap SDFs or hardware with strict occupancy limits. The Coverage Search algorithm was developed by the author of the source material as an effort to solve ray hit/miss determination in fewer iterations than standard sphere tracing. It was designed to address cases where standard raymarching requires substantially more iterations, such as hitting an object dead-on, hitting at an acute angle, or running parallel to an object without hitting it. The algorithm was initially analyzed in a non-shader implementation and later ported to GLSL. SDF Raymarching, https://zone.dog/braindump/sdfmarching/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching
head: Bipolar ray marcher, Distance fields (SDF), SDF-accelerated volumetric rendering, Signed Distance Field (SDF) Ray Marching for Volumetrics
body: SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Ray Marching is a technique to accelerate volumetric ray marching by using a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to skip large empty spaces. The SDF stores the distance to the nearest surface of the volume, allowing the ray to advance by that distance in empty space without missing intersections. Unlike uniform sampling, this method spends samples only where clouds exist, avoiding expensive calculations for empty space. It solves the problem of wasting GPU cycles calculating zero-value samples in sparse cloud volumes, which previously led to 'soft, undefined volumes' or 'horrible banding/noisy output' if sample counts were low. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin rayStart, ray direction rayDir (normalized), SDF texture MapVolume, fixed inner step size StepSize, maximum steps RAYMAXSTEPS. Outputs: Accumulated color and transmittance float4. Data Structures: SDF Texture: A signed, half-precision floating point 3D texture. Resolution: 128x32x128. Sampling: Non-uniform, stretched by a factor of 6 horizontally to cover a larger area. Tiling: Horizontal tiling for infinite extension. Value: Distance to the shell of the cloud volume. Sign: Negative if inside the volume, positive if outside. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize scattering/transmission accumulator intScattTrans to float4(0, 0, 0, 1). Initialize distance along ray t to 0. 2. Loop: Iterate u from 0 to RAYMAXSTEPS. 3. Position: Calculate current ray position: rayPos = rayStart + rayDir t. 4. SDF Evaluation: Sample the SDF texture at rayPos to get sdf. Function: float sdf = MapVolume(rayPos). 5. Inside Volume Check: If sdf < 0 (inside volume): Calculate extinction using DensityFunction(sdf) = max(-sdf, 0). Calculate transmittance: transmittance = exp(-extinction StepSize). Get luminance luminance = Luminance(rayPos). Integrate scattering: integScatt = luminance - luminance transmittance. Update accumulator: intScattTrans.rgb += integScatt intScattTrans.a. Update alpha: intScattTrans.a = transmittance. Opaque Check: If intScattTrans.a < 0.003, set intScattTrans.a = 0.0 and break loop. 6. March Forward: Update t. If inside volume (sdf < 0), step by StepSize. If outside (sdf >= 0), step by max(sdf, StepSize). 7. Return: Return float4(intScattTrans.rgb, 1-intScattTrans.a). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Raymarch(rayStart, rayDir, MapVolume, StepSize, RAYMAXSTEPS): # Scattering in RGB, transmission in A intScattTrans = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Current distance along ray t = 0.0 for u in range(RAYMAXSTEPS): # Current ray position rayPos = rayStart + rayDir t # Evaluate our signed distance field at the current ray position sdf = MapVolume(rayPos) # Only evaluate the cloud color if we're inside the volume if sdf < 0: # Density function: max(-sdf, 0) extinction = max(-sdf, 0.0) # Transmittance calculation transmittance = exp(-extinction StepSize) # Get the luminance for the current ray position # Luminance is assumed to be a function returning float3 luminance = Luminance(rayPos) # Integrate scattering integScatt = luminance - luminance transmittance intScattTrans[0] += integScatt[0] intScattTrans[3] intScattTrans[1] += integScatt[1] intScattTrans[3] intScattTrans[2] += integScatt[2] intScattTrans[3] intScattTrans[3] = transmittance # Opaque check if intScattTrans[3] < 0.003: intScattTrans[3] = 0.0 break # March forward; step size depends on if we're inside the volume or not if sdf < 0: t += StepSize else: t += max(sdf, StepSize) return [intScattTrans[0], intScattTrans[1], intScattTrans[2], 1.0 - intScattTrans[3]] Parameters: StepSize: Fixed step size used for ray marching when inside the cloud volume. Type: float (uniform). RAYMAXSTEPS: Maximum number of ray march steps allowed per ray. Pitfalls: Performance of SDF Generation: Recalculating the SDF texture is expensive (approx 200ms on GTX1070 for a 3-pass compute shader). Solution: Use static cloud volumes. Movement is achieved by scrolling the volume texture rather than regenerating the SDF. A technique to accelerate real-time volumetric cloud rendering by using a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to skip empty space and determine step sizes, allowing for high sample counts without performance loss. It solves the problem of wasting GPU cycles calculating zero-value samples in sparse cloud volumes, which previously led to 'soft, undefined volumes' or 'horrible banding/noisy output' if sample counts were low. Unlike uniform sampling, this method spends samples only where clouds exist, avoiding expensive calculations for empty space. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of expensive volume evaluations by skipping empty space. Adaptively sampled distance fields (ADFs) achieve rendering speedups of up to 20 times compared to uniform sampling in complex scenes. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the SDF texture. The example uses a 128x32x128 half-precision 3D texture. Measured Performance: SDF generation takes about 200ms using a 3-pass compute shader on a GTX1070. Strengths: Avoids banding/noise by allowing high sample counts where it matters; skips empty space quickly. Limitations: Requires static cloud volumes if SDF regeneration is too expensive; low-resolution SDFs may lose detail. When to use: Real-time volumetric cloud rendering in VR to avoid banding/noise and improve performance by skipping empty space. When not to use: Dynamic volumes where SDF regeneration cannot be avoided or amortized. Origin: The technique is used in the UHawk VR engine for real-time volumetric cloud rendering in VR. History: The method was described in a blog post by the UHawk VR team, referencing GPU Gems 2: Chapter 8 for the visualization of empty space skipping. Usage: Used in the UHawk VR engine.
