name: SDF-Accelerated Volumetric Cloud Rendering
head: Ray marching with Signed Distance Fields
body: A technique to accelerate real-time volumetric cloud rendering by using a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to skip empty space and determine step sizes, allowing for high sample counts without performance loss. It solves the problem of wasting GPU cycles calculating zero-value samples in sparse cloud volumes, which previously led to 'soft, undefined volumes' or 'horrible banding/noisy output' if sample counts were low. Unlike uniform sampling, this method spends samples only where clouds exist, avoiding expensive calculations for empty space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static cloud volume represented by an SDF texture and a density/coverage texture. A ray origin and direction. Output: The final color and alpha of the ray, integrating scattering and transmittance. Data Structures: 1. SDF Texture: A signed, half-precision floating point 3D texture. Resolution: 128 \times 32 \times 128. Layout: Each entry contains the distance to the nearest point of the cloud volume shell. Inside the volume, values are negative. Scaling: The texture is stretched by a factor of 6 horizontally to cover a larger area and must tile horizontally for an infinitely extending cloud plane. 2. Cloud Volume Texture: An RG16 3D texture of the same resolution as the SDF. Red Channel: Coverage. Green Channel: Density. Pre-computation: The SDF is pre-computed using a layered system where a compute shader runs for each cloud layer, adding to the RG16 3D texture. The method for generating cloud shapes is similar to the method described by Sébastien Hillaire. Recalculating the distance field texture is expensive (takes about 200ms using a 3-pass compute shader on a GTX1070), so the system is limited to a static cloud volume. Movement is achieved by scrolling the volume itself. Ray Marching Algorithm: The ray marcher operates in two modes: 1. SDF Mode: Used when outside the cloud volume. The step size is determined by the SDF value. 2. Regular Mode: Used when inside the cloud volume. The step size is fixed. Areas outside of the cloud volume are skipped entirely. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SDFRESOLUTION = (128, 32, 128) HORIZONTALSCALE = 6.0 FIXEDSTEPSIZE = 0.1 # Uniform variable StepSize MAXRAYDIST = 1000.0 # Standard ray marching bound def worldtosdfcoords(worldpos): # Apply horizontal stretch and tiling to map to [0, 1) x = ((worldpos[0] HORIZONTALSCALE) % SDFRESOLUTION[0]) / SDFRESOLUTION[0] y = (worldpos[1] % SDFRESOLUTION[1]) / SDFRESOLUTION[1] z = (worldpos[2] % SDFRESOLUTION[2]) / SDFRESOLUTION[2] return (x, y, z) def densityfunction(sdfvalue): # Inside volume (negative SDF), density is positive distance to shell return max(-sdfvalue, 0.0) def raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 currentpos = list(rayorigin) rayt = 0.0 # Sample initial SDF value sdfval = samplesdf(currentpos) isinside = sdfval < 0 while rayt < MAXRAYDIST and accumulatedalpha < 1.0: if isinside: stepsize = FIXEDSTEPSIZE else: stepsize = sdfval if stepsize < 1e-6: break # Advance ray rayt += stepsize currentpos = [currentpos[i] + raydirection[i] stepsize for i in range(3)] # Sample SDF at new position nextsdfval = samplesdf(currentpos) nextisinside = nextsdfval < 0 if isinside: extinction = densityfunction(sdfval) transmittance = math.exp(-extinction stepsize) luminance = getluminance(currentpos) scatteredlight = [l (1.0 - transmittance) for l in luminance] # Front-to-back blending accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + scatteredlight[i] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) for i in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) (1.0 - transmittance) sdfval = nextsdfval isinside = nextisinside return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha def samplesdf(pos): coords = worldtosdfcoords(pos) return texture3d(sdftexture, coords) def getluminance(pos): # Sample cloud volume texture for density/coverage and compute luminance return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Implementation-specific Parameters: SDF Texture Resolution: 128 \times 32 \times 128. Horizontal Stretch Factor: 6. SDF Texture Format: Signed, half-precision floating point 3D texture. Fixed Step Size: Uniform variable StepSize. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The SDF texture uses half-precision floats, which may introduce quantization artifacts in distance calculations. Static Volume: The SDF pre-computation is expensive (~200ms on GTX1070), so the cloud volume must be static. Dynamic clouds are not supported without significant performance cost or alternative techniques. Tiling: The SDF texture must tile horizontally to support an infinitely extending cloud plane. Inside/Outside Transition: The switch between SDF and Regular modes must be handled carefully to avoid gaps or overlaps in the ray march. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the SDF texture, but is done offline. Ray marching is O(M) where M is the number of samples taken. The SDF allows skipping large empty spaces, reducing M significantly compared to uniform sampling. Memory Complexity: O(R^3) for the SDF texture, where R is the resolution. For 128 \times 32 \times 128, this is 524,288 half-floats, which is relatively small. Measured Performance: Pre-computation takes ~200ms on a GTX1070. Real-time rendering is possible with changing time of day and directional shadows. Strengths: High visual fidelity with well-defined cloud shapes. Efficient use of sample budget by skipping empty space. Limitations: Static cloud volume only. Pre-computation cost. Requires careful tuning of step sizes and texture resolution. When to Use: Real-time rendering of static volumetric clouds where visual quality is prioritized over dynamic cloud formation. When Not to Use: Dynamic cloud simulations, mobile platforms with very limited memory, or scenes requiring frequent updates to the cloud volume. This technique was developed by the author of the blog post "Rendering volumetric clouds using signed distance fields". It was implemented in the author's game engine 'UHawk' and demonstrated in a video of the game. The author was inspired by observing sparse but dense cumulus cloud formations and the frustration of achieving well-defined shapes with uniform sampling. The concept of using SDFs for ray marching is based on the work of Jamie Wong, who provided a full overview of signed distance fields. The cloud shape generation method is similar to the method described by Sébastien Hillaire. name: Adaptive SDF Ray Marching with Cell Acceleration
body: This method renders signed distance field (SDF) scenes by marching a ray through the field using an acceleration structure to skip empty space, adaptive step sizing, and sign-change detection for surface refinement. It differs from standard sphere tracing by integrating a spatial acceleration structure that provides lower bounds on distance, allowing larger steps in empty regions while maintaining precision near surfaces. Inputs: Ray origin ro, ray direction rd, scene bounds (boundsEnter, boundsExit), acceleration structure data, maximum distance MAX\DIST, maximum steps MAX\STEPS. Outputs: Hit distance dist, termination code. Data Structures: Acceleration Cell: Contains accelStart, accelCount, and cellExit (distance to cell boundary). Shape Data: Metadata for SDF primitives (scale, rotation, etc.) accessed via texture lookups if needed for exact evaluation. Parameters: SPHERE\TRACE\SAFETY: Multiplier for sphere tracing step size to prevent overshooting. ACCEL\EXACT\REFINE\DIST: Threshold for d{Lower} to trigger exact SDF evaluation instead of using the lower bound. ACCEL\MIN\CELL\EXIT\REFINE: Minimum cell exit distance to trigger refinement. over\relax: Over-relaxation factor for step size calculation. Steps: 1. Compute ray origin ro and direction rd. 2. Intersect scene bounds to get boundsEnter and boundsExit. 3. Initialize marchDist = boundsEnter, marchEnd = \min(MAX\DIST, boundsExit). 4. Loop i from 0 to MAX\STEPS: a. If i \ge MAX\STEPS, break. b. Evaluate current position: hitPos = ro + rd \cdot marchDist. c. Query acceleration cell: Call getAccelCellData(hitPos, cell, accelStart, accelCount, forceFullScan). d. Determine distance d{Scene}: i. If cell found and not forceFullScan: Compute cellExit. If accelCount > 0, get d{Lower} = sceneSDFDistanceLowerBoundForAccelRange(accelStart, accelCount, hitPos). If d{Lower} \le ACCEL\EXACT\REFINE\DIST or cellExit \le ACCEL\MIN\CELL\EXIT\REFINE, set d{Scene} = sceneSDFDistanceExact(hitPos). Else, set d{Scene} = d{Lower}. ii. Else if accelCount == 0, set d{Scene} = cellExit. iii. Else (no cell or full scan), set d{Scene} = sceneSDFDistanceExact(hitPos). e. Compute adaptive epsilon: hitEps = getAdaptiveHitEpsilon(marchDist). f. Check for surface hit: If |d{Scene}| < hitEps, set dist = marchDist, terminationCode = 1, break. g. Check for surface crossing: If havePrev and prevDist > 0.0 and d{Scene} < 0.0: i. Call refineSurfaceCrossing(ro, rd, prevT, marchDist). ii. Set dist, terminationCode = 2, break. h. Compute step size: stepDist = \max(|d{Scene}| \cdot SPHERE\TRACE\SAFETY \cdot over\relax, hitEps \cdot 0.33). i. If in cell, stepDist = \min(stepDist, cellExit + hitEps \cdot 0.5). j. Update state: havePrev = true, prevDist = d{Scene}, prevT = marchDist. k. marchDist += stepDist. l. If marchDist > marchEnd, break. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivesdfraymarching(ro, rd, boundsenter, boundsexit, maxdist, maxsteps, accelstructure): marchdist = boundsenter marchend = min(maxdist, boundsexit) haveprev = False prevdist = 0.0 prevt = 0.0 SPHERETRACESAFETY = 1.0 # Standard sphere tracing multiplier ACCELEXACTREFINEDIST = 1e-4 # Typical threshold ACCELMINCELLEXITREFINE = 1e-4 # Typical threshold overrelax = 1.0 # Over-relaxation factor for i in range(maxsteps): if i >= maxsteps: break hitpos = ro + rd marchdist # Query acceleration structure cell, accelstart, accelcount, forcefullscan = getaccelcelldata(hitpos, accelstructure) # Determine distance if cell is not None and not forcefullscan: cellexit = computecellexit(cell, hitpos, rd) if accelcount > 0: dlower = scenesdfdistancelowerboundforaccelrange(accelstart, accelcount, hitpos) if dlower <= ACCELEXACTREFINEDIST or cellexit <= ACCELMINCELLEXITREFINE: dscene = scenesdfdistanceexact(hitpos) else: dscene = dlower else: dscene = cellexit else: dscene = scenesdfdistanceexact(hitpos) # Adaptive epsilon hiteps = getadaptivehitepsilon(marchdist) # Termination: Exact hit if abs(dscene) < hiteps: return marchdist, 1 # Termination: Sign change crossing if haveprev and prevdist > 0.0 and dscene < 0.0: dist, = refinesurfacecrossing(ro, rd, prevt, marchdist) return dist, 2 # Step size calculation stepdist = max(abs(dscene) SPHERETRACESAFETY overrelax, hiteps 0.33) if cell is not None: stepdist = min(stepdist, cellexit + hiteps 0.5) # Update state haveprev = True prevdist = dscene prevt = marchdist marchdist += stepdist if marchdist > marchend: break return marchdist, 0 def getaccelcelldata(hitpos, accelstructure): # Standard spatial hash or BVH query to find containing cell return None, 0, 0, False def computecellexit(cell, hitpos, rd): # Ray-cell intersection to find exit distance return 1e9 def scenesdfdistancelowerboundforaccelrange(start, count, hitpos): # Query precomputed lower bounds for the cell's primitives return 1e9 def scenesdfdistanceexact(hitpos): # Evaluate full SDF at hitpos return 1e9 def getadaptivehitepsilon(marchdist): # Scale epsilon with distance or use fixed value return 1e-4 def refinesurfacecrossing(ro, rd, prevt, currt): # Bisection or linear interpolation between prevt and currt mid = (prevt + currt) / 2.0 return mid, 0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surface Crossing: Detection relies on sign change between previous and current d{Scene}. If prevDist > 0 and d{Scene} < 0, refineSurfaceCrossing is called to interpolate the exact hit position, preventing missed thin geometry. Precision: Using lower bounds from acceleration structures can lead to overshooting if not refined. The ACCEL\EXACT\REFINE\DIST threshold ensures exact evaluation when close to surfaces. Cell Boundaries: Step size is clamped by cell exit distance to ensure the ray does not skip over potential intersections within a cell. SDF Raymarching & Rendering is a fragment shader technique that renders signed distance field (SDF) scenes by marching a ray through the field to find surface intersections and computing lighting at the hit point. It samples the SDF volume via a procedural function or texture, compares the sampled distance against a threshold to determine surface intersection, and applies procedural coloring and shading. This method builds on Adaptive SDF Ray Marching with Cell Acceleration by performing the final surface refinement, shading, and texturing after the acceleration structure has narrowed the search space. Time Complexity: Depends on the acceleration structure query cost and the number of steps. In empty space, steps are large due to lower bounds. Near surfaces, steps are small due to adaptive epsilon and exact evaluation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the acceleration structure and scene bounds. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space, handles complex SDF scenes, precise surface detection. Limitations: Requires an acceleration structure, potential for missed thin geometry if sign change detection is not robust. When to Use: Rendering complex SDF scenes where empty space is significant. When Not to Use: Simple scenes where standard sphere tracing is sufficient, or when volumetric rendering is required. This method is derived from techniques described in, which combines sphere tracing with acceleration structures for efficient SDF rendering. It addresses the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing in large, sparse scenes. name: SDF Raymarching & Rendering
head: SDFRenderer, unlit SDF fragment shader
body: SDF Raymarching & Rendering is a fragment shader technique that renders signed distance field (SDF) scenes by marching a ray through the field to find surface intersections and computing lighting at the hit point. It samples the SDF volume via a procedural function or texture, compares the sampled distance against a threshold to determine surface intersection, and applies procedural coloring and shading. This method builds on Adaptive SDF Ray Marching with Cell Acceleration by performing the final surface refinement, shading, and texturing after the acceleration structure has narrowed the search space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Vertex shader outputs world position and view direction; SDF texture or procedural function; scene parameters (light position, shadow settings, AO settings). Output: Fragment color with shading, shadows, and ambient occlusion. Data Structures: v2f (Vertex Output): vertex: SVPOSITION (clip space position) worldVertex: TEXCOORD0 (world space vertex position, float3) vectorToSurface: TEXCOORD1 (direction from camera to vertex, float3) Uniforms: sphereRadius (float): Radius of the SDF bounding sphere. sdfRadius (float): Radius used for ray-sphere intersection start point. maxRaymarchSteps (int): Maximum number of steps per ray. shadowIntensity (float), shadowSoftness (float): Shadow parameters. aoSamples (int), aoKernelSize (float): Ambient occlusion parameters. planetTex (sampler2D): Texture for base color. sunPos (float3): Light source position. debugMode (int, default 0): Enables debug visualization. boidCount (float), boidPositions[256] (uniform float3 array), boidRadii[256] (uniform float array): Boid/SDF interaction parameters. planetTexHeight (float): Texture height parameter. sdfTexIn (texture): Input SDF texture. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Shader: Compute world position o.worldVertex = mul(unityObjectToWorld, v.vertex) and camera-to-surface vector o.vectorToSurface = o.worldVertex - WorldSpaceCameraPos. 2. Fragment Shader - Ray Initialization: Set rayOrigin = i.worldVertex and compute rayDirection = normalize(i.worldVertex - WorldSpaceCameraPos). 3. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Calculate distance dist from rayOrigin to the SDF bounding sphere using raySphereIntersect(rayOrigin, rayDirection, float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), sdfRadius). Advance rayOrigin by dist + 0.01 to start inside or just outside the field. 4. Ray Marching: Call worldRayMarch(rayOrigin, rayDirection, 16.0, res, hitPos, colAtHit). This function iteratively samples the SDF volume via sdfWorld(pos) to get signed distance, compares against hitThreshold() to determine surface intersection, and steps forward by the sampled distance until a surface is hit or max steps are exceeded. It returns hit > 0.0 if a surface is found. 5. Shading: If hit > 0.0: Compute surface normal normal = worldNormal(hitPos). Compute shadow: Cast a shadow ray from hitPos + normal 0.001 towards sunPos. Use shadowIntensity and shadowSoftness to modulate the result. Compute Ambient Occlusion (AO): Sample the SDF along the normal in multiple directions using aoSamples and aoKernelSize. Compute base color: Sample planetTex using UVs derived from uv and sphereRadius. Falls back to float3(0.8, 0.8, 0.8) if distance exceeds threshold. Combine lighting, shadow, AO, and base color to produce final col. 6. Debug Mode: If debugMode == 1, skip raymarching. Compute d = worldSample(rayOrigin, c). Color based on signed distance d using exponential falloff and cosine modulation. Formulas: Ray-Sphere Intersection: Standard quadratic solution for |rayOrigin + t \cdot rayDirection - center|^2 = radius^2. Shadow Ray: shadow = 1.0 - \text{smoothstep}(0.0, \shadowSoftness, \text{distanceToLight}) \cdot \shadowIntensity. AO: ao = 1.0 - \frac{\sum{i=0}^{\aoSamples} \text{clamp}(0.0, 1.0, \text{sdf}(hitPos + normal \cdot i \cdot \aoKernelSize))}{\aoSamples}. Debug Coloring: col = \text{float3}(\text{step}(0.0, d), \text{step}(d, 0.0), 0.0) \cdot (1.0 - e^{-5.0 |d|}) \cdot (0.8 + 0.2 \cos(512.0 |d|)); then col = \text{lerp}(col, \text{float3}(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), 1.0 - \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.005, |d|)). Parameters: maxRaymarchSteps: Not given in the sources. aoSamples: Not given in the sources. aoKernelSize: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Small offsets (0.001) are used to prevent self-intersection in shadow rays. Boundaries: Ray-sphere intersection ensures the ray starts within the SDF volume, preventing infinite loops in empty space. Degenerate Input: If debugMode is enabled, the raymarching logic is bypassed, which may lead to incorrect lighting if not handled separately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchrender(worldvertex, worldcamerapos, sdffunc, params): rayorigin = worldvertex raydirection = normalize(worldvertex - worldcamerapos) # Ray-sphere intersection dist = raysphereintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), params.sdfradius) rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection (dist + 0.01) # Ray marching hit, hitpos, colathit = worldraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, 16.0, params.maxsteps) if hit > 0.0: normal = worldnormal(hitpos) # Shadow shadowrayorigin = hitpos + normal 0.001 shadow = computeshadow(shadowrayorigin, params.sunpos, params.shadowintensity, params.shadowsoftness) # AO ao = computeao(hitpos, normal, params.aosamples, params.aokernelsize) # Color uv = (0.5, length(uv) / params.sphereradius) basecolor = sampletexture(params.planettex, uv) # Final color finalcolor = basecolor shadow ao return finalcolor else: return (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) def raysphereintersect(origin, direction, center, radius): oc = (origin[0]-center[0], origin[1]-center[1], origin[2]-center[2]) a = dot(direction, direction) b = 2.0 dot(oc, direction) c = dot(oc, oc) - radius radius disc = b b - 4 a c if disc < 0: return -1.0 sqrtdisc = sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) return t1 if t1 > 0 else t2 def worldraymarch(origin, direction, maxdist, maxsteps): t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return False, origin, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) dist = sdffunc(origin) if dist < 0.001: return True, origin, (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) t += dist origin = origin + direction dist return False, origin, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def worldnormal(pos): eps = 0.001 dx = (sdffunc((pos[0]+eps, pos[1], pos[2])) - sdffunc((pos[0]-eps, pos[1], pos[2]))) / (2eps) dy = (sdffunc((pos[0], pos[1]+eps, pos[2])) - sdffunc((pos[0], pos[1]-eps, pos[2]))) / (2eps) dz = (sdffunc((pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]+eps)) - sdffunc((pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]-eps))) / (2eps) return normalize((dx, dy, dz)) def computeshadow(origin, sunpos, intensity, softness): dirtolight = normalize(sunpos - origin) dist = length(sunpos - origin) shadowval = smoothstep(0.0, softness, dist) return 1.0 - shadowval intensity def computeao(pos, normal, samples, kernelsize): totalocclusion = 0.0 for i in range(samples): samplepos = pos + normal i kernelsize dist = sdffunc(samplepos) totalocclusion += clamp(0.0, 1.0, dist) return 1.0 - totalocclusion / samples def sampletexture(tex, uv): # Standard texture sampling implementation return tex.sample(uv) Renders the signed distance field directly as a 2D cross-section or 3D volume, using color to indicate sign and magnitude. Useful for debugging SDF generation. Debug SDF Visualization Optimized function to find the entry point of a ray into a bounding sphere, used to initialize the raymarch. Ray-Sphere Intersection Computes the surface normal from the SDF gradient at a given point. World Normal Computation Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of raymarch steps. Each step involves an SDF query. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, plus storage for the SDF texture. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and the number of rays (pixels). SDF query cost depends on texture size or procedural complexity. Strengths: No geometry required; infinite detail; easy to modify shapes. Limitations: No occlusion culling beyond the acceleration structure; high computational cost per pixel; no support for transparent surfaces without additional logic. When to Use: Real-time rendering of simple, smooth, or procedural shapes. When Not to Use: Complex scenes with many objects, or when high precision is required for thin structures. Originated from the use of signed distance fields in real-time graphics, popularized by tools like Unity and Unreal Engine. name: SDF Ray Marching with Eikonal Correction
head: Eikonal-corrected ray marching, distance field ray marching with step correction
body: This method marches a ray through a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to find surface intersections while applying a correction factor to counteract distance elongation along non-cardinal directions caused by the Eikonal equation. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by explicitly scaling step sizes based on ray direction to prevent overshooting and jitter. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). SDF field SDF(x, y, z). Maximum ray march steps N{max} (typical value: 128, range 8–512). Hit threshold distance \epsilon (implicit in hitThreshold()). Progress multiplier k (16.0 for ray origin march, 32.0 for shadow march). Eikonal correction factor C{eikonal}, computed from ray direction D. Outputs: Hit distance t. Hit status flag. Data Structures: The SDF is stored as a 3D texture or voxel grid, accessed via world-space coordinates mapped to texture coordinates. No additional complex data structures are required beyond standard ray parameters and SDF lookup. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize current ray distance t = 0.0 and progress accumulator res = 1.0. 2. Loop up to N{max} iterations: a. Calculate current world position: P = O + D \cdot t. b. Check bounds: If P is out of the SDF volume, return 0.0. c. Sample SDF: d = SDF(P). d. Check hit: If d \le \epsilon, set hit position to P, set res = 0.0, and return 1.0. e. Apply Eikonal correction: Clamp d to a minimum positive value (0.0001), then multiply by the correction factor: d{corrected} = \max(d, 0.0001) \cdot C{eikonal}. f. Update progress: res = \min(res, k \cdot d{corrected} / t). g. Advance ray: t = t + d{corrected}. 3. Return 1.0 if the loop finishes without hitting. Formula: The core step advancement formula is: t{new} = t{old} + \max(d, 0.0001) \cdot C{eikonal} where d is the raw SDF value at the current position, and C{eikonal} is the correction factor derived from the ray direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarcheikonalcorrected(origin, direction, sdfsample, maxsteps=128, k=16.0, hitthreshold=0.001): t = 0.0 res = 1.0 eikonalfix = calceikonalcorrection(direction) for in range(maxsteps): currentpos = origin + direction t if not iswithinsdfbounds(currentpos): return 0.0 dist = sdfsample(currentpos) if dist <= hitthreshold: return 1.0 correcteddist = max(dist, 0.0001) eikonalfix if t > 0: res = min(res, k correcteddist / t) t += correcteddist return 1.0 def calceikonalcorrection(direction): # Standard geometric correction for non-cardinal ray directions # Returns a scalar multiplier >= 1.0 based on direction alignment with grid axes. return 1.0 def iswithinsdfbounds(pos): # Standard AABB boundary check return True Parameters: maxsteps: 128 (typical), range 8–512. k: 16.0 for ray origin march, 32.0 for shadow march. eikonalfix: Calculated by calcEikonalCorrection(dir). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance Elongation: The Eikonal equation causes distance values to be larger than the true Euclidean distance along non-cardinal directions, leading to larger step sizes than necessary. The eikonalfix factor corrects this. Zero Distance: If dist is 0 or negative, it is clamped to 0.0001 to prevent zero-step stalls. Out of Bounds: Rays leaving the SDF volume must be handled explicitly to avoid sampling errors. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of ray march steps (up to maxsteps). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, plus the SDF texture storage. Performance: The correction factor calculation adds minimal overhead; the main cost is SDF sampling. The correction improves accuracy for non-cardinal rays but may increase step counts if the correction factor is large. Strengths: Improves accuracy of ray marching in SDFs, especially for rays not aligned with grid axes. Limitations: Requires a method to calculate the Eikonal correction factor, which is not detailed in the source. When to use: When high accuracy is required in SDF ray marching, particularly for non-axis-aligned rays. When not to use: If performance is critical and approximate results are acceptable, or if rays are always aligned with cardinal directions. This method is part of the implementation of signed distance fields in Unity, as described in an unofficial GitHub repository by samuelbigos. It addresses a known issue in SDF rendering where the Eikonal equation introduces directional bias in the distance values, which is corrected during ray marching to ensure accurate surface intersection detection. samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, https://github.com/samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with SDFs and Soft Accumulation
head: Jellyfish Ray Marching with Soft Accumulation, Soft Accumulation for Thin Geometry
body: A rendering technique for hair-thin geometry (such as jellyfish tentacles) that prevents flickering by replacing hard surface intersection with soft accumulation. Instead of stopping at the first hit, each ray march step adds a contribution based on the distance to the surface, fading in smoothly via an exponential falloff. This sets it apart from standard SDF ray marching, which typically terminates on hard intersection, and from Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF, which focuses on step size optimization rather than anti-aliasing thin strands. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin ro, ray direction d, time t, phase offset \phi, scene parameters (bell radius, tentacle length, school count), and SDF functions for the bell (sdBell), tentacles (sdTentacles), and arms (sdArms). Outputs: Final color col for the pixel. Data Structures: Ray State: travel (float, accumulated distance), trans (float, transparency, initialized to 1.0), rad (vec3, accumulated radial color), strands (float, accumulated strand contribution). Scene Constants: MARCHSTEPS (120), TENTLEN (3.0), ARMLEN (1.5), SCHOOL (5), GLOW, HOT (lighting intensity parameters). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsdfsoftaccumulation(ro, d, t, ph): # Camera/ray setup (from evidence) ro = vec3(0.0, 0.10 + 0.16 sin(t 0.08), 5.60) ro.xz = rot(0.07 sin(t 0.11)) ro.xz uv = (2.0 glFragCoord.xy - uresolution) / uresolution.y d = normalize(fw 1.85 + rt uv.x + upv uv.y) col = vec3(0.0) for i in range(SCHOOL): # Compute centre with sinusoidal drift centre = computecentresinusoidaldrift(i, t, ph) # Transform ray origin relative to center o = (ro - centre) / data.w # Apply tilt rotations o.xy = rot(tilt.x) o.xy o.zy = rot(tilt.y) o.zy # Ray-sphere intersection for marching bounds bo = o - vec3(0.0, -1.4, 0.0) b = dot(bo, d) disc = b b - dot(bo, bo) + 2.7 2.7 tmax = -b + sqrt(disc) # Initialize marching state pc = pulse(t 0.42 + ph 0.37) travel = max(-b - sq, 0.0) + dither # sq and dither not defined in sources trans = 1.0 strands = 0.0 rad = vec3(0.0) for s in range(MARCHSTEPS): if travel > tmax or trans < 0.05: break p = o + d travel # SDF evaluation db = sdBell(p, pc, t, ph) dt = sdTentacles(p, pc, t, ph) da = sdArms(p, t, ph) # Step size stride = clamp(min(db, min(dt, da)) 0.70, 0.010, 0.18) # Soft accumulation for strands taper = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.55, 1.05, -p.y / TENTLEN) strands += exp(-max(dt, 0.0) 95.0) stride 8.5 taper strands += exp(-max(da, 0.0) 45.0) stride 3.0 # Bell surface shading if db < 0.012: # Compute normal via finite differences n = bellNormal(p, pc, t, ph) # Uses e = vec2(0.0035, 0.0) fres = pow(1.0 - abs(dot(n, -d)), 2.4) lam = 0.35 + 0.65 abs(dot(n, normalize(vec3(-0.35, 1.0, 0.45)))) ribs = pow(0.5 + 0.5 cos(16.0 atan(p.z, p.x)), 14.0) op = 0.075 + 0.42 fres + ribs 0.12 rad += trans op (GLOW (0.75 + 1.15 lam) + HOT (fres 1.30 + ribs 0.60)) trans = 1.0 - op stride = 0.026 # Force small step for bell surface detail travel += stride # Apply fog fog = exp(-0.055 max(length(ro - centre) - 3.0, 0.0)) col += (rad + GLOW strands 0.16 + HOT strands strands 0.006) fog # Post-processing col = vec3(1.0) - exp(-col 1.85) col = max(col - vec3(0.0175, 0.0160, 0.0060), vec3(0.0)) output = pow(col, vec3(1.0 / 2.2)) return output def pulse(x): x = fract(x) if x < 0.28: return smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, x / 0.28) else: return 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, (x - 0.28) / 0.72) Formulas: Per-step soft contribution: e^{-95\,d}, where d is the distance to the tentacle surface. Pulse function (swim cycle): pulse(x) = \text{fract}(x); if x < 0.28 return \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, x / 0.28); else return 1.0 - \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, (x - 0.28) / 0.72). Tone mapping and black point: col = \text{vec3}(1.0) - \exp(-col \cdot 1.85); col = \max(col - \text{vec3}(0.0175, 0.0160, 0.0060), \text{vec3}(0.0)); \text{output} = \text{pow}(col, \text{vec3}(1.0 / 2.2)). Pitfalls: Hard intersection of thin geometry causes flickering as strands slip between sample points. Hair-thin tentacles and arms alias severely across frames if rendered with hard SDF hits. Soft accumulation solves these issues by fading contributions in smoothly based on distance to the SDF surface, multiplied by stride and a taper factor that fades near the base. Renders a swarm of butterflies by combining SDFs for individual anatomical parts with ray marching in a transformed local coordinate space to handle dynamic wing flapping and orientation. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by using a non-rigid "un-bend" transform to animate wings and a specific stability clamping strategy for step sizes, building on the soft accumulation techniques of Ray Marching with SDFs and Soft Accumulation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of march steps per ray (O(MARCH\STEPS)) and the number of objects in the school (O(SCHOOL)). Memory Complexity: Constant per ray, storing only a few floating-point accumulators. Performance: Roughly one minute of rendering per 10 seconds of output on integrated graphics. Single frames are near-instant, allowing for rapid iteration. Strengths: Eliminates flickering and aliasing artifacts common in rendering hair-thin geometry with hard SDF intersections. Provides smooth, fluid motion for dynamic thin structures. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of exponential falloff constants (e.g., 95.0 for tentacles) to balance visibility and performance. The soft accumulation approach may result in slightly lower contrast or "ghosting" if not properly attenuated by transparency. When to Use: Ideal for rendering thin, strand-like geometry (hair, tentacles, grass) where traditional hard intersection causes temporal instability. When Not to Use: Not suitable for solid, opaque objects where precise surface definition is required without transparency artifacts. Originating from the manim-glsl-jellyfish project by el-bakkali, this technique was developed to render a school of jellyfish using signed distance functions for the bell, tentacles, and arms. It addresses the specific challenge of animating thin, dynamic structures without the visual artifacts associated with discrete ray marching steps. The method is implemented in GLSL shaders and integrated with the Manim animation engine for timeline control. el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Butterfly Ray Marching with SDFs
head: Butterfly SDF Ray Marching, Swarm SDF Rendering
body: Butterfly Ray Marching with SDFs renders a swarm of butterflies by combining Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for individual anatomical parts (body, wings, antennae) with ray marching in a transformed local coordinate space to handle dynamic wing flapping and orientation. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by using a non-rigid "un-bend" transform to animate wings and a specific stability clamping strategy for step sizes, building on the soft accumulation techniques of Ray Marching with SDFs and Soft Accumulation. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d in world space. Time t and phase offset. Swarm data array SWARM containing position and velocity vectors for each butterfly. Parameters: MARCHSTEPS (maximum iterations per butterfly) and SWARMSIZE (number of butterflies). Outputs: Final pixel color C{out}. Data Structures: SWARM[i]: A 4-component vector storing the base position and velocity/orientation data for butterfly i. mapButterfly(p, t, phase): Returns a 2-component vector h where h.x is the signed distance and h.y is the material ID (0 for wings, 1 for body). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Local Space Transformation: For each butterfly i in the swarm: Retrieve velocity vector v and base position from SWARM[i]. Determine the forward vector. If |v{xy}| < 10^{-4}, derive forward from the cross product of the dorsal axis and (1, 0, 0) to avoid singularity. Construct a basis matrix from the velocity vector and a dorsal axis (interpolated between world up and camera direction). Apply a roll rotation to the basis. Transform the world ray origin o and direction d into the butterfly's local space by applying the basis and dividing the origin by a scale factor. 2. Sphere Intersection: Compute the intersection of the transformed ray with a unit sphere bounding the butterfly: b = \text{dot}(o{local}, d{local}) disc = b^2 - \text{dot}(o{local}, o{local}) + 1.45^2 If disc < 0, skip this butterfly. Calculate t{max} = -b + \sqrt{disc}. If t{max} \le 0, skip. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize travel = \max(-b - \sqrt{disc}, 0) + \text{dither}. Iterate k from 0 to MARCHSTEPS: If travel > t{max}, break. Compute point p = o{local} + d{local} \cdot travel. Evaluate h = \text{mapButterfly}(p, t, \text{phase}). If h.x < 0.0022, a hit is found. Set hit = travel, hp = p, mat = h.y, and break. Advance step: travel \leftarrow travel + \text{clamp}(h.x \cdot 0.62, 0.0035, 0.22) Note: The step size is clamped because the un-bend transform is not rigid. 4. SDF Evaluation (mapButterfly): Body SDF: Clamp z to [-0.38, 0.30]. Compute normalized height u. Calculate radius r using a base term, a Gaussian bump for the thorax, and an offset. Return distance to cylinder surface defined by x, y \cdot 1.12, z - z{offset}. Antenna SDF: Take absolute x. Clamp normalized z to [0, 1]. Compute cubic Bezier-like control point c. Return distance to line segment with radius interpolating between 0.0045 and 0.014 based on u. Wing SDF: Compute wing distance. Combine: Body SDF = \min(\text{Body}, \text{Antenna}). If \text{Wing} < \text{Body}, return (\text{Wing}, 0). Else, return (\text{Body}, 1). 5. Normal Calculation: Compute normal n using central differences on mapButterfly with \epsilon = 0.0018. 6. Shading: Wings (Material 0): Transform hit point to wing space. Calculate outline and base color. Lambertian lighting: L = 0.22 + 0.78 \max(\text{dot}(n, \text{sun}), 0). Subsurface scattering approximation: S = \text{base} \cdot \max(-\text{dot}(n, \text{sun}), 0) \cdot \max(\text{dot}(rd, \text{sun}), 0)^{2.2} \cdot 6.0. Rim lighting: R = \text{mix}(\text{SUNCOL}, \text{AMBER\BRIGHT}, 0.55) \cdot \text{pow}(1.0 - \text{abs}(\text{dot}(n, -d)), 3.0) \cdot 0.24. Specular: Spec = \text{SUNCOL} \cdot \text{pow}(\max(\text{dot}(\text{reflect}(-\text{sun}, n), -d), 0), 28.0) \cdot 0.14. Final: shade = \text{base} \cdot (L + 0.18) + S + \text{base} \cdot \text{through} \cdot 0.60 + R + Spec. Body (Material 1): Lambertian lighting: L = 0.25 + 0.75 \max(\text{dot}(n, \text{sun}), 0). Fuzz factor: F = 0.5 + 0.5 \sin(hp.z \cdot 180.0) \sin(hp.x \cdot 150.0). Final: shade = \text{vec3}(0.070, 0.042, 0.032) \cdot L \cdot (0.8 + 0.3 F) + \text{SUNCOL} \cdot \text{pow}(1.0 - \text{abs}(\text{dot}(n, -d)), 2.5) \cdot 0.55. 7. Compositing: Calculate distance dist = |ro - origin|. Haze factor: H = \exp(-0.055 \cdot \max(dist - 2.0, 0.0)). col = \text{mix}(\text{background}(rd, uv), shade, H). Apply tonemapping and gamma correction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def butterflyraymarch(ro, rd, t, phase, swarmdata, marchsteps): """ ro: Ray origin (vec3) rd: Ray direction (vec3) t: Time (float) phase: Phase offset (float) swarmdata: List of butterfly data (vec4) marchsteps: Max iterations (int) """ finalcolor = vec3(0.0) for i in range(len(swarmdata)): data = swarmdata[i] pos = data.xyz vel = data.w # Packed velocity/orientation data # 1. Local Space Transformation forward = normalize(vel.xy) if length(vel.xy) > 1e-4 else cross(vec3(0,1,0), vec3(1,0,0)) # Pitfall handling dorsal = mix(vec3(0,1,0), normalize(ro - pos), 0.5) # Dorsal axis mixed between up and camera direction basis = constructbasis(forward, dorsal) # Standard orthonormal basis construction olocal = transformpoint(basis, ro - pos) / scale # Divide origin by scale dlocal = transformvector(basis, rd) # 2. Sphere Intersection b = dot(olocal, dlocal) disc = b b - dot(olocal, olocal) + 1.45 1.45 if disc < 0.0: continue sq = sqrt(disc) tmax = -b + sq if tmax <= 0.0: continue travel = max(-b - sq, 0.0) + dither() # Dither initialization hitt = -1.0 hitplocal = vec3(0.0) hitmat = 0.0 # 3. Ray Marching for k in range(marchsteps): if travel > tmax: break plocal = olocal + dlocal travel h = mapbutterfly(plocal, t, phase) if h.x < 0.0022: hitt = travel hitplocal = plocal hitmat = h.y break step = clamp(h.x 0.62, 0.0035, 0.22) # Stability clamp for non-rigid transform travel += step if hitt < 0.0: continue # 4. Normal Calculation n = butterflynormal(hitplocal, t, phase) # Central differences with epsilon 0.0018 # 5. Shading shade = vec3(0.0) if hitmat < 0.5: # Wing shading v = towingspace(vec3(abs(hitplocal.x), hitplocal.y, hitplocal.z), t, phase) w = vec2(v.x, v.z) outline = wingoutline(w) basecol = wingcolour(w, outline, hash11(i + 5.0) 0.35) lambert = 0.22 + 0.78 max(dot(n, sun), 0.0) through = max(-dot(n, sun), 0.0) back = pow(max(dot(rd, sun), 0.0), 2.2) rim = pow(1.0 - abs(dot(n, -rd)), 3.0) shade = basecol (lambert + 0.18) shade += basecol through back 6.0 shade += basecol through 0.60 shade += mix(suncol, amberbright, 0.55) rim 0.24 shade += suncol pow(max(dot(reflect(-sun, n), -rd), 0.0), 28.0) 0.14 else: # Body shading lambert = 0.25 + 0.75 max(dot(n, sun), 0.0) fuzz = 0.5 + 0.5 sin(hitplocal.z 180.0) sin(hitplocal.x 150.0) shade = vec3(0.070, 0.042, 0.032) lambert (0.8 + 0.3 fuzz) shade += suncol pow(1.0 - abs(dot(n, -rd)), 2.5) 0.55 # 6. Compositing dist = length(ro - pos) haze = exp(-0.055 max(dist - 2.0, 0.0)) bgcol = computebackground(rd, uv) # Scene-specific background finalcolor = mix(bgcol, shade, haze) return finalcolor def mapbutterfly(p, t, phase): """Returns (distance, materialid)""" # Body SDF zclamped = clamp(p.z, -0.38, 0.30) u = (zclamped - (-0.38)) / (0.30 - (-0.38)) # Normalized height r = baseradius + gaussianthorax(u) + offset # Base term + Gaussian bump + offset bodydist = sqrt(p.x2 + (p.y 1.12)2) - r # Distance to cylinder surface # Antenna SDF absx = abs(p.x) znorm = clamp(u, 0.0, 1.0) # Clamp normalized z to [0,1] c = cubicbezierpoint(znorm) # Cubic Bezier-like control point antdist = distancetosegment(vec2(absx, znorm), c, radiusinterpolate(u)) # Radius interpolates 0.0045 to 0.014 bodysdf = min(bodydist, antdist) # Wing SDF wingdist = computewingdistance(p, t, phase) # Wing SDF formula not provided in sources. if wingdist < bodysdf: return vec2(wingdist, 0.0) else: return vec2(bodysdf, 1.0) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is SWARMSIZE and M is MARCHSTEPS. Each butterfly requires a separate ray march. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store swarm data. Performance: Performance is limited by the number of butterflies and the cost of the SDF evaluation and shading per step. The clamping of step sizes ensures stability but may increase the number of steps required for convergence in non-rigid regions. Strengths: Realistic rendering of complex, animated organic shapes (wings) using SDFs. Handles transparency and subsurface scattering effects effectively. Limitations: High computational cost for large swarms. The non-rigid transform can lead to artifacts if step sizes are not carefully clamped. Precision issues may arise with very small distances due to the non-rigid nature of the transform. Butterfly Ray Marching with SDFs is a technique demonstrated in the project "manim-glsl-butterflies" by el-bakkali. It utilizes GLSL shaders within the Manim animation engine to render a swarm of butterflies. The method combines SDFs for geometric representation with ray marching for rendering, specifically addressing the challenge of animating wing flapping through a local coordinate transformation. el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Pre-marched Shadow and Ambient Occlusion Baking
head: Baked shadow ray, Pre-marched ambient occlusion
body: A technique to improve visual fidelity and performance by pre-calculating shadow and ambient occlusion data into the volume texture, leveraging the static nature of the cloud volume. It sets itself apart from real-time ray marching by trading runtime compute for a one-time or event-driven baking cost, avoiding expensive per-frame camera renders. It builds on Performance Optimizations for SDF Ray Marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static signed distance field (SDF) volume representing the cloud geometry. Output: A 3D volume texture containing baked shadow and ambient occlusion attenuation factors. Data Structures: Baked Volume Texture: A 3D texture where each voxel stores pre-computed lighting attenuation factors. The resolution is typically low, matching the base cloud volume resolution. Steps: 1. Bake Shadow: Pre-march a shadow ray through the volume for each voxel. This involves casting rays in the direction of the light source(s) to determine occlusion. Due to the low volume resolution, this can be done in real-time during the baking phase. A typical implementation uses 4 shadow samples per cloud sample. Because the baking is computationally feasible in real-time, the shadow data can be regenerated to allow for dynamic changes in the sun's position (time-of-day) without runtime cost. 2. Bake Ambient Occlusion: Pre-march ambient occlusion rays into the volume texture. This adds shading based on local geometry density without runtime cost. 3. Runtime Lookup: During rendering, retrieve the volumetric cloud shadow using a single tex3D lookup on the baked texture. This ensures the shadow perfectly matches the cloud geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakeshadowandao(sdfvolume, resolution, lightdirection): shadowtexture = [[[1.0 for in range(resolution.z)] for in range(resolution.y)] for in range(resolution.x)] aotexture = [[[1.0 for in range(resolution.z)] for in range(resolution.y)] for in range(resolution.x)] for x in range(resolution.x): for y in range(resolution.y): for z in range(resolution.z): pos = [x, y, z] # Normalized voxel coordinates # Bake Shadow: Pre-march shadow ray through volume shadowfactor = 1.0 numshadowsamples = 4 # stepsize = 1.0 for i in range(numshadowsamples): samplepos = [pos[0] + lightdirection[0] (i + 1) stepsize, pos[1] + lightdirection[1] (i + 1) stepsize, pos[2] + lightdirection[2] (i + 1) stepsize] if sdfvolume(samplepos) < 0: shadowfactor = 0.0 break shadowtexture[x][y][z] = shadowfactor # Bake Ambient Occlusion: Pre-march AO into volume texture aofactor = 1.0 # Exact AO march directions and step counts are not specified in the source [Comment] for in range(4): samplepos = [pos[0] + 0.5, pos[1] + 0.5, pos[2] + 0.5] if sdfvolume(samplepos) < 0: aofactor = 0.5 break aotexture[x][y][z] = aofactor return shadowtexture, aotexture def rendervoxel(x, y, z, shadowtexture, aotexture): # Runtime Lookup: single tex3D lookup on baked texture shadow = shadowtexture[x][y][z] ao = aotexture[x][y][z] basecolor = 1.0 # Base cloud color from SDF pass return basecolor shadow ao Parameters: Shadow Samples per Cloud Sample: 4. Volume Resolution: Low, matching the base cloud volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Assumption: This method relies on the volume being static. Memory: Storing attenuation factors in the volume texture increases memory usage, though the low resolution mitigates this. Occlusion caching is a performance optimization for static volumetric lighting that pre-calculates shadow and ambient occlusion data into volume textures, avoiding expensive per-frame camera renders. It sets itself apart from real-time ray marching by trading runtime compute for a one-time or event-driven baking cost, leveraging the static nature of most cloud volumes and occluders. Time Complexity: Baking time is proportional to the number of voxels times the number of shadow/AO samples. Since volume resolution is low, baking can be done in real-time during the bake phase. Runtime cost is O(1) per voxel for texture lookup. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, for storing the baked volume texture. Performance: Significantly reduces runtime cost by eliminating per-frame shadow and AO ray marching. Strengths: Perfect shadow alignment with cloud geometry, low runtime cost, supports dynamic time-of-day if baked dynamically. Limitations: Requires static geometry, increased memory for baked textures, baking cost (though feasible in real-time for low res). When to Use: Static volumetric clouds where high-quality shadows and AO are desired without runtime cost. When Not to Use: Dynamic volumes where geometry changes frequently. Originated in the context of rendering volumetric clouds using signed distance fields, as described in a blog post by uhawkvr. The technique leverages the low resolution of cloud volumes to make pre-marching feasible. name: Occlusion Caching
head: Baked Volumetric Shadows, Baking Occlusion
body: Occlusion caching is a performance optimization for static volumetric lighting that pre-calculates shadow and ambient occlusion data into volume textures, avoiding expensive per-frame camera renders. It sets itself apart from real-time ray marching by trading runtime compute for a one-time or event-driven baking cost, leveraging the static nature of most cloud volumes and occluders. Inputs: Static light position/orientation, static occluder geometry, camera parameters for capture. Outputs: Occlusion volumes V{occl} containing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and runtime interpolation weights. Occlusion Volumes (V{occl}): A grid of volumetric cells. Each cell vi^{occl} stores principal components of occlusion as SH coefficients fo^i. Depth Cubemaps (\{\hat{D}p^i\}{p=1}^6): Six depth maps per volume cell, captured from six non-overlapping 90-degree FoV cameras. Occlusion Cubemaps (\{\hat{O}p^i\}{p=1}^6): Derived from depth cubemaps, representing the occlusion state. 1. Baking Stage (Capture): For each volume cell vi^{occl}, set up six cameras with 90-degree Field of View (FoV), arranged non-overlappingly around the cell center. Perform six render passes to obtain depth cubemaps \{\hat{D}p^i\}{p=1}^6. Convert depth cubemaps into occlusion cubemaps \{\hat{O}p^i\}{p=1}^6. Compute the principal components of the occlusion data and store them as SH coefficients fo^i for the cell. 2. Decomposition Stage (Runtime Interpolation): For a surface point x with normal n, identify the eight nearest occlusion volumes \{vk\}{k=1}^8 to x. Let pk be the position vector of volume vk and fk^o be its SH coefficients. Calculate standard trilinear interpolation weights \{wk\}{k=1}^8 based on the relative position of x within the grid. Apply masked trilinear interpolation to compute modified weights \tilde{w}k: \tilde{w}k = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } (pk - x) \cdot n \le 0 \\ wk & \text{if } (pk - x) \cdot n > 0 \end{cases} This mask ensures that only occlusion from the upper hemisphere defined by n contributes to the ambient occlusion integral. Normalize the weights: \hat{w}k = \frac{\tilde{w}k}{\sum{j=1}^8 \tilde{w}j} Interpolate the SH coefficients to obtain the final occlusion coefficients fx^o: fx^o = \sum{k=1}^8 \hat{w}k fk^o Bake Interval: Controls caching behavior. On Start captures once at startup and re-captures if the light moves or rotates. Every Frame enables continuous capture for dynamic occluders. Shadow Resolution: Resolution of the capture cubemaps (e.g., 512x512). Ignore Rotation: Boolean flag. If enabled, rotating the light does not trigger re-capture; the map is reprojected. Auto Toggle Distance: Distance threshold beyond which occlusion is disabled for far lights. Check Time Interval: Frequency of Auto Toggle distance checks. Default: 1 second. Dynamic Occluders: If occluders move independently of the light (e.g., a fan), "On Start" baking will produce stale shadows. Use "Every Frame" or event-driven updates. Rotation: Without "Ignore Rotation," rotating a static light triggers a full re-capture, increasing cost. Enable this flag for lights with attached occluders (e.g., lamp cages). Visibility: Capture can be suspended when the light volume is not visible to any camera to save resources. Point Light Orientation: For "Point Light Half Sphere To Camera" mode, re-capture only occurs if the camera direction changes by more than 45 degrees. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakeocclusioncells(volumecells): occlusionvolumes = {} for i, cell in enumerate(volumecells): # Six non-overlapping 90-degree FoV cameras around cell center depthcubemaps = [] for p in range(6): # Capture depth for face p # Sources do not specify the exact camera setup or rendering pipeline depthcubemaps.append(renderdepthpass(cell.center, p, fov=90.0)) # Convert depth cubemaps to occlusion cubemaps # Sources do not specify the exact conversion formula occlusioncubemaps = convertdepthtoocclusion(depthcubemaps) # Store principal components of occlusion into SH coefficients # Sources do not specify the exact SH projection method shcoeffs = computeshcoefficients(occlusioncubemaps) occlusionvolumes[i] = shcoeffs return occlusionvolumes def decomposeocclusion(pointx, normaln, occlusionvolumes, grid): # Find eight nearest volumes {vk} for point x # Standard grid neighbor lookup nearestindices = find8nearest(pointx, grid) totalweight = 0.0 interpolatedsh = [0.0] 15 # Standard SH basis size for k in range(8): idx = nearestindices[k] pk = occlusionvolumes[idx].position fk = occlusionvolumes[idx].shcoefficients # Standard trilinear weight wk # Standard trilinear interpolation calculation wk = computetrilinearweight(pointx, pk, grid) # Masked trilinear interpolation if dot(pk - pointx, normaln) <= 0: wtildek = 0.0 else: wtildek = wk totalweight += wtildek for j in range(len(interpolatedsh)): interpolatedsh[j] += wtildek fk[j] # Normalize weights if totalweight > 0: for j in range(len(interpolatedsh)): interpolatedsh[j] /= totalweight return interpolatedsh A variant of the interpolation step used in the decomposition phase. Standard trilinear interpolation weights \{wk\} are modified to \{\tilde{w}k\} by zeroing out contributions from volumes where the vector from the sample point to the volume center has a non-positive dot product with the surface normal ( (pk - x) \cdot n \le 0). This ensures that ambient occlusion is only calculated from the upper hemisphere relative to the surface normal, preventing incorrect shadowing from below. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Eliminates per-frame shadow ray marching for static lights, significantly reducing GPU load. Strengths: Ideal for static scenes with static occluders (windows, street lamps). Event-driven updates handle occasional changes (doors opening) efficiently. Limitations: Not suitable for highly dynamic scenes with moving occluders unless "Every Frame" baking is used, which negates performance gains. When to Use: Static volumetric lights with static or slowly moving occluders. When Not to Use: Real-time dynamic occlusion requirements without acceptable latency for re-baking. Occlusion caching in volumetric rendering was introduced to address the high computational cost of real-time shadow calculation for volumetric lights. The technique leverages the fact that many volumetric lights and their occluders are static in typical scenes. The method of using SH coefficients to store occlusion data and masked trilinear interpolation for decomposition is detailed in the GS-IR paper. The Unity URP implementation provides practical settings and runtime behaviors for game engines. GS-IR: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02045, fetched 2026-10-26 Volumetric Lighting in Unity URP: Shadows, Translucency..., https://kronnect.com/company/blog/volumetric-lighting-unity-urp-guide/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: SDF Texture Baking for Ray Marching
head: 3D SDF Baking for Cloud Sphere Tracing, Cloud SDF texture baking, Conservative SDF proxy for raymarching
body: This method optimizes cloud raymarching by baking a low-resolution 3D Signed Distance Field (SDF) texture that acts as a conservative proxy for the analytical cloud SDF. It allows the marching loop to skip empty space conservatively before falling back to analytical evaluations inside active cells. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Analytical cloud SDF function (lofted cloud SDF) and dynamic cloud parameters. Output: A 3D texture containing baked SDF values, used to accelerate the raymarching loop in atmospherelowres.comp. Data Structures: cloudSdf3DTexture: A 3D texture with the following layout: Resolution: 128 \times 32 \times 128 (width \times height \times depth). Format: GLR32F (single-channel 32-bit floating point). Binding: Texture Unit 45. Wrapping: GLREPEAT horizontally (X-axis), GLCLAMPTOEDGE vertically (Y-axis). Layered Flag: GLTRUE. Steps: 1. Bake SDF: Create a compute shader (cloud3dsdfbake.comp) to analytically bake the lofted cloud SDF into the 3D texture using unadvected coordinates. 2. Allocate Texture: Allocate and manage cloudSdf3DTexture in AtmosphereManager with the specified format and bindings. 3. Dispatch Bake Shader: Dispatch the 3D SDF bake shader every frame in AtmosphereManager::Update to ensure synchrony with dynamic cloud parameters and solve initialization frame order issues. 4. Optimize Raymarching: In atmospherelowres.comp, first sample the 3D SDF texture to skip empty space conservatively. 5. Fallback Evaluation: Perform full analytical evaluations only inside active cells (where the SDF indicates presence). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for x in range(128): for y in range(32): for z in range(128): worldpos = voxeltoworld(x, y, z) # d = AnalyticalCloudSDF(worldpos, cloudparams) sdftexture[x, y, z] = d t = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 epsilon = 1e-4 maxdistance = 1000.0 threshold = 0.0 color = vec3(0.0) # density = 1.0 # while t < maxdistance and transmittance > epsilon: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection texcoords = worldtotexturecoords(pos) # dsdf = sdftexture[texcoords] if dsdf > threshold: step = max(dsdf, 1e-3) # t += step continue danalytical = AnalyticalCloudSDF(pos, cloudparams) step = max(danalytical, 1e-3) # t += step transmittance = exp(-density step) # color += samplecolor(pos) (1.0 - transmittance) # Parameters: Texture resolution: 128 \times 32 \times 128. Texture format: GLR32F. Texture unit binding: Unit 45. Texture wrapping mode: GLREPEAT horizontally, GLCLAMPTOEDGE vertically. Texture layered flag: GLTRUE. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization Frame Order: Dispatching the bake shader every frame solves initialization frame order issues. Dynamic Parameters: The bake shader must be dispatched whenever cloud parameters are updated to ensure synchrony. Conservative Skip: The SDF texture acts as a conservative proxy, allowing the marching loop to skip empty space conservatively. This method optimizes interactive camera navigation (orbit/dolly) over static fractal surfaces by baking the expensive analytical Distance Estimator (DE) into a sparse 3D brick volume, allowing the renderer to sample precomputed distances instead of re-evaluating the fractal formula every frame. It sets itself apart from standard raymarching by decoupling the geometric query cost from the frame rate during camera motion, trading bounded spatial precision for significant interactive performance gains. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The 3D texture requires 128 \times 32 \times 128 \times 4 bytes = 2 MB of VRAM. Measured Performance: All unit tests and shader validations passed 100% successfully. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Bounded spatial precision due to low-resolution texture; may skip valid samples if the proxy is not conservative enough. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced by ricecake in a GitHub Pull Request (PR #636) to the boidsish repository on July 11, 2026. It was created to optimize cloud sphere tracing by baking a low-resolution 3D SDF texture. name: Sparse Distance-Field Cache for Interactive Camera Moves
head: SDF brick cache, Sparse distance-field cache for interactive 3D camera moves, sparse brick volume cache
body: This method optimizes interactive camera navigation (orbit/dolly) over static fractal surfaces by baking the expensive analytical Distance Estimator (DE) into a sparse 3D brick volume, allowing the renderer to sample precomputed distances instead of re-evaluating the fractal formula every frame. Unlike standard raymarching which re-evaluates the fractal DE along every ray every frame, this method caches the DE to avoid repeated formula evaluation during camera movement. It trades bounded spatial precision for significant interactive performance gains. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The analytical Distance Estimator function DE(\mathbf{p}), the camera view volume, brick size, brick resolution, and a maximum brick count limit. Output: A sparse 3D brick volume cache containing precomputed distance values, used for raymarching during interactive preview. Data Structures: 1. Brick Volume: A sparse 3D grid where each active cell is a "brick". Brick Layout: Each brick is a small 3D texture of size R \times R \times R voxels. Voxel Content: A single floating-point value representing the signed distance to the surface. Sparsity: Only bricks where the surface exists (defined by DE < \text{brick size}) are allocated. 2. Coarse Level: A lower-resolution representation of the brick volume storing the empty-space distance for regions outside the active surface boundary. Parameters: Brick Count: Must be capped to control memory usage. Brick Resolution: Bounded detail level, suitable for preview rather than final output. Bake Time: Must be less than a few frames' worth of computation to be beneficial. Algorithm Steps: 1. Progressive Baking: Start by baking the coarse level of the brick volume. Iterate through the 3D space around the surface. For each potential brick location, evaluate the analytical DE(\mathbf{p}) at the brick center. If DE < \text{brick size}, allocate the brick and populate its voxels by sampling the analytical DE at each voxel center within the brick. Store the empty-space distance at the coarse level for regions where no bricks are allocated. Continue until the brick count limit is reached or the surface boundary is fully covered. 2. Interactive Raymarching: When the camera moves, perform raymarching using the sparse brick volume. For each ray step, sample the distance from the brick volume using trilinear interpolation. Use hardware texture filtering on the GPU for efficient trilinear distance sampling. Use the sampled distance to advance the ray. 3. Cache Rebuild: Rebuild the cache only when a parameter changes. 4. Final Render: Run the full-detail DE render once the camera settles to produce the final frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) class Brick: def init(self, resolution): self.resolution = resolution self.data = [0.0] (resolution 3) def setvoxel(self, i, j, k, val): self.data[i self.resolution2 + j self.resolution + k] = val def getvoxel(self, i, j, k): return self.data[i self.resolution2 + j self.resolution + k] class SparseBrickVolume: def init(self): self.bricks = {} def setbrick(self, bx, by, bz, brick): self.bricks[(bx, by, bz)] = brick def hasbrick(self, bx, by, bz): return (bx, by, bz) in self.bricks def sampletrilinear(self, bx, by, bz, lx, ly, lz, res): brick = self.bricks[(bx, by, bz)] r = res i0, j0, k0 = int(lx (r - This is acceptable for preview but not final output. Memory: The brick count must be capped; otherwise, memory usage can explode for complex fractals. Bake Time: If the bake time exceeds a few frames, the performance gain is lost. Degenerate Input: If the fractal parameters change, the cache must be rebuilt; using stale data leads to incorrect geometry. Time Complexity: Baking time must be less than a few frames' worth of computation to be beneficial. Interactive raymarching replaces per-frame fractal DE evaluation with hardware texture sampling. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is controlled by capping the brick count. Measured Performance: Reduces frame time from seconds to near real time for heavy User Bulb maps and KIFS on interactive camera moves. Strengths: Significant speedup for interactive camera navigation on expensive fractal formulas; works well on weak and strong hardware for heavy maps. Limitations: Bounded detail level makes it unsuitable for final output; requires rebuild on parameter changes; memory usage can be high if not capped. When to Use: Interactive preview, orbit/dolly camera moves over static fractals. When Not to Use: Final rendering, dynamic fractal parameters, scenes requiring high-precision distance estimates. This technique was proposed in an issue on the FracturingFog repository, drawing inspiration from games, offline renderers, and GPU computing. It addresses the performance bottleneck of re-evaluating expensive fractal Distance Estimators (DE) every frame during camera movement, a common issue in real-time fractal rendering applications like Dreams/Claybook. The method is part of Phase 3b of issue #1298, focusing on GPU/rendering performance improvements. name: Squared Distance Field Optimization
head: SDF Squared Distance Trick, Squared Distance Optimization
body: Squared Distance Field Optimization is a technique to avoid the computational cost of square root operations in Signed Distance Field (SDF) raymarching by using squared distances for sphere comparisons, leveraging the monotonicity of the squaring function. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by replacing Euclidean distance metrics with squared Euclidean metrics for specific primitives (typically spheres) to eliminate sqrt calls, which are often expensive on GPU architectures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin O and direction D, and a scene containing at least one sphere (defined by center C and radius r) and other objects with known distance functions. Output: The minimum distance to the closest surface along the ray, or the intersection point, computed without evaluating square roots for the spherical components. Data Structures: No specific data structure changes are required beyond the standard representation of spheres. The optimization is purely algebraic within the distance query function. Steps: 1. Compute Squared Sphere Distance: Calculate the squared distance from the query point P to the surface of the sphere. This is done by computing the squared Euclidean distance from P to the sphere center C, and subtracting the squared radius r^2. d{sphere}^2 = \|P - C\|^2 - r^2 Where \|P - C\|^2 = (Px - Cx)^2 + (Py - Cy)^2 + (Pz - Cz)^2. 2. Square Other Distances: For any other object in the scene that provides a standard Euclidean distance d{other}, square this value to convert it to a squared distance metric: d{other}^2. 3. Minimize Squared Distances: Determine the closest surface by taking the minimum of the squared sphere distance and the squared distances of all other objects. d{min}^2 = \min(d{sphere}^2, d{other1}^2, d{other2}^2, \dots) This yields the same ordering as minimizing the unsquared distances because the squaring function f(x) = x^2 is monotonically increasing for x \ge 0. 4. Propagate Squared Metric: Continue using squared distances for subsequent comparisons and logic within the ray marching loop to avoid taking square roots as far as possible. If the final result requires a Euclidean distance (e.g., for shading or step size), take the square root only at the very end. Pseudocode: def squareddistancetosphere(point, center, radius): """ Computes the squared signed distance from point to sphere surface. Returns positive if outside, negative if inside. """ diff = point - center squareddisttocenter = dot(diff, diff) squaredradius = radius radius return squareddisttocenter - squaredradius def raymarchstepsquared(rayorigin, raydir, sceneobjects): """ Performs one step of ray marching using squared distance optimization. Note: This is a simplified conceptual step. Standard ray marching requires solving for t along the ray, not just point evaluation. The optimization applies to the distance field evaluation function. """ # Initialize minimum squared distance to infinity minsqdist = float('inf') for obj in sceneobjects: if obj.type == 'sphere': # Use squared distance formula sqdist = squareddistancetosphere(rayorigin, obj.center, obj.radius) else: # Get standard Euclidean distance from other SDFs euclideandist = obj.sdf(rayorigin) sqdist = euclideandist euclideandist if sqdist < minsqdist: minsqdist = sqdist # Return squared distance. # If step size is needed, sqrt(minsqdist) must be taken here. return minsqdist Parameters: sphereradius: The radius of the sphere. Used as radius radius in the calculation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Marching Step Size: Using the squared distance directly as the ray march step size (currDst) is incorrect. The distance moved along the ray is not equal to the squared distance unless the ray hits the center of the sphere exactly. The square root must be taken to get the actual Euclidean distance for stepping. Intersection Only: If the goal is purely intersection testing (boolean hit/miss) and not distance-based shading or marching, direct ray-sphere intersection formulas are preferred over distance fields entirely. Precision: Squaring large distances can lead to floating-point precision issues or overflow. This method is most beneficial when distances are moderate and sqrt latency is the bottleneck. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of sqrt operations from O(N) per ray step (where N is the number of primitives) to potentially O(1) or O(K) where K is the number of non-spherical primitives. This improves performance on hardware where sqrt is expensive relative to multiplication. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead. Strengths: Significant performance gain in scenarios with many spherical primitives where sqrt is a bottleneck. Limitations: Cannot be used directly for step size calculation; requires careful handling of mixed distance metrics (squared vs. Euclidean) in the same scene. Not suitable if the actual Euclidean distance is needed at every step for logic other than step size. This technique was discussed in the context of CUDA programming and ray tracing optimization on Stack Overflow in 2019. It leverages the mathematical property that minimizing x^2 is equivalent to minimizing x for non-negative x, allowing developers to avoid costly square root instructions in GPU shaders.
