name: Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping
head: Dynamic Synchronized Inference
body: Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping is a parallelization technique for differentiable sphere tracing that maintains a dynamic mask of unfinished rays to prevent wasted computation on rays that have already converged or exited the scene. It differs from its siblings, such as Beam Optimization which prunes low-probability paths, and Performance Optimizations for SDF Ray Marching which may use static acceleration structures, by explicitly managing the active set of rays at every iteration to handle heterogeneous convergence rates across the image plane. Inputs: Camera rays: origin \mathbf{o}i and direction \mathbf{d}i for each pixel i \in [0, H \times W - 1]. SDF function f(\mathbf{p}): returns signed distance value for a query point. Outputs: Rendered depth, normal, color, or silhouette for each pixel. Gradients for optimization (if differentiable). Data Structures: marchingzdepth: Array of size N, storing accumulated distance along each ray. unfinishedmask: Boolean array of size N, initially True for all rays within the valid viewing frustum or unit sphere bounds. raypositions: Array of size N \times 3, storing current 3D position of each ray. queryhistory: List of arrays storing query positions for backpropagation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set marchingzdepth to zeros. Set raypositions to ray origins \mathbf{o}i. Set unfinishedmask to True for all rays within the valid viewing frustum or unit sphere bounds. 2. Iteration Loop: For step k from 1 to maxsteps: a. Select Active Rays: Identify indices where unfinishedmask is True. Concatenate these rays into a single batch tensor. b. Query SDF: Evaluate dj = f(\mathbf{p}j) for each active ray j in the batch. c. Update Positions: Compute step size using the SDF value and a multiplier. Update position and accumulated depth. d. Check Convergence: If the ray meets convergence criteria, set its mask entry to False. e. Gradient Handling: Save query locations globally. Perform minimization of absolute SDF over a detached tensor graph to find the minimum K queries per ray. Re-evaluate these specific queries with gradients attached. 3. Final Compositing: Map results back to original image resolution. Formulas: Step size: \text{step\size}j = \max(dj, \text{min\step}) \times \alpha Position update: \mathbf{p}j \leftarrow \mathbf{p}j + \mathbf{d}j \times \text{step\size}j Depth update: \text{marching\zdepth}j \leftarrow \text{marching\zdepth}j + \text{step\size}j Convergence: |dj| < \text{threshold} or ray exits bounding volume. Symbols: dj is signed distance at \mathbf{p}j, \alpha is step multiplier, \text{min\step} prevents backward movement when inside the object, \text{threshold} is convergence tolerance, \mathbf{d}j is ray direction, \mathbf{p}j is current position. Parameters: maxsteps: Maximum marching iterations. Default is 100. alpha (\alpha): Step multiplier scaling the SDF value. Typical range is 1.2–1.8. threshold: Convergence stop threshold. Default is 5 \times 10^{-5}. K: Number of queries to keep for backpropagation. K=1 for depth rendering, K=3 for shape completion, K=1 for multi-view reconstruction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When close to the surface, SDF values are small, leading to slow convergence. The threshold must be chosen relative to the rendering resolution and object scale. Thin Structures: Large alpha values can cause rays to overshoot thin surfaces, creating holes. Empirical values range from 1.2 to 1.8. Memory: Storing all query positions for backpropagation is memory-intensive. The detached tensor minimization trick is essential for high-resolution rendering (e.g., 2048x2048). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def recursiveraymarchingwithearlystopping(rays, sdffunc, maxsteps=100, alpha=1.5, threshold=5e-5, K=1): """ rays: list of (origin, direction) tuples, each 3D vector sdffunc: callable returning distance (float) """ N = len(rays) positions = [ray[0] for ray in rays] directions = [ray[1] for ray in rays] zdepth = [0.0] N unfinishedmask = [True] N queryhistory = [] minstep = 1e-4 # Guard against backward movement inside object for step in range(maxsteps): activeindices = [i for i in range(N) if unfinishedmask[i]] if not activeindices: break activepositions = [positions[i] for i in activeindices] distances = [sdffunc(p) for p in activepositions] queryhistory.append(activepositions) for idx, i in enumerate(activeindices): d = distances[idx] stepsize = max(d, minstep) alpha positions[i] = [positions[i][j] + directions[i][j] stepsize for j in range(3)] zdepth[i] += stepsize if abs(d) < threshold: unfinishedmask[i] = False # Sources do not specify the exact autograd hook implementation for the detached minimization trick. return zdepth, positions Dynamically adjusts the number of steps per ray based on the count of currently active rays, differing from this method which uses a fixed step count per iteration but variable active set size. Processes rays in explicit batches with a fixed step count per batch, differing from this method which updates a single active set with variable steps per iteration. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S{active}), where N is the number of rays and S{active} is the average number of steps per active ray. Early stopping reduces S{active} for converged rays, improving performance over fixed-step marching. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot K) for storing query history for backpropagation, where K is the number of queries kept per ray. Performance: Enables high-resolution rendering (2048x2048) on single GPUs (e.g., GTX-1080Ti) by avoiding wasted computation on converged rays. Strengths: Efficient for scenes with varying depth complexity; reduces compute for background and converged foreground pixels. Limitations: Requires tuning of the step multiplier \alpha (typically 1.2–1.8) to balance convergence speed and hole formation in thin areas. The method was introduced as "Dynamic Synchronized Inference" in the DIST framework. It addresses the inefficiency of naive parallel sphere tracing where all rays are updated synchronously, leading to wasted computation when some rays converge earlier than others. The implementation details were further explored in unofficial repositories such as B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer. DIST: Rendering Deep Implicit Signed Distance Function With Differentiable Sphere Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr42600.2020.00209, fetched 2026-10-26 B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, https://github.com/B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Dynamic Step Count
head: CUDA Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count
body: Adaptive Ray Marching with Dynamic Step Count is an iterative volume rendering algorithm that samples rays until they are occluded or a maximum step count is reached, using a density grid for acceleration. It differs from its parent, Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping, by dynamically adjusting the number of steps per ray based on the count of currently active rays. The method operates in an iterative loop that determines the number of currently active rays and calculates a step batch size for them. It proceeds by marching these rays, querying densities and colors, and compositing the results. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [B, N, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [B, N, 3]. near, far: Near and far clipping planes. bound: Bounding box parameters. densitygrid: Acceleration structure (density grid). meandensity: Mean density value for normalization or thresholding. bgcolor: Background color, default 1.0. perturb: Boolean flag for ray perturbation. alphapremultiplied: Boolean flag determining output normalization. B: Batch size. N: Number of rays per batch. Outputs: image: Rendered image, shape [B, N, 4]. The first three channels are RGB, and the fourth channel is the accumulated weight sum (transparency mask). raysalive: A ping-pong buffer array of two boolean tensors, shape [2, B, N]. raysalive[i % 2] indicates which rays are still active in the current iteration i. rayst: A ping-pong buffer array of two float tensors, shape [2, B, N]. rayst[i % 2] stores the current accumulated distance along the ray for active rays. alivecounter: An integer scalar tracking the total number of active rays across the batch. weightssum: Accumulated weight (opacity) per ray, shape [B, N]. depth: Accumulated depth per ray, shape [B, N]. nstep: Number of steps to process per alive ray in the current iteration. B: Batch size. N: Number of rays per batch. nalive: Number of currently active rays. 1. Initialization: Initialize raysalive[0] to all True (all rays start alive). Initialize rayst[0] to near. Initialize weightssum and depth to 0. Initialize step (global step counter) to 0. Initialize alivecounter to B \times N. 2. Loop Condition: While alivecounter > 0: a. Calculate Alive Rays: Determine nalive = alivecounter.item(). b. Exit Check: If nalive <= 0, break the loop. c. Calculate Steps: Compute nstep = max(min(B N // nalive, 8), 1). d. Ray Marching: Call raymarching.marchrays with nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], rayso, raysd, bound, densitygrid, meandensity, near, far, 128, perturb. This function updates raysalive[(i+1) % 2] and rayst[(i+1) % 2] for the next iteration, marking rays as dead if they hit a surface or exceed bounds. It returns sampled positions xyzs and directions dirs for the active steps. e. Neural Network Query: Compute densities (sigmas) and colors (rgbs) by passing xyzs and dirs through the neural network: sigmas, rgbs = self(xyzs, dirs). f. Compositing: Call raymarching.compositerays with nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], sigmas, rgbs, deltas, weightssum, depth, image. This function updates weightssum, depth, and image based on volume rendering integration. g. Update Step Counter: step += nstep. h. Background Compositing: If alphapremultiplied is true, image = image + (1 - weightssum).unsqueeze(-1) bgcolor (default bgcolor = 1). If alphapremultiplied is false, image /= (weightssum + 1e-9).unsqueeze(-1). i. Concatenate Weight Sum: image = torch.cat([image, weightssum.unsqueeze(-1)], -1). j. Swap Buffers: Swap raysalive and rayst buffers for the next iteration (toggle i % 2). k. Update Alive Counter: Recalculate alivecounter based on the new raysalive mask. 3. Final Reshape: Reshape image to [B, N, 4]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def adaptiveraymarching(rayso, raysd, near, far, bgcolor=1.0, alphapremultiplied=False, perturb=False, bound=None, densitygrid=None, meandensity=None, B=1, N=1): # Initialize ping-pong buffers and accumulators raysalive = [[True] (B N), [False] (B N)] rayst = [[near] (B N), [0.0] (B N)] weightssum = [0.0] (B N) depth = [0.0] (B N) image = [0.0] (B N 3) alivecounter = B N step = 0 i = 0 while alivecounter > 0: nalive = alivecounter if nalive <= 0: break nstep = max(min((B N) // nalive, 8), 1) # GPU kernel: marches rays, checks bounds/density, updates alive mask and t # Returns: xyzs, dirs, deltas, newalivemask, newt xyzs, dirs, deltas, newalivemask, newt = marchrays( nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], rayso, raysd, bound, densitygrid, meandensity, near, far, 128, perturb) # Neural network forward pass sigmas, rgbs = networkforward(xyzs, dirs) # Composite rays: updates weightssum, depth, image weightssum, depth, image = compositerays( nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], sigmas, rgbs, deltas, weightssum, depth, image) step += nstep # Background compositing or normalization if alphapremultiplied: for k in range(B N): image[k3] += (1.0 - weightssum[k]) bgcolor image[k3+1] += (1.0 - weightssum[k]) bgcolor image[k3+2] += (1.0 - weightssum[k]) bgcolor else: for k in range(B N): denom = weightssum[k] + 1e-9 image[k3] /= denom image[k3+1] /= denom image[k3+2] /= denom # Swap ping-pong buffers raysalive[(i + 1) % 2] = newalivemask rayst[(i + 1) % 2] = newt # Update alive counter alivecounter = sum(1 for x in newalivemask if x) i += 1 # Concatenate weight sum to image channels and reshape to [B, N, 4] image.extend(weightssum) return image def compositerays(nalive, nstep, raysalive, rayst, sigmas, rgbs, deltas, weightssum, depth, image): for r in range(nalive): wacc = 0.0 dacc = 0.0 rgbacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] T = 1.0 for s in range(nstep): sigma = sigmas[r nstep + s] rgb = rgbs[r nstep + s] dt = deltas[r nstep + s] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma dt) w = alpha T wacc += w dacc += (rayst[r] + dt) w rgbacc[0] += rgb[0] w rgbacc[1] += rgb[1] w rgbacc[2] += rgb[2] w T = (1.0 - alpha) weightssum[r] = wacc depth[r] = dacc image[r3] = rgbacc[0] image[r3+1] = rgbacc[1] image[r3+2] = rgbacc[2] return weightssum, depth, image def marchrays(nalive, nstep, raysalive, rayst, rayso, raysd, bound, densitygrid, meandensity, near, far, blocksize, perturb): # GPU kernel: marches rays, checks bounds/density, updates alive mask and t # Returns: xyzs, dirs, deltas, newalivemask, newt return [], [], [], [], [] def networkforward(xyzs, dirs): # Neural network forward pass return [], [] Division by Zero: When alphapremultiplied is false, the normalization step divides by weightssum. If a ray has zero accumulated opacity (e.g., passed through empty space), this causes division by zero. The implementation adds 1e-9 to the denominator to avoid this. Zero Alive Rays: The loop checks nalive <= 0 to exit early, preventing unnecessary computation. Step Count Calculation: The formula max(min(B N // nalive, 8), 1) ensures that nstep is at least 1. If nalive is very small, nstep becomes 1, processing rays one by one in terms of step batches, which may reduce efficiency but prevents excessive steps per ray. This variant uses a hash grid (specifically a density bitfield) for acceleration instead of a dense grid. It calculates the number of samples per ray based on the scene scale and a step factor. For each alive ray, it marches along the ray, checking the hash grid for occupied voxels. If a voxel is occupied, it samples the neural network; otherwise, it skips to the next occupied voxel. The step size is calculated using an exponential step factor (expstepfactor), which is 1/256 if the scene scale is greater than 0.5, otherwise 0. The hash grid uses morton codes for indexing, and the density bitfield is stored as a bitfield of uint8 values. Parameters include gridsize (resolution of the hash grid), cascades (number of levels in the density bitfield), and scale (size of the scene bounding box). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for ping-pong buffers (raysalive, rayst), neural network weights, and the acceleration structure (density grid or hash grid). Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient handling of sparse scenes, reduced computation on terminated rays, good hardware utilization. Limitations: Performance may degrade if the number of active rays is very small (leading to small batch sizes) or very large (leading to many iterations). The fixed step cap (8) may limit accuracy in highly detailed regions. This method is derived from implementations in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and instant-NGP, where adaptive ray marching is used to optimize rendering speed. The specific implementation with dynamic step count and hash grid acceleration is found in unofficial repositories. megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, https://github.com/Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Ray Marching (Test)
head: Iterative volume rendering, Progressive ray marching
body: Adaptive Ray Marching (Test) is an iterative volume rendering technique that marches rays in batches, composites results, and stops rays that have converged (transmittance below a threshold) to save computation. It differs from standard fixed-step ray marching by dynamically reducing the number of active rays over iterations, and from Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping by processing rays in explicit batches with a fixed step count per batch rather than updating a single active set with variable steps. Inputs: Ray origins rayso and directions raysd (shape: N{rays} \times 3). Hit bounds hitst (shape: N{rays} \times 2, start and end distances). Neural network model evaluating density (sigmas) and color (rgbs) at sample points. Background color rgbbg. Parameters: Tthreshold (default 10^{-4}), MAXSAMPLES (default 1024), expstepfactor (default 0). Outputs: Final RGB image rgb (shape: N{rays} \times 3). Final opacity opacity (shape: N{rays}). Final depth depth (shape: N{rays}). Data Structures: aliveindices: 1D tensor of indices into the ray batch that have not yet converged. Initialized to [0, 1,..., Nrays - 1]. opacity, depth, rgb: Accumulators initialized to zeros. samples: Integer counter for total samples processed per ray. Steps: 1. Initialize opacity, depth, rgb to zeros. Set aliveindices to all ray indices. Set samples = 0. Set minsamples = 1 (or 4 if expstepfactor != 0). 2. While samples < MAXSAMPLES: a. Let N{alive} = \text{len}(alive\indices). If N{alive} == 0, break.. b. Calculate batch size N{samples} = \max(\min(N{rays} // N{alive}, 64), min\samples). c. Increment samples by N{samples}. d. Generate sample points for the N{alive} rays using raymarchingtest. This returns xyzs (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3), dirs (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3), deltas (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples}), ts (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples}), and Neffsamples. e. Flatten xyzs and dirs to 2D: (N{alive} \times N{samples}) \times 3. f. Compute validmask where dirs are not zero vectors: validmask = ~torch.all(dirs==0, dim=1). If validmask.sum() == 0, break. g. Initialize sigmas and rgbs tensors of size (N{alive} \times N{samples}) and (N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3) with zeros. Evaluate the neural network at xyzs[validmask] and dirs[validmask] to get sigmas and rgbs, filling only the valid entries. h. Reshape sigmas and rgbs back to (N{alive} \times N{samples}) and (N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3) respectively. i. Call compositetestfw with sigmas, rgbs, deltas, ts, hitst[:, 0], aliveindices, Tthreshold, Neffsamples, and the accumulators opacity, depth, rgb to update them in-place. j. Filter aliveindices to keep only valid indices (aliveindices >= 0). 3. After the loop, add background color: rgb += rgbbg (1 - opacity). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarchingtest(rayso, raysd, hitst, model, rgbbg, Tthreshold=1e-4, MAXSAMPLES=1024, expstepfactor=0): Nrays = rayso.shape[0] device = rayso.device # Initialize accumulators opacity = torch.zeros(Nrays, device=device) depth = torch.zeros(Nrays, device=device) rgb = torch.zeros(Nrays, 3, device=device) # Initialize alive indices aliveindices = torch.arange(Nrays, device=device) samples = 0 minsamples = 4 if expstepfactor != 0 else 1 while samples < MAXSAMPLES: Nalive = len(aliveindices) if Nalive == 0: break # Calculate batch size Nsamples = max(min(Nrays // Nalive, 64), minsamples) samples += Nsamples # Generate sample points xyzs, dirs, deltas, ts, Neffsamples = raymarchingtest( rayso, raysd, hitst[:, 0], aliveindices, model.densitybitfield, model.cascades, model.scale, expstepfactor, model.gridsize, MAXSAMPLES, Nsamples) # Flatten for network evaluation xyzs = xyzs.reshape(-1, 3) dirs = dirs.reshape(-1, 3) # Filter invalid directions validmask = ~torch.all(dirs == 0, dim=1) if validmask.sum() == 0: break # Evaluate neural network sigmas = torch.zeros(len(xyzs), device=device) rgbs = torch.zeros(len(xyzs), 3, device=device) sigmasvalid, rgbsvalid = model(xyzs[validmask], dirs[validmask]) sigmas[validmask] = sigmasvalid rgbs[validmask] = rgbsvalid.float() # Reshape back sigmas = sigmas.reshape(Nalive, Nsamples) rgbs = rgbs.reshape(Nalive, Nsamples, 3) # Composite and update accumulators in-place compositetestfw( sigmas, rgbs, deltas, ts, hitst[:, 0], aliveindices, Tthreshold, Neffsamples, opacity, depth, rgb) # Filter valid indices aliveindices = aliveindices[aliveindices >= 0] # Add background rgb = rgb + rgbbg (1 - opacity) return rgb, opacity, depth def raymarchingtest(rayso, raysd, hitst, aliveindices, densitybitfield, cascades, scale, expstepfactor, gridsize, maxsamples, nsamples): # Sources do not provide the internal implementation. pass def compositetestfw(sigmas, rgbs, deltas, ts, hitst, aliveindices, Tthreshold, Neffsamples, opacity, depth, rgb): # Sources do not provide the internal implementation. pass Parameters: Tthreshold: Transmittance threshold below which a ray is considered converged. Default: 10^{-4}. MAXSAMPLES: Maximum total samples per ray across iterations. Default: 1024. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-direction rays: Filtered by validmask to prevent division by zero or invalid sampling. Convergence: Rays stop contributing to computation once transmittance drops below Tthreshold, but the loop continues until MAXSAMPLES is reached for remaining rays. Batch size calculation: minsamples ensures a minimum computational load per iteration, preventing excessive overhead from very small batches. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the total number of samples processed, which is bounded by N{rays} \times MAX\SAMPLES. Memory complexity is Not given in the sources.. Measured Performance: On the Lego scene with an RTX 2080 Ti, the method achieved 36.2 FPS and 32.96 PSNR, compared to 18.2 FPS and 31.46 PSNR for torch-ngp. Scaling: Performance scales with scene emptiness; faster rendering occurs when most of the scene is empty, allowing more rays to converge early. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant speedup in transparent/empty regions due to early stopping; simple batching logic. Limitations: Slower than instant-ngp (60 FPS on 3090) due to iterative Python loop overhead and lack of fully fused kernels; quality may fluctuate across runs. This method is part of the ngppl project by kwea123, an unofficial PyTorch Lightning implementation of instant-NGP. name: Ray Grouping
head: Ray grouping approach for Visualization of Medical Data
body: Ray grouping is an optimization technique for distance-field ray marching that reduces computational complexity by grouping rays originating from similar successive voxels into a single representative ray. It solves the problem of excessive interpolation and ray casting costs in high-resolution volume rendering by lowering the total number of initial rays. Unlike Beam Optimization, which optimizes the traversal path, or Block Culling, which discards empty space, ray grouping merges active rays based on local variance. It is distinct from Bounding Shape Optimization as it operates on the ray origin distribution rather than scene geometry bounds. Inputs: A 2D input slice (image plane) of resolution W \times H, a user-defined variance threshold T, and a maximum group size G{max}. Outputs: A rendered image where rays are cast from grouped or individual voxels based on variance. Data Structures: The input slice is conceptually divided into non-overlapping blocks of size B \times B. For each block, the algorithm computes the intra-block variance of the ray origins or associated scalar field values. Parameters: T: User-defined threshold for variance. G{max}: Maximum group size. In practice, implementations tested group sizes of 2, 4, and 8. A group size of 1 implies no grouping. Steps: 1. Block Division: Divide the input slice into smaller blocks of the same size. 2. Variance Measurement: Measure the intra-block variance for each block. Let Vb be the variance of block b. 3. Threshold Comparison: Compare Vb to the threshold T. 4. Grouping Decision: If Vb \le T (variance lies within the threshold range), group every voxel in the block into a single unit. Cast only one representative ray for the group. If Vb > T (deviation found), ungroup the voxels. Cast rays from individual voxels in the block. 5. Rendering: During rendering, consider information from both grouped and non-grouped voxels to ensure no information is lost. For grouped rays, the representative ray's result is applied to the group members. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raygroupingrender(inputslice, threshold, groupsize): """ Renders a volume slice using ray grouping optimization. Args: inputslice: 2D array of ray origins or scalar values. threshold: Variance threshold T. groupsize: Block dimension B x B. Returns: renderedimage: 2D array of final colors. """ height, width = inputslice.shape renderedimage = zeroslike(inputslice) # Iterate over blocks for y in range(0, height, groupsize): for x in range(0, width, groupsize): # Extract block yend = min(y + groupsize, height) xend = min(x + groupsize, width) block = inputslice[y:yend, x:xend] # Calculate intra-block variance # Note: Variance calculation details (mean subtraction, squaring) are standard # but not explicitly defined in sources beyond "intra-block variance mechanism" variance = calculatevariance(block) if variance <= threshold: # Grouped: Cast one representative ray # The representative is typically the center or first voxel of the block repx, repy = x + groupsize // 2, y + groupsize // 2 # Handle edge cases for block center if groupsize is even if groupsize % 2 == 0: repx = x + groupsize // 2 - 1 repy = y + groupsize // 2 - 1 # Get ray from representative voxel ray = getray(inputslice, repy, repx) color = castray(ray) # Apply color to all voxels in the block for by in range(y, yend): for bx in range(x, xend): renderedimage[by, bx] = color else: # Ungrouped: Cast individual rays for by in range(y, yend): for bx in range(x, xend): ray = getray(inputslice, by, bx) renderedimage[by, bx] = castray(ray) return renderedimage def calculatevariance(block): """Calculates the variance of the values in the block.""" mean = sum(block.flatten()) / len(block.flatten()) variance = sum((x - mean) 2 for x in block.flatten()) / len(block.flatten()) return variance def getray(slicedata, y, x): """Retrieves the ray origin/direction for a specific voxel.""" # Implementation depends on the specific ray casting setup (e.g., perspective projection) # This is a placeholder for the standard ray generation logic return Ray(origin=slicedata[y, x], direction=...) def castray(ray): """Performs the actual ray marching and compositing.""" # Standard distance-field ray marching loop # Uses the formula: C ≈ Σ (Π (1 - αj)) αi ci color = 0.0 alphaaccum = 1.0 # Marching steps... return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The variance calculation must be robust to floating-point errors, especially for uniform regions. Boundary Conditions: Blocks at the image edges may be smaller than B \times B. The variance calculation must handle these partial blocks correctly. Over-splitting: Implementations may be "slightly too eager to split groups," leading to suboptimal performance. This suggests the threshold T or variance metric may need tuning to avoid unnecessary ungrouping. Information Loss: While grouping reduces rays, care must be taken to ensure that grouping does not obscure fine details. The sources state that information from grouped and non-grouped voxels is considered to prevent loss. Time and Memory Complexity: The method reduces computational complexity by minimizing the number of interpolations and ray casts. The absolute number of interpolations would otherwise be m \times n \times s (where m, n are dimensions and s is steps), but grouping reduces the number of initial rays. The exact formula for the reduced complexity is not provided. The cost at each step for a given group is not dependent on the number of rays in the group, making it efficient for high resolutions. Measured Performance: Tests were conducted on 64x64 and 128x128 pixel displays with a scene containing 3 spheres at varying distances. Group Size 2: Lowered execution time significantly. Group Size 4 and 8: Did not decrease execution time significantly further compared to size 2. Resolution Scaling: Improvements were more significant for higher resolutions (128x128). | Group Size | 64x64 Display (Clock Cycles) | 128x128 Display (Clock Cycles) | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 1 (No Grouping) | 128k | 512k | | 2 | 84k | 328k | | 4 | 80k | 312k | | 8 | 82k | 313k | Table 5.2 from Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces total number of marching steps; effective on high-resolution displays; works well on GPUs with dynamic thread creation. Limitations: Significant overhead from splitting groups; diminishing returns for large group sizes; less effective on traditional lockstepped GPU architectures compared to custom GPUs. The implementation's eagerness to split groups can reduce potential gains. When to Use: Use when rendering high-resolution volumes where ray casting is the bottleneck and the scene has regions of low variance (smooth or uniform areas). Avoid on hardware with strict lockstep execution if the variance metric causes frequent group splitting. Origin: The technique was introduced in the context of medical data visualization. It is described as a method to reduce computational complexity in ray casting by grouping rays based on intra-block variance. History and Development: The method was implemented and evaluated in a study on sphere tracing on a custom GPU. The implementation was done in GLSL shaders. The authors noted that while the optimization improved performance, the gains were less than expected due to overhead and implementation specifics. Usage: Used in volume rendering of medical data and 3D geospatial information. It is particularly relevant for distance-field ray marching where many rays traverse similar paths. name: Block Culling
head: RT+Cull
body: Block culling is an optimization technique for volume rendering that reduces the time required to reach content values inside RGBA volumes by skipping blocks that do not contribute to the visible result. It is particularly effective when sparsity in the volume data results from runtime parameters, such as a narrower allowed density range, rather than inherent data sparsity. Block culling integrates with hardware ray tracing (RT) to evaluate whether a block contains relevant content before performing expensive ray marching or traversal steps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical volume data structure (e.g., bricks or blocks), a user-defined content range (density/opacity thresholds), and ray intersection data. Output: A rendered image with reduced computation time by skipping irrelevant blocks. Data Structures: The method relies on the existing block hierarchy. Each block stores metadata indicating its content range (min/max density or opacity). If this metadata is not explicitly stored, it must be computed or approximated. Steps: 1. Ray-Block Intersection: Determine if a ray intersects a block in the hierarchy. 2. Content Range Check: Compare the block's stored content range against the user-requested content range. 3. Culling Decision: If the block's content range does not overlap with the user-requested range, the block is culled (skipped). If there is an overlap, the block is processed (traversed or ray-marched). 4. Traversal/Rendering: Proceed with standard ray tracing or block walking for non-culled blocks. Parameters: User-requested content range: The density/opacity interval of interest. Block content range: Precomputed min/max values for each block. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Culling Benefit: If the user-requested content range is greater than or equal to the actual content range of the volume, block culling provides no significant performance gain. Performance Regression: The method does not cause significant performance regression when it cannot impact performance (i.e., when no blocks are culled). Sparse Content: If the volume is inherently too sparse, block culling may not be as effective as block walking, and the overhead of checking ranges might outweigh benefits if not optimized. Pseudocode: def blockculling(rayorigin, raydirection, block, userrangemin, userrangemax): # 1. Ray-Block Intersection (AABB slab method) tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < block.boundsmin[i] or rayorigin[i] > block.boundsmax[i]: return None # Ray misses block else: t1 = (block.boundsmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (block.boundsmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax or tmax < 0: return None # Ray misses block # 2. Content Range Check if block.contentmax < userrangemin or block.contentmin > userrangemax: return None # Cull this block # 3. Process block if block.isleaf: return raymarchblock(rayorigin, raydirection, block.data, userrangemin, userrangemax) # 4. Recurse into children results = [] for child in block.children: result = blockculling(rayorigin, raydirection, child, userrangemin, userrangemax) if result is not None: results.append(result) return compositeresults(results) def raymarchblock(origin, direction, data, rangemin, rangemax): # Standard ray marching/shading for leaf blocks return 0.0 def compositeresults(results): # Accumulate results from children return sum(results) Edit culling is a technique used during the construction of Signed Distance Field (SDF) bricks to reduce the number of edits evaluated per brick, thereby reducing construction latency. It determines which edits affect a sub-brick based on the principle that a sub-brick is entirely encapsulated by its parent, ensuring that no edit affecting the child is missed while culling those that do not. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the hierarchical relationship between parent and child bricks to minimize redundant distance evaluations during the critical construction phase. Block walking with culling combines block walking and block culling algorithms to reduce the time to reach content values inside RGBA volumes. In block traversal mode, 'RT+Walk+Cull' achieved 5.543ms on Fish (a) and 6.945ms on Fish (c). In blend mode, 'RT+Walk+Cull' achieved 107.725ms on Fish (a) and 11.892ms on Fish (c). The combination results in the best performance on average compared to using either technique alone or standard ray tracing. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Time complexity is reduced by skipping irrelevant blocks, with gains most significant when sparsity results from runtime parameters. Memory: Memory complexity requires storing content range metadata for each block, with no additional significant overhead noted. Measured Performance: Block Traversal Mode: Fish (c): RT+Cull achieved 4.823ms vs 7.375ms for RT. Fish (a): RT+Cull achieved 9.740ms vs 9.745ms for RT. Chip (d): RT+Cull achieved 2.309ms vs 2.310ms for RT. Rock (e): RT+Cull achieved 7.949ms vs 7.949ms for RT. Blend Mode: Fish (c): RT+Cull achieved 8.079ms vs 10.798ms for RT. Fish (a): RT+Cull achieved 113.780ms vs 113.983ms for RT. Chip (d): RT+Cull achieved 15.132ms vs 15.098ms for RT. Scaling: Performance gains are consistent across different datasets (Fish, Chip, Rock) when sparsity is present. No significant performance regression occurs when no blocks are culled. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Strengths include effectiveness for runtime-adjustable density ranges and no significant penalty when ineffective. Limitations: Limitations include reduced effectiveness when content is inherently too sparse and the requirement for precomputed content ranges. When to Use: Use when sparsity is due to runtime parameters rather than inherent data sparsity. Use in conjunction with block walking for optimal performance. When Not to Use: Avoid when the user-requested content range covers the entire actual content range, as no culling benefit is realized. Avoid when content is inherently too sparse, as block walking may be more effective. Block culling is applied in sparse volume rendering using hardware ray tracing. It addresses performance challenges of rendering large, sparse RGBA volumes by leveraging the hierarchical block structure to skip irrelevant data. The technique is part of a broader set of optimizations including block walking. name: Edit Culling
body: Edit culling is a technique used during the construction of Signed Distance Field (SDF) bricks to reduce the number of edits evaluated per brick, thereby reducing construction latency. It determines which edits affect a sub-brick based on the principle that a sub-brick is entirely encapsulated by its parent, ensuring that no edit affecting the child is missed while culling those that do not. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the hierarchical relationship between parent and child bricks to minimize redundant distance evaluations during the critical construction phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A parent brick's index buffer (list of active edits), the edit definitions (including smooth blending dependencies), and the brick geometry (size and midpoint). Output: A new index buffer for the sub-brick containing indices of edits that affect the sub-brick, guaranteed to be unique and in ascending order. Data Structures: Bitfield: A 32-element array of 32-bit unsigned integers (uint32[32]), totaling 1024 bits. This supports a maximum of 1024 edits. Index Buffer: A list of integers representing the indices of the set bits in the bitfield. Dependency Buffer: A structure mapping smooth edits to their required dependencies. Parameters: Max Edits: 1024. Brick Size: The physical size of the brick volume. Steps: 1. Initialize a 1024-bit bitfield (32 uint32 words) to all zeros. 2. Iterate through each edit index i present in the parent brick's index buffer. a. Evaluate the edit's distance function at the midpoint of the sub-brick, denoted as d{mid}. b. Compare d{mid} to the brick size S. c. If d{mid} > S, the edit is culled and its bit remains unset. d. If d{mid} \le S, set the i-th bit in the bitfield to 1. e. If the edit is smooth, retrieve its dependencies from the dependency buffer and set the corresponding bits for each dependency in the bitfield to 1. 3. Construct the index buffer by performing a prefix sum on the bitfield to compact it, then writing the indices of the set bits to the global index buffer. Indices are guaranteed to be both unique and in ascending order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def editculling(parentindexbuffer, edits, brickmidpoint, bricksize, maxedits=1024): # Step 1: Initialize bitfield (32 uint32s) bitfield = [0] 32 def setbit(i): bitfield[i // 32] |= (1 << (i % 32)) # Step 2: Evaluate edits against midpoint for editidx in parentindexbuffer: dist = edits[editidx].distance(brickmidpoint) # Culling condition: if distance > brick size, cull if dist > bricksize: continue # Set bit for this edit setbit(editidx) # Handle smooth blending dependencies if edits[editidx].issmooth: for depidx in edits[editidx].dependencies: setbit(depidx) # Step 3: Construct index buffer via prefix sum # Convert bitfield to binary counts counts = [0] maxedits for i in range(maxedits): if (bitfield[i // 32] >> (i % 32)) & 1: counts[i] = 1 # Prefix sum to determine output positions for i in range(1, maxedits): counts[i] += counts[i-1] # Scatter indices into sorted, unique buffer indexbuffer = [0] counts[maxedits-1] if counts[maxedits-1] > 0 else [] for i in range(maxedits): if counts[i] > 0: indexbuffer[counts[i]-1] = i counts[i] -= 1 return indexbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation Error: The method relies on evaluating the distance at the midpoint, which acts as a bounding sphere approximation. This approximation can result in more edits being evaluated per brick than an optimal solution using precise signed distance function intersection calculation. Smooth Blending Overhead: High edit counts with smooth blending significantly increase the number of edits per brick because dependencies are added, increasing the index buffer size. Bounding Sphere Limitation: The source notes that bounding spheres are used for intersection detection in this context, which is an approximation that may evaluate more edits than necessary. Time Complexity: The algorithm iterates through the parent's index buffer and performs constant-time bit operations. The prefix sum is linear in the number of edits (1024). It significantly reduces the total amount of work compared to evaluating all edits. Memory Complexity: Requires a fixed 1024-bit bitfield per brick during construction and an index buffer for the output. The index buffer size varies; in optimal cases (e.g., Fractal scene), it references less than 10 edits, but in worst cases (e.g., Drops scene with 1024 edits and smooth blending), it can be much larger. Performance: In the "Drops" scene at a brick size of 0.0625, enabling edit culling increased construction performance by a factor of 32, reducing construction times to less than 100 milliseconds, whereas without it, construction took multiple seconds. Strengths: Dramatically reduces construction latency for scenes with many edits; ensures correct geometry by maintaining sorted, unique indices; leverages hierarchical encapsulation. Limitations: The midpoint evaluation is an approximation and may cull edits that actually intersect the brick or keep edits that do not, compared to precise intersection methods. Smooth blending increases memory overhead. When to Use: When constructing SDF bricks hierarchically and the number of edits is large (up to 1024). When Not to Use: When precise intersection is required and the cost of midpoint approximation is unacceptable. Edit culling was introduced in the context of real-time rendering and construction of Signed Distance Fields, specifically within hierarchical brick-based representations. It addresses the bottleneck of evaluating hundreds of edits per brick during construction, which is critical for interactive applications. The technique was developed to make real-time reconstruction of SDF geometry feasible, as construction without it was too slow for interactive use. name: Bounding Shape Optimization
head: Bounding Shape Culling
body: Bounding Shape Optimization accelerates volumetric rendering by skipping density evaluations in empty space using pre-defined bounding shapes. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space by restricting ray marching to regions where density is non-zero. Unlike Beam Optimization which optimizes for caustic beams, or Block Culling which uses grid-based culling, this method generalizes the concept of space-leaping by allowing arbitrary closed geometry (e.g., spheres, cylinders) to define the volume extent. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{O}, ray direction \mathbf{D}, density field \rho(\mathbf{x}), bounding shape parameters (e.g., sphere center C and radius R), initial step size s0, light color \mathbf{L}, and background color \mathbf{C}{bg}. Output: Rendered color and opacity for the ray. Data Structures: The bounding shape B is defined by its geometric parameters. For a sphere, this is the center C and radius R. For other shapes, the intersection function must be defined. The density field is sampled only within the bounds of B. Steps: 1. Define Boundaries: Identify the region where density is non-zero. The closer B is to the actual density field, the fewer "useless" steps are performed. 2. Compute Intersections: Use a surface rendering technique to find the intersection points of the ray (\mathbf{O}, \mathbf{D}) with the bounding shape B. This yields the entry and exit distances along the ray. 3. Ray Marching: Perform classical volumetric rendering only for samples located between the entry and exit distances. 4. Step Size Adaptation: To improve performance, step sizes can increase as the ray progresses through the medium, as imprecisions have less impact further along the ray. Formulas: For a sphere intersection, the ray \mathbf{P}(t) = \mathbf{O} + t\mathbf{D} intersects the sphere when: a = \mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{D} \mathbf{oc} = \mathbf{O} - C b = 2(\mathbf{oc} \cdot \mathbf{D}) c = \mathbf{oc} \cdot \mathbf{oc} - R^2 \Delta = b^2 - 4ac t{enter} = \frac{-b - \sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}, \quad t{exit} = \frac{-b + \sqrt{\Delta}}{2a} where t{enter} and t{exit} are the distances along the ray to the entry and exit points, respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraywithboundingshape(rayorigin, raydirection, densityfield, spherecenter, sphereradius, initialstepsize, lightcolor, backgroundcolor): # Step 1 & 2: Compute ray-sphere intersection oc = rayorigin - spherecenter a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) c = dot(oc, oc) - sphereradius sphereradius discriminant = b b - 4.0 a c # If no intersection, return background color if discriminant < 0: return vec4(backgroundcolor, 1.0) sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) tenter = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) texit = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) # If the ray starts inside, adjust tenter to avoid backward marching if tenter < 0.0: tenter = 0.0 color = vec3(0.0) opacity = 0.0 t = tenter stepsize = initialstepsize # Step 3 & 4: Volumetric rendering inside bounds while t < texit and opacity < 1.0: pos = rayorigin + raydirection t density = densityfield.sample(pos) attenuation = exp(-density stepsize) color += (1.0 - opacity) density stepsize lightcolor opacity += (1.0 - opacity) (1.0 - attenuation) # Adaptive step size: increase step size as we go deeper # Specific formula not provided in sources; heuristic multiplier applied stepsize = stepsize 1.1 t += stepsize return vec4(color, opacity) Parameters: Bounding Shape Choice: The type of geometry used (e.g., Sphere, Cylinder, Box). Sphere Marching is selected in the reference implementation for its simplicity and efficiency. Container Definition Fineness: Finer container definitions (tighter bounds) improve volume render efficiency by reducing the number of samples taken in empty space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Origin Inside: If the ray origin is inside the bounding shape, t{enter} must be clamped to 0 or the negative root must be ignored to avoid backward marching. Tightness: Loose bounding shapes result in unnecessary density evaluations. The optimization gain is directly proportional to how tightly the shape fits the non-zero density region. Intersection Precision: Floating-point errors in intersection calculation can cause rays to miss the volume or march slightly outside it, leading to artifacts or wasted computation. Convex Polyhedron Bounding is a space-leaping technique for direct volume rendering that accelerates ray traversal by enclosing objects within a convex polyhedron. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space by allowing rays to skip large volumes of non-data voxels. Unlike Bounding Shape Optimization which generalizes the concept, this method specifically constructs a convex hull around the object, and differs from Bounding Volume Extrusion by using a general polyhedron rather than a prism tailored for caustic beams. Container-based Ray Marching uses closed geometry as a bounding container to ray march only where there actually is density, improving efficiency. It restricts ray marching to regions where density exists, using closed geometry as a bounding container. Finer container definitions improve volume render efficiency compared to coarse or non-existent containers. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of density evaluations from O(N) (where N is the total ray length in steps) to O(N{inside}), where N{inside} is the number of steps within the bounding shape. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the bounding shape parameters and the density field. No additional large data structures are needed beyond the shape definition. Strengths: Significant performance boost in scenes with mostly empty density fields. Simple to implement for basic shapes like spheres and boxes. Limitations: Requires pre-defining or computing the bounding shape. If the density field is dense or irregularly shaped, the bounding shape may not provide significant culling benefits. When to Use: Ideal for procedural noise fields, interstellar dust, or solar flares where large portions of the volume are empty. When Not to Use: When the density field fills the entire volume or when the bounding shape computation cost outweighs the savings from culling. Bounding Shape Optimization was introduced in the context of real-time rendering of interstellar dust clouds and solar flares. The method leverages the hypothesis that such density fields are mostly empty, allowing for significant performance gains by skipping empty space. It is also discussed in the context of production volume rendering, where closed geometry containers are used to optimize ray marching efficiency. name: Convex Polyhedron Bounding
head: PARC (Polygon assisted ray casting)
body: Convex Polyhedron Bounding is a space-leaping technique for direct volume rendering that accelerates ray traversal by enclosing objects within a convex polyhedron. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space by allowing rays to skip large volumes of non-data voxels. The method is specifically recommended for volumes containing only a few objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset containing one or few distinct objects. Output: A convex polyhedron that encloses the object, used to cull empty space during ray marching. Data Structures: The exact layout is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Object Identification: Identify the voxels belonging to the object(s) in the volume. 2. Polyhedron Construction: Compute a convex polyhedron that encloses all identified object voxels. 3. Ray Traversal Setup: For each ray, determine the entry and exit points of the ray with respect to the convex polyhedron. 4. Space Leaping: If the ray does not intersect the polyhedron, skip the ray entirely. If it intersects, traverse only the segment within the polyhedron using standard volume rendering techniques. Formulas: The exact mathematical formulation is not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of Objects: The method is recommended for volumes with "few objects". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Objects: If the volume contains many objects, the convex hull may become too large or complex, reducing efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convexpolyhedronbounding(volumedata, objectmask): # 1. Identify object voxels objectvoxels = [] for z in range(volumedata.shape[0]): for y in range(volumedata.shape[1]): for x in range(volumedata.shape[2]): if objectmask[z, y, x]: objectvoxels.append((x, y, z)) # 2. Build convex polyhedron # Note: Specific algorithm for convex hull construction is not provided in sources polyhedronplanes = [] # 3. For each ray for rayorigin, raydirection in rays: # 4. Intersect ray with polyhedron tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') miss = False for n, d in polyhedronplanes: denom = n[0]raydirection[0] + n[1]raydirection[1] + n[2]raydirection[2] if abs(denom) > 1e-8: t = (d - (n[0]rayorigin[0] + n[1]rayorigin[1] + n[2]rayorigin[2])) / denom if denom > 0: if t < tmax: tmax = t else: if t > tmin: tmin = t else: if n[0]rayorigin[0] + n[1]rayorigin[1] + n[2]rayorigin[2] > d: miss = True break if miss or tmax < tmin: continue # 5. March ray within the bounding volume step = 0.01 t = tmin while t <= tmax: pos = (rayorigin[0] + traydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + traydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + traydirection[2]) rendersegment(pos, volumedata) t += step def rendersegment(pos, volumedata): # Standard volume rendering step at pos pass Computes tight convex hulls for caustic beams using 6-triangle hulls, superior to planar prism approximations for warped beams. Represents the bound as a reduced set of half-spaces for efficient distance queries, clustering orientations to minimize plane count. Decomposes point sets into a union of tighter convex volumes via recursive cutting planes, better for concave shapes than a single hull. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Bounding Volume Extrusion
head: 6-triangle convex hull method for caustic beams, Tight Bounding Volume Computation
body: Bounding Volume Extrusion is a technique to compute tight convex hull bounding volumes for caustic beams, enabling efficient rasterization of inscattered light while minimizing fill-rate overhead. Unlike the standard bounding prism method, which approximates bilinear beam sides with planar prisms and suffers from poor accuracy on strongly warped or focused beams, this method constructs a 6-triangle convex hull that tightly encloses the beam geometry. Inputs: Caustic beam defined by a base triangle vertices v0, v1, v2 and corresponding beam direction vectors d0, d1, d2 at each vertex. Scene geometry for occlusion testing. View frustum parameters. Outputs: A set of 6 triangles forming the bounding volume of the caustic beam. Data Structures: Beam Space Coordinate System: A local coordinate system is established for each beam: Origin: Coincides with vertex v0 of the base triangle. Y-axis: Aligned with the normal of the base triangle. Direction Vectors: The beam direction vectors di are scaled such that their y-coordinate is exactly 1.0. Area Function Coefficients: Three coefficients for the second-order area function A(y), precomputed during beam generation. Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the beam vertices and direction vectors into the local beam space defined above. 2. Precompute Area Function: Calculate the coefficients for the cross-sectional area function A(y). In this coordinate system, the area of the parallel cross-section of the beam is a second-order expression over the local y-coordinate. A(y) = c2 y^2 + c1 y + c0 where c0, c1, c2 are the precomputed coefficients. This allows evaluation of the cross-section with a single dot product later. 3. Determine Extrusion Length: Compute the maximum possible length by intersecting beam edges with the view frustum. Refine the length by intersecting beam edges with surrounding scene geometry using approximate ray tracing (Szirmay-Kalos et al. [2005]) within the geometry shader. Apply energy approximation for divergent beams: if the beam is divergent, limit the extrusion length to the distance where the contribution becomes negligible, maximizing extrusion only up to that point. 4. Generate Bounding Volume (6-Triangle Method): For each of the three edges of the base triangle, identify the corresponding vertex on the top triangle (the end of the extrusion). Construct a plane for each edge containing the base edge and the opposite top vertex, such that the entire beam lies in the negative half-space of the plane (touching plane). Simplify the computation: Instead of intersecting full prisms, take the triangle formed by one base edge and one top vertex directly as one side of the bounding volume. Select one such triangle for each of the three base edges, resulting in 3 side triangles. The base and top triangles form the remaining 2 faces. The 6th is likely the top triangle or a specific hull face. The text says "bounding volume is defined by six triangles". 5. Watertightness Check: Check if multiple consistent triangulations exist for any edge (i.e., the beam side is close to planar). If multiple candidates exist, revert to the bounding prism method to ensure a watertight volume. If no ambiguity exists, emit the 6 triangles from the geometry shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeboundingvolume(basevertices, beamdirections, scenegeometry, viewfrustum): """ Computes the 6-triangle convex hull bounding volume for a caustic beam. Args: basevertices: List of 3 vec3s [v0, v1, v2] beamdirections: List of 3 vec3s [d0, d1, d2] scenegeometry: Data structure for approximate ray tracing viewfrustum: View frustum planes Returns: List of 6 triangles (each triangle is 3 vec3s) or None if fallback is needed """ # Step 1: Coordinate Transformation # Origin at v0, y-axis is triangle normal v0, v1, v2 = basevertices d0, d1, d2 = beamdirections trianglenormal = normalize(cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0)) # Scale directions so y-coordinate is 1 # dscaled.y = 1 => dscaled = d / (d. normal) # Note: If d. normal is 0 or negative, beam is parallel or backward, handle as edge case scalefactors = [dot(d, trianglenormal) for d in [d0, d1, d2]] # Check for degenerate directions if any(sf <= 0 for sf in scalefactors): return fallbackprismmethod(basevertices, beamdirections) scaleddirections = [d / sf for d, sf in zip([d0, d1, d2], scalefactors)] # Step 2: Precompute Area Function Coefficients # A(y) = c2y^2 + c1y + c0 # Exact coefficient calculation from bilinear patch area is not detailed in sources c0, c1, c2 = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Step 3: Determine Extrusion Length # Max length from view frustum # Exact frustum intersection algorithm is not detailed in sources maxlengthfrustum = 100.0 # Refine with scene geometry using approximate ray tracing (Szirmay-Kalos et al. [2005]) # Exact ray tracing implementation is not detailed in sources maxlengthscene = 50.0 # Energy approximation for divergent beams # Exact energy threshold function is not detailed in sources energylimitlength = 10.0 # Combine lengths extrusionlength = min(maxlengthfrustum, maxlengthscene, energylimitlength) # Calculate top vertices topvertices = [v + d extrusionlength for v, d in zip(basevertices, scaleddirections)] v0top, v1top, v2top = topvertices # Step 4: Generate Bounding Volume (6-Triangle Method) # Construct side triangles: each edge of base + opposite top vertex tri1 = [v0, v1, v2top] tri2 = [v1, v2, v0top] tri3 = [v2, v0, v1top] # Base and Top triangles tribase = [v0, v1, v2] tritop = [v0top, v1top, v2top] # Step 5: Watertightness Check # Check if multiple consistent triangulations exist for any edge # Exact ambiguity check algorithm is not detailed in sources if isambiguoustriangulation(tri1, tri2, tri3, basevertices, topvertices): return fallbackprismmethod(basevertices, beamdirections) # The source specifies the volume is defined by six triangles, selected for each edge independently return [tri1, tri2, tri3, tribase, tritop, tritop] def fallbackprismmethod(basevertices, beamdirections): # Revert to Ernst et al. [2005] bounding prism method # Exact implementation is not detailed in sources return [] def isambiguoustriangulation(tri1, tri2, tri3, base, top): # Check if any side is close to planar, leading to multiple consistent triangulations # Exact implementation is not detailed in sources return False Time Complexity: The method adds overhead to the geometry shader for extrusion length calculation (ray tracing) and triangle selection. The precomputation of area coefficients is done during beam generation. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory; coefficients are stored per beam. Performance: Significantly reduces fill-rate compared to the bounding prism method, especially for strongly warped or focused beams where the prism method yields a poor approximation. Strengths: Tighter convex hull approximation than prisms; efficient rasterization; handles dynamic scenes without precomputation. Limitations: Numerical instability can lead to non-watertight volumes if multiple triangulations are consistent; requires fallback to less efficient prism method in such cases. Approximate ray tracing may miss thin occluders. Origin: Proposed by Liktor et al. in "Real-time volume caustics with adaptive beam tracing" (2011). History: Builds on earlier caustic beam tracing methods. The bounding prism method by Ernst et al. [2005] was the prior standard for bounding caustic beams. Usage: Used in real-time volume caustics rendering to accumulate inscattered light efficiently. name: Implicit Convex Hulls
head: Convex Hull Bounding Volumes, Simplified Convex Hulls
body: Implicit Convex Hulls construct a compact convex bounding volume for the point set generated by Sphere Carving, representing it as an intersection of a reduced set of oriented half-spaces. By clustering half-space orientations and projecting cluster centers back to the original hull, the method preserves the convex bounding property while enabling significantly more efficient distance evaluation than the full-resolution hull. Inputs: S: Final sphere set from Sphere Carving. P: Point set generated by S. H: Full set of half-spaces \{\Pii\} defining the convex hull H(P). m: Target number of half-spaces for the simplified volume (typical value: 20). Outputs: He: Reduced set of half-spaces defining the simplified bounding volume \mathcal{B}. d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}): Distance from query point \mathbf{p} to \mathcal{B}. Data Structures: Half-space \Pii: Defined by unit normal vector \mathbf{n}i and scalar offset di, representing the inequality \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{x} + di \le 0 for all \mathbf{x} \in H. Steps: 1. Extract the normal vectors \{\mathbf{n}i\} from the full half-space set H. 2. Apply a k-means clustering algorithm to the set of orientations \{\mathbf{n}i\} to find m clusters. 3. Compute the cluster centers (mean vectors) for each cluster. 4. Project each cluster center onto the existing half-spaces in H by selecting the half-space whose normal \mathbf{n}k maximizes the dot product with the center. 5. Form the reduced set He from the selected half-spaces, preserving the convex bounding property. 6. Evaluate distance: d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) = \max{\Pii \in He} (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{p} + di). 7. Compute the final field value: \tilde{f} = d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) if d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) > \varepsilon, otherwise \tilde{f} = f(\mathbf{p}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return tuple(vi / mag for vi in v) if mag > 0 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def argmaxindex(values): bestidx = 0 bestval = values[0] for i, v in enumerate(values): if v > bestval: bestval = v bestidx = i return bestidx def initializecentroids(normals, m): # Deterministic initialization: pick first m normals return [tuple(n) for n in normals[:m]] def computesimplifiedconvexhull(halfspaces, m): normals = [hs[0] for hs in halfspaces] centroids = initializecentroids(normals, m) maxiterations = 100 tolerance = 1e-6 for in range(maxiterations): assignments = [[] for in range(m)] for i, n in enumerate(normals): scores = [dot(n, c) for c in centroids] bestidx = argmaxindex(scores) assignments[bestidx].append(i) newcentroids = [] for clusterindices in assignments: if not clusterindices: newcentroids.append(centroids[0]) else: meann = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for idx in clusterindices: meann = [meann[j] + normals[idx][j] for j in range(3)] newcentroids.append(normalize(meann)) converged = all(math.sqrt(sum((c[j] - nc[j])2 for j in range(3))) < tolerance for c, nc in zip(centroids, newcentroids)) centroids = newcentroids if converged: break simplifiedhalfspaces = [] for centroid in centroids: scores = [dot(centroid, hs[0]) for hs in halfspaces] bestidx = argmaxindex(scores) simplifiedhalfspaces.append(halfspaces[bestidx]) return simplifiedhalfspaces def distancetosimplifiedhull(p, simplifiedhalfspaces): maxdist = -float('inf') for n, d in simplifiedhalfspaces: dist = dot(n, p) + d if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist return maxdist Edge Cases: Empty clusters: Re-initialized to the first centroid to avoid undefined centroids. Degenerate input: Collinear or coplanar points yield fewer unique normals; the algorithm naturally handles reduced N. Precision: Dot product comparisons use a tolerance threshold; epsilon \varepsilon in the distance check prevents z-fighting artifacts. A bounding volume \mathcal{B} constructed as the geometric convex hull H(P) of the point set P generated by Sphere Carving, represented as an intersection of oriented half-spaces. This serves as the base representation before simplification. Construction time: O(N \cdot m \cdot I), where N is the number of half-spaces in H, m is the cluster count, and I is the number of k-means iterations. Distance query time: O(m), requiring one dot product and addition per half-space in He. Memory: O(m) for the simplified volume versus O(N) for the full hull. Using m \approx 20 half-spaces yields a shape almost equivalent to the full resolution (e.g., 768 half-spaces) while significantly improving distance evaluation efficiency. The evaluation cost remains negligible compared to the underlying SDF function f. Strengths: Compact representation, preserves convex bounding property, fast queries for ray marching. Limitations: Approximation error increases as m decreases; preprocessing adds clustering overhead. Use when a tight convex bound is needed for acceleration and the SDF is expensive. Avoid when exact bounding is required or the scene is highly non-convex. The method originates from the Sphere Carving algorithm, which produces a final sphere set S and an associated point set P. The convex hull of P bounds the object and is exploited to build efficient bounding volumes. Clustering half-space orientations was introduced to address the computational intensity of evaluating distance against a high-resolution convex hull. name: Approximate Convex Decomposition
head: Plane Cutting Decomposition, Recursive Convex Decomposition
body: Approximate Convex Decomposition (ACD) is a post-processing method that decomposes a point set P (generated by Sphere Carving) into a union of tighter convex bounding volumes by recursively cutting the set with planes. Unlike a single convex hull, which can be loose for concave shapes, ACD creates a union of simpler convex shapes that conform more closely to the object's surface. It sets itself apart from siblings like Bounding Volume Extrusion and Implicit Convex Hulls by explicitly using a cutting-plane strategy inspired by mesh decomposition to minimize the total volume of the resulting hulls. Inputs: Point set P: A dense set of points close to the object surface, generated by Sphere Carving. Sphere set S: The set of spheres used in the preceding Sphere Carving step. V0: The volume of the initial bounding volume. ni: Number of iterations used in Sphere Carving (determines point cloud density). Outputs: A set of convex polyhedra (or ellipsoids) whose union bounds the object \mathcal{O}. Data Structures: P: List of 3D points. S: List of spheres (center, radius). \Pi: Cutting plane defined by normal \mathbf{n} and distance d from origin, or implicitly by the infinite sphere S\infty. Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample a set of candidate cutting planes \{\Pii\} (typically hundreds) from the space surrounding the point set P. 2. Selection: For each candidate plane \Pii, split P into two disjoint subsets \mathcal{L} (left) and \mathcal{R} (right) based on the signed distance d(\Pii, \mathbf{p}): \mathcal{L} = \{\mathbf{p} \in P, d(\Pii, \mathbf{p}) < 0\} \mathcal{R} = \{\mathbf{p} \in P, d(\Pii, \mathbf{p}) \geq 0\} Compute the score \sigma(P, \Pii) as the sum of the volumes of the convex hulls of these subsets: \sigma(P, \Pii) = V(H(\mathcal{L})) + V(H(\mathcal{R})) where V is the volume function and H is the convex hull operator. Select the plane \Pi that minimizes this score: \Pi = \arg \mini \sigma(P, \Pii) 3. Bounding Maintenance (Infinite Sphere): To ensure the resulting hulls bound the object, the cutting plane \Pi is treated as an infinite sphere S\infty added to the sphere set S. The convex hull created by trilaterating the extended sphere set \mathcal{S} \cup S\infty bounds the intersection of the object and the plane: H(\widetilde{T}(\mathcal{S} \cup S\infty)) \supset \mathcal{O} \cap \Pi where \widetilde{T} denotes the trilateration operation. 4. Finite Sphere Replacement: Replace S\infty with a large finite sphere tangent to \Pi. Radius: Set to the size of V0 (the initial volume). Center: Located on the line perpendicular to \Pi passing through the centroid of the subset (\mathcal{L} or \mathcal{R}). This replacement maintains the bounding guarantee and allows reuse of Sphere Carving intersection calculations. 5. Recursion: Recursively apply steps 2-4 to subsets \mathcal{L} and \mathcal{R} until a user-defined number of convex parts is reached or a stopping criterion is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximateconvexdecomposition(P, S, V0, maxparts, currentparts=0): """ Recursively decomposes point set P into convex hulls. P: list of 3D points (tuples or arrays) S: list of spheres (tuples of (center, radius)) V0: initial volume size (scalar) maxparts: target number of convex parts currentparts: number of parts generated so far """ if len(P) == 0: return [] # Base case: reached target parts or subset is too small if currentparts >= maxparts or len(P) < 4: # Compute convex hull from the current sphere set context return [computeconvexhullfromspheres(S)] # 1. Sample candidate planes (hundreds) # Sources do not specify the exact sampling strategy candidateplanes = samplecandidateplanes(P, count=200) bestplane = None minscore = float('inf') bestL = None bestR = None # 2. Evaluate scores for plane in candidateplanes: # Split P based on signed distance to plane L = [p for p in P if signeddistance(plane, p) < 0] R = [p for p in P if signeddistance(plane, p) >= 0] if not L or not R: continue # Compute score: sum of volumes of convex hulls of subsets volL = computeconvexhullvolume(L) volR = computeconvexhullvolume(R) score = volL + volR if score < minscore: minscore = score bestplane = plane bestL = L bestR = R if bestplane is None: return [computeconvexhullfromspheres(S)] # 3. Create bounding spheres for L and R # Treat bestplane as infinite sphere Sinf, then replace with finite sphere centroidL = computecentroid(bestL) sphereL = createlargesphere(bestplane, centroidL, V0) centroidR = computecentroid(bestR) sphereR = createlargesphere(bestplane, centroidR, V0) # 4. Recurse with extended sphere sets hullsL = approximateconvexdecomposition(bestL, S + [sphereL], V0, maxparts, currentparts + 1) hullsR = approximateconvexdecomposition(bestR, S + [sphereR], V0, maxparts, currentparts + 1) return hullsL + hullsR def signeddistance(plane, point): """Signed distance from point to plane defined by (normal, d).""" n, d = plane return float(n[0]point[0] + n[1]point[1] + n[2]point[2]) + d def computecentroid(points): n = len(points) return (sum(p[0] for p in points)/n, sum(p[1] for p in points)/n, sum(p[2] for p in points)/n) def computeconvexhullvolume(points): """Computes the volume of the 3D convex hull of points.""" # Standard 3D convex hull volume algorithm implementation pass def computeconvexhullfromspheres(S): """Computes the convex hull bounding the intersection region of the sphere set.""" # Standard convex hull computation from sphere constraints pass def samplecandidateplanes(P, count): """Samples candidate planes around the bounding box of P.""" # Sources do not specify the sampling strategy pass def createlargesphere(plane, centroid, V0): """ Creates a large finite sphere tangent to the plane, centered on the perpendicular line through the centroid. Radius equals V0. """ n, d = plane radius = V0 # Distance from centroid to plane dist = signeddistance(plane, centroid) # Center is shifted from centroid by (radius - dist) along the normal # to ensure the sphere is tangent to the plane and covers the subset side shift = radius - dist center = (centroid[0] + n[0]shift, centroid[1] + n[1]shift, centroid[2] + n[2]shift) return (center, radius) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The cutting plane selection requires multiple convex hull computations, which is computationally expensive and can be sensitive to numerical precision in volume calculations. Boundaries: Simply taking the convex hull of split point sets \mathcal{L} and \mathcal{R} is not sufficient to guarantee the bounding property (\mathcal{O} \not\subset H(\mathcal{L}) \cup H(\mathcal{R})). The sphere intersection logic is mandatory. Degenerate Input: If the point set P is not dense enough (too few iterations ni in Sphere Carving), the decomposition may not accurately capture the shape, leading to loose bounds. Time Complexity: The cutting plane selection step is the bottleneck, requiring multiple convex hull computations for hundreds of candidate planes. The decomposition process usually takes a few seconds to complete. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of points in P and the number of convex parts generated. Using large finite spheres instead of infinite spheres or planes creates slight overlaps between different convex hulls, but this never breaks the bounding guarantee and allows reuse of Sphere Carving intersection calculations. Measured Performance: For models like "House" (17 iterations, 4 parts), decomposition took 2.7 seconds. For "Amphora" (7 iterations, 29 parts), it took 49.9 seconds. Strengths: Produces tighter bounding volumes than a single convex hull, leveraging the detailed information in the point set P. Maintains the bounding guarantee. Limitations: Slow due to the exhaustive search for the optimal cutting plane. The method draws inspiration from mesh decomposition and could be replaced with more efficient methods. When to use: When tighter bounds are needed for ray marching acceleration and the object has significant concavity. Suitable for real-time applications if the pre-processing time is acceptable. Approximate Convex Decomposition in this context is a post-processing step for the Sphere Carving algorithm. It draws inspiration from approximate convex decomposition methods typically applied to meshes, specifically citing [Thul et al. 2018]. The method was introduced in the paper "Sphere Carving: Bounding Volumes for Signed Distance Fields". name: Out-of-core brick-based volume rendering
head: Brick pyramid rendering, Volume virtualization
body: Out-of-core brick-based volume rendering is a technique that streams multi-GB volumetric datasets over HTTP and renders them interactively with a fixed VRAM budget by decoupling logical 3D grid coordinates from physical GPU memory using a brick pyramid and indirection texture. It solves the problem of rendering datasets too large to fit in memory or download monolithically by fetching only the visible bricks via HTTP range reads. It sets itself apart from Sectioning by using fixed-size spatial chunks (bricks) rather than view-dependent slabs, and from Hardware-Assisted Volume Streaming by relying on a software-managed page cache and indirection texture rather than hardware texture streaming features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source volumetric dataset (e.g., 16-bit raw, OME-Zarr) and a camera view (position, orientation, field of view). Output: A rendered 2D image (framebuffer) and a fixed-size GPU page cache containing active bricks. Data Structures: 1. Brick Pyramid: A multi-resolution hierarchy where each level is a downsampled version of the previous one, with all levels split into fixed-size chunks called bricks. Logical Brick Size: 64^3 voxels. Physical Brick Size: 66^3 voxels (to facilitate interpolation during sampling). Storage: Compressed, stored server-side in structured binary blobs. 2. Indirection Texture: A compact 2D or 3D texture storing cache slot indices. Each texel corresponds to a logical brick coordinate in the pyramid and points to its current physical location (slot index) in the GPU page cache. 3. GPU Page Cache (Atlas): A fixed-size array of slots holding decompressed bricks. Default Size: 512 slots. Scalable Size: Up to 768^3 or 1024^3 slots for larger volumes or high-DPI screens. VRAM Footprint: Approximately 300 MB at 512 slots for 16-bit data, remaining fixed regardless of total dataset size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Split the source dataset into fixed-size bricks (64^3 logical, 66^3 physical). Generate downsampled LOD levels to create the brick pyramid. Compress the bricks and store the pyramid server-side. 2. Runtime Initialization: Initialize the GPU page cache with empty slots. Initialize the indirection texture (mapping logical coordinates to cache slots, initially invalid/null). 3. View Update and Fetching: Identify bricks relevant to the current camera view. For each relevant brick not currently in the cache: Fetch the compressed brick data from the server using HTTP range reads. Decompress the brick asynchronously in dedicated worker threads. Upload the decompressed brick to the GPU page cache. Update the indirection texture: map the logical brick coordinate to the new cache slot index. Cache Eviction: If the cache is full, evict the Least Recently Used (LRU) brick and update the indirection texture to mark the old logical coordinate as unmapped or pointing to a new slot if re-fetched. 4. Rendering (Compute Shader Ray Marching): For each pixel in the output image, cast a ray through the volume. For each sample point along the ray: Calculate the logical brick coordinate (Bx, By, Bz) containing the sample point. Sample the Indirection Texture at (Bx, By, Bz) to retrieve the cache slot index S. If S is valid: Calculate the local coordinates (Lx, Ly, Lz) within the brick. Perform density lookup and compositing using the data in cache slot S at local coordinates (Lx, Ly, Lz). If S is invalid (brick not in cache), skip compositing for this sample or use a coarse proxy value. Composite the accumulated color and opacity for the pixel. Formulas: Logical brick coordinate: B = \lfloor P / 64 \rfloor, where P is the world-space voxel coordinate. Local brick coordinate: L = P \mod 64. Physical interpolation padding: Bricks are stored as 66^3 to provide a 1-voxel halo for trilinear interpolation at brick boundaries. Parameters: Brick Logical Size: 64^3 voxels. Brick Physical Size: 66^3 voxels. Cache Slots: 512 (default), scalable to 768^3 or 1024^3. Render Scale: May need reduction (e.g., 0.25) on older/mobile GPUs to maintain 60 FPS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bandwidth Limitation: Volume ray marching is texture bandwidth intensive. Older or mobile GPUs may drop below 60 FPS at full resolution. Pre-processing Requirement: Raw volume files cannot be rendered directly; they must be pre-processed and compressed, adding an offline ingestion step and increasing total storage requirements by ~15–20%. Network Dependency: User experience is tied to internet connection quality. Lack of smart prefetching or offline capabilities means performance degrades with poor connectivity. Scalability Limit: Tested up to ~2048^3 voxels. Larger datasets require manual adjustment of indirection table dimensions and page cache size. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
