It sets itself apart from Out-of-core brick-based volume rendering by tightly integrating algorithm-specific prefetching with the ray casting traversal to ensure data is available exactly when needed, rather than relying on general-purpose disk prefetching or fixed memory budgets. Unlike program-driven approaches where the renderer controls the I/O, this method uses a dedicated prefetch thread that mirrors the ray caster's traversal logic to hide latency. Out-of-core bricking is a technique to create bricks of volumetric data along with a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the relative distance of each brick along a single view direction. Bricks are aligned with cropped subvolumes. A heuristic is used to evaluate the coherency of a series of data slices, which are parsed into a set of bricks sized for rendering hardware. Limitations: Requires pre-processing; storage overhead ~15-20%; dependent on network quality; no smart prefetching; limited tested scale (~2048³); texture bandwidth bound on GPUs. When to use: Interactive web-based visualization of large bioimaging or scientific datasets where VRAM is constrained and network bandwidth is sufficient. When not to use: Offline scenarios; datasets requiring immediate full-volume access without streaming latency; environments with very low-end GPUs lacking WebGPU support. name: I/O-Conscious Volume Rendering
head: Data-driven block-based volume rendering, I/O-Conscious Ray Casting, Prefetching ray casting, data-driven ray casting, out-of-core rendering, program-driven approach
body: I/O-Conscious Volume Rendering is an out-of-core rendering technique that minimizes end-to-end rendering time by overlapping disk I/O with rendering computation using a data-driven execution model where data blocks are accessed as indivisible units. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Out-of-core brick-based volume rendering, by tightly integrating algorithm-specific prefetching with the ray casting traversal to ensure data is available exactly when needed, rather than relying on general-purpose disk prefetching or fixed memory budgets. Unlike program-driven approaches where the renderer controls the I/O, this method uses a dedicated prefetch thread that mirrors the ray caster's traversal logic to hide latency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset stored on disk, decomposed into cubic macro-voxels of size B \times B \times B. Output: A 2D image (e.g., 128 \times 128 pixels). Data Structures: Macro-voxel: A cubic block of voxels stored contiguously on disk and fetched as an indivisible unit. Ray Group: A set of rays cast concurrently to exploit processing parallelism. Thread State: Two threads are used: one for ray casting and one for prefetching, chosen to minimize context switch overhead compared to processes. Parameters: Macro-voxel size (B): The dimension of the cubic block. B must be chosen such that prefetching rays spaced by B pixels cover the entire volume. Ray group size: Tested sizes include 128, 64, 32, and 16. Larger groups improve performance by increasing parallelism, outweighing state maintenance overhead. Sampling distance: Fixed at 1 along rays for both rendering and prefetching. Numbered Steps: 1. Decomposition: Decompose the volumetric dataset into 3D sub-cubes (macro-voxels) of size B \times B \times B, stored contiguously on disk. 2. Thread Initialization: Initialize two threads: a rendering thread and a prefetching thread. 3. Ray Group Casting: Cast a group of rays concurrently rather than one at a time to enable processing parallelism and reduce CPU idle time. 4. Prefetching Traversal: The prefetching module executes the same traversal code as the ray casting module to determine which macro-voxels to fetch. 5. Macro-voxel Check: During prefetching traversal, check if each sample on each ray steps into a new macro-voxel. 6. Disk Fetch: If a new macro-voxel is entered, fetch it from disk; otherwise, continue sampling along the ray. 7. Rendering: The rendering thread samples the volume using the fetched macro-voxels, ensuring a data block is completed exercised once brought into memory to achieve ideal overlap. 8. Optimization: Approximate floating-point computation with integer arithmetic without causing perceptible loss of quality. 9. Interpolation Optimization: Speed up address generation for the eight voxels used in tri-linear interpolation by exploiting fixed relationships among them. 10. Vectorization: Employ MMX instructions to execute multiple instructions simultaneously during computation. Formulas: Minimum End-to-End Time: T{\text{min}} = T{\text{fetch\first}} + T{\text{memory\resident}} Where T{\text{fetch\first}} is the time to fetch the first macro-voxel and T{\text{memory\resident}} is the time to render the dataset when completely memory-resident. Prefetching Ray Spacing: Ray origins for prefetching must be at most B pixels apart on the image plane, with sampling distance along rays remaining at 1, to ensure all macro-voxels are covered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getmacrovoxelid(x, y, z, B): """Calculate the unique ID for the macro-voxel containing (x, y, z).""" return (x // B, y // B, z // B) def fetchmacrovoxel(mvid): """Simulate blocking I/O to load a BxBxB macro-voxel from disk.""" # Blocks until the contiguous block is read from storage into memory pass def trilinearinterpolation(v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111, fx, fy, fz): """ Perform tri-linear interpolation. Integer arithmetic approximation exploits fixed relationships among 8 voxels """ return (v000 (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) + v100 fx(1-fy)(1-fz) + v010 (1-fx)fy(1-fz) + v110 fxfy(1-fz) + v001 (1-fx)(1-fy)fz + v101 fx(1-fy)fz + v011 (1-fx)fyfz + v111 fxfyfz) def raymarch(o, d, step, B, Dx, Dy, Dz, cache): """March a single ray, fetching macro-voxels and compositing.""" color, opacity = 0.0, 0.0 x, y, z = o currentmv = getmacrovoxelid(int(x), int(y), int(z), B) if currentmv not in cache: cache[currentmv] = fetchmacrovoxel(currentmv) while x >= 0 and x < Dx and y >= 0 and y < Dy and z >= 0 and z < Dz: fx, fy, fz = x % 1, y % 1, z % 1 # Extract 8 neighboring voxel values from the loaded macro-voxel cache voxels = [cache[currentmv][i] for i in range(8)] value = trilinearinterpolation(voxels, fx, fy, fz) alpha = 1.0 - value color += value (1.0 - opacity) opacity += alpha (1.0 - opacity) if opacity >= 1.0: break x += d[0] step y += d[1] step z += d[2] step nextmv = getmacrovoxelid(int(x), int(y), int(z), B) if nextmv != currentmv: if nextmv not in cache: cache[nextmv] = fetchmacrovoxel(nextmv) currentmv = nextmv return color, opacity def prefetchthread(B, W, H, Dx, Dy, Dz, cache): """Prefetch thread: casts rays spaced by B pixels with step 1 to detect boundaries.""" for y in range(0, H, B): for x in range(0, W, B): # Standard ray setup for pixel (x, y) o = (x, y, 0.0) d = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) raymarch(o, d, 1.0, B, Dx, Dy, Dz, cache) def renderthread(B, W, H, Dx, Dy, Dz, cache): """Rendering thread: casts all rays, compositing as it marches.""" for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # Standard ray setup for pixel (x, y) o = (x, y, 0.0) d = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) raymarch(o, d, 1.0, B, Dx, Dy, Dz, cache) def main(): B = 16 W, H = 128, 128 Dx, Dy, Dz = 128, 128, 128 cache = {} # Prefetch thread precedes rendering thread for each macro-voxel accessed prefetcher = threading.Thread(target=prefetchthread, args=(B, W, H, Dx, Dy, Dz, cache)) renderer = threading.Thread(target=renderthread, args=(B, W, H, Dx, Dy, Dz, cache)) prefetcher.start() renderer.start() renderer.join() prefetcher.join() Time Complexity: The minimum end-to-end time is T{\text{min}} = T{\text{fetch\first}} + T{\text{memory\resident}}. Memory Complexity: Insensitive to main memory size. Rendering times for a 256 \times 256 \times 256 dataset varied by less than 8% when memory capacity increased from 1MB to 16MB. Measured Performance: On a 300-MHz Pentium-II, rendering a 128 \times 128 \times 128 dataset to a 128 \times 128 image took an average of 1 second end-to-end (including disk I/O), compared to 0.68-1.0 seconds for memory-resident rendering and 0.33 seconds for disk retrieval. Scaling: Performance gain from parallelism outweighs state maintenance overhead as ray group size increases. Tested sizes: 128, 64, 32, 16. Strengths: Hides most disk I/O delay; insensitive to main memory size; data-driven approach is faster than program-driven approach (e.g., 1.10s vs 1.25s for 128^3 data). Limitations: Achieving ideal overlap between disk I/O and rendering computation is difficult in practice; implementation must ensure a data block is completed exercised once brought into memory. When to use: When rendering large volumetric datasets that do not fit in main memory on hardware with slow disk I/O, and when end-to-end latency is critical. When not to use: When datasets fit entirely in memory, or when compression is preferred over computation optimization. Origin: Developed by researchers investigating volume rendering on desktop personal workstations. Paper: "I/O-Conscious Volume Rendering" (2001). History: The work re-examined implementation strategies of ray casting, taking into account both computation and I/O overheads. It proposed a data-driven execution model to achieve maximum overlap between rendering computation and disk I/O. Usage: Used for out-of-core visualization of large-scale volumetric datasets where traditional in-core assumptions fail. name: Dynamic SDF Ray Marching with Structured Buffers
head: Procedural Geometry Ray Marching, SDF Ray Marching with Dynamic Object Buffers, SDF Ray Marching with GPU Buffers
body: This method renders dynamic, complex scenes by streaming object definitions from the CPU to the GPU in structured buffers, allowing for per-pixel evaluation of multiple objects without hardcoding the scene geometry in the shader. Unlike static SDF implementations where the scene is hardcoded in GLSL, this approach enables dynamic worlds with many moving characters and objects by replacing CPU-side ray termination logic with a GPU-side buffer of object structs that return a composite type (distance, color, ID) from the distance function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A subset of scene objects (culled from the full scene), passed as a structured buffer on the GPU. Each element defines the object's type, position, rotation, scale, and average color. Output: For each pixel, the final color and depth, derived from the closest object hit by the ray. Data Structures: 1. Render Input Buffer (GPU Structured Buffer): Layout: Array of ObjectDefinition structs. ObjectDefinition fields: id: Integer identifier (inferred from buffer index during search). type: Enum or integer indicating the SDF primitive type (e.g., sphere, box). position: float3 (world space position). rotation: float3 or quat (orientation). scale: float3 (uniform or non-uniform scaling). color: float3 (average/base color). 2. Distance Function Return Struct: Layout: struct { float distance; float3 color; int id; }. distance: The local signed distance to the object's surface. color: The color associated with the hit object. id: The ID of the object in the input buffer that produced this distance. Numbered Steps: 1. Culling: Cull the scene into a manageable subset of objects visible in the view frustum. Ray-marching performs automatic partial occlusion culling, and frustum/occlusion culling are partly automatic. 2. Buffer Preparation: Pass the subset of objects into a render input buffer on the CPU. Create a typed buffer (e.g., C-style struct) where each element defines the object's function type, position, rotation, scale, and average color. 3. Upload: Transfer the buffer to the GPU if it is not already present. 4. Ray Marching Loop (Per Pixel): Initialize ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. For each iteration k: Buffer Search: Perform a per-step search through the input buffer to evaluate which item is closest to the current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Transform Application: Apply transforms to either the rays (inverting figure rotations before GPU upload) or the distance functions (moving function origin for position changes, adjusting side lengths for scale changes). The simplest approach is to modify the rays before passing them to the core distance function. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF for each object. The distance function returns a complex type (struct) containing the local distance, local color, and an ID tied to the input buffer element. ID Inference: The ID is inferred from the loop counter of the buffer search, as the mapping function loops through the input buffer to find the closest figure. Color Determination: Determine the color from the average color of the buffer element corresponding to the ID, or procedurally (e.g., mapping iteration count to a palette weighted towards the stored average). Step Size: Use the minimum distance found across all objects in the buffer as the step size for the next iteration. Termination: If the minimum distance < \epsilon (convergence threshold), the ray has hit the closest object. Terminate the loop. 5. Shading: Pass the output color directly to the screen or into lighting code based on the collision point and the returned ID/color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vec3sub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def vec3len(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) class ObjectDefinition: def init(self, objid, objtype, position, rotation, scale, color): self.id = objid self.type = objtype self.position = position self.rotation = rotation self.scale = scale self.color = color class SDFResult: def init(self, distance, color, objid): self.distance = distance self.color = color self.id = objid def sdfsphere(p, center, radius): return vec3len(vec3sub(p, center)) - radius def evaluateobjectsdf(p, obj): # Transform point to local object space # Rotation transformation omitted; apply inverse rotation matrix to localp localp = [(p[i] - obj.position[i]) / obj.scale[i] for i in range(3)] dist = float('inf') if obj.type == 0: # Sphere dist = sdfsphere(localp, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 1.0) elif obj.type == 1: # Box d = [abs(localp[0]) - 1.0, abs(localp[1]) - 1.0, abs(localp[2]) - 1.0] dist = max(d[0], max(d[1], d[2])) return SDFResult(distance=dist, color=obj.color, objid=obj.id) def raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, objects, maxsteps=64, epsilon=0.001, maxdist=100.0): t = 0.0 hitcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(maxsteps): currentpos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] minresult = SDFResult(distance=float('inf'), color=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], objid=-1) for i in range(len(objects)): obj = objects[i] result = evaluateobjectsdf(currentpos, obj) if result.distance < minresult.distance: minresult = result if minresult.distance < epsilon: hitcolor = minresult.color break elif t > maxdist: break t += minresult.distance return hitcolor Parameters: Transform Strategy: Either transform rays (requires inverting rotations on CPU) or transform distance functions (adjust origin for position, side lengths for scale). Color Generation: Can use average color from buffer element or procedural color weighted towards stored average. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The method requires a per-step search through the input buffer for every ray iteration, which can be computationally expensive compared to static scenes. Precision: Transforming points to local space for SDF evaluation requires careful handling of rotation and scale to avoid precision issues, especially with large scenes or extreme scales. Buffer Size: The number of objects in the buffer directly impacts performance. Culling is essential to keep the buffer size manageable. Defines the basic building blocks (spheres, boxes, etc.) used in the buffer. SDF Primitive Definitions Details on how to apply rotation and scale to objects in the buffer. Deformation and Transformation Handling Techniques to reduce the cost of the per-step buffer search. Acceleration and Optimization Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) per pixel, where N is the number of objects in the buffer and M is the number of ray-marching steps. This is significantly slower than static SDF rendering where N is effectively constant or hardcoded. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the structured buffer on the GPU. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Dynamic scenes, easy to add/remove objects, no need to recompile shaders for scene changes. Not given in the sources. Limitations: Performance degrades linearly with the number of objects. Not suitable for very large numbers of objects without additional acceleration structures (e.g., BVH, which is not covered in the basic structured buffer approach). Not given in the sources. When to Use: Real-time rendering of dynamic scenes with a moderate number of objects where procedural geometry is desired. Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Scenes with thousands of objects, or where maximum performance is critical and the scene is static. Not given in the sources. This method was described in the context of implementing Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching for dynamic worlds, specifically addressing how to stream objects to the GPU and handle multiple colors without hardcoding the scene in GLSL. It is used in procedural geometry engines and real-time SDF rendering, such as in the Claybook engine. The approach leverages GPU structured buffers (or equivalent typed buffers in HLSL/GLSL) to pass complex object data to the shader, allowing the distance function to return a composite type including distance, color, and ID. name: Naive SDF Raymarching with Brute-Force Sphere SDF
head: Flat Array SDF Evaluation, Unoptimized Sphere SDF Raymarching
body: This method renders a scene of spheres by evaluating the Signed Distance Field (SDF) for every sphere in a flat GPU buffer per fragment and returning the minimum distance to find the closest surface. It differs from its parent Dynamic SDF Ray Marching with Structured Buffers by skipping spatial acceleration structures (like trees or BVHs) and structured buffer optimizations, instead performing a linear scan over all sphere definitions in the fragment shader. This approach is chosen for its implementation simplicity and suitability for scenes with a small, dynamic number of spheres, trading performance for code clarity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A flat buffer containing numsdfspheres sphere definitions. Each sphere has a color (Vec4), center (Vec3), and radius (f32). Input: Ray origin (camera position) and ray direction (computed in vertex shader). Output: Fragment color (sphere color modulated by diffuse lighting). Data Structures: The sphere data is stored in a flat array SdfBuffer: 1. numspheres: u32, the count of spheres. 2. sdfs: Vec<SdfSphere>, an array of sphere structs. SdfSphere layout: color: Vec4 (RGBA). center: Vec3 (XYZ). radius: f32. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Setup: In the vertex shader, compute the initial ray direction: \text{Initial\Ray\Direction} = \text{normalize}(\text{world\position}.xyz - \text{Position}.xyz) where \text{world\position} = \text{Model} \times \text{vec4}(\text{Vertex\Position}, 1.0) and \text{Position} is the camera position. 2. SDF Evaluation Loop: In the fragment shader, iterate through all spheres to find the minimum distance: Initialize mindist to 10000.0. For each sphere i from 0 to \text{num\sdf\spheres} - 1: Compute distance: di = \| \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}i \| - ri, where \mathbf{p} is the current point (ray origin), \mathbf{c}i is the sphere center, and ri is the radius. If di < \text{min\dist}, update \text{min\dist} = di and store the closest sphere index. 3. Normal Calculation: Compute the surface normal at the ray origin using central finite differences with step h = 0.0001 and kernel k = \text{vec2}(1, -1): \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}\left( kx \cdot \text{sdSphere}(\mathbf{p} + kx \cdot h \cdot \mathbf{e}x, r{\text{closest}}) + ky \cdot \text{sdSphere}(\mathbf{p} + ky \cdot h \cdot \mathbf{e}y, r{\text{closest}}) + kz \cdot \text{sdSphere}(\mathbf{p} + kz \cdot h \cdot \mathbf{e}z, r{\text{closest}}) \right) Note: The source formula uses a specific kernel application k.xyy, k.yyx, etc., which implies a weighted sum of directional derivatives. The standard central difference for gradient \nabla f at \mathbf{p} is \frac{f(\mathbf{p}+h\mathbf{e}i) - f(\mathbf{p}-h\mathbf{e}i)}{2h}. The source code snippet k.xyy sdSphere(...) suggests a specific implementation detail where k components are used as weights or signs for the finite difference approximation. 4. Lighting: Calculate diffuse intensity: I = \max(0, \text{dot}(\text{normalize}(-\text{ray\origin}), \mathbf{n})) 5. Output: Return \text{color}{\text{closest}} \times I. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. H = 0.0001 K = vec2(1.0, -1.0) # Kernel for finite differences INFDIST = 10000.0 def sdsphere(p: vec3, center: vec3, radius: f32) -> f32: return length(p - center) - radius def getnormal(p: vec3, center: vec3, radius: f32) -> vec3: # Central finite differences # Note: Source uses specific kernel application. Standard central diff: # gradx = (sd(p + hex) - sd(p - hex)) / (2h) # The source snippet: k.xyy sdSphere((point + k.xyy h) - center, radius) # implies a direct weighted sum. We implement the standard central difference # for clarity and correctness, as the source's specific kernel usage is ambiguous # without the exact vector component mapping. eps = H dx = sdsphere(p + vec3(eps, 0.0, 0.0), center, radius) - sdsphere(p - vec3(eps, 0.0, 0.0), center, radius) dy = sdsphere(p + vec3(0.0, eps, 0.0), center, radius) - sdsphere(p - vec3(0.0, eps, 0.0), center, radius) dz = sdsphere(p + vec3(0.0, 0.0, eps), center, radius) - sdsphere(p - vec3(0.0, 0.0, eps), center, radius) return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz) / (2.0 eps)) def renderfragment(rayorigin: vec3, spheres: list[SdfSphere]) -> vec4: mindist = INFDIST closestidx = -1 # Brute-force loop over all spheres for i in range(len(spheres)): sphere = spheres[i] dist = sdsphere(rayorigin, sphere.center, sphere.radius) # Floating point comparison instability mitigation # Using a small epsilon for comparison stability if dist < mindist - 1e-6: mindist = dist closestidx = i if closestidx == -1: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Background color closestsphere = spheres[closestidx] # Calculate normal at the ray origin (point on surface approximation) # Note: The ray origin is the camera position. The normal is calculated # at the point on the sphere closest to the ray origin. # However, the source calculates normal at 'point' which is the ray origin. # This implies the ray origin is assumed to be on or very close to the surface, # or the normal is approximated at the camera position relative to the sphere. # Given the context of "raymarching", usually we march along the ray. # But this "naive" method seems to evaluate the SDF at the ray origin directly # for a single-hit or billboard-like effect, or assumes the ray origin is the surface point. # Based on source: "computes the normal at the ray origin" normal = getnormal(rayorigin, closestsphere.center, closestsphere.radius) # Diffuse lighting # Light direction is assumed to be -rayorigin (light at camera?) or normalized ray direction? # Source: dot(normalize(-rayorigin), normal) lightdir = normalize(-rayorigin) intensity = max(0.0, dot(lightdir, normal)) return closestsphere.color intensity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Point Instability: Direct comparison of floats can be unstable. Mitigated by a custom CmpFloat wrapper using partialcmp with unwrapor(Ordering::Equal). Ray Origin on Surface: The normal calculation assumes the ray origin is close to the sphere surface. If the ray origin is far away, the finite difference normal at the origin will be incorrect for the actual intersection point. This method is likely intended for simple visualizations or specific camera positions rather than full raymarching with multiple bounces. Performance: Linear scan O(N) per fragment. Not suitable for large N. Time Complexity: O(N) per fragment, where N is the number of spheres. No acceleration structure build time. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the flat buffer. Performance: Suitable for small scenes (N < 100). Performance degrades linearly with sphere count. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structures, easy to debug, dynamic sphere addition/removal is trivial. Limitations: Poor scalability, no support for complex geometry beyond spheres, no shadowing/reflections beyond basic diffuse lighting. When to Use: Prototyping, educational purposes, or scenes with very few dynamic spheres. When Not to Use: Large scenes, complex geometries, or when performance is critical. This technique is part of an attempt to create a game-ready SDF and raymarching-based graphics engine built on a traditional rasterization pipeline. It leverages the work of Inigo Quilez on performant SDFs. name: RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing
head: RBF volume rendering, SPH volume rendering, Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) volume rendering
body: RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing renders volumetric particle data by modeling the scene as a continuous scalar field composed of additive weighted radial basis functions (RBFs), specifically Gaussians. It solves the visual clutter and pathological BVH performance issues of overlapping splatted particles by treating the volume as a unified field, enabling full path tracing through integration into a volume sampling kernel API. The method builds on Distance-field ray marching. Inputs: Particle dataset: N particles, each defined by position \mathbf{x}i, radius ri, and weight wi. Rendering parameters: radiusSupportFactor (\sigma, default 3), clampMaxCumulativeValue (optional threshold). Transfer functions: Color map C(\cdot) and opacity map \alpha(\cdot) mapping scalar field values to color and extinction. Ray: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \omega. Outputs: Radiance L(0, \omega) along the ray. 1. Particle Volume: Arrays of size N: positions (\mathbb{R}^3), radii (\mathbb{R}), weights (\mathbb{R}). 2. BVH: Built using Embree. Leaf nodes: Each leaf corresponds to a single particle. Node bounds: Determined by the particle's base radius multiplied by radiusSupportFactor (\sigma ri). Value Ranges: Each node stores the minimum and maximum scalar field values \Phi achievable within its bounding volume. These are estimated during preprocessing. 1. Preprocessing: a. BVH Construction: Build a BVH over the N particles. The bounding box for particle i is expanded by a factor of \sigma (default 3) to account for the Gaussian kernel's support. b. Value Range Estimation: For each leaf node (particle i), evaluate the RBF field \Phi on a small grid (e.g., 10^3 points) within the support radius \sigma ri. Determine the local minimum and maximum values for that leaf. Propagate these ranges up the tree to update interior node ranges. Store the global minimum and maximum values for the entire dataset. Estimate \sigma{t,\max}, the maximum extinction coefficient along the ray, using these ranges or manual specification. 2. Ray Marching Loop (per pixel): a. Initialize: Set accumulated radiance L{acc} = 0, optical depth \tau = 0, and current ray distance t{curr} = 0. b. Sample Distance: Sample distance t using the Delta Tracking formula with \sigma{t,\max}. c. Compute Position: Compute sample position \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + t\omega. d. Evaluate Field: i. Traverse BVH to find all particles whose support radius intersects \mathbf{x}. ii. For each intersecting particle i, compute di(\mathbf{x}). iii. If di(\mathbf{x}) < \sigma ri, compute \phii(\mathbf{x}) = wi e^{-\frac{1}{2}(di(\mathbf{x})/ri)^2}. iv. Accumulate \Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \sum \phii(\mathbf{x}). v. If clampMaxCumulativeValue is set and \Phi(\mathbf{x}) exceeds it, clamp \Phi(\mathbf{x}) to this value and stop summing further particles. e. Apply Transfer Function: i. Compute \sigmat = \alpha(\Phi(\mathbf{x})). ii. Compute L^e = C(\Phi(\mathbf{x})). f. Check Virtual Event: i. Generate \xi \in [0, 1). If \xi < 1 - \sigmat/\sigma{t,\max}, the event is virtual; continue loop without advancing t{curr}. ii. If accepted, update accumulated radiance: L{acc} \leftarrow L{acc} + e^{-\tau} \cdot \sigmae L^e / \sigma{t,\max}. iii. Update optical depth: \tau \leftarrow \tau + \sigmat \cdot t. iv. Advance ray: t{curr} \leftarrow t{curr} + t. 3. Return L{acc}. 1. RBF Scalar Field The scalar field \Phi(\mathbf{x}) at query point \mathbf{x} is the sum of Gaussian kernels from all contributing particles i: \Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \sumi \phii(di(\mathbf{x})) where di(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\| is the distance from particle center \mathbf{x}i. 2. Gaussian Kernel The kernel for particle i with weight wi and radius ri is: \phii(\mathbf{x}) = wi e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{di(\mathbf{x})}{ri}\right)^2} The kernel is truncated at a support radius of \sigma ri. Outside this radius, the contribution is zero. 3. Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) Assuming non-scattering media (\sigmas = 0), the RTE simplifies to: L(0, \omega) = \int0^\infty T(0, t) \cdot \sigmae(t) L^e(t, \omega) dt where T(0, t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \sigmat(s) ds\right) is the transmittance, \sigmae(t) is the emission coefficient, and \sigmat(t) is the extinction coefficient. 4. Transfer Function Application The emission and extinction coefficients are derived from the scalar field \Phi(t) evaluated along the ray: L^e(t, -\omega) = L^e(C(\Phi(t)), -\omega) T(t, -\omega) = T(\alpha(\Phi(t)), -\omega) Where C is a color map and \alpha is an opacity/extinction map. 5. Delta Tracking (Woodcock Tracking) To sample distances unbiasedly in the non-homogeneous medium defined by \Phi(t): Sample a distance t to the next event: t = -\frac{\ln(1-\xi)}{\sigma{t,\max}} where \xi \in [0, 1) is a uniform random number. Evaluate \sigmat(t) at the sampled point. Reject the event as "virtual" with probability: P[\text{virtual}] = 1 - \frac{\sigmat(t)}{\sigma{t,\max}} If rejected, sample a new distance t from the current position and repeat. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rbfvolumepathtrace(rayorigin, raydirection, bvh, particles, transferfunc, sigmatmax, clampmax, radiussupportfactor=3.0, maxtransmittancethreshold=1e-4): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 bvh: BVH structure built on particles particles: list of {position, radius, weight} transferfunc: function(phi) -> (sigmat, emissioncolor) sigmatmax: float, maximum extinction coefficient clampmax: float, optional clamp for accumulated phi radiussupportfactor: float, kernel truncation multiplier maxtransmittancethreshold: float, ray termination threshold """ accumulatedradiance = 0.0 opticaldepth = 0.0 tcurrent = 0.0 while True: if exp(-opticaldepth) < maxtransmittancethreshold: break # 1. Sample distance using Delta Tracking xi = uniform(0.0, 1.0) tstep = -log(1.0 - xi) / sigmatmax tsample = tcurrent + tstep # 2. Evaluate Scalar Field Phi at sample point samplepos = rayorigin + tsample raydirection phivalue = evaluaterbffield(samplepos, bvh, particles, clampmax, radiussupportfactor) # 3. Apply Transfer Function sigmat, emissioncolor = transferfunc(phivalue) # 4. Check for Virtual Event acceptanceprob = sigmat / sigmatmax if uniform(0.0, 1.0) < acceptanceprob: # Event is real transmittance = exp(-opticaldepth) accumulatedradiance += transmittance emissioncolor / sigmatmax opticaldepth += sigmat tstep tcurrent = tsample # If virtual, loop continues and samples a new distance from current position return accumulatedradiance def evaluaterbffield(samplepos, bvh, particles, clampmax, radiussupportfactor): phi = 0.0 candidates = bvh.traverse(samplepos) for particle in candidates: delta = samplepos - particle.position distsq = dot(delta, delta) radiussq = particle.radius particle.radius supportradiussq = (radiussupportfactor particle.radius) 2 if distsq < supportradiussq: val = particle.weight exp(-0.5 distsq / radiussq) phi += val if clampmax > 0.0 and phi >= clampmax: phi = clampmax break return phi radiusSupportFactor (\sigma): Multiple of base particle radius for BVH bounds and kernel truncation. Default: 3. Smaller values improve performance but may cause truncation artifacts. clampMaxCumulativeValue: Threshold for accumulated \Phi. If exceeded, evaluation terminates early. Useful in regions of high overlap to preserve contours at the cost of dynamic range. Overlapping Particles: In splatting, overlapping particles cause visual clutter and BVH performance issues. RBF volume rendering handles this by treating the volume as a continuous field. \sigma{t,\max} Estimation: Worst-case complexity O(N) for value estimation. Costly for large datasets. It is only necessary for small datasets with unpredictable overlap or if the user cannot guess the cumulative maximum. For large datasets, manual specification of clampMaxCumulativeValue is recommended to skip preprocessing. Truncation Artifacts: Setting radiusSupportFactor too low can cause visible artifacts where the Gaussian kernel is abruptly cut off. Time Complexity: The preprocessing step for value estimation has worst-case time complexity O(N), where N is the number of particles. Performance: Allows interactive rendering of hundreds of millions of particles at high resolution (e.g., 4000) without simplification or proxy geometry. Strengths: Handles overlapping particles without visual clutter. Supports full path tracing (unlike previous RBF implementations restricted to ray casting). Adjustable smoothing/sharpening via kernel radius and weight. Analytical derivatives available for shading. Limitations: Value estimation for \sigma{t,\max} can be costly for large, complex datasets. Requires careful tuning of radiusSupportFactor to balance performance and artifact avoidance. RBF volume rendering is frequently referred to as a Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) approach due to its use in visualizing SPH fluid dynamics codes. The method was implemented in Intel OSPRay and the Open Volume Kernel Library (VKL) using ISPC. It builds on the Woodcock-tracking volume path tracer of Raab and integrates RBF reconstruction into a volume sampling kernel API, leveraging interval iterators for space skipping. The approach addresses limitations of earlier RBF implementations that were restricted to ray casting. Path Tracing RBF Particle Volumes, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4842-7185-844, fetched 2026-10-25 (book)

name: Sphere Tracing and Step Rules
head: Ray Marching, Distance Field Ray Marching
body: Sphere tracing is a geometric method for rendering implicit surfaces by iteratively stepping along a ray using the distance to the nearest surface as the step size. It solves the problem of rendering complex, continuous geometry without explicit polygonal meshes by leveraging the mathematical guarantee that the Signed Distance Function (SDF) provides a lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface. It differs from its siblings, such as FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration and Coarse-to-Fine Sphere Tracing, by relying on the exact Lipschitz property of the SDF for step sizing rather than hierarchical acceleration structures or multi-resolution sampling strategies. The method operates on the principle that a Signed Distance Function f(\mathbf{p}) provides a lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface. For any point \mathbf{p} in space, f(\mathbf{p}) returns the shortest Euclidean distance to the implicit surface, with a sign indicating position: f(\mathbf{p}) < 0 inside, f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 on the surface, and f(\mathbf{p}) > 0 outside. The core algorithm, known as sphere tracing, proceeds as follows for each pixel: 1. Ray Definition: A ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. 2. Initialization: The accumulated distance t is initialized to 0 (or a near-plane value). 3. Marching Loop: Evaluate the scene SDF at the current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to get the distance d = f(\mathbf{p}). Termination Check: If d < \epsilon (a small convergence threshold, e.g., 0.001), the ray has hit the surface. If t > t{max} (maximum ray distance), the ray has escaped. Step: Advance the ray by the distance value: t \leftarrow t + d. This step size is guaranteed not to penetrate the surface because the SDF satisfies the Lipschitz condition with constant 1. 4. Shading: Upon hit, compute surface properties (normal, color) and lighting. Scene composition is typically achieved by combining primitive SDFs using Boolean operations: Union is \min(d1, d2), Intersection is \max(d1, d2), and Subtraction is \max(-d1, d2). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} to the local space of the primitive via M^{-1}\mathbf{p} before evaluation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, maxsteps, maxdistance, epsilon): """ Core sphere tracing algorithm. Args: rayorigin: Camera origin (vec3) raydirection: Normalized ray direction (vec3) sdf: Signed Distance Function callable sdf(p) maxsteps: Maximum number of iterations maxdistance: Maximum ray travel distance epsilon: Convergence threshold for surface hit Returns: hitdistance: Distance along ray to surface, or None hitpoint: 3D position of hit, or None """ t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdistance: break p = rayorigin + t raydirection d = sdf(p) if d < epsilon: return t, p t += d return None, None This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by computing valid Sphere Distance Bounds (SDB) and adaptive step sizes using a dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) derived from the FBM structure itself. It reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness, by progressively evaluating octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach supports features like Adaptive Lipschitz constants, Sub-stepping, Early Stop+k, and Quadratic Taylor inclusion functions. This method extends standard sphere tracing to render scenes composed of primitive shapes, character segments (letters), and arcs using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex geometric text and decorative arcs alongside standard diffuse geometry by treating them as distinct hit types with specialized distance queries and normal estimation. Unlike standard sphere tracing which typically handles uniform primitives, this approach integrates a composite SDF evaluation that prioritizes character and arc geometry when the ray is near a surrounding bounding box, and employs variance-based adaptive sampling to converge path-traced lighting. Non-Linear Sphere Tracing (NLST) is a rendering method for directly visualizing deformed Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) without converting them to explicit meshes. It solves the incompatibility between standard sphere tracing and non-linear deformation techniques (such as Linear Blend Skinning or Free-Form Deformations), which invalidate the Euclidean distance metric required for safe stepping. Unlike meshing approaches like Marching Cubes, NLST maintains infinite resolution and sharp features, and unlike methods requiring inverse deformations, it works with general forward deformation functions by integrating the ray path as a curve in object space. This family defines the logic for determining the distance \Delta t to advance a ray along its direction \mathbf{d} and the conditions under which the marching loop terminates. It solves the problem of balancing rendering accuracy (avoiding missed geometry or aliasing) against computational cost (minimizing samples in empty space). It is distinguished from Sphere Tracing by relaxing the strict Lipschitz safety constraint (\Delta t \le f(\mathbf{p})) in favor of heuristic, error-based, or geometric bounds that allow larger steps in safe regions, and from Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by dynamically varying \Delta t per sample rather than using a global constant. Coarse-to-fine sphere tracing is an acceleration strategy for rendering deep implicit signed distance functions (SDFs) that reduces computational cost by initializing ray marching at a lower resolution and progressively refining it. It differs from standard single-resolution sphere tracing by leveraging the spatial coherence of nearby rays; since neighboring rays often traverse similar paths, information from coarse passes allows fine-resolution rays to start closer to the surface, significantly reducing the number of SDF evaluations required for convergence. Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit is a deferred rendering technique that extends standard sphere tracing by tracking two distinct hit points per pixel: a primary surface hit (the nearest geometric intersection) and a represent hit (a proxy for the surface at the pixel's radius). This dual-pass approach is designed to handle transparency and aliasing artifacts at object edges by evaluating visibility and occlusion from both points and selecting the ray with greater visual impact (higher alpha). It differs from standard sphere tracing by explicitly maintaining a "represent" state to capture edge information that would otherwise be missed by a single convergence check. Bidirectional sphere tracing is a robust surface extraction technique that mitigates the convergence failures of standard sphere tracing when rays miss surface edges or intersect surfaces non-orthogonally. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which relies on a single forward march that may stall or overshoot, this method uses forward and backward traces to narrow the candidate range of the surface position, then refines the zero-level set using additional solvers. It is distinct from FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration and Coarse-to-Fine Sphere Tracing by replacing the iterative step-size heuristic with a bounded search interval derived from two opposing traces. Relaxed sphere tracing is an acceleration technique for distance-field ray marching that increases the step size beyond the conservative SDF value to reduce iteration counts. It scales the step by a relaxation factor \omega, reverting to the standard safe step if the new sample indicates the ray has jumped over the surface (i.e., the unbounding spheres of consecutive steps are disjoint). It is distinguished from Enhanced Sphere Tracing by its simpler geometric assumption; while relaxed tracing uses a fixed scalar multiplier, enhanced tracing computes an optimal tangential step size for planar surfaces, offering superior convergence at the cost of higher per-step complexity. Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids renders volumetric clouds by tracing rays through a set of implicit surfaces (pseudo-spheroids) and sampling noise only within those volumes. It differs from general sphere tracing by explicitly managing a list of intersected cloud primitives, sorting them by depth, and using a distance-based Level of Detail (LOD) to vary step size, optimizing the trade-off between visual fidelity and computational cost. An optimization to eliminate unnecessary distance computations for collections of objects by using the triangle inequality to bound the distance to an object based on previous evaluations and ray traversal. An optimization using the triangle inequality to reduce unnecessary distance evaluations, particularly effective for large assortments of objects. If all primitives (e.g., 14 Bezier curves) are nearly equidistant from the eye, the triangle inequality does not significantly reduce unnecessary distance evaluations until sphere tracing has traversed much of each ray. For 9 spheres/plane, triangle inequality reduced execution time from 2:53 to 1:19 (46% relative time). For the zeno logo, triangle inequality reduced execution time from 26:29 to 19:23 (73% relative time). When combined with convexity, triangle inequality enhances ordinary sphere tracing by 60%. Get total number of rays N from raybundle.origins.shape[0]. Initialize empty list chunkcolors. Loop over chunks: for chunkstart in range(0, N, self.chunksize). Slice raybundle for current chunk: curraybundle = raybundle[chunkstart: chunkstart + self.chunksize]. Call parent forward method: curcolor = super().forward(sampler, implicitfn, curraybundle). Append color to list: chunkcolors.append(curcolor). Concatenate all chunk colors along dimension 0: color = torch.cat(chunkcolors, dim=0). Return concatenated color. chunksize: maximum number of rays processed in a single forward pass. The term "sphere tracing" and the geometric method for antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces were introduced in [Kay & Kajiya, 1986]. The method was presented as a geometric alternative to standard ray tracing, particularly suited for implicit surfaces defined by distance fields. It gained prominence for its ability to handle complex geometric modeling operations and its inherent support for antialiasing through symbolic prefiltering. (PDF) Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2792108SphereTracingAGeometricMethodfortheAntialiasedRayTracingofImplicitSurfaces, fetched 2026-10-27 Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Quadric Tracing
body:
Quadric tracing is a method to accelerate sphere tracing by precomputing an augmented distance field using quadric surfaces (second-degree algebraic surfaces) to bound or unbound scene geometry, reducing the number of Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluations. It solves the slowdown of sphere tracing near surfaces and with increasing scene complexity, where function evaluation time and convergence slow drastically. Unlike relaxed sphere tracing (which uses a scalar to determine step size and reverts if too large) or enhanced sphere tracing (which uses previous two radii to approximate planar surfaces), quadric tracing uses precomputed geometric bounds to accelerate convergence. It stops when the computed distance value dips below a threshold, switching to enhanced sphere tracing for final convergence. Inputs: A 3D grid of precomputed quadric parameters and SDF values; a ray defined by origin p0 and direction v (|v|2 = 1). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray. Data Structures: The accelerator data structure is a regular 3D grid. Each cell stores: Quadric of Revolution: 96 bits (3 floats). Defined relative to the grid point pc. The axis of revolution direction n \in \mathbb{R}^3 (|n|2 = 1) is multiplied by 2 + k to store the quadric parameters. The scalar parameter k \in [-1, 1] encodes the shape (eccentricity and curvature). SDF Value: 32 bits (1 float). A signed distance function value d stored for the cell. Total: 128 bits per cell. Preprocessing: For every cell in parallel on the GPU, starting from the quadric origin pc: 1. Shoot rays in N uniformly sampled directions vi (i = 1, \dots, N). 2. Sphere trace each ray pc + t vi until the surface or the bounding box is reached. 3. For each ray-surface intersection (xi, yi, zi):= pc + ti vi, compute the unique ki \in [-1, 1] value defining the quadric of revolution touching the surface at that point. Operate in the 2D plane defined by vi and normal n. Let q = (qx, qy) \in \mathbb{R}^2 be the rotated projection where n is the y-axis. Solve for k using the quadratic equation: qx^2 k^2 + (2 \operatorname{sgn}(qy) qy^2 - qy) k - qy^2 = 0 Select the smaller solution for ki. 4. To obtain the unbounding quadric within the cell, we need the narrowest candidate unbounding quadric region from all rays; therefore, k:= \min \{ki \mid i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\}. 5. Store the axis direction n (normalized gradient -
abla f(p)/|
abla f(p)|) scaled by 2+k, and the SDF value. Rendering: 1. For each evaluation point along the ray, query the closest grid cell to get k, n, and d. 2. Intersect the ray with the precomputed quadric to accelerate tracing convergence. 3. If the quadric intersection yields a valid step that does not skip the surface, take it. Otherwise, fall back to standard sphere tracing or enhanced sphere tracing. 4. Stop when the distance value dips below a threshold. Conic Section Definitions: The quadric is a revolution of a conic section. The conic section coefficients A, B, C are functions of k: A(k) = k^2, \quad B(k) = 2(k - 1/2), \quad C(k) = -k These define the implicit equation in the 2D plane (y-axis is axis of revolution): A \cdot x^2 + B \cdot y^2 + C \cdot y = 0 \quad (1) The polar parametrization of the conic section is s(t) = [\cos(t) \cdot r(t), \sin(t) \cdot r(t)]^T, where: r(t) =  rac{-C \cdot \sin(t)}{A \cdot \cos^2(t) + B \cdot \sin^2(t)} The interval L(k) restricts the parameter t to avoid unwanted hyperbola branches: L(k) =  egin{cases}  rac{\pi}{2}, & 	ext{if } A(k) \cdot B(k) \geq 0 \ \arctan\left(\sqrt{ rac{-A}{B}}ight), & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (k \in [-1, 1]) \quad (2) The implicit equation of the unbounding quadric of revolution in 3D (z-axis is axis of revolution) is: A \cdot (x^2 + y^2) + B \cdot z^2 + C \cdot z = 0 \quad (3) Ray-Quadric Intersection: Given ray p0 + t \cdot v (p0 = (x0, y0, z0), v = (vx, vy, vz)), substitute into (3) to solve at^2 + bt + c = 0: a = A \cdot vx^2 + A \cdot vy^2 + B \cdot vz^2 b = 2A \cdot x0 vx + 2A \cdot y0 vy + 2B \cdot z0 vz + C vz c = A \cdot (x0^2 + y0^2) + B \cdot z0^2 + C \cdot z0 Let roots be t1 \leq t2. If no real roots, I:= [-\infty, +\infty]. If 0 
eq |k| < 1/2 (hyperbolas), omit the unwanted branch: I:=  egin{cases} [-\infty, t2] & 	ext{if } (z0 + t1 vz) \cdot k < 0 \ [t1, +\infty] & 	ext{if } (z0 + t2 vz) \cdot k < 0 \end{cases} If none of the conditions apply, I remains as previously defined. Selecting Intersection t: Evaluate the following conditional assignments in order to find the first valid intersection t \geq 0: 1. t:= t2 if t1 = -\infty 2. t:= t1 if 0 < t2 < +\infty 3. t:= \infty if t1 < 0 4. t:= 0 if otherwise Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def intersectquadric(p0, v, A, B, C, k): # Quadratic coefficients for ray p0 + tv against A(x^2+y^2) + Bz^2 + Cz = 0 a = A (v.x2 + v.y2) + B v.z2 b = 2 A (p0.x v.x + p0.y v.y) + 2 B p0.z v.z + C v.z c = A (p0.x2 + p0.y2) + B p0.z2 + C p0.z # Solve quadratic equation if abs(a) < 1e-9: if abs(b) < 1e-9: return float('inf') t1 = -c / b t2 = float('inf') else: disc = b2 - 4 a c if disc < 0: t1 = float('-inf') t2 = float('inf') else: sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 # Omit unwanted hyperbola branch if |k| < 0.5 and k != 0 if abs(k) < 0.5 and k != 0: z1 = p0.z + t1 v.z z2 = p0.z + t2 v.z if z1 k < 0: t1 = float('-inf') if z2 k < 0: t2 = float('inf') # Select first valid intersection t >= 0 per source assignment order t = float('inf') if t1 == float('-inf'): t = t2 elif 0 < t2 < float('inf'): t = t1 elif t1 < 0: t = float('inf') else: t = 0 return t def quadrictrace(p0, v, grid, maxsteps=100, threshold=1e-4): """ Quadric tracing algorithm. grid.query(p) returns a cell struct with.A,.B,.C,.k,.d (SDF value). """ p = p0 for in range(maxsteps): cell = grid.query(p) d = cell.d if d < threshold: return p # Query quadric parameters for current cell A, B, C, k = cell.A, cell.B, cell.C, cell.k # Compute acceleration step from quadric intersection tq = intersectquadric(p, v, A, B, C, k) # Take quadric step if valid and does not skip the surface, else fall back to SDF step if tq > 0 and tq <= d: t = tq else: t = d p = p + t v return p # Non-convergence or max steps reached Combines regular or improved quadratic Taylor bounds with enhancements: Sub-stepping, ES+1, and Adaptive computation of \gamma{Fn}. Using k > 1 was never found to be faster when using quadratic bounds. On the Sponge scene with all enhancements, Linear bounds have 362.3 avg steps, 3815.0 avg octaves, 65.0 ms time. Regular Quad has 70.0 avg steps, 651.1 avg octaves, 16.3 ms time, offering a 	imes 4.0 speedup vs Linear and 	imes 6.7 speedup vs naive. On Sponge (far) scene, Linear (far) has 147.8 avg steps, 749.6 avg octaves, 16.7 ms time. Regular Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.8 ms time (	imes 1.7 vs Linear, 	imes 4.1 vs naive). Improved Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.7 ms time (	imes 1.7 vs Linear, 	imes 4.2 vs naive). With enhancements, quadratic bounds provide massive performance gains over linear bounds with same enhancements (	imes 4.0 and 	imes 1.7 speedups on test scenes) and 	imes 6.7 and 	imes 4.1 speedups over the naive method. Quadric tracing offers a 20% to 100% speedup in rendering static scenes. It amortizes the slowdown caused by the complexity of the geometry. The method takes much larger steps along the ray, often skipping several grid cells without skipping ray-surface intersections. However, sometimes the quadric does not contain the whole cell it is assigned to, so the acceleration is zero or negligible for some positions. About 20% of expensive signed distance function evaluations are saved. Quadric tracing was introduced to accelerate sphere tracing for implicit surfaces defined by signed distance functions (SDFs). Most implicit surface representations require conversion to a triangle list for efficient, real-time visualization, but distance-based representations allow sphere tracing to enable raytracing for the whole scene within milliseconds using the GPU. The representation supports set operations such as union, intersection, subtraction, and real-time offsets, allowing any CSG tree to be constructed from a large set of primitives. However, function evaluation time and convergence slow drastically with scene complexity. The method generalizes the unbounding sphere and separating plane approach to unbounding quadrics for any SDF. It is applicable to light visibility computation such as soft shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination, as well as room impulse response estimation and deep learning based implicit signed distance functions. A Geometric Method for Accelerated Sphere Tracing of Implicit Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.14232/actacyb.290007, fetched 2026-10-26 Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70072, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Raymarched SDF Volume Rendering
head: Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields, Raymarching Signed Distance Fields, SDF Raycasting, SDF Raymarching
body: Raymarched SDF Volume Rendering is a technique for rendering 3D scenes defined by implicit surfaces (Signed Distance Fields) without rasterizing triangle meshes. It solves the problem of displaying complex, procedural, or fractal geometry by casting rays from the camera and stepping along them using distance estimates provided by the SDF. Unlike traditional rasterization or standard ray tracing with explicit geometry, this method relies entirely on mathematical functions to define shape, offering infinite sharpness and precision for primitive-based SDFs, which is crucial for CAD and professional graphic design. The method renders a pixel by casting a ray into the scene and iteratively advancing it until it intersects a surface or escapes the scene. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, maximum ray distance t{max}, convergence threshold \epsilon, and the scene SDF function f(\mathbf{p}) which returns the signed distance to the nearest surface. Outputs: Pixel color (and optionally alpha) based on the hit surface's material and lighting, or background color if no hit occurs. Data Structures Ray: Defined as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where t is the distance along the ray. SDF Function: A procedural function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. For primitives, it returns the Euclidean distance. For example: Sphere: f(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\| - r. Box: f(\mathbf{p}) = \|\max(|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}| - \mathbf{s}, 0)\|. Scene Composition: Complex shapes are built using Boolean operations on primitive SDFs: Union: f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Intersection: f{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Subtraction: f{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), -f2(\mathbf{p})). Material ID (Optional): Some implementations return a vector where the x-component is the distance and the y-component is a material ID. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Construction: For each pixel, construct the ray direction \mathbf{d} from the camera basis vectors and pixel UV coordinates. The ray is defined as p(s) = o + s\,\hat{r}. 2. Initialization: Initialize the accumulated distance t = 0 (or near-plane value) and current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate up to a maximum number of steps N{max} (e.g., 64 or 130): Evaluate SDF: Compute d = f(\mathbf{p}). Termination Check: If d < \epsilon (e.g., 0.005 or 0.001), the ray has hit the surface. Break loop. If t > t{max} (e.g., 400.0), the ray has escaped. Break loop. Step: Advance the ray. The standard safe step is t \leftarrow t + d. However, some implementations use a conservative step size, such as t \leftarrow t + d \times 0.5, to prevent tunnelling through thin structures or due to non-rigid transforms. Update Position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 4. Shading: If a hit occurred (d < \epsilon): Normal Estimation: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} using finite differences (gradient of the SDF): \mathbf{n} = \frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|\nabla f(\mathbf{p})\|} Approximated numerically with epsilon \epsilon{grad} (e.g., 0.02): \mathbf{n} \approx \text{normalize}\left( \begin{bmatrix} f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon{grad}\hat{x}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon{grad}\hat{x}) \\ f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon{grad}\hat{y}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon{grad}\hat{y}) \\ f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon{grad}\hat{z}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon{grad}\hat{z}) \end{bmatrix} \right) Lighting: Compute diffuse lighting using the light direction \mathbf{l} and ambient light \mathbf{a}: \mathbf{C}{diffuse} = \mathbf{C}{light} \cdot \max(\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0) \mathbf{C}{final} = (\mathbf{C}{diffuse} + \mathbf{a} \cdot 2.0) \cdot \mathbf{C}{base} Fog: Apply exponential fog based on distance from camera dist = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}\|: f{fog} = e^{-dist \cdot \rho} \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{fog} \cdot (1 - f{fog}) + \mathbf{C}{final} \cdot f{fog} Alpha: Set alpha based on lighting or material properties (e.g., shadow transparency). 5. Background: If no hit occurred, return the background color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsdf(cameraorigin, cameradirection, maxsteps, maxdist, epsilon, sdffunc, stepscale=1.0, backgroundcolor=vec3(0.0)): """ Renders a single pixel using raymarched SDF. Args: cameraorigin (vec3): The position of the camera. cameradirection (vec3): The normalized direction vector for the pixel. maxsteps (int): Maximum number of marching iterations (e.g., 64 or 130). maxdist (float): Maximum ray distance (e.g., 400.0). epsilon (float): Convergence threshold for surface hit (e.g., 0.005). sdffunc (function): Function f(p) returning signed distance to nearest surface. stepscale (float): Multiplier for step size (1.0 standard, 0.5 conservative). backgroundcolor (vec3): Color returned if ray escapes. Returns: vec4: Final pixel color with alpha. """ t = 0.0 pos = cameraorigin for i in range(maxsteps): # Evaluate SDF at current position d = sdffunc(pos) # Check for surface hit if d < epsilon: break # Check for escape if t > maxdist: return vec4(backgroundcolor, 1.0) # Advance ray by safe distance t += d stepscale pos = cameraorigin + t cameradirection # If loop finished without break, check if we hit or escaped if d < epsilon: # Shading # 1. Compute Normal via Finite Differences epsgrad = 0.02 dx = vec3(epsgrad, 0.0, 0.0) dy = vec3(0.0, epsgrad, 0.0) dz = vec3(0.0, 0.0, epsgrad) gradx = sdffunc(pos + dx) - sdffunc(pos - dx) grady = sdffunc(pos + dy) - sdffunc(pos - dy) gradz = sdffunc(pos + dz) - sdffunc(pos - dz) normal = normalize(vec3(gradx, grady, gradz)) # 2. Lighting lightdir = normalize(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) lightcolor = vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) ambientcolor = vec3(0.2, 0.2, 0.2) diffuse = lightcolor max(dot(lightdir, normal), 0.0) finallight = diffuse + ambientcolor 2.0 basecolor = vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) color = basecolor finallight # 3. Fog distancefromcam = length(pos - cameraorigin) fogdensity = 0.1 fogcolor = vec3(0.8, 0.8, 0.8) fogfactor = exp(-distancefromcam fogdensity) outcolor = fogcolor (1.0 - fogfactor) + color fogfactor # 4. Alpha alpha = max(dot(lightdir, normal), 0.0) return vec4(outcolor, alpha) else: return vec4(backgroundcolor, 1.0) Parameters MARCHSTEPS: Maximum iterations. Typical values: 64, 130. epsilon: Convergence threshold. Typical values: 0.005, 0.001. maxdist: Maximum ray distance. Typical values: 400.0. focallength: Camera parameter. Typical value: 0.62. stepscale: Multiplier for step size. Typical value: 1.0, 0.5 (conservative). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Tunnelling: If the step size is too large or the SDF is not a true Euclidean distance (e.g., due to non-rigid transforms like wing flapping), rays may skip over thin geometry. Solution: Use conservative step sizes (e.g., 0.5 \times d) or increase iteration count. Precision: Primitive-based SDFs offer infinite sharpness, but numerical precision issues can arise with very small distances or large coordinate values. Clipping: The rendering quad must be positioned beyond the camera's near clipping plane (e.g., z=0.32 if near clip is 0.3). Layer Culling: In engine implementations, use separate cameras or layer masks to ensure the volume renders in the correct depth order relative to other scene elements. Renders fractals using iterative SDFs. Chosen when infinite self-similar detail is required, but suffers from normal noise and distance estimator inaccuracy at high zoom. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C), where N is the number of pixels and C is the average number of marching steps per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, as the scene is defined procedurally. This results in a reduced memory footprint compared to mesh-based rendering. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on GPU ALU capabilities rather than memory bandwidth, as pure mathematical SDFs are compute-bound. Modern GPUs have evolved to support this efficiently. Strengths: Infinite sharpness and precision for primitives; small memory footprint; easy to create complex procedural geometry and fractals; no need for mesh generation or UV unwrapping. Limitations: Thin structures may require conservative stepping, reducing performance; normal estimation via finite differences can be noisy for complex SDFs. When to Use: Demoscene, Shadertoy art, procedural content generation, fractal rendering, CAD visualization where precision is key. Origin: The concept of implicit surfaces using boolean operations (min/max) dates back to 1972 by A. Ricci and later B. Wyvill and G. Wyvill in 1989. History: The first mention of raymarching SDFs for rendering 3D fractals was in a paper by Sandin, Hart, and Kauffman, though they did not coin the term "SDF". C. Hart documented the technique in 1995, incorrectly calling it "Sphere Tracing". Modern SDFs: Modern SDFs, characterized by constraining the field to be a Euclidean Distance, were explored by Inigo Quilez starting in 2007, influenced by Alex Evan's 2006 work and Keenan Crane's 2005 work. Usage: The technique became popular in the demoscene and Shadertoy communities for art-directed content with sophisticated modeling, shading, and animation. It is also used at Pixar for procedural content and reduced memory footprint. el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) AJKKinney/Mandelbulb, https://github.com/AJKKinney/Mandelbulb, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Raymarching Distance Fields, https://iquilezles.org/articles/raymarchingdf/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Advanced shaders in Unity - Volume render a death star | Habrador, https://www.habrador.com/tutorials/shaders/1-volume-rendering-death-star/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Mandelbulb Sphere Tracing
head: Mandelbulb Fractal Rendering, Mandelbulb Ray Marching, Mandelbulb SDF Raymarching, Mandelbulb Tracing, mandelSphereTracing
body: Mandelbulb Sphere Tracing is a volume rendering technique that renders the Mandelbulb fractal by raymarching through 3D space using a specific Signed Distance Function (SDF) based on iterative spherical power operations. It differs from standard primitive sphere tracing by replacing simple geometric distance calculations with a computationally expensive iterative formula that approximates the fractal's boundary. Unlike recursive polyhedral fractals (e.g., Menger sponge) which have finite depth, the Mandelbulb possesses infinite self-similar detail, requiring adaptive iteration counts and suffering from increasing distance estimator inaccuracy and normal noise as the camera zooms in. Inputs: Camera position (Ox, Oy, Oz) and direction vectors (right, up, forward). Screen resolution (W, H) and pixel coordinates (x, y). Fractal parameters: power (exponent, typically 8), maxmarchdist (2000), hitthreshold (0.01). Iteration count per raymarch step: approximately 10. Outputs: Pixel color (RGB) based on surface hit, lighting, and shadows. Background color if no hit. Data Structures: minDistances[x][y][5]: A 3D array storing per-pixel data. Indices: [0] distance, [1] hit flag (0=light, 1=shadow), [2] R, [3] G, [4] B, [5] auxiliary value (e.g., for mu calculation). Vector3: Represents 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and camera offsets. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel (x, y), construct the ray origin P at the camera position and direction D based on screen coordinates, zoom, and view range. Initialize minDist to a large value. 2. Raymarching Loop: While minDist > hitthreshold (0.01) AND minDist < maxmarchdist (2000): a. Evaluate the Mandelbulb SDF at the current ray position P using distMandelBulb(P). b. If minDist <= hitthreshold, the ray has hit the surface. Break loop. c. Advance the ray position: P \leftarrow P + D \times \text{minDist}. d. Increment iteration counter. 3. Hit Processing: If minDist <= hitthreshold: a. Estimate surface normal N by sampling the SDF at four nearby points around P and computing the gradient. b. Apply lighting: Calculate diffuse component (dot product of N and light direction), ambient lighting, and soft shadows. c. Store color in minDistances[x][y]. 4. Miss Processing: If minDist > maxmarchdist or loop exits without hit: a. Store distance as 10000 and iteration count. b. Paint background color. Formulas: Mandelbulb Iteration: The core SDF calculation iterates the transformation: z{n+1} = zn^{\text{power}} + c Where z is a 3D vector represented in spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi). The "spherical power" operation raises the radius r to the power exponent and multiplies the angles \theta and \phi by the power. Specifically, for a point (x, y, z): 1. Convert to spherical coordinates: r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}, \theta = \arctan2(y, x), \phi = \arccos(z/r). 2. Apply power: r' = r^{\text{power}}, \theta' = \theta \times \text{power}, \phi' = \phi \times \text{power}. 3. Convert back to Cartesian: x' = r' \sin(\phi') \cos(\theta'), y' = r' \sin(\phi') \sin(\theta'), z' = r' \cos(\phi'). 4. Add constant c (usually the original pixel coordinate or a fixed offset). 5. Repeat for numiterations (approx. 10). Distance Estimator (Hubbard-Douady): The distance estimate d is derived from the iteration's escape behavior using the Hubbard-Douady distance estimator. It is an approximate lower bound. d \approx \frac{rn \ln rn}{|\frac{\partial zn}{\partial z0}|} Where rn is the magnitude of the final iterate and the denominator is the derivative of the iteration function with respect to the initial point, tracked during iteration. Note: Exact formula not provided in sources, described as "Hubbard-Douady distance estimator" using "escape behavior". Normal Estimation: N = \frac{\partial SDF}{\partial P} \approx \frac{SDF(P + \epsilon) - SDF(P - \epsilon)}{2\epsilon} Sampled at four nearby points to compute the gradient. o.x, self.y - o.y, self.z - o.z) def normalize(v): m = math.sqrt(v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2) return Vector3(v.x / m, v.y / m, v.z / m) if m > 0 else Vector3(0, 0, 0) def dot(a, b): return a.x b.x + a.y b.y + a.z b.z backgroundcolor = (0, 0, 0) def distmandelbulb(x, y, z, power=8, iterations=10): """Computes the approximate distance to the Mandelbulb fractal surface.""" r = math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) if r == 0: return 0.0 theta = math.atan2(y, x) phi = math.acos(z / r) dr = 1.0 for in range(iterations): r = pow(r, power) theta = power phi = power dr = power r x = r math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = r math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = r math.cos(phi) if dr == 0: return 2000.0 return (r math.log(r)) / dr def renderpixel(px, py, campos, camdir, power=8, maxmarch=2000, hitthresh=0.01): """Renders a single pixel of the Mandelbulb.""" raypos = campos raydir = camdir mindist = 0.0 hit = False for in range(1000): dist = distmandelbulb(raypos.x, raypos.y, raypos.z, power) if dist < hitthresh: hit = True mindist = dist break if dist > maxmarch: mindist = 10000.0 break raypos = raypos + raydir dist if hit: eps = 0.01 dx = distmandelbulb(raypos.x + eps, raypos.y, raypos.z, power) - distmandelbulb(raypos.x - eps, raypos.y, raypos.z, power) dy = distmandelbulb(raypos.x, raypos.y + eps, raypos.z, power) - distmandelbulb(raypos.x, raypos.y - eps, raypos.z, power) dz = distmandelbulb(raypos.x, raypos.y, raypos.z + eps, power) - distmandelbulb(raypos.x, raypos.y, raypos.z - eps, power) normal = normalize(Vector3(dx, dy, dz)) lightdir = normalize(Vector3(0, 1, 0)) diff = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) ambient = 0.2 return (int((diff + ambient) 255), int((diff + ambient) 255), int((diff + ambient) 255)) else: return backgroundcolor def renderchunk(starty, endy, campos, camdir, power=8): """Processes a horizontal strip of pixels.""" results = [] for y in range(starty, endy): for x in range(600): # Assuming fixed width for example color = renderpixel(x, y, campos, camdir, power) results.append((x, y, color)) return results Renders a recursive cube-based fractal. Unlike the Mandelbulb, it has finite depth at reasonable zoom levels, making distance estimation more stable and normals less noisy. Renders basic shapes (spheres, boxes) using exact distance formulas. Significantly faster than Mandelbulb as it avoids iterative calculations. Time Complexity: The Mandelbulb SDF call requires approximately 10 iterations of spherical power (involving trigonometric functions) plus derivative tracking per raymarch step. This is roughly 100x the work of a simple sphere SDF. Since the SDF is called dozens of times per pixel during raymarching, the total cost is thousands of math operations per pixel per frame. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storage for the image buffer and camera state. Measured Performance: Real-time rendering is possible on modern GPUs due to parallel pixel processing, but high-resolution or high-iteration renders are computationally expensive. Strengths: Can render complex, organic, infinitely detailed fractal structures that are impossible to model with polygons. Limitations: Approximate Distance: The Hubbard-Douady estimator is a lower bound, not exact. It can be loose, leading to smaller raymarch steps and higher GPU cost. Noise: Normal estimation amplifies noise because it computes differences between approximate SDF samples. Small numerical errors in distance become large errors in normals, causing bumpy shading artifacts. Zoom Limitations: As the camera zooms in, more iterations are needed, the distance estimator becomes less accurate, and normal estimation gets noisier, with no Level of Detail (LOD) fallback. When to Use: When rendering 3D fractals or implicit surfaces with infinite detail. When Not to Use: When high precision is required at close zoom levels, or when performance is critical and the geometry is simple. The Mandelbulb is a 3D generalization of the 2D Mandelbrot set, defined by iterating a "spherical power" operation. It was popularized in the demoscene and by graphics engineers like Inigo Quilez. The technique of rendering it via sphere tracing was implemented in projects such as haydenparker3/3D-Sphere-Tracing and AJKKinney/Mandelbulb. The method relies on the Hubbard-Douady distance estimator, which is an approximation suitable for fractals where exact distance calculation is intractable. haydenparker3/3D-Sphere-Tracing, https://github.com/haydenparker3/3D-Sphere-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) AJKKinney/Mandelbulb, https://github.com/AJKKinney/Mandelbulb, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density
head: Raymarching with a twist, Signed distance field (SDF) ray marching, Volumetric Raymarching
body: Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density adapts sphere tracing principles to render volumetric objects by treating the Signed Distance Function (SDF) as a density field rather than a surface boundary. Unlike standard sphere tracing which terminates upon surface intersection, this method marches through the object's interior using a constant step size, accumulating color and alpha based on the SDF's positive values. It enables the compact, procedural representation of intricate volumes like clouds or smoke without explicit voxelization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, a density function f(\mathbf{p}) derived from an SDF, maximum step count N{\text{max}}, constant step size s, and convergence threshold \epsilon. Outputs: Accumulated color C{\text{out}} and alpha \alpha{\text{out}}. Data Structures: Density Function f(\mathbf{p}): A scalar field where f(\mathbf{p}) > 0 inside the volume, f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 on the boundary, and f(\mathbf{p}) < 0 outside. Note that this is the negation of the standard SDF definition (f{\text{std}}(\mathbf{p}) = -f(\mathbf{p})). Parameters: MARCHSIZE (s): Constant step size. Typical value: 0.08. MAXSTEPS (N{\text{max}}): Maximum iterations. Typical value: 100. \epsilon: Small tolerance for convergence checks if used, though constant stepping often bypasses dynamic step sizing. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set accumulated distance t = 0, current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, and result color/alpha C{\text{res}} = (0,0,0,0). 2. Loop: For i from 0 to N{\text{max}}-1: a. Sample Density: Evaluate d = f(\mathbf{p}). b. Check Density: If d > 0: i. Compute sample color C{\text{sample}} and alpha \alpha{\text{sample}}. A simple mapping uses density directly for alpha: \alpha{\text{sample}} = d. Color is interpolated between white and black based on density: C{\text{sample}} = \text{mix}(\text{white}, \text{black}, d). ii. Apply lighting/attenuation if applicable (e.g., C{\text{sample}}.\text{rgb} = C{\text{sample}}.\text{a}). iii. Front-to-Back Blending: Update result: C{\text{res}} = C{\text{res}} + C{\text{sample}} \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{res}}) \alpha{\text{res}} = \alpha{\text{res}} + \alpha{\text{sample}} \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{res}}) c. Step: Advance ray: t \leftarrow t + s, \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. 3. Return: C{\text{res}} and \alpha{\text{res}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetricraymarchsdfdensity(rayorigin, raydirection, densityfunc, maxsteps=100, marchsize=0.08): """ Renders a volume using SDF density with constant step marching. Args: rayorigin: vec3, camera origin raydirection: vec3, normalized ray direction densityfunc: callable, returns positive value inside volume, 0 on boundary, negative outside maxsteps: int, maximum number of march steps marchsize: float, constant step size (default 0.08) Returns: vec4: Accumulated color (RGB) and alpha (A) """ t = 0.0 p = rayorigin + t raydirection rescolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] resalpha = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): # Sample density from the SDF-derived function # Note: The function must return positive values inside the volume density = densityfunc(p) if density > 0.0: # Map density to color and alpha # Simple example: White to Black based on density # Alpha is directly proportional to density alphasample = density # Interpolate color: mix(white, black, density) # In Python-like logic: color = white (1 - density) + black density # Assuming density is normalized or scaled appropriately r = 1.0 (1.0 - density) + 0.0 density g = 1.0 (1.0 - density) + 0.0 density b = 1.0 (1.0 - density) + 0.0 density samplecolor = [r, g, b] # Attenuate color by alpha (as per source) samplecolor[0] = alphasample samplecolor[1] = alphasample samplecolor[2] = alphasample # Front-to-back blending # Cres = Cres + Csample (1 - alphares) # alphares = alphares + alphasample (1 - alphares) weight = 1.0 - resalpha rescolor[0] += samplecolor[0] weight rescolor[1] += samplecolor[1] weight rescolor[2] += samplecolor[2] weight resalpha += alphasample weight # Constant step advancement t += marchsize p = rayorigin + t raydirection return rescolor + [resalpha] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Density Scaling: The SDF must be transformed to return positive values inside the volume. Standard SDFs return negative values inside. Step Size: Using a constant step size ignores the Lipschitz property of the SDF for stepping, potentially leading to aliasing or missed thin features if s is too large. Uses a cone-shaped volume and SDFs for light shafts, differing by operating in screen space on pre-computed textures and tapering from light sources. Time Complexity: O(N{\text{max}}) per ray, where N{\text{max}} is the maximum number of steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as it is procedural and does not store voxel grids. Performance: Efficient for real-time rendering of procedural volumes like clouds or smoke. Performance depends heavily on N{\text{max}} and s. Strengths: No precomputation or voxelization required; watertight traversal; compact representation. Limitations: Constant step size may cause aliasing in thin features; less efficient than adaptive sphere tracing for surface rendering. Originating from the adaptation of sphere tracing to volumetric rendering, this method leverages the continuous nature of SDFs to encode density. It gained popularity through real-time shader communities, notably Shadertoy scenes by Inigo Quilez and others, for rendering procedural clouds and smoke.
