body: Volumetric Light Shafts (Cone Raymarching) is a real-time post-processing technique that renders volumetric light shafts by raymarching through a cone-shaped volume originating from a light source, using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) to define the volume shape and noise for density variation. It solves the problem of rendering visible light beams in fog or haze by accumulating scattered light along the view ray only within the light's defined geometry. It differs from its parent Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density by focusing specifically on light shafts in a post-process context, using the SDF primarily for volume boundary definition and shadow occlusion rather than just surface distance. Outputs: Final color buffer with volumetric light shafts composited over the scene. SDF Light Shaping defines the geometry of volumetric light shafts using Signed Distance Functions during raymarching. It solves the problem of arbitrary light volume boundaries by allowing the renderer to accumulate light only when a sample point lies within a mathematically defined shape (e.g., cylinder, cone, sphere). It differs from standard cone raymarching by decoupling the light's physical geometry from the ray's direction, enabling complex, non-conical volumes to be rendered in post-processing. Choose it when precise, mathematically defined volume boundaries are required without explicit mesh geometry. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps per ray and the number of lights. Each light marches only inside its own volume (cone, sphere, or box) instead of across the whole screen. Memory Complexity: Low, primarily requiring storage for the shadow map, depth texture, and blue noise texture. Measured Performance: Performance scales with the number of pixels covered, the number of steps per ray, and the number of lights. Scaling: Step length is not fixed; it uses Min Step Size + log(Path Length / Raymarch Quality). Long rays through big volumes take longer steps, so their cost stays under control, and Max Steps caps the number of steps per ray. Strengths: Real-time capability; decoupled geometry allows for complex light shapes; jittering and blue noise reduce banding artifacts. Limitations: Cost grows with the number of lights; requires shadow maps for occlusion; banding can occur with few steps. When to Use: Real-time rendering of volumetric light shafts in fog or haze, especially for spot lights or directional lights with defined volumes. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity, physically accurate light scattering is required over real-time constraints, or when the scene has an extremely high number of volumetric lights. Volumetric Light Shafts (Cone Raymarching) is a post-processing technique that renders volumetric light shafts by raymarching through a cone-shaped volume originating from a light source, using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) to define the volume shape and noise for density variation. It is a real-time technique where the shader walks along the view ray in small steps inside a light's volume (cone, sphere, or box) to evaluate light and medium density, adding up scattered light toward the camera. The method uses a cone SDF to define the volume shape rather than a box or sphere, allowing for directional light shafts that taper from the light source. name: SDF Light Shaping
head: Cylindrical light shaping, Raymarched Light Shaping, SDF-Based Light Shaping
body: SDF Light Shaping is a technique for defining the geometry of volumetric light shafts using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) during raymarching. It solves the problem of arbitrary light volume boundaries by allowing the renderer to accumulate light only when a sample point lies within a mathematically defined shape (e.g., cylinder, cone, sphere). It differs from standard cone raymarching by decoupling the light's physical geometry from the ray's direction, enabling complex, non-conical volumes like cylinders or toruses to be rendered in post-processing. Inputs and Outputs The method takes the ray origin, ray direction, light position, light direction, shape radius, step size, depth limits, and smooth edge width as inputs. It outputs the accumulated light color for the current pixel. Data Structures No complex data structures are required; the method operates on scalar values and 3D vectors. SDF Definition The core of the method is an SDF function that returns the signed distance from a point p to the surface of the light shape. For a cylinder, the function is defined as follows: 1. Calculate the vector from the sample point to the light's axis origin: p\to\origin = p - axisOrigin 2. Calculate the projection length of this vector onto the light's axis direction: projectionLength = dot(p\to\origin, axisDir) 3. Find the closest point on the axis to the sample point: closestPointOnAxis = axisOrigin + axisDir \times projectionLength 4. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the sample point to this closest point on the axis: distanceToAxis = length(p - closestPointOnAxis) 5. Return the signed distance by subtracting the radius: sdfVal = distanceToAxis - radius Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize the raymarching loop with a distance variable t set to 0.0. 2. For each step, calculate the sample position: samplePos = rayOrigin + rayDir \times t 3. Check boundary conditions: if t > sceneDepth or t > cameraFar, terminate the loop. 4. Evaluate the SDF for the current samplePos using the light's parameters (lightPos, lightDir, radius). 5. Calculate the shape factor to determine if the point is inside the light volume and to soften the edges: shapeFactor = smoothstep(0.0, -smoothEdgeWidth, sdfVal) Here, smoothEdgeWidth controls the transition softness. 6. Early Exit Optimization: If shapeFactor < 0.1, the point is considered outside the light volume. Increment t by STEP\SIZE and continue to the next iteration without accumulating light. 7. If shapeFactor \ge 0.1, proceed with light accumulation using the shapeFactor to modulate the result. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcylinder(p, axisorigin, axisdir, radius): """ Calculates the signed distance from point p to a cylinder defined by axisorigin, axisdir, and radius. """ axisdir = normalize(axisdir) # Standard requirement for correct projection ptoorigin = p - axisorigin projectionlength = dot(ptoorigin, axisdir) closestpointonaxis = axisorigin + axisdir projectionlength distancetoaxis = length(p - closestpointonaxis) return distancetoaxis - radius def raymarchlightshaping(rayorigin, raydir, lightpos, lightdir, radius, smoothedgewidth, stepsize, scenedepth, camerafar): """ Raymarches through a volume shaped by an SDF. Returns accumulated light color as a vec4. """ accumulatedlight = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) t = 0.0 maxdist = min(scenedepth, camerafar) # Reference implementation uses a fixed step count for in range(1000): if t > maxdist: break samplepos = rayorigin + raydir t # Evaluate SDF sdfval = sdcylinder(samplepos, lightpos, lightdir, radius) # Calculate shape factor for soft edges # smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) shapefactor = smoothstep(0.0, -smoothedgewidth, sdfval) # Early exit if outside the light volume if shapefactor < 0.1: t += stepsize continue # Standard volumetric accumulation: add light modulated by shape factor and step size lightcolor = vec3(1.0) accumulatedlight.rgb += lightcolor shapefactor stepsize t += stepsize return accumulatedlight Parameters smoothEdgeWidth: Width of the smooth edge for the cylinder shape, set to 0.1. radius: The radius of the cylinder in the example, set to 2.0. STEPSIZE: The distance advanced per raymarch step. Not explicitly defined in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Smoothstep Direction: The smoothstep parameters are ordered (0.0, -smoothEdgeWidth, sdfVal). Since smoothEdgeWidth is positive, the second argument is negative. This ensures that when sdfVal is negative (inside the cylinder), the result is 1.0, and it fades to 0.0 as sdfVal becomes positive (outside). Threshold Selection: The threshold 0.1 for early exit is taken directly from the reference implementation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of raymarch steps per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory as no voxel grids or textures are required for the shape definition. Strengths: Allows for arbitrary light shapes (cylinders, cones, spheres, toruses) without modifying the raymarching geometry logic. Efficient due to early exit optimization. Limitations: The light shape is static relative to the light source's coordinate system. When to use: When volumetric light needs to conform to specific geometric constraints (e.g., light passing through a cylindrical window or shaft). The technique was demonstrated by Kenny Pirman in his habitat demo scene, a 3D reconstruction of an O’Neil cylindrical world, where volumetric light was shaped as a cylinder using SDFs. The method builds upon general raymarching techniques and SDF primitives. name: Bidirectional Sphere Tracing
head: Forward-Backward Sphere Tracing, Zero-level set solver
body: Bidirectional Sphere Tracing is a robust surface extraction technique that mitigates the convergence failures of standard sphere tracing when rays miss surface edges or intersect surfaces non-orthogonally. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which relies on the Signed Distance Function (SDF) to guarantee convergence by stepping along the ray, this method uses forward and backward sphere tracing to narrow the candidate range of the surface position, then refines the zero-level set using additional solvers. It is distinct from sibling methods like Relaxed Sphere Tracing because it does not attempt to correct the step size via gradient adjustments in every iteration; instead, it bounds the search space and delegates precision to a separate refinement phase. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{r}o, normalized ray direction \mathbf{r}d, SDF function S(\mathbf{p}), forward iteration count n=16, convergence threshold \epsilon{mask} = 5 \times 10^{-5}, gradient adjustment threshold 0.005, denominator clamp 0.01, candidate sample count N{samples}=100, and sectioning steps N{sec}=8. Outputs: Refined zero-level set position \hat{\mathbf{x}}n or a flag indicating no surface intersection. Data Structures Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Forward Sphere Tracing: Initialize \mathbf{x}0^0 = \mathbf{r}o. Iterate i from 0 to n-1 (where n=16): Evaluate d = S(\mathbf{x}i^i). Update position: \mathbf{x}i^{i+1} = \mathbf{x}i^i + d \cdot \mathbf{r}d. Let \mathbf{x}{nn} = \mathbf{x}n^n be the near zero-level set estimate. 2. Convergence Check: If |S(\mathbf{x}{nn})| < \epsilon{mask}, the ray has converged. Set \hat{\mathbf{x}}n = \mathbf{x}{nn} and terminate. 3. Backward Sphere Tracing: For rays that did not converge, initialize the backward trace from the rear intersection of the ray with a unit sphere. Calculate tf as the rear intersection of \mathbf{r}d with a unit sphere centered at the origin. Set \mathbf{x}f^0 = \mathbf{r}o + tf \mathbf{r}d. The source defines the iteration as \mathbf{x}f^{i+1} = \mathbf{x}0^i - S(\mathbf{x}f^i) \mathbf{r}d. Interpreting \mathbf{x}0^i as a typo for the previous iteration's position \mathbf{x}f^i, the update is: \mathbf{x}f^{i+1} = \mathbf{x}f^i - S(\mathbf{x}f^i) \mathbf{r}d The source does not specify the number of backward iterations. It implies solving until a "far zero-level set" \mathbf{x}{fn} is found. In practice, a symmetric count or a fixed maximum is used to bracket the surface. Let \mathbf{x}{fn} be the resulting position. 4. Candidate Range Validation: Determine the range [\mathbf{x}{nn}, \mathbf{x}{fn}]. If \mathbf{x}{fn} is closer to the camera than \mathbf{x}{nn} (i.e., the distance along \mathbf{r}d from \mathbf{r}o to \mathbf{x}{fn} is less than to \mathbf{x}{nn}), conclude that no surface exists along this ray. 5. Zero-Crossing Search: Evaluate N{samples}=100 samples uniformly distributed within the candidate range [\mathbf{x}{nn}, \mathbf{x}{fn}]. Identify the first zero crossing of S within this range. 6. Refinement (Sectioning): Assuming S is locally monotonic, refine the zero-crossing location using N{sec}=8 steps of sectioning (bisection) to obtain the final zero-level set \hat{\mathbf{x}}n. 7. Gradient Adjustment (Optional Final Step): For performance and stability, the main procedure is non-differentiable. An extra step of forward sphere tracing with gradient tracking is executed to achieve differentiability. Apply gradient direction adjustment to get the final zero-level set: \hat{\mathbf{x}}n = \hat{\mathbf{x}}n - \frac{S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n)}{\nabla{\mathbf{x}} S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n) \cdot \mathbf{r}d} \mathbf{r}d This adjustment is applied only if |S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n)| < 0.005. To avoid division by zero, clamp the denominator: only apply the adjustment if |\nabla{\mathbf{x}} S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n) \cdot \mathbf{r}d| > 0.01. Pseudocode def bidirectionalspheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, nforward=16, epsilonmask=5e-5, epsilonclamp=0.01, nsamples=100, nsectioning=8): """ Bidirectional sphere tracing for robust surface extraction. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera origin. raydirection: 3D vector, normalized ray direction. sdf: Callable, returns signed distance at point p. nforward: Number of forward sphere tracing iterations. epsilonmask: Threshold to consider a ray converged. epsilonclamp: Denominator clamp for gradient adjustment. nsamples: Number of samples in candidate range. nsectioning: Number of bisection steps for refinement. Returns: hitpoint: 3D vector, refined surface position, or None. """ def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def scale(a, s): return (a[0]s, a[1]s, a[2]s) # 1. Forward Sphere Tracing xcurr = rayorigin for in range(nforward): d = sdf(xcurr) xcurr = add(xcurr, scale(raydirection, d)) xnn = xcurr # Near zero-level set # 2. Convergence Check if abs(sdf(xnn)) < epsilonmask: return xnn # 3. Backward Sphere Tracing # Calculate rear intersection with a unit sphere centered at origin. # Ray: r(t) = ro + t rd. |ro + trd|^2 = 1 # t^2 + 2(ro. rd)t + (|ro|^2 - 1) = 0 a = 1.0 b = 2.0 dot(rayorigin, raydirection) c = dot(rayorigin, rayorigin) - 1.0 discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: # Ray does not intersect unit sphere. # Fallback to a large distance or return None. return None sqrtdisc = discriminant0.5 t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) tf = max(t1, t2) # Rear intersection xfcurr = add(rayorigin, scale(raydirection, tf)) # Note: Source does not specify iteration count for backward trace. # Using nforward for symmetry as a standard implementation detail. for in range(nforward): d = sdf(xfcurr) xfcurr = sub(xfcurr, scale(raydirection, d)) xfn = xfcurr # Far zero-level set # 4. Candidate Range Validation distnn = dot(sub(xnn, rayorigin), raydirection) distfn = dot(sub(xfn, rayorigin), raydirection) if distfn < distnn: return None # No surface exists # 5. Zero-Crossing Search # Ensure we sample from near to far if distnn > distfn: xstart, xend = xfn, xnn else: xstart, xend = xnn, xfn candidates = [] for i in range(nsamples + 1): t = i / nsamples p = add(xstart, scale(sub(xend, xstart), t)) candidates.append((p, sdf(p))) # Find first zero crossing zerocrossingidx = -1 for i in range(len(candidates) - 1): s1 = candidates[i][1] s2 = candidates[i+1][1] if s1 s2 <= 0: zerocrossingidx = i break if zerocrossingidx == -1: return None # No zero crossing found in the range # 6. Refinement (Sectioning) pleft, sleft = candidates[zerocrossingidx] pright, sright = candidates[zerocrossingidx + 1] xhat = pleft for in range(nsectioning): mid = scale(add(pleft, pright), 0.5) smid = sdf(mid) if sleft smid < 0: pright = mid sright = smid else: pleft = mid sleft = smid xhat = mid # 7. Gradient Adjustment (Differentiable Step) shat = sdf(xhat) if abs(shat) < 0.005: # Exact threshold from source # Compute gradient numerically eps = 1e-4 grad = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for j in range(3): pplus = list(xhat) pplus[j] += eps grad = add(grad, (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat) / eps, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Simplified gradient accumulation for clarity: grad = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for j in range(3): pplus = list(xhat) pplus[j] += eps grad = (grad[0] + (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat)/eps, grad[1] + (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat)/eps, grad[2] + (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat)/eps) denom = dot(grad, raydirection) if abs(denom) > epsilonclamp: xhat = sub(xhat, scale(raydirection, shat / denom)) return xhat Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method performs n forward iterations, n backward iterations, N{samples} SDF evaluations, and N{sec} bisection steps. With n=16, N{samples}=100, and N{sec}=8, the total SDF evaluations are approximately 16 + 16 + 100 + 8 = 140 per ray, plus potentially one gradient computation for the differentiable step. This is significantly more expensive than standard sphere tracing (16 steps) but ensures convergence where standard tracing fails. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The algorithm requires O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, as no global structures are required. Strengths: Robust against rays that miss surface edges or intersect surfaces at shallow angles, where standard sphere tracing may stall or diverge. It guarantees a bounded search range. Limitations: Higher computational cost due to the bidirectional trace and sampling phase. The backward trace requires calculating the rear intersection with a bounding volume (unit sphere in the source), which may not be applicable to all scene representations without modification. The method is non-differentiable by default; differentiability requires an extra forward step with gradient tracking. Bidirectional Sphere Tracing was introduced by Yariv et al. in the context of Neural Volumes and later adapted for Neural Lumigraph Rendering and IDR (Implicit Disentangled Representation). It addresses the limitation that standard sphere tracing convergence is not guaranteed for general shape configurations, particularly when the SDF underestimates the optimal step length due to non-orthogonal surface intersections. The technique was cited from Yariv et al. [60] in the source. Neural Lumigraph Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00427, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Relaxed Sphere Tracing
head: Keinert et al. sphere tracing
body: Relaxed sphere tracing is a sphere tracing variant that scales up the signed distance function estimate (SDFE) value to take larger steps, thereby improving rendering performance. It reverts to the basic conservative step size if the unbounding spheres of two consecutive steps are disjoint, ensuring that no surface intersections are skipped. It is distinguished from its sibling Enhanced Sphere Tracing by its simpler geometric approximation; while relaxed tracing uses a fixed relaxation factor, enhanced tracing optimally approximates planar surfaces by ensuring consecutive unbounding spheres are tangential, resulting in decisively better error-decrease velocity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray direction \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 with |\mathbf{v}|=1, Signed Distance Function Estimate f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, relaxation parameter \omega, maximum iteration count i{\max}, and convergence threshold \epsilon. Output: Distance t \in 0, \infty) traveled along the ray to the surface. Data Structures: Scalar variables: t (current distance), ri ([SDF value at previous step), r{i+1} (SDF value at current step), di (step size), i (iteration counter). Parameters: \omega: Relaxation parameter. A typical example value is 0.6, yielding a step size factor of 1.6. The sources do not specify a general optimal range, but it must be positive. i{\max}: Maximum number of iterations to prevent infinite loops in empty space. \epsilon: Convergence threshold for surface hit, typically near machine epsilon or a predefined resolution limit. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, i = 0, and evaluate the initial distance ri = f(\mathbf{p}). 2. Loop while i < i{\max} and ri \ge \epsilon: a. Calculate the relaxed step size: di = ri(1 + \omega). b. Sample the SDF at the new position: r{i+1} = f(\mathbf{p} + (t + di)\mathbf{v}). c. Safety Check: If the unbounding spheres of the previous step (radius ri) and the current step (radius r{i+1}) are disjoint, the step di was too large and might have skipped the surface. The condition for disjointness is di > ri + r{i+1}. d. If disjoint (di > ri + r{i+1}): Revert to the conservative step size di = ri and re-sample the SDF at the corrected position r{i+1} = f(\mathbf{p} + (t + di)\mathbf{v}). e. Update distance and state: t \leftarrow t + di, ri \leftarrow r{i+1}. f. Increment iteration: i \leftarrow i + 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def relaxedspheretracing(p, v, f, omega, imax, epsilon): """ Relaxed sphere tracing algorithm. Args: p: Ray origin (vec3) v: Normalized ray direction (vec3) f: Signed Distance Function Estimate callable f(p) omega: Relaxation parameter (scalar) imax: Maximum number of iterations epsilon: Convergence threshold Returns: t: Distance along ray to surface, or None hitpoint: 3D position of hit, or None """ t = 0.0 rprev = f(p) # Initialize with SDF at origin to avoid wasted iteration for in range(imax): if rprev < epsilon: return t, p + t v d = rprev (1.0 + omega) rcurr = f(p + (t + d) v) if d > rprev + rcurr: d = rprev rcurr = f(p + (t + d) v) t += d rprev = rcurr return None, None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The check di > ri + r{i+1} relies on floating-point arithmetic. In degenerate cases where the surface is extremely close, precision errors might cause unnecessary fallbacks or missed detections. Lipschitz Constant: The SDF f is assumed to have a Lipschitz constant \text{Lip } f \le 1. This property ensures that the distance function does not change faster than the Euclidean distance, which is fundamental to the correctness of sphere tracing. Transformation for Boundary Inspection: An alternative formulation by Bálint and Valasek incorporates a transformation into the SDF to prevent overstepping the nonzero boundary without explicit branching. Let \alpha = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{p \cdot \text{width}^2 \cdot \text{Cheigh} \cdot t^2} (where p, \text{width}, \text{Cheigh}, and t are scene-specific parameters). One can inspect g(t) = f(\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v}) - \alpha t. The modified SDF is: F(t) = \frac{f(\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v})}{1 + \alpha - \alpha t} This transformation efficiently offsets the surface by a value that increases with distance, allowing the use of standard sphere tracing logic on F(t) without special termination conditions. Incremental Minimum Step Relaxed Sphere Tracing is a ray marching algorithm that accelerates traversal through empty space by combining the step-scaling logic of relaxed sphere tracing with an incrementally increasing minimum step size. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing in large empty volumes by allowing the step size to grow as the ray travels further from the origin, while retaining the safety checks of relaxed sphere tracing to prevent skipping intersections. It is distinguished from basic sphere tracing by its adaptive step growth and from standard relaxed sphere tracing by the explicit addition of a growing minimum step component. Relaxed Sphere Tracing with Backward Correction is a ray marching algorithm that uses a relaxed sphere tracing step combined with a backward correction if the step size decreases significantly. It initializes t=0, pft=0, or=\text{TRACE\OR}, and loops i from 0 to \text{stepcount}-1. It evaluates the SDF ft = \text{sdf}(\text{RAY}(r,t)), and if ft < pft \times (or - 1), it applies backward correction t -= (or - 1) \times pft and re-evaluates ft. If ft \le 0, it returns vec2(t - \text{stepsize}, t); otherwise it advances t += ft \times or + \text{stepsize}, and returns vec2(t - \text{stepsize}, t) after the loop. BlobTree Distance Bound Correction is a method to correct the signed distance bound for BlobTree models to allow large steps in sphere tracing outside the object's compact support. Let b: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} be the scalar field function of a BlobTree, T be the threshold, and \lambda be the Lipschitz bound of b. Let d(\mathbf{p}, \Omega) be the distance to the boundary of the domain \Omega. The corrected function is f(\mathbf{p}) = \begin{cases} (T - b(\mathbf{p}))/\lambda & \text{if } \mathbf{p} \in \Omega \\ T/\lambda + d(\mathbf{p}, \Omega) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. For standard BlobTrees, b(\mathbf{p}) = 0 for \mathbf{p} \notin \Omega, making the distance bound constant and equal to T/\lambda outside the object, which yields small values and slows algorithms such as sphere tracing. Performance: Relaxed sphere tracing offers a performance increase over basic sphere tracing by taking larger steps in empty space or far from surfaces. Enhanced sphere tracing is decisively better than relaxed sphere tracing in performance metrics (error-decrease velocity) across all iteration counts. Enhanced tracing outperforms relaxed tracing on every iteration count because its optimal approximation of smooth surfaces allows for longer steps and rarely branches execution by falling back to the standard sphere tracing step. Complexity: Time complexity is O(k) where k is the number of iterations, similar to basic sphere tracing, but with a potentially smaller k due to larger steps. Memory complexity is O(1) as it only stores a few scalar values per ray. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a good balance between speed and safety compared to basic sphere tracing. Limitations: The fixed relaxation factor \omega is not adaptive. In regions with high curvature or complex geometry, the fallback mechanism may trigger frequently, reducing the performance benefit. It is less efficient than enhanced sphere tracing. Relaxed sphere tracing was introduced by Keinert et al. [KSK14] as a faster algorithm via relaxation of the original sphere tracing method. It was later used in the Claybook project to implement a real-time simulation-based computer game. The method was analyzed and compared against basic and enhanced sphere tracing by Csaba Bálint and Gábor Valasek in their 2018 paper "Accelerating Sphere Tracing". The authors noted that while Keinert's method scales up the conservative step size, it requires a check for disjoint unbounding spheres to maintain correctness. body: Incremental Minimum Step Relaxed Sphere Tracing is a ray marching algorithm that accelerates traversal by combining the step-scaling logic of Relaxed Sphere Tracing with an incrementally increasing minimum step size. It adjusts the step size based on the previous distance estimate to handle glassy artifacts at low step counts. The method advances a ray along a parameter t using a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to determine step sizes. It maintains a minimum step size msp that increases linearly with each iteration, ensuring that steps do not shrink below a growing threshold. It also implements a backward correction mechanism to handle cases where the distance estimate drops significantly, which can occur with glassy artifacts or rapid changes in geometry. Inputs: r: Ray origin and direction (normalized). sdf(p): Signed Distance Function returning distance to surface. stepcount: Maximum number of iterations. stepsize: Initial step size scalar. TRACE\STEPINCR: Constant increment for the minimum step size. TRACE\OR: Overstep ratio (typically > 1). Outputs: A vec2 (or pair) containing the hit position t{hit} and the end position t{end} of the traversal. If no intersection is found within stepcount, it returns the last valid interval. No complex data structures are required. The algorithm uses scalar variables for ray parameter t, previous distance pft, current distance ft, minimum step msp, and overstep ratio components. The implementation varies slightly depending on whether backward correction is enabled. The core logic involves initializing variables, looping, evaluating the SDF, checking for intersections, applying backward correction if necessary, incrementing the minimum step, and advancing the ray. 1. Initialization: Set t = 0. Set msp = stepsize. If backward correction is used: Set pft = 0. Set orm1 = TRACE\OR - 1. 2. Iteration Loop (for i from 0 to stepcount - 1): Evaluate SDF: ft = sdf(RAY(r, t)). Backward Correction (if enabled): If ft < pft \times orm1: t = t - orm1 \times pft. ft = sdf(RAY(r, t)). Increment Minimum Step: msp = msp + TRACE\STEPINCR. Intersection Test: If ft \le 0: Return vec2(t - msp, t). Advance Ray: t = t + TRACE\OR \times ft + msp. Update pft = ft at the end of the loop to serve as the previous distance for the next iteration, as the source notes do not explicitly show this assignment. 3. Termination: If the loop completes without returning: Return vec2(t - msp, t). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalminsteprelaxedspheretrace(ray, sdf, stepcount, stepsize, TRACESTEPINCR, TRACEOR): t = 0.0 msp = stepsize pft = 0.0 orm1 = TRACEOR - 1.0 for i in range(stepcount): ft = sdf(ray.origin + ray.direction t) if ft < pft orm1: t = t - orm1 pft ft = sdf(ray.origin + ray.direction t) msp = msp + TRACESTEPINCR if ft <= 0: return (t - msp, t) t = t + TRACEOR ft + msp # Update previous distance for next iteration pft = ft return (t - msp, t) TRACE\STEPINCR: The amount added to msp per step. Not given in the sources. TRACE\OR: Overstep ratio. Not given in the sources. stepsize: Initial minimum step. Not given in the sources. stepcount: Max iterations. Not given in the sources. Initial pft=0: On the first iteration, pft is 0. The condition ft < 0 \times (TRACE\OR - 1) becomes ft < 0. This correctly triggers if the ray starts inside an object, but does not trigger false positives for empty space. Precision: Floating point errors in t updates can accumulate. The backward correction helps mitigate overshooting but relies on accurate SDF evaluation. Glassy Artifacts: The method is specifically noted to handle glassy artifacts at low step counts by adjusting step size based on previous distance. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps taken, up to stepcount. The incremental step size reduces the number of steps required for long empty traversals compared to constant step size methods. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Accelerates traversal in empty space compared to basic sphere tracing. The "faster raymarch" alias suggests it is optimized for speed. Strengths: Handles large empty volumes efficiently; reduces glassy artifacts; simple implementation. Limitations: Requires tuning of TRACE\STEPINCR and TRACE\OR; backward correction adds computational overhead per step; may overshoot if parameters are not set correctly. The method is derived from the Interactive-SDF-Renderer project by Csabix. It is an unofficial implementation combining relaxed sphere tracing with an incrementing minimum step size. It appears in shader code labeled 02Shaders and is associated with aliases like Raytracer02 and faster raymarch. name: Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids
head: Apodaca’s code (variant)
body: Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids renders volumetric clouds by tracing rays through a set of implicit surfaces (pseudo-spheroids or ellipsoids) and sampling noise only when the ray traverses these volumes. It differs from standard sphere tracing by using a list of randomized bounded-surface volumes rather than a single global Signed Distance Function (SDF), optimizing performance by discarding positions outside the cloud and using a collision detection method based on quadratic discriminants. Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized) for each pixel. List of N pseudo-spheroids, each defined by center \mathbf{c}i, nominal radius R{nominal}, distortion parameter k, and maximum density \rho{max}. 3D noise function fBm(\mathbf{p}) (fractional Brownian motion), normalized to [0, 1]. Density threshold \rho{thresh} for termination. Bounding box for spatial culling. Outputs: Final color R for each pixel, blended with the sky background. Data Structures: candidates: A list of indices of pseudo-spheroids intersected by the ray. sortedcandidates: The candidates list sorted by intersection distance (back-to-front). Formulas: 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection: For a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and sphere i with center \mathbf{c}i and effective radius Ri, the intersection is determined by the discriminant \Delta of the quadratic equation |\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{c}i|^2 = Ri^2. \Delta = (\mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}i))^2 - (|\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}i|^2 - Ri^2) If \Delta \ge 0, the ray intersects the sphere. The entry and exit distances are: t{entry, exit} = -(\mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}i)) \pm \sqrt{\Delta} 2. Effective Radius: The nominal radius is modulated by a random component k to create a pseudo-spheroid shape: Ri = R{nominal} \pm k (Note: The source describes scaling the nominal sphere radius by \pm k using Euclidean distance, effectively creating a distorted boundary.) 3. Density Modulation: The density \rho at a point \mathbf{p} inside the pseudo-spheroid is calculated as: \rho(\mathbf{p}) = \rho{max} \cdot fBm(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{||\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}i||}{Ri}\right) (Inferred from Equation (2) description: Density is modulated by position inside the pseudo-spheroid with a random component. The term (1 - \frac{||\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}i||}{Ri}) ensures density drops to zero at the boundary.) 4. Level of Detail (LOD) Step Size: The step increment \Delta t is controlled by the distance from the cloud center to balance detail and performance: \Delta t = f(\text{distance from center}) Longer steps are taken when close to the camera (or far from center?), and smaller steps when far. (Note: The source states "longer steps when close to camera, smaller steps when far" in the context of distance from the center of the cloud. This implies an inverse relationship or a specific LOD function not fully detailed in the text.) Algorithm Steps: 1. Culling: For each pixel, identify pseudo-spheroids within the bounding box. 2. Collision Detection: For each candidate sphere, compute the discriminant \Delta. If \Delta \ge 0, add the sphere index to the candidates list. 3. Sorting: Sort the candidates list by intersection distance using insertion sort, ensuring back-to-front processing. 4. Ray Marching: For each pixel: Initialize accumulated color C = 0 and opacity \alpha = 0. For each sphere in sortedcandidates: Calculate intersection interval [t{entry}, t{exit}]. If the ray does not intersect the sphere, skip. March from t{entry} to t{exit} with step size \Delta t (LOD adjusted). At each step point \mathbf{p}: Calculate density \rho(\mathbf{p}) using the formula above. If \rho(\mathbf{p}) < \rho{thresh}, continue. Compute lighting L(\mathbf{p}) (e.g., using normal derived from SDF gradient or noise gradient). Update color and opacity using volume rendering integration (e.g., standard front-to-back compositing, though the source mentions back-to-front tracing, standard alpha blending is implied for "Blend the result R with the sky"). If \alpha \ge 1.0 (or sufficient opacity), break the marching loop for this sphere. Blend the accumulated cloud color R with the sky background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cloudtracing(rayorigin, raydirection, spheres, noisefunc, rhothresh): """ Render clouds using pseudo-spheroids. Args: rayorigin: Camera origin (vec3) raydirection: Normalized ray direction (vec3) spheres: List of dicts with keys: 'center', 'Rnominal', 'k', 'rhomax' noisefunc: Function fBm(p) returning normalized noise [0,1] rhothresh: Density threshold for termination Returns: color: Final pixel color (vec3) """ candidates = [] # 1. Culling and Collision Detection for i, sphere in enumerate(spheres): c = sphere['center'] R = sphere['Rnominal'] + sphere['k'] # Effective radius oc = rayorigin - c a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) cval = dot(oc, oc) - R R discriminant = b b - 4 a cval if discriminant >= 0: # Ray intersects sphere sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) candidates.append({'index': i, 'tentry': t1, 'texit': t2}) # 2. Sort Candidates (Back-to-Front) # Insertion sort as per source for i in range(1, len(candidates)): key = candidates[i] j = i - 1 while j >= 0 and candidates[j]['tentry'] > key['tentry']: candidates[j + 1] = candidates[j] j -= 1 candidates[j + 1] key # 3. Ray Marching and Integration accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for cand in candidates: tstart = max(cand['tentry'], 0.0) tend = cand['texit'] if tstart >= tend: continue # LOD Step Size: Simplified assumption based on distance # Source: "longer steps when close to camera, smaller steps when far" # We use a distance-based step size. # Note: Exact LOD formula not provided in source disttocenter = length(rayorigin - spheres[cand['index']]['center']) stepsize = 0.1 (1.0 + disttocenter) # Placeholder for LOD function t = tstart while t < tend: p = rayorigin + t raydirection sphere = spheres[cand['index']] c = sphere['center'] R = sphere['Rnominal'] + sphere['k'] # Density Calculation disttoc = length(p - c) if disttoc < R: noiseval = noisefunc(p) density = sphere['rhomax'] noiseval (1.0 - disttoc / R) if density > rhothresh: # Lighting Calculation (Placeholder) # Source mentions lighting(p) but no formula light = vec3(1.0) color = light density # Volume Rendering (Front-to-Back Compositing) # Note: Source says "trace from back to front" but standard # compositing is front-to-back. We assume standard alpha blending. alpha = density stepsize # Approximation alpha = min(alpha, 1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedalpha += alpha (1.0 - alpha) # Simplified if accumulatedalpha >= 0.99: break t += stepsize if accumulatedalpha >= 0.99: break # 4. Blend with Sky skycolor = vec3(0.5, 0.7, 1.0) # Placeholder finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + skycolor (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Discriminant calculation must handle floating-point errors near \Delta = 0. Boundary: Density drops to zero at the effective radius Ri. Points outside this radius should not be sampled. LOD: The exact LOD equation is not provided in the source. A distance-based heuristic is used as a placeholder. Sorting: Insertion sort is efficient for small lists of candidates but may be slow for very large N. A ray-tracing algorithm over a list of N randomized bounded-surface volumes (pseudo-spheroids) to render clouds, using collision detection and insertion sort for optimization. It differs from the general method by explicitly detailing the candidate selection and sorting steps. It is chosen when a simple, GPU-friendly implementation with spatial culling is required. Link: Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of spheres and M is the number of steps per sphere. The insertion sort adds O(K^2) where K is the number of intersected spheres. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sphere data and O(K) for candidates. Performance: The method reduces computational effort by discarding positions outside the cloud and using a short list of intersected spheres. Strengths: Efficient culling, simple geometry (spheres/ellipsoids), good for real-time GPU rendering. Limitations: Approximation of cloud shape (pseudo-spheroids), LOD step size is heuristic. When to use: Real-time cloud rendering where performance is critical and high-fidelity global noise is not required. When not to use: When complex, non-spherical cloud structures are needed. Originated in the context of real-time GPU volumetric cloud rendering. The method is an improved version of Apodaca’s code [27] and is described in. It builds on the principle of using implicit surfaces to define cloud volumes and sampling noise only within those volumes. name: Ray Marching with Spherical Harmonics (SH) Basis
head: JNeRF Forward/Backward Ray Marching
body: This method performs differentiable volume rendering by ray marching through a 3D grid where color is represented as Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients, enabling gradient-based optimization of the SH basis during training. It differs from standard ray marching by maintaining a logtransmit accumulator for exponential transmission and computing gradients for both the SH color coefficients and the volume density (\sigma) simultaneously within the marching loop. It is specifically designed for neural radiance field (NeRF) training frameworks that utilize SH for view-dependent appearance. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Grid data structures containing SH coefficients (grid.shdata), density values (grid.sigma), and spatial links (grid.links). Parameters: opt.stepsize, opt.stopthresh, sparsityloss, betaloss, gout (gradient output scaling). Outputs: Accumulated color \mathbf{C}. Gradients for SH coefficients (gradshout), density (graddensityout), and mask (maskout). Data Structures: grid.shdata: Array of SH coefficients. Layout depends on grid.shdatadim and grid.basisdim. grid.links: Spatial indexing for trilinear interpolation. Shared memory (CUDA context): sphfuncval[TRACERAYBKWDCUDARAYSPERBLOCK][9]: Stores SH basis function values. gradsphfuncval[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK][9]: Accumulates SH basis gradients. rayspec[TRACERAYBKWDCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Ray-specific state. tempstorage[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Temporary storage for warp reductions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize logtransmit to 0.0 (or input value). Initialize accum (color accumulator) to 0.0. Initialize gradsphfuncval to 0.0. Initialize currgradsigma to 0.0. 2. Marching Loop: Loop over ray steps t with increment opt.stepsize. Termination: If \exp(\text{log\transmit}) < \text{opt.stop\thresh}, break loop. Sample: Evaluate density \sigma and SH coefficients at current ray position \mathbf{p}. Compute Transmission: Calculate pixel coverage factor: \text{pcnt} = \text{ray.world\step} \times \sigma. Calculate weight: w = \exp(\text{log\transmit}) \times (1 - \exp(-\text{pcnt})). Update transmission: \text{log\transmit} \leftarrow \text{log\transmit} - \text{pcnt}. Accumulate Color: Evaluate SH basis functions \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}) for direction \mathbf{d}. Compute color: \mathbf{C}{\text{step}} = \sum{i} \text{coeff}i \times Yi(\mathbf{d}). Accumulate: \text{accum} \leftarrow \text{accum} - w \times \mathbf{C}{\text{step}}. Compute Gradients: Determine if color is in valid range: \text{color\in\01} = (\text{total\color} == \text{lane\color\total}). Compute common gradient factor: \text{grad\common} = w \times \text{color\in\01} \times \text{gout}. Compute SH gradient contribution: \text{curr\grad\color} = \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}) \times \text{grad\common}. Compute density gradient: \text{curr\grad\sigma} = \text{ray.world\step} \times (\mathbf{C}{\text{step}} \times \exp(\text{log\transmit}) - \text{accum}). Sparsity Loss: If \text{sparsity\loss} > 0, add Cauchy regularization gradient: \text{curr\grad\sigma} \leftarrow \text{curr\grad\sigma} + \text{sparsity\loss} \times \frac{4\sigma}{1 + 2\sigma^2}. Backpropagate to Grid: Call trilerpbackwardcuvolone to propagate currgradcolor to SH coefficients. Call trilerpbackwardcuvolonedensity to propagate currgradsigma to density grid. 3. Finalization: Apply betaloss: \text{accum} \leftarrow \text{accum} - \text{beta\loss}. Perform warp shuffle reductions for totalcolor and colorin01. Return accumulated color and gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raymarchingshbackward(rayso, raysd, grid, opt, sparsityloss, betaloss, gout): """ Differentiable ray marching with SH basis and backward pass. """ # Initialize accumulators logtransmit = 0.0 accum = 0.0 # Initialize gradient arrays with zeros (fixes sequence multiplication bug) gradshout = [0.0] grid.shdatadim graddensityout = 0.0 gradsphfuncval = [0.0] grid.basisdim t = 0.0 while t < opt.maxdistance: # Termination check based on transmission if math.exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh: break # Sample grid pos = [rayso[i] + t raysd[i] for i in range(3)] sigma = sampledensity(grid, pos) shcoeffs = sampleshcoeffs(grid, pos) # Compute weight and update transmission pcnt = opt.stepsize sigma weight = math.exp(logtransmit) (1.0 - math.exp(-pcnt)) logtransmit -= pcnt # Compute color from SH coefficients shbasis = computeshbasis(raysd, grid.basisdim) colorstep = sum(shcoeffs[i] shbasis[i] for i in range(grid.basisdim)) # Accumulate color (backward pass convention from source) accum -= weight colorstep # Determine if color is in valid range [0, 1] totalcolor = colorstep colorin01 = 1.0 if (totalcolor >= 0.0 and totalcolor <= 1.0) else 0.0 # Compute common gradient factor gradcommon = weight colorin01 gout # Gradient for SH coefficients for i in range(grid.basisdim): gradsphfuncval[i] += shbasis[i] gradcommon # Gradient for density currgradsigma = opt.stepsize (totalcolor math.exp(logtransmit) - accum) # Sparsity loss gradient if sparsityloss > 0.0: currgradsigma += sparsityloss (4.0 sigma / (1.0 + 2.0 sigma2)) # Backpropagate to grid trilerpbackwardcuvolone(grid, pos, gradsphfuncval, gradshout) trilerpbackwardcuvolonedensity(grid, pos, currgradsigma, graddensityout) t += opt.stepsize # Final adjustment accum -= betaloss return accum, gradshout, graddensityout def sampledensity(grid, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation of grid.sigma at pos return grid.sigma[pos] def sampleshcoeffs(grid, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation of grid.shdata at pos return grid.shdata[pos] def computeshbasis(direction, dim): # Standard evaluation of SH basis functions Yi(d) for i in [0, dim) return [math.cos(direction[0] i) for i in range(dim)] def trilerpbackwardcuvolone(grid, pos, gradsphfuncval, gradshout): # Propagate color gradients to SH coefficients via trilinear backward pass for i in range(grid.basisdim): gradshout[i] += gradsphfuncval[i] def trilerpbackwardcuvolonedensity(grid, pos, currgradsigma, graddensityout): # Propagate density gradients to density grid graddensityout += currgradsigma An endless cloud animation illuminated by sunlight and skylight with multiple scattering, using precomputed spherical harmonics and binary tree clustering. The binary tree contains sample points in leaf nodes, and error and mean values in interior nodes. The transmittance for each lighted voxel is clustered through sample points using a binary tree structure. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of ray steps and D is the SH basis dimension. Each step requires SH evaluation and gradient computation. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot D), where V is the number of voxels in the grid. SH coefficients are stored per voxel. Performance: Optimized for CUDA with warp-level reductions. Shared memory is used to store SH basis values and gradients to minimize global memory access. Strengths: Enables view-dependent appearance modeling with differentiable SH basis. Efficient gradient computation for both color and density. Limitations: High memory usage for large SH bases. Sensitive to opt.stopthresh and sparsityloss parameters. This method is part of the JNeRF framework, which uses Jittor for differentiable rendering. It extends standard volume rendering by incorporating Spherical Harmonics for view-dependent shading and providing backward pass implementations for training. The approach is similar to PlenOctrees and SNeRG in its use of SH and sparsity regularization. name: Adaptive Step Size and Termination
head: Adaptive Ray Marching, Adaptive Step Rules
body: This family defines the control flow logic for ray-marching loops, determining how far a ray advances per iteration (\Delta t) and when the loop halts. It solves the trade-off between computational efficiency (skipping empty space) and visual fidelity (avoiding missed geometry or aliasing). It sets itself apart from specific implementations like Sphere Tracing or Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by providing the general framework for adaptive stepping, early termination, and safety constraints applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields. All methods in this family operate on a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by accumulated distance t. The core loop evaluates a scene function (SDF, density field, or volume texture) at the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to determine the next step size \Delta t and check for termination. Termination Conditions: 1. Surface Hit: The ray has intersected the target geometry. For SDFs, this is typically |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon or f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0. For volumes, this may be a density threshold or opacity accumulation. 2. Escape/Miss: The ray has traveled beyond a maximum distance t{max} or exceeded a maximum iteration count N{max}. 3. Early Termination (Volumes): Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1 - \epsilon), or accumulated transmission falls below a minimum threshold, allowing the ray to stop early as further contributions are negligible. Step Size Determination: The step size \Delta t is computed based on the local scene properties: SDF-based: \Delta t is often derived from the SDF value f(\mathbf{p}), potentially scaled by a relaxation factor or Lipschitz constant \lambda. Volume-based: \Delta t may be fixed, adaptive based on density gradients, or constrained by minimum/maximum bounds to prevent aliasing or excessive computation. Safety: Steps must be chosen to ensure the ray does not penetrate the surface or skip over significant volumetric features, often requiring conservative clamping. Pseudocode Structure: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchloop(rayorigin, raydirection, scenefunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): """ Generic ray marching loop with adaptive step size and termination. Args: rayorigin (vec3): The starting point of the ray. raydirection (vec3): The normalized direction of the ray. scenefunc (function): A function evaluating the scene (SDF or density) at point p. maxdist (float): The maximum distance the ray can travel. maxsteps (int): The maximum number of iterations allowed. epsilon (float): The convergence threshold for hit detection. Returns: tuple: (hit: bool, distance: float) """ t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): # Check for escape if t > maxdist: return False, t # Calculate current position p = rayorigin + raydirection t # Evaluate scene function val = scenefunc(p) # Termination: Hit if ishit(val, epsilon): return True, t # Termination: Early Exit (Volume specific) if isearlyexit(val, t): return False, t # Or handle partial contribution # Step Size Calculation step = computestepsize(val, t, i) # Safety Clamp step = max(step, minstep) step = min(step, maxstep) t += step # Max steps reached return False, t Step Size and Termination Rules defines the general framework for adaptive stepping, early termination, and safety constraints applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields. It sets itself apart from specific implementations like Sphere Tracing or Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by providing the general framework for adaptive stepping, early termination, and safety constraints applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields. Adaptive Step Size Adjustment refers to a family of techniques in distance-field ray marching that dynamically modify the step length during traversal to optimize the trade-off between rendering performance and visual fidelity. Unlike fixed-step methods, these algorithms adjust the step size based on local geometry (via Signed Distance Functions) or screen-space error metrics, often incorporating mechanisms to handle the risks of non-conservative stepping such as overshooting. This family is distinct from Step Size and Termination Rules by its focus on dynamic adjustment logic rather than static thresholds, and from Step Size and Tracing Geometry by its reliance on SDF properties rather than purely geometric bounding volumes. Step Size and Tracing Geometry defines how a ray advances through a volume or implicit field, determining the distance to the next sampling point and the conditions for termination. It solves the problem of balancing rendering accuracy (avoiding missed surfaces or artifacts) with computational performance (minimizing expensive volume or SDF evaluations). It sets apart from its siblings by focusing on the geometric interpretation of the step: Non-Linear Sphere Tracing handles deformed spaces via ODE integration, Cone Tracing uses expanding apertures for lighting approximation, and Occlusion-Aware Raycasting clips rays against foreground geometry to reduce overdraw. A speed function F for the Fast Marching method that varies between [0, 1] and depends on image gradient magnitude and intensity. Pre-process datasets with edge-preserving denoising using curvature flow method with time-step t{cf} = 0.1 and iterations n{cf} = 10. Suppress artificial boundaries caused by contrast agent structures using a global intensity threshold tc \approx 125. In cases with thin pericardium and pleura, reinsert the sternum using an intensity-based region growing operation seeded anywhere in the sternum to prevent contour leakage. F(I(\mathbf{x})) = \begin{cases} SIG(\operatorname{RGM}(I(\mathbf{x}))); & I(\mathbf{x}) > tl \\ 0; & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where tl is a global threshold. RGM(I(\mathbf{x})) = \left\| \nabla (G(\mathbf{x}, \sigmag) I(\mathbf{x})) \right\| where RGM is the gradient magnitude computed using recursive filters approximating convolution with the first derivative of a Gaussian. SIG(I(\mathbf{x})) = \left[ 1 + \exp\left( \frac{-I(\mathbf{x}) - \beta}{\alpha} \right) \right]^{-1} where SIG is the non-linear monotonic sigmoid mapping function. The concept of adaptive stepping in ray marching evolved from the need to optimize the computational cost of evaluating implicit surfaces and volumetric data. While standard sphere tracing uses a fixed conservative step based on the SDF value, adaptive methods allow for larger steps in empty space or smoother regions, and smaller steps near complex geometry. The specific "Edge-based Speed Function" described in the minor variants originates from medical imaging applications, specifically for tagged volume rendering of the heart, where accurate contour propagation is critical. name: Step Size and Termination Rules
head: Ray Marching Parameters and Compositing
body: Step Size and Termination Rules define the control flow logic for ray-marching loops, determining how far a ray advances per iteration (\Delta t) and when the loop halts. This family solves the trade-off between computational efficiency (skipping empty space) and visual fidelity (avoiding missed geometry or aliasing). It sets itself apart from specific implementations like Sphere Tracing or Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by providing the general framework for adaptive stepping, early termination, and safety constraints applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields. All methods in this family operate on a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by accumulated distance t. The core loop evaluates a scene function (SDF, density field, or volume texture) at the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to determine the next step size \Delta t and check for termination. Termination Conditions: 1. Surface Hit: The ray has intersected the target geometry. For SDFs, this is typically |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon or f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0. For volumes, early termination often relies on an accumulated opacity threshold (e.g., \alpha{acc} \ge 0.995). 2. Escape/Miss: The ray has traveled beyond a maximum distance t{max} or exceeded a maximum iteration count N{max}. 3. Early Termination (Volumes): Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold, or accumulated transmission falls below a minimum threshold, allowing the ray to stop early as further contributions are negligible. Step Size Determination: The step size \Delta t is computed based on the local scene properties. SDF-based: \Delta t is often derived from the SDF value f(\mathbf{p}), potentially scaled by a relaxation factor or Lipschitz constant \lambda. Volume-based: \Delta t may be fixed, adaptive based on density gradients, or constrained by minimum/maximum bounds to prevent aliasing or excessive computation. Safety: Steps must be chosen to ensure the ray does not penetrate the surface or skip over significant volumetric features, often requiring conservative clamping. Pseudocode Structure: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchloop(rayorigin, raydirection, scenefunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon, minstep=1e-6, maxstep=1.0): """ Generic ray marching loop with adaptive step size and termination. """ t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return False, t p = rayorigin + raydirection t val = scenefunc(p) # Termination: Surface Hit (SDF) if abs(val) < epsilon: return True, t # Termination: Early Exit (Volume specific) - Not given in the sources. # if isearlyexit(val, t): # return False, t # Step Size Calculation step = val # Safety Clamp step = max(minstep, min(maxstep, step)) t += step return False, t Standard Constant Step Ray Marching uses a predefined constant step size \Delta t, simplifying implementation but requiring careful tuning to avoid aliasing or missed details. It differs from Sphere Tracing by ignoring local geometry constraints for performance, and from SDF Ray Marching with Grid Lookup by not using interpolation for precise intersection detection. Choose when scene scale is uniform and computational overhead of adaptive stepping is undesirable. Sphere Tracing uses the SDF value at the current position as a safe lower bound for the distance to the nearest surface, allowing the ray to "jump" forward by that exact distance. This guarantees that the ray never overshoots or penetrates the surface, provided the function satisfies the Lipschitz condition. It is distinguished from its siblings by its adaptive step sizing which significantly reduces the number of function evaluations required to converge on a surface. Choose for implicit surfaces where guaranteed no-overshoot is required. Step Size Optimization encompasses techniques that dynamically determine the distance \Delta t to advance a ray, replacing fixed-step methods to balance computational cost and visual fidelity. It differs from Sphere Tracing in that while sphere tracing strictly uses the SDF value as a lower bound for the step (often with a relaxation factor), step size optimization includes broader strategies like error estimation, gap limiting, and integration-based adaptive stepping that may not rely solely on the geometric distance bound. Choose when scene complexity varies significantly along the ray. Adaptive Minimum Step Size dynamically increases the minimum sampling interval (\Delta t{min}) based on the ray's distance from the camera and the accumulated density along the path. It solves the problem of excessive sampling in regions where visual detail is less critical (far from the camera) or where light contribution is negligible (behind dense volumes), thereby reducing computational cost without significantly degrading image quality. Unlike fixed step sizes, it allows for coarser sampling in the background and deep within volumetric structures. Choose for large, sparse volumetric scenes. Termination Criteria define the conditions under which a ray-marching loop halts, ensuring the algorithm returns a valid intersection point or correctly identifies a miss without infinite iteration. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sphere Tracing by focusing on the general control flow logic applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields, rather than the specific geometric step-size constraints of sphere tracing or the fixed-step simplicity of constant marching. Choose when robust loop exit conditions are needed across different rendering backends. Cone step mapping and relaxed cone step mapping are space leaping acceleration techniques used in ray marching. They provide a safety distance that allows the ray to move along the path without intersecting geometry, or without intersecting and then leaving geometry so that it misses it. Conservative Sphere Tracing Step Sizing is a fix for volumetric cloud rendering where sphere tracing takes overly aggressive step sizes, skipping cloud boundaries and leaving circular/scalloped density artifacts. It resolves issues by clamping the pre-computed 2D organic cell SDF to a conservative maximum of 30000.0 uWorldScale, reducing the sphere tracing step size multiplier from 0.8 to 0.4, and clamping the empty space skipping step size to a maximum of 2000.0 worldScale. In empty regions of the weather map, uncapped SDF values (up to 1e14) caused bilinear filtering to interpolate extremely large values near cloud edges, while an aggressive step multiplier of 0.8 with no upper bound resulted in rays jumping past the actual cloud surface. The concept of step size and termination is fundamental to all ray-marching techniques. Early implementations often used fixed steps due to simplicity, but this led to aliasing and missed geometry in complex scenes. The introduction of Sphere Tracing by John Hart provided a mathematically safe adaptive step size based on SDFs. Subsequent developments, such as those in volumetric cloud rendering, introduced adaptive minimum step sizes to optimize performance in large, sparse volumes. Specific implementations, like the conservative step sizing fixes for volumetric clouds, highlight the ongoing need to balance aggressive space-leaping with visual fidelity. steubengineer/imaginaryVolumes, https://github.com/steubengineer/imaginaryVolumes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) What is Ray Marching? name: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching
head: Constant Step Distance Sampling, Constant step ray marching, March Calculation
body: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching is an iterative root-finding technique for determining the intersection of a ray with an implicit surface or evaluating volumetric fields by stepping along the ray at fixed intervals. It solves the problem of rendering implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or scalar fields without requiring analytical intersection solutions or polygonal mesh rasterization. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which dynamically adjusts step size based on the local SDF value to guarantee no overshooting, this method uses a predefined constant step size \Delta t, simplifying implementation but requiring careful tuning to avoid aliasing or missed details. It differs from Step Size Optimization by ignoring local geometry constraints for performance, and from SDF Ray Marching with Grid Lookup by not using interpolation for precise intersection detection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, fixed step size \Delta t, maximum travel distance t{max}, maximum iteration count N{max}, and convergence threshold \epsilon. Outputs: Intersection distance t{hit} (or null if missed), and optionally the hit position \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Ray State: A scalar t representing accumulated distance, initialized to t{min} (near clipping plane). Scene Function: A function f(\mathbf{p}) that returns a scalar value. For SDFs, f(\mathbf{p}) is the signed distance to the nearest surface; for boolean volumes, it may return a boolean or density. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set accumulated distance t \leftarrow t{min} and step counter k \leftarrow 0. 2. Position Calculation: Compute the current sample point \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d}. 3. Sampling: Evaluate the scene function at \mathbf{p}k to get value v = f(\mathbf{p}k). 4. Termination Check: If v \le 0 (for SDFs) or v indicates a hit (e.g., density threshold), the ray has intersected the surface. Return t as the intersection distance. If t > t{max} or k \ge N{max}, the ray has escaped or exceeded resources. Return null/miss. 5. Step Advancement: Advance the ray by the constant step size: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. 6. Increment: Increment step counter k \leftarrow k + 1. 7. Loop: Repeat from Step 2. Formulas: The ray position at step k is defined as: \mathbf{r}(k) = \mathbf{o} + k \Delta t \mathbf{d} where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin, \mathbf{d} is the unit ray direction, \Delta t is the predefined constant step size, and k \in \{0, 1, 2,...\} is the step number. For SDFs, the intersection is detected when: f(\mathbf{r}(k)) \le 0 Parameters with Typical Values: \Delta t: Fixed step size. Typical values range from 0.001 to 0.1 depending on scene scale and desired precision. t{max}: Maximum ray distance. Typical values: 10.0 to 100.0. N{max}: Maximum iterations. Typical values: 50 to 255. \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Typical value: 0.001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overshooting: If \Delta t is too large relative to the scene's high-frequency details, the ray may jump over thin objects or surfaces, resulting in missed intersections. Aliasing: Large \Delta t can cause jagged edges or "staircasing" artifacts on curved surfaces. Performance: Unlike Sphere Tracing, constant step marching does not adapt to empty space, leading to unnecessary samples in large voids. Precision: For SDFs, checking f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0 may return a point slightly inside the surface. Midpoint approximation (t - 0.5 \Delta t) can improve accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def standardconstantstepraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): """ Performs standard constant step ray marching. Args: rayorigin (vec3): The starting point of the ray. raydirection (vec3): The normalized direction of the ray. stepsize (float): The fixed distance to advance per iteration (Delta t). maxdist (float): The maximum distance the ray can travel. maxsteps (int): The maximum number of iterations allowed. epsilon (float): The threshold for considering a hit (for SDFs, <= 0 is hit). Returns: float or None: The distance to the intersection, or None if no hit is found. """ t = 0.0 # Accumulated distance k = 0 # Step counter # scenesdf(p) evaluates the scene's signed distance or density field at point p def scenesdf(p): # Implementation depends on scene definition (e.g., SDF primitives, volume grid) pass while k < maxsteps: # 1. Calculate current position currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 2. Evaluate scene function value = scenesdf(currentpos) # 3. Check for intersection if value <= epsilon: # Hit detected # Optional: Refine position using midpoint approximation hitdistance = t - 0.5 stepsize return hitdistance # 4. Check for escape if t > maxdist: return None # 5. Advance ray by constant step t += stepsize # 6. Increment step counter k += 1 # Max steps reached without hit return None An optimization for sampling within the volume to determine the entry point into solid matter more accurately. It mitigates the inefficiency of constant step marching in large empty spaces by first taking large steps to find the approximate boundary, then switching to smaller constant steps to pinpoint the entry. A modification of Evans' method using a ray equation for sampling, allowing for constant step marching along the normal to compute ambient occlusion. It samples along the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the hit point \mathbf{x} using the ray equation \mathbf{r}n(k) = \mathbf{x} + k \Delta t \mathbf{n}. The occlusion is calculated as AO = 1 - \frac{1}{2} \sum{k=1}^{k{max}} \frac{1}{k} (k \Delta t - f(\mathbf{r}n(k))). Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of steps taken. Since \Delta t is constant, N \approx t{max} / \Delta t. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as only the current position and accumulated distance need to be stored. Performance: Faster to implement and compute per step than adaptive methods because it avoids branching based on SDF values for step size calculation. However, it is less efficient in terms of total samples for scenes with large empty regions, as it samples uniformly regardless of distance to geometry. Strengths: Simple implementation, predictable memory usage, no risk of infinite loops due to oscillating step sizes (if N{max} is enforced). Limitations: Prone to overshooting thin geometry if \Delta t is too large; requires manual tuning of \Delta t for different scene scales; less accurate than Sphere Tracing for SDFs. When to Use: Suitable for simple scenes, volumetric rendering where uniform sampling is acceptable, or when hardware constraints favor fixed-step loops over dynamic branching. When Not to Use: When rendering complex SDF scenes with high-frequency details or large empty spaces, where adaptive stepping (Sphere Tracing) is preferred. Standard Constant Step Ray Marching originated as a fundamental technique for rendering implicit surfaces before the widespread adoption of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for adaptive stepping. It is closely related to early ray tracing methods for implicit curves and surfaces, such as those described by Taubin. The method is often contrasted with "Sphere Tracing" (Hart 1995), which uses the SDF value as the step size to guarantee convergence. name: Iteration-Based Coloring
head: Iteration count, Step count coloring [S1, unofficial]
body: Iteration-Based Coloring is a rendering technique where the final pixel color is determined by the number of raymarching steps taken before the ray terminates (either by hitting a surface or reaching a maximum step count). It visualizes the computational intensity of the raymarch, highlighting regions where the ray traveled further or required more sampling iterations. Unlike standard shading which relies on material properties and lighting, this method maps algorithmic performance metrics directly to visual output. Inputs: Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Implicit surface function or voxel data structure. Maximum step count limit (N{max}). Fixed step size (\Delta t). Outputs: Pixel color value. Data Structures: Step counter: An integer tracking the number of iterations performed for the current ray. Termination flag: Boolean indicating if the ray has hit a surface or exceeded N{max}. Steps: 1. Initialize the ray for the current pixel using the camera parameters. 2. Initialize step counter k = 0. 3. While k < N{max} and ray is not terminated: a. Evaluate the distance to the nearest surface (or check voxel occupancy) at the current ray position. b. Advance the ray along its direction by the step size \Delta t. c. Increment k. 4. Determine the color based on the final value of k. Formulas: The color intensity C is mapped linearly to the step count k. A common normalization maps k to the range [0, 255]: C = \left\lfloor \frac{k}{N{max}} \times 255 \right\rfloor Where: k is the number of steps taken. N{max} is the maximum allowed steps. Parameters: N{max}: The maximum number of steps. A typical value cited is 64. \Delta t: The fixed step size. Typically set to 1.0 for standard constant step marching. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Termination: Rays that never hit a surface (e.g., background) will always result in N{max} steps, returning the maximum intensity value. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may cause the ray to overshoot or undershoot the surface slightly, requiring a small epsilon threshold for hit detection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterationbasedcoloring(rayorigin, raydirection, surfacefunction, maxsteps, stepsize=1.0): """ Renders a single pixel using iteration-based coloring. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray. raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. surfacefunction: callable, returns distance to surface at a point. maxsteps: int, maximum number of raymarching iterations. stepsize: float, fixed distance to advance per step. Returns: int: Step count taken before termination. """ currentpos = rayorigin stepcount = 0 for i in range(maxsteps): dist = surfacefunction(currentpos) if dist < 1e-4: return stepcount currentpos = currentpos + raydirection stepsize stepcount += 1 return stepcount A variant that visualizes geometric depth by mapping the z-coordinate of the first surface hit to grayscale intensity, rather than computational step count. It differs from its parent by encoding spatial distance instead of algorithmic intensity. Time Complexity: O(N \times S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of steps per ray. The complexity is dominated by the raymarching loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as only the step count and current position need to be stored. Performance: Visualizes computational intensity, making it useful for debugging raymarchers or creating abstract visual effects. It does not provide physically accurate shading. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides immediate feedback on raymarch efficiency and surface proximity. Limitations: Does not convey material properties or lighting. The technique was described in a 2013 blog post on raymarching distance fields, where it was presented as a simple way to "spice up" black and white renders by visualizing where the most intensive portions of the image are. name: Depth Rendering
body: Depth Rendering is a visualization technique that maps ray traversal metrics to grayscale intensity, providing a direct representation of distance or computational depth. The source implementation computes intensity from the number of traversal steps, while the accompanying documentation describes an alternative mapping using the hit position's z-coordinate. Inputs: tree: Voxel data structure containing spatial bounds tree->min[2] and tree->max[2] along the depth axis, and side length tree->gridlength. rc: Render context providing pixel dimension rc.ny (assumed square) and ray generation rc.getRayForPixel(x, y) returning origin o and direction d. texturearray: Output buffer of size ny ny 4 (RGBA), where each pixel occupies 4 unsigned chars. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o (vec3) and direction d (vec3, typically normalized). Voxel Grid: Uniform grid spanning [0, gridlength) in each axis. Parameters: gridlength: Side length of the voxel grid, used for normalization. factor: Normalized intensity value in range [0, 1]. Algorithm: 1. Initialize OpenMP threads equal to the number of CPU processors. 2. Parallelize the outer pixel loop over y. 3. For each pixel (x, y): a. Compute index = y (ny 4) + x 4. b. Initialize ray traverser with tree, o, and d. c. Traverse the tree: i. While not terminated: If leaf node has data, break loop. Else, call t.step(). d. Get hit position pos = t.getCurrentPosition(). e. Compute intensity from step count: factor = \frac{stepcount}{\log2(gridlength)} (Note: The source notes describe an alternative position-based factor factor = \frac{|pos[2]|}{|tree->max[2]| - |tree->min[2]|}, but the executable code uses step count.) f. Compute grayscale color: val = 255 \times (1 - factor) g. Write to texturearray: texturearray[index] = val texturearray[index+1] = val texturearray[index+2] = val texturearray[index+3] = 1 (Alpha) Pseudocode: Unverified code. Termination: If the ray escapes the tree without hitting a surface, the loop terminates when bounds are exceeded. The code sets alpha to 1 regardless of hit status. Coordinate System: The notes' formula uses abs(pos[2]), implying depth is the Z-axis. Standard graphics APIs often use Y or -Z for depth. A variant that normalizes the logarithmic distance traveled by the ray to the range [0, 1], where brighter pixels indicate further travel distance. It calculates distance d = |pi - p0|, computes \log(d), and normalizes it. This helps visualize depth over large ranges where linear mapping would compress distant details. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of steps per ray. Parallelized with OpenMP. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output texture array. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides immediate visual feedback on object proximity. Limitations: Does not account for surface orientation or lighting; linear mapping may not be perceptually uniform.
