name: Depth Shading
head: Depth-Only Shading
body: Depth shading is a 2D discrete shading technique that computes pixel intensity solely from the depth coordinate of the closest surface voxel, without considering surface orientation. It differs from gradient-based methods by ignoring normals, resulting in a simple inverse-depth mapping where closer features appear brighter and distant features appear darker. Inputs: 1. A depth shaded pre-image: a 2D array (Z-buffer) where each pixel (x, y) stores the distance to the closest non-empty surface voxel along the viewing ray. 2. A second framebuffer for storing the pre-image data. Outputs: 1. A 2D intensity image where pixel brightness is determined by the stored depth value. Data Structures: Z-buffer: A 2D array of depth values where each element stores a scalar distance z to the closest non-empty voxel. Steps: 1. Ray Casting / Data Traversal: Execute the underlying ray casting algorithm to identify surface voxels and yield their depth coordinates along the viewing axis. 2. Depth Storage: For each pixel (x, y), store the distance to the closest non-empty voxel found along the viewing ray into the Z-buffer at index (x, y). 3. Intensity Calculation: Compute the output intensity I(x, y) for each pixel based on its depth value z = D(x, y). The intensity is inversely proportional to the depth: I(x, y) \propto \frac{1}{z} In the specific implementation described by, this relationship is discretized by mapping the depth coordinate to one of 128 possible values. 4. Lookup Table Application: Populate a hardware output lookup table with intensity values calculated as a function of these 128 depth levels, then apply the table to the Z-buffer to generate the final shaded image. Pitfalls: Loss of Detail: Because surface orientation (normals) is not considered, surface discontinuities and object boundaries are lost. Complexity: The shading step runs in O(1) time per pixel once the Z-buffer is populated, as it only requires a table lookup. Performance: The shading stage is computationally inexpensive because it relies on a precomputed lookup table rather than per-pixel geometric calculations. Strengths: Simple to implement; requires minimal additional computation after depth acquisition; effective for highlighting proximity to the viewer. Limitations: Lacks geometric detail due to the absence of normal vectors; produces flat, silhouette-like shading. It is described as a "depth shaded pre-image" technique, serving as a foundational step before more complex shading methods like binary gradient shading. It is categorized under 2D discrete shading techniques in volume visualization literature. name: Step Size Selection
head: Constant Step Ray Marching, Constant step marching, Fixed-step volume rendering, Ray Marching with Fixed Step Count, Simple ray marching, Step Size Determination, Step Size Heuristic, Volumetric Raymarching with Constant Step
body: Step Size Selection determines the distance between consecutive samples (\Delta t) along a ray during volume rendering, balancing rendering speed against the accuracy of the Riemann sum approximation of the light transport integral. Unlike adaptive methods that vary step size based on local density or geometry, this method employs a fixed or heuristically derived constant step count, simplifying implementation but risking aliasing if the step is too large for the scene's frequency content. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Entry distance t{min} and exit distance t{max} of the volume bounding box. Camera Field of View (FOV) in radians. Image resolution (width W, height H). Volume dataset (3D texture or implicit function). Parameters: NumSteps (fixed iteration count) or STEPSIZE (fixed distance). Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity (transmittance) for the pixel. Ray State: A vector \mathbf{p} representing the current position along the ray. Accumulator: A scalar or vector (e.g., result) storing the accumulated color/opacity. Step Vector: A precomputed vector \mathbf{s} representing the displacement per step. 1. Ray Initialization: Determine the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. For screen-space rendering, transform screen coordinates to world space using the inverse Model-View-Projection matrix. 2. Step Size Determination: Calculate the step size \Delta t. This can be: Fixed by a user-defined constant STEPSIZE. Derived from a fixed NumSteps over the total ray length L = t{max} - t{min}. Heuristically estimated based on the projected pixel size at t{min}. 3. Iteration Loop: For i from 0 to N-1 (where N is NumSteps): a. Sample: Evaluate the volume density \sigma at the current position \mathbf{p}. b. Composite: Update the accumulator using front-to-back compositing: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - C{in}) \cdot \sigma \cdot \Delta t (Note: Specific implementations may normalize \sigma by N or scale it, e.g., multiplying by 4.0, depending on data range.) c. Advance: Update position \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \Delta t. d. Boundary Check: Verify if \mathbf{p} remains within the volume bounds (e.g., unit cube [-1, 1]). If outside, add zero contribution and continue the loop. 4. Termination: Return the accumulated color. If early termination is used, stop if accumulated opacity reaches 1.0. Projected Pixel Width Heuristic: \text{projPixWidth} = 2 \cdot \tan\left(\frac{\text{fov}}{2}\right) \cdot t{min} Where \text{fov} is in radians and t{min} is the distance to the volume entry. Fixed Step from Count: \Delta t = \frac{t{max} - t{min}}{\text{NumSteps}} Sphere Hit Test (for implicit volumes): \text{distance}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{C}) < R Where \mathbf{C} is the sphere center and R is the radius. NumSteps: Fixed number of samples per ray. Typical value: 64. STEPSIZE: Fixed distance units per step. Typical value: 0.01. fov: Field of view angle. Typically in degrees in code, converted to radians for trigonometric functions. tmin: Distance to volume entry. Centre, Radius: Sphere geometry parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatedensity(pos): # Evaluates volume density at pos pass def stepsizeselection(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, numsteps): # 1. Calculate step size based on fixed count totaldistance = tmax - tmin stepsize = totaldistance / numsteps # 2. Initialize state currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection tmin accumulatedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # 3. Iterate for i in range(numsteps): # Boundary check: unit cube [-1, 1] using strict inequality inside = (-1.0 < currentpos.x < 1.0) and \ (-1.0 < currentpos.y < 1.0) and \ (-1.0 < currentpos.z < 1.0) if inside and accumulatedopacity < 1.0: # Map to [0, 1] for texture sampling texcoord = (currentpos + 1.0) 0.5 # Sample density, scale by 4.0, normalize by numsteps density = evaluatedensity(texcoord) samplecontribution = density 4.0 / numsteps # Front-to-back compositing accumulatedcolor += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) samplecontribution accumulatedopacity += samplecontribution # Advance ray currentpos += raydirection stepsize return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity Aliasing/Filtering: If STEPSIZE is too large, small frequency features (clouds, smoke) are missed, causing a filtering issue. Shadow Misses: Large step sizes may skip over small solid objects casting shadows on the volume, missing shadow effects. Boundary Exclusion: Strict inequality checks (e.g., < 1.0) may exclude points exactly at the boundary, affecting the last few samples. Data Scaling: Texture sampling assumes specific data ranges (e.g., [0,1]); incorrect scaling (e.g., missing the 4.0 factor in some implementations) leads to incorrect density values. This method normalizes the volume dataset's physical dimensions to a unit cube to ensure consistent sampling density regardless of resolution or aspect ratio. It computes a base step size from the maximum volume dimension and an optional axis-wise scaling factor. Choose this when rendering arbitrary voxel grids that need uniform visual density across different aspect ratios. This method scales the step size based on the viewing angle relative to the volume, using a cone angle parameter to balance speed and quality in atmospheric clouds. It varies the step count dynamically based on geometry orientation, unlike standard constant step marching. Choose this for horizon views where more steps are needed compared to top-down views. A Monte Carlo importance sampling technique that constructs a PDF matching the exponential transmittance component to cancel it analytically. It treats the integration domain as trapezoidal segments defined by the bounding box corners, allowing direct sampling of free path length. Choose this when avoiding fixed-step iteration errors in complex light transport is required. A scheme where the step size \tau grows exponentially with distance t along the ray: \tau:= t/256, clamped to [\text{diag}/1024, \text{size} \times \text{diag}/1024]. This allows computation cost to grow logarithmically with scene diameter while maintaining quality. Choose this for large scenes where uniform sampling would be prohibitively expensive, accepting a variable number of steps. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the fixed number of steps per ray. Total time is proportional to pixel count \times N. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, excluding the volume texture storage. Performance: Fast and predictable, as it avoids branching for adaptive decisions or complex distance queries. However, it may waste samples in empty regions or undersample dense regions compared to adaptive methods. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structures, predictable memory usage. Limitations: Prone to aliasing if step size is not carefully chosen relative to scene scale and pixel size; inefficient for large empty spaces. When to Use: Uniform media, simple volumes, or when implementation simplicity is prioritized over optimal sampling efficiency. When Not to Use: Complex scenes with high-frequency details requiring adaptive sampling, or very large scenes where exponential or sparse stepping is needed. Originating from early volumetric rendering techniques, constant step ray marching was popularized in tutorials and real-time graphics for its simplicity. It is a core component of many volume rendering pipelines, often serving as the baseline before introducing adaptive or sparse techniques. The method is widely used in real-time applications like procedural terrain and cloud rendering, where fixed-step approximations provide sufficient visual quality with low computational overhead. name: Raycasting Step Size & Aspect Ratio Normalization
head: Aspect Ratio Normalized Ray Marching, Fixed-Step Ray Marching Setup, Fixed-Step Ray Marching with Steps Per Voxel, Fixed-Steps, Normalized Step Size Calculation, Step Size Calculation, Step-based voxel raymarching
body: This method establishes a uniform step size for volume rendering by normalizing the volume dataset's physical dimensions to a unit cube, ensuring consistent sampling density regardless of the volume's aspect ratio or resolution. It sets itself apart from adaptive methods like Adaptive Step Size Calculation by using constant intervals rather than density-based acceleration, and from Dartmouth Distance Sampling by relying on fixed increments rather than analytical intersection math. Inputs: Volume dimensions: W (width), H (height), D (depth) in voxels. Optional aspect ratio scaling factors: \mathbf{a} = (ax, ay, az). Step scale multiplier: s{scale}. Maximum ray distance: d{max}. Camera ray origin: \mathbf{p}0. Camera ray direction: \mathbf{d} (normalized). Outputs: Step size vector: \mathbf{s}. Marching results: Hit coordinates and previous coordinates. Data Structures: stepSize: A 3-component vector (float32) representing the distance to advance along each axis. currpos: A 3-component vector (float32) tracking the current ray position. Steps: 1. Calculate Max Dimension: Determine the largest dimension of the volume dataset. M = \max(W, H, D) 2. Compute Base Step Size: Calculate the step size for each axis. The sources provide two variations for this calculation. Variation A (Simple Normalization): \mathbf{s}{base} = \left( \frac{1}{M}, \frac{1}{M}, \frac{1}{M} \right) Variation B (Aspect-Ratio Aware): If aspect ratios \mathbf{a} are provided, compute a scaling factor to map arbitrary dimensions into a unit cube. \mathbf{s}{base} = \left( \frac{1}{W \cdot (M/W)}, \frac{1}{H \cdot (M/H)}, \frac{1}{D \cdot (M/D)} \right) Note: In Variation B, the term (M/W) effectively normalizes the axis length relative to the max dimension. If aspect ratios are used to adjust the scale factor, the formula becomes: \text{scaleFactor} = \frac{1}{(1 \cdot M) / (\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{a})} where \mathbf{d} is the dimension vector (W, H, D). 3. Apply Step Scale: Multiply the base step size by the user-defined scale factor s{scale} (default 1.0). \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}{base} \cdot s{scale} The step scale is typically clamped to a minimum of 0.1f to prevent excessively small steps. 4. Initialize Ray Marching: Set current position \mathbf{p}{curr} = \mathbf{p}0. Normalize the look vector \mathbf{d}. If \|\mathbf{d}\| < 10^{-5}, terminate immediately. Calculate maximum iterations: N{max} = \lceil d{max} / \|\mathbf{s}\| \rceil. Note: Some implementations use M \cdot (1/s{scale}) \cdot 2 as a heuristic for iterations. 5. Marching Loop: For i from 0 to N{max}: Check voxel at \mathbf{p}{curr}. If a solid voxel is detected, return (\mathbf{p}{curr}, \mathbf{p}{prev}) and stop. Store \mathbf{p}{prev} = \mathbf{p}{curr}. Advance position: \mathbf{p}{curr} = \mathbf{p}{curr} + \mathbf{s} \cdot \|\mathbf{d}\| (or simply \mathbf{p}{curr} + \mathbf{s} if \mathbf{d} is already normalized and \mathbf{s} is direction-agnostic). If \mathbf{p}{curr} exceeds bounds or distance limit, terminate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def calculatestepsize(width: int, height: int, depth: int, stepscale: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray: """ Calculate normalized step size vector for ray marching. Based on. """ # 1. Calculate max dimension maxdim = max(width, height, depth) if maxdim == 0: return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # 2. Compute base step size (Variation B from) # Note: The formula 1.0 / (dim (maxdim / dim)) simplifies to 1.0 / maxdim # However, we retain the structure if aspect ratios are intended to be applied later. # For pure normalization without aspect ratios, this is uniform. stepx = 1.0 / (width (maxdim / width)) stepy = 1.0 / (height (maxdim / height)) stepz = 1.0 / (depth (maxdim / depth)) stepsize = np.array([stepx, stepy, stepz], dtype=np.float32) # 3. Apply step scale stepsize = stepscale # Clamp minimum step scale if necessary (implementation detail from) # stepsize = np.maximum(stepsize, 0.1) # Usually applied to scale factor, not step directly return stepsize def performraycast( startpos: np.ndarray, lookvector: np.ndarray, stepsize: np.ndarray, maxdist: float = 8.0, voxelchecker=None) -> tuple: """ Perform fixed-step ray marching. Based on. """ # Normalize look vector norm = np.linalg.norm(lookvector) if norm < 1e-5: return None direction = lookvector / norm # Initialize currpos = startpos.copy() prevpos = startpos.copy() # Calculate max iterations based on maxdist and step magnitude # Using the magnitude of the step size vector as the increment distance stepmag = np.linalg.norm(stepsize) if stepmag == 0: return None maxiterations = int(maxdist / stepmag) + 1 for in range(maxiterations): # Check voxel at current position # voxelchecker should return True if solid voxel is detected if voxelchecker is not None and voxelchecker(currpos): return (currpos, prevpos) prevpos = currpos.copy() # Advance along the direction by the step size # Note: stepsize is a vector, direction is a vector. # In many implementations, stepsize is isotropic or applied along the ray direction. # Based on, it advances by stepsize along the normalized look vector. # If stepsize is a scalar magnitude, it would be: currpos += direction stepsize # If stepsize is a vector representing the max axis step, it needs projection. # The sources imply a scalar stepsize or a vector applied directly. # Assuming stepsize is the magnitude to advance per step along the ray: currpos = currpos + direction stepmag return None Parameters: fixedStepSize: Boolean uniform enabling fixed step size ray marching. Set to true. stepsPerVoxel: Integer uniform controlling ray step granularity relative to voxel size. Typical value is 2, meaning each ray step covers half a voxel. stepScale: Multiplier for the base step size. Clamped to a minimum of 0.1f. aspectRatios: vec3 defining relative scaling of volume axes. Clamped to a minimum of vec3(0). maxdist: Maximum distance the ray travels. Typically 8.0 blocks. stepsize: Increment distance. Typically 0.1 blocks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Dimensions: If W, H, or D is 0, division by zero occurs in step size calculation. Guard against this. Degenerate Ray: If the look vector norm is near zero, the ray direction is undefined. Return immediately. Precision: Using float32 for positions and step sizes is standard, but accumulation of error over many steps may require periodic re-normalization or double precision for long rays. Aspect Ratio Distortion: Without aspect ratio normalization, non-cubic volumes will have stretched sampling, leading to aliasing or gaps. Uniform Ray Marching is a sampling strategy that generates 3D sample positions along rays within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a fixed spacing between consecutive samples. It serves as a debug rendering mode for direct atlas sampling without brick traversal, a PyTorch-native fallback for environments lacking custom CUDA extensions, and a dense uniform sampler for Line-of-Sight (LOS) integral visualization. It sets itself apart from adaptive methods like NeRF Ray Marching Optimizations by using constant intervals rather than density-based acceleration, and from Oversampled 3D Ray March by not enforcing strict slab ownership at LOD boundaries. Calculates a scaling factor for ray marching step sizes based on camera FOV and pixel tolerance to ensure consistent visual quality across resolutions. Formula: F = \frac{1}{2 \tan(\frac{\theta}{2})} \cdot \frac{Wy}{\text{pixelTolerance}} where \theta is vertical FOV, Wy is screen height, and pixelTolerance is in pixels. Parameters: fovy: Vertical field of view in radians. pixelTolerance: Desired pixel tolerance for step sizing. screenDivisor: Resolution divisor (default 1.0f, or 8.0f for min-depth pass). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps along the ray. N is determined by d{max} / \text{step\size}. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, excluding the volume texture storage. Performance: Fixed-step marching is computationally predictable and easy to parallelize on GPUs. However, it is less efficient than adaptive methods in sparse volumes because it samples empty space uniformly. Strengths: Simple to implement, deterministic, no branching overhead for step size adjustment. Limitations: Inefficient for large empty regions; requires careful tuning of stepScale to balance quality and speed. When to Use: Debugging, uniform density volumes, or when hardware lacks advanced branching capabilities. When Not to Use: Sparse volumes where adaptive methods like Adaptive Step Size Calculation would skip empty space efficiently. Originating from early voxel-based rendering techniques, this method was popularized in game engines for block-based worlds (e.g., Minecraft-like environments) due to its simplicity and robustness. It is widely used in medical imaging viewers (e.g., qt-viewer-pro) for consistent visualization across different dataset resolutions. The aspect ratio normalization component addresses the issue of distorted sampling in non-cubic volumes, a common problem in medical and scientific datasets. wpop/qt-viewer-pro, https://github.com/wpop/qt-viewer-pro, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) aryaman-gupta/LiV-renderer, https://github.com/aryaman-gupta/LiV-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) herbal1st/pyvorengi-sdk-demo, https://github.com/herbal1st/pyvorengi-sdk-demo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 3D Texture Only interpolates on Y-Axis, https://gamedev.stackexchange.com/questions/166205, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) RvanderLaan/SVDAG-Compression, https://github.com/RvanderLaan/SVDAG-Compression, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Uniform Ray Marching
head: Fixed-Step Ray Marching Setup, Normalized Step Size Calculation, Parallel Ray Sampling (Fallback), Ray-to-Sample Generation, Simple ray marching (debug view), Uniform Ray Marching for Visualization
body: Uniform Ray Marching is a sampling strategy that generates 3D sample positions along rays within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a fixed spacing between consecutive samples. It serves as a debug rendering mode for direct atlas sampling without brick traversal, a PyTorch-native fallback for environments lacking custom CUDA extensions, and a dense uniform sampler for Line-of-Sight (LOS) integral visualization. It sets itself apart from adaptive methods like NeRF Ray Marching Optimizations by using constant intervals rather than density-based acceleration, and from Oversampled 3D Ray March by not enforcing strict slab ownership at LOD boundaries. Inputs: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray origins. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray directions. aabbmin, aabbmax: Vectors defining the AABB boundaries. renderstepsize: Scalar float defining the fixed distance between sample points. rmaxrsun: Optional float specifying an outer sphere radius in solar radii (R{sun}) for clipping. atlasSize: Scalar for volume texture normalization (used in debug/atlas mode). numSteps: Integer specifying the number of steps (alternative input to renderstepsize). Outputs: samplepositions: Tensor of 3D coordinates along the rays. ts: Tensor of segment start times (depths). te: Tensor of segment end times (depths). rayidx: Tensor mapping samples to original rays. valid: Boolean mask indicating rays with valid intersections. Data Structures: Rays are typically stored as (N, 6) arrays where the first 3 columns are origins and the last 3 are directions. Depth values are masked with MAXDEPTH (constant 10000.0) to mark invalid entries before sorting and trimming. Steps: 1. Ray Preparation: Extract origins and directions. Normalize directions and compute inverse directions if using slab-based intersection. 2. AABB Intersection: Compute near (tmin) and far (tmax) intersection distances for each ray against the AABB. Filter rays where tmin < tmax. Initialize a valid mask ok = (tmax > tmin). 3. Optional Sphere Clipping: If rmaxrsun is provided, clip the ray interval to an outer sphere. Calculate coefficients for the quadratic equation |o + t d|^2 = (r{max}/scale)^2: A = \sum (rays\d^2) B = 2.0 \sum (rays\o \cdot rays\d) C = \sum (rays\o^2) - \rho^2 where \rho = r{max\rsun} / aabb\scale. Solve for intersection times t{in} and t{out} using the quadratic formula. Handle numerical safety by clamping A to 10^{-20} and the discriminant disc = B^2 - 4AC to 0.0. Update interval bounds: t{min} = \max(t{min}, t{in}) and t{max} = \min(t{max}, t{out}). Update valid mask: ok = ok & hit. 4. Step Size Calculation: Determine the step size and number of steps. If using renderstepsize: Calculate steps per ray as \lceil (t{max} - t{min}) / render\step\size \rceil, clamped to a minimum of 1. If using numSteps: Calculate stepSize = rayLength / numSteps. 5. Sample Generation: Generate uniform sample points along the valid intervals. Method A (Edge-based): Create linearly spaced points u in [0, 1]. Compute edge coordinates edges = t{min} + (t{max} - t{min}) \cdot u. Flatten to get start times ts and end times te. Method B (Offset-based): Generate delta offsets scaled by MARCHSIZE (or renderstepsize). Add deterministic noise (0.5) or uniform noise [0.01, 0.99] if required. Compute sampled depths and sort them. 6. Position Computation: Compute 3D positions as pos = ori + t \cdot dir. For atlas debugging: Compute UV coordinates as atlasUV = (pos / normalizedSize) + 0.5. 7. Post-Processing: Identify invalid depths by comparing against mindepth and maxdepth. Mask invalid depths with MAXDEPTH and sort them to the end. Trim outputs to nummaxsteps (maximum valid steps per ray). Construct rayidx mapping each sample to its source ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformraymarching(rayso, raysd, aabbmin, aabbmax, renderstepsize, rmaxrsun=None, aabbscale=1.0): """ Generates uniform samples along rays within an AABB. rayso: (N, 3) raysd: (N, 3) aabbmin: (3,) aabbmax: (3,) """ rayso = torch.astensor(rayso, dtype=torch.float32) raysd = torch.astensor(raysd, dtype=torch.float32) aabbmin = torch.astensor(aabbmin, dtype=torch.float32) aabbmax = torch.astensor(aabbmax, dtype=torch.float32) N = rayso.shape[0] # 1. AABB Intersection # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero invdir = torch.where(raysd.abs() > 1e-8, 1.0 / raysd, 0.0) t1 = (aabbmin - rayso) invdir t2 = (aabbmax - rayso) invdir tmin = torch.maximum(t1, t2).min(dim=1).values tmax = torch.minimum(t1, t2).max(dim=1).values validmask = tmax > tmin tmin = tmin.maskedfill(~validmask, 0.0) tmax = tmax.maskedfill(~validmask, 0.0) # 2. Optional Sphere Clipping if rmaxrsun is not None: rho = rmaxrsun / aabbscale A = (raysd raysd).sum(dim=1) B = 2.0 (rayso raysd).sum(dim=1) C = (rayso rayso).sum(dim=1) - rho rho A = torch.maximum(A, torch.tensor(1e-20)) disc = BB - 4.0AC disc = torch.maximum(disc, torch.tensor(0.0)) sqrtdisc = torch.sqrt(disc) tin = (-B - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) tout = (-B + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) tmin = torch.maximum(tmin, tin) tmax = torch.minimum(tmax, tout) hitsphere = (disc >= 0) & (tmax > tmin) validmask = validmask & hitsphere # 3. Step Size and Count raylengths = tmax - tmin nsteps = torch.ceil(raylengths / renderstepsize).long() nsteps = torch.maximum(nsteps, torch.oneslike(nsteps)) maxsteps = nsteps.max().item() idx = torch.arange(maxsteps, device=rayso.device).unsqueeze(0) nstepsexp = nsteps.unsqueeze(1) stepmask = idx < nstepsexp ts = tmin.unsqueeze(1) + idx.float() renderstepsize ts = ts.maskedfill(~stepmask, 0.0) te = ts + renderstepsize te = torch.minimum(te, tmax.unsqueeze(1)) tsflat = ts[stepmask] teflat = te[stepmask] rayindices = torch.arange(N, device=rayso.device).repeatinterleave(nsteps) # 4. Zero Direction Components: Division by zero in inverse direction calculation must be guarded, typically by clamping the denominator or using a safe division function. Enforces strict slab ownership and corrected exit-face probing to resolve LOD boundary discontinuities. Choose when visual artifacts from empty-space skipping are present. Replaces fixed intervals with adaptive step sizes (exponential stepping, empty space skipping). Choose for performance optimization in NeRFs. Samples only within intersected voxels with probabilities proportional to distance. Choose for sparse voxel fields with variable intersection counts. name: Oversampled 3D Ray March
head: slab tiling fix
body: Oversampled 3D Ray March is a sampling strategy for distance-field ray marching that resolves discontinuities at Level-of-Detail (LOD) boundaries by ensuring every fine sample owns the slab it represents as its midpoint, clipped to the brick's segment. It solves the problem of unprobed material at chunk exit faces caused by previous empty-space skip logic, which led to zero contribution and visual artifacts. It sets itself apart from standard uniform marching by enforcing strict slab ownership and corrected exit-face probing, and from NeRF Ray Marching Optimizations by focusing on geometric tiling correctness rather than density-based acceleration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D, brick segment bounds [0, len] along the ray, and LOD interface boundaries. Output: A sequence of sample positions and associated density/color values that tile exactly across LOD boundaries without gaps. Data Structures: Sample Point: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the position in world space. Slab: Defined by the interval [t{start}, t{end}] along the ray parameter t. Steps: 1. Calculate Ray Segment: Determine the intersection of the ray with the current brick's AABB to find the entry t{entry} and exit t{exit} parameters. The segment length is len = t{exit} - t{entry}. 2. Determine Sample Count: Calculate the number of fine samples N required based on the desired spatial resolution or step size s. N = \lceil len / s \rceil. 3. Compute Slab Thickness: The thickness of each slab is \Delta t = len / N. 4. Assign Slab Ownership: For each sample index i from 0 to N-1: The slab for sample i is defined by the interval [t{entry} + i \cdot \Delta t, t{entry} + (i+1) \cdot \Delta t]. The sample position Pi is the midpoint of this slab: Pi = O + D \cdot (t{entry} + (i + 0.5) \cdot \Delta t) This midpoint is clipped to the brick's segment to ensure it lies within [t{entry}, t{exit}]. 5. Correct Empty-Space Skip Probing: When skipping empty space, the probe must extend one stride past each cube's exit face. This ensures that material in the last sub-stride is probed, preventing the cube from contributing zero and eliminating discontinuities at exit faces. If using a stride S{stride}, the probe position is P{probe} = P{current} + D \cdot S{stride}. The next iteration starts from this probe position, ensuring coverage of the boundary region. Parameters: Step size s: Determined by the LOD level and brick size. Not given in the sources. Stride for empty-space skip: The previous implementation strode 1.9 level voxels, which was incorrect. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: LOD Interfaces: Slab thicknesses must tile [0, len] exactly at LOD interfaces to avoid gaps or overlaps. Exit Face Discontinuities: Failing to probe past the exit face leaves material unprobed, causing zero contribution and visual discontinuities. Precision: Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient to handle small slab thicknesses at high LODs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def oversampledraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, brickentryt, brickexitt, stepsize): """ Performs oversampled 3D ray marching with correct slab tiling and exit-face probing. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray (normalized). brickentryt: float, t parameter where ray enters the brick. brickexitt: float, t parameter where ray exits the brick. stepsize: float, desired distance between sample midpoints. Returns: list of 3D vectors, sample positions. """ length = brickexitt - brickentryt if length <= 0: return [] numsamples = math.ceil(length / stepsize) slabthickness = length / numsamples samples = [] for i in range(numsamples): tmid = brickentryt + (i + 0.5) slabthickness tclipped = max(brickentryt, min(tmid, brickexitt)) samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection tclipped samples.append(samplepos) return samples def correctemptyspaceskip(rayorigin, raydirection, currentt, stride): """ Calculates the next probe position for empty-space skipping, ensuring one stride past the exit face is probed. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. currentt: float, current t parameter. stride: float, distance to skip. Returns: float, next t parameter. """ nextt = currentt + stride return nextt A raymarching loop that uses stable, uniform linear marching between bounding bounds to eliminate artifacts like spots, missing clouds, noise, and banding, replacing unstable backing-up/bifurcated stepping loops. It corrects empty space skipping using a robust positive-step bifurcated step size logic to handle coordinate jumping and infinite loops. Choose this when rendering low-resolution volumes where unstable stepping causes visible artifacts. It is a variant focused on stability in low-resolution contexts, whereas Oversampled 3D Ray March focuses on LOD tiling correctness. Measured Performance: CPU replica worst-case two-cube split error: -3.99% to +0.68%. Browser A/B (HOA heart, pinned L4, 64 chunks, WebGPU): whole-image TV -2.7% x / -2.2% y. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Eliminates discontinuities at LOD boundaries and exit faces; ensures exact tiling of slabs. Limitations: Requires careful calculation of slab thickness and midpoint positioning; may increase sample count slightly. When to Use: Use when rendering multi-LOD volumes where discontinuities at chunk boundaries are visible. Use when empty-space skipping causes artifacts due to unprobed material at exit faces. When Not to Use: Not needed for single-level rendering, which takes an exact path and is bit-identical to previous methods. Not needed if high-resolution rendering does not exhibit LOD-related artifacts. Originated in the context of streamed multi-LOD rendering fixes, specifically addressing ray-march ringing and slab tiling issues in the Niivue project. It was developed to correct errors in empty-space skip logic that caused material to be unprobed at chunk exit faces. The method was implemented and tested on both CPU and WebGPU backends, with measured improvements in visual consistency. feat(niivue): streamed multi-LOD rendering fixes, LOD compensation, budget plans, and block inspection, https://github.com/niivue/mono/pull/138, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Optimize cloud rendering with eroded Voronoi weather maps and stable linear raymarching, https://github.com/ricecake/boidsish/pull/679, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: NeRF Ray Marching Optimizations
head: Accelerated NeRF Ray Marching, Occupancy Grids for Empty Space Skipping
body: A set of three techniques to optimize NeRF ray marching performance with imperceptible error: exponential stepping, empty space skipping, and sample compaction. It builds on Uniform Ray Marching by replacing fixed uniform intervals with adaptive step sizes and skipping empty regions via multiscale occupancy grids. Inputs: Ray origin o, ray direction d, scene bounding box size s (largest axis), NeRF model f{\theta}, current training step count. Outputs: Sample positions along the ray, transmittance, accumulated color. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy Grids: A cascade of K grids. Each grid has resolution 128^3. Cells are laid out in Morton (z-curve) order. Each cell stores occupancy as a single bit. 2. Density Grids: A second set of K grids with the same layout, storing full-precision floating-point density values. Parameters: Fixed step size for unit cube scenes: \Delta t = \sqrt{3}/1024. Transmittance stopping threshold: 10^{-4}. Number of grids K: 1 for synthetic NeRF scenes; K \in [1, 5] for larger real-world scenes. Grid resolution: 128^3. Update frequency: Every 16 training iterations. Density decay factor: 0.95. Occupancy threshold t: 0.01 \cdot 1024/\sqrt{3}. Number of candidate cells M: K \cdot 128^3 for first 256 steps; K \cdot 128^3 / 2 for subsequent steps. Steps: 1. Step Size Selection: If the scene is bounded to the unit cube [0,1]^3, set \Delta t = \sqrt{3}/1024. Otherwise, set \Delta t = t/256, where t is the current distance along the ray. Clamp \Delta t to [-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1024} \cdot s, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{1024} \cdot s], where s is the size of the largest axis of the scene's bounding box. 2. Grid Query: For a sample position x, determine which grid to query. Among the grids covering x, select the finest one with cell side-length larger than the current step size \Delta t. The domain for grid k is [-2^{k-1}+0.5, 2^{k-1}+0.5]^3, centered around (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). 3. Empty Space Skipping: Query the occupancy bit of the cell containing x in the selected grid. If the bit is low (0), skip the sample. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize transmittance T = 1.0. While T > 10^{-4}: Calculate next sample position x = o + t \cdot d. Check occupancy. If occupied, query NeRF model f{\theta}(x) to get density \sigma and color C. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t). Accumulate color: C{out} \leftarrow C{out} + T \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t)) \cdot C. Update distance: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. Recalculate \Delta t based on new t if using exponential stepping. 5. Grid Update (Every 16 iterations): Decay density values in all cells by a factor of 0.95. Sample M candidate cells: If training step < 256: Sample M = K \cdot 128^3 cells uniformly without repetition. If training step \ge 256: Set M = K \cdot 128^3 / 2. Partition into two sets: First M/2 cells sampled uniformly among all cells. Remaining M/2 cells sampled via rejection sampling restricted to currently occupied cells. For each candidate cell, set its density value to \max(\text{current}, \text{NeRF density at random location in cell}). Update occupancy bits by thresholding density with t = 0.01 \cdot 1024/\sqrt{3}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def morton3d(x, y, z): code = 0 for i in range(7): code |= (x & (1 << i)) << (2 i) code |= (y & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 1) code |= (z & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 2) return code def mortondecode3d(code, bits=7): x, y, z = 0, 0, 0 for i in range(bits): x |= (code & (1 << (3 i))) << i y |= (code & (1 << (3 i + 1))) << i z |= (code & (1 << (3 i + 2))) << i return x, y, z def samplepointincell(grididx, cellidx, resolution=128): x, y, z = mortondecode3d(cellidx) k = grididx + 1 minval = -2(k-1) + 0.5 width = 2k cellsize = width / resolution return (minval + x cellsize + random.random() cellsize, minval + y cellsize + random.random() cellsize, minval + z cellsize + random.random() cellsize) def queryoccupancygrid(x, grids, stepsize): bestk = -1 for kidx in range(len(grids) - 1, -1, -1): k = kidx + 1 minval = -2(k-1) + 0.5 width = 2k if not (minval <= x[0] <= minval + width and minval <= x[1] <= minval + width and minval <= x[2] <= minval + width): continue cellside = width / 128.0 if cellside > stepsize: bestk = kidx break if bestk == -1: return 0 k = bestk + 1 minval = -2(k-1) + 0.5 width = 2k cellside = width / 128.0 u = int((x[0] - minval) / cellside) v = int((x[1] - minval) / cellside) w = int((x[2] - minval) / cellside) u = max(0, min(127, u)) v = max(0, min(127, v)) w = max(0, min(127, w)) idx = morton3d(u, v, w) return grids[bestk][idx] def updategrids(grids, densitygrids, step, kcount, nerfmodel): if step % 16 != 0: return for i in range(kcount): for j in range(len(densitygrids[i])): densitygrids[i][j] = 0.95 if step < 256: M = kcount 1283 selectedindices = random.sample(range(1283), M) else: M = kcount 1283 // 2 selectedindices = random.sample(range(1283), M // 2) occupiedindices = [i for grid in grids for i, bit in enumerate(grid) if bit == 1] occupiedset = set(occupiedindices) for in range(M // 2): while True: cand = random.randint(0, 1283 - 1) if cand in occupiedset: selectedindices.append(cand) break threshold = 0.01 1024 / math.sqrt(3) for idx in selectedindices: grididx = idx // (1283) cellidx = idx % (1283) point = samplepointincell(grididx, cellidx) sigma, = nerfmodel(point) densitygrids[grididx][cellidx] = max(densitygrids[grididx][cellidx], sigma) grids[grididx][cellidx] = 1 if densitygrids[grididx][cellidx] > threshold else 0 def nerfraymarching(o, d, s, nerfmodel, grids, densitygrids, step): t = 0.0 T = 1.0 Cout = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if s <= 1.0: deltat = math.sqrt(3) / 1024.0 else: deltat = math.sqrt(3) / 1024.0 s while T > 1e-4: x = (o[0] + t d[0], o[1] + t d[1], o[2] + t d[2]) occ = queryoccupancygrid(x, grids, deltat) if occ == 1: sigma, C = nerfmodel(x) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma deltat) T = T math.exp(-sigma deltat) Cout[0] += T alpha C[0] Cout[1] += T alpha C[1] Cout[2] += T alpha C[2] t += deltat if s > 1.0: deltat = t / 256.0 maxdeltat = math.sqrt(3) / 1024.0 s deltat = max(0.0, min(maxdeltat, deltat)) return Cout Time Complexity: Computation cost grows only logarithmically in scene diameter due to exponential step size growth. Memory Complexity: K \times 128^3 bits for occupancy grids and K \times 128^3 floats for density grids. Performance: One order of magnitude faster than using triangle BVH for rayshape intersections on RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Imperceptible error, significant speedup for large scenes. Limitations: Requires maintaining and updating grids, which adds complexity. Originated in "Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding" by Müller et al. (2022). Used in Instant-NGP for fast NeRF training and rendering. name: Voxel-Aware Masked Ray Sampling
head: Hierarchical Sampling for Sparse Feature Volume, Inside-Voxel Sampling, NSVF Hierarchical Ray Sampling with Voxel-Aware Masking, NSVF parallel ray sampling, NSVF voxel intersection sampling, Ray-Voxel Intersection Sampling
body: Voxel-Aware Masked Ray Sampling is a ray sampling strategy for sparse voxel fields that ensures all sampling points lie strictly within intersected voxels, preventing invalid "air" samples common in unconstrained hierarchical sampling. It handles variable numbers of voxel intersections per ray by padding and masking tensors, supporting hierarchical sampling ratios where coarse and fine passes are constrained to valid sparse regions. Unlike standard NeRF which uses uniform or stratified sampling along the entire ray, this method restricts integration to occupied sparse voxels, offering significant memory and compute savings for sparse scenes. Inputs: Ray origins and directions for a batch of rays. Sparse voxel grid structure (defining voxel bounds and IDs). Parameters: chunksize (default 4096), maxhits (default 60), raymarchingstepsize (default 0.01), finenumsampleratio (default 0), inversedistancecoarsesampling (default 'none'), backgrounddepth (default 5.0), fixednumsamples (default 0). Outputs: sampleddists: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxsteps) containing distances from camera origin for each sample point. sampledidx: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxsteps) containing voxel IDs for each sample point. sampledmasks: Boolean tensor indicating valid samples. Rendered colors, depths, and other attributes after compositing. Data Structures: 1. Intersection Outputs Dictionary: mindepth: Tensor of shape (numrays,), distance to voxel entry. maxdepth: Tensor of shape (numrays,), distance to voxel exit. intersectedvoxelidx: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxhits), voxel IDs. probs: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxhits), sampling probabilities. steps: Tensor of shape (numrays,), number of samples per ray. 2. All Results Dictionary (Post-processing): missed: Tensor of shape (fullsize,), boolean mask for rays hitting no voxels. colors: Tensor of shape (fullsize, 3). depths: Tensor of shape (fullsize,). normal: Tensor of shape (fullsize, 3) (optional). voxeldepth: Tensor of shape (fullsize,) (optional). voxeledges: Tensor of shape (fullsize, 3) (optional). featn2: Tensor of shape (fullsize,) (optional). Steps: 1. Ray-Voxel Intersection Sampling: Identify pairs P = \{(r, v)\} where ray r intersects voxel v. For each ray, determine the entry (mindepth) and exit (maxdepth) distances in world space, and the corresponding voxel indices. Calculate sampling probabilities probs proportional to the distance within each voxel: \text{dists}i = \max(0, \text{max\depth}i - \text{min\depth}i) Mask out invalid voxels (where ptsidx == -1) by setting their dists to 0: \text{probs}i = \frac{\text{dists}i}{\sumj \text{dists}j} Determine the number of steps steps for each ray. If fixednumsamples > 0, steps is constant. Otherwise: \text{steps} = \frac{\sumi \text{dists}i}{\text{raymarching\stepsize}} If finenumsampleratio > 0 (hierarchical fine pass), update steps: \text{steps} = (\text{intersected\voxel\idx} \neq -1).\text{sum}(-1).\text{float}() \times \text{fine\num\sample\ratio} 2. Inside-Voxel Sampling: For each intersected voxel v and ray r, sample points. Convert world-space distance dw to sparse-space distance ds using the ray-voxel exit positions: ds = dw - (dw^{(r,v)} - ds^{(r,v)}) where dw^{(r,v)} is the world-space distance of the ray-voxel exit, and ds^{(r,v)} is the sparse-space distance of the same exit point. Perform uniform coarse sampling and importance sampling in the sparse space to generate Nc coarse and Ni importance samples. 3. Parallel Processing and Padding: If the total number of rays fullsize exceeds chunksize (4096), split rays into chunks. Process each chunk independently. Find maxlen, the maximum number of steps across all chunks. Pad outputs: sampledidx: Fill masked/invalid positions with -1. sampleddepth: Fill masked/invalid positions with MAXDEPTH. sampleddists: Fill masked/invalid positions with 0.0. Concatenate chunks and truncate to maxlen. 4. Masking and Truncation: Identify rays that hit the maximum depth boundary: \text{sampled\masks} = (\text{sampled\depth} == \text{MAX\DEPTH}) Calculate the maximum valid steps across all rays: \text{num\max\steps} = \maxi (\sim \text{sampled\masks}i).\text{sum}() Truncate tensors to nummaxsteps: \text{sampled\dists} = \text{sampled\dists}[:,: \text{num\max\steps}] \text{sampled\idx} = \text{sampled\idx}[:,: \text{num\max\steps}] 5. Compositing and Background Handling: Render colors and depths. Identify missed rays (those with no valid voxel intersections). \text{missed} = \text{fill\in}((\text{fullsize},), \text{hits}, \text{all\results}['\text{missed}'], 1.0) Fill missed rays with background values: \text{colors} = \text{fill\in}((\text{fullsize}, 3), \text{hits}, \text{all\results}['\text{colors}'], 0.0) \text{depths} = \text{fill\in}((\text{fullsize},), \text{hits}, \text{all\results}['\text{depths}'], 0.0) Add background contribution: \text{colors} += \text{missed}.\text{unsqueeze}(-1) \times \text{bg\color} \text{depths} += \text{missed} \times \text{BG\DEPTH} where bgcolor is derived from allresults['colors'] and BGDEPTH is self.field.bgcolor.depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def voxelawaremaskedraysampling(rays, voxelgrid, args): """ rays: (numrays, 3) origins, (numrays, 3) directions voxelgrid: Sparse voxel structure args: Configuration object """ fullsize = rays.shape[0] chunksize = args.chunksize if hasattr(args, 'chunksize') else 4096 maxhits = args.maxhits if hasattr(args, 'maxhits') else 60 raymarchingstepsize = args.raymarchingstepsize if hasattr(args, 'raymarchingstepsize') else 0.01 finenumsampleratio = args.finenumsampleratio if hasattr(args, 'finenumsampleratio') else 0.0 fixednumsamples = args.fixednumsamples if hasattr(args, 'fixednumsamples') else 0 bgdepth = args.backgrounddepth if hasattr(args, 'backgrounddepth') else 5.0 MAXDEPTH = 1e9 # Ray-box intersection logic to compute mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps. mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps = rayvoxelintersection(rays, voxelgrid, maxhits) # Mask invalid voxels (idx == -1) validmask = intersectedvoxelidx != -1 dists = (maxdepth - mindepth).maskedfill(~validmask, 0.0) # Normalize probabilities distssum = dists.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) probs = dists / distssum.maskedfill(distssum == 0, 1.0) # Determine number of samples per ray if fixednumsamples > 0: steps = torch.full((fullsize,), fixednumsamples, dtype=torch.float32, device=rays.device) else: steps = dists.sum(dim=-1) / raymarchingstepsize # Hierarchical fine pass adjustment if finenumsampleratio > 0: validcount = validmask.sum(dim=-1).float() steps = validcount finenumsampleratio # Inside-voxel sampling sampleddists, sampledidx, sampleddepth = insidevoxelsampling( rays, mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps, args) # Parallel processing with chunking if fullsize > chunksize: chunksdists, chunksidx, chunksdepth = [], [], [] for i in range(0, fullsize, chunksize): cdists, cidx, cdepth = insidevoxelsampling( rays[i:i+chunksize], mindepth[i:i+chunksize], maxdepth[i:i+chunksize], intersectedvoxelidx[i:i+chunksize], probs[i:i+chunksize], steps[i:i+chunksize], args) chunksdists.append(cdists) chunksidx.append(cidx) chunksdepth.append(cdepth) maxlen = max(c.shape[1] for c in chunksdists) paddeddists = [padtensor(c, maxlen, 0.0) for c in chunksdists] paddedidx = [padtensor(c, maxlen, -1) for c in chunksidx] paddeddepth = [padtensor(c, maxlen, MAXDEPTH) for c in chunksdepth] sampleddists = torch.cat(paddeddists, dim=0) sampledidx = torch.cat(paddedidx, dim=0) sampleddepth = torch.cat(paddeddepth, dim=0) else: maxsteps = sampleddists.shape[1] sampleddists = padtensor(sampleddists, maxsteps, 0.0) sampledidx = padtensor(sampledidx, maxsteps, -1) sampleddepth = padtensor(sampleddepth, maxsteps, MAXDEPTH) # Masking and Truncation sampledmasks = sampleddepth.eq(MAXDEPTH) nummaxsteps = (~sampledmasks).sum(dim=-1).max().item() # Generate orderedindex for gathering (standard sequential indices per ray) orderedindex = torch.arange(nummaxsteps, device=rays.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(fullsize, -1) sampleddists = sampleddists.gather(1, orderedindex).maskedfill(sampledmasks, 0.0)[:,:nummaxsteps] sampledidx = sampledidx.gather(1, orderedindex).maskedfill(sampledmasks, -1)[:,:nummaxsteps] sampleddepth = sampleddepth.gather(1, orderedindex).maskedfill(sampledmasks, MAXDEPTH)[:,:nummaxsteps] # Compositing # Volume rendering/compositing step aggregating sampled SDF and color values. colors, depths = rendervolume(sampleddists, sampledidx, rays, voxelgrid) # Handle missed rays missed = (sampledidx[:, 0] == -1) bgcolor = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], device=rays.device) # Derived from field colors = fillin(colors, ~missed, 0.0) depths = fillin(depths, ~missed, 0.0) colors += missed.unsqueeze(-1) bgcolor depths += missed bgdepth return colors, depths, sampleddists, sampledidx def insidevoxelsampling(rays, mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps, args): """ Samples points inside voxels using distance conversion. """ numrays = rays.shape[0] maxsteps = steps.max().int().item() sampleddists = torch.zeros((numrays, maxsteps), device=rays.device) sampledidx = torch.full((numrays, maxsteps), -1, dtype=torch.long, device=rays.device) sampleddepth = torch.full((numrays, maxsteps), 1e9, dtype=torch.float32, device=rays.device) for i in range(numrays): nsamples = int(steps[i].item()) if nsamples == 0: continue voxelindices = intersectedvoxelidx[i] validvoxels = voxelindices != -1 validvoxelindices = voxelindices[validvoxels] dmin = mindepth[i][validvoxels] dmax = maxdepth[i][validvoxels] # Generate sample offsets within each intersected voxel # Uniform coarse sampling + importance sampling in sparse space offsets = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nsamples, device=rays.device) voxellengths = dmax - dmin sampleoffsets = offsets voxellengths.unsqueeze(0) # World-space distances dw = dmin.unsqueeze(0) + sampleoffsets # Distance conversion: ds = dw - (dwout - dsout) # dwout is dmax, dsout is the sparse-space exit distance (assumed equal to dmax for uniform sparse grid) ds = dw - (dmax.unsqueeze(0) - dmax.unsqueeze(0)) # Fill tensors sampleddists[i,:nsamples] = ds sampledidx[i,:nsamples] = validvoxelindices sampleddepth[i,:nsamples] = dw return sampleddists, sampledidx, sampleddepth def padtensor(tensor, maxlen, padvalue): currentlen = tensor.shape[1] if currentlen < maxlen: padding = torch.full((tensor.shape[0], maxlen - currentlen), padvalue, device=tensor.device) if tensor.dtype == torch.bool: padding = padding.bool() tensor = torch.cat([tensor, padding], dim=1) return tensor def fillin(tensor, mask, fillvalue): tensor = tensor.clone() tensor[~mask] = fillvalue return tensor A rendering pipeline that dynamically allocates voxels only where objects and surfaces exist, restricting ray marching and volume integration to occupied regions. It performs ray-voxel intersection tests to identify sparse voxels traversed by camera rays, samples points within them, and applies volume rendering. Pitfalls include reduced throughput in high-complexity or noisy scenarios. Operating frequencies are typically 5 Hz for tracking and 2 Hz for optimization on the synthetic Replica dataset. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of intersected voxels per ray and the number of samples per voxel. Parallel processing with chunking (default 4096 rays) helps manage memory and latency. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of rays and the maximum number of voxel intersections (maxhits, default 60) plus samples per intersection. Padding ensures uniform tensor shapes. Performance: On a single NVIDIA RTX 3090, per-frame tracking takes ~150-200 ms and joint frame/map optimization takes 450-550 ms. Typical operating frequencies are 5 Hz for tracking and 2 Hz for optimization on the synthetic Replica dataset. Strengths: Efficient for sparse scenes by ignoring empty space. Prevents invalid sampling outside voxels, which is crucial for sparse feature volumes. Limitations: Performance degrades in highly complex or noisy scenes. Requires careful handling of variable intersection counts via padding and masking. Originating from the NSVF (Neural Sparse Voxel Fields) framework, this method was developed to address the inefficiency of dense volume rendering in sparse environments. It builds on the concept of sparse voxel grids, where only occupied regions are stored and processed. The hierarchical sampling strategy ensures that sampling points remain within valid voxels, avoiding the "air" sampling issues of unconstrained methods. It is used in neural implicit reconstruction and rendering pipelines, particularly for dynamic scenes and SLAM systems. facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) MonoNeuralFusion: Online Monocular Neural 3D Reconstruction with Geometric Priors, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2209.15153, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Vox-Fusion: Dense Tracking and Mapping with Voxel-based Neural Implicit Representation, https://doi.org/10.1109/ismar55827.2022.00066, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Step Size Calculation
head: Cone-angle based step size, Step Size Calculation, Step Size Determination, Step Size Heuristic
body: Adaptive Step Size Calculation determines the distance between samples during ray marching by varying the step size based on the ray's position and a cone angle parameter. It differs from standard constant step ray marching by dynamically adjusting the step size rather than using a fixed value. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current ray time t, cone angle \alpha, minimum step size dt{min}, maximum step size dt{max}. Output: Step size dt. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute the raw step size by multiplying the current ray time by the cone angle. 2. Clamp the result to the range [dt{min}, dt{max}]. Formula: The step size is calculated as: dt = \text{clamp}(t \cdot \alpha, dt{min}, dt{max}) Where: t: Current ray time. \alpha: Cone angle for volume rendering. dt{min}: Minimum step size. dt{max}: Maximum step size. Parameters: dt{min}: Not given in the sources. dt{max}: Not given in the sources. \alpha: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateadaptivestepsize(t: float, coneangle: float, dtmin: float, dtmax: float) -> float: """ Calculate adaptive step size based on cone angle heuristic. Args: t: Current ray time/distance. coneangle: Cone angle for volume rendering. dtmin: Minimum step size. dtmax: Maximum step size. Returns: Clamped step size. """ rawstep = t coneangle stepsize = max(dtmin, min(dtmax, rawstep)) return stepsize Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If t=0, the step size becomes 0, which may cause infinite loops or degenerate behavior. A guard should ensure t > 0 or use a minimum step size. Precision issues may arise if t \cdot \alpha is very small or very large relative to floating-point limits. Renders volumetric clouds by adaptively selecting the number of ray march steps based on the viewing angle and using cone sampling to approximate light transport within the volume. It balances rendering performance and visual quality by using fewer steps for top-down views and more steps for horizon views. It differs from standard constant step ray marching by varying the step count dynamically and from sibling methods by using a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors rotated towards the light source for density estimation along the light path. Choose it when rendering volumetric clouds where viewing angle significantly impacts visual quality and performance. Performs volume rendering by combining adaptive ray marching with temporal accumulation to reduce noise and flickering in animated scenes. It builds on Adaptive Step Size Calculation by using density thresholds to vary step size, and extends standard ray marching by reprojection of the previous frame's color and alpha into the current frame's screen space. It is distinct from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling by relying on spatial reprojection rather than cone-based filtering for temporal stability. Choose it when rendering animated volumetric scenes requiring temporal stability and noise reduction. Time and Memory Complexity: The calculation is O(1) in time and memory, as it involves simple arithmetic operations on scalar values. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling
head: Adaptive Step Count with Cone Sampling
body: This method renders volumetric clouds by adaptively selecting the number of ray march steps based on the viewing angle and using cone sampling to approximate light transport within the volume. It balances rendering performance and visual quality by using fewer steps for top-down views and more steps for horizon views, while cone sampling mitigates artifacts from single-sample lighting. It differs from standard constant step ray marching by varying the step count dynamically and from sibling methods by using a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors rotated towards the light source for density estimation along the light path. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). Ray segment bounds t{start} and t{end} in world space. Pixel identifier (integer) for jittering. Time variable T for wind animation. Light direction L (normalized). Earth center position C{earth}. Parameters: baseDensityFactor, jitterfactor, eccentricity, silverintensity, silverspread, brightness. Outputs: Accumulated color C{out} (RGB). Accumulated density \alpha{accum} (scalar, clamped to 1.0). The method uses a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors defined in local space and rotated to align with the light direction. Kernel Offsets (Local): 1. (0.1, 0.25, -0.15) 2. (0.2, 0.5, 0.2) 3. (-0.2, 0.1, -0.1) 4. (-0.05, 0.75, 0.05) 5. (-0.1, 1.0, 0.0) 6. (0.0, 3.0, 0.0) 1. Calculate Adaptive Step Count: Compute the dot product of the ray direction D and the world up vector U = (0, 1, 0). Calculate the number of steps N{steps} using linear interpolation between 35 and 60 steps based on the viewing angle. Top-down views (d \approx 1) use 35 steps; horizon views (d \approx 0) use 60 steps. d = \text{dot}(D, U) N{steps} = \lfloor \text{mix}(35.0, 60.0, 1.0 - d) \rfloor 2. Initialize Variables: Compute the step size \Delta t = (t{end} - t{start}) / N{steps}. Initialize transmittance T{trans} = 1.0 and accumulated density \alpha{accum} = 0.0. Initialize output color C{out} = (0, 0, 0). 3. Construct Light Rotation Matrix (TBN): Find the axis with the largest absolute component in L, denoted V{max}. Compute Z{comp} = \text{cross}(L, V{max}) and X{comp} = \text{cross}(Z{comp}, L). Form the rotation matrix M{sun} with columns X{comp}, L, and Z{comp}. M{sun} = \begin{bmatrix} X{comp} & L & Z{comp} \end{bmatrix} 4. Precompute Cone Sampling Offsets: Transform the 6 local kernel offsets K{local}[i] into world space aligned with the light: K{world}[i] = M{sun} \times K{local}[i] for i \in [0, 5]. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate j from 0 to N{steps} - 1. a. Calculate Sample Position: Compute current t = t{start} + j \cdot \Delta t. Generate a jitter offset using pixelID and t to select an index modulo 16, then retrieve jitterLocation. Update position P: P = O + t \cdot (D + (\text{jitterLocation}.x, (\text{jitterLocation}.x + \text{jitterLocation}.y) \cdot \text{jitterfactor}, \text{jitterLocation}.y)) b. Sample Density: Transform P to relative atmospheric coordinates and divide by 8.0 to control noise frequency. Skew the sample point using wind direction and time T. Calculate relative height h from P and C{earth}. Sample low-frequency density: \rho{base} = \text{SampleLowFreq}(P{skewed}, P, h, C{earth}) \cdot \text{baseDensityFactor}. If \rho{base} > 0.0, erode with high-frequency noise: \rho{high} = \text{ErodeCloud}(\rho{base} \cdot 1.4, D, P{skewed}, h). Update accumulated density: \alpha{accum} \leftarrow \alpha{accum} + \rho{high} \cdot 0.5. Check for early termination: if \alpha{accum} \ge 1.0, set \alpha{accum} = 1.0 and break the loop. c. Cone Sampling for Lighting: Initialize densityAlongLight = 0.0. Loop i from 0 to 5. Calculate light sample position: P{light} = P + \Delta t \cdot K{world}[i] \cdot i. Sample density at P{light}. If density > 0.0, erode with high-frequency noise and add to densityAlongLight. d. Compute Light Energy and Update Color: Calculate total light energy using GetLightEnergy with parameters: relative height h, densityAlongLight, \rho{base}, Henyey-Greenstein phase function value p(\theta) with eccentricity eccentricity, cosine of the angle between light and view direction, step size \Delta t, and brightness multiplier brightness. Update transmittance and color: T{trans} = \text{mix}(T{trans}, E{light}, 1.0 - \alpha{accum}) C{out} \leftarrow C{out} + T{trans} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchadaptivecone(rayorigin, raydir, tstart, tend, pixelid, time, lightdir, earthcenter, params): # 1. Adaptive step count dotval = dot(raydir, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) maxsteps = floor(mix(35.0, 60.0, 1.0 - dotval)) stepsize = (tend - tstart) / maxsteps # 2. Initialize transmittance = 1.0 accumdensity = 0.0 returncolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 3. TBN matrix for light maxcompidx = argmax(abs(lightdir)) maxcompunit = vec3([1.0 if i == maxcompidx else 0.0 for i in range(3)]) zcomp = cross(lightdir, maxcompunit) xcomp = cross(zcomp, lightdir) sunrotmatrix = mat3(xcomp, lightdir, zcomp) # 4. Precompute cone offsets localoffsets = [ vec3(0.1, 0.25, -0.15), vec3(0.2, 0.5, 0.2), vec3(-0.2, 0.1, -0.1), vec3(-0.05, 0.75, 0.05), vec3(-0.1, 1.0, 0.0), vec3(0.0, 3.0, 0.0) ] noisekernel = [sunrotmatrix @ k for k in localoffsets] # 5. Marching loop for step in range(maxsteps): t = tstart + step stepsize # Jitter jitteridx = hash(pixelid, t) % 16 jitterloc = getjitter(jitteridx) # Standard lookup/pseudo-random retrieval jitteroffset = vec3(jitterloc.x, (jitterloc.x + jitterloc.y) params.jitterfactor, jitterloc.y) pos = rayorigin + t (raydir + jitteroffset) # Density sampling relcoords = transformtoatmosphere(pos) / 8.0 skewedpoint = skewwithwind(relcoords, time) relheight = computerelativeheight(pos, earthcenter) basedensity = samplelowfrequency(skewedpoint, pos, relheight, earthcenter) params.baseDensityFactor if basedensity > 0.0: highfreqdensity = erodecloudwithhighfrequency(basedensity 1.4, raydir, skewedpoint, relheight) accumdensity += highfreqdensity 0.5 if accumdensity >= 1.0: accumdensity = 1.0 break # Cone sampling densityalonglight = 0.0 for i in range(6): lightpos = pos + stepsize noisekernel[i] float(i) lightbase = samplelowfrequency(lightpos, lightpos, relheight, earthcenter) if lightbase > 0.0: lighthigh = erodecloudwithhighfrequency(lightbase 1.4, raydir, lightpos, relheight) densityalonglight += lighthigh # Light energy & update cosangle = dot(raydir, lightdir) hgvalue = heneygreenstein(cosangle, params.eccentricity, params.silverintensity, params.silverspread) totallightenergy = getlightenergy(relheight, densityalonglight, basedensity, hgvalue, cosangle, stepsize, params.brightness) transmittance = mix(transmittance, totallightenergy, 1.0 - accumdensity) returncolor += transmittance return returncolor baseDensityFactor: Controls cloud density center intensity. Default: 0.380. jitterfactor: Multiplier for jitter offset in Y component. Default: 1.180. eccentricity: Henyey-Greenstein scattering parameter. Default: 0.6. silverintensity: Parameter for modified Henyey-Greenstein function. Default: 0.7. silverspread: Parameter for modified Henyey-Greenstein function. Default: 0.1. brightness: Lighting brightness multiplier. Default: 5.0. Precision: The mixing of transmittance and light energy requires careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid banding, especially at low densities. Boundaries: The ray segment bounds t{start} and t{end} must correctly clip against the volume boundaries (e.g., sphere intersection with atmosphere). Degenerate Input: If the ray direction is parallel to the world up vector, the dot product is 1 or -1. The formula handles d \approx 1 (top-down) well. If d is negative (viewing from below), the mix parameter 1.0-d exceeds 1, potentially exceeding 60 steps. The source specifies "horizon views" for d near 0, implying the method is optimized for viewing from above or the horizon. Kernel Alignment: The TBN matrix construction assumes L is not parallel to the chosen maxComp axis. If L is parallel, the cross product becomes zero. A fallback axis selection is not explicitly detailed in the source but is a standard implementation requirement. Time Complexity: O(N{steps} \cdot K), where N{steps} is the adaptive step count (35-60) and K=6 is the number of cone samples. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of steps and constant with respect to the scene size (assuming texture lookups are O(1)). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, excluding the noise texture/sampler state. Specific performance metrics (FPS, resolution) are not provided in the sources. The method scales well with resolution as it is a per-pixel operation. The adaptive step count reduces computational load for top-down views, providing a performance benefit in scenes with significant vertical viewing angles. Strengths: Reduces artifacts from single-sample lighting via cone sampling. Adaptive steps optimize performance based on viewing angle. Limitations: Fixed kernel size (6 samples) may not capture complex light transport in very dense volumes. The method relies on procedural noise, which may lack the detail of texture-based approaches. Use for real-time volumetric cloud rendering where performance is critical and visual quality needs to be maintained across varying camera angles. Not suitable for offline rendering where higher fidelity light transport (e.g., multiple scattering) is required. Not suitable for scenes with dynamic light sources that change rapidly, as the TBN matrix must be recomputed per ray. The method is derived from the implementation in the open-source project "realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes" by erickTornero. The technique combines adaptive step sizing, which is common in ray marching to optimize performance, with cone sampling, a technique used to approximate the integration of light through a volume by sampling along a cone aligned with the light direction. The method is used in real-time graphics applications, specifically for rendering atmospheric clouds in games or simulations. erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Temporal Reprojection
head: HZL Fluid Effects Studio volume renderer, field mode shading
body: This method performs volume rendering by combining adaptive ray marching with temporal accumulation to reduce noise and flickering in animated scenes. It builds on Adaptive Step Size Calculation by using density thresholds to vary step size, and extends standard ray marching by reprojection of the previous frame's color and alpha into the current frame's screen space. It is distinct from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling by relying on spatial reprojection rather than cone-based filtering for temporal stability. Inputs: Ray origin and direction. Volume density field (accessed via ray marching). stepSize: Base step length for ray marching through the volume. densityScale: Scaling factor applied to density in the opacity calculation. absorption: Absorption coefficient multiplier used in the opacity exponent. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: Boolean flag that doubles the step size (multiplies by 4.0) when density falls below 0.004. historyTexture: Previous frame's accumulated color and alpha buffer. historyWeight: Base weight for temporal history blending, modulated by alpha difference. emittedLight: Emissive contribution per unit step. smokeColor: Base color of the volume. fieldMode: Integer switch (0-7) controlling the smoke color mapping logic via conditional branches. Outputs: Final accumulated color (accumulated.rgb) and alpha (accumulated.a). Data Structures: accumulated: A vector or struct holding rgb (float3) and a (float). Initialized to zero. history: Sampled from historyTexture at reprojected UV coordinates. Holds rgb and a. representativePosition: World or view space position of the current ray step, used for reprojection. Parameters: stepSize: Base step length. densityScale: Scaling factor. absorption: Absorption multiplier. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: Boolean. historyWeight: Base blend weight. emissionStrength: Multiplier for emitted light (used in emittedLight calculation). fieldMode: Integer (0-7). Steps: 1. Initialize accumulated.rgb and accumulated.a to zero. 2. Loop through ray steps: a. Compute currentStep. If adaptiveSteppingEnabled is true and current density < 0.004, set currentStep = stepSize 4.0. Otherwise, currentStep = stepSize. b. Calculate opacity: opacity = 1.0 - \exp(-density \cdot densityScale \cdot currentStep \cdot absorption \cdot 4.0). c. Update accumulated color: accumulated.rgb \leftarrow accumulated.rgb + (1.0 - accumulated.a) \cdot (opacity \cdot smokeColor + emittedLight \cdot currentStep). d. Update accumulated alpha: accumulated.a \leftarrow accumulated.a + (1.0 - accumulated.a) \cdot opacity. e. If accumulated.a > 0.985, break the loop. f. Increment distanceAlongRay by currentStep. 3. If accumulated.a < 0.002, discard the fragment (do not write to color buffer). 4. If temporalEnabled is true and foundVolume is true: a. Project representativePosition to previous clip space. b. Compute UV coordinates from previous clip space. c. Clamp UV to [0.0, 1.0]. d. Sample historyTexture at clamped UV to get history. e. Compute responsiveWeight: responsiveWeight = historyWeight \cdot (1.0 - |history.a - accumulated.a|). f. Blend: accumulated = mix(accumulated, history, clamp(responsiveWeight, 0.0, 0.95)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarchingwithtemporalreprojection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumesampler, historytexture, camerastate, params): # Initialize accumulation accumulatedrgb = vec3(0.0) accumulateda = 0.0 # Parameters stepsize = params.stepSize densityscale = params.densityScale absorption = params.absorption adaptiveenabled = params.adaptiveSteppingEnabled historyweight = params.historyWeight emittedlight = params.emittedLight smokecolor = params.smokeColor fieldmode = params.fieldMode # Temporal reprojection state temporalenabled = params.temporalEnabled foundvolume = False # Ray marching loop distancealongray = 0.0 while True: # Get density at current position rayposition = rayorigin + raydirection distancealongray density = volumesampler.sample(rayposition) # Adaptive step size if adaptiveenabled and density < 0.004: currentstep = stepsize 4.0 else: currentstep = stepsize # Opacity calculation opacity = 1.0 - exp(-density densityscale currentstep absorption 4.0) # Color accumulation accumulatedrgb += (1.0 - accumulateda) (opacity smokecolor + emittedlight currentstep) # Alpha accumulation accumulateda += (1.0 - accumulateda) opacity # Termination if accumulateda > 0.985: foundvolume = True break distancealongray += currentstep # Max step limit not given in sources; implementation requires a loop bound or distance threshold. # Discard transparent fragments if accumulateda < 0.002: return None # Temporal reprojection if temporalenabled and foundvolume: # Project representative position to previous frame's clip space prevclippos = camerastate.previousviewprojection @ rayposition # Compute UV if prevclippos.w > 0.0: prevuv = vec2(prevclippos.x / prevclippos.w, prevclippos.y / prevclippos.w) prevuv = vec2(clamp(prevuv.x, 0.0, 1.0), clamp(prevuv.y, 0.0, 1.0)) # Sample history history = historytexture.sample(prevuv) # Responsive weight responsiveweight = historyweight (1.0 - abs(history.a - accumulateda)) # Blend blendfactor = clamp(responsiveweight, 0.0, 0.95) accumulatedrgb = mix(accumulatedrgb, history.rgb, blendfactor) accumulateda = mix(accumulateda, history.a, blendfactor) return vec4(accumulatedrgb, accumulateda) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Reprojection Bounds: If the previous frame projection has w <= 0.0, the UV calculation is invalid. Clamp UV to [0.0, 1.0] to avoid sampling outside bounds. Ghosting: Mitigated by scaling historyWeight with (1.0 - abs(history.a - accumulated.a)) and clamping the blend factor to [0.0, 0.95]. Transparent Pixels: Fragments with final opacity below 0.002 are discarded to avoid rendering transparent pixels. Field Mode: The fieldMode parameter (0-7) controls smoke color mapping logic via conditional branches, but the specific logic is not detailed in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces temporal noise and flickering through reprojection. Adaptive stepping reduces steps in low-density regions. Limitations: Ghosting is mitigated by alpha-difference weighting and blend clamping. Requires valid previous frame projection. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method is associated with the HZL Fluid Effects Studio volume renderer, as implemented in the pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio repository. It combines adaptive ray marching with temporal accumulation techniques. HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, https://github.com/pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Predictive Adaptive SDF Ray Marching
head: Raytracer 30
body: Predictive Adaptive SDF Ray Marching is a ray marching algorithm for Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering that determines step size using a prediction derived from the previous two distance estimates, scaled by a reduction factor to prevent overshooting. It differs from standard adaptive methods by incorporating a temporal component (previous step history) into the step size calculation, allowing for smoother convergence in empty space compared to methods relying solely on the current distance estimate. Inputs: Ray r (origin and direction). SDF function SDF(p). Maximum step count stepcount. Reduction factor STEPSIZEREDUCTION (typically 0.87). Outputs: A vec2 containing the final distance to the surface (t) and the final step size used (t + \text{stepsize}). Data Structures: Floating-point variables: t (current ray distance), ft (SDF value at t), pft (SDF value at previous step), dt (step size), nft (SDF value at next step). Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, ft = SDF(ray(r, t)), pft = 0, dt = 0. 2. Loop for i from 0 to stepcount: a. Calculate the predicted step size dt using the formula: dt = ft \times \left(1 - \text{STEP\SIZE\REDUCTION} \times \frac{pft - ft - dt}{pft - ft + dt}\right). b. Evaluate the SDF at the new position: nft = SDF(ray(r, t + dt)). c. Check for overshooting: If dt < ft + nft: Update ft = nft. Update t = t + dt. Else (overshoot detected): Update t = t + ft (step back to the previous valid position). Update ft = SDF(ray(r, t)). 3. Return vec2(t, t + stepsize). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictiveadaptivesdfraymarching(ray, sdf, stepcount, stepsizereduction=0.87): t = 0.0 ft = sdf(rayat(ray, t)) pft = 0.0 dt = 0.0 for i in range(stepcount): # Calculate predicted step size # Note: Division by zero check for (pft - ft + dt) is implied by robust implementation numerator = pft - ft - dt denominator = pft - ft + dt if denominator == 0: dt = ft # Fallback to simple step if denominator is zero else: dt = ft (1.0 - stepsizereduction (numerator / denominator)) # Evaluate SDF at new position nft = sdf(rayat(ray, t + dt)) # Check for overshooting if dt < ft + nft: ft = nft t = t + dt else: t = t + ft ft = sdf(rayat(ray, t)) return vec2(t, t + stepcount) # Note: Source returns t + stepsize, but stepsize variable is not explicitly tracked as a separate accumulator in the loop description. # The source says "Return vec2(t, t + stepsize)". Assuming stepsize refers to the last dt or a specific final metric. # Given the ambiguity, we return t and the last computed dt as a proxy for stepsize if not tracked. # However, strictly following source: return vec2(t, t + dt) is the most logical interpretation of the final state. return vec2(t, t + dt) Parameters: STEPSIZEREDUCTION: A constant float value of 0.87 used to scale the correction term. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero in the step size formula if pft - ft + dt = 0. A guard is required. The condition dt < ft + nft is used to detect overshooting. If this condition fails, the algorithm steps back by ft rather than dt, which may cause oscillation if not handled carefully. Uses predicted distances from previous steps for adaptive skipping via an octree, unlike the continuous adjustment of this method.
