name: Segment Tracing
body: Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm that computes local Lipschitz bounds on candidate segments to determine adaptive step sizes, reducing the number of field function queries compared to global Lipschitz bound methods like Sphere Tracing. It works for a particular class of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, leveraging the composition of distance functions and kernel functions to compute directional Lipschitz bounds. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which uses a global bound that limits step size efficiency, Segment Tracing allows larger, safer steps by adapting to the local gradient and field values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray \delta(t), a hierarchical skeletal implicit surface model where primitives and operators support local Lipschitz bound queries, an initial candidate step distance \varepsilon0, an amplification factor \kappa, and a threshold \mu. Output: The intersection parameter t along the ray, or the domain exit parameter. Data Structures: The method requires the implicit model to implement specific queries for each primitive and operator node: 1. Field function evaluation f(p). 2. Local Lipschitz bound over a segment \lambda(e), where e is a segment of the ray. 3. Local Lipschitz bound over a sphere \lambda(S) (used in some implementations for tighter bounds). Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the intersection between the ray and the domain [t-, t+] = \Delta \cap \Omega, and initialize t = t-. 2. Set the initial candidate stepping distance \varepsilon0. 3. While t < t+: 1. Compute the field function value f(t) at the current position. 2. If |f(t)| < \mu, an intersection has occurred; terminate and return t. 3. Define the candidate segment e(t, \varepsiloni) = [\delta(t), \delta(t + \varepsiloni)]. 4. Compute the local directional Lipschitz bound \lambda(e(t, \varepsiloni)) for the candidate segment. This step leverages the fact that primitives are defined as a composition of a distance function and a kernel function. 5. Evaluate f(pi^) (where pi^ is the current point) and compute the safe stepping increment s(t, \varepsiloni) using the formula: s(t, \varepsiloni) = \min \left( \frac{|f(t)|}{\lambda(e(t, \varepsiloni))}, \varepsiloni \right) where s is the effective stepping distance, f(t) is the field function value, \lambda(e) is the local Lipschitz bound on segment e, and \varepsiloni is the candidate distance. 6. Update the position: t \leftarrow t + s(t, \varepsiloni). 7. Compute the next candidate stepping distance \varepsilon{i+1} = \kappa \cdot s(t, \varepsiloni), where \kappa is the geometric amplification factor. Parameters: \mu: The threshold value from which an intersection is considered to have occurred (|f(t)| < \mu). \varepsilon0: The initial candidate step distance. Its value has little impact on performance; if too large, the initial Lipschitz bound is large, leading to small subsequent steps. \kappa: The geometric amplification factor for the next candidate step. Typical value is \kappa \approx 2. Must be > 1. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: If \varepsilon0 is too large, the computed Lipschitz bound \lambda(e(t0, \varepsilon0)) is large (upper bound), causing the next candidate distance \varepsilon1 to be small. If \varepsilon0 \to \infty, \lambda(e) becomes the global bound. If the computation of local bounds is too complex or computationally intensive for a given operator or primitive, the algorithm automatically reverts to the standard Sphere Tracing framework locally. The method works only for a particular class of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces and is not directly applicable to a wide range of volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def segmenttracing(rayorigin, raydirection, domainmin, domainmax, fieldfunction, locallipschitzsegment, epsilon0, kappa, mu): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 (normalized) domainmin: float (tmin) domainmax: float (tmax) fieldfunction: function(p) -> float locallipschitzsegment: function(t, epsilon) -> float epsilon0: float kappa: float (> 1) mu: float """ t = domainmin epsilon = epsilon0 while t < domainmax: # Evaluate field function at current position p = rayorigin + t raydirection fval = fieldfunction(p) # Check for intersection if abs(fval) < mu: return t # Compute local Lipschitz bound for candidate segment [t, t + epsilon] lambdabound = locallipschitzsegment(t, epsilon) # Compute safe stepping increment if lambdabound == 0: step = epsilon else: step = min(abs(fval) / lambdabound, epsilon) # Clamp step to domain boundary to prevent overshoot and fix boundary precision step = min(step, domainmax - t) # Update position t = t + step # Amplify candidate step for next iteration epsilon = kappa step return domainmax # No intersection within domain The parent method using a global Lipschitz bound. Choose when simplicity is preferred and local bound computation is not feasible. [1674-sphere-tracing.md] Uses cone intersection tests for tighter bounds. Choose when higher precision is needed for complex primitives. [1553-cone-intersection.md] Uses quadric approximations for step size. Choose for quadric-based implicit surfaces. [1866-quadric-tracing.md] Uses L1 distance fields. Choose for grid-based volumes where L1 metrics are appropriate. [2752-chamfer-l1-distance-computation.md] Uses over-stepping heuristics. Choose for a simple speedup over standard Sphere Tracing without local bound computation. [3805-over-relaxation-sphere-tracing.md] Reduces queries by a factor of 1.2. Choose for a minor improvement over Sphere Tracing. [3811-enhanced-sphere-tracing.md] Uses non-linear transformations. Choose for specific non-linear field representations. [4079-non-linear-sphere-tracing.md] Time Complexity: Increases the overall complexity of the shader due to the implementation of extra functions for computing the Lipschitz bound over a segment, a ray, or a spherical domain. Memory Complexity: Does not require accelerating data structures such as voxel grids or octrees for storing the local Lipschitz bound. Measured Performance: Reduces field function queries by up to three orders of magnitude compared to Sphere Tracing, resulting in accelerations of up to \times 10, despite the extra computational cost of Lipschitz bound queries. Scaling: Performance gains are most significant for hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces where local bounds can be computed efficiently. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of field function queries; no need for precomputed acceleration structures; adapts to local gradient variations. Limitations: Requires primitives and operators to implement complex local Lipschitz bound queries; not directly applicable to a wide range of volumes; overhead from bound computation can negate benefits if not optimized. When to use: When rendering hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces and field function evaluation is expensive. When not to use: When the implicit model does not support local Lipschitz bound queries, or when the overhead of computing these bounds exceeds the savings from fewer field evaluations. Introduced in, the method was developed to address the limitations of Sphere Tracing, which uses a global Lipschitz bound that limits efficiency. The method leverages the structure of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, where primitives are defined as a composition of a distance function and a kernel function, allowing for the computation of local directional Lipschitz bounds. It has been used in the context of ray tracing compactly supported primitives combined in a Blobtree. name: Enhanced Sphere Tracing
head: Aggressive Marching, Aggressive Ray Marching, Aggressive Sphere Tracing, Bálint and Valasek method, Over-relaxed sphere tracing, Sphere tracing with over-relaxation
body: Enhanced Sphere Tracing is a family of ray-marching optimizations that accelerate convergence toward implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by taking steps larger than the strict Lipschitz bound or by predicting optimal step sizes based on local surface geometry. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing, which becomes prohibitively slow when rays graze surfaces at shallow angles or when the surface is locally planar. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which uses the queried distance value as the step size, enhanced variants either over-relax the step size by a constant factor or infer the next step size from the previous two distance queries to approximate the surface as locally flat. The term "Enhanced Sphere Tracing" refers to two distinct but related algorithmic strategies: Aggressive/Over-relaxed Marching (accelerating convergence via scalar multiplication) and Geometric Enhancement (predicting step size via historical data). Both require a conservative SDF (one that never overstates the distance to the surface) to ensure robustness. Input: Ray origin p \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray direction v \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized, |v|=1), SDF query function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, maximum iteration count i{max}, convergence threshold \epsilon, and method-specific parameters (\alpha, \omega, or \sigma). Output: Distance t \in [0, +\infty) traveled along the ray to the surface, or a failure state if i{max} is exceeded. History State: Stores the SDF values from the previous two steps (r{i-1}, ri) and the step size taken to reach the current step (di). Accumulator: Total distance traveled t. This variant multiplies the safe step size by a factor \alpha > 1 (or \omega > 1) to accelerate convergence, particularly for grazing rays. It requires a safety check to prevent skipping the surface if the SDF is non-conservative or the geometry is too thin. Parameters: \alpha: Aggressive multiplier. Default 1.5. Range 1.2–1.8. \omega: Over-relaxation factor. Value 1.6. \sigma: Overstepping factor in [0, 1]. Typical value \approx 1.2. \lambda: Global Lipschitz bound of the SDF. Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, r{prev} = 0, r{curr} = 0. 2. Loop while t < b (max distance) and iterations < i{max}: 3. Query SDF: d = f(p + t \cdot v). 4. Calculate safe step: s = |d| / \lambda. 5. Calculate over-step: o = (1 + \sigma) \cdot s. 6. Safety Check: If the over-step o causes the new sphere to not overlap with the previous safe sphere (i.e., the step is too large relative to the local geometry or d is negative/inside), revert to standard sphere tracing step s. Alternative Implementation (Keinert et al.): Calculate over-relaxed step step = \omega \cdot |d|. If step > |d| (overshoots safe radius), retreat to t + |d| (back to safe boundary). 7. Update position: t \leftarrow t + step. 8. Update history: r{prev} \leftarrow r{curr}, r{curr} \leftarrow d. 9. Check convergence: If |d| < \epsilon, break and return t. This variant assumes the surface is locally flat and calculates the optimal step size using the radii of the two previous unbounding spheres. It is more expensive per step than aggressive marching but converges faster on smooth surfaces. Parameters: \omega: Relaxation parameter for locally concave regions. Range \omega \in (0, 1]. Typical range (0.7, 1]. Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, r{i-1} = 0, ri = 0, r{i+1} = \infty, di = 0. 2. Loop for i from 0 while i < i{max} and r{i+1} is not too small: 3. Calculate Step Size: Compute di using the geometric formula derived from similar triangles: di = ri + \omega \cdot ri \cdot \frac{di - r{i-1} + ri}{di + r{i-1} - ri} Note: In the first iteration, r{i-1}=0, di=0. The formula simplifies or requires a fallback to standard step size ri for the very first step if division by zero occurs. 4. Step: Advance ray: t \leftarrow t + di. 5. Query: Evaluate SDF at new position: r{i+1} = f(p + t \cdot v). 6. Safety Check (Fallback): If the spheres are disjoint (di > ri + r{i+1}), the step was too large and may have missed the surface. Reset step to conservative size: di \leftarrow ri. Re-evaluate SDF at the corrected position: r{i+1} = f(p + (t{old} + di) \cdot v). Update t to reflect the corrected step. 7. Update History: Shift values: r{i-1} \leftarrow ri, ri \leftarrow r{i+1}. 8. Convergence: If |r{i+1}| < \epsilon, break and return t. Thin Geometry: Aggressive marching (\alpha > 1) can cause the ray to trespass two surfaces in a single step if the geometry is super thin, leaving the ray front end outside the shape and causing infinite marching or small holes. Non-Conservative SDFs: Over-relaxation is unsound if the SDF overstates the distance (is not 1-Lipschitz or conservative). It may skip surfaces entirely. Non-Smooth Surfaces: On fractals or non-smooth surfaces (e.g., Mandelbulb), the geometric enhancement provides only marginal improvement over basic sphere tracing, as the "locally flat" assumption fails. Grazing Incidence: Standard sphere tracing is slow when the angle \theta between the ray and surface normal is small. Enhanced methods mitigate this, but aggressive marching requires careful tuning of \alpha to avoid instability. The Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm is a method for automatically computing tight bounding volumes for objects defined by a conservative signed distance field (SDF). It solves the problem of accelerating implicit surface queries (such as sphere tracing or polygonization) by generating a lightweight bounding proxy function fe that avoids expensive SDF evaluations outside the object. Unlike sphere tracing, which discards empty segments along a ray to find an intersection, Sphere Carving discards empty volumes (spheres) in space to find a bounding volume of the surface. It is agnostic of the function representation, requiring only a conservative SDF query, and provides strict bounding guarantees that neural or interval-arithmetic methods may lack. A technique where you march a small distance further outside the Minimum Distance Sphere (MDS) edge to decrease the number of times marched, increasing performance. March to the edge of the MDS, then march a small distance further outside. Compare the original MDS with the new MDS; if they overlap, continue marching further. If the two MDSs do not overlap, step back to the edge of the first MDS and continue normally. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF queries significantly compared to standard sphere tracing. For grazing angles, the minimum number of steps k decreases from k{std} to k{enh}. Formula for aggressive marching convergence: k > k{min} = \frac{\log \epsilon - \log d}{\log |1 - \alpha \sin \theta|}. Example: For d=1.0, \epsilon=5 \times 10^{-5}, \theta=10^\circ, steps decrease from 52 (conventional) to 33 (aggressive \alpha=1.5). Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storing only a few scalar values (t, r{i-1}, ri, di) per ray. Performance: Aggressive marching with \sigma \approx 1.2 reduces field function queries by a factor of 1.2 and speeds up computation by the same factor. Geometric enhancement (Bálint & Valasek) outperforms relaxed sphere tracing by up to 1.5 times on smooth surfaces and up to 50% better than Hart and Keinert et al.'s variant in error-decrease velocity. On non-smooth surfaces (Mandelbulb), it performs slightly better than basic tracing but is on par with relaxed tracing within error margins. Strengths: Faster convergence on planar/smooth surfaces; stabilizes training in neural rendering by allowing sampling behind the surface; prevents geometry vanishing at grazing angles under non-uniform scaling. Limitations: Risk of missing thin geometry; requires conservative SDFs; higher computational cost per step for geometric enhancement due to formula evaluation. Enhanced Sphere Tracing originated from the need to accelerate real-time rendering of implicit surfaces. The "Relaxed Sphere Tracing" variant was introduced by Keinert et al. in 2014, proposing over-relaxation to accelerate convergence. The "Enhanced Sphere Tracing" variant, specifically the geometric approach using historical step data, was proposed by Bálint and Valasek in 2018, optimizing for locally planar surfaces. The aggressive marching strategy was also independently applied in differentiable neural rendering contexts to stabilize training and speed up forward propagation. name: Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm
body: The Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm is a method for automatically computing tight bounding volumes for objects defined by a conservative signed distance field (SDF). It solves the problem of accelerating implicit surface queries (such as sphere tracing or polygonization) by generating a lightweight bounding proxy function fe that avoids expensive SDF evaluations outside the object. Unlike sphere tracing, which discards empty segments along a ray to find an intersection, Sphere Carving discards empty volumes (spheres) in space to find a bounding volume of the surface. It is agnostic of the function representation, requiring only a conservative SDF query, and provides strict bounding guarantees that neural or interval-arithmetic methods may lack. The algorithm iteratively carves an initial large bounding volume V0 using spheres defined by the SDF, extracting intersection points to compute a bounding volume. The process is parallelized into four kernels per iteration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A conservative signed distance field function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, where |f(p)| \le d(p, \partial \mathcal{O}). An initial large bounding volume V0 (typically an icosphere). A distance threshold \tau (typical value: 0.1). Outputs: A set of empty spheres S and a point set P whose convex hull bounds the object surface \partial \mathcal{O}. Data Structures: S: Array of empty spheres (center and radius). P: Array of 3D points. P': Temporary array of intermediate intersection points. pairs: Array of sphere index pairs (a, b). All arrays are pre-allocated with sufficient memory. Parallel updates to arrays require one atomic counter per array. The Empty Sphere Criterion: For any point p, the sphere S(p, |f(p)|) does not intersect the object's surface \partial \mathcal{O}: \forall \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \ S(\mathbf{p}, |f(\mathbf{p})|) \cap \partial \mathcal{O} = \emptyset Here, f is a conservative SDF where |f(p)| \le d(p, \partial O). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Sample points P on the surface of V0. Create initial sphere set S0 = \{ \text{sphere}(p, |f(p)|) \mid p \in P \}. Verify coverage: for an icosphere, ensure every triangle \Delta(a,b,c) is contained in the union of spheres at its vertices: \Delta(a,b,c) \subset S(a) \cup S(b) \cup S(c). If not, increase subdivision. 2. Iteration Loop: While \max{p \in P} f(p) > \tau: Kernel 1 (Gather Pairs): Identify intersecting sphere pairs. Kernel 2 (Compute Intersections): Calculate 3-sphere intersections (trilateration) for triplets. Kernel 3 (Filter Points): Discard points inside the current sphere set. Kernel 4 (Augment Spheres): Add new spheres based on filtered points. 3. Termination: The loop ends when \max(f(P)) \le \tau. The result is the final sphere set S and point set P. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Callable def parallelspherecarving(f: Callable, V0, tau: float) -> Tuple[List, List]: # Initialization: sample points on V0 surface P = samplesurface(V0) # Create initial sphere set S0 = { sphere(p, |f(p)|) | p in P } S = [(p, abs(f(p))) for p in P] # Verify coverage: for an icosphere, ensure every triangle is covered by vertex spheres if not isicospherecovered(V0, S): raise ValueError("Initial coverage constraint not met") while P and max(f(p) for p in P) > tau: pairs = [] # Kernel 1: Gather intersecting sphere pairs for a in range(len(S)): for b in range(a + 1, len(S)): if spheresintersect(S[a], S[b]): pairs.append((a, b)) Pprime = [] # Kernel 2: Compute intersection points for triplets (trilateration) for (a, b) in pairs: for c in range(b + 1, len(S)): pts = intersectthreespheres(S[a], S[b], S[c]) Pprime.extend(pts) Pnew = [] # Kernel 3: Filter points inside the volume for p in Pprime: isinside = False for s in S: # Discard if distance to center < radius, accounting for precision if math.dist(p, s[0]) < s[1]: isinside = True break if not isinside: Pnew.append(p) # Kernel 4: Augment sphere set for p in Pnew: if f(p) > tau: S.append((p, abs(f(p)))) P = Pnew return S, P def samplesurface(V0): # Returns vertices of the recursively subdivided icosahedron V0 return V0.vertices def isicospherecovered(V0, S): # Checks if every triangle of V0 is contained in the union of spheres at its vertices for tri in V0.triangles: a, b, c = tri Sa, Sb, Sc = S[a], S[b], S[c] if not triangleinsphereunion(a, b, c, Sa, Sb, Sc): return False return True def triangleinsphereunion(a, b, c, Sa, Sb, Sc): # Standard geometric coverage test # Checks if triangle vertices and centroid are within the union of spheres centers = [Sa[0], Sb[0], Sc[0]] radii = [Sa[1], Sb[1], Sc[1]] points = [a, b, c, ((a[0]+b[0]+c[0])/3, (a[1]+b[1]+c[1])/3, (a[2]+b[2]+c[2])/3)] return all(any(math.dist(p, ctr) <= rad for ctr, rad in zip(centers, radii)) for p in points) def spheresintersect(s1, s2): c1, r1 = s1 c2, r2 = s2 return math.dist(c1, c2) <= r1 + r2 def intersectthreespheres(s1, s2, s3): c1, r1 = s1 c2, r2 = s2 c3, r3 = s3 d = math.dist(c1, c2) if d > r1 + r2 or d < abs(r1 - r2): return [] # Trilateration formulas from Appendix A.2 x = (r12 - r22 + d2) / (2 d) ysq = r12 - x2 if ysq < 0: return [] y = math.sqrt(ysq) # Basis vectors ex = ((c2[0]-c1[0])/d, (c2[1]-c1[1])/d, (c2[2]-c1[2])/d) # ey perpendicular to ex and in plane of c1,c2,c3 v = (c3[0]-c1[0], c3[1]-c1[1], c3[2]-c1[2]) dotvex = v[0]ex[0] + v[1]ex[1] + v[2]ex[2] ey = (v[0]-dotvexex[0], v[1]-dotvexex[1], v[2]-dotvexex[2]) eylen = math.sqrt(ey[0]2 + ey[1]2 + ey[2]2) if eylen < 1e-9: return [] # Spheres are collinear ey = (ey[0]/eylen, ey[1]/eylen, ey[2]/eylen) ez = (ex[1]ey[2]-ex[2]ey[1], ex[2]ey[0]-ex[0]ey[2], ex[0]ey[1]-ex[1]ey[0]) # Solve for z using third sphere offset = (xex[0] + yey[0] + c1[0] - c3[0], xex[1] + yey[1] + c1[1] - c3[1], xex[2] + yey[2] + c1[2] - c3[2]) zsq = r32 - (offset[0]2 + offset[1]2 + offset[2]2) if zsq < 0: return [] z = math.sqrt(zsq) # Return points in original frame p1 = (c1[0] + xex[0] + yey[0] + zez[0], c1[1] + xex[1] + yey[1] + zez[1], c1[2] + xex[2] + yey[2] + zez[2]) p2 = (c1[0] + xex[0] + yey[0] - zez[0], c1[1] + xex[1] + yey[1] - zez[1], c1[2] + xex[2] + yey[2] - zez[2]) return [p1, p2] Parameters: \tau: Distance threshold for stopping. Typical value: 0.1. V0: Initial volume. Size: Usually two orders of magnitude larger than the object. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Conservative SDFs: Underestimating distance causes slow convergence and high computational cost due to O(n^3) intersection calculations and many spheres. Overestimated SDFs: Break the bounding guarantee. The algorithm progresses, but the result is not guaranteed to bound the object. Initialization Coverage: The initial sphere set S0 must cover the entire surface of V0. For an icosphere, this is checked per triangle. Precision: Filtering points inside the sphere set volume accounts for floating-point precision by discarding a point if its distance to any sphere center is less than the sphere radius. A strategy for initializing the Sphere Carving algorithm using a recursively subdivided icosahedron (icosphere) as the initial bounding volume V0. It is chosen because sampling is straightforward (using vertices) and the coverage constraint can be checked per triangle \Delta(a,b,c) using only the spheres at its vertices. If the triangle is not contained in the union of the spheres at its vertices, the subdivision level is increased. Time Complexity: The complexity of the sphere intersection routine is O(n^3), where n is the number of spheres, due to evaluating every possible triplet of sphere intersections. Memory Complexity: Compact representation. The bounding volume is stored as a set of convex polyhedra or ellipsoids, which is more memory-efficient than external acceleration structures like grids or octrees. Performance: Requires a small number of field function queries (#f), from a few thousand for complex objects to less than one hundred for an exact SDF. The algorithm typically converges in less than 20 iterations. Strengths: Agnostic of function representation; provides strict bounding guarantees; terminates in seconds; no training time required. Limitations: Computationally intensive for overly conservative SDFs (underestimated distances), which require more iterations and spheres. Overly conservative functions may require a larger initial volume or denser sampling. Sphere Carving was introduced by Hugo Schott, Theo Thonat, Thibaud Lambert, Eric Guérin, and Axel Paris. It is designed to accelerate queries in sphere tracing, polygonization, and simulation by generating a bounding proxy signed distance function fe. The method draws inspiration from techniques that carve space using empty spheres, similar to how sphere tracing discards empty segments. It is particularly useful for procedurally defined implicit surfaces such as exact or Lipschitz functions, BlobTrees, or neural representations. name: Uniform Sphere Tracing
head: Ray Marching for Volumes, Rustgpu Sphere Tracing Implementation, Uniform Density Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering with Ray Marching (Uniform Sphere)
body: Uniform Sphere Tracing is a volume rendering technique that uses ray marching along a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to detect volume boundaries and applies Beer's Law for optical depth integration under a uniform density assumption. It solves the problem of rendering participating media with constant optical properties by stepping through the volume, accumulating absorption and scattering, and blending the result with the background. It is distinguished from its parent Sphere Tracing by its specific application to uniform density volume rendering and its reliance on fixed or clamped step sizes for the marching phase, while using SDF evaluation primarily for surface detection rather than purely adaptive step sizing for optical integration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), SDF function f(P), maximum iterations N{max}, minimum step size d{min}, maximum step size d{max}, cutoff threshold d{cut}, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, volume scatter color C{vol}, background color C{bg}. Outputs: Final pixel color C{final}, boolean hit flag, final position, iteration count. Data Structures: Sphere Class (for bounding/intersection): center: vec3 (e.g., [0, 0, -4]) radius: float (e.g., 1.0) sigmaa: float (e.g., 0.1) scatter: vec3 (e.g., [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]) intersect: Method returning intersection distances t0, t1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, compute ray origin O and direction D. 2. Bounding Intersection: Check if the ray intersects the volume's bounding object (e.g., a sphere). If no intersection, return C{bg}. If intersection exists, calculate entry point P1 = O + D \cdot t0 and exit point P2 = O + D \cdot t1. Calculate total distance through volume L = t1 - t0 (assuming normalized D). 3. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize itercount = 0, hitsdf = false, currentpos = O, priord = \infty, terminated = false, and distance = 0.0001. While itercount < N{max}: Update currentpos = O + \text{distance} \cdot D. Evaluate SDF: s = f(\text{current\pos}). Check termination: If s \le d{cut}, set hitsdf = true and break loop. Determine step increment: d{step} = \text{clamp}(s, d{min}, d{max}). Update distance += d{step}. Increment itercount. 4. Optical Integration (Beer's Law): Calculate transmittance T through the volume based on the straight-line distance L. Formula: T = e^{-L \cdot \sigmaa}. 5. Color Blending: Calculate final color: C{final} = T \cdot C{bg} + (1 - T) \cdot C{vol}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def uniformspheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, sphereobj, minstep=0.0001, maxstep=0.001, cutoff=0.05, itermax=1000): # 1. Bounding Intersection t0, t1 = sphereobj.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if not t0: return sphereobj.backgroundcolor, False, rayorigin, 0, 0.0 # Distance through volume (straight line for uniform density) distancethroughvolume = t1 - t0 # 2. Ray Marching for SDF Hit Detection itercount = 0 hitsdf = False currentpos = rayorigin priord = float('inf') terminated = False distance = 0.0001 while itercount < itermax: currentpos = rayorigin + distance raydirection increment = sdffunc(currentpos, itercount, priord) # Check termination before advancing to prevent overshoot if increment <= cutoff: hitsdf = True break # Clamp step size and advance clampedincrement = max(minstep, min(increment, maxstep)) distance += clampedincrement priord = increment itercount += 1 # 3. Optical Integration sigmaa = sphereobj.sigmaa transmittance = math.exp(-distancethroughvolume sigmaa) # 4. Color Blending backgroundcolor = sphereobj.backgroundcolor volumecolor = sphereobj.scatter finalcolor = transmittance backgroundcolor + (1.0 - transmittance) volumecolor return finalcolor, hitsdf, currentpos, itercount, distance Parameters: minstep: Minimum allowed step increment. Typical: 0.0001. maxstep: Maximum allowed step increment. Typical: 0.001 for clamped ray marching, or larger for pure sphere tracing. cutoff: Threshold below which the surface is considered hit. Typical: 0.05. itermax: Maximum number of iterations. sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. Typical: 0.1. scatter: Volume scatter color. Typical: [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]. backgroundcolor: Background color. Typical: [0.572, 0.772, 0.921]. Pitfalls: SDF Scaling: Scaling the input position vector to the SDF closure (e.g., v 10.0) without adjusting the step size or SDF output accordingly breaks the sphere tracing property, causing the ray to overshoot collisions. The SDF distance does not scale linearly with the ray step in a way that preserves the tracing logic when the position is scaled but the step is not adjusted. Step Clamping: Using very small maxstep values effectively turns sphere tracing into uniform ray marching, losing the benefit of large steps in empty space. Spectral tracking is a volume rendering technique that efficiently handles per-wavelength optical properties by decomposing the medium's scattering and absorption coefficients into spectral components, using a single majorant density to drive the sampling process for all wavelengths simultaneously. Unlike naive delta tracking which handles each wavelength separately, spectral tracking invokes the tracker only once for all wavelengths, computing a spectrally resolved collision weight at each collision to counteract the discrepancy between the single sampling distribution and the true per-wavelength free-path distribution. This reduces the number of tracker invocations and leverages vectorized operations, making it particularly effective for spectrally heterogeneous media. Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing is a robust sphere tracing method that automatically scales step sizes based on data from previous iterations, using a scalar hyperparameter similar to the learning rate of gradient descent methods. It sets itself apart from its parent Uniform Sphere Tracing by replacing fixed or heuristic step rules with an adaptive scaling mechanism that reduces the frequency of invalid, over-relaxed step sizes, thereby minimizing the need for robustness-preserving fallback steps. Compared to Spectral Tracking, it exhibits a smaller effect on performance from its step-scale hyperparameters and performs up to par with or outperforms the most efficient concurrent methods depending on iteration count limits. A technique to reduce visual discontinuities (jagged edges/artifacts) between adjacent rays by allowing a tolerance error in the intersection condition that scales with screen-space distance from the origin. Unlike standard sphere tracing which requires f(p)=0, this method accepts a larger error for rays further away (in screen space), reducing step count and discontinuities without affecting visual quality. The update rule becomes p{i+1} = pi + d \cdot (f(pi) - \text{err}(\|pi - o\|2)), where \text{err}(\|pi - o\|2) is an error function based on the screen-space distance from the ray origin o to the current point pi. This allows for coarser intersection checks at a distance, mitigating the "wavy" artifacts caused by non-continuous step sizes between neighboring pixels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance depends on maxstep and SDF evaluation cost. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it only stores current position, distance, and iteration count. Performance: Small maxstep values result in more iterations but stable convergence, while larger values reduce iteration count but risk overshooting if the SDF is improperly scaled. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for convex shapes, efficient for uniform density volumes. Limitations: Struggles with non-convex shapes without additional logic. Sensitive to SDF scaling errors. Discontinuities between adjacent rays can cause visual artifacts if not handled. When to use: Rendering simple volumetric effects like fog, smoke, or clouds with uniform density. When not to use: Rendering complex, non-uniform, or highly heterogeneous media where delta tracking or spectral tracking is more appropriate. Uniform Sphere Tracing for volumes combines SDF-based ray marching for boundary detection with uniform density optical depth integration. The specific implementation details, such as the Rust-based closure-based SDF evaluator and step clamping, are documented in community resources. The volume rendering aspect, including Beer's Law application and sphere object structure, is detailed in tutorials on volume rendering. The technique has been adapted to reduce visual discontinuities by relaxing intersection conditions based on screen-space distance. name: Spectral Tracking
head: Single-Distribution Spectral Tracking, Vectorized Weighted Delta Tracking
body: Spectral Tracking is a volumetric rendering technique that efficiently handles spectrally resolved optical properties by decomposing the medium's scattering and absorption coefficients into spectral components (e.g., RGB) and using a single majorant density to drive the sampling process for all wavelengths simultaneously. Unlike naive delta tracking, which invokes the tracker separately for each wavelength, spectral tracking invokes the tracker only once, computing a spectrally resolved collision weight at each step to counteract the discrepancy between the single sampling distribution and the true per-wavelength free-path distribution. It differs from its parent, Uniform Sphere Tracing, by replacing the scalar transmittance accumulation with a vectorized throughput update that accounts for spectral variance, and from its sibling, Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing, by explicitly managing spectral weights rather than relaxing the majorant bound. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Volume Scene Definition (vsdf) containing the density volume, emission volume, and a global scattering ratio (scatter); a ray (ray) with origin o and direction d; a maximum travel distance (maxdistance); and a random number generator state (rng). Output: A pair containing the total path length traveled and a spectral throughput vector (f) representing the accumulated contribution. Data Structures: vec3f: A 3-component vector representing spectral values (Red, Green, Blue). sigmat, sigmas, sigmaa, sigman: Spectral vectors for total extinction, scattering, absorption, and null (non-interaction) coefficients. Pt, Ps, Pn, Pa: Scalar probabilities for total, scattering, null, and absorption events, derived from the spectral coefficients and the majorant. wD (or contrib): A spectral vector used to track the weight correction factor. In the implementation, this is updated element-wise. Parameters: majorantdensity: The upper bound on the total extinction coefficient across all wavelengths and space. Typically set to maxdensity. imaxdensity: The inverse of the majorant density (1 / \text{majorant\density}). scatter: A scalar representing the albedo or scattering ratio of the medium. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Retrieve maxdensity from the volume object (densityvol->maxvoxel object->densitymult). Set majorantdensity = maxdensity and imaxdensity = 1.0 / majorantdensity. Initialize pathlength = 0.0. Initialize spectral throughput vectors: tr = vec3f(1.0) (transmittance) and f = vec3f(1.0) (final contribution/throughput). Calculate initial scattering coefficient vector: sigmas = vsdf.scatter maxdensity. Calculate scattering probability: Ps = sigmas imaxdensity. Initialize spectral weight vector wD to ones, though the specific implementation handles weights via the contrib vector logic below. The theoretical formulation initializes wD \leftarrow (1, \dots, 1)^{N\lambda}. 2. Loop: Generate a uniform random number \zeta \in 0, 1) using rng. Compute tentative distance: t = -\ln(1 - \zeta) / \text{majorant\density}. Update pathlength += t. (Note: Source uses pathlength -= log(1 - rand1f(rng)) imaxdensity, which is mathematically equivalent to adding -\ln(\dots)/\text{majorant}). Termination Check: If pathlength >= maxdistance, break the loop. Calculate current position: \mathbf{x} = \text{ray}.o + \text{path\length} \times \text{ray}.d. Evaluate total extinction coefficient at \mathbf{x}: \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) = \text{vec3f}(\text{eval\vpt\density}(vsdf, \mathbf{x})). Calculate null (non-interaction) coefficient: \sigman(\mathbf{x}) = \text{majorant\density} - \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Calculate [absorption coefficient: \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) = \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) - \sigmas. (The implementation assumes a homogeneous scattering ratio vsdf.scatter applied to the local total extinction or uses a pre-computed constant sigmas. Based on code, sigmas is constant, but sigmat varies. This implies the albedo varies spectrally via sigmat while the scattering ratio is fixed, or sigmas is derived differently. The code sigmaa = sigmat - sigmas implies sigmas is the scattering part of the majorant, which is constant. This is a specific implementation detail.) Calculate Pt(\mathbf{x}) = \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) \times \text{imax\density}. Calculate Pn(\mathbf{x}) = \sigman(\mathbf{x}) \times \text{imax\density}. Calculate Pa(\mathbf{x}) = 1.0 - Ps - Pn(\mathbf{x}). (Note: Ps is constant from initialization). Generate a random number \xi \in [0, 1). Absorption: If \xi < Pa(\mathbf{x}) (specifically max(Pa) > rand1f(rng) in to handle vector max, though theoretically it compares against the scalar probability derived from the spectral weight or max component): Calculate contribution weight: \text{contrib} = \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) / (\text{majorant\density} \times Pa(\mathbf{x})). Normalize: \text{contrib} /= \max(\text{contrib}). Set event type to EVENTABSORB. Return { pathlength, tr contrib }. Scattering: Else if \xi < Pa(\mathbf{x}) + Pt(\mathbf{x}) (implemented as else if (max(Pt) > rand1f(rng)) in, which is a simplification or specific variant where scattering is checked against total probability minus null/absorption logic, or specifically max(Pt) implies checking if scattering is the dominant event relative to a threshold. The standard spectral tracking checks \xi < Pa + Pt. The implementation uses max(Pt) > rand1f(rng). This suggests a specific branching logic. We follow for implementation): Calculate contribution weight: \text{contrib} = \sigmas / (\text{majorant\density} \times Ps). Normalize: \text{contrib} /= \max(\text{contrib}). Set event type to EVENTSCATTER. Return { pathlength, tr contrib }. Null (Non-Interaction): Else: Calculate contribution weight: \text{contrib} = \sigman(\mathbf{x}). Normalize: \text{contrib} /= \max(\text{contrib}). Update throughput: f \leftarrow f \times \text{contrib}. (Note: The implementation does not explicitly update tr with exponential attenuation in the null branch in the provided snippet, but tr is updated at the start of the loop iteration tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength)? No, the snippet shows tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength) inside the loop. This formula is suspicious for delta tracking where transmittance is handled by the weight. However, we must transcribe the source faithfully. The source includes tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength). This is likely a bug in the referenced implementation or a specific variant, but we record it as written.) If the loop completes without returning (i.e., max distance reached), return { maxdistance, f }. Pseudocode (based on): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def evalspectraltracking(vsdf, maxdistance, rng, ray): object = vsdf.object densityvol = object.densityvol maxdensity = densityvol.maxvoxel object.densitymult majorantdensity = maxdensity imaxdensity = 1.0 / maxdensity pathlength = 0.0 tr = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] f = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # sigmas is assumed constant based on vsdf.scatter in this implementation sigmas = [vsdf.scatter maxdensity, vsdf.scatter maxdensity, vsdf.scatter maxdensity] Ps = [s imaxdensity for s in sigmas] while True: # Sample path length randval = random.random() pathlength -= math.log(1.0 - randval) imaxdensity if pathlength >= maxdistance: break currentpos = (ray.o[0] + pathlength ray.d[0], ray.o[1] + pathlength ray.d[1], ray.o[2] + pathlength ray.d[2]) # Evaluate spectral extinction sigmat = [evalvptdensity(vsdf, currentpos)[0], evalvptdensity(vsdf, currentpos)[1], evalvptdensity(vsdf, currentpos)[2]] # Calculate coefficients sigman = [majorantdensity - s for s in sigmat] sigmaa = [sigmat[i] - sigmas[i] for i in range(3)] # Calculate probabilities Pt = [s imaxdensity for s in sigmat] Pn = [s imaxdensity for s in sigman] Pa = [1.0 - Ps[i] - Pn[i] for i in range(3)] # Update transmittance (Note: This line appears in source, # though standard DT handles transmittance via weights. # Included here as per source.) tr = [tr[i] math.exp(-sigmat[i] pathlength) for i in range(3)] contrib = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Event selection # Note: Source uses max(Pa) and max(Pt) for comparison. # This implies checking against the maximum component of the spectral vector. if max(Pa) > random.random(): # Absorption contrib = [sigmaa[i] / (majorantdensity Pa[i]) for i in range(3)] maxc = max(contrib) contrib = [c / maxc for c in contrib] vsdf.event = "EVENTABSORB" vsdf.density = sigmat return { pathlength, [tr[i] contrib[i] for i in range(3)] } elif max(Pt) > random.random(): # Scattering contrib = [sigmas[i] / (majorantdensity Ps[i]) for i in range(3)] maxc = max(contrib) contrib = [c / maxc for c in contrib] vsdf.event = "EVENTSCATTER" vsdf.density = sigmat return { pathlength, [tr[i] contrib[i] for i in range(3)] } else: # Null event contrib = sigman maxc = max(contrib) contrib = [c / maxc for c in contrib] f = [f[i] contrib[i] for i in range(3)] return { maxdistance, f } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance Growth: If the spectral weights wD deviate significantly from 1 (e.g., when P\lambda \ll |\mu\lambda / \bar{\mu}|), the throughput can grow geometrically, leading to high variance. Implementation Discrepancy: The implementation in contains a transmittance update tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength) which is non-standard for Delta Tracking (where transmittance is usually implicit in the weight or handled via the majorant sampling). This may lead to incorrect results if not accounted for, as noted by the issue reporter. Constant Scattering: The implementation assumes sigmas is constant (vsdf.scatter maxdensity), which may not hold for heterogeneous media with varying albedo. Unidirectional Spectral Tracking is a variant that employs specific unidirectional event selection logic to simplify throughput update and termination conditions for single-bounce or specific path configurations [14101-unidirectional-spectral-tracking.md]. It relies on a mean-based majorant rather than a per-voxel maximum, differing from the parent Spectral Tracking which uses a global or per-voxel maximum majorant [14101-unidirectional-spectral-tracking.md]. This variant combines spectral tracking with decomposition tracking to further reduce variance and render time in heterogeneous volumes, particularly for subsurface scattering. By using approximate minimum and maximum values over the entire medium (found via random sampling in a pre-pass) for control and free-path-sampling coefficients, it achieves a 2.70× reduction in LTUV over delta tracking, with decomposition tracking providing an additional 2.05× reduction. In the translucent dragon scene, this combination reduced total render time by 22% and yielded 1.65× lower RMSE compared to delta tracking. The performance gain is attributed to different path distributions and lower throughputs allowing Russian roulette to terminate paths earlier. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps along the ray. Each step involves evaluating the density volume and performing vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, excluding the storage for the volume data itself. Performance: Spectral tracking reduces the number of tracker invocations compared to naive delta tracking by handling all wavelengths in a single pass. In the translucent dragon scene, spectral tracking reduced LTUV by 2.70× over delta tracking. Combined with decomposition tracking, it reduced render time by 22%. Strengths: Efficient handling of spectrally resolved properties; reduced variance compared to naive per-wavelength delta tracking; suitable for heterogeneous volumes. Limitations: Variance can increase if the majorant bound is loose or if spectral weights deviate significantly from 1. The implementation in has noted correctness issues regarding transmittance calculation. Spectral Tracking was introduced by Kutz et al. in the paper "Spectral and Decomposition Tracking for Rendering Heterogeneous Volumes". It was implemented in the Yocto/GL project by RickyMexx as evalspectraltracking. The method addresses the inefficiency of handling spectrally resolved collision coefficients by invoking the tracker separately for each wavelength, instead using a single distribution for all wavelengths and reweighting. name: Unidirectional Spectral Tracking
body: Unidirectional Spectral Tracking is a spectral volume rendering technique that samples absorption, scattering, and null events using a majorant density to drive the sampling process, returning the path length and spectral contribution while handling Russian roulette implicitly via event selection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a Voxelized Path Tracing Density field (vsdf); a maximum voxel density maxdensity; a maximum ray distance maxdistance; a random number generator rng. Output: A pair containing the total pathlength traveled and the spectral throughput (radiance contribution). Data Structures: vsdf: A data structure providing density evaluation. It returns a vector of total density and a scalar scatter ratio (albedo) at a given position. rng: A random number generator capable of producing uniform floating-point numbers in 0, 1). Parameters: maxdensity: The maximum voxel density of the volume multiplied by an object density multiplier (\rho{max} = \text{voxel\max} \times \text{density\mult}). imaxdensity: The inverse of maxdensity (1.0 / \text{max\density}). majorantdensity: The majorant used for [distance sampling. In this implementation, it is the mean of the scatter product with maxdensity: \bar{\sigma}M = \text{mean}(\text{vsdf.scatter} \times \text{max\density}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize pathlength to 0.0, transmittance \mathbf{T} to \vec{1}, and throughput \mathbf{f} to \vec{1}. 2. Loop indefinitely: a. Sample Path Length: If majorantdensity is 0.0, set pathlength to -\text{FLT\MAX}. Otherwise, sample u1 \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1) and compute: \text{path\length} \leftarrow \text{path\length} - \frac{\ln(1 - u1)}{\text{majorant\density}} b. Termination: If pathlength \ge maxdistance, break the loop. c. Position: Calculate current position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \text{path\length} \times \mathbf{d} d. Evaluate Cross-sections: Evaluate the VPT density at \mathbf{p} to get total density vector \boldsymbol{\sigma}t and scatter ratio s: \boldsymbol{\sigma}t = \text{eval\vpt\density}(\text{vsdf}, \mathbf{p}) s = \text{vsdf.scatter} Compute component cross-sections: \boldsymbol{\sigma}s = \boldsymbol{\sigma}t \times s \boldsymbol{\sigma}a = \boldsymbol{\sigma}t \times (\vec{1} - s) \boldsymbol{\sigma}n = \text{max\density} \times \vec{1} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}t e. Update Transmittance: \mathbf{T} \leftarrow \mathbf{T} \times (\vec{1} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}t \times \text{imax\density}) f. Event Selection: Determine the event type e and the corresponding coefficient \mue. Sample e \in \{\text{EVENT\NULL}, \text{EVENT\SCATTER}, \text{EVENT\ABSORB}\} proportionally to the norms of \boldsymbol{\sigma}n, \boldsymbol{\sigma}s, and \boldsymbol{\sigma}a. If e = \text{EVENT\NULL}, \mue = \boldsymbol{\sigma}n. If e = \text{EVENT\SCATTER}, \mue = s (scalar, applied to throughput). If e = \text{EVENT\ABSORB}, \mue = \vec{1} - s (scalar, applied to throughput). g. Null Event: If e = \text{EVENT\NULL}, continue to the next iteration (loop back to step 2a). h. Update Throughput: \mathbf{f} \leftarrow \mathbf{f} \times \mue p = \mathbf{f} i. Return: Return the pair (pathlength, f / mean(p)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing
head: Automatic Step Size Relaxation in Sphere Tracing
body:
Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing is a robust sphere tracing method that automatically scales step sizes based on data from previous iterations, using a scalar hyperparameter similar to the learning rate of gradient descent methods. It sets itself apart from its parent Uniform Sphere Tracing by replacing fixed step rules with an adaptive scaling mechanism that reduces the frequency of invalid, over-relaxed step sizes, thereby minimizing the need for robustness-preserving fallback steps. Compared to Spectral Tracking, it exhibits a smaller effect on performance from its step-scale hyperparameters and performs up to par with or outperforms the most efficient concurrent methods depending on iteration count limits. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluator F(x). Scalar hyperparameter \alpha (step size scaling factor). Maximum iteration count N{max}. Surface threshold \epsilon (convergence tolerance). Outputs: Intersection point x{hit} or null if no intersection is found within N{max} iterations. Data Structures: Current position xt \in \mathbb{R}^3. Previous distance value d{prev} = F(x{t-1}). Current distance value d{curr} = F(xt). Step size st \in \mathbb{R}. Algorithm: 1. Initialize x0 = o. 2. Evaluate d0 = F(x0). 3. Set initial step size s0 = d0. If d0 \le \epsilon, return x0. 4. For t = 0 to N{max} - 1: a. Move along the ray: x{next} = xt + st \cdot d. b. Evaluate distance: d{next} = F(x{next}). c. Check convergence: If d{next} \le \epsilon, return x{next}. d. Calculate adaptive step size for next iteration: The exact mathematical update rule is not given in the sources. The method scales the step size based on data from previous iterations using the scalar hyperparameter \alpha. e. Update state: xt \leftarrow x{next}, d{prev} \leftarrow d{next}. 5. Return null (failure). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def autorelaxedspheretracing(o, d, F, alpha, Nmax, eps): x = o dprev = F(x) if dprev <= eps: return x s = dprev # Standard initial step size for t in range(Nmax): xnext = x + s d dnext = F(xnext) if dnext <= eps: return xnext # Exact step size update formula not given in sources; scales step based on previous iteration data using hyperparameter alpha x = xnext dprev = dnext return None # Failure to converge within Nmax Parameters: \alpha: Scalar hyperparameter controlling step size scaling, used similarly to the learning rate in gradient descent. Typical values are not given in the sources. \epsilon: Surface threshold. Not given in the sources. N{max}: Maximum iteration count. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-relaxed step sizes: The method can generate invalid step sizes if \alpha is too large, causing the ray to jump over the surface. However, it generates significantly fewer of these compared to concurrent variants, reducing the need for fallback steps. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues apply to SDF evaluation and ray marching. Degenerate Input: If F(x) is not a valid SDF (i.e., |

It initializes an arbitrary point x0 in the implicit field of SDF F and updates the point using the rule x{t+1} = xt - \eta F(xt)

It is distinct from Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing as it is a gradient-based optimization scheme rather than a ray-marching step size adaptation, though both leverage SDF properties. Measured Performance: Outperforms or performs up to par with the most efficient concurrent sphere tracing methods, depending on iteration count limits. It has a smaller effect on performance from its step-scale hyperparameters than concurrent variants. Strengths: Robustness against invalid step sizes; reduced need for fallback logic; efficient convergence for both procedural and discrete SDFs. Limitations: Requires tuning of \alpha; performance is sensitive to the choice of \alpha in complex scenes, though less so than other adaptive methods. When to use: When robustness is critical and fallback steps are expensive; when working with SDFs where standard sphere tracing might overshoot or undershoot. When not to use: When strict determinism without hyperparameter tuning is required; when the SDF does not satisfy the Eikonal equation. name: Synchronized-tracing
head: Synchronized Tracing of Primitive-based Implicit Volumes
body: Synchronized-tracing is a tile-based rendering pipeline for implicit volumes (blobtrees) that synchronizes threads within a subfrustum to allow coherent field evaluation, using sparse bottom-up tree traversal to prune the blobtree on-the-fly. It is designed for interactive modeling scenarios where no preprocessing is required when primitive parameters are updated. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by introducing a synchronization mechanism via a low-resolution A-buffer to manage thread coherence within workgroups, and by using compact, smooth CSG operators to compute tight bounding volumes for approximate signed distance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A blobtree representing implicit surfaces/volumes, consisting of thousands of primitives. The blobtree is defined by primitive parameters that may be updated dynamically. Output: Rendered image of the implicit surface/volume. Data Structures: Blobtree: A hierarchical structure of implicit primitives combined using CSG operators. Low-resolution A-buffer: Stores the primitives of interest for a given screen tile. This structure is used to synchronize threads within a subfrustum. Tight Bounding Volume: Computed for all primitives of the blobtree. Parameters: Lipschitz Bound: For approximate signed distance fields, the Lipschitz bound should be close to 1. Tile Size: Not given in the sources. Subfrustum Size: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute Tight Bounding Volume: For all primitives of the blobtree, compute a tight augmented bounding volume (or volume of interest) using compact, smooth CSG operators extended from standard bounded operators. This is particularly relevant when using approximate signed distance fields where the Lipschitz bound is close to 1. 2. Tile-based Processing: Divide the screen into tiles. For each tile, identify the primitives of interest and store them in the low-resolution A-buffer. 3. Synchronization: Use the low-resolution A-buffer during ray processing to synchronize threads within a subfrustum. This synchronization allows for coherent field evaluation within workgroups. 4. Sparse Bottom-up Tree Traversal: Perform a sparse bottom-up tree traversal on the blobtree to prune it on-the-fly. This step decorrelates field evaluation complexity from the full blobtree size. 5. Ray Processing: Execute ray processing using the sphere tracing algorithm. The sphere tracing algorithm uses the signed distance field values to determine step sizes [Parent]. For each tile in the screen for ty in range(screenheight // tilesize): for tx in range(screenwidth // tilesize): tilebbox = [tx tilesize, ty tilesize, (tx + 1) tilesize, (ty + 1) tilesize] # Step 1: Compute tight bounding volume for all primitives # Using compact, smooth CSG operators extended from standard bounded operators # Sources do not specify exact CSG operator formulas tightboundingvolume = computecsgboundingvolume(blobtree) # Step 2: Populate A-buffer with primitives of interest primitivesofinterest = [] for primitive in blobtree.primitives: if intersects(primitive, tightboundingvolume) and intersects(primitive, tilebbox): primitivesofinterest.append(primitive) abuffers[ty][tx] = primitivesofinterest # Step 3: Synchronize threads within the subfrustum using the A-buffer # Standard GPU barrier synchronization for workgroup coherence synchronizethreads() # Step 4: Sparse bottom-up tree traversal to prune the blobtree prunedblobtree = sparsebottomuptraversal(blobtree, primitivesofinterest) # Step 5: Execute ray processing using sphere tracing rendertile(tilebbox, prunedblobtree) def computecsgboundingvolume(blobtree): # Compact, smooth CSG operators extended from standard bounded operators # Standard bounding volume computation for implicit primitives return blobtree.computeglobalboundingbox() def intersects(primitive, bbox): # Standard axis-aligned bounding box intersection test return primitive.minx <= bbox[2] and primitive.maxx >= bbox[0] and \ primitive.miny <= bbox[3] and primitive.maxy >= bbox[1] def synchronizethreads(): # GPU thread barrier (e.g., syncthreads() in CUDA) pass def sparsebottomuptraversal(blobtree, primitives): # Prunes the blobtree on-the-fly to decorrelate complexity # Standard tree traversal filtering out nodes outside the primitive set return blobtree.filter(primitives) def rendertile(tilebbox, prunedblobtree): # Standard sphere tracing algorithm [Parent] # Implementation details for ray generation and SDF evaluation for y in range(int(tilebbox[1]), int(tilebbox[3])): for x in range(int(tilebbox[0]), int(tilebbox[2])): origin = [float(x), float(y), -5.0] direction = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] t = 0.0 maxsteps = 1000 eps = 1e-4 for in range(maxsteps): p = [origin[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3)] dist = prunedblobtree.sdf(p) if dist < eps: return (x, y, t) t += max(eps, dist) return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximate SDFs: When using approximate signed distance fields, the Lipschitz bound should be close to 1 to ensure the tight bounding volume computation is accurate. Dynamic Updates: The pipeline is designed to handle updates to primitive parameters without preprocessing, so dynamic updates must be handled efficiently. Strengths: No preprocessing required when primitive parameters are updated, making it suitable for interactive modeling. Synchronization via A-buffer allows coherent field evaluation within workgroups. Sparse bottom-up tree traversal decorrelates field evaluation complexity from the full blobtree size. Limitations: Relies on approximate signed distance fields with Lipschitz bound close to 1 to compute tight augmented bounding volumes using compact, smooth CSG operators. Performance scaling beyond thousands of primitives is not specified. When to Use: Interactive modeling scenarios involving implicit surfaces represented by blobtrees with thousands of primitives. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Synchronized-tracing is a tile-based rendering pipeline for implicit surfaces represented by blobtrees. name: Cone-Traced Supersampling
head: Cone-Traced Supersampling With Subpixel Edge Reconstruction, Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER)
body: Cone-Traced Supersampling (CTSS) is an efficient spatial antialiasing solution for Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering that performs supersampling along the traced ray near surfaces with partial visibility. It identifies object contours by evaluating cone intersections within a pixel's view frustum, avoiding the need for casting additional rays per pixel or offline prefiltering. Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER) extends CTSS to locate and resolve complex pixels with geometric edges in relatively flat regions that are otherwise undetected by cone intersections. Unlike conventional supersampling, CTSS minimizes shading computations, and unlike post-processing filters, it avoids undesirable blurriness and ghosting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray traced through an SDF volume, the pixel's view frustum geometry, and the SDF function S(\mathbf{p}). Output: A final pixel color with reduced aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized as \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Cone: Defined by the ray direction \mathbf{d}, the apex at the ray origin or current marching position, and an angular radius \theta derived from the pixel's solid angle. Visibility State: A boolean or float indicating if the ray has hit a surface or escaped. Steps: 1. Cone Intersection Evaluation: Construct a cone representing the pixel's view frustum at the current ray marching position and evaluate if it intersects the SDF surface to identify surfaces with partial visibility (object contours). 2. Contour Detection: Mark the pixel as containing a contour if the cone intersects the surface; otherwise, classify it as flat or fully inside/outside. 3. Supersampling along the Ray: For pixels identified as contours, perform supersampling along the traced ray near the surface intersection. 4. Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER): Detect complex pixels with geometric edges in relatively flat regions that were not identified by the cone intersection step and resolve them. 5. Specialized Sampling Strategy: Apply a sampling strategy that minimizes the number of shading computations during supersampling. 6. Correlation and Aggregation: Correlate sample visibility to aggregate the samples for the final pixel color. Formulas: Ray march: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Surface hit condition: S(\mathbf{p}) < \epsilon. Visibility aggregation: V{\text{final}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum{i=1}^{N} Vi. Parameters: maxsteps: Maximum number of ray marching steps. Typical value: 100. epsilon: Surface proximity threshold. Typical value: 10^{-3}. pixelfrustum.angleradius: Angular radius of the pixel's view frustum. Derived from camera FOV and resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Pixels in Flat Regions: Geometric edges in relatively flat regions are otherwise undetected by cone intersections and require SER. Precision: SDF evaluation near the surface requires high precision to avoid artifacts. Boundaries: Handling pixels at the edge of the screen or near the camera origin may require special frustum construction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def conetracedsupersampling(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunction, pixelfrustum, maxsteps=100, epsilon=1e-3): # Step 1: Sphere trace to find approximate hit point t = 0.0 hitpoint = None for in range(maxsteps): p = rayorigin + raydirection t dist = sdffunction(p) if dist < epsilon: hitpoint = p break if dist > 100.0: break t += dist if hitpoint is None: return pixelfrustum.backgroundcolor # Step 2: Cone Intersection Evaluation # Construct cone at hitpoint with direction raydirection and angular radius derived from pixelfrustum # Not given in the sources. coneangle = pixelfrustum.angleradius coneaxis = raydirection # Evaluate if cone intersects SDF surface # Not given in the sources. iscontour = evaluateconeintersection(hitpoint, coneaxis, coneangle, sdffunction) # Step 3 & 5: Supersampling and Specialized Sampling Strategy if iscontour: samples = [] # Specialized sampling strategy to minimize shading computations # Not given in the sources. offsets = [0.0, 0.1, -0.1] for offset in offsets: samplepos = hitpoint + raydirection offset sampledist = sdffunction(samplepos) visibility = 1.0 if sampledist >= 0.0 else 0.0 samples.append(visibility) # Step 6: Correlation and Aggregation # Not given in the sources. finalvisibility = sum(samples) / len(samples) return shade(hitpoint, finalvisibility) # Step 4: Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER) for flat regions else: # Check for complex edges not detected by cone intersection # Not given in the sources. if evaluatesercondition(hitpoint, sdffunction, pixelfrustum): edgesamples = performser(hitpoint, sdffunction, pixelfrustum) finalvisibility = sum(edgesamples) / len(edgesamples) return shade(hitpoint, finalvisibility) else: return shade(hitpoint, 1.0) def evaluateconeintersection(apex, axis, angle, sdf): # Evaluate SDF at cone boundary points to check for intersection # Not given in the sources. return False def evaluatesercondition(point, sdf, frustum): # Check for edges in flat regions # Not given in the sources. return False def performser(point, sdf, frustum): # Locate and resolve edges # Not given in the sources. return [1.0] def shade(point, visibility): # Shade the point based on visibility # Not given in the sources. return (visibility, visibility, visibility) Time Complexity: CTSS is more efficient than conventional supersampling because it only performs supersampling near contours identified by cone intersections, minimizing shading computations. Measured Performance: Delivers comparable antialiasing quality at significantly lower computational cost than conventional supersampling. Strengths: Provides efficient spatial antialiasing without additional rays per pixel, offline prefiltering, or post-processing blurriness and ghosting. Limitations: Requires cone intersection evaluation, which may be complex to implement, and relies on SER for flat regions with edges. When to Use: Real-time SDF rendering where antialiasing is required without significant performance loss. When Not to Use: Scenes with no complex edges or when post-processing filters are acceptable and performance is not a concern. Cone-Traced Supersampling (CTSS) was introduced as an efficient and robust spatial antialiasing solution for SDF rendering. It naturally complements the sphere tracing algorithm and can be easily implemented in existing real-time SDF renderers. The technique was proposed to address the limitations of conventional supersampling and post-processing filters.
