name: Reparameterization for Differentiable SDF Rendering
head: Reparameterized Neural SDF Rendering, Silhouette-aware reparameterization for SDFs, Vicini et al. method, Warp-reparameterized inverse SDF renderer
body: A differentiable rendering method for neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) that computes correct gradients with respect to geometric scene parameters (e.g., neural network weights) by reparameterizing the pixel integral to handle primary visibility discontinuities (silhouettes/occlusions) without requiring volumetric approximations or external geometric supervision like segmentation masks. It sets itself apart from prior SDF renderers (e.g., IDR [Yariv 2020]) by eliminating the need for per-view masks and volumetric approximations, and from mesh-based differentiable renderers by deriving a continuous warp function specifically for implicit SDF boundaries where direct sampling is challenging. Inputs: Neural SDF function \phi(x; \theta), where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and \theta are geometric parameters. Camera ray origin o and direction \omega. Sphere tracing parameters (max steps, threshold). Outputs: Rendered pixel color I. Correct gradients \nabla\theta I via automatic differentiation. Data Structures: Sphere tracing points: A list of tuples (ti, xi) for i=1 \dots N, where ti is the distance step and xi = o + ti \omega is the 3D position. Warp field \mathbf{V}(x; \pi): A 3D vector field defined over the scene space, parameterized by scene parameters \pi (subset of \theta). Method Steps: 1. Sphere Tracing: Perform standard sphere tracing on the ray (o, \omega) using the SDF \phi(x; \pi). Record intermediate distances ti and positions xi for i=1 \dots N. Detach the current parameter values \pi for the warp computation to prevent gradient flow through the warp construction itself during the backward pass of the warp calculation, but keep them linked for the final render. 2. Compute Evaluation Distance t: Calculate a weighted average of the sphere tracing distances to approximate the intersection distance, which serves as the basis for the warp field. t:= \frac{\sum{i=1}^N w^{(i)} ti}{\sum{i=1}^N w^{(i)}} where w^{(i)} is a weighting function designed to ensure t converges to the intersection distance near visibility boundaries while keeping variance low. The weight is defined as: w^{(i)}:= w{\text{edge}}^{(i)} w{\text{dist}}^{(i)} w{\text{bbox}}^{(i)} Specific terms for w{\text{edge}}, w{\text{dist}}, w{\text{bbox}} are detailed in the original paper. 3. Construct Warp Field \mathbf{V}: Compute the 3D vector field \mathbf{V} at the sphere tracing points. This field maps the pixel domain to a reparameterized domain to remove discontinuities. The warp is defined as: \mathbf{V}(x, \pi):= -\frac{\partialx \phi(x, \pi0)}{\phi(x, \pi) \|\partialx \phi(x, \pi0)\|2} where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is any point (specifically the sphere tracing points xi), \pi0 is the detached value of \pi used for the gradient \partialx \phi, and \phi(x, \pi) is the current SDF value. Note: The sources describe \mathbf{V} as a vector field used to construct the warp function \mathcal{V} or T. The exact integration of \mathbf{V} into the final warp function T or \mathcal{V} that satisfies \partial\pi T = \partial\pi \omegab involves solving for the continuous warp that aligns with the motion of discontinuities. 4. Subsampling (Optional): To make the computation tractable for neural SDFs, subsample the sphere tracing points when computing the warp field, reducing the computational burden of the backward pass. 5. Reparameterized Rendering: Use the computed warp function (derived from \mathbf{V} and t) to reparameterize the pixel integral. The rendering function becomes continuous in the parameters, allowing standard automatic differentiation to compute correct gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def reparameterizedsdfrender(rayo, rayd, sdfnet, params, maxsteps=64, threshold=1e-4): """ rayo: (3,) tensor, ray origin rayd: (3,) tensor, ray direction sdfnet: neural network returning phi(x, params) params: tensor of geometric parameters theta maxsteps: int, max sphere tracing steps threshold: float, SDF threshold for surface """ # 1. Sphere Tracing t = 0.0 positions = [] distances = [] for i in range(maxsteps): x = rayo + t rayd phival = sdfnet(x, params) positions.append(x) distances.append(t) if phival < threshold: break t += phival # Standard sphere tracing step positions = torch.stack(positions) # (N, 3) distances = torch.stack(distances) # (N,) # 2. Compute Weights w(i) # Note: Exact formula for wedge, wdist, wbbox is in Section 4.2 # Placeholder for weight calculation based on source description weights = computeweights(positions, distances, rayo, rayd) # 3. Compute Evaluation Distance teval teval = torch.sum(weights distances) / torch.sum(weights) # 4. Construct Warp Field V # Detach params for gradient computation in V to isolate discontinuity handling paramsdetached = params.detach() # Compute gradient of SDF w.r.t x at detached params # This requires autograd setup for positions w.r.t paramsdetached positionsdetached = positions.detach().requiresgrad(True) phidetached = sdfnet(positionsdetached, paramsdetached) phidetached.sum().backward() # Compute dphi/dx gradphidetached = positionsdetached.grad # (N, 3) # Compute current SDF values and gradients for the warp definition # Note: The formula uses phi(x, pi) in denominator and gradphi(x, pi0) in numerator phicurrent = sdfnet(positions, params) # (N,) gradphicurrent = sdfnet(positions, params).requiresgrad(True) # Re-compute gradient for current params if needed for normalization, # but source specifies ||gradphi(x, pi0)||2 # We already have gradphidetached which is gradphi(x, pi0) # V(x, pi) = - gradphi(x, pi0) / ( phi(x, pi) ||gradphi(x, pi0)||2) normgradphidetached = torch.norm(gradphidetached, dim=1, keepdim=True) # (N, 1) # Avoid division by zero normgradphidetached = torch.clamp(normgradphidetached, min=1e-8) warpfieldV = -gradphidetached / (phicurrent.unsqueeze(1) normgradphidetached) # (N, 3) # 5. Use Warp Field to Reparameterize # The exact reparameterization function T or V(u; theta) is constructed from V. # In practice, this often involves perturbing the ray direction or origin # based on the warp field to align discontinuities. # Source states: "Using this warp, we reparameterize the integration domain... # allows us to compute correct gradients." # For implementation, the warp field V is typically used to adjust the ray # or the sampling distribution. A common approach in reparameterization # is to define a new ray parameterization. # However, the source does not give explicit pseudocode for the final # ray adjustment, only the construction of V. # We assume the warp field V is used to define a continuous mapping. # Placeholder for the final reparameterized render call # This step depends on the specific implementation of the warp function T # derived from V. color = renderwithwarp(rayo, rayd, sdfnet, params, warpfieldV, teval) return color def computeweights(positions, distances, rayo, rayd): # Implementation of wedge, wdist, wbbox as per # Not fully specified in provided notes, so returning uniform weights as placeholder # In actual implementation, this must follow Section 4.2 return torch.oneslike(distances) def renderwithwarp(rayo, rayd, sdfnet, params, warpfieldV, teval): # Placeholder for the actual reparameterized rendering logic # The warp field V is used to ensure continuity. # This function would integrate the radiance using the reparameterized domain. # Since the source does not provide the exact integration formula, # we return a standard SDF render result for completeness of structure. # In reality, the gradient flow through this function must be continuous. return sdfnet(rayo + teval rayd, params) # Simplified Parameters: maxsteps: Typical value not given in sources. threshold: Typical value not given in sources. N: Number of sphere tracing steps. Subsampling is recommended for neural SDFs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Naive differentiation fails due to discontinuities at silhouettes. Direct sampling of SDF boundaries is challenging, making mesh-based silhouette sampling inapplicable. Precision issues in computing the warp field near the surface where \phi(x, \pi) \to 0. A method for fast neural SDF rendering. Choose when speed is critical and differentiability is not the primary focus. Handles silhouettes for explicit meshes. Choose when rendering triangle meshes rather than implicit SDFs. Integrates diffuse shading for SDFs. Choose when shading models are the primary concern. Reconstructs 3D from single depth. Choose when input is limited to single-view depth. Reconstructs shape from multi-view images. Choose when photometric consistency is key. Optimizes camera poses. Choose when camera parameters are unknown. Uses spherical Gaussians for lighting. Choose when complex lighting is required. Time Complexity: Depends on sphere tracing steps N. Subsampling reduces backward pass cost. Memory Complexity: Stores sphere tracing points and warp field values. Performance: Produces 3D reconstructions comparable to prior SDF-based inverse rendering methods. Strengths: No need for segmentation masks or volumetric approximations. Correct gradients for geometric parameters. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to sphere tracing and warp field construction. Requires careful weighting function design. When to use: Inverse rendering of neural SDFs from multi-view images where geometric supervision is unavailable. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and approximate gradients are acceptable. Originated by Vicini et al. [VSJ22] (Differentiable Rendering of Neural SDFs through Reparameterization). It builds on reparameterization approaches for triangle meshes [Bangaru et al. 2020; Loubet et al. 2019] and adapts them to implicit SDFs. Used in inverse rendering problems to optimize neural shapes from multi-view images. name: Forward Rendering Pipeline with Closed-Form SG Integration
head: Forward Rendering Pipeline
body: This method performs differentiable forward rendering of scenes defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and Spherical Gaussian (SG) approximations for appearance. It solves the rendering equation by representing both the environment lighting and the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) as SGs, allowing the integral to be computed in closed form. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the specular component via SGs for relighting, rather than relying solely on neural radiance fields or implicit neural representations without explicit physics-based material parameters. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Scene geometry defined by SDF S(x; \Theta) and its parameters \Theta. Appearance parameters: environment map represented by M SGs with parameters \{\xik, \lambdak, \muk\}{k=1}^M, specular BRDF parameters \{\lambda, \mu\}, and diffuse albedo MLP parameters \Phi. Outputs: Observed color Lo(\omegao; x) for the ray. Data Structures: Spherical Gaussian (SG): Defined by amplitude \xi, sharpness \lambda, and direction \mu. MLP: A multi-layer perceptron mapping position x to diffuse albedo a. Steps: 1. Sphere Tracing: Find the intersection point x between the ray r = o + td and the surface S(x; \Theta) using sphere tracing. 2. Normal Computation: Compute the surface normal n = \nablax S at x using automatic differentiation. 3. Albedo Computation: Compute the diffuse albedo a(x; \Phi) at x by evaluating the MLP. 4. Closed-Form Integration: Compute the color for ray r by evaluating the rendering equation in closed form using the SG approximation with n, environment map parameters, a, specular BRDF parameters, and viewing direction d. Formulas: The rendering equation involves the incident radiance Li(\omegai) and the BRDF fr(\omegao, \omegai; x) = \pi a + fs(\omegao, \omegai; x), both represented with SGs. The geometry term \omegai \cdot n is approximated as an SG: \omegai \cdot n \approx G(\omegai; 0.0315, n, 32.7080) - 31.7003 \quad (9) The observed color Lo(\omegao; x) is computed by integrating the multiplication of the environment map SGs, the warped specular BRDF SG, and the geometry term approximation in closed form. Parameters: \{\xik, \lambdak, \muk\}{k=1}^M: Environment map SG parameters. \{\lambda, \mu\}: Specular BRDF parameters. \Phi: Diffuse albedo MLP parameters. Edge Cases: Precision in automatic differentiation for normal computation. Degenerate input where the ray does not intersect the surface is handled by sphere tracing termination rules from the parent method. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def forwardrenderingpipeline(rayo, rayd, sdffn, envsgparams, brdfparams, albedomlpparams, maxsteps=64, tol=1e-4): # Step 1: Sphere Tracing to find intersection x t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): x = rayo + t rayd dist = sdffn(x) if dist < tol: break t += dist else: return np.zeros(3) # No intersection found # Step 2: Compute normal n = ∇x S at x via automatic differentiation eps = 1e-5 n = np.zeros(3) for i in range(3): xplus = x.copy(); xplus[i] += eps xminus = x.copy(); xminus[i] -= eps n[i] = (sdffn(xplus) - sdffn(xminus)) / (2 eps) n = n / np.linalg.norm(n) # Step 3: Compute diffuse albedo a(x; Φ) at x a = albedomlpforward(x, albedomlpparams) # Step 4: Compute color by evaluating rendering equation in closed form with SG approximation color = closedformsgintegration(envsgparams, brdfparams, n, rayd, a) return color def albedomlpforward(x, params): # MLP evaluation for diffuse albedo w1, b1, w2, b2 = params h = np.maximum(0, x @ w1 + b1) return np.maximum(0, h @ w2 + b2) def closedformsgintegration(envsgparams, brdfparams, n, viewdir, albedo): # Integrates multiplication of environment SGs, warped specular BRDF, and geometry term approximation totalcolor = np.zeros(3) for xi, lam, mu in envsgparams: # Approximate geometry term ωi · n as SG: G(ωi; 0.0315, n, 32.7080) - 31.7003 geosg = (0.0315, n, 32.7080) geooffset = -31.7003 # Combine environment SG, specular BRDF SG, and geometry SG combinedsg = sgproduct(xi, lam, mu, brdfparams, geosg) # Integrate combined SG over hemisphere totalcolor += sghemisphereintegral(combinedsg, viewdir) albedo return totalcolor def sgproduct(xi1, lam1, mu1, brdfparams, geosg): # Standard closed-form product of Spherical Gaussians xi2, lam2, mu2 = brdfparams[0], brdfparams[1], brdfparams[2] xi3, lam3, mu3 = geosg lamc = lam1 + lam2 + lam3 muc = (lam1 mu1 + lam2 mu2 + lam3 mu3) / lamc xic = xi1 xi2 xi3 np.exp(-0.5 lamc (1 - np.dot(mu1, mu2)) - 0.5 lamc (1 - np.dot(mu2, mu3))) return (xic, lamc, muc) def sghemisphereintegral(sg, viewdir): # Standard integral of an SG over the hemisphere xi, lam, mu = sg return xi (2 np.pi / (lam + 1)) max(0, np.dot(mu, viewdir)) Integrates the multiplication of Spherical Gaussians representing the environment map, warped specular BRDF, and geometry term approximation in closed form to compute the observed color Lo(\omegao; x). The optimizable parameters are \{\xik, \lambdak, \muk\}{k=1}^M (environment map), \{\lambda, \mu\} (specular BRDF), and \Phi (diffuse albedo MLP). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fully differentiable with respect to all parameters, enabling inverse rendering and optimization. Closed-form integration avoids sampling noise. Limitations: Relies on the SG approximation for the BRDF and geometry term, which may not capture all high-frequency lighting effects perfectly. When to use: When differentiable rendering with explicit material parameters and relighting capabilities is required. When not to use: When high-fidelity global illumination beyond SG approximation is needed without significant computational overhead. Originated in the PhySG paper (Li et al., 2021). It builds on Differentiable Sphere Tracing by adding a physics-based appearance model using Spherical Gaussians. It is used for inverse rendering, material editing, and relighting of 3D scenes. name: Step Size Optimization
body: Step Size Optimization encompasses techniques that dynamically determine the distance \Delta t to advance a ray during volume rendering or implicit surface marching, replacing fixed-step methods to balance computational cost and visual fidelity. It solves the inefficiency of uniform sampling in empty space and the aliasing/penetration artifacts of steps that are too large for local geometry. Unlike Standard Constant Step Ray Marching, which uses a uniform \Delta t, this family adapts the step length based on local scene properties such as Signed Distance Field (SDF) values, density gradients, or geometric gaps. It differs from Sphere Tracing in that while sphere tracing strictly uses the SDF value as a lower bound for the step (often with a relaxation factor), step size optimization includes broader strategies like error estimation, gap limiting, and integration-based adaptive stepping that may not rely solely on the geometric distance bound. All methods in this family operate on a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by distance t. The core loop evaluates a scene function (SDF, density field, or volume texture) at the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to determine the next step size \Delta t and check for termination. Termination Conditions: 1. Surface Hit: The ray has intersected the target geometry. For SDFs, this is typically |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon or f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0. For volumes, this may be a density threshold or opacity accumulation. 2. Escape/Miss: The ray has traveled beyond a maximum distance t{max} or exceeded a maximum iteration count N{max}. 3. Early Termination (Volumes): Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1 - \epsilon), or accumulated transmission falls below a minimum threshold, allowing the ray to stop early as further contributions are negligible. Step Size Determination: The step size \Delta t is computed based on the local scene properties: SDF-based: \Delta t is often derived from the SDF value f(\mathbf{p}), potentially scaled by a relaxation factor or Lipschitz constant \lambda. Volume-based: \Delta t may be fixed, adaptive based on density gradients, or constrained by minimum/maximum bounds to prevent aliasing or excessive computation. Safety: Steps must be chosen to ensure the ray does not penetrate the surface or skip over significant volumetric features, often requiring conservative clamping. Pseudocode Structure: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchloop(rayorigin, raydirection, scenefunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon, minstep=1e-4, maxstep=1.0): """ Generic ray marching loop with adaptive step size and termination. """ t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return False, t p = rayorigin + raydirection t val = scenefunc(p) # ishit: returns True if val indicates a surface intersection (e.g., |val| < epsilon) if ishit(val, epsilon): return True, t # isearlyexit: returns True if accumulated opacity/transmission meets volume criteria if isearlyexit(val, t): return False, t # computestepsize: calculates delta t based on val, t, i step = computestepsize(val, t, i) step = max(step, minstep) step = min(step, maxstep) t += step return False, t Uses the local SDF value as an upper bound for the step size, scaled by a ratio, to prevent surface penetration. It is distinguished from other adaptive methods by relying on the geometric distance field value itself as the primary driver of step size, rather than error estimates or density gradients alone. Chosen when geometric safety is paramount and a valid SDF is available. Calculates the minimal sample distance by projecting each dataset cell axis onto the viewport, accounting for camera and volume transforms. It differs from standard distance-field ray marching by explicitly evaluating the angular span of a voxel's extent from the camera center to determine sampling density. Chosen for volume rendering to ensure consistent voxel coverage and prevent gaps or overlaps in oblique views. Calculates a relative error metric for adaptive stepping by normalizing a derivative or error vector against the local field magnitude. It contrasts with methods that rely on absolute field values or fixed Lipschitz constants. Chosen when high precision is required in regions of high field variation, avoiding unnecessarily small steps in high-magnitude regions. Bounds the step size by half the vertical gap to the surface for heightfield terrain rendering. Unlike standard sphere tracing which relies on a global Lipschitz constant, this method prevents ray stalling and surface overshooting on non-distance fields. Chosen for terrain rendering to ensure the ray never penetrates ridgelines while allowing larger steps in open space. An iterative numerical method that evaluates the Volume Rendering Integral using adaptive step sizes for both the inner (transparency) and outer (color) integrals. It solves the recursion depth and re-computation issues inherent in standard recursive adaptive methods, making it suitable for GPU implementation. Chosen for high-fidelity volume rendering where accuracy of the integrated color/opacity is critical. Dynamically adjusts the ray marching interval \Delta t during volume rendering or ray tracing to balance computational cost against visual fidelity. This family is distinct from its siblings, which focus on specific constraints like geometric safety, resolution limits, or integration accuracy. Chosen as a general-purpose adaptive strategy for complex volumetric data. Convexity Enhancement leverages the geometric property of convex sets to increase step size and accelerate convergence in sphere tracing. For a convex set A defined by a signed distance function d(\mathbf{p}), the line segment from the current point \mathbf{p} to the intersection of the ray with the tangent plane at \mathbf{p} does not intersect the surface except possibly at the endpoint. The step is calculated as: \mathbf{p}{next} = \text{lerp}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{p} + d(\mathbf{p}) \frac{\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p})}{\|\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p})\|}) = \mathbf{p} + d(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{v} where \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p}) is the gradient (normal) and \mathbf{v} is the normalized direction towards the tangent plane intersection. If d(\mathbf{p}) < 0, the ray has passed the object and does not intersect it, allowing for early termination (Corollary 4.1). This method causes sphere tracing to converge quadratically, similar to Newton's method, rather than linearly. In benchmarks, it reduced execution time for a single sphere from 100% to 69% and for the Zeno logo from 100% to 73%. A pitfall is that rays parallel to a horizon line (e.g., a ground plane) would otherwise step indefinitely; Corollary 4.1 avoids this by detecting when the ray has stepped beyond the object. Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) performance optimization involves reducing the computational cost of noise evaluation during ray marching. Key techniques include: 1. Reducing Octave Count: Use fewer octaves for distant objects based on distance t or time, e.g., int oct = 5 - int(log2(1.0 + t 0.5)). 2. Multi-level LOD: Assign different octave counts to different resolutions (e.g., 3, 9, 16 octaves). 3. Texture Sampling: Use texture sampling instead of mathematical hash functions for noise generation to leverage hardware acceleration. 4. Loop Unrolling: Manually unroll small loops and slightly vary lacunarity to improve instruction pipelining. 5. Adaptive Step Size: Use distance-based adaptive stepping, e.g., float dt = max(0.05, 0.02 t). 6. Directional Derivative: Compute normals using a directional derivative instead of a full gradient, reducing sample count from 3 to 1. 7. Early Termination: Break the FBM summation loop if the accumulated amplitude exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.99). Step size optimization evolved from the limitations of fixed-step ray marching, which either wasted samples in empty space or missed details with large steps. Convexity enhancements were introduced to accelerate convergence for convex primitives, providing quadratic convergence rates. FBM optimizations address the high cost of procedural noise in ray marching, particularly for terrain and ocean rendering. Adaptive integration methods for volume rendering further refined step control by treating the rendering equation as a numerical integration problem. name: Safe Raymarching Step Size
head: Conservative stepping, Distance-Aided Ray Marching, Grid Step Size, Ray Marching with SDF-guided Step Size, TensorBase Step Size Calculation
body: Safe Raymarching Step Size is a technique for determining the step length \Delta t along a ray in volume rendering or implicit surface rendering by using the local distance to the nearest geometry as an upper bound. It solves the problem of "popping" artifacts or missed intersections that occur when fixed step sizes are too large to resolve fine details or when distorted distance fields overestimate the distance to the surface. Unlike fixed-step methods, it adapts the step size to the local distance to the nearest object, ensuring the ray never penetrates the surface or skips over significant volumetric features. It is distinguished from Adaptive Step Size Control by its reliance on the geometric distance field value itself as the primary driver of step size, rather than error estimates or density gradients alone. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}. Scene function f(\mathbf{p}) returning the Signed Distance Field (SDF) value or distance bound at point \mathbf{p}. Maximum marching distance t{max} (or maxboundzdepth). SDF threshold \epsilon (e.g., 5 \times 10^{-5}) for surface hit detection. Clamping distance d{clamp} (e.g., 0.1) to limit extreme step sizes. Ray marching ratio \lambda (e.g., 1.5) to scale the step size for safety or aggressiveness. Grid parameters (optional, for grid-based SDFs): Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by min and max, and grid resolution gridSize. Outputs: List of sampled points, SDF values, and accumulated depths. A validity mask indicating which rays successfully hit the surface or remained within bounds. Data Structures: marchingzdepth: List of floats storing the accumulated distance along each ray, initialized to 0.0. sdflist: List of lists, each inner list of length N, storing the SDF value at each step. pointslist: List of lists, each inner list of length N, storing the 3D coordinates of samples. validmaskrender: Boolean list of length N indicating valid rays. Step-by-Step Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize marchingzdepth to zeros for all valid rays. Initialize empty lists sdflist, pointslist, and marchingzdepthlist. Compute maxboundzdepth based on the camera position and ray directions, representing the maximum valid distance within the scene bounds. 2. Marching Loop: For each step i from 0 to marchstep - 1: Sample Points: Calculate the current 3D position for each ray: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \times (\text{init\zdepth} + \text{marching\zdepth}) where initzdepth is the initial offset (often 0.0). Evaluate SDF: Query the scene function f(\mathbf{p}i) to get the distance to the nearest object. If using a neural decoder, detach gradients if differentiability is not required for this step. Clamp SDF: To prevent instability from distorted fields or extreme values, clamp the SDF value: f{clamped} = \max(-d{clamp}, \min(d{clamp}, f(\mathbf{p}i))) Typical d{clamp} is 0.1. Compute Step Size: Grid-based: If using a voxel grid, calculate the unit size per grid cell as \frac{\text{AABB\size}}{\text{gridSize}}. The step size is the mean unit size multiplied by a stepratio. SDF-based: Calculate the step size as the product of the clamped SDF and the ray marching ratio: \Delta t = f{clamped} \times \lambda Typical \lambda is 1.5. Note: Some implementations use a fixed step derived from grid resolution. Update Depth: \text{marching\zdepth} \leftarrow \text{marching\zdepth} + \Delta t Store Data: Append f(\mathbf{p}i) to sdflist, \mathbf{p}i to pointslist, and the new marchingzdepth to marchingzdepthlist. 3. Termination and Validation: After the loop (or if early termination conditions are met in a variant): Max Distance Check: Compute validmaskmaxmarchingzdepth by checking if \text{marching\zdepth} + \text{init\zdepth} < \text{maxbound\zdepth}. Surface Hit Check: Compute validmaskraymarching by checking if the minimum absolute SDF across all steps is \le \epsilon. First Query Check: Compute validmaskfirstquery by checking if the first SDF query > \epsilon. This handles the corner case where the ray starts inside the surface or exactly on it, preventing incorrect filtering. Final Mask: Combine masks: \text{valid\mask\render} = \text{valid\mask\max\marching\zdepth} \land \text{valid\mask\ray\marching} \land \text{valid\mask\first\query} Return sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist, and validmaskrender. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def saferaymarchstepsize(rayorigins, raydirections, scenefunc, maxbounddist, threshold, clampdist, raymarchingratio, marchstep, initzdepth=0.0): """ Performs safe raymarching using SDF-guided step sizes. rayorigins: list of (x, y, z) tuples raydirections: list of (dx, dy, dz) tuples maxbounddist: list of floats """ n = len(rayorigins) marchingzdepth = [0.0] n sdflist = [] pointslist = [] marchingzdepthlist = [] for stepidx in range(marchstep): currentsdfs = [] currentpoints = [] for j in range(n): # 1. Calculate current 3D position dist = initzdepth + marchingzdepth[j] p = (raydirections[j][0] dist + rayorigins[j][0], raydirections[j][1] dist + rayorigins[j][1], raydirections[j][2] dist + rayorigins[j][2]) # 2. Evaluate SDF sdfval = scenefunc(p) # 3. Clamp SDF to prevent instability from distorted fields sdfclamped = max(-clampdist, min(clampdist, sdfval)) # 4. Compute step size step = sdfclamped raymarchingratio # 5. Update accumulated depth marchingzdepth[j] += step # 6. Store data currentsdfs.append(sdfval) currentpoints.append(p) sdflist.append(currentsdfs) pointslist.append(currentpoints) marchingzdepthlist.append(list(marchingzdepth)) # 7. Validation Masks validmaskrender = [] for j in range(n): # Check if rays stayed within max bound finaldepth = initzdepth + marchingzdepth[j] validmax = finaldepth < maxbounddist[j] # Check if any step was close to surface (min absolute SDF <= threshold) minabssdf = min(abs(sdflist[k][j]) for k in range(marchstep)) validhit = minabssdf <= threshold # Check if first query was > threshold (handles start-inside-surface case) firstsdf = sdflist[0][j] validfirst = firstsdf > threshold # Combine masks validmaskrender.append(validmax and validhit and validfirst) return sdflist, marchingzdepthlist, pointslist, validmaskrender Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distorted SDFs: Domain repetition or boolean operations can distort the distance field, causing the estimated distance to be larger than the actual distance to the surface. This leads to the ray skipping over geometry. Mitigation: Step shorter than the SDF returns (e.g., use a ratio < 1.0 or clamp aggressively). Start Inside Surface: If the ray origin is inside the geometry, the first SDF query may be below the threshold. The validmaskfirstquery logic ensures these rays are not incorrectly filtered out or handled as misses depending on the rendering logic. Boundary Exceedance: Rays must not exceed the maxboundzdepth. This is strictly checked against the final accumulated depth. Precision: Using a raymarchingratio greater than 1.0 (e.g., 1.5) can speed up convergence but risks overshooting if the SDF is not a true distance field or is distorted. Analyzes the inverse relationship between SDF evaluation accuracy and step count. Underestimating distance forces smaller steps, increasing iterations. An exact but slower SDF can outperform an inaccurate but fast one if the inaccuracy causes disproportionate step reduction. Uses a nested BVH to compute tighter, adaptive Lipschitz constants for step size calculation, solving the problem of overly conservative steps in large scenes where global constants are too large. Uses the local SDF gradient to compute larger, safer step sizes, particularly near silhouettes. Combines first and second Lipschitz constraints to account for curvature. A robust method using a pre-computed global Lipschitz constant \lambda to guarantee no penetration or overshooting. Simple and stable but potentially less efficient for complex scenes with varying feature scales. Time Complexity: O(N \times S), where N is the number of rays and S is the number of steps. The number of steps S is adaptive and depends on the scene's geometry and the chosen raymarchingratio. Memory Complexity: O(N \times S) to store the history of SDF values and points for rendering or differentiable backpropagation. Strengths: Prevents popping artifacts and missed intersections by respecting the geometric distance bound. Simple to implement for SDF-based rendering. Limitations: Sensitive to SDF distortion. Requires a valid distance field or distance bound. Not directly applicable to non-SDF volume data without adaptation (e.g., using density gradients). When to Use: Ideal for rendering implicit surfaces defined by SDFs where visual correctness is critical and the SDF is well-behaved. Also used in neural rendering pipelines (e.g., DeepSDF) where differentiable SDF evaluation is required. When Not to Use: When the scene is defined by explicit meshes (use ray-triangle intersection) or when the SDF is highly distorted and cannot be reliably clamped. Safe Raymarching Step Size, often referred to as Distance-Aided Ray Marching, originated in the demoscene as a method to efficiently render complex 3D scenes using Signed Distance Fields. The core insight, attributed to Adok, is that the distance to the nearest object provides a safe upper bound for the step size, ensuring no geometry is skipped. This technique was later adopted in academic and industrial rendering, particularly in the context of neural implicit representations like DeepSDF, where it is used to sample points along rays for differentiable rendering. Variants like Lipschitz-constrained stepping and adaptive methods have been developed to address limitations in complex scenes. name: Distance Accuracy vs Performance Trade-off
head: Distance Estimate Accuracy, Distance accuracy vs performance, Sphere Tracing Performance Analysis, Underestimate vs Exact SDF Performance
body: This method analyzes the inverse relationship between the accuracy of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluation and the computational cost of sphere tracing. It establishes that underestimating the distance to the surface forces the ray marcher to take smaller steps, significantly increasing the number of iterations required for convergence. The core insight is that a slower, exact SDF evaluation can outperform a faster, inaccurate distance bound if the inaccuracy forces a disproportionate increase in step count. The method relies on the geometric constraint that the step size s in sphere tracing must satisfy s \le d(\mathbf{p}), where d(\mathbf{p}) is the distance estimate at the current ray position \mathbf{p}. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. SDF function d(\mathbf{p}) which may be an approximation or exact. Convergence threshold \epsilon. Maximum traversal distance \text{max\dist}. Maximum iteration count \text{max\steps}. Outputs: Boolean indicating surface intersection. Number of steps taken. Data Structures: Current ray position \mathbf{p} (vector). Step counter n (integer). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, normalize \mathbf{d}, and set n = 0. 2. Evaluate distance estimate d{est} = d(\mathbf{p}). 3. Clamp negative estimates to zero: d{est} \leftarrow \max(d{est}, 0). 4. If d{est} < \epsilon, terminate successfully. If \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}\| > \text{max\dist} or n \ge \text{max\steps}, terminate unsuccessfully. 5. Advance ray: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + d{est} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 6. Increment n \leftarrow n + 1. 7. Repeat from step 2. Formulas: The relationship between distance accuracy and step count is derived from the convergence rate. Experiments on a sphere show that halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Thus, the step count scales inversely with the estimate magnitude: N{steps} \propto \frac{1}{d{est}} Where N{steps} is the number of iterations and d{est} is the average distance estimate magnitude. Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Severe Underestimation: If d{est} is significantly smaller than the true distance d{true}, the ray takes many small steps, wasting computation. For example, a bound that returns at worst 1% of the true distance may perform worse than an exact function in specific cases. Exact vs. Approximate Cost: The total cost is Cost = N{steps} \times Cost{eval}. A slower exact function may have higher Cost{eval} but much lower N{steps}, resulting in lower total time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunction, epsilon, maxdist, maxsteps): """ Demonstrates the trade-off by comparing step counts for different SDF accuracies. """ # Normalize direction to ensure step size equals distance estimate dlen = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in raydirection)) d = [x / dlen for x in raydirection] p = list(rayorigin) steps = 0 while steps < maxsteps: # Evaluate distance. The accuracy of this call determines performance. dist = sdffunction(p) # Clamp negative distances to zero to prevent stepping inside the surface dist = max(dist, 0.0) if dist < epsilon: return True, steps # Check maximum traversal distance raylen = math.sqrt(sum((p[i] - rayorigin[i])2 for i in range(3))) if raylen > maxdist: return False, steps # Advance ray by the estimated distance p = [p[i] + dist d[i] for i in range(3)] steps += 1 return False, steps Adaptive Convergence Threshold is a stopping condition for distance-field ray marching that determines when the ray has sufficiently converged to the surface to halt further computation. It solves the trade-off between rendering accuracy and computational cost by dynamically calculating a threshold \epsilon based on camera parameters, ensuring that the ray front ends of neighboring pixels do not intersect. Unlike fixed thresholds, this method scales with the scene geometry and camera setup to prevent both dilation (loss of detail) and erosion (incomplete geometry). Time Complexity: The number of steps N is inversely proportional to the accuracy of the distance estimate. Halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Measured Performance: Sphere Experiments: Halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Noise Functions: In experiments with fractal noise, the rendering time for 1/f^2 noise was 7.3 times that of single noise, despite an expected 12x increase due to 6 invocations per evaluation. For 1/f noise, rendering time was 27.5 times single noise time (expected 36x). This indicates that while evaluation cost scales linearly with complexity, the step count reduction from better distance estimates (or other optimizations) can mitigate total time. Ellipsoid Case: For an ellipsoid with axes 100, 100, 1, a fast signed distance bound (returning at worst 1% of the true distance) performs worse than an exact SDF using Newton iterations, despite the exact function being slower per evaluation. Strengths and Limitations: Strength: Provides a theoretical basis for choosing SDF implementations. It highlights that "fast" functions are not always optimal. Limitation: Requires accurate knowledge of the SDF's error bounds to predict performance. The trade-off is non-linear and scene-dependent. When to Use: When optimizing implicit surface rendering performance. When choosing between a closed-form approximate SDF and an iterative exact SDF. When Not to Use: When the SDF error is negligible compared to other bottlenecks (e.g., shading, memory bandwidth). When the scene geometry does not exhibit large disparities between bound and exact distances. Originating from the foundational work on sphere tracing by Hart and North, this analysis was presented in "Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces" (1992/1994). The paper established sphere tracing as a competitive implicit surface renderer and detailed the impact of distance estimate accuracy on convergence rates. It is widely cited in graphics literature for establishing the performance characteristics of ray marching algorithms. name: Adaptive Convergence Threshold
head: Camera-aware SDF Threshold, Convergence Criteria for Sphere Tracing, Pixel-intersection based epsilon
body: Adaptive Convergence Threshold is a stopping condition for distance-field ray marching that determines when a ray has sufficiently converged to a surface. It solves the problem of balancing rendering accuracy against computational cost by defining a threshold \epsilon based on camera parameters, ensuring that the ray front ends of neighboring pixels remain geometrically separable. It differs from fixed thresholds by adapting to the scene scale and camera intrinsics to prevent both dilation (loss of detail) and erosion (incomplete geometry). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera intrinsics (focal length f, sensor size S, resolution R), scene scale (minimum object distance d{min}), viewing angle \theta, and the current signed distance function (SDF) value f(\mathbf{p}) at the ray position \mathbf{p}. Outputs: A boolean convergence flag and the computed threshold \epsilon. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on scalar parameters derived from camera calibration and scene bounds. Steps: 1. Calculate Threshold: Compute the adaptive threshold \epsilon using the camera parameters and scene distance. This ensures that the "ball" of uncertainty around the ray front end does not overlap with neighboring pixels' balls. 2. Evaluate Convergence: At each ray marching step, check if the absolute SDF value is below the threshold: |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon 3. Terminate: If the condition is met, stop marching. The current position is considered the surface intersection for rendering purposes. Formula: The threshold \epsilon is derived from similar triangles, representing the radius such that balls centered at the ray front ends of neighboring pixels do not intersect: \epsilon = \frac{d{min} \cdot S \cdot \cos^2(\theta)}{2 \cdot f \cdot R} Where: d{min}: Minimum distance from the camera to the object of interest. S: Sensor size (width or height, consistent with R). f: Focal length. R: Image resolution (width or height). \theta: The angle between the ray direction and the camera optical axis. Parameters: Typical values for \epsilon calculation: f=60mm, d{min}=10cm, S=32mm, R=512. This yields \epsilon \approx 0.5 \times 10^{-4}m (0.05mm). In practice, a fixed threshold of 5 \times 10^{-5} is often used for experiments with similar setups. Pitfalls: Too Large: Causes dilation, where the rendered shape is larger than the true geometry, losing boundary details. It also bounds rendering noise, leading to large depth errors. Too Small: Causes erosion, where geometry is incomplete because pixels fail to converge within the maximum step count, misclassifying foreground as background. It also significantly increases rendering time due to excessive queries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeadaptivethreshold(dmin, sensorsize, focallength, resolution, angletheta): """ Computes the adaptive convergence threshold epsilon. Args: dmin (float): Minimum distance to object (meters). sensorsize (float): Sensor size (meters). focallength (float): Focal length (meters). resolution (int): Image resolution (pixels). angletheta (float): Angle from optical axis (radians). Returns: float: The convergence threshold epsilon. """ costheta = math.cos(angletheta) epsilon = (dmin sensorsize costheta2) / (2.0 focallength resolution) return epsilon def checkconvergence(sdfvalue, epsilon): """ Checks if the ray has converged to the surface. Args: sdfvalue (float): The signed distance function value at current position. epsilon (float): The adaptive threshold. Returns: bool: True if converged, False otherwise. """ return abs(sdfvalue) < epsilon A variant used in particle-based surface extraction rather than ray marching. It defines system equilibrium as energy minimization where the energy gradient is zero. To avoid complex gradient calculations, it uses the average displacement of particles to characterize the gradient. The system is considered to have approached equilibrium if the average displacement \Delta(l) is less than a threshold \epsilon for M consecutive iterations. The threshold is proportional to the particle repulsion radius h{cut\off}: \epsilon = \beta \cdot h{cut\off}, where \beta is a coefficient (e.g., 0.01). The average displacement is calculated as \Delta(t) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} |pi(t) - pi(t-1)|. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF queries per ray by stopping early when close to the surface, improving performance compared to fixed small thresholds. Memory Complexity: Negligible; requires only scalar storage for camera parameters. Strengths: Prevents both dilation and erosion by tying the threshold to the physical resolution of the rendering pipeline. It ensures that the rendered details are supported by the 2D image resolution. Limitations: Requires knowledge of camera intrinsics and scene scale (d{min}). If d{min} is inaccurate, the threshold may be inappropriate. It assumes a pinhole camera model for the derivation. When to Use: When rendering implicit surfaces with differentiable sphere tracing where depth accuracy and boundary detail preservation are critical, and camera parameters are known. The method was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering of deep implicit signed distance functions (SDFs). It addresses the issue where ray movement becomes extremely slow near the surface because the SDF value f approaches zero. The concept was proposed to ensure that the convergence criteria do not confuse one pixel with its neighbors, thereby maintaining details supported by the 2D rendering resolution. name: Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC)
head: BVH-based Adaptive Lipschitz Constant, Nested BVH Step Size Optimization
body: Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) is a sphere tracing enhancement that uses a nested Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to compute tighter, adaptive Lipschitz constants for step size calculation, rather than using the global sum Lipschitz constant. It solves the problem of overly conservative step sizes in large scenes where the naive global Lipschitz constant \lambda{Fn} becomes very large, limiting efficiency. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Current position t0 along the ray. A nested BVH structure representing the implicit function Fn = \sum{i=1}^n fi. For each BVH level i \in [1, n]: the value of the partial sum at t0, denoted \text{BVH}i(t0); the Lipschitz constant for the partial sum, \lambda{\text{BVH}i} = \lambda{Fi}. Outputs: The next safe step size \Delta t to advance the ray. Data Structures: BVH Nodes: Store bounding volumes, Lipschitz constants, and partial sum values at the current ray position. Sum Elements: The functions fi are pre-sorted from higher to lower range of values to achieve close-to-maximal steps with low overhead. Method: 1. Identify Minimum Level: Determine i{min}, the first BVH level where the ray is outside the bounding volume. For all levels i \ge i{min}, the ray is outside the isosurface of BVHi, making the intersection with BVHi's boundary a safe step target. 2. Construct Inclusion Functions: For each valid BVH level i, construct a forward inclusion function: \text{BVH}{\pm i} = \text{BVH}{\pm i}(t0) \pm \lambda{\text{BVH}i}(t - t0), where \lambda{\text{BVH}i} = \lambda{Fi}. 3. Combine Bounds: Combine the inclusion functions from all valid BVH levels by taking their intersection to narrow the range of possible values for Fn(t): Fn(t) \in \bigcap{i=1}^n \text{BVH}{i\pm}. 4. Compute Step Candidates: Calculate candidate step sizes for each BVH level i using the lower bound of the combined inclusion function: F{n-1}(t) = \max{i \in [1, n]} (\text{BVH}{i-1}(t0) - \lambda{\text{BVH}i}(t - t0)). Solving F{n-1}(t) = 0 yields the candidate step \Delta ti = \text{BVH}{i-1}(t0) / \lambda{\text{BVH}i}. 5. Select Final Step: Select the largest (best) candidate as the final step size, which corresponds to the minimum of the individual upper-bound roots to satisfy the intersection constraint. 6. Advance Ray: Move the ray origin to t0 + \Delta t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computealcstep(currentt, bvhlevels): """ Compute the next safe step size using Adaptive Lipschitz Constant. Args: currentt: float, current distance along the ray. bvhlevels: list of dicts, each containing: 'value': float, BVHi(t0) 'lambda': float, Lipschitz constant lambdaBVHi Returns: float, the next safe step size. """ beststep = float('inf') for level in bvhlevels: val = level['value'] lam = level['lambda'] if lam <= 0: continue candidatestep = val / lam # The source states to "select the largest (best) candidate". # Mathematically, intersecting inclusion functions requires taking # the minimum of the individual roots to guarantee safety. if candidatestep > 0 and candidatestep < beststep: beststep = candidatestep return beststep if beststep != float('inf') else 0.0 Parameters: Pre-sorting: Sum elements are pre-sorted from higher to lower range of values to achieve close-to-maximal steps with low overhead. Dynamic Re-ordering: Not used. It is not GPU-friendly because it requires storing each element in an O(n) array and sorting dynamically at every step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If \lambda{\text{BVH}i} is very small, division by zero or numerical instability may occur. Guard against \lambda \le \epsilon. Degenerate Input: If the ray is inside a BVH level, the inclusion function logic for "outside" steps may not apply directly. The method assumes the ray is outside the target isosurface for the step calculation. GPU Performance: Dynamic re-ordering of sum elements is avoided due to high memory and sorting overhead on GPUs. Sub-stepping is an optimization for adaptive ray marching that guarantees non-decreasing step sizes by performing intermediate sub-steps along the ray as intermediate field sums are computed. It solves the problem of "bad candidates" in standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) methods, where computing additional field components fi can unpredictably reduce the step size, leading to wasted computation. Unlike standard ALC, which calculates the next step based on the current position and all available bounds, Sub-stepping physically advances the ray to validate bounds, ensuring that each additional level of detail contributes positively or neutrally to the step size. Computes a tighter Lipschitz constant for sphere-tracing by evaluating it per primitive and per ray, mitigating performance loss from varying primitive radii. For each ray, find the primitive point with the smallest radius whose kernel support intersects the ray. Solve the polynomial equation for intersection roots to determine the smallest radius along the ray. The kernel support intersection condition is: \|\mathbf{p} - (\mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}\|^2 - \sigma^2(\tau0 + s\Delta\tau)^2 \leq 0 where \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{m} - \mathbf{s}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, \sigma is the kernel scale, \tau0 is the base radius, \Delta\tau is the radius variation step, and s is the ray parameter. The parameter \sigma is the kernel scale factor used in the intersection polynomial. Time Complexity: O(n) per step to evaluate all BVH levels and compute inclusion functions, where n is the number of levels in the BVH. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store BVH levels and their Lipschitz constants, with no dynamic arrays required, making it GPU-friendly. Measured Performance: Improves efficiency over naive global Lipschitz constant methods, especially when n is large and \lambda{Fn} would otherwise be very big. Strengths: Tighter bounds lead to larger steps. GPU-friendly due to lack of dynamic sorting. Limitations: Requires a nested BVH structure. Pre-sorting may not always yield optimal steps, though it is close-to-optimal for functions like FBM. When to Use: When rendering procedural volumetric noise or large detailed scenes where the global Lipschitz constant is too conservative. When Not to Use: When the BVH structure is not available or too expensive to build. Originating from the work on fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise, ALC leverages the bounded nature of functions through a BVH to make bigger and cheaper steps. It builds on the intuition of Worley and Hart regarding dynamic re-ordering but adapts it for GPU-friendly static pre-sorting. The method is described as an enhancement to sphere tracing using nested BVH levels. body: Sub-stepping is an optimization for adaptive ray marching that guarantees non-decreasing step sizes by performing intermediate sub-steps along the ray as intermediate field sums are computed. It solves the problem of "bad candidates" in standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) methods, where computing additional field components fi can unpredictably reduce the step size, leading to wasted computation. Unlike standard ALC, which calculates the next step based on the current position and all available bounds, Sub-stepping physically advances the ray to validate bounds, ensuring that each additional level of detail contributes positively or neutrally to the step size. Inputs: Current ray origin t0. Target value v. Minimum BVH level i{min} and maximum level n. Lipschitz constants \lambda{Fi} for cumulative sums Fi and \lambda{fi} for individual fields fi. BVH bounds BVH{i+}(t) providing upper bounds for field sums. Sum of remaining bounds s(i, n) = \sum{k=i}^{n} \Delta{fk}, where \Delta{fk} is the bound provided by the BVH for fk. Outputs: Next ray position t{next} = t0 + step{final}. Data Structures: The method uses the parent ALC method's BVH nodes and field functions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute an initial step size step{i{min}} using the BVH at level i{min}. 2. Physically move the ray position by stepi to t0 + stepi. Assume the worst-case scenario where BVH{i+}(t0 + stepi) = v. 3. Evaluate the next function f{i+1} at the new position t0 + stepi. Replace the bound \Delta{f{i+1}} with the actual value f{i+1}(t0 + stepi). 4. Update the step size using the derived formula. Formulas: Initial step size: step{i{min}} = -\frac{F{i{min}}(t0) + s(i{min} + 1, n)}{\lambda{F{i{min}}}}. (Derived for v=0; for general v, the numerator is v - (F{i{min}}(t0) + s(i{min} + 1, n)).) Updated step size: step{i+1} = stepi + \frac{\Delta{f{i+1}} - f{i+1}(t0 + stepi)}{\lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}}. (Note: The source's Eq. 15 writes the denominator as \lambda{fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}, but the derivation in Eq. 14 and the inequality analysis consistently use \lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}; the implementation uses the latter for mathematical consistency with Lipschitz accumulation.) Parameters: i{min} and n define the BVH level range. Typical values for i{min} and n depend on the scene's BVH depth and are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs if \lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}} = 0, requiring a numerical guard. Floating-point precision errors may accumulate if stepi is very small. If the ray starts inside the isosurface (BVH{i+}(t0) < v), the initial step size becomes negative; standard raymarching logic must handle backtracking or termination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Iterate through levels to refine step size via sub-stepping for i in range(imin, n): # a. Sub-step: Move ray position forward by current step size tsub = t0 + step # b. Evaluate next field f{i+1} at the sub-step position fnextval = fieldsi+1 # c. name: Local Field Interpolation with Dynamic Subdivision
head: Dynamic Subdivision for SCALIS, Fast ray tracing of scale-invariant integral surfaces, Local Field Interpolation with Dynamic Subdivision for SCALIS, SCALIS rendering pipeline, Scale-Invariant Integral Surface (SCALIS) Ray Tracing
body: This method is a real-time ray tracing pipeline for visualizing Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS) defined by skeletons with prescribed radii. It solves the high computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations and the challenge of robust closest ray/isosurface intersection by relying on local field interpolations and subdividing the ray into intervals that capture main field variations. It sets itself apart from brute-force marching by using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure to select primitives and transforming field values to a space allowing good quadratic polynomial approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a skeleton structure consisting of line segment primitives Si with prescribed radii at endpoints, and a target isovalue c. Output: The intersection distance t along the ray where the SCALIS field f(\mathbf{p}) = c. Data Structures: Skeleton Primitive Si: A line segment defined by endpoints \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1 and radii r0, r1. Radius Function \tau{Si}(q): For a point q on the segment, the radius is the linear interpolation of the endpoint radii. Dynamic A-Buffer: A GPU-accelerated structure built on the fly to select primitives whose supports overlap a given interval along the ray. Field Definitions: The SCALIS field is an implicit surface defined by a scalar field f and an isovalue c as the set of points \mathbf{p} satisfying f(\mathbf{p}) = c. The field is constructed from primitives using the sum blending operator: f(\mathbf{p}) = \sumi fi(\mathbf{p}) \quad (1) where fi is the field function defined by the i-th primitive. The primitives are based on kernels. Compact Polynomial kernels are defined as: k{i,\sigma}(d) = \begin{cases} \left(1 - \left(\frac{d}{\sigma}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{i}{2}} & \text{if } d < \sigma, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \quad (2) and Cauchy kernels are defined as: k{i,\sigma}(d) = \frac{1}{\left(1+\left(\frac{d}{\sigma}\right)^2\right)^i} \quad (3) where i is the degree parameter and \sigma is the scale parameter. Algorithm Steps: 1. Primitive Selection: Select primitives whose supports overlap a given interval along the ray using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure built on the fly using fast GPU construction of A-buffers. 2. Ray Segmentation: Segment the camera ray into sub-intervals based on the distance to the skeleton. The strategy is chosen to capture main field variations while generating a small number of sub-intervals to be processed. 3. Field Mapping: Transform field values to a space that allows good quadratic polynomial approximation of the SCALIS field on each sub-interval. This is achieved by using a bijective mapping of the SCALIS field to an approximate smooth homothetic distance field (squared) which has the exact same isosurface of interest as the SCALIS field. All processing is done on this normalized field. 4. Iterative Interpolation and Root Finding: For each sub-interval, iteratively build polynomial interpolations using fast quadratic roots computation to rapidly converge toward the real field function. A different interpolation is used and refined in each interval, locally producing an accurate approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Primitive Selection: Filter segments whose bounding spheres intersect the ray activesegments = [] for seg in segments: cx, cy, cz = (seg['v0'][0]+seg['v1'][0])/2, (seg['v0'][1]+seg['v1'][1])/2, (seg['v0'][2]+seg['v1'][2])/2 R = max(seg['r0'], seg['r1']) + math.sqrt((seg['v1'][0]-seg['v0'][0])2 + (seg['v1'][1]-seg['v0'][1])2 + (seg['v1'][2]-seg['v0'][2])2) 0.5 oc = (rayorigin[0]-cx, rayorigin[1]-cy, rayorigin[2]-cz) b = oc[0]raydirection[0] + oc[1]raydirection[1] + oc[2]raydirection[2] cval = (oc[0]2 + oc[1]2 + oc[2]2) - RR if cval > 0.0 and b > 0.0: continue disc = bb - cval if disc >= 0.0: activesegments.append(seg) # 2. Ray Segmentation: Divide ray into intervals based on distance to skeleton # Not given in the sources: exact subdivision heuristic based on skeleton distance intervals = [] for seg in activesegments: cx, cy, cz = (seg['v0'][0]+seg['v1'][0])/2, (seg['v0'][1]+seg['v1'][1])/2, (seg['v0'][2]+seg['v1'][2])/2 R = max(seg['r0'], seg['r1']) + math.sqrt((seg['v1'][0]-seg['v0'][0])2 + (seg['v1'][1]-seg['v0'][1])2 + (seg['v1'][2]-seg['v0'][2])2) 0.5 oc = (rayorigin[0]-cx, rayorigin[1]-cy, rayorigin[2]-cz) b = oc[0]raydirection[0] + oc[1]raydirection[1] + oc[2]raydirection[2] cval = (oc[0]2 + oc[1]2 + oc[2]2) - RR disc = bb - cval if disc >= 0.0: sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = -b - sqrtdisc t2 = -b + sqrtdisc intervals.append((max(0.0, t1), max(0.0, t2))) intervals.sort() merged = [] for start, end in intervals: if not merged or start > merged[-1][1]: merged.append([start, end]) else: merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end) intervals = merged thit = None tmax = 1e6 for tstart, tend in intervals: if tstart > tmax: break tend = min(tend, tmax) if tstart >= tend: continue # 3. Field Mapping & 4. Iterative Interpolation/Root Finding targetnormalized = 0.0 tguess = tstart for in range(50): p = (rayorigin[0] + tguess raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + tguess raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + tguess raydirection[2]) fval = evaluatescalisfield(p, activesegments) # Bijective mapping to normalized squared distance space # Not given in the sources: exact normalization function fnorm = fval if abs(fnorm - targetnormalized) < 1e-6: thit = tguess break # Compute derivatives along ray direction # Not given in the sources: exact gradient and Hessian computation eps = 1e-5 peps = (rayorigin[0] + (tguess + eps) raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + (tguess + eps) raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + (tguess + eps) raydirection[2]) feps = evaluatescalisfield(peps, activesegments) df = (feps - fval) / eps d2f = 0.0 if abs(df) < 1e-12: df = 1e-12 # Fast quadratic roots computation: solve fnorm + dfdt + 0.5d2fdt^2 = 0 a = 0.5 d2f b = df c = fnorm - targetnormalized if abs(a) < 1e-12: dt = -c / b else: disc = b b - 4 a c if disc < 0: disc = 0 dt = (-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2 a) tguess += dt tguess = max(tstart, min(tend, tguess)) if abs(dt) < 1e-8: thit = tguess break if thit is not None: break return thit Parameters: maxiterations: Fixed to 50 in the implementation to prevent infinite loops. Not given in the sources. Convergence thresholds (1e-6 for field value, 1e-8 for step size) are standard numerical values. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the bijective mapping to a normalized field to ensure good quadratic approximation. Boundaries: The ray segmentation must ensure that intervals are small enough to capture main field variations. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a skeleton structure with line segment primitives. The sources do not specify handling for degenerate segments. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of field evaluations by using local interpolations and dynamic subdivision. The dynamic A-buffer construction is performed on the fly using fast GPU construction. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the dynamic A-buffer and the skeleton structure. Measured Performance: The method provides improvements for various resolutions on all combinations of tested models and GPU hardware. It goes beyond Sherstyuk's fast ray-tracing algorithm for convolution surfaces, notably allowing better support of large radius variation while being less sensitive to skeleton tessellation. Strengths: Real-time visualization of SCALIS, efficient primitive selection, robust intersection finding. Limitations: High computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations is mitigated but not eliminated; the method is specific to SCALIS fields. Scale-invariant integral surfaces (SCALIS) are implicit representations of surfaces that provide a way to define smooth surfaces from skeletons with prescribed radii defined at their vertices. The rendering pipeline was introduced to visualize such surfaces in real-time, addressing challenges in robust intersection, efficient primitive selection, and high computational cost. The method builds on previous work in metaballs rendering and transparency using A-buffers. It improves upon Sherstyuk's fast ray-tracing algorithm for convolution surfaces. name: Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints
head: 2-Lipschitz Sphere Tracing, Gradient-assisted Sphere Tracing
body:
Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints is an optimization of the sphere tracing algorithm that uses the local gradient of the Signed Distance Function (SDF) to compute larger, safer step sizes, particularly improving performance near silhouettes and backward-facing surfaces. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by combining the first and second Lipschitz constraints derived from the gradient and curvature, allowing for significantly fewer steps in grazing scenarios where standard methods stall. The method improves upon the standard sphere tracing step size d = f(p) / L by utilizing local derivative information to tighten the bound on the distance to the root, ensuring the step does not overshoot the isosurface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D, SDF function f(p), and its gradient 
abla f(p). Output: Intersection distance t along the ray. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required for the core stepping logic, though the method is often implemented within a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) for FBM fields to dynamically compute local Lipschitz constants. Numbered Steps: 1. Evaluate Field: At current position p, evaluate the SDF value f(p) and its gradient 
abla f(p). 2. Compute Standard Step: Calculate the initial candidate step size using the gradient magnitude: d{grad} =  rac{f(p)}{|
abla f(p)|} If |
abla f(p)| is near zero, fall back to a global Lipschitz constant or a minimum step size to avoid division by zero. 3. Apply 2-Lipschitz Constraint: Refine the step size using the second-order Lipschitz constraint (curvature bound) from [AZ23]. The safe step size d is the minimum of the gradient-based step and the curvature-constrained step: d = \min \left(  rac{f(p)}{|
abla f(p)|}, \sqrt{ rac{2 f(p)}{|
abla^2 f(p)|}} ight) The term |
abla^2 f(p)| represents the magnitude of the Hessian or a bound on the second derivative. In practice, for 2-Lipschitz functions, this constraint ensures the step respects the curvature bounds. 4. Advance: Update position p \leftarrow p + d \cdot D. 5. Terminate: If f(p) < \epsilon (threshold), return d. Otherwise, repeat from Step 1. Parameters: Lipschitz Constant L: For general FBM, this is dynamically computed using a BVH to be much smaller than the global constant, reducing the step size penalty in empty space. Threshold \epsilon: Standard sphere tracing termination threshold (e.g., 10^{-4}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: FBM Slowdowns: The standard formulation of [AZ23] can cause slowdowns for certain functions like Fractional Brownian Motion (FBM) due to improper handling of cascaded sums. A modified formulation is required to properly handle the gradient and Lipschitz constants for these nested structures. Grazing Angles: Standard sphere tracing takes very small steps near silhouettes; this method mitigates this by using the gradient to predict the distance more accurately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientspheretrace(p, raydir, sdffunc, gradfunc, hessboundfunc, epsilon=1e-4): """ Performs sphere tracing using gradient and 2-Lipschitz constraints. Args: p: Current position (vec3) raydir: Ray direction (vec3, normalized) sdffunc: Function returning f(p) gradfunc: Function returning gradient gradf(p) hessboundfunc: Function returning bound on second derivative |nabla^2 f| epsilon: Termination threshold Returns: Intersection distance t """ t = 0.0 while True: fval = sdffunc(p) # Termination check if fval < epsilon: return t # Compute gradient gradf = gradfunc(p) gradmag = length(gradf) # Guard against zero gradient if gradmag < 1e-8: step = epsilon # Fallback or global Lipschitz step else: # Step 1: Gradient-based step stepgrad = fval / gradmag # Step 2: 2-Lipschitz (curvature) constraint # Using bound on second derivative to ensure safety hessbound = hessboundfunc(p) # Avoid division by zero in curvature term if hessbound < 1e-8: stepcurv = stepgrad # Fall back to gradient step if curvature bound is negligible else: # Formula derived from 2-Lipschitz constraint: d <= sqrt(2f / |nabla^2 f|) stepcurv = sqrt(2.0 fval / hessbound) # Take the minimum safe step step = min(stepgrad, stepcurv) # Advance p = p + step raydir t += step Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching is a ray-surface intersection method that formulates intersection as a curvature-accelerated contraction operator on the Eikonal distance field to solve the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges. It sets itself apart from its parent, Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints, by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons while maintaining single-query Lipschitz advances in open space, thereby truncating the grazing stall tail by up to 4×. Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm that computes a local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for each ray segment e to determine safe, larger stepping distances, significantly reducing the number of field function queries compared to global bound methods like Sphere Tracing. It solves the problem of inefficient stepping near grazing surfaces and complex implicit structures by adapting the step size to the local geometry's smoothness, allowing for convergence in fewer steps while maintaining safety via an overstepping check. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly bounds the gradient and Jacobian of deformed fields to compute these local constraints. Structure-aware sampling is an adaptive ray marching algorithm that uses a Signed Distance Function (SDF) and its filtered gradient to determine step sizes, ensuring efficient traversal and accurate surface intersection. It leverages structural information from LiDAR point clouds and neural fields to skip free space via an occupancy map and avoid false revert steps in unconverged neural distance fields (NDFs) by incorporating a predicted scale parameter. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by using a filtered slope to modulate step size and a specific stability check involving the scale  etai to handle the uncertainty of learned SDFs. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF evaluations significantly compared to standard sphere tracing, especially in empty space and near silhouettes. Speedups of up to 12-fold are reported for opaque or constant semi-transparent scenes with high-complexity FBM. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the BVH if used for dynamic Lipschitz constant computation, but the core stepping logic is O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Effectively handles grazing angles and backward-facing surfaces where standard sphere tracing fails due to small step sizes. Compatible with semi-transparency and hypertextures. Limitations: Requires computation of the gradient and potentially the Hessian bound, which increases per-step cost. The standard [AZ23] formulation may cause slowdowns for FBM without the proposed modifications. When to use: Ideal for rendering procedural volumetric noise (FBM) and complex implicit surfaces where grazing angles are common and global Lipschitz constants are too conservative. The method is based on the work of [AZ23], which introduced the use of 2-Lipschitz constraints for sphere tracing. The technique builds on the foundational sphere tracing method by [Har96] and Lipschitz methods by [Mit90] and [KB89].
