name: Field Error Metric
head: Error Estimation Methods, Field Error Measurement, Scalar Value Difference Error, Surface Error Measurement
body: The Field Error Metric estimates approximation error in simplified meshes by measuring discrepancies in scalar field values between the original and simplified representations. It complements surface boundary error metrics by evaluating internal data variations within the mesh domain. Inputs: 1. Original scalar field defined on a tetrahedral mesh domain. 2. Simplified mesh representation. 3. Scalar field range R = \max(f) - \min(f) of the original field. Outputs: 1. Normalized field error percentage. Data Structures: Sample points P: 3D coordinates including original mesh vertices and interpolated points inside each tetrahedron. Scalar values f(p): Field value at point p. Steps: 1. Sample points P inside the domain of the original mesh, including vertices and interior interpolated points of each tetrahedron. 2. For each point p \in P, check if it lies inside the domain of the simplified mesh. 3. Discard points outside the simplified mesh domain; these are excluded from field error and contribute to surface boundary error instead. 4. For remaining points, compute the difference between the original scalar value f{\text{orig}}(p) and the simplified mesh scalar value f{\text{simp}}(p). 5. Aggregate the differences and normalize by the original field range R to express the result as a percentage. Formula: Let P{\text{valid}} be the set of sample points inside the simplified mesh domain. The field error E{\text{field}} is: E{\text{field}} = \frac{\sum{p \in P{\text{valid}}} |f{\text{orig}}(p) - f{\text{simp}}(p)|}{|P{\text{valid}}| \cdot R} \times 100\% The sources specify computing "differences between their scalar values" and normalizing field error percentages relative to the field range, without specifying squared differences. Parameters: R: Range of the original scalar field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Points outside the simplified mesh domain must be explicitly ignored to avoid double-counting with surface boundary error metrics. Interpolation accuracy for f{\text{simp}}(p) depends on the method used within the simplified mesh elements. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefielderrormetric(originalfield, simplifiedmesh, originalrange): """ Computes the normalized field error metric. Args: originalfield: Function or data structure providing forig(p). simplifiedmesh: Data structure providing fsimp(p) and isinside(p). originalrange: The scalar range (max - min) of the original field. Returns: float: Normalized field error percentage. """ # 1. Generate sample points P inside the original domain # The sources do not specify the sampling strategy; implementers must generate points including vertices and interior tetrahedron points. samplepoints = [] totalerror = 0.0 count = 0 for p in samplepoints: # 2. Check if point is inside simplified mesh domain if not simplifiedmesh.isinside(p): # 3. Ignore points outside simplified domain continue # 4. Get scalar values forig = originalfield.evaluate(p) fsimp = simplifiedmesh.evaluate(p) # 5. Compute difference diff = abs(forig - fsimp) totalerror += diff count += 1 if count == 0: return 0.0 # 6. Normalize by range and count normalizederror = totalerror / (count originalrange) return normalizederror 100.0 A method to measure approximation quality by computing the Euclidean distance between the output mesh and the implicit surface. It globally increases accuracy by subdividing each triangle three times to increase the number of error sampling points. The error at point p is approximated by e(p) \approx \frac{|f(p)|}{\|\nabla f(p)\|}, where f(p) is the implicit function value and \nabla f(p) is its gradient. The sources do not provide measured performance, time/memory complexity, or specific usage conditions for this metric. Not given in the sources. The Field Error Metric was introduced in the context of streaming simplification of tetrahedral meshes. It was proposed alongside surface boundary error measurement (using Metro [30]) as an alternative method to evaluate the quality of simplified field data using scalar value differences. The implementation differs from prior approaches by explicitly ignoring points outside the simplified mesh domain to separate field error from surface boundary error. name: Stepsize Annealing
head: Sampling Annealing
body: Stepsize Annealing is a training strategy for differentiable volume rendering and neural radiance fields that varies the sampling density along rays over the course of training epochs or iterations. It addresses the trade-off between convergence speed and geometric accuracy by starting with coarse sampling (large step sizes or few points) to accelerate early learning and progressively refining the sampling (smaller step sizes or more points) to recover fine details. It is distinct from static error-based adaptive stepping (see Error Estimate) because the sampling schedule is determined by training progress rather than local field gradients or error metrics at inference time. The method modifies the number of samples or the step size used during the ray marching process as a function of the training iteration u or epoch e. There are two primary formulations found in the literature: one based on sampling rate scaling and one based on linear point count increase. Inputs: Current training iteration/epoch (u or e), total training iterations/epochs (U or E), hyperparameters defining the range and speed of annealing. Outputs: The number of sampling points Nt or the sampling rate s(e) to be used for the current training step. No specific complex data structures are required; the method relies on scalar values for the current progress and hyperparameters. This method varies the sampling rate s within a range [sl, sh]. s(e) = sl \left(1 - \left(\frac{e}{E}\right)^2\right) + \left(\frac{e}{E}\right)^2 sh s(e): Sampling rate at epoch e. sl: Lower bound of sampling rate. Typical value: 0.1. sh: Upper bound of sampling rate. Typical value: 2.0. e: Current epoch. E: Total number of epochs. This method increases the number of sampling points Nt linearly to address near-field artifacts. Nt = \min(N{\max}, \lfloor u/\eta \rfloor + N{start}) Nt: Number of sampling points along a ray at iteration u. N{\max}: Maximum number of sampling points. u: Current training iteration. N{start}: Number of sampling points at the start of training. \eta: Hyperparameter controlling the increasing speed of sampling points. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getsamplingrate(epoch, totalepochs, sl=0.1, sh=2.0): """Computes sampling rate s(e) for stepsize annealing.""" progress = epoch / totalepochs progress = min(1.0, max(0.0, progress)) return sl (1.0 - progress2) + (progress2) sh def getnumsamples(iteration, nmax, nstart, eta): """Computes number of sampling points Nt for linear annealing.""" rawcount = (iteration // eta) + nstart return min(nmax, rawcount) Near-Field Artifacts: In forward-facing real-world scenes, floating artifacts often appear close to the camera. Linear point count annealing (Nt) addresses this by increasing sampling points over training iterations. Memory Bottlenecks: Early training with dense sampling can cause peak memory costs. Max time-step scaling mitigates this by starting with a reduced maximum time step (e.g., 2) and restoring it (e.g., 8) once sampling stabilizes. Surface Compactness: Without a shrinking sampling procedure, learned occupancy fields may result in noisy normal maps and dents in surface geometry, even if rendered images look realistic. A strategy to keep training stable under large maximum time steps (T). It starts with a reduced maximum time step (e.g., 2) in the initial epoch of each training stage to avoid peak memory costs from dense early samples, then restores T (e.g., 8) once sampling becomes stable. This preserves full temporal capacity while removing the initial memory bottleneck. A training schedule that progressively reduces the sampling interval around the surface to force the learned occupancy field to converge tightly to the true geometry. It initializes the sampling region to cover the entire volume and gradually shrinks it to a minimal neighborhood around the predicted surface, using root-finding on alpha values to locate the surface within the shrinking bounds. Without this, normal maps contain random noise and face shapes develop dents. A strategy used to address near-field artifacts in forward-facing scenes. It is implemented via the linear point count increase formula Nt = \min(N{\max}, \lfloor u/\eta \rfloor + N{start}) to progressively increase sampling density during training. A training strategy to avoid high-density values at ray origins by gradually increasing the sample range along the ray. It starts sampling in a small range around the middle of the ray and gradually increases the sample range as training progresses. This keeps the 99%-mass band \ell(s) proportional to the minimum voxel size, yielding stable early training (thick bands) and progressively sharper surfaces. Learning thickness \ell(s) is defined as the surface band capturing 99% of weight: \ell(s) \approx 2 \ln(199) / s. Normalized thickness \tilde{\ell}(s) = \ell(s) / hL, where hL is the minimum voxel size in scene resolution 2^L. Within each octree level L, it ramps \log s(\tau) = \log sL + 0.07 \cdot rL(\tau), where rL: 0 \to 1. When moving to the next level, it updates base \log s{L+1} = \log sL + \ln(hL / h{L+1}) (so if h halves, \log s rises by \ln 2). Convergence: It benefits from faster convergence at low sampling rates in early epochs for rough approximation and increases sampling rate towards the end to refine the optimized transfer function. Quality: Produces visual results comparable to training with a fixed high sampling rate (e.g., s=2.0). Limitations: The method is a training-time optimization; it does not inherently improve inference-time rendering speed unless the final model is configured to use the final annealed parameters. It requires careful tuning of hyperparameters like sl, sh, \eta, N{start}, N{max}. Stepsize annealing was introduced as a training acceleration method for differentiable volume rendering models. It was proposed to address the diminishing returns of increasing sampling rates beyond a certain point (e.g., s=1.0) and to accelerate training by starting with a high rendering step size in early epochs. Variants have been developed to address specific issues in neural radiance fields, such as near-field artifacts in forward-facing scenes, memory bottlenecks from dense early samples in spike-based NeRFs, and surface compactness in generative occupancy fields. name: Embedded Error Norm Calculation
head: ODE Error Norm, RMS Error Scaling
body: Embedded Error Norm Calculation computes a scalar error metric from a vector of local truncation errors and the current solution state, enabling adaptive step size control in ray marching. It differs from Data-Dependent Error Metric for Scalar Fields by relying on the numerical integration error (ODE residual) rather than field derivatives, and from Stepsize Annealing by providing a rigorous tolerance-based acceptance criterion rather than a heuristic decay schedule. Inputs: err: Vector of local error estimates (e.g., difference between two integration orders). y: Vector of the current solution state (e.g., accumulated opacity, transmittance, or position). rtol: Relative tolerance (scalar). atol: Absolute tolerance (scalar). Outputs: norm: A scalar error value representing the weighted magnitude of err. Data Structures: err: Array of floats, length N (number of components). y: Array of floats, length N. rtol, atol: Floats. Steps: 1. Compute the scale factor for each component i: si = \text{atol} + \text{rtol} \cdot |yi| 2. Compute the weighted error for each component: ei = \frac{|erri|}{si} 3. Compute the RMS norm of the weighted errors: \text{norm} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} ei^2} Parameters: rtol: Typical value 10^{-6}. atol: Typical value 0. Edge Cases: If si = 0 (both atol and yi are zero), the division is undefined. In practice, if yi=0 and atol=0, the error contribution is treated as 0 if erri=0, or requires a safeguard (e.g., treating the ratio as 1 if erri \neq 0). For single-component fields (N=1), the norm collapses to |err| / s1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def embeddederrornorm(err: list[float], y: list[float], rtol: float, atol: float) -> float: n = len(err) if n == 0: return 0.0 sumsq = 0.0 for i in range(n): # Compute scale factor scale = atol + rtol abs(y[i]) # Handle division by zero if scale == 0.0: if err[i] == 0.0: weightederr = 0.0 else: # Guard: if scale is 0 but error is non-zero, treat as max error weightederr = 1.0 else: weightederr = abs(err[i]) / scale sumsq += weightederr weightederr return (sumsq / n) 0.5 This variant provides a theoretical upper bound on the error of approximated opacity \hat{O} in volume rendering, derived from Lipschitz continuity of the density field. It is used when rigorous error guarantees are required rather than heuristic ODE norms. The bound is given by |O(t) - \hat{O}(t)| \leq \exp(-\hat{R}(t)) \left( \exp(\hat{E}(t)) - 1 \right), where \hat{E}(t) = \frac{\alpha}{4\beta} \left( \sum{i=1}^{k-1} \deltai^2 e^{-\frac{di^}{\beta}} + (t - tk)^2 e^{-\frac{dk^}{\beta}} \right). This method is chosen when the density field \sigma is known to be Lipschitz continuous with constant \alpha/\beta, and step sizes \deltai and distances di^ are available. It differs from the standard ODE norm by providing a worst-case bound rather than an estimate based on step differences. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of components in the error vector. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simple, robust, and widely applicable to any adaptive integration scheme. The RMS scaling ensures that errors in different components are balanced according to their physical significance (via rtol and atol). Limitations: Requires the error vector err to be computed by a higher-order method or difference estimator. Does not account for spatial coherence or field smoothness directly (unlike Data-Dependent Error Metric for Scalar Fields). When to use: When integrating coupled ODEs in ray marching (e.g., position, opacity, transmittance) and a tolerance-based step acceptance is desired. When not to use: When the field has known smoothness properties that can be exploited for tighter bounds (use Error Bound for Approximated Opacity) or when heuristic step size adjustment is sufficient. The Embedded Error Norm Calculation is a standard technique in numerical analysis for Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs), particularly in Runge-Kutta methods where local error is estimated by comparing two approximations of different orders. It was adapted for volume rendering ray marching to provide a rigorous criterion for adaptive step size selection, ensuring that the accumulated error in opacity and transmittance remains within user-defined tolerances. The specific implementation details and typical parameter values are documented in the webpic library. The theoretical error bound for opacity approximation, which serves as an alternative rigorous metric, was derived in the context of volume rendering neural implicit surfaces. webpic, https://github.com/rusaitis/webpic, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering of Neural Implicit Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.12052, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Step Method
head: Adaptive RK2
body: The Adaptive Step Method is a numerical integration technique for volume rendering that dynamically adjusts the ray marching step size to maintain a specified error tolerance. It solves the problem of balancing rendering speed and accuracy by estimating the local truncation error at each step and modifying the step length accordingly. Unlike fixed-step methods, it uses a user-defined tolerance parameter rather than a fixed step count, making it more user-friendly. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Data-Dependent Error Metric for Scalar Fields by using order-difference estimation (Euler vs. RK2) rather than field-specific gradients, and from Stepsize Annealing by its explicit error-based feedback loop. Inputs: Current position Pn and direction D. Radiance transfer function parameters (scattering coefficient \sigmas, emission Le, extinction \sigmat). Target relative error tolerance E. Current step size dt. Outputs: Next position P{n+1}. Accumulated radiance contribution. Updated step size dt{new}. Data Structures: Position P: 3D vector (x, y, z). Step size dt: Scalar float. Error tolerance E: Scalar float. Method Steps: 1. Euler Estimate: Compute the next position using Euler’s method (first-order) with the current step size dt. P{Euler} = Pn + dt \cdot V(Pn) Where V(P) is the derivative of the state (e.g., radiance or position in phase space) at P. In standard volume rendering, this often refers to the radiance integration step. 2. RK2 Estimate: Compute the next position using a second-order Runge-Kutta method (midpoint) with the same step size dt. k1 = V(Pn) k2 = V(Pn + \frac{dt}{2} k1) P{RK2} = Pn + dt \cdot k2 3. Error Estimation: Calculate the relative error between the two estimates. error = \frac{|P{RK2} - P{Euler}|}{|P{RK2}| + \epsilon} Where \epsilon is a small constant to prevent division by zero. 4. Step Size Adjustment: Compare the estimated error against the tolerance E and adjust dt. If error > E: Reduce step size. dt{new} = dt \cdot \left( \frac{E}{error} \right)^{1/2} If error \le E: Increase step size. dt{new} = dt \cdot \left( \frac{error}{E} \right)^{1/3} The exponents 1/2 and 1/3 are standard stability factors for order-difference adaptation. 5. Integration: Advance the ray using the RK2 estimate P{RK2} as P{n+1} and accumulate radiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivestep(Pn, dt, tolerance, velocityfunc): # 1. Euler step (1st order) Vn = velocityfunc(Pn) Peuler = Pn + dt Vn # 2. RK2 step (2nd order) - Midpoint method Vmid = velocityfunc(Pn + 0.5 dt Vn) Prk2 = Pn + dt Vmid # 3. Error estimation # Use relative error to handle scale denom = max(norm(Prk2), 1e-8) error = norm(Prk2 - Peuler) / denom # 4. Adjust step size if error > tolerance: dt = dt (tolerance / error) 0.5 else: dt = dt (error / tolerance) (1.0/3.0) # 5. Finalize step using the more accurate method (RK2) Pnext = Prk2 return Pnext, dt Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Illumination: In scenes with sharp light beams or high-frequency illumination, the method may increase the step size in dark, low-error regions, causing the ray to skip over the high-frequency light beams entirely. Maximum Step Size: To mitigate the skipping of high-frequency features, a maximum step size constraint is required. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in the error estimation can lead to oscillating step sizes. A variant used for particle tracing or steady flow integration that keeps integration error constant by adjusting the time step dt. It is described in the context of unsteady flow volumes and references Press et al. [12] for its derivation. It uses 11 function evaluations per step and applies a conservative factor of 0.9 for dt changes. It uses specific exponents for shrinking and growing dt: SHRINK is 1/2 for second-order RK and 1/4 for fourth-order RK; GROW is 1/3 for second-order RK and 1/5 for fourth-order RK. The algorithm evaluates velocity at the current position, performs a half-step RK, a full-step RK, evaluates velocity at the half-step position, and then performs a final correction step to estimate error. Time Complexity: Variable per step due to multiple function evaluations (Euler + RK2 = 2-3 evaluations per step vs. 1 for Euler). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Provides better accuracy than Euler for the same render time at low tolerances. For lower tolerances, the effect of step size is ignored, as the method adapts its step size to the desired overall error. Strengths: User-friendly via tolerance parameter; adapts to scene complexity. Limitations: Can fail on high-frequency illumination without a maximum step size constraint; artifacts may persist even with restrictive tolerances if the scene has sharp discontinuities (e.g., shadows). Hardware: Tested on Intel Core i5 at 2.4GHz with 4GB RAM, parallelized using threads. Scaling: Not given in the sources. The method was tested and described in the context of differential ray marching for participating media. It was evaluated against fixed-step methods (Euler, RK2) in scenes including green fog and car headlights with sharp shadows. name: Adaptive Time Integration (Steady/Particle)
head: Adaptive RK Integration, Adaptive Step Size Control for ODEs
body: Adaptive Time Integration is a numerical method for particle tracing in vector fields that dynamically adjusts the integration step size to maintain a constant local truncation error. It solves the problem of inefficient or inaccurate particle paths by shortening steps in regions of high field curvature and lengthening them in smooth regions. It sets itself apart from fixed-step methods by using an embedded error estimate to control step size, and from general adaptive step methods by its specific implementation using Runge-Kutta schemes with a conservative scaling factor. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current particle position Pn, current step size dt, error tolerance E, velocity field function velocity(P). Output: Next particle position P{n+1}, updated step size dt for the next iteration. Data Structures: Pn: 3D vector representing particle position at step n. dt: Scalar float representing the time step size. E: Scalar float representing the maximum allowable error. V: 3D vector representing velocity. Parameters: SHRINK: Exponent for reducing dt when error exceeds E. Value is 1/2 for second-order Runge-Kutta (RK), 1/4 for fourth-order RK. GROW: Exponent for increasing dt when error is within E. Value is 1/3 for second-order RK, 1/5 for fourth-order RK. Conservative Factor: 0.9, applied to prevent aggressive step size changes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Evaluate velocity at current position: V = velocity(Pn). 2. Compute a mid-point estimate using half step: P{n+1, mid} = RungeKutta(Pn, 0.5 \cdot dt). 3. Compute a full-step estimate: P{n+1} = RungeKutta(Pn, dt). 4. Evaluate velocity at the mid-point position: V{n+1, mid} = velocity(P{n+1, mid}). 5. Refine the full-step estimate using the mid-point velocity: P{n+1} = RungeKutta(P{n+1, mid}, 0.5 \cdot dt, V{n+1, mid}). Note: This step implies a specific embedded RK scheme (likely Heun or similar 2nd/3rd order pair) where the final position is corrected using the mid-velocity. The source describes this as requiring 11 function evaluations, suggesting a complex embedded pair or repeated evaluations not fully detailed in the pseudocode snippet. 6. Calculate error: error = |P{n+1} - P{n+1, mid}|. 7. Update step size: If error > E: dt = 0.9 \cdot SHRINK \cdot dt \cdot (E / error) Else: dt = 0.9 \cdot GROW \cdot dt \cdot (error / E) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivetimeintegration(Pn, dt, E, velocity, order): # Determine exponents based on RK order if order == 2: SHRINK = 0.5 GROW = 1.0 / 3.0 elif order == 4: SHRINK = 0.25 GROW = 0.2 else: raise ValueError("Unsupported RK order") # Step 1: Evaluate velocity at current position V = velocity(Pn) # Step 2: Mid-point estimate (half step) # Note: RungeKutta function signature assumed to handle internal stages Pn1mid = rungekuttastep(Pn, 0.5 dt, V) # Step 3: Full-step estimate Pn1full = rungekuttastep(Pn, dt, V) # Step 4: Evaluate velocity at mid-point position Vn1mid = velocity(Pn1mid) # Step 5: Refine full-step estimate using mid-point velocity # This step corrects the position using the mid-velocity information Pn1final = rungekuttarefine(Pn1mid, 0.5 dt, Vn1mid) # Step 6: Calculate error error = abs(Pn1final - Pn1mid) # Step 7: Update step size if error > E: dt = 0.9 SHRINK dt (E / error) else: dt = 0.9 GROW dt (error / E) return Pn1final, dt def rungekuttastep(P, h, V): # Placeholder for specific RK stage calculation # In a standard 2nd order RK, this might be Euler or Midpoint # The source implies 11 evaluations total, so this is a simplification return P + h V def rungekuttarefine(Pmid, h, Vmid): # Placeholder for refinement step return Pmid + h Vmid Note: The pseudocode above simplifies the "11 function evaluations" claim. The source text provides a specific sequence of calls that does not map directly to a standard 4-stage RK4. The implementation must follow the source's specific call sequence: RungeKutta(Pn, 0.5 dt), RungeKutta(Pn, dt), velocity(Pn+1, mid), RungeKutta(Pn+1, mid, 0.5 dt, Vn+1, mid). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in small dt can accumulate. The conservative factor of 0.9 helps mitigate oscillation in dt. Boundaries: If dt becomes too small, integration may stall. If too large, error tolerance E is violated. Degenerate Input: Zero velocity or singularities in the vector field may cause undefined behavior in velocity(P). Uses eigenvalues and grid geometry to bound step size for stability, unlike error-based adaptive methods. Choose when numerical stability is more critical than error tolerance. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of function evaluations per step. The source specifies 11 evaluations per step, which is higher than the 8 evaluations of a standard RK4 without adaptation. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring storage for current position, velocity, and intermediate estimates. Performance: Improves efficiency by reducing steps in smooth regions and increasing accuracy in complex regions. Strengths: Maintains constant error tolerance, adapts to local field complexity. Limitations: Higher computational cost per step due to extra evaluations; requires careful tuning of E and exponents. This method is described in the context of unsteady flow volume rendering, specifically for particle tracing in smoke or flow volumes. It references Press et al. [12] for the derivation of exponents and the adaptive scheme. The technique is used to visualize flow fields by integrating particle paths, potentially combined with solid geometry rendering. name: Stability-constrained Integration Step
head: Stability Condition
body: The Stability-constrained Integration Step is a method for determining the maximum allowable step length in the numerical integration of vector or tensor fields to ensure numerical stability. It solves the problem of integration divergence or oscillation that occurs when the step size is too large relative to the local field curvature and grid resolution. It sets itself apart from general adaptive step methods by explicitly incorporating the eigenvalues of the transformation tensor and the local grid geometry into the stability bound, rather than relying solely on error estimates of the integration scheme. The method calculates a conservative upper bound for the time step \Delta\tau based on the local properties of the tensor field and the spatial discretization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: P: The current integration point. T(P): The tensor field value at P. G(P): The length of the neighboring grid lines at P. s(\lambda): A scaling factor representing ray flexibility. Outputs: \Delta\tau{max}: The maximum stable time step. Data Structures: Tensor Field: Stored as a grid of tensors. Each tensor T is a 3 \times 3 matrix. Grid Geometry: Stored as a uniform or structured grid where the spacing (or neighbor distances) G(P) is known or computable for each point P. Steps: 1. Compute Eigenvalues: For the tensor T(P) at the current point P, compute the eigenvalues. Let e(P) be the magnitude of the eigenvalue with the largest absolute value (or the specific eigenvalue relevant to the integration direction, as defined by the source context). Note: The source defines e(P) as "the magnitude of any of its eigenvalues" in the inequality context, implying the bound must hold for the worst-case eigenvalue. Typically, this refers to the spectral radius or the maximum magnitude eigenvalue to ensure stability across all principal directions. 2. Determine Grid Spacing: Identify G(P), defined as the length of any of the neighboring grid lines at point P. In a uniform grid with spacing h, G(P) would be h. 3. Apply Stability Constraint: Calculate the maximum step size using the stability condition: s(\lambda)\Delta\tau < \frac{1}{2} \minP \frac{G(P)}{|e(P)|} Rearranging for \Delta\tau: \Delta\tau < \frac{1}{2 s(\lambda)} \minP \frac{G(P)}{|e(P)|} 4. Select Step Size: Choose \Delta\tau such that it satisfies the inequality. A safety factor may be applied to ensure strict inequality. Parameters: s(\lambda): A scaling factor related to ray flexibility. The source notes that large values of s(\lambda) require smaller time steps. No specific default value is given. \Delta\tau: The integration time step. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Large Ray Flexibility: If s(\lambda) is very large, the required \Delta\tau becomes very small, leading to high computational cost. The source suggests that implicit methods could address this problem when large ray flexibility is necessary for complicated data sets. Singular Tensors: If |e(P)| is zero or near-zero, the bound becomes trivial or unstable. Care must be taken to handle degenerate tensors. Grid Anisotropy: G(P) should represent the smallest relevant grid dimension to ensure stability in all directions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestabilityconstrainedstep(tensorfield, gridspacing, pointp, scalingfactorslambda): """ Computes the maximum stable integration step size. Args: tensorfield: A function or data structure providing T(P) for any point P. gridspacing: The length of neighboring grid lines G(P). Assumes uniform grid for simplicity. pointp: The current integration point. scalingfactorslambda: The scaling factor s(lambda). Returns: maxdt: The maximum stable time step. """ # 1. Get tensor at current point T = tensorfield(pointp) # 2. Compute eigenvalues of T # Eigenvalues are roots of det(T - eI) = 0 eigenvalues = computeeigenvalues(T) # 3. Find the magnitude of the eigenvalue with the largest absolute value # The source uses |e(P)| in the denominator. To satisfy the condition for # "any of its eigenvalues", we must consider the worst case (largest magnitude). maxeigenvaluemagnitude = max(abs(e) for e in eigenvalues) # Handle potential division by zero if tensor is zero if maxeigenvaluemagnitude == 0: # If tensor is zero, there is no curvature constraint from eigenvalues. # The step is limited only by other factors (e.g., error estimates). # For this stability constraint specifically, the bound is infinite. return float('inf') # 4. Get grid spacing G(P) # Source defines G(P) as the length of any of its neighboring grid lines. G = gridspacing # 5. Apply stability formula: s(lambda) dt < 0.5 G(P) / |e(P)| # dt < (0.5 G(P) / |e(P)|) / s(lambda) numerator = 0.5 G denominator = maxeigenvaluemagnitude scalingfactorslambda if denominator == 0: # If scaling factor is 0, the constraint is vacuous (infinite step) return float('inf') maxdt = numerator / denominator return maxdt Alternative approach for handling large s(\lambda) where explicit step constraints become prohibitive. Implicit Methods Method that adjusts step size based on local truncation error estimates rather than stability bounds. Error Estimate Time Complexity: The cost is dominated by the eigenvalue decomposition of the tensor T(P) at each step. For a 3 \times 3 tensor, this is O(1) but involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per step, assuming the tensor field is accessed from memory. Strengths: Provides a rigorous guarantee against numerical instability due to large field gradients or high flexibility. Simple to implement. Limitations: Can be overly conservative, leading to very small step sizes and slow rendering/tracing, especially when s(\lambda) is large. Does not account for local truncation error, only stability. When to use: When numerical stability is the primary concern, or when the tensor field exhibits high variability or large eigenvalues. When not to use: When performance is critical and the field is smooth, or when implicit methods are available to handle large flexibility. The stability constraint for integration steps in tensor fields was introduced in the context of visualizing light interaction with tensor fields. The method ensures that the updating rule for ray positions remains stable by limiting the step length relative to the local tensor eigenvalues and grid geometry. name: Gap-Limited Ray Marching
head: Distance-Proportional Step with Gap Bound, Terrain Ray Marching with Gap Limiting
body: Gap-Limited Ray Marching is a step-size optimization technique for heightfield terrain rendering that prevents ray stalling and surface overshooting on non-distance fields. Unlike standard sphere tracing which relies on a global Lipschitz constant, this method bounds the step size by half the vertical gap to the surface, ensuring the ray never penetrates ridgelines while allowing larger steps in open space. It builds on Step Size Optimization by combining distance-proportional growth with a local geometric constraint. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz), normalized ray direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz), heightfield lookup function heightAtExtended(field, x, z), maximum distance t{max}, maximum iterations N{max}, step scale factor s, minimum step size \delta{min}, and refinement iterations N{refine}. Outputs: Intersection distance t{hit} or miss indicator. Data Structures: heightAtExtended(field, x, z): Returns the height H(x, z) at the given world coordinates, typically via bilinear interpolation of the four surrounding grid points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaplimitedraymarch(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, field, heightAtExtended, tmax, maxsteps, stepscale, minstep, refinesteps): t = 0.0 tprev = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): if t >= tmax: return -1 # miss # Calculate current position and vertical gap x = ox + dx t z = oz + dz t yray = oy + dy t h = yray - heightAtExtended(field, x, z) # Surface hit check if h <= 0: lo, hi = tprev, t for in range(refinesteps): mid = (lo + hi) 0.5 xmid = ox + dx mid zmid = oz + dz mid ymid = oy + dy mid hmid = ymid - heightAtExtended(field, xmid, zmid) if hmid <= 0: hi = mid else: lo = mid return hi # intersection distance # Step size calculation distancestep = t stepscale gapstep = h 0.5 step = min(distancestep, gapstep) if step < minstep: step = minstep # Advance ray tprev = t t += step return -1 # miss Parameters: s (stepScale): Multiplier for the distance-proportional step term. \delta{min} (minStep): Minimum step size to prevent infinite loops on flat surfaces or precision issues. N{max} (maxSteps): Maximum number of march iterations. N{refine} (refineSteps): Number of bisection iterations to find the precise surface intersection after crossing. Pitfalls: Without the gap limiting term (h \cdot 0.5), the ray can step through the surface on ridgelines, causing holes. The gap step ensures the ray never steps more than half the vertical clearance, preventing overshoot. Precision issues on flat surfaces may require \delta{min} to avoid stalling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Prevents surface penetration on complex terrain (ridgelines); efficient for large open areas due to distance-proportional steps; simple to implement. Limitations: Specific to heightfields; requires a height function. When to use: Terrain rendering where heightfields are available and ridgeline accuracy is critical. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originating from the theme1 renderer by mingderwang, this method was developed to efficiently render heightfield-based terrain without relying on distance fields. It addresses the specific challenge of ray marching over terrain where the surface is not a distance field, preventing the common issue of rays stepping over ridgelines. mingderwang/theme1, https://github.com/mingderwang/theme1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Volume Rendering Integration
head: Adaptive Integration Strategy, Adaptive Numerical Integration for Volume Rendering, Adaptive VRI evaluation, Iterative Adaptive Simpson's Rule for Volume Rendering
body: Adaptive Volume Rendering Integration (VRI) is an iterative numerical method that evaluates the Volume Rendering Integral using adaptive step sizes for both the inner (transparency) and outer (color) integrals. It solves the problem of balancing accuracy and performance in volume rendering by avoiding the recursion depth and re-computation issues inherent in standard recursive adaptive methods, making it suitable for GPU implementation. Unlike naive adaptive procedures that recursively integrate the inner integral for every outer evaluation, this method advances both integrals iteratively in consonance, caching function evaluations where possible. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray start parameter t, initial step size h^0, error tolerance \epsilon, minimum step size h{min}, maximum step size h{max}, and ray end parameter t{final}. Outputs: The accumulated color and opacity vector I = [R, G, B, A] and the final step size used. Data Structures: Integration State: Variables t (current position), h (current step size), \epsilon (current tolerance), lastsucceeded (boolean flag), and I (accumulator). Simpson's Rule Values: Temporary storage for S(t,h) (full step) and D(t,h) (two half steps) to compute error. Formulas: The Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) is defined as: I = \int0^D C(s(t)) \tau(s(t)) \exp\left(-\int0^t \tau(s(t')) dt'\right) dt where D is the ray length, C is emitted light, \tau is extinction coefficient, and s is the scalar field. Simpson's rule approximates the integral of a function f in [t, t+h] as: S(t,h) = \frac{h}{6} \left[ f(t) + 4f(t + \frac{h}{2}) + f(t + h) \right] The error estimate E(t,h) is calculated by comparing a full step with two half steps: D(t, h) = S(t, \frac{h}{2}) + S(t + \frac{h}{2}, \frac{h}{2}) E(t,h) = \frac{1}{15} |D(t,h) - S(t,h)| Parameters: h^0: Initial step size. Default experiment value: 0.5 voxel units. h{min}: Minimum step size. Default: 0.1 voxel units. Prevents infinite halving. h{max}: Maximum step size. Default: 2.0 voxel units. Prevents missing high-frequency features. \epsilon: User-specified error tolerance. Tested at 0.01, 0.005, 0.001. Pseudocode: The method consists of three main components: the core iterative loop (Algorithm 2), the Inner Integral routine (RI), and the Outer Integral routine (RO), combined in the main VRI evaluation (Algorithm 3). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simpsonsfull(t, h, f): """Evaluate Simpson's rule for a full step.""" return (h / 6.0) (f(t) + 4.0 f(t + h / 2.0) + f(t + h)) def simpsonshalfsum(t, h, f): """Evaluate sum of two Simpson's half steps.""" h2 = h / 2.0 return simpsonsfull(t, h2, f) + simpsonsfull(t + h2, h2, f) def errorestimate(t, h, f): """Calculate error estimate E(t,h) using Simpson's rule.""" sfull = simpsonsfull(t, h, f) dhalf = simpsonshalfsum(t, h, f) return (1.0 / 15.0) abs(dhalf - sfull) def integrateinterval(t, tfinal, h, hmin, hmax, epsilon, f): """ Iterative integration for a single scalar function f. Returns accumulated integral I, updated t, and final step size h. Based on Algorithm 2 from. """ I = 0.0 currenth = min(h, tfinal - t) lastsucceeded = True while t < tfinal: # Clamp step to remaining distance currenth = min(currenth, tfinal - t) # Calculate error e = errorestimate(t, currenth, f) if e <= epsilon: # Success: accumulate result # D(t,h) is the more accurate estimate from two half steps dval = simpsonshalfsum(t, currenth, f) I += dval + e t += currenth if lastsucceeded: # Double step and tolerance for faster progression in smooth regions currenth = 2.0 currenth epsilon = 2.0 epsilon else: lastsucceeded = True # Cap step size at maximum currenth = min(currenth, hmax) else: # Failure: halve step and tolerance currenth = currenth / 2.0 epsilon = epsilon / 2.0 lastsucceeded = False # If step size hits minimum, take it anyway to prevent infinite loop if currenth <= hmin: dval = simpsonshalfsum(t, currenth, f) I += dval t += currenth lastsucceeded = True currenth = min(2.0 currenth, hmax) return I, t, currenth def innerintegral(t, tfinal, h, hmin, hmax, epsilon, densityfunc): """ Computes the inner integral (transparency) using adaptive integration. Returns integral value and the step size hinner. Based on. """ Iinner, tnew, hinner = integrateinterval(t, tfinal, h, hmin, hmax, epsilon, densityfunc) return Iinner, hinner def outerintegral(t, tfinal, hinner, houter, hmin, hmax, epsilon, colorfunc): """ Computes the outer integral (color) using adaptive integration. Uses regular Simpson's rule for the inner integral evaluation within the outer loop because the error is already bounded by hinner selection. Based on. """ return integrateinterval(t, tfinal, houter, hmin, hmax, epsilon, colorfunc) def adaptivevri(t, h0, epsilon, hmin, hmax, colorfunc, densityfunc): """ Main Adaptive VRI Evaluation (Algorithm 3). Implements Coupled strategy: houter = hinner. """ I = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # R, G, B, A tfinal = t + h0 hinner = min(h0, tfinal - t) houter = hinner while t < tfinal: # 1. Evaluate Inner Integral Iinner, hinner = innerintegral(t, tfinal, hinner, hmin, hmax, epsilon, densityfunc) if Iinner != 0: # 2. Coupled Strategy: houter = hinner houter = hinner # 3. Evaluate Outer Integral Iouter, t, houter = outerintegral(t, tfinal, hinner, houter, hmin, hmax, epsilon, colorfunc) # 4. Accumulate for k in range(4): I[k] += Iouter[k] return I Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Halving: If the error cannot be estimated precisely, the step size may hit h{min}. The algorithm must take the step even if error > tolerance to prevent infinite loops. Missing Features: Without h{max}, high-frequency variations (e.g., thin leaves) may be missed because the adaptive step size becomes too large. Numerical Inaccuracy: Even with strict tolerance, some rays may exceed the limit due to numerical error evaluation inaccuracies and the h{min} floor. High-Frequency Ignorance: High-frequency regions may be wrongly ignored if the error evaluation sampling strategy fails to detect them, especially if the initial step size is too large. GPU Recursion: Recursive adaptive methods cannot be re-initialized after a succeeded step because they store execution context in the call stack. The iterative method allows re-initialization, which is crucial for controlling inner and outer step sizes. Time Complexity: The method avoids excessive re-computations by advancing step-by-step and reusing function evaluations shared by adjacent intervals, similar to caching in recursive Simpson's rule but with constant memory overhead per step. Memory Complexity: Constant memory overhead per step, unlike recursive methods which use stack memory. Performance: CPU architecture favors adaptive algorithms. GPU SIMD architecture favors Riemann summation because adaptive approaches require different step sizes per thread, reducing parallel efficiency. Accuracy: Adaptive VRI offers better accuracy for similar or lower computational cost compared to Riemann summation. Riemann summation requires prohibitive computational costs to reach similar accuracy with constant small step sizes. Coupled vs. Decoupled: The coupled strategy is slightly more efficient; the decoupled strategy is slightly more accurate. Both are equivalent in practice for most cases. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Accurate Volume Rendering based on Adaptive Numerical Integration". History: It addresses the challenge of computing the Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) accurately while maintaining performance, specifically tackling the mapping of recursive adaptive methods to GPU architectures. Usage: Tested on datasets from volvis.org (Bonsai, BluntFin, Teapot, Engine) on a 2.66 GHz Quad Core CPU and GeForce GTX 560 GPU. Accurate Volume Rendering based on Adaptive Numerical Integration, https://lhf.impa.br/ftp/papers/sib2015.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Adaptive Step Size Control
head: Adaptive Step Size Controller, Integrator Step Controller, Step Safety Factor
body: Adaptive Step Size Control is a family of techniques that dynamically adjusts the ray marching interval \Delta t during volume rendering or ray tracing to balance computational cost against visual fidelity. Unlike fixed-step methods, which enforce a uniform trade-off between quality and efficiency, these methods vary the sampling density based on local scene properties (such as density gradients, transmittance, or statistical variance) or global constraints (such as target frame rates). This family is distinct from its siblings: Safe Raymarching Step Size focuses on geometric safety bounds, Compute Minimal Sample Distance Per Pixel on resolution limits, Error Estimate on local error metrics, Gap-Limited Ray Marching on feature gaps, and Adaptive Volume Rendering Integration on integration accuracy. All methods in this family operate on a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by distance t. The core loop evaluates a scene function (SDF, density field, or volume texture) at the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to determine the next step size \Delta t and check for termination. Termination Conditions: 1. Surface Hit: The ray has intersected the target geometry. For SDFs, this is typically |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon or f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0. For volumes, this may be a density threshold or opacity accumulation. 2. Escape/Miss: The ray has traveled beyond a maximum distance t{max} or exceeded a maximum iteration count N{max}. 3. Early Termination (Volumes): Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1 - \epsilon), or accumulated transmission falls below a minimum threshold, allowing the ray to stop early as further contributions are negligible. Step Size Determination: The step size \Delta t is computed based on the local scene properties: SDF-based: \Delta t is often derived from the SDF value f(\mathbf{p}), potentially scaled by a relaxation factor or Lipschitz constant. Volume-based: \Delta t may be fixed, adaptive based on density gradients, or constrained by minimum/maximum bounds to prevent aliasing or excessive computation. Safety: Steps must be chosen to ensure the ray does not penetrate the surface or skip over significant volumetric features, often requiring conservative clamping. Pseudocode Structure: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchloop(rayorigin, raydirection, scenefunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon, minstep=1e-4, maxstep=1.0): """ Generic adaptive ray marching loop implementing shared principles. scenefunc(p) returns (val, alpha) where val is SDF/density and alpha is opacity. """ t = 0.0 alphaacc = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): # Escape/Miss check if t >= maxdist: return False, t, alphaacc # Evaluate scene p = rayorigin + raydirection t val, alpha = scenefunc(p) # Surface Hit check (SDF) if abs(val) < epsilon: return True, t, alphaacc # Early Exit check (Volume) if alphaacc >= 1.0 - epsilon: return False, t, alphaacc # Adaptive Step Calculation # Use SDF/density magnitude as base step, fallback to maxstep if negative/zero step = abs(val) if val > 0 else maxstep step = max(minstep, min(step, maxstep)) # Guard against zero/negative steps to prevent infinite loops if step <= 0: step = minstep t += step alphaacc += alpha (1.0 - alphaacc) return False, t, alphaacc Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching is a volume rendering technique that optimizes computational cost by varying the sampling interval along a ray based on local density changes and transmittance. Unlike fixed-step linear sampling, which forces a trade-off between quality and efficiency, this method uses fine steps in high-density regions and coarse steps in empty space or at distance. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment by explicitly coupling step size to density gradients and transmittance thresholds, and from Variance-based Step Size Adaptation by relying on deterministic density thresholds rather than statistical variance. Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment is a ray marching optimization technique that accelerates traversal through empty or homogeneous regions of a volume by exponentially increasing the step size when no density is detected. It solves the problem of redundant sampling in sparse areas, such as the sky in atmospheric rendering, by skipping large distances until a feature is encountered. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching by using a binary "empty/non-empty" heuristic rather than continuous gradient or variance metrics to drive step changes, and from Variance-based Step Size Adaptation by relying on mip-level offsets rather than statistical error bounds. Adaptive Step Size for Interaction is a performance optimization technique that dynamically increases the ray marching step size during user interaction (e.g., viewpoint changes) to maintain frame rate, then restores smaller step sizes for high-quality final image generation. It differs from continuous adaptive methods like Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching by decoupling the step size from local geometric features during the interaction phase, relying instead on a global state switch to trade visual fidelity for speed. Variance-based Step Size Adaptation is a preprocessing technique that determines the adaptive ray traversal step size (\Delta t) for volume rendering by calculating the statistical variance of voxel data within spatial bricks. It solves the problem of selecting an appropriate step size for sparse or local traversal without the computational cost of calculating iso-surface normals at runtime. Unlike fixed-step methods, it adjusts \Delta t based on local data complexity: high variance (frequent normal changes) yields smaller steps, while low variance allows larger steps. Time-Aware Adaptive Step Size is a technique for controlling rendering frame rate by dynamically adjusting the ray step size based on a predicted rendering time. It solves the problem of maintaining a target frame rate during interactive exploration, particularly when scene complexity changes due to camera movement or transfer function adjustments. It sets itself apart from reactive methods like OLP and PID controllers by predicting rendering time proactively before rendering each frame, thereby avoiding the one-frame lag inherent in reactive approaches. A rendering method where the ray marching step size is provided per-pixel via an input tensor, allowing for variable sampling density across the image. The PyTorch wrapper adaptiveStepsizeRendering asserts that the input stepsizes tensor has shape B1HW and C=1. The stepsizes tensor is moved to the CUDA device. For each batch item, the renderer settings are sent to update the renderer state. The viewport dimensions are extracted from settings and asserted to match the H and W of the stepsizes tensor. The stepsizes tensor is padded to match the viewport requirements (code snippet cuts off, but padding is initiated). fdepsilon: A float parameter with default value 1e-5, used for gradient propagation support. Input tensor stepsize is a float tensor on the GPU of size HxW with only positive values. Output tensor output is a float tensor on the GPU of size BxHxW with B=8 channels: 0=mask, 1=normalX, 2=normalY, 3=normalZ, 4=depth, 5=ao, 6=flowX, 7=flowY. Unlike standard rendering which uses a uniform or pre-computed step size, this method accepts a per-pixel tensor of step sizes, enabling adaptive sampling based on importance maps. A reactive feedback-loop controller that adjusts the ray step size based on the error between actual and target rendering times. Calculate the error as the difference between the actual rendering time and the target rendering time of the previous frame. Apply proportional, integral, and derivative coefficients to the error to compute the control signal. Update the ray step size using the computed control signal. Proportional coefficient: 0.3. Integral coefficient: 0.05. Derivative coefficient: 0.1. A technique to adapt ray step size during volume rendering by constructing a lookup table from median measured rendering times across discrete step sizes, then using linear interpolation to predict rendering time for arbitrary step sizes. Measure rendering times for a set of discrete ray step sizes to generate sampled δ-tnorm curves. Compute the median rendering time at each ray step size across all measured curves to form the adaptation curve G. Store G as a lookup table indexed by ray step size. Query the lookup table for a desired step size using linear interpolation to estimate rendering time. Lookup table mapping ray step size (input) to predicted rendering time (output), accessed via linear interpolation between stored points. Integrated into an interactive widget for Use Case 1 based on the CUDA-raycaster, enabling real-time transfer function adjustment and volume exploration with live frame rate feedback. Adaptive step size control originated from the need to optimize ray marching in volumetric data, where fixed sampling rates lead to either aliasing in dense regions or wasted computation in empty space. Early methods focused on density-gradient-based adaptation for cloud rendering. More recently, the focus has shifted towards performance-aware adaptation, using predictive models like ENTIRE to proactively adjust step sizes for target frame rates, avoiding the lag of reactive PID controllers. These techniques are widely used in interactive volume visualization, medical imaging, and real-time cloud/atmospheric rendering. rusaitis/webpic, https://github.com/rusaitis/webpic, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Learning adaptive sampling and reconstruction for Volume Visualization, https://github.com/shamanDevel/AdaptiveSampling, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ENTIRE: Learning-based Volume Rendering Time Prediction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2501.12119, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching
head: Adaptive Step Size Volume Rendering, CSRayMarch, DDVR, DDVR Raymarching Shader, Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Size and Temporal Accumulation, Volume Rendering via Ray Marching
body: Adaptive Step Size Ray Marching is a volume rendering technique that optimizes computational cost by varying the sampling interval along a ray based on local density changes and transmittance. Unlike fixed-step linear sampling, which forces a trade-off between quality and efficiency, this method uses fine steps in high-density regions and coarse steps in empty space or at distance. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment by explicitly coupling step size to density gradients and transmittance thresholds, and from Variance-based Step Size Adaptation by relying on deterministic density thresholds rather than statistical variance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized direction \mathbf{d}, 3D volume texture(s), transfer function/color map, camera parameters, and configuration parameters (step size, thresholds). Outputs: Final pixel color (RGB) and alpha (A). Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture (sampler3D) storing density/scalar values. For 4D volumes, two textures are used: volumeTexture and volumeTexture4DNextFrame. Noise Image: 2D image buffer (image2D, format rg32f) storing per-pixel noise data. Component.r stores the current step size (or 0 for default); component.g stores the ray offset for jittering. Position Depth Buffer: 2D image buffer (image2D, format rgba32f) storing the world position of the first hit (.xyz) and depth t (.w). Motion Vector Image: 2D image buffer (image2D, format rgba8) storing motion vectors in UV space (.xy). Output Image: 2D image buffer (image2D, format rgba8) storing the final rendered color. Parameters: stepSize: Base step size for ray marching. ZEROTHRESHOLD: Threshold for density and transmittance to skip empty space or terminate ray. EARLYSTOPTHRESHOLD: Transmittance value below which the ray march terminates early (e.g., 0.05). STEPSIZEFINE: Maximum size of a fine step. COARSESTEPSIZEMULTIPLIER: Multiplier to determine coarse step size from fine step size. MAXNUMMISSEDSTEPS: Threshold for switching from fine to coarse steps after missing cloud density. scalarMinMax: Vec2 containing min/max scalar values for density normalization. accumulation: Boolean flag enabling temporal accumulation. bVolume4D: Boolean flag indicating time-varying volume. pingpong4D: Boolean flag for swapping 4D volume textures. interpolationFactor: Float value to mix between two 4D volume frames. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Construct ray from camera position and UV coordinates. Perform ray-box intersection against the volume bounding box to find entry (t{entry}) and exit (t{exit}) distances. If no intersection, output black color and return. Initialize transmittance T = 1.0, accumulated color C{acc} = \mathbf{0}, and light energy L = 0.0. Load noise offset from noiseImage for the current pixel. If.r is 0, use default stepSize; otherwise, use.r as mstepSize. Initialize step offset rayOffset from noiseImage.g. 2. Step Size Calculation (Cloud-Specific Variant): If using cloud rendering with fine/coarse steps: Calculate totalDst = t{exit} - t{entry}. Set curFineStepSize = \min(\text{STEPSIZE\FINE}, \text{totalDst} / \text{MIN\NUM\FINE\STEPS}). Set curCoarseStepSize = curFineStepSize \times COARSESTEPSIZEMULTIPLIER. Set curThreshold = MAXNUMMISSEDSTEPS. Set initial dt = curCoarseStepSize. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate t from t{entry} + \text{rayOffset} to t{exit} with step mstepSize (or dt for cloud variant). Position Calculation: Calculate current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Volume Sampling: Convert \mathbf{p} to texture coordinates uvw. If bVolume4D is true, sample density from volumeTexture and volumeTexture4DNextFrame, mixing them using interpolationFactor and pingpong4D. If bVolume4D is false, sample density directly from volumeTexture. Density Threshold Check: If density > 0.01 (or > 0 for clouds), proceed to color mapping and compositing. Cloud Variant: Decrement curThreshold. If curThreshold \le 0, switch to curCoarseStepSize. Color Mapping & Compositing (if density > threshold): Calculate colorMappingCoord = clamp((density - scalarMinMax.x) / (scalarMinMax.y - scalarMinMax.x), 0, 1). Sample color map to get s (vec4: RGB color, A extinction). Calculate alpha: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{extinction} \times \text{m\stepSize}). Calculate contribution: C{contrib} = T \times \text{s.rgb} \times \alpha. Update accumulated color: C{acc} += C{contrib}. Update transmittance: T = (1.0 - \alpha). Lighting (Optional): If density is above threshold, calculate light contribution (e.g., single scattering toward sun). For clouds, update light energy: lightEnergy = phaseVal; cloudColor = lightEnergy sunColor. First Hit Storage: If !firstHit and \alpha > 0, set firstHit = true and store \mathbf{p} and t in positionDepthBufferImage. Early Termination: If 1.0 - T > 0.95 (or T < \text{EARLY\STOP\THRESHOLD}), break loop. Step Size Adaptation (General Variant): Calculate density difference dDensity = current density - previous density. Compute adaptive step size: newStep = GetStep(dDensity, T, density, stepScale). Update step: step = (step + newStep) \times 0.5. Update prevDensity = current density. Advance Position: \mathbf{p} += \mathbf{d} \times \text{m\stepSize} (or dt). 4. Post-Processing: Apply gamma correction: C{acc}.rgb = \text{pow}(C{acc}.rgb, 1.0/2.2). Calculate final alpha: \alpha{final} = 1.0 - T. Apply illumination scale: C{final} = C{acc} \times \text{illuminationScale}. Temporal Accumulation: If accumulation is true and camera has not moved, blend C{final} with previous frame color using \alpha{final} as weight. Motion Vectors: If enabled, calculate motion vector by reprojecting positionDepthBufferImage to previous frame coordinates. Update Noise: Update noiseImage with new step size and offset for next frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, tentry, texit, volumetexture, colormap, config): # Initialization t = tentry + config.rayoffset transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] firsthit = False prevdensity = 0.0 # Determine step size from noise image mstepsize = config.stepsize if config.noiser == 0 else config.noiser # Cloud-specific variables (if applicable) if config.usecloudsteps: totaldst = texit - tentry curfinestep = min(config.STEPSIZEFINE, totaldst / config.MINNUMFINESTEPS) curcoarsestep = curfinestep config.COARSESTEPSIZEMULTIPLIER curthreshold = config.MAXNUMMISSEDSTEPS dt = curcoarsestep else: dt = mstepsize while t < texit: # Position calculation pos = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] # Volume sampling (explicit coordinate conversion and trilinear interpolation) uvw = [(pos[i] - config.bbmin[i]) / (config.bbmax[i] - config.bbmin[i]) for i in range(3)] uvw = [max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) for u in uvw] # Sample density if config.bVolume4D: d1 = sample3dtexture(uvw, volumetexture) d2 = sample3dtexture(uvw, config.volumetexture4dnext) density = d1 (1.0 - config.interpolationFactor) + d2 config.interpolationFactor else: density = sample3dtexture(uvw, volumetexture) # Density threshold check if density > 0.01: # Color mapping normdensity = clamp((density - config.scalarmin) / (config.scalarmax - config.scalarmin), 0.0, 1.0) s = samplecolormap(normdensity, colormap) # s is [r, g, b, extinction] # Compositing alpha = 1.0 - exp(-s[3] dt) contribution = [transmittance s[0] alpha, transmittance s[1] alpha, transmittance s[2] alpha] accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + contribution[i] for i in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # First hit storage if not firsthit: firsthit = True # storepositiondepth(pos, t) # Handled externally # Early termination if 1.0 - transmittance > 0.95: break prevdensity = density # Step size adaptation (General Variant from S2) ddensity = density - prevdensity newstep = getstep(ddensity, transmittance, density, config.stepscale) dt = (dt + newstep) 0.5 else: # Empty space handling if config.usecloudsteps: curthreshold -= 1 if curthreshold <= 0: dt = curcoarsestep else: # Increase step size in empty space dt = min(dt 2.0, config.maxstep) # Advance t += dt # Post-processing accumulatedcolor = [pow(c, 1.0/2.2) for c in accumulatedcolor] finalalpha = 1.0 - transmittance finalcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] config.illuminationscale for i in range(3)] # Temporal accumulation if config.accumulation and not config.cameramoved: lastcolor = config.lastframecolor finalcolor = [lastcolor[i] (1.0 - finalalpha) + finalcolor[i] finalalpha for i in range(3)] return finalcolor, finalalpha def clamp(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) def sample3dtexture(uvw, tex): # Trilinear interpolation of 3D volume texture at normalized coordinates uvw return tex.trilinearsample(uvw) def samplecolormap(coord, cmap): # 1D color/transfer function lookup return cmap.sample(coord) def getstep(ddensity, transmittance, density, stepscale): # Standard adaptive step function based on density gradient and transmittance return stepscale (1.0 + abs(ddensity)) transmittance Screen-Space Ray Casting with Adaptive Step Size is a pixel shader technique that renders volumetric scattering by casting rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D texture, accumulating in-scattered radiance using an adaptive step size based on density changes and transmittance. It distinguishes itself from fixed-step ray marching by dynamically adjusting the sampling interval to maintain visual fidelity in high-density regions while skipping empty space, and it operates entirely in screen space without requiring explicit geometry intersection beyond depth buffer occlusion. A volumetric rendering technique for clouds that uses raymarching with single scattering toward the sun, optimized with adaptive step sizing and early termination to maintain interactive frame rates. Adaptive step sizing increases step length with ray distance and in empty regions; upon entering a cloud volume, the ray backsteps and resumes with finer steps. Early termination halts the marching loop immediately when accumulated transmittance falls below a predefined threshold, skipping further sampling in that region. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. Adaptive step size reduces the effective N by skipping empty space, but increases overhead per step due to density gradient calculations and conditional branching. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, plus storage for volume textures and auxiliary buffers (noise, depth, motion vectors). Performance: Generates high-quality images with SSIM of 0.95 compared to source, with significant speedup over linear sampling. Interactive frame rates are achievable for cloud rendering with early termination and adaptive steps. Strengths: Reduces computational cost in empty regions; maintains quality in dense areas; supports temporal accumulation for denoising. Limitations: Branch divergence in GPU shaders due to variable step sizes; requires careful tuning of thresholds and multipliers; 4D volumes require double the texture memory. When to use: Real-time volume rendering where performance is critical and density fields have large empty regions (e.g., clouds, smoke). When not to use: Uniform density fields where adaptive steps provide no benefit; scenes requiring precise surface intersection without approximation. Adaptive sampling for volume rendering was proposed to tackle the excessive computational cost of GPU-based 3-D volume rendering, making a trade-off between performance and rendering quality. The method reduces the number of sampling points through a non-linear sampling function, inspired by photography where far objects are vague and close objects are clear. It is implemented in various projects including DDVR (Direct Volume Renderer) which supports 3D and 4D volumes with temporal accumulation and denoising, and cloud renderers using procedural noise. The technique builds on Adaptive Step Size Control principles. name: Screen-Space Ray Casting with Adaptive Step Size
head: In-scattered Radiance with Inverted Transmittance, PSRayCast
body: Screen-Space Ray Casting with Adaptive Step Size is a pixel shader technique that renders volumetric scattering by casting rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D texture, accumulating in-scattered radiance using an adaptive step size based on density changes and transmittance. It distinguishes itself from fixed-step ray marching by dynamically adjusting the sampling interval to maintain visual fidelity in high-density regions while skipping empty space, and it operates entirely in screen space without requiring explicit geometry intersection beyond depth buffer occlusion. Inputs and Outputs Input: Pixel shader input structure PSIn containing Pos (float4) and UV (float2). Global constants include gworldViewProjI (inverse world-view-projection matrix), geyePt (eye position), gworldI (inverse world matrix), gstep (initial step size), gnumSamples (maximum samples), ZEROTHRESHOLD (empty/occlusion threshold), ABSORPTION (accumulation constant), ghasLightProbes (boolean), groSHCoeffs (light probe coefficients), and optionally a depth texture controlled by HASDEPTHMAP. Output: Accumulated in-scattered radiance scatter (float4). Data Structures PSIn: Pos (float4, clip-space position), UV (float2, normalized texture coordinates). shCoeffs: Array of SHNUMCOEFF spherical harmonic coefficients (size not specified). Step-by-Step Method 1. Ray Origin Calculation: Convert screen UV to local space ray origin. Transform UV to clip space: pos.xy = uv 2.0 - 1.0; pos.zw = float2(0.0, 1.0); Flip Y axis: pos.y = -pos.y; Transform to world space: pos = mul(pos, gworldViewProjI); Divide by W: rayOrigin = pos.xyz / pos.w; 2. Ray Direction Calculation: Transform eye position to local space: localSpaceEyePt = mul(float4(geyePt, 1.0), gworldI); Compute direction: rayDir = normalize(rayOrigin - localSpaceEyePt); 3. Ray Validation: Call ComputeRayOrigin(rayOrigin, rayDir); if invalid, discard pixel. 4. Update State: prevDensity = color.w; (Required for next iteration's dDensity calculation) 8. Final Normalization: scatter.xyz /= 2.0 PI; Pseudocode Unverified code. name: Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment
head: Adaptive Step Doubling, Adaptive step volume rendering, Empty Space Step Doubling, Ray-casting with variable step size, Volume rendering with configurable sampling distance
body: Dynamic Sampling Step Adjustment is a volume rendering technique where the distance between sampled points along projection rays is explicitly controlled to balance image quality, resolution, and rendering performance. It solves the problem of excessive rendering time caused by uniform high-density sampling in homogeneous or empty regions, while maintaining high resolution in areas with significant features. Unlike fixed-step ray marching, it dynamically trades off between rendering time and profile smoothness/full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) by adjusting the sampling distance parameter. The method operates by initializing a ray cast with a base sampling distance and iteratively adjusting this distance based on the local content of the volume (density or SDF values). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized direction \mathbf{d}, volume data (density field or SDF), base sampling distance \Delta t{base}, maximum distance t{max}, maximum iterations N{max}. Output: Composed color/opacity for the pixel, final ray distance t. Data Structures: Ray State: Current distance t, accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}, current step size \Delta t. Volume Access: Function sample(p) returning density \rho or SDF value f. Parameters: Base Sampling Distance (\Delta t{base}): The initial step size. Typical values tested include 0.010, 0.025, 0.050, 0.100, 0.170, 0.195, and 1.0 mm. An optimal value for clinical data was found to be 0.025 mm. Empty Space Threshold: A density threshold below which a voxel is considered "empty" or "transparent". Doubling Factor: The multiplier applied to the step size when empty space is detected (typically 2). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, \alpha{acc} = 0, \Delta t = \Delta t{base}. 2. For each iteration i from 0 to N{max}: a. Escape Check: If t \ge t{max}, terminate. b. Evaluate: Compute position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Sample the volume at \mathbf{p} to get density \rho (or SDF f). c. Termination Check: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1 - \epsilon (early exit) or surface hit (|f| < \epsilon), terminate. d. Adaptive Step Logic: i. Empty Space Detection: If \rho is empty (below threshold) for multiple consecutive samples: Double the step size: \Delta t \leftarrow \Delta t \times 2. Optionally increase mip-map offset to sample lower-resolution textures, reducing memory bandwidth. ii. Non-Empty Detection: If \rho is non-empty (above threshold): Step back one step: t \leftarrow t - \Delta t{previous} (where \Delta t{previous} is the step size used in the previous iteration before any doubling). Restore step size: \Delta t \leftarrow \Delta t{base}. Restore mip-map offset if used. e. Advance: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. f. Composite: Accumulate opacity and color contribution from the sample at \mathbf{p} using standard front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
