name: Offset Surface Evaluation
head: Distance to Offset Surfaces, Global offset, Local offset, Point-to-set distance
body: Offset Surface Evaluation computes the distance from a query point to a surface generated by offsetting a skeleton geometry by a fixed distance. It defines smooth, thickened representations of curves, surfaces, or meshes for implicit modeling and ray marching. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a global point-to-set distance search (global offset) rather than a local parametric displacement, which avoids the interior self-intersections and high-degree algebraic artifacts common in local offset methods. The method evaluates the distance to an offset surface by finding the closest point on the underlying skeleton geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point \mathbf{p}, skeleton geometry S (e.g., a space curve or surface), constant offset distance c. Output: Signed distance d(\mathbf{p}) to the offset surface. Data Structures: Skeleton representation: Parametric form \mathbf{s}(t) for curves or \mathbf{s}(u,v) for surfaces, or a mesh vertex list with normals. Distance metric: Euclidean distance. Steps: 1. Search Skeleton: Search the entire set S for the closest point \mathbf{s}^ to \mathbf{p}. 2. Solve for Curves: For a parametric curve \mathbf{s}(t), find the point where the tangent is perpendicular to the vector pointing to \mathbf{p} by solving (\mathbf{s}(t) - \mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{s}'(t) = 0. This can be converted to a degree-5 Bernstein polynomial and solved via convex hull bounding. 3. Search for Meshes: For meshes, iterate over vertices or primitives to find the minimum distance. 4. Compute Distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance d{\text{raw}} = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}^\|. 5. Apply Offset: The signed distance to the offset surface is d(\mathbf{p}) = d{\text{raw}} - c. Parameters: c: Constant offset distance applied to the skeleton. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Interior Surfaces: Global offsets avoid interior surfaces, whereas local offsets can cause gradient discontinuities or result in high-degree algebraic representations. Mesh Self-Intersection: When offsetting a mesh by moving vertices along normals, self-intersections are not handled automatically. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def offsetsurfacedistance(p, skeletonprimitives, c): """ Computes distance from point p to the offset surface of a skeleton by distance c. skeletonprimitives: list of objects with a closestpoint(p) method. c: float, constant offset distance. """ mindistsq = float('inf') for prim in skeletonprimitives: # Primitive-specific closest point search (curve parameter solve or triangle test) pt = prim.closestpoint(p) distsq = (p[0] - pt[0])2 + (p[1] - pt[1])2 + (p[2] - pt[2])2 if distsq < mindistsq: mindistsq = distsq rawdist = mindistsq0.5 return rawdist - c Creates an offset surface from a mesh by moving vertices along their computed normals by a given distance. It is a local offset method, distinct from the global point-to-set distance approach. It is chosen for mesh-based modeling where normals are available. It does not handle self-intersections, as vertices are moved independently along their original normals. Definition: Parametric displacement of mesh vertices. Steps: 1. Ensure normals are computed: mesh->neednormals(). 2. Iterate over all vertices i from 0 to nv-1. 3. Update vertex position: mesh->vertices[i] += amount mesh->normals[i]. 4. Invalidate bounding box and bounding sphere flags. Parameters: amount: distance to offset along normals. Pitfalls: Does not handle self-intersections; vertices are moved independently along their original normals. Time Complexity: Depends on the skeleton search. For a mesh, it is O(N) where N is the number of primitives, unless accelerated by a BVH or grid. For parametric curves, it involves solving polynomial equations, which is constant time but potentially expensive per evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the skeleton geometry. Strengths: Global offsets avoid interior surfaces and are more desirable for ray-tracing and CSG operations. They provide smooth, continuous distance fields. Limitations: Local offsets can cause gradient discontinuities. Mesh-based local offsets do not handle self-intersections. When to use: When a smooth, thickened representation of a curve or surface is needed for ray marching or implicit modeling. When not to use: When the skeleton has high curvature leading to self-intersections, or when performance is critical and the skeleton is a large mesh without acceleration structures. The concept of offset surfaces is rooted in computer-aided geometric design (CAGD) and implicit surface rendering. Global offsets are defined geometrically by the implicit equation d(\mathbf{p}) = 0, where d(\mathbf{p}) is the point-to-set distance to a closed skeleton geometry S. When d is constant, the surface fleshes out the skeleton. The formulation of point-to-set distance reduces the search space for closest point determination to primitives such as parametric surfaces. Global offsets are usually defined as geometric implicit surfaces, whereas local offsets are usually defined parametrically. Global offsets are considered more desirable [Hoffman, 1989] as they avoid interior surfaces which can cause problems in ray-tracing and CSG [van Wijk, 1984]. The offset of an algebraic implicit surface is algebraic, though of higher degree in general. name: Boolean Operations on Distance Fields
head: Boolean Operations on SDFs, Boolean SDF Operations, CSG Operations on Signed Distance Fields, Constructive Solid Geometry, SDF Boolean Operations, SDF Boolean Operators, SDF Set Operations, SDF Surface Boolean Combination (Subtraction)
body:
Boolean operations on Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) are Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) primitives that combine the scalar fields of two or more shapes to create complex geometries. By applying component-wise minimum or maximum functions to the distance values, these operations define the union, intersection, and difference of volumes. Unlike Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) which may focus on specific blending or hierarchical structures, this method provides the fundamental algebraic operators for exact CSG composition, ensuring the resulting field remains a valid SDF for use in sphere tracing. The method evaluates two SDFs, f1(\mathbf{p}) and f2(\mathbf{p}), at a query point \mathbf{p} and combines their scalar outputs. The result is a new SDF f{result}(\mathbf{p}) representing the combined shape. Inputs: Two SDF functions f1, f2: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R}, and a query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: A scalar distance value d{result} \in \mathbb{R}. Optionally, a material ID or normal vector may be returned alongside the distance. The core data structure is the scalar distance value. When tracking material identity (e.g., for shading different primitives differently), the SDF evaluation returns a pair: a vec2 or struct { distance: float, materialid: int }. The distance component (.x) is used for ray marching. The material ID component (.y) is used for shading logic. Let d1 = f1(\mathbf{p}) and d2 = f2(\mathbf{p}). 1. Union: The volume occupied by either shape. The distance is the minimum of the two, as the surface is defined by the closest boundary. d{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(d1, d2) 2. Intersection: The volume occupied by both shapes. The distance is the maximum of the two, as the surface is defined by the farthest boundary that still keeps the point inside both volumes. d{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(d1, d2) 3. Subtraction (Difference): The volume of the first shape minus the second. The second shape's distance is negated before taking the maximum. d{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(d1, -d2) Note: Some sources define subtraction as A - B using \max(dA, -dB), while others describe it as removing object 1 from object 2 using \max(-d1, d2). The standard CSG interpretation A \setminus B uses \max(dA, -dB). The following implementation handles both scalar distance and material ID tracking, consistent with and. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatesdfunion(p, sdf1, sdf2): """ Computes the union of two SDFs. Returns (distance, materialid). """ d1, id1 = sdf1(p) d2, id2 = sdf2(p) if d1 < d2: return d1, id1 else: return d2, id2 def evaluatesdfintersection(p, sdf1, sdf2): """ Computes the intersection of two SDFs. Returns (distance, materialid). """ d1, id1 = sdf1(p) d2, id2 = sdf2(p) if d1 > d2: return d1, id1 else: return d2, id2 def evaluatesdfsubtraction(p, sdf1, sdf2): """ Computes the difference (subtraction) of two SDFs: sdf1 - sdf2. Returns (distance, materialid). """ d1, id1 = sdf1(p) d2, id2 = sdf2(p) negd2 = -d2 if d1 > negd2: return d1, id1 else: return negd2, id2 def scenesdf(p, primitives): """ Combines multiple primitives using union. primitives: list of (sdffunc, materialid) """ currentdist = float('inf') currentid = 0 for sdffunc, matid in primitives: d, = sdffunc(p) if d < currentdist: currentdist = d currentid = matid return currentdist, currentid Operation Type: Enum or string indicating 'union', 'intersection', or 'difference'. csgPrimitiveValueMultiplier: A constant multiplier applied to primitive SDF values to narrow the interval of small values near the isosurface, limiting perturbation of nearby SDFs. Value: 7.5f. maxdistancecustommaterial: The maximum distance between surfaces at which materials are merged. Default value is 0.05. Smoothness (Optional): Standard boolean operations produce sharp edges. Smooth variants use a blending parameter k to interpolate between min/max, but this breaks the exact SDF property and is not a strict boolean operation. Lipschitz Condition: The min/max of 1-Lipschitz functions is also 1-Lipschitz, preserving the validity of sphere tracing. Normals: The normal at the surface is the gradient of the resulting SDF. For boolean operations, the normal is simply the normal of the primitive that determined the minimum/maximum distance. If d{union} = d1, then \mathbf{n} = 
abla f1(\mathbf{p}). Degenerate Intersection: If two shapes touch exactly, the distance is 0. The normal may be undefined or ambiguous if the gradients are opposite. In practice, sphere tracing handles this by stopping at the surface. Precision: When d1 \approx d2, floating-point precision errors may cause flickering or incorrect normal selection. Using a small epsilon for comparison can help, but strict equality is rare in continuous space. Interior Distance Problem: Set operations (union, intersection, subtraction) break the exact distance field (interior for union, exterior for others), requiring case-by-case solutions or Jump Flooding Algorithm (JFA). Lower Bound: Using min/max operators only results in a lower bound to the actual distance, increasing the number of sphere tracing steps after subtraction and intersection operations. FRep R-function Boolean Operations perform set-theoretic operations (union, intersection, subtraction) on implicit surfaces defined by scalar fields f1 and f2 using R-functions, ensuring specific continuity properties based on the parameter \alpha. Unlike the standard SDF operations (min/max) which produce C^1 discontinuities along the entire bisector plane where f1 = f2, R-functions allow for the construction of surfaces with C^1 continuity restricted only to the intersection of the zero-level sets, or smooth blending. This method is distinct from basic SDF primitives by providing a mathematical framework for constructing complex, continuous implicit models from simpler components without explicit mesh topology. The Contact Operator produces a contact surface between two distinct phases \mathcal{A} and \mathcal{B} within their intersection \mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}, simulating collision without deformation. It interpolates between the Over and Under operators defined in Boolean Operations on Distance Fields using a weight parameter \alpha, allowing for a tunable boundary between the two materials. The under operator is a non-commutative Boolean operator for multiphase Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) that performs a union of phases while replacing the phase labels of the first operand with those of the second operand. It solves the problem of assembling composite objects where one material (e.g., cement) must visually "cover" or replace the identity of another (e.g., rock blocks) in overlapping regions, without altering the underlying geometric distance values of the covering material. It differs from the standard commutative union (min) by enforcing a strict occlusion order, and from the Contact Operator by not generating an internal interface surface between phases. An unsolved problem where set operations (union, intersection, subtraction) break the exact distance field (interior for union, exterior for others), requiring case-by-case solutions or Jump Flooding Algorithm (JFA). A scene construction function that combines a floor with a rounded box from which a sphere has been subtracted. The subtraction is performed first, and the result is unioned with the floor. Steps: 1. Compute the SDF of the floor at point p: objfloor(p). 2. Compute the SDF of the rounded box at point p: objroundbox(p). 3. Compute the SDF of the sphere at point p: objsphere(p). 4. Perform boolean subtraction on the rounded box and sphere: opsub(objroundbox(p), objsphere(p)). 5. Perform boolean union between the floor and the result of step 4: objunion(floorresult, subtractionresult). 6. Return the resulting vec2 (distance and material ID). Code: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. vec2 distancetoobj(in vec3 p) { return objunion(objfloor(p), opsub(objroundbox(p), objsphere(p))); } Performs a hard union on two pointrecords, returning the one with the smaller distance. Steps: 1. If p1.dist < p2.dist, return p1. 2. Else, return p2. Parameters: p1: First point record. p2: Second point record. Computes the intersection or difference of a multiphase object \mathcal{A} with an external shape \mathcal{S} defined by SDF f. The intersection is \mathcal{B} = \mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{S}. A variant computes intersection/difference only for a specified set of phase indexes, preserving others. This is useful for cutting parts of objects while preserving other phases. The second term in the phase k equation enforces phase exclusivity by preventing overlaps with competing phases. Formula: For all phases i \in [1, n], the intersection phase function is: \phii = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, f) The difference operator uses -f instead of f. For intersection with shape \mathcal{S} on a single phase k (\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{A} \capk \mathcal{S}): \phii = \phi{\mathcal{A}i} \quad  orall i 
eq k \phik = \max \left( \min(\phi{\mathcal{A}k}, f), -\min{j 
eq k} \phi{\mathcal{A}j} ight). Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive pair. For N primitives combined via union, the complexity is O(N) per ray step, as each primitive must be evaluated to find the minimum distance. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per operation. No additional data structures are required beyond the primitive definitions. Performance: The operations are extremely fast, consisting of basic arithmetic comparisons. They are highly parallelizable on GPUs. Strengths: Exact CSG representation. No tessellation required. Easy to animate and transform. Limitations: Intersection breaks the exterior distance field. Using min/max operators only results in a lower bound to the actual distance, increasing the number of sphere tracing steps after subtraction and intersection operations. Boolean operations on SDFs were popularized by Inigo Quilez in his articles on distance functions and raymarching. The technique leverages the mathematical properties of distance fields to allow constructive solid geometry without explicit mesh representation. It is a cornerstone of procedural raymarching, enabling the creation of complex scenes from simple primitives like spheres, boxes, and tori. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, https://github.com/Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, https://github.com/nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, https://github.com/ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Tantenfisch/Voxels, https://github.com/Tantenfisch/Voxels, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 6 – Raymarching: Floor + Union of Rounded Box and Sphere, http://www.geeks3d.com/20130524/building-worlds-with-distance-functions-in-glsl-raymarching-glslhacker-tutorial-opengl/6/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 7 – Raymarching: Floor + Rounded Box minus Sphere, http://www.geeks3d.com/20130524/building-worlds-with-distance-functions-in-glsl-raymarching-glslhacker-tutorial-opengl/7/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) holger-kibur/sdf, https://github.com/holger-kibur/sdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Skipping Spheres: SDF Scaling & Early Ray Termination for Fast Sphere..., https://diglib.eg.org/items/7f21e58c-639e-4359-bf94-414738612006, fetched 2026-10-27 PDF Further Graphics - name: FRep R-function Boolean Operations
head: Function Representation Boolean Operations, R-function logic
body: FRep R-function Boolean Operations perform set-theoretic operations (union, intersection, subtraction) on implicit surfaces defined by scalar fields f1 and f2 using R-functions, ensuring specific continuity properties based on the parameter \alpha. Unlike the standard SDF operations (min/max) which produce C^1 discontinuities along the entire bisector plane where f1 = f2, R-functions allow for the construction of surfaces with C^1 continuity restricted only to the intersection of the zero-level sets, or smooth blending. This method is distinct from basic SDF primitives by providing a mathematical framework for constructing complex, continuous implicit models from simpler components without explicit mesh topology. Inputs: Two scalar fields f1(\mathbf{x}) and f2(\mathbf{x}) representing the distance or implicit functions of two objects. A continuity parameter \alpha \in \{0, 1\} selecting the R-function class. Optional parameters for variants (e.g., blending coefficients a0, a1, a2, lattice frequencies q, phases p, thresholds l, offsets d). Outputs: A resulting scalar field f3(\mathbf{x}) representing the union, intersection, or subtraction of the input objects. The method operates on scalar fields. In a procedural implementation, these are functions mapping 3D coordinates to real numbers. No explicit grid or voxel structure is required for the definition, though evaluation occurs at query points \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z). The core operations are defined by the R-function logic \lor\alpha, \land\alpha, \setminus\alpha. Class \alpha = 1 (Standard SDF-like): These functions are C^1 discontinuous at all points where f1 = f2. Union: f3 = f1 \lor1 f2 = \max(f1, f2) Intersection: f3 = f1 \land1 f2 = \min(f1, f2) Subtraction: f3 = f1 \setminus1 f2 = \min(f1, -f2) Class \alpha = 0 (Smooth R-functions): These functions have C^1 discontinuity only at points where both arguments are equal to zero (f1 = 0 \land f2 = 0). Union: f3 = f1 \lor0 f2 = \sqrt{f1^2 + f2^2 + \sqrt{f1^4 + f2^4}} Intersection: f3 = f1 \land0 f2 = \sqrt{f1^2 + f2^2 - \sqrt{f1^4 + f2^4}} Subtraction: f3 = f1 \setminus0 f2 = \sqrt{f1^2 + f2^2} - \sqrt{f1^4 + f2^4} This variant models infinite regular 3D lattices by combining periodic slabs. Step 1: Define Parallel Slabs Define three sets of infinite parallel slabs orthogonal to the coordinate axes using trigonometric functions: sx(x,y,z) = \sin(qx x + px) - lx sy(x,y,z) = \sin(qy y + py) - ly sz(x,y,z) = \sin(qz z + pz) - lz q: Frequency/distance between slabs. p: Phase/position of slabs relative to the origin. l: Threshold defining slab thickness, where -1 < l < 1. Step 2: Define Rods (Intersection of Slabs) Intersect orthogonal slab sets to form rods parallel to one axis. Optional offsets dx, dy, dz can be applied to adjust cross-section shape: rx = sy \land\alpha sz + dx ry = sx \land\alpha sz + dy rz = sx \land\alpha sy + dz If dx = dy = dz, rods have circular cross-sections. Otherwise, rods have elliptical cross-sections. Step 3: Define Lattice (Union of Rods) Union the rods to form the infinite lattice: g(x,y,z) = rx \lor\alpha ry \lor\alpha rz Explicitly: g = (sy \land\alpha sz) \lor\alpha (sx \land\alpha sz) \lor\alpha (sx \land\alpha sy) This variant combines an infinite microstructure lattice g with an external object shape F. Step 1: Define Internal Offset Create an internal offset of the external shape F using threshold lo > 0: Fo(x,y,z) = F(x,y,z) - lo Step 2: Define Object Shell Subtract the offset from the original shape to create a thin shell: Fs(x,y,z) = F \setminus\alpha Fo Step 3: Truncate Lattice Intersect the infinite lattice with the original external shape to fit it inside: Fg = g \land\alpha F Step 4: Combine Shell and Lattice Union the shell and the truncated lattice to form the final scaffold: Fm(x,y,z) = Fs \lor\alpha Fg = (F \setminus\alpha Fo) \lor\alpha (g \land\alpha F) This variant produces smooth transitions between surfaces instead of sharp edges by adding a displacement term. Blending Intersection Formula: f1 \landb f2 = (f1 \land\alpha f2) + a0 \left( \left(\frac{f1}{a1}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{f2}{a2}\right)^2 \right) a0, a1, a2: Parameters controlling the blend shape. a0 < 0: Corresponds to a blend with removed material (chamfer). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rfunctionunion(f1, f2, alpha=0): """ Computes the R-function union of two scalar fields. alpha=1: max(f1, f2) alpha=0: sqrt(f1^2 + f2^2 + sqrt(f1^4 + f2^4)) """ if alpha == 1: return max(f1, f2) elif alpha == 0: f1sq = f1 f1 f2sq = f2 f2 f14 = f1sq f1sq f24 = f2sq f2sq innersqrt = math.sqrt(f14 + f24) return math.sqrt(f1sq + f2sq + innersqrt) else: raise ValueError("Alpha must be 0 or 1") def rfunctionintersection(f1, f2, alpha=0): """ Computes the R-function intersection of two scalar fields. alpha=1: min(f1, f2) alpha=0: sqrt(f1^2 + f2^2 - sqrt(f1^4 + f2^4)) """ if alpha == 1: return min(f1, f2) elif alpha == 0: f1sq = f1 f1 f2sq = f2 f2 f14 = f1sq f1sq f24 = f2sq f2sq innersqrt = math.sqrt(f14 + f24) return math.sqrt(f1sq + f2sq - innersqrt) else: raise ValueError("Alpha must be 0 or 1") def rfunctionsubtraction(f1, f2, alpha=0): """ Computes the R-function subtraction of two scalar fields. alpha=1: min(f1, -f2) alpha=0: sqrt(f1^2 + f2^2) - sqrt(f1^4 + f2^4) """ if alpha == 1: return min(f1, -f2) elif alpha == 0: f1sq = f1 f1 f2sq = f2 f2 f14 = f1sq f1sq f24 = f2sq f2sq return math.sqrt(f1sq + f2sq) - math.sqrt(f14 + f24) else: raise ValueError("Alpha must be 0 or 1") def slabfunctionx(x, y, z, qx, px, lx): return math.sin(qx x + px) - lx def slabfunctiony(x, y, z, qy, py, ly): return math.sin(qy y + py) - ly def slabfunctionz(x, y, z, qz, pz, lz): return math.sin(qz z + pz) - lz def latticefunction(x, y, z, qx, px, lx, qy, py, ly, qz, pz, lz, alpha=0, dx=0, dy=0, dz=0): """ Computes the infinite regular lattice function. """ # Step 1: Slabs sx = slabfunctionx(x, y, z, qx, px, lx) sy = slabfunctiony(x, y, z, qy, py, ly) sz = slabfunctionz(x, y, z, qz, pz, lz) # Step 2: Rods (Intersection of orthogonal slabs) # Note: The source defines rods as intersections. # rx is intersection of sy and sz. rx = rfunctionintersection(sy, sz, alpha) + dx ry = rfunctionintersection(sx, sz, alpha) + dy rz = rfunctionintersection(sx, sy, alpha) + dz # Step 3: Lattice (Union of rods) lattice = rfunctionunion(rx, ry, alpha) lattice = rfunctionunion(lattice, rz, alpha) return lattice def microstructurescaffold(Ffunc, gfunc, x, y, z, lo, alpha=0): """ Computes the microstructure scaffold combining external shape F and lattice g. Ffunc: function returning F(x,y,z) gfunc: function returning g(x,y,z) lo: offset threshold > 0 """ Fval = Ffunc(x, y, z) gval = gfunc(x, y, z) # Step 1: Internal offset Foval = Fval - lo # Step 2: Shell (Subtraction) Fsval = rfunctionsubtraction(Fval, Foval, alpha) # Step 3: Truncated Lattice (Intersection) Fgval = rfunctionintersection(gval, Fval, alpha) # Step 4: Final Scaffold (Union) Fmval = rfunctionunion(Fsval, Fgval, alpha) return Fmval def blendingintersection(f1, f2, alpha=0, a0=0, a1=1, a2=1): """ Computes the blending intersection. a0 < 0 corresponds to removed material (chamfer). """ baseintersection = rfunctionintersection(f1, f2, alpha) blendterm = a0 ((f1 / a1)2 + (f2 / a2)2) return baseintersection + blendterm Continuity Discontinuities: The \alpha=1 class functions are C^1 discontinuous at all points where f1 = f2. The \alpha=0 class has C^1 discontinuity only at points where both arguments are equal to zero. Lattice Continuity: For the regular lattice using \alpha=0, the function is C^1 continuous in the entire domain except at surface edges resulting from intersection and union operations. Offset Constraint: The offset threshold lo in the microstructure combination must be positive (lo > 0) to define the internal offset for the thin shell. Slab Threshold: The slab threshold l must satisfy -1 < l < 1. A method to model infinite regular 3D lattices by defining parallel slabs using periodic trigonometric functions, intersecting them to form rods, and uniting the rods. It is chosen when a periodic, infinite cellular structure is required. It differs from finite lattice representations by being defined analytically over the entire domain. A method to combine an infinite microstructure lattice with a given external object shape by creating a thin shell and intersecting the lattice with the object. It is chosen when embedding internal structures within a specific boundary. It differs from simple clipping by using R-function subtraction to maintain smooth shell thickness. A method to produce smooth transitions between surfaces instead of sharp edges by adding a displacement term to standard R-functions. It is chosen when chamfering or smoothing the edges of boolean operations is desired. It differs from standard boolean operations by introducing parameters a0, a1, a2 to control the blend shape. Time Complexity: Evaluation is O(1) per point query, involving a constant number of trigonometric, square root, and arithmetic operations. The cost depends on the depth of the boolean tree (number of nested operations). Memory Complexity: O(1) for procedural evaluation, as no grid or mesh data is stored. Parameters are stored in constant space. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales well with resolution since it is procedural. However, evaluating deep boolean trees or complex lattices with many parameters increases computational cost per sample. Strengths: Compact representation, arbitrary parameterization, ability to model infinite structures, and control over continuity properties (C^1). Limitations: C^1 discontinuities still exist at specific boundaries (edges of intersections/unions) even with \alpha=0. Blending requires tuning parameters. When to use: Procedural modeling of microstructures, implicit surfaces requiring specific continuity, and infinite periodic patterns. When not to use: When explicit mesh topology is required or when exact C^\infty continuity everywhere is needed without blending. The method originates from the Function Representation (FRep) approach to procedural modeling, which addresses the drawbacks of Boundary Representation (BRep) and voxel-based models. R-functions were introduced by Rabinovich and later developed by Shapiro and others for implicit modeling. The specific application to microstructures and lattices using trigonometric functions was proposed in the paper "Procedural function-based modelling of volumetric microstructures". This work builds on earlier applications of implicit surfaces to periodic structures like chess boards. name: Contact Operator
head: Phase Contact Operator, Weighted SDF Combination
body: The Contact Operator produces a contact surface between two distinct phases \mathcal{A} and \mathcal{B} within their intersection \mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}, simulating collision without deformation. It interpolates between the Over and Under operators defined in Boolean Operations on Distance Fields using a weight parameter \alpha, allowing for a tunable boundary between the two materials. Inputs: Two Signed Distance Fields (SDFs): \phi{\mathcal{A}i} for phase i of object \mathcal{A}, and \phi{\mathcal{B}j} for phase j of object \mathcal{B}. Weight parameter \alpha \in [0, 1]. Outputs: Updated multiphase function \Phi where phases i and j are modified to reflect contact, and all other phases k \neq i, j are set to infinity. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar fields. For implementation, \phi{\mathcal{A}i} and \phi{\mathcal{B}j} are typically stored as 3D grids or evaluated procedurally. The output \Phi is a multiphase representation where each voxel or point stores the active phase ID and its distance value. Steps: 1. Compute the Contact Field f: Calculate the 1-Lipschitz signed distance field f(\mathbf{p}) at every point \mathbf{p} using the weighted sum of the input SDFs: f(\mathbf{p}) = \alpha \phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{p}) - (1 - \alpha) \phi{\mathcal{B}j}(\mathbf{p}) 2. Define Regions: Identify the regions \Omega^+ and \Omega^- based on the sign of f(\mathbf{p}): \Omega^+ = \{\mathbf{p} \mid f(\mathbf{p}) > 0\} \Omega^- = \{\mathbf{p} \mid f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0\} Note: \Omega^+ \cup \Omega^- = \mathbb{R}^3 and \Omega^+ \cap \Omega^- = \{\mathbf{p} \mid f(\mathbf{p}) = 0\}. 3. Update Phase i (\mathcal{A}): The new distance field for phase i, denoted \phii, is the maximum of the original phase distance and the negated contact field: \phii(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{p}), -f(\mathbf{p})) This effectively subtracts the region \Omega^+ from \mathcal{A} (\tilde{\mathcal{A}} = \mathcal{A} - \Omega^+). 4. Update Phase j (\mathcal{B}): The new distance field for phase j, denoted \phij, is the maximum of the original phase distance and the contact field: \phij(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\phi{\mathcal{B}j}(\mathbf{p}), f(\mathbf{p})) This effectively subtracts the region \Omega^- from \mathcal{B} (\tilde{\mathcal{B}} = \mathcal{B} - \Omega^-). 5. Invalidate Other Phases: For all other phases k \neq i, j, set their distance values to infinity to indicate they are not present in the contact region: \phik(\mathbf{p}) = \infty Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def contactoperator(phiAi, phiBj, alpha): """ Computes the contact surface between phase i of A and phase j of B. Args: phiAi: SDF function or grid for phase i of object A. phiBj: SDF function or grid for phase j of object B. alpha: Weight parameter in [0, 1]. Returns: phii: Updated SDF for phase i. phij: Updated SDF for phase j. """ # Step 1: Compute the weighted contact field f # f(p) = alpha phiAi(p) - (1 - alpha) phiBj(p) f = alpha phiAi - (1 - alpha) phiBj # Step 2 & 3: Update phase i # phii = max(phiAi, -f) # This corresponds to A - Omega^+ where Omega^+ is f > 0 phii = max(phiAi, -f) # Step 4: Update phase j # phij = max(phiBj, f) # This corresponds to B - Omega^- where Omega^- is f <= 0 phij = max(phiBj, f) # Step 5: Other phases are set to infinity (not returned here, # but implied in the multiphase structure) return phii, phij Parameters: \alpha \in [0, 1]: Weight parameter. \alpha \to 0: f \to \phi{\mathcal{B}j}, \Omega^+ \to \Omega{\mathcal{B}}. The operator approaches the Under operator. \alpha \to 1: f \to \phi{\mathcal{A}i}, \Omega^- \to \Omega{\mathcal{A}}. The operator approaches the Over operator. \alpha = 1/2: The implicit surface \partial\Omega\alpha = \{\mathbf{p} \mid f(\mathbf{p}) = 0\} separates space into domains where \phi{\mathcal{A}i} > \phi{\mathcal{B}j} and \phi{\mathcal{A}i} < \phi{\mathcal{B}j}. Edge Cases: Precision: The boundary is defined by f(\mathbf{p}) = 0. Floating-point precision errors near this zero-crossing may cause artifacts in the contact surface. Non-intersecting Phases: If \mathcal{A} and \mathcal{B} do not intersect, the behavior is determined by the global SDF values, but the "contact" surface may not be visually meaningful as a collision interface. Uses smooth R-functions for Boolean operations. Choose when smooth blending of shapes is required rather than distinct phase contact. A specific non-commutative union. Choose when one object must strictly occlude another without a shared contact interface. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of points/voxels, as it requires a single pass to compute f and two max operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the intermediate field f and the output fields. Strengths: Provides a tunable interface between two phases, allowing for a smooth transition or specific collision boundary defined by \alpha. It avoids the deformation complexity of earlier contact models. Limitations: Only applies to two specific phases at a time. Other phases are invalidated (\infty), which may require careful management in complex multiphase scenes. When to use: When simulating contact between two distinct materials (e.g., rock and cement) where a specific boundary surface is desired within their overlap. The Contact Operator is described in The PhaseTree: Multiphase Signed Distance Fields. It draws inspiration from the work of Gascuel et al. [1993] but focuses on collision without deformation. It is used in multiphase SDF representations, such as synthesizing a rock wall by combining Voronoi cells (rock blocks) with a cement phase. The PhaseTree: Multiphase Signed Distance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811379, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Under Operator (Non-commutative Union)
head: Non-commutative under operator, Over Operator, Non-commutative Union, symmetric over operator, union with replacement
body:
The under operator is a non-commutative Boolean operator for multiphase Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) that performs a union of phases while replacing the phase labels of the first operand with those of the second operand. It solves the problem of assembling composite objects where one material must visually cover or replace the identity of another in overlapping regions, without altering the underlying geometric distance values of the covering material. It differs from the standard commutative union (min) by enforcing a strict occlusion order, and from the Contact Operator by not generating an internal interface surface between phases. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two multiphase objects \mathcal{A} and \mathcal{B}, each defined by a vector of n signed distance fields \{\phi{\mathcal{A}1}, \dots, \phi{\mathcal{A}n}\} and \{\phi{\mathcal{B}1}, \dots, \phi{\mathcal{B}n}\}. Output: A resulting multiphase object \mathcal{C} = \mathcal{A} \cup- \mathcal{B} with n phases, where each phase i has a signed distance field \phii. Data Structures: Each phase i is represented by its scalar SDF value \phii at a given point in space. Formulas: The set-theoretic definition for the i-th phase of the result is: \mathcal{C}i = (\mathcal{A}i \cup \mathcal{B}i) -  igcup{j 
eq i} \mathcal{B}j where \cup denotes standard set union and - denotes set difference. The corresponding signed distance field computation for each phase i \in [1, n] is: \phii = \max(\min(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, \phi{\mathcal{B}i}), -\min(\phi{\mathcal{B}i})) where \phi{\mathcal{A}i} and \phi{\mathcal{B}i} are the SDF values of phase i in objects \mathcal{A} and \mathcal{B} respectively. Parameters: n: The number of phases. Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize an output array phiC of length n. 2. Iterate over each phase index i from 1 to n. 3. Compute the standard union of phase i from both objects: u = \min(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, \phi{\mathcal{B}i}). 4. Compute the replacement term: r = -\min(\phi{\mathcal{B}i}). 5. Assign the result: \phii = \max(u, r). 6. Return phiC. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def underoperator(phiA, phiB): """Computes the non-commutative under operator for multiphase SDFs. Args: phiA: List of n SDF values for object A. phiB: List of n SDF values for object B. Returns: phiC: List of n SDF values for the result. """ n = len(phiA) phiC = [0.0] n for i in range(n): phiC[i] = max(min(phiA[i], phiB[i]), -min(phiB[i])) return phiC Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Standard floating-point precision applies. Boundaries: The formula applies for all i \in [1, n]. The Local Phase Change operator modifies the phase labels of a multiphase SDF within a specific spatial region defined by another SDF. It differs from global phase reassignment by being spatially localized and from geometric Boolean operations by preserving the distance values of the target phase while only updating the label. Choose it when selectively reassigning material identities in a composite object without altering the underlying geometry's shape is required. A phase-specific smooth union with a shape S over other phases, denoted \mathcal{B} =  igcup+^(\mathcal{A}, S, k). It smooths the union of phase k and shape S, while subtracting this result from all other phases. The set operations are \mathcal{B}k = \mathcal{A}k \cup^ S and \mathcal{B}i = \mathcal{A}i - (\mathcal{A}k \cup^ S) for all i 
eq k, where \cup^ is the smooth union with blending radius r. The phase functions are computed as \phi{\mathcal{B}k} = \widetilde{\phik} and \phi{\mathcal{B}i} = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, \widetilde{\phik}) for all i 
eq k, where \widetilde{\phik} = s(\phi{\mathcal{A}k}, f) and f is the SDF of shape S. The function s represents the smooth union formulation. Choose it when blending geometries smoothly while enforcing phase replacement behavior is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows for the construction of complex composite materials (e.g., rocks with cement) where the occluding material's phase identity is preserved in the overlap. Limitations: Non-commutative, so the order of operands matters. When to use: When assembling multiphase objects where one phase should visually replace another in overlapping regions. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The under operator was introduced in the context of multiphase Signed Distance Fields to address the limitations of standard Boolean operators (union, intersection, difference) which do not directly adapt to multiphase models. It is part of the PhaseTree framework for representing and manipulating multiphase implicit surfaces. The operator is symmetric to the over operator, where \mathcal{A} \cup+ \mathcal{B} is equivalent to \mathcal{B} \cup- \mathcal{A}. name: Local Phase Change
head: Phase Change Operator, Phase Replacement
body: The Local Phase Change operator modifies the phase labels of a multiphase Signed Distance Field (SDF) within a specific spatial region defined by another SDF. It solves the problem of selectively reassigning material identities (phases) in a composite object without altering the underlying geometry's shape, effectively performing a "cut and paste" of phase labels. It differs from global phase reassignment by being spatially localized and from geometric Boolean operations by preserving the distance values of the target phase while only updating the label. Inputs: A multiphase SDF object \mathcal{A}, represented by a set of phase functions \{\phii\}. A region \mathcal{S} defined by a signed distance field f. Two phase indices: i (source phase to be removed from the region) and k (target phase to be assigned to the region). Outputs: A new multiphase SDF object \mathcal{B} with updated phase functions \{\phi'j\}. Data Structures: The implementation assumes a structure capable of storing multiple scalar fields (one per phase) or a vector field where each component corresponds to a phase index. For an object with N phases, the state is typically stored as an array or vector of N scalar fields. Algorithm: The operator performs two logical steps: 1. Subtraction: Remove phase i from the region \mathcal{S}. This is achieved by taking the maximum of the original phase i distance and the negative of the region SDF. This ensures that inside \mathcal{S} (where f < 0), the distance for phase i becomes positive (outside), effectively removing it. 2. Addition: Assign phase k to the intersection of the region \mathcal{S} and the original phase i. The new phase k distance is the minimum of the original phase k and the maximum of the original phase i (after subtraction) and the region SDF. Formulas: The resulting phase functions \Phi are computed as follows: \Phi = \begin{cases} \phii = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, -f) \\ \phik = \min(\phi{\mathcal{A}k}, \max(\phii, f)) \\ \phij = \phi{\mathcal{A}j} & \forall j \neq i, k \end{cases} Where: \phi{\mathcal{A}i} is the original distance field for phase i. \phi{\mathcal{A}k} is the original distance field for phase k. f is the signed distance field defining region \mathcal{S}. \phii in the second equation refers to the updated value from the first line. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode computes the new phase fields for a given voxel or point evaluation. It assumes phases is a list/array of scalar fields, f is the region SDF, and i, k are integer indices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localphasechange(phases, f, i, k): """ Computes the new phase fields after applying local phase change. Args: phases: List of scalar fields (functions or arrays) for each phase. f: Signed distance field defining the region S. i: Index of the source phase (to be removed from S). k: Index of the target phase (to be added to S). Returns: List of updated scalar fields. """ nphases = len(phases) newphases = [None] nphases # Step 1: Update phase i # phii = max(phiAi, -f) # Note: In a voxel-based implementation, this is element-wise max. # In a procedural evaluation, this is computed on the fly. phiiold = phases[i] phiinew = elementwisemax(phiiold, negate(f)) # Step 2: Update phase k # phik = min(phiAk, max(phiinew, f)) phikold = phases[k] phikintermediate = elementwisemax(phiinew, f) phiknew = elementwisemin(phikold, phikintermediate) # Step 3: Copy other phases unchanged for j in range(nphases): if j == i: newphases[j] = phiinew elif j == k: newphases[j] = phiknew else: newphases[j] = phases[j] return newphases def elementwisemax(a, b): # Placeholder for vectorized max operation return [max(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)] def elementwisemin(a, b): # Placeholder for vectorized min operation return [min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)] def negate(f): # Placeholder for negation operation return [-x for x in f] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Identity of Indices: If i = k, the operation is a no-op for the phase labels, but the distance field for phase k is still modified by the region S. Specifically, \phik = \min(\phi{\mathcal{A}k}, \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}k}, f)). If f < \phi{\mathcal{A}k}, the distance is clamped to f. This effectively clips the phase k boundary to the region S. Precision: When f is close to zero (boundary of region \mathcal{S}), floating-point precision errors in the max and min operations can cause artifacts in the resulting distance field. Region Definition: The region \mathcal{S} must be well-defined. If f is not a valid SDF, the topological guarantees of the phase change are lost. A high-level operator that deforms a specific target phase k within a multiphase set \mathcal{A}, while optionally preserving or replacing other phases using over/under operators. It generalizes the local phase change by applying a deformation map \omega and scaling factor \lambda to the target phase. The operator is defined as D(\mathcal{A}, k) = D(\mathcal{A}k) \cup+ (\mathcal{A} - \mathcal{A}k), where \cup+ is the over operator. The resulting phase functions are: \Phi = \begin{cases} \phii = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, -\phi{\mathcal{A}i} \circ \omega^{-1}/\lambda) & \forall i \neq k \\ \phik = \phi{\mathcal{A}k} \circ \omega^{-1}/\lambda & \end{cases} where \omega is the deformation map, \lambda is a scaling factor, and \circ denotes composition. This allows for warping specific materials within a composite object. Time Complexity: O(N) per evaluation point, where N is the number of phases. The operation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations per phase. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where V is the number of voxels or evaluation points, as all phase fields must be stored or recomputed. Strengths: Allows for complex material editing without reconstructing the geometry. Efficient for interactive editing of multiphase models. Limitations: The resulting distance field may not be a perfect SDF if the region \mathcal{S} is not convex or if the phase change creates topological inconsistencies. The distance values for phase k are clamped, which may affect subsequent smoothing or offsetting operations. The Local Phase Change operator was introduced in the context of the PhaseTree model for multiphase Signed Distance Fields. It is part of a suite of smooth-Boolean operators designed to handle complex multiphase objects in computer graphics and geometric modeling. The operator enables the manipulation of material identities in implicit surfaces, extending the capabilities of traditional Boolean operations to multiphase contexts. The PhaseTree: Multiphase Signed Distance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811379, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Layered Operator
head: Layering operator, L operator
body: The Layered Operator is a unary SDF operation that embeds a set of existing phases \mathcal{A}i within a new outer layer \mathcal{A}{n+1} of specified thickness t, creating a distinct new phase. It generalizes standard SDF offsetting to multiphase environments by ensuring the new layer surrounds the union of all underlying phases without penetrating them. Unlike the Under Operator which modifies existing phase boundaries, this operator strictly adds a new phase index n+1. Inputs: A set of n existing phase functions \{\phi{\mathcal{A}1}, \dots, \phi{\mathcal{A}n}\}, where \phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{x}) is the signed distance to phase i. Thickness parameter t > 0. Optional blending radius r for smooth union mode. Outputs: The original n phase functions unchanged. A new phase function \phi{\mathcal{A}{n+1}} representing the layer. Data Structures: Phase functions are typically stored as scalar fields or evaluated on the fly. No specific bit-packing is mandated by the definition, but standard float32 or float16 precision is implied for SDF values. Steps: 1. Compute the signed distance to the union of all existing phases, denoted \phi{\mathcal{A}0}. By definition, \mathcal{A}0 is the complement of the union of all phases \mathcal{A}i (i \in [1, n]). The distance function is: \phi{\mathcal{A}0}(\mathbf{x}) = -\min{i \in [1, n]} \phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{x}) This value is negative inside the union of existing phases and positive outside. 2. Determine the mode of operation: Normal Mode: Use standard union. Smooth Mode: Use smooth union with radius r. 3. Compute the new layer phase function \phi{\mathcal{A}{n+1}}: Normal Mode: The layer is defined as the offset of the complement of the existing union, intersected with the complement itself: \mathcal{A}{n+1} = I(\overline{\mathcal{A}}0, t) \cap \mathcal{A}0 The resulting phase function is: \phi{\mathcal{A}{n+1}}(\mathbf{x}) = \max(-\phi{\mathcal{A}0}(\mathbf{x}) - t, \phi{\mathcal{A}0}(\mathbf{x})) Here, I(\cdot, t) represents the offsetting operator. The term -\phi{\mathcal{A}0} - t represents the offset surface of the existing geometry, and \phi{\mathcal{A}0} ensures the layer does not penetrate the existing phases (intersection with \mathcal{A}0). Smooth Mode: To obtain a smooth coating effect, replace the standard union with a smooth union \cup^: \mathcal{A}{n+1} = I\left(\bigcup{i \in [1, n]}^ \mathcal{A}i, t\right) \cap \mathcal{A}0 The smooth union of two phases i and j with blending radius r is defined as: \phi{\mathcal{A}i \cup^ \mathcal{A}j} = \min(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, \phi{\mathcal{A}j}) - \frac{1}{6} r \left( \max\left(1 - \frac{|\phi{\mathcal{A}i} - \phi{\mathcal{A}j}|}{r}, 0\right) \right)^3 For n > 2 phases, the smooth union is applied iteratively or via a generalized smooth min operator. The resulting \phi{\mathcal{A}{n+1}} is computed using the same max formula as the normal mode, but with the smooth union distance replacing \phi{\mathcal{A}0} in the offset calculation. Parameters: t: Thickness of the new layer. Must be positive. r: Blending radius for the smooth union operator. Must be positive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If t is very small relative to the precision of the SDF, the layer may disappear or exhibit artifacts. In smooth mode, if r is too large, the blending may extend too far, potentially causing the layer to merge visually with distant phases if not carefully bounded. The definition assumes \phi{\mathcal{A}i} are valid signed distance fields. If inputs are not normalized or have incorrect signs, the min operation for \phi{\mathcal{A}0} will fail to represent the correct union boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def layeredoperator(phases, thickness, smooth=False, radius=0.0): """ Computes the new layer phase function for a set of existing phases. Args: phases: List of callable functions phii(x) returning signed distance. thickness: Float, thickness of the new layer. smooth: Boolean, whether to use smooth union. radius: Float, blending radius for smooth union (ignored if smooth=False). Returns: A callable function phinew(x) for the new layer phase. Time Complexity: O(n) per evaluation point, where n is the number of existing phases, as it requires evaluating all phase functions to find the minimum (or smooth union). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per evaluation, assuming phase functions are evaluated on the fly. If precomputed, it depends on the storage of the phase fields. Strengths: Allows incremental construction of complex multiphase objects by adding layers without modifying existing phase definitions. Efficient for creating coatings or shells around existing geometry. Limitations: The layer thickness t is uniform in the normal mode. In smooth mode, the blending radius r affects the shape of the layer near phase boundaries, which may require tuning. name: Implicit Surface Representation
head: Grid-based SDF, Tricubic SDF, Zero-level set surface
body: This method represents an implicit surface as a grid-based Signed Distance Function (SDF) using tricubic interpolation to ensure continuous surface normals. It defines the surface geometry as the zero-level set of a scalar field f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}). It builds on SDF Primitive Definitions but replaces analytical formulas with a discrete grid evaluated via higher-order interpolation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D grid of floating-point values representing the signed distance to the surface at grid vertices. Output: A continuous scalar field f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}) and its gradient \nabla f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}) for any query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures The core data structure is a 3D array (grid) of floating-point values. Let G be a grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Each vertex (i, j, k) stores the distance value d{i,j,k} at the corresponding grid point. The grid spacing (resolution) is uniform, denoted by \Delta. Formulas The implicit surface S{implicit} is defined as the set of points where the function evaluates to zero: S{implicit} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f{implicit}(x, y, z) = 0 \right\} Parameters Grid Resolution: Determines the spatial frequency of the SDF. Interpolation Order: Tricubic (order 3) is specified to ensure continuous normals. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatetricubicsdf(grid, p, spacing): """ Evaluates the implicit surface function and its gradient at point p using tricubic interpolation on a uniform grid. Args: grid: 3D numpy array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) containing distance values. p: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the query point. spacing: float, the uniform distance between grid vertices. Returns: value: float, the signed distance f(p). normal: 3D vector, the gradient df/dp (surface normal). """ # 1. Map world point to grid coordinates gx = p[0] / spacing gy = p[1] / spacing gz = p[2] / spacing # 2. Find base cell indices and fractional offsets ix = int(gx) iy = int(gy) iz = int(gz) tx = gx - ix ty = gy - iy tz = gz - iz # 3. Boundary clamping ix = max(0, min(ix, grid.shape[0] - 2)) iy = max(0, min(iy, grid.shape[1] - 2)) iz = max(0, min(iz, grid.shape[2] - 2)) # 4. Retrieve 8 corner values corners = [] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): corners.append(grid[ix + i, iy + j, iz + k]) # 5. Tricubic interpolation basis functions and derivatives def h0(t): return 2t3 - 3t2 + 1 def h1(t): return t3 - 2t2 + t def h2(t): return -2t3 + 3t2 def h3(t): return t3 - t2 def dh0(t): return 6t2 - 6t def dh1(t): return 3t2 - 4t + 1 def dh2(t): return -6t2 + 6t def dh3(t): return 3t2 - 2t # 6. Evaluate value and gradient via tensor product value = 0.0 gradx = 0.0 grady = 0.0 gradz = 0.0 idx = 0 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): vi = [h0(tx), h1(tx), h2(tx), h3(tx)][i] vj = [h0(ty), h1(ty), h2(ty), h3(ty)][j] vk = [h0(tz), h1(tz), h2(tz), h3(tz)][k] dvi = [dh0(tx), dh1(tx), dh2(tx), dh3(tx)][i] dvj = [dh0(ty), dh1(ty), dh2(ty), dh3(ty)][j] dvk = [dh0(tz), dh1(tz), dh2(tz), dh3(tz)][k] val = corners[idx] value += vi vj vk val gradx += (dvi / spacing) vj vk val grady += vi (dvj / spacing) vk val gradz += vi vj (dvk / spacing) val idx += 1 normal = (gradx, grady, gradz) return value, normal Edge Cases Boundary Conditions: Points outside the grid bounds require clamping or extrapolation. Precision: Floating-point errors in interpolation can cause artifacts near the zero-level set. Memory: Not given in the sources. Time: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Continuous surface normals enable smooth shading and differentiable rendering without explicit mesh extraction. Limitations: Memory usage scales with volume rather than surface area. High resolution is needed for fine details. This representation is used in differentiable rendering pipelines, specifically in the implementation based on the cudaadrgb backend of Mitsuba 3. name: Standard Solid Primitives
body: Standard Solid Primitives provide exact, closed-form Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for canonical geometric shapes, enabling efficient distance-field ray marching without explicit mesh tessellation. Unlike Distance to Natural Quadrics, which focuses on the geometric properties of conic sections, this family emphasizes the practical implementation of exact distance bounds for spheres, boxes, tori, and their combinations, guaranteeing that sphere tracing steps do not overshoot surfaces. The family operates on the principle that a scene is defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) where the zero-level set f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 represents the surface. For sphere tracing to be valid, the function must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring |f(\mathbf{p}1) - f(\mathbf{p}2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2\|. This guarantees that the value f(\mathbf{p}) is a safe lower bound on the distance to the surface, allowing the ray marcher to step forward by exactly f(\mathbf{p}) without tunneling. Composition is achieved through Boolean operations on the distance values: Union: f{\text{union}}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})) Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination). Intersection: f{\text{intersect}}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})) Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination). Subtraction: f{\text{sub}}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(-f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})) Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} into the local coordinate space of the primitive using the inverse transformation matrix M^{-1} before evaluation. The general definition for a shape centered at the origin with radius r is d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - r. Specific primitives are defined as follows: Sphere: Center \mathbf{c}, radius r. d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\| - r Box (AABB): Half-extents \mathbf{b} = (bx, by, bz), centered at origin. \mathbf{d} = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b} d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\max(\mathbf{d}, 0)\| + \min(\max(\mathbf{d}x, \max(\mathbf{d}y, \mathbf{d}z)), 0) Note: A cheaper, non-exact approximation is \max(|\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b}). Cylinder (Infinite): Axis-aligned with Y, radius r. d(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r Cylinder (Capped): Radius r, half-height h. dx = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r, \quad dy = |py| - h d(\mathbf{p}) = \min(\max(dx, dy), 0) + \|\max(dx, dy, 0)\| Cone: Radius r, height h, axis-aligned with Y. Let \phi = \arctan(r/h). d(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}\cos(\phi) - |py|\sin(\phi), \max(py - h, -py)) Implementation detail: Requires checking distance to tip and base ring if the projection falls outside the mantle. Plane: Normal \mathbf{n} (unit length), offset d{\text{offset}}. d(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + d{\text{offset}} Torus: Major radius R{\text{out}}, tube radius R{\text{in}}. d(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R{\text{out}})^2 + py^2} - R{\text{in}} Capsule: Endpoints \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, radius r. \mathbf{ab} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} t = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{ab}}{\|\mathbf{ab}\|^2}, 0, 1\right) d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{ab} - \mathbf{p}\| - r Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def vec3sub(v1, v2): return (v1[0]-v2[0], v1[1]-v2[1], v1[2]-v2[2]) def vec3add(v1, v2): return (v1[0]+v2[0], v1[1]+v2[1], v1[2]+v2[2]) def vec3scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def vec3abs(v): return (abs(v[0]), abs(v[1]), abs(v[2])) def vec3max(v, s): return (max(v[0], s), max(v[1], s), max(v[2], s)) def vec3min(v, s): return (min(v[0], s), min(v[1], s), min(v[2], s)) def vec3maxcomponent(v): return max(v[0], v[1], v[2]) def vec3mincomponent(v): return min(v[0], v[1], v[2]) def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def sdfsphere(p, center, radius): return length(vec3sub(p, center)) - radius def sdfbox(p, center, halfextents): plocal = vec3sub(p, center) d = vec3abs(plocal) - halfextents distoutside = length(vec3max(d, 0)) distinside = vec3mincomponent(vec3min(d, 0)) return distoutside + distinside def sdftorus(p, majorradius, tuberadius): q = (length((p[0], p[2])) - majorradius, p[1]) return length(q) - tuberadius def sdfcylindercapped(p, radius, halfheight): dx = length((p[0], p[2])) - radius dy = abs(p[1]) - halfheight distoutside = length(vec3max((dx, dy, 0), 0)) distinside = vec3mincomponent(vec3min((dx, dy, 0), 0)) return distoutside + distinside def sdfunion(d1, d2): return min(d1, d2) def sdfintersection(d1, d2): return max(d1, d2) def sdfsubtraction(d1, d2): return max(d1, -d2) def sdfsmoothunion(d1, d2, k): h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 (d2 - d1) / k, 0.0, 1.0) return mix(d2, d1, h) - k h (1.0 - h) def spheretrace(origin, direction, scenefunc, maxsteps=64, maxdist=100.0, epsilon=0.001): t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): p = (origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], origin[2] + t direction[2]) d = scenefunc(p) if d < epsilon: return t, p if t > maxdist: return -1.0, None t += d return -1.0, None A method for representing 3D geometry using analytical scalar functions that return the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point \mathbf{p} to the surface of a canonical shape, with a sign indicating whether the point is inside (negative) or outside (positive) the shape. It solves the problem of defining complex scene geometry without explicit mesh tessellation, replacing discrete triangle lists with continuous, closed-form algebraic solutions for primitives like spheres, boxes, and tori. Unlike Distance to Natural Quadrics, which focuses on the geometric properties of conic sections, SDF primitives provide exact distance bounds required for safe sphere tracing in ray marching. Provides closed-form Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for standard solid modeling primitives, including the plane, sphere, cylinder, cone, and torus. These functions compute the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of the primitive, enabling valid sphere tracing in volume rendering and constructive solid geometry (CSG). Unlike general implicit surface solvers, these methods offer high efficiency and analytical precision, serving as the foundational building blocks for complex scene composition. A technique for rendering implicit geometry defined by SDFs using ray marching, specifically for cap cylinder shapes. The capCylinder function computes the distance as d = \text{abs}(\text{vec2f}(\text{length}(p.yz), p.x)) - \text{vec2}(r, h), returning \min(\max(d.x, d.y), 0.) + \text{length}(\max(d, \text{vec2f}(0.))). Nested cylinder calculations are used for complex lighting or structural details, such as calculating outer and inner cylinder distances and returning a boolean-like SDF via \max(-d1, d2). Normals are calculated using finite differences with h=0.001 and kernel k=\text{vec2f}(1, -1). Ray marching initializes d = \text{map}(pp), t = \text{abs}(d), and loops while counter < 30 and d > 0.001, updating d = \text{map}(pp + t \times \text{rayReflect}) and t += \text{abs}(d), stepping pp if d \le 0.01. Parameters include OUTERRADIUS (0.4255), INNERRADIUS (0.385), and LIGHTPOS (0.035). Not given in the sources. name: Signed Distance Field (SDF) Primitive Definition
head: SDF Function, SDF Shapes, Signed Distance Field (SDF), Signed Distance Function (SDF), Signed Distance Function Primitives
body: A Signed Distance Field (SDF) Primitive Definition is a method for representing 3D geometry using analytical scalar functions that return the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point \mathbf{p} to the surface of a canonical shape, with a sign indicating whether the point is inside (negative) or outside (positive) the shape. It solves the problem of defining complex scene geometry without explicit mesh tessellation, replacing discrete triangle lists with continuous, closed-form algebraic solutions for primitives like spheres, boxes, and tori. Unlike Distance to Natural Quadrics, which focuses on the geometric properties of conic sections, SDF primitives provide exact distance bounds required for safe sphere tracing in ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D query point \mathbf{p} = (px, py, pz) in world or local space, and primitive-specific parameters (e.g., radius, center, half-extents). Output: A scalar float d = \text{SDF}(\mathbf{p}) representing the signed distance. Data Structures: Primitives are typically defined by simple structs or parameter sets: Sphere: struct sph { float r; vec3 c; } where r is radius and c is center. Box: struct box { vec3 p; vec3 size; } where p is position and size is full extent (halved in calculation). Cylinder: struct cylinder { vec2 p; float r; } (infinite) or struct cylinderCapped { float r; float h; } (capped, h is half-height). Cone: struct cone { float r; float h; vec3 c; } where c is center/offset. Plane: struct plane { vec4 k; } where k.xyz is the normal vector \mathbf{n} and k.w is the offset d{offset}. Torus: struct tor { float inR; float outR; } where inR is tube radius and outR is major radius. Numbered Steps: 1. Transform Point: If the primitive is transformed (rotated, translated, scaled), map the query point \mathbf{p} into the primitive's local coordinate space using the inverse transformation matrix M^{-1}. 2. Evaluate Local Distance: Compute the distance to the nearest point on the untransformed primitive surface using the specific analytical formula for the shape. 3. Apply Sign: The result is positive if \mathbf{p} is outside the surface, negative if inside, and zero if on the surface. 4. Return Value: Return the signed distance d. Formulas: The general definition for a shape centered at the origin with radius r is d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - r. Specific primitives are defined as follows: Sphere: Center \mathbf{c}, radius r. d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\| - r Box (AABB): Half-extents \mathbf{b} = (bx, by, bz), centered at origin. \mathbf{d} = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b} d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\max(\mathbf{d}, 0)\| + \min(\max(\mathbf{d}x, \max(\mathbf{d}y, \mathbf{d}z)), 0) Note: A cheaper, non-exact approximation is \max(|\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{b}). Cylinder (Infinite): Axis-aligned with Y, radius r. d(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r Cylinder (Capped): Radius r, half-height h. dx = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r, \quad dy = |py| - h d(\mathbf{p}) = \min(\max(dx, dy), 0) + \|\max(dx, dy, 0)\| Cone: Radius r, height h, axis-aligned with Y. Let \phi = \arctan(r/h). d(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}\cos(\phi) - |py|\sin(\phi), \max(py - h, -py)) Implementation detail: Requires checking distance to tip and base ring if the projection falls outside the mantle. Plane: Normal \mathbf{n} (unit length), offset d{offset}. d(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + d{offset} Torus: Major radius R{out}, tube radius R{in}. d(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R{out})^2 + py^2} - R{in} Capsule: Endpoints \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, radius r. \mathbf{ab} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} t = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{ab}}{\|\mathbf{ab}\|^2}, 0, 1\right) d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{ab} - \mathbf{p}\| - r Parameters: Smoothing Constant (k): Used in smooth minimum blending (e.g., k=0.2). Gradient Step (\epsilon): Used for normal approximation, typically 0.0001. Lipschitz Bound: The SDF guarantees that |f(\mathbf{p}1) - f(\mathbf{p}2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2\|, ensuring d(\mathbf{p}) is a safe lower bound for ray marching. Arbitrary meshes require approximate SDFs (e.g., baked into 3D textures or BVH traversal). Gradient Noise: The GDF (Generalized Distance Function) implementation with variable exponent e is slow and may not produce correct distances, though it allows for bulging. Driver Issues: Loop unrolling issues on some hardware (e.g., Nvidia 350.12) can cause slowdowns for complex GDF primitives like fIcosahedron. Sharp Discontinuities: Taking the min() or max() of two SDFs yields sharp corners; smooth blending requires specific approximation functions like smin. SDF Primitives & Operations provide the foundational analytical functions and geometric operators used to define scene geometry implicitly for distance-field ray marching, replacing explicit mesh tessellation with continuous scalar fields. They solve the problem of representing complex 3D shapes and their compositions using closed-form algebraic solutions for canonical shapes (spheres, boxes, tori) and boolean/domain operators. Unlike SDF Transformation which modifies coordinates, or CSG Operations on Implicit Functions which combines distinct shapes, this method focuses on the definition of base primitives and the immediate application of min/max operators for union/intersection. SDF Transformation is a technique for applying geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling, and deformation) to Signed Distance Field primitives by manipulating the query point coordinates before evaluating the base distance function. It solves the problem of positioning and animating implicit surfaces in world space without modifying the underlying primitive definition, preserving the mathematical integrity of the distance field for ray marching. Unlike Uniform Scaling of SDFs, which handles exact distance compensation for uniform factors, or Lipschitz Transformation Bounds, which derives safety bounds for non-linear deformations, standard SDF Transformation relies on the inverse mapping of isometries (which preserve distance) or explicit scaling factors. k-SDF is a representation for real-time view synthesis of fuzzy geometries using k lightweight, semi-transparent mesh shells rendered via rasterization in a fixed order, bounding the number of sampling locations per ray to a small range (3 \le k \le 9). It models implicit geometry as k distinct signed distance fields combined with a view-dependent transparency field and a color field. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting or SMERF, it is sorting-free and bounds samples per ray, enabling real-time rendering on low-cost smartphones. Unlike AdaptiveShells, it learns multiple SDFs and finds sampling locations via rasterization using 2D textures rather than volume rendering. The SDF Representation DOP creates a volumetric signed distance field (SDF) from geometry to enable fast inside/outside testing for collision detection. It differs from general volume rendering methods by focusing on the topological correctness of the distance field for rigid body dynamics rather than visual appearance, utilizing specific modes like Laser Scanning to handle non-watertight geometry. A float grid where the active values describe the distance to a surface. Negative values are on the inside and positive on the outside, and the surface is where the values are zero. Boolean operations on SDF grids allow for efficient boolean operations with smooth transitions, which are hard to perform on meshes. Smoothing is often applied using an SDF Grid Mean node. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. The cost scales linearly with the number of primitives in the scene if evaluated naively, or logarithmically if accelerated with a BVH or grid structure. Memory Complexity: O(1) for analytical primitives (only parameters stored). O(N) for grid-based SDFs where N is the number of voxels. Strengths: Exact representation of smooth surfaces; easy composition via CSG; efficient rendering of complex procedural geometry; robust inside/outside testing. Limitations: Limited to shapes with known analytical SDFs; sharp corners from boolean operations can cause aliasing or require smoothing; non-uniform scaling breaks the Lipschitz condition unless compensated. When to Use: Real-time rendering of procedural scenes, ray marching, collision detection, and implicit modeling. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring exact triangle-level detail (e.g., texturing with high-frequency UV maps), or when the geometry cannot be approximated by analytical functions. The concept of Signed Distance Fields originates from computational geometry and level set methods, where they are used to track interfaces and represent orientable manifolds. In computer graphics, SDFs were popularized for real-time rendering by Inigo Quilez's work on "Modeling with Distance Functions" and the subsequent adoption of sphere tracing (ray marching) techniques.
