name: CSG Distance Field Evaluation (Batched)
head: Scalar CSG Evaluation
body: This method computes the signed distance and material indices for a batch of points against a Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) tree. It serves as the core evaluation kernel for ray marching or point-in-solid tests by processing multiple coordinates simultaneously. Unlike the single-point variant, this batched approach maintains arrays of distances and material indices, allowing for efficient traversal of the CSG tree structure across a set of samples. Inputs and Outputs: Input: pos: Array of N 3D points (vectors). normaldist: Optional array of N floats used for normal approximation logic. d: Pointer to the root of the CSG tree. box: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defining the region of interest for the current evaluation batch. num: Integer N, the number of points in the batch. Outputs: dist: Array of N floats, storing the signed distance from each point to the CSG surface. matindex: Array of N integers, storing the material index for each point. Data Structures: CSG Node (d): Contains a type (CUNION, CINTERSECTION, CDIFFERENCE, CREPLACE, CTRANSLATION, CROTATION, CPLANE, CCYLINDERXY, CCYLINDERXZ, CCYLINDERYZ, CSPHERE, CBOX), pointers to children (left, right, n), and primitive-specific data (e.g., p for plane, c for cylinder, s for sphere, b for box, t for translation, r for rotation). AABB (box): Defined by pmin and pmax vectors. Constants: MATAIRINDEX represents empty space. FLTMAX represents infinity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize dist[i] = FLTMAX and matindex[i] = MATAIRINDEX for all i \in [0, N-1]. 2. Recursive Evaluation (distr): The function distr is called recursively on the CSG tree nodes. For each node type, the algorithm checks if the node's bounding box intersects the query box. If not, the branch is skipped. Union (CUNION): 1. Check if box intersects d->left->box. If yes, recursively call distr on d->left. 2. Initialize temporary arrays tempdist to FLTMAX and tempmatindex to MATAIRINDEX. 3. Check if box intersects d->right->box. If yes, recursively call distr on d->right, writing results to tempdist and tempmatindex. 4. Update main arrays: matindex[i] = max(matindex[i], tempmatindex[i]). If normaldist is provided: If abs(tempdist[i]) < normaldist[i], set dist[i] = tempdist[i]. Otherwise, keep dist[i]. If normaldist is not provided: dist[i] = min(dist[i], tempdist[i]). Intersection (CINTERSECTION): 1. Check if box intersects d->left->box. If not, return. 2. Recursively call distr on d->left. 3. Initialize tempdist to FLTMAX. 4. Check if box intersects d->right->box. If not, return. 5. Recursively call distr on d->right, writing to tempdist. 6. Update main arrays: dist[i] = max(dist[i], tempdist[i]). If dist[i] >= 0, set matindex[i] = MATAIRINDEX. Difference (CDIFFERENCE): 1. Check if box intersects d->left->box. If not, return. 2. Recursively call distr on d->left. 3. Check if box intersects d->right->box. If not, return. 4. Initialize tempdist to FLTMAX and tempmatindex to default. 5. Recursively call distr on d->right, writing to tempdist and tempmatindex. 6. Update main arrays: dist[i] = max(dist[i], -tempdist[i]). If dist[i] >= 0, set matindex[i] = MATAIRINDEX. Replace (CREPLACE): 1. Check if box intersects d->left->box. If not, return. 2. Recursively call distr on d->left. 3. Check if box intersects d->right->box. If not, return. 4. Initialize tempdist and tempmatindex. 5. Recursively call distr on d->right, writing to tempdist and tempmatindex. 6. Update main arrays: If tempdist[i] < 0 and dist[i] < 0 (both inside), set matindex[i] = tempmatindex[i]. If normaldist is provided: If dist[i] < 0 and abs(tempdist[i]) < normaldist[i], set dist[i] = tempdist[i]. Otherwise, keep dist[i]. Translation (CTRANSLATION): 1. Check if box intersects n->box (where n is the child node). If not, return. 2. Get translation vector t->p. 3. For each point i: tpos[i] = pos[i] - t->p. tbox.pmin = box.pmin - t->p tbox.pmax = box.pmax - t->p. 4. Recursively call distr on t->n with tpos, normaldist, dist, matindex, num, and tbox. Rotation (CROTATION): 1. Check if box intersects n->box. If not, return. 2. Get rotation quaternion r->q. 3. For each point i: tpos[i] = xfmpoint(conj(r->q), pos[i]). 4. Recursively call distr on r->n with tpos, normaldist, dist, matindex, num, and aabb::all() (unbounded box). Plane (CPLANE): 1. Check if box intersects n->box. If not, return. 2. For each point i: dist[i] = dot(pos[i], p->p.xyz()) + p->p.w. If dist[i] < 0, matindex[i] = p->matindex. Cylinder (CCYLINDERXY, CCYLINDERXZ, CCYLINDERYZ): 1. Check if box intersects n->box. If not, return. 2. For each point i: Let COORD be the relevant 2D coordinates (xy, xz, or yz). dist[i] = length(pos[i].COORD() - c->cCOORD) - c->r. If dist[i] < 0, matindex[i] = c->matindex. Sphere (CSPHERE): 1. Check if box intersects n->box. If not, return. 2. For each point i: dist[i] = length(pos[i]) - s->r. If dist[i] < 0, matindex[i] = s->matindex. Box (CBOX): 1. Check if box intersects n->box. If not, return. 2. Get box extent b->extent. 3. For each point i: pd = abs(pos[i]) - extent. dist[i] = min(max(pd.x, max(pd.y, pd.z)), 0.0f) + length(max(pd, vec3f(0))). If dist[i] < 0, matindex[i] = b->matindex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. else keep dist[i] else: dist[i] = min(dist[i], tempdist[i]) elif nodetype == CINTERSECTION: if not aabbintersects(d.left.box, box): return distr(pos, normaldist, d.left, box, num, dist, matindex) tempdist = [FLTMAX] num if not aabbintersects(d.right.box, box): return distr(pos, normaldist, d.right, box, num, tempdist, [MATAIRINDEX] num) for i in range(num): dist[i] = max(dist[i], tempdist[i]) if dist[i] >= 0.0: matindex[i] = MATAIRINDEX elif nodetype == CDIFFERENCE: if not aabbintersects(d.left.box, box): return distr(pos, normaldist, d.left, box, num, dist, matindex) if not aabbintersects(d.right.box, box): return tempdist = [FLTMAX] num tempmatindex = [MATAIRINDEX] num distr(pos, normaldist, d.right, box, num, tempdist, tempmatindex) for i in range(num): dist[i] = max(dist[i], -tempdist[i]) if dist[i] >= 0.0: matindex[i] = MATAIRINDEX elif nodetype == CREPLACE: if not aabbintersects(d.left.box, box): return distr(pos, normaldist, d.left, box, num, dist, matindex) if not aabbintersects(d.right.box, box): return tempdist = [FLTMAX] num tempmatindex = [MATAIRINDEX] num distr(pos, normaldist, d.right, box, num, tempdist, tempmatindex) for i in range(num): if tempdist[i] < 0 and dist[i] < 0: matindex[i] = tempmatindex[i] if normaldist is not None: if dist[i] < 0 and abs(tempdist[i]) < normaldist[i]: dist[i] = tempdist[i] # Boundaries: Bounding box intersection checks are critical for pruning. Incorrect intersection logic can lead to incorrect distance values or infinite recursion if not handled properly. Degenerate Input: Empty batches or invalid CSG trees (e.g., null pointers) are not explicitly handled in the provided snippets, but standard guards should be applied. Strengths: Efficient for evaluating many points against complex CSG structures. Supports various primitive types and transformations. Limitations: The non-SIMD nature may limit performance on modern hardware compared to vectorized implementations. The batched approach requires more memory than the single-point variant. When to use: When evaluating a large number of points (e.g., for ray marching steps or voxelization). When not to use: When memory is constrained or when evaluating a single point is sufficient. name: CSG Distance Field Evaluation (Single Point)
body: A recursive algorithm to compute the signed distance from a single point to a Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) tree, supporting Union, Intersection, Difference, Replace, Translation, Rotation, Plane, Cylinder, Sphere, and Box primitives. It differs from the batched variant by operating on a single coordinate vector and returning a scalar distance, serving as the fundamental evaluation kernel for ray marching or point-in-solid tests. Input: pos (3D point, vec3f), node (pointer to CSG node structure), box (axis-aligned bounding box, aabb, used for culling). Output: float signed distance. Returns FLTMAX if the point is outside the node's bounding box or if the node is empty. The algorithm assumes a node structure n with a type field n->type and child pointers or primitive data: n->type: Enum indicating the operation (CUNION, CINTERSECTION, CDIFFERENCE, CREPLACE, CTRANSLATION, CROTATION, CPLANE, CCYLINDERXZ, CCYLINDERXY, CCYLINDERYZ, CSPHERE, CBOX, CEMPTY). n->left, n->right: Pointers to child nodes for binary operations. n->n: Pointer to child node for unary operations (Translation, Rotation, Replace). Primitive data fields (e.g., p->p for plane normal/w, c->cCOORD for cylinder axis/center, s->r for sphere radius, box.extent for box half-extents). 1. Culling: Compute the intersection of the query box with the node's bounding box n->box. Let isec be the intersection box. If any(gt(isec.pmin, isec.pmax)), return FLTMAX. 2. Dispatch: Based on n->type, perform the following: Union (CUNION): Return min(dist(u->left, pos, box), dist(u->right, pos, box)). Intersection (CINTERSECTION): Return max(dist(i->left, pos, box), dist(i->right, pos, box)). Difference (CDIFFERENCE): Return max(dist(d->left, pos, box), -dist(d->right, pos, box)). Replace (CREPLACE): Return dist(r->left, pos, box). Translation (CTRANSLATION): Let t be the translation vector t->p. Return dist(t->n, pos - t->p, aabb(box.pmin - t->p, box.pmax - t->p)). Rotation (CROTATION): Let r->q be the rotation quaternion. Compute posrot = xfmpoint(conj(r->q), pos). Return dist(r->n, posrot, aabb::all()). Plane (CPLANE): Let p->p be the plane equation ax + by + cz + w = 0. Return dot(pos, p->p.xyz()) + p->p.w. Cylinder (CCYLINDERXZ, CCYLINDERXY, CCYLINDERYZ): Let c->cCOORD be the axis-aligned center point and c->r be the radius. The function pos.COORD() selects the two coordinates perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Return length(pos.COORD() - c->cCOORD) - c->r. Sphere (CSPHERE): Let s->r be the radius. Return length(pos) - s->r. Box (CBOX): Let box.extent be the half-extents. Compute d = abs(pos) - box.extent. Return min(max(d.x, max(d.y, d.z)), 0.0f) + length(max(d, vec3f(0.0f))). Empty (CEMPTY): Return FLTMAX. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dist(pos, node, box): """ Compute signed distance from pos to the CSG tree rooted at node. box: AABB used for culling. """ # Step 1: Culling # Compute intersection of box and node's bounding box n->box # isec.pmin = max(box.pmin, node.box.pmin) # isec.pmax = min(box.pmax, node.box.pmax) # If any component of isec.pmin > isec.pmax, return FLTMAX if any(isec.pmin > isec.pmax): return float('inf') n = node t = n.type if t == CUNION: return min(dist(pos, n.left, box), dist(pos, n.right, box)) elif t == CINTERSECTION: return max(dist(pos, n.left, box), dist(pos, n.right, box)) elif t == CDIFFERENCE: return max(dist(pos, n.left, box), -dist(pos, n.right, box)) elif t == CREPLACE: return dist(pos, n.left, box) elif t == CTRANSLATION: # t->p is the translation vector newpos = pos - n.p newboxmin = box.pmin - n.p newboxmax = box.pmax - n.p newbox = AABB(newboxmin, newboxmax) return dist(newpos, n.n, newbox) elif t == CROTATION: # r->q is the rotation quaternion # xfmpoint applies quaternion conjugate rotation to point posrot = xfmpoint(conj(n.q), pos) # aabb::all() implies an infinite or sufficiently large box return dist(posrot, n.n, AABB.infinite()) elif t == CPLANE: # p->p is a vec4f representing ax+by+cz+w return dot(pos, n.p.xyz()) + n.p.w elif t in (CCYLINDERXZ, CCYLINDERXY, CCYLINDERYZ): # c->cCOORD is the center point on the axis # c->r is the radius # pos.COORD() selects the 2D coordinates perpendicular to the axis center2d = pos.COORD() - n.cCOORD.COORD() return length(center2d) - n.r elif t == CSPHERE: return length(pos) - n.r elif t == CBOX: # box.extent is vec3f of half-extents d = abs(pos) - n.extent return min(max(d.x, max(d.y, d.z)), 0.0f) + length(max(d, vec3f(0.0f))) elif t == CEMPTY: return float('inf') else: # Unknown type return float('inf') def xfmpoint(q, p): """Apply quaternion rotation q to point p. q is assumed normalized.""" # Standard quaternion rotation: p' = q p q^-1 # For unit quaternion, q^-1 = conj(q) # Implementation depends on vector/quaternion library conventions. # Here we assume a standard implementation. t = 2.0 cross(q.xyz(), p) return p + q.w t + cross(t, q.xyz()) def conj(q): return vec4f(q.x, -q.y, -q.z, q.w) Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise near the surface of primitives. The box SDF formula is robust but relies on correct extent values. Boundaries: The culling step is critical for performance. If the bounding box intersection is invalid (empty), the recursion stops immediately. Degenerate Input: Empty nodes return FLTMAX. Primitives with zero radius or extent may produce incorrect distances if not handled, though standard SDF formulas generally handle zero-size primitives gracefully (e.g., sphere radius 0 returns distance to origin). Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case, where N is the number of nodes in the CSG tree, as it may traverse the entire tree. Pruning via bounding box culling reduces average case complexity. Memory Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the CSG tree, due to recursion stack. Strengths: Simple, recursive structure; supports complex CSG operations; efficient culling. Limitations: Single-point evaluation; no batch optimization; recursion depth limits for very deep trees. When to use: When evaluating distance for a single point is sufficient, or as a kernel for batched evaluation. The algorithm is described in the mini.q repository by bsegovia. It is a standard implementation of CSG operations on Signed Distance Fields, commonly used in ray marching and implicit surface rendering. bsegovia/mini.q, https://github.com/bsegovia/mini.q, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stack-Based SDF Editor
head: Post-order SDF construction, RPN-style SDF editor [S1, unofficial]
body: An interactive editor that constructs Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), implicitly representing a tree with postorder traversal. It differs from explicit tree editors by deferring structure resolution until compilation, allowing users to build complex scenes by pushing operations onto a linear stack where only the top item is visible until combined. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of operations pushed onto a stack, categorized as Shapes, Transformations, or CSG Operations. Output: A compiled GLSL shader string containing the SDF evaluation function. Data Structures: Operation Stack: A list of operation objects representing the postorder traversal of the scene graph. AST Tree: A recursive structure built from the stack where nodes are either leaves (primitive shapes annotated with domain-modifying transformations) or internal nodes (CSG operations acting on range values). Numbered Steps: 1. Push Operation: Operations are pushed onto the stack. The editor only considers the first item by default; subsequent items are not visible until joined via union or other operations. 2. Invalidate Cache: Modifying any parameter calls #invalidate, which clears the cached shader program to trigger recompilation on the next access. 3. Build SDF (Tree Reconstruction): The buildSDF function iterates over the stack, popping off previous operations according to the arity of the current operation to reconstruct the tree structure. 4. Generate GLSL: The system recursively traverses the AST, transforming nodes to appropriate calls. At leaves, it composes domain-modifying functions in the opposite order of application. Internal nodes generate range operations (e.g., min for union). 5. Compile: The generated GLSL string is spliced into a template and compiled. Formulas: Union: S{union}(p) = \min(SA(p), SB(p)). Domain Transformation Composition: If transformations T1, T2, \dots are applied to a shape, the input position p is transformed by composing them in the opposite order: Tn(\dots T2(T1(p)) \dots). Parameters: Primitive Types: Box and Sphere (e.g., radius 1.0). Transformations: Translate (vec3 offset) and Rotate (float angle). CSG Operations: Union and Intersection. Configuration: Uses lazy evaluation and caching via getter/setter methods that call #invalidate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility: Subsequent stack items remain invisible until a union or similar operation combines them with the top item. AST vs Conceptual Tree: The generated AST differs from the conceptual operation tree because domain modifications (transformations) are attached to leaves, while range modifications (CSG operations) form internal nodes. Performance: Without #invalidate caching, the shader would be reassembled and compiled on every frame, causing severe inefficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsdf(stack): aststack = [] for op in stack: if op['type'] == 'Shape': aststack.append({ 'type': 'Leaf', 'shape': op['shape'], 'params': op.get('params', {}), 'transforms': [] }) elif op['type'] == 'Transform': if aststack: aststack[-1]['transforms'].append(op['transform']) elif op['type'] == 'CSG': if len(aststack) >= 2: right = aststack.pop() left = aststack.pop() aststack.append({ 'type': 'CSG', 'op': op['op'], 'left': left, 'right': right }) return aststack[0] if aststack else None def generateglsl(node): if node['type'] == 'Leaf': p = "p" for t in reversed(node['transforms']): if t['type'] == 'Translate': p = f"opTx({p}, vec3({t['x']}, {t['y']}, {t['z']}))" elif t['type'] == 'Rotate': p = f"opRotX({p}, {t['angle']})" size = node['params'].get('size', 'vec3(1, 1, 1)') return f"sd{node['shape'].upper()}({p}, {size})" elif node['type'] == 'CSG': leftcode = generateglsl(node['left']) rightcode = generateglsl(node['right']) if node['op'] == 'Union': return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" elif node['op'] == 'Intersection': return f"max({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return "" Caching via #invalidate prevents recompilation on every frame, making runtime evaluation efficient. The Config class uses lazy evaluation and caching to avoid unnecessary shader recompilation. The interface is described as intuitive once the input model is understood. The Stack-Based SDF Editor was developed as a final project for COS 426. It demonstrates building SDFs from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to RPN notation. PDF COS 426 Final Project Writeup Raymarching with Signed Distance Fields, https://jbaum98.github.io/cos426finalproject/writeup.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Rounding
head: Distance Offset, Rounded, Rounded Corners in SDFs, Rounding Transformation, SDF Domain Manipulation, SDF Offset, SDF Rounding/Offset
body: SDF Rounding is a geometric transformation that modifies a Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitive by subtracting a constant scalar value from its distance result, effectively rounding off hard edges and corners with a specified radius. It solves the problem of creating smooth, organic, or chamfered geometry from sharp primitives without altering the underlying mesh or topology. Unlike CSG operations which combine shapes, or Elongation which stretches them, Rounding uniformly expands or contracts the implicit surface by a fixed distance. It is a specific instance of domain manipulation where the distance value itself is offset rather than the query position. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a base SDF function d{base}(\mathbf{p}). Parameter: A scalar radius r (or offset value) representing the rounding amount. If r > 0, the shape shrinks (or edges round inward); if r < 0, the shape expands (or edges round outward). Output: The rounded signed distance d{rounded}. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The operation is a pure function evaluation. In object-oriented implementations, the radius is often stored as a field within the rounding operator struct. Steps: 1. Evaluate the base SDF at the query point \mathbf{p} to obtain the raw distance d = d{base}(\mathbf{p}). 2. Subtract the rounding radius r from d. 3. Return the result. Formula: d{rounded}(\mathbf{p}) = d{base}(\mathbf{p}) - r Where: d{base}(\mathbf{p}) is the signed distance from \mathbf{p} to the unrounded primitive. r is the rounding radius (scalar). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfrounding(p: Vec3, basesdf: Callable[[Vec3], float], radius: float) -> float: """ Rounds the edges of a shape defined by basesdf by a specified radius. Args: p: The query point in 3D space. basesdf: A function that returns the signed distance of the base primitive at p. radius: The radius of rounding. Positive values round inward (shrink), negative values round outward (expand). Returns: The rounded signed distance. """ # Step 1: Query the base SDF at the original point d = basesdf(p) # Step 2: Subtract the radius from the SDF value # Note: Subtracting a positive radius reduces the distance, # effectively moving the isosurface (d=0) inward. drounded = d - radius # Step 3: Return the result return drounded Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When r is large relative to the primitive size, the shape may disappear entirely if the entire volume is rounded away. The SDF becomes positive everywhere inside the original volume and negative outside, but the "surface" may vanish if r exceeds the minimum feature size. Sign Convention: Ensure consistency with the base SDF's sign convention. If d{base} is positive outside and negative inside, subtracting r moves the zero-crossing inward. If the base SDF is inverted, the effect is reversed. Degenerate Input: If the base SDF is not a valid distance field (e.g., discontinuous), the rounded result will also be invalid. The SDF Onion operation creates a hollow shell or layered structure from a solid SDF primitive by taking the absolute value of the distance and subtracting a specified radius. It is a specific application of SDF Rounding that inverts the interior of the shape to create a void. It is chosen when a hollow object or a series of concentric shells is required. Link: SDF Onion. This variant applies a spatially varying offset to the SDF, effectively creating a displacement map on the implicit surface. The offset is calculated as a function of position and time, allowing for dynamic, organic deformation. It is chosen when procedural noise or wave-like distortions are needed on a surface. The formula adds a variable offset to the base SDF: d{result} = d{base}(\mathbf{p}) + \text{offset}(\mathbf{p}, t). Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per query point. The operation involves one function call to the base SDF and one subtraction. It does not increase the computational cost of ray marching, only the cost of each step. Memory: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond storing the radius parameter. Measured Performance: Performance is identical to the base SDF evaluation. On modern GPUs, the subtraction is negligible compared to the cost of evaluating complex primitives (e.g., torus, box with rounding). Scaling: Scales linearly with the complexity of the base SDF. Rounding a simple sphere is faster than rounding a complex CSG combination, but the rounding operation itself adds no overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Extremely fast; creates perfectly smooth, mathematically accurate rounded edges; no tessellation artifacts; works with any base SDF. Limitations: Cannot create sharp features; large rounding radii can distort the shape significantly or cause it to vanish; does not support varying radius across the surface (unless combined with displacement maps). When to Use: Use when you need smooth, organic, or chamfered geometry from sharp primitives. Ideal for UI elements, soft-body physics approximations, or stylized graphics. When Not to Use: Do not use when sharp edges are required, or when the rounding radius is too large relative to the object size, causing topological changes or disappearance of the object. SDF Rounding is a fundamental technique in ray marching and implicit surface rendering, popularized by Inigo Quilez in his seminal articles on ray marching and SDFs. It leverages the mathematical property that the signed distance function represents the distance to the surface, so offsetting this distance uniformly shifts the isosurface. name: SDF Onion
head: Onion, Onion SDF, SDF Absolute Value Offset, SDF Shell
body: The SDF Onion operation creates a hollow shell or layered structure from a solid Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitive by taking the absolute value of the distance and subtracting a specified radius. It is a specific application of SDF Rounding that inverts the interior of the shape to create a void. Inputs: 1. sdf: A callable returning the signed distance d for a query point p. 2. radius: A scalar float r \ge 0 defining the shell offset. Outputs: A callable returning the signed distance to the shell surface. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the operation is a point-wise mathematical transformation applied to the output of the parent SDF. Steps: 1. Evaluate the parent SDF at the query coordinates to obtain the signed distance d = \text{sdf}(p). 2. Compute the absolute value of the signed distance: d{abs} = |d|. 3. Subtract the radius r from the absolute distance: d{onion} = d{abs} - r. 4. Return d{onion}. Formula: d{onion}(p) = |\text{sdf}(p)| - r Where: p is the 3D query point. \text{sdf}(p) is the signed distance from p to the original solid shape. r is the shell radius/thickness. Parameters: radius (r): The shell thickness. Typical values depend on the scale of the parent primitive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Thickness: If r=0, the result is |d|, representing the unsigned distance to the surface. Large Radius: If r exceeds the distance from the center to the nearest surface of the parent shape, the resulting SDF may be positive everywhere inside the original volume, creating a large void. Degenerate Shapes: For shapes with zero volume or thin surfaces, the absolute value operation combined with subtraction may produce artifacts if the radius is not carefully chosen relative to the shape's curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfonion(sdffunc, radius): """ Creates an SDF for a hollow shell from a solid SDF. Args: sdffunc: A callable that takes a 3D point p and returns the signed distance. radius: The thickness of the shell (r >= 0). Returns: A callable that returns the signed distance to the shell surface. """ def onionsdf(p): d = sdffunc(p) dabs = abs(d) donion = dabs - radius return donion return onionsdf The operation requires O(1) time per query point, involving only absolute value and subtraction arithmetic on top of the parent SDF evaluation. Memory complexity is O(1) as no additional data structures are stored. It is computationally cheap and effective for creating hollow objects, but produces uniform shell thickness and cannot generate variable thickness without more complex operations. The interior of the shell is empty, which may require additional ray marching logic if the ray must stop at the inner surface. Use this when a hollow version of a solid primitive is required, and avoid it when variable thickness or complex internal structures are needed. The SDF Onion operation is used in ray marching and implicit surface rendering to create hollow objects. The onion function can be applied recursively to a sphere with different radii to create layered structures. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Elongation
head: Elongation operator, elongation transform
body: Elongation is a domain manipulation operator for Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) that stretches a primitive along a specific axis or direction by modifying the query position vector. It solves the problem of creating elongated or tapered geometric shapes from standard primitives without altering the underlying primitive definition. It sets itself apart from siblings like SDF Rounding (which modifies distance values) and Finite Repetition (which tiling) by operating on the spatial coordinates to scale or shear the shape's extent. Inputs: A query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a base SDF function d{base}(\mathbf{p}). An elongation vector \mathbf{s} or scaling factor defines the stretch. Outputs: The signed distance d{result} at the transformed point. Data Structures: \mathbf{p}: Input position vector (px, py, pz). \mathbf{q}: Transformed position vector. \mathbf{s}: Elongation offset vector. Steps: 1. Transform Position: The input position \mathbf{p} is modified to \mathbf{q} using arithmetic operations involving the elongation parameters. In the specific implementation found in, the transformation involves: Computing an intermediate value m = h^2 + 0.25. Separating components: px, pz are processed via absolute values and max/min operations to handle symmetry. Constructing \mathbf{q} from px, py, pz and a height parameter h: qx = pz qy = h \cdot py - 0.5 \cdot px qz = h \cdot px + 0.5 \cdot py Applying the elongation offset \mathbf{s}: \mathbf{s} = \text{relu}(-qx) \mathbf{q}' = \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{s} 2. Evaluate Base SDF: The base SDF is evaluated at the transformed point \mathbf{q}'. The specific primitive in computes a distance d based on quadratic forms a and b: a = m(qx + s)^2 + qy^2 b = m(qx + 0.5t)^2 + (qy - mt)^2 where t = \text{clamp}((qy - 0.5pz) / (m + 0.25), 0.0, 1.0). The distance is selected via: d = \sqrt{\frac{\min(a, b) + qz^2}{m}} \cdot \text{sign}(\max(qz, -py)) 3. Return Result: The computed distance d is returned. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def elongationsdf(p, h): # Unpack input px, py, pz = p.x, p.y, p.z # Symmetry handling for x and z px, pz = abs(px), abs(pz) px, pz = max(px, pz), min(pz, px) # Offset px, pz = px - 0.5, pz - 0.5 # Construct q qz = pz qx = h py - 0.5 px qy = h px + 0.5 py # Elongation offset s s = max(-qx, 0.0) # Intermediate calculations m = h2 + 0.25 t = clamp((qy - 0.5 pz) / (m + 0.25), 0.0, 1.0) a = m (qx + s)2 + qy2 b = m (qx + 0.5 t)2 + (qy - m t)2 # Select distance cond = min(qy, -qx m - qy 0.5) > 0.0 dsq = where(cond, a, min(a, b)) d = sqrt((dsq + qz2) / m) sign(max(qz, -py)) return d Edge Cases: Precision errors near the elongation boundary where qx \approx 0 may cause discontinuities if not clamped properly. Degenerate input where h=0 results in division by zero or undefined behavior in the transformation matrix. The End-point Corrector addresses radius shrinkage and field variation divergence near skeleton end-points in vector field visualization. Time Complexity: O(1) per query, involving basic arithmetic and trigonometric operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only temporary variables for the transformation. Strengths: Efficiently creates complex elongated shapes from simple primitives; differentiable for gradient-based optimization. Limitations: The specific implementation in is tailored to a specific primitive (likely a sphere or capsule variant) and may not generalize to all base SDFs without modification. When to use: When creating tapered or stretched objects in ray marching. When not: When uniform scaling is sufficient (use simple scaling instead). The specific algorithmic implementation of elongation as described in originates from the Torch-Sphere-Tracer repository by skmhrk1209. It is part of a collection of SDF primitives and domain manipulation operators designed for differentiable rendering and neural implicit surfaces. The technique builds on standard SDF domain manipulation principles where position vectors are transformed to create periodic, mirrored, or reflected structures. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: End-point Corrector
head: Line Width Adjustment, Streamline End-point Adjustment
body: The End-point Corrector addresses radius shrinkage and field variation divergence near skeleton end-points in vector field visualization. It forces an additional sampling position near end-points to increase the correlation between the minima of individual primitives and the global field. Alternatively, it adjusts the start and end points of a streamline to account for line width, either by expanding from the midpoint or by setting fixed bounds. The method operates in two contexts: correcting implicit surface radius errors in SCALIS fields and adjusting streamline geometry for line width in CUDA-based visualization. Inputs: Start point (m{startPt}) and end point (m{endPt}) of the primitive or streamline. Prescribed radius (r) or line width (m{lineWidth}). Field volume dimensions (m{vfInfo.realSize}). Boolean flags: mwingLine (wing line mode) and moritentationX (X orientation mode). Outputs: Adjusted start and end points (m'{startPt}, m'{endPt}). Or, an additional sampling position near the end-point. Points are represented as 3D vectors, stored as float3 structures in the CUDA implementation. Field information includes realSize, a vector representing the physical or voxel dimensions of the volume. This method addresses the issue where the prescribed radius is not achieved in the tangential direction near skeleton end-points. 1. Identify skeleton end-points where the field diverges from the expected behavior. 2. Add a segment primitive with a constant radius at these end vertices. 3. Determine the length of this segment, which is proportional to the prescribed radius at the end vertices and a constant depending on the kernel used. 4. Force an additional sampling position near the skeleton end-points. Note: If end-point correctors are absent, a heuristic presented in section 6.2 of the source can compensate for this shortcoming. In structures without end-points (e.g., truss structures), all assumptions related to the presence of end-point correctors can be used. This method adjusts the start and end points of a streamline to account for line width, either by expanding from the midpoint (wing line) or by setting fixed bounds. 1. Retrieve the start point (m{startPt}) and end point (m{endPt}). 2. Retrieve the line width parameter (m{lineWidth}). 3. Check the mwingLine flag: If mwingLine is true: 1. Calculate the midpoint: mid = \frac{m{startPt} + m{endPt}}{2.0}. 2. Calculate the start vector: startVect = m{startPt} - mid. 3. Calculate the end vector: endVect = m{endPt} - mid. 4. Update start point: m{startPt} = mid + startVect \times (m{lineWidth} + 0.5). 5. Update end point: m{endPt} = mid + endVect \times (m{lineWidth} + 0.5). 6. Return. If mwingLine is false: 1. Check the moritentationX flag. 2. If moritentationX is true: 1. Set m{startPt}.y = (1.0 - m{lineWidth}) \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.y}}{2}. 2. Set m{endPt}.y = m{lineWidth} \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.y}}{2} + \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.y}}{2}. 3. Else: 1. Set m{startPt}.z = (1.0 - m{lineWidth}) \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.z}}{2}. 2. Set m{endPt}.z = m{lineWidth} \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.z}}{2} + \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.z}}{2}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adjustendpoints(startpt, endpt, linewidth, fieldsize, wingline, orientationx): """ Adjusts streamline endpoints based on line width and orientation. Args: startpt: Tuple (x, y, z) of start point. endpt: Tuple (x, y, z) of end point. linewidth: Float, width of the streamline. fieldsize: Tuple (ysize, zsize) representing realSize.y and realSize.z. wingline: Boolean, if True uses midpoint expansion. orientationx: Boolean, if True adjusts Y axis, else Z axis. Returns: Tuple (newstartpt, newendpt) """ if wingline: midx = (startpt[0] + endpt[0]) / 2.0 midy = (startpt[1] + endpt[1]) / 2.0 midz = (startpt[2] + endpt[2]) / 2.0 startvectx = startpt[0] - midx startvecty = startpt[1] - midy startvectz = startpt[2] - midz endvectx = endpt[0] - midx endvecty = endpt[1] - midy endvectz = endpt[2] - midz scale = linewidth + 0.5 newstartx = midx + startvectx scale newstarty = midy + startvecty scale newstartz = midz + startvectz scale newendx = midx + endvectx scale newendy = midy + endvecty scale newendz = midz + endvectz scale return (newstartx, newstarty, newstartz), (newendx, newendy, newendz) else: ysize = fieldsize[0] zsize = fieldsize[1] if orientationx: newstarty = (1.0 - linewidth) (ysize / 2.0) newendy = linewidth (ysize / 2.0) + (ysize / 2.0) newstartx = startpt[0] newstartz = startpt[2] newendx = endpt[0] newendz = endpt[2] return (newstartx, newstarty, newstartz), (newendx, newendy, newendz) else: newstartz = (1.0 - linewidth) (zsize / 2.0) newendz = linewidth (zsize / 2.0) + (zsize / 2.0) newstartx = startpt[0] newstarty = startpt[1] newendx = endpt[0] newendy = endpt[1] return (newstartx, newstarty, newstartz), (newendx, newendy, newendz) Line Width (mlineWidth): The width of the streamline. Wing Line (mwingLine): Boolean flag to enable wing line mode. Orientation X (moritentationX): Boolean flag to enable X orientation mode. Kernel Constant: In the SCALIS method, the length of the corrector segment depends on a constant related to the kernel used. Not given in the sources. Absence of Correctors: In structures without end-points (e.g., truss structures), all assumptions related to the presence of end-point correctors can be used. If correctors are absent, a heuristic presented in section 6.2 can compensate for this shortcoming. Precision: The calculation involves floating-point arithmetic for midpoint and scaling, using standard float precision in the CUDA implementation. Boundary Conditions: The fixed bound method assumes the field size is centered or aligned such that the calculated bounds fit within the volume. If linewidth is outside the range [0, 1], the bounds may exceed the field size. Time Complexity: O(1) per streamline or primitive, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively reduces radius shrinkage artifacts at skeleton end-points. Provides flexible adjustment of streamline geometry for visual continuity. Limitations: Requires knowledge of field dimensions or kernel constants. The heuristic alternative for missing correctors may not be as accurate. When to use: When visualizing vector fields with skeleton-based primitives where end-point artifacts are visible, or when rendering streamlines with specific line width requirements. The concept of end-point correction in vector field visualization originated from the need to accurately render implicit surfaces defined by skeleton-based primitives. The SCALIS method, described in, addresses the divergence of field values near skeleton end-points, a problem related to radius shrinkage observed in [ZBQC13]. The CUDA-based implementation adapts similar concepts for streamline visualization, allowing for line width adjustments via wing lines or fixed bounds. name: Finite Repetition
head: Bounded Tiling, Finite Domain Repetition, Limited Repetition
body: Finite Repetition creates a bounded, tiled instance of a base Signed Distance Function (SDF) within a specified limit l along each axis, preventing the infinite periodicity found in standard tiling operators. Unlike Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset or standard infinite tiling, this method clamps the replication count to a finite range, making it suitable for rendering localized clusters of objects without artifacts at infinity. Inputs: Query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Period vector \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, defining the cell dimensions along each axis. Limit vector \mathbf{l} \in \mathbb{R}^3, defining the maximum number of cells to replicate in the positive and negative directions for each axis. Outputs: Transformed position \mathbf{p}' mapped to the nearest valid cell within the bounds [-\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{l}]. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{l} are typically 3-component floating-point vectors (e.g., Vec3). Steps: 1. Normalize the query point by the period: \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{p} / \mathbf{c}. 2. Round \mathbf{u} to the nearest integer to find the cell index: \mathbf{q}{raw} = \text{round}(\mathbf{u}). 3. Clamp the cell index to the finite limits: \mathbf{q} = \text{clamp}(\mathbf{q}{raw}, -\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{l}). 4. Map the point back to the local coordinate system of the clamped cell: \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{q}. 5. Evaluate the base SDF at \mathbf{p}': d = d{base}(\mathbf{p}'). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def repeatfinite(p: Vec3, c: Vec3, l: Vec3) -> Vec3: """ Maps p to the nearest cell within bounds [-l, l] with period c. """ # Step 1 & 2: Divide by period and round to nearest integer qraw = (p / c).round() # Step 3: Clamp to finite limits q = qraw.clamp(-l, l) # Step 4: Transform point to local cell coordinates pprime = p - c q return pprime Parameters: \mathbf{c}: Must be non-zero. If any component is zero, division is undefined. \mathbf{l}: Non-negative integers or floats. If \mathbf{l} = 0, the point is clamped to the origin cell. Edge Cases: Zero Period: Division by zero in \mathbf{p}/\mathbf{c} if any component of \mathbf{c} is 0. Boundary Precision: Rounding errors near half-integer boundaries of cells may cause jitter if \mathbf{p} is extremely close to a cell boundary. Limit Exceedance: Points outside the limit \mathbf{l} are mapped to the boundary cell (index \pm \mathbf{l}), not discarded. Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset creates a perfect, interlocking hexagonal honeycomb pattern by combining two separate rectangular repetition grids that are offset from each other. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Involves basic arithmetic operations (division, rounding, clamping, subtraction). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures required. Strengths: Efficiently renders bounded clusters; avoids infinite recursion or memory issues associated with infinite tiling; simple implementation. Limitations: Creates sharp discontinuities in the derivative of the SDF at the boundaries of the limit \mathbf{l}, which may affect ray marching convergence or shading smoothness at the edges of the tiled region. When to use: When a localized, finite number of repeated objects is needed. When not to use: When infinite periodicity is required (use Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset or standard infinite tiling) or when seamless interlocking patterns are needed without boundary artifacts. Finite Repetition is a domain manipulation operator used in Signed Distance Field rendering to create bounded tiled structures. It is commonly implemented in GLSL and Rust-based SDF libraries for procedural geometry generation. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset
head: Hexagonal Honeycomb Repetition, Hexagonal Honeycomb Repetition via Dual Offset Repetition, OR-Composite Honeycomb, Two-Cell Honeycomb
body: Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset creates a perfect, interlocking hexagonal honeycomb pattern by combining two separate rectangular repetition grids that are offset from each other. Unlike the skew method, which applies a single coordinate transformation, this method uses a boolean OR operation (minimum of distances) on two distinct distance functions to ensure that the "interlocking" parts of adjacent hexagons are correctly rendered without clipping. It is computationally more expensive than skew-based approaches but allows for different shape functions or properties (such as color) per column. Inputs: Point p in 3D space (or 2D for the tiling plane). Side length s of the regular hexagon. Outputs: Signed distance d to the nearest hexagon boundary. Data Structures: No complex structures required. The method relies on standard vector arithmetic and two calls to a rectangular repetition function. Steps: 1. Define the two repetition patterns: The honeycomb is formed by two interleaved rectangular grids. Let the vertical repetition step be hy and the horizontal step be hx. For a regular hexagon with side length s: the horizontal period is hx = 2s. The vertical period is hy = 2\sqrt{3}s. This is derived from the height of an equilateral triangle with side s (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s) multiplied by 4. The two grids are offset. Typically, one grid is aligned with the origin, and the other is shifted to ensure their cells interlock. A common implementation places the centers of the two rectangular cells at Grid 1: (0, 0) and Grid 2: (s, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s) or equivalent offset that ensures the hexagons from Grid 1 and Grid 2 touch at their edges to form the honeycomb. 2. Calculate the distance function for the first pattern (d1): Apply the rectangular repetition operator to point p using periods (hx, hy) centered at the origin. Let p1 be the wrapped point. Calculate the signed distance from p1 to the hexagon shape defined within this cell. Let this be d1. 3. Calculate the distance function for the second pattern (d2): Apply the rectangular repetition operator to point p using the same periods (hx, hy) but with the offset center for the second grid. Let p2 be the wrapped point relative to this second grid's origin. Calculate the signed distance from p2 to the hexagon shape. Let this be d2. 4. Combine using minimum operation: The final distance is the minimum of the two distances: d = \min(d1, d2) This corresponds to the boolean OR operation for signed distance fields, ensuring that if a point is inside or near a hexagon from either grid, the distance reflects the nearest boundary. Parameters: s: Side length of the hexagon. Typical value: 1.0. hx = 2s. hy = 2\sqrt{3}s \approx 3.464s. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clipping in Single-Grid Approaches: If one attempts to create a honeycomb by simply shifting every other row by half the cell width (brick-like layout) using a single distance function per cell, the interlocking parts of tightly packed hexagons will extend outside the defined rectangular repetition cell. Since a single distance function defines the shape within one cell, these protruding parts are clipped/cut off at the cell boundaries. The Dual Offset method avoids this by ensuring the "missing" parts of one cell are covered by the adjacent cell from the other grid. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is sufficient for typical scene scales. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector2: def init(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y def sub(self, other): return Vector2(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y) def repeatrect(p, periodx, periody): """Wraps point p into the fundamental domain of a rectangular grid.""" x = p.x % periodx y = p.y % periody if x > periodx / 2: x -= periodx if y > periody / 2: y -= periody return Vector2(x, y) def hexagonsdf(p, s): """Signed distance to a regular hexagon centered at origin with side length s.""" q = Vector2(abs(p.x), abs(p.y)) if q.x > q.y: d = q.x 0.5 + q.y math.sqrt(3)/2 - s math.sqrt(3)/2 else: d = q.y - s return d def infiniterepetitiondualoffset(p, sidelength): """Computes the distance to an infinite honeycomb pattern using dual offset repetition.""" s = sidelength hx = 2 s hy = 2 math.sqrt(3) s p1 = repeatrect(p, hx, hy) d1 = hexagonsdf(p1, s) offset = Vector2(s, math.sqrt(3)/2 s) p2 = repeatrect(p - offset, hx, hy) d2 = hexagonsdf(p2, s) return min(d1, d2) A variant that creates a honeycomb pattern by shifting every other row of a rectangular grid by half the cell width, creating a brick-like layout. It is simpler to conceptualize but suffers from a critical pitfall: when using convex shapes like hexagons that are tightly packed, the 'interlocking' parts of the shape may extend outside the defined rectangular repetition cell. Since a single distance function defines the shape within one cell, these protruding parts are clipped/cut off at the cell boundaries, resulting in incorrect geometry. A variant that applies a 2D skew transformation matrix that shears the xy-plane by 30 degrees while maintaining unit vector lengths. This transformation is applied to the input coordinates before passing them to the infinite repetition function. A pitfall is that the primitive shape itself must be defined in the skewed coordinate space; for example, a right-angled triangle in the skewed space becomes an equilateral triangle in the final rendered space. It is computationally lighter than the dual offset method because it requires only one transformation and one distance function evaluation, whereas the alternative requires two distance function evaluations and a boolean OR. Time Complexity: Requires calculating two distance functions and combining them with a minimum operation, making it approximately twice the cost of a single repetition pattern. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory; only requires storing the offset parameters. Strengths: Produces a perfect, interlocking honeycomb without clipping artifacts. Allows different shape functions or properties (e.g., color, material) to be applied to each column/grid independently. Limitations: More computationally expensive than the skew method. Requires careful tuning of the offset to ensure proper interlocking. When to use: When perfect interlocking is required and different properties per column are desired. When not to use: When performance is critical and the skew method suffices for the visual requirement. Originated from practical shader art and procedural geometry techniques, specifically discussed in the context of Sphere Tracing and domain operations. The method is highlighted as a solution to the clipping issues inherent in simple row-offsetting methods for hexagonal tiling. It leverages the property that the union of two offset rectangular grids can form a hexagonal lattice. name: Quadric SDF (First-Order Approximation)
body: Computes an approximate signed distance from a query point to a general quadric surface defined by a quadratic implicit equation, using a first-order Taylor approximation. It differs from exact SDF primitives by handling arbitrary second-order surfaces (ellipsoids, hyperboloids, paraboloids) at the cost of geometric accuracy, trading precision for the ability to model complex algebraic shapes without analytical distance formulas. Inputs: Query point v = (x, y, z). Quadric coefficients: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j defining the surface ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + dxy + eyz + fzx + gx + hy + iz + j = 0. Outputs: Approximate signed distance d{approx}. (Optional) Normal vector n at the closest point approximation. Data Structures: Coefficients stored as 10 floating-point values. Point v as a 3D vector. Steps: 1. Evaluate the implicit function value f0 at v: f0 = ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + dxy + eyz + fzx + gx + hy + iz + j. 2. Compute the gradient components (partial derivatives) at v: dx = 2ax + dy + fz + g dy = 2by + ez + dx + h dz = 2cz + fx + ey + i. 3. Compute the gradient magnitude f1: f1 = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}. 4. Return the approximate signed distance: d{approx} = \frac{f0}{f1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quadricsdfapprox(x, y, z, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j): # 1. Evaluate implicit function f0 f0 = (a x x + b y y + c z z + d x y + e y z + f z x + g x + h y + i z + j) # 2. Compute gradient components gradx = 2 a x + d y + f z + g grady = 2 b y + e z + d x + h gradz = 2 c z + f x + e y + i # 3. Compute gradient magnitude gradmag = math.sqrt(gradx gradx + grady grady + gradz gradz) # 4. Return approximate distance # Guard against division by zero when gradient vanishes if gradmag == 0.0: return f0 return f0 / gradmag def quadricnormal(x, y, z, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j): gradx = 2 a x + d y + f z + g grady = 2 b y + e z + d x + h gradz = 2 c z + f x + e y + i gradmag = math.sqrt(gradx gradx + grady grady + gradz gradz) if gradmag == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (gradx / gradmag, grady / gradmag, gradz / gradmag) Parameters: a, b, c: Coefficients of squared terms x^2, y^2, z^2. d, e, f: Coefficients of cross terms xy, yz, zx. g, h, i: Coefficients of linear terms x, y, z. j: Constant term. Typical values depend on the specific quadric shape being modeled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Near Zero: If the gradient magnitude is near zero (e.g., at critical points or far from the surface), the division by f1 becomes unstable, leading to incorrect or infinite distance estimates. Signed Distance Accuracy: This is an approximation. The sign is determined by the sign of f0, but the magnitude is only accurate to first order. It is not a true Euclidean distance, which can lead to inaccuracies in ray marching convergence or normal estimation. Degenerate Quadrics: If the quadratic form is degenerate (e.g., representing parallel planes or a line), the gradient behavior may be singular or non-uniform, requiring specific handling. Diagonalizes the quadratic form matrix of a general quadratic function to identify principal curvatures and axes. This method maps a generic quadratic surface to a standard prototype (paraboloid or hyperbolic paraboloid) to enable optimal, error-bounded triangulation of its zero-level set. It is chosen when exact geometric analysis or mesh generation is required rather than just ray marching distance queries. Represents complex 3D geometry using a continuous real-valued describing function F(X) \ge 0, where X=(x1,x2,x3). The object is the closed subset of Euclidean space where the function is non-negative. It allows visualization of both the surface and internal structure. The base surface is a quadric F(x,y,z) \ge 0, and freeform shapes are created by adding perturbation functions Ri(x,y,z), which are cubes of perturbing quadrics Qi clamped to zero where Qi < 0. This reduces object construction to quadric surface deformation rather than approximation by primitives (polygons or B-spline patches). Estimating the maximum value of the combined function requires calculating the maximum of the perturbation function on the same interval, based on the inequality \max[Q + R] \le \max[Q] + \max[R]. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (10 multiplications, 9 additions, 1 square root for distance; 1 square root for normal). Memory Complexity: O(1) storage for coefficients. Scaling: Performance is independent of resolution or scene complexity, as it is a point-wise evaluation. Strengths: Handles arbitrary quadric surfaces (ellipsoids, hyperboloids, etc.) without needing complex analytical SDF derivations. Simple to implement. Limitations: Approximate distance. Not a true Euclidean distance, which can lead to inaccuracies in ray marching convergence or normal estimation. Unstable near critical points where the gradient vanishes. When to use: When modeling complex algebraic surfaces that are quadrics, and high precision is not critical, or as a fallback when no exact SDF is available. When not to use: When exact Euclidean distance is required for correct ray marching behavior (e.g., in constructive solid geometry with smooth blending), or when the surface has regions with vanishing gradients. The method originates from John C. Hart's 1995 work on analytic distance fields, as referenced in the implementation code. The concept of using implicit functions for geometric modeling, including quadrics, has roots in computer graphics literature. The specific first-order approximation for general quadrics is a practical technique to extend SDF ray marching beyond basic primitives. The related concept of freeform surfaces via quadric perturbation is described in a paper on GPU-based volume-oriented rendering of functionally defined objects. name: Principal Axis Transformation for Quadratic Surfaces
head: Eigenvalue Analysis of Quadratic Forms, Principal Component Analysis of Quadrics
body: The Principal Axis Transformation (PAT) diagonalizes the quadratic form matrix of a general quadratic function to identify principal curvatures and axes. This method maps a generic quadratic surface to a standard prototype (paraboloid or hyperbolic paraboloid) to enable optimal, error-bounded triangulation of its zero-level set. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Quadratic function coefficients c{20}, c{11}, c{02}, c{10}, c{01}, c{00}. Output: Eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, normalized eigenvectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2, and the classification of the surface type (Elliptic, Hyperbolic, or Parabolic). Data Structures: Matrix C: A 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix representing the quadratic form. C = \begin{pmatrix} c{20} & c{11} \\ c{11} & c{02} \end{pmatrix} Eigenvalues: Scalars \lambda1, \lambda2. Eigenvectors: Normalized 2D vectors \mathbf{e}1 = (e{11}, e{12})^T, \mathbf{e}2 = (e{21}, e{22})^T. Steps: 1. Construct Matrix C: Extract the quadratic coefficients from the input function. The linear and constant terms do not affect the principal axes or curvature classification. 2. Compute Eigenvalues: Solve the characteristic equation \det(C - \lambda I) = 0 for \lambda1 and \lambda2. 3. Compute Eigenvectors: For each \lambdai, solve (C - \lambdai I)\mathbf{v} = 0 and normalize the resulting vector \mathbf{v} to obtain \mathbf{e}i. 4. Classify Surface: Determine the surface type based on the product of the eigenvalues: Elliptic if \lambda1 \lambda2 > 0. Hyperbolic if \lambda1 \lambda2 < 0. Parabolic if \lambda1 \lambda2 = 0. Formulas: The quadratic function is represented as: f(x, y) = (x \ y) \begin{pmatrix} c{20} & c{11} \\ c{11} & c{02} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + (c{10} \ c{01}) \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + c{00} The quadratic form is \mathbf{x}^T C \mathbf{x} = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def principalaxistransformation(c20, c11, c02, c10, c01, c00): # Step 1: Construct Matrix C # C is symmetric: [[c20, c11], [c11, c02]] # Linear and constant terms are ignored for axis determination # Step 2: Compute Eigenvalues # Characteristic equation: lambda^2 - trace(C)lambda + det(C) = 0 traceC = c20 + c02 detC = c20 c02 - c11 c11 discriminant = traceC2 - 4 detC sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) lambda1 = (traceC + sqrtdisc) / 2 lambda2 = (traceC - sqrtdisc) / 2 # Step 3: Compute Eigenvectors # For lambda1 if abs(c11) > 1e-9: e1 = (1.0, (lambda1 - c20) / c11) else: e1 = (0.0, 1.0) if abs(lambda1 - c02) < 1e-9 else (1.0, 0.0) norm1 = math.sqrt(e1[0]2 + e1[1]2) e1 = (e1[0] / norm1, e1[1] / norm1) # For lambda2 if abs(c11) > 1e-9: e2 = (1.0, (lambda2 - c20) / c11) else: e2 = (0.0, 1.0) if abs(lambda2 - c02) < 1e-9 else (1.0, 0.0) norm2 = math.sqrt(e2[0]2 + e2[1]2) e2 = (e2[0] / norm2, e2[1] / norm2) # Step 4: Classify Surface product = lambda1 lambda2 if product > 0: surfacetype = "Elliptic" elif product < 0: surfacetype = "Hyperbolic" else: surfacetype = "Parabolic" return { "lambda1": lambda1, "lambda2": lambda2, "e1": e1, "e2": e2, "surfacetype": surfacetype } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If c{11} is near zero, eigenvector calculation may suffer from division by zero; handle via conditional checks. Degenerate Input: If both eigenvalues are zero, the surface is planar and the cluster region can be triangulated by only considering the vertices of its convex boundary polygon. Generates a mesh for elliptic quadrics (\lambda1 \lambda2 > 0) by mapping an optimal equilateral prototype triangle from a canonical paraboloid space (g = \bar{x}^2 + \bar{y}^2) to the target surface. It is distinguished by its use of the paraboloid prototype and reliance on PAT to preserve error bounds analytically. See Elliptic Case Triangulation. Generates a mesh for hyperbolic quadrics (\lambda1 \lambda2 < 0) by placing vertices exactly on the surface to minimize interpolation error. It uses the prototype h(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \bar{x}^2 - \bar{y}^2. The transformation from prototype to original function (for \lambda1 > 0, \lambda2 < 0) is \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = H \begin{pmatrix} \bar{x} \\ \bar{y} \end{pmatrix}, where H = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{11} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{-\lambda2}} e{21} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{12} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{-\lambda2}} e{22} \end{pmatrix}. If \lambda1 < 0 and \lambda2 > 0, the triangulation is obtained by considering the quadratic form of -f. Optimal triangle vertices for h are (\sqrt{\epsilon}, \sqrt{\epsilon})^T, (\sqrt{\epsilon}, -\sqrt{\epsilon})^T, and ((1-\sqrt{5})\sqrt{\epsilon}, 0)^T. The maximal error for any edge ab is \varepsilon{\text{ab}} = \frac{1}{4} |(ax - bx)^2 - (ay - by)^2|. The final triangulation is established by transforming two edges according to H. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of multiresolution modeling for scientific visualization, specifically for the triangulation of quadratic surface graphs. The method leverages classical linear algebra techniques (eigenvalue decomposition) to simplify quadratic forms. name: Elliptic Case Triangulation
body: Elliptic Case Triangulation generates a mesh approximation for the graph surface of a quadratic function f of elliptic type, which is equivalent to the paraboloid g(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \bar{x}^2 + \bar{y}^2. It converts the continuous quadratic surface into a discrete triangular mesh by mapping an optimal equilateral prototype triangle from canonical space to the target surface space via a principal axis transformation. It is distinguished from the Hyperbolic Case Triangulation by its paraboloid prototype and from general meshing methods by its analytical error bound preservation. Inputs: Quadratic function f (or its symmetric matrix C), error tolerance \epsilon > 0, cluster region boundary, and cluster centroid c. Outputs: A set of triangles forming a triangulation of the surface within the cluster region. Data Structures: Prototype Triangle: Defined in canonical coordinates (\bar{x}, \bar{y}). Transformation Matrix G: 2 \times 2 matrix mapping canonical to physical coordinates. Edge Vectors: Two vectors defining the regular triangulation lattice. Steps: 1. Eigen-decomposition: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and normalized eigenvectors e1 = (e{11}, e{12})^T, e2 = (e{21}, e{22})^T of the quadratic matrix C. For the elliptic case, the eigenvalues are positive. 2. Handle Negative Eigenvalues: If eigenvalues are negative, replace f with -f to imply positive eigenvalues. 3. Construct Transformation Matrix G: The transformation maps the canonical paraboloid g(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \bar{x}^2 + \bar{y}^2 to the quadratic form f. The matrix G is constructed from the eigenvectors scaled by the inverse square roots of the eigenvalues: G = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{11} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda2}} e{21} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{12} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda2}} e{22} \end{pmatrix} The source text contains a typo in equation (2.9) writing \frac{1}{\sqrt{1}} and \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} instead of \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} and \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda2}}. 4. Define Prototype Triangle: In the canonical space (\bar{x}, \bar{y}), the optimal triangle is equilateral with a circumscribed circle radius R = \sqrt{2\epsilon}. The vertices are: v1 = \begin{pmatrix} -\sqrt{2\epsilon} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad v2 = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{0.5\epsilon} \\ \sqrt{1.5\epsilon} \end{pmatrix}, \quad v3 = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{0.5\epsilon} \\ -\sqrt{1.5\epsilon} \end{pmatrix} This triangle maximizes area for a given maximal error \epsilon, which occurs at the center and vertices. 5. Transform Edges: Compute edge vectors u = v2 - v1 and v = v3 - v1. Transform only these two edges according to G: U = G u, V = G v. 6. Generate Triangulation: Establish a regular triangulation emanating from the cluster centroid c using U and V. For positive eigenvalues, place vertices below the surface by \epsilon (if f was flipped to -f, place vertices above by \epsilon). Only generate triangles that lie entirely within the cluster region, leaving untriangulated gaps at boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ellipticcasetriangulation(C, centroid, isinside, epsilon): """ Generates triangulation for elliptic quadratic SDF. C: 2x2 symmetric matrix [[c11, c12], [c12, c22]] centroid: (cx, cy) isinside: function(x, y) -> bool epsilon: float, error tolerance """ # 1. Eigen-decomposition c11, c12, c22 = C[0][0], C[0][1], C[1][1] trace = c11 + c22 det = c11 c22 - c122 discriminant = math.sqrt(max(0, trace2 - 4 det)) lambda1 = (trace + discriminant) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - discriminant) / 2 if lambda1 <= 0 or lambda2 <= 0: raise ValueError("Not an elliptic case: eigenvalues must be positive.") # Compute normalized eigenvectors if abs(c12) > 1e-9: e1 = (1.0, -(c11 - lambda1) / c12) else: e1 = (0.0, 1.0) norme1 = math.sqrt(e1[0]2 + e1[1]2) e1 = (e1[0] / norme1, e1[1] / norme1) e2 = (-e1[1], e1[0]) # Orthogonal to e1 # 2. Construct G matrix invsqrtl1 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(lambda1) invsqrtl2 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(lambda2) G = [ [e1[0] invsqrtl1, e2[0] invsqrtl2], [e1[1] invsqrtl1, e2[1] invsqrtl2] ] # 3. Prototype triangle vertices in canonical space sqrteps = math.sqrt(epsilon) v1 = (-math.sqrt(2) sqrteps, 0.0) v2 = (math.sqrt(0.5) sqrteps, math.sqrt(1.5) sqrteps) v3 = (math.sqrt(0.5) sqrteps, -math.sqrt(1.5) sqrteps) # 4. Transform edge vectors def matvecmul(M, v): return (M[0][0]v[0] + M[0][1]v[1], M[1][0]v[0] + M[1][1]v[1]) u = (v2[0] - v1[0], v2[1] - v1[1]) v = (v3[0] - v1[0], v3[1] - v1[1]) U = matvecmul(G, u) V = matvecmul(G, v) # 5. Generate triangulation triangles = [] # Iterate over a grid centered at the centroid; range depends on cluster size maxidx = 200 # Implementation-dependent bound for i in range(-maxidx, maxidx): for j in range(-maxidx, maxidx): p0x = centroid[0] + i U[0] + j V[0] p0y = centroid[1] + i U[1] + j V[1] p1x = p0x + U[0] p1y = p0y + U[1] p2x = p0x + V[0] p2y = p0y + V[1] # Boundary culling: only triangles entirely inside the cluster if isinside(p0x, p0y) and isinside(p1x, p1y) and isinside(p2x, p2y): # Apply offset: place vertices below the surface by epsilon # In practice, shift each vertex along the surface normal by epsilon triangles.append(((p0x, p0y), (p1x, p1y), (p2x, p2y))) return triangles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The square roots of eigenvalues can be small, leading to large scaling factors in G. Use double precision. Boundary Gaps: The method explicitly leaves gaps at cluster boundaries. Degenerate Input: If eigenvalues are zero, the surface is not elliptic (parabolic or planar). Uses prototype h = \bar{x}^2 - \bar{y}^2. Choose when eigenvalues have opposite signs. Link Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The approach leverages the rotational symmetry of the canonical paraboloid to define an optimal equilateral triangle, then maps this triangle to the general elliptic case via principal axis transformation. name: SDF Tiling via Modulo
head: Tiled SDF, Tiling SDF, Modulo Tiling, Tiling via Modulo
body: SDF Tiling via Modulo creates a periodic tiling of a base signed distance field by folding 3D coordinates into a fundamental domain centered at the origin. It segments space into infinite parallel regions of repeated distance by taking the modulus of a point’s position along one or more axes before computing the signed distance. This allows for the infinite repetition of geometry for no extra computational cost in terms of scene complexity. It differs from SDF Domain Manipulation Operators by specifically using arithmetic wrapping to create periodicity rather than general transformations, and from Basic Primitive Definitions by enabling complex, repeated structures from simple primitives. Inputs: pt: The 3D point in world space (x, y, z). period: The spacing between repetitions along each axis (f32). basesdf: A function that computes the signed distance for the fundamental tile. Outputs: The signed distance value at pt within the tiled scene. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The operation is stateless and computed per-point. Parameters: period: The size of the repeating unit. In the standard implementation, the period is 4.0, and the offset is 2.0 to center the tile. offset: Half the period, used to center the fundamental domain at the origin. Typically offset = period / 2.0. Steps: 1. For each coordinate c in \{x, y, z\}, apply the modulo tiling transformation to fold the coordinate into the fundamental domain centered at 0: c' = \text{mod}(c + \text{offset}, \text{period}) - \text{offset} Where \text{mod}(a, b) is the floating-point modulo operation returning a value in [0, b). 2. Construct the transformed point \mathbf{p}' = (x', y', z'). 3. Pass \mathbf{p}' to the basesdf function to compute the distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modtilingsdf(pt: Vec3, period: float, basesdf: Callable[[Vec3], float]) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance of a point in a periodically tiled scene. Args: pt: The 3D point to evaluate. period: The spacing between repetitions. basesdf: The SDF function for the single tile. Returns: The signed distance value. """ offset = period / 2.0 # Apply modulo tiling to x and z axes (y is often left un-tiled for floor/ceiling effects, # but can be tiled similarly if desired) xtiled = mod(pt.x + offset, period) - offset ytiled = pt.y # Not tiled in standard example ztiled = mod(pt.z + offset, period) - offset transformedpt = Vec3(xtiled, ytiled, ztiled) return basesdf(transformedpt) def mod(a: float, b: float) -> float: """ Standard floating-point modulo. Returns a value in [0, b). """ return a - b floor(a / b) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Symmetry: Simple modulo tiling works seamlessly for symmetrical shapes (e.g., circles, squares). For irregular shapes that are not symmetrical along the tiling axis (e.g., stars not symmetrical vertically), the simple mod approach may produce artifacts at the boundaries. Irregular Shapes Solution: For irregular shapes, one must sample the distance field at multiple shifted positions (e.g., one unit above and below) and take the minimum to ensure seamless tiling. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise with very large coordinates or very small periods, potentially causing discontinuities in the gradient. An infinite multiphase primitive defined as a set of parallel slices orthogonal to a prescribed direction \mathbf{u}. It uses a similar fractional part calculation but defines a two-phase space-filling structure. Let \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{p}\mathbf{u} (as per source notation), compute the fractional part \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{u} - [\mathbf{u}]. The signed distance field is defined as \phii = s \min(\mathbf{q}, 1 - \mathbf{q}), where the sign s is determined by s = +1 if [\mathbf{u}] is even, and -1 otherwise. Note: The source notation \mathbf{q} and \mathbf{p}\mathbf{u} appears to contain typos or specific variable mappings not fully clarified in the excerpt, but the core mechanism relies on the integer part parity of the projected coordinate. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per point evaluation, independent of the number of repetitions. Memory: O(1), as no geometry data is stored. Measured Performance: Infinite repetition of geometry incurs no extra cost in terms of scene complexity or memory usage. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Extremely efficient for creating complex, repetitive environments (e.g., floors, walls, grids) without increasing draw calls or memory footprint. Limitations: Limited to periodic, regular structures. Cannot easily represent non-periodic or irregular tiling without additional logic. May produce visual artifacts at tile boundaries for non-symmetric primitives. When to Use: Use for creating infinite floors, walls, grids, or any scene requiring regular, periodic repetition of a base shape. When Not to Use: Do not use for irregular, non-periodic, or asymmetric tiling without the additional sampling techniques described in. The technique is widely popularized in the context of ray marching and signed distance fields, particularly through the work of Inigo Quilez and educational resources from the University of Cambridge. It is a fundamental building block in procedural geometry generation, allowing for the creation of complex scenes from simple primitives. The concept of using modulo for repetition is also related to fractal generation techniques described by John C. name: Basic Primitive Definitions
head: Standard Solid Primitives, Canonical SDFs, Atomic SDFs
body: Basic Primitive Definitions provide exact Euclidean Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for fundamental geometric shapes, serving as the atomic building blocks for procedural geometry in distance-field ray marching. They differ from sibling primitives like the Ellipsoid or Capsule by defining canonical, analytically simple volumes (sphere, box, plane) that form the basis for complex scene construction via boolean operations. These functions compute the shortest distance from a query point in 3D space to the surface of a primitive, enabling ray marching to determine object boundaries without mesh intersection tests. The method consists of evaluating analytical distance formulas for specific canonical shapes. To place a primitive at an arbitrary location, orientation, or scale, the query point is transformed into the primitive's local coordinate system before evaluation. Input: A 3D query point p = (px, py, pz) in world or local space. Input: Primitive parameters (e.g., radius, half-extents, normal). Output: A scalar signed distance d. d > 0 indicates the point is outside the surface, d < 0 indicates inside, and d = 0 indicates the surface. No complex data structures are required for the primitives themselves. Parameters are typically passed as scalars or vectors: p: vec3 (query point). r or s: float (radius). b or d: vec3 (half-extents for boxes). t or c: vec2 or vec3 (torus radii or cylinder parameters). A sphere of radius r centered at the origin. Formula: d(p, r) = \|p\| - r. Steps: 1. Calculate the Euclidean length of the point vector: \|p\| = \sqrt{px^2 + py^2 + pz^2}. 2. Subtract the radius r. Pitfall: If the sphere is not centered at the origin, translate p by p - center before computing length. An axis-aligned box centered at the origin with half-extents b = (bx, by, bz). Formula: d(p, b) = \|\max(q, 0)\| + \min(\max(qx, \max(qy, qz)), 0), where q = |p| - b. Steps: 1. Compute q = (|px| - bx, |py| - by, |pz| - bz). 2. Calculate the outside distance: d{out} = \|\max(q, 0)\|. This is the Euclidean distance to the nearest corner or edge if outside. 3. Calculate the inside distance: d{in} = \min(\max(qx, \max(qy, qz)), 0). This is the negative distance to the nearest face if inside. 4. Return d{out} + d{in}. Pitfall: Ensure b represents half-extents, not full dimensions. An infinite plane defined by a normalized normal vector n and a scalar offset d{offset} (distance from origin along n). Formula: d(p, n, d{offset}) = p \cdot n + d{offset}. Steps: 1. Compute the dot product of p and n. 2. Add the offset d{offset}. Pitfall: The normal n must be normalized. A torus in the XZ plane with major radius R (hole radius) and minor radius r (tube radius). Formula: d(p, R, r) = \|(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R, py)\| - r. Steps: 1. Compute the distance from the Y-axis in the XZ plane: dist{xz} = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}. 2. Construct a 2D vector q = (dist{xz} - R, py). 3. Return \|q\| - r. Pitfall: The torus lies in the XZ plane by default; rotation is required to align it with other axes. A cylinder aligned with the Y-axis, with radius r and half-height h. Formula: d(p, r, h) = \min(\max(dx, dy), 0) + \|\max(d)\|, where d = (|\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}| - r, |py| - h). Steps: 1. Compute radial distance: r{dist} = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}. 2. Compute 2D distance vector d = (r{dist} - r, |py| - h). 3. Return \min(\max(dx, dy), 0) + \sqrt{\max(dx, 0)^2 + \max(dy, 0)^2}. Pitfall: This computes the distance to the capped cylinder (side walls and top/bottom caps). A capsule defined by endpoints a, b and radius r. Formula: d(p, a, b, r) = \|p - (a + ba \cdot h)\| - r, where ba = b - a and h = \text{clamp}(\frac{pa \cdot ba}{ba \cdot ba}, 0, 1) with pa = p - a. Steps: 1. Compute segment vector ab = b - a and point vector ap = p - a. 2. Compute parameter t = \text{clamp}(\frac{ap \cdot ab}{ab \cdot ab}, 0.0, 1.0). 3. Compute closest point on segment: closest = a + ab \cdot t. 4. Return \|p - closest\| - r. A regular tetrahedron centered at the origin.
