name: Arc Signed Distance Function
head: SDF Arc, sdArc
body: The Arc Signed Distance Function computes the Euclidean distance from a query point to a 3D tube of constant radius wrapping a circular arc. It solves the problem of defining smooth, analytically continuous boundaries for curved, open-ended tubular structures in ray marching and implicit modeling. It is distinguished from the Capsule Signed Distance Function by its curved path rather than a straight line segment, and from the Torus by its limited angular aperture. Inputs: Query point p = (px, py, pz). arccenter: Center of the arc's circular path in 3D space. orientationangle: Angle of the arc's starting plane relative to the global X-axis (in degrees). apertureangle: Total angular span of the arc (in degrees). ra: Radius of the circular path defining the arc's curvature. rb: Radius of an inner circle, used for complex shapes (default 0.0). arctuberadius: Radius of the tube surrounding the arc path. depth: A global Z-coordinate value used to define the arc's plane if the arc is not centered at pz (implementation detail from). Outputs: Signed distance d to the arc surface. Positive outside, negative inside. Data Structures: The implementation typically precomputes trigonometric values to avoid repeated calls during evaluation. The Arc struct layout is: vec3 arccenter: Center position. float arctuberadius: Tube radius. float orientationangle: Orientation in degrees. float apertureangle: Aperture in degrees. float scacos: \cos(\text{orientation\angle}). float scasin: \sin(\text{orientation\angle}). float scbcos: \cos(\text{aperture\angle}). float scbsin: \sin(\text{aperture\angle}). float ra: Path radius. float rb: Inner radius. Steps: 1. Position Construction: Construct a position vector from the query point, replacing the Z component with a global depth value to align the arc's plane. pos = (px, py, \text{depth}) 2. Translation: Translate the position by the arc center. pos = pos - \text{arc\center} 3. Rotation: Rotate the position into the arc's local coordinate system using the precomputed sine and cosine of the orientation angle. x = posx \cdot \text{sca\cos} - posy \cdot \text{sca\sin} y = posx \cdot \text{sca\sin} + posy \cdot \text{sca\cos} posx = x, \quad posy = y 4. Symmetry: Take the absolute value of the X component to exploit symmetry across the arc's mid-plane. posx = |posx| 5. Intermediate Value Calculation: Compute an intermediate value k based on the aperture angle. This step effectively projects the point onto the arc's bounding geometry. k = \begin{cases} posx \cdot \text{scb\sin} + posy \cdot \text{scb\cos} & \text{if } \text{scb\cos} \cdot posx > \text{scb\sin} \cdot posy \\ \sqrt{posx^2 + posy^2} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 6. Project Distance: Compute the distance to the circular path defined by radius ra and inner radius rb. \text{project\distance} = \sqrt{pos \cdot pos + ra^2 - 2 \cdot ra \cdot k} - rb Note: The source code uses sqrt14, an approximation of square root. 7. Final Distance: Combine the project distance with the Z-component (depth difference) and subtract the tube radius. d = \sqrt{\text{project\distance}^2 + pz^2} - \text{arc\tube\radius} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdarc(p: Vec3, arc: Arc) -> float: # 1. Construct position vector using global depth # Note: 'depth' is assumed to be a global variable or passed context pos = Vec3(p.x, p.y, depth) # 2. Translate by arc center pos = pos - arc.arccenter # 3. Rotate by orientation angle x = pos.x arc.scacos - pos.y arc.scasin y = pos.x arc.scasin + pos.y arc.scacos pos.x = x pos.y = y # 4. Absolute value of x pos.x = abs(pos.x) # 5. Compute intermediate value k # Condition: scbcos pos.x > scbsin pos.y if arc.scbcos pos.x > arc.scbsin pos.y: k = pos.x arc.scbsin + pos.y arc.scbcos else: k = length(pos.x, pos.y) # 6. Compute project distance # Using standard sqrt for clarity; source uses FT::sqrt approximation projectdistance = sqrt(dot(pos, pos) + arc.ra arc.ra - 2.0 arc.ra k) - arc.rb # 7. Final distance return sqrt(projectdistance projectdistance + p.z p.z) - arc.arctuberadius def length(x: float, y: float) -> float: return sqrt(x x + y y) def dot(v: Vec3, w: Vec3) -> float: return v.x w.x + v.y w.y + v.z w.z Parameters: ra: Radius of the circle defining the arc path. Typical value varies by instance (e.g., 1.75f). rb: Radius of an inner circle, used for interesting shapes. Default is 0.0f. arctuberadius: Radius of the tube running along the arc. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Angle Conversion: The constructor must convert orientationangle and apertureangle from degrees to radians by multiplying by \pi/180.0 before computing sine and cosine values. Precision: The source implementation uses fast trigonometric approximations (FT::sqrt, FT::atan) which may introduce minor precision errors compared to standard library functions. Depth Dependency: The method relies on a global depth variable to define the Z-coordinate of the arc plane. If depth does not match the intended plane of the arc, the distance calculation will be incorrect. Computes the exact length of a quadratic geodesic arc defined by z = at^2. The integral l(a, \rho0) = \int \sqrt{1 + (2at)^2} dt is solved via substitution u=2at and x=\arctan(u), resulting in l(a, \rho0) = \frac{u\sqrt{1+u^2} + \ln(u + \sqrt{1+u^2})}{4a}. This is used for high-quality surface reconstruction in Gaussian Splatting, distinct from the SDF distance query. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. The calculation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and trigonometric lookups (precomputed). Memory Complexity: O(1) for the primitive parameters. Strengths: Provides smooth, continuous distance fields for curved tubes without tessellation. Efficient for ray marching due to analytic derivatives (if computed) and simple structure. Limitations: Limited to specific geometric shapes. The approximation of square roots in the source code may affect precision in critical applications. The reliance on a global depth variable makes it less portable in generic SDF libraries unless adapted. When to use: When rendering curved, tubular structures with constant cross-sections where a torus is too complex or a capsule is too straight. It appears in the repository AlerianEmperor/SDF-Sphere-Tracing, which implements various SDF primitives including spheres, boxes, and arcs. The implementation utilizes fast trigonometric approximations and SSE optimizations as noted in the source comments. name: Basic Geometric Primitives
head: Basic SDF Primitives, Standard Solid Primitives
body: Basic Geometric Primitives provide exact Euclidean signed distance functions (SDFs) for fundamental shapes, serving as the atomic building blocks for procedural geometry in distance-field ray marching. They differ from sibling primitives like the Ellipsoid or Capsule by defining canonical, analytically simple volumes (sphere, box, plane) that form the basis for complex scene construction via boolean operations. All primitives in this family compute a scalar field d(p) representing the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point p to the surface of the shape. The sign of d(p) indicates spatial containment: d(p) < 0: The point p is inside the volume. d(p) = 0: The point p lies exactly on the surface. d(p) > 0: The point p is outside the volume. This signed distance property ensures that ray marching steps are safe: the step size never exceeds the distance to the surface, preventing ray overshooting and intersection errors. The functions are differentiable almost everywhere, allowing the gradient \nabla d to be used as the surface normal for shading [Parent]. Computes the exact distance to an axis-aligned box. It distinguishes interior from exterior space and maintains sharp 90-degree corners, unlike rounded variants. Defines an infinite plane using a normal and offset. It is computationally trivial and serves as a ground plane or boundary for boolean operations [Parent]. Computes the distance to a sphere surface. It is the fundamental 3D volumetric primitive, enabling efficient step-size estimation in ray marching. Signed Distance Functions for basic primitives were popularized in computer graphics by Martin Held and later refined by Ian McEwan, Andrew Kensler, and others for real-time ray marching. The sphere SDF is among the oldest and most widely used implicit primitives due to its simplicity and rotational symmetry. The box SDF requires careful implementation to avoid underestimation in corner regions, a pitfall noted in early implementations.

body: The Signed Box Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point p to the surface of an axis-aligned box, returning a signed scalar where the sign indicates spatial containment (d < 0 inside, d > 0 outside). It solves the problem of defining a robust, differentiable implicit volume primitive for ray marching and implicit modeling, ensuring that step sizes in sphere tracing are safe lower bounds to prevent ray overshooting. Unlike the cheaper approximation that intersects half-spaces, this method correctly calculates the distance to corners and edges, preventing the underestimation artifacts that cause incorrect ambient occlusion and slower convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3; Box definition. Two common parameterizations exist: 1. Center c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and side lengths s \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Center c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and half-extents (bounds) b \in \mathbb{R}^3, where bi = si / 2. Output: Signed distance d(p) \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The function operates on scalar values and 3D vectors. If the box is part of a scene graph, it may be stored as a struct containing two corner vectors c1, c2 or center/side-length pairs. Algorithm (Version 2 - Exact): This is the standard, correct implementation that handles inside/outside cases separately to ensure Euclidean accuracy at corners. 1. Shift and Scale: Compute the vector q representing the distance from the point to the box boundary in each axis. Using half-extents b: q = |p - c| - b Where | \cdot | is the component-wise absolute value. 2. Inside Distance: Calculate the maximum component of q. If the point is inside, all components of q are negative. The distance to the nearest face is the magnitude of the largest negative component (closest to zero). d{inside} = \max(qx, \max(qy, qz)) Note: If the point is inside, d{inside} will be negative. 3. Outside Distance: If the point is outside (d{inside} > 0), the distance is the Euclidean length of the positive components of q (the parts of the vector extending beyond the box faces). d{outside} = \| \max(q, 0) \|2 Where \max(q, 0) is the component-wise maximum of q and the zero vector, and \| \cdot \|2 is the L2 norm (Euclidean length). 4. Combine: If d{inside} > 0 (point is outside), return d{outside}. Otherwise (point is inside or on surface), return d{inside}. This can be written compactly as: d(p) = \max(qx, \max(qy, qz)) + \| \max(q, 0) \|2 Wait, this compact form is actually Version 1 and is incorrect for corners. The correct logic is: d(p) = \begin{cases} \| \max(q, 0) \|2 & \text{if } \max(q) > 0 \\ \max(q) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Actually, the standard compact formula often cited as "correct" in GLSL libraries (like) is: d(p) = \text{length}(\max(q, 0)) + \min(\max(qx, \max(qy, qz)), 0) Let's verify this compact formula. If inside: \max(q) < 0. \max(q, 0) = 0. Length is 0. Result is \max(q), which is negative. Correct. If outside: \max(q) > 0. \max(q, 0) has positive components. Length is d{outside}. \min(\max(q), 0) = 0. Result is d{outside}. Correct. This compact formula is mathematically equivalent to the if/else logic and is the standard implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def signedboxdistance(p: Vector3, center: Vector3, halfextents: Vector3) -> float: """ Computes the signed Euclidean distance from point p to an axis-aligned box. Args: p: Query point (Vector3). center: Center of the box (Vector3). halfextents: Half-lengths of the box along x, y, z axes (Vector3). Returns: Signed distance. Negative if inside, positive if outside. """ # 1. Shift point to box-centered coordinates and take absolute value # q = |p - center| - halfextents q = Vector3( abs(p.x - center.x) - halfextents.x, abs(p.y - center.y) - halfextents.y, abs(p.z - center.z) - halfextents.z) # 2. Calculate the maximum component of q (distance to nearest face if inside) maxq = max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)) # 3. Calculate the Euclidean distance of the positive components (distance to edge/corner if outside) # max(q, 0) clamps negative components to 0 positiveq = Vector3( max(q.x, 0.0), max(q.y, 0.0), max(q.z, 0.0)) outsidedist = positiveq.length() # 4. Combine # If inside (maxq < 0), outsidedist is 0, so result is maxq (negative). # If outside (maxq > 0), maxq term is clamped to 0 by min(..., 0) logic implicitly # handled by the addition: maxq + outsidedist? # No, the formula is: length(max(q,0)) + min(max(q), 0) insideterm = min(maxq, 0.0) return outsidedist + insideterm Parameters: center: The 3D coordinates of the box center. Default: (0,0,0). halfextents (or b): The distance from the center to the faces along each axis. For a 1 \times 1 \times 1 box, b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Version 1 Artifact: A common incorrect implementation is d = \max(q) + \| \max(q, 0) \|2? No, the incorrect one is often cited as d = \min(\max(q), \| \max(q, 0) \|2) or simply using the max of the two without the conditional logic correctly, or specifically the formula d = \max(|p|-b) which underestimates distance at corners. Underestimation: Using the "cheap" approximation d = \max(|p-c| - s) (where s is side length, not half-extent) or the uncorrected max/min logic leads to underestimating the distance in corner regions. This causes ray marching to take smaller steps than necessary (slower convergence) and produces incorrect ambient occlusion (dark spots). Overestimation: Any function that overestimates the distance risks the ray overshooting the surface, leading to intersection errors. The exact SDF guarantees no overestimation. Computes the Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box centered at the origin, returning only non-negative values regardless of whether the point lies inside or outside the volume. Unlike its sibling, the Signed Box Distance Function, which distinguishes interior from exterior space, this method treats the box as a solid boundary where internal points are measured by their distance to the nearest face. Computes the signed Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box whose edges and corners are rounded by a constant radius. It solves the problem of defining smooth, organic variations of standard rectangular primitives for ray marching and implicit modeling. It differs from the Signed Box Distance Function by replacing sharp 90-degree corners with spherical fillets, allowing for continuous normals and softer visual interactions. Computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the boundary of an axis-aligned rectangle centered at the origin. It is the 2D analog of the Signed Box Distance Function. Computes the signed Euclidean distance from a 2D point to a line segment of arbitrary length and thickness, effectively representing a 2D box with rounded corners oriented along the segment axis. It differs from the Unsigned Box Distance Function by providing signed output and from the Signed Box Distance Function by operating in 2D with a specific segment-based orientation rather than a general 3D axis-aligned or oriented box. It serves as a primitive for constructing 2D shapes in ray marching or implicit modeling. Computes the signed distance from a point to an Oriented Bounding Box (OBB). It transforms the input point into the box's local coordinate system using the inverse of the box's transformation matrix, computes the distance to the unit box scaled by the box's dimensions, and adjusts for being inside or outside. Steps: 1. Transform point p to local space: trans = fullinverse (p, 1.0). 2. Compute local difference: qlocal = (abs(trans.xyz) - 1.0) scale. 3. Compute distance using the same logic as the axis-aligned box: dist = length(max(qlocal, 0)) + min(max(qlocal), 0). Time Complexity: O(1). The function involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (subtractions, absolute values, max/min, and one square root for the L2 norm). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are needed. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time ray marching. The square root operation is the most expensive part, but it is only computed for the outside distance. Strengths: Exact Euclidean distance; safe for sphere tracing (no overshooting); differentiable almost everywhere (gradient provides surface normal); handles inside/outside correctly. Limitations: The square root operation is slightly more expensive than the "cheap" approximation. The cheap approximation is sometimes used for performance when visual quality (AO) is not critical, but it is technically incorrect. When to use: Standard choice for axis-aligned boxes in ray marching, implicit modeling, and collision detection. When not to use: If the box is rotated, use the Oriented Box SDF. If performance is critical and visual artifacts are acceptable, the cheap approximation might be used, but it is generally discouraged for high-quality rendering. The Signed Box Distance Function is a fundamental primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching. The exact formulation (Version 2) was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online articles on distance functions. Earlier or simpler approximations (Version 1) were used in early GPU ray marching implementations but were shown to produce artifacts in ambient occlusion due to distance underestimation at corners. The function is widely implemented in GLSL libraries and graphics engines. name: Unsigned Box Distance Function
head: Unsigned Box, udBox
body: The Unsigned Box Distance Function computes the Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box centered at the origin, returning only non-negative values regardless of whether the point lies inside or outside the volume. Unlike the Signed Box Distance Function, which distinguishes interior from exterior space, this method treats the box as a solid boundary where internal points are measured by their distance to the nearest face. Inputs and outputs: Input: p (vec3), the query point in 3D space. Input: b (vec3), the half-extents of the box along the X, Y, and Z axes. The box is centered at (0,0,0) and spans [-bx, bx] \times [-by, by] \times [-bz, bz]. Output: d (float), the unsigned Euclidean distance from p to the box surface. Data structures: No complex data structures are required. The function operates on standard 3D vectors. Formula: The distance is calculated using the following formula: d = \|\max(|p| - b, 0)\| Where: |p| denotes the component-wise absolute value of vector p, i.e., (|px|, |py|, |pz|). \max(v, 0) denotes the component-wise maximum of vector v and the scalar 0, i.e., (\max(vx, 0), \max(vy, 0), \max(vz, 0)). \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm (length) of the resulting vector. Step-by-step derivation: 1. Compute the absolute coordinates of the point: q = |p|. 2. Subtract the box half-extents: r = q - b. 3. Clamp negative values to zero: s = \max(r, 0). This step discards interior distances. 4. Compute the Euclidean length of the remaining vector: d = \sqrt{sx^2 + sy^2 + sz^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def udBox(p, b): """ Computes the unsigned distance from point p to an axis-aligned box centered at the origin with half-extents b. Args: p: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) b: tuple or list of 3 floats (bx, by, bz) Returns: Non-negative Euclidean distance to the box surface. """ # Step 1: Component-wise absolute value of p q = (abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]), abs(p[2])) # Step 2: Subtract half-extents r = (q[0] - b[0], q[1] - b[1], q[2] - b[2]) # Step 3: Component-wise max with 0 (clamp negatives to zero) s = (max(r[0], 0.0), max(r[1], 0.0), max(r[2], 0.0)) # Step 4: Euclidean norm (length) distance = (s[0]2 + s[1]2 + s[2]2)0.5 return distance Parameters and typical values: b: Must be non-negative. If any component is zero, the box degenerates into a plane, line, or point. p: Any real-valued 3D coordinate. Edge cases and pitfalls: Inside the box: If the point is strictly inside the box, the intermediate r vector will have negative components. The clamping step sets these to 0. The formula yields a zero vector when |pi| \le bi for all i, resulting in a distance of 0. Precision: Near the box edges and corners, the function is continuous but not differentiable. Floating-point precision issues may arise when |pi| \approx bi. Degenerate input: If b contains negative values, the geometric interpretation is invalid. Evaluates the signed distance from a point to an axis-aligned cuboid, handling both outside and inside distances. It transforms the point using the cuboid's 4x4 matrix, calculates distances to faces, and combines outside and inside distance components. The cuboid struct layout is: transform (Mat4, 64 bytes), dimensions (Vec3, 12 bytes), padding (u32, 4 bytes), totaling 80 bytes with 16-byte alignment. Construction uses Cuboid::new(dimensions).translate(v).rotate(v). Time complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (absolute value, subtraction, comparison, square root). Memory complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are allocated. Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation, suitable for real-time ray marching and collision detection where interior/exterior distinction is not required. Limitations: Does not provide information about whether the point is inside or outside the volume. Not suitable for operations requiring signed distance properties (e.g., smooth unions, boolean operations with SDFs). The Unsigned Box Distance Function is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering, often used in GLSL-based ray marchers. It is part of the collection of SDF primitives popularized by the glsl-sdf-primitives library. While the signed variant is more common in constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations, the unsigned variant is useful for simple boundary checks or when the interior is treated as empty space. marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Box with Edge Rounding SDF
head: Box with Edge Rounding, Rounded Box Distance Function, Rounded Box SDF, SDF Primitive: Box with Edge Rounding, sdBoxRounded
body: Computes the signed Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box whose edges and corners are rounded by a constant radius. It solves the problem of defining smooth, organic variations of standard rectangular primitives for ray marching and implicit modeling. It differs from the Signed Box Distance Function by replacing sharp 90-degree corners with spherical fillets, allowing for continuous normals and softer visual interactions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, box half-extents b = (bx, by, bz), edge/corner rounding radius e. Output: Signed distance d. Positive outside, negative inside, zero on the surface. Data Structures: p: vec3 (float x, y, z). b: vec3 (float x, y, z), representing half-width, half-height, half-depth. e: float, the radius of the rounding. Must satisfy 0 \le e \le \min(bx, by, bz). Steps: 1. Compute the absolute coordinates of the point relative to the box center: p{abs} = |p|. 2. Compute the distance to the unrounded box faces: q = p{abs} - b. 3. Clamp negative components to zero to isolate the region outside the box faces: q{pos} = \max(q, 0.0). 4. Compute the distance to the rounded corners/edges. This is done by treating the "excess" distance from the box as a vector from the corner center. The corner centers are located at (\pm bx, \pm by, \pm bz). The vector from the nearest corner to the point is q{pos}. The distance to the corner sphere is k = \|q{pos}\|. 5. The raw distance to the rounded geometry is d{raw} = k - e. 6. Adjust for the signed nature. If the point is inside the unrounded box (q has negative components), the distance is determined by the closest face. If outside, it is determined by the closest edge/corner sphere. A unified formula often used is: d = \| \max(|p| - b, 0) \| - e. However, this returns unsigned distance for the outer shell. For a signed distance function (SDF), we must account for the interior. The standard SDF implementation combines the box distance and the rounding. Let d{box} be the distance to the sharp box. Let d{round} be the distance to the rounded corners. A common robust implementation (derived from and) calculates the distance to the rounded box as: d = \text{length}(\max(|p| - b, 0.0)) - e This formula alone is unsigned for the outer region. To make it signed, we check if the point is inside the sharp box. d{signed} = \begin{cases} d{box} & \text{if } d{box} < 0 \\ \max(d{box}, \| \max(|p| - b, 0.0) \| - e) & \text{if } d{box} \ge 0 \end{cases} Actually, a simpler and widely cited SDF for rounded boxes (e.g., Inigo Quilez's style) is: d = \text{length}(\max(|p| - b, 0.0)) - e This is technically an unsigned distance to the rounded box surface from the outside. For a true SDF that is negative inside, we use: d = \text{length}(\max(|p| - b, 0.0)) - e Wait, if p is inside the sharp box, \max(|p|-b, 0) is zero (or has zeros). The length is 0. d = -e. This is incorrect for the interior of the sharp box, which should be close to 0 or negative based on face distance. Correct SDF logic: 1. q = |p| - b 2. d{box} = \text{length}(\max(q, 0.0)) + \min(\max(q, 0.0), 0.0) (This is the standard box SDF) 3. For rounded box, we replace the corner contribution. 4. The distance to the rounded box is: d = \text{length}(\max(|p| - b, 0.0)) - e This formula is valid for the outside. For the inside, the distance is determined by the closest face of the sharp box, but clipped by the rounding. Let's look at: float d = length(max(abs(p)-vec3(2.0,0.5,2.0),0.0))-0.2; This returns a value that is negative inside the "rounded" volume? No, if p=0, |p|-b = -b. \max(-b, 0) = 0. length(0) - 0.2 = -0.2. If p is far outside, d is positive. If p is inside the sharp box but outside the rounded volume? The "rounded box" volume is the intersection of the sharp box and the expanded box? No, it's the sharp box with corners cut off. The interior of the rounded box is the set of points where d < 0. The formula d = \| \max(|p| - b, 0) \| - e works as a signed distance function if we consider the "rounded box" to be the shape where the corners are rounded. However, strictly speaking, the distance to the surface is what is needed. Let's refine the algorithm based on and: 1. q = |p| - b 2. d{out} = \| \max(q, 0.0) \| - e 3. d{in} = \min(q) + e? No. Standard SDF for rounded box (from Quilez): glsl float sdRoundedBox( vec3 p, vec3 b, float r) { vec3 q = abs(p) - b; return length(max(q,0.0)) + min(max(q.x,max(q.y,q.z)),0.0) - r; } This is the correct SDF. max(q, 0.0) isolates the outside components. length(...) computes distance to the corner sphere. min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0.0) computes the distance to the nearest face if inside, or 0 if outside. Subtracting r shifts the surface inward by the radius. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdroundedbox(p: Vec3, b: Vec3, r: float) -> float: """ Computes signed distance to a rounded box. p: query point b: half-extents (width/2, height/2, depth/2) r: rounding radius """ # Step 1: Absolute coordinates minus half-extents q = abs(p) - b # Step 2: Distance to the outside corner spheres # max(q, 0) keeps only positive components (outside the box faces) outsidedist = length(max(q, 0.0)) # Step 3: Distance to the inside faces # min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0) is negative if inside, 0 if outside # It represents the distance to the nearest face if inside the box insidedist = min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0.0) # Step 4: Combine and subtract radius d = outsidedist + insidedist - r return d Parameters: r (or e): Rounding radius. Typical values depend on b. r should be < \min(bx, by, bz). If r \ge \min(b), the shape degenerates (e.g., to a capsule or sphere). Edge Cases: r = 0: Reduces to Signed Box Distance Function. r \ge \min(bx, by, bz): The box corners meet or overlap. The shape becomes a capsule-like form or a sphere. The SDF remains valid but may lose the "box" character. Precision: Near the boundaries where the face distance transitions to edge/corner distance, the function is C^1 continuous (smooth normals), but numerical precision issues can arise if r is very small relative to floating-point epsilon. Computes the signed distance to a 2D rounded rectangle. It is defined as the distance to a sharp 2D box with half-extents b-r, minus the radius r. Formula: \text{box2d}(p, b - r) - r. It is chosen when working in 2D space or extruding 2D profiles. Computes the unsigned distance from a point to an axis-aligned box with rounded corners. Formula: d = \|\max(|p| - b, 0)\| - r. It returns negative values if the point is inside the rounded box. It is simpler than the SDF version as it does not calculate the interior face distance separately, making it suitable for collision detection where only the boundary matters. Time Complexity: O(1). Involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations, vector subtractions, absolute values, max/min, and a square root (length). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time ray marching in fragment shaders. The square root is the most expensive operation, but it is unavoidable for Euclidean distance. Strengths: Provides smooth, organic shapes; continuous normals for lighting; simple parameterization. Limitations: Cannot represent sharp features; rounding radius limits the aspect ratio of the box (cannot round a very thin box fully). The Signed Distance Field for a rounded box is a staple in procedural geometry and ray marching, popularized by Inigo Quilez's tutorials on distance functions. It allows for the creation of soft, mechanical, or organic shapes without the need for mesh tessellation. It is widely used in real-time graphics, voxel engines, and implicit modeling. erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 5 – Raymarching: Floor + Rounded Box, http://www.geeks3d.com/20130524/building-worlds-with-distance-functions-in-glsl-raymarching-glslhacker-tutorial-opengl/5/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Rectangle Signed Distance Function
head: 2D Rectangle SDF, sdRect
body: Computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the boundary of an axis-aligned rectangle centered at the origin in 2D space. It distinguishes itself from the Signed Box Distance Function by operating in two dimensions, reducing computational overhead for planar primitives, and serving as the foundational 2D case for higher-dimensional box SDFs. Inputs: p: Query point in 2D space (\mathbb{R}^2). hsize: Half-extents of the rectangle (\mathbb{R}^2), defining the rectangle as [-hsizex, hsizex] \times [-hsizey, hsizey]. Outputs: d: Signed distance. Positive outside, negative inside, zero on boundary. Data Structures: Vectors p and hsize are 2-component floating-point vectors. Steps: 1. Calculate the vector dv representing the displacement from the rectangle's boundary to the query point, clamped to zero for components inside the bounds: dv = |p| - hsize where |p| is the component-wise absolute value of p. 2. Calculate the distance to the exterior (or zero if inside): outside = \| \max(dv, 0) \| where \max(dv, 0) applies the maximum operator component-wise, and \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean norm. 3. Calculate the distance to the interior (or zero if outside): inside = \min(\max(dvx, dvy), 0) This term is non-zero only when the point is inside the rectangle's infinite extrusion but outside the rectangle itself (i.e., in the corner regions if we consider the box logic, but for a 2D rectangle, this specific formula handles the transition correctly by checking if both components are negative). 4. Return the sum: d = outside + inside Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdRect(p: Vec2, hsize: Vec2) -> float: # Component-wise absolute value absp = Vec2(abs(p.x), abs(p.y)) # Displacement from half-extents dv = Vec2(absp.x - hsize.x, absp.y - hsize.y) # Clamp negative components to zero for outside distance dvclamped = Vec2(max(dv.x, 0.0), max(dv.y, 0.0)) # Euclidean norm of the clamped vector outsidedist = sqrt(dvclamped.x2 + dvclamped.y2) # Minimum of the components, clamped to zero for inside distance # min(max(dv.x, dv.y), 0.0) mincomponent = min(dv.x, dv.y) insidedist = min(mincomponent, 0.0) return outsidedist + insidedist Edge Cases: If hsize contains zeros, the rectangle degenerates to a line or point. The formula remains valid but may exhibit reduced precision near the degenerate geometry. Precision issues may arise if p is very close to the boundary and floating-point errors cause sign flips. A 3D extension of the rectangle SDF for a cube centered at the origin with side length 2.0 (half-extents of 1.0). It follows the same logic: d = \| \max(|p| - 1, 0) \| + \min(\max(|p|x, |p|y, |p|z), 0). It is chosen when 3D volumetric primitives are required. A primitive SDF representing a hollow box frame. It is defined by dimensions (x, y, z) and a thickness parameter. In the source implementation, it is identified by opid 5 and stored in an SdfOpSpecificBlock where vec4s[0] holds dimensions and floats[0] holds thickness. It is used for creating wireframe-like structures or hollow containers. Time Complexity: O(1) constant time. Requires a few arithmetic operations, a square root, and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Exact distance calculation; no approximation errors; efficient for ray marching in 2D. Limitations: Limited to axis-aligned rectangles. For rotated rectangles, the Oriented Box2D SDF is required. The 2D rectangle SDF is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field rendering, popularized by Inigo Quilez's online tutorials and widely adopted in shader coding communities. name: Oriented Box2D SDF
head: Rotated Box2D SDF
body: Computes the signed Euclidean distance from a 2D point to a line segment of arbitrary length and thickness, effectively representing a 2D box with rounded corners oriented along the segment axis. It differs from the Unsigned Box Distance Function by providing signed output and from the Signed Box Distance Function by operating in 2D with a specific segment-based orientation rather than a general 3D axis-aligned or oriented box. It serves as a primitive for constructing 2D shapes in ray marching or implicit modeling. Inputs: Point p \in \mathbb{R}^2. Segment endpoints a, b \in \mathbb{R}^2. Full thickness th \in \mathbb{R} (width of the box perpendicular to the segment). Outputs: Signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: Vectors are 2D floats. No complex packing required. Steps: 1. Calculate segment length l = \|b - a\|. 2. Edge Case: If l \le 10^{-6}, the segment is degenerate. Return the distance to a circle centered at a with radius th \cdot 0.5: d = \|p - a\| - th \cdot 0.5. 3. Calculate unit direction vector d{vec} = (b - a) / l. 4. Calculate center of segment c = (a + b) \cdot 0.5. 5. Calculate vector from center to point q = p - c. 6. Rotate q into the local frame aligned with d{vec}. The local x-axis aligns with the segment, and the y-axis is perpendicular: local.x = d{vec}.x \cdot q.x + d{vec}.y \cdot q.y local.y = -d{vec}.y \cdot q.x + d{vec}.x \cdot q.y 7. Calculate half-extents h = (l \cdot 0.5, th \cdot 0.5). 8. Compute the 2D box distance using the standard axis-aligned box SDF formula: d = \|\max(|local| - h, 0)\| + \min(\max(local.x - h.x, local.y - h.y), 0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def orientedbox2dsdf(p, a, b, th): # Step 1: Segment length diff = (b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]) l = math.hypot(diff[0], diff[1]) # Step 2: Degenerate case if l <= 1e-6: return math.hypot(p[0] - a[0], p[1] - a[1]) - (th 0.5) # Step 3: Direction dx = diff[0] / l dy = diff[1] / l # Step 4 & 5: Center and relative vector centerx = (a[0] + b[0]) 0.5 centery = (a[1] + b[1]) 0.5 qx = p[0] - centerx qy = p[1] - centery # Step 6: Rotate into local frame localx = dx qx + dy qy localy = -dy qx + dx qy # Step 7: Half extents hx = l 0.5 hy = th 0.5 # Step 8: Standard 2D box SDF dx = abs(localx) - hx dy = abs(localy) - hy qxbox = max(dx, 0.0) qybox = max(dy, 0.0) return math.hypot(qxbox, qybox) + min(max(dx, dy), 0.0) Parameters: th: Typical values depend on scene scale. Must be positive. 1e-6: Threshold for degenerate segment detection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Segment: If a \approx b, the direction vector is undefined. The method falls back to a circle. Precision: Division by small l causes instability. The threshold 10^{-6} prevents division by zero. Thickness: If th is zero, the shape becomes a line segment. The distance function still works but represents a 1D object in 2D space. A variant representing a glass panel with variable thickness and surface perturbations. It constructs an SDF by deforming an axis-aligned box SDF using elevation profiles f and g for the front and back faces. The thickness t(\mathbf{x}) is defined as t + f(\mathbf{x}x, \mathbf{x}y) for \mathbf{x}z > 0 and t + g(\mathbf{x}x, \mathbf{x}y) otherwise, where f and g are differentiable functions (e.g., procedural noise). This allows modeling hand-blown glass with bubbles and surface irregularities. However, replacing t with t(\mathbf{x}) in the standard box SDF definition creates a discontinuity around xz = 0 and inaccurate distance evaluation near the center plane. Time Complexity: O(1). Constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Efficient primitive for 2D ray marching; handles arbitrary orientation and thickness; robust to degenerate inputs. Limitations: Only applicable in 2D; assumes uniform thickness along the segment; not suitable for complex 3D box orientations directly (requires 3D extension). When to use: When rendering 2D shapes with rounded corners defined by a central spine or segment. When not to use: For 3D boxes or non-uniform thickness profiles. The Oriented Box2D SDF is documented in the sdf-math-rs repository. It is used in procedural generation and ray marching of 2D implicit surfaces. The specific handling of degenerate segments as circles is a practical implementation detail from. bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Parabolic Sphere Tracing of Signed Distance Fields for Old Glass Modelling and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3613853, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Plane Signed Distance Function
head: Plane SDF, Plane distance, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Plane, Signed Plane, sdPlane
body: The Plane Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point to an infinite plane, with the sign indicating which side of the plane the point resides on. It serves as a fundamental building block for procedural geometry in ray marching, providing a differentiable surface normal for shading and a safe step size for sphere tracing. Unlike bounded primitives such as the Sphere Signed Distance Function or Signed Box Distance Function, the plane extends infinitely in all directions perpendicular to its normal, making it ideal for representing ground planes, clipping boundaries, or half-space constraints. Inputs and Outputs Input: A query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and plane definition parameters (unit normal n and offset h, or normal n and a point r on the plane). Output: A scalar value d(p) representing the signed distance. Data Structures The plane is defined by two primary components: 1. Normal (n): A unit vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) perpendicular to the plane surface. 2. Offset/Position: Either a scalar offset h representing the signed distance from the origin to the plane along the normal, or a point \mathbf{r} lying on the plane. Formulas There are two common parameterizations, which are mathematically equivalent: 1. Normal-Offset Form: d(p) = p \cdot n + h Where h is the signed distance from the origin to the plane. If the plane passes through the origin, h=0. The sign of h depends on the direction of n relative to the origin. Specifically, if n points away from the origin, h is negative for planes "in front" of the origin in the direction of n. More precisely, h = -r \cdot n where r is any point on the plane. 2. Normal-Point Form: d(p) = (p - r) \cdot n Where r is a specific point known to lie on the plane. This is often more intuitive for construction (e.g., "plane passing through origin with normal up"). Parameters n: Must be a unit vector (\|n\| = 1). If not normalized, the result is scaled by the length of n, leading to incorrect step sizes in ray marching. h: Scalar offset. r: 3D point on the plane. Numbered Steps 1. Ensure the normal vector n is normalized. If using a point r and an unnormalized normal v, compute n = v / \|v\|. 2. Compute the dot product of the query point p and the normal n. 3. Add the offset h (if using normal-offset form) or subtract the dot product of r and n (if using normal-point form, effectively p \cdot n - r \cdot n). 4. Return the result. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdplane(p: Vector3, n: Vector3, h: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a plane defined by unit normal n and offset h. Args: p: Query point (Vector3). n: Unit normal vector of the plane (Vector3). Must be normalized. h: Offset from the origin. The plane equation is n.xx + n.yy + n.zz + h = 0. Alternatively, h = -dot(r, n) where r is a point on the plane. Returns: Signed distance. Positive if p is on the side of n, negative if on the opposite side. """ # Guard: Ensure normal is normalized to guarantee correct Euclidean distance # In production code, assert or normalize here if n is not guaranteed unit length. if length(n) != 1.0: n = normalize(n) # Formula: d = dot(p, n) + h # This is equivalent to dot(p - r, n) where r is a point on the plane and h = -dot(r, n) return dot(p, n) + h def sdplanefrompoint(p: Vector3, n: Vector3, r: Vector3) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a plane defined by unit normal n and a point r on the plane. Args: p: Query point (Vector3). n: Unit normal vector of the plane (Vector3). r: A point known to lie on the plane (Vector3). Returns: Signed distance. """ # Guard: Ensure normal is normalized if length(n) != 1.0: n = normalize(n) # Formula: d = dot(p - r, n) return dot(p - r, n) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Unnormalized Normal: If n is not a unit vector, the result is not the Euclidean distance but the projection scaled by \|n\|. This causes ray marching to overshoot or undershoot. Sign Convention: The sign of the distance indicates containment. d(p) < 0 means the point is on the side opposite to the normal direction (inside the half-space defined by -n), and d(p) > 0 means it is on the side of the normal. Consistency with the rest of the scene's SDFs is crucial for boolean operations (e.g., unions, intersections). Infinite Extent: The plane is infinite. It does not have edges. If a bounded plane is required, it must be combined with other primitives (e.g., using min/max operations with box SDFs). A geometric data structure for dual contouring that exposes the distance parameter and shortest distance vector for iterative constraint solving, differing from the standard SDF by its explicit interface for constraint handling. Time Complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a single dot product and an addition. Memory Complexity: O(1). Requires storing the normal vector (3 floats) and the offset (1 float), or the normal and a point (6 floats). Performance: Extremely fast, often one of the fastest SDF evaluations. Suitable for real-time ray marching and dense volume rendering. Strengths: Analytically exact, differentiable everywhere except at the plane itself (where the gradient is discontinuous, but the normal is well-defined as \pm n). Provides a safe, tight bound for sphere tracing steps. Limitations: Represents an infinite surface. Cannot model bounded planar regions without composition with other primitives. When to use: Ground planes, infinite walls, clipping planes, or as a component in complex CSG (Constructive Solid Geometry) operations. When not to use: When a bounded planar surface is needed (use a Box or custom mesh SDF instead). The signed distance function for a plane is a fundamental result in computational geometry and implicit surface rendering. It is widely cited in the context of sphere tracing and ray marching for implicit surfaces. Hart (1994) provided early formalizations of SDFs for basic primitives, including the plane. The specific formulation d(x) = x \cdot n - h is commonly attributed to Hart and appears in various graphics literature and educational resources on GPU ray marching. The GLSL implementation sdPlane popularized by Inigo Quilez's online resources further cemented the normal-offset parameterization in the real-time graphics community. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching of Distance Fields, https://www2.compute.dtu.dk/pubdb/edoc/imm6392.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Plane Representation for Dual Contouring
head: Plane Class for Dual Contouring, Plane Constraint Representation, Plane Representation
body: The Plane Representation for Dual Contouring is a geometric data structure used to define linear constraints for locating feature points in dual contouring algorithms. It represents a plane via a unit normal vector and a scalar distance from the origin, enabling efficient signed distance queries. It differs from the parent Plane Signed Distance Function by explicitly exposing the distance parameter and shortest distance vector calculation as part of its interface for iterative constraint solving. Inputs and Outputs Input: A point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and an unnormalized normal vector \mathbf{n}{\text{in}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for construction; a query point \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for distance evaluation. Output: A signed distance scalar and a shortest distance vector for a given query point. Data Structures The representation consists of a single class or struct with two fields: normal: A Vector3 representing the unit normal \mathbf{n}, guaranteed to be normalized (\|\mathbf{n}\| = 1). distance: A float representing the scalar d in the plane equation \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Numbered Steps 1. Construction from Point and Normal: a. Normalize the input normal: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{n}{\text{in}}}{\|\mathbf{n}{\text{in}}\|}. b. Calculate the distance parameter using the dot product: d = -\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}. c. Store \mathbf{n} and d in the structure. 2. Signed Distance Query: a. Compute the signed distance: d{\text{signed}} = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{q} + d. b. Return d{\text{signed}}. 3. Shortest Distance Vector: a. Compute the signed distance d{\text{signed}} using Step 2. b. Compute the vector from the point to the plane: \mathbf{v} = d{\text{signed}} \cdot \mathbf{n}. c. Return \mathbf{v}. Formulas Plane Equation: \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Distance Parameter: d = -\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}. Signed Distance: D(\mathbf{q}) = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{q} + d. Shortest Vector: \mathbf{v} = D(\mathbf{q}) \mathbf{n}. Parameters Normalization: The normal vector must be normalized before storing. Iterative Solving Context: In dual contouring, these planes are used to iteratively move a feature point. A typical step size factor is ~0.7 along the resultant average vector to stabilize convergence. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Normal: Not given in the sources. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Plane: def init(self, point: Vector3, normal: Vector3): self.normal = normal.normalize() self.distance = -self.normal.dot(point) def signeddistance(self, point: Vector3) -> float: return self.normal.dot(point) + self.distance def shortestdistancevector(self, point: Vector3) -> Vector3: dist = self.signeddistance(point) return self.normal dist Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This representation originates from practical implementations of dual contouring for real-time graphics, specifically discussed in the context of finding feature points by averaging vectors to intersecting planes. It is commonly used in voxel-based mesh generation where planar constraints are derived from surface normals at grid edges. name: Sphere Signed Distance Function
head: SDF Primitive: Sphere, SDF Sphere, SDF Sphere Primitive, Signed Distance Field (SDF) Sphere, Signed Distance Function (SDF) Sphere, Sphere SDF, Sphere SDF Primitive
body: The Sphere Signed Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point p to the surface of a sphere defined by a center c and radius r. It returns a negative value if the point is inside the sphere, a positive value if outside, and zero if on the surface. This function serves as the fundamental building block for procedural geometry in ray marching, providing a differentiable field where the gradient \nabla d yields the surface normal. It is distinguished from the Signed Box Distance Function by its rotational symmetry and from the Plane Signed Distance Function by its non-linear curvature [Parent]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, sphere center c \in \mathbb{R}^3, sphere radius r \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}. Optionally, a transformation matrix M if the sphere is not axis-aligned or centered at the origin. Output: Scalar signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: The sphere is typically defined by two parameters: 1. Center (c): A 3D vector (cx, cy, cz). In some implementations, this is learnable or stored in a specific block (e.g., floats[0] for radius, with center implied or stored separately). 2. Radius (r): A scalar float. In some implementations, this is learnable. 3. Transform (Optional): A 4 \times 4 matrix for non-uniform scaling, rotation, or translation. Formula: The signed distance d(p) is calculated as the length of the vector from the center to the point, minus the radius: d(p) = \| p - c \| - r where \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean norm (length). If a transformation matrix M is applied to the point (e.g., to handle local-to-world transformations or non-uniform scaling in a generalized SDF context), the point is transformed first: p' = M \cdot [p, 1]^T, and the distance is computed on p'. Note that for non-uniform scaling, the Euclidean SDF is an approximation unless the inverse transpose of the linear part of the matrix is used for normal computation, but the distance value itself remains \|p'\| - r in the transformed space if the sphere is defined in that space. Parameters: r: Radius. Typical values depend on scene scale. Default is often 1.0 or 0.5 in examples. c: Center. Default is (0, 0, 0). M: Transformation matrix. Not given in the sources for standard origin-centered sphere, but required for general placement. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: 1. Precision: For points very close to the surface, floating-point precision errors in the square root calculation can cause jitter in normals if not handled carefully. However, the SDF itself is robust. 2. Zero Radius: If r=0, the function returns the distance to the center point. This is valid but may cause issues in ray marching if not handled (step size becomes 0 at the center). 3. Negative Radius: Radii must be non-negative. A negative radius is physically invalid and should be clamped or rejected. 4. Gradient Normalization: The gradient \nabla d = \frac{p-c}{\|p-c\|} is already a unit vector (normal) everywhere except at the center p=c where it is undefined. Ray marching steps should use the SDF value directly, not the gradient magnitude, for safety [Parent]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spheresdf(p: list, c: list, r: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a sphere with center c and radius r. Args: p: List of 3 floats [x, y, z] representing the query point. c: List of 3 floats [cx, cy, cz] representing the sphere center. r: Float representing the sphere radius. Returns: Float: Signed distance. Positive outside, negative inside, zero on surface. """ # Calculate vector from center to point dx = p[0] - c[0] dy = p[1] - c[1] dz = p[2] - c[2] # Calculate Euclidean distance from center disttocenter = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Subtract radius to get signed distance return disttocenter - r def spheresdfwithtransform(p: list, c: list, r: float, M: list) -> float: """ Computes SDF after applying a 4x4 transformation matrix M to the point. Note: This assumes M transforms world coordinates to the sphere's local space where the sphere is centered at origin with radius r. Args: p: World space point. c: Not used directly if M includes translation, but kept for signature consistency. r: Radius in local space. M: 4x4 transformation matrix (list of lists or flat list). Returns: Float: Signed distance in local space. """ # Transform point p using matrix M # Assuming M is 4x4, p is treated as [x, y, z, 1] # This is a simplified matrix-vector multiplication x, y, z = p[0], p[1], p[2] # Row 0 tx = M[0][0]x + M[0][1]y + M[0][2]z + M[0][3] # Row 1 ty = M[1][0]x + M[1][1]y + M[1][2]z + M[1][3] # Row 2 tz = M[2][0]x + M[2][1]y + M[2][2]z + M[2][3] # Row 3 (w component, usually 1 for points) # tw = M[3][0]x + M[3][1]y + M[3][2]z + M[3][3] # Compute SDF in transformed space (centered at origin) disttocenter = math.sqrt(txtx + tyty + tztz) return disttocenter - r The Circle Signed Distance Function computes the signed distance from a 2D query point to the perimeter of a circle centered at the origin. It returns a negative value inside the circle, a positive value outside, and zero on the boundary. It serves as the 2D analog of the Sphere Signed Distance Function. A Distance Estimator is a function that computes the minimum distance from a query point to any object in a scene, returning that distance along with the color of the closest object. Definition: It aggregates SDFs of multiple primitives to find the closest surface. Step: Initialize minimum distance to DRAW-DISTANCE (typically 1000) and color to [0, 0, 0]. For each object, compute its SDF. If the computed distance is less than the current minimum, update the minimum distance and store the object's color. Return the minimum distance and associated color. Parameter: DRAW-DISTANCE: The initial maximum distance for the estimator, set to 1000. Comparison: It returns color alongside distance to avoid recomputing the color lookup for the endpoint later. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. The computation involves a few subtractions, multiplications, and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1). Only the center and radius need to be stored. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time ray marching on GPUs. The square root operation is the most expensive part but is well-optimized in hardware. Strengths: Exact distance, differentiable, simple to implement, robust for ray marching steps. Limitations: Only represents spherical shapes. Cannot represent complex geometry without CSG operations. When to use: When rendering spheres or using them as primitives in CSG operations. When not to use: When the scene contains non-spherical objects without CSG, or when performance is critical and the square root is too expensive (though rare). The Sphere SDF is a fundamental primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching, popularized by Inigo Quilez and others in the demoscene and computer graphics community. It is derived from the geometric definition of a sphere as the locus of points equidistant from a center. The function has been used in various contexts including real-time rendering, implicit surface reconstruction, and neural radiance fields (NeRFs) as a baseline or regularizer. The concept of using distance functions for ray marching was introduced by John C. Hart in 1994 with "Sphere Tracing". name: Circle Signed Distance Function
head: 2D Circle SDF, 2D Sphere SDF, Circle SDF, sdCircle
body: The Circle Signed Distance Function computes the signed distance from a 2D query point to the perimeter of a circle centered at the origin. It returns a negative value inside the circle, a positive value outside, and zero on the boundary. It serves as the 2D analog of the Sphere Signed Distance Function. Inputs: p: A 2D query point, represented as a vector (px, py). r: The radius of the circle, a scalar. Outputs: d: The signed distance from p to the circle boundary. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Formula: The signed distance is calculated as the Euclidean norm of the query point minus the radius: d = \|p\| - r where \|p\| = \sqrt{px^2 + py^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcircle(p: tuple, r: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a circle of radius r centered at origin. Args: p: Tuple (x, y) representing the 2D query point. r: Float representing the radius of the circle. Returns: Float representing the signed distance. Negative if inside, positive if outside. """ return (p[0] 2 + p[1] 2) 0.5 - r Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sign Interpretation: A negative result indicates the point is inside the circle, zero indicates it is on the boundary, and a positive result indicates it is outside. Zero Radius: If r=0, the function returns the distance to the origin. This is mathematically valid but may cause degenerate behavior in ray marching if not handled. Negative Radius: The radius r should be non-negative. If a negative radius is passed, the sign of the distance will be inverted relative to the geometric expectation. Off-Center Circles: For circles not centered at the origin, the query point must be translated by the circle's center vector before evaluation. Time Complexity: O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation; analytically exact distance. Limitations: Only applies to circles centered at the origin. When to use: Ideal for 2D ray marching and procedural texture generation. The Circle SDF is the 2D analog of the Sphere Signed Distance Function. Its implementation relies on the standard definition of Euclidean distance. erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ellipsoid Signed Distance Function
head: Ellipsoid SDF, Ellipsoidal Prior SDF, Approximate Ellipsoid SDF
body: The Ellipsoid Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an ellipsoid defined by three semi-axes. It serves as a fundamental building block for procedural geometry in volume rendering and ray marching, enabling the representation of smooth, organic shapes and thin objects (via degenerate 2D disks). Unlike the Sphere SDF, which assumes uniform scaling, the Ellipsoid SDF handles anisotropic scaling, making it distinct from siblings like the Box or Capsule primitives [Parent]. It is particularly noted for its ability to handle non-watertight surfaces when one axis radius is set to zero, reducing the function to a Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF) for 2D disks. Inputs: p \in \mathbb{R}^3: The query point in the ellipsoid's local coordinate frame. r \in \mathbb{R}^3: The semi-axes lengths (rx, ry, rz), where ri > 0. For a 2D disk, one component (typically rz) is set to 0. Outputs: d \in \mathbb{R}: The signed distance. d < 0 if inside, d = 0 on surface, d > 0 if outside. Data Structures: Vectors p and r are typically stored as 3-component floating-point arrays or SIMD registers. Method: There are two primary implementations: an approximate version (fast, widely used in real-time graphics) and a more accurate iterative or analytical approximation. The sources provide specific formulas for both. This version scales the distance from the unit sphere by the minimum semi-axis. It is computationally cheap but less accurate for highly anisotropic ellipsoids. 1. Normalize the point by the radii: p' = p / r (component-wise division). 2. Compute the length of the normalized point: k1 = \|p'\|. 3. Compute the minimum semi-axis: r{min} = \min(rx, ry, rz). 4. Calculate distance: d = (k1 - 1.0) \cdot r{min}. This version provides better accuracy by correcting the step size based on the gradient magnitude at the closest point on the unit sphere. 1. Normalize the point by the radii: p' = p / r (component-wise division). 2. Compute the length of the normalized point: k1 = \|p'\|. 3. Compute the gradient magnitude factor: k2 = \|p' / r\| (Note: sources define this as length of p divided by squared radii, effectively \|p / r^2\| in local space, but geometrically it relates to the gradient of the implicit function f(x) = \sum (xi/ri)^2 - 1). Specifically, k2 = \|p / (r \cdot r)\| where r \cdot r is component-wise squaring. 4. Calculate distance: d = \frac{k1 (k1 - 1.0)}{k2}. When rz = 0, the ellipsoid becomes a flat disk in the xy-plane. The standard SDF is ill-posed for sign in non-watertight objects, so a Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF) is used for ray marching. Inputs: p': Ray origin in local frame. v': Ray direction in local frame. rx, ry: Non-zero semi-axes. Steps: 1. Compute the cross product w' = p' \times v'. 2. Check intersection indicator: i(p, v; E) = (rx ry v'z)^2 - rx^2 w'z^2 - ry^2 w'y^2 3. If i(p, v; E) < 0, the ray does not intersect the disk. Return \infty or handle as miss. 4. If i(p, v; E) \ge 0, compute the signed distance: d = -\frac{p'z}{v'z} Pitfall: If v'z = 0, the function returns \infty (no intersection). Pitfall: If the ray points away from the disk (v'z > 0 and p'z \le 0, or v'z < 0 and p'z \ge 0), the formula yields invalid negative values. The intersection check i \ge 0 is required to validate the result. Pseudocode (Improved V2 for 3D Ellipsoid): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ellipsoidsdf(p: list, r: list) -> float: """ Computes the improved approximate signed distance to an ellipsoid. p: [px, py, pz] query point in local space r: [rx, ry, rz] semi-axes lengths """ # Component-wise division p / r px, py, pz = p rx, ry, rz = r # Avoid division by zero if r contains 0 (use V1 or handle separately) # For standard 3D ellipsoid, ri > 0 # Step 1: Normalize point pxr = px / rx pyr = py / ry pzr = pz / rz # Step 2: Compute k1 = length(p / r) k1 = math.sqrt(pxr2 + pyr2 + pzr2) # Step 3: Compute k2 = length(p / (r r)) # Note: p / (rr) means component-wise pi / (ri^2) pxrr = px / (rx rx) pyrr = py / (ry ry) pzrr = pz / (rz rz) k2 = math.sqrt(pxrr2 + pyrr2 + pzrr2) # Step 4: Return distance # Guard against k2 being zero (origin case) if k2 == 0: return -min(rx, ry, rz) # Inside, distance to closest surface d = (k1 (k1 - 1.0)) / k2 # Sign correction: The formula above yields positive outside, negative inside? # Standard SDF: positive outside, negative inside. # k1 > 1 implies outside. k1 < 1 implies inside. # If k1 > 1, k1-1 > 0, d > 0. # If k1 < 1, k1-1 < 0, d < 0. # The formula naturally handles the sign. return d Pseudocode (2D Disk SDDF): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ellipsoiddisksddf(p: list, v: list, rx: float, ry: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed directional distance for a 2D disk (rz=0). p: [px, py, pz] ray origin in local space v: [vx, vy, vz] ray direction in local space rx, ry: semi-axes of the disk """ px, py, pz = p vx, vy, vz = v # Step 1: Compute w' = p' x v' wx = py vz - pz vy wy = pz vx - px vz wz = px vy - py vx # Step 2: Check intersection indicator # i = (rx ry vz)^2 - rx^2 wz^2 - ry^2 wy^2 term1 = (rx ry vz) 2 term2 = (rx 2) (wz 2) term3 = (ry 2) (wy 2) i = term1 - term2 - term3 if i < 0: return float('inf') # No intersection # Step 3: Handle degenerate direction if vz == 0: return float('inf') # Parallel to disk plane, no intersection # Step 4: Compute distance # d = -pz / vz d = -pz / vz # Pitfall check: If ray points away, d might be invalid relative to geometry # The intersection check i >= 0 ensures we hit the disk plane within bounds, # but the sign of d depends on vz. # If vz > 0 and pz <= 0, ray starts "below" and goes "up" through disk? # Actually, the formula -pz/vz gives the parameter t. # If t < 0, the intersection is behind the ray origin. # The source notes say: "If vz > 0 and pz <= 0... gives invalid negative values." # This implies we should check if the intersection is in front of the ray. if d < 0: return float('inf') # Intersection behind ray origin return d Time Complexity: O(1) per query. The improved version requires a few multiplications, additions, and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Accuracy: The V1 approximation is fast but can have errors up to several percent for extreme aspect ratios. The V2 approximation is significantly more accurate and is the standard choice for high-quality rendering. Strengths: Handles arbitrary ellipsoids; V2 is smooth and differentiable almost everywhere, providing good normals for shading [Parent]. The 2D disk variant allows rendering of thin, non-watertight objects like walls or curtains without geometry thickness. Limitations: The V2 formula involves division by k2, which can be numerically unstable if the point is very close to the center (origin) or if radii are extremely small/large. The 2D disk SDDF is not a true SDF (it is directional) and requires careful ray intersection checks to avoid artifacts. The concept of using ellipsoids as priors for scene representation has been explored in neural rendering and implicit surface modeling. The specific SDDF formulation for 2D disks using ellipsoidal priors was introduced to handle non-watertight objects in neural radiance fields and similar frameworks. The approximate SDF formulas (V1 and V2) are widely attributed to Inigo Quilez's articles on distance functions, which are standard references in the real-time graphics community. The V2 formula is a refinement over the simple scaling method (V1) to better approximate the true Euclidean distance. name: Capsule Signed Distance Function
head: 3D Capsule SDF, Capsule Rendering via Distance Check, Capsule SDF, Capsule3D SDF, Signed Capsule, sdCapsule
body: The Capsule Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point p to the surface of a capsule, defined as a cylinder of radius r capped by hemispheres at its endpoints. It solves the problem of efficiently determining spatial containment and proximity for volumetric rendering or collision detection of elongated, rounded shapes. It differs from the Sphere SDF by supporting an arbitrary axis and length, and from the Cone SDF by maintaining a constant radius along its central axis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3; Capsule endpoints a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3; Radius r \in \mathbb{R}^+. Output: Signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The computation uses temporary vectors and scalars. Parameters: r: Radius of the capsule. uses 0.12 as a hardcoded example, but r is a general parameter. a, b: The two endpoints defining the capsule's central axis. Algorithm: The function calculates the distance by projecting the query point onto the line segment defined by a and b, clamping the projection to the segment bounds, and computing the distance from the point to this closest point on the segment, then subtracting the radius. 1. Compute the vector from endpoint a to the query point p: pa = p - a 2. Compute the vector representing the capsule's axis: ba = b - a 3. Compute the squared length of the axis vector: len\sq = ba \cdot ba 4. Determine the projection parameter h along the axis. If the axis has negligible length (len\sq < \epsilon), h is 0. Otherwise, project pa onto ba and clamp the result to [0, 1]: h = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{pa \cdot ba}{len\sq}, 0.0, 1.0\right) where \text{clamp}(v, min, max) returns min if v < min, max if v > max, and v otherwise. 5. Compute the closest point on the segment to p: closest = a + ba \cdot h Alternatively, using the precomputed pa and ba: closest\relative = pa - ba \cdot h 6. Compute the Euclidean distance from p to the closest point: dist = \| closest\relative \| 7. Subtract the radius to get the signed distance: d = dist - r Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-Length Capsule: If a = b, len\sq = 0. Division by zero must be avoided. The sources handle this by clamping h to 0.0 if len\sq is below a threshold (e.g., 1e-12). In this case, the capsule degenerates to a sphere centered at a with radius r. Precision: Using squared lengths avoids square roots in the projection step, improving performance and stability. Sign Convention: The sign is determined by the final subtraction. d < 0 implies the point is inside the capsule volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdcapsule(p, a, b, r): """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a capsule defined by endpoints a, b and radius r. Args: p: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) a: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) b: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) r: float, radius of the capsule Returns: float: signed distance """ # Vector from a to p pax = p[0] - a[0] pay = p[1] - a[1] paz = p[2] - a[2] # Vector from a to b bax = b[0] - a[0] bay = b[1] - a[1] baz = b[2] - a[2] # Squared length of the capsule axis lensq = bax bax + bay bay + baz baz # Projection parameter h if lensq < 1e-12: h = 0.0 else: # Dot product of pa and ba dotpaba = pax bax + pay bay + paz baz # Clamp h to [0, 1] h = dotpaba / lensq if h < 0.0: h = 0.0 elif h > 1.0: h = 1.0 # Closest point on the segment relative to a # closestrelative = pa - h ba closestrelx = pax - h bax closestrely = pay - h bay closestrelz = paz - h baz # Distance from p to the closest point on the segment dist = math.sqrt(closestrelx closestrelx + closestrely closestrely + closestrelz closestrelz) # Signed distance return dist - r Subtopics: Segment Signed Distance Function: Computes distance to a 1D line segment. The capsule SDF is essentially the segment SDF with an offset by radius r. Choose the segment SDF when radius is zero or for pure geometric line queries. Cone Signed Distance Function: Computes distance to a cone. Choose the cone SDF when the shape tapers to a point or has a varying radius. Time Complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (subtractions, multiplications, dot products, one square root). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are needed. Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation, making it suitable for real-time ray marching and GPU-based volume rendering. It provides smooth, differentiable surfaces (except at the junction of the cylinder and hemispheres, where the normal is continuous but the derivative might have discontinuities depending on implementation, though standard SDFs are generally considered smooth enough for shading). Limitations: Only represents a specific shape. Cannot represent arbitrary meshes. Precision issues may arise with very small radii or very long capsules if not handled carefully, though the clamping logic mitigates most numerical instability. When to use: When rendering or detecting collisions with capsule-shaped objects (e.g., character skeletons, pipes, cables). When not to use: For complex, non-convex, or highly detailed geometries where mesh-based or voxel-based representations are more appropriate. The capsule SDF is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field rendering, popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online articles and GLSL code snippets. It is widely used in ray marching demos and real-time graphics engines due to its simplicity and efficiency. The function is often implemented as sdCapsule in GLSL libraries. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) quertzuiop/Volumetric-display, https://github.com/quertzuiop/Volumetric-display, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
