name: Cone Signed Distance Function
head: Cone SDF, Exact Cone SDF, Signed Capped Cone, Signed Cone, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Cone, sdCone
body: The Cone Signed Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point p to the surface of a capped cone, defined by its base radius r, height h, and orientation. It solves the problem of efficiently determining spatial containment and proximity for ray marching or collision detection against conical geometry. Unlike linear approximations, this method provides the true signed distance, ensuring safe step sizes in ray marching. It is distinct from the infinite cone SDF, which lacks base and tip caps, and from the cylinder, which has parallel sides. Inputs: p: Query point in 3D space (vec3). r: Base radius of the cone (float). h: Height of the cone (float). Coordinate System: The implementation assumes the cone is aligned with the Y-axis. The apex (tip) is located at the origin (0, 0, 0). The base is centered at (0, -h, 0) with radius r. The cone opens downward along the negative Y-axis. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The computation relies on 2D vector projections in the radial-vertical plane. Algorithm: 1. Radial Projection: Project the 3D point p into a 2D plane containing the cone's axis of symmetry. Let q be a 2D vector where the x-component is the radial distance from the Y-axis and the y-component is the height along the Y-axis: q = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}, py) 2. Define Geometry in 2D: Define the tip and base points in this 2D cross-section: \text{tip} = (0, 0) \text{base} = (r, -h) 3. Compute Distances: Calculate the distance to the side slope (mantle) and the distance to the base cap. Side Distance: The shortest distance from q to the line segment connecting \text{tip} and \text{base}. Let ba = \text{base} - \text{tip}. Let d1 = q - \text{tip}. Compute the projection parameter u of d1 onto ba: u = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{d1 \cdot ba}{ba \cdot ba}, 0.0, 1.0\right) The squared length of ba is m2 = r^2 + h^2. The closest point on the segment is p{seg} = \text{tip} + ba \cdot u. The side distance is: \text{side\dist} = \| q - p{seg} \| Base Cap Distance: The distance from q to the base disk. The base disk lies in the plane y = -h with radius r. Clamp the radial component of q to the base radius to find the closest point on the disk boundary if outside, or the projection if inside. Let q{base} = (\text{clamp}(qx, 0.0, r), -h). \text{cap\dist} = \| q - q{base} \| Unsigned Distance: \text{dist} = \min(\text{side\dist}, \text{cap\dist}) 4. Sign Determination (Inside Test): Determine if the point p is inside the cone volume. A point is inside if its height qy is between the tip and base (-h \le qy \le 0) and it lies "below" the slope line connecting the tip and base. The condition for being inside is: \text{inside} = (qy \le 0.0) \land (qy \ge -h) \land (qx \cdot h + qy \cdot r \le 0.0) Note: The term qx \cdot h + qy \cdot r \le 0.0 checks if the point is on the inner side of the line segment from (0,0) to (r,-h). The line equation is y = -\frac{h}{r}x \implies hx + ry = 0. For points inside (closer to axis), the value is negative. 5. Return Result: \text{result} = \begin{cases} -\text{dist} & \text{if inside} \\ \text{dist} & \text{if outside} \end{cases} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdcone(p: tuple, r: float, h: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a capped cone. Cone apex at (0,0,0), base center at (0,-h,0), radius r. Opens downward along -Y. """ # 1. Radial projection rad = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) q = (rad, p[1]) # 2. Define 2D geometry tip = (0.0, 0.0) base = (r, -h) # 3. Side distance calculation # Vector from tip to base ba = (base[0] - tip[0], base[1] - tip[1]) # Vector from tip to q d1 = (q[0] - tip[0], q[1] - tip[1]) # Squared length of ba m2 = ba[0]2 + ba[1]2 # Projection parameter u if m2 == 0: u = 0.0 else: u = (d1[0]ba[0] + d1[1]ba[1]) / m2 # Clamp u to segment u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) # Closest point on segment closestsidex = tip[0] + ba[0] u closestsidey = tip[1] + ba[1] u sidedist = math.sqrt((q[0] - closestsidex)2 + (q[1] - closestsidey)2) # 4. Base cap distance calculation # Clamp radial component to radius r qbasex = max(0.0, min(r, q[0])) qbasey = -h capdist = math.sqrt((q[0] - qbasex)2 + (q[1] - qbasey)2) # 5. Unsigned distance dist = min(sidedist, capdist) # 6. Inside test # q.y <= 0 (below tip) AND q.y >= -h (above base) AND inside slope # Slope line: y = -(h/r)x => hx + ry = 0. Inside is hx + ry <= 0 inside = (q[1] <= 0.0) and (q[1] >= -h) and ((q[0] h + q[1] r) <= 0.0) if inside: return -dist else: return dist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Cone: If r=0 or h=0, the cone degenerates to a line segment or a disk. The formula for m2 becomes 0, requiring a guard clause to avoid division by zero. Precision: The inside test relies on floating-point comparisons. Points very close to the surface may flip signs due to precision errors. Using a small epsilon for the inside test boundary can help stabilize shading normals. Axis Alignment: This specific implementation assumes the cone is aligned with the Y-axis. For arbitrary orientations, the point p must be transformed into the cone's local coordinate system before applying the function. Computes distance to an unbounded cone. Simpler formula but does not account for base or tip caps. Use when the cone is part of a larger structure where caps are handled by other primitives or when the cone extends to infinity. A cylinder with flat caps. Use for shapes with constant radius. The cone SDF is a generalization where the radius varies linearly with height. Time Complexity: O(1). The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations, square roots, and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are needed. Strengths: Provides exact distances, ensuring robust ray marching without overshooting. Differentiable almost everywhere, allowing for accurate normal computation via gradient \nabla d [Parent]. Limitations: The closed-form solution is more complex than simple primitives like spheres or boxes. The inside test logic is specific to the capped geometry and must be implemented carefully to avoid sign errors. When to use: When rendering or simulating conical objects (e.g., funnels, horns, certain architectural elements) where exact distance is required for correct marching steps or collision response. When not to use: If the cone is infinite or if approximate distance is sufficient and performance is critical, a simpler approximation or infinite cone SDF might be preferred. The exact signed distance function for a cone was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his article on distance functions for ray tracing. The derivation involves projecting the 3D point onto the 2D plane containing the cone's axis and computing the distance to the line segment representing the cone's profile in that plane. This method is widely used in ray marching shaders and implicit surface rendering. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, https://github.com/tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nschaievitch/sdf-editor, https://github.com/nschaievitch/sdf-editor, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Segment Signed Distance Function
head: Segment SDF, sdSegment, Distance to line segment
body: The Segment Signed Distance Function computes the shortest Euclidean distance from a query point p to a finite line segment defined by endpoints a and b. It solves the problem of defining a 1D geometric primitive in 3D space for ray marching, ensuring the distance field correctly accounts for the segment's finite bounds rather than treating it as an infinite line. It differs from infinite line distance functions by clamping the projection parameter to the segment's extent, and from point-to-segment distance by returning a scalar signed distance value suitable for marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p (vector), segment endpoints a and b (vectors). Output: Scalar signed distance d. Note: For a simple line segment (zero thickness), the "signed" aspect is often treated as unsigned distance in practice, or the sign is determined by a separate containment check. However, standard implementations return the non-negative Euclidean distance. The parent article defines sign for volumes; for a 1D curve, d \ge 0 always. If a signed field is required for a capsule (see Subtopics), the radius is subtracted. Data Structures: Vectors p, a, b are typically 3D floats (vec3) or 2D floats (vec2) depending on the dimensionality of the scene. Steps: 1. Compute the segment vector: ab = b - a. 2. Compute the vector from the start point to the query point: ap = p - a. 3. Compute the squared length of the segment: len\sq = ab \cdot ab. 4. Handle degenerate segments (where len\sq is near zero): If len\sq < \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-12}), the segment is effectively a point. The closest point is a. Return \|p - a\|. 5. Compute the projection parameter t (or h): t = \frac{ap \cdot ab}{len\sq} Clamp t to the range [0, 1]: t = \text{clamp}(t, 0.0, 1.0). 6. Compute the closest point on the segment: closest = a + ab \cdot t. 7. Compute the distance vector: diff = p - closest. 8. Return the Euclidean distance: d = \|diff\|. Formula: d(p) = \| p - (a + \text{clamp}(\frac{(p-a)\cdot(b-a)}{\|b-a\|^2}, 0, 1) \cdot (b-a)) \| Parameters: \epsilon: Threshold for degenerate segment length. Typical value: 10^{-12} or 10^{-8} depending on precision. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Segment: If a = b, division by zero occurs in step 5. Must check len\sq against a small epsilon. Precision: In floating-point arithmetic, very short segments may suffer from precision loss. Using squared lengths avoids square roots until the final step. Sign: For a pure line segment, the distance is always non-negative. To obtain a signed distance for a volume (like a capsule), subtract the radius. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdsegment(p, a, b, epsilon=1e-12): """ Computes the Euclidean distance from point p to the line segment [a, b]. Args: p: Query point (vec3 or vec2) a: Segment start point (vec3 or vec2) b: Segment end point (vec3 or vec2) epsilon: Threshold for degenerate segment check Returns: float: Distance from p to the segment """ # Step 1: Segment vector ab = b - a # Step 2: Vector from a to p ap = p - a # Step 3: Squared length of segment lensq = dot(ab, ab) # Step 4: Handle degenerate segment if lensq < epsilon: return length(p - a) # Step 5: Projection parameter t = dot(ap, ab) / lensq # Clamp t to [0, 1] t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Step 6: Closest point on segment closest = a + ab t # Step 7 & 8: Distance return length(p - closest) Computes the Euclidean distance from a query point p to a line segment defined by endpoints l0 and l1. It differs from infinite line distance by checking projection bounds before computing the final distance, ensuring the result correctly handles points outside the segment endpoints. This method is used as a signed distance field (SDF) primitive in ray marching. The Point on Segment Check determines whether a query point Q lies exactly on the line segment defined by endpoints Pi and Pj. It solves the geometric containment problem for 1D segments embedded in 2D or 3D space. It is distinguished from Line Segment Distance and Point-to-Segment Distance by returning a binary boolean result rather than a scalar distance value, serving as a primitive predicate within the Segment Signed Distance Function. Computes the closest point on a line segment [a, b] to a query point p. It differs from infinite line projection by clamping the projection parameter to [0, 1], ensuring the output lies on the closed segment. Signed distance to a 2D capsule (stadium) between points a and b with radius r. Formula: \text{segment}(p, a, b) - r. Unverified code. The computation involves a constant number of vector operations (subtraction, dot product, clamp, length). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are required. name: Line Segment Distance
head: Point-to-Line Distance Calculation, Segment SDF, sdSegment
body: Computes the Euclidean distance from a query point p to a line segment defined by endpoints l0 and l1. It differs from infinite line distance by checking projection bounds before computing the final distance, ensuring the result correctly handles points outside the segment endpoints. This method is used as a signed distance field (SDF) primitive in ray marching. Inputs: p: Query point (vec3). l0: Segment start point (vec3). l1: Segment end point (vec3). Outputs: dist: Euclidean distance (float). Data Structures: None required; scalar/vector operations only. Steps: 1. Compute vector v = l1 - l0. 2. Compute vector w = p - l0. 3. Compute dot product c1 = dot(v, w). 4. If c1 <= 0.0, the closest point is l0. Return length(p - l0). 5. Compute dot product c2 = dot(v, v). 6. If c2 <= c1, the closest point is l1. Return length(p - l1). 7. Compute projection parameter b = c1 / c2. 8. Compute projection point pb = l0 + b v. 9. Return length(p - pb). Formulas: v = l1 - l0 w = p - l0 c1 = v · w c2 = v · v b = c1 / c2 pb = l0 + b v dist = ||p - pb|| Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linesegmentdistance(p, l0, l1): v = l1 - l0 w = p - l0 c1 = dot(v, w) if c1 <= 0.0: return length(p - l0) c2 = dot(v, v) if c2 <= c1: return length(p - l1) b = c1 / c2 pb = l0 + b v return length(p - pb) Parameters: None. Edge Cases: Degenerate Segment: If l0 == l1, c2 is 0. Division by zero occurs in step 7. Guard against this by checking c2 < epsilon and returning length(p - l0) if true. Precision: Near-boundary cases may suffer from floating-point inaccuracies. Use a small epsilon for comparisons if high precision is required. Computes the distance from a point to an infinite line defined by two points. It differs from segment distance by omitting endpoint clamping, making it suitable for directional constraints or unbounded ray approximations. Choose it when the query geometry extends infinitely in both directions rather than being bounded by endpoints. Time Complexity: O(1). Fixed number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). name: Point-to-Line Distance
head: DistToLineSq, Distance to Line Squared, Point-to-Line Vector
body: Computes the vector from a point to the closest point on an infinite line, or the squared Euclidean distance to that line. It serves as the geometric core for Line Segment Distance, which clamps this result to segment bounds. Unlike segment distance, this method assumes an infinite extent, making it suitable for directional constraints or unbounded ray approximations. Inputs: p: The query point (3D vector). o: A point on the line (origin, 3D vector). d: The direction vector of the line (3D vector). Outputs: qp: The vector from the closest point on the line to p (3D vector). distSq: The squared Euclidean distance (scalar). Data Structures: Standard 3D floating-point vectors. No complex packing required. Steps: 1. Compute the projection scale factor scalefactor representing the position along the direction vector d closest to p: \text{scale\factor} = \frac{\mathbf{op} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}} where \mathbf{op} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}. 2. Compute the closest point q on the line: \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{o} + \text{scale\factor} \times \mathbf{d}. 3. Compute the residual vector qp from the closest point to the query point: \mathbf{qp} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}. 4. Compute the squared distance: \text{distSq} = \|\mathbf{qp}\|^2. Formula: The squared distance is computed via orthogonal projection subtraction: \text{distSq} = \| (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}) - \frac{(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}) \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}} \mathbf{d} \|^2 where \mathbf{op} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointtolinedistance(p, o, d): # Vector from line origin to point op = p - o # Dot products dotopd = dot(op, d) dotdd = dot(d, d) # Guard against zero-length direction vector if dotdd == 0.0: # Direction is zero; closest point is the origin itself qp = p - o distsq = dot(qp, qp) return qp, distsq # Projection scale factor scalefactor = dotopd / dotdd # Closest point on the infinite line q = o + scalefactor d # Vector from closest point to original point qp = p - q # Squared Euclidean distance distsq = dot(qp, qp) return qp, distsq Parameters: d must be non-zero. If d is zero, the line is undefined. Implementation should handle dot(d, d) == 0 to avoid division by zero. Edge Cases: Zero Direction: If \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{0}, the line collapses to a single point \mathbf{o}. The distance is \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}\|. Precision: For very long lines or small distances, floating-point cancellation may occur in \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}. Using the projection formula directly on the normalized direction may improve stability if \mathbf{d} is normalized beforehand. Time Complexity: O(1) constant time. Requires a few dot products and vector additions. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Extremely fast; no branching required if direction is guaranteed non-zero. Limitations: Does not account for segment endpoints. Using this for a segment without clamping yields incorrect distances near the ends. This method is a fundamental linear algebra operation used in computer graphics, physics engines, and geometric modeling. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Real-time BC6H compression on GPU, https://github.com/knarkowicz/GPURealTimeBC6H, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Point on Segment Check
head: onSegment, point-on-segment test
body: The Point on Segment Check determines whether a query point Q lies exactly on the line segment defined by endpoints Pi and Pj. It solves the geometric containment problem for 1D segments embedded in 2D or 3D space. It is distinguished from Line Segment Distance and Point-to-Segment Distance by returning a binary boolean result rather than a scalar distance value, serving as a primitive predicate within the Segment Signed Distance Function. Inputs: Pi: First endpoint of the segment (vector). Pj: Second endpoint of the segment (vector). Q: Query point (vector). \epsilon: Floating-point tolerance for equality comparison. Outputs: true if Q lies on the segment Pi Pj; false otherwise. Data Structures: Vectors Pi, Pj, Q are typically 3D Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). Distance is Euclidean: d(A, B) = \sqrt{(Ax-Bx)^2 + (Ay-By)^2 + (Az-Bz)^2}. Steps: 1. Compute the distance from Pi to Q: d1 = \text{distance}(Pi, Q). 2. Compute the distance from Pj to Q: d2 = \text{distance}(Pj, Q). 3. Compute the length of the segment Pi Pj: d3 = \text{distance}(Pi, Pj). 4. Compare the sum of the sub-segments to the total length using the tolerance \epsilon. If d3 + \epsilon < d1 + d2, return false. Otherwise, return true. Formulas: d1 = \| Q - Pi \| d2 = \| Q - Pj \| d3 = \| Pj - Pi \| Condition for containment: d1 + d2 \le d3 + \epsilon Parameters: \epsilon: Epsilon for floating-point comparison. Typical value is 10^{-8}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Segments: If Pi = Pj, then d3 = 0. The check returns true only if Q is also equal to Pi (within \epsilon). Floating Point Precision: Direct equality checks fail due to precision errors. The distance-sum method is preferred over ratio-based methods (checking if Q divides Pi Pj in a specific ratio) because ratio methods fail when the segment aligns with a primary axis, causing division by zero. Rounding Tolerance: Some implementations use rounding (e.g., Math.Round(dist2 + dist3, 3) == Math.Round(dist1, 3)) instead of additive epsilon, though additive epsilon is more standard in continuous geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def onsegment(Pi, Pj, Q, eps=1e-8): """ Check if point Q lies on the segment between Pi and Pj. Args: Pi: Tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) Pj: Tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) Q: Tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) eps: Floating point tolerance (default 1e-8) Returns: bool: True if Q is on the segment, False otherwise """ def distance(A, B): return math.sqrt((A[0]-B[0])2 + (A[1]-B[1])2 + (A[2]-B[2])2) dis1 = distance(Pi, Q) dis2 = distance(Pj, Q) dis3 = distance(Pi, Pj) if dis3 + eps < dis1 + dis2: return False return True Time Complexity: O(1) constant time. Requires 3 distance calculations (each involving 3 subtractions, 3 multiplications, 2 additions, and 1 square root) and 2 additions/comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Numerically stable; avoids division by zero errors associated with parametric/ratio checks; simple to implement. Limitations: Sensitive to the choice of \epsilon in high-precision or large-scale coordinate systems. The square root operations are computationally more expensive than squared-distance checks, but necessary here because the triangle inequality (d1 + d2 \ge d3) holds for Euclidean distances, not squared distances. The method is a standard geometric primitive used in computational geometry and computer graphics. It appears in implementations of volumetric photon mapping and voxel game engines as a helper for collision detection or point-in-segment validation. The distance-sum approach is cited as a robust alternative to ratio-based methods which suffer from axis-alignment singularities. jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, https://github.com/jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) TerryLyons16/MonoGameVoxelGameEngine, https://github.com/TerryLyons16/MonoGameVoxelGameEngine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Point-to-Segment Distance
head: Closest Point on Line Segment, Distance to line segment, closestPointOnSegment, closestPointOnSegmentToPoint
body: Computes the closest point on a line segment [a, b] to a query point p. It differs from infinite line projection by clamping the projection parameter to [0, 1], ensuring the output lies on the closed segment. Inputs: a: First endpoint of the segment (vector). b: Second endpoint of the segment (vector). p: Query point (vector). Outputs: closest: The point on the segment [a, b] closest to p (vector). Data Structures: Vectors must support arithmetic operations (+, -, scalar) and dot product (dot(u, v)). Steps: 1. Calculate the segment vector: segVec = b - a. 2. Calculate the projection parameter t using the dot product: t = \frac{\text{dot}(p - a, \text{segVec})}{\text{dot}(\text{segVec}, \text{segVec})}. 3. Clamp t to the range [0, 1] to ensure the point lies on the segment rather than the infinite line passing through it. 4. Calculate the destination point: closest = a + segVec t. 5. Return closest. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def closestPointOnSegment(a, b, p): segVec = b - a segLenSq = dot(segVec, segVec) # Guard for zero-length segment if segLenSq == 0: return a t = dot(p - a, segVec) / segLenSq # Clamp t to [0, 1] if t < 0.0: t = 0.0 elif t > 1.0: t = 1.0 return a + segVec t Parameters: Vec3T: Any vector type supporting arithmetic and dot product. Edge Cases: Degenerate Segment: If a == b, segLenSq is zero. Division by zero must be handled, typically by returning a. Precision: Floating-point inaccuracies may cause t to slightly exceed [0, 1] before clamping, but explicit clamping handles this. Time Complexity: O(1) constant time operations (vector subtractions, dot products, division, clamping). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Extremely fast and numerically stable for non-degenerate segments. Limitations: Requires special handling for zero-length segments to avoid division by zero. name: Higher Order Algebraic Signed Distance Fields
head: HOASDFs
body: Higher Order Algebraic Signed Distance Fields (HOASDFs) generalize traditional signed distance fields by approximating the distance function over a larger area using local Taylor approximations or least squares fit polynomials. Inputs: A set of sample points with associated distance values and, optionally, partial derivatives for Hermite interpolation. Outputs: A query function D(\mathbf{x}) that returns the signed distance and potentially geometric properties such as surface normals at any point \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The field stores coefficients for polynomial approximations. Taylor Fields: Store the value and partial derivatives up to order n at each sample point. Least Squares Fields: Store coefficients of a polynomial fitted to a local neighborhood of samples. Steps: 1. Formulation: Formulate the sampling and reconstruction process as a function approximation problem combining local Taylor approximations. 2. Accuracy Characterization: Derive the error bound for arbitrary sampling topologies and interpolation schemes by noting that the error bound of a combination of Taylor approximations is closed under convex barycentric combination. 3. Extension to Least Squares: Extend the framework to least squares fit polynomial fields. 4. Implementation: For regular grids, utilize GPU filtering to implement highly efficient queries on both Taylor and least squares fields. 5. Hermite Interpolation: Store partial derivatives directly in the field data and use Hermite interpolation for queries, trading query time for higher accuracy. 6. Conversion: Convert traditional zero order signed distance fields to higher order representations using a general framework. 7. Optimization: Decrease filtering footprint size via simplicial interpolation schemes to balance performance and storage. Formulas: The Taylor expansion of the distance function D around a sample point \mathbf{s} up to order n is: D(\mathbf{x}) \approx D(\mathbf{s}) + \nabla D(\mathbf{s}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{s}) + \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{s})^T \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{s}) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{s}) + \dots where \nabla D(\mathbf{s}) is the gradient and \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{s}) is the Hessian matrix at \mathbf{s}. The final query result is computed as a convex barycentric combination of these local expansions. Parameters: Order (n): The degree of the Taylor approximations or polynomial fields used to represent the distance function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Higher order expansions amplify floating-point errors near the surface; clamping or fallback to zero-order queries may be required. Boundaries: Sampling irregularities at domain edges break barycentric weight computation; padding or boundary-aware interpolation is needed. Degenerate Input: Collinear or coplanar sample points produce singular barycentric systems; fallback to inverse-distance weighting or grid-aligned queries is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryhoasdf(x, samples, order): # samples: list of dicts with keys 'pos', 'val', 'grad', 'hess' weights = computebarycentricweights(x, samples) result = 0.0 for i, s in enumerate(samples): delta = [x[j] - s['pos'][j] for j in range(3)] polyval = s['val'] if order >= 1: polyval += sum(s['grad'][j] delta[j] for j in range(3)) if order >= 2: polyval += 0.5 sum(s['hess'][j][k] delta[j] delta[k] for j in range(3) for k in range(3)) result += weights[i] polyval return result def computebarycentricweights(x, samples): # Compute barycentric coordinates for a simplex (4 points in 3D) # Fallback to inverse-distance weighting if topology is not a simplex if len(samples) == 4: p0, p1, p2, p3 = [s['pos'] for s in samples] v0 = [p1[j]-p0[j] for j in range(3)] v1 = [p2[j]-p0[j] for j in range(3)] v2 = [p3[j]-p0[j] for j in range(3)] d00 = sum(v0[j]v0[j] for j in range(3)) d01 = sum(v0[j]v1[j] for j in range(3)) d02 = sum(v0[j]v2[j] for j in range(3)) d11 = sum(v1[j]v1[j] for j in range(3)) d12 = sum(v1[j]v2[j] for j in range(3)) d22 = sum(v2[j]v2[j] for j in range(3)) denom = d00 d11 - d01 d01 w1 = (d11 d02 - d01 d12) / denom w2 = (d00 d12 - d01 d02) / denom w3 = 1.0 - w1 - w2 w0 = 1.0 - w1 - w2 - w3 return [w0, w1, w2, w3] else: dists = [sum((x[j] - s['pos'][j])2 for j in range(3)) for s in samples] invdists = [1.0 / (d + 1e-8) for d in dists] total = sum(invdists) return [w / total for w in invdists] Use local Taylor expansions. Sets apart by leveraging derivative data for higher accuracy. Choose when query accuracy is prioritized over raw speed. Link Fit polynomials to local neighborhoods. Sets apart by smoothing noise across samples. Choose when robustness to sampling irregularities is needed. Link Stores partial derivatives directly. Sets apart by enabling exact gradient reconstruction at sample points. Choose when surface normals or precise geometric properties are required. Link Time Complexity: Query time is higher than zero-order SDFs, especially for Hermite interpolation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the order and number of coefficients stored per sample. Performance: GPU filtering can be utilized for efficient queries on regular grids. Accuracy: Higher order fields provide better accuracy and can infer geometric properties like normals. Storage: Techniques decrease filtering footprint size to balance performance and storage, improving quality without increasing footprint. When to use: When higher accuracy is needed without increasing sampling density, or when geometric properties like normals are required. When not to use: When query performance is critical and lower accuracy is acceptable. Proposed by Gábor Valasek and Róbert Bán in January 2022. It addresses limitations of classical sphere tracing and zero-order SDFs by leveraging higher-order derivative information. name: Smooth Blending and CSG Operations
head: Smooth Minimum, SDF Boolean Operations, Constructive Solid Geometry with SDFs
body: This family defines the mathematical operators and coordinate transformations required to construct complex procedural geometry from primitive Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). It solves the problem of combining simple shapes into complex models and positioning them in world space. It is distinguished from exact Boolean operations by its support for smooth blending approximations, which allow for continuous gradients and organic transitions between shapes, at the cost of distance field accuracy. The core mechanism involves evaluating primitive SDF functions Si(\mathbf{p}) at query points \mathbf{x}, applying coordinate transformations, and combining the resulting scalar distances using specific binary operators. Coordinate Transformation: To evaluate a primitive in world space, the query point \mathbf{x} is transformed into the primitive's local space. This involves: 1. Subtracting translation \mathbf{t}: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}. 2. Applying rotation \mathbf{R}: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{R}^T \mathbf{p} (assuming \mathbf{R} is orthonormal). 3. Applying scale s: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p} / s. The resulting distance di must be divided by the scale factor |s| to maintain correct distance metric properties. Domain Repetition (Tiling): For periodic structures, a modulo operation is applied to local coordinates before evaluation: \mathbf{p}{mod} = \mathbf{p} - \lfloor \mathbf{p} / \mathbf{period} + 0.5 \rfloor \cdot \mathbf{period} Exact Boolean Operations: These operators combine distances d1 and d2 to form unions, intersections, and subtractions: Union: d{union} = \min(d1, d2). This returns the distance to the closest shape exterior edge. Intersection: d{intersect} = \max(d1, d2). Subtraction: d{sub} = \max(d1, -d2) (subtracting shape 2 from shape 1). Smooth Blending: Approximate unions/subtractions are achieved with a transition controlled by parameter k. These are no longer exact distance fields but distorted approximations. Two primary formulations are used: 1. Exponential Smooth Minimum: \text{smin}(a, b, k) = -k \cdot \log2(2^{-a/k} + 2^{-b/k}) Alternatively using natural base e: \text{smin}(a, b, k) = -k \cdot \ln(e^{-a/k} + e^{-b/k}) 2. Polynomial (Hermite) Smooth Minimum: h = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{0.5 + 0.5(b - a)}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) \text{smin}(a, b, k) = \text{lerp}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where \text{lerp}(b, a, h) = (1.0 - h)a + hb. Data Structures: Operations are often stored in a tree structure within GPU buffers. The specific layout for an SDF operation block is defined as: SdfOpSpecificBlock mat4s: Array of 2 Mat4 matrices. vec4s: Array of 3 Vec4 vectors. floats: Array of 2 f32 scalars. SdfBoundingBoxBlock matrix: Mat4. scale: Vec4. fullinverse: Mat4. transinverse: Mat4. SdfOpBlock (Parent container) opcode: u32 (Operation identifier). isprimitive: bool. parentisunion: bool. len: u32. level: u32. opspecific: SdfOpSpecificBlock. boundingbox: SdfBoundingBoxBlock. otherbox: SdfBoundingBoxBlock. This method defines the mathematical operators and coordinate transformations required to construct complex procedural geometry from primitive Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). It solves the problem of combining simple shapes into complex models and positioning them in world space. It is distinguished from exact Boolean operations by its support for smooth blending approximations, which allow for continuous gradients and organic transitions between shapes, at the cost of distance field accuracy. A function used in Dreams to blend primitive shapes over a fixed radius, allowing for smoothed addition and subtraction in CSG operations. The specific formula is not provided in the text, but it is noted that the standard smooth minimum has an infinite range (reaching zero at infinity). Dreams uses a modified formula that blends over a fixed radius. Blend radius: A specified radius over which shapes blend. This replaces the infinite range of the standard smooth minimum. Used in Dreams for creating intuitive sculpting tools for user-generated content. The SDF for bubbles is defined as the union of N ellipsoids. Since ellipsoid SDFs lack a simple closed form, a lower bound of the signed distance field is used. Each bubble i has position \mathbf{x}i, semi-axis lengths \mathbf{r}i, and orientation angles \thetai, \phii in the \{X, Z\} and \{Y, Z\} planes. The full bubble field SDF is the union of all N individual distance functions: S{bubbles}(\mathbf{x}) = \bigcup{i=1}^N Bi(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{r}i, \thetai, \phii), where the union operator \mathcal{S} is defined by \mathcal{S}(S1, S2) = \min(S1, S2). The bubbles are subtracted from the displaced panel using the intersection operator \bigcap, defined by \bigcap(S1, S2) = \max(S1, -S2). The final distance function is S{final} = \bigcap(S{panel}, S{bubbles}). To manage a high number of bubbles efficiently, a regular voxel grid is defined inside the panel. Each voxel contains a maximum of one bubble to prevent overlapping. This allows S{bubbles} to be interpreted as a single SDF and traversed using a fast voxel traversal algorithm. The application of SDFs to Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) allows for the construction of 3D shapes through unions and subtractions of primitives, enabling simple and intuitive sculpting tools. This approach is particularly favorable in user-generated content games like Dreams, where objects are constructed from lists of edits (primitive shapes) applied in a linear, right-leaning CSG tree. The use of smooth blending functions, such as the smooth minimum, facilitates organic transitions between shapes, although these functions traditionally have an infinite range, requiring modification for fixed-radius blending in specific applications. In scientific and industrial contexts, such as the modeling of old glass, SDFs are used to represent complex features like bubbles. These are modeled as unions of ellipsoids (using lower-bound approximations due to the lack of closed-form ellipsoid SDFs) and subtracted from base panels. To handle high densities of such features, spatial partitioning structures like regular voxel grids are employed to enable efficient traversal and evaluation. Apply rotation: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{R}^T \mathbf{p} (assuming \mathbf{R} is orthonormal). Apply scale: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p} / s. The resulting distance di must be divided by the scale factor |s| to maintain correct distance metric properties. 2. Domain Repetition (Tiling): For periodic structures, apply a modulo operation to the local coordinates before evaluation: \mathbf{p}{mod} = \mathbf{p} - \lfloor \mathbf{p} / \mathbf{period} + 0.5 \rfloor \cdot \mathbf{period} Evaluate the primitive at \mathbf{p}{mod}. 3. Exact Boolean Operations: Combine distances d1 and d2: Union: d{union} = \min(d1, d2). This returns the distance to the closest shape exterior edge. Intersection: d{intersect} = \max(d1, d2). Subtraction: d{sub} = \max(d1, -d2) (subtracting shape 2 from shape 1). 4. Smooth Blending: Approximate unions/subtractions with a transition controlled by parameter k. These are no longer exact distance fields but distorted approximations. Exponential Smooth Minimum: \text{smin}(a, b, k) = -k \cdot \log2(2^{-a/k} + 2^{-b/k}) Alternatively using natural base e: \text{smin}(a, b, k) = -k \cdot \ln(e^{-a/k} + e^{-b/k}) Polynomial (Hermite) Smooth Minimum: h = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{0.5 + 0.5(b - a)}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) \text{smin}(a, b, k) = \text{lerp}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where \text{lerp}(b, a, h) = (1.0 - h)a + hb. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def transformpoint(x, t, R, s): """ Transform world point x to local space. t: translation vector R: rotation matrix (orthonormal) s: scale factor (scalar) """ p = x - t p = R.transpose() @ p p = p / s return p def domainrepetition(p, period): """ Apply modulo tiling to local coordinates. p: local point vector period: period vector """ # floor(p / period + 0.5) period shift = (p / period + 0.5).floor() period return p - shift def exactunion(d1, d2): return min(d1, d2) def exactintersection(d1, d2): return max(d1, d2) def exactsubtraction(d1, d2): """Subtract shape 2 from shape 1.""" return max(d1, -d2) def smoothminexponential(a, b, k): """ Exponential smooth minimum. k: blend factor (smaller k = sharper transition) """ if k == 0: return min(a, b) r = math.exp2(-a / k) + math.exp2(-b / k) return -k math.log2(r) def smoothminpolynomial(a, b, k): """ Polynomial (Hermite) smooth minimum. k: blend factor """ if k == 0: return min(a, b) h = max(0.0, min(1.0, (0.5 + 0.5 (b - a)) / k)) lerpval = (1.0 - h) a + h b return lerpval - k h (1.0 - h) def evaluatesdf(x, primitives, transforms, blendfunc, k): """ Evaluate combined SDF. primitives: list of SDF functions transforms: list of (t, R, s) tuples blendfunc: function for combining distances k: blend parameter """ # Assuming binary tree structure or sequential combination # This is a simplified example for two primitives p1local = transformpoint(x, transforms[0]) d1 = primitives0 / transforms[0][2] # Divide by scale p2local = transformpoint(x, transforms[1]) d2 = primitives1 / transforms[1][2] # Divide by scale return blendfunc(d1, d2, k) Parameters: k: The smoothness parameter. Smaller values yield sharper transitions closer to exact Boolean operations. Typical values depend on the scale of the scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interior Distance Breaks: Union breaks the interior distance field, returning a greater distance than it should. This can break outline thickness or require more raymarching steps. Exterior Distance Breaks: Subtraction and intersection break the exterior distance field. Approximation Errors: Smooth blending functions are no longer exact distance fields but distorted approximations. The more distorted they become, the more difficult they may be to work with. A data structure for storing SDF operations in a buffer, typically used in GPU compute shaders. It contains operation codes, primitive flags, and specific transformation data. Layout (repr C): opcode (u32), isprimitive (bool), parentisunion (bool), len (u32), level (u32), opspecific (SdfOpSpecificBlock), boundingbox (SdfBoundingBoxBlock), otherbox (SdfBoundingBoxBlock). The distance to the closest shape exterior edge is the lesser of the two distances. Can be repeated for 3 or more shapes by chaining the operation. Pitfall: Union breaks the interior distance field, returning a greater distance than it should. This can break outline thickness or require more raymarching steps. To subtract shape 2 from shape 1: take the maximum of shapedist1 and the negation of shapedist2. To subtract shape 1 from shape 2: take the maximum of shapedist2 and the negation of shapedist1. Pitfall: Subtraction breaks the exterior distance field. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. Complex scenes require traversing the operation tree, so complexity is proportional to the number of primitives. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the operation tree. The SdfOpBlock structure requires fixed-size buffers. Strengths: Allows for infinite resolution and compact storage of complex geometry. Smooth blending enables organic shapes. Limitations: Smooth blending is not an exact distance field, which can affect shading and normal calculation accuracy. Exact Boolean operations can break distance field properties (interior/exterior), requiring more raymarching steps or specialized handling. When to use: When procedural generation, infinite resolution, or smooth blending is required. When not to use: When exact distance field properties are critical for all operations, or when the scene complexity exceeds the capacity of the operation tree structure. Inigo Quilez produced the first results recognizable as modern SDF in 2007, demonstrating techniques for efficient soft shadows, smooth blending, and domain repetition. This work built upon earlier foundations by Alex Evan (2006) and Keenan Crane (2005). The method has since become a standard technique in procedural rendering and raymarching. name: Gradient-SDF
head: Gradient-SDF representation
body:
Gradient-SDF is a hybrid 3D geometry representation that augments a voxel-based implicit Signed Distance Field (SDF) with the SDF gradient vector field at each voxel, combining implicit topology handling with explicit surface feature access. It solves the problem of costly neighbor lookups required for gradient computation in sparse SDF storage (e.g., hash maps) by storing gradients directly, enabling efficient interpolation via first-order Taylor expansion without accessing multiple voxels. Unlike standard sparse SDFs which require accessing 8 voxels for interpolation or gradient computation, Gradient-SDF allows direct access to the gradient per voxel, facilitating direct SDF tracking from depth images and photometric bundle adjustment directly in the voxel representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of depth images (and optionally RGB images), camera poses (initially estimated or optimized), and a voxel size vs. Output: A set of voxels vj, each storing an SDF value \psij, a weight Wj, and an accumulated gradient vector gj. Optionally, extracted surface points, normals, or meshes. Data Structures: Each voxel vj stores three fields: 1. SDF value \psij: A scalar representing the signed distance to the closest surface point. 2. Weight Wj: A scalar indicating the reliability of the SDF estimate. 3. Accumulated gradient vector gj: A 3D vector storing the weighted sum of surface normals. Voxels are stored in a hash map (one voxel per entry) rather than contiguous memory, allowing compact storage where voxels far from the surface (zero weight) are not explicitly stored. Implementation uses single precision floats for GradSdfVoxels. Numbered Steps: 1. Voxel Indexing: For a query point p, compute the voxel index j^ by rounding p/vs (voxel size), leveraging the regular grid structure to avoid neighbor search. j^ = 	ext{round}(p / vs) The rounding operation maps the continuous coordinate to the integer grid index of the voxel containing p. 2. SDF Update: For a new distance estimate d(vj) at voxel vj with weight w(vj), update the SDF value and total weight: Wj \leftarrow Wj + w(vj) \psij \leftarrow  rac{Wj \psij + w(vj) d(vj)}{Wj + w(vj)} If Wj is initially 0, \psij becomes d(vj). 3. Gradient Update: Update the accumulated gradient vector gj by adding the weighted inwards-pointing surface normal n(vj) at the closest surface point: gj \leftarrow gj + w(vj) n(vj) In most applications, normals are already computed from the incoming data (e.g., depth maps) for filtering or rendering, so the computation does not introduce overhead. 4. Gradient Normalization: Normalize the accumulated gradient to get the actual gradient estimate \hat{g}j at vj: \hat{g}j =  rac{gj}{|gj|} If |gj| \approx 0, the gradient is undefined; the voxel may be ignored or treated as non-surface. 5. Distance and Gradient Approximation: To evaluate the distance dS(p) and its gradient 
abla dS(p) for a point p near voxel v{j^}, use the first-order Taylor expansion: d^{our}S(p) = \psi{j^} + (p - v{j^}) \cdot \hat{g}{j^} 
abla d^{our}S(p) = \hat{g}{j^} where j^ = \arg \minj \|p - vj\|. Since vj are on a regular grid, j^ is computed by rounding p/vs. 6. Closest Surface Point: Compute the closest surface point ps for a voxel vj: ps(vj) = vj - \psij \hat{g}j 7. Photometric Bundle Adjustment (Optional): If optimizing poses and geometry using RGB data, minimize the energy E(R, t): E(R, t) = \sumk wk dS(R pk + t)^2 where pk are points in the world frame, and R, t are rotation and translation. Optimize by alternating minimization of poses and distances to reduce computational cost. Limit pose optimization to voxels containing surface points. Use a Gauss-Newton solver with Cholesky decomposition for the linear system. Project the real surface point vj - \psij \hat{g}j into RGB images Ii rather than voxel centers. Compute voxel color ho^cj after optimization: ho^cj =  rac{1}{Nj} \sumi 
u{ij} I^c{ij} where 
u{ij} is a visibility indicator and Nj is the number of valid observations. 8. Surface Extraction (Oriented Point Cloud): Extract surface points ps(vj) and normals -\hat{g}j from voxels where |\psij \hat{g}j| \le vs^2 (component-wise). This results in a homogeneously sampled, consistently oriented point cloud. 9. Geometry Upsampling: Subdivide each voxel into four subvoxels, determine distance using Taylor expansion, and extract surfels from subvoxels where |\psij \hat{g}j| \le vs^2/4. 10. Mesh Extraction (Layered Marching Cubes): Extract min/max x, y, z coordinates to get bounding box. Allocate two voxel layers of size (x{max}-x{min}) 	imes (y{max}-y{min}). Fill with first two z-layers (weights, colors, distances). Apply Marching Cubes on the layer interface. Shift layers: refill the first layer with the next z-values and repeat. Parameters: Voxel size vs: Determines grid resolution. Typical values are not given in the sources. Weight w(vj): Reliability of the estimate. Typical values are not given in the sources. Precision: Single precision floats. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Storage Cost: In sparse storage (hash maps), standard SDF gradient computation is costly because neighbor lookups require additional hash table accesses, especially for voxels near block boundaries (57.8% of voxels in an 8^3 block). Gradient-SDF avoids this by storing gradients directly. Zero Gradient: If gj is zero (no surface evidence), normalization fails. Check for a zero vector before normalization. Time Complexity: Distance and gradient evaluation is O(1) per query due to direct voxel lookup via rounding, avoiding neighbor searches. Pose optimization uses Gauss-Newton with Cholesky decomposition, complexity depends on the number of active voxels and points. Memory Complexity: Hash map storage scales with the number of non-zero weight voxels. On the 00577 sofa sequence, the hash map-based Gradient-SDF method uses more than 20x less memory than dense storage of SDF Tracker [8], despite having three more entries per voxel. Measured Performance: On synthetic data, mean angular deviation for Gradient-SDF gradients within 10 voxel sizes from surface is 5.07°, compared to 9.49° for central finite differences. On the 00577 sofa sequence, it achieves comparable ATE to SDF-Fusion but is much faster. Strengths: Efficient interpolation without neighbor lookups; accurate gradient estimates; compact sparse storage; enables direct photometric bundle adjustment in voxel space. Limitations: Requires storing an extra 3D vector per voxel; hash map overhead may be higher than contiguous arrays for very dense grids. When to use: When sparse storage is needed for large scenes, and efficient gradient-based optimization (tracking, BA) is required. When not to use: When dense volumetric operations are needed, or when memory overhead of hash maps is prohibitive compared to contiguous storage. Gradient-SDF was proposed in "Gradient-SDF: A Semi-Implicit Surface Representation for 3D Reconstruction" (2022). It builds on the idea of combining implicit voxel SDFs with explicit surfel features to overcome the limitations of pure voxel or surfel representations, particularly in sparse storage scenarios. It is used for direct SDF tracking from depth images and photometric bundle adjustment directly in voxel representation. name: SDF Transformation
head: SDF Transforms, Transformed SDF, Transforming SDFs, SDF Affine Transformation, SDF Model Transformations, SDF Inverse Transformation, SDF Spatial Transformations, Rigid Body Transformation of SDFs, Inverse Transformation for Rotation/Translation
body: SDF Transformation is a technique for applying geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling, and deformation) to Signed Distance Field primitives by manipulating the query point coordinates before evaluating the distance function. It solves the problem of positioning, orienting, and scaling implicit surfaces without modifying the underlying primitive definitions or requiring mesh regeneration. Unlike Spatial and nD transforms which describe the general coordinate change, this method specifically details the inverse-application strategy and the necessary distance compensation for non-isometric transforms. It sets itself apart from Uniform Scaling of SDFs by handling general affine and non-linear deformations, though uniform scaling is a specific sub-case requiring distance multiplication. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{p} in world space, a transformation T (defined by parameters such as translation vector \mathbf{d}, rotation matrix R, scale factor s, or deformation function), and a base SDF function f(\mathbf{x}). Output: The signed distance d from \mathbf{p} to the transformed surface, and optionally the surface normal \mathbf{n}. Data Structures: Transformation Matrix: A 4 \times 4 homogeneous matrix M representing the local-to-world transform (Scale, Rotation, Translation). Inverse Matrix: M^{-1}, used to transform the query point from world space to the primitive's local space. Parameters: Translation \mathbf{d}: 3D vector. Rotation: Angle \theta and axis (e.g., Y-axis). Scale s: Scalar (uniform) or vector (non-uniform). Deformation: Coefficients for bending, twisting, or warping. Steps: 1. Compute Inverse Transform: Determine the inverse of the transformation T that maps world coordinates to the primitive's local coordinates. For rigid body transformations (rotation/translation), this is the inverse matrix T^{-1}. 2. Transform Query Point: Apply T^{-1} to the world-space query point \mathbf{p} to obtain the local-space point \mathbf{p}{local}. For affine transforms: \mathbf{p}{local} = T^{-1}(\mathbf{p}). For specific operations like translation by \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{p}{local} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{d}. For rotation by angle \theta around Y-axis: \mathbf{p}{local} = \text{rotateY}(-\theta) \cdot \mathbf{p} (using transpose for inverse in GLSL). 3. Evaluate Base SDF: Query the base distance function with the transformed point: d' = f(\mathbf{p}{local}). 4. Compensate Distance (Non-Isometric): If the transformation is not an isometry (e.g., scaling or non-linear deformation), adjust the returned distance d' to preserve the signed distance property. For uniform scale s: d = s \cdot d'. For non-linear deformations: Use Lipschitz bounds or accept that the result is an approximation. 5. Return Result: Return the compensated distance d. Formulas: General Transformed Surface: f(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) = 0. Isometry Distance Preservation: d(\mathbf{x}, I \circ f^{-1}(0)) = d(I^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), f^{-1}(0)). No distance adjustment needed. Uniform Scale: S(\mathbf{x}) = s\mathbf{x}. Inverse: S^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{s}\mathbf{x}. Distance: d(\mathbf{x}, S(f^{-1}(0))) = s \cdot d(S^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), f^{-1}(0)). Twist: \mathbf{q} = \text{rotateY}(\mathbf{p}, 0.5 \times py). Bend: Rotation in X-Y plane by angle proportional to X. Repetition (Infinite Tile): \mathbf{p}' = \text{mod}(\mathbf{p} + 0.5c, c) - 0.5c. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def transformsdf(p: Vector3, transform: Transform, basesdf: Callable[[Vector3], float]) -> float: """ Evaluate an SDF with a geometric transformation applied. Args: p: Query point in world space. transform: Object containing transformation parameters (matrix, scale, etc.). basesdf: The underlying SDF function (e.g., sphere, box). Returns: Signed distance to the transformed surface. """ # Step 1 & 2: Transform point to local space # For affine transforms (Rotation, Translation, Uniform Scale) if transform.isaffine: # Compute inverse transform matrix # Note: In GLSL, inverse of rotation is transpose (negative angle) invmatrix = transform.getinversematrix() # Convert point to homogeneous coordinates phomogeneous = Vector4(p.x, p.y, p.z, 1.0) # Apply inverse transform plocalhomogeneous = invmatrix phomogeneous # Extract xyz plocal = Vector3(plocalhomogeneous.x, plocalhomogeneous.y, plocalhomogeneous.z) else: # For non-linear deformations (Twist, Bend, Warp) plocal = transform.applyinverse(p) # Step 3: Evaluate base SDF dlocal = basesdf(plocal) # Step 4: Compensate distance for non-isometric transforms if transform.isscale: # Uniform scaling requires multiplying distance by scale factor # dnew = s dold dcompensated = transform.scalefactor dlocal elif transform.isdeformation: # Non-linear deformations break strict SDF properties. # For accurate bounds, Lipschitz constants are required. # Here we return the raw value, noting it may not be a true distance. dcompensated = dlocal else: # Isometries (Rotation, Translation) preserve distance dcompensated = dlocal return dcompensated def getgradient(p: Vector3, transform: Transform, basesdf: Callable[[Vector3], float]) -> Vector3: """ Compute the gradient (normal) for a transformed SDF. Requires transforming the gradient vector back to world space. """ # Transform point to local space if transform.isaffine: invmatrix = transform.getinversematrix() phomogeneous = Vector4(p.x, p.y, p.z, 1.0) plocal = Vector3((invmatrix phomogeneous).xyz) else: plocal = transform.applyinverse(p) # Get local gradient gradlocal = basesdf.gradient(plocal) # Transform gradient to world space # The gradient transforms with the inverse transpose of the position transform # For rigid body transforms, this is just the rotation part of the forward matrix if transform.isaffine: worldmatrix = transform.getforwardmatrix() # Extract rotation part (upper 3x3) rotmatrix = worldmatrix.getrotationmatrix() gradworld = rotmatrix gradlocal else: # For non-linear, Jacobian is needed gradworld = gradlocal # Approximation return gradworld Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GLSL Matrix Inversion: WebGL/GLSL lacks a built-in matrix inversion routine. For rotation matrices, use the transpose (negative angle) as the inverse. Non-Uniform Scaling: Non-uniform scaling distorts distances anisotropically. Simple multiplication by a scalar is insufficient; conservative bounds or Lipschitz constants are required to prevent ray tunneling. Non-Linear Deformation: Deformations like twist or bend modify space as a function of position, breaking local linearity. This can invalidate normal estimation and step sizes in ray marching. Repetition Boundaries: Infinite tiling requires the position to be in the positive quadrant for modulo operations to work correctly, otherwise the shape may disappear. Lipschitz Transformation Bounds provide a method for computing accurate distance fields for implicitly defined surfaces after applying spatial transformations (such as scaling, rotation, or deformation) by adjusting the distance estimate using the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation. Unlike standard Euclidean ray marching which assumes the metric is preserved, this method compensates for the distortion introduced by non-isometric transforms, preventing ray tunneling and ensuring the distance function remains a valid lower bound. It sets itself apart from Uniform Scaling of SDFs by handling general non-uniform and non-linear deformations, and from Spatial and nD transforms by explicitly deriving and applying the Lipschitz bound to correct the distance value rather than just transforming the query point. Implicit Surface Field Function Evaluation computes the signed distance (or density) value d = f(\mathbf{p}) for a 3D point \mathbf{p} relative to a target surface. It solves the problem of determining whether a point lies inside, outside, or on the boundary of a geometric primitive or voxelized field, which is the fundamental query required for ray marching, mesh extraction, and differentiable rendering. It differs from sibling methods like Batched SDF Inference by focusing on the mathematical evaluation of a single or small set of points rather than large-scale batched inference, and from SDF Validity Check with Relaxation by providing the raw metric value rather than a binary validity classification. Uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an implicit surface by a uniform factor while preserving the correctness of the distance value for ray marching. It solves the problem that scaling is not a rigid body transformation and distorts distances; without correction, the ray marching algorithm may overestimate the distance to the surface, causing the object to disappear. Unlike Non-Uniform Scaling of SDFs, which requires conservative bounds to avoid overestimation, uniform scaling allows for an exact compensation of distance distortion. Spatial and nD transforms allow the application of geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling, and permutation) to Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitives and discrete data structures by applying the inverse transformation to the query point rather than transforming the geometry itself. This approach ensures that the underlying data structures remain unmodified, preserving local linearity and allowing constant-time affine queries per dimension. It differs from direct geometry transformation by deferring the coordinate change to the evaluation step, which avoids distorting the stored data and supports non-uniform or spatially varying distortions. A technique to create a 'blob effect' by perturbing the position \mathbf{p} with trigonometric functions before querying the SDF. This is noted as 'cheating' because it breaks the strict mathematical properties of the SDF. Step: Perturb coordinates: px += 0.02 \cos(8 py + 3 pz) py += 0.02 \sin(6 pz + 7 px) pz += 0.02 \cos(8 px + 9 px). Time Complexity: O(1) per query, assuming the transformation matrix inversion is precomputed. The cost is dominated by the base SDF evaluation and the matrix-vector multiplication. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for storing the transformation matrix and parameters. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to the lack of branching and simple arithmetic operations. Strengths: No need to regenerate geometry; supports dynamic animations (e.g., time-varying rotation/translation). Limitations: Non-isometric transforms (scaling, deformation) require distance compensation or result in invalid SDFs (overestimation). Non-linear deformations break the guarantee of the distance field being a true metric, potentially causing ray marching artifacts. SDF transformations are a fundamental technique in ray marching and implicit surface rendering, popularized by shaders and demos in the demoscene and real-time graphics. The mathematical foundation relies on the properties of isometries and the chain rule for distance functions. Key references include Hart's work on GPU ray marching of distance fields and Quilez's tutorials on SDF operations. The technique is widely used in real-time rendering for procedural geometry, animation, and scene composition. name: Lipschitz Transformation Bounds
head: Distances to Transformed Objects, SDF Transformation with Lipschitz Bounds, Transformed implicit surfaces
body: Lipschitz Transformation Bounds provide a method for computing accurate distance fields for implicitly defined surfaces after applying spatial transformations (such as scaling, rotation, or deformation) by adjusting the distance estimate using the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation. Unlike standard Euclidean ray marching which assumes the metric is preserved, this method compensates for the distortion introduced by non-isometric transforms, preventing ray tunneling and ensuring the distance function remains a valid lower bound. It sets itself apart from Uniform Scaling of SDFs by handling general non-uniform and non-linear deformations, and from Spatial and nD transforms by explicitly deriving and applying the Lipschitz bound to correct the distance value rather than just transforming the query point. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base Signed Distance Field (SDF) function f(\mathbf{x}), a spatial transformation T(\mathbf{x}), and a query point \mathbf{x} in the transformed space. Output: The corrected distance d to the transformed implicit surface at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The transformation T is defined by its inverse T^{-1}, which maps the query point back to the object's local space. The Lipschitz constant L is a scalar value derived from the maximum norm of the Jacobian of T^{-1} over the relevant domain. Method Steps: 1. Define the Transformed Surface: The transformed implicit surface is defined as the set of points where the base function evaluated at the inverse-transformed coordinates is zero: f(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) = 0 \quad \text{(Eq. 44)} 2. Compute Local Distance: Evaluate the base SDF at the inverse-transformed point to get the uncorrected distance: d{local} = f(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) Note: In practice, T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) is computed, and f is evaluated there. 3. Determine Lipschitz Constant (L): Calculate the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation T^{-1}. The Lipschitz constant of the composition is no greater than the product of the component Lipschitz constants. The specific method for determining L depends on the type of transformation: Isometry: If T is an isometry (rotation, translation, reflection), distances are preserved. The distance returned by the base SDF needs no adjustment: d(T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})) = d(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) - T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})) \quad \text{(Eq. 45)} Here, the effective Lipschitz constant is 1. Uniform Scale: If T is a uniform scale by factor s, the inverse is a scale by 1/s. The distance is scaled by 1/s: d(s T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})) = \frac{1}{s} d(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) - T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})) \quad \text{(Eq. 47)} The Lipschitz constant of the inverse scale is 1/s. Linear Deformation: For a general linear transformation, the Lipschitz constant is the largest singular value of the inverse transformation matrix, found via the power method. Taper: For a taper deformation scaling two axes by a function \alpha(z) of the third axis, the Lipschitz constant is determined by the "tightest" tapering: Lip{taper} = \min \frac{1}{\alpha(z)} \quad \text{(Eq. 49)} See Lipschitz Bound Computation for Tapering Transformation for the exact Jacobian norm calculation. Twist: For a twist deformation rotating two axes by a linear function \theta(z) of the third axis, the transformation is not Lipschitz over unbounded domains. It must be constrained to a domain like a unit cylinder along the twisting axis. The Lipschitz constant is computed from the worst-case scenario within these bounds: Lip{twist} = \sqrt{4 + \frac{\theta^2}{4}} \quad \text{(Eq. 51)} 4. Apply Bound Correction: The final distance is the local distance divided by the Lipschitz constant L of the inverse transformation. This ensures the resulting function satisfies the 1-Lipschitz condition (or a known bound), providing a safe lower bound for ray marching: d{corrected} = \frac{d{local}}{L} If the base SDF is not 1-Lipschitz, it must first be normalized by its own bound K (see Lipschitz Normalization) before applying the transformation bound. Parameters: s: Uniform scale factor. \alpha(z): Tapering coefficient function along the vertical axis. \theta: Twist angle parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Twist: Twisting is not Lipschitz on unbounded domains because the distance between transformed points can grow arbitrarily large relative to the original distance. It must be constrained to a specific domain (e.g., a unit cylinder) to compute a valid bound. Precision: The Lipschitz constant must be computed accurately. For tapering, interval analysis or exact derivative evaluation is recommended to avoid underestimating the bound, which would cause ray tunneling. Composition: When multiple transformations are composed, the total Lipschitz constant is the product of the individual constants. Care must be taken to compute the bound of the inverse composition, which is not simply the inverse of the forward composition's bound. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelipschitzboundtransformationdistance(basesdf, inversetransform, querypoint, transformtype, params): """ Computes the distance to a transformed implicit surface using Lipschitz bounds. Args: basesdf: Function f(x) returning the distance to the base object. inversetransform: Function Tinv(x) returning the inverse-transformed coordinates. querypoint: The point x in world space to query. transformtype: String identifying the transformation ('isometry', 'uniformscale', 'taper', 'twist'). params: Dictionary of transformation parameters (e.g., 'scale', 'alphafunc', 'theta'). Returns: The corrected distance to the transformed surface. """ # Step 1: Transform query point to local space localpoint = inversetransform(querypoint) # Step 2: Evaluate base SDF localdistance = basesdf(localpoint) # Step 3: Determine Lipschitz constant L of the inverse transformation if transformtype == 'isometry': L = 1.0 elif transformtype == 'uniformscale': s = params['scale'] L = 1.0 / s elif transformtype == 'taper': # Compute min(1/alpha(z)) over the relevant domain # This requires evaluating the taper function and its derivative alphafunc = params['alphafunc'] # Example: if alpha(z) is linear, find the minimum value in the domain # For complex cases, use interval analysis or numerical optimization minalpha = computeminalphataper(params['domain'], alphafunc) if minalpha == 0: raise ValueError("Taper function alpha(z) cannot be zero") L = 1.0 / minalpha elif transformtype == 'twist': theta = params['theta'] # Constrained to unit cylinder; worst-case bound L = math.sqrt(4 + (theta 2) / 4) else: # Generic linear deformation: compute largest singular value of Jacobian of Tinv # This involves computing the Jacobian matrix and finding its spectral norm jacobian = computejacobianinversetransform(inversetransform, localpoint) L = computespectralnorm(jacobian) # Step 4: Apply correction # Ensure distance is non-negative if we are outside the object # Note: basesdf should return signed distance; for ray marching, we often use abs or check sign correcteddistance = localdistance / L return correcteddistance def computeminalphataper(domain, alphafunc): """ Computes the minimum value of alpha(z) over a given domain. This is a placeholder for the specific analytical or numerical method required for the taper function. """ # For a linear taper alpha(z) = az + b, the min is at one of the endpoints # For more complex functions, use interval analysis or optimization # suggests developing the equation or using interval analysis return alphafunc(domain.minz) # Simplified example Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching is a technique for rendering scenes with regularly spaced geometry (such as urban environments) by defining the scene in a sheared coordinate space ("road space") where buildings are axis-aligned, simplifying distance field computation. It differs from standard Euclidean ray marching by applying a safety factor to the computed distances to compensate for the non-Euclidean metric introduced by the spatial transformation, preventing the ray from tunneling through walls. It is a specific application of Lipschitz bounds where the transformation is a shear. SDF Deformations apply a non-uniform spatial distortion to a Signed Distance Field by warping the coordinate space, allowing for the creation of twisted, bent, or otherwise distorted geometric shapes. It solves the problem of generating complex, organic, or mechanical deformations (such as twisted cables) from simple primitive SDFs without requiring explicit mesh topology. It is distinguished from Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching by its explicit handling of multiphase SDFs and the mathematical constraint of the Lipschitz constant to preserve distance accuracy. A method to compute the bound of the norm of the Jacobian for a tapering transformation to determine the Lipschitz bound. For a tapering transformation \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{p}) = (\alpha(z)x, \alpha(z)y, z) where \beta = \alpha', the Jacobian matrix is: \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & 0 & \beta \\ 0 & \alpha & 0 \\ \beta & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} The Euclidean norm of the Jacobian is: \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^-}\| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{\alpha^2 + 2\beta^2 + 1 + (1 + \alpha)\sqrt{\alpha^2 - 2\alpha + 4\beta^2 + 1}} For a given input interval, this norm can be obtained by developing the equation or by interval analysis. A preprocessing step that transforms any signed distance function f into a lower-bound distance function satisfying the 1-Lipschitz condition by dividing it by a known Lipschitz bound K. The formula is: f{normalized} = \frac{f}{K} where K is the Lipschitz bound of the original field function f, ensuring \|\nabla f\| \le 1 everywhere. The value of K depends on the primitive/operator and must be computed or known a priori. Time Complexity: The core computation involves evaluating the inverse transformation and the base SDF, which is O(1) per query. Computing the Lipschitz constant may require additional operations (e.g., eigenvalue decomposition for linear transforms, or interval analysis for tapering), but these are typically precomputed or cached for uniform transformations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for storing the Lipschitz constant. No additional data structures are required beyond those for the base SDF. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the complexity of the base SDF and the transformation. For simple primitives, the overhead of computing the Lipschitz bound is negligible. For complex deformations, the cost of evaluating the Jacobian or its bound may become significant. Scaling: The method scales well with scene complexity as it is a local operation. However, for scenes with many different transformations, precomputing and caching Lipschitz bounds is recommended. Strengths: Provides mathematically guaranteed lower bounds for distances, preventing ray tunneling in transformed spaces. Works with any transformation where the Lipschitz constant of the inverse can be computed. Limitations: Requires the Lipschitz constant to be known or computable. For complex non-linear transformations, computing the bound can be difficult. Twisting requires domain constraints. When to Use: When rendering scenes with scaled, rotated, or deformed SDF primitives where distance accuracy is critical. When Not to Use: When the transformation is complex and the Lipschitz bound is difficult to compute or varies significantly across the domain, making a single bound too conservative. The concept of using Lipschitz constants to bound distances in transformed spaces originates from the foundational work on Sphere Tracing by John C. Hart et al.. The paper "Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces" (1992) introduced the use of Lipschitz bounds to ensure the safety of the sphere tracing algorithm when applied to transformed implicit surfaces. The specific formulas for isometries, uniform scales, tapers, and twists were derived in this context. Later work, such as "Segment Tracing Using Local Lipschitz Bounds" and "Lipschitz Pruning: Hierarchical Simplification of Primitive‐Based SDFs", extended these ideas to more complex deformations and hierarchical scene structures.
