name: Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching
head: Road-space SDF, Sheared SDF
body: Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching is a technique for rendering scenes with regularly spaced geometry (such as urban environments) by defining the scene in a sheared coordinate space ("road space") where buildings are axis-aligned, simplifying distance field computation. It differs from standard Euclidean ray marching by applying a safety factor to the computed distances to compensate for the non-Euclidean metric introduced by the spatial transformation, preventing the ray from tunneling through walls. Inputs: Ray query point p{world} in world space. Scene definition: A set of buildings, each defined by a center c and half-extents h in road space. Road geometry function roadX(z), which returns the lateral offset of the road center at longitudinal position z. Ground plane height y{ground}. Safety factor \alpha = 0.8. Outputs: Marched distance d{out} and material ID. Data Structures: Buildings are stored in a grid or hash map indexed by longitudinal cell. Each building entry contains: center: vec3 (cx, cy, cz) in road space. halfExt: vec3 (hx, hy, hz) in road space. materialID: integer. Steps: 1. Transform to Road Space: For a given world point p, compute its road space coordinate q: q = (px - roadX(pz), py, pz) This transformation shears the world such that the road runs along the z-axis in road space. 2. Cell Identification: Determine the longitudinal cell index for the current z-coordinate: baseCz = \lfloor qz / BLOCK\DEPTH \rfloor where BLOCK\DEPTH is the grid cell size in the z-direction. 3. Neighbor Iteration: Iterate over 2 sides, NROWS rows, and 3 z-neighbors (dz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}). 4. Distance Computation: For each present building, compute the signed distance to the axis-aligned box: d{box} = sdBox(q - b.center, b.halfExt). 5. Take Minimum: Track the minimum distance found across all buildings as best. 6. Apply Safety Factor: Multiply best by 0.8. 7. Ground Comparison: Compare best with the ground plane distance; return the smaller distance and corresponding material ID. Formulas: Coordinate transformation: q = (px - roadX(pz), py, pz). Warped distance: d{warped} = d{box}(q - b.center, b.halfExt) \times 0.8. Parameters: \alpha = 0.8: Safety factor. Chosen because |roadX'| \le \sim 0.52, so the compression factor peaks at \sim 1.13. Since 0.8 < 1/1.13, this ensures a valid Lipschitz lower bound, preventing tunneling. BLOCK\DEPTH: Grid cell size in z. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tunneling: Because the warped space is not Euclidean, the box distance is compressed by |\nabla qx| = \sqrt{1 + roadX'(z)^2}. Without the 0.8 factor, the marcher could step too far and pass through walls. Degenerate Input: If roadX'(z) is large, the compression factor increases. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import floor, abs, max, inf GROUNDMATERIALID = 0 def raymarchwarped(pworld, roadXfunc, buildingsgrid, BLOCKDEPTH, yground, alpha=0.8): """ Performs a single distance query in warped space. pworld: tuple/list of 3 floats (x, y, z) in world space. roadXfunc: callable returning lateral offset for a given z. buildingsgrid: dict mapping cellz -> list of building dicts. BLOCKDEPTH: float, longitudinal cell size. yground: float, ground plane height. alpha: float, safety factor (default 0.8). Returns: (distance, materialid) """ # 1. Transform world point to road space pz = pworld[2] roadoffset = roadXfunc(pz) q = (pworld[0] - roadoffset, pworld[1], pz) # 2. Determine longitudinal cell index basecz = int(floor(q[2] / BLOCKDEPTH)) bestdist = inf bestmatid = -1 # 3. Iterate over 3 z-neighbors (dz=-1 to 1) # Source iterates over 2 sides, NROWS rows, and 3 z-neighbors; # here we iterate over buildings in the relevant cells. for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: cellz = basecz + dz cellbuildings = buildingsgrid.get(cellz, []) for b in cellbuildings: # 4. Compute box distance in road space v = (q[0] - b.center[0], q[1] - b.center[1], q[2] - b.center[2]) dx = abs(v[0]) - b.halfExt[0] dy = abs(v[1]) - b.halfExt[1] dzbox = abs(v[2]) - b.halfExt[2] # Standard AABB SDF dbox = max(dx, max(dy, dzbox)) # 5. Take minimum distance if dbox < bestdist: bestdist = dbox bestmatid = b.materialid # 6. Apply safety factor bestdist = alpha # 7. Compare with ground plane distance dground = pworld[1] - yground if dground < bestdist: return dground, GROUNDMATERIALID else: return bestdist, bestmatid Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of buildings in the current and adjacent longitudinal cells. Typically small due to spatial partitioning. Memory Complexity: O(B) where B is the total number of buildings, stored in a grid/hash structure. Strengths: Simplifies building placement and SDF computation by aligning geometry with the coordinate axes in road space. Efficient for dense, regular urban layouts. Limitations: Only suitable for scenes with a dominant directional structure (e.g., roads). Requires careful tuning of the safety factor based on the maximum shear rate. Not suitable for arbitrary curved paths without complex roadX(z) definitions. When to use: Urban environments, highways, or any scene with a strong linear or gently curving central axis. When not to use: Scenes with no dominant direction, or where high precision is required without the overhead of dynamic safety factor calculation. The technique is described in the context of a WebGL raymarcher implementation, specifically for rendering urban environments efficiently. It leverages the concept of Lipschitz transformation bounds to ensure valid distance queries in non-Euclidean spaces. name: SDF Deformations
head: Non-uniform spatial distortion, Space Deformation, Twist deformation, Warping Operator
body: SDF Deformations apply a non-uniform spatial distortion to a Signed Distance Field by warping the coordinate space. This technique generates complex, organic, or mechanical deformations (such as twisted cables) from simple primitive SDFs without requiring explicit mesh topology. It is distinguished from Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching by its explicit handling of multiphase SDFs and the mathematical constraint of the Lipschitz constant to preserve distance accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A warping function \omega: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3, a base SDF \Phi{\mathcal{A}} (potentially multiphase), and a scaling factor \lambda. Output: A deformed SDF \Phi(\mathbf{p}) that preserves the signed distance property. Data Structures: Warping Function \omega: A mapping from world coordinates to deformed coordinates. The implementation requires the inverse function \omega^{-1} to evaluate the distance at the deformed point. Lipschitz Constant \lambda: A scalar value \lambda \geq \sup \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\|, where \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} is the Jacobian matrix of the inverse warping function. This ensures the deformed field remains a valid distance field. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Inverse Warp: For a query point \mathbf{p}, determine the pre-warp coordinate \mathbf{p}' = \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{p}). 2. Evaluate Base SDF: Compute the base distance \phi{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{p}') at the pre-warp coordinate. 3. Scale Distance: Divide the base distance by \lambda to obtain the deformed distance: \phi{\text{def}} = \phi{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{p}') / \lambda. 4. Multiphase Handling (Optional): If deforming only a specific phase k within a multiphase structure \mathcal{A}, apply the over operator to combine the deformed phase with undeformed phases. For the target phase k: \phik = \phi{\mathcal{A}k}(\mathbf{p}') / \lambda. For all other phases i \neq k: \phii = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{p}), -\phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{p}') / \lambda). Formulas: For global warping of all phases: \Phi(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{1}{\lambda} \Phi{\mathcal{A}} \circ \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{p}) where \lambda \geq \sup \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\|. For partial phase deformation D(\mathcal{A}, k): D(\mathcal{A}, k) = D(\mathcal{A}k) \cup+ (\mathcal{A} - \mathcal{A}k) Function evaluation: \phii = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}, -\phi{\mathcal{A}i} \circ \omega^{-1}/\lambda) \quad \forall i \neq k \phik = \phi{\mathcal{A}k} \circ \omega^{-1}/\lambda. Parameters: \lambda: Scaling factor constrained by the supremum of the Jacobian norm of the inverse warping function to preserve the signed distance property. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lipschitz Violation: If \lambda is too small, the resulting field is no longer a valid signed distance field, leading to incorrect ray marching steps and visual artifacts. Inverse Solving: Computing \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{p}) may require iterative numerical methods if \omega is complex, which can impact performance. Phase Boundaries: When deforming only a subset of phases, the interaction between deformed and undeformed regions must be handled carefully to avoid gaps or overlaps, typically using the max operator as defined. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfdeformation(p, basesdf, omegainv, lambdaval, phasek=None, numphases=None): """ Computes the deformed SDF value at point p. Args: p: vec3, query point in world space. basesdf: function, returns SDF value(s) at a point. omegainv: function, returns omega^-1(p). lambdaval: float, Lipschitz constant >= sup||Jomegainv||. phasek: int or None, if set, deforms only this phase. numphases: int or None, required if phasek is set. Returns: float or vecN, deformed SDF value(s). """ # Step 1: Compute inverse warp pprime = omegainv(p) # Step 2 & 3: Evaluate base SDF and scale if phasek is None: # Global warping phibase = basesdf(pprime) return phibase / lambdaval else: # Partial phase warping # Evaluate base SDF at both original and deformed points phibaseoriginal = basesdf(p) phibasedeformed = basesdf(pprime) resultphases = [] for i in range(numphases): if i == phasek: # Deform only phase k phik = phibasedeformed[i] / lambdaval resultphases.append(phik) else: # Combine undeformed phase i with deformed phase k # phii = max(phiAi, -phiAicomposed / lambda) phii = max(phibaseoriginal[i], -phibasedeformed[i] / lambdaval) resultphases.append(phii) return resultphases Applies a rotation angle that varies linearly with position (e.g., along the Y-axis) to create helical or twisted structures like cables. It is chosen for generating twisted geometries without explicit mesh topology. Applies deformation to only a subset of phases in a multiphase SDF, chosen when only specific components of a complex assembly need to be distorted while others remain static. It is implemented using the over operator to preserve undeformed phases. Time Complexity: Dominated by the evaluation of \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{p}) and the base SDF. If \omega^{-1} requires iteration, complexity increases. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per query, assuming \omega^{-1} is computed on the fly. Strengths: Enables complex, organic shapes from simple primitives; supports multiphase structures for detailed internal geometry. Limitations: Requires careful calculation of \lambda to preserve distance accuracy; inverse warping can be computationally expensive or numerically unstable. When to Use: When creating twisted, bent, or distorted geometries that are difficult to model with standard primitives. When Not to Use: When high performance is critical and \omega^{-1} is expensive to compute, or when the deformation is uniform (use simple transformation instead). The concept of space deformation for SDFs was formalized in the context of multiphase SDFs by the PhaseTree authors. The warping operator allows for the deformation of space following classical formulations, enabling the creation of complex scenes like twisted electrical cables. The technique is widely used in ray marching for procedural geometry, as demonstrated by examples such as twisting deformations and displacement maps. name: Implicit Surface Field Function Evaluation
head: Field Function Evaluation, SDF Query, Isosurface Density Evaluation
body:
Implicit Surface Field Function Evaluation computes the signed distance (or density) value d = f(\mathbf{p}) for a 3D point \mathbf{p} relative to a target surface. It solves the problem of determining whether a point lies inside, outside, or on the boundary of a geometric primitive or voxelized field, which is the fundamental query required for ray marching, mesh extraction, and differentiable rendering. It differs from sibling methods like Batched SDF Inference by focusing on the mathematical evaluation of a single or small set of points rather than large-scale batched inference, and from SDF Validity Check with Relaxation by providing the raw metric value rather than a binary validity classification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) in world space. Input: The implicit surface definition (analytical formula or voxel grid). Input: A transformation matrix T representing the surface's placement in world space. Output: The scalar field value d = f(\mathbf{p}). By convention, d < 0 indicates the point is inside the volume, d > 0 indicates outside, and d = 0 indicates the point is on the contour. Optional Output: The gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) for normal computation. Data Structures: 1. Analytical Primitive: Stores parameters (e.g., radius R for a sphere) and the bounding box. 2. Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor (e.g., mi.TensorXf with shape (res, res, res, 1)) storing pre-computed distance values. 3. Interpolation Mode: A string parameter utils.SDFMODE selecting between 'linear' or 'cubic' interpolation for grid-based evaluation. Steps: 1. Validation: If the SDF is loaded from a named registry, validate the name. If invalid, raise an error (e.g., std::runtimeerror("unknown SDF '...'")). 2. Transformation Inversion: If the surface has a transformation T, compute the inverse transformation T^{-1}. Transform the query point \mathbf{p} to the surface's local coordinate system: \mathbf{p}{local} = T^{-1} \mathbf{p}. If no transformation is applied, T^{-1} is the identity, and \mathbf{p}{local} = \mathbf{p}. 3. Field Evaluation: Analytical: Evaluate the closed-form function f(\mathbf{p}{local}). For a sphere of radius R, f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - R^2. Voxel Grid: Query the grid at \mathbf{p}{local}. If utils.SDFMODE is 'linear', perform trilinear interpolation. If utils.SDFMODE is 'cubic', perform tricubic interpolation. 4. Batch Processing (Optional): For performance, evaluate the function for a sequence of points starting at (x0, y0, z0) along the +z axis with step size dz for numpoints iterations. Formulas: Sphere: f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - R^2. Gradient (Linear Mode): Computed via central finite differences with step size \epsilon = 10^{-5}: 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) \approx \left[  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \hat{x}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \hat{x})}{2\epsilon},  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \hat{y}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \hat{y})}{2\epsilon},  rac{f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \hat{z}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \hat{z})}{2\epsilon} ight] Gradient (Cubic Mode): Extracted directly from the interpolation kernel's derivative output. Directional Derivative: D{\mathbf{d}} f = 
abla f \cdot  rac{\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|}. Parameters: utils.SDFMODE: 'linear' or 'cubic'. Cubic is smoother and theoretically more robust but slower. epsilon: Finite difference step size, default 10^{-5}. dz: Delta step size along the +z axis for batch evaluation. numpoints: Number of points in a batch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluatesdfanalyticalsphere(plocal: np.ndarray, radius: float) -> float: """ Evaluates the SDF for a sphere centered at origin. plocal: (3,) array [x, y, z] in local coordinates. radius: float, radius of the sphere. Returns: float, signed distance. """ x, y, z = plocal return np.sqrt(x2 + y2 + z2) - radius def evaluatesdfvoxel(plocal: np.ndarray, grid: np.ndarray, mode: str, epsilon: float = 1e-5) -> float: """ Evaluates SDF from a 3D voxel grid. plocal: (3,) array [x, y, z] in local coordinates. grid: (res, res, res) numpy array of SDF values. mode: 'linear' or 'cubic'. epsilon: step size for finite differences if mode is 'linear'. Returns: float, signed distance. """ # Note: Actual interpolation requires clamping or boundary handling. # This pseudocode assumes a helper interpolate exists. if mode == 'linear': return interpolatelinear(grid, plocal) elif mode == 'cubic': return interpolatecubic(grid, plocal) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown SDF mode: {mode}") def computegradientvoxel(plocal: np.ndarray, grid: np.ndarray, mode: str, epsilon: float = 1e-5) -> np.ndarray: """ Computes the gradient of the SDF at plocal. """ if mode == 'linear': # Central finite differences grad = np.zeros(3) for i in range(3): pplus = plocal.copy() pminus = plocal.copy() pplus[i] += epsilon pminus[i] -= epsilon grad[i] = (evaluatesdfvoxel(pplus, grid, mode) - evaluatesdfvoxel(pminus, grid, mode)) / (2 epsilon) return grad elif mode == 'cubic': # Return gradient from cubic interpolation kernel return interpolatecubicgradient(grid, plocal) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown SDF mode: {mode}") def querysdf(pworld: np.ndarray, transformationmatrix: np.ndarray, sdfsource: dict) -> float: """ Main entry point for SDF evaluation. pworld: (3,) array, query point in world space. transformationmatrix: (4,4) or (3,3) matrix T. sdfsource: dict containing 'type' ('sphere' or 'voxel'), 'params', and 'grid'. Returns: float, signed distance. """ # Step 2: Transform to local space # Assuming homogeneous coordinates if 4x4, otherwise 3x3 if transformationmatrix.shape == (4, 4): phomogeneous = np.append(pworld, 1.0) plocalhomogeneous = np.linalg.inv(transformationmatrix) @ phomogeneous plocal = plocalhomogeneous[:3] else: plocal = np.linalg.inv(transformationmatrix) @ pworld # Step 3: Evaluate if sdfsource['type'] == 'sphere': return evaluatesdfanalyticalsphere(plocal, sdfsource['radius']) elif sdfsource['type'] == 'voxel': return evaluatesdfvoxel(plocal, sdfsource['grid'], sdfsource['mode']) else: raise ValueError("Unknown SDF source type") A memory-efficient method to extract boundaries between multiple materials by storing the blended Extended Signed Distance Function (ESDF) in a Z-buffer. It differs from standard SDF evaluation by handling multi-material boundaries simultaneously using a Z-buffer approach rather than evaluating a single scalar field. It is chosen when extracting non-manifold meshes from time-varying segmented volumes, such as modeling a human heart. The algorithm stores the blended ESDF of one material in a Z-buffer, successively processes other materials, and updates the Z-buffer at each pixel where the current entry is greater than the current ESDF, simultaneously storing the material index in a frame buffer. The material index at pixel (x,y) is determined by m(x, y) = \arg \minm \{sm(x, y)\}, where sm is the ESDF for material m. Time Complexity: O(1) for analytical primitives (e.g., sphere). O(1) for voxel grid evaluation assuming constant-time interpolation, but dependent on grid resolution and interpolation order (cubic is slower than linear). Memory Complexity: O(1) for analytical primitives. O(N^3) for voxel grids, where N is the resolution. Performance: Cubic interpolation provides smoother geometry and is theoretically more robust but is significantly slower than linear interpolation. Strengths: Compact representation for precise surfaces; supports transformations via inverse mapping. Limitations: Analytical bounding box computation can be difficult for complex field functions. Voxel grids suffer from discretization artifacts and high memory usage for high resolution. Implicit surfaces were introduced as a compact and precise way to describe volumes in 3D space, avoiding the need for explicit polygon lists. The concept of evaluating a field function d = f(x,y,z) where d represents density or distance is foundational to computer graphics. The specific implementation details regarding voxel grid interpolation modes (linear vs cubic) and finite difference gradient computation are documented in recent differentiable rendering pipelines for SDFs. The batched evaluation along the +z axis for performance optimization is described in early implicit surface implementation guides. hbaktash/subgrid-marching, https://github.com/hbaktash/subgrid-marching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Non-manifold Mesh Extraction from Time-varying Segmented Volumes used for Modeling a Human Heart, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/eurovis05/199-206, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Batched SDF Inference
head: Batched SDF Evaluation
body: Batched SDF Inference evaluates Signed Distance Function values for a large set of spatial samples in batches to manage memory constraints during inference. It differs from single-sample evaluation by processing multiple points simultaneously, and from training methods by focusing solely on forward evaluation without gradient accumulation. Inputs: A list of 3D query points \mathbf{p}i, an SDF evaluation function, and maxbatch (default 32^3). Outputs: An array of SDF values d(\mathbf{p}i) corresponding to each input point. Data Structures: samples is a 2D array of shape (N, 4) where columns 0–2 store coordinates (x, y, z) and column 3 stores the computed SDF value. Steps: 1. Disable automatic differentiation for the inference process. 2. Determine the total number of samples N. 3. Initialize a head pointer h = 0. 4. While h < N: a. Calculate the batch end: e = \min(h + \text{max\batch}, N). b. Extract the subset of samples from index h to e-1. c. Evaluate the SDF for this subset and store the results in column 3 of the samples array for indices h to e-1. d. Increment h by \text{max\batch}. 5. Return the SDF values from column 3 of the samples array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def batchedsdfinference(samples, evaluatesdf, maxbatch=323): """ Evaluates SDF values for a large set of samples in batches. Args: samples: Array of shape (N, 4) where columns 0-2 are coordinates and column 3 is for output. evaluatesdf: Function that takes an array of points and returns an array of distances. maxbatch: Integer maximum batch size. Default 32768. Returns: Array of SDF values of shape (N,). """ # Disable gradients for memory efficiency numsamples = len(samples) head = 0 while head < numsamples: end = min(head + maxbatch, numsamples) batchpoints = [samples[i][:3] for i in range(head, end)] batchsdfs = evaluatesdf(batchpoints) for i, val in enumerate(batchsdfs): samples[head + i][3] = val head += maxbatch return [sample[3] for sample in samples] Parameters: maxbatch: Integer maximum batch size for inference, default 32^3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If maxbatch exceeds N, the loop executes exactly once. Precision and memory limits depend entirely on the underlying SDF evaluation function and hardware constraints. Evaluates SDFs for volumetric structures across multiple joint configurations and query points simultaneously, enabling efficient batched inference for robotic kinematics. name: SDF Value Computation
head: IsoVal.compute
body: SDF Value Computation is a compute shader kernel that calculates the Signed Distance Function (SDF) value for each voxel in a grid. It transforms grid coordinates to world space, evaluates the SDF function, and stores the result. It serves as the atomic evaluation step within batched inference pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A linearized 3D grid of voxel indices (IDs), a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix ShapeToWorld mapping local shape coordinates to world space, and the shape's intrinsic size SHAPESIZE. Output: A 1D array or texture IsoVals storing the computed SDF value for each voxel. Data Structures: IsoVals: A 1D array storing SDF values, indexed by a linearized 3D coordinate ID. ShapeToWorld: A 4 \times 4 matrix. SHAPESIZE: A scalar defining the scale or extent of the primitive shape. Steps: 1. Grid Coordinate Retrieval: For each voxel, determine its 3D grid coordinates from its linear ID. 2. Local Position Calculation: Convert the grid coordinates into a local surface position using a helper GetPosSurface(id). 3. World Space Transformation: Transform the local position \mathbf{p}{local} to world space \mathbf{p}{world} using the transformation matrix: \mathbf{p}{world} = \mathbf{M}{shape\to\world} \cdot \mathbf{p}{local} where \mathbf{M}{shape\to\world} is ShapeToWorld. 4. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF function F(\mathbf{p}) at the world position. The function depends on the specific primitive shape defined by SHAPESIZE. d = \text{SDF}(\mathbf{p}{world}, \text{SHAPE\SIZE}) 5. Storage: Store the computed distance d in the output array IsoVals at the index corresponding to the voxel ID. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfvalue(voxelid, shapetoworldmatrix, shapesize, griddims, gridorigin): # Step 1 & 2: Get local position from grid ID using GetPosSurface(id) # Standard linear ID to 3D coordinate conversion for a regular grid x = (voxelid % griddims[0]) / griddims[0] y = ((voxelid // griddims[0]) % griddims[1]) / griddims[1] z = (voxelid // (griddims[0] griddims[1])) / griddims[2] localpos = (x, y, z) # Step 3: Transform to world space using ShapeToWorld worldposx = shapetoworldmatrix[0][0] localpos[0] + shapetoworldmatrix[0][1] localpos[1] + shapetoworldmatrix[0][2] localpos[2] + shapetoworldmatrix[0][3] worldposy = shapetoworldmatrix[1][0] localpos[0] + shapetoworldmatrix[1][1] localpos[1] + shapetoworldmatrix[1][2] localpos[2] + shapetoworldmatrix[1][3] worldposz = shapetoworldmatrix[2][0] localpos[0] + shapetoworldmatrix[2][1] localpos[1] + shapetoworldmatrix[2][2] localpos[2] + shapetoworldmatrix[2][3] worldpos = (worldposx, worldposy, worldposz) # Step 4: Evaluate SDF function at the world position with SHAPESIZE # The specific primitive function depends on the shape type and uses shapesize as a parameter. # Common implementations: sphere (length(point) - size), box (length(max(abs(point) - size, 0.0)) - size) sdfvalue = evaluatesdfprimitive(worldpos, shapesize) # Step 5: Store result in IsoVals at index voxelid return sdfvalue def evaluatesdfprimitive(point, size): # Shape-specific SDF evaluation. Sources do not specify the exact primitive function. raise NotImplementedError("Specific SDF primitive function not defined in source.") Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in the transformation matrix multiplication can cause slight inaccuracies in the distance value, potentially affecting marching convergence. Boundary Conditions: The definition of GetPosSurface must correctly handle grid boundaries to avoid out-of-bounds access or incorrect coordinate mapping. Shape Definition: The SDF evaluation must be consistent with the SHAPESIZE interpretation (e.g., radius vs. half-extent). Calculates SDF and RGB for 3D points relative to a single camera view, solving geometric and photometric consistency. It differs by incorporating view-dependent color and depth comparison, whereas this method is view-agnostic and geometry-only. Not given in the sources. name: Per-Frame SDF Computation
body: Per-Frame SDF Computation calculates the signed distance function (SDF) and RGB color for a set of 3D points by projecting them into a single camera view and comparing their projected depth against a reference depth map. It differs from batched inference by operating on a per-view basis, allowing for incremental fusion or single-view analysis, and serves as the core evaluation step within multi-view fusion pipelines like Unbounded TSDF Fusion. Inputs: points: A tensor of 3D points with shape (N, 3), where N is the number of points. fullprojtransform: A 4 \times 4 projection matrix mapping world coordinates to clip space. depthmap: A 2D tensor representing the reference depth map for the current view. rgbmap: A 2D tensor representing the reference RGB color map for the current view. invcontraction (optional): A boolean flag or function indicating if the space is contracted (used in Unbounded TSDF Fusion). Outputs: sdf: A tensor of shape (N, 1) containing the signed distance values. rgb: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the sampled RGB colors. mask: A boolean tensor of shape (N, 1) indicating valid projections. Data Structures: Points are stored as floating-point tensors. Depth and RGB maps are stored as 2D tensors (height \times width). Masks are boolean tensors. Steps: 1. Homogenization: Append a column of ones to points to create homogeneous coordinates (x, y, z, 1). 2. Clip Space Projection: Multiply the homogeneous points by fullprojtransform to obtain clip space coordinates (xc, yc, zc, wc). 3. Perspective Division: Compute pixel coordinates by dividing xc and yc by zc (assuming wc=1 or already handled in projection matrix). Let z{proj} = zc. u = \frac{xc}{z{proj}}, \quad v = \frac{yc}{z{proj}} 4. Projection Masking: Create a mask where: -1 \le u \le 1 -1 \le v \le 1 z{proj} > 0 Points failing any condition are marked invalid. 5. Depth Sampling: Sample the depthmap at (u, v) using bilinear interpolation (gridsample with border padding). Reshape to (N, 1). Let this be d{sampled}. 6. Color Sampling: Sample the rgbmap at (u, v) using bilinear interpolation (gridsample with border padding). Reshape to (N, 3). Let this be c{sampled}. 7. SDF Calculation: Compute the signed distance as the difference between the sampled depth and the projected depth: \text{SDF} = d{sampled} - z{proj} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfperframe(points, fullprojtransform, depthmap, rgbmap): # points: (N, 3) # fullprojtransform: (4, 4) # depthmap: (H, W) # rgbmap: (H, W, 3) # 1. Homogenize ones = torch.ones(points.shape[0], 1, device=points.device) pointshomo = torch.cat([points, ones], dim=1) # (N, 4) # 2. Project to clip space clipcoords = torch.matmul(pointshomo, fullprojtransform.T) # (N, 4) xc, yc, zc, wc = clipcoords[:, 0], clipcoords[:, 1], clipcoords[:, 2], clipcoords[:, 3] # 3. Perspective division # Note: In standard OpenGL/DirectX projections, wc is often -z or similar. # Assuming fullprojtransform handles w correctly for division. # If wc is not 1, we divide by wc. If the matrix is set up such that # zc is already the depth after division, adjust accordingly. # Standard GL projection: zc is clip z, wc is -viewz. # Here we assume zc represents the depth value to compare against depthmap. # The source implies zc is the projected z. zproj = zc # 4. Pixel coordinates u = xc / zproj v = yc / zproj # 5. Masking validu = (u >= -1.0) & (u <= 1.0) validv = (v >= -1.0) & (v <= 1.0) validz = zproj > 0.0 mask = validu & validv & validz # 6. Sampling # Normalize u, v to [-1, 1] for gridsample if they are in [-1, 1] already. # gridsample expects normalized coordinates in [-1, 1]. # u, v are already in [-1, 1] for valid points. # Reshape to (N, 1, 1, 2) for gridsample: (N, 1, 1, 2) -> (N, 1, 1, 2) # gridsample input: (N, H, W, 2) or (N, 1, 1, 2) depending on implementation. # PyTorch gridsample: grid is (N, Hout, Wout, 2). # We need to sample at specific points. # Create grid for sampling # u, v are (N,) # Reshape to (N, 1, 1, 2) grid = torch.stack([u, v], dim=-1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 1, 2) # Sample depth # depthmap needs to be (1, 1, H, W) for gridsample depthmapexpanded = depthmap.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, H, W) sampleddepth = torch.nn.functional.gridsample( depthmapexpanded, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border', aligncorners=False).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # (N, 1) # Sample RGB # rgbmap needs to be (1, 3, H, W) rgbmapexpanded = rgbmap.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 3, H, W) sampledrgb = torch.nn.functional.gridsample( rgbmapexpanded, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border', aligncorners=False).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # (N, 3) # 7. SDF Calculation sdf = sampleddepth - zproj.unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1) return sdf, sampledrgb, mask Fuses SDF values from multiple frames in contracted space with adaptive truncation, then uncontracts the space. It differs from standard TSDF fusion by handling unbounded scenes via a contraction mapping that compresses infinity into a unit sphere. Choose this when dealing with large-scale outdoor scenes or when the volume of interest extends beyond a fixed bounding box. It calls computesdfperframe for each view in the viewpointstack. The truncation parameter sdftrunc is set to 5 \times \text{voxel\size}. For points outside the unit sphere (||x|| > 1), the truncation is scaled by 1/(2-||x||) if invcontraction is provided; otherwise, it remains constant. The fusion uses a weighted average update: new = (old \times w + val) / (w + 1), with weights initialized to 1 and incremented per view. A volumetric shape representation where the signed distance of a 3D point X is defined by the depth prediction of a specific camera j along the viewing ray passing through X, rather than the shortest distance in any direction. Unlike standard SDF which uses the shortest distance along any direction, or SDDF which uses a fixed direction, SRDF uses the direction of the viewing ray from a specific camera. It is defined as SRDFj(X) = Dj(X) - Zj(X), where Dj(X) is the predicted depth and Zj(X) is the point's depth along the ray. It is differentiable at any point in the 3D observation volume. Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of points N for a single view, dominated by the projection and bilinear sampling operations. Memory complexity is O(N) for storing the SDF and RGB values. Performance scales with the resolution of the depth/RGB maps due to the sampling cost, but is generally efficient on GPU due to parallelizable tensor operations. Strengths include simplicity and direct integration with differentiable rendering pipelines. Limitations include sensitivity to depth map accuracy and occlusion handling, as it relies on a single view's depth map. Not suitable for scenes with significant self-occlusion without multi-view fusion. Originated in the context of 2D Gaussian Splatting and multi-view reconstruction, specifically in the 2d-gaussian-splatting repository by Inria's GRAPHDECO research group. The method is used to evaluate the consistency of 3D points against 2D observations, facilitating colorization and SDF-based regularization. It builds on the concept of projecting 3D points to 2D to leverage 2D image data for 3D attribute estimation. hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, https://github.com/hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Multi-View Reconstruction Using Signed Ray Distance Functions (SRDF), https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01602, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Point Colorization via Projective SDF
head: Projective SDF Colorization, Projective SDF Filtering & Color Sampling
body: Point Colorization via Projective SDF assigns RGB colors to a set of 3D points by projecting them into training views, filtering based on alpha confidence and projective depth consistency, and sampling the closest valid color from the rendered reference frames. It differs from standard nearest-neighbor colorization by enforcing geometric consistency through a projective Signed Distance Field (SDF) metric, ensuring that sampled colors correspond to the visible surface rather than occluded geometry or background. Inputs: pts: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D point coordinates in world space. voxelmodel: A sparse voxel representation capable of rendering color, depth, and alpha. camlst: List of training camera objects, each providing position, lookat, project, and render methods. args.alphathres: Scalar threshold for alpha filtering (e.g., 0.5). args.usemean: Boolean flag to select mean depth (True) or median depth (False) from the renderer. Outputs: closestcolor: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the assigned RGB color for each point. closestdist: Tensor of shape (N) containing the minimum projective SDF distance for each point. Data Structures: closestcolor: Initialized to [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] for all points. closestdist: Initialized to +\infty for all points. validptsidx: Indices of points currently considered valid, initially all points projected within the image bounds. Parameters: mode='bilinear': Interpolation mode for gridsample. aligncorners=False: Coordinate alignment setting for gridsample to prevent edge bias. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set closestcolor to 0.5 for all N points. Set closestdist to +\infty for all N points. 2. Iterate over Training Cameras: For each camera cam in camlst: a. Render Reference Frame: Call renderpkg = voxelmodel.render(cam, colormode="sh0", outputdepth=True, outputT=True). Extract framecolor from renderpkg['color']. Select framedepth: if args.usemean is true, use renderpkg['rawdepth'][[0]] (mean); otherwise, use renderpkg['rawdepth'][[2]] (median). Compute framealpha = 1 - renderpkg['rawT']. Get image dimensions H, W from framedepth.shape[-2:]. b. Project Points: Compute projected UV coordinates: ptsuv = cam.project(pts). Filter points outside the image bounds [-1, 1]: filteridx = torch.where((ptsuv.abs() <= 1).all(-1))[0]. Update valid indices and points: validptsidx = filteridx. validpts = pts[filteridx]. ptsuv = ptsuv[filteridx]. If validpts is empty, skip to the next camera. c. Alpha Filtering: Sample alpha at projected UVs using bilinear interpolation: \text{pts\frame\alpha} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{frame\alpha}.view(1,1,H,W), \text{pts\uv}.view(1,1,-1,2), \text{mode}='bilinear', \text{align\corners}=False).flatten(). Filter points with alpha below threshold: filteridx = torch.where(ptsframealpha > args.alphathres)[0]. Update valid arrays: validptsidx = validptsidx[filteridx]. validpts = validpts[filteridx]. ptsuv = ptsuv[filteridx]. If validpts is empty, skip to the next camera. d. Compute Projective SDF Distance: Sample frame depth at projected UVs: \text{pts\frame\depth} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{frame\depth}.view(1,1,H,W), \text{pts\uv}.view(1,1,-1,2), \text{mode}='bilinear', \text{align\corners}=False).flatten(). Compute camera-space depth for each point: \text{pts\depth} = (\text{valid\pts} - \text{cam.position}) \cdot \text{cam.lookat}. Compute absolute projective distance: \text{pts\dist} = |\text{pts\frame\depth} - \text{pts\depth}|. e. Update Closest Color: Identify points with smaller distance than current best: filteridx = torch.where(ptsdist < closestdist[validptsidx])[0]. Update valid indices for this iteration: validptsidx = validptsidx[filteridx]. ptsuv = ptsuv[filteridx]. ptsdist = ptsdist[filteridx]. validpts = validpts[filteridx]. If validpts is empty, continue to next camera. Sample color at filtered UVs: \text{pts\color} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{frame\color}.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), \text{pts\uv}.view(1,1,-1,2), \text{mode}='bilinear', \text{align\corners}=False).squeeze().T. Update global closest arrays: closestdist[validptsidx] = ptsdist. closestcolor[validptsidx] = ptscolor. 3. Return: Return closestcolor and closestdist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def pointcolorizationviaprojectivesdf(pts, voxelmodel, camlst, args): """ Args: pts: (N, 3) tensor of 3D points voxelmodel: SparseVoxelModel with render method camlst: List of camera objects args: Object with alphathres, usemean Returns: closestcolor: (N, 3) tensor closestdist: (N,) tensor """ N = pts.shape[0] closestcolor = torch.full((N, 3), 0.5, dtype=torch.float32, device=pts.device) closestdist = torch.full((N,), float('inf'), dtype=torch.float32, device=pts.device) for cam in camlst: # 1. Render reference frame renderpkg = voxelmodel.render(cam, colormode="sh0", outputdepth=True, outputT=True) framecolor = renderpkg['color'] if args.usemean: framedepth = renderpkg['rawdepth'][[0]] else: framedepth = renderpkg['rawdepth'][[2]] framealpha = 1 - renderpkg['rawT'] H, W = framedepth.shape[-2:] # 2. Project points ptsuv = cam.project(pts) # Filter points outside image bounds [-1, 1] validmask = (ptsuv.abs() <= 1).all(dim=-1) validindices = torch.where(validmask)[0] if validindices.numel() == 0: continue validpts = pts[validindices] ptsuvvalid = ptsuv[validindices] # 3. Alpha filtering ptsframealpha = F.gridsample( framealpha.view(1, 1, H, W), ptsuvvalid.view(1, 1, -1, 2), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).flatten() alphamask = ptsframealpha > args.alphathres validindices = validindices[alphamask] validpts = validpts[alphamask] ptsuvvalid = ptsuvvalid[alphamask] if validindices.numel() == 0: continue # 4. Compute Projective SDF ptsframedepth = F.gridsample( framedepth.view(1, 1, H, W), ptsuvvalid.view(1, 1, -1, 2), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).flatten() # Camera space depth: dot product of point offset and look-at vector ptsdepth = (validpts - cam.position) @ cam.lookat # Absolute distance ptsdist = (ptsframedepth - ptsdepth).abs() # 5. Update closest currentclosest = closestdist[validindices] updatemask = ptsdist < currentclosest updateindices = validindices[updatemask] updateptsuv = ptsuvvalid[updatemask] updateptsdist = ptsdist[updatemask] if updateindices.numel() == 0: continue # Sample color (permute to (C, H, W) for gridsample) ptscolor = F.gridsample( framecolor.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), updateptsuv.view(1, 1, -1, 2), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze().T # Update global arrays closestdist[updateindices] = updateptsdist closestcolor[updateindices] = ptscolor return closestcolor, closestdist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Points projected exactly to the image edge may suffer from interpolation bias if aligncorners=True; the method uses aligncorners=False to mitigate this. Degenerate Input: If no training views cover a point (all projections outside bounds or low alpha), the point retains the initial color [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] and distance \infty. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C), where N is the number of points and C is the number of training cameras. Each camera requires rendering and grid sampling operations proportional to N. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing closestcolor and closestdist. Strengths: Robust to occlusion by using projective depth consistency; leverages existing sparse voxel rendering infrastructure. Limitations: Requires access to training views and their depth/alpha outputs; performance scales linearly with the number of cameras. This method is part of the SVaR (Sparse Voxel Rasterization) pipeline for 3D reconstruction and colorization. It builds on Per-Frame SDF Computation to assign colors to points derived from adaptive sparse voxels. The approach was introduced in the context of efficient mesh extraction and colorization from sparse voxel representations. leonhardrobin/svraster-win10, https://github.com/leonhardrobin/svraster-win10, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Batched SDF Query with Joint Configuration
body: This method evaluates Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for volumetric structures across multiple joint configurations and query points simultaneously to manage memory during batched inference. It differs from single-configuration queries by integrating Forward Kinematics (FK) chains to support automatic differentiation with respect to joint angles, enabling gradient-based optimization such as trajectory optimization for collision avoidance. Inputs and Outputs: points: Input tensor of shape (N, d) representing N geometric points in d dimensions. jointconfiguration: Input tensor of shape (B, J) representing B batched configurations, each with J joint angles. rangeperdim: Input tensor of shape (d, 2) specifying the minimum and maximum range for each dimension. computegrad: Boolean parameter for the CachedSDF class; if False, gradient computation is skipped entirely to improve performance. sdfval: Output tensor of shape (B, N) containing signed distance values. sdfgrad: Output tensor of shape (B, N, d) containing gradients with respect to points, or None if computegrad is False. Data Structures: The implementation uses a custom PyTorch Function subclass (e.g., ObjectFrameSDF) to manage the forward and backward passes for automatic differentiation. The forward pass evaluates the SDF and saves the gradient tensor for the backward pass. The backward pass computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the input points by multiplying the upstream gradient by the saved SDF gradient. Steps: 1. Range Validation: Check if query points lie within the specified rangeperdim using the isinside helper function, which returns a boolean tensor indicating membership. 2. Configuration Application: Apply the batched joint configuration to the SDF object via setjointconfiguration, which internally computes the Forward Kinematics (FK) chain to transform points into the object frame. 3. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF value at the transformed points. If computegrad is True, compute the gradient of the SDF with respect to the points in the object frame. 4. Gradient Accumulation (Backward): If computegrad is True, the backward pass computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the input points using element-wise multiplication. Formulas: The isinside helper function evaluates membership as: \text{is\inside}(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{R}) = \bigwedge{i=0}^{d-1} (R{i,0} \le P{:,i} \le R{i,1}) where \mathbf{P} is the points tensor of shape (N, d) and \mathbf{R} is the range tensor of shape (d, 2). The backward pass computes the gradient with respect to the points as: \frac{\partial \text{loss}}{\partial \mathbf{P}{\text{obj}}} = \frac{\partial \text{loss}}{\partial \text{sdf\val}} \otimes \text{sdf\grad} where \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication broadcasted appropriately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def isinside(points: torch.Tensor, rangeperdim: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Check if points are within the specified range per dimension.""" return torch.all((rangeperdim[:, 0] <= points) & (points <= rangeperdim[:, 1]), dim=-1) class CachedSDF(torch.autograd.Function): """Batched SDF query supporting automatic differentiation.""" @staticmethod def forward(ctx, points, jointconfig, computegrad=True): # Expand points to (B, N, d) for batched evaluation if points.dim() == 2: B = jointconfig.shape[0] points = points.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1) # Evaluate SDF values and gradients w.r.t points in object frame # The underlying C++/CUDA kernel handles FK transformation and SDF evaluation sdfval, sdfgrad = evaluatesdfkernel(points, jointconfig, computegrad) ctx.saveforbackward(sdfgrad) ctx.computegrad = computegrad return sdfval, sdfgrad @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutputs): if not ctx.computegrad: return None, None, None sdfgrad, = ctx.savedtensors dsdfvalsdpoints = gradoutputs[0].unsqueeze(-1) sdfgrad return dsdfvalsdpoints, None, None def query(points: torch.Tensor, jointconfig: torch.Tensor, rangeperdim: torch.Tensor, computegrad: bool = True) -> tuple: """Query SDF for batched joint configurations.""" # Validate points are within range isinrange = isinside(points, rangeperdim) # Set configuration and evaluate sdfval, sdfgrad = CachedSDF.apply(points, jointconfig, computegrad) return sdfval, sdfgrad Parameters: computegrad: Boolean. Default True. If False, skips gradient computation, improving performance. points: Input tensor of shape (N, d). rangeperdim: Input tensor of shape (d, 2). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Points outside rangeperdim may yield undefined or incorrect SDF values if not pre-filtered. Degenerate Input: Empty point sets or zero-sized batches should be handled gracefully by the underlying batched kernel. Precision: Not given in the sources. Computes SDF values for a single configuration. Use when batch processing is not required. Returns both SDF values and gradients for a single configuration. Use when gradients are needed but batched joint configurations are not. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity scales linearly with the number of points N and the number of batched configurations B. Memory complexity is dominated by the storage of B \times N SDF values and gradients. Measured Performance: On an RTX 4070 with an 8-link Kuka robot: Single configuration with 100K points: 3.1 ms. 1000 configurations x 10K points: 198 ms. 5000 configurations x 10K points: 997 ms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High throughput for batched queries; supports autograd for optimization. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Use for trajectory optimization, collision avoidance, and any scenario requiring gradient-based optimization over joint configurations. When Not to Use: Avoid for single-point queries where overhead of batching is not justified. This method originates from the pytorchvolumetric library by the University of Michigan ARM Lab. It is designed to integrate volumetric SDF representations with robotic kinematics, enabling efficient collision checking and optimization in high-dimensional configuration spaces. name: SDF Value and Gradient Query
head: Live Cursor Measurement Caliper, ObjectFrameSDF query, Step Ruler Caliper, measureSdfRayCaliper
body:
SDF Value and Gradient Query inspects Signed Distance Field (SDF) properties at specific 3D coordinates in real-time for debugging and spatial interaction. It outputs the signed distance d(\mathbf{p}), the analytical normal 
abla d(\mathbf{p}), and a hit classification for a given point \mathbf{p}. It differs from SDF Value Computation by focusing on interactive, single-point or sparse inspection rather than bulk volume evaluation, and from Batched SDF Query with Joint Configuration by handling static object frames rather than articulated joint hierarchies. The method supports two primary implementation patterns: interactive ray-casting inspection (caliper) and programmatic object-frame queries. Inputs: A 3D point \mathbf{p} in world or object coordinates; a boolean flag computegrad (default True). Outputs: Signed distance d(\mathbf{p}) \in \mathbb{R}; gradient/normal 
abla d(\mathbf{p}) \in \mathbb{R}^3; hit classification (e.g., COURSE SURFACE, GLASS MARBLE, ABYSS, SKY RAY). Raycasting Scene: A spatial acceleration structure storing triangle meshes to compute closest points. Query Points: A tensor or array of shape (N, 3) or (B, N, 3) for batched queries. 1. Point Acquisition: Cast a ray from the camera through the mouse cursor to determine the 3D world point \mathbf{p}. Alternatively, generate query points using a grid resolution and query range. 2. Distance and Gradient Computation: Query the SDF representation at \mathbf{p}. Compute the raw gradient vector as the difference between the closest surface point and the query point: \mathbf{g} = \mathbf{p}{	ext{closest}} - \mathbf{p}. Normalize the gradient: 
abla d(\mathbf{p}) =  rac{\mathbf{g}}{\|\mathbf{g}\|} if \|\mathbf{g}\| > 0. If computegrad is False, skip gradient calculation to improve speed. 3. Verification and Classification: Verify the normal magnitude \|
abla d(\mathbf{p})\| \approx 1.000. Classify the hit target based on material properties or depth. Apply a +1.0 m free-space probe offset to the measured distance for visualization. 4. Args: raycastscene: A raycasting scene object supporting closest point queries. point: A list or tuple of shape (3,) representing [x, y, z]. computegrad: Boolean flag. If False, gradient computation is skipped. Returns: distance: Float, the signed distance. gradient: List of shape (3,), the normalized gradient/normal. hitinfo: String, classification of the hit target. """ # 1. Find closest point on the mesh surface closestpoint = raycastscene.computeclosestpoint(point) # 2. Compute raw gradient vector and distance rawgradient = [closestpoint[i] - point[i] for i in range(3)] distance = math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in rawgradient)) # 3. Handle edge cases if distance < 1e-6: # Point is on the surface or inside; gradient is undefined or zero gradient = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] hitinfo = "SURFACE" else: # 4. Normalize gradient gradient = [v / distance for v in rawgradient] # 5. Classify hit based on distance thresholds # Classification logic depends on specific scene materials if distance < 0.1: hitinfo = "COURSE SURFACE" elif distance < 1.0: hitinfo = "GLASS MARBLE" elif distance < 10.0: hitinfo = "ABYSS" else: hitinfo = "SKY RAY" # 6. Apply free-space probe offset if needed for visualization displaydistance = distance + 1.0 return distance, gradient, hitinfo def batchedquerysdf(raycastscene, points, computegrad=True): """ Queries SDF for a batch of points. Args: points: List of lists of shape (N, 3) or list of lists of shape (B, N, 3). Returns: sdfvals: List of shape (N,) or (B, N). sdfgrads: List of shape (N, 3) or (B, N, 3). """ # Flatten for processing if batched if isinstance(points[0][0], (list, tuple)): pointsflat = [p for batch in points for p in batch] originalshape = (len(points), len(points[0])) else: pointsflat = points originalshape = (len(points),) n = len(pointsflat) sdfvals = [0.0] n sdfgrads = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(n)] for i in range(n): d, g, = querysdfvalueandgradient(raycastscene, pointsflat[i], computegrad) sdfvals[i] = d sdfgrads[i] = g # Reshape back to original batch structure if len(originalshape) == 2: sdfvals = [sdfvals[i originalshape[1]: (i + 1) originalshape[1]] for i in range(originalshape[0])] sdfgrads = [sdfgrads[i originalshape[1]: (i + 1) originalshape[1]] for i in range(originalshape[0])] return sdfvals, sdfgrads computegrad: Boolean. Zero Distance: If the query point is exactly on the surface, the gradient vector is zero. Precision: Normalization errors can accumulate; verification of \|
abla d\| = 1.000 is recommended for debugging. CSG Latency: Real-time CSG operations may introduce latency (e.g., 0.0018 ms) which should be monitored. SDF Snapping queries the VoxelGenerator at floating-point positions to approximate the surface, snapping instances closer to the surface. It uses at least 2 nearby SDF samples to interpolate the surface distance: P{	ext{snapped}} = P{	ext{mesh}} + 	ext{interpolation}(SDF(P{	ext{mesh}}), 	ext{samples}). It is slower than non-snapping but improves positioning significantly, preferably used when lodindex > 0. Pitfalls include failure to work if terrain is modified after initial generation (workaround: set instances as persistent) and far-distance artifacts where instances may "bury" or "float" when low-resolution meshes are active. name: Cached SDF
head: CachedSDF, Voxel Grid SDF
body:
Cached SDF accelerates Signed Distance Field queries by storing quantized distance values in a voxel grid, falling back to a ground truth SDF for points outside the cache. It differs from standard SDF primitives by trading far-field precision for significant memory savings and query speed, using Int8 quantization to compress the field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ground truth SDF function S{gt}(p), a voxel cell size resolution (or VOXEL), a bounding box defined by range\per\dim with padding, and an outofboundsstrategy. Output: A voxel grid storing quantized signed distances, and a query function returning (d, 
abla d) for any point p. Data Structures: The core structure is a 3D voxel grid of type Int8 (8-bit signed integer). Grid dimensions W 	imes H 	imes D are derived from the object's bounding box divided by VOXEL. A border of PAD voxels (e.g., 2) surrounds the active region to handle boundary conditions. Typical parameters include VOXEL = 0.25 meters, SDF\SCALE = 32, SDF\MAX = 127, and CHUNK = 32 voxels. Quantization Formula: The signed distance d at a voxel center is quantized to an 8-bit integer v using the scale factor SDF\SCALE: v = 	ext{clamp}\left( 	ext{round}\left(  rac{d}{VOXEL} 	imes SDF\SCALE ight), -128, 127 ight) Decoding back to distance: d{decoded} =  rac{v}{SDF\SCALE} 	imes VOXEL Precision is approximately 1/32 of a voxel within \pm 4 voxels of the surface. Query Algorithm: 1. Transform: Convert query point p from world frame to object frame using the inverse transformation matrix. 2. Grid Lookup: Determine if p lies within the cached voxel grid bounds. If inside: Perform trilinear interpolation of the 8 neighboring Int8 values to get a floating-point distance d{cached}. Compute the gradient 
abla d via finite differences of the interpolated values or by querying the ground truth SDF at the same point if gradient accuracy is critical. If outside: Apply the outofboundsstrategy. Default strategy: Compare p against the object's bounding box. Alternative strategy (LOOKUPGTSDF): Query the ground truth SDF S{gt}(p) directly. 3. Return: Return (d, 
abla d). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class CachedSDF: def init(self, sdfgt, voxelsize=0.25, scale=32, padding=2): self.sdfgt = sdfgt self.voxelsize = voxelsize self.scale = scale self.padding = padding self.grid = None self.boundsmin = None self.boundsmax = None self.dims = None def build(self, boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax): dims = np.ceil((boundingboxmax - boundingboxmin) / self.voxelsize).astype(int) self.dims = dims self.boundsmin = boundingboxmin self.boundsmax = boundingboxmax self.grid = np.zeros(dims, dtype=np.int8) for x in range(dims[0]): for y in range(dims[1]): for z in range(dims[2]): pworld = boundingboxmin + np.array([x, y, z]) self.voxelsize + self.voxelsize / 2.0 pobj = pworld d = self.sdfgt(pobj) val = int(round(d / self.voxelsize self.scale)) val = np.clip(val, -128, 127) self.grid[x, y, z] = val def query(self, pworld): pobj = pworld coords = (pobj - self.boundsmin) / self.voxelsize ix, iy, iz = coords if not (0 <= ix < self.dims[0] and 0 <= iy < self.dims[1] and 0 <= iz < self.dims[2]): d, grad = self.sdfgt(pobj) return d, grad ix0, iy0, iz0 = np.floor(coords).astype(int) ix1, iy1, iz1 = np.clip(ix0 + 1, 0, self.dims[0]-1), np.clip(iy0 + 1, 0, self.dims[1]-1), np.clip(iz0 + 1, 0, self.dims[2]-1) fx, fy, fz = coords - np.floor(coords) c000 = self.grid[ix0, iy0, iz0] c100 = self.grid[ix1, iy0, iz0] c010 = self.grid[ix0, iy1, iz0] c110 = self.grid[ix1, iy1, iz0] c001 = self.grid[ix0, iy0, iz1] c101 = self.grid[ix1, iy0, iz1] c011 = self.grid[ix0, iy1, iz1] c111 = self.grid[ix1, iy1, iz1] d00 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx d01 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx d10 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx d11 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx d0 = d00 (1 - fy) + d01 fy d1 = d10 (1 - fy) + d11 fy dcached = d0 (1 - fz) + d1 fz dcached = dcached / self.scale self.voxelsize eps = self.voxelsize 0.1 dx = (self.interpolate(pobj + np.array([eps, 0, 0])) - dcached) / eps dy = (self.interpolate(pobj + np.array([0, eps, 0])) - dcached) / eps dz = (self.interpolate(pobj + np.array([0, 0, eps])) - dcached) / eps grad = np.array([dx, dy, dz]) return dcached, grad def interpolate(self, pobj): coords = (pobj - self.boundsmin) / self.voxelsize ix, iy, iz = coords ix0, iy0, iz0 = np.floor(coords).astype(int) ix1, iy1, iz1 = np.clip(ix0 + 1, 0, self.dims[0]-1), np.clip(iy0 + 1, 0, self.dims[1]-1), np.clip(iz0 + 1, 0, self.dims[2]-1) fx, fy, fz = coords - np.floor(coords) c000 = self.grid[ix0, iy0, iz0] c100 = self.grid[ix1, iy0, iz0] c010 = self.grid[ix0, iy1, iz0] c110 = self.grid[ix1, iy1, iz0] c001 = self.grid[ix0, iy0, iz1] c101 = self.grid[ix1, iy0, iz1] c011 = self.grid[ix0, iy1, iz1] c111 = self.grid[ix1, iy1, iz1] d00 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx d01 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx d10 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx d11 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx d0 = d00 (1 - fy) + d01 fy d1 = d10 (1 - fy) + d11 fy return d0 (1 - fz) + d1 fz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Distances beyond \pm 4 voxels from the surface are saturated to SDF\MAX (127) or -128, losing precision for far-field queries. Out-of-Bounds: The default bounding box comparison for out-of-bounds points always under-approximates the SDF value, but is empirically sufficient for most applications. Truncation: Using a Truncated SDF (TSDF) variant reduces grid size significantly (e.g., 150x smaller) by only storing values within truncationdistance of the surface, but out-of-bounds points return the truncation value. A variant where truncationdistance creates a smaller voxel grid covering only the near-surface region. Out-of-bounds points return the truncation value. The underlying analytic or high-resolution SDF used to populate the cache and handle out-of-bounds queries. Time Complexity: Query time is O(1) for in-bounds points and O(1) for out-of-bounds if using bounding box check, or O(N) if falling back to ground truth SDF. Memory Complexity: O(W 	imes H 	imes D) bytes, where W,H,D are grid dimensions. Performance: Dramatically faster than using the ground truth SDF for out-of-bounds queries. Strengths: Low memory footprint, fast query times, suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: Loss of precision for far-field queries, under-approximation for out-of-bounds points with default strategy. Cached SDF was introduced as a method to optimize SDF queries in volumetric representations, particularly in robotics and simulation contexts where frequent distance queries are needed. It leverages the spatial coherence of SDFs to store values in a voxel grid, reducing the computational cost of evaluating complex implicit surfaces. name: SDF Validity Check with Relaxation
body: SDF Validity Check with Relaxation determines whether a sample point in a Signed Distance Field (SDF) is sufficiently close to the zero-level set (the surface) to be considered "valid" for rendering or optimization purposes. It solves the problem of discrete boundary detection by replacing hard Boolean thresholds with a continuous validity range, preventing discontinuities in differentiable pipelines. It differs from sibling methods like Batched SDF Inference by focusing on local sample classification rather than global inference, and from Eikonal SDF Refinement by using a simple threshold check rather than solving the Eikonal equation for gradient correction. Inputs: d: The signed distance value at a specific point x. v{size}: The voxel size or characteristic length scale of the grid/resolution. \alpha: The relaxation constant (default 1.5). Outputs: A classification of the sample as positive, negative, or valid (near-zero). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the operation is point-wise. Steps: 1. Calculate the relaxation threshold T = v{size} \times \alpha. 2. Compare the absolute SDF value |d| against T. 3. Classify the sample based on the following conditions: If d > T, the sample is positive (outside the valid surface band). If -d > T (i.e., d < -T), the sample is negative (inside the valid surface band). If |d| \le T, the sample is valid (on or near the surface). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checkvalid(d: float, voxelsize: float, relaxation: float = 1.5) -> str: """ Classifies an SDF sample as positive, negative, or valid based on relaxation. Args: d: Signed distance value. voxelsize: The characteristic size of the voxel/grid unit. relaxation: The relaxation constant factor (default 1.5). Returns: 'positive', 'negative', or 'valid'. """ threshold = voxelsize relaxation if d > threshold: return 'positive' elif d < -threshold: return 'negative' else: return 'valid' Parameters: relaxation: A constant factor defining the width of the "valid" band around the zero-level set. Typical value is 1.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If d is extremely close to zero but non-zero due to floating-point noise, it will be classified as valid. This is generally desired for surface sampling. Voxel Size Dependency: The validity band scales with voxelsize. In adaptive grids or non-uniform resolutions, voxelsize must be the local cell size at the query point, not a global average. Eikonal SDF Refinement corrects inaccurate SDF values near the zero-level set by solving the Eikonal equation |\nabla \phi| = 1 using a fast-marching style approach over neighboring voxels. It differs from simple relaxation methods by computing an analytical Eikonal solution in 3D and 2D planes to enforce the exact gradient magnitude constraint. It builds on SDF Validity Check with Relaxation. Choose this when gradient accuracy is critical for normal-based shading or physics, rather than just visibility sampling. Continuous Validity Check determines path validity continuously between 0 and 1, avoiding Boolean discontinuities. It identifies conditions causing discontinuities (e.g., object blocking, incorrect coordinate placement) and applies a smoothing function s(x0 - x1; \alpha) to replace conditional checks like x0 > x1. This returns a continuum of values where 1 is valid and 0 is invalid. A key pitfall is that assuming infinitely large objects during initial path coordinate determination can cause placement errors, which this method handles by smoothing the validity output. SDF Threshold Sensitivity Handling addresses the bias-variance tradeoff of the relaxation threshold \epsilon. Increasing \epsilon smooths the boundary (increasing bias) but improves the sampling probability of relaxed silhouette points, thereby decreasing gradient variance. The recommended value is \epsilon = 10^{-4} for objects within a unit cube. Pitfalls include: if \epsilon is too large (e.g., 10^{-2}), excessive silhouette blurring creates tiny floaters; if \epsilon is too small (e.g., 10^{-6}), insufficient silhouette sampling prevents full convergence. The method is robust across wide scales of \epsilon, requiring only order-of-magnitude tuning. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The check involves only basic arithmetic comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary storage is needed. Strengths: Simple to implement; differentiable if the threshold function is smoothed (see Continuous Validity Check); effective at isolating surface samples for rendering or optimization. Limitations: Does not correct the SDF value itself, only classifies it. The "valid" band width is fixed by the relaxation parameter and voxel size, which may not adapt to local geometry complexity. When to use: When sampling points for volume rendering, shadow optimization, or training where only points near the surface contribute significantly to the loss or image. When not to use: When the SDF values themselves are inaccurate and need correction (use Eikonal SDF Refinement) or when global path validity is required rather than local sample validity. The concept of relaxing hard thresholds in SDF-based rendering originates from the need to make visibility and surface intersection checks differentiable. The specific "checkvalid" implementation with a relaxation factor of 1.5 appears in the DIST-Renderer codebase. The broader context of threshold sensitivity and bias-variance tradeoffs in SDF rendering is detailed in "A Simple Approach to Differentiable Rendering of SDFs", which highlights the importance of \epsilon tuning for silhouette sampling. Continuous validity checks for ray tracing discontinuities are discussed in "Fully Differentiable Ray Tracing via Discontinuity Smoothing for Radio Network Optimization". name: Eikonal SDF Refinement
head: Eikonal Distance Field Solver, Fast Marching SDF Correction
body: Eikonal SDF Refinement corrects inaccurate Signed Distance Field (SDF) values near the zero-level set by solving the Eikonal equation |\nabla \phi| = 1 using a fast-marching style approach over neighboring voxels. It differs from simple relaxation methods by computing an analytical Eikonal solution in 3D and 2D planes to enforce the exact gradient magnitude constraint. It builds on SDF Validity Check with Relaxation. Inputs: A 3D grid of SDF values \phi and grid spacing g. Outputs: Updated SDF values \phi' where the Eikonal constraint is satisfied. Data Structures: phi: 3D array of floats, indexed by (x, y, z). g: Scalar float representing the distance between adjacent voxel centers. Parameters: g: Grid spacing, calculated as g = sdfRadius 2.0 / sdfTexSizeX. Steps: 1. Iterate over every voxel (x, y, z) in the grid. 2. Compute distances to immediate neighbors along the X, Y, and Z axes using neighborMin, which returns min(abs(a), abs(b)) where a and b are the SDF values at kernel + delta and kernel - delta for that axis. 3. Pass the three neighbor distances to eikonal3d. If it returns true, use the result as the candidate distance e. Otherwise, fallback to 2D combinations (eikonal2d for XY, XZ, and YZ planes) and take the minimum valid result. 4. If the computed Eikonal distance e is less than the current voxel value current and current > g, update current = e. Formulas: 3D Eikonal Solution: Given neighbor distances u1, u2, u3 and grid spacing g: e = \frac{1}{n} \left( \sum{i=1}^{n} ui + \sqrt{ \left(\sum{i=1}^{n} ui\right)^2 - n \left( \sum{i=1}^{n} ui^2 - g^2 \right) } \right) where n=3. Returns false if the discriminant d = \left(\sum ui\right)^2 - n \left( \sum ui^2 - g^2 \right) < 0. 2D Eikonal Solution: Given two neighbor distances h, v and grid spacing g: If |h - v| \ge g: e = \min(h, v) + g Else: e = \frac{1}{2} \left( (h+v) + \sqrt{(h+v)^2 - 2(h^2 + v^2 - g^2)} \right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def eikonal2d(h, v, g): if abs(h - v) >= g: return min(h, v) + g sumhv = h + v sumsq = h2 + v2 discriminant = sumhv2 - 2 (sumsq - g2) if discriminant < 0: return None return 0.5 (sumhv + math.sqrt(discriminant)) def eikonal3d(u, g): n = 3 sumu = sum(u) sumusq = sum(val2 for val in u) discriminant = sumu2 - n (sumusq - g2) if discriminant < 0: return None, False e = (1.0 / n) (sumu + math.sqrt(discriminant)) return e, True def neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, axis): if axis == 0: n1, n2 = phi[x+1, y, z], phi[x-1, y, z] elif axis == 1: n1, n2 = phi[x, y+1, z], phi[x, y-1, z] else: n1, n2 = phi[x, y, z+1], phi[x, y, z-1] return min(abs(n1), abs(n2)) def refinesdf(phi, g): height, width, depth = phi.shape for x in range(1, width - 1): for y in range(1, height - 1): for z in range(1, depth - 1): current = phi[x, y, z] if current <= g: continue u = [ neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, 0), neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, 1), neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, 2) ] beste = current e3d, valid3d = eikonal3d(u, g) if valid3d: beste = min(beste, e3d) else: candidates = [] exy = eikonal2d(u[0], u[1], g) if exy is not None: candidates.append(exy) exz = eikonal2d(u[0], u[2], g) if exz is not None: candidates.append(exz) eyz = eikonal2d(u[1], u[2], g) if eyz is not None: candidates.append(eyz) if candidates: beste = min(beste, min(candidates)) if beste < current: phi[x, y, z] = beste Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The 3D Eikonal solver returns false if the discriminant d < 0, forcing a fallback to 2D planes. This handles degenerate cases where the gradient direction does not align with a single axis or plane. Boundary conditions: The pseudocode assumes interior voxels and requires padding or clamping for grid edges. Precision: The square root and discriminant calculations require floating-point stability. name: SDF Training with Eikonal Loss
head: Implicit Geometric Regularization, IGR, SDF Surface Training with Eikonal Loss, Neural SDF Training with Eikonal Regularization, Implicit neural representations with Eikonal regularization
body:
SDF Training with Eikonal Loss trains a neural network to represent a surface as the zero-level set of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) by enforcing the Eikonal equation (||
abla f|| = 1) alongside data constraints. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-fidelity 3D shapes from raw point clouds or images without requiring pre-computed 3D supervision (like occupancy grids). Unlike occupancy-based methods, it explicitly regularizes the gradient magnitude to ensure the output is a valid metric distance field, distinguishing it from siblings like DeepSDF Neural Network which focuses on latent code optimization, and SDF Optimization via Finite Differences which may lack the global geometric regularization. Inputs: A set of oriented points X = \{xi\} with normals N = \{ni\}, or posed images Ij with projection matrices Wj. Outputs: Network parameters 	heta defining the SDF f(x; 	heta). Data Structures: MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron f: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R} with parameters 	heta. Common architectures include 8 layers with 256 hidden units or configurations like D8-W45 (8 depth, 45 width). Activation: Softplus is recommended for smoothness. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Center the input point cloud by subtracting its mean. Normalize the 3D space to a bounding box, typically [-1, 1]^3. 2. Sampling: Sample points X{data} from the input point cloud. Sample points X{eik} uniformly from the bounding box (e.g., 1024 points) to enforce the Eikonal constraint everywhere. Optional: For image-based training, sample pixels and cast rays. 3. Forward Pass: Query the network for distances and gradients at sampled points: (d, 
abla d) = (f(x), 
ablax f(x)) for x \in X{data} \cup X{eik}. Compute gradients using automatic differentiation. 4. Loss Computation: Data Loss (L{data}): Enforces f(x) \approx 0 for points on the surface and aligns 
abla f with normals n. L{data} =  rac{1}{|X{data}|} \sum{x \in X{data}} \left( f(x)^2 + (1 - \langle 
abla f(x), n(x) angle)^2 ight) Eikonal Loss (L{eikonal}): Enforces unit gradient magnitude for all sampled points. L{eikonal} =  rac{1}{|X{eik}|} \sum{x \in X{eik}} \left( \|
abla f(x)\|2 - 1 ight)^2 Note: Some implementations use the absolute difference |\|
abla f(x)\|2 - 1|. Interior/Off-surface Regularization: Penalizes points inside the object to ensure correct sign. L{inter} = \exp(-100 \cdot |f(x)|) Applied to X{eik} points. Total Loss: L = L{data} + \lambda{eik} L{eikonal} + \lambda{inter} L{inter} 5. Optimization: Update 	heta using Adam optimizer. Learning rate: 10^{-3}. Scheduler: LambdaLR or exponential decay.
