name: MLP Distillation
head: Knowledge Distillation for SDF, SDF Distillation
body: MLP Distillation compresses a large Signed Distance Function (SDF) network into a smaller MLP by minimizing the output discrepancy between the two networks at sampled points. The teacher network f uses 256 hidden channels, while the student network f{\text{small}} uses 16 hidden channels. The method transfers geometric knowledge from the teacher to the student over a fixed number of iterations before replacing the teacher for subsequent finetuning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained large SDF network f (teacher) with 256 hidden channels, a randomly initialized small SDF network f{\text{small}} (student) with 16 hidden channels, and a set of training rays \mathbf{r} sampled from the training dataset. Output: The updated weights of the distilled small SDF network f{\text{small}}. Data Structures: Teacher Network f: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 256 hidden units. Student Network f{\text{small}}: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 16 hidden units. Sampled Points \mathbf{x}i: 3D coordinates along the training rays. Parameters: Distillation Iterations: 5,000 iterations. Loss Function: L1 loss. Gradient Handling: Stop gradient applied to teacher outputs. Algorithm: 1. Sampling: For each of the 5,000 distillation iterations, sample a batch of random rays \mathbf{r} from the training set. 2. Point Evaluation: For each ray, evaluate the teacher network f and the student network f{\text{small}} at the sampled points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the distillation loss \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} using the L1 norm of the difference between the teacher's and student's SDF outputs. A stop gradient operation is applied to the teacher's output to prevent it from updating during this phase. \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}(\mathbf{r}):= \sum{i=0}^{N-1} |f(\mathbf{x}i) - f{\text{small}}(\mathbf{x}i)| where N is the number of sampled points per ray. 4. Optimization: Update the weights of f{\text{small}} by minimizing \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} using gradient descent. 5. Replacement: After 5,000 iterations, discard the original teacher network f and replace it with the distilled network f{\text{small}} for subsequent finetuning stages. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mlpdistillation(teachermodel, studentmodel, trainingrays, iterations=5000): # teachermodel: MLP with 256 channels # studentmodel: MLP with 16 channels for iteration in range(iterations): # 1. Sample random rays from the training set raysbatch = sampletrainingrays(trainingrays) # 2. Extract 3D coordinates xi along the rays points = raysbatch.points # 3. Evaluate teacher network with stop gradient teacheroutputs = teachermodel.forward(points, stopgradient=True) # 4. Evaluate student network studentoutputs = studentmodel.forward(points) # 5. Compute L1 loss: Ldist(r) = sum{i=0}^{N-1} |f(xi) - fsmall(xi)| loss = sum(abs(teacheroutputs - studentoutputs)) # 6. Update student weights via gradient descent gradients = computegradients(loss, studentmodel.parameters()) studentmodel.updateweights(gradients) # 7. Discard original teacher and switch to distilled counterpart for finetuning return studentmodel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure the student network is initialized with appropriate weights to avoid vanishing gradients during the initial distillation steps. Boundaries: The method assumes the sampled points \mathbf{x}i are within the domain where the teacher model provides meaningful SDF values. Degenerate Input: If the training rays do not cover the scene uniformly, the distilled model may inherit biases from the teacher's sampling distribution. Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic method for converting trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models between heterogeneous architectures, including MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, and hash tables. It solves the problem of architectural incompatibility by constructing a unified two-level view of volume representations and performing distillation progressively from shallower to deeper levels. Unlike methods that distill only between identical architectures, PVD enables any-to-any conversion while maintaining teacher performance, leveraging a block-wise training strategy to accelerate the process significantly. Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) Training is a method for learning implicit surface representations from oriented point clouds by supervising a neural network to output a probability distribution over depths rather than a single scalar value. It solves the problem of representing discontinuous directed distance fields (DDFs) with a continuous (C^1) network, enabling accurate modeling of surface occlusions and visibility transitions. It distinguishes itself from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling depth as a discrete mixture of delta functions and enforcing view consistency inequalities to ensure geometric coherence across different viewing directions. Time Complexity: The distillation process requires 5,000 iterations of forward and backward passes through both networks. Memory Complexity: The student network uses significantly less memory than the teacher (16 channels vs. 256 channels). Measured Performance: The method enables the use of a small 16-channel MLP for inference while maintaining the geometric accuracy of a 256-channel MLP. Strengths: Significant reduction in model size and inference latency; preserves high-quality geometry learned by the teacher. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained large teacher model; distillation quality depends on the coverage of sampled points. When to Use: When real-time rendering is required but the initial training used a large, slow network. When Not to Use: When the teacher model is not available or when the scene geometry is too complex for a small MLP to capture even with distillation. MLP Distillation was introduced in the context of HybridNeRF, an efficient neural rendering method that combines volumetric and surface-based approaches. The method addresses the challenge of complex backgrounds and the high cost of separate NeRF background models. By distilling a large SDF into a smaller one, it enables real-time rendering without doubling inference costs. The approach builds on SDF Training with Eikonal Loss, using the large network to learn accurate scene geometry before compression. name: Progressive Volume Distillation
head: PVD
body: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic method for converting trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models between heterogeneous architectures, including MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, and hash tables. It solves the problem of architectural incompatibility by constructing a unified two-level view of volume representations and performing distillation progressively from shallower to deeper levels. Unlike methods that distill only between identical architectures, PVD enables any-to-any conversion while maintaining teacher performance, leveraging a block-wise training strategy to accelerate the process significantly. Inputs and Outputs Input: A trained teacher model \phi^ (of any architecture: Hash, VM, MLP, or Tensor) and a target student architecture (different from or same as the teacher). Output: A trained student model \phis that approximates the teacher's radiance field. Data Structures and Unified View PVD maps all NeRF architectures to a unified two-level view consisting of a feature extraction stage \phi1^ and a decoding stage \phi2^. The teacher model is split into two cascaded modules: \phi^(x, d) = \phi2^(\phi1^(x, d)) where x is the 3D coordinate and d is the view direction. The split depends on the architecture: 1. Hybrid Representations: \phi1^ is the explicit part (e.g., hash table lookup, tensor grid access) and \phi2^ is the implicit part (e.g., MLP decoder). 2. Purely Implicit (MLP): The network is split by depth. \phi1^ comprises the first K layers, and \phi2^ comprises the remaining layers. Default K=4. 3. Purely Explicit (Plenoxels): \phi2^ is set to an identity function, as the explicit grid directly outputs density and color. Loss Functions The total loss L combines volume-aligned loss, density loss, color loss, RGB loss, and regularization: L = \omega1 L{v2} + \omega2 L{\sigma 2} + \omega3 L{c 2} + \omega4 L{rgb 2} + \omega5 L{reg} where \|\cdot\|^2 denotes the squared L2 norm. 1. Volume-Aligned Loss (L{v2}): Aligns the intermediate feature outputs of the teacher and student. L{v2} = \| \phi{1t}^(x, d) - \phi{1s}^(x, d) \|^2 where \phi{1t}^ and \phi{1s}^ are the outputs of the first stage for the teacher and student, respectively. 2. Density Loss (L{\sigma 2}): Matches the density \sigma after clipping to a constrained range [a, b] to ensure numerical stability. L{\sigma 2} = \| \min(\max(\sigmat, a), b) - \min(\max(\sigmas, a), b) \|^2 where \sigmat and \sigmas are the teacher and student densities. The range [a, b] limits values that are physically consistent (transparent or opaque) but numerically unstable. 3. Color Loss (L{c 2}): Matches the color outputs. L{c 2} = \| ct - cs \|^2 where ct and cs are the color outputs. 4. RGB Loss (L{rgb 2}): Matches the final rendered RGB values. L{rgb 2} = \| \text{RGB}t - \text{RGB}s \|^2 5. Regularization (L{reg}): Applied only to specific explicit or hybrid students. For Plenoxels and VM-decomposition: Add L1 sparsity loss and Total Variation (TV) regularization loss. For other architectures: Not applied (or zero). Parameters Loss Weights: \omega1 = 2 \times 10^{-3} (volume-aligned), \omega2 = 2 \times 10^{-3} (density), \omega3 = 2 \times 10^{-3} (color), \omega4 = 1 (RGB). \omega5 is not explicitly given in the sources. Density Range [a, b]: Specific values for a and b are not given in the sources, but the clipping function \min(\max(\sigma, a), b) is mandatory. Optimization: Adam Optimizer with initial learning rate 0.02. Batch Size: 4096 rays. Total Steps: 20,000 steps. Algorithm: Block-wise Distillation To accelerate training, PVD uses a block-wise strategy that progressively unfreezes deeper stages of the student network, leveraging the volume-aligned loss to stabilize early training. 1. Stage 1 (Steps 1–3,000): Forward pass only through the student's first stage \phi{1s}^ to compute L{v2} and L{\sigma 2} (using teacher's \phi{1t}^ and \sigmat). Backpropagate gradients to update \phi{1s}^. Note: The teacher's \phi{1t}^ is frozen and used as a reference. 2. Stage 2 (Steps 3,001–8,000): Forward pass through student's \phi{1s}^ and \phi{2s}^ to compute intermediate outputs. Compute L{v2}, L{\sigma 2}, L{c 2}, and L{reg} (if applicable). Backpropagate gradients to update \phi{1s}^ and \phi{2s}^. 3. Stage 3 (Steps 8,001–20,000): Forward pass through the full student network \phis^ to compute final rendered RGB. Compute full loss L including L{rgb 2}. Backpropagate gradients to update all student parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivevolumedistillation(teachermodel, studentmodel, numsteps=20000, batchsize=4096, lr=0.02, a=0.0, b=10.0): # Loss weights from wv2, ws2, wc2, wrgb = 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 1.0 wreg = 1.0 # Not given in sources optimizer = Optimizer(studentmodel.parameters(), lr=lr) for step in range(1, numsteps + 1): rays = samplerays(batchsize) # Teacher forward pass (frozen) with torch.nograd(): tfeat = teachermodel.phi1(rays.x, rays.d) tsigma = getdensity(tfeat) tcolor = getcolor(tfeat, rays.d) trgb = renderray(teachermodel, rays) # Student forward pass Stage 1 sfeat = studentmodel.phi1(rays.x, rays.d) ssigma = getdensity(sfeat) scolor = getcolor(sfeat, rays.d) # Losses lossv2 = mse(sfeat, tfeat) losss2 = mse(clip(tsigma, a, b), clip(ssigma, a, b)) lossc2 = mse(scolor, tcolor) if step <= 3000: loss = wv2 lossv2 + ws2 losss2 optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() elif step <= 8000: lossreg = regularizationloss(studentmodel) if studentmodel.isexplicit else 0.0 loss = wv2 lossv2 + ws2 losss2 + wc2 lossc2 + wreg lossreg optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() else: srgb = renderray(studentmodel, rays) lossrgb = mse(srgb, trgb) lossreg = regularizationloss(studentmodel) if studentmodel.isexplicit else 0.0 loss = wv2 lossv2 + ws2 losss2 + wc2 lossc2 + wrgb lossrgb + wreg lossreg optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() def mse(a, b): return sum((x - y)2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) / len(a) def clip(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) def samplerays(n): return [(randompoint(), randomdirection()) for in range(n)] def getdensity(feat): return feat # Simplified for pseudocode def getcolor(feat, d): return feat # Simplified for pseudocode def renderray(model, rays): return [integrateray(model, r) for r in rays] def regularizationloss(model): return l1norm(model.weights) + tvnorm(model.weights) class Optimizer: def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params; self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): [p.grad.zero() for p in self.params] def step(self): [p.data -= self.lr p.grad for p in self.params] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Numerical Instability: Optimizing density \sigma directly is unstable. Clipping \sigma to [a, b] is required. Gradient Saturation: Applying density loss on \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is inefficient due to gradient saturation and high computational cost of exponentials during block-wise implementation. Architecture Split: For purely explicit models (Plenoxels), \phi2^ is identity, so no MLP decoding occurs. A method for mutual conversion between different NeRF architectures (implicit, explicit, hybrid) using a unified two-level view and active learning strategies to accelerate distillation and improve synthesis quality. Time Complexity: Distillation is significantly faster than training from scratch. An MLP-based NeRF distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model takes 1.5 hours compared to 25 hours for training from scratch. Speedup Factor: 10x to 20x faster than training the original NeRF from scratch. Memory Complexity: Depends on the student architecture. The method itself does not add significant memory overhead beyond storing the teacher and student models. Performance: Maintains teacher performance levels. Conversions between Hash, VM, MLP, and Tensors maintain performance comparable to the teacher model and training from scratch. Strengths: Enables any-to-any conversion; accelerates training; improves synthesis quality via density clipping and volume-aligned loss. Limitations: Requires a trained teacher model; performance depends on the quality of the teacher. Hardware: Experiments performed on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. Progressive Volume Distillation was proposed in the paper "One Is All: Bridging the Gap between Neural Radiance Fields Architectures with Progressive Volume Distillation". It addresses the diversity of NeRF architectures (MLP, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables) which have different trade-offs in training speed, rendering speed, and geometric manipulability. Prior methods focused on distilling between models of the same architecture, whereas PVD provides a systematic framework for heterogeneous conversion. The method was validated on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples datasets. name: Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning
head: PVD-AL
body: Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning (PVD-AL) is a method for mutual conversion between different Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architectures (implicit, explicit, and hybrid). It accelerates distillation and improves synthesis quality by splitting the teacher and student models into cascaded modules and applying active learning strategies to select important camera poses, rays, and sample points. It sets itself apart from standard distillation by using a block-wise training schedule that spares networks from forwarding the entire network and rendering RGB outputs in early phases, and by dynamically selecting hard examples across three levels of granularity. Inputs: Teacher model \phi^t (architecture can be MLP, hybrid, or Plenoxels). Student model \phi^s (target architecture). Training dataset containing camera poses and rays. Hyperparameters: \omega1, \dots, \omega5 (loss weights), K (split point for MLP layers), N{sp} (number of important sample points). Outputs: Distilled student model \phi^s. The method operates on three levels of active learning sets, updated per epoch: 1. TCP (Important Camera Poses): A set of camera poses identified as difficult for the student. 2. TSR (Important Sample Rays): A set of rays identified as difficult. 3. TSP (Important Sample Points): A set of 3D points along rays identified as difficult, selected based on weight metrics. The core mechanism splits any model \phi^ into a cascade of two modules: \phi^(x, d) = \phi^2(\phi^1(x, d)) For MLP NeRF: \phi^1 consists of the first K layers; \phi^2 consists of the remaining layers. For Hybrid Representations: \phi^1 is the explicit part (e.g., voxel grid); \phi^2 is the implicit part (e.g., MLP). For Plenoxels (Purely Explicit): \phi^1 is the full grid; \phi^2 is the identity function. The total loss L is a weighted sum of five terms: L = \omega1 L{v2} + \omega2 L{\sigma 2} + \omega3 L{c 2} + \omega4 L{\text{rgb} 2} + \omega5 L{\text{reg}} 1. Volume-aligned loss (L{v2}): Aligns the outputs of the first module \phi1 between teacher and student: L{v2} = || \phi{1t}(x, d) - \phi{1s}(x, d) ||2^2 where \phi{1t} and \phi{1s} are the outputs of the first module for the teacher and student, respectively. 2. Density loss (L{\sigma 2}): Mean-squared error (MSE) between teacher and student density \sigma. 3. Color loss (L{c 2}): MSE between teacher and student color c. 4. RGB loss (L{\text{rgb} 2}): MSE between rendered RGB images. 5. Regularization (L{\text{reg}}): Depends on the student model; for Plenoxels and VM-decomposition, it includes L1 sparsity loss and Total Variation (TV) regularization. 1. Initialization: Initialize TCP, TSR, and TSP sets. 2. Epoch Loop: For each training epoch: a. Pose Selection: Generate random poses and select important poses from TCP to form trainposes. b. Ray Sampling: Sample rays from trainposes to form allbatchrays. c. Batch Processing: For each batch of rays: i. Ray Selection: Generate random rays and select important rays from TSR to form trainrays. ii. Point Sampling: Sample points from trainrays to form traindata. iii. Forward Pass: Forward traindata through both teacher (teamodel) and student (stumodel) to get outputs teaout and stuout. iv. Point Selection (Active Learning): Extract weight metrics PW from teaout and stuout (specifically density/color weights). Sort points by PW to get indices sortedPW. Select the top N{sp} points as TSP: TSP = sortedPW[:Nsp]. v. Loss Calculation: Calculate L{\sigma 2} and L{c 2} using only the points in TSP. Calculate L{v2} using all points in traindata. Calculate L{\text{rgb} 2} and L{\text{reg}} as appropriate. vi. Backpropagation: Update student model parameters using total loss L. 3. Update Active Sets: Update TCP, TSR, and TSP based on training progress (details of update logic not fully specified in source, but implied by "continually analyze"). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainpvdal(teamodel, stumodel, traindataset, hyperparams): """ teamodel: Teacher NeRF model stumodel: Student NeRF model traindataset: Dataset containing camera poses and rays hyperparams: Dictionary containing omega weights, K, Nsp, numepochs """ # Initialize active learning sets TCP = set() # Important Camera Poses TSR = set() # Important Sample Rays TSP = set() # Important Sample Points # Split models based on architecture # For MLP: teamodel1 = teamodel[:K], teamodel2 = teamodel[K:] # For Hybrid: teamodel1 = explicitpart, teamodel2 = implicitpart # For Plenoxels: teamodel1 = fullgrid, teamodel2 = identity for epoch in range(hyperparams.numepochs): # 1. Active Learning: Camera Poses # Generate random poses randomposes = [traindataset.getpose(i) for i in range(hyperparams.numposes)] # Select important poses from TCP selectedtcpposes = random.sample(list(TCP), min(10, len(TCP))) trainposes = randomposes + selectedtcpposes # 2. Sample Rays allbatchrays = [traindataset.sampleraysfrompose(p) for p in trainposes] for batchrays in allbatchrays: # 3. Active Learning: Rays # Generate random rays randomrays = [traindataset.sampleray() for in range(len(batchrays))] # Select important rays from TSR selectedtsrrays = random.sample(list(TSR), min(10, len(TSR))) trainrays = randomrays + selectedtsrrays # 4. Sample Points traindata = [traindataset.samplepointsonray(r) for r in trainrays] # 5. Forward Pass teaout = teamodel(traindata) stuout = stumodel(traindata) # 6. Active Learning: Points (TSP) # Extract weights (e.g., density or color magnitude) teaweights = [abs(o.density) for o in teaout] stuweights = [abs(o.density) for o in stuout] combinedweights = [t + s for t, s in zip(teaweights, stuweights)] # Sort points by weight (descending) sortedindices = sorted(range(len(combinedweights)), key=lambda i: combinedweights[i], reverse=True) # Select top Nsp points TSPindices = sortedindices[:hyperparams.Nsp] # 7. Loss Calculation # Volume-aligned loss on all points Lv2 = sum((t.phi1 - s.phi1)2 for t, s in zip(teaout, stuout)) / len(teaout) # Density and Color losses on TSP only teaouttsp = [teaout[i] for i in TSPindices] stuouttsp = [stuout[i] for i in TSPindices] Lsigma2 = sum((t.density - s.density)2 for t, s in zip(teaouttsp, stuouttsp)) / len(teaouttsp) Lc2 = sum((t.color - s.color)2 for t, s in zip(teaouttsp, stuouttsp)) / len(teaouttsp) # RGB and Regularization losses # Note: RGB loss requires rendering full images, which is skipped in early block-wise phases # For simplicity, assuming standard rendering for these losses Lrgb2 = computergbloss(teamodel, stumodel, trainrays) Lreg = computeregularization(stumodel) # Total Loss L = (hyperparams.omega1 Lv2 + hyperparams.omega2 Lsigma2 + hyperparams.omega3 Lc2 + hyperparams.omega4 Lrgb2 + hyperparams.omega5 Lreg) # 8. Backpropagation stumodel.zerograd() L.backward() stumodel.step() # 9. Update Active Sets (Simplified) # Add current difficult poses/rays/points to sets TCP.update(trainposes) TSR.update(trainrays) TSP.update(TSPindices) def computergbloss(teamodel, stumodel, rays): """Renders RGB images for teacher and student and computes MSE.""" # Implementation depends on renderer; returns scalar MSE pass def computeregularization(model): """Computes L1 sparsity and TV regularization based on student architecture.""" # Implementation depends on student model type pass Numerical Instability in Density Loss: The density loss L{\sigma 2} is hard to optimize directly because density reflects light transmittance, leading to numerical instability when \sigma is very high or very low (completely transparent or opaque). Mitigation: This is handled by: 1. Density Range Constraint: Clipping the density values. 2. Volume-Aligned Loss: Using L{v2} to stabilize training by aligning intermediate representations rather than just final outputs. 3. Block-wise Distillation: In early training phases, only forward stage 1 (\phi1) to spare networks from forwarding the entire network and rendering RGB outputs, which significantly accelerates the distillation process. Time: The block-wise strategy accelerates distillation by sparing networks from forwarding the entire network and rendering RGB outputs in early phases. Active learning reduces the number of samples needed to grasp complex concepts compared to traditional supervised learning. Memory: Memory usage depends on the student architecture (MLP, sparse tensor, etc.) and the size of the active learning sets (TCP, TSR, TSP). Strengths: Enables mutual conversion between different NeRF architectures (implicit, explicit, hybrid). Significantly improves synthesis quality and accelerates training compared to standard distillation. Three-level active learning (poses, rays, points) efficiently transfers knowledge by focusing on difficult examples. Limitations: Density loss optimization remains challenging without the specific mitigations (clipping, volume-aligned loss). Use when converting between different NeRF architectures (e.g., MLP to Plenoxels) and needing high-quality results with faster training. Use when computational resources are limited and active learning can reduce the number of required training samples. PVD-AL was introduced in the paper "Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning for Efficient NeRF Architecture Conversion". It builds upon the Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) method [Parent], which allows any-to-any conversions between NeRF architectures by distilling progressively on different levels of volume representations [Parent]. The method addresses the inefficiency of traditional distillation by introducing active learning strategies and a block-wise training schedule. It leverages the observation that different parts of a NeRF model correspond to different learning objectives, allowing for modular distillation. name: Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) Training
head: DDF Learning and Loss Functions, PDDF Optimization, Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF), View Consistency Inequality
body:
Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) Training is a method for learning implicit surface representations from oriented point clouds by supervising a neural network to output a probability distribution over depths rather than a single scalar value. It solves the problem of representing discontinuous directed distance fields (DDFs) with a continuous (C^1) network, enabling accurate modeling of surface occlusions and visibility transitions. It distinguishes itself from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling depth as a discrete mixture of delta functions and enforcing view consistency inequalities to ensure geometric coherence across different viewing directions. Inputs and Outputs: The network takes an oriented point 	au = (p, v) as input, where p \in B is a 3D position and v \in S^2 is a viewing direction. The network predicts a visibility scalar \xib(p, v) \in [0, 1] and a probabilistic depth distribution P{p,v}(d). The distribution is a mixture of K Dirac delta functions: P{p,v}(d) = \sum{i=1}^K wi(p, v) \delta(d - di(p, v)) where wi are mixture weights (\sum wi = 1) and di are delta locations. The final predicted depth is d{i^} where i^ = \arg\maxi wi. Data Structures: The network outputs K+1 values per oriented point: \xib (visibility prediction), di (depth component i for i=1 \dots K), and wi (weight component i for i=1 \dots K). The weights are constrained such that \sum{i=1}^K wi = 1. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Extraction: Generate six types of samples (p, v) from the mesh to train the network: (U) Uniform: Random (p, v) within the bounding volume and sphere. (A) At-surface: Samples where ground truth visibility \xi(p, v) = 1. (B) Bounding: Samples where p \in \partial B (boundary of bounding volume) and v points interior. (S) Surface: Samples where p \in S (on the surface) and v is uniformly distributed on the sphere U[S^2]. (T) Tangent: Samples where v lies in the tangent space of the surface point q(p, v) \in S. (O) Offset: Samples where p is offset from (T) samples along the surface normal n(p, v) by a small value. 2. View Consistency Inequality Enforcement: Ensure that if a surface point q1 is visible from 	au1 = (p1, v1) (i.e., q1 = p1 + d(	au1)v1 \in S) and q1 also lies on the ray from 	au2 = (p2, v2) (i.e., \exists t > 0 such that p2 + t v2 = q1), then: (i) \xi(	au2) = 1 (the point is visible from 	au2) and (ii) d(	au2) \le ||p2 - q1||2 = t (the depth from 	au2 is no greater than the distance to the known surface point). 3. Loss Computation: Compute the following loss terms per oriented point: Minimum Distance Loss: Trains the highest probability depth component i^ = \arg\maxj wj: \mathcal{L}d = \xi |d{b i^} - d|. Visibility Loss: Binary cross-entropy between ground truth \xi and prediction \xib: \mathcal{L}\xi = 	ext{BCE}(\xi, \xib). First-Order Normals Loss: Matches surface normals derived from 
ablap d{b i^} to ground truth normals n: \mathcal{L}n = -\xi |n^T n{b i^}(p, v)|. Directed Eikonal Regularization: Applied to visibility and each delta component di: \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} = \gamma{	ext{E},d} \sum{i=1}^K \xi [
ablai \widehat{d}i v + 1]^2 + \gamma{	ext{E},\xi} [
abla\xi \widehat{\xi} v]^2. Weight Field Regularization: Encourages low entropy (preventing unnecessary switching of i^) and transition at discontinuities: \mathcal{L}W = \gammaV \mathcal{L}V + \gammaT \mathcal{L}T. 4. Optimization: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}d + \mathcal{L}\xi + \mathcal{L}n + \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} + \mathcal{L}W using gradient descent. Parameters: K: Number of Dirac delta components. Typical value is K=2 to represent discontinuities without sacrificing efficiency. \gamma{	ext{E},d}, \gamma{	ext{E},\xi}: Eikonal regularization weights. \gammaV, \gammaT: Weight field regularization weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: Standard DDFs are discontinuous at surface collisions and occlusions. PDDF handles this by allowing the weight field w(p, v) to smoothly transition from one index i^ to another j at discontinuities, causing the selected delta component d{i^} to jump to dj, creating the desired discontinuity in d while keeping the network C^1. Precision: The use of \arg\max for i^ introduces a non-differentiable step. The smooth transition of weights ensures that the distribution is differentiable, but the final depth selection is discrete. The loss functions are designed to train the components such that the correct component has the highest weight. The PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss (\mathcal{L}S) is the primary training objective for Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields, designed to supervise the network's prediction of visibility, surface normals, and a mixture of depth components. It solves the problem of learning accurate implicit surface representations from oriented point clouds by combining geometric consistency, visibility prediction, and regularization of the probabilistic weight fields. It distinguishes itself from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling depth as a discrete mixture of delta functions (PDDF) and enforcing transitions between these components at surface discontinuities via a dedicated weight transition loss. Time Complexity: Rendering is a single forward pass per pixel, independent of mesh complexity. Training requires generating samples and computing gradients for all loss terms. Memory Complexity: The network stores weights for K depth components and visibility. For K=2, this is minimal overhead over a standard DDF. Strengths: Handles discontinuities (occlusions, self-occlusions) naturally via the probabilistic mixture. View consistency is enforced. Efficient rendering. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of weight field regularization to prevent unnecessary switching of i^. The discrete selection of i^ is non-differentiable, though the underlying distribution is smooth. When to use: When learning implicit surfaces from oriented point clouds or meshes where occlusions and visibility changes are significant. When not to use: For simple, convex, or non-occluding shapes where a standard SDF or DDF suffices. Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields were introduced to address the limitations of standard Directed Distance Fields (DDFs) in representing discontinuous fields with continuous neural networks. The method builds on the properties of DDFs, specifically the View Consistency Inequality, which ensures geometric coherence across viewing directions. The key innovation is the modification of the depth field d to output a probability distribution over depths, allowing a C^1 network to represent discontinuous fields. This approach is particularly useful for differentiable rendering and shape reconstruction from oriented point clouds. Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3594225, fetched 2026-10-29

name: PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss
head: PDDF loss
body:
The PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss (\mathcal{L}S) is the training objective for Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDF), a method that represents 3D shapes using a probabilistic distribution over directed distance components. It solves the problem of training neural networks to predict depth, visibility, and surface normals from oriented point data by combining a minimum distance loss, visibility and normal matching, Directed Eikonal regularization, and weight field regularizations. It sets itself apart from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling the uncertainty and switching between multiple delta components via a probabilistic weight field, rather than predicting a single deterministic distance value. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Oriented points (p, v) where p is position and v is view direction. Ground truth data includes visibility \xi, surface normal n, and depth d. Predictions from the network are visibility \hat{\xi}, depth components \hat{d}i, and weights wi for i \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}S. Data Structures: K: Number of delta components. Sources specify K=2. i^: The maximum likelihood index, defined as i^ = \arg \maxj wj. \hat{d}{b{i^}}: The depth component corresponding to the maximum likelihood index. n{b{i^}}(p, v): The surface normal derived from the gradient of the predicted depth at the maximum likelihood index, 
ablap \hat{d}{b{i^}}. Formulas: The total loss is a weighted sum of five components: \mathcal{L}S = \gammad \mathcal{L}d + \gamma\xi \mathcal{L}\xi + \gamman \mathcal{L}n + \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} + \mathcal{L}W \quad (2) 1. Minimum Distance Loss (\mathcal{L}d): Trains the highest probability depth component to match the ground truth depth. \mathcal{L}d = \xi | \hat{d}{b{i^}} - d | where \xi is the ground truth visibility. 2. Visibility Objective (\mathcal{L}\xi): Binary cross-entropy between the visibility prediction and the ground truth. \mathcal{L}\xi = 	ext{BCE}(\hat{\xi}, \xib) 3. Normals Loss (\mathcal{L}n): Matches the predicted surface normal (derived from 
ablap \hat{d}{b{i^}}) to the ground truth normal n. \mathcal{L}n = -\xi | n^T n{b{i^}}(p, v) | 4. Directed Eikonal Regularization (\mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}}): Applied to the visibility and each delta component of depth, analogous to SDF work. \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} = \gamma{	ext{E},d} \sumi \xi \left[ 
ablai \hat{d}i \cdot v + 1 ight]^2 + \gamma{	ext{E},\xi} \left[ 
abla\xi \hat{\xi} \cdot v ight]^2 where 
ablai denotes the gradient with respect to the i-th component. 5. Weight Field Regularization (\mathcal{L}W): Encourages low entropy outputs and controlled transitions. \mathcal{L}W = \gammaV \mathcal{L}V + \gammaT \mathcal{L}T Weight Variance Loss (\mathcal{L}V): Encourages low entropy PDDF outputs to prevent i^ from switching unnecessarily. \mathcal{L}V = \sumi wi Weight Transition Loss (\mathcal{L}T): Encourages the maximum likelihood delta component to change i^ when a discontinuity is required. \mathcal{L}T = \max(0, \varepsilonT - |
ablap w1|)^2 where \varepsilonT is a hyper-parameter controlling the desired transition speed. Parameters: \gammad, \gamma\xi, \gamman, \gammaV, \gammaT, \gamma{	ext{E},d}, \gamma{	ext{E},\xi}: Weighting hyper-parameters for each loss term. \varepsilonT: Hyper-parameter for transition speed. K=2: The number of delta components. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def norm(a): return dot(a, a) 0.5 def bce(pred, target): return -(target math.log(pred) + (1 - target) math.log(1 - pred)) def gradient(fieldval, pos): # Returns the spatial gradient ∇pos fieldval, computed via automatic differentiation return autogradgrad(fieldval, pos) def pddfshapefittingloss(p, v, dgt, ngt, xigt, xibgt, dpred, xipred, wpred, gammad, gammaxi, gamman, gammaV, gammaT, gammaEd, gammaExi, epsilonT): # p, v: list of 3D vectors (positions, view directions) # dgt, ngt, xigt: list of scalars (ground truth depth, normal, visibility) # xibgt: list of scalars (ground truth visibility for BCE) # dpred: list of lists [K][N] (predicted depth components) # xipred: list of scalars (predicted visibility) # wpred: list of lists [K][N] (predicted weights) K = 2 # Number of delta components N = len(p) # 1. Find maximum likelihood index i = argmaxj wj istar = [max(range(K), key=lambda k: wpred[k][n]) for n in range(N)] # 2. Gather predicted depth and normal for i dbistar = [dpred[istar[n]][n] for n in range(N)] nbistar = [gradient(dbistar[n], p[n]) for n in range(N)] # 3. Minimum Distance Loss Ld = ξ |dbi - d| Ld = [xigt[n] abs(dbistar[n] - dgt[n]) for n in range(N)] # 4. Visibility Objective Lξ = BCE(ξ, ξb) Lxi = [bce(xipred[n], xibgt[n]) for n in range(N)] # 5. Normals Loss Ln = -ξ |n^T nbi| Ln = [-xigt[n] abs(dot(ngt[n], nbistar[n])) for n in range(N)] # 6. Directed Eikonal Regularization LDE # LDE = γE,d Σi ξ [∇i d̂i · v + 1]^2 + γE,ξ [∇ξ ξ̂ · v]^2 LDEd = [0.0] N for i in range(K): graddi = [gradient(dpred[i][n], p[n]) for n in range(N)] for n in range(N): LDEd[n] += xigt[n] (dot(graddi[n], v[n]) + 1) 2 LDEd = [gammaEd x for x in LDEd] gradxi = [gradient(xipred[n], p[n]) for n in range(N)] LDExi = [gammaExi (dot(gradxi[n], v[n])) 2 for n in range(N)] LDE = [x + y for x, y in zip(LDEd, LDExi)] # 7. Weight Field Regularization LW # LV = Σi wi LV = [sum(wpred[i][n] for i in range(K)) for n in range(N)] # LT = max(0, εT - |∇p w1|)^2 (using w1 alone is sufficient for K=2) gradw1 = [gradient(wpred[0][n], p[n]) for n in range(N)] LT = [max(0, epsilonT - norm(gradw1[n])) 2 for n in range(N)] LW = [gammaV LV[n] + gammaT LT[n] for n in range(N)] # 8. Total Loss LS = γd Ld + γξ Lξ + γn Ln + LDE + LW LS = [gammad Ld[n] + gammaxi Lxi[n] + gamman Ln[n] + LDE[n] + LW[n] for n in range(N)] return sum(LS) / N Edge Cases and Pitfalls: \mathcal{L}T is only applied to oriented points that are surface (S) and tangent (T) data, where a discontinuity is desired. Applying it to other data types (e.g., occluded points) is incorrect. The index i^ is determined by the maximum weight wj. If weights are equal, the behavior is not specified. Precision issues may arise in gradient computation for \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} and \mathcal{L}T if the network outputs are not smooth. The Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF) is a generative method that encodes 3D shapes into a latent vector and decodes it into a depth field for efficient rendering. It builds on PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss by conditioning the probabilistic distance field on a learned latent representation zs rather than a fixed parameterization. This allows for the generation of diverse shapes from a Gaussian prior while maintaining the rendering efficiency of directed distance fields. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Encourages low entropy outputs to prevent unnecessary switching of the maximum likelihood component, while allowing transitions at discontinuities. Uses directed Eikonal regularization for better surface alignment. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyper-parameters (\gamma values, \varepsilonT). The transition loss \mathcal{L}T is only applicable to specific data types (S and T). When to use: When training PDDF models for ray-based shape representations where probabilistic depth prediction is beneficial. The PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss was introduced in the paper "Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations". It is part of the broader development of Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDF) for representing 3D shapes. The method builds on prior work in SDF training and directed distance fields. name: Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF)
head: CPDDF decoder, Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF) with Shape VAE, Shape VAE
body: The Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF) is a generative method that encodes 3D shapes into a latent vector and decodes it into a depth field for efficient rendering. It builds on PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss by conditioning the probabilistic distance field on a learned latent representation zs rather than a fixed parameterization. This allows for the generation of diverse shapes from a Gaussian prior while maintaining the rendering efficiency of directed distance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud P with associated normals N (fixed size of 1024 points). Output: A latent shape vector zs (dimension d{zs}) and, via the decoder, a depth value d(p, v | zs) for a query point p and view direction v. Data Structures: 1. PointNet Encoder Output: A vector of size 2 d{zs}. 2. Latent Vector zs: A vector of size d{zs}. 3. Posterior Parameters: Mean \mu and diagonal log-variance \Sigma, each of size d{zs}. Architecture Details: 1. PointNet Encoder: Consists of four Conv1D-BatchNorm-ReLU blocks with channel sizes 64, 64, 128, and 1024, followed by global max pooling and a multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers of size 512 (Linear-BatchNorm-ReLU, dropout 0.1). The final output size is 2 d{zs}. 2. Variational Posterior Networks: Two separate networks compute the parameters for the approximate posterior q(zs | P, N) = \mathcal{N}(zs | \mu(P, N), \Sigma(P, N)). Each network is structured as Linear-ReLU-Linear with layer dimensions equal to d{zs}. The first network takes the first half of the PointNet output to compute \mu, and the second takes the second half to compute \Sigma. 3. CPDDF Decoder: An eight-layer modulated SIREN network. The layer sizes are 512, 512, 512, 512, 256, 256, 256, 256. It takes the latent vector zs and spatial/view inputs to compute the depth field. Training Objective: The model is trained using a \beta-VAE loss: \mathcal{E}{\text{VAE}} = \mathcal{E}S + \beta \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}} is the KL divergence between the approximate posterior and a standard Gaussian prior \mathcal{N}(0, I), and \mathcal{E}S is the reconstruction likelihood loss. The total loss includes weighted terms for depth, normals, and other constraints: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \gammad \mathcal{L}d + \gamma\xi \mathcal{L}\xi + \gamman \mathcal{L}n + \gammaV \mathcal{L}V + \gamma{E,d} \mathcal{L}{E,d} + \gamma{E,\xi} \mathcal{L}{E,\xi} + \gamma{V,\xi} \mathcal{L}{V,\xi} + \gammaT \mathcal{L}T. Parameters: d{zs} (latent dimension): 400. \beta (KL weight): 0.05. Loss weights: \gammad=5, \gamma\xi=10, \gamman=10, \gammaV=1, \gamma{E,d}=0.1, \gamma{E,\xi}=0.1, \gamma{V,\xi}=0.1, \gammaT=0.1. Optimizer: Adam (lr=10^{-4}, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999). Training iterations: 100,000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class PointNetEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, dimzs): super().init() self.conv1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(4, 64, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(64), nn.ReLU()) self.conv2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(64, 64, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(64), nn.ReLU()) self.conv3 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(64, 128, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(128), nn.ReLU()) self.conv4 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(128, 1024, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(1024), nn.ReLU()) self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.BatchNorm1d(512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.1), nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.BatchNorm1d(512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, 2 dimzs)) def forward(self, x): # x shape: (B, 4, 1024) x = self.conv1(x) x = self.conv2(x) x = self.conv3(x) x = self.conv4(x) x = torch.max(x, 2, keepdim=True)[0] x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) return self.mlp(x) class PosteriorNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, dimzs): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(dimzs, dimzs), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(dimzs, dimzs)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class ModulatedSIRENLayer(nn.Module): def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures, w0=30.0): super().init() self.linear = nn.Linear(infeatures, outfeatures) self.w0 = w0 self.initweights() def initweights(self): with torch.nograd(): self.linear.weight.uniform(-1 / self.linear.infeatures, 1 / self.linear.infeatures) def forward(self, x, zs=None): if zs is not None: x = x + zs # Additive modulation of input by latent vector return torch.sin(self.linear(x) self.w0) class CPDDFDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self, dimzs): super().init() sizes = [512, 512, 512, 512, 256, 256, 256, 256] self.layers = nn.ModuleList() currentdim = dimzs for size in sizes: self.layers.append(ModulatedSIRENLayer(currentdim, size)) currentdim = size def forward(self, zs, query): # query shape: (B, 3) or (B, 4) x = query for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): x = layer(x, zs if i == 0 else None) return x def computevaeloss(mu, logvar, beta=0.05): klloss = -0.5 torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp()) return klloss beta def trainstep(pointcloud, normals, encoder, posteriormu, posteriorlogvar, decoder, optimizer): # pointcloud: (B, 1024, 3), normals: (B, 1024, 3) x = torch.cat([pointcloud, normals], dim=2).permute(0, 2, 1) encoderout = encoder(x) mu = posteriormu(encoderout[:,:encoderout.size(1)//2]) logvar = posteriorlogvar(encoderout[:, encoderout.size(1)//2:]) std = torch.exp(0.5 logvar) eps = torch.randnlike(std) zs = mu + eps std # queries: (B, N, 3) for depth evaluation depth = decoder(zs, queries) kl = computevaeloss(mu, logvar) reconloss = 0 # Reconstruction loss ES computed against sampled points totalloss = reconloss + kl optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The PointNet encoder expects a fixed input size of 1024 points with normals. The posterior networks split the encoder output evenly; incorrect splitting will break the independence assumption of the mean and variance networks. The modulated SIREN decoder requires careful initialization of frequencies (typically w0=30) to avoid high-frequency artifacts, as per standard SIREN practice. Time Complexity: Training requires 100,000 iterations with a minibatch size of 32 shapes. Each shape uses 1,200 points (for A/U categories) or 300 points (for S/B/T/O categories). Memory Complexity: The latent vector size is 400. The encoder output is 800. The decoder has 8 layers with up to 512 units. Measured Performance: Evaluated on single categories of ShapeNet-v1 cars. Strengths: Enables efficient rendering of diverse shapes via latent sampling. The directed distance field allows for fast depth estimation. Limitations: Limited to single categories of ShapeNet (e.g., cars). Requires point cloud input with normals. When to use: When generating diverse 3D shapes from a latent space and rendering them efficiently as directed distance fields. When not to use: When multi-category generalization without retraining is required, or when point cloud inputs with normals are unavailable. The CPDDF method was introduced in "Representing 3D Shapes with Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields" (CVPR 2022). It extends the Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) framework by incorporating a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) structure to learn a latent space of shapes. The method uses a PointNet encoder and a modulated SIREN decoder. Representing 3D Shapes with Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01874, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SDDF with Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals
head: Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF), Scene-level SDDF
body: This method learns a scene-level Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF) by combining an explicit ellipsoidal prior with an implicit neural residual network. It solves the problem of reconstructing complex 3D environments from sensor data (LiDAR or RGB-D depth) while maintaining differentiability for novel view synthesis and avoiding the iterative sphere tracing required by standard SDFs. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly models occlusions via ellipsoids to handle discontinuities, while the neural network recovers fine details, satisfying the directional Eikonal constraint by construction. Inputs: A set of sensor measurements \{Tt, Zt\}{t=1}^T, where Tt \in SE(3) is the sensor pose and Zt contains viewing directions vi \in S^2 and range measurements r{t,i} \in \mathbb{R}{>0}. Query inputs: a 3D position p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction v \in S^2. Outputs: The predicted SDDF value \hat{f}(p, v), representing the signed distance to the observed surface along direction v from position p. Data Structures: 1. Ellipsoid Prior: A set of M learnable ellipsoids. Each ellipsoid j is defined by parameters \thetaj (center, orientation, scale). The total number of ellipsoids M is typically 128 (256 for Gibson Allensville). 2. Latent Feature Network (L): A neural network that maps the intersection point and viewing direction to a latent feature vector z \in \mathbb{R}^m. 3. Residual Decoder (R): A neural network that takes the latent feature z and outputs the residual prediction \deltaf(p, v). Definitions: SDDF Definition: For a query (p, v), the SDDF f^(p, v) is the signed distance to the first intersection of the ray p + dv with the occupied space boundary \partial O. The sign is positive if p is in free space and negative if p is inside the occupied space. The function is continuous when entering occupied space from free space, but discontinuous when leaving occupied space (inside-out). This discontinuity is handled by assuming sensors remain in free space, observing the scene from outside-in. Directional Eikonal Constraint: The gradient of the SDDF with respect to position p in the direction v must have unit magnitude: \nablap f(p, v) \cdot v = 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ellipsoids: Initialize the M ellipsoids to approximate the coarse shape of the scene. Do not use K-means++ initialization alone, as it causes excessive ellipsoids for planar surfaces and larger errors. Use a method that provides a balanced initial coverage. 2. Compute Ellipsoid Prior f(p, v): For a query (p, v), compute the distance to the nearest ellipsoid surface along v. Let dj(p, v) be the distance from p to the surface of ellipsoid j along direction v. The prior f(p, v) is the minimum of these distances, considering the sign based on whether p is inside or outside the ellipsoid. Note: The exact closed-form solution for dj(p, v) involves solving a quartic equation for the intersection of a ray and an ellipsoid. The sources state that gradients are derived in closed-form to accelerate training, but do not provide the explicit quartic solver code. 3. Find Intersection Point: Identify the ellipsoid j^ that provides the minimum distance f(p, v). Compute the intersection point p{\text{int}} = p + f(p, v)v to pass to the latent network. 4. Construct Latent Feature z: Pass p{\text{int}} and v through the Latent Feature Network L to obtain z = L(p{\text{int}}, v). The network is designed such that the resulting residual satisfies the directional Eikonal constraint. 5. Predict Residual \deltaf(p, v): Pass z through the Residual Decoder R to obtain the residual: \deltaf(p, v) = R(z). 6. Compute Final SDDF: Combine the prior and the residual: \hat{f}(p, v) = f(p, v) + \deltaf(p, v) Training: Loss Function: Minimize the difference between \hat{f}(p, v) and the ground truth SDDF derived from sensor measurements. Negative Sample Augmentation: Include negative SDDF samples (points inside the object) in the training data. Without this, ellipsoids regress into the interior of objects, leading to missing ray intersections and wrong ellipsoid selection. Embedding: Use polynomial embedding for the neural networks. Fourier embedding is inferior due to the need for scene-specific spatial frequency tuning. Fourier embedding formula (for ablation comparison): \mathbf{m} = [\sin(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{p}}\mathbf{p}), \cos(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{p}}\mathbf{p}), \sin(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{v}}\mathbf{v}), \cos(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{v}}\mathbf{v})] where \mathbf{B}p, \mathbf{B}v \in \mathbb{R}^{25 \times 3} are random Fourier features sampled from \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Parameters: Number of ellipsoids M: 128 (default), 256 for Gibson Allensville. RGB-D Downsampling: 20× for most datasets, 5× for Replica Hotel, to match LiDAR ray density. Fourier Feature Dimensions: 25 (for ablation). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The SDDF is discontinuous when a ray leaves the occupied space from inside out. This is handled by assuming sensors remain in free space. Too Few Ellipsoids: Prevents accurate approximation of object shapes. Too Many Ellipsoids: Causes the model to learn spurious occlusions between ellipsoids and moves redundant ellipsoids out of the scene during testing. Missing Negative Samples: Causes ellipsoids to regress into object interiors, leading to missing ray intersections. K-means++ Initialization: Causes larger errors due to excessive ellipsoids for planar surfaces. The explicit geometric representation using learnable ellipsoids to approximate coarse shapes and handle occlusions. It provides an analytic, differentiable prior that satisfies the directional Eikonal equation by construction. Time Complexity: Inference is a single forward pass through the ellipsoid prior and the neural network, making it faster than iterative sphere tracing methods. It is 1.5× faster than SDF-Instant-NGP sphere tracing and 4× faster than Nerfacto. Memory Complexity: Low GPU memory usage. On Replica-Hotel, max training GPU memory is 3.3 GB, significantly lower than RaDe-GS (18.7 GB) and Nerfacto (4.7 GB). Performance: On Replica-Hotel (Intel 14900K CPU, NVIDIA RTX-3090 GPU), training time is 100 minutes, inference time is 69 ms/frame, and the model has 2.7M parameters. Strengths: Single-query differentiable novel view synthesis. Handles occlusions explicitly. Low memory footprint. Robust to varying viewing distances due to Eikonal constraint satisfaction. Works with LiDAR and depth-only data. Limitations: Slower inference than highly optimized Gaussian Splatting methods like RaDe-GS (69 ms vs 7 ms). Requires careful tuning of the number of ellipsoids. Sensitive to initialization. When to Use: When geometric reconstruction accuracy with low memory usage is required, and differentiable depth rendering is needed without RGB supervision. When Not to Use: Avoid when maximum inference speed is required (use RaDe-GS) or when photometric rendering with RGB supervision is the primary goal (use Nerfacto). The method was introduced in "Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals". It addresses the limitations of previous SDDF formulations: object-level SDDF ignores objects behind the viewing position, and PDDF lacks sign information and has discontinuities. This method defines a scene-level SDDF that is continuous when entering occupied space and retains sign information, enabling accurate scene reconstruction from sensor data. name: Ellipsoid SDDF Prior
head: Ellipsoid Signed Directional Distance Function, Single Ellipsoid SDDF, Ellipsoid-based Prior Network, Prior network P
body:
The Ellipsoid SDDF Prior is an explicit geometric representation that approximates the coarse shape of an environment using a set of M learnable ellipsoids. It serves as the foundational prior for a Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF), handling occlusions explicitly and providing a closed-form analytical solution for the distance field. It differs from implicit neural fields by offering an analytic, differentiable geometric prior that satisfies the directional Eikonal equation by construction, leaving fine details to be recovered by a subsequent neural residual network. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray direction \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{S}^2 (unit vector), and ellipsoid parameters: center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation matrix \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3}, and radii vector \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3+. Outputs: SDDF value f(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}; \mathcal{E}), intersection indicator i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}), and sign indicator s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}). Data Structures: Ellipsoid Parameters: \mathbf{c}: Center position. \mathbf{R}: Rotation matrix. Parameterized via Lie algebra: \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}0 \exp(\xi^\wedge), where \mathbf{T}0 is a fixed initial pose, \xi = ( oldsymbol{ho},  oldsymbol{	heta}) \in \mathbb{R}^6 is learnable,  oldsymbol{ho} is translation,  oldsymbol{	heta} maps to rotation via skew-symmetric matrix \xi^\wedge and matrix exponential. \mathbf{r}: Radii vector. Parameterized as \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}0 \exp(\mathbf{s}), where \mathbf{r}0 \in \mathbb{R}^3+ is fixed initialization and \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is learnable. This ensures \mathbf{r} remains positive. \mathbf{Q}0 = 	ext{diag}(\mathbf{r}). Formulas and Definitions: 1. Local Frame Transformation: Transform world-space coordinates to the ellipsoid's local frame: \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{R}^	op (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}) \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{R}^	op \mathbf{v} \mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{p}' 	imes \mathbf{v}' \mathbf{Q}1 = \det(\mathbf{Q}0) \mathbf{Q}0^{-1} 2. Intersection Indicator: Determines if the ray intersects the ellipsoid. i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{v}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}' - \mathbf{w}'^	op \mathbf{Q}0^2 \mathbf{w}' If i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0, the ray does not intersect the ellipsoid. 3. Sign Indicator: Determines if the point is inside or outside the ellipsoid. s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{p}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{p}' - \det(\mathbf{Q}0)^2 s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 means \mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{E} (inside); s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) > 0 means \mathbf{p} 
otin \mathcal{E} (outside). This form is used for better numerical stability than \mathbf{p}'^	op \mathbf{Q}0^{-2} \mathbf{p}' - 1. 4. Validity Function: Handles cases where the ellipsoid is behind the ray.  eta = \max(i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}), 0) + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon > 0 v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = - rac{\det(\mathbf{Q}0)\sqrt{ eta} + \mathbf{p}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'}{\mathbf{v}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'} s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 indicates the ellipsoid is behind the view ray. 5. SDDF Prior Value: f(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}; \mathcal{E}) =  egin{cases} - rac{\det(\mathbf{Q}0)\sqrt{ eta} + \mathbf{p}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^	op \mathbf{v}'}{\mathbf{v}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^	op \mathbf{v}'}, & v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) \geq 0 \ \infty, & v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 \end{cases} When i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 (no intersection) and valid, this simplifies to the distance to a virtual plane: - rac{\mathbf{p}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'}{\mathbf{v}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ellipsoidsddfprior(p, v, c, R, r): # 1. Compute Q0 and Q1 Q0 = diag(r) detQ0 = det(Q0) Q1 = detQ0 inv(Q0) # 2. Transform to local frame pprime = R.T @ (p - c) vprime = R.T @ v wprime = cross(pprime, vprime) # 3. Compute Intersection Indicator # i = v'^T Q1^2 v' - w'^T Q0^2 w' vQ1sqv = dot(vprime, (Q1 @ Q1) @ vprime) wQ0sqw = dot(wprime, (Q0 @ Q0) @ wprime) i = vQ1sqv - wQ0sqw # 4. Compute Sign Indicator # s = p'^T Q1^2 p' - det(Q0)^2 pQ1sqp = dot(pprime, (Q1 @ Q1) @ pprime) s = pQ1sqp - detQ02 # 5. Compute Validity and SDDF epsilon = 1e-8 beta = max(i, 0.0) + epsilon # Denominator for validity and SDDF denomvalid = dot(vprime, (Q1 @ Q1) @ vprime) denomsddf = dot(vprime, (Q1.T @ Q1) @ vprime) # Note: Q1 is symmetric in standard ellipsoid def, but formula uses Q1^T # Numerator for validity numvalid = detQ0 sqrt(beta) + dot(pprime, (Q1 @ Q1) @ vprime) # Validity function if denomvalid == 0: vval = 0 # Guard against division by zero else: vval = -(numvalid / denomvalid) s if vval < 0: return infinity, i, s # Numerator for SDDF numsddf = detQ0 sqrt(beta) + dot(pprime, (Q1.T @ Q1) @ vprime) if denomsddf == 0: fval = infinity # Guard else: fval = -numsddf / denomsddf return fval, i, s The pseudocode assumes standard matrix operations. Q1 is defined as \det(\mathbf{Q}0)\mathbf{Q}0^{-1}. Since \mathbf{Q}0 is diagonal, \mathbf{Q}1 is also diagonal and symmetric, so \mathbf{Q}1^	op = \mathbf{Q}1. The term \mathbf{v}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^	op \mathbf{v}' in the denominator of Eq. 7 is equivalent to \mathbf{v}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}' only if \mathbf{Q}1 is symmetric, which it is. However, Eq. 12 uses \mathbf{Q}1^2 in the validity numerator. The pseudocode reflects the specific terms in the source equations. Parameters: M: Number of ellipsoids. Defines the capacity of the explicit prior. Typical value not specified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Intersection: If i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0, the SDDF is \infty. This must be handled to avoid numerical issues. Ellipsoid Behind Ray: If s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) > 0 (point outside) and the ellipsoid is behind the ray, the standard formula yields a negative value, but the true SDDF should be \infty. The validity function v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) detects this and returns \infty. Numerical Stability: A small \epsilon > 0 is added to  eta in the square root term to ensure stable backward propagation. A neural network component that predicts a correction term \deltaf(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) to refine the coarse geometric prior. It uses a degree-2 monomial embedding \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{p}) = [px^2, px py, px pz, py^2, py pz, pz^2, px, py, pz, 1]^	op \in \mathbb{R}^{10}. The latent feature \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{W}{jf} \mathbf{m}, where \mathbf{m} = 	ext{vec}(\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{v}')^	op) \in \mathbb{R}^{100} is the outer product of embeddings of the intersection point \mathbf{q} and local direction \mathbf{v}', and \mathbf{W}{jf} \in \mathbb{R}^{m 	imes 100} is a weight matrix specific to the intersected ellipsoid index jf. The residual decoder is an MLP mapping \mathbb{R}^m 	o \mathbb{R}^3 producing (\deltai, \deltas, \deltaf). Final predictions are \hat{i} = 	anh(\alpha i) + \deltai, \hat{s} = 	anh(\alpha s) + \deltas, \hat{f} = f + \deltaf. Residuals are added after tanh to prevent gradient clipping. Computes the SDDF for a union of M ellipsoids by aggregating individual properties. Intersection Indicator: i{	ext{union}} = \maxj ij(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}). Sign Indicator: s{	ext{union}} = \minj sj(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}). SDDF Value: f{	ext{union}} = \min{j: ij \geq 0} fj(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) if any ellipsoid is intersected; otherwise f{	ext{union}} = \minj fj(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}). Time complexity is O(M) per ray. The network is differentiable with respect to \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{T}j, \mathbf{r}j. Manual gradient implementation to optimize GPU memory and speed, replacing automatic differentiation. Intermediate Variables: t0 = \mathbf{v}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}', t1 = \mathbf{w}'^	op \mathbf{Q}0^2 \mathbf{w}', t2 = \mathbf{p}'^	op \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'. Gradients: Computed via chain rule for 
abla{\mathbf{p}'} \mathcal{L}P, 
abla{\mathbf{v}'} \mathcal{L}P, 
abla{\mathbf{r}} \mathcal{L}P using the simplified forms i = t0 - t1 and f = -(\det(\mathbf{Q}0)\max(i, 0) + \epsilon + t2)/t0. Complexity: The prior network computation is O(M) per ray due to the min/max operations over M ellipsoids. Strengths: Provides a closed-form, differentiable geometric prior that satisfies the directional Eikonal equation by construction. Handles occlusions explicitly. Compatible with unsigned DDF by setting one axis radius to 0 (forming a 2D disk) for non-watertight objects. Limitations: The prior network alone provides only a coarse approximation; fine details require the residual network. Numerical stability requires careful handling of the validity function and \epsilon. When to use: When a coarse, analytic geometric prior is needed for scene-level SDDF reconstruction, especially for differentiable rendering or SLAM where Eikonal constraints are beneficial. The method originates from the paper "Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals". It addresses the challenge of learning a continuous, implicit representation of scene-level SDDFs, which are sensitive to both position and direction. The approach builds on the definition of SDDF as a function measuring signed distance from a point to an occupied space along a viewing direction, extending object-level SDDFs to scene-level representations. name: SDF-Instant-NGP Training
head: SDDF Training, SDF baseline training
body:
This method defines the training procedure for a Signed Distance Function (SDF) baseline network, specifically referred to as SDF-Instant-NGP in the source literature. It is distinguished from its parent method, SDF Training with Eikonal Loss, by the explicit inclusion of a sign loss term applied to free-space samples to enforce positive SDF values outside the surface, and by the specific hyperparameter configuration (batch size, learning rate, epochs) used for the SDF baseline in the RaDe-GS context. Inputs: A set of near-surface samples \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} with corresponding distance labels yi \in \mathbb{R}. A set of free-space positions \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}. A differentiable SDF model f(\mathbf{x}; 	heta). Outputs: Trained network parameters 	heta that minimize the combined loss function. The training data consists of two sets of 3D points: \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} containing near-surface points with distance labels yi \in \mathbb{R}, and \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}} containing free-space positions that provide only sign supervision. 1. Sample Generation: Generate two types of training samples: SDF samples \mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} with distance labels yi, and free space positions \mathbf{x}j \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}. 2. Forward Pass: For each batch of samples, compute the predicted SDF values f(\mathbf{x}) and their gradients 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) with respect to the input coordinates using automatic differentiation. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the three components of the loss function: SDF loss (l{	ext{SDF}}) for near-surface samples, sign loss (l{	ext{sign}}) for free-space samples, and Eikonal loss (l{	ext{eik}}) for all samples. 4. Optimization: Update the network parameters using the Adam optimizer to minimize the total loss. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for 300 epochs. The total loss is the sum of three terms: l{	ext{SDF}} =  rac{1}{\|\mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}\|} \sum{\mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}} |f(\mathbf{x}i) - yi| \quad (63) l{	ext{sign}} =  rac{1}{\|\mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}\|} \sum{\mathbf{x}j \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}} \exp(-\lambda f(\mathbf{x}j)) \quad (64) l{	ext{eik}} =  rac{1}{\|\mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}\| + \|\mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}\|} \sum{\mathbf{x}k \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} \cup \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}} \| |
abla f(\mathbf{x}k)| - 1 \| \quad (65) Where: \|\mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}\| and \|\mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}\| are the number of samples in each set. f(\mathbf{x}) is the SDF model output. yi is the ground truth distance label. 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) is the gradient of the SDF with respect to the input position. \lambda is a parameter for the sign loss. Not given in the sources. Batch size: 60. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate: 0.0001. Epochs: 300. \lambda: Value not specified in the source section. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def computesdfloss(prednear, labelsnear): return torch.mean(torch.abs(prednear - labelsnear)) def computesignloss(predfree, lambdaparam): return torch.mean(torch.exp(-lambdaparam predfree)) def computeeikonalloss(prednear, inputsnear, predfree, inputsfree): gradnear = torch.autograd.grad( prednear, inputsnear, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(prednear), creategraph=False, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] gradfree = torch.autograd.grad( predfree, inputsfree, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(predfree), creategraph=False, retaingraph=False, onlyinputs=True)[0] gradnormnear = torch.norm(gradnear, dim=1, keepdim=True) gradnormfree = torch.norm(gradfree, dim=1, keepdim=True) return torch.mean(torch.abs(gradnormnear - 1.0)) + torch.mean(torch.abs(gradnormfree - 1.0)) def trainsdfbaseline(model, nearsamples, nearlabels, freesamples, lambdaparam, batchsize=60, lr=0.0001, epochs=300): optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr) for epoch in range(epochs): nearindices = torch.randperm(nearsamples.size(0)) freeindices = torch.randperm(freesamples.size(0)) for i in range(0, nearsamples.size(0), batchsize): nearidx = nearindices[i:i+batchsize] xnear = nearsamples[nearidx] ynear = nearlabels[nearidx] freeidx = freeindices[i:i+batchsize] xfree = freesamples[freeidx] optimizer.zerograd() prednear = model(xnear) predfree = model(xfree) losssdf = computesdfloss(prednear, ynear) losssign = computesignloss(predfree, lambdaparam) losseik = computeeikonalloss(prednear, xnear, predfree, xfree) totalloss = losssdf + losssign + losseik totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() The source does not specify the value of \lambda, the sampling strategy for \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}, or how to handle precision issues and degenerate inputs. What it is: A method that uses spherical priors or constraints to regularize the SDF. Difference: Focuses on geometric priors rather than just point-wise supervision. When to choose: When scene geometry can be approximated by spheres or when spherical priors improve convergence. Link: Sphere Loss What it is: A technique where a smaller network is trained to mimic a larger, pre-trained SDF network. Difference: Focuses on model compression and inference speed rather than initial training from scratch. When to choose: When deployment constraints require a smaller model. Link: MLP Distillation What it is: The primary method in the source paper, which uses ellipsoidal priors and neural residuals to learn a Signed Directional Distance Function. Difference: This is the advanced method; SDF-Instant-NGP is the baseline used for comparison. When to choose: For higher accuracy and robustness, especially in complex scenes. Link: SDDF with Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals The method trains for 300 epochs. The source does not report time or memory complexity, measured performance metrics, specific limitations, or usage guidelines for this baseline. The method is described in the paper "Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals". It is presented as a baseline (SDF-Instant-NGP) for the proposed SDDF method in the RaDe-GS framework. It is used for training a standard SDF network to serve as a comparison point for the more advanced SDDF method. name: TetraSDF Training Procedure
head: SDF neural network training, TetraSDF optimization
body: TetraSDF Training Procedure optimizes a neural network to represent a signed distance field (SDF) using a multi-resolution tetrahedral grid, combining L1 regression, Eikonal regularization, and weight normalization constraints. It differs from standard MLP-based SDF training by utilizing a tetrahedral grid structure for spatial representation, which allows for efficient multi-resolution handling and specific mesh extraction via sub-polygonization. Inputs and Outputs Input: A dataset of 3D points with ground truth SDF values, typically sampled from a mesh (e.g., Stanford 3D scanning models). Output: A trained TetraSDF neural network model capable of evaluating SDF values and gradients at arbitrary 3D coordinates. Data Structures TetraSDF Network: A neural network defined by numlayers, numhidden, levels, rmin, rmax, and T. numlayers: Number of hidden layers (default 4). numhidden: Number of hidden units per layer (default 12). levels: Multi-resolution levels (default 4). rmin, rmax: Resolution bounds for the tetrahedral grid, dependent on the chosen resolution preset (small, medium, large). T: A parameter related to the tetrahedral grid structure (default 21). useA: Boolean flag for using a preconditioner (default True). StanfordDataset: A custom dataset class that provides point-cloud samples and ground truth SDF labels. DataLoader: A standard iterator that shuffles data and yields batches of size BATCHSIZE. Parameters BATCHSIZE: 1000. lr (Adam learning rate): 1 \times 10^{-3}. eikonalweight: 5 \times 10^{-3}. EPOCH: 10. Tmax (for scheduler): EPOCH \times \frac{\text{len(training\data)}}{BATCH\SIZE}. Resolution presets: small: r{min}=2, r{max}=32. medium: r{min}=4, r{max}=64. large: r{min}=8, r{max}=128. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Set random seeds for Python, NumPy, and PyTorch. Create the TetraSDF network instance with specified hyperparameters. Load the training dataset (StanfordDataset) and create a DataLoader with BATCHSIZE=1000 and shuffle=True. Initialize the Adam optimizer with lr=1e-3. Initialize the CosineAnnealingLR scheduler with Tmax calculated as above. Define the L1 Loss criterion (nn.L1Loss). 2. Epoch Loop: Iterate for EPOCH times (default 10). Resampling: If epoch == 0, call traindataloader.dataset.resample() to resample the dataset. 3. Batch Loop: Iterate through each batch in traindataloader. Data Loading: Retrieve inputs (points) and labels (ground truth SDF) from the batch and move them to the GPU. Gradient Zeroing: Reset accumulated gradients to zero. Forward Pass: Compute predicted SDF values: predsdf = net.sdf(inputs)[:, 0]. L1 Loss Calculation: Compute L{L1} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N | \hat{y}i - yi | where \hat{y}i is predsdf and yi is labels. Eikonal Loss Calculation: Set points = inputs.detach().clone().requiresgrad(True). Compute the gradient of the SDF output with respect to the input points: J = torch.autograd.grad(net.sdf(points).sum(), points, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0]. Compute the Eikonal loss: L{eik} = \mathbb{E} [ (\| \nabla \phi(\mathbf{x}) \|2 - 1)^2 ] using eik = (J.norm(p=2, dim=1) - 1.0).pow(2).mean(). Weight Norm Loss Calculation: Compute L{wn} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^M \mathbb{E} [ (1 - \| \mathbf{W}i \|2)^2 ] where \mathbf{W}i are the layer weights in net.fc. Total Loss: Sum the losses: loss = L1Loss + eikonalweight Leik + Lwn. Backward Pass: Compute gradients of the total loss with respect to all network parameters. Optimizer Step: Update network parameters using the Adam algorithm. Scheduler Step: Update the learning rate using cosine annealing. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn from torch.utils.data import DataLoader def l1loss(pred, target): return torch.mean(torch.abs(pred -
