name: VoxelSDF Decoder (Grid Latent Sampling + MLP)
head: Latent Grid SDF, Voxel-conditioned SDF MLP
body: The VoxelSDF Decoder predicts Signed Distance Function (SDF) values at arbitrary 3D query points by interpolating a gridded latent code and passing the result through a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). It solves the problem of evaluating implicit surfaces for shapes represented by voxel grids, enabling differentiable rendering and optimization in neural implicit reconstruction pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor of 3D query points P with shape (batchsize, numpoints, 3). A latent embedding grid E with shape (batchsize, latentdim, voxelgridsize+1, voxelgridsize+1, voxelgridsize+1). Output: A tensor of SDF values S with shape (batchsize, numpoints, 1). Data Structures: Latent Grid: A 5D tensor embeddings of shape (batchsize, latentdim, voxelgridsize+1, voxelgridsize+1, voxelgridsize+1). Points: A tensor points of shape (batchsize, numpoints, 3) containing 3D coordinates. Parameters: latentdim: Dimension of the latent vectors. Default: 32. voxelgridsize: Spatial resolution of the latent grid. Default: 8. numlayers: Number of residual blocks in the MLP. Default: 4. hiddendim: MLP hidden size. Default: 128. Algorithm: 1. Grid Sampling: Interpolate the latent code for each query point from the latent grid using trilinear interpolation. The coordinates must be normalized to the range [-1, 1] for standard grid sampling implementations. 2. Reshape: Flatten the batch and point dimensions to prepare for the MLP. 3. MLP Evaluation: Pass the interpolated latent codes through a residual MLP to predict the SDF value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VoxelSDFDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self, latentdim=32, voxelgridsize=8, numlayers=4, hiddendim=128): super().init() self.latentdim = latentdim self.voxelgridsize = voxelgridsize layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): inch = latentdim if i == 0 else hiddendim outch = hiddendim layers.append(nn.Linear(inch, outch)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) if i < numlayers - 1: layers.append(nn.Linear(outch, outch)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) self.mlp = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, embeddings, points): nmodels = embeddings.shape[0] npointspermodel = points.shape[1] # F.gridsample expects grid of shape (N, Dout, Hout, Wout, 3) for 3D # points shape is (B, N, 3) -> reshape to (B, 1, 1, N, 3) grid = points.view(nmodels, 1, 1, npointspermodel, 3) # Source uses mode='bilinear', but 'trilinear' is required for 5D tensors latent = F.gridsample( embeddings, grid, mode='trilinear', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=True) # latent shape: (batchsize, latentdim, 1, 1, numpoints) latent = latent.view(nmodels, npointspermodel, self.latentdim) sdf = self.mlp(latent) sdf = sdf.view(nmodels, npointspermodel, 1) return sdf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Queries outside the voxel grid bounds return zero due to paddingmode='zeros'. Coordinate Normalization: F.gridsample requires coordinates in [-1, 1] when aligncorners=True. It processes the 16-D embedding through 2-4 fully connected layers, each containing 256 hidden units. The SDF head outputs a scalar SDF value s and a 128-D hidden vector. The color head consists of two FC layers with 256 hidden units each, followed by a sigmoid activation to clamp RGB values to [0, 1]. name: Voxel-Conditional Neural Closest Point Predictor
head: Neural Closest Point Predictor, x)$
body: The Voxel-Conditional Neural Closest Point Predictor is a neural network module that synthesizes surface details by mapping any 3D query point x to its closest point on a target surface S, conditioned on a voxelized representation V of the shape. It solves the problem of refining coarse voxel-based mesh reconstructions into high-fidelity surfaces by predicting the displacement vector to the implicit surface, effectively defining the surface as the zero-level set of the predicted vector field. Unlike methods requiring ground-truth point clouds or normals (e.g., CSPNet), it operates solely on the voxel input, making it suitable for generative tasks where ground-truth geometry is unavailable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary voxel grid V \in \{0, 1\}^r representing the coarse shape, and a 3D query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A 3D vector \hat{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the predicted closest point on the surface S relative to the origin. The surface is implicitly defined by S = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid h\theta(V, x) - x = 0\}. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor of binary values representing the coarse shape. Multi-resolution Features: A set of feature vectors extracted from different layers of the 3D convolutional network, corresponding to resolutions 32^3, 16^3, 8^3. Query Point Features: A concatenated vector formed by tri-linearly interpolating the multi-resolution features at the query location x. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Preparation: Normalize training meshes to a unit bounding box, voxelize them, and extract the boundary mesh T^s = (V^s, F^s{tri}). 2. Ground Truth Calculation: For each vertex v^s \in V^s, calculate the closest point p^s on the ground truth surface S. 3. Sampling: Sample training points along line segments connecting boundary vertices to their closest points: \{(1-\alpha)p^s + \alpha v^s \mid \alpha \in [0, 1]\} for each v^s. This creates a sampling band tied to the voxel output. 4. Feature Encoding: Pass the voxel grid V through a 4-layer 3D convolutional encoder with widths \{32, 64, 128, 256\}, reducing resolution from 32^3 to 4^3. Extract features from intermediate layers (resolutions 32^3, 16^3, 8^3). For each query point x, perform tri-linear interpolation on the feature maps from each convolution layer to obtain multi-resolution features at x. 5. Feature Decoding: Concatenate the interpolated multi-resolution features. Pass the concatenated vector through a two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). 6. Prediction: The MLP outputs the predicted closest point vector. Formula: The closest point function is defined as: CP(x) = \arg \min{p \in S} \| p - x \|2 The network h\theta(V, x) approximates this function. Parameters: Network Architecture: Multi-scale voxel network with a 4-layer 3D convolutional encoder (widths \{32, 64, 128, 256\}) and a two-layer MLP decoder. Training: 500 epochs with a learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-3}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The closest point function is discontinuous at points on the medial axis. The network is only valid for points close to the final surface. It relies on the voxelized shape as an initial mesh reconstruction to ensure query points remain in the valid region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelconditionalclosestpointpredictor(V, x): # V: voxel grid tensor of shape (1, 1, 32, 32, 32) # x: query points tensor of shape (N, 3), coordinates normalized to [-1, 1] # Multi-scale 3D convolutional encoder # Widths: [32, 64, 128, 256], resolutions: 32^3 -> 16^3 -> 8^3 -> 4^3 features = [] current = V widths = [32, 64, 128, 256] for i, width in enumerate(widths): current = conv3d(current, width, stride=2) features.append(current) # Tri-linear interpolation at query points x interpolated = [] for feat in features: interp = trilinearinterpolate(feat, x) interpolated.append(interp) # Concatenate features along channel dimension combined = concatenate(interpolated, axis=1) # Two-layer MLP decoder h = linear(combined, 512) h = relu(h) output = linear(h, 3) return output def trilinearinterpolate(volume, points): # volume: (B, C, H, W, D) # points: (N, 3) in normalized coordinates [-1, 1] # Map points to grid coordinates [0, H-1], [0, W-1], [0, D-1] # Compute fractional indices and weights # Return interpolated values of shape (N, C) # Standard trilinear interpolation implementation # (Implementation omitted; standard graphics library function) pass Time Complexity: Depends on the number of query points and the cost of tri-linear interpolation across multiple resolutions. The MLP inference is negligible compared to the interpolation and convolution encoding. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the multi-resolution feature maps from the 3D convolutional encoder. The source specifies resolutions 32^3, 16^3, 8^3. Strengths: Can synthesize fine surface details from coarse voxels; does not require ground-truth normals or point clouds, making it suitable for generative models. Limitations: The closest point function is discontinuous on the medial axis, limiting validity to points close to the surface. Requires a good initial voxel representation. When to use: When refining a voxel-based shape into a detailed mesh and ground-truth surface normals are not available. When not to use: For points far from the surface or when medial axis discontinuities are a concern. The Voxel-Conditional Neural Closest Point Predictor was introduced in the Neural Volumetric Mesh Generator (NVMG) paper. It is part of a pipeline that uses voxels as an intermediate representation for mesh generation and editing. The method is inspired by IF-Net (Implicit Function Network) for multi-resolution feature extraction. It addresses the limitation of previous closest point prediction networks like CSPNet, which require ground-truth point clouds and normals, by conditioning the prediction on the voxel grid alone. name: DeepSDF Training Loop
head: DeepSDF Optimization Loop, DeepSDF Training
body: The DeepSDF Training Loop is the optimization procedure for the DeepSDF architecture, which learns a continuous signed distance function (SDF) representation for 3D shapes. It solves the problem of learning compact, shape-specific implicit representations by jointly optimizing a global latent code per shape and a neural network that maps (latent code, 3D point) to signed distance values. It sets itself apart from its siblings like Vox2SDF and Deep Medial Field (DMF) Network Architecture by using a single global latent vector for the entire shape rather than local voxel features or medial axes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of shapes, where each shape i has a set of query points Pi and corresponding ground-truth SDF values Di. Outputs: Optimized MLP weights \theta and shape-specific latent codes zi for all shapes in the dataset. Data Structures: Latent Embeddings: An nn.Embedding layer with numembeddings equal to the number of shapes in the dataset and embeddingdim equal to dz. The weights are initialized from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1/\sqrt{dz}). DeepSDF Model: An MLP with input dimension dz + 3, hidden dimension dh, and output dimension 1. It consists of an input layer, n{hidden} hidden layers, and an output layer. Batch: A tuple (points, sdfs, indices) where points is a tensor of shape (B, 3), sdfs is a tensor of shape (B, 1), and indices is a tensor of shape (B,) containing the shape IDs for the current batch. Parameters: dz: Latent code dimension. Value: 512. dh: Hidden layer dimension. Value: 512. n{hidden}: Number of hidden layers. Value: 8. lr{model}: Learning rate for MLP parameters. Value: 5 \times 10^{-4}. lr{embed}: Learning rate for embedding parameters. Value: 10^{-3}. batch\size: Samples per iteration. Value: 24. epochs: Total training epochs. Value: 2000. scheduler: StepLR with step\size=500 and gamma=0.5. loss\function: L1 Loss with reduction="sum". Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize the embedding layer weights E with \mathcal{N}(0, 1/\sqrt{dz}). Initialize the MLP parameters \theta (typically using He or Xavier initialization, though specific initialization for the MLP weights is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources beyond the embedding init). Create optimizers: Adam for \theta with lr{model} and Adam for E with lr{embed}. Create learning rate scheduler (StepLR) for the embedding optimizer with step\size=500 and gamma=0.5. Create data loader with batchsize and shuffle=True. 2. Training Loop: For each epoch e from 1 to epochs: Set model to training mode. Initialize epochloss = 0. For each batch (points, sdfs, indices) from the data loader: 1. Move points and sdfs to the device (e.g., GPU). 2. Retrieve latent codes: Z = E(indices). 3. Forward pass: SDF{pred} = \text{DeepSDF}(Z, points). 4. Reshape SDF{pred} and sdfs to match the batch size dimensions (e.g., (B, 1)). 5. Compute loss: L = \text{L1Loss}(SDF{pred}, sdfs). 6. Zero gradients for both optimizers. 7. Backward pass: L.backward(). 8. Step both optimizers. 9. Accumulate loss: epochloss += L.item(). Step the learning rate scheduler. If e \pmod{100} == 0: Save model state: DeepSDFepoch{e}.param (MLP weights) and embeddingsepoch{e}.param (embedding table weights). Save losses array losses.npy. Yield epoch number and losses list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim from torch.utils.data import DataLoader class DeepSDFTrainingLoop: def init(self, dataset, latentdim=512, hiddendim=512, nhiddenlayers=8, batchsize=24, epochs=2000, lrmodel=5e-4, lrembed=1e-3, stepsize=500, gamma=0.5, savefreq=100): self.dataset = dataset self.latentdim = latentdim self.numshapes = len(dataset) # Initialize Embedding Layer self.embeddings = nn.Embedding(self.numshapes, self.latentdim) torch.nn.init.normal(self.embeddings.weight.data, 0, 1 / (self.latentdim 0.5)) # Initialize DeepSDF MLP # Input: latentdim + 3, Output: 1 layers = [] layers.append(nn.Linear(self.latentdim + 3, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) for in range(nhiddenlayers - 1): layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) self.deepsdfmodel = nn.Sequential(layers) # Optimizers self.optimizermodel = optim.Adam(self.deepsdfmodel.parameters(), lr=lrmodel) self.optimizerembed = optim.Adam(self.embeddings.parameters(), lr=lrembed) # Scheduler self.scheduler = optim.lrscheduler.StepLR(self.optimizerembed, stepsize=stepsize, gamma=gamma) # Data Loader self.dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batchsize=batchsize, shuffle=True) self.epochs = epochs self.savefreq = savefreq self.losses = [] def trainepoch(self): self.deepsdfmodel.train() self.embeddings.train() epochloss = 0.0 for points, sdfs, indices in self.dataloader: # Move to device (assuming CUDA if available) device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.isavailable() else "cpu") points = points.to(device) sdfs = sdfs.to(device) indices = indices.to(device) # Forward pass latents = self.embeddings(indices) # Concatenate latent code and point coordinates # latents shape: (batchsize, latentdim) # points shape: (batchsize, 3) # x shape: (batchsize, latentdim + 3) x = torch.cat([latents, points], dim=-1) sdfpreds = self.deepsdfmodel(x) # Compute Loss loss = nn.functional.l1loss(sdfpreds.view(-1), sdfs.view(-1), reduction="sum") # Backward pass self.optimizermodel.zerograd() self.optimizerembed.zerograd() loss.backward() # Step optimizers self.optimizermodel.step() self.optimizerembed.step() epochloss += loss.item() self.scheduler.step() self.losses.append(epochloss) return epochloss def run(self): for epoch in range(1, self.epochs + 1): epochloss = self.trainepoch() if epoch % self.savefreq == 0: # Save model state torch.save(self.deepsdfmodel.statedict(), f"deepsdfepoch{epoch}.param") torch.save(self.embeddings.statedict(), f"embeddingsepoch{epoch}.param") # Save losses import numpy as np np.save("losses.npy", np.array(self.losses)) yield epoch, self.losses H3D is a variant that uses a two-stage training process for head modeling. First, an SDF network is trained on a large dataset of 3D scans, and its parameters are fixed. Second, an implicit neural rendering model is trained using the fixed SDF as a prior. After convergence, the SDF parameters are unfrozen, and training continues for fine-tuning. This approach leverages pre-trained SDF knowledge to improve reconstruction quality for complex structures like heads. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The memory usage is dominated by the embedding table size (N \times dz) and the MLP weights (O(dz \cdot dh + dh^2 \cdot n{hidden})). The batch size determines the GPU memory required for the forward/backward pass. Time: Each epoch processes all shapes in the dataset. The complexity per iteration is linear in the number of query points per batch. Measured Performance: Trained for 2000 epochs with a batch size of 24. Learning rate decay is applied every 500 epochs. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Compact representation via global latent codes; continuous surface representation. Limitations: Global latent code may struggle with high-frequency details compared to local feature methods like VoxelSDF. Training requires joint optimization of latent codes and network weights, which can be sensitive to initialization. When to Use: Use when a compact, global representation is sufficient and the shapes are relatively smooth or low-frequency. Do not use when high-frequency geometric details are critical and local feature interpolation (as in VoxelSDF) is preferred. DeepSDF was introduced by Park et al. in 2019. It represents shapes as continuous signed distance functions parameterized by a neural network conditioned on a latent code. The training loop jointly optimizes these latent codes and the network weights using L1 loss on sampled points. It is widely used in 3D reconstruction and generative modeling. name: VoxelSDF Training Loop
head: Training Procedure (L1 Loss + Adam + StepLR), VoxelSDF Training Procedure
body: The VoxelSDF Training Loop is the optimization procedure for the VoxelSDF architecture, which predicts Signed Distance Function (SDF) values by interpolating features from a voxelized latent embedding grid. It solves the problem of learning compact, spatially-aware implicit representations by conditioning a neural network on local voxel features rather than global latent codes. It sets itself apart from global implicit representations like DeepSDF by using a structured voxel grid to store latent codes, allowing for localized feature interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of 3D points and their corresponding ground-truth SDF values, indexed by shape identifier (e.g., ShapeNetSDF). Output: Updated parameters for the VoxelSDF decoder (MLP) and the GridEmbedding (lookup table of latent codes). Data Structures: GridEmbedding: A learnable tensor storing latent codes for each voxel in the grid. Accessed via embeddings(index) where index maps shapes to specific voxel coordinates or embeddings. Model: The VoxelSDF decoder, typically an MLP that takes latent codes and 3D points as input. Optimizer State: Maintained by Adam optimizer for both model parameters and embedding parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the GridEmbedding tensor for the dataset size. Initialize the Adam optimizer with separate learning rates for the model and embeddings. Initialize a StepLR scheduler. 2. Epoch Loop: Iterate through epochs from startepoch to epochs. 3. Batch Iteration: For each batch in the dataloader: a. Move points, sdfs, and index to the target device (e.g., GPU). b. Retrieve latent codes: latentcodes = embeddings(index). c. Forward pass: sdfpred = model(latentcodes, points). d. Reshape sdfpred and sdfs to (realbatchsize, -1). e. Compute L1 loss: loss = criterion(sdfpred, sdfs). f. Zero gradients: optimizer.zerograd(). g. Backward pass: loss.backward(). h. Update parameters: optimizer.step(). 4. Scheduler Step: After each epoch, step the learning rate scheduler. 5. Checkpointing: Every 100 epochs, save the model state dict and embedding state dict. 6. Logging: Record epoch loss. Formulas: L1 Loss: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} | \hat{y}i - yi |, where \hat{y}i is the predicted SDF and yi is the ground truth SDF. Adam Optimizer: Uses adaptive moment estimation with separate learning rates for model and embeddings. StepLR Scheduler: Reduces learning rate by a factor (gamma) every stepsize epochs. Parameters: Learning Rate (Model): 1 \times 10^{-4}. Learning Rate (Embeddings): 1 \times 10^{-2}. Step Size (Scheduler): 100 epochs (default). Batch Size: Not given in the sources. Total Epochs: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Device Placement: Points, SDFs, and indices must be moved to the correct device (CPU/GPU) before computation. Reshaping: Predictions and targets must be reshaped to match the batch dimension before loss computation. Gradient Zeroing: Gradients must be zeroed before each backward pass to prevent accumulation. Checkpointing: Models are saved every 100 epochs; intermediate epochs are not saved by default. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np import os class VoxelSDFTrainer: def init(self, model, embeddings, dataloader, epochs=1000, startepoch=0, resultdir="./results"): self.model = model self.embeddings = embeddings self.dataloader = dataloader self.epochs = epochs self.startepoch = startepoch self.resultdir = resultdir self.device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.isavailable() else "cpu") # Initialize optimizer with separate learning rates self.optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([ {"params": self.model.parameters(), "lr": 1e-4}, {"params": self.embeddings.parameters(), "lr": 1e-2} ]) # Initialize scheduler self.scheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.StepLR(self.optimizer, stepsize=100, gamma=0.1) # Initialize criterion self.criterion = nn.L1Loss() self.losses = [] def trainepoch(self, epoch): self.model.train() epochloss = 0.0 for points, sdfs, index in self.dataloader: # Move data to device points = points.to(self.device) sdfs = sdfs.to(self.device) index = index.to(self.device) realbatchsize = index.shape[0] # Forward pass latentcodes = self.embeddings(index) sdfpred = self.model(latentcodes, points) # Reshape for loss computation sdfpred = sdfpred.view(realbatchsize, -1) sdfs = sdfs.view(realbatchsize, -1) # Compute loss loss = self.criterion(sdfpred, sdfs) # Backward pass and optimization self.optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() epochloss += loss.item() return epochloss / len(self.dataloader) def train(self): for e in range(self.startepoch, self.epochs + 1): epochloss = self.trainepoch(e) self.losses.append(epochloss) # Step scheduler self.scheduler.step() # Save model every 100 epochs if e % 100 == 0: self.savemodel(e) np.save(os.path.join(self.resultdir, "losses.npy"), np.array(self.losses)) yield e, self.losses def savemodel(self, epoch): modelpath = os.path.join(self.resultdir, f"voxelsdfepoch{epoch}.param") embeddingpath = os.path.join(self.resultdir, f"embeddingsepoch{epoch}.param") torch.save(self.model.statedict(), modelpath) torch.save(self.embeddings.statedict(), embeddingpath) def loadmodel(self, epoch): modelpath = os.path.join(self.resultdir, f"voxelsdfepoch{epoch}.param") embeddingpath = os.path.join(self.resultdir, f"embeddingsepoch{epoch}.param") self.model.loadstatedict(torch.load(modelpath, weightsonly=True)) self.embeddings.loadstatedict(torch.load(embeddingpath, weightsonly=True)) MetaSDF is a method for learning a prior over signed distance function (SDF) shape spaces by treating shape reconstruction as a meta-learning problem, where a neural network is specialized to a new shape via few steps of gradient descent on context observations. It sets itself apart from auto-decoder frameworks by performing specialization in the forward pass via a fixed number of gradient steps, making it an order of magnitude faster at inference, and from pooling-based set-encoders by avoiding the underfitting of context sets. The SDF Training Step is the core optimization routine for the VoxelSDF architecture, which predicts Signed Distance Function (SDF) values for 3D points by interpolating features from a voxelized latent embedding grid. It solves the problem of learning compact, spatially-aware implicit representations by conditioning a neural network on local voxel features rather than global latent codes. It sets itself apart from global implicit representations like DeepSDF by using a structured voxel grid to store latent codes, allowing for localized feature interpolation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of training points and epochs. Each epoch requires a forward and backward pass through the model and embeddings. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the GridEmbedding tensor and the model parameters. The batch size also affects memory usage during training. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The use of a voxel grid allows for localized feature interpolation, which can improve scalability compared to global latent codes for large datasets. Strengths: Combines the benefits of voxel-based representations (spatial locality) with implicit representations (continuous SDF values). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rates for model and embeddings. The voxel grid size can impact memory usage. When to Use: Suitable for learning compact, spatially-aware implicit representations for 3D shape reconstruction. When Not to Use: Not suitable for applications requiring real-time inference without pre-trained models, or when memory constraints are severe. The VoxelSDF Training Loop is based on the VoxelSDF architecture, which integrates voxel-based latent embeddings with a neural network decoder for SDF prediction. It builds on the DeepSDF framework by introducing a voxelized latent code structure. The method was introduced in the context of 3D shape reconstruction and representation learning. name: MetaSDF
head: Gradient-based meta-learning of shape spaces, Meta-learning Signed Distance Functions
body:
MetaSDF is a method for learning a prior over signed distance function (SDF) shape spaces by treating shape reconstruction as a meta-learning problem, where a neural network is specialized to a new shape via few steps of gradient descent on context observations. It sets itself apart from auto-decoder frameworks by performing specialization in the forward pass via a fixed number of gradient steps, making it an order of magnitude faster at inference, and from pooling-based set-encoders by avoiding the underfitting of context sets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset \mathcal{D} of N shapes. Each shape i is represented by a set of K point samples from its ground-truth SDF: Xi = \{(xj, sj): sj = 	ext{SDF}i(xj)\}{j=1}^K, where xj \in \mathbb{R}^3 are spatial coordinates and sj \in \mathbb{R} are signed distances. Output: Meta-parameters 	heta and per-parameter inner learning rates \alpha for a neural network \Phi that approximates the SDF. Data Structures: Meta-parameters 	heta: The initial weights of the neural network \Phi, shared across all tasks/shapes. Inner learning rates \alpha: A vector of per-parameter learning rates for the inner loop, initialized to 1 	imes 10^{-1}. Outer learning rate  eta: A scalar used to update meta-parameters and inner learning rates. Network \Phi: A fully connected ReLU-MLP. In 2D experiments, it has 4 layers and 256 hidden units. Formulas: The surface of the shape is represented implicitly as the zero-level set of the neural network \Phii: L0(\Phii) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \Phii(x) = 0\}, \quad \Phii: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R} The inner-loop update rule for shape i at step j is: \phi{j+1}^i = \phij^i - \alpha \odot 
abla{\phij^i} \mathcal{L}(\Phi(x; \phij^i), s) where \phi0^i = 	heta, \odot denotes element-wise multiplication, and \mathcal{L} is the loss function. Parameters: k: The number of inner-loop gradient descent steps. In 2D MNIST experiments, k=5. \alpha: Per-parameter inner learning rates, initialized to 1 	imes 10^{-1}.  eta: Outer learning rate. In 2D experiments,  eta = 1 	imes 10^{-4}. Steps: 1. Initialize inner, per-parameter learning rates \alpha and meta-parameters 	heta. 2. Sample a batch of shape datasets Xi \sim \mathcal{D}. 3. For each shape i in the batch: a. Split Xi into a training set Xi^{	ext{train}} and a test set Xi^{	ext{test}}. b. Initialize inner parameters \phi0^i = 	heta and training loss \mathcal{L}{	ext{train}} = 0. c. For j from 0 to k-1: i. Chan, Noah Snavely, Richard Tucker, and Gordon Wetzstein in 2020. name: SDF Training Step
head: Voxel-Conditioned SDF Decoder, VoxelSDF, VoxelSDF MLP
body: The SDF Training Step is the core optimization routine for the VoxelSDF architecture, which predicts Signed Distance Function (SDF) values for 3D points by interpolating features from a voxelized latent embedding grid. It solves the problem of learning compact, spatially-aware implicit representations by conditioning a neural network on local voxel features rather than global latent codes. It sets itself apart from global implicit representations like DeepSDF by using a structured voxel grid to store latent codes, allowing for localized feature interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of 3D query points P \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} and their corresponding ground-truth SDF values D \in \mathbb{R}^{N}. Output: Predicted SDF values \hat{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N} and a scalar loss value. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid Embedding: A 5D tensor of shape (N{models}, L, V+1, V+1, V+1), where N{models} is the batch size (number of models), L is the latent dimension, and V is the voxelgridsize. The grid stores learnable latent codes for each voxel. 2. Training Batch Matrix: A matrix containing the shuffled query points, shaped (N, 3). 3. Training Target Matrix: A matrix containing the shuffled target distances, shaped (N, 1). Parameters: voxelgridsize: Resolution of the voxel grid. Default: 8. numlayers: Number of hidden layers in the SDF MLP. Default: 4. hiddendim: Dimensionality of hidden layers in the SDF MLP. Default: 128. latentdim: Dimensionality of the latent codes stored in the voxel grid. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Shuffle Data: To de-correlate data and improve training stability, shuffle the positions and distances within the training batch. 2. Reshape Inputs: Reshape the voxel grid embeddings into a 5D tensor (N{models}, L, V+1, V+1, V+1). Reshape the input query points into a 5D tensor (N{models}, N{points}, 1, 1, 3) to align with the interpolation grid dimensions. 3. Feature Sampling: Sample latent features at the query points using bilinear interpolation (e.g., gridsample) with zero padding and aligned corners. This retrieves the latent code z corresponding to the spatial location of each point. 4. Concatenation: Concatenate the sampled latent features z with the original 3D coordinates of the points p along the feature dimension, resulting in a vector of size L + 3. 5. MLP Prediction: Pass the concatenated vector through the SDF MLP to predict the SDF value. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the loss (typically L1) between the predicted SDF values and the ground-truth distances. 7. Optimization Step: Perform the gradient update using the optimizer (e.g., Adam). 8. Update State: Increment the training step counter and update the loss scalar if required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdftrainingstep(voxelgrid, points, targets, trainer, voxelgridsize=8, latentdim=128, hiddendim=128, numlayers=4): """ Performs one training step for the VoxelSDF model. Args: voxelgrid: Tensor of shape (Nmodels, latentdim, V+1, V+1, V+1) points: Tensor of shape (Npoints, 3) targets: Tensor of shape (Npoints,) trainer: Object with trainingstep and loss methods voxelgridsize: int, resolution of the voxel grid latentdim: int, dimension of latent codes hiddendim: int, dimension of MLP hidden layers numlayers: int, number of MLP hidden layers Returns: loss: float, computed loss value """ # 1. Shuffle data to de-correlate # Note: In a real implementation, this might be handled by DataLoader shuffling. # Here we assume points and targets are already shuffled or shuffled externally. # If not, shuffle them: indices = torch.randperm(points.size(0)) points = points[indices] targets = targets[indices] # 2. Reshape inputs for interpolation # voxelgrid is already (Nmodels, L, V+1, V+1, V+1) # Reshape points to (Nmodels, Npoints, 1, 1, 3) for gridsample # Assuming points are grouped by model in the batch. # If points are flat, we need to reshape them to match the batch structure. # Let's assume points are already structured as (Nmodels, Npointspermodel, 3) # or we flatten and reshape. For simplicity, assume points is (Ntotal, 3) # and we need to map it to the voxel grid structure. # The source says: "Reshape input points into 5D tensor: (nmodels, npointspermodel, 1, 1, 3)" # This implies the input batch is already organized by model. # 3. Sample latent features using bilinear interpolation # gridsample expects input (N, C, H, W, D) and grid (N, Hout, Wout, Dout, 3) # We need to adapt the point coordinates to the gridsample format. # Normalize points to [-1, 1] range if they are not already. # Let's assume points are normalized. # Create grid for sampling # The gridsample function in PyTorch expects the grid to be in normalized coordinates [-1, 1] # We need to convert our 3D points to this format. # Assuming points are in [0, 1] or [-1, 1]. Let's assume [-1, 1]. # Reshape points to (Nmodels, Npoints, 1, 1, 3) # If points is (Ntotal, 3), we need to know Nmodels and Npointspermodel. # Let's assume we have a batch of models, each with Npoints. # For this pseudocode, we assume points is already reshaped to (Nmodels, Npoints, 3) # and we expand it to (Nmodels, Npoints, 1, 1, 3) # Note: The exact reshaping depends on the data loader structure. # We will assume points is (Nmodels, Npoints, 3) # Expand dimensions for gridsample # gridsample input: (N, C, H, W, D) # gridsample grid: (N, Hout, Wout, Dout, 3) # We need to convert points to the grid format. # Let's assume points are in [-1, 1]. # Reshape points to (Nmodels, Npoints, 1, 1, 3) points5d = points.unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(2) # (Nmodels, Npoints, 1, 1, 3) # Sample features # voxelgrid is (Nmodels, L, V+1, V+1, V+1) # gridsample output: (Nmodels, L, Npoints, 1, 1) sampledfeatures = torch.nn.functional.gridsample( voxelgrid, points5d, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=True) # Squeeze the last two dimensions sampledfeatures = sampledfeatures.squeeze(3).squeeze(3) # (Nmodels, L, Npoints) # Transpose to (Nmodels, Npoints, L) sampledfeatures = sampledfeatures.permute(0, 2, 1) # 4. Concatenate sampled features with original points # points is (Nmodels, Npoints, 3) # sampledfeatures is (Nmodels, Npoints, L) # Concatenate along the last dimension concatenated = torch.cat([sampledfeatures, points], dim=2) # (Nmodels, Npoints, L+3) # Flatten for MLP # (Nmodels Npoints, L+3) concatenatedflat = concatenated.view(-1, latentdim + 3) # 5. Pass through MLP # MLP: Linear(L+3, hiddendim) -> ReLU ->... -> Linear(hiddendim, 1) -> Tanh x = concatenatedflat for i in range(numlayers): x = torch.nn.functional.relu(torch.nn.Linear(latentdim + 3 if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)(x)) output = torch.tanh(torch.nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)(x)) # Flatten output to (Ntotal,) predictedsdf = output.squeeze(1) # 6. Compute loss # L1 loss loss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(predictedsdf, targets) # 7. Optimization step # This is handled by the trainer object # trainer.step(loss) return loss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Points outside the voxel grid bounds must be handled correctly by the interpolation method (zero padding is used). Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise during interpolation and MLP computation. Using aligncorners=True in gridsample ensures consistent coordinate mapping. Degenerate Input: Empty batches or points with identical coordinates should be handled by the shuffling and batching logic. PatchNet represents a 3D object as a collection of learnable surface patches, where each patch models the geometry within a specific radius from its center using a neural implicit function. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of query points and the size of the voxel grid. The dominant operation is the bilinear interpolation and the MLP forward pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the voxel grid embedding (N{models} \times L \times (V+1)^3) and the batch size. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with batch size due to parallelizable operations (interpolation, MLP). The voxel grid size V affects memory linearly with V^3. Strengths: Localized feature interpolation allows for detailed geometry representation. Structured latent codes improve training stability compared to global codes. Limitations: Memory usage grows cubically with voxel grid resolution. Interpolation artifacts may occur at low resolutions. When to Use: When learning implicit representations for multiple objects with shared structure or when localized features are beneficial. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained and high-resolution voxel grids are not feasible. The VoxelSDF method was introduced as an extension of DeepSDF, aiming to improve generalization and training efficiency by using voxelized latent codes. It builds on the idea of implicit surface representations but structures the latent space spatially. jaeyeol816/Dynamic-NGPs, https://github.com/jaeyeol816/Dynamic-NGPs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) TurtleJayWang/VC-SDFGen2, https://github.com/TurtleJayWang/VC-SDFGen2, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: PatchNet
head: Patch-Based Generalizable Deep Implicit 3D Shape Representations
body: PatchNet represents a 3D object as a collection of learnable surface patches, where each patch models the geometry within a specific radius from its center using a neural implicit function. It solves the problem of generalizable surface reconstruction by treating patch latent codes and extrinsic parameters (position, orientation, radius) as free variables optimized directly during training (auto-decoding), rather than regressing them from an encoder. This approach allows for controllable deformation and generalization across object categories, outperforming global implicit representations like DeepSDF and structured approaches like DSIF, particularly when training data is limited. Inputs: A watertight mesh (for training) or point samples with truncated signed distance field (SDF) values (for test-time optimization). Outputs: A blended SDF field gi(x) representing the object surface, from which meshes can be extracted via Marching Cubes. Patch Extrinsic Parameters (e{i,p}) Each patch p of object i is defined by 7 parameters e{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^7: Radius r{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}: The spherical radius of the patch. Center c{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D position of the patch center. Orientation \phi{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Euler angles defining the rotation of the patch's canonical frame. Patch Latent Code (z{i,p}) z{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^{128}: A vector describing the intrinsic geometry of the patch surface. Network Weights (\theta) Parameters of the fully-connected neural network that maps (z, x) to SDF values. 1. Preprocessing: Center the input mesh and fit it tightly into the unit sphere. Sample points mostly close to the surface and compute their truncated signed distance to the object surface, truncating at 0.1. 2. Latent Codes: Initialize all patch latent codes z{i,p} to zero. 3. Positions: Initialize patch centers c{i,p} using greedy farthest point sampling of the object's surface point samples. 4. Radii: Set each patch radius r{i,p} to the minimum value such that every surface point sample is covered by its closest patch. 5. Orientation: Align the z-axis of the patch coordinate system with the surface normal at the closest point to the patch center. The network f(x, z, \theta) takes a query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a latent code z \in \mathbb{R}^{128} as input and outputs a scalar SDF value. Structure: Eight weight-normalized fully-connected layers with 128 output dimensions and ReLU activations. Concatenation: The latent code z and query point x are concatenated to the input of the fifth layer. Output: The last layer outputs a single scalar, passed through a \tanh activation to bound the SDF value. Training minimizes the total loss L over network weights \theta, patch latent codes \{zi\}, and extrinsics \{ei\} for all objects i: \arg\min{\theta, \{zi\}, \{ei\}} \sumi L(zi, ei, \theta) The total loss is defined as: L(zi, ei, \theta) = L{recon}(zi, ei, \theta) + L{ext}(ei) + L{reg}(zi) 1. Reconstruction Loss (L{recon}) Minimizes the difference between predicted and ground truth SDF values for points within each patch's bounds: L{recon}(zi, ei, \theta) = \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} \frac{1}{|S(e{i,p})|} \sum{x \in S(e{i,p})} |f(x, z{i,p}, \theta) - s(x)| Where: NP = 30 is the number of patches. S(e{i,p}) is the set of normalized point samples within the bounds of patch p. s(x) is the ground truth truncated SDF value. 2. Extrinsic Loss (L{ext}) Guides the placement and orientation of patches: L{ext}(ei) = L{sur}(ei) + L{cov}(ei) + L{rot}(ei) + L{scl}(ei) + L{var}(ei) Surface Loss (L{sur}): Ensures patches stay close to the surface: L{sur}(ei) = \omega{sur} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} \max\left( \frac{1}{|Oi|} \sum{x \in Oi} \|c{i,p} - x\|^2, t \right) Where Oi is the set of surface points of object i, and t = 0.06 is a threshold. Coverage Loss (L{cov}): Encourages uncovered surface points Ui to be covered by at least one patch: L{cov}(ei) = \omega{cov} \cdot \frac{1}{|Ui|} \sum{x \in Ui} \frac{w{i,p,x}}{\sum{p} w{i,p,x}} (\|c{i,p} - x\|^2 - r{i,p}) Where w{i,p,x} = \exp\left(-0.5 \cdot \left(\frac{\|c{i,p} - x\|^2 - r{i,p}}{\sigma}\right)^2\right) with \sigma = 0.05. Rotation Loss (L{rot}): Aligns patch orientation with surface normals: L{rot}(ei) = \omega{rot} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} (1 - \langle \phi{i,p} \cdot [0,0,1]^T, n{i,p} \rangle)^2 Where n{i,p} is the surface normal at o{i,p} = \arg\min{x \in Oi} \|x - c{i,p}\|^2. Scale Loss (L{scl}): Encourages small patch radii to prevent overlap: L{scl}(ei) = \omega{scl} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} r{i,p}^2 Variance Loss (L{var}): Encourages similar patch sizes: L{var}(ei) = \omega{var} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} (r{i,p} - mi)^2 Where mi is the mean patch radius of object i. 3. Regularization (L{reg}) L2 regularizer on latent codes assuming a Gaussian prior: L{reg}(zi) = \omega{reg} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} \|z{i,p}\|^2 For a new object given point samples and SDF values, optimize for patch latent codes and extrinsics using the same initialization, while keeping network weights \theta fixed. To obtain a smooth SDF field gi(x) for rendering or meshing, blend overlapping patches using isotropic Gaussian weights: gi(x) = \frac{\sum{p \in P{i,x}} w{i,p,x} f(x, z{i,p}, \theta)}{\sum{p \in P{i,x}} w{i,p,x}} Where P{i,x} is the set of patches covering point x, and the weight w{i,p,x} is defined as: w{i,p,x} = \exp\left(-\frac{\|c{i,p} - x\|^2}{2\sigma}\right) - \exp\left(-\frac{\|c{i,p} - x\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) With \sigma = r{i,p}/3, ensuring the weight is zero at the patch boundary. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np class PatchNetNetwork(nn.Module): """ Neural network for implicit patch representation. Input: x (3,), z (128,) Output: scalar SDF """ def init(self): super().init() # 8 weight-normalized FC layers, 128 dims, ReLU self.layers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(3, 128)), # Layer 0 nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), # Layer 1 nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), # Layer 2 nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), # Layer 3 nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), # Layer 4 # Layer 5 input is concat(z, x) -> 128 + 3 = 131 nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(131, 128)), # Layer 5 nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), # Layer 6 nn.utils.weightnorm(nn.Linear(128, 128)), # Layer 7 nn.Linear(128, 1) # Output layer ]) def forward(self, x, z): h = x for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): if i == 5: # Concatenate z and x at the input of the 5th layer (index 5) h = torch.cat([z, h], dim=-1) h = layer(h) if i < 7: # ReLU for all layers except the last h = torch.relu(h) # Last layer: tanh activation return torch.tanh(h) def farthestpointsample(points, numpatches): """ Greedy farthest point sampling. points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) Returns: centers (numpatches, 3) """ N = points.shape[0] centers = torch.zeros(numpatches, 3, device=points.device) centers[0] = points[0] dists = torch.full((numpatches,), float('inf'), device=points.device) for i in range(1, numpatches): # Compute distances from all points to the last added center disttolast = torch.norm(points.unsqueeze(1) - centers[i-1].unsqueeze(0), dim=2).squeeze(1) # Update minimum distances dists = torch.minimum(dists, disttolast) # Pick the farthest point idx = torch.argmax(dists) centers[i] = points[idx] return centers def preprocessmesh(mesh): """ Preprocess a watertight mesh: center, fit to unit sphere, sample points, compute truncated SDF. Returns: surfacepoints (N, 3), sdfvalues (N,) """ # Standard preprocessing: center mesh, normalize to unit sphere, # sample points near surface, compute truncated SDF at truncation=0.1. # Placeholder for actual mesh processing pipeline. surfacepoints = torch.randn(3000, 3) # Dummy data sdfvalues = torch.randn(3000) # Dummy data return surfacepoints, sdfvalues def computeextrinsicloss(centers, radii, normals, surfacepoints, objectnormals, params): """ Compute Lext = Lsur + Lcov + Lrot + Lscl + Lvar """ # Lsur: Surface loss distssur = torch.cdist(centers, surfacepoints) # (numpatches, Nsurf) meansqdists = torch.mean(distssur2, dim=1) # (numpatches,) Lsur = torch.mean(torch.clamp(meansqdists - params['t'], min=0)) # max(meansq, t) logic approximated for gradient flow, but exact max is used in formula # Lcov: Coverage loss for uncovered points distscov = torch.cdist(centers, surfacepoints) # (numpatches, Nsurf) covered = torch.any(distscov2 <= radii.unsqueeze(1)2, dim=0) # (Nsurf,) uncoveredmask = ~covered uncoveredpoints = surfacepoints[uncoveredmask] if len(uncoveredpoints) == 0: Lcov = torch.tensor(0.0) else: distsuncovered = torch.cdist(centers, uncoveredpoints) # (numpatches, Nuncovered) sqdists = distsuncovered2 weights = torch.exp(-0.5 ((sqdists - radii.unsqueeze(1)) / params['sigmacov'])2) weightsums = torch.sum(weights, dim=0) # (Nuncovered,) weightsums = torch.clamp(weightsums, min=1e-8) lossterms = sqdists - radii.unsqueeze(1) weightedloss = torch.sum(weights lossterms, dim=0) / weightsums Lcov = torch.mean(weightedloss) # Lrot: Rotation loss dotproducts = torch.sum(normals objectnormals, dim=1) # (numpatches,) Lrot = torch.mean((1 - dotproducts)2) # Lscl: Scale loss Lscl = torch.mean(radii2) # Lvar: Variance loss meanradius = torch.mean(radii) Lvar = torch.mean((radii - meanradius)2) totalext = (params['wsur'] Lsur + params['wcov'] Lcov + params['wrot'] Lrot + params['wscl'] Lscl + params['wvar'] Lvar) return totalext def computereconstructionloss(network, centers, radii, normals, zcodes, pointsamples, sdfvalues, params): """ Compute Lrecon """ numpatches = zcodes.shape[0] totalloss = 0.0 count = 0 for p in range(numpatches): dists = torch.cdist(centers[p:p+1], pointsamples) # (1, N) mask = dists[0] <= radii[p] patchpoints = pointsamples[mask] patchsdfs = sdfvalues[mask] if len(patchpoints) == 0: continue # Transform points to patch-local canonical frame localpoints = transformpointstopatchframe(patchpoints, centers[p], normals[p]) zp = zcodes[p] zbatch = zp.unsqueeze(0).expand(localpoints.shape[0], -1) sdfpred = network(localpoints, zbatch).squeeze(-1) loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(sdfpred - patchsdfs)) totalloss += loss count += 1 if count == 0: return torch.tensor(0.0) return totalloss / count def transformpointstopatchframe(points, center, normal): """ Transform global points to patch-local canonical frame. Aligns z-axis with normal. """ translated = points - center R = rotationmatrixfromnormal(normal) localpoints = torch.matmul(translated, R.T) return localpoints def rotationmatrixfromnormal(normal): """ Create a rotation matrix that aligns [0,0,1] with normal. """ zaxis = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], device=normal.device) axis = torch.cross(zaxis, normal) angle = torch.acos(torch.clamp(torch.dot(zaxis, normal), -1.0, 1.0)) # Rodrigues' rotation formula K = torch.tensor([[0, -axis[2], axis[1]], [axis[2], 0, -axis[0]], [-axis[1], axis[0], 0]], device=normal.device) I = torch.eye(3, device=normal.device) R = I + torch.sin(angle) K + (1 - torch.cos(angle)) torch.matmul(K, K) return R def trainpatchnet(meshes, network, optimizerz, optimizere, optimizertheta, numepochs=1000): """ Main training loop. """ for epoch in range(numepochs): for obj in meshes: surfacepoints, sdfvalues = preprocessmesh(obj) if not hasattr(obj, 'patchesinitialized'): centers, radii, normals = initializepatches(surfacepoints) obj.centers = centers obj.radii = radii obj.normals = normals obj.zcodes = torch.zeros(30, 128) obj.patchesinitialized = True optimizerz.zerograd() optimizere.zerograd() optimizertheta.zerograd() reconloss = computereconstructionloss( network, obj.centers, obj.radii, obj.normals, obj.zcodes, surfacepoints, sdfvalues, params) extloss = computeextrinsicloss( obj.centers, obj.radii, obj.normals, surfacepoints, obj.normals, params) regloss = torch.mean(obj.zcodes2) totalloss = reconloss + extloss + regloss totalloss.backward() optimizertheta.step() optimizerz.step() optimizere.step() if epoch % 200 == 0 and epoch > 0: for paramgroup in optimizertheta.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = 0.5 for paramgroup in optimizerz.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = 0.5 for paramgroup in optimizere.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = 0.5 def testtimeoptimization(obj, pointsamples, sdfvalues, network, numiterations=10000): """ Optimize z and e for a new object with fixed network weights. """ centers, radii, normals = initializepatches(pointsamples) zcodes = torch.zeros(30, 128) optimizerz = torch.optim.Adam([zcodes], lr=1e-3) optimizere = torch.optim.Adam([centers, radii, normals], lr=1e-3) for i in range(numiterations): optimizerz.zerograd() optimizere.zerograd() reconloss = computereconstructionloss( network, centers, radii, normals, zcodes, pointsamples, sdfvalues, params) extloss = computeextrinsicloss( centers, radii, normals, pointsamples, normals, params) regloss = torch.mean(zcodes2) totalloss = reconloss + extloss + regloss totalloss.backward() optimizerz.step() optimizere.step() if i % 2000 == 0 and i > 0: for paramgroup in optimizerz.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = 0.5 for paramgroup in optimizere.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = 0.5 return zcodes, centers, radii, normals Number of patches (NP): 30. Threshold (t): 0.06 for L{sur}. \sigma (Coverage): 0.05 for L{cov}. \sigma (Noise): Standard deviation of Gaussian noise added to ground truth SDF values during robustness testing; tested values include 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, and 0. \omega{reg}: Linearly increased from 0 to 10^{-4} for 400 epochs, then constant. Learning Rate (Network \theta): Initially 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. Learning Rate (Latent/Extrinsics): Initially 10^{-3}. Batch Size: 64. SDF Point Samples per Object: 3k. Patch Latent Size: 128. Baseline Patch Latent Size: 4050. ICL-NUIM Specifics: 800 patches, 50 million SDF samples, extrinsics fixed, 10k iterations, learning rate halved every 2k iterations, 25k SDF samples per iteration. Wasteful Distribution: Due to extrinsics initialization and L{var}, all patches tend to have similar sizes, leading to a potentially wasteful distribution of coverage. Generalization on Extrinsics: Unlike DSIF, PatchNet does not regress extrinsics, avoiding issues with predicting extrinsics for shapes very different from training data. Scaling: For datasets with different scales (e.g., ICL-NUIM), the standard deviation for SDF sample generation must be adjusted (e.g., reduced by a factor of 100). Training Time: 2 hours on Nvidia V100 GPU for PatchNets (NP=10, size=512) vs 156 hours for the full dataset baseline. Memory: The representation is compact, storing only latent codes and extrinsics per object, unlike voxel grids. ShapeNet Test Set: Mean IoU: 92.1 (PatchNets) vs 77.4 (DeepSDF) and 76.5 (Baseline). Mean Chamfer Distance: 0.044 (PatchNets) vs 0.075 (DeepSDF) and 0.111 (Baseline). Mean F-Score: 94.8 (PatchNets) vs 89.9 (DeepSDF) and 80.6 (Baseline). Robustness (Reduced Test Set): \sigma=0.1: IoU 81.2, Chamfer 0.037, F-Score 85.3. \sigma=0.01: IoU 90.3, Chamfer 0.045, F-Score 94.3. \sigma=0.001: IoU 91.5, Chamfer 0.047, F-Score 94.4. \sigma=0: IoU 91.6, Chamfer 0.045, F-Score 94.5. Cross-Dataset Generalization: ~70% improvement in F-score compared to global-patch baseline when evaluating on Dynamic FAUST. Strengths: Outperforms DeepSDF, OccupancyNetworks, Structured Implicit Functions, and DSIF on most ShapeNet categories, despite being trained on a smaller subset (~4% of training data). Better generalization with few training shapes (1-100 per category). Avoids the need for input geometry representation for an encoder. Limitations: Patches have similar sizes due to initialization and regularization, which may not be optimal for all geometries. Use for surface reconstruction and generalizable 3D shape representation when training data is limited or when cross-dataset generalization is required. PatchNet was introduced by Tretschk et al. in the paper "PatchNets: Patch-Based Generalizable Deep Implicit 3D Shape Representations". The method builds upon DeepSDF by introducing a patch-based representation with learnable extrinsics. It was developed to address the limitations of global implicit representations and structured implicit functions, particularly in terms of generalization and handling articulated deformations. It was compared against concurrent work such as Deep Structured Implicit Functions (DSIF). PatchNet is used for surface reconstruction and generalizable 3D shape representation on datasets like ShapeNet and Dynamic FAUST. name: Deep Medial Field (DMF) Network Architecture
head: DMF Network
body:
The Deep Medial Field (DMF) Network is a neural implicit surface representation that extends the DeepSDF Neural Network by predicting the medial field in addition to the signed distance field (SDF) and its gradient. While DeepSDF outputs only the SDF value \Phi(x), DMF predicts two medial field components M^+(x) and M^-(x), the SDF \Phi(x), and the SDF gradient 
abla\Phi(x). This extension enables efficient computation of medial field ambient occlusion (MFAO) and provides local shape thickness information. It is distinct from Vox2SDF, which uses voxel grids, and builds on DeepSDF by adding specific heads to handle the discontinuous nature of the medial field. Inputs: A 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Four values: 1. M^+(x) \in \mathbb{R}: Medial field value for the outside of the shape (x \in O^+). 2. M^-(x) \in \mathbb{R}: Medial field value for the inside of the shape (x \in O^-). 3. \Phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}: Signed distance value. 4. 
abla\Phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^3: Gradient of the SDF. Data Structures: The network consists of a shared fully connected backbone (MLP) and four separate fully connected heads. Shared Backbone: An MLP with 6 hidden layers. It takes the transformed input coordinates and outputs a shared feature vector. Heads: Four separate MLPs, each with 2 hidden layers containing 64 neurons and a linear output layer. Head 1: Outputs M^+(x). Head 2: Outputs M^-(x). Head 3: Outputs \Phi(x). Head 4: Outputs 
abla\Phi(x). Parameters: Random Fourier Features (RFF): 64 bands transform input coordinates. Weighting Constant (\alpha): Set to 10^{-3}. Activation: The backbone and heads use the activation functions described in [Gropp et al. 2020], with the architecture diagram explicitly specifying Softplus. Algorithm: 1. Input Transformation: Transform input coordinate x into 64-band Random Fourier Features. Let fi be the i-th Fourier feature band. 2. Feature Weighting: Weight each Fourier feature fi by wi = \alpha ||fi||, where ||fi|| is the frequency of the i-th band and \alpha = 10^{-3}. This preserves the network's bias towards spherical topology. 3. Concatenation: Concatenate the weighted Fourier features with the original un-transformed coordinates x. 4. Shared Encoding: Pass the concatenated vector through the shared backbone MLP (6 hidden layers) to obtain a shared feature vector h. 5. Head Decoding: Pass h through each of the four separate heads to obtain M^+(x), M^-(x), \Phi(x), and 
abla\Phi(x). 6. Medial Field Combination: Compute the final medial field M(x) using the sign of \Phi(x) to handle the discontinuity at the surface \partial O: M(x) =  egin{cases} M^+(x) & 	ext{if } \Phi(x) > 0 \ M^-(x) & 	ext{if } \Phi(x) < 0 \end{cases} This formulation allows the network to model the discontinuity of the medial field at the surface, which ordinary Lipschitz MLPs cannot approximate directly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def randomfourierfeatures(x, numbands=64, alpha=1e-3, B=None, b=None): """Transforms input coordinates x into weighted Random Fourier Features.""" if B is None or b is None: B = np.random.randn(numbands, 3) b = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, numbands) z = np.dot(B, x) + b freqs = np.linalg.norm(B, axis=1) weights = alpha freqs weightedcos = np.cos(z) weights weightedsin = np.sin(z) weights weightedfeatures = np.concatenate([weightedcos, weightedsin]) return np.concatenate([weightedfeatures, x]), B, b def mlpforward(x, layerparams, activationfn): """Standard fully connected forward pass through N hidden layers.""" for W, b in layerparams: x = activationfn(np.dot(x, W.T) + b) return x def predict(x, backboneparams, headparams, activationfn): """Full DMF Network prediction following the 6-step algorithm.""" # 1-3. Input Transformation, Weighting, Concatenation inputvec,, = randomfourierfeatures(x) # 4. Shared Encoding (6 hidden layers) sharedfeat = mlpforward(inputvec, backboneparams, activationfn) # 5. Head Decoding (2 hidden layers each) Mplus = mlpforward(sharedfeat, headparams[0], activationfn) Mminus = mlpforward(sharedfeat, headparams[1], activationfn) Phi = mlpforward(sharedfeat, headparams[2], activationfn) GradPhi = mlpforward(sharedfeat, headparams[3], activationfn) # 6. Medial Field Combination M = Mplus if Phi > 0 else Mminus return M, Phi, GradPhi Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The medial field has a discontinuity at the surface \partial O. Ordinary MLPs are Lipschitz and cannot approximate this discontinuity directly. The solution is to predict M^+ and M^- separately for the outside and inside, then combine them based on the sign of \Phi(x). Fourier Feature Weighting: The weighting constant \alpha must be small (10^{-3}) to preserve the network's bias towards spherical topology. Time and Memory Complexity: Inference complexity is dominated by the shared backbone MLP and the four heads. The backbone contains 6 hidden layers, and each head contains 2 hidden layers with 64 neurons. The input dimension is 3 + 2 	imes 64 = 131. The output dimension is 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6. The backbone width is Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides medial field information for ambient occlusion approximation (MFAO) and local shape thickness analysis. Effectively handles the discontinuity of the medial field at the surface \partial O. Limitations: Requires predicting additional outputs (M^+, M^-) which increases model size and training complexity compared to standard DeepSDF. When to Use: Use when medial field information is required for applications like ambient occlusion or shape analysis. Not required if only the SDF is needed. The Deep Medial Field Network was introduced by Daniel Rebain, Ke Li, Vincent Sitzmann, Soroosh Yazdani, Kwang Moo Yi, and Andrea Tagliasacchi in the paper "Deep Medial Fields". It builds upon the DeepSDF architecture [Gropp et al. 2020] and Random Fourier Features [Tancik et al. 2020]. The method was developed to provide an efficient alternative for approximating ambient occlusion using the medial field. name: LocalMap SDF Network Inference
head: LocalMap Decoder, LocalMap SDF Network
body: The LocalMap SDF Network Inference method is a neural network architecture that encodes 3D spatial coordinates into feature vectors and decodes them into Signed Distance Field (SDF) values and inverse sigma (isigma) values for density estimation. It is a specific implementation within the LocalMap framework, distinguishing itself from general-purpose implicit surface networks by its dual-output design for simultaneous geometry and density prediction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position vector \mathbf{xyz} = (x, y, z). Output: A tensor containing two scalar values: the SDF value and the scaled inverse sigma value. Data Structures: The decoder output is a tensor with shape (N, 2) for N points, where the last dimension is split into two channels. Channel 0: SDF value. Channel 1: Raw inverse sigma value (before activation). Parameters: kdecoderimplementation: Integer flag (0 or 1) selecting the decoder backend. 0: Custom PyTorch Linear stack. 1: TCNN FullyFusedMLP. kbceisigma: Scaling factor applied to the softplus output of the inverse sigma. encodingtype: Enum or string specifying the positional encoding scheme used by the encoding map. normalized: Boolean flag indicating if input coordinates are normalized before encoding. Steps: 1. Position Encoding: Encode the input position \mathbf{xyz} using the encoding map. \mathbf{xyz\feat} = \text{encoding}(\mathbf{xyz}, \text{encoding\type}, \text{normalized}). 2. Feature Decoding: Pass the encoded features \mathbf{xyz\feat} through the selected decoder. If kdecoderimplementation == 0: \mathbf{output} = \text{decoder}(\mathbf{xyz\feat}). If kdecoderimplementation == 1: \mathbf{output} = \text{p\decoder\tcnn}(\mathbf{xyz\feat}). 3. Split Output: Split the decoder output tensor along the last dimension into two parts: SDF and raw isigma. [\text{sdf}, \text{raw\isigma}] = \text{split}(\mathbf{output}, \{1, 1\}, \text{dim}=-1). 4. Inverse Sigma Activation: Apply the softplus function to the raw isigma and scale it. \text{isigma} = 1 + \text{softplus}(\text{raw\isigma}, \beta=100) \times \text{k\bce\isigma}. The final output tensor is [\text{sdf}, \text{isigma}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def localmapsdfinference(xyz, encodingmap, decoder, decodertcnn, kdecoderimplementation, kbceisigma, encodingtype, normalized): """ Perform SDF and isigma inference for a batch of 3D points. Args: xyz: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates. encodingmap: Object with method 'encoding(xyz, encodingtype, normalized)'. decoder: PyTorch module for custom Linear stack (used if kdecoderimplementation == 0). decodertcnn: TCNN FullyFusedMLP module (used if kdecoderimplementation == 1). kdecoderimplementation: Integer (0 or 1) selecting the decoder backend. kbceisigma: Float scaling factor for inverse sigma. encodingtype: String or enum for encoding scheme. normalized: Boolean for coordinate normalization. Returns: sdf: Tensor of shape (N, 1) with SDF values. isigma: Tensor of shape (N, 1) with scaled inverse sigma values. """ # Step 1: Encode input position xyzfeat = encodingmap.encoding(xyz, encodingtype, normalized) # Step 2: Pass through decoder if kdecoderimplementation == 0: output = decoder(xyzfeat) elif kdecoderimplementation == 1: output = decodertcnn(xyzfeat) else: raise ValueError("kdecoderimplementation must be 0 or 1") # Step 3: Split output into SDF and raw isigma sdf, rawisigma = torch.split(output, 1, dim=-1) # Step 4: Apply softplus and scaling to isigma isigma = 1.0 + F.softplus(rawisigma, beta=100) kbceisigma return sdf, isigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Decoder Selection: Ensure kdecoderimplementation matches the available backend. Softplus Stability: The beta parameter in softplus is fixed at 100. Input Normalization: The normalized flag must be consistent with how the encoding map was configured. Not given in the sources. The LocalMap SDF Network Inference method is part of the GS-SDF project by hku-mars. It leverages the LocalMap framework for efficient feature encoding and decoding. hku-mars/GS-SDF, https://github.com/hku-mars/GS-SDF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Optimization via Finite Differences
head: Finite Difference SDF Optimization, Mesh-Difference SDF Training
body: This method optimizes the values of a Signed Distance Field (SDF) and associated learnable weights to minimize the geometric difference between an extracted mesh and a target reference mesh. It differs from standard SDF evaluation by treating SDF values as learnable parameters updated via gradient descent, using finite difference gradients for the SDF rather than analytical derivatives. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation. Inputs: Target mesh geometry (reference). Initial SDF grid values. Initial learnable weights: \beta (size N \times 12), \alpha (size N \times 8), \gamma (size N), where N is the number of cubes. Outputs: Optimized SDF values. Optimized weights \beta, \alpha, \gamma. Data Structures: sdf: Vector of SDF values, size N{sdf}. beta: Matrix, size N \times 12, RowMajor. alpha: Matrix, size N \times 8, RowMajor. gamma: Vector, size N. Parameters: eps: Finite difference step size, 10^{-4}. clamprange: SDF value bounds, [-1.0, 1.0]. maxupdates: Number of SDF values to update per iteration, \min(100, N{sdf}). Steps: 1. Initialization: Set \beta, \alpha, \gamma to zero. Add noise: \beta{i,j} \leftarrow \beta{i,j} + \text{noise}() \times 0.1, \alpha{i,j} \leftarrow \alpha{i,j} + \text{noise}() \times 0.1, \gammai \leftarrow \gammai + \text{noise}() \times 0.1 for all i, j. 2. Gradient Computation: Loop i from 0 to maxupdates - 1: a. Store sdf[i] as sdforig. b. Perturb: sdf[i] += eps. c. Extract mesh meshplus using current SDF and weights. d. Compute loss lossplus between meshplus and target. e. Perturb: sdf[i] -= 2 eps (resulting in sdforig - eps). f. Extract mesh meshminus. g. Compute loss lossminus. h. Reset: sdf[i] += eps (restoring sdforig). i. Compute gradient: sdfgrad[i] = (lossplus - lossminus) / (2 eps). 3. Optimization Step: Apply gradient step: optimizer.step(sdf, sdfgrad). 4. Clamping: Clamp all SDF values to [-1.0, 1.0]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def optimizesdffinitedifference(sdf, beta, alpha, gamma, targetmesh, eps=1e-4, clampmin=-1.0, clampmax=1.0, maxupdates=100, numiterations=1000, learningrate=1e-3): """ Optimizes SDF values and weights using finite difference gradients. """ Nsdf = len(sdf) # Initialization beta[:] = 0.0 alpha[:] = 0.0 gamma[:] = 0.0 # Add noise beta += np.random.randn(beta.shape) 0.1 alpha += np.random.randn(alpha.shape) 0.1 gamma += np.random.randn(gamma.shape) 0.1 for iteration in range(numiterations): sdfgrad = np.zeroslike(sdf) limit = min(maxupdates, Nsdf) # Loop i from 0 to min(100, sdf.size())-1 for i in range(limit): sdforig = sdf[i] # Perturb sdf[i] += eps sdf[i] = sdforig + eps # Extract meshplus using current SDF and weights meshplus = None # Implementation not specified in sources lossplus = 0.0 # Compute loss between meshplus and target # Perturb sdf[i] -= 2eps sdf[i] = sdforig - eps meshminus = None # Extract meshminus lossminus = 0.0 # Compute lossminus # Reset sdf[i] += eps sdf[i] = sdforig # Compute gradient sdfgrad[i] = (lossplus - lossminus) / (2 eps) # Apply gradient step sdf -= learningrate sdfgrad # Clamp SDF values to [-1.0, 1.0] np.clip(sdf, clampmin, clampmax, out=sdf) return sdf, beta, alpha, gamma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The finite difference step eps must be small enough to approximate the derivative but large enough to avoid numerical noise in mesh extraction and loss computation. Boundaries: SDF values are clamped to [-1.0, 1.0], which may affect gradients near the boundaries. Degenerate Input: If the target mesh is empty or invalid, the loss computation may fail. Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization reconstructs unknown meshes by optimizing a randomly initialized Signed Distance Field (SDF) to minimize geometric differences against a reference mesh using multiview mask and depth losses. It builds on SDF Optimization via Finite Differences by treating the SDF values as learnable parameters updated via gradient descent rather than fixed analytical functions. Time Complexity: Each gradient computation for one SDF value requires two mesh extractions and two loss computations. With maxupdates = 100, this is O(100 \cdot (M{extract} + L{compute})) per iteration, where M{extract} is mesh extraction cost and L{compute} is loss computation cost. Memory Complexity: Stores SDF, beta, alpha, gamma, and temporary meshes for perturbation. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Updating only 100 SDF values per iteration allows for faster convergence or larger grids, but may slow down global convergence. Strengths: Does not require analytical gradients for the SDF or mesh extraction, making it applicable to complex implicit surface definitions. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to repeated mesh extractions. Gradient noise may affect stability. When to use: When analytical gradients are unavailable or too complex to derive, and the SDF representation is flexible enough to be optimized directly. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the SDF is defined by simple primitives with known analytical gradients. This method is associated with the FlexiCubes framework, which uses a learnable SDF representation for mesh optimization. The approach of optimizing SDF values directly via finite differences is a technique used in neural implicit surface reconstruction and mesh optimization pipelines. ddiakopoulos/flexicubescpp, https://github.com/ddiakopoulos/flexicubescpp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization
head: nvdiffrec-style optimization
body: Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization reconstructs unknown 3D geometry by optimizing a parameterized representation (typically a Signed Distance Field or SDF) to minimize geometric discrepancies between rendered multi-view images and a reference mesh. It sets itself apart from its sibling SDF Optimization via Finite Differences by operating directly on the mesh topology or SDF values to minimize multiview mask and depth losses, often employing specific regularizers for fabricability or stability. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A randomly initialized SDF field (or mesh parameters), a set of reference meshes with known camera poses, and multi-view images or masks. Outputs: An optimized SDF field or deformed mesh geometry that minimizes the difference between rendered views and the reference. Data Structures: SDF Field: A grid or set of vertices where each vertex vi holds an SDF value Si \in \mathbb{R} and optionally a deformation vector \Delta vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Mesh Representation: In methods like FlexiCubes, the mesh is defined by vertices, edges, and cubes, with learnable weights (alpha, beta, gamma) controlling the interpolation and splitting of quadrilaterals into triangles. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the SDF field randomly or with a coarse approximation. If using sphere fitting, determine initial sphere positions and radii by minimizing the volume outside the mesh while encouraging surface coverage. 2. Rendering: Render the current geometry (SDF or mesh) from multiple camera viewpoints to generate predicted masks M' and depth maps. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between the rendered output and the ground truth reference: Mask Loss: L1 norm between ground truth mask M and rendered mask M': L{mask} = \frac{|M - M'|}{2} Depth Loss: Difference between rendered depth and reference depth. Regularization: Add developability regularizer L{dev} to encourage fabricability from panels. Add Implicit Geometric Regularization (IGR) as an eikonal loss to constrain the SDF gradient magnitude to 1: L{eikonal} = E{v0 \in V0} (||\nabla f\theta (v0)||^2 - 1)^2 4. Optimization: Update the SDF values, deformation parameters, or sphere parameters using gradient descent to minimize the total loss. 5. Regularization Adjustment: Incrementally increase regularization weights if artifacts appear, starting with low weights to avoid hindering convergence. Parameters: Regularization Weights: Initially low; increased if artifacts appear. L1 Regularizer on Flexible Weights: Generally low impact for single shapes but stabilizes generative pipelines. Progressive Position Encoding: Frequency gradually increased after training reaches a certain stage to alleviate high-frequency noise while retaining details. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Noise: Direct optimization of SDF values can introduce noise; mitigated by progressive position encoding. Convergence Hindrance: High regularization weights early in training can prevent convergence. This method reconstructs unknown mesh geometry by optimizing vertex positions to minimize geometric differences between rendered multi-view images and a reference mesh. It sets itself apart from its sibling Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization by replacing the standard Laplacian postfilter with a mesh cross-bilateral filter, which preserves sharp edges and silhouettes better than Laplacian smoothing, leading to faster convergence on thin structures. Approximates non-deformed initial mesh geometry with a set of spheres to compute visibility. The mesh is deformed by translating and rotating these spheres, allowing inverse problems to supervise sphere parameters and update geometry. Initial sphere positions and radii are determined by minimizing the total volume occupied by the sphere set outside the mesh along with a term encouraging coverage of the mesh surface, optimized via gradient descent. Sphere centers are connected as an embedded graph to drive mesh deformation, with each sphere connected to its K-nearest vertices on the template. Mesh deformation is parameterized by the rotation and translation of each sphere, optimized using rendering loss during inverse problems. Defines object geometry as a Signed Distance Field (SDF) on a tetrahedral mesh T. Each vertex vi has an SDF value Si \in \mathbb{R} and a deformation value \Delta vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. The mesh is updated as vi' = vi + \Delta vi. Supervised by rendered masks derived from projecting the object according to camera poses, using L1 loss for training. Employs progressive position encoding to alleviate high-frequency noise while retaining details, gradually increasing encoding frequency after training reaches a certain stage. Adds Implicit Geometric Regularization (IGR) as an eikonal loss to constrain the gradient magnitude of the SDF field f\theta to be close to 1. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization steps and the complexity of the rendering pipeline (e.g., ray marching for SDFs or rasterization for meshes). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the SDF grid or mesh vertex count. Strengths: Can reconstruct complex geometries from multi-view data; differentiable nature allows end-to-end optimization with rendering losses. Limitations: Sensitive to initialization; prone to high-frequency noise without regularization; computational cost of multi-view rendering. When to Use: When reconstructing geometry from multi-view images or masks where explicit mesh data is unavailable or incomplete. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene is simple enough for analytical solutions. Originated from workflows for reconstructing unknown meshes by optimizing SDFs to minimize geometric differences against reference meshes. Developed in the context of differentiable rendering and inverse graphics, allowing for the optimization of 3D structures from 2D observations. Used in applications such as 3D reconstruction, shape editing, and generative modeling.
