name: Inverse Mesh Recovery with Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering
head: Edge-aware cross-bilateral filter for mesh recovery, Spatiotemporal optimizer for inverse recovery
body: This method reconstructs unknown mesh geometry by optimizing vertex positions to minimize geometric differences between rendered multi-view images and a reference mesh. It sets itself apart from its sibling Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization by replacing the standard Laplacian postfilter with a mesh cross-bilateral filter, which preserves sharp edges and silhouettes better than Laplacian smoothing, leading to faster convergence on thin structures. Inputs: A reference mesh (e.g., a cube or dragon model). A set of N camera views (10 views for the cube, 25 views for the dragon). Initial mesh geometry (sphere with ~10k vertices). Outputs: Optimized mesh vertex positions. Data Structures: Mesh: Defined by vertices V and connectivity. Intermediate Variables: mt (current parameter state), vt (intermediate variable for filtering). Gradients: \nabla L computed via differentiable rendering. Parameters: Learning rate \alpha: 1 \cdot 10^{-2} for cube, 3 \cdot 10^{-2} for dragon. Adam momentum \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99. Regularization weight \lambda = 19. Cross-bilateral filter range parameter \sigma\phi = 0.4. Cross-bilateral filter spatial distance parameter \sigmad = 0.5. Learning rate scheduler: Exponential reduction to factor 0.6 at the end of optimization. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the mesh as a sphere with approximately 10,000 vertices. 2. Iteration Loop: For each optimization iteration t: a. Upsampling (Conditional): If optimizing the dragon model, upsample the mesh at iterations 10, 30, and 60 by remeshing to reduce the average edge length by a factor of 2. The cube does not require remeshing. b. Rendering: Render all N views. Use 16 samples per pixel for forward rendering and 1 sample per pixel for gradient computation. c. Loss Computation: Compute the loss L using the L1 norm between the rendered images and the reference images. d. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient \nabla L with respect to vertex positions. e. Optimizer Step: Update parameters using the UniformAdam optimizer with the infinity norm, using \alpha, \beta1, and \beta2. f. Filtering: Apply the spatiotemporal bilateral filtering to the gradients/parameters as described below. 3. Termination: Stop when the learning rate scheduler completes or convergence criteria are met. Filtering Procedure (Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering): The method follows the Large Steps framework (Algorithm 3) but replaces the postfilter on mt with a mesh cross-bilateral filter. The optimal configuration identified is a Laplacian prefilter and a bilateral postfilter on mt, while keeping the UniformAdam infinity norm. 1. Prefiltering (Laplacian): Apply a Laplacian prefilter to the gradient or intermediate state to provide initial smoothing. This step is crucial as a bilateral prefilter alone is not sufficient to diffuse silhouette gradients. 2. Postfiltering (Cross-Bilateral): Apply the mesh cross-bilateral filter to mt. This filter uses vertex normals to guide smoothing, preserving sharp edges and silhouettes. The filter weights are determined by the photometric difference (range parameter \sigma\phi = 0.4) and the spatial distance (distance parameter \sigmad = 0.5). Unlike Laplacian smoothing, which dilutes silhouette gradients, this edge-aware filter retains values on silhouettes, interpolating gradients in the interior using values on the silhouettes. Limitations: Assumes spatial coherence of parameters; hyperparameter tuning is tedious; bilateral filtering on vt can cause cracks. name: Bilateral gradient filtering for meshes
head: Generalized bilateral filter for meshes
body: This method replaces the standard Laplacian postfilter in inverse mesh recovery with a cross-bilateral filter that preserves sharp edges and silhouettes. It sets itself apart from its sibling Inverse Mesh Recovery with Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering by using vertex normals to guide the smoothing, preventing the over-smoothing of thin structures and leading to faster convergence. Inputs: h: The vector of values to be filtered (e.g., vertex position updates or displacements). \hat{n}: The vector of vertex normals for the mesh. L: The cotangent Laplacian matrix of the mesh. \lambda: The regularization parameter for the Laplacian term. \sigmad: The data term bandwidth parameter. \sigma\phi: The partition of unity bandwidth parameter. N: The number of sampling directions (typically 32). Outputs: \tilde{h}: The filtered vector. Data Structures: W(\hat{n}, si): A diagonal matrix where the j-th diagonal element is Wj = \exp(\hat{n}j \cdot si / \sigmad). \Phi(\hat{n}, si): A diagonal matrix where the j-th diagonal element is \Phij = \exp(\hat{n}j \cdot si / \sigma\phi). M: A matrix of size V \times 2N, where V is the number of vertices. The columns are formed by concatenating the vectors W(\hat{n}, si)h and W(\hat{n}, si)\mathbf{1} for all i=1 \dots N. Steps: 1. Sample N=32 directions si uniformly on the unit sphere S^2 using the Sobol sequence [Sobol’ 1967]. 2. For each direction si, compute the diagonal data matrix Wi = W(\hat{n}, si) and the diagonal partition of unity matrix \Phii = \Phi(\hat{n}, si). 3. Construct the matrix M by concatenating the vectors Wi h and Wi \mathbf{1} as columns: M = \left[ \begin{array}{c|c} W1 h & W1 \mathbf{1} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ WN h & WN \mathbf{1} \end{array} \right] 4. Solve the linear system (I + \lambda L) X = M for X using a single matrix solve (e.g., Cholesky decomposition). Let X = [Xh | X\phi], where Xh contains the solutions for the Wi h columns and X\phi contains the solutions for the Wi \mathbf{1} columns. 5. Compute the filtered vector \tilde{h} using component-wise operations: \tilde{h} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N \Phii X{h,i}}{\sum{i=1}^N \Phii X{\phi,i}} where X{h,i} is the i-th column of Xh and X{\phi,i} is the i-th column of X\phi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bilateralgradientfiltermesh(h, nhat, L, lambdareg, sigmad, sigmaphi, N=32): """ Filter vector h using bilateral gradient filtering for meshes. Args: h: (V,) array, values to filter. nhat: (V, 3) array, vertex normals. L: (V, V) sparse matrix, cotangent Laplacian. lambdareg: float, regularization parameter. sigmad: float, data term bandwidth. sigmaphi: float, partition of unity bandwidth. N: int, number of sampling directions. Returns: htilde: (V,) array, filtered values. """ import numpy as np from scipy.sparse import eye, diags from scipy.sparse.linalg import splu # 1. Sample directions using Sobol sequence # Note: In practice, use a Sobol sequence generator. # Here we assume a function sobolsample(N) returns (N, 3) unit vectors. s = sobolsample(N) # Shape: (N, 3) V = h.shape[0] ones = np.ones(V) # Precompute dot products: (V, N) # nhat is (V, 3), s is (N, 3). We need (V, N) where entry (v, i) is nhat[v]. s[i] dotproducts = np.dot(nhat, s.T) # Shape: (V, N) # 2. Compute diagonal weights # Wi diagonal elements: exp(nhat. si / sigmad) # Phii diagonal elements: exp(nhat. si / sigmaphi) Wweights = np.exp(dotproducts / sigmad) # Shape: (V, N) Phiweights = np.exp(dotproducts / sigmaphi) # Shape: (V, N) # 3. Construct matrix M # M columns: [W1 h,..., WN h, W1 1,..., WN 1] # Wi h is element-wise multiplication of Wweights[:, i] and h # Wi 1 is element-wise multiplication of Wweights[:, i] and ones # Compute Wi h for all i # Wweights is (V, N), h is (V,) -> broadcast to (V, N) Wh = Wweights h[:, np.newaxis] # Shape: (V, N) # Compute Wi 1 for all i W1 = Wweights ones[:, np.newaxis] # Shape: (V, N) # Concatenate horizontally M = np.hstack([Wh, W1]) # Shape: (V, 2N) # 4. Solve (I + lambda L) X = M # I + lambda L I = eye(V, format='csr') A = I + lambdareg L # Solve for X # Using sparse LU or Cholesky if symmetric positive definite # Assuming L is symmetric positive semi-definite, A is SPD try: cholesky = splu(A.tocsc()) # Or use a Cholesky solver if available X = cholesky.solve(M) except: # Fallback to general sparse solver if Cholesky fails from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve X = spsolve(A, M) # X is (V, 2N) # Split X into Xh and Xphi Xh = X[:,:N] # Shape: (V, N) Xphi = X[:, N:] # Shape: (V, N) # 5. Compute htilde # Numerator: sumi Phii (Wi h filtered) = sumi Phiweights[:, i] Xh[:, i] # Denominator: sumi Phii (Wi 1 filtered) = sumi Phiweights[:, i] Xphi[:, i] # Element-wise multiplication and sum over axis 1 (the N dimension) numerator = np.sum(Phiweights Xh, axis=1) # Shape: (V,) denominator = np.sum(Phiweights Xphi, axis=1) # Shape: (V,) # Avoid division by zero denominator = np.maximum(denominator, 1e-8) htilde = numerator / denominator return htilde Parameters: N=32: Number of sampling directions. \sigmad, \sigma\phi: Bandwidth parameters for the von Mises-Fisher kernel. Not given in the sources. \lambda: Regularization parameter for the Laplacian. Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: The Laplacian matrix L must be positive semi-definite, and I + \lambda L must be positive definite for the Cholesky solver to work. Division by zero in the denominator should be guarded against. The Sobol sequence sampling ensures uniform coverage of the sphere, which is critical for the filter's isotropy. This method optimizes high-frequency surface details of a mesh by backpropagating image-space gradients into spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients within a TetWeave representation. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the single matrix solve (I + \lambda L)^{-1} M, which is O(V) for sparse matrices if using iterative solvers or O(V^{1.5}) to O(V^2) for direct solvers depending on the fill-in. The overhead over standard Laplacian smoothing is minor (<10%). Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing the mesh and O(V \cdot N) for the intermediate matrices M and X. Performance: Implemented on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU. Strengths: Preserves sharp edges and silhouettes better than Laplacian smoothing, leading to faster convergence on thin structures. Limitations: More complex to implement than Laplacian smoothing. Requires vertex normals. This method is based on the generalized bilateral filter from Solomon et al. [2014] and is used in the context of inverse mesh recovery. It was introduced to improve the quality of reconstructed meshes by preserving geometric details that are lost with standard smoothing techniques. name: Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization via Spherical Harmonics
head: Geometric texture generation, Paparazzi-style optimization
body: This method optimizes high-frequency surface details of a mesh by backpropagating image-space gradients into spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients within a TetWeave representation. It solves the problem of generating geometric textures or refining mesh details without altering the coarse topology or significantly deviating from a reference shape. Unlike direct vertex displacement, it adjusts normals to tilt surface details, making it suitable for applications like photogrammetry refinement or artistic texture generation. Inputs: A reference mesh or coarse shape M{ref}. A TetWeave representation initialized with a point cloud, SDF values, and SH coefficients. An image filter F (e.g., Guided filter, L0-Smoothing, or K-means quantization). A loss function L combining mask, depth, and normal map differences against a target. Outputs: An optimized TetWeave representation with updated SH coefficients. Data Structures: TetWeave Parameters: Point positions \mathbf{p}i (fixed after initial fit). SDF values si (fixed after initial fit). Spherical Harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{l,m} for each point or local region. SH Degree: Degree L=2 for initial fitting. Degree L=1 for refinement stages. Steps: 1. Initialization: Fit the TetWeave representation to the reference shape M{ref} using SH of degree 2. Optimize point positions and SDF values to minimize reconstruction error. 2. Freeze Geometry: Once the fit is complete, fix the point positions \mathbf{p}i and SDF values si. Only SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{l,m} remain trainable. 3. Reference Update: Periodically update the reference shape with the current mesh during optimization to avoid being constrained too much by the initial reference. 4. Rendering: Render the normal map \mathbf{N}{render} of the current mesh \tilde{M} from a randomly sampled camera view. 5. Filtering: Apply the chosen image filter F to the rendered normal map to obtain \mathbf{N}{filtered} = F(\mathbf{N}{render}). 6. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient as the difference between the filtered and rendered normal maps: \nabla = \mathbf{N}{filtered} - \mathbf{N}{render}. 7. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the gradient through the differentiable renderer and TetWeave representation to update only the SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{l,m}. 8. Loss Calculation: Compute a loss L on the mask, depth map, and normal map compared to the reference mesh to ensure the generated shape remains close to the reference and does not degenerate. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 4-8 until convergence or a specified number of iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegeometrictexture(tetweavemodel, referencemesh, imagefilter, numiterations): # Step 1: Initial fit with degree 2 SH tetweavemodel.fittoreference(referencemesh, shdegree=2) # Step 2: Fix point positions and SDF values tetweavemodel.freezegeometry() # Step 3: Set SH degree to 1 for refinement tetweavemodel.setshdegree(1) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Step 3: Periodically update reference if iteration % updatefrequency == 0: referencemesh = tetweavemodel.getcurrentmesh() # Step 4: Render normal map from random camera camera = samplerandomcamera() normalmap = tetweavemodel.rendernormalmap(camera) # Step 5: Apply image filter filterednormalmap = imagefilter(normalmap) # Step 6: Compute gradient gradient = filterednormalmap - normalmap # Step 7: Backpropagate to update SH coefficients loss = computeloss(normalmap, gradient, referencemesh) loss.backward() tetweavemodel.optimizer.step() tetweavemodel.optimizer.zerograd() return tetweavemodel Parameters: SH Degree: 2 for initial fitting, 1 for refinement. Image Filters: Guided filter [He et al. 2013], L0-Smoothing [Xu et al. 2011], or K-means image quantization [MacQueen 1967]. Pitfalls: Adjusting SH coefficients primarily tilts normals to affect high-frequency details without deviating significantly from the reference shape. Ensure the reference shape is updated periodically to avoid stagnation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations, camera samples, and filter complexity. Differentiable rendering and backpropagation are computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Low, as point positions and SDF values are fixed after initialization. Only SH coefficients are stored and updated. Strengths: Efficiently generates high-frequency geometric textures without altering coarse geometry. Supports user-defined energies (e.g., CLIP loss, developability energy) via automatic differentiation. Limitations: May not recover large-scale geometric changes. Performance depends on the quality of the initial fit and the choice of image filter. When to Use: Geometric texture generation, photogrammetry refinement, artistic mesh editing. When Not to Use: When significant topological or large-scale geometric changes are required. This method is part of the TetWeave pipeline, which uses on-the-fly Delaunay tetrahedral grids for gradient-based mesh optimization. It builds on the Paparazzi method for geometric texture generation [Liu et al. 2018] and integrates with differentiable rendering frameworks like NVDiffRec [Munkberg et al. 2022] for photogrammetry. The approach leverages spherical harmonics to represent high-frequency details, allowing for efficient optimization via backpropagation. name: Mandelbulb SDF Evaluation
head: Fractal SDF, Mandelbulb, Mandelbulb Distance Estimator, Mandelbulb Fractal SDF, Mandelbulb distance function, sdMandelbulb
body: The Mandelbulb SDF Evaluation computes the signed distance from a 3D point to the boundary of the Mandelbulb fractal using an iterative derivative-based estimation. It differs from standard primitives by using polar coordinate transformations and derivative tracking to approximate the distance to a non-algebraic surface. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation. The method uses the distance estimation technique for iterated function systems, where the distance is approximated by the radius of the current point scaled by the logarithm of its magnitude and divided by the accumulated derivative of the iteration function. Input: point (vec3): The 3D query point in world space. center (vec3): The center of the Mandelbulb. scale (float): Global scaling factor applied to the input point offset and the final returned distance. power (float): Exponent for the fractal mapping that controls the geometric complexity and shape of the Mandelbulb. maxiterations (int): Maximum number of fractal iterations performed per point evaluation. bailout (float): Maximum radius threshold to break iteration early and prevent numerical overflow. Output: distance (float): The estimated signed distance from point to the Mandelbulb surface. No persistent data structures are required. Temporary variables include: z (vec3): Current position in the transformed space. dr (float): Accumulated derivative of the iteration function with respect to the initial position. r (float): Magnitude (radius) of z. theta, phi (float): Spherical angles. 1. Initialization: Translate and scale the input point: z = \frac{\text{point} - \text{center}}{\text{scale}}. Initialize derivative: dr = 1.0. Initialize radius: r = 0.0. 2. Iteration Loop: For i from 0 to maxiterations - 1: Calculate current radius: r = \|z\|. Bailout Check: If r > \text{bailout}, break the loop. Convert to spherical coordinates: \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{zz}{r}\right). \phi = \operatorname{atan2}(zy, zx). Update derivative: dr = r^{\text{power} - 1} \cdot \text{power} \cdot dr + 1.0. Calculate radial power: zr = r^{\text{power}}. Scale angles: \theta \leftarrow \theta \cdot \text{power}. \phi \leftarrow \phi \cdot \text{power}. Transform back to Cartesian coordinates: z \leftarrow zr \cdot (\sin\theta\cos\phi, \sin\theta\sin\phi, \cos\theta) + \frac{\text{point} - \text{center}}{\text{scale}}. 3. Distance Calculation: Calculate distance: d = \frac{0.5 \cdot \ln(r) \cdot r}{dr}. Scale the result: d = d \cdot \text{scale}. Return d. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdMandelbulb(point: vec3, center: vec3, scale: float, power: float, maxiterations: int, bailout: float) -> float: # 1. Initialize z = (point - center) / scale dr = 1.0 r = 0.0 # 2. Iterate for i in range(maxiterations): r = length(z) if r > bailout: break # Guard against division by zero in acos if r < 1e-6: break # Spherical coordinates theta = acos(z.z / r) phi = atan2(z.y, z.x) # Update derivative dr = pow(r, power - 1.0) power dr + 1.0 # Radial power zr = pow(r, power) # Scale angles theta = theta power phi = phi power # Transform back to Cartesian and add constant offset z.x = zr sin(theta) cos(phi) z.y = zr sin(theta) sin(phi) z.z = zr cos(theta) z = z + (point - center) / scale # 3. Distance Estimator if r < 1e-6: return 0.0 distance = 0.5 log(r) r / dr distance = distance scale return distance power: 8.0 is the classic Mandelbulb exponent. maxiterations: Defined as an integer. One implementation fixes it at 6. Not given in the sources. bailout: 2.0 is standard for escape radius. scale: Depends on the desired size of the object in the scene. Division by Zero: If r=0 (the point is exactly at the origin of the iteration space), \arccos(zz/r) is undefined. Guard against r < \epsilon. Precision: Floating point precision issues can cause jitter in the distance estimate for points very close to the surface, especially with high power values. Inside the Fractal: The distance estimator d = \frac{0.5 \ln(r) r}{dr} is valid for points outside the fractal (where r \to \infty). For points inside, the distance is not well-defined by this formula, and ray marching may fail or require a different estimator. Time Complexity: O(I), where I is the number of iterations. Each iteration involves trigonometric functions and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary memory is required. Performance: The Mandelbulb SDF is computationally expensive per evaluation due to the trigonometric functions (sin, cos, atan2, acos) and power calculations. It is significantly slower than primitive SDFs but allows for infinitely detailed geometry. Strengths: Generates complex, organic-looking fractal geometry with a single function. No mesh storage required. Limitations: High computational cost. The distance estimate is an approximation and may not be perfectly tight, potentially leading to slightly larger step sizes in ray marching or visual artifacts if the derivative is inaccurate. name: SDF and Material Optimization Pipeline
head: SDF training loop, relaxed boundary optimization
body: This method optimizes a voxelized signed distance field (SDF) and associated material volumes (albedo, roughness, metallic) by minimizing the L1 difference between rendered images and reference images. It differs from pure geometry optimization by jointly updating material grids, and from neural SDF methods by using explicit grid-based representations with periodic upsampling. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation for the forward rendering pass. Inputs: Scene definition containing geometry and initial material volumes. Reference images rendered from multiple sensor viewpoints. Configuration parameters: sdfres, sphereradius, lr, batchsize, spp, sppgrad, laplacianweight, lrdecay, upsample epochs, lrdownsample epochs, checkpoint interval. Outputs: Optimized SDF grid stored as.npy. Optimized material grids (albedo, roughness, metallic) stored as.npy and.vol. Loss curves and intermediate optimization videos. Data Structures: SDF Grid: 3D tensor of shape (res, res, res) representing the signed distance field. Initialized as a sphere. Material Grids: 3D tensors for basecolor (albedo), roughness, and metallic. Resampled to match sdfres. Optimizer State: Adam optimizer state for the SDF grid and material grids. Checkpoint Format: 1D array where the first element is the resolution res, followed by the flattened grid values grid.flatten(). Parameters: lr: Base learning rate for Adam. lralbedoscale, lrroughnessscale, lrmetallicscale: Multipliers for material learning rates relative to lr. laplacianweight: Weight for the Laplacian regularization term. lrdecay: Factor by which lr is divided during upsample/lrdownsample epochs. batchsize: Number of sensor images processed per epoch. sdfres: Target resolution for SDF and material volumes. spp, sppgrad: Samples per pixel for rendering and gradient estimation. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the scene and sensors. Render reference images using a non-differentiable integrator. Initialize the SDF as a SphereSDF with resolution sdfres and radius sphereradius. Enable gradients on the SDF grid tensor. Traverse scene parameters to identify material volumes (basecolor, reflectance, roughness, metallic). If material volumes exist, upsample their resolution to sdfres using upsampleto and update the scene parameters. Configure the Adam optimizer with base learning rate lr. Add the SDF grid to the optimizer. If materials are enabled, add their grids to the optimizer and set per-parameter learning rates: lralbedo = lr lralbedoscale lrroughness = lr lrroughnessscale lrmetallic = lr lrmetallicscale. 2. Optimization Loop: Calculate steps per epoch: steps = ceil(numsensor / batchsize). For each epoch: Calculate number of indices: numindices = min(batchsize, numsensor). Generate indices: indices = [(j steps + epoch % steps) % numsensor for j in range(numindices)]. Shuffle indices. Initialize losssum = 0. For each index i in indices: Render image using the SDF integrator with spp, sppgrad, and seed epoch numsensor + i. Compute L1 loss: loss = l1loss(image, refimages[i]) / batchsize. Accumulate loss: losssum += loss. Backpropagate: dr.backward(loss). Compute regularization loss: regloss = laplacianweight laplacianloss(sdf.grid.tensor()). If epoch in upsample list: Decay learning rate: lr /= lrdecay. Update optimizer learning rates for grid and materials. Upsample SDF: upsamplesdf. Upsample materials: upsamplegrid (only if resolution != 256). If epoch in lrdownsample list: Decay learning rate: lr /= lrdecay. Update optimizer learning rates for grid and materials. If epoch % checkpoint == 0: Save checkpoint: flatten grid, prepend resolution, save as [resolution] + grid.tolist() to.npy. Repeat for materials if enabled. 3. Finalization: Save final SDF and material grids in [resolution] + grid.tolist() format to.npy. Write material grids to.vol files via mi.VolumeGrid. Generate optimization video (24 FPS) from optdir. Plot L1 loss over epochs and save as loss.pdf, loss.png, loss.npy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Augmented SDF
head: Conservative Proxy, Conservative SDF Construction from Bounding Volume, Conservative Signed Distance Field Construction, Discontinuous Proxy, Proxy Nodes, tilde f
body: Augmented SDF is a conservative variant of a signed distance field (SDF) that embeds a bounding volume to accelerate field queries outside the volume. It replaces the expensive original SDF evaluation with a simpler, inexpensive distance-to-boundary function for points outside the volume, creating a discontinuous but conservative signed distance field. Unlike its siblings, it prioritizes query speed over continuity, making it unsuitable for smooth Boolean operators but highly effective for sphere tracing and polygonization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The original signed distance field function f(\mathbf{p}), a bounding volume B (derived from Sphere Carving points), and a small positive constant \varepsilon. Output: The augmented field function fe(\mathbf{p}) (also denoted \tilde{f}). Data Structures: The bounding volume B is represented as a compact signed distance field d(\mathbf{p}, B). The sources specify two primary types of bounding volumes: 1. Convex Polyhedra: Constructed as the geometric convex hull H(P) of a point set P generated by Sphere Carving. The property H(P) \supseteq O (where O is the object) is guaranteed. 2. Ellipsoids/Simple Shapes: Defined as spheres, ellipsoids, or unions thereof. The memory footprint is compact, embedded directly in the function definition, avoiding external acceleration structures like grids or octrees. Parameters: \varepsilon: A small positive constant ensuring the 0-level set of fe matches f. Typical/Default value: 0.01. Formally, it represents a lower bound of the distance to the object surface \partial O. Steps: 1. Bounding Volume Construction: Generate the bounding volume B. If using convex hulls, compute H(P) from the point set P obtained via Sphere Carving. 2. Query Evaluation: For a query point \mathbf{p}: Compute the distance to the bounding volume: dB = d(\mathbf{p}, B). If dB > \varepsilon, return dB (or the proxy function value). Otherwise, return f(\mathbf{p}). Formulas: The conservative SDF definition is given by: \tilde{f}(\mathbf{p}) = \begin{cases} d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) > \varepsilon \\ f(\mathbf{p}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Alternatively, described as a proxy node P replacing f outside volume V with a simpler function b: fe(\mathbf{p}) = \begin{cases} f(\mathbf{p}) & \text{if } \mathbf{p} \in V \\ b(\mathbf{p}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where the exterior proxy function b is defined as: b = d(\mathbf{p}, \partial V) + \varepsilon Here, d(\mathbf{p}, \partial V) is the Euclidean distance to the volume boundary, and \varepsilon is formally defined as: \varepsilon = \min{\mathbf{p} \in V} f(\mathbf{p}) If the proxy is used to accelerate evaluation inside the object O (where b(\mathbf{p}) < 0), the interior proxy is defined as: b = -d(\mathbf{p}, \partial V) - \varepsilon Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def augmentedsdf(p, foriginal, boundingvolume, epsilon=0.01): """ Evaluate the augmented SDF at point p. Args: p: 3D point (vector). foriginal: Function evaluating the original SDF f(p). boundingvolume: Object representing the bounding volume B, providing a method distancetoboundary(p). epsilon: Small positive constant (default 0.01). Returns: The augmented SDF value fe(p). """ # Compute distance to the bounding volume boundary # Note: For convex hulls, this is the distance to the hull surface. # For simple shapes (sphere/ellipsoid), this is standard analytic distance. disttobound = boundingvolume.distancetoboundary(p) # Check if point is sufficiently outside the bounding volume if disttobound > epsilon: # Return the conservative proxy value # This is equivalent to disttobound + epsilon if using the # specific proxy definition b = d(p, dV) + epsilon return disttobound + epsilon else: # Point is inside or very close to the bounding volume boundary. # Fall back to the expensive original SDF evaluation. return foriginal(p) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The function fe is discontinuous at the boundary \partial V. It is piecewise Lipschitz but not globally continuous. Operator Compatibility: Because of the discontinuity, proxy nodes cannot be inserted below nodes requiring Lipschitz or continuous fields, such as smooth union operators. Doing so produces rendering artifacts. They are only safe with Boolean or warping operators. GPU Artifacts: In per-pixel cost comparison visualizations (e.g., sphere tracing), GPU memory access pattern inconsistencies can cause visible artifacts. Conservativeness: The method produces a conservative SDF. The 0-level set is preserved by \varepsilon, but the distance values outside B are approximations. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Compact. The bounding volume is embedded in the function definition, avoiding the overhead of external acceleration structures like grids or octrees. Time: Significantly faster for queries outside the bounding volume. The expensive f(\mathbf{p}) is skipped if d(\mathbf{p}, B) > \varepsilon. Measured Performance: In tests with ~1 million queries in a box surrounding the object, fe performs 3.3 to 4.9 times faster on average than the base field f. Using a convex bound in a Sphere Tracing scenario can provide up to a 50% speedup. In ray-object intersection performance tests using Sphere Tracing, proxy nodes achieved an average speedup of \times 7 compared to the reference object. On the Temple model, using capsule, half-sphere, and cylinder proxy volumes resulted in an average speedup factor of approximately \times 6.86. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fast queries for points outside the volume; compact memory footprint; compatible with Sphere Tracing and Segment Tracing. Limitations: Discontinuous at \partial V; cannot be used with smooth Boolean operators; only yields conservative distance fields. When to Use: Use when query speed is critical and the object is complex. Use when the construction tree involves only Boolean or warping operators above the proxy node. Use for sphere tracing or polygonization where points far from the surface are common. When Not to Use: Do not use if smooth blending or continuous field properties are required (e.g., smooth unions). Do not use if exact distance values outside the bounding volume are required. Origin: The Augmented SDF (specifically the conservative variant using bounding volumes from Sphere Carving) was introduced in the paper "Sphere Carving: Bounding Volumes for Signed Distance Fields". The concept of proxy nodes (P) as discontinuous simplification nodes was further detailed in "Accelerating Signed Distance Functions". History and Development: The method relies on "Sphere Carving," an algorithm that generates a set of empty spheres and a point set P whose convex hull bounds the object surface. The bounding volume is constructed from this point set without requiring supplementary queries of f. The approach was developed to address the computational cost of evaluating complex SDFs, particularly in real-time rendering contexts like sphere tracing. Usage: It is used to provide fast SDF queries for points outside the bounding volume while maintaining accuracy inside. It is applicable in sphere tracing, polygonization, and simulation. name: Sweep-based SDF Generation
head: Approximate Distance Field computation, Marching Parabolas, SDF Generation via Sweep Passes
body: Sweep-based SDF Generation is an algorithm to compute an approximate Signed Distance Field (SDF) texture efficiently without brute-force per-pixel distance calculation. It is intended for use in Sphere Tracing. The method sets itself apart from exact analytical SDF evaluations by using a multi-pass sweep approach that propagates distance information from rendered surface primitives through the volume, trading geometric precision for computational speed and texture-based storage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D or 3D texture containing initial distance values, typically resulting from an initial sweep along the X-axis or direct rasterization of surfaces. Output: A quantized Signed Distance Field texture where each texel stores an approximate distance value. Data Structures: Texture Storage: The SDF is stored in a quantized format to avoid floating-point storage requirements. Common formats include UNORMR8 (range 0–255) or SNORMR8 (range -127 to 127). Shared Memory: A local memory buffer (sharedMem) used within a compute shader workgroup to store a segment of the row being processed. Intermediate Textures: If the quantization factor requires high precision during intermediate calculations, intermediate result textures may require twice the bits of the input storage to prevent overflow during parabolic addition. Parameters: EDFRANGE: The maximum quantizable distance. For UNORMR8, this is 255; for SNORMR8, this is 127. QUANITZATIONFACTOR: A rescaling factor used to convert floating-point distances to integer storage. LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX: The local workgroup size, typically 256 due to mobile device constraints. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initial Rasterization (2D Context): Render surfaces into the distance field texture. In 2D, this is done by drawing lines a couple of pixels wide to get accurate subpixel distances for the immediate vicinity of surfaces. 2. X-Axis Sweep: The input texture is assumed to have already been swept in the X direction. 3. Y-Axis Sweep: Perform a sweep along the Y axis using an extension compute shader. 4. Synchronization: Insert a memory barrier to ensure synchronization between passes. 5. Z-Axis Sweep: Perform a sweep along the Z axis. 6. Completion: The SDF generation is complete. Row Processing Logic (The Sweep Pass): The core computation occurs when processing a single row (or column) of the texture. The algorithm processes a row by: 1. Loading the input value for the current invocation. 2. Quantizing the value: out = uint(input QUANITZATIONFACTOR). Values greater than EDFRANGE EDFRANGE indicate "infinity". 3. Storing the quantized value to sharedMem[rowInvocationID]. 4. Synchronizing all threads in the workgroup (BARRIER()). 5. Iterating over a range of offsets i from -EDFRANGE to EDFRANGE - 1 (excluding 0 for optimization). 6. For each offset, calculating the wrap-around coordinate and the distance between the current invocation and the neighbor. 7. Updating the local minimum using the parabolic distance approximation. Formula: The distance update rule for each neighbor in the sweep is: \text{newDist} = \min(\text{currentDist}, \text{sharedMem}[\text{newCoordinate}] + \text{distanceBetween}^2) Where: \text{currentDist} is the current minimum distance found for the invocation. \text{sharedMem}[\text{newCoordinate}] is the quantized distance value stored in shared memory at the neighbor's position. \text{distanceBetween} = \text{rowInvocationID} - \text{newCoordinate}. \text{newCoordinate} = \text{coordinateWrapAround}(\text{rowInvocationID} + i), which is typically x % ROWLENGTH. Post-Processing: After the loop, the final result is de-quantized: \text{result} = \text{float}(\text{out}) \times \text{QUANITZATIONFACTOR\RCP} Where QUANITZATIONFACTORRCP is the reciprocal of the quantization factor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sweeprow(inputtex, outputtex, rowlength, rowInvocationID, sharedMem, barrierfunc): # Constants from evidence EDFRANGE = 255 # For UNORMR8 QUANITZATIONFACTOR = 255.0 QUANITZATIONFACTORRCP = 1.0 / QUANITZATIONFACTOR # 1. Load and Quantize inputval = inputtex[rowInvocationID] # Standard texel fetch out = int(inputval QUANITZATIONFACTOR) # uint cast # 2. Store to Shared Memory sharedMem[rowInvocationID] = out # 3. Synchronize barrierfunc() # 4. Sweep Loop # Evidence loop: for i from -EDFRANGE to EDFRANGE - 1 for i in range(-EDFRANGE, EDFRANGE): # Wrap-around coordinate newCoordinate = (rowInvocationID + i) % rowlength # Distance between distanceBetween = rowInvocationID - newCoordinate # Update minimum candidate = sharedMem[newCoordinate] + distanceBetween distanceBetween if candidate < out: out = candidate # 5. De-quantize and Store result = float(out) QUANITZATIONFACTORRCP outputtex[rowInvocationID] = result # Standard texel store # Note: If rowlength > LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX, sharedMem must be # pre-loaded with LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX + 2EDFRANGE samples # to handle wrap-around and range access. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Row Length vs. Workgroup Size: If the row length exceeds LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX, sharedMem must be pre-loaded with LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX + 2EDFRANGE samples to handle wrap-around and range access. Overflow: Intermediate result textures require twice the bits of the input storage to prevent overflow during the parabolic addition (\text{distanceBetween}^2). Infinity Handling: Values exceeding EDFRANGE EDFRANGE after quantization should be treated as infinity to avoid incorrect minimums. Time Complexity: The non-optimal version (without prefix-sum/scan) has a complexity proportional to O(\text{EDF\RANGE}) per pixel per sweep pass. Performance: On a 320GB/s GDDR5 desktop GPU, the performance bound is around 6ms for SDF computation. The non-optimal algorithm is expected to take between 500-1000ms assuming 2TB/s shared memory speed and EDFRANGE=255. Memory Complexity: Requires shared memory proportional to the workgroup size plus a halo for the sweep range. Intermediate textures may require double the bit-depth of the final output. Strengths: Efficient generation of approximate SDFs for sphere tracing; avoids expensive per-pixel analytical distance calculations; suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs. Limitations: The result is an approximation, not an exact Euclidean distance field; accuracy depends on EDFRANGE and the initial rasterization quality; performance degrades with larger EDFRANGE in the non-optimized version. When to use: When an approximate SDF is sufficient for sphere tracing, though the non-optimal version is slow (500–1000 ms) and requires optimizations like prefix-sum/scan or warp shuffles for performance-critical applications. When not to use: When exact Euclidean distances are required for collision detection or precise ray marching. The method is described in the context of adding an "Approximate Distance Field computation extension" to the Irrlicht engine. It builds upon the "Marching Parabolas" technique, which is analogous to blur functions in shared memory. The concept of rendering surfaces to get accurate subpixel distances and then sweeping to propagate them was discussed in the context of fast pixelshader 2D raytracing. The non-optimal version can be optimized using prefix-sum/scan algorithms or warp-level primitives like NVshuffle. name: Uniform Scaling of SDFs
head: Uniform Scaling of Signed Distance Functions, SDF Scaling, Scaling SDFs, SDF Scale
body: Uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an implicit surface by a uniform factor while preserving the correctness of the distance value for ray marching. It solves the problem that scaling is not a rigid body transformation and distorts distances; without correction, the ray marching algorithm may overestimate the distance to the surface, causing the object to disappear. Unlike Non-Uniform Scaling of SDFs, which requires conservative bounds to avoid overestimation, uniform scaling allows for an exact compensation of distance distortion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base SDF function f(p), a query point p in world space, and a uniform scaling factor s (where s > 0). Output: The signed distance from p to the scaled surface. Data Structures: The scaling factor is stored as a scalar floating-point value (e.g., f32) as the second field of the Scaled struct. Steps: 1. Inverse Transform Point: Divide the query point p by the scaling factor s to compress the evaluation space. If the primitive has a center offset o, the operation is (p - o) / s. p' = \frac{p}{s} 2. Evaluate Base SDF: Query the base SDF function with the transformed point p' to get the raw distance d'. d' = f(p') 3. Rescale Distance: Multiply the returned distance d' by the scaling factor s to compensate for the distortion caused by the non-rigid scaling. d = d' \times s Formula: The general formula for a uniformly scaled SDF is: d{scaled}(p) = f\left(\frac{p}{s}\right) \times s For a specific primitive like a sphere with center o and base radius r, the scaled SDF is: d{sphere}(p) = \left( \left\| \frac{p - o}{s} \right\| - r \right) \times s where \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. Parameters: s: The uniform scaling factor. Values s > 1 enlarge the surface footprint; values s < 1 shrink it. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Overestimation: If the distance is overestimated (e.g., scaling down without correction: sphereSDF(samplePoint / 0.5)), the ray marching algorithm may step past the surface, causing the object to disappear completely. Underestimation: If the distance is underestimated (e.g., using no correction or a smaller correction factor), the ray marching algorithm still works but requires more iterations, resulting in slower performance. Sign Preservation: The sign of the distance is preserved regardless of the scaling correction factor, so the object remains visible even with incorrect distance values, but the geometric accuracy is lost. Zero Scaling: s=0 is undefined and should be guarded against. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scalesdfuniform(sdffunc, point, scalefactor): """ Computes the signed distance to a uniformly scaled SDF. Args: sdffunc: A function that takes a point and returns the signed distance. point: The query point in world space (tuple or list of 3 floats). scalefactor: The uniform scaling factor (scalar > 0). Returns: The signed distance from point to the scaled surface. """ if scalefactor == 0: raise ValueError("Scaling factor must be non-zero.") # Step 1: Inverse transform point (component-wise division) scaledpoint = (point[0] / scalefactor, point[1] / scalefactor, point[2] / scalefactor) # Step 2: Evaluate base SDF rawdistance = sdffunc(scaledpoint) # Step 3: Rescale distance finaldistance = rawdistance scalefactor return finaldistance Non-uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an SDF primitive by scaling its axes by different factors, ensuring the ray marching algorithm does not overestimate the distance to the surface. Unlike uniform scaling, which allows for exact distance compensation, non-uniform scaling distorts distances anisotropically; this method uses the minimum scaling factor as a conservative correction multiplier to guarantee distance underestimation, which is safe for ray marching convergence. Strengths: Exact distance preservation prevents overestimation, which would cause the ray marching algorithm to step past the surface and miss the object. Limitations: Only applicable to uniform scaling. Non-uniform scaling requires different techniques. The technique applies the inverse transformation to the query point before evaluating the base SDF, then scales the returned distance to compensate for non-rigid distortion. head: Anisotropic SDF Scaling, Non-Uniform Scaling of Signed Distance Functions
body: Non-uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an SDF primitive by scaling its axes by different factors, ensuring the ray marching algorithm does not overestimate the distance to the surface. Unlike uniform scaling, which allows for exact distance compensation, non-uniform scaling distorts distances anisotropically; this method uses the minimum scaling factor as a conservative correction multiplier to guarantee distance underestimation, which is safe for ray marching convergence. Inputs: samplePoint: The 3D coordinate in world space where the SDF is being evaluated. s: A 3D vector (sx, sy, sz) representing the non-uniform scaling factors for the X, Y, and Z axes. baseSDF: A function that evaluates the base SDF primitive. Outputs: dist: The corrected signed distance value. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Transform the sample point: Divide the samplePoint by the scaling vector s. p{local} = \frac{samplePoint}{s} = \left( \frac{x}{sx}, \frac{y}{sy}, \frac{z}{sz} \right) 2. Evaluate the SDF: Compute the distance by calling the base SDF function at the transformed point. d{local} = baseSDF(p{local}) 3. Apply correction factor: Multiply the local distance by the minimum of the scaling factors. dist = d{local} \times \min(sx, sy, sz) Formula: For a general SDF baseSDF scaled by vector s = (sx, sy, sz), the transformed SDF S{scaled}(x, y, z) is: S{scaled}(x, y, z) = baseSDF\left(\frac{x}{sx}, \frac{y}{sy}, \frac{z}{sz}\right) \times \min(sx, sy, sz) Example Derivation (Unit Sphere): Consider a unit sphere scaled to half its size along the X-axis (sx=0.5, sy=1, sz=1). The unscaled unit sphere SDF is \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} - 1. Applying the coordinate transformation without the correction multiplier yields the naive scaled SDF: sphereSDF{naive}(x, y, z) = \sqrt{(2x)^2 + y^2 + z^2} - 1 Evaluating this at (2, 0, 0) yields 3, while the true distance is 1.5. Applying the correction method multiplies the result by \min(0.5, 1, 1) = 0.5 to prevent overestimation. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Overestimation Risk: Non-uniform scaling cannot exactly compensate for distance distortion because the correction factor varies depending on the location of the closest point on the surface relative to the sampling point, which is unknown during evaluation. Using the minimum scaling factor is a safe approximation that ensures the returned distance is never greater than the true distance, preventing ray marching from skipping the surface. Directional Variance: The overestimation factor varies depending on where the sampling point and the closest surface point are located. Zero/Negative Scaling: Scaling factors must be positive. Zero or negative scaling breaks the geometric interpretation of the distance field and the validity of the minimum factor heuristic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nonuniformscaledsdf(samplepoint, scalingfactors, basesdf): """ Evaluates an SDF with non-uniform scaling. Args: samplepoint: tuple or list of 3 floats (x, y, z) scalingfactors: tuple or list of 3 floats (sx, sy, sz) basesdf: function that takes (x, y, z) and returns float distance Returns: float: The corrected signed distance """ sx, sy, sz = scalingfactors # Step 1: Transform sample point to local space localx = samplepoint[0] / sx localy = samplepoint[1] / sy localz = samplepoint[2] / sz # Step 2: Evaluate base SDF in local space localdist = basesdf(localx, localy, localz) # Step 3: Multiply by the minimum scaling factor minscale = min(sx, sy, sz) correcteddist = localdist minscale return correcteddist This technique is described in the context of ray marching and Signed Distance Functions, specifically addressing the limitations of applying non-rigid transformations to distance fields. Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions, http://jamie-wong.com/2016/07/15/ray-marching-signed-distance-functions/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions, https://github.com/guevara/read-it-later/issues/4535, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spatial and nD transforms
head: Transforming SDF Geometry, hierarchical transforms, inverse transform query
body: Spatial and nD transforms allow the application of geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling, and permutation) to Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitives and discrete data structures by applying the inverse transformation to the query point rather than transforming the geometry itself. This approach ensures that the underlying data structures remain unmodified, preserving local linearity and allowing constant-time affine queries per dimension. It differs from direct geometry transformation by deferring the coordinate change to the evaluation step, which avoids distorting the stored data and supports non-uniform or spatially varying distortions. The method operates by mapping a world-space query point back to the local space of the primitive or data grid using the inverse of the desired transformation matrix. This applies to both continuous SDFs and discrete multi-dimensional data structures. Input: A query point P{world} in world coordinates. Input: A transformation matrix T (or its components: scale, offset, permutation) defining the local-to-world mapping. Output: A transformed point P{local} (or transformed tolerance) suitable for evaluating the base distance function or accessing the data grid. For discrete multi-dimensional data (e.g., voxel grids or splatting indices), transforms are stored per node or dimension: Affine Transform: Defined by a scale factor s and an offset o. Permutation Transform: Defined by a permutation array perm mapping indices. Composition: Affine transforms compose as s = sp sc and o = sp oc + op; permutations compose as r[i] = permp[permc[i]]. 1. Construct Inverse Transform: Determine the inverse of the local-to-world transformation T. For a composite transformation T = S \cdot R \cdot T{trans}, compute T^{-1}. 2. Apply Inverse to Query Point: For SDFs: Transform the query point P{world} to P{local} using T^{-1}. For Discrete Data: Inverse-transform the slice query per dimension rather than per point to maintain constant work for affine transforms. 3. Evaluate Base Function: Use P{local} to evaluate the base distance function or access the data grid. Affine Transform (Continuous/Discrete): Given a world position P{world} and tolerance T{world}, and affine parameters scale s and offset o: P{raw} = \frac{P{world} - o}{s} T{raw} = \frac{T{world}}{|s|} Permutation Transform (Discrete): Given a permutation array perm, the inverse mapping is: inverse[perm[i]] = i Matrix Inverse (SDF): For a 4x4 transformation matrix M (combining scale S, rotation R, and translation T), the transformed point P{local} is: P{local} = (P{world} \cdot M^{-1}).xyz where P{world} is treated as a homogeneous vector (x, y, z, 1). Scale (s): Non-uniform scaling factors. A zero scale is accepted but triggers a validation warning, leaving the query untransformed. Offset (o): Translation vector. Permutation (perm): Array mapping discrete indices. Norm: In nD geometric transformation contexts, if norm != 0, the result is projected onto the z=norm plane. The following pseudocode demonstrates the application of an inverse transform to an SDF query point, combining translation, rotation, and scaling. Unverified code. Args: ptworld: tuple of 3 floats, the query point in world space. transformmatrix: list of lists, 4x4 matrix representing the local-to-world transform. Returns: tuple of 3 floats, the transformed point in local space. """ pthomogeneous = (ptworld[0], ptworld[1], ptworld[2], 1.0) invmatrix = invertmatrix4x4(transformmatrix) ptlocalx = invmatrix[0][0]pthomogeneous[0] + invmatrix[0][1]pthomogeneous[1] + invmatrix[0][2]pthomogeneous[2] + invmatrix[0][3]pthomogeneous[3] ptlocaly = invmatrix[1][0]pthomogeneous[0] + invmatrix[1][1]pthomogeneous[1] + invmatrix[1][2]pthomogeneous[2] + invmatrix[1][3]pthomogeneous[3] ptlocalz = invmatrix[2][0]pthomogeneous[0] + invmatrix[2][1]pthomogeneous[1] + invmatrix[2][2]pthomogeneous[2] + invmatrix[2][3]pthomogeneous[3] return (ptlocalx, ptlocaly, ptlocalz) def evaluatetransformedsdf(ptworld, transformmatrix, basesdffunc): """ Evaluates an SDF after applying a spatial transform. Args: ptworld: tuple of 3 floats, query point. transformmatrix: list of lists, 4x4 matrix, local-to-world transform. basesdffunc: function, the base distance function (e.g., sphere). Returns: float, the signed distance. """ ptlocal = inversetransformquery(ptworld, transformmatrix) return basesdffunc(ptlocal) def sphere(pt): return (pt[0]2 + pt[1]2 + pt[2]2)0.5 - 1.0 def ftranslate(ptworld): # Translation by (0, 3, 0) # Inverse translation is (0, -3, 0) ptlocal = (ptworld[0], ptworld[1] - 3.0, ptworld[2]) return sphere(ptlocal) For discrete nD geometric transformations, the exact tensor operations are not given in the sources. The method instead inverse-transforms the slice query per dimension to maintain constant work for affine transforms. Zero Scale: A zero scale factor is accepted but triggers a validation warning. The query remains untransformed in this case. Discrete Grid Alignment: On a discrete axis, the world value is rounded onto the declared grid. If a value has no local preimage (i.e., it falls between grid points), it selects nothing. Non-Uniform Distortion: Non-uniform spatial distortion modifies 'all of space' with the same transform, so distance functions retain their local linearity. Spatially varying distortion can also be applied by making the transform a function of the point's position. Precision: Inverse transformation queries must handle floating-point precision carefully, especially when dealing with large translation offsets or small scale factors. SDF Rotation applies a rotational transformation to a signed distance field primitive by rotating the sampling point before evaluating the base distance function. It is chosen when an object needs to be oriented in world space without modifying its underlying SDF definition. It is a specific case of the general inverse transform method, focusing solely on the rotational component of the transformation matrix. See SDF Rotation. Time Complexity: For affine transforms, the query time is constant per dimension, independent of the data size, as it involves simple arithmetic operations. For permutations, it requires one pass over the category list. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required for the transformation itself, as the inverse is applied on-the-fly to the query point. Strengths: Preserves the integrity of the underlying data structure; supports non-uniform and spatially varying distortions; efficient for discrete data by avoiding per-point transformation. Limitations: Requires computing the inverse transformation matrix, which can be computationally expensive if done per-query (though typically done once per frame/object). Zero scale leads to undefined behavior unless handled. When to Use: When transforming SDF primitives or discrete data structures for rendering or visualization, especially when the underlying data should remain unmodified. When Not to Use: When the transformation is simple enough to be baked into the data structure, or when the inverse transformation is not available or difficult to compute. The concept of applying inverse transformations to query points in SDF rendering is a standard technique in ray marching, popularized by tutorials and resources such as those by Inigo Quilez. The application of hierarchical and nD transforms to discrete scientific data (e.g., microscopy data) for scalable web visualization was detailed in the Luxar paper, which introduced per-node affine and permutation transforms for multi-dimensional data. The geometric transformation application in nD spaces is supported by deep learning frameworks, though the exact tensor implementation details are not provided in the sources. name: SDF Rotation
head: Rotating SDFs, SDF Rotate
body: SDF Rotation applies a rotational transformation to a signed distance field primitive by rotating the sampling point before evaluating the base distance function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p in world space, rotation representation (quaternion q or axis-angle). Output: Signed distance value d from the base primitive at the rotated location. Data Structures: Rotation representation: Stores the orientation as a quaternion. Query point: 3D vector p = (x, y, z). Steps: 1. Retrieve the stored rotation representation (quaternion q). 2. Compute the inverse rotation of q. For a unit quaternion, the inverse is the conjugate: q^{-1} = (w, -x, -y, -z). 3. Apply the inverse rotation to the query point p to obtain the rotated point p'. If using a quaternion q^{-1}: p' = q^{-1} \otimes (0, p) \otimes q (where \otimes is quaternion multiplication). If using axis-angle: Rotate p around the specified axis by the stored angle. 4. Evaluate the base SDF function using the rotated point p': d = \text{BaseSDF}(p'). 5. Return d. Parameters: Quaternion q: The rotation to apply. Stored as the second field of the Rotation struct. It is inverted at query time. Axis and angle: Alternative representation where the axis is a 3D vector and the angle is in radians. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-unit quaternions: If the stored quaternion is not normalized, the inverse rotation will scale the point incorrectly. Normalization is required. Precision errors: Repeated rotations can accumulate floating-point errors. Renormalizing the quaternion periodically is recommended. Degenerate input: An axis of zero length in axis-angle representation is undefined. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Callable @dataclass class Vec3: x: float y: float z: float @dataclass class Quaternion: w: float x: float y: float z: float def rotatesdf(p: Vec3, q: Quaternion, basesdf: Callable[[Vec3], float]) -> float: # Step 2: Compute inverse quaternion (conjugate for unit quaternion) qinv = Quaternion(q.w, -q.x, -q.y, -q.z) # Step 3: Apply inverse rotation to p # Convert point to quaternion (w=0) pq = Quaternion(0.0, p.x, p.y, p.z) # Quaternion multiplication: qinv pq q temp = quaternionmultiply(qinv, pq) protatedq = quaternionmultiply(temp, q) # Extract rotated point protated = Vec3(protatedq.x, protatedq.y, protatedq.z) # Step 4: Evaluate base SDF distance = basesdf(protated) # Step 5: Return distance return distance def quaternionmultiply(a: Quaternion, b: Quaternion) -> Quaternion: """Standard Hamilton product for quaternion multiplication.""" w = a.w b.w - a.x b.x - a.y b.y - a.z b.z x = a.w b.x + a.x b.w + a.y b.z - a.z b.y y = a.w b.y - a.x b.z + a.y b.w + a.z b.x z = a.w b.z + a.x b.y - a.y b.x + a.z b.w return Quaternion(w, x, y, z) Positions a primitive by transforming the sampling point via vector subtraction. Choose it when only placement is needed, as it avoids rotation overhead. Time complexity: O(1) per query, dominated by quaternion multiplication. Memory complexity: O(1) additional memory for the inverse quaternion calculation. Strengths: Efficient orientation of primitives without modifying the base SDF code; supports arbitrary rotations via quaternions. Limitations: Requires careful handling of quaternion normalization; slightly more expensive than translation due to quaternion multiplication overhead. When to use: When primitives need to be oriented at arbitrary angles in the scene. When not to use: When performance is critical and only axis-aligned rotations are needed (matrix multiplication might be faster on some hardware). name: SDF Translation
head: Moving SDFs, Positioning SDFs, SDF Move
body: SDF Translation positions a signed distance field primitive at a specific coordinate by transforming the sampling point in the opposite direction of the desired object movement before querying the base primitive. Unlike SDF Rotation, which applies an inverse rotation matrix to the query point, translation uses a simple vector subtraction. This method allows for the static definition of primitive shapes while dynamically placing them within a scene without modifying the primitive's internal geometry. Inputs: p: The query point in world space (vec3). t: The translation vector representing the desired position of the SDF object in world space (vec3). basesdf: The function evaluating the untransformed primitive (e.g., sdSphere, sdBox). Outputs: d: The signed distance from p to the translated primitive surface. Data Structures: The translation vector t is stored as a field within a scene descriptor struct, specifically as the second field of the Translation struct in the reference implementation. Steps: 1. Compute the inverse-transformed query point p' by subtracting the translation vector t from the world-space query point p: p' = p - t 2. Evaluate the base SDF function at p': d = \text{base\sdf}(p') 3. Return d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def translatesdf(p: Vec3, t: Vec3, basesdf: Callable[[Vec3], float]) -> float: # Inverse transform: move the sampling point opposite to the object's movement ptransformed = p - t # Evaluate base primitive at transformed point distance = basesdf(ptransformed) return distance Parameters: t (Vec3): The 3D offset vector defining the object's position. Typical values depend on scene scale; for a unit sphere centered at (0, 1, 0), t = (0, 1, 0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: A common error is adding the translation vector to the query point (p + t) or modifying the primitive's internal coordinates directly. The correct approach is moving the sampling point in the opposite direction of the desired object movement. If you move the object right, you must move the sampling point left to maintain the same relative distance. Standard floating-point precision is sufficient for most scene scales. However, for very large translation vectors, precision loss in the subtraction p - t may affect distance accuracy near the surface. Not given in the sources. It relies on the principle that transforming the query point inversely is equivalent to transforming the object in the forward direction. This concept is introduced alongside rotation and scaling in introductory raymarching guides. Implementation details, such as storing translation vectors in uniform buffers for GPU rendering, are demonstrated in open-source raymarcher projects. unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Painting with Math: A Gentle Study of Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/painting-with-math-a-gentle-study-of-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: k-SDF
head: Volumetric Surfaces, k-SDF network
body: k-SDF is a representation for real-time view synthesis of fuzzy geometries using k lightweight, semi-transparent mesh shells rendered via rasterization in a fixed order, bounding the number of sampling locations per ray to a small range (3 \le k \le 9). It models implicit geometry as k distinct signed distance fields combined with a view-dependent transparency field and a color field. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting or SMERF, it is sorting-free and bounds samples per ray, enabling real-time rendering on low-cost smartphones. Unlike AdaptiveShells, it learns multiple SDFs and finds sampling locations via rasterization using 2D textures rather than volume rendering. Inputs: Multi-view images of a fuzzy scene. Outputs: A set of k simplified meshes, UV atlases, and baked neural texture images (PNGs) representing color and transparency. Data Structures: 1. k-SDF Network: Encodes 3D points to output a signed distance d and a geometric feature vector z. 2. Offset MLP Heads: k-1 tiny MLPs, each taking z as input to predict relative offsets \hat{o}i. 3. Appearance Network: Encodes position, view direction, normal, and feature vector to predict SH coefficients for color and transparency. 4. Neural Textures: Hash-grid based representation discretized into (deg+1)^2 PNG images per mesh, storing RGBA channels. 5. Occupancy Grid: Binary 256^3 grid marking occupied space. Parameters: k: Number of shells, typically 3 \le k \le 9. \beta: Controls density spread in the logistic distribution. Scheduled during training. \Deltao: Initialization spacing for support surfaces, \Deltao = \frac{1}{\beta2} \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}. Grid resolution: 256^3. Texture resolutions: Base color at 2048^2, highest SH degree coefficients at 256^2. Range [v{min}, v{max}]: [-15, 15] for texture rescaling. Steps: 1. Implicit Surface Training: Train a standard NeuS-like model for 100k iterations to learn a single opaque main SDF d. Schedule \beta exponentially from \phi{\beta1} to \phi{\beta2}. Initialize k-1 support surfaces as shells uniformly spaced from the main surface by \Deltao. Initialize all on the inside to increase capacity. Train the k-SDF model for 50k iterations starting from \phi{\beta2} until \phi{\beta3}, where densities are peaked. Loss function: L = Lc + \lambdae Le + \lambdas Ls, with \lambdae = 0.04, \lambdas = 0.65. 2. Sampling: Compute per-surface binary occupancy: a voxel is occupied if its center's |d| value, combined with \beta and the voxel's space diagonal, allows any point in the volume to have density > 10^{-4}. Aggregate occupancy with OR operation to form a single binary grid. Traverse grid to sample n points uniformly in occupied space. Perform hierarchical importance sampling: Evaluate all k SDFs to compute k CDFs, sum and normalize to get probability distribution. Sample m/2 additional points, add to previous n. Repeat once to add m/2 more. Total samples per ray: n+m. In the first importance sampling iteration, use \beta half of the rendering value; in the second, match it. 3. Rendering (Implicit): For each surface i, compute color \mathcal{C}i(\mathbf{r}) and transparency \mathcal{A}i(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{C}j(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^n w{i,j} \xi(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{n}{i,j}, \mathbf{z}i) \mathcal{A}j(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^n w{i,j} \alpha(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{n}{i,j}, \mathbf{z}i) where w{i,j} are sample weights. Compute final color: \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^k \mathcal{C}i(\mathbf{r}) \mathcal{A}i(\mathbf{r}) wi, \quad wi = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \mathcal{A}j(\mathbf{r})) Apply transparency attenuation: \alphaw = 2 \cdot \text{Sigmoid}(10 \cdot |\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}|) - 1. Multiply predicted transparencies by \alphaw. 4. Mesh Extraction and Baking: Extract zero-level sets of d{1:k} as high-resolution meshes using marching cubes. Simplify meshes to 0.02% of original triangle count. Generate UV atlases using xatlas. Train per-surface view-dependent appearance model using neural textures (hash-grid + small decoder MLP) on the fixed geometry. Discretize neural textures: Map x \in \mathbb{R}^3 to x \in [0,1]^2 in UV space. Predict SH coefficients via bilinear interpolation of texel centers. Squeeze values: \hat{sh} = \text{Sigmoid}(sh). Quantize: q(x) = \text{round}(255x)/255. Rescale: sh = v{min} + (v{max}-v{min})q(\hat{sh}). Bake to (deg+1)^2 PNG images per mesh, where the i-th image stores the i-th coefficient of RGBA channels. 5. Rasterization (Explicit): Rasterize all meshes in a fixed order (outermost to innermost) in a WebGL renderer. Blend them in the final frame buffer using the baked textures. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trainksdf(images, poses, k=5): # Phase 1: Single opaque SDF model = NeuSModel() for i in range(100000): beta = schedulebeta(i, start=beta1, end=beta2) loss = computeneusloss(model, images, poses, beta) model.update(loss) # Phase 2: k-SDF mainsdf = model.sdf # Initialize offsets uniformly spaced inside offsets = [Deltao for in range(k-1)] for i in range(50000): beta = schedulebeta(i, start=beta2, end=beta3) # Compute occupancy grid occupancygrid = computeoccupancy(mainsdf, offsets, beta, threshold=1e-4) # Sample points points = sampleuniform(occupancygrid, n) points = importancesample(points, mainsdf, offsets, beta, m) # Render and compute loss color = renderksdf(points, mainsdf, offsets, beta) loss = L1loss(color, targetimage) + lambdae eikonalloss + lambdas curvatureloss model.update(loss) return model, offsets def renderksdf(points, mainsdf, offsets, beta): # Compute absolute SDFs # d1 = mainsdf # d2 = mainsdf + offsets[0] #... sdfvalues = [mainsdf] + [mainsdf + o for o in offsets] # Compute densities densities = [phibeta(d, beta) for d in sdfvalues] # Compute weights for each surface # wi = product(1 - Aj) for j < i # Aj = sum(wij alphaj) totalcolor = 0 alphaaccumulator = 1.0 for i in range(len(sdfvalues)): # Compute surface color and alpha Ci, Ai = rendersurface(points, sdfvalues[i], densities[i], beta) # Apply transparency attenuation # alphaw = 2 Sigmoid(10 |v. n|) - 1 # Ai = Ai alphaw totalcolor += Ci Ai alphaaccumulator alphaaccumulator = (1 - Ai) return totalcolor def baketextures(meshes, ksdfmodel, deg=3): # For each mesh for mesh in meshes: uvatlas = xatlas(mesh) # Create hash grid for neural texture hashgrid = HashGrid(inputdim=2, outputdim=4(deg+1)2) # Train hash grid on UV coordinates for sample in meshsamples: uv = maptouv(sample, uvatlas) # Predict SH coefficients sh = hashgrid.predict(uv) # Decode to RGBA using view direction rgba = decodesh(sh, viewdirection) loss = L1loss(rgba, targetrgba) hashgrid.update(loss) # Discretize and bake for texel in hashgrid.texels: sh = texel.value shsigmoid = sigmoid(sh) shquant = round(255 shsigmoid) / 255 shfinal = vmin + (vmax - vmin) shquant savepng(shfinal, filename) A neural network architecture that encodes 3D points to output a signed distance d and a geometric feature vector z, used to predict relative offsets for layered meshes. Input: 3D point coordinates. Encoding: Trainable positional encoding from Rosu and Behnke. Main MLP: Three layers, each with 32 features. Hidden layers use GELU activations. Final layer uses linear activation. Output: Signed distance d and geometric feature vector z. Offset Prediction: Tiny MLP heads (single layer, 32 units) with independent parameters. Input is only z. Step: Enforce sign of predicted offset: Apply softplus activation multiplied by the desired sign. Step: Compute final ordered offsets: Perform a cumulative sum over the predicted relative offsets, separately for negative and positive values. A training schedule for the parameter \beta that controls the sharpness of the logistic distribution used for density peaks in the k-SDF model. Step: During the main surface training phase, v linearly transitions from v1 = 0.3 to v2 = 0.7. Step: During the training of k-SDF, v further progresses from v2 = 0.7 to v3 = 1.0. Parameter: At \beta2 (corresponding to v2=0.7), the logistic distribution standard deviation is approximately 0.001. This value is used to initialize offsets as constants (\Deltao). Parameter: By the end of implicit surface training (\beta3, corresponding to v3=1.0), the standard deviation decreases to 0.00008, resulting in fully peaked densities. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(k \cdot n) per ray, where k is the number of shells and n is the number of samples. Since k is small (3-9) and n is bounded by the occupancy grid and importance sampling, it is significantly faster than dense volume rendering. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the neural textures. With mixed resolutions (2048^2 for base color, 256^2 for high SH degrees), memory footprint is approximately 14 MB per mesh. Meshes are simplified to 0.02% of original triangle count. Measured Performance: Enables real-time rendering on low-cost smartphones, outperforming 3DGS and SMERF in speed on mobile hardware. Strengths: Sorting-free rendering, bounded samples per ray, high quality for fuzzy geometry, efficient mobile rendering. Limitations: Requires training phase to bake textures; less flexible than splatting for dynamic scenes without retraining. When to use: Real-time view synthesis of fuzzy geometries on mobile or low-power devices. When not to use: Scenes requiring frequent dynamic updates without retraining, or where extreme geometric complexity exceeds the capacity of k shells. k-SDF, also known as Volumetric Surfaces, was proposed by Stefano Esposito, Anpei Chen, Christian Reiser, Samuel Rota Bulò, Lorenzo Porzi, Katja Schwarz, Christian Richardt, Michael Zollhofer, Peter Kontschieder, and Andreas Geiger from the University of Tübingen and Meta Reality Labs. It was published in CVPR 2025. The method builds on NeuS and is inspired by textured shells used in game production.
