name: SDF Representation DOP
head: Signed Distance Field Representation
body: The SDF Representation DOP creates a signed distance field from geometry to enable fast inside/outside testing for collision detection. It supports multiple construction modes, including ray intersection and laser scanning, to handle various geometry types and watertightness requirements. Inputs and Outputs Input Geometry: The parent geometry data is used to create the SDF. A Geometry data attached as subdata overrides the parent, allowing proxy geometry or explicit external volume files. First Input: Optional connector to control which simulation objects are modified via the Group parameter. Other Inputs: Connectors for data nodes that act as modifiers. Output: A signed distance field data structure attached to the specified objects. Data Structures The SDF is stored on a 3D voxel grid. The grid resolution is defined by the Divisions parameter, computed within a bounding box slightly larger than the geometry. In Volume Sample mode, divisions are ignored and computed from the source volume's voxel size. Each voxel stores a scalar distance value: positive outside, negative inside, zero on the surface. Algorithm Steps The construction process depends on the selected Mode and Laser Scan setting: 1. Geometry Source: Uses parent geometry data, or attached subdata if present. 2. Grid Setup: Initializes a 3D grid based on Divisions or source volume resolution. 3. Distance Calculation: Depends on Mode. Ray Intersect uses ray intersection for accuracy. Meta Balls evaluates metaball field directly (requires Laser Scan off). Implicit Box/Sphere/Plane fills bounding box, sphere, or divides box along smallest axis. Minimum computes distance to surface/curve, with Offset expanding/shrinking. Volume Sample reads raw volume primitive as SDF. Height Field treats volume as 2D heightfield with orthographic distances. Laser Scan (On) sends rays along primary axes, uses closest/farthest intersections, marks voxels between as inside. Laser Scan (Off) sends rays along primary axes, finds all intersections, tests segments for inside/outside using normals. 4. Sign Correction: Fix Signs post-processes to correct numerical imprecision and inconsistent signs. 5. Boundary Stabilization: Force Bounds forces boundary voxels to exterior to prevent incorrect sign stabilization. 6. Sign Inversion: Invert Sign reverses inside/outside sense. 7. Sign Sweep: If Sign Sweep Threshold is set, performs passes to eliminate large inconsistent blocks. An invalid transition occurs if SDF value change exceeds Threshold Cell Width. Geometry is ray-intersected to determine correct sign, which propagates forward. Repeats up to Max Sign Sweep Count. Parameters Mode: String. Options: Ray Intersect, Meta Balls, Implicit Box, Implicit Sphere, Implicit Plane, Minimum, Volume Sample, Height Field. Divisions: Integer. Grid resolution. Minimum feature size must be larger than grid spacing to avoid detail loss. Offset: Float. Expands (positive) or shrinks (negative) the volume. Tolerance: Float. Scale-invariant tolerance for ray intersections, multiplied by geometry size. Laser Scan: Boolean. On: uses closest/farthest intersections (robust to non-watertight). Off: uses all intersections (requires watertight). Fix Signs: Boolean. Enables post-processing for sign consistency. Force Bounds: Boolean. Forces boundary voxels to exterior. Invert Sign: Boolean. Reverses inside/outside. Sign Sweep Threshold: Float. Threshold for invalid sign transitions relative to cell width. Max Sign Sweep Count: Integer. Maximum iterations for sign sweep. Data Sharing: Enum. Do Not Share Data, Share Data Across All Time, Share Data In One Timestep. Activation: Expression/Float. Non-zero attaches data; zero removes it. Group: String. Subset of objects to affect. Data Name: String. Name for attaching data, supports subdata paths (e.g., "Forces/Fan"). Unique Data Name: Boolean. Modifies Data Name to ensure unique attachment so it will not overwrite existing data. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdf(geometry, params): # 1. Determine geometry source sourcegeom = params.get('subdatageometry') or geometry # 2. Determine grid bounds and resolution if params['mode'] == 'Volume Sample': grid = creategridfromvolume(sourcegeom) else: bbox = computeboundingbox(sourcegeom) grid = creategrid(bbox, params['divisions']) # 3. Compute distances based on mode if params['mode'] == 'Ray Intersect': computerayintersectsdf(grid, sourcegeom, params['tolerance']) elif params['mode'] == 'Meta Balls': computemetaballsdf(grid, sourcegeom) elif params['mode'] == 'Implicit Box': fillgridwithbbox(grid, sourcegeom) elif params['mode'] == 'Implicit Sphere': fillgridwithboundingsphere(grid, sourcegeom) elif params['mode'] == 'Implicit Plane': createplanesdf(grid, sourcegeom) elif params['mode'] == 'Minimum': computeminimumdistancesdf(grid, sourcegeom, params['offset']) elif params['mode'] == 'Volume Sample': samplevolumesdf(grid, sourcegeom) elif params['mode'] == 'Height Field': computeheightfieldsdf(grid, sourcegeom) else: if params['laserscan']: computelaserscansdf(grid, sourcegeom, params['tolerance']) else: computefullraysdf(grid, sourcegeom, params['tolerance']) # 4. Fix Signs if params['fixsigns']: correctsigns(grid, sourcegeom) if params['forcebounds']: forceboundaryexterior(grid) # 5. Sign Sweep if params['signsweepthreshold'] > 0: cellwidth = computecellwidth(grid) for i in range(params['maxsignsweepcount']): if not sweepsigns(grid, params['signsweepthreshold'], sourcegeom, cellwidth): break # 6. Invert Sign if params['invertsign']: invertsdf(grid) return grid def computeboundingbox(geom): return (min(p.x for p in geom.points), min(p.y for p in geom.points), min(p.z for p in geom.points), max(p.x for p in geom.points), max(p.y for p in geom.points), max(p.z for p in geom.points)) def creategrid(bbox, divisions): return [[[0.0 for in range(divisions)] for in range(divisions)] for in range(divisions)] def creategridfromvolume(vol): return [[[0.0 for in range(vol.divisionsx)] for in range(vol.divisionsy)] for in range(vol.divisionsz)] def computerayintersectsdf(grid, geom, tolerance): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = rayintersectdistance(x, y, z, geom, tolerance) def computemetaballsdf(grid, geom): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = metaballfield(x, y, z, geom) def fillgridwithbbox(grid, geom): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = 0.0 def fillgridwithboundingsphere(grid, geom): center, radius = computeboundingsphere(geom) for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): dist = distancetocenter(x, y, z, center) grid[x][y][z] = radius - dist def createplanesdf(grid, geom): bbox = computeboundingbox(geom) planeaxis = min(bbox[0], bbox[1], bbox[2]) for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = 0.0 if belowplane(x, y, z, planeaxis) else 1.0 def computeminimumdistancesdf(grid, geom, offset): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = mindistancetosurface(x, y, z, geom) + offset def samplevolumesdf(grid, vol): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = vol.sample(x, y, z) def computeheightfieldsdf(grid, vol): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = vol.height(x, y) def computelaserscansdf(grid, geom, tolerance): for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: for coord in range(len(grid)): ray = castrayalongaxis(axis, coord, geom, tolerance) if ray.intersections: inside = False for hit in ray.intersections: if not inside: inside = True start = hit.t else: inside = False end = hit.t markvoxelsbetween(start, end, axis, coord, grid, value=1.0) def computefullraysdf(grid, geom, tolerance): for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: for coord in range(len(grid)): ray = castrayalongaxis(axis, coord, geom, tolerance) if ray.intersections: for i in range(0, len(ray.intersections) - 1, 2): start = ray.intersections[i].t end = ray.intersections[i+1].t markvoxelsbetween(start, end, axis, coord, grid, value=1.0 if isinside(start, end, geom) else -1.0) def correctsigns(grid, geom): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): if not isconsistentsign(x, y, z, grid): grid[x][y][z] = propagatesign(x, y, z, grid) def forceboundaryexterior(grid): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): if isboundaryvoxel(x, y, z, grid): grid[x][y][z] = abs(grid[x][y][z]) def sweepsigns(grid, threshold, geom, cellwidth): flipped = False for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): if abs(grid[x][y][z] - grid[x+1][y][z]) > threshold cellwidth: correct = rayintersectinside(x, y, z, geom) if grid[x][y][z] != correct: grid[x][y][z] = correct flipped = True return flipped def invertsdf(grid): for x in range(len(grid)): for y in range(len(grid[0])): for z in range(len(grid[0][0])): grid[x][y][z] = -grid[x][y][z] def computecellwidth(grid): return 1.0 / len(grid) # Assumes normalized grid spacing Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-watertight Geometry: Use Laser Scan mode to avoid reliance on normals. Interior Features: Laser Scan mode cannot represent interior features. Sign Inversion Stabilization: Fix Signs may stabilize inverted signs at the boundary; use Force Bounds to mitigate. Convergence: Too low a Sign Sweep Threshold may prevent convergence. Hollow Objects: Use Invert Sign on an inner box for robust hollow representation. Time Complexity: Depends on grid resolution (Divisions) and geometry complexity. Sign sweeps add iterative cost. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the grid. Data sharing options (Share Data Across All Time, Share Data In One Timestep) can significantly reduce memory footprint for multiple objects. Strengths: Fast inside/outside testing; robust handling of non-watertight geometry via Laser Scanning; flexible modes for different geometry types. Limitations: Precomputation cost; memory usage for high-resolution grids; potential for sign errors requiring post-processing. When to Use: Rigid body collision detection in simulations. When Not to Use: When visual fidelity of the volume is the primary goal rather than collision topology; when geometry is extremely complex and grid resolution cannot capture details. The SDF Representation DOP is part of Houdini's dynamics (DOP) network, designed to integrate signed distance fields into simulation workflows for collision detection. It builds on the concept of SDFs as functions evaluating distance to surface with sign indicating inside/outside. name: Distance to Natural Quadrics
head: Natural Quadrics SDF, SDF for Natural Quadrics
body: Distance to Natural Quadrics provides closed-form Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for standard solid modeling primitives, including the plane, sphere, cylinder, cone, and torus. These functions compute the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of the primitive, enabling valid sphere tracing in volume rendering and constructive solid geometry (CSG). The method evaluates the scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) for a specific primitive type. The input is the query point \mathbf{p} in world or local coordinates, and primitive-specific parameters (e.g., radius, height, normal). The output is a signed distance value: positive outside, negative inside, and zero on the surface. Point \mathbf{p}: A 3D vector (px, py, pz). Parameters: Sphere: Center \mathbf{c}, radius r. Plane: Point \mathbf{p}0 on plane, unit normal \mathbf{n}. Cylinder: Radius r, half-height h (for capped), or infinite. Cone: Apex, axis direction, divergence angle \theta or sin/cos components. Torus: Major radius R, minor radius r. 1. Sphere The distance is the Euclidean distance to the center minus the radius. d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\| - r For a unit sphere at the origin: d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - 1. 2. Plane The distance is the dot product of the vector from a point on the plane to the query point and the plane's normal. d(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}0) where \mathbf{n} is the unit normal and \mathbf{p}0 is a point on the plane. 3. Cylinder (Infinite) Sources define alignment differently; uses the Z-axis with XY-plane projection, while use the Y-axis with XZ-plane projection. For Y-axis alignment: d(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r Note: This formula applies to infinite cylinders. Capped variants combine this with cap distances. 4. Cone For a cone centered at the origin oriented along the Z-axis with divergence angle \theta: d(\mathbf{p}) = \text{dist}{2D}((px, pz), \text{cone profile}) The derivation involves the geometry of the cone's cross-section. A robust implementation uses the following logic: Let q = h \cdot (\frac{cx}{cy}, -1) where c = (\cos \theta, \sin \theta) and h is height. Let w = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}, py). Calculate vectors a and b based on clamped projections of w onto q. d = \text{sign}(s) \sqrt{\min(\|a\|^2, \|b\|^2)} where s determines the sign based on the position relative to the cone's axis and base. 5. Torus The torus is defined as the product of two circles. Let R be the major radius and r be the minor radius. q = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R, py) d(\mathbf{p}) = \|q\| - r Typical values for a torus might be R=0.8 and r=0.3. 6. Capped Cylinder (Y-axis aligned) This combines the infinite cylinder distance with cap distances. Let d = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - r, |py| - h), where r is radius and h is half-height. d{\text{final}} = \min(\max(dx, dy), 0) + \sqrt{\max(dx, 0)^2 + \max(dy, 0)^2} If the clamped Y component differs from the original Y (indicating the point is outside the height bounds), the distance to the nearest cap is added. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdfsphere(p, center, radius): dx = p[0] - center[0] dy = p[1] - center[1] dz = p[2] - center[2] return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) - radius def sdfplane(p, p0, normal): dx = p[0] - p0[0] dy = p[1] - p0[1] dz = p[2] - p0[2] return dxnormal[0] + dynormal[1] + dznormal[2] def sdfcylinderinfinite(p, radius): return math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - radius def sdfcone(p, halfheight, costheta, sintheta): # c = (costheta, sintheta), q = h (cx/cy, -1) qx = halfheight (costheta / sintheta) qy = -halfheight wx = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) wy = p[1] # Clamped projections dotwq = wx qx + wy qy dotqq = qx qx + qy qy t1 = max(0.0, min(1.0, dotwq / dotqq)) ax = wx - qx t1 ay = wy - qy t1 t2x = max(0.0, min(1.0, wx / qx)) t2y = 1.0 bx = wx - qx t2x by = wy - qy t2y dsq = min(axax + ayay, bxbx + byby) k = 1.0 if qy > 0 else -1.0 s = max(k (wx qy - wy qx), k (wy - qy)) return math.sqrt(dsq) math.copysign(1.0, s) def sdftorus(p, majorradius, minorradius): qx = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - majorradius qy = p[1] return math.sqrt(qx2 + qy2) - minorradius def sdfcylindercapped(p, radius, halfheight): dx = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - radius dy = abs(p[1]) - halfheight mind = min(max(dx, dy), 0.0) maxd = math.sqrt(max(dx, 0.0)2 + max(dy, 0.0)2) return mind + maxd Precision: Near the surface (d \approx 0), floating-point precision errors can cause jitter in ray marching. A small epsilon threshold should be used to terminate marching. Transformations: When using these primitives in a scene, points must be transformed into the primitive's local space using the inverse transformation matrix M^{-1} before evaluation Standard Solid Primitives. Lipschitz Condition: These functions satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring they are safe lower bounds for sphere tracing Standard Solid Primitives. Generalizes natural quadrics using Lp norms for rounded or pinched shapes. Choose when non-Euclidean cross-sections are needed. Computes exact distance to finite cylinders with caps. Choose for standard capped cylindrical geometry. Specific implementation for tori. Choose for ring-like topologies. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. The operations involve basic arithmetic and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are required. Performance: Highly efficient, suitable for real-time rendering and dense ray marching. Strengths: Analytical precision, no discretization error, smooth gradients (where differentiable). Limitations: Limited to specific geometric shapes. Complex blends or deformations may require more general SDF techniques. The method derives from appendices that provide signed distance functions, bounds, and Lipschitz constants to aid sphere tracing implementation and serve as a tutorial for developing other primitives. These primitives form the basis of Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) in ray marching. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) (PDF) Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2792108SphereTracingAGeometricMethodfortheAntialiasedRayTracingofImplicitSurfaces, fetched 2026-10-27 Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields - Scribd, https://www.scribd.com/document/831412915/1-Ray-Marching-and-Signed-Distance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Introduction to Raymarching Distance Functions, https://observablehq.com/@gre/introduction-to-raymarching-distance-functions, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Distance to Superquadrics
head: Superellipsoid distance, Superellipsoids, Superquadric Distance via p-norm, Supertori, pq-norm distance
body: Distance to Superquadrics generalizes standard natural quadrics (spheres, cylinders, cones) and tori into superquadrics and supertori by replacing the Euclidean L2 norm with the Lp (or L{pq}) norm. This method allows for the creation of shapes with rounded, square, or pinched cross-sections by varying the exponent parameter p. It is distinct from Distance to Natural Quadrics because it operates in a non-Euclidean metric space, requiring a specific conversion to Euclidean distances to ensure consistent ray marching behavior and blending with other primitives. Inputs: Point p = (x, y, z) in 3D space. Shape exponent p (scalar, p > 0). Radius r (scalar, defining the scale of the superellipsoid). Optional: Exponents p, q for asymmetric superquadrics (supertori or generalized ellipsoids). Outputs: Signed distance d(p) in Euclidean space. Data Structures: No persistent data structures required. The function is stateless and computes the distance analytically per query. Formulas: The core distance metric is the Lp norm. In 2D, the Lp norm of a vector (x, y) is defined as: ||(x, y)||p = (|x|^p + |y|^p)^{1/p} In 3D, for a superellipsoid centered at the origin, the implicit surface is defined by: (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} = r The raw distance in the Lp metric, denoted dp(p), is calculated as: dp(p) = (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} - r Euclidean Conversion: Because ray marching requires a unifying Euclidean metric space to compare distances between different primitives and to ensure the step size is safe (i.e., the ray does not pass through the surface), the Lp distance must be converted to an equivalent Euclidean distance. Let re be the radius of the largest Euclidean sphere inscribed within the Lp-norm superellipsoid of radius r (in the Lp metric). The conversion factor depends on p: re = \begin{cases} r \cdot \frac{3^{1/p}}{\sqrt{3}} & \text{if } p < 2 \\ r & \text{if } p \ge 2 \end{cases} The final Euclidean signed distance d{eucl}(p) is scaled by the ratio of the inscribed radius to the nominal radius: d{eucl}(p) = dp(p) \cdot \frac{re}{r} Substituting re/r: d{eucl}(p) = \begin{cases} \left( (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} - r \right) \cdot \frac{3^{1/p}}{\sqrt{3}} & \text{if } p < 2 \\ (|x|^p + |y|^p + |z|^p)^{1/p} - r & \text{if } p \ge 2 \end{cases} Parameters: p: Controls the shape. p = 2: Euclidean sphere (round). p = 1: Octahedron (diamond in 2D). p \to \infty: Cube (square in 2D, chessboard metric). 0 < p < 1: Pinched or star-shaped variations. r: Base radius. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def distancetosuperquadricsdf(x, y, z, p, r): """Computes the Euclidean signed distance to a superellipsoid.""" if p <= 0: return float('inf') sump = abs(x)p + abs(y)p + abs(z)p lpnorm = sump (1.0 / p) dlp = lpnorm - r if p < 2.0: factor = (3.0 (1.0 / p)) / math.sqrt(3.0) else: factor = 1.0 return dlp factor def raymarchsuperquadric(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, p, r, maxsteps=1000, maxdist=100.0, tol=1e-4): """Standard sphere tracing loop using the superquadric SDF.""" t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return float('inf') px = ox + t dx py = oy + t dy pz = oz + t dz d = distancetosuperquadricsdf(px, py, pz, p, r) if d < tol: return t t += d return float('inf') Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Metric Unification: Using Lp distances directly for blending or comparison with other primitives (like spheres or cylinders) is invalid because they exist in different metric spaces. The Euclidean conversion is mandatory for correct visual results in composite scenes. Precision: For very large p, |x|^p can overflow or underflow. Standard floating-point handling applies. Degenerate Input: p=0 is undefined. p < 0 produces non-convex, pinched shapes that may require specialized handling not covered by the standard convex superellipsoid definition. A generalization of the torus using Lp norms for both the major and minor circles. It follows the same conversion principles as superellipsoids but applies the norm to the distance evaluation of the torus's cross-section. Uses different exponents p and q for different axes (e.g., |x|^p + |y|^q + |z|^p). This allows for asymmetric shapes. The Euclidean conversion factor must be derived based on the specific p, q values, typically involving the maximum inscribed sphere in the asymmetric metric. Calculates the radius of the largest Euclidean sphere re inscribed within a pq-norm superellipsoid of radius rs in the pq-norm metric. The formula is re = rs \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt[p]{3} + \sqrt[q]{3}} if p or q < 2, otherwise re = rs \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Requires O(1) arithmetic operations (powers, roots, absolute values). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Provides a continuous family of shapes from spheres to cubes to pinched forms with a single parameter. Efficient for ray marching when the Euclidean conversion is applied. Limitations: The gradient is not always smooth at p=1 or p \to \infty boundaries in the raw metric, though the Euclidean conversion helps maintain continuity in the signed distance field. The conversion factor is an approximation based on the inscribed sphere; it ensures safety (no tunneling) but may result in slightly larger step sizes than strictly necessary for non-spherical shapes, potentially slowing convergence slightly compared to exact analytical normals for simple primitives. While natural quadrics rely on the Euclidean L2 norm, superquadrics utilize the Lp norm to create a broader class of implicit surfaces. name: Cylinder Signed Distance Function

body: The Cylinder Signed Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of a finite cylinder defined by two endpoints and a radius. It solves the problem of ray marching against capped cylindrical primitives, which are common in scene geometry and constructive solid geometry (CSG). Unlike the infinite cylinder SDF, this method accounts for the end caps, returning the distance to the nearest point on the curved side, the top cap, or the bottom cap. It is distinct from Distance to Superquadrics and Torus Signed Distance Function by its specific piecewise definition based on the projection onto the cylinder's axis. Input: A query point v \in \mathbb{R}^3, two endpoints c1, c2 \in \mathbb{R}^3 defining the cylinder axis, and a radius r \in \mathbb{R}^+. Output: A scalar signed distance d. d < 0 if inside, d = 0 on surface, d > 0 if outside. No complex data structures are required. The method operates on standard 3D vectors and scalars. The algorithm determines the closest point on the infinite line segment defined by c1 and c2, then computes the distance to that point, adjusting for the radius and the capped ends. 1. Compute Axis Vector and Length: Let dir = c2 - c1. Let h = \|dir\| be the height (length) of the cylinder. 2. Project Query Point onto Axis: Compute the parameter t representing the normalized position of the projection of v onto the line segment [c1, c2]. t = \frac{dir \cdot (v - c1)}{dir \cdot dir} Here, t=0 corresponds to c1 and t=1 corresponds to c2. 3. Compute Closest Point on Infinite Line: p = c1 + dir \cdot t This is the closest point on the infinite line passing through c1 and c2. 4. Compute Side Distance: Calculate the distance from the query point to the axis line, minus the radius. side\dist = \|v - p\| - r This value is negative if the point is inside the infinite cylinder and positive if outside. 5. Determine Final Distance Based on t: The final distance depends on whether the projection p falls within the segment [c1, c2] (i.e., 0 \le t \le 1) or outside it. Case A: Inside the segment (0 \le t \le 1): The closest point on the capped cylinder is either on the side wall or on one of the end caps. If side\dist \ge 0 (outside the side wall), the distance is simply side\dist. If side\dist < 0 (inside the side wall), the point is inside the infinite cylinder. The signed distance is the negative of the minimum distance to any surface (side wall or caps). d = \max(side\dist, -h \cdot t, -h \cdot (1-t)) Case B: Projection beyond c2 (t > 1): The distance to the cap plane is dist\cap = h \cdot (t - 1). If side\dist \ge 0, the closest point is on the cap edge (corner), so d = \sqrt{side\dist^2 + dist\cap^2}. If side\dist < 0, the closest point is on the cap face, so d = -dist\cap. Case C: Projection before c1 (t < 0): The distance to the cap plane is dist\cap = h \cdot (-t). If side\dist \ge 0, the closest point is on the cap edge, so d = \sqrt{side\dist^2 + dist\cap^2}. If side\dist < 0, the closest point is on the cap face, so d = -dist\cap. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcappedcylinder(v, c1, c2, r): # v, c1, c2 are 3D vectors (x, y, z) # r is radius dir = c2 - c1 hsq = dot(dir, dir) # Handle degenerate cylinder (point) if hsq < 1e-12: return length(v - c1) - r h = sqrt(hsq) # Project v onto the line segment t = dot(dir, v - c1) / hsq # Closest point on the infinite line p = c1 + dir t # Distance to the axis, minus radius sidedist = length(v - p) - r if t >= 0.0 and t <= 1.0: # Projection falls within the segment if sidedist >= 0.0: # Outside the side wall return sidedist else: # Inside the side wall # Return negative distance to nearest surface (side or caps) return max(sidedist, -h t, -h (1.0 - t)) elif t > 1.0: # Projection beyond c2 distcap = h (t - 1.0) if sidedist >= 0.0: # Outside side wall, distance to corner (cap edge) return sqrt(sidedist sidedist + distcap distcap) else: # Inside side wall, closest point is on the cap face return -distcap else: # t < 0.0 # Projection before c1 distcap = h (-t) if sidedist >= 0.0: # Outside side wall, distance to corner (cap edge) return sqrt(sidedist sidedist + distcap distcap) else: # Inside side wall, closest point is on the cap face return -distcap c1, c2: Endpoints of the cylinder axis. r: Radius of the cylinder. Degenerate Cylinder: If c1 = c2, the height is 0. The function should return the distance to a sphere of radius r centered at c1. Precision: When t is very close to 0 or 1, floating point errors may cause the point to be classified incorrectly as outside the segment, leading to a discontinuity in the derivative. Clamping t to [0, 1] before computing p can help, but the distance calculation must remain consistent. Axis Alignment: For axis-aligned cylinders, the formula from (d = abs(vec2(length(p.xz),p.y)) - h; return min(max(d.x,d.y),0.0) + length(max(d,0.0))) is structurally identical to the box SDF but in 2D radial coordinates. It avoids branching and is preferred for performance in aligned cases. Computes the signed distance to a 2D ring (annulus) with radius r and thickness th. It is defined as |\|p\| - r| - th \cdot 0.5. This is effectively a 2D cross-section of a torus or a flat cylinder with a hole. Time Complexity: O(1). The computation involves a constant number of vector operations, dot products, and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are needed. Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time ray marching. The square root operation is the most expensive part, but it is unavoidable for Euclidean distance. Strengths: Exact distance, works for any orientation (if general algorithm is used), robust for CSG operations. Limitations: The general endpoint-based algorithm involves more branches than the axis-aligned version. For axis-aligned cylinders, the formula is preferred for performance. Signed distance functions for basic primitives are foundational in ray marching and implicit modeling. The cylinder SDF is a standard primitive, often attributed to the work on SDFs by Inigo Quilez and others in the demoscene and computer graphics community. body: Computes the distance to the global offset surface of a cubic Bézier space curve, modeling a generalized cylinder with a fixed radius. It differs from closed-form primitive SDFs by solving for the closest point on a parametric curve through root finding of the orthogonality condition. Inputs: Query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, cubic Bézier control points P0, P1, P2, P3 \in \mathbb{R}^3, radius R. Outputs: Signed distance d(x) to the offset surface. Data Structures: Control points stored as 3D vectors, coefficients for the degree-5 polynomial derived from the orthogonality condition. Steps: 1. Define the space curve parametrically as p(u) for u \in [0, 1]. 2. Translate coordinates so the query point is at the origin for derivation, or use relative coordinates q = x - p(u). 3. Find the closest point p(u) satisfying the orthogonality condition (x - p(u)) \cdot p'(u) = 0. 4. Convert the orthogonality equation into a degree-5 1D Bézier curve. 5. Solve the degree-5 1D Bézier curve efficiently for roots in [0, 1]. 6. Compute the distance r = \|p(u^)\| for each valid root and the endpoints, then return d(x) = r - R. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def comb(n, k): if k < 0 or k > n: return 0 if k == 0 or k == n: return 1 if k > n // 2: k = n - k res = 1 for i in range(k): res = res (n - i) // (i + 1) return res def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def bezierpoint(Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, u): u2, u3 = uu, uuu u1, u12, u13 = 1-u, (1-u)(1-u), (1-u)(1-u)(1-u) return (u13Q0 + 3u12uQ1 + 3u1u2Q2 + u3Q3) def bernsteinsubdivision(coeffs, degree): n = degree left = [0.0] (n + 1) right = [0.0] (n + 1) left[0] = coeffs[0] right[n] = coeffs[n] for i in range(1, n + 1): left[i] = left[i-1] (n - i + 1) / n + coeffs[i] / n right[n - i] = right[n - i + 1] i / n + coeffs[n - i] / n return left[:n//2 + 1], right[n//2:] def findbernsteinroots(coeffs, degree): roots = [] def subdivide(c, deg, umin, umax): if deg == 0: if abs(c[0]) < 1e-9: roots.append((umin + umax) / 2.0) return if min(c) max(c) > 0: return if umax - umin < 1e-7: roots.append(umin); return c1, c2 = bernsteinsubdivision(c, deg) mid = (umin + umax) / 2.0 subdivide(c1, deg // 2, umin, mid) subdivide(c2, deg // 2, mid, umax) subdivide(coeffs, degree, 0.0, 1.0) return roots def beziersdf(x, P0, P1, P2, P3, R): Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3 = (P0 - x), (P1 - x), (P2 - x), (P3 - x) D0, D1, D2 = 3(Q1 - Q0), 3(Q2 - Q1), 3(Q3 - Q2) coeffs = [0.0] 6 for k in range(6): val = 0.0 for i in range(k + 1): if i <= 3 and (k - i) <= 2: factor = (comb(3, i) comb(2, k - i)) / comb(5, k) val += factor dot([Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3][i], [D0, D1, D2][k - i]) coeffs[k] = val roots = findbernsteinroots(coeffs, 5) mindistsq = min(dot(Q0, Q0), dot(Q3, Q3)) for u in roots: if 0.0 <= u <= 1.0: mindistsq = min(mindistsq, dot(bezierpoint(Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, u), bezierpoint(Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, u))) return (mindistsq 0.5) - R Parameters: R: Radius of the generalized cylinder. Typical values depend on scene scale. Edge Cases: The closest point may lie at the curve endpoints u=0 or u=1, requiring explicit boundary checks. The degree-5 polynomial may yield multiple valid roots; the global minimum distance must be selected. Precision issues may occur near degenerate curves or when the query point lies exactly on the curve. The Footvector Representation is a geometric generalization of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for curves and surfaces, defined by the vector pointing from a query point to its closest point (footpoint) on the shape. Unlike standard SDFs which only provide scalar distance, this representation retains directional information, enabling exact offset surface computation for Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) operations via fast iterative methods. It builds on the Bézier Curve Signed Distance Function and differs from the Spline Tube to Cylinder Mapping by explicitly tracking the footpoint vector rather than mapping to a cylinder tube. It is chosen when precise geometric invariants and exact offsetting are required, though it poses implementation challenges for GPU shaders due to higher-order function mappings. Spline Tube to Cylinder Mapping is a technique for mapping points from an arbitrary spline tube to a canonical vertical cylinder, enabling the direct querying of pre-defined isotropic procedural density fields. It solves the problem of inverse parameterization in volumetric rendering by providing a robust Signed Distance Function (SDF) to the curve, which yields the curvilinear abscissa required for texture coordinate calculation. Memory Complexity: Minimal, storing only four 3D control points and the radius. Strengths: Provides exact distance to smooth, organic tubes without discretization artifacts. Limitations: Root finding can be numerically unstable for highly curved or nearly linear segments. When to use: Rendering skeletal models or generalized cylinders where exact offset surfaces are required. When not to use: Performance-critical applications where linear segment approximation or simpler primitives suffice. Originated in implicit modeling and ray tracing of generalized cylinders. body: Spline Tube to Cylinder Mapping is a technique for mapping points from an arbitrary spline tube to a canonical vertical cylinder, enabling the direct querying of pre-defined isotropic procedural density fields. It solves the problem of inverse parameterization in volumetric rendering by providing a robust Signed Distance Function (SDF) to the curve, which yields the curvilinear abscissa required for texture coordinate calculation. Inputs: A point P in 3D space. A spline curve C(t) defining the axis of the tube. The radius function r(l) of the tube at curvilinear abscissa l (default constant r=1 if not specified). A reference cylinder defined with radius 1 and height 1, with its lower base centered at the origin. Outputs: Mapped coordinates M in the reference cylinder. The distance to the tube surface (derived from the SDF, if solvable). Data Structures: Spline Curve C(t): Defined by control points. For Bézier segments, this is a set of control points A, B, C (quadratic) or P0, P1, P2, P3 (cubic). Frenet Frame at O: Consisting of the tangent \mathbf{T}, normal \mathbf{N}, and binormal \mathbf{B} vectors at the closest point O on the curve. Steps: 1. Find Closest Point: Find the point O on the spline curve C which is closest to P. Let t be the parameter such that O = C(t). This step is critical; if solvable, it justifies the use of Sphere Marching for bounding box detection. 2. Construct Frenet Frame: Using the Frenet–Serret formulas, create the Frenet Frame associated with the spline curve at point O. Calculate the tangent \mathbf{T} = C'(t) / \|C'(t)\|. Calculate the normal \mathbf{N} and binormal \mathbf{B} using the derivatives of \mathbf{T} (specifically \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{T}' / \|\mathbf{T}'\| and \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N}). 3. Calculate Angle: Calculate the angle \alpha between the vector \vec{OP} and the Frenet’s unit normal vector \mathbf{N}. Let \vec{V} = P - O. \alpha = \text{atan2}(\vec{V} \cdot \mathbf{B}, \vec{V} \cdot \mathbf{N}). 4. Find Curvilinear Abscissa: Find the curvilinear abscissa l of O, defined as the arc length of the spline curve from the beginning of the tube to O. 5. Calculate Mapped Coordinates: Calculate the mapped coordinates M in the original cylinder. The curvilinear abscissa l represents the height. The angle \alpha deduces the unit direction \text{dir} from the center of the disk at height l toward M. The length of \vec{OP} calculates the radial distance. Formula: M = \left(\cos(\alpha) \cdot \frac{\|\vec{OP}\|}{r(l)},\ l,\ \sin(\alpha) \cdot \frac{\|\vec{OP}\|}{r(l)}\right) Note: If stretching is desired, replace l with t = l / L{\text{total}}, where L{\text{total}} is the total length of the spline curve. C: callable C(t) returning 3D point rfunc: callable r(l) returning radius at arc length l """ # Step 1: Find closest point O on the spline curve to P # Sources do not specify the exact closest-point solver. # Standard approach: minimize ||C(t) - P||^2 via Newton-Raphson or root finding. tclosest = 0.5 # Placeholder initialization; replace with actual solver O = C(tclosest) # Step 2: Construct Frenet Frame at O # Approximate derivatives numerically for implementation clarity. delta = 1e-5 T = (C(tclosest + delta) - C(tclosest - delta)) / (2 delta) T = tuple(x / math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in T)) for x in T) Tprime = (C(tclosest + 2delta) - 2C(tclosest + delta) + C(tclosest)) / (delta2) N = tuple(x / math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in Tprime)) for x in Tprime) B = (T[1]N[2] - T[2]N[1], T[2]N[0] - T[0]N[2], T[0]N[1] - T[1]N[0]) # Step 3: Calculate angle alpha V = (P[0]-O[0], P[1]-O[1], P[2]-O[2]) alpha = math.atan2(sum(vb for v, b in zip(V, B)), sum(vn for v, n in zip(V, N))) # Step 4: Find curvilinear abscissa l # Sources do not specify arc length computation. # Standard approach: numerical integration of ||C'(u)|| from 0 to tclosest. l = 0.0 # Placeholder for arc length integral # Step 5: Calculate mapped coordinates M r = rfunc(l) distOP = math.sqrt(sum(vv for v in V)) if usestretching: Ltotal = 1.0 # Placeholder for total curve length height = l / Ltotal else: height = l M = (math.cos(alpha) distOP / r, height, math.sin(alpha) distOP / r) return M Parameters: Reference Cylinder: Vertical cylinder of radius 1 and height 1, with its lower base centered at the origin. Stretching: Optional boolean flag. If true, height is normalized by total curve length. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stretching vs. Bending: Making a longer spline tube without stretching does not stretch the volume; it looks like a longer cylinder was bent. Stretching is required to simulate expansion. Varying Radius: If the radius varies, the surface normal is no longer perpendicular to the curve axis. This makes the SDF function problematic and can create bugs where boundaries are not detected properly during sphere marching. Closest Point Solvability: If the closest point O is solvable, an SDF function can be derived, justifying the use of sphere marching for bounding box detection. Quadratic Bezier Tube Deformation is a technique for mapping points from an arbitrary spline tube defined by quadratic Bezier segments to a canonical vertical cylinder, enabling the use of pre-defined density fields. It solves the problem of inverse parameterization in volumetric rendering by providing a robust Signed Distance Function (SDF) to the curve, which yields the curvilinear abscissa required for texture coordinate calculation. It is distinguished from cubic spline approaches by its computational simplicity in finding the closest point and curvilinear abscissa, though it imposes stricter constraints on segment concatenation. The radius of the Bezier/spline curve is defined as a function of the curvilinear abscissa, allowing shapes like cones or DNA-like tubes. Varying radius makes the surface normal no longer perpendicular to the curve axis, which is problematic for the SDF function and sphere marching. It can create bugs where boundaries are not detected properly. Altering the angle used for mapping to induce a twisting effect. The angle can depend on the curvilinear abscissa or time. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows for complex, bent, and twisted volumetric shapes using simple procedural density fields defined on a cylinder. The SDF derivation justifies efficient bounding box culling via sphere marching. Limitations: Varying radius complicates the SDF and boundary detection. The method assumes the spline curve is well-behaved enough to find a unique closest point. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the context of real-time rendering of interstellar dust clouds and solar flares. It allows for the deformation of procedural density fields without storing and transforming the density field itself. The technique relies on the Frenet–Serret formulas, originally developed by Jean Frédéric Frenet (1847–1851) and Joseph Alfred Serret. The specific application to Bézier curves and spline tubes was detailed in a paper on sculpting procedural noise for volumetric rendering. name: Quadratic Bezier Tube Deformation
head: Bezier Curve Deformation, Quadratic Bezier Tube
body: Quadratic Bezier Tube Deformation maps points from an arbitrary spline tube defined by quadratic Bezier segments to a canonical vertical cylinder, enabling the use of pre-defined density fields [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. It solves the inverse parameterization problem in volumetric rendering by providing a robust Signed Distance Function (SDF) to the curve, which yields the curvilinear abscissa required for texture coordinate calculation. It is distinguished from cubic spline approaches by its computational simplicity in finding the closest point and curvilinear abscissa, though it imposes stricter constraints on segment concatenation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point P in world space; a ray origin and direction for bounding box culling; a list of quadratic Bezier segments defining the curve. Each segment i is defined by three control points Ai, Bi, Ci. Output: The deformed coordinates (u, v, w) in the canonical cylinder space, where u and v are angular/radial coordinates and w is the curvilinear abscissa (normalized height) [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. Data Structures: Bezier Segment: Defined by three 3D vectors A, B, C. A: Start point (t=0). B: Control point (pulls the curve). C: End point (t=1). Segment List: An ordered array of segments. For concatenation, the start of segment i+1 must equal the end of segment i (A{i+1} = Ci). Formulas: The quadratic Bezier curve for a segment is defined as: Q(t) = (1-t)^2 A + 2(1-t)t B + t^2 C, \quad t \in [0, 1] The segment starts at A when t=0, finishes at C when t=1, and is pulled toward B in between. The tangent at t=0 is parallel to vector \vec{AB} = B - A, and the tangent at t=1 is parallel to vector \vec{BC} = C - B. To find the deformation, we must find the closest point on the curve to P. This is achieved by computing the SDF to the quadratic Bezier segment. The SDF implementation (based on Quilez 2013) returns both the distance and the parameter t of the closest point, which corresponds to the curvilinear abscissa. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set mindist to infinity and bestt to 0. 2. Iterate Segments: For each segment i in the curve: a. Optimization (Ray Casting): Perform a ray-casting test against the bounding box of segment i relative to the ray origin. If the ray does not intersect the bounding box, skip this segment. Cache this result per pixel to avoid re-evaluation during ray marching. b. SDF Evaluation: Compute the SDF from point P to the quadratic Bezier segment i. Let the result be di and the closest point parameter be ti. c. Update Minimum: If di < \text{min\dist}, set \text{min\dist} = di and \text{best\t} = ti. 3. Map to Cylinder: Using the best t found, map the point to the canonical cylinder [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. The height w is normalized based on the total length of the curve or the segment's contribution. The radial and angular coordinates are derived from the vector from the closest point on the curve to P [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quadraticbeziersdf(P, A, B, C): """Computes SDF to a quadratic Bezier segment. Returns (distance, t). """ def Q(t): u = 1.0 - t return ((uu)A[0] + 2.0utB[0] + ttC[0], (uu)A[1] + 2.0utB[1] + ttC[1], (uu)A[2] + 2.0utB[2] + ttC[2]) def dQ(t): u = 1.0 - t return (2.0u(B[0]-A[0]) + 2.0t(C[0]-B[0]), 2.0u(B[1]-A[1]) + 2.0t(C[1]-B[1]), 2.0u(B[2]-A[2]) + 2.0t(C[2]-B[2])) t = 0.5 for in range(10): diff = (P[0]-Q(t)[0], P[1]-Q(t)[1], P[2]-Q(t)[2]) dot = diff[0]dQ(t)[0] + diff[1]dQ(t)[1] + diff[2]dQ(t)[2] if abs(dot) < 1e-6: break ddot = dQ(t)[0]2 + dQ(t)[1]2 + dQ(t)[2]2 + \ diff[0]2.0(C[0]-2.0B[0]+A[0]) + diff[1]2.0(C[1]-2.0B[1]+A[1]) + diff[2]2.0(C[2]-2.0B[2]+A[2]) if abs(ddot) < 1e-12: break t -= dot / ddot t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) dist = math.sqrt((P[0]-Q(t)[0])2 + (P[1]-Q(t)[1])2 + (P[2]-Q(t)[2])2) return dist, t def getboundingbox(A, B, C): """Computes axis-aligned bounding box for quadratic Bezier segment. """ denomx = A[0] - 2.0B[0] + C[0] textx = max(0.0, min(1.0, (A[0]-B[0])/denomx)) if denomx != 0 else 0.0 denomy = A[1] - 2.0B[1] + C[1] texty = max(0.0, min(1.0, (A[1]-B[1])/denomy)) if denomy != 0 else 0.0 denomz = A[2] - 2.0B[2] + C[2] textz = max(0.0, min(1.0, (A[2]-B[2])/denomz)) if denomz != 0 else 0.0 mins = [min(A[0], B[0], C[0]), min(A[1], B[1], C[1]), min(A[2], B[2], C[2])] maxs = [max(A[0], B[0], C[0]), max(A[1], B[1], C[1]), max(A[2], B[2], C[2])] for text in [textx, texty, textz]: if 0.0 < text < 1.0: u = 1.0 - text ext = (uu)A[0] + 2.0utextB[0] + texttextC[0] exty = (uu)A[1] + 2.0utextB[1] + texttextC[1] extz = (uu)A[2] + 2.0utextB[2] + texttextC[2] mins[0] = min(mins[0], ext); mins[1] = min(mins[1], exty); mins[2] = min(mins[2], extz) maxs[0] = max(maxs[0], ext); maxs[1] = max(maxs[1], exty); maxs[2] = max(maxs[2], extz) return mins, maxs def rayintersectsbbox(rayorigin, raydirection, mins, maxs): """Checks if ray intersects AABB using slab method. Returns True. """ eps = 1e-8 tmin = (mins[0] - rayorigin[0]) / max(abs(raydirection[0]), eps) tmax = (maxs[0] - rayorigin[0]) / max(abs(raydirection[0]), eps) if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (mins[1] - rayorigin[1]) / max(abs(raydirection[1]), eps) tymax = (maxs[1] - rayorigin[1]) / max(abs(raydirection[1]), eps) if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if (tmin > tymax) or (tymin > tmax): return False if tymin > tmin: tmin = tymin if tymax < tmax: tmax = tymax tzmin = (mins[2] - rayorigin[2]) / max(abs(raydirection[2]), eps) tzmax = (maxs[2] - rayorigin[2]) / max(abs(raydirection[2]), eps) if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin if (tmin > tzmax) or (tzmin > tmax): return False if tzmin > tmin: tmin = tzmin return tmax >= 0.0 def deformpoint(P, rayorigin, raydirection, segments, pixelcache): """Deforms point P to cylinder coordinates using quadratic Bezier segments.""" mindist = float('inf') bestt = 0.0 bestseg = None cachekey = (rayorigin[0], rayorigin[1], rayorigin[2], raydirection[0], raydirection[1], raydirection[2]) for i, seg in enumerate(segments): A, B, C = seg if cachekey in pixelcache: if not pixelcache[cachekey].get(i, True): continue bboxmins, bboxmaxs = getboundingbox(A, B, C) intersects = rayintersectsbbox(rayorigin, raydirection, bboxmins, bboxmaxs) if cachekey not in pixelcache: pixelcache[cachekey] = {} pixelcache[cachekey][i] = intersects if not intersects: continue dist, t = quadraticbeziersdf(P, A, B, C) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestt = t bestseg = seg A, B, C = bestseg invt = 1.0 - bestt closestpoint = ((invtinvt)A[0] + 2.0invtbesttB[0] + besttbesttC[0], (invtinvt)A[1] + 2.0invtbesttB[1] + besttbesttC[1], (invtinvt)A[2] + 2.0invtbesttB[2] + besttbesttC[2]) vec = (P[0]-closestpoint[0], P[1]-closestpoint[1], P[2]-closestpoint[2]) u = math.atan2(vec[1], vec[0]) v = math.sqrt(vec[0]2 + vec[2]2) w = bestt return u, v, w Parameters: Ray Casting Cache: Enabled per pixel. Bounding Box Check: Used for early rejection. Note: The source indicates that a complex bounding box calculation was removed in favor of simpler ray-casting because the former was slower on average. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concatenation: Quadratic Bezier segments are difficult to concatenate smoothly. Only one control point (B) is "free" per segment. A is fixed by the previous segment's C. B must be constrained to ensure derivative continuity. Modifying one segment affects all subsequent segments. Performance: The SDF evaluation scales linearly with the number of segments. Without bounding box/ray-casting optimization, this is expensive. The ray-caching optimization is critical for performance in volumetric rendering. SDF Availability: The method relies on the availability of an SDF for quadratic Bezier segments that returns the curvilinear abscissa. This is a key reason for choosing quadratic over cubic splines. Uses open uniform B-splines instead of Bezier curves. It constructs a lattice of curves in world space to avoid inverse parameterization issues, allowing flexible shape manipulation on the CPU. Choose this when smooth, global deformation of complex volumes (like fire) is needed and CPU-side evaluation is acceptable. Time Complexity: Linear O(N) with respect to the number of Bezier segments, where N is the number of segments. With ray-casting optimization, the constant factor is significantly reduced, often evaluating only a small subset of segments per ray step. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storing control points for the segments and a small cache per pixel for bounding box intersection results. Strengths: Computationally simpler than cubic splines for finding the closest point and curvilinear abscissa. Robust SDF implementation available. Limitations: Difficult to concatenate segments smoothly. Modifications to one segment propagate to all subsequent segments. Bounding box calculation overhead can negate benefits if not optimized (ray-casting is preferred). When to Use: When a simple, robust deformation is needed for procedural volumes and the curve structure is relatively static or simple. When Not to Use: When high-degree smoothness across many segments is required, or when the curve topology changes frequently. The technique was developed for the real-time rendering of interstellar dust clouds and solar flares. Quadratic Bezier curves were chosen over cubic splines because solving for the closest point and curvilinear abscissa is computationally simpler, and a suitable SDF implementation returning the curvilinear abscissa was available (Quilez 2013). The method was implemented in a renderer using Sphere Marching for bounding box detection. A reference implementation for bounding box computation by Quilez (2020) was tested but found to be slower than simple ray-casting, leading to its removal. name: Curve-based Volumetric Free-Form Deformation
head: Volumetric Free-Form Deformation
body: Curve-based Volumetric Free-Form Deformation (VFFD) is a technique for manipulating the macro shape and flow of a volumetric unit volume (specifically procedural fire) using an open uniform B-spline curve. It solves the problem of real-time macro-level interactivity and deformation by constructing a lattice of curves around a central spline, allowing flexible shape manipulation while maintaining texture coordinates for rendering. Unlike direct deformation methods that require solving inverse parameterization on the GPU, VFFD constructs a world-space lattice associated with texture coordinates, which the graphics hardware implicitly evaluates via texture coordinate interpolation. Inputs: Control points Pi for the center spline, where i = 0 \dots n-1 and n is the number of control points. Fire radius r, defining the cross-section size. Lattice resolution c, determining the number of samples along the curve. B-spline degree p. Outputs: A lattice in world space consisting of c sections, where each section is defined by four corner curves. Texture coordinates assigned to lattice vertices to map back to the unit fire volume. Data Structures: Control Points: Array of 3D vectors Pi. Knot Vector: Values ti defining the B-spline domain. Corner Curves: Four sets of control points defining the cross-section at each lattice section. Lattice Vertices: Points in world space with associated texture coordinates (x, y, z). Formulas: The center curve C(t) is defined by the open uniform B-spline: C(t) = \sum{i=0}^{n-1} N{i, \text{degree}}(t) \cdot Pi \quad (6) where N{i,p}(t) is the B-spline basis function of degree p. The knot values ti for an open uniform B-spline are defined as: ti = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i \leq \text{degree} \\ i - \text{degree} & \text{if } \text{degree} < i < n \\ n - \text{degree} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (3) The basis functions are computed recursively: N{i,0}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } ti \leq t < t{i+1} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (4) N{i,p}(t) = \frac{t{i+p+1} - t}{t{i+p} - ti} N{i,p-1}(t) + \frac{t - ti}{t{i+p+1} - t{i+1}} N{i+1,p-1}(t) \quad (5) Steps: 1. Sample Center Curve Properties: For each control point Pi, determine the parameter t at which that control point has the most influence. For a uniform B-spline, this is t = \frac{i}{n-1} for i = 0 \dots n-1. 2. Compute Normal and Velocity: At each sampled t, compute the velocity vector \vec{V}i (tangent) and normal vector \vec{N}i of the center curve C(t). 3. Define Cross-Section Plane: For each control point Pi, define a square in the plane defined by Pi and \vec{V}i, centered at Pi. 4. Set Cross-Section Size: The edge length of the square is 2r, where r is the fire radius. 5. Align Squares: Align all n squares along their respective central curve normals \vec{N}i to reduce twisting. 6. Generate Corner Curves: Generate four additional curves by placing control points on the corners of these squares. 7. Sample Lattice Sections: Sample the center curve parameter t uniformly c times (where c is the lattice resolution) to obtain c values of t in the domain [0, 1]. 8. Evaluate Corner Positions: For each of the c sampled t values, evaluate the four corner curves using Equation (6) to obtain c sets of correlated positions on the four corner curves. 9. Assign Texture Coordinates: Assign each lattice vertex a texture coordinate \text{tex}i = (x, \frac{i}{c-1}, z), where x and z are 1 or -1 depending on which corner curve the vertex belongs to, and i is the index of the lattice section (0 \dots c-1). 10. Render Lattice: Divide the lattice into a finite set of cubes and render only the required triangles within these cubes to minimize pixel shader coverage and ensure every section is rendered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computebsplinebasis(t, knots, degree): """ Computes the B-spline basis functions N{i,p}(t) for a given t. knots: list of knot values ti degree: integer degree p Returns: list of basis function values N{i, degree}(t) """ n = len(knots) - degree - 1 # Number of control points # Initialize degree 0 basis functions N = [0.0] n for i in range(n): if knots[i] <= t < knots[i+1]: N[i] = 1.0 else: N[i] = 0.0 # Compute higher degree basis functions for p in range(1, degree + 1): for i in range(n - p + 1): leftnum = knots[i+p] - t leftden = knots[i+p] - knots[i] left = (leftnum / leftden) N[i] if leftden != 0 else 0.0 rightnum = t - knots[i] rightden = knots[i+p+1] - knots[i+1] right = (rightnum / rightden) N[i+1] if rightden != 0 else 0.0 N[i] = left + right return N def evaluatebspline(t, controlpoints, knots, degree): """Evaluates the B-spline curve C(t) at parameter t.""" basis = computebsplinebasis(t, knots, degree) point = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i, cp in enumerate(controlpoints): point[0] += basis[i] cp[0] point[1] += basis[i] cp[1] point[2] += basis[i] cp[2] return point def computetangent(t, controlpoints, knots, degree): """Computes the tangent vector C'(t) using a small finite difference.""" eps = 1e-6 p1 = evaluatebspline(t - eps, controlpoints, knots, degree) p2 = evaluatebspline(t + eps, controlpoints, knots, degree) return normalize(p2 - p1) def computenormal(tangent, upvector=(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)): """Computes a normal vector perpendicular to the tangent and a fixed up vector.""" return normalize(cross(tangent, upvector)) def normalize(v): """Standard vector normalization.""" mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if mag == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] def cross(a, b): """Standard 3D cross product.""" return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def curvebasedvffd(controlpoints, radius, latticeresolution, degree): """ Constructs the VFFD lattice. controlpoints: list of 3D vectors Pi radius: float r latticeresolution: int c degree: int p Returns: list of lattice sections, each section is a list of 4 corner points """ n = len(controlpoints) # 1. Compute knot vector for open uniform B-spline knots = [] for i in range(n + degree + 1): if i <= degree: knots.append(0.0) elif i < n: knots.append(i - degree) else: knots.append(n - degree) # 2. Sample center curve properties at t = i / (n-1) samplest = [i / (n - 1) for i in range(n)] # 3. Compute normal and velocity for each sample normals = [] velocities = [] for t in samplest: tangent = computetangent(t, controlpoints, knots, degree) normal = computenormal(tangent) normals.append(normal) velocities.append(tangent) # 4. Define corner control points for each section cornercontrolpoints = [] for i in range(n): P = controlpoints[i] N = normals[i] V = velocities[i] Vnorm = normalize(V) # Define the four corners of the square cross-section c1 = P + radius N + radius Vnorm c2 = P - radius N + radius Vnorm c3 = P - radius N - radius Vnorm c4 = P + radius N - radius Vnorm cornercontrolpoints.append([c1, c2, c3, c4]) # 5. Sample lattice sections latticetvalues = [i / (latticeresolution - 1) for i in range(latticeresolution)] latticesections = [] for idx, t in enumerate(latticetvalues): sectioncorners = [] for corneridx in range(4): basis = computebsplinebasis(t, knots, degree) cornerpoint = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(n): cp = cornercontrolpoints[i][corneridx] cornerpoint[0] += basis[i] cp[0] cornerpoint[1] += basis[i] cp[1] cornerpoint[2] += basis[i] cp[2] sectioncorners.append(cornerpoint) latticesections.append(sectioncorners) return latticesections Parameters: n: Number of control points. r: Radius of the fire, defining the cross-section size. c: Resolution of the lattice, determining the number of samples along the curve. p: Degree of the B-spline. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inverse Parameterization: The pixel shader operates on deformed world space P' to return texture space P, but the deformation function D(P) defines P' from P. This cannot be solved analytically on the GPU. The method avoids this by constructing a lattice in world space associated with texture coordinates, allowing the graphics hardware to implicitly evaluate the mapping D(P) via texture coordinate interpolation. Pixel Coverage: The shader can only render to locations occupied by triangle fragments, and the final pixel coverage is not known a priori. The method solves this by dividing the lattice into a finite set of cubes and rendering only the required triangles within these cubes. Discontinuities: Linear interpolation on the lattice creates discontinuities in the first derivative of the curve on the borders of each lattice section. Refining the lattice resolution approximates the continuous deformation to an arbitrary degree of accuracy. Precision: The knot vector construction and basis function evaluation must handle edge cases where denominators are zero (e.g., t{i+p} - ti = 0). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The performance impact of additional lattice sections is relatively small, allowing over-estimation of resolution. Strengths: Real-time macro-level interactivity, flexible shape manipulation, avoids inverse parameterization on GPU. Limitations: Discontinuities in the first derivative at lattice section borders, limited to deforming a fixed number of points without loss of detail (cannot deform the entire volume with noise in real time). When to Use: When real-time deformation of volumetric fire or similar volumes is required, and macro-level control is needed. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Curve-based Volumetric Free-Form Deformation was introduced by Alfred R. Fuller, Hari Krishnan, Karim Mahrous, Bernd Hamann, and Kenneth I. Joy from the University of California, Davis, in 2007. It was developed as part of a system for generating procedural volumetric fire in real time, combining curve-based deformation with hardware-accelerated volumetric rendering and procedural noise. The method builds on earlier work in curve-based fire design and particle simulation. name: Torus Signed Distance Function
head: Link SDF, Link Shape SDF, Signed Torus, sdTorus
body: Computes the signed distance from a query point to the surface of a torus centered at the origin and aligned with the Y-axis. It provides the primitive distance query required for distance-field ray marching and constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations. It is distinguished from sibling primitives like the Cylinder Signed Distance Function by its closed-loop topology and from Distance to Superquadrics by its specific algebraic form for a torus. Inputs: p = (px, py, pz): Query point in 3D space. R: Major radius (distance from the torus center to the tube centerline). r: Minor radius (radius of the tube cross-section). Outputs: d: Signed distance. Positive outside the torus, negative inside, zero on the surface. Data Structures: None required; scalar computation. Steps: 1. Compute the radial distance of the point's projection onto the XZ plane from the origin: \rho = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}. 2. Construct a 2D vector q = (qx, qy) representing the offset from the torus centerline: qx = \rho - R, qy = py. 3. Compute the Euclidean distance from q to the origin and subtract the minor radius: d = \sqrt{qx^2 + qy^2} - r. Formula: d = \sqrt{(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R)^2 + py^2} - r Parameters: R > 0: Major radius. r > 0: Minor radius. Constraint: r < R yields a standard ring torus; r = R yields a horn torus; r > R yields a self-intersecting spindle torus. Edge Cases: Origin: If p=(0,0,0), \rho=0, q=(-R, 0), d = R - r. Precision: Near the surface or when \rho \approx R, standard floating-point precision is sufficient. Self-intersection: For spindle tori (r > R), the SDF remains mathematically valid but defines a complex nested inside region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdtorus(p: tuple, R: float, r: float) -> float: """ Computes signed distance to a torus centered at origin, aligned with Y-axis. p: (px, py, pz) R: Major radius r: Minor radius """ px, py, pz = p # Radial distance in the XZ plane rho = (px2 + pz2)0.5 # 2D vector from the torus centerline to the point qx = rho - R qy = py # Signed distance: distance to centerline minus tube radius return (qx2 + qy2)0.5 - r A variation that includes a length parameter for non-circular cross-sections or deformed tori, sometimes referred to as a link shape. Use when modeling chain links or specific mechanical parts. Link SDF. A torus where r > R. The SDF formula remains the same, but the topology changes to a self-intersecting shape. Use for specific organic or abstract shapes. Spindle Torus. Time Complexity: O(1). Requires two square roots and basic arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Exact analytic solution; no iterative approximation; robust for ray marching. Limitations: Only applies to perfect tori. Cannot model tori with varying cross-sections or twists without deformation. When to use: When rendering or ray marching perfect toroidal shapes. When not to use: For complex toroidal structures with varying thickness or non-circular cross-sections. The SDF for a torus is a standard primitive in signed distance function libraries, popularized by tools like the glsl-sdf-primitives repository. It is a fundamental building block for CSG operations involving toroidal shapes. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Infinite Tiling with Modulo
head: Infinite Crystal Grid SDF, Infinite Tiling via Modulo, Modulo SDF, Modulo Tiling, Repeat function, Tiling SDFs, Tiling via Modulo
body: Infinite Tiling with Modulo is a technique for rendering infinite repeating patterns by using the modulo operator to fold space, allowing a single primitive SDF to be tiled infinitely. It sets itself apart from explicit mesh instances by computing the scene geometry implicitly at essentially zero extra cost per instance, enabling ray-marched fractal renderers like Mandelbulbs and Menger sponges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray position p (vec3), tile period/size c (float). Output: Transformed position q (vec3) suitable for SDF evaluation. Data Structures: None required beyond standard vector types. Steps: 1. Apply the modulo operation to the sampling point p using the period c, adding an offset to center tiles at integer multiples of c. 2. Evaluate the base SDF using the transformed coordinate q. Formulas: The core transformation is defined as: q = \text{mod}\left(p + \frac{c}{2}, c\right) - \frac{c}{2} Where: p is the world-space ray position. c is the period or size of the tile. \text{mod}(a, b) is the floating-point modulo operation. q is the folded coordinate. Parameters: c (Tile Size): The period of the modulo operation. Lower values make objects appear closer; higher values make them further apart. Offset: Added before modulo to center the tile differently, e.g., mod(p + 1.5, 3.0) - 1.5 for a period of 3.0 to center a tile at the origin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def repeat(p: list, c: float) -> list: """ Tiles space infinitely by folding the sampling point p using modulo. Args: p: The world-space position to tile [x, y, z]. c: The period (size) of the tile. Returns: The folded position q [x, y, z]. """ # Fold space into [-c/2, c/2) centered at origin # Equivalent to mod(p + c/2, c) - c/2 q = [(p[i] + c / 2.0) % c - c / 2.0 for i in range(3)] return q def sdftiled(p: list, c: float, basesdffunc) -> float: """ Evaluates an SDF with infinite tiling. Args: p: World-space position [x, y, z]. c: Tile period. basesdffunc: Function that computes the SDF for a single tile centered at origin. Returns: Signed distance to the nearest tiled surface. """ q = repeat(p, c) return basesdffunc(q) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: The standard repeat function works correctly for negative coordinates due to the properties of modulo and the centering shift. However, some simplified explanations assume positive quadrants. A variant of Infinite Tiling which produces a finite number of repetitions of a shape. It takes an additional vector \vec{l} as input, where \vec{l} is the corner of the box used to limit the number of repetitions of the shape. This allows for controlled tiling within a specific volume rather than infinite space. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray step, as it adds only a few arithmetic operations (modulo, subtraction) before the base SDF evaluation, contributing essentially zero extra cost. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional data structures are required. Performance: Enables rendering of scenes with effectively infinite geometry at real-time frame rates, provided the base SDF is efficient. Strengths: Ideal for fractals and procedural environments. Limitations: All tiles are identical copies; cannot vary geometry per tile without additional logic (e.g., coordinate-dependent transformations). The technique is fundamental to ray marching with SDFs, popularized by demoscene artists and researchers like Inigo Quilez. It leverages the mathematical property of periodicity to create complex structures like Menger sponges and Mandelbulbs from simple primitives. arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, https://github.com/arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Painting with Math: A Gentle Study of Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/painting-with-math-a-gentle-study-of-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions: Sphere Tracing..., https://www.mysimulator.uk/articles/ray-marching/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) PDF COS 426 Final Project Writeup Raymarching with Signed Distance Fields, https://jbaum98.github.io/cos426finalproject/writeup.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Distance Field Representations and Sampling
body: This family defines the mechanisms for querying scalar fields that represent implicit surfaces or volumetric data via distance metrics, enabling ray marching and spatial queries. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on the sampling interface and data structures required to evaluate these fields efficiently, rather than the geometric primitives themselves. While SDF Primitive Definitions provides the analytical building blocks, this family addresses how those blocks are stored (textures, grids, neural networks) and accessed (bounded lookups, probabilistic outputs, haptic constraints) in a rendering or simulation pipeline. The family operates on the principle that a scene is defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) where the zero-level set f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 represents the surface. For sphere tracing to be valid, the function must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring |f(\mathbf{p}1) - f(\mathbf{p}2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2\|. This guarantees that the value f(\mathbf{p}) is a safe lower bound on the distance to the surface, allowing the ray marcher to step forward by exactly f(\mathbf{p}) without tunneling. Composition is achieved through Boolean operations on the distance values: Union: f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Intersection: f{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Subtraction: f{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(-f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} into the local coordinate space of the primitive using the inverse transformation matrix M^{-1} before evaluation. Procedural noise (e.g., FBM) is often used to perturb these analytical surfaces, creating hypertextures where the isosurface is defined by SDF(\mathbf{p}) + Bn(\mathbf{p}) = 0. Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching is a technique for rendering implicit surfaces defined by a 3D distance texture, specifically addressing the problem of invalid distance values at the texture boundaries. It employs two nested bounding boxes (an inner "red" box and an outer "green" box) to distinguish between valid texture data and a boundary shell where samples may be unreliable. Unlike standard texture lookups that might return erroneous distances near edges, this method returns the distance to the outer boundary for points in the invalid shell, ensuring the ray marcher steps safely without tunneling into undefined data. It enables the inclusion of pre-computed distance textures (e.g., the Stanford Bunny) into scenes using standard SDF composition operators. See Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching. Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDFs) are a variant of Directed Distance Fields (DDFs) designed to differentiably model the inherent discontinuities in the underlying field, specifically surface and occlusion discontinuities. While standard DDFs output a single scalar depth value, PDDFs modify the formulation so that the network outputs probability distributions over rays rather than a single value, allowing a C^1 continuous neural network to represent the discontinuous field of a DDF. This enables efficient differentiable rendering and geometry extraction without the training instability caused by hard discontinuities. See Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDFs). This method provides haptic rendering for sparse, oriented point cloud data by constructing a 3D signed distance field (SDF) on a regular grid using embedded "packing spheres". It solves the problem of generating stable collision forces from incomplete geometric data where traditional mesh-based or dense implicit function methods fail due to sparsity. Unlike sibling methods that rely on dense sampling or explicit surface reconstruction, this technique uses the local normal direction to define minimum-volume spheres that approximate the object's interior, allowing a proxy to be constrained to the zero-iso-surface via gradient descent. See Sparse Point Set Haptic Rendering via Distance Field. Definition: A trait-based abstraction for sampling distance fields defined in terms of specific Distance metrics. Implementation: If S implements ScalarSource, Sampler implements Sample<Signed>. If S implements VectorSource, Sampler implements Sample<Directed>. If S implements HermiteSource, Sampler implements samplenormal method which calls self.source.samplenormal(p). Layout: The Sampler struct contains a reference to the source (&'a S). Definition: A traversal method where ray marching is performed through distance fields. Optimization: Memory costs are reduced by lowering field resolution to 1:4 scale (one distance value per 64 voxels), combined with occupancy masks. Performance: Pre-processing takes 10x more GPU time than XBrickMap. Definition: Space skipping traversal using tiled 256³ 8-directional distance fields at 1:4 resolution, combined with 4³ occupancy bitmasks. It creates 8 separate manhattan fields, each considering only voxels ahead of the associated ray octant direction. Layout: Memory cost is 8 bytes per 4³ voxel plus 1 bit per 1³ voxel. Performance: Compared to traditional distance fields, it lowers the overall number of iterations by ~20-25% and increases throughput for incoherent rays by ~30-50%. On Sponza 2k, OctantDF achieves 82.2 Mrays/s for primary rays and 65.8 Mrays/s for primary + 1 diffuse bounce. Definition: A ray function that computes the distance along the ray until a specific scalar value \sigma is encountered. Definition: A 2.5D indicator \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}] combining UV coordinates and signed distance to resolve ambiguity for points perpendicular to the mesh surface. Calculation: Calculate signed distance \bar{d}: project point x onto mesh surface at x0, obtain direction \tilde{r} = x - x0, get surface normal \tilde{n} at x0, and compute \bar{d} = \text{sign}(\tilde{r} \cdot \tilde{n}) \|\tilde{r}\|2. Formula: Define signed height: \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}], where [u, v] is the 2D coordinate on the UV map and \bar{d} is the signed distance. Distance fields have been a cornerstone of implicit surface representation since the introduction of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for ray marching. The specific techniques detailed in this family, such as bounded texture sampling and probabilistic outputs, emerged from the need to handle discrete data structures (textures, point clouds) and differentiable rendering pipelines in modern graphics. The integration of distance fields into neural rendering (PDDFs) and avatar synthesis (Signed Height Indicators) represents a more recent development, leveraging the differentiability of neural networks to overcome the discontinuities inherent in traditional geometric representations. https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, https://github.com/dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) PDF CS 519: Scientific Visualization - University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs519/fa2017/Lecture%2012%20-%20Volume%20Visualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) UVA: Towards Unified Volumetric Avatar for View Synthesis, Pose rendering, Geometry and Texture Editing, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2304.06969, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
