name: Implicit Surface Taxonomy
head: Lipschitz Scalar Fields, SDF Classification
body:
This taxonomy categorizes implicit surface models into four distinct types based on their mathematical properties: Distance Field, Pseudo Signed Distance Field, Conservative Distance Field, and Lipschitz Scalar Field. It distinguishes these types to determine which implicit operators (such as Boolean combinations or inflation) can be applied without introducing geometric artifacts or discontinuities. Unlike SDF Primitive Definitions which focuses on specific shapes, this article defines the validity conditions for general functions within a construction tree. The taxonomy classifies a scalar field function f(\mathbf{p}) based on its relationship to the true Euclidean signed distance d(\mathbf{p}) and the magnitude of its gradient \|
abla f\|. The classification is defined by the following constraints: 1. Distance Field: Condition: f(\mathbf{p}) = d(\mathbf{p}). Properties: Exact Euclidean distance. Satisfies the eikonal equation \|
abla f\| = 1 everywhere except at singularities (medial axes). 2. Pseudo Signed Distance Field: Condition: Piecewise differentiable function satisfying the eikonal property \|
abla f\| = 1 wherever the gradient is well-defined. Properties: Often arises from geometric editing or Boolean operations on exact SDFs. May lack continuity or exact distance values. 3. Conservative Distance Field: Condition: |f(\mathbf{p})| \le |d(\mathbf{p})|. Properties: The field value is a lower bound on the true distance. It does not need to be continuous and may exhibit unexpected high gradients in certain regions. 4. Lipschitz Scalar Field: Condition: Satisfies the Lipschitz property with constant 1, implying \|
abla f\| \le 1. Properties: Continuous and has a bounded gradient. These properties are stronger than those of conservative distance fields. The choice of field type dictates which implicit operators can be safely applied in a construction tree. Sphere Tracing: The original algorithm is applicable to Lipschitz scalar fields. It is also applicable to conservative distance fields, provided the conservative property (|f| \le |d|) ensures the step size remains a safe lower bound. Smooth Boolean Operators: These operators require the input functions to be Lipschitz or at least continuous. Applying smooth Boolean operators to discontinuous conservative distance fields may produce fields that are not continuous and fail to consistently define an implicit surface. General Implicit Operators: Most implicit operators require a true signed distance field to function correctly. Feeding them with a pseudo signed distance or a conservative field may introduce artifacts. Inflation Operator: The inflate operator, defined as I(\epsilon) = f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{n}) - k (or conceptually shifting the isosurface), is impacted by the degradation of surface quality in non-exact fields. Applying this operator to conservative or pseudo fields results in visible artifacts compared to exact distance fields. The following pseudocode demonstrates how to verify if a field satisfies the Lipschitz condition, a prerequisite for many smooth operators. Note that exact verification is generally impossible for arbitrary functions; this checks the gradient bound where differentiable. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def islipschitzfield(f, p, epsilon=1e-6): """ Checks if the field f satisfies the Lipschitz condition ||grad f|| <= 1 at point p by numerical differentiation. Args: f: Function evaluating the scalar field. p: 3D point (vector). epsilon: Step size for numerical gradient. Returns: True if ||grad f|| <= 1 + tolerance, False otherwise. """ # Numerical gradient calculation gradx = (f(p + [epsilon, 0, 0]) - f(p - [epsilon, 0, 0])) / (2 epsilon) grady = (f(p + [0, epsilon, 0]) - f(p - [0, epsilon, 0])) / (2 epsilon) gradz = (f(p + [0, 0, epsilon]) - f(p - [0, 0, epsilon])) / (2 epsilon) gradientmagnitude = sqrt(gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2) # Tolerance for numerical error return gradientmagnitude <= 1.0 + 1e-5 def classifyfield(f, p, truedistancefunc=None): """ Classifies the field f at point p based on available ground truth. Args: f: The implicit function. p: 3D point. truedistancefunc: Optional function for exact distance d(p). Returns: String: 'Distance', 'Pseudo', 'Conservative', or 'Lipschitz' """ val = f(p) # Check for Exact Distance Field if truedistancefunc is not None: d = truedistancefunc(p) if abs(val - d) < 1e-5: return 'Distance' elif val <= d and val >= -d: # |f| <= |d| # Further check for Lipschitz vs Conservative # Conservative fields may not be continuous or have bounded gradients # Lipschitz fields have ||grad f|| <= 1 if islipschitzfield(f, p): return 'Lipschitz' else: return 'Conservative' # If we cannot compare to true distance, we rely on gradient properties # Pseudo SDFs satisfy ||grad f|| = 1 # Lipschitz fields satisfy ||grad f|| <= 1 # Note: Without true distance, distinguishing Pseudo from Lipschitz # requires checking if ||grad f|| == 1 strictly. # This is a heuristic classification. gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(f, p) if abs(gradmag - 1.0) < 1e-5: return 'Pseudo' # Or Lipschitz if <= 1 elif gradmag <= 1.0: return 'Lipschitz' else: return 'Unknown' # Violates Lipschitz Modeling Complexity: Using exact Distance Fields is computationally expensive to compute for complex shapes but guarantees artifact-free results for all operators. Artifact Risk: Using Conservative or Pseudo fields reduces computational cost or simplifies construction but risks artifacts when using smooth Boolean operators or inflation. Rendering Compatibility: Sphere tracing works with Conservative and Lipschitz fields, but smooth blending requires Lipschitz continuity. The taxonomy was introduced in [MSLJ23] and completed with the inclusion of Lipschitz scalar fields, referencing foundational work by [KB89] and [Har96]. The classification highlights the trade-offs in implicit modeling trees, where internal nodes combine values from sub-trees. Accelerating Signed Distance Functions, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70258, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Signed Euclidean Distance Field (SDF) Representation
head: Signed Distance Field (SDF), Signed Distance Function (SDF)
body: A Signed Euclidean Distance Field (SDF) is a continuous implicit representation that maps any 3D point to a scalar value representing the shortest Euclidean distance to the nearest surface, with a sign indicating whether the point lies inside or outside the watertight boundary. It differs from occupancy fields, which only indicate binary presence, by providing metric distance information that enables robust sphere tracing and smooth surface reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and, in neural implementations, an observation context \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} (e.g., image data or identity parameters). Output: A scalar value s \in \mathbb{R} representing the signed distance. Data Structures: Grid-based: A 3D voxel grid where each voxel stores a single floating-point value. The value is -d for voxels outside the object boundary and +d for voxels inside, where d is the Euclidean distance to the nearest boundary. Neural Implicit: A parameterized function f\theta (e.g., a Multi-Layer Perceptron) that approximates the mapping. Formulas: The fundamental mapping is defined as: s: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \quad In the context of neural implicit representations conditioned on observations \mathbf{x}, the function is expressed as: f\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \quad Steps to Compute/Store: 1. Define Boundary: Identify the watertight surface boundary of the object. 2. Compute Distance: For every point (voxel center or query location), calculate the Euclidean distance d to the nearest point on the boundary. 3. Assign Sign: If the point is outside the boundary, assign value -d. If the point is inside the boundary, assign value +d. Note on Neural Variants: Some neural implementations (like O-Net) map to [0,1] where the surface is the 0.5-level set, but the standard SDF definition maps to \mathbb{R} with the zero-level set at 0. Parameters: Resolution: For grid-based SDFs, the voxel grid resolution determines the precision of the distance approximation. Neural Parameters: \theta represents the weights and biases of the neural network approximating the field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: In grid-based representations, the distance is only exact at voxel centers or interpolated values; aliasing can occur at high frequencies. Non-Watertight Surfaces: The definition assumes a watertight surface to define a clear inside/outside region. Pseudocode (Grid-based Construction): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfgrid(mesh, gridresolution, bounds): """ Computes a Signed Euclidean Distance Field on a 3D grid. Args: mesh: A watertight surface mesh defining the boundary. gridresolution: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) defining the voxel count. bounds: Tuple (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) defining the grid extent. Returns: A 3D numpy array of shape (nx, ny, nz) containing signed distances. """ nx, ny, nz = gridresolution minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = bounds # Initialize grid with zeros sdfgrid = np.zeros((nx, ny, nz)) # Calculate voxel size dx = (maxx - minx) / nx dy = (maxy - miny) / ny dz = (maxz - minz) / nz # Iterate over all voxels for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): # Calculate center of the voxel in world space x = minx + (i + 0.5) dx y = miny + (j + 0.5) dy z = minz + (k + 0.5) dz point = np.array([x, y, z]) # Compute Euclidean distance to the mesh boundary # This requires a nearest-point query on the mesh triangles distancetoboundary = computeeuclideandistancetomesh(point, mesh) # Determine if point is inside or outside # Using ray casting or winding number for point-in-mesh test isinside = ispointinsidemesh(point, mesh) if isinside: sdfgrid[i, j, k] = distancetoboundary else: sdfgrid[i, j, k] = -distancetoboundary return sdfgrid def computeeuclideandistancetomesh(point, mesh): """ Computes the shortest Euclidean distance from a point to a mesh. Implementation detail: Iterate over all triangles, compute distance to triangle plane, clamp to triangle bounds, find minimum distance. """ mindist = infinity for triangle in mesh.triangles: dist = distancepointtotriangle(point, triangle) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist return mindist def ispointinsidemesh(point, mesh): """ Determines if a point is inside a watertight mesh. Implementation detail: Cast a ray from point to infinity, count intersections with mesh triangles. Odd count implies inside. """ raydirection = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Arbitrary direction intersections = 0 for triangle in mesh.triangles: if rayintersectstriangle(point, raydirection, triangle): intersections += 1 return intersections % 2 == 1 Defines analytical SDFs for basic shapes (spheres, boxes, cylinders) which serve as building blocks for complex scenes. Choose when procedural geometry is preferred over mesh-based SDFs. SDF Primitive Definitions Discusses various ways to store and sample distance fields (e.g., sparse grids, hash tables) beyond dense voxel grids. Choose when memory efficiency is critical for large scenes. Distance Field Representations and Sampling Details how to apply affine transformations (rotation, translation, scaling) to SDFs by transforming the query point. Choose when objects need to move or deform. SDF Transformations Addresses the challenge of computing accurate SDFs for large scenes by blending local high-resolution SDFs with a global low-resolution field. Choose for large-scale outdoor environments. Global Distance Query via Local-Global Blending Specializes in generating SDFs from vector fonts for efficient text rendering. Choose when rendering text with smooth scaling and anti-aliasing. SDF Text Rendering Classifies different types of implicit surfaces, including SDFs, occupancy fields, and level sets. Choose for understanding the broader context of implicit representations. Implicit Surface Taxonomy Time Complexity: Computing the SDF for a mesh-based object requires a nearest-point query for each voxel, which is O(N \cdot M) for N voxels and M mesh primitives without acceleration structures. With spatial acceleration (e.g., BVH), this reduces significantly. Neural SDF evaluation is O(1) per query but requires training time. Memory Complexity: Dense grid SDFs require O(N^3) memory for 3D resolution N. Sparse representations or neural networks reduce this to O(N) or constant size, respectively. Strengths: Provides metric distance information enabling robust sphere tracing; smooth gradients facilitate normal estimation; Boolean operations are simple and efficient. Limitations: High memory usage for dense grids; difficult to represent non-watertight or open surfaces; neural SDFs require training and may suffer from artifacts if not regularized. When to Use: Ideal for procedural geometry, sphere tracing, and applications requiring smooth surface interpolation or normal estimation. When Not to Use: Not suitable for non-watertight surfaces or when exact mesh topology preservation is required without smoothing. The Signed Distance Field was introduced as a continuous implicit representation mapping 3D points to signed distances, where the sign indicates inside/outside status and the amplitude represents distance from the watertight surface. It is widely used in non-linear registration techniques and shape skeletonization algorithms. In recent years, it has become a fundamental component in Implicit Neural Representations (INR) for 3D avatar modeling and human body reconstruction, often denoted as f\theta. Human 3D Avatar Modeling with Implicit Neural Representation: A Brief Survey, https://doi.org/10.1109/icsps58776.2022.00148, fetched 2026-10-26 Virtual mastoidectomy performance evaluation through multi-volume analysis., https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-012-0687-4, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Multiphase Signed Distance Field Interface Extraction
head: Multiphase Interface Extraction, Multiphase SDF evaluation, PhaseTree interface computation, Thin Volume Interface
body: This method extracts the complete set of thin, non-manifold interfaces separating distinct material phases within a multiphase Signed Distance Field (SDF) model. It solves the problem of explicitly defining the boundaries between multiple coexisting phases, including complex junctions where three or more phases meet, which are often ambiguous or lost in monolithic SDF representations. Unlike solid-textured implicit surfaces where phases are indistinguishable, or object-space multiphase fields that lack Lipschitz guarantees, this method preserves the 1-Lipschitz property of individual phases to enable standard SDF algorithms like Sphere Tracing while providing explicit geometric handles for each phase. The method computes a signed distance field representing the interface between two specific phases i and j by intersecting their "inflated" regions. This intersection creates a thin volume \mathcal{S} that embeds the boundary \partial\Omega{ij}. The process relies on the PhaseTree construction, which maintains a 1-Lipschitz SDF for each phase \mathcal{A}k. Inputs: n: The total number of phases in the model. \phi{\mathcal{A}k}(\mathbf{p}): The 1-Lipschitz signed distance field function for phase k, where k \in [1, n]. \varepsilon: A small positive offset value used to inflate the phases for intersection calculation. The specific numerical value is not provided in the sources. Outputs: \Phi: A vector of n signed distance fields, where each entry \phik represents the phase function for phase k in the context of the extracted interfaces. f{ij}(\mathbf{p}): The SDF of the thin interface volume between phases i and j. The method operates on procedural functions. No explicit grid or voxel data structure is required; the SDFs are evaluated analytically or via neural networks (e.g., SIREN) or hierarchical trees (e.g., BlobTree). The output \Phi is a logical collection of n scalar fields. 1. Ensure 1-Lipschitz Continuity: Each phase's SDF \phi{\mathcal{A}k} must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, i.e., |\phi{\mathcal{A}k}(\mathbf{p}1) - \phi{\mathcal{A}k}(\mathbf{p}2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2\|. For BlobTree models, convert the tree to a 1-Lipschitz SDF. For SIREN (neural) models, compute the theoretical Lipschitz bound \lambda or sample the maximum gradient magnitude \lambda. Define the normalized function as f/\lambda to ensure 1-Lipschitz continuity. Restrict queries to the learned area using a proxy sphere. 2. Compute Minimum Inter-Phase Distance (f): Calculate the global minimum distance between any pair of distinct phases, inflated by \varepsilon. This value f serves as a lower bound for the interface thickness and ensures that interfaces do not overlap incorrectly. f = \min{(i,j) \in [1, n]^2, i \neq j} \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{p}) - \varepsilon, \phi{\mathcal{A}j}(\mathbf{p}) - \varepsilon) Here, f is a scalar field (or a conservative lower bound scalar if precomputed) representing the tightest gap between any two phases minus the inflation radius. 3. Compute Two-Phase Interface SDF (f{ij}): For a specific pair of phases i and j, the SDF of the thin interface volume \mathcal{S} is computed by intersecting the inflated phases: f{ij}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(\phi{\mathcal{A}i}(\mathbf{p}) - \varepsilon, \phi{\mathcal{A}j}(\mathbf{p}) - \varepsilon) The operator I(\mathcal{A}k, \varepsilon) denotes the inflation of phase k by \varepsilon. The intersection is defined as \mathcal{S} = I(\mathcal{A}i, \varepsilon) \cap I(\mathcal{A}j, \varepsilon). 4. Construct Complete Interface Set (\Phi): To extract the complete set of interfaces for all n phases, update the phase functions \phik in the output vector \Phi. For a two-phase representation (isolating interface between i and j): \phik = \begin{cases} \max(f, \phi{\mathcal{A}k}) & \forall k \in \{i, j\} \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} For the complete set of interfaces (all phases): \Phi = (\phi1, \phi2, \dots, \phin) Where for each k \in [1, n]: \phik(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f(\mathbf{p}), \phi{\mathcal{A}k}(\mathbf{p})) Note: In the complete set formulation, f is the field computed in Step 2. The use of \max(f, \phi{\mathcal{A}k}) effectively clips the phase distance, ensuring that the phase boundary is defined relative to the nearest other phase's inflated boundary, thereby creating the thin interface volume. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemultiphaseinterfaces(phases, epsilon): """ Computes the thin interface SDFs for a multiphase model. Args: phases: A list of n callable functions [phiA1,..., phiAn]. Each phiAk(p) returns the signed distance for phase k. It is assumed these are 1-Lipschitz. epsilon: Float, the inflation radius for interface extraction. Returns: phioutput: A list of n callable functions representing the multiphase interface SDFs. ffield: The scalar field representing the minimum inter-phase distance. """ n = len(phases) # Step 1: Ensure 1-Lipschitz (Assumed pre-condition for inputs) # If using SIREN, inputs should already be normalized by lambda. # Step 2: Compute ffield = min{i!=j} max(phiAi - eps, phiAj - eps) # We evaluate this field at query points. For implementation, we define # a function that computes f(p) on the fly. def ffield(p): minval = infinity for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): # Compute inflated distances disti = phasesi - epsilon distj = phasesj - epsilon # Intersection of inflated phases interfaceval = max(disti, distj) if interfaceval < minval: minval = interfaceval return minval # Step 3 & 4: Construct the output phase functions phioutput = [] for k in range(n): def phik(p, k=k): # phik = max(f, phiAk) # Note: f is the field from Step 2. # In a real renderer, f(p) might be precomputed or cached. # Here we compute it directly, which is O(n^2) per query. # Optimization: Precompute ffield if memory allows. fval = ffield(p) return max(fval, phasesk) phioutput.append(phik) return phioutput, ffield \varepsilon: Inflation radius. Not given in the sources. \lambda: Lipschitz bound for SIREN models. Computed theoretically or via sampling. Sphere Tracing Performance: Near interfaces between phases, the signed distance value may become locally smaller due to the \max(f, \phi{\mathcal{A}k}) operation. This causes Sphere Tracing to take shorter steps, increasing the number of iterations required for convergence. Monolithic Merging: Aggressively merging multiple phases into a single mono-phase SDF when the geometry contains many internal interfaces significantly degrades ray-object intersection performance. Lipschitz Violation: If the input phases are not 1-Lipschitz, Sphere Tracing may tunnel. SIREN models require normalization by \lambda. Boundary Queries: For SIREN models, queries should be restricted to the learned area using a proxy sphere to avoid undefined behavior outside the training domain. Time Complexity: The computation of the complete interface set \Phi requires evaluating the minimum over all pairs of phases. For n phases, this involves O(n^2) comparisons per query point if f is computed on-the-fly. This can be a bottleneck for scenes with many phases. Memory Complexity: The PhaseTree representation is highly compact, requiring only a few kilobytes of storage for the construction tree, compared to several megabytes for sampled vector volumes. Strengths: Fully resolution-independent and procedural. Preserves 1-Lipschitz continuity, ensuring compatibility with Sphere Tracing and other SDF algorithms. Explicitly encodes phase geometry, allowing individual phases to be manipulated as first-class primitives. Can be compiled into GLSL for efficient GPU execution. Limitations: Performance degrades with an increasing number of phases due to the O(n^2) pairwise comparisons for f. Requires careful handling of Lipschitz bounds for neural representations (SIREN). Current authoring workflow relies on scripting construction trees, which may be less intuitive than direct modeling. The method is part of the PhaseTree framework, which extends traditional SDFs with native multiphase capabilities. It builds on the principle that a scene can be defined by a scalar field where the zero-level set represents the surface. Origin: The PhaseTree concept was introduced in the paper "The PhaseTree: Multiphase Signed Distance Fields". Related Models: SIREN: Sinusoidal Implicit Neural Representations, introduced by Sitzmann et al. in 2020, are compatible with this method when normalized to be 1-Lipschitz. BlobTree: Introduced by Wyvill et al. in 1999, BlobTrees can be converted to 1-Lipschitz SDFs and integrated into the PhaseTree framework. Comparison to Alternatives: Unlike solid-textured implicit surfaces, PhaseTree explicitly encodes phase geometry. Unlike multiscale vector volumes, it uses compact trees instead of sampled fields, preserving resolution independence and Lipschitz guarantees. Unlike object-space multiphase implicit functions (e.g., Yuan et al. 2012), it guarantees 1-Lipschitz continuity, enabling standard SDF algorithms without reinitialization. Unlike unsigned distance field reconstruction methods, it partitions space into labeled regions with explicit phase information, ensuring consistent non-manifold interfaces. The PhaseTree: Multiphase Signed Distance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811379, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multiphase Signed Distance Field
head: Multiphase SDF
body:
Multiphase Signed Distance Fields (MP-SDFs), also known as the PhaseTree, extend classical signed distance functions by integrating phase information directly into a construction tree, enabling the native representation of multi-material and multiphase objects. Unlike standard SDFs that model a single scalar field, MP-SDFs maintain a vector of phase functions \Phi(\mathbf{p}) = (\phi1(\mathbf{p}), \dots, \phin(\mathbf{p})) that partition space into distinct material regions while preserving the 1-Lipschitz property required for algorithmic compatibility with Sphere Tracing. This approach supports constructive solid geometry (CSG) workflows and novel operators like thin shells and phase merging, which are not directly supported by monolithic SDF representations. Input: A construction tree (PhaseTree) where leaves are monophase SDFs or standard SDF primitives, and internal nodes are operators (conversion, thin shell, merging, combination). Output: A multiphase field \Phi: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R}^n and an associated empty-phase function \phi0, allowing ray marching to determine both geometry and material identity. The core data structure is the PhaseTree, a binary or n-ary tree where each node evaluates to a multiphase model. Leaf Node: Represents a monophase SDF f. It is converted into a multiphase model with n phases using the Set k conversion operator. Internal Node: Represents an operator combining child nodes. It maintains the 1-Lipschitz property if its children do and the operator is Lipschitz-preserving. Phase Vector: At any point \mathbf{p}, the state is defined by the vector \Phi(\mathbf{p}) = [\phi1(\mathbf{p}), \dots, \phin(\mathbf{p})]. The MP-SDF model relies on the Single-Negative-Phase Invariant: for any point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, there exists a unique index k \in [1, n] such that \phik(\mathbf{p}) < 0. If no phase is negative, the point is in the empty region \Omega0. The Phase Type \mu(\mathbf{p}) at a point is the index of the minimum phase function value: \mu(\mathbf{p}) = \arg \min{i \in [1,n]} \phii(\mathbf{p}) If \mini \phii(\mathbf{p}) > 0, then \mu(\mathbf{p}) = 0 (empty space). The Phase Regions \Omegai are defined as the partition of space where phase i is negative and all other phases j 
eq i are positive: \Omegai = \{\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \phii(\mathbf{p}) < 0, 	ext{ and } \phij(\mathbf{p}) > 0  orall j

The Interface between phase i and j is the set of points where both phase functions are zero: \Omega{ij} = \{\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \phii(\mathbf{p}) = 0 	ext{ and } \phij(\mathbf{p}) = 0\} At these interfaces, the gradients

All operators described below preserve the 1-Lipschitz property if their inputs are 1-Lipschitz. Converts a standard SDF f into a multiphase model where phase k is f and all other phases i

Phase i represents the shell surface, and phase j represents the interior/exterior depending on the sign convention. \Phi =  egin{cases} \phii = |f(\mathbf{p})| - t \ \phij = f + t \end{cases} Here, t is the thickness of the generated shell. The shell exists where \phii < 0. Fuses a subset of phases \mathcal{K} into a single standard SDF f. This is useful for applying single-phase algorithms to a subset of materials. f = \min{i \in \mathcal{K}} \phii The resulting function f is 1-Lipschitz. However, f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 at the interfaces \partial\Omega{ij} between the original phases in \mathcal{K}, which may require handling for smooth rendering or further operations. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the evaluation of a multiphase SDF at a point \mathbf{p}, assuming a tree structure where each node has an evaluate method. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluatenode(node, p): """ Evaluates a PhaseTree node at point p. Returns a numpy array of size nphases + 1: [phi1,..., phin, phi0]. """ if node.isleaf(): f = node.sdfvalue(p) k = node.phaseindex # 1-based index phi = np.full(node.nphases, np.inf) phi[k - 1] = f phi0 = -np.min(phi) return np.append(phi, phi0) elif node.op == 'under': phia = evaluatenode(node.left, p) phib = evaluatenode(node.right, p) phasesa = phia[:-1] phasesb = phib[:-1] resultphases = np.zeros(node.nphases) for i in range(node.nphases): resultphases[i] = max(min(phasesa[i], phasesb[i]), -phasesb[i]) phi0 = -np.min(resultphases) return np.append(resultphases, phi0) elif node.op == 'thinshell': f = node.left.sdfvalue(p) t = node.thickness iidx = node.phasei - 1 jidx = node.phasej - 1 phi = np.full(node.nphases, np.inf) phi[iidx] = abs(f) - t phi[jidx] = f + t phi0 = -np.min(phi) return np.append(phi, phi0) elif node.op == 'merge': f = node.sdfvalue(p) k = node.phaseindex phi = np.full(node.nphases, np.inf) phi[k - 1] = f phi0 = -np.min(phi) return np.append(phi, phi0) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown operator: {node.op}") def computenormal(tree, p, phaseidx): """Computes the normal via central finite differences on the active phase.""" eps = 1e-4 dx = np.array([eps, 0.0, 0.0]) dy = np.array([0.0, eps, 0.0]) dz = np.array([0.0, 0.0, eps]) phip = evaluatenode(tree, p)[phaseidx - 1] phix = evaluatenode(tree, p + dx)[phaseidx - 1] phiy = evaluatenode(tree, p + dy)[phaseidx - 1] phiz = evaluatenode(tree, p + dz)[phaseidx - 1] grad = np.array([(phix - phip) / eps, (phiy - phip) / eps, (phiz - phip) / eps]) return grad / np.linalg.norm(grad) def raymarchmpsdf(origin, direction, tree, maxsteps=100, maxdist=100.0): t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return False, t, 0, np.zeros(3) p = origin + t direction phi = evaluatenode(tree, p) minphi = np.min(phi[:-1]) if minphi < 1e-4: phaseidx = np.argmin(phi[:-1]) + 1 normal = computenormal(tree, p, phaseidx) return True, t, phaseidx, normal t += max(1e-4, minphi) return False, t, 0, np.zeros(3) Thickness (t): Used in the Thin Shell operator to define the thickness of the generated shell. Phase Indices (i, j, k): Integer indices identifying specific phases in the vector \Phi. Merging Interfaces: When using the Phase Merging operator, the resulting function satisfies f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 at the interfaces \partial\Omega{ij} between the original phases, which may require handling for smooth rendering or further operations. Conservative Functions: Conservative functions (where |\phii(\mathbf{p})| \leq d(\mathbf{p}, \partial\Omegai)) can be used but generally do not accommodate smooth or extended blending operations, unlike 1-Lipschitz functions. The MP-SDF formulation prioritizes 1-Lipschitz continuity to ensure robust CSG and blending. Infinity Handling: The Set k conversion operator uses \infty for non-active phases. Standard IEEE 754 floating-point infinity is used, where \min(\infty, x) = x and \max(\infty, x) = \infty for finite x, ensuring correct propagation without special guards. Time Complexity: Evaluation of a point \mathbf{p} is proportional to the depth of the PhaseTree. Each node performs constant-time operations (min, max, abs) on vectors of size n (number of phases). Thus, evaluation is O(D \cdot n), where D is tree depth. Ray marching step count is similar to standard SDFs, depending on the Lipschitz constant (which is 1). Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is proportional to the number of nodes in the PhaseTree and the number of phases n. Each node stores operator metadata and references to children. The phase vector size is O(n). Strengths: Native support for multi-material objects; compatibility with Sphere Tracing; supports complex operators like thin shells and phase merging; preserves 1-Lipschitz property for robust marching. Limitations: Increased computational cost per evaluation due to vector operations on n phases; complexity in implementing gradient computation for normals in multiphase contexts; merging phases can introduce zero-level set artifacts at interfaces. When to Use: When rendering scenes with multiple distinct materials or phases that interact geometrically (e.g., shells, composites) and require efficient ray marching. When Not to Use: For simple single-material scenes where standard SDFs are sufficient; when smooth blending between phases is required without the overhead of multiphase management (though MP-SDF supports blending, it is more complex). The Multiphase Signed Distance Field, also known as the PhaseTree, was introduced by Hubert-Brierre et al. in 2025. It extends the classical SDF framework to support multi-material objects while maintaining the efficiency and robustness of sphere tracing. The work builds on the BlobTree [Wyvill et al. 1999] and addresses limitations of conservative distance fields in handling smooth blending [Dekkers et al. 2004]. It is used in computer graphics for modeling and rendering complex multiphase objects. The PhaseTree: Multiphase Signed Distance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811379, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Infinite Floor Projection
head: testFloor
body: Infinite Floor Projection is a technique for rendering an infinite textured floor by projecting screen coordinates into world space using perspective division, then applying player rotation and a checkerboard pattern. It calculates world-space coordinates directly per pixel using perspective division, allowing for seamless infinite tiling without UV wrapping artifacts. Inputs: Screen dimensions: SCRWIDTH, SCRHEIGHT. Player state: player.lookAngle (rotation), player.x, player.y, player.z (position). Constants: MOVEVERTICALSCALE = 16.0, LOOKANGLEMULTIPLIER = 6.2 (approximates 2\pi). Outputs: Pixel colors for a checkerboard pattern. Data Structures: Scalar variables and simple iteration loops. Steps: 1. Calculate Look Angle Offset: Compute lookAngle = -player.lookAngle 6.2. Clamp the result to the range [0, SCRHEIGHT]. 2. Calculate Vertical Scale: Compute moveVertical = player.z / 16.0. If moveVertical equals zero, set it to 0.0001 to prevent division by zero. 3. Iterate Screen Rows: Loop y from yStart to yEnd. 4. Iterate Screen Columns: Loop x from -SCRWIDTHHALF to SCRWIDTHHALF. 5. Compute Depth Proxy: Calculate z = y + lookAngle. If z <= 0, set z = 0.0001. 6. Project to World Space: Calculate intermediate coordinates: fx = \frac{x}{z} \times moveVertical fy = \frac{200}{z} \times moveVertical. 7. Apply Player Rotation: Rotate the coordinates using the player's look angle (referred to as angle in the source): rx = fx \times \sin(\text{lookAngle}) - fy \times \cos(\text{lookAngle}) + \frac{\text{player.y}}{60.0} ry = fx \times \cos(\text{lookAngle}) + fy \times \sin(\text{lookAngle}) - \frac{\text{player.x}}{60.0}. 8. Mirror Coordinates: Handle negative values for seamless tiling: If rx < 0, set rx = -rx + 1. If ry < 0, set ry = -ry + 1. 9. Cull Invalid Tiles: Skip rendering if rx <= 0 or ry <= 0 or rx >= 5 or ry >= 5. 10. Determine Pattern: Draw red if rx % 2 == ry % 2, otherwise draw blue. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderinfinitefloor(player, scrwidth, scrheight, ystart, yend): LOOKANGLEMULTIPLIER = 6.2 MOVEVERTICALSCALE = 16.0 MINZ = 0.0001 MINMOVEVERTICAL = 0.0001 FLOOROFFSET = 60.0 TILELIMIT = 5 RED = (255, 0, 0) BLUE = (0, 0, 255) sin = math.sin cos = math.cos # 1. Calculate Look Angle Offset lookangle = -player.lookAngle LOOKANGLEMULTIPLIER lookangle = max(0.0, min(lookangle, scrheight)) # 2. Calculate Vertical Scale movevertical = player.z / MOVEVERTICALSCALE if movevertical == 0: movevertical = MINMOVEVERTICAL # 3 & 4. Iterate Screen Pixels for y in range(ystart, yend): # Exact bounds not specified in sources for x in range(-scrwidth // 2, scrwidth // 2): # 5. Compute Depth Proxy z = y + lookangle if z <= 0: z = MINZ # 6. Project to World Space fx = (x / z) movevertical fy = (200 / z) movevertical # 7. Apply Player Rotation rx = fx sin(lookangle) - fy cos(lookangle) + (player.y / FLOOROFFSET) ry = fx cos(lookangle) + fy sin(lookangle) - (player.x / FLOOROFFSET) # 8. Mirror Coordinates if rx < 0: rx = -rx + 1 if ry < 0: ry = -ry + 1 # 9. Cull Invalid Tiles if rx <= 0 or ry <= 0 or rx >= TILELIMIT or ry >= TILELIMIT: continue # 10. Determine Pattern screenx = x + scrwidth // 2 if (rx % 2) == (ry % 2): setpixelcolor(screenx, y, RED) # Implementation detail else: setpixelcolor(screenx, y, BLUE) # Implementation detail Parameters: moveVertical scaling factor: 16.0. Look angle multiplier: 6.2 (approximates 2\pi). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: z and moveVertical are clamped to 0.0001 to prevent division by zero errors. Coordinate Wrapping: The mirroring step (rx = -rx + 1) handles negative world coordinates to create a seamless tiling effect without explicit modulo operations on negative numbers. Tiling Limit: The culling step (rx >= 5, ry >= 5) restricts rendering to a 5 \times 5 tile area. Floor Rendering via Ray Casting is a technique for rendering an infinite textured floor by casting rays from the camera plane through screen pixels to the world grid, interpolating world coordinates (x, y) based on the distance from the camera to the screen row. It differs from standard texture mapping by calculating world-space coordinates directly per pixel using perspective division, allowing for seamless infinite tiling without UV wrapping artifacts. It builds on Infinite Floor Projection by explicitly deriving the world coordinate increments from the view frustum geometry rather than relying on pre-projected screen coordinates. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels rendered, as each pixel is processed in a nested loop. Memory Complexity: O(1), as only scalar variables are required. Strengths: Direct world-space coordinate calculation and seamless infinite tiling without UV mapping. Limitations: Fixed 5 \times 5 tile culling limit and approximate perspective projection using screen coordinates rather than full 3D ray casting. Not given in the sources. name: Floor Rendering via Ray Casting
head: DDA Floor Casting, Raycast Floor Projection
body: Floor Rendering via Ray Casting is a technique for rendering an infinite textured floor by casting rays from the camera plane through screen pixels to the world grid, interpolating world coordinates (x, y) based on the distance from the camera to the screen row. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Screen dimensions (SCREEN\WIDTH, SCREEN\HEIGHT), horizon line (HORIZON), player position in world/grid space (playerX, playerY), player orientation vector (dirX, dirY), and camera plane vector (planeX, planeY). Outputs: A pixel buffer where each pixel (x, y) below the horizon is colored based on the floor grid cell (cellX, cellY) intersected by the ray. Data Structures: normalizedLeft: A 2D vector (normalizedLeftX, normalizedLeftY) representing the normalized direction to the left edge of the view frustum at the near plane. normalizedRight: A 2D vector (normalizedRightX, normalizedRightY) representing the normalized direction to the right edge of the view frustum at the near plane. floorXStart, floorYStart: Floating-point accumulators for the current world grid coordinates at the left edge of the current screen row. floorXDirInc, floorYDirInc: Floating-point increments for advancing the world grid coordinates across one screen pixel horizontally. Steps: 1. Calculate Frustum Edge Vectors: Compute the unnormalized direction vectors for the left and right edges of the view frustum at the near plane. \begin{aligned} nearPlaneX1 &= dirX - planeX \\ nearPlaneY1 &= dirY - planeY \\ nearPlaneX2 &= dirX + planeX \\ nearPlaneY2 &= dirY + planeY \end{aligned} Normalize these vectors to unit length: \begin{aligned} normalizedLeftX &= \frac{nearPlaneX1}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX1^2 + nearPlaneY1^2}} \\ normalizedLeftY &= \frac{nearPlaneY1}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX1^2 + nearPlaneY1^2}} \\ normalizedRightX &= \frac{nearPlaneX2}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX2^2 + nearPlaneY2^2}} \\ normalizedRightY &= \frac{nearPlaneY2}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX2^2 + nearPlaneY2^2}} \end{aligned} 2. Iterate Screen Rows: Loop through screen rows y from the bottom of the screen (SCREEN\HEIGHT) down to the horizon (HORIZON). The floor is rendered for y > HORIZON. 3. Calculate Distance and Increments: For each row y, calculate the perspective distance factor yDistance and the horizontal world coordinate increments per pixel: yDistance = \frac{HORIZON}{y - HORIZON} \begin{aligned} floorXDirInc &= yDistance \times \frac{normalizedRightX - normalizedLeftX}{SCREEN\WIDTH} \\ floorYDirInc &= yDistance \times \frac{normalizedRightY - normalizedLeftY}{SCREEN\WIDTH} \end{aligned} The value yDistance represents the distance from the camera to the floor plane at row y. In the source implementation, HORIZON is equated to PLAYER\HEIGHT (camera height). 4. Initialize Row Start Coordinates: Calculate the starting world grid coordinates for the left edge of the current row. This is the player's grid position plus the offset to the left edge of the view frustum scaled by the distance: \begin{aligned} floorXStart &= worldToGrid(playerX) + yDistance \times normalizedLeftX \\ floorYStart &= worldToGrid(playerY) + yDistance \times normalizedLeftY \end{aligned} 5. Iterate Screen Columns: For each column x from 0 to SCREEN\WIDTH - 1: a. Determine the grid cell indices: \begin{aligned} cellX &= \lfloor |floorXStart| \rfloor \\ cellY &= \lfloor |floorYStart| \rfloor \end{aligned} b. Update the start coordinates for the next pixel in the row: \begin{aligned} floorXStart &+= floorXDirInc \\ floorYStart &+= floorYDirInc \end{aligned} c. Render the pixel using cellX and cellY. For example, a checkerboard pattern can be applied: \text{if } ((cellX + cellY) \pmod 2) \neq 0 \text{ then color} = (0, 0, 255, 255) \text{ else color} = (255, 255, 255, 255) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderfloor(SCREENWIDTH, SCREENHEIGHT, HORIZON, playerX, playerY, dirX, dirY, planeX, planeY, worldToGrid): # 1. Calculate normalized frustum edge vectors nearPlaneX1 = dirX - planeX nearPlaneY1 = dirY - planeY nearPlaneX2 = dirX + planeX nearPlaneY2 = dirY + planeY lenLeft = math.sqrt(nearPlaneX12 + nearPlaneY12) lenRight = math.sqrt(nearPlaneX22 + nearPlaneY22) normalizedLeftX = nearPlaneX1 / lenLeft normalizedLeftY = nearPlaneY1 / lenLeft normalizedRightX = nearPlaneX2 / lenRight normalizedRightY = nearPlaneY2 / lenRight # Pre-calculate constant differences for increments diffX = normalizedRightX - normalizedLeftX diffY = normalizedRightY - normalizedLeftY # Player grid position gridPlayerX = worldToGrid(playerX) gridPlayerY = worldToGrid(playerY) # 2. Iterate screen rows from bottom to horizon for y in range(SCREENHEIGHT, HORIZON, -1): # 3. Calculate distance factor yDistance = HORIZON / (y - HORIZON) # Calculate increments per pixel floorXDirInc = yDistance diffX / SCREENWIDTH floorYDirInc = yDistance diffY / SCREENWIDTH # 4. Initialize start coordinates for this row floorXStart = gridPlayerX + yDistance normalizedLeftX floorYStart = gridPlayerY + yDistance normalizedLeftY # 5. Iterate screen columns for x in range(SCREENWIDTH): # Determine grid cell cellX = math.floor(abs(floorXStart)) cellY = math.floor(abs(floorYStart)) # Update for next pixel floorXStart += floorXDirInc floorYStart += floorYDirInc # Render pixel (Example: Checkerboard) if (cellX + cellY) % 2 != 0: color = (0, 0, 255, 255) # Blue else: color = (255, 255, 255, 255) # White # Write to buffer at index (y SCREENWIDTH + x) # buffer[(y SCREENWIDTH + x) 4: (y SCREENWIDTH + x) 4 + 4] = color Parameters: PLAYER\HEIGHT: The vertical position of the camera. In the source implementation, this is equated to HORIZON. HORIZON: The y-coordinate on the screen corresponding to the camera height (vanishing line). Floor rendering occurs for screen y values from SCREEN\HEIGHT down to HORIZON + 1. SCREEN\HEIGHT: The total height of the canvas in pixels. The bottom pixel is at y = SCREEN\HEIGHT. SCREEN\WIDTH: The total width of the canvas in pixels. Used to calculate ray increment and floor step increments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Wall/Floor Sync: The floor rendering may appear 'out of sync' with wall rendering, where floor tiles appear to slide or change color near walls as the player moves. This is attributed to a discrepancy between the distance used for wall height calculation (from DDA) and the distance used for floor interpolation (yDistance), although the author notes they are 'two different types of distances'. Horizon Division: The formula for yDistance involves division by (y - HORIZON), requiring y > HORIZON to avoid division by zero. Not given in the sources. This technique is described in the context of implementing a raycaster with both wall and floor rendering. It is presented as a method to solve the problem of rendering an infinite floor in a raycasting engine, where the floor coordinates are interpolated based on the distance from the camera. The source notes that the basic idea uses PLAYER\HEIGHT (position of camera) and the formula PLAYER\HEIGHT / (y - HORIZON) to interpolate floor coordinates. name: Parametric Surface Density Model
head: 3D object model with six parameters
body: The Parametric Surface Density Model is a 3D object representation defined by six scalar quantities: three separating surfaces and the density fields defined on these interfaces. It solves the problem of reconstructing a 3D volumetric field from density fields defined on these interfaces. The method separates the geometric definition (the surfaces) from the volumetric definition (the densities), using an adaptive elliptic operator to fill the volume. Inputs: Data defining three planar curves that generate the separating surfaces. A set of example deformations for PCA-based surface deformation. Outputs: A 3D volumetric representation defined by the three separating surfaces and the interpolated density fields. Data Structures: Separating Surfaces: Represented by their planar generators (curves) rotated around an axis. Exact field layouts and bit packing are not given in the sources. Density Fields: Scalar fields \rhoi(\mathbf{p}) defined on the surface Si. Volumetric Field: A 3D scalar field V(\mathbf{p}) reconstructed from the surface densities. Steps: 1. Define Separating Surfaces: Construct three separating surfaces S1, S2, S3 by rotating three planar curves around an axis. 2. Define Surface Densities: Assign a density field \rhoi to each surface Si. 3. Reconstruct Volumetric Field: Fill the 3D volume with a scalar field based on the surface densities using an adaptive elliptic operator. Let V(\mathbf{p}) be the reconstructed field. The operator solves a partial differential equation (PDE) such that V(\mathbf{p}) matches \rhoi on Si and is smooth elsewhere. 4. Iterative Refinement: For tomographic reconstruction, iterate a 1D approach across slices, adding a smoothing term between slices to ensure consistency. Formulas: Surface generation: Si is generated by rotating a planar curve around an axis. Field matching: V(\mathbf{p}) = \rhoi(\mathbf{p}) for \mathbf{p} \in Si. Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of separating surfaces: 3. Number of density fields: 3. Axis of rotation: Not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Curves: If the planar curves do not generate valid closed surfaces, the separation of space may be ill-defined. Precision: The adaptive elliptic operator requires careful numerical implementation to maintain stability near boundaries. This variant addresses the deformation of the separating surfaces (the planar generators) using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). It is chosen when the object's shape varies across a set of examples and a compact basis of deformations is needed. Definition: Deformation is characterized by finding an optimal basis of deformations obtained via PCA on a set of examples. Steps: 1. Construct a random example set where realizations are obtained by integrating the solution of a linear stochastic differential equation. 2. Apply PCA to the set of example deformations to obtain a basis. 3. Search for an optimal basis from the PCA results to characterize surface deformation. When to choose: Use this when the object exhibits natural variations in shape that can be modeled as stochastic processes, allowing for efficient representation and generation of new shapes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The iterative reconstruction and PDE solving steps likely dominate, depending on the resolution of the adaptive elliptic operator. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of parameters defining the planar curves and the density fields, plus the storage for the reconstructed 3D volume if explicitly stored. Strengths: Explicitly models boundaries and internal properties; allows for adaptive smoothing; supports iterative 1D reconstruction with smoothing between slices. Limitations: Requires defining three specific surfaces; complex to implement the adaptive elliptic operator; limited to objects that can be separated by three rotating planar curves. When to use: Ideal for reconstructing 3D objects from limited tomographic data where the object can be approximated by three distinct regions separated by smooth surfaces. The Parametric Surface Density Model was proposed in the context of tomographic reconstruction from a small number of views. The work, authored by an unnamed researcher (thesis/report), focuses on defining a 3D object model characterized by six quantities: three separating surfaces and density fields on these interfaces. The primary difficulty addressed was filling a 3D field from the density fields on the interfaces, leading to the proposal of an adaptive elliptic operator. The model also incorporates deformation via PCA on stochastic examples, allowing for the characterization of surface variations. name: Neural and Implicit Representations
body: Neural and Implicit Representations render scenes by evaluating continuous scalar fields—parameterized as neural networks, Gaussian mixtures, or radial basis functions—along camera rays to compute geometry and appearance [1036-ray-marching-on-3d-gaussians.md][2409-ray-marching-with-neural-sdf.md][9641-rbf-particle-volume-path-tracing.md][15259-metanlr.md]. This family replaces analytical primitives or explicit meshes with learned or weighted fields, enabling high-fidelity rendering of complex structures through ray marching or path tracing. Evaluates a continuous Gaussian mixture field along camera rays to compute accurate volumetric integrals, explicitly handling primitive overlap and self-attenuation [1036-ray-marching-on-3d-gaussians.md]. It serves as a ground-truth baseline to analyze approximations in standard rasterization-based 3D Gaussian Splatting, such as ignoring spatial overlap and using approximate projected shapes [1036-ray-marching-on-3d-gaussians.md]. Unlike rasterization, it performs adaptive sampling along rays to resolve the exact order and contribution of overlapping Gaussians, ensuring precision governed by sample count rather than rasterization artifacts [1036-ray-marching-on-3d-gaussians.md]. Choose when exact volumetric integration of Gaussian primitives is required. Approximates the Signed Distance Field using a deep neural network and renders images by marching rays along the estimated distance field [2409-ray-marching-with-neural-sdf.md]. It differs from traditional SDF rendering by replacing the analytical distance function with a learned implicit representation, allowing for the reconstruction of complex geometries from data rather than explicit modeling [2409-ray-marching-with-neural-sdf.md]. Choose when data-driven surface reconstruction from a neural network is preferred over analytical primitives. Renders volumetric data represented as particles by modeling the scene as a continuous scalar field composed of additive weighted radial basis functions (RBFs), specifically Gaussians [9641-rbf-particle-volume-path-tracing.md]. It solves the visual clutter and pathological performance issues associated with BVH-based ray tracing of overlapping splatted particles by treating the volume as a single unified field rather than discrete geometric proxies [9641-rbf-particle-volume-path-tracing.md]. Unlike splatting, it allows for adjustable smoothing via kernel parameters and supports full path tracing through Delta Tracking [9641-rbf-particle-volume-path-tracing.md]. Choose when unbiased path tracing of particle-based volumes is required. Combines a neural implicit shape representation (SDF) with 2D CNN-based image feature extraction, aggregation, and re-projection for novel view synthesis [15259-metanlr.md]. It solves slow training and rendering times of previous neural lumigraph methods by leveraging meta-learning to specialize initializations, enabling high-quality convergence in minutes and real-time rendering [15259-metanlr.md]. Unlike volumetric methods, it renders explicit surfaces via sphere tracing, and uses deep feature blending to inpaint geometry errors and avoid artifacts from imperfect shape reconstruction [15259-metanlr.md]. Choose when fast, high-quality novel view synthesis with explicit surface rendering is needed. A neural mesh-based implicit field method that disentangles geometry and texture codes for editing. Step: Pre-compute near-far bounds for each ray by counting the minimum and maximum distances of ray-to-mesh intersections. Sample 64 coarse points along the ray. Adopt a progressive up-sampling strategy to guide the sampling of 64 fine points, yielding 128 samples for each ray. Formula: Distillation loss: Supervised with output from the teacher model (NeuS) for queried color and SDF value. Formula referenced as Eq.(4) in Sec 3.2. Background supervision: Binary cross-entropy loss using foreground masks for unbounded backgrounds. Parameter: Batch size: 512 rays. Optimizer: Adam with initial learning rate 0.0005 and cosine annealing scheduler with 5000 warm-up steps. Hardware: Single Nvidia RTX3090-24G GPU. Training time: Approximately 16 hours for each model. Layout: Model Architecture: Geometry Code lg(x) (dim 32), Texture Code lt(x) (dim 32), Sign Distance h(x) (dim 1). Interpolated Items include lt(x) (dim 32), gradient of SDF |\nablax s| (dim 256), s (dim 256), \gamma (dim 256), h(x) (dim 1), d (dim 160), \gamma (dim 32). Geometry Decoder outputs (256, 256, 256). Radiance Decoder outputs (3). A rendering architecture that combines an implicit function (scene representation), a sampling scheme (raymarching), and a renderer to produce images from ray bundles [15197-implicit-function-rendering-pipeline.md]. Choose when a modular pipeline separating implicit representation, sampling, and rendering is desired. The concept of implicit surfaces dates back to constructive solid geometry, but neural implicit representations emerged with the advent of deep learning. NeuMesh builds on distillation from the NeuS teacher model to optimize disentangled geometry and texture codes. MetaNLR++ leverages meta-learning with the Reptile algorithm to accelerate convergence on new scenes [15259-metanlr.md]. RBF-based methods integrate radial basis functions into unbiased path tracing frameworks for particle volumes [9641-rbf-particle-volume-path-tracing.md]. name: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians
body: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians is a volume rendering method that evaluates the continuous Gaussian mixture field along camera rays to compute accurate volumetric integrals, explicitly handling primitive overlap and self-attenuation. It serves as a ground-truth baseline to analyze the approximations inherent in standard rasterization-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), such as ignoring spatial overlap and using approximate projected shapes. Unlike 3DGS, which relies on screen-space sorting and alpha blending, this method performs adaptive sampling along rays to resolve the exact order and contribution of overlapping Gaussians, ensuring precision governed by sample count rather than rasterization artifacts. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position, a covariance matrix (or scale and rotation), an opacity, and a color value. Input: Camera ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for each pixel. Output: Final pixel color and accumulated opacity. Data Structures The method reuses the standard 3DGS data structures: Tensors: Arrays storing positions, scales, rotations (quaternions), opacities, and colors. Algorithm Steps 1. Adaptive Sampling: Determine sample points along the ray. Unlike fixed-step marching, adaptive sampling increases density in regions where the Gaussian mixture field changes rapidly to accurately resolve overlap. 2. Field Evaluation: At each sample point tk, evaluate the Gaussian mixture. The density \sigma(tk) and color c(tk) are computed by aggregating contributions from all active Gaussians i: \sigma(tk) = \sum{i} \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} di^2(tk)\right) c(tk) = \frac{\sum{i} \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} di^2(tk)\right) ci}{\sigma(tk) + \epsilon} where di^2(tk) is the squared Mahalanobis distance from the ray point to the Gaussian center, \alphai is the Gaussian opacity, ci is the color, and \epsilon prevents division by zero. 3. Integration: Perform volumetric integration using the evaluated density and color. The standard volume rendering integral is discretized: C = \sum{k} Tk \cdot (1 - e^{-\sigma(tk) \Delta tk}) \cdot c(tk) T{k+1} = Tk \cdot e^{-\sigma(tk) \Delta tk} where \Delta tk is the step size between samples, Tk is the transmittance at step k, and T0 = 1. 4. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity for the final pixel. Parameters Sample Count: The number of samples per ray, governing integration precision. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate during long ray marches or when evaluating very small Gaussian contributions. Boundary Handling: Gaussians truncated at their support radius may cause artifacts if the ray passes near the boundary without sufficient sampling. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raymarchgaussians(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, maxsamples=1000): """ Ray-marches through a set of 3D Gaussians. rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (x, y, z), normalized gaussians: List of dicts with keys: 'center' (3,), 'covinv' (3x3 list of lists), 'scale' (3,), 'opacity' (float), 'color' (3,) """ # 1. Adaptive Sampling: Collect ray bounds from Gaussian extents and subdivide bounds = [] for g in gaussians: diff = (g['center'][0] - rayorigin[0], g['center'][1] - rayorigin[1], g['center'][2] - rayorigin[2]) tcenter = diff[0]raydirection[0] + diff[1]raydirection[1] + diff[2]raydirection[2] r = math.sqrt(g['scale'][0]2 + g['scale'][1]2 + g['scale'][2]2) bounds.append(max(0.0, tcenter - r)) bounds.append(tcenter + r) bounds = sorted(set(bounds)) if not bounds: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 tpoints = [] for i in range(len(bounds) - 1): tstart, tend = bounds[i], bounds[i+1] tpoints.append(tstart) tpoints.append((tstart + tend) / 2.0) tpoints.append(bounds[-1]) tpoints = sorted(set(tpoints)) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(len(tpoints) - 1): tstart = tpoints[i] tend = tpoints[i+1] if tend <= tstart: continue tmid = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 deltat = tend - tstart point = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0]tmid, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1]tmid, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2]tmid) density = 0.0 weightedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for g in gaussians: diff = (point[0] - g['center'][0], point[1] - g['center'][1], point[2] - g['center'][2]) distsq = 0.0 for ridx in range(3): rowsum = 0.0 for cidx in range(3): rowsum += g['covinv'][ridx][cidx] diff[cidx] distsq += diff[ridx] rowsum if distsq > 9.0: continue weight = g['opacity'] math.exp(-0.5 distsq) density += weight weightedcolor[0] += weight g['color'][0] weightedcolor[1] += weight g['color'][1] weightedcolor[2] += weight g['color'][2] if density < 1e-6: continue color = [c / density for c in weightedcolor] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density deltat) accumulatedcolor[0] += transmittance alpha color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += transmittance alpha color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += transmittance alpha color[2] accumulatedopacity += transmittance alpha transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity A volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Choose it when exact volumetric integration and overlap resolution are required over rasterization speed. A representation for the view-dependent color (radiance) of a 3D Gaussian primitive as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics coefficients. It solves the problem of storing directional color variation compactly without requiring per-ray neural network queries. Choose it when capturing specular effects and directional shading is necessary. It is distinct from its siblings in the tree: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians uses this representation for color evaluation during rasterization, whereas OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm and Physics-based Gaussian Simulation do not inherently rely on this specific view-dependent color encoding. A method that integrates continuum mechanics or particle dynamics directly into 3D Gaussian Splatting, treating each Gaussian kernel as a discrete physical particle with volume. This approach creates a unified simulation-to-rendering pipeline where the geometric representation serves as the simulation mesh, enabling physically accurate dynamics, real-time interaction, and editing of high-fidelity virtual content. Choose it when dynamic scenes or physical editing are required. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes static appearance, these methods decouple or tightly couple physical state from radiometric properties to support dynamic scenes. A sort-free, image-order rendering technique for 3D Gaussians that resolves the hidden-surface problem by computing a weighted average of all ray-Gaussian intersection depths. Unlike NeRF-style methods that sort intersections and use closer Gaussians to attenuate further ones, this method blends all intersections simultaneously without sorting, extending Order Independent Transparency principles to 3D opaque surfaces. Choose it when order-independent transparency is needed without sorting overhead. A post-processing refinement method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples geometric alignment from material and lighting optimization. It corrects accumulated camera pose errors and refines coarse scene geometry in the first stage, then locks the Gaussian geometry to optimize material and lighting parameters using pre-computed per-Gaussian visibility. Choose it when high-fidelity material/lighting optimization is needed after initial geometry reconstruction. A ray marching-based renderer that follows the 3DGS model of opacity, reusing the data structures, activation functions, and learning rates of 3DGS. Differs from OTS Marcher in the model of opacity/extinction used, but shares the same ray marching pipeline structure. Choose it when compatibility with standard 3DGS training pipelines is prioritized over extinction-based accuracy. A custom ray tracing solution for physically accurate volumetric integration of 3D Gaussians, potentially including scattering. Uses icosahedrons to bound Gaussians and proposes an alternative kernel function to increase compactness. Choose it when physical accuracy and scattering effects are required. A proposal by Sun et al. to accelerate the ray tracing of pretrained 3D Gaussians using stochastic subsampling. Does not offer a backward pass and reaches frame rates about 3× below 3DGS. Choose it for inference-only acceleration of pretrained scenes where training speed is irrelevant. Time Complexity: Naive evaluation scales linearly with the number of Gaussians and samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian parameters. Performance: Significantly slower than rasterization-based 3DGS due to the per-ray evaluation and lack of GPU-friendly parallelism in early implementations. Stochastic subsampling can improve speed but still trails 3DGS by ~3×. Strengths: Accurately handles overlapping Gaussians and self-attenuation, providing a ground-truth reference for 3DGS approximations. Limitations: High computational cost makes real-time rendering challenging without significant optimization or hardware acceleration. The method was introduced to systematically analyze the approximations made in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), specifically regarding spatial overlap and sorting. It was developed as part of the work "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?". The study demonstrated that while 3DGS approximations have negligible impact on still images with many Gaussians. Subsequent works like Condor have explored ray-tracing variants for performance and physical accuracy. name: OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm
head: Adaptive Binning Ray Marching, OTS Marcher, OTS Marching, Ray Marching (OTS scheme)
body: The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm is a volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Unlike raytracing solutions for Gaussians, this method explicitly accounts for primitive overlap in the integration process. The algorithm performs adaptive sampling along each viewing ray to resolve Gaussian overlap. It iterates over the Gaussian mixture twice: first to establish bin borders adapted to the Gaussian data, and second to perform analytical integration into bins of variable extent. The bins are then blended together following the volume integral equation. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, scale, rotation, and color; a viewing ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a maximum ray depth or opacity threshold. Outputs: The final pixel color I(\mathbf{x}) and accumulated transmittance. Density Section Buffer: A fixed-size buffer storing sections. Each section is defined by: start: The start parameter t along the ray. end: The end parameter t along the ray. density: The sampling density for this section. Bin: A segment of the ray defined by start and end t values, storing integrated color and extinction. 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization: Create a fixed-size density section buffer. Iterate over all Gaussians to fill the buffer. For each Gaussian, compute its intersection interval with the ray. Define the start and end of the sampling section using the Gaussian's position \pm 3 standard deviations along the ray direction. Compute the density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit within the space defined by start and end. 2. Section Merging: Add the new section to the density section buffer. Combine existing and new sections to ensure they are ordered and non-overlapping. If sections overlap, the section with the higher sampling density takes precedence in the overlap area. Combining two sections can result in up to three new sections. Sections that fall outside the buffer capacity are deferred to the next batch. 3. Bin Creation: Traverse the merged sections to create bins. The size of each bin is inversely proportional to the density of the section it belongs to. 4. Blending Integral Computation (Batching): Divide the work into batches of bins (e.g., 128 bins per batch). Initialize the first batch at t=0. Subsequent batches start at the end-border of the last bin of the previous batch. Iterate over the Gaussian mixture again to compute integrals for each bin in the current batch. For each bin, compute 4 values: Red, Green, Blue, and integrated extinction (opacity). Colors are multiplied by the per-Gaussian integrated extinction. Stop when all Gaussians are processed or accumulated opacity reaches a high threshold. 5. Blending: Blend the bin evaluations together using the following equation: I(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{\infty} \gammai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} + cb \prod{j=0}^{\infty} e^{-\rhoj} Where: \gammai is the color contribution of bin i. \rhoj is the integrated extinction (opacity) of bin j. The term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} is the transmittance factor, cached between iterations to avoid redundant computation. cb is the background color. 6. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients manually using a front-to-back strategy. Two variants exist: Attached: Considers the numerical integration procedure and border positions in the gradient calculation. Detached: Assumes the numerical method can be ignored, keeping sampling and border positions constant with respect to differentiation. The detached variant performs significantly better. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def otsmarchingraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, backgroundcolor, maxsectionsbuffer, binsperbatch=128, opacitythreshold=0.99, binspergaussian=10): """ Renders a single ray using the OTS Marching Algorithm. """ # 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization sections = [] for g in gaussians: # Compute intersection interval along ray using position +/- 3 standard deviations tstart = g.position - 3.0 g.scale tend = g.position + 3.0 g.scale if tstart > tend: tstart, tend = tend, tstart # Compute density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit in the space length = tend - tstart density = binspergaussian / length if length > 0 else 0.0 newsection = Section(start=tstart, end=tend, density=density) sections = mergesections(sections, newsection, maxsectionsbuffer) # 2. Bin Creation bins = createbins(sections) # 3. Blending Integral Computation (Batching) totalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for batchstart in range(0, len(bins), binsperbatch): batchend = min(batchstart + binsperbatch, len(bins)) currentbatchbins = bins[batchstart:batchend] for bin in currentbatchbins: bincolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] binextinction = 0.0 # Iterate over Gaussians again to compute integrals for each bin for g in gaussians: # Check overlap and compute analytical integral if g.overlapssegment(bin.start, bin.end): c, e = g.integrateoversegment(bin.start, bin.end) bincolor[0] += c[0] bincolor[1] += c[1] bincolor[2] += c[2] binextinction += e # Front-to-back blending matching Eq. 3 transmittancefactor = exp(-binextinction) totalcolor[0] += bincolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += bincolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += bincolor[2] transmittance transmittance = transmittancefactor # Check accumulated opacity threshold if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break # Add background totalcolor[0] += backgroundcolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += backgroundcolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += backgroundcolor[2] transmittance return totalcolor, transmittance def mergesections(existing, newsec, maxsize): """ Combines newsec with existing sections ensuring order and no overlap. Higher density wins in overlap. Combining 2 sections creates up to 3 new sections. """ merged = existing + [newsec] merged.sort(key=lambda s: s.start) result = [] for sec in merged: if not result: result.append(sec) continue last = result[-1] if sec.start < last.end: # Overlap exists if sec.density >= last.density: # Higher density wins: extend last section, discard lower density part last.end = max(last.end, sec.end) else: # Lower density wins in overlap: split last section last.end = sec.start result.append(sec) else: result.append(sec) # Defer excess sections to next batch if buffer full if len(result) > maxsize: result = result[:maxsize] return result def createbins(sections): """ Traverse sections to create bins. Bin size is inversely proportional to density. """ bins = [] for sec in sections: if sec.density <= 0: continue binwidth = 1.0 / sec.density t = sec.start while t < sec.end: binend = min(t + binwidth, sec.end) bins.append(Bin(start=t, end=binend)) t = binend return bins class Section: def init(self, start, end, density): self.start = start self.end = end self.density = density class Bin: def init(self, start, end): self.start = start self.end = end Batch Size: Typically 128 bins per batch. Activation Function: Softplus with \beta = 2 is used instead of sigmoid to allow Gaussians to become fully opaque. Standard Deviation Factor: 3 standard deviations are used to define the start and end of sampling sections. Buffer Overflow: Sections that fall out of the fixed-size density section buffer are deferred to the next batch. Opacity Convergence: Using a constant opacity initialization can prevent convergence for large Gaussian counts. A power function fitting opacity to the number of Gaussians is recommended for initialization. Gradient Choice: The attached gradient variant is computationally more expensive and performs worse than the detached variant. Performance: The algorithm is considerably slower than splatting, typically between one and two orders of magnitude slower, depending on the scene. Accuracy: It provides accurate resolution of Gaussian overlap and precise perspective projection, serving as a testbed to examine the importance of these factors in 3DGS. Complexity: The algorithm requires iterating over the Gaussian mixture twice per batch (once for binning, once for integration), leading to higher computational cost compared to single-pass splatting. Strengths: Accurate volumetric rendering, handles overlap correctly, accounts for primitive overlap in integration unlike some raytracing solutions. Limitations: Low performance compared to splatting; implementation complexity is higher. The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm was introduced in the paper "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?". It was developed as part of an implementation to study the impact of approximations like spatial overlap and sorting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The implementation builds on the original 3DGS code base to enable meaningful comparisons.
