name: View-dependent color with Spherical Harmonics
head: Spherical Harmonics Color Evaluation, Spherical Harmonic Colour Model, Spherical Harmonic Color Modeling, Spherical Harmonic Evaluation, SH Color Representation, SH to RGB, SH Render, Rendering with Spherical Harmonics, Spherical Harmonics for View-Dependent Color
body: This method represents the view-dependent color (radiance) of a 3D Gaussian primitive as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It solves the problem of storing directional color variation (such as highlights and reflections) compactly without requiring per-ray neural network queries. Unlike simple point colors or view-independent RGB values, this model captures specular effects and directional shading. It is distinct from its siblings in the tree: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians uses this representation for color evaluation during rasterization, whereas OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm and Physics-based Gaussian Simulation do not inherently rely on this specific view-dependent color encoding. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians. For each Gaussian i: Position \mathbf{p}i. Camera parameters (position \mathbf{c}, orientation). SH coefficients \mathbf{k}i (see Data structures). Maximum SH degree L=3. Outputs: For each Gaussian projected onto the image plane, an RGB color value \mathbf{C}i corresponding to the viewing direction. Data structures: Each Gaussian stores 48 SH coefficients in a contiguous array of 32-bit floats. The layout is interleaved by coefficient index across the three color channels. Indices 0–2: Degree 0 (DC) coefficients for R, G, B. Indices 3–47: Higher-order coefficients for R, G, B. Specifically, the coefficients are stored in increasing order of degree and order. The first 3 elements are the DC color (f{dc\0..2}), and the next 45 elements are the rest coefficients (f{rest\0..f{rest\44}). Constants: The following normalization constants are used: SH\C0 = 0.28209479177387814 SH\C1 = 0.4886025119029199 SH\C2\0 = 1.0925484305920792 SH\C2\1 = -0.3153915652525201 SH\C2\2 = 0.5462742152960396 SH\C2\3 = -0.3153915652525201 SH\C2\4 = 0.1084622861184793 SH\C3\0 = -0.5900435899266435 SH\C3\1 = 2.890611442640554 SH\C3\2 = -0.4576460222995229 SH\C3\3 = 0.3731763325901154 SH\C3\4 = -0.4576460222995229 SH\C3\5 = 1.445305721320277 SH\C3\6 = -0.5900435899266435 Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Viewing Direction: For a given Gaussian with mean position \mathbf{p} and camera center \mathbf{c}, compute the normalized viewing direction vector \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}}{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\|}. Let \mathbf{d} = (x, y, z). 2. Evaluate Spherical Harmonics: Compute the color Cc(\mathbf{d}) for each color channel c \in \{R, G, B\} using the stored coefficients \mathbf{k}c and the direction \mathbf{d}. The basis functions Yl^m(\mathbf{d}) are fixed polynomials of x, y, z. The evaluation follows the formula: \begin{aligned} Cc(\mathbf{d}) = \max\Big(0, \quad & SH\C0 \cdot k{0,c} \\ & - SH\C1 \cdot y \cdot k{1,c} + SH\C1 \cdot z \cdot k{2,c} - SH\C1 \cdot x \cdot k{3,c} \\ & + SH\C2\0 \cdot xy \cdot k{4,c} - SH\C2\1 \cdot yz \cdot k{5,c} + SH\C2\2 \cdot (2z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{6,c} \\ & - SH\C2\3 \cdot xz \cdot k{7,c} + SH\C2\4 \cdot (x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{8,c} \\ & - SH\C3\0 \cdot y(3x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{9,c} + SH\C31 \cdot xyz \cdot k{10,c} \\ & - SH\C32 \cdot y(4z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{11,c} + SH\C33 \cdot z(2z^2 - 3x^2 - 3y^2) \cdot k{12,c} \\ & - SH\C34 \cdot x(4z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{13,c} + SH\C35 \cdot z(x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{14,c} \\ & - SH\C36 \cdot x(x^2 - 3y^2) \cdot k{15,c} \quad + 0.5 \Big) \end{aligned} Where k{i,c} are the coefficients for channel c at index i in the coefficient array. The term +0.5 is a bias added before the ReLU activation to handle negative SH values, as colors must be non-negative. The \max(0, \dots) operation acts as a ReLU. 3. Composite: Use the computed RGB color \mathbf{C}i in the front-to-back compositing rule for the Gaussian splat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 SHC1 = 0.4886025119029199 SHC20 = 1.0925484305920792 SHC21 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC22 = 0.5462742152960396 SHC23 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC24 = 0.1084622861184793 SHC30 = -0.5900435899266435 SHC31 = 2.890611442640554 SHC32 = -0.4576460222995229 SHC33 = 0.3731763325901154 SHC34 = -0.4576460222995229 SHC35 = 1.445305721320277 SHC36 = -0.5900435899266435 def evalsh(shcoeffs, viewdir): """ Evaluate view-dependent color for a single Gaussian. Args: shcoeffs: Array of 48 floats. Layout is interleaved by coefficient index: [R0, G0, B0, R1, G1, B1,..., R15, G15, B15]. viewdir: Tuple (x, y, z) of the normalized viewing direction. Returns: Tuple (r, g, b) """ x, y, z = viewdir # Extract coefficients for all channels at once # Degree 0 r0, g0, b0 = shcoeffs[0], shcoeffs[1], shcoeffs[2] # Degree 1 r1, g1, b1 = shcoeffs[3], shcoeffs[4], shcoeffs[5] r2, g2, b2 = shcoeffs[6], shcoeffs[7], shcoeffs[8] r3, g3, b3 = shcoeffs[9], shcoeffs[10], shcoeffs[11] # Degree 2 r4, g4, b4 = shcoeffs[12], shcoeffs[13], shcoeffs[14] r5, g5, b5 = shcoeffs[15], shcoeffs[16], shcoeffs[17] r6, g6, b6 = shcoeffs[18], shcoeffs[19], shcoeffs[20] r7, g7, b7 = shcoeffs[21], shcoeffs[22], shcoeffs[23] r8, g8, b8 = shcoeffs[24], shcoeffs[25], shcoeffs[26] # Degree 3 r9, g9, b9 = shcoeffs[27], shcoeffs[28], shcoeffs[29] r10, g10, b10 = shcoeffs[30], shcoeffs[31], shcoeffs[32] r11, g11, b11 = shcoeffs[33], shcoeffs[34], shcoeffs[35] r12, g12, b12 = shcoeffs[36], shcoeffs[37], shcoeffs[38] r13, g13, b13 = shcoeffs[39], shcoeffs[40], shcoeffs[41] r14, g14, b14 = shcoeffs[42], shcoeffs[43], shcoeffs[44] r15, g15, b15 = shcoeffs[45], shcoeffs[46], shcoeffs[47] # Compute contributions r = SHC0 r0 g = SHC0 g0 b = SHC0 b0 # Degree 1 r += -SHC1 y r1 + SHC1 z r2 - SHC1 x r3 g += -SHC1 y g1 + SHC1 z g2 - SHC1 x g3 b += -SHC1 y b1 + SHC1 z b2 - SHC1 x b3 # Degree 2 xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz r += SHC20 xy r4 - SHC21 yz r5 + SHC22 (2zz - xx - yy) r6 - SHC23 xz r7 + SHC24 (xx - yy) r8 g += SHC20 xy g4 - SHC21 yz g5 + SHC22 (2zz - xx - yy) g6 - SHC23 xz g7 + SHC24 (xx - yy) g8 b += SHC20 xy b4 - SHC21 yz b5 + SHC22 (2zz - xx - yy) b6 - SHC23 xz b7 + SHC24 (xx - yy) b8 # Degree 3 r += -SHC30 y(3xx - yy) r9 + SHC31 xyz r10 - SHC32 y(4zz - xx - yy) r11 + SHC33 z(2zz - 3xx - 3yy) r12 - SHC34 x(4zz - xx - yy) r13 + SHC35 z(xx - yy) r14 - SHC36 x(xx - 3yy) r15 g += -SHC30 y(3xx - yy) g9 + SHC31 xyz g10 - SHC32 y(4zz - xx - yy) g11 + SHC33 z(2zz - 3xx - 3yy) g12 - SHC34 x(4zz - xx - yy) g13 + SHC35 z(xx - yy) g14 - SHC36 x(xx - 3yy) g15 b += -SHC30 y(3xx - yy) b9 + SHC31 xyz b10 - SHC32 y(4zz - xx - yy) b11 + SHC33 z(2zz - 3xx - 3yy) b12 - SHC34 x(4zz - xx - yy) b13 + SHC35 z(xx - yy) b14 - SHC36 x(xx - 3yy) b15 # Apply bias and ReLU r = max(0.0, r + 0.5) g = max(0.0, g + 0.5) b = max(0.0, b + 0.5) return (r, g, b) Training Schedule: Optimization begins with only the degree-0 band (base color) active. One further band is unlocked every 1,000 iterations until all four bands (degrees 0-3) are active. This ensures the diffuse base color is correct before fitting higher-order components. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The basis functions Yl^m(\mathbf{d}) are fixed polynomials and are never updated during training; only the coefficients k are learned. If the viewing direction is not normalized, the polynomial evaluation will be incorrect. High-degree SH coefficients can cause memory bandwidth pressure during rendering. Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory bandwidth pressure caused by high-degree spherical harmonics (SH) by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame. It alleviates the bottleneck where loading high-degree SH coefficients consumes more memory than the splat's geometric attributes, storing the evaluated results in a "baked" color buffer. Unlike standard per-frame SH evaluation, this method trades immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance, converging to the correct view-dependent color within a short, fixed number of frames. Spherical Beta (SB) is a specular appearance model that adds explicit specular lobes on top of a diffuse base color, used for view-dependent color in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is distinct from Spherical Harmonics (SH) by using a parametric lobe function rather than a global basis expansion, allowing for sharper highlights with fewer parameters. It is orthogonal to SH, where SH (typically degree 0) supplies the diffuse base and SB adds the specular component. The Spherical Beta (SB) function is a directional appearance representation used to model view-dependent effects, such as specular reflections, in 3D Gaussian splatting. It replaces spherical harmonics (SH) to capture higher-frequency directional variations by using asymmetric, bounded-support lobes. Unlike SH, which uses global basis functions, SB uses localized kernels that can model skewed and sharper directional variation, offering greater flexibility at the cost of increased optimization difficulty. A representation where each point in the point cloud carries spherical harmonics parameters to model directional appearance, as opposed to directionally invariant RGB values. Using spherical harmonics yields better rendering quality than using learnable directionally invariant RGB values. On the Blender dataset, removing spherical harmonics ('w/o sh') reduces PSNR from 30.3 dB to 27.1 dB, SSIM from 0.945 to 0.932, and increases LPIPS from 0.078 to 0.155. A ray-traced variant of 3D Gaussians that treats Gaussians as volumetric primitives and ray marches them in a NeRF-like manner to achieve high quality at the cost of performance. It introduces a slab-by-slab integration scheme and augments spherical harmonics with a spherical Gaussian encoding to better capture view-dependent color. While this yields higher PSNR than 3DGS, it comes with a 6× training slowdown and approximately 25× lower frame rates. Strategies to reduce storage by removing or reducing the order of Spherical Harmonics coefficients, which represent view-dependent color. [44] introduces adaptive adjustment: calculate average transmittance per pixel and per view; if minimal variation per view, reduce SH coefficients to lower bands or remove them completely. Self-Organizing-Gaussians [40] trains scenes without higher-degree spherical harmonics, achieving competitive quality with smaller storage. LightGaussian [12] uses Knowledge Distillation with pseudo-view augmentation to encapsulate information from higher-order coefficients into a condensed form. Removing SH bands/degrees eliminates higher frequency color components, leading to loss of fine detail in view-dependent effects and sacrificing information on subtle lighting/shading variations. 3D Gaussians have 59 attributes total; 48 are SH coefficients across three bands, with 45 of these 48 responsible for view-dependent colors. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Each Gaussian stores 48 coefficients (16 per channel × 3 channels). This is significantly more than a single RGB triplet (3 floats). Time: Evaluation is a fixed number of polynomial operations per Gaussian, described as costing "almost nothing at display time". However, loading 48 floats per Gaussian can cause memory bandwidth bottlenecks. Measured Performance: On the Average-30K dataset, using full SH (degree 3) achieves a PSNR of 26.05, whereas removing SH (No-SH) reduces PSNR to 25.35. On the Blender dataset, using SH yields a PSNR of 30.3 dB, SSIM of 0.945, and LPIPS of 0.078, compared to 27.1 dB, 0.932, and 0.155 without SH. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Captures view-dependent effects like highlights and reflections. Compact representation compared to per-ray queries or simple point colors. Limitations: High memory usage for high degrees. Can introduce artifacts if not trained properly (e.g., weird colors on poorly observed sides). When to use: When view-dependent appearance (specularities, reflections) is important for photorealism. When rendering speed is critical and neural network queries are too slow. When not to use: When memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and view-dependent effects are negligible. When only diffuse, view-independent color is required. Spherical harmonics were repurposed from irradiance environment maps to represent the view-dependent color of 3D Gaussians in the 3D Gaussian Splatting method. The method was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The SH expansion is analogous to a Fourier series on the sphere, where low-degree harmonics capture smooth diffuse shading and higher degrees capture sharper directional variations. name: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking
head: Baked view-dependent color buffer, Progressive SH evaluation, Progressive Spherical Harmonics
body: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory bandwidth pressure caused by high-degree spherical harmonics (SH) by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame. It alleviates the bottleneck where loading high-degree SH coefficients consumes more memory than the splat's geometric attributes, storing the evaluated results in a "baked" color buffer. Unlike standard per-frame SH evaluation, this method trades immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance, converging to the correct view-dependent color within a short, fixed number of frames. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian splats with stored SH coefficients (e.g., Degree 3), camera view direction, and a convergence parameter N (number of frames to fully update all visible splats). Output: A "baked" view-dependent color buffer containing the evaluated RGB color for each visible splat. Data Structures: Splat Attributes: Position, scale, orientation, base color, and flags, consuming 52 bytes per splat. SH Coefficients: For Degree 3, 45 additional floating-point values (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Baked Color Buffer: Stores the evaluated RGB color for each splat. Size depends on the number of visible splats. For Degree 3, the SH data adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging memory load, which is more than triple the 52 bytes of geometric data. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Create a baked color buffer for all visible splats and initialize it with the base color or the previous frame's baked color. 2. Progressive Update Loop: For each frame f (where f=1, 2, \dots, N): a. Determine the subset of splats to update, targeting a fraction of 1/N of the total visible splats per frame. b. Select a subset of splats (e.g., sequential or random) comprising 1/N of the total visible splats. c. For each selected splat i: i. Evaluate the spherical harmonics function C(\mathbf{v}i) using the splat's SH coefficients and the view direction \mathbf{v}i. ii. Write the resulting RGB color to the baked color buffer for splat i. d. For splats not selected in this frame, retain their previously baked color value. 3. VR Handling: In Virtual Reality, account for different camera directions for left and right eyes. It is sufficient to progressively bake color values for only one eye and reuse them for the other, or evaluate based on the direction to the center of both eyes. 4. Rendering: Use the baked color buffer for shading during the current frame's rasterization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressiveshbaking(splats, viewdirections, numframestoconverge=10): """ splats: List of splat objects with.shcoeffs (45 floats for Degree 3) and.basecolor viewdirections: List of 3D view direction vectors numframestoconverge: N, frames to fully update all visible splats """ numsplats = len(splats) bakedcolors = [splat.basecolor for splat in splats] # Initialize with base color splatsperframe = max(1, numsplats // numframestoconverge) currentsplatidx = 0 for frame in range(numframestoconverge): for in range(splatsperframe): if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break # Evaluate spherical harmonics: C(v) = sum{l=0}^{L} sum{m=-l}^{l} c{lm} Y{lm}(v) # Standard SH evaluation routine bakedcolors[currentsplatidx] = splats[currentsplatidx].basecolor currentsplatidx += 1 if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break return bakedcolors Parameters: Convergence Frames (N): Number of frames to fully update all visible splats. Typical value: 10. SH Degree: Degree 3 is used, requiring 45 additional coefficients per splat (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VR Eye Discrepancy: Left and right eyes have different view directions. Reusing baked colors from one eye for the other may cause slight inaccuracies, but is deemed sufficient. Motion Artifacts: Under sufficiently high frame rates, progressive updates cause little to no apparent lag even under motion. Memory Bandwidth: High-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) adds 180 bytes per splat to staging memory, which is a significant bottleneck compared to 52 bytes of geometric data. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Storing Degree 3 SH coefficients adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging pass memory load. This is more than triple the 52 bytes used for position, scale, orientation, color, and flags. Time: Updating all harmonics per frame is expensive. On the Kinuta scene, updating all harmonics takes 1.6 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 0.6 ms and 1/30th takes 0.5 ms. On the Campus scene, updating all harmonics takes 4.4 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 1.5 ms and 1/30th takes 1.1 ms. Measured Performance: Kinuta Scene: All: 1.6 ms, 1/10th: 0.6 ms, 1/30th: 0.5 ms. Campus Scene: All: 4.4 ms, 1/10th: 1.5 ms, 1/30th: 1.1 ms. Berlin Scene: All: 0.4 ms, 1/10th: 0.2 ms, 1/30th: 0.1 ms. Garden Scene: All: 2.6 ms, 1/10th: 1.9 ms, 1/30th: 1.8 ms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduces memory bandwidth pressure and staging time for high-degree SH. Convergence is typically fast enough (e.g., 10 frames) to cause barely noticeable artifacts. Limitations: Progressive updates introduce a temporary lag in view-dependent color updates, but under sufficiently high frame rates, this causes little to no apparent lag even under motion. Requires additional memory for the baked color buffer. When to Use: Use when rendering high-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Use in VR where per-eye evaluation is expensive. When Not to Use: Use when SH degree is low (e.g., Degree 0 or 1) and bandwidth is not a concern. Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for large models and VR rendering. It addresses the performance bottleneck caused by the large memory footprint of high-degree spherical harmonics coefficients. The technique was developed as part of the Splatshop project, which focuses on efficiently editing large Gaussian Splat models. name: Spherical Beta View-Dependent Color
head: Spherical Beta, Spherical Beta (SB) appearance model, Spherical Beta lobes
body: Spherical Beta (SB) is a specular appearance model that adds explicit specular lobes on top of a diffuse base color for view-dependent rendering in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It replaces higher SH bands with parametric lobes, achieving sharper highlights with fewer parameters while remaining orthogonal to the SH diffuse base. Inputs: Gaussian splat parameters: position, covariance (or scale/rotation), opacity, and base color. SH coefficients (optional, typically degree 0 for SB-only specular, or degree 3 for hybrid). SB lobe parameters: number of lobes, axis direction, sharpness, and color. Outputs: Final pixel color for each splat during rasterization. Each SB lobe stores 6 floats in the following order: [r, g, b, \theta, \phi, \beta]. r, g, b: Color components of the lobe. \theta, \phi: Spherical angles defining the lobe axis direction. \beta: Sharpness parameter. During preprocessing (load time), lobe parameters are converted and stored as half floats (16-bit). One 16-byte texel is stored per lobe per splat. Lobes are packed into an RGBA32F texture atlas with 2 texels per lobe, indexed by splat.index. 1. Preprocessing: At load time, convert lobe parameters (axis from spherical angles \theta, \phi, sharpness \beta, and activated color rgb) into half-floats. 2. Densification: Handle the sbnumber parameter through densification strategies (DefaultStrategy and MCMCStrategy). 3. Rendering: For each splat, compute the color contribution of each lobe. 4. Composition: Add the lobe contributions to the base color (from SH or base color). 5. Clamping: Clamp the base color to zero before adding lobe contributions to prevent negative base colors from absorbing part of the highlight. 6. Export: Export SB parameters to PLY files via additive properties named sbparams, matching the reference implementation's naming convention. Leave standard fdc / frest schema untouched. For mixed lobe counts during merge, columns are channel-major (sbparams{channel lobes + lobe}). Absent lobes are padded with a raw value that activates to zero, since softplus(0) ≈ 0.1 would add a visible specular term. The color contribution of each lobe is calculated as: C{lobe} = \text{softplus}(rgb) \cdot \max(\text{dot}(dir, axis), 0)^{4 \cdot \exp(\beta)} Where: dir: View direction vector. axis: Lobe axis direction vector derived from \theta, \phi. rgb: Color components of the lobe. \beta: Sharpness parameter. \text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x). The final color is: C{final} = \max(C{base}, 0) + \sum{i=1}^{N{lobes}} C{lobe, i} Where C{base} is the color from SH degree 0 or base color. Number of lobes (N{lobes}): Up to 4 lobes are rendered. The trainers default to 2 lobes. shdegree: The degree of spherical harmonics used for the diffuse base. Typical value: 0 (for SB-only specular) or 3 (default in nerfstudio). sbnumber: The number of SB lobes to use. Typical values: 0 (purely diffuse), 2 (Beta Splatting setting). SBMAXLOBES: The maximum number of lobes supported, set to 2 in the implementation. It bounds the shader loop and atlas size. Negative Base Colors: The base color must be clamped to zero before adding lobe contributions. Many splats have negative base colors, which would otherwise absorb part of the highlight. Format Support: Compressed PLY, SOG, and SPZ formats currently do not support lobe data storage. Only uncompressed PLY is supported. Beta Kernel: This implementation only covers the Spherical Beta color lobes, not the Beta kernel. The Beta kernel replaces the Gaussian falloff with opacity (1 - r^2)^\beta and a hard cutoff, and requires changes to quad extent, bounds/culling, and per-splat values. Files using the kernel will not render correctly with this PR. Splat with Lobes but no SH: For splats with lobes but no SH, the color is re-evaluated as the camera moves. Rejection of Unsupported Formats: The splat and plycompressed formats reject SB lobes rather than dropping them silently. Preprocessor Guard: PlayCanvas's preprocessor treats bare #if NAME as #ifdef NAME. Therefore, #if SBLOBES > 0 is used instead of #if SBLOBES to ensure a 0-valued define is treated as false. Column Validation: If the count of sbparams columns is not a whole number of lobes or exceeds the supported count, the file is rejected with a warning to prevent misinterpreting one channel as another. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesphericalbetacolor(splat, viewdir): """ Compute the final color for a splat using Spherical Beta lobes. Args: splat: Object containing: basecolor: Color from SH degree 0 or base color (3 floats) lobes: List of lobe parameters, each being [r, g, b, theta, phi, beta] sbnumber: Number of lobes to use viewdir: View direction vector (3 floats) Returns: Final color (3 floats) """ # Clamp base color to zero to prevent absorption of highlights basecolor = [max(c, 0.0) for c in splat.basecolor] totallobecolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Iterate over the specified number of lobes for i in range(splat.sbnumber): lobe = splat.lobes[i] r, g, b, theta, phi, beta = lobe # Convert spherical angles to axis vector axis = [sin(theta) cos(phi), sin(theta) sin(phi), cos(theta)] # Compute dot product dotproduct = viewdir[0] axis[0] + viewdir[1] axis[1] + viewdir[2] axis[2] # Compute lobe contribution # softplus(rgb) softplusrgb = [log(1 + exp(r)), log(1 + exp(g)), log(1 + exp(b))] # max(dot(dir, axis), 0)^(4 exp(beta)) exponent = 4.0 exp(beta) lobefactor = max(dotproduct, 0.0) exponent # Add to total lobe color totallobecolor[0] += softplusrgb[0] lobefactor totallobecolor[1] += softplusrgb[1] lobefactor totallobecolor[2] += softplusrgb[2] lobefactor # Final color finalcolor = [ basecolor[0] + totallobecolor[0], basecolor[1] + totallobecolor[1], basecolor[2] + totallobecolor[2] ] return finalcolor Note: sin, cos, log, exp, and max are standard mathematical functions. A method for baking view-dependent color into textures, differing from SB's parametric lobe approach by using baked textures for view-dependent effects. Choose when hardware supports texture sampling efficiently and when pre-baking is feasible. Time Complexity: The shader computes one pow operation per lobe. With up to 4 lobes, this is a constant number of operations per splat. Memory Complexity: Each lobe stores 6 floats. With 2 lobes, this is 12 floats per splat, compared to 45 floats for SH bands 1-3. Measured Performance: On MipNeRF-360 (7 scenes, 30k steps, RTX 4090): MCMC SH0/SB2: 29.602 dB PSNR, 104 MB PLY size, 0.91 GB Peak VRAM, 52.0 FPS, 487s train time. Default SH0/SB2: 29.465 dB PSNR, 332 MB PLY size, 2.17 GB Peak VRAM, 31.1 FPS, 616s train time. Comparison to SH3/SB0: MCMC SH0/SB2 vs MCMC SH3/SB0: +0.15 dB PSNR, -56% PLY size, -39% Peak VRAM, +19% Render speed, -5% Train time. Default SH0/SB2 vs Default SH3/SB0: +0.30 dB PSNR, -54% PLY size, -53% Peak VRAM, +5% Render speed, -16% Train time. Strengths: Higher PSNR, smaller model size (44-46% of SH3), roughly half the peak VRAM, faster render speed, and faster training time compared to SH degree 3. Limitations: Only uncompressed PLY is supported for lobe data storage. The Beta kernel is not included, which would require more extensive changes to the renderer. When to Use: When view-dependent specular highlights are important and computational efficiency is a priority. SB is a strict win over SH3 in terms of PSNR, size, VRAM, and speed. When Not to Use: When compressed PLY, SOG, or SPZ formats are required, as they do not support lobe data storage. When the Beta kernel is required, as this implementation only covers the Spherical Beta color lobes. Spherical Beta (SB) is the specular model from Deformable Beta Splatting (Liu et al., SIGGRAPH 2025). It was integrated into the PlayCanvas engine (Pull Request #9729) for WebGL2 and WebGPU, and into the nerfstudio-project/gsplat (Pull Request #1056) for training and export. The model was designed to provide higher PSNR and faster speed at half the size and memory than SH degree 3. name: Spherical Harmonics Per Point
head: Point-based SH Representation, SH Per Point
body: Spherical Harmonics Per Point is a technique for modeling view-dependent appearance in point-based radiance field representations, where each point carries spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients to define directional color, rather than storing a single static RGB value. It sets itself apart from directionally invariant point representations by significantly improving rendering quality and view synthesis fidelity, as evidenced by higher PSNR and SSIM scores on standard datasets. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 3D points \{Pi\}, each with position \mathbf{p}i, opacity \alphai, and a set of spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Output: A rendered image pixel color C for a given camera ray. Data Structures Each point i stores: Position: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1] SH Coefficients: \mathbf{c}i. The dimension depends on the degree L of the spherical harmonics used. For degree L, there are (L+1)^2 coefficients per color channel (R, G, B). The coefficients are typically stored as a flat array or a tensor of shape [(L+1)^2, 3]. Method Steps 1. Ray-Point Intersection: For a camera ray, identify the set of points \mathcal{P} that contribute to the pixel. In point-based splatting, this often involves projecting points to screen space and determining coverage, or using a spatial acceleration structure (e.g., voxel grid) to find nearby points. 2. View Direction Calculation: For each contributing point i, compute the view direction \mathbf{v}i from the camera center to the point position \mathbf{p}i. Normalize \mathbf{v}i. 3. SH Evaluation: Evaluate the spherical harmonics basis functions \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{v}i) at the view direction \mathbf{v}i. The basis functions depend on the chosen degree L. 4. Color Computation: Compute the view-dependent color \mathbf{C}i for point i by taking the dot product of the SH coefficients and the basis functions: \mathbf{C}i = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{i, l, m} \cdot Y{l, m}(\mathbf{v}i) where c{i, l, m} are the SH coefficients for point i at degree l and order m, and Y{l, m} are the real spherical harmonics basis functions. This is performed for each color channel (R, G, B). 5. Compositing: Composite the colors \mathbf{C}i and opacities \alphai of all contributing points along the ray using standard alpha compositing to produce the final pixel color. Parameters SH Degree (L): Determines the complexity of the view-dependent appearance. Higher L allows for more detailed reflections but increases memory and computation. Common values are L=0 (constant color), L=1 (linear), or L=2 (quadratic). The sources do not specify the exact degree used in the ablation study, but the improvement from "w/o sh" implies L \ge 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: SH evaluation involves trigonometric functions and polynomial evaluations. Numerical stability should be maintained, especially for higher degrees. Boundary Conditions: The SH basis is defined on the unit sphere. Ensure view directions are normalized. Degenerate Input: If a point has zero opacity, its SH coefficients do not contribute to the final color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluateshbasis(v, degree): """ Evaluates real spherical harmonics basis functions for a given view direction v and degree. v: numpy array of shape (3,), normalized view direction. degree: integer, the degree L of the spherical harmonics. Returns: numpy array of shape ((degree+1)2,), the basis values. """ # Implementation of real spherical harmonics basis functions # This is a standard mathematical function, not a library call # For degree 0: [1] # For degree 1: [z, x, y] (normalized appropriately) # For degree 2: [sqrt(3)xy, sqrt(3)yz, sqrt(3)(2z^2-x^2-y^2), sqrt(3)xz, sqrt(3)yz]... # Note: Exact normalization factors depend on the specific SH convention used. # A common convention uses real solid harmonics. # Placeholder for actual SH basis evaluation logic # The exact formula for real SH basis functions is required here. # For example, for L=1: # Y0^0 = 1/(2sqrt(pi)) # Y1^-1 = sqrt(3/(4pi)) y # Y1^0 = sqrt(3/(4pi)) z # Y1^1 = sqrt(3/(4pi)) x # The coefficients c{l,m} are scaled accordingly. # For simplicity, assume a precomputed basis function evaluator exists or is implemented. # Here we return a dummy array for structure. numcoeffs = (degree + 1) 2 return np.ones(numcoeffs) def computepointcolor(p, v, shcoeffs, degree): """ Computes the view-dependent color for a single point. p: point position (unused in color computation, but part of point struct) v: view direction (normalized) shcoeffs: numpy array of shape ((degree+1)2, 3) for R, G, B degree: integer, SH degree Returns: numpy array of shape (3,), the RGB color """ basis = evaluateshbasis(v, degree) # Dot product between coefficients and basis for each channel color = np.dot(basis, shcoeffs) return color def renderpointcloud(points, rayorigin, raydirection, degree): """ Renders a point cloud using spherical harmonics per point. points: list of dicts with keys 'pos', 'opacity', 'shcoeffs' rayorigin: numpy array (3,) raydirection: numpy array (3,) degree: integer, SH degree Returns: numpy array (3,), final pixel color """ # 1. Find contributing points (simplified: all points for this example) # In practice, use a spatial index or screen-space projection contributingpoints = points # 2. Initialize accumulated color and opacity acccolor = np.zeros(3) accopacity = 0.0 # 3. Sort points by distance to camera (back-to-front for alpha compositing) # Sorting is crucial for correct alpha compositing distances = [np.linalg.norm(p['pos'] - rayorigin) for p in contributingpoints] sortedindices = np.argsort(distances) for idx in sortedindices: p = contributingpoints[idx] # 4. Compute view direction v = p['pos'] - rayorigin v = v / np.linalg.norm(v) # 5. Compute view-dependent color c = computepointcolor(p['pos'], v, p['shcoeffs'], degree) # 6. Alpha compositing alpha = p['opacity'] acccolor = acccolor + c alpha (1.0 - accopacity) accopacity = accopacity + alpha (1.0 - accopacity) if accopacity > 0.99: # Early ray termination break return acccolor Octahedral Surface Texture is a per-cell appearance representation that replaces spherical harmonics with an 8 \times 8 RGB texture projected onto a Voronoi cell's surface. It solves the problem of limited spatial appearance variation within a single primitive by allowing color to vary across the cell's image footprint, enabling larger cells to represent spatial detail that would otherwise require additional primitives. It sets itself apart from its parent Spherical Harmonics Per Point by halving the appearance values required for each cell evaluation while providing continuous, singularity-free directional mapping. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of contributing points per pixel and the degree of the spherical harmonics. Evaluating SH basis functions is O(L^2) per point. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of points times the number of SH coefficients per point. For degree L, this is O(N \cdot (L+1)^2 \cdot 3) floats, where N is the number of points. Measured Performance: On the Blender dataset, using spherical harmonics yields a PSNR of 30.3 dB, SSIM of 0.945, and LPIPS of 0.078. Removing spherical harmonics ('w/o sh') reduces PSNR to 27.1 dB, SSIM to 0.932, and increases LPIPS to 0.155. Strengths: Significantly improves rendering quality over directionally invariant RGB values. Allows for compact representation of view-dependent effects like reflections. Limitations: Higher degrees increase memory and computation. May struggle with very high-frequency view-dependent details if the degree is low. When to use: When view-dependent appearance is important and a point-based representation is preferred over volumetric or neural field representations. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and low-degree SH is insufficient for the desired visual quality, or when the scene has very complex, high-frequency view-dependent effects that require higher degrees than feasible. Spherical Harmonics Per Point is part of the broader field of differentiable point-based radiance fields for efficient view synthesis. It departs from volumetric representations and coordinate-network representations, which require ray-marching with hundreds of network evaluations per ray. The method was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Point-Based Radiance Fields for Efficient View Synthesis". The authors investigated an alternate radiance field representation based on points without giving up end-to-end differentiability. The use of spherical harmonics for view-dependent color in point-based representations has been validated through ablation experiments, showing that it jointly achieves the best view synthesis performance when combined with other components like a coarse-to-fine strategy and a consistency filter function. Differentiable Point-Based Radiance Fields for Efficient View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1145/3550469.3555413, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Octahedral Surface Texture
head: Paired Octahedral Surface and View-Dependent Textures, Octahedral Appearance Textures
body: Octahedral Surface Texture is a per-cell appearance representation that replaces spherical harmonics with an 8 \times 8 RGB texture projected onto a Voronoi cell's surface. It solves the problem of limited spatial appearance variation within a single primitive by allowing color to vary across the cell's image footprint, enabling larger cells to represent spatial detail that would otherwise require additional primitives. It sets itself apart from its parent Spherical Harmonics Per Point by halving the appearance values required for each cell evaluation while providing continuous, singularity-free directional mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The hit point \mathbf{x} of a ray intersecting a Voronoi cell Vi, the site position \mathbf{p}i of that cell, and the per-cell texture Ti (an 8 \times 8 RGB texture). Output: The sampled color \mathbf{c} at the hit point. Data Structures: Texture Ti: An 8 \times 8 grid of RGB values. Each texel stores 3 floating-point components. Total size: 64 \times 3 floats per cell. Steps: 1. Compute Direction: Calculate the unit direction vector \mathbf{d} from the site to the hit point: \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\|} 2. Project to Octahedron: Project \mathbf{d} onto the unit octahedron using \ell1 normalization to obtain coordinates \mathbf{q}: \mathbf{q} = \frac{\mathbf{d}}{|dx| + |dy| + |dz|} 3. Map to Texture Coordinates: Convert \mathbf{q} to 2D texture coordinates (u, v) \in [-1, 1]^2 based on the sign of dz: (u, v) = \begin{cases} (qx, qy) & \text{if } dz \geq 0 \\ ((1 - |qy|) \operatorname{sign}(qx), (1 - |qx|) \operatorname{sign}(qy)) & \text{if } dz < 0 \end{cases} If dz \geq 0 (upper hemisphere), the mapping is direct. If dz < 0 (lower hemisphere), the mapping unfolds the lower face to the corners of the square domain to maintain continuity across the texture boundary. 4. Sample Texture: Rescale (u, v) from [-1, 1]^2 to the texel space of Ti (e.g., [0, 7] or normalized [0, 1] depending on implementation) and perform bilinear interpolation to retrieve the color \mathbf{c}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octahedralsurfacetexture(hitpoint: Vector3, site: Vector3, texture: Texture8x8) -> Vector3: # 1. Compute unit direction direction = hitpoint - site d = normalize(direction) # 2. Project to unit octahedron (l1 normalization) l1norm = abs(d.x) + abs(d.y) + abs(d.z) q = Vector3(d.x / l1norm, d.y / l1norm, d.z / l1norm) # 3. Map to texture coordinates (u, v) in [-1, 1] if d.z >= 0: u = q.x v = q.y else: u = (1 - abs(q.y)) sign(q.x) v = (1 - abs(q.x)) sign(q.y) # 4. Sample texture # Rescale u, v from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] for standard texture lookup unorm = (u + 1.0) / 2.0 vnorm = (v + 1.0) / 2.0 # Bilinear interpolation on the 8x8 RGB texture color = texture.samplebilinear(unorm, vnorm) return color Parameters: Texture Size: 8 \times 8 RGB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction: If \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p}i, the direction is undefined. In practice, this occurs only if the ray origin is exactly at the site, which is rare in ray marching. A guard should handle division by zero in normalization. Boundary Continuity: The mapping is designed to be continuous across the texture boundary. Incorrect handling of the \operatorname{sign}(0) case in the lower hemisphere mapping can cause artifacts. \operatorname{sign}(0) is typically defined as 0 or 1 depending on convention, but since qx, qy are non-zero at the exact center of the lower face (where dz < 0 and qx=qy=0 is impossible for a valid direction on the octahedron surface unless dz=0), this is generally stable. A technique to store view-dependent color using octahedral maps to add spatial and directional detail while keeping appearance traffic bounded, replacing spherical harmonics. It is chosen when the primary goal is to reduce per-cell appearance cost while maintaining spatial variation within a cell, as opposed to using spherical harmonics which require more coefficients for similar directional accuracy. Time Complexity: O(1) per cell evaluation. The operations involve a few vector arithmetic operations and a texture lookup. Memory Complexity: O(1) per cell. Each cell stores a fixed 8 \times 8 RGB texture (64 \times 3 floats). This is significantly less than spherical harmonics, which require more coefficients for comparable directional accuracy. Performance: The method reduces appearance traffic and per-cell evaluation cost compared to spherical harmonics. It allows for larger cells, reducing the total number of primitives needed to represent spatial detail. Strengths: Low distortion, no polar singularities, continuous across texture boundaries, reduced memory footprint compared to SH. Limitations: The 8 \times 8 resolution may not capture high-frequency spatial details as well as denser primitives or higher-resolution textures. It is limited to the specific Voronoi cell structure where the site is interior and the map from direction to surface is a bijection. When to use: When rendering with a fixed budget of primitives and needing to balance spatial and directional appearance detail with memory constraints. When not to use: When extremely high-frequency spatial detail is required within a single cell, or when the primitive structure does not allow for a bijection between direction and surface point. The method was introduced in "Differentiable Voronoi Ray Tracing Beyond Rasterization Speeds". It builds on the concept of textured Gaussians [Chao et al. 2025] but adapts it for Voronoi-based rendering where appearance lookup is part of the per-cell traversal loop. The octahedral mapping technique itself is based on [Cigolle et al. 2014]. The approach is part of a broader effort to optimize explicit radiance-field methods by reducing per-cell appearance cost and enabling larger cells to represent spatial detail. Differentiable Voronoi Ray Tracing Beyond Rasterization Speeds, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17682, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: RayGauss
head: Volumetric Gaussian-Based Ray Casting
body: RayGauss is a differentiable volume ray casting algorithm that approximates radiance and density fields using ray casting of irregularly distributed anisotropic Gaussian primitives to generate photorealistic novel views. It treats 3D Gaussians as volumetric primitives and ray marches them in a NeRF-like manner, introducing a slab-by-slab integration scheme and augmenting spherical harmonics with spherical Gaussian encoding to better capture view-dependent color. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting, which uses a splatting algorithm that inherently produces rendering artifacts such as flickering, RayGauss uses volume ray casting which promises to produce minimal artifacts. Unlike grid-based methods (e.g., Instant NGP, TetraNeRF) which are limited by the resolution of the underlying structure, RayGauss uses irregularly distributed points/primitives that efficiently adapt to scene geometry. Inputs: A set of n anisotropic Gaussian primitives, each defined by a mean position \mathbf{\mu}, a covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation and scale parameters), and view-dependent color coefficients. A set of camera viewpoints with corresponding images for optimization. Ray origins and directions for rendering. Outputs: Rendered images (radiance) for given camera viewpoints. Optimized primitive parameters (position, covariance, color coefficients) after training. Data Structures: 1. Primitive: An anisotropic Gaussian function. \mathbf{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \mathbf{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix, ensuring elliptical shape. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Scalar opacity/density amplitude. \mathbf{c}{SH} \in \mathbb{R}^{k}: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color. \mathbf{c}{SG} \in \mathbb{R}^{m}: Spherical Gaussian coefficients for view-dependent color. 2. Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH): Acceleration structure storing Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) for each primitive. AABB: Defined by min/max coordinates [\mathbf{b}{min}, \mathbf{b}{max}]. Construction: Uses a dedicated API (e.g., OptiX). Formulas: The global density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and radiance L(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) fields are derived from the radiative transfer equation for a medium containing n independent entities. The individual density of a primitive i is: \sigmai(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \cdot \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{\mu}i, \mathbf{\Sigma}i) where \mathcal{N} is the anisotropic Gaussian function: \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{\mu}, \mathbf{\Sigma}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{\mu})^T \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{\mu})\right) The radiance emitted by primitive i in direction \mathbf{v} is parameterized by a combination of spherical harmonics (SH) and spherical Gaussians (SG): Li(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = \text{SH}(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{c}{SH,i}) + \text{SG}(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{c}{SG,i}) The global density and radiance are the superposition of individual primitives: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{n} \sigmai(\mathbf{x}) L(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Li(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) Rendering Steps: 1. Bounding Primitives: Since anisotropic Gaussian functions have unbounded support, restrict evaluation to the region where density exceeds a threshold \tau. Compute the AABB for each primitive based on this threshold. 2. BVH Construction: Calculate AABBs and build the BVH using an API like OptiX. 3. Ray Traversal: For each pixel, cast a ray. Traverse the BVH to find intersected primitives. 4. Slab-by-Slab Integration: Evaluate the discretized rendering equation over successive segments (slabs) containing multiple samples. Compute intersections of multiple samples with primitives directly to reduce intersection costs. 5. Volume Rendering: Integrate density and radiance along the ray using standard volume rendering accumulation (alpha blending). Optimization: Optimize primitive parameters (position, covariance, SH/SG coefficients) using gradient descent on the difference between rendered images and ground truth images from known viewpoints, similar to NeRF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussiandensity(x, mu, Sigmainv): """ Compute anisotropic Gaussian density. x: (3,) point mu: (3,) mean Sigmainv: (3,3) inverse covariance """ diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diff, np.dot(Sigmainv, diff)) return np.exp(exponent) def viewdependentcolor(v, shcoeffs, sgcoeffs): """ Compute radiance from view direction using SH and SG. v: (3,) normalized view direction shcoeffs: array of SH coefficients sgcoeffs: array of SG coefficients """ # Placeholder for actual SH and SG evaluation functions # In practice, these are standard mathematical functions shval = evaluatesphericalharmonics(v, shcoeffs) sgval = evaluatesphericalgaussians(v, sgcoeffs) return shval + sgval def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, primitives, threshold=1e-4): """ Render a single ray using volume ray casting. primitives: list of dicts with keys 'mu', 'Sigmainv', 'alpha', 'shcoeffs', 'sgcoeffs', 'aabb' """ # 1. Traverse BVH to get relevant primitives # This step is abstracted as finding primitives whose AABB intersects the ray relevantprimitives = traversebvh(rayorigin, raydirection, primitives) # 2. Collect intersection intervals and sort by distance intervals = [] for prim in relevantprimitives: # Compute intersection of ray with primitive's AABB tmin, tmax = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, prim['aabb']) if tmax > 0: intervals.append((tmin, tmax, prim)) # Sort intervals by tmin intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # 3. Slab-by-slab integration totaltransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) # Define ray segment length for sampling stepsize = 0.01 # Not given in sources, typical value for ray marching currentt = 0.0 for tmin, tmax, prim in intervals: # Sample points along the ray within the slab tstart = max(currentt, tmin) tend = tmax # Number of samples in this slab numsamples = int((tend - tstart) / stepsize) if numsamples == 0: numsamples = 1 for i in range(numsamples): t = tstart + (i + 0.5) stepsize if t > tend: break # Sample point on ray x = rayorigin + t raydirection # Compute density density = prim['alpha'] gaussiandensity(x, prim['mu'], prim['Sigmainv']) # Compute radiance # View direction is opposite to ray direction for outgoing light v = -raydirection radiance = viewdependentcolor(v, prim['shcoeffs'], prim['sgcoeffs']) # Volume rendering equation: dL = L (1 - exp(-sigma dt)) # Approximation for small dt: dL = L sigma dt alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density stepsize) accumulatedcolor += totaltransmittance alpha radiance totaltransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if totaltransmittance < 1e-4: break currentt = tend return accumulatedcolor def optimizeprimitives(primitives, images, cameras, lr=0.01): """ Optimize primitive parameters using gradient descent. """ for epoch in range(1000): # Not given in sources, typical training loop for image, camera in zip(images, cameras): # Render image renderedimage = renderimage(camera, primitives) # Compute loss (e.g., MSE) loss = np.mean((renderedimage - image) 2) # Backpropagate and update parameters # This requires differentiable rendering of the Gaussian primitives gradients = computegradients(loss, primitives) updateparameters(primitives, gradients, lr) Parameters: Threshold (\tau): Density threshold for bounding primitives. Not given in the sources. Step Size: Distance between samples along the ray. Not given in the sources. Spherical Harmonics Degree: Determines the number of SH coefficients. Not given in the sources. Spherical Gaussian Order: Determines the number of SG coefficients. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Support: Anisotropic Gaussians have infinite support. Must be truncated using a threshold to compute AABBs for BVH construction. Precision: High precision required for density and radiance calculations to avoid artifacts. Degenerate Input: If primitives are too small or too large, rendering quality may suffer. Optimization must handle this. A technique to bake view-dependent color into textures over time. Choose when real-time performance is critical and offline baking is acceptable. Uses spherical beta functions for view-dependent color. Choose when smooth, physically plausible view-dependent effects are needed. Assigns SH coefficients to each point. Choose when simple view-dependent effects are sufficient. A mathematical function for view-dependent color. Choose as a building block for other methods. Time Complexity: Slower than 3D Gaussian Splatting due to volume ray marching. Training is 6× slower than 3DGS. Frame rates are approximately 25× lower than 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives. BVH construction adds overhead. Measured Performance: Yields higher PSNR than 3DGS. Strengths: High quality, minimal artifacts compared to splatting, adapts to scene geometry. Limitations: Slow performance, high training time. When to use: When high quality is more important than speed, and artifacts from splatting are unacceptable. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical. RayGauss was introduced by Blanc et al. in 2025. It is inspired by point cloud inspired representations and aims to develop a differentiable volume ray casting algorithm capable of rendering primitives represented by elliptical basis functions. The work validates modeling choices through empirical tests, demonstrating that anisotropic Gaussians combined with spherical harmonics and spherical Gaussians achieve accurate rendering. RayGauss: Volumetric Gaussian-Based Ray Casting for Photorealistic Novel View Synthesis, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F8tg0CTBiCo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804496, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Spherical Beta Function
head: SB color representation
body: The Spherical Beta (SB) function is a directional appearance representation used in 3D Gaussian splatting to model view-dependent effects. It replaces spherical harmonics (SH) to capture higher-frequency directional variations. It provides a compact, bounded alternative that ensures radiance continuity while enabling sharper directional modeling. It builds on View-dependent color with Spherical Harmonics by trading the global basis of SH for localized, asymmetric lobes. The SB function represents the directional intensity or color component of a Gaussian surfel as a sum of K directional lobes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Viewing direction \omega \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit vector), number of lobes K, set of principal directions \{sk\}{k=1}^K, and shape parameters \{\alphak, \betak\}{k=1}^K. Output: Scalar value f{SB}(\omega) representing the directional intensity or color component. Data Structures: For each Gaussian primitive, the view-dependent color is stored as: K: Integer, number of lobes. sk: 3D vector, principal direction of the k-th lobe, normalized to unit length. \alphak: Scalar, shape parameter > 0 controlling the "rise" side of the lobe. \betak: Scalar, shape parameter > 0 controlling the "fall" side of the lobe. Formula: The standard formulation computes the sum of lobe contributions as follows: f{SB} (\omega; \alpha, \beta, s) = \sum{k=1}^{K} (1+sk \cdot \omega)^{\alphak -1} (1-sk \cdot \omega)^{\betak -1} Where: sk \cdot \omega is the dot product between the principal direction and the viewing direction. \alphak, \betak > 0. The term (1+sk \cdot \omega) is non-negative because sk \cdot \omega \in [-1, 1] for unit vectors. Steps: 1. Initialize an accumulator to zero. 2. For each lobe k from 1 to K: 3. Compute the dot product d = sk \cdot \omega. 4. Compute the terms (1+d)^{\alphak-1} and (1-d)^{\betak-1}. 5. Multiply the terms and add the result to the accumulator. 6. Return the accumulator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalbetafunction(omega, lobes): total = 0.0 for lobe in lobes: s = lobe['s'] alpha = lobe['alpha'] beta = lobe['beta'] dot = sum(a b for a, b in zip(s, omega)) term1 = (1.0 + dot) (alpha - 1.0) term2 = (1.0 - dot) (beta - 1.0) total += term1 term2 return total Parameters: K: Number of lobes. Not given in the sources. \alphak, \betak: Optimized during training. Typical values are not given in the sources, but they must be > 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The function is well-defined for all \omega on the unit sphere since 1 \pm sk \cdot \omega \ge 0. Ill-conditioned Gradients: Extreme values of \alphak or \betak generate very sharp and flat regions, causing ill-conditioned gradients. A directional appearance representation that extends Spherical Gaussians by enabling asymmetric and bounded-support lobes for skewed directional variation. Chosen when SH ringing or SG unbounded support is problematic, as SB provides a compact, bounded alternative that ensures radiance continuity. Time Complexity: O(K) per evaluation, where K is the number of lobes. Memory Complexity: Stores K directions (3 floats each) and 2K shape parameters (2 floats each), totaling 5K floats per Gaussian. Performance: In DP-GES, using SB slightly increases FLIP error compared to GES because the function enables higher-frequency view-dependent effects that FLIP interprets as warping error, but it improves view-dependent appearance. Reverting to SH reduces FPS from 472 to 480 and PSNR from 28.11 to 27.72 on MipNeRF360, indicating SB is slightly more expensive but yields higher quality. Strengths: Captures higher-frequency view-dependent effects than SH. Limitations: Increases the risk of overfitting, as observed in Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS). The Spherical Beta function was introduced in the context of Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering to model higher-frequency view-dependent effects. It is used in DP-GES (Depth Peeling for High-Fidelity Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering). Depth Peeling for High-Fidelity Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25345, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Betas (SB)
head: SB color representation
body: Spherical Betas (SB) is a directional appearance representation that extends Spherical Gaussians (SG) by enabling asymmetric and bounded-support lobes to model skewed and sharper directional variation. It is used in Deformable Beta Splatting to model view-dependent specular color. Unlike SG, which has unbounded support requiring truncation, SB provides a compact, bounded alternative that ensures radiance continuity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: View direction \hat{V}, primitive parameters (base color, lobe directions, shape parameters). Output: View-dependent color c(\hat{V}). Data Structures: A 3D Beta primitive stores features that scale linearly with the number of reflection lobes M. The feature dimension is 3 + 6M: c0: Diffuse/base color (3 components). For each lobe m \in \{1, \dots, M\}: \hat{R}m: Reflection direction (3 components, normalized). cm: Lobe color (3 components). bm: Shininess parameter (1 component, scalar). Formulas: The general Spherical Beta function for a direction \omega with K lobes is defined as: f{SB} (\omega; \alpha, \beta, s) = \sum{k=1}^{K} (1+sk \cdot \omega)^{\alphak -1} (1-sk \cdot \omega)^{\betak -1} where sk is the principal direction and \alphak, \betak > 0 control the shape. In the specular lobe variant, appearance is modeled as a sum of a base diffuse color and specular lobes: c(\hat{V}) = c0 + \sum{m \in \mathcal{M}} \mathcal{B}(1 - \hat{R}m \cdot \hat{V}; bm) cm where c0 is the diffuse/base color, \mathcal{M} is the set of SB lobes, \hat{R}m is the reflection direction derived from surface normal and light source, \hat{V} is the view direction, cm is the lobe color, bm is the shininess coefficient, and \mathcal{B} is the Beta Kernel function. Parameters: M: Number of reflection lobes per primitive. Default value is M=2 (sb=2). bm: Shininess parameter. Initialized to zero to make the Beta Kernel initially resemble the Gaussian Kernel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalbetacolor(basecolor, lobes, viewdir): """ Computes view-dependent color using Spherical Beta lobes. Args: basecolor (vec3): Diffuse/base color c0. lobes (list of dict): List of M lobes. Each lobe contains: 'R': reflection direction (vec3, normalized) 'c': lobe color (vec3) 'b': shininess parameter (float) viewdir (vec3): View direction (vec3, normalized). Returns: vec3: Final view-dependent color. """ totalspecular = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for lobe in lobes: R = lobe['R'] cm = lobe['c'] b = lobe['b'] # Calculate argument for Beta kernel: 1 - R. V # Source states input range is confined to [0, 1] costheta = dot(R, viewdir) x = 1.0 - costheta x = max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) # Clamp to [0, 1] per source claim # Standard unnormalized Beta kernel form: x^(alpha-1) (1-x)^(beta-1) # Mapping shininess b to symmetric shape parameters for implementation. alpha = b + 1.0 betashape = b + 1.0 if x <= 0.0 or x >= 1.0: betaval = 0.0 else: betaval = (x (alpha - 1.0)) ((1.0 - x) (betashape - 1.0)) totalspecular += betaval cm return basecolor + totalspecular Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioned Gradients: Extreme values of \alphak or \betak (or bm) generate very sharp and flat regions, causing ill-conditioned gradients and stronger sensitivity to initialization compared to Spherical Gaussians. Truncation Artifacts: Unlike Spherical Gaussians, which have unbounded support and require truncation (causing radiance discontinuities when view and reflection directions are orthogonal), Spherical Beta is inherently bounded. Its input range is confined to [0, 1], ensuring radiance naturally drops to zero when \hat{R}m \cdot \hat{V} = 0. Extends SG with asymmetric, bounded-support lobes for sharper directional variation. Harder to optimize due to gradient ill-conditioning at extreme shape parameters. Models outgoing reflected radiance by merging ambient and diffuse into a base color c0. Uses learnable bounded Beta kernels for specular lobes. Chosen for efficiency (3+6M dimension) and continuity (no truncation artifacts) compared to SG. Default uses M=2 lobes per primitive. Time Complexity: Evaluation is O(M) per primitive. Memory Complexity: Feature dimension per primitive is 3 + 6M. For default M=2, this is 15 floats per primitive. Performance: Fully explicit and differentiable, implemented in CUDA for optimized performance. Convergence speed varies by scene, with default training at 30,000 iterations. Strengths: Bounded support eliminates truncation artifacts and radiance discontinuities at orthogonal view/reflection angles. More flexible than SG for modeling skewed/sharp lobes. Limitations: Harder to optimize than SG due to ill-conditioned gradients and sensitivity to initialization. Spherical Betas were introduced as an extension of Spherical Gaussians to provide asymmetric and bounded-support lobes. They are used in Deformable Beta Splatting. The Deformable Beta Splatting implementation builds upon the 3DGS-MCMC framework and GSplat library. Spherical Voronoi: Directional Appearance as a Differentiable Partition of the Sphere, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2512.14180, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Deformable Beta Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3721238.3730716, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Physics-based Gaussian Simulation
body: Physics-based Gaussian Simulation integrates continuum mechanics or particle dynamics directly into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), treating each Gaussian kernel as a discrete physical particle with volume. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes static appearance, this approach decouples or tightly couples physical state (position, velocity, deformation) from radiometric properties to enable physically accurate dynamics, real-time interaction, and editing of high-fidelity virtual content. Inputs: 1. Initial 3DGS representation: A set of N Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gi is defined by mean position \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color ci. 2. Physical parameters: Mass mi, damping coefficients, and material properties (e.g., stiffness, viscosity). 3. External forces: Gravity, collisions, or user interactions. Outputs: 1. Updated Gaussian parameters: New positions \mu'i, covariances \Sigma'i, and potentially updated colors/opacities if coupled with rendering. 2. Rendered image: Computed via standard 3DGS rasterization using the updated physical state. The core data structure extends the standard 3DGS attribute list with physics-specific fields: Position (\mu): 3D vector (x, y, z). Velocity (v): 3D vector (vx, vy, vz). Mass (m): Scalar value, potentially learned from input video or assigned based on volume. Covariance (\Sigma): 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix representing the Gaussian kernel shape. Physical State Flags: Boolean or integer flags indicating if a Gaussian is part of the active simulation domain (e.g., fluid vs. solid). 1. Initialization: Reconstruct initial 3DGS from input images or video. Assign physical properties: mass mi is learned from input video dynamics or estimated from Gaussian volume, and velocity vi is initialized to zero or estimated from temporal changes. Define material parameters (stiffness, damping) based on object type (solid, fluid). 2. Physics Simulation Step: Compute forces Fi acting on each Gaussian i: Fi = F{gravity} + F{collision} + F{interaction} + F{internal} F{gravity} = mi \cdot g. F{collision}: Derived from contact detection with other Gaussians or static meshes. F{internal}: Depends on the chosen physics model: Continuum Mechanics (PhysGaussian): Uses continuum deformation of Gaussian kernels, treating the cloud as a deformable body. Position-Based Dynamics (Gaussian Splashing): Uses Position-Based Fluids (PBD) constraints to enforce incompressibility and cohesion. Spring-Mass (Spring-Gaus): Applies spring forces between neighboring Gaussians based on a spring-mass model. Update velocity and position using a numerical integrator (e.g., Verlet or Euler): vi^{t+1} = vi^t + \frac{Fi}{mi} \Delta t \mui^{t+1} = \mui^t + vi^{t+1} \Delta t. Update covariance \Sigmai to reflect deformation: For continuum deformation, \Sigmai is transformed by the local deformation gradient. For PBD, \Sigmai may be adjusted to maintain volume consistency. 3. Rendering Step: Rasterize the updated Gaussians using standard 3DGS alpha blending. Deferred Shading: Some methods (e.g., VR-GS) use deferred shading to avoid blending artifacts from multiple shading calculations. Material Rendering: For fluids/solids, material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, normals) are applied to each Gaussian to enhance physical appearance. Normals are aligned with surface normals to improve reflection accuracy. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def physicsbasedgaussiansimulation(gaussians, dt, externalforces): """ Simulate physics for a set of 3D Gaussians. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: (3,) position vector v: (3,) velocity vector m: float mass Sigma: (3,3) covariance matrix type: str ('solid', 'fluid', 'particle') collisionradius: float interaction range dt: float time step externalforces: dict of force functions, e.g., {'gravity': lambda m: m 9.81} Returns: Updated list of Gaussians """ for g in gaussians: F = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 1. name: Weighted Blending (Fuzzy Metaballs)
head: Blending intersections, Fuzzy Metaballs rendering, Hidden-surface solution for Fuzzy Metaballs, Sort-free Gaussian rendering, Weighted Blending of Intersections
body: Weighted Blending is a sort-free, image-order rendering technique for 3D Gaussians that resolves the hidden-surface problem by computing a weighted average of all ray-Gaussian intersection depths. Unlike NeRF-style methods that sort intersections and use closer Gaussians to attenuate further ones, this method blends all intersections simultaneously without sorting, extending Order Independent Transparency (OIT) principles to 3D opaque surfaces. Inputs: Ray direction \vec{v} (normalized), set of N 3D Gaussians. Outputs: Blended intersection depth tf, opacity \alpha, and optionally normal \vec{n}f or color \vec{c}f. Data Structures: Gaussian i: \mui (vector), \Sigmai^{-1} (matrix), \lambdai (scalar). Per-ray accumulators: tf (scalar), \alpha (scalar), \vec{n}f (vector), \vec{c}f (vector). Steps: 1. For each Gaussian i, compute the intersection distance ti along the ray \vec{v} using the linear approach (point of maximum likelihood): ti = \frac{\mui^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}}{\vec{v}^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}} 2. Compute the unnormalized log distance di for Gaussian i: di = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ (ti \vec{v} - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (ti \vec{v} - \mui) \right] + \log(\lambdai) 3. Compute the unnormalized Gaussian density \deltai: \deltai = \exp(di) 4. Compute the weight wi for each intersection: wi = \exp \left( \beta1 di \sigma \left( \frac{\beta3}{\eta} ti \right) - \frac{\beta2}{\eta} ti \right) where \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} is the sigmoid function. The term h(ti) = \sigma \left( \frac{\beta3}{\eta} ti \right) down-weights intersections behind the camera. 5. Compute the final blended depth tf: tf = \frac{1}{\sumi wi} \sumi wi ti 6. Compute opacity \alpha: \alpha = \sigma \left( \beta4 \sumi \deltai + \beta5 \right) 7. For other properties like normal \vec{n}i or color \vec{c}i, apply the same weighted average using wi. Parameters: \beta1, \beta2: Balance high-quality hits (high di) vs. camera proximity (low ti). \beta3: Controls sigmoid decay for behind-camera intersections. \beta4, \beta5: Control opacity scaling and offset. \eta: Rough scale of the object, used to normalize ti for scale invariance. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intersections behind the camera (ti < 0) are down-weighted by the sigmoid term in the original model. The original formulation assumes \sum \lambdai = 1. Losing this global normalization causes minor differences in pose estimation but is negligible for shape estimation. Precision issues may arise if \lambdai is very small, causing \log(\lambdai) to underflow. Ensure \lambdai is bounded away from zero or use log-sum-exp tricks if necessary. Fuzzy Metaballs is an algebraic, implicit surface representation that defines geometry as the zero level set of a function composed of multidimensional Gaussians (ellipsoids) rather than isotropic ones. It serves as the foundational object representation for differentiable rendering pipelines, enabling robust optimization by relaxing hard thresholds to ensure smooth gradients during ray-tracing. Unlike Weighted Blending, which focuses on sort-free image-order rendering, Fuzzy Metaballs provides the underlying implicit field definition that allows for the computation of surface normals and distance-based losses. A simplified rendering model for shape reconstruction that reduces the original 5 hyperparameters to 2 (\beta1, \beta2) by removing the sigmoid term for behind-camera contributions and replacing the sigmoid alpha function with a decaying exponential. Weight: wi = \exp \left( \beta1 di - \frac{\beta2}{\eta} ti \right). Alpha: \alpha = 1 - \exp \left( - \sumi \deltai \right). Pitfall: Losing the global normalization condition (\sum \lambdai = 1) causes minor differences in pose estimation, but these are negligible for shape estimation. A hyperparameter-free rendering variant that requires sorting intersections and uses alpha compositing (transmission) to compute weights, enabling differentiable rendering without tunable parameters. Step: Sort all ray-Gaussian intersections by depth ti. Compute accumulated transmission Ti for each intersection based on earlier (closer) intersections. Transmission: Ti = \exp \left( -\sumj \deltaj 1[tj < ti] \right), where 1[\cdot] is the indicator function. Weight: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\deltai)). Comparison: This approach is slower than the sort-free models but performs nearly identically in quality, while requiring no hyperparameters. Time Complexity: O(N) evaluations of Gaussians for each ray, where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a Quadro P2000 (CUDA), Fuzzy Metaballs forward pass takes 3.0 \pm 0.2 ms and backward pass 9.6 \pm 0.5 ms for 160x120 images. On an i5-7287U (CPU), forward pass takes 3.0 \pm 0.15 ms and backward pass 13.2 \pm 1.4 ms for 80x60 images. Strengths: Sort-free, differentiable, scale-invariant (with \eta), simple implementation (60 lines of JAX code). Limitations: The original model requires tuning 5 hyperparameters. The Zero Parameter Model is slower due to sorting. When to use: When differentiable rendering of 3D Gaussians is required without the overhead of sorting, particularly for shape reconstruction. Originated from the Fuzzy Metaballs paper and further detailed in "Flexible Techniques for Differentiable Rendering with 3D Gaussians". The method was developed to provide a sort-free solution to the hidden-surface problem for 3D Gaussian representations, extending Order Independent Transparency (OIT) to opaque surfaces. It is used in differentiable rendering pipelines for shape reconstruction from video. name: Fuzzy Metaballs
head: Fuzzy Metaballs representation, differentiable renderer for GMMs
body: Fuzzy Metaballs is an algebraic, implicit surface representation that defines geometry as the zero level set of a function composed of multidimensional Gaussians (ellipsoids) rather than isotropic ones. It serves as the foundational object representation for differentiable rendering pipelines, enabling robust optimization by relaxing hard thresholds to ensure smooth gradients during ray-tracing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multidimensional Gaussian components \{Gi\}, each defined by a center \mui, a covariance matrix \Sigmai, and a weight \lambdai. Training views \{Ij\} are used for supervision. Outputs: An implicit field function F(x,y,z) and, in optimization contexts, updated Gaussian parameters \mut, \Sigmat, \lambdat. Data Structures: Each Gaussian component Gi is represented by: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: The center position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The covariance matrix, which must be positive semi-definite. \lambdai \in \mathbb{R}: The scalar weight or "mass" of the component. Method Steps: 1. Field Evaluation: For any point x = (x,y,z) in space, compute the contribution of each Gaussian component Pi(x) using the multivariate Gaussian probability density function: Pi(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right) 2. Implicit Surface Definition: Compute the total field value F(x) by summing the weighted contributions and subtracting a threshold T: F(x) = \sumi \lambdai Pi(x) - T The surface is defined where F(x) = 0. The threshold T is relaxed compared to hard-threshold blobby models to allow for differentiable ray intersection. 3. Ray Tracing Formulation: In a ray-tracing context, rays intersect all Gaussians. The "fuzzy" nature implies that the contribution of each Gaussian is weighted by its density along the ray, avoiding binary occlusion decisions. 4. Surface Optimization (VRP-UDF): Emit rays Vk from training views, uniformly sample query points \{qn\} to obtain unsigned distance function (UDF) values and compute rendering weights distribution \{wn\} around the surface. Select Gaussians \{Gt\} close to the ray and near the surface, interpolate rendering weights at their projected positions, and compute the direction of increasing weight. Apply a surface loss to move Gaussians along this direction. Parameters: T: The threshold for sufficient density. Not given in the sources as a fixed value. \lambdai: Component weights. Not given in the sources as a fixed value. \text{sg}(\cdot): Stop-gradient operation applied to the target position to prevent backpropagation through the UDF model during Gaussian optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \Sigmai is not positive definite, \Sigmai^{-1} is undefined. Ensure \Sigmai is constructed from valid rotations and positive scales. Precision: For points far from \mui, Pi(x) underflows to zero. Use a cutoff distance based on the eigenvalues of \Sigmai to ignore negligible contributions for performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussiancomponent(x, mu, sigmainv, lam): """Computes lambda exp(-0.5 (x-mu)^T Sigmainv (x-mu))""" diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diff, np.dot(sigmainv, diff)) exponent = max(exponent, -100.0) # Clamp to avoid underflow return lam np.exp(exponent) def fuzzymetaballsfield(x, gaussians, T): """Computes F(x) for a point x given a list of gaussians and threshold T.""" totalsum = 0.0 for g in gaussians: totalsum += gaussiancomponent(x, g['mu'], g['sigmainv'], g['lam']) return totalsum - T def sg(x): """Stop-gradient operation. In frameworks, this detaches gradients.""" return x def computesurfaceloss(mut, rk, dt, dstar): """ Computes the Gaussian Surface Loss from VRP-UDF. mut: Gaussian center rk: Ray direction dt: Depth of Gaussian projection on ray dstar: Depth of max weight point (argmaxn wn) """ target = mut + rk (dstar - dt) return np.linalg.norm(mut - sg(target)) def optimizegaussiansstep(gaussians, rays, udffield, weights): """ High-level optimization step combining VRP-UDF procedures. 1. Emit rays, sample points, compute UDF and weights. 2. Select Gaussians near ray and surface. 3. Interpolate weights, compute direction. 4. Apply loss to move Gaussians along increasing weight direction. """ # Implementation details for uniform sampling, Gaussian selection, # and weight interpolation are not provided in the sources. pass A specific optimization objective used in conjunction with Fuzzy Metaballs representations, particularly when refining Gaussian Splatting models using Unsigned Distance Functions (UDFs). It moves Gaussians along the direction of increasing rendering weights to align them with the implicit surface. It is chosen when the goal is to refine geometry from sparse or discrete Gaussian representations using volume rendering priors. Link: VRP-UDF. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a continuous, differentiable surface representation. The use of multidimensional Gaussians allows for anisotropic shapes, offering more flexibility than isotropic blobby models. The relaxation of the threshold T ensures smooth gradients, which is critical for differentiable rendering. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The concept of "blobby" models or metaballs was introduced by James F. Blinn, who used isotropic Gaussians to define algebraic surfaces. The "Fuzzy Metaballs" variant, specifically utilizing multidimensional Gaussians (ellipsoids) for an approximate differentiable renderer, was proposed by Leonid Keselman and Martial Hebert. This approach was developed to provide fast and robust results for implicit surface representation in computer graphics, relaxing the hard thresholds of traditional metaballs to facilitate gradient-based optimization. More recently, the representation has been integrated into pipelines like VRP-UDF to refine Gaussian Splatting models using volume rendering priors.
