name: Two-Stage Optimization Pipeline
head: Finalizing Neural Scene Reconstruction
body: The Two-Stage Optimization Pipeline is a post-processing refinement method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples geometric alignment from material and lighting optimization. It corrects accumulated camera pose errors and refines coarse scene geometry in the first stage, then locks the Gaussian geometry to optimize material and lighting parameters using pre-computed per-Gaussian visibility. Inputs: A set of registered images, initial camera poses (with seed image pose fixed), and an initial 3D Gaussian point cloud. Outputs: Optimized camera poses, refined 3D Gaussian primitives, and optimized material and lighting parameters. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitive: Position, covariance matrix (or scale/rotation), opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients, and an additional normal vector \mathbf{n}. Camera Pose: 6-DoF transformation matrix. Visibility Map: Per-Gaussian visibility V(\omegai) pre-computed over the hemispherical domain defined by normal \mathbf{n}. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Pose Correction. Optimize all camera poses using point-to-camera ray consistency loss (Eq. 8 in) to correct accumulated errors, fixing only the seed image pose. Use poses from previous training epochs as initial values. 2. Stage 1: Geometry Refinement. Optimize a vanilla 3D Gaussian point cloud augmented with normal vectors \mathbf{n}, applying normal gradient-based densification. 3. Stage 2: Visibility Pre-computation. Pre-compute per-Gaussian visibility V(\omegai) across the hemispherical domain determined by \mathbf{n} using ray tracing. 4. Stage 2: Material and Lighting Optimization. Lock the geometry of all 3D Gaussians and optimize material and lighting parameters using the pre-computed visibility. Refine scene details using explicit 3D Gaussian primitives densification and pruning strategies from [28] to improve rendering quality beyond the coarse geometry of the scene regressor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostageoptimization(images, initialposes, initialgaussians): # Stage 1: Pose Correction fixedposeidx = 0 # Seed image pose is fixed optimizedposes = initialposes.copy() # Standard gradient descent on 6-DoF pose parameters, excluding fixedidx, using point-to-camera ray consistency loss (Eq. 8) optimizedposes = optimizeposes(images, optimizedposes, fixedposeidx) # Stage 1: Geometry Refinement gaussians = initialgaussians # Augment each Gaussian with a normal vector n for g in gaussians: g.normal = computeinitialnormal(g) # Differentiable rasterization optimization of positions, opacities, and normals gaussians = optimizegeometry(gaussians, images, optimizedposes) # Normal gradient-based densification as specified in the method gaussians = applynormalgradientdensification(gaussians) # Stage 2: Visibility Pre-computation for g in gaussians: # Pre-compute visibility V(omegai) over the hemispherical domain defined by n using ray tracing g.visibility = precomputevisibility(g.normal) # Stage 2: Material and Lighting Optimization # Lock geometry (positions, covariances, opacities, normals) lockedgaussians = lockgeometry(gaussians) # Inverse rendering optimization of BRDF and lighting parameters using pre-computed visibility materialparams, lightingparams = optimizemateriallighting(lockedgaussians, images, optimizedposes) # Explicit 3D Gaussian primitives densification and pruning strategies from [28] to refine scene details gaussians = applydensificationpruning(gaussians) return optimizedposes, gaussians, materialparams, lightingparams Parameters: Seed Image Pose: Fixed during Stage 1. Densification/Pruning Strategy: From [28] (Not given in the sources). Visibility Domain: Hemispherical domain determined by normal \mathbf{n}. Edge Cases: Accumulated Pose Errors: Addressed by Stage 1 pose optimization. Coarse Geometry: Addressed by Stage 2 densification/pruning and material optimization. GPU Memory Limitations: Initial scene regressor uses low-resolution images, necessitating Stage 2 refinement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves rendering quality beyond coarse geometry. Enables realistic relighting. Strengths: Corrects accumulated pose errors, refines geometry, enables relighting. Limitations: Requires two stages, increasing complexity. Initial geometry may be coarse. When to Use: When finalizing reconstruction after incremental registration or when relighting is required. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Proposed in for finalizing neural scene reconstruction and in for point-based relighting. History: Developed to address limitations of incremental registration and coarse geometry in scene regressors. Usage: Used in 3DGS-based pose-free methods and point-based relighting pipelines. name: NeuMesh Rendering Pipeline
head: NeuMesh
body:
NeuMesh is a neural rendering method that represents scenes using a deformable mesh scaffold to decouple geometry and texture, enabling efficient ray marching with high-frequency detail synthesis. It solves the limitation of standard neural implicit fields (like NeuS) by providing an explicit mesh structure that supports geometry editing while maintaining the rendering quality of neural SDFs. It replaces generic SDF evaluation with a mesh-based interpolation of learned codes. The method renders a scene by marching rays through a neural implicit field defined on a mesh. The core innovation is the disentanglement of geometry and texture into separate learnable codes associated with mesh vertices, which are interpolated during ray marching. Inputs: Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), a triangular mesh scaffold (vertices \mathbf{V}, faces \mathbf{F}), and pre-trained neural network parameters. Outputs: Final pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}). The model architecture consists of two main components: the Geometry Code and the Texture Code, stored per vertex or interpolated. 1. Geometry Code \mathbf{l}g(\mathbf{x}): A vector of dimension 32. 2. Texture Code \mathbf{l}t(\mathbf{x}): A vector of dimension 32. 3. Sign Distance h(\mathbf{x}): A scalar value of dimension 1. 4. Interpolated Items: During ray marching, these are computed for each sample point \mathbf{x}: 
abla{\mathbf{x}} s: Gradient of the SDF, dimension 256. s: SDF value, dimension 256. \gamma^{(i)}: Positional encoding or frequency components, dimension 256 or 32. h(\mathbf{x}): Sign distance, dimension 1. \mathbf{d}: Auxiliary vector, dimension 160. 5. Decoders: Geometry Decoder: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 3 hidden layers, size 256, using SoftPlus activation. Outputs SDF-related features. Radiance Decoder: MLP with 4 hidden layers, size 256, using ReLU activation. Outputs radiance (color) with dimension 3. 1. Pre-computation of Bounds: For each ray \mathbf{r}, compute the near and far bounds by finding the minimum and maximum distances of ray-to-mesh intersections. 2. Coarse Sampling: Sample 64 coarse points along the ray within the pre-computed bounds. 3. Fine Sampling (Progressive Up-sampling): Use a progressive up-sampling strategy (as described in Wang et al. [55], referenced in) to guide the sampling of 64 fine points. This results in a total of 128 samples per ray (64 coarse + 64 fine). 4. Neural Field Evaluation: For each sample point \mathbf{p} on the ray: Interpolate the Geometry Code \mathbf{l}g, Texture Code \mathbf{l}t, and Sign Distance h from the mesh vertices surrounding \mathbf{p}. Compute the SDF value s and its gradient 
abla{\mathbf{x}} s using the Geometry Decoder. Compute the radiance (color) using the Radiance Decoder. 5. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color and transmittance using standard volume rendering integration over the 128 samples. Distillation Loss: Supervised with output from the teacher model (NeuS) for queried color and SDF value. Background Supervision: Binary cross-entropy loss using foreground masks for unbounded backgrounds. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, mesh, geometrydecoder, radiancedecoder, geometrycodes, texturecodes, signdistances): # Step 1: Pre-compute near-far bounds tmin, tmax = computeraymeshbounds(rayorigin, raydirection, mesh) # Step 2: Sample 64 coarse points coarsets = samplelinear(tmin, tmax, numsamples=64) coarsesamples = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in coarsets] # Step 3: Progressive up-sampling for 64 fine points # Guided by coarse samples to find SDF zero-crossings finets = progressiveupsample(coarsesamples, geometrydecoder, geometrycodes, texturecodes, signdistances, numfine=64) finesamples = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in finets] allsamples = coarsesamples + finesamples accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 beta = 100.0 # Temperature parameter for p in allsamples: # Interpolate codes from mesh vertices at p lg = interpolategeometrycode(p, mesh, geometrycodes) lt = interpolatetexturecode(p, mesh, texturecodes) h = interpolatesigndistance(p, mesh, signdistances) # Evaluate Geometry Decoder s, grads = geometrydecoder(lg, lt, h) # Evaluate Radiance Decoder c = radiancedecoder(lg, lt, h, grads) # Volume rendering step alpha = computealpha(s, beta) weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + weight c[i] for i in range(3)] accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor def computeraymeshbounds(origin, direction, mesh): tvals = [] for face in mesh.faces: t = raytriangleintersect(origin, direction, face) if t is not None: tvals.append(t) return (min(tvals), max(tvals)) if tvals else (0.0, float('inf')) def samplelinear(tmin, tmax, numsamples): return [tmin + i (tmax - tmin) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] def progressiveupsample(coarsesamples, geometrydecoder, geometrycodes, texturecodes, signdistances, numfine): # Samples points near coarse samples where SDF crosses zero finets = [] for p in coarsesamples: lg = interpolategeometrycode(p, mesh, geometrycodes) # Query SDF to find zero-crossing interval, sample midpoint finets.append(rayorigin + p direction) return finets[:numfine] def interpolategeometrycode(point, mesh, codes): face = findcontainingface(point, mesh) weights = computebarycentricweights(point, face) return sum(w codes[v] for w, v in zip(weights, face.vertices)) def interpolatetexturecode(point, mesh, codes): face = findcontainingface(point, mesh) weights = computebarycentricweights(point, face) return sum(w codes[v] for w, v in zip(weights, face.vertices)) def interpolatesigndistance(point, mesh, distances): face = findcontainingface(point, mesh) weights = computebarycentricweights(point, face) return sum(w distances[v] for w, v in zip(weights, face.vertices)) def computealpha(s, beta): return 1.0 - math.exp(-beta max(0.0, s)) Batch Size: 512 rays. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Initial 0.0005. Scheduler: Cosine annealing with 5000 warm-up steps. Hardware: Single Nvidia RTX3090-24G GPU. Training Time: Approximately 16 hours per model. Unbounded Backgrounds: Standard NeuMesh assumes bounded scenes. For unbounded backgrounds, foreground masks must be used with binary cross-entropy loss during training to prevent background artifacts. Geometry Editing Consistency: When deforming the mesh, the local consistency of learnable signed distances must be maintained. Rotations of surface normals must be compensated in the learnable signed indicator h(\mathbf{x}) to ensure the interpolated SDF remains consistent. Precision: The SDF gradient 
abla{\mathbf{x}} s is used in the radiance decoder. Numerical instability in gradient computation can affect shading quality. A pipeline that integrates neural objects with traditional mesh rendering to support dynamic shadow casting across both in a single scene. Uses shared camera and light settings to generate rendering buffers, integrates scenes via depth-based composition, and applies shadow mapping for the final result. Time Complexity: Rendering involves 128 samples per ray (64 coarse + 64 fine). Pre-computing ray-mesh bounds accelerates the marching loop. Memory Complexity: Stores geometry codes (dim 32), texture codes (dim 32), and sign distances per vertex, plus the MLP parameters for the decoders (3-4 layers, 256 hidden units). Performance: Trains in ~16 hours on a single RTX3090. Rendering quality shows better appearance details than NeuS and NeuTex on DTU and NeRF Synthetic datasets. Strengths: Explicit mesh scaffold allows for geometry editing; disentangled codes improve high-frequency detail synthesis; efficient ray marching via pre-computed bounds. Limitations: Requires a pre-existing mesh scaffold; unbounded scenes require hybrid background modeling. NeuMesh was introduced to address the limitations of neural implicit fields in supporting geometry editing and efficient rendering. It builds on the principles of neural SDFs (like NeuS) but introduces a mesh-based representation to decouple geometry and texture. The method is used in 3D editing applications. name: Implicit Function Rendering Pipeline
head: Neural Implicit Rendering, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) Rendering, Differentiable Rendering with Implicit Functions
body: The Implicit Function Rendering Pipeline is a rendering architecture that combines an implicit scene representation, a sampling scheme (typically ray marching), and a differentiable renderer to produce images from arbitrary viewpoints. It differs from explicit mesh-based rendering by avoiding mesh extraction and from standard volume rendering by using a neural network to define the scene's geometry and appearance continuously in space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray bundle (origin O and direction D for each pixel), camera parameters, and a trained implicit function model. Output: A rendered image tensor of shape (H, W, 3) representing RGB values. Data Structures: Implicit Function Model: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that maps 3D coordinates (and optionally viewing directions) to density (\sigma) and color (C) or signed distance (SDF) and color. Ray Bundle: A tensor of shape (N, 3) for origins and (N, 3) for directions, where N = H \times W. Sampling Points: A tensor of shape (N, K, 3) representing K points sampled along each of the N rays. Method Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel (u, v), compute the ray origin O and direction D based on camera intrinsics and extrinsics. 2. Point Sampling: Sample K points Pi along each ray within the viewing frustum. Positions are typically determined by uniform or stratified sampling between near and far planes. 3. Implicit Function Evaluation: Query the neural network for each point Pi to obtain density \sigmai and color Ci. If using SDF-based representation, convert SDF di to density, e.g., \sigmai = \max(0, -\frac{di}{\epsilon}) or via a softplus function. 4. Volume Rendering Integration: Compute the accumulated color C and opacity \alpha for each ray using the standard volume rendering integral approximation: C = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti \alphai Ci Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where \deltai is the distance between adjacent sample points. 5. Image Assembly: Reshape the output feature tensor to (H, W, 3) and convert to a numpy array or image format. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class ImplicitRenderer: def init(self, mlpmodel, nsamples=128): self.mlp = mlpmodel self.nsamples = nsamples def samplepoints(self, origins, directions, near, far): """Sample points along rays.""" tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., self.nsamples, device=origins.device) tvals = near + (far - near) tvals points = origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) return points def queryimplicitfunction(self, points): """Query MLP for density and color.""" # points shape: (N, K, 3) # Flatten for MLP input: (NK, 3) flatpoints = points.view(-1, 3) density, color = self.mlp(flatpoints) # Reshape back: (N, K, 1) and (N, K, 3) density = density.view(points.shape[0], points.shape[1], 1) color = color.view(points.shape[0], points.shape[1], 3) return density, color def volumerender(self, points, density, color): """Perform volume rendering integration.""" # Compute distances between samples deltas = torch.diff(points, dim=1, append=torch.zeroslike(points[:, -1:,:])) deltas = deltas.norm(dim=2, keepdim=True) # Compute alpha alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-density deltas) # Compute transmittance transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=1) # Prepend 1.0 for the first segment transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1,:]), transmittance[:,:-1,:]], dim=1) # Compute final color weights = alpha transmittance finalcolor = torch.sum(weights color, dim=1) return finalcolor def forward(self, origins, directions, near, far): points = self.samplepoints(origins, directions, near, far) density, color = self.queryimplicitfunction(points) image = self.volumerender(points, density, color) return image Parameters: nsamples: Number of points sampled per ray. Typical values: 64-256. near, far: Near and far clipping planes. Edge Cases: Precision: Floating point errors in cumulative product for transmittance can cause artifacts. Use log-space computation if necessary. Boundaries: Points outside the training domain may produce undefined outputs. Clamp or mask these points. Degenerate Input: Zero-length rays or identical origins/directions should be handled by skipping or adding small epsilon. Uses SDFs for geometry and RGB for appearance, guiding ray marching via SDF values. Choose for high-quality surface reconstruction without mesh extraction. Uses 3D Gaussians as the implicit representation. Choose for faster rendering and explicit control over geometry. Combines neural implicit fields with explicit meshes. Choose for hybrid rendering benefits. A variant for light field rendering. Choose for light field applications. Uses kernel modulation for light fields. Choose for light field rendering with kernel-based efficiency. Extends INR to 4D with motion fields. Choose for dynamic volumetric data like 4D-CT. Monocular SDF reconstruction. Choose for single-image SDF estimation. Uses hypernetworks for object-specific embeddings. Choose for multi-object scenes with distinct appearances. Uses a single MLP for the entire scene. Choose for simple scenes or baseline implementations. Focuses on inverse rendering for translucent materials. Choose for material estimation and rendering of translucent objects. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K \cdot D), where N is the number of pixels, K is the number of samples per ray, and D is the MLP depth/width. The MLP evaluation dominates. Memory Complexity: O(M), where M is the number of MLP parameters. No large voxel grids or point clouds are stored. Measured Performance: Rendering speed is significantly slower than rasterization or traditional ray tracing due to MLP evaluations. Typical frame rates are low (1-10 FPS) for high-resolution images without optimization. Scaling: Scales well with scene complexity as the MLP size is independent of scene size, but inference time scales linearly with resolution and sample count. Strengths: Continuous representation, high-quality anti-aliasing, compact storage, differentiable. Limitations: Slow rendering, requires training, sensitive to sampling density. When to Use: High-quality offline rendering, novel view synthesis, scenes with complex geometry. When Not to Use: Real-time applications, scenes with extremely large scale or high-frequency details without acceleration structures. The Implicit Function Rendering Pipeline, particularly in the form of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It revolutionized novel view synthesis by using neural networks to represent continuous 3D scenes. The method builds on earlier work in neural implicit representations and volume rendering. name: Neural Implicit Surface Rendering
head: Implicit Differentiable Rendering, Neural Signed Distance Field (SDF) Rendering
body: Neural Implicit Surface Rendering is a method that uses a neural network to represent a scene as an implicit function, typically outputting signed distance values (SDF) for geometry and RGB values for appearance, to render images from arbitrary viewpoints. It differs from explicit mesh-based rendering by avoiding mesh extraction and from standard volume rendering by using the SDF to guide ray marching or convert geometry into density for volumetric integration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters (origin o, direction v), neural network weights \theta, and optionally a feature grid \Phi\theta. Outputs: Pixel color \hat{C}(r), depth \hat{D}(r), and surface normal \hat{N}(r) for each ray r. Data Structures: Neural Network: An MLP that maps 3D coordinates x to SDF \hat{s} and color \hat{c}. Feature Grid (Optional): A sparse or dense grid storing local feature vectors, interpolated at query points x to condition the MLP. Octree (Optional): A sparse octree structure used to accelerate ray tracing by skipping empty space. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray r from camera center o along view direction v. 2. Sampling: Sample M points xi^r = o + ti^r v along the ray. 3. Implicit Function Evaluation: Query the neural network to obtain SDF \hat{s}i^r and color \hat{c}i^r for each sample point. 4. Density Conversion (Volume Rendering Variant): Convert SDF \hat{s} to density \sigma using a learnable parameter \beta: \sigma\beta(s) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2\beta} \exp(s/\beta) & \text{if } s \le 0 \\ \frac{1}{2\beta} (1 - \exp(-s/\beta)) & \text{if } s > 0 \end{cases} 5. Alpha Calculation: Compute alpha \alphai^r based on density \sigmai^r and step size \deltai^r (distance to next sample): \alphai^r = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai^r \deltai^r) 6. Transmittance Calculation: Compute transmittance Ti^r as the product of non-alpha terms of previous samples: Ti^r = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^r) 7. Color Computation: Render color via numerical integration: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti^r \alphai^r \hat{c}i^r 8. Depth and Normal Computation (Optional): Compute depth and normal similarly using weights Ti^r \alphai^r: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti^r \alphai^r ti^r \hat{N}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti^r \alphai^r \hat{n}i^r Note: In sphere tracing variants, steps 4-7 are replaced by iterative ray marching until surface intersection is found. Parameters: \beta: Learnable parameter controlling the sharpness of the SDF-to-density conversion. M: Number of sample points per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Sphere tracing is iterative and can be expensive. Geometry-Appearance Ambiguity: Joint estimation from 2D images is ambiguous. Solutions include using foreground masks for geometry supervision [NMOG20, YKM20, KJJ21, BKW21], formulating the surface function into volumetric rendering [OPG21, YGKL21b], or using pseudo ground truth SDF values from monocular depth estimation [ZYQ21]. This variant formulates the implicit surface function into a volumetric rendering framework, converting SDF values to density using a learnable parameter \beta to enable differentiable volume rendering. It allows for the computation of depth and normals alongside color. It is chosen when robust handling of transparency or complex lighting via volume integration is needed, or when 2D supervision ambiguity is addressed via volumetric formulations. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples M per ray and the neural network inference cost. Sphere tracing variants depend on the number of iterations to reach the surface. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the neural network size and, if used, the feature grid or octree size. Strengths: High-quality geometry and appearance representation; differentiable; handles complex shapes without explicit meshing. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to iterative sampling or dense grid queries; ambiguity in joint geometry-appearance estimation from 2D data. When to Use: High-quality novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction from sparse views. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring very low latency without hardware acceleration; scenes with extreme detail requiring very high sample counts. Originated from the combination of implicit surface representations (SDFs) and differentiable rendering. Key developments include the use of sphere tracing for intersection [Har96], adaptation to sparse octrees for performance [TLY21], and the formulation of volumetric rendering for implicit surfaces to address supervision ambiguity. It is used in neural rendering, 3D reconstruction, and computer graphics. name: MetaNLR++
head: MetaNLR, MetaNLR++ / NLR++, MetaNLR++ Training and Optimization Procedure, NLR++, NLR++ training, Neural Lumigraph Representation training, SVS* training
body: MetaNLR++ is a neural rendering method for novel view synthesis that combines a neural implicit shape representation (a Signed Distance Function) with 2D CNN-based image feature extraction, aggregation, and re-projection. It solves the problem of slow training and rendering times associated with previous neural lumigraph methods by leveraging meta-learning to specialize initializations, enabling high-quality convergence in minutes and real-time rendering. Unlike volumetric methods like NeRF, MetaNLR++ renders explicit surfaces via sphere tracing, and unlike earlier neural surface methods like NLR++, it uses deep feature blending to inpaint geometry errors and avoid artifacts from imperfect shape reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with corresponding binary foreground masks \{Mi\}{i=1}^N and camera parameters Ci (intrinsics and extrinsics). Target: A synthesized image \hat{I}t from a target viewpoint Ct. Learnable Parameters: \xi (encoder), \psi (decoder), \theta (SDF shape network), \zeta (aggregation MLP weights). Data Structures: Neural Shape Network \Phi\theta: A 5-layer MLP with 128 hidden units per layer (SIREN architecture) mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. The surface is the zero-level set L0(\Phi\theta) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \Phi\theta(x) = 0\}. Feature Encoder E\xi: A resolution-preserving CNN mapping \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \to \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d}. Target Decoder D\psi: A resolution-preserving CNN mapping \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} \to \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Aggregation MLP \gamma\zeta: A pixel-wise MLP taking re-sampled features and viewing direction to produce weight maps. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sphere Tracing for Surface Points: For each pixel in the target image defined by camera Ct, perform sphere tracing on the neural SDF \Phi\theta to find the surface intersection point \mathbf{p}t. 2. Feature Re-projection (P{i \to t}): For each source view i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, project the target surface point \mathbf{p}t into the image plane of source view i to obtain 2D coordinates, then sample interpolated features from the source feature map Fi = E\xi(Ii) at these coordinates. 3. Occlusion Check: Perform sphere tracing from source view i using \Phi\theta to find the source surface point \mathbf{p}i. Check if the L2-distance between the target view surface position projected into the source view and the source view surface position is smaller than threshold \tau. Discard occluded features by setting them to zero. 4. Feature Aggregation (\Gamma\zeta): Compute the aggregated target feature map Ft \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} using a weighted average of the re-sampled features, modulated by the target viewing direction Vt \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. 5. Decoding: Decode the aggregated feature map into the final RGB image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertargetview(Ct, {Ii}, {Mi}, {Ci}, Phitheta, Exi, Dpsi, gammazeta, Vt, tau): # 1. Sphere trace target ray to find surface point pt t = 0.0 for step in range(8): d = Phitheta(rayorigin(Ct) + t raydirection(Ct)) if abs(d) < 5e-5: # Converged break t += d # Standard sphere tracing update pt = rayorigin(Ct) + t raydirection(Ct) # 2. Feature re-projection and occlusion check resampledfeatures = [] for i in range(N): # Project pt to source view i coords2d = projecttoimage(pt, Ct, Ci) Fi = Exi(Ii) Fsampled = bilinearsample(Fi, coords2d) # Occlusion check: sphere trace source ray to find pi ti = 0.0 for step in range(8): di = Phitheta(rayorigin(Ci) + ti raydirection(Ci)) if abs(di) < 5e-5: break ti += di pi = rayorigin(Ci) + ti raydirection(Ci) # Check L2 distance between projected pt and pi ptprojected = projecttoimage(pt, Ct, Ci) if L2distance(ptprojected, pi) > tau: Fsampled = 0 # Discard occluded features resampledfeatures.append(Fsampled) # 3. Feature aggregation L = gammazeta(resampledfeatures, Vt) # Weight map Ft = sum((Li / sum(L)) Fsampled for Li, Fsampled in zip(L, resampledfeatures)) # Weighted average # 4. Decoding Ihatt = Dpsi(Ft) return Ihatt Formulas: Image Formation: \hat{I}t = D\psi (\Gamma\zeta (\{P{i \to t} (E\xi (Ii))\}{i=1}^N, Vt)). Feature Aggregation: \Gamma\zeta (\{Fi\}{i=1}^N, Vt) = \sum{i=1}^N (Li / \sum{j=1}^N Lj) \circ Fi = Ft, where \circ is the Hadamard product and L is the weight map. Weight Map: L = \gamma\zeta(\{Fi\}{i=1}^N, Vt). Decoder: D\psi: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} \to \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Loss Function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}R + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}M + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}E. Image Reconstruction Loss: \mathcal{L}R(\hat{I}t, \{It, Mt\}) = \frac{1}{|Mt|} \sum{p | Mt[p]=1} |It[p] - \hat{I}t[p]|. Parameters: DTU Dataset: Shape optimization parameters t1 = 50, t2 = 7. Shape gradient batch size 4. Total image batch size 7. Learning rate for shape \eta1 = 1 \times 10^{-4} (halved at [500, 1000, 3000, 7000, 15000, 31000]). Learning rate for feature networks \eta2 = 5 \times 10^{-5} (halved every 2000 iterations). Mask softness \alpha = 50 (doubled at [2000, 4000, 6000]). Occlusion threshold \tau starts at 1 \times 10^{-3}, changes to 1 \times 10^{-4} at 5000 iterations, and 1 \times 10^{-5} at 10000 iterations. Meta-learning rate \beta = 1 \times 10^{-1}. NLR Dataset: Shape optimization parameters t1 = 100, t2 = 3. Shape hidden dimension increased to 256. Decoder UNet blocks decreased to 2 with half channels. Meta-learning rate \beta = 1 \times 10^{-1}. ShapeNet Dataset: Shape optimization parameters t1 = 2,000, t2 = 5. Shape gradient batch size 10 (out of 21 training images). Meta-learning rate \beta = 2 \times 10^{-2}. Sphere Tracing: Limited to 8 steps. Rays with SDF value within 5 \times 10^{-5} of 0 are marked as converged. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Overfitting: On the NLR dataset, if the neural shape model capacity is not increased (hidden dim 128 to 256) and the decoder capacity is not decreased (UNet blocks 3 to 2, half channels), the representation overfits to training views. The decoder memorizes falsely blended features instead of the shape capturing geometry, causing blurriness in interpolated views. Geometry Errors: Using RGB pixels directly with a learned aggregation function introduces distortion in training. Using RGB pixels directly without an encoder/decoder fails to inpaint and correct geometry errors, leading to missing colored areas around object boundaries and falsely blended/occluded features. Mask Sensitivity: SVS exhibits flickering artifacts between views and large holes in rendered images when ground truth masks are not used, due to inaccurate rendering masks in COLMAP-produced geometry and overfitting of feature processing networks with limited training views. Camera Consistency: Using images from different cameras with an encoder/decoder that learns image priors causes undesirable artifacts around occluded regions (e.g., nose on faces). Solved by using only single-camera views for training. Early Training Inaccuracy: Cached surface points may be inaccurate during early training, but optimizing feature networks more frequently allows them to adapt to evolving shape representations. Training Speed: MetaNLR++ achieves significantly faster shape convergence than volumetric methods like NeRF and faster than other neural surface-based methods like NLR. On the ShapeNet chairs split, MetaNLR++ reaches 30dB PSNR in 1.5 min, compared to NLR++ in 3.6 min. It reaches 35dB PSNR in 50.0 min, compared to NLR++ in 125.0 min. MetaNLR++ achieves a maximum PSNR of 40.7dB, compared to NLR++'s 37.0dB. Iteration Time: 2.19 sec/iteration with no shape optimization, 7.69 sec/iteration with shape optimization (Nvidia RTX6000 GPU). Iterations take longer than NeRF/IDR because MetaNLR++ optimizes the representation for multiple entire images instead of randomly selected rays, resulting in significantly larger ray-batch sizes, though it requires significantly fewer iterations to converge. Rendering Time: 0.031 sec/frame (assuming mesh and encoders pre-computed). For comparison, NeRF takes 32 sec/frame, IBRNet takes 33.3 sec/frame, NLR takes 0.025 sec/frame, and SVS takes 0.031 sec/frame. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability, fast training via meta-learning, robustness to geometry errors via feature-based inpainting. Limitations: Requires binary foreground masks for best results; sensitive to decoder/shape capacity balance; slower per-iteration than ray-based methods due to full-image batch optimization. MetaNLR++ was introduced by Alexander W. Bergman, Petr Kellnhofer, and Gordon Wetzstein at Stanford University in 2021. It builds upon the NLR++ framework, which itself combines neural implicit surfaces with neural lumigraph representations. The method addresses the limitations of slow training in neural scene representations by incorporating meta-learning (Reptile algorithm) to learn priors for rapid adaptation to new scenes. The meta-initialization is trained on 15 distinct DTU scenes and 5 distinct NLR scenes. It is applied to the DTU dataset (7 training views, 800×600 resolution), NLR dataset (6 training views, 800×600 resolution), and ShapeNet dataset (24 views, 64×64 resolution). name: Kernel-Modulated Neural Representation for Light Fields
head: Descriptor and Modulator Network, Implicit Convolutional Network for Light Fields
body: Kernel-Modulated Neural Representation (KMNR) is a compact implicit neural representation for light fields that avoids parameter explosion at high angular resolutions by decomposing network kernels into shared descriptors and view-specific modulators. Unlike standard Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) that map spatial coordinates to color, KMNR maps uniform noise to Single Aperture Images (SAIs) conditioned on angular coordinates, enabling efficient compression and view synthesis. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like NeuMesh Rendering Pipeline by explicitly modeling angular dependencies through switchable convolutional kernels rather than geometric primitives or explicit coordinate encoding. Input: A uniform noise tensor \epsilon (typically same spatial dimensions as the target SAI) and angular coordinates (u, v) indexing the desired view in the light field. Output: A predicted SAI \hat{I}{u,v} with 3 channels (RGB). Training Target: A ground truth SAI I{u,v} corresponding to angular position (u, v) from the light field L. Network Architecture: The network consists of 6 layers (L1–L5 + Decoder). Layers L1–L4: Convolutional layers followed by Bicubic Upsampling (up2, scale 2), Batch Normalization (BN), and GELU activation. Kernel size: 3 \times 3. Stride: 1. Dilation: 2 (to expand receptive field without increasing parameters). Layer L5: Convolutional layer followed by BN and GELU activation. Kernel size: 3 \times 3. Stride: 1. Dilation: 1. Decoder: Convolutional layer followed by Sigmoid activation. Kernel size: 1 \times 1. Stride: 1. Output channels: 3 (RGB). Kernel Decomposition: Each layer i (for i=1 \dots 5) has weights Ki and bias bi. These are composed of a Descriptor and Modulators: Descriptor (K^di, b^di): Shared across all views. Stores common scene information. Modulator (K^{m}{u,v}, b^{m}{u,v}): Switched per view. Stores view-specific information. Directional Allocation: To reduce parameters, modulators are not allocated per (u,v) pair but split along orthogonal angular directions u (horizontal) and v (vertical): K^{m}{u,v} = K^{m}{u} \oplus K^{m}{v} (Concatenation in the last dimension). b^{m}{u,v} = b^{m}{u} + b^{m}{v} (Element-wise addition). The channel count for K^{m}{u} and K^{m}{v} is half that of a full modulator K^{m}{u,v}. Tensor Sizes: K^di, K^{m}{u}, K^{m}{v}: Size k \times k \times C{in} \times C{out} (where k=3 for L1-L5). Ki: Size k \times k \times C{in} \times (C{out}^{d} + C{out}^{m}). bi: Size C{out}^{d} + C{out}^{m}. C{in}, C{out}: Input and output channels for the layer. Total Parameter Count (N): N \approx l k^2 C{in} \left[ \frac{1}{2} (U + V) C{out} + C{out} \right] Where: l: Number of layers (5 for the modulated layers). k: Kernel size (3). C{in}: Input channels. C{out}: Output channels. U, V: Angular resolutions (number of views in horizontal and vertical directions). Note: The modulator parameters scale with \frac{1}{2}(U+V) instead of UV. 1. Initialization: Initialize descriptor weights K^di, b^di and modulator weights K^{m}{u}, b^{m}{u}, K^{m}{v}, b^{m}{v} for all layers i=1 \dots 5 and angular indices u \in [0, U-1], v \in [0, V-1]. 2. Sampling: Randomly select an angular position (u, v) and retrieve the corresponding ground truth SAI I{u,v} from the light field L. 3. Noise Generation: Generate a uniform noise tensor \epsilon with the same spatial dimensions as I{u,v}. 4. Modulator Selection: Retrieve the modulator weights K^{m}{u}, K^{m}{v} and biases b^{m}{u}, b^{m}{v} corresponding to the selected (u, v). 5. Kernel Assembly: For each layer i=1 \dots 5, assemble the effective kernel Ki and bias bi: Ki = K^di \oplus (K^{m}{u} \oplus K^{m}{v}) bi = b^di + b^{m}{u} + b^{m}{v} (Note: Concatenation \oplus occurs in the last dimension for kernels; addition for biases). 6. Forward Pass: Feed \epsilon through the network using the assembled kernels and biases: Pass through L1–L4: Conv3x3 (dilation 2) \rightarrow Bicubic Upsample (scale 2) \rightarrow BN \rightarrow GELU. Pass through L5: Conv3x3 (dilation 1) \rightarrow BN \rightarrow GELU. Pass through Decoder: Conv1x1 \rightarrow Sigmoid. Output is \hat{I}{u,v}. 7. Loss Computation: Compute the Mean Square Error (MSE) between \hat{I}{u,v} and I{u,v}: E = \frac{1}{Np} \sum (\hat{I}{u,v} - I{u,v})^2 Where Np is the number of pixels. 8. Optimization: Update all weights (descriptors and modulators) via backpropagation to minimize E. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–8 for a new random SAI. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class KernelModulatedLightField(nn.Module): def init(self, U, V, Cin, Cout, l=5, k=3): """ U: Horizontal angular resolution V: Vertical angular resolution Cin: Input channels for convolution Cout: Output channels for convolution l: Number of modulated layers (1 to 5) k: Kernel size (3) """ super().init() self.U = U self.V = V self.l = l self.k = k # Descriptor parameters (shared) # Descriptors have Cout channels self.desckernels = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Cin, Cout, k, k)) for in range(l) ]) self.descbiases = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(Cout)) for in range(l) ]) # Modulator parameters (split by direction) # Each directional modulator has Cout / 2 channels halfcout = Cout // 2 # Horizontal modulators: U instances self.modkernelsu = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Cin, halfcout, k, k)) for in range(U) ]) self.modbiasesu = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(halfcout)) for in range(U) ]) # Vertical modulators: V instances self.modkernelsv = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Cin, halfcout, k, k)) for in range(V) ]) self.modbiasesv = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(halfcout)) for in range(V) ]) # Decoder layers (no modulation) self.decoderconv = nn.Conv2d(Cout, 3, kernelsize=1, stride=1) self.sigmoid = nn.Sigmoid() # Batch Norms for L1-L5 self.bnlist = nn.ModuleList([ nn.BatchNorm2d(Cout) for in range(l) ]) # Bicubic upsampling self.upsample = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2, mode='bicubic', aligncorners=False) def forward(self, epsilon, uidx, vidx): """ epsilon: Noise tensor [B, Cin, H, W] uidx: Integer index for horizontal view [B] vidx: Integer index for vertical view [B] Returns: Predicted SAI [B, 3, Hout, Wout] """ x = epsilon batchsize = x.size(0) for i in range(self.l): # 1. Assemble Kernel: Descriptor + Modulator U + Modulator V # Ki = K^di || K^mu || K^mv # Biasi = b^di + b^mu + b^mv # Get descriptors kd = self.desckernels[i] # [Cin, Cout, k, k] bd = self.descbiases[i] # [Cout] # Get modulators for current view # Note: In practice, gather from parameter lists based on uidx, vidx # For simplicity in pseudocode, assuming single view per call or batched gather kmu = self.modkernelsu[uidx] # [Cin, halfcout, k, k] bmu = self.modbiasesu[uidx] # [halfcout] kmv = self.modkernelsv[vidx] # [Cin, halfcout, k, k] bmv = self.modbiasesv[vidx] # [halfcout] # Concatenate kernels along channel dimension (dim 1) # Shape: [Cin, Cout + halfcout + halfcout, k, k] -> [Cin, Cout, k, k] effectively if we sum channels? # The source says Ki = K^di || K^m{u,v}. And K^m{u,v} = K^mu || K^mv. # So total output channels = Cout (desc) + halfcout (u) + halfcout (v) = Cout + Cout = 2Cout? # Wait, source says: "K^di and K^m{u,v} have sizes... Cout". # And "K^m{u,v} = K^mu || K^mv". # If K^mu and K^mv have half channels, their concatenation has Cout channels. # So Ki concatenates K^d (Cout) and K^m (Cout). Loss loss = F.mseloss(Ipred, Igt.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).unsqueeze(0)) # Assuming Igt is [H,W,3] # 5. name: Implicit Neural Representation (INR) with Parametric Motion Field for 4D-CT
head: Differentiable Analysis-by-Synthesis 4D-CT, Warp Template Scene with Motion Field
body: This method reconstructs a 4D dynamic scene (3D volume evolving over time) from limited-view sinogram data without requiring training data or phase information. It jointly estimates a static 3D scene template via an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) and a parametric motion field that warps the template over time. Unlike traditional 4D-CT methods that require sparse measurements spanning 360 degrees or phase-gating for periodic motion, this approach works with limited-view sampling (partial angular ranges) and self-supervised analysis-by-synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Captured sinogram measurements p{\theta}(r, z) corresponding to specific view angles \theta(t) and times t. Output: Optimized INR network weights representing the static scene template and optimized motion field parameters representing the dynamic deformation. Data Structures: 1. INR Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with positional encoding that maps 3D spatial coordinates (x, y, z) to the linear attenuation coefficient (LAC) \tilde{\sigma} of the static template. The network outputs a scalar value for density at any queried coordinate. 2. Motion Field Parameters: A set of parameters \phi defining a parametric warping function that transforms static coordinates to dynamic coordinates based on time t. The specific mathematical form of the parametric field is not detailed in the sources, but it is treated as a differentiable function W(x, y, z, t; \phi). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the INR network weights and the motion field parameters \phi. 2. Scene Generation: For a given time t, query the INR to get the static template density \tilde{\sigma}(x, y, z). Apply the motion field to warp the coordinates: (x', y', z') = W(x, y, z, t; \phi). The dynamic scene density at time t is \sigma(x, y, z, t) = \tilde{\sigma}(x', y', z'). 3. Differentiable Projection: Apply the 3D Radon transform to the generated 4D scene frame \sigma(x, y, z, t) to project it into sinogram space, producing synthesized measurements p{\theta}^{syn}(r, z). 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss function between the synthesized sinogram measurements and the ground truth (captured) sinogram measurements. 5. Optimization: Backpropagate the loss to update the INR network weights and the motion field parameters \phi. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence. Formulas: The forward imaging model uses the 3D Radon transform for parallel-beam CT: p{\theta}(r, z) = \iint \sigma(x, y, z, t) \delta(x \cos(\theta(t)) + y \sin(\theta(t)) - r) \, dx \, dy Where: p{\theta}(r, z) is the synthesized sinogram measurement at view angle \theta, detector pixel r, and height z. \sigma(x, y, z, t) is the linear attenuation coefficient (LAC) of the dynamic scene at coordinates (x, y, z) and time t. \theta(t) is the view angle at time t. \delta(\cdot) is the Dirac delta function. Assumptions and Parameters: Fixed LAC during exposure: The scene's LAC remains fixed for a single projection exposure time dt. This is mathematically expressed as: ||\sigma(x, y, z, t + dt) - \sigma(x, y, z, t)||1 = 0 Parallel-Beam Geometry: The method assumes parallel-beam geometry, typical of synchrotron CT scanners. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Mismatch: The method assumes parallel-beam geometry. It does not support cone-beam or helical measurements directly. To support these, the Radon transform must be replaced with a differentiable volume ray tracer. Pre-processing Requirements: The method assumes CT measurements have undergone pre-processing for beam hardening and truncation. Synchrotron systems use monochromatic sources (no beam hardening), but other systems require correction methods. Limited View Ambiguity: While robust, rapid motion combined with limited view sampling can lead to spatiotemporal ambiguities. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Validated on a synthetic dataset for parallel beam CT generated with an accurate physics simulator, and on publicly available thoracic CT reconstructions where x-ray measurements were resimulated. The method outperforms competitive baselines in these scenarios. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Works with limited-view sampling (partial angular ranges in a single revolution); does not require phase information for reconstruction; self-supervised (no training data required). Limitations: Restricted to parallel-beam geometry; requires pre-processed sinograms (beam hardening/truncation correction); performance may degrade with very rapid motion due to spatiotemporal ambiguities. When to use: When reconstructing 4D scenes from limited-view sinogram data where phase information is unavailable and traditional 360-degree sampling is not feasible. When not: When cone-beam or helical CT data is used without modification; when beam hardening/truncation corrections are not applied. Origin: Proposed in "Dynamic CT Reconstruction from Limited Views with Implicit Neural Representations and Parametric Motion Fields" (ICCV 2021). History and Development: The method builds on recent advances in Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) using positional encoding to map input coordinates to volume density. It addresses limitations in traditional 4D-CT methods that require sparse measurements spanning 360 degrees or phase-gating. Usage: Validated on synthetic parallel-beam CT data and resimulated thoracic CT data. name: MonoSDF
head: MonoSDF: Exploring Monocular Geometric Cues for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction
body: MonoSDF is a neural implicit surface reconstruction framework that integrates data-driven monocular geometric priors (depth and surface normals) into the optimization of signed distance functions (SDFs). It solves the problem of poor reconstruction quality in textureless regions and limited-view scenarios, where standard photometric consistency fails. Unlike Manhattan-SDF, which relies on dense multi-view stereo (MVS) depth maps and strict Manhattan world assumptions requiring semantic segmentation, MonoSDF uses general-purpose monocular estimators, removing the need for semantic labels and enabling scalability to larger, unstructured scenes. Inputs: A set of N posed RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known camera poses. Pretrained monocular depth and normal estimators are used to generate initial depth maps Di and normal maps Ni for each input image. Outputs: A neural implicit SDF field f\theta(\mathbf{x}) and a color field c\theta(\mathbf{x}) (or equivalent appearance representation) that reconstruct the 3D scene geometry and appearance. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a neural network f\theta (e.g., an MLP or multi-resolution feature grid) parameterized by \theta. The network takes a 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 as input and outputs a scalar SDF value d = f\theta(\mathbf{x}) and a color vector \mathbf{c} = c\theta(\mathbf{x}). Numbered Steps: 1. Monocular Prior Estimation: For each input image Ii, compute the predicted depth map Di and surface normal map Ni using a general-purpose pretrained monocular estimator. 2. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in the input images, cast a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} into the scene. Sample points along the ray. To reconstruct surfaces, points are typically sampled near the zero-level set of the SDF. 3. Volume Rendering: Evaluate the SDF f\theta(\mathbf{r}(t)) and color c\theta(\mathbf{r}(t)) at sampled points. Compute the volume rendering integral for RGB color, depth, and normal at each pixel. The rendered normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} is derived from the gradient of the SDF: \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \nabla f\theta(\mathbf{x}) / \|\nabla f\theta(\mathbf{x})\|. 4. Loss Computation: The total loss \mathcal{L} combines photometric and geometric terms: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}{depth} + \lambdan \mathcal{L}{normal} Where: \mathcal{L}{rgb} is the photometric reconstruction loss between rendered RGB and input image RGB. \mathcal{L}{depth} is the consistency loss between rendered depth and the monocular depth prior Di. \mathcal{L}{normal} is the consistency loss between rendered normals and the monocular normal prior Ni. \lambdad, \lambdan are weighting hyperparameters. 5. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L} with respect to network parameters \theta using gradient descent. Parameters: Image resolution: 384 \times 384 pixels. Loss weights (\lambdad, \lambdan): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Textureless Regions: Standard photometric loss fails here; monocular normals provide necessary constraints. Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth is inherently scale-ambiguous. The SDF optimization must handle this, potentially through scale-invariant losses or normalization, though specific scaling strategies are not detailed in the provided notes. Error Propagation: Errors in monocular depth/normal predictions can mislead the SDF optimization. The complementary nature of photometric and recognition cues helps mitigate this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmonosdf(images, poses, monocularestimator, sdfnetwork, numepochs): """ Train MonoSDF using monocular geometric priors. """ optimizer = Adam(sdfnetwork.parameters()) # Precompute monocular priors monoculardepths = [] monocularnormals = [] for img in images: depth, normal = monocularestimator.predict(img) monoculardepths.append(depth) monocularnormals.append(normal) for epoch in range(numepochs): totalloss = 0 for i, (img, pose) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # 1. Sample rays from image pixels rays = sampleraysfromimage(img, pose) # 2. Sample points along rays (e.g., near SDF zero-level set) points, tvals = samplepointsalongrays(rays, sdfnetwork) # 3. Evaluate SDF and Color sdfvalues = sdfnetwork(points) colors = sdfnetwork.getcolor(points) # 4. Volume Render renderedrgb, rendereddepth, renderednormal = volumerender( points, sdfvalues, colors, tvals) # 5. Compute Losses # Photometric loss lossrgb = mse(renderedrgb, img) # Geometric losses against monocular priors # Note: Rendering depth/normal must be aligned with input image coordinates lossdepth = consistencyloss(rendereddepth, monoculardepths[i]) lossnormal = consistencyloss(renderednormal, monocularnormals[i]) # Total Loss loss = lossrgb + lambdad lossdepth + lambdan lossnormal # 6. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() totalloss += loss.item() print(f"Epoch {epoch}: Loss {totalloss / len(images)}") volumerender implements the standard volume rendering integral using the SDF to compute opacity weights (e.g., via the cumulative distribution function of the SDF). consistencyloss typically uses L1 or L2 distance. samplepointsalongrays should prioritize points near the zero-crossing of the SDF for surface reconstruction. MonoNeRD is a monocular 3D target detection framework that models the scene as a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to achieve dense 3D geometric and occupancy representation. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF-based detection by treating intermediate frustum representations as SDF-based NeRFs, which effectively masks out free space and reduces ambiguity in the feature volume. This approach was the first to introduce volume rendering into the monocular 3D detection (M3D) domain, demonstrating the potential for implicit reconstruction of image-based 3D perception. Time Complexity: Optimization is iterative and depends on the neural network size and number of sampled points per ray. Monocular priors are computed once offline, reducing per-iteration cost compared to MVS. Memory Complexity: Depends on the neural network architecture (MLP or feature grid) and the number of rays sampled. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality in textureless regions; scales to larger scenes; removes need for semantic segmentation and Manhattan world assumptions. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of pretrained monocular estimators; scale ambiguity of monocular depth. When to use: When multi-view stereo is unreliable due to textureless regions or sparse views, and semantic segmentation is unavailable. When not to use: When high-precision metric depth is required without scale ambiguity, or when monocular priors are known to be inaccurate for the specific scene type. MonoSDF was introduced in the paper "MonoSDF: Exploring Monocular Geometric Cues for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction" published at NeurIPS 2022. It builds on neural implicit surface reconstruction methods like NeuS. It addresses limitations of previous works like Manhattan-SDF, which required dense MVS depth and semantic segmentation. The method leverages the complementary nature of photometric consistency and monocular recognition cues. name: MonoNeRD
head: MonoNeRD, SDF-based NeRF for Monocular 3D Detection
body: MonoNeRD is a monocular 3D target detection framework that models the scene as a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to achieve dense 3D geometric and occupancy representation. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF-based detection by treating intermediate frustum representations as SDF-based NeRFs, which effectively masks out free space and reduces ambiguity in the feature volume. This approach was the first to introduce volume rendering into the monocular 3D detection (M3D) domain, demonstrating the potential for implicit reconstruction of image-based 3D perception. Inputs: Monocular images, camera parameters, and initial frustum features. Outputs: 3D voxel features, densities, RGB images, depth maps, and 3D bounding boxes for detected targets. Data Structures: Frustum Features: Intermediate feature representations aligned with the camera frustum. 3D Voxel Grid: Regular 3D grid constructed from sampled frustum features. SDF Field: Signed Distance Function values associated with the voxel grid. Radial Fields: Auxiliary fields used in conjunction with the SDF for volume rendering. Steps: 1. SDF Modeling: Model the scene geometry and occupancy using a Signed Distance Function (SDF). 2. Grid Sampling: Perform grid sampling on the frustum features to construct regular 3D voxel features. 3. Density Estimation: Compute corresponding densities for the voxel features. The optimization process allows the detection branch to use gradient flow from the NeRF to estimate opacity fields, effectively masking out free space. 4. Volume Rendering: Employ volume rendering techniques to recover RGB images and depth maps from the SDF and radial fields. This step optimizes the frustum representations. 5. Detection: Input the resulting voxel features into detection modules to identify 3D targets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mononerdepipeline(image, cameraparams): # Step 1: Initialize SDF-based representation # The scene is modeled as a Signed Distance Function (SDF) sdffield = initializesdffield() # Step 2: Construct Frustum Features # Intermediate frustum representations are created frustumfeatures = getfrustumfeatures(image, cameraparams) # Step 3: Grid Sampling # Perform grid sampling on frustum features to construct regular 3D voxel features voxelfeatures, densities = gridsamplefrustumfeatures(frustumfeatures) # Step 4: Optimization with Volume Rendering # Optimize frustum representations using volume rendering # This recovers RGB images and depth maps from the SDF and radial fields # The gradient flow from NeRF helps estimate opacity fields and mask free space rgbimage, depthmap = volumerendersdf(sdffield, voxelfeatures, densities) # Update SDF and features based on rendering loss sdffield, voxelfeatures = optimizestep(sdffield, voxelfeatures, rgbimage, depthmap) # Step 5: Detection # Input voxel features into detection modules boundingboxes = detectionmodule(voxelfeatures) return boundingboxes, rgbimage, depthmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Free Space Ambiguity: Without the SDF-based opacity masking, standard NeRF approaches may suffer from ambiguity in free space regions. Long-range and Occluded Objects: The method is specifically noted for its superiority in handling long-range and occluded objects compared to explicit reconstruction methods. Strengths: Handles long-range and occluded objects effectively; reduces ambiguity in feature volume by masking free space; establishes a new standard in monocular 3D detection using NeRFs. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Performance: Demonstrates superiority in handling challenging scenarios like occlusion and long-range detection. Complexity: Not given in the sources. MonoNeRD was proposed in 2023. It represents a novel approach to monocular 3D target detection by integrating SDFs with NeRFs. It was the first method to introduce volume rendering into the M3D domain, highlighting the potential for implicit reconstruction in image-based 3D perception. The method builds on the concept of using NeRFs for 3D detection but enhances it by considering intermediate frustum representations as SDF-based. name: Hypernetwork-based Object Embedding
head: Hypernetwork
body: Hypernetwork-based Object Embedding generalizes neural scene representations across a class of objects by assuming that the weights of individual scene representation networks lie in a low-dimensional subspace. It maps a compact embedding vector to the full weight vector of a scene network, enabling the inference of new object instances via optimization rather than direct network evaluation. This approach differs from single MLP implicit functions by decoupling the network architecture from the specific instance parameters, allowing for efficient adaptation to new views or objects within a known category. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An embedding vector z \in \mathbb{R}^k representing a specific object instance; a pre-trained Hypernetwork HN; a frozen Scene Representation Network (SRN) architecture; and target image data for optimization. Output: The optimized embedding vector z that reconstructs the target scene, and the generated weights w for the SRN. Data Structures: Embedding Vector (z): A vector of dimension k. Weight Vector (w): A vector of dimension l, containing all parameters of the SRN. Constraint: k < l, ensuring the embedding is a compressed representation of the weights. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Randomly initialize the embedding vector z \in \mathbb{R}^k. 2. Freezing: Freeze the weights of the Hypernetwork HN, the Scene Representation Network (SRN) architecture (though its weights are generated dynamically), and the differentiable rendering pipeline (RGB Renderer, Segmentation Renderer, Ray Marcher). 3. Weight Generation: Compute the SRN weights w by passing z through the Hypernetwork: w = HN(z) where HN: \mathbb{R}^k \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^l. 4. Rendering: Use the generated weights w to configure the SRN. Render the scene from the current camera viewpoint using the differentiable renderer to produce predicted images (RGB and/or semantic labels). 5. Optimization: Update z to minimize the reconstruction error between the rendered output and the target image data. The loss function L typically includes image reconstruction loss and/or cross-entropy loss (L{co}) if semantic labels are available. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inferscene(HN, SRNarch, targetimage, targetsemantics=None, lr=0.01, steps=1000): # 1. Initialize embedding vector z randomly z = torch.randn(k, requiresgrad=True) # 2. Freeze all network weights (HN, SRN, Renderers) # Note: SRN weights are not stored; they are generated from z. # The rendering pipeline is frozen. optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([z], lr=lr) for step in range(steps): optimizer.zerograd() # 3. Generate SRN weights from embedding w = HN(z) # 4. Configure SRN with generated weights # The SRNarch is a blueprint; we apply weights w to it. # This step is implementation-specific but conceptually: # srn = SRNarch.applyweights(w) # 5. Render scene using differentiable renderer # renderedrgb, renderedsemantics = renderer(srn, cameraparams) # 6. Compute loss loss = 0.0 if targetimage is not None: loss += torch.mean((renderedrgb - targetimage) 2) if targetsemantics is not None: loss += crossentropyloss(renderedsemantics, targetsemantics) # 7. Backpropagate to update z loss.backward() optimizer.step() return z Parameters: k: Dimension of the embedding vector. Must be less than l. l: Dimension of the weight vector of the SRN. Loss functions: Image reconstruction loss and/or cross-entropy loss (L{co}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimization Stability: Since z is optimized directly, the process is sensitive to initialization and learning rate. Local minima may result in poor reconstructions. Dimensionality Constraint: The method requires k < l. If k is too small, the subspace may not capture the variability of the object class. If k is too large, the compression benefit is lost. Frozen Weights: The Hypernetwork and rendering pipeline must be pre-trained and frozen during inference. If they are not frozen, the optimization may collapse to trivial solutions. This variant explicitly frames the inference process as an optimization problem at test time. It involves freezing all network weights (HN, SRN, RGB Renderer, SEG), initializing a new code vector z, and optimizing z to minimize image reconstruction and/or cross-entropy losses. It allows inference from either RGB information, semantic segmentation information, or both. Time Complexity: The method requires iterative optimization at test time for each new scene, making it significantly slower than direct inference methods. The complexity depends on the number of optimization steps and the cost of differentiable rendering. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the Hypernetwork and the rendering pipeline. The embedding vector z is small (k < l), reducing the storage required for scene representation compared to storing full SRN weights. Strengths: Enables generalization across object classes; allows for semantic-aware scene representations; flexible input modalities (RGB, semantics). Limitations: Slow inference due to optimization; requires pre-training of the Hypernetwork on a dataset of object classes; sensitive to optimization hyperparameters. When to Use: When generalizing to new instances of known object classes is required, and computational time for inference is not the primary constraint. When Not to Use: For real-time applications requiring immediate inference; for scenes outside the trained object class. The Hypernetwork-based Object Embedding method was introduced in "Semantic Implicit Neural Scene Representations With Semi-Supervised Training" (2020). It builds on the concept of Hypernetworks, which map embedding vectors to network weights, allowing for efficient representation of multiple instances within a low-dimensional subspace. The method extends this to semantic-aware scene representations, enabling semi-supervised learning of 3D semantic segmentation. name: Single MLP Implicit Function
head: Coordinate-based Neural Implicit, Single-Layer MLP SDF, Fixed-PE MLP
body: This family encompasses methods that represent 3D geometry or volumetric properties as the output of a single Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) f\theta mapping 3D coordinates to a scalar value, such as a Signed Distance Function (SDF) or density. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts and storage overhead inherent in voxel grids by providing a continuous, differentiable representation. Unlike hierarchical grid-based methods (e.g., HIGS) that rely on learned feature grids, this approach relies entirely on the MLP's capacity to approximate the function, often augmented with fixed positional encoding. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of evaluating a continuous function f\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} defined by a neural network. 1. Coordinate Input: The input is a 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, typically normalized to a domain such as [-1, 1]^3. 2. Positional Encoding: To enable the MLP to fit high-frequency details, input coordinates are transformed via an encoding function \gamma(\mathbf{x}) before entering the network. Common encodings include: Gaussian Random Fourier Features (GRFF): \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = [\cos(2\pi \kappa \mathbf{B} \mathbf{x}), \sin(2\pi \kappa \mathbf{B} \mathbf{x})] Where \mathbf{B} is a random vector sampled from \mathcal{N}(0, I) and \kappa is a bandwidth factor. Fixed Positional Encoding: A deterministic mapping involving sines and cosines at different frequencies. 3. MLP Architecture: The network consists of fully connected layers. A common configuration is a single hidden layer with dimension 64, though deeper networks (e.g., 4 layers) are also used. 4. Activation Functions: The choice of activation \phi depends on the target property: Sine (\phi = \sin): Used for surface reconstruction and SDFs. ReLU: Used with Fourier feature mapping for image-based reconstruction. 5. Output: The network outputs a scalar value representing the physical property (e.g., SDF value, density, or Linear Attenuation Coefficient). A rendering technique that approximates the Space Distance Field (SDF) using a deep neural network and renders images by marching rays along the estimated distance field. It is chosen when explicit ray marching integration is required for visualization. Encodes volumetric or geometric data as the output of a continuous function, typically an MLP, mapping 3D coordinates to physical properties like density or SDF. It solves discretization artifacts and integrates seamlessly with gradient-based optimization for reconstruction from sparse projections. It is distinct from Single MLP SDF by its broader application to various physical properties and potential use of hashgrid encodings. Specifically parameterizes a Signed Distance Field (SDF) using a single MLP f\theta. It is distinct from Ray Marching with Neural SDF in that it denotes the decoder architecture rather than the rendering pipeline, and from INR by its specific application to SDFs with a single-layer structure. The concept of implicit neural representations for 3D geometry emerged as an alternative to explicit mesh or voxel representations. The use of MLPs to represent SDFs allows for continuous, resolution-independent geometry. The application of Fourier feature mappings to neural networks for high-frequency fitting was introduced in earlier works on neural radiance fields and implicit surfaces. The specific "Single MLP SDF" variant with fixed positional encoding and a single hidden layer of dimension 64 is documented in recent implementations.

name: Ray Marching with Neural SDF
head: DeepSDF Rendering, Neural SDF Ray Marching
body: Ray Marching with Neural SDF is a rendering technique that approximates the Space Distance Field (SDF) using a deep neural network and renders images by marching rays along the estimated distance field. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained neural network model representing the SDF, camera parameters, and lighting configuration. Outputs: A 2D image representing the rendered scene. Data Structures: Camera: width (int), height (int), fov (float, default \pi/3), position (torch.Tensor), aspectratio (float, width/height). Distances tensor: Shape [width height, 1], initialized to zeros on the GPU. Parameters: maxsteps: Maximum number of ray marching iterations. Default is 30. epsilon: Convergence threshold. If all distances are less than epsilon, the loop breaks. Default is 10^{-3}. maxdist: Maximum distance a ray can travel before being clipped. Default is 10.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize distances tensor to zeros with shape [width height, 1] on the GPU. 2. Calculate ray origins from the camera and initial positions as \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \text{distances} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 3. Loop up to maxsteps times: a. Query the neural SDF for distances at current positions. b. If all distances are less than epsilon, break the loop. c. Update distances by adding the sampled SDF value and recalculate positions. d. Check if all rays have either converged (distance < epsilon) or exceeded maxdist. If so, break. 4. Estimate normals at the final positions using central finite differences with step size e = 10^{-3}. Compute offsets: \mathbf{dx} = (e, 0, 0), \mathbf{dy} = (0, e, 0), \mathbf{dz} = (0, 0, e). Calculate normal components: nx = f(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{dx}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{dx}), ny = f(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{dy}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{dy}), nz = f(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{dz}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{dz}). Normalize the resulting vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz). 5. Calculate brightness using a single directional light by clamping the dot product of normals and light direction to [0, 1]: \text{brightness} = \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}). 6. Set brightness to 0 for pixels where the final distance exceeds maxdist. 7. Reshape brightness to height \times width, convert to numpy, scale by 255, and cast to uint8 for the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def renderneuralsdf(camera, sdfmodel, latentcode, lights, maxsteps=30, epsilon=1e-3, maxdist=10.0): device = next(sdfmodel.parameters()).device dtype = next(sdfmodel.parameters()).dtype numpixels = camera.width camera.height distances = torch.zeros((numpixels, 1), device=device, dtype=dtype) y, x = torch.meshgrid( torch.linspace(-1, 1, camera.height, device=device, dtype=dtype), torch.linspace(-1, 1, camera.width, device=device, dtype=dtype), indexing='ij') directions = torch.stack([x, y, torch.fulllike(x, 1.0)], dim=-1) directions = torch.nn.functional.normalize(directions, dim=-1) directions = directions.reshape((numpixels, 3)) positions = camera.position.unsqueeze(0).expand(numpixels, -1) latentcodeexpanded = latentcode.expand(numpixels, -1) for step in range(maxsteps): sdfvalues = sdfmodel(latentcodeexpanded, positions) if torch.all(sdfvalues < epsilon): break distances = distances + sdfvalues positions = camera.position.unsqueeze(0).expand(numpixels, -1) + distances directions if torch.all(distances.squeeze() > maxdist): break e = 1e-3 dx = torch.tensor([e, 0, 0], device=device, dtype=dtype) dy = torch.tensor([0, e, 0], device=device, dtype=dtype) dz = torch.tensor([0, 0, e], device=device, dtype=dtype) nx = sdfmodel(latentcodeexpanded, positions + dx) - sdfmodel(latentcodeexpanded, positions - dx) ny = sdfmodel(latentcodeexpanded, positions + dy) - sdfmodel(latentcodeexpanded, positions - dy) nz = sdfmodel(latentcodeexpanded, positions + dz) - sdfmodel(latentcodeexpanded, positions - dz) normals = torch.nn.functional.normalize(torch.stack([nx, ny, nz], dim=-1), dim=-1) lightdir = lights[0].direction brightness = torch.clamp(torch.sum(normals lightdir, dim=-1), 0.0, 1.0) finaldistances = distances.squeeze() brightness[finaldistances > maxdist] = 0.0 image = brightness.reshape(camera.height, camera.width) imagenp = image.cpu().numpy() imagenp = (imagenp 255).astype(np.uint8) return np.stack([imagenp] 3, axis=-1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The reference implementation contains a hardcoded index for the first object (objects[0]) when estimating normals, which fails if multiple objects are present. The PyGame screen initialization is hardcoded to 1280x720 in the reference implementation. Reconstructs surfaces represented by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by making the ray marching and shading process differentiable. A neural network represents an SDF, outputting the distance to the nearest surface for any 3D point. A differentiable ray marcher steps along a ray, querying the SDF network to find the zero-crossing (the surface). The surface normal is computed via automatic differentiation of the SDF network. A shading model (e.g., Phong) is applied, and the final pixel color is compared to the target image. Frameworks like NeuS use this for high-fidelity 3D shape reconstruction. Not given in the sources. The technique is based on the concept of DeepSDF, which uses a deep neural network to represent a continuous signed distance field. The specific implementation described in the sources is an unofficial project exploring the approximation of SDFs using deep machine learning for ray marching rendering.
