name: Implicit Neural Representation (INR)
head: Continuous volume representation, Hashgrid INR, Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for CT Template, MLP INR, MLP-based LAC estimation, Network Architecture for INR
body: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) encode volumetric or geometric data as the output of a continuous function, typically a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), mapping 3D coordinates to physical properties like density or signed distance. This method solves the problem of discretization artifacts and storage overhead associated with voxel grids by providing a differentiable representation suitable for volume rendering and tomography. Unlike discrete voxel-based methods, INRs integrate seamlessly with gradient-based optimization for reconstruction from sparse or limited view projections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D coordinates \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z) sampled from the scene domain, typically normalized to [-1, 1]^3. Output: A scalar value representing the physical property (e.g., Linear Attenuation Coefficient (LAC) for CT, or Signed Distance Function (SDF) for geometry). Data Structures: MLP Parameters: A set of weights \mathbf{W}i and biases \mathbf{b}i for each layer i. Encoding Parameters: For Fourier-based methods, a random vector \mathbf{B} and bandwidth \kappa. For hashgrid methods, hash tables mapping coordinates to feature vectors to accelerate computation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Sampling: Sample a grid of coordinates \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{\beta \times 3} from the scene boundaries [-1, 1]^3. To enforce continuity and prevent the network from memorizing discrete grid points, perturb each coordinate randomly within its respective voxel. Parameter: Voxel grid resolution \beta. Typical value: \beta = 80, resulting in 80^3 sampled coordinates per iteration. 2. Positional Encoding: Apply an encoding function \gamma(\mathbf{v}) to the input coordinates before the first MLP layer to improve high-frequency fitting. Gaussian Random Fourier Features (GRFF): \gamma(\mathbf{v}) = [\cos(2\pi \kappa \mathbf{B} \mathbf{v}), \sin(2\pi \kappa \mathbf{B} \mathbf{v})] Where \mathbf{v}=(x,y,z), \mathbf{B} is a vector randomly sampled from \mathcal{N}(0, I), and operations are element-wise. Parameter: Bandwidth factor \kappa. Controls the sharpness of the output. If \kappa is too low, high-frequency content is lost; if too high, the network fits spurious noise in the measurements (e.g., sinogram). Hashgrid Encoding: Maps coordinates to dense feature vectors via hash tables, significantly speeding up training and rendering compared to Fourier features. Fourier Feature Mapping (ReLU variant): Projects the input onto a list of sines and cosines in the first layer, followed by ReLU activations in subsequent layers. 3. Network Forward Pass: Compute the network output f(\mathbf{p}) using the MLP composition: f(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{W}n \circ f{n-1} \circ \dots \circ f0(\mathbf{p}) + \mathbf{b}n Where fi(\mathbf{p}i) = \phi(\mathbf{W}i \mathbf{p}i + \mathbf{b}i). Architecture: Typically 4 fully connected layers. Activation Function \phi: Sine (\phi = \sin): Used for powerful INR architectures in surface reconstruction. ReLU: Used with Fourier feature mapping for image-based reconstruction. 4. Loss Computation and Optimization: Compute the loss between the network output and the target data (e.g., measured sinogram values or SDF ground truth) and optimize the MLP parameters \theta using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplecoordinates(beta, bounds=(-1.0, 1.0)): # Generate beta^3 linearly spaced coordinates in [-1, 1]^3 coords = np.linspace(bounds[0], bounds[1], beta) grid = np.meshgrid(coords, coords, coords) V = np.stack(grid, axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3) # Perturb randomly within voxels to enforce continuity perturbation = np.random.uniform(0, 1.0/beta, V.shape) return V + perturbation def grffencode(v, kappa, B): # v: (N, 3), B: (3,), element-wise multiplication per evidence return np.concatenate([np.cos(2 np.pi kappa B v), np.sin(2 np.pi kappa B v)], axis=-1) def mlpforward(p, weights, biases, activation): x = p for W, b in zip(weights, biases[:-1]): x = activation(W @ x + b) return weights[-1] @ x + biases[-1] def traininr(V, targets, weights, biases, kappa, B, activation, lr, epochs): for epoch in range(epochs): encoded = grffencode(V, kappa, B) pred = mlpforward(encoded, weights, biases, activation) loss = np.mean((pred - targets) 2) # Gradient descent step (conceptual) grad = np.gradient(loss, weights, biases) weights -= lr grad[0] biases -= lr grad[1] return weights, biases Pitfalls: Bandwidth Selection: Setting \kappa in GRFF incorrectly leads to either underfitting (low \kappa) or overfitting to noise (high \kappa). Training Speed: Standard Fourier feature MLPs train slowly; hashgrid encodings are recommended for speed. Misalignment: In tomography, uncorrected tilt-axis errors cause streaking artifacts. The INR must be trained with pose optimization or pre-aligned data. Pre-training phase for Variational Compression of Implicit Neural Representations (VC-INR). Learns a shared network parameterization and latent modulation initialization for rapid adaptation to new data instances with minimal storage overhead. Sets itself apart by optimizing the initialization itself via meta-learning rather than training weights for a single instance. Choose when rapid adaptation to new data with minimal storage is required. Uses a continuous complex Gabor wavelet as the activation nonlinearity to achieve high accuracy, fast training, and robustness to noise by leveraging optimal space-frequency compactness. Sets itself apart by combining Gaussian spatial compactness with complex exponential frequency compactness. Choose when high-frequency fitting and noise robustness are prioritized over standard activations. Reparameterization method that encodes semantic priors into the weights of an INR using a pre-trained Semantic Neural Network (SNN) and Weight Generation Network (WGN) to enhance representational capacity without increasing inference cost. Sets itself apart by decoupling semantic feature extraction from implicit function learning. Choose when injecting specific semantic context into weights is needed for a target signal. A technique where the full 3D orientation of the volume corresponding to each tilt image is directly optimized during the INR training process to correct for tilt axis errors and misalignment. Sets itself apart by jointly optimizing network weights and pose parameters rather than assuming fixed poses. Choose when dealing with electron tomography data subject to rotational misalignment. Large misalignment increases convergence epochs, so coarse preprocessing is recommended. Time Complexity: Training time is generally slower than traditional algebraic reconstruction techniques (ART/SIRT) for a single instance due to the iterative nature of neural optimization. Hashgrid-based INRs significantly reduce training and rendering times compared to Fourier-feature-based INRs. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is determined by the MLP weights and encoding tables. Performance: INRs can achieve high Structural Similarity (SSIM) (e.g., average SSIM of 0.974) even with limited views or significant misalignment when combined with pose optimization. Strengths: Differentiable nature allows for gradient-based optimization, compact storage, and robustness to noise when properly regularized. Limitations: Slow convergence for high-resolution details without advanced encodings; sensitive to hyperparameters like \kappa; requires careful handling of misalignment in tomographic applications. When to use: When dealing with sparse or limited view data, or when integrating geometric priors into the reconstruction process. When not to use: When real-time inference on low-power hardware is critical without pre-trained models, or when the scene is static and high-resolution voxel storage is not a constraint. Implicit Neural Representations originated from the need to represent continuous signals and geometric shapes without discretization. The use of MLPs to approximate continuous functions for graphics was popularized by works such as SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Networks). In the context of volume rendering and tomography, INRs have been applied to reconstruct dynamic scenes from limited views using parametric motion fields and to inpaint missing wedges in electron tomography while jointly optimizing alignment. The method builds on Single MLP Implicit Function by introducing specific encoding strategies (Fourier, Hashgrid) and training protocols (meta-training, pose optimization) to enhance performance and efficiency. name: VC-INR Meta-Training
head: INR Meta-training stage
body:
VC-INR Meta-Training is the pre-training phase for Variational Compression of Implicit Neural Representations (VC-INR), designed to learn a shared network parameterization and a latent modulation initialization that enables rapid adaptation to new data instances. It solves the problem of initializing an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) such that a small set of latent parameters can quickly adapt the shared weights to fit specific data (e.g., images or audio) with minimal storage overhead. Unlike standard INR training which optimizes weights for a single instance, this method uses meta-learning to optimize the initialization itself, allowing the model to generalize across a distribution of data types. It differs from siblings like WIRE by focusing on the meta-initialization of modulations rather than positional encoding, and from SPW by optimizing latent codes for compression rather than semantic priors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset \{xi, yi\}{i=1}^N where x represents input coordinates (e.g., pixel positions, audio samples) and y represents target values (e.g., pixel intensities, audio amplitudes). Output: A shared network parameter vector 	heta and a latent modulation initialization vector \phi0. Data Structures: Shared Network (	heta): A neural network f(x, 	heta, \phi) parameterized by 	heta. The architecture typically uses LayerNorm to stabilize training. Latent Modulation Initialization (\phi0): A vector of parameters that modulate the shared network. Adapted Latent Modulation (\phij): The result of adapting \phi0 for a specific instance j. Parameters: \alpha: Inner-loop step size (meta-learned).  eta: Outer-loop step size. B: Batch size for sampling. Algorithm: The method minimizes the expected loss after one step of inner-loop adaptation. The inner loop adapts the latent modulation \phi0 to fit a specific instance, and the outer loop updates the shared parameters 	heta and the initialization \phi0 to minimize the loss on the adapted model. 1. Initialize shared network parameters 	heta and latent modulation initialization \phi0. 2. While not converged: a. Sample a batch of data B = \{(xj, yj)\}{j=1}^B. b. For each instance j in B: i. Compute the adapted latent modulation \phij by taking one gradient step on \phi0: \phij = \phi0 - \alpha 
abla{\phi0} L{MSE}(f(xj, 	heta, \phi0), yj) c. Compute the outer-loop gradients using the adapted models \phij: i. Update \phi0: \phi0 \leftarrow \phi0 -  eta \mathbb{E}{j \in B} [
abla{\phi0} L{MSE}(f(xj, 	heta, \phij), yj)] ii. Update 	heta: 	heta \leftarrow 	heta -  eta \mathbb{E}{j \in B} [
abla{	heta} L{MSE}(f(xj, 	heta, \phij), yj)] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vcinrmetatraining(dataset, sharednetwork, initialphi0, alpha, beta, batchsize, maxiterations): """ VC-INR Meta-Training Algorithm. Args: dataset: List of tuples (x, y). sharednetwork: Function f(x, theta, phi) returning prediction. initialphi0: Initial latent modulation vector phi0. alpha: Inner-loop step size (meta-learned). beta: Outer-loop step size. batchsize: Number of samples per batch. maxiterations: Maximum number of outer-loop updates. Returns: theta: Shared network parameters. phi0: Optimized latent modulation initialization. """ # Initialize shared network parameters theta theta = initializesharednetworkparameters() # Current phi0 is passed in or initialized phi0 = initialphi0 for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Sample batch batch = samplebatch(dataset, batchsize) # Accumulators for outer-loop gradients gradphi0sum = zeroslike(phi0) gradthetasum = zeroslike(theta) for xj, yj in batch: # Inner-loop adaptation: compute phij # phij = phi0 - alpha gradphi0 LMSE(f(xj, theta, phi0), yj) # We need the gradient of the loss with respect to phi0 at phi0 lossatphi0 = mseloss(sharednetwork(xj, theta, phi0), yj) gradphi0atphi0 = gradient(lossatphi0, phi0) phij = phi0 - alpha gradphi0atphi0 # Outer-loop update: compute gradients using the adapted phij # We need gradients of LMSE(f(xj, theta, phij), yj) w.r.t phi0 and theta lossatphij = mseloss(sharednetwork(xj, theta, phij), yj) # Gradient w.r.t phi0 # Note: phij depends on phi0, so we compute the full gradient gradphi0atphij = gradient(lossatphij, phi0) gradphi0sum += gradphi0atphij # Gradient w.r.t theta gradthetaatphij = gradient(lossatphij, theta) gradthetasum += gradthetaatphij # Update phi0 and theta batchsizeactual = len(batch) phi0 = phi0 - beta (gradphi0sum / batchsizeactual) theta = theta - beta (gradthetasum / batchsizeactual) return theta, phi0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instability: Meta-learning is highly unstable by default, especially with large dimensions of \phi. This requires extensive hyperparameter search. LayerNorm: LayerNorm is essential to smooth the loss landscape and bound the norm of \phi, preventing divergence. Step Size: The step size \alpha is meta-learned (MetaSGD) and acts as a preconditioner for the gradient. A Geometric INR is a neural network f: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R} that approximates a Signed Distance Function (SDF) of a regular surface S, characterized by the property that the magnitude of its gradient is approximately unity (\|
abla f\| \approx 1). It solves the problem of reconstructing 3D geometry from sparse or noisy input data (such as oriented point clouds or posed images) by enforcing geometric constraints, specifically the Eikonal equation and normal alignment, during training. Unlike standard INRs that may only fit data values, Geometric INRs explicitly regularize the differential properties of the implicit function to ensure the zero-level set represents a clean, regular surface without spurious components. Time Complexity: The method requires two forward and backward passes per instance per batch (one for inner-loop adaptation, one for outer-loop gradient computation), making it computationally expensive compared to standard INR training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradients for both 	heta and \phi0 for the outer loop, and temporary storage for \phij during the inner loop. Performance: VC-INR achieves compression performance comparable to JPEG and JPEG-2000 on standard benchmarks like Kodak and CIFAR-10, with PSNR values ranging from 22.76 to 48.32 depending on the bit-per-pixel (bpp) rate. Strengths: Effectively utilizes increasing network capacity (width), unlike methods like Functa which show decreasing performance for non-linear mappings. Limitations: Highly sensitive to hyperparameters due to instability; requires LayerNorm for stable training. VC-INR Meta-Training was introduced in the paper "Modality-Agnostic Variational Compression of Implicit Neural Representations" by Schwarz et al. (2023). It builds upon the MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning) framework, adapting it for implicit neural representations to enable efficient compression by learning a good initialization for latent modulations. The method is part of a broader effort to compress INRs for storage and transmission, leveraging the fact that a small number of bits can encode a latent code that adapts a shared network to a specific instance. name: Geometric Implicit Neural Representation
head: Geometric INR, Implicit Neural Representation for SDFs, Neural SDF with geometric losses
body:
A Geometric Implicit Neural Representation (Geometric INR) is a neural network f: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R} that approximates a Signed Distance Function (SDF) of a regular surface S, characterized by the property that the magnitude of its gradient is approximately unity (\|
abla f\| \approx 1). It solves the problem of reconstructing 3D geometry from sparse or noisy input data (such as oriented point clouds or posed images) by enforcing geometric constraints, specifically the Eikonal equation and normal alignment, during training. Unlike standard INRs that may only fit data values, Geometric INRs explicitly regularize the differential properties of the implicit function to ensure the zero-level set represents a clean, regular surface without spurious components. Inputs and Outputs Input Data: Either an oriented point cloud \{pi, Ni\}{i=1}^n sampled from the surface S (where pi \in S and Ni is the normal at pi), or a set of posed images \{Ij\} with projection matrices Wj mapping screen coordinates to world coordinates. Output: A trained neural network f	heta: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R} approximating the SDF, from which the geometry is extracted as the zero-level set S \approx f^{-1}(0). Data Structures Neural Network f	heta: A coordinate-based neural network (e.g., MLP) with parameters 	heta. Training Domain \Omega: The spatial region over which the Eikonal regularization integral is computed. Point Sets: Surface points P = \{pi\} with normals N = \{Ni\}, and additional regularization points Q = \{qk\} sampled outside the surface to mitigate noise. Loss Function The total loss L(	heta) combines data constraints and geometric regularization: L(	heta) = L{data}(	heta) + L{Eik}(	heta) 1. Eikonal Regularization (L{Eik}): Enforces the SDF property \|
abla f\| = 1 throughout the training domain \Omega: L{Eik}(	heta) = \int{\Omega} (\|
abla f\| - 1)^2 dp 2. Normal Alignment: Enforces alignment between the network gradient and surface normals on S: L{normal}(	heta) = \int{S} (1 - \langle 
abla f, N angle) dS 3. Data Constraint (L{data}): For point clouds, enforces f(pi) = 0 and 
abla f(pi) = Ni. For images, enforces photometric consistency I(	heta, Wj) = Ij via differentiable rendering. Numbered Steps 1. Define Input Data: Acquire either an oriented point cloud \{pi, Ni\} or posed images \{Ij\} with projection matrices Wj. 2. Sample Regularization Points: If using point clouds, sample additional points \{qk\} outside the surface points \{pi\} to prevent spurious zero-level set components. 3. Define Network: Initialize the neural network f	heta: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R} with parameters 	heta. 4. Construct Loss: Formulate L(	heta) using the Eikonal term over \Omega, the normal alignment term over S, and the data term (L{data}). 5. Optimize: Use a variant of gradient descent with mini-batches to minimize L(	heta). Mini-batches are necessary because computing the full gradient 
abla L is often infeasible due to dataset size. 6. Inference: Extract the geometry by computing the zero-level set S \approx f^{-1}(0). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingeometricinr(points, normals, domainsamples, numepochs=1000, lr=1e-4): """ Trains a Geometric INR to approximate an SDF. Args: points: Array of shape (N, 3) representing surface points pi. normals: Array of shape (N, 3) representing normals Ni. domainsamples: Array of shape (M, 3) representing points qk in domain Omega. numepochs: Number of training iterations. lr: Learning rate. Returns: theta: Trained network parameters. """ # Initialize network parameters theta (weights and biases of an MLP) theta = initializeparameters() for epoch in range(numepochs): # 1. Sample mini-batches of surface points batchpoints, batchnormals = samplebatch(points, normals) # 2. Sample mini-batch of domain points for Eikonal regularization if domainsamples is not None: batchdomain = samplebatch(domainsamples) else: batchdomain = randomsampleinboundingbox(batchpoints) # 3. Compute forward pass for surface points fsurface = forwardmodel(batchpoints, theta) gradsurface = computegradient(fsurface, batchpoints) # 4. Compute forward pass for domain points fdomain = forwardmodel(batchdomain, theta) graddomain = computegradient(fdomain, batchdomain) # 5. Compute Loss Terms # Data Loss: Enforce f(p) = 0 and grad(f)(p) = N losssdf = meansquarederror(fsurface, zeroslike(fsurface)) lossnormal = meansquarederror(gradsurface, batchnormals) lossdata = losssdf + lossnormal # Eikonal Loss: Enforce ||grad(f)|| = 1 in domain Omega gradnormdomain = vectornorm(graddomain, axis=1) losseikonal = meansquarederror(gradnormdomain, oneslike(gradnormdomain)) # Total Loss loss = lossdata + losseikonal # 6. Backpropagate and optimize gradtheta = computegradient(loss, theta) theta = updateparameters(theta, gradtheta, lr) return theta def computegradient(output, inputs): """ Computes the gradient of the network output with respect to input points using reverse-mode automatic differentiation. """ # Standard autograd implementation builds a computational graph # and propagates gradients backwards. grad = autogradgrad(output, inputs, gradoutputs=oneslike(output), creategraph=True)[0] return grad def updateparameters(theta, gradtheta, lr): """Performs a gradient descent step.""" return theta - lr gradtheta def samplebatch(data): """Randomly samples a subset of data points.""" return data[torch.randint(0, len(data), size=(batchsize,))] def randomsampleinboundingbox(points): """Samples points uniformly within the axis-aligned bounding box of the input points.""" mincoords = points.min(axis=0) maxcoords = points.max(axis=0) return mincoords + torch.rand(batchsize, 3) (maxcoords - mincoords) def forwardmodel(x, theta): """Evaluates the MLP forward pass.""" # Standard MLP: x -> Linear -> Activation -> Linear ->... -> scalar output return applymlp(x, theta) def vectornorm(v, axis=1): """Computes the L2 norm along the specified axis.""" return torch.sqrt(torch.sum(v2, axis=axis)) def meansquarederror(pred, target): """Computes the mean squared error between predictions and targets.""" return torch.mean((pred - target)2) def initializeparameters(): """Initializes network weights and biases.""" return torch.nn.ParameterDict({ 'W1': torch.randn(3, 64), 'b1': torch.zeros(64), 'W2': torch.randn(64, 64), 'b2': torch.zeros(64), 'W3': torch.randn(64, 1) }) def applymlp(x, params): """Standard MLP forward pass.""" x = torch.relu(x @ params['W1'] + params['b1']) x = torch.relu(x @ params['W2'] + params['b2']) return x @ params['W3'] + params['b3'] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparse Sampling Noise: Sparse sampling near the surface can introduce noise in regions with no data. This is handled by imposing the Eikonal equation on additional points outside the surface samples. Spurious Components: Enforcing f(pi)=0 and 
abla f(pi)=Ni on oriented point clouds alone may result in spurious components on the zero-level set. Mitigation involves sampling additional points \{qk\} outside \{pi\}. Infeasible Gradients: Computing the full gradient 
abla L may be infeasible due to dataset size; mini-batches must be used. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training time depends on the number of network parameters, the size of the mini-batches, and the number of epochs. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the neural network parameters and the active mini-batches of points and normals during training. Strengths: Produces smooth, regular surfaces; leverages differential properties (normals, curvatures) for robust reconstruction; suitable for dynamic scenes by extending domain to space-time \mathbb{R}^3 	imes \mathbb{R}. Limitations: Requires careful sampling of the training domain \Omega to avoid noise; inference requires extracting the zero-level set via sphere tracing or level-set methods. When to Use: 3D reconstruction from oriented point clouds or posed images, surface animation, and dynamic geometric INRs. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Geometric INRs are part of the broader family of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), also known as neural fields or neural implicits. The specific focus on geometric constraints, particularly the Eikonal equation \|
abla f\| = 1, stems from the need to regularize INRs trained on sparse data. Traditional implicit representations encode surfaces as zero-level sets of functions, but without geometric constraints, neural networks may produce irregular zero-level sets. The use of the Eikonal equation as a regularization term was introduced to ensure that the learned function behaves like a true Signed Distance Function, providing stable normals and enabling applications like sphere tracing and surface evolution. Recent frameworks enhance training performance by exploring geometric losses and curvature information for adaptive sampling. name: WIRE (Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations)
head: Gabor Wavelet INR, Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations
body: WIRE is an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) that uses a continuous complex Gabor wavelet as the activation nonlinearity in its Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to achieve high accuracy, fast training, and robustness to noise by leveraging optimal space-frequency compactness. It differs from SIREN by adding a Gaussian window to provide spatial compactness, and from pure Gaussian activations by adding a complex exponential term to provide frequency compactness. This combination allows WIRE to decompose images as a linear combination of sparse images, providing high representational capacity for a given parameter count. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Coordinates x \in \mathbb{R}^{Di} (e.g., 2D image coordinates or 3D spatial coordinates). Output: A real-valued scalar (e.g., pixel intensity, density, or color component). Data Structures: Weights and Biases: The MLP weights Wm and biases bm are complex-valued to preserve phase relationships throughout the network. Layer Outputs: Intermediate activations ym are complex-valued. Final Output: The real part of the final network output is taken; the imaginary part is discarded. Activation Function: The core nonlinearity is the Gabor wavelet \sigma(x), defined as: \sigma(x) = \psi(x; \omega0, s0) = e^{j\omega0 x} e^{-|s0 x|^2} where: \omega0 controls the frequency of the sinusoid. s0 controls the spread (width) of the Gaussian envelope. j is the imaginary unit. An alternate form for problems where complex weights are infeasible uses the real (or imaginary) part of the complex Gabor wavelet: \psi(x; \omega0, s0) = \sin(\omega0 x)e^{-(s0 x)^2} Note that setting s0 = 0 results in the pure sine nonlinearity used in SIREN, and setting \omega0 = 0 results in the Gaussian nonlinearity. Multi-dimensional Localization (2D WIRE): For multidimensional localization, the output of each unit is computed by augmenting the Gabor wavelet with additional Gaussian windows: ym = \psi(Wm y{m-1} + b^{(1)}m; \omega0, s0) \cdot e^{-\sum{k=2}^{Dm} |s0 (Wm y{m-1} + bm)|^2} This ensures activations are compact along both spatial axes, unlike 1D WIRE which may blur features along one axis. Parameters: \omega0, s0: Default hyperparameters for standard image representation are \omega0 = 20 and s0 = 10. A Constant-Q embodiment sets \omega0 s0 = Q for constant fractional bandwidth. Learning Rate: WIRE performs best with a high learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-2}. Hidden Layers: Fixed to 2 for standard image representation experiments. Using \ge 3 layers causes performance to converge to SIREN/Gaussian levels, increases computational cost, and often causes instability. Hidden Features: For NeRF applications, 128 features are used per layer (calculated as 182/\sqrt{2}) to account for parameter doubling from complex weights. Initialization: WIRE is robust to initialization and works with standard uniform initialization. However, SIREN-like initialization yields up to 1 dB higher accuracy: First layer weights: U(-1/N, 1/N) Subsequent layer weights: U(-6/(\omega0 N), 6/(\omega0 N)) where N is the number of input features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def gaborwavelet(x, omega0, s0, usecomplex=True): if usecomplex: term1 = torch.exp(1j omega0 x) term2 = torch.exp(- (s0 x).abs() 2) return term1 term2 else: return torch.sin(omega0 x) torch.exp(-(s0 x) 2) def gaborwavelet2d(x, omega0, s0): z1 = x[..., 0:1] zrest = x[..., 1:] gaborval = torch.sin(omega0 z1) torch.exp(-(s0 z1) 2) gaussianval = torch.exp(-(s0 zrest) 2) return gaborval torch.prod(gaussianval, dim=-1, keepdim=True) def linear(x, weight, bias): return torch.matmul(x, weight.t()) + bias class WIREMLP: def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim, outputdim, numhiddenlayers=2, omega0=20.0, s0=10.0, usecomplexweights=True): self.numhiddenlayers = numhiddenlayers self.omega0 = omega0 self.s0 = s0 self.usecomplexweights = usecomplexweights self.weights = [] self.biases = [] n = inputdim self.weights.append(torch.empty(hiddendim, n)) self.biases.append(torch.empty(hiddendim)) for in range(numhiddenlayers - 1): self.weights.append(torch.empty(hiddendim, hiddendim)) self.biases.append(torch.empty(hiddendim)) self.weights.append(torch.empty(outputdim, hiddendim)) self.biases.append(torch.empty(outputdim)) self.initweights(omega0, inputdim, hiddendim) def initweights(self, omega0, inputdim, hiddendim): for i in range(len(self.weights)): n = self.weights[i].shape[1] if i == 0: limit = 1.0 / n else: limit = 6.0 / (omega0 n) self.weights[i].uniform(-limit, limit) self.biases[i].zero() nout = self.weights[-1].shape[1] self.weights[-1].uniform(-1.0 / nout, 1.0 / nout) self.biases[-1].zero() def forward(self, x): h = x for i in range(self.numhiddenlayers + 1): h = linear(h, self.weights[i], self.biases[i]) if i < self.numhiddenlayers: h = gaborwavelet(h, self.omega0, self.s0, self.usecomplexweights) return h.real if self.usecomplexweights else h Time and Memory Complexity: WIRE converges an order of magnitude faster than SIREN and Gaussian INRs. However, using a large number of hidden layers (\ge 3) increases computational cost and often causes an unstable learning regime. Measured Performance: Image Representation: 43.2 dB PSNR on Kodak dataset (vs 42.4 dB SIREN, 40.0 dB Gauss). Occupancy Volume: 0.99 IOU on Thai statue mesh (vs 0.97 SIREN/Gauss). Denoising: 30.2 dB PSNR on DIV2K with 17.6 dB input noise (vs 28.1 dB DIP, 30.1 dB Gauss). Super-Resolution: 27.3 dB PSNR for 4x single image SR (vs 26.4 dB Bilinear, 25.6 dB SIREN). NeRF: WIRE achieves 0.1–0.4 dB higher accuracy than SIREN across 25–100 training images. Strengths: High accuracy, fast training, robustness to noise and undersampling, sparse second-layer outputs enabling high approximation capacity for high-frequency signals. Limitations: Performance degrades to SIREN/Gaussian levels with \ge 3 hidden layers, increases computational cost, and often causes instability. 1D WIRE blurs features along one axis compared to 2D WIRE. When to use: Ideal for image representation, denoising, super-resolution, CT reconstruction, and NeRF training, especially when data is noisy or undersampled. WIRE was introduced in the paper "WIRE: Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations" by Vishwanath et al., published on arXiv in January 2023. It was developed to address the trade-off between high accuracy and robustness in INRs, leveraging the optimal space-frequency compactness of Gabor wavelets from harmonic analysis. It builds on the properties of SIREN (sinusoidal activations) and Gaussian activations, inheriting their favorable traits while mitigating their weaknesses (global ringing for SIREN, compact but large error at edges for Gauss). name: SPW (Semantic Priors in Weights)
body: SPW is a reparameterization method that encodes semantic priors into the weights of an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) model to enhance its representational capacity without increasing inference cost. It differs from standard INR training by decoupling semantic feature extraction from the implicit function learning, using a pre-trained Semantic Neural Network (SNN) to generate a semantic vector that conditions a Weight Generation Network (WGN). Unlike VC-INR Meta-Training which learns task-specific meta-initializations, SPW injects specific semantic context into the weights for a given target signal. Unlike WIRE (Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations) which modifies the activation function to improve high-frequency fitting, SPW modifies the weight initialization and structure based on semantic content. Inputs: Target visual signal (e.g., image I \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times H \times 3}). INR architecture definition (number of layers, hidden dimensions Cm). Pre-trained SNN (e.g., EfficientNet-B7). Outputs: Semantic weights W^s for the INR layers. The INR model parameterized by W^s. Data Structures: 1. Semantic Vector (vs): A 1D vector of size 1 \times (C1 + C2 + \dots + C7), where Cn is the channel count of stage n in the SNN. 2. Weight Generation Network (WGN): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with an inverted residual bottleneck structure. For the m-th INR layer, the WGN takes vs as input and outputs a vector of size 1 \times (C{m-1} \times Cm). 3. INR Weights (W^s): A set of matrices \{W^s1, W^s2, \dots, W^sL\}, where W^sm \in \mathbb{R}^{C{m-1} \times Cm}. Parameters: Expansion factor (E): Multiplier for hidden channels in the first two layers of the WGN. Default: 6. PE-MLP Fourier bases: 10. SIREN frequency parameter (\omega0): 30. WIRE frequency parameter (\omega): 20. WIRE spread parameter (s): 10. Optimizer: Adam. Initial learning rate: 2 \times 10^{-4}. Training iterations: 50,000. WGN Initialization: LeCun random initialization. Steps: 1. Extract Semantic Features: Pass the target visual signal through the fixed SNN (e.g., EfficientNet-B7). Extract feature maps from the final layer of each of the 7 stages of the SNN. For stage n, let the feature maps be Fn \in \mathbb{R}^{Hn \times Wn \times Cn}. 2. Compute Semantic Vector: Globally average-pool Fn along the spatial dimensions (Hn, Wn) to obtain a vector pn \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times Cn}: pn = \text{GAP}(Fn) Concatenate p1, p2, \dots, p7 to form the Semantic Vector vs \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times (C1 + \dots + C7)}: vs = \text{Concat}(p1, p2, \dots, p7) Compute vs once at the beginning of training. 3. Initialize WGNs: For each layer m of the INR (where m=1 \dots L), initialize a WGN Gm. The WGN Gm consists of three fully connected layers: Layer 1: Input size D{in} = \sum{i=1}^7 Ci. Output size D{mid} = E \times C{m-1} \times Cm. Layer 2: Input size D{mid}. Output size D{mid}. Layer 3: Input size D{mid}. Output size D{out} = C{m-1} \times Cm. Initialize weights using LeCun random initialization. 4. Train WGNs: The SNN is frozen. The INR backbone weights are not directly optimized; instead, the WGN parameters are optimized. For each training iteration: a. For each INR layer m, compute the generated weight vector um = Gm(vs). b. Reshape um into the weight matrix W^sm \in \mathbb{R}^{C{m-1} \times Cm}. c. Construct the INR forward pass using W^sm for all layers. d. Compute the loss (e.g., MSE) between the INR output and the target signal values at sampled coordinates. e. Back-propagate the gradient through the WGNs to update their parameters. 5. Inference Preparation: After training, the SNN and WGNs are fixed. Compute the final semantic weights W^sm for all layers m by passing vs through the trained WGNs Gm. Discard the SNN and WGNs. Store only the matrices W^sm. 6. Inference: Use the INR model with weights W^s to map coordinates to signal values. No additional computational or memory cost compared to a standard INR with the same architecture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim from torchvision import models class WeightGenerationNetwork(nn.Module): """ WGN with inverted residual bottleneck structure. """ def init(self, semanticdim, outchannels, expansionfactor=6): super(WeightGenerationNetwork, self).init() self.expansionfactor = expansionfactor midchannels = expansionfactor outchannels self.fc1 = nn.Linear(semanticdim, midchannels) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(midchannels, midchannels) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(midchannels, outchannels) # LeCun initialization for m in self.modules(): if isinstance(m, nn.Linear): nn.init.kaiminguniform(m.weight, a=0, mode='fanin') if m.bias is not None: fanin, = nn.init.calculatefaninandfanout(m.weight) bound = 1 / (fanin 0.5) nn.init.uniform(m.bias, -bound, bound) def forward(self, vs): x = torch.relu(self.fc1(vs)) x = torch.relu(self.fc2(x)) out = self.fc3(x) return out class SPWINRTrainer: def init(self, inrmodelclass, inrconfig, semanticmodelname='efficientnetb7'): """ inrmodelclass: Class defining the INR architecture (e.g., SIREN, PE-MLP). inrconfig: Dict containing hidden layers and features. semanticmodelname: Name of the pre-trained SNN. """ self.inrconfig = inrconfig self.inrmodelclass = inrmodelclass # Load SNN self.snn = models.efficientnetb7(pretrained=True) self.snn.eval() # Remove the classifier/head to get feature maps from stages # Note: EfficientNet-B7 stages correspond to specific blocks. # For implementation, one must hook the outputs of the 7 stages. # This is a placeholder for the specific feature extraction logic. self.snnfeatures = None # Initialize WGNs # EfficientNet-B7 stage channel sizes: [C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7] # These are typically [32, 24, 64, 160, 448, 1536, 2560] for B7. # We assume these are known or extracted from the model. self.stagechannels = [32, 24, 64, 160, 448, 1536, 2560] self.semanticdim = sum(self.stagechannels) self.wgns = nn.ModuleList() layers = inrconfig['layers'] hiddenfeatures = inrconfig['features'] for m in range(1, layers + 1): prevc = hiddenfeatures if m > 1 else 3 # Assuming 3 channels for input image currc = hiddenfeatures wgn = WeightGenerationNetwork(self.semanticdim, prevc currc, expansionfactor=6) self.wgns.append(wgn) self.optimizer = optim.Adam(self.wgns.parameters(), lr=2e-4) def extractsemanticvector(self, image): """ Extracts semantic vector from image using SNN. image: Tensor of shape (1, 3, H, W) """ self.snn.eval() with torch.nograd(): # Hooking stages is required. Here we assume a helper function # that returns feature maps from the 7 stages. featuremaps = self.getefficientnetb7stages(image) pooledvectors = [] for fm in featuremaps: # Global Average Pooling along H and W pooled = torch.mean(fm, dim=(2, 3), keepdim=True) pooledvectors.append(pooled) vs = torch.cat(pooledvectors, dim=1) return vs def getefficientnetb7stages(self, x): # Placeholder for actual EfficientNet-B7 stage extraction. # In practice, one would use forward hooks or modify the model # to return intermediate features. # This function returns a list of 7 tensors. return [] def train(self, targetimage, numiterations=50000): vs = self.extractsemanticvector(targetimage) for i in range(numiterations): self.optimizer.zerograd() # Generate weights for all layers generatedweights = [] layers = self.inrconfig['layers'] hiddenfeatures = self.inrconfig['features'] for m in range(1, layers + 1): prevc = hiddenfeatures if m > 1 else 3 currc = hiddenfeatures wgn = self.wgns[m-1] # Generate weight vector wvec = wgn(vs) # Reshape to matrix wmat = wvec.view(prevc, currc) generatedweights.append(wmat) # Create INR instance with generated weights # The INR model class must accept weights or be constructed dynamically inr = self.inrmodelclass(weights=generatedweights, config=self.inrconfig) # Sample coordinates (e.g., random pixels from target image) coords = self.samplecoordinates(targetimage) targetvalues = self.samplevalues(targetimage, coords) # Forward pass predvalues = inr(coords) # Loss loss = nn.MSELoss()(predvalues, targetvalues) loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() if i % 1000 == 0: print(f"Iteration {i}, Loss: {loss.item()}") def getinferencemodel(self): """ Returns an INR model with the final semantic weights. """ # This method is not fully defined in sources, but implies # saving the weights W^s. # We assume the trainer has access to the final vs and wgns. # In practice, one would re-run the forward pass of WGNs # to get the final weights and save them. pass def samplecoordinates(self, image): # Placeholder for coordinate sampling return torch.randn(1000, 2) def samplevalues(self, image, coords): # Placeholder for value sampling return torch.randn(1000, 3) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SNN Compatibility: The method relies on the SNN providing feature maps from multiple stages. If the SNN does not expose intermediate features, the semantic vector cannot be constructed. WGN Capacity: The WGN must be sufficiently large to map the semantic vector to the INR weights. The expansion factor E=6 is recommended. Training Stability: The WGNs are trained via back-propagation through the INR. If the INR architecture is sensitive to weight initialization, the WGN must learn to stabilize the weights. Inference Cost: While SPW adds no cost at inference, the training cost is higher due to the WGNs and the need to compute vs. Time Complexity: Training time is increased compared to standard INR due to the WGNs and the SNN feature extraction. However, inference time is identical to standard INR. Memory Complexity: Training memory includes the SNN, WGNs, and INR weights. Inference memory is only the INR weights W^s, identical to standard INR. Performance: On the Kodak dataset (24 RGB images, 768x512 resolution), SPW improved PSNR by up to 1.4dB for image fitting tasks compared to original INR models. Specifically, for the [10x28] architecture, SPW SIREN achieved 26.61 PSNR vs 25.52 for standard SIREN. Strengths: Enhances representational capacity without inference overhead; generalizable to various INR models (SIREN, PE-MLP, MFN, WIRE). Limitations: Requires a pre-trained SNN; training is more complex due to the two-stage process (SNN fixed, WGN trained). SPW was proposed by Qiu Shen et al. in 2024. It addresses the limitation that standard INR coordinates contain no semantic information, which can hinder performance in tasks where semantic context is beneficial. The method builds on the idea that semantic features extracted from pre-trained networks can guide the learning of implicit representations. It is applicable to 2D image fitting, compression, CT reconstruction, MRI reconstruction, and novel view synthesis. name: Single MLP SDF
head: MLP SDF, SDF decoder, Single MLP
body: Single MLP SDF is a coordinate-based neural implicit representation that parameterizes a signed distance field (SDF) using a single Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) f\theta. It solves the problem of representing continuous 3D geometry without voxelization or explicit mesh extraction by mapping 3D coordinates directly to distance values. Unlike hierarchical grid-based methods (e.g., HIGS) that rely on learned feature grids, this method relies entirely on the MLP's capacity to approximate the distance function, often augmented with fixed positional encoding. It is distinct from Ray Marching with Neural SDF in that it specifically denotes the decoder architecture (a single MLP) rather than the rendering pipeline, and from Implicit Neural Representation (INR) by its specific application to SDFs using a single-layer network structure. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A scalar signed distance value \hat{s} \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures MLP Parameters \theta: A single set of weights and biases for the decoder network. The network is a single-layer MLP (one hidden layer) with a hidden dimension of 64. Positional Encoding \gamma(x): A fixed mapping that transforms the input coordinate x into a higher-dimensional space to increase the network's expressiveness. The specific implementation of \gamma is not detailed in the provided notes, but it is described as a "fixed positional encoding". Algorithm 1. Positional Encoding: Compute the encoded representation \gamma(x) of the input point x. 2. MLP Forward Pass: Pass \gamma(x) through the single-layer MLP f\theta to compute the predicted SDF value \hat{s}. Formula The computation is defined as: \hat{s} = f\theta(\gamma(x)) where: \hat{s} is the predicted SDF value. f\theta is the single-layer MLP parameterized by \theta. \gamma(x) is the fixed positional encoding of point x. Training Procedure The method is trained offline using a joint optimization strategy. 1. Dataset Compilation: Compile an offline training dataset using six scenes from the Replica dataset. 2. View Simulation: Randomly simulate 128 camera views with ground truth poses for each scene. 3. Optimization Setup: Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10^{-3}. Train for a total of 1200 epochs. Use the SDF loss defined in Problem 1 of the source. 4. Coarse-to-Fine Strategy: Activate all fine-level features after 200 epochs. Note: This step implies the context of hierarchical features, but for the pure "Single MLP" definition, the core inference remains f\theta(\gamma(x)). 5. Finalization: After training, discard any associated grid features (if applicable in the broader context) and save only the decoder parameters \theta. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class SingleMLPSDF: def init(self, hiddendim=64): """ Initializes a single-layer MLP for SDF prediction. Note: The exact weight initialization and activation functions are not specified in the sources. Standard practices (e.g., He initialization, ReLU/Swish) are assumed. """ self.hiddendim = hiddendim # Weights and biases for a single hidden layer # Input dim depends on gamma(x), output dim is 1 self.W1 = None self.b1 = None self.W2 = None self.b2 = None def positionalencoding(self, x, numfrequencies=10): """ Placeholder for fixed positional encoding gamma(x). Standard implementation involves sin/cos functions at different frequencies. """ # Not given in the sources. Standard NeRF-style PE assumed. # x: (N, 3) # Returns: (N, 2 numfrequencies 3 + 3) pass def forward(self, x): """ Computes the SDF value for point x. Args: x: numpy array of shape (N, 3) representing 3D points. Returns: s: numpy array of shape (N,) representing predicted SDF values. """ # 1. Positional Encoding xenc = self.positionalencoding(x) # 2. First Layer (Hidden) # z = W1 @ xenc + b1 z = np.dot(xenc, self.W1.T) + self.b1 # Activation function not specified in sources # Assuming ReLU or similar standard activation a = np.maximum(0, z) # 3. Second Layer (Output) # s = W2 @ a + b2 s = np.dot(a, self.W2.T) + self.b2 return s.squeeze() def trainstep(self, x, targetsdf, optimizer, lossfn): """ Performs one training step. """ # Forward pass predsdf = self.forward(x) # Compute loss (SDF loss from Problem 1 in) loss = lossfn(predsdf, targetsdf) # Backward pass and update (using Adam) # Gradients are computed w.r.t theta (W1, b1, W2, b2) # Optimizer step with lr=1e-3 pass Parameters Hidden Dimension: 64. Learning Rate: 10^{-3}. Total Epochs: 1200. Coarse-to-Fine Threshold: Fine level features activated after 200 epochs. Dataset: 6 scenes from Replica. Views per Scene: 128 simulated views with ground truth poses. Time Complexity: Inference is O(1) with respect to spatial resolution, but depends on the MLP depth and width. For a single-layer MLP with hidden dimension 64, the cost is low per query. However, ray marching requires many queries per pixel, making it slower than grid-based lookups. Memory Complexity: O(D^2) where D is the hidden dimension (64). It stores only the MLP weights, resulting in very low memory footprint compared to dense grids. Strengths: Resolution-independent representation; compact storage (only \theta is saved); simple architecture. Limitations: High query cost for ray marching; potential difficulty in capturing high-frequency details with a single-layer MLP compared to deeper networks or hybrid methods. When to use: When memory is constrained and the geometry is relatively smooth or can be represented by a simple MLP. When not to use: For high-resolution scenes requiring fine details where grid-based methods (e.g., HIGS) or deeper networks might perform better. The Single MLP SDF approach originates from the use of coordinate-based neural networks for implicit surface reconstruction. It was popularized by the introduction of positional encoding for novel view synthesis. The specific configuration of a single-layer MLP with hidden dimension 64 for SDF decoding is detailed in the HIGS paper. The use of fixed positional encoding \gamma(x) to map coordinates to a higher-dimensional space is a standard technique in neural implicit representations. name: Inverse Rendering of Translucent Objects
head: Homo Translucent Inverse Rendering
body: Inverse Rendering of Translucent Objects is a framework that jointly estimates 3D shape, spatially-varying surface reflectance, homogeneous subsurface scattering (SSS) parameters, and environment illumination from a single viewpoint using only a pair of captured images: one with a flash and one without. It solves the ambiguity inherent in inverse rendering by decomposing the scene into surface reflectance and homogeneous SSS components, handling both simultaneously for arbitrary shapes under environment illumination. Unlike methods that assume pure SSS or ignore surface reflectance, this approach models glossy translucent materials where light undergoes multiple bounces inside the object, distinguishing it from glossy transparent materials that assume straight-line travel. It employs a hybrid rendering pipeline combining a physically-based renderer for direct illumination and a neural renderer for SSS, enabling efficient global illumination estimation without the high memory and compute costs of Monte Carlo path tracing. Input images are assumed to be size 256 \times 256. Outputs: Depth map (D): Rough representation of object shape. Normal map (N): Local surface details. Roughness map (R): Spatially-varying BSDF parameters. SSS parameters: Homogeneous subsurface scattering coefficients: Extinction coefficient (\sigmat): Controls optical density. Volumetric albedo (\alpha): Probability of scattering vs. absorption. Henyey-Greenstein phase function parameter (g): Defines scattering direction. Illumination: Spherical harmonics coefficients (sh) for environment lighting. Flashlight intensity (i): Radiance of the flash source. The method uses a deep neural network estimator with a specific encoder-decoder architecture. All physical parameters (\sigmat, \alpha, g, i) and pixel values are normalized to the range [-1, 1]. Network parameters are initialized using Normal Initialization with mean 0 and variance 0.02. 1. Output: H/64 \times W/64 \times 32. Decoder (Table 6): ResNet Blocks: 9 blocks. Each block contains two 3 \times 3 convolutions, 288 channels, stride 1 \times 1, BN, ReLU. Input is concatenated Surface and Scattering encoders. Output: H/4 \times W/4 \times 256. Upsample 1: 3 \times 3, 128 ch, stride 2 \times 2, BN, ReLU. Output: H/2 \times W/2 \times 128. Outgoing Light Radiance: The outgoing light radiance L(wo) at point p is defined by the sum of reflected and transmitted light integrals over the outside hemisphere \Omega and inside hemisphere \Omega0 respectively: L(wo) = \int{\Omega} L(wi) fr(wi, wo, R(p), N(p)) \max(wi \cdot N(p), 0) dwi + \int{\Omega0} L(wi) ft(wi, wo, R(p), N(p)) \max(wi \cdot N(p), 0) dwi Where: wo is the outgoing direction. wi is the incident direction. name: SDFPerf Raymarching Shader
head: Node-based SDF Editor Raymarching, SDFPerf
body: The SDFPerf Raymarching Shader is a fragment shader generated from a node-based graph editor that constructs Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) using basic primitives, CSG operations, and domain manipulations. It differs from generic sphere tracing implementations by providing a specific, optimized set of domain transformation operators (bend, twist) and shading modes (ambient occlusion, depth, normals) directly integrated into the generated code, rather than relying on external scene graphs or complex hierarchical structures. It builds on Distance-field ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: vstexcoord (vec2, location 0): Vertex shader texture coordinates, typically in range [0, 1]. ucameraposition (vec3): Camera origin in world space. ucamerafront (vec3): Camera forward direction vector. ushading (uint): Enum selecting the shading mode (0-4). utime (float): Current time in seconds. paramsblock (SSBO, binding 0, std430): A variable-size array of vec4 parameters used by domain manipulation nodes (e.g., bend angle, twist angle, primitive dimensions). Outputs: ocolor (vec4, location 0): The final rendered color. Data Structures: Params Block: Defined as layout (std430, binding = 0) buffer paramsblock { vec4 params[]; };. The shader accesses specific vec4 elements based on the node graph connections. Hit Info: A custom structure or tuple containing id (primitive identifier) and distance (SDF value) returned by the map(p) function. Parameters: MAXSTEPS: 256 (maximum iterations per ray). MAXTRACEDISTANCE: 64.0 (maximum ray length). MINHITDISTANCE: 0.001 (convergence threshold for surface hit). SDF Primitives and Operations: The generated shader evaluates a composite SDF function map(p) which returns the distance to the nearest surface. The following formulas are used for basic primitives and operations: 1. Sphere: Center c, Radius r. d = \|p - c\| - r 2. Box: Half-extents b = (bx, by, bz). d = \min(\max(dx, \max(dy, dz)), 0.0) + \|\max(d, 0.0)\| where d = |p| - b. 3. Plane: Height h (normal along Y). d = py - h 4. Torus: Major radius tx, Minor radius ty. d = \sqrt{(\|p{xz}\| - tx)^2 + py^2} - ty 5. Union: d = \min(da, db) 6. Intersection: d = \max(da, db) 7. Subtraction: d = \max(-da, db) 8. Smooth Minimum: Parameter k. h = \text{clamp}(0.5 + 0.5 \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0) d = \text{mix}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Domain Manipulations: These functions transform the query point p before evaluation, effectively deforming the space. 1. Twist: Rotate XZ plane around Y axis by angle t \cdot py. 2. Bend: Rotate XY plane around Z axis by angle t \cdot py. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Convert vstexcoord to UV range [-1, 1]. Compute camera right vector from ucamerafront and up vector. Calculate pixel position using camera position, front, right, up vectors, and a fixed FOV of 50 degrees. Construct ray r with origin ucameraposition and normalized direction. 2. Raymarching Loop: Initialize res.id = -1, totaldistance = 0, totalsteps = 0. Loop while totalsteps < MAXSTEPS: Calculate current point p = r.o + r.d \times \text{total\distance}. Evaluate hit\info = \text{map}(p). Add hit\info.distance to totaldistance. If hit\info.distance < \text{MIN\HIT\DISTANCE}: Set res.id = hitinfo.id. Break loop. If \text{total\distance} > \text{MAX\TRACE\DISTANCE}: Reset totaldistance = 0.0. Break loop (discarding the ray). Increment totalsteps. 3. Normal Estimation: If a hit occurred, compute the normal n using central finite differences with epsilon \epsilon = 0.001: e = (0.001, 0.0, 0.0) nx = \text{map}(p + e{xyy}).y - \text{map}(p - e{xyy}).y ny = \text{map}(p + e{yxy}).y - \text{map}(p - e{yxy}).y nz = \text{map}(p + e{yyx}).y - \text{map}(p - e{yyx}).y n = \text{normalize}(nx, ny, nz) Note: The source code snippet uses.y to access the distance component of the hit info tuple, implying the SDF returns a vec2 or similar where the second component is the distance. 4. Ambient Occlusion (AO): Compute AO using 5 steps along the normal: \text{attenuation} = 0.5 \text{accum} = 0.0 \text{scale} = 1.0 \text{ao} = 1.0 For step from 0 to 4: hr = 0.01 + 0.02 \times (\text{step}^2) aopos = p + n \times hr dist = \text{map}(aopos).y ao = -(dist - hr) \text{accum} += ao \times \text{scale} \text{scale} = \text{attenuation} \text{ao} = 1.0 - \text{clamp}(\text{accum}, 0.0, 1.0) 5. Shading: Based on ushading mode: 0 (Depth): \sqrt{\frac{pz}{\text{MAX\TRACE\DISTANCE}}} (Note: Source says hit.z, likely referring to distance or depth component). 1 (Steps): Map totalsteps percentage to colors using smoothstep. 2 (AO): \text{pow}(\text{ao}, 3.0). 3 (Normals): n \times 0.5 + 0.5. 4 (Diffuse): Diffuse lighting with light at (0, 2, 3) and AO \text{pow}(\text{ao}, 3.0).
