pi)2 for pi, c in zip(p, center))) - radius def sdfbox(p, b): d = (abs(p[0]) - b[0], abs(p[1]) - b[1], abs(p[2]) - b[2]) return min(max(d[0], max(d[1], d[2])), 0.0) + math.sqrt(max(d[0], 0.0)2 + max(d[1], 0.0)2 + max(d[2], 0.0)2) def sdfplane(p, h): return p[1] - h def sdftorus(p, t): dxz = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - t[0] dy = p[1] return math.sqrt(dxz2 + dy2) - t[1] def sdfunion(a, b): return min(a, b) def sdfintersection(a, b): return max(a, b) def sdfsubtraction(a, b): return max(-a, b) def sdfsmoothmin(a, b, k): h = max(0.0, min(1.0, 0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / k)) return b - h (b - a) - k h (1.0 - h) def domaintwist(p, t): c = math.cos(t p[1]) s = math.sin(t p[1]) return (c p[0] - s p[2], p[1], s p[0] + c p[2]) def domainbend(p, t): c = math.cos(t p[1]) s = math.sin(t p[1]) return (c p[0] - s p[1], s p[0] + c p[1], p[2]) def map(p): # Example scene: twisted box ptwisted = domaintwist(p, 0.5) d = sdfbox(ptwisted, (1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) return (0.0, d) # id=0, distance=d def getnormal(p): e = 0.001 nx = map((p[0]+e, p[1], p[2]))[1] - map((p[0]-e, p[1], p[2]))[1] ny = map((p[0], p[1]+e, p[2]))[1] - map((p[0], p[1]-e, p[2]))[1] nz = map((p[0], p[1], p[2]+e))[1] - map((p[0], p[1], p[2]-e))[1] mag = math.sqrt(nx2 + ny2 + nz2) return (nx/mag, ny/mag, nz/mag) def getao(p, n): attenuation = 0.5 accum = 0.0 scale = 1.0 for step in range(5): hr = 0.01 + 0.02 (step step) aopos = (p[0] + n[0]hr, p[1] + n[1]hr, p[2] + n[2]hr) dist = map(aopos)[1] aoval = -(dist - hr) accum += aoval scale scale = attenuation return 1.0 - max(0.0, min(1.0, accum)) def raymarch(rayorigin, raydir): resid = -1 totaldistance = 0.0 totalsteps = 0 while totalsteps < MAXSTEPS: p = (rayorigin[0] + raydir[0]totaldistance, rayorigin[1] + raydir[1]totaldistance, rayorigin[2] + raydir[2]totaldistance) hitinfo = map(p) dist = hitinfo[1] totaldistance += dist if dist < MINHITDISTANCE: resid = hitinfo[0] break if totaldistance > MAXTRACEDISTANCE: totaldistance = 0.0 break totalsteps += 1 return resid, totaldistance, totalsteps def fragmentshader(vstexcoord, ucameraposition, ucamerafront, ushading): # 1. Ray Generation uv = (vstexcoord[0] 2.0 - 1.0, vstexcoord[1] 2.0 - 1.0) aspect = 1.0 # Assume square for simplicity fovrad = math.radians(FOVDEGREES) raydir = (uv[0], uv[1] / aspect, 1.0 / math.tan(fovrad / 2.0)) mag = math.sqrt(raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2) raydir = (raydir[0]/mag, raydir[1]/mag, raydir[2]/mag) rayorigin = ucameraposition # 2. March hitid, hitdist, steps = raymarch(rayorigin, raydir) # 3. Shading if hitid != -1: phit = (rayorigin[0] + raydir[0]hitdist, rayorigin[1] + raydir[1]hitdist, rayorigin[2] + raydir[2]hitdist) n = getnormal(phit) ao = getao(phit, n) if ushading == 0: # Depth color = math.sqrt(phit[2] / MAXTRACEDISTANCE) elif ushading == 1: # Steps color = max(0.0, min(1.0, steps / MAXSTEPS)) # smoothstep approximation elif ushading == 2: # AO color = ao 3.0 elif ushading == 3: # Normals color = (n[0]0.5 + 0.5, n[1]0.5 + 0.5, n[2]0.5 + 0.5) elif ushading == 4: # Diffuse l = (LIGHTPOS[0]-phit[0], LIGHTPOS[1]-phit[1], LIGHTPOS[2]-phit[2]) magl = math.sqrt(l[0]2 + l[1]2 + l[2]2) l = (l[0]/magl, l[1]/magl, l[2]/magl) diff = max(0.0, n[0]l[0] + n[1]l[1] + n[2]l[2]) color = diff ao 3.0 else: color = 0.0 else: color = 0.0 return color This method renders large worlds composed of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by partitioning the scene into tiles, pruning irrelevant primitives per tile, and evaluating the remaining SDF expression in the fragment shader using a Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) interpreter. It solves the problem of shader compilation latency and memory constraints when dealing with complex, large-scale SDF scenes. Unlike SDFPerf, which generates static shader code, this approach uses a dynamic interpreter pattern with command and operand buffers, allowing for on-the-fly simplification and avoiding the prohibitive cost of recompiling shaders for every tile. See Tile-based SDF Rendering with RPN Interpreter. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the average number of steps per ray (up to MAXSTEPS). The complexity of the map(p) function depends on the number of primitives and operations in the node graph. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, plus O(P) for the paramsblock where P is the number of parameters. Measured Performance: Tested on NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970M and GTX 980. Performance is highly dependent on the complexity of the SDF graph and the number of steps. Scaling: Scales linearly with resolution. Does not scale well with increasing SDF complexity due to the lack of spatial acceleration structures. Strengths: Simple implementation, no need for external scene graphs or BVH construction, easy to edit via node-based interface, good for real-time procedural geometry. Limitations: No spatial acceleration (slow for complex scenes), fixed step count can lead to aliasing or slow convergence, limited to convex primitives and simple CSG, no native support for shadows or reflections without additional raymarching passes. When to use: Real-time visualization of procedural geometry, educational purposes, simple VFX, scenes with low primitive count. When not to use: Complex scenes with many primitives, scenes requiring shadows/reflections, high-resolution rendering where aliasing is unacceptable. The SDFPerf project was created by mwalczyk as a work-in-progress node-based editor for creating and manipulating signed-distance fields. It was tested on Windows 8.1, Windows 10, and Ubuntu 18.04, using NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970M and GTX 980 GPUs, and built with Rust compiler version 1.37.0-nightly. The project generates a raymarching shader string from a graph of operators, supporting basic SDF primitives, domain manipulation, and CSG operations. mwalczyk/sdfperf, https://github.com/mwalczyk/sdfperf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tile-based SDF Rendering with RPN Interpreter
head: Chunked SDF rendering, SDF interpreter with command buffers
body: This method renders large worlds composed of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by partitioning the scene into tiles, pruning irrelevant primitives per tile, and evaluating the remaining SDF expression in the fragment shader using a Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) interpreter. It solves the problem of shader compilation latency and memory constraints when dealing with complex, large-scale SDF scenes. Unlike SDFPerf Raymarching Shader, which generates static shader code, this approach uses a dynamic interpreter pattern with command and operand buffers, allowing for on-the-fly simplification and avoiding the prohibitive cost of recompiling shaders for every tile. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A world defined by a set of SDF primitives and their transformations. Output: A rendered image where each tile displays the SDF evaluation for that region. Data Structures: The shader requires two input buffers, one for each tile: 1. Command Buffer: An integer array containing opcodes (e.g., union, add, multiply, pointprimitive, segmentprimitive). 2. Operand Buffer: A float array containing numerical values, such as primitive parameters and transformation matrices, consumed by the commands. Algorithm Steps: 1. Define Usefulness Bounds: Assign each primitive a "usefulness bound," a finite distance beyond which its contribution to the SDF is considered zero. This requires selecting or modifying the distance-to-height mapping curve so it reaches zero at a finite distance. 2. Tile Partitioning: Split the world into tiles (chunks) small enough to fit within the shader's memory constraints for the command and operand buffers. 3. Pruning: For each tile, identify primitives whose usefulness bounds do not intersect the tile. Remove these primitives from the local SDF expression. 4. Tree Simplification: Simplify the remaining operation tree by applying algebraic identities to eliminate zero contributions. Specifically: Replace x \times 0 with 0. Replace x + 0 with x. Repeat until no further simplification is possible. This step reduces the number of operations required. 5. RPN Conversion (CPU): Rewrite the simplified SDF expression into Reverse Polish Notation (RPN). Generate the corresponding integer command buffer and float operand buffer for the tile. 6. Shader Execution (GPU): In the fragment shader, execute a loop over the command buffer. Maintain a stack of float values. For each command: Pop the required number of operands from the operand buffer. Perform the operation using the stack. Push the result back onto the stack. The final value on the stack is the SDF value for the fragment. Parameters: Stack Size: The maximum depth of the evaluation stack must be determined during the simplification phase and fixed in the shader implementation. It must be reasonably small to fit within shader memory limits. Pitfalls: Shader Compilation Time: Generating unique shader code for each tile (e.g., via string concatenation) is prohibitively slow for large unions (e.g., thousands of primitives can take 30+ seconds to compile). The RPN interpreter approach avoids this by using a single generic shader program. Stack Overflow: If the simplification step is insufficient, the stack depth may exceed the fixed size allocated in the shader, leading to incorrect results or crashes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processtile(primitives, tilebounds): # Step 1 & 3: Prune primitives based on usefulness bounds activeprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: if intersectsbounds(prim.usefulnessbounds, tilebounds): activeprimitives.append(prim) # Step 4: Simplify the operation tree # This function returns a simplified expression tree simplifiedtree = simplifytree(buildsdftree(activeprimitives)) # Step 5: Convert to RPN and generate buffers rpncommands, operands = converttorpn(simplifiedtree) return rpncommands, operands def evaluatesdf(): # Initialize stack pointer stackptr = 0 # Loop through all commands in the buffer while commandptr < len(commandbuffer): cmd = commandbuffer[commandptr] commandptr += 1 if cmd == UNION: b = stack[stackptr - 1] a = stack[stackptr - 2] stack[stackptr - 2] = min(a, b) stackptr -= 1 elif cmd == ADD: b = stack[stackptr - 1] a = stack[stackptr - 2] stack[stackptr - 2] = a + b stackptr -= 1 elif cmd == MULTIPLY: b = stack[stackptr - 1] a = stack[stackptr - 2] stack[stackptr - 2] = a b stackptr -= 1 elif cmd == POINTPRIMITIVE: # Pop parameters from operand buffer center = readoperands(3) # x, y, z radius = readoperand(1) # r # Push result onto stack stack[stackptr] = distance(center, currentfragmentpos) - radius stackptr += 1 elif cmd == SEGMENTPRIMITIVE: # Pop parameters from operand buffer p1 = readoperands(3) p2 = readoperands(3) radius = readoperand(1) # Push result onto stack stack[stackptr] = distancetosegment(currentfragmentpos, p1, p2) - radius stackptr += 1 else: # Unknown command or placeholder for other operations pass return stack[0] def readoperand(count): val = operandbuffer[operandptr] operandptr += count return val def readoperands(count): # Returns a vector of size count return [operandbuffer[operandptr + i] for i in range(count)] Renders each SDF object as a separate quad. It is simpler to implement and optimal in terms of primitive evaluation count but may struggle to keep GPU cores busy due to overdraw and state changes. It is preferred when overlapping per pixel is low. Generates a unique shader string for the entire scene or large chunks. It is simple but suffers from extreme compilation times for complex scenes (thousands of primitives). Time Complexity: The CPU side complexity depends on the pruning and simplification algorithms. For millions of primitives, spatial hierarchies (e.g., BVH, Octree) are required to scale the pruning process efficiently. The GPU side complexity is linear with respect to the number of commands in the RPN buffer for the tile. Memory Complexity: The shader memory usage is fixed per tile, determined by the size of the command buffer, operand buffer, and the maximum stack depth. This allows rendering of large worlds by tiling, as only a subset of primitives is loaded per tile. Strengths: Avoids shader compilation overhead; allows dynamic simplification; scales to large worlds via tiling. Limitations: Requires a fixed stack size; simplification logic can be complex; tiling introduces boundary artifacts if not handled carefully (not detailed in sources). When to Use: Large worlds with many overlapping SDF primitives where static shader generation is too slow. When Not to Use: Scenes with very few primitives where the overhead of tiling and interpretation outweighs the benefits; scenes where dynamic stack depth is unpredictable and cannot be bounded. This method was proposed in a 2020 discussion on Computer Graphics Stack Exchange as a solution to the problem of rendering large SDF worlds without incurring the high cost of on-the-fly shader compilation. It builds on the concept of tile-based rendering to manage local complexity and applies the interpreter pattern with RPN to decouple the SDF expression structure from the shader code. SDF rendering for large world, https://computergraphics.stackexchange.com/questions/9708/sdf-rendering-for-large-world, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: L-Tracing
head: Light Visibility Estimation on Neural Surfaces by Sphere Tracing, Light Visibility Tracing, Volume Integration for Light Visibility, Volume Rendering Visibility
body: L-Tracing is a method for estimating light visibility on neural implicit surfaces by replacing continuous volumetric integration with binary sphere tracing. It computes whether a light path is occluded by a solid surface using the Signed Distance Function (SDF), producing binary visibility values (0 or 1) instead of continuous probabilities. This approach yields sharper shadows and specular highlights compared to volumetric integration, which models translucent occlusion, while achieving approximately 10–13× faster computation. Inputs: xl: Light source position (3D vector). xs: Surface point position (3D vector) on the neural implicit surface \mathcal{S}. f: Neural implicit surface function returning the Signed Distance Function (SDF) value at a query point. T: Maximum number of tracing iterations (default 20). Outputs: v: Binary light visibility (1 if visible, 0 if occluded). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required; the method is stateless per point-light pair. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Setup: Calculate the vector from the light to the surface point: \mathbf{r} = xs - xl. 2. Range Bound: Compute the maximum tracing distance (far plane) as the Euclidean norm: far = \|\mathbf{r}\|2. 3. Direction: Normalize the ray direction: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{r} / \|\mathbf{r}\|2. 4. Initialization: Set the accumulated distance t = 0. 5. Iteration Loop: For i from 0 to T-1: a. Query: Evaluate the SDF at the current tracing point pts = xl + \mathbf{d} \cdot t: sd = f(pts). b. Step: Advance the ray: t \leftarrow t + sd. c. Termination Check: If t > far or t < 0, return v = 1 (unoccluded). 6. Final Check: If the loop completes without returning, return v = 0 (occluded). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ltracing(xl, xs, f, T=20): """ Compute binary light visibility using sphere tracing on an SDF. Args: xl: Light position (3,) xs: Surface point position (3,) f: SDF function f(p) -> float T: Max iterations (int) Returns: v: Visibility (1.0 if visible, 0.0 if occluded) """ # 1. Ray Setup r = xs - xl far = torch.norm(r) d = r / far # 2. Initialization t = 0.0 # 3. Iteration Loop for in range(T): # Query SDF pts = xl + d t sd = f(pts) # Step t = t + sd # Termination Check if t > far or t < 0: return 1.0 # 4. Final Check return 0.0 Formulas: Convergence Inequality: For convex surfaces, the error \epsilonk (distance between tracing point Ok and surface point Q) converges linearly: 0 < \frac{\epsilon{k+1}}{\epsilonk} \leq 1 - \sin\theta where \theta is the angle between the ray and the surface normal. Minimum Iterations: The theoretical lower bound for iterations T to achieve accuracy \epsilon is: T \geq \frac{\log \frac{\epsilon}{\epsilon0}}{\log(1-\sin\theta)} where \epsilon0 is the initial distance (max range 2) and \epsilon is the target accuracy (0.001). Parameters: T: Maximum iterations. Set to 20 in experiments. Theoretical minimum for \epsilon=0.001 and \theta{min}=5^\circ is 83, but 20 is sufficient in practice. \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Default 0.001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tangential Rays: If the ray is nearly parallel to the surface (\theta \approx 0), convergence slows. The theoretical bound assumes \theta{min}=5^\circ. Range Violation: If t exceeds far or becomes negative, the light is considered visible (v=1). Iteration Limit: If T iterations are exhausted without t exceeding bounds, the ray is considered trapped/occluded (v=0). Time Complexity: Linear in the number of iterations T. Each iteration requires one SDF query. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per point-light pair. Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 3090, L-Tracing takes 1.07 seconds for 1024 points with 512 lights, compared to 13.36 seconds for Volumetric Integration, a ~13× speedup. Strengths: Produces binary, hard shadows and speculars; significantly faster than volumetric integration; respects solid geometry occlusions. Limitations: Assumes solid, non-translucent objects; binary visibility may not model soft shadows from translucent materials. When to Use: When rendering solid objects with neural implicit surfaces and requiring efficient, sharp shadowing. When Not to Use: When modeling translucent materials or soft shadows from volumetric media. L-Tracing was introduced by Ziyu Chen et al. in the paper "L-Tracing: Fast Light Visibility Estimation on Neural Surfaces by Sphere Tracing" at ECCV 2022. It was developed to address the inefficiency and physical inaccuracy of volumetric integration for light visibility in neural implicit surface reconstruction. The method is used in reflectance factorization frameworks to decompose material and reflectance from multiview images. L-Tracing: Fast Light Visibility Estimation on Neural Surfaces by Sphere Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19784-013, fetched 2026-10-31 ziyc/L-Tracing, https://github.com/ziyc/L-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Lighting, Shading, and Visualization
head: SDF Lighting, Ray Marched Shading
body: This family covers the computation of visual properties (color, opacity, lighting) for surfaces and volumes defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) during the ray marching process. While the parent Distance-field ray marching defines the geometric traversal, this family defines how the traversed data is converted into pixels. It differs from sibling methods like Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion by relying on implicit geometry evaluation rather than explicit depth buffers, and from Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering by focusing primarily on surface-based SDF shading, though it shares the marching infrastructure. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the SDF f(\mathbf{p}) at points \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. The visual output depends on the value of f(\mathbf{p}) relative to a threshold (typically 0 for surfaces). 1. Surface Detection: A hit is recorded when |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon. The normal \mathbf{n} is estimated via finite differences of the SDF. 2. Lighting Models: Standard shading models (Phong, Blinn-Phong) are applied using the estimated normal and light positions. 3. Volume Integration: For volumetric SDFs, the density \sigma is derived from f(\mathbf{p}), and transmittance is accumulated via the Beer-Lambert law. 4. Anti-aliasing: Techniques like Antialiasing (AA) are often integrated by jittering the ray origin or direction within the pixel footprint. Accelerates sphere tracing for Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) isosurfaces by computing Sphere Distance Bounds (SDB) and adaptive step sizes using a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) derived from the FBM structure. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM sum at every step, this approach progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and larger step sizes. It builds on Sphere Tracing and Step Rules by replacing explicit spatial acceleration structures with a procedural hierarchy that reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. Adapts distance-field ray marching to simulate LiDAR sensor data by detecting surface intersections from a camera viewpoint and projecting them onto a framebuffer as a sparse point cloud, rather than rendering a continuous geometric or volumetric surface. It differs from standard sphere tracing by discarding surface shading and normal estimation in favor of storing hit positions in a bounded point cloud buffer and rendering them with an occlusion-aware color map. A deferred rendering technique for Signed Distance Fields (SDF) that tracks both a primary surface hit and a 'represent' hit (a proxy for the surface at the pixel radius) to handle transparency and aliasing at object edges. It writes results to two render targets: index 0 for the surface and index 1 for the represent hit. The integration of lighting and shading into sphere tracing was pioneered by Inigo Quilez in the mid-2000s, who demonstrated how to compute normals and apply lighting models directly within the SDF evaluation loop. The specific techniques for FBM acceleration [1728-fbm-sphere-tracing-with-bvh-acceleration.md] and represent hits [6684-sphere-tracing-with-represent-hit.md] are more recent developments in procedural rendering, aimed at improving performance and visual quality for complex noise-based geometries.

name: FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration
head: High-level view algorithm of how step size is computed during the FBM loop, Procedural FBM Sphere Tracing
body: This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by computing valid Sphere Distance Bounds (SDB) and adaptive step sizes using a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) derived from the FBM structure itself. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM sum at every step, this approach progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and larger step sizes. It builds on Sphere Tracing and Step Rules by replacing explicit spatial acceleration structures with a procedural hierarchy that reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. The algorithm integrates the FBM summation loop with the sphere tracing step computation. Instead of evaluating all n octaves to get a single distance value, it computes the FBM value F, the derivative along the ray dF, and a valid step size incrementally. It uses a bounding volume BVH representing the maximum possible contribution of the remaining uncomputed octaves to decide whether to compute a step size and whether to terminate the octave loop early. Inputs: p: Current 3D position in space. n: Total number of octaves in the FBM sum. v: Threshold function (hypertexture), typically approximated by its 1st order affine Taylor polynomial. u: Normalized ray direction vector. k: Early Stop threshold parameter (integer). \lambda{noise}, \gamma{noise}: Lipschitz constants for the base noise function (e.g., Perlin noise [Per85] or Worley noise [Wor96]). Default values depend on the specific noise implementation. Outputs: F: The final FBM value at the hit point or current position. step: The computed step size to advance the ray. Data Structures: F: Scalar accumulator for the FBM sum. dF: Scalar accumulator for the directional derivative along the ray. step: Scalar accumulator for the total step size. BVH: Scalar bounding volume representing the upper bound of the remaining FBM contribution. inclFuncParams: Tuple (BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma) passed to the intersection function. Parameters: n: Typical value 20 (as used in Sponge scene tests). k: Typical values tested: 0, 1, 2, 3. \epsilon: Convergence threshold for surface hit (from parent algorithm). t{max}: Maximum ray distance (from parent algorithm). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize F \leftarrow 0, dF \leftarrow 0, step \leftarrow 0. Set global Lipschitz constants \lambda \leftarrow \lambda{Fn} and \gamma \leftarrow \gamma{Fn}, where \lambda{Fn} and \gamma{Fn} are the Lipschitz constants for the full FBM sum. 2. Octave Loop: Iterate i from 1 to n: a. Accumulate Octave: Add the current octave value to the sum: F \leftarrow F + oi(p), where oi(p) is the i-th octave of the noise function evaluated at p. b. Accumulate Derivative: Add the derivative of the current octave along the ray direction: dF \leftarrow dF + (u \cdot o'i(p)), where o'i(p) is the gradient of the octave. c. Compute Bounding Volume: Calculate the bounding volume for the remaining octaves: BVH \leftarrow F + s(i+1, n), where s(i+1, n) is the sum of the absolute maximum bounds of the remaining octaves from i+1 to n. d. Determine Step Computation: Determine if a step size needs to be computed: compStep \leftarrow (i == n) OR (BVH - v(0) < 0). This condition is true if it is the last octave or if the bounding volume indicates the ray is outside the threshold region (empty space). e. Compute Step Size: If compStep is true: i. Adaptive Lipschitz: Replace global constants with local values for the current partial sum: \lambda \leftarrow \lambda{Fi}, \gamma \leftarrow \gamma{Fi}. ii. Prepare Parameters: Set inclFuncParams \leftarrow (BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma). iii. Intersect: Compute the current step size increment: curr\step \leftarrow intersect(inclFuncParams, v). The intersect function solves for the distance t such that the inclusion function (based on BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma) intersects the threshold v. iv. Update Step: step \leftarrow step + curr\step. v. Sub-stepping Guard: If Sub-stepping is enabled, enforce minimum step: step \leftarrow \max(step, curr\step). f. Sub-stepping (Optional): If Sub-stepping is enabled: i. Move ray position: p \leftarrow p + u \cdot curr\step. ii. Update sum: F \leftarrow v(curr\step). iii. Update threshold: v \leftarrow v at curr\step. iv. Update derivative: dF \leftarrow dF + \gamma \cdot curr\step. v. Clamp derivative: dF \leftarrow \max(dF, \lambda). g. Early Stop + k: Decrement k \leftarrow k - 1. If k < 0, break the loop. 3. Return: Return F and step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbmspheretracingstep(p, n, vfunc, u, k, lambdanoise, gammanoise, noisefunc): """ Compute FBM value and step size using BVH acceleration. Args: p: Current 3D position (vec3) n: Number of octaves (int) vfunc: Threshold function (callable, approximated by 1st order Taylor) u: Ray direction (vec3, normalized) k: Early stop threshold (int) lambdanoise: Lipschitz constant for base noise gammanoise: Second Lipschitz constant for base noise noisefunc: Base noise function (e.g., Perlin) Returns: F: Final FBM value (float) step: Computed step size (float) """ F = 0.0 dF = 0.0 step = 0.0 # Global Lipschitz constants for the full FBM sum # Note: Exact formulas for lambdaFn and gammaFn depend on the specific noise composition. # For standard Perlin FBM, these are often derived from the sum of octave contributions. lambdaFn = lambdanoise n # Simplified approximation; source uses lambdaFn gammaFn = gammanoise n # Simplified approximation; source uses gammaFn lambda = lambdaFn gamma = gammaFn for i in range(1, n + 1): # Evaluate current octave oi = noisefunc(p, octave=i) oigrad = noisefuncgradient(p, octave=i) # Accumulate FBM sum and derivative F += oi dF += dot(u, oigrad) # Compute Bounding Volume for remaining octaves # s(i+1, n) is the sum of absolute bounds of remaining octaves # For standard FBM, this is often a geometric series sum remainingoctaves = n - i # Assuming standard FBM decay, s(i+1, n) can be precomputed or approximated # Source uses s(i+1, n) directly sremaining = computesremaining(i, n, lambdanoise, gammanoise) BVH = F + sremaining # Determine if step size computation is required compStep = (i == n) or (BVH - vfunc(0) < 0) if compStep: # Adaptive Lipschitz: use local constants for current partial sum lambdaFi = lambdanoise i gammaFi = gammanoise i lambda = lambdaFi gamma = gammaFi # Prepare inclusion function parameters inclFuncParams = (BVH, lambda, dF, gamma) # Compute current step size # intersect solves for t where inclusion function intersects v(t) currstep = intersect(inclFuncParams, vfunc) # Update total step size step += currstep # Sub-stepping guard (optional) # step = max(step, currstep) # Commented out if SS is on, as per source # Sub-stepping related updates # Move along ray p = p + u currstep # Update sum and threshold F = vfunc(currstep) vfunc = vfuncatstep(vfunc, currstep) # Update threshold function state # Update derivative dF += gamma currstep dF = max(dF, lambda) # If Improved Quadratic (not detailed in source, assumed part of inclFuncParams) pass # Early Stop + k k -= 1 if k < 0: break return F, step def computesremaining(i, n, lambdanoise, gammanoise): """ Computes the sum of absolute bounds for octaves i+1 to n. This is a placeholder for the specific formula used in the source. Typically, for FBM, this is a geometric series. """ # Not given in the sources. Implementer must derive based on specific FBM definition. return 0.0 def intersect(inclFuncParams, vfunc): """ Computes the step size by intersecting the inclusion function with the threshold. inclFuncParams = (BVH, lambda, dF, gamma) """ # Not given in the sources. Implementer must derive based on the specific inclusion function. # Typically involves solving a quadratic or linear equation derived from Taylor expansion. return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thread Divergence: The Early Stop feature causes thread divergence within a warp, as different rays may exit the octave loop at different iterations. However, rays from the same warp are spatially coherent, so divergence is typically limited to a single octave. GPU Memory Usage: The method avoids O(n) per-thread data storage required by dynamic re-ordering methods [WH96], making it more suitable for fast GPU implementation. Threshold Approximation: The threshold function v(p) is approximated by its 1st order (affine) Taylor polynomial. Higher order approximations were not implemented as they showed no noticeable error improvement. Noise Parameters: The algorithm requires \lambda{noise} and \gamma{noise} for arbitrary noise functions. Default values depend on the specific noise implementation (e.g., Perlin with or without abs()). This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by treating the cascaded sum of octaves as a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and empty space skipping. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. It builds on FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration by replacing the explicit spatial tree with a procedural hierarchy derived from the FBM structure itself. Time Complexity: The average cost per step is reduced from O(N) to O(k), where k is the number of octaves computed before early termination or bounding volume check. Memory Complexity: O(1) per thread, avoiding the O(n) storage required by dynamic re-ordering methods. Measured Performance: Tested on an Nvidia RTX 4080 Ti at 1024×1024 resolution on a "Sponge" scene (20-octave Perlin noise FBM): Ray Marching (Early Stop): Reduced average octaves from 49,596.3 to 24,252.6 (close view) and 56,577.8 to 10,347.0 (far view). Time reduced from 770.0ms to 399.8ms (1.9x speedup) and 843.0ms to 178.4ms (4.7x speedup). Sphere Tracing (Adaptive Lipschitz): Reduced average steps from 428.1 to 331.7 (close view) and 223.7 to 154.5 (far view). Time reduced from 110.2ms to 87.1ms (1.3x speedup) and 42.4ms to 28.3ms (1.5x speedup). Sphere Tracing (Sub-stepping): Further reduced time from 87.1ms to 72.5ms (1.2x speedup over Adaptive Lipschitz) in close view, and 28.3ms to 22.0ms (1.3x speedup) in far view. Sphere Tracing (Early Stop + k=1): Reduced time from 72.5ms to 65.0ms (1.1x speedup) in close view, and 22.7ms to 16.7ms (1.4x speedup) in far view. Strengths: Significant performance gains in scenes with large empty spaces or intricate details where FBM evaluation is costly. Low memory overhead makes it GPU-friendly. Limitations: Step sizes may be slightly smaller than those from dynamic re-ordering methods [WH96], but the overhead is much lower. Thread divergence from Early Stop is minimal due to spatial coherence. When to Use: Rendering procedural volumetric noise (FBM) where evaluation cost is high and empty space skipping is beneficial. When Not to Use: Scenes where FBM evaluation is cheap or where dynamic re-ordering's slightly better step sizes are critical and memory is not a constraint. The method was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It was implemented in GLSL fragment shaders and tested on high-end GPUs. The approach leverages the mathematical properties of FBM to create an implicit BVH, avoiding the need for external acceleration structures. It addresses the computational bottleneck of evaluating high-octave FBM noise in sphere tracing, particularly in large, detailed scenes. name: FBM Sphere Tracing with Implicit BVH
head: Dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchy for FBM, Progressive evaluation of octaves
body: This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by treating the cascaded sum of octaves as a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and empty space skipping. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. It builds on FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration by replacing the explicit spatial tree with a procedural hierarchy derived from the FBM structure itself. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. FBM parameters: octave count N, amplitude Ai and frequency Fi for each octave i \in [0, N-1]. Base noise function n(\mathbf{p}) with range [-1, 1]. Isosurface threshold v (typically 0). Outputs: Distance to the nearest surface intersection or empty space indicator. Accumulated density (for volume rendering). Data Structures: No explicit tree nodes are stored; the hierarchy is implicit in the loop order of octave evaluation. Variables: val (current accumulated FBM value) and rem (remaining maximum possible contribution of uncomputed octaves). Algorithm: The core optimization occurs within the FBM evaluation loop. Instead of computing all N octaves, the algorithm maintains a bound on the maximum possible value the remaining octaves can add. If the current value plus this maximum bound cannot reach the threshold v, the point is guaranteed to be outside the object (assuming the object exists where f(\mathbf{p}) > v), and the loop terminates early. 1. Initialize val = 0. 2. Initialize rem = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ai. This represents the worst-case contribution if all remaining noise samples were at their maximum positive value (1). 3. Iterate through octaves i from 0 to N-1: a. Compute noise sample ni = n(\mathbf{p} \cdot Fi). b. Update val: val = val + Ai \cdot ni. c. Update rem: rem = rem - Ai. Since the base noise is bounded in [-1, 1], removing Ai correctly bounds the maximum possible contribution of all remaining unprocessed octaves. d. Early Termination Check: If val + rem < v, terminate the loop immediately. The point is outside the object. 4. If the loop completes, val is the full FBM value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbmwithimplicitbvh(p, octaves, threshold): """ Computes FBM with early termination based on implicit BVH bounds. Args: p: 3D point position. octaves: List of tuples (amplitude, frequency) for each octave. threshold: The isosurface threshold (typically 0). Returns: The FBM value if fully computed, or the partial value if early terminated. Note: The caller must handle the 'early terminated' state to skip ray marching steps. """ val = 0.0 # Initialize rem as the sum of all amplitudes (worst-case potential of all octaves) rem = sum(a for a, f in octaves) for i, (amplitude, frequency) in enumerate(octaves): # Evaluate base noise at scaled position. # Standard 3D noise function bounded in [-1, 1]. noiseval = noise(p frequency) # Add current octave contribution val += amplitude noiseval # Update remaining bound: remove current amplitude from potential max # The remaining octaves can contribute at most their sum of amplitudes rem -= amplitude # Check if it's impossible to reach the threshold # If val + rem < threshold, even if all remaining noise samples are 1, # the total will be below the threshold. if val + rem < threshold: return val, True # True indicates early termination return val, False # False indicates full computation Parameters: Threshold v: The density threshold defining the object boundary. Default is 0. Object exists where f(\mathbf{p}) > v. Octave count N: The number of noise layers. Higher counts increase complexity and the Lipschitz constant. Amplitude Ai: Typically decreases with octave index (e.g., Ai = A0 \cdot \text{lacunarity}^{-i}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accumulation of val and rem must be done with sufficient precision to avoid false positives in the early termination check, especially when rem is small. Noise Range: The method assumes the base noise function is strictly bounded in [-1, 1]. Gradient Calculation: For sphere tracing step sizes, gradients are still required. If early termination occurs, the gradient is undefined or incomplete. The algorithm must ensure that sphere tracing steps are only taken when the full FBM (or a sufficiently accurate approximation) is available, or use the partial value with caution. This method accelerates the ray marching of implicit surfaces defined by a sum of bounded functions Fn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^n fi(\mathbf{p}) by exploiting the known value ranges of individual terms. It constructs an implicit hierarchy where partial sums serve as bounding volumes for the final sum, allowing early termination when the potential range of the total function excludes the isosurface threshold. It differs from explicit BVH approaches by computing bounds on-the-fly from pre-sorted function ranges rather than traversing a spatial tree structure. A technique to render hypertextures by modulating a smooth main shape function with FBM noise, while preserving the ability to use the implicit BVH and gradient-based sphere tracing optimizations. It defines a smooth base shape function S(\mathbf{p}) (e.g., a sphere or plane) and computes the FBM noise N(\mathbf{p}). Unlike naive hypertexture rendering which might require full evaluation of complex modulated functions, this method keeps the structure compatible with the progressive octave evaluation and gradient-based stepping. Time Complexity: Reduces average evaluation cost per step in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves needed to prove emptiness. In dense regions, the cost remains O(N) as all octaves must be evaluated. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory is required, as no explicit tree structure is stored. The hierarchy is implicit in the evaluation order. Measured Performance: Speedups up to 12-fold on opaque or constant semi-transparent scenes compared to classical sphere tracing, and up to 2-fold on non-constant density volumetric scenes. Gains of up to \times 1.8 are attributed specifically to the progressive octave evaluation. Strengths: Real-time performance on large, detailed scenes; no precomputation or storage overhead; compatible with animated content due to proceduralism. Limitations: Effectiveness depends on the distribution of the noise; if the object is dense and fills most of the scene, early termination opportunities are reduced. The method assumes the base noise is bounded in [-1, 1]. Originating from the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes", this method addresses the high rendering cost of procedural 3D noise in real-time applications. Precomputing volumes is storage-prohibitive for large open worlds and prevents animation. The method leverages the structure of FBM, treating cascaded sums as nested bounding volumes to enable efficient empty space skipping. It is part of a broader effort to accelerate sphere tracing for general Signed Distance Functions (SDF) by combining progressive evaluation with Lipschitz-based stepping. name: Implicit BVH for Sum of Bounded Functions
head: Procedural Bounding Volume Hierarchy
body: This method accelerates the ray marching of implicit surfaces defined by a sum of bounded functions Fn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^n fi(\mathbf{p}) by exploiting the known value ranges of individual terms. It constructs an implicit hierarchy where partial sums serve as bounding volumes for the final sum, allowing early termination when the potential range of the total function excludes the isosurface threshold. It differs from explicit BVH approaches by computing bounds on-the-fly from pre-sorted function ranges rather than traversing a spatial tree structure. Inputs: A set of n scalar functions fi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}, where each fi is bounded within [-\Delta{fi}, \Delta{fi}]. A target threshold value v (typically 0 for isosurfaces). A ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for ray marching. Outputs: The intersection distance t along the ray, or a failure indicator if no intersection exists within the marching bounds. Data Structures: Precomputed Range Sum Array: An array S of size n+1 where S[k] = s(k, n) = \sum{m=k}^{n} \Delta{fm} for k \in [1, n+1], with S[n+1] = 0. Sorted Functions: The functions fi must be sorted such that \Delta{f1} \geq \Delta{f2} \geq \dots \geq \Delta{fn}. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute \Delta{fi} for all i. Sort fi in descending order of \Delta{fi}. Compute the suffix sums s(i+1, n) for all i \in [1, n]. 2. Ray Marching Initialization: Start at t=0 (or ray origin offset). 3. Iteration: For each marching step: a. Evaluate the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Initialize partial sum F{current} = 0 and current index i=1. c. Early Termination Check Loop: While i \leq n: i. Evaluate fi(\mathbf{p}) and update F{current} \leftarrow F{current} + fi(\mathbf{p}). ii. Compute the inclusion interval for the final sum Fn based on the current partial sum: Fn = F{current} \pm s(i+1, n). iii. Check if the threshold v lies outside this interval. If v < F{current} - s(i+1, n) or v > F{current} + s(i+1, n), then no root exists for Fn at this \mathbf{p} in the current direction. Terminate the ray march (return failure). iv. Increment i. d. If the loop completes, Fn(\mathbf{p}) = F{current} is the exact function value. e. Check if |Fn(\mathbf{p}) - v| < \epsilon (convergence). If yes, return t. f. Compute step size h (e.g., using Lipschitz constants if available, or fixed step) and advance t \leftarrow t + h. Formulas: Inclusion Function for Intermediate Sum: F{i+1} = Fi(\mathbf{p}) \pm \Delta{f{i+1}} \quad (4) where \Deltaf is the bound such that f \in [-\Deltaf, \Deltaf]. Sum of Ranges: s(i, j) = \sum{m=i}^{j} \Delta{fm} \quad \text{for } j \geq i. Inclusion Function for Final Sum from Partial Sum: Fn = Fi(\mathbf{p}) \pm s(i+1, n) \quad (6). Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence tolerance for ray marching. Not given in the sources. Step size strategy: Not given in the sources (depends on Lipschitz continuity assumptions in later sections). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unsorted Functions: If functions are not sorted by descending \Delta{fi}, the early termination guarantee is weakened or invalid, potentially leading to incorrect skips or missed intersections. Invalid Bounds: If \Delta{fi} is not a tight bound, the inclusion interval becomes loose, reducing the effectiveness of early termination but maintaining correctness. Lipschitz Continuity: This method assumes only boundedness. If the derivative is not Lipschitz continuous, standard sphere tracing step sizes may be invalid, requiring alternative marching strategies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsumofboundedfunctions(rayorigin, raydirection, functions, deltas, threshold, maxsteps, stepsizefunc): """ functions: list of callable fi(p) deltas: list of float Deltafi, sorted descending threshold: float v """ n = len(functions) # Precompute suffix sums s(i+1, n) # s[k] corresponds to s(k+1, n) for k in 0..n-1 # s[n] = 0 suffixsums = [0.0] (n + 1) currentsum = 0.0 for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): currentsum += deltas[i] suffixsums[i] = currentsum t = 0.0 for step in range(maxsteps): p = rayorigin + t raydirection partialsum = 0.0 earlystop = False for i in range(n): partialsum += functionsi # Inclusion interval for final sum Fn based on partial sum F{i+1} # Fn = partialsum +/- s(i+1, n) # Note: suffixsums[i] is s(i+1, n) because i is 0-indexed # i=0 -> suffixsums[0] = s(1, n) # i=1 -> suffixsums[1] = s(2, n) lowerbound = partialsum - suffixsums[i] upperbound = partialsum + suffixsums[i] if threshold < lowerbound or threshold > upperbound: earlystop = True break if earlystop: return None # No intersection # If loop completes, partialsum is the exact Fn(p) if abs(partialsum - threshold) < 1e-6: return t # Advance ray t += stepsizefunc(partialsum, deltas) # Implementation depends on Lipschitz info return None # Max steps reached Uses derivative bounds to compute safe step sizes. Chosen when functions are differentiable and Lipschitz constants are known. Link: Lipschitz Sphere Tracing. Uses explicit spatial subdivision. Chosen for sparse scenes or when functions have complex spatial locality not captured by range bounds. Link: Octree BVH. Time Complexity: O(n) per ray marching step in the worst case (evaluating all functions). Best case is O(1) if early termination occurs at the first function. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store precomputed range sums and function references. Strengths: No spatial data structure construction overhead; efficient for functions with rapidly decaying ranges (e.g., FBM octaves). Limitations: Requires prior knowledge of tight bounds \Delta{fi}; sorting overhead; less effective if bounds are loose or functions have similar ranges. When to Use: When the implicit function is a sum of many bounded terms with known, decreasing ranges (e.g., procedural noise). When Not to Use: When functions are not bounded or bounds are unknown; when spatial coherence is high and explicit BVH is more efficient. Originated in the context of fast sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise. The method was introduced to exploit the hierarchical nature of FBM (Fractional Brownian Motion) noise, where higher-frequency octaves have smaller amplitudes, allowing them to be treated as bounding volumes for lower-frequency sums. It is used in real-time rendering of procedural landscapes and materials. Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70072, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Lighting and Shading Models
body:
Lighting and Shading Models compute the color of surface points identified by distance-field ray marching by estimating surface normals and applying reflectance models to determine how light interacts with the geometry. This family solves the problem of shading ray-marched geometry without explicit mesh topology, distinguishing itself from Distance Color Blending by calculating geometric lighting contributions (diffuse/specular) rather than relying solely on distance-based color mapping, and from Ray-marched Shadows by focusing on local reflectance properties rather than global occlusion calculations. All methods in this family operate on a surface point \mathbf{p} and its associated geometric data, primarily the surface normal \mathbf{n}. The normal is typically derived from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) using the gradient: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|} where 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) is estimated via finite differences, such as solving a linear system based on values at vertices of a tetrahedron, or via back-propagation. The core shading computation generally follows this structure: 1. Geometric Setup: Determine the view direction \mathbf{v} (from \mathbf{p} to camera) and light direction \mathbf{l} (from \mathbf{p} to light source). 2. Occlusion/Ambient Occlusion: Calculate shadow factors or ambient occlusion values to determine how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from the environment or specific lights. 3. Reflectance Model: Compute the diffuse and specular components based on the angle between \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, and the reflection vector \mathbf{r}. 4. Color Accumulation: Combine the base material color with the lighting contributions, often modulated by depth cueing or atmospheric effects. Enhances depth perception by blending sampled voxel colors with a background color based on distance from the viewer. It solves the foreground/background distinction problem in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff that dims distant objects and shifts their hue, simulating atmospheric haze or aerial perspective. Unlike standard lighting models that compute surface reflectance, this method operates on the accumulated color along the ray, modulating it with depth. Choose it when foreground/background distinction is needed in dense volumetric data without explicit mesh topology. Determines if a surface point is occluded from a light source by performing a sphere trace from the point towards the light. Unlike rasterization-based shadow maps, this method computes occlusion directly from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) of the scene, producing alias-free hard shadows with a single additional traversal per light. It sets itself apart from Soft Shadow Ray Marching by returning a binary occlusion result rather than a continuous penumbra factor, and from Shadow Casting Algorithm by marching from surface points toward lights rather than projecting light through a volumetric dataset. Choose it for alias-free hard shadows directly from SDFs, avoiding rasterization shadow maps. Approximates the darkening of crevices and contact points by sampling the signed distance function (SDF) along the surface normal. It detects occlusion by comparing the actual distance to nearby geometry against the expected distance if the surface were isolated; a smaller actual distance indicates an obstacle is closer, reducing the ambient light contribution. Unlike screen-space methods or shadow maps, this technique requires no separate rendering pass, relying solely on the scene's distance function sampled differently. It is computationally cheaper than full ray-marched shadows but provides a local approximation of global illumination effects. Choose it for computationally cheaper local approximation of global illumination without separate rendering passes. Extends standard distance-field ray marching by iteratively casting new rays upon surface intersection to simulate specular reflections. It solves the problem of rendering mirror-like or glossy surfaces in implicit geometry by continuing the ray path after a hit, rather than terminating at the first surface. It sets itself apart from Distance Color Blending by handling geometric specular bounces rather than volumetric color blending, and from Screen-Space Reflections by operating in 3D space via Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) rather than 2D screen-space depth buffers. Choose it for mirror-like or glossy surfaces in implicit geometry, operating in 3D space rather than screen-space. Renders iridescent surfaces by modulating a cosine-based palette function with a perturbed surface normal, simulating thin-film interference colors, while combining this base color with multi-component specular highlights and directional shadowing. It differs from standard diffuse or simple specular models by generating color variation through geometric perturbation rather than wavelength-dependent physics, and it differs from physically accurate thin-film models by using a computationally cheaper, artistic approximation driven by position and normal noise. Choose it for artistic thin-film interference simulation via geometric perturbation rather than wavelength-dependent physics. Computes eight distinct visualization layers simultaneously in a single forward pass, returning them as a tuple of tensors. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Distance Color Blending or Ray-marched Shadows by decoupling geometric, photometric, and stylistic attributes into parallel outputs rather than combining them into a single RGB image, allowing for flexible post-processing or neural network ingestion. Choose it when decoupling geometric, photometric, and stylistic attributes into parallel outputs is required for post-processing or neural ingestion. Approximates complex lighting environments and specular reflections by decomposing incident radiance into a sum of Spherical Gaussians, which are then rendered as discrete point lights or integrated into a microfacet BRDF model. It solves the problem of efficient relighting in scenes with spatially variant lighting, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), by avoiding the high computational cost of full spherical harmonic integration. Unlike Diffuse Lighting Models which ignore view-dependent effects, SG Shading explicitly models specular highlights and view-dependent reflectance. Choose it for efficient relighting in scenes with spatially variant lighting like NeRFs, avoiding full spherical harmonic integration. A family of techniques used in distance-field ray marching to suppress banding and layering artifacts caused by low step counts or discrete sampling intervals. Unlike standard fixed-step marching which produces visible intensity bands, these methods introduce controlled randomness to the sampling process—either by perturbing the ray's UV coordinates based on hit distance, offsetting the initial depth using a blue noise texture, or jittering the step size itself. This breaks up coherent aliasing patterns while maintaining the sharpness of volumetric features like god rays. Choose it to break up coherent aliasing patterns from low step counts while maintaining sharp volumetric features. Provide a mechanism for users to define arbitrary illumination logic for volume rendering, bypassing standard predefined lighting equations. They solve the problem of rigid lighting constraints by allowing per-voxel or per-surface-point computation of color based on user-defined material properties, geometric data, and environmental factors. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the architectural approach to integration: some methods inject custom logic via API callbacks into a rendering pipeline, while others implement self-contained mathematical models or procedural rules directly within the shading step. Choose it when rigid lighting constraints must be bypassed via API callbacks or self-contained mathematical models. A real-time shading technique for procedural neon city scenes that computes diffuse, specular, ambient occlusion, metallic reflection, and emissive contributions per pixel. It distinguishes itself by integrating a metalness-driven specular model and a Fresnel-weighted metallic reflection term tailored for high-contrast, emissive aesthetics. Choose it for high-contrast, emissive aesthetics with metalness-driven specular and Fresnel-weighted reflections. Calculate the illumination of surfaces by simulating the scattering of light, providing the primary visual cue for surface orientation and shape in ray-marched and rasterized rendering. This family distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Reflections or Iridescent Material with Perturbation by focusing exclusively on non-specular, non-directional reflectance, often serving as the base layer for more complex shading. Choose it as the base layer for non-specular, non-directional reflectance in ray-marched or rasterized rendering. Renders scenes defined by implicit surfaces (Signed Distance Fields) by casting rays from a camera, iteratively marching them to a surface, and shading the hit point using the Blinn-Phong reflectance model. It differs from analytical ray tracing by using iterative distance estimation to handle complex, non-analytic geometry, and it differs from pure SDF rendering by applying a specific local lighting approximation (Blinn-Phong) rather than global illumination or complex material models. Choose it for applying a specific local lighting approximation (Blinn-Phong) to complex, non-analytic geometry via iterative distance estimation. Write a material ID, the distance, and the local coordinate p into global variables whenever an object's distance is smaller than the stored distance. At the end of the rendering process, evaluate the material to get color, roughness, etc., and perform shading. A modern approach offloading meshing and AO to compute shaders to achieve smooth, high-fidelity AO that avoids the rigid look of per-vertex discrete levels. Voxel chunk data is held in a 3D texture, and a compute shader evaluates the local density field within a small spherical kernel (e.g., a 3 	imes 3 	imes 3 or 5 	imes 5 	imes 5 window) around each surface point. If the procedural generation pipeline generates a distance field rather than raw block binaries, short-range cone tracing through the local SDF provides smooth, realistic contact shadows baked directly into the output mesh buffers during the surface extraction pass (such as Marching Cubes or Surface Nets). Kernel window sizes for local density field evaluation are typically 3 	imes 3 	imes 3 or 5 	imes 5 	imes 5. name: Distance Color Blending
head: Depth-Cued Colors, Exponential fog, Intensity Depth-Cuing, Aerial perspective, Chroma-depth, Pseudo chroma-depth
body: Distance Color Blending is a shading technique that enhances depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels and shifting their color toward a background hue, simulating aerial perspective. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear color and intensity falloff based on the sample's distance from the camera. Unlike simple intensity depth-cuing which only reduces brightness, this method modulates the color spectrum (typically adding blue) to exploit the human visual tendency for cool colors to recede. It is distinct from Ambient Occlusion via SDF as it relies on view-dependent distance rather than local geometric curvature, and from Multi-Layer Shading / OmniShader by being a per-sample color modulation rather than a complex multi-pass lighting integration. Inputs: cv: Original voxel color (RGB) at the current sample point. cb: Background color (RGB), typically a shade of blue or gray. dv: Fractional distance of the sample through the volume, normalized to [0, 1]. k{ds}: Magnitude of the blending effect (default 1.0). k{de}: Rate of application (exponent) for the depth falloff (default 0.5). Outputs: cd: Final depth-cued color (RGB). Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond the standard ray-marching state (current position, accumulated color, step size). The fractional depth dv is maintained as a scalar accumulator. Steps: 1. Calculate Fractional Depth: Determine the total length of the ray segment traversing the volume (L{total}) and the current distance traveled from the camera origin (L{current}). Compute dv = L{current} / L{total}. If the total length is zero, set dv = 0. 2. Compute Blending Factor: Calculate the blending weight B using the exponential power function: B = k{ds} \cdot dv^{k{de}} Clamp B to the range [0, 1] to prevent overflow or negative values due to precision errors. 3. Blend Colors: Interpolate between the original voxel color cv and the background color cb using B: cd = (1 - B) cv + B cb 4. Output: Use cd as the color contribution for the current sample in the volume integration loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancecolorblending(cv, cb, dv, kds=1.0, kde=0.5): """ Applies distance color blending to a voxel color. Args: cv: vec3, original voxel color. cb: vec3, background color (e.g., blue or gray). dv: float, fractional distance through volume [0.0, 1.0]. kds: float, magnitude of blending effect. kde: float, exponent for depth falloff. Returns: vec3, the depth-cued color. """ # Calculate blending factor B = kds dv ^ kde # Clamp dv to [0, 1] to handle edge cases where ray extends slightly beyond bounds dvclamped = max(0.0, min(1.0, dv)) # Compute B B = kds (dvclamped kde) # Clamp B to [0, 1] B = max(0.0, min(1.0, B)) # Blend colors: cd = (1 - B) cv + B cb cd = (1.0 - B) cv + B cb return cd Parameters: k{ds}: Controls the size of the color blending effect. Typical value: 1.0. k{de}: Controls the rate of application of color blending. Typical value: 0.5. cb: Background color. If cb is a shade of gray (a, a, a), only intensity depth-cuing (dimming) occurs. If cb is blue-shifted (a, b, c with c > a, b), it introduces a cool shift in distant regions. Example: cb = (0, 0, 0.15). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hard Transfer Functions: This technique avoids the information loss associated with hard transfer functions by modulating existing colors rather than masking them. Precision: Ensure dv is correctly normalized. If the ray does not fully traverse the volume (e.g., clipped by near/far planes), dv should reflect the fraction of the visible segment or the absolute distance relative to a global max depth, depending on implementation. Color Perception: Using a non-gray background color significantly alters the perceived depth. A blue background simulates atmospheric haze, while a gray background only simulates fog density. Exponential Depth Cueing is a shading technique that simulates atmospheric fog to enhance depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff based on normalized depth. Unlike linear cueing, it uses an exponential function to control how rapidly objects recede into darkness, allowing for more natural aerial perspective effects. See Exponential Depth Cueing. A technique to simulate atmospheric attenuation as depth cuing, blending colors of distant objects with the background color to indicate distance. The blending factor s is calculated as: s = \frac{1 + \text{depth} \times z}{1 + z{\max}} where depth is the attenuation parameter, z is the z-value of the fragment, and z{\max} is the maximal z-value in the scene. The final color intensity I is modified to: sI + (1 - s)I{bg} where I is the original intensity and I{bg} is the background color intensity. This method is simpler but less perceptually accurate than exponential variants for large depth ranges. A color modification technique based on the eye's lens refracting colored light at different angles to enhance depth perception in angiography images. It assigns reddish tones to closer objects and blueish tones to further ones, leveraging the chromatic aberration of the human eye. Time and Memory Complexity: The time complexity of the blending calculation is O(1) per sample, as it involves only basic arithmetic operations (power, multiplication, addition). The memory complexity is O(1) as no additional buffers are required beyond the standard ray-marching state. Measured Performance: Performance is independent of the number of light sources and geometry complexity, depending only on the resolution of the input image or the number of volume samples. It is highly efficient and suitable for real-time rendering. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enhances depth perception significantly with minimal computational cost; avoids the "flat" look of un-cued volumes. Limitations: It is an empirical approximation and does not simulate true physical light scattering (participating media). The effect is view-dependent and may not accurately represent the physical density of the volume. When to Use: Use when depth perception is critical and computational resources are limited, or when a stylized "aerial perspective" look is desired. When Not to Use: Do not use when physically accurate light transport (e.g., volumetric shadows, scattering) is required, as this method only modulates color and intensity. Distance Color Blending is an extension of intensity depth-cuing, a technique documented by Segal and Akeley in the specification of the first version of OpenGL. It was adapted for volume rendering by Interrante et al. to enhance the perception of depth in medical and scientific visualization. The method relies on the artistic principle of aerial perspective, where distant objects appear cooler and less saturated, a technique used by painters for centuries. It is commonly used in medical imaging (e.g., OCT, CT) to distinguish overlapping structures. name: Exponential Depth Cueing
head: Fog Depth Cueing
body: Exponential Depth Cueing is a shading technique that simulates atmospheric fog to enhance depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff based on normalized depth. Unlike linear cueing, it uses an exponential function to control how rapidly objects recede into darkness, allowing for more natural aerial perspective effects. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: frontfactor (fog transparency at the front plane), density (fog density parameter), and depth (normalized distance of the voxel from the viewer). Outputs: A transparency factor T used to modulate the voxel's color components. Data Structures: The method relies on scalar parameters and a single computed transparency value. No complex data structures are required beyond the standard volume rendering context. Steps: 1. Enable depth cueing in the rendering context. 2. Set the depth cueing parameters (frontfactor and density). 3. For each voxel or sample point along the ray: a. Determine the normalized depth value (0 at front, 1 at back). b. Calculate T using the formula below. c. Multiply the voxel's color components by T. Formula: The fog transparency T is calculated as: T = \text{front\factor} \times \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{depth}) where T is fog transparency, depth is 0 at the front plane and 1 at the back plane, and each voxel color component is multiplied by T during rendering. Parameters: frontfactor: Transparency of the fog at the front plane. Must be positive. Usually < 1.0. Larger values brighten the foreground. density: Controls the fog density, determining how rapidly objects recede into darkness. depth: Normalized depth value, where 0 is at the front plane of the viewing volume and 1 is at the back plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter Constraints: frontfactor must be positive. Boundaries: depth must be strictly normalized between 0 and 1 as defined by the viewing volume planes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def exponentialdepthcueing(frontfactor: float, density: float, depth: float) -> float: """Calculate fog transparency for exponential depth cueing.""" return frontfactor math.exp(-density depth) def applycueingtovoxel(color: tuple, frontfactor: float, density: float, depth: float) -> tuple: """Multiply each voxel color component by the fog transparency.""" T = exponentialdepthcueing(frontfactor, density, depth) return (color[0] T, color[1] T, color[2] T) An efficient ray marching algorithm designed to accurately generate spatial-temporal points for deformable tissue reconstruction, balancing rendering speed and reconstruction quality. It outperforms the Depth-Cueing method in PSNR (33.374 vs 31.325) and SSIM (0.907 vs 0.897) on the EndoNeRF dataset, while maintaining competitive inference speed (1.73 fps vs 1.95 fps). The Depth-Cueing method suffers from suboptimal performance due to reliance on noisy and incomplete stereo depth data and is inapplicable for temporal interpolation due to the absence of stereo depth in certain contexts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Comparative data for the "Depth-Cueing" method on the EndoNeRF dataset shows a test speed of 1.95 fps, PSNR of 31.325, SSIM of 0.897, and LPIPS of 0.132. Strengths: Introduces black "fog" to make distant voxels appear darker than close ones, aiding foreground/background distinction. Limitations: Relies on noisy and incomplete stereo depth data, and is inapplicable for temporal interpolation due to the absence of stereo depth in certain contexts. When to Use: When distinguishing foreground objects from background objects in volumetric data. When Not to Use: In dynamic scenes requiring temporal interpolation or when stereo depth data is noisy/incomplete. Exponential Depth Cueing was introduced as part of the VolPack volume rendering library. It is designed to introduce black "fog" to make distant voxels appear darker than close ones, thereby aiding in the distinction of foreground objects from background objects. The technique is implemented via specific API calls (vpEnable and vpSetDepthCueing) within the VolPack context. name: Linear Depth Cueing
head: Atmospheric Attenuation Depth Cuing, Color attenuation, Depth-based Attenuation, depth cuing
body: Linear Depth Cueing is a technique to simulate atmospheric attenuation by blending the colors of distant objects with a background color to indicate distance and enhance depth perception. It differs from Exponential Depth Cueing by using a linear interpolation factor based on depth rather than an exponential decay function. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Original color intensity I, background color intensity I{bg}, current fragment depth z, maximum scene depth z{\max}, and a depth cueing parameter depth. Outputs: Modified color intensity I'. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar values for depth and color components. The implementation relies on computing a scalar blending factor s. Steps: 1. Determine the maximum depth z{\max} for the scene. 2. For each fragment at depth z, calculate the blending factor s using the linear formula: s = \frac{1 + \text{depth} \times z}{1 + z{\max}} 3. Compute the final color intensity I' by blending the original intensity I with the background intensity I{bg} using s: I' = sI + (1 - s)I{bg} 4. Optionally apply desaturation (reduce saturation while maintaining hue and brightness) or darkening (reduce brightness while maintaining hue and saturation), or combine both methods. Parameters: depth: A non-zero argument specifying whether depth cuing is used; if zero, attenuation is not applied. Typical values observed in examples include 0.3. z{\max}: The maximal z-value in the scene, computed by the rendering code. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If depth is zero, attenuation is explicitly disabled per the source specification. Applying the formula blindly would yield s = \frac{1}{1 + z{\max}}, which does not represent the intended "no cueing" state. Precision issues may arise if z{\max} is very large or very small relative to z and depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lineardepthcueing(I, Ibg, z, zmax, depthparam): """ Applies linear depth cueing to a color intensity. Args: I: Original color intensity (scalar or vector). Ibg: Background color intensity. z: Current fragment depth. zmax: Maximum depth in the scene. depthparam: Depth cueing strength parameter. Returns: Modified color intensity. """ # If depthparam is zero, no cueing is applied if depthparam == 0: return I # Calculate blending factor s s = (1 + depthparam z) / (1 + zmax) # Blend original intensity with background intensity Iprime = s I + (1 - s) Ibg return Iprime Uses an exponential function for non-linear depth progression, offering different visual characteristics than linear blending. See Exponential Depth Cueing. Time Complexity: The time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The memory complexity is not given in the sources. Strengths: The method is simple to implement and effectively simulates atmospheric haze or fog to enhance depth perception. Limitations: The limitations are not given in the sources. When to use: It should be used when a simple, computationally inexpensive method is needed to enhance depth perception in volume or surface rendering. When not to use: The conditions for not using it are not given in the sources. Linear Depth Cueing was introduced in the context of computing and displaying isosurfaces in R, specifically for visualizing elevation data such as the Maunga Whau volcano. It is also discussed in the context of dense geometric flow visualization, where it is combined with desaturation and darkening techniques to enhance depth perception in vector field data.
