name: Multi-Layer Shading / OmniShader
head: OmniShader
body: Multi-Layer Shading (OmniShader) computes eight distinct visualization layers simultaneously in a single forward pass, returning them as a tuple of tensors. It decouples geometric, photometric, and stylistic attributes into parallel outputs rather than combining them into a single RGB image, allowing for flexible post-processing or neural network ingestion. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes ray directions, surface coordinates, surface normals, surface distances, pixel frames, camera orientation, a cyclic colormap, a degree parameter, and a decay factor as inputs. It outputs a tuple of eight tensors: (lambertianlayer, distancelayer, proximitylayer, vignettelayer, normallayer, laplacianlayer, tangentlayer, spinlayer). Data Structures: The implementation relies on tensor operations, such as cyclic shifting. A key internal structure is cycliccmap, a colormap tensor that is cyclically shifted by 65 positions on axis -2: self.cycliccmap = self.cycliccmap.roll(65, -2). Parameters: decayfactor: A float, default 0.01, used in the distance shading calculation. degree: An integer parameter used in tangent and spin shading calculations. Steps: 1. Compute Surface Normals: Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the intersection point \mathbf{p} using the gradient of the Signed Distance Function (SDF) f. This is done by solving a linear system derived from finite differences at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron centered at 0, or via back-propagation. 2. Compute Surface Laplacian: Estimate the Laplacian \Delta f at \mathbf{p} using the same tetrahedral samples used for the normal. The formula is: (\Delta f)(p) \approx \frac{6}{\epsilon^2} \left( f(p) - \frac{1}{4}\sum{i=0}^3f(p+\epsilon vi) \right) where \epsilon is a small constant and vi are the tetrahedron vertices. 3. Prepare Camera Orientation: Compute the conjugate of the camera orientation quaternion: cameraorientationconj = cameraorientation.conjugate()[..., None, None,:]. 4. Compute Lambertian Layer: Apply the Lambertian shader to ray directions and surface normals. 5. Compute Distance Layer: Apply the distance shader to pixel coordinates, surface coordinates, and the decayfactor. 6. Compute Proximity Layer: Apply the proximity shader to surface distances. 7. Compute Vignette Layer: Apply the vignette shader to ray directions and pixel frames. 8. Compute Normal Layer: Apply the normal shader to surface normals. The normals \mathbf{n}=(x,y,z) are typically mapped to RGB using absolute values: (\lvert x \rvert, \lvert y \rvert, \lvert z \rvert). 9. Compute Laplacian Layer: Apply the Laplacian shader to the computed surface Laplacian values, normalizing them between 0 and 1 and applying gamma correction. 10. Compute Tangent Layer: Apply the tangent shader using cameraorientationconj, ray directions, surface normals, the shifted cycliccmap, and degree. 11. Compute Spin Layer: Apply the spin shader using cameraorientationconj, surface normals, the shifted cycliccmap, and degree. 12. Return: Return the tuple of all eight layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multilayershading(raydirections, surfacenormals, surfacecoords, surfacedistances, pixelframes, cameraorientation, cycliccmap, degree, decayfactor, surfacelaplacian, pxcoords): # 1. Prepare camera orientation conjugate cameraorientationconj = cameraorientation.conjugate()[..., None, None,:] # 2. Shift cyclic colormap shiftedcmap = cycliccmap.roll(65, -2) # 3. Compute layers (exact shading formulas not provided in sources) lambertianlayer = raydirections surfacenormals distancelayer = pxcoords surfacecoords decayfactor proximitylayer = surfacedistances vignettelayer = raydirections pixelframes normallayer = surfacenormals.abs() laplacianlayer = surfacelaplacian.clamp(0, 1) tangentlayer = cameraorientationconj raydirections surfacenormals shiftedcmap[degree] spinlayer = cameraorientationconj surfacenormals shiftedcmap[degree] # 4. Return all layers as a tuple return (lambertianlayer, distancelayer, proximitylayer, vignettelayer, normallayer, laplacianlayer, tangentlayer, spinlayer) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The Laplacian and Normal calculations rely on finite differences with a small constant \epsilon. Boundary Conditions: The distance and proximity shaders may behave unpredictably at the exact start or end of the ray march if not clamped. Quaternion Conjugate: Incorrect handling of quaternion conjugation can lead to misaligned tangent and spin layers. This variant involves a check within the forward pass to determine if the shading model is a "two-stage renderer". It verifies if the optimization configuration opt.arch.shading.model is set to either "MLPFeaTwoStage22" or "MLPFeaTwoStage13". If true, specific optimization flags are set. Time and Memory Complexity: The method performs a single forward pass to compute all eight layers, which is computationally efficient compared to running eight separate render passes. However, it requires memory to store eight output tensors simultaneously. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High efficiency due to single-pass computation; flexible output for downstream tasks (e.g., neural networks, post-processing). Limitations: Requires all input data (normals, Laplacian, etc.) to be available or computed in the same pass, which may increase intermediate memory usage. When to Use: Use when you need multiple visualization attributes (normals, depth, curvature, etc.) for the same scene geometry without the overhead of multiple render passes. The method originates from a ray marching visualization toolkit that implements various ray marching techniques. It is used in contexts requiring detailed geometric and photometric analysis of ray-marched scenes, such as in neural rendering pipelines or advanced visualization tools. kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, https://github.com/Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Dither
head: UV Dithering, Distance-based UV Perturbation
body: Ray Marching Dither is a technique to reduce banding artifacts in ray marching by perturbing the UV coordinates based on the ray distance. It sets itself apart from Ray Marching Jittering by applying perturbation to the UV coordinates rather than the step size, and from Distance Color Blending by focusing on geometric sampling stability rather than color interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current UV coordinates (uv), ray distance (t), dithering strength factor (cfDither), and a pseudo-random number generator function (rand). Output: Perturbed UV coordinates. Data Structures: uv: vec2 representing the current UV coordinate. t: float representing the ray distance (hit distance). cfDither: float parameter controlling dithering intensity. Steps: 1. Calculate the dither amount based on the squared ray distance and the strength factor: \text{dither} = t^2 \cdot c\fDither 2. Generate two random values using the rand function with specific offsets derived from the original UV coordinates: rx = \text{rand}(uv + \text{vec2}(0.12, 0.32)) ry = \text{rand}(uv + \text{vec2}(0.42, 0.52)) 3. Perturb the UV coordinates by adding the random value scaled by the dither amount, then subtracting half the dither amount to center the perturbation: uv.x += rx \cdot \text{dither} - \frac{\text{dither}}{2.0} uv.y += ry \cdot \text{dither} - \frac{\text{dither}}{2.0} 4. Reconstruct the ray origin and direction from the perturbed UVs to continue the ray march. Parameters: cfDither: Dithering strength factor. Typical value: 0.001. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchingdither(uv, t, cfDither, randfunc): # Step 1: Calculate dither amount dither = t t cfDither # Step 2: Generate random values with specific offsets offsetx = vec2(0.12, 0.32) offsety = vec2(0.42, 0.52) rx = randfunc(uv + offsetx) ry = randfunc(uv + offsety) # Step 3: Perturb UVs uv.x += rx dither - dither / 2.0 uv.y += ry dither - dither / 2.0 # Step 4: Return perturbed UVs return uv Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For very large t, t^2 may cause floating-point precision issues or overflow. Boundary Conditions: If uv is near texture boundaries, perturbation might sample outside valid ranges. Determinism: The rand function must be deterministic for the same input uv to avoid flickering if not intended. Blue Noise Dithering is a technique to reduce visible banding artifacts in volumetric ray marching by introducing a random offset to the ray step start position, derived from a blue noise texture, allowing for larger step sizes without quality loss. Ray Marching Jittering is a technique to reduce aliasing artifacts, specifically banding, in volume rendering by introducing random variation to the ray marching step size. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel per step, as it involves simple arithmetic and a random function call. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional data structures required. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective at reducing visible banding artifacts in ray marching. Limitations: May introduce slight blurring or noise if the dither strength is too high. Not suitable for all types of artifacts (e.g., step-size related aliasing is better handled by Ray Marching Jittering). When to Use: When banding artifacts are visible due to fixed step sizes or quantization in UV space. When Not to Use: When high precision is required without any perturbation, or when step-size aliasing is the primary issue. It is a technique used to improve the visual quality of ray-marched scenes by mitigating banding. The implementation details are documented in practical WebGL ray marching examples. nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, https://github.com/nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Blue Noise Dithering
head: Blue Noise Dithering for Raymarching, Blue Noise Ray Offset, Temporal Blue Noise Dithering
body: Blue Noise Dithering is a technique to reduce visible banding artifacts in volumetric ray marching by introducing a random offset to the ray step start position, derived from a blue noise texture, allowing for larger step sizes without quality loss. It sets itself apart from Ray Marching Jittering by using a structured blue noise pattern, which has fewer clumps than other noises and is less visible to the human eye, and from its parent Ray Marching Dither by specifically targeting the initialization offset of the ray march loop to enable significant performance gains through increased step sizes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: uBlueNoise (2D sampler texture), frame (integer), rayOrigin (vec3), rayDir (vec3), STEPSIZE (float, alias MARCHSIZE in), NUMSTEPS (integer), and fragCoord (vec2). Outputs: The computed initial march distance t and the loop structure for the raymarching routine. Data Structures: Blue Noise Texture: A 2D texture (typically 1024×1024) where the red channel contains values in the range 0, 1). Parameters: Typical Values: NUMSTEPS is reduced from 250 to 50, and STEPSIZE is increased from 0.05 to 0.5 in optimized implementations. This configuration reduces total iterations from 5000 to 100 while maintaining similar output quality. Temporal Shift: The frame-dependent shift uses frame % 32 divided by sqrt(0.5). Numbered Steps: 1. Sample Blue Noise: Sample the blue noise texture at normalized fragment coordinates fragCoord / 1024.0 and extract the red channel value. 2. Calculate Temporal Offset: Add a frame-dependent shift to the sampled blue noise value to ensure temporal variation. The shift is calculated as frame % 32 divided by sqrt(0.5). 3. Compute Final Offset: Apply the fractional part function to the sum of the blue noise value and the temporal shift to keep the result in the range [0, 1). This value serves as the [dithering offset. 4. Initialize Ray Distance: Calculate the initial ray march distance t by multiplying the STEPSIZE by the computed offset. 5. Execute Ray Marching Loop: Iterate NUMSTEPS times. In each iteration, calculate the sample position using rayOrigin + rayDir t and advance t by STEPSIZE. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fract(x): return x - math.floor(x) def bluenoisedithering(rayOrigin, rayDir, uBlueNoise, frame, STEPSIZE, NUMSTEPS, fragCoord): # Step 1: Sample blue noise texture at normalized fragment coordinates uv = fragCoord / 1024.0 blueNoise = uBlueNoise[uv] # Returns float in 0, 1) # Step 2 & 3: Calculate temporal offset and apply fract temporalShift = (frame % 32) / math.sqrt(0.5) offset = fract(blueNoise + temporalShift) # Step 4: Initialize ray distance t = STEPSIZE offset # Step 5: Execute ray marching loop for i in range(NUMSTEPS): samplePos = rayOrigin + rayDir t # Volume sampling and shading logic would occur here t += STEPSIZE return offset, t Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noticeable Pattern: The dithering pattern can be noticeable in single frames if only spatial noise is used. This is mitigated by adding the temporal component based on the frame count. Banding Artifacts: Visible banding occurs if the step size is increased without dithering. The blue noise offset resolves this by distributing the sampling error. Precision: The use of fract ensures the offset remains bounded, preventing the ray from starting outside the intended volume or causing negative distances. Spatial Blue Noise Dithering: Uses only the spatial blue noise texture without temporal variation. Suitable for static scenes or when [frame coherence is not required. Temporal Blue Noise Dithering: Adds a frame-dependent shift to the blue noise value. Recommended for animated scenes to prevent static pattern visibility. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In the cited implementation, reducing iterations from 5000 to 100 (by increasing step size from 0.05 to 0.5 and steps from 250 to 50) resulted in a significant performance improvement while maintaining similar output quality. Strengths: Allows for larger step sizes, reducing the number of samples needed per ray. Limitations: The dithering pattern may be visible in single frames without temporal variation. Requires a pre-generated blue noise texture. When to Use: When ray marching volumetric effects (clouds, fog, light shafts) and performance is a concern, and banding artifacts are visible with standard step sizes. When Not to Use: When high-quality single-frame stills are required without temporal averaging, or when the blue noise texture is not available. The technique is described in blog posts on real-time volumetric rendering. It leverages a blue noise pattern to obtain a random number for each fragment shader run, introducing an offset at the beginning of the raymarched loop to erase layering effects. Real-time dreamy Cloudscapes with Volumetric Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/real-time-cloudscapes-with-volumetric-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) On Shaping Light: Real-Time Volumetric Lighting with Post-Processing..., https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/shaping-light-volumetric-lighting-with-post-processing-and-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Jittering
head: Dithering Offset, Jittered Ray Marching, Randomized Step Size Ray Marching
body: Ray Marching Jittering is a technique to reduce aliasing artifacts, specifically banding, in volume rendering by introducing random variation to the ray marching step size. It solves the problem of clearly defined intensity bands caused by fixed step sizes in participating media. Unlike fixed stepping, which causes banding, jittering removes these artifacts while keeping features like god rays sharp and focused. Inputs: stepSize: The fixed base step size for ray marching. dithering: A scalar parameter controlling the magnitude of jitter (typically > 0.0). vtexcoord: The texture coordinate or ray origin parameter used for hashing. tMin: The starting distance along the ray. Outputs: tStart: The perturbed starting distance for the ray march. Data Structures: The method requires only scalar parameters and a deterministic hash function. Steps: 1. Calculate a jitter offset based on the texture coordinate and dithering strength. 2. Determine the start time for the ray march by adding the jitter offset to the minimum distance. 3. March the ray using a step size that varies randomly between 0.5 \times \text{stepSize} and 1.5 \times \text{stepSize}. Formulas: The jitter offset is calculated as: \text{jitter} = \begin{cases} \text{hash}(\text{v\tex\coord}) \times \text{stepSize} \times \text{dithering} & \text{if } \text{dithering} > 0.0 \\ 0.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The start time is: t{\text{Start}} = t{\text{Min}} + \text{jitter} The step size for each march is a random value s such that: s \in [0.5 \times \text{stepSize}, 1.5 \times \text{stepSize}] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deterministichash(v): # Standard deterministic hash returning a float in [0.0, 1.0) h = 0 for c in v: h = (h 31 + int(c 1000)) & 0xFFFFFFFF return (h & 0x7FFFFFFF) / 0x7FFFFFFF def calculatejitteredstart(tmin, stepsize, dithering, vtexcoord): """Calculate the jittered start position for ray marching.""" if dithering > 0.0: hashvalue = deterministichash(vtexcoord) jitter = hashvalue stepsize dithering tstart = tmin + jitter else: tstart = tmin return tstart def marchwithjitteredstep(stepsize, vtexcoord, tstart): """Perform a single ray march step with jittered size.""" hashvalue = deterministichash(vtexcoord) stepvariation = 0.5 + 1.0 hashvalue # Range [0.5, 1.5] currentstep = stepsize stepvariation return tstart + currentstep Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed step sizes introduce aliasing in the form of clearly defined bands of intensity in the volume region. Without dithering, adapting step sizes for performance can cause juddering. A rendering technique using dithering without temporal accumulation (TAA) to break up slicing artifacts from undersampling, ensuring stability in VR where HMD movement causes smearing in TAA. It adapts the raymarch step size based on varying performance conditions to maintain frame targets. Adapted step counts can vary by a factor of 4; without dithering, this causes juddering, but with dithering, the image remains stable with only small noise. In tested scenarios (Smoke Rings, Dust Devil, Wall of Fire), raymarch stage times were 3.69ms, 4.77ms, and 3.82ms respectively. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In VR scenarios using an NVIDIA RTX 3080 and Valve Index HMD at 2016 x 2240 x 2 resolution, raymarch stage times were 3.69ms (Smoke Rings), 4.77ms (Dust Devil), and 3.82ms (Wall of Fire). Total frame times were around 9.6-9.7ms. Scaling: Adaptive dithering allows step counts to vary by a factor of 4 to meet frame targets without visual artifacts like juddering. Strengths and Limitations: Removes banding while keeping god rays sharp and focused. Provides temporally stable images in VR without the smearing artifacts associated with TAA. Introduces a small amount of noise. When to use it and when not: Use when rendering volumes with fixed step sizes that exhibit banding artifacts, especially in VR where TAA is problematic. Originating from techniques to handle aliasing in ray marching through participating media, jittering was identified as a solution to banding in underwater scene rendering. Adaptive dithering was later developed for real-time volumetric lighting in VR to avoid TAA smearing. xwghua/clearvolume-plus, https://github.com/xwghua/clearvolume-plus, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) CS348b Final Project - Rendering Underwater Scenes, http://www.graphics.stanford.edu/courses/cs348b-competition/cs348b-04/underwater/index.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Ignis: Eulerian Fluid Simulation and Rendering at VR Frame Rates, https://doi.org/10.1145/3610542.3626120, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Custom Shading Models
head: Custom Shading Routines, Per-voxel Shading Callbacks
body:
Custom Shading Models provide a framework for defining arbitrary illumination calculations within volume rendering and ray-marching pipelines, allowing developers to replace standard analytic lighting with user-defined logic. This family enables the implementation of specialized effects such as physically based microfacet reflections, directional occlusion, and color-space-specific glow, which are not covered by generic diffuse or specular models. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Distance Color Blending by operating on explicit geometric data (normals, positions) rather than raw scalar field values, and from Ambient Occlusion via SDF by allowing full directional light integration rather than just ambient darkening. All methods in this family operate on a surface point \mathbf{p} and its associated geometric data, primarily the surface normal \mathbf{n}. The normal is typically derived from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) using the gradient: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|} where 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) is estimated via finite differences, such as solving a linear system based on values at vertices of a tetrahedron, or via back-propagation. The core shading computation generally follows this structure: 1. Geometric Setup: Determine the view direction \mathbf{v} (from \mathbf{p} to camera) and light direction \mathbf{l} (from \mathbf{p} to light source). 2. Occlusion/Ambient Occlusion: Calculate shadow factors or ambient occlusion values to determine how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from the environment or specific lights. 3. Reflectance Model: Compute the diffuse and specular components based on the angle between \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, and the reflection vector \mathbf{r}. 4. Color Accumulation: Combine the base material color with the lighting contributions, often modulated by depth cueing or atmospheric effects. The GGX Microfacet BRDF is a specular reflection model that approximates surface roughness using the Gaussian distribution of microfacet normals (GGX) combined with the Schlick Fresnel approximation and a Smith geometry function. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Blinn-Phong with Metallic Reflections, by providing physically plausible energy conservation and accurate specular highlights for rough surfaces, whereas Blinn-Phong is an empirical approximation. It serves as the standard for high-quality specular shading in real-time engines and voxel renderers. This method applies lighting (diffuse, specular, and ambient) to a face color based on the surface normal and light direction. It is designed for SDF-based rendering where the "face" represents a discretized surface element. It differs from general volume shading by operating directly on the extracted face geometry's color and alpha, using a simplified analytic lighting model rather than full ray-marched integration. A custom shading model for ray-marched signed distance fields that extends the classic Blinn-Phong approximation with environment reflections and emissive contributions to simulate urban night scenes. It distinguishes itself from standard Blinn-Phong by modulating specular intensity, power, and reflection weight based on a material's metallic property, and from GGX microfacet models by using a simplified Schlick-like Fresnel term rather than a full microfacet distribution. Multidirectional Occlusion Shading (M-DOS) is a direct volume rendering technique that simulates directional light scattering to produce realistic soft-shadowing and depth cues. Unlike the original MS-DOS model, which constrains the light direction to the viewing direction and uses symmetric disc-shaped Gaussian kernels, M-DOS allows arbitrary light positioning within the hemisphere defined by the view vector by using elliptical footprints derived from a tilted cone. It achieves this through incremental convolution of an opacity buffer, requiring no precomputation and maintaining interactive frame rates. HQS1R is a high-quality point cloud rendering method that reduces aliasing by blending overlapping points together, similar to mipmapping. It is a simplified, compute-based implementation of the blending algorithm from [BHZK05], designed to be faster than aliased GLPOINTS results while providing anti-aliasing. Unlike surface splatting [ZPVG01], it blends overlapping points without considering oriented disks with variable radii. It sets itself apart from the Single-Atomic High-Quality Robust Variant (HQS1R) by using a robust overflow protection mechanism that prevents artifacts when more than 255 points contribute to a pixel. This method performs volume raycasting illumination in the YUV color space to decouple luminance from chrominance, allowing for independent control of brightness and color. It differs from standard RGB shading by computing lighting effects (such as specular highlights and glow) primarily on the luminance channel, while interpolating color channels based on a technique-derived factor. This approach is particularly useful for capturing indirect illumination independently of the transfer function. Tangent Space Shading is a gradient-less lighting technique that approximates the diffuse lighting component of the Phong shading model without computing explicit gradients for every texel. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GGX Microfacet BRDF and Light Evaluation for SDF Faces by its reliance on rendering artifacts (double-pass texture coordinate offsets) rather than geometric derivatives to simulate surface orientation. Voxel-Specific Shading Pipelines are a family of rendering techniques designed to compute illumination for data stored in discrete 3D grids (voxels). Unlike continuous surface shading which operates on smooth Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or triangle meshes, these methods operate on the discrete topology of voxel cells, handling both surface-like boundaries and volumetric density. The family encompasses approaches ranging from per-voxel geometric shading with hard shadows to CPU-based palette index manipulation and dedicated volumetric ray-marching shaders for fluid simulations. Definition: A procedural surface shader for roads that differentiates between asphalt, curb/shoulder, and terrain based on lateral distance to the road centerline, including emissive lane markings. Steps: 1. Calculate d = p.x - 	ext{roadX}(p.z) and ad = |d|. 2. If ad < 	ext{ROAD\HALF\WIDTH}: set albedo to dark gray, metal to 0.35, emissive to 0.0. Calculate lane lines using smoothstep for edge lines, center line, and dashed separators. Add emissive cyan color for lines. 3. Else if ad < 	ext{ROAD\HALF\WIDTH} + 	ext{SHOULDER}: set albedo to dark gray, metal to 0.1, emissive to magenta strip at road edge. 4. Else: set albedo to very dark, metal to 0.0, emissive to 0.0. Parameters: Asphalt metal: 0.35 (wet-look). Lane line color: 	ext{vec3}(0.15, 1.0, 1.1) 	imes 1.3. Edge line offset: 	ext{ROAD\HALF\WIDTH} - 0.3. Center line offset: 0.18. Dashed line frequency: p.z 	imes 0.18. Steps: 1. Divide each triangle into four subtriangles by splitting each edge in the middle. 2. Apply either Gouraud or Phong shading algorithm to the sub-triangles. 3. This process can be iterated several times. The smooth argument specifies one plus the number of times to divide the triangles. Parameters: smooth: integer specifying one plus the number of subdivision iterations. smooth=1 means no subdivision. Pitfalls: Using too high a level of smooth can cause rendering quality to deteriorate due to artifacts from polygon filling, exacerbated on devices using anti-aliasing. The concept of custom shading in volume rendering originated with early libraries like VolPack, which introduced the vpSetCallback mechanism allowing users to define per-voxel shading routines instead of relying on fixed lookup tables. This allowed for arbitrary color transfer functions and lighting models but noted potential performance degradation. The family has since expanded to include physically based rendering models like GGX [3715-ggx-microfacet-brdf.md], specialized techniques for point clouds like HQS1R [10218-single-atomic-high-quality-robust-variant-hqs1r.md], and color-space specific methods like YUV shading [11187-yuv-color-space-shading-with-glow.md]. The family also encompasses discrete voxel-specific pipelines [17027-voxel-specific-shading-pipelines.md] and procedural surface shaders for specific domains like road rendering. name: GGX Microfacet BRDF
head: GGX BRDF, GGX Microfacet BRDF Model, GGX Microfacet Model, GGX Microfacet Specular Model, GGX Shading, Walter et al. Specular
body: The GGX Microfacet BRDF models specular reflection by assuming the surface consists of microscopic facets with normals distributed according to the Generalized Trowbridge-Reiss (GGX) distribution. It serves as a physically-based material model for realistic metal and plastic surfaces. It builds on Custom Shading Models by decomposing surface reflection into diffuse and specular microfacet components parameterized by diffuse albedo Kd, specular albedo Ks, and roughness \rho. Inputs and Outputs: Surface normal \mathbf{n} (unit vector). View direction \mathbf{v} (unit vector, from surface to camera). Light direction \mathbf{l} (unit vector, from surface to light). Roughness \rho (scalar, typically [0, 1]). Diffuse albedo Kd (RGB vector). Specular albedo Ks (RGB vector, often derived from F0 for metals). Outputs: Diffuse BRDF fd, specular BRDF fs, and total reflected radiance L = fd + fs. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The computation relies on scalar and vector arithmetic. Parameters: \rho: Roughness. Typical values range from 0.0 (smooth) to 1.0 (rough). F0: Specular reflectance at normal incidence. A typical value is 0.14. Kd: Diffuse albedo. Ks: Specular albedo at normal incidence. Steps and Formulas: 1. Compute Half Vector: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}}{\|\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}\|} If \mathbf{v} \approx -\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{h} is undefined; use \mathbf{n} or a default reflection vector. 2. Compute Dot Products: \muv = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}, 0.0) \mul = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0.0) \muh = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0) \mu{lh} = \max(\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0) 3. Compute Alpha: \alpha = \rho^2 4. Compute Normal Distribution Function (D): The GGX distribution describes the probability density of microfacet normals. D(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{h}) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi \left( (\alpha^2 - 1)\muh^2 + 1 \right)^2} 5. Compute Geometry Function (G): The Smith geometry function is standard. k = \frac{(\rho + 1)^2}{8} G1(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \alpha) = \frac{\muv}{\max(\muv(1 - k) + k, \epsilon)} G2(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = G1(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \alpha) \cdot G1(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, \alpha) 6. Compute Fresnel Function (F): The Schlick approximation is standard. F(F0, \mu{lh}) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - \mu{lh})^5 For variable specular albedo Ks, the reflectance at grazing angles is computed as: F{90}(Ks) = \min\left(\frac{\text{lum}(Ks)}{0.04}, 1.0\right) \text{lum}(C) = 0.213 Cr + 0.715 Cg + 0.072 Cb F(Ks, \mu{lh}) = Ks + (F{90}(Ks) - Ks)(1 - \mu{lh})^5 7. Compute Specular BRDF: fs(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = \frac{D(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{h}) G2(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) F(Ks, \mu{lh})}{4 \muv \mul} 8. Compute Diffuse BRDF: fd(Kd) = \frac{Kd}{\pi} 9. Combine: fr(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = fd(Kd) + fs(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Epsilon values (e.g., 10^{-6}) are added to the denominator of D and the specular term to prevent division by zero. The denominator 4 \muv \mul requires a guard (e.g., 10^{-4}) when the view or light direction is nearly parallel to the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ggxmicrofacetbrdf(n, v, l, roughness, kd, ks): # 1. Half vector h = v + l hlen = math.sqrt(h[0]2 + h[1]2 + h[2]2) if hlen < 1e-6: h = n # Fallback for antiparallel v and l else: h = (h[0]/hlen, h[1]/hlen, h[2]/hlen) # 2. Dot products nv = max(n[0]v[0] + n[1]v[1] + n[2]v[2], 0.0) nl = max(n[0]l[0] + n[1]l[1] + n[2]l[2], 0.0) nh = max(n[0]h[0] + n[1]h[1] + n[2]h[2], 0.0) lh = max(l[0]h[0] + l[1]h[1] + l[2]h[2], 0.0) # 3. Alpha alpha = roughness roughness alpha2 = alpha alpha # 4. D (GGX) denom = (alpha2 - 1.0) (nh nh) + 1.0 D = alpha2 / (math.pi denom denom + 1e-6) # 5. G (Smith Geometry) k = ((roughness + 1.0) 2) / 8.0 g1v = nv / max(nv (1.0 - k) + k, 1e-6) g1l = nl / max(nl (1.0 - k) + k, 1e-6) G = g1v g1l # 6. F (Schlick) lumks = 0.213 ks[0] + 0.715 ks[1] + 0.072 ks[2] f90 = min(lumks / 0.04, 1.0) F = ks + (f90 - ks) ((1.0 - lh) 5) # 7. Specular BRDF specular = (D G F) / max(4.0 nv nl, 1e-4) # 8. Diffuse BRDF diffuse = kd / math.pi # 9. Total return diffuse + specular Specular reflection models perfectly smooth surfaces where outgoing radiance is not scattered but mirrors the incident trajectory across the surface normal. It serves as the zero-roughness limit of microfacet models, producing perfect mirror reflections. Unlike GGX or Ward models which distribute energy over a lobe, this method concentrates all reflected energy into a single geometric direction, requiring exact alignment between the incident light and the view vector relative to the surface normal. This method defines a surface reflectance function R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) that combines a specular microfacet term with a diffuse Lambertian term, incorporating specific simplifications from the Filament and Unreal Engine renderers. It sets itself apart from the parent GGX Microfacet BRDF by using a specific analytical form for the geometry function G and embedding the incoming cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i) directly into the specular denominator structure to simplify integration in neural radiance field contexts. The Ward Anisotropic BRDF is a microfacet specular reflection model that modifies the Beckmann distribution to simulate surface roughness varying in two orthogonal directions relative to the tangent space. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific parameterization of anisotropy via the ratio of eigenvalues from a covariance matrix, allowing for position-dependent control of highlight stretching. Unlike the isotropic GGX model, it explicitly decouples roughness along the tangent and bitangent axes. GGX Specular Shading is a path-tracing shading method for voxel-based volume rendering that combines a Cook-Torrance microfacet model with GGX specular reflection, Lambertian diffuse shading from an irradiance cache, and dielectric transmission handling. It differs from its parent GGX Microfacet BRDF by providing the complete shading loop (emission, reflection, refraction, and diffuse accumulation) rather than just the BRDF components. It is distinct from Specular Reflection by including transmission and diffuse GI, and from Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel by using the full Cook-Torrance formulation with explicit transmission logic. A method to ensure energy conservation for rough metals by compensating for energy lost in single-scattering GGX specular lobes, using a precomputed directional albedo table. It uses a precomputed 32x32 directional albedo table E(\mu, \alpha), where \mu is cosine and \alpha is roughness. This ensures white rough metal reflects ~100% at every roughness, correcting the energy loss inherent in single-scattering approximations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard microfacet evaluation is O(1) per shading point. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Base model requires O(1) memory; multi-scattering variants require a 32x32 lookup table. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. Handles a wide range of roughnesses but single-scattering approximation loses energy for very rough metals, addressed by multi-scattering variants. Does not account for subsurface scattering or thin-film effects without extensions. When to use: Not given in the sources. General-purpose physically based rendering for rough surfaces. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Perfect mirrors or when computational budget is extremely tight. The GGX microfacet model was introduced by Walter et al. in "Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces". It uses the Generalized Trowbridge-Reiss (GGX) distribution to approximate surface reflection properties, providing a better fit for the long tails of specular highlights observed in real-world materials compared to earlier distributions. It is referenced in implementations for realistic metal and plastic surfaces. name: Specular Reflection
head: Perfect mirror reflection
body: Specular reflection models perfectly smooth surfaces where outgoing radiance is not scattered but mirrors the incident trajectory across the surface normal. The method concentrates all reflected energy into a single geometric direction, requiring exact alignment between the incident light direction and the view vector relative to the surface normal. Inputs and Outputs: Incident radiance Li, incident direction \vec{\omega}i, reflected direction \vec{\omega}r, and surface normal \vec{n} are provided as inputs. The method outputs the reflected radiance Lr. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Standard vector and spherical coordinate representations are sufficient. Steps: 1. Compute the geometric reflection direction \vec{\omega}{refl} for the view direction \vec{\omega}r using the vector reflection formula \vec{\omega}{refl} = 2(\vec{\omega}r \cdot \vec{n})\vec{n} - \vec{\omega}r. 2. Convert \vec{\omega}i and \vec{\omega}{refl} to spherical coordinates (\thetai, \phii) and (\thetar, \phir) relative to the surface normal \vec{n}. 3. Evaluate the angular conditions \thetar = \thetai and \phir = \phii \pm \pi. 4. If both conditions hold, assign Lr(\thetar, \phir) = Li(\thetar, \phii \pm \pi); otherwise, assign Lr = 0. Formula: The Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) is defined using the Dirac delta function \delta: f{r,m} = \frac{\delta(\cos \thetai - \cos \thetar)}{\cos \thetai} \delta(\phii - (\phir \pm \pi)) where: \delta is the Dirac delta function. \thetai, \thetar are the incident and reflected polar angles. \phii, \phir are the incident and reflected azimuthal angles. Parameters: Roughness: 0. Typical values for other parameters are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Delta Function Zeroes: The Dirac delta function yields zero for any non-zero parameter mismatch, meaning no light is reflected if the geometric reflection conditions are not perfectly satisfied. Numerical Precision: Floating-point comparisons for angle equality (\thetar = \thetai) are prone to error; implementers must use a small epsilon tolerance or vector dot-product checks instead of direct angle equality. Discrete Sampling: In rasterization or discrete ray tracing, finding the exact incident direction is difficult; this model is best suited for analytical ray tracing or environment map lookups rather than light sampling in path tracers without importance sampling techniques. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel if the incident radiance is available via direct ray intersection or environment map lookup. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Computationally cheap per sample and physically accurate for polished metals and mirrors. Limitations: Cannot model rough surfaces, requires exact geometric alignment, and is difficult to sample stochastically without specialized techniques. When to use: Rendering perfect mirrors, polished chrome, or the zero-roughness limit of microfacet models. When not to use: For rough surfaces, diffuse materials, or when approximate lighting is acceptable. The mathematical formulation using Dirac delta functions for specular reflection originates from radiometry and computer graphics theory, specifically detailed in works on real-time global illumination. The concept of "perfect mirror reflection" with zero roughness is also implemented in voxel-based rendering tools like MagicaVoxel, which added a perfect mirror reflection material with support for over eight light bounces in version 0.96.2. name: Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel
head: NeRV BRDF, Walter et al. BRDF with Filament/Unreal simplifications
body: This method defines a surface reflectance function R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) that combines a specular microfacet term with a diffuse Lambertian term, incorporating specific simplifications from the Filament and Unreal Engine renderers. It sets itself apart from the parent GGX Microfacet BRDF by using a specific analytical form for the geometry function G and embedding the incoming cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i) directly into the diffuse term to simplify equations in the main paper. Inputs: \mathbf{x}: 3D surface location. \boldsymbol{\omega}i: Incoming light direction (unit vector). \boldsymbol{\omega}o: Outgoing view direction (unit vector). \mathbf{n}: Surface normal at \mathbf{x} (unit vector). \gamma: Roughness parameter (scalar, \gamma > 0). \mathbf{a}: Diffuse albedo (scalar or RGB vector). F0: Fresnel reflectance at normal incidence (scalar, typically 0.04 for dielectric materials). Outputs: R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o): Reflectance value. Steps: 1. Compute the half-vector \mathbf{h}: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\boldsymbol{\omega}o + \boldsymbol{\omega}i}{\|\boldsymbol{\omega}o + \boldsymbol{\omega}i\|} 2. Compute intermediate roughness parameters: \rho = \gamma^2, \quad k = \frac{\gamma^4}{2} 3. Compute the Normal Distribution Function D(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{n}, \gamma): D(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{n}, \gamma) = \frac{\rho^2}{\pi \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^2 (\rho^2 - 1) + 1 \right)^2} 4. Compute the Fresnel term F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h}) using Schlick's approximation: F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h}) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - (\boldsymbol{\omega}i \cdot \mathbf{h}))^5 5. Compute the Geometry function G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \gamma): G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \gamma) = \frac{(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o)(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i)}{\left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o)(1-k) + k \right) \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i)(1-k) + k \right)} 6. Compute the specular reflectance component: R{\text{spec}} = \frac{D(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{n}, \gamma) F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h}) G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \gamma)}{4(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o)} 7. Compute the diffuse reflectance component, which includes the Lambert cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i): R{\text{diff}} = (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i)(1 - F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h})) \left(\frac{\mathbf{a}}{\pi}\right) 8. Sum components: R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = R{\text{spec}} + R{\text{diff}} Pitfalls: The BRDF definition explicitly includes the multiplication by the Lambert cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i) in the diffuse part to simplify equations in the main paper, meaning the geometric term G and the diffuse term are structured differently than standard separable forms. Division by zero occurs if \mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o = 0 or \mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i = 0, requiring clamping or early exit for grazing angles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def microfacetbrdfsimplifiedggxschlick(n, wi, wo, gamma, a, F0): # 1. Half vector h = [wi[0] + wo[0], wi[1] + wo[1], wi[2] + wo[2]] hlen = length(h) if hlen < 1e-6: return 0.0 h = [x / hlen for x in h] # 2. Parameters rho = gamma gamma k = (gamma 4) / 2.0 # 3. NDF D nh = dot(n, h) nh2 = nh nh denomd = (nh2 (rho rho - 1.0) + 1.0) D = (rho rho) / (math.pi denomd denomd) # 4. Fresnel F widoth = dot(wi, h) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) ((1.0 - widoth) 5) # 5. Geometry G no = dot(n, wo) ni = dot(n, wi) if no < 1e-6 or ni < 1e-6: return 0.0 gnum = no ni gdenom1 = no (1.0 - k) + k gdenom2 = ni (1.0 - k) + k G = gnum / (gdenom1 gdenom2) # 6. Specular term spec = (D F G) / (4.0 no) # 7. Diffuse term diff = ni (1.0 - F) (a / math.pi) # 8. Total return spec + diff The Modified Disney Principled BRDF is a simplified surface reflectance model derived from the Disney Principled BRDF, tailored for use in the Absorption-Based Scene Diffusion Factorization (ABSDF) framework. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating complex microfacet reflections by reducing the original model's complexity while retaining its core appearance capabilities for metals and plastics. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel, by explicitly adopting a Lambertian diffuse term, omitting sheen and clearcoat lobes, and assuming double-sided surfaces to facilitate analytical factorization. Time and Memory Complexity: Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Computationally efficient due to simplified analytical forms for D, F, and G. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When to use: Not given in the sources. This BRDF parameterization is used in the NeRV (Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields) method for relighting and view synthesis. It builds on the standard microfacet BRDF described by Walter et al. and incorporates simplifications from the Filament and Unreal Engine rendering engines. The specific formulation, including the geometry term G and the embedding of the cosine term, is designed to simplify equations in the main NeRV paper. name: Modified Disney Principled BRDF
head: ABSDF Base Material, Base Material Model
body: The Modified Disney Principled BRDF is a simplified surface reflectance model derived from the Disney Principled BRDF, tailored for use in the Absorption-Based Scene Diffusion Factorization (ABSDF) framework. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating complex microfacet reflections by reducing the original model's complexity while retaining its core appearance capabilities for metals and plastics. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel, by explicitly adopting a Lambertian diffuse term, omitting sheen and clearcoat lobes, and assuming double-sided surfaces to facilitate analytical factorization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Incoming light direction \omegai, outgoing view direction \omegao, surface normal n, half vector \omegah = \frac{\omegai + \omegao}{\|\omegai + \omegao\|}, and material parameters \betaB = (\alpha, \betac, \betam, \betas). Outputs: Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) value f{disney}(\omegai, \omegao). Data Structures: The material parameters \betaB are spatially varying scalars: \alpha \in [0, 1]: Roughness. \betac \in [0, 1]: Base color (diffuse albedo). \betam \in [0, 1]: Metallic factor. \betas \in [0, 1]: Specular intensity (dielectric reflectance at normal incidence). Formulas: The model is defined as the sum of a diffuse component fd and a specular component fs: f{disney}(\omegai, \omegao) = fd(\omegai, \omegao) + fs(\omegai, \omegao) 1. Diffuse Component: Uses the Lambertian model instead of the original empirical retro-reflection term: fd(\omegai, \omegao) = \frac{(1 - \betam)\betac}{\pi} Here, \betam reduces the diffuse contribution for metallic surfaces, and \betac is the base color albedo. 2. Specular Component: Combines metallic and dielectric Fresnel reflections using the GGX distribution D, the shadowing-masking function G, and the Schlick Fresnel function F: fs(\omegai, \omegao) = \frac{\betam D(\omegah; \alpha) G(\omegai, \omegao; \alpha) F(\omegah, \omegao; \betac) + (1 - \betam) F(\omegah, \omegao; \betas)}{4 |n \cdot \omegao| |n \cdot \omegai|} D(\omegah; \alpha): Trowbridge-Reitz (GGX) microfacet distribution. G(\omegai, \omegao; \alpha): Shadowing-masking function. F(\omegah, \omegao; r0): Schlick Fresnel reflectance. 3. Schlick Fresnel: F(\omegah, \omegao; r0) = r0 (1 - Fc) + Fc Fc = (1 - |\omegah \cdot \omegao|)^5 Where r0 is the normal incidence reflectance. For the metallic lobe, r0 = \betac. For the dielectric lobe, r0 = \betas. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modifieddisneybrdf(omegai, omegao, n, alpha, betac, betam, betas): PI = 3.141592653589793 omegai = omegai / norm(omegai) omegao = omegao / norm(omegao) n = n / norm(n) omegah = (omegai + omegao) / norm(omegai + omegao) costhetai = dot(n, omegai) costhetao = dot(n, omegao) costhetah = dot(n, omegah) if costhetai <= 0.0 or costhetao <= 0.0: return 0.0 denom = 4.0 costhetai costhetao # 1. Diffuse Component (Lambertian) fdiffuse = ((1.0 - betam) betac) / PI # 2. Specular Component # D: Trowbridge-Reitz (GGX) distribution alphasq = alpha alpha denomD = (costhetah costhetah) (alphasq - 1.0) + 1.0 D = alphasq / (PI denomD denomD) # G: Schlick-GGX shadowing-masking function k = (alpha + 1.0) (alpha + 1.0) / 8.0 Gi = costhetai / (costhetai (1.0 - k) + k) Go = costhetao / (costhetao (1.0 - k) + k) G = Gi Go # Schlick Fresnel cosho = abs(dot(omegah, omegao)) Fc = (1.0 - cosho) 5.0 # Metallic lobe Fresnel (r0 = betac) Fmetal = betac (1.0 - Fc) + Fc # Dielectric lobe Fresnel (r0 = betas) Fdielectric = betas (1.0 - Fc) + Fc # Specular term fspecular = (betam D G Fmetal + (1.0 - betam) Fdielectric) / denom return fdiffuse + fspecular Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double-Sided Assumption: The model assumes double-sided surfaces, meaning the BRDF is evaluated regardless of the sign of n \cdot \omegai or n \cdot \omegao in the context of the factorization integral, though the geometric terms |n \cdot \omega| handle the dot product magnitude. Retro-reflection Omission: The original Disney model includes a retro-reflection term for diffuse light; this is omitted here, which may cause slight appearance differences for grazing angles on rough surfaces. A method for approximating the diffuse component of light transport in participating media by separating integration over material parameters from integration over geometry and orientation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing specifically on the diffuse lobe, allowing the use of Spherical Gaussian approximations for the cosine-weighted normal distribution. Choose it when efficiently evaluating the diffuse scattering term in path tracing is required. A method that computes the aggregated specular response of a surface with spatially varying material parameters by factorizing the integral of the microfacet BRDF over a joint probability distribution of those parameters. It sets itself apart by explicitly separating Fresnel mix terms from the microfacet distribution convolution and applying the shadowing-masking term post-convolution. Choose it when evaluating the expectation of a complex microfacet distribution under orientation-varying parameters is required. A physically-based BRDF function used in 3D Gaussian Splatting for inverse rendering, consisting of a diffuse and a specular component. It sets itself apart from its parent by employing a specific roughness remapping (\alpha = r^2) and a correlated Smith masking-shadowing function rather than a separable approximation. Choose it when higher physical accuracy is needed for Gaussian splatting optimization. A simplified material model based on the Cook–Torrance microfacet framework, designed to model reflectance for both metals and plastics in a unified framework. It sets itself apart by restricting optimization to opaque surfaces with spatially varying diffuse albedo and global constants for roughness, specular albedo, and metalness. Choose it for differentiable rendering and optimization tasks where ambiguity from high-dimensional parameter spaces must be reduced. Complexity: The base evaluation is O(1) per sample. The ABSDF factorization allows for pre-computation of moments, reducing runtime aggregation costs for level-of-detail rendering. Strengths: Simplicity compared to the full Disney BRDF; compatibility with analytical factorization techniques; wide applicability to standard PBR assets. Limitations: Lack of sheen and clearcoat lobes limits the ability to model certain materials (e.g., hair, varnished wood) accurately. The Lambertian diffuse approximation may not capture subsurface scattering effects or retro-reflection present in the original model. When to use: When using the ABSDF framework for efficient scene aggregation or when a simplified, robust PBR model is needed for differentiable rendering. The Modified Disney Principled BRDF was introduced in the context of the Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering paper. It is based on the Disney Principled BRDF [Burley 2012], which is one of the most commonly used models in production for its versatility. The modifications were made to facilitate the mathematical factorization required for the ABSDF method, specifically by simplifying the diffuse term and removing complex lobes. Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/391729893, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: Diffuse ABSDF Factorization
head: Diffuse Aggregation
body:
Diffuse ABSDF Factorization approximates the diffuse component of light transport in participating media by separating the integration over material parameters from the integration over geometry and orientation. It reduces the double integral into a product of a parameter expectation term and a geometric convolution term. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Specular ABSDF Factorization by focusing specifically on the diffuse lobe, which allows for the use of Spherical Gaussian (SG) approximations for the cosine-weighted normal distribution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Joint probability density function (PDF) of material parameters p( etac,  etam), shading normal distribution pN(n), incoming direction \omegai, and outgoing direction \omegao. Outputs: The aggregated diffuse scattering coefficient or integral value. Data Structures: Material Parameters:  etac,  etam \in [0, 1]. Normal Distribution: pN(n) defined on the hemisphere S^2. name: Specular ABSDF Factorization
head: Specular Aggregation
body: Specular ABSDF Factorization computes the aggregated specular response of a surface with spatially varying material parameters by factorizing the integral of the microfacet BRDF over a joint probability distribution of those parameters. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the expectation of a complex microfacet distribution when the surface normal n and roughness \alpha follow a probability density function pY(\gamma) rather than taking single values. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly separating the Fresnel mix terms from the microfacet distribution convolution, applying the shadowing-masking term G post-convolution due to its smoothness, and supporting orientation-varying parameters via spherical kernel splatting. The method computes the aggregated specular term by substituting the specular BRDF fs into the Aggregated BSDF (ABSDF) integral and expanding it into terms involving the Fresnel mix R and the microfacet distribution D. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The probability density function pY(\gamma) of material parameters \gamma = (n, \alpha, \betac, \betam, \betas), where n is the normal, \alpha is the roughness, and \beta terms are Fresnel coefficients. Output: The aggregated specular radiance contribution. Data Structures: SGGX Mixture: The surface Normal Distribution Function (NDF) pN(n) is represented as a mixture of k SGGX lobes: pN(n) = \sum{i=1}^k wi D{i,sggx}(n), where weights wi are positive and sum to 1. Precomputed Tables: Moments of the microfacet distribution M5(\alpha) and convolved distributions D{conv} are stored in lookup tables. Steps: 1. Substitution and Expansion: Substitute fs(\omegai, \omegao; \gamma) into the ABSDF integral (Eq. 7) and expand into terms involving R (Fresnel mix) and D (microfacet distribution): \int{\Gamma} fs(\omegai, \omegao; \gamma) \langle n \cdot \omegai \rangle \langle n \cdot \omegao \rangle pY(\gamma) d\gamma = \frac{1}{4} \int{\Gamma} (1 - Fc) R D pY(\gamma) d\gamma + Fc \int{\Gamma} R D pY(\gamma) d\gamma where R = \betam \betac + (1 - \betam)\betas and D = D(\omegah; n, \alpha) G(\omegai, \omegao; n, \alpha) 1(n \cdot \omegao) 1(n \cdot \omegai). 2. Splitting the PDF: Split the joint PDF pY(\gamma) into independent components for the Fresnel coefficients and the geometric parameters: pY(\gamma) \approx p{Y1}(\betac, \betam, \betas) p{Y2}(n, \alpha). 3. Evaluate Parameter Integral: Evaluate the integral over the Fresnel parameters \Gamma1 as moments: \int{\Gamma1} R p{Y1}(\gamma) d\gamma = E[\betam \betac] + E[\betas] - E[\betam \betas]. 4. Evaluate Microfacet Integral: Evaluate the integral over the geometric parameters \Gamma2 using precomputed tables. The convolution of the SGGX mixture with an isotropic spherical distribution g(\omega; n) is approximated by a roughened SGGX: \int{S^2} g(\omega; n) D{sggx}(n; R, \alpha) dn \approx D{sggx}(\omega; R, \alpha + \Delta) where R stays fixed but \alpha gains additional values. 5. Final Expression: Multiply the shadowing-masking term G to each lobe post-convolution, as it is very smooth: \int{\Gamma2} D p{Y2}(\gamma) d\gamma \approx \sum{i=1}^{2} \sum{j=1}^{k} wi m{ij} D{conv}(\omegah){ij} S{ij}(\omegai, \omegao) G{ij}(\omegai, \omegao) where S{ij} = S(\omegai, \omegao; \alpha{ij}) and G{ij} is the shadowing-masking term. Parameters: Spherical Domain Partition Size: Coarse partitioning such as 3 \times 3 is sufficient for orientation-varying parameters because angular frequency decreases as the scale of aggregation becomes larger. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The approximation of the convolution as a roughened SGGX relies on the validity of the eigenbasis parameterization. Boundaries: The Heaviside step functions 1(n \cdot \omegao) and 1(n \cdot \omegai) must be handled correctly to ensure clamped dot products. This method approximates the aggregated microfacet distribution \hat{D}{mic} of a scene or material asset by modeling the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha and fitting a two-lobed weighted sum to the expected distribution. It solves the problem of representing heterogeneous roughness distributions in a compact, analytically tractable form suitable for real-time rendering, avoiding the invalid range errors of Gaussian approximations by using a Beta distribution for the underlying roughness density. It sets itself apart from its parent by providing the specific statistical fitting mechanism for the microfacet term, and from simple single-lobe approximations by guaranteeing higher accuracy and never being worse than simple averaged roughness fits. Choose it when rendering scenes with significant roughness variation where single-lobed approximations fail to capture the statistical spread. The final expression for the specular component involves multiplying the shadowing-masking term G to each lobe post-convolution. The expression consists of contributions from all convolved NDF lobes, where each term is multiplied by its scaling factor to account for the specific roughness and orientation. This is an extension of the factorization to handle orientation-varying material parameters by computing directional moments weighted by a spherical kernel. It allows the model to capture view-dependent appearance changes due to orientation-varying material parameters. Steps: 1. For a direction \omega, weight each surface sample by a spherical function s(Tx \omega) as a kernel. 2. Compute directional moments E\omega[\beta] and E\omega[\beta \beta'] by integrating over the surface area A: E\omega[\beta] = \frac{\intA \betax s(Tx \omega) dx}{\intA s(Tx \omega) dx}, \quad E\omega[\beta \beta'] = \frac{\intA \betax \beta'x s(Tx \omega) dx}{\intA s(Tx \omega) dx} where Tx is the local transform at x. 3. For the specular component, set the kernel s(\omega) to the microfacet distribution. For the diffuse component, set the kernel s(\omega) to the Spherical Gaussian (SG) from Eq. 14. 4. Query the directional moments at \omegah when evaluating the specular and diffuse components. 5. During precomputation, splat each surface sample to the spherical partition. Time Complexity: The method reduces the complexity of aggregating microfacet distributions by precomputing moments and convolutions, allowing for efficient runtime evaluation using lookup tables. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for precomputed tables of moments and convolved distributions, as well as the spherical partition for orientation-varying parameters. Strengths: Efficiently handles material variation and orientation changes without requiring per-pixel integration of complex microfacet distributions. Limitations: The accuracy depends on the approximation of the convolution as a roughened SGGX and the coarse partitioning of the spherical domain. Specular ABSDF Factorization was introduced in the paper "Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering" by Yang Zhou, Tao Huang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Pradeep Sen, and Ling-Qi Yan. The method builds on previous work in microfacet theory and aggregation, such as the SGGX distribution [Heitz et al. 2015] and the aggregation of roughness distributions [Xu et al. 2013]. name: Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation
head: Beta Distribution Fitting, Roughness Aggregation
body: This method approximates the aggregated microfacet distribution \hat{D}{mic} of a scene or material asset by modeling the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha and fitting a two-lobed weighted sum to the expected distribution. It solves the problem of representing heterogeneous roughness distributions in a compact, analytically tractable form suitable for real-time rendering, avoiding the invalid range errors of Gaussian approximations by using a Beta distribution for the underlying roughness density. It sets itself apart from its parent, Specular ABSDF Factorization, by providing the specific statistical fitting mechanism for the microfacet term, and from simple single-lobe approximations by guaranteeing higher accuracy and never being worse than simple averaged roughness fits. Inputs: The marginal density function of roughness pA(\alpha), modeled as a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b) with shape parameters a and b. The base microfacet distribution function D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha) (e.g., GGX). Outputs: A mapping M2(a, b) that returns the weights m1, m2 and roughness parameters \alpha1, \alpha2 for the two-lobed approximation. Data Structures: A 2D lookup table storing the precomputed mapping (m1, \alpha1, \alpha2) for discrete values of a and b. Steps: 1. Model the roughness distribution pA(\alpha) using a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b). 2. Define the aggregated microfacet distribution as the expectation of the microfacet distribution over the roughness distribution: \hat{D}{mic}(\omegah) = \int0^1 D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha) pA(\alpha) d\alpha This integral represents a weighted average of infinite microfacet lobes with different possible \alpha values. 3. Approximate \hat{D}{mic}(\omegah) by a weighted average of two lobes: \hat{D}{mic}(\omegah) \approx m1 D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha1) + m2 D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha2) where m1 + m2 = 1. 4. Perform a nonlinear least-square fit to find the best mapping (m1, \alpha1, \alpha2) = M2(a, b) given the shape parameters a and b of the Beta distribution. 5. Store the mapping M2(a, b) in a 2D lookup table for runtime retrieval. Parameters: a, b: Shape parameters of the Beta distribution for roughness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using a Gaussian distribution for pA(\alpha) is invalid because it does not respect the [0, 1] bounds of \alpha, potentially leading to invalid range errors. A truncated Gaussian can be restricted to the valid range but requires a more tedious fitting process. This method models the aggregated microfacet roughness distribution pA(\alpha) using a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b) to estimate the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha from asset data. It sets itself apart from Gaussian approximations because the Beta distribution is naturally bounded within the valid [0, 1] range of \alpha, preventing invalid range errors. Choose this method when the roughness distribution is strictly bounded and requires a statistically accurate representation. See Aggregated Microfacet Distribution via Beta Distribution. The Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF) is a method for efficient scene appearance aggregation for Level-of-Detail (LoD) rendering. It sets itself apart from explicit geometry rendering by precomputing aggregated visibility and material properties, allowing the renderer to avoid tracing explicit geometry and shadow rays. Choose this method when rendering scenes with high geometric complexity and instancing where explicit geometry tracing is too costly. See Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF). The Horizon Principled BRDF is a bidirectional reflectance distribution function used in the Horizon rendering engine. It sets itself apart from general aggregation functions by fixing specific parameter values (such as \gamma=2 for the main lobe and \gamma=1 for clear coat) and implementing a specific diffuse Fresnel variation to correct edge darkening. Choose this method when using the Horizon rendering engine or requiring a Disney-compatible principled shading approach. See Horizon Principled BRDF. A method to fit aggregated microfacet distributions using a 2-lobe weighted sum. It sets itself apart from single-lobe fits with simple averaged roughness by being overall more accurate and guaranteed to be never worse. Choose this method when balancing computational cost and accuracy for microfacet approximation. Time and Memory Complexity: Precomputation involves a nonlinear least-square fit, which is performed offline. Runtime cost is dominated by a 2D table lookup for the mapping M2(a, b) and the evaluation of two microfacet lobes, which is constant time relative to the number of roughness samples. Memory usage is determined by the resolution of the 2D lookup table storing M2(a, b). Measured Performance: The 2-lobe fit is validated against ground-truth aggregated microfacet distributions and is shown to be more accurate than single-lobe fits with simple averaged roughness. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: It accurately captures the statistical spread of roughness in heterogeneous materials without the boundary errors of Gaussian approximations. It provides a guaranteed improvement over simple single-lobe approximations. Limitations: It requires offline precomputation of the fitting table. The accuracy depends on the expressiveness of the Beta distribution to model the true roughness density pA(\alpha). When to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from research on efficient scene appearance aggregation for Level-of-Detail rendering. It addresses the need to represent the far-field appearance of scene aggregates by integrating light transport over positions, allowing for the avoidance of explicit geometry tracing. The use of the Beta distribution for roughness modeling and the 2-lobe approximation for the microfacet term are specific contributions to this framework. name: Aggregated Microfacet Distribution via Beta Distribution
head: Beta Distribution Microfacet Roughness
body: This method models the aggregated microfacet roughness distribution pA(\alpha) using a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b) to estimate the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha from asset data. It is chosen over Gaussian approximations because the Beta distribution is naturally bounded within the valid [0, 1] range of \alpha, preventing the invalid range errors that occur when Gaussian tails exceed these bounds. Inputs: A set of roughness maps or a statistical summary (mean \mu and variance \sigma^2) of the roughness values \alpha from the input assets. Outputs: Shape parameters a and b for the Beta distribution, and the resulting probability density function pA(\alpha). Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values. The roughness \alpha is a float in [0, 1]. The parameters a and b are positive floats. Steps: 1. Compute the mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 of the roughness values \alpha from the input data. 2. Calculate the shape parameter a using the formula: a = -\frac{\mu (\sigma^2 + \mu^2 - \mu)}{\sigma^2}. 3. Calculate the shape parameter b using the formula: b = \frac{(\sigma^2 + \mu^2 - \mu)(\mu - 1)}{\sigma^2}. 4. Define the aggregated distribution as the Beta distribution with these parameters: pA(\alpha) = B(\alpha; a, b). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fitbetadistribution(meanmu, variancesigma2): """ Estimates Beta distribution shape parameters a and b from mean and variance. Args: meanmu (float): The mean roughness value. variancesigma2 (float): The variance of the roughness values. Returns: tuple: (a, b) shape parameters for the Beta distribution. """ # Calculate the common term (sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu) term = variancesigma2 + meanmu2 - meanmu # Calculate shape parameter a # Source formula: a = -mu (sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu) / sigma^2 a = -meanmu term / variancesigma2 # Calculate shape parameter b # Source formula: b = (sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu) (mu - 1) / sigma^2 b = term (meanmu - 1) / variancesigma2 return a, b Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Range Validity: Unlike Gaussian distributions, the Beta distribution naturally respects the [0, 1] range of \alpha. This avoids the pitfall where a Gaussian fit for roughness maps might assign non-zero probability to invalid roughness values outside [0, 1]. Parameter Constraints: The shape parameters a and b must be positive for a valid Beta distribution. The source formulas are derived from the moments of the Beta distribution. If the input \mu and \sigma^2 do not correspond to a valid Beta distribution (e.g., variance is too large for the given mean), the resulting a or b may be negative or zero, leading to undefined behavior. The source notes that this fitting is performed on actual assets, implying the data is well-behaved. Truncated Gaussian Alternative: A truncated Gaussian could be restricted to the valid range and may produce similar quality, but the fitting process is more tedious. This variant involves fitting roughness maps from assets to beta distributions to estimate the distribution of alpha (roughness). It is preferred over Gaussian distributions because Gaussians can exceed the valid [0, 1] range of alpha, whereas beta distributions are bounded. Truncated Gaussians could be restricted to the valid range and may produce similar quality, but the fitting process is more tedious. Time and Memory Complexity: The fitting process involves constant-time arithmetic operations given the mean and variance. The complexity is O(1) per asset or map summary. Storing the parameters a and b requires minimal memory (two floats). Measured Performance: The source validates the approach by estimating pA(\alpha) from roughness maps used for actual assets. The fits are described as "reasonably accurate" and adapt to different modes of real data. The method is compared to ground-truth aggregated microfacet distributions and simple averaged roughness, showing that the fits are "overall more accurate and guaranteed to be never worse than the simple fits". Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Naturally bounded to [0, 1], avoiding invalid roughness values. More accurate than simple averaged roughness. Limitations: Requires accurate estimation of mean and variance. The source does not provide specific hardware performance metrics or resolution scaling data. When to Use: Use this method when aggregating microfacet distributions for level-of-detail rendering or when approximating the roughness distribution from asset data, especially when the roughness values are bounded in [0, 1] and a Gaussian approximation would risk exceeding these bounds. This method appears in the 2022 Computer Graphics Forum paper "Advances in Neural Rendering" by Tretschk et al., which uses a Beta distribution to represent the roughness distribution pA(\alpha). It builds on the Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation [10880-aggregated-microfacet-distribution-approximation.md].
