name: Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF)
head: ABSDF-based method, Scene Appearance Aggregation for LoD Rendering
body: The Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF) is a method for efficient scene appearance aggregation for Level-of-Detail (LoD) rendering, designed to handle scenes with high geometric complexity and instancing. It defines a 4D function of incident and outgoing directions that describes the far-field appearance of a scene aggregate by integrating the 8D light transport function over positions, effectively capturing the aggregated appearance of all surfaces within a volume. Unlike explicit geometry rendering, ABSDF precomputes aggregated visibility and material properties, allowing the renderer to avoid tracing explicit geometry and shadow rays, thereby reducing the sample count required for convergence. It builds on Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation by providing a closed-form factorization that supports all-frequency and view-dependent effects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene composed of multiple aggregated objects and instances, defined by their geometry, materials (modeled via Disney Principled BRDF with GGX microfacets), and spatial layout. Output: A rendered image at a specified LoD resolution (e.g., 64^3, 128^3, 256^3, 512^3) with precomputed aggregated data structures. Data Structures: The method relies on a voxel grid representation of the scene. Each voxel stores aggregated data derived from the surfaces within it. 1. Aggregated Interior Visibility (AIV): A high-dimensional data structure representing visibility within the volume. It is compressed using Compact Principal Component Analysis (CPCA). 2. Aggregated Boundary Visibility (ABV): A data structure representing visibility at the boundaries of the voxel, used to compute partial occlusion between different instances. 3. NDF Lobes: The material appearance is approximated using up to 4 surface Normal Distribution Function (NDF) lobes in the "maximum" configuration. Parameters: LoD Resolution: The spatial subdivision resolution (e.g., 64^3, 128^3). NDF Lobes: Number of lobes for material approximation (up to 4). Truncation Thresholds: Coefficient truncation for AIV and ABV data (e.g., 1%, 10%). CPCA Representatives: Number of representatives kept for CPCA compression (1 or more). Steps: 1. Spatial Subdivision: Subdivide the scene into voxels at a resolution suitable for the pixel footprint, ensuring each voxel satisfies the far-field assumption. 2. Precomputation: For each voxel, integrate the product of base material, foreshortening factors, and bidirectional visibility over the underlying surfaces to compute the ABSDF. Compute Aggregated Interior Visibility (AIV) and Aggregated Boundary Visibility (ABV). Apply CPCA to compress the high-dimensional AIV data. Apply coefficient truncation to AIV and ABV data to reduce memory footprint. Use a truncated ellipsoid primitive to approximate the voxel shape, improving the preservation of local correlation compared to a cubic primitive. 3. Instance Selection: For scenes with multiple aggregated objects and instancing, each instance selects its LoD level based on its screen-space projection size. 4. Rendering: Trace rays through the voxel grid. For each voxel hit, evaluate the ABSDF to determine the outgoing radiance. The ABSDF factorization allows for efficient evaluation and sampling. Use ABV to compute partial occlusion between different instances, treating them as uncorrelated. Use precomputed AIV to determine visibility, avoiding the tracing of shadow rays. Perform splitting to allocate more samples for lighting (e.g., Next Event Estimation) since the representation is already anti-aliased. Formulas: The ABSDF \hat{f}(\omegai, \omegao) is defined by integrating the product of base material, foreshortening factors, and bidirectional visibility over the underlying surfaces. The normalization term uses the projected area |A|{\omegao} for simplicity, though the visible projected area |Av(\omegao)| could also be used as it cancels out in accumulation equations. The symmetry property of the ABSDF is: |A|{\omegao} \hat{f}(\omegai, \omegao) = |A|{\omegai} \hat{f}(\omegao, \omegai) where |A|{\omegao} is the projected area of the voxel in the direction \omegao. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Independence Assumptions: Eq. 6 assumes independence between visibility and material in a single voxel, which can lead to artifacts, especially at coarse scales. Eq. 25 assumes independence between visibility along two directions, which can lead to incorrect occlusion when the camera and light source are collocated. Angular Resolution: At the coarsest scale, the multi-lobe NDF may not have sufficient angular resolution to resolve all highlights, resulting in a slightly darker look. Truncation Errors: Hard shadows may have small imperfections due to visibility coefficient truncation and compression. 1% truncation results in visible inaccuracy, while 10% truncation introduces barely recognizable error. CPCA Compression: Using only 1 CPCA representative reduces CPCA to simple vector quantization and approximates per-cluster subspaces poorly. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is largely independent of the original scene complexity, providing asymptotic benefits for larger scenes. It requires more memory than HybridLoD and NonExp mainly due to high-dimensional aggregated visibility data even after compression. The memory cost is agnostic to whether the original scene contains instanced geometry. Performance: The method is comparable to the PT (Path Tracing) baseline in terms of rendering speed, whereas HybridLoD and NonExp are significantly slower, likely due to the complexity of nested ray marching or sampling. The method avoids spending a large number of samples to trace explicit geometry, allowing for more samples to be allocated for lighting. Quality: The method achieves superior quality compared to existing methods (HybridLoD, NonExp) and DAP on various scenes, as shown by lower RMSE in comparisons. Scaling: The memory footprint scales quadratically with respect to LoD resolution. If a model only occupies a small portion of the rendered image, a coarser LoD level with much smaller memory is needed. When to Use: Suitable for large, complex scenes with high geometric complexity and instancing, where explicit rendering is infeasible due to memory constraints. When Not to Use: Not suitable for small scenes where explicit representation is more efficient. Currently limited to direct illumination; supporting global illumination would require modeling multiple scattering between scene parts. The Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF) method was presented in the paper "Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering" by Yang Zhou, Tao Huang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Pradeep Sen, and Ling-Qi Yan, published in October 2024. The method addresses the challenge of rendering large, complex scenes with high geometric detail by aggregating the appearance of surfaces within a volume into a compact representation. It builds upon previous work in appearance aggregation and LoD rendering, aiming to provide a scalable solution for physically based rendering of massive scenes. Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/391729893, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: Horizon Principled BRDF
head: Disney Principled BRDF variant, Horizon PBR
body: The Horizon Principled BRDF is a bidirectional reflectance distribution function used in the Horizon rendering engine, designed to be compatible with Disney's principled shading approach. It solves the problem of providing a physically plausible, energy-conserving shading model that supports a wide range of material types (dielectric, metallic, clear coat, sheen) through a unified set of normalized parameters. It sets itself apart from its parent, Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation, by fixing specific parameter values (such as \gamma=2 for the main lobe and \gamma=1 for clear coat) and implementing a specific diffuse Fresnel variation to correct edge darkening, rather than using a general aggregation function. The Horizon BRDF computes the total reflected radiance fr(l, v) as the sum of a diffuse component fd and a specular component fs: fr(l, v) = fd + fs where l is the incoming light vector, v is the outgoing view vector, and n is the surface normal vector. The method requires the following inputs and parameters, all normalized between 0 and 1 unless specified: albedo: Surface color at the point. roughness: Controls microfacet alignment. 0 is smooth, 1 is rough. F0: Base reflectivity constant for the material. anisotropic: Controls anisotropy. 0 is isotropic, 1 is highly anisotropic. Subsurface: Blends diffuse with a Hanrahan-Krueger inspired subsurface BRDF. 0 is no subsurface, 1 is full blending. Metallic: 0 is dielectric, 1 is metallic. Specular: Intensity of specular light. 0 is low, 1 is high. Specular Tint: Interpolates specular color between achromatic (white, 0) and base color (1). Sheen: Intensity of edge reflections. 0 is low, 1 is high. Sheen Tint: Tint for sheen reflections. Clear Coat: Intensity of the second specular lobe. 0 is none, 1 is full. Clear Coat Gloss: Smoothness of the clear coat lobe. 0 is matte, 1 is satin. absorption coefficient (\alpha), distance (l), concentration (c): Used for translucent materials via Beer-Lambert law. The method operates on standard 3D vectors for l, v, n, h, x, y. The halfway vector h is computed as: h = \frac{l + v}{|l + v|} The diffuse component uses a modified Lambertian model with a Fresnel factor to prevent edge darkening. 1. Calculate the base Lambertian diffuse: f{Lambert} = \frac{albedo}{\pi} 2. Calculate the diffuse Fresnel factor FD{90}: FD{90} = 0.5 + 2(h \cdot v)^{roughness} 3. Compute the final diffuse term: fd = f{Lambert} \left[1 + (FD{90} - 1)(1 - (l \cdot n))^5\right] \left[1 + (FD{90} - 1)(1 - (n \cdot v))^5\right] This factor accounts for the portion of light reflected vs. refracted based on viewing angle, reducing incident reflectance by half at sharp angles for smooth surfaces and increasing response for rough surfaces. The specular component follows the Cook-Torrance microfacet model: fs = \frac{D(h) F(h, v) G(l, h, v)}{4(l \cdot n)(n \cdot v)} where D is the Normal Distribution Function (NDF), F is the Fresnel coefficient, and G is the Geometry Shadowing Function. Uses the Schlick approximation: F{Schlick}(F0, h, v) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - (h \cdot v))^5 Horizon uses the Generalized Trowbridge-Reiss (GTR) distribution with fixed \gamma values. Main Lobe (\gamma = 2): Equivalent to GGX. Used for the base material. D{GGX} = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi \left[1 + (\alpha^2 - 1)(h \cdot n)^2\right]^2} where \alpha = roughness^2. Clear Coat Lobe (\gamma = 1): Used for the clear coat layer. This lobe is always isotropic and non-metallic. Due to a singularity at \gamma=1, the limit form is used: D{GTR1} = \frac{\alpha^2 - 1}{2\pi \log(\alpha^2) \left[1 + (\alpha^2 - 1)(h \cdot n)^2\right]} Anisotropic Main Lobe: If anisotropic > 0, the main lobe uses an anisotropic GTR form: D{GTR2, anisotropic} = \frac{1}{\pi \alphax \alphay \left[\frac{(h \cdot x)^2}{\alphax^2} + \frac{(h \cdot y)^2}{\alphay^2} + (h \cdot n)^2\right]^2} where x and y are tangent and binormal vectors. The anisotropic roughness parameters are: \alphax = \frac{roughness^2}{ar}, \quad \alphay = roughness^2 \cdot ar The aspect ratio ar is derived from the anisotropic parameter: ar = \sqrt{1 - 0.9 \cdot anisotropic} The factor 0.9 limits the aspect ratio to 10:1. Uses the separable Smith GGX function. Isotropic: G{GGX} = \frac{1}{(l \cdot h) + \sqrt{\alpha^2 + (l \cdot h)^2 - \alpha^2(l \cdot h)^2}} Anisotropic: G{GGX, anisotropic} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \sqrt{(l \cdot h)^2 + \alphax^2(l \cdot x)^2 + \alphay^2(l \cdot y)^2 + (l \cdot h)^2}} Subsurface Blending: The Subsurface parameter blends the calculated fd with a Hanrahan-Krueger inspired subsurface BRDF. This is not a substitute for full subsurface transport; it does not bleed light into shadows or through the surface. Beer-Lambert Law: For translucent materials (glass, liquids), light absorption is modeled independently: \frac{I1}{I0} = e^{-\alpha l c} where I0 is incident intensity, I1 is transmitted intensity, \alpha is the absorption coefficient, l is the distance light travels, and c is the concentration of absorbing elements. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def horizonprincipledbrdf(l, v, n, albedo, roughness, F0, anisotropic, metallic, specular, speculartint, sheen, sheentint, clearcoat, clearcoatgloss, subsurface, tangentx, tangenty, absorptioncoeff, distance, concentration): # 1. Precompute vectors h = [l[i] + v[i] for i in range(3)] hlen = math.sqrt(dot(h, h)) h = [x / hlen for x in h] costhetal = dot(l, n) costhetav = dot(v, n) costhetah = dot(h, n) costhetahv = dot(h, v) # 2. Compute Diffuse Component flambert = [x / math.pi for x in albedo] fd90 = 0.5 + 2.0 (costhetahv roughness) terml = 1.0 + (fd90 - 1.0) ((1.0 - costhetal) 5) termv = 1.0 + (fd90 - 1.0) ((1.0 - costhetav) 5) fd = [x terml termv for x in flambert] # 3. Compute Specular Component (Main Lobe) alpha = roughness 2 if anisotropic > 0: ar = math.sqrt(1.0 - 0.9 anisotropic) alphax = alpha / ar alphay = alpha ar denomndf = costhetah 2 + (dot(h, tangentx) 2) / (alphax 2) + (dot(h, tangenty) 2) / (alphay 2) Dmain = 1.0 / (math.pi alphax alphay (denomndf 2)) gdenomsq = 2.0 (costhetah 2) + (alphax 2 dot(l, tangentx) 2) + (alphay 2 dot(l, tangenty) 2) Gmain = 1.0 / (math.sqrt(2.0) math.sqrt(gdenomsq)) else: denomndf = 1.0 + (alpha - 1.0) (costhetah 2) Dmain = alpha / (math.pi (denomndf 2)) gdenom = costhetah + math.sqrt(alpha 2 + (costhetah 2) - (alpha 2 (costhetah 2))) Gmain = 1.0 / gdenom Fmain = F0 + (1.0 - F0) ((1.0 - costhetahv) 5) specdenom = 4.0 costhetal costhetav if specdenom < 1e-8: fsmain = 0.0 else: fsmain = (Dmain Fmain Gmain) / specdenom # 4. Compute Clear Coat Specular Component (Isotropic, gamma=1) ccalpha = clearcoatgloss 2 alphasq = ccalpha 2 denomndfcc = 1.0 + (alphasq - 1.0) (costhetah 2) logalphasq = math.log(alphasq) if abs(logalphasq) < 1e-8: Dcc = 1.0 / math.pi else: Dcc = (alphasq - 1.0) / (2.0 math.pi logalphasq denomndfcc) Fcc = F0 + (1.0 - F0) ((1.0 - costhetahv) 5) gdenomcc = costhetah + math.sqrt(ccalpha 2 + (costhetah 2) - (ccalpha 2 (costhetah 2))) Gcc = 1.0 / gdenomcc fscc = (Dcc Fcc Gcc) / specdenom if specdenom > 1e-8 else 0.0 fs = fsmain + clearcoat fscc # 5. Subsurface Blending # The Hanrahan-Krueger formula is not provided in the sources. # A linear blend with a placeholder subsurface term would be: fd = lerp(fd, fsubsurface, subsurface) # fdfinal = fd # 6. Sheen # The Sheen BRDF formula is not provided in the sources. fsheen = 0.0 # 7. Total fr = [fd[i] + fs + fsheen for i in range(3)] # 8. Translucency (Beer-Lambert) # Applied to transmitted light: Itransmitted = Iincident exp(-absorptioncoeff distance concentration) return fr Singularity at \gamma=1: The GTR NDF has a singularity at \gamma=1. The source specifies using the limit form D{GTR1} for the clear coat lobe. Edge Darkening: Standard Lambertian diffuse is darker at grazing angles. The Horizon model addresses this with the FD{90} Fresnel variation. Subsurface Limitations: The subsurface blending parameter does not perform full subsurface transport; it does not bleed light into shadows or through the surface. Clear Coat Constraints: The clear coat lobe is always isotropic and non-metallic, regardless of the main lobe's settings. Not given in the sources. The Horizon Principled BRDF was introduced in the Horizon rendering engine. It is inspired by Disney's "principled" shading approach, adhering to its usability and interactivity principles. The engine is used for visualizing large medical imaging datasets, such as fiber tracking algorithms generating millions of streamlines, and translucent materials like glass and liquids. The BRDF was published in a preprint in 2023. name: Phys3DGS BRDF Function
head: Phys3DGS BRDF
body: A physically-based BRDF function used in 3D Gaussian Splatting for inverse rendering, consisting of a diffuse and a specular component. It differs from its parent, Modified Disney Principled BRDF, by employing a specific roughness remapping (\alpha = r^2) and a correlated Smith masking-shadowing function rather than a separable approximation. Inputs: \omegai: Incident light direction. \omegao: Outgoing view direction. \bm{n}: Surface normal. \bm{a}: Base color (diffuse albedo). m: Metallic value (scalar). r: Roughness parameter (scalar). Outputs: f(\omegao, \omegai): Reflected radiance factor. Steps: 1. Compute Roughness Remapping: \alpha = r^2. 2. Compute Half Vector: \bm{h} = (\omegai + \omegao) / \|\omegai + \omegao\|. 3. Compute Fresnel Term (F): F0 = 0.04(1 - m) + \bm{a}m. Then F(\bm{h}, \bm{n}) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - \bm{h} \cdot \bm{n})^5. 4. Compute Normal Distribution Function (D): D(\alpha, \bm{h}, \bm{n}) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi ((\bm{h} \cdot \bm{n})^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2}. 5. Compute Masking-Shadowing Function (G): G{\lambda}(\alpha, \bm{n} \cdot \omegai) = \frac{1}{2(\sqrt{1 + \alpha(1 - (\bm{n} \cdot \omegai)^2)/(\bm{n} \cdot \omegai)^2} - 1)}. G(\alpha, \bm{n}, \omegai, \omegao) = \frac{1}{1 + G{\lambda}(\alpha, \bm{n} \cdot \omegai) + G{\lambda}(\alpha, \bm{n} \cdot \omegao)}. 6. Compute Final BRDF: f(\omegao, \omegai) = \frac{1-m}{\pi}\bm{a} + \frac{DFG}{4(\omegai \cdot \bm{n})(\omegao \cdot \bm{n})}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phys3dgsbrdf(omegai, omegao, n, a, m, r): # 1. Roughness remapping alpha = r r # 2. Half vector h = normalize(omegai + omegao) # 3. Fresnel F0 = 0.04 (1 - m) + a m costhetah = dot(h, n) F = F0 + (1 - F0) (1 - costhetah)5 # 4. Normal Distribution Function (GGX) costhetahsq = costhetah costhetah denomD = costhetahsq (alpha alpha - 1) + 1 D = (alpha alpha) / (pi denomD denomD) # 5. Masking-Shadowing Function (Correlated Smith) def lambdaggx(alpha, costheta): # costheta is n. omega if costheta == 0: return 0.0 term = 1 + (alpha (1 - costheta costheta)) / (costheta costheta) term = max(term, 0.0) return 1.0 / (2.0 (sqrt(term) - 1.0)) costhetai = dot(n, omegai) costhetao = dot(n, omegao) lambdai = lambdaggx(alpha, costhetai) lambdao = lambdaggx(alpha, costhetao) G = 1.0 / (1.0 + lambdai + lambdao) # 6. Final BRDF denomspec = 4.0 costhetai costhetao if denomspec == 0: return 0.0 specular = (D F G) / denomspec diffuse = ((1 - m) / pi) a return diffuse + specular Parameters: m (metallic): Optimized during training. Regularizer weight \lambda{smooth} is 0.02. r (roughness): Optimized during training. Regularizer weight \lambda{smooth} is 0.02. \bm{a} (base color): Optimized during training. Regularizer weight is 0.06. Edge Cases: Grazing Angles: If \bm{n} \cdot \omegai or \bm{n} \cdot \omegao approaches 0, the specular denominator approaches 0. Zero Half Vector: If \omegai = -\omegao, the half vector is undefined. Precision in Lambda: The term inside the square root for G{\lambda} must be non-negative; numerical errors at grazing angles require a max(term, 0.0) guard. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard vector operations are O(1) per evaluation. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. The Phys3DGS BRDF function was introduced in "Phys3DGS: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering" (ECCV 2024 Submission #12158). It provides a differentiable, physically-based material model within the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for inverse rendering. name: Isotropic Disney BRDF
head: Cook-Torrance based Disney BRDF, Disney BRDF Material Model, Simplified Disney BRDF, Unreal Engine 4 BRDF
body: The Isotropic Disney BRDF is a simplified material model based on the Cook–Torrance microfacet framework, designed to model reflectance for both metals and plastics in a unified framework. It is a restricted subset of the full Disney Principled BRDF, optimized for differentiable rendering and optimization tasks where ambiguity from high-dimensional parameter spaces must be reduced. Unlike the full model, it restricts optimization to opaque surfaces with spatially varying diffuse albedo and global constants for roughness, specular albedo, and metalness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface position \mathbf{x}, incoming light direction \mathbf{l} (or \omegai), outgoing view direction \mathbf{v} (or \omegao), surface normal \mathbf{n}. Parameters: c{\text{base}} \in [0, 1]^3: Base color / diffuse albedo, spatially varying a(\mathbf{x}). s \in [0, 1]: Specular albedo, global constant. r \in [0, 1]: Surface roughness (denoted \beta in some sources), global constant. m \in [0, 1]: Metalness, global constant. Output: Reflected radiance Lr(\mathbf{v}). Data Structures: The diffuse albedo c{\text{base}} is stored as a 3-channel texture or array indexed by \mathbf{x}. The parameters s, r, and m are scalar constants or global uniforms. Formulas: The BRDF fr(\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{v}) combines a diffuse term and a specular term: fr(\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{c{\text{diffuse}}}{\pi} + \frac{D F G}{4(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})} Where: c{\text{diffuse}} = (1 - m) c{\text{base}} c{\text{specular}} = (1 - m) 0.08 s + m c{\text{base}} \alpha = r^2 k = \frac{r + 1}{8} \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}\|} D = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1 \right)^2} G = \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})(1 - k) + k \right) \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})(1 - k) + k \right) F = c{\text{specular}} + (1 - c{\text{specular}})^{2^{-5.55473(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{h}) - 6.98316}} Steps: 1. Retrieve base color c{\text{base}} at \mathbf{x}. 2. Compute half-vector \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}). 3. Compute \alpha = r^2 and k = (r + 1) / 8. 4. Evaluate NDF D using \alpha and \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}. 5. Evaluate geometry term G using \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}, and k. 6. Compute c{\text{specular}} from m, s, and c{\text{base}}. 7. Evaluate Fresnel term F using c{\text{specular}} and \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{h}. 8. Compute specular BRDF: f{\text{spec}} = (D F G) / (4 (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})). 9. Compute diffuse BRDF: f{\text{diff}} = c{\text{base}} / \pi. 10. Return fr = f{\text{diff}} + f{\text{spec}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isotropicdisneybrdf(x, omegai, omegao, n, cbase, s, r, m): # 1. Retrieve base color cbaseval = cbase.sample(x) # 2. Compute half vector h = omegai + omegao hlen = sqrt(dot(h, h)) if hlen == 0: return 0.0 h = h / hlen # 3. Precompute alpha and k alpha = r r k = (r + 1.0) / 8.0 # 4. Evaluate NDF D nh = dot(n, h) if nh <= 0: return 0.0 denom = (nh nh) (alpha alpha - 1.0) + 1.0 D = (alpha alpha) / (3.141592653589793 denom denom) # 5. Evaluate Geometry G nl = dot(n, omegai) nv = dot(n, omegao) if nl <= 0 or nv <= 0: return 0.0 G = ((nl (1.0 - k) + k) (nv (1.0 - k) + k)) # 6. Compute cspecular cspec = (1.0 - m) 0.08 s + m cbaseval # 7. Evaluate Fresnel F vh = dot(omegao, h) exponent = 2.0 (-5.55473 vh - 6.98316) F = cspec + (1.0 - cspec) exponent # 8. Compute specular term fspec = (D F G) / (4.0 nl nv) # 9. Compute diffuse term fdiff = cbaseval / 3.141592653589793 # 10. Blend return fdiff + fspec Parameters: c{\text{base}}: Base color / diffuse albedo, range [0, 1]^3. s: Specular albedo, range [0, 1]. r: Roughness (or \beta), range [0, 1]. m: Metalness, range [0, 1]. Edge Cases: Backface or grazing angles where \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} \le 0 or \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} \le 0 yield zero contribution. The denominator in D approaches 1 when \alpha \to 0 or \alpha \to 1, preventing division by zero. To evaluate the rendering equation at point \mathbf{x} with normal \mathbf{n} and view direction \omegao, the distribution D is spherically warped and M (Fresnel/shadowing) is approximated by a constant at \mathbf{x}. The warped distribution is Dx(\mathbf{h}) = G(\mathbf{h}; \mathbf{n}, \frac{\lambda}{4\mathbf{h} \cdot \omegao}, \mu), and the constant approximation is Mx(\omegao, \omegai) \approx M(\omegao, 2(\omegao \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} - \omegai). The specular BRDF becomes fs(\omegao, \omegai; \mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{h}; \mathbf{n}, \frac{\lambda}{4\mathbf{h} \cdot \omegao}, Mx \mu), combining the warped distribution and constant M into a single SG representation. Evaluation is a direct formula computation per sample. The model is used in Monte Carlo shading, requiring N importance-sampled light directions to compute the final pixel color as an average. Strengths include a unified framework for metals and plastics, intuitive parameters, and reduced optimization ambiguity by restricting to opaque surfaces. Limitations include the simplified nature compared to the full Disney Principled BRDF (e.g., missing clearcoat/sheen) and the isotropic specular assumption. It is chosen when optimizing material parameters for opaque surfaces in differentiable rendering pipelines. The model originates from the Disney Principled BRDF, a widely adopted material model in movies and games that captures versatile appearances with intuitive controls. The simplified isotropic version was adapted for differentiable rendering contexts, such as DIB-R++ and texture-space differentiable rendering, to facilitate learning and optimization of lighting and material parameters while restricting ambiguity. name: Ward Anisotropic BRDF
head: Wald Anisotropic BRDF, Ward Anisotropic Mapping, Ward BRDF parameter mapping, Ward model, anisotropic material standardized by Wald model
body: The Ward Anisotropic BRDF is a microfacet specular reflection model that modifies the Beckmann distribution to simulate surface roughness varying in two orthogonal directions relative to the tangent space. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific parameterization of anisotropy via the ratio of eigenvalues from a covariance matrix, allowing for position-dependent control of highlight stretching. Unlike the isotropic GGX model, it explicitly decouples roughness along the tangent and bitangent axes. The method computes the specular reflection using the Cook-Torrance framework, where the Ward model specifically defines the Normal Distribution Function (NDF). The core innovation described in the sources is the "Ward Anisotropic Mapping," which derives position-dependent anisotropy parameters from global user controls and local surface geometry. Inputs: \kappaw: Global glossiness parameter (analogous to Blinn-Phong exponent). Range: \kappaw > 0. \gammaw: Global anisotropy scaling factor. Range: \gammaw \ge 0. \lambda1(x), \lambda2(x): Eigenvalues of the local covariance matrix describing surface anisotropy at position x, where \lambda1(x) \le \lambda2(x). \alphax, \alphay: Roughness parameters in the tangent space x and y directions. \mathbf{h}: Half-vector between incident and outgoing directions. \mathbf{n}: Surface normal. Outputs: D(\mathbf{h}): The Ward Normal Distribution Function value. uw(x), vw(x): Position-dependent anisotropy parameters used in the NDF. The method requires the storage of: 1. Global parameters \kappaw and \gammaw. 2. Local eigenvalues \lambda1(x) and \lambda2(x) derived from surface analysis. 3. Tangent space basis vectors (\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{b}) to define the x and y roughness directions. 1. Compute Anisotropy Mapping: Calculate the position-dependent parameters uw(x) and vw(x) using the global glossiness \kappaw, the anisotropy scaling \gammaw, and the ratio of the eigenvalues: uw(x) = \kappaw \left( \frac{\lambda2(x)}{\lambda1(x)} \right)^{\gammaw} vw(x) = \kappaw \left( \frac{\lambda1(x)}{\lambda2(x)} \right)^{\gammaw} Note: The source equations (32) and (33) in show uw scaling with \lambda2/\lambda1 and vw scaling with the inverse ratio (implied by symmetry and the condition uw=vw when \lambda1=\lambda2). The source text explicitly writes: uw(x) = \kappaw \left( \frac{\lambda2(x)}{\lambda1(x)} \right)^{\gammaw}, \quad vw(x) = \kappaw \left( \frac{\lambda1(x)}{\lambda2(x)} \right)^{\gammaw}. 2. Evaluate NDF: Compute the Ward distribution function D(\mathbf{h}). The source states the model modifies the Beckmann distribution factor. The standard Ward NDF is: D(\mathbf{h}) = \frac{1}{\pi uw vw \cos^4 \thetah} \exp \left( -\tan^2 \thetah \left( \frac{\cos^2 \phih}{uw^2} + \frac{\sin^2 \phih}{vw^2} \right) \right) Where: \thetah is the angle between \mathbf{h} and \mathbf{n}. \phih is the azimuth angle of \mathbf{h} in the tangent space. uw, vw are the parameters from Step 1. 3. Importance Sampling (Optional): To sample the distribution, generate two uniform random variables u1, u2 \in [0, 1]. Solve for the azimuth angle \phi and altitude angle \theta. The source notes that it is "easy to solve the equations" but does not provide the explicit inverse sampling formulas. Isotropy Condition: When \lambda1(x) = \lambda2(x), the ratio is 1. Consequently, uw(x) = vw(x) = \kappaw. The distribution becomes isotropic, determined solely by \kappaw. Anisotropy Scaling: When \lambda1(x) < \lambda2(x), the ratio > 1. The parameter \gammaw scales this anisotropy. If \gammaw > 1, anisotropy is amplified. If \gammaw < 1, it is damped. If \gammaw = 0, uw = vw = \kappaw, resulting in isotropic shading regardless of the eigenvalue ratio. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wardanisotropicmapping(lambda1, lambda2, kappaw, gammaw): """ Computes position-dependent anisotropy parameters for the Ward BRDF. Args: lambda1 (float): Smaller eigenvalue of the covariance matrix. lambda2 (float): Larger eigenvalue of the covariance matrix. kappaw (float): Global glossiness parameter (> 0). gammaw (float): Global anisotropy scaling factor (>= 0). Returns: tuple: (uw, vw) anisotropy parameters. """ # Guard against division by zero if lambda1 is 0 if lambda1 == 0: # If lambda1 is 0, the surface is perfectly aligned in one direction. # The ratio lambda2/lambda1 approaches infinity. # If gammaw > 0, uw -> infinity, vw -> 0. # This represents extreme anisotropy. # For numerical stability, clamp or handle as limit. # Standard practice: if lambda1 is effectively 0, # treat as highly anisotropic. uw = float('inf') vw = 0.0 else: ratio = lambda2 / lambda1 uw = kappaw (ratio gammaw) vw = kappaw (ratio (-gammaw)) return uw, vw def wardndf(hdotn, cosphih, sinphih, uw, vw): """ Computes the Ward Normal Distribution Function value. Args: hdotn (float): Cosine of the angle between half-vector and normal. cosphih (float): Cosine of azimuth angle of half-vector in tangent space. sinphih (float): Sine of azimuth angle of half-vector in tangent space. uw (float): X-direction anisotropy parameter. vw (float): Y-direction anisotropy parameter. Returns: float: NDF value. """ # Guard against division by zero if uw == 0 or vw == 0: return 0.0 costhetah = hdotn sinthetahsq = 1.0 - costhetah costhetah # tan^2(thetah) if costhetah == 0: tanthetahsq = float('inf') else: tanthetahsq = sinthetahsq / (costhetah costhetah) # Exponent term exponent = -tanthetahsq ( (cosphih cosphih) / (uw uw) + (sinphih sinphih) / (vw vw)) # Prefactor: 1 / (pi uw vw cos^4(thetah)) costhetah4 = costhetah costhetah costhetah costhetah if costhetah4 == 0: return 0.0 prefactor = 1.0 / (3.141592653589793 uw vw costhetah4) return prefactor math.exp(exponent) Isotropic Regions: In regions where \lambda1(x) = \lambda2(x), the ratio is 1. This results in uw(x) = vw(x) = \kappaw, yielding isotropic shading regardless of \gammaw. Zero Anisotropy Scaling: If \gammaw = 0, the exponent in the mapping function becomes 0, making uw = vw = \kappaw. This forces isotropic shading even if \lambda1 \neq \lambda2. Eigenvalue Ratio: The mapping relies on \lambda1(x) > 0. If \lambda1(x) = 0, the ratio is undefined/infinite, leading to extreme anisotropy values. A parameterization technique that maps global glossiness and anisotropy controls to position-dependent BRDF parameters using eigenvalue ratios. It allows artists to control the "stretch" of highlights globally while respecting local surface structure. Choose when you need position-dependent anisotropy driven by surface covariance. The specific probability distribution function used in the Cook-Torrance model. It differs from GGX by using a Gaussian-like exponent in the tangent space. Choose when simulating brushed metals or surfaces with elliptical highlights. Time Complexity: The evaluation of the mapping function is O(1). The NDF evaluation involves exponentials and divisions, also O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1) for parameters. Requires storage of eigenvalues if precomputed. Strengths: Provides intuitive global control (\kappaw, \gammaw) over local anisotropy. Handles the transition from isotropic to anisotropic smoothly via \gammaw. Limitations: The source does not provide closed-form importance sampling equations, making efficient path tracing harder to implement compared to GGX. The Beckmann-based NDF may not match measured data as well as GGX for certain materials. When to use: When simulating anisotropic materials like brushed metal or hair, and when the surface anisotropy is derived from a covariance matrix analysis. When not to use: When high-performance importance sampling is required and closed-form solutions are not available. The Ward BRDF was introduced by Ward in 1992. It is a modification of the Cook-Torrance microfacet model, specifically altering the Beckmann distribution factor to account for anisotropy. The "Ward Anisotropic Mapping" technique described in was developed later (2015) to standardize the parameterization of anisotropic materials, allowing for global control parameters (\kappaw, \gammaw) that are independent of the specific BRDF implementation. It is used in rendering systems that support anisotropic materials, such as the path tracer described in. name: GGX Specular Shading
body: GGX Specular Shading is a path-tracing shading method for voxel-based volume rendering that combines a Cook-Torrance microfacet model with GGX specular reflection, Lambertian diffuse shading from an irradiance cache, and dielectric transmission handling. It differs from its parent GGX Microfacet BRDF by providing the complete shading loop (emission, reflection, refraction, and diffuse accumulation) rather than just the BRDF components. It is distinct from Specular Reflection by including transmission and diffuse GI, and from Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel by using the full Cook-Torrance formulation with explicit transmission logic. Inputs: rayDir: Current ray direction (normalized). normal: Surface normal at hit point (normalized). material: Material properties including albedo (RGB), metallic (float), roughness (float), transmission (float), ior (float), emissioncolor (RGB), emissionstrength (float). ugi: Irradiance cache texture for diffuse GI. ugiscale: Scale factor for GI contribution. rng: Random number generator state. umaxbounces: Maximum path depth. Outputs: radiance: Accumulated radiance value. Data Structures: Material: Defined in. Fields: id, name, usevoxelcolor, albedo (tuple), metallic, roughness, emissioncolor, emissionstrength, emissionusevoxelcolor, transmission, ior, flags, extra. VoxelGrid: Defined in. Fields: rgba (4D array), materialid (3D array), dims. Steps: 1. Initialize radiance = 0, throughput = 1. 2. Loop bounce from 0 to umaxbounces: a. Add throughput material.emission material.emissionstrength to radiance. b. If material.transmission > 0.0: i. Compute viewFresnel using Schlick approximation or similar for dielectric: F0 = mix(vec3(0.04), material.albedo, material.metallic). For dielectric transmission, use ior to compute Fresnel reflectance. ii. Sample random01(rng). If random01(rng) < fresneldielectric(abs(dot(rayDir, normal)), material.ior), set rayDir to reflected direction and continue. iii. Else, call transmitblock. If transmitblock returns false, add throughput sampleenv(rayDir) to radiance and break loop. c. If landed is true (hit surface): i. Update hit point, cell, normal, and material. ii. If material is opaque (or after reflection): 1. Compute view = -rayDir. 2. Compute ndv = max(dot(normal, view), 1e-4). 3. Compute Fresnel F0: fresnelF0 = mix(vec3(0.04), material.albedo, material.metallic). 4. Compute diffuse term: diffuse = (1.0 - viewFresnel) (1.0 - material.metallic) material.albedo. 5. Add diffuse radiance: throughput diffuse texelFetch(ugi,...).rgb ugiscale. 6. Sample GGX microfacet normal: microNormal = ggxsample(normal, material.roughness, rng). 7. Compute reflected direction using microNormal and view. 8. Update throughput by multiplying with BRDF value and ndv. 9. Update rayDir to reflected direction. d. If landed is false (missed or transmitted out), break loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ggxspecularshading(raydir, normal, material, ugi, ugiscale, rng, umaxbounces): radiance = 0.0 throughput = 1.0 raydir = normalize(raydir) normal = normalize(normal) for bounce in range(umaxbounces): # Add emission emission = material.emissioncolor material.emissionstrength radiance += throughput emission # Handle transmission if material.transmission > 0.0: # Dielectric Fresnel ndv = abs(dot(normal, raydir)) # Simplified Schlick for dielectric with IOR f0 = 0.04 # Default for dielectric # More accurate: f0 = ((ior - 1) / (ior + 1))2 fresnel = f0 + (1.0 - f0) (1.0 - ndv)5 if random01(rng) < fresnel: # Reflect raydir = reflect(raydir, normal) continue else: # Transmit if not transmitblock(raydir, normal, material.ior, rng): # Hit environment or failed transmission radiance += throughput sampleenv(raydir) break # Handle opaque/reflected shading # Assume landed is true if we are shading a surface view = -raydir ndv = max(dot(normal, view), 1e-4) # Fresnel for metal/dielectric mix fresnelF0 = mix(vec3(0.04), material.albedo, material.metallic) viewFresnel = fresnelF0 + (1.0 - fresnelF0) (1.0 - ndv)5 # Diffuse term diffuse = (1.0 - viewFresnel) (1.0 - material.metallic) material.albedo # Add diffuse GI # texelFetch depends on UV coordinates, assumed to be available gicolor = texelFetch(ugi,...) # Placeholder for UV lookup radiance += throughput diffuse gicolor ugiscale # Specular term micronormal = ggxsample(normal, material.roughness, rng) halfvec = normalize(view + micronormal) # For reflection, halfvec is not directly used for direction, but micronormal is # Reflected direction raydir = reflect(raydir, micronormal) # Update throughput # BRDF = D G F / (4 |n.o| |n.i|) # D = ggxdistribution(micronormal, normal, material.roughness) # G = schlickggx(micronormal, normal, view, material.roughness) # F = fresnelschlick(ndv, fresnelF0) # throughput = D G F / (4.0 ndv ndv) # Simplified, actual G and D needed # For simplicity, assuming throughput update is handled by BRDF evaluation # throughput = brdfvalue ndv # Standard path tracing throughput update # If opaque, we might break or continue depending on implementation # The source implies continuing the loop for bounces Parameters: umaxbounces: Maximum number of bounces. Typical value: Not given in the sources. ugiscale: Scale for GI contribution. Typical value: Not given in the sources. roughness: GGX roughness parameter. Typical value: 0.5 (from Material default). ior: Index of refraction. Typical value: 1.45 (from Material default). Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: Use 1e-4 for ndv to avoid division by zero. Boundaries: Handle transmission failures gracefully by sampling environment. Degenerate input: Ensure normal and raydir are normalized. A modification of the Cook-Torrance model for surface-to-surface refraction by recalculating the Jacobian matrix for the transform between half-vector and outgoing vector. The refraction BSDF is given by fr = \frac{D \cdot G \cdot F}{4 \cdot |n \cdot o| \cdot |n \cdot i| \cdot |J|}, where D is the microfacet distribution function (Beckmann), G is the shadowing term (numerical approximation to Smith shadowing function), F is Fresnel, and J is the Jacobian determinant. The half-vector in refraction indicates the normal of the sampled microfacet, obtained by h = \text{normalize}(v + l) if BSDF needs to be determined from arbitrary incoming and outgoing radiance. For anisotropic materials, the roughness coefficient inside the shadowing term G is substituted by 1/\sqrt{\text{roughness}x \cdot \text{roughness}y}. Time complexity: Linear in the number of bounces, with GGX sampling and Fresnel calculations per bounce. Memory complexity: Depends on the irradiance cache size and material library. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with resolution and scene complexity. Strengths: Physically based, handles both reflection and transmission, integrates with GI. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to path tracing and GGX sampling. When to use: For realistic rendering of dielectric and metallic surfaces in voxel environments. When not: For real-time applications requiring high performance, or for non-physically based rendering. Originated from the Cook-Torrance microfacet model and GGX distribution, adapted for voxel-based volume rendering. The refraction variant with Jacobian calculation is based on Walter et al. (2007). Used in voxel-based rendering systems like Voxmat. name: Light Evaluation for SDF Faces
body: This method applies diffuse, specular, and ambient lighting to a face color based on a surface normal and light direction. It operates directly on discretized face geometry data rather than integrating light along a ray. Inputs: faceColor: A float4 containing the base RGB color and alpha (\alpha) of the surface face. n: The surface normal vector (\mathbf{n}), typically derived from the SDF gradient. LightAngle: A scalar defining the light direction via sine and cosine parameters. Diffuse: A scalar diffuse intensity factor. Ambient: A scalar ambient intensity factor. Outputs: color: A float4 representing the final lit color and alpha. Data Structures: The normal \mathbf{n} is a normalized 3D vector. The light direction \mathbf{l} is constructed from LightAngle. Steps: 1. Normal Adjustment: Set the z-component of the normal to its absolute value: nz = |nz|. 2. Light Direction Construction: Construct the light direction vector \mathbf{l} from the sine and cosine of LightAngle, then normalize it. 3. Specular Addition: Compute the base color clamped to zero, add the specular contribution scaled by the face alpha: \mathbf{c} = \max(\text{faceColor.rgb}, 0) + \text{GetSpecular}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}) \times \text{faceColor.a}. 4. Diffuse Modulation: Multiply the color by the factor (1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \times \Diffuse): \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} \times (1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \times \Diffuse). 5. Ambient/Height Modulation: Multiply the color by a linear interpolation between Ambient and 1 controlled by the squared z-component of the normal: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} \times \text{lerp}(\Ambient, 1, nz^2). 6. Output Assembly: Set the final color to \text{float4}(\mathbf{c}, \text{faceColor.a}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def evaluatelightface(facecolor, normal, lightangle, diffuse, ambient): # 1. Normal adjustment: n.z = abs(n.z) n = [normal[0], normal[1], abs(normal[2])] # 2. Light direction: normalize light vector from sin/cos of LightAngle sinval = math.sin(lightangle) cosval = math.cos(lightangle) lightdir = [cosval, sinval, 0.0] mag = math.sqrt(lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2) lightdir = [lightdir[i] / mag for i in range(3)] # 3. Specular addition: col = max(faceColor.rgb, 0) + GetSpecular(n, light) faceColor.a # GetSpecular implementation not provided in sources # Standard Blinn-Phong specular calculation specular = computespecular(n, lightdir) basergb = [max(facecolor[i], 0.0) for i in range(3)] litcolor = [basergb[i] + specular[i] facecolor[3] for i in range(3)] # 4. Diffuse modulation: col = (1 - dot(n, light) Diffuse) dotnl = n[0]lightdir[0] + n[1]lightdir[1] + n[2]lightdir[2] litcolor = [litcolor[i] (1.0 - dotnl diffuse) for i in range(3)] # 5. Ambient/Height modulation: col = lerp(Ambient, 1, n.z n.z) heightfactor = n[2] n[2] ambientblend = ambient + (1.0 - ambient) heightfactor finalcolor = [litcolor[i] ambientblend for i in range(3)] # 6. Output assembly: color = float4(col, faceColor.a) return [finalcolor[0], finalcolor[1], finalcolor[2], facecolor[3]] def computespecular(n, l): # Standard Blinn-Phong specular calculation halfvec = [l[i] + n[i] for i in range(3)] hmag = math.sqrt(halfvec[0]2 + halfvec[1]2 + halfvec[2]2) halfvec = [halfvec[i] / hmag for i in range(3)] dotnh = max(halfvec[0]n[0] + halfvec[1]n[1] + halfvec[2]n[2], 0.0) specval = dotnh 32 return [specval, specval, specval] This variant integrates lighting directly into the SDF gradient evaluation loop. It calculates the gradient at the current ray-marched position to determine the normal dynamically, rather than relying on pre-computed normals. Steps: Calculate the gradient at the current position: \mathbf{g} = \nabla f(\mathbf{p}). Calculate the magnitude: m = \|\mathbf{g}\|. Normalize to get the normal: \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{g} / m. Calculate lighting using the color, normal, light direction, and view direction: \text{col.rgb} = \text{calculateLighting}(\text{col.rgb}, \mathbf{n}, \text{getLightDirection}(-\text{ray.direction}), -\text{ray.direction}, 0.15). Set alpha to 1.0 and break the marching loop: \text{col.a} = 1.0; \text{break}. Parameters: MinGradient is the minimum gradient magnitude threshold required to consider a voxel as a surface for lighting calculation. MinVal is the minimum density value threshold for surface detection. MaxVal is the maximum density value threshold for surface detection. Pitfalls: If the gradient magnitude is zero or very small, division by zero occurs during normalization. The code assumes gradMag > MinGradient before normalizing, implying a check or clamp is handled elsewhere or MinGradient prevents zero division. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. This method originates from implementations in Unity-based SDF renderers, specifically the unity-nanovdb-renderer and UnityVolumeRendering projects. andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GitHub - mlavik1/UnityVolumeRendering: Volume rendering, implemented in..., https://github.com/mlavik1/UnityVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Blinn-Phong with Metallic Reflections
head: Neon City Lighting, Wet Asphalt Shader
body: A custom shading model for ray-marched signed distance fields that extends the classic Blinn-Phong approximation with environment reflections and emissive contributions to simulate urban night scenes. It distinguishes itself from standard Blinn-Phong by modulating specular intensity, power, and reflection weight based on a material's metallic property, and from GGX microfacet models by using a simplified Schlick-like Fresnel term rather than a full microfacet distribution. Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p} in world space. Ray direction \mathbf{rd} (from camera to \mathbf{p}, normalized). Material structure sf containing albedo (base color), metal (float in [0, 1]), and emissive (self-illuminated color). Scene functions: calcNormal(p), softShadow(p, l, radius), calcAO(p, n), skyColor(r). Outputs: Final color vec3. Data Structures: The material structure sf is determined by a material ID derived from the SDF evaluation (e.g., via hashing cell coordinates). Steps: 1. Calculate normal \mathbf{n} = \text{calcNormal}(\mathbf{p}). 2. Determine surface properties (sf.albedo, sf.metal, sf.emissive) based on material ID. 3. Define light direction \mathbf{l} = \text{normalize}(\text{vec3}(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25)) and light color \mathbf{c}L = \text{vec3}(0.5, 0.65, 1.0). 4. Calculate diffuse factor d = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0.0). 5. Calculate shadow factor s = \text{softShadow}(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \cdot 0.03, \mathbf{l}, 12.0). 6. Apply shadow to diffuse: d \leftarrow d \cdot s. 7. Calculate half-vector \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{rd}). 8. Calculate specular intensity \text{spec} = \text{pow}(\max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0), \text{mix}(32.0, 140.0, \text{sf.metal})) \cdot s. 9. Calculate ambient occlusion \text{ao} = \text{calcAO}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{n}). 10. Calculate base color \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} = \text{sf.albedo} \cdot (\text{ambient} \cdot \text{ao}) + \text{sf.albedo} \cdot \mathbf{c}L \cdot d + \mathbf{c}L \cdot \text{spec} \cdot \text{mix}(0.4, 2.0, \text{sf.metal}). 11. Calculate Fresnel term F = \text{pow}(1.0 - \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot (-\mathbf{rd}), 0.0), 5.0). 12. Calculate reflected color \mathbf{c}{\text{refl}} = \text{skyColor}(\text{reflect}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n})). 13. Add reflection contribution: \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} \leftarrow \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} + \mathbf{c}{\text{refl}} \cdot \text{mix}(0.03, 0.6, \text{sf.metal}) \cdot (0.25 + 0.75 \cdot F) \cdot \text{ao}. 14. Add emissive contribution: \mathbf{c}{\text{final}} = \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} + \text{sf.emissive}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def reflect(I, N): return I - 2.0 dot(I, N) N def blinnphongmetallic(p, rd, sf, ambient=0.16): n = calcNormal(p) l = normalize(vec3(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25)) cL = vec3(0.5, 0.65, 1.0) d = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) s = softShadow(p + n 0.03, l, 12.0) d = d s h = normalize(l - rd) spec = pow(max(dot(n, h), 0.0), mix(32.0, 140.0, sf.metal)) s ao = calcAO(p, n) cbase = sf.albedo (ambient ao) + sf.albedo cL d + cL spec mix(0.4, 2.0, sf.metal) F = pow(1.0 - max(dot(n, -rd), 0.0), 5.0) crefl = skyColor(reflect(rd, n)) cbase = cbase + crefl mix(0.03, 0.6, sf.metal) (0.25 + 0.75 F) ao cfinal = cbase + sf.emissive return cfinal Parameters: Light Direction: \text{vec3}(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25) Light Color: \text{vec3}(0.5, 0.65, 1.0) Ambient Intensity: 0.16 Specular Power: Interpolated between 32.0 (non-metal) and 140.0 (metal) Specular Intensity Multiplier: Interpolated between 0.4 (non-metal) and 2.0 (metal) Fresnel Power: 5.0 Reflection Intensity: Interpolated between 0.03 (non-metal) and 0.6 (metal) Fresnel Reflection Weight: 0.25 + 0.75 \cdot F Edge Cases: If \mathbf{n} is zero (degenerate SDF), the normal must be clamped or defaulted to \text{vec3}(0,1,0) to avoid division by zero in normalization. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. The model is defined in the referenced codebase as a lighting model combining Blinn-Phong diffuse/specular, metallic environment reflections weighted by a Schlick-like Fresnel term, and emissive contributions for neon effects. name: Multidirectional Occlusion Shading
head: Elliptical Kernel Convolution, M-DOS, Multidirectional OS, Multidirectional Occlusion Model
body: Multidirectional Occlusion Shading (M-DOS) is a direct volume rendering technique that simulates directional light scattering to produce realistic soft-shadowing and depth cues. Unlike the original MS-DOS model, which constrains the light direction to the viewing direction and uses symmetric disc-shaped Gaussian kernels, M-DOS allows arbitrary light positioning within the hemisphere defined by the view vector by using elliptical footprints derived from a tilted cone. It achieves this through incremental convolution of an opacity buffer, requiring no precomputation and maintaining interactive frame rates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume dataset, camera parameters (view direction \mathbf{v}), light source parameters (position or direction \mathbf{l}), aperture angle \theta, tilt angle \alpha. Outputs: Final rendered image with shading effects. Data Structures: Opacity Buffer (Oi): A 2D texture storing the accumulated opacity for slice i, initialized to zero. Color Buffer (Ci): A 2D texture storing the accumulated color for slice i. Kernel Texture (G\epsilon): A 128 \times 128 texture storing the elliptical weighting function. Parameters: \theta (theta): Aperture angle of the conical phase function. \alpha (alpha): Tilt angle of the conical phase function, determining the light direction relative to the view. R: Distance from the scattering point to the slice plane, derived from the geometric setup. Geometric Setup: The method approximates light transport using a tilted cone-shaped phase function \Phi{\theta,\alpha}. The axis of the cone is parallel to the light direction \mathbf{l}. The intersection of this cone with the viewing plane (slice plane) forms an ellipse \epsilon. The ellipse is defined by its major axis A and minor axis B. 1. Calculate Ellipse Axes: The distances a1 and a2 from the center O to the edges of the ellipse along the major axis are: a1 = R \frac{\sin(\pi/2 - \theta)}{\sin(\pi/2 + \theta - \alpha)} a2 = R \frac{\sin(\pi/2 + \theta)}{\sin(\pi/2 - \theta - \alpha)} The major axis A is: A = \frac{a1 + a2}{2} The distance from the center O to the ellipse center C is: kOCk = \frac{|a2 - a1|}{2} The minor axis B is calculated using a modified radius R' and modified distance d': B = \sqrt{R'^2 - kOCk^2 + d'^2} where R' and d' are derived from the geometric intersection analysis involving the circle \kappa intersecting at C. 2. Define Weighting Function: The weighting function WL(x,y) at position (x,y) relative to the ellipse center is defined implicitly by k: WL(x, y) = 1 - k where k is the solution to the quadratic equation: \frac{(x - (1-k)kOCk)^2}{A^2} + \frac{y^2}{B^2} = k^2 The point O represents the projection of the light vector and has the highest incident energy. 3. Kernel Alignment: The kernel G\epsilon is aligned with the light direction by rotating it so its major axis aligns with the 2D projection of the light vector \mathbf{L'} on the viewing plane: \frac{\mathbf{L'}}{k\mathbf{L'}k} = \frac{\mathbf{OC}}{kOCk} The kernel is stored in a texture and updated whenever lighting parameters change. Algorithm Steps: The rendering proceeds slice-by-slice in front-to-back order. For each slice i: 1. Compute Modulation Factor: Calculate the visibility \lambdai for the current slice using the previous slice's opacity buffer O{i-1} and the elliptical kernel G\epsilon: \lambdai = \frac{1}{1 + G\epsilon O{i-1}} where denotes convolution. 2. Update Opacity Buffer: Convolve the previous opacity buffer with the kernel and add the current slice's opacity \alphai: Oi = G\epsilon O{i-1} + \alphai 3. Modulate Color: Multiply the current slice's color contribution ci by the modulation factor \lambdai: c'i = ci \cdot \lambdai 4. Composite: Propagate the modified color c'i and the current opacity \alphai to the next composite step using traditional alpha-blending with the over operator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multidirectionalocclusionshading(volumeslices, viewportwidth, viewportheight, theta, alpha, lightdir): # Initialize buffers Oprev = [[0.0] viewportwidth for in range(viewportheight)] Cprev = [[0.0] viewportwidth for in range(viewportheight)] # Generate elliptical kernel Gepsilon # R is derived from slice distance; compute a1, a2, A, B, kOCk # Solve implicit quadratic for WL(x,y) to fill kernel texture Gepsilon = generateellipticalkernel(theta, alpha, R, viewportwidth, viewportheight) # Rotate kernel to align major axis with 2D projection of lightdir Gepsilon = rotatekernel(Gepsilon, lightdir) for slice in volumeslices: # 1. Get current slice opacity and color alphai = min(1.0, max(0.0, slice.opacity)) ci = slice.color # 2. Calculate modulation factor lambdai blurredopacity = convolve2d(Oprev, Gepsilon) lambdai = [1.0 / (1.0 + rowval) for rowval in blurredopacity] # 3. Update opacity buffer for next slice Onext = [[blurredopacity[r][c] + alphai for c in range(viewportwidth)] for r in range(viewportheight)] # 4. Modulate color cmodulated = [[ci[r][c] lambdai[r][c] for c in range(viewportwidth)] for r in range(viewportheight)] # 5. Composite using over operator Cnext = [[(cmodulated[r][c] alphai) + (Cprev[r][c] (1.0 - alphai)) for c in range(viewportwidth)] for r in range(viewportheight)] # Update buffers for next iteration Oprev = Onext Cprev = Cnext return Cprev def zeroslike(shape): return [[0.0] shape[1] for in range(shape[0])] def convolve2d(buffer, kernel): # Standard 2D convolution with boundary clamping h, w = len(buffer), len(buffer[0]) kh, kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0]) result = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] padh, padw = kh // 2, kw // 2 for r in range(h): for c in range(w): acc = 0.0 for kr in range(kh): for kc in range(kw): br, bc = r + kr - padh, c + kc - padw if 0 <= br < h and 0 <= bc < w: acc += buffer[br][bc] kernel[kr][kc] result[r][c] = acc return result def generateellipticalkernel(theta, alpha, R, width, height): # Compute a1, a2, A, B, kOCk from formulas # Solve WL(x,y) = 1 - k for each pixel relative to ellipse center # Scale and rotate to fit texture bounding box pass # Implementation follows standard implicit surface rasterization def rotatekernel(kernel, lightdir): # Apply 2D rotation matrix to align major axis with light projection pass # Standard matrix rotation applied to kernel coordinates Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Geometry: The tilt angle \alpha must be limited to 0, \pi/2 - \theta) to prevent the cone-section from degenerating into hyperbolas or parabolas. Precision Loss: Massive downscaling of the coordinate system to fit the kernel into the texture bounding box may lead to a loss of precision. Light Direction: The method assumes the light source is within the hemisphere defined by the view vector; traversal reversal for opposite hemisphere lights is a potential extension but not part of the core method. Kernel Updates: The kernel G\epsilon is only recomputed when tilt, aperture, light direction, or slice distance changes, which may cause artifacts if parameters change rapidly without triggering an update. Time Complexity: The method performs an incremental convolution per slice. The convolution cost depends on the kernel size, which is fixed at 128 \times 128 in the source. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two render targets (intermediate image and occlusion buffer) per slice and one kernel texture (128 \times 128). Performance: Performs at interactive frame-rates with negligible performance penalty compared to state-of-the-art models. No precomputation is required. Strengths: Allows arbitrary light positioning within the view hemisphere; gradient-free (suitable for noisy data like ultrasound); no precomputation or additional data storage compared to shadow maps or light volumes. Limitations: Precision loss due to kernel scaling; limited to the hemisphere defined by the view vector without traversal reversal; artifacts may occur if the light direction changes rapidly without kernel updates. Origin: Developed by Veronika Šoltészová, Daniel Patel, Stefan Bruckner, and Ivan Viola. Paper: "A Multidirectional Occlusion Shading Model for Direct Volume Rendering" (2010). Development: Extends the original MS-DOS model by Mathias [Schott et al. (2009), which constrained light to the viewing direction and used symmetric disc-shaped Gaussian kernels. M-DOS removes this constraint using elliptical footprints derived from a tilted cone. Usage: Implemented as a plugin to VolumeShop using C++ and OpenGL/GLSL. Used to visualize CT datasets (gecko, carp, human foot, human hand, human thorax) and 3D cardiac ultrasound. User studies showed high preference for directional lighting over headlamp or raycasting for depth cues.
