name: Single-Atomic High-Quality Robust Variant (HQS1R)
head: Compute-based blending, High-Quality Shader, High-Quality Shader with Single Atomic Reduction, Robust high-quality shading with overflow protection
body: HQS1R is a high-quality point cloud rendering method that reduces aliasing by blending overlapping points together, similar to mipmapping. It is a simplified, compute-based implementation of the blending algorithm from [BHZK05], designed to be faster than aliased GLPOINTS results while providing anti-aliasing. Unlike surface splatting [ZPVG01], it blends overlapping points without considering oriented disks with variable radii. It sets itself apart from the Single-Atomic High-Quality Variant (HQS1x) by using a robust overflow protection mechanism that prevents artifacts when more than 255 points contribute to a pixel. HQS1R operates on a set of points, each with a position and color. It computes the average color of overlapping points within a depth range using a single 64-bit atomic operation per point in the fast path, with overflow protection via fallback buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of points, each defined by a 3D position \mathbf{p} and a color \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b). Output: A framebuffer containing the average color for each pixel, resolved from the main buffer and fallback buffers. Data Structures: The method uses a custom 64-bit integer layout to pack color and count data. 1. Main Buffer (ssRGBA): A 64-bit integer per pixel. Bits 0-15: Count (Alpha/Counter). Bits 16-31: Blue component (b). Bits 32-47: Green component (g). Bits 48-63: Red component (r). Format: 16-16-16-16 bit pattern. 2. Fallback Buffers: Two 64-bit integer buffers per pixel, used when the main buffer count exceeds 255. fallback[2 pixelID + 0]: Stores Red (bits 32-63) and Green (bits 0-31). fallback[2 pixelID + 1]: Stores Blue (bits 32-63) and Alpha/Count (bits 0-31). Format: 16-16-16-16 bit pattern. Numbered Steps: 1. Depth Map Pass (Required for high-quality variations): Compute a depth map over all points, resulting in a total of two geometry passes and one screen pass. 2. Screen Pass (Render Pass): For each point: a. Transform the point position to screen space and determine the pixel ID (pixelID) it covers. b. Encode the point's color (r, g, b) and a count of 1 into a 64-bit integer rgba: \text{rgba} = (r \ll 48) \mid (g \ll 32) \mid (b \ll 16) \mid 1 where r, g, b are 16-bit unsigned integers. c. Perform an atomic addition of rgba to the main framebuffer buffer ssRGBA at pixelID, storing the previous value in old: \text{old} = \text{atomicAdd}(\text{ssRGBA}[\text{pixelID}], \text{rgba}) d. Extract the lower 16 bits of old to get the previous count: \text{count} = \text{old} \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} e. Check if count >= 255. If true, an overflow condition is detected. f. If count == 255 (indicating this is the first thread to overflow for this pixel): i. Atomically exchange the main buffer value to 0 to reset it: \text{atomicExchange}(\text{ssRGBA}[\text{pixelID}], 0) ii. Extract the previous color components from old and accumulate them into local variables r, g, b, and set a=1: r += (\text{old} \gg 48) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} g += (\text{old} \gg 32) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} b += (\text{old} \gg 16) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} a = 1 iii. Add 255 to a to account for the points already counted in the buffer before the reset: a += 255 g. If overflow was detected (count >= 255): i. Encode the accumulated color (r, g) and accumulated alpha/count (b, a) into two 64-bit integers: \text{rg} = (r \ll 32) \mid g \text{ba} = (b \ll 32) \mid a ii. Write the accumulated values to the two separate fallback buffers using atomicAdd. Indices are fallback[2 pixelID + 0] for rg and fallback[2 pixelID + 1] for ba: \text{atomicAdd}(\text{fallback}[2 \times \text{pixelID} + 0], \text{rg}) \text{atomicAdd}(\text{fallback}[2 \times \text{pixelID} + 1], \text{ba}) 3. Resolve Pass: Combine the results from the main buffer and fallback buffers to compute the final average color for each pixel. a. For each pixel, read ssRGBA, fallback[2 pixelID + 0], and fallback[2 pixelID + 1]. b. Extract the total count and color components from all buffers. c. Normalize the accumulated color by dividing by the total count to get the average color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atomicAdd(arr, idx, val): arr[idx] += val return arr[idx] - val def atomicExchange(arr, idx, val): old = arr[idx] arr[idx] = val return old OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD = 255 def renderpoint(position, color): # 1. Transform point to screen space # Not given in the sources. pos = position pixelid = 0 # 2. Encode color and count into 64-bit integer r = int(color[0] 65535.0) g = int(color[1] 65535.0) b = int(color[2] 65535.0) rgba = (r << 48) | (g << 32) | (b << 16) | 1 # 3. Atomic addition to main buffer old = atomicAdd(ssRGBA, pixelid, rgba) # 4. Extract previous count count = old & 0xFFFF # 5. Check for overflow if count >= OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD: a = 1 # 6. If this is the first thread to overflow (count == 255) if count == OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD: # Reset main buffer atomicExchange(ssRGBA, pixelid, 0) # Accumulate previous values from 'old' r += (old >> 48) & 0xFFFF g += (old >> 32) & 0xFFFF b += (old >> 16) & 0xFFFF a += OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD # 7. Encode accumulated values for fallback buffers rg = (r << 32) | g ba = (b << 32) | a # 8. Write to fallback buffers atomicAdd(fallback, 2 pixelid + 0, rg) atomicAdd(fallback, 2 pixelid + 1, ba) Parameters: Overflow Threshold: 255. If the counter reaches exactly 255, the current pixel's buffer is reset to zero and data is moved to fallback buffers. Bit Pattern: 16 bits for Red, 16 bits for Green, 16 bits for Blue, 16 bits for Counter (Alpha/Count). Total 64 bits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overflow: If more than 1023 points contribute to a pixel, the naive 18-18-18-10 bit pattern (used in HQS1×) overflows. The 16-16-16-16 pattern handles up to 255 points in the main buffer before falling back, with a safety margin of 65,536 - 256 counts. Simultaneous Accesses: The unused 2^{16} - 256 counts serve as a safety margin for potentially several thousand simultaneously executing threads to detect the overflow. If more or significantly fewer than 65k simultaneous accesses to a pixel are expected, the bit pattern may be changed accordingly. A variant of HQS that reduces atomic operations by encoding RGB channels and counter into a single 64-bit integer. It uses a 18-18-18-10 bit pattern, where the 10-bit counter allows correct computation of the sum of up to 1023 points per pixel. However, this naive approach is prone to overflow artifacts when more than 1023 points contribute to a pixel's average color value, leading to strongly noticeable rendering artifacts in larger scenes. HQS1R is robust against these overflow artifacts compared to HQS1×, with negligible overhead. Time Complexity: The method requires two geometry passes and one screen pass for high-quality variations. The render pass performs a single atomic operation per point in the fast path, reducing memory bandwidth usage compared to the standard HQS. Memory Complexity: Uses a 64-bit integer per pixel for the main buffer and two 64-bit integers per pixel for fallback buffers. Performance: Achieves higher frame rates than aliased GLPOINTS results while providing anti-aliasing. The robust variant, HQS1R, shows negligible overhead compared to the unstable HQS1× version. Strengths: Reduces aliasing, robust against overflow artifacts, efficient memory access pattern. Limitations: Requires fallback buffers for overflow handling, which increases memory usage. When to use: Point cloud rendering where anti-aliasing is desired and performance is critical. When not to use: Scenes with extremely high point density per pixel where fallback buffers might become a bottleneck. HQS1R was introduced in the paper "Rendering Point Clouds with Compute Shaders and Vertex Order Optimization". It is a compute-based implementation of the blending algorithm from [BHZK05]. The method was developed to address the limitations of traditional GLPOINTS rendering, such as aliasing and performance issues, by leveraging compute shaders for parallel processing. The HQS1R variant was specifically designed to handle overflow conditions robustly, ensuring high-quality rendering even in dense point clouds. Rendering Point Clouds with Compute Shaders and Vertex Order Optimization, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14345, fetched 2026-10-26

name: YUV Color Space Shading with Glow
body: This method performs volume raycasting illumination in the YUV color space to decouple luminance from chrominance. It differs from standard RGB shading by computing lighting effects primarily on the luminance channel, while interpolating color channels based on a technique-derived factor. Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p} and normal \mathbf{n} (derived from SDF gradient). View direction \mathbf{v} and light direction \mathbf{l}. Base color values \mathbf{C}1, \mathbf{C}2 in YUV space. Interpolation factor \alpha derived from the technique's output. Glow mapping function G(\cdot) and additional texture fetch for glow. Outputs: Final shaded color \mathbf{C}{final} in YUV space. Data Structures: YUV Color Vector: \mathbf{C} = [Y, U, V]^T. Glow Texture: 2D or 3D texture storing glow intensity. Steps: 1. Geometric Setup: Compute normal \mathbf{n}, view vector \mathbf{v}, and light vector \mathbf{l}. 2. Luminance Calculation: Calculate the luminance component Y as the minimum of two values, Y1 and Y2: Y = \min(Y1, Y2) 3. Color Interpolation: Interpolate the chrominance components (U, V) between two color states \mathbf{C}1 and \mathbf{C}2 using the factor \alpha: \mathbf{C}{interp} = (1 - \alpha) \mathbf{C}1 + \alpha \mathbf{C}2 4. Specular Highlight (Optional): Add specular highlights to the luminance channel. 5. Volumetric Glow: Realize volumetric glow by exploiting an additional texture fetch and a glow mapping function: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C}{interp} + [G(\text{GlowTexture}(\mathbf{p})), 0, 0]^T This allows indirect illumination to be captured independently of the transfer function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def yuvshadingwithglow(p, n, v, l, C1yuv, C2yuv, alpha, glowtexture, glowfunc): # Step 1: Geometric Setup # n, v, l are assumed normalized # Step 2: Luminance Calculation Y1 = C1yuv[0] Y2 = C2yuv[0] Y = min(Y1, Y2) # Step 3: Color Interpolation U = (1.0 - alpha) C1yuv[1] + alpha C2yuv[1] V = (1.0 - alpha) C1yuv[2] + alpha C2yuv[2] # Step 4: Specular Highlights h = (v[0] + l[0], v[1] + l[1], v[2] + l[2]) hlen = math.sqrt(h[0]2 + h[1]2 + h[2]2) h = (h[0]/hlen, h[1]/hlen, h[2]/hlen) spec = math.pow(max(n[0]h[0] + n[1]h[1] + n[2]h[2], 0.0), 32.0) Y += spec # Step 5: Volumetric Glow glowintensity = glowtexture.fetch(p) glowcontribution = glowfunc(glowintensity) Y += glowcontribution return [Y, U, V] Parameters: \alpha: Interpolation factor derived from the technique's output. Edge Cases: Precision: YUV conversion and interpolation may introduce precision errors. Converts RGB images to YUV color space and back using JPEG standard conversion matrices. Definition: Linear transformation using fixed 3x3 matrices. Parameters: RGBTOYUV: Matrix [[0.299, 0.587, 0.114], [-0.168736, -0.331264, 0.5], [0.5, -0.418688, -0.081312]]. YUVTORGB: Matrix [[1.0, 0.0, 1.402], [1.0, -0.34414, -0.71414], [1.0, 1.772, 0.0]]. YUVOFFSET: Array [0, 128.0, 128.0] reshaped to (1,1,-1), added to YUV output. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for YUV color vectors and glow texture. Strengths: Decouples luminance and chrominance. Can capture indirect illumination independently of the transfer function. Limitations: Requires conversion steps if input/output is RGB. Glow implementation adds texture fetch overhead. Originated in Timo Ropinski's work on advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume raycasting. The method leverages the YUV color space to simplify lighting calculations and enhance visual effects like glow. The RGB to YUV conversion matrices are based on JPEG standards. GPU-Based Volume Ray-Casting with Advanced Illumination, https://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/websiteuniulm/iui.inst.100/institut/Papers/viscom/2008/advancedillumination.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tangent Space Shading
head: vzTMTangentSpaceShader, vzTangentSpaceShader
body: Tangent Space Shading is a gradient-less lighting technique that approximates the diffuse lighting component of the Phong shading model without computing explicit gradients for every texel. It uses a double-pass rendering approach with offset texture coordinates to effectively compute the component of the gradient along the light vector. Inputs: Volume texture data. Light direction vector \mathbf{l}. Outputs: Rendered image with diffuse shading approximation. Data Structures: Volume texture (bricked or continuous). Steps: 1. First Pass: Draw the volume slice using standard texture coordinates. 2. Second Pass: Draw the volume slice again using slightly offset texture coordinates. 3. Gradient Approximation: The difference between the two passes effectively computes the component of the gradient along the light vector. 4. Lighting Model: Apply an approximation to the diffuse lighting component of the Phong shading model. Parameters: Light direction: User-adjustable. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bricking Artifacts: The technique produces visible seams for bricked shapes along the borders of the bricks. Incorrect Lighting: The shader does not generate physically correct lighting; it creates a visual effect via a system-dependent technique. Recommendation: Use vzTMGradientShader for correct volumetric lighting if bricking artifacts are a concern. Performance: Efficient as it avoids per-texel gradient computation. Quality: Provides higher image quality and better depth cues. Limitations: Not suitable for applications requiring correct volumetric lighting or where bricking seams are unacceptable. Tangent Space Shading was introduced by Brian Cabral in SIGGRAPH 1997. It was implemented in the SGI OpenGL Volumizer library as vzTMTangentSpaceShader. Chapter 4. Texture Mapping Render Action, https://techpubs.jurassic.nl/library/manuals/4000/007-4389-010/sgihtml/ch04.html, fetched 2026-10-27 Appendix A. Volume Rendering Examples, https://techpubs.jurassic.nl/library/manuals/3000/007-3720-002/sgihtml/apa.html, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Voxel-Specific Shading Pipelines
body: Voxel-Specific Shading Pipelines compute illumination for data stored in discrete 3D voxel grids, handling both surface-like boundaries and volumetric density. They differ from continuous surface shading by operating on discrete voxel coordinates and neighbor-dependent lighting calculations, and include Voxel Shading Pipeline, Fast Shading for Voxel Engines, Voxel Shader Volumetric Ray Marching, and Voxmat Path Tracer. All methods operate on a 3D voxel grid indexed by integer coordinates (x, y, z). Lighting calculations frequently depend on immediate neighboring voxels to determine occlusion or shading factors, rather than casting long-distance rays for every sample, except in explicit ray-marching variants. Inputs include block types, palette indices, or continuous scalar/vector fields stored in the voxel cells. Computes final voxel color by combining albedo sampling, Lambertian diffuse lighting, rim lighting, and specular integration. It differs by operating on discrete voxel coordinates and using hard shadow rays with per-voxel specular highlights rather than smooth surface approximations. Choose this for foundational voxel-specific rendering where discrete neighbor dependence is required. A CPU-based lighting algorithm that modifies voxel palette indices to simulate lighting by checking immediate neighbors, assuming vertical sun rays. It differs by using fewer neighbor checks and operating on palettes grouped into dark-to-light gradients, making it faster but less visually detailed than geometric pipelines. Choose this for performance-critical voxel engines where speed is prioritized over visual fidelity. A shading method for volumetric data (fire, smoke) that reads voxel grid data from simulators or volume grids. It differs by explicitly tracing camera and shadow rays through the grid with configurable step sizes and sampling filters, supporting both pure volumetric ray marching and procedural geometry modes. Choose this for rendering volumetric effects where standard surface materials cannot shade directly. A real-time path tracer for per-voxel physically based rendering and global illumination. It differs by performing full path tracing (including specular reflections and refractions) on a per-voxel basis using a pre-computed irradiance cache for indirect diffuse lighting, rather than relying on static shading or simple ray marching. Choose this for physically accurate voxel rendering with global illumination. Not given in the sources.

name: Voxel Shading Pipeline
head: Block Shading, Shading and Lighting, Voxel Lighting
body: The Voxel Shading Pipeline computes the final color of a voxel hit during ray marching by combining albedo sampling, Lambertian diffuse lighting, rim lighting, and specular integration. It distinguishes itself from continuous shading by operating on discrete voxel coordinates and neighbor-dependent lighting calculations, specifically using hard shadow rays and per-voxel specular highlights rather than smooth surface approximations. Inputs: hitPosition: World-space position of the ray-voxel intersection. hitCell: Integer coordinates (x, y, z) of the hit voxel. hitFaceNormal: Normal vector of the hit voxel face. rayDir: Camera ray direction. sunVec: World-space sun direction. time: Current simulation time (for sun rotation). tLimit, maxSteps: Parameters for shadow ray tracing. camPos: Camera position. Outputs: finalColor: The computed RGB color of the pixel. Data Structures: TraceResult: Struct containing hit (bool), t (float, distance), cell (ivec3), normal (vec3). BLOCKEMISSIVE: Integer constant identifying emissive block types. Steps: 1. Intersection Validation: If the ray hits a voxel (tr.hit is true): If tr.t <= 0.0, set hitPosition = camPos. Else, set hitPosition = camPos + rayDir (tr.t + 1e-5). Extract hitCell = tr.cell and hitFaceNormal = tr.normal. 2. Vector Normalization: N = \text{normalize}(\text{hitFaceNormal}). L = \text{normalize}(\text{sunVec}(time \times \text{SUN\ROT\SPEED})). V = \text{normalize}(\text{rayDir}). 3. Local Coordinate Calculation: Compute local position within the voxel: \text{local} = \text{hitPosition} - \text{vec3}(\text{float}(\text{hitCell}.x), \text{float}(\text{hitCell}.y), \text{float}(\text{hitCell}.z)) Apply fracturing for texture sampling: \text{localPos} = \text{fract}(\text{local}). 4. Albedo and Environment Sampling: Sample block albedo: albedo = sampleBlockAlbedoTexmanual(hitCell, localPos, hitFaceNormal). Compute absorption color: absorpColor = absorp(...). Compute sky color: If atmosphere enabled: sky = 1.0 - exp(-atmosphere(...)) Else: sky = absorpColor. 5. Lighting Components: Diffuse: nDotL = \max(0.0, N \cdot L) \text{lambert} = nDotL. Rim Lighting: \text{rim} = \text{pow}(1.0 - \max(0.0, N \cdot V), 2.2) \times 0.12. Constants: lightColor = vec3(1.0, 0.96, 0.85) ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.14, 0.18). 6. Shadow Casting: Initialize shadow = 1.0. If shadows enabled: Trace voxel from hitPosition + N 0.01 in direction L. If sh.hit is true, shadow = 0.0. 7. Direct and Indirect Light: directLight = lightColor lambert indirectLight = 0.25 albedo. Emissive Handling: If block type is BLOCKEMISSIVE: emission = getEmissiveColor(hitCell) getEmissiveIntensity(hitCell) indirectLight += 0.35 emission directLight += emission 0.5. 8. Final Color Composition: diffAlbedo = albedo absorpColor Base lit color: \text{lit} = (\text{shadow} \times \text{directLight} + \text{ambient}) \times \text{diffAlbedo} + (\text{indirectLight} \times \text{absorpColor}) + \text{rim} \times 0.6 \times \text{absorpColor}. 9. Specular Integration (Microfacet/GGX-like): Parameters: roughness = 0.54, F0 = 0.14. Compute half vector: H = \text{normalize}(L - V) Compute dot products: dotLH = \max(0.0, L \cdot H) dotNH = \max(0.0, N \cdot H) dotNL = \max(0.0, N \cdot L) Compute D (Normal Distribution): \alpha = \text{roughness}^2 \alphaSqr = \alpha^2 \text{denom} = dotNH^2 \times (\alphaSqr - 1.0) + 1.0 D = \frac{\alphaSqr}{\pi \times \text{denom}^2 + 1e-6} Compute F (Fresnel): F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) \times \text{pow}(1.0 - dotLH, 5.0) Compute Geometry/Approximation term: k = 0.5 \times \alpha k2 = k^2 \text{specularTerm} = \frac{dotNL \times D \times F}{\max(1e-6, dotLH^2 \times (1.0 - k2)) + k2} Add to lit: \text{lit} += \text{shadow} \times \text{specularTerm} \times \text{absorpColor} \times \text{lit}. Apply shadow modifier to final lit: \text{lit} = \max(0.7, \text{shadow}). 10. Tone Mapping: finalColor = 1.0 - exp(-2.0 lit). 11. Miss Case: If no hit, finalColor = sky. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math PI = 3.14159265359 BLOCKEMISSIVE = 0 class vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def mul(self, s): return vec3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def add(self, o): return vec3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return vec3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def truediv(self, s): return vec3(self.x/s, self.y/s, self.z/s) def normalize(v): return v / math.sqrt(v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2) def dot(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def fract(v): return v - math.floor(v) def max(a, b): return a if a > b else b def pow(b, e): return be def exp(x): return math.exp(x) def tracevoxel(origin, direction, tlimit, maxsteps): # Standard voxel DDA traversal pass def sampleblockalbedo(cell, localpos, normal): # Texture lookup for block at cell using localpos pass def computeabsorption(cell, campos, lightdir): # Environment absorption calculation pass def voxelshadingpipeline(hit, campos, raydir, time, sunrotspeed, tlimit, maxsteps): if not hit: return computeabsorption(hit.cell, campos, raydir) if hit.t <= 0.0: hitposition = campos else: hitposition = campos + raydir (hit.t + 1e-5) hitcell = hit.cell hitnormal = hit.normal N = normalize(hitnormal) L = normalize(vec3(1.0, 0.5, 0.2)) V = normalize(raydir) local = hitposition - vec3(float(hitcell.x), float(hitcell.y), float(hitcell.z)) localpos = fract(local) blocktype = 0 albedo = sampleblockalbedo(hitcell, localpos, hitnormal) absorpcolor = computeabsorption(hitcell, campos, L) sky = absorpcolor ndotl = max(0.0, dot(N, L)) rim = pow(1.0 - max(0.0, dot(N, V)), 2.2) 0.12 lightcolor = vec3(1.0, 0.96, 0.85) ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.14, 0.18) shadow = 1.0 sh = tracevoxel(hitposition + N 0.01, L, tlimit, maxsteps) if sh.hit: shadow = 0.0 directlight = lightcolor ndotl indirectlight = 0.25 albedo if blocktype == BLOCKEMISSIVE: emission = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) indirectlight += 0.35 emission directlight += emission 0.5 diffalbedo = albedo absorpcolor lit = (shadow directlight + ambient) diffalbedo + (indirectlight absorpcolor) + rim 0.6 absorpcolor roughness = 0.54 F0 = 0.14 alpha = roughness roughness alphasqr = alpha alpha H = normalize(L - V) dotLH = max(0.0, dot(L, H)) dotNH = max(0.0, dot(N, H)) dotNL = max(0.0, dot(N, L)) denom = dotNH dotNH (alphasqr - 1.0) + 1.0 D = alphasqr / (PI denom denom + 1e-6) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) pow(1.0 - dotLH, 5.0) k = 0.5 alpha k2 = k k specterm = (dotNL D F) / (max(1e-6, dotLH dotLH (1.0 - k2)) + k2) lit += shadow specterm absorpcolor lit lit = max(0.7, shadow) finalcolor = 1.0 - exp(-2.0 lit) return finalcolor This method extends the basic pipeline by adding shadow ray casting, Phong-like specular highlights, and recursive or discrete refraction bounces. It is distinguished by its support for recursive light transport through semi-transparent volumes and specific handling of voxel-space coordinate offsets for shadow and refraction ray origins. A lighting optimization that computes illumination per voxel block rather than per pixel, then applies per-pixel modifiers to retain shading detail. It calculates base lighting values for an entire voxel block and applies per-pixel adjustments to prevent uniform shading and maintain surface variation. Strengths: Fast enough for interactive frame rates on simple scenes; hard shadows and per-voxel speculars provide strong visual cues for voxel structure. Limitations: Hard shadows are generated via secondary rays and may appear aliased; specular highlights are discrete per voxel via grid rounding, which may look blocky at high resolutions. When to use: Real-time voxel games where performance is critical and stylized, blocky lighting is acceptable. The method originates from early interactive voxel world shaders, specifically those implementing ray-marched voxel rendering with basic lighting models. It was developed to provide visually distinct lighting for voxel-based environments without the computational cost of full path tracing. The specific implementation details, such as the GGX-like specular approximation and tone mapping, were popularized in community-driven GLSL shader repositories. name: Shading with Shadows, Specular, and Refraction
head: Voxel Shading with Shadows, Specular, and Refraction
body: This method computes the final color of a hit voxel by combining diffuse and specular lighting from multiple light sources, handling shadow casting to occlude lights, and managing refraction through volumetric structures. It extends the basic voxel shading pipeline by adding shadow ray casting, Phong-like specular highlights, and recursive or discrete refraction bounces. It is distinguished from simpler shading models by its support for recursive light transport through semi-transparent volumes and its specific handling of voxel-space coordinate offsets for shadow and refraction ray origins. Inputs: renderingattributes: Contains lightcount, an array of light sources (each with diffuse and specular color vectors), ambientcolour, and flags for shadow/refraction enablement. hit: The hit point structure from the ray marcher, containing hitpos (world position), hitscale (log2 of voxel size or similar scale factor), and hitt (distance along ray). shadingattributes: Contains normal (surface normal at hit point), colour (RGBA color sampled from voxel, where a is alpha), and refractiveindex (material refractive index). eyeray: The primary ray, containing direction (view direction). tree: The volume data structure for ray casting. stack: Auxiliary stack for recursive ray casting. incidentrefractiveindex: Refractive index of the medium the ray is currently traveling through. recursions: Current recursion depth counter. shadowsenabled, refractionenabled, refractionmode, refractiondiscretestepsmax, refractiondiscretestep: Configuration flags and parameters controlling shadow casting, refraction mode (CONTINUOUS or DISCRETE), and discrete stepping limits. Outputs: out: A vec4 representing the final computed color (RGB + alpha, though alpha handling in output is implicit in the accumulation logic). The method relies on structures defined in the parent Voxel Shading Pipeline and the ray marcher. Key fields include: hit.hitscale: Used to compute geometric offsets. MAXSCALE is a constant defining the maximum scale (smallest voxel). HALFSQRT2 is a constant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}. shadingattributes.colour.a: Alpha value of the hit voxel. refractionmode: Enum indicating CONTINUOUS or DISCRETE refraction. refractiondiscretestepsmax: Maximum number of steps for discrete refraction. refractiondiscretestep: Step size for discrete refraction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def vec4(x, y, z, w): return (x, y, z, w) def vec3add(a, b): return vec3(a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def vec3sub(a, b): return vec3(a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def vec3mul(a, s): return vec3(a[0]s, a[1]s, a[2]s) def vec4add(a, b): return vec4(a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2], a[3]+b[3]) def vec4mul(a, s): return vec4(a[0]s, a[1]s, a[2]s, a[3]s) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return vec3(v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) if l > 1e-8 else v def reflect(I, N): return vec3(I[0] - 2dot(I, N)N[0], I[1] - 2dot(I, N)N[1], I[2] - 2dot(I, N)N[2]) def refract(I, N, eta): costheta = min(dot(-I, N), 1.0) routperp = vec3(eta(I[0] + N[0]costheta), eta(I[1] + N[1]costheta), eta(I[2] + N[2]costheta)) routparallel = vec3(-N[0]math.sqrt(max(1.0 - dot(routperp, routperp), 0.0)), -N[1]math.sqrt(max(1.0 - dot(routperp, routperp), 0.0)), -N[2]math.sqrt(max(1.0 - dot(routperp, routperp), 0.0))) return vec3add(routperp, routparallel) def exp2f(x): return 2.0 x def maxval(a, b): return a if a > b else b def minval(a, b): return a if a < b else b def raycast(tree, origin, direction, stack): # Standard volume ray traversal returning a Hit structure pass def lookupattachment(tree, hit): # Unpacks voxel data at hit position to retrieve material properties pass def shade(renderingattributes, eyeray, hit, shadingattributes, stack, tree, incidentrefractiveindex, recursions): MAXSCALE = 23.0 HALFSQRT2 = math.sqrt(2.0) / 2.0 MINFLOAT = exp2f(-MAXSCALE) # 1. Normalize normal normal = normalize(shadingattributes.normal) # 2. Initialize output and view direction out = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) viewdir = eyeray.direction # 3. Iterate over lights for i in range(renderingattributes.lightcount): light = renderingattributes.lights[i] lightdir = normalize(vec3sub(light.position, hit.hitpos)) lightdistance = exp2f(23.0) attenuation = 1.0 # 4. Shadow Ray Casting if shadowsenabled and dot(lightdir, normal) < 0.0: shadowraydir = vec3mul(lightdir, -1.0) shadowrayorigin = vec3add(hit.hitpos, vec3mul(shadowraydir, HALFSQRT2 exp2f(hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE))) shadowhit = raycast(tree, shadowrayorigin, shadowraydir, stack) # Boundary Conditions: The check shadowhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE ensures that only valid voxel hits are considered for occlusion. if shadowhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE and shadowhit.hitt < lightdistance: continue # 5. Diffuse Contribution diffusefactor = attenuation maxval(0.0, dot(normal, vec3mul(lightdir, -1.0))) diffusecolour = vec3mul(shadingattributes.colour.rgb, light.diffuse) out = vec4add(out, vec4(vec3mul(diffusefactor, diffusecolour), 0.0)) # 6. Specular Contribution if dot(normal, lightdir) < 0.0: reflection = reflect(lightdir, normal) specularfactor = pow(maxval(0.0, dot(reflection, viewdir)), 32.0) speccolour = vec3mul(shadingattributes.colour.rgb, light.specular) out = vec4add(out, vec4(vec3mul(specularfactor, speccolour), 0.0)) # 7. Refraction Handling if refractionenabled and shadingattributes.colour.a < 1.0: oneminusalpha = 1.0 - shadingattributes.colour.a out = vec4mul(out, shadingattributes.colour.a) refractnormal = normal if dot(normal, eyeray.direction) > 0.0: refractnormal = vec3mul(normal, -1.0) eta = incidentrefractiveindex / shadingattributes.refractiveindex refractdir = refract(eyeray.direction, refractnormal, eta) refractrayorigin = vec3add(hit.hitpos, vec3mul(refractdir, HALFSQRT2 exp2f(hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE))) if refractionmode != "CONTINUOUS": # Discrete Refraction currentrefractiveindex = shadingattributes.refractiveindex discreterayorigin = vec3add(refractrayorigin, vec3mul(refractdir, HALFSQRT2 exp2f(hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE))) discreteraydir = vec3mul(refractdir, -1.0) refractedtimes = 0 for step in range(refractiondiscretestepsmax): refractionhit = raycast(tree, discreterayorigin, discreteraydir, stack) if refractionhit.hitscale == MAXSCALE or refractionhit.hitt <= MINFLOAT: break refractionattachment = lookupattachment(tree, refractionhit) if refractionattachment.refractiveindex != currentrefractiveindex: refractedtimes += 1 eta = currentrefractiveindex / refractionattachment.refractiveindex refnormal = normalize(refractionhit.normal) if dot(refnormal, refractdir) > 0.0: refnormal = vec3mul(refnormal, -1.0) refractdir = refract(refractdir, refnormal, eta) discreteraydir = vec3mul(refractdir, -1.0) currentrefractiveindex = refractionattachment.refractiveindex discreterayorigin = vec3add(discreterayorigin, vec3mul(refractdir, refractiondiscretestep)) else: # Continuous Refraction refractionhit = raycast(tree, refractrayorigin, refractdir, stack) if refractionhit.hitscale >= MAXSCALE: out = vec4add(out, vec4(vec3mul(oneminusalpha, renderingattributes.ambientcolour), 0.0)) else: refractionattachment = lookupattachment(tree, refractionhit) refnormal = normalize(refractionhit.normal) if dot(refnormal, refractdir) > 0.0: refnormal = vec3mul(refnormal, -1.0) eta = refractionattachment.refractiveindex / incidentrefractiveindex refractdir = refract(refractdir, refnormal, eta) refractrayorigin = vec3add(refractionhit.hitpos, vec3mul(refractdir, HALFSQRT2 exp2f(refractionhit.hitscale - MAXSCALE))) refractionhit = raycast(tree, refractrayorigin, refractdir, stack) if refractionhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: out = vec4add(out, shade(renderingattributes, refractrayorigin, refractionhit, shadingattributes, stack, tree, refractionattachment.refractiveindex, recursions + 1)) return out MAXSCALE: Constant defining the smallest voxel scale. exp2f(MAXSCALE) is the minimum voxel size. HALFSQRT2: Constant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 0.7071. 32.0: Exponent for specular highlight (Shininess). exp2f(23): Approximation for infinity in shadow ray distance checks. refractiondiscretestepsmax: Number of steps for discrete refraction. Not given in the sources. refractiondiscretestep: Step size for discrete refraction. Not given in the sources. Precision: The use of exp2f for scale calculations requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially for very small or large scales. Boundary Conditions: The check shadowhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE ensures that only valid voxel hits are considered for occlusion. Hits at MAXSCALE (empty space) are ignored. Normal Orientation: The normal must be reversed if the dot product with the view/refraction direction is positive, indicating the ray is exiting the surface. Recursion Depth: The method supports recursive bounces up to a template parameter. Deep recursion can lead to performance issues or stack overflow. Discrete Refraction Logic: The source code negates the direction in discrete refraction (discreterefractionray.direction = -refractionray.direction). This appears to be a specific implementation detail that may need verification against the intended physics. A recursive ray marching loop for volumetric rendering that handles opaque surfaces, diffuse irradiance caching, GGX specular microfacet reflection, and glass refraction, including a specific guide generation step for denoising refracted pixels. It differs from standard volumetric shading by explicitly decoupling the denoising guide computation from the radiance accumulation, tracing refracted rays through glass blocks to find the first surface behind them to provide accurate albedo and normal data to the denoiser. Time Complexity: O(L \cdot (1 + R)), where L is the number of lights and R is the number of refraction bounces. Each light requires a shadow ray cast. Refraction adds recursive ray casts. Memory Complexity: O(R) for the recursion stack, where R is the maximum refraction depth. Not given in the sources. Performance scales linearly with the number of lights and refraction depth. High refraction depths can significantly impact performance. Strengths: Supports complex lighting effects including shadows, specular highlights, and refraction. Handles semi-transparent volumes. Limitations: Recursive refraction can be computationally expensive. Discrete refraction logic is complex and may not accurately model continuous refraction. Use when realistic lighting with shadows and refraction is required for volumetric data. Avoid for real-time applications with strict performance constraints and high refraction depths. name: Volumetric Ray Marching with Glass Refraction and Denoising Guides
head: dielectric guide, voxmat shading loop
body: A recursive ray marching loop for volumetric rendering that handles opaque surfaces, diffuse irradiance caching, GGX specular microfacet reflection, and glass refraction, including a specific guide generation step for denoising refracted pixels. It differs from standard volumetric shading by explicitly decoupling the denoising guide computation from the radiance accumulation, tracing refracted rays through glass blocks to find the first surface behind them to provide accurate albedo and normal data to the denoiser. Inputs: uresolution: vec2 (width, height) of the output buffer. uforward, uright, uup: vec3 camera basis vectors. uaspect: float camera aspect ratio. utanhalffov: float tangent of half the vertical field of view. uframe: uint current frame number. ugiscale: float scale factor for irradiance cache contribution. ugi: sampler2D irradiance cache texture. uaccum: sampler2D temporal accumulation buffer. gAlbedo, gNormal: image2D (or equivalent) for writing denoising guides. Outputs: fcolor: vec4 final color output. gAlbedo, gNormal: Updated denoising guide textures. Material: Contains id (int), name (string), albedo (vec3), metallic (float), roughness (float), transmission (float), ior (float). Voxel Hit: Returns cell (ivec3), normal (vec3), hitDistance (float). Medium March: Returns exitDistance (float), exitNormal (vec3), beyondCell (ivec3), exitToEmpty (bool). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def random01(rngstate): # Implementation of a simple PRNG step using rngstate # Returns float in [0, 1) pass def fresnelschlick(costheta, f0): return f0 + (1.0 - f0) pow(1.0 - costheta, 5.0) def smithg(NdotV, NdotL, roughness): # Approximate Smith geometry term # Using standard Schlick-GGX approximation alpha = roughness roughness r = alpha / 2.0 return 1.0 / (NdotV + NdotL - NdotV NdotL (1.0 - r)) def ggxsample(N, roughness, rng): # Importance sample GGX normal distribution # Returns a micro-normal vector in local space transformed to world space pass def tracevoxel(origin, direction, startcell, skipempty, outcell, outnormal, outdistance): # Marches ray through voxel grid # Returns True if hit, False if escaped pass def fetchmaterial(cell): # Returns Material struct for the voxel at cell pass def sampleenv(raydir): # Samples environment map or background color pass def atlascoord(cell, face): # Maps 3D cell and face to 2D UV coordinate for irradiance cache pass def materialrow(cell): # Returns material properties for the medium inside the cell pass def dielectricguide(hitpoint, raydir, cell, normal, material, galbedoimg, gnormalimg): """ Traces a refracted ray through a glass block to find the first surface behind it. Provides albedo and normal to the denoiser to prevent blurring of the refracted image. """ # Orient normal against ray direction entrynormal = normal if dot(raydir, entrynormal) < 0.0: entrynormal = -entrynormal # Refract ray # ior is material.ior dir = refract(raydir, entrynormal, 1.0 / material.ior) # Check for total internal reflection (TIR) if dot(dir, dir) < 1e-6: galbedoimg[cell] = material.albedo gnormalimg[cell] = entrynormal return # March through medium to find exit exitdistance = 0.0 exitnormal = vec3(0.0) beyondcell = ivec3(0) exittoempty = False # marchmedium is a helper that advances along dir until exit marchmedium(hitpoint + dir 1e-6, dir, materialrow(cell), exitdistance, exitnormal, beyondcell, exittoempty) exitpoint = hitpoint + dir 1e-6 + dir exitdistance # Determine exit direction if exittoempty: outdir = refract(dir, -exitnormal, material.ior) else: outdir = dir # Handle TIR at exit if dot(outdir, outdir) < 1e-6: outdir = reflect(dir, exitnormal) # Trace voxel from exit point gc = ivec3(0) gn = vec3(0.0) gt = 0.0 if tracevoxel(exitpoint + outdir 1e-6, outdir, beyondcell, False, gc, gn, gt): galbedoimg[gc] = fetchmaterial(gc).albedo gnormalimg[gc] = gn else: # Sky galbedoimg[gc] = vec3(1.0) gnormalimg[gc] = outdir def shade(hitpoint, raydir, cell, normal, material, rng): """ Computes radiance for a single bounce. """ color = vec3(0.0) throughput = vec3(1.0) # View vector and Fresnel view = -raydir ndv = max(dot(normal, view), 1e-4) fresnelf0 = mix(vec3(0.04), material.albedo, material.metallic) # Diffuse term viewfresnel = fresnelschlick(ndv, fresnelf0) diffuse = (1.0 - viewfresnel) (1.0 - material.metallic) material.albedo # Add diffuse irradiance from cache # atlascoord maps cell and face to 2D UV giuv = atlascoord(cell, faceof(normal)) color += throughput diffuse texelfetch(ugi, giuv).rgb ugiscale # Specular term (GGX) micronormal = ggxsample(normal, material.roughness, rng) lightdir = reflect(raydir, micronormal) # Check if light direction is below horizon if dot(lightdir, normal) <= 0.0: return color ndl = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 1e-4) ndh = max(dot(normal, micronormal), 1e-4) vdh = max(dot(view, micronormal), 1e-4) # Specular weight weight = fresnelschlick(vdh, fresnelf0) smithg(ndv, ndl, material.roughness) vdh / (ndv ndh) # Clamp throughput to prevent fireflies throughput = min(weight, vec3(4.0)) # Break if throughput is negligible if max(throughput.r, max(throughput.g, throughput.b)) < 0.01: return color # Trace next voxel hit along light direction nextcell = ivec3(0) nextnormal = vec3(0.0) nextdistance = 0.0 if not tracevoxel(hitpoint + normal 1e-6, lightdir, cell, False, nextcell, nextnormal, nextdistance): # Escape to sky color += throughput sampleenv(lightdir) return color # Advance hit point and update state hitpoint = hitpoint + normal 1e-6 + lightdir nextdistance cell = nextcell normal = nextnormal material = fetchmaterial(nextcell) raydir = lightdir # Recursive call or loop continuation? # The source implies a loop structure for bounces, but shade() is called once per pixel in the main loop. # However, the notes describe a "recursive ray marching loop". # Let's assume shade() handles one bounce and the main loop handles recursion, # OR shade() is iterative. Given the structure, it's likely iterative within the main loop. # But the pseudocode below shows the main loop handling the recursion. return color def main(): # Initialize RNG rng = uint(glFragCoord.x) 1973u + uint(glFragCoord.y) 9277u + uint(uframe) 26699u + 1u # Compute jittered NDC and ray direction jitter = vec2(random01(rng), random01(rng)) - 0.5 ndc = ((glFragCoord.xy + jitter) / uresolution) 2.0 - 1.0 raydir = normalize(uforward + uright (ndc.x uaspect utanhalffov) + uup (ndc.y utanhalffov)) # Trace initial voxel hit cell = ivec3(-9999) normal = vec3(0.0) hitdistance = 0.0 if not tracevoxel(vec3(0.0), raydir, ivec3(-9999), False, cell, normal, hitdistance): color = sampleenv(raydir) else: material = fetchmaterial(cell) hitpoint = vec3(0.0) + raydir hitdistance # Generate denoising guide if material.transmission > 0.0: dielectricguide(hitpoint, raydir, cell, normal, material, gAlbedo, gNormal) else: gAlbedo[cell] = material.albedo gNormal[cell] = normal # Shade color = shade(hitpoint, raydir, cell, normal, material, rng) # Temporal accumulation prev = vec3(0.0) if uframe > 0: prev = texelfetch(uaccum, ivec2(glFragCoord.xy), 0).rgb fcolor = vec4(prev + max(color, vec3(0.0)), 1.0) 1. Initialize RNG: Seed the random number generator using fragment coordinates and frame number. 2. Compute Ray: Calculate jittered normalized device coordinates (NDC) and transform to world space ray direction. 3. Trace Initial Hit: Cast a ray from the camera origin. If no hit, sample the environment and return. 4. Fetch Material: Retrieve material properties for the hit voxel. 5. Generate Guide: If the material is dielectric (transmission > 0.0), call dielectricguide to trace the refracted ray through the glass block and write the albedo/normal of the first surface behind it to the guide buffers. If opaque, write the surface albedo and normal directly to the guide buffers. 6. Shade: Call the shade function to compute radiance for the current hit, including diffuse irradiance from cache and GGX specular reflection. 7. Accumulate: Add the computed color to the temporal accumulation buffer using nearest neighbor fetch to avoid drift. Dielectric Guide: A helper function that traces a refracted ray through a glass block to find the first surface behind it, providing albedo and normal to the denoiser to prevent blurring of the refracted image. Choose this when rendering transparent/translucent materials in a denoised pipeline. GGX Specular: Uses importance sampling of the GGX microfacet normal distribution and Schlick Fresnel for specular reflection. Choose this for realistic metallic/dielectric surfaces. Irradiance Cache: Uses a precomputed irradiance cache for diffuse lighting, sampled based on voxel position and surface normal. Choose this for performance in scenes with static lighting. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of bounces and voxel traversal steps. The dielectricguide adds an additional traversal for dielectric materials. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the irradiance cache and the denoising guide buffers. Strengths: Handles complex glass refraction with denoising support; efficient diffuse lighting via irradiance cache. Limitations: Requires precomputed irradiance cache; guide generation adds overhead for dielectrics. When to use: Real-time or interactive volumetric rendering with glass and denoising. When not to use: Offline path tracing where full integration is required; scenes without denoising needs where simpler shading suffices. Originated in the Voxmat project by HollaFoil. It is part of a custom shading pipeline for volumetric rendering, specifically designed to handle dielectric materials and integrate with denoisers. HollaFoil/Voxmat, https://github.com/HollaFoil/Voxmat, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)
