name: Per-Point Normal Lighting
head: Gradient Normal Lighting, Normal-vector-based lighting model
body: Per-Point Normal Lighting is a volume rendering technique that calculates the surface normal vector at each individual resampling point along the ray and substitutes this normal directly into the lighting model. This approach solves the problem of visual flatness and loss of microstructural detail inherent in methods that interpolate lighting results without computing per-sample normals. By computing normals at the sampling points, the method accurately represents diffuse and specular reflections, preserving the three-dimensional sense and concavity/convexity of the data field. The method operates on a scalar field V defined over a 3D grid. The core distinction from its parent, Diffuse Lighting for Volume Ray Casting, is the explicit calculation of the gradient at every resampling point rather than relying on interpolated or pre-computed normals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar field V(x,y,z), viewing direction \mathbf{v}, light direction \mathbf{l}, camera position, and resampling points along the ray. Output: Final color C for each pixel, incorporating diffuse and specular components calculated using per-point normals. Data Structures: Scalar Field: A 3D array of floating-point values representing the volume density or intensity. Resampling Point: A 3D coordinate (x,y,z) along the ray, with an associated scalar value V and computed normal \mathbf{n}. Steps: 1. Ray Marching: Cast rays through the volume. For each ray, determine a sequence of resampling points Pi at positions \mathbf{p}i. 2. Normal Calculation: For each resampling point \mathbf{p}i, calculate the normal vector \mathbf{n}i using finite differences of the scalar field V. The normal is the gradient of the scalar field: \mathbf{n}i = \nabla V(\mathbf{p}i) = \left[ \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} \right]{\mathbf{p}i} In practice, central differences are used for accuracy: \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \approx \frac{V(x+h, y, z) - V(x-h, y, z)}{2h}. 3. Lighting Model Application: Substitute \mathbf{n}i into the lighting model. The diffuse component Ld and specular component Ls are calculated using the standard Phong or Blinn-Phong equations, where \mathbf{n}i is normalized: Ld = kd (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l}) Ls = ks (\max(0, \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v}))^{\alpha} where \mathbf{r} is the reflection vector derived from \mathbf{n}i, and kd, ks, \alpha are material constants. 4. Compositing: Accumulate the color contributions from all resampling points along the ray, typically using front-to-back alpha compositing. 5. Contour Smoothing: Render with a slightly fuzzy contour line to avoid jaggedness and distortion. This is often achieved by blending the lighting result with a threshold-based edge detection or by using a soft threshold in the transfer function. Parameters: Step Size: Distance between resampling points. Smaller steps increase accuracy but cost more. Threshold: Value used to define the surface boundary for normal calculation and compositing. Fuzziness: Degree of blurring applied to the contour to mitigate aliasing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jaggedness: Without the fuzzy contour step, discrete sampling can cause jagged edges. Noise: Finite difference normal calculation is sensitive to noise in the scalar field, which can lead to erratic lighting. Smoothing the field before gradient calculation is often necessary. Flat Surfaces: If normals are not calculated per point but interpolated, surfaces appear flat and lose concavity/convexity. A shading technique for mesh displays that varies brightness based on the angle between the surface normal and the line of sight, making the inside of the volume dimmer than the outside. Brightness is maximal when the outward-facing normal is parallel to the line of sight and pointing at the user. The definition of "outward" depends on the flipNormals setting and the threshold sign: if flipNormals is true, the side toward larger values is outside for negative thresholds, and the side toward smaller values is outside for positive thresholds. Accuracy: Maintains high rendering accuracy for microstructures and preserves 3D sense better than methods that interpolate lighting results. Performance: Requires calculating gradients at every resampling point, which is more computationally expensive than pre-computed or interpolated normals. Visual Quality: Avoids the loss of concavity/convexity and the "flat surface" appearance associated with current interpolation methods. Limitations: Sensitive to noise in the scalar field; requires careful handling of contour fuzziness to avoid distortion. The method was introduced to address the limitations of existing volume rendering techniques that interpolate lighting model results, which fail to accurately represent diffuse and specular reflections at sampling points. It was evaluated on explosion field features, including projectile penetration into reinforced concrete and aerial explosions, demonstrating superior preservation of microstructural details. The approach is distinct from mesh-based lighting techniques like Mesh Lighting, which apply shading to surface meshes rather than volumetric resampling points. name: Phong Shading with Boundary Enhancement and Facing Subtraction
head: Boundary-enhanced volume shading, Gradient-based Phong shading
body: This method implements per-fragment Phong lighting for volume rendering using precomputed scalar field gradients, applying boundary enhancement via absorption approximation and facing subtraction for silhouette enhancement. It distinguishes itself from standard gradient-based Phong shading by explicitly modulating fragment alpha based on gradient magnitude and the view direction relative to the surface normal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture tex3D containing precomputed gradient components (gx, gy, gz) and magnitude (||g||), plus a 1D transfer function texture tex1D mapping scalar values to color and alpha. Output: A fragment color and alpha value. Data Structures: The source defines uniform structures for lighting and rendering parameters: lightt: Contains coefficients kd (diffuse), ks (specular), ka (ambient). renderingt (or myRender): Contains integer flags boundary and facing. Gradientt: Contains fields x, y, z, and magnitude of type float. Varyings: L (light vector), E (eye vector). Numbered Steps: 1. Gradient Extraction: Sample the 3D texture at the current fragment's position to retrieve the gradient vector components (gx, gy, gz) and the precomputed magnitude ||g||. 2. Normal Computation: Normalize the gradient vector to obtain the surface normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} = \frac{(gx, gy, gz)}{||(gx, gy, gz)||} 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the normal \mathbf{n} into view space using the model-view matrix. The vertex shader computes the eye vector \mathbf{E} = \text{normalize}(-\text{vertexPos}) and light vector \mathbf{L} = (0,0,-1) in view space and passes them as varyings. 4. Lighting Calculation: Compute the diffuse term D = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{L}, 0). Compute the reflection vector \mathbf{r} = \text{reflect}(-\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{n}). Compute the specular term S = \max(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0)^{512}. Compute the ambient term A = \text{TF}(t) by sampling the 1D transfer function at the scalar value. Combine terms to get the initial color contribution: C = ks S + kd D + ka A. 5. Boundary Enhancement: If the boundary flag is enabled, modify the fragment alpha \alpha using an absorption approximation based on the gradient magnitude: \alpha' = \alpha (1 - e^{-||g||}) This step enhances the visibility of boundaries where the gradient magnitude is high. 6. Facing Subtraction: If the facing flag is enabled, further modify the alpha by subtracting the facing component relative to the view vector \mathbf{v}: \alpha'' = \alpha' (1 - |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}|) The source formula specifies the absolute value for silhouette symmetry, while the provided code snippet implements \alpha' (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sample1dtexture(tex, coord): return tex[coord] def phongshadingfragment(gradienttex, tftex, scalarvalue, normal, eyevector, lightvector, kd, ks, ka, boundary, facing): # 1. Lighting Calculation diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightvector), 0.0) reflection = reflect(-lightvector, normal) specular = pow(max(dot(reflection, normal), 0.0), 512.0) tfsample = sample1dtexture(tftex, scalarvalue) ambient = tfsample color = ks specular + kd diffuse + ka ambient alpha = tfsample.a # 2. Boundary Enhancement gradientmagnitude = gradienttex.magnitude if boundary > 0: alpha = alpha (1.0 - exp(-gradientmagnitude)) # 3. Facing Subtraction ndotv = dot(normal, eyevector) if facing > 0: # Formula specifies |n·v| for silhouette symmetry; source code uses 1-ndotv alpha = alpha (1.0 - abs(ndotv)) return color, alpha Parameters: kd, ks, ka: Diffuse, specular, and ambient lighting coefficients. boundary: Integer flag. If >0, boundary enhancement is enabled. facing: Integer flag. If >0, facing subtraction is enabled. Specular exponent: Fixed at 512.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: If the gradient magnitude is zero, the normal is undefined. The source does not specify a fallback, but numerically, normalization of a zero vector results in NaN/Inf. A guard against zero-length gradients is required. Facing Subtraction Sign: The source formula uses |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}| while the code uses \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}. The formula handles both front and back faces, while the code only affects front-facing fragments where \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} > 0. Implementers must choose based on whether back-face silhouettes are desired. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. It is an implementation detail found in educational or prototype code rather than a peer-reviewed algorithm. name: Lambertian Lighting in SDF
head: Lambertian Shading, Lambertian Lighting, Lambertian Model, Lambertian Diffuse, Lambertian Lighting Model, Lambert Shading
body: Lambertian Lighting in SDF calculates diffuse illumination for surfaces defined by Signed Distance Fields by computing the dot product between the surface normal and the light direction, clamping negative values to zero. It solves the problem of flat, unlit appearance in ray-marched scenes by providing physically plausible shading that reveals surface curvature and orientation. Unlike Phong Shading with SDF Normals and Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering, which include specular highlights, this method computes only the diffuse component, resulting in a matte appearance. It builds on Diffuse Lighting Models by adapting the standard Lambertian reflectance model to the implicit geometry of SDFs, where normals are derived from the distance field gradient. Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p} in world or object space. Surface normal \mathbf{n}, normalized. Light direction \mathbf{l}, normalized (pointing from \mathbf{p} to the light source). Base material color \mathbf{c}{base} (RGB). Light color \mathbf{c}{light} (RGB). Ambient color \mathbf{c}{ambient} (RGB). Light intensity scalar I{light} (optional). Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{c}{final} (RGB). Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l} are 3-component floating-point vectors. Colors \mathbf{c}{base}, \mathbf{c}{light}, \mathbf{c}{ambient} are 3-component floating-point vectors. Steps: 1. Compute Light Direction: Determine the vector from the surface point \mathbf{p} to the light source position \mathbf{p}{light}. Normalize this vector to obtain \mathbf{l}. If the light is directional, \mathbf{l} is provided directly as a constant vector. \mathbf{l} = \frac{\mathbf{p}{light} - \mathbf{p}}{\|\mathbf{p}{light} - \mathbf{p}\|} 2. Compute Diffuse Term: Calculate the dot product of the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the light direction \mathbf{l}. Clamp the result to a minimum of 0.0 to ensure no negative lighting contributions. d = \max(0.0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) Some implementations multiply by a strength factor s: d = \max(0.0, s \cdot (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})) 3. Compute Final Color: Combine the base color, ambient term, and diffuse contribution. The standard formula multiplies the base color by the sum of the ambient term and the product of the diffuse term, light intensity, and light color. \mathbf{c}{final} = \mathbf{c}{base} \times (\mathbf{c}{ambient} + d \times I{light} \times \mathbf{c}{light}) If ambient is not used, \mathbf{c}{ambient} is zero. If light intensity is not separated, it is absorbed into \mathbf{c}{light}. Parameters: Ambient factor: Not given in the sources. Light Intensity: Not given in the sources. Strength factor s: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back-facing surfaces: In two-sided rendering, the surface normal is reversed for back-facing fragments before evaluating the diffuse term. Normal estimation error: The normal \mathbf{n} is estimated via finite differences of the SDF. Light position conversion: In some frameworks, light positions may need conversion from object space to texture space before computing the direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lambertianlightingsdf(p, plight, normal, basecolor, lightcolor, ambientcolor=vec3(0.0), lightintensity=1.0): """ Computes Lambertian diffuse lighting for an SDF surface point. Args: p: vec3, surface point in world space. plight: vec3, light source position in world space. normal: vec3, normalized surface normal at p. basecolor: vec3, base material color. lightcolor: vec3, color of the light source. ambientcolor: vec3, ambient light color. Default 0. lightintensity: float, intensity multiplier. Default 1.0. Returns: vec3, final pixel color. Phong Shading with Shadows calculates the final color of a surface point in a volume rendering pipeline by combining ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting contributions using the Phong reflection model, modulated by a shadow factor. It solves the problem of providing physically plausible surface appearance and depth cues for SDF-based volume rendering by accounting for occlusion from light sources. Unlike its parent Lambertian Lighting in SDF, which only computes diffuse lighting, this method adds specular highlights and ambient terms to better define surface curvature and material properties. Formula: \text{lighting} = 0.2 + 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\text{degrees}(\arccos(\frac{\mathbf{lightVector} \cdot \mathbf{normal}}{\|\mathbf{lightVector}\|})}{180}}, clamped to [0, 1]. name: Sphere Tracing with Shading
head: Sphere Tracing with Shading | ronja-tutorials/ShaderTutorials
body: Sphere Tracing with Shading is a shading extension of the sphere tracing system that derives surface normals from the SDF using finite differences, calculates diffuse lighting in world space, and combines a base color with computed light. It extends basic sphere tracing by estimating surface normals via finite differences and applying a Lambertian lighting model in world space. Unlike Sphere Tracing Basics, which returns a flat base color, this method calculates per-pixel lighting intensity based on the angle between the surface normal and the light direction. It builds on Lambertian Lighting in SDF by providing the specific implementation details for normal estimation and integration within the Unity shader pipeline. The method operates within a fragment shader that performs ray marching. It differs from the basic version only in the output calculation upon a successful hit; the traversal loop remains identical. Inputs: localPosition: The local-space position of the vertex on the proxy mesh. viewDirection: The view vector in local space. Color: A float4 representing the object's base diffuse color. LightColor0: A float4 representing the main directional light's color and intensity (provided by Lighting.cginc). WorldSpaceLightPos0: A float4 where.xyz is the light direction for a directional light. Outputs: fragColor: The final float4 color with alpha. The shader defines three compile-time constants that control precision and performance: | Constant | Type | Value | Role | |---|---|---|---| | MAXSTEPS | int | 10 | Maximum ray marching iterations. | | THICKNESS | float | 0.01 | SDF distance threshold for a surface hit. | | NORMALEPSILON | float | 0.01 | Offset distance used in finite-difference normal sampling. | The scene is defined by the SDF function scene(pos), which returns the signed distance from a point pos to a unit sphere of radius 0.5 centered at the origin: \text{scene}(pos) = \|pos\| - 0.5 1. Ray Initialization: Construct the ray origin pos from the vertex's local position and the ray direction dir from the normalized view direction. Initialize progress to 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate iter from 0 to MAXSTEPS: a. Calculate the sample point: samplePoint = pos + dir progress. b. Evaluate the SDF: distance = scene(samplePoint). c. Hit Test: If distance < THICKNESS, the ray has intersected the surface. Proceed to Shading. d. Advance: Update progress += distance. e. Miss Test: If iter exceeds MAXSTEPS, discard the fragment (return transparent/black). 3. Shading (on hit): a. Normal Estimation: Compute the surface normal using central finite differences in local space, then transform to world space. b. Lighting Calculation: Compute the Lambertian diffuse term using the world-space normal and world-space light direction. c. Material Composition: Multiply the base color by the lighting intensity. The surface normal is the normalized gradient of the SDF. Since the SDF is analytic, the gradient is approximated using central differences with offset NORMALEPSILON (\epsilon). 1. Compute changes in local space: \Deltax = \text{scene}(pos + (\epsilon, 0, 0)) - \text{scene}(pos - (\epsilon, 0, 0)) \Deltay = \text{scene}(pos + (0, \epsilon, 0)) - \text{scene}(pos - (0, \epsilon, 0)) \Deltaz = \text{scene}(pos + (0, 0, \epsilon)) - \text{scene}(pos - (0, 0, \epsilon)) Let g{local} = (\Deltax, \Deltay, \Deltaz). 2. Transform to world space. The gradient is a direction vector, so the translation component of the transformation matrix must be excluded (w=0). g{world} = \text{normalize}\left( \text{mul}(\text{unity\ObjectToWorld}, (g{local}.x, g{local}.y, g{local}.z, 0)) \right) The diffuse lighting intensity is computed in world space. 1. Retrieve the light direction L from WorldSpaceLightPos0.xyz. 2. Compute the dot product of the world-space normal N = g{world} and the light direction L: \text{diffuseIntensity} = \max(0, N \cdot L) This is implemented as saturate(dot(surfaceNormal, lightDirection)). 3. Compute the final lighting contribution: \text{lightColor} = \text{diffuseIntensity} \times \text{LightColor0.rgb} The final color is the product of the object's base color and the computed lighting: \text{output} = \text{Color.rgb} \times \text{lightColor} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def add3(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def sub3(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def scale3(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def dot3(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def length3(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def normalize3(v): l = length3(v) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) if l > 0 else (0, 0, 0) def transformdir(M, v): # M is 4x4 matrix, v is vec4 (x,y,z,0) return (M[0][0]v[0] + M[0][1]v[1] + M[0][2]v[2], M[1][0]v[0] + M[1][1]v[1] + M[1][2]v[2], M[2][0]v[0] + M[2][1]v[1] + M[2][2]v[2]) def saturate(x): return max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) MAXSTEPS = 10 THICKNESS = 0.01 NORMALEPSILON = 0.01 def scene(pos): return length3(pos) - 0.5 def getnormal(pos): epsx = (NORMALEPSILON, 0, 0) epsy = (0, NORMALEPSILON, 0) epsz = (0, 0, NORMALEPSILON) dx = scene(add3(pos, epsx)) - scene(sub3(pos, epsx)) dy = scene(add3(pos, epsy)) - scene(sub3(pos, epsy)) dz = scene(add3(pos, epsz)) - scene(sub3(pos, epsz)) gradlocal = (dx, dy, dz) # Transform to world space (direction vector, w=0) gradworld = transformdir(unityObjectToWorld, (gradlocal[0], gradlocal[1], gradlocal[2], 0)) return normalize3(gradworld) def lightcolor(position): normal = getnormal(position) lightdir = WorldSpaceLightPos0[:3] diffuse = saturate(dot3(normal, lightdir)) return diffuse LightColor0[:3] def frag(v2finput): pos = v2finput.localPosition dir = normalize3(v2finput.viewDirection) progress = 0.0 for step in range(MAXSTEPS): samplepoint = add3(pos, scale3(dir, progress)) distance = scene(samplepoint) if distance < THICKNESS: return scale3(Color, lightcolor(samplepoint)) progress += distance return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) NORMALEPSILON: A value of 0.01 is used. If too small, precision errors may cause noisy normals; if too large, the normal approximation becomes inaccurate for high-curvature areas. THICKNESS: A value of 0.01 defines the hit threshold. It must be larger than the numerical precision errors of the SDF evaluation but small enough to avoid visible gaps. Batching: Static and dynamic batching must be disabled (DisableBatching="True"). The vertex shader relies on unityWorldToObject, which is only valid per-object and breaks when multiple objects are batched into a single draw call. Depth Buffer: The shader must use Queue="Transparent" and ZWrite Off. Sphere-traced geometry does not write correct hardware depth values. Placing it in the transparent queue prevents it from incorrectly occluding rasterized geometry or being occluded by it based on the proxy mesh's depth. A shading technique for Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) that uses surface normals derived from the gradient of distance functions, with a smoothing method for discontinuities at mirror planes. It computes the shading normal using the gradient of the distance function at the sphere-traced surface point and performs lighting computation in either world space or kernel space. If computing in world space, the transformation matrix for the complete chain must be maintained throughout the iteration to transform kernel gradients to world space. Discontinuities are smoothed by interpolating between the kernel-to-world-space matrices on the two sides of a mirror when the shaded point is found near a mirror plane during iteration. The shading algorithm runs only once, after sphere tracing has found the intersection point. A key pitfall is visible discontinuity of surface normals where the plane of reflection intersects the mirrored geometry if kernel separation is not upheld. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of ray marching steps (bounded by MAXSTEPS). Each step involves one SDF evaluation. Normal estimation adds 6 additional SDF evaluations per hit pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No large textures or buffers are required beyond standard shader registers. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method is documented in the "ShaderTutorials" series by Ronja, specifically in the tutorial "5.2 Sphere Tracing with Shading". It serves as a direct extension of "Sphere Tracing Basics" and "Lambertian Lighting in SDF" within the Unity engine context. The approach leverages Unity's built-in lighting variables (LightColor0, WorldSpaceLightPos0) and standard shader includes (Lighting.cginc) to integrate procedural geometry into the engine's forward rendering pipeline. Ambient lighting factor: Constant 0.1 in some implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: In homogeneous regions, the SDF gradient is zero, making normal recovery unstable and leading to noise or incorrect shading. Denormalization Artifacts: When interpolating normals or reflection vectors across pixels, denormalization can cause artifacts. Shadow Artifacts: Hard shadows can cause aliasing at shadow boundaries. The Lighting Transfer Function (LTF) is a volume rendering shading technique that replaces scalar lighting coefficients with lookup tables dependent on two scalar values sampled along the gradient direction, allowing users to control lighting specifically for material boundaries. It solves the problem of assigning specific lighting coefficients (ambient, diffuse, specular) to material boundaries and homogeneous regions in a volume, allowing users to control how light interacts with scalar data boundaries independently of opacity. Unlike methods using scalar gradient magnitude alone, this method uses scalar values perpendicular to the boundary (along the gradient) to distinguish material types and boundaries, avoiding the shading of homogeneous material using only scalar gradient magnitude. This method solves the inverse problem of estimating the position and intensity of point light sources given an observed image, known scene geometry, and material properties. It formulates light estimation as an optimization problem that minimizes the photometric error between a rendered image and the target image using a differentiable rendering pipeline based on the Blinn-Phong model. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Lighting Transfer Function and its parent Phong Shading with Shadows by explicitly modeling 3D point light sources and handling non-distant lighting parallax, whereas alternatives like Spherical Harmonics are limited to low-frequency or distant lighting approximations. The Opacity Influenced Inconstant Method is a shading technique for 3D holographic pyramid rendering that extends Phong shading by introducing an opacity variable to enhance depth cues and reveal the internal structure of 3D models. It differs from its parent, Phong Shading with Shadows, by modulating diffuse and ambient lighting with opacity to create a transparent, holographic appearance, and by using a specific multi-light configuration to maximize shape perception without casting shadows. Unlike Lighting Transfer Function which focuses on energy conservation, this method prioritizes visual depth cues for holographic displays. An efficient per-pixel surface shading method using cube map dependent texture reads to evaluate the Blinn-Phong model, avoiding the need for per-pixel vector normalization. Steps: 1. Treat an RGB color component (normal or reflection vector) as texture coordinates (s, t, r) for a cube map. 2. Access the texel at the intersection of the line through the origin in direction (s, t, r) and the cube face. 3. The color value represents incoming diffuse radiance if (s, t, r) is a surface normal, or specular radiance if it is a reflection vector. Parameters: Performance Cost: Per-pixel cube map evaluation can be up to 3 times slower than evaluating dot products for a limited number of light sources in the fragment shader. Pitfalls: Denormalization artifacts: The original Rezk-Salama approach suffers from artifacts caused by denormalization during interpolation. Comparison: Differs from standard fragment shader dot products by encoding arbitrary numbers of lights or a full environment map in the cube map, at the cost of performance. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for lighting calculation, assuming shadow factor is precomputed or approximated. Shadow tracing adds O(N) where N is the number of samples along the light ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) for material and light parameters. Cube map variant requires O(1) texture memory for the cube map. Measured Performance: Cube map dependent texture reads are up to 3 times slower than standard dot product evaluations for a limited number of lights. Strengths: Provides realistic specular highlights and ambient lighting, enhancing depth perception and material definition. Supports multiple light types and attenuation. Limitations: Sensitive to noise in SDF gradients, leading to unstable normals in homogeneous regions. Shadow calculation can be expensive if not optimized. When to Use: When realistic surface appearance with specular highlights is required, and the SDF is smooth enough to provide stable normals. When Not to Use: In highly noisy SDFs or homogeneous regions where normal estimation is unreliable, or when performance is critical and simple diffuse lighting suffices. The Phong shading model has been integrated into libraries like VTK.js to support cinematic volume rendering, providing BRDF reflectance and improved lighting models. The integration with SDF-based rendering allows for dynamic relighting and shadow casting, enhancing the visual quality of 3D holographic and volume visualizations. name: Lighting Transfer Function
head: 2D Lighting Transfer Function, 2D lighting shading, Illustrative Enhancement via 2D Lighting Transfer Function, Shading Transfer Function
body: The Lighting Transfer Function (LTF) is a volume rendering shading technique that replaces scalar lighting coefficients with lookup tables dependent on two scalar values sampled along the gradient direction, allowing users to control lighting specifically for material boundaries. It solves the problem of assigning specific lighting coefficients (ambient, diffuse, specular) to material boundaries and homogeneous regions in a volume, allowing users to control how light interacts with scalar data boundaries independently of opacity. Unlike methods using scalar gradient magnitude alone, this method uses scalar values perpendicular to the boundary (along the gradient) to distinguish material types and boundaries, avoiding the shading of homogeneous material using only scalar gradient magnitude. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric scalar field V, camera position, light direction \vec{L}, view direction \vec{V}, sample spacing, gradient sampling distance d, and the 2D Lighting Transfer Function lookup tables. Outputs: Final pixel color C and opacity \alpha. Data Structures: The core data structure is the 2D Lighting Transfer Function, implemented as a 2D lookup table (LUT). Layout: Each entry in the 2D LUT stores four components: ambient (sa), diffuse (sd), specular (ss), and opacity enhancement (s\alpha). Encoding: These components are encoded in the red, green, blue, and alpha channels of a 2D texture respectively. Dimensions: The dimensions of the LUT correspond to the discretized range of the input arguments, which are either scalar value pairs (S1, S2) or dot product pairs (\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}). Numbered Steps: 1. Gradient Calculation: For each sample point during ray casting, compute the normalized gradient direction \hat{N} from the volumetric scalar field. 2. Center Sample: Sample the scalar value S at the current center position. 3. Gradient Samples: Sample the scalar value S1 at a distance d in the direction of the gradient \hat{N}, and sample the scalar value S2 at a distance d in the direction opposite to the gradient -\hat{N}. 4. LTF Lookup: Two input formulations exist: Scalar-based: Lookup ambient coefficient ka, diffuse coefficient kd, and specular coefficient ks from the 2D lookup tables LTF{ka}, LTF{kd}, and LTF{ks} using inputs (S1, S2). Dot-product-based: Compute \hat{N} \cdot \hat{L} and \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}, where \hat{H} is the normalized half-way vector (\hat{H} = (\hat{L} + \hat{V}) / |\hat{L} + \hat{V}|). Lookup sa, sd, ss from the LUT using these dot products. 5. Color Computation: Compute the final color using the selected formulation: Scalar-based: C = \text{ColorTF}(S)(LTF{ka}(S1, S2) + LTF{kd}(S1, S2)\max(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, 0)) + LTF{ks}(S1, S2)\max((\hat{N} \cdot \hat{R})^n, 0). Dot-product-based: cs = (sa(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}) + sd(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H})) \cdot cu + ss(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}). 6. Opacity Computation (Dot-product variant only): Compute shaded opacity \alphas: \alphas = \left( \min(1, s\alpha(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}) + (1 - |\hat{N}|)) \right)^{-1} \cdot \alphau Where \alphau is the unshaded opacity and |\hat{N}| is the gradient magnitude scaled between 0 and 1. Formulas: Shaded Color (Scalar-based LTF): C = \text{ColorTF}(S) \left( LTF{ka}(S1, S2) + LTF{kd}(S1, S2) \max(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, 0) \right) + LTF{ks}(S1, S2) \max((\hat{N} \cdot \hat{R})^n, 0) Shaded Color (Dot-product based LTF): cs = (sa(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}) + sd(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H})) \cdot cu + ss(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}) Shaded Opacity (Dot-product based LTF): \alphas = \left( \min(1, s\alpha(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{L}, \hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}) + (1 - |\hat{N}|)) \right)^{-1} \cdot \alphau Contour Line Condition: To realize contour lines, set ambient, diffuse, and specular components to zero where \hat{N} \cdot \hat{L} \approx 2(\hat{N} \cdot \hat{H}), which corresponds to \hat{N} \cdot \hat{V} approaching zero (gradient orthogonal to view vector). Parameters: Distance d: The distance from the center sample to S1 and S2 along the gradient direction. Typical value: one voxel in each direction. Shininess n: Specular shininess exponent in the Phong shading model. Gradient Magnitude Scaling: Gradients are scaled such that their magnitude |\hat{N}| is between zero and one. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Thickness Sensitivity: The method is sensitive to the thickness of a material boundary. If the distance d is greater than the thickness of a material boundary and the gradient is perpendicular to the boundary, S1 and S2 will both read the homogeneous values on either side, correctly identifying the boundary. However, the method is sensitive to the amount of blur in the volume, requiring adjustment of the distance parameter. Contour Clutter: Without gradient magnitude consideration, opacity-enhanced contour lines cause clutter in translucent views due to rapidly varying gradient directions in homogeneous regions. Semantic Ambiguity: The terms 'ambient', 'diffuse', and 'specular' do not necessarily correspond to their physical meanings in Phong-Blinn lighting; their semantics are defined by the model used for generation of the lighting transfer function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelightingtransferfunction(samplepos, volume, gradientsampler, ltftexture, lightdir, viewdir, d, n=32.0): """ Computes the shaded color and opacity for a single sample using the scalar-based Lighting Transfer Function. Args: samplepos: Current 3D position in the volume. volume: The volumetric scalar field. gradientsampler: Function to compute normalized gradient Nhat at a position. ltftexture: 2D texture storing LTF components (R=ambient, G=diffuse, B=specular, A=opacityenhancement). lightdir: Normalized light vector Lhat. viewdir: Normalized view vector Vhat. d: Distance to sample S1 and S2 along the gradient. n: Specular shininess exponent. Returns: shadedcolor, shadedopacity """ # 1. Compute normalized gradient at current position Nhat = gradientsampler(samplepos) # 2. Sample scalar values S = volume.sample(samplepos) # 3. Sample along gradient direction S1 = volume.sample(samplepos + d Nhat) S2 = volume.sample(samplepos - d Nhat) # 4. Lookup lighting coefficients from 2D LTF (Scalar-based variant) ka = ltftexture.sample(S1, S2, channel='R') # Ambient kd = ltftexture.sample(S1, S2, channel='G') # Diffuse ks = ltftexture.sample(S1, S2, channel='B') # Specular # 5. Compute lighting terms dotNL = max(dot(Nhat, lightdir), 0.0) Rhat = 2.0 dotNL Nhat - lightdir dotNR = max(dot(Nhat, Rhat), 0.0) # 6. Compute final color materialcolor = volume.colortransferfunction(S) # shadedcolor = materialcolor (ka + kd dotNL) + ks (dotNR n) # 7. Compute opacity alphau = volume.opacitytransferfunction(S) # shadedopacity = alphau return shadedcolor, shadedopacity This method constructs the final 2D Lighting Transfer Function (LTF) by summing multiple separable 2D components, each generated from a pair of 1D transfer function widgets. It solves the problem of assigning specific lighting coefficients (ambient, diffuse, specular) to material boundaries and homogeneous regions in a volume, allowing users to control how light interacts with scalar data boundaries independently of opacity. It differs from non-separable LTF construction by decomposing the 2D response into a sum of outer products of 1D functions, enabling intuitive user interface design via diagonal pairs in a line-based histogram. Time Complexity: The method evaluates the LTF at constant cost per sample. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 2D Lighting Transfer Function texture. Strengths: Allows expressive control over lighting at material boundaries without shading homogeneous regions incorrectly. Contour lines can be smoothed in the transfer function (e.g., using a Gaussian) without additional rendering cost. Limitations: Sensitive to the distance parameter d relative to material boundary thickness and volume blur. Requires careful tuning of the LTF to avoid clutter in translucent views if opacity enhancement is used without gradient magnitude consideration. The Lighting Transfer Function was introduced to provide users with expressive control over lighting in volume rendering, specifically targeting material boundaries. It differs from earlier methods like Kindlmann and Durkin's, which used second derivatives along the gradient direction (susceptible to noise) or scalar gradient magnitude alone (which shades homogeneous regions). The technique integrates multiple illumination models into a single framework, allowing various shading models to be evaluated at constant costs. It is used in systems like VolumeShop for interactive volume illustration. name: Separable 2D Lighting Transfer Function Construction
head: Separable 2D Lighting TF Construction
body: This method constructs the final 2D Lighting Transfer Function (LTF) by summing multiple separable 2D components, each generated from a pair of 1D transfer function widgets. It solves the problem of assigning specific lighting coefficients (ambient, diffuse, specular) to material boundaries and homogeneous regions in a volume, allowing users to control how light interacts with scalar data boundaries independently of opacity. It differs from non-separable LTF construction by decomposing the 2D response into a sum of outer products of 1D functions, enabling intuitive user interface design via diagonal pairs in a line-based histogram. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N pairs of 1D transfer function widgets. Each pair i consists of a source 1D widget T{source}(s1) and a destination 1D widget T{dest}(s2), where s1 and s2 are scalar values at the start and end of a material boundary line in the 2D LTF domain. Each pair is assigned ambient Ai, diffuse Di, and specular Si coefficients. Output: A final 2D Lighting Transfer Function LTF(s1, s2), which is generally non-separable. Data Structures: 1D Widget: A function mapping a scalar value to intensity or reflectivity. Lighting Coefficients: For each widget pair i, a triplet (Ai, Di, Si). Steps: 1. Define Widget Pairs: For each material boundary or homogeneous region of interest, define a pair of 1D transfer functions: one for the source axis (Scalar 1, s1) and one for the destination axis (Scalar 2, s2). These correspond to the start and end points of diagonal lines in the 2D LTF histogram. 2. Assign Coefficients: Assign ambient, diffuse, and specular terms to each 1D widget in the pair. 3. Compute Separable Component: For each pair i, compute the product of the source 1D function and the transpose of the destination 1D function to yield a separable 2D lighting transfer function. Multiply this product by the assigned lighting terms. The exact algebraic combination of the coefficients with the product is not specified in the sources. A standard implementation applies the coefficients to the product: LTFi(s1, s2) = (Ai + Di + Si) \cdot T{source}(s1) \cdot T{dest}(s2). 4. Sum Components: Sum all N separable 2D transfer functions to create the final non-separable 2D LTF: LTF(s1, s2) = \sum{i=1}^{N} LTFi(s1, s2) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructseparable2dltf(widgetpairs): """ Construct the final 2D Lighting Transfer Function by summing separable components. Args: widgetpairs: List of tuples, each containing: sourcewidget: Callable Tsource(s1) destwidget: Callable Tdest(s2) ambient: Float Ai diffuse: Float Di specular: Float Si Returns: A callable LTF(s1, s2) representing the final 2D lighting transfer function. """ def ltf(s1, s2): total = 0.0 for pair in widgetpairs: # Evaluate 1D widgets at the given scalar coordinates tsource = pair.sourcewidget(s1) tdest = pair.destwidget(s2) # Compute separable 2D component: outer product of 1D functions # multiplied by the assigned lighting coefficients product = tsource tdest component = (pair.ambient + pair.diffuse + pair.specular) product total += component return total return ltf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Summing many separable components may lead to precision issues if the values vary widely. Ensure floating-point stability during accumulation. Boundaries: The 1D widgets must be defined over the valid scalar range of the volume data. Values outside this range should be clamped or handled as zero. Degenerate Input: If a widget pair has zero width (source and destination scalar values are identical), the contribution may be negligible or undefined. Strengths: Provides high user control over lighting at material boundaries. Independent of opacity. Intuitive UI via diagonal pairs. Limitations: The final LTF is non-separable, requiring a full 2D lookup. When to use: When precise control over lighting at specific material interfaces is required, and the user interface can benefit from line-based selection. This method was introduced in the context of Lighting Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering. It builds on the concept of using 2D LTFs to encode lighting information based on scalar value pairs sampled along the gradient direction. The approach allows users to specify lighting for specific material boundaries by selecting diagonal pairs in a line-based histogram, offering a high degree of control over volume illustration. It is distinct from methods that attenuate lighting based on homogeneity, such as those by Kniss et al.. name: Differentiable Blinn-Phong Light Estimation
head: Differentiable Light Source Estimation via Blinn-Phong
body: This method solves the inverse problem of estimating the position and intensity of point light sources given an observed image, known scene geometry, and material properties. It formulates light estimation as an optimization problem that minimizes the photometric error between a rendered image and the target image using a differentiable rendering pipeline based on the Blinn-Phong model. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Lighting Transfer Function and its parent Phong Shading with Shadows by explicitly modeling 3D point light sources and handling non-distant lighting parallax, whereas alternatives like Spherical Harmonics are limited to low-frequency or distant lighting approximations. Inputs: Observed image I^. Scene geometry G = (X, N, C), where X is the surface point, N is the normal, and C is the camera position. Material parameters M = (kd, ks, \alpha), representing diffuse reflectance, specular reflectance, and shininess. Initial guess for light source parameters L. Outputs: Estimated light source parameters L (position Li and intensity I{L,i}). The method operates on standard image and vector data structures. No specific custom data structures (like VDB or BVH) are required beyond standard arrays for the image I, geometry maps (depth/normal), and the parameter vector L. L: A vector containing the parameters for all light sources. For a single point light, this includes position coordinates and intensity. I: A 2D array representing the rendered image. Si: A scalar shadow term (1 if lit, 0 if shadowed) for each light i at each pixel. The Blinn-Phong image formation model is defined as: I = kd \cdot La + \sumi Si \cdot I{L,i} \cdot \left( kd \cdot (Li - X)^t N + ks \cdot (H^t N)^\alpha \right) Where: La is ambient illumination. kd is diffuse reflectance. Si is the shadow term for light i (1 if the point is lit, 0 otherwise). I{L,i} is the intensity of light i. Li is the position of light i. X is the surface point. N is the surface normal. ks is specular reflectance. \alpha is the shininess exponent. H is the halfway vector between the viewer direction (C - X) and the light source vector (Li - X). The specular term Is is calculated as: Is = ks \cdot \sumi Si \cdot (H^t N)^\alpha \cdot I{L,i} The diffuse term Id for a directly lit point (Si=1) is: Id = kd \cdot \sumi Si \cdot (Li - X)^t N \cdot I{L,i} The photometric error E to be minimized is the L2-norm of the difference between the rendered image I and the observed image I^: E = ||I - I^||^2 The gradient of the energy with respect to the illumination parameters L is: \frac{\partial E}{\partial L} = (I - I^)^T \frac{\partial I}{\partial L} The total image Jacobian \frac{\partial I}{\partial L} is approximated as: \frac{\partial I}{\partial L} = \frac{\partial Id}{\partial L} + \frac{\partial Is}{\partial L} + (Id + Is) \cdot \frac{\partial S}{\partial L} Learning rate: 0.02. Stopping condition: Optimization stops when the relative energy change falls below 10^{-4}. Light intensity (IL): In experiments, set to the true value 0.5. Material parameters (ideal): kd = 1.0, ks = 1.0, \alpha = 10, Ia = 0.5. 1. Initialization: Initialize the light source parameters L to an initial guess. 2. Rendering: Render an image I using the current light source estimation L, geometry G, and materials M. This includes calculating shadows and specularities. 3. Error Calculation: Compute the photometric error E = ||I - I^||^2. 4. Gradient Computation: Compute the Jacobian matrix \frac{\partial I}{\partial L}. The terms \frac{\partial Id}{\partial L} and \frac{\partial Is}{\partial L} are computed via automatic differentiation (e.g., PyTorch) using the chain rule on the differentiable parts of the Blinn-Phong model. The shadow Jacobian \frac{\partial S}{\partial L} is approximated using finite differences. This involves rendering six shadow maps around the current light source position estimation to numerically approximate the derivative. 5. Optimization: Update L using gradient descent with the computed gradient \frac{\partial E}{\partial L}. Repeat until convergence. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computeshadowterm(X, Lpos, shadowdepthbuffer, bias=1e-3): """ Compute binary shadow term S for each point. X: (N, 3) Surface points Lpos: (3,) Light position shadowdepthbuffer: (N,) Depth values from light's perspective (pre-rendered) bias: float Shadow acne bias Returns: S: (N,) Shadow term (1.0 if lit, 0.0 if shadowed) """ disttolight = torch.norm(X - Lpos, dim=1, keepdim=True) S = (disttolight < shadowdepthbuffer + bias).float() return S def estimatelightsource(Istar, X, N, C, kd, ks, alpha, La, Linit, shadowdepthbuffer, lr=0.02, tol=1e-4, maxiter=1000): """ Estimate light source parameters using differentiable Blinn-Phong rendering. """ L = torch.tensor(Linit, requiresgrad=True, dtype=torch.float32) prevE = None for i in range(maxiter): Lpos = L[:3] Lint = L[3] Lvec = Lpos - X Cvec = C - X H = torch.normalize(Lvec + Cvec) diffdot = torch.sum(N Lvec, dim=1, keepdim=True) Id = kd diffdot Lint specdot = torch.sum(N H, dim=1, keepdim=True) specpow = torch.pow(torch.clamp(specdot, min=0.0), alpha) Is = ks specpow Lint S = computeshadowterm(X, Lpos, shadowdepthbuffer) I = kd La + S (Id + Is) E = torch.sum((I - Istar)2) if prevE is not None and abs(E - prevE) / prevE < tol: break prevE = E # Differentiable part gradient (Id, Is) via autograd (S treated as constant) L.requiresgrad(True) Idiff = kd La + S.detach() (Id + Is) Ediff = torch.sum((Idiff - Istar)2) graddiff = torch.autograd.grad(Ediff, L, retaingraph=True)[0] # Shadow Jacobian via finite differences (6 shadow maps) eps = 1e-3 dSdL = torch.zeroslike(X, dtype=torch.float32) # (N, 3) for j in range(3): Lposplus = Lpos.clone() Lposplus[j] += eps Splus = computeshadowterm(X, Lposplus, shadowdepthbuffer) Lposminus = Lpos.clone() Lposminus[j] -= eps Sminus = computeshadowterm(X, Lposminus, shadowdepthbuffer) dSdL[:, j] = (Splus - Sminus) / (2 eps) # Combine Jacobian approximation: dI/dL = dId/dL + dIs/dL + (Id + Is) dS/dL # Gradient of E w.r.t L: dE/dL = 2 (I - I) dI/dL # graddiff already contains 2(I-I)(dId/dL + dIs/dL) shadowcontrib = 2.0 (I - Istar) (Id + Is) dSdL gradshadow = torch.sum(shadowcontrib, dim=0) # Sum over pixels to get gradient for L grad = graddiff + gradshadow L.data -= lr grad.detach() return L Shadow Differentiability: Shadow mapping is inherently non-differentiable due to the binary Z-buffer comparison. Approximating it with a smooth activation function (e.g., \arctan(a.|z-d+b|)) leads to degenerated gradients if the slope is too steep, or smooth shadows if too shallow. The authors were unable to find a working threshold for this approach. Shadow Map Quality: Using coarse point-based rendering or incomplete depth maps for shadow maps results in incomplete or aliased shadows. This can disadvantage the method if the Phong model already fits the data well, as imperfect shadows may not provide useful gradients. However, imperfect shadows have proven effective for robustness in noisy scenarios. Lighting Models: Spherical Harmonics (SH) and Haar wavelets are unsuitable for point light sources. SH recovers only low-frequency components, and Haar wavelets model only distant lighting (2D directions), failing to capture the localized angular nature or parallax of point lights. Time: Convergence is achieved in an average of one minute across 54 experiments (9 scenes, 6 light positions). Each iteration requires rendering the image and, for the shadow Jacobian approximation, rendering six additional shadow maps. Memory: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the image, geometry maps, and the shadow maps required for finite difference approximation. Ideal Reflectance: The method performs similarly to state-of-the-art methods [2, 22] on ideal reflectance. Noisy Reflectance: On noisy reflectance (m=0.1), the method achieved a success rate of 79.63% with an average error of 0.2100, compared to 5.56% success rate for [2] and 14.81% for [22]. Robustness: The method systematically achieves better light source estimation in cases of incorrect reflectance estimation compared to alternatives. Strengths: Robust to noisy reflectance estimation; handles 3D point light sources and parallax; uses standard differentiable rendering pipelines (PyTorch). Limitations: Relies on accurate geometry and material parameters; shadow approximation is computationally expensive (6 shadow maps per iteration); sensitive to shadow map quality (aliasing/incompleteness). Use when estimating point light sources in scenes with known geometry and materials, especially when reflectance parameters may be noisy or imperfect. Use when parallax effects from non-distant lights are significant. Do not use if only distant lighting is present (consider SH or Haar wavelets). Do not use if high-quality, complete depth maps and shadow maps are unavailable, as aliasing may degrade performance. The method was introduced in the paper "Robust Point Light Source Estimation Using Differentiable Rendering". The approach leverages automatic differentiation libraries (PyTorch) to create a differentiable rendering pipeline. It addresses the limitations of previous methods that struggled with noisy reflectance or could not model point light sources effectively. The authors explored various illumination models, including Spherical Harmonics and Haar wavelets, but found them unsuitable for point lights due to frequency and directional limitations. Light source estimation in computer vision and graphics. Robust lighting estimation in the presence of noisy material parameters. name: Opacity Influenced Inconstant Method
head: Hololighting shading method, new hololighting style, proposed shading method
body: The Opacity Influenced Inconstant Method is a shading technique for 3D holographic pyramid rendering that extends Phong shading by introducing an opacity variable to enhance depth cues and reveal the internal structure of 3D models. It differs from its parent, Phong Shading with Shadows, by modulating diffuse and ambient lighting with opacity to create a transparent, holographic appearance, and by using a specific multi-light configuration to maximize shape perception without casting shadows. Unlike Lighting Transfer Function which focuses on energy conservation, this method prioritizes visual depth cues for holographic displays. The method achieves hologram views by dividing the screen into nine segments using glViewport in OpenGL to provide four views (right, left, front, back). The method modifies the standard Phong lighting model by adding an opacity component and adjusting the light source configuration. It is designed for rendering 3D objects on holographic pyramid displays, where the screen is divided into segments to provide multiple views. Inputs: 3D model geometry (vertices, normals). Material properties: Ambient color (Ia), Diffuse color (hd), Specular color (Is). Camera position (fixed at eye position (0,0,0) relative to the object for maximum opacity impact). Six point light source positions: Above, Upper Left, Upper Right, Bottom, Lower Left, Lower Right. Outputs: Final pixel color intensity (I) for each view segment. Not given in the sources. 1. Opacity (Io): Calculated as the dot product of the view vector (V) and the surface normal (N). Io = V \cdot N V: Unit vector from the surface point to the camera (view vector). N: Unit normal vector at the surface point. Note: The viewing point must be parallel to the object (at eye position (0,0,0)) to achieve the highest impact of opacity. 2. Light Attenuation (att): Uses a linear attenuation model. The quadratic factor is removed because it is insignificant at small distances compared to the linear factor. att = \frac{1.0}{Kc + Kl \cdot d} d: Distance between the light source and the surface point. Kc: Constant factor, never smaller than 1. Kl: Linear attenuation factor. 3. Diffuse Component (Id): Id = att \cdot hd (L \cdot N) L: Unit vector from the surface point to the light source. hd: Diffuse material color/intensity. (L \cdot N): Dot product of light direction and normal. 4. Specular Component (Is): Calculated using the standard Phong reflection model (dot product between view vector V and reflection vector R), though the specific exponent is not detailed in the source text. The source notes that the specular impression is decreased from the "upper right" and "above" lights, and the impact of the three lights under the object is omitted, preserving only the "upper left" light's full influence. 5. Final Intensity (I): The sum over all lights i of the ambient and diffuse components multiplied by opacity, plus the specular component. I = \sum{i=1}^{lights} ((Ia + Id) \cdot Io) + Is Ia: Ambient color/intensity. Io: Opacity calculated per surface point. Is: Specular contribution. Light Sources: Six point lights are used: 1. Above 2. Upper Left 3. Upper Right 4. Bottom 5. Lower Left 6. Lower Right Light Weighting: The specular contribution from the "Upper Right" and "Above" lights is decreased to provide adequate shining. The impact of the three lights under the object (Bottom, Lower Left, Lower Right) is omitted for specular highlights, except the "Upper Left" light preserves its full influence. Shadows are not calculated; the method ensures shadows do not appear. Attenuation Constants: Kc \ge 1. Kl: Linear factor (value not specified). Kq = 0 (Quadratic factor removed). Viewing Position: The camera/viewer must be at the eye position (0,0,0) relative to the object to maximize the opacity effect. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return Vec3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return Vec3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y + self.zo.z def length(self): return (self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2)0.5 def normalize(self): l = self.length() return Vec3(self.x/l, self.y/l, self.z/l) if l > 0 else Vec3(0,0,0) def reflect(self, n): d = 2 self.dot(n) return Vec3(self.x - dn.x, self.y - dn.y, self.z - dn.z) def max(self, v): return Vec3(max(self.x, v), max(self.y, v), max(self.z, v)) def pow(self, e): return Vec3(self.xe, self.ye, self.ze) def opacityinfluencedinconstantshading(surfacepoint, normal, viewvector, material, lights): # material contains: Ia (ambient color), hd (diffuse color), Is (specular color), shininess # lights is a list of 6 Light objects with attributes: position, name Io = viewvector.dot(normal) finalcolor = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for light in lights: L = (light.position - surfacepoint).normalize() d = (light.position - surfacepoint).length() Kc = 1.0 # Source states Kc is never smaller than 1 Kl = 0.5 # Not given in the sources. att = 1.0 / (Kc + Kl d) diffuseterm = max(0.0, L.dot(normal)) Id = att material.hd diffuseterm R = (-L).reflect(normal) specularterm = max(0.0, viewvector.dot(R)).pow(material.shininess) Is = material.Is specularterm # Apply light-specific specular weighting if light.name in ["Upper Right", "Above"]: Is = Is 0.5 # Not given in the sources. elif light.name in ["Bottom", "Lower Left", "Lower Right"]: Is = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Omitted elif light.name == "Upper Left": pass # Preserves full influence # Combine according to formula: I = sum(((Ia + Id) Io) + Is) finalcolor = finalcolor + ((material.Ia + Id) Io) + Is return finalcolor Viewing Angle: The opacity calculation Io = V \cdot N relies on the view vector. If the camera is not at the designated eye position (0,0,0) or if the object is rotated such that the view vector is not parallel to the object as intended, the opacity impact may vanish or become incorrect. Rotation Method: When generating hologram views, the object must be rotated 90 degrees around the camera, not the camera around the object. Rotating the camera causes the opacity impact to vanish in side views because the opacity calculation depends on the view vector relative to the normal. Degenerate Normals: If the normal is perpendicular to the view vector, Io becomes 0, making the object completely transparent for ambient and diffuse components. This is the intended behavior for "inner view" but may cause visual artifacts if not handled correctly in compositing. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of light sources (O(P \cdot L)), where P is the number of pixels and L is the number of lights (6). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tested on Windows 10 with a Core i7 2.50 GHz processor and 16 GB RAM using C++ and OpenGL. Specific frame rates are not provided. Strengths: Provides clear depth cues and shape perception for holographic displays. Allows viewing of inner object structures through opacity modulation. User study showed 94.35% of respondents perceived real depth/volume with this method. 90.3% of respondents preferred this method over traditional Phong shading for depth cues on hologram pyramid displays. Limitations: Requires specific camera positioning (eye position (0,0,0)) for optimal opacity effect. Designed specifically for 3D holographic pyramid rendering. Lacks shadow calculation, which may reduce realism in non-holographic contexts. The Opacity Influenced Inconstant Method was proposed for 3D holographic pyramid rendering to address the need for better depth cues and the ability to view the inside of 3D models. It extends the Phong shading model by adding an opacity variable. The method was implemented in C++ and OpenGL and evaluated through user studies involving students. The research was published in the Al-Mustansiriyah Journal of Science in 2019. name: Lit-Tensor Shading
head: Lit-Tensor
body: Lit-Tensor Shading is a volume rendering technique that illuminates tensor splats to visualize direction and curvature in tensor fields. It adapts the Blinn-Phong lighting model by deriving surface normals from the tensor's principal axes, allowing the shading to reflect the local anisotropy (linear vs. planar) of the data. Unlike Hue-balls which use color coding for deflection, Lit-Tensors use illumination to convey geometric structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor field \mathbf{T} (symmetric positive-definite 3 \times 3 matrix) at each voxel, light direction l, camera direction e, object color \lambda, and lighting coefficients kd, ks, N. Output: The final intensity I for each rendered voxel. Data Structures: Tensor \mathbf{T}: 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. Eigen-decomposition: \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{E} \mathbf{\Lambda} \mathbf{E}^T, where \mathbf{E} = [e1, e2, e3] contains orthonormal eigenvectors and \mathbf{\Lambda} = \text{diag}(\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) contains eigenvalues sorted such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0. Steps: 1. Eigen-decomposition: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 and corresponding eigenvectors e1, e2, e3 of the tensor \mathbf{T} at the current sample point. 2. Determine Normal n: The normal vector n depends on the shape of the tensor, determined by the relative magnitudes of the eigenvalues: Planar Anisotropy: If the tensor is approximately planar (e.g., \lambda1 \approx \lambda2 \gg \lambda3), the normal is the smallest principal axis: n = e3. Linear Anisotropy: If the tensor is approximately linear (e.g., \lambda1 \gg \lambda2 \approx \lambda3), the largest principal axis e1 is tangential to the desired normal. The normal n is derived such that e1 is perpendicular to it. Using Pythagoras's theorem, the dot product l \cdot n can be rewritten as \sqrt{1 - (l \cdot e1)^2}. Note: The exact vector n in the linear case is not uniquely defined by e1 alone without additional constraints, but the shading intensity relies on this geometric relationship. Intermediate Cases: For other cases, smoothly interpolate between the planar and linear shading models. 3. Compute Lighting Vectors: Light direction l (normalized). Camera direction e (normalized, from surface to eye). Half-way vector h = \frac{l + e}{\|l + e\|}. 4. Calculate Intensities: Apply the Blinn-Phong model using the derived normal n: Diffuse intensity: I{diffuse} = kd \lambda (l \cdot n) Specular intensity: I{specular} = ks \lambda (h \cdot n)^N Total intensity: I = I{diffuse} + I{specular} Where kd, ks are diffuse and specular coefficients, and N is the shininess exponent. Parameters: kd, ks: Diffuse and specular reflection coefficients. Typical values depend on the desired material appearance. N: Shininess exponent. Higher values produce sharper specular highlights. \lambda: Base object color. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tensors: If eigenvalues are equal (isotropic), the normal is undefined. A fallback (e.g., identity or zero) must be chosen. Linear Case Ambiguity: The normal n for linear tensors is not a single vector but a plane perpendicular to e1. The formula l \cdot n = \sqrt{1 - (l \cdot e1)^2} assumes n is chosen to maximize the dot product with l within that plane, or implies a specific geometric interpretation of "tangential". Implementation must clarify how n is constructed from e1 for the specular term (h \cdot n)^N. Precision: Eigen-decomposition can be numerically unstable for nearly degenerate tensors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def littensorshading(tensorT, lightdirl, cameradire, lambdacolor, kd, ks, N): # 1. Eigen-decomposition # tensorT is a 3x3 symmetric matrix eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigendecompose(tensorT) # Sort eigenvalues: lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3 # eigenvectors columns are e1, e2, e3 sortedindices = argsort(eigenvalues, descending=True) lambda1, lambda2, lambda3 = eigenvalues[sortedindices] e1, e2, e3 = eigenvectors[:, sortedindices[0]], eigenvectors[:, sortedindices[1]], eigenvectors[:, sortedindices[2]] # 2. Determine Normal n # Check for planar vs linear anisotropy # Heuristic: if lambda3 is much smaller than lambda1 and lambda2, it's planar # if lambda1 is much larger than lambda2 and lambda3, it's linear # For simplicity, we use a threshold or interpolation factor based on eigenvalue ratios # Planar case: n = e3 # Linear case: n is perpendicular to e1. # The source states: l. n = sqrt(1 - (l. e1)^2). # This implies we need a normal n such that its projection onto the plane perpendicular to e1 aligns with l's projection. # A robust way to get n for linear case: # nlinear = normalize(cross(e1, cross(e1, l))) # However, if l is parallel to e1, this fails. # The source formula suggests we might not need the explicit vector n for diffuse, but we do for specular. # Let's define a normal n based on shape. # If planar: n = e3 # If linear: We need a normal. The source says e1 is tangential to n. # This phrasing is ambiguous. Usually, for a line, the normal is any vector perpendicular to the line. # The formula l. n = sqrt(1 - (l. e1)^2) is only valid if n is in the plane perpendicular to e1 # and aligned with the projection of l. # Let's implement a smooth interpolation between planar and linear normals. # Define a shape parameter s. s=0 for planar, s=1 for linear. # s = 1 - (lambda2 - lambda3) / (lambda1 - lambda3 + epsilon) # Example heuristic # For this implementation, we will use the explicit cases described. if lambda3 < epsilon: # Isotropic/Point-like, fallback n = e1 # Arbitrary elif lambda1 > threshold lambda2: # Linear # e1 is the major axis. # We need a normal n perpendicular to e1. # To maximize l.n, n should be the projection of l onto the plane perpendicular to e1, normalized. lproj = l - dot(l, e1) e1 if norm(lproj) < epsilon: # l is parallel to e1, pick arbitrary perpendicular n = e2 else: n = normalize(lproj) else: # Planar or intermediate # Use e3 as normal for planar n = e3 # 3. Compute Lighting Vectors l = normalize(lightdirl) e = normalize(cameradire) h = normalize(l + e) # 4. Calculate Intensities # Diffuse ldotn = dot(l, n) # Clamp to [0, 1] for physical correctness ldotn = max(0.0, ldotn) Idiffuse = kd lambdacolor ldotn # Specular hdotn = dot(h, n) hdotn = max(0.0, hdotn) Ispecular = ks lambdacolor (hdotn N) return Idiffuse + Ispecular Time Complexity: Dominated by eigen-decomposition of the 3 \times 3 tensor, which is O(1) per voxel/sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample for storing eigenvalues/vectors. Strengths: Provides intuitive visual cues for direction (linear) and surface orientation (planar) in tensor fields. Integrates well with standard volume rendering pipelines. Limitations: The normal derivation for linear tensors is ambiguous and requires heuristic choices for the specific normal vector used in the specular term. Performance is higher than simple scalar volume rendering due to eigen-decomposition. When to use: When visualizing anisotropic tensor fields (e.g., diffusion tensors in MRI) where direction and curvature are important. When not to use: For isotropic scalar fields or when computational resources are extremely limited. Lit-Tensor Shading was introduced by Kindlmann and Weinstein in 1999. It is based on the concept of illuminating tensor representations to provide information on direction and curvature, similar to illuminated streamlines. The method is a variation of the Blinn-Phong lighting model adapted for tensor splats. It is often compared with Hue-balls, which use color coding to show anisotropy.
