name: Lambertian Diffuse Shading with Fog
head: Lambertian Diffuse with Fog, Lambertian Fog Shading
body: This method computes lighting using Lambertian diffuse reflection, ambient light, and exponential fog, then maps the result to terminal colors with optional gamma correction. Inputs: materialColor: A 3-component vector (X, Y, Z) representing the base surface color. normal: The surface normal vector at the hit point. LightDirection: A normalized vector pointing to the light source. Default: (0.5, 1.0, -0.3). distance: The raymarch distance from the camera to the hit point. FogDensity: A scalar parameter controlling fog thickness. Default: 0.03f. EnableFog: A boolean flag to toggle fog application. settings.MapColorsWithGamma: A boolean flag to toggle gamma correction. lighting: An initial intensity value, typically initialized with the diffuse term or ambient light intensity 0.25f. Outputs: An ANSI escape sequence string representing the colored character to be printed to the console. Data Structures: materialColor: 3-component vector with components X, Y, Z. normal: 3-component vector. LightDirection: 3-component vector. Steps: 1. Compute the Lambertian diffuse factor: \text{diffuse} = \max(0, \text{dot}(\text{normal}, \text{LightDirection})) where dot is the standard dot product. 2. Initialize lighting with the diffuse term (or add ambient light intensity 0.25f if required by the implementation). 3. Compute the fog factor using exponential decay: \text{fogFactor} = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{distance} \times \text{FogDensity}) where exp is the natural exponential function. 4. Apply fog attenuation if enabled: \text{lighting} = \text{lighting} \times (1.0 - \text{fogFactor}) \quad \text{if } \text{EnableFog} \text{ is true}. 5. Compute the average material brightness: \text{colorIntensity} = \frac{\text{materialColor.X} + \text{materialColor.Y} + \text{materialColor.Z}}{3.0}. 6. Modulate the lighting intensity: \text{lighting} = \text{lighting} \times (0.7 + \text{colorIntensity} \times 0.3). 7. Map the computed lighting to a color: If !settings.MapColorsWithGamma, call MapToColor(lighting, materialColor, theme). Else, call MapToColorWithGamma(lighting, materialColor, theme). 8. In MapToColor: finalColor = materialColor intensity (where intensity is the final lighting value). Clamp each component of finalColor to [0, 1]. Multiply each component by 255 and round to the nearest integer to get r, g, b. Return the ANSI escape sequence "\u001b[38;2;{r};{g};{b}m". 9. In MapToColorWithGamma: finalColor = materialColor intensity. Clamp each component of finalColor to [0, 1]. Apply gamma correction with gamma value 0.8: r = \text{pow}(\text{clamped\X}, 1.0 / 0.8) g = \text{pow}(\text{clamped\Y}, 1.0 / 0.8) b = \text{pow}(\text{clamped\Z}, 1.0 / 0.8). Multiply each component by 255 and cast to integer. Return the ANSI escape sequence "\u001b[38;2;{r};{g};{b}m". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lambertiandiffuseshadingwithfog(materialcolor, normal, lightdirection, distance, fogdensity, enablefog, usegamma): # 1. Compute diffuse lighting diffuse = max(0.0, math.fsum(normal) math.fsum(lightdirection) if not hasattr(normal, 'dot') else normal.dot(lightdirection)) # 2. Initialize lighting with diffuse term lighting = diffuse # 3. Apply fog attenuation if enablefog: fogfactor = 1.0 - math.exp(-distance fogdensity) lighting = lighting (1.0 - fogfactor) # 4. Modulate by material color intensity colorintensity = (materialcolor.x + materialcolor.y + materialcolor.z) / 3.0 lighting = lighting (0.7 + colorintensity 0.3) # 5. Map to Color finalcolor = (materialcolor.x lighting, materialcolor.y lighting, materialcolor.z lighting) # Clamp to [0, 1] r = max(0.0, min(1.0, finalcolor[0])) g = max(0.0, min(1.0, finalcolor[1])) b = max(0.0, min(1.0, finalcolor[2])) if usegamma: gamma = 0.8 r = math.pow(r, 1.0 / gamma) g = math.pow(g, 1.0 / gamma) b = math.pow(b, 1.0 / gamma) # Convert to 0-255 integer rint = int(round(r 255)) gint = int(round(g 255)) bint = int(round(b 255)) # Return ANSI code return f"\u001b38;2;{rint};{gint};{bint}m" Parameters: LightDirection: Normalized vector. Default: (0.5, 1.0, -0.3). AmbientLightIntensity: Scalar. Default: 0.25f. FogDensity: Scalar. Default: 0.03f. Gamma: Scalar. Default: 0.8f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If distance is 0, fogFactor is 0, so no fog attenuation occurs. Precision: Standard IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic is sufficient for exp and pow operations. [Clamping: Values outside [0, 1] are clamped before integer conversion to prevent overflow. Time Complexity: O(1) per hit point. Memory Complexity: O(1). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple arithmetic operations; provides basic atmospheric depth perception via exponential fog. Limitations: The fog model is a simple exponential decay without light scattering or multiple bounces. When to use: Real-time ASCII raymarching where performance is critical and visual fidelity is secondary to readability. When not to use: High-fidelity rendering or scenes requiring physically accurate light transport. This method is derived from the csRaymarching project, which focuses on raymarching signed distance fields (SDFs) for console output. It adapts standard Lambertian shading for the specific constraints of ANSI color codes and half-block character rendering. The use of gamma 0.8 and specific color mapping suggests an optimization for terminal display characteristics rather than physical accuracy. 0gecco/csRaymarching, https://github.com/0gecco/csRaymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering
head: Shaded Volume Rendering (SVR)
body: Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering is a technique that applies the Blinn-Phong lighting model to volume data during ray marching to provide surface-like shading cues. It differs from unshaded volume rendering by computing per-sample normals via central differences and combining diffuse, specular, and ambient terms to enhance depth perception and material appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture (volumeTexture), a 1D transfer function texture (tfTexture), a transformation matrix (transform), and lighting parameters (lightPos, lightColour, diffuse, specular, ambient, tfSize). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and alpha. Data Structures: Uniforms struct: transform: mat4x4<f32> lightPos: vec3<f32> lightColour: vec3<f32> diffuse: f32 specular: f32 ambient: f32 tfSize: f32 Texture Bindings: volumeTexture: texture3d<f32> at binding 0 volumeSampler: sampler at binding 1 tfTexture: texture1d<f32> at binding 3 Steps: 1. Vertex Shader: Generate a full-screen triangle using vertex indices to produce positions (-1, 3), (-1, -1), and (3, -1) in clip space. 2. Ray Origin/Direction: For each fragment with screen coordinate coord.xy, compute ray origin pos and direction dir by transforming screen coordinates: pos = transform vec4(coord.xy, 0.0, 1.0) and dir = transform vec4(0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0). 3. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute entry (near) and exit (far) distances by calculating inverse direction, bounding box distances, and taking min/max of axis intersections. Clamp near to 0 if negative. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from near to far: Intensity Sampling: Sample the 3D volume texture at coords. Convert the RG8 format sample to a normalized 16-bit value: \text{intensity} = \frac{\text{sample}.x + \text{sample}.y \times 255}{256} Normal Calculation: Compute the gradient using central differences. For each axis, sample the intensity at pos + offset and pos - offset, subtract them, and normalize the resulting vector delta. Transfer Function Lookup: Map the sampled intensity val to a 1D texture index tfIndex = \text{int32}(val \times \text{uniforms.tfSize}) and load the color from tfTexture. Blinn-Phong Lighting: Calculate light direction lightDir, view direction viewDir, and half vector halfDir. Compute: Diffuse: \max(0.0, \text{dot}(\text{norm}, \text{lightDir})) \times \text{uniforms.diffuse} Specular: \text{pow}(\max(0.0, \text{dot}(\text{norm}, \text{halfDir})), \text{shininess}) \times \text{uniforms.specular} Ambient: \text{uniforms.ambient} Combined: \text{litColor} = \text{uniforms.lightColour} \times (\text{colour.rgb} \times (\text{diffuse} + \text{ambient}) + \text{specular}) Front-to-Back Composition: Update accumulated color accColour using alpha blending: \alpha = (1.0 - \text{accColour}.a) \times \text{colour}.a \text{accColour}.rgb += \alpha \times \text{colour}.rgb \text{accColour}.a += \alpha Break if \text{accColour}.a \ge 0.95. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texturesample(tex, coords): return tex.sample(coords) def rayboxintersection(bboxmin, bboxmax, pos, dir): invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0.0 else 1e9 for d in dir] bot = [invdir[i] (bboxmin[i] - pos[i]) for i in range(3)] top = [invdir[i] (bboxmax[i] - pos[i]) for i in range(3)] rmin = [min(top[i], bot[i]) for i in range(3)] rmax = [max(top[i], bot[i]) for i in range(3)] tnear = max(rmin[0], max(rmin[1], rmin[2])) tfar = min(rmax[0], min(rmax[1], rmax[2])) return (tnear, tfar) def fragmain(coord, uniforms, volumetexture, tftexture): size = (volumetexture.shape[0], volumetexture.shape[1], volumetexture.shape[2]) pos = uniforms.transform vec4(coord.x, coord.y, 0.0, 1.0) dir = uniforms.transform vec4(0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0) intersect = rayboxintersection((0.0, 0.0, 0.0), size, pos.xyz, dir.xyz) near = max(0, int(intersect[0])) far = int(intersect[1]) acccolour = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for k in range(near, far + 1): transformed = uniforms.transform vec4(coord.x, coord.y, float(k), 1.0) coords = vec3(transformed.x / size[0], transformed.y / size[1], transformed.z / size[2]) sample = texturesample(volumetexture, coords) intensity = (sample.x + sample.y 255.0) / 256.0 # Normal calculation using central differences offset = vec3(0.001, 0.001, 0.001) grad = vec3( texturesample(volumetexture, pos + offset vec3(1, 0, 0)).x - texturesample(volumetexture, pos - offset vec3(1, 0, 0)).x, texturesample(volumetexture, pos + offset vec3(0, 1, 0)).x - texturesample(volumetexture, pos - offset vec3(0, 1, 0)).x, texturesample(volumetexture, pos + offset vec3(0, 0, 1)).x - texturesample(volumetexture, pos - offset vec3(0, 0, 1)).x) norm = normalize(grad) # Transfer function lookup tfindex = int(intensity uniforms.tfSize) colour = texturesample(tftexture, vec4(float(tfindex) / uniforms.tfSize, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Blinn-Phong lighting lightdir = normalize(uniforms.lightPos - pos.xyz) viewdir = normalize(-pos.xyz) halfdir = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) diffuse = max(0.0, dot(norm, lightdir)) uniforms.diffuse specular = pow(max(0.0, dot(norm, halfdir)), 10.0) uniforms.specular ambient = uniforms.ambient litcolour = uniforms.lightColour (colour.rgb (diffuse + ambient) + specular) # Front-to-back composition alpha = (1.0 - acccolour.a) colour.a acccolour.rgb += alpha litcolour.rgb acccolour.a += alpha if acccolour.a >= 0.95: break return acccolour Parameters: shininess: 10.0 Edge Cases: Precision issues in normal calculation due to small offsets. Boundary conditions when ray exits volume. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples along the ray. Strengths: Provides realistic shading cues. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple texture samples for normal calculation. Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering was implemented in the ossium project for WebGPU. fraserlove/ossium, https://github.com/fraserlove/ossium, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gouraud Shading
head: intensity interpolation shading, smooth shading
body: Gouraud shading is a surface shading technique that computes illumination colors at mesh vertices and linearly interpolates these colors across the resulting primitives to approximate smooth lighting. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by interpolating the final color value rather than the geometric normal vector, as done in Phong Shading with SDF Normals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh defined by vertices, vertex normals, and a directional light source. Output: A rasterized image with per-pixel colors. Data Structures: Vertex Attributes: Each vertex stores a position and a normal vector \mathbf{n}. Interpolation: Linear interpolation of scalar color values across triangle edges and interior. Steps: 1. Compute Vertex Normals: For curved surfaces, calculate the normal for each vertex by averaging the normals of all adjacent faces sharing that vertex. For planar surfaces, the same normal is applied to all defining vertices. 2. Calculate Vertex Colors: For each vertex, compute the color using the lighting model. The intensity depends on the angle between the light source direction and the vertex normal vector. 3. Interpolate Colors: During rasterization, linearly interpolate the computed vertex colors across the surface of the primitive to determine the color of each pixel. Formulas: The sources do not specify an exact mathematical lighting equation. The vertex color is determined by the angle between the light source direction and the vertex normal vector. The interpolated color at any point on the primitive is a linear combination of the vertex colors. Parameters: Normal Vector: A vertex attribute pointing perpendicular to the surface, used to estimate light reflection. Shading Model Flag: In OpenGL, glShadeModel(GLSMOOTH) enables this method. Pitfalls: Faceted Appearance: If normals are not averaged for curved surfaces, the discontinuity in slope between faces results in a faceted or gem-like appearance. Intensity Discontinuities: Without shading, curved surfaces approximated by polygons exhibit Mach band effect intensity discontinuities along edges. Complexity: Computation is performed per-vertex, making it faster than per-pixel shading methods like Phong shading. Strengths: Provides a smoother appearance than flat shading by diminishing intensity discontinuities. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Gouraud shading, also known as intensity interpolation shading, was introduced as an approach to render approximate surfaces with smoother color variations than flat shading. It is implemented in systems such as Smokeview for visualizing fire dynamics simulation data, where it is referred to as smooth shading. name: Ray Marching with Blinn-Phong Lighting
head: GPU Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields
body:
This method renders scenes defined by implicit surfaces (Signed Distance Fields) by casting rays from a camera, iteratively marching them to find intersections, and shading the resulting surface points using the Blinn-Phong reflectance model. It differs from analytical ray tracing by using iterative distance estimation to handle complex, non-analytic geometry, and it differs from pure SDF rendering by explicitly applying a local lighting model (diffuse, specular, ambient) rather than just color blending or occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position (ucamPos), inverse projection matrix (ucamInvProjMat), world transformation matrix (ucamToWorldMat), maximum marching distance (umaxDis), light direction (ulightDir), light color (ulightColor), diffuse intensity (udiffIntensity), shininess exponent (ushininess), specular intensity (uspecIntensity), ambient intensity (uambientIntensity), and background color (uclearColor). Outputs: A fragment color (glFragColor) for each pixel. Data Structures: The implementation typically resides in a fragment shader applied to a plane fixed to the camera's near plane. Shader code is stored in string variables (vertCode, fragCode) and passed to a shader material. The core logic requires a scene SDF evaluation function, a ray marching loop, a normal estimation function, and a scene color retrieval function. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Obtain normalized screen coordinates uv. Calculate ray origin ro from the uniform ucamPos. Calculate ray direction rd by transforming uv through the inverse projection matrix and world matrix, then normalizing: \mathbf{rd} = 	ext{normalize}(\mathbf{u\camToWorldMat} \cdot (\mathbf{u\camInvProjMat} \cdot 	ext{vec4}(\mathbf{uv} \cdot 2 - 1, 0, 1)).xyz) 2. Ray Marching: Call rayMarch(ro, rd) to find the total distance disTravelled along the ray to the nearest surface. 3. Hit Point Calculation: Compute the hit point position hp: \mathbf{hp} = \mathbf{ro} + 	ext{disTravelled} \cdot \mathbf{rd} 4. Normal Estimation: Compute the surface normal n at hp using a normal(hp) function. This is typically the normalized gradient of the SDF: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{hp})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{hp})\|} where 
abla f is estimated via finite differences (e.g., sampling the SDF at small offsets along axes). 5. Termination Check: If disTravelled >= umaxDis, the ray did not hit a surface within bounds. Output the clear color: 	ext{gl\FragColor} = 	ext{vec4}(\mathbf{u\clearColor}, 1) 6. Lighting Calculation (Blinn-Phong): If a hit occurs, compute the diffuse term diff: 	ext{diff} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{u\lightDir}, 0.0) \cdot \mathbf{u\diffIntensity} Compute the specular term spec using the diffuse term as the basis for the shininess exponent (as per the source code logic): 	ext{spec} = 	ext{pow}(	ext{diff}, \mathbf{u\shininess}) \cdot \mathbf{u\specIntensity} Retrieve the ambient intensity: 	ext{ambient} = \mathbf{u\ambientIntensity} 7. Color Accumulation: Retrieve the scene color at the hit point: \mathbf{sceneCol} = 	ext{sceneCol}(\mathbf{hp}). Compute the final color: \mathbf{color} = \mathbf{u\lightColor} \cdot (\mathbf{sceneCol} \cdot (	ext{spec} + 	ext{ambient} + 	ext{diff})) Output the result: 	ext{gl\FragColor} = 	ext{vec4}(\mathbf{color}, 1) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(uv, ucamPos, ucamInvProjMat, ucamToWorldMat, umaxDis, uclearColor, ulightDir, udiffIntensity, ushininess, uspecIntensity, uambientIntensity, ulightColor, scenefunc, scenecolfunc): # 1. Ray Generation ro = ucamPos ndc = vec4(uv 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) rd = ucamInvProjMat ndc rd = vec3(rd.x, rd.y, rd.z) rd = ucamToWorldMat vec4(rd, 0.0) rd = vec3(rd.x, rd.y, rd.z) rd = normalize(rd) # 2. Ray Marching (Sphere Tracing) disTravelled = rayMarch(ro, rd, umaxDis, scenefunc) # 3. Hit Point hp = ro + disTravelled rd # 4. Normal n = normal(hp, scenefunc) # 5. Termination Check if disTravelled >= umaxDis: return vec4(uclearColor, 1.0) # 6. Lighting dotNL = dot(n, ulightDir) diff = max(dotNL, 0.0) udiffIntensity spec = pow(diff, ushininess) uspecIntensity ambient = uambientIntensity # 7. Color Accumulation sc = scenecolfunc(hp) color = ulightColor (sc (spec + ambient + diff)) return vec4(color, 1.0) def rayMarch(ro, rd, umaxDis, scenefunc): t = 0.0 epsilon = 0.001 while t < umaxDis: p = ro + t rd d = scenefunc(p) if d < epsilon: return t t += d return t def normal(p, scenefunc): # Finite difference gradient estimation eps = 0.001 dx = scenefunc(p + vec3(eps, 0.0, 0.0)) - scenefunc(p - vec3(eps, 0.0, 0.0)) dy = scenefunc(p + vec3(0.0, eps, 0.0)) - scenefunc(p - vec3(0.0, eps, 0.0)) dz = scenefunc(p + vec3(0.0, 0.0, eps)) - scenefunc(p - vec3(0.0, 0.0, eps)) return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) Parameters: ushininess: Specular shininess exponent. Typical values are not given in the sources. umaxDis: Maximum ray marching distance. Prevents infinite loops and defines the visible depth range. udiffIntensity, uspecIntensity, uambientIntensity: Multipliers for the respective lighting components. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Finite difference normal estimation can be noisy if the step size is not chosen carefully relative to the SDF's scale. Boundary: Rays exceeding umaxDis must be handled to avoid rendering artifacts or undefined behavior. Light Direction: ulightDir is assumed to be a uniform direction. For point lights, the direction would need to be calculated per-pixel as normalize(lightPos - hp), which is not described in the source but is a common extension. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of ray march steps, as each step requires an SDF evaluation. The lighting calculation is constant time per hit. Memory Complexity: Low. Primarily requires storage for uniforms and temporary variables in the shader. No large buffers are needed for geometry. Strengths: Efficiently renders complex, smooth implicit surfaces without explicit mesh topology. Simple to implement in WebGL/Three.js as a post-process or overlay shader. Limitations: The Blinn-Phong model is a local approximation and does not account for global illumination effects like indirect lighting or soft shadows (unless added via additional ray marches). The specific specular calculation using pow(diff, shininess) is a simplification and may not match standard Blinn-Phong implementations which use the half-vector. When to use: Real-time rendering of SDF-based scenes where performance is critical and high-fidelity global illumination is not required. Suitable for stylized or abstract visuals. This technique is a practical implementation of GPU ray marching for Signed Distance Fields, popularized in the context of WebGL and libraries like Three.js. It combines the geometric power of SDFs with the simplicity of the Blinn-Phong shading model. The specific implementation details, including the shader structure and parameter names, are documented in guides for implementing ray marching in Three.js. Ray Marching with Three.js Guide, https://www.scribd.com/document/882338593/Ray-Marching-in-Three-js, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Specular and Reflective Shading
head: Reflective Shading, Specular Shading
body:
This family covers techniques for rendering specular highlights, mirror-like reflections, and iridescent effects in distance-field ray marching. It solves the problem of simulating view-dependent surface reflectance in implicit geometry, where standard rasterization techniques are not directly applicable. It sets itself apart from Distance Color Blending by handling geometric specular bounces rather than volumetric color blending, and from Diffuse Lighting Models by explicitly modeling view-dependent reflectance. All methods in this family operate on a surface point \mathbf{p} and its associated geometric data, primarily the surface normal \mathbf{n}. The normal is typically derived from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) using the gradient: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|} where 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) is estimated via finite differences, such as solving a linear system based on values at vertices of a tetrahedron, or via back-propagation. The core shading computation generally follows this structure: 1. Geometric Setup: Determine the view direction \mathbf{v} (from \mathbf{p} to camera) and light direction \mathbf{l} (from \mathbf{p} to light source). 2. Occlusion/Ambient Occlusion: Calculate shadow factors or ambient occlusion values to determine how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from the environment or specific lights. 3. Reflectance Model: Compute the diffuse and specular components based on the angle between \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, and the reflection vector \mathbf{r}. 4. Color Accumulation: Combine the base material color with the lighting contributions, often modulated by depth cueing or atmospheric effects. Extends distance-field ray marching by iteratively scattering rays specularly upon surface intersection to simulate mirror-like or metallic materials. It distinguishes itself from Approximate Refraction by handling surface reflection rather than transmission, and from Screen-Space Reflections by operating in full 3D volume space rather than restricted screen-space depth buffers. Choose this method when simulating recursive mirror-like or metallic surfaces. Generates an iridescent appearance on ray-marched surfaces by mapping a perturbed surface normal to a color via a cosine palette function, simulating thin-film interference colors. It differs from Ray Marching with Reflections by using a procedural color palette driven by normal perturbation rather than recursive ray tracing for color, and from Spherical Gaussian Shading by using a fixed cosine palette rather than analytically approximated lobes for the base color. Choose this method for artistic thin-film interference effects. Approximates direct illumination and specular BRDFs using a mixture of Spherical Gaussian basis functions to enable fast, analytic integration and automatic differentiation. It distinguishes itself from Monte Carlo integration by being less expensive and more robust to roughness variations, though it sacrifices high-frequency detail accuracy. Choose this method in differentiable rendering and inverse rendering pipelines where lighting and material parameters must be optimized jointly. A real-time shading technique designed for procedural neon city scenes, computing diffuse, specular, ambient occlusion, metallic reflection, and emissive contributions per pixel. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Ray Marching with Reflections by integrating a specific metallic Fresnel weighting scheme and a fixed-step shadow ray implementation optimized for the compressed distance field of the neon city geometry, rather than relying on general-purpose path tracing or complex environment maps. Choose this method for high-contrast, emissive neon or cyberpunk aesthetics. Not given in the sources.

name: Ray Marching with Reflections
head: GLSL reflect function for raymarching, Metal Material Scattering, Ray Marching with Recursive Reflections, Reflection and Refraction in Raymarching, Spherical Marching with Reflections, raytraced reflections, renderReflection
body:
Ray Marching with Reflections extends distance-field ray marching by iteratively scattering rays specularly upon surface intersection to simulate mirror-like or metallic materials. Unlike standard ray marching which terminates at the first hit, this method continues the ray path in the reflected direction, accumulating color contributions weighted by material reflectivity. It distinguishes itself from Approximate Refraction by handling surface reflection rather than transmission, and from Screen-Space Reflections by operating in full 3D volume space rather than restricted screen-space depth buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial ray origin \mathbf{r}o and direction \mathbf{r}d; Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}); reflection coefficient c{	ext{refl}}; maximum reflection bounces N{	ext{max}}. Output: Final accumulated color \mathbf{C}{	ext{out}}. Data Structures: Ray: Struct containing origin (vec3) and direction (vec3). HitRecord: Struct containing t (distance to hit, float), hitpoint (vec3), normal (vec3), and material properties. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set accumulated color \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} = \mathbf{0}, transmission mask \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{1}, and current ray \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{r}o, \mathbf{r}d). 2. Loop: For bounce index i from 0 to N{	ext{max}}-1: a. March: Perform SDF ray marching along \mathbf{r} to find the closest intersection distance t. b. Hit Handling: i. If intersection found (t \ge 0): 1. Compute intersection point: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}.	ext{origin} + t \cdot \mathbf{r}.	ext{direction}. 2. Compute surface normal \mathbf{n} using the SDF gradient: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|} where 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) is estimated via finite differences. 3. Compute direct illumination \mathbf{C}{	ext{light}} at \mathbf{p} using \mathbf{n}, view direction, and light sources. 4. Accumulate color: \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} + \mathbf{M} \odot \mathbf{C}{	ext{light}}. 5. Update mask: \mathbf{M} \leftarrow \mathbf{M} \cdot c{	ext{refl}}. 6. Check termination: If \|\mathbf{M}\| < \epsilon (e.g., 0.001), break loop. 7. Prepare next ray: Compute reflected direction: \mathbf{r}{	ext{new\d}} = \mathbf{r}.	ext{direction} - 2(\mathbf{r}.	ext{direction} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n}. Guard against degenerate normals: If \|\mathbf{r}{	ext{new\d}}\| < 10^{-8}, set \mathbf{r}{	ext{new\d}} = \mathbf{n}. Offset origin to prevent self-intersection (shadow acne): \mathbf{p}{	ext{new}} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \cdot \delta, where \delta = 0.05 or \delta = 0.001. Set \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{p}{	ext{new}}, \mathbf{r}{	ext{new\d}}). ii. If no intersection found: 1. If i=0 (primary ray missed), set \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} = (0.3, 0.2, 0.8). 2. Else, add background contribution: \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} + \mathbf{M} \odot \mathbf{C}{	ext{background}}(\mathbf{r}). 3. Break loop. 3. Post-Processing: a. Apply tone mapping: \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} =  rac{\mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}}}{\mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}} + \mathbf{1}}. b. Apply gamma correction: \mathbf{C}{	ext{out}} = \mathbf{C}{	ext{acc}}^{(1/\gamma)}, typically \gamma = 1.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchwithreflections(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, maxbounces, crefl, epsilon=0.001): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 (normalized) sdffunc: function(x) -> float maxbounces: int crefl: float (reflection coefficient, 0.0 to 1.0) epsilon: float (transmittance threshold) """ accum = vec3(0.0) mask = vec3(1.0) currrayorigin = rayorigin currraydir = raydirection MAXDIST = 100.0 for i in range(maxbounces): # 1. March hitdist = marchsdf(currrayorigin, currraydir, sdffunc, MAXDIST) if hitdist is not None: # 2. Hit Found p = currrayorigin + hitdist currraydir # 3. Compute Normal grad = computesdfgradient(p, sdffunc) n = normalize(grad) # 4. Direct Illumination lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) diff = max(dot(n, lightdir), 0.0) color = vec3(0.8) diff # 5. Accumulate accum = accum + mask color # 6. Update Mask mask = mask crefl # 7. Termination Check if length(mask) < epsilon: break # 8. Prepare Next Ray newdir = currraydir - 2.0 dot(currraydir, n) n # Guard degenerate case if length(newdir) < 1e-8: newdir = n # Offset origin to prevent self-intersection delta = 0.05 neworigin = p + n delta currrayorigin = neworigin currraydir = newdir else: # 9. Miss if i == 0: accum = vec3(0.3, 0.2, 0.8) # Sky color else: bgcolor = vec3(0.1, 0.1, 0.1) # Background color accum = accum + mask bgcolor break # 10. Post-processing accum = accum / (accum + vec3(1.0)) gamma = 1.1 accum = pow(accum, vec3(1.0/gamma)) return accum def marchsdf(origin, direction, sdffunc, maxdist): t = 0.0 maxsteps = 64 for in range(maxsteps): p = origin + t direction d = sdffunc(p) if d < 0.001: return t if t > maxdist: return None t += d return None def computesdfgradient(p, sdffunc): eps = 0.001 x = vec3(1, 0, 0) y = vec3(0, 1, 0) z = vec3(0, 0, 1) dx = sdffunc(p + x eps) - sdffunc(p - x eps) dy = sdffunc(p + y eps) - sdffunc(p - y eps) dz = sdffunc(p + z eps) - sdffunc(p - z eps) return vec3(dx, dy, dz) / (2 eps) Parameters: c{	ext{refl}}: Reflection coefficient multiplier. Controls the attenuation of color per bounce. Default value: 0.3. N{	ext{max}}: Number of reflection bounces. If 1, uses a single bounce path. Default value: 0 (no recursion) or 1. \epsilon: Transmittance threshold. Stops recursion when mask magnitude drops below this value. Default value: 0.001. \delta: Offset distance for ray origin. Prevents self-intersection. Value: 0.05 or 0.001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection (Shadow Acne): Casting a ray from the exact intersection point causes the ray to immediately hit the same surface. Mitigated by offsetting the origin along the normal by \delta. Degenerate Normals: If the reflection vector becomes near-zero (e.g., grazing angles or numerical instability), it should be clamped to the normal direction to prevent undefined behavior. Infinite Recursion: Without a termination condition based on transmittance (\epsilon) or max bounces, reflective scenes can cause stack overflows or infinite loops. Extends basic raycasting by continuing the ray path after intersection to realize reflections, distinguishing raytracing (interaction continuation) from raycasting (single throw). Renders glass with Fresnel reflection and per-channel refraction for chromatic dispersion (n = 1.48/1.50/1.52). Falls back to reflected ray on total-internal-reflection and applies distance-compounding tint. The 3-trace dispersion path is gated to grazing angles. Interpolates between specular lighting and environment reflection color based on a blend factor. Computes environment reflection color via an environment map and mixes it with specular sum, resetting specular sum and light Y to 1.0 after blending. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originating from the generalization of raycasting to raytracing, this method allows for the simulation of light interaction with surfaces beyond the first hit. It is commonly implemented in GLSL-based raymarchers using the reflect function. name: Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption
head: renderRefraction, transparent raymarching
body: This method extends distance-field ray marching to simulate transparent dielectric objects by handling refraction, total internal reflection (TIR), and exponential light absorption (Beer's Law) over multiple bounces. Unlike standard ray marching which terminates at the first surface hit, this approach continues the ray through transparent boundaries, flipping the normal direction to track interior traversal and accumulating distance for attenuation. It distinguishes itself from Approximate Refraction by explicitly computing the refracted ray direction and handling TIR, and from Cone Marching by using a single ray path rather than volumetric cone integration for absorption. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{ro}, ray direction \mathbf{rd}, scene signed distance function (SDF) sceneSDF, maximum refraction bounces MAXREFRACTIONS, and per-material absorption vector \mathbf{a} (RGB). Outputs: Final pixel color C{out}. Data Structures: SdResult: Struct containing dist (float, signed distance) and mat (material struct). dist < 0 indicates the ray is inside the object. Material: Contains refractionindex (float, IOR) and absorption (vec3). Parameters: MAXREFRACTIONS: Integer, typically 4. absorption: RGB vector controlling exponential light attenuation per unit distance inside the medium. Algorithm: 1. Initialize color = vec3(0), invert = -1.0 (indicating interior state), and absorbdist = 0.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to MAXREFRACTIONS - 1: a. Cast ray: if invert < 0, call castRayDI(ro, rd) (interior cast); else call castRayD(ro, rd) (exterior cast). b. If invert < 0, add sd.dist to absorbdist. c. If sd.dist < 0, render background if invert > 0 and break the loop. d. Compute intersection point: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{ro} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot sd.dist. e. Compute normal: \mathbf{n} = \text{getNormalFast}(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \text{invert}. f. Compute reflection direction: \mathbf{ref} = \text{reflect}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n}). g. Add lighting contribution: color += light(sd.mat, ro, ref, p, n). h. If invert > 0, break the loop (ray exited object). i. Compute Index of Refraction (IOR): if invert < 0 (inside), ior = sd.mat.refractionindex; if invert > 0 (outside), ior = 1.0 / sd.mat.refractionindex. j. Compute refraction direction: \mathbf{raf} = \text{refract}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n}, \text{ior}). k. If \mathbf{raf} == \mathbf{0} (Total Internal Reflection), set \mathbf{rd} = \mathbf{ref}; else set \mathbf{rd} = \mathbf{raf}. l. Update ray origin to prevent self-intersection: \mathbf{ro} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot (0.01 / |\mathbf{rd} \cdot \mathbf{n}|). m. Update invert: if TIR occurred, keep invert; else invert = invert -1.0. 3. Apply Beer's Law absorption: C{out} = \text{color} \cdot e^{-\mathbf{a} \cdot \text{absorb\dist}}. Formulas: Beer's Law Absorption: C{out} = C{in} \cdot e^{-\mathbf{a} \cdot d} where \mathbf{a} is the absorption vector and d is the accumulated distance traveled inside transparent media. Self-intersection offset: \mathbf{ro}{new} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot \frac{0.01}{|\mathbf{rd} \cdot \mathbf{n}|} This offset prevents floating-point inaccuracies at sharp angles from causing immediate re-intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrefraction(ro, rd, maxrefractions=4, absorption=vec3(0.0)): color = vec3(0.0) invert = -1.0 # -1 for inside state, 1 for outside state absorbdist = 0.0 for i in range(maxrefractions): # Cast ray based on current state if invert < 0: sd = castRayDI(ro, rd) else: sd = castRayD(ro, rd) # Accumulate distance if inside if invert < 0: absorbdist += sd.dist # Handle exit or background if sd.dist < 0: if invert > 0: return background(ro, rd) # else: ray exited object, loop continues, invert flips next # Intersection point p = ro + rd sd.dist # Normal with correct orientation n = getNormalFast(p) invert # Reflection component ref = reflect(rd, n) color += light(sd.mat, ro, ref, p, n) # If we hit from outside (invert > 0), break loop if invert > 0: break # Compute IOR for refraction if invert < 0: ior = sd.mat.refractionindex else: ior = 1.0 / sd.mat.refractionindex # Compute refraction raf = refract(rd, n, ior) # Check for Total Internal Reflection (TIR) tif = (raf == vec3(0.0)) if tif: rd = ref else: rd = raf # Offset origin to prevent self-intersection ro = p + rd (0.01 / abs(dot(rd, n))) # Update invert state if tif: pass # Keep invert else: invert = invert -1.0 # Apply Beer's Law color = exp(-dot(absorption, absorbdist)) return color The pseudocode assumes castRayDI and castRayD are distinct SDF casters handling interior/exterior distance queries appropriately, and refract returns a zero vector on TIR. Standard vector operations (vec3, dot, abs, exp, reflect, refract, getNormalFast, light, background) are assumed available or implemented per standard graphics conventions. Edge cases and pitfalls: At sharp angles, floating-point inaccuracies cause self-intersection, mitigated by the origin offset. The method assumes invert correctly tracks interior traversal state and that sd.dist < 0 reliably indicates exiting the medium. This method extends Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption by simulating chromatic dispersion, where the index of refraction (IOR) varies by wavelength. It splits the ray into Red, Green, and Blue channels, refracting each with a distinct IOR to produce spectral separation effects, while falling back to a single IOR when dispersion is negligible. A shading model for dielectric materials that handles transparency and absorption using stochastic ray selection and Beer-Lambert law. It performs stochastic selection between reflection and refraction rays, and applies Beer-Lambert absorption to the transmitted ray intensity based on distance and absorption density. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to MAXREFRACTIONS and the cost of SDF evaluation per bounce. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), as it only stores current ray state and accumulated color/distance. Strengths: Physically plausible transparency, handles complex internal reflections and absorption. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple bounces. Sensitive to floating-point precision at grazing angles (mitigated by offset). Does not account for subsurface scattering or volumetric scattering within the medium, only surface refraction and path absorption. When to use: Rendering transparent dielectrics like glass, water, or gems where internal reflections and color absorption are important. When not to use: Opaque objects, or when performance is critical and approximate transparency suffices. This method is implemented in the cahekp/Raymarching repository. It builds upon standard ray marching techniques by adding transparency handling. The use of Beer's Law for absorption is a standard technique in computer graphics for simulating light attenuation in participating media or transparent solids. cahekp/Raymarching, https://github.com/cahekp/Raymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, https://github.com/NiekMSoftware/bad-apple-voxel-raytracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Transmission & Chromatic Dispersion Ray Marching
head: Chromatic Dispersion Ray Marching
body: This method extends Ray Marching with Refraction and Beer's Law Absorption by simulating chromatic dispersion, where the index of refraction varies by wavelength. It handles light transmission through transparent surfaces using refraction, optionally splitting rays into Red, Green, and Blue channels based on an IOR spread. Inputs: Ray origin O, direction D, surface normal N, view direction V, transmission T, index of refraction n, dispersion factor d, hit position hitPos, epsilon hitEpsAtHit, scene parameters throughHitPos, throughHitRes, transmissionSamples, ambient light ambientLight, base transmission throughBase, and emission throughEmission. Outputs: Transmitted color C{trans} = [R, G, B]. Data Structures: Material struct fields relevant to this step: transmission (float), ior (float), dispersion (float). Steps: 1. If T > 0.001, compute incident vector I = -V. 2. If d \le 10^{-4}, compute \eta = 1.0/\max(n, 1.0001), compute refracted direction D{refr} = \text{refract}(I, N, \eta), and if \|D{refr}\|^2 < 10^{-6}, replace D{refr} with the reflected fallback direction. 3. March the refracted ray: marchSceneTransmission(hitPos + D{refr} (hitEpsAtHit 6.0), D{refr}, throughHitPos, throughHitRes, transmissionSamples). 4. If a hit occurs, compute transmitted color: C{trans} = \text{ambientLight} \times \text{throughBase} + \text{throughEmission}. 5. If d > 10^{-4}, compute channel IORs (nR, nG, nB), refract I and N for each channel, and apply the same TIR fallback if \|D{refr,c}\|^2 < 10^{-6}. 6. March each refracted ray independently. 7. Combine the transmitted R, G, B channels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def refract(I, N, eta): costheta = dot(-I, N) r = eta eta (1.0 - costheta costheta) if r > 1.0: return vec3(0.0) return eta I + (eta costheta - sqrt(1.0 - r)) N def marchchromaticdispersion(hitpos, normal, viewdir, transmission, ior, dispersion, hitEpsAtHit, throughHitPos, throughHitRes, transmissionSamples, ambientLight, throughBase, throughEmission): # 1. Check transmission if transmission <= 0.001: return vec3(0.0) # Not given in the sources. I = -viewdir refracteddirs = [] # 2 & 5. Dispersion handling if dispersion <= 1e-4: eta = 1.0 / max(ior, 1.0001) refracted = refract(I, normal, eta) if dot(refracted, refracted) < 1e-6: refracted = reflect(I, normal) # reflectedFallback refracteddirs.append(refracted) else: iorspread = dispersion 0.35 iorvals = [ior + iorspread, ior, ior - iorspread] # iorR, iorG, iorB for iorval in iorvals: eta = 1.0 / max(iorval, 1.0001) refracted = refract(I, normal, eta) if dot(refracted, refracted) < 1e-6: refracted = reflect(I, normal) # reflectedFallback refracteddirs.append(refracted) # 3 & 6. March each refracted ray independently transmittedcolors = [] for refrdir in refracteddirs: startpos = hitpos + refrdir (hitEpsAtHit 6.0) # marchSceneTransmission(startpos, refrdir, throughHitPos, throughHitRes, transmissionSamples) # Ray marching implementation details are not provided in the sources. hit = True # Assumed for the accumulation step per evidence if hit: # 4. Accumulate transmitted = ambientLight throughBase + throughEmission transmittedcolors.append(transmitted) # 7. Combine return vec3(transmittedcolors[0], transmittedcolors[1], transmittedcolors[2]) Parameters: dispersion: Chromatic dispersion factor, typically in [0, 1]. ior: Index of refraction, clamped to \ge 1.0. Edge Cases: Total Internal Reflection (TIR): Detected by checking if the squared length of the refracted direction is less than 10^{-6}. If true, the refracted ray is replaced with the reflected fallback direction to prevent NaN or invalid directions. Not given in the sources. This method is implemented in the RayMarchingtool repository by TeoGrajqevci. It builds on standard ray marching with refraction by adding spectral separation to transparent materials. name: Nested Raymarching for Refraction
head: GLASSREFLECT, Glass Refraction via Nested Raymarching, Glass-like surface modeling
body: Nested Raymarching for Refraction models a glass-like surface by refracting the ray direction upon entering the object, marching inside the object, and refracting again upon exiting. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, a signed distance field function S(\mathbf{p}), a refractive index ratio \eta (ratio of the incident medium to the glass), and a maximum march step count as inputs. It outputs the color at the final intersection point, or a background color if the ray escapes without hitting a surface. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains standard raymarching state variables for the current position \mathbf{p} and current direction \mathbf{d}. No additional complex data structures are required beyond the SDF evaluation. Steps: 1. Initial March: Perform standard raymarching along \mathbf{d} using S(\mathbf{p}) until a surface is intersected at \mathbf{p}{entry}. 2. Entry Refraction: Compute the new ray direction \mathbf{d}{in} using the standard refraction formula with incident direction \mathbf{d}, surface normal \mathbf{n}{entry}, and ratio \eta. 3. Nested March (Inside Glass): Initialize a nested loop for marching inside the glass. Set the current position \mathbf{p}{curr} = \mathbf{p}{entry} and direction \mathbf{d}{curr} = \mathbf{d}{in}. Because the ray is inside the object, the signed distance values returned by S are negative. To march forward, subtract the negative distance (i.e., use its absolute value) when calculating the step size. Loop: evaluate d = S(\mathbf{p}{curr}). If d > 0, the ray has exited the object; break the nested loop. Otherwise, step forward: \mathbf{p}{curr} \leftarrow \mathbf{p}{curr} + \mathbf{d}{curr} \cdot \max(|d|, \epsilon). 4. Exit Refraction: When the loop breaks because d > 0, the current position \mathbf{p}{exit} is near the exit surface. Compute the exit normal \mathbf{n}{exit} = \nabla S(\mathbf{p}{exit}). The normal at the exit point points away from the object center (outward). For the refraction calculation from glass to air, use the negated normal -\mathbf{n}{exit} and the reciprocal of the entry refractive index, 1/\eta. Compute the final direction \mathbf{d}{out} = \text{refract}(\mathbf{d}{curr}, -\mathbf{n}{exit}, 1/\eta). 5. Final March: Continue raymarching along \mathbf{d}{out} in the external medium to find the final intersection or background. Pitfalls: Normal Direction: When exiting, the SDF normal points outward. It must be negated (-\mathbf{n}) for the refraction formula to correctly compute the transmission from inside to outside. Index Ratio: The refractive index ratio must be inverted (1/\eta) upon exit, as the ray travels from the denser medium (glass) to the rarer medium (air). Negative Distances: Inside the object, SDF values are negative. The marching logic must subtract these negative distances to step forward correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nestedraymarchrefraction(rayorigin, raydir, sdf, eta, maxsteps): # 1. Initial March pos = rayorigin dir = raydir hit = False for in range(maxsteps): dist = sdf(pos) if dist < 0.001: hit = True break pos += dir max(dist, 0.001) if not hit: return BACKGROUNDCOLOR # 2. Entry Refraction normalin = normalize(sdfgradient(pos, sdf)) dirin = refract(dir, normalin, eta) # 3. Nested March (Inside Glass) pos = pos + dirin 0.001 # Offset to avoid self-intersection for in range(maxsteps): dist = sdf(pos) if dist > 0.0: # Exit detected break # Inside glass, SDF values are negative. Subtract distances to march forward. stepsize = max(abs(dist), 0.001) pos += dirin stepsize # 4. Exit Refraction normalout = normalize(sdfgradient(pos, sdf)) # Normal points away from surface; negate for internal-to-external refraction. # Index ratio is inverted (glass to air). dirout = refract(dirin, -normalout, 1.0 / eta) # 5. Final March pos = pos + dirout 0.001 for in range(maxsteps): dist = sdf(pos) if dist < 0.001: break pos += dirout max(dist, 0.001) return computecolor(pos) def refract(i, n, eta): # Standard vector refraction formula dot = sum(ab for a,b in zip(i, n)) k = 1.0 - eta eta (1.0 - dot dot) if k < 0.0: return i # Total internal reflection fallback return [eta i[j] + (eta dot - (k 0.5)) n[j] for j in range(len(i))] def sdfgradient(p, sdffunc, eps=0.001): # Finite difference approximation of the SDF normal return normalize([ sdffunc([p[0]+eps, p[1], p[2]]) - sdffunc([p[0]-eps, p[1], p[2]]), sdffunc([p[0], p[1]+eps, p[2]]) - sdffunc([p[0], p[1]-eps, p[2]]), sdffunc([p[0], p[1], p[2]+eps]) - sdffunc([p[0], p[1], p[2]-eps]) ]) def computecolor(p): return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Shading logic not specified in sources def normalize(v): l = (sum(xx for x in v))0.5 return [x/l for x in v] if l > 0 else v BACKGROUNDCOLOR = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) A method to handle light passing through transparent objects by computing refraction beams at both front and back intersections simultaneously. It runs the refinement process once for both reflection and refraction, as the heuristic depends only on geometry. It computes the refraction beam at the first intersection and immediately computes the second refraction. To intersect rays from inside the objects, it uses a distance impostor: a cube map storing surface normals and distance from a reference point (typically the object's center). This speeds up rendering but cannot render caustics inside the object. Not given in the sources. This method was described in the COS 426 Final Project Writeup on Raymarching with Signed Distance Fields. It is presented as a "relatively simple glass-like effect" that is "the most tricky to get right" among reflection types. The authors note that a more sophisticated approach modeling glass as a material that both reflects and refracts light was attempted but unsuccessful.
