name: Real-time Reflection of Clouds
head: Panoramic Cloud Reflection, SSR for Clouds, Sky Light Cloud Reflections, Volumetric Cloud Reflection Tracing
body: This method provides scene reflections for volumetric clouds by ray marching reflection surfaces using data from the Sky Light component. It addresses the limitation of standard Screen-Space Reflections (SSR), which can only reflect clouds currently visible within the screen space. To capture clouds outside the current view, it renders a low-resolution panoramic view in an extra pass and blends it into the sky cubemap. Inputs: Volumetric cloud data (position, normal). Sky Light component containing the environment cubemap. Camera view direction. Reflection Sample Count Scale and Shadow Reflection Sample Count Scale parameters. Outputs: Reflection contribution to the final cloud shading. Data Structures: Panoramic Cloud Texture: A low-resolution texture, typically 256 \times 128 pixels. Sky Cubemap: The environment map updated with the panoramic cloud data. Sample Count Scalars: Multipliers for reflection and shadowed reflection ray marching. Parameters: Reflection Sample Count Scale: Slider in the Volumetric Cloud Details panel under Cloud Tracing. Progressive values: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 (Default), 2, 4, 8. Clamped by default. Max count controlled by console command r.VolumetricCloud.ReflectionRaySampleMaxCount. Shadow Reflection Sample Count Scale: Slider in the Volumetric Cloud Details panel under Cloud Tracing. Progressive values: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 (Default), 2, 4, 8. Clamped by default. Max count controlled by console command r.VolumetricCloud.Shadow.ReflectionRaySampleMaxCount. Steps: 1. Render Panoramic Cloud View: In a separate render pass, render a low-resolution (256 \times 128) panoramic view of the clouds. 2. Blend into Sky Cubemap: Blend the rendered panoramic cloud data into the Sky Light's cubemap. 3. Ray March Reflections: During the main cloud shading pass, use the Sky Light component to ray march reflection surfaces in the scene. 4. Sample Count Application: Scale the number of samples used for tracing the cloud's reflection ray based on the Reflection Sample Count Scale. 5. Shadowed Reflections: Apply Shadow Reflection Sample Count Scale to determine the sample count for shadowed reflections of clouds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecloudreflection(cloudposition, cloudnormal, viewdirection, skycubemap, reflectionscale, shadowreflectionscale, basesamplecount): # Clamp scales to valid range [0.25, 8] reflectionscale = max(0.25, min(8.0, reflectionscale)) shadowreflectionscale = max(0.25, min(8.0, shadowreflectionscale)) # Calculate sample counts reflectionsamples = int(basesamplecount reflectionscale) shadowreflectionsamples = int(basesamplecount shadowreflectionscale) # Compute reflection direction reflectiondirection = reflect(viewdirection, cloudnormal) # Ray march reflection surfaces using the calculated sample counts # For blurry reflections, this typically samples the environment map reflectedcolor = sampleenvironment(skycubemap, reflectiondirection, reflectionsamples) shadowedreflectedcolor = sampleenvironment(skycubemap, reflectiondirection, shadowreflectionsamples) return reflectedcolor, shadowedreflectedcolor def sampleenvironment(environmentmap, direction, samplecount): # Standard environment sampling return environmentmap.sample(direction) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Screen Space Limitation: Standard SSR only reflects clouds within screen space. This method extends that by using the panoramic pass, but the panoramic texture itself has low precision. Precision: The method has low precision and is suitable only for blurry reflections. Water Reflections: For water surfaces, this method is insufficient; separate specular handling is required for cloud reflections on water. Controls the sample counts for cloud reflections via the Volumetric Cloud Details panel. Scalable modes (reactive to cinematic) that affect how cloud intersections with opaque surfaces are handled, influencing the underlying ray marching performance. Time Complexity: Dependent on the Reflection Sample Count Scale and Shadow Reflection Sample Count Scale. The base cost includes an extra render pass for the 256 \times 128 panoramic cloud view. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the low-resolution panoramic texture and the updated Sky Cubemap. Performance: The low resolution (256 \times 128) of the panoramic pass keeps the overhead manageable for real-time applications. However, the low precision limits its use to blurry reflections. Strengths: Captures reflections of clouds outside the current screen space, which SSR cannot do. Limitations: Low precision; not suitable for sharp reflections or water surfaces. When to use: When blurry, screen-space-independent cloud reflections are needed in real-time volumetric cloud rendering. When not to use: When sharp reflections are required, or for water surface reflections. This method is part of the volumetric cloud rendering pipeline in Unreal Engine, specifically leveraging the Sky Light component for environmental reflections. It addresses the artifacts and limitations of pure screen-space approaches by incorporating a panoramic capture pass. The implementation details, including the sample count scales and console commands, are documented in the Unreal Engine 5.8 documentation for the Volumetric Cloud Component. The conceptual basis for handling reflections in atmospheric scattering and cloud rendering, including the use of transmittance LUTs and depth blending, is discussed in general volumetric cloud implementation guides. 体积云效果的实现，游戏世界的云合雾集, https://leihuo.163.com/institution/news/20230719/384231099592.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Volumetric Cloud Component in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.8 Documentation | Epic Developer Community, https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/volumetric-cloud-component-in-unreal-engine, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Approximate Refraction
body: Approximate refraction is a technique to make a fluid surface appear to refract objects behind it, which is faster and simpler to implement than ray tracing. Convex regions of the surface magnify the image behind them, concave regions shrink it, and flat regions allow rays to pass straight through. Inputs: A background scene rendered into a texture. A volume representing the fluid surface. View direction V and up vector z. Scalar parameter \beta > 0. Outputs: Final image with refracted appearance. Data Structures: 1. Background Texture: Stores the color of objects behind the fluid. 2. Hit Location Texture: Stores the 2D screen-space coordinates p of the nearest ray-surface intersection. Alpha channel is 1 if an intersection exists, 0 otherwise. 3. Shading Normal Texture: Stores the surface normal N at the intersection point. Steps: 1. Render Background: Render all scene geometry located behind the fluid volume into a background texture. 2. Ray Marching: For each pixel, march through the volume to find the nearest intersection with the fluid surface. Store the screen-space hit location p in the Hit Location Texture. Store the shading normal N at the hit point in the Shading Normal Texture. Set the alpha of the Hit Location Texture to 0 if no intersection is found, 1 otherwise. 3. Compute Basis Vectors: Calculate the orthonormal basis vectors Ph and Pv for the image plane based on the view direction V and up vector z. 4. Calculate Texture Offset: For each pixel with a valid hit (alpha = 1), compute the texture coordinate offset using the surface normal N and parameter \beta. 5. Sample Background: Look up the color in the Background Texture using the calculated texture coordinate t. 6. Composite: Use the sampled background color in the shading equation for the fluid surface. Add foreground objects to create the final image. Formulas: The texture coordinate t is calculated as: t = p - \beta(N \cdot Ph, N \cdot Pv) Where: p is the location of the pixel being shaded (screen-space coordinates). N is the surface normal at the hit point. \beta is a scalar parameter controlling the severity of the refraction effect (\beta > 0). Ph and Pv are orthonormal basis vectors for the image plane. The vertical basis vector Pv is calculated as: Pv = \frac{z - (z \cdot V)V}{\|z - (z \cdot V)V\|} Where: z is the up vector. V is the view direction. The horizontal basis vector Ph is calculated as: Ph = Pv \times V Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeapproximaterefraction(backgroundtexture, hitlocationtexture, normaltexture, viewdirection, upvector, beta): # Precompute basis vectors for the image plane zproj = upvector - (dot(upvector, viewdirection) viewdirection) normzproj = length(zproj) if normzproj < 1e-6: # Fallback when upvector is parallel to viewdirection Pv = normalize(cross(viewdirection, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0))) else: Pv = zproj / normzproj Ph = cross(Pv, viewdirection) finalimage = createemptytexturelike(hitlocationtexture) for y in range(hitlocationtexture.height): for x in range(hitlocationtexture.width): pxy = hitlocationtexture[x, y].xy alpha = hitlocationtexture[x, y].a N = normaltexture[x, y].xyz if alpha == 0: finalimage[x, y] = backgroundtexture[x, y] continue offsetx = dot(N, Ph) offsety = dot(N, Pv) tx = pxy.x - beta offsetx ty = pxy.y - beta offsety # Standard texture sampling refractedcolor = backgroundtexture.sample(tx, ty) finalimage[x, y] = refractedcolor return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate View Direction: If the up vector z is parallel to the view direction V, the denominator in the Pv calculation becomes zero. A fallback basis vector must be chosen. Boundary Conditions: Texture coordinates t may fall outside the [0, 1] range. Standard texture wrapping or clamping modes should be applied when sampling the background texture. Precision: The offset magnitude depends on \beta and the magnitude of the normal's projection. Large normals or large \beta values can cause significant displacement, potentially sampling incorrect background regions. Physically based refraction with absorption. Choose when accurate light transport through the volume is required. Handles reflections. Choose when mirror-like surfaces are needed. Uses cone intersections for better volume accuracy. Choose when high-quality volume rendering is needed and performance allows. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the refraction offset calculation, assuming constant-time texture lookups. The dominant cost is the ray marching step to find the surface intersection. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the background texture, hit location texture, and normal texture. Performance: Significantly faster than ray tracing for refraction, as it avoids casting secondary rays into the scene. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast, suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: Does not account for the actual path of light through the volume; can produce artifacts if the background scene is complex or if the surface curvature is extreme. Ray tracing is an alternative but is expensive and may fail to find intersections with other scene geometry. The method was described in "Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids". It was developed as a practical alternative to ray tracing for fluid animation in interactive environments, where performance is critical. The technique leverages the fact that for many fluid simulations, the visual impact of refraction can be approximated by distorting the background image based on the surface normal. Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cone Marching
head: Cone Marching in patches, Two-pass Cone Marching
body: Cone Marching is a GPU optimization technique for Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching that reduces redundant distance calculations by grouping rays into cones. It addresses the problem where adjacent rays in a pixel bundle march similar distances, causing repeated evaluations of the same scene geometry. Unlike standard ray marching which processes pixels independently, Cone Marching computes a coarse approximation of the intersection distance in a lower-resolution pass (or vertex shader) and feeds this starting distance to a fine per-pixel pass. This sets it apart from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Reflections by specifically optimizing the traversal phase before shading, rather than optimizing the shading or reflection logic itself. Cone Marching typically employs a two-pass architecture or a vertex-to-fragment data pipeline. The method relies on the geometric property that a bundle of rays from a camera center forms a cone, allowing the algorithm to skip steps where the cone does not intersect the scene. Inputs: Camera position (ro), camera direction/orientation, field of view (FOV), screen resolution, SDF scene function (scene(p)), maximum marching distance (u\maxDis), and maximum steps (u\maxSteps). Outputs: Final ray distance (for shading) and hit position. In the two-pass variant, the first pass outputs starting distances and step counts; the second pass outputs the final color. The core data structure passed between passes (or from vertex to fragment shader) is a March struct: dis (float): Total distance travelled by the cone so far. steps (int): Number of steps taken during the cone march. u\camTanFov: Tangent of half the camera's field of view. Calculated as \tan(\frac{FOV}{2}). u\camPlaneSubdivisions: The number of subdivisions used to define the marching grid or vertex plane. A typical value is 32. padding: A multiplier applied to the cone radius to prevent artifacts at SDF edges. Typical value is 1.25. 1. Setup Marching Plane: Create a geometry representing the screen or marching plane. To avoid artifacts caused by rectangular aspect ratios, vertices must be evenly spaced (square). If using a plane of width 1 with 32 height subdivisions, the width subdivisions should be \lfloor aspect \times 32 \rfloor. 2. Compute Ray Direction (World Space): For each vertex in the marching plane: Transform UV coordinates to clip space. Unproject using the inverse projection matrix. Transform to world space using the camera world matrix. Normalize the resulting vector to get the cone ray direction (crd). 3. Cone Marching Loop: Iterate to find the approximate intersection distance: Initialize total distance d = 0 and step counter i = 0. Calculate current position: p = cro + d \cdot crd, where cro is the cone ray origin (camera position). Calculate current scene distance: cd = scene(p). Calculate current cone radius: ccr = \frac{d \cdot u\camTanFov \cdot 2.0}{u\camPlaneSubdivisions}. Break Condition: If cd < ccr \cdot 1.25 OR d \ge u\maxDis, exit the loop. The padding factor (1.25) is used instead of a small epsilon to check for intersection. Advance: If not broken, d \leftarrow d + cd and i \leftarrow i + 1. 4. Return Coarse Result: Return the March struct containing d and i. 5. Fine Ray Marching (Fragment Pass): Receive vDisTravelled (distance) and vSteps (steps) from the coarse pass. Initialize fine ray distance d = vDisTravelled and loop counter i = vSteps. Compute per-pixel ray direction rd from UV. Iterate while i < u\maxSteps: p = ro + d \cdot rd. cd = scene(p). If cd < \epsilon (standard epsilon) OR d \ge u\maxDis, break. d \leftarrow d + cd. Return final distance d for shading. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct March: dis: float steps: int ucamTanFov: float ucamPlaneSubdivisions: int umaxDis: float umaxSteps: int ueps: float def scene(p: vec3) -> float: # Returns signed distance to nearest object pass def conemarch(cro: vec3, crd: vec3) -> March: d = 0.0 i = 0 while i < umaxSteps: p = cro + d crd cd = scene(p) ccr = (d ucamTanFov 2.0) / ucamPlaneSubdivisions # Break if cone intersects scene (with padding) or max distance reached if cd < ccr 1.25 or d >= umaxDis: break d += cd i += 1 return March(dis=d, steps=i) def raymarch(startdis: float, stepstaken: int, ro: vec3, rd: vec3) -> float: d = startdis i = stepstaken while i < umaxSteps: p = ro + d rd cd = scene(p) # Standard epsilon check for precise intersection if cd < ueps or d >= umaxDis: break d += cd i += 1 return d Aspect Ratio Artifacts: Using rectangular screen vertices without accounting for the camera aspect ratio causes uneven spacing and visual artifacts. Vertices must be adjusted to ensure square/evenly spaced distribution. Padding Factor: The break condition uses a padding factor (1.25) on the cone radius. Using a standard epsilon here may cause artifacts at the edges of the SDF. Precision: The cone radius calculation assumes a linear relationship between distance and radius. For pixels far from the screen center, using the central focal distance may be inaccurate; using the specific pixel's distance from the camera is more precise. A method to estimate the radius of the ray cone at any given distance to implement cone-marching and minimize steps. It addresses the inaccuracy of exponential radius growth approximations by using a linear relationship: radius(distance) = \frac{distance \cdot initialRadius}{focalDistance}. This requires recalculating the radius at every step because the distance from the camera changes. For pixels not in the center of the screen, using the distance of the specific pixel on the screen plane from the camera is more accurate than the central focal distance. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF evaluations in the coarse phase by marching a single cone per patch/vertex instead of per pixel. The fine phase still requires per-pixel marching but starts from a closer distance, reducing total steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate results (distance and steps) between passes or shader stages. Performance: Reported to double FPS in simple scenes (e.g., 50 FPS to 100 FPS on a single CPU core for recursive algorithms, though GPU gains vary). The simple Three.js approach offers a good balance of complexity and gain, whereas multi-pass approaches (decreasing cone size until it equals pixel size) are theoretically ideal but more complex to implement. Strengths: Significant reduction in redundant calculations for bundles of rays; easy to implement in vertex shaders or simple multi-pass setups. Limitations: Requires additional passes or uniform data transfer; less effective if the scene has high-frequency details that cause cones to intersect early and frequently. Cone Marching was popularized in the context of real-time SDF rendering and fractal visualization. It is described in "Cone Marching in less than 5 minutes," "Rendering Mandelbox fractals faster with Cone Marching," and "Cone Marching in Three.js". The technique was also highlighted in "DD2018: Sebastian Aaltonen - GPU based clay simulation and ray tracing tech in Claybook". The underlying principle of linear cone radius growth is discussed in community forums such as Stack Overflow. A Recursive Algorithm to Render Signed Distance Fields, https://pointersgonewild.com/2026-03-06-a-recursive-algorithm-to-render-signed-distance-fields/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Cone Marching in Three.js, https://medium.com/@nabilnymansour/cone-marching-in-three-js-6d54eac17ad4, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) How to calculate the viewing cone radius (ie. size of a pixel) at a distance in raymarching?, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10492590/how-to-calculate-the-viewing-cone-radius-ie-size-of-a-pixel-at-a-distance-in, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Refracted Ray Directions
head: Vector Snell's Law Refraction, refract
body: Calculates the direction of a ray after it passes through a discrete interface between two media with different refractive indices, handling both entry and exit scenarios. It differs from Nested Raymarching for Refraction and Piecewise evaluation of Snell's law by treating the medium as homogeneous within the object and applying refraction only at the boundary, rather than integrating a gradient or recursively marching through nested volumes. Inputs: ray: Incident ray direction (normalized vector). N: Surface normal at the intersection point (normalized vector, pointing outward from the object surface). ref: Current refractive index of the medium the ray is traveling in. nobj: Refractive index of the object being intersected. Outputs: directionrefracted: The new ray direction after refraction (normalized vector). refnew: The refractive index of the medium the ray is now traveling in. Data Structures: Vectors are 3D floating-point vectors. Scalars are double-precision floats. Steps: 1. Compute the dot product s = \text{dot}(\text{ray}, N). 2. Determine the relative refractive index \mu and the indices n1, n2: If the ray is exiting the object (detected by checking if the object is a sphere and s > 0, or generally if the normal points in the same direction as the ray), swap indices: n1 = n{obj}, n2 = ref, and \mu = n{obj} / ref. The normal N remains as computed. If the ray is entering the object, n1 = ref, n2 = n{obj}, and \mu = n{obj} / ref. Note: In standard implementations, the normal N is always the outward surface normal. If s > 0, the ray is exiting, and the effective normal for Snell's law calculation should be -N to maintain the convention that the normal points into the incident medium, or the formula must account for the sign of s. The source code implies handling the swap of n1/n2 and potentially the normal direction. 3. Compute the dot product c = \text{dot}(\text{ray}, N). 4. Calculate the intermediate variable tmp: tmp = 1 - \mu^2 (1 - c^2) 5. Check for Total Internal Reflection (TIR): If tmp < 0, TIR occurs. The ray does not refract. The caller should handle this (e.g., by reflecting the ray or terminating the path). 6. Calculate the refracted direction: \text{direction\refracted} = \sqrt{tmp} \cdot N + \mu \cdot (\text{ray} - c \cdot N) 7. Normalize \text{direction\refracted}. 8. Update the current refractive index: ref{new} = n2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def refract(ray, N, ref, nobj): """ ray: incident ray direction (normalized) N: surface normal (normalized, outward) ref: current medium refractive index nobj: object refractive index returns: (refracteddirection, newrefindex) """ s = dot(ray, N) # Determine direction of travel relative to surface # If s > 0, ray is exiting (normal points same way as ray) # If s < 0, ray is entering (normal points opposite to ray) if s > 0: # Exiting n1 = nobj n2 = ref mu = nobj / ref # Normal N is outward. For Snell's law vector form, # we typically use the normal pointing into the incident medium. # However, the formula derived in uses N directly with specific mu definitions. # Let's follow logic: # S1 says: if exiting, swap n1/n2. # S1 formula: directionrefracted = sqrt(tmp) normals + mu (directions - c normals) # This formula assumes N is the normal used in the dot product c. # If we are exiting, the ray goes from nobj to ref. # The standard vector refraction formula is: # vout = (n1/n2) vin + ((n1/n2)cos(thetai) - sqrt(1 - (n1/n2)^2 sin^2(thetai))) N # where N is the normal pointing OUT of the surface. # Let's stick to the specific implementation details. # Code snippet: # float n1 = ref; float n2 = ob->getRefractive(); # if(exiting) swap n1, n2. # So if exiting: n1=nobj, n2=ref. # mu = n1/n2 ? No, says mu = next / nlens for entering. # Let's re-read carefully. # S2: mu = next / nlens for entering. # S2: mu = nlens / next for exiting. # This implies mu = nincident / ntransmitted. mu = n1 / n2 # nincident / ntransmitted # c = dot(ray, N) c = dot(ray, N) # tmp = 1 - mu^2 (1 - c^2) tmp = 1.0 - mu mu (1.0 - c c) if tmp < 0: return None # Total Internal Reflection # directionrefracted = sqrt(tmp) N + mu (ray - c N) dirref = sqrt(tmp) N + mu (ray - c N) dirref = normalize(dirref) return dirref, n2 else: # Entering n1 = ref n2 = nobj mu = n1 / n2 # nincident / ntransmitted c = dot(ray, N) tmp = 1.0 - mu mu (1.0 - c c) if tmp < 0: return None # Total Internal Reflection dirref = sqrt(tmp) N + mu (ray - c N) dirref = normalize(dirref) return dirref, n2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Total Internal Reflection: If tmp < 0, the square root is invalid. This occurs when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. The method must detect this and return a failure flag or handle reflection instead. Precision: Near grazing angles, tmp may be very close to 0. Use epsilon guards if necessary. Normal Orientation: The formula relies on consistent normal orientation. If N is not the outward normal, the sign of s and the resulting direction will be incorrect. Calculates the Fresnel reflectance for unpolarized light at an interface between two media with different indices of refraction. It determines the ratio of reflected to refracted light based on the angle of incidence, enabling realistic rendering of transparent and reflective surfaces. Unlike basic glass models that ignore angular dependence, this method produces characteristic darkening of glass sides at grazing angles and more accurate caustics beneath the object. It serves as the core weighting function for combining reflected and refracted ray contributions in path tracing and ray marching. An approximation technique for continuous refraction that repeatedly evaluates Snell's law at discrete steps along a ray path. It serves as a middle ground between constant refraction (single-step) and higher-order numerical integration (e.g., RK4) for rays traversing media with spatially varying refractive indices. Unlike Refracted Ray Directions, which handles discrete interfaces, this method approximates the curved trajectory within a gradient medium by treating it as a sequence of small, homogeneous slabs. Models a thick lens using Snell's law at two spherical interfaces, accounting for lens thickness and curvature. It differs from thin lens approximations by explicitly computing ray propagation through the lens material volume. Time Complexity: O(1) per interface intersection. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Exact solution for planar or spherical interfaces between homogeneous media. Computationally inexpensive. Limitations: Does not handle gradient-index (GRIN) media. Requires accurate surface normals. Fails for total internal reflection without additional handling. When to use: Rendering transparent objects with constant refractive indices (glass, water, plastic). When not to use: Rendering atmospheric effects, heat haze, or GRIN lenses where refraction varies continuously. Originated from standard geometric optics and Snell's Law. The specific vector formulation and implementation details for ray tracing are found in early ray tracing literature and graphics programming repositories. It is a fundamental building block for rendering transparent and refractive materials. jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, https://github.com/jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) magis-slac/gradoptics, https://github.com/magis-slac/gradoptics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fresnel Reflection/Refraction
head: Fresnel Reflection
body: Calculates the Fresnel reflectance for unpolarized light at an interface between two media with different indices of refraction. It determines the ratio of reflected to refracted light based on the angle of incidence, enabling realistic rendering of transparent and reflective surfaces. Unlike basic glass models that ignore angular dependence, this method produces characteristic darkening of glass sides at grazing angles and more accurate caustics beneath the object. It serves as the core weighting function for combining reflected and refracted ray contributions in path tracing and ray marching. Inputs: incom: Incoming light direction or view direction (normalized vector). normal: Surface normal at the intersection point (normalized vector). indexinternal: Refractive index of the internal medium (scalar). indexexternal: Refractive index of the external medium (scalar). Outputs: reflectance: Scalar value between 0.0 and 1.0 representing the fraction of light reflected. Data Structures: None required beyond standard scalar and vector types. Steps: 1. Calculate the ratio of indices of refraction: \eta = \frac{\text{index\internal}}{\text{index\external}} 2. Calculate the cosine of the angle of incidence (\theta1): \cos\theta1 = \text{dot}(\text{incom}, \text{normal}) Note: The sign of dot depends on whether incom points towards or away from the surface relative to the normal. Standard implementations often assume incom is the view direction pointing out, or handle the sign explicitly. The source uses dot(incom, normal) directly. 3. Calculate the squared cosine of the angle of refraction (\theta2) using Snell's law derived identity: \cos^2\theta2 = 1.0 - \eta^2 \cdot (1.0 - \cos\theta1 \cdot \cos\theta1) 4. Check for Total Internal Reflection (TIR): If \cos^2\theta2 < 0.0, return 1.0 (all light is reflected). 5. Calculate the cosine of the angle of refraction: \cos\theta2 = \sqrt{\cos^2\theta2} 6. Calculate the Fresnel s-polarized reflectance term (rs): rs = \frac{\text{index\internal} \cdot \cos\theta1 - \text{index\external} \cdot \cos\theta2}{\text{index\internal} \cdot \cos\theta1 + \text{index\external} \cdot \cos\theta2} 7. Calculate the Fresnel p-polarized reflectance term (rp): rp = \frac{\text{index\internal} \cdot \cos\theta2 - \text{index\external} \cdot \cos\theta1}{\text{index\internal} \cdot \cos\theta2 + \text{index\external} \cdot \cos\theta1} 8. Return the average reflectance for unpolarized light: \text{reflectance} = \frac{rs^2 + rp^2}{2} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fresnelreflectance(incom: Vec3, normal: Vec3, indexinternal: float, indexexternal: float) -> float: # 1. Calculate eta eta = indexinternal / indexexternal # 2. Calculate costheta1 costheta1 = dot(incom, normal) # 3. Calculate costheta2 squared # Using identity: sin^2(theta2) = eta^2 sin^2(theta1) # cos^2(theta2) = 1 - sin^2(theta2) costheta2sq = 1.0 - (eta eta) (1.0 - costheta1 costheta1) # 4. Check for Total Internal Reflection if costheta2sq < 0.0: return 1.0 # 5. Calculate costheta2 costheta2 = sqrt(costheta2sq) # 6. Calculate Fresnel s-polarized reflectance term numerators = indexinternal costheta1 - indexexternal costheta2 denominators = indexinternal costheta1 + indexexternal costheta2 fresnelrs = numerators / denominators # 7. Calculate Fresnel p-polarized reflectance term numeratorp = indexinternal costheta2 - indexexternal costheta1 denominatorp = indexinternal costheta2 + indexexternal costheta1 fresnelrp = numeratorp / denominatorp # 8. Return average reflectance for unpolarized light return (fresnelrs fresnelrs + fresnelrp fresnelrp) 0.5 Usage in Shading: In a fragment shader or path tracer, the Fresnel factor kR is used to blend reflected and refracted colors: 1. Calculate kR = \text{fresnel\reflectance}(-\text{eye}, \text{normal}, 1.0, \text{IOR}). 2. Calculate transmission factor kT = 1.0 - kR. 3. Combine colors: \text{color} = kR \cdot \text{reflectColor} + kT \cdot \text{refractColor}. Parameters: incom: Incoming light direction (or view direction). normal: Surface normal. indexinternal: Refractive index of the internal medium. indexexternal: Refractive index of the external medium. The Fresnel Glass Material is a shading model for transparent dielectric objects (such as glass, water, or diamond) that simulates the bending of light (refraction) and partial reflection at boundaries. It solves the problem of rendering realistic transparent surfaces by dynamically adjusting the ratio of reflected to refracted light based on the angle of incidence, using the Schlick approximation. Unlike basic glass models that ignore angular dependence, this method produces characteristic darkening of glass sides at grazing angles and more accurate caustics beneath the object. This method models light transmission through a planar window (a medium with a refractive index between two parallel surfaces) in a ray-marching context. It calculates the refracted ray direction using Snell's law and applies Fresnel coefficients to determine the transmission loss, updating the ray's luminosity accordingly. It is distinct from simple transmission models by explicitly accounting for the angular dependence of reflectance at the interface boundaries. An OpenPBR-style edge coloring technique for metals using complex-indexed Fresnel calculations, allowing for non-white edge highlights. It uses an edgeTint parameter to control the color of the edge tint; a white value reproduces the Schlick approximation exactly. A key pitfall is that standard real-index Fresnel must not be used; complex-indexed Fresnel calculations are required to correctly model metallic edge colors. Traces a ray through a homogeneous glass block, handling entry refraction, Beer-Lambert absorption, exit refraction, and total internal reflection (TIR). It determines the oriented normal, refracts the ray, marches through the medium to find the exit, applies absorption based on uglassdensity, and refracts the ray out upon exit. If the ray exits to a different solid, it sets the landing state; if the depth limit is exhausted, it returns false. Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in WebGPU-based voxel cone tracing and path tracing contexts. It is part of advanced material features in photon engines, including conductor (metal), dielectric, and thin-film implementations. It is also used in voxel-based ray marching for glass blocks with absorption. name: Fresnel Glass Material
head: Dielectric Scattering, Glass scattering, Refraction with Schlick approximation
body: The Fresnel Glass Material is a shading model for transparent dielectric objects that simulates light bending (refraction) and partial reflection at boundaries like glass or water. It dynamically adjusts the ratio of refracted to reflected light based on the angle of incidence using the Fresnel equations. Unlike basic glass models that ignore angular dependence, this method produces characteristic darkening of glass sides at low-incidence viewing angles and more accurate caustics beneath the base. Inputs: Incident ray direction, surface normal, index of refraction (n), and a random number generator. Outputs: A new ray direction (either reflected or refracted) and attenuation color (default white). hitrecord: Stores the intersection point p, the surface normal \vec{n}, the distance t, a material pointer, and a boolean frontface indicating if the ray hit from outside or inside. ray: Defined by an origin point and a direction vector. n (Index of Refraction): A double-precision floating-point value. Typical values are 1.5 for glass, 1.33 for water, and 2.4 for diamond. 1. Set attenuation to white. 2. Determine refraction ratio: 1.0/n if front face, n if back face. 3. Compute unit direction \vec{u}. 4. Calculate \cos\theta clamped to 1.0. 5. Compute \sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2\theta}. 6. Check for total internal reflection (TIR): if \text{refraction\ratio} \times \sin\theta > 1.0, TIR occurs. 7. Compute Schlick reflectance: R0 = \left(\frac{1 - n}{1 + n}\right)^2, Reflectance = R0 + (1 - R0)(1 - \cos\theta)^5. 8. If TIR or Schlick reflectance > random double, reflect; else refract. 9. Create new ray with the computed direction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): s = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/s, v[1]/s, v[2]/s) class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def fresnelglassmaterial(ray, hitrecord, n, rng): # 1. Set attenuation to white (implicit) # 2. Determine refraction ratio: 1.0/n if front face, n if back face refractionratio = 1.0 / n if hitrecord.frontface else n # 3. Compute unit direction u = normalize(ray.direction) # 4. Calculate costheta clamped to 1.0 # hitrecord.normal is already oriented per setfacenormal in costheta = dot(u, hitrecord.normal) costheta = min(costheta, 1.0) # 5. Compute sintheta = sqrt(1 - cos^2theta) sintheta = (1.0 - costheta costheta)0.5 # 6. Check for TIR: refractionratio sintheta > 1.0 istir = (refractionratio sintheta > 1.0) # 7. Compute Schlick reflectance r0 = ((1.0 - n) / (1.0 + n)) 2 reflectance = r0 + (1.0 - r0) (1.0 - costheta) 5 # 8. If TIR or Schlick reflectance > random double, reflect; else refract if istir or rng() > reflectance: # Reflect: dnew = u - 2(u. n)n direction = u - 2.0 dot(u, hitrecord.normal) hitrecord.normal else: # Refract vector formula not given in sources discriminant = 1.0 - refractionratio refractionratio (1.0 - costheta costheta) if discriminant < 0.0: direction = u - 2.0 dot(u, hitrecord.normal) hitrecord.normal else: direction = refractionratio u - (refractionratio costheta + discriminant0.5) hitrecord.normal # 9. Create new ray with the computed direction neworigin = (ray.origin[0] + direction[0]1e-4, ray.origin[1] + direction[1]1e-4, ray.origin[2] + direction[2]1e-4) return Ray(neworigin, direction) Grazing Angles: At grazing angles, reflectance approaches 1.0. The Schlick approximation handles this probabilistically, ensuring realistic darkening of edges. Total Internal Reflection: Must be handled explicitly. If the condition \text{refraction\ratio} \times \sin\theta > 1.0 is met, the ray falls back to pure reflection. Numerical Precision: Clamping \cos\theta to 1.0 prevents invalid square root calculations when computing sine. Handles light bending (refraction) and partial reflection at transparent boundaries like glass or water, using probabilistic reflection at grazing angles. Choose when rendering flat transparent panes. Link Time Complexity: O(1) per intersection for the shading calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Produces visually accurate glass with realistic edge darkening and caustics. Computationally efficient due to the Schlick approximation. When to use: For rendering transparent dielectric objects like glass, water, or plastic where surface reflections and refractions are dominant. When not to use: For materials with significant internal scattering or absorption without extension. The Fresnel Glass Material is based on the principles of optics, specifically the Fresnel equations, which describe the reflection and transmission of light at an interface between two media. The Schlick approximation is a widely used simplification for computational efficiency. This model was notably implemented in ray tracers to improve the realism of glass objects, such as martini glasses, by capturing the darkening of sides at low-incidence angles and accurate caustics. name: Window Refraction and Fresnel Transmission
head: Fresnel Transmission, Window Refraction
body: This method models light transmission through a planar window (a medium with a refractive index between two parallel surfaces) in a ray-marching context. It calculates the refracted ray direction using Snell's law and applies Fresnel coefficients to determine the transmission loss, updating the ray's luminosity accordingly. It is distinct from simple transmission models by explicitly accounting for the angular dependence of reflectance at the interface boundaries. Inputs: Ray origins: origins (array of shape (N, 3)). Ray directions: directions (array of shape (N, 3)), assumed normalized. Incident luminosity: incidentrays.luminosities (array of shape (N,)). Window parameters: leftinterfacexposition, rightinterfacexposition, next, nglass, diameter, eps. Window normal: windownormal (typically [1, 0, 0] for a window perpendicular to the x-axis). Outputs: Refracted ray directions: directionrefractedrays (array of shape (N, 3)). Updated luminosity: outputrays.luminosities (array of shape (N,)). Data Structures: The Window object holds the following fields: leftinterfacexposition (float), rightinterfacexposition (float), next (float), nglass (float), diameter (float), eps (float), and w2obj (SimpleTransform object). Parameters: next: Refractive index of the external medium. Typical value: 1.000293. nglass: Refractive index of the medium (glass). Typical value: 1.494. diameter: Diameter of the interfaces. Typical value: 0.137. eps: Parameter used for numerical stability in division operations. Default value: 1e-15. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection with Left Interface: Calculate the intersection time t with the left interface plane at x = \text{left\interface\x\position}. t = \frac{\text{left\interface\x\position} - \text{origins}[:, 0]}{\text{directions}[:, 0] + \epsilon} where \epsilon is a small value to prevent division by zero. 2. Compute Intersection Coordinates: Calculate the y and z coordinates of the intersection point on the left interface. y = \text{origins}[:, 1] + t \times \text{directions}[:, 1] z = \text{origins}[:, 2] + t \times \text{directions}[:, 2] 3. Filter Invalid Intersections: Check if the intersection is within the valid time range and inside the circular aperture. \text{condition} = (t > 10^{-3}) \ \& \ (y^2 + z^2 < (\text{diameter} / 2)^2) If the condition is false, set t to infinity to discard the ray. 4. Calculate Refracted Direction: Use Snell's law in vector form to compute the refracted direction. Let \mu = n{ext} / n{glass}. Let \mathbf{n} be the windownormal. Let \mathbf{d} be the directions. c = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} \text{tmp} = 1 - \mu^2 (1 - c^2) \text{direction\refracted\rays} = \sqrt{\text{tmp}} \times \mathbf{n} + \mu \times (\mathbf{d} - c \times \mathbf{n}) Note: \sqrt{\text{tmp}} must be real; if \text{tmp} < 0, total internal reflection occurs, and transmission is zero. 5. Calculate Fresnel Transmission Coefficient: Compute the reflectance for s-polarized (rs) and p-polarized (rp) light. Let \thetai be the angle of incidence such that \cos(\thetai) = c = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. Let n1 = n{ext} and n2 = n{glass}. rs = \left| \frac{n1 \cos(\thetai) - n2 \sqrt{1 - (\frac{n1}{n2} \sin(\thetai))^2}}{n1 \cos(\thetai) + n2 \sqrt{1 - (\frac{n1}{n2} \sin(\thetai))^2}} \right|^2 rp = \left| \frac{n1 \sqrt{1 - (\frac{n1}{n2} \sin(\thetai))^2} - n2 \cos(\thetai)}{n1 \sqrt{1 - (\frac{n1}{n2} \sin(\thetai))^2} + n2 \cos(\thetai)} \right|^2 The transmission coefficient is: \text{trans\coeff} = 1 - 0.5 \times (rs + rp) 6. Update Luminosity: \text{output\rays.luminosities} = \text{incident\rays.luminosities} \times \text{trans\coeff} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def windowrefractionandfresneltransmission( origins, directions, incidentluminosities, leftinterfacexposition, rightinterfacexposition, next, nglass, diameter, eps=1e-15): """ Models refraction and Fresnel transmission through a planar window. Parameters: origins: (N, 3) array of ray origins. directions: (N, 3) array of ray directions (normalized). incidentluminosities: (N,) array of incident ray luminosities. leftinterfacexposition: float, x-coordinate of the left interface. rightinterfacexposition: float, x-coordinate of the right interface. next: float, refractive index of the external medium. nglass: float, refractive index of the glass medium. diameter: float, diameter of the circular interfaces. eps: float, numerical stability parameter. Returns: refracteddirections: (N, 3) array of refracted ray directions. outputluminosities: (N,) array of updated ray luminosities. """ N = origins.shape[0] refracteddirections = np.zeroslike(directions) outputluminosities = np.zeros(N) # Step 1: Compute intersection time t with the left interface t = (leftinterfacexposition - origins[:, 0]) / (directions[:, 0] + eps) # Step 2: Compute intersection coordinates y and z y = origins[:, 1] + t directions[:, 1] z = origins[:, 2] + t directions[:, 2] # Step 3: Filter invalid intersections validmask = (t > 1e-3) & ((y 2 + z 2) < (diameter / 2) 2) t[~validmask] = np.inf # Set t to infinity for invalid rays as per evidence # Initialize output arrays refracteddirections[:] = directions[:] outputluminosities[:] = 0.0 # Only process valid rays if np.any(validmask): validdirections = directions[validmask] validincidentluminosities = incidentluminosities[validmask] # Step 4: Calculate refracted direction using Snell's law windownormal = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) mu = next / nglass # c = dotproduct(windownormal, directions) c = np.sum(windownormal validdirections, axis=1) # tmp = 1 - mu 2 (1 - c 2) tmp = 1.0 - mu 2 (1.0 - c 2) # Handle total internal reflection where tmp < 0 sqrttmp = np.sqrt(np.maximum(tmp, 0.0)) # directionrefractedrays = sqrt(tmp) windownormal + mu (directions - c windownormal) refracteddirections[validmask] = ( sqrttmp[:, np.newaxis] windownormal + mu (validdirections - c[:, np.newaxis] windownormal)) # Step 5: Calculate Fresnel transmission coefficient n1 = next n2 = nglass # cos(theta) = c costheta = c # sin(theta) = sqrt(1 - cos(theta)^2) sintheta = np.sqrt(np.maximum(1.0 - costheta 2, 0.0)) # term = n1/n2 sin(theta) term = (n1 / n2) sintheta # sqrt(1 - term^2) sqrtterm = np.sqrt(np.maximum(1.0 - term 2, 0.0)) # rs = abs((n1cos(theta) - n2sqrtterm) / (n1cos(theta) + n2sqrtterm)) 2 numerators = n1 costheta - n2 sqrtterm denominators = n1 costheta + n2 sqrtterm # Avoid division by zero denominators = np.where(np.abs(denominators) < eps, eps, denominators) rs = (numerators / denominators) 2 # rp = abs((n1sqrtterm - n2cos(theta)) / (n1sqrtterm + n2cos(theta)) 2 numeratorp = n1 sqrtterm - n2 costheta denominatorp = n1 sqrtterm + n2 costheta # Avoid division by zero denominatorp = np.where(np.abs(denominatorp) < eps, eps, denominatorp) rp = (numeratorp / denominatorp) 2 # Transmission = 1 - 0.5 (rs + rp) transcoeff = 1.0 - 0.5 (rs + rp) # Step 6: Update ray luminosity outputluminosities[validmask] = validincidentluminosities transcoeff return refracteddirections, outputluminosities Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of rays. The operations are vectorized element-wise arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing intermediate arrays (t, y, z, tmp, etc.). Strengths: Accurately models the angular dependence of transmission loss at dielectric interfaces. Simple to implement for planar windows. Limitations: Assumes a planar window with parallel surfaces. Does not account for multiple internal reflections within the glass (only the first transmission is modeled). Total internal reflection is handled by setting transmission to zero (implicitly via sqrt(tmp) clamping and subsequent luminosity update). When to use: When rendering scenes with planar glass windows or transparent planar barriers where Fresnel effects are important. When not to use: For curved glass surfaces, thick glass with significant internal scattering, or when multiple internal reflections are required. This method is derived from the gradoptics library, which focuses on Gaussian optics and ray tracing for atom clouds and similar media. The specific implementation for window refraction and Fresnel transmission is found in the gradoptics repository. It is used in simulations involving light propagation through optical elements like windows or lenses in atomic physics experiments. magis-slac/gradoptics, https://github.com/magis-slac/gradoptics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Piecewise evaluation of Snell's law
body:
An approximation technique for continuous refraction that repeatedly evaluates Snell's law at discrete steps along a ray path. Unlike Refracted Ray Directions, which handles discrete interfaces, this method approximates the curved trajectory within a gradient medium by treating it as a sequence of small, homogeneous slabs. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{D}. Refractive index field n(\mathbf{x}). Outputs: Ray trajectory points and final exit direction. Data Structures: Current position \mathbf{x}i and direction \mathbf{d}i. Refractive index ni = n(\mathbf{x}i) and gradient 
abla ni = 
abla n(\mathbf{x}i). Steps: 1. Initialize \mathbf{x}0 = \mathbf{O}, \mathbf{d}0 = \mathbf{D}. 2. For each step i = 0, 1, \dots: a. Compute the refractive index gradient 
abla ni at \mathbf{x}i. b. Determine the normal to the isophote at \mathbf{x}i: \mathbf{N}i =  rac{
abla ni}{\|
abla ni\|}. c. Calculate the angle of incidence 	hetai between -\mathbf{d}i and \mathbf{N}i: \cos 	hetai = -\mathbf{d}i \cdot \mathbf{N}i. d. Calculate the refractive index at the next step \mathbf{x}{i+1} = \mathbf{x}i + h \mathbf{d}i: n{i+1} = n(\mathbf{x}{i+1}). e. Apply Snell's law to find the new direction \mathbf{d}{i+1}. The change in direction \Delta \mathbf{d} is proportional to the gradient component perpendicular to the ray. f. Update \mathbf{x}i \leftarrow \mathbf{x}{i+1}, \mathbf{d}i \leftarrow \mathbf{d}{i+1}. g. Check termination condition (exit volume or max steps). Parameters: Step size h: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Fails to sufficiently reproduce the shape of caustics and introduces significant discrepancies compared to analytical or RK4 solutions. Total internal reflection must be handled if the ray attempts to exit a high-index region into a lower-index one at a steep angle. Precision errors accumulate over many steps. Modeling the porcine eye lens as a Gradient Refractive Index (GRIN) medium by dividing it into two regions (anterior and middle) and converting a polar-coordinate profile to a Cartesian polynomial for Zemax 'Gradient 3' surfaces. Definition: The GRIN profile is defined in polar coordinates as: n(ho,	heta) = nN - (nN - nS) \cdot \left( rac{ho}{hoS}ight)^{p(	heta)} where hoS is the distance from lens center to surface, ho is distance from center to point, 	heta is angle from optical axis, and p(	heta) is an exponent function. Formula: For Zemax compatibility, the profile is converted to a Cartesian polynomial n(z) along the optical axis (	heta=0): n(z) = n0 + N{z1} \cdot z + N{z2} \cdot z^2 where z is distance from surface vertex, and N{z1}, N{z2} are solved by matching n(z) at midpoint and endpoint of lens thickness. Parameters: nN = 1.443 (center index), nS = 1.362 (surface index). Exponent axial value p1 = 2.62; Exponent meridional range p2 = 3.56 to 5.18. Simplified model uses p(0) = p1 = 2.62. Layout: Table 2: GRIN Parameters with fields: Surface, n0, N{z1}, N{z2}. Anterior Lens: n0=1.362, N{z1}=0.063, N{z2}=-0.012. Middle Lens: n0=1.443, N{z1}=6.481 	imes 10^{-3}, N{z2}=-5.734 	imes 10^{-3}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The piecewise approximation shows significant discrepancies compared to analytical or RK4 solutions, particularly in reproducing caustic shapes. Strengths: Simpler to implement than RK4; more accurate than constant refraction for smooth gradients. Limitations: Fails to accurately reproduce caustics; accuracy depends heavily on step size. Originated in the context of refractive radiative transfer equation simulations. It was compared against constant refraction and RK4 methods in studies involving photon trajectories through gradient media. The GRIN modeling variant was developed for simulating porcine eye lenses in intraoperative OCT applications. name: Thick Lens (Snell's Law Refraction)
body: Models a thick lens using Snell's law at two spherical interfaces, accounting for lens thickness and curvature. It differs from thin lens approximations by explicitly computing ray propagation through the lens material volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin o, ray direction d (normalized), lens radius of curvature R, lens thickness d{lens}, lens refractive index n{lens}, external refractive index n{ext}. Output: Refracted ray direction after exiting the second interface, or the original direction if no intersection occurs. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar and vector parameters without complex data structures. Steps: 1. Define two spherical interfaces separated by distance d{lens} along the optical axis. 2. Compute ray-sphere intersection coefficients for the current interface: a = |d|^2, b = 2(o - c) \cdot d, c{val} = |o - c|^2 - R^2. 3. Compute discriminant \text{pho} = b^2 - 4ac{val}. 4. If \text{pho} > 0, calculate t1 = (-b + \sqrt{\text{pho}}) / 2a and t2 = (-b - \sqrt{\text{pho}}) / 2a. 5. Set virtual intersections (t < 0) and non-intersecting cases (\text{pho} \le 0) to \infty to ignore them. 6. Select the smallest positive t as the intersection distance, compute the intersection point, and compute the surface normal oriented towards the center of curvature using \text{normalize}(c - p), where c = -\text{sign}(px) \cdot R for batched point evaluation. 7. Apply Snell's law to compute the refracted direction inside the lens material. 8. Repeat steps 2–7 for the second interface using the refracted direction and the second center. 9. Apply Snell's law to compute the final refracted direction exiting into the external medium. Formulas: Approximate focal length: f{approx} = \frac{1}{(\frac{n{ext}}{n{lens}} - 1) (\frac{1}{R1} - \frac{1}{R2})}, where R1 = R and R2 = -R. Ray-sphere intersection discriminant: \text{pho} = b^2 - 4ac{val}. Parameters: n{lens}: Index of refraction of the lens material (float). n{ext}: Index of refraction of the external medium (float). R: Radius of curvature of the lens surfaces (float). d{lens}: Thickness of the lens (float). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Virtual intersections (t < 0) are set to \infty to be ignored. Non-intersecting rays (\text{pho} \le 0) have t1 and t2 set to \infty. Precision issues may arise if the ray is tangent to the surface (\text{pho} \approx 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Assumes n points into the incident medium for standard Snell's law formulation.""" costheta1 = -dot(n, d) sintheta1sq = 1.0 - costheta12 sintheta2sq = (n1 / n2)2 sintheta1sq if sintheta2sq > 1.0: return reflectvector(d, n) costheta2 = math.sqrt(1.0 - sintheta2sq) return n2 / n1 d + (n2 / n1 costheta1 - costheta2) n def reflectvector(d, n): return d - 2 dot(n, d) n def thicklensrefraction(o, d, R, dlens, nlens, next): # Centers of the two spherical interfaces c1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] c2 = [0.0, 0.0, dlens] # First intersection a = dot(d, d) b = 2 dot([o[i] - c1[i] for i in range(3)], d) cval = dot([o[i] - c1[i] for i in range(3)], [o[i] - c1[i] for i in range(3)]) - R2 pho = b2 - 4 a cval if pho <= 0: t1, t2 = float('inf'), float('inf') else: t1 = (-b + math.sqrt(pho)) / (2 a) t2 = (-b - math.sqrt(pho)) / (2 a) # Set virtual intersections to Inf if t1 < 0: t1 = float('inf') if t2 < 0: t2 = float('inf') tin = min(t1, t2) if tin == float('inf'): return d pin = [o[i] + tin d[i] for i in range(3)] # Normal oriented towards center n1 = normalize([c1[i] - pin[i] for i in range(3)]) drefracted = refractvector(d, n1, next, nlens) # Second intersection a = dot(drefracted, drefracted) b = 2 dot([pin[i] - c2[i] for i in range(3)], drefracted) cval = dot([pin[i] - c2[i] for i in range(3)], [pin[i] - c2[i] for i in range(3)]) - R2 pho = b2 - 4 a cval if pho <= 0: t1, t2 = float('inf'), float('inf') else: t1 = (-b + math.sqrt(pho)) / (2 a) t2 = (-b - math.sqrt(pho)) / (2 a) if t1 < 0: t1 = float('inf') if t2 < 0: t2 = float('inf') tout = min(t1, t2) if tout == float('inf'): return drefracted pout = [pin[i] + tout drefracted[i] for i in range(3)] n2 = normalize([c2[i] - pout[i] for i in range(3)]) dfinal = refractvector(drefracted, n2, nlens, next) return dfinal def dot(v1, v2): return sum(v1[i] v2[i] for i in range(len(v1))) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) if mag == 0: return v return [v[i] / mag for i in range(len(v))] The Porcine Eye Model Construction method defines the precise geometric and optical parameters of an ex vivo porcine eye to enable accurate ray tracing for distortion correction in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) systems. name: Porcine Eye Model Construction
head: Ex vivo porcine eye geometric model, Porcine eye optical model
body: The Porcine Eye Model Construction method defines the precise geometric and optical parameters of an ex vivo porcine eye to enable accurate ray tracing for distortion correction in Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) systems. It differs from human eye models by accounting for specific differences in corneal curvature, lens thickness, and gradient refractive index properties inherent to porcine tissue. This model serves as the physical substrate for the Thick Lens (Snell's Law Refraction) method, providing the surface curvatures, thicknesses, and refractive indices required to compute ray paths through the eye's optical components. Inputs: Refractive power of anterior and posterior corneal surfaces in diopters (P); refractive indices of air, cornea, aqueous humor, and vitreous humor at the operating wavelength; physical measurements of corneal thickness, anterior chamber depth, and lens dimensions. Outputs: A structured representation of the eye's optical surfaces, including radius of curvature and thickness for each interface, and the refractive indices of the media. The model is represented as a sequence of optical surfaces. Each surface entry contains: Surface: Identifier (e.g., "Anterior Cornea"). Radius: Radius of curvature in millimeters (mm). Positive values indicate convex surfaces facing the incident light; negative values indicate concave surfaces. \infty indicates a planar surface. Thickness: Axial distance to the next surface in millimeters (mm). The specific layout for the porcine eye model is defined as follows: | Surface | Radius (mm) | Thickness (mm) | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Anterior Cornea | 8.68 | 0.833 | | Posterior Cornea | 8.35 | 1.770 | | Anterior Lens | 7.08 | 3.034 | | Middle Lens | \infty | 4.366 | | Posterior Lens | -5.08 | 0.000 | The radius of curvature for each corneal surface is calculated from its refractive power using the following formula: R = \frac{(n2 - n1) \cdot 1000}{P} Where: R is the radius of curvature in millimeters. P is the refractive power of the surface in diopters (D). n1 is the refractive index of the medium preceding the surface. n2 is the refractive index of the medium following the surface. Anterior Cornea Calculation: P = 43.27 D. n1 = 1.0003 (air at 1050 nm). n2 = 1.376 (cornea). R{ca} = \frac{(1.376 - 1.0003) \cdot 1000}{43.27} \approx 8.68 mm. Posterior Cornea Calculation: P = -5.15 D. n1 = 1.376 (cornea). n2 = 1.333 (aqueous humor). R{cp} = \frac{(1.333 - 1.376) \cdot 1000}{-5.15} \approx 8.35 mm. Lens Geometry: Anterior lens radius: 7.08 mm. Posterior lens radius: -5.08 mm. Total lens thickness: 7.40 mm, composed of an anterior region (3.034 mm) and a middle region (4.366 mm). The middle lens surface is planar (\infty radius), separating the anterior and posterior lens regions. Refractive Indices: The approximate refractive index of the eye tissue (n{eye}) is 1.344 at 1050 nm. Cornea: 1.376. Aqueous humor: 1.333. Vitreous humor: Computed by optical design software based on 1050 nm properties. Operating Wavelength: 1050 nm. Anterior Corneal Radius (R{ca}): 8.68 mm. Posterior Corneal Radius (R{cp}): 8.35 mm. Corneal Thickness: 0.833 mm. Anterior Chamber Depth: 1.77 mm. Lens Anterior Radius: 7.08 mm. Lens Posterior Radius: -5.08 mm. Lens Total Thickness: 7.40 mm. Eye Refractive Index (n{eye}): 1.344. Gradient Refractive Index (GRIN): The anterior and middle lens surfaces are designated as "Gradient 3" type in optical design software to model the gradient refractive index of the lens material, rather than treating the lens as a homogeneous medium. This requires specific handling in ray tracing algorithms that support GRIN media. Sign Convention: The posterior lens radius is negative (-5.08 mm), indicating a concave surface relative to the incident light direction from the anterior chamber. Implementations must adhere to the sign convention used in the source (standard optical design convention) to ensure correct refraction calculations. Ex Vivo Conditions: The model is specific to ex vivo porcine eyes. In vivo conditions or human eyes will have different parameters, requiring separate model construction. Accuracy: Provides high geometric accuracy for ex vivo porcine eye ray tracing at 1050 nm, enabling distortion correction in OCT images. Complexity: The model involves 5 surfaces and GRIN lens handling, increasing computational complexity compared to simple homogeneous eye models. Applicability: Specifically designed for indirect viewing systems using ex vivo porcine eyes. Not directly applicable to human eyes or in vivo porcine eyes without parameter adjustment. The Porcine Eye Model Construction method was developed to address the significant differences in curvature and thickness between human and porcine eyes, which contribute to distortion in OCT images. Since experiments were conducted on ex vivo porcine eyes, a specific geometric optical model was required to achieve accurate ray tracing for distortion correction. The parameters were derived from mean refractive powers reported in literature [25], physical measurements [25, 26], and lens dimensions [27]. The model was implemented in Zemax OpticStudio for optical design and simulation. 3D fast ray-traced distortion correction of indirectly viewed intraoperative retinal OCT for surgical tool path reconstruction, https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13671697, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Screen-Space Reflections
head: Screen Space Ray Tracing (SSR)
body: Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) is a real-time global illumination method that traces rays in screen space against the depth buffer to achieve effects like reflections and color bleeding, which direct illumination cannot produce. It operates entirely within the 2D screen coordinate system using the existing depth buffer, distinguishing it from sibling methods that march through 3D volumes or scene graphs. This approach is significantly cheaper than full ray tracing but is strictly limited to geometry currently visible on screen. Inputs: Shaded point position in view space (P{view}). View vector (V) from the camera to P{view}. Surface normal (N) at P{view}. Depth buffer (Z-buffer) containing depth values for all visible pixels. Color buffer containing radiance/color values for all visible pixels. Screen resolution (W \times H). Outputs: Reflected color contribution (C{refl}) for the shaded point. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: A 2D array of size W \times H, storing depth values (z) in view space. Color Buffer: A 2D array of size W \times H, storing RGB(A) color values. Steps: 1. Reflect View Vector: Calculate the reflection direction R by reflecting the view vector V along the surface normal N. R = V - 2(V \cdot N)N Where V and N are normalized. The ray direction for tracing is R. 2. Initialize Ray: Start a ray at P{view} with direction R. 3. Iterate Ray Steps: Advance the ray in screen space. For each step i: a. Compute the current view position Pi of the ray. b. Project Pi into screen space to get pixel coordinates (ui, vi). c. Fetch the depth value z{buffer} from the Depth Buffer at (ui, vi). d. Fetch the depth value z{ray} of the current ray point Pi in view space. e. Intersection Test: If z{ray} > z{buffer} (assuming depth increases away from camera), the point is further away from the camera than the geometry in the depth buffer, meaning the ray is inside the geometry. If z{ray} < z{buffer}, the ray is in front of the geometry; continue to the next step. If the ray goes off-screen or exceeds a maximum distance, terminate. 4. Binary Search Refinement: If an intersection is detected between step i-1 and step i, perform a binary search between these two positions to find a more precise intersection point P{hit}. This improves accuracy because the initial intersection location is imprecise due to the unknown distance traveled between steps. 5. Sample Color: Once P{hit} is determined, project it to screen space (u{hit}, v{hit}). Sample the Color Buffer at (u{hit}, v{hit}) to obtain the incident radiance value C{refl}. 6. Shade: Utilize C{refl} to shade the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def screenspacereflections(Pview, V, N, depthbuffer, colorbuffer, W, H, maxsteps, stepsize): # Reflect view vector to get ray direction R = V - 2 dot(V, N) N prevpos = Pview currentpos = Pview for i in range(maxsteps): # Advance ray currentpos = prevpos + R stepsize # Project currentpos to screen space u, v = projecttoscreen(currentpos, W, H) # Check bounds if not (0 <= u < W and 0 <= v < H): return 0.0 # Off-screen # Get depth values zray = getviewdepth(currentpos) zbuffer = depthbuffer[v][u] # Check for intersection # Assuming depth buffer stores depth away from camera if zray > zbuffer: # Intersection occurred between prevpos and currentpos # Perform binary search to refine intersection point hitpos = binarysearchdepth(prevpos, currentpos, depthbuffer, W, H) # Sample color buffer at hit position uhit, vhit = projecttoscreen(hitpos, W, H) if 0 <= uhit < W and 0 <= vhit < H: return colorbuffer[vhit][uhit] else: return 0.0 else: prevpos = currentpos return 0.0 # No intersection found def projecttoscreen(Pview, W, H): # Standard perspective projection to screen coordinates # Assumes camera looks down -Z, depth increases away from camera if Pview.z == 0: return 0, 0 xclip = Pview.x / -Pview.z yclip = Pview.y / -Pview.z u = int((xclip 0.5 + 0.5) W) v = int((yclip 0.5 + 0.5) H) return u, v def getviewdepth(Pview): # Return depth in view space (distance from camera) return -Pview.z def binarysearchdepth(startpos, endpos, depthbuffer, W, H): low = startpos high = endpos for in range(10): # Fixed iterations for stability mid = low + (high - low) 0.5 u, v = projecttoscreen(mid, W, H) if not (0 <= u < W and 0 <= v < H): return mid # Fallback zray = getviewdepth(mid) zbuffer = depthbuffer[v][u] if zray > zbuffer: high = mid else: low = mid return low Parameters: maxsteps: Maximum number of ray steps. Typical value: Not given in the sources. stepsize: Distance to advance the ray per step. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lambertian Limitation: The approach only works on Lambertian surfaces. Screen Boundary: It can only reflect what is currently on screen. Geometry outside the viewport is not reflected. Precision: Initial intersection location is imprecise due to unknown distance traveled between steps, necessitating binary search. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of ray steps and pixels processed. Each pixel requires a depth buffer lookup and potentially a binary search. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the depth and color buffers. Strengths: Real-time performance; leverages existing rasterization buffers; effective for mirror and glossy surfaces. Limitations: Limited to visible geometry; artifacts at screen edges; requires depth buffer; limited to Lambertian surfaces according to source. When to use: Real-time rendering of reflections and color bleeding where full ray tracing is too expensive. When not to use: When reflections of off-screen objects are required, or for non-Lambertian surfaces if the source constraint is strict. Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) was first presented by Sousa. It is commonly found in real-time scenarios to render reflections. It is considered the most general method in real-time rendering for global illumination using screen space techniques, achieving honorable global illumination effects for both mirror and glossy surfaces. It is used in Jrender to depict global illumination for mirror and glossy surfaces.
