name: Flipped Reflection Ray Masking
head: Flipped Reflection Rays
body: Flipped Reflection Ray Masking is a regularization method for few-shot novel view synthesis that generates additional training rays from input viewing directions and estimated surface normals, casting them toward the identical target pixels as the original rays. It filters out ineffective rays based on the angle between the viewing direction and the normal to stabilize training and reduce floating artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Original input ray directions (\mathbf{d}{in}), estimated surface normal vectors (\mathbf{n}), and a threshold angle parameter (\tau). Outputs: A filtered set of flipped reflection rays (\mathbf{d}{flip}) used for training supervision. Data Structures: The method operates on standard 3D vector arrays for ray directions and surface normals. Steps: 1. Derive the flipped reflection rays from the original input ray directions and the estimated surface normals. 2. Cast the derived rays toward the identical target pixels as the original input rays. 3. Compute \theta, the angle between the input viewing direction \mathbf{d}{in} and the surface normal vector \mathbf{n} at each pixel. 4. If \theta > \tau, discard the corresponding flipped reflection ray; otherwise, retain it for training supervision. Formulas: The flipped reflection direction is computed as: \mathbf{d}{flip} = 2(\mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{d}{in} where \mathbf{d}{in} is the original viewing direction and \mathbf{n} is the surface normal. The angle \theta is calculated as: \theta = \arccos\left( \frac{\mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n}}{\|\mathbf{d}{in}\| \|\mathbf{n}\|} \right) The term "flipped" refers to the reflected ray having an opposite direction relative to the camera, effectively pointing from the object surface back toward the camera's general hemisphere. Parameters: \tau (tau): Threshold angle in degrees for ray masking. The optimal value is 90^\circ. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computeflippedreflectionmasking(inputraydirs, surfacenormals, thresholddegrees=90.0): """ Computes flipped reflection rays and masks ineffective ones based on the angle between the input viewing direction and the surface normal. Args: inputraydirs (np.ndarray): Array of shape (N, 3) representing input ray directions. surfacenormals (np.ndarray): Array of shape (N, 3) representing estimated surface normals. thresholddegrees (float): The threshold angle tau in degrees. Default 90.0. Returns: np.ndarray: Array of shape (N, 3) containing the flipped reflection rays. Pixels where the ray was masked are set to zero vectors. """ # Normalize input vectors for accurate angle calculation din = inputraydirs / np.linalg.norm(inputraydirs, axis=1, keepdims=True) n = surfacenormals / np.linalg.norm(surfacenormals, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Step 1: Compute the flipped reflection direction dotproduct = np.sum(din n, axis=1) dflip = 2.0 dotproduct[:, np.newaxis] n - din # Step 2: Compute the angle theta between input direction and normal costheta = np.clip(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0) thetadegrees = np.degrees(np.arccos(costheta)) # Step 3: Apply masking # If theta > tau, discard the ray; otherwise, retain it mask = thetadegrees <= thresholddegrees dflipmasked = np.where(mask[:, np.newaxis], dflip, 0.0) return dflipmasked Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Normals: If surface normals are zero vectors or poorly estimated (common in early training phases), the angle calculation becomes unstable. The masking strategy effectively filters these invalid additional rays at the initial training phase, leading to high-quality supervision and stabilizing training. Precision: Ensure dot products are clipped to [-1, 1] before arccos to avoid numerical domain errors. A complementary loss function used with flipped rays to reduce floating artifacts based on uncertainty. Ensures consistency between bottleneck features of original and flipped rays. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method adds a parallel branch of ray supervision without increasing the number of ray march steps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing additional ray directions and normals for the flipped rays during training. Performance: On the Realistic Synthetic 360° dataset, the 90^\circ masking strategy yields the highest PSNR (19.55), SSIM (0.767), and lowest LPIPS (0.180) and Average Error (0.101) among masking variants. Strengths: Stabilizes training in few-shot scenarios by filtering invalid rays at the initial phase and reducing floating artifacts. Limitations: Using too strict a threshold (e.g., \tau = 30^\circ or 60^\circ) degrades quality by filtering too many rays, reducing supervision. Using no masking yields inferior results due to noise from ineffective rays. When to use: Few-shot novel view synthesis where surface normal estimation is available or learnable. When not to use: Dense-view scenarios where standard supervision is sufficient, or when normal estimation is unreliable. Flipped Reflection Ray Masking was introduced in the FlipNeRF paper in 2023. It is built upon MixNeRF, leveraging a mixture model framework. The method addresses the limited input views in novel view synthesis by using flipped reflection rays as effective additional training resources. It is particularly relevant for few-shot learning where accurate depth and normal estimation are critical. FlipNeRF: Flipped Reflection Rays for Few-shot Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.02092, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Specular Radiance Calculation
head: Direct Specular Radiance, Indirect Specular Radiance via Cone Tracing, Specular Lighting
body: Specular radiance calculation determines the view-dependent specular contribution of a surface in real-time volume rendering, a component that cannot be precomputed in a voxel texture due to its dependency on camera position and surface reflection. It distinguishes itself by splitting the calculation into indirect specular radiance (computed via cone tracing through the voxel volume) and direct specular radiance (computed via a geometric visibility term). Inputs: I: Incoming camera direction vector (view direction). N: Surface normal vector. \theta: Cone width (diameter), determined by surface roughness. P: Surface position (3D fragment position). L: Light direction vector. V: Visibility factor (occlusion). Outputs: R{indirect}: Indirect specular radiance. R{direct}: Direct specular radiance. Data Structures: The method relies on a voxel texture for sampling during cone tracing. Steps: 1. Calculate Reflected Direction: Compute the direction of reflection based on the incident view direction and surface normal. \text{Reflect Direction} = \text{normalize}(I - 2.0 \cdot \text{dot}(N, I) \cdot N) where I is the incoming camera direction and N is the surface normal. 2. Determine Cone Width: The cone width \theta is derived from the surface roughness. For a completely smooth surface, the cone diameter is close to 1^\circ of the hemisphere. As roughness increases, the diameter increases up to a maximum of 180^\circ coverage to emulate light spreading on uneven surfaces. 3. Calculate Indirect Specular Radiance: Perform cone tracing from the surface position in the reflected direction to gather indirect specular light from the environment/volume. \text{Indirect Specular Radiance} = \text{cone trace}(\theta, P, \text{Reflect Direction}) The cone trace function implements iterative distance stepping and voxel sampling with occlusion accumulation. 4. Calculate Direct Specular Radiance: Compute the direct specular contribution using a geometry term that depends on the camera's point of view hitting the surface and the light's direction, scaled by PBR shininess. \text{direct specular radiance} = V \cdot \max(0, \text{dot}(\text{reflectDir}, L)) where reflectDir is the result from Step 1, L is the light direction, and V accounts for occlusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatespecularradiance(I, N, P, L, V, roughness): # Step 1: Calculate Reflected Direction reflectdir = normalize(I - 2.0 dot(N, I) N) # Step 2: Determine Cone Width from roughness # Smooth surface: ~1 degree, Rough surface: up to 180 degrees conewidthdeg = 1.0 + roughness 179.0 conewidthrad = conewidthdeg 3.141592653589793 / 180.0 # Step 3: Calculate Indirect Specular Radiance via Cone Tracing indirectradiance = conetrace(conewidthrad, P, reflectdir) # Step 4: Calculate Direct Specular Radiance directradiance = V max(0.0, dot(reflectdir, L)) return indirectradiance, directradiance def conetrace(theta, startpos, direction): distance = 0.0 radiance = 0.0 occlusion = 0.0 # Cone tracing loop from source while occlusion < 1.0: pos = startpos + direction distance distance = distance + 2.0 tan(theta / 2.0) distance lodlevel = log2(distance) sample = samplevoxels(pos, lodlevel) radiance = radiance + sample (1.0 - occlusion) occlusion = occlusion + (1.0 - occlusion) radiance return radiance def samplevoxels(pos, lodlevel): # Standard voxel texture lookup at position and LOD return texturelookup(pos, lodlevel) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The calculation is view-dependent and must be performed in real-time; precomputing it in a voxel texture is not feasible. Roughness Mapping: The cone width must correctly map from 0 to 1 roughness to 1 degree to 180 degrees to accurately simulate surface scattering. Visibility: The visibility term must accurately reflect occlusion to prevent light leaking through geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires access to the voxel texture for cone tracing. Performance: Evaluated by timing the overall program and specific functions like rendering and light calculation, varying with voxel texture size and scene complexity. Strengths: Provides accurate, view-dependent specular reflections in real-time by leveraging cone tracing for indirect light and geometric terms for direct light. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to iterative cone tracing. When to use: When real-time, view-dependent specular reflections are required in a voxel-based rendering pipeline. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the evaluation of voxel cone tracing for real-time applications, specifically focusing on the specular radiance component of the lighting model. It builds on the principles of physically based rendering (PBR) and cone tracing techniques for approximating indirect lighting in voxel environments. PDF Voxel Cone Tracing Evaluation for Real-Time Applications, https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1886204/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Iridescent Material with Perturbation
head: Iridescent Material (Cosine Palette), Iridescent Material with Specular and Shadow
body: This method generates an iridescent appearance on ray-marched surfaces by mapping a perturbed surface normal to a color via a cosine palette function, simulating thin-film interference colors. It combines this base iridescent layer with a multi-component specular highlight and a directional shadow term. It differs from Ray Marching with Reflections by using a procedural color palette driven by normal perturbation rather than recursive ray tracing for color, and from Spherical Gaussian Shading by using a fixed cosine palette rather than analytically approximated lobes for the base color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin (rayOrigin), ray direction (rayDirection), surface position (pos), surface normal (nor), light position (lightPos), and a gamma exponent (GAMMA, typically 2.2). Outputs: A linear RGB color vector (color) before gamma correction, or a screen-space RGB vector after correction. Data Structures: vec3: 3-component floating-point vector (x, y, z). float: 32-bit floating-point scalar. pal parameters: Vectors a, b, c, d of type vec3. Formulas: 1. Cosine Palette: pal(t, a, b, c, d) = a + b \cdot \cos(2\pi (c \cdot t + d)) Where t is a scalar input, and a, b, c, d are vec3 parameters. The code approximates 2\pi as 6.28318. 2. Spectrum Function: spectrum(n) = pal(n, \mathbf{0.5}, \mathbf{0.5}, \mathbf{1.0}, \mathbf{d}) Where \mathbf{0.5} and \mathbf{1.0} are vec3 vectors with all components equal to the scalar value, and \mathbf{d} = (0.0, 0.33, 0.67). 3. Gamma Correction: \text{linearToScreen}(C) = C^{1/\text{GAMMA}} Where C is a vec3 and the power operation is component-wise. Parameters: GAMMA: Gamma correction exponent. Typical value: 2.2. Perturbation scale: 0.05 (multiplier for perturb). Perturbation frequency: 10.0 (multiplier for pos in sin). Base layer intensity multiplier: 2.0 (multiplier for the dot product input to spectrum). Specular modulation frequency: 20.0. Specular modulation phase offset: -3.0. Specular power: 32.0. Specular base weight: 0.1. Secondary specular additive constant: 0.3. Secondary specular power: 8.0. Secondary specular weight: 0.1. Shadow dome direction: (0, 1, 0). Shadow slope: 0.5. Shadow bias: 1.2. Shadow power: 3.0. Steps: 1. Calculate Reflection Vector: Compute the reflection vector of the ray direction against the surface normal: \text{reflection} = \text{reflect}(\text{rayDirection}, \text{nor}). 2. Calculate Perturbation: Compute a perturbation vector based on the surface position: \text{perturb} = \sin(\text{pos} \times 10.0). 3. Calculate Base Iridescent Color: a. Compute the dot product between the perturbed normal and the eye direction (normalized vector from surface to ray origin): \text{dotVal} = \text{dot}(\text{nor} + \text{perturb} \times 0.05, \text{eyeDirection}) \times 2.0 b. Map this value to color using the spectrum function: \text{color} = \text{spectrum}(\text{dotVal}). 4. Calculate Specular Highlights: a. Compute the primary specular term: i. Clamp the dot product of the reflection vector and light direction to [0, 1]: s = \text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{reflection}, \text{lightDirection}), 0.0, 1.0) ii. Modulate with a sine wave and raise to a power: \text{specular} = \text{pow}((\sin(s \times 20.0 - 3.0) \times 0.5 + 0.5) + 0.1, 32.0) \times s iii. Scale by 0.1: \text{specular} = \text{specular} \times 0.1 b. Add a secondary specular component: i. Compute a new clamped dot product (same as step 4.a.i): s2 = \text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{reflection}, \text{lightDirection}), 0.0, 1.0) ii. Add offset, raise to power, and scale: \text{secondary} = \text{pow}(s2 + 0.3, 8.0) \times 0.1 iii. Add to specular: \text{specular} = \text{specular} + \text{secondary}. 5. Calculate Shadow: a. Define dome direction as \text{dome} = (0, 1, 0). b. Compute shadow factor: \text{shadow} = \text{pow}(\text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{nor}, \text{dome}) \times 0.5 + 1.2, 0.0, 1.0), 3.0). 6. Combine Colors: \text{color} = \text{color} \times \text{shadow} + \text{specular}. 7. Gamma Correction: Convert linear RGB to screen space: \text{color} = \text{linearToScreen}(\text{color}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Tuple def vec3add(a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]) def vec3sub(a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1], a[2] - b[2]) def vec3mulscalar(v: Tuple[float, float, float], s: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (v[0] s, v[1] s, v[2] s) def vec3dot(a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> float: return a[0] b[0] + a[1] b[1] + a[2] b[2] def vec3normalize(v: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: s = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0] / s, v[1] / s, v[2] / s) def vec3sin(v: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (math.sin(v[0]), math.sin(v[1]), math.sin(v[2])) def vec3clamp(v: Tuple[float, float, float], lo: float, hi: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (max(lo, min(hi, v[0])), max(lo, min(hi, v[1])), max(lo, min(hi, v[2]))) def vec3reflect(I: Tuple[float, float, float], N: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: dotval = vec3dot(I, N) return (I[0] - 2 dotval N[0], I[1] - 2 dotval N[1], I[2] - 2 dotval N[2]) def pal(t: float, a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float], c: Tuple[float, float, float], d: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Cosine palette function.""" arg = (c[0]t + d[0], c[1]t + d[1], c[2]t + d[2]) cosarg = (math.cos(6.28318 arg[0]), math.cos(6.28318 arg[1]), math.cos(6.28318 arg[2])) return (a[0] + b[0]cosarg[0], a[1] + b[1]cosarg[1], a[2] + b[2]cosarg[2]) def spectrum(n: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Spectrum function using specific palette parameters.""" a = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) c = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) d = (0.0, 0.33, 0.67) return pal(n, a, b, c, d) def gamma(color: Tuple[float, float, float], g: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Apply gamma correction component-wise.""" return (color[0]g, color[1]g, color[2]g) def lineartoscreen(linearrgb: Tuple[float, float, float], gammaval: float = 2.2) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Convert linear RGB to screen space.""" return gamma(linearrgb, 1.0 / gammaval) def iridescentmaterial(rayorigin: Tuple[float, float, float], raydirection: Tuple[float, float, float], pos: Tuple[float, float, float], nor: Tuple[float, float, float], lightpos: Tuple[float, float, float], gammaval: float = 2.2) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """ Calculate iridescent shading with perturbation, specular, and shadow. """ eyedirection = vec3normalize(vec3sub(rayorigin, pos)) lightdirection = vec3normalize(vec3sub(lightpos, pos)) reflection = vec3reflect(raydirection, nor) perturb = vec3sin(vec3mulscalar(pos, 10.0)) perturbednor = vec3add(nor, vec3mulscalar(perturb, 0.05)) dotval = vec3dot(perturbednor, eyedirection) 2.0 color = spectrum(dotval) dotreflight = vec3dot(reflection, lightdirection) s = vec3clamp(dotreflight, 0.0, 1.0) sinterm = math.sin(s 20.0 - 3.0) modulated = sinterm 0.5 + 0.5 modulated += 0.1 specular = (modulated 32.0) s specular = 0.1 s2 = vec3clamp(dotreflight, 0.0, 1.0) secondary = ((s2 + 0.3) 8.0) 0.1 specular += secondary dome = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) dotnordome = vec3dot(nor, dome) shadowarg = dotnordome 0.5 + 1.2 shadowclamped = vec3clamp(shadowarg, 0.0, 1.0) shadow = shadowclamped 3.0 color = (color[0] shadow + specular, color[1] shadow + specular, color[2] shadow + specular) color = lineartoscreen(color, gammaval) return color A technique for rendering iridescence in thin films (soap bubbles, oil films) using Airy summation for s/p polarization over multiple wavelengths. It samples 9 wavelengths to compute the interference pattern and applies the model over a dielectric or metal base. For metal bases, it derives the complex Index of Refraction (IOR) from F0 and edge tint using Gulbrandsen's inversion. A key pitfall is handling thin films at zero thickness as a special case to avoid numerical instability or incorrect reflection. A technique to blend Blinn-Phong lighting with iridescent lighting to create tinted iridescent objects. It calculates a Blinn-Phong specular term (power) multiplied by a tint color to get baseColor. It calculates the standard iridescent color (color shadow + specular). It then blends the two using mix(baseColor, color, mixBaseAndIridescent). The parameter mixBaseAndIridescent controls the blend factor, typically in range [0,1]. Time Complexity: Constant number of trigonometric, power, and vector operations per surface hit. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time ray marching. Strengths: Produces vibrant, procedural iridescent colors without complex physics simulation; easy to tune via palette parameters. Limitations: Physically approximate; the "cosine palette" is an artistic approximation of thin-film interference, not a rigorous physical model. When to use: When a stylized, colorful iridescent effect is desired for ray-marched objects (e.g., crystals, soap bubbles) and physical accuracy is not required. When not to use: When physically accurate thin-film interference is required (use Thin-Film Interference via Airy Summation instead). The method originates from community-driven shader art, specifically popularized by Thomas Hooper's "Crystals" shader and discussed in tutorials on ray marching with Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). It leverages the "cosine palette" technique, a common tool in Shadertoy programming for generating smooth, periodic color gradients. The specific combination of perturbation, specular, and shadow terms was detailed in a tutorial by Varun (Show HN: Iridescent crystal with raymarching and signed distance fields). name: Spherical Gaussian Shading
head: SG Shading, SG-Based Rendering, Shading Rendering of Spherical Gaussians, Specular BRDF Approximation
body: Spherical Gaussian (SG) Shading is a technique that approximates direct illumination and specular BRDFs using a mixture of Spherical Gaussian basis functions to enable fast, analytic integration and automatic differentiation. It distinguishes itself from Monte Carlo (MC) integration by being less expensive and more robust to roughness variations, though it sacrifices high-frequency detail accuracy. It is primarily used in differentiable rendering and inverse rendering pipelines where lighting and material parameters must be optimized jointly. The method operates on a surface point \mathbf{p} with normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{v}, and incident light direction \mathbf{l}. It approximates the rendering equation by representing both the incident radiance and the BRDF lobes as sums of Spherical Gaussians. 1. Spherical Gaussian (SG) Kernel: Defined by four parameters: \omega \in S^2 (input direction), \xi \in S^2 (axis/center), \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+ (sharpness), and \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{3+} (amplitude/HDR RGB color). 2. Lighting Representation: A mixture of K SGs representing the environment map or spatially variant lights, with parameters \gamma = \{ \xi{lk}, \lambda{lk}, \mu{lk} \}{k=1}^K. Typical K is 128 for fitting HDR environment maps. 3. Volumetric SG (VSG) Layout: Stored as an 8-channel tensor \mathcal{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times X \times Y \times Z}. Each voxel contains opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], HDR RGB intensity c \in \mathbb{R}^3, lobe axis \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, and sharpness \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+. The Spherical Gaussian function is defined as: G(\omega; \xi, \lambda, \mu) = \mu e^{\lambda(\xi \cdot \omega - 1)} Cosine foreshortening is approximated by a single SG: |\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai| \approx Gc(\omegai; \mathbf{n}, 2.133, 1.17) The specular lobe of the BRDF is fitted to a single monochromatic SG, denoted fr^{(SG)}, forming a sum of diffuse and specular lobes. The final pixel color S^{(SG)} is computed by integrating the product of the BRDF, incident radiance, and cosine term: S^{(SG)}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{n}, \omegao; \theta, \gamma) = \int{S^2} fr^{(SG)}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao; \theta) Li^{(SG)}(\omegai; \gamma) Gc(\omegai) d\omegai where Li^{(SG)} is the incident radiance represented by K SGs. Alternatively, each SG can be rendered as 5 point lights (1 center + 4 sampled around). For k point lights with intensity \mathbf{I}i, the shading is: \mathbf{S}{SG}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^k \frac{\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r})}{|\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r})| |\mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r})|} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{I}i}{\gamma \cdot \mathbf{Dis}i(\mathbf{r})^2} where \mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r}) is the direction from light to point, \mathbf{Dis}i(\mathbf{r}) is the distance, and \gamma is a hyperparameter controlling luminance. For VSG, incident radiance R(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{l}, \mathcal{L}) at point \mathbf{p} in direction \mathbf{l} is calculated via alpha compositing along N equi-spaced points: R(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{l}, \mathcal{L}) = \left( \prod{i=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphai) \right) \sum{k=1}^{N} \alphak G(-\mathbf{l}; ck, \muk, \sigmak) The total image for ray \mathbf{r} combines diffuse, specular, and SG shading: I(\mathbf{r}) = Id(\mathbf{r}) + Is(\mathbf{r}) + V(\mathbf{r})\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r})S{SG}(\mathbf{r}) where V is shadow visibility and \mathcal{R} is reflectance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalgaussianshading(surfacepoint, normal, viewdir, lightingparams, method="pointlight"): """ Compute shading using Spherical Gaussians. Args: surfacepoint: 3D position p. normal: Surface normal n. viewdir: View direction v. lightingparams: Dictionary containing 'K', 'SGs' (list of dicts with 'xi', 'lambda', 'mu'), or 'VSGvolume' for volumetric method. method: 'analytic' for direct integration, 'pointlight' for 5-light approximation. Returns: Color C. """ if method == "pointlight": totalshading = np.zeros(3) gamma = lightingparams.get('gamma', 1.0) for sg in lightingparams['SGs']: lights = generatepointlightsfromsg(sg['xi']) for lightdir, lightintensity in lights: ldir = normalize(lightdir) dist = 1.0 cosine = max(dot(normal, ldir), 0.0) attenuation = lightintensity / (gamma dist2) totalshading += cosine attenuation return totalshading elif method == "analytic": cosinesg = {'xi': normal, 'lambda': 2.133, 'mu': 1.17} specularsg = fitspecularsg(normal, viewdir, roughness=0.1, metalness=0.5) color = np.zeros(3) for sg in lightingparams['SGs']: # The analytic integral of the product of SGs on a sphere is not provided in the sources. # Standard closed-form integration applies. color += integratesgproduct(cosinesg, specularsg, sg) return color def sphericalgaussian(direction, axis, sharpness, amplitude): """Evaluate a single Spherical Gaussian: G(w; xi, lambda, mu) = mu exp(lambda (xi. w - 1)).""" return amplitude exp(sharpness (dot(axis, direction) - 1.0)) def generatepointlightsfromsg(centeraxis): """Generate 5 light directions around the SG center axis.""" lights = [(centeraxis, 1.0)] for i in range(4): offset = orthogonalvector(centeraxis) lights.append((normalize(centeraxis + 0.5 offset), 0.5)) return lights def fitspecularsg(normal, viewdir, roughness, metalness): """Fit a single monochromatic SG to the specular lobe of the BRDF.""" halfvec = normalize(normal + viewdir) sharpness = 2.0 / (roughness2 + 1e-6) return {'xi': halfvec, 'lambda': sharpness, 'mu': 1.0} def integratesgproduct(sg1, sg2, sg3): # The analytic integral of the product of SGs on a sphere is not provided in the sources. # Standard closed-form integration applies. return np.zeros(3) K: Number of SGs. Typical value is 128 for fitting HDR environment maps. \gamma: Hyperparameter for luminance control in point-light approximation. \beta: Surface roughness. SG shading is robust to variations in \beta. \sigma: VSG sharpness. If \sigma \gg 1, VSG reduces to RGB\alpha. High Frequency Loss: SGs smooth out high-frequency details and sharp corners. They are not precise enough for real-time scenarios requiring high fidelity without a very large number of coefficients. HDR Lighting: If the environment is HDR, SGs should be placed far from the scene to assume distant lighting. VSG Degeneracy: If \sigma \gg 1 in VSG, the representation loses directional lighting capability and becomes a standard RGB\alpha volume. Coefficient Count: Accurate reconstruction may require significantly more coefficients than dense pixel maps (e.g., 896 SGs vs 98,304 pixels for an HDR map). A specific application of SG shading within Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for relighting. It combines diffuse (Id), specular (Is), and SG shading (S{SG}) modulated by shadow visibility (V) and reflectance (\mathcal{R}). It allows for material editing and scene relighting by optimizing SG parameters. A voxel-based representation for 3D spatially-varying lighting where each voxel acts as a light source parameterized by SG lobes. It captures view-dependent effects and directional lighting in 3D space, unlike standard RGB\alpha volumes. It is calculated via alpha compositing along rays. Assumes full light source visibility, ignoring self-occlusions and assuming all light sources in the upper hemisphere above any surface are fully visible. It accelerates rendering by representing environment lighting and scene BRDFs as mixtures of spherical Gaussians, enabling the hemispherical integral of incoming light multiplied by the BRDF to be computed in closed form. Assuming full light source visibility is unable to simulate effects such as cast shadows due to occlusion of light sources by scene geometry, though it works well for mostly convex objects. Time Complexity: Faster than Monte Carlo (MC) integration because it uses analytic integration of SG products. The cost scales linearly with the number of SGs K. Memory Complexity: Compact. Requires significantly fewer parameters than dense environment maps (e.g., 896 parameters for K=128 SGs vs 98,304 for a dense HDR map). VSG adds spatial storage overhead (8 \times X \times Y \times Z). Performance: Robust to roughness variations. MC is better for mirror-like objects (low roughness) where high frequencies are preserved, but SG is more efficient for moderate-to-high roughness. Limitations: Loses high-frequency details. Not suitable for real-time rendering if high precision is required without large K. When to Use: Differentiable rendering, inverse rendering, optimization of lighting/materials, and scenes with moderate roughness. When Not to Use: Real-time rendering requiring high-fidelity specular highlights with sharp features, or scenes with very low roughness (mirrors) where MC is superior. Spherical Gaussian shading was introduced as a compact approximation for direct illumination in differentiable rendering frameworks, specifically within the DIB-R++ pipeline. It builds on the mathematical properties of Spherical Gaussians to allow analytic integration of the rendering equation, facilitating gradient-based optimization of lighting and materials. It has been applied in various contexts including intrinsic decomposition, relighting in NeRFs, and 3D inverse rendering with spatially varying lighting.
