name: Neon Raymarcher Shading Model
head: Milestone 2 shading, Procedural Neon Shading
body: The Neon Raymarcher Shading Model is a real-time shading technique for procedural neon city scenes that computes diffuse, specular, ambient occlusion, metallic reflection, and emissive contributions per pixel. It uses a fixed-step shadow ray and a metallic Fresnel weighting scheme tailored to the compressed distance field geometry of the scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{rd} (from \mathbf{p} to camera), light direction \mathbf{lightDir} (from \mathbf{p} to light), material properties: albedo \mathbf{c}{albedo}, metalness m \in [0,1], emissive color \mathbf{c}{emissive}, and light color \mathbf{c}{light}. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{c}{final}. Data Structures: The material state sf contains: albedo: vec3 metal: float (0.0 to 1.0) emissive: vec3. Steps: 1. Geometric Setup: Calculate the half-vector \mathbf{h} between the view direction \mathbf{rd} and light direction \mathbf{lightDir}: \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{lightDir} - \mathbf{rd}) Calculate the dot products for diffuse, specular, and Fresnel terms: d{diff} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{lightDir}, 0.0) d{spec} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0) d{fresnel\dot} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot (-\mathbf{rd}), 0.0). 2. Shadow Calculation: Compute the shadow factor S by casting a shadow ray from an origin offset along the normal to prevent self-shadowing artifacts: \mathbf{p}{shadow} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \times 0.03 The shadow function returns a value in [0, 1] indicating occlusion, using a fixed maximum distance of 12.0 units: S = \text{Shadow}(\mathbf{p}{shadow}, \mathbf{lightDir}, 12.0) The effective diffuse lighting is modulated by this shadow: L{diff} = d{diff} \times S. 3. Ambient Occlusion Calculation: Compute the ambient occlusion factor A using the function calcAO(p, n). 4. Specular Reflection: Calculate the specular contribution using a power exponent mixed based on metalness: C{spec} = \text{pow}(d{spec}, \text{mix}(32.0, 140.0, m)) \times S. 5. Metallic Reflection: Calculate the Fresnel factor F using a power of 5.0: F = \text{pow}(1.0 - d{fresnel\dot}, 5.0) Get the sky color \mathbf{c}{sky} by reflecting the view direction \mathbf{rd} about the normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{r} = \text{reflect}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{c}{sky} = \text{skyColor}(\mathbf{r}) Calculate the metallic reflection intensity I{metal}: I{metal} = \text{mix}(0.03, 0.6, m) \times (0.25 + 0.75 \times F) The metallic reflection contribution is: C{metal} = \mathbf{c}{sky} \times I{metal} \times A. 6. Color Accumulation: Combine the components. The base color is the albedo modulated by ambient light and AO, plus the diffuse light contribution. The specular and metallic reflections are added. Finally, the emissive color is added: \mathbf{c}{final} = \mathbf{c}{albedo} \times (\text{ambient} \times A) + \mathbf{c}{albedo} \times \mathbf{c}{light} \times L{diff} + \mathbf{c}{light} \times C{spec} \times \text{mix}(0.4, 2.0, m) + C{metal} + \mathbf{c}{emissive}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neonraymarchershading(p, n, rd, lightDir, lightCol, sf, ambient): # 1. Geometric Setup halfVec = normalize(lightDir - rd) diffdot = max(dot(n, lightDir), 0.0) specdot = max(dot(n, halfVec), 0.0) fresneldot = max(dot(n, -rd), 0.0) # 2. Shadow Calculation # Offset normal to prevent self-shadowing pshadow = p + n 0.03 # Source does not provide implementation for shadowray def shadowray(origin, dir, maxdist): # Standard distance-field shadow raymarcher omitted by source return 1.0 shadow = shadowray(pshadow, lightDir, 12.0) diffterm = diffdot shadow # 3. Ambient Occlusion # Source does not provide implementation for calcao def calcao(point, normal): # Standard hemisphere visibility estimation omitted by source return 1.0 ao = calcao(p, n) # 4. Specular Reflection speccontrib = pow(specdot, mix(32.0, 140.0, sf.metal)) shadow # 5. Metallic Reflection fresnel = pow(1.0 - fresneldot, 5.0) r = reflect(rd, n) # Source does not provide implementation for skycolorfunction def skycolorfunction(reflecteddir): # Environment map lookup omitted by source return vec3(0.0) skycolor = skycolorfunction(r) metalbase = mix(0.03, 0.6, sf.metal) metalgrazingboost = 0.25 + 0.75 fresnel metalcontrib = skycolor metalbase metalgrazingboost ao # 6. Color Accumulation basecolor = sf.albedo (ambient ao) + sf.albedo lightCol diffterm color = basecolor + lightCol speccontrib mix(0.4, 2.0, sf.metal) + metalcontrib color += sf.emissive return color Parameters: Shadow ray origin offset: 0.03 units along \mathbf{n}. Shadow ray max distance: 12.0 units. Specular exponent range: 32.0 (non-metal) to 140.0 (metal). Specular intensity range: 0.4 (non-metal) to 2.0 (metal). Fresnel power: 5.0. Metallic reflection base intensity: 0.03 (non-metal) to 0.6 (metal). Metallic reflection grazing boost: 0.25 (normal) to 0.75 (grazing). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: The normal offset of 0.03 is critical to prevent the shadow ray from intersecting the surface itself, which causes dark artifacts. Sky Color: The skyColor function is an external dependency not defined in the shading model; it must be implemented to return appropriate environment colors for the reflection. Time Complexity: The shading cost is dominated by the shadowray and calcao functions, which involve additional distance field evaluations. The core shading formula is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, storing only intermediate vectors and scalars. Strengths: Real-time performance on modern hardware due to a simplified shading model tailored for the neon city aesthetic. Limitations: The shadow ray is cast in a fixed direction with a fixed max distance, which may not accurately represent complex lighting scenarios. The ambient occlusion approximation may lack detail compared to screen-space or baked solutions. When to use: Ideal for real-time rendering of stylized, neon-lit urban environments where performance is critical. When not to use: Not suitable for physically accurate rendering or scenes requiring complex dynamic lighting. The Neon Raymarcher Shading Model is implemented in the "neon-raymarcher" project by PIGJET, a real-time raymarched demo of a procedural neon city. It is designed to complement the specific distance field geometry of the scene, which includes compressed building distances and a ground plane. PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, https://github.com/PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Lidar Sphere Tracing
body: Lidar Sphere Tracing is a rendering technique that adapts distance-field ray marching to simulate LiDAR sensor data by detecting surface intersections from a camera viewpoint and projecting them onto a framebuffer as a sparse point cloud, rather than rendering a continuous geometric or volumetric surface. It differs from standard sphere tracing by discarding surface shading and normal estimation in favor of storing hit positions in a bounded point cloud buffer and rendering them with an occlusion-aware color map. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Signed Distance Function (SDF) world representation, camera parameters (center, orientation, focal length, resolution), and rendering parameters (maxspheres, spheredetectsize, lidardensity, maxlidarpoints). Output: A 1D array of uint32t representing an ARGB8888 framebuffer, and a deque of 3D points representing the Lidar scan. Data Structures: Framebuffer: A 1D array of size imagewidth imageheight. Memory layout is row-major, indexed by screenx + imagewidth screeny. Format is ARGB8888 (Alpha 8, Red 8, Green 8, Blue 8). Lidar Point Cloud: A std::deque<vec3> storing 3D hit coordinates. It acts as a bounded buffer with a maximum capacity maxlidarpoints. Parameters: maxspheres: Maximum iterations per ray before the trace is considered failed. Default: 100. spheredetectsize: Convergence threshold for hit detection. Default: 0.01. lidardensity: Sampling rate control. A ray is cast only if (int)((double)rand() / RANDMAX lidardensity) == 1. Higher values result in sparser clouds. Default: 2. maxlidarpoints: Maximum capacity of the point cloud buffer. Default: 1,400,000. Algorithm Steps: 1. Camera Initialization: Calculate viewport dimensions based on fov, aspectratio, and focallength: \text{viewport\width} = 2 \cdot \text{focal\length} \cdot \tan(\text{fov}/2) \text{viewport\height} = \text{viewport\width} / \text{aspect\ratio} Calculate pixel dimensions: \text{pixel\width} = \text{viewport\width} / \text{image\width} \text{pixel\height} = \text{viewport\height} / \text{image\height} Define the top-left pixel center in camera space (before rotation): \mathbf{p}{00} = \mathbf{c} + \left( -\frac{\text{viewport\width}}{2}, -\frac{\text{viewport\height}}{2}, \text{focal\length} \right) where \mathbf{c} is cameracenter. 2. Ray Casting Loop (Lidar Generation): For each pixel (i, j) in the image grid: a. Ray Origin: \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{c}. b. Ray Direction: Calculate the unrotated pixel direction vector: \mathbf{v}{\text{raw}} = \mathbf{p}{00} + (i \cdot \text{pixel\width}, j \cdot \text{pixel\height}, 0) + \left( \frac{\text{pixel\width}}{2}, \frac{\text{pixel\height}}{2}, 0 \right) Translate to origin-relative: \mathbf{v}{\text{trans}} = \mathbf{v}{\text{raw}} - \mathbf{c} Apply camera rotation (Yaw angley, Pitch anglex): \mathbf{d} = \text{rotateX}(\text{rotateY}(\mathbf{v}{\text{trans}}, angley), anglex) Normalize \mathbf{d} to unit length. c. Sampling Check: If (int)((double)rand() / RANDMAX lidardensity) != 1, skip this pixel. d. Sphere Tracing: Initialize length = 0. Loop k from 0 to maxspheres: i. Current position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \text{length}. ii. Distance query: d{\text{obj}} = \text{world.minDist}(\mathbf{p}). iii. Hit Test: If d{\text{obj}} < \text{sphere\detect\size}, record \mathbf{p} as a Lidar point and break. iv. Step: \text{length} \leftarrow \text{length} + d{\text{obj}}. e. Buffer Management: If a hit was recorded, add \mathbf{p} to lidarpoints. If lidarpoints.size() > maxlidarpoints, remove the oldest point (popfront). 3. Projection and Rendering: For each point \mathbf{p} in lidarpoints: a. Transform to Camera Space: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} \mathbf{v} = \text{rotateY}(\mathbf{v}, -anglex) \mathbf{v} = \text{rotateX}(\mathbf{v}, -angley). b. Depth Check: If \mathbf{v}z \le 10^{-6}, the point is behind or on the camera plane; skip. c. Screen Coordinates: x{\text{img}} = \frac{\text{focal\length} \cdot \mathbf{v}x}{\mathbf{v}z} y{\text{img}} = \frac{\text{focal\length} \cdot \mathbf{v}y}{\mathbf{v}z} \text{screen\x} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{image\width}}{2} + \frac{x{\text{img}}}{\text{pixel\width}} \right\rfloor \text{screen\y} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{image\height}}{2} + \frac{y{\text{img}}}{\text{pixel\height}} \right\rfloor. d. Bounds Check: If \text{screen\x} < 0 or \ge \text{image\width} or \text{screen\y} < 0 or \ge \text{image\height}, skip. e. Color Calculation: The color depends on whether the point is a primary Lidar hit or an occlusion check. Primary Lidar Hit: Write color 0xFFFF0000 (Red, Alpha 255). Occlusion Count (Standard Pixels): If rendering occlusion for a pixel (via sphereCastOcclusion), let stepcount be the number of iterations. If 0x00030303 \cdot \text{step\count} > 0x00FFFFFF, set pixel to 0xFF000000 (Black). Otherwise, set pixel to: \text{Color} = 0xFF000000 + 0x00FFFFFF - (0x00030303 \cdot \text{step\count}) This results in a grayscale value that darkens as stepcount increases. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rotatey(v, angle): c = math.cos(angle) s = math.sin(angle) return (c v[0] + s v[2], v[1], -s v[0] + c v[2]) def rotatex(v, angle): c = math.cos(angle) s = math.sin(angle) return (v[0], c v[1] - s v[2], s v[1] + c v[2]) def unitvector(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if mag == 0: return (0, 0, 0) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def spheretrace(rayorigin, raydir, world, maxspheres, spheredetectsize): length = 0.0 for in range(maxspheres): pos = (rayorigin[0] + raydir[0] length, rayorigin[1] + raydir[1] length, rayorigin[2] + raydir[2] length) dist = world.mindist(pos) if dist < spheredetectsize: return pos length += dist return None def spheretraceocclusion(rayorigin, raydir, world, maxspheres, spheredetectsize): length = world.mindist(rayorigin) steps = 0 for in range(maxspheres): pos = (rayorigin[0] + raydir[0] length, rayorigin[1] + raydir[1] length, rayorigin[2] + raydir[2] length) dist = world.mindist(pos) steps += 1 if dist < spheredetectsize: return steps length += dist return steps def renderlidar(camera, world, framebuffer, imagewidth, imageheight): fov = camera.fov focallength = camera.focallength aspectratio = camera.aspectratio viewportwidth = 2 focallength math.tan(fov / 2) viewportheight = viewportwidth / aspectratio pixelwidth = viewportwidth / imagewidth pixelheight = viewportheight / imageheight p00 = (camera.cameracenter[0] - viewportwidth / 2, camera.cameracenter[1] - viewportheight / 2, camera.cameracenter[2] + focallength) halfoffset = (pixelwidth 0.5, pixelheight 0.5, 0) lidarpoints = [] for i in range(imagewidth): for j in range(imageheight): if int((random.random() camera.lidardensity)) != 1: continue pixelloc = (p00[0] + i pixelwidth + halfoffset[0], p00[1] + j pixelheight + halfoffset[1], p00[2] + halfoffset[2]) translated = (pixelloc[0] - camera.cameracenter[0], pixelloc[1] - camera.cameracenter[1], pixelloc[2] - camera.cameracenter[2]) rotatedy = rotatey(translated, camera.angley) rotatedx = rotatex(rotatedy, camera.anglex) raydir = unitvector(rotatedx) rayorigin = camera.cameracenter hit = spheretrace(rayorigin, raydir, world, camera.maxspheres, camera.spheredetectsize) if hit is not None: lidarpoints.append(hit) if len(lidarpoints) > camera.maxlidarpoints: lidarpoints.pop(0) for point in lidarpoints: v = (point[0] - camera.cameracenter[0], point[1] - camera.cameracenter[1], point[2] - camera.cameracenter[2]) v = rotatey(v, -camera.anglex) v = rotatex(v, -camera.angley) if v[2] <= 1e-6: continue ximg = (focallength v[0]) / v[2] yimg = (focallength v[1]) / v[2] screenx = int(imagewidth / 2 + ximg / pixelwidth) screeny = int(imageheight / 2 + yimg / pixelheight) if 0 <= screenx < imagewidth and 0 <= screeny < imageheight: idx = screenx + imagewidth screeny framebuffer[idx] = 0xFFFF0000 def renderocclusion(camera, world, framebuffer, imagewidth, imageheight): fov = camera.fov focallength = camera.focallength aspectratio = camera.aspectratio viewportwidth = 2 focallength math.tan(fov / 2) viewportheight = viewportwidth / aspectratio pixelwidth = viewportwidth / imagewidth pixelheight = viewportheight / imageheight p00 = (camera.cameracenter[0] - viewportwidth / 2, camera.cameracenter[1] - viewportheight / 2, camera.cameracenter[2] + focallength) halfoffset = (pixelwidth 0.5, pixelheight 0.5, 0) for i in range(imagewidth): for j in range(imageheight): pixelloc = (p00[0] + i pixelwidth + halfoffset[0], p00[1] + j pixelheight + halfoffset[1], p00[2] + halfoffset[2]) translated = (pixelloc[0] - camera.cameracenter[0], pixelloc[1] - camera.cameracenter[1], pixelloc[2] - camera.cameracenter[2]) rotatedy = rotatey(translated, camera.angley) rotatedx = rotatex(rotatedy, camera.anglex) raydir = unitvector(rotatedx) rayorigin = camera.cameracenter steps = spheretraceocclusion(rayorigin, raydir, world, camera.maxspheres, camera.spheredetectsize) idx = i + imagewidth j term = 0x00030303 steps if term > 0x00FFFFFF: framebuffer[idx] = 0xFF000000 else: framebuffer[idx] = 0xFF000000 + 0x00FFFFFF - term Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels sampled (determined by lidardensity) and M is the average number of sphere tracing iterations per ray. Memory Complexity: O(P), where P is maxlidarpoints. The framebuffer is O(W \cdot H). Strengths: Efficiently visualizes sparse depth data; simple implementation using standard SDF primitives; parallelizable ray casting. Limitations: Produces a point cloud rather than a solid surface; occlusion rendering is a separate pass or combined logic that may not accurately represent true depth buffering for all pixels; sparse sampling can lead to visual gaps. When to use: Simulating LiDAR sensor output, point cloud visualization, or stylized depth visualization. When not to use: When continuous surface rendering, accurate shading, or high-density point coverage is required. Lidar Sphere Tracing is an open-source implementation found in educational and hobbyist graphics projects that adapts the classic sphere tracing algorithm to generate point clouds mimicking LiDAR sensor data, projecting these points onto a 2D plane using standard perspective projection matrices. Lidar Sphere Tracing Renderer, https://github.com/kuvsamja/lidar-sphere-tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering
head: Standard 3ds Max atmospheric
body: Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering is a family of techniques that visualize participating media by integrating light transport along view rays through a density field. It solves the problem of rendering non-surface-based phenomena such as smoke, fire, clouds, and planetary atmospheres, which lack explicit geometric boundaries. It is distinguished from sibling methods like SDF Cloud Rendering by its reliance on sampled density fields or explicit atmospheric models rather than implicit Signed Distance Fields, and from Ray Marching with Single Scattering by its broader scope encompassing global atmospheric scattering and temporal accumulation strategies. The family operates on the principle of discretizing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. The integration computes the accumulated color C and transmittance T by marching through a medium defined by density \rho(\mathbf{p}), scattering coefficient \sigmas, and absorption coefficient \sigmaa. The core integration step for a segment of length \Delta t is: 1. Density Evaluation: Sample \rho at the current position \mathbf{p}. 2. Extinction: Compute the extinction coefficient \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa. 3. Transmittance Update: Update the ray's transmittance T using Beer-Lambert law: T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\sigmat \rho \Delta t}. 4. Inscattering: Compute the light contributed by the segment. For single scattering, this involves the phase function P(\theta) and the light source radiance L{source} attenuated by the optical depth to the light. 5. Accumulation: Add the inscattered light to the accumulated color, weighted by the current transmittance: C \leftarrow C + T \cdot \sigmas \rho \Delta t \cdot L{scattered}. The process terminates when T falls below a threshold (e.g., 0.01) or the ray exits the volume bounds. Focuses on general volumetric single scattering without specific planetary geometry or atmospheric density models. Choose when rendering generic fog or clouds rather than a planet's sky. Resolves a complete ray by compositing terrain, water, sky, cloud volume, and aerial perspective. Choose when managing the sequential evaluation and compositing order of heterogeneous scene elements in distance-field ray marching. Adds temporal stability to the ray marching process by blending the current frame's result with a history texture. Choose when flickering artifacts in dynamic scenes are a concern. Specializes in planetary atmospheres using spherical geometry and Rayleigh phase functions. Choose when rendering skyboxes or planetary atmospheres. Encodes directional color variation into SH coefficients evaluated per sample, allowing view-dependent shading via algebraic projections. Choose when replacing scalar transfer function lookups with continuous SH basis evaluation for sparse voxel grids. Computes the average density along a ray rather than integrating light transport. Choose when visualizing internal structures without depth cues or opacity accumulation. Simulates the irregular density of water droplets in clouds by generating fractal Brownian motion (fBm) noise from a pre-computed 3D noise cube. It transforms uniform random noise into a Gaussian-like distribution suitable for atmospheric vapour simulation, serving as the density field input for ray-marching algorithms. It differs from procedural noise generation by relying on a static, pre-calculated texture lookup, which trades memory bandwidth for computational simplicity and deterministic results. Renders volumetric data in a single GPU pass using WebGPU, performing analytic ray-box intersection, early-alpha termination, and optional central-difference Phong shading. It differs from standard sphere tracing by operating on explicit 3D texture volumes rather than implicit Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), allowing for complex, non-uniform density distributions. Casts rays from the camera through a volumetric scalar field, sampling the field at discrete intervals to accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. Unlike SDF Cloud Rendering, which relies on signed distance fields for surface-like rendering, this method integrates density directly, and unlike Atmospheric Ray Marching, which often targets specific post-processing effects like god rays, this method provides a general-purpose integration of the radiative transfer equation for arbitrary volume textures. Raymarches the interior volume of a glass container to simulate wax. It computes the surface normal using the gradient of the density field and sets fragment depth explicitly using glFragDepth in the opaque pass. The shading model includes wrap lighting, soft Fresnel, fake subsurface scattering based on traversed thickness, and emission driven by temperature and proximity to a light bulb. Artifacts are minimal, with 0.00% of surface voxels causing a round-trip to the threshold, even at 60 Hz with ±30% jitter. A unified rendering implementation for volumetric clouds and atmosphere using raymarching as the main method. It renders the atmosphere using an approach with multiple precomputed Look-up tables (LUTs) proposed by Sébastien Hillaire, and renders volumetric clouds using a pre-computed three dimensional texture setup storing procedurally generated noise described by Andrew Schneider. It renders images in high dynamic range before applying post-processing effects and uses adaptive luminance to transform the image into LDR for presentation. The term "Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering" in this context is closely associated with the "Standard 3ds Max atmospheric" rendering mode provided by Phoenix for 3ds Max. This mode visualizes grid content (such as fire and smoke simulations) as a standard atmospheric volume without generating a mesh surface, thereby preventing the use of standard 3ds Max and V-Ray materials for shading. Instead, shading is handled by Volumetric Render Settings using color gradients and graphs. Key parameters defined in this implementation include: Step % (rendstep): The ray marching step of camera rays as a percentage of cell size. Values >100 skip cells causing artifacts; values <90% are needed for render curves or texture maps to capture sub-voxel details. Shadow Step % (rendshadstep): The ray marching step for shadow rays, usually higher than Step % to speed up rendering. Border Fade (borderFade): Distance from grid boundaries where content becomes transparent to prevent sharp edges. Sampler Type (sampler): Blending method between adjacent voxels. Options include Box (fastest, no blending), Linear (20-30% faster than Spherical, may show grid structure), and Spherical (smoothest, weight-based sampling). This approach is distinct from surface render modes which generate a mesh and allow standard material shading. FireSmoke Rendering - Phoenix for 3ds Max, https://documentation.chaos.com/space/PHX4MAX/124396558, fetched 2026-10-27 Étape 4: surface de cire raymarchée et liquide volumique, https://github.com/nathanddrl/lava-lamp/pull/4, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Atmosphere and Cloud Rendering in Real-time | DCGI, https://dcgi.fel.cvut.cz/en/theses/2022/sakmamat/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SDF Cloud Rendering
body: SDF Cloud Rendering is a fragment-shader-based technique for rendering volumetric cloud-like structures using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and ray marching. It solves the problem of generating complex, organic volumetric shapes without explicit mesh data by composing simple geometric primitives (spheres) via smooth unions and fractal warping. It differs from standard ray marching by relying on procedural noise-based warping of the coordinate space to create "cloudy" topology, rather than sampling a 3D texture or voxel grid. The method operates in a single-pass fragment shader. It defines a scene using a hierarchy of warped spheres, marches a ray to find the intersection with the implicit surface, and computes lighting via a shadow ray. Inputs: Fragment coordinates (glFragCoord), screen resolution (screenSize), camera field of view (45.0 degrees), and a random seed (seed). Outputs: A final color vector (glFragColor) in the range [0, 1]. No complex data structures are used. The state is maintained via local variables in the shader. Constants define the scene bounds and marching parameters. 1. Calculate the ray direction from fragment coordinates, screen size, and field of view. 2. Initialize ray depth to MINDIST and iterate up to MAXMARCHINGSTEPS. 3. Evaluate the scene SDF at the current ray position; if the returned distance is less than EPSILON, return the current depth as a surface hit. 4. Advance the ray depth by dist STEPSCALE; if the new depth exceeds MAXDIST, terminate and return MAXDIST. 5. If a hit occurs, compute a shadow ray along the light direction and blend between dark and light colors; otherwise, render a sky gradient. 6. Apply Hable tone mapping and exposure scaling to output the final color. 1. Sphere SDF The distance from a point p to a sphere centered at c with radius r: d{sphere}(p) = \|p - c\| - r where p is the query point, c is the sphere center, and r is the radius. 2. Smooth Union Blends two SDFs d1 and d2 with a blending factor k: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \frac{d2 - d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d{union} = \text{mix}(d2, d1, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) where d1 and d2 are the input SDF values, and k controls the smoothness of the blend. 3. Jitter (Fractal Noise) Generates a pseudo-random offset based on a seed and coordinate: \text{jitter}(mixAmount, offset, seed) = 0.09 \sum{i=0}^{2} \frac{\sin((offset \cdot 1234.0 + mixAmount) \cdot 2^i)}{2^i} where the loop runs three times, scaling the sine argument and divisor by powers of two. 4. Warp Distorts the input vector v using jittered offsets: \text{warp}(v, scale, seed) = v + scale \cdot \text{vec3}(\text{jitter}(v.x, 0.0, seed), \text{jitter}(v.y, 0.2, seed), \text{jitter}(v.z, 0.5, seed)) where scale controls the intensity of the coordinate distortion. 5. Hable Tone Mapping Maps linear color x to [0, 1]: \text{toneMap}(x) = \frac{x(Ax + CB) + DE}{x(Ax + B) + DF} - \frac{E}{F} where A=0.15, B=0.50, C=0.10, D=0.20, E=0.02, F=0.30. MAXMARCHINGSTEPS: 100. MINDIST: 0.0. MAXDIST: 100.0. EPSILON: 0.0001. STEPSCALE: 0.67. EXPOSURE: 1.0. WHITE: 200.0. LIGHTPOS: vec3(-10.0, 10.0, 3.0). LIGHTCOLOR: vec3(100.0, 100.0, 100.0). DARKCOLOR: vec3(5.0, 8.0, 20.0). Precision: The source shader uses mediump float precision. Lower precision may lead to jittering artifacts or incorrect SDF evaluations in high-resolution renders. Seed Dependency: The visual appearance is deterministic based on the seed parameter. Changing the seed alters the cloud shape significantly due to the fractal warping. Step Scaling: STEPSCALE is set to 0.67 to prevent overshooting caused by coordinate warping. Computes lighting by sampling volumetric density along the ray and applying a single-scattering phase function. It sets itself apart by modeling light absorption and emission within the volume rather than just surface reflection. Choose it when rendering semi-transparent volumetric media like fog or smoke. See Ray-marched Shadows. Renders volumetric data over multiple frames and blends results to reduce noise and stabilize animated sequences. It differs from single-frame marching by leveraging temporal coherence to lower per-frame sample counts. Choose it for real-time animated volumetric effects where performance is constrained. See Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering. Simulates large-scale light transport in planetary atmospheres using phase functions and density profiles. It distinguishes itself by integrating density variations over long ray segments and accounting for multiple scattering approximations. Choose it for planetary or skybox rendering. See Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering. Accumulates density and transparency along rays to produce projection-like images of internal structures. It differs from surface-focused SDF marching by integrating transmittance rather than stopping at the first hit. Choose it for medical or industrial inspection visualizations. See WebGL2 Volume Raycasting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. SDF Cloud Rendering was developed by Dave Pagurek as a small experiment for Graphics Interface 2019. It demonstrates the capability of Signed Distance Fields to create organic, volumetric-looking structures through procedural warping and smooth unions, rather than traditional mesh or voxel representations. davepagurek/sdf-clouds, https://github.com/davepagurek/sdf-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Primary Ray Integrator
head: Composite Ray Marcher, renderRay
body: The Primary Ray Integrator is a single-function ray integrator that resolves a complete ray by compositing terrain, water, sky, cloud volume, and aerial perspective. It serves as the core rendering loop for distance-field ray marching in terrain and atmospheric scenes, handling the sequential evaluation of distinct environmental layers. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing the compositing order of heterogeneous scene elements (solid surfaces vs. volumetric clouds) and handling secondary ray recursion to prevent infinite loops. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: ctx: A RenderContext object containing scratch buffers, theme parameters, and camera state. ox, oy, oz: The ray origin coordinates. dx, dy, dz: The normalized ray direction vector components. tMax: The maximum ray distance for traversal. depth: An integer recursion depth counter. Primary rays pass 0; secondary rays (reflections/refractions) pass 1. Outputs: result: An Rgb color value representing the final pixel color. Data Structures: RenderScratch: A struct used for intermediate calculations, initialized to zero upon creation. It contains: result (Rgb): Accumulated color. secondary (Rgb): Color for secondary ray contributions. surface (SurfaceShade): Surface shading data (albedo, normal, etc.). Algorithm Steps: 1. Secondary Ray Guard: If depth > 0, disable water and cloud passes to prevent infinite recursion. 2. Water Plane Intersection: If depth == 0, test for intersection with the water plane. Compute limit as the minimum of the water hit distance and tMax, or tMax if no water hit. 3. Terrain/Water/Sky Trace: Trace the ray from the origin along the direction up to limit. Determine the hitKind (KINDTERRAIN, KINDWATER, KINDSKY) and distance to the hit. 4. Surface Shading: If KINDTERRAIN: Compute hit position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t{\text{terrain}}. Call shadeTerrain with the hit position and a ditherAngle. Copy the resulting surface color to result. If KINDWATER: Compute hit position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t{\text{water}}. Call shadeWater with ctx.waterShade parameters. Copy the resulting surface color to result. If KINDSKY or no hit: Call skyRadiance with the ray direction to fill result. 5. Atmospheric Compositing: If KINDSKY: Apply sky haze using the vertical component of the direction vector, dy. Else (Terrain/Water hit): Compute the hit Y coordinate y{\text{hit}} = oy + dy \cdot \text{distance}. Apply aerial perspective using distance, y{\text{hit}}, and the ray direction to composite the atmosphere over the surface color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderRay(ctx, ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, tMax, depth): # Initialize scratch buffers to zero result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] secondary = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] surface = {"color": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "normal": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]} # Step 1: Secondary Ray Guard disablewater = depth > 0 disablecloud = depth > 0 # Step 2: Water Plane Intersection limit = tMax if not disablewater: # Intersect ray with water plane waterhitdist = intersectwaterplane(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz) if waterhitdist is not None and waterhitdist < tMax: limit = waterhitdist # Step 3: Trace ray up to limit # Sphere tracing implementation from parent method hitkind, distance = traceray(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, limit) # Step 4: Surface Shading if hitkind == "KINDTERRAIN": px, py, pz = ox + dx distance, oy + dy distance, oz + dz distance # Theme-specific terrain shading shadeTerrain(px, py, pz, surface, ctx.ditherAngle) result = surface["color"] elif hitkind == "KINDWATER": px, py, pz = ox + dx distance, oy + dy distance, oz + dz distance # Theme-specific water shading shadeWater(px, py, pz, surface, ctx.waterShade) result = surface["color"] else: # Sky radiance calculation result = skyRadiance(dx, dy, dz) # Step 5: Atmospheric Compositing if hitkind == "KINDSKY": # Sky haze computation hazefactor = computehaze(dy) result = compositehaze(result, hazefactor) else: yhit = oy + dy distance # Aerial perspective compositing result = applyaerialperspective(result, distance, yhit, dx, dy, dz) return result Parameters: ditherAngle: Used in terrain shading to reduce banding artifacts. ctx.waterShade: Configuration object for water rendering properties. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Recursion: Secondary rays (water reflections/refractions) calling back into the primary integrator can cause infinite loops. This is handled by checking depth > 0 and disabling water/cloud passes for recursive calls. Boundary Conditions: If tMax is not respected, rays may escape the scene bounds without proper termination. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles multiple scene types (terrain, water, sky, clouds) in a single pass; robust against recursion issues via depth checking. Limitations: Limited to specific scene compositions defined in the integrator; does not handle complex volumetric scattering beyond simple aerial perspective and cloud compositing. When to use: Not given in the sources. The Primary Ray Integrator is described in the context of the theme1 project by mingderwang. It is part of a larger system that includes CLI tools for rendering, theme validation, and batch processing. The method builds on the principles of distance-field ray marching, specifically sphere tracing, as detailed in the parent article. mingderwang/theme1, https://github.com/mingderwang/theme1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Rendering with Spherical Harmonics
head: Volume Rendering with Spherical Harmonics (Forward)
body: Volumetric Rendering with Spherical Harmonics is a direct volume ray casting method that traces rays through a sparse grid represented by spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, computing color output and optionally log-transmittance for background compositing. It encodes directional color variation into SH coefficients evaluated per sample, allowing view-dependent shading via algebraic projections during compositing. It differs from standard direct volume rendering by replacing scalar transfer function lookups with continuous SH basis evaluation, and from Neural volume rendering by using explicit SH basis functions rather than implicit neural fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel grid where each active voxel stores a scalar density/opacity proxy and a vector of spherical harmonic coefficients. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}) and ray bounds [t{near}, t{far}]. Output: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and optionally accumulated log-transmittance for background compositing. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid. Each active voxel contains: density: Scalar value representing extinction coefficient or opacity proxy. shcoeffs: Array of K floats, where K depends on the SH degree L (K = (L+1)^2). Ray Data: For Q rays, arrays of origin \mathbf{o}i, direction \mathbf{d}i, and sample positions. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel/ray i, define the ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] by intersecting the ray with the volume bounding box. Discretize the segment into N samples (default N=512 or 100) at positions tj = t{near} + j \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N. Sample positions are often parameterized in [0.05, 0.95] to avoid boundary artifacts. 2. Voxel Interpolation: At each sample position \mathbf{p}j, perform trilinear interpolation on the voxel grid to retrieve the local density/opacity proxy \sigmaj and the SH coefficient vector \mathbf{c}j. Extract opacity proxy: \sigmaj = \text{interp}(\text{density}). Extract SH coefficients: \mathbf{c}j = \text{interp}(\text{sh\coeffs}). 3. SH Basis Evaluation: Compute the SH basis functions \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}i) for the viewing direction \mathbf{d}i of the ray. The basis evaluation depends on the chosen degree L (typically 1 or 2). Let \mathbf{y}i = \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}i) be the vector of basis values. 4. Color Computation: Compute the view-dependent color \mathbf{C}j at sample j by taking the dot product of the interpolated SH coefficients and the basis vector: \mathbf{C}j = \mathbf{c}j \cdot \mathbf{y}i Note: In some implementations, the SH coefficients are reshaped to separate color channels before projection. 5. Transmittance and Opacity Calculation: Compute the optical depth and transmittance for each sample. Compute step sizes: \Delta tj = t{j+1} - tj (for j=0 \dots N-2). Compute weighted optical depth deltas: \deltaj = -\Delta tj \cdot \sigmaj. Compute cumulative transmittance Tj from front to back: T0 = 1 T{j+1} = \exp\left(\sum{k=0}^{j} \deltak\right) Compute per-sample opacity contribution: \alphaj = 1 - \exp(\deltaj). 6. Front-to-Back Compositing: Composite the samples into the final color: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{j=0}^{N-1} Tj \cdot \alphaj \cdot \mathbf{C}j \alpha{out} = \sum{j=0}^{N-1} Tj \cdot \alphaj Or in iterative form: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + Tj \cdot \mathbf{C}j \cdot \alphaj T{j+1} \leftarrow Tj \cdot (1 - \alphaj) 7. Background Compositing (Optional): If background rendering is enabled, compute the log-transmittance for the ray and composite the background color using the accumulated transmittance. Log-transmittance: \log T{final} = \sum{j=0}^{N-1} \deltaj. Composite with background color \mathbf{C}{bg}: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C}{out} + T{final} \cdot \mathbf{C}{bg} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sphericalharmonicsbasis(direction, degree): """ Computes the spherical harmonic basis vector for a given direction. direction: (3,) array, normalized viewing direction. degree: int, SH degree (0, 1, or 2). Returns: (K,) array of basis values, where K = (degree + 1)2. """ x, y, z = direction basis = [] # Degree 0 basis.append(0.28209479177387814) # 1 / sqrt(4pi) if degree >= 1: # Degree 1 basis.append(-0.4886025119029199 y) basis.append(0.4886025119029199 z) basis.append(-0.4886025119029199 x) if degree >= 2: # Degree 2 basis.append(1.0925484305920792 x y) basis.append(-1.0925484305920792 y z) basis.append(0.31539156525252005 (3 z2 - 1)) basis.append(-1.0925484305920792 x z) basis.append(0.5462742152960396 (x2 - y2)) return np.array(basis) def rendervolumetricsh(voxelgrid, rayorigins, raydirections, tnear, tfar, numsamples=512, shdegree=1, backgroundenabled=False, backgroundcolors=None): """ Renders a volume using spherical harmonics for view-dependent color. Args: voxelgrid: Sparse grid object supporting trilinear interpolation. Must support query(pos) -> (density, shcoeffs). rayorigins: (Q, 3) array of ray origins. raydirections: (Q, 3) array of ray directions (normalized). tnear: (Q,) array of ray entry parameters. tfar: (Q,) array of ray exit parameters. numsamples: int, number of samples per ray. shdegree: int, degree of spherical harmonics (0, 1, 2). backgroundenabled: bool, whether to composite with background. backgroundcolors: (Q, 3) array of background colors. Returns: colors: (Q, 3) array of final pixel colors. transmittances: (Q,) array of final transmittance (if background enabled). """ Q = rayorigins.shape[0] K = (shdegree + 1)2 # Precompute SH basis for all ray directions # Shape: (Q, K) rayshbases = np.array([sphericalharmonicsbasis(raydirections[i], shdegree) for i in range(Q)]) colors = np.zeros((Q, 3)) transmittances = np.ones(Q) for i in range(Q): # Sample positions along the ray tsamples = np.linspace(tnear[i], tfar[i], numsamples + 1) # Sample points in world space samplepoints = rayorigins[i] + tsamples[:, None] raydirections[i] # Interpolate density and SH coefficients at sample points # Note: In a real implementation, this is done in bulk or via GPU kernel # Here we simulate the interpolation result # interpdata shape: (numsamples + 1, 1 + K) # Column 0: density/opacity proxy, Columns 1:K+1: shcoeffs interpdata = voxelgrid.interpolate(samplepoints) interpopacities = interpdata[:, 0] interpshcoeffs = interpdata[:, 1:] # Compute SH basis for the ray direction (constant for all samples on the ray) raybasis = rayshbases[i] # Compute color at each sample # Color = dot(shcoeffs, raybasis) # shcoeffs shape: (numsamples + 1, K) # raybasis shape: (K,) samplecolors = np.dot(interpshcoeffs, raybasis) # Shape: (numsamples + 1, 3) # Compute optical depth deltas deltas = np.diff(tsamples) # Weighted deltas for transmittance (matches S2: deltastimessigmas = - deltas interpopacities[:-1]) deltastimessigmas = -deltas interpopacities[:-1] # Cumulative transmittance (matches S2: cumsum prepended with 0) cumweighteddeltas = np.concatenate(([0], np.cumsum(deltastimessigmas))) T = np.exp(cumweighteddeltas) # Per-sample opacity (matches S2: tmp2 = 1 - exp(deltastimessigmas)) alpha = 1 - np.exp(deltastimessigmas) # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = sum(Tj alphaj Cj) # Tj here is transmittance BEFORE sample j # alphaj is opacity of sample j contribution = T[:-1] alpha samplecolors[:-1] colors[i] = np.sum(contribution, axis=0) transmittances[i] = T[-1] # Transmittance after last sample if backgroundenabled and backgroundcolors is not None: colors = colors + transmittances[:, None] backgroundcolors return colors, transmittances Parameters: numsamples: Default 512 or 100. shdegree: Typically 1 or 2. cudanthreads: Number of CUDA threads per block for ray tracing (macro TRACERAYCUDATHREADS). TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS: Number of CUDA threads per block for background rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Sampling at exact boundaries can cause interpolation errors. Using parameterized ranges like [0.05, 0.95] helps. SH Degree Limits: Higher SH degrees increase memory usage and reduce the maximum number of splats/voxels that can be rendered due to memory constraints (e.g., Degree 2 limits splat count to ~8,000,000 vs ~16,000,000 for Degree 0). Precision: Floating-point precision in cumulative transmittance calculation can lead to artifacts in deep volumes. Log-transmittance is computed for background compositing. Spherical Harmonics (SH) provide an orthonormal basis for representing directional functions defined on the unit sphere S^2, enabling the compact storage and efficient manipulation of volumetric radiance distributions. This family of methods solves the problem of expensive numerical integration for directional signals (such as in-scattering or visibility) by projecting them into a coefficient space where operations like rotation and integration become analytic or linear algebraic. It differs from its siblings, such as Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer and Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading, by serving as the fundamental mathematical representation layer; while the siblings apply this representation to specific shading or transfer pipelines, the core SH family focuses on the basis definition, coefficient projection, and the algebraic properties (like the product convolution) that make these applications feasible. Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer (VSH-PRT) is a technique for rendering semi-transparent volumetric datasets with dynamic lighting by precomputing the scene's response to illumination. It solves the problem of expensive real-time volume rendering by compressing the 6D Volume Radiance Transfer function into spherical harmonic coefficients stored on a surface mesh, allowing for fast runtime evaluation under arbitrary distant lighting. It sets itself apart from direct volume rendering by decoupling the expensive volume integration from the render loop, and from standard surface PRT by explicitly handling the volumetric scattering process to determine the exit radiance. Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading is a method for computing diffuse illumination in Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) by approximating the non-linear shading operator (specifically the \max(N \cdot L, 0) term) using spherical harmonics. It solves the problem of interactive relighting in the frequency domain, where traditional methods require expensive recomputation of 3D Fourier transforms for every change in light direction. Unlike Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer, which precomputes transfer functions for specific geometries, this method operates directly on the volume's gradient-derived normals in the Fourier domain, allowing light direction changes to be handled via simple coefficient updates without re-transforming the volume data. The Ray Tracing Backward Pass computes the gradients of a differentiable volume rendering loss with respect to the scene representation (spherical harmonic coefficients and density) and auxiliary parameters, given the rendered image and ground truth. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the forward ray casting pass, enabling end-to-end training of volumetric models like Plenoxels. Unlike the forward pass which accumulates color and transmittance, this method propagates error signals backward through the ray integration, handling RGB normalization and optional regularization losses (beta, sparsity). The Zonal Method (Bhate and Tokuta) is a global illumination technique for participating media that extends the classical zonal method by incorporating spherical harmonics to handle anisotropic scattering and surface-volume interactions. Unlike the standard zonal method which assumes isotropic media and ignores surface effects, this method represents the phase function and radiance using spherical harmonics, allowing for the approximation of Mie scattering while maintaining ideal diffuse surfaces. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific use of an extended hemicube technique to compute spherical harmonic form factors and a Gauss-Seidel solver for the coupled volume-surface system. Renders RGB values by projecting spherical harmonics coefficients along viewing directions, then compositing with weights. Reshapes SH coefficients to separate color channels, computes SH basis components for given directions, multiplies coefficients by components, sums over SH components and adds bias, applies optional activation function to RGB, and composites using RGBRenderer.combinergb. The activation function defaults to nn.Sigmoid(). A known pitfall in some source implementations is that the code overwrites the RGB tensor in the sum step (rgb = torch.sum(sh, dim=-1) + 0.5), discarding the channel multiplication result. Time Complexity: O(Q \cdot N \cdot K), where Q is the number of rays, N is the number of samples per ray, and K is the number of SH coefficients (K=(L+1)^2). Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot K), where V is the number of active voxels and K is the number of SH coefficients per voxel. Measured Performance: Limits on splat count depend on SH degree: Degree 0 allows ~16,000,000 splats, Degree 1 allows ~11,000,000, and Degree 2 allows ~8,000,000. Strengths: Efficient view-dependent shading without per-sample transfer function lookups; compact representation of directional data. Limitations: Memory intensive for high SH degrees; fixed basis may not capture complex directional effects as well as learned bases. When to Use: When view-dependent color effects are important and computational resources allow for the memory overhead of SH coefficients. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or view-dependent effects are minimal (use Degree 0 or standard scalar transfer functions). The method originates from CUDA-based volume rendering implementations that use sparse grids represented by spherical harmonic coefficients. It is part of the broader family of spherical harmonic methods for directional data representation. name: Spherical Harmonics
head: SH basis, SH coefficients, Spherical Harmonic Representation of Radiance, Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Rendering, Spherical Harmonics (SH) Basis
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) provide a complete, orthonormal basis for representing directional functions defined on the unit sphere S^2. In volume rendering, they serve as a fixed, non-learnable basis for directional signals, where switching between max degree 3 (SH-16) and 4 (SH-25) yields negligible differences in metrics or visual quality. They differ from their siblings, such as Spherical Harmonics Approximation and Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer, by defining the fundamental mathematical basis itself, whereas the siblings focus on specific application pipelines or optimization techniques built upon this basis. The SH basis consists of an infinite set of functions Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) indexed by degree \ell \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\} and order m \in \{-\ell, \dots, \ell\}. The complex-valued basis functions are defined as: Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) = \sqrt{\frac{2\ell + 1}{4\pi} \frac{(\ell - m)!}{(\ell + m)!}} P\ell^m(\cos \theta) e^{im\phi} where P\ell^m are the associated Legendre polynomials. For real-valued rendering applications, the basis is constructed to avoid imaginary numbers for m \neq 0. The real-valued basis Y{lm} is defined piecewise: Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2} K{lm} \cos(m\phi) Pl^m(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m > 0 \\ K{l0} Pl^0(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m = 0 \\ \sqrt{2} K{lm} \sin(-m\phi) Pl^{-m}(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m < 0 \end{cases} where K{lm} = \sqrt{\frac{2l + 1}{4\pi} \frac{(l - m)!}{(l + m)!}}. Source provides an alternative real-valued construction using Y\ell^m = \sqrt{2}(-1)^m\text{Im}[Y\ell^{|m|}] for m < 0, Y\ell^0 for m = 0, and \sqrt{2}(-1)^m\text{Re}[Y\ell^m] for m > 0. A directional signal f(\omega) is represented by a finite set of coefficients \mathbf{f} of size n = (L+1)^2, where L is the maximum degree (bandwidth) Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection. The coefficients are computed by projecting the function onto the basis Spherical Harmonics Approximation: fi = \int{\Omega} f(\omega) yi(\omega) d\omega The signal is reconstructed by summing the basis functions weighted by the coefficients Spherical Harmonics Approximation: \tilde{f}(\omega) = \sum{i=0}^{n-1} fi yi(\omega) The linear index i maps the degree l and order m via i = l^2 + l + m Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection. Convolution of two functions \tilde{a}(\omega) and \tilde{b}(\omega) in the SH domain is performed using a precomputed transfer matrix C{ijk} Spherical Harmonics Approximation: (a b)i = \sum{j=0}^{n-1} \sum{k=0}^{n-1} C{ijk} aj bk where C{ijk} = \int{\Omega} yi(\omega) yj(\omega) yk(\omega) d\omega Spherical Harmonics Approximation. The integral of the product of two approximated functions is the dot product of their coefficient vectors Spherical Harmonics Approximation: \int{\Omega} \tilde{a}(\omega)\tilde{b}(\omega)d\omega = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} Typical implementations use the lowest 3-5 levels of SH to keep the representation compact. SH approximations containing higher frequencies become too large to be practical, and SH functions exhibit 'ringing' artifacts (high-frequency noise) near sharp value changes, especially when many coefficients are used. Represents a spherical function using a finite SH subset for efficient, differentiable computation. Sets it apart by focusing on projection and reconstruction mechanics with a fixed bandwidth rather than determining optimal bandwidth. Choose it for inverse problems requiring algebraic integration and convolution. Determines the maximum bandwidth L to balance reconstruction fidelity against memory consumption. Sets it apart by focusing on the capacity limit (bandwidth) rather than the projection or fitting process itself. Choose it when optimizing memory and compute constraints for a given signal's frequency content. Stores position- and direction-dependent scattered radiance in a 3D grid using SH basis functions. Sets it apart by enabling fast integration via sparse matrix multiplication during rendering. Choose it for efficient multiple scattering in volumes (e.g., hair) where storage compactness and organized memory access are critical. (Link only; details in child article). (Link only; details in child article). (Link only; details in child article). (Link only; details in child article). A basis used to encode a hemispherical signal, requiring fewer coefficients to achieve the same quality as 3rd order spherical harmonics. A coordinate system local to the surface is required to orient the hemisphere, commonly utilizing a tangent frame resulting from uv-parameterization. If encoded in textures, the texture needs sufficient resolution to adapt to changes in the underlying tangent space. If two triangles cover the same texel and have significantly different tangents, it leads to a lack of precision in the reconstructed signal. Spherical Harmonics originated in mathematical physics as a complete basis for functions on the sphere. In computer graphics, they were adopted for Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) to efficiently represent lighting and reflection. They are used in volume rendering to represent the directional distribution of scattered radiance, allowing for efficient rotation and integration. Recent applications include representing neural radiance fields (NeRFs) via PlenOctrees, where SH basis functions replace standard color representations to enable real-time rendering. name: Spherical Harmonics Approximation
head: SH Approximation, Spherical Harmonics Basis Approximation
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Approximation is a technique to represent a spherical function f(\omega) using a finite subset of the SH basis functions, enabling efficient and differentiable computation for inverse problems in volume rendering. It solves the problem of expensive Monte Carlo integration by projecting directional data (such as lighting, visibility, and in-scattering) into the SH domain, where integrals become simple dot products and convolutions become matrix-vector multiplications. Inputs: A spherical function f(\omega) defined over the domain \Omega (the unit sphere), and a maximum bandwidth L (or number of bands n). Outputs: A vector of SH coefficients \mathbf{f} of size n = (L+1)^2. Data Structures: The coefficients are stored in a 1D array \mathbf{f} of length n. The linear index i maps the degree l and order m via: i = l^2 + l + m where l \in \{0, \dots, L\} and m \in \{-l, \dots, l\}. Steps: 1. Projection: Compute the SH coefficients fi by projecting the function f(\omega) onto the basis functions yi(\omega): fi = \int{\Omega} f(\omega) yi(\omega) d\omega. In practice, for inverse problems, this integral is often precomputed or solved via numerical integration at initialization to ensure differentiability with respect to scene parameters. 2. Reconstruction: Approximate the original signal \tilde{f}(\omega) by summing the basis functions weighted by the coefficients: \tilde{f}(\omega) = \sum{i=1}^{n} fi yi(\omega). The accuracy increases with n. 3. Integration via Dot Product: The integral of the product of two approximated functions \tilde{a}(\omega) and \tilde{b}(\omega) is computed as the dot product of their coefficient vectors: \int{\Omega} \tilde{a}(\omega)\tilde{b}(\omega)d\omega = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}. 4. Convolution (Multiplication Projection): The SH projection of the product of two functions, denoted a b, is computed using a precomputed transfer matrix C{ijk}: (a b)i = \sum{j=1}^{n} \sum{k=1}^{n} C{ijk} aj bk where C{ijk} = \int{\Omega} yi(\omega)yj(\omega)yk(\omega)d\omega. Parameters: Bandwidth n: The number of bands used. A value of n=8 is cited as providing good low-frequency approximations for inverse problems. Typical implementations use the lowest 3-5 levels of SH to keep the representation compact. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshcoefficients(functionf, basisfunctionsy, domainsamples): """ Computes SH coefficients fi by numerically integrating f(w) yi(w) over the sphere. functionf: callable, returns f(w) for a direction w. basisfunctionsy: callable, returns yi(w) for a direction w and index i. domainsamples: list of (w, weight) tuples representing the discretized sphere. """ n = len(basisfunctionsy) f = [0.0] n for w, weight in domainsamples: valf = functionf(w) for i in range(n): valy = basisfunctionsy(i, w) f[i] += valf valy weight return f def reconstructshsignal(coefficientsf, basisfunctionsy, directionw): """ Reconstructs the signal at a specific direction using SH coefficients. coefficientsf: list of SH coefficients fi. basisfunctionsy: callable, returns yi(w). directionw: the direction vector w. """ signal = 0.0 for i, coeff in enumerate(coefficientsf): signal += coeff basisfunctionsy(i, directionw) return signal def computeconvolutioncoefficients(coefficientsa, coefficientsb, transfermatrixC): """ Computes the SH coefficients of the product of two functions a and b. coefficientsa: list of SH coefficients for a. coefficientsb: list of SH coefficients for b. transfermatrixC: 3D array C[i][j][k]. """ n = len(coefficientsa) result = [0.0] n for i in range(n): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(n): for k in range(n): sumval += transfermatrixC[i][j][k] coefficientsa[j] coefficientsb[k] result[i] = sumval return result def computeintegraldotproduct(coefficientsa, coefficientsb): """ Computes the integral of the product of two SH approximated functions. """ return sum(a b for a, b in zip(coefficientsa, coefficientsb)) Spherical Harmonic Projection is the process of approximating an arbitrary spherical function f(\omega) by computing the coefficients of its expansion in the SH basis [Child 11243]. It differs from the parent Spherical Harmonics Approximation by focusing specifically on the computational mechanics of deriving these coefficients via least-squares minimization and leveraging the basis's orthonormality for efficient GPU-based integration [Child 11243]. It is chosen when efficient representation of complex angular data (lighting, reflectance) is required for volume rendering [Child 11243]. This variant reformulates the computation of the hemisphere visibility term H(x) to be differentiable with respect to the surface normal n(x). Instead of direct integration, it uses a linear rotation function \phi{SH} to rotate a standard z-axis symmetric integral: H(x) = \phi{SH}(n(x)) \int{\Omega} \max(iz \cdot \omega, 0)y(\omega)d\omega where iz = (0, 0, 1)^T. The integral is solved using numerical integration at initialization and does not need to be differentiable, as only the SH coefficients of the environment map are updated. This method approximates an SH vector f as a sum of rotated Zonal Harmonic (ZH) basis functions by minimizing the L2 error \psi = \|f - g\|. It iterates through ZH levels from lowest to highest frequency. For each level, it calculates several hundred rotations uniformly distributed on the hemisphere, solves for the optimal SH coefficients g^l for each rotation, and keeps the rotation with the lowest error. The optimal coefficients for a fixed rotation \hat{z} are: g^l = \frac{4\pi}{2l + 1} \sum{m=-l}^{l} Y{lm}(\hat{z}) f{lm}. The selected ZH function is projected into the SH basis and subtracted from the target vector before proceeding to the next level. Zonal Harmonics are a subset of SH defined by m=0, consisting of functions symmetric about the vertical axis. A ZH function g is a sum of the n lowest-order ZH functions: g = \sum{l=1}^{n} gl Y{l0}. To rotate a ZH vector g and project it into the SH basis, each coefficient f{lm} is calculated as: f{lm} = g^l Y{lm}(\hat{z}l) where g^l = gl \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{2l + 1}} and \hat{z}l is the rotation axis for level l. Projecting an SH vector into the ZH basis is a hard problem solved by minimizing the L2 norm \psi = \|f - g\|. Time Complexity: Projection is typically precomputed or solved via numerical integration at initialization to avoid expensive Monte Carlo integration. Convolution is O(n^3) due to the triple summation in the transfer matrix. Reconstruction is O(n). Memory Complexity: Storing coefficients is O(n). The transfer matrix C{ijk} is precomputed. Hardware, Resolution, and Scene Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables differentiable computation for inverse problems; converts expensive integrals into dot products; allows real-time rendering of global illumination effects via PRT. Limitations: Low-pass filtering nature limits high-frequency detail representation; requires precomputation of transfer matrices or integrals; rotation of general SH functions is complex, often requiring conversion to ZH or other bases. When to use: When global illumination or in-scattering effects need to be represented compactly and differentially for optimization or real-time rendering. When not to use: When high-frequency directional details are critical and cannot be captured by low-bandwidth SH. The method applies spherical harmonic function approximation to Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) for real-time global illumination. Sloan et al. introduced the use of SH for representing light transport and the rotation of Zonal Harmonics. The specific application to differentiable shadow computation and inverse problems in volume rendering was detailed by in 2021. Zonal Harmonics were popularized by Sloan et al. (2005) for efficient rotation and projection. name: Spherical Harmonic Projection
head: SH Compression, SH Integration, Spherical Harmonic (SH) Projection for Volume Rendering
body: Spherical Harmonic (SH) Projection computes the coefficients of a spherical function f(\omega)'s expansion in the spherical harmonics basis to approximate it. It solves the problem of efficiently representing complex angular data (lighting, material reflectance, in-scattering) for volume rendering by leveraging the basis's orthonormality for fast integration. It builds on Spherical Harmonics Approximation by focusing on the least-squares derivation of coefficients and GPU-accelerated dot-product integration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A spherical function f(s) defined over the domain S (the unit sphere). Output: A vector of coefficients cj representing the projection of f onto the SH basis. Data Structures: The coefficients are stored as a flat array. Field coeffs: Array of size (L+1)^2. Field L: Integer, maximum band order. Parameters: L: Maximum SH band order. Typical value: L=3. This results in (3+1)^2 = 16 coefficients per channel. Steps: 1. Define Basis: Select the orthonormal spherical harmonics basis functions Yj(s) up to order L. 2. Compute Coefficients: For each basis function index j (where 0 \le j < (L+1)^2), compute the coefficient cj by integrating the product of the basis function and the target function over the sphere: cj = \intS Yj(s) f(s) ds \quad (1) This is a least-squares projection that minimizes the squared error between the approximation and the original function f. 3. Store Coefficients: Store the computed cj values in the coefficient vector. Integration of Projected Functions: Once functions f and g are projected to coefficients c and d respectively, their integration is computed as the dot product of their coefficient vectors: I(\tilde{f}, \tilde{g}) = \sumi ci di \quad (2) This property allows integration to be performed efficiently on the GPU using a single dot product operation, avoiding the reconstruction and integration of the original functions. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Three-Function Integration: Integrating three functions (Material M, In-scattering L{mi}^0, and Light Li) is complex. While techniques exist [Sny06], a simpler, non-physical approximation is used for performance reasons. Precision: Approximation quality improves with more samples, but the number of SH bands must remain consistent across projections to simplify the rendering pipeline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalharmonicprojection(fsample, L=3): """ Computes SH coefficients for a spherical function f. Args: fsample: A callable representing the function f(s) on the sphere. L: Maximum band order (default 3). Returns: coeffs: List of (L+1)^2 coefficients. """ numcoeffs = (L + 1) 2 coeffs = [0.0] numcoeffs # The exact numerical integration method (e.g., Monte Carlo, quadrature) # is not specified in the sources. The implementer must approximate # the integral cj = \intS Yj(s) f(s) ds using a chosen sampling strategy. for j in range(numcoeffs): # Evaluate integral for coefficient j integralvalue = 0.0 # Integration routine would sample directions si with weights wi # and accumulate: integralvalue += wi Yj(si) fsample(si) coeffs[j] = integralvalue return coeffs def integrateshfunctions(coeffsf, coeffsg): """ Computes the integral of two SH-projected functions via dot product. Args: coeffsf: Coefficients of function f. coeffsg: Coefficients of function g. Returns: The scalar integral value. """ # I(f, g) = sumi ci di return sum(c d for c, d in zip(coeffsf, coeffsg)) Adaptive Monte-Carlo SH Projection computes SH coefficients by integrating the product of the environment and SH basis functions over a domain that adapts to local material properties. It distinguishes itself from standard SH projection by dynamically adjusting the integration domain from a full sphere to a hemisphere (plus a transitional ring) based on voxel transparency and gradient magnitude, thereby optimizing the approximation for both translucent volumes and opaque surface-like boundaries. Computes SH coefficients for material reflectance by integrating over a hemisphere using 1250 samples. It uses data from the MERL BRDF library [MPBM03] to describe material function M for surface-like structures with high reflectance. To simplify the rendering pipeline, it uses the same number of SH bands as other projections, relying on the increased sample count to improve approximation quality. Time Complexity: Projection requires evaluating the integral for each coefficient. Integration of two functions is O(K) where K=(L+1)^2, computed as a dot product. Memory Complexity: O(K) per function/channel to store coefficients. Performance: Dot-product integration is highly efficient on GPUs. Precomputing material projections (e.g., 1250 samples for BRDFs) is done once and does not impact runtime. Strengths: Rotational invariance allows direct application of rotations to SH coefficients, useful for rotating light sources. Efficient integration via dot products. Limitations: Three-function integration requires non-physical simplifications for performance. When to use: When efficient representation of spherical functions is needed for volume rendering, particularly for lighting and material effects. When not to use: When high-fidelity three-function integration is required and performance constraints allow for more complex techniques. The method is described in the context of advanced light-material interaction for direct volume rendering. It is implemented in a GPU-based volume ray-caster using C++, OpenGL, and GLSL. It leverages the orthonormality and rotational invariance of spherical harmonics to simplify complex integrations in rendering equations. The approach uses data from the MERL BRDF library [MPBM03] for material representation. name: Adaptive Monte-Carlo SH Projection
head: Adaptive Sampling SH, Green's SH projection, Modified Monte-Carlo Integration, SH Environment Projection via Monte Carlo Integration, SH lighting projection
body:
Adaptive Monte-Carlo SH Projection computes Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for an arbitrary spherical environment function by integrating the product of the environment and SH basis functions over a domain that adapts to local material properties. It distinguishes itself from standard SH projection by dynamically adjusting the integration domain from a full sphere to a hemisphere (plus a transitional ring) based on voxel transparency and gradient magnitude, thereby optimizing the approximation for both translucent volumes and opaque surface-like boundaries. Inputs: Spherical environment function h(S), where S is a direction on the unit sphere. Local material properties at position \vec{x}: Transparency 	au(f(\vec{x})) assigned via a transfer function. Gradient length |

Outputs: SH coefficients \hat{c}l^m for the local environment. Data Structures: Random sample set X = \{x1,..., xn\}, where each xi is a 3D unit vector uniformly distributed on the sphere S. SH basis functions Y{lm}(S). Parameters: Below-surface angle \alpha: A parameter proportional to voxel transparency, lying between 0 and \pi/2. \alpha = 0 corresponds to an opaque, surface-like boundary (hemisphere only). \alpha = \pi/2 corresponds to high transparency (full sphere). Threshold angle for sampling: \pi/2 + \alpha. Method Steps: 1. Determine Integration Domain: If 	au(f(\vec{x})) is high and |
abla 	au(f(\vec{x}))| is small, assume the whole unit sphere affects illumination. If 	au(f(\vec{x})) is low (opaque) and |
abla 	au(f(\vec{x}))| is large, assume only the front-facing hemisphere affects illumination. For intermediate cases, use the angle \alpha to define a transitional region. 2. Define Probability Density Function (PDF): The SH coefficient calculation is reformulated as the expected value E of a random variable r using a PDF p(r): cj = \int\Omega  rac{h(s)Yj(s)}{p(r)} ds = E(r) The PDF normalization factor depends on \alpha. The base value for a hemisphere is 2\pi. The additional ring below the surface given by \alpha adds 2\pi \cdot \sin \alpha. The total normalization factor is: Z = 2\pi(\sin \alpha + 1) This factor equals 2\pi for \alpha=0 (hemisphere) and 4\pi for \alpha=\pi/2 (full sphere). The PDF p(r) is defined such that \int\Omega p(r) ds = 1. 3. Generate Samples: Generate n uniformly distributed random samples X = \{x1,..., xn\} on the sphere S. 4. Filter Samples: During Monte-Carlo sampling, only consider rays if their angle with the gradient 
abla 	au(f(\vec{x})) is less than or equal to \pi/2 + \alpha. Let S{valid} be the set of samples satisfying this condition. 5. Compute Coefficients: Approximate the integral using the filtered samples. The coefficient \hat{c}l^m is calculated as: \hat{c}l^m =  rac{Z}{n} \sum{i=1}^n h(xi) Y{lm}(xi) \cdot \mathbb{I}(	ext{angle}(xi, 
abla 	au) \le \pi/2 + \alpha) Standard Monte-Carlo integration over the full sphere uses  rac{4\pi}{n}. Here, the normalization factor Z replaces 4\pi to account for the restricted integration domain \Omega\alpha. The indicator function \mathbb{I} restricts the sum to valid samples, effectively implementing the adaptive domain. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: h: Function returning environment value for a direction vector (3D unit vector). gradientdirection: Normalized gradient vector of transparency at the current voxel. transparency: Scalar transparency value tau(f(x)). nsamples: Number of random samples. shorder: Order of SH basis (determines number of coefficients). Returns: List of SH coefficients cl^m. """ # Calculate below-surface angle alpha based on transparency # Source: alpha is proportional to transparency, lies between 0 and pi/2. # Exact mapping not specified, assume linear for implementation. alpha = transparency (math.pi / 2) # Calculate normalization factor Z # Source: Z = 2 pi (sin(alpha) + 1) Z = 2 math.pi (math.sin(alpha) + 1) # Threshold angle for sampling # Source: Consider rays if angle with nabla tau <= pi/2 + alpha thresholdangle = math.pi / 2 + alpha # Number of SH coefficients for a given order numcoeffs = (shorder + 1) 2 coefficients = [0.0] numcoeffs for in range(nsamples): # Generate uniform random sample on sphere # Source: X = x1,..., xn uniformly distributed on S x = randomuniformspheresample() # Calculate angle between sample direction and gradient # Source: angle with nabla tau cosangle = dotproduct(x, gradientdirection) angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosangle))) # Clamp for precision # Check if sample is within valid domain if angle <= thresholdangle: # Evaluate environment function hval = h(x) # Update SH coefficients for l in range(shorder + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): idx = l (l + 1) + (m + l) # Standard SH basis evaluation Yl^m yval = evaluateshbasis(l, m, x) coefficients[idx] += hval yval # Normalize by Z/n # Source: cl^m = (4pi/n) sum... # Source: Adapted to Z for idx in range(numcoeffs): coefficients[idx] = (Z / nsamples) coefficients[idx] return coefficients def randomuniformspheresample(): """Generates a uniformly distributed random point on the unit sphere.""" # Standard method: uniform phi, cos(theta) uniform u = random.random() v = random.random() theta = 2 math.pi u phi = math.acos(2 v - 1) x = math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = math.cos(phi) return (x, y, z) def dotproduct(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def evaluateshbasis(l, m, direction): # Standard SH basis evaluation Yl^m # Implementation uses associated Legendre polynomials and trigonometric functions. # Returns the value of the spherical harmonic basis function for the given l, m, and direction. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Clamping the dot product to [-1, 1] before acos is necessary to avoid NaNs due to floating-point errors. Degenerate Input: If the gradient is zero, the direction is undefined. A default direction (e.g., view vector) or full sphere sampling should be used. Boundary Conditions: The transition between hemisphere and full sphere is continuous via \alpha, but sharp changes in transparency between adjacent voxels may cause visual artifacts if not smoothed. Assumes the entire sphere contributes. Used for highly translucent media. Link: Spherical Harmonic Projection. Assumes only the front-facing hemisphere contributes. Used for opaque surfaces. Link: Spherical Harmonic Projection. Time Complexity: O(n \cdot L^2) per voxel, where n is the number of samples and L is the SH order (number of coefficients). The adaptive filtering step adds a constant overhead per sample. Memory Complexity: O(L^2) to store the SH coefficients per voxel. The random samples can be generated on the fly, requiring O(1) additional memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of samples n and the square of the SH order. The adaptive nature does not significantly change the asymptotic complexity but may reduce the effective number of samples needed for convergence in opaque regions. Strengths: Adapts to local material properties, providing accurate lighting for both translucent and opaque regions without requiring separate passes or assumptions. Limitations: Requires evaluation of the environment function h at random points, which can be expensive if h is complex. The approximation error depends on the number of samples and the smoothness of h. When to use: When rendering direct volume data with varying transparency and when environmental lighting (e.g., color bleeding) needs to be approximated efficiently. When not: For real-time applications with very high SH orders or extremely noisy environment functions where deterministic integration might be preferred. Origin: The method was introduced by Lindemann and Ropinski in "Advanced Light Material Interaction for Direct Volume Rendering" (2010). It builds on standard SH projection techniques and Monte-Carlo integration methods [Green, 2003] cited in. History: The use of SH for lighting in graphics dates back to PRT (Precomputed Radiance Transfer). The adaptive approach specifically addresses the challenge of volume rendering where material properties vary spatially. Usage: Used in direct volume rendering to compute color bleeding effects and diffuse shadowed radiance transfer.
