name: Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection
head: SH basis selection
body: Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection determines the maximum bandwidth L of the SH basis used to represent directional signals (such as radiance or color) in volumetric rendering. It balances reconstruction fidelity against memory consumption, as higher degrees increase the number of coefficients quadratically. It differs from Spherical Harmonics Approximation by focusing on the capacity limit (bandwidth) rather than the projection or fitting process itself. Inputs: Target maximum degree L{\text{target}} (integer \ge 0). Source directional coefficients, potentially at a higher degree L{\text{source}}. Outputs: A coefficient vector truncated or padded to degree L{\text{target}}. Metadata indicating the effective bandwidth. Data Structures: Coefficients are stored as a flat vector of size N = (L+1)^2 for a given degree L [Parent]. For real-valued rendering, coefficients correspond to the real basis functions Y{lm} [Parent]. The linear index i maps degree l and order m via i = l^2 + l + m [Parent]. Steps: 1. Calculate Capacity: Compute the required coefficient count for the target degree: N{\text{target}} = (L{\text{target}} + 1)^2. 2. Check Compatibility: Compare L{\text{source}} with L{\text{target}}. 3. Pad (if necessary): If L{\text{source}} < L{\text{target}}, extend the coefficient vector with zeros up to index N{\text{target}} - 1. 4. Truncate (if necessary): If L{\text{source}} \ge L{\text{target}}, discard all coefficients corresponding to degrees l > L{\text{target}} by keeping only the first N{\text{target}} elements of the flat vector. 5. Validate: Ensure L{\text{target}} \ge 0. If L{\text{target}} = 0, retain only the DC component (l=0, m=0). Parameters: L{\text{target}}: Not given in the sources. L{\text{source}}: Determined by the data generation method or training configuration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Scaling: Memory usage scales as O(L^2). Higher degrees require significantly more memory. Precision: Truncation introduces approximation error. SH functions exhibit 'ringing' artifacts (high-frequency noise) near sharp value changes when many coefficients are used [Parent]. Boundary: L=0 represents a constant color field with no directional variation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectshdegree(coefficients, lsource, ltarget): """ Selects or truncates SH coefficients to a target degree. Operates on a flat coefficient array of size (L+1)^2. """ # Calculate required size for target degree ntarget = (ltarget + 1) 2 # If source is smaller, pad with zeros if lsource < ltarget: currentsize = (lsource + 1) 2 paddedcoeffs = list(coefficients) + [0.0] (ntarget - currentsize) return paddedcoeffs # If source is larger or equal, truncate else: return list(coefficients[:ntarget]) SH Degree Truncation is a preprocessing step that reduces the spherical harmonics (SH) degree of loaded splats to match a target parameter, thereby lowering memory and compute requirements. It differs from dynamic degree selection methods by performing a static, in-place reduction of the SH coefficients at load time rather than during rendering or training. Spherical Harmonic Irradiance Gradients store the rate at which irradiance changes with respect to translations about a sample point, allowing extrapolation of irradiance to nearby points to reduce error from moving away from the sample location. The technique projects 6 additional irradiance functions into spherical harmonics at small offsets in the +Y, -Y, +X, -X, +Z, and -Z directions relative to the original sample. For each SH coefficient, partial derivatives are computed via central differencing by subtracting the coefficient from the offset sample in the negative direction from the positive direction sample, then dividing by the distance between samples. This yields a 3D gradient vector for each coefficient. At render time, the gradient extrapolates a new irradiance function using Ii' = Ii + (\nabla Ii \cdot d), where Ii' is the i-th SH coefficient of the extrapolated irradiance, Ii is the stored sample's coefficient, \nabla Ii is the irradiance gradient for that coefficient, and d is the non-unit vector from the original sample location to the point being rendered. Time Complexity: Selection is O(N) for copying or truncating the coefficient array, where N = (L+1)^2. Computational cost for rendering is not obviously affected by SH degree. Memory Complexity: O(L^2). Each coefficient typically requires 3 floats (RGB) or 4 floats (RGBA). Performance: PSNR generally increases with SH degree. On a 256^3 grid, PSNR rises from 26.13 (Degree 0) to 27.22 (Degree 1), 26.99 (Degree 2), 28.29 (Degree 3), and 27.89 (Degree 4). On a 512^3 grid, it rises from 26.99 (Degree 0) to 28.29 (Degree 1), 29.44 (Degree 2), 28.30 (Degree 3), and 29.98 (Degree 4). Trade-offs: Higher degrees improve visual fidelity but significantly increase memory usage. When to use: Use low degrees for memory-constrained environments; use higher degrees for high-fidelity rendering where directional detail is critical. The concept of limiting spherical harmonic expansions to a finite bandwidth is fundamental to signal processing on the sphere. In volumetric rendering, specifically Direct Volume Ray Casting and Neural Radiance Fields, SH degree selection became a critical hyperparameter for balancing quality and resource usage. Empirical studies on DVGO (Direct Voxel Grid Optimization) demonstrated the quantitative impact of degree selection on PSNR. name: SH Degree Truncation
head: SH Capping, Spherical Harmonics Degree Reduction
body: SH Degree Truncation is a preprocessing step that reduces the spherical harmonics (SH) degree of loaded splats to match a target parameter, lowering memory and compute requirements. It performs a static, in-place reduction of the SH coefficients at load time rather than during rendering or training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A splat data structure containing SH coefficients up to a maximum loaded degree, and a target degree parameter L{\text{target}} (where L{\text{target}} \ge 0). Output: The same splat data structure with SH coefficients truncated to degree L{\text{target}}. Data Structures: The splat data structure stores SH coefficients. Standard implementations store coefficients in a flat array or tensor, typically ordered by degree l and order m, with (L+1)^2 coefficients per color channel for degree L. Steps: 1. Check if the target parameter params.shdegree is \ge 0 and differs from the loaded splat's getmaxshdegree(). 2. If the condition is met, call truncateSHDegree(splat, params.shdegree) to modify the splat data in-place. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def truncateshdegree(splat, targetdegree): """ Truncates the spherical harmonics coefficients of a splat to a target degree. Assumes splat.sh[l][m] stores coefficients for degree l and order m. """ currentmax = splat.getmaxshdegree() if targetdegree >= 0 and targetdegree != currentmax: # Zero out coefficients for degrees strictly greater than targetdegree for l in range(targetdegree + 1, currentmax + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): splat.sh[l][m] = 0.0 return splat Parameters: targetdegree: The maximum SH degree to retain. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method preserves the majority of radiance energy in an L2 sense, but the discarded residual energy is highly correlated with intrinsic Gaussian attributes such as spatial position and anisotropic scale. Not given in the sources. A variant approach for reducing SH degree (specifically from 3rd to 1st order) by aggregating the residual energy of higher-order terms into a compact latent representation rather than simply discarding coefficients. It samples K unit direction vectors dk on the sphere using spherical coordinates: \phik \sim U(0, 2\pi), \thetak = \arccos(1 - 2\xik), \xik \sim U(0, 1), then converts to Cartesian dk = [\sin \thetak \cos \phik, \sin \thetak \sin \phik, \cos \thetak]. It evaluates the photometric residual c{\text{res}}(dk) = ci(dk) - c^2i(dk) between the 3rd-order SH radiance ci and 2nd-order SH radiance c^2i. The energy magnitude is E{\text{mag}} = \max(0, c{\text{res}}(dk)) and the directional energy is E{\text{dir}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} dk \otimes E{\text{mag}}. The Gaussian position \hat{\mu} is normalized via f(\hat{\mu}) = \hat{\mu} if \|\hat{\mu}\|2 \le 1, else f(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{2-1}{\|\hat{\mu}\|2} \frac{\hat{\mu}}{\|\hat{\mu}\|2}. A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) \Psi maps the base color c{\text{dc}}, E{\text{dir}}, and f(\hat{\mu}) to first-order SH coefficients c'. This eliminates expensive distillation and reduces SH storage memory overhead compared to 3rd-order baselines, with no per-frame decoding overhead as coefficients are decoded once before inference. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Reduces SH storage memory overhead compared to third-order baselines. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates expensive distillation; achieves significant compression in SH storage memory overhead; no per-frame decoding overhead. Limitations: Projecting higher-order bands inevitably degrades overall color fidelity and scene structure. When to use: When memory or compute is constrained and high-frequency details are not critical. When not to use: When high-fidelity view-dependent effects are required. SH Degree Truncation is a standard technique in Gaussian Splatting and radiance field rendering to manage the computational cost of spherical harmonics. A more advanced variant, Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregation, is proposed in Mobile-4DGS to preserve high-frequency details while reducing degree. name: Real Spherical Harmonic Basis Functions
head: Condon-Shortley Phase SH, SH Basis Functions
body: Real Spherical Harmonic (SH) basis functions provide a real-valued, orthonormal basis for representing directional signals on the unit sphere S^2, avoiding the complex arithmetic required by the standard complex SH basis. They are constructed by combining complex SH basis functions Y\ell^m into real linear combinations, typically incorporating the Condon-Shortley phase factor (-1)^m. This method is essential in volumetric and atmospheric rendering to efficiently store and evaluate directional lighting and radiance fields Spherical Harmonics. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Direction vector \omega = (\theta, \phi) in spherical coordinates, or Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) with r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}. Output: A vector of basis function values \mathbf{y}(\omega) = [y0, y1, \dots, y{n-1}]^T, where n = (L+1)^2 and L is the maximum degree. Data Structures: The basis functions are indexed by degree l \in \{0, \dots, L\} and order m \in \{-l, \dots, l\}. The linear index i maps (l, m) to the array position: i = l^2 + l + m This mapping ensures that for a given degree l, the orders m are stored contiguously Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection. Formulas: The real-valued basis function Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) is defined piecewise based on the sign of m: Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2} K{lm} \cos(m\phi) Pl^m(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m > 0 \\ K{l0} Pl^0(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m = 0 \\ \sqrt{2} K{lm} \sin(-m\phi) Pl^{-m}(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m < 0 \end{cases} where K{lm} is the normalization constant: K{lm} = \sqrt{\frac{2l + 1}{4\pi} \frac{(l - m)!}{(l + m)!}} and Pl^m are the associated Legendre polynomials. Source provides an alternative construction using the Condon-Shortley phase (-1)^m: Y{lm} = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2}(-1)^m\text{Im}[Yl^{|m|}], & m < 0 \\ Yl^0, & m = 0 \\ \sqrt{2}(-1)^m\text{Re}[Yl^m], & m > 0 \end{cases} where Yl^m are the standard complex SH basis functions. Both constructions yield real-valued bases, but the phase factor affects the sign of specific coefficients. Explicit Cartesian Forms (Degrees 0-3): For implementation, it is often efficient to evaluate these functions in Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) where r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}: Degree 0 (l=0): Y{0,0} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}} \approx 0.2820947917738781 Degree 1 (l=1): Y{1,-1} = -\sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}} \frac{y}{r} Y{1,0} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}} \frac{z}{r} Y{1,1} = -\sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}} \frac{x}{r} Degree 2 (l=2): Y{2,-2} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{15}{\pi}} \frac{xy}{r^2} Y{2,-1} = -\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{15}{\pi}} \left(-\frac{yz}{r^2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{15}{\pi}} \frac{yz}{r^2} Y{2,0} = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{5}{\pi}} \frac{3z^2 - r^2}{r^2} Y{2,1} = -\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{15}{\pi}} \left(-\frac{xz}{r^2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{15}{\pi}} \frac{xz}{r^2} Y{2,2} = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{15}{\pi}} \frac{x^2 - y^2}{r^2} Degree 3 (l=3): Y{3,-3} = -\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{35}{2\pi}} \frac{y(3x^2 - y^2)}{r^3} Y{3,-2} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{105}{\pi}} \frac{xyz}{r^3} Y{3,-1} = -\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{21}{2\pi}} \frac{y(5z^2 - r^2)}{r^3} Y{3,0} = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{7}{\pi}} \frac{z(5z^2 - 3r^2)}{r^3} Y{3,1} = -\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{21}{2\pi}} \frac{x(5z^2 - r^2)}{r^3} Y{3,2} = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{105}{\pi}} \frac{z(x^2 - y^2)}{r^3} Y{3,3} = -\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{35}{2\pi}} \frac{x(x^2 - 3y^2)}{r^3} Parameters: L: Maximum degree. Typical values in rendering are 3-5. r: Euclidean distance from origin. For direction vectors, r=1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def realshbasis(theta, phi, maxdegree): """ Computes real spherical harmonic basis functions for a given direction. Args: theta: Polar angle in radians [0, pi]. phi: Azimuthal angle in radians [0, 2pi]. maxdegree: Maximum degree L of the basis. Returns: List of basis function values [y0, y1,..., y{n-1}]. """ n = (maxdegree + 1) 2 basis = [0.0] n # Precompute trigonometric values costheta = math.cos(theta) sintheta = math.sin(theta) cosphi = math.cos(phi) sinphi = math.sin(phi) for l in range(maxdegree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Calculate linear index i = l^2 + l + m i = l l + l + m # Calculate normalization constant Klm # Klm = sqrt( (2l+1)/(4pi) (l-m)! / (l+m)!) # Note: factorial of negative numbers is undefined, but the formula # uses (l-m)! and (l+m)!. Since m ranges from -l to l, # l-m >= 0 and l+m >= 0. # Compute factorials factlminusm = math.factorial(l - m) factlplusm = math.factorial(l + m) klm = math.sqrt((2 l + 1) / (4 math.pi) factlminusm / factlplusm) # Compute Associated Legendre Polynomial Pl^m(cos(theta)) # For m < 0, Pl^m(x) = (-1)^m (l-m)!/(l+m)! Pl^{-m}(x) # However, the real SH definition uses Pl^{|m|} with sin/cos terms. # We use the standard definition for Pl^m where m >= 0. if m == 0: # Yl0 = Kl0 Pl^0(cos(theta)) plm = associatedlegendre(l, 0, costheta) basis[i] = klm plm elif m > 0: # Ylm = sqrt(2) Klm cos(mphi) Pl^m(cos(theta)) plm = associatedlegendre(l, m, costheta) basis[i] = math.sqrt(2) klm cosphim(m, phi) plm else: # m < 0 # Ylm = sqrt(2) Klm sin(-mphi) Pl^{-m}(cos(theta)) # Note: Pl^{-m} is not directly used in the real basis formula # for m<0 in the piecewise definition provided in. # The formula uses Pl^{-m} but with sin(-m phi). # Actually, the standard real SH for m<0 uses Pl^{|m|}. # Let's re-read: "sqrt(2) Klm sin(-m phi) Pl^{-m}(cos(theta))" # Wait, standard definition usually uses Pl^{|m|}. # Let's check cartesian forms. They are consistent with Pl^{|m|}. # The formula in might have a typo or specific convention. # Standard real SH: Yl^{-m} = sqrt(2) (-1)^m Klm sin(m phi) Pl^m(cos theta) # Or Yl^{-m} = sqrt(2) Klm sin(m phi) Pl^m(cos theta) depending on phase. # The prompt says: "sqrt(2) Klm sin(-m phi) Pl^{-m}(cos(theta))" for m < 0. # If we assume Pl^{-m} means Pl^{|m|}, then: absm = -m plm = associatedlegendre(l, absm, costheta) basis[i] = math.sqrt(2) klm math.sin(-m phi) plm return basis def associatedlegendre(l, m, x): """ Computes the associated Legendre polynomial Pl^m(x). Uses recurrence relations. """ if m < 0: # Pl^{-m}(x) = (-1)^m (l-m)! / (l+m)! Pl^m(x) # But we usually compute Pl^m for m>=0. # If called with m<0, we might need to handle it, but the loop above # calls it with m>=0 for the Plm part in the m>0 case. # For m<0 case in realshbasis, we use Pl^{|m|}. pass if m > l: return 0.0 # Compute Pl^m(x) for m >= 0 # P0^0(x) = 1 # P1^0(x) = x # Pl^m(x) = (2l-1)/(l-m) x P{l-1}^m(x) - (l+m-1)/(l-m) P{l-2}^m(x) # Initialize P0^m and P1^m # Pm^m(x) = (-1)^m (2m-1)!! (1-x^2)^(m/2) # P{m+1}^m(x) = (2m+1) x Pm^m(x) if m == 0: pmm = 1.0 else: pmm = 0.0 for i in range(1, m + 1): pmm = -pmm (2 i - 1) math.sqrt(1 - x x) if l == m: return pmm pmp1 = (2 m + 1) x pmm if l == m + 1: return pmp1 pll = 0.0 for ll in range(m + 2, l + 1): pll = ((2 ll - 1) x pmp1 - (ll + m - 1) pmm) / (ll - m) pmm = pmp1 pmp1 = pll return pll def cosphim(m, phi): return math.cos(m phi) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Near the poles (\theta = 0, \pi), \sin(\theta) approaches 0, which can cause numerical instability in the associated Legendre polynomials if not handled carefully. Boundary Conditions: The basis functions are defined on the unit sphere. For vectors not normalized to length 1, the Cartesian forms require division by r^l to maintain correctness. Condon-Shortley Phase: The inclusion of (-1)^m affects the sign of the basis functions. Implementations must be consistent with the source of the SH coefficients. A method to convert SH basis functions into homogeneous polynomials in Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) to avoid numerical inaccuracies associated with monomial bases like x^4. It involves identifying monomials for desired SH bands (e.g., 0, 2, 4), homogenizing monomials of degree d < k by multiplying by (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{(k-d)/2}, and combining them into a vector-valued function. This preserves values on the unit sphere while ensuring the polynomial is homogeneous of degree k. Time Complexity: Evaluating the basis functions for a single direction is O(L^2), where L is the maximum degree. The number of basis functions is n = (L+1)^2 Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection. Memory Complexity: Storing the basis functions explicitly is not required if computed on the fly. Storing coefficients for a directional field requires O(L^2) memory per channel Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection. Performance: Typical implementations use L=3 or L=4 to balance accuracy and performance. Higher degrees lead to larger representations and increased computational cost. Strengths: Real-valued, orthonormal, and efficient for representing smooth directional functions. The Cartesian forms allow for fast evaluation without trigonometric functions if precomputed. Limitations: SH approximations exhibit "ringing" artifacts (Gibbs phenomenon) near sharp discontinuities or high-frequency details. This limits their effectiveness for highly detailed or sharp lighting conditions. Real spherical harmonic basis functions are derived from the complex spherical harmonics, which are eigenfunctions of the angular part of the Laplacian in spherical coordinates Spherical Harmonics. The real-valued formulation is widely used in computer graphics for its computational efficiency and compatibility with real-valued data. The Condon-Shortley phase is a standard convention in physics and chemistry, adopted in some graphics implementations for consistency. The homogeneous polynomial construction is a technique used to improve numerical stability in specific rendering contexts. name: Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer
head: Pre-computed Volume Radiance Transfer, Precomputed Radiance Transfer, Spherical Harmonics PRT, Volume Radiance Transfer, Volumetric PRT
body: Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer (VSH-PRT) is a technique for rendering semi-transparent volumetric datasets with dynamic lighting by precomputing the scene's response to illumination. It solves the problem of expensive real-time volume rendering by compressing the 6D Volume Radiance Transfer function into spherical harmonic coefficients stored on a surface mesh, allowing for fast runtime evaluation under arbitrary distant lighting. It sets itself apart from direct volume rendering by decoupling the expensive volume integration from the render loop, and from standard surface PRT by explicitly handling the volumetric scattering process to determine the exit radiance. Inputs: A volumetric dataset (e.g., electronic density function). A set of distant light sources (direction and intensity). A surface representation (isosurface) extracted from the volume data. Outputs: A rendered image of the volumetric object under the specified lighting. Precomputed spherical harmonic coefficients associated with each vertex of the surface mesh. Data Structures: Surface Mesh: A triangle mesh extracted from the volume. Each vertex v stores a vector of spherical harmonic coefficients. SH Coefficients: For a given vertex, the coefficients represent the Volume Radiance Transfer function compressed into the spherical harmonic basis. The size of this vector depends on the number of bands L. The number of coefficients N for order L is (L+1)^2. Volume Radiance Transfer (VRT): Defined as a 6D function: two dimensions for incoming light direction, two dimensions for the location of the exiting radiance point (surface position), and two dimensions for the viewing direction. Parameters: L: The order of the spherical harmonic basis. The number of basis functions is N = (L+1)^2. Typical values tested include L=6 (49 SHs), L=9 (100 SHs), L=13 (196 SHs), and L=19 (400 SHs). N{views}: The number of view directions sampled during precomputation. Example: 4000 directions. Steps: 1. Surface Extraction: Generate a surface representation (isosurface) of the volume data. For objects with a well-defined boundary, record the ray at the surface point where it exits the volume. Note that for distant illumination, the ray direction does not change after exiting the surface. 2. Volume Radiance Sampling: For each vertex on the extracted surface, sample the volume-scattered radiance along a sufficient number of incoming light directions and viewing directions using direct volume rendering algorithms. This computes the raw 6D VRT function for the surface points. Note: This step is computationally expensive and is performed offline. Tools like OpenSplat can be used for this sampling. 3. Spherical Harmonic Compression: Compress the sampled volume radiance transfer function for each vertex using spherical harmonic basis functions. This involves projecting the sampled radiance data onto the SH basis to obtain the coefficients. Let Li(\omega) be the precomputed unit contribution of light i in direction \omega. The scene's response is modeled as a distribution defined by SH basis functions. The coefficients c{lm} are calculated by integrating the sampled radiance against the SH basis functions Y{lm}(\omega). 4. Runtime Rendering: At runtime, for a given viewing direction and lighting setup: a. Re-sample the surface-mapped volume radiance transfer for the given viewing direction. b. Evaluate the SH coefficients to determine the radiance contribution. c. The final radiance L(p) for a point p is computed by combining the precomputed coefficients with the current light intensities. L(p) = \sum{i} Wi \cdot Li(p) Where Wi is the brightness of light i and Li(p) is the precomputed unit contribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputevrt(volumedata, surfacemesh, numbands): """ Precompute Volume Radiance Transfer coefficients for a surface mesh. Args: volumedata: 3D array representing the volumetric dataset. surfacemesh: List of vertices and triangles extracted from volumedata. numbands: Integer L, defining the SH order. Total coefficients N = (L+1)^2. Returns: vertexshcoeffs: Dictionary mapping vertexid to list of SH coefficients. """ vertexshcoeffs = {} # Step 1: Sample VRT for each vertex # For each vertex, we need to sample radiance for various incoming light directions # and viewing directions. numsamples = 4000 # Example from source lightdirections = samplesphericaldirections(numsamples) for vertex in surfacemesh.vertices: # Sample the volume-scattered radiance along sufficient number of directions # using direct volume rendering algorithms. # This involves casting rays through the volume from the vertex position # in various directions and accumulating scattering. sampledradiance = [] for lightdir in lightdirections: # Direct volume rendering integration from vertex position # along the light direction (or viewing direction, depending on # specific VRT definition implementation). # The source states: "sample the volume-scattered radiance # along sufficient number of directions... and compress this VRT". radiancevalue = directvolumerendersample(volumedata, vertex.position, lightdir) sampledradiance.append(radiancevalue) # Step 2: Compress with Spherical Harmonics # Project sampledradiance onto SH basis functions. # The SH basis functions Ylm are defined for the sphere. shcoeffs = compresstosphericalharmonics(sampledradiance, lightdirections, numbands) vertexshcoeffs[vertex.id] = shcoeffs return vertexshcoeffs def renderruntime(surfacemesh, vertexshcoeffs, lightintensities, viewdirection): """ Render the scene using precomputed VRT coefficients. Args: surfacemesh: The surface mesh. vertexshcoeffs: Precomputed SH coefficients per vertex. lightintensities: List of light source intensities Wi. viewdirection: Current camera/view direction. Returns: Image buffer. """ image = createimagebuffer() for triangle in surfacemesh.triangles: # Interpolate vertex coefficients for the current pixel/fragment # If using the "Interpolated" method without SH compression, # linearly interpolate among the four pre-computed radiance values # closest to the current viewing position. # With SH, we evaluate the SH function. # For each vertex in the triangle, retrieve SH coefficients coeffsv0 = vertexshcoeffs[triangle.v0.id] coeffsv1 = vertexshcoeffs[triangle.v1.id] coeffsv2 = vertexshcoeffs[triangle.v2.id] # Interpolate coefficients across the triangle (barycentric interpolation) # Standard barycentric interpolation is assumed for mesh shading. bary = computebarycentriccoords(triangle, fragmentuv) interpolatedcoeffs = (bary[0] coeffsv0 + bary[1] coeffsv1 + bary[2] coeffsv2) # Evaluate the SH function for the view direction and light directions # The final radiance Li(p) is the precomputed unit contribution. # L(p) = sum(Wi Li(p)) radiance = 0.0 for i, intensity in enumerate(lightintensities): # Evaluate SH basis at view direction and light direction # The exact evaluation of SH basis Ylm(omega) is a standard math operation. shvalue = evaluatesh(interpolatedcoeffs, viewdirection, lightdirections[i]) radiance += intensity shvalue image.setpixel(triangle, radiance) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ringing Artifacts: The method exhibits ringing artifacts due to the truncation of the spherical harmonic series. Prefiltering can mitigate this but leads to undesirable smoothening of the lighting. Precision Loss: If two triangles cover the same texel and have significantly different tangent spaces, there is a lack of precision in the reconstructed signal. High Costs: The method presents relatively high memory and bandwidth costs, as well as high runtime cost compared to simpler interpolation methods. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The memory requirement per vertex scales with the number of spherical harmonic basis functions N = (L+1)^2. For the Neghip dataset (64^3 volume), memory per vertex ranges from 294 bytes (49 SHs) to 12K bytes (Interpolated method). Runtime: The rendering speed declines as the number of SH basis functions increases. The run-time algorithm has lower time complexity than direct volume rendering algorithms. Measured Performance: Test results on the Neghip dataset (64^3 volume, 70569 triangles, 35435 vertices) on a 2GHz Pentium 4 PC with nVIDIA GeForceFX 5900: OpenSplat (Direct Volume Rendering): 0.042 fps. 49 SHs: 15.8 fps. 100 SHs: 12.5 fps. 196 SHs: 7.9 fps. 400 SHs: 4.5 fps. Interpolated (No SH compression): 31.5 fps. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows for efficient synthesis of the appearance of volumetric objects at runtime for any given view direction under arbitrary lighting. Provides consistent lighting between static and dynamic geometry. Limitations: High memory and bandwidth costs. High runtime cost compared to interpolation. Ringing artifacts require prefiltering, which smooths lighting. When to Use: Use when dynamic lighting is required for volumetric data and direct volume rendering is too slow. Use when the volume has a well-defined boundary. When Not to Use: Do not use if memory bandwidth is a critical bottleneck. Do not use if high-frequency lighting details are required and ringing artifacts are unacceptable without smoothing. The concept of Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) was introduced by Sloan et al., who stored the scene's response to light with a distribution defined by spherical harmonic basis functions, allowing rendering of scenes with arbitrary lighting setups. Lehtinen et al. described a volumetric approach to calculate precomputed transfer, allowing querying at any location in 3D space and providing consistent lighting between static and dynamic geometry. The specific application of Spherical Harmonics to Volumetric Radiance Transfer was detailed in research on fast volume visualization, demonstrating the compression of the 6D VRT function. name: Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading
head: SH Volume Shading, SH Volumes, Spherical Harmonic Volumes, Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Shading
body:
Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading is a method for computing diffuse illumination in Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) by approximating the non-linear shading operator (specifically the \max(N \cdot L, 0) term) using spherical harmonics. It solves the problem of interactive relighting in the frequency domain, where traditional methods require expensive recomputation of 3D Fourier transforms for every change in light direction. Unlike Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer, which precomputes transfer functions for specific geometries, this method operates directly on the volume's gradient-derived normals in the Fourier domain, allowing light direction changes to be handled via simple coefficient updates without re-transforming the volume data. Inputs: Volume data f(x,y,z) (scalar field). Light direction L (unit vector (xL, yL, zL)). Truncation order M (typically M=2, covering l=0,1,2). Outputs: Shaded 2D slice image (via inverse Fourier transform) or shaded 3D volume in frequency domain. Data Structures: Volume Normals: Three 3D arrays Nx, Ny, Nz storing the components of the unit normal vector N(x,y,z) for each voxel. Precomputed Fourier Volumes: A set of 3D complex Fourier volumes T(Y{lm}(Nx, Ny, Nz)) for each harmonic basis function Y{lm} up to order M. For M=2, there are 9 such volumes (l=0,1,2; -l \le m \le l). Light Coefficients: A set of real scalars Y{lm}(xL, yL, zL) representing the spherical harmonic expansion of the light direction. Steps: 1. Compute Per-Voxel Normals: Calculate the gradient of the volume data and normalize it to obtain unit normals: N(x,y,z) =  rac{
abla f(x,y,z)}{|
abla f(x,y,z)|} = (nx, ny, nz) Guard against division by zero if 
abla f = 0 by setting N = (0,0,1) or a default normal. 2. Precompute Fourier Transforms of Basis Functions (Offline/Once): For each spherical harmonic basis function Y{lm} (where 0 \le l \le M and -l \le m \le l), compute the 3D Fourier transform of the function evaluated at the voxel normals: T{lm} = \mathcal{F}\{ Y{lm}(nx, ny, nz) \} These terms are independent of the light direction and are stored as complex 3D volumes. 3. Compute Light Coefficients (Per-Frame/Per-Light): For the current light direction (xL, yL, zL), compute the spherical harmonic coefficients: L{lm} = Y{lm}(xL, yL, zL) Note: The sources define the light term expansion as L(	hetaL, \phiL) = \sum \sum L{lm} Y{lm}(	hetaL, \phiL), and for a directional light, the coefficient is simply the basis function value at the light's spherical coordinates. 4. Assemble Shaded Frequency Domain Representation: Combine the precomputed Fourier volumes with the light coefficients and the constant shading coefficients c'{l0}: T(E) =  rac{|L|}{\pi} \sum{l=0}^{M} \sum{m=-l}^{l} L{lm} c'{l0} T{lm} Where c'{l0} =  rac{4\pi}{2l+1} c{l0}, and c{l0} are the coefficients of the \max(\cos 	heta, 0) expansion. The constant |L| is the light intensity. If L is a unit vector, |L|=1. 5. Reconstruct Image (Optional/For Display): To render a specific 2D slice (e.g., at depth z=k): a. Extract the k-th slice from each of the 9 (or M(M+2)) precomputed Fourier volumes T{lm}. b. Multiply each slice by the corresponding scalar L{lm} c'{l0}. c. Sum the slices to form the composite frequency domain slice T(E{slice}). d. Apply the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform to T(E{slice}) to get the shaded pixel values. Formulas: Real Spherical Harmonics Basis: Y{lm}(	heta, \phi) = \sqrt{ rac{(2l+1)(l-|m|)!}{4\pi(l+|m|)!}} Pl^{|m|}(\cos 	heta)  egin{cases} \cos(m\phi) & 	ext{for } m \ge 0 \ \sin(|m|\phi) & 	ext{for } m < 0 \end{cases} Where Pl^{|m|} are the associated Legendre polynomials. Diffuse Shading Equation (Simplified): The final shading equation in the Fourier domain is derived from the convolution of the light and the shading kernel: E =  rac{|L|}{\pi} \sum{l} \sum{m} \sqrt{ rac{4\pi}{2l+1}} Y{lm}(	hetaL, \phiL) c{l0} Y{lm}(\alpha,  eta) Where (\alpha,  eta) are the spherical coordinates of the normal vector. Alternative form used in implementation: E(x,y,z) =  rac{|L|}{\pi} \sum{l} \sum{m} c'{l0} Y{lm}(xL, yL, zL) Y{lm}(nx, ny, nz) With c'{l0} =  rac{4\pi}{2l+1} c{l0}. Max Function Expansion Coefficients (c{l0}): The sources cite the expansion of \max(\cos 	heta, 0) but do not provide the explicit numerical values for c{l0} in the text. Standard SH coefficients for the hemispherical cosine lobe are required. For l=0, c{00} =  rac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \int \max(\cos 	heta, 0) d\omega =  rac{\pi}{\sqrt{4\pi}} =  rac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}. For l>0, odd l terms are zero due to symmetry, and even l terms can be computed via integration. The sources do not list these values. Parameters: Truncation Order M: Typically M=2 (l=0,1,2), capturing over 98% of image energy. Ambient Term: An ambient term of 0.3 or 0.4 is often added to the final image to handle unlit areas, though it is not part of the core SH shading equation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Estimation: Volume data lacks explicit surfaces. Normals are estimated via the gradient operator 
abla f. This approximation is inaccurate in noisy regions or flat areas where the gradient is near zero. Memory Consumption: Storing the Fourier transforms of 9 (or more) harmonic planes requires significant memory. Each complex Fourier volume requires 8 times the storage of the original byte-size data set. Performance: Slicing 10 volumes (9 SH + 1 ambient/data) to assemble one image results in a five-fold increase in rendering time compared to methods that only slice two volumes (like linear/cubic illumination). This method computes physically based multiple scattering in hair volumes by representing the incident scattered radiance field as spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, allowing the complex scattering integral to be evaluated via a precomputed sparse matrix multiplication. It solves the high computational cost of directional multiple scattering by exploiting the smoothness of the indirect radiance distribution, reducing the per-ray shading cost from sampling-based integration to a fixed-size linear algebra operation. It differs from its parent Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading by specifically addressing the anisotropic, fiber-based scattering properties of hair and using a voxelized light-tracing approach to populate the SH coefficients, rather than relying on Fourier transforms or local basis approximations alone. Time Complexity: The core shading operation is a linear combination of precomputed volumes. The cost is dominated by the number of harmonic planes sliced and summed. For M=2, 9 volumes are sliced and summed per frame. Memory Complexity: Requires storing O(M^2) complex 3D Fourier volumes of the normal components. For M=2, this is 9 volumes. Each complex volume is 8x the size of the original byte data. Measured Performance: Synthetic Sphere: 21 fps without depth cueing, 13 fps with depth cueing. UNC Brain: 5 fps without depth cueing, 3 fps with depth cueing. reports 8 fps (no depth cueing) and 6 fps (with depth cueing) for the sphere, and notes that for constant light sources, a cubic illumination model can achieve 35 fps, which is a 5x improvement over the interactive SH method. Strengths: Allows interactive relighting (changing light direction) without recomputing the 3D Fourier transform of the volume. Accurately models the \max(N \cdot L, 0) non-linearity compared to hemispherical approximations. Limitations: High memory usage due to storing multiple Fourier volumes. Slower than simpler shading models (linear/cubic) due to the need to slice and sum more volumes (10 vs 2). Normal estimation from volume gradients can be noisy. The method builds on Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) and uses spherical harmonics to handle the non-linearity of the shading operation, as described in [1] and [8] (Ramamoorthi and Hanrahan, SIGGRAPH 2001). It was introduced to address the lack of efficient illumination models in the Fourier domain, where lighting is essentially non-linear and traditionally required expensive recomputation upon light changes. The work is based on Ramamoorthi and Hanrahan's research on efficient representation for irradiance environment maps and the relationship between radiance and irradiance. name: Efficient multiple scattering in hair using spherical harmonics
head: SH Hair Scattering, SH-based multiple scattering for hair, Spherical Harmonic Multiple Scattering in Hair, Volumetric Hair Multiple Scattering
body:
This method computes physically based multiple scattering in hair volumes by representing the incident scattered radiance field as spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, allowing the complex scattering integral to be evaluated via a precomputed sparse matrix multiplication. It solves the high computational cost of directional multiple scattering by exploiting the smoothness of the indirect radiance distribution, reducing the per-ray shading cost from sampling-based integration to a fixed-size linear algebra operation. It differs from its parent Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading by specifically addressing the anisotropic, fiber-based scattering properties of hair and using a voxelized light-tracing approach to populate the SH coefficients, rather than relying on Fourier transforms or local basis approximations alone. The method consists of four main phases: Voxelization, Light Tracing, Filtering, and Shading (which includes optional Scattering Matrix Precomputation). Inputs: Hair geometry (segments), light source definitions, fiber properties (diameter 2r, eccentricity), grid resolution, SH degree D. Outputs: Rendered image with multiple scattering; optionally, a sparse scattering matrix F for future frames. Voxel Grid A 3D rectilinear grid. Each active voxel stores: meandirection:  ar{\omega}, a 3D vector (normalized). stddev: 
u, a scalar (standard deviation of dot products with  ar{\omega}). attenuation: \sigmat^\perp, a scalar (perpendicular attenuation coefficient). coefficients: A vector of size (D+1)^2 containing SH coefficients ck in the world frame. Scattering Matrix F: A sparse matrix of size (D+1)^2 	imes (D+1)^2. Non-zero entries: Approximately 2% of total entries. Estimate hair density and direction distribution by rasterizing hair segments into the voxel grid. 1. Initialize all voxels as empty. 2. For each hair segment, identify all voxels within a search distance d. 3. For each sample point near the fiber within distance d, add contributions to the voxel's direction list. The weight drops linearly to zero at distance d. 4. After processing all segments, for each voxel: Sum the nearby segment directions weighted by their linear distance drop-off. Normalize the sum to obtain the mean direction  ar{\omega}. Calculate 
u as the standard deviation of the dot products of the normalized segment directions with  ar{\omega}. Calculate the perpendicular attenuation coefficient \sigmat^\perp using formula (6): \sigmat^\perp =  rac{2r N}{\pi d^2} where 2r is the fiber diameter, N is the number of nearby fibers, and d is the voxelization search distance. 5. Mark voxels with no contribution as empty. 6. Mark voxels far from any non-empty cell (unable to participate in lookup) as inactive. Do not allocate coefficients for inactive cells. Estimate scattered radiance in all directions by tracing paths from light sources. 1. Trace paths from light sources proportional to emitted power. 2. After the first geometric scattering event, walk through the voxel grid along each path segment. 3. For each intersected grid cell j with volume \Delta V: Let lp be the length of the intersection between path segment p and cell j. Let \Delta \Phip be the power associated with the light particle. Add contribution to the SH coefficients ck of cell j according to the density definition: 	ext{Contribution} \propto  rac{lp \cdot \Delta \Phip}{\Delta V} The contribution is distributed into the SH basis functions Yk based on the direction of the path segment. 4. Scattering within the volume occurs according to \sigmat(\omega) derived from the voxel's  ar{\omega} and 
u. 5. Upon scattering, choose a fiber direction u from the distribution described by  ar{\omega} and 
u. 6. Sample the scattered direction \omegai using a table-driven procedure: Precompute several thousand random directions for each possible inclination based on the refracted direction for a rough elliptical fiber (simulating roughness by randomizing surface normals). During simulation, randomly choose one of these stored directions. Incident rays have a random azimuthal angle and random position across the fiber width. Reduce noise and Gibbs phenomenon ringing. 1. Spectral Filtering: Apply a gentle lowpass filter to the SH coefficients. Attenuate coefficients by a factor that drops smoothly to zero just beyond the maximum degree D. This prevents ringing caused by sharp peaks in the accumulated radiance. 2. Spatial Filtering: Convolve the grid of coefficients with a box filter with spherical support. The radius is typically between 1.5 and 3 grid cells. Use more aggressive filtering for animations to prevent temporal flicker. Compute exitant radiance for a point \mathbf{x} on a hair fiber. 1. Retrieve Coefficients: Trilinearly interpolate the SH coefficients ck(\mathbf{x}) from the grid (stored in world frame). 2. Rotate to Local Frame: Rotate the interpolated coefficients c to the local fiber frame at \mathbf{x} using the rotation matrix R(\mathbf{x}): c0 = R(\mathbf{x}) c 3. Compute Exitant Coefficients: Option A (Precomputed Matrix): Multiply the precomputed scattering matrix F by the rotated incident coefficients: d0 = F c0 where d0 are the coefficients of the exitant scattered radiance. Option B (Stabbing - Fallback): If F is not precomputed or parameters change frequently, generate 20 to 50 directional "stabs" by sampling the phase function fs(\mathbf{x}, \omegao, \omegai) \sin(\omegai, u). Use the filtered grid values to evaluate incident radiance for each stab direction, weight by attenuation, and average. 4. Reconstruct Radiance: Convert exitant coefficients d0 back to world frame and evaluate the SH basis functions to get the exitant radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao). 5. Add Direct Illumination: Calculate direct illumination separately using standard ray tracing and add to the result. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def voxelize(segments, gridsize, d, fiberdiameter2r): grid = {} for seg in segments: # Not given in the sources: determine voxels intersected by segment within distance d for vkey in voxelsnearsegment(seg, d): if vkey not in grid: grid[vkey] = {'dirs': [], 'count': 0} dist = segmentvoxeldistance(seg, vkey) w = max(0.0, 1.0 - dist / d) grid[vkey]['dirs'].append((seg.dir, w)) grid[vkey]['count'] += 1 for vkey in list(grid.keys()): data = grid[vkey] if not data['dirs']: del grid[vkey] continue wsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for dvec, w in data['dirs']: wsum[0] += dvec[0] w wsum[1] += dvec[1] w wsum[2] += dvec[2] w norm = math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in wsum)) meandir = [v / norm for v in wsum] if norm > 0 else [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dots = [sum(ab for a, b in zip(dvec, meandir)) for dvec, in data['dirs']] meandot = sum(dots) / len(dots) stddev = math.sqrt(sum((x - meandot)2 for x in dots) / len(dots)) N = data['count'] sigmatperp = (fiberdiameter2r N) / (math.pi d 2) grid[vkey] = { 'meandirection': meandir, 'stddev': stddev, 'sigmatperp': sigmatperp, 'coeffs': [0.0] ((15 + 1) 2) } return grid def lighttrace(lights, grid): for light in lights: for path in tracepathsfromlight(light): for seg in path.segmentsafterfirstscatter: # Not given in the sources: traverse grid along segment for vkey in voxelsintersectedbysegment(seg): if vkey in grid: vol = voxelvolume(vkey) contrib = seg.lengthinvoxel(vkey) path.power / vol # Not given in the sources: project direction onto SH basis and add to coeffs accumulateshcoefficients(grid[vkey]['coeffs'], seg.dir, contrib) # Not given in the sources: compute scattering probability if random.random() < scatteringprobability(grid[vkey]['sigmatperp']): u = samplefiberdirection(grid[vkey]['meandirection'], grid[vkey]['stddev']) omegai = samplescattereddirectiontable(u) path.continue(omegai) def filtergrid(grid): for vkey in grid: coeffs = grid[vkey]['coeffs'] for k in range(len(coeffs)): # Not given in the sources: compute lowpass attenuation factor factor = smoothstep(k, 15) coeffs[k] = factor radius = 2.0 for vkey in grid: # Not given in the sources: find neighbors within radius neighbors = getsphericalneighbors(vkey, radius) neighborcoeffs = [grid[n]['coeffs'] for n in neighbors if n in grid] if neighborcoeffs: # Not given in the sources: average vectors grid[vkey]['coeffs'] = averagecoefficients(neighborcoeffs) return grid def shade(x, diro, grid, F=None): # Not given in the sources: trilinear interpolation cworld = trilinearinterp(grid, x) # Not given in the sources: compute rotation matrix to local frame Rx = rotationtolocal(x, diro) # Not given in the sources: rotate SH coefficients clocal = rotatesh(cworld, Rx) if F is not None: # Not given in the sources: sparse matrix-vector multiplication dlocal = matvecmul(F, clocal) else: # Not given in the sources: fallback stabbing method dlocal = stabbing(cworld, diro, grid) # Not given in the sources: rotate SH coefficients back dworld = rotatesh(dlocal, transpose(Rx)) # Not given in the sources: evaluate SH basis functions Lo = evalsh(dworld, diro) # Not given in the sources: compute direct illumination Ld = tracedirect(x, diro) return Lo + Ld SH Degree (D): Typically up to 15, resulting in 256 coefficients per grid point. Fiber Diameter (2r): Used in \sigmat^\perp calculation. Voxelization Search Distance (d): Determines the spatial extent of fiber influence per voxel. Smoothing Factor: Values range from 2.0 to 2.2 cells across tested scenes. Grid Cell Parameter (r): Values range from 8 to 10 cells across tested scenes. Paths Traced: Ranges from 100M to 160M depending on the scene. Image Resolution: 600 x 600 pixels. Rays per Pixel: 64. Gibbs Phenomenon: Directly using accumulated coefficients with sharp peaks leads to ringing. Increasing SH degree does not reduce this until the peak is fully resolved. Solution: Apply lowpass filter. Temporal Incoherence: Spatial noise in static images is hard to notice, but becomes perceptible flicker in animations. Solution: Use more aggressive spatial filtering for animations. Sampling Difficulty: The Marschner et al. phase function model is difficult to sample directly. Solution: Use table-driven scattering with precomputed random directions based on refracted directions for rough elliptical fibers. Smoothness Assumption: The method limits accuracy for highly directional radiance distributions, as they cannot be accurately represented by the SH basis. Spatial Resolution: Constrained by rectilinear grid spacing, causing spatial and angular blurring comparable to photon mapping. Time Complexity: The shading step is O(1) per ray (matrix multiplication or stabbing). The dominant cost is light tracing, which scales with the number of paths traced (100M-160M paths). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active voxels times the number of SH coefficients. For a 33x109x49 grid with 46,074 active cells and 256 coefficients, memory usage is significantly lower than photon mapping (270 MB vs 1.5 GB). Measured Performance: On a 3.0 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo workstation, single-threaded, 1 GB RAM: Voxelization: ~10 seconds. Attenuation/Scattering function tabulation: ~3 seconds each. Scattering matrix precomputation: 700 seconds (500,000 evaluations). Multiple scattering rendering: 13 minutes per frame (animations), 5 minutes for stills (vs 1.5 hours for photon mapping). Direct illumination: Additional 10 minutes. Strengths: Significantly faster than photon mapping for hair multiple scattering; preserves directionally varying effects; low memory footprint. Limitations: Limited by SH basis smoothness; spatial blurring from grid resolution; requires precomputation for optimal speed. When to use: Production hair rendering where multiple scattering is required and performance is critical. When not to use: Scenes with highly directional, non-smooth indirect lighting that cannot be captured by SH; real-time applications requiring dynamic hair geometry changes without re-voxelization. This method was introduced by to address the high cost of physically based multiple scattering in hair. It builds on the fiber radiance cache concept from Moon and Marschner [2006] but replaces the directional stabbing approach with spherical harmonics to exploit the smoothness of multiple scattering. The implementation was done in Java using a hierarchical grid for ray-hair intersection acceleration. Efficient multiple scattering in hair using spherical harmonics, https://doi.org/10.1145/1360612.1360630, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Ray Tracing Backward Pass
head: Backward Ray Tracing with Spherical Harmonics, Plenoxel Ray Tracing (Backward), volume_render_cuvol_backward [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial]
body: The Ray Tracing Backward Pass computes the gradients of a differentiable volume rendering loss with respect to the scene representation (spherical harmonic coefficients and density) and auxiliary parameters, given the rendered image and ground truth. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the forward ray casting pass, enabling end-to-end training of volumetric models like Plenoxels. Unlike the forward pass which accumulates color and transmittance, this method propagates error signals backward through the ray integration, handling RGB normalization and optional regularization losses (beta, sparsity). Inputs: gradoutput: Gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered RGB color (shape: [N, 3] or flattened). colorcache: Cached accumulated color components from the forward pass (shape: [N, 3] or similar structure storing intermediate accumulation terms). rayspec: Ray origins and directions. grid: Volumetric grid containing density data and spherical harmonic coefficients. betaloss: Scalar weight for beta distribution sparsity loss. sparsityloss: Scalar weight for sparsity loss. logtransmitin: Logarithm of transmittance at the start of the ray segment. opt: Configuration options (e.g., gradoutisrgb, basisdim, shdatadim). Outputs: grads: Gradients for spherical harmonic coefficients and density. accumout (optional): Accumulated gradient values. logtransmitout (optional): Gradient of log transmittance. Data Structures: sphfuncval: Shared memory array storing spherical harmonic function values for the current ray. gradsphfuncval: Shared memory array storing gradients of SH function values. rayspec: Struct containing ray origin (\mathbf{o}) and direction (\mathbf{v}). tempstorage: Warp-level reduction buffer. Steps: 1. Compute the initial gradient accumulator accum from the color cache and output gradient: accum = colorcache[0]gradoutput[0] + colorcache[1]gradoutput[1] + colorcache[2]gradoutput[2]. 2. Calculate global thread ID and derive rayid, rayblkid, and laneid (warp lane index). If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, return early, as this thread does not contribute to SH gradient computation. 3. If betaloss > 0, compute transmitin = exp(logtransmitin) and update betaloss = (1 - transmitin / (1 - transmitin + 1e-3)), then add to accum. 4. Initialize shared memory arrays sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, rayspec, and tempstorage for warp reduction. 5. Set rayspec from origins and directions, extracting the direction vector \mathbf{v}{\text{dir}}. 6. If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the ray is invalid. Write accum to accumout (if not null) and 0 to logtransmitout (if not null), then return. 7. Compute gradient output: if gradoutisrgb, calculate resid = colorcache - gradoutput, then gradout[i] = resid normfactor where normfactor = 2.f / (3 Q); otherwise gradout[i] = gradoutput[i]. 8. Synchronize warps within the SH data dimension mask to ensure shared memory consistency. 9. Call traceraycuvolbackward with gradout, colorcache, rayspec, opt, laneid, sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, tempstorage, logtransmitin, betaloss, sparsityloss, grads, and optional output pointers. This function performs the core integration of gradients along the ray, interpolating density and SH coefficients, and computing gradients for the grid parameters. 10. Call calcsphfuncbackward to compute the gradients for the spherical harmonic basis coefficients based on the accumulated gradients in gradsphfuncval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraybackwardkernel( gradoutput, # Tensor [N, 3] colorcache, # Tensor [N, 3] rayspec, # Struct with origin, direction, tmin, tmax grid, # Object with densitydata, shcoeffs, shdatadim, basisdim betaloss, # Float sparsityloss, # Float logtransmitin, # Float opt, # Struct with gradoutisrgb, shdatadim, etc. accumout, # Optional pointer/tensor logtransmitout # Optional pointer/tensor): # 1. Initialize Accumulation accum = 0.0 for i in range(3): accum += colorcache[i] gradoutput[i] # 2. Thread Identification # Derived from global thread ID: rayid = tid >> 5, rayblkid = threadid >> 5, laneid = threadid & 0x1F laneid = threadid & 0x1F if laneid >= grid.shdatadim: return # 3. Beta Loss Gradient if betaloss > 0.0: transmitin = exp(logtransmitin) betagrad = betaloss (1.0 - transmitin / (1.0 - transmitin + 1e-3)) accum += betagrad # 4. Shared Memory Init # Layout: sphfuncval[RAYPERBLOCK][9], gradsphfuncval[RAYPERBLOCK][9], rayspec[RAYPERBLOCK], tempstorage[RAYPERBLOCK] sphfuncval = [0.0] grid.basisdim gradsphfuncval = [0.0] grid.basisdim tempstorage = [0.0] 32 # Warp reduction buffer # 5. Ray Setup vdir = rayspec.direction # 6. Degenerate Ray Check if rayspec.tmin > rayspec.tmax: if accumout is not None: accumout[0] = accum if logtransmitout is not None: logtransmitout[0] = 0.0 return # 7. Gradient Output Normalization if opt.gradoutisrgb: resid = [colorcache[i] - gradoutput[i] for i in range(3)] normfactor = 2.0 / (3.0 Q) gradout = [r normfactor for r in resid] else: gradout = gradoutput # 8. Warp Sync # Synchronize threads in the warp based on the SH data dimension mask # (CUDA syncwarp primitive) # 9. Core Backward Trace # Sources do not provide the internal implementation of this function. # It performs trilinear interpolation of density and SH values, # and accumulation of gradients along the ray. traceraycuvolbackward( grid=grid, gradout=gradout, colorcache=colorcache, rayspec=rayspec, opt=opt, laneid=laneid, sphfuncval=sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval=gradsphfuncval, tempstorage=tempstorage, logtransmitin=logtransmitin, betaloss=betaloss, sparsityloss=sparsityloss, grads=grid.grads, accumout=accumout, logtransmitout=logtransmitout) # 10. SH Gradient Computation # Sources do not provide the internal implementation of this function. # It computes gradients for the spherical harmonic basis coefficients based on # the accumulated gradients in gradsphfuncval. calcsphfuncbackward( grid=grid, laneid=laneid, rayid=rayid, vdir=vdir, sphfuncval=sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval=gradsphfuncval, gradbasisout=grid.grads.gradbasisout) Parameters: betaloss: Scalar weight for beta distribution sparsity loss. If > 0, gradient contribution is added to accum. sparsityloss: Scalar weight for sparsity loss. Passed to traceraycuvolbackward. Q: Scaling factor used in RGB normalization. Edge Cases: If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the kernel returns early, writing zero to logtransmitout. Numerical stability is handled by adding \epsilon = 10^{-3} in the beta loss denominator. The Background Rendering Backward Pass computes the gradients of the loss with respect to the background volumetric field (typically a sparse grid of spherical harmonic coefficients or density values) and the accumulated transmittance, given the rendered background color, ground truth, and ray parameters. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the concentric sphere sampling and trilinear interpolation used in the forward background rendering pass. Unlike the foreground ray casting which traverses a dense or sparse voxel grid, this method specifically handles the unbounded background field, often using a separate sparse grid structure. It is distinct from the general Ray Tracing Backward Pass by isolating the gradient computation for the background component, allowing for specialized handling of RGB normalization and sparsity regularization specific to the background layer. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Implemented as a CUDA kernel for GPU acceleration. The Ray Tracing Backward Pass is part of the svox2 library, developed by Alex Yu and others. It is designed to support differentiable volume rendering with spherical harmonics, enabling efficient training of neural radiance fields and related representations. The method is integrated into the NeRF-Factory framework by POSTECH, KAIST, and Kakao Brain Corp. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sxyu/svox2, https://github.com/sxyu/svox2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) OSHMOS/IPRF, https://github.com/OSHMOS/IPRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Background Rendering Backward Pass
head: Background Backpropagation
body: Computes gradients for the background rendering pass, backpropagating through concentric sphere sampling and trilinear interpolation to update the background volumetric field and accumulated transmittance. It handles RGB gradient normalization and calls the background backward function. Unlike the foreground pass, it operates on a separate sparse grid structure for unbounded backgrounds. Inputs: grid (SparseGridSpec), rgbgt (ground truth RGB tensor), rgbout (rendered RGB tensor), rays (RaysSpec with origins, directions, IDs), opt (RenderOptions: backgroundnlayers, stepsize, usebackground, gradoutisrgb), logtransmit (per-ray log-transmittance tensor), accum (per-ray accumulated color tensor), sparsityloss (boolean flag), gradoutput (loss gradient w.r.t. output RGB). Outputs: grads.gradbackgroundout (gradient buffer for background volumetric data). Data structures: SparseGridSpec: Contains layout for the background sparse grid. Internal layout (hash map keys, leaf node sizes) is defined by the parent Background Volume Rendering with Sparse Grid implementation. SingleRaySpec: Temporary structure holding interpolated values (ray.pos, ray.l, invrmid) for the current sampling step. Parameters: backgroundnlayers: Number of layers in the background grid. Default 32. stepsize: Step size for concentric sphere sampling. Not given in the sources. TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS: Number of CUDA threads per block. Default 256. sparsityloss: Weight for Cauchy sparsity regularization. Passed as argument. usebackground: Boolean flag to enable/disable the background backward pass. Steps: 1. Check usebackground. If false, return. 2. Get rayid for the current thread. If logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0f, return early. 3. Initialize totalcolor = 0.0f. 4. Initialize concentric sphere intersector with ray.origin and ray.dir. Calculate innerradius = max(distraytoorigin(ray.origin, ray.dir) + 1e-3f, 1.0f). Calculate nsteps = int(grid.backgroundnlayers / opt.stepsize) + 2. Initialize invrlast = 1.0f / innerradius. 5. Prepare gradout: if gradoutisrgb is true, gradout = (rgbgt - rgbout) (2.0f / (3.0f Q)); else gradout = gradoutput. 6. Loop i from 0 to nsteps - 1: Calculate radius r = nsteps / (nsteps - i - 0.5). If r < innerradius or ray-sphere intersection fails, continue. Calculate position ray.pos = origin + t dir. Calculate invrmid = 1.0f / norm(ray.pos). Normalize ray.pos = invrmid. Convert to equirectangular coordinates. Calculate layer index and integer lattice ray.l, clamp to grid bounds, and compute fractional part ray.pos. Trilinearly interpolate sigma: sigma = trilerp(grid, ray.l, ray.pos). If sigma > 0.0f: pcnt = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) sigma. weight = exp(logtransmit[rayid]) (1.0f - exp(-pcnt)). logtransmit[rayid] -= pcnt. For each RGB channel i: color = trilerp(grid, ray.l, ray.pos) C0 + 0.5f (where C0 is the base color coefficient). totalcolor += max(color, 0.0f) gradout[i]. If color > 0.0f: currgradcolor = C0 weight gradout[i]. Backpropagate to background data using trilinear interpolation backward. invrlast = invrmid. 7. Accumulate color gradient: accum[rayid] -= weight totalcolor. 8. Sparsity loss gradient (if sparsityloss): currgradsigma = sparsityloss (4.0f sigma / (1.0f + 2.0f sigma sigma)). Backpropagate to background data using trilinear interpolation backward. 9. Sigma gradient from color: currgradsigma = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) (totalcolor exp(logtransmit[rayid]) - accum[rayid]). Backpropagate to background data using trilinear interpolation backward. 10. Calculate blocks: blocks = CUDANBLOCKSNEEDED(Q, TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS). Launch kernel. Check CUDA errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbackgroundbackward(grid, rgbgt, rgbout, rays, opt, logtransmit, accum, sparsityloss, gradoutput): """ Computes gradients for the background rendering pass. """ if not opt.usebackground: return Q = rays.numrays threads = 256 # TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS blocks = (Q + threads - 1) // threads grads = GradientBuffer(grid) for rayid in range(Q): ray = rays[rayid] # Early exit check if logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0: continue totalcolor = 0.0 innerradius = max(distraytoorigin(ray.origin, ray.dir) + 1e-3, 1.0) nsteps = int(grid.backgroundnlayers / opt.stepsize) + 2 invrlast = 1.0 / innerradius # Prepare gradient output if opt.gradoutisrgb: normfactor = 2.0 / (3.0 Q) resid = rgbgt[rayid] - rgbout[rayid] gradout = resid normfactor else: gradout = gradoutput[rayid] for i in range(nsteps): r = nsteps / (nsteps - i - 0.5) if r < innerradius: continue t = intersectsphere(ray.origin, ray.dir, r) if t is None: continue raypos = ray.origin + t ray.dir invrmid = 1.0 / norm(raypos) rayposnorm = raypos invrmid eqcoords = unitvec2equirect(rayposnorm) lattice, frac = getlatticeandfrac(eqcoords, grid.backgroundreso) sigma = trilerp(grid, lattice, frac) if sigma > 0.0: pcnt = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) sigma weight = exp(logtransmit[rayid]) (1.0 - exp(-pcnt)) logtransmit[rayid] -= pcnt for ch in range(3): color = trilerp(grid, lattice, frac) C0 + 0.5 totalcolor += max(color[ch], 0.0) gradout[ch] if color[ch] > 0.0: currgradcolor = C0 weight gradout[ch] trilerpbackward(grads, lattice, frac, currgradcolor) if sparsityloss: currgradsigma = sparsityloss (4.0 sigma / (1.0 + 2.0 sigma sigma)) trilerpbackward(grads, lattice, frac, currgradsigma) currgradsigma = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) (totalcolor exp(logtransmit[rayid]) - accum[rayid]) trilerpbackward(grads, lattice, frac, currgradsigma) invrlast = invrmid accum[rayid] -= weight totalcolor return grads def distraytoorigin(origin, dir): return norm(origin) def intersectsphere(origin, dir, radius): # Returns distance t along dir to sphere of given radius centered at origin # Simplified for concentric spheres centered at origin return radius def norm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def unitvec2equirect(v): # Converts unit vector to equirectangular (theta, phi) theta = acos(v[2] / norm(v)) phi = atan2(v[1], v[0]) return (theta, phi) def getlatticeandfrac(coords, reso): # Converts equirectangular coords to grid lattice and fractional part theta, phi = coords x = int(theta reso / pi) y = int(phi reso / (2 pi)) fracx = (theta reso / pi) - x fracy = (phi reso / (2 pi)) - y return ((x, y), (fracx, fracy)) def trilerp(grid, lattice, frac): # Standard trilinear interpolation on grid at lattice with fractional offset frac # Returns interpolated value return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual grid lookup and interpolation def trilerpbackward(grads, lattice, frac, gradval): # Accumulates gradval to the gradient buffer at lattice and frac pass class GradientBuffer: def init(self, grid): self.data = [0.0] grid.size Transmittance Saturation: If logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0f, the thread returns early to avoid numerical instability and wasted computation. Precision: The use of float (single precision) is standard in the CUDA implementation. Care must be taken with the exp and log operations to avoid underflow/overflow. Boundary Conditions: The innerradius calculation ensures that rays do not sample inside the origin sphere, preventing division by zero or invalid intersections. CUDA Errors: The kernel launch must be followed by error checking to catch invalid memory accesses or configuration errors. A technique for rendering unbounded or distant background elements using a separate sparse grid structure. It allows for efficient rendering by treating the background as a distinct volumetric field, enabling different resolution and sampling strategies compared to the foreground. Choose this when the scene has large unbounded backgrounds that do not fit efficiently into a dense voxel grid. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays Q and the number of sampling steps n{steps}. The complexity is O(Q \cdot n{steps}). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays for storing logtransmit and accum gradients, and proportional to the size of the background sparse grid for storing gradients. Performance: The CUDA kernel is optimized for parallel execution, with 256 threads per block. Performance scales with the number of rays and the complexity of the background grid traversal. Strengths: Efficiently handles unbounded backgrounds; separates background and foreground computations for modular optimization; supports sparsity regularization. Limitations: Requires a separate sparse grid structure for the background; performance may degrade if the background grid is very large or has high resolution. When to Use: When rendering scenes with large, unbounded backgrounds (e.g., sky, distant geometry) that are distinct from the foreground scene. When Not to Use: When the background is simple (e.g., a solid color or environment map) and does not require volumetric rendering. The Background Rendering Backward Pass is part of the NeRF-Factory project by Kakaobrain, which includes custom CUDA kernels for sparse voxel volume rendering. It is also implemented in Svox2 by sxyu, which uses spherical harmonics for background rendering. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering, specifically adapting the backward pass for the concentric sphere sampling technique used for background rendering. The implementation in NeRF-Factory is described in the context of a PyTorch sparse voxel volume extension. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sxyu/svox2, https://github.com/sxyu/svox2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Background Volume Rendering with Sparse Grid
body: Background Volume Rendering with Sparse Grid is a technique for rendering unbounded or distant background elements (e.g., sky, distant geometry) using a separate sparse grid structure distinct from the foreground scene representation. It allows for efficient rendering of background content by treating it as a separate volumetric field accessed via ray traversal, enabling different resolution and sampling strategies for background versus foreground. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins and directions, background sparse grid data (grid.backgrounddata), background grid links (grid.backgroundlinks), optional gradient output (gradoutput), and optimization parameters (opt.stopthresh, sparsityloss). Outputs: Rendered RGB color and transmittance for the background contribution; gradients for background density/color (gradbackgroundout) and mask/visibility (maskbackgroundout) if in backward mode. Data Structures: PackedGridOutputGrads: A structure containing: gradbackgroundout: Gradient for background density/color data. maskbackgroundout: Gradient for background mask/visibility data. Background Grid: Accessed via grid.backgroundlinks and grid.backgrounddata, distinct from foreground grids. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization and Bounds: For each ray, determine the spatial bounds of the intersection with the background grid using rayfindboundsbg. 2. Transmittance Check (Skip Condition): If the logarithmic transmittance logtransmit is less than -25.0, skip the ray entirely to save computation, assuming negligible contribution. 3. Forward Pass (renderbackgroundforward): Iterate through ray samples within the background bounds. Accumulation: Accumulate color and transmittance. The color contribution is computed as totalcolor += max(color, 0.0) weight. Note: The source snippet uses gradoutput[i] in the forward accumulation formula, which is a variable name reuse for the weight/transmission factor. Transmittance Update: Update logtransmit based on density and step size. Termination: If the transmittance drops below a threshold, terminate the ray: if exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh, break. Sparsity Regularization (Optional): If sparsityloss > 0.0, add a regularization term to the density gradient currgradsigma. Two variants are mentioned: Cauchy version (from SNeRG): currgradsigma += sparsityloss (4 sigma / (1 + 2 (sigma sigma))). Alphs version (from PlenOctrees): currgradsigma += sparsityloss exp(-pcnt) ray.worldstep. 4. Gradient Computation (Backward Pass): Sigma Gradient: Compute the gradient for density (currgradsigma) using the chain rule involving accumulated color, transmittance, and step size: currgradsigma = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) (totalcolor exp(logtransmit) - accum). Where invrlast and invrmid are inverse ray positions, and accum is the accumulated transmittance/color term. Gradient Normalization (if gradoutisrgb): If the gradient output is RGB, normalize the residual: normfactor = 2.0 / (3 Nrays) and gradout[i] = resid normfactor. Otherwise, copy gradoutput directly. Propagate Gradients: Update PackedGridOutputGrads using trilerpbackwardbgone. This function updates gradbackgroundout and optionally maskbackgroundout based on currgradsigma (or currgradcolor for color gradients). Parameters: sparsityloss: Scalar weight for sparsity regularization. Typical values are > 0.0 to encourage transparency in background regions. stopthresh: Transmittance threshold for early ray termination. Expressed as a value for logtransmit in the check \exp(\log\transmit) < opt.stop\thresh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rayfindboundsbg(ray, grid): """Standard AABB intersection for background grid.""" # Returns (tmin, tmax) or None if no intersection # Implementation depends on grid coordinate system; assumes axis-aligned bounds return (0.0, 1000.0) # Placeholder bounds for demonstration def trilerpbackwardbgone(grid, ray, gradsigma, gradcolor, grads): """Standard trilinear interpolation backward pass for sparse grid gradient scatter.""" pos = ray.position # Scatter gradient to 8 neighboring grid vertices for dx in (0, 1): for dy in (0, 1): for dz in (0, 1): corner = pos + [dx, dy, dz] weight = math.prod([abs(corner[i] - pos[i]) for i in range(3)]) grads.gradbackgroundout[corner] += gradsigma weight if gradcolor is not None: grads.maskbackgroundout[corner] += gradcolor weight def renderbackgroundforward(ray, grid, opt): """Forward pass for background volume rendering.""" bounds = rayfindboundsbg(ray, grid) if bounds is None: return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 totalcolor = 0.0 logtransmit = 0.0 accum = 0.0 currgradsigma = 0.0 for sample in ray.march(bounds): sigma, color = grid.samplebackground(sample.position) color = max(color, 0.0) step = ray.worldstep weight = math.exp(logtransmit) (1.0 - math.exp(-sigma step)) totalcolor += color weight logtransmit += -sigma step if math.exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh: break if opt.sparsityloss > 0.0: # Cauchy version from SNeRG currgradsigma += opt.sparsityloss (4.0 sigma / (1.0 + 2.0 (sigma sigma))) # Alphs version from PlenOctrees: currgradsigma += opt.sparsityloss math.exp(-pcnt) step return totalcolor, math.exp(logtransmit), currgradsigma def renderbackgroundbackward(ray, grid, gradoutput, opt, gradoutisrgb=False): """Backward pass for background volume rendering.""" if ray.logtransmit < -25.0: return PackedGridOutputGrads() if gradoutisrgb: Nrays = len(ray.origins) normfactor = 2.0 / (3.0 Nrays) gradoutput = gradoutput normfactor currgradsigma = ray.worldstep (ray.invrlast - ray.invrmid) (ray.totalcolor math.exp(ray.logtransmit) - ray.accum) grads = PackedGridOutputGrads() trilerpbackwardbgone(grid, ray, currgradsigma, gradoutput, grads) return grads class PackedGridOutputGrads: def init(self): self.gradbackgroundout = None self.maskbackgroundout = None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Transmittance Rays: Rays with logtransmit < -25.0 are skipped. This assumes negligible contribution but may miss subtle background details in very transparent regions. Variable Name Reuse: The source snippet uses gradoutput in the forward accumulation formula, which is likely a misnomer for weight/transmission. Implementers should use standard volume rendering accumulation weight color. Sparsity Regularization: The choice between Cauchy and Alphs versions depends on the specific background representation (SNeRG vs. PlenOctrees). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of ray samples within the background grid bounds. Early termination based on stopthresh reduces average case complexity. Skipping rays with logtransmit < -25.0 further optimizes performance. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the background sparse grid (grid.backgrounddata, grid.backgroundlinks). Separate from foreground grid memory. Strengths: Efficient rendering of unbounded backgrounds; separate resolution/sampling for background vs. foreground; early termination and ray skipping optimize performance. Limitations: Requires separate grid management; sparsity regularization parameters need tuning; low transmittance ray skipping may lose detail. When to Use: When rendering scenes with significant distant or unbounded background elements that benefit from sparse representation. This method is part of the JNeRF project, an unofficial implementation of NeRF using the Jittor framework. It extends standard volume rendering by introducing a separate sparse grid for background elements, allowing for more flexible and efficient handling of large-scale scenes.
