name: Zonal Method (Bhate and Tokuta)
head: Bhate et al. Method, Bhate's method
body: The Zonal Method (Bhate and Tokuta) is a global illumination technique for participating media that extends the classical zonal method to handle interactions between volumes and ideal diffuse surfaces while eliminating the assumption of medium isotropy. It distinguishes itself from standard zonal methods by representing the phase function and radiance using spherical harmonics to approximate Mie scattering, and by computing the resulting form factors using an extended hemicube technique. Inputs: A scene containing v volume elements (voxels) and s ideal diffuse surfaces. Outputs: The radiance distribution within the volumes and reflected radiance from the surfaces. Data Structures: 1. Spherical harmonic coefficient vectors of size M for each volume and surface to store radiance expansions. 2. Form factor matrices F{ik} and F{isj} for volume-volume and volume-surface interactions, computed per spherical harmonic term. Steps: 1. Approximate the scattering phase function by the first M terms of its spherical harmonics expansion to approximate Mie scattering. 2. Compute the form factors between all volume elements and between volumes and surfaces, accounting for the spherical harmonics, using the extended hemicube technique. 3. Set up a system of linear equations consisting of M \times v equations for the v volumes plus s related equations for the s surfaces. 4. Solve the resulting system using a Gauss-Seidel iterative technique. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: M is the number of spherical harmonic terms; only the first few are necessary for a convincing image, but computational cost scales significantly with M. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The direct application of this method is impractical for large scenes due to the prohibitive cost of computing form factors. A hierarchical acceleration technique for the Zonal Method that reduces form factor computation cost by dynamically determining interaction levels and skipping unnecessary refinements. It is chosen for complex scenes where direct computation is prohibitive, distinguishing itself from standard zonal methods by avoiding iterative hierarchy refinement. Time Complexity: The cost to compute form factors in a regular grid of v = n^3 voxels is O(n^7 + M^2 n^6). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles anisotropic scattering (Mie approximation) and surface-volume interactions, which standard zonal methods cannot. Limitations: Extremely high computational cost for form factor calculation makes it impractical for large-scale scenes without acceleration techniques. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Bhate and Tokuta as an extension to the classical zonal method. It addresses the limitations of previous zonal method implementations which assumed isotropic media and ignored effects between surfaces and volumes. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Global Illumination Techniques for the Simulation of Participating Media, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00510096v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Progressive Refinement Zonal Method
head: Bhate and Tokuta's progressive refinement, Bhate's method, Progressive Refinement Approach (Bhate's method)
body: The Progressive Refinement Zonal Method is a hierarchical acceleration technique for the Zonal Method [12221-zonal-method-bhate-and-tokuta.md] that reduces the computational cost of computing form factors between volumes and surfaces. It establishes a fixed hierarchy during preprocessing and employs a shooting strategy during rendering, avoiding the iterative refinement of the hierarchy itself. Unlike standard zonal methods that compute interactions between all elements, this method determines interaction levels dynamically based on heuristics, skipping unnecessary refinements when transmittance is high or form factors are negligible. Inputs: Scene geometry consisting of volumes (participating media) and surfaces (ideal diffuse emitters/reflectors); optical properties (absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, phase function); light source definitions. Outputs: Radiosity (radiance) values for all volume elements and surface patches at their respective hierarchy levels. The method relies on a hierarchical tree structure for volumes and surfaces. Hierarchy Node: Represents a volume or surface element. level: Integer indicating the depth in the hierarchy (0 = global, higher = finer). children: List of child nodes (if not a leaf). links: List of links to other nodes (volumes or surfaces) at specific levels. Link: Represents an interaction between two elements. targetnode: The node being linked to. interactionlevel: The hierarchy level at which the interaction is computed. formfactor: Precomputed or estimated form factor between the source and target at the specified level. transmittance: Estimated transmittance between the elements. 1. Preprocessing Step 1: Subdivision Subdivide global volumes and surfaces into a hierarchy. Recursively subdivide until a minimum size or maximum depth is reached. 2. Preprocessing Step 2: Link Creation Create links between volume-volume pairs and surface-volume pairs. Determine the interactionlevel for each pair using heuristics. Volume-Volume Heuristics: Compute a rough estimate of the total form factor. If it is below a specified threshold, the elements can interact at the current level without further refinement. Estimate visibility between the volumes. Compute the optical depth of the intervening medium. Condition: If the transmittance between two elements is too high, no further refinement is needed. Volume-Surface Heuristics: Use a brightness factor heuristic for light sources. For each pair of elements, calculate the bounding volume intersection and approximate form factor. Set the interaction level to the coarsest level satisfying the heuristics. 3. Rendering Phase: Shooting Strategy Iterate through the hierarchy from coarse to fine levels. For each node, shoot energy to its linked targets at their determined interactionlevel. Accumulate radiosity contributions. The sources state there is no Push-Pull procedure. This implies radiosity is computed locally at each level and accumulated, but not corrected across levels during the shooting phase. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD = 0.0 TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD = 1.0 BRIGHTNESSTHRESHOLD = 0.0 class Link: def init(self, source, target, interactionlevel, formfactor, transmittance): self.source = source self.target = target self.interactionlevel = interactionlevel self.formfactor = formfactor self.transmittance = transmittance def buildhierarchy(elements): # Standard spatial subdivision (e.g., octree) until minimum size/depth. return [Element(level=0, children=[], links=[]) for in elements] def getleafnodes(node): # Recursively collect leaf elements. if not node.children: return [node] leaves = [] for child in node.children: leaves.extend(getleafnodes(child)) return leaves def estimateformfactor(a, b): # Standard geometric form factor approximation between bounding volumes. return 0.5 def estimatetransmittance(a, b): # Standard transmittance calculation: exp(-opticaldepth). return 0.95 def islightsource(element): # Check if element has non-zero emission. return hasattr(element, 'emission') and element.emission > 0 def createrefinedlinks(a, b): # Recursively link children at finer levels. links = [] for childa in a.children: for childb in b.children: ff = estimateformfactor(childa, childb) tt = estimatetransmittance(childa, childb) level = childa.level links.append(Link(childa, childb, level, ff, tt)) return links def initializeradiosity(scene): # Allocate zero radiosity for all elements. return {elem: 0.0 for elem in scene.allelements} def computeenergytransfer(source, target, formfactor, transmittance): # Standard radiosity transfer: Esource formfactor transmittance. return source.emission formfactor transmittance def progressiverefinementzonalmethod(scene): volumehierarchy = buildhierarchy(scene.volumes) surfacehierarchy = buildhierarchy(scene.surfaces) links = [] for vola in volumehierarchy: for volb in volumehierarchy: if vola is volb: links.extend(createselflinks(vola)) continue ff = estimateformfactor(vola, volb) tt = estimatetransmittance(vola, volb) if ff < FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD and tt > TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: links.append(Link(vola, volb, vola.level, ff, tt)) else: links.extend(createrefinedlinks(vola, volb)) for vol in volumehierarchy: for surf in surfacehierarchy: if islightsource(surf) and surf.emission < BRIGHTNESSTHRESHOLD: continue ff = estimateformfactor(vol, surf) tt = estimatetransmittance(vol, surf) if ff < FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD and tt > TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: links.append(Link(vol, surf, vol.level, ff, tt)) else: links.extend(createrefinedlinks(vol, surf)) radiosity = initializeradiosity(scene) for link in links: energy = computeenergytransfer(link.source, link.target, link.formfactor, link.transmittance) radiosity[link.target] += energy return radiosity def createselflinks(volume): # Handle self-refinement issue: link each pair of smallest volume elements. links = [] smallestelements = getleafnodes(volume) for i, elema in enumerate(smallestelements): for j, elemb in enumerate(smallestelements): links.append(Link(elema, elemb, elema.level, 1.0, 1.0)) return links FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD: Threshold for rough estimate of form factor. Not given in the sources. TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: Threshold for transmittance. Not given in the sources. BRIGHTNESSTHRESHOLD: Threshold for light source brightness. Not given in the sources. Self-Refinement Issue: Participating media are modeled by a set of global volumes. Each global volume is refined against each other, but not against itself (no self-refinement). Therefore, links must be set between each pair of the smallest volume element considered within a given global volume, otherwise its self-illumination won’t be correctly computed. A self-refinement strategy would be better as it would reduce the number of interactions. Push-Pull Issue: There is no Push-Pull procedure to set correctly the values of the radiosity at all levels of the hierarchies. Such a procedure would be needed after each shooting iteration to obtain a correct solution. This is a significant limitation of the method. Time Complexity: The computation of all form factors in a naive zonal method takes O(n^7) where n is the number of intervening voxels. The progressive refinement method reduces this cost by using hierarchies and heuristics to skip unnecessary interactions. The exact complexity is not given, but it is significantly lower than the naive approach. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces computational cost by avoiding unnecessary refinements; uses heuristics to determine interaction levels efficiently. Limitations: No Push-Pull procedure leads to potentially incorrect radiosity values at different hierarchy levels; lack of self-refinement requires explicit handling of self-illumination. When to use: When computational cost is a concern and the scene has large volumes with low interaction between distant parts. When not to use: When high accuracy is required for self-illumination or when the scene has complex interactions that require fine-grained refinement across all levels. The Progressive Refinement Zonal Method, also known as Bhate's method, is a progressive refinement version of the zonal method. It was proposed by Bhate and Tokuta. The method builds on the Zonal Method [12221-zonal-method-bhate-and-tokuta.md] by introducing hierarchies to reduce computational cost. It is part of the family of deterministic multiple scattering methods for participating media rendering. name: Spherical Harmonics Rendering
head: SH Rendering, SH coefficient interpolation, SH-based Volume Rendering, SHRenderer, SLF evaluation, Spherical Harmonic Radiance Field Evaluation
body: Spherical Harmonics Rendering evaluates a 5D Spherical Harmonic Field (SLF) at a 3D location and viewing direction by interpolating SH coefficients from a tree structure and projecting them along the viewing direction to estimate RGB radiance. It distinguishes itself from standard volume rendering by encoding angular view-dependent effects as a compact set of coefficients rather than storing explicit RGB values per sample, reducing memory overhead while preserving directional lighting variation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tensor of SH coefficients with shape (batch, numsamples, numcoeffs) and a tensor of viewing directions with shape (batch, numsamples, 3). Output: A tensor of RGB values with shape (batch, numsamples, 3). Data Structures The SH coefficients are stored in a flat tensor where the last dimension contains the coefficients, which are reshaped to separate color channels. Steps 1. Reshape coefficients to (batch, numsamples, 3, numcoeffs // 3) to separate color channels. 2. Calculate the number of levels from the number of coefficients per channel: levels = int(math.sqrt(numcoeffsperchannel)). 3. Compute SH basis components for the viewing directions: components = componentsfromsphericalharmonics(degree=levels - 1, directions=directions). 4. Multiply coefficients by components: rgb = sh components[..., None,:]. 5. Sum over SH components and add bias: rgb = torch.sum(sh, dim=-1) + 0.5. (Note: Source contains a bug here where it sums sh instead of the product from step 4; the correct operation sums the product). 6. Apply optional activation function to RGB. 7. Composite using weights and background color. 8. If not in training mode, replace NaN values with 0 and clamp RGB to [0.0, 1.0]. Formula \widehat{L}0(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{l=0}^{b} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{l,m}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot Y{l,m}(\mathbf{v}) where \widehat{L}0 is the raw unconstrained RGB radiance, c{l,m}(\mathbf{x}) are the interpolated SH coefficients for band l and order m, Y{l,m}(\mathbf{v}) are the SH basis functions evaluated at direction \mathbf{v}, and b is the maximum band index. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def sphericalharmonicsrendering(shcoeffs, directions, activation=None, training=True): """ Render RGB values from SH coefficients and viewing directions. Args: shcoeffs: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, numcoeffs) directions: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, 3) activation: Optional activation function (e.g., torch.sigmoid) training: Boolean flag for training mode Returns: rgb: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, 3) """ # Step 1: Reshape coefficients to separate color channels shchannels = shcoeffs.view(shcoeffs.shape[:-1], 3, shcoeffs.shape[-1] // 3) # Step 2: Determine SH degree numcoeffsperchannel = shcoeffs.shape[-1] // 3 levels = int(math.sqrt(numcoeffsperchannel)) degree = levels - 1 # Step 3: Compute SH basis components for the given directions components = componentsfromsphericalharmonics(degree=degree, directions=directions) # Step 4 & 5: Project coefficients to RGB, sum, and add bias # Corrected from source bug where sh was summed instead of the product rgb = torch.sum(shchannels components[..., None,:], dim=-1) + 0.5 # Step 6: Apply activation function if specified if activation is not None: rgb = activation(rgb) # Step 7: Composite with weights/background (placeholder for renderer-specific logic) # rgb = RGBRenderer.combinergb(rgb, weights, backgroundcolor) # Step 8: Handle NaNs and clamping in inference mode if not training: rgb = torch.nantonum(rgb, nan=0.0) rgb = torch.clamp(rgb, 0.0, 1.0) return rgb def componentsfromsphericalharmonics(degree, directions): """ Compute spherical harmonic basis components for given directions. Args: degree: SH degree L directions: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, 3) Returns: components: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, (degree+1)^2) """ directions = directions / (torch.norm(directions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) x, y, z = directions[..., 0], directions[..., 1], directions[..., 2] theta = torch.acos(z) phi = torch.atan2(y, x) numcoeffs = (degree + 1) 2 components = torch.zeros(directions.shape[:-1], numcoeffs, device=directions.device, dtype=directions.dtype) sintheta = torch.sin(theta) costheta = torch.cos(theta) sinphi = torch.sin(phi) cosphi = torch.cos(phi) idx = 0 for l in range(degree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Real SH basis evaluation if l == 0 and m == 0: components[..., idx] = 1.0 / math.sqrt(4 math.pi) elif l == 1 and m == -1: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) sintheta sinphi elif l == 1 and m == 0: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) costheta elif l == 1 and m == 1: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) sintheta cosphi elif l == 2 and m == -2: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) sintheta2 sin(2 phi) / 2 elif l == 2 and m == -1: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) sintheta costheta sinphi elif l == 2 and m == 0: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(5 / (4 math.pi)) (3 costheta2 - 1) / 2 elif l == 2 and m == 1: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) sintheta costheta cosphi elif l == 2 and m == 2: components[..., idx] = math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) sintheta2 cos(2 phi) / 2 else: # Higher degrees follow standard recurrence relations components[..., idx] = 0.0 idx += 1 return components Parameters Band limit b: The number of SH bands stored. Typically b=3 to store low-frequency components and save memory, resulting in 3 \times (b+1)^2 coefficients per node per color channel. Activation: Optional activation function, default nn.Sigmoid(). Edge Cases and Pitfalls NaN values in non-training mode must be replaced with 0. RGB values must be clamped to [0.0, 1.0] in non-training mode. The coefficient tensor reshaping assumes a specific memory layout; if coefficients are grouped by channel rather than interleaved, the reshape operation must be adjusted. Source contains a known bug where the summation step overwrites the channel multiplication result, discarding the projection. Time and Memory Complexity Memory usage scales with the number of SH coefficients per sample. For band limit b, there are (b+1)^2 coefficients per channel, totaling 3(b+1)^2 coefficients per sample. Time complexity is dominated by the evaluation of the SH basis functions and the dot product with the coefficients. Measured Performance Not given in the sources. Scaling The method scales linearly with the number of samples and the batch size. Strengths and Limitations Strengths include a compact representation of view-dependent effects and reduced memory overhead compared to storing full RGB tensors per sample. Limitations include the inability to capture high-frequency angular details when using low band limits. When to Use Use when view-dependent effects are important and memory is constrained. When Not to Use Do not use when high-frequency angular details are required and cannot be captured by low-degree SH. Spherical Harmonics Rendering is used in neural radiance fields and implicit surface representations to model view-dependent shading. It was popularized by works such as "NeRF--Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" and subsequent extensions incorporating SH for view-dependent effects. The method is implemented in frameworks like Nerfstudio and SDFStudio. name: Spherical Harmonics Raycaster (Shell Density)
head: SH Shell Volume Rendering, Shell Density Raycasting
body: A volumetric raycasting method that renders a shell-shaped density field defined by spherical harmonics (specifically Y{l3,m0}), using additive color accumulation, normalization, and saturation-based early termination. It differs from general SH volume rendering by restricting the density function to a specific harmonic degree and using a binary shell thickness model rather than continuous density gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position (camPos), ray direction (rayDirection), ray start distance (startT), ray end distance (endT), step size (stepSize), shell thickness (thickness), saturation threshold (saturationThreshold). Outputs: Final color (finalColor), a float4 with normalized RGB and alpha=1.0. Data Structures: finalColor: float4 (R, G, B, A). location: float3 representing the current ray position. currentt: float representing the current distance along the ray. isSaturated: bool flag for early termination. Spherical Harmonics Definitions: The density field is based on the spherical harmonic Y{l3,m0}. The general form for Y{l,0} depends on the polar angle \theta. The specific functions used are: Y{l1,m0}(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{3}{\pi}} \cos(\theta) Y{l2,m0}(\theta) = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{5}{\pi}} (3\cos^2(\theta) - 1) Y{l3,m0}(\theta) = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{\frac{7}{\pi}} (5\cos^3(\theta) - 3\cos(\theta)) Parameters: thickness: float, default 0.4f. Defines the radial thickness of the shell around the Y{l3,m0} surface. saturationThreshold: int (used as float comparison), default 0. Used to stop raymarching when any RGB channel exceeds this value. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize finalColor to (0, 0, 0, 0). 2. Initialize location to camPos + startT rayDirection. 3. Initialize currentt to startT. 4. Initialize isSaturated to false. 5. Loop while currentt < endT and !isSaturated: a. Update location by adding stepSize rayDirection. b. Increment currentt by stepSize. c. Check if location is inside the rendering extent (bounding box/sphere). If not, continue to next iteration. d. Transform location to spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi): r = \| \text{location} \| \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\text{location}.z}{r}\right) \phi = \operatorname{atan2}(\text{location}.y, \text{location}.x) e. Compute the harmonic value: val = Y{l3,m0}(\theta). f. Compute density using densityFunc(val, thickness): \text{density} = \begin{cases} \operatorname{sign}(\text{val}) & \text{if } |2|\text{val}| - r| < \text{thickness} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Note: The source formula |2|val| - r| < thickness is interpreted as the condition for being inside the shell. The term 2|val| likely refers to a scaling factor or specific implementation detail where the harmonic value is scaled. Given the standard definition, val is the harmonic value. The condition checks if the point is within thickness of the surface defined by the harmonic. However, the source explicitly states val = Yl3m0(theta) and the condition |2|val| - r| < thickness. This implies the shell surface is defined by r = 2|Y{l3,m0}(\theta)|. We follow the source literally. g. Compute color using colorFunc(density): If density > 0: return float4(0, 0, 1, 1) (Blue). If density < 0: return float4(1, 1, 0, 1) (Yellow). Else: return float4(0, 0, 0, 1) (Black). h. Add computed color to finalColor: finalColor += color. i. Check saturation: \text{isSaturated} = (\text{finalColor}.R > \text{saturationThreshold}) \lor (\text{finalColor}.G > \text{saturationThreshold}) \lor (\text{finalColor}.B > \text{saturationThreshold}) 6. Normalize finalColor: \text{normalizer} = \max(1.0f, \max(\text{finalColor}.R, \max(\text{finalColor}.G, \text{finalColor}.B))) \text{finalColor} = \text{finalColor} / \text{normalizer} \text{finalColor}.A = 1.0f 7. Return finalColor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sphericalharmonicl3m0(theta): """ Computes Yl3m0(theta) = (1/4) sqrt(7/pi) (5cos^3(theta) - 3cos(theta)) """ costheta = math.cos(theta) return 0.25 math.sqrt(7.0 / math.pi) (5.0 costheta3 - 3.0 costheta) def densityfunc(val, r, thickness): """ Computes density based on the shell condition. Shell surface is defined by r = 2 |val|. """ # Condition from source: |2|val| - r| < thickness if abs(2.0 abs(val) - r) < thickness: return math.copysign(1.0, val) # sign(val) return 0.0 def colorfunc(density): """ Returns color based on density sign. """ if density > 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Blue elif density < 0: return (1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Yellow else: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Black def raycast(campos, raydir, startt, endt, stepsize, thickness, saturationthreshold): """ Renders the SH Shell Volume. """ finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] location = [ campos[0] + startt raydir[0], campos[1] + startt raydir[1], campos[2] + startt raydir[2] ] currentt = startt issaturated = False # Note: 'isInside(extent, location)' check is assumed to be handled by # the caller or a bounding volume check. For this implementation, # we assume the ray is already within the extent or the check is implicit. # If the source implies a bounding box, it is not specified. # We proceed with the spherical coordinate conversion which assumes # the point is valid. while currentt < endt and not issaturated: # Update location location = [ location[0] + stepsize raydir[0], location[1] + stepsize raydir[1], location[2] + stepsize raydir[2] ] currentt += stepsize # Convert to spherical coordinates r = math.sqrt(location[0]2 + location[1]2 + location[2]2) # Avoid division by zero if r == 0: continue theta = math.acos(location[2] / r) phi = math.atan2(location[1], location[0]) # Compute harmonic value val = sphericalharmonicl3m0(theta) # Compute density density = densityfunc(val, r, thickness) # Compute color color = colorfunc(density) # Additive accumulation finalcolor[0] += color[0] finalcolor[1] += color[1] finalcolor[2] += color[2] # Alpha is not accumulated in the loop, only normalized at the end # Check saturation if (finalcolor[0] > saturationthreshold or finalcolor[1] > saturationthreshold or finalcolor[2] > saturationthreshold): issaturated = True # Normalize maxval = max(1.0, max(finalcolor[0], max(finalcolor[1], finalcolor[2]))) finalcolor[0] /= maxval finalcolor[1] /= maxval finalcolor[2] /= maxval finalcolor[3] = 1.0 return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Camera Inside Sphere: If the camera is inside the sphere and the ray intersects the sphere boundary at t1 > 0 but t0 <= 0, the raymarch should start at t=0.0 instead of t0. Zero Radius: If r=0 (camera at origin), acos is undefined. The code should handle this by skipping or returning a default value. Precision: Floating point precision in acos and atan2 can affect the shell boundary detection. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps along the ray. Early termination via saturation can reduce this. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray. No large data structures are stored per pixel. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast evaluation of the density function, early termination improves performance for opaque regions. Limitations: Limited to a specific harmonic shape (Y{l3,m0}), additive blending does not account for occlusion in the traditional sense (no alpha compositing with background), saturation threshold is a crude early termination method. When to use: When a specific shell-like volumetric effect is desired and performance is critical. When not to use: When complex lighting, occlusion, or arbitrary density fields are required. This method is derived from the VolumetricRayCasting-GL repository by Balázs Banto. It is part of a broader set of techniques for volumetric rendering using spherical harmonics. The specific use of Y{l3,m0} for shell density is a specialized application within this framework. balazsbanto/VolumetricRayCasting-GL, https://github.com/balazsbanto/VolumetricRayCasting-GL, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Color MLP with Primitive-Aware Bias
head: Color MLP, MLP Color Representation, Primitive-Aware Color MLP, tiny MLP for representing color
body: A small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) used to represent view-dependent color in the linear RAW color space, replacing Spherical Harmonics (SH) to enhance expressiveness and optimization stability. It addresses the inability of SH to adequately represent RAW linear color data, which causes strange color representations early in training and negatively affects final structural reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera pose v (concatenated with feature vector), Gaussian index i. Output: View-dependent color ci in linear RAW space. Data Structures Each Gaussian i maintains two learnable parameters: 1. Color Feature (fi): A vector sampled from a normal distribution. 2. Color Bias (bi): A scalar initialized based on projected pixel colors. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: For each Gaussian i derived from the scattered point set S': Project the point s'i onto all training images to obtain the set of pixel colors \{c^p{pix}\}i. Initialize the bias bi^{(0)} = \log(\text{avg}(\{c^p{pix}\}i)). Initialize the feature fi^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigmaf). 2. Cloning/Splitting: During Gaussian cloning or splitting operations, copy and assign the current fi and bi values to the new Gaussians. 3. Color Computation: To render color for a specific view: Concatenate the camera pose v with the feature vector fi. Feed the concatenated vector into the tiny MLP F\theta. Add the bias bi to the MLP output. Apply the exponential activation function to simulate the unbounded HDR color space. Formulas The final color ci is computed as: ci = \exp(F\theta(fi, v) + bi) where: F\theta is the tiny MLP with parameters \theta. fi is the color feature vector. v is the camera pose. bi is the color bias. \exp is the exponent activation function. Parameters \sigmaf: Standard deviation for the normal distribution sampling fi^{(0)}. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls SH Inadequacy: Using Spherical Harmonics instead of the Color MLP results in strange color representations early in training because SH cannot adequately represent the RAW linear color space. This negatively impacts the final structural reconstruction, even if the rendered image appears similar initially. HDR Range: The exponential activation is necessary because the HDR color space theoretically has no upper bound on color values. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializecolormlpgaussian(pointsprime, trainingimages): """ Initialize color feature and bias for a single Gaussian. Args: pointsprime: The 3D point coordinates. trainingimages: List of training image views containing the point. Returns: fi: Color feature vector. bi: Color bias scalar. """ # 1. Project point onto all training images to get pixel colors # Note: Implementation of projection depends on camera intrinsics/extrinsics # which are assumed available in the broader context. projectedcolors = [] for view in trainingimages: if pointsprime is visible in view: color = getpixelcoloratpoint(view, pointsprime) projectedcolors.append(color) # 2. Initialize bias bi^(0) = log(avg({c^ppix}i)) if len(projectedcolors) > 0: avgcolor = np.mean(projectedcolors, axis=0) # Assuming avgcolor is in linear space, take log component-wise or scalar? # Source implies scalar log of average, but color is vector. # Standard practice for HDR bias is often per-channel or scalar magnitude. # Source text: "bi^(0) is setted by the log value of the average of {c^ppix}i" # We assume scalar bias applied to the MLP output which produces a vector? # Or bias is vector? Source says "color bias bi". # Formula: exp(Ftheta(...) + bi). If Ftheta outputs vector, bi must be vector. # However, source says "bi^(0) = log(avg(...))". # Let's assume bi is a vector of same dimension as MLP output (e.g., 3 for RGB). bi = np.log(avgcolor + 1e-8) # Guard against log(0) else: # Fallback if not visible in any training image bi = np.zeros(3) # # 3. Initialize feature fi^(0) ~ N(0, sigmaf) sigmaf = 0.1 # Not given in sources fi = np.random.normal(0, sigmaf, size=3) # Assuming 3D feature vector return fi, bi def rendercolormlp(fi, bi, v, mlpmodel): """ Compute view-dependent color using the Color MLP. Args: fi: Color feature vector. bi: Color bias vector. v: Camera pose vector. mlpmodel: The tiny MLP Ftheta. Returns: ci: Rendered color in linear RAW space. """ # Concatenate feature and camera pose inputvector = np.concatenate([fi, v]) # Forward pass through MLP mlpoutput = mlpmodel(inputvector) # Add bias and apply exponential activation # Source: ci = exp(Ftheta(fi, v) + bi) ci = np.exp(mlpoutput + bi) return ci Expressiveness: Provides better stability and linear color space representation compared to Spherical Harmonics. Optimization: Introduces greater stability during the optimization process. HDR Support: Enables realistic exposure variation and HDR tone-mapping in real-time by rendering in the linear color space. Structural Impact: Avoids the negative impact on final structural reconstruction caused by SH's inability to handle RAW data. This method is part of the LE3D framework, which is based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It was introduced to address issues with missing distant points in nighttime scenes and to improve HDR view synthesis. The approach replaces the standard SH color representation in Gaussian attributes with a tiny MLP. name: X-Ray Visualization
head: Average Density Projection, X-Ray Rendering, n-D X-ray projection
body: X-Ray Visualization is a volume rendering technique that projects a dataset into a 2D image by computing the average density along each ray, producing a grey-scale image similar to medical X-rays. Unlike standard ray marching which accumulates color and opacity based on depth ordering, this method treats ordering as irrelevant to simplify the user interface and reveal topological information in high-dimensional or complex data. It discards depth cues and inscattering, focusing solely on the mean density value encountered along the ray path. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset defined by density values \rho(\mathbf{p}) at discrete grid positions; a viewing direction defined by camera origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction vector \mathbf{d}; and rotation parameters for the view axes. Output: A 2D grey-scale image where pixel intensity corresponds to the average density along the corresponding ray. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array of density values. Ray Parameters: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and step size \Delta t. Steps: 1. View Transformation: The user defines the viewing orientation by rotating the system of axis vectors in any of the 3 directions (X, Y, Z axes) in degrees within the range [-360, 360]. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the output image, cast a ray through the data set in the desired viewing direction. 3. Density Sampling: March along the ray, sampling the density \rho at each step. 4. Average Density Calculation: Compute the arithmetic mean of the sampled density values along the ray segment contained within the volume. Let N be the number of samples and \rhoi be the density at the i-th sample. The average density \bar{\rho} is: \bar{\rho} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \rhoi 5. Image Formation: Map the calculated \bar{\rho} to a grey-scale intensity value for the corresponding pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderxray(volumedata, volumebounds, cameraorigin, cameradirection, imagewidth, imageheight, numsamples): """Renders an X-ray projection of a volume.""" def zeros(shape): return [[0.0 for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): return bounds[0][0] <= pos[0] <= bounds[0][1] and bounds[1][0] <= pos[1] <= bounds[1][1] and bounds[2][0] <= pos[2] <= bounds[2][1] def samplevolume(vol, pos): # Interpolation method (trilinear, etc.) is not specified in the sources ix, iy, iz = int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2]) return vol[ix][iy][iz] def maptogreyscale(val): return min(255, max(0, int(val))) image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) raylength = 10.0 # Not given in the sources stepsize = raylength / numsamples for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Projection matrix mapping not specified in the sources rayo = [cameraorigin[0] + x 0.1, cameraorigin[1] + y 0.1, cameraorigin[2]] rayd = cameradirection densitysum = 0.0 count = 0 for t in range(numsamples): currentpos = [rayo[i] + t stepsize rayd[i] for i in range(3)] if isinsidevolume(currentpos, volumebounds): density = samplevolume(volumedata, currentpos) densitysum += density count += 1 if count > 0: avgdensity = densitysum / count image[y][x] = maptogreyscale(avgdensity) else: image[y][x] = 0 return image Parameters: View Rotation: Rotation angles for X, Y, and Z axes in degrees, typically ranging from -360 to 360. Num Samples: Number of integration steps per ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Empty Rays: If a ray does not intersect the volume, the average density is undefined or zero. High-Dimensional Data: The method is designed for n-D volume rendering (n>3) where ordering is irrelevant, but implementation requires projection into 3D or 2D viewing spaces. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot N), where W and H are image dimensions and N is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Strengths: Simplifies user interface by eliminating occlusion exploration; reveals topological information in n-D spaces. Limitations: Lacks depth cues; ordering of structures is irrelevant, which may obscure spatial relationships; limited to density visualization. When to use: When exploring topological features of high-dimensional or complex datasets where depth ordering is less important than average density distribution. When not to use: When realistic lighting, shadows, or depth perception is required. The method was introduced by Bajaj et al. for n-D volume rendering (n>3) to simplify the user interface by treating ordering as irrelevant, thereby eliminating the need for occlusion exploration. It allows users to change viewpoints in n-D space by stretching and rotating axis vectors. The technique is also implemented in educational visualization tools, such as the application described by Thomas Lidy, where it computes average density values along rays and visualizes them as grey-scale images, similar to medical X-rays. name: fBm Noise Generation
head: Water Vapour Emulation (fBm Noise Generation), fBm Noise Generation for Cloud Density, fBm density simulation, fractal Brownian motion noise, uniform noise cube
body: This method simulates the irregular density of water droplets in clouds by generating fractal Brownian motion (fBm) noise from a pre-computed 3D noise cube. It transforms uniform random noise into a Gaussian-like distribution suitable for atmospheric vapour simulation, serving as the density field input for ray-marching algorithms. It differs from procedural noise generation (e.g., Perlin or Simplex noise computed on-the-fly) by relying on a static, pre-calculated texture lookup, which trades memory bandwidth for computational simplicity and deterministic results. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D texture (volume) containing pre-computed uniform random noise values. Input: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for spatial sampling coordinates. Input: Number of octaves N, scale factor w, and sampling factor s. Output: A scalar density value \rho(\mathbf{p}) at position \mathbf{p}, derived from the fBm sum. Data Structures Noise Cube: A 3D array of dimensions 64 \times 64 \times 64. Data Type: Single-precision floating-point values (32-bit). Content: Uniform random noise values. Storage: Transferred from host CPU to GPU memory. Algorithm Steps 1. Pre-computation (Host CPU): Generate a 64 \times 64 \times 64 grid of single-precision floats. Fill each voxel with a uniform random noise value. Transfer this 3D cube to GPU memory. 2. Sampling (GPU Fragment Shader): For each pixel, compute the ray position \mathbf{p} along the ray. Initialize totalNoise = 0.0. Iterate through octaves i from 0 to N-1 (where N=5): Sample the noise cube at position \mathbf{p} \cdot s^i. Retrieve the uniform noise value Ui from the texture. Accumulate the weighted noise: totalNoise += w^i Ui. The implementation uses an unrolled version of this summation in the fragment shader to improve performance. Parameters Number of octaves (N): 5. Increasing beyond 5 does not improve vapour deformation shape and decreases frame performance. Octave scale factor (w): Amplitude attenuation factor, with w < 1. Noise sampling factor (s): Frequency multiplier for each octave, with s > 1. Note: The source specifies the constraints w < 1 and s > 1 but omits the exact numerical values chosen for the implementation. Formula The fBm noise value at position \mathbf{x} is defined as: fBm(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} w^i \cdot Noise(s^i \cdot \mathbf{x}) Where: N = 5 is the number of octaves. w is the octave scale factor (amplitude decay), with w < 1. s is the noise sampling factor (frequency increase), with s > 1. Noise(\cdot) is the lookup function returning the uniform random value from the pre-computed 3D cube. \mathbf{x} is the 3D spatial coordinate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Single-precision floats are used for the noise cube. Performance: Increasing octaves beyond 5 yields diminishing returns for vapour shape while reducing frame rate. Determinism: Pre-computed noise ensures identical results across frames for the same coordinates. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplenoisecube(coord, cube, size=64): # Standard clamping for out-of-bounds coordinates x = max(0, min(size - 1, int(coord.x (size - 1)))) y = max(0, min(size - 1, int(coord.y (size - 1)))) z = max(0, min(size - 1, int(coord.z (size - 1)))) return cube[x][y][z] def computefbm(position, noisecube, w, s, octaves=5): # Unrolled summation for 5 octaves as specified in the source # Octave 0 p0 = position (s 0) n0 = samplenoisecube(p0, noisecube) # Octave 1 p1 = position (s 1) n1 = samplenoisecube(p1, noisecube) # Octave 2 p2 = position (s 2) n2 = samplenoisecube(p2, noisecube) # Octave 3 p3 = position (s 3) n3 = samplenoisecube(p3, noisecube) # Octave 4 p4 = position (s 4) n4 = samplenoisecube(p4, noisecube) # Summation with amplitude decay w < 1 return (w0 n0) + (w1 n1) + (w2 n2) + (w3 n3) + (w4 n4) Generates noise on-the-fly using gradient vectors and interpolation. More flexible but computationally heavier than pre-computed cubes. Choose when memory is constrained or dynamic noise evolution is needed. Uses explicit voxel grids rather than noise functions. Better for sharp, structured clouds but requires more memory for high resolution. Choose for non-stochastic, geometric cloud shapes. Time Complexity: O(N) per sample, where N is the number of octaves (fixed at 5). The unrolled implementation ensures constant time overhead per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the volume of the noise cube. For 64^3 single-precision floats, this is 64 \times 64 \times 64 \times 4 bytes \approx 1 MB. Measured Performance: The source states that increasing octaves above 5 decreases frame performance. Pre-calculating the noise on the host and transferring it to the GPU achieves higher frames-per-second compared to procedural generation. Strengths: Fast sampling (texture lookup), deterministic results, low computational cost per sample. Limitations: Fixed resolution (64^3) limits detail at high zoom levels; requires memory transfer; less flexible than procedural noise. When to use: Real-time volumetric cloud rendering where performance is critical and static noise patterns are acceptable. When not to use: When dynamic noise evolution or infinite resolution is required. This method was described in the context of efficient algorithms for real-time GPU volumetric cloud rendering. It builds on the concept of fractal Brownian motion (fBm) as a fractal sum of noise functions, referencing Iñigo Quilez’s work on noise generation. The specific implementation uses uniform random noise instead of Perlin noise for the base layer, transforming it into a Gaussian-like distribution via octave accumulation. The technique is applied to simulate water vapour density in clouds, leveraging the stochastic properties of noise to emulate natural textures. name: Single-pass WebGPU volume raymarching
head: raymarchScene, volume raymarcher
body: This method renders volumetric data (such as magnetic field magnitude) in a single GPU pass using WebGPU, performing analytic ray-box intersection, early-alpha termination, and optional central-difference Phong shading. It differs from standard sphere tracing Distance-field ray marching by operating on explicit 3D texture volumes rather than implicit Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), allowing for complex, non-uniform density distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture containing volume data (e.g., density or field magnitude), camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), and rendering parameters (steps, density scale, shading flags). Output: A 2D color buffer (RGBA) representing the rendered volume. Data Structures: Volume Texture: A 3D texture (e.g., texture3d<f32> in WGSL). The object space is defined as the unit box [-0.5, 0.5]^3. Texture coordinates are computed as \mathbf{pos} + 0.5 to map the box to [0, 1]^3. Transfer Function: Maps sampled density values to color and opacity, supporting linear, logarithmic, or symlog modes. Parameters: steps: Number of samples per ray across the clipped segment. Default: 256. density: Opacity scale factor for the emission-absorption transfer function. shaded: Boolean flag to enable Phong shading. Default: false. EARLYALPHA: Threshold for early ray termination. Default: 0.98. SHADETFLOOR: Minimum accumulated opacity threshold to enable gradient computation for shading. Default: 1/255. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances along the ray for the unit box [-0.5, 0.5]^3. Calculate inverse direction components: inv\diri = 1.0 / di. Pitfall Handling: If any component of \mathbf{d} is near zero (e.g., |di| < 1.0e-8), substitute inv\diri with a large finite slope (1.0e30) to avoid 0 \times \infty = \text{NaN} results from axis-parallel rays. Compute axis-aligned intersections: t{axis\min} = (\mathbf{box\min} - \mathbf{o}) \cdot inv\dir t{axis\max} = (\mathbf{box\max} - \mathbf{o}) \cdot inv\dir Determine entry and exit: t0 = \max(t{axis\min}) t1 = \min(t{axis\max}) If t0 > t1, the ray misses the box. 2. Ray Marching Loop: March along the ray from t0 to t1 in N steps (where N = \text{steps}), with step size \Delta t = (t1 - t0) / N. For each step i: Position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t0 + i \cdot \Delta t) \mathbf{d}. Sampling: Sample the volume texture at normalized coordinates \mathbf{p} + 0.5 to get density D. Transfer Function: Compute opacity \alpha and color C from D using the transfer function scaled by density. Accumulation: Use front-to-back blending: C{out} = C{in} + C \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{in} = \alpha{in} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) Early Termination: If accumulated opacity exceeds EARLYALPHA (0.98), break the loop. 3. Shading (Optional): If shaded is true and current sample opacity t \ge \text{SHADE\T\FLOOR}, compute the gradient \nabla D at the current sample position using central differences (6 gradient taps per step) to generate a Phong lighting normal. Normalize \nabla D to get the surface normal \mathbf{n}. Apply Phong lighting model using \mathbf{n}, view direction, and light direction. If accumulated opacity < \text{SHADE\T\FLOOR}, skip gradient computation to stay within the 8 ms budget. Pseudocode (Python-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EARLYALPHA = 0.98 SHADETFLOOR = 1.0 / 255.0 MAXINVDIR = 1.0e30 EPSILON = 1.0e-8 BOXMIN = [-0.5, -0.5, -0.5] BOXMAX = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] def samplevolume(texture, texcoords): # Standard 3D texture lookup with clamping to [0, 1] return texture.sample(texcoords) def transferfunction(densityval, densityscale): # Emission-absorption transfer function scaled by density alpha = 1.0 - exp(-densityscale densityval) color = densityval # Simplified linear mapping; actual implementation uses a lookup or function return color, alpha def computegradient(texture, pos): # Central differences: 6 taps (±1 along each axis) eps = 1.0 / texture.resolution dx = samplevolume(texture, pos + [eps, 0, 0]) - samplevolume(texture, pos - [eps, 0, 0]) dy = samplevolume(texture, pos + [0, eps, 0]) - samplevolume(texture, pos - [0, eps, 0]) dz = samplevolume(texture, pos + [0, 0, eps]) - samplevolume(texture, pos - [0, 0, eps]) grad = [dx, dy, dz] length = sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if length > 1e-8: return [g/length for g in grad] return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def applyphong(color, normal, viewdir, lightdir): # Standard Phong lighting model diff = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) return color (0.5 + 0.5 diff) def raymarchvolume(rayorigin, raydir, volumetexture, steps, density, shaded): # Ray-Box Intersection invdir = [MAXINVDIR if abs(d) < EPSILON else 1.0/d for d in raydir] tmin = [(BOXMIN[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmax = [(BOXMAX[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] t0 = max(tmin) t1 = min(tmax) if t0 > t1: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dt = (t1 - t0) / steps acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for i in range(steps): t = t0 + i dt pos = rayorigin + raydir t texpos = [p + 0.5 for p in pos] # Map object space [-0.5, 0.5] to texture space [0, 1] densityval = samplevolume(volumetexture, texpos) color, alpha = transferfunction(densityval, density) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[j] + color[j] weight for j in range(3)] accalpha = accalpha + weight if accalpha > EARLYALPHA: break if shaded and accalpha >= SHADETFLOOR: normal = computegradient(volumetexture, texpos) acccolor = applyphong(acccolor, normal, raydir, [0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) return [acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha] Extends this method by adding temporal filtering and explicit 4D data handling for time-varying volumetric fields like plasma simulations. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of steps. With early termination, the average case is often significantly less than N. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for accumulation; O(V) for the volume texture storage, where V is the texture resolution. Performance: Designed to run within an 8 ms budget on modern GPUs. Performance is heavily dependent on the steps parameter and the density of the volume. Strengths: Single-pass execution allows for real-time interaction. Analytic ray-box intersection is efficient. Early-alpha termination optimizes rendering of transparent regions. Limitations: Fixed step size can lead to aliasing in sparse regions or slow convergence in dense regions. Central-difference shading increases texture fetch count by 6x for shaded samples. This method is implemented in the webpic project by Ruslan Saitis, which provides a WebGPU-based visualization tool for scientific data. It is designed to run in the browser, leveraging WebGPU for high-performance parallel computation. The implementation includes features like HMR (Hot Module Replacement) for shader editing and support for various transfer functions. rusaitis/webpic, https://github.com/rusaitis/webpic, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: WebGPU Ray Marching for 4D Volumes
head: Volume4D Viewer Ray Marching, WASM Volume Rendering
body: A real-time volume rendering technique using WebGPU (WGSL) to ray march through 3D spatial data with a temporal dimension (4D), supporting interpolation between time steps and clipping via axis-aligned bounding boxes. It extends the single-pass WebGPU volume raymarching method by adding temporal filtering and explicit 4D data handling, allowing for the visualization of time-varying volumetric fields such as plasma simulations. Inputs: Volume Textures: Two 3D textures (volume, volumenext) storing scalar field values for consecutive time steps, formatted as texture3d<f32>. Color Map: A 2D texture (cmap) storing the transfer function (RGB colors), formatted as texture2d<f32>. Camera Uniforms: View, view inverse, projection, and projection inverse matrices. Settings Uniform: AABB bounds, clipping bounds, time parameters, step size, temporal filter mode, distance scale, value range (vmin, vmax), and gamma correction flag. Screen Coordinates: Vertex index used to generate a full-screen quad. Output: Color Buffer: A 3-component float color (vec3<f32>) for each pixel, optionally converted to sRGB. The following structures are passed via uniform buffers or bind groups in WGSL: Unverified code. Ray Creation: Compute far point in NDC: far = vec4<f32>((px 2. - 1.), -1., 1.). Flip Y: far.y = -1.. Transform to world: farw = viewinv projinv far. Normalize W: farw /= farw.w + 1e-4 to avoid division by zero. Compute near point: near = vec4<f32>((px 2. - 1.), 1., 1.). Flip Y: near.y = -1.. Transform to world: nearw = viewinv projinv near. Normalize W: nearw /= nearw.w + 1e-4. Ray origin: nearw.xyz. Direction: normalize(farw.xyz - nearw.xyz). 3. AABB Intersection: tMin = (boxmin - ray.orig) / ray.dir. tMax = (boxmax - ray.orig) / ray.dir. t1 = min(tMin, tMax). t2 = max(tMin, tMax). tNear = max(max(t1.x, t1.y), t1.z). tFar = min(min(t2.x, t2.y), t2.z). If tNear > tFar, return transparent black vec4<f32>(0.). 4. Clipping AABB Adjustment: aabbsize = aabb.max - aabb.min. aabbmin = aabb.min + (slicemin aabbsize). aabbmax = aabb.max - ((1. - slicemax) aabbsize). Note: Source comments indicate 'zxy for tensorf alignment', implying potential coordinate axis permutation in the underlying tensor format. Re-calculate tNear and tFar with adjusted bounds. If no intersection, return black. 5. Ray Initialization: start = max(0., tNear) + 1e-4. ray.orig += start ray.dir. iters = 0u. color = vec3<f32>(0.). transmittance = 1.. distancescale = settings.distancescale. pos = ray.orig. earlystoppingt = 1. / 255.. stepsizeg = settings.stepsize. 6. Marching Loop: Call nextpos(&pos, stepsizeg, ray.dir) to get samplepos (vec4 containing normalized sample position and stepsize). Extract stepsize = samplepos.w. Sample volume at samplepos.xyz. Apply transfer function. sigma = colortf.a (1. - 1e-6) to prevent artifacts from sigma exactly one. ai = 1. - pow(1. - sigma, stepsize distancescale). color += transmittance ai samplecolor. transmittance = 1. - ai. Early stopping: if exp(-transmittance) <= earlystoppingt, break. Clipping check: slicetest = any(samplepos.xyz < settings.clipping.min) || any(samplepos.xyz > settings.clipping.max). If true, break. Increment iters by 1u. 7. Next Position Calculation: samplepos = ((pos) - aabb.min) / aabbsize. pos += raydir stepsize. Return vec4<f32>(samplepos, stepsize). 8. Temporal Sampling: If temporalfilter == FILTERNEAREST, return samplecurr. Else, timefraction = fract(settings.time f32(settings.timesteps - 1)). Return mix(samplecurr, samplenext, timefraction). 9. Volume Sampling: Flip Y: posm = vec3<f32>(pos.x, 1. - pos.y). samplecurr = textureSampleLevel(volume, volumesampler, posm, 0.).r. samplenext = textureSampleLevel(volumenext, volumesampler, posm, 0.).r. 10. Color Map Sampling: valuen = (value - settings.vmin) / (settings.vmax - settings.vmin). textureSampleLevel(cmap, cmapsampler, vec2<f32>(valuen, 0.5), 0.). 11. Gamma Correction: If settings.gammacorrection == 1u, apply linear to sRGB conversion. Cutoff: color.rgb < vec3<f32>(0.0031308). Higher: vec3<f32>(1.055) pow(color.rgb, vec3<f32>(1.0 / 2.4)) - 0.055. Lower: color.rgb 12.92. Return mix(higher, lower, cutoff) with original alpha. 12. Render Pass: Set bind group 0 and bind group 1. Draw 4 vertices (0..4) for 1 instance. Unverified code. settings.volumeaabb.min) / aabbsize # Clipping Check if any(sampleposnorm < settings.clipping.min) or any(sampleposnorm > settings.clipping.max): break # Temporal & Volume Sampling samplecolor = samplevolume(sampleposnorm, settings) # Marching sigma = samplecolor.a (1.0 - The number of steps is determined by the volume depth divided by stepsize. Memory Complexity: Constant per pixel, plus storage for the two 3D volume textures and the 2D color map texture. Performance: Real-time performance is achieved on WebGPU-compatible hardware. Performance scales with resolution and the number of time steps (though only two textures are loaded at once). When to use: Real-time visualization of time-varying volumetric data in a browser. When not to use: High-fidelity offline rendering requiring adaptive sampling or complex transfer functions not supported by 1D lookup. name: Volume Ray Casting with Marching
head: Marching along the point of view, Ray Casting with Adaptive Step Size and Early Ray Termination, Volume Rendering via Ray Casting, Volume ray tracing
body: Volume Ray Casting with Marching is an image-order rendering technique that casts rays from the camera through a volumetric scalar field, sampling the field at discrete intervals to accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar data (such as medical CT scans or atmospheric density) by projecting it onto a 2D screen while preserving depth cues and transparency. It integrates color and opacity along a ray. Builds on Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering. The method computes the final pixel color by integrating light contribution along a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. The integration proceeds from the camera outward (front-to-back) through the volume bounds. Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}. Volume 3D texture with dimensions V{dims} = (Vx, Vy, Vz) and bounding box [box{min}, box{max}]. 2D colormap texture for the transfer function. Parameters: step size scale dt{scale}, early termination threshold (default 0.95 opacity). Outputs: Final pixel color and accumulated opacity. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values; 16-bit data is normalized by 65536.0. Colormap Texture: 2D texture mapping normalized scalar values (x-axis) to RGBA, with y-axis fixed at 0.5. Ray State: Tracks entry/exit distances (t{entry}, t{exit}), current position p, and accumulators C, A. 1. Calculate Back Plate Position: Determine the position of the back of the volume bounding box relative to the camera to establish the maximum ray extent. 2. Calculate Ray Direction: Normalize the view ray direction vector \mathbf{d}. 3. Calculate Front Plate Position: Determine the position of the front of the volume bounding box. 4. Intersect Ray with Volume Bounds: Compute the entry distance t0 and exit distance t1 where the ray intersects the bounding box defined by box{min} and box{max}. If t0 > t1, discard the ray (the ray does not intersect the volume). Clamp the entry distance to non-negative values: t{entry} = \max(t0, 0.0). 5. Calculate Step Size: Determine the step size \Delta t based on the volume dimensions, ray direction, and a scaling factor dt{scale}. The base step is derived from the voxel traversal rates: \Delta t = dt{scale} \times \min \left( \frac{1}{|dx| \cdot Vx}, \frac{1}{|dy| \cdot Vy}, \frac{1}{|dz| \cdot Vz} \right). Note: In implementation, this is often computed as 1.0 / (vec3(volumedims) abs(raydir)). 6. Generate Jitter Offset: To reduce aliasing artifacts (specifically "wood grain" patterns), generate a random offset for the starting position within the first voxel. The offset is calculated using a hash function (e.g., wanghash) on the fragment coordinates: \text{offset} = \text{wang\hash}(\text{int}(gl\FragCoord.x + 640.0 \cdot gl\FragCoord.y)). 7. Initialize Sample Position: Set the initial sample position p at the entry point plus the jittered offset: p = \mathbf{o} + (t{entry} + \text{offset} \cdot \Delta t) \cdot \mathbf{d}. 8. Marching Loop: Iterate along the ray from t{entry} to t{exit} with step \Delta t. In each iteration: a. Sample Volume Value: Sample the scalar value v from the volume texture at position p. For 16-bit data: v = \text{texture}(\text{volume}, p).r / 65536.0. For 8-bit/float data: v = \text{texture}(\text{volume}, p).r. b. Map to Color: Sample the colormap texture using the normalized value v to get the transfer function output: \text{trans\sample} = \text{texture}(\text{colormap}, \text{vec2}(v, 0.5)). c. Combine Color and Opacity: Construct the sample color C{sample} and opacity A{sample}: C{sample} = \text{trans\sample}.rgb A{sample} = v \cdot \text{trans\sample}.a. d. Apply Opacity Correction: Correct the sample opacity for the step size to approximate the integral of absorption over the segment: A{corrected} = 1 - (1 - A{sample})^{dt{scale}}. e. Front-to-Back Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity into the running totals C and A: C \leftarrow C + (1.0 - A) \cdot A{corrected} \cdot C{sample} A \leftarrow A + (1.0 - A) \cdot A{corrected}. f. Advance Position: Move to the next sample point: p \leftarrow p + \mathbf{d} \cdot \Delta t. g. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If the accumulated opacity A \ge 0.95, break the loop. 9. Update Controller and View Matrix: After the marching pass, update the controller and view matrix based on the previous state, applying rescaling if necessary. 10. Draw Frame and Generate Color Maps: Render the frame around the volume and generate any necessary color maps for the current frame. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def rmul(self, s): return self.mul(s) def add(self, o): return Vec3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return Vec3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def truediv(self, s): return Vec3(self.x/s, self.y/s, self.z/s) def abs(self): return Vec3(abs(self.x), abs(self.y), abs(self.z)) def min(self): return min(self.x, self.y, self.z) def max(self): return max(self.x, self.y, self.z) def volumeraycasting(cameraorigin, cameradirection, volumetexture, colormaptexture, volumedims, boxmin, boxmax, dtscale, tthresh, is16bit, fragcoord): # 1. Intersect ray with bounding box [boxmin, boxmax] t0, t1 = intersectbox(cameraorigin, cameradirection, boxmin, boxmax) if t0 is None or t1 is None: return Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 tentry = max(t0, 0.0) texit = t1 # 2. Calculate step size dtvec = Vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) / (volumedims cameradirection.abs()) dt = dtscale dtvec.min() # 3. Generate jitter offset offset = wanghash(int(fragcoord.x + 640.0 fragcoord.y)) # 4. Initialize position and accumulators p = cameraorigin + (tentry + offset dt) cameradirection acccolor = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 t = tentry + offset dt # 5. name: Shadow Occlusion via Occlusion Camera
head: Light-space shadow maps, Volumetric shadow maps
body: This method uses a dedicated child camera (the "Occlusion Camera") to render a depth map from the light's perspective, allowing scene geometry to block volumetric light beams. Unlike standard URP shadows which depend on the light's Shadow Type and global URP shadow settings, this occlusion map operates independently, enabling volumetric shadows even when the light casts no regular geometric shadows. It is integrated into the ray marching shader, which computes shadow coordinates at the ray's entry and exit points from the volume. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Scene geometry (filtered by Culling Mask), light parameters (type, position, orientation), and the Occlusion Camera configuration. Outputs: A depth texture (Occlusion Map) and the final volumetric lighting contribution where shadow density is applied. Data Structures Occlusion Map: A depth texture generated by the Occlusion Camera. Resolution is configurable from 32 to 4096, with a default of 256. Shadow Coordinates: Computed at the ray's entry and exit points from the volume, then interpolated along the ray for each marching step. Steps 1. Render Occlusion Map: The system adds a lightweight depth-only renderer to the URP Asset's renderer list if not already present. The Occlusion Camera renders a depth-only pass of the scene, respecting the Culling Mask and Near Clip Distance. For Spot Lights: The capture projection uses a perspective frustum matching the spot angle. For Rect/Disc Area Lights: The capture projection is orthographic. For Point Lights: A specific Bake Mode is required: Half Sphere: Captures a 160-degree view in one render, oriented either toward the camera or a fixed direction. Cubemap One Face Per Frame: Captures one face of a cubemap per frame. Cubemap All 6 Faces Per Frame: Captures all six faces per frame (slowest). 2. Compute Shadow Coordinates: In the ray marching shader, shadow coordinates are calculated at the ray's entry point into the volume and at its exit point. 3. Interpolate: Shadow coordinates are interpolated between the entry and exit points along the ray for each marching step. 4. Sample Occlusion: The shader samples the Occlusion Map texture at the interpolated coordinates to determine shadow density. 5. Apply Shadow: The volumetric beam intensity is blended toward the configured Shadow Color (Intensity and Color parameter) based on the sampled density, rather than blending to pure black. Parameters Resolution: 32 to 4096. Default 256. Higher values are needed for fine patterns like window bars, grilles, or foliage. Intensity and Color: Defines the color the shadowed part of the beam blends toward. Culling Mask: Layers that occlude the beam. The TransparentFX layer is excluded by default. Include Transparent: If enabled, transparent geometry and 2D sprites block light, provided their material writes depth via a DepthOnly pass. Near Clip Distance: The near plane of the Occlusion Camera. Used when the light is inside a model (e.g., a lamp). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Point Light Performance: Cubemap modes are significantly slower than Half Sphere. All 6 Faces Per Frame is the slowest option. Thin Occluders: Raymarch Quality controls sampling fineness; thin occluders may appear blurry on lower presets. Transparent Geometry: Transparent objects only occlude if they explicitly write depth. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Depends on the Occlusion Camera's resolution and the Point Light Bake Mode. Half Sphere is the fastest; Cubemap All 6 Faces Per Frame is the slowest. Strengths: Independent of standard shadow settings; allows volumetric shadows on lights that do not cast geometric shadows. Limitations: Requires a depth-writing pass from transparent objects for full occlusion; point lights have high performance costs for full coverage. When to use/not: Use when volumetric beams need to be blocked by geometry without relying on standard URP shadow settings. Avoid when point light performance is critical and full cubemap coverage is required. This technique is implemented in Unity's Universal Render Pipeline (URP) via third-party volumetric lighting assets (e.g., Kronnect). It addresses the visual artifact where volumetric beams pass through walls and props, creating "glowing cone mesh" appearances without occlusion. name: Basic Volumetric Cone Lighting
head: First light ray, Volumetric raymarching loop, Depth-Based Stopping, Scene depth culling
body: Basic Volumetric Cone Lighting is a post-processing technique that renders a volumetric light beam shaped like a cone originating from a light position and pointing in a specific direction, using screen-space raymarching. It solves the problem of rendering visible light shafts in real-time by accumulating light density along rays cast from the camera into the scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: inputColor (current frame buffer color), uv (screen coordinates), depthBuffer (scene depth texture), cameraPosition (world space), cameraFar (max render distance), lightPosition (world space), lightDirection (normalized world space vector), coneAngle (aperture in degrees), STEPSIZE (march increment), NUMSTEPS (loop count). Outputs: outputColor (final pixel color). Data Structures: depthBuffer: Texture containing depth values for each pixel. projectionMatrixInverse: Inverse of the camera's projection matrix, used to convert coordinates from clip-space to view-space. viewMatrixInverse: Inverse of the camera's view matrix (world matrix), used to convert coordinates from view-space to world-space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mainImage(inputColor, uv, depthBuffer, cameraFar, projectionMatrixInverse, viewMatrixInverse, cameraPosition, lightPosition, lightDirection, coneAngle, STEPSIZE, NUMSTEPS): # 1. Sample depth and reconstruct world position depth = readDepth(depthBuffer, uv) worldPosition = getWorldPosition(uv, depth, projectionMatrixInverse, viewMatrixInverse) # 2. Define ray parameters rayOrigin = cameraPosition rayDir = normalize(worldPosition - rayOrigin) lightPos = lightPosition lightDir = normalize(lightDirection) # 3. Calculate scene depth for culling sceneDepth = length(worldPosition - cameraPosition) # 4. Initialize lighting variables coneAngleRad = radians(coneAngle) halfConeAngleRad = coneAngleRad 0.5 fogAmount = 0.0 lightIntensity = 1.0 t = STEPSIZE # 5. Raymarching loop for i in range(NUMSTEPS): # Calculate current sample position samplePos = rayOrigin + rayDir t # Depth-based stopping: break if beyond scene geometry or camera far plane if t > sceneDepth or t > cameraFar: break # Cone shape check: calculate angle between sample-to-light vector and light direction toSample = normalize(samplePos - lightPos) cosAngle = dot(toSample, lightDir) # Skip samples outside the cone aperture if cosAngle < cos(halfConeAngleRad): t += STEPSIZE continue # Attenuation based on distance to light source distanceToLight = length(samplePos - lightPos) attenuation = exp(-0.05 distanceToLight) # Accumulate light fogAmount += attenuation lightIntensity # Advance ray t += STEPSIZE # 6. Combine with input color outputColor = inputColor + fogAmount return outputColor def readDepth(depthBuffer, uv): return depthBuffer[uv] def getWorldPosition(uv, depth, projectionMatrixInverse, viewMatrixInverse): clipx = uv[0] 2.0 - 1.0 clipy = uv[1] 2.0 - 1.0 clipy = -clipy viewspace = [clipx, clipy, -1.0, 1.0] viewspace = matmul(projectionMatrixInverse, viewspace) viewspace = [v / viewspace[3] for v in viewspace[:3]] worldspace = matmul(viewMatrixInverse, [viewspace[0], viewspace[1], viewspace[2], 1.0]) return (worldspace[0], worldspace[1], worldspace[2]) def matmul(matrix, vector): return tuple(sum(matrix[r][c] vector[c] for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)) def normalize(v): mag = length(v) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def length(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] import math def radians(deg): return deg math.pi / 180.0 def cos(x): return math.cos(x) def exp(x): return math.exp(x) Parameters: cameraFar: Depth limit beyond which nothing is visible or rendered. coneAngle: Represents how wide the spotlight aperture is. STEPSIZE: Step size for raymarching. NUMSTEPS: Number of steps in the raymarching loop. 0.05: Exponential decay constant for light attenuation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Through-wall leakage: Without depth-based stopping, the light ray continues marching beyond visible geometry, causing light to appear through walls and objects, breaking realism and wasting performance on intensive raymarching beyond visible areas.
