name: WebGL2 Volume Raycasting
head: VolRen, Volume Raycasting Fragment Shader (Colormap/Segmentation/Scalar), Web-based volumetric data explorer
body: WebGL2 Volume Raycasting is a lightweight, web-based volumetric data explorer that renders 3D scalar fields using WebGL2 raymarching within a fragment shader. It supports 8-bit, 16-bit, and float data types, with optional segmentation masks and clipping planes. Unlike general-purpose SDF-based sphere tracing which targets implicit surfaces, this method performs front-to-back alpha blending over a discrete 3D texture grid to visualize scalar fields. It is distinguished by its specific WebGL2 implementation details, including handling of integer texture formats for 16-bit data and a fixed 180x1 colormap texture. The method operates by casting rays from a camera through a 3D volume texture, sampling scalar values, and compositing them into a 2D image using alpha blending. Inputs: Volume Texture: A 3D texture (gl.TEXTURE0) containing the scalar field with dimensions volDims[0], volDims[1], volDims[2]. 8-bit: Format R8, Type UNSIGNEDBYTE, Filter LINEAR. 16-bit: Format R16UI, Type UNSIGNEDSHORT, Filter NEAREST. Float: Format R32F, Type FLOAT, Filter LINEAR. Colormap Texture: A 2D texture (gl.TEXTURE1) of size 180x1 pixels, format RGBA8. Segmentation Texture (Optional): A 3D texture (gl.TEXTURE2) of dimensions volDims, format R8, Type UNSIGNEDBYTE, Filter NEAREST, Wrapping CLAMPTOEDGE. Uniforms: highp usampler3D volume: The volume texture sampler. highp sampler2D colormap: The colormap texture sampler. bool usecolormap: Enables colormap mode. bool useseg: Enables segmentation mode. vec3 volumescale: Scaling factor for the volume. vec3 volumedims: Dimensions of the volume. float dtscale: Step size scaling factor (Default: 1.0). ivec2 comp: Comparison coordinates for inversion logic. vec3 colors[25]: Array of colors for segmentation IDs (implied global constant or defined elsewhere). Vertex Shader Inputs: pos: Vertex position. eyepos: Camera eye position in world space. Outputs: out vec4 color: The final fragment color. The volume is stored as a 3D texture where the internal format depends on the bit depth of the source data. The colormap is a 1D lookup table represented as a 180x1 2D texture. 1. Vertex Shader Transformation: Compute volume translation: volumetranslation = vec3(0.5) - volumescale 0.5. Transform vertex position: glPosition = projview vec4(pos volumescale + volumetranslation, 1.0). Compute transformed eye position: transformedeye = (eyepos - volumetranslation) / volumescale. Compute ray direction in object space: vraydir = pos - transformedeye. 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Normalize ray direction: raydir = normalize(vraydir). Intersect ray with the volume bounding box defined by boxmin and boxmax using the slab method to obtain entry and exit distances thit.x (t0) and thit.y (t1). If thit.x > thit.y, discard the fragment (ray misses the volume). Clamp start distance: thit.x = max(thit.x, 0.0). 3. Step Size Calculation: Compute step vector components: dtvec = 1.0 / (vec3(volumedims) abs(raydir)). Compute step size: dt = dtscale min(dtvec.x, min(dtvec.y, dtvec.z)). 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize accumulated color: color = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). Initialize current position: p = transformedeye + thit.x raydir. Loop t from thit.x to thit.y with step dt: Sample Volume: Sample the volume texture at p: valraw = texture(volume, p).r. Normalization: If data type is 16-bit: val = float(valraw) / 65536.0. If p is outside [0.0, 1.0] in any dimension, set val = 0.0. Color/Alpha Computation: Determine valcolor based on mode: Colormap Mode (usecolormap == true): transsample = texture(colormap, vec2(val, 0.5)). valcolor = vec4(transsample.rgb, val transsample.a). Segmentation Mode (useseg == true): Convert segmentation value to integer: seg = int(texture(segvolume, p).r). Loop k from 0 to min(seg, 24): If k == seg, valcolor = vec4(colors[k], 1.0). Scalar Mode (Default): valcolor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, val). Inversion Logic: Check inversion condition: invert = (comp.x == int(glFragCoord.x)) || (comp.y == int(glFragCoord.y)). If invert is true: Colormap/Segmentation Modes: valcolor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Scalar Mode: valcolor.a = 1.0 - val. Opacity Correction: Apply Beer-Lambert law approximation for step size: valcolor.a = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - valcolor.a, dtscale). Alpha Blending: color.rgb += (1.0 - color.a) valcolor.a valcolor.rgb. color.a += (1.0 - color.a) valcolor.a. Early Termination: If color.a >= 0.95, break loop. Advance Ray: p += raydir dt. 5. Final Output: Set glFragColor = color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastvolume(projview, volumescale, eyepos, pos, volumesampler, colormapsampler, usecolormap, useseg, volumedims, dtscale, comp, colors, fragcoord): # Vertex shader logic volumetranslation = vec3(0.5) - volumescale 0.5 transformedeye = (eyepos - volumetranslation) / volumescale vraydir = pos - transformedeye # Fragment shader logic raydir = normalize(vraydir) # Slab intersection with box [0,1]^3 t0 = (vec3(0.0) - transformedeye) / raydir t1 = (vec3(1.0) - transformedeye) / raydir tmin = min(t0, t1) tmax = max(t0, t1) thitx = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z) thity = min(min(tmax.x, tmax.y), tmax.z) if thitx > thity: return None # Discard fragment thitx = max(thitx, 0.0) dtvec = 1.0 / (volumedims abs(raydir)) dt = dtscale min(dtvec.x, min(dtvec.y, dtvec.z)) p = transformedeye + thitx raydir acccolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) invert = (comp.x == int(fragcoord.x)) or (comp.y == int(fragcoord.y)) t = thitx while t < thity: valraw = volumesampler.sample(p).r # Normalize 16-bit data if volumesampler.is16bit: val = float(valraw) / 65536.0 else: val = valraw # Boundary check if not (0.0 <= p.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= p.y <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= p.z <= 1.0): val = 0.0 if usecolormap: transsample = colormapsampler.sample(vec2(val, 0.5)) valcolor = vec4(transsample.rgb, val transsample.a) elif useseg: segval = int(volumesampler.sampleseg(p).r) valcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for k in range(min(segval, 24) + 1): if k == segval: valcolor = vec4(colors[k], 1.0) break else: valcolor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, val) if invert: if usecolormap or useseg: valcolor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) else: valcolor.a = 1.0 - val valcolor.a = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - valcolor.a, dtscale) acccolor.rgb += (1.0 - acccolor.a) valcolor.a valcolor.rgb acccolor.a += (1.0 - acccolor.a) valcolor.a if acccolor.a >= 0.95: break p += raydir dt t += dt return acccolor dtscale: Controls step size scaling. Default is 1.0. Lower values increase sampling density and quality but reduce performance. targetFrameTime: JavaScript variable set to 32 ms to manage frame rate. Non-uniform Volumes: The vertex shader transformation assumes a specific centering logic. Non-uniform size volumes may require different transformation to center properly, as noted in the source's TODO comment. Offset Initialization: The initialization of the ray start position affects visual quality. "With offset is bad for flat surfaces, without has wood grain". Missing Uniforms: The colors array used in segmentation mode is not declared as a uniform in the provided shader code, implying it is a global constant or defined elsewhere. The segmentation texture sampler is also not explicitly passed as a uniform in the provided list, though logic exists. Filtering: LINEAR filtering is used for 8-bit and float volumes, while NEAREST filtering is used for 16-bit volumes, likely due to integer texture limitations. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps along the ray, which is determined by the volume dimensions, ray direction, and dtscale. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D volume texture and the 2D colormap texture. Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on the volume resolution and the dtscale parameter. WebGL2 allows for efficient texture sampling, but fragment shader execution time can be high for large volumes or small step sizes. Strengths: Lightweight, web-based, supports multiple data types (8-bit, 16-bit, float), supports segmentation masks. Limitations: Limited to scalar field visualization, no advanced lighting models (default is white scalar), potential precision issues with 16-bit integer textures, missing uniform declarations in source code. name: Atmospheric scattering models
head: Atmospheric scattering, Planetary atmosphere rendering, Volumetric atmospheric rendering
body: Atmospheric scattering models render the light interaction within a planetary atmosphere or volumetric cloud layer by solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along view rays. This family is distinguished from generic volume rendering by its reliance on analytical density profiles (e.g., exponential falloff) and specific phase functions (Rayleigh, Henyey-Greenstein) tailored to gaseous or particulate media, rather than arbitrary voxel densities. It differs from billboard-based methods by providing true volumetric depth and internal shadowing. The family operates on the principle of discretizing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. The integration computes the accumulated color C and transmittance T by marching through a medium defined by density \rho(\mathbf{p}), scattering coefficient \sigmas, and absorption coefficient \sigmaa. The core integration step for a segment of length \Delta t is: 1. Density Evaluation: Sample \rho at the current position \mathbf{p}. 2. Extinction: Compute the extinction coefficient \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa. 3. Transmittance Update: Update the ray's transmittance T using Beer-Lambert law: T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\sigmat \rho \Delta t}. 4. Inscattering: Compute the light contributed by the segment. For single scattering, this involves the phase function P(\theta) and the light source radiance L{source} attenuated by the optical depth to the light. 5. Accumulation: Add the inscattered light to the accumulated color, weighted by the current transmittance: C \leftarrow C + T \cdot \sigmas \rho \Delta t \cdot L{scattered}. The process terminates when T falls below a threshold (e.g., 0.01) or the ray exits the volume bounds. A real-time technique for rendering volumetric clouds by discretizing the RTE along view rays and approximating light transport with a single scattering event. It combines procedural noise for density generation with a physically-based lighting model to produce dynamic, three-dimensional cloudscapes. It is distinguished from multi-scattering methods by its computational efficiency, trading physical accuracy for performance, and from billboard-based methods by its ability to render volumetric depth and internal structure. See Ray Marching with Single Scattering. A technique for rendering planetary atmospheres using single scattering, exponential density falloff, and the Rayleigh phase function. It solves the RTE for a spherical atmosphere by marching along view rays and light rays to compute inscattered sunlight and shadowing. It is distinguished from Ray Marching with Single Scattering by its specific application to planetary spheres with analytical density profiles and its handling of shadow rays for occlusion. See Atmospheric Ray Marching. A unified rendering implementation for volumetric clouds and atmosphere using raymarching as the main method. It renders the atmosphere using an approach with multiple precomputed Look-up tables (LUTs) proposed by Sébastien Hillaire, and volumetric clouds using a pre-computed three-dimensional texture setup storing procedurally generated noise described by Andrew Schneider. Images are rendered in high dynamic range before applying post-processing effects and using adaptive luminance to transform the image into LDR for presentation. A method where atmospheric scattering effects are precomputed and stored, using an octree-based LOD to provide cloud density for lightning scattering. The unified approach of combining atmosphere LUTs and cloud noise textures was presented by Matěj Sakmary in a 2022 bachelor thesis. The underlying survey of cloud modeling and rendering techniques, including precomputation methods, was published in a 2020 survey. name: Ray Marching with Single Scattering
head: Real-time Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Real-time Volumetric Rendering, Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Ray Marching
body: Ray marching with single scattering is a real-time technique for rendering volumetric clouds by discretizing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along view rays and approximating light transport with a single scattering event. It combines procedural noise for density generation with a physically-based lighting model to produce dynamic, three-dimensional cloudscapes. It is distinguished from multi-scattering methods by its computational efficiency, trading physical accuracy for performance, and from billboard-based methods by its ability to render volumetric depth and internal structure. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o}, normalized view direction \mathbf{d}, sun direction \mathbf{d}{\text{sun}}, sun color \mathbf{C}{\text{sun}}, ambient color \mathbf{C}{\text{amb}}, cloud bounding box (AABB), cloud layer height limits (h{\min}, h{\max}), and procedural noise textures (Weather Map, Base Noise, Edge Detail). Outputs: Final pixel color C{\text{final}}. Data Structures: 1. Weather Map (2D Texture): Format: RGBA, Float32. Red Channel: Base cloud coverage (0.0 to 1.0). Blue Channel: Cloud type (0.0=stratus, 0.5=stratocumulus, 1.0=cumulus). 2. Base Noise Texture (3D Texture, 128 \times 128 \times 128): Red Channel: Combined Perlin-Worley noise. Green, Blue, Alpha Channels: Low-frequency inverse Worley noise at increasing frequencies. 3. Edge Detail Texture (3D Texture, 32 \times 32 \times 32): Channels: High-frequency inverse Worley noise at increasing frequencies. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{s} - \mathbf{o}), where \mathbf{s} is the screen position and \mathbf{o} is the eye position. Compute sky color using \mathbf{d}. Initialize main transmittance T = 1.0, accumulated color C = 0, and distance t = 0.0. Set scene variables (scattering/absorption coefficients) based on time of day. 2. Main Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to MAXSTEPS. Calculate position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d}. Bounding Check: If \mathbf{p} is outside the cloud bounding box or cloud layer height limits, skip or break. Density Evaluation: Sample base noise \rho{\text{base}} from the 3D texture at \mathbf{p}. Sample edge detail \rho{\text{edge}} from the 32x32x32 texture at \mathbf{p}. Combine noise: Use fBm of low-frequency inverse Worley channels to modulate the Perlin-Worley noise. Apply height modulation: Modulate density with a linear gradient from h{\min} to h{\max}. Apply weather map: Scale density by coverage from the Weather Map Red channel. Final density \rho = \text{clamp}(\text{combined noise}, 0.0, 1.0). Optimization: If \rho < 0.01, increment t by STEPSIZE and continue. Light Marching (Single Scattering): Initialize light transmittance T{\text{light}} = 1.0, light distance t{\text{light}} = 0.0. Compute light direction \mathbf{d}{\text{light}} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{d}{\text{sun}} - \mathbf{p}). Iterate j from 0 to MAXSTEPSLIGHT. Calculate light position \mathbf{p}{\text{light}} = \mathbf{p} + t{\text{light}} \mathbf{d}{\text{light}}. Sample density \rho{\text{light}} at \mathbf{p}{\text{light}}. Update light transmittance: T{\text{light}} \leftarrow T{\text{light}} \cdot e^{-\rho{\text{light}} \cdot \text{extinctionCoeff} \cdot \text{STEP\SIZE\LIGHT} \cdot 1.5}. If T{\text{light}} < 0.05, break light loop. Increment t{\text{light}} by STEPSIZELIGHT. Scattering Calculation: Compute phase function value fp using \mathbf{d} and \mathbf{d}{\text{light}}. Compute Ls = \mathbf{C}{\text{sun}} \cdot T{\text{light}} \cdot fp \cdot 6.0. Compute La = \mathbf{C}{\text{amb}} \cdot 0.7. Compute local scattering contribution: S = (Ls + La) \cdot T \cdot \rho \cdot \text{STEP\SIZE}. Accumulation: C \leftarrow C + S. Update main transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\rho \cdot \text{extinctionCoeff} \cdot \text{STEP\SIZE} \cdot 1.5}. If T < 0.01, break main loop. Increment t by STEPSIZE. If t > 20.0, break main loop. 3. Final Composition: C{\text{final}} = C + T \cdot \text{sky}. Output C{\text{final}}. Formulas: Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: fp(\cos \theta) = \left( \text{mix}(F, B, 0.4) \right) \cdot 0.4 Where: F = \frac{1 - g1^2}{(1 + g1^2 - 2 g1 \cos \theta)^{1.5}} B = \frac{1 - g2^2}{(1 + g2^2 - 2 g2 \cos \theta)^{1.5}} In-scattered Radiance (Ls): Ls = L{\text{sun}} T fp Ambient Radiance (La): La = L{\text{ambient}} (1 - e^{-\rho}) Transmittance Update: Tk = T{k-1} e^{-\alpha \rho \Delta s} Radiance Update: Lk = L{k-1} + (La + Ls) Tk \Delta s Sky Color: \text{sky} = \text{mix}(\text{skyBottom}, \text{skyTop}, \text{clamp}(\mathbf{d}y \cdot 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0)) Parameters: MAXSTEPS: 50. STEPSIZE: 0.08. MAXSTEPSLIGHT: 5. STEPSIZELIGHT: 0.6. scatteringCoeff: 1.5 (sunset), 1.2 (day). absorptionCoeff: 0.4 (sunset), 0.2 (day). extinctionCoeff: scatteringCoeff + absorptionCoeff. alpha (\alpha): Light absorption coefficient. g1: 0.7 (forward anisotropy). g2: -0.2 (backward anisotropy). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision & Boundaries: The algorithm uses a fixed maximum distance of 20.0 and a transmittance threshold of 0.01 to terminate early. WebGL 1 does not support dynamic loop bounds, requiring STEPSIZE and STEPSIZELIGHT to be hardcoded constants. Degenerate Input: Aliasing artifacts become noticeable when the camera is positioned inside the cloud volume. The method cannot render two clouds vertically layered at the same position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsinglescattering(cameraorigin, cameradir, sundir, suncolor, ambientcolor, weathermap, basenoise, edgedetail, boundsmin, boundsmax, hmin, hmax, maxsteps=50, stepsize=0.08, maxstepslight=5, stepsizelight=0.6): # Initialize transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) t = 0.0 # Sky color calculation skytop = vec3(0.2, 0.4, 0.8) # Day default skybottom = vec3(0.7, 0.85, 1.0) # Day default screenrange = clamp(cameradir.y 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) sky = mix(skybottom, skytop, screenrange) # Scene variables (simplified for day) scatteringcoeff = 1.2 absorptioncoeff = 0.2 extinctioncoeff = scatteringcoeff + absorptioncoeff for i in range(maxsteps): p = cameraorigin + t cameradir # Bounding box check if not isinsidebox(p, boundsmin, boundsmax): t += stepsize continue # Height check if p.y < hmin or p.y > hmax: t += stepsize continue # Density evaluation # 1. Base noise (Perlin-Worley) density = samplebasenoise(p) # 2. Edge detail erosion edge = sampleedgedetail(p) density = edge # Simplified erosion # 3. Weather map modulation weather = sampleweathermap(p.xy) # Project to 2D density = weather.r # Coverage # 4. Height modulation heightfactor = smoothstep(hmin, hmax, p.y) density = heightfactor density = clamp(density, 0.0, 1.0) # Optimization: Skip low density if density < 0.01: t += stepsize continue # Light marching lightdir = normalize(sundir - p) transmittancelight = 1.0 tlight = 0.0 for j in range(maxstepslight): plight = p + tlight lightdir densitylight = samplebasenoise(plight) # Simplified: using same noise for light path # Beer-Lambert for light transmittancelight = exp(-densitylight extinctioncoeff stepsizelight 1.5) if transmittancelight < 0.05: break tlight += stepsizelight # Scattering costheta = dot(cameradir, lightdir) phase = henyeygreenstein(costheta, g1=0.7, g2=-0.2) # In-scattered light ls = suncolor transmittancelight phase 6.0 la = ambientcolor 0.7 # Accumulate scattered = ls + la accumulatedcolor += transmittance density scattered stepsize # Update transmittance transmittance = exp(-density extinctioncoeff stepsize 1.5) if transmittance < 0.01: break t += stepsize if t > 20.0: break finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + transmittance sky return finalcolor def henyeygreenstein(costheta, g1=0.7, g2=-0.2): denom1 = 1.0 + g1g1 - 2.0g1costheta forward = (1.0 - g1g1) / pow(denom1, 1.5) denom2 = 1.0 + g2g2 - 2.0g2costheta backward = (1.0 - g2g2) / pow(denom2, 1.5) return mix(forward, backward, 0.4) 0.4 def isinsidebox(p, min, max): return p.x >= min.x and p.x <= max.x and p.y >= min.y and p.y <= max.y and p.z >= min.z and p.z <= max.z def samplebasenoise(p): # Returns density from 3D texture (128x128x128) return texture3D(basenoise, p).r def sampleedgedetail(p): # Returns erosion factor from 3D texture (32x32x32) return texture3D(edgedetail, p).r def sampleweathermap(p): # Returns coverage from 2D texture return texture2D(weathermap, p) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) per pixel, where N is the number of main ray steps and M is the number of light ray steps. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D noise textures (128^3 and 32^3) and the 2D weather map. Performance: Achieves 2.6 ms frame time at 1440p on an AMD Ryzen 5 7600X CPU and AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT GPU. Strengths: Real-time performance; dynamic wind simulation via texture scrolling; configurable cloud types and weather patterns. Limitations: Single scattering approximation lacks physical accuracy for thick clouds. Noticeable aliasing occurs when the camera is inside the cloud volume. The approach cannot render two clouds vertically layered at the same position. Scaling: Performance scales with cloud layer thickness; reducing thickness yields major performance gains by enabling smaller/fewer ray marching steps. When to use: Suitable for real-time applications requiring dynamic, volumetric cloudscapes where performance is prioritized over strict physical accuracy. When not to use: Unsuitable for offline rendering requiring multiple scattering, or for close-up camera shots inside the volume where aliasing becomes prominent. The method originates from real-time volumetric rendering techniques for games and simulations, specifically focusing on cloud rendering. It builds on the principles of ray marching and procedural noise. The specific implementation details, such as the combination of Perlin-Worley noise and the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, are documented in recent academic and open-source projects. gmanishaa/volumetric-rendering, https://github.com/gmanishaa/volumetric-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) M4trixStrike/WebGL-Volumetric-clouds, https://github.com/M4trixStrike/WebGL-Volumetric-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Real-time volumetric cloud rendering for games and simulations, https://erk.fe.uni-lj.si/2025/papers/loboda(realtimevolumetric).pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Atmospheric Ray Marching
head: Basic Volumetric Rendering Atmosphere
body: Atmospheric Ray Marching is a technique for rendering planetary atmospheres using single scattering, exponential density falloff, and the Rayleigh phase function. It solves the Radiative Transfer Equation for a spherical atmosphere by marching along view rays and light rays to compute inscattered sunlight and shadowing. It is distinguished from Ray Marching with Single Scattering by its specific application to planetary spheres with analytical density profiles and its handling of shadow rays for occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, planet radius R{planet}, atmosphere radius R{atm}, sun direction \mathbf{s}, scale height H, and physical coefficients (scattering, absorption). Outputs: Final pixel color L{out}. Data Structures: Uniforms: cameraMatrices (std140) containing viewMatrix, projectionMatrix, cameraMatrix; cameraUniforms (std140) containing cameraPosition (vec3), cameraExposure (float), cameraFOV (float). Constants: rayleigh = vec3(5.802, 13.558, 33.1) \times 10^{-6}; ozone = vec3(0.650, 1.881, 0.085) \times 3 \times 10^{-6}; sigmaS (scattering coefficient) = rayleigh; sigmaT (extinction coefficient) = rayleigh + ozone; STEPSPRIMARY = 32; STEPSLIGHT = 32; GAMMA = 2.2. Formulas: Rayleigh Phase Function: P(\theta) = \frac{3}{16\pi} (1 + \cos^2\theta), where \theta is the scattering angle between the view direction and the sun direction. Exponential Density Falloff: \rho(h) = e^{-h / H}, where h is the height above the planet surface and H is the scale height. Sphere Intersection: For a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and sphere radius R, solve at^2 + bt + c = 0 with a=1, b=2\mathbf{o}\cdot\mathbf{d}, c=\mathbf{o}\cdot\mathbf{o}-R^2. Roots are t = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Direction: Calculate the view ray direction \mathbf{d} from fragment coordinates (x, y) and resolution res: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}\left( \left( \frac{x}{res.x} - 0.5, \frac{y}{res.y} - 0.5, -z \right) \right) where z = \frac{0.5 \cdot res.y}{\tan(0.5 \cdot FOV)}. 2. Intersect Atmosphere: Compute the entry and exit points of the view ray with the atmosphere sphere (R{atm}) and planet sphere (R{planet}) using the quadratic formula. Determine the valid segment [t{start}, t{end}] for marching. 3. Initialize Accumulators: Set total transmittance T{total} = 1.0 and accumulated radiance L{out} = 0. 4. March View Ray: Loop i from 0 to STEPS\PRIMARY - 1: a. Calculate step size \Delta s = \frac{t{end} - t{start}}{STEPS\PRIMARY}. b. Compute current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t{start} + i \cdot \Delta s) \mathbf{d}. c. Compute height h = \|\mathbf{p}\| - R{planet}. d. Evaluate density \rho = e^{-h / H}. e. Shadow Test: Cast a shadow ray from \mathbf{p} towards the sun \mathbf{s}. Intersect this ray with a sphere of radius 0.95 R{planet} to determine if the point is in shadow. Using 0.95 R{planet} avoids banding artifacts at sunset. f. Inscattering Calculation: If not in shadow: i. Compute optical depth to the sun \tau{light} by marching STEPS\LIGHT steps towards the sun, summing \rho \cdot \Delta s{light}. ii. Compute inscattered radiance L{in} = S{sun} C{sun} e^{-\sigmaT \tau{light}}, where S{sun} is solar spectral irradiance and C{sun} is a constant. g. Update Transmittance: T{total} \leftarrow T{total} \cdot e^{-\sigmaT \rho \Delta s}. h. Accumulate: L{out} \leftarrow L{out} + T{total} \cdot \sigmaS \cdot \rho \cdot P(\theta) \cdot L{in} \cdot \Delta s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def atmosphericraymarching(camerapos, cameradir, sundir, planetradius, atmradius, scaleheight, solarirradiance): # Constants rayleigh = [5.802e-6, 13.558e-6, 33.1e-6] ozone = [0.650e-6, 1.881e-6, 0.085e-6] sigmas = rayleigh[:] sigmat = [rayleigh[i] + ozone[i] for i in range(3)] stepsprimary = 32 stepslight = 32 lightstep = 100.0 # Step size for light ray not given in sources dir = normalize(cameradir) # Intersect view ray with atmosphere and planet spheres tatmstart, tatmend = intersectsphere(camerapos, dir, atmradius) tplanetstart, tplanetend = intersectsphere(camerapos, dir, planetradius) # Determine valid marching segment tstart = max(tatmstart, tplanetstart) tend = min(tatmend, tplanetend) if tend < tstart: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] deltas = (tend - tstart) / stepsprimary ttotaltransmittance = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] lout = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(stepsprimary): t = tstart + i deltas p = add(camerapos, scale(dir, t)) h = length(p) - planetradius rho = math.exp(-h / scaleheight) # Shadow test: ray from p towards sun, intersect with 0.95Rplanet inshadow = isinshadow(p, sundir, planetradius 0.95) lin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if not inshadow: taulight = computeopticaldepthtosun(p, sundir, stepslight, lightstep, scaleheight, planetradius) # Lin = Ssun Csun exp(-sigmaT taulight) lin = [solarirradiance[j] math.exp(-sigmat[j] taulight) for j in range(3)] # Phase function costheta = dot(sundir, dir) phase = (3.0 / (16.0 math.pi)) (1.0 + costheta costheta) # Update transmittance for j in range(3): ttotaltransmittance[j] = math.exp(-sigmat[j] rho deltas) # Accumulate radiance for j in range(3): lout[j] += ttotaltransmittance[j] sigmas[j] rho phase lin[j] deltas return lout def intersectsphere(rayo, rayd, radius): a = 1.0 b = 2.0 dot(rayo, rayd) c = dot(rayo, rayo) - radius radius discriminant = b b - 4.0 a c if discriminant < 0.0: return -1.0, -1.0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) return t1, t2 def isinshadow(point, sundir, shadowradius): # Ray from point towards sun rayo = point rayd = sundir t1, t2 = intersectsphere(rayo, rayd, shadowradius) # If intersection distance is positive, the planet blocks the sun return t1 > 0.0 or t2 > 0.0 def computeopticaldepthtosun(point, sundir, steps, stepsize, scaleheight, planetradius): tau = 0.0 for i in range(steps): p = add(point, scale(sundir, i stepsize)) h = length(p) - planetradius rho = math.exp(-h / scaleheight) tau += rho stepsize return tau def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def length(v): return math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) def normalize(v): l = length(v); return [x / l for x in v] def add(a, b): return [x + y for x, y in zip(a, b)] def scale(v, s): return [x s for x in v] A post-processing technique that renders volumetric atmospheric scattering (Rayleigh, Mie, and Ozone absorption) over a scene by tracing rays through a spherical atmosphere shell, accounting for occlusion by scene geometry. It differs from in-scene atmospheric rendering by operating on the final screen buffer, using the depth map to determine ray termination distances, and applying tonemapping and saturation adjustments to the accumulated light. Choose this when atmospheric effects need to be applied uniformly across a rendered scene without modifying the primary geometry pipeline. Complexity: Time complexity is O(N \cdot M) per pixel, where N is STEPSPRIMARY and M is STEPSLIGHT. Memory complexity is O(1) per pixel as it computes values on the fly without storing volumetric grids. Performance: The method is computationally expensive due to the nested ray marching (view ray and light ray) and exponential density calculations. The method originates from the "Basic Volumetric Rendering" workshop at the Graphics Programming Conference in Breda, 2024. It is based on the repository al-ro/volumetrics. The technique is a specific application of ray marching for atmospheric rendering, utilizing the Rayleigh phase function and exponential density profiles. al-ro/volumetrics, https://github.com/al-ro/volumetrics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Atmospheric Scattering Post-Process
head: Post-process Atmospheric Rendering, Screen-space Atmospheric Scattering
body: A post-processing technique that renders volumetric atmospheric scattering (Rayleigh, Mie, and Ozone absorption) over a scene by tracing rays through a spherical atmosphere shell, accounting for occlusion by scene geometry. It differs from in-scene atmospheric rendering by operating on the final screen buffer, using the depth map to determine ray termination distances, and applying tonemapping and saturation adjustments to the accumulated light. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Screen color texture, depth texture, camera position, sun position, planet parameters (radius, atmosphere radius), and scattering coefficients. Outputs: Final rendered color buffer. Data Structures The method relies on a uniform structure AtmosphereSettings containing the following fields: planetRadius: Radius of the planet in meters. atmosphereRadius: Radius of the atmosphere in meters. rayleighHeight: Height falloff of Rayleigh scattering. Default: 8 \times 10^3. rayleighScatteringCoefficients: Rayleigh scattering coefficients (R, G, B). Default: (5.8 \times 10^{-6}, 13.5 \times 10^{-6}, 33.1 \times 10^{-6}). mieHeight: Height falloff of Mie scattering. Default: 1.2 \times 10^3. mieScatteringCoefficients: Mie scattering coefficients (R, G, B). Default: (3.9 \times 10^{-6}, 3.9 \times 10^{-6}, 3.9 \times 10^{-6}). mieAsymmetry: Mie scattering asymmetry factor, between -1 and 1. Default: 0.8. ozoneHeight: Height of the ozone layer in meters above the planet surface. Default: 25 \times 10^3. ozoneAbsorptionCoefficients: Ozone absorption coefficients (R, G, B). Default: (0.6 \times 10^{-6}, 1.8 \times 10^{-6}, 0.085 \times 10^{-6}). ozoneFalloff: Ozone absorption falloff around the ozone layer height in meters. Default: 5 \times 10^3. lightIntensity: Intensity of the sun. Default: 20. Numbered Steps 1. Sample Input Data: Read the screen color and depth value for the current pixel UV coordinates. 2. Compute Ray Origin and Direction: Transform the depth value to world space to find the deepest visible point, then compute the ray direction from the camera position. 3. Clamp Ray Length for Planet Sphere Intersection: Intersect the ray with the planet sphere to get entry distance t0. If the ray intersects and the computed maximum distance is greater than t0 - 1.0 (to avoid precision artifacts from imperfect sphere discretization), clamp the maximum distance to t0. This clamping logic should not be used if the planet has landmasses or non-spherical geometry. 4. Atmosphere Intersection: Call the scatter function with the screen color, camera position, ray direction, and maximum distance. Inside scatter: a. Intersect the ray with the atmosphere sphere to get impact point impactPoint and escape point escapePoint. b. If no intersection occurs, return the original screen color. c. Clamp impactPoint to \max(0.0, \text{impactPoint}). d. Clamp escapePoint to \min(\text{maximumDistance}, \text{escapePoint}). e. Calculate the distance through the atmosphere: \text{distanceThroughAtmosphere} = \max(0.0, \text{escapePoint} - \text{impactPoint}). f. Compute the first point in the atmosphere: \text{firstPointInAtmosphere} = \text{rayOrigin} + \text{rayDir} \times \text{impactPoint}. g. Call calculateLight with firstPointInAtmosphere, ray direction, distanceThroughAtmosphere, and original color. 5. Calculate Scattering (calculateLight): a. Define the number of sample points POINTSFROMCAMERA. b. Compute step size: s = \text{rayLength} / (\text{POINTS\FROM\CAMERA} - 1). c. Initialize accumulators: inScatteredRayleigh = 0, inScatteredMie = 0, totalOpticalDepth = 0. d. Iterate i from 0 to POINTSFROMCAMERA - 1: i. Current sample point: P{sample} = P{start} + \text{rayDir} \times (i \times s). ii. Compute Sun Ray Optical Depth: Calculate initial distance from light source through atmosphere: L{sun} = \text{atmosphereRadius} - \text{length}(P{sample} - \text{planetPosition}). If ray from P{sample} in sun direction intersects atmosphere sphere, update L{sun} to the intersection distance t1. Compute optical depth from sun to sample point: OD{sun} = \text{opticalDepth}(P{sample}, \text{sunDir}, L{sun}). iii. Compute View Ray Optical Depth: Distance from sample point to camera along view ray: L{view} = s \times i. Compute optical depth from sample point to camera: OD{view} = \text{opticalDepth}(P{sample}, -\text{rayDir}, L{view}). iv. Compute Transmittance: T = \exp(-\text{rayleighCoeffs} \times (OD{sun}.x + OD{view}.x) - \text{mieCoeffs} \times (OD{sun}.y + OD{view}.y) - \text{ozoneCoeffs} \times (OD{sun}.z + OD{view}.z)). v. Update Total Optical Depth: Get local density at sample point: \rho = \text{densityAtPoint}(P{sample}). OD{total} += \rho \times s. vi. Accumulate Scattered Light: inScatteredRayleigh += \rho.x \times T \times s. inScatteredMie += \rho.y \times T \times s. e. Compute Phase Functions: Cosine of angle between view and sun directions: c = \text{dot}(\text{rayDir}, \text{sunDir}). Rayleigh Phase Function: PR = \frac{3}{16\pi} (1 + c^2). Mie Phase Function: Let g = \text{mieAsymmetry}. PM = \frac{3(1-g^2)}{2(2+g^2)} \frac{1+c^2}{(1+g^2-2gc)^{1.5}}. f. Apply Phase Functions and Coefficients: inScatteredRayleigh = PR \times \text{rayleighCoeffs}. inScatteredMie = PM \times \text{mieCoeffs}. g. Compute Opacity (Transmittance to Camera): O = \exp(-(\text{mieCoeffs} \times OD{total}.y + \text{rayleighCoeffs} \times OD{total}.x + \text{ozoneCoeffs} \times OD{total}.z)). h. Return Final Color: \text{final} = (\text{inScatteredRayleigh} + \text{inScatteredMie}) \times \text{lightIntensity} + \text{originalColor} \times O. 6. Post-Processing: a. Apply exposure: \text{finalColor} \times 1.2. b. Apply ACES tonemapping. c. Apply saturation (factor 1.2) using grayscale luminance weights (0.299, 0.587, 0.114): \text{grayscale} = \text{vec3}(0.299, 0.587, 0.114) \times \text{finalColor} \text{finalColor} = \text{mix}(\text{grayscale}, \text{finalColor}, 1.2). d. Clamp to [0.0, 1.0] and output. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rayintersectsphere(origin, direction, spherecenter, radius): oc = [origin[j] - spherecenter[j] for j in range(3)] a = sum(dd for d in direction) b = 2.0 sum(oc[j]direction[j] for j in range(3)) c = sum(oc[j]oc[j] for j in range(3)) - radiusradius disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return None, None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t0 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t1 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) return t0, t1 def opticaldepth(point, direction, length, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff): # Note: exact implementation of opticaldepth is not provided in the sources. # It integrates exponential density falloff along the ray path. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def densityatpoint(point, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff): # Note: exact implementation of densityatpoint is not provided in the sources. # It computes local density based on height falloff parameters. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def worldfromuv(uv, depth, inverseprojection, inverseview): # Standard inverse projection to world space clip = [uv[0]2-1, uv[1]2-1, 0.0, 1.0] # Apply inverse view and projection matrices, then divide by w # Simplified for pseudocode: returns world position at given depth return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for matrix math; implement using inverseprojection inverseview def atmosphericscatteringpostprocess(screencolor, depth, uv, cameraposition, sunposition, planetposition, planetradius, atmosphereradius, rayleighcoeffs, miecoeffs, ozonecoeffs, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff, lightintensity, pointsfromcamera): screencolor = texture2D(screencolor, uv) depthval = texture2D(depth, uv).r deepestpoint = [worldfromuv(uv, depthval, inverseprojection, inverseview)[j] - cameraposition[j] for j in range(3)] maximumdistance = math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in deepestpoint)) raydir = [d / maximumdistance for d in deepestpoint] t0, t1 = rayintersectsphere(cameraposition, raydir, planetposition, planetradius) if t0 is not None and maximumdistance > t0 - 1.0: maximumdistance = t0 finalcolor = scatter(screencolor, cameraposition, raydir, maximumdistance, sunposition, planetposition, atmosphereradius, rayleighcoeffs, miecoeffs, ozonecoeffs, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff, lightintensity) finalcolor = [c 1.2 for c in finalcolor] finalcolor = acestonemap(finalcolor) saturation = 1.2 grayscale = [0.299finalcolor[0], 0.587finalcolor[1], 0.114finalcolor[2]] finalcolor = [grayscale[j] + saturation (finalcolor[j] - grayscale[j]) for j in range(3)] finalcolor = [max(0.0, min(1.0, c)) for c in finalcolor] return finalcolor def scatter(originalcolor, rayorigin, raydir, maximumdistance, sunposition, planetposition, atmosphereradius, rayleighcoeffs, miecoeffs, ozonecoeffs, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff, lightintensity): impactpoint, escapepoint = rayintersectsphere(rayorigin, raydir, planetposition, atmosphereradius) if impactpoint is None: return originalcolor impactpoint = max(0.0, impactpoint) escapepoint = min(maximumdistance, escapepoint) distancethroughatmosphere = max(0.0, escapepoint - impactpoint) firstpointinatmosphere = [rayorigin[j] + raydir[j] impactpoint for j in range(3)] return calculatelight(firstpointinatmosphere, raydir, distancethroughatmosphere, originalcolor, sunposition, planetposition, atmosphereradius, rayleighcoeffs, miecoeffs, ozonecoeffs, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff, lightintensity) def calculatelight(rayorigin, raydir, raylength, originalcolor, sunposition, planetposition, atmosphereradius, rayleighcoeffs, miecoeffs, ozonecoeffs, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff, lightintensity): sundir = normalize(sunposition, planetposition) stepsize = raylength / (pointsfromcamera - 1) inscatteredrayleigh = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] inscatteredmie = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] totalopticaldepth = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(pointsfromcamera): samplepoint = [rayorigin[j] + raydir[j] (i stepsize) for j in range(3)] sunraylengthinatm = atmosphereradius - math.sqrt(sum((samplepoint[j] - planetposition[j])2 for j in range(3))) t0, t1 = rayintersectsphere(samplepoint, sundir, planetposition, atmosphereradius) if t0 is not None: sunraylengthinatm = t1 sunrayopticaldepth = opticaldepth(samplepoint, sundir, sunraylengthinatm, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff) viewraylengthinatm = stepsize i viewrayopticaldepth = opticaldepth(samplepoint, [-d for d in raydir], viewraylengthinatm, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff) transmittance = [math.exp(-(rayleighcoeffs[j] (sunrayopticaldepth[j] + viewrayopticaldepth[j]) + miecoeffs[j] (sunrayopticaldepth[j+1] if j<2 else 0) + ozonecoeffs[j] (sunrayopticaldepth[j+2] if j<1 else 0))) for j in range(3)] # Simplified vector math for pseudocode localdensity = densityatpoint(samplepoint, rayleighheight, mieheight, ozoneheight, ozonefalloff) totalopticaldepth = [totalopticaldepth[j] + localdensity[j] stepsize for j in range(3)] inscatteredrayleigh = [inscatteredrayleigh[j] + localdensity[0] transmittance[j] stepsize for j in range(3)] inscatteredmie = [inscatteredmie[j] + localdensity[1] transmittance[j] stepsize for j in range(3)] costheta = sum(raydir[j] sundir[j] for j in range(3)) costheta2 = costheta costheta phaserayleigh = 3.0 / (16.0 math.pi) (1.0 + costheta2) g = mieasymmetry g2 = g g phasemie = ((3.0 (1.0 - g2)) / (2.0 (2.0 + g2))) ((1.0 + costheta2) / pow(1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g costheta, 1.5)) inscatteredrayleigh = [c phaserayleigh rayleighcoeffs[j] for j, c in enumerate(inscatteredrayleigh)] inscatteredmie = [c phasemie miecoeffs[j] for j, c in enumerate(inscatteredmie)] opacity = math.exp(-(miecoeffs[1] totalopticaldepth[1] + rayleighcoeffs[0] totalopticaldepth[0] + ozonecoeffs[2] totalopticaldepth[2])) return [(inscatteredrayleigh[j] + inscatteredmie[j]) lightintensity + originalcolor[j] opacity for j in range(3)] Formulas Rayleigh Phase Function: PR(\theta) = \frac{3}{16\pi} (1 + \cos^2 \theta) where \theta is the scattering angle. Mie Phase Function (Henyey-Greenstein variant): PM(\theta) = \frac{3(1-g^2)}{2(2+g^2)} \frac{1+\cos^2 \theta}{(1+g^2-2g\cos \theta)^{3/2}} where g is the asymmetry factor. Optical Depth: The optical depth is computed based on the density falloff of Rayleigh, Mie, and Ozone layers. The specific opticaldepth function implementation is not fully detailed in the provided notes, but it integrates density along the ray path. Transmittance: T = \exp\left(-\sum{k \in \{R, M, O\}} \sigmak \cdot ODk\right) where \sigmak are the scattering/absorption coefficients and ODk are the optical depths for Rayleigh (R), Mie (M), and Ozone (O). Parameters POINTSFROMCAMERA: Number of sample points along the view ray. Not given in the sources. (Typical values in similar implementations range from 16 to 64, but must be defined by the implementer). sunPosition: Position of the sun. Provided as uniform.. cameraPosition: Position of the camera. Provided as uniform.. planetPosition: Position of the planet center. Provided as uniform.. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Intersection: If the ray does not intersect the atmosphere sphere, return the original color immediately. Negative Impact Point: Clamp the impact point to \max(0.0, t{in}). Negative Distance: Clamp the distance through atmosphere to \max(0.0, t{out} - t{in}). Non-Spherical Planets: The clamping logic for maximumDistance using t0 - 1.0 should not be used if the planet has landmasses or imperfect discretized geometry, as it may incorrectly truncate the ray. Precision Artifacts: Use a tolerance of -1.0 when clamping maximumDistance to t0 to avoid precision artifacts from imperfect sphere discretization. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points POINTSFROMCAMERA per pixel. The complexity is O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel, excluding the input and output textures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and sample count. Strengths: Post-process approach allows for easy integration into existing rendering pipelines without modifying scene geometry. Accounts for occlusion by scene geometry via depth buffer. Limitations: Limited to screen-space; rays are only traced for visible pixels. Approximates atmospheric scattering with a fixed number of samples. Relies on a spherical atmosphere model. When to Use: When rendering a spherical planet with an atmosphere and occlusion by terrain is required, and performance constraints allow for per-pixel ray marching. When Not to Use: For non-spherical planets, or when high-fidelity multi-scattering is required (this method uses single scattering approximation). Originated from the GitHub repository BarthPaleologue/volumetric-atmospheric-scattering. It is an implementation of atmospheric scattering using post-processing techniques, likely inspired by standard volumetric rendering principles and Rayleigh/Mie scattering theory. name: Ray Marching Volumetric Rendering with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering
head: GLSL Volumetric Rendering, TouchDesigner Volumetric Rendering
body: This method renders volumetric scenes by discretizing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along camera rays using fixed-step ray marching, evaluating density via a procedural fractal Signed Distance Field (SDF), and computing single-scattering light contributions using the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SDF Cloud Rendering by explicitly mixing forward and backward scattering coefficients to control anisotropy, and from Volumetric Rendering with Spherical Harmonics by avoiding frequency-domain approximations in favor of direct spatial integration. Inputs: fragCoord: Pixel coordinates (u, v) in the output image resolution. iResolution: Image width and height (W, H). iTime: Global animation time variable. Parameters: RAYITER: Number of ray marching steps (default: 120). LIGHTITER: Number of shadow sampling steps (default: 16). RAYSTEPSIZE: Distance advanced per ray step (default: 0.01). LIGHTATTEN: Light attenuation coefficient (default: 64.0). FOWARD: Forward scattering anisotropy parameter gf (default: 0.8). BACKWARD: Backward scattering anisotropy parameter gb (default: -0.2). Outputs: fragColor: Final RGBA color for the pixel. No complex data structures are used; the method relies on scalar variables and 3D vectors. The density field is defined implicitly by the sdf function. 1. Initialization: Map pixel coordinates to normalized device coordinates: \mathbf{uv} = \left(\frac{u}{W} - 0.5\right) \cdot 2.0, \left(\frac{v}{H} - 0.5\right) \cdot 2.0. Set camera origin \mathbf{o} = (0.0, 0.0, -2.0). Compute ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}((\mathbf{uv}, 0.0) - \mathbf{o}). Initialize accumulated color \mathbf{C} = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) and transmittance T = 1.0. Set current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} (initial step offset). Compute dynamic light position \mathbf{l} using a Lissajous curve (see below). 2. Ray Marching Loop (iterate i from 0 to RAYITER): Advance position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \text{RAY\STEP\SIZE}. Evaluate density \rho = \text{sampleDensity}(\mathbf{p}). Pitfall: If \rho \le 0.0, skip to the next iteration (empty space). Early Termination: If T < 0.01, break the loop. 3. Lighting and Scattering: Compute light direction vector \mathbf{l}{dir} = \mathbf{l} - \mathbf{p}. Compute light distance Dl = \|\mathbf{l}{dir}\|. Normalize light direction: \mathbf{l}{dir} \leftarrow \mathbf{l}{dir} / Dl. Compute light step size: \Delta tl = Dl / \text{LIGHT\ITER}. Compute dot product for phase function: \mu = \text{dot}(\mathbf{d}, -\mathbf{l}{dir}). Compute scattering weight S = \text{getScattering}(\mu) (see Phase Function below). 4. Shadow Density Accumulation: Initialize shadow density \rho{shadow} = 0.0. Set light ray position \mathbf{p}l = \mathbf{p}. Iterate j from 0 to LIGHTITER: \rho{shadow} \leftarrow \rho{shadow} + \text{sampleDensity}(\mathbf{p}l) \cdot \Delta tl. \mathbf{p}l \leftarrow \mathbf{p}l + \mathbf{l}{dir} \cdot \Delta tl. 5. Color and Transmittance Update: Compute attenuated external light: \mathbf{L}{ext} = \exp(-\rho{shadow} \cdot \text{LIGHT\ATTEN}) \cdot S. Update accumulated color: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + T \cdot \mathbf{L}{ext} \cdot \rho. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot \exp(-\rho \cdot \text{RAY\STEP\SIZE} \cdot \text{LIGHT\ATTEN}). 6. Post-Processing: Apply gamma correction: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}^{(1/2.2)}. Output \mathbf{C} as fragColor. Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: P(\mu, g) = \frac{1 - g^2}{(1 + g^2 - 2g\mu)^{1.5}} Where \mu = \cos \theta = \text{dot}(\mathbf{d}, -\mathbf{l}{dir}) and g is the anisotropy parameter. Scattering Mix: S(\mu) = 0.5 \cdot P(\mu, gf) + 0.5 \cdot P(\mu, gb) Where gf = \text{FOWARD} and gb = \text{BACKWARD}. Density Sampling: \rho(\mathbf{p}) = 10.0 \cdot \max(-\text{sdf}(\mathbf{p}), 0.0)^{1.3} Where sdf is the procedural fractal distance field. Light Position (Lissajous Curve): \mathbf{l}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} A \sin(a t + \delta) \\ B \sin(b t) \\ C \sin(c t) \end{bmatrix} With A=1.5, B=1.2, C=1.1, a=3.1, b=2.2, c=4.3, \delta=0.2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def rotatevector(z, axis, angle): """Rotate vector z around axis by angle.""" s = math.sin(angle) c = math.cos(angle) ax, ay, az = axis # Rotation matrix components c1 = 1.0 - c m00 = c + ax ax c1 m01 = ax ay c1 - az s m02 = ax az c1 + ay s m10 = ay ax c1 + az s m11 = c + ay ay c1 m12 = ay az c1 - ax s m20 = az ax c1 - ay s m21 = az ay c1 + ax s m22 = c + az az c1 # Apply rotation newx = m00 z[0] + m01 z[1] + m02 z[2] newy = m10 z[0] + m11 z[1] + m12 z[2] newz = m20 z[0] + m21 z[1] + m22 z[2] return np.array([newx, newy, newz]) def fractalsdf(p, time): """Compute procedural fractal SDF.""" currentp = p.copy() for i in range(8): # Rotate around X and Y axes currentp = rotatevector(currentp, np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), time 0.2) currentp = rotatevector(currentp, np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), time 0.1) # Reflective symmetry checks if currentp[0] + currentp[1] < 0.0: currentp[0], currentp[1] = -currentp[1], -currentp[0] if currentp[1] + currentp[2] < 0.0: currentp[1], currentp[2] = -currentp[2], -currentp[1] if currentp[2] + currentp[0] < 0.0: currentp[2], currentp[0] = -currentp[0], -currentp[2] # Scale down and translate currentp -= 0.06 return np.linalg.norm(currentp) - 0.15 def sampledensity(p, time): """Convert SDF to density.""" d = fractalsdf(p, time) return max(-d, 0.0) 1.3 10.0 def henyeygreenstein(mu, g): """Henyey-Greenstein phase function.""" gg = g g denom = 1.0 + gg - 2.0 g mu if denom <= 0: return 0.0 return (1.0 - gg) / (denom 1.5) def getscattering(mu, gforward, gbackward): """Mix forward and backward scattering.""" return 0.5 henyeygreenstein(mu, gforward) + 0.5 henyeygreenstein(mu, gbackward) def lightposlissajous(t): """Compute light position using Lissajous curve.""" A, B, C = 1.5, 1.2, 1.1 a, b, c = 3.1, 2.2, 4.3 delta = 0.2 x = A math.sin(a t + delta) y = B math.sin(b t) z = C math.sin(c t) return np.array([x, y, z]) def renderpixel(u, v, resolution, time, params): """Render a single pixel.""" W, H = resolution RAYITER = params['RAYITER'] LIGHTITER = params['LIGHTITER'] RAYSTEPSIZE = params['RAYSTEPSIZE'] LIGHTATTEN = params['LIGHTATTEN'] FOWARD = params['FOWARD'] BACKWARD = params['BACKWARD'] # UV mapping uv = np.array([(u / W - 0.5) 2.0, (v / H - 0.5) 2.0, 0.0]) # Camera setup campos = np.array([0.0, 0.0, -2.0]) raydir = uv - campos raydir = raydir / np.linalg.norm(raydir) # Light setup lightpos = lightposlissajous(time 0.2) # Initialization col = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) transmittance = 1.0 raypos = campos + raydir for i in range(RAYITER): # Advance ray raypos += raydir RAYSTEPSIZE # Sample density density = sampledensity(raypos, time) # Skip empty space if density <= 0.0: continue # Early termination if transmittance < 0.01: break # Lighting calculation lightdirvec = lightpos - raypos lightdist = np.linalg.norm(lightdirvec) lightdir = lightdirvec / lightdist lightstep = lightdist / LIGHTITER # Phase function input mu = np.dot(raydir, -lightdir) scattering = getscattering(mu, FOWARD, BACKWARD) # Shadow density accumulation shadowdensity = 0.0 lightraypos = raypos for j in range(LIGHTITER): shadowdensity += sampledensity(lightraypos, time) lightstep lightraypos += lightdir lightstep # Color update externallight = np.array([math.exp(-shadowdensity LIGHTATTEN) scattering] 3) col += transmittance externallight density # Transmittance update transmittance = math.exp(-density RAYSTEPSIZE LIGHTATTEN) # Gamma correction col = col (1.0 / 2.2) return col Empty Space: If sampleDensity returns \le 0.0, the iteration must be skipped to avoid division by zero or invalid scattering calculations in subsequent steps, although the primary loop guard handles this. Transmittance Threshold: Breaking the loop when T < 0.01 is a standard optimization but may cause artifacts in very dense volumes if the threshold is too high. Singularity: The Henyey-Greenstein denominator (1 + g^2 - 2g\mu) approaches zero if g \approx 1 and \mu \approx 1 (perfect forward scattering). The implementation should guard against division by zero or negative denominators. Uses a fractal SDF with rotational symmetry and reflection to create complex volumetric shapes without texture maps. Chosen when memory bandwidth is limited or dynamic deformation is required. The light source moves along a parametric curve. Chosen to demonstrate dynamic lighting effects in real-time ray marching. Time Complexity: O(R \cdot L) per pixel, where R is RAYITER and L is LIGHTITER. With typical values (120 \times 16), this is computationally expensive for high-resolution images. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, as the density field is procedural and no voxel grids are stored. Performance: Suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs (GLSL/WebGPU) due to the lack of data structure traversal overhead, but limited by the nested loop for shadow density. Strengths: Simple implementation, no pre-computation required, supports dynamic geometry via the SDF. Limitations: Single-scattering approximation only; no multiple scattering or global illumination effects. This method originates from GLSL shader programming tutorials, specifically popularized by the "Okdalto" blog post detailing a "rigorous" version of volumetric rendering in GLSL. It is frequently implemented in creative coding environments like TouchDesigner to demonstrate real-time volumetric effects using procedural noise and SDFs. The use of the Henyey-Greenstein phase function is standard in atmospheric and particulate rendering to model anisotropic scattering. name: Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit
head: RayMarch, Sphere Tracing with Surface/Represent Passes, SphereTracingFPass, SphereTracingKPass, Surface/Represent Ray Marching
body: Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit is a deferred rendering technique for Signed Distance Fields (SDF) that tracks both a primary surface hit and a 'represent' hit (a proxy for the surface at the pixel radius) to handle transparency and aliasing at object edges. It writes results to two render targets: index 0 for the surface and index 1 for the represent hit. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), SDF map function Map(\mathbf{p}) returning a float2 (distance, material ID), clipping planes [ClippingPlanes.x, ClippingPlanes.y], maximum sphere tracing steps N{steps}, and pixel radius factor RadiusPixel. Outputs: Two hit structures: surfaceHit and representHit, each containing DistanceToWorld, TraceDistance, MaterialId, Position, and Alpha. Data Structures: HitRecord: A structure containing: DistanceToWorld: float, distance from camera origin to hit point. TraceDistance: float, total distance traveled along ray. MaterialId: int, material identifier from SDF map. Position: vec3, 3D world position of the hit. Alpha: float, opacity value (0.0 to 1.0). currentMap: float2, current SDF sample (distance, material ID). nextMap: float2, next SDF sample. Parameters: N{steps}: Maximum number of marching iterations (e.g., 64). RadiusPixel: Scaling factor for pixel radius approximation. ClippingPlanes: Near and far clipping distances. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize surfaceHit and representHit with near plane clipping distance (ClippingPlanes.x) and far plane (ClippingPlanes.y). Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = -1 and representHit.MaterialId = -1. Set representHit.DistanceToWorld = 1000000 (large value). Set representHit.Alpha = 0. Initialize ray distance t = ClippingPlanes.x. Sample SDF at \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to get currentMap. Initialize loop counter i = 0 and representFound = false. 2. Marching Loop: Loop i from 0 to N{steps} - 1: Calculate adaptive epsilon: \epsilon = 0.0015 \times t. Surface Hit Check: If currentMap.x \le \epsilon: Set surfaceHit.DistanceToWorld = t + currentMap.x. Set surfaceHit.TraceDistance = t + currentMap.x. Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = currentMap.y. Set surfaceHit.Position = \mathbf{o} + (t + currentMap.x)\mathbf{d}. Break loop. Represent Hit Logic: Sample next point: \mathbf{p}{next} = \mathbf{o} + (t + \text{currentMap}.x)\mathbf{d}. Get nextMap = Map(\mathbf{p}{next}). Check if inside pixel radius: If currentMap.x < (t \times RadiusPixel): If nextMap.x > currentMap.x (moving away from surface) and representFound == false: Set representFound = true. If currentMap.x < representHit.DistanceToWorld and (representHit.MaterialId == -1 or representHit.MaterialId == currentMap.y): Update representHit.DistanceToWorld = t. Update representHit.MaterialId = currentMap.y. Update representHit.TraceDistance = t. Update representHit.Position = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Advance Ray: t \leftarrow t + \text{currentMap}.x. currentMap = nextMap. Far Clipping Check: If t > ClippingPlanes.y: Set surfaceHit.TraceDistance = ClippingPlanes.y. Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = -1. Break loop. 3. Post-Processing: If loop finished without hit (i == N{steps}): Use latest currentMap data for surfaceHit (fallback hit). Set surfaceHit.DistanceToWorld = t. Set surfaceHit.TraceDistance = t. Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = currentMap.y. Set surfaceHit.Position = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. If representHit.MaterialId >= 0: Calculate representHit.Alpha = 1.0 - representHit.DistanceToWorld / (representHit.TraceDistance RadiusPixel). Update representHit.Position. If surfaceHit.MaterialId < 0 or representHit.MaterialId < 0: Set corresponding Alpha to 0. 4. Final Evaluation: Perform ray marching: If DisableAntiAliasing is true, call RayMarchNoAA(r, surfaceHit, representHit); else call RayMarch(r, surfaceHit, representHit). Evaluate hits: Call EvaluateHit(id.xy, r, surfaceHit, surface) and EvaluateHit(id.xy, r, representHit, represent). Write final data: Call WriteSphereTracingData(id.xy, 0, surface) and WriteSphereTracingData(id.xy, 1, represent). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretracingwithrepresenthit(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfmap, clippingplanes, maxsteps, radiuspixel): """ Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit algorithm. Args: rayorigin: vec3, camera origin raydirection: vec3, normalized ray direction sdfmap: callable, returns (distance: float, materialid: int) for a point clippingplanes: tuple (near: float, far: float) maxsteps: int, maximum number of marching steps radiuspixel: float, scaling factor for pixel radius Returns: surfacehit: dict with keys 'DistanceToWorld', 'TraceDistance', 'MaterialId', 'Position', 'Alpha' representhit: dict with keys 'DistanceToWorld', 'TraceDistance', 'MaterialId', 'Position', 'Alpha' """ nearplane, farplane = clippingplanes # Initialize surface hit surfacehit = { 'DistanceToWorld': nearplane, 'TraceDistance': nearplane, 'MaterialId': -1, 'Position': rayorigin + nearplane raydirection, 'Alpha': 0.0 } # Initialize represent hit representhit = { 'DistanceToWorld': 1000000.0, 'TraceDistance': nearplane, 'MaterialId': -1, 'Position': rayorigin + nearplane raydirection, 'Alpha': 0.0 } t = nearplane currentmap = sdfmap(rayorigin + t raydirection) representfound = False for i in range(maxsteps): # Adaptive epsilon (clamp to avoid zero at t=0) epsilon = 0.0015 t if t > 0.0 else 0.0015 # Surface hit check if currentmap[0] <= epsilon: surfacehit['DistanceToWorld'] = t + currentmap[0] surfacehit['TraceDistance'] = t + currentmap[0] surfacehit['MaterialId'] = currentmap[1] surfacehit['Position'] = rayorigin + (t + currentmap[0]) raydirection break # Sample next point nextpoint = rayorigin + (t + currentmap[0]) raydirection nextmap = sdfmap(nextpoint) # Represent hit logic if currentmap[0] < (t radiuspixel): if nextmap[0] > currentmap[0] and not representfound: representfound = True if currentmap[0] < representhit['DistanceToWorld']: if representhit['MaterialId'] == -1 or representhit['MaterialId'] == currentmap[1]: representhit['DistanceToWorld'] = t representhit['MaterialId'] = currentmap[1] representhit['TraceDistance'] = t representhit['Position'] = rayorigin + t raydirection # Advance ray t += currentmap[0] currentmap = nextmap # Far clipping check if t > farplane: surfacehit['TraceDistance'] = farplane surfacehit['MaterialId'] = -1 break # Post-processing if i == maxsteps - 1 and surfacehit['MaterialId'] == -1: # Fallback hit if loop finished without explicit hit surfacehit['DistanceToWorld'] = t surfacehit['TraceDistance'] = t surfacehit['MaterialId'] = currentmap[1] surfacehit['Position'] = rayorigin + t raydirection if representhit['MaterialId'] >= 0: # Calculate alpha for represent hit denom = representhit['TraceDistance'] radiuspixel representhit['Alpha'] = 1.0 - representhit['DistanceToWorld'] / denom if denom != 0 else 0.0 if surfacehit['MaterialId'] < 0: surfacehit['Alpha'] = 0.0 if representhit['MaterialId'] < 0: representhit['Alpha'] = 0.0 return surfacehit, representhit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Adaptive epsilon \epsilon = 0.0015 \times t scales with distance, which may cause issues at very large distances or very small scales if not clamped. Boundaries: Far clipping plane must be handled to prevent infinite loops or invalid hits. Degenerate Input: If TraceDistance is zero or RadiusPixel is zero, division by zero occurs in alpha calculation. Guard against this. Material ID Consistency: The represent hit only updates if the material ID matches the current hit or is uninitialized (-1). This prevents mixing materials in the represent pass. Hit Distance Offset: The hit distance must be calculated as t + \text{currentMap}.x rather than t to avoid underestimating the true intersection point by the adaptive epsilon margin. Time Complexity: O(N{steps}) per pixel, where N{steps} is the maximum number of sphere tracing iterations. The represent hit logic adds constant overhead per step. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for hit records. Requires two render targets (surface and represent). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and maximum steps. The represent hit pass does not significantly increase computational cost as it shares the same marching loop. Strengths: Handles transparency and aliasing at object edges by tracking a 'represent' hit. Deferred rendering allows for efficient lighting calculations. Limitations: Requires two render targets. Alpha calculation for represent hit is heuristic and may not be physically accurate. When to use: When rendering SDFs with transparency or soft edges where standard sphere tracing produces aliasing artifacts. When not to use: When memory bandwidth is limited (due to two render targets) or when hard-edged opaque SDFs are sufficient. Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit is an unofficial technique described in a GitHub repository. It extends standard sphere tracing by introducing a secondary 'represent' hit to improve visual quality at object boundaries. The technique is implemented in a deferred rendering pipeline, integrating with ambient occlusion and environment mapping passes.
