name: Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture
head: Multi-core time-sliced pipeline, Time-slicing
body: The Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture is a hardware design methodology for volume rendering that achieves real-time performance by overlapping distinct pipeline stages through time-slicing. It solves sequential processing bottlenecks by allowing multiple tasks to run simultaneously on shared or replicated functional blocks, enabling continuous hardware-software communication and interactive frame rates. The architecture decomposes the volume rendering pipeline into independent functional blocks that are configured or replicated as sub-cores based on processing requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data (voxels), transformation matrices (Model-View-Projection), and rendering parameters (opacity, shading models). Output: Final rendered image frame. Data Structures: Context Memory: A shared RAM structure used for inter-component communication. It stores intermediate results (e.g., dot products) for several clock cycles so they can be accessed by other components. Normal Mode Registers: Provide a common interface for components to access context memory. Context Address Snooping Mechanism: Allows components to monitor and access stored information in the context memory. Sub-cores: Basic functional blocks (multipliers, adders, inner product processors) that are physically considered as sub-cores. They are configured or replicated to execute specific operations. Numbered Steps: 1. Pipeline Decomposition: Divide the rendering pipeline into functional blocks: classifier, gradient calculator, shearing-warping block, shader, and composer. 2. Component Implementation: Implement these blocks as independent, reusable components/sub-cores. The gradient calculator, shearer-composer, shading processor, and matrix multiplication processor are composed from basic functional blocks like multipliers, adders, or inner product processors. 3. Configuration/Replication: Based on the processing required by the calling module, the embedded sub-core is configured or replicated to execute a specific operation. 4. Time-Sliced Execution: Use time-slicing to overlap execution stages. This allows the simultaneous processing of several tasks, such as calculating a dot product for a voxel in the classifier and using that same value in the shader and composer within the same time frame. 5. Inter-Component Communication: Components communicate via the common interface provided by context RAM, normal mode registers, and the context address snooping mechanism. Calculated values (e.g., dot products) are stored in corresponding RAM cells to be called up by another component. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class TimeSlicedPipeline: def init(self): self.contextmemory = {} self.stagestages = ['classifier', 'gradientcalculator', 'shearwarp', 'shader', 'composer'] self.pipelinebuffer = [None] len(self.stagestages) def processvoxel(self, voxeldata): # Stage 1: Classifier self.pipelinebuffer[0] = self.executeblock('classifier', voxeldata) # Stage 2: Gradient Calculator self.pipelinebuffer[1] = self.executeblock('gradientcalculator', voxeldata) # Stage 3: Shear-Warp self.pipelinebuffer[2] = self.executeblock('shearwarp', voxeldata) # Stage 4: Shader (reads gradient from context memory) gradient = self.pipelinebuffer[1] dotproduct = self.dotproduct(self.pipelinebuffer[2], gradient) self.contextmemory['dotproduct'] = dotproduct self.pipelinebuffer[3] = self.executeblock('shader', self.pipelinebuffer[2], dotproduct) # Stage 5: Composer (reads dotproduct from context memory) self.pipelinebuffer[4] = self.executeblock('composer', self.pipelinebuffer[3], self.contextmemory['dotproduct']) return self.pipelinebuffer[4] def executeblock(self, blockname, args): # Hardware mapping: functional blocks are composed of sub-cores # (multipliers, adders, inner product processors) configured per operation # Exact sub-core configuration logic is not specified in the sources return args[0] if args else None def dotproduct(self, vec1, vec2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(vec1, vec2)) def starttimeslicing(self, voxelstream): # In hardware, time-slicing overlaps stages so multiple voxels are processed concurrently # while stage N processes voxel i, stage N+1 processes voxel i-1 results = [] for voxel in voxelstream: results.append(self.processvoxel(voxel)) return results Parameters: Time-Slice Duration: Not given in the sources. Number of Sub-cores: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. The Vg500 Parallel Pipeline Architecture is a highly parallel, template-based ray-casting hardware implementation designed for real-time volume rendering. It solves the bandwidth and computation bottlenecks of single-pipeline ray casters by employing four identical rendering pipelines that process adjacent voxel values in the x-direction simultaneously. Unlike general-purpose GPU approaches or the larger VIRIM architecture, the Vg500 integrates the entire ray-casting pipeline (interpolation, gradient estimation, shading, classification, and compositing) into a single ASIC, enabling the rendering of 256^3 volumes at 30 fps on a standard PCI card. Time Complexity: Enables real-time rendering by overlapping execution stages. Memory Complexity: Uses context memory for inter-component communication, storing intermediate results for several clock cycles. Measured Performance: Provides real-time frame rates for volumetric datasets through time-sliced multi-core execution. Scaling: Component reusability and multi-core layout allow users to choose required functions, simplifying layout and enabling scalability. Strengths: Real-time performance, continuous hardware-software communication, interactive user interface, simplified layout through component reusability. Limitations: Specific limitations are not detailed in the sources. When to Use: When real-time rendering of volumetric datasets is required, and hardware integration is feasible. When Not to Use: When software-only solutions are preferred, or when the overhead of hardware design is prohibitive. The Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture was developed as part of the Shear-warp factorization volume rendering visualization system (SWE). It was designed to provide real-time rendering capabilities by implementing a multi-core structure compliant with the rendering pipeline. The architecture emphasizes component reusability and hierarchical design to simplify layout and improve efficiency. It is used in systems like the VolumePro, where the Vg500 ASIC implements a similar pipelined approach. name: Vg500 Parallel Pipeline Architecture
head: Cube-4, EM-Cube, VolumePro / vg500 ASIC
body: The Vg500 Parallel Pipeline Architecture is a highly parallel, template-based ray-casting hardware implementation designed for real-time volume rendering. It solves the bandwidth and computation bottlenecks of single-pipeline ray casters by employing four identical rendering pipelines that process adjacent voxel values in the x-direction simultaneously. Unlike general-purpose GPU approaches or the larger VIRIM architecture, the Vg500 integrates the entire ray-casting pipeline (interpolation, gradient estimation, shading, classification, and compositing) into a single ASIC, enabling the rendering of 256^3 volumes at 30 fps on a standard PCI card. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data stored in off-chip Voxel Memory (SDRAM), camera parameters, and transfer function lookup tables. Output: Final image pixels written to off-chip Pixel Memory. Data Structures: Voxel Memory: Consists of 16-bit wide SDRAM modules. Data is organized into "miniblocks" of 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighboring voxels. Miniblocks are stored linearly but with a specific skewing pattern to ensure cache locality. Miniblocks are read/written in bursts of eight voxels. Miniblock Addressing: A miniblock at position [x, y, z] in the volume is assigned to memory module k using the formula: k = \left(\lfloor x/2 \rfloor + \lfloor y/2 \rfloor + \lfloor z/2 \rfloor\right) \mod 4 This linear skewing guarantees that rendering pipelines always have access to four adjacent miniblocks in any of the three slice orientations. Pipeline State: Each pipeline maintains internal shift registers to hold intermediate values (such as interpolated samples and gradients) for communication with neighboring pipelines. Algorithm Steps: The architecture implements template-based ray-casting. Rays are projected from each pixel on a base plane (co-planar to the volume face most parallel to the image plane). The resulting base-plane image is subsequently warped onto the final image plane by off-chip graphics hardware. Within the Vg500 ASIC, the processing per sample along the ray proceeds as follows: 1. Voxel Fetch: Each pipeline reads voxel data from the Voxel Memory. The memory system is organized such that each voxel is read exactly once per frame. 2. Interpolation: Sample values along the ray are calculated using tri-linear interpolation of the fetched voxel data. 3. Gradient Estimation: A 3D gradient is computed using central differences between the tri-linear samples. 4. Shading: The gradient is used in the shader stage to compute sample intensity according to the Phong illumination model. 5. Classification: Lookup tables in the classification stage assign color and opacity to each sample point based on the intensity and gradient. 6. Compositing: Illuminated samples are accumulated into base plane pixels using front-to-back compositing. Parallelism and Data Flow: The four pipelines (Pipeline 0–3) operate in parallel, processing adjacent voxel or sample values in the x-direction. Each pipeline is connected to its immediate neighbor by shift registers in each major unit (Interpolation, Gradient, Shading, Classification, Compositing). These shift registers provide values to neighbors in the same cycle. The pipelines on the far left (Pipeline 0) and far right (Pipeline 3) are connected in a wrap-around fashion. Specifically, the shift registers of the rightmost pipeline recirculate values needed in the next cycle and send them to the leftmost pipeline. An off-chip Voxel Memory supplies data to all pipelines, and all pipelines write pixel values to an off-chip Pixel Memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processpipeline(pipelineid, raystep): # 1. Fetch Voxel Data # The memory controller handles the linear skewing and burst reads. # Each pipeline receives its specific slice of the miniblock. voxeldata = fetchvoxeldata(pipelineid, raystep) # 2. Tri-linear Interpolation # Interpolate sample value from the 2x2x2 miniblock. samplevalue = trilinearinterpolate(voxeldata, raystep) # 3. Gradient Estimation # Compute 3D gradient using central differences between tri-linear samples. # Requires access to neighboring samples, provided via shift registers. gradient = computegradientcentraldiff(samplevalue, pipelineid) # 4. Shading (Phong Illumination) # Compute intensity based on gradient and light model. intensity = phongshading(gradient, raystep.direction) # 5. Classification # Assign color and opacity using lookup tables. color, opacity = classifysample(intensity, lookuptable) # 6. Compositing # Accumulate into base plane pixel using front-to-back compositing. # Requires current accumulated color/opacity from previous steps. basepixel = fronttobackcomposite(basepixel, color, opacity) # 7. Shift Register Update # Pass intermediate values to neighbors for next cycle. # Pipeline 3 sends to Pipeline 0 (wrap-around). sendtoneighbors(pipelineid, samplevalue, gradient) return basepixel Parameters: Clock Speed: 133 MHz. Memory Bandwidth: 533 million 16-bit voxels per second (4 \times 133 \times 10^6). Volume Memory: 32, 64, or 128 MBytes of SDRAM. Performance: Over 500 million tri-linear samples per second, sufficient to render 256^3 volumes at 30 frames per second. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Miniblock Skewing: Linear skewing of miniblocks is required to guarantee that rendering pipelines always have access to four adjacent miniblocks in any of the three slice orientations. Failure to implement this skewing results in cache misses or incorrect gradient calculations. Wrap-around Logic: The shift registers of the rightmost pipeline must correctly recirculate values to the leftmost pipeline to maintain continuity across the x-direction boundaries. A hardware architecture for real-time volume rendering using the Pixel-Planes 5 system, consisting of graphics processors and pixel processors, where pixel processors store voxel function values and gradients, and graphics processors handle ray tracing and compositing. It separates the heavy classification and shading computations from the ray traversal logic to leverage massive parallelism in the pixel processor array. Time Complexity: Real-time performance is achieved for 256^3 volumes at 30 fps. The architecture processes 4 voxels per clock cycle across 4 pipelines. Memory Complexity: Requires 32–128 MBytes of off-chip SDRAM for volume storage and off-chip Pixel Memory for frame buffer output. The ASIC itself contains approximately 2 Mbits of on-chip SRAM. Measured Performance: Renders 256^3 datasets at 30 fps. Memory bandwidth is 533 million 16-bit voxels/second. Strengths: High throughput via parallel pipelines; single-ASIC implementation reduces physical size and cost compared to DSP-based solutions like VIRIM; efficient memory access via miniblock skewing and burst mode. Limitations: Limited to template-based ray-casting (base-plane warping required for arbitrary view angles); does not allow arbitrary intermixing of volumes and polygons. When to use: Real-time volume visualization on PC-class hardware where high frame rates for moderate-resolution volumes (256^3) are required. When not to use: Applications requiring dynamic polygon-volume interaction or arbitrary view angles without warping artifacts. The Vg500 architecture is the core of the VolumePro system, developed by Mitsubishi Electric. It is based on the Cube-4 technology, which Mitsubishi licensed and developed into the Enhanced Memory Cube-4 (EM-Cube) architecture. The VolumePro system was an improved commercial version of EM-Cube, implemented as a PCI card for Windows NT computers. The vg500 ASIC contains approximately 3.2 million random logic transistors and is fabricated in 0.35 \mum technology. It was designed to overcome the limitations of earlier architectures like VIRIM, which required 16 DSPs and achieved only 2.5 fps for similar volume sizes, while being physically larger. name: Pixel-Planes 5 Volume Rendering Architecture
head: Pixel-Planes 5 Architecture
body: A hardware architecture for real-time volume rendering using the Pixel-Planes 5 system, consisting of graphics processors and pixel processors, where pixel processors store voxel function values and gradients, and graphics processors handle ray tracing and compositing. It separates the heavy classification and shading computations from the ray traversal logic to leverage massive parallelism in the pixel processor array. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D voxel dataset (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 256), classification mapping, shading parameters, and observer position. Output: A color image in the frame buffer. Data Structures Pixel Processor Backing Store: Stores function value and gradient for several voxels. In the reference implementation, each pixel processor is assigned 64 voxels. Hierarchical Enumeration: A pyramid of binary volumes installed in each graphics processor to encode coherence. Local Cache: Retains voxels received by a graphics processor for reuse. Numbered Steps 1. Voxel Storage: Pixel processors store function value and gradient for their assigned voxels in their backing store. 2. Classification and Shading: Pixel processors perform classification and shading calculations for all voxels in their backing store. 3. Ray Tracing Initiation: Graphics processors trace rays to generate an image. 4. Voxel Request: Graphics processors request sets of voxels from pixel processors as necessary. 5. Interpolation and Compositing: Graphics processors perform tri-linear interpolation and compositing operations on the requested voxels. 6. Frame Buffer Update: Graphics processors transmit resulting pixel colors to the frame buffer. Strategies for Optimization 1. Hierarchical Enumeration: Install a pyramid of binary volumes in each graphics processor to encode coherence and tell the graphics processor which voxels are interesting (non-transparent) and worth requesting. 2. Adaptive Sampling: Use an adaptive sampling scheme to reduce the number of rays required to generate an initial image. 3. Caching: Retain all voxels received by a graphics processor in a local cache. If the observer does not move, cached voxels drive successive refinement. If the observer moves, cached voxels may still be useful depending on movement distance. Formulas and Parameters Shading Time: Applying a monochrome Phong shading model at a single voxel using a pixel processor takes about 1 msec. Total Classification/Shading Time: For a 256 \times 256 \times 256 voxel dataset, with each pixel processor assigned 64 voxels, the time to classify and shade the entire dataset is about 64 msec. Pitfalls Recomputation: If the user changes the classification mapping such that the set of interesting voxels changes, the hierarchical enumeration must be recomputed, taking several seconds. Hardware Layout: 32 graphics processors (10-20 MFLOP each), 1/4 million pixel processors, 1024 x 768 pixel color frame buffer, 5 Gbit/sec ring network. Performance Estimate (Classification/Shading): For a 256 \times 256 \times 256 voxel dataset, the time to classify and shade the entire dataset is about 64 msec. Frame Rate Estimate (Observer Position Change): 10 fps for slightly coarse images, 1 fps for high-quality images. Frame Rate Estimate (Shading/Classification Change): 20 fps for coarse images, 2 fps for high-quality images, if the hierarchical enumeration is not invalidated. Strengths: High parallelism for shading/classification; potential for real-time interaction. Limitations: Recomputation of hierarchical enumeration is slow (several seconds) if classification mapping changes significantly. The Pixel-Planes 5 architecture was developed under joint funding by DARPA and the NSF, with development starting in the late summer of 1986. It was expected to become operational during the summer or fall of 1989. Although not explicitly designed for volume rendering, its flexibility made it well suited to the task. name: Screen Quad Rendering
head: FBO composition pass, Screen Render Pass, Two-pass rendering pipeline
body: Screen Quad Rendering is the final compositing stage in a two-pass splatting pipeline, where pre-rendered volumetric data stored in off-screen Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) is composited into the default framebuffer. It solves the problem of transferring intermediate rendering results (such as color and auxiliary buffers) from GPU memory to the display surface. It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the volume splatting geometry pass from the final screen composition. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: colorTexture: 2D texture containing the accumulated splat color, bound to unit 0. Format: GLRGBA, type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. positionTexture: 2D texture containing auxiliary data (e.g., world-space positions), bound to unit 3. Format: GLRGBA32F, type GLFLOAT. viewportSize: Vector2 uniform specifying the target resolution. upscale: Scalar uniform dividing the first-pass texture resolution. Default value 1. crossSection: Scalar uniform for debug overlay positioning, clamped to [0, 1]. Outputs: Default framebuffer (screen) with the composited image. Data Structures: The intermediate rendering state is stored in an FBO with two attachments: 1. GLCOLORATTACHMENT0: colorTexture (RGBA, Unsigned Byte). 2. GLCOLORATTACHMENT3: positionTexture (RGBA32F, Float). Draw buffers are configured as drawBuffers[] = {GLCOLORATTACHMENT0, GLNONE, GLNONE, GLCOLORATTACHMENT3}. Steps: 1. Pass 1 (Splatting): Render the volume primitives into the FBO described above. The texture resolution is scaled by upscale (default 1). 2. Pass 2 (Screen Render Pass): a. Bind the default framebuffer (ID 0). b. Bind colorTexture to texture unit 0 and positionTexture to texture unit 3. c. Set uniforms: viewportSize, upscale, and crossSection. d. Clear the color attachment with {r:0.0, g:0.0, b:0.0, a:1.0} and set loadOp to 'clear', storeOp to 'store'. e. Draw a full-screen triangle using the screen pass shader. f. End the render pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def screenquadrenderpass(colortexture, positiontexture, viewportsize, upscale, crosssection): # Clamp cross-section to [0, 1] if crosssection < 0: crosssection = 0 if crosssection > 1: crosssection = 1 # Bind default framebuffer (ID 0) bindframebuffer(0) # Bind textures to units 0 and 3 bindtexture(colortexture, unit=0) bindtexture(positiontexture, unit=3) # Set uniforms setuniform("viewportSize", viewportsize) setuniform("upscale", upscale) setuniform("crossSection", crosssection) # Begin render pass with clear value {r:0.0, g:0.0, b:0.0, a:1.0} beginrenderpass( colorattachment=colortexture, clearvalue=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0), loadop="clear", storeop="store") # Draw full-screen triangle drawfullscreentriangle() # End render pass endrenderpass() def bindframebuffer(id): pass def bindtexture(tex, unit): pass def setuniform(name, val): pass def beginrenderpass(colorattachment, clearvalue, loadop, storeop): pass def drawfullscreentriangle(): pass def endrenderpass(): pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Wayland Compositing: On Wayland, forcing output alpha to 1.0 in the fragment shader prevents compositing artifacts. Upscale Factor: If upscale > 1, the intermediate textures are smaller than the viewport, requiring filtering during the final draw. Performs a screen-space copy with injected debug logic and alpha forcing. Uses a single oversized triangle to avoid diagonal seams and double-shading artifacts. Time Complexity: Depends only on screen resolution, not volume size. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the intermediate FBO attachments. Strengths: Decouples volume rendering from display output, enabling post-processing and debug overlays. Limitations: Requires two passes; intermediate FBOs consume VRAM. When to use: When post-processing, debug overlays, or separate auxiliary buffer handling is required. This method originates from standard OpenGL and WebGPU rendering pipelines. It is implemented in real-time volume visualization applications. It leverages hardware-accelerated rasterization for the final composition step. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dongeronimo/webgpuvolumerendererdemo, https://github.com/dongeronimo/webgpuvolumerendererdemo, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Screen-space blit / Resample copy
head: Fullscreen Blit with Crosshair, Resample copy, Screen-space blit, blit.wgsl
body: This method performs a screen-space copy (blit) of a source texture, typically a compute-shader output, into a target render target. It simultaneously overlays a debug crosshair and forces the output alpha to 1.0 to prevent compositing artifacts on certain windowing systems like Wayland. It differs from a standard blit by injecting pixel-level crosshair logic and alpha forcing directly in the fragment shader. Input: A source texture accessed via a Shader Resource View (SRV) bound at slot uSRVSlot. Output: A target render target view (RTV) identified by slice uSlice and mip level uMip, cleared to transparent before drawing. Parameters: pSRVSrc (source SRV handle), pShader (shader object containing vertex and pixel shaders), uSRVSlot, uSlice, and uMip. The implementation relies on Direct3D 11 API objects for state management, including render target views, depth stencil views, and viewport structures. 1. Context Acquisition: Get the immediate device context (pDXContext) from the device. 2. Save State: Retrieve the current render target view (pRTVBack) and depth stencil view (pDSVBack) using OMGetRenderTargets. 3. Set Target: Bind the target render target mvvpRTVs[uSlice][uMip] using OMSetRenderTargets. 4. Clear: Clear the target render target to transparent using ClearRenderTargetView. 5. Set Viewport: Create a viewport matching the texture dimensions (VpDepth) and set it using RSSetViewports. Save the previous viewport (VpBack) for restoration. 6. Bind Resources: Bind the source SRV (pSRVSrc) at slot uSRVSlot using PSSetShaderResources. 7. Set Topology: Set the primitive topology to D3D11PRIMITIVETOPOLOGYTRIANGLESTRIP. 8. Bind Shaders: Set the vertex shader guVSScreenQuad using VSSetShader and the pixel shader guPSResample using PSSetShader. 9. Draw: Issue a draw call for 3 vertices using Draw(3, 0). 10. Unbind: Unbind the source SRV, vertex shader, and pixel shader by setting them to nullptr (or null SRV) at their respective slots. 11. Restore State: Restore the original viewport using RSSetViewports with VpBack. 12. Restore Targets: Restore the original render and depth-stencil targets using OMSetRenderTargets. The vertex shader renders a single oversized triangle using vertex indices 0, 1, 2. Positions are (-1.0, -1.0), (3.0, -1.0), (-1.0, 3.0). UVs are (0.0, 1.0), (2.0, 1.0), (0.0, -1.0). This covers the entire screen and extends beyond to ensure full coverage. The fragment shader samples the source texture at the interpolated UV coordinate. It calculates screen dimensions and the absolute offset in pixels from the screen center (0.5, 0.5). It determines if the pixel is inside the crosshair arms: Horizontal arm checks offsetpx.x <= 12.0 AND offsetpx.y <= 2.0 (outer) or <= 1.0 (inner); Vertical arm checks offsetpx.y <= 12.0 AND offsetpx.x <= 2.0 (outer) or <= 1.0 (inner). It returns white (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) for inner crosshair, black (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) for outer crosshair, and the sampled color with alpha forced to 1.0 otherwise. The alpha forcing prevents alpha-compositing issues on Wayland when TAA resolve smuggles grass-blade markers in the alpha channel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertargetpopulate(pSRVSrc, pShader, uSRVSlot, uSlice, uMip): # 1. Get immediate device context pDXContext = getimmediatedevicecontext() # 2. Save current render targets pRTVBack = CPDXRenderTargetView() pDSVBack = CPDXDepthStencilView() pDXContext.OMGetRenderTargets(1, pRTVBack, pDSVBack) # 3. Set target render target targetrtv = mvvpRTVs[uSlice][uMip] pDXContext.OMSetRenderTargets(1, targetrtv, None) # 4. Clear target to transparent pDXContext.ClearRenderTargetView(targetrtv, Colors.Transparent) # 5. Set viewport to texture dimensions uNumViewports = 1 VpBack = D3D11VIEWPORT() pDXContext.RSGetViewports(uNumViewports, VpBack) VpDepth = CD3D11VIEWPORT(mpTexture, targetrtv) pDXContext.RSSetViewports(uNumViewports, VpDepth) # 6. Bind source SRV pDXContext.PSSetShaderResources(uSRVSlot, 1, pSRVSrc) # 7. Set primitive topology pDXContext.IASetPrimitiveTopology(D3D11PRIMITIVETOPOLOGYTRIANGLESTRIP) # 8. Bind shaders vs = pShader.GetVertexShader(guVSScreenQuad) ps = pShader.GetPixelShader(guPSResample) pDXContext.VSSetShader(vs, None, 0) pDXContext.GSSetShader(None, None, 0) pDXContext.PSSetShader(ps, None, 0) # 9. Draw 3 vertices pDXContext.Draw(3, 0) # 10. Unbind resources pNullSRV = LPDXShaderResourceView(None) pDXContext.PSSetShaderResources(uSRVSlot, 1, pNullSRV) pDXContext.VSSetShader(None, None, 0) pDXContext.PSSetShader(None, None, 0) # 11. Restore viewport pDXContext.RSSetViewports(uNumViewports, VpBack) # 12. Restore render targets pDXContext.OMSetRenderTargets(1, pRTVBack, pDSVBack) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentshader(uv: vec2<f32>, screendims: vec2<f32>, sourcetexture: Texture2D) -> vec4<f32>: # Sample source color = sourcetexture.sample(uv) # Calculate pixel offset from center center = vec2<f32>(0.5, 0.5) pixelpos = uv screendims offsetpx = abs(pixelpos - center screendims) # Check crosshair arms # Horizontal arm houter = offsetpx.x <= 12.0 and offsetpx.y <= 2.0 hinner = offsetpx.x <= 12.0 and offsetpx.y <= 1.0 # Vertical arm vouter = offsetpx.y <= 12.0 and offsetpx.x <= 2.0 vinner = offsetpx.y <= 12.0 and offsetpx.x <= 1.0 isinner = hinner or vinner isouter = (houter or vouter) and not isinner if isinner: return vec4<f32>(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) elif isouter: return vec4<f32>(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) else: # Force alpha to 1.0 to prevent TAA resolve issues on Wayland return vec4<f32>(color.rgb, 1.0) Wayland TAA Artifacts: Failing to force alpha to 1.0 can result in grass-blade markers from the TAA resolve process leaking into the alpha channel, causing compositing issues. Viewport Mismatch: The viewport must be set to the texture dimensions, not the window dimensions, to ensure correct sampling coordinates. State Restoration: Failing to restore the original render targets and viewport can corrupt subsequent rendering passes. Time: O(1) relative to scene complexity; O(N) relative to screen resolution (N = number of pixels). The cost is dominated by the fragment shader execution over the screen area. Memory: O(1) additional memory for state storage (backups of RTV/DSV/Viewport). The source and target textures occupy their respective memory. Hardware: Tested on Direct3D 11 hardware. Resolution: Performance scales linearly with screen resolution. Scene: Independent of scene geometry or voxel count, as it operates on screen-space textures. Strengths: Efficient screen-space data transfer. Built-in debug visualization (crosshair). Avoids CPU-GPU synchronization overhead by using immediate context commands. Limitations: Specific to Direct3D 11 API in the provided implementation. Crosshair logic is hardcoded and not configurable via parameters in the base method. Alpha forcing may be undesirable for non-debug blits. Use when transferring compute shader output to a render target for display or further processing. Use when a debug crosshair is needed for screen-space alignment. Use when targeting Wayland compositors to avoid TAA-related alpha artifacts. Do not use for general-purpose texture copying where alpha preservation is critical and the Wayland TAA issue is not present. Do not use if the crosshair overlay is not desired. The method originates from the voxelG and VoxelizerX projects, which are unofficial implementations of voxel rendering techniques. The specific blit implementation with crosshair overlay is documented in the RenderTarget::Populate function of VoxelizerX and the associated shader code in voxelG. The technique is part of the rendering pipeline for screen-space blitting in voxel renderers. The crosshair overlay was added to assist with debugging screen-space coordinates and alignment. The alpha forcing was introduced to address specific artifacts observed on Wayland compositors with TAA. Used in voxel rendering pipelines for transferring data between render targets and providing debug visualization. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) StarsX/VoxelizerX, https://github.com/StarsX/VoxelizerX, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: Fullscreen Triangle Rendering
head: Fullscreen Texture Blit, Post-Process Quad, Screen Quad Texture Display, gl_VertexID fullscreen quad
body: Fullscreen Triangle Rendering displays an off-screen render texture onto the entire viewport using a dedicated shader, enabling HUD overlays and screenshot captures. It differs from sibling methods by generating a single oversized triangle via glVertexID to avoid diagonal seams and double-shading artifacts inherent in standard quad strip approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source render texture and viewport dimensions (width, height). Output: The color buffer of the default framebuffer (screen). Data Structures: Explicit VBO layout: 4 vertices, each containing 3 position floats and 2 texture coordinate floats, totaling 20 floats per quad. Vertex 0: (-1, -1, 0, 0, 0) Vertex 1: (-1, 1, 0, 0, 1) Vertex 2: (1, -1, 0, 1, 0) Vertex 3: (1, 1, 0, 1, 1) glVertexID layout: No explicit VBO is required; geometry is generated procedurally in the vertex shader. Steps: 1. Bind the default framebuffer (ID 0). 2. Clear the color buffer. 3. Bind the render texture to a sampler unit. 4. Bind the dedicated shader program. 5. Set uniforms: screenWidth, screenHeight, and crosshairType. 6. Draw geometry using GLTRIANGLESTRIP with 4 vertices. Formulas: For the glVertexID approach: 1. Compute UV coordinates: uv = \text{vec2}((\text{gl\VertexID} \ll 1) \& 2, \text{gl\VertexID} \& 2) 2. Compute clip-space position: \text{gl\Position} = \text{vec4}(uv \times 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fullscreentrianglerender(sourcetexture, width, height): # State initialization activeframebuffer = 0 colorbuffer = [0.0] (width height 4) samplerunit = [None] activeshader = None # 1. Bind default framebuffer activeframebuffer = 0 # 2. Clear color buffer for i in range(len(colorbuffer)): colorbuffer[i] = 0.0 # 3. Bind source texture samplerunit[0] = sourcetexture # 4. Bind shader activeshader = fullscreentriangleshader # 5. Set uniforms activeshader.uniforms["screenWidth"] = width activeshader.uniforms["screenHeight"] = height activeshader.uniforms["crosshairType"] = 0 # Default value not specified in sources # 6. Draw using triangle strip # Issue draw call: primitive=GLTRIANGLESTRIP, first=0, count=4 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Diagonal Seams: Standard quad rendering can cause seams if the diagonal is shared incorrectly. Double-Shading: Overlapping triangles in quad strips can cause double-shading. Aspect Ratio: If the source texture does not match the viewport aspect ratio, distortion occurs. Performance: While theoretically more optimal by avoiding duplicated ray tracing along the quad edge, no measurable performance difference was observed at the granularity used. Time Complexity: O(1) relative to scene complexity; depends only on screen resolution. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for vertex data (if using explicit VBO) or O(0) if using glVertexID. Strengths: Simple implementation, no vertex buffer management required with glVertexID, avoids diagonal seams and double-shading. Limitations: Limited to displaying a single texture; not suitable for complex geometry or multiple textures without additional passes. When to Use: Post-processing, HUD overlays, screenshot capture. When Not to Use: Complex 3D scene rendering, multi-texture blending in a single pass. The technique is used in real-time graphics for displaying textures on the screen, particularly in voxel raytracing and post-processing pipelines. The glVertexID approach generates the geometry procedurally, avoiding explicit vertex buffer overhead. name: Fullscreen Actor Pass
head: Single Fullscreen Actor Pass
body: The Fullscreen Actor Pass is a rendering stage in the Met3D volume rendering pipeline that renders a single selected 3D actor to a fullscreen quad using an internal rendering resolution. It solves the problem of isolating the rendering of a specific volume actor for debugging, analysis, or high-quality upscaling, distinct from the standard multi-actor compositing pass. It differs from the Multisampled 3-D Actors Pass by rendering only one actor and from the 2-D UI Actors Pass by targeting the 3D scene depth buffer rather than a UI layer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene view configuration where "single fullscreen actor mode" is enabled, and a specific actor selected in the scene view properties. Output: A framebuffer containing the rendered geometry/volume of the selected actor at the internal rendering resolution. Data Structures: MSceneViewGLWidget: Manages the current render step state. MActor: The actor instance to be rendered. Internal Framebuffer: A render target with dimensions defined by the internal rendering resolution, not the viewport resolution. Steps: 1. The rendering system sets the current render step to RENDERSCENE by calling MSceneViewGLWidget::renderStep(). 2. The scene view identifies the actor selected in the scene view properties. 3. The scene view calls MActor::renderToFullScreen() on the selected actor. 4. The actor is rendered into the internal framebuffer. Parameters: Resolution: The pass uses an internal rendering resolution instead of the viewport resolution. This allows rendering at a fixed resolution or using upscaling techniques (e.g., FSR) to reach the target resolution. If FSR is disabled, the original framebuffer is copied into a new framebuffer at the target resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fullscreenactorpass(sceneview, selectedactor): # Step 1: Set render step to RENDERSCENE sceneview.renderstep = RENDERSCENE # Step 2: Render the selected actor to fullscreen # The actor is rendered into an internal framebuffer # using an internal resolution, not the viewport resolution. selectedactor.rendertofullscreen() # Note: If single fullscreen actor mode is disabled, # this pass is skipped in favor of the multisampled pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If single fullscreen actor mode is disabled, this pass is not executed. The internal resolution may differ from the viewport resolution, requiring upscaling or copying. This variant renders all actors participating in the RENDERUI pass to a UI layer. It sets the render step to RENDERUI and calls MActor::renderToUiLayer() for each actor. If single fullscreen actor mode is enabled, only the fullscreen actor is rendered during this pass. It is primarily used for rendering 2-D interface elements (e.g., colour bars) at the target resolution without upscaling. This variant renders all enabled actors participating in the RENDERSCENE pass when single fullscreen actor mode is disabled. It calls MActor::render() for each actor and uses an internal rendering resolution. It employs Order Independent Transparency for transparency rendering. Time Complexity: Proportional to the rendering cost of a single actor (or all actors in the multisampled variant). Memory Complexity: Requires an internal framebuffer at the internal rendering resolution. Strengths: Allows focused rendering of a single actor for debugging or high-quality upscaling. Limitations: Only one actor can be rendered in single fullscreen actor mode. Overlapping volumes are composited incorrectly if more than one actor is rendered in the DVR pass (though this is a separate pass). When to use: When debugging a specific volume actor or when upscaling techniques are required for a single actor. When not to use: When multiple actors need to be composited together in a single pass. The Fullscreen Actor Pass is part of the Met3D rendering pipeline, as documented in the Met3D developer manual. It is used in conjunction with other passes such as the Multisampled DVR pass and the Label pass to produce the final scene. The pass is designed to support internal rendering resolutions and upscaling techniques like FSR. Rendering, https://met3d.readthedocs.io/en/latest/05developermanual/04rendering/index.html, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Scatter Samples to Image
head: Sample Scattering to Image, ScatterSamplesToImage
body: Scatter Samples to Image is a post-processing step that scatters computed sample values from arbitrary screen-space positions into a regular image grid. It maps non-uniformly distributed samples to a standard raster image for visualization. Unlike Splatting, which uses geometric kernels to blur and accumulate contributions, this method performs a direct assignment of values to pixel coordinates without filtering. Inputs and Outputs: samplepositions: A tensor of shape 2 \times N, where N is the number of samples. samples: A tensor of shape C \times N, where C is the number of channels. imageout: A tensor of shape C \times H \times W. samplemaskout: A tensor of shape 1 \times H \times W, containing 1 where samples were taken and 0 elsewhere. defaultvalues: A vector of doubles providing default values for the 8 channels, used in the PyTorch interface ScatterSamplesToImage. Data Structures: samplepositions: 2 \times N tensor. samples: C \times N tensor. imageout: C \times H \times W tensor. samplemaskout: 1 \times H \times W tensor. Steps: 1. Initialize imageout and samplemaskout. 2. Initialize samplemaskout to all zeros. 3. For each sample index k from 0 to N-1: a. Retrieve position (xk, yk) from samplepositions[:, k]. b. Retrieve values v{k,1}, \dots, v{k,C} from samples[:, k]. c. Convert (xk, yk) to integer pixel coordinates (i, j) by flooring or rounding. d. Check if (i, j) is within the image boundaries [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1]. If outside, ignore this sample. e. For each channel c from 0 to C-1: write v{k,c} to imageout[c, j, i]. f. Set samplemaskout[0, j, i] = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def scattersamplestoimage(samplepositions, samples, imageshape, defaultvalues=None): C, N = samples.shape H, W = imageshape # Initialize output tensors imageout = [[[0.0] W for in range(H)] for in range(C)] samplemaskout = [[[0.0] W for in range(H)] for in range(1)] # Apply default values if provided; otherwise pixels receiving no samples remain untouched if defaultvalues is not None: for c in range(C): for r in range(H): for col in range(W): imageout[c][r][col] = defaultvalues[c] # Scatter samples for k in range(N): x = samplepositions[0][k] y = samplepositions[1][k] col = math.floor(x) row = math.floor(y) # Check boundaries if 0 <= col < W and 0 <= row < H: for c in range(C): imageout[c][row][col] = samples[c][k] samplemaskout[0][row][col] = 1.0 return imageout, samplemaskout Parameters: defaultvalues: A vector of doubles providing default values for the 8 channels, used in the PyTorch interface ScatterSamplesToImage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Samples located outside the image boundaries are ignored. Pixels in the output image that receive no samples are left untouched (no default value overwriting). Multiple samples may map to the same pixel; the last sample processed overwrites previous values. A variant that uses scatter-like logic to render a 2D heatmap from trace data. It initializes a canvas of width traceCount 2 and height sampleCount. It computes min and max values across the 2D array samples[traceCount][sampleCount], calculating range as max - min (defaulting to 1 if 0 to avoid division by zero). For each pixel (i, j), it calculates normalized value v = (samples[i][j] - min) / range, computes color intensity color = \lfloor v \times 255 \rfloor, and sets RGBA to (color, color, color, 255). Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples, as each sample is processed once. Memory Complexity: O(C \times H \times W) for the output image and mask. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Extremely fast for direct mapping; no kernel evaluation or sorting required. Limitations: No anti-aliasing or smoothing; artifacts appear if samples are sparse or misaligned with pixels. When to use: When samples are already on a grid or when a raw, unfiltered representation is desired. When not to use: When smooth visualization or blending is required; use Splatting instead. The method is described in the context of adaptive sampling and reconstruction for volume visualization. Learning adaptive sampling and reconstruction for Volume Visualization, https://github.com/shamanDevel/AdaptiveSampling, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) SeismicDataCompressor, https://github.com/rubensrudio/SeismicDataCompressor, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Surface Rendering with Scatter Accumulation
head: Scatter Accumulation for Surface Properties
body: This method is a rendering pass that queries surface properties (albedo, BRDF, normals) at ray-object hit points and scatters them into per-ray maps using a scatter operation, handling optional noise jittering and relighting outputs. It differs from volume-based splatting by operating exclusively on discrete surface intersections rather than volumetric samples, enabling direct extraction of material properties and visibility masks for downstream relighting or metric evaluation. Inputs: Ray hit data: positions, normals, intersection masks (intersectmask), and ray indices. Model parameters: noisestd, albedoscales, rendercfg flags (relightolat, relightprobes, relightenvmap, whitebkgd). Hit properties: raw albedo, BRDF parameters, and normals queried at hit points. Outputs: Per-ray maps: rgb, lvis (light visibility), normals, albedo, brdfprop. Optional relighting maps: olat (object-local albedo), probe (probe contributions), env (environment map contributions). Accumulation mask: accmap indicating valid hits. Data Structures: Maps are stored as tensors with shape (B, Nrays,...) where B is batch size and Nrays is the number of rays. rgb: (B, Nrays, 3) lvis: (B, Nrays, 1) or (B, Nrays, 3) depending on implementation. normals: (B, Nrays, 3) albedo: (B, Nrays, 3) brdfprop: (B, Nrays, Nbrdfparams) olat: (B, Nrays, 512, 3) if enabled. probe: (B, Nrays, Nprobes, 3) if enabled. env: (B, Nrays, Nenvcoeffs, 3) if enabled. accmap: (B, Nrays) boolean or float mask. Steps: 1. Query Properties: Use batchifyquery to retrieve albedo, BRDF, and normals at hit points. If model.noisestd > 0, also query jittered versions: albedojitter and brdfzjitter. 2. Scale Albedo: If albedoscales is provided, apply scaling: albedo = albedoscales.reshape(1, 3) albedo. 3. Squeeze Dimensions: Remove batch/ray dimensions from hit properties to prepare for rendering: albedohit = albedo.squeeze(-2).squeeze(0). 4. Render Surface Points: Call model.rendersurfpts with hit positions, albedo, BRDF props, and normals to compute RGB, olat, probe, env, and lvis. 5. Identify Hits: Determine valid hit indices using torch.where(intersectmask)[0]. 6. Scatter Hit Properties: Use scatternd to scatter hit properties into full ray maps: rgb, lvis, normals, albedo, and brdfprop. 7. Scatter Jittered Maps: If noise is enabled, scatter albedojitter and brdfzjitter into their respective maps. 8. Conditionally Scatter Relighting Maps: Based on rendercfg flags, scatter olat, probe, and env maps if relightolat, relightprobes, or relightenvmap are true. 9. Initialize Non-Hit Rays: For rays with no intersection, initialize all maps to zeros with appropriate shapes (e.g., olatmap shape (B, Nrays, 512, 3) if enabled). 10. Accumulation and Background Compensation: Compute accmap from intersectmask. If whitebkgd is true, apply white background compensation: rgbmap = rgbmap + (1.0 - accmap[..., None]). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfacerenderwithscatteraccumulation( intersectmask, hitpositions, hitnormals, hitbrdfprops, model, rendercfg, albedoscales=None, noisestd=0.0): # Step 1: Query properties albedo, brdf, normals = batchifyquery(hitpositions, hitnormals, hitbrdfprops) albedojitter = None brdfzjitter = None if noisestd > 0: albedojitter, brdfzjitter = queryjitteredversions(albedo, brdf, noisestd) # Step 2: Scale albedo if albedoscales is not None: albedo = albedoscales.reshape(1, 3) albedo # Step 3: Squeeze dimensions albedohit = albedo.squeeze(-2).squeeze(0) normalshit = normals.squeeze(-2).squeeze(0) brdfhit = brdf.squeeze(-2).squeeze(0) # Step 4: Render surface points rgb, olat, probe, env, lvis = model.rendersurfpts( hitpositions, albedohit, brdfhit, normalshit) # Step 5: Identify hits hitindices = torch.where(intersectmask)[0] # Step 6: Scatter hit properties rgbmap = scatternd(hitindices, rgb, shape=(B, Nrays, 3)) lvismap = scatternd(hitindices, lvis, shape=(B, Nrays, 1)) normalsmap = scatternd(hitindices, normalshit, shape=(B, Nrays, 3)) albedomap = scatternd(hitindices, albedohit, shape=(B, Nrays, 3)) brdfpropmap = scatternd(hitindices, brdfhit, shape=(B, Nrays, Nbrdfparams)) # Step 7: Scatter jittered maps if noisestd > 0: albedojittermap = scatternd(hitindices, albedojitter, shape=(B, Nrays, 3)) brdfzjittermap = scatternd(hitindices, brdfzjitter, shape=(B, Nrays, Nbrdfparams)) # Step 8: Conditionally scatter relighting maps olatmap = None probemap = None envmap = None if rendercfg.relightolat: olatmap = scatternd(hitindices, olat, shape=(B, Nrays, 512, 3)) if rendercfg.relightprobes: probemap = scatternd(hitindices, probe, shape=(B, Nrays, Nprobes, 3)) if rendercfg.relightenvmap: envmap = scatternd(hitindices, env, shape=(B, Nrays, Nenvcoeffs, 3)) # Step 9: Initialize non-hit rays # Initialize all maps to zeros for non-hit rays # This is implicitly handled by scatternd if it initializes the output tensor to zeros # and only updates hitindices. Explicit initialization: rgbmap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, 3), device=rgbmap.device) lvismap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, 1), device=lvismap.device) normalsmap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, 3), device=normalsmap.device) albedomap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, 3), device=albedomap.device) brdfpropmap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, Nbrdfparams), device=brdfpropmap.device) if noisestd > 0: albedojittermap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, 3), device=albedojittermap.device) brdfzjittermap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, Nbrdfparams), device=brdfzjittermap.device) if rendercfg.relightolat: olatmap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, 512, 3), device=olatmap.device) if rendercfg.relightprobes: probemap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, Nprobes, 3), device=probemap.device) if rendercfg.relightenvmap: envmap = torch.zeros((B, Nrays, Nenvcoeffs, 3), device=envmap.device) # Re-scatter hits into initialized maps rgbmap[hitindices] = rgb lvismap[hitindices] = lvis normalsmap[hitindices] = normalshit albedomap[hitindices] = albedohit brdfpropmap[hitindices] = brdfhit if noisestd > 0: albedojittermap[hitindices] = albedojitter brdfzjittermap[hitindices] = brdfzjitter if rendercfg.relightolat: olatmap[hitindices] = olat if rendercfg.relightprobes: probemap[hitindices] = probe if rendercfg.relightenvmap: envmap[hitindices] = env # Step 10: Accumulation and background compensation accmap = intersectmask.float() if rendercfg.whitebkgd: rgbmap = rgbmap + (1.0 - accmap[..., None]) return { 'rgb': rgbmap, 'lvis': lvismap, 'normals': normalsmap, 'albedo': albedomap, 'brdfprop': brdfpropmap, 'olat': olatmap, 'probe': probemap, 'env': envmap, 'accmap': accmap } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when scattering sparse hits into dense maps, especially for large scenes. Use appropriate data types (e.g., float32). Boundaries: Ensure that scatternd handles boundary conditions correctly, especially when hit indices are out of bounds. Degenerate Input: Handle cases where intersectmask is all False (no hits) by initializing maps to zeros and skipping scattering steps. Time Complexity: O(Nrays) for querying and scattering, where Nrays is the number of rays. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of rays and hit points. Memory Complexity: O(Nrays Nproperties) for storing per-ray maps, where Nproperties is the number of properties (RGB, normals, albedo, etc.). Measured Performance: Performance depends on the hardware and resolution. For high-resolution scenes, memory usage can become a bottleneck. Scaling: Scales well with batch size and number of rays, but memory usage increases linearly with the number of rays. Strengths: Direct extraction of surface properties, support for noise jittering, and flexible relighting options. Limitations: Memory-intensive for large scenes, sensitive to precision issues, and requires careful handling of boundary conditions. When to Use: Suitable for applications requiring detailed surface property extraction, such as material analysis, relighting, and metric evaluation. When Not to Use: Not ideal for real-time applications with strict memory constraints or when volumetric effects are required. This method originates from the L-Tracing framework, which focuses on surface-based rendering and property extraction. It is used in research contexts for evaluating novel view synthesis, material estimation, and relighting techniques. ziyc/L-Tracing, https://github.com/ziyc/L-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Rendering Pipeline Architecture
body: Rendering Pipeline Architecture refers to the structural organization of hardware-accelerated splatting techniques, where volumetric or point-cloud data is decomposed into primitives (splats) and rasterized to form an image. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large-scale volumetric datasets in real-time by leveraging GPU rasterization pipelines for transformation, projection, and compositing. It differs from ray-marching methods by using screen-space accumulation (compositing along sheets) rather than per-ray sampling, and from single-pass mesh rendering by explicitly handling transparency and depth occlusion through multi-stage or specialized accumulation buffers. The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized. 1. Primitive Representation: The volume is decomposed into primitives. These may be explicit geometric shapes (cubes, cells, splats) or implicit functions sampled via texture hardware. Each primitive k is defined by its position \mathbf{p}k, density/extinction coefficient gk or \rhok, and a reconstruction kernel h (typically a Gaussian). 2. Transformation: Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp). For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening. 3. Rasterization: The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane. This step leverages hardware-accelerated scan-conversion, depth testing, and blending. The contribution of a voxel D to a screen point (x,y) is determined by the footprint function F(x,y), which is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view direction: F(x,y) = \int h(x-xD, y-yD, z) \, dz The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density: P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) where \text{weight}(x,y) = F(x-xD, y-yD). 4. Compositing: Contributions are accumulated to form the final image. This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly. Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time). 5. Hardware Acceleration: Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity. A fragment-processing stage that reconstructs continuous and cardinal attributes (normals, colors) into a G-Buffer using weighted blending and ternary depth tests. Choose this when accurate per-splat attribute reconstruction with transparency is required. Combines splat and mesh rendering to enable high-quality shader effects in a single pass by interpolating attributes in object space via elevation map patches. Choose this when avoiding multi-pass blending artifacts and blurring is critical. Separates depth testing, color accumulation, and normalization into distinct passes to ensure exact perspective-correct filtering without explicit sorting. Choose this when exact weight normalization and correct occlusion handling are prioritized over single-pass performance. The concept of splatting was introduced by Levoy as a method for volume visualization. The family evolved to address the limitations of early software-based rendering by leveraging GPU hardware acceleration. Subsequent developments focused on improving attribute quality [1066-splat-attributes-pass.md], reducing pass counts [1254-single-pass-splat-rendering-pipeline.md], and ensuring numerical correctness in perspective projection [2837-three-pass-gpu-point-rendering-pipeline.md].
