name: Splat Attributes Pass
head: Blending Pass, G-Buffer Pass
body: The Splat Attributes Pass is the fragment processing stage in hardware-accelerated surface splatting that reconstructs continuous attributes from overlapping splats into a reconstruction buffer (G-Buffer). It solves the problem of correctly accumulating per-fragment data (such as normals and colors) from translucent, overlapping point sprites by applying a weighted blending scheme based on radial distance and depth proximity. It differs from standard alpha blending by incorporating a depth-proximity falloff factor to prioritize splats closer to the visible surface. The pass processes each fragment generated by the rasterization of a splat (point sprite). It calculates a composite weight for the splat based on its position within the sprite and its depth relative to the scene geometry, then accumulates weighted attributes into the G-Buffer textures. Inputs: Splat Data: Per-splat attributes including center position, radius, color, and linear depth in view space. Depth Buffer: The current depth buffer containing the depth of the closest visible surface at each pixel. Viewport Size: The dimensions of the render target, used to normalize fragment coordinates for depth buffer sampling. Outputs: G-Buffer Textures: gnormal (vec4, location 0): Stores the accumulated weighted normal vector in the RGB channels. gcolor (vec4, location 1): Stores the accumulated weighted color in the RGB channels and the accumulated weight in the Alpha channel. The G-Buffer is implemented as two 2D textures (or render targets): 1. gnormal: Format RGBA (or RGB with unused alpha), type float. Layout: xyz = weighted normal sum, w = unused or padding. 2. gcolor: Format RGBA, type float. Layout: rgb = weighted color sum, a = weight sum. epsilon: A small constant used to normalize the depth-proximity falloff. Typical value: 0.25. 1. Fragment Position Calculation: Calculate the 2D offset of the fragment from the center of the point sprite in screen space. \mathbf{p}{offset} = \text{gl\PointCoord} - (0.5, 0.5) 2. Radius Check: Calculate the squared magnitude of the offset. m^2 = \mathbf{p}{offset} \cdot \mathbf{p}{offset} If m^2 > 0.25, discard the fragment. 3. World-Space Offset Conversion: Convert the screen-space offset to a world-space offset proportional to the splat's radius. \mathbf{p}{world\offset} = \mathbf{p}{offset} \times 2 \times r where r is the splat radius. 4. Depth Offset Calculation: Calculate the depth offset from the center of the splat sphere to the fragment's position on the sphere surface. d{offset} = \sqrt{r^2 - \mathbf{p}{world\offset} \cdot \mathbf{p}{world\offset}} 5. Fragment Depth in View Space: Calculate the depth of the fragment on the splat surface in view space by subtracting the depth offset from the linear depth of the splat center. z{frag} = z{linear} - d{offset} where z{linear} is the linear depth of the splat center. 6. Surface Depth Retrieval: Sample the depth buffer at the fragment's screen coordinates to get the depth of the visible surface. z{surface} = \text{LinearDepth}(\text{Texture}(\text{DepthBuffer}, \frac{\text{gl\FragCoord.xy}}{\text{ViewportSize}}).x) 7. Occlusion Test: If the splat fragment is behind the visible surface (z{frag} > z{surface}), discard the fragment. 8. Weight Calculation: Compute two falloff weights and combine them. Radial Falloff (w1): Decreases with distance from the splat center. w1 = 1 - \frac{\sqrt{m^2}}{0.5} Depth-Proximity Falloff (w2): Increases as the splat surface approaches the visible surface (smaller gap). w2 = \frac{z{surface} - z{frag}}{\epsilon} where \epsilon is the epsilon parameter (e.g., 0.25). Combined Weight (w): w = w1 \times w2 9. Normal Calculation: Compute the view-space normal at the fragment's position on the splat sphere. \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{world\offset}, d{offset}) The reference code constructs the normal vector from the world-space offset and the depth offset component. 10. Attribute Accumulation: Accumulate the weighted attributes into the G-Buffer using additive blending (or manual accumulation in a compute shader). Normal: \mathbf{g\normal.xyz} \leftarrow \mathbf{g\normal.xyz} + w \cdot \mathbf{n} Color: \mathbf{g\color.rgb} \leftarrow \mathbf{g\color.rgb} + w \cdot \mathbf{c} where \mathbf{c} is the splat color. Weight: \mathbf{g\color.a} \leftarrow \mathbf{g\color.a} + w Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def lineardepth(depthvalue): """Converts depth buffer value to linear view space depth.""" return depthvalue def sampletexture(depthbuffer, coords): """Samples the depth buffer texture at normalized coordinates.""" return depthbuffer[coords] def computesplatfragment(glPointCoord, radius, linearDepth, color, depthbuffer, viewportsize, epsilon, glFragCoord): # 1. Fragment position calculation fromcenterptspc = np.array(glPointCoord) - 0.5 # 2. Radius check magsq = np.dot(fromcenterptspc, fromcenterptspc) if magsq > 0.25: return None # Discard fragment # 3. World-space offset conversion fromcenterwldspc = fromcenterptspc 2.0 radius # 4. Depth offset calculation depthoffset = math.sqrt(radius radius - np.dot(fromcenterwldspc, fromcenterwldspc)) # 5. Fragment depth in view space depth = linearDepth - depthoffset # 6. Surface depth retrieval texcoords = np.array(glFragCoord) / viewportsize surfacedepth = lineardepth(sampletexture(depthbuffer, texcoords)) # 7. Occlusion test if depth > surfacedepth: return None # Discard fragment # 8. Weight calculation w1 = 1.0 - (math.sqrt(magsq) / 0.5) w2 = (surfacedepth - depth) / epsilon weight = w1 w2 # 9. Normal calculation normal = np.array(list(fromcenterwldspc) + [depthoffset]) normal = normal / np.linalg.norm(normal) # 10. Attribute accumulation values normalcontrib = weight normal colorcontrib = weight color weightcontrib = weight return normalcontrib, colorcontrib, weightcontrib This configuration sets up the blending state for the Splat Attributes Pass to ensure correct accumulation of translucent splats. It involves clearing the color buffer to RGBA(0,0,0,0) to ensure zero initial alpha, disabling depth testing, and enabling blending with separate blend factors: RGB uses GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA / GLONE, and Alpha uses GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA / GLONE, with the blend equation set to GLFUNCADD for both. This setup is typically used when rendering instanced quads representing splats. A full-screen triangle pass that reads an intermediate sRGB-blended splat accumulation texture, converts it to linear space, and outputs the result for premultiplied alpha blending onto the final SceneColor buffer. It takes parameters including an intermediate texture (IntermediateTexture) and a sampler (IntermediateSampler). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot F), where N is the number of splats and F is the average number of fragments per splat (determined by the splat radius and screen resolution). The depth buffer sampling and discard operations are constant time per fragment. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the G-Buffer textures, where W and H are the viewport dimensions. Performance: The pass is highly parallelizable and benefits from hardware-accelerated rasterization and blending. The depth test and discard logic can reduce the effective workload if splats are largely occluded. Strengths: Provides physically plausible attribute reconstruction (normals, colors) for surface splatting by considering depth proximity. It is efficient as it leverages standard GPU fragment processing. Limitations: The accuracy of the normal and color reconstruction depends on the density of splats and the correctness of the depth buffer. If splats are too sparse, the G-Buffer may contain gaps or inaccurate normals. When to use: When surface splatting is required for rendering point clouds or Gaussian splats, and accurate per-pixel normals and colors are needed for lighting or further processing. When not to use: If only a simple color accumulation is needed without normal reconstruction, or if the depth buffer is not available or unreliable. The Splat Attributes Pass is part of the rendering pipeline for surface splatting, a technique used to render point clouds and Gaussian splats as smooth surfaces. The method of using depth-proximity falloff to weight attributes is described in the context of point cloud rendering using OpenGL. The broader context of splatting as a volume rendering technique involves treating volumetric data as geometric primitives rasterized onto the screen. The specific implementation details, including the G-Buffer layout and weight calculation, are derived from open-source point cloud rendering projects. arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, https://github.com/YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Splat Depth Pass
head: Front-Face Depth Pass, Visibility Pass
body: The Splat Depth Pass computes the depth of the front surface of a point sprite (splat) for each fragment, enabling correct occlusion handling during surface splatting. It differs from standard binary depth testing by applying a small epsilon shift to the calculated depth, which prevents z-fighting and gaps between overlapping splats by ensuring consistent blending at surface boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: Fragment shader context including glFragCoord (window-space coordinates), glPointCoord (normalized texture coordinates within the point sprite, range [0,1]), and vertex attributes i.radius (splat radius in world space) and i.depth (or equivalent linear depth of the point center). Output: glFragDepth (window-space depth value written to the depth buffer). Data Structures No explicit data structures are required; the method operates on per-fragment state provided by the graphics API. Steps 1. Calculate offset from center: Compute the 2D vector from the center of the point sprite to the current fragment. 2. Check circular boundary: Calculate the squared magnitude of the offset. If the squared magnitude exceeds 0.25, the fragment lies outside the unit circle and is discarded. 3. Compute world-space offset: Scale the normalized offset by the splat's radius to get the world-space 2D offset vector. 4. Calculate depth offset: Determine the z-offset from the center of the sphere to the front surface at the current 2D position using the Pythagorean theorem. 5. Compute final depth: Subtract the depth offset from the center's linear depth and add an epsilon value to shift the depth slightly towards the camera. 6. Write depth: Assign the computed depth to the fragment depth output. Formulas Boundary Check: |\mathbf{v}{center}|^2 \le 0.25. Depth Offset: d{offset} = \sqrt{r^2 - |\mathbf{v}{world}|^2}. Final Depth: z{frag} = z{center} - d{offset} + \epsilon. Parameters epsilon (\epsilon): A small constant added to the depth to blend splats close to the surface. Value: 0.25. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Z-fighting and Gaps: Without the epsilon shift, overlapping splats at the same depth may cause z-fighting or visible gaps due to precision errors. The epsilon ensures splats near the surface are blended correctly. Precision: The calculation assumes linear depth. If non-linear depth is used, a conversion function must transform window-space Z to linear eye-space Z before subtraction. Radius Zero: If the radius is zero, the depth offset is zero, and the depth equals the center depth minus epsilon. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesplatdepth(glfragcoordz: float, glpointcoord: tuple, radius: float, centerlineardepth: float, epsilon: float) -> float: # 1. Calculate offset from center vcenter = (glpointcoord[0] - 0.5, glpointcoord[1] - 0.5) # 2. Check circular boundary magsq = vcenter[0]2 + vcenter[1]2 if magsq > 0.25: return None # Fragment outside splat boundary # 3. Compute world-space offset vworld = (vcenter[0] 2.0 radius, vcenter[1] 2.0 radius) # 4. Calculate depth offset dotval = vworld[0]2 + vworld[1]2 radiussq = radius radius depthoffset = (max(radiussq - dotval, 0.0)) 0.5 # 5. Compute final depth # centerlineardepth replaces linearDepth(glFragCoord.z) as a standard conversion finaldepth = centerlineardepth - depthoffset + epsilon # 6. Write depth return finaldepth A technique that maintains exactly one surface layer per pixel using a depth band to decide blending, replacing, or discarding fragments. It differs from the standard Splat Depth Pass by accommodating depth uncertainty, though it may cause occlusion artifacts in complex geometry. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment. The calculation involves basic arithmetic operations and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No additional buffers are allocated; it writes directly to the depth buffer. Strengths: Simple to implement in the fragment shader. It effectively handles occlusion for point-based surface rendering. It prevents z-fighting via epsilon adjustment. Limitations: It relies on the assumption that splats are spherical and uniformly sized. It does not handle transparency or volume accumulation directly, as those are handled by subsequent passes. When to use: When rendering point clouds as surfaces where correct occlusion is required before color accumulation. When not to use: For volume rendering where depth is integrated along rays, or when splats are not spherical. The method is derived from implementations of point cloud surface rendering, specifically those using spherical splats to approximate surfaces. The specific epsilon adjustment technique is documented in the PointCloudRendering repository. arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Single-Layer Ternary Depth Test
head: Single-layer depth test, Ternary Depth Test, Ternary Depth Test for Surface Reconstruction, Three-way z-test, Weyrich et al. depth test, Z-blend test
body: The Single-Layer Ternary Depth Test is a rasterization technique for surface splatting that maintains exactly one surface layer per pixel, using a depth band to decide whether to blend, replace, or discard incoming fragments. It solves the problem of handling overlapping splats during surface reconstruction by replacing the standard binary pass/fail depth test with a ternary logic that accommodates depth uncertainty. It differs from depth-interval grouping by maintaining only a single layer per pixel, which simplifies the pipeline but causes visibility and occlusion artifacts in complex geometry. Inputs and Outputs Input: A stream of splat fragments, each with a depth value zd, color, and weight. State: Each pixel maintains a single stored depth value zs and a running accumulated sum (e.g., EWA sum) for the single surface layer. Output: The final color and opacity for the pixel, representing the single closest surface layer. Data Structures Pixel State: A single depth value zs is stored in the depth buffer or a dedicated surface layer buffer. No multi-layer stack is maintained. Parameters \varepsilon{\Delta z}: A scaling factor for the depth extents of the splat. Typically set to 1.0. \varepsilon{bias}: A bias term accounting for numerical inaccuracies, comparable to glPolygonOffset's parameter unit. hz: The depth extent (or half-height) of the splat. Algorithm Steps 1. Compute Epsilon Band: For each incoming splat, compute the epsilon band size \varepsilon based on the splat's depth range hz: \varepsilon:= hz \cdot \varepsilon{\Delta z} + \varepsilon{bias} 2. Compare Depths: For each incoming fragment with depth zd, compare it to the currently stored depth zs for that pixel. 3. Apply Ternary Test: Determine the action based on the difference between the fragment depth and the stored depth: Z-Blend: If the fragment depth falls within the \varepsilon-band of the stored value, i.e., |zd - zs| \le \varepsilon, blend the fragment into the running EWA sum. Z-Fail (Discard): If the fragment is significantly behind the stored layer (zd < zs - \varepsilon), discard the fragment. Z-Pass (Replace): If the fragment is significantly in front of the stored layer (zd > zs + \varepsilon), replace the stored layer with this new fragment (updating zs and resetting the accumulation). 4. Normalization: After processing all fragments for a pixel, the accumulated color and weight are normalized. Because no coverage-based opacity is involved, the normalized output is always fully opaque wherever any surfel contributes, even at silhouette pixels where only a few surfels partially cover the pixel footprint and the accumulated weight is low. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlelayerternarydepthtest(fragment, pixelstate, epsilondeltaz=1.0, epsilonbias=0.0): """ fragment: object with attributes.depth (zd),.color,.weight,.hz pixelstate: object with attributes.storeddepth (zs),.accumulatedcolor,.accumulatedweight epsilondeltaz: scaling factor for depth extents (default 1.0) epsilonbias: bias for numerical inaccuracies (default 0.0) Returns: Updated pixelstate """ # 1. Compute epsilon band size epsilon = fragment.hz epsilondeltaz + epsilonbias zd = fragment.depth zs = pixelstate.storeddepth # 2. Ternary Depth Test if zd < zs - epsilon: # Z-Fail: Fragment is significantly behind the stored layer # Discard fragment, do not update pixel state return pixelstate elif zd > zs + epsilon: # Z-Pass: Fragment is significantly in front of the stored layer # Replace the stored layer pixelstate.storeddepth = zd pixelstate.accumulatedcolor = fragment.color fragment.weight pixelstate.accumulatedweight = fragment.weight return pixelstate else: # Z-Blend: Fragment is within the epsilon band # Blend into the running sum pixelstate.accumulatedcolor += fragment.color fragment.weight pixelstate.accumulatedweight += fragment.weight return pixelstate The pseudocode assumes fragment.hz is available from the splat's geometry. The "Replace" action resets the accumulation, which is consistent with maintaining a single layer where the new front-most fragment becomes the sole contributor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Hard Opaque Fringes: Because the normalized output is always fully opaque wherever any surfel contributes, even at silhouette pixels where only a few surfels partially cover the pixel footprint and the accumulated weight is low, the method produces hard, opaque fringes along object boundaries. This results in a "crusty" shell appearance rather than a gradual opacity falloff. Self-Occlusion Artifacts: The single-layer constraint exacerbates self-occlusion errors at concavities (e.g., inside ears or under chins). Deeper surfels that should form a second layer are incorrectly rejected by the ternary test, resulting in holes or translucent patches that reveal the background through what should be an opaque, self-occluding object. Usage Context: The ternary depth test is used only for surface reconstruction; regular depth tests are still required for triangle pipelines. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of splats per pixel, as each splat is processed once with constant-time depth comparisons. Memory complexity is O(1) per pixel, as only a single depth value and accumulation buffer are maintained. Performance: The method is computationally efficient due to the lack of multi-layer management and sorting overhead associated with depth-interval grouping. Strengths: Simple implementation; low memory footprint; effective for simple, convex surfaces where single-layer assumption holds. Limitations: Fails to handle complex geometry with self-occlusion or multiple surface layers per pixel. Produces aliasing and silhouette artifacts due to the lack of coverage-based opacity. When to use: Suitable for simple surface splatting where performance is critical and geometry is relatively simple (e.g., convex objects). When not to use: Unsuitable for complex scenes with concavities, self-occlusion, or where accurate silhouette rendering is required. The Single-Layer Ternary Depth Test was introduced by Weyrich et al. in 2007 as a method for surface splatting. It was designed to handle overlapping splats during surface reconstruction by providing a more robust depth test than the standard binary pass/fail test. It serves as a baseline for comparison against more advanced techniques like depth-interval grouping, which was introduced to address the limitations of the single-layer approach. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A hardware architecture for surface splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/1275808.1276490, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Radix Sort for Splat Depth
head: 16-bit Radix Sort for Splatting, Depth Sorting via Radix Sort, Tsplat depth sort
body: This method sorts projected 3D Gaussian splats by their depth values to establish a front-to-back rendering order, which is critical for correct alpha blending of translucent splats. It distinguishes itself from comparison-based sorts by leveraging the bit-pattern ordering of IEEE 754 floating-point numbers to achieve O(n) time complexity with small constants, resulting in performance that is consistently 2 times faster for ~100k–200k elements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of projected splats, where each splat contains a depth field (f32). Output: The projected list sorted in ascending order of depth (front-to-back). Auxiliary: aux buffer of same size as projected; countslo, countshi histogram arrays; offsets prefix sum array. Data Structures: projected: Array of splat structs. Each struct has depth: f32. countslo, countshi: Arrays of u32 with size 65,536 (2^{16}). offsets: Array of u32 with size 65,536. aux: Array of splat structs, same size as projected. Parameters: Parallel sort threshold: 50,000 splats. If splat count < 50,000 or no thread pool is available, use sequential radix sort. Otherwise, use a parallel unstable sort on depth bit patterns. Algorithm Steps: 1. Edge Case: If the number of splats is \le 1, return immediately. 2. Histogram Initialization: Initialize countslo and countshi to zero. 3. Histogram Population: Iterate through each splat in projected: Let k be the bit pattern of splat.depth reinterpreted as a u32. Increment countslo[(k & 0xFFFF)]. Increment countshi[(k >> 16)]. 4. Pass 1 (Low 16 bits): Compute prefix sums of countslo into offsets. Scatter splats from projected to aux based on the low 16 bits of their depth bit pattern (k \& 0xFFFF). 5. Pass 2 (High 16 bits): Compute prefix sums of countshi into offsets. Scatter splats from aux back to projected based on the high 16 bits of their depth bit pattern (k >> 16). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sortbydepth(projected: list, aux: list, countslo: list, countshi: list, offsets: list) -> None: n = len(projected) if n <= 1: return # Parallel threshold check if n >= 50000: # Use a parallel unstable sort on depth bit patterns projected.sort(key=lambda s: s.depth.tobits()) return # Reset histograms for i in range(65536): countslo[i] = 0 countshi[i] = 0 # Populate histograms for splat in projected: k = splat.depth.tobits() # Reinterpret f32 bits as u32 countslo[k & 0xFFFF] += 1 countshi[k >> 16] += 1 # Pass 1: Sort by low 16 bits # Compute exclusive prefix sums for offsets offsets[0] = 0 for i in range(1, 65536): offsets[i] = offsets[i-1] + countslo[i-1] # Scatter to aux for splat in projected: k = splat.depth.tobits() bucket = k & 0xFFFF idx = offsets[bucket] aux[idx] = splat offsets[bucket] += 1 # Pass 2: Sort by high 16 bits # Compute exclusive prefix sums for offsets offsets[0] = 0 for i in range(1, 65536): offsets[i] = offsets[i-1] + countshi[i-1] # Scatter back to projected for splat in aux: k = splat.depth.tobits() bucket = k >> 16 idx = offsets[bucket] projected[idx] = splat offsets[bucket] += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Float Bit Pattern: This method relies on positive float bit patterns preserving ordering when reinterpreted as u32. Precision: The method uses the full 32-bit float representation. No precision loss occurs during the bit reinterpretation, but sorting stability is not guaranteed unless the secondary key (e.g., original index) is included, which is not done in this basic variant. Gaussian Sorting orders 3D Gaussians by their distance from the camera to ensure correct alpha blending during rasterization. It solves the transparency accumulation problem by establishing a front-to-back draw order, which is critical because Gaussians with non-zero opacity must be rendered in depth order. It builds on Radix Sort for Splat Depth by applying the radix sort to a global index buffer of Gaussian attributes rather than just projected splat depths. Fast Splat Sorting is an optimization for volume rendering pipelines that replaces the single 48-bit combined tileID+depth radix sort with two sequential, smaller-key sorts: a 32-bit depth sort of visible splats followed by a 16-bit tileID sort of generated fragments. It sets itself apart from its parent Radix Sort for Splat Depth by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, and from Gaussian Sorting by relying on explicit fragment duplication rather than implicit spatial partitioning. This separation reduces computational complexity by leveraging the fact that the number of visible splats (n) is typically smaller than the number of fragments (m). Gaussian Splat Sorting sorts projected 3D Gaussian splats front-to-back within screen-space tiles to enable correct alpha blending. It differs from its parent Radix Sort for Splat Depth by operating on a per-tile basis using a combined tile-ID and depth key, and from Gaussian Sorting by relying on a simple monotonic depth proxy rather than complex geometric comparisons. Default Camera Sort is a compositing technique for oriented Gaussian ellipses (splats) that sorts them back-to-front relative to a camera viewpoint to ensure correct translucent blending. It differs from its siblings by automatically binding the sort order to the active scene camera without requiring explicit provider configuration. This method compresses the conventional 64-bit depth sorting key into 32 bits to reduce sorting traffic and the number of radix passes required for splat sorting. It differs from popular CUDA implementations that use 64-bit keys by mapping depth to a specific range where only the lower 23 mantissa bits vary, allowing tile IDs to occupy the minimum necessary higher bits. This optimization is particularly beneficial for Vulkan sorting implementations, which are often slower than CUDA's built-in sorting, while maintaining quality metrics comparable to 64-bit approaches. DistWar is a method that accelerates sorting by exploiting hardware-accelerated visibility ordering in the rasterizer to perform a fast depth test and bypass the CUDA radix sort. This method converts float16 values to uint16 such that lexicographical comparison of the uint16 representation preserves the original float16 ordering. It operates by viewing the tensor as uint16, casting to int32, XORing with the sign mask 0x8000, and casting back to uint16. The constant 0x8000 flips the sign bit to ensure correct unsigned integer sorting. Time Complexity: O(n) for the radix sort passes, where n is the number of splats. The constant factor is small due to the fixed 2-pass structure. Memory Complexity: O(n) for the auxiliary buffer aux and O(1) for the histogram arrays (fixed size 65,536). Performance: Consistently 2 times faster than comparison-based sorts for ~100k–200k elements. Strengths: Linear time complexity, predictable performance, no recursion depth issues, efficient use of cache due to sequential memory access in scatter/gather phases. Limitations: Requires positive depth values. Not stable by default. Parallelization threshold must be tuned for specific hardware. When to Use: When sorting large numbers of splats for front-to-back rendering where performance is critical and depth values are positive. When Not to Use: When stability is required without additional overhead, or when depth values include negative numbers that are not handled by bit manipulation. This method is described in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipelines. It is part of the broader effort to accelerate splatting by replacing slower comparison-based sorts with hardware-friendly radix sorts. The use of a 2-pass 16-bit radix sort on float bit patterns is a standard optimization for depth sorting in GPU rendering. name: Gaussian Sorting
head: Depth Sorting for Alpha Blending, Gaussian Depth Sorting
body: Gaussian Sorting orders 3D Gaussians by their distance from the camera to ensure correct alpha blending during rasterization. It solves the transparency accumulation problem by establishing a front-to-back draw order, which is critical because Gaussians with non-zero opacity must be rendered in depth order. It builds on Radix Sort for Splat Depth by applying the radix sort to a global index buffer of Gaussian attributes rather than just projected splat depths. Inputs: A list of N Gaussians, each defined by a position \mathbf{p}i, opacity \alphai, and other attributes (color, covariance, etc.). A view matrix \mathbf{V} transforming world space to camera space. A regular buffer (not sparse residency) storing Gaussian attributes. Outputs: A sorted index buffer \mathcal{I} of length N, where \mathcal{I}[k] is the index of the k-th closest Gaussian to the camera. Data Structures: Gaussian Attribute Buffer: A contiguous GPU StorageBuffer containing one entry per Gaussian. Index Buffer: An array of uint32 of size N, initialized to [0, 1, \dots, N-1]. Depth Buffer: An array of float or uint32 of size N to store computed depths for sorting. Steps: 1. Transform to Camera Space: For each Gaussian i, compute \mathbf{p}'i = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{p}i. The depth is the z-component zi = \mathbf{p}'i.z. 2. Compute Distances: Use zi as the sort key for each Gaussian. 3. Radix Sort Indices: Perform a radix sort on the index buffer \mathcal{I} based on the computed depths z{\mathcal{I}[j]} using compute shaders. 4. Render: Pass the sorted index buffer to the vertex shader to fetch attributes from the storage buffer in front-to-back order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiansort(gaussians, viewmatrix): """ Sorts Gaussians by depth for alpha blending. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: pos: (x, y, z) in world space opacity: float viewmatrix: 4x4 matrix transforming world to camera space. Returns: sortedindices: List of integers, indices into gaussians list, sorted front-to-back. """ n = len(gaussians) indices = list(range(n)) depths = [] # Step 1 & 2: Transform to camera space and extract z-depth for i in range(n): p = gaussians[i].pos # Homogeneous transformation: pcam = V [p.x, p.y, p.z, 1]^T w = viewmatrix[3][0]p[0] + viewmatrix[3][1]p[1] + viewmatrix[3][2]p[2] + viewmatrix[3][3] z = (viewmatrix[2][0]p[0] + viewmatrix[2][1]p[1] + viewmatrix[2][2]p[2] + viewmatrix[2][3]) / w depths.append(z) # Step 3: Stable radix sort indices by depths sortedindices = stablesortbykey(indices, depths) return sortedindices def stablesortbykey(keys, values): """ Stable sort that returns indices sorted by values. Python's built-in sort is stable; GPU implementations use a 2-pass radix sort on uint32 reinterpreted floats. """ return sorted(range(len(keys)), key=lambda i: values[i]) Parameters: Buffer Type: Regular buffer is used instead of sparse residency buffers. Sorting Algorithm: Radix sort. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Residency Buffers: Avoid using sparse residency buffers. They require indirection texture lookups for UV coordinates in virtual texturing, adding lookup overhead. Furthermore, support is limited: less than a third of desktop GPUs and just over 10% of Android devices support sparseResidencyBuffer. MoltenVK (Apple) generally lacks this feature. Even on hardware that supports it, performance may be unsatisfactory. Precision: The depth values must be compared accurately. Using the z-coordinate in camera space is standard. Degenerate Input: If multiple Gaussians share identical depths, a stable sort or a secondary key must be used to impose a weak ordering, such as comparing original indices or base vertices. A method that introduces a temporal coherence heuristic into the tile sorting phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, avoiding the computational cost of re-sorting Gaussians whose depth order has not changed between consecutive frames. It sets itself apart from standard per-frame sorting by leveraging the high degree of similarity between adjacent video frames to skip redundant sorting operations. An ordering technique that sorts draw calls front-to-back based on the dot product of the vector between chunk positions and the camera position, reducing z-buffer burden and increasing speed for alpha blending. It is applied by calling vertpool.order with a lambda comparing two DAICs a and b: if \text{dot}(b.\text{pos} - a.\text{pos}, \text{cam}.\text{pos}) < 0 return true; if > 0 return false; otherwise return (a.\text{baseVert} < b.\text{baseVert}) to impose a weak ordering. Sorts Gaussians in z-order at regular intervals during training to resolve cache contention in the alpha blending backward pass. It significantly slows down training when the number of Gaussians is small due to massive atomic contention and false sharing, where threads in different tiles write to the same cache line. When the per-Gaussian backward pass is enabled, omitting repeated z-ordering during densification reduces this false sharing issue. Time Complexity: O(N) for radix sort on fixed-width keys. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the index buffer and depth arrays. Performance: Using regular buffers avoids the indirection texture lookup overhead required by sparse residency buffers, leading to better performance on supported hardware. Strengths: Ensures correct alpha blending for transparent Gaussians. Works on a wide range of hardware due to the avoidance of sparse residency features. Limitations: Sorting is required for every frame to maintain correct alpha blending order. Sparse residency buffers are not recommended due to poor support and performance. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussians with opacity that require correct alpha blending. When not to use: When Gaussians are opaque and depth sorting is not required for correctness. Gaussian Sorting originated with the introduction of 3D Gaussian Splatting by Kerbl et al., where Gaussians with opacity require alpha blending and must be sorted by distance from the camera. The method was further detailed in implementations such as "Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting", which highlighted the use of compute shaders for depth calculation and radix sorting of indices. The approach is also referenced in unofficial implementations like thomasantony/splat and adapted in voxel engine contexts for front-to-back rendering of chunks. name: Temporal Coherence Heuristic for Gaussian Sorting
body: A method that introduces a temporal coherence heuristic into the tile sorting phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, avoiding the computational cost of re-sorting Gaussians whose depth order has not changed between consecutive frames. It sets itself apart from standard per-frame sorting by leveraging frame-to-frame similarity to skip redundant sorting operations. Inputs: Screen-projected 3D Gaussians with their camera-space depth z, and the sorted depth order from the previous frame. Outputs: A depth-sorted list of Gaussians per tile, ready for front-to-back alpha compositing. Gaussian List: An array of Gaussian primitives per tile, each containing screen-space position, covariance, opacity, and depth z. Tile Sort State: For each tile, a record of the sorted Gaussian indices from the previous frame. 1. Initialize: For the first frame, perform a standard depth sort of Gaussians within each tile. 2. Frame Start: For subsequent frames, iterate through all tiles. 3. Check Coherence: For each tile, compare the current depth z of the Gaussians against the depth order stored from the previous frame. 4. Skip or Re-sort: If the relative depth order of all Gaussians in the tile remains unchanged, skip sorting for that tile. If any Gaussian's depth order has changed relative to its neighbors, re-sort the tile. 5. Composite: Render all tiles using the resulting sorted Gaussian lists. SortMode: Enum defining sorting frequency (Always, SortEveryNFrames, CutoutsEveryNSorts). SortRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between sorts when SortEveryNFrames is active. CutoutsRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between cutout updates when CutoutsEveryNSorts is active. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalcoherencesort(gaussianspertile, previoustilesorts, frameindex): currenttilesorts = [] for tileidx, gaussians in enumerate(gaussianspertile): if frameindex == 0: currenttilesorts.append(sortbydepth(gaussians)) else: prevsort = previoustilesorts[tileidx] currentsort = sortbydepth(gaussians) if isdepthorderchanged(currentsort, prevsort): currenttilesorts.append(currentsort) else: currenttilesorts.append(prevsort) return currenttilesorts def sortbydepth(gaussians): return sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depth) def isdepthorderchanged(currentsort, previoussort): if len(currentsort) != len(previoussort): return True epsilon = 1e-6 # Tolerance for floating-point precision for curr, prev in zip(currentsort, previoussort): if abs(curr.depth - prev.depth) > epsilon: return True return False Controls how frequently the depth sorting pass executes to balance performance and visual stability. SortMode: Enum defining sorting frequency (Always, SortEveryNFrames, CutoutsEveryNSorts). SortRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between sorts when SortEveryNFrames is active. CutoutsRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between cutout updates when CutoutsEveryNSorts is active. Reduces sorting overhead when depth order is stable across frames. Memory overhead: stores previous frame's sort order per tile. Performance gain depends on scene dynamics; diminishes in highly dynamic scenes. Not given in the sources for exact complexity metrics or hardware-specific performance. The method was introduced in the context of large-scale and scalable formulations for 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically in the work referred to as "Gaufre". It addresses efficient Gaussian sorting in large-scale scenes, building on earlier spatial partitioning lessons from scaling NeRFs. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Static-Dynamic Depth Sorting with Exact Reuse Certificate
head: Depth Travel Bound reuse, Depth-Order Certificate, Mobile-4DGS sorting, Static-Dynamic separation sorting, Two-Stream Depth Order
body: Static-Dynamic Depth Sorting with Exact Reuse Certificate is a rendering optimization for 4D Gaussian Splatting that reduces computational overhead during playback by selectively reusing previously committed depth orders. It solves the problem of expensive per-frame re-projection, sorting, merging, and index-buffer updates by separating Gaussians into static and dynamic sets, caching the static depth order, and verifying the validity of the global draw list using a closed-form depth-motion bound. It sets itself apart from its parent Temporal Coherence Heuristic for Gaussian Sorting by providing a mathematically exact certificate for reuse (or a bounded budget-based relaxation) rather than relying solely on heuristic temporal coherence, thereby guaranteeing visual consistency for reused frames. The method operates on a binary partition of Gaussians into a static set S and a dynamic set D, where gi=0 for i \in S and gi=1 for i \in D. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Committed draw list \pic, its commit time tc, streams S and D, precomputed bounds V, A, t'{\min}, t'{\max}, mean Gaussian radius \bar{s}, budget tolerance r, current time t, and camera parameters (depth row n, depth range [z{\min}, z{\max}]). Outputs: A draw list \pi (either reused \pic or newly computed) and a status flag indicating reuse or commit. Data Structures Static Cache: Stores the sorted indices of S for a fixed camera configuration. Invalidated if n or [z{\min}, z{\max}] changes. Global Bounds: Scalars V = \max{i \in D} \|vi\|2, A = \max{i \in D} \|ai\|2, t'{\min} = \min{i \in D} t'i, t'{\max} = \max{i \in D} t'i. Committed List \pic: Array of N indices representing the sorted order at tc. Algorithm Steps 1. Check Camera Change: If the camera depth mapping (n or [z{\min}, z{\max}]) has changed since tc: Invalidate static cache. Re-project and sort S (refresh static cache). Re-project and sort D. Merge streams S and D to produce \pi. Update \pic \leftarrow \pi, tc \leftarrow t. Recompute g{\min} if r=0. Return \pi and commit status. 2. Compute Motion Bound: Calculate the maximum quantized key shift M(t) for dynamic Gaussians: Compute temporal offset bound: \tau(t) = \max(|t - t'{\min}|, |t - t'{\max}|). Compute depth motion bound: \Delta z(t) = |t - tc| \|n\|2 \times V + \frac{1}{2} A (\tau(t) + \tau(tc)). Compute quantized bound: M(t) = \kappa \Delta z(t), where \kappa = \frac{B-1}{z{\max}-z{\min}} and B=2^{16}. 3. Evaluate Reuse Certificate: Case r=0 (Exact): Identify relevant neighboring pairs in \pic: Kc = \{k: \pic(k) \in D \text{ or } \pic(k+1) \in D\}. Compute g{\min} = \min{k \in Kc} (q{\pic(k+1)}(tc) - q{\pic(k)}(tc)). If 2M(t) < g{\min}, acknowledge reuse. If g{\min}=0 (tie), reject reuse. Case r>0 (Budget): If M(t) \leq \lceil \kappa r \bar{s} \|n\|2 \rceil, acknowledge reuse. This allows small local ordering changes. 4. Handle Reuse or Commit: Reuse: Worker keeps \pic, performs no re-projection/sort/merge, returns O(1) acknowledgement. Main thread skips index upload. Commit: Re-project and sort D only (static cache is valid). Merge S and D to produce \pi. Update \pic \leftarrow \pi, tc \leftarrow t. Recompute g{\min} if r=0. Return \pi and commit status. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivedepthorderreuse(pic, tc, S, D, V, A, tmin, tmax, sbar, r, t, n, zmin, zmax, B=65536): """ Adaptive depth-order reuse for 4D Gaussian Splatting. Args: pic: Committed draw list (array of indices) tc: Time of commit S: Static Gaussian stream (indices) D: Dynamic Gaussian stream (indices) V: Max velocity magnitude in D A: Max acceleration magnitude in D tmin: Min temporal support in D tmax: Max temporal support in D sbar: Mean Gaussian radius r: Budget tolerance (0 for exact, >0 for relaxed) t: Current time n: Camera depth row vector zmin: Near plane depth zmax: Far plane depth B: Number of quantization bins (2^16) Returns: pi: Draw list reused: Boolean, True if pic was reused """ # 1. Check for camera change if cameradepthmappingchanged(n, zmin, zmax): # Invalidate static cache and recompute everything pis = sortstream(S, n, zmin, zmax, B) pid = sortstream(D, n, zmin, zmax, B) pi = mergestreams(pis, pid) pic = pi tc = t if r == 0: gmin = computegmin(pic, D) return pi, False # 2. Compute motion bound taut = max(abs(t - tmin), abs(t - tmax)) tautc = max(abs(tc - tmin), abs(tc - tmax)) # Depth motion bound deltaz = abs(t - tc) norm(n) V + 0.5 A (taut + tautc) # Quantization factor kappa = (B - 1) / (zmax - zmin) M = kappa deltaz # 3. Evaluate reuse certificate if r == 0: # Exact reuse if 2 M < gmin: return pic, True else: # Commit new order pid = sortstream(D, n, zmin, zmax, B) pis = getcachedstaticstream(S) # Static cache valid pi = mergestreams(pis, pid) pic = pi tc = t gmin = computegmin(pic, D) return pi, False elif r > 0: # Budget reuse threshold = ceil(kappa r sbar norm(n)) if M <= threshold: return pic, True else: # Commit new order pid = sortstream(D, n, zmin, zmax, B) pis = getcachedstaticstream(S) pi = mergestreams(pis, pid) pic = pi tc = t # gmin not needed for r > 0 in this branch logic, # but recomputed if r changes to 0 later return pi, False def sortstream(stream, n, zmin, zmax, B): """ Stable counting sort for a stream of Gaussians. """ kappa = (B - 1) / (zmax - zmin) keys = [] for i in stream: # Project to view-space depth zi = dot(n, getcenter(i)) # Quantize qi = clip(kappa (zi - zmin), 0, B - 1) keys.append((qi, i)) # Stable counting sort # Since input is ordered by row-id, stable sort preserves row-id for ties return argsort(keys) def mergestreams(pis, pid): """ Standard two-pointer merge of two sorted streams. """ result = [] i, j = 0, 0 while i < len(pis) and j < len(pid): # Compare (key, index) tuples if pis[i] <= pid[j]: result.append(pis[i]) i += 1 else: result.append(pid[j]) j += 1 result.extend(pis[i:]) result.extend(pid[j:]) return result def computegmin(pic, D): """ Compute minimum depth-key gap between relevant neighbors. """ gmin = infinity for k in range(len(pic) - 1): idxcurr = pic[k] idxnext = pic[k+1] # Check if at least one is dynamic if idxcurr in D or idxnext in D: keycurr = getquantizedkey(idxcurr) keynext = getquantizedkey(idxnext) gap = keynext - keycurr if gap < gmin: gmin = gap return gmin Parameters B = 2^{16}: Number of quantization bins. r: Tolerance parameter. Default 0.5 (mean radii). r=0 for exact certificate. \bar{s}: Mean Gaussian radius, computed once from decoded scales. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Ties: If two relevant Gaussians share the same key, g{\min}=0, and exact reuse is conservatively rejected. Camera Change: If n or [z{\min}, z{\max}] changes, the static cache is invalidated, requiring full recomputation. Precision: The certificate guarantees exact reuse only for the 16-bit quantized ordering. An algorithm that determines if the previously computed global draw list can be reused for a playback frame, avoiding re-sorting. It extends the basic certificate by supporting a "budget branch" (r>0) that allows small local ordering changes relative to the mean Gaussian radius, providing a practical relaxation for dense scenes where the exact certificate might be too conservative. It is chosen when visual quality can tolerate minor depth-order swaps within overlapping footprints, whereas the exact mode (r=0) is chosen for strict consistency. Time Complexity: Reused frame cost is O(1) for certificate computation on the worker and O(1) communication. Committed frame cost is O(N+B) for projection/sort/merge on the worker and O(N) for index upload on the main thread. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the committed draw list (4N bytes) and precomputed bounds (constant space). The counting-sort scratch space (B=2^{16}) is reused across frames. Performance: On mobile devices, this method substantially reduces rendering overhead by skipping re-projection, sorting, merging, and index uploads for frames that pass the certificate. Strengths: Eliminates redundant computation for static scenes and reduces load for dynamic scenes by bounding motion. Limitations: The exact certificate can be conservative in dense scenes with small depth-key gaps. The budget branch may allow minor visual artifacts due to local ordering changes. The method was introduced in Mobile-4DGS, a framework for unified static-dynamic real-time mobile Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the binary static-dynamic partition learned during optimization, enabling continuous-time modeling without runtime deformation networks. The Depth-Order Certificate (DOC) leverages this partition to cache static depth orders and bound dynamic motion, enabling real-time 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting on mobile devices. name: Fast Splat Sorting
head: Depth and TileID Sorting, Split Radix Sort for Splatting, Separating Depth and Tile Sorting, Splat Sorting Dispatch
body: Fast Splat Sorting is an optimization for volume rendering pipelines that replaces the single 48-bit combined tileID+depth radix sort with two sequential, smaller-key sorts: a 32-bit depth sort of visible splats followed by a 16-bit tileID sort of generated fragments. It sets itself apart from its parent Radix Sort for Splat Depth by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, and from Gaussian Sorting by relying on explicit fragment duplication rather than implicit spatial partitioning. This separation reduces computational complexity by leveraging the fact that the number of visible splats (n) is typically smaller than the number of fragments (m). The method replaces the standard 48-bit radix sort (used in 3DGS) which sorts fragments by a combined key of tileID and depth. Instead, it performs two distinct sorting passes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n visible splats, each with a 32-bit depth value, plus camera parameters and sorting flags. Intermediate: A set of m fragments, where each fragment corresponds to a splat intersecting a specific tile. Each fragment carries a 16-bit tileID. Output: An ordering array of indices, sorted such that splats are ordered by depth within each tile, and tiles are processed in raster order. Data Structures: 1. Splat Data: Each visible splat i has a depth value di (stored as f32). 2. Fragment Data: Each fragment j has a tileID tj (stored as u16). 3. Ordering Array: Uint32Array of size m, storing indices to the fragment list. Steps: 1. Depth Sort (Visible Splats): Collect all n visible splats. Perform a radix sort on the 32-bit depth values. This step produces a list of splats sorted by depth. 2. Fragment Generation: For each splat in the depth-sorted list, determine which tiles it intersects. Generate a fragment for each intersected tile. Each fragment inherits the splat's depth and is assigned the tile's 16-bit ID. Note: The sources mention using tighter AABBs and approximate tile-ellipse intersection tests to reduce false-positive fragments, but the sorting logic itself assumes the fragments are already generated. 3. TileID Sort (Fragments): Perform a radix sort on the m fragments using their 16-bit tileID as the key. Because the splats were already sorted by depth in Step 1, and radix sort is stable, the resulting list is sorted primarily by tileID (raster order) and secondarily by depth (front-to-back). Formulas: The total complexity is split as follows: T{48\text{-bit}}(m) \approx T{32\text{-bit}}(n) + T{16\text{-bit}}(m) Where T{48\text{-bit}}(m) \approx 3 \times T{16\text{-bit}}(m) assuming linear scaling of radix sort runtime with the number of bits. Parameters: numsplats (u32): Total number of splats to process. camerax, cameray, cameraz (f64): Camera position coordinates. directionx, directiony, directionz (f32): Camera viewing direction vector. radial (bool): Enables radial sorting mode. fastsort (bool): Enables fast sorting mode. frontsort (bool): Selects between 16-bit front sort and 32-bit sort. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode implements the dispatch logic described in the sources. It includes validation checks and inline stable radix sort implementations to avoid external dependencies. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastsplatsort(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction, radial, fastsort, frontsort, ordering): # Copy sorted indices to output array if activesplats > 0: ordering[0:activesplats] = buffers.ordering[0:activesplats] return activesplats def sort16centersfrontinternal(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction): # Performs 16-bit radix sort on fragment tileIDs return stableradixsort16(buffers.fragmenttileids, buffers.fragmentindices, numsplats) def sort32centersinternal(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction, radial, fastsort): # Performs 32-bit radix sort on visible splat depths return stableradixsort32(buffers.splatdepths, buffers.splatindices, numsplats) def stableradixsort16(keys, indices, n): # Standard 16-bit stable radix sort (counting sort per 8-bit digit) for digit in [0, 1]: counts = [0] 256 for i in range(n): counts[(keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] output = [0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): d = (keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF output[counts[d] - 1] = indices[i] counts[d] -= 1 indices[:] = output return n def stableradixsort32(keys, indices, n): # Standard 32-bit stable radix sort (counting sort per 8-bit digit) for digit in [0, 1, 2, 3]: counts = [0] 256 for i in range(n): counts[(keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] output = [0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): d = (keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF output[counts[d] - 1] = indices[i] counts[d] -= 1 indices[:] = output return n Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fragment Count: The number of fragments m can be significantly larger than n. The 16-bit sort must handle this larger dataset efficiently. False Positives: Without tight bounding boxes, the fragment generation step may create unnecessary fragments, increasing m and slowing down the 16-bit sort. The sources recommend using tight AABBs and approximate tile-ellipse intersection tests to mitigate this. Validation: The implementation must validate that range arrays and update arrays have consistent lengths and bounds to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Sort Stability: The algorithm relies on stable radix sort to preserve the depth ordering established in Step 1 when sorting by tileID in Step 2. A variant that explicitly splits the generation of depth-sorted per-tile splat lists into two separate radix sort routines. It sets itself apart by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, allowing the use of smaller key sizes (32-bit and 16-bit) instead of a single large key. Time Complexity: The total sorting time is the sum of a 32-bit sort on n splats and a 16-bit sort on m fragments. Assuming linear scaling with bit-width, the 48-bit sort is approximately three times as expensive as the 16-bit sort. Measured Performance: Berlin Scene: 0.24 ms total (0.11 ms depth + 0.13 ms tileID) vs. 0.39 ms for 48-bit sort. Campus Scene: 1.00 ms total (0.38 ms depth + 0.62 ms tileID) vs. 1.86 ms for 48-bit sort. Scaling: Performance improves significantly when the majority of splats contribute to the rendered image across multiple tiles, as the depth sort operates on a smaller set of visible splats. Strengths: Reduced computational complexity and better GPU utilization by avoiding large 48-bit sorts. Limitations: Requires an additional fragment generation step. Performance depends on the ratio of fragments to splats (m/n). If m is very large, the 16-bit sort may become a bottleneck. When to Use: Use when rendering large Gaussian Splat models where the 48-bit sort is a bottleneck and the number of visible splats is significantly smaller than the number of fragments. When Not to Use: Avoid if the fragment generation step is already expensive or if the scene has a very high ratio of fragments to splats. Fast Splat Sorting was introduced in the "Splatshop" paper (2025) as part of an efficient CUDA-based splat editing system. It was developed to address the performance limitations of the original 3DGS rendering pipeline, which used a combined 48-bit tileID+depth radix sort. The method leverages the observation that sorting visible splats by depth first, and then sorting the resulting fragments by tileID, is more efficient than sorting all fragments by a combined key. name: Two-Stage Sorting
head: Schutz et al. sorting, Separate Sorting, Two-pass sorting
body: Two-Stage Sorting is a sorting optimization for volume rendering pipelines that splits the generation of depth-sorted per-tile splat lists into two separate radix sort routines to reduce VRAM usage and computational complexity. It sets itself apart from single-stage approaches by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, allowing the use of smaller key sizes (32-bit and 16-bit) instead of a single large key. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n visible Gaussians, each with a depth value \hat{\mu}z and a spatial position determining its tile assignment. Output: Depth-sorted lists of splats for each tile, ready for rasterization. Data Structures: 1. Compacted Depth Buffer: Stores indices of visible Gaussians and their 32-bit depth values. 2. Intermediate Gaussian Values: Stores attributes needed for rasterization and blending. These are not compacted to avoid indirection during gradient computation. 3. Tile Index Buffer: Stores the tile index for each Gaussian. Parameters: Tile Size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Max Resolution for 16-bit Tile Indices: 2^{16} \times 256 (roughly 16 megapixels). Note that this limit is slightly lower when image dimensions are not a multiple of 16. Sorting Algorithm: Must be stable (e.g., radix sort) to maintain the order established in the first stage. Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Identify indices of all visible Gaussians and their depth \hat{\mu}z. Write these to compacted buffers using an atomic counter. 2. First Sort (Depth): Perform a radix sort using 32-bit keys to establish depth ordering of the Gaussians. 3. Second Sort (Tile): Perform a radix sort using 16-bit keys (or 32-bit for very high resolutions) to sort splats into per-tile lists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagesort(gaussians, tilesize=16, imagewidth=1920, imageheight=1080): # Step 1: Pre-processing # Identify indices of all visible Gaussians and their depth, writing them to compacted buffers using an atomic counter. # In a GPU implementation, an atomic counter manages buffer writes to avoid race conditions. visibleindices = [i for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if g.visible] depthbuffer = [gaussians[i].depth for i in visibleindices] gaussianindices = visibleindices # Intermediate Gaussian values are kept in original order/structure and NOT compacted to avoid indirection during gradient computation. # Step 2: First Sort (Depth) # Perform a radix sort using 32-bit keys to establish depth ordering of the Gaussians. # Standard LSD radix sort for 32-bit integers. Stability is required. depthsortedperm = stableradixsort32bit(depthbuffer, gaussianindices) depthsortedindices = [gaussianindices[i] for i in depthsortedperm] # Step 3: Second Sort (Tile) # Calculate tile indices for each Gaussian. numtilesx = (imagewidth + tilesize - 1) // tilesize tileindices = [] for idx in depthsortedindices: tilex = int(gaussians[idx].pos.x) // tilesize tiley = int(gaussians[idx].pos.y) // tilesize tileidx = tiley numtilesx + tilex tileindices.append(tileidx) # Perform a radix sort using 16-bit keys (or 32-bit for very high resolutions) to sort splats into per-tile lists. # Stability preserves depth order within tiles. tilesortedperm = stableradixsort16bit(tileindices, range(len(depthsortedindices))) tilesortedindices = [depthsortedindices[i] for i in tilesortedperm] # Construct per-tile lists pertilelists = buildpertilelists(tilesortedindices, tileindices, numtilesx) return pertilelists def stableradixsort32bit(keys, values): # Standard LSD radix sort for 32-bit integers. return [v for, v in sorted(zip(keys, values), key=lambda x: x[0])] def stableradixsort16bit(keys, values): # Standard LSD radix sort for 16-bit integers. return [v for, v in sorted(zip(keys, values), key=lambda x: x[0])] def buildpertilelists(sortedindices, tileindices, numtilesx): # Constructs a flat buffer or list-of-lists mapping tile IDs to splat indices. tilemap = {} for idx in sortedindices: tidx = tileindices[idx] if tidx not in tilemap: tilemap[tidx] = [] tilemap[tidx].append(idx) return tilemap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Limit: Tile indices must fit in 16 bits. For resolutions exceeding roughly 16 megapixels, 32-bit keys must be used for the second sort. Non-Multiples of 16: If image dimensions are not a multiple of 16, the effective max resolution for 16-bit tile indices is slightly lower. Gradient Computation: Compacting intermediate Gaussian values needed for rasterization and blending should be avoided to prevent additional indirection during the backward pass. Time and Memory Complexity: Original 3DGS: Uses a single 64-bit key sort. Assuming a 48-bit effective key size and an average of 8 tiles per Gaussian, the complexity is O(8 \cdot (16 + 32)n) = O(384n). Two-Stage Sorting: First Sort (Depth): O(32n). Second Sort (Tile): O(8 \cdot 16n) = O(128n). Combined Complexity: O(32n) + O(128n) = O(160n). VRAM Usage: Reduced because it eliminates the need for 64-bit data types to store sorting keys. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in sorting time and VRAM usage compared to single-stage sorting, with benefits increasing as the number of Gaussians increases. Limitations: Requires a stable sorting algorithm. The 16-bit tile index limit restricts maximum resolution unless 32-bit keys are used for the second stage. When to Use: Use when VRAM is constrained or when sorting performance is a bottleneck. Suitable for resolutions up to ~16 megapixels with 16-bit tile keys. When Not to Use: For very high resolutions (>16MP) where 32-bit keys for the second stage negate some VRAM benefits. If the rendering pipeline does not support stable radix sorts. Two-Stage Sorting was introduced by Schutz et al. [73] as an optimization for Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines. It addresses the computational inefficiency of single-stage radix sorts that use large keys to encode both depth and tile information. The method is implemented in Faster-GS. name: Gaussian Splat Sorting
head: Clip-space w depth sorting, Tile-based sorting using clip-space w
body: Gaussian Splat Sorting sorts projected 3D Gaussian splats front-to-back within screen-space tiles to enable correct alpha blending. It uses clip-space w as a monotonic distance proxy to handle reverse-z projection. Inputs: clipposw: Clip-space w component of the splat position. tileid: Screen-space tile identifier. id: Unique splat identifier. Outputs: sortkeys: Array of 32-bit sort keys. sortvalues: Array of splat IDs corresponding to the keys. Data Structures: sortkeys: 32-bit integer array where the upper 16 bits store tileid and the lower 16 bits store the quantized depth. sortvalues: 32-bit integer array storing the original splat id. Steps: 1. Calculate View Depth: Extract the clip-space w component and clamp to zero. d{\text{view}} = \max(0.0, \text{clip\pos\w}) 2. Normalize Depth: Map the view depth to [0, 1] using a rational function. d{01} = \frac{d{\text{view}}}{1.0 + d{\text{view}}} 3. Quantize Depth: Convert the normalized depth to a 16-bit unsigned integer. d{16} = \lfloor d{01} \times 65535.0 \rfloor \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} 4. Create Sort Key: Combine the tile ID and quantized depth into a single 32-bit key. \text{key} = (\text{tile\id} \ll 16) \ | \ d{16} 5. Store Keys and Values: Write the key and the splat ID to the respective sort buffers at the current offset. \text{sort\keys}[\text{offset}] = \text{key} \text{sort\values}[\text{offset}] = \text{id} Parameters: Depth quantization bits: 16. Depth normalization constant: 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiansplatsort(clipposw: float, tileid: int, splatid: int, sortkeys: list[int], sortvalues: list[int], offset: int) -> None: # Step 1: Calculate view depth viewdepth = max(0.0, clipposw) # Step 2: Normalize depth to 0-1 range depth01 = viewdepth / (1.0 + viewdepth) # Step 3: Quantize depth to 16-bit integer depth16 = int(depth01 65535.0) & 0xFFFF # Step 4: Create sort key by combining tile ID and depth key = (tileid << 16) | depth16 # Step 5: Store key and splat ID in sort buffers sortkeys[offset] = key sortvalues[offset] = splatid Not given in the sources. The method uses clip-space w as a monotonic distance proxy to handle reverse-z projection for front-to-back sorting within tiles. name: Tile-based Gaussian Sorting with Comparison-Free Sorter
head: Comparison-free key sorter, Stage 2 Gaussian Sorting
body: This method is a hardware sorting module designed for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that outputs the current maximum depth value in a linear delay, tailored to match the one-point-at-a-time consumption of alpha-blending. It differs from pipelined heap designs [20] by emitting <tile-id, depth> keys and consuming tiles front-to-back, yielding fixed per-output latency and avoiding O(\log n) priority-queue operations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 15-bit unsigned depth values (sign bit skipped as all numbers are positive) and associated values for Gaussian splats within a tile. Output: The address of the largest element every 2 cycles, allowing the renderer to consume the front-most splat. Data Structures: Sub-sorter Buffer: Each of the four parallel sub-sorters has a 4 KB key buffer and a 4 KB value buffer, capable of holding 256 data elements. Global Buffer: A shared 12 KB key buffer and 12 KB value buffer for excess points beyond the local 2000-point limit per tile. Bit Grouping: The 15-bit data is divided into groups of sizes (3, 4, 4, 4) bits. Parameters: Tile Size: 16×16 pixels. Sub-sorter Capacity (N): 256 data elements. This value was chosen because a capacity of 512 elements resulted in a critical path delay (N-input OR gate) that limited the frequency to below 500 MHz in a 28 nm process, failing to meet the target of 800 MHz. Processing Rate: One maximum value output every 2 cycles. Algorithm Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the 15-bit depth values into four bit groups: 3 bits, 4 bits, 4 bits, and 4 bits. 2. Clustering: Send these bit groups to the cluster stage for sorting. 3. Sequencing: Process the sorted clusters in the sequence stage to determine the address of the largest element. 4. Output: Emit the address of the maximum value every 2 cycles. 5. Buffer Management: If a tile contains more than 2000 points (exceeding the 4 KB local buffer capacity), excess points are stored in the shared global buffers (12 KB key/value) to prevent image holes caused by discarding points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sortgaussiansplats(depthvalues15bit): # Extract 15-bit unsigned depth values (sign bit skipped) groups = [] shift = 14 for size in (3, 4, 4, 4): groups.append((depthvalues15bit >> shift) & ((1 << size) - 1)) shift -= size # The sources do not specify the internal algorithm for the cluster and sequence stages. # In comparison-free hardware sorters, these typically use fixed permutation networks # or radix-decoding to route bits to the correct output position. maxaddress = 0 # Hardware-specific address generation return maxaddress Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Variability in Point Density: Gaussian point density per tile varies significantly (from a few hundred to 5000 points). Setting a strict upper bound on processed points per tile and discarding the rest causes image "holes". The shared global buffer mitigates this. Frequency Constraints: Increasing sub-sorter capacity to 512 elements reduces the maximum operating frequency below 500 MHz in a 28 nm process due to the critical path delay of the N-input OR gate. Time Complexity: Linear sorting delay for outputting the maximum value, avoiding the O(\log n) operations found in heap-based approaches. Memory Complexity: Each sub-sorter uses 8 KB (4 KB key + 4 KB value) for 256 elements. A global buffer of 24 KB (12 KB key + 12 KB value) is shared among four sub-sorters. Performance: The design targets 800 MHz in a 28 nm process. It outputs one maximum value every 2 cycles. Strengths: Fixed per-output latency, high sustained throughput, and reduced memory requirements for rasterization compared to heap-based methods. It aligns well with the one-point-at-a-time consumption of alpha-blending. Limitations: The critical path delay limits the sub-sorter capacity to 256 elements to maintain the target frequency. Requires shared global buffers to handle high variability in point density, adding complexity to memory management. This method was proposed as a hardware accelerator for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the inefficiencies of previous pipelined heap designs [20] which reorder splats by tile index for cache coherence, imposing a cyclic tile scan and extra complexity. The comparison-free sorter is tailored specifically for the monotonic depth consumption of 3DGS alpha-blending. name: Front-to-Back Gaussian Splat Rendering
head: Gaussian Splat Sorting and Rendering
body: Renders semi-transparent 2D Gaussian splats in correct depth order to enable accurate alpha blending. It differs from instanced rendering by using a CPU-side loop to issue sequential draw calls, ensuring the GPU processes splats in a specific sorted order rather than in parallel. Inputs: Centroids of all splats. Covariance matrices (or 2D basis parameters) for all splats. Model-view and projection matrices. Number of actual splats (N) and padded splats (dummy splats added to fill tile or batch boundaries). Outputs: Rendered image with correct front-to-back alpha blending. Data Structures: centroid: Array of N vectors (e.g., vec3<f32>). covariance: Array of N vectors/matrices representing the Gaussian spread. basis: Array of N vectors (e.g., vec4<f32>) storing the projected 2D basis. distance: Array of N unsigned 32-bit integers (u32). Stores the sorted key. id: Array of N unsigned 32-bit integers (u32). Stores the original index or instance ID. Steps: 1. Compute Distances and Basis: For each splat i, compute the projected 2D basis and the distance to the camera. This is typically done in a compute shader. The distance is calculated as a monotonic proxy for depth (e.g., using clip-space w or Euclidean distance in view space). The distance value is converted to an integer in the range [0, 0xFFFFFFFF \gg 8] (effectively 24-bit precision) to serve as the sort key. For dummy/padded splats, assign the maximum possible distance value (0xFFFFFFFF) so they sort to the end of the array. 2. GPU Radix Sort: Sort the distance array (and corresponding id and basis arrays) in ascending order (front-to-back) using a GPU radix sort algorithm. The sort key is the integer distance. The sort is stable to preserve relative order of splats at the same depth if necessary, though distinct depths are preferred. 3. Sequential Rendering Loop: Iterate through the sorted splats and issue individual draw calls. The source code iterates from actualSplatSize - 1 down to 0. Note on Order: The source states this is "front-to-back rendering" but the loop index i goes from largest to smallest. If distance is sorted ascending (smallest distance = closest = index 0), then distance[last] is the farthest. Iterating backwards draws the farthest splats first. Standard alpha blending requires front-to-back (closest first). However, the source explicitly labels this loop as applying "front-to-back rendering" and cites the reason for the loop as maintaining order. We follow the source's implementation: python # Pseudocode based on # sortedindices is the result of the radix sort on the distance array # actualSplatSize is the number of real splats (excluding padding) for i from actualSplatSize - 1 down to 0: currentsplatid = sortedindices[i] # Set vertex buffer to the position/basis of currentsplatid # Issue draw call for this single splat drawcall(splatid=currentsplatid) Pitfall: Instanced rendering cannot be used because it does not guarantee the rendering order of instances, which is required for correct alpha blending of semi-transparent splats. The CPU loop ensures sequential processing. Parameters: Distance precision: 24-bit integer range [0, 0xFFFFFF]. Padding: Dummy splats with distance 0xFFFFFFFF. Edge Cases: Padded Splats: Must be assigned the maximum distance value to ensure they are sorted to the end and not rendered (or rendered last, effectively transparent if alpha is 0). Precision: The conversion to integer distance must be monotonic with respect to actual depth to ensure correct sorting. Time Complexity: Dominated by the GPU radix sort O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the radix sort implementation, plus O(N) draw calls. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing distances, IDs, and bases. Strengths: Ensures correct alpha blending for semi-transparent splats. Limitations: High CPU overhead due to N individual draw calls. Instanced rendering is not viable for ordered blending. When to use: When correct depth ordering is critical for semi-transparent rendering and the number of splats is manageable for the draw call overhead. Originated in the context of WebGPU implementations of 2D Gaussian Splatting. The method leverages existing GPU radix sort algorithms to reorder splats by camera distance, addressing the need for front-to-back rendering of semi-transparent primitives. name: Default Camera Sort
head: Back-to-front sort, Splat Painter's Sort, sort splats for the scene camera by default
body: Default Camera Sort is a compositing technique for oriented Gaussian ellipses (splats) that sorts them back-to-front relative to a camera viewpoint to ensure correct translucent blending. It differs from its siblings by automatically binding the sort order to the active scene camera without requiring explicit provider configuration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A cloud of splats managed by SplatNode, and a camera viewpoint (either the scene camera or a custom provider). Output: A compositing order of splats sorted back-to-front relative to the camera. Data Structures: The SplatNode manages the SplatCloud and triggers the sort operation on a background thread whenever the camera moves. Steps: 1. Determine Viewpoint: Check if a cameraPositionProvider is set. If null (the default), use the scene camera position. If provided, invoke the lambda to retrieve the Position object representing the custom viewpoint. 2. Calculate Depths: For each splat i, calculate the distance di from the splat's center position Pi to the camera position C: di = \| Pi - C \| 3. Sort: Sort the splats in descending order of di (back-to-front). The sort executes on a background thread to avoid blocking the main rendering loop. 4. Update Compositing Order: The node automatically applies the sorted order to the rendering pipeline. Formulas: di = \| Pi - C \|: Euclidean distance from splat center Pi to camera position C. Sort order: descending di ensures back-to-front compositing. Parameters: cameraPositionProvider: A lambda returning a Position object representing the camera's world position. If null, the scene camera is used (default). If provided, it enables the back-to-front painter's sort for that specific viewpoint. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Orbiting Artifacts: If cameraPositionProvider is explicitly set to null in older versions where it was required for sorting, or if the automatic default sort is inactive, the compositing order remains as loaded. This causes visual popping artifacts when orbiting the camera because the splat order does not update to match the new viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatesortorder(splatcloud, camerapositionprovider): if splatcloud is None: return # Step 1: Determine camera position if camerapositionprovider is not None: camerapos = camerapositionprovider() else: # Default: use scene camera camerapos = scenecamera.position # Standard engine call to retrieve active camera # Step 2: Calculate depths depths = [] for i in range(splatcloud.count): splat = splatcloud.splats[i] # Euclidean distance diffx = splat.pos.x - camerapos.x diffy = splat.pos.y - camerapos.y diffz = splat.pos.z - camerapos.z depth = (diffx2 + diffy2 + diffz2)0.5 depths.append((depth, i)) # Step 3: Sort back-to-front (descending depth) # Stable sort is preferred to maintain original order for equal depths depths.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Step 4: Apply order # Reorder the splat cloud or update the index buffer sortedindices = [item[1] for item in depths] splatcloud.applyrenderorder(sortedindices) Sorts visible meshes in ascending order of squared distance to the camera position. Choose when a distance-based metric is preferred over Euclidean depth for visibility culling or rendering order. See Camera Distance Sorting. General term for ordering splats by depth. Choose when implementing custom sort logic outside the default node behavior. See Gaussian Sorting. Optimized sorting techniques for performance-critical rendering. Choose when the default sort is too slow. See Fast Splat Sorting. Specific implementations tailored for Gaussian splat rendering pipelines. Choose for specialized Gaussian rendering workflows. See Gaussian Splat Sorting. Tile-based sorting approach that pairs tile IDs with depth values. Choose for tile-based renderers or when depth precision issues arise with standard sorting. See 32-bit Tile-Depth Pair Sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The sort is executed on a background thread to prevent frame drops during camera movement. Strengths: Eliminates visual popping artifacts during camera orbiting by automatically updating the compositing order. Removes the need for manual camera position tracking in standard use cases. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Standard Gaussian splat rendering where correct translucent blending is required and the camera moves. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Default Camera Sort was introduced as part of the SplatNode implementation in the SceneView library, specifically in commit e7e8fd4. It was developed to address visual popping artifacts that occurred when orbiting cameras in Gaussian splat visualizations, which previously relied on a static load order or required an explicit cameraPositionProvider. The change was part of a broader effort to improve the robustness of Gaussian splatting on platforms like iOS and VisionOS, removing potential AI-generated bugs associated with previous default sort sources.
