name: Multi-Pass and Sequential Stage Architectures
body: Multi-pass and sequential stage architectures decompose volume rendering into distinct, ordered computational phases to manage complexity, memory bandwidth, or specific visual effects that cannot be achieved in a single rasterization pass. Unlike single-pass splatting or ray-marching methods, these architectures explicitly separate data traversal, shading, compositing, or post-processing into separate GPU passes, often utilizing intermediate Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) or fragment lists. They are chosen when the rendering workload requires decoupling geometry processing from shading logic, managing complex fragment storage for accurate transparency, or integrating screen-space effects like ambient occlusion. The family shares the fundamental mechanism of decomposing the rendering workload into sequential, ordered stages that communicate via intermediate buffers or lists. Each stage performs a specific transformation or accumulation step, allowing complex lighting, transparency, and post-processing effects to be computed without re-rasterizing geometry or recomputing ray samples. Common implementation patterns include: 1. Stage Separation: Geometry traversal, shading, compositing, and post-processing are isolated into distinct shader programs or pipeline states. 2. Intermediate Storage: Results are written to dedicated buffers (e.g., FBOs, fragment lists, or texture arrays) and read back in subsequent passes. 3. Sequential Execution: Passes execute in a strict order, with later stages depending on the accumulated or filtered data from earlier stages. 4. Hardware Utilization: Stages leverage GPU rasterization pipelines, z-buffers, and parallel fragment processing to maintain real-time performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def executemultipasspipeline(stages, buffers): """ Executes a sequence of rendering passes, writing intermediate results to dedicated buffers and synchronizing memory between stages. """ for stage in stages: bindframebuffer(stage.outputbuffer) clearbuffer(stage.outputbuffer) stage.shaderprogram.bind() stage.shaderprogram.setuniforms(stage.uniforms) if stage.requiresgeometry: drawgeometry(stage.geometry) else: drawfullscreenquad() unbindframebuffer() # Memory barrier ensures subsequent stages see written data syncmemory(stage.outputbuffer) A standard implementation structure for direct volume rendering that processes scalar field data through a sequence of stages to produce a 2D image without fitting geometric primitives. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D volumetric data by discretizing the continuous volume rendering integral along light rays, mapping scalar values to optical properties, and compositing the results. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as the Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline or the Deferred Rendering Pipeline, is its explicit separation of classification (opacity assignment) and shading (color assignment) into distinct, often parallel, steps before ray casting, allowing for independent control of surface appearance and transparency. A multi-pass architecture for real-time smoke volume rendering that processes geometry through four distinct stages to store per-pixel fragment data in GPU memory structures. It is chosen to maintain high accuracy and circumvent the self-intersection and global intersection problems inherent in raytracing approaches. Unlike the Volume Rendering Pipeline which typically evaluates rays directly, or the Deferred Rendering Pipeline which separates shading from geometry, this method explicitly decouples fragment construction and insertion from their final evaluation to manage complex storage requirements. A multi-pass deferred rendering sequence that computes depth, position/normal, materials, filtered normals, shadows, SSAO, blurred AO, and final shading in separate framebuffer objects. It sets itself apart from the Volume Rendering Pipeline by decoupling geometry traversal from shading logic, and from the Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline by relying on screen-space post-processing for effects like ambient occlusion rather than explicit fragment lists. Definition: Renders volumetric data in three sequential passes: eye pass (direct lighting/color), light pass (opacity accumulation for shadows), and composite pass (blends results). Steps: 1. Eye pass: Render volume to meyeBuffer with direct lighting, using meyePipeline and meyeSet. 2. Light pass: Accumulate opacity into mlightBuffer using mlightPipeline and mvolSet, transitioning layout from ColorAttachmentOptimal to ShaderReadOnlyOptimal. 3. Composite pass: Bind mcompositePipeline and mcompSet, draw 3 triangles (full-screen quad) using meyeBuffer as a sampled texture. Layout: Buffers include meyeBuffer (eye pass output), mlightBuffer (light pass opacity accumulation), mvolumeTex (3D volume data, R8G8Unorm), and mtfTex (transfer function). Definition: A modular differentiable rendering pipeline containing four stages: vertex processing, rasterization, fragment shading, and post-processing. Steps: Supports various rasterization algorithms and shading models through efficient interpolation between Jittor and CUDA. Usage: Supports surface rendering for 3D meshes and volume rendering for 3D volumes. Supports PBR materials and shading effects such as soft shadows, ambient occlusions, subsurface scattering, and global illumination. Definition: A pass that renders scene labels into the framebuffer produced by the previous pass, utilizing existing depth information for depth testing. Steps: Render all labels into the framebuffer from the previous pass. Pitfall: Depth testing can be enabled for labels because the framebuffer still contains depth information from previous passes. Definition: A method using historical order to overlap stages. Steps: Reuses previously computed order to avoid sorting every list from scratch, locally reordering previous frame’s lists to reduce sorting work and list storage. Definition: A GPU-accelerated rendering method for multiplanar volumetric displays that maps Cartesian geometry to the GPU, leverages the GPU z-buffer for per-pixel depth, and projects synchronized 2D slices onto a stack of liquid crystal panels. Steps: 1. Render scene to GPU frame buffer using 3D texture maps, vertex/fragment shaders, and multiple passes. 2. Read rendered frame buffer contents back to main memory. 3. Transfer data to DepthCube via API or GLInterceptor. 4. High-speed digital projector illuminates successive planar regions of the multiplanar optical element (MOE). 5. MOE driver synchronizes projector to the single light-scattering panel at the target depth. 6. Process repeats 50 times per second in noninterlaced mode. Parameters: Frame rate: 50 Hz in noninterlaced mode. Resolution: 1,024 × 768 × 20 voxels. Color depth: 15-bit per voxel. Update rate: <15 Hz for images containing single 3D surfaces. Layout: Dual-volume buffer in computer subsystem holds sequence; digital projector relays sequence into MOE; each relayed image corresponds to single liquid crystal panel. Multi-pass rendering in volume visualization evolved to handle complex lighting and transparency effects that single-pass rasterization could not efficiently support. Early direct volume rendering methods established the separation of opacity and color assignment to improve visual fidelity. As GPU architectures advanced, fragment list-based approaches emerged to handle complex smoke and fire simulations by decoupling fragment storage from evaluation, addressing issues like self-intersection in ray-tracing. Deferred rendering techniques were adapted for volume rendering to integrate screen-space effects like ambient occlusion and shadows without the performance penalty of explicit ray casting. The rise of differentiable rendering has further refined these pipelines, allowing for gradient computation through the entire multi-stage process for applications in computer vision and optimization. Modern implementations also leverage historical order overlap to reduce sorting overhead in tile-based splatting pipelines, and specialized hardware pipelines like DepthCube utilize multi-pass GPU rendering to drive multiplanar volumetric displays at 50 Hz. sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, https://github.com/sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Jrender: An efficient differentiable rendering library based on Jittor, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1524070323000322, fetched 2026-11-01 Rendering, https://met3d.readthedocs.io/en/latest/05developermanual/04rendering/index.html, fetched 2026-10-27 From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06157, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Volumetric 3D displays and application infrastructure, https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2005.276, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: CRIO Process, Classification, Reflection, Illumination, Opacity, Rendering Stages, Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) Pipeline, Shading and Classification Pipeline, VolumeRenderer forward method
body: The Volume Rendering Pipeline is a conceptual and implementation structure for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) that processes volumetric data through a sequence of stages to produce a 2D image. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields by mapping sample properties to optical attributes (color, opacity) and compositing them along viewing rays. It is distinct from splatting methods, which decompose the volume into geometric primitives for rasterization, by treating each sample as a semi-transparent cloud that is shaded and projected directly without intermediate geometric fitting. The pipeline typically consists of six sequential stages: Data Traversal, Interpolation, Gradient Computation, Classification, Shading/Illumination, and Compositing. Input: A 3D scalar field f0(\mathbf{x}i) defined at voxel locations \mathbf{x}i = (xi, yj, zk). Output: A 2D image where each pixel (u,v) has a final color C\lambda(u,v) and opacity \alpha(u,v). Voxel Database: An array of scalar values. In some implementations (e.g., DVR 1.0), this is stored in a simple binary format with width, height, and depth specified first, followed by 16-bit little-endian data values. Prepared Values Array: An intermediate array f1(\mathbf{x}i) resulting from data preparation steps. Color Array: An array of RGB colors c\lambda(\mathbf{x}i) for each voxel, where \lambda \in \{r, g, b\}. Opacity Array: An array of scalar opacities \alpha(\mathbf{x}i) for each voxel. Ray Bundle: A set of rays defined by origin and direction, often generated from camera parameters. 1. Data Traversal and Preparation: The pipeline begins by traversing the 3D scalar field. This step may include corrections for non-orthogonal sampling grids, patient motion, contrast enhancement, or interpolation of additional samples. The output is an array of prepared values f1(\mathbf{x}i). 2. Interpolation: Since sampling positions along a ray usually do not coincide with voxel centers, values must be interpolated. For ray-casting pipelines, this occurs during ray traversal. For pre-classification pipelines, interpolation may occur on the voxel grid itself or during the ray casting phase. 3. Gradient Computation: The gradient of the scalar field \nabla f is computed at sample positions to provide visual cues for shading. This is typically approximated using central differences. The gradient vector serves as a surface normal for lighting calculations. 4. Classification: A classification procedure maps the prepared values (or interpolated sample values) to optical properties. Transfer functions are applied to assign an opacity \alpha and potentially a color to each sample based on features like density or gradient magnitude. Unwanted data values are faded out (opacity set to zero). 5. Shading and Illumination: A shading model calculates the final color c\lambda for each sample. This uses the assigned color, the position of the light source, and the view point. Models range from simple identity functions to directional lighting like Phong shading. 6. Compositing: Rays are cast from the observer eyepoint through the volume. For each ray, samples are taken at K evenly spaced locations \tilde{\mathbf{x}}i along the ray. The color and opacity at these locations are determined by resampling the pre-computed color and opacity arrays using trilinear interpolation from the eight closest voxels. These samples are composited back-to-front using the transparency formula to produce the final pixel color. Transparency Formula (Compositing): The color C{out, \lambda} of the ray leaving a sample is related to the color C{in, \lambda} entering the sample, the sample color c\lambda, and opacity \alpha by: C{out, \lambda} = C{in, \lambda}(1 - \alpha) + c\lambda \alpha This is applied recursively from back to front. Ray Sampling: Sample locations \tilde{\mathbf{x}}i along a ray are computed as: \tilde{\mathbf{x}}i = \mathbf{x}0 + i \frac{d}{K} where \mathbf{x}0 is the observer eyepoint, d is the ray length through the volume, and K is the number of evenly spaced sample locations. Trilinear Interpolation: The value V at a sample location is interpolated from the eight surrounding voxels V{ijk} using weights wx, wy, wz derived from the fractional distance to the voxel corners. K: Number of evenly spaced sample locations along a viewing ray. Light Source Position: Adjustable parameter for shading. View Point: Adjustable parameter for shading and ray origin. Transfer Function Parameters: Define the mapping from scalar values to color and opacity. Performance Cost: Shading and trilinear interpolation between eight voxels are high-cost operations. In some implementations, these can be switched off to improve performance, potentially reducing visual quality. Precision: The input data format may require specific endianness (e.g., little-endian 16-bit) which must be handled correctly during loading. Clipping: Standard pipelines apply clipping globally. Specialized variants are needed to render important structures differently if they lie within a clipped area. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumerenderingpipeline(volumedata, width, height, depth, rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, transferfunctions): """ Implements the standard Direct Volume Rendering pipeline. Args: volumedata: 3D list of scalar values indexed as [x][y][z]. width, height, depth: Dimensions of the volume. rayorigin: Tuple (ox, oy, oz) for the observer eyepoint. raydirection: Tuple (dx, dy, dz) for the ray direction. numsamples: Integer K, number of samples per ray. transferfunctions: List of functions mapping scalar value to (color, opacity). Returns: image: 2D list of RGB colors. alphaimage: 2D list of opacities. """ image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] alphaimage = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Pre-compute voxel colors and opacities (Pre-classification approach) voxelcolors = [[[None for in range(depth)] for in range(height)] for in range(width)] voxelopacities = [[[0.0 for in range(depth)] for in range(height)] for in range(width)] for x in range(width): for y in range(height): for z in range(depth): val = volumedata[x][y][z] color, opacity = applytransferfunction(val, transferfunctions) voxelcolors[x][y][z] = color voxelopacities[x][y][z] = opacity for v in range(height): for u in range(width): raylength = computeraylength(rayorigin, raydirection, width, height, depth) stepsize = raylength / numsamples currentcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentopacity = 1.0 # Traverse ray from back to front for k in range(numsamples, 0, -1): t = (k - 0.5) stepsize samplepos = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) if not isinsidevolume(samplepos, width, height, depth): continue samplecolor = trilinearinterpolate(voxelcolors, samplepos) sampleopacity = trilinearinterpolate(voxelopacities, samplepos) currentcolor = (currentcolor[0] (1 - sampleopacity) + samplecolor[0] sampleopacity, currentcolor[1] (1 - sampleopacity) + samplecolor[1] sampleopacity, currentcolor[2] (1 - sampleopacity) + samplecolor[2] sampleopacity) currentopacity = currentopacity (1 - sampleopacity) if currentopacity >= 1.0: break image[v][u] = currentcolor alphaimage[v][u] = 1.0 - currentopacity return image, alphaimage def applytransferfunction(value, transferfunctions): color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) opacity = 0.0 for tf in transferfunctions: c, a = tf(value) opacity += a (1 - opacity) color = (color[0] (1 - a) + c[0] a, color[1] (1 - a) + c[1] a, color[2] (1 - a) + c[2] a) return color, opacity def computeraylength(rayorigin, raydirection, width, height, depth): # Computes the length of the ray segment inside the volume AABB return 10.0 # Simplified for example def isinsidevolume(point, width, height, depth): return 0 <= point[0] < width and 0 <= point[1] < height and 0 <= point[2] < depth def trilinearinterpolate(dataarray, point): x, y, z = point ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz ix = max(0, min(ix, len(dataarray) - 2)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(dataarray[0]) - 2)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(dataarray[0][0]) - 2)) c000 = dataarray[ix][iy][iz] c100 = dataarray[ix+1][iy][iz] c010 = dataarray[ix][iy+1][iz] c110 = dataarray[ix+1][iy+1][iz] c001 = dataarray[ix][iy][iz+1] c101 = dataarray[ix+1][iy][iz+1] c011 = dataarray[ix][iy+1][iz+1] c111 = dataarray[ix+1][iy+1][iz+1] c00 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx c01 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx c10 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx c11 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c01 fy c1 = c10 (1 - fy) + c11 fy result = c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz return result The Post-classification Shading Pipeline (also known as Post-DVRI) is a volume rendering model where raw volume density values are interpolated by the ray first, and the resulting interpolated values are then mapped to color and opacity via transfer functions, followed by shading. This approach solves the blurring artifacts inherent in pre-classification methods by ensuring that high-frequency details in transfer functions are resolved after interpolation. It is distinct from the Pre-classification Shading Pipeline, which classifies discrete voxel values before interpolation, resulting in blurry edges and loss of fine detail under magnification. A pipeline split into two parallel stages to render important pathological structures with different parameters even if they lie in a clipping area, while rendering anatomical structures normally. Stage 1 renders anatomical structures that are not clipped away using standard volume rendering steps. Stage 2 renders important structures (e.g., vessels, pathological tissue) that are excluded from clipping, using specific rendering parameters (gradient computation, classification, lighting). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of samples per ray (O(W \cdot H \cdot K)). Gradient computation and classification are typically O(V) where V is the volume size, if done pre-pass, or O(W \cdot H \cdot K) if done per-sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) to store the volume data. Performance: High computational cost due to shading and interpolation per sample. Performance can be improved by switching off shading/interpolation or using early ray termination. Strengths: High visual quality, ability to handle complex transfer functions, independence of shading and classification allows for undistorted visualization of 3D shape. Limitations: Blurring in pre-classification methods; high cost of per-voxel shading and interpolation; global clipping limitations in standard pipelines. When to use: When high-quality visualization of internal structures is required, and interactive frame rates are not the primary constraint, or when hardware acceleration is available. When not to use: When real-time performance on low-end hardware is critical without optimization, or when the volume data is extremely large and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. The volume rendering pipeline was formalized in the late 1980s. Key early work includes the presentation of the "Display of Surfaces from Volume Data" technique by Marc Levoy at the SPIE Medical Imaging II conference in January 1988. This work described the pipeline stages of classification, shading, and back-to-front compositing. The term "CRIO" (Classification, Reflection, Illumination, Opacity) was used to describe the conceptual feed-forward process in splatting algorithms. The pipeline structure is widely cited in volume rendering literature, such as Engel's survey. name: Post-classification Shading Pipeline
head: Post-DVRI, Post-classification DVR, Post-classified DVR, Post-classified Rendering, Post-shaded DVRI
body: The Post-classification Shading Pipeline (also known as Post-DVRI) is a volume rendering model where raw volume density values are interpolated by the ray first, and the resulting interpolated values are then mapped to color and opacity via transfer functions, followed by shading. This approach solves the blurring artifacts inherent in pre-classification methods by ensuring that high-frequency details in transfer functions are resolved after interpolation. It is distinct from the Pre-classification Shading Pipeline, which classifies discrete voxel values before interpolation, resulting in blurry edges and loss of fine detail under magnification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume grid fd(x,y,z) representing density; a ray defined by origin \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{r}; transfer functions for color C\lambda and opacity \alpha; shading function C\lambda (which may depend on gradient); ray step size \Delta s; and ray length L. Output: The accumulated color I\lambda(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) for each pixel. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array of scalar density values. Transfer Functions: Lookup tables (LUTs) mapping density values to color and opacity. Gradient Field: Pre-computed or on-the-fly computed gradient vectors \nabla f for shading. Steps: 1. Ray Marching: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume and sample at intervals \Delta s along the ray. 2. Interpolation: For each sample position si = \mathbf{x} + i\Delta s \mathbf{r}, interpolate the raw density value f(si) and the gradient vector g(si) from the volume grid fd using a 3D interpolation kernel. 3. Classification: Map the interpolated density f(si) to opacity \alpha(f(si)) and base color using the transfer function \alpha. 4. Shading: Compute the shading color C\lambda based on the interpolated density f(si) and the interpolated gradient g(si). The gradient g(i\Delta s) is passed to the shading function to approximate surface orientation. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the color contributions using front-to-back alpha blending. Formula: The final image intensity I\lambda(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) is computed as: I\lambda(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=0}^{L/\Delta s - 1} C\lambda(f(i\Delta s), g(i\Delta s)) \alpha(f(i\Delta s)) \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(f(j\Delta s))) Where: L is the total length of the ray within the volume. \Delta s is the step size. f(i\Delta s) is the interpolated volume function value at sample i. g(i\Delta s) is the interpolated gradient vector at sample i. \alpha(f(i\Delta s)) is the opacity derived from the transfer function applied to the interpolated density. C\lambda(f(i\Delta s), g(i\Delta s)) is the color contribution, determined by transfer and shading functions using the interpolated density and gradient. The product term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(f(j\Delta s))) represents the transmittance from previous samples. Note: Some sources define the summation limit as L/\Delta s without the -1, implying an inclusive upper bound indexing. The standard front-to-back accumulation typically iterates up to the last sample within the volume bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def postclassificationshadingpipeline(volumegrid, rayorigin, raydirection, transferfunctionalpha, transferfunctioncolor, shadingfunction, stepsize, volumebounds): """ Implements the Post-classification Shading Pipeline. Args: volumegrid: 3D array of density values. rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z). raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), normalized. transferfunctionalpha: Function or LUT mapping density -> opacity. transferfunctioncolor: Function or LUT mapping density -> base color. shadingfunction: Function mapping (density, gradient) -> shaded color. stepsize: Float, distance between samples. volumebounds: Object defining the AABB of the volume. Returns: Color vector (R, G, B). """ # 1. Intersect ray with volume bounds to get tmin and tmax tmin, tmax = intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) if tmax < 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Ray misses volume # Clamp start to 0 to handle rays originating inside the volume tstart = max(0.0, tmin) numsamples = max(1, int(round((tmax - tstart) / stepsize))) # Initialize accumulators accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) transmittance = 1.0 # 2. Ray march: iterate i from 0 to numsamples-1 to match formula bounds for i in range(numsamples): t = tstart + i stepsize pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 3. Interpolate raw density and gradient from volume grid fval = interpolatedensity(volumegrid, pos) gvec = interpolategradient(volumegrid, pos) # 4. Classification: Map density to opacity alpha = transferfunctionalpha(fval) # 5. Shading: Compute color based on density and gradient color = shadingfunction(fval, gvec) # 6. Compositing: Front-to-back blending contribution = color alpha transmittance accumulatedcolor = ( accumulatedcolor[0] + contribution[0], accumulatedcolor[1] + contribution[1], accumulatedcolor[2] + contribution[2]) # Update transmittance for next sample transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early ray termination optimization if transmittance <= 1e-6: break return accumulatedcolor def intersectrayaabb(origin, direction, bounds): """Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection.""" tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds.min[i] or origin[i] > bounds.max[i]: return (float('inf'), -float('inf')) else: t1 = (bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) def interpolatedensity(grid, pos): """Clamp coordinates to grid bounds and perform trilinear interpolation.""" x, y, z = pos nx, ny, nz = grid.shape x = max(0, min(nx - 1, x)) y = max(0, min(ny - 1, y)) z = max(0, min(nz - 1, z)) return grid[int(x), int(y), int(z)] # Simplified nearest-neighbor for brevity; replace with trilinear def interpolategradient(grid, pos): """Compute central difference gradient, clamped to bounds.""" x, y, z = pos nx, ny, nz = grid.shape dx = (grid[min(nx-1, int(x)+1), int(y), int(z)] - grid[max(0, int(x)-1), int(y), int(z)]) / 2.0 dy = (grid[int(x), min(ny-1, int(y)+1), int(z)] - grid[int(x), max(0, int(y)-1), int(z)]) / 2.0 dz = (grid[int(x), int(y), min(nz-1, int(z)+1)] - grid[int(x), int(y), max(0, int(z)-1)]) / 2.0 return (dx, dy, dz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Partial Volume Effect: Interpolated density values may fall into a range classified as a material not actually present at the sample location, leading to false colors. Narrow Transfer Function Peaks: If the transfer function has very narrow peaks, standard ray sampling might miss these peaks entirely, failing to render thin structures. Pre-integrated transfer functions can mitigate this but are not part of the basic pipeline definition. Staircasing Artifacts: Avoiding false colors via prior segmentation can introduce high-frequency artifacts and staircasing. Classifies and shades discrete voxel values before interpolation. Chosen for performance or when partial volume effects are less critical; results in blurrier images at high resolutions compared to post-classification. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray (O(L/\Delta s)) and the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the volume grid and transfer function LUTs. Gradient computation can be done on-the-fly (increasing compute) or pre-computed (increasing memory). Performance: Generally faster than methods requiring complex geometric primitives but slower than pre-classification if gradient computation is expensive. Strengths: Produces considerably sharper images than pre-classified rendering because classification is performed after interpolation, eliminating blurry edges introduced by the interpolation filter. Fine detail in transfer functions is readily expressed in the final image. Limitations: Susceptible to partial volume artifacts (false colors). Can miss narrow peaks in transfer functions if ray sampling is too coarse. When to Use: When image sharpness and accurate representation of high-frequency transfer function details are prioritized over the avoidance of partial volume artifacts. When Not to Use: When partial volume artifacts are unacceptable and segmentation is not feasible, or when extreme performance is required and blur is tolerable (use Pre-classification). The Post-classification Shading Pipeline, also referred to as Post-DVRI (Post-shaded Direct Volume Rendering Integration), was developed as an alternative to the pre-classified model to address blurring issues in volume visualization. It is based on the principle that interpolating raw data before applying transfer functions allows for better resolution of high-frequency details. The mathematical formulation is derived from the generalized volume rendering integral, adapted for discrete sampling and interpolation. It is widely used in modern volume rendering systems where image quality is paramount. name: Pre-classification Shading Pipeline
head: Pre-DVRI, Pre-shaded DVR, Pre-shaded DVRI
body: The Pre-classification Shading Pipeline (also known as Pre-DVRI) is a volume rendering method where voxel values are mapped to optical properties (color and opacity) and shaded before ray sample interpolation occurs. Unlike the Post-classification Shading Pipeline, which interpolates raw density values first, this approach classifies and shades the discrete grid samples, then composites them along the ray. It is distinct from post-classification primarily in its handling of partial voluming and its susceptibility to blurring at high image resolutions. Input: A scalar volume grid V where each voxel v has a scalar value sv, optionally augmented with material indices and probabilities from a segmentation process. Output: A 2D image where each pixel represents the integrated light I\lambda(x, r) along the viewing ray r. The core data structure for a pre-classified voxel is a vector of four components: (R\alpha, G\alpha, B\alpha, \alpha). This is called associated color or opacity-weighted color. Let \tilde{C} denote the associated color vector, defined as \tilde{C} = C\alpha where C is the original color and \alpha is the opacity. 1. Classification and Shading (Pre-processing): Apply transfer functions to voxels to compute color C and opacity \alpha. If segmentation is available, use material indices and probabilities to resolve partial voluming. 2. Pre-multiplication: Pre-multiply the color of each voxel with its opacity before interpolation to form the associated color \tilde{C} = C\alpha. 3. Interpolation: Interpolate the associated color \tilde{C} and opacity \alpha from the grid to sample positions si along the ray. 4. Compositing: Composite the samples along the ray using the discretized volume rendering integral. I\lambda(x,r) = \sum{i=0}^{L/\Delta s} \tilde{C}\lambda(si) \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(sj)) Where: L is the length of ray r. \Delta s is the step size. \tilde{C}\lambda(si) is the associated color at sample i. \alpha(sj) is the opacity at sample j. The term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(sj)) represents the transmittance from the ray start to sample i. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preclassificationshadingpipeline(volumegrid, transferfunction, rayorigin, raydirection, imagewidth, imageheight, stepsize, raylength): # Pre-processing: Classify and shade the entire volume grid preclassifiedvolume = [] for voxel in volumegrid: scalarvalue = voxel.value color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarvalue) associatedcolor = color opacity preclassifiedvolume.append({'associatedcolor': associatedcolor, 'opacity': opacity}) image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Standard ray generation for pixel (x, y) rayoriginpixel = rayorigin + raydirection (x 0.01 + y 0.01) transmittance = 1.0 pixelcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] numsamples = int(raylength / stepsize) for i in range(numsamples): samplepos = rayoriginpixel + raydirection (i stepsize) # Standard trilinear interpolation def trilinearinterpolate(grid, pos, field): # Compute grid coordinates and fractional offsets ix, iy, iz = int(pos.x), int(pos.y), int(pos.z) fx, fy, fz = pos.x - ix, pos.y - iy, pos.z - iz # Fetch 8 neighbors (clamped to grid bounds) def getval(x, y, z): x = max(0, min(x, gridwidth - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, gridheight - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, griddepth - 1)) return grid[z][y][x][field] # Interpolate c00 = getval(ix, iy, iz) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy, iz) fx c10 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz) fx c01 = getval(ix, iy, iz+1) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy, iz+1) fx c11 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz+1) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) fx c0 = c00 (1-fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1-fy) + c11 fy return c0 (1-fz) + c1 fz associatedcolorsample = trilinearinterpolate(preclassifiedvolume, samplepos, 'associatedcolor') opacitysample = trilinearinterpolate(preclassifiedvolume, samplepos, 'opacity') contribution = associatedcolorsample transmittance pixelcolor += contribution transmittance = (1.0 - opacitysample) if transmittance < 0.001: break image[y][x] = pixelcolor return image Step Size (\Delta s): Not given in the sources. Partial Voluming: A major source of error where a single voxel represents multiple materials. This is mitigated by using segmented volumes with material indices and probabilities during the pre-classification step. Blurring: Pre-classification tends to cause excessive blurring when the image resolution exceeds the volume resolution (e.g., zoomed viewing or wide perspectives). Interpolation Error: Interpolating color and opacity separately and then multiplying them introduces artifacts because interpolation is a linear operation and the product is non-linear. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles segmented anatomical parts effectively in medical imaging. Prevents partial voluming errors when segmentation data is available. Compatible with pre-integration techniques. Limitations: Prone to excessive blurring at high image resolutions or wide perspectives. Harder to implement than post-classification due to the requirement of pre-multiplying color and opacity. Cannot easily re-classify data without re-processing the entire volume. The concept of pre-classification was introduced by Drebin et al. in 1988, who defined associated color (opacity-weighted color). Wittenbrink et al. (1998) further analyzed the pipeline, highlighting the necessity of pre-multiplying color and opacity before interpolation to avoid artifacts. The term Pre-DVRI (Pre-shaded Direct Volume Rendering Integration) was used to distinguish this pipeline from post-shaded variants. It remains a critical tool in medical imaging for handling segmented data. name: Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline
head: 4-Stage Rendering Pipeline, Smoker Rendering Pipeline
body: The Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline is a multi-pass architecture designed for real-time smoke volume rendering that processes volumetric primitives through four distinct stages: Clear, Construction, Insertion, and Evaluation. It solves the problem of maintaining high accuracy in transparent volume visualization while circumventing the computational complexity and self-intersection artifacts inherent in raytracing methods. Unlike standard ray-casting which accumulates contributions along rays, this method rasterizes primitives into per-pixel fragment lists, deferring the final compositing and visualization to a dedicated evaluation pass. The pipeline executes four sequential stages using three distinct shader programs: Clear, Render (combining Construction and Insertion), and Display (Evaluation). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Smoke volume data (density, flow tangents), geometry primitives (triangles representing volume slices or particles), and screen resolution. Output: Final rendered image buffer. Data Structures: Fragment Lists: Per-pixel storage structures (e.g., linked lists, atomic counters, or fixed-size arrays) that accumulate fragment data during the Insertion stage. OpenGL Buffer Objects: Used to store intermediate states, reset per frame, and pass data between stages. Numbered Steps: 1. Clear Stage: Reset all OpenGL buffer objects and fragment list storage structures required for the subsequent frame. Initiated by rendering a single screen-filling quad using the Clear shader program. 2. Construction Stage: Vertex Shader: Performs perspective transformation of vertices from volume space to screen space. Vertex Shader: Assigns additional vertex data such as density (\rho) and flow tangents. Geometry Shader: Assembles primitives (e.g., triangles) from the transformed vertices. Geometry Shader: Processes triangle-related data including orientation, topology, and volume information. Geometry Shader: Forwards the constructed primitives to the Insertion stage. This stage is part of the Render shader program. 3. Insertion Stage: Rasterization: The primitives constructed in the previous stage are rasterized. Fragment Shader: Processes incoming fragments. Fragment Shader: The processing logic varies by visualization method, ranging from a simple pixel counter to inserting fragment data into a complicated storage data structure (fragment list). Constraint: The type of fragment processing must be strictly compatible with the subsequent Evaluation step. This stage is part of the Render shader program. 4. Evaluation Stage: Render a single screen-filling quad using the Display shader program. Interpret and visualize the per-pixel information (e.g., accumulated density, color, depth) that was prepared and stored by the Insertion stage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentlistpipeline(volumedata, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize per-pixel fragment lists fragmentlists = [[[] for in range(screenheight)] for in range(screenwidth)] # 1. Clear Stage clearbuffers(fragmentlists) # 2. Construction & 3. Insertion Stage (Render Program) for primitive in volumedata.primitives: # Vertex Shader: Perspective transform and assign data transformedvertices = [] for vertex in primitive.vertices: screenpos = perspectivetransform(vertex.position) transformedvertices.append({ 'screenpos': screenpos, 'density': vertex.density, 'flowtangent': vertex.flowtangent }) # Geometry Shader: Assemble primitives and process topology constructedprimitives = assembleprimitives(transformedvertices) # Rasterization and Fragment Shader: Insertion for fragment in rasterize(constructedprimitives, screenwidth, screenheight): insertfragment(fragmentlists, fragment) # 4. Evaluation Stage evaluateandrender(fragmentlists, screenwidth, screenheight) def clearbuffers(fragmentlists): for x in range(len(fragmentlists)): for y in range(len(fragmentlists[0])): fragmentlists[x][y].clear() def perspectivetransform(position): # Standard MVP matrix multiplication return mvpmatrix @ position def assembleprimitives(vertices): # Form triangles from vertex triplets return [createtriangle(v0, v1, v2) for v0, v1, v2 in vertextriplets(vertices)] def vertextriplets(vertices): return [(vertices[i], vertices[i+1], vertices[i+2]) for i in range(0, len(vertices)-2, 3)] def createtriangle(v0, v1, v2): return {'vertices': [v0, v1, v2], 'orientation': v0['screenpos'], 'topology': 'triangle'} def rasterize(primitives, width, height): # Simplified rasterization returning fragments for each covered pixel fragments = [] for prim in primitives: for x in range(width): for y in range(height): if isinsidetriangle(x, y, prim['vertices']): fragments.append({ 'screenpos': (x, y), 'density': interpolateattribute('density', x, y, prim['vertices']), 'flowtangent': interpolateattribute('flowtangent', x, y, prim['vertices']) }) return fragments def isinsidetriangle(x, y, vertices): # Barycentric coordinate check v0, v1, v2 = vertices d1 = sign((x, y), v0['screenpos'], v1['screenpos']) d2 = sign((x, y), v1['screenpos'], v2['screenpos']) d3 = sign((x, y), v2['screenpos'], v0['screenpos']) hasneg = (d1 < 0) or (d2 < 0) or (d3 < 0) haspos = (d1 > 0) or (d2 > 0) or (d3 > 0) return not (hasneg or haspos) def sign(p1, p2, p3): return (p1[0] - p3[0]) (p2[1] - p3[1]) - (p2[0] - p3[0]) (p1[1] - p3[1]) def interpolateattribute(attr, x, y, vertices): # Barycentric interpolation return vertices[0][attr] def insertfragment(fragmentlists, fragment): # Critical section: Concurrent modification of shared memory # In GPU implementation, this uses atomic operations to avoid inconsistent states fragmentlists[fragment['screenpos'][0]][fragment['screenpos'][1]].append(fragment) def evaluateandrender(fragmentlists, width, height): # Render screen-filling quad to interpret per-pixel information for x in range(width): for y in range(height): fragments = fragmentlists[x][y] # Visualization logic depends on fragment list structure renderpixel(x, y, fragments) def renderpixel(x, y, fragments): # Interpret and visualize per-pixel information prepared by Insertion pass Parameters: Pipeline Stages: Clear, Construction, Insertion, Evaluation. Shader Programs: Clear, Render (Construction + Insertion), Display (Evaluation). Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concurrent Modification: The Insertion step is the greatest bottleneck due to simultaneous access to shared indexing mechanisms. Inconsistent States: Unmanaged access to shared memory by shader threads can leave the memory in an inconsistent state because threads cannot check if a shared address is currently being modified. Compatibility: The fragment processing method in the Insertion stage must be strictly compatible with the Evaluation stage; mismatched data structures will result in incorrect visualization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance is heavily influenced by the complexity of the fragment list insertion and the number of primitives per pixel. Memory Complexity: Depends on the fragment list storage structure. Measured Performance: Implemented in the Smoker application for real-time smoke volume rendering. Strengths: Maintains high accuracy and circumvents problems arising from raytracing, self-intersections, and global intersections. Limitations: The Insertion stage is a significant bottleneck due to concurrent memory access issues and requires careful management of shared memory states. When to use: Real-time smoke volume rendering where accuracy is prioritized over the simplicity of ray-casting and where self-intersection artifacts must be avoided. When not to use: Scenes with extremely high primitive density per pixel where fragment list management overhead becomes prohibitive, or when hardware does not support efficient atomic operations for fragment list insertion. The Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline was developed as part of the "Smoker" application for real-time smoke volume rendering. It was chosen over raytracing techniques to maintain the best possible accuracy and to circumvent problems arising from raytracing and self or global intersections. The method is detailed in a master's thesis by Sowinski (2012). name: Deferred Rendering Pipeline
head: 8-Pass Deferred Rendering Pipeline
body: A multi-pass deferred rendering sequence that computes depth, position/normal, materials, filtered normals, shadows, SSAO, blurred AO, and final shading in separate framebuffer objects. It separates geometry processing from lighting calculations, allowing complex lighting effects to be applied per-pixel without re-rasterizing geometry. It is distinct from the Volume Rendering Pipeline by deferring shading to a post-process stage, and from the Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline by using fixed-screen-space framebuffers rather than dynamic fragment lists. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (accessed via OctreeDDARenderer), camera matrices (view, projection, inverse), light position, and material parameters. Output: Final shaded image in the default framebuffer. Data Structures: The method uses a sequence of Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) and associated textures. The following textures are bound to texture units TEXNUM during resetState(): 1. glTexDepth: Depth buffer. 2. glTexHitPos: Position buffer. 3. glTexHitNorm: Normal buffer. 4. glTexHitMaterial: Material buffer. 5. glTexHitNormFiltered: Filtered normal buffer. 6. glTexShadows: Shadow map buffer. 7. glTexAO: Ambient Occlusion buffer. 8. glTexAOBlurred: Blurred AO buffer. 9. glTexAONoise: Noise texture for AO. 10. glTexTBOMaterials: Texture for TBO materials. Framebuffers glFBO[0] through glFBO[6] are used sequentially. Steps: 1. Depth Pass: Bind glFBO[0], clear, set OctreeDDARenderer mode to DEPTH, and draw the volume geometry. 2. Position/Normal Pass: Bind glFBO[1], clear, use programPosNorm, set uniforms viewMatInv, projMatInv, useDif, and draw a full-screen quad. 3. Material Pass: If useMaterials is true, bind glFBO[2], clear, use programMaterial, set uniforms, and draw a full-screen quad. 4. Normal Filtering Pass: If filterNormals is true, bind glFBO[3], clear, use programNormFilter, set uniforms sigma and bsigma, and draw a full-screen quad. 5. Shadow Pass: If doShadows is true, bind glFBO[4], clear, set lightPos, set OctreeDDARenderer mode to SHADOW, and draw the volume geometry. Otherwise, clear glFBO[4] to white (1.0). 6. SSAO Pass: If doSSAO is true, bind glFBO[5], clear, use programSSAO, set uniforms projMat, viewMat, camPos, radius, and draw a full-screen quad. 7. AO Blur Pass: Bind glFBO[6], clear, use programBlur, and draw a full-screen quad. 8. Final Shading Pass: Bind the default framebuffer, clear, use programShading, set uniforms isYUp, camPos, projMatInv, viewMatInv, lightPos, renderMode, useMaterials, and draw a full-screen quad. Pitfalls: Pass 5 (Shadows) clears to white (1.0) when disabled, which acts as a default fully lit state. Pass 6 (SSAO) is wrapped in #if 0/#else in the source, indicating the original octree-based AO path is disabled in favor of the screen-space quad pass. Not given in the sources. This specific 8-pass implementation is part of the ssvdag project, which uses an octree-based DDA renderer for volume visualization. ajaspe/ssvdag, https://github.com/ajaspe/ssvdag, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Interactive Forward Rendering with Approximate Splatting
head: Fast Rendering, OpenGL Approximation
body: This method provides an efficient, hardware-accelerated approximation of point reprojection for high-quality free-viewpoint rendering, enabling interactive frame rates by replacing full soft rasterization with a global depth layering system. It differs from sibling methods by using a fixed number of global depth layers rather than processing slices sequentially, and by explicitly managing opacity accumulation via logarithmic blending in screen space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input views (images and camera poses), a multi-view stereo (MVS) mesh, and a pre-trained neural network for image synthesis. Outputs: A synthesized novel view image. Data Structures: Depth Layers: A stack of kd texture buffers representing global depth intervals. Each layer stores accumulated opacity and depth information. MVS Mesh Depth Map: A low-resolution depth map used to determine the relevant depth interval for the scene. Parameters: kd: Number of global depth layers. Typical value: 10. Resolution: Target output resolution (e.g., 900×600). Steps: 1. Camera Selection: Choose a subset of input views relevant to the novel view. 2. Depth Interval Determination: Rasterize the MVS mesh depth at a low resolution (1/16 of target) and construct a min-max mipmap to determine the relevant depth range. 3. Splatting into Depth Layers: Project points from all selected input views into the kd global depth layers in parallel. Opacity accumulation uses hardware-accelerated additive blending of \log(1 - \alpha) to achieve multiplicative opacity accumulation. Formula for opacity accumulation: If \alpha is the splat opacity, the stored value V is updated as V{\text{new}} = V{\text{old}} + \log(1 - \alpha). The final accumulated opacity is 1 - \exp(V{\text{total}}). 4. Compositing: Composite the depth layers back-to-front in parallel over all re-projected pixels of all input images. 5. Probabilistic Depth Test: Apply a probabilistic depth test considering at most kd alpha-weighted depth samples to refine visibility. 6. Neural Synthesis: Run the neural network to synthesize the final image using the accumulated depth and color information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interactiveforwardrendering(inputviews, mvsmesh, neuralnet, kd=10, targetres=(900, 600)): # 1. Camera Selection: Choose relevant input views # Camera selection algorithm not specified in sources selectedviews = inputviews # 2. Determine Depth Interval: Rasterize MVS mesh at 1/16 resolution, build min-max mipmap lowres = (targetres[0] // 16, targetres[1] // 16) lowresdepth = rasterizemesh(mvsmesh, lowres) # Standard GPU rasterization depthmin = lowresdepth.min() depthmax = lowresdepth.max() # 3. Initialize Depth Layers: Stack of kd texture buffers for log(1-alpha) accumulation depthlayers = [[0.0] (targetres[0] targetres[1]) for in range(kd)] # 4. Splat Points into Depth Layers: Project all pixels of selected views in parallel for view in selectedviews: for point in view.points: # Points extracted from input view # Project to screen space screenx = int((point.screenu targetres[0]) % targetres[0]) screeny = int((point.screenv targetres[1]) % targetres[1]) depth = point.depth # Map depth to layer index layeridx = int(((depth - depthmin) / (depthmax - depthmin)) kd) layeridx = max(0, min(kd - 1, layeridx)) # Compute opacity and update layer with additive blending of log(1-alpha) alpha = point.alpha logval = math.log(1.0 - alpha) depthlayers[layeridx][screeny targetres[0] + screenx] += logval # 5. Composite Depth Layers Back-to-Front in parallel # Sum log values across layers to get total accumulated log opacity totallogalpha = [0.0] (targetres[0] targetres[1]) for layer in depthlayers: for i in range(len(totallogalpha)): totallogalpha[i] += layer[i] finalalpha = [1.0 - math.exp(val) for val in totallogalpha] # 6. Probabilistic Depth Test: Consider at most kd alpha-weighted depth samples # Probabilistic depth test logic not specified in sources refineddepth = depthlayers # 7. Neural Synthesis: Run neural network to synthesize image finalimage = neuralnet(refineddepth, finalalpha, selectedviews) return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Consumption: High memory usage due to batching all input views and depth layers. Compression: Memory can be reduced through standard texture compression methods. Time Complexity: The method is designed for interactive performance. An unoptimized implementation runs at 4.5 fps. Breakdown: Camera selection: 87 ms, point splatting: 36 ms, depth test: 38 ms, network evaluation: 59 ms. Memory Complexity: High. Depth layers consume ~4 GB for 900×600 resolution, 10 layers, 9 views. PyTorch reports 4.5 GB total memory usage for this configuration. Strengths: Enables interactive viewing with marginal quality degradation compared to full soft rasterization. Limitations: High memory consumption; requires pre-trained neural network. When to use: When interactive frame rates are required for free-viewpoint rendering and sufficient GPU memory is available. When not to use: When memory is constrained or offline rendering quality is prioritized over speed. This method was introduced by Kopanas et al. in "Point-Based Neural Rendering with Per-View Optimization". It is part of a differentiable multi-view pipeline used for applications such as image-based rendering (IBR), multi-view harmonization, and multi-view style transfer. The implementation was done in PyTorch with custom OpenGL-based approximations for the forward pass. name: INPC Inference & Rendering Pipeline
head: INPC Pipeline
body: The INPC (Implicit Neural Point Cloud) Inference & Rendering Pipeline is a splatting-based method that renders high-quality radiance fields by blending multisampled splats into feature images, applying global sorting, and refining the output via a U-Net and tone mapping module. It distinguishes itself from explicit point-based siblings like 3D Gaussian Splatting 3DGS or TRIPS TRIPS by using an implicit point cloud formulation with a view-independent sampling algorithm, which allows for superior image quality at the cost of higher computational overhead during the sorting and post-processing stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained implicit neural point cloud model (defined by an octree structure and neural networks for attributes), camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, resolution), and a configuration setting (e.g., 8M or 33M samples). Output: A final rendered image (color and/or feature map). Data Structures: The method relies on an octree-based data structure to manage the point cloud. The specific field layouts of the octree nodes and the neural network weights are not detailed in the sources. The pipeline processes points defined by position \mathbf{p} and associated implicit attributes. Steps: 1. Sampling: Generate a set of points for the current viewpoint using a view-independent sampling algorithm. For the default configuration, this involves 33 million samples per training iteration; for the fast configuration, 8 million samples. During inference, 4× multisampling is applied, meaning each point is sampled 4 times to reduce aliasing. 2. Splatting: Transform the sampled points into screen space and rasterize them as splats. The splats are blended into feature images. The number of blended splats depends on the configuration: up to 528 million splats (4×33M points) for the default configuration, or 128 million splats (4×8M points) for the fast configuration. 3. Global Sorting: Perform a global sort of the splats. This step is identified as the primary rendering bottleneck. 4. Post-Processing: Apply a U-Net architecture followed by a tone mapping module to the rendered feature images. This step corrects artifacts and enhances high-frequency details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinpc(model, camera, config): # 1. Sampling: Generate points using a view-independent sampling algorithm # config.numsamples is 8M or 33M; 4x multisampling is applied during inference points = model.sampleviewindependent(numsamples=config.numsamples, multisample=4) # 2. Splatting: Transform points to screen space and rasterize into feature images # Blends up to 528M splats (4x33M) or 128M splats (4x8M) per feature image featureimages = [] for point in points: screenpos = camera.project(point.position) contribution = point.computesplatcontribution(screenpos) featureimages.append(contribution) renderedfeatures = accumulatesplats(featureimages) # 3. Global Sorting: Sort all splats globally (identified as the rendering bottleneck) # The sources do not provide the specific sorting algorithm details. sortedfeatures = sortsplatsglobally(renderedfeatures) # 4. Post-Processing: Apply U-Net architecture followed by tone mapping # The sources do not provide the exact U-Net architecture or tone mapping formula. refinedfeatures = applyunet(sortedfeatures) finalimage = applytonemapping(refinedfeatures) return finalimage def accumulatesplats(splats): # Standard accumulation of splat contributions into feature images return [[sum(s[i] for s in splats) for i in range(len(splats[0]))] for splats in zip(splats)] def sortsplatsglobally(features): # Global sort of splats; algorithm details not provided in sources return sorted(features, key=lambda f: f.depth) def applyunet(features): # U-Net architecture pass; exact architecture not provided in sources return features def applytonemapping(features): # Tone mapping pass; exact formula not provided in sources return features Parameters: numsamples: The number of samples per training iteration. Default is 33M; Fast configuration is 8M. multisample: Set to 4 for inference to blend multiple splats per point. resolution: Standard resolutions tested include 2000×1085 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting Bottleneck: Global sorting significantly impacts real-time performance, making it slower than explicit point-based methods. Pixel Budget Limits: Pre-extracting a global point cloud (e.g., 67M points) may be insufficient for high-resolution scenes like Tanks and Temples due to pixel budget limits. Thin Structures: The sampling algorithm may miss thin structures if multisampling is disabled. Temporal Stability: Minor temporal instability may occur during inference, a common issue with CNN-based post-processing. Fine Detail Near Camera: The method may struggle to reconstruct fine geometric details close to the camera, similar to 3DGS and Zip-NeRF. The underlying representation uses an octree-based data structure and a view-independent sampling algorithm to manage the point cloud. Link to Implicit Neural Point Clouds A convolutional neural network (U-Net) is used to refine rasterized features and address artifacts, followed by a tone mapping module. Link to U-Net Rendering Time Complexity: The global sorting step is the bottleneck, leading to higher latency compared to explicit point-based methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On an RTX 4090 GPU at 2000×1085 resolution with the 8M configuration: Sampling: 51ms Rendering: 16ms Total: 37ms (~9 fps). With pre-extracted global point cloud: Total 26ms. Scaling: The method scales with the number of samples (8M vs 33M), with the 33M configuration blending up to 528 million splats. Strengths: High image quality, outperforming Zip-NeRF and comparable to explicit methods in perceived quality. Limitations: Slower than 3DGS, TRIPS, and ADOP due to sorting and post-processing overhead. The INPC method was introduced in the paper "INPC: Implicit Neural Point Clouds for Radiance Field Rendering". It builds upon the splatting family of volume rendering techniques, leveraging implicit neural representations to enhance the quality of point-based rendering. The method was evaluated on benchmarks such as Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks and Temples. name: Rasterization-based Splatting Pipeline
head: Point Splatting Rasterization, RASTERIZE
body: The Rasterization-based Splatting Pipeline renders volumetric data by decomposing it into primitives (points or Gaussians), transforming them to screen space, and rasterizing them as 2D footprints (splats) that are accumulated via alpha blending. It differs from ray-marching methods by leveraging standard GPU rasterization hardware for high-performance, real-time rendering, and from pure screen-space quad methods by explicitly managing primitive-to-pixel sorting and blending to handle transparency and depth complexity correctly. The pipeline processes a set of volumetric primitives to produce a 2D image. It consists of projection, rasterization of attributes, sorting, and compositing. Inputs: C: Camera model (intrinsic and extrinsic parameters). P: Point positions (3D coordinates). A: Opacities and features (per-primitive attributes). F: Feature data (e.g., color, normal) associated with splats. Output: I: Rendered image (2D pixel buffer). Primitives: Defined by position \mathbf{p}k, opacity \alphak, and features \mathbf{f}k. Splat Attributes: After rasterization, each pixel may receive multiple splat contributions. These are stored as: A': Rasterized attributes (position, opacity, features) mapped to screen space. K: Keys (pixel coordinates or tile indices) identifying which pixel each splat contributes to. N: Counts (number of splats per pixel). L: Exclusive sum of counts, used to compute starting indices for sorting and blending. 1. Project and Cull: Transform primitive positions from world space to clip space using the camera model C. Cull primitives that are outside the view frustum or behind the camera. P' \leftarrow \text{PROJECTANDCULL}(P, C) 2. Bilinear Splatting: Rasterize the projected primitives onto the screen. For each primitive, compute its contribution to nearby pixels using a bilinear or Gaussian footprint. Compute the screen-space attributes A', the pixel keys K, and the splat counts N per pixel. A', K, N \leftarrow \text{BILINEARSPLATTING}(P', A) 3. Exclusive Sum: Compute the exclusive prefix sum of the counts N to determine the starting index in the sorted output array for each pixel's splats. This allows for efficient parallel sorting and blending. L \leftarrow \text{EXCLUSIVESUM}(N) 4. Radix Sort: Sort the splats based on their keys K and their depth (or sort order) using the exclusive sums L as offsets. This groups splats by pixel and orders them for correct alpha blending (typically front-to-back). \text{RADIXSORTPAIRS}(K, L) 5. Blend Sorted Splats: Iterate through the sorted splats. For each pixel, accumulate the color and opacity using alpha blending. The blending order is determined by the sorted depth of the splats. I \leftarrow \text{BLENDSORTEDSPLATS}(A', F, L, N) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RASTERIZE(C, P, A, F): # Step 1: Project and cull primitives Pprime = PROJECTANDCULL(P, C) # Step 2: Rasterize primitives to screen, computing attributes, keys, and counts Aprime, K, N = BILINEARSPLATTING(Pprime, A) # Step 3: Compute exclusive sum of counts to determine start indices L = EXCLUSIVESUM(N) # Step 4: Sort splats by pixel key and depth using radix sort # K contains pixel indices, L contains start indices for each pixel's splats RADIXSORTPAIRS(K, L) # Step 5: Blend sorted splats per pixel to form the final image I = BLENDSORTEDSPLATS(Aprime, F, L, N) return I Sorting Order: Correct alpha blending requires splats to be sorted front-to-back relative to the camera. The RADIXSORTPAIRS step must handle depth comparison correctly, especially for anisotropic splats where the depth varies across the footprint. Precision: Floating-point precision in position and depth calculations can affect culling and sorting accuracy, particularly for distant or small primitives. Empty Pixels: Pixels with no splats should be initialized to a background color or transparent value. The tile-based Gaussian rasterizer is a GPU-accelerated rendering method for 3D Gaussian splats that pre-sorts primitives across the entire image to enable approximate alpha-blending for anisotropic splats. It distinguishes itself from previous per-pixel sorting approaches by eliminating hard limits on the number of blended primitives receiving gradient updates, thereby supporting arbitrary depth complexity without scene-specific hyperparameter tuning. Rendering a 4D volume by slicing it into multiple 3D cross-sections, rendering each slice to a texture, and then blending these textures together to form a 3D voxel cloud image. Steps: Render each 3D cross-section slice to a frame buffer (texture). Use Alpha Blending to overlay the textures of the slices. Render one layer, project it to the 2D canvas, and reuse the frame buffer texture for the next layer to save memory. Formula: Opacity can be adjusted per pixel based on the angle between the view direction and the slice normal, following exponential decay. Light passing through layers at a steep angle travels a longer distance and should be more attenuated (less transparent). Parameters: Opacity can be assigned per object (e.g., ground/sky transparent, objects opaque) to improve visibility. Slicing direction is typically aligned with coordinate axes; arbitrary directions are possible but may incur high computational overhead. A renderer that takes point clouds, rasterizes them to fragments, computes splat weights based on a quadratic form Q and a scaler, and composites the point colors into an image with an occupancy mask. Steps: 1. Rasterize the input point clouds using the configured rasterizer to obtain fragments and filtered point clouds. 2. Permute the weights tensor from shape (N, H, W, C) to (N, C, H, W) to align with the compositor's expected input format. 3. Extract point colors from the filtered point clouds, permute from (C, N) to (N, C), and clamp values to [0, 1]. 4. Extract the fragment indices (idx), permute from (N, H, W, C) to (N, C, H, W), and convert to long integer type. 5. Composite the image using either a custom compositor or the default weightedsum function from pytorch3d, passing fragment indices, weights, and point colors. 6. Permute the resulting image tensor from (N, C, H, W) to (N, H, W, C) and concatenate the occupancy mask (fragments.occupancy) as an additional channel. Formula: Weights are computed as w = \exp(-0.5 \cdot Q) \cdot \text{scaler}, where Q is the quadratic form from fragments.qvalue and scaler is from fragments.scaler. The weights are then clamped to [0, 2000]. Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step, which is O(N \log N) or O(N) with radix sort, where N is the number of primitives. Rasterization is O(N) if the footprint size is bounded. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for primitive attributes, sorted splat lists, and frame buffers. The tile-based variant reduces memory pressure by processing tiles independently. Performance: Enables real-time rendering on modern GPUs due to hardware acceleration of rasterization and sorting. Strengths: High performance, supports arbitrary depth complexity, and is compatible with standard graphics APIs. Limitations: Sorting can be expensive for very high primitive counts. Anisotropic splats require careful handling of depth sorting to avoid artifacts. The rasterization-based splatting pipeline has evolved from early point-based rendering techniques to support complex volumetric and neural representations. The INPC method (Implicit Neural Point Clouds) formalized this pipeline for radiance field rendering, integrating view-specific sampling and efficient GPU-based sorting and blending. The 4D voxel cloud rendering approach extends these concepts to higher-dimensional data by slicing and blending. Surface splatting techniques have been adapted for point cloud rendering and diffusion models, emphasizing efficient weight computation and compositing.
