name: Tile-based Gaussian Rasterizer
head: Fast Differentiable Rasterizer for Gaussians
body: The tile-based Gaussian rasterizer is a GPU-accelerated rendering method for 3D Gaussian splats that pre-sorts primitives across the entire image to enable approximate alpha-blending for anisotropic splats. It distinguishes itself from previous per-pixel sorting approaches by eliminating hard limits on the number of blended primitives receiving gradient updates, thereby supporting arbitrary depth complexity without scene-specific hyperparameter tuning. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (mean, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), camera projection matrices, image resolution. Outputs: Final color buffer, depth buffer, and gradient tensors for training. Data Structures: Gaussian Instances: Each Gaussian is instantiated once per overlapping tile. Key: A composite key combining view-space depth and tile ID, used for sorting. Tile Ranges: For each tile, the start and end indices in the sorted global Gaussian array. Shared Memory: Used by thread blocks to load packets of Gaussians for a tile. Per-Pixel State: Stores the final accumulated opacity \alpha{final} and the depth of the last contributing point z{last} for backward pass optimization. Parameters: Tile size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Culling threshold: 99% confidence interval of the Gaussian. Alpha saturation threshold: \alpha \geq 1.0 (or a value very close to 1, e.g., 1 - \epsilon). Steps: 1. Culling: Reject Gaussians whose 99% confidence interval does not intersect the view frustum. Apply a guard band to trivially reject Gaussians with means close to the near plane or far outside the view frustum to prevent unstable 2D covariance computation. 2. Instantiation and Key Assignment: For each surviving Gaussian, determine the set of tiles it overlaps. Instantiate one Gaussian object per overlapping tile. Assign each instance a key K = (\text{tile\ID}, \text{view\space\depth}). 3. Sorting: Perform a single global radix sort on all Gaussian instances based on their keys K. This produces a globally depth-sorted list of Gaussian instances per tile. 4. Tile Range Identification: Identify the start and end indices in the sorted array for each tile. 5. Forward Rasterization (Per Tile): Launch one thread block per tile. Collaboratively load packets of Gaussians from global memory into shared memory. For each pixel (u, v) in the tile: Initialize accumulated color C = 0 and accumulated opacity \alpha = 0. Traverse the tile's Gaussian list front-to-back. For each Gaussian, compute its 2D projection and coverage at (u, v). Compute the Gaussian's alpha \alphag and color Cg. Update accumulation: \alpha{new} = \alpha + \alphag (1 - \alpha) C{new} = C + Cg \alphag (1 - \alpha) Store the current \alpha{new} as the final accumulated opacity for this pixel if it is the last contributing point. Store the depth zg of the current Gaussian if it contributes to the color (i.e., \alphag > 0 and \alpha{new} > \alpha). If \alpha{new} \geq 1.0 (saturation), stop processing further Gaussians for this pixel. After processing all pixels, check if all pixels in the tile have saturated. If so, terminate tile processing early. 6. Backward Pass (Gradient Computation): Traverse the tile's Gaussian list back-to-front. Start from the last point that affected any pixel in the tile. Collaboratively load points into shared memory. For each pixel (u, v): Retrieve the final accumulated opacity \alpha{final} and the depth of the last contributing point z{last} from the forward pass. If the current Gaussian's depth zg > z{last}, skip overlap testing and processing. Otherwise, perform expensive overlap testing and compute gradients. Recover intermediate accumulated opacity \alpha{prev} for gradient computation by dividing the final accumulated opacity by the current point's alpha: \alpha{prev} = \frac{\alpha{final}}{\alphag} This allows computation of the gradient with respect to the current Gaussian's contribution without storing the full history of opacities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilebasedgaussianrasterize(gaussians, camera, tilesize=16): # 1. Culling validgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if not intersectsviewfrustum(g, camera, threshold=0.99): continue if isoutsideguardband(g, camera): continue validgaussians.append(g) # 2. Instantiation and Key Assignment instances = [] for g in validgaussians: tiles = getoverlappingtiles(g, camera, imagedims) for t in tiles: key = (t.id, g.viewspacedepth) instances.append({ 'gaussian': g, 'tileid': t.id, 'key': key, 'starttileidx': t.startidx, # Placeholder for logic 'endtileidx': t.endidx }) # 3. Sorting # Sort instances by key (tileid, then depth) instances.sort(key=lambda x: x['key']) # 4. Tile Ranges tileranges = {} for i, inst in enumerate(instances): tid = inst['tileid'] if tid not in tileranges: tileranges[tid] = {'start': i, 'end': i} else: tileranges[tid]['end'] = i # 5. Forward Rasterization colorbuffer = zeros(imagedims) alphabuffer = zeros(imagedims) lastcontribdepth = zeros(imagedims) for tid, rangeinfo in tileranges.items(): startidx = rangeinfo['start'] endidx = rangeinfo['end'] tilegaussians = instances[startidx:endidx+1] # Launch thread block for tile # Shared memory allocation for tilegaussians packets for y in range(tid.y tilesize, (tid.y + 1) tilesize): for x in range(tid.x tilesize, (tid.x + 1) tilesize): if y >= imagedims.height or x >= imagedims.width: continue acccolor = 0.0 accalpha = 0.0 lastz = -1.0 for ginst in tilegaussians: g = ginst['gaussian'] # Project and compute coverage alphag, colorg, zg = projectandsample(g, x, y, camera) if alphag <= 0: continue newalpha = accalpha + alphag (1.0 - accalpha) newcolor = acccolor + colorg alphag (1.0 - accalpha) accalpha = newalpha acccolor = newcolor if accalpha > accalphaprev: # Contribution detected lastz = zg if accalpha >= 1.0: break colorbuffer[y, x] = acccolor alphabuffer[y, x] = accalpha lastcontribdepth[y, x] = lastz return colorbuffer, alphabuffer, lastcontribdepth def backwardpass(gaussians, instances, tileranges, lastcontribdepth, alphabuffer, tilesize=16): # 6. Backward Pass for tid, rangeinfo in tileranges.items(): startidx = rangeinfo['start'] endidx = rangeinfo['end'] tilegaussians = instances[startidx:endidx+1] # Traverse back-to-front for ginst in reversed(tilegaussians): g = ginst['gaussian'] zg = g.viewspacedepth # Check if this Gaussian could have contributed to any pixel in the tile # Optimization: only process if depth <= lastcontribdepth for relevant pixels # This requires checking per-pixel or using a tile-level bound for y in range(tid.y tilesize, (tid.y + 1) tilesize): for x in range(tid.x tilesize, (tid.x + 1) tilesize): if y >= imagedims.height or x >= imagedims.width: continue zlast = lastcontribdepth[y, x] alphafinal = alphabuffer[y, x] if zg > zlast: continue # Compute gradients # Recover intermediate opacity alphag, colorg, = projectandsample(g, x, y, camera) if alphag > 0: alphaprev = alphafinal / alphag # Compute gradients w.r.t. Gaussian parameters using alphaprev computegradients(g, alphaprev, alphafinal, colorg) Time Complexity: Dominated by the global radix sort O(N \log N) where N is the number of Gaussian instances. Rasterization is O(T \cdot P) where T is the number of tiles and P is the number of pixels per tile, but early termination reduces effective complexity for saturated pixels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian instances and sorted arrays. Constant overhead per pixel for storing final opacity and last contributing depth. Performance: Enables real-time rendering and efficient training on GPUs. Avoids the memory overhead of storing per-pixel lists of blended points. Strengths: Handles arbitrary depth complexity; no hard limit on gradient updates; efficient use of GPU parallelism via tile-based processing and shared memory. Limitations: Alpha-blending is approximate due to pre-sorting; artifacts may appear in highly complex scenes with significant depth interleaving within a tile, though these are negligible in converged scenes. When to use: Real-time rendering and training of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. When not to use: Applications requiring exact per-pixel depth sorting for alpha-blending where visual fidelity is critical over performance. The tile-based Gaussian rasterizer was introduced in "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering" by Kerbl et al.. It builds on software rasterization approaches by Lassner and Zollhofer and addresses limitations in previous alpha-blending solutions by Kopanas et al.. The method was designed to enable efficient backpropagation over an arbitrary number of blended Gaussians with low additional memory consumption. 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering [pdf], https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/3dgaussiansplattinglow.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-View Point Splatting
head: deferred blending multi-view splatting, single-pass multi-view point splatting
body: Multi-View Point Splatting is a rendering algorithm designed for auto-stereoscopic displays that generates N simultaneous perspective views in a single GPU rendering pass. It solves the linear performance degradation (N \times t) and memory overhead associated with standard multi-pass rendering by calculating view-specific intersections on a per-fragment basis. Unlike conventional approaches that render N full-resolution frame buffers and combine them via masking, this method exploits GPU programmability to interleave views directly into the final spatial image, supporting full resolution without sub-resolution artifacts. The method renders point splats (typically Gaussian or disk primitives) once per frame. For each fragment generated by the rasterizer, the shader calculates the intersection with the splat for each required view zone. In systems using wavelength-selective filters, the Red, Green, and Blue sub-pixels correspond to three different view zones, requiring three distinct intersection calculations per fragment. Inputs: Point set S: A collection of point samples \mathbf{p}i with associated properties (position, normal \mathbf{n}i, radius ri, density/color). Display parameters: Number of views N, focal distance fd, maximal view eccentricity vd, and horizontal LCD panel resolution m. Camera parameters: View matrices for the N virtual cameras, positioned to create off-axis asymmetric sheared view frusta with parallel view directions. Outputs: A single spatial image buffer where pixels are interleaved to form view zones for the auto-stereoscopic display. The point set S is stored as a buffer of primitives. Each primitive i contains: \mathbf{p}i: 3D position vector (x, y, z). \mathbf{n}i: Normal vector. ri: Projected radius in screen space (or object space, transformed later). Color/Density attributes. 1. Calculate Covering Quad: For each splat, compute an enlarged quadrilateral in screen space that covers the splat's projection across all N views. This accounts for parallax shifts. Determine the horizontal offset off required to cover the worst-case orientation where the splat normal \mathbf{n} is orthogonal to the focal and camera planes. Calculate offset using the formula: off = vd \cdot (d - fd) \cdot d^{-1} Where d is the depth of the splat (distance from camera), fd is the focal distance, and vd is the maximal view eccentricity. The quad corners \mathbf{q} are defined by extending the projected splat radius r horizontally by off and vertically by the projected height. The horizontal extent includes the parallax shift term vd \cdot (\mathbf{p}.z \cdot fd^{-1}). Note: The source provides the start of the corner formula but cuts off. The vertical extent is simply the projected height of the splat. The horizontal extent is p.x \pm (r + off + \text{parallax term}). 2. Rasterization with Per-Fragment View Calculation: Rasterize the enlarged quads. For each fragment covered by a quad: Identify which view zone the fragment belongs to. For wavelength-selective displays, the view index V is determined by the sub-pixel component (R, G, or B). Calculate the intersection of the fragment's screen position with the splat for the specific view V. This involves transforming the splat center \mathbf{p} and the fragment position into the view space of camera V. Compute the contribution (color/density) based on the splat kernel (e.g., Gaussian) evaluated at the intersection point for view V. 3. Deferred Blending: Accumulate contributions from all overlapping splats for the specific view zone of the current fragment using alpha blending. Since the geometry is processed once, the \epsilon-z-buffering (fuzzy visibility test) must handle occlusion across the different view perspectives. 4. Image Composition: The final image is written directly to the frame buffer. No separate masking or compositing pass is required because the view assignment is handled during the per-fragment intersection calculation. Horizontal Display Resolution: For wavelength-selective filter arrays, the effective horizontal resolution X{Res} for N views is: X{Res} = \frac{m}{N} \cdot 3 Where m is the horizontal pixel resolution of the LCD panel. Splat Covering Offset: off = vd \cdot \frac{d - fd}{d} Where: vd: Maximal view eccentricity. d: Depth of the splat. fd: Focal distance. Quad Corners (Horizontal): \mathbf{q}.x = \mathbf{p}.x \pm \left( r + vd \cdot \frac{\mathbf{p}.z}{fd} + off \right) Note: The source formula is incomplete: \mathbf{q}.x = (\mathbf{p}.x \pm (r + vd \cdot (\mathbf{p}.z \cdot fd^{-1}).... The term vd \cdot (\mathbf{p}.z \cdot fd^{-1}) represents the parallax shift. The offset off is added to ensure coverage of the worst-case orientation. N: Number of views (view zones). Typical values depend on the display (e.g., N=8 in benchmarks). K: Sub-pixel resolution constant. K=3 for RGB wavelength-selective views. fd: Focal distance, matching the focal plane of the auto-stereoscopic display. vd: Maximal view eccentricity, used to calculate the horizontal offset. Parallax Handling: For multiple viewpoints, projections of the same pixel may not lie on the same surface element. The algorithm must correctly handle splat intersections per view to avoid artifacts. Filter Arrays: The method is optimized for wavelength-selective filters. For lenticular sheets (no sub-pixel view resolution), the performance advantage increases by up to a factor of three compared to conventional rendering, but the constant K changes (likely K=1 or requires different handling). Quad Size: The enlarged quad must be large enough to cover the splat's movement across all views. Failure to account for the worst-case orientation (normal orthogonal to focal plane) will result in missing pixels at the edges of view zones. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. function RenderMultiViewSplat(splat): # Calculate the enlarged covering quad for all N views # d is the depth of the splat center in camera space d = splat.position.z # Calculate horizontal offset for worst-case parallax coverage # vd: maximal view eccentricity, fd: focal distance off = vd (d - fd) / d # Parallax shift term based on splat depth and focal distance parallaxshift = vd (splat.position.z / fd) # Base projected radius r (computed from MVP matrix and splat radius) r = splat.projectedradius # Define quad corners in screen space # Horizontal extent covers all view zones left = splat.screenx - (r + off + parallaxshift) right = splat.screenx + (r + off + parallaxshift) # Vertical extent covers the splat height (h) top = splat.screeny + splat.screenheight / 2 bottom = splat.screeny - splat.screenheight / 2 # Output quad vertices to rasterizer return Quad(left, top, right, bottom) function FragmentShader(fragmentpos, fragmentcolorchannel): # fragmentcolorchannel identifies the view zone (e.g., 0 for R, 1 for G, 2 for B) # For wavelength-selective displays, this maps to a specific view index V # Determine the view index V based on the sub-pixel channel # Assuming N views and 3 channels, mapping logic depends on display layout # Simplified: V = fragmentcolorchannel (for K=3 case) V = fragmentcolorchannel # Get the current splat being rasterized splat = GetActiveSplat() # Transform splat center and fragment position to View V's space # This accounts for the different camera positions for each view viewmatrixV = GetViewMatrix(V) splatcenterV = viewmatrixV splat.position fragposV = viewmatrixV fragmentpos # Calculate the distance from the fragment to the splat center in View V # This determines the kernel weight for this specific view dx = fragposV.x - splatcenterV.x dy = fragposV.y - splatcenterV.y # Evaluate splat kernel (e.g., Gaussian) # sigma is the splat's standard deviation in view space weight = exp(-(dxdx + dydy) / (2 sigmasigma)) # Apply alpha blending with existing buffer content # This handles the deferred blending and occlusion (epsilon-z-buffering) currentalpha = FrameBuffer[fragmentpos].alpha newalpha = weight splat.alpha # Blend color FrameBuffer[fragmentpos].color = Blend(currentalpha, FrameBuffer[fragmentpos].color, newalpha, weight splat.color) FrameBuffer[fragmentpos].alpha = currentalpha + newalpha (1 - currentalpha) Extends the basic multi-view approach by adding fill-rate filtering to handle high-density splatting scenarios, reducing overdraw Link. Discusses the general compositing order (back-to-front) required for correct alpha blending, which is implicitly handled in the per-fragment deferred blending of this method Link. Details the mathematical definition of the splat shape (Gaussian, disk) used in the intersection calculation Link. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot t), where t is the time for a single mono-view rendering pass and K is the sub-pixel resolution constant (typically 3 for RGB). This is independent of the number of views N. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for frame buffers compared to single-view rendering, as it avoids storing N full-resolution buffers. Performance: Benchmarks for N=8 views and a 512 \times 512 window show: Balljoint (137k points): 18 fps. Female (303k points): 15 fps. Dragon (1,100k points): 10 fps. Strengths: Eliminates the N-fold cost of multi-pass rendering. Supports full resolution without sub-resolution artifacts. No post-processing masking or compositing passes required. Limitations: Requires programmable GPUs (fragment shaders). Performance advantage is most significant for large N and large datasets where geometry processing is the bottleneck. Relies on specific display hardware (auto-stereoscopic with wavelength-selective filters or lenticular sheets). The method was introduced by Thomas Hübner, Yanci Zhang, and Renato Pajarola from the Visualization and MultiMedia Lab at the University of Zürich. It addresses the limitations of existing auto-stereoscopic libraries like the Interactive Stereo Library (ISL) from SGI, which rendered N views individually into N frame buffers, incurring N \times t cost and requiring masking. The work builds on point splatting techniques described by Pfister et al.. Multi-view point splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/1174429.1174479, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Slice-by-Slice (Sheet Buffer) Splatting
head: Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffer Compositing, Muller sheet-buffer, Sheet Buffer Splatting, Sheet-Buffer Method, slice-based composition
body: Slice-by-Slice (Sheet Buffer) Splatting is a volume rendering optimization that organizes splats into cache-sheets aligned parallel to the volume face most closely parallel to the image plane, then composites these sheets slice-by-slice. It sets itself apart from ray-casting and screen-quad methods by compositing splats into aligned sheet buffers rather than sampling along rays or rendering full-screen quads, trading the "sparkling" of per-splat compositing for "popping" artifacts when the view crosses 45° relative to the data axes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset (regular grid), camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix), transfer function. Output: 2D image (color and alpha buffer). Data Structures: 1. Sheet Buffer: A 2D array (texture or render target) matching the screen resolution that accumulates the weighted contributions of splats belonging to a specific depth slice. 2. Cache Image: The current accumulated result of composited slices. 3. Splat List: A list of transformed splats, typically sorted or bucketed by their depth coordinate along the alignment axis. Method Steps: 1. Sheet Alignment: Determine the volume axis (x, y, or z) most parallel to the image plane. Switch the compositing axis at 45° to maintain alignment with the view. 2. Splat Transformation: Transform splat centers from volume space to screen space. Compute new positions using interpolation so that they lie on the slice, since the buffer does not correspond to voxel positions in space. 3. Bucketing: Assign each splat to a specific sheet buffer corresponding to its depth slice index k along the alignment axis. 4. Rasterization: Rasterize all splats assigned to sheet k onto the sheet buffer. The contribution of a voxel D to a screen point (x,y) is determined by the footprint function F(x,y), which is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view direction: F(x,y) = \int h(x-xD, y-yD, z) \, dz The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density: P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) where \text{weight}(x,y) = F(x-xD, y-yD). 5. Compositing: Traverse the sheet buffers in depth order (back-to-front for opacity). For each sheet buffer: Composite the sheet buffer into the cache image using alpha blending. This step effectively adds voxel contributions slice-by-slice. Whenever a sheet buffer has received all contributions, it is composited with the current image and the next slice is processed. 6. Output: The cache image is the final rendered image. Parameters: Switching Threshold: The view angle at which the alignment axis switches (typically 45°). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: Occur when the orientation of the sheets suddenly changes, specifically when the view angle crosses the 45-degree switching threshold (e.g., from 44.7° to 45.2°). Interpolation: Since the sheet buffer does not correspond directly to voxel positions in space, new positions for splats must be computed using interpolation to lie on the slice. Orthographic vs. Perspective: The method works best for orthographic views because it requires only a single footprint table and reconstruction kernel, which is constant except for screen space offset. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def slicebyslicesplatting(volume, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): # 1. Determine alignment axis based on camera view direction # Align with volume axis most parallel to image plane viewdir = normalize(camera.viewmatrix[2][:3]) axes = [vec(1,0,0), vec(0,1,0), vec(0,0,1)] alignmentaxis = max(axes, key=lambda a: abs(dot(viewdir, a))) # 2. Initialize sheet buffers and cache image # Sheet buffers are 2D arrays matching screen resolution numslices = volume.shape[alignmentaxis] sheetbuffers = [createzero2darray(imagewidth, imageheight) for in range(numslices)] cacheimage = createzero2darray(imagewidth, imageheight) # 3. Transform and bucket splats splats = transformsplats(volume, camera) bucketsplatsintosheets(splats, sheetbuffers, alignmentaxis) # 4. Rasterize splats into sheet buffers for k, sheet in enumerate(sheetbuffers): clearsheet(sheet) for splat in sheet.splats: # Compute footprint F(x,y) and weight footprint = computefootprint(splat.kernel, splat.center, camera) weight = footprint.evaluate(splat.centerscreen) color = splat.color weight # Rasterize onto sheet buffer rasterizesplat(sheet, splat, color) # 5. Composite sheets into cache image # Traverse in depth order (back-to-front for standard alpha blending) sortedindices = sortsheetsbydepth(sheetbuffers, alignmentaxis, camera) for k in sortedindices: compositesheetintoimage(sheetbuffers[k], cacheimage) return cacheimage def determinealignmentaxis(viewmatrix): # Returns 'x', 'y', or 'z' based on which volume axis is most parallel to the image plane viewdir = normalize(viewmatrix[2][:3]) axes = [vec(1,0,0), vec(0,1,0), vec(0,0,1)] return ['x', 'y', 'z'][max(range(3), key=lambda i: abs(dot(viewdir, axes[i])))] def transformsplats(volume, camera): # Applies MVP matrix to volume centers, computes screen positions and projected kernel parameters splats = [] for voxel in volume: center3d = voxel.position center4d = vec4(center3d, 1.0) projected = camera.mvpmatrix @ center4d centerscreen = projected.xy / projected.w kernel = projectkernel(voxel.kernel, camera) splats.append({'center': center3d, 'centerscreen': centerscreen, 'kernel': kernel, 'color': voxel.color}) return splats def bucketsplatsintosheets(splats, sheetbuffers, axis): # Assigns each splat to sheetbuffers[depthindex] along the chosen axis for splat in splats: depthidx = int(round(splat['center'][axis] / volume.voxelsize[axis])) if 0 <= depthidx < len(sheetbuffers): sheetbuffers[depthidx].splats.append(splat) def computefootprint(kernel, center, camera): # Computes 2D footprint function F(x,y) by integrating 3D kernel along view direction # For orthographic views, footprint is constant per kernel type return kernel.integratealongview(camera.projectiontype) def rasterizesplat(sheet, splat, color): # Rasterizes the footprint of the splat onto the 2D sheet buffer bounds = splat.kernel.boundingbox2d(splat['centerscreen']) for y in range(bounds.miny, bounds.maxy): for x in range(bounds.minx, bounds.maxx): if 0 <= x < sheet.width and 0 <= y < sheet.height: alpha = splat.kernel.evaluate(vec2(x, y) - splat['centerscreen']) sheet[y, x] = blend(sheet[y, x], color, alpha) def sortsheetsbydepth(sheets, axis, camera): # Returns indices of sheets sorted back-to-front relative to view sheetdepths = [(i, sheet.splats[0]['center'][axis] if sheet.splats else 0) for i, sheet in enumerate(sheets)] return [idx for idx, in sorted(sheetdepths, key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)] def compositesheetintoimage(sheet, cacheimage): # Blends the accumulated sheet buffer into the main cache image for y in range(sheet.height): for x in range(sheet.width): pixelcolor, pixelalpha = sheet[y, x] cacheimage[y, x] = blend(cacheimage[y, x], (pixelcolor, pixelalpha), 1.0) def blend(src, dst, alpha): # Standard alpha compositing: out = src (1 - alpha) + dst alpha return src (1.0 - alpha) + dst alpha Image-Aligned Sheet-Buffer Compositing is a variant that eliminates "popping" artifacts by aligning the sheet buffer compositing axis with the image plane, rather than the volume axes. Unlike standard axis-aligned sheet buffers, which suffer from discontinuities when the viewing angle crosses 45° relative to the data axes, this method slices interpolation kernels into sections parallel to the image plane. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Slice-by-Slice (Sheet Buffer) Splatting, by using image-aligned cutting planes and alpha-compositing kernel sections to ensure smooth color transitions across varying optical properties and resolutions. However, it has a high computational cost and requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point. Sheet-based Splatting, proposed by Westover, accumulates splats onto a 2D sheet aligned with the volume axis most parallel to the view plane, then composites the sheets in depth order into the image with a matting operation. It is a foundational concept for the sheet-buffer approach, improving image quality over simple splat-every-sample composition by handling depth ordering more effectively. Performance: Slice-based composition produces brighter images due to correct visibility determination but is slower than splat-every-sample composition because it avoids per-slice additions in the other method. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated, good image quality compared to simple splatting, avoids sparkling artifacts. Limitations: Popping artifacts at 45° view angles, high computational cost for image-aligned variants, best suited for orthographic views. When to use: When real-time performance is needed and the view angle is stable or orthographic. When not to use: When the view angle frequently crosses 45° thresholds and popping artifacts are unacceptable. The sheet-buffer method was proposed by Müller and Yagel [Müller96] and Müller [Müller98] as an optimization for CPU-based volume rendering. It builds on Westover's earlier work on sheet-based accumulation. Müller and Crawfis later proposed image-aligned kernel-slicing to mitigate popping artifacts, though this increased computational cost. name: Image-Aligned Sheet-Buffer Compositing
body: Image-aligned sheet-buffer compositing is a volume rendering technique that eliminates popping artifacts by aligning compositing sheets with the image plane regardless of viewing direction. Unlike Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, which organizes voxels into fixed volume slices, this method advances a slab across the volume, slicing kernels into sections and projecting them into image-aligned sheet buffers. Inputs: Volume data, viewing parameters, sheet buffer resolution. Outputs: Final composited image. Data Structures: Sheet Buffer: A 2D buffer aligned with the image plane, storing accumulated color and opacity for each pixel. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. Compositing Buffer: The final image buffer where sheet buffers are composited. Steps: 1. Slab Advancement: Advance a slab across the volume so that the slab cuts kernels into sections. 2. Footprint Mapping: For each voxel or point within the current slab, perform footprint mapping as usual. This requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point to account for the intersection of the kernel with the image-aligned sheet. 3. Kernel Section Addition: Add the resulting kernel sections into the sheet buffer. 4. Compositing: Composite the sheet buffers into the final image. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: Axis-aligned methods suffer from popping when the viewing angle crosses thresholds near 45° (e.g., 44.7° vs 45.2°). Image-aligned methods eliminate this by aligning with the image plane. Computational Cost: Requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point, increasing computational expense. A variant that aligns compositing sheets with the image plane regardless of viewing direction, eliminating popping artifacts. It sets itself apart from axis-aligned sheet-buffered splatting by advancing a slab across the volume rather than using fixed volume slices. Choose it when accurate voxel field reconstruction and smooth anti-aliasing are required, accepting higher computational cost due to multiple splatting of voxels. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts. Limitations: Higher computational expense due to multiple splatting of individual voxels. Requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point. When to use: Ideal for rendering where popping artifacts must be avoided. When not to use: When computational resources are limited. Originated from work by Mueller ('98) on volumetric points and sheet buffers. The method addresses limitations of axis-aligned splatting, such as popping artifacts observed at specific viewing angles (e.g., 44.7° vs 45.2°). name: Image-aligned Splatting
head: Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, Image-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, Image-aligned Splatting with Alpha Composition, Kernel section composition, Mueller 76, Sheet-bucket splatting, slab-based splatting
body: Image-aligned splatting is a volume rendering technique that eliminates color bleeding and popping artifacts by aligning the compositing sheet with the image plane at all times, regardless of the viewing direction. Unlike its sibling Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, which organizes voxels into fixed volume slices parallel to the viewing axis, image-aligned splatting advances a slab across the volume, slicing and projecting all intersecting kernels into sheet buffers. This approach provides the most accurate reconstruction of the voxel field prior to compositing and produces smoother images with better anti-aliasing characteristics than raycasting, though at a higher computational cost due to multiple splatting of voxels. Inputs: Volume dataset containing density, color, and opacity fields. Viewing parameters including viewpoint, direction, and projection matrix. Slab width \Delta s. Kernel base distribution and scaling factor. Outputs: Final composited image buffer. Data Structures: 1. Sheet Buffer: A 2D buffer aligned with the image plane, storing accumulated color C and opacity \alpha for the current slab. 2. Occlusion Map: A dynamically computed screen-space map used for early splat elimination, updated via convolution after each sheet composite. 3. Kernel Sections: Pre-integrated footprints of voxel kernels, stacked to form a single kernel representation. Steps: 1. Kernel Preparation: Compute kernel sections using a kernel base distribution and a scaling factor. Stack sections to form a single kernel representation. 2. Slab Advancement: Define a slab of width \Delta s aligned parallel to the image plane. 3. Voxel Selection and Transformation: Identify all voxel kernels that overlap the current slab. Transform the center of each relevant voxel into screen space. 4. Early Splat Elimination: Index the occlusion map using the transformed screen coordinates to test for visibility. If the voxel is occluded, skip it, noting that transformation is still required even if the voxel is culled. 5. Clipping and Projection: For visible voxels, clip the voxel kernels to the slab boundaries. Slice and project the intersecting kernels. 6. Sheet Buffer Accumulation: Sum the clipped kernels into the sheet buffer. All splats within a single sheet are added together; they are not composited within the sheet. 7. Sheet Composition: Composite the current sheet buffer with the previous accumulated result. 8. Occlusion Map Update: Perform a convolution operation on the occlusion map to update it based on the current sheet's contributions. This operation can be limited to buffer tiles that received splat contributions in the current slab to save time. 9. Iteration: Advance the slab across the volume and repeat steps 2–8 until the volume is fully processed. Formulas: The color, opacity, and feature terms are calculated as averages over the slab interval \Delta s: C\lambda(si) = \frac{\int{i\Delta s}^{(i+1)\Delta s} C\lambda(s) ds}{\Delta s} \alpha(si) = \frac{\int{i\Delta s}^{(i+1)\Delta s} \alpha(s) ds}{\Delta s} f(si) = \frac{\int{i\Delta s}^{(i+1)\Delta s} f(s) ds}{\Delta s} Where si represents the slab index, and C\lambda, \alpha, and f are the color, opacity, and feature values respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imagealignedsplatting(volume, viewparams, slabwidthdeltas, kernelbase, scalingfactor): # Initialize final composited image and opacity buffers finalimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] finalopacity = [[0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] # Initialize occlusion map for early splat elimination occlusionmap = [[0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] # Pre-compute kernel sections and stack them kernelsections = computekernelsections(kernelbase, scalingfactor) # Determine slab range along the view direction slabstart = volume.bounds.minz slabend = volume.bounds.maxz currentslabz = slabstart while currentslabz < slabend: slab = Slab(zmin=currentslabz, zmax=currentslabz + slabwidthdeltas) currentsheet = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] currentsheetopacity = [[0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] # Identify voxels intersecting the current slab for voxel in volume.voxels: if not voxel.intersectsslab(slab): continue # Transform voxel center to screen space screenpos = transformtoscreen(voxel.center, viewparams) # Early splat elimination: test visibility against occlusion map if not isvisible(screenpos, occlusionmap): continue # Clip kernel to slab boundaries and project clippedkernel = clipkerneltoslab(voxel.kernel, slab) rasterizefootprint(currentsheet, currentsheetopacity, clippedkernel, screenpos) # Composite current sheet with previous accumulated result compositesheetintoimage(finalimage, finalopacity, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity) # Update occlusion map via convolution on tiles with contributions updateocclusionmap(occlusionmap, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity) currentslabz += slabwidthdeltas return finalimage def computekernelsections(kernelbase, scalingfactor): # Returns a list of kernel sections with weights based on base distribution and scaling sections = [] for i in range(kernelbase.numsections): weight = kernelbase.basedistribution(i) scalingfactor sections.append(KernelSection(weight=weight, footprint=kernelbase.footprint)) return sections def transformtoscreen(voxelcenter, viewparams): # Standard perspective projection to screen coordinates x = viewparams.projmatrix[0][0] voxelcenter.x + viewparams.projmatrix[0][3] y = viewparams.projmatrix[1][1] voxelcenter.y + viewparams.projmatrix[1][3] return Point(x, y) def isvisible(screenpos, occlusionmap): # Checks if screen position exceeds occlusion threshold h, w = len(occlusionmap), len(occlusionmap[0]) y, x = int(screenpos.y), int(screenpos.x) if 0 <= y < h and 0 <= x < w: return occlusionmap[y][x] < 0.95 return True def clipkerneltoslab(kernel, slab): # Returns kernel scaled/weighted for slab intersection return Kernel(weight=kernel.weight slab.intersectionratio(kernel), footprint=kernel.footprint) def rasterizefootprint(sheet, sheetopacity, kernel, screenpos): # Additive accumulation within the sheet buffer h, w = len(sheet), len(sheet[0]) for dy, dx in kernel.footprintoffsets: y, x = int(screenpos.y + dy), int(screenpos.x + dx) if 0 <= y < h and 0 <= x < w: sheet[y][x][0] += kernel.weight kernel.color[0] sheet[y][x][1] += kernel.weight kernel.color[1] sheet[y][x][2] += kernel.weight kernel.color[2] sheetopacity[y][x][0] += kernel.weight def compositesheetintoimage(finalimage, finalopacity, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity): # Standard back-to-front alpha compositing between sheets h, w = len(finalimage), len(finalimage[0]) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): oc = currentsheetopacity[y][x][0] if oc <= 0.0: continue fc = currentsheet[y][x] fo = finalopacity[y][x][0] alpha = oc (1.0 - fo) finalimage[y][x][0] += fc[0] alpha finalimage[y][x][1] += fc[1] alpha finalimage[y][x][2] += fc[2] alpha finalopacity[y][x][0] += alpha def updateocclusionmap(occlusionmap, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity): # Convolve sheet opacity into occlusion map, limited to tiles with contributions h, w = len(occlusionmap), len(occlusionmap[0]) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): if currentsheetopacity[y][x][0] > 0.0: occlusionmap[y][x] = min(1.0, occlusionmap[y][x] + currentsheetopacity[y][x][0]) Parameters: \Delta s: Slab width. Typical values are not explicitly given, but it must be chosen to balance between aliasing reduction and computational cost. Kernel Base Distribution: Defines the shape of the splat kernel (e.g., Gaussian). Scaling Factor: Used to adjust kernel radius based on cutting plane distance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The integration over \Delta s assumes smooth variation within the slab. If \Delta s is too large, high-frequency details may be lost due to low-pass filtering. Classification: If data values (density) are splatted before classification, the original density is smoothed and accumulated, making classification an unsolved problem that aggravates the partial volume effect. Occlusion Map Cost: Early splat elimination requires transforming invisible voxels to screen space to determine occlusion, saving only the rasterization cost. Viewing Direction Switch: Aligning the compositing sheet with the image plane eliminates the popping artifacts caused by sudden switches to orthogonal slice stacks in axis-aligned methods. Time Complexity: Higher than axis-aligned sheet-buffered splatting because each voxel may be considered more than once (multiple splatting) as the slab advances. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for sheet buffers and a dynamically updated occlusion map. Performance: Slower than raycasting for datasets with a low number of non-contributing samples. Faster than raycasting for datasets with a small number of relevant voxels and sheet buffers. Strengths: Eliminates color bleeding and popping artifacts; provides accurate reconstruction of the voxel field; produces smoother images with better anti-aliasing due to z-averaged kernels and Gaussian filters. Limitations: More expensive due to multiple splatting of voxels; early splat elimination still requires transformation of occluded voxels; classification is problematic if density is splatted first. When to Use: Best suited for post-classified rendering where accurate density/gradient reconstruction is needed; beneficial for rotational angiography visualization. When Not to Use: Not ideal for datasets with many non-contributing samples where raycasting would be faster; avoid if pre-classification is required without density smoothing issues. Image-aligned splatting was introduced by Mueller (referred to as Mueller 76) to address the drawbacks of earlier axis-aligned sheet-buffered approaches, which suffered from severe brightness variations and did not allow variable DVRI interval distances. It builds on the concept of sheet-buffered compositing but aligns the compositing sheet with the image plane to ensure consistent visual quality regardless of viewing angle. The method utilizes analytical pre-integration of kernel slices and fast footprint rasterization for efficient projection. name: Image-Parallel Sheet Buffer Splatting
head: New sheet buffer-based splatting method, Slicing slab method, new image-parallel sheet-buffer method, slicing-slab splatting
body: Image-Parallel Sheet Buffer Splatting is a volume rendering algorithm that eliminates color popping artifacts inherent in traditional sheet-buffer splatting by maintaining sheet buffers parallel to the image plane regardless of camera orientation. Unlike its sibling Image-aligned Splatting, which aligns splats with image rows, this method accumulates pre-integrated kernel sections (slabs) within fixed-width slicing slabs, approximating the discrete volume rendering integral more closely by compositing kernel parts along the viewing axis rather than adding entire voxel contributions at once. Inputs: Volume dataset with voxel values and opacities. Camera position and orientation. Splatting kernel (e.g., Gaussian). Slab width parameter w{slab} (typically 1.0 voxel units). Outputs: Final composited image. Data Structures: 1. Pre-integrated Kernel Sections Array: An array of 128 overlapping, pre-integrated kernel sections. Spacing \Delta s = (\text{kernel-Extent} + w{slab}) / 128. Each section represents a slab of thickness w{slab} integrated against the kernel function f(r) = 0.446 \cdot e^{-2.0 \cdot r^2}. The overlapping kernels sum to 1.0 in a unity volume. 2. Sheet Buffer: A 2D buffer parallel to the image plane, accumulating color and opacity contributions. 3. Relevant Voxel List (Lr): A list of voxels intersecting the current view frustum, sorted by distance from the viewing plane. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Compute the array of 128 pre-integrated kernel sections using the Gaussian kernel f(r). If using thick slabs for performance, normalize the footprint tables to correct for intensity differences between adding and compositing operations. For a thick slab composed of two thin slabs with section integrals hf (front) and hb (back), and voxel opacity \alphav, the normalization factor subtracted from the footprint is 2 hb hf + 0.5 hb^2 hf (assuming average \alphav=0.5). This allows building slab hierarchies with thicknesses of powers of 2. 2. Initialization: Define a slicing slab of fixed width w{slab} parallel to the image plane. Initialize the sheet buffer to zero. 3. Voxel Processing Loop: For each voxel in the relevant list Lr (sorted by distance from the viewing plane): Determine which pre-integrated kernel sections intersect the current slicing slab. Retrieve the appropriate pre-integrated kernel section(s) based on the voxel's position relative to the slab boundaries. Scale the kernel section by the voxel's color cv and opacity \alphav. Add the scaled contribution to the sheet buffer. Note: Shading is performed once per voxel, prior to or during this step, and does not repeat for each slab section. 4. Compositing: Once all voxels contributing to the current slicing slab have been processed, composite the accumulated sheet buffer into the cache image using front-to-back compositing. The compositing of two thin slabs with integrals hf and hb and voxel opacity \alphav results in color: c{comp} = \alphav cv (hb^2 - hb^2 \alphav hf + hf^2) Advance the slicing slab forward along the viewing ray. 5. Hardware Acceleration: Use 2D texture mapping hardware to project the footprint mappings and perform the compositing into the sheet buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageparallelsheetbuffersplatting(volume, camera, kernelextent, slabwidth=1.0): # 1. Pre-compute kernel sections numsections = 128 deltas = (kernelextent + slabwidth) / numsections kernelsections = precomputekernelsections(numsections, deltas, slabwidth) # 2. Initialize structures sheetbuffer = initializesheetbuffer(camera.resolution) cacheimage = initializecacheimage(camera.resolution) relevantvoxels = getrelevantvoxels(volume, camera) sortbydistance(relevantvoxels, camera.viewingplane) # 3. Define slicing slab range # The slab moves along the viewing ray. # In a full implementation, this loop iterates through depth. # Here we assume a single pass or simplified depth iteration for clarity. slabstart = camera.nearplane slabend = slabstart + slabwidth while slabend <= camera.farplane: clearsheetbuffer(sheetbuffer) for voxel in relevantvoxels: # Determine intersection of voxel kernel with current slab # This involves checking if the voxel's splat footprint overlaps the slab # and selecting the appropriate pre-integrated section # Calculate relative position of voxel within the slab context # to index into kernelsections sectionindex = getkernelsectionindex(voxel, slabstart, slabend, deltas) if sectionindex is valid: section = kernelsections[sectionindex] # Apply normalization if using thick slabs/hierarchies # Normalize factor: 2hbhf + 0.5hb^2hf # This is pre-computed and stored in the section or applied here # Scale by voxel properties contribution = voxel.color voxel.opacity section # Add to sheet buffer using 2D texture mapping hardware logic # In software simulation: addtosheetbuffer(sheetbuffer, voxel.screenposition, contribution) # Composite sheet buffer to cache image compositefronttoback(cacheimage, sheetbuffer) # Advance slab slabstart += slabwidth slabend += slabwidth return cacheimage def precomputekernelsections(numsections, deltas, slabwidth): sections = [] for i in range(numsections): # Compute integral of Gaussian kernel over the slab interval # f(r) = 0.446 exp(-2.0 r^2) # The integration is done radially or along the slab thickness # depending on the specific projection geometry. # The source states these are "pre-integrated kernel sections". integral = integrategaussianslab(i deltas, (i + 1) deltas, slabwidth) sections.append(integral) return sections Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Slab Width Selection: A slab width of 2.0 produces strong periodic artifacts because slice planes section kernels differently depending on their location on the cube face, causing bright regions where thick kernel sections are composited close to the image plane. A width of 0.5 shows minor improvements but increases cost. A width of 1.0 is recommended. Intensity Normalization: Thinner slabs produce darker images due to the inequivalence of adding and compositing operations. Normalization via footprint manipulation is required to maintain similar color intensity across different slab widths. Performance: Increasing the number of sheet buffers (or reducing slab width) increases the number of compositing operations proportionally to the number of footprint mappings per voxel. Time Complexity: The run time is dominated by polygon transform and rasterization operations. The added complexity relative to the traditional sheet-buffer method is determined by the factor \text{splatExtent} / \text{slabWidth}, which affects largely only the projection operations. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the sheet buffer, cache image, and the array of 128 pre-integrated kernel sections. Measured Performance: On an SGI Onyx with InfiniteReality engine: MRI-brain dataset (1.2M relevant voxels): 16.6s for the new method vs 4.2s for the traditional method (sorting took an extra 7s). Nerve dataset (0.9M relevant voxels): 2.8s for the new method vs 9.0s for the traditional method. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts; reduces color bleeding; provides smoother surface appearance; allows control of accuracy via slab width. Limitations: Slower than traditional sheet-buffer splatting for some datasets due to increased compositing operations; requires careful normalization for different slab widths. When to Use: When visual quality (absence of popping) is critical and hardware acceleration for texture mapping/compositing is available. When Not to Use: When maximum rendering speed is required and popping artifacts are acceptable or can be mitigated by other means. Origin: The method was introduced to address color popping artifacts in sheet-buffer-based splatting, which occur when the orientation of compositing sheets changes suddenly as the image screen becomes more parallel to another volume face. Development: It builds on the discretized volume rendering model, approximating the integral by slicing the volume into parallel images (slabs) and compositing them. It differs from Laur and Hanrahan’s scheme of increasing the Gaussian exponent by using footprint table manipulation. Usage: Used in animated viewing of medical datasets (MRI-brain, nerve cells) where smooth illumination changes are critical. The parent method that this technique refines. It uses sheet buffers aligned with volume axes, leading to popping artifacts. Image-Aligned Sheet-Buffer Compositing. A sibling method that aligns splats with image rows. It differs in how it handles the sheet buffer orientation and splat projection. Image-aligned Splatting. Eliminating Popping Artifacts in Sheet Buffer-Based Splatting, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/papers/pop.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting
head: Texture-Atlas Splatting
body: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting is a learned sparse scene representation that eliminates runtime neural network inference by baking view-independent high-frequency texture into a hardware-accelerated 2D texture atlas. It represents the scene as a sparse set of oriented 2D Beta kernels, separating low-frequency view-dependent appearance (stored per-surfel) from high-frequency spatial texture (stored in the atlas). This approach achieves 7–9× faster rendering than 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on common benchmarks by reducing overdraw via flat Beta kernels and replacing expensive ray-surfel intersection shaders with an exact rational reformulation. Inputs: A set of optimized 2D surfels (position \boldsymbol{\mu}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity oi, and view-dependent color parameters) and a trained multi-resolution hash grid E\theta with MLP decoder f\theta. Outputs: A compressed RGB texture atlas (55–320 MB for typical scenes) and the surfel attributes. The final rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Surfel Attributes: For each surfel i: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^2: 2D scale. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. f{SV}(\mathbf{d}): View-dependent color function parameters (stored per-surfel). 2. Texture Atlas: A 2D RGB texture where each surfel i maps to a rectangular region. The texels store the signed residual color \rho(\mathbf{x}) = f\theta(E\theta(\mathbf{x})). The atlas is allocated once after sparsification. Numbered Steps: 1. Primitive Representation: Represent the scene as a sparse set of oriented 2D surfels. Each surfel i is defined by its position, rotation, scale, and opacity. 2. Kernel Selection: Use the Deformable Beta kernel \mathcal{B}(x;b) instead of a Gaussian. The kernel shape is controlled by a parameter b \in \mathbb{R}: \mathcal{B}(x;b) = (1-x)^{\beta(b)} where x \in [0,1] is the squared radial distance from the kernel center normalized to 1 at the edge of the support, and \beta(b) = 5\sigma(b) with \sigma being the sigmoid function. Small b values produce flat, hard-edged disks to reduce overdraw; large b values produce soft, Gaussian-like profiles. The parameter b is restricted to lie between a flat disk and a soft Gaussian. 3. Appearance Decomposition: Decompose the fragment color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) into a per-surfel view-dependent term and a view-independent residual: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \text{ReLU}\left(\text{ReLU}(f{SV}(\mathbf{d}) + b{SV}) + f\theta(\mathbf{E}\theta(\mathbf{x}))\right) where b{SV} = 0.5 is a fixed offset providing a neutral gray baseline, f{SV} is the per-surfel view-dependent color, and f\theta(\mathbf{E}\theta(\mathbf{x})) is the residual from the hash grid E\theta and MLP decoder f\theta. 4. Training: Query the hash grid at every fragment along the surfel's surface during training to absorb fine spatial texture. Per-surfel attributes remain constant across the surfel to absorb low-frequency view-dependent appearance. Use signed texture residuals (positive and negative color offsets) to provide representational power, allowing a single surfel to reproduce color variation that positive-only textures cannot. Train jointly with the multi-view error criterion of FastGS to limit densification. Introduce a falloff prior using Beta kernels to regularize kernels toward flat, hard-edged profiles, dampening positional gradients and reducing primitive count. 5. Baking: Sample the hash-grid across the surface of each primitive during training. Bake the output of the hash-grid sampling into a compressed RGB texture atlas. Finetune the atlas texels directly against the training images to overcome hash collisions from training. 6. Rendering: Perform fast, per-fragment texture fetches from the atlas. Evaluate the ray-surfel intersection using an exact rational reformulation of the intersection test. Composite the surfels in front-to-back order using alpha blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def betakernel(x, b): """Compute the Deformable Beta kernel value.""" beta = 5.0 sigmoid(b) x = max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) return (1.0 - x) beta def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def projectscreenbounds(surfel, camera): # Standard projection of surfel bounding box to screen coordinates # Returns object with xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax pass def intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydir, surfel): # Exact rational reformulation of ray-surfel intersection # Returns t, u, v parameters pass def transformtolocal(surfel, worldpos): # Transforms world position to surfel's local 2D coordinate system pass def renderscene(surfels, camera, textureatlas): # Initialize output image with zeros image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height camera.width)] # Sort surfels front-to-back by depth along view direction sortedsurfels = sorted(surfels, key=lambda s: dot(s.position, camera.viewdirection)) for surfel in sortedsurfels: screenbounds = projectscreenbounds(surfel, camera) for y in range(screenbounds.ymin, screenbounds.ymax): for x in range(screenbounds.xmin, screenbounds.xmax): # Exact rational ray-surfel intersection test rayorigin = camera.center raydir = normalize(camera.screentoray(x, y) - rayorigin) t, u, v = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydir, surfel) if t > 0 and 0.0 <= u <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= v <= 1.0: # Compute normalized squared distance from surfel center localpos = transformtolocal(surfel, rayorigin + t raydir) distsq = dot(localpos, localpos) kernelval = betakernel(distsq, surfel.bparam) alpha = surfel.opacity kernelval if alpha > 0.0: # Sample baked texture atlas at local UV coordinates residual = textureatlas.sample(u, v) # Compute view-dependent color fsv = surfel.computeviewdependentcolor(raydir) bsv = 0.5 basecolor = max(0.0, fsv + bsv) finalcolor = max(0.0, basecolor + residual) # Front-to-back alpha compositing idx = y camera.width + x c = image[idx] image[idx] = [ c[0] + (1.0 - c[0]) finalcolor[0] alpha, c[1] + (1.0 - c[1]) finalcolor[1] alpha, c[2] + (1.0 - c[2]) finalcolor[2] alpha ] return image Parameters: b{SV} = 0.5: Fixed offset inside the inner ReLU activation. Texture atlas size: 55–320 MB for typical scenes. \beta(b) = 5\sigma(b): Shape parameter scaling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: Hash collisions from training can degrade quality. Finetuning the atlas texels directly against training images mitigates this. Overdraw: Soft Gaussian tails cause redundant overlaps. Using flat Beta kernels (small b) reduces overdraw and primitive count. Sparsity: Pipelines using per-primitive textures start from a converged dense model with densification frozen, capping sparsity. This method allocates the atlas once after sparsification, allowing higher sparsity. A kernel family defined by \mathcal{B}(x;b) = (1-x)^{\beta(b)} that interpolates between flat disks and soft Gaussians via the parameter b. Chosen to reduce overdraw compared to standard Gaussians. The process of converting view-independent neural queries (hash grid + MLP) into a static 2D texture map. Enables hardware-accelerated sampling without runtime neural inference. When a block requiring rendering is encountered, the UE4 submodule supplies the block and level index information, while the inference submodule provides corresponding regional meshes and feature maps. If feature maps are not ready, inference is carried out to generate them. Uses dynamic inference instead of storing all texture maps to reduce storage overhead for large-scale scenes. Time Complexity: Rendering is dominated by texture fetches and simple arithmetic, avoiding neural network evaluations. The rational intersection test is computationally cheaper than standard ray-surfel shaders. Memory Complexity: Requires a texture atlas of 55–320 MB for typical scenes, which is larger than memory-optimized 3DGS representations but fits on low-to-mid-range GPUs. Performance: Renders 7.1–9.1× faster than 3DGS and 1.2–1.8× faster than FastGS and Speedy-Splat on common benchmarks. Strengths: High rendering speed due to elimination of runtime neural inference; reduced overdraw via flat kernels; high sparsity. Limitations: Larger memory footprint than some compressed 3DGS variants; requires training to bake the atlas; signed residuals require careful handling of negative values in texture formats. When to Use: Real-time rendering of high-fidelity scenes where GPU compute is limited by neural network inference overhead. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and smaller scene representations are prioritized over rendering speed. Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting was introduced by Petkov and Klaus from Siemens Healthineers in 2026. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) and FastGS, aiming to solve the rendering overhead caused by runtime neural network evaluations in neural radiance representations. The method leverages the observation that view-independent high-frequency texture can be baked into a texture atlas, while view-dependent low-frequency appearance remains per-surfel.
