name: Lighting and Material Interaction
body: This family defines how photometric properties and illumination are computed for splatted primitives, addressing the gap between raw geometric density and visually plausible appearance. It differs from sibling methods by injecting per-primitive shading calculations or baked lighting data into the rendering pipeline, allowing for dynamic lighting interactions, baked global illumination, or direct user editing of material properties per primitive. Photon Splatting captures direct illumination by rasterizing a light-view map and projecting photons into a sparse voxel octree structure [2832-photon-splatting.md]. It solves the problem of efficiently storing incoming radiance as a direction distribution and energy proportional to the subtended solid angle of the light source [2832-photon-splatting.md]. It differs from Per-Splat Relighting by baking lighting information directly into the voxel data structure during a pre-computation phase, rather than computing shading dynamically per splat during rendering [2832-photon-splatting.md, 3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. Choose this method when pre-computing direct illumination into a sparse voxel octree is preferred for static lighting or radiance storage [2832-photon-splatting.md]. Per-Splat Relighting computes a dynamic lighting multiplier for each Gaussian splat based on its world position, normal, ambient occlusion, and confidence, enabling real-time dynamic illumination [3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. It differs from pre-shading by deferring photometric calculations to the rendering pass, allowing interactive light changes while avoiding the complexity of full path tracing by treating each splat as an independent shading unit [3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. Choose this method when dynamic, real-time lighting changes are required without full path tracing overhead [3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. Definition: Recolorization or shadow additions by checking if a splat center intersects with a spherical brush and adjusting its color value. Parameters: Color channels are stored in 16-bit format to support brushes with smooth falloff and low opacity. Pitfalls: Splat models often do not lend themselves well to painting detailed features (text, lines, symbols) because they represent sparse geometry; models from images use few splats on clean surfaces, preventing detailed color changes. Color leaks may occur into differently colored parts of a surface if state-of-the-art Gaussian splat reconstructions rarely feature clean and opaque surfaces. Choose this method when artistic recolorization or shadow additions are needed directly on sparse geometry. The techniques described herein originate from the practical requirements of editing and rendering large-scale Gaussian Splat models, specifically detailed in the development of "Splatshop". Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Photon Splatting
head: Capturing Direct Illumination (Photon Splatting)
body: Photon Splatting captures direct illumination by projecting photons from light sources onto scene geometry and storing them in a sparse voxel octree. It solves the problem of efficiently accumulating incoming radiance for subsequent indirect illumination calculations by treating light-view map pixels as photons. It differs from Per-Splat Relighting by focusing on the initial capture and storage of direct light energy into the voxel structure rather than per-surface lighting updates. Inputs: Light-view map: A world position map rendered from the light's perspective, where each pixel represents a photon. Sparse Voxel Octree: A hierarchical data structure representing the scene, where leaf nodes store photon data. Outputs: Updated Octree: Leaf nodes contain direction distributions and energy values proportional to the subtended solid angle of the light-view map pixel. Data Structures: Light-View Map: Stores world positions and depth. Octree Leaf Node: Stores photon data. Brick Structure: Voxels are repeated at brick boundaries to enable hardware filtering. Atomic Operations: Hardware atomic adds are limited to integer textures. Empty Voxels: Photons are stored at the surface, and empty voxels are collapsed. Steps: 1. Render Light-View Map: Render the scene from the light's view using standard rasterization to generate a world position map. 2. Splat Photons: Launch a fragment shader with one thread per light-view-map pixel. For each pixel, determine the corresponding leaf node in the octree based on the world position. Calculate the photon's energy, which is proportional to the subtended solid angle of the pixel as seen from the light. Store the photon as a direction distribution and energy in the leaf node. 3. Handle Atomic Operations: Since atomic add operations are only available for integer textures, use a 16-bit normalized texture format for storage. Denormalize the values when accessing them later. 4. Resolve Brick Boundary Inconsistencies: Because voxels are repeated for adjacent bricks, direct copying causes thread collisions and bandwidth issues. Use the "Value Transfer to Neighboring Bricks" method to ensure coherence. Formulas: E \propto \Omega, where E is the stored photon energy and \Omega is the subtended solid angle of the light-view map pixel as seen from the light. Parameters: Light-View Map Resolution: Typically higher than the lowest level of the voxel grid to avoid gaps. Texture Format: 16-bit normalized (e.g., RG16F) to support atomic adds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomic Operations: Hardware atomic adds are limited to integer textures, requiring 16-bit normalized formats and careful denormalization. Thread Collisions: Copying photons directly to all required locations in adjacent bricks leads to significant performance degradation due to parallel random scattering and bandwidth issues. Empty Voxels: Photons are stored at the surface, and empty voxels are collapsed, ensuring photons are always placed at the finest level of the voxel structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatphotons(lightviewmap, octreeleaves): # One thread per pixel in lightviewmap for pixel in lightviewmap: worldpos = pixel.worldposition solidangle = pixel.subtendedsolidangle # Find leaf node in octree based on world position leaf = octreeleaves.findleaf(worldpos) # Photon data: direction and energy proportional to solid angle energy = solidangle direction = normalize(lightposition - worldpos) # Atomic add required for concurrent updates on 16-bit normalized buffer leaf.buffer.atomicadd(energy, direction) def transfertoneighbors(octreeleaves): # Six passes, two for each axis (x, y, z) for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: # Pass 1: Add current node's data to the neighbor in positive direction for leaf in octreeleaves: neighbor = leaf.getneighbor(axis, direction=+1) neighbor.buffer += leaf.buffer # Pass 2: Copy summed data from neighbor back to current node for leaf in octreeleaves: neighbor = leaf.getneighbor(axis, direction=+1) leaf.buffer = neighbor.buffer This method addresses the inconsistency of duplicated voxels at brick boundaries. It uses six passes (two per axis: x, y, z) to propagate data. In the first pass of an axis, each thread adds its voxel data to the neighbor in the positive direction. In the second pass, it copies the summed data from the neighbor back. This ensures coherence along each axis without atomic operations or thread collisions, leveraging neighbor pointers for efficient access. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient for scenes with high-resolution light-view maps. Strengths: Avoids atomic operations in the transfer step and prevents thread collisions. Limitations: Requires a complete octree assumption for the simplified explanation of value transfer. Photon Splatting was introduced in Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing (2011). It builds on the idea of using light-view maps to capture direct illumination for subsequent indirect illumination calculations. The method was developed to address the challenges of storing photons in a sparse voxel octree while maintaining performance and accuracy. PDF Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing, https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/publications/GIVoxels-pg2011-authors.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2011.02063.x, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Splat Painting
head: Interactive Splat Editing, Splat Brushing
body: Splat Painting is a direct manipulation technique for editing the appearance of Gaussian Splatting models by applying color changes via a 3D brush. It solves the problem of post-hoc recolorization, such as restoring faded pigments or adding shadows, without requiring full scene re-optimization. Unlike methods that reoptimize primitive colors (which preserves texture but may alter shading) or direct painting (which erases shading and texture), Splat Painting modifies only the albedo parameters to achieve sharper boundaries and preserve existing shading effects. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (centers, covariances, colors, opacities); a spherical brush defined by center, radius, and target color. Outputs: Modified Gaussian primitives with updated color values. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: center: 3D vector (x, y, z). color: 16-bit per channel (RGB) to support smooth falloff and low opacity brushes. opacity: Scalar. covariance: 3x3 matrix (or quaternion/scale representation). Brush: center: 3D vector. radius: Scalar. targetcolor: 16-bit RGB vector. Algorithm: 1. Selection: Iterate through all Gaussian primitives. For each primitive i with center ci, calculate the Euclidean distance d to the brush center b: d = \| ci - b \|2 2. Intersection Check: If d \leq \text{radius}, the primitive is selected for editing. 3. Color Update: Adjust the primitive's color. Basic Mode: Replace the color with the target color. Hue/Saturation Mode: Adjust only hue and saturation to the target color, preserving the original value/brightness to retain texture and ambient occlusion. Albedo-Only Mode (Variant): If the model uses intrinsic decomposition, update only the albedo Gaussian parameters while keeping shading Gaussians untouched. 4. Falloff (Optional): For smooth edges, apply a falloff function based on d to blend the original color with the target color. The sources note the use of 16-bit channels to support this smooth falloff and low opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatpaint(primitives, brushcenter, brushradius, targetcolor, mode="basic"): """ primitives: list of Gaussian objects with attributes.center,.color brushcenter: tuple (x, y, z) brushradius: float targetcolor: tuple (r, g, b) with 16-bit precision mode: "basic", "huesat", or "albedoonly" """ for prim in primitives: # Calculate distance from splat center to brush center dx = prim.center.x - brushcenter[0] dy = prim.center.y - brushcenter[1] dz = prim.center.z - brushcenter[2] distancesq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz # Check intersection if distancesq <= brushradius brushradius: if mode == "basic": # Direct replacement prim.color = targetcolor elif mode == "huesat": # Adjust hue and saturation, preserve value/brightness # Implementation detail: Convert RGB to HSV, modify H/S, convert back # Standard HSV conversion logic assumed orighsv = rgbtohsv(prim.color) targethsv = rgbtohsv(targetcolor) newhsv = (targethsv[0], targethsv[1], orighsv[2]) prim.color = hsvtorgb(newhsv) elif mode == "albedoonly": # Update only albedo component if intrinsic decomposition is used # Assumes prim has.albedo and.shading attributes prim.albedo = targetcolor # Note: Smooth falloff blending is supported by 16-bit channels # Implementation of specific falloff function not detailed in sources Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Geometry: Splat models are sparse; painting detailed features (text, lines) is difficult because individual splats are visible and undersampling occurs. Clean Surfaces: Models from images focus splats on high-frequency regions. Clean, single-colored surfaces (e.g., walls) use few splats, preventing detailed color changes. Color Leaks: In reconstructions with non-opaque surfaces, splats may contribute to multiple surface parts. Changing appearance can cause color leaks into differently colored areas. This variant modifies only the albedo parameters of the Gaussian primitives while leaving shading and residual Gaussians untouched. It is chosen when the goal is to change surface color without altering existing lighting effects (shadows, ambient occlusion). It achieves sharper boundaries around the edited area compared to methods that reoptimize all color channels. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of primitives N for the selection phase (O(N)). If optimization is involved (e.g., ReCoGS), complexity increases significantly; however, basic Splat Painting and SplatShop are direct updates without optimization. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the primitive data. Undo/redo history poses memory challenges, requiring compact storage of differences to avoid VR stutters. Strengths: Interactive speed (no optimization required for direct painting); preserves shading if using intrinsic decomposition. Limitations: Cannot create detailed features due to sparse geometry; color leaks on non-opaque surfaces; limited to modifying existing primitives rather than generating new geometry. When to use: Quick recolorization, fading restoration, or shadow addition where shading preservation is desired. When not to use: When detailed texture addition is required or when the underlying reconstruction is too sparse to support the desired brush strokes. Splat Painting originated as a feature within Gaussian Splatting editing tools, specifically discussed in the context of Splatshop and intrinsic decomposition methods. It addresses the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting, which lacks native editing capabilities for appearance. The method distinguishes itself from ReCoGS (which reoptimizes colors under a mask) and SplatShop (which paints directly but erases shading) by offering a middle ground, particularly through albedo-only updates. Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31 Intrinsic decomposition and editing of 3D Gaussian splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804495, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Per-Splat Relighting
body: Per-Splat Relighting computes a lighting multiplier for a splat based on lights, normal, ambient occlusion, and confidence. It differs from Photon Splatting by calculating lighting analytically per-splat rather than accumulating photon densities, allowing real-time updates when light positions or intensities change without re-radiating photons. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: splatlighting buffer (packed lighting records), lightrig buffer (light definitions), worldposition of the splat center, unlitlevel (base color), ambient color, gain scalar. Output: Relit color value. Data Structures: The splatlighting buffer stores per-splat metadata packed into a 4-component vector where rg is an octahedral normal, b is ambient occlusion, and a is confidence. The lightrig buffer is an array where each light occupies 4 consecutive elements: i4+0 is a vec3 representing light position or direction, i4+1 contains a vec3 tint and a float alpha for the light type, i4+2 holds setup parameters (r for inverse range, g for decay, b for spot cone cosine threshold, a for spot exponent), and i4+3 is a vec3 spot direction vector. Numbered Steps: 1. Unpack Lighting Record: Retrieve the lighting record for the current splat index from splatlighting and extract the octahedral normal (rg), AO (b), and confidence (a). 2. Normalize Normal: Convert the octahedral normal to a 3D vector, calculate its length, and normalize it if the length is greater than zero; otherwise, default the normal to (0, 0, 1). 3. Initialize Direct Light: Set direct illumination to zero. 4. Loop Over Lights: For each light i in the lightrig: extract tint from lightrig[i4+1], setup from lightrig[i4+2], and determine type by rounding tint.a to the nearest integer; initialize tolight from lightrig[i4+0].xyz and attenuation to 1.0; if type is not 0, calculate relative as lightrig[i4+0].xyz - worldposition, compute dist, skip if dist < 1e-6, normalize tolight to relative / dist, and compute attenuation using the omniattenuation formula with dist, setup.r, and setup.g; if type equals 2, calculate conecosine as max(dot(-tolight, lightrig[i4+3].xyz), setup.b), compute rim as (1.0 - conecosine) / max(1e-4, 1.0 - setup.b), and update attenuation by multiplying it by 1.0 - pow(clamp(rim, 0, 1), setup.a); finally, accumulate direct by adding tint.rgb attenuation max(dot(worldnormal, tolight), 0). 5. Compute Irradiance: Calculate irradiance as ambient ao + direct confidence. 6. Return Result: Return unlitlevel + gain irradiance. Formulas: Omni Attenuation: \text{omni\attenuation}(dist, inv\range, decay) = \max(1.0 - (dist \cdot inv\range)^4, 0)^2 \cdot dist^{-decay} Where dist is the distance from splat to light, inv\range is the inverse range of the light (setup.r), and decay is the decay exponent (setup.g). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodeoctnormal(oct): v = vec3(oct.x, oct.y, 1.0 - abs(oct.x) - abs(oct.y)) if v.z < 0: v.xy = 1.0 - abs(v.yx) vec2(sign(v.x), sign(v.y)) return normalize(v) def persplatrelight(splatindex, worldposition, unlitlevel, ambient, gain, splatlighting, lightrig): record = splatlighting[splatindex] octnormal = record.rg ao = record.b confidence = record.a decodednormal = decodeoctnormal(octnormal) normallength = length(decodednormal) worldnormal = decodednormal / normallength if normallength > 0 else vec3(0, 0, 1) direct = vec3(0, 0, 0) numlights = len(lightrig) // 4 for i in range(numlights): baseidx = i 4 tint = lightrig[baseidx + 1] setup = lightrig[baseidx + 2] lightdata = lightrig[baseidx + 0] lighttype = int(tint.a + 0.5) tolight = lightdata.xyz attenuation = 1.0 if lighttype != 0: relative = lightdata.xyz - worldposition dist = length(relative) if dist < 1e-6: continue tolight = relative / dist invrange = setup.r decay = setup.g term = max(1.0 - (dist invrange)4, 0.0) attenuation = (term 2) (dist -decay) if lighttype == 2: spotdir = lightrig[baseidx + 3].xyz conecosine = max(dot(-tolight, spotdir), setup.b) rim = (1.0 - conecosine) / max(1e-4, 1.0 - setup.b) attenuation = 1.0 - pow(clamp(rim, 0.0, 1.0), setup.a) diff = max(dot(worldnormal, tolight), 0.0) direct += tint.rgb attenuation diff irradiance = ambient ao + direct confidence return unlitlevel + gain irradiance Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Normal: If the decoded normal has zero length, it defaults to (0,0,1), which can cause incorrect shading for flat surfaces or degenerate splats. Division by Zero: The spot light rim calculation uses max(1e-4, 1.0 - setup.b) to prevent division by zero when the cone angle is very narrow (setup.b close to 1.0). Near-Zero Distance: Lights at the exact splat position are skipped (dist < 1e-6) to avoid NaNs or infinite attenuation. Time Complexity: O(L) per splat, where L is the number of lights, executed per fragment during splat rendering. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per splat for the lighting record packed in splatlighting. Strengths: Real-time capable; supports dynamic light movement and intensity changes without precomputation. Limitations: Only handles direct lighting and simple AO; no indirect bounces; performance scales linearly with light count. When to use: Real-time applications with dynamic lighting. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring global illumination or very high light counts where performance is critical. Per-Splat Relighting is a technique used in real-time Gaussian Splatting renderers, such as the one implemented in the godot-gaussian-splatting repository, which adapts traditional lighting concepts to the splat-based rendering pipeline by storing lighting metadata within the splat data structure. ReconWorldLab/godot-gaussian-splatting, https://github.com/ReconWorldLab/godot-gaussian-splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Metal Gaussian Splat Relighting
head: MetalSplatter, Ref-Gaussian Relighting
body: Metal Gaussian Splat Relighting is a real-time, GPU-accelerated method for rendering Gaussian Splatting scenes with physically based rendering (PBR) materials and dynamic indirect lighting. It solves the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which relies on spherical harmonics (SH) for view-dependent color but lacks material definitions for realistic light interaction. By integrating PBR shading and Ambient Sphere Gaussians (ASG) for indirect illumination, this method enables dynamic relighting of splat clouds. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Soft-Lit Sphere Sprite Generator by using explicit material properties and environment maps rather than pre-computed sprite lighting. Inputs: Splat data: Position, covariance (or 2DGS surfel geometry), SH coefficients, and optional PBR material properties (albedo, roughness, metallic, normal). Lighting data: Environment map (prefiltered for indirect lighting), irradiance environment map, BRDF LUT, and camera position. Relighting configuration: Flags for enabling/disabling relighting, SH degree, and material buffer availability. Outputs: Final color buffer: Linear HDR RGB with alpha, ready for presentation (tonemapping/exposure handled in a separate post-process pass). ChunkedSplatIndex Identifies a specific splat within a chunk. Total size: 8 bytes. chunkIndex: UInt16 (2 bytes). Index of the chunk in the chunk array. padding: UInt16 (2 bytes). Reserved for alignment. splatIndex: UInt32 (4 bytes). Index of the splat within the chunk's splat array. SplatChunk Contains batches of splats and their associated data. splats: Array of splat structures. materials: Optional pointer to an array of SplatMaterial structures. If nullptr, standard 3DGS SH color is used. shCoefficients: Buffer for higher-order SH coefficients. shDegree: Integer indicating the SH degree (0, 1, 2, or 3). enabled: Boolean flag. If false, the chunk is skipped. splatCount: Number of valid splats in the chunk. SplatMaterial Defines PBR properties for a splat. albedo: float3 (RGB). Base color. roughness: float. Surface roughness (0.0 to 1.0). metallic: float. Metalness factor (0.0 to 1.0). normal: float3. Surface normal (normalized). Splat Basic geometric and radiometric data. position: float3. Center of the Gaussian. shCoefficients: Array of coefficients for view-dependent color. color: float4 (RGBA). Base color and opacity (used if SH degree is 0). 1. Vertex Shader: Splat Identification and Validation Calculate splatID from instanceID, uniforms.indexedSplatCount, and vertexID. If splatID >= uniforms.splatCount, return a fragment with position (1, 1, 0, 1) to discard. Retrieve ChunkedSplatIndex from splatIndexArray using splatID. If idx.chunkIndex >= uniforms.chunkCount, return discard position. Retrieve ChunkInfo for idx.chunkIndex. If idx.splatIndex >= chunk.splatCount, return discard position. If chunk.enabled is false, return discard position. 2. Vertex Shader: Data Retrieval and SH Evaluation Retrieve the Splat from chunk.splats[idx.splatIndex]. Call splatVertex with the splat, uniforms, vertexID % 4, chunk.shCoefficients, chunk.shDegree, and idx.splatIndex to compute FragmentIn. This step evaluates the SH coefficients to determine the base color and opacity at the fragment's relative position. 3. Vertex Shader: PBR Relighting (Conditional) If relight.enabled != 0 and chunk.materials != nullptr: Retrieve SplatMaterial from chunk.materials[idx.splatIndex]. Call shadePBR with out.color.rgb, material, splat.position, uniforms.cameraPosition, relight, prefilteredEnv, irradianceEnv, brdfLUT, and iblSampler. This updates out.color.rgb with the result of the PBR shading calculation, including direct and indirect lighting. 4. Fragment Shader: Alpha Compositing Calculate alpha using splatFragmentAlpha with in.relativePosition and in.color.a. Return half4(alpha in.color.rgb, alpha). Spherical Harmonics (SH) Coefficients The number of coefficients depends on the SH degree. Values are stored as Float16. SH Degree 0: 1 coefficient (3 RGB channels). Total: 3 values. SH Degree 1: 4 coefficients (3 RGB channels). Total: 12 values. (Note: Source lists 9 values for Degree 1, which implies 3 coefficients × 3 RGB. Standard SH Degree 1 has 4 coefficients (l=0,1). The source note "9 Float16 values per splat (3 coefficients × 3 RGB)" suggests a specific implementation detail or a typo in the source's coefficient count vs. value count. We follow the source's explicit value count: 9 values for Degree 1, 24 for Degree 2, 45 for Degree 3). Correction based on Source: SH Degree 1: 9 Float16 values per splat (3 coefficients × 3 RGB). SH Degree 2: 24 Float16 values per splat (8 coefficients × 3 RGB, cumulative). SH Degree 3: 45 Float16 values per splat (15 coefficients × 3 RGB, cumulative). ASG Coefficients: 160 Float16 values per splat (32 lobes × 5 channels, lobe-major). Approx. 320 bytes/splat. Normal Orientation for 2DGS/Ref-Gaussian For 2DGS surfels, normals are sign-ambiguous because disks are two-sided. To prevent noise in shading: 1. Compute the centroid of all splat positions in the chunk. 2. For each splat, calculate the dot product of its normal and the vector from the centroid to the splat position: d = \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}). 3. If d < 0, flip the normal sign: \mathbf{n} = -\mathbf{n}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(instanceid, vertexid, uniforms, splatindexarray, chunkarray): # Step 1: Splat Identification splatid = computesplatid(instanceid, uniforms.indexedsplatcount, vertexid) if splatid >= uniforms.splatcount: return discardfragment(position=(1, 1, 0, 1)) # Retrieve ChunkedSplatIndex chunkedidx = splatindexarray[splatid] if chunkedidx.chunkindex >= uniforms.chunkcount: return discardfragment() # Retrieve ChunkInfo chunk = chunkarray[chunkedidx.chunkindex] if chunkedidx.splatindex >= chunk.splatcount: return discardfragment() if not chunk.enabled: return discardfragment() # Step 2: Data Retrieval and SH Evaluation splat = chunk.splats[chunkedidx.splatindex] fragmentin = splatvertex( splat=splat, uniforms=uniforms, vertexoffset=vertexid % 4, shcoefficients=chunk.shcoefficients, shdegree=chunk.shdegree, splatindex=chunkedidx.splatindex) # Step 3: PBR Relighting if uniforms.relightenabled and chunk.materials is not None: material = chunk.materials[chunkedidx.splatindex] # Ensure normal is oriented outward for 2DGS if chunk.shdegree > 0: # Assuming this flag indicates 2DGS/Ref-Gaussian mode material.normal = orientnormal(material.normal, splat.position, chunk.centroid) shadepbr( outcolor=fragmentin.color.rgb, material=material, splatposition=splat.position, cameraposition=uniforms.cameraposition, relight=uniforms.relight, prefilteredenv=uniforms.prefilteredenv, irradianceenv=uniforms.irradianceenv, brdflut=uniforms.brdflut, iblsampler=uniforms.iblsampler) return fragmentin def fragmentshader(fragmentin): # Step 4: Alpha Compositing alpha = splatfragmentalpha(fragmentin.relativeposition, fragmentin.color.a) return half4(alpha fragmentin.color.rgb, alpha) def orientnormal(normal, position, centroid): """ Orient normal outward from the cloud centroid. """ tocentroid = centroid - position if dot(normal, tocentroid) < 0: return -normal return normal def shadepbr(outcolor, material, position, cameraposition, relight, prefilteredenv, irradianceenv, brdflut, iblsampler): """ Computes PBR shading with indirect lighting. """ # Calculate direct lighting (if any) and indirect lighting from environment # Indirect lighting uses prefilteredenv and irradianceenv indirectlighting = computeindirectlighting( material.normal, material.roughness, material.metallic, prefilteredenv, irradianceenv, brdflut, iblsampler) # Combine with base color outcolor = material.albedo indirectlighting # Note: Direct lighting might be added here if relight includes direct lights # outcolor += directlighting material.albedo 2DGS Normal Ambiguity: 2DGS surfels have sign-ambiguous normals because disks are two-sided. If not corrected, normals point randomly inward/outward, causing noise in shading. Solution: Orient normals consistently outward from the cloud centroid. Missing ASG Coefficients: Missing ASG coefficients in a chunk can cause unbounded reflections in the shader (e.g., exp(ep - 3)). Solution: Fill missing ASG data with zeros. Precision: SH coefficients are stored as Float16. For high dynamic range scenes, ensure that the accumulation of SH terms does not lose precision. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of splats. Each splat is processed in constant time per fragment, with shading cost depending on the complexity of the PBR evaluation and environment map sampling. Memory Complexity: O(N) for splat data. Additional memory for PBR materials and ASG coefficients. ASG coefficients add ~320 bytes per splat. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of splats. Chunking allows for efficient culling and batch processing. Strengths: Enables dynamic relighting with PBR materials. Supports indirect lighting via ASG. Real-time performance on mobile GPUs (Metal). Limitations: Requires additional memory for materials and ASG coefficients. 2DGS normal orientation requires a centroid calculation pass. When to use: When realistic material appearance and dynamic lighting are required for Gaussian Splatting scenes. When not to use: When memory is constrained and ASG coefficients cannot be afforded. When static lighting is sufficient and SH-only rendering is preferred. Metal Gaussian Splat Relighting is an implementation of PBR relighting for Gaussian Splatting, specifically designed for the Metal API. It is associated with the "MetalSplatter" and "Ref-Gaussian" projects. The method extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by adding PBR materials and ASG for indirect lighting, enabling dynamic relighting. It is used in real-time rendering applications, particularly on Apple devices, where Metal is the primary graphics API. john-rocky/MetalGaussianSplatRelighting, https://github.com/john-rocky/MetalGaussianSplatRelighting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Soft-Lit Sphere Sprite Generator
head: CPU Point Sprite Renderer, Rough-Plastic Sphere Sprite
body: Generates a 2D RGBA sprite representing a softly lit sphere with a restrained rough-plastic highlight, optimized for CPU-based point-cloud rendering without external renderer dependencies. It differs from GPU-accelerated splatting methods by providing a lightweight, self-contained procedural texture that approximates diffuse and rim lighting for individual points, serving as the visual primitive for the Per-Splat Relighting pipeline. Inputs: radius: Integer, sprite radius in pixels. basecolor: Tuple of three integers (red, green, blue), each in range [0, 255]. Outputs: A 2D RGBA image (PIL Image or equivalent array) of size (2 radius + 1, 2 radius + 1, 4) with uint8 data type. Data Structures: The sprite is stored as a 2D grid of pixels. Each pixel contains four channels: Red, Green, Blue, and Alpha. Coordinates are normalized to the range [-1, 1] relative to the sprite center. Parameters: radius: Clamped to a minimum of 2 (radius = max(radius, 2)). Light direction: Fixed vector [-0.48, -0.58, 0.66]. Lighting weights: Ambient 0.64, Diffuse 0.29, Rim 0.07. Highlight offset: (0.32, 0.38). Highlight spread: 0.23. Highlight intensity: 38.0. Steps: 1. Grid Generation: Create a grid of coordinates xx, yy ranging from -radius to radius. Normalize these to nx, ny by dividing by radius. 2. Sphere Masking: Compute squaredradius = nx2 + ny2. Determine if a pixel is inside the sphere: inside = squaredradius <= 1.0. For inside pixels, compute the z-component of the normal: nz = sqrt(clip(1.0 - squaredradius, 0.0, 1.0)). For outside pixels, nz is undefined but masked out later. 3. Lighting Calculation: Define light direction light = [-0.48, -0.58, 0.66] and normalize it to unit length. Compute diffuse term: diffuse = clip(nxlx + nyly + nzlz, 0.0, 1.0). Compute rim term: rim = clip(nz, 0.0, 1.0). Combine: illumination = 0.64 + 0.29 diffuse + 0.07 rim. 4. Highlight Calculation: Compute a 2D Gaussian highlight centered at (-0.32, -0.38) with standard deviation 0.23: highlight = exp(-(((nx + 0.32)/0.23)2 + ((ny + 0.38)/0.23)2)). 5. Color Compositing: Scale base RGB by illumination: rgb = basecolor illumination[..., None]. Add highlight: rgb += 38.0 highlight[..., None]. Clip RGB values to [0, 255]. 6. Alpha Generation: Compute edge alpha: edge = clip((1.03 - sqrt(squaredradius)) radius, 0.0, 1.0). Set alpha channel to edge 255.0 for inside pixels, 0.0 for outside. 7. Output: Concatenate RGB and Alpha channels, convert to uint8, and return as an image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from PIL import Image def generatesoftlitspheresprite(radius: int, basecolor: tuple) -> Image.Image: # Clamp radius radius = max(radius, 2) # 1. Grid Generation # Create coordinates from -radius to radius x = np.arange(-radius, radius + 1) y = np.arange(-radius, radius + 1) xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x, y) # Normalize to [-1, 1] nx = xx / radius ny = yy / radius # 2. Sphere Masking squaredradius = nx2 + ny2 inside = squaredradius <= 1.0 # Compute nz for inside pixels nz = np.zeroslike(nx) nz[inside] = np.sqrt(np.clip(1.0 - squaredradius[inside], 0.0, 1.0)) # 3. Lighting Calculation light = np.array([-0.48, -0.58, 0.66]) light = light / np.linalg.norm(light) lx, ly, lz = light # Diffuse: dot product of normal (nx, ny, nz) and light diffuse = np.clip(nx lx + ny ly + nz lz, 0.0, 1.0) # Rim: based on nz rim = np.clip(nz, 0.0, 1.0) # Combine lighting illumination = 0.64 + 0.29 diffuse + 0.07 rim # 4. Highlight Calculation # Gaussian highlight centered at (-0.32, -0.38) highlight = np.exp(-(((nx + 0.32) / 0.23)2 + ((ny + 0.38) / 0.23)2)) # 5. Color Compositing # Base color is (R, G, B) baser, baseg, baseb = basecolor # Apply illumination to base color rgbr = baser illumination rgbg = baseg illumination rgbb = baseb illumination # Add highlight rgbr += 38.0 highlight rgbg += 38.0 highlight rgbb += 38.0 highlight # Clip to [0, 255] rgbr = np.clip(rgbr, 0, 255) rgbg = np.clip(rgbg, 0, 255) rgbb = np.clip(rgbb, 0, 255) # 6. Alpha Generation # Edge alpha edge = np.clip((1.03 - np.sqrt(squaredradius)) radius, 0.0, 1.0) alpha = edge 255.0 # Set alpha to 0 for outside pixels alpha[~inside] = 0.0 # 7. Output # Convert to uint8 rgbr = rgbr.astype(np.uint8) rgbg = rgbg.astype(np.uint8) rgbb = rgbb.astype(np.uint8) alpha = alpha.astype(np.uint8) # Stack channels: H x W x 4 sprite = np.stack([rgbr, rgbg, rgbb, alpha], axis=-1) return Image.fromarray(sprite, mode='RGBA') Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Radius < 2: The algorithm clamps radius to 2 to ensure sufficient resolution for the highlight and edge effects. Precision: Floating-point operations should be performed in float32 or higher to avoid quantization artifacts in the highlight and alpha gradients. Boundary Conditions: The clip function is critical for nz and diffuse to prevent NaNs or negative values when squaredradius slightly exceeds 1.0 due to floating-point error. Time Complexity: O(R^2) where R is the sprite radius. The operations are element-wise and highly parallelizable, but the method is designed for CPU execution. Memory Complexity: O(R^2) for the output sprite. No auxiliary data structures are required. Performance: Optimized for CPU-based rendering, avoiding the overhead of GPU kernel launches for simple point sprites. Suitable for real-time applications where GPU resources are constrained or for preprocessing assets. Strengths: No external renderer dependencies; lightweight; produces visually pleasing "rough-plastic" highlights that approximate complex lighting. Limitations: Fixed light direction; does not support dynamic lighting changes per-splat without regenerating the sprite; limited to spherical primitives. The Soft-Lit Sphere Sprite Generator is part of the Gaussian-JEPA project, specifically used in the context of CPU-based point-cloud rendering. It provides a procedural alternative to pre-baked textures or complex GPU-based shading for individual points in a scene. name: BCC Grid Rendering
head: BCC vs CC Grid Rendering, Body-Centered Cartesian Grid
body: BCC Grid Rendering is a volume rendering technique that utilizes a Body-Centered Cartesian (BCC) lattice for spatial sampling instead of the standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid. It solves the problem of excessive memory and computational cost in point-based volume rendering by reducing the required number of sample points to 70.3% of a CC grid while maintaining lossless compression for spherically bandlimited signals. It is distinct from CC rendering by its higher packing efficiency for isotropic signals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset defined on a BCC lattice, camera parameters (view and projection matrices), and a rendering kernel. Output: A 2D raster image. Data Structures: The data is stored in a BCC lattice structure. A BCC lattice can be viewed as two interleaved simple cubic lattices, or as a cubic lattice with an additional point at the center of each cube. Lattice Points: Defined by integer coordinates (i, j, k) and a parity bit or offset indicating whether the point belongs to the primary cubic sublattice or the body-centered sublattice. Attributes: Each lattice point stores density/extinction coefficient \rho and potentially other scalar/vector fields. Steps: 1. Lattice Generation: Construct the BCC grid from the input data. If the input is on a CC grid, resample or interpolate onto the BCC lattice. Not given in the sources. 2. Transformation: Transform the BCC lattice points from world space to clip space using the standard Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix, identical to CC rendering. 3. Slicing/Sorting: Sort the transformed points by depth (Z-buffer) to ensure correct front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. 4. Rasterization (Splatting): For each point, project its 3D footprint onto the 2D image plane. Shift: When rendering BCC grids, slices must be shifted by 1/2 relative to the CC grid alignment to account for the body-centered offset. Footprint: Compute the 2D footprint F(x,y) for each point. The evidence states that BCC grids assume spherically bandlimited signals, under which assumption compression is lossless. Weighting: Calculate the weight based on the distance from the pixel center to the point's projected center, modulated by the point's density \rho. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the splatted contributions into the frame buffer using alpha blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbccgrid(points, camera, width, height, kernelradius=3.0): """ points: List of dicts with keys 'pos' (x,y,z), 'density', 'type' ('primary'/'center') camera: Object with 'mvp' (4x4 matrix), 'shiftoffset' (0.5) width, height: int kernelradius: float, radius of the splat footprint """ # Initialize frame buffer (RGBA) fb = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # 1. Transform to clip space clippoints = [] for p in points: # MVP transform clipw = (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][3] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][3] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][3] + camera.mvp[3][3]) if clipw <= 0.0: continue clippoints.append({ 'x': (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][0] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][0] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][0] + camera.mvp[3][0]) / clipw, 'y': (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][1] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][1] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][1] + camera.mvp[3][1]) / clipw, 'z': (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][2] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][2] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][2] + camera.mvp[3][2]) / clipw, 'density': p['density'] }) # 2. Sort back-to-front for standard alpha blending clippoints.sort(key=lambda p: p['z']) # 3. Rasterize (Splat) for p in clippoints: # NDC to screen coordinates sx = (p['x'] + 1.0) 0.5 width sy = (1.0 - (p['y'] + 1.0) 0.5) height # Apply BCC slice shift by 1/2 sx += camera.shiftoffset width sy += camera.shiftoffset height # Splat footprint for dy in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): for dx in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): px, py = int(sx + dx), int(sy + dy) if 0 <= px < width and 0 <= py < height: distsq = dxdx + dydy # Gaussian/quadratic kernel weight weight = max(0.0, 1.0 - distsq / (kernelradius kernelradius)) alpha = weight p['density'] if alpha <= 0.0: continue # Front-to-back alpha blending oldrgba = fb[py][px] newa = alpha + oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha) if newa > 0.0: # Monochromatic density visualization fb[py][px] = ( (p['density'] alpha + oldrgba[0] oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha)) / newa, (p['density'] alpha + oldrgba[1] oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha)) / newa, (p['density'] alpha + oldrgba[2] oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha)) / newa, newa) return fb Parameters: Shift Offset: 0.5 in normalized screen coordinates or lattice units. Kernel: Spherical/Gaussian, optimized for isotropic signals. Edge Cases: Non-Spherical Signals: If the signal is not spherically bandlimited, the BCC grid may not provide lossless compression, and artifacts may appear. Boundary Conditions: Not given in the sources. BCC Grid Sampling uses a Body-Centered Cartesian (BCC) lattice to store volume data, requiring fewer sample points than a standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid while maintaining lossless compression for spherically bandlimited signals. It is distinct from CC sampling by its higher packing efficiency for isotropic signals. The BCC grid reduces required point samples to 70.3% of a cubic grid, while a 4D BCC grid requires only 50% of the equivalent 4D cubic grid samples. In practice, BCC grid rendering took 70% of the time of CC grid rendering for the Foot dataset, although renderings were almost identical. For the Turbulent Jet 4D example, BCC rendering took 1.01s (71% of CC time) with 138 time steps, compared to 1.23s for CC with 99 time steps. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of sample points. Since BCC reduces the number of required points to 70.3% of a CC grid, the theoretical rendering time is reduced by a similar factor, assuming constant cost per point. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by approximately 29.7% compared to CC grids for the same spatial resolution and signal fidelity. Measured Performance: In the Turbulent Jet 4D example, BCC rendering took 1.01s (71% of CC time) with 138 time steps, compared to 1.23s for CC with 99 time steps. The BCC grid had 87M total points vs 168M for CC, but only 7.4M relevant voxels vs 9.4M for CC. For the Foot dataset, BCC rendering took 70% of the time of CC rendering, although renderings were almost identical. Strengths: Significant reduction in memory and computation for isotropic, spherically bandlimited signals. Lossless compression under the spherical bandlimit assumption. Limitations: Only optimal for spherically bandlimited signals. Requires careful handling of the 1/2 shift during rasterization. When to Use: Point-based volume rendering of isotropic data where memory and performance are critical. When Not to Use: Non-isotropic signals, or when compatibility with standard CC-based tools is required. The BCC grid was introduced as an alternative to the Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid for volumetric data representation. The concept is based on the work of Theussl ('01) and Neophytou ('02). The BCC lattice is known in mathematics and signal processing for its optimal packing density for spheres, which translates to fewer sample points needed for reconstruction of bandlimited signals. It has been applied to time-varying datasets such as turbulent jets and flows. name: BCC Grid Sampling
head: BCC Lattice Sampling, Body Centered Cartesian
body: BCC Grid Sampling is a 3D sampling method that uses a Body-Centered Cartesian (BCC) lattice to store volume data, requiring fewer sample points than a standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid for spherically bandlimited signals. It is distinguished from its sibling FCC Lattice Sampling by its application: BCC is best used with point-based object-order methods employing spherical filters, whereas FCC is optimal when the signal spectrum is spherical. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A continuous volumetric signal f(\mathbf{x}) assumed to be bandlimited with a spherical frequency spectrum. Output: A discrete set of sample values located at the nodes of a BCC lattice. Data Structures: The BCC lattice is defined as the dual of the Face-Centered Cartesian (FCC) lattice in the spatial domain. In the spatial domain, this structure gives rise to two interleaved CC grids. The lattice consists of two interpenetrating simple cubic sublattices. The sources describe the sampling interval separation as involving \sqrt{2} and 1/\sqrt{2}, which dictates the density relationship between the lattices. Numbered Steps: 1. Define the spatial bounding box and a base lattice spacing parameter. 2. Generate the first sublattice by sampling a simple cubic grid at intervals of basespacing. 3. Generate the second sublattice by sampling a simple cubic grid at intervals of basespacing, offset by half the spacing along each axis. 4. Discard any generated points that fall outside the bounding box. 5. During reconstruction, evaluate a radially symmetric filter at the distance between the query point and each sample point. Formulas: Sample Count Reduction: N{\text{BCC}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} N{\text{CC}} \approx 0.71 N{\text{CC}}. N{\text{BCC}}: Number of samples required for the BCC grid. N{\text{CC}}: Number of samples required for an equivalent-resolution CC grid. \sqrt{2}/2: Density ratio derived from the lattice geometry for equivalent spherical bandlimiting. 4D Extension: N{\text{BCC,4D}} = 0.50 N{\text{CC,4D}}. Parameters: basespacing: Controls the lattice constant. Typical values are not given in the sources. To achieve the 71% reduction relative to a target CC grid, basespacing is typically scaled by \sqrt{2} relative to the CC grid spacing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing with Trilinear Filters: Reconstruction of a BCC grid with trilinear filters leads to aliasing. This occurs because the trilinear filter's frequency response is not radially symmetric, causing it to include higher spectra during interpolation. Boundary Handling: Points generated near the bounding box edges must be explicitly clamped or discarded to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatebccsamples(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax, basespacing): """ Generates sample points for a BCC lattice within a bounding box. The BCC lattice is constructed as two interleaved CC grids. Sources do not specify exact iteration bounds or boundary clamping rules. """ samples = [] step = basespacing halfstep = step / 2.0 # Sublattice 1: Simple cubic grid at integer multiples of step x = xmin while x <= xmax: y = ymin while y <= ymax: z = zmin while z <= zmax: samples.append((x, y, z)) z += step y += step x += step # Sublattice 2: Offset by (step/2, step/2, step/2) x = xmin + halfstep while x <= xmax: y = ymin + halfstep while y <= ymax: z = zmin + halfstep while z <= zmax: samples.append((x, y, z)) z += step y += step x += step return samples def reconstructbcc(samples, querypoint, filterfunc): """ Reconstructs the value at querypoint using BCC samples. Must use a radially symmetric filter to avoid aliasing. Sources do not specify normalization or accumulation logic. """ value = 0.0 for samplepos, sampleval in samples: dx = querypoint[0] - samplepos[0] dy = querypoint[1] - samplepos[1] dz = querypoint[2] - samplepos[2] dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) weight = filterfunc(dist) value += sampleval weight return value BCC Lattice Storage refers to the specific data organization of the BCC grid, which arises as the dual of the FCC lattice in the spatial domain. It consists of two interleaved CC grids with a sampling interval separation involving \sqrt{2} and 1/\sqrt{2}. This structure requires 71% of the samples of a usual cubic Cartesian (CC) grid. For 4D volumes (time-varying), a 4D BCC storage requires only 50% of the 4D CC samples. It is best used in conjunction with point-based object-order methods using spherical (radially symmetric) filters to preserve the spherical shape of the frequency spectrum. Reconstruction with trilinear filters leads to aliasing due to the lack of radial symmetry in the filter's frequency response. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: BCC sampling requires approximately 71% of the memory of a CC grid for the same volume resolution. In 4D, it requires 50%. Time: BCC rendering took 70% of the time of CC rendering for the Foot dataset. Measured Performance: On the Foot dataset, BCC rendering achieved 70% of the time required by CC rendering. The UltraVis system, which optimizes cache performance, can render a 256^3 volume at 10 frames/s. While not exclusively BCC, the system highlights that cache management is key to fast volume rendering due to massive data sizes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in sample count (and thus memory and potentially computation) for spherically bandlimited signals. Limitations: Trilinear interpolation causes aliasing because the filter is not radially symmetric. It is less common than CC grids. When to Use: Use BCC grids with point-based object-order methods that employ spherical (radially symmetric) filters. Do not use with trilinear filters if aliasing is a concern. The BCC lattice is the dual of the Face-Centered Cartesian (FCC) lattice in the spatial domain. The spacing of samples in the BCC lattice is the reciprocal of that in the frequency domain, according to the Fourier scaling theorem. The concept extends to higher dimensions, such as 4D volumes. The efficiency of BCC grids is particularly relevant for signals with spherical frequency spectra, which are common in volume generation due to the sampling kernels used. name: FCC Lattice Sampling
head: FCC dataset lattice, FCC lattice, Face Centered Cubic (FCC) Lattice, Face-centered cartesian lattice
body: FCC Lattice Sampling is a 3D sampling method that defines a volume grid as a subset of the Cartesian lattice, offering superior sampling efficiency and optimality for signals sampled at a depressed rate compared to standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grids. It is distinguished from its sibling BCC Grid Sampling by its optimality conditions: while BCC is optimal for band-limited and isotropic signals, FCC is optimal when the signal spectrum is spherical or when sampling rates are depressed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D signal (volume data) defined over space. Output: A set of sample points located on the FCC lattice, and the corresponding scalar values at those points. Data Structures: The lattice is defined by a generator matrix G or an integer constraint. Generator Matrix (G): A 3 \times 3 matrix where columns are the basis vectors of the lattice. G = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} Integer Constraint: A point (x, y, z) belongs to the lattice if x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z} and x + y + z is even. Parameters: Generator Matrix G: Must be non-singular (\det(G) \neq 0). For the standard FCC lattice, \det(G) = 2. Applicability Condition: The method is most effective if the frequency spectrum of the signal is spherical. Steps: 1. Define Lattice Basis: Choose the generator matrix G for the FCC lattice. 2. Generate Sample Coordinates: For every integer vector \mathbf{v} = [i, j, k]^T \in \mathbb{Z}^3, compute the physical coordinate \mathbf{p} = G \cdot \mathbf{v}. Alternatively, iterate over integer coordinates (x, y, z) and include the point only if (x + y + z) \pmod 2 = 0. 3. Sample Signal: Evaluate the volume signal at each generated coordinate \mathbf{p}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatefcclatticepoints(boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax, stepsize=1.0): """ Generates coordinates for an FCC lattice within a bounding box. Uses the integer constraint definition: x + y + z is even. """ points = [] # Determine integer range covering the bounding box minx = math.floor(boundingboxmin[0] / stepsize) maxx = math.ceil(boundingboxmax[0] / stepsize) miny = math.floor(boundingboxmin[1] / stepsize) maxy = math.ceil(boundingboxmax[1] / stepsize) minz = math.floor(boundingboxmin[2] / stepsize) maxz = math.ceil(boundingboxmax[2] / stepsize) for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): # FCC condition: sum of coordinates must be even if (x + y + z) % 2 == 0: # Convert integer lattice index to physical space points.append((x stepsize, y stepsize, z stepsize)) return points Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: The integer constraint method requires careful clamping to ensure points fall exactly within the desired bounding box. Precision: When converting between the generator matrix representation and the integer constraint representation, floating-point errors may occur. The integer constraint method is generally more robust for storage and indexing. Degenerate Input: If the signal is not band-limited or has a non-spherical spectrum, the sampling efficiency advantage over CC grids may diminish. A water field defined by fixed Gaussian centers on an FCC lattice with fixed covariance, optimizing only two non-negative RGB density vectors per center (direct and backscatter attenuation) to prevent transport mass changes via geometric resizing. Time Complexity: Sampling time is proportional to the number of lattice points within the volume. The density of FCC points is half that of a CC grid with the same spacing, reducing the number of samples by approximately 50% compared to CC for equivalent spatial coverage, though the exact savings depend on the specific implementation and bounding box alignment. Memory Complexity: Storage is reduced compared to CC grids. The FCC lattice provides the densest packing of equal-sized spheres, making it space-efficient for storage. Performance: GPU ray casting implementations for FCC datasets have shown superior performance due to efficient empty space skipping and spline value evolution. Strengths: Better sampling efficiency than Cartesian lattices; optimal for signals sampled at a depressed rate; densest sphere packing. Limitations: Not optimal for all signal types (specifically, BCC is preferred for band-limited isotropic signals). When to use: Medical and scientific datasets, GPU ray casting, mobile volume rendering where memory and bandwidth are constrained. The FCC lattice was introduced as a more efficient alternative to Cartesian lattices for volume rendering. Kim implemented a real-time GPU iso-surface ray caster for FCC datasets, demonstrating the practical benefits of this approach. The theoretical basis for its optimality in specific signal conditions was indicated by Künsch et al.. The FCC lattice is the dual of the BCC lattice in the spatial domain. name: Normalized Free-Space Water Field
head: Optical-Mass Water Gaussians
body: The Normalized Free-Space Water Field is a volumetric representation for underwater rendering that models light attenuation and backscatter using fixed Gaussian bases on an FCC lattice. It solves the problem of simulating participating media by optimizing only two non-negative RGB density vectors per lattice point (direct and backscatter attenuation) while keeping geometry fixed to prevent transport mass changes via geometric resizing. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the spatial sampling lattice (FCC) from the optical parameter optimization, ensuring that the integral of the optical mass remains consistent under lattice refinement. Inputs: Scene bounds defined by Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points plus a fixed world-space margin. Lattice resolution parameter N (cells per axis). Standard deviation parameter s\Delta for the Gaussian covariance. Initial RGB density vectors \rho{D,i} and \rho{B,i} for each lattice point i. Outputs: Continuous direct extinction field \sigmaD(x). Continuous backscatter attenuation field \sigmaB(x). The method uses a fixed face-centered-cubic (FCC) lattice. Lattice Generation: For N cells per axis, there are 4N^3 centers. Each axis-aligned cell contains four offsets. Center Position (\mui): Fixed 3D coordinates on the FCC lattice within the axis-aligned bounds. Covariance (\Sigmai): Fixed axis-aligned diagonal matrix with standard deviation s\Delta along each dimension. Optimized Parameters: Two RGB vectors per center i: \rho{D,i}: Direct extinction density. \rho{B,i}: Backscatter attenuation density. The basis function is a normalized 3D Gaussian: \phii(x) = \frac{\exp \left[ -\frac{1}{2} (x - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui) \right]}{(2\pi)^{3/2} |\Sigmai|^{1/2}} Where \int{\mathbb{R}^3} \phii(x) dx = 1. The volume assigned to each lattice point is derived from the cell volume \Delta V = \Delta x \Delta y \Delta z: Vi = \frac{\Delta V}{4} Optical mass is assigned using the softplus function to ensure non-negativity: m{D,i} = Vi \text{softplus}(\rho{D,i}) m{B,i} = Vi \text{softplus}(\rho{B,i}) The continuous optical fields are computed as the sum of weighted basis functions: \sigmaD(x) = \sumi m{D,i} \phii(x) \sigmaB(x) = \sumi m{B,i} \phii(x) Standard Deviation (s\Delta): The compact configuration uses s = 1.3. An initial layout with s = 0.7 is retained as a control. Softplus: \text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computewaterfield(latticecenters, latticecovariances, cellvolume, rhoD, rhoB): """ Compute continuous optical fields for the Normalized Free-Space Water Field. Args: latticecenters: Array of shape (Ncenters, 3) containing mui. latticecovariances: Array of shape (Ncenters, 3) containing standard deviations sdelta for each axis. cellvolume: Scalar Delta V. rhoD: Array of shape (Ncenters, 3) for direct extinction densities. rhoB: Array of shape (Ncenters, 3) for backscatter attenuation densities. Returns: sigmaD: Function or array representing direct extinction field. sigmaB: Function or array representing backscatter attenuation field. """ Ncenters = latticecenters.shape[0] Vi = cellvolume / 4.0 # Calculate covariance determinants and inverses for each center # Covariance is diagonal: diag(s^2, s^2, s^2) # |Sigma| = s^6, Sigma^-1 = diag(1/s^2, 1/s^2, 1/s^2) ssq = latticecovariances 2 detSigma = np.prod(ssq, axis=1) # Shape (Ncenters,) invSigma = 1.0 / ssq # Shape (Ncenters, 3) # Precompute normalization constant denominator part # (2pi)^(3/2) |Sigma|^(1/2) normconst = (2 np.pi) 1.5 np.sqrt(detSigma) # Shape (Ncenters,) # Compute optical masses # softplus(x) = log(1 + exp(x)) softplusD = np.log(1 + np.exp(rhoD)) softplusB = np.log(1 + np.exp(rhoB)) mD = Vi softplusD # Shape (Ncenters, 3) mB = Vi softplusB # Shape (Ncenters, 3) # To evaluate at a query point xquery (shape (3,)): # sigmaD(x) = sumi mD,i phii(x) # phii(x) = exp(-0.5 (x-mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x-mu)) / normconsti def evaluatefields(xquery): # xquery shape (3,) # Broadcast to (Ncenters, 3) diff = latticecenters - xquery # Shape (Ncenters, 3) # Quadratic form: (x-mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x-mu) # Since Sigma^-1 is diagonal, this is sum over dims of diff^2 invSigma # diffsq = diff 2 # exponentarg = np.sum(diffsq invSigma, axis=1) # Shape (Ncenters,) # More efficient vectorized calculation exponentarg = np.sum(diff 2 invSigma, axis=1) # Basis functions phi = np.exp(-0.5 exponentarg) / normconst # Shape (Ncenters,) # Weighted sum sigmaDval = np.sum(mD phi[:, np.newaxis], axis=0) # Shape (3,) sigmaBval = np.sum(mB phi[:, np.newaxis], axis=0) # Shape (3,) return sigmaDval, sigmaBval return evaluatefields Truncation: Gaussian bases are not truncated at declared bounds. The method distinguishes between assigned full-space mass and mass inside the hard box. Implementers must account for the infinite support of the Gaussian when integrating or bounding the field. Mass Conservation: Keeping position and covariance fixed prevents transport mass from changing through geometric resizing. Optimizing only density vectors ensures optical mass scales with the assigned volume under lattice refinement. Complexity: The number of centers scales as 4N^3 for N cells per axis. Evaluation of the field at a point requires summing over all centers, leading to O(N^3) complexity per evaluation unless spatial acceleration structures are used. Memory: Requires storing 4N^3 centers, covariances, and two RGB density vectors. Strengths: Fixed geometry prevents artifacts from geometric resizing. The FCC lattice offers better sampling efficiency than Cartesian grids. Limitations: The infinite support of Gaussians requires careful handling of bounds for integration. The method is specific to underwater rendering scenarios requiring direct and backscatter attenuation modeling. The Normalized Free-Space Water Field was introduced in the context of optical-mass water Gaussians for per-scene underwater rendering. It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques but modifies the splatted surface statistics query by the water field. The approach uses a face-centered-cubic (FCC) lattice for sampling, which is a subset of the Cartesian lattice offering better sampling efficiency. name: FCC/BCC Subsampling via Voronoi Filtering
head: Granular 3D Multiresolution Transform, Granular Multiresolution Transform, Lattice-based Subsampling
body: This method provides a 3D multi-resolution scheme that represents volumetric data at resolutions that are powers of two (1/2, 1/4, 1/8 of original), resolving the rigidity of Cartesian schemes that only allow resolution changes by a factor of eight. It achieves this by subsampling a Cartesian volume onto Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) and Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) lattices using discrete filters designed to match the Nyquist regions of the target lattices. Unlike standard Cartesian downsampling, which loses information or requires larger kernels, this approach leverages the geometric properties of FCC and BCC lattices to maintain lossless compression for spherically bandlimited signals while reducing sample counts by half and quarter, respectively. Inputs: A volumetric dataset sampled on a 3D Cartesian lattice (\mathbb{Z}^3) at resolution N^3. Target resolution levels: FCC (1/2 density), BCC (1/4 density), and Cartesian (1/8 density). Outputs: Three volumes stored in compacted-Cartesian memory space: 1. FCC volume at N^3/2 samples. 2. BCC volume at N^3/4 samples. 3. Cartesian volume at N^3/8 samples. The data is stored in a 1-dimensional array (or 3D array) representing compacted-Cartesian-space. Canonical Lattice Spacing: Cartesian: Distance between neighboring points is 1. FCC/BCC: Distance between neighboring points is 2. Compacted-Cartesian Layout: To store non-Cartesian lattices efficiently, coordinates are transformed into a standard Cartesian grid: 1. BCC Storage: Odd-numbered z-slices are shifted by an offset of 1 along the x and y axes to align with even slices. The x and y axes are compacted (scaled) by a factor of 2. Result: A standard Cartesian grid where every other voxel corresponds to a BCC point. 2. FCC Storage: Each z-slice is decomposed into two sub-slices. The second sub-slice is pushed halfway between the current z-slice and the one behind it. All sub-slices are aligned along the z-axis. Scaling is applied to transform into a canonical-Cartesian-lattice. Result: A standard Cartesian grid where specific indices map to FCC points. Lattice Definitions: FCC Lattice: A sub-lattice of \mathbb{Z}^3 where the sum of coordinates is even. Density is 1/2 of Cartesian. BCC Lattice: A sub-lattice of \mathbb{Z}^3 where all three coordinates have the same parity (all even or all odd). Density is 1/4 of Cartesian. Duality: FCC and BCC are dual lattices of each other. Sampling Density: The sampling density is the inverse of the volume of the Voronoi cell: \text{Density} = \frac{1}{\text{Volume}(\text{Voronoi Cell})} FCC Voronoi Cell: Rhombic dodecahedron. BCC Voronoi Cell: Truncated octahedron. Nyquist Regions: To subsample properly, the original spectrum must be band-limited to the Voronoi cell of the dual lattice. FCC Subsampling: The Nyquist region is the Voronoi cell of the BCC lattice (truncated octahedron). This occupies exactly half the volume of the original cubic spectrum. BCC Subsampling: The Nyquist region is the Voronoi cell of the FCC lattice (rhombic dodecahedron). This occupies exactly one-quarter the volume of the original cubic spectrum. Goal: Design a bandpass filter whose support in the frequency domain resembles the Voronoi cell of the dual lattice of the subsampling lattice. Ideal filters are band-limited but have infinite spatial support, so compact support filters derived from reconstruction kernels are used. Filters: 1. FCC Linear Filter: Linear filter on the first neighbors cell of the FCC (a cub-octahedron). 2. FCC Cubic Filter: Convolution of the linear element FCC with itself. 3. BCC Linear Filter: Linear box spline BCC filter whose support is a rhombic dodecahedron. 4. BCC Cubic Filter: Convolution of the linear box spline with itself. Algorithm Steps: 1. Reconstruct Continuous Volume: Interpolate the original Cartesian volume to a continuous function using a high-quality filter (e.g., tri-cubic B-spline). 2. Band-Limit for FCC (1/2 Resolution): Apply a filter to the continuous volume such that the resulting spectrum is contained within the truncated octahedron (BCC Voronoi cell). Resample the filtered continuous volume onto the FCC lattice points. Implementation Note: The filter size must be chosen to ensure proper band-limiting before resampling. 3. Band-Limit for BCC (1/4 Resolution): Apply a filter to the continuous volume such that the resulting spectrum is contained within the rhombic dodecahedron (FCC Voronoi cell). Resample the filtered continuous volume onto the BCC lattice points. Implementation Note: Similar computation to FCC, but with the stricter quarter-volume constraint. 4. Cartesian Subsampling (1/8 Resolution): Standard Cartesian downsampling (typically by factor of 2 in each dimension) is used for the 1/8 resolution level, as FCC/BCC nesting does not provide a direct 1/8 sub-lattice. 5. Coordinate Transformation (Storage): Transform the sampled points from canonical-lattice-space to compacted-Cartesian-space. Map coordinates to 1-dimensional indices for file storage. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def granularmultiresolutiontransform(volumecartesian): """ volumecartesian: 3D array of shape (N, N, N) on Cartesian lattice. Returns: volumefcc: 3D array of shape (N, N, N/2) in compacted-Cartesian space. volumebcc: 3D array of shape (N/2, N/2, N/2) in compacted-Cartesian space. volumecart18: 3D array of shape (N/2, N/2, N/2) in Cartesian space. """ # 1. Reconstruct continuous volume from Cartesian samples # Use a tri-cubic B-spline filter for high-quality reconstruction # This step effectively creates a continuous function f(x,y,z) continuousvol = reconstructcontinuous(volumecartesian, filtertype='tricubicbspline') # 2. Generate FCC samples (1/2 resolution) # FCC points are those (x,y,z) in Z^3 where (x+y+z) is even. # Canonical spacing is 2. fccpoints = generatefcclatticepoints(originalsize=N, spacing=2) # Filter for FCC: Band-limit to BCC Voronoi cell (Truncated Octahedron) # Use FCC Linear Filter (support: cub-octahedron) or Cubic Filter filteredfcc = applyfilter(continuousvol, fccpoints, filtertype='fcclinear') # Store in compacted-Cartesian space volumefcc = compacttocartesianfcc(filteredfcc) # 3. Generate BCC samples (1/4 resolution) # BCC points are those (x,y,z) in Z^3 where x,y,z have same parity. # Canonical spacing is 2. bccpoints = generatebcclatticepoints(originalsize=N, spacing=2) # Filter for BCC: Band-limit to FCC Voronoi cell (Rhombic Dodecahedron) # Use BCC Linear Filter (support: rhombic dodecahedron) or Cubic Filter filteredbcc = applyfilter(continuousvol, bccpoints, filtertype='bcclinear') # Store in compacted-Cartesian space volumebcc = compacttocartesianbcc(filteredbcc) # 4. Generate Cartesian samples (1/8 resolution) # Standard downsampling by factor of 2 in each dimension volumecart18 = downsamplecartesian(volumecartesian, factor=2) return volumefcc, volumebcc, volumecart18 def generatefcclatticepoints(size, spacing): """ Generates FCC lattice points within the volume bounds. FCC: sum of coordinates is even. """ points = [] # Iterate over canonical grid with spacing 2 # Note: Implementation details of 'generate' depend on specific lattice generation algorithm # Standard approach: iterate x,y,z from 0 to size/spacing, check parity for x in range(0, size, spacing): for y in range(0, size, spacing): for z in range(0, size, spacing): if (x + y + z) % 2 == 0: points.append((x, y, z)) return points def generatebcclatticepoints(size, spacing): """ Generates BCC lattice points within the volume bounds. BCC: all coordinates have same parity (all even or all odd relative to origin). """ points = [] for x in range(0, size, spacing): for y in range(0, size, spacing): for z in range(0, size, spacing): # Check if x, y, z are all even or all odd if (x % 2 == y % 2 == z % 2): points.append((x, y, z)) return points def compacttocartesianfcc(samples): """ Transforms FCC samples to compacted-Cartesian storage. 1. Decompose each z-slice into two sub-slices. 2. Push second sub-slice halfway between current and previous z-slice. 3. Align all sub-slices along z-axis. 4. Scale to canonical Cartesian. """ # Specific indexing logic from Figure 6. # The output array shape will be (N, N, N/2) if original was N^3. # This function maps the irregular FCC grid to a regular Cartesian grid. outputshape = (N, N, N // 2) outputarray = zeros(outputshape) for (x, y, z) in samples: # Map (x,y,z) to compacted index (ix, iy, iz) # Logic: # z is split. If z is even, it goes to one set of slices. # If z is odd, it goes to the "halfway" slices. # The exact mapping requires implementing the decomposition described in. # For brevity, we assume a helper function exists that performs this specific geometric compaction. ix, iy, iz = mapfcctocompactedcartesian(x, y, z) outputarray[ix, iy, iz] = samples[(x, y, z)] return outputarray def compacttocartesianbcc(samples): """ Transforms BCC samples to compacted-Cartesian storage. 1. Shift odd z-slices by offset 1 in x and y. 2. Compact x and y axes by factor of 2. """ # Specific indexing logic from Figure 5. # The output array shape will be (N/2, N/2, N/2) if original was N^3. outputshape = (N // 2, N // 2, N // 2) outputarray = zeros(outputshape) for (x, y, z) in samples: # Determine if z is even or odd if z % 2 == 1: # Shift odd slices xadj = x - 1 yadj = y - 1 else: xadj = x yadj = y # Compact by factor of 2 ix = xadj // 2 iy = yadj // 2 iz = z // 2 outputarray[ix, iy, iz] = samples[(x, y, z)] return outputarray Infinite Support: Ideal subsampling filters are band-limited in frequency but have infinite support in space. Practical implementations must use compact support filters (like the linear/cubic filters described), which may introduce approximation errors. Girdering Artifacts: The linear FCC filter can exhibit "girdering" artifacts. Cubic filters or other specialized filters may be required to mitigate this. Precision: Ensure that the filter size is sufficient to capture the necessary frequency content for proper band-limiting before resampling. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method reduces memory usage by half (FCC) and quarter (BCC) compared to the original Cartesian volume at those respective levels. Storage is efficient due to compacted-Cartesian layout. Time: The filtering step involves convolution with compact support filters (linear/cubic). The complexity depends on the filter kernel size. Resampling is linear in the number of output samples. Performance: Quality: The FCC/BCC pipeline preserves more detail than a comparable Cartesian multi-resolution pipeline at the same reduction ratios (1/2, 1/4). Benchmark: Tested on ML dataset (40^3) and Skull dataset (128^3). The FCC volume has half the samples, and BCC has quarter samples of the original. Strengths: Allows resolution changes by powers of two (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) in 3D, unlike Cartesian schemes which typically jump by 1/8. Superior representation accuracy compared to Cartesian resampling. Limitations: Requires complex coordinate transformations for storage (compaction). Linear FCC filters may produce artifacts. Origin: The method was introduced by Alireza Entezari, Tai Meng, Steven Bergner, and Torsten Möller in the paper "A Granular Three Dimensional Multiresolution Transform" (EuroVis 2006). History: The work addresses the limitations of separable Cartesian multi-resolution schemes in 3D, which are rigid and only allow resolution changes by powers of eight. By leveraging the properties of FCC and BCC lattices, which are dual to each other and have higher packing densities, the authors created a more flexible multi-resolution framework. Usage: Used in volume rendering pipelines where efficient multi-resolution representation is needed for ray-casting. It enables rendering of continuous volumes from sampled data on FCC, BCC, and Cartesian lattices using appropriate reconstruction kernels (linear/cubic element FCC, linear/cubic box spline BCC).
