name: Hierarchical and Multi-Resolution Splatting
head: Multi-Resolution Splatting, Hierarchical Splatting, LOD Splatting
body: Hierarchical and Multi-Resolution Splatting optimizes the rendering of dense volumetric data and point clouds by organizing primitives into a spatial hierarchy, allowing the renderer to select primitives of varying granularity based on screen-space footprint or error metrics. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering high-density data by replacing clusters of fine primitives with single, aggregated coarse primitives in homogeneous or distant regions, while preserving detail in complex or foreground areas. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by its reliance on explicit error metrics or fixed downsampling rates to drive the selection of the appropriate resolution level, rather than relying solely on static distance thresholds or fixed grid subdivisions. The methods in this family share the mechanism of hierarchical decomposition and error-driven or distance-driven primitive selection, building on Splatting. 1. Hierarchical Decomposition: The input data (volume, point cloud, or Gaussian set) is organized into a tree structure or grid (e.g., octree, pyramid, or uniform grid cells). Each node or cell represents a spatial region and stores aggregate properties derived from its children or contained points. 2. Error Metric Computation: For each internal node, a local error metric E is computed to quantify the approximation cost of representing the node's children with the node's aggregate properties. Not given in the sources. 3. Adaptive Traversal and Selection: During rendering, the hierarchy is traversed from the root to the leaves or cells are traversed in front-to-back order. A node or cell is selected as a leaf (and thus rendered as a single primitive) if its error E is below a user-defined threshold \epsilon or if its projected screen-space footprint is smaller than a pixel threshold. If the error exceeds the threshold, the algorithm recurses to the children. 4. Primitive Aggregation: When a node is selected, its children are merged into a single representative primitive. The primitive's attributes (position, size, color, opacity) are computed as weighted averages or sums of the children's attributes. For Gaussian splats, this involves merging covariances and spherical harmonics coefficients. 5. Multi-Resolution Rendering: The final image is composed of primitives from various levels of the hierarchy, allowing for efficient culling of distant or homogeneous regions while maintaining fidelity in foreground or complex areas. Multi Resolution Alpha Blending is a fragment accumulation strategy used in hierarchical point splatting to resolve depth-ordering ambiguities when multiple splats project to the same pixel. It solves the problem of correct alpha compositing in scenes with varying point densities by collecting, sorting, and blending fragments on a per-pixel basis rather than globally. It differs from global sorting methods by operating on small, localized lists, which reduces computational overhead and memory bandwidth usage. Multi-Resolution and Level of Detail (LOD) techniques optimize volume and point cloud rendering by decomposing data into hierarchical structures, allowing the renderer to select primitives of varying granularity based on spatial error or screen-space footprint. This family solves the performance bottleneck of rendering high-density data by replacing clusters of fine primitives with single, aggregated coarse primitives in homogeneous or distant regions, while preserving detail in complex or foreground areas. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by its reliance on explicit error metrics or fixed downsampling rates to drive the selection of the appropriate resolution level, rather than relying solely on static distance thresholds or fixed grid subdivisions. Definition: A splatting implementation using Rational Basis Functions (RBFs) located by an octree, evaluated via fragment programs on cache-sheets. Steps: Add an octree to locate the Rational Basis Functions (RBFs) intersecting the cache-sheets. For each sheet plane pixel, use a fragment program to evaluate the exponential Gaussian function of the RBFs. Performance: 7 to 70 fps for Blunt-fin rendering at 400^2 resolution, caused by large variation of RBFs. Hardware: 2.8 GHz Pentium-IV, nVidia GeForce FX 5900. Definition: A method that organizes deformation as a mergeable tree, where each node represents a rigid part of an articulated object, and the overall deformation is computed by traversing the kinematic chain. Definition: A splatting strategy that converts rasterized surface points into Gaussian splats and uses a multi-layer accumulation strategy based on depth to handle occlusion boundaries and disocclusions, producing smooth derivatives. Steps: Render multiple layers of G-buffers. Maintain three accumulation buffers during splatting: S^+ for splats occluding the target pixel, S^- for occluded splats, and S^o for splats at the same depth as the target pixel. To determine splat depth relation, pair up multi-layer surface intersections at splat center p with closest intersections at target pixel q in depth. The p layer paired with the front-most q layer is assigned to S^o, layers in front of it to S^+, and the rest to S^-. After all splats are rendered, buffers are separately normalized following Eq. 3 and composited in S^-, S^o, S^+ order using over-compositing to produce the final result S. Pitfall: Single-layer splatting treats all splats at the same depth, ignoring occlusions and producing spurious derivatives for occluded objects. Multi-layer splatting corrects this by distinguishing front, back, and coincident depths. Definition: Reduces Gaussian splat sizes to improve rendering speed while minimizing visual quality impact. Parameter: SplatDownscaleFactor: Float parameter in range [0, 1] controlling the degree of size reduction. Definition: Copying a nearest-neighbour splat cluster into an empty adjacent voxel cell to fill space. Pitfall: Visual coherence issues: only 60% of source voxels find an empty adjacent cell on the butterfly scene; SH coefficients are not copied resulting in slightly flat shading; noticeable visual seam at source/target boundary. Performance: p95 10.6 ms across 200-op session; 121/200 ops committed; 4,735 splats stacked; subjective coherence rated 3/5. Definition: A rendering algorithm that traverses out-of-core hierarchical structures (uniform grid cells) in front-to-back order, dynamically selecting the Level of Detail (LOD) for each cell based on distance to the viewpoint to balance performance and quality. Steps: Generate a discretization of the scene using a uniform grid, storing cells out-of-core. Produce multiple simplified versions for each cell by decimating points by a factor of 10 for each decreasing LOD level, keeping these in main memory. Traverse cells overlapping the view frustum in front-to-back order. Dynamically select the most appropriate LOD for each cell based on the distance from the cell center to the viewpoint. Manually tune scaling factors for points at each LOD level to achieve visually pleasing results. If interaction stops and the viewpoint is held still, load from disk and display cells containing original points (finest LOD). Performance: Tested on Intel Core i7-4790K CPU and GeForce GTX 970 with ~150 million points: 600 fps for far-away views, 300-600 fps for closer ones. Render quality remains good even with aggressive pruning (1 point out of 100) for areas with uniform sampling density. The concept of hierarchical splatting emerged alongside the need for real-time volume rendering. Early implementations focused on accelerating the evaluation of splats using spatial data structures. For instance, Jang et al. [Jang04] added an octree to locate rational basis functions (RBFs) intersecting cache-sheets, evaluating them via fragment programs. This approach allowed for interactive frame rates on mid-sized datasets, though performance varied significantly based on the variation of RBFs. Later, Neophytou et al. [Neophytou06] utilized floating-point rasterization facilities to avoid expensive fragment programs, achieving near-interactive frame rates on irregular data. In the context of Gaussian Splatting, hierarchical methods have been adapted to handle dynamic deformations and multi-resolution rendering. TreeSplat, for example, organizes deformation as a mergeable tree for articulated objects. Depth-aware multi-layer splatting was introduced to handle occlusion boundaries in differentiable rendering, ensuring accurate derivatives by distinguishing between occluding, occluded, and coincident splats. Optimization techniques like Splat Downscaling adjust splat sizes to improve rendering speed. Splat Stacking copies nearest-neighbour splat clusters into empty adjacent voxel cells to fill space, though it introduces visual seams and flat shading due to uncopied SH coefficients. Hierarchical Point Cloud Rendering traverses out-of-core uniform grid cells in front-to-back order, dynamically selecting LOD based on distance to the viewpoint. name: Multi Resolution Alpha Blending
body: Multi Resolution Alpha Blending is a fragment accumulation strategy used in hierarchical point splatting to resolve depth-ordering ambiguities when multiple splats project to the same pixel. It solves the problem of correct alpha compositing in scenes with varying point densities by collecting, sorting, and blending fragments on a per-pixel basis rather than globally. It differs from global sorting methods by operating on small, localized lists, which reduces computational overhead and memory bandwidth usage. Inputs: A set of splatted points projected to screen space, each with position (x, y), depth z, opacity \alpha, color c, and a reference to its hierarchical layer index l. Outputs: A final color value C\Lambda for each pixel. Data Structures: Per-pixel list (\Lambda{li, xi, yi}): A dynamic array storing fragments for pixel (xi, yi) at layer li. Fragment record: Contains depth z, opacity \alpha, color c, and layer index l. Maximum size: 16 elements per list. Steps: 1. Collection: For each point, project it to screen space. For every pixel covered by the splat, append the fragment to the corresponding per-pixel list \Lambda{li, xi, yi}. Store the pair (z, \text{index}) to allow efficient sorting. 2. Clamping: If a list exceeds 16 elements, keep only the 16 fragments with the smallest depth values (closest to the camera) to maintain the limit. 3. Sorting: Sort each list by depth z in ascending order (front-to-back). Use GPU-friendly sorting algorithms, specifically warp-local (32 threads) and shuffle-based bitonic sorts. The sorting process iteratively replaces the last 16 elements with new unsorted ones until all fragments are processed. 4. Blending: Perform front-to-back alpha blending on the sorted list in the same pass as sorting, leveraging register storage for intermediate values. Formulas: The final color C\Lambda for a pixel is computed as: C\Lambda = \sum{m=1}^{|\Lambda|} Tm \cdot \alpham \cdot cm The transmittance Tm at fragment m is: Tm = \prod{i=1}^{m-1} (1 - \alphai) Where: |\Lambda| is the number of fragments in the list (up to 16). \alpham is the opacity of fragment m. cm is the color of fragment m. Tm is the transmittance, representing the probability that light passes through all preceding fragments 1 to m-1. Parameters: Max list size: 16. Minimum contribution weight: \epsilon = 0.25. To prevent the contribution of points from finer levels from disappearing during blending, their weight is clamped to at least this value. Edge cases and pitfalls: Occlusion errors: In scenes with large deviations in point density, the neural network may fail to correctly evaluate occlusion in edge cases. Mitigation: Include points from coarser layers during blending to ensure robust occlusion handling. The additional cost is minimal (< 0.5ms). Precision: The approximation of limiting lists to 16 elements causes no significant loss of quality because the blending contribution of later (distant) points is very low. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiresolutionalphablending(fragments): """ fragments: list of dicts with keys 'x', 'y', 'z', 'alpha', 'color', 'layer' """ # 1. Initialize per-pixel lists pixellists = {} for frag in fragments: key = (frag['x'], frag['y'], frag['layer']) if key not in pixellists: pixellists[key] = [] pixellists[key].append(frag) finalcolors = {} # 2. Process each pixel list for key, fraglist in pixellists.items(): x, y, layer = key # 3. Sort by depth ascending (front-to-back) # GPU implementation uses warp-local (32 threads) and shuffle-based bitonic sorts fraglist.sort(key=lambda f: f['z']) # 4. Clamp to max size 16, keeping front-most (smallest z) if len(fraglist) > 16: fraglist = fraglist[:16] # 5. Front-to-back blending transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for frag in fraglist: alpha = frag['alpha'] color = frag['color'] # Clamp contribution to epsilon=0.25 if required for fine layers weight = transmittance alpha accumulatedcolor = [ accumulatedcolor[i] + weight color[i] for i in range(3) ] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) finalcolors[(x, y)] = accumulatedcolor return finalcolors A compact neural network that consolidates a feature image pyramid of n layers into a single full-resolution image, resembling a U-Net decoder. It incorporates a single gated convolution [YLY 19] in each layer with a self-bypass connection and a feature size of 32. It requires a significantly smaller and more efficient network than hole-filling networks because the renderer fills gaps autonomously and generates smooth output. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of splats and pixels, optimized by the 16-element list limit. Per-pixel sorting is faster than global sorting for this approach due to the higher amount and smaller sizes of points. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of pixels times the maximum list size (16). Performance: The sorting and accumulation pass is critical. The use of GPU-friendly sorting (warp-local, shuffle-based) ensures high throughput. The additional cost of including coarser layer points for occlusion handling is < 0.5ms. Strengths: Efficient handling of varying point densities; avoids global sorting overhead; robust occlusion via coarse layer inclusion. Limitations: Approximation of limiting to 16 fragments may miss very distant but significant contributions (though deemed negligible); requires careful handling of minimum weight contributions for fine layers. Multi Resolution Alpha Blending is a core component of the TRIPS (Trilinear Point Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering) method. It was introduced to address the inefficiencies of global sorting in hierarchical point-based rendering, leveraging the fact that per-pixel lists are small and numerous, making local sorting more efficient on GPU architectures. name: Neural Reconstruction Network
head: Feature Pyramid Consolidation Network, U-Net Decoder for Volume Rendering
body: The Neural Reconstruction Network (NRN) is a compact neural network that consolidates a feature image pyramid of n layers into a single full-resolution image, resembling a U-Net decoder. It builds on Multi Resolution Alpha Blending by taking the blended output from multiple splatting resolutions and fusing them to produce the final view. Unlike hole-filling networks, the NRN is significantly smaller and more efficient because the underlying renderer autonomously fills gaps and generates smooth output via trilinear splatting, allowing the network to focus on high-quality texture reconstruction and minimal outlier removal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A feature image pyramid comprising n layers, where each layer corresponds to a different resolution level of the rasterized scene. Output: A single full-resolution RGB image. Data Structures: The input is a list of n feature maps. The exact channel dimensions are not specified, but the internal feature size is fixed at 32. The output is a tensor of shape (H, W, 3) for RGB, where H, W are the highest resolution dimensions. Steps: 1. Initialize the network with a U-Net decoder-like architecture. 2. For each layer l in the pyramid (from coarsest to finest, excluding the final layer): a. Apply a bilinear upsampling operation to the current feature map to match the resolution of the next finer layer. b. Merge the upsampled output with the subsequent (finer) level's features via concatenation or addition (standard U-Net skip connection behavior implied by "merging"). c. Process the merged features through a single gated convolution block. 3. For the final layer: a. Process the features through a single gated convolution block without subsequent upsampling. 4. Output the resulting full-resolution image. Gated Convolution Block Details: Each layer incorporates a single gated convolution [YLY 19]. The block includes a self-bypass connection (residual connection). The feature size (number of channels) is 32. The gated convolution mechanism typically splits the output channels into two halves: one passed through a sigmoid activation (gate) and the other multiplied element-wise. Parameters: Feature size: 32. Number of pyramid layers: n (variable, determined by the renderer's multi-resolution setup). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The network assumes the renderer has already produced a pyramid with sufficient coverage. If the renderer fails to fill gaps, the NRN may still produce artifacts, though it is designed to handle minor holes. Precision issues in bilinear upsampling should be managed using standard floating-point operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neuralreconstructionnetwork(pyramidlayers): """ Consolidates a feature image pyramid into a single full-resolution image. Args: pyramidlayers: List of feature maps [L1, L2,..., Ln] from coarsest to finest. Returns: Full-resolution RGB image. """ # Assume pyramidlayers has n elements n = len(pyramidlayers) # Start with the coarsest layer currentfeatures = pyramidlayers[0] # Process intermediate layers for i in range(n - 1): # Bilinear upsampling to match the resolution of the next layer # Note: Standard bilinear interpolation upscaled = bilinearupsample(currentfeatures, targetsize=pyramidlayers[i+1].shape) # Merge with the subsequent finer level # Assuming concatenation along channel dimension as per typical U-Net decoder merged = concatenate(upscaled, pyramidlayers[i+1], axis=-1) # Apply gated convolution with self-bypass currentfeatures = gatedconvblock(merged, featuresize=32) # Process the final layer # No upsampling for the final layer finaloutput = gatedconvblock(currentfeatures, featuresize=32) return finaloutput def gatedconvblock(features, featuresize=32): """ Applies a single gated convolution with a self-bypass connection. Args: features: Input feature map. featuresize: Number of channels in the output. Returns: Output feature map with residual connection. """ # Standard gated convolution implementation # Split output into two halves: linear and gate # Typically: conv -> split -> sigmoid -> multiply # For simplicity, we assume a standard gated conv block exists # The block has featuresize channels # Apply convolution to get 2 featuresize channels convoutput = convolution2d(features, outchannels=2 featuresize, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Split into linear and gate parts linearpart, gatepart = split(convoutput, axis=-1) # Apply sigmoid to gate part gate = sigmoid(gatepart) # Element-wise multiplication gatedoutput = linearpart gate # Self-bypass (residual) connection # Note: If input and output dimensions differ, a 1x1 conv might be needed for the skip # Assuming dimensions match for simplicity as per "self-bypass" output = gatedoutput + features return output def bilinearupsample(features, targetsize): """ Performs bilinear upsampling to the target size. Args: features: Input feature map. targetsize: Tuple (height, width) for the output. Returns: Upsampled feature map. """ # Standard bilinear interpolation # Implementation depends on framework, but logically: # Resize using bilinear kernel return resizebilinear(features, targetsize) def concatenate(a, b, axis=-1): """ Concatenates two tensors along the specified axis. """ return torch.cat([a, b], dim=axis) def convolution2d(features, outchannels, kernelsize, padding): """ Applies a 2D convolution. """ # Standard 2D convolution # Assuming input channels are inferred from features return torch.nn.functional.conv2d(features, weight, bias, padding=padding) def sigmoid(x): """ Sigmoid activation function. """ return 1 / (1 + torch.exp(-x)) def split(tensor, axis=-1): """ Splits a tensor into two equal halves along the specified axis. """ mid = tensor.shape[axis] // 2 return tensor[...,:mid], tensor[..., mid:] def resizebilinear(features, targetsize): """ Resizes features using bilinear interpolation. """ # Standard bilinear resize return torch.nn.functional.interpolate(features, size=targetsize, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) A variant that explicitly integrates adversarial training. It processes the pyramid of rasterized raw images to generate a full-resolution RGB image in one pass, fusing coarse and fine details to cover bleeding surfaces. Unlike the basic NRN, it renders views at down-sampled resolutions in addition to the highest resolution to pair with a multi-scale discriminator, enabling joint adversarial-rasterization training for better generalization and artifact reduction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, the network is described as "significantly smaller and more efficient" than hole-filling networks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The restrained number of features (32) and convolutional operations suggests low memory usage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient due to small size; leverages the renderer's ability to fill gaps autonomously; focuses on high-quality texture reconstruction. The adversarial variant handles bleeding surfaces and generates realistic outputs even with insufficient point cloud information. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the input pyramid; if the renderer produces poor coverage, the network may struggle. When to use: When real-time or efficient rendering is required, and the underlying splatting renderer provides good initial coverage. Use the adversarial variant when high visual fidelity and generalization to unseen inputs are critical. When not to use: When the renderer fails to produce a coherent pyramid or when computational resources are extremely limited and even the small network is too heavy. The Neural Reconstruction Network was introduced in the TRIPS paper (Trilinear Point Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering). It was designed to replace traditional hole-filling networks with a more efficient decoder-like architecture, capitalizing on the smooth output generated by trilinear point splatting. The U-Net Synthesizer variant was later proposed in CE-NPBG (Connectivity Enhanced Neural Point-Based Graphics for Novel View Synthesis in Autonomous Driving Scenes) to address bleeding surfaces and improve realism through adversarial training. name: Multi-Resolution and Level of Detail (Pyramid, LOD, Downsampling)
body: Multi-Resolution and Level of Detail (LOD) techniques optimize volume and point cloud rendering by decomposing data into hierarchical structures, allowing the renderer to select primitives of varying granularity based on spatial error or screen-space footprint. This family solves the performance bottleneck of rendering high-density data by replacing clusters of fine primitives with single, aggregated coarse primitives in homogeneous or distant regions, while preserving detail in complex or foreground areas. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by its reliance on explicit error metrics or fixed downsampling rates to drive the selection of the appropriate resolution level, rather than relying solely on static distance thresholds or fixed grid subdivisions. The methods in this family share the mechanism of hierarchical decomposition and error-driven or distance-driven primitive selection, building on Splatting. Uses a fixed-resolution pyramid structure where each level is 1/8th the resolution of the previous, aggregating 2 \times 2 \times 2 voxels. It is chosen when a regular, predictable hierarchy is preferred over adaptive spatial partitioning. Groups points into clusters based on a local RMS error metric to replace many small points with one large point. It is chosen for dense point clouds where overdraw is the primary bottleneck. Adapts 3D Gaussian properties (covariance, opacity, SH) into hierarchies or compressed codebooks. It is chosen for large-scale 3DGS scenes to manage memory and rendering latency. Generates a flat, contiguous buffer of splat indices by iteratively downsampling a voxel occupancy mask. It is chosen when a flat buffer structure is required for efficient GPU indexing, avoiding tree traversal overhead. The concept of multi-resolution rendering for volumes originated with the need to interactively visualize large medical and scientific datasets. Early work by Laur and Hanrahan (1991) introduced hierarchical point clouds using error metrics. Subsequent developments extended these ideas to volumetric splatting using pyramidal structures and more recently to 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle the memory constraints of neural radiance fields. The technique is widely used in scientific visualization, medical imaging, and real-time rendering of large-scale 3D scenes.

name: Hierarchical Splatting
head: Progressive refinement splatting, Pyramid Splatting, Pyramidal volume splatting
body: Hierarchical splatting is a progressive refinement algorithm for volume rendering that uses a pyramidal volume representation to achieve real-time interactive rendering. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering large, high-resolution volume datasets by decomposing the volume into cubes of varying sizes based on homogeneity, approximating each homogeneous section with a single large splat projected onto the image plane. Unlike standard splatting which treats all voxels equally, hierarchical splatting adapts the resolution of the rendering primitives to the visual complexity of the data, allowing for efficient culling of distant or homogeneous regions while maintaining fidelity in complex areas. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset of size N^3 samples. A user-specified error threshold \epsilon that measures the desired homogeneity for the volume decomposition. Outputs: A rendered image composed of RGBA Gouraud-shaded polygons approximating the splats. Data Structures: The core data structure is a Volume Pyramid. Structure: A sequence of \log2 N volumes. Level 0: The original dataset of size N^3. Level k (k > 0): Created from Level k-1 by averaging each 2 \times 2 \times 2 group of samples. This results in a volume with one-eighth the resolution (linear dimensions halved) of the previous level. Node Content: Each node (voxel) in the pyramid stores: Average RGB color. Average Alpha (opacity). Estimated Error (E): The approximation cost of representing the node's children with the node's aggregate properties. This error quantifies the deviation if the region is rendered with one average splat instead of the original data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pyramid Construction: Build the pyramid from the input volume. For each level k from 1 to \log2 N: Iterate through all 2 \times 2 \times 2 blocks of voxels in Level k-1. Compute the average RGB and Alpha for the block to form the voxel at the corresponding position in Level k. Compute the error E for the new voxel. The error represents the variance or deviation of the 8 child values from the parent's average. 2. Octree Fitting (Traverse and Select): Traverse the pyramid to determine which nodes are rendered as single splats and which are subdivided. Start at the root (Level \log2 N). For a given node, compare its error E against the user threshold \epsilon. If E \le \epsilon: The node is homogeneous enough. It is selected as a leaf node. A single splat is generated for this node, scaled to match the projection of the corresponding volume cell. If E > \epsilon: The node is too heterogeneous. Recursively traverse its children in the next finer level. The traversal continues down the pyramid until the error in a node is less than or equal to the desired threshold. 3. Footprint Table Generation: For every level of the pyramid, calculate proper-sized footprint tables. These tables define the screen-space footprint (polygon shape and size) for projecting and compositing cells of that specific level. The footprint size scales with the resolution of the pyramid level; higher levels (coarser resolution) have larger footprints. 4. Rendering (Splatting): Identify the set of leaf nodes from the traversal step. Sort these leaf nodes in back-to-front order based on the viewing direction. For each leaf node: Project the volume cell onto the image plane. Approximate the splat as an RGBA Gouraud-shaded polygon. Use the pre-calculated footprint table for the node's pyramid level to determine the polygon's geometry. Rasterize the polygon using standard graphics hardware. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildpyramid(volumedata): """ Constructs the volume pyramid. volumedata: 3D list of shape (N, N, N) containing (R, G, B, A) tuples. Returns: List of pyramid levels, where level 0 is original data. """ pyramid = [volumedata] currentlevel = volumedata n = len(currentlevel) while n > 1: nextn = n // 2 nextlevel = [] nexterror = [] for x in range(nextn): levelx = [] errorx = [] for y in range(nextn): levely = [] errory = [] for z in range(nextn): # Extract 2x2x2 block from current level block = [] for dx in range(2): for dy in range(2): for dz in range(2): block.append(currentlevel[2x+dx][2y+dy][2z+dz]) # Compute average RGB and Alpha avgr = sum(v[0] for v in block) / 8.0 avgg = sum(v[1] for v in block) / 8.0 avgb = sum(v[2] for v in block) / 8.0 avga = sum(v[3] for v in block) / 8.0 avg = (avgr, avgg, avgb, avga) levely.append(avg) # Compute error (variance of children from parent mean) err = sum((v[0]-avgr)2 + (v[1]-avgg)2 + (v[2]-avgb)2 + (v[3]-avga)2 for v in block) / 8.0 errory.append(err) levelx.append(levely) errorx.append(errory) nextlevel.append(levelx) nexterror.append(errorx) pyramid.append({'data': nextlevel, 'error': nexterror}) currentlevel = nextlevel n = nextn return pyramid def traverseandselect(pyramid, threshold): """ Traverses the pyramid to select leaf nodes for splatting. pyramid: List of pyramid levels (index 0 is finest, index -1 is coarsest root) threshold: User-specified error threshold epsilon Returns: List of leaf nodes, each containing (levelindex, x, y, z, rgb, alpha) """ leaves = [] numlevels = len(pyramid) def recurse(levelidx, x, y, z): node = pyramid[levelidx] error = node['error'][x][y][z] rgbalpha = node['data'][x][y][z] # If error is below threshold, select this node as a leaf if error <= threshold: leaves.append({ 'level': levelidx, 'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z, 'rgb': rgbalpha[:3], 'alpha': rgbalpha[3] }) else: # Recurse to children (finer level) if levelidx + 1 < numlevels: basex = 2 x basey = 2 y basez = 2 z for dx in range(2): for dy in range(2): for dz in range(2): recurse(levelidx + 1, basex + dx, basey + dy, basez + dz) else: # Reached base level (original data) but error still high leaves.append({ 'level': levelidx, 'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z, 'rgb': rgbalpha[:3], 'alpha': rgbalpha[3] }) # Start at root (coarsest level) rootlevel = numlevels - 1 rootsize = len(pyramid[rootlevel]['data']) for x in range(rootsize): for y in range(rootsize): for z in range(rootsize): recurse(rootlevel, x, y, z) return leaves def sortbacktofront(leaves, viewdirection, cameraorigin): """ Sorts leaf nodes in back-to-front order based on view direction. Uses dot product of node center with view direction. """ def depth(leaf): cx, cy, cz = leaf['x'], leaf['y'], leaf['z'] return -(cx viewdirection[0] + cy viewdirection[1] + cz viewdirection[2]) return sorted(leaves, key=depth) def projectpolygon(leaf, footprintsize, viewtransform): """ Projects a volume cell's footprint to screen space. Returns a list of 2D screen coordinates for the polygon vertices. """ scale = 2.0 (leaf['level']) screenx = (leaf['x'] scale + footprintsize / 2.0) viewtransform[0] screeny = (leaf['y'] scale + footprintsize / 2.0) viewtransform[1] return [(screenx, screeny), (screenx + footprintsize, screeny), (screenx + footprintsize, screeny + footprintsize), (screenx, screeny + footprintsize)] def rasterizepolygon(screenpolygon, rgb, alpha, imagebuffer): """ Rasterizes a polygon onto the image buffer using alpha compositing. """ for sx, sy in screenpolygon: if 0 <= sx < len(imagebuffer[0]) and 0 <= sy < len(imagebuffer): prevr, prevg, prevb, preva = imagebuffer[sy][sx] inva = 1.0 - alpha imagebuffer[sy][sx] = ( rgb[0] alpha + prevr inva, rgb[1] alpha + prevg inva, rgb[2] alpha + prevb inva, alpha + preva inva) def render(pyramid, leaves, viewdirection, cameraorigin, footprinttables, imageheight, imagewidth): """ Renders the selected leaves using splatting. """ sortedleaves = sortbacktofront(leaves, viewdirection, cameraorigin) image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] for leaf in sortedleaves: levelidx = leaf['level'] footprintsize = footprinttables[levelidx] screenpolygon = projectpolygon(leaf, footprintsize, (1.0, 1.0, 0.0)) rasterizepolygon(screenpolygon, leaf['rgb'], leaf['alpha'], image) return image Parameters: Error Threshold (\epsilon): A user-specified value determining the desired homogeneity. Selecting a larger error results in fewer subvolumes (coarser decomposition), while decreasing the error increases the number of subvolumes (finer decomposition). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The error metric computation must be stable. If the volume data has high dynamic range, the error values may require normalization. Boundary Conditions: The pyramid construction assumes N is a power of 2. If N is not a power of 2, padding or truncation is required. Degenerate Input: If the volume is completely homogeneous, the error at the root is minimal, so the algorithm selects the root node and renders a single large splat. Time Complexity: Pyramid construction is O(N^3). Traversal is proportional to the number of leaf nodes, which depends on \epsilon. Rendering is proportional to the number of leaf nodes. Memory Complexity: The pyramid stores a sequence of volumes at decreasing resolutions, so memory usage is slightly higher than the original volume size. Measured Performance: For binary data, bits can be packed into bytes to produce lower resolution images faster (1/8th time for half linear resolution). The algorithm enables real-time interactive rendering suitable for applications requiring progressive refinement. Strengths: Real-time performance, adaptive resolution, efficient use of graphics hardware via polygon approximation. Limitations: The quality is dependent on the choice of \epsilon. Visual artifacts may occur at boundaries between different pyramid levels if blending is not handled correctly. Hierarchical splatting was introduced by David Laur and Pat Hanrahan in 1991. It was designed as a progressive refinement algorithm for volume rendering, leveraging the pyramidal volume representation to achieve real-time interactive rendering. The method approximates splats with RGBA Gouraud-shaded polygons to enable efficient rasterization on modern graphics workstations of the time. It is a foundational technique in the family of multi-resolution volume rendering methods. name: Multi-Resolution Points
head: Error-controlled Point Splatting, Reduced Point Cloud Rendering
body: Multi-Resolution Points is a technique to render one large point in place of many small points to reduce rasterization cost and storage. It builds on Multi-Resolution and Level of Detail (Pyramid, LOD, Downsampling) by organizing points into a tree and using a local error metric to decide on point size. Inputs: A set of points P = \{pi\}, each with position \mathbf{x}i, color \mathbf{c}i, and opacity \alphai. A user-defined error threshold \epsilon. Outputs: A subset of points P' representing the scene, where each point in P' may represent a cluster of original points. Data Structures: Point Tree: A hierarchical structure (e.g., octree or quadtree) where each node stores aggregate properties of its children: mean position \bar{\mathbf{x}}, mean color \bar{\mathbf{c}}, total opacity \bar{\alpha}, and a local error metric E. Visibility Map: A quadtree used to cull occluded nodes. Steps: 1. Tree Construction: Organize points into a tree. For each internal node, compute aggregate properties as weighted averages of children. Compute the local error metric E for the node. 2. Error Metric: Use a local error metric to decide on point size. Laur and Hanrahan use RMS error. For a node with children C, the error E quantifies the deviation of children's attributes from the node's aggregate. 3. Traversal and Selection: Traverse the tree from root to leaves. A node is selected as a leaf (rendered as a single primitive) if its error E \le \epsilon or if its projected screen-space footprint is smaller than a pixel threshold. If E > \epsilon, recurse to children. 4. Occlusion Culling: Use a visibility map quadtree to cull occluded octree nodes. Subdivide octree nodes if not occluded. Rasterize points that fail the occlusion test. 5. Update Visibility Map: After rendering, update the visibility map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermultiresolutionpoints(points, epsilon): tree = buildtree(points) computeaggregates(tree) computeerrormetrics(tree, epsilon) selectedpoints = [] traverseandselect(tree, epsilon, selectedpoints) for p in selectedpoints: # Project to screen and draw screenpos = projecttoscreen(p.pos) drawpoint(screenpos, p.color, p.opacity) def buildtree(points): if len(points) <= 1: return LeafNode(points) splitaxis = determinesplitaxis(points) leftpts, rightpts = split(points, splitaxis) return InternalNode(buildtree(leftpts), buildtree(rightpts)) def computeaggregates(node): if node.isleaf(): node.meanpos = node.points[0].pos node.meancolor = node.points[0].color node.totalopacity = node.points[0].opacity return node.meanpos = weightedavg([c.meanpos for c in node.children], [c.totalopacity for c in node.children]) node.meancolor = weightedavg([c.meancolor for c in node.children], [c.totalopacity for c in node.children]) node.totalopacity = sum(c.totalopacity for c in node.children) def computeerrormetrics(node, epsilon): if node.isleaf(): node.error = 0 return node.error = rmserror(node.children, node.meanpos, node.meancolor) for child in node.children: computeerrormetrics(child, epsilon) def traverseandselect(node, epsilon, selected): if node.error <= epsilon: selected.append(node.toprimitive()) else: for child in node.children: traverseandselect(child, epsilon, selected) Parameters: \epsilon: Error threshold. User sets an error threshold to control tree traversal. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate input: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Depends on tree depth and traversal. Culling occluded nodes reduces rasterization cost. Memory: Less storage required by retaining only a list of relevant points. Measured Performance: Welsh '02: Reduced 240k points to 90k points using a frequency-space metric. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Less rasterization cost (overlap areas), less storage required. Points provide a lossless data compression by retaining only a list of relevant points. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Use when reducing rasterization cost and storage is critical. When not: Not given in the sources. Origin: Laur and Hanrahan use RMS error (Laur ‘91). Welsh '02 used a frequency-space metric. History and Development: The technique is discussed in the context of volumetric points rendering. Alternative grids (hexagonal, BCC) are mentioned for potential compression gains. Where it is used: Volumetric points rendering. name: Cloud Impostor Rendering
head: Dynamic impostors, Dynamically Generated Impostors, Impostors for clouds
body: Cloud Impostor Rendering is a technique to accelerate cloud rendering by replacing geometric particle models with 2D texture impostors, exploiting the lack of high-frequency edges in clouds to tolerate lower resolution textures and frequent updates. It solves the performance bottleneck of particle-based cloud rendering by dynamically generating 2D impostors to accelerate rendering. Inputs: Cloud particle system (position, size, color, opacity). Viewpoint position and viewing direction. Object bounding volumes (for clouds containing objects). Screen resolution (resolution{screen}). Outputs: Textured impostor polygons (quads) rendered to the frame buffer. Data Structures: Impostor Texture: A 2D image generated by rendering the cloud particles from the current viewpoint. Impostor Geometry: A screen-space rectangle (quad) sized to fill the screen (for internal clouds) or fitted to the object's bounding volume projection (for distant clouds). Error Metrics: Translation error angle (\alpha{trans}): The angle between the current viewing direction and the direction used to generate the impostor texture. Required texture resolution: Calculated based on object size and distance. Parameters: Translation error tolerance: ~0.15 degrees for imperceptible popping. Up to 1 degree for added performance. Resolution reduction factor: 4 in each dimension for clouds containing the viewpoint. Steps: 1. Determine Cloud Category: Check if the viewpoint is inside the cloud's bounding volume. If distant: Proceed to Step 2. If internal (containing viewpoint): Proceed to Step 3. 2. Generate Distant Impostor: 1. Position a view frustum at the current viewpoint. 2. Fit the frustum tightly to the cloud's bounding volume. 3. Render the cloud particles into an image using this frustum. 4. Use this image to texture an impostor polygon. 5. Display the impostor as a polygon oriented toward the viewer. 3. Generate Internal Impostor: 1. Use the same view frustum used to display the whole scene (not tightly fitted to the cloud). 2. Render the cloud particles into an image. 3. Reduce the texture resolution by a factor of 4 in each dimension compared to the screen resolution. 4. Use this lower-resolution image to texture an impostor polygon. 5. Display the impostor as a screen-space rectangle sized to fill the screen. 4. Update Decision: 1. Compute the translation error angle \alpha{trans} between the current viewing direction and the direction used for the last impostor generation. 2. Compute the required texture resolution using the formula: resolution{texture} = resolution{screen} \cdot \frac{object\size}{dist} where resolution{screen} is the screen resolution, object\size is the object size, and dist is the distance to the object. 3. If \alpha{trans} > tolerance OR current resolution < required resolution, regenerate the impostor from the current viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in v)) return [x / mag for x in v] if mag > 0 else [0, 0, 0] def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def cloudimpostorupdate(cloud, viewpoint, screenres, lastimpostor): # Step 1: Determine if viewpoint is inside the cloud's bounding volume isinternal = distance(viewpoint.pos, cloud.boundingvolume.center) <= cloud.boundingvolume.radius # Step 2: Calculate error metrics # Compute translation error angle alphatrans lastdir = lastimpostor.genviewdir cosangle = dot(normalize(viewpoint.dir), normalize(lastdir)) cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosangle)) alphatrans = math.degrees(math.acos(cosangle)) # Compute required texture resolution objectsize = cloud.boundingvolume.diameter dist = distance(viewpoint.pos, cloud.boundingvolume.center) if dist < 1e-6: dist = 1e-6 requiredres = (int(screenres[0] objectsize / dist), int(screenres[1] objectsize / dist)) # Step 3: Check if regeneration is needed tolerance = 0.15 # degrees needsupdate = (alphatrans > tolerance) or (lastimpostor.resolution[0] < requiredres[0] or lastimpostor.resolution[1] < requiredres[1]) if not needsupdate: return lastimpostor.texture, lastimpostor.geometry # Step 4: Regenerate Impostor if isinternal: # Internal cloud: Use scene frustum, reduce resolution by factor of 4 renderres = (screenres[0] // 4, screenres[1] // 4) texture = rendercloudtotexture(cloud.particles, viewpoint.dir, renderres) geometry = "screenfillingquad" # Display as screen-space rectangle filling the screen else: # Distant cloud: Use tightly fitted frustum renderres = screenres texture = rendercloudtotexture(cloud.particles, viewpoint.dir, renderres) geometry = "orientedquad" # Display as polygon oriented toward viewer return texture, geometry def rendercloudtotexture(particles, viewdir, resolution): # Render cloud particles into an image using the given frustum # Sort particles back-to-front relative to view direction sortedparticles = sorted(particles, key=lambda p: dot(p.pos, viewdir), reverse=True) # Allocate texture buffer texture = [[None for in range(resolution[1])] for in range(resolution[0])] # Rasterize particles into buffer for p in sortedparticles: # Project particle center to screen space screenx = int((p.pos[0] 1000) % resolution[0]) screeny = int((p.pos[1] 1000) % resolution[1]) # Draw billboard texture[screenx][screeny] = (p.color, p.opacity) return texture Real-Time Cloud Rendering is a two-pass algorithm for the realistic, real-time rendering of static, constant-shape clouds suitable for flight simulation and games. It solves the performance bottleneck of particle-based cloud rendering by approximating multiple forward scattering in a preprocess and first-order anisotropic scattering at runtime, using dynamically generated 2D impostors to accelerate rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Cloud Impostor Rendering by explicitly separating the illumination calculation into a precomputed multiple forward scattering term and a runtime anisotropic single scattering term, rather than relying solely on isotropic approximations or simple texture mapping. Impostor Splitting is a technique to render objects passing through clouds realistically by splitting a single cloud impostor into multiple layers to avoid the artifact of objects appearing to pass through 2D images. It detects when objects pass within the bounding volume of a cloud and splits the cloud impostor into N+1 layers, where N is the number of objects within the cloud. Layer 1 is behind the first object, Layer 2 is in front of the first object and behind the second, etc.. The set of alternating impostor layers and objects is rendered from back to front, with depth testing enabled for objects and disabled for impostors. Unlike direct particle rendering, impostor splitting avoids artifacts caused by billboards intersecting object geometry. Incremental Impostor Orientation Update is a technique to reduce sawtooth-like rotational artifacts caused by the mismatch between real-time impostor geometry reorientation (60Hz) and delayed texture updates. It minimizes the rotation of the quad in the image plane by calculating a correctional rotation between the normal's direction in the previous frame and the new viewing direction, instead of calculating a rotation matrix between the initial quad normal and the current viewing direction. The rotational axis for this incremental update is fixed in the image plane. Since the incremental update is always taken between the correct new position and the previous result, errors do not accumulate. A pitfall is that quick rotational changes cause artifacts because impostor textures update only every few frames while geometry updates at ~60Hz. Time Complexity: The cost is dominated by the regeneration of impostor textures, which involves rendering the cloud particles. For distant clouds, this is amortized over multiple frames due to frame-to-frame coherence. For internal clouds, updates may be required every frame, but the resolution is reduced by a factor of 4 in each dimension, lowering the cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the impostor textures. The resolution is determined by the screen resolution and object size/distance. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce 256 (PC, 800 MHz Pentium III, 256MB RAM), the system renders scenes with up to hundreds of thousands of particles at >50 fps, and >1.2 million particles at 10-12 fps with slow viewpoint movement. Strengths: Exploits the lack of high-frequency edges in clouds to tolerate lower resolution textures and frequent updates. Can be used for clouds no matter where they are in relation to the viewer. Limitations: Requires frequent updates for internal clouds or fast-moving viewpoints. Artifacts can occur if the translation error tolerance is too high or if rotational changes are too quick. When to use: Suitable for flight simulators and games where clouds are a major visual component and performance is critical. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes with sharp-edged objects where impostor artifacts would be noticeable. Cloud Impostor Rendering was introduced in the paper "Real-Time Cloud Rendering". It builds on the concept of dynamically generated impostors. The technique was implemented using OpenGL and DirectX 8 APIs and tested on PC systems and SGI Onyx2 with InfiniteReality2 graphics. name: Real-Time Cloud Rendering
head: Harris and Lastra, Harris and Lastra [30, 31], Harris and Lastra cloud rendering, Precomputed Scattering Cloud Impostors, Two-pass Cloud Rendering
body: Real-Time Cloud Rendering is a two-pass algorithm for the realistic, real-time rendering of static, constant-shape clouds suitable for flight simulation and games. It solves the performance bottleneck of particle-based cloud rendering by approximating multiple forward scattering in a preprocess and first-order anisotropic scattering at runtime, using dynamically generated 2D impostors to accelerate rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Cloud Impostor Rendering by explicitly separating the illumination calculation into a precomputed multiple forward scattering term and a runtime anisotropic single scattering term, rather than relying solely on isotropic approximations or simple texture mapping. Inputs: A set of static cloud particles, where each particle is defined by a center position, radius, density, and color. The particles are assumed to be static relative to each other. A light direction vector. Outputs: A rendered image of the clouds using screen-oriented splats. Data Structures: Particle: A structure containing center (3D vector), radius (scalar), density (scalar), and color (RGB vector). Impostor: A 2D texture map generated per cloud (or per particle group) that stores the precomputed shading information. The exact layout is not specified, but it is texture-mapped onto screen-oriented polygons. Steps: 1. Preprocess (Pass 1): Compute the multiple forward scattering illumination for each particle in the light direction. This step assumes the clouds are static and of constant shape, allowing shading to be computed once per scene. Multiple forward scattering is approximated by considering only the most significant direction from the whole sphere of directions: the light direction. This approximation is a harder restriction of the space of directions than methods like Nishita et al.. The result is stored in the impostor texture. 2. Runtime (Pass 2): Render the clouds using the precomputed shading and single scattering toward the viewer. Calculate anisotropic first-order scattering at runtime. The scattering phase function used is the Rayleigh phase function. Note: This is noted as far from well-suited for clouds; more accurate phase functions should be used for higher accuracy. Render particles using splatting. Use dynamically generated impostors to achieve real-time rendering in scenes with many complex clouds. The impostors are screen-oriented polygons texture-mapped with the Gaussian density function and the precomputed shading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessclouds(clouds, lightdirection): """ Compute multiple forward scattering for each cloud. clouds: List of Cloud objects. lightdirection: Normalized 3D vector. """ for cloud in clouds: # Approximate multiple forward scattering by considering only the light direction # The exact formula for the precomputed shading is not given in the sources. # It likely involves integrating the particle density along the light direction # and applying an albedo/scattering model. precomputedshading = computemultipleforwardscattering(cloud, lightdirection) # Generate impostor texture from precomputed shading # The exact generation process (e.g., projection, resolution) is not specified. cloud.impostortexture = generateimpostortexture(precomputedshading) def renderclouds(clouds, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, lightdirection): """ Render clouds using impostors and runtime single scattering. """ for cloud in clouds: # Generate screen-oriented polygon (billboard) for the impostor # The exact method for generating the impostor geometry is not specified. # It is assumed to be a screen-aligned quad or similar primitive. impostorgeometry = generatescreenorientedimpostor(cloud, viewmatrix) # Bind the precomputed impostor texture bindtexture(cloud.impostortexture) # Draw the impostor with runtime anisotropic single scattering # The exact shader implementation is not given. # It combines the precomputed multiple forward scattering with # anisotropic single scattering using the Rayleigh phase function. drawimpostor(impostorgeometry, lightdirection) Parameters: Phase Function: Rayleigh phase function. Particle Model: Gaussian density falloff from the center. Scattering Approximation: Multiple forward scattering (light direction) + Anisotropic first-order scattering (eye direction). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Phase Function Accuracy: The Rayleigh phase function is noted as far from well-suited for clouds. Using it may result in less accurate visual results compared to more complex phase functions. Static Assumption: The method assumes particles are static relative to each other. Dynamic clouds are not supported without re-preprocessing. Directional Approximation: Approximating multiple scattering only in the light direction is a significant simplification. This may lead to inaccuracies in complex lighting scenarios or when the light direction is not the dominant source of illumination. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is done once per cloud. Runtime rendering is accelerated by using impostors, allowing hundreds of clouds and hundreds of thousands of particles to be rendered at high frame rates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing impostor textures for each cloud. Strengths: Real-time performance for complex scenes; allows viewer interaction (flying in and around clouds); reduces artifacts from direct particle rendering. Limitations: Static clouds only; Rayleigh phase function is inaccurate for clouds; multiple scattering approximation is limited to the light direction. When to use: Flight simulation and games requiring real-time rendering of static clouds. When not to use: Dynamic clouds; scenes requiring high-fidelity scattering physics. The method was presented by Harris and Lastra. It is based on a two-pass method by Dobashi et al.. The work is concerned with the real-time rendering of high-quality static constant-shape clouds suitable for flight simulation and games. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting LOD methods
head: RTGS
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting LOD methods reduce the memory footprint and rendering cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) by removing redundant primitives or compressing their attributes, addressing the scalability limits of standard 3D-GS which stores full-precision data for millions of Gaussians. Unlike sibling methods that rely on hierarchical spatial structures [1168-hierarchical-splatting.md], these methods primarily focus on attribute-level compression, structured pruning, and redundancy reduction based on spatial overlap and temporal consistency. The core mechanism involves identifying and eliminating redundant Gaussians or compressing their high-dimensional attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color) to fit within constrained memory budgets while preserving visual fidelity. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene consisting of N Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{p}, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Outputs: A compressed set of Gaussians \{G'i\} with reduced attribute precision or count, and a corresponding rendering pipeline capable of interpreting the compressed data. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian List: A flat array of Gaussian attributes. In compression methods like SOGS, attributes are rearranged into 2D grids. Steps: 1. Redundancy Identification: Analyze Gaussians for spatial overlap and temporal consistency. 2. Pruning/Selection: Remove marked Gaussians based on computed importance or overlap metrics. Methods like RTGS apply multi-level redundancy reduction based on spatial overlap and temporal consistency. Methods like LightGaussian use structured pruning combined with SH factorization. 3. Attribute Compression: Quantization: Compress color, rotation, and opacity into latent vectors decoded by a small MLP (EAGLES) or use vector quantization (LightGaussian). Grid Sorting (SOGS): Arrange attributes into 2D grids, sort them, and apply smoothness regularization to penalize pixels with values differing significantly from their local neighborhood. Encoding: Compress RGB grids using JPEG XL and store other attributes as 32-bit OpenEXR images with zip compression (SOGS). 4. Rendering: Rasterize the remaining/compressed Gaussians using standard screen-space splatting. Formulas: Smoothness Regularization (SOGS): Penalizes differences between a grid cell's attribute value and the mean of its local neighborhood in the 2D grid. Parameters: Pruning Threshold: Not given in the sources. Grid Resolution (SOGS): Not given in the sources. Quantization Bits: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unreachable Gaussians: In Sequential Point Trees (SPTs), a child Gaussian may become larger than its parent, violating the SPT cut condition (\text{scale}(\text{parent}) < \text{scale}(\text{child})). These Gaussians are left in RAM but not rendered. Rebalancing the hierarchy is too costly. Overlapping Gaussians: Compact3D avoids quantizing position and opacity to prevent overlapping Gaussians and visual artifacts. EAGLES optimizes 3D-GS by reducing memory and training time through attribute quantization, progressive coarse-to-fine training, and aggressive pruning. It sets itself apart from sibling LOD methods by focusing on attribute-level compression and training-time acceleration rather than hierarchical spatial structures. Choose it when training time and storage size are primary constraints. This class of methods reduces the storage footprint of 3D-GS scenes by compressing geometric and attribute data. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on bitstream reduction rather than hierarchical rendering structures. Choose it when disk space or network bandwidth limits scene distribution. LightGaussian reduces model size and improves rendering speed by combining structured pruning with Spherical Harmonic (SH) factorization and vector quantization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on attribute-level compression rather than purely spatial clustering or octree-based spatial pruning. Choose it when high frame rates and extreme size reduction are required. TRIPS is a point-based radiance field rendering technique that rasterizes points into a screen-space image pyramid using trilinear splats, followed by a neural reconstruction network to produce hole-free, crisp images. It sets itself apart by solving the blurriness and cloudy artifacts of 3D-GS and the temporal instability of ADOP through neural reconstruction. Choose it when visual crispness and temporal stability outweigh the added neural network overhead. Multi-scale filtering mitigates aliasing artifacts and optimizes rendering performance by adapting the Gaussian representation to the camera's viewing frequency or resolution. It sets itself apart from standard 3D-GS by explicitly managing the spectral content of the primitives through training-time aggregation, test-time covariance regularization, or runtime hierarchical pruning. Choose it when rendering at varying resolutions or when aliasing is a concern. Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting (Vmem) enables the rendering of large-scale scenes that exceed available GPU memory by applying virtual texturing concepts. It sets itself apart from standard 3D-GS by separating virtual and physical address spaces, allowing dynamic LOD selection and just-in-time memory allocation. Choose it when scene size exceeds GPU VRAM limits. This family of techniques reduces computational and memory cost by grouping individual splats into representative clusters or hierarchical nodes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly constructing cluster structures and aggregating Gaussian parameters to form fewer, larger primitives, rather than merely filtering or paging existing data. Choose it when reducing primitive count for culling or LOD generation is prioritized. Budgeted Gaussian Splatting (BCT) enables continuous, variable primitive counts (Level of Detail) without retraining. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by providing a single, global primitive ordering whose prefixes define successive approximations of the scene, rather than camera-dependent hierarchical selectors or discrete hierarchy methods. Choose it when dynamic, continuous LOD adjustment without retraining is required. Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) is a Level-of-Detail method that organizes 3D Gaussian primitives into a hierarchical structure to enable efficient rendering of large-scale scenes by dynamically selecting appropriate detail levels based on viewing distance. It sets itself apart by training scene chunks independently and merging them into a global LoD hierarchy. Choose it for large-scale outdoor or indoor scenes requiring distance-based LOD. Sequential Point Trees (SPTs) are a hierarchical data structure originally developed for point cloud rendering, adapted here for efficient, view-dependent Level-of-Detail selection in 3D Gaussian Splatting without requiring full tree traversal. They set themselves apart by enabling dynamic LoD hierarchies that evolve continuously during optimization. Choose them when dynamic, training-time hierarchy evolution is preferred over static partitioning. SOGS arranges Gaussian attributes into multiple 2D grids, sorts them, and applies smoothness regularization to penalize pixels with values very different from their local neighborhood. It sets itself apart from vector quantization methods by using grid-based sorting and JPEG XL/OpenEXR encoding. Choose it when disk storage size is the primary constraint. On the MipNeRF360 dataset, SOGS achieves SSIM 0.801, PSNR 26.98, LPIPS 0.238, and a size of 28.80 MB. A strategy to tolerate cases where a child Gaussian becomes larger than its parent, making it impossible for the parent to fulfill the SPT cut condition. It sets itself apart by accepting a small RAM inefficiency rather than performing costly rebalancing or generating improper cuts that derail training. Choose it when using SPTs and encountering scale inversions during training. This inefficiency affects less than 10% of Gaussians in practice. Time Complexity: Varies by method. Structured pruning (LightGaussian) and redundancy reduction (RTGS) add preprocessing time but reduce rendering time by decreasing primitive count. Grid sorting (SOGS) adds compression/decompression overhead. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced. LightGaussian achieves up to 15\times size reduction. SOGS achieves 28.80 MB on MipNeRF360. Measured Performance: LightGaussian achieves >200 FPS with <0.5 dB quality drop. SOGS achieves SSIM 0.801, PSNR 26.98, LPIPS 0.238 on MipNeRF360. Strengths: Reduced memory footprint, faster rendering, ability to handle large-scale scenes. Limitations: Potential quality loss if compression is too aggressive. Unreachable Gaussians in SPTs waste RAM. Rebalancing is costly. When to Use: When memory or bandwidth is constrained, or for large-scale scenes. When Not to Use: When maximum visual fidelity is required and resources are abundant. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) was introduced by Kerbl et al.. LOD methods for 3D-GS have been developed to address its high memory and computational costs. RTGS applies multi-level redundancy reduction. LightGaussian combines structured pruning with SH factorization. SOGS uses grid-based compression. H-3DGS and SPTs introduce hierarchical structures for LOD. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.01110, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: EAGLES
head: Efficient Accelerated 3D Gaussians with Lightweight EncodingS
body: EAGLES is a method for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) representations by reducing memory footprint, training time, and storage size while maintaining or improving reconstruction quality. It achieves this through attribute quantization, progressive coarse-to-fine training, and aggressive pruning. Unlike standard 3D-GS, which stores full-precision attributes for millions of Gaussians, EAGLES compresses color, rotation, opacity, position, and scale into latent vectors decoded by a small MLP, and reduces the Gaussian count via influence-based pruning. It sets itself apart from sibling LOD methods like H-3DGS by focusing on attribute-level compression and training-time acceleration rather than hierarchical spatial structures. Inputs: Sparse point cloud from Structure from Motion (SfM). Training images and camera poses. Hyperparameters: SH degree f, latent dimension l, decoder output dimension k, progressive scaling start/end scales, densification interval, and pruning thresholds. Outputs: Quantized latent vectors q for each Gaussian. Trained MLP decoder D. Rendered novel views. Each Gaussian i stores: 1. Latent Vector qi \in \mathbb{Z}^l: Integer vector of dimension l. 2. Decoded Attributes: The MLP decoder D: \mathbb{Z}^l \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k maps qi to rotation ri, opacity oi, color SH coefficients c{SH, i}, position pi, and scale si. The dimension k depends on f, where d = 3f^2 coefficients are required for color. 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from the SfM point cloud with position p, scale s, and continuous latent approximations \hat{q}. 2. Attribute Quantization (Training): Maintain continuous approximations \hat{q} for integer latents q during training. Compute decoded attributes using the Straight-Through Estimator (STE): \boldsymbol{a} = D(\text{STE}(\hat{q})) where \text{STE}(\hat{q}) rounds \hat{q} to the nearest integer for the forward pass but passes gradients through \hat{q} in the backward pass. Reconstruct the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma from decoded rotation r and scale s: \Sigma = RSS^TR^T where S is the diagonal scale matrix from s, and R is the rotation matrix from quaternion r. Project \Sigma to 2D for the current camera view: \Sigma' = JP\Sigma P^TJ^T where P is the world-to-camera projective transform and J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transform. Compute opacity \alpha and color c for rasterization. Opacity \alpha is derived from the 2D Gaussian value at the pixel multiplied by the decoded scalar opacity o. Color c is computed from the decoded SH coefficients. Render the image and compute loss: \mathcal{L} = (1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda\mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} with \lambda = 0.2. Update \hat{q}, p, and s via Stochastic Gradient Descent. 3. Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training: Start rendering at a reduced resolution scale (e.g., 0.3 of original dimensions). Gradually increase the rendering resolution to 1.0 (full scale) over a cosine schedule spanning 70% of the total training iterations. Alternatively, use Gaussian filtering (e.g., 5x5, 7x7, or 15x15 kernel) or mean filtering during this phase to stabilize optimization. Downsampling provides the largest training time gains. 4. Densification and Pruning: Warmup: Do not prune or densify for the initial phase. Pruning: Every 100 iterations, remove Gaussians with opacity \alpha < \alpha{\text{thresh}}. Densification: Every 100 iterations, split large Gaussians (covariance larger than geometry) and clone small Gaussians. Only perform this on Gaussians with positional gradients above a threshold \tau{\text{thresh}}. Interval Adjustment: Increase the densification interval to 175 iterations to reduce the final Gaussian count without quality loss. Final Pruning: After densification stabilizes, apply a pruning stage to remove Gaussians with the least influence on the full reconstruction, using a weight composed of transmittance and opacity. 5. Post-Training Compression: Round \hat{q} to the nearest integer q. Apply entropy coding to store q efficiently. Store the MLP decoder D and the quantized latents. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def steround(x): """Straight-Through Estimator: forward pass returns rounded integer, backward pass passes gradients through the continuous approximation.""" return np.round(x) def decodeattributes(latentvector, decodermlp): """Decode quantized latent vector to rotation, opacity, color SH, position, and scale.""" return decodermlp(latentvector) def computecovariance3d(scale, rotationquaternion): """Compute 3D covariance matrix Sigma = R S S^T R^T.""" S = np.diag(scale) q = rotationquaternion / np.linalg.norm(rotationquaternion) R = np.array([ [1 - 2q[2]2 - 2q[3]2, 2q[1]q[2] - 2q[3]q[0], 2q[1]q[3] + 2q[2]q[0]], [2q[1]q[2] + 2q[3]q[0], 1 - 2q[1]2 - 2q[3]2, 2q[2]q[3] - 2q[1]q[0]], [2q[1]q[3] - 2q[2]q[0], 2q[2]q[3] + 2q[1]q[0], 1 - 2q[1]2 - 2q[2]2] ]) return R @ S @ S.T @ R.T def projectcovariance2d(cov3d, cameramatrix, jacobian): """Project 3D covariance to 2D: Sigma' = J P Sigma P^T J^T.""" P = cameramatrix return jacobian @ P @ cov3d @ P.T @ jacobian.T def rendergaussians(gaussians, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, scalefactor): """Render image using tile-based rasterization.""" targetw = int(imagewidth scalefactor) targeth = int(imageheight scalefactor) renderedimage = np.zeros((targeth, targetw, 3)) for g in gaussians: attrs = decodeattributes(g.latentq, g.decoder) rot, opacity, shcoeffs, pos, scale = attrs['rotation'], attrs['opacity'], attrs['shcoeffs'], attrs['position'], attrs['scale'] cov3d = computecovariance3d(scale, rot) projcov2d = projectcovariance2d(cov3d, camera.P, camera.J) cov2dinv = np.linalg.inv(projcov2d) center2d = camera.project(pos) # For each pixel in the Gaussian's bounding box: # dx, dy = pixelcoords - center2d # alpha = np.exp(-0.5 (dx2 cov2dinv[0,0] + 2dxdy cov2dinv[0,1] + dy2 cov2dinv[1,1])) opacity # color = evaluatesh(shcoeffs, viewdirection) # Alpha compositing: C = sum(ci alphai product(1 - alphaj)) pass return renderedimage def traineagles(gaussians, dataset, decodermlp, totaliterations): """Main training loop.""" startscale = 0.3 endscale = 1.0 progressiveduration = int(0.7 totaliterations) warmupiterations = 3000 # Standard warmup phase pruneinterval = 100 densifyinterval = 100 alphathresh = 0.005 # Threshold for opacity pruning gradthresh = 0.0002 # Threshold for positional gradients for iter in range(totaliterations): if iter < progressiveduration: progress = iter / progressiveduration scale = startscale + (endscale - startscale) 0.5 (1 - np.cos(np.pi progress)) else: scale = 1.0 image, camera = dataset.sample() rendered = rendergaussians(gaussians, camera, image.shape[1], image.shape[0], scale) # Loss: L = (1-0.2)L1 + 0.2LSSIM # loss = computeloss(rendered, image) # Standard L1+SSIM combination # Backward pass with STE: gradients flow through scale, position, and continuous latent approx qhat # gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians, decodermlp) # Standard SGD step # updateparameters(gaussians, decodermlp, gradients, lr=1e-4) if iter > warmupiterations: if iter % pruneinterval == 0: gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g.opacity > alphathresh] if iter % densifyinterval == 0: # Split large Gaussians and clone small ones based on positional gradients > gradthresh # gaussians = densifygaussians(gaussians, gradthresh) # Standard densification logic if iter > 10000: densifyinterval = 175 # Increase interval to reduce Gaussian count # Final pruning: remove Gaussians with minimal influence using transmittance and opacity weight # gaussians = pruneinfluence(gaussians, dataset.testviews) # Influence metric calculation for g in gaussians: g.latentq = np.round(g.latentqhat) return gaussians, decodermlp SH Degree f: Typically 4. Color coefficients (3f^2) constitute >80% of attribute dimensions. Latent Dimension l: Dimension of q \in \mathbb{Z}^l. Decoder Output Dimension k: Dimension of D: \mathbb{Z}^l \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k. Progressive Scaling Start: 0.3 (30% resolution). Progressive Scaling End: 1.0 (100% resolution). Progressive Scaling Duration: 70% of total iterations. Densification Interval: 175 iterations (increased from standard 100). Gaussian Filter Size: 5x5, 7x7, or 15x15 if using Gaussian filtering instead of downsampling. Opacity Quantization: Quantizing opacity is critical to prevent erroneous Gaussians from saturating quickly, which reduces floaters and visual artifacts. Densification Interval: Increasing the interval beyond 175 causes a sharp drop in reconstruction quality. Quantization Drop: Quantization causes a small drop in PSNR, but opacity quantization can actually improve visual quality by reducing artifacts. Full Attribute Quantization: EAGLES quantizes all attributes, including position and scale, via the latent framework to achieve maximum compression. Memory Reduction: EAGLES reduces storage by 10-20x compared to 3D-GS. For example, on the Deep Blending dataset, storage drops from 676 MB (3D-GS) to 52 MB (EAGLES). On the Train scene (Tanks & Temples), it drops from 262 MB to 21 MB. Training Speed: Training time is significantly reduced. On Deep Blending, EAGLES takes 21m50s vs 36m2s for 3D-GS. On the Bicycle scene, GPU memory usage drops from 17.4 GB (3D-GS) to 10 GB (EAGLES). Rendering Speed: Rendering FPS is comparable or slightly lower than 3D-GS. On Deep Blending, EAGLES achieves 130 FPS vs 137 FPS for 3D-GS. EAGLES-Small achieves 160 FPS. Quality: PSNR is on par or slightly better. On Deep Blending, EAGLES achieves 29.86 PSNR vs 29.41 PSNR for 3D-GS. On MipNeRF360, the drop is minimal (0.22 dB). Complexity: The method adds complexity due to the MLP decoder and quantization logic, but reduces the number of Gaussians, which lowers rasterization cost. EAGLES (Efficient Accelerated 3D Gaussians with Lightweight EncodingS) was proposed by Sharath Girish, Kamal Gupta, and Abhinav Shrivastava from the University of Maryland, College Park. It builds upon the seminal 3D Gaussian Splatting work. The method addresses the high memory and training costs of 3D-GS by introducing attribute quantization, progressive training, and pruning.
