name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression
head: Compact3D, EGGS (Explicitly Granular 3D Gaussian Splatting), Explicitly Granular 3D Gaussian Splatting
body:
3D Gaussian Splatting Compression reduces the storage footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by compressing geometric and attribute data. Compact3D avoids quantizing position and opacity to prevent overlapping Gaussians and visual artifacts. EGGS employs Luma-Aware and Volume-Preserving Attribute Factorization. These methods build on 3D Gaussian Splatting LOD methods by focusing on bitstream reduction rather than hierarchical rendering structures. The EGGS pipeline compresses Gaussian means using G-PCC (Geometry-based Point Cloud Compression). Other attributes are handled separately or via factorization. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance (scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Output: A binary file containing a compressed geometry stream and a header. The output binary file structure is: 1. Header: 24 bytes. meansmin: 3 floats (float32), the minimum x, y, z coordinates of the Gaussian means. meansmax: 3 floats (float32), the maximum x, y, z coordinates of the Gaussian means. 2. Length: 4 bytes (uint32), the size in bytes of the compressed geometry stream. 3. Compressed Data: Variable length, the binary stream output from the GPCC encoder. VOXELIZESCALEFACTOR: 16. The bit depth used for voxelizing Gaussian means, defining an integer range of [0, 2^{16}-1]. GPCC Encoder Flags (used for tmc3): mode=0, trisoupNodeSizeLog2=0, mergeDuplicatedPoints=0, neighbourAvailBoundaryLog2=8, positionQuantisationEnabled=1, intrapredmaxnodesizelog2=3, positionQuantizationScale=1, inferredDirectCodingMode=3, maxNumQtBtBeforeOt=2, minQtbtSizeLog2=0, planarEnabled=0, planarModeIdcmUse=0, cabacbypassstreamenabledflag=1. GPCC Decoder Flags: mode=1, outputBinaryPly=1. 1. Voxelization of Means: Calculate the bounding box of all Gaussian means: \mathbf{p}{min} = \mini (\mathbf{p}i) and \mathbf{p}{max} = \maxi (\mathbf{p}i). Normalize each mean \mathbf{p}i = [xi, yi, zi]^T to [0, 1]: \mathbf{p}'i =  rac{\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}{min}}{\mathbf{p}{max} - \mathbf{p}{min}}. Convert to 16-bit integers: \mathbf{v}i = 	ext{round}(\mathbf{p}'i 	imes (2^{16} - 1)). 2. Sorting by Morton Code: Calculate the Morton code for each voxelized mean \mathbf{v}i as the dot product of the voxelized coordinates and powers of (	ext{max\coordinate} + 1), where 	ext{max\coordinate} = 2^{16} - 1. Sort the voxelized means \mathbf{v}i in ascending order of their Morton codes. 3. PLY File Generation: Write the sorted voxelized means to an ASCII PLY file containing x, y, z properties. 4. GPCC Compression: Execute the external GPCC encoder (tmc3) with the specified flags. Input is the ASCII PLY file; output is a binary compressed stream. 5. File Assembly: Write the 24-byte header (meansmin, meansmax), followed by the 4-byte length of the compressed stream, followed by the compressed binary stream. 1. Header and Stream Extraction: Read the first 24 bytes to extract meansmin and meansmax. Read the next 4 bytes to determine the length L of the compressed stream. Read the next L bytes into a temporary binary file. 2. GPCC Decompression: Execute the external GPCC decoder (tmc3) with flags mode=1 and outputBinaryPly=1. Input is the temporary binary file; output is a reconstructed binary PLY file. 3. Reading Voxelized Means: Parse the binary PLY file to retrieve the voxelized means \mathbf{v}i from the x, y, z properties. 4. Re-sorting: Sort the decoded voxelized means by their Morton codes, as the GPCC decoder may unsort them. 5. Devoxelization: Convert the sorted integer voxelized means \mathbf{v}i back to float32 coordinates: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{p}{min} + \left(  rac{\mathbf{v}i}{2^{16} - 1} ight) 	imes (\mathbf{p}{max} - \mathbf{p}{min}). Returns: bytes of the final file content. """ # 1. Calculate bounding box pmin = np.min(means, axis=0) pmax = np.max(means, axis=0) rangevec = pmax - pmin # Handle degenerate case where range is zero rangevec = np.where(rangevec == 0, 1.0, rangevec) # 2. Returns: Nx3 array of float32 positions. """ # 1. Parse Header offset = 0 pmin = np.array(struct.unpack('fff', filedata[offset:offset+12])) offset += 12 pmax = np.array(struct.unpack('fff', filedata[offset:offset+12])) offset += 12 # 2. Parse Length length = struct.unpack('I', filedata[offset:offset+4])[0] offset += 4 compresseddata = filedata[offset:offset+length] # 3. Write Compressed Data with open("tempcompressed.bin", "wb") as f: f.write(compresseddata) # 4. Devoxelize rangevec = pmax - pmin rangevec = np.where(rangevec == 0, 1.0, rangevec) precovered = pmin + (vsorted / (216 - 1)) rangevec # Cleanup os.remove("tempcompressed.bin") os.remove("tempoutput.ply") return precovered Unsorted Decoded Data: The GPCC decoder does not guarantee output points are sorted by Morton code. Empty Scene / Degenerate Bounding Box: If all Gaussian means are identical, the range is zero. The normalization step must handle division by zero by clamping the range to a minimum positive value. Comparison: Compact3D has lower SSIM (0.808) than 3DGS (0.815) and LightGaussian (0.857), and higher LPIPS (0.228) than 3DGS (0.214) and LightGaussian (0.210). Strengths: Avoids quantization of position and opacity, reducing artifacts from overlapping Gaussians. Limitations: Requires external GPCC encoder/decoder (tmc3). It is a compression method that specifically avoids quantizing opacity and position to prevent visual artifacts caused by overlapping Gaussians. EGGS (Explicitly Granular 3D Gaussian Splatting): Cited in. It uses Luma-Aware and Volume-Preserving Attribute Factorization. The implementation relies on G-PCC for geometry compression. name: LightGaussian
body: LightGaussian is a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces model size and improves rendering speed by combining structured pruning with Spherical Harmonic (SH) factorization and vector quantization. It achieves significant size reduction (up to 15\times) and high frame rates (>200 FPS) with minimal quality degradation (<0.5 dB drop). It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on attribute-level compression (SH factorization, vector quantization, and G-PCC position compression) rather than purely spatial clustering or octree-based spatial pruning. LightGaussian reduces the computational and memory footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting through a five-stage pipeline: importance-based pruning, SH distillation/factorization, vector quantization, and position compression. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model with N Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{l,m} for bands l=0 \dots L. Output: A compressed model with N' < N Gaussians, where attributes are quantized and SH coefficients are reduced in dimensionality. Data Structures: 1. Pruned Gaussian Set: A subset of the original N Gaussians selected by importance ranking. 2. Quantized Attributes: Position compressed using octree-based lossless compression (G-PCC). SH coefficients factorized and reduced to lower bands, then vector quantized. Opacity, scale, and rotation quantized (e.g., opacity to 8-bit). Steps: 1. Importance Scoring: Calculate an importance score for each Gaussian based on its contribution to the training views, typically the average alpha-weighted contribution. 2. Structured Pruning: Rank Gaussians by importance and prune those with the lowest scores, typically dropping the bottom 30–80%. 3. SH Distillation: Apply knowledge distillation to transfer information from higher-order SH bands to lower-order bands, reducing SH dimensionality. 4. Vector Quantization: Apply vector quantization to the remaining SH coefficients and other attributes (scale, rotation) to further reduce size. 5. Position Compression: Encode the positions of the remaining Gaussians using octree-based lossless compression (G-PCC) due to rasterization accuracy sensitivity to position errors. Formulas: Importance Score Ii: Average alpha-weighted contribution across training views. Size Reduction: Up to 15\times reduction with <0.5 dB quality drop. Parameters: Pruning Ratio: 30–80%. SH Bands: Reduced to lower bands. Edge Cases: Position sensitivity: Rasterization accuracy is sensitive to position errors, hence lossless compression for positions. Quality trade-off: Pruning and quantization introduce quality loss, kept below 0.5 dB. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def lightgaussiancompress(gaussians, trainingviews, targetretention=0.2): # Step 1: Importance Scoring importancescores = [] for g in gaussians: totalcontribution = 0.0 for view in trainingviews: totalcontribution += g.opacity computeviewimpact(g, view) importancescores.append(totalcontribution / len(trainingviews)) # Step 2: Structured Pruning sortedindices = sorted(range(len(importancescores)), key=lambda i: importancescores[i], reverse=True) numtokeep = int(len(gaussians) targetretention) keepindices = sortedindices[:numtokeep] prunedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in keepindices] # Step 3: SH Distillation for g in prunedgaussians: g.shcoeffs = distillshtolowerbands(g.shcoeffs, targetbands=2) # Step 4: Vector Quantization for g in prunedgaussians: g.shcoeffs = vectorquantize(g.shcoeffs) g.opacity = quantize8bit(g.opacity) g.scale = vectorquantize(g.scale) g.rotation = vectorquantize(g.rotation) # Step 5: Position Compression positions = [g.position for g in prunedgaussians] compressedpositions = octreecompresspositions(positions) compressedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(prunedgaussians): g.position = compressedpositions[i] compressedgaussians.append(g) return compressedgaussians def computeviewimpact(gaussian, view): # Standard rasterization contribution calculation return gaussian.opacity gaussian.shcoeffs[0] def distillshtolowerbands(shcoeffs, targetbands): # Distillation redistributes higher-band energy to lower bands # Not given in the sources. Standard practice projects higher bands to lower. return shcoeffs[:,:targetbands] def vectorquantize(data): # Find nearest codebook entry and replace # Codebook is typically pre-trained; here we assume a fixed codebook C C = np.random.randn(256, data.shape[1]) # Placeholder for pre-trained codebook indices = [np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(data - c)) for c in C] return [C[idx] for idx in indices] def quantize8bit(value): # Scale and round to 8-bit integer range return int(max(0, min(255, round(value 255)))) def octreecompresspositions(positions): # G-PCC octree compression for position attributes # Not given in the sources. Uses standard octree quantization and entropy coding. return positions Performance: Achieves over 200 FPS. Quality: On the MipNeRF360 dataset, LightGaussian achieves SSIM 0.857, PSNR 28.45, and LPIPS 0.210. Size: Reduces model size to 42.48 MB on MipNeRF360, a 15\times reduction compared to the original. Strengths: High compression ratio, fast rendering, minimal quality loss. Limitations: Pruning may remove important Gaussians if not done carefully; SH distillation may lose high-frequency details. LightGaussian was introduced in NeurIPS'23. It addresses the need for efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting for mobile/web/streaming applications by compressing the Gaussian attributes. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: TRIPS
head: TRIPS, Trilinear Point Splatting, TRIPS: Neural Feature Attachment and Pyramid Rendering for 3DGS
body: TRIPS is a point-based radiance field rendering technique that rasterizes points into a screen-space image pyramid using trilinear splats, followed by a neural reconstruction network to produce hole-free, crisp images. It solves the blurriness and cloudy artifacts of 3D Gaussian Splatting and the temporal instability and large-gap handling issues of ADOP by projecting neural color descriptors into an image pyramid using trilinear writes to two neighboring resolution layers based on projected point size, avoiding overdraw by rendering only 2x2 splats. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Point positions \mathbf{x}w, world-space sizes sw, neural feature descriptors \tau, point opacities \alpha, camera intrinsics C (including focal length f), and camera extrinsics (R, t). Outputs: Final RGB image. Data Structures: Image Pyramid: A set of n layers. Layer L has resolution 2^L \times 2^L relative to the finest layer 0. Each pixel in each layer stores a depth-sorted list of fragments \Lambda{l,x,y} containing colors and alpha values, clamped to a maximum size of 16 elements. Neural Reconstruction Network: A small decoder consisting of gated convolutions, with only a single gated convolution per layer. Spherical Harmonics Module: Optional module applied after the neural network to model view-dependent artifacts. Steps: 1. Projection: For each point, project its position \mathbf{x}w = (xw, yw, zw) to continuous screen space coordinates (x, y, z) using camera intrinsics C and extrinsics (R, t). Calculate the screen space size s from the world space size sw and depth z: s = \frac{f \cdot sw}{z} where f is the focal length. 2. Layer Selection: Determine the two resolution layers for each point based on its projected size s: L{lower} = \lfloor \log2(s) \rfloor L{upper} = \lceil \log2(s) \rceil Points are rasterized as 2x2x2 trilinear splats into these two layers. 3. Trilinear Splatting: For each of the eight pixels (2x2 in each of the 2 selected layers), compute the contribution of the point. The final opacity value \gamma written to the image pyramid for pixel (xi, yi, si) with si = 2^L is: \gamma = \beta \cdot \iota \cdot \alpha where \alpha is the point opacity. Bilinear Weight (\beta): Computed inside the image layer based on continuous screen coordinates (x, y) and pixel coordinates (xi, yi): \beta = (1 - |x - xi|) \cdot (1 - |y - yi|) Linear Layer Weight (\iota): Interpolates between the two selected layers based on projected size s and layer sizes s{lower}=2^{L{lower}} and s{upper}=2^{L{upper}}: \iota = \begin{cases} 1 - \frac{|s - si|}{2^{L{upper}} - 2^{L{lower}}} & s \geq 1 \\ \epsilon + (1 - \epsilon)s & si = 0 \wedge s < 1 \end{cases} where \epsilon = 0.25 is a minimum weight constant to ensure far-away points with pixel size < 1 do not disappear. 4. Alpha Blending: Collect all fragments in per-pixel lists \Lambda{l,x,y} for each layer. Sort lists by depth. Compute the color C\Lambda for each pixel using front-to-back alpha blending: C\Lambda = \sum{m=1}^{|\Lambda|} Tm \cdot \alpham \cdot cm Tm = \prod{i=1}^{m-1} (1 - \alphai) where cm is the color of the m-th fragment, \alpham is its opacity, and Tm is the transmittance. 5. Neural Reconstruction: Feed the feature image pyramid through the compact neural reconstruction network. The network harmonizes the various layers, addresses remaining gaps, and conceals rendering artifacts. 6. Optional View Dependency: Apply the spherical harmonics module to the output of the neural network to preserve high levels of detail and model view-dependent artifacts. 7. Tone Mapping: Apply a tone mapping module to transform the resulting features into RGB colors. Parameters: Splat Size: Points are rasterized as 2x2x2 trilinear splats. Minimum Weight: \epsilon = 0.25. Feature Descriptors: Default is 4 feature vectors per point. Network Architecture: Small decoder made out of gated convolutions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tripsrender(points, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, pyramidlayers, usesh=False): """ points: List of dicts with keys 'pos' (x,y,z), 'size' (sw), 'features' (tau), 'alpha' cameraintrinsics: Dict with 'f' (focal length in pixels) cameraextrinsics: Tuple (R, t) where R is 3x3 rotation matrix, t is 3x1 translation vector pyramidlayers: List of layer indices Llower to Lupper usesh: Boolean flag for spherical harmonics """ R, t = cameraextrinsics imagepyramid = {L: {} for L in pyramidlayers} for point in points: xw, yw, zw = point['pos'] # Apply extrinsics xc = R[0][0]xw + R[0][1]yw + R[0][2]zw + t[0] yc = R[1][0]xw + R[1][1]yw + R[1][2]zw + t[1] zc = R[2][0]xw + R[2][1]yw + R[2][2]zw + t[2] f = cameraintrinsics['f'] xscreen = f xc / zc yscreen = f yc / zc zscreen = zc sw = point['size'] s = (f sw) / zscreen Llower = math.floor(math.log2(s)) Lupper = math.ceil(math.log2(s)) if s < 1: Llower = 0 Lupper = 0 selectedlayers = [Llower, Lupper] for L in selectedlayers: si = 2 L if s >= 1: iota = 1 - abs(s - si) / (2Lupper - 2Llower) else: iota = 0.25 + (1 - 0.25) s xi = math.floor(xscreen) yi = math.floor(yscreen) for dx in [0, 1]: for dy in [0, 1]: px = xi + dx py = yi + dy betax = 1 - abs(xscreen - px) betay = 1 - abs(yscreen - py) beta = betax betay gamma = beta iota point['alpha'] if (px, py) not in imagepyramid[L]: imagepyramid[L][(px, py)] = [] imagepyramid[L][(px, py)].append({ 'z': zscreen, 'color': point['features'], 'alpha': gamma }) blendedpyramid = {} for L, pixels in imagepyramid.items(): blendedpyramid[L] = {} for (px, py), fragments in pixels.items(): fragments.sort(key=lambda f: f['z']) fragments = fragments[:16] T = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for frag in fragments: alpha = frag['alpha'] c = frag['color'] color = [color[k] + T alpha c[k] for k in range(3)] T = T (1 - alpha) blendedpyramid[L][(px, py)] = color # Neural reconstruction: gated convolution decoder reconstructedfeatures = blendedpyramid if usesh: # Spherical harmonics evaluation reconstructedfeatures = blendedpyramid # Reinhard tone mapping finalimage = {} for L, pixels in reconstructedfeatures.items(): finalimage[L] = {} for (px, py), color in pixels.items(): finalimage[L][(px, py)] = [c / (1 + c) for c in color] return finalimage Uses an octree structure to manage Gaussian primitives at different levels of detail, allowing for efficient rendering and compression. Choose it when memory efficiency and compression are prioritized over raw rasterization speed. Link Organizes points into a tree structure to facilitate efficient rendering and LOD management. Choose it when streaming large point clouds with dynamic level-of-detail is required. Link Time Complexity: Real-time performance is maintained. For the OFFICE scene with 72.5M points, render time is 15.0ms. On the PLAYGROUND scene (12.5M points), rasterization takes 6.2ms (counting/memory allocation 1.9ms, splatting 2.6ms, sorting/blending 1.7ms), and the neural network takes 4.5ms. Memory Complexity: Uses 4 feature descriptors per point by default. Performance: Maintains a real-time frame rate of 60 frames per second on readily available hardware (RTX4090 for rendering, Nvidia A100 for training). Strengths: Crisper images than 3D Gaussian Splatting, better gap filling and temporal consistency than ADOP, efficient handling of large point clouds. Limitations: Requires an initial dense reconstruction. Lack of anisotropic splat formulation causes noisy artifacts around silhouettes of elongated, slender objects during strong hole-filling. Hole-filling near the camera exhibits fuzzy edges and shine-through artifacts. Slight flickering can occur in areas with too many or too few points. When to use: When crisp, hole-free images are required and temporal consistency is important, especially for scenes with intricate geometry or expansive landscapes. When not to use: When an initial dense reconstruction is unavailable, or when strong hole-filling of elongated, slender objects is required (which causes noisy silhouette artifacts due to the lack of anisotropic splatting). TRIPS was introduced by Linus Franke, Darius Rückert, Laura Fink, and Marc Stamminger from Visual Computing Erlangen, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Germany. It combines ideas from 3D Gaussian Splatting and ADOP. It is used on datasets such as Tanks&Temples, MipNeRF-360, BOAT, OFFICE, GARDEN, PLAYGROUND, HORSE, and FAMILY. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 TRIPS: Trilinear Point Splatting for Real‐Time Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.15012, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Multi-scale filtering
body: Multi-scale filtering is a family of techniques in 3D Gaussian Splatting that mitigate aliasing artifacts and optimize rendering performance by adapting the Gaussian representation to the camera's viewing frequency or resolution. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by explicitly managing the spectral content of the primitives—either through training-time aggregation, test-time covariance regularization, or runtime hierarchical pruning—to ensure the rendered image remains consistent across varying scales. All methods in this family address the mismatch between the discrete sampling of the image sensor and the continuous representation of 3D Gaussians. The core mechanism involves modifying the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} to account for the sampling frequency or pixel size. 1. Covariance Regularization: To prevent aliasing (high-frequency artifacts) when zooming out or rendering at low resolution, a low-pass filter is applied. This is achieved by adding a variance term \sigma^2{test} (derived from the pixel size or testing frequency) to the projected 2D covariance: \Sigma{reg} = \Sigma{2D} + \sigma^2{test} I where I is the identity matrix. 2. Opacity Preservation: Adding variance spreads the Gaussian, reducing its peak height. To preserve the integral (total mass/energy) of the Gaussian, the opacity \alpha is scaled by a normalization factor C: C = \frac{\sqrt{|\Sigma{2D}|}}{\sqrt{|\Sigma{reg}|}} \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} \cdot C This ensures that the total contribution of the Gaussian remains constant despite the blurring. 3. Frequency Matching: The filter parameters are tuned to match the Nyquist limit of the rendering resolution. For training-time methods, this involves constraining the 3D representation frequency to the training data's sampling rate, as detailed in MIP-Splatting. For test-time methods, it involves adapting to the specific camera distance and resolution, as detailed in Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting and FilterGS. MIP-Splatting eliminates aliasing by combining a 3D smoothing filter, a 2D Mip filter, and multi-scale Gaussian selection. It sets itself apart by constraining the 3D representation frequency to the training data's Nyquist limit during training and replacing the empirical dilation filter with a physics-based box filter approximation during rendering. It uses a 4-level hierarchy (1x, 4x, 16x, 64x) and aggregates small Gaussians into coarser levels to prevent missing parts in the rendered image. Choose this method when training a new scene and you need to prevent high-frequency artifacts during optimization and rendering at arbitrary scales. Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting (SA-GS) is a training-free, test-time plugin that improves anti-aliasing by applying 2D scale-adaptive filters. Unlike MIP-Splatting, which modifies training and uses filters unaware of testing frequency, SA-GS operates on any pretrained Gaussian field, ensuring consistent primitive distribution across different rendering resolutions and camera distances by dynamically adjusting the covariance based on the target resolution. Choose this method when you need a post-processing step that adapts to specific test-time resolutions without retraining. FilterGS is a rendering acceleration method for large-scale Level-of-Detail (LoD) 3D Gaussian Splatting. It eliminates inefficient serial tree traversal and reduces redundant Gaussian-tile pairs through parallel filtering and adaptive shrinking. It addresses the critical challenges of LoD methods by using a traversal-free, parallel filtering structure that selects a single scale for each Gaussian via a learned network, avoiding expensive tree traversal at render time. Choose this method when rendering large-scale hierarchical scenes and need to decouple computational cost from tree depth. Progressively applies low-pass filtering to avoid 2D Gaussian projections becoming smaller than a pixel. The problem of aliasing in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises because standard 3DGS systematically underestimates the scale parameter during optimization, leading to erosion effects when zooming in and high-frequency artifacts when zooming out. MIP-Splatting was introduced to address these resolution-dependent artifacts by integrating multi-scale representations. Subsequent works like Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting and FilterGS expanded the family to include test-time adaptations and performance optimizations. The theoretical basis relies on treating the camera sensor as a box filter and ensuring the Gaussian's spectral content does not exceed the Nyquist limit of the sampling grid. name: 2D Mip Filter
head: Mip-Splatting 2D filter, View-dependent 2D Gaussian filter
body: The 2D Mip Filter mitigates aliasing artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting when rendering from camera distances or focal lengths larger than those encountered during training. It extends the standard 2D Gaussian filter by introducing a view-dependent opacity compensation factor that prevents excessive blurring as Gaussians become smaller relative to the pixel grid. Unlike the basic 2D Gaussian filter which dilates the covariance matrix uniformly, this method dynamically adjusts opacity based on the ratio of the original to the dilated covariance determinant. The method modifies the projected 2D covariance matrix and the opacity of each Gaussian during the rendering pass. It is typically combined with a 3D smoothing filter, which requires a smaller base variance for the 2D filter to avoid over-smoothing. Inputs: \Sigma{2D}: The projected 2D covariance matrix of a Gaussian. o: The original opacity of the Gaussian. \kappa{3D}: The variance parameter for the 2D filter dilation. Outputs: \hat{\Sigma}{2D}: The dilated covariance matrix used for rasterization. \hat{o}: The compensated opacity used for alpha blending. Data Structures: \Sigma{2D}: A 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix. \mathbf{I}: The 2 \times 2 identity matrix. Parameters: \kappa{3D}: The added variance. Default value is 0.1 when combined with the 3D smoothing filter. (Note: The original 3DGS uses 0.3 for the 2D filter alone, but this value is reduced in the Mip-Splatting context). Steps: 1. Dilate Covariance: Add the variance parameter to the diagonal of the projected covariance matrix to prevent aliasing from undersampling: \hat{\Sigma}{2D} = \Sigma{2D} + \kappa{3D} \mathbf{I} 2. Compute Compensation Factor: Calculate the square root of the ratio of the determinants of the original and dilated covariance matrices. This factor represents the relative volume change: \text{factor} = \sqrt{\frac{|\Sigma{2D}|}{|\hat{\Sigma}{2D}|}} 3. Compensate Opacity: Multiply the original opacity by the compensation factor to maintain visual consistency at different scales: \hat{o} = \text{factor} \cdot o 4. Bounding Box Update: Use the compensated opacity \hat{o} (rather than the original o) when computing opacity-aware bounding boxes for culling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compute2dmipfilter(Sigma2D: list, opacity: float, kappa3D: float = 0.1) -> tuple: """ Computes the dilated covariance and compensated opacity for the 2D Mip Filter. Args: Sigma2D: 2x2 list of lists representing the projected 2D covariance matrix [[a, b], [c, d]]. opacity: Original opacity scalar. kappa3D: Variance parameter for dilation (default 0.1). Returns: Tuple of (dilatedSigma2D, compensatedopacity) """ # Extract matrix elements a, b = Sigma2D[0] c, d = Sigma2D[1] # Step 1: Dilate covariance matrix # Add kappa3D to the diagonal elements dilatedSigma2D = [[a + kappa3D, b], [c, d + kappa3D]] # Step 2: Compute determinants detoriginal = a d - b c detdilated = (a + kappa3D) (d + kappa3D) - b c # Guard against numerical instability if determinant is near zero or negative # Clamp determinants to a small positive epsilon to avoid NaNs in sqrt epsilon = 1e-8 detoriginal = max(detoriginal, epsilon) detdilated = max(detdilated, epsilon) # Step 3: Compute compensation factor # factor = sqrt(|Sigma2D| / |Sigmahat2D|) factor = math.sqrt(detoriginal / detdilated) # Step 4: Compensate opacity compensatedopacity = factor opacity return dilatedSigma2D, compensatedopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Instability: The analytical derivatives of the opacity compensation factor with respect to \Sigma{2D} are numerically unstable and can cause gradients to explode during training. Bounding Box Accuracy: Failing to use the compensated opacity \hat{o} for bounding box calculations can lead to incorrect culling decisions, potentially rendering Gaussians that should be culled or missing those that should be included. A technique to prevent exploding gradients in the 2D Mip filter by detaching the compensation factor from the gradient computation for the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D}. The original implementation [98] frequently clips extreme values, while other re-implementations [56, 65] use non-analytical gradients that do not match the analytical derivative. Detaching the factor ensures stable gradients while maintaining the analytical form of the forward pass. A stable implementation for the full analytical derivative is optionally available but not recommended for standard training. Time Complexity: The additional computation involves determinant calculation and square root operations per Gaussian, which is negligible compared to the rasterization cost. The authors report that their simplifications effectively eliminate any training overhead compared to the original implementation. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the stored Gaussian parameters. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, enabling full anti-aliasing (including the 2D Mip Filter) improves PSNR at 0.5x resolution from 25.11 to 28.39, while maintaining comparable PSNR at 1x resolution (27.56 vs 27.54). Strengths: Significantly reduces aliasing artifacts when rendering at resolutions different from training resolution or from distant cameras. Limitations: Can lead to increasingly blurry renderings if the compensation factor is not applied, as the dilated covariance dominates at large distances. The 2D Mip Filter was introduced by Yu et al. as part of the Mip-Splatting framework. It builds upon the 2D Gaussian filter used in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by Kerbl et al. [37], which adds a constant variance to prevent aliasing when Gaussians fall between pixels. Yu et al. identified that this uniform dilation causes excessive blurring during inference when the camera is far away, and introduced the view-dependent opacity compensation to mitigate this. The method is cited as [98] in the Faster-GS paper. Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting
head: SA-GS
body: Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting (SA-GS) is a training-free, test-time plugin for 3D Gaussian Splatting that improves anti-aliasing by applying 2D scale-adaptive filters to each Gaussian primitive. It solves the mismatch between Gaussian scales learned during training and the sampling frequency encountered at test time, which causes aliasing artifacts when zooming out or rendering at low resolutions. Unlike Mip-Splatting, which modifies the training procedure and uses 3D smoothing/2D Mip filters unaware of testing frequency, SA-GS operates at test-time and uses filters informed by testing frequency. Inputs: Pre-trained 3D Gaussian field (positions, covariances, opacities, colors); camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, focal length); rendering resolution (W, H). Outputs: Rendered image. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Defined by mean position \mu, 3D covariance \Sigma{3D} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Projected Covariance: \Sigma{2D}, a 2 \times 2 matrix representing the Gaussian's spread in screen space. Steps: 1. Calculate Testing Frequency: Determine the effective sampling frequency based on the rendering resolution and camera distance. 2. Project and Regularize Covariance: Project the 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space to obtain \Sigma{2D}. Apply a 2D scale-adaptive low-pass filter by adding a variance term \sigma^2{test} to the projected covariance: \Sigma{reg} = \Sigma{2D} + \sigma^2{test} I where I is the 2 \times 2 identity matrix and \sigma^2{test} is derived from the testing frequency (resolution and camera distance). 3. Adjust Opacity: To preserve the integral (total mass) of the Gaussian after blurring, scale the opacity \alpha by a normalization factor C: C = \frac{\sqrt{|\Sigma{2D}|}}{\sqrt{|\Sigma{reg}|}} \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} \cdot C This ensures the Gaussian's contribution remains consistent despite the scale adaptation. 4. Integrate within Pixels: Instead of simple point sampling, integrate the projected 2D Gaussian within each pixel area. This acts as a limiting case of super-sampling, handling sampling rates smaller than the scene frequency. The integration can be approximated by evaluating the cumulative distribution function or using a fixed number of samples within the pixel bounds weighted by the Gaussian PDF. Parameters: \sigma^2{test}: Adaptive variance term. Not given in the sources as a fixed formula, but described as being informed by testing frequency (resolution and camera distance). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jaggedness without Filtering: Super-sampling and integration are only effective when the scale-adaptive filtering is activated; without it, scale inconsistency leads to jaggedness at low sampling rates. Scale Mismatch: If the Gaussian scale does not match the testing frequency, high-frequency artifacts appear. Eliminates high-frequency artifacts in dynamic scenes by adapting the dilation scale using the ratio of Gaussian scales before and after temporal changes, unlike Mip-Splatting's fixed dilation scale. Choose for dynamic 4D scenes. A training-stage module that corrects scale-dependent color mismatch by applying a learnable, scale-specific RGB offset to the SH DC coefficient. Choose when color fidelity across scales is critical and training modification is acceptable. Time Complexity: Adds a constant-time filter application per Gaussian during rendering. Integration within pixels may increase per-pixel cost slightly compared to vanilla splatting. Memory Complexity: No additional memory required for training data structures as it is training-free. Performance: Performs comparably with or better than Mip-Splatting in various settings and both bounded and unbounded scenes. Strengths: Training-free; can be applied to any pre-trained Gaussian splatting field as a plugin; explicitly aware of testing frequency. Limitations: Requires modification of the rendering pipeline to implement the adaptive filter and integration; does not address view-dependent effects as directly as methods like VDGS. SA-GS was introduced to address the limitations of Mip-Splatting, which requires modifying the training procedure and uses 3D smoothing/2D Mip filters that are unaware of testing frequency. It builds on the principle that observing Gaussians at different frequencies leads to mismatches between training and testing scales. The method was proposed by Z. Song et al.. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 SA-GS: Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Anti-Aliasing, https://core.ac.uk/download/620273869.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive-Scale Color Offset
body: Adaptive-Scale Color Offset (ACO) is a training-stage module for multi-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting that corrects scale-dependent color mismatch by applying a learnable, scale-specific RGB offset to the shared base color of each Gaussian. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Alias-free 4D Gaussian Splatting by modifying only the Spherical Harmonics (SH) DC coefficient to adapt color per scale, while keeping Gaussian geometry and higher-order view-dependent SH coefficients unchanged. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: N: Number of Gaussians. S: Number of rendering scales. B: Number of SH basis functions. f{i,b} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The original SH coefficients for Gaussian i and basis b. Yb(d): The value of the b-th SH basis function evaluated at view direction d. s{target}: The index of the target rendering scale during inference (0 \le s{target} < S). Outputs: c{i, s{target}}(d): The corrected color of Gaussian i at scale s{target} for view direction d. Data Structures SH Coefficients (f): A tensor of shape (N, B, 3). f{i,b} stores the RGB coefficients for Gaussian i and basis b. ACO Offsets (\Delta): A learnable parameter tensor of shape (N, S, 3). \Delta{i,s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the RGB offset for Gaussian i at scale s. Initialized to zero: \Delta{i,s} = \mathbf{0} for all i, s. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the ACO offset matrix \Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times S \times 3} with zeros. 2. Training Loop: a. Select a training scale s from the set of S scales. b. Render the scene at scale s using the standard 3DGS splatting algorithm. c. Compute the reconstruction loss \mathcal{L} between the rendered image and the ground truth image. d. Back-propagate \mathcal{L} to update the corresponding offset \Delta{i,s} for the selected scale s. 3. Inference/Rendering: a. Given a target rendering scale s{target}. b. For each Gaussian i and view direction d: i. Retrieve the original DC coefficient f{i,0}. ii. Retrieve the scale-specific offset \Delta{i, s{target}}. iii. Compute the adapted DC coefficient: f{i,0}^{s{target}} = f{i,0} + \Delta{i, s{target}}. iv. Compute the color using the adapted DC coefficient and the shared higher-order coefficients: c{i, s{target}}(d) = Y0(d) f{i,0}^{s{target}} + \sum{b=1}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b}. v. Use c{i, s{target}}(d) for splatting. Formulas The base color representation for Gaussian i along view direction d is given by the SH expansion: ci(d) = \sum{b=0}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b} where Yb(d) is the b-th SH basis function and f{i,b} is the corresponding SH coefficient. The scale-adapted color at scale s is defined as: c{i,s}(d) = Y0(d) f{i,0}^s + \sum{b=1}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b} where the adapted DC coefficient is f{i,0}^s = f{i,0} + \Delta{i,s}. Here, \Delta{i,s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the learnable DC color offset for Gaussian i at scale s. Parameters Number of Scales (S): Not given in the sources. SH Degree: Not given in the sources, but B is the number of basis functions. Initialization: \Delta{i,s} = 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Geometry Independence: ACO modifies only the DC color term. Shared Higher-Order Coefficients: The higher-order SH coefficients (b > 0) remain shared across all scales and are not modified by the offset. Optimization Scope: The DC offsets are optimized through the backbone reconstruction loss alone. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def evaluateshbases(d, degree): # Standard spherical harmonic basis evaluation x, y, z = d[:, 0], d[:, 1], d[:, 2] invsqrt4pi = 1.0 / (4 3.141592653589793) 0.5 bases = [torch.fulllike(x, invsqrt4pi)] if degree >= 1: bases.append(torch.fulllike(x, y invsqrt4pi)) if degree >= 2: bases.append(torch.fulllike(x, z invsqrt4pi)) if degree >= 3: bases.append(torch.fulllike(x, x invsqrt4pi)) # Higher degrees follow standard formulas return torch.stack(bases, dim=1)[:,:degree] class AdaptiveScaleColorOffset(nn.Module): def init(self, numgaussians, numscales): super().init() # ACO offsets: shape (N, S, 3), initialized to zero self.offsets = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(numgaussians, numscales, 3)) def forward(self, shcoeffs, viewdirections, targetscale): # shcoeffs: (N, B, 3) # viewdirections: (N, 3) # targetscale: int in [0, S-1] dccoeff = shcoeffs[:, 0,:] # (N, 3) higherordercoeffs = shcoeffs[:, 1:,:] # (N, B-1, 3) # Retrieve scale-specific offset scaleoffset = self.offsets[:, targetscale,:] # (N, 3) adapteddc = dccoeff + scaleoffset # (N, 3) # Evaluate SH basis functions for view directions Y0 = torch.full((shcoeffs.size(0), 1), 1.0 / (4 3.141592653589793) 0.5, device=shcoeffs.device) Yhigher = evaluateshbases(viewdirections, shcoeffs.size(1) - 1) # (N, B-1, 1) # Compute scale-adapted color: c{i,s}(d) = Y0 f{i,0}^s + sum{b=1}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b} colordc = Y0 adapteddc.unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 3) colorhigher = torch.sum(Yhigher higherordercoeffs, dim=1) # (N, 3) return colordc.squeeze(1) + colorhigher # (N, 3) A companion module that redistributes low-contribution Gaussians toward high-error regions to fix primitive allocation imbalance. It differs from ACO by modifying geometry and primitive placement rather than color offsets. Choose it when coarse-scale regions lack sufficient Gaussian coverage. Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation The parent method that ACO extends is Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting. It applies 2D scale-adaptive filters to improve anti-aliasing by matching Gaussian scales to testing frequency. It differs from ACO by filtering geometry/scales rather than correcting color offsets. Choose it as the base rendering pipeline before applying color corrections. A sibling method that addresses aliasing in dynamic scenes using frequency-domain filtering. It differs from ACO by not using scale-specific color offsets but rather temporal and spatial anti-aliasing techniques. Choose it for dynamic scenes where temporal consistency is critical. Alias-free 4D Gaussian Splatting Time Complexity: Rendering time is not significantly increased by ACO, as it only adds a vector addition to the DC coefficient per Gaussian. The training time increases slightly due to the optimization of the offset parameters \Delta. Memory Complexity: ACO adds N \times S \times 3 parameters to the model, where N is the number of Gaussians and S is the number of scales. Strengths: Corrects color mismatch at coarse rendering scales without altering Gaussian geometry. It provides scale-dependent color adaptation. Limitations: Only corrects color, not geometry or view-dependent shading (higher-order SH). It requires training at multiple scales. When to use: When rendering multi-scale 3DGS and observing color inaccuracies at coarse scales. When not to use: When geometry accuracy is the primary concern, or when single-scale rendering is sufficient. ACO was proposed in the paper "Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting" published in Mathematics in 2026. It addresses the issue where coarse-scale error regions remain underrepresented in multi-scale 3DGS, leading to color mismatch because the same color representation is shared across rendering scales. The method is part of the ACO-EGR framework, which also includes Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR). Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14152713, fetched 2026-11-01

name: 2D-GES Anti-Aliasing via Object Space Filtering
head: Back-projected EWA filter, Object space scaling adjustment
body: This method provides a training-free, test-time anti-aliasing technique for 2D Gaussian Splatting (2D-GES) by avoiding screen-space filtering. Instead, it back-projects the screen-space Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) filter into object space, implementing the anti-aliasing effect as a simple scaling adjustment of the 2D Gaussians. This approach is distinct from screen-space filters, which are unsuitable for per-splat rendering in 2D-GES due to the use of planar depth and accurate perspective projection. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Alias-free 4D Gaussian Splatting by operating directly on the 2D Gaussian scaling parameters rather than modifying the 4D representation or color offsets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The original 2D Gaussian parameters: covariance \Sigmai, scaling matrix (implicitly or explicitly defined), opacity \sigmai, and the affine approximation of the object-to-screen transformation Ji. Output: Adjusted scaling and opacity parameters ready for rendering, which eliminate aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: Covariance Matrix (\Sigmai): A 2 \times 2 symmetric positive-definite matrix representing the Gaussian spread in object space. Scaling Matrix (\mathbf{S}i): A diagonal matrix \text{diag}(s{i,1}, s{i,2}) used to approximate the filtered covariance. Transformation Matrix (Ji): The 2 \times 2 affine approximation of the object-to-screen transformation. Filter Size (r): A scalar representing the EWA filter radius. Parameters: r: EWA filter size. Typical value is not explicitly given in the sources, but it is a standard parameter in EWA splatting. [G: Commonly r=2 or 3 pixels in screen space, but must be consistent with the filter definition used in the renderer]. \Sigmai: Set to Identity matrix I for the unit 2D Gaussian in object space. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Screen-Space Filtered Covariance: Calculate the effective covariance of the Gaussian in screen space. This accounts for the transformation Ji and the EWA filter r. The filtered Gaussian in screen space is defined as: \rhoi(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \frac{1}{|Ji^{-1}|} G{Ji \Sigmai Ji^T + rI}(\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}) where: \hat{\mathbf{x}} is the pixel position in screen space. \hat{\mathbf{p}} is the rasterized position of the Gaussian center in screen space. Ji is the affine approximation of the object-to-screen transformation. r is the EWA filter size. I is the 2 \times 2 identity matrix. |Ji^{-1}| is the determinant of the inverse transformation matrix. 2. Back-Project to Object Space: Transform the screen-space filter back into the local Gaussian object space. The filtered Gaussian in object space \rho'i(\mathbf{x}) is given by: \rho'i(\mathbf{x}) = G{\Sigmai + r Ji^{-1} Ji^{-T}}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}) where: \mathbf{x} is the position in object space. \mathbf{p} is the Gaussian center in object space. Note: The source writes Ji^{-1} Ji^{-1} T, which denotes Ji^{-1} (Ji^{-1})^T or Ji^{-1} Ji^{-T}. 3. Approximate with Scaling Matrix: Since the method uses a unit 2D Gaussian in object space, set \Sigmai = I. The covariance matrix of the filtered Gaussian becomes I + r Ji^{-1} Ji^{-T}. To simplify computation, approximate this covariance matrix using a diagonal scaling transformation \mathbf{S}i = \text{diag}(s{i,1}, s{i,2}) such that: \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^T \approx I + r Ji^{-1} Ji^{-T} This implies: s{i,1}^2 \approx 1 + r (Ji^{-1} Ji^{-T}){0,0} s{i,2}^2 \approx 1 + r (Ji^{-1} Ji^{-T}){1,1} [G: In practice, one might compute the eigenvalues of I + r Ji^{-1} Ji^{-T} and take the square roots, or simply use the diagonal elements if the off-diagonal terms are negligible or rotated out. The source states "approximate... using a scaling transformation", implying a diagonal approximation is sufficient for the shader implementation]. 4. Adjust Rendering Parameters: Multiply the original scaling of the 2D Gaussians by \mathbf{S}i. If the original scaling is represented by a matrix \mathbf{S}{orig}, the new scaling is \mathbf{S}{new} = \mathbf{S}{orig} \mathbf{S}i. Multiply the original opacity \sigmai by 1/(s{i,1}s{i,2}) to preserve the integral (energy) of the Gaussian after scaling. \sigma{new} = \frac{\sigmai}{s{i,1} s{i,2}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def applyobjectspacefiltering(gaussiancovariance, gaussianopacity, Jinv, r): """ Applies anti-aliasing via object space filtering to a 2D Gaussian. Args: gaussiancovariance (np.ndarray): 2x2 covariance matrix Sigmai in object space. gaussianopacity (float): Original opacity sigmai. Jinv (np.ndarray): 2x2 inverse of the object-to-screen transformation matrix. r (float): EWA filter size. Returns: tuple: (newscalingmatrix, newopacity) """ # Step 1 & 2: Compute the back-projected covariance in object space # Covariance = Sigmai + r Jinv @ Jinv.T # Note: The source uses Sigmai = I for the unit Gaussian assumption in the approximation step, # but the general formula includes Sigmai. We follow the general formula first. backprojectedcov = gaussiancovariance + r (Jinv @ Jinv.T) # Step 3: Approximate with scaling matrix Si = diag(s1, s2) # We approximate backprojectedcov with Si @ Si.T # A simple approximation is to take the square root of the diagonal elements # if we assume the off-diagonal elements are small or handled by rotation. # However, a more robust approximation for a diagonal scaling matrix # matching the variance is to use the eigenvalues or just the diagonal. # The source says "approximate... using a scaling transformation". # Let's use the diagonal elements of the back-projected covariance as the squared scales. # This assumes the principal axes align with the coordinate system or the error is acceptable. s1sq = backprojectedcov[0, 0] s2sq = backprojectedcov[1, 1] # Guard against negative values due to numerical precision s1sq = max(s1sq, 1e-6) s2sq = max(s2sq, 1e-6) s1 = np.sqrt(s1sq) s2 = np.sqrt(s2sq) # Step 4: Adjust scaling and opacity # The original scaling is not explicitly passed as a matrix, but implied by the covariance. # If the Gaussian is defined by scaling Sorig and rotation R, then Sigma = Sorig R R^T Sorig^T. # The method says "multiply the original scaling... by Si". # So we return the scaling factors s1, s2 to be multiplied with the existing scale. # And the opacity adjustment. opacityscalefactor = 1.0 / (s1 s2) newopacity = gaussianopacity opacityscalefactor # Return the scaling adjustment factors # The caller should multiply their existing scale parameters by s1 and s2 respectively. return (s1, s2), newopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure s{i,1} and s{i,2} are positive. If the back-projected covariance diagonal elements are negative due to numerical error, clamp them to a small positive value. Boundaries: The method assumes the affine approximation Ji is valid. For highly non-linear projections, this approximation may introduce artifacts. Degenerate Input: If Ji is singular (e.g., Gaussian is viewed edge-on or at infinity), Ji^{-1} is undefined. Check for singularity before inversion. Extends anti-aliasing to 4D (3D space + time) by modifying the 4D Gaussian representation. Choose when temporal consistency and 4D scenes are required. Link Adjusts color based on scale to reduce aliasing. Choose when color bleeding is a primary concern. Link Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, as it involves matrix multiplication and square root operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per Gaussian for storing the scaling factors. Measured Performance: The method is described as "concise and efficient" for shader implementation. It does not increase the number of primitives. Table 6 in shows that 2D-GES uses 0.18M surfels + 2.21M Gaussians for the Garden scene, comparable to other methods. Strengths: Training-free, test-time plugin, efficient shader implementation, no need for screen-space filtering. Limitations: Relies on the affine approximation Ji, which may be inaccurate for extreme perspectives. Approximates the covariance with a diagonal scaling matrix, potentially losing rotational information. When to use: When rendering 2D Gaussian Splatting scenes with high-frequency details and aliasing artifacts are visible, and a lightweight, training-free solution is preferred. When not to use: When high accuracy in rotational covariance is required, or when the scene contains extreme perspective distortions that violate the affine approximation. The method originates from the paper "When Gaussian Meets Surfel: Ultra-fast High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". It builds on the concept of back-projecting screen-space filters into object space, a technique previously used in [Ren et al. 2002b] for EWA splatting. The specific application to 2D-GES addresses the limitations of screen-space filters in per-splat rendering with planar depth and accurate perspective projection. When Gaussian Meets Surfel: Ultra-fast High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3730925, fetched 2026-10-26

name: FilterGS
head: Traversal-Free Parallel Filtering, Adaptive Shrinking, Parallel filtering structure for Gaussian scale selection
body: FilterGS is a rendering acceleration method for large-scale Level-of-Detail (LoD) 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates inefficient serial tree traversal and reduces redundant Gaussian-tile pairs through parallel filtering and adaptive shrinking. It proposes a traversal-free, parallel filtering structure that selects a single scale for each Gaussian, avoiding expensive tree traversal at render time. Unlike sibling methods that rely on serial level-by-level traversal, FilterGS completes filtering in two parallel steps regardless of tree depth, decoupling computational cost from hierarchical depth. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A hierarchical LoD Gaussian tree model (trained from SfM points and images), a camera view (position, orientation, intrinsics), and a pre-computed scene-adaptive shrinking threshold \tau. Outputs: A set of filtered 2D Gaussians ready for standard \alpha-blending rasterization, with redundant pairs removed and influence radii adaptively shrunk. Data Structures LoD Gaussian Tree: Nodes encapsulate full Gaussian primitives. Node Parameters: Center position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color c, rotation q, and scale s. Hierarchy Construction: For a parent node v with rotation R(qv) and scale sv, children are placed using oriented offsets ok \in \{\pm xv/2, \pm yv/2, \pm zv/2\}: \mu{uk} = \muv + R(qv) ok Children shrink geometrically: s{uk} = \gamma sv with 0 < \gamma < 1. Children inherit parent orientation, color, and opacity: q{uk} = qv, c{uk} = cv, \alpha{uk} = \alphav. Ancestor Path (AP{i,j}): For every node N{i,j} at level i, a pre-computed ordered list of serial numbers of all ancestor nodes from the direct parent up to the root node. Algorithm Steps 1. Preprocessing (Offline): Perform a pre-rendering pass over all training views following the standard 3DGS pipeline. Compute the Global Tile Coverage (GTC) metric \bar{G}, defined as the average Gaussian-to-Tile Contribution (GTC) across all views. Derive the scene-adaptive shrinking threshold \tau = f(\bar{G}). The exact functional form of f and the directional relationship between \bar{G} and \tau are not given in the sources. 2. Parallel Filtering (Per Frame): Step 1: Radius and Leaf (R&L) Filter: Project all Gaussians inside the view frustum into 2D Gaussians. Compute the 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} and its eigenvalues \sigma (standard deviations along screen-space principal axes). Calculate the pixel radius R{2D} = 3\sigma. Retention Rule: Retain any node where R{2D} \leq \tauR (default \tauR = 3). Leaf Exemption: Exempt all leaf nodes from the pruning threshold; preserve every leaf node at least once to prevent holes in the rendered image. Step 2: Ancestor Filter: For every node N{i,j} that passed R&L filtering, traverse its pre-computed ancestor path AP{i,j}. Culling Rule: If any ancestor node N{i^,j^} \in AP{i,j} is an internal node that passed R&L filtering, cull the descendant node N{i,j}. This ensures that branches with a valid coarser node retain only a single, highest-level Gaussian node. 3. Adaptive Shrinking: During Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) formation, adaptively scale the filtered Gaussians by the pre-computed factor \tau to significantly reduce redundant key-value pairs before sorting and \alpha-blending. Calculate the effective influence radius r at which opacity decays to threshold \tau: r = \sqrt{2\sigma{max} \ln(\alpha0 / \tau)} where \sigma{max} is the maximum standard deviation and \alpha0 is the central opacity. 4. Rasterization: Sort the filtered Gaussians by depth. Compute pixel color C by blending N ordered 2D Gaussians: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai Ti, \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is color, \alphai is opacity, and Ti is residual transmittance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def filtergsrender(tree, camera, taushrink, taur=3.0): # 1. Project Gaussians in frustum infrustum = [] for node in tree.allnodes: if node.isinfrustum(camera): # Standard 3DGS 2D covariance projection node.sigma2d = projectcovariance2d(node.sigma3d, camera) infrustum.append(node) # 2. Parallel Filtering Step 1: R&L Filter for node in infrustum: eig = computeeigenvalues2x2(node.sigma2d) sigmamax = max(eig) node.r2d = 3.0 sigmamax node.passedrl = False for node in infrustum: if node.isleaf or node.r2d <= taur: node.passedrl = True # 3. Parallel Filtering Step 2: Ancestor Filter # Identify internal nodes that passed R&L qualifiedinternalids = { node.id for node in infrustum if node.passedrl and not node.isleaf } for node in infrustum: if not node.passedrl: continue hasqualifiedancestor = False for ancid in node.ancestorpath: if ancid in qualifiedinternalids: hasqualifiedancestor = True break if hasqualifiedancestor: node.passedrl = False # 4. Adaptive Shrinking & Collection finalgaussians = [] for node in infrustum: if node.passedrl: # Scale Gaussian parameters by taushrink during AABB formation node.scale = taushrink node.sigma3d = taushrink 2 finalgaussians.append(node) # 5. Rasterization finalgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) image = zerosliketargetimage() for g in finalgaussians: alpha = g.alpha transmittance = 1.0 for j in range(len(finalgaussians)): if finalgaussians[j].id == g.id: break transmittance = (1.0 - finalgaussians[j].alpha) image += g.color alpha transmittance return image def projectcovariance2d(sigma3d, camera): # Standard 3DGS covariance projection using view Jacobian # Returns 2x2 matrix return [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]] def computeeigenvalues2x2(matrix): # Standard eigenvalue decomposition for 2x2 symmetric matrix # Returns tuple of eigenvalues return [1.0, 1.0] def zerosliketargetimage(): # Returns a zero-initialized image buffer matching target dimensions return [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(1920)] Parameters \tauR: Radius threshold for pruning. Default value is 3. Smaller values retain finer primitives. \tau: Scene-adaptive shrinking threshold derived from GTC. Determined by \lambdaG = 0.2 scaling factor in experiments. \gamma: Geometric shrinking factor for child node scales in the LoD tree, must satisfy 0 < \gamma < 1. Redundancy Threshold: Key-value pairs with Key-value Pair Contribution (KPC) below 0.01 are defined as redundant. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Holes in Rendering: Directly applying the radius pruning threshold may remove entire branches of Gaussians with uniformly large radii. The leaf exemption rule is critical to prevent this. Congestion: In highly congested scenes, a fixed threshold (e.g., \tau = 1/255) is overly conservative. The scene-adaptive \tau derived from GTC is necessary to mitigate congestion effectively. Precision: The calculation of R{2D} = 3\sigma assumes a standard deviation-based cutoff. Precision in eigenvalue computation for \Sigma{2D} is required for accurate radius estimation. Time Complexity: Filtering time scales with the total number of in-frustum Gaussians N and is independent of the hierarchical depth L (Depth Decoupling). T{parallel} = T{synch.} + T{calcu.}(N) where T{synch.} is the fixed overhead of kernel launch and synchronization, and T{calcu.}(N) is the time for radius estimation and filtering. Memory Complexity: Requires pre-computation of ancestor paths for all nodes, adding static memory overhead proportional to the number of nodes and tree depth. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art rendering speeds across multiple large-scale datasets (tested at 1080p resolution on RTX 4090) while maintaining competitive visual quality. Strengths: Eliminates serial traversal overhead (which can consume >60% of rendering time in LoG methods); maximizes GPU concurrency via parallel processing; reduces redundant Gaussian-tile pairs. Limitations: Requires a pre-rendering pass to compute GTC and \tau; relies on the correctness of the hierarchical tree structure; performance depends on the efficiency of the parallel filtering implementation. FilterGS was introduced to address critical challenges in large-scale Level-of-Detail 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically inefficient serial traversal and redundant Gaussian-tile pairs. The method was developed to improve upon serial strategies like LoG, which require steps proportional to tree depth. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) FilterGS: Traversal-Free Parallel Filtering and Adaptive Shrinking for Large-Scale LoD 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.23891, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Page-based Rendering, Virtual Texturing for 3DGS, Vmem
body: Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting (Vmem) enables the rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes that exceed available GPU memory by applying virtual texturing concepts. It groups Gaussians into fixed-size pages, uses a proxy mesh for visibility culling, and streams only visible pages into a limited GPU buffer. Unlike standard 3DGS which loads all Gaussians or relies on simple distance culling, Vmem separates virtual and physical address spaces, allowing dynamic LOD selection and just-in-time memory allocation to maintain stable frame rates in memory-constrained environments. Inputs: A trained 3DGS scene containing Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Camera position and orientation. Configuration parameters including Page Size (N{page}), Staging Buffer Size, Rendering Buffer Size, and Adaptive LOD memory targets. Outputs: Rendered image frame. Updated GPU memory state containing resident pages. Scene File (Preprocessed): Proxy Mesh: A coarse mesh approximating the scene geometry, used for visibility determination. Page IDs: An array mapping each Gaussian to a page index. Page Links: Adjacency list where each page ID maps to a list of overlapping page IDs. LOD Levels: Precomputed Gaussian sets for each page at different levels of detail. Size: Typically < 20 MiB. Page Structure: Each page contains a fixed number of Gaussians (N{page}). LOD Levels: For each page, multiple LOD levels exist. Level 0 contains the original Gaussians. Level L contains \frac{1}{2^L} of the Gaussians of Level 0, generated by merging or clustering Gaussians within the page. Note: The source notes that LOD creation may have flaws regarding incorrect scale and lack of level blending. GPU Buffers: Staging Buffer: A temporary buffer for copying data from CPU to GPU. Size is typically ~18.4 MiB (e.g., 40 pages of 2048 Gaussians). Rendering Buffer: A resident GPU buffer holding visible pages. Size is configurable, e.g., 500 pages for the Berlin scene which uses 489 pages. Page Table: Maps virtual page IDs to physical locations in the Rendering Buffer. Supports sparse residency or reserved resources via APIs like Vulkan or Direct3D 12. 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Mesh Extraction: Generate a proxy mesh from the 3DGS scene using techniques like marching cubes or Gaussian Opacity Fields, tailored to the scene. 2. Page Assignment: Group Gaussians into pages based on spatial position and assign a unique Page ID to each Gaussian. 3. Page Linking: Identify overlapping pages and link them if their spatial extents overlap. This ensures that pages occluded by the proxy mesh but visible via Gaussian spread are included. Pitfall: Unchecked overlaps can negate occlusion culling. A threshold should be used to ignore small overlaps. 4. LOD Generation: For each page, generate lower LOD levels by merging Gaussians so that Level L has half the count of Level L-1. 5. File Creation: Store the proxy mesh, page IDs, links, and LOD data in a single file. 2. Runtime (Per Frame): 1. Visibility Determination: Render the proxy mesh to a visibility buffer to identify which pages are potentially visible. Expand the list of visible pages by including all linked pages that overlap with directly visible pages. 2. LOD Selection: Calculate the distance from the camera to each visible page. Determine the required LOD level for each page based on distance and current memory usage. Adaptive LOD: Dynamically adjust the distance thresholds for LOD transitions to keep physical memory usage between 50% and 80%. Constraint: A single physical page in the rendering buffer can store up to 2, 4, or 8 logical pages at higher LOD levels (Level 1, 2, 3) to save space. 3. Memory Management (Streaming): Compare the set of required pages with selected LOD levels against the currently resident pages in the Rendering Buffer. Identify pages to evict if the buffer is full and pages to load. Copy non-resident pages from the staging buffer to the Rendering Buffer. Update the Page Table to map virtual IDs to physical buffer locations. 4. Rendering: Sort the resident Gaussians by depth (back-to-front). Rasterize the Gaussians to the screen. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(camera, scenefile, config): # 1. Visibility Determination # Render proxy mesh to get visible tile/page IDs visiblepageids = renderproxymeshvisibility(scenefile.proxymesh, camera) # Expand to include linked pages allrequiredpageids = set(visiblepageids) for pid in visiblepageids: if pid in scenefile.pagelinks: allrequiredpageids.update(scenefile.pagelinks[pid]) # 2. LOD Selection and Memory Budgeting # Calculate distance to each page center pagedistances = {} for pid in allrequiredpageids: pagedistances[pid] = euclideandistance(camera.position, getpagecenter(scenefile, pid)) # Determine LOD level for each page # Adaptive LOD adjusts thresholds to keep memory usage in [50%, 80%] requiredpages = [] for pid in allrequiredpageids: dist = pagedistances[pid] # Select LOD level L such that memory fits budget # Higher L means fewer Gaussians (halved per level) lodlevel = selectlodlevel(dist, config.adaptivelodthresholds, config.memorybudget) requiredpages.append((pid, lodlevel)) # 3. Memory Management # Identify resident pages in GPU buffer residentpages = getresidentpages(config.renderingbuffer) # Determine pages to load and evict pagestoload = [] pagestoevict = [] currentmemoryusage = calculatememoryusage(residentpages, config.renderingbuffercapacity) for pid, lod in requiredpages: if (pid, lod) not in residentpages: pagestoload.append((pid, lod)) # If buffer is full, evict least recently used or lowest priority pages if len(residentpages) + len(pagestoload) > config.renderingbuffercapacity: pagestoevict = selectpagestoevict(residentpages, pagestoload, config.renderingbuffercapacity) # Execute streaming for pid, lod in pagestoevict: evictpagefromgpu(config.renderingbuffer, pid, lod) for pid, lod in pagestoload: # Copy from staging buffer or disk copypagetogpu(config.stagingbuffer, config.renderingbuffer, pid, lod) # Update page table updatepagetable(config.pagetable, residentpages, pagestoload, pagestoevict) # 4. Rendering # Gather all resident Gaussians for the current frame residentgaussians = getgaussiansfrombuffer(config.renderingbuffer) # Sort by depth sortedgaussians = sortgaussiansbydepth(residentgaussians, camera) # Rasterize image = rasterizegaussians(sortedgaussians, camera, config.resolution) return image def selectlodlevel(distance, thresholds, memorybudget): """ Selects LOD level based on distance and memory constraints. Level 0: Original Gaussians. Level L: 1/2^L Gaussians. """ # Base selection from distance lod = 0 for i, threshold in enumerate(thresholds): if distance > threshold: lod = i + 1 # Adaptive adjustment: if memory is high, increase LOD (reduce Gaussians) # This is a simplified representation of the adaptive mechanism described # The source notes that thresholds are dynamically modified to keep memory in 50-80% range. if memorybudget > 0.8: lod = min(lod + 1, maxlodlevel) elif memorybudget < 0.5: lod = max(lod - 1, 0) return lod def renderproxymeshvisibility(mesh, camera): # Renders proxy mesh to a visibility buffer and returns visible page IDs return [pid for pid in mesh.visiblepages] def getpagecenter(scenefile, pid): # Returns the centroid of Gaussians in the specified page return scenefile.pagecentroids[pid] def getresidentpages(buffer): # Returns set of (pageid, lodlevel) tuples currently in GPU memory return set(buffer.residentpages) def calculatememoryusage(residentpages, capacity): # Calculates ratio of used pages to total capacity return len(residentpages) / capacity def selectpagestoevict(resident, toload, capacity): # Evicts pages to make room for toload, prioritizing higher LOD or least recently used needed = len(toload) - (capacity - len(resident)) evictcandidates = sorted(resident, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) # Evict highest LOD first return evictcandidates[:needed] def evictpagefromgpu(buffer, pid, lod): # Unmaps virtual page from physical buffer buffer.unmap(pid, lod) def copypagetogpu(staging, target, pid, lod): # Copies page data from staging to target buffer target.map(pid, lod, staging.data[pid][lod]) def updatepagetable(table, resident, load, evict): # Updates virtual-to-physical mapping for pid, lod in load: table[pid] = lod for pid, lod in evict: del table[pid] def getgaussiansfrombuffer(buffer): # Retrieves all Gaussian data from resident pages return buffer.gatherall() def sortgaussiansbydepth(gaussians, camera): # Sorts back-to-front based on camera projection return sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depthfrom(camera)) def rasterizegaussians(sortedgaussians, camera, resolution): # Standard 3DGS splatting rasterization return rasterize(sortedgaussians, camera, resolution) Page Size (N{page}): 2048 Gaussians. Smaller sizes increase page table overhead; larger sizes reduce cache locality and increase false visibility. Staging Buffer Size: ~18.4 MiB (e.g., 40 pages of 2048 Gaussians). Rendering Buffer Size: Configurable to hold visible pages, e.g., 500 pages for the Berlin scene which uses 489 pages. Camera FoV: 90° (used in evaluation paths). Adaptive LOD Memory Target: 50% to 80%. LOD Page Capacity: A single physical page can store up to 2, 4, or 8 logical pages at higher LOD levels. Page Overlap: If page overlaps are not guarded during preprocessing, occlusion culling may be negated, increasing memory overhead. LOD Artifacts: Merging Gaussians for higher LOD levels creates artifacts, especially near the camera. Reducing page overlaps and adjusting Gaussian scales can decrease these. Buffer Too Small: If the rendering buffer is too small, holes and popping artifacts occur. Page Linking Trade-off: Page links increase memory usage and can degrade image quality by forcing poorer LOD selection. Omitting links causes rendering artifacts. Mitigation: use careful page assignments and set a threshold to ignore small overlaps. LOD System Flaws: The source notes incorrect scale during LOD creation and a lack of level blending during rendering. Preprocessing: Highly parallel. For the 'Residence' scene, preprocessing takes >1 hour, with 85% spent on LOD generation. For other scenes, page assignment, linking, and LOD each take ~0.5s per page. Page Table Update: 0.9ms (Page Size 2048), 0.5ms (4096), 0.3ms (8192). Depth Sort: 2.0ms (2048), 3.0ms (4096), 6.7ms (8192). Render Time: 8.0ms (2048), 9.7ms (4096), 10.6ms (8192). Memory Usage: Drastically reduced compared to baseline. In 'Alameda', memory never exceeds 50%. In 'Residence', memory is quickly saturated without LOD but reduces drastically with LOD. Hardware: Tested on NVIDIA GTX 1070 (Desktop) and Apple M1 SoC (Mobile). Quality: With Page Links and LOD: PSNR 47.19, SSIM 0.99. Baseline (No Virtual Memory): PSNR 42.89, SSIM 0.99. Mobile Performance: iPad M1 experiences a fourfold increase in Gaussian sorting time compared to desktop due to slower integrated GPU memory access. However, Vmem reduces the number of Gaussians sorted, justifying the overhead. Strengths: Enables rendering of scenes exceeding GPU memory. Improves frame times by reducing the number of Gaussians processed. Good cache locality due to page grouping. Limitations: LOD artifacts near the camera. Page linking increases memory overhead. Streaming overhead on mobile devices. LOD system lacks level blending. Large-scale 3DGS scenes (e.g., city streets, large open scenes) where GPU memory is insufficient to hold all Gaussians. Scenarios with significant occlusions (e.g., 'Alameda') where visibility culling is effective. Small scenes with negligible occlusions (e.g., single object novel view synthesis), as the overhead of page management may not be justified. Scenes where high-fidelity LOD blending is critical and the current LOD flaws (scale, blending) are unacceptable. Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting is based on the concept of Virtual Texturing, originally applied to GPU textures by Barrett [30] and analyzed by Mayer [31]. The method adapts these concepts to 3DGS by using a proxy mesh for visibility and grouping Gaussians into pages. The specific implementation described in the source was tested on large-scale scenes like ArtSci, Residence, Alameda, and Berlin. The method is used in large-scale 3DGS rendering to handle scenes exceeding GPU memory. It was tested on desktop and mobile hardware across various scene types. The implementation avoids compression to test the virtual memory methods in isolation. Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://zenodo.org/records/19690968, fetched 2026-10-26
