name: Gaussian clustering and merging
body: Gaussian clustering and merging refers to a family of techniques that reduce the computational and memory cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by grouping individual splats into representative clusters or hierarchical nodes. These methods solve the problem of rendering large-scale scenes with millions of Gaussians by enabling Level of Detail (LOD) generation, spatial culling, and memory management. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like Multi-scale filtering or Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting is the explicit construction of cluster structures (flat or hierarchical) and the aggregation of Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) to form fewer, larger primitives, rather than merely filtering or paging existing data. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}, where each Gi is defined by position \mathbf{t}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and color coefficients ci (often spherical harmonics). The core mechanism involves partitioning G into disjoint subsets (clusters) and replacing each subset with a single representative Gaussian G'j. The aggregation of parameters generally follows one of two paradigms: 1. Arithmetic Averaging: Simple mean of position, opacity, color, and sometimes scale. This is computationally cheap but may introduce geometric artifacts if the cluster is large or heterogeneous. 2. Moment Matching: Preserving the first and second spatial moments of the cluster to minimize integrated squared error (L2 loss). For a cluster Cj, the total weight is Wj = \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai. The representative position is \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}i, and the covariance is \mathbf{\Sigma}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \left( \mathbf{\Sigma}i + (\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)(\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)^T \right). Clustering is typically performed in one of two spaces: Attribute Space: Clustering based on similarity of position, color, and scale (e.g., k-means). World Space: Clustering based on geometric proximity, often using spatial hashing, Morton codes, or hierarchical bounding volumes. Most methods support hierarchical structures (trees) to enable multi-resolution rendering, where leaf nodes contain raw splats and internal nodes contain merged representatives. A level-of-detail technique that reduces scene complexity by combining K splats into a single representative. It distinguishes itself by using moment matching for geometry and L2-optimal amplitude optimization for opacity, ensuring the merged Gaussian preserves the first and second spatial moments while minimizing integrated squared error. Choose it when geometric fidelity and minimal visual error are prioritized over computational simplicity. Generates multiple LOD levels by iteratively clustering and averaging Gaussian parameters. It differs by using simple arithmetic averaging for position, opacity, and color, while explicitly excluding scale from averaging. Choose it for computational simplicity and unified buffer formats over strict geometric fidelity. Reduces Gaussian count by merging based on k-means clustering in multidimensional attribute space. It is distinguished by its use of a virtual memory framework where pages are mapped to LOD levels, and dynamic threshold adjustment to prevent visual popping. Choose it when integrating with page-based virtual memory management and dynamic thresholding. Focuses on the culling and selection phase of a hierarchical structure. It operates via compute shaders to perform frustum culling and screen-space error-based LOD selection on pre-computed clusters. Choose it when performance scaling similar to Unreal Engine's Nanite system is required, focusing on selection rather than merge logic. Constructs hierarchical cluster structures using Morton code sorting and recursive merging. It differs by focusing on tree construction via spatial locality (Z-order curve) rather than direct optimization of a flat set. Choose it when explicit reliance on Morton code sorting for spatial locality and configurable LOD generation is needed. A preprocessing technique that converts 2D screen-space pixel coverage into world-space coordinates and applies single-linkage hierarchical clustering. It differs by relying exclusively on geometric proximity in world space rather than color or scale similarity, primarily for noise removal and coverage management. Choose it for removing foreground or background pixels that do not contribute to the primary surface representation. A minor variant focusing on the structural assembly of the cluster tree. Step: Calculate the global bounding box of all splats using CalculateGlobalBounds. Build parent levels by merging child clusters using BuildParentLevel, specifying MaxChildrenPerCluster, ParentLODLevel, and NextClusterID. Parameter: SplatsPerCluster (default 128), MaxChildrenPerCluster (default 8), bReorderSplats (default true), bGenerateLOD (default true), and LODReductionRatio (default 4). Layout: Uses FSplatSortEntry with fields uint64 MortonCode and int32 OriginalIndex, compared by MortonCode. A post-processing step that merges neighboring Gaussian blocks across leaf node boundaries to form larger Gaussians for homogeneous regions. Definition: Assesses sets of neighboring blocks in a second pass to find cross-leaf homogeneous regions for merging. Step: Store intermediate LOD refinement results as individual leaf nodes. Run spatial variance estimation on these results sequentially in groups of 26 neighbors (considering faces, edges, and corners of a 2x2x2 node). If variance is below a threshold, replace the group with a single merged Gaussian. Calculate the new position as the merged centroid and radii/opacity using standard methods. Formula: The bounding box of the merged region is defined by bboxmin = \mini cmini and bboxmax = \maxi cmaxi, where ci are the corner coordinates of the bounding boxes of the regions being merged. The need for clustering and merging in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the high memory bandwidth and compute requirements of rendering millions of splats. Early 3DGS implementations rendered all splats, leading to performance bottlenecks in large scenes. Subsequent research introduced hierarchical structures and LOD techniques to mitigate this. The concept of merging Gaussians to reduce complexity has roots in Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and volumetric representations. The specific application to 3DGS LOD generation gained traction with the introduction of methods like Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) and Sequential Point Trees (SPTs). The "Nanite-style" approach, popularized by Cluster Culling and Gaussian Cluster Builder, adapts virtual geometry techniques from film rendering to real-time rasterization. The Inter-leaf node clustering variant originates from research into approximating VDB datasets with 3D Gaussians, aiming to improve data fidelity by merging across spatial boundaries. The K-wise moment-matched merging approach emphasizes mathematical optimality in the merging process, ensuring minimal visual error compared to simple averaging. name: K-wise moment-matched merging with L2-optimal amplitude
head: cost-aware merging, substitutive LOD merging
body: K-wise moment-matched merging with L2-optimal amplitude is a level-of-detail technique that reduces scene complexity by partitioning K splats into a single representative splat. It solves the substitutive-LOD problem by preserving the first and second spatial moments of the cluster to minimize geometric distortion, while explicitly optimizing the amplitude (opacity) of the merged splat to minimize the L2 integrated squared error. It distinguishes itself from simple arithmetic averaging by preserving spatial statistics and from culling methods by retaining all visual information in a compressed form. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}, where each Gi is defined by position \mathbf{t}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color coefficients ci, plus a target cluster size K. Outputs: A reduced set of N/K representative Gaussians G' = \{G'j\}. Data Structures: Cluster: A list of indices \{i1, i2,..., iK\} mapping to the original splats. Representative Gaussian G'j: \mathbf{t}'j: Position (float32). \mathbf{\Sigma}'j: Covariance matrix (float32, 3x3 symmetric). \alpha'j: Amplitude/Opacity (float32, optimized). c'j: Color coefficients (float32, weighted average). Algorithm Steps: 1. Partitioning: Partition the set of splats G into disjoint clusters Cj of size K using one of three algorithms: greedy hierarchical (à la Runnalls), cost-increment relocation, or joint relaxation. Cost-increment relocation matches greedy merging performance within 5.5% at compression factors of four and above. 2. Moment Matching (Position and Covariance): For each cluster Cj, compute the total weight Wj = \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai, the representative position \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}i, and the covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \left( \mathbf{\Sigma}i + (\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)(\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)^T \right). 3. L2-Optimal Amplitude: Optimize the amplitude \alpha'j of the representative splat to minimize the L2 integrated squared error between the original cluster and the merged splat. The optimal amplitude is derived analytically to minimize \int \| \sum{i \in Cj} Gi(\mathbf{x}) - G'j(\mathbf{x}) \|^2 d\mathbf{x}. 4. Color Aggregation: Compute the color c'j as the weighted average of the cluster colors: c'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai ci. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Gaussian: def init(self, t, Sigma, alpha, c): self.t = t self.Sigma = Sigma self.alpha = alpha self.c = c def outerproduct(v1, v2): return [[v1[i] v2[j] for j in range(len(v2))] for i in range(len(v1))] def kwisemomentmatchedmerge(splats, K, partitionmethod='costincrement'): clusters = partition(splats, K, partitionmethod) mergedsplats = [] for cluster in clusters: W = sum(s.alpha for s in cluster) tprime = [sum(s.alpha s.t[i] for s in cluster) / W for i in range(3)] Sigmaprime = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for s in cluster: diff = [s.t[i] - tprime[i] for i in range(3)] covadd = outerproduct(diff, diff) for r in range(3): for c in range(3): Sigmaprime[r][c] += s.alpha (s.Sigma[r][c] + covadd[r][c]) for r in range(3): for c in range(3): Sigmaprime[r][c] /= W cprime = [sum(s.alpha s.c[i] for s in cluster) / W for i in range(len(cluster[0].c))] # Sources do not provide the exact closed-form scalar equation for alphaprime. # Standard L2 amplitude optimization requires solving the normal equations for the integral of squared differences. alphaprime = 1.0 mergedsplats.append(Gaussian(t=tprime, Sigma=Sigmaprime, alpha=alphaprime, c=cprime)) return mergedsplats def partition(splats, K, method): # Supports: 'greedyhierarchical', 'costincrement', 'jointrelaxation' # Simple chunking for demonstration; production code implements the specified algorithm. return [splats[i:i+K] for i in range(0, len(splats), K)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Quantization fidelity (uint16 centres, uint8 Cholesky factors) impacts results, with PSNR changes of at most -0.679 dB on fresh float32 fits. Sparse Subsamples: On sparse subsamples, mass-ranked culling may outperform this merging method in the median. Provides the closed-form framework for merging two Gaussians by minimizing L2 error, serving as the core primitive for this method. Time Complexity: Depends on the partitioning algorithm; cost-increment relocation is noted to be efficient, matching greedy performance. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory usage by a factor of K. Performance: On full fits, cost-aware merging outperforms mass-ranked culling regardless of amplitude refit. On sparse subsamples, culling wins in the median. Strengths: Preserves visual fidelity better than culling on dense data. Limitations: May be less effective than culling on sparse data. The method is described in supplementary documentation for a Gaussian splatting visualization framework, detailing cost-metric design spaces (L2, Cauchy–Schwarz, gKL, W2, MMD, L∞) for the substitutive-LOD problem. name: Analytical Merging of Gaussian Splats
head: Amplitude-optimised moment-matched template merging, Closed-form L2 integrated squared-error merging
body: Analytical merging of Gaussian splats is a closed-form framework for merging two Gaussian splats by minimizing the L2 integrated squared-error between the original pair and a single representative splat. It provides a geometric interpretation of the relative merging error, relating it to a geometric angle parameter between the splats' covariance matrices and means. This method serves as the core merging primitive for the parent technique, K-wise moment-matched merging with L2-optimal amplitude, enabling efficient level-of-detail reduction and fitting optimization. The method computes a single representative Gaussian splat from two input splats such that the L2 error between the sum of the two original splats and the single merged splat is minimized. The solution is derived analytically, ensuring the merged splat matches the first and second moments of the input pair while optimizing the amplitude to minimize the residual error. Inputs: Two Gaussian splats, G1 and G2. Each splat is defined by mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite), amplitude a \in \mathbb{R}, and color/feature vector c \in \mathbb{R}^k. Outputs: A single merged Gaussian splat G{merged} with parameters \mu', \Sigma', a', c'. Data Structures: The implementation requires storing the mean, covariance, amplitude, and color for each splat. The covariance is typically stored in a symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix or its 6 unique elements. Steps: 1. Compute Merged Mean and Covariance: The merged mean \mu' and covariance \Sigma' are calculated as the moment-matched average of the two input splats. This ensures the spatial distribution of the merged splat approximates the combined distribution of G1 and G2. \mu' = \frac{a1 \mu1 + a2 \mu2}{a1 + a2}. \Sigma' = \frac{a1 (\Sigma1 + (\mu1 - \mu')(\mu1 - \mu')^T) + a2 (\Sigma2 + (\mu2 - \mu')(\mu2 - \mu')^T)}{a1 + a2}. 2. Compute Merged Amplitude: The amplitude a' is optimized to minimize the L2 error. The optimal amplitude is the sum of the input amplitudes, adjusted by the geometric relationship between the splats. The relative merging error \epsilon is given by \epsilon = \sin^2 \alpha, where \alpha is the geometric angle parameter derived from the covariance matrices and means. The optimal amplitude is a' = (a1 + a2) \sqrt{1 - \epsilon}. 3. Compute Merged Color/Feature: The color c' is a weighted average of the input colors, weighted by their amplitudes. c' = \frac{a1 c1 + a2 c2}{a1 + a2}. Formulas: Relative Merging Error: \epsilon = \sin^2 \alpha. Geometric Angle \alpha: The angle \alpha is determined by the relative orientation and scale of the covariance matrices \Sigma1 and \Sigma2 and the distance between means \mu1 and \mu2. The exact formula for \alpha is not provided in the sources. Optimal Amplitude: a' = (a1 + a2) \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \alpha} = (a1 + a2) |\cos \alpha|. Parameters: No free parameters are required for the core merging algorithm. The method is closed-form and deterministic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Covariance: If either \Sigma1 or \Sigma2 is singular or near-singular, the geometric angle \alpha may be ill-defined. Regularization of the covariance matrices (e.g., adding a small identity matrix) may be required. Zero Amplitude: If both a1 and a2 are zero, the merged splat is undefined. This case should be handled by skipping the merge or returning a null splat. Precision: The calculation of \sin^2 \alpha requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially when the splats are very similar (\alpha \approx 0) or very different (\alpha \approx \pi/2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def outer(v1, v2): return [[v1[i] v2[j] for j in range(len(v2))] for i in range(len(v1))] def matadd(A, B): return [[A[i][j] + B[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def matscale(A, s): return [[A[i][j] s for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def mergegaussians(g1, g2): mu1, Sigma1, a1, c1 = g1 mu2, Sigma2, a2, c2 = g2 totalamplitude = a1 + a2 if totalamplitude == 0: return (mu1, Sigma1, 0.0, c1) muprime = [(a1 mu1[i] + a2 mu2[i]) / totalamplitude for i in range(3)] diff1 = [mu1[i] - muprime[i] for i in range(3)] diff2 = [mu2[i] - muprime[i] for i in range(3)] Sigmaprime = matadd( matadd(Sigma1, outer(diff1, diff1)), matadd(Sigma2, outer(diff2, diff2))) Sigmaprime = matscale(Sigmaprime, 1.0 / totalamplitude) # Compute geometric angle alpha from covariance matrices and mean distance. # Exact formula for alpha is not provided in the sources. alpha = 0.0 epsilon = math.sin(alpha) 2 aprime = totalamplitude math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - epsilon)) cprime = [(a1 c1[i] + a2 c2[i]) / totalamplitude for i in range(len(c1))] return (muprime, Sigmaprime, aprime, cprime) Stage-dependent merging is a technique for progressively refining Gaussian representations by partitioning candidate Gaussians into groups and merging them using geometry-conditioned soft weights, exposing only coarse representations at early training stages. It sets itself apart from its sibling Analytical Merging of Gaussian Splats by using a learned, soft-weighted aggregation rather than a closed-form L2-optimal geometric merge, allowing for a smooth transition from coarse to fine detail during training. Time Complexity: The merging of two splats is O(1) if the geometric angle \alpha is precomputed or approximated. Memory Complexity: O(1) per merge operation, as it only requires storing the parameters of the two input splats and the one output splat. Measured Performance: Implemented in Luxar for merging Gaussian splats during fitting or LOD reduction. Strengths: Closed-form solution ensures deterministic and fast merging. The geometric interpretation of the error provides insight into the quality of the merge. Limitations: The exact formula for the geometric angle \alpha is not provided, which may hinder implementation. The method is limited to merging two splats at a time; merging more than two requires iterative application. When to use: When efficient LOD reduction or fitting optimization is required for Gaussian splatting representations. When not to use: When the geometric angle \alpha cannot be reliably computed or when merging more than two splats simultaneously is required without iterative application. The method was introduced in the context of Luxar, a tool for Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualisation of multidimensional scientific data. The supplementary materials provide a closed-form L2 integrated squared-error framework for merging two Gaussian splats, with a geometric interpretation of the relative merging error. The method is part of a broader effort to improve the efficiency and scalability of Gaussian splatting techniques. name: Stage-dependent merging
head: Grouped merging, Soft-weighted merging
body: Stage-dependent merging is a technique for progressively refining Gaussian representations by partitioning candidate Gaussians into groups and merging them using geometry-conditioned soft weights, exposing only coarse representations at early training stages. It sets itself apart from its sibling Analytical Merging of Gaussian Splats by using a learned, soft-weighted aggregation rather than a closed-form L2-optimal geometric merge, allowing for a smooth transition from coarse to fine detail during training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 16 candidate Gaussians per token, each with attributes \mathbf{z}{p,g,i} and a gate logit \ell{p,g,i}. Outputs: A merged representation \mathbf{z}^{(s)} for the current training stage. Data Structures: Candidates are stored as a list of 16 items. Each candidate contains a vector or matrix of attributes \mathbf{z} and a scalar gate logit \ell. Steps: 1. Partition the 16 candidates into G = 2^s groups, where each group has size bs = 16 / G. 2. Calculate normalized gate weights for each candidate i in group g using a softmax function. 3. Compute the merged output for attribute \mathbf{z} in group g by taking the weighted sum of the candidates' attributes. 4. Apply a smooth stage transition to avoid abrupt changes between stages. Formulas: Normalized gate weight for candidate i in group g: w{p,g,i} = \frac {\exp (\ell {p,g,i}/\tau)} {\sum {j=1}^{bs}\exp (\ell {p,g,j}/\tau)}. Merged output for attribute \mathbf{z} in group g: \bar {\mathbf {z}}{p,g} = \sum {i=1}^{bs} w{p,g,i}\,\mathbf {z}{p,g,i}. Smooth stage transition: \mathbf {z}^{(s)} = (1-\lambda)\,\mathbf {z}^{(s-1)} + \lambda \,\bar {\mathbf {z}}^{(s)}. This procedure does not introduce new candidates but progressively relaxes the merging applied to the same underlying set of predictions. Parameters: \tau: Temperature parameter for the softmax gate. \lambda: Transition coefficient for stage interpolation, \lambda \in [0, 1]. Edge cases and pitfalls: Numerical stability requires subtracting the maximum logit before exponentiation in the softmax calculation. The transition coefficient \lambda must be clamped to [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def stagedependentmerge(candidates, gatelogits, stages, tau, lambdaval, prevstagerepr): """ candidates: list of 16 attribute vectors/matrices z{p,g,i} gatelogits: list of 16 floats l{p,g,i} stages: int, current training stage s tau: float, temperature parameter lambdaval: float, transition coefficient in [0, 1] prevstagerepr: list of merged attribute vectors from stage s-1 """ numcandidates = 16 numgroups = 2 stages groupsize = numcandidates // numgroups currentstagerepr = [] for g in range(numgroups): groupcandidates = candidates[g groupsize: (g + 1) groupsize] grouplogits = gatelogits[g groupsize: (g + 1) groupsize] # Softmax weights with numerical stability maxlogit = max(grouplogits) explogits = [math.exp((l - maxlogit) / tau) for l in grouplogits] sumexp = sum(explogits) weights = [e / sumexp for e in explogits] # Weighted sum of attributes mergedz = [0.0] len(groupcandidates[0]) for i, z in enumerate(groupcandidates): for k in range(len(z)): mergedz[k] += weights[i] z[k] currentstagerepr.append(mergedz) # Smooth stage transition finalrepr = [] for i, mergedz in enumerate(currentstagerepr): if prevstagerepr and i < len(prevstagerepr): prevz = prevstagerepr[i] interpolatedz = [ (1 - lambdaval) prevz[k] + lambdaval mergedz[k] for k in range(len(mergedz)) ] finalrepr.append(interpolatedz) else: finalrepr.append(mergedz) return finalrepr A variant used in large-scale reconstruction where cells are optimized independently and then merged. After optimization, 3D Gaussians outside the original region (before boundary expansion) are deleted for each cell to prevent floaters in other cells. The non-overlapping cells are then merged. The merged scene is seamless in appearance and geometry without obvious border artifacts because some training views are common between adjacent cells, eliminating the need for further appearance adjustment. Complexity: The merging operation is linear with respect to the number of candidates per group (bs) and the number of groups (G). Since bs \times G = 16, the complexity per token is constant O(1) with respect to the total number of candidates. Performance: Exposes only coarse representations at early stages, potentially reducing computational load during initial training phases. Strengths: Allows for progressive refinement and smooth transitions between levels of detail. Limitations: Requires learning gate logits and managing stage transitions. Stage-dependent merging was introduced in GlobalSplat: Efficient Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Global Scene Tokens. It is designed to enable efficient feed-forward rendering by managing the complexity of Gaussian representations through a staged merging process. name: Hierarchical Gaussian Merging
head: Gaussian Merging for LOD, LOD Generation via Merging, LOD Level Generation, Unified LOD Approach
body: Hierarchical Gaussian Merging generates multi-resolution representations of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by iteratively reducing the Gaussian count through averaging-based merging. It solves the problem of rendering large Gaussian sets at varying distances by creating a hierarchy of simplified LOD levels, where each level contains half the Gaussians of the previous one. Unlike moment-matching approaches that preserve spatial covariance structure, this method uses simple arithmetic averaging for most properties, prioritizing computational simplicity and unified buffer formats over geometric fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians G^{(0)} at Level 0, and a target maximum page size N{max} for spatial grouping. Output: A sequence of Gaussian sets G^{(0)}, G^{(1)}, \dots, G^{(L)}, where |G^{(l+1)}| \approx \frac{1}{2}|G^{(l)}|. Data Structures: Gaussians are grouped into "pages" to manage memory and visibility checks. Page: A container holding up to N{max} Gaussians. Gaussian: Defined by position \mathbf{t}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, and color coefficients c. Unified Buffer: LOD splats use the same memory format as original splats to facilitate efficient rendering. Steps: 1. Page Assignment: Initially, assign each mesh face a separate page. Assign each Gaussian to the page of the nearest mesh face. If a page exceeds N{max}, subdivide the corresponding mesh face (e.g., by adding a vertex at an edge midpoint) and reassign Gaussians. Repeat subdivision until each face has no more Gaussians than the target page size. To prevent thin triangles from repeated subdivisions, rotate the vertex order and choose different edges for subsequent subdivisions. 2. LOD Generation (Merging): For each level l from 0 to L-1: Group Gaussians from G^{(l)} into clusters (typically one cluster per page or spatial unit). For each cluster, compute the representative Gaussian G'{new} for G^{(l+1)} by averaging properties: Position: \mathbf{t}' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{t}i Opacity: \alpha' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai Color: c' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} ci Rotation: \mathbf{q}' = \text{Normalize}\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{q}i\right) (Standard quaternion averaging for unit quaternions) Scale: Not averaged. The source explicitly states merging is done with an average for all properties but their scale. The specific handling of scale is not given in the sources. Parameters: N{max}: Maximum Gaussians per page. Not given in the sources. L: Number of LOD levels. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Scale Ambiguity: The method explicitly excludes scale from averaging. The implementation must define how scale is derived (e.g., max, mean, or inherited). Page Subdivision: Repeated subdivision can create degenerate thin triangles, requiring careful vertex rotation and edge selection to maintain mesh quality. Time Complexity: LOD generation is linear with respect to the number of Gaussians for the averaging step, plus the cost of mesh subdivision for page balancing. Memory Complexity: Requires storing L levels of Gaussians, with each level halving the count from the previous one. Strengths: Simple implementation; unified buffer format allows efficient GPU memory management; fast generation. Limitations: Arithmetic averaging of position and rotation can introduce geometric artifacts and blurring, especially for large clusters or heterogeneous regions. Scale handling is undefined, potentially leading to visual inconsistencies. When to use: When rendering performance and memory bandwidth are critical, and visual fidelity of merged splats is secondary to simplicity. This method is described in the context of "Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting," which introduces page-based memory management for 3DGS. It is also referenced in the OpenSplat4D project. name: LOD Generation for 3DGS
head: 3DGS LOD Generation, Gaussian Clustering for LOD
body: This method reduces the number of 3D Gaussians copied, stored, sorted, and rendered by merging Gaussians into clusters based on similar attributes, minimizing distant appearance impact without altering scene creation. It operates on a virtual memory system where Gaussians are organized into pages; unlike virtual texturing where mip levels are uniform-sized pages, this method reduces the Gaussian count with each LOD level, allowing multiple virtual pages to reside within one physical page. It is distinct from K-wise moment-matched merging by using arithmetic averaging and fixed scaling factors rather than L2-optimal moment matching, and from Hierarchical Gaussian Merging by its specific integration with page-based virtual memory management and dynamic thresholding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians G assigned to spatial pages. Each Gaussian Gi has position \mathbf{t}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients ci. Output: A set of merged representative Gaussians G' for each LOD level, and a page table mapping virtual pages to physical memory with associated LOD indices. Data Structures: Page Table: An array of entries. Each entry contains: pageid: Identifier for the virtual page. lodlevel: Integer index indicating the current detail level (0 = highest detail/raw Gaussians, 1+ = merged). lastuse: Timestamp or frame counter for LRU eviction. physicaladdress: Pointer to the GPU memory buffer containing the merged Gaussians for this LOD. Gaussian Buffer: Stores the merged Gaussians. Since the count decreases with LOD, buffers for higher LODs are smaller. Algorithm Steps: 1. Clustering: For each page, identify clusters of Gaussians using the k-means algorithm in a multidimensional attribute space. The feature vector for each Gaussian includes position \mathbf{t}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, and color ci. Priority: Position attributes are prioritized during clustering to prevent dispersed clusters. This is implemented by weighting the position components higher in the distance metric used by k-means. Constraint: Only Gaussians residing on the same page can be merged into a cluster. 2. Merging: Replace each cluster Cj with a single representative Gaussian G'j. Translation: Arithmetic mean: \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{|Cj|} \sum{i \in Cj} \mathbf{t}i. Rotation: Arithmetic mean of quaternions, followed by normalization. Opacity: Arithmetic mean: \alpha'j = \frac{1}{|Cj|} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai. Color: Arithmetic mean of spherical harmonic coefficients. Scale: Arithmetic mean is not used directly. Merging scales directly causes the resulting Gaussian to be too small, creating visual gaps. Instead, the merged Gaussian is scaled up by a fixed factor k{\text{scale}} to fill gaps. The factor k{\text{scale}} is determined during training using average pixel coverage. \mathbf{s}'j = k{\text{scale}} \cdot \frac{1}{|Cj|} \sum{i \in Cj} \mathbf{s}i. 3. LOD Threshold Management: Assign an initial LOD level to each page based on distance from the camera. Dynamic Adjustment: Thresholds move away from the camera when GPU memory usage exceeds a limit, and closer when memory is available. Step Size Adaptation: To prevent rapid flipping (popping/flickering) between levels, the step size for threshold changes is dynamically adjusted based on previous moves. If a move caused overshooting (drastic memory change), the step size is reduced; if adaptation is too slow, it is increased. 4. Page Table Update: Mark page table entries with their current LOD level. When a page's LOD changes, the corresponding merged Gaussian buffer is loaded or evicted. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import sqrt, pi class Gaussian: t: tuple[float, float, float] q: tuple[float, float, float, float] s: tuple[float, float, float] alpha: float sh: tuple[float, float, float] color: tuple[float, float, float] def normalizequaternion(q: tuple[float, float, float, float]) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]: norm = sqrt(sum(cc for c in q)) return tuple(c / norm for c in q) def computeclustermean(cluster: list[Gaussian]) -> Gaussian: n = len(cluster) sumt = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sumq = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sumalpha = 0.0 sumsh = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sums = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for g in cluster: sumt = tuple(sumt[i] + g.t[i] for i in range(3)) sumq = tuple(sumq[i] + g.q[i] for i in range(4)) sumalpha += g.alpha sumsh = tuple(sumsh[i] + g.sh[i] for i in range(3)) sums = tuple(sums[i] + g.s[i] for i in range(3)) meant = tuple(v / n for v in sumt) meanq = normalizequaternion(tuple(v / n for v in sumq)) meanalpha = sumalpha / n meansh = tuple(v / n for v in sumsh) rawmeans = tuple(v / n for v in sums) return Gaussian(meant, meanq, rawmeans, meanalpha, meansh, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) def standardkmeans(points: list, k: int, maxiters: int = 10, positionweight: float = 10.0) -> list[list[int]]: """Standard Lloyd's k-means algorithm. Returns list of cluster indices.""" n = len(points) if k > n: k = n centroids = points[:k] assignments = [0] n for in range(maxiters): newassignments = [] for p in points: mindist = float('inf') bestc = 0 for i, c in enumerate(centroids): # Weight position higher to prevent dispersed clusters dist = positionweight sum((p[j] - c[j])2 for j in range(3)) + sum((p[j] - c[j])2 for j in range(3, len(p))) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestc = i newassignments.append(bestc) if newassignments == assignments: break assignments = newassignments for i in range(k): clusterpts = [points[j] for j in range(n) if assignments[j] == i] if clusterpts: centroids[i] = tuple(sum(pts[d] for pts in clusterpts) / len(clusterpts) for d in range(len(points[0]))) clusters = [[] for in range(k)] for idx, c in enumerate(assignments): clusters[c].append(idx) return clusters def generatelodgaussians(pagegaussians: list[Gaussian], clustercount: int, scalefactor: float) -> list[Gaussian]: features = [tuple(g.t + g.q + g.color) for g in pagegaussians] clusters = standardkmeans(features, k=clustercount) mergedgaussians = [] for clusterindices in clusters: clustergs = [pagegaussians[i] for i in clusterindices] mean = computeclustermean(clustergs) s = tuple(v scalefactor for v in mean.s) mergedgaussians.append(Gaussian(mean.t, mean.q, s, mean.alpha, mean.sh, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0))) return mergedgaussians def updatelodthresholds(currentmemoryusage: float, memorylimit: float, currentthresholds: list[float], prevstepdirection: int, basestep: float) -> tuple[list[float], int, float]: newthresholds = currentthresholds.copy() step = basestep # Dynamically adjust step size based on previous moves to prevent popping/flickering if prevstepdirection != 0: step = basestep 0.8 if prevstepdirection == 1 else basestep 1.2 if currentmemoryusage > memorylimit: for i in range(len(newthresholds)): newthresholds[i] += step return newthresholds, 1, step else: for i in range(len(newthresholds)): newthresholds[i] = max(0.0, newthresholds[i] - step) return newthresholds, -1, step This variant combines strategic pruning of low-impact Gaussians (e.g., volume-based masking) with clustering. Neighboring Gaussians are represented using properties stored within a "local anchor" obtained via clustering. It specifically employs a hash-grid for clustering to improve efficiency in large-scale scenes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Enables real-time rendering (60+ FPS) by reducing sorting and rendering overhead for distant geometry. Strengths: Arithmetic averaging is computationally cheap. Dynamic thresholding adapts to varying memory constraints. Limitations: Arithmetic averaging can introduce geometric artifacts if clusters are large or heterogeneous. Fixed scale factor may not be optimal for all scenes. Rapid flipping (popping) can occur if threshold adaptation is poorly tuned. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in "Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the scalability and memory demands of 3DGS in large-scale scenes. The approach is inspired by virtual texturing techniques used in computer graphics, where mip levels are used to manage memory bandwidth and capacity. The specific use of k-means clustering with position prioritization and fixed scale adjustment was proposed to minimize distant appearance impact while keeping the implementation simple. name: Cluster Culling (Nanite-style)
head: FClusterCullingCS, FClusterCullingResetCS
body: Cluster Culling (Nanite-style) is a hierarchical frustum culling and Level of Detail (LOD) selection system for 3D Gaussian Splatting, designed to efficiently cull invisible or low-priority clusters from the rendering pipeline. It operates on a pre-computed hierarchy of Gaussian clusters, testing each cluster's bounding volume against the view frustum and calculating screen-space error to determine the appropriate LOD level. Unlike sibling methods that focus on the merging of Gaussians (e.g., K-wise moment-matched merging or Hierarchical Gaussian Merging), this method focuses on the selection and culling of those clusters for rendering, enabling performance scaling similar to Unreal Engine's Nanite system. The method consists of two primary compute shader stages: a reset stage to initialize buffers and a culling stage to determine visibility and LOD. Inputs: ClusterBuffer: A structured buffer containing FGaussianGPUCluster objects. FrustumPlanes: An array of 6 plane vectors defining the view frustum in world space. LocalToWorld: A 4 \times 4 transformation matrix from local cluster space to world space. WorldToClip: A 4 \times 4 projection matrix from world space to clip space. CameraPosition: The camera's position in world space. ScreenHeight: The height of the viewport in pixels. ErrorThreshold: The maximum allowable screen-space error for a cluster to be rendered at a lower LOD. LODBias: A bias added to the calculated screen-space error to favor lower LODs. MaxDrawDistance: The maximum distance from the camera at which clusters are considered for visibility. LeafClusterCount: The number of leaf clusters in the hierarchy. ClusterCount: The total number of clusters in the hierarchy. UseLODRendering: A flag indicating whether LOD rendering is enabled. DebugForceLODLevel: A debug parameter to force a specific LOD level (-1 for auto, 0 for leaf, 1+ for specific level). Outputs: VisibleClusterBuffer: A buffer containing indices of visible clusters. VisibleClusterCountBuffer: A counter for the number of visible clusters. IndirectDrawArgsBuffer: Indirect draw arguments for the rendering engine. ClusterVisibilityBitmap: A bitmap indicating the visibility status of each cluster. SelectedClusterBuffer: A buffer of selected cluster indices for rendering. LODClusterBuffer: A buffer of clusters selected for specific LOD levels. LODClusterCountBuffer: A counter for clusters at each LOD level. LODClusterSelectedBitmap: A bitmap for LOD cluster selection. LODSplatTotalBuffer: Total number of splats in visible LOD clusters. LODSplatOutputCountBuffer: Count of splats to be output. FGaussianGPUCluster: Layout details are Not given in the sources. The culling stage accesses at minimum Center (world-space position), Radius (bounding sphere radius), LODLevel (current LOD index), and SplatCount (number of Gaussians in the cluster). 1. Reset Stage (FClusterCullingResetCS): Initialize VisibleClusterCountBuffer to 0, initialize IndirectDrawArgsBuffer with default values, and clear ClusterVisibilityBitmap, SelectedClusterBuffer, LODClusterBuffer, LODClusterCountBuffer, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, LODSplatTotalBuffer, and LODSplatOutputCountBuffer. 2. Culling Stage (FClusterCullingCS): For each cluster i in ClusterBuffer: If DebugForceLODLevel is not -1, override LODLevel to DebugForceLODLevel. Extract the cluster's world-space bounding sphere center \mathbf{c} and radius r. Frustum Culling: Test the bounding sphere against each of the 6 frustum planes. A sphere is inside the frustum if the distance from the sphere center to each plane is greater than or equal to the radius: di = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{c} + di \ge r for all i \in \{0, \dots, 5\}. If the sphere is outside any plane, mark the cluster as invisible and skip further processing. Distance Culling: Calculate the distance from the camera to the cluster center: dist = \| \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{CameraPosition} \|. If dist > MaxDrawDistance, mark the cluster as invisible. LOD Selection: If the cluster is visible and UseLODRendering is enabled, project the cluster's bounding sphere to screen space to estimate its screen-space radius r{screen}. Calculate the screen-space error E based on the cluster's size and distance. If E > ErrorThreshold + LODBias, select a higher LOD level (coarser cluster) if available. If no higher LOD is available or the error is within threshold, select the current cluster. Visibility Update: If the cluster is selected, append its index to SelectedClusterBuffer. Update ClusterVisibilityBitmap to mark the cluster as visible. Add its SplatCount to LODSplatTotalBuffer. 3. Update VisibleClusterCountBuffer with the number of selected clusters and update IndirectDrawArgsBuffer with the total number of instances and splats. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def length(v): return (sum(x x for x in v)) 0.5 def matmulvec(M, v): # M is 4x4 row-major, v is 4-component vector return [dot(M[r], v) for r in range(4)] def FClusterCullingResetCS( VisibleClusterCountBuffer, IndirectDrawArgsBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmap, SelectedClusterBuffer, LODClusterBuffer, LODClusterCountBuffer, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, LODSplatTotalBuffer, LODSplatOutputCountBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmapSize, LeafClusterCount, DebugForceLODLevel): # Initialize counters VisibleClusterCountBuffer[0] = 0 IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[0] = 0 # Draw count IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[1] = 0 # Instance count IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[2] = 0 # Start index IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[3] = 0 # Start offset # Clear bitmaps and buffers for i in range(ClusterVisibilityBitmapSize): ClusterVisibilityBitmap[i] = 0 LODClusterSelectedBitmap[0] = 0 LODSplatTotalBuffer[0] = 0 LODSplatOutputCountBuffer[0] = 0 def FClusterCullingCS( ClusterBuffer, VisibleClusterBuffer, VisibleClusterCountBuffer, IndirectDrawArgsBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmap, SelectedClusterBuffer, LODClusterBuffer, LODClusterCountBuffer, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, LODSplatTotalBuffer, LocalToWorld, WorldToClip, ClusterCount, LeafClusterCount, FrustumPlanes, CameraPosition, ScreenHeight, ErrorThreshold, LODBias, MaxDrawDistance, UseLODRendering, DebugForceLODLevel): visiblecount = 0 totalsplats = 0 for i in range(ClusterCount): cluster = ClusterBuffer[i] # Debug force LOD lodlevel = cluster.LODLevel if DebugForceLODLevel != -1: lodlevel = DebugForceLODLevel # Transform center to world space if not already center = cluster.Center radius = cluster.Radius # Frustum Culling visible = True for plane in FrustumPlanes: # plane is (normal, distance) dist = dot(plane.normal, center) + plane.distance if dist < radius: visible = False break if not visible: continue # Distance Culling disttocamera = length([center[0] - CameraPosition[0], center[1] - CameraPosition[1], center[2] - CameraPosition[2]]) if disttocamera > MaxDrawDistance: continue # LOD Selection if UseLODRendering and DebugForceLODLevel == -1: # Project radius to screen space clipcenter = matmulvec(WorldToClip, center + [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) if clipcenter[3] > 0.0: ndcradius = radius / clipcenter[3] ScreenHeight / 2.0 # Calculate error error = ndcradius / (lodlevel + 1) if error > ErrorThreshold + LODBias: # LOD selection logic not specified in sources lodlevel = lodlevel + 1 # Mark as visible ClusterVisibilityBitmap[i] = 1 SelectedClusterBuffer[visiblecount] = i visiblecount += 1 # Count splats totalsplats += cluster.SplatCount # Update output buffers VisibleClusterCountBuffer[0] = visiblecount IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[1] = visiblecount # Instance count IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[0] = totalsplats # Draw count LODSplatTotalBuffer[0] = totalsplats FrustumPlanes: Array of 6 plane vectors. ErrorThreshold: Threshold for screen-space error calculation. Typical value: Not given in the sources. LODBias: Bias applied to LOD selection. Typical value: Not given in the sources. MaxDrawDistance: Maximum distance for cluster visibility. Typical value: Not given in the sources. DebugForceLODLevel: Debug parameter to force a specific LOD level. Typical value: -1 (auto). THREADGROUPSIZE: Compilation define set to 64 for FClusterCullingCS. Precision: Frustum culling tests should use sufficient precision to avoid false negatives/positives for clusters on the frustum boundary. Degenerate Input: Clusters with zero radius or splat count should be handled gracefully (e.g., skipped or treated as invisible). LOD Selection: The exact formula for screen-space error and LOD selection is not provided in the sources. Implementers must derive this based on the specific Gaussian representation and desired visual quality. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of clusters, as each cluster is processed once in the culling stage. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing cluster data and visibility buffers. Performance: Performance scales with the number of clusters and the complexity of the frustum culling test. The use of compute shaders allows for parallel processing of clusters. Strengths: Efficient culling of invisible clusters, adaptive LOD selection based on screen-space error, integration with hierarchical clustering structures. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the pre-computed cluster hierarchy. LOD selection logic is not fully specified in the sources. When to use: When rendering large scenes with many Gaussian splats and requiring efficient frustum culling and LOD management. When not to use: For small scenes where the overhead of hierarchical culling is not justified. Cluster Culling (Nanite-style) is inspired by Unreal Engine's Nanite virtualized geometry system, which uses hierarchical clustering and culling to render large amounts of geometry efficiently. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, it adapts this concept to manage the rendering of Gaussian splats by clustering them and culling invisible or low-priority clusters. The method is implemented in the OpenSplat4D project, which provides a native 4D implementation of Gaussian splatting. name: Gaussian Cluster Builder
head: FGaussianClusterBuilder
body: The Gaussian Cluster Builder constructs a hierarchical cluster structure from a set of 3D Gaussians to enable multi-resolution rendering and efficient culling. It partitions the Gaussians into disjoint subsets and replaces each subset with a single representative Gaussian. It is distinguished by its use of spatial sorting for locality and configurable Level of Detail (LOD) generation for parent clusters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}, where each Gaussian Gi is defined by position \mathbf{t}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and color coefficients ci. Output: A hierarchical tree structure where leaf nodes contain original or grouped splats, and internal nodes contain merged representative Gaussians. Data Structures: The builder uses a configuration structure FBuildSettings with the following fields: int32 SplatsPerCluster: Number of splats per leaf cluster. Default: GaussianClusterConstants::DefaultSplatsPerCluster. int32 MaxChildrenPerCluster: Maximum children per parent cluster. Default: GaussianClusterConstants::MaxChildrenPerCluster. bool bReorderSplats: Whether to reorder splat data for cluster locality. Default: true. bool bGenerateLOD: Whether to generate LOD splats for parent clusters. Default: true. int32 LODReductionRatio: How many original splats per LOD splat. Default: 4. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sort: If bReorderSplats is true, sort the input splats by their Morton code (Z-order curve) to ensure spatial locality. 2. Leaf Clustering: Group the sorted splats into leaf clusters, each containing SplatsPerCluster splats. 3. Recursive Merging: Recursively merge clusters into parent nodes. A parent cluster is formed by grouping up to MaxChildrenPerCluster child clusters. 4. Aggregation: For each parent cluster, calculate the bounding volume and the representative Gaussian parameters. The aggregation follows the moment-matching paradigm defined in the parent article Gaussian clustering and merging: Wj = \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}i \mathbf{\Sigma}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \left( \mathbf{\Sigma}i + (\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)(\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)^T \right). 5. LOD Generation: If bGenerateLOD is true, generate LOD splats for parent clusters. The number of original splats represented by one LOD splat is determined by LODReductionRatio (default 4). 6. Reordering: If bReorderSplats is true, reorder the splat data in memory to reflect the cluster hierarchy, improving cache locality during rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildgaussianclusters(splats, settings): """ splats: List of dicts with keys 'pos' (3-tuple), 'cov' (3x3 list of lists), 'alpha' (float), 'color' (list). settings: dict with keys SplatsPerCluster, MaxChildrenPerCluster, bReorderSplats, bGenerateLOD, LODReductionRatio. """ if settings['bReorderSplats']: # Sort splats by Morton code for spatial locality splats = sorted(splats, key=lambda s: computemortoncode(s['pos'])) # Step 1: Create leaf clusters leafclusters = [] splatspercluster = settings['SplatsPerCluster'] for i in range(0, len(splats), splatspercluster): clustersplats = splats[i: i + splatspercluster] leafclusters.append(createleafcluster(clustersplats)) # Step 2: Recursively build hierarchy currentlevelclusters = leafclusters while len(currentlevelclusters) > 1: nextlevelclusters = [] maxchildren = settings['MaxChildrenPerCluster'] for i in range(0, len(currentlevelclusters), maxchildren): children = currentlevelclusters[i: i + maxchildren] parentcluster = createparentcluster(children) nextlevelclusters.append(parentcluster) currentlevelclusters = nextlevelclusters # Step 3: Generate LOD if enabled if settings['bGenerateLOD']: for cluster in currentlevelclusters: generatelodsplats(cluster, settings['LODReductionRatio']) # Step 4: Reorder splats in memory if requested if settings['bReorderSplats']: reordersplatsinmemory(currentlevelclusters) return currentlevelclusters def computemortoncode(pos): # Standard 3D Morton code interleaving of x, y, z coordinates. def interleavebits(x): x = (x | (x << 16)) & 0x00030000FF x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x0300F00FF x = (x | (x << 4)) & 0x030C30C3 x = (x | (x << 2)) & 0x09249249 return x return interleavebits(pos[0]) | (interleavebits(pos[1]) << 1) | (interleavebits(pos[2]) << 2) def createleafcluster(splats): totalalpha = sum(s['alpha'] for s in splats) if totalalpha == 0: return {'pos': (0,0,0), 'cov': [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]], 'alpha': 0, 'color': [0,0,0], 'children': splats, 'isleaf': True} meanpos = tuple(sum(s['alpha'] s['pos'][k] for s in splats) / totalalpha for k in range(3)) cov = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for s in splats: diff = [s['pos'][k] - meanpos[k] for k in range(3)] for r in range(3): for c in range(3): cov[r][c] += s['alpha'] (s['cov'][r][c] + diff[r] diff[c]) cov = [[v / totalalpha for v in row] for row in cov] # Arithmetic mean for color coefficients meancolor = [sum(s['color'][k] for s in splats) / len(splats) for k in range(len(splats[0]['color']))] return {'pos': meanpos, 'cov': cov, 'alpha': totalalpha, 'color': meancolor, 'children': splats, 'isleaf': True} def createparentcluster(children): representatives = [child if child['isleaf'] else child for child in children] totalalpha = sum(r['alpha'] for r in representatives) if totalalpha == 0: return {'pos': (0,0,0), 'cov': [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]], 'alpha': 0, 'color': [0,0,0], 'children': children, 'isleaf': False} meanpos = tuple(sum(r['alpha'] r['pos'][k] for r in representatives) / totalalpha for k in range(3)) cov = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for r in representatives: diff = [r['pos'][k] - meanpos[k] for k in range(3)] for rowidx in range(3): for colidx in range(3): cov[rowidx][colidx] += r['alpha'] (r['cov'][rowidx][colidx] + diff[rowidx] diff[colidx]) cov = [[v / totalalpha for v in row] for row in cov] # Arithmetic mean for color coefficients meancolor = [sum(r['color'][k] for r in representatives) / len(representatives) for k in range(len(representatives[0]['color']))] return {'pos': meanpos, 'cov': cov, 'alpha': totalalpha, 'color': meancolor, 'children': children, 'isleaf': False} def generatelodsplats(cluster, reductionratio): # LOD generation logic not specified in sources. pass def reordersplatsinmemory(rootcluster): # Reorders splat data in memory to reflect cluster hierarchy for cache locality. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Alpha: If a cluster has zero total alpha, it should be handled gracefully (e.g., skipped or represented by a zero-opacity Gaussian) to avoid division by zero in moment matching. Boundary Conditions: When SplatsPerCluster does not evenly divide the total number of splats, the last leaf cluster will contain fewer splats. The algorithm must handle this variable-sized cluster correctly. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when calculating covariance matrices for very small or very large clusters. Using double precision for intermediate calculations is recommended. A strategy that implements hierarchical structuring of Gaussians to enable simulations to be performed exclusively on selected Core Gaussians, accelerating the process. It organizes Gaussians into a hierarchy through clustering methods and performs simulation only on the Core Gaussians (highest level of hierarchy). This approach speeds up computations, especially when using particle-based engines such as Taichi. Time Complexity: Sorting by Morton code takes O(N \log N) where N is the number of splats. Clustering and merging are linear with respect to the number of clusters, but the recursive nature means the total time is proportional to N with a small constant factor depending on the tree depth. Memory Complexity: The hierarchical structure requires storing additional metadata for each cluster (bounding volumes, parent/child pointers). The memory overhead is proportional to the number of clusters, which is N / \text{SplatsPerCluster}. Strengths: Efficient spatial locality due to Morton code sorting. Configurable LOD generation allows for flexible trade-offs between quality and performance. Spatial clustering is effective for culling. Limitations: The quality of the merged Gaussians depends on the heterogeneity of the cluster. Large or heterogeneous clusters may introduce geometric artifacts. The method assumes a static scene; dynamic scenes may require frequent rebuilding of the hierarchy. When to Use: Suitable for large-scale 3D Gaussian splatting applications where multi-resolution rendering and efficient culling are required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for highly dynamic scenes where the hierarchy would need to be rebuilt frequently. Not suitable for scenes with very small clusters where the overhead of the hierarchy outweighs the benefits. The Gaussian Cluster Builder is a method for constructing hierarchical cluster structures from Gaussian splat data. It builds on the principles of hierarchical clustering and moment-matched merging described in the parent article Gaussian clustering and merging. name: World Space Clustering
head: Single linkage merging
body: World Space Clustering is a preprocessing step in 3D Gaussian Splatting that groups sampling pixels into clusters based on their geometric proximity in world space. It solves the problem of redundant or noisy Gaussian primitives by removing foreground or background pixels that do not contribute to the primary surface representation. Inputs: A set of 2D sampling pixels, each associated with a 3D Gaussian kernel. For each pixel, the algorithm obtains the corresponding world-space coordinate covered by the Gaussian kernel. Outputs: A set of disjoint clusters of pixel indices. Pixels belonging to the same cluster are merged or processed together; isolated pixels (outliers) are removed. Data Structures: Point Set: A list of 3D world-space coordinates \mathbf{p}k for each pixel k covered by a Gaussian. Clusters: A dictionary mapping cluster IDs to sets of pixel indices. Initially, each pixel forms its own cluster. Parameters: Initial Threshold (T0): 5 \cdot \deltad, where \deltad is the world-space distance between two adjacent pixels at the depth of the Gaussian kernel’s central pixel. Failure Multiplier: 1.5 (used if clustering fails). Opacity Pruning Threshold: 0.005 (Gaussians with opacity below this are pruned prior to clustering). Pixel Coverage Threshold: 25 pixels (Gaussians covering fewer than this are pruned). Steps: 1. Pruning: Remove any Gaussian primitives with opacity \alpha < 0.005 or those covering fewer than 25 pixels. 2. Coordinate Extraction: For each remaining Gaussian, compute the world-space coordinates \mathbf{p}k for all pixels k covered by the 2D Gaussian kernel. 3. Distance Calculation: Compute \deltad, the world-space distance between two adjacent pixels at the depth of the central pixel of the Gaussian kernel. 4. Initialization: Set the termination threshold T = T0 = 5 \cdot \deltad. Initialize each pixel coordinate as a separate cluster. 5. Iterative Merging (Single Linkage): Find the pair of distinct clusters (Ca, Cb) with the minimum distance between any two points from distinct clusters: d(Ca, Cb) = \min{\mathbf{p}i \in Ca, \mathbf{p}j \in Cb} \| \mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}j \| If d(Ca, Cb) < T, merge Ca and Cb into a single cluster. Repeat until only one cluster remains or no pair of clusters has a distance less than T. 6. Failure Handling: If the process fails to produce a valid clustering, update T \leftarrow 1.5 \cdot T and repeat steps 5–6. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def worldspaceclustering(gaussians): # Step 1: Pruning validgaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g.opacity >= 0.005 and g.pixelcount >= 25] # Step 2: Coordinate Extraction points = [] for g in validgaussians: for k in g.coveredpixels: points.append((k, g.worldcoordinate(k))) if not points: return [] # Step 3: Distance Calculation centralpixelidx = points[0][0] depth = points[0][1].z deltad = 2.0 depth (0.5 / 1000.0) # Approximate world distance between adjacent pixels at depth # Step 4: Initialization threshold = 5.0 deltad clusters = {p[0]: {p[0]} for p in points} pointmap = {p[0]: p[1] for p in points} # Step 5: Iterative Merging (Single Linkage) def runsinglelinkage(clusters, pointmap, threshold): while True: mindist = float('inf') mergepair = None clusterids = list(clusters.keys()) for i in range(len(clusterids)): for j in range(i + 1, len(clusterids)): c1, c2 = clusterids[i], clusterids[j] dist = min( computeeuclideandistance(pointmap[p1], pointmap[p2]) for p1 in clusters[c1] for p2 in clusters[c2]) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist mergepair = (c1, c2) if mergepair is None or mindist >= threshold: break c1, c2 = mergepair clusters[c1].update(clusters[c2]) del clusters[c2] return clusters clusters = runsinglelinkage(clusters, pointmap, threshold) # Step 6: Failure Handling # If clustering fails (e.g., too many small clusters remain), repeat with increased threshold if len(clusters) > len(points) // 2: threshold = 1.5 clusters = runsinglelinkage(clusters, pointmap, threshold) return clusters def computeeuclideandistance(p1, p2): return ((p1.x - p2.x)2 + (p1.y - p2.y)2 + (p1.z - p2.z)2)0.5 A variant that groups 3D Gaussians based on approximate view-independent colors rather than pure spatial proximity. It serves as a coarse-level decomposition of the scene, aligning with transfer-function-based classification. Definition: Groups Gaussians by color similarity in RGB space. Steps: 1. Approximate view-independent color \tilde{c} for each Gaussian by averaging view-dependent colors cd across sampled directions D: \tilde{c} \approx \frac{1}{\|D\|} \sum{d \in D} cd 2. Apply a clustering algorithm (e.g., k-means) to group Gaussians based on \tilde{c} using Euclidean distance in RGB space. 3. Outlier Removal: For each Gaussian, search for neighbors within a small-radius sphere. Remove the Gaussian if the neighbor count falls below a predefined threshold. When to choose: When semantic or material-based segmentation is required prior to fine-level affinity-based segmentation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of pixels N and the clustering algorithm. Single linkage merging can be O(N^2) or O(N \log N) with efficient data structures (e.g., KD-trees) for nearest-neighbor searches. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store point coordinates and cluster assignments. Strengths: Effective at removing noise and redundant background/foreground pixels. Computationally lightweight compared to full optimization. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation for \deltad. May merge distinct objects if they are spatially close but semantically different (addressed by color-based variants). When to use: As a preprocessing step before projecting Gaussians into world space. When not: When fine-grained structural separation is required without color cues. Originating from the need to optimize 3D Gaussian Splatting representations, this method adapts single linkage merging (Sibson 1973) to the context of Gaussian primitives. It is used in frameworks like Augmented Radiance Field to enhance Gaussian Splatting by reducing redundancy. The color-based variant is used in VolSegGS for volumetric scene segmentation. name: Budgeted Gaussian Splatting
body: Budgeted Gaussian Splatting (BCT) is a training and deployment method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables continuous, variable primitive counts (Level of Detail) without retraining. It solves the problem of fixed-budget compression by constructing a Morton-ordered tree of primitives and a coverage-preserving prefix cut, allowing for near-lossless quality at low compression ratios. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) by providing a single, global primitive ordering whose prefixes define successive approximations of the scene, rather than camera-dependent hierarchical selectors or discrete hierarchy methods. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (means, scales, rotations, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a set of training views. Outputs: A compact binary file containing primitives in Morton order, and a runtime scheduler that selects a subset of primitives for rendering based on a budget parameter c. Data Structures: 1. Morton-Ordered Tree: Primitives are sorted by their 3D Morton code, enabling efficient prefix traversal. 2. Compact Binary Format: Stores raw primitives in Morton order, per-band equivalent planks, and SH first moments of all degrees. DC-only Compact Path: Stores 3 floats per primitive (DC component), enabling selection of up to 13.1M primitives in 3.9 GB. Full Export: Standard 3DGS PLY format with SH zero-padded to degree 3, scales/opacities in log/logit domain. 3. Residuals (for Adaptive Selection): Per cluster, two residuals are stored: Geometric spread: \sigma{geo} = \frac{p \cdot \text{tr}(T^)}{W} (world units), projected to pixels by \sigma \cdot f / d. SH residual ratio: \rho{sh} (cluster-internal SH variance vs. global RMS). Parameters: c: Compression factor or LOD tier parameter. Typical values: c \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\}. K: Capacity or maximum primitive count for the trajectory (e.g., K=2\text{M}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Construct a Morton-order tree on the trained primitives. Takes 1.5 s with 19.4 GiB peak memory on an A100 GPU for 8.56M primitives. 2. (Optional) Compute LightGaussian significance scores for pure primitive-count budgets: score every primitive with accumulated per-pixel T^\alpha over all training views via a one-pass forward scan. Validate CUDA accumulation using the telescoping identity \sumi si = \sump (1 - T^{\text{final}}), matched to 10^{-5} relative. Select top-N primitives based on this score for a given budget. 2. Runtime Selection (Per Frame): 1. Determine the target budget based on c or K. 2. Traverse the coverage-preserving prefix cut on the GPU. 3. Gather the selected prefix directly into rasterizer buffers, fusing SH evaluation and opacity compensation. No CPU-side collection or host-to-device upload is required. 4. (Adaptive Mode) Use \sigma{geo} and \rho{sh} to refine selection if content-aware pruning is enabled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocess(primitives, trainingviews): # 1. Compute 3D Morton codes for each primitive's mean position mortoncodes = [interleavebits(p.mean.x, p.mean.y, p.mean.z) for p in primitives] # 2. Sort primitives by Morton code indices = sorted(range(len(primitives)), key=lambda i: mortoncodes[i]) sortedprimitives = [primitives[i] for i in indices] # 3. Build implicit Morton tree (sorted array enables prefix traversal) tree = sortedprimitives # 4. Compute Adaptive Residuals (if enabled) clusters = spatialhashcluster(sortedprimitives) for cluster in clusters: pcount = len(cluster.primitives) # T is accumulated front-to-back transmittance over training views Tstarsum = sum(computetransmittance(p, v) for p in cluster.primitives for v in trainingviews) W = cluster.bounds.volume cluster.sigmageo = (pcount Tstarsum) / W # SH residual ratio: cluster-internal SH variance / global RMS clustervariance = variance(cluster.shcoeffs) globalrms = rms(allprimitives.shcoeffs) cluster.rhosh = clustervariance / globalrms return tree, clusters def renderframe(tree, clusters, camera, budgetc, capacityk, adaptivemode=False): # 1. Determine selection criteria if budgetc is not None: selectedindices = getprefixcutbyfactor(tree, compressionfactor=budgetc) else: selectedindices = getprefixcutbycapacity(tree, capacity=capacityk) # 2. Gather primitives into rasterizer buffers on GPU # Fuses SH evaluation and opacity compensation, no CPU upload splats = [] for idx in selectedindices: prim = tree[idx] color = evaluatesh(prim.shcoeffs, camera.direction) cov2d = projectcovariance(prim.scale, prim.rotation, camera) opacity = prim.opacity opacitycompensation(prim, camera) splats.append({'mean': prim.mean, 'cov2d': cov2d, 'color': color, 'opacity': opacity}) # 3. Rasterize image = alphablendrasterize(splats, camera.resolution) return image def computetransmittance(primitive, view): # Accumulated per-pixel Talpha contribution for scoring return primitive.opacity gaussianprojection(primitive, view) def getprefixcutbyfactor(tree, compressionfactor): # Returns indices for a coverage-preserving prefix cut total = len(tree) length = total // compressionfactor return list(range(length)) def getprefixcutbycapacity(tree, capacity): return list(range(min(capacity, len(tree)))) def interleavebits(x, y, z): # Standard 3D Morton code interleaving of x, y, z bits return (z << 2) | (y << 1) | x def spatialhashcluster(points): # Standard grid-based spatial clustering return gridcluster(points, cellsize=1.0) def variance(coeffs): mean = sum(coeffs) / len(coeffs) return sum((c - mean)2 for c in coeffs) / len(coeffs) def rms(coeffs): mean = sum(coeffs) / len(coeffs) return (sum((c - mean)2 for c in coeffs) / len(coeffs)) 0.5 def evaluatesh(shcoeffs, direction): # Evaluate spherical harmonics at given direction return evaluateshfunction(shcoeffs, direction) def projectcovariance(scale, rotation, camera): # Jacobian-based projection of 3D covariance to 2D return camera.jacobian @ rotation @ scale @ rotation.T @ camera.jacobian.T def opacitycompensation(prim, camera): # Compensation factor for depth/size return 1.0 def alphablendrasterize(splats, resolution): # Standard alpha-blending rasterization image = zeros(resolution) for s in sorted(splats, key=lambda x: x.depth): image = blendpixel(image, s) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Redundancy Blind Spot: A primitive can be geometrically redundant yet visually load-bearing (occludes neighbors, carries unique color) or geometrically isolated yet invisible (fully occluded). Aggressive geometry-only pruning removes primitives a contribution-aware score would keep. View-Direction Reversals: Large-count outliers in per-frame selection coincide with view-direction reversals where leaves entering/leaving selection are back-facing and never rasterized. Zero-Score Primitives: A significant portion of primitives (e.g., 24.3% on BlockA) may score exactly zero in LightGaussian significance, being never visible from any training view. Also known as KoalaGS. A global, view-independent LoD formulation that provides a single primitive ordering whose prefixes define successive approximations of a scene. It solves the problem of variable-quality rendering by enabling progressive streaming and continuous budget adjustment without retraining, distinguishing itself from camera-dependent hierarchical selectors like FlexGS and discrete hierarchy methods like Octree-GS. It analyzes degradation across complexity levels by projecting image complexity maps onto Gaussians, grouping them into five bins, and measuring allocation, survival rate, and quality per bin. At 0.1% budget, it retains 2.02% of Gaussians in the simplest bin [0,1) vs 0.02% in the most complex bin [4,5], achieving higher PSNR (+2.25 dB at 0.1%) despite lower survival in complex bins. Time Complexity: Preprocessing (tree construction) is fast: 1.5 s for 8.56M primitives on A100. Per-frame selection and gather is 0.8 ms for 7.07M primitives at 1920×1080. LightGaussian scoring takes 234 s for 4565 views at 7.94M primitives on RTX 4080. Memory Complexity: Compact binary storage is efficient. DC-only path uses 3 floats per primitive, selecting 13.1M primitives in 3.9 GB on 8 GB GPUs. Memory-quality Pareto on MatrixCity: 1240 MB → 34 MB at 28.4 → 17.5 dB. Matching ~20.8 dB operating point needs 110.6 MB vs. 1926 MB (GPS full), a 17× saving. Performance: BCT wall-clock time is 78±7 min over three seeds on room@529k with one A100, compared to ≈175 min for the traditional train-prune-finetune route (2.2× faster). BCT achieves higher quality (31.9 dB vs. 30.5 dB). Quality: BCT reaches near-lossless quality at low compression ratios. At c=4, quality loss is -0.05 dB. On Lego scene, BCT stop rule reaches within 0.34 dB of Vanilla quality at 44% of primitives. BCT beats random subsampling by +5.5/+7.5/+8.0 dB at matched budgets. Stability: Per-frame count stability is high: median change of 1.1% between consecutive views on a 207-view trajectory at K=2M. GPU selection accuracy matches offline Python reference exactly (5/5 views at c=1, 10/10 at c=8). Strengths: Fast preprocessing, low memory footprint, high quality at low budgets, renderer-agnostic export, continuous LOD without retraining. Limitations: Geometric redundancy blind spot, view-direction reversal outliers, requires careful tuning of c or K. Budgeted Gaussian Splatting (BCT) was introduced in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It addresses the limitations of traditional compression methods (train-prune-finetune) which are slow and lose quality. BCT provides a continuous budget-quality curve, allowing for variable primitive counts without retraining. It is used in large-scale Gaussian Splatting applications where real-time rendering and memory efficiency are critical.
