name: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting
head: KoalaGS
body: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail (LoD) for Gaussian Splatting, also known as KoalaGS, is a global, view-independent LoD formulation that provides a single primitive ordering whose prefixes define successive approximations of a scene. It solves the problem of variable-quality rendering in 3D Gaussian Splatting by enabling progressive streaming and continuous budget adjustment without retraining, distinguishing itself from camera-dependent hierarchical selectors like FlexGS and discrete hierarchy methods like Octree-GS. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 3D Gaussians (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients) initialized from a standard 3DGS or 3DGS-MCMC training run; input images for complexity estimation. Output: A sorted list of primitives based on a computed "complexity" metric, allowing any prefix of the list to be rendered to achieve a specific budget (primitive count). Data Structures Complexity Map: A precomputed field associated with each Gaussian. For a newly added or relocated Gaussian, the complexity is initialized to the minimum possible value until observed by a training view. Primitive Ordering: A static array of indices sorted by descending complexity. This ordering is view-independent and fixed after training. Parameters Receptive Field: 32 pixels (fixed). Stride: 4 to 8 pixels, depending on image resolution. Training Steps: 30,000 steps. Initial Full-Capacity Steps: First 500 steps render only at full capacity. Budget Sampling: \tau \sim U(0, 1), sampled uniformly at each training step. Complexity Dropout Rate (\delta): Default 0.2. Spatial-Variance Loss Weight (\lambda{var}): 2.0. Importance-Score Weight (\lambda): 2.0. Complexity EMA Rate (\eta): 0.8. Steps 1. Complexity Map Computation (Pre-training): Compute complexity maps once per scene before training. This is implemented in PyTorch on the GPU. Use a fixed receptive field of 32 pixels. Use a stride of 4 to 8 pixels depending on image resolution. Cache the results to disk. Cost: 20–60 seconds per scene. 2. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a standard 3DGS or 3DGS-MCMC checkpoint. Set the complexity of any newly added or relocated Gaussian to the minimum value. 3. Training Loop (30,000 steps): For each step t: If t < 500: Render the training view at full capacity (all primitives). If t \ge 500: Sample a budget \tau \sim U(0, 1). Render the training view twice: 1. At full capacity (\hat{I}i^{full}). 2. At the sampled budget \tau (\hat{I}i^{\tau}), using the prefix of the sorted primitive list corresponding to \tau. Compute the loss L using the formula below. Perform gradient descent. 4. Relocation and Complexity Update: During training, when a Gaussian is relocated or added: If it has no complexity estimate (newly added/relocated), rank it by opacity alone until a training view observes it and updates its complexity via the EMA. Apply complexity dropout during relocation selection with rate \delta=0.2. With probability \delta, the complexity term is set to zero, causing the Gaussian to compete based only on opacity. Formula The total objective L is defined as: L = \frac{1}{2} L{rec} (\hat{I}i^{full}, Ii) + L{rec} (\hat{I}i^{\tau}, Ii) + \lambda{var} L{var} + \lambda{\alpha} \bar{\alpha} + \lambda{\sigma} \bar{\sigma} Where: L{rec} is the L1+D-SSIM loss of 3DGS. \hat{I}i^{full} is the rendered image at full capacity. \hat{I}i^{\tau} is the rendered image at budget \tau. Ii is the ground truth image. L{var} is the spatial-variance loss (Eq. 6 in). \bar{\alpha} is the mean opacity of the primitives. \bar{\sigma} is the mean scale of the primitives. \lambda{var}, \lambda{\alpha}, \lambda{\sigma} are weighting hyperparameters. Pitfalls and Edge Cases New/Relocated Gaussians: A newly added or relocated Gaussian has no complexity estimate until a training view observes it. It is handled by setting its complexity to the minimum, so relocation ranks it by opacity alone until the update assigns it a value. Complexity Dropout: The dropout rate \delta interpolates between applying complexity always (\delta=0) and dropping it always (\delta=1, reducing to original opacity sampling). A default \delta=0.2 prevents relocation from repeatedly targeting the same high-complexity regions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computecomplexitymap(gaussians, images, receptivefield=32, stride=4): """Pre-compute complexity maps for all Gaussians once before training.""" # Not given in the sources: Exact functional form of 'delentropy' or other metrics. complexity = torch.zeros(len(gaussians)) return complexity def rendergaussians(gaussians, camera, numprimitives=None): """Render Gaussians. If numprimitives is specified, only render the top-k primitives.""" if numprimitives is not None: sortedindices = torch.argsort(gaussians.complexity, descending=True) selectedgaussians = gaussians[sortedindices[:numprimitives]] else: selectedgaussians = gaussians # Standard 3DGS rasterization is assumed here. return torch.zeros(3, camera.height, camera.width) def l1dssimloss(pred, target): """L1 + D-SSIM loss as used in 3DGS.""" # Not given in the sources: Exact D-SSIM implementation. return F.l1loss(pred, target) def computespatialvarianceloss(gaussians): """Spatial variance loss to discourage abrupt degradation across budgets.""" # Not given in the sources: Exact formulation of Eq. 6. return torch.tensor(0.0) def trainstep(gaussians, camera, groundtruthimage, tau, lambdavar=2.0, lambdaalpha=0.0, lambdasigma=0.0, dropoutrate=0.2): """Single training step.""" imgfull = rendergaussians(gaussians, camera) numprimitives = int(tau len(gaussians)) imgtau = rendergaussians(gaussians, camera, numprimitives=numprimitives) lrecfull = l1dssimloss(imgfull, groundtruthimage) lrectau = l1dssimloss(imgtau, groundtruthimage) lvar = computespatialvarianceloss(gaussians) meanalpha = torch.mean(gaussians.opacity) meansigma = torch.mean(gaussians.scale) loss = 0.5 lrecfull + lrectau + lambdavar lvar + lambdaalpha meanalpha + lambdasigma meansigma loss.backward() return loss def main(): # 1. Pre-training: Compute complexity maps complexitymaps = computecomplexitymap(gaussians, trainingimages) gaussians.complexity = complexitymaps # 2. Training Loop for step in range(30000): camera, groundtruth = sampletrainingdata() if step < 500: tau = 1.0 else: tau = torch.rand(1).item() loss = trainstep(gaussians, camera, groundtruth, tau) # Update Gaussians (densify, prune, etc.) # Not given in the sources: Exact densification/pruning thresholds. # updategaussians(gaussians) # Update complexity EMA for observed Gaussians # Not given in the sources: Exact EMA update logic for new observations. # gaussians.complexity = (1 - 0.8) gaussians.complexity + 0.8 newcomplexityobserved Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 15 minutes on a single NVIDIA H100 for a scene with ~2M primitives. Pre-processing (complexity map computation) takes 20–60 seconds per scene. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the complexity map for each Gaussian. No additional hierarchical data structures are needed compared to standard 3DGS. Performance: On Tanks and Temples, the default dropout rate \delta=0.2 improves AUC PSNR by 0.14 dB (24.02 vs. 23.88) compared to original opacity sampling (\delta=1). On Deep Blending, it improves AUC PSNR by 0.23 dB (29.51 vs. 29.28). Strengths: Continuous LoD allows any budget within the range; progressive streaming is enabled by the fixed ordering; view-independent selection simplifies deployment. Limitations: Requires a one-time pre-processing step; the ordering is fixed, so it may not adapt to specific camera viewpoints as well as camera-dependent methods. KoalaGS was introduced in the paper "KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the 3DGS-MCMC framework and addresses the limitations of discrete LoD methods (like Octree-GS) and camera-dependent selectors (like FlexGS) by providing a global, view-independent ordering. name: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS)
head: H-3DGS, Hierarchical-3DGS, Inria H-3DGS
body: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) is a Level-of-Detail (LoD) method that organizes 3D Gaussian primitives into a hierarchical structure to enable efficient rendering of large-scale scenes by dynamically selecting appropriate detail levels based on viewing distance. It addresses the memory bottlenecks of standard 3DGS by training scene chunks independently and merging them into a global LoD hierarchy. H-3DGS and its siblings share the core principle of spatial partitioning to manage the memory and computational load of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in large scenes. The general mechanism involves: 1. Hierarchical Organization: Primitives (Gaussians) are grouped into nodes of a tree structure (e.g., octree, cluster tree). Each node represents a spatial region and contains a summary or a set of Gaussians. 2. Level-of-Detail (LoD) Selection: During rendering, the hierarchy is traversed based on the camera's distance to the scene regions. Coarser levels (fewer, larger Gaussians) are used for distant regions, while finer levels (more, smaller Gaussians) are used for nearby regions. 3. Distance-Based Cuts: The selection of the LoD level is typically determined by a threshold distance. If the camera is closer than the threshold, the children of the current node are processed; otherwise, the current node's Gaussians are rendered, and its children are culled. 4. Memory Efficiency: By not loading or rendering all Gaussians simultaneously, the method reduces VRAM usage and increases rendering throughput for large scenes. CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian are methods for large-scale urban reconstruction that partition scenes into overlapping or disjoint blocks, train independent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models per block, and merge them at render time using a Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchy. They solve the memory and training bottlenecks of standard 3DGS in city-scale scenes by enabling distributed or block-wise training and streaming. They set themselves apart from sibling methods like Octree-GS by relying on tile-based training and merging rather than a single unified anchor-based hierarchy, and from Iterative Gaussian Synopsis by using explicit spatial partitioning for training rather than iterative synopsis generation. Octree-GS is a Level-of-Detail (LoD) method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that organizes Gaussian primitives into a sparse octree structure to enable consistent real-time rendering across varying viewing distances and scene complexities. It solves the problem of inefficient primitive usage and visual artifacts in large-scale scenes by dynamically selecting appropriate LOD levels based on camera distance, ensuring rendering speed remains stable regardless of trajectory changes. Unlike concurrent methods that require multi-resolution inputs, post-processing, or manual threshold tuning, Octree-GS achieves LoD effects in a single end-to-end training round using an accumulative LOD strategy. Iterative Gaussian Synopsis is a top-down strategy for constructing a hierarchy of Level-of-Detail (LOD) representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It addresses the challenges of deploying large-scale 3DGS models for progressive and adaptive rendering by deriving coarser levels from a full-fidelity model through adaptive, learnable pruning and downsampling, ensuring coherent simplification without the error accumulation typical of bottom-up training. It sets itself apart from siblings like Octree-GS and CityGaussian / VastGaussian / DoGaussian by using a unified top-down unfolding framework that extracts all LODs from a single optimization, rather than building independent models or using bottom-up enhancement layers. A level-of-detail framework for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables efficient rendering by dynamically selecting appropriate detail levels. A technique to prevent overfitting of Gaussians to specific viewing distances by introducing noise into the hierarchy cut distances, ensuring coarser levels are trained occasionally. For each training iteration, multiply the distances to the SPT (Split Point Tree) centers by a factor calculated as 1 + 5^{\frac{u}{4}}, where u \in (0, 1) is a uniformly random variable. The base of the exponent in the noise factor is 5. Without this noise, Gaussians of a specific scale overfit to views from a particular distance, leading to LoD popping artifacts. A method to account for differing focal lengths in datasets by using a relative distance metric for HSPT cuts, ensuring the required LoD is consistent across cameras with different projections. Choose a base focal length f{\text{base}}. For the current camera with focal length f, calculate the relative distance metric \tilde{d} for HSPT cuts as \tilde{d} = \frac{f}{f{\text{base}}} d, where d is the actual distance. Unlike standard methods that use only Euclidean distance, this method scales the cut distance by the ratio of the current focal length to a base focal length. A variant inspired by Levels of Detail (LoD) that stores splats in a tree structure where each node is represented in greater detail by its children, using non-layered models (“Separate”) with different target sizes. Lower-version splats are set as root nodes and higher-version splats as child nodes, sharing the same object ID and highest similarity score. Unlike the layered approach, no splats are shared across levels of the tree, requiring replacement of multiple splats and leading to bandwidth inefficiencies, though it allows finer-grained progressive replacement than the coarse-grained per-scene replacement of the original Separate baseline. Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. (the original 3DGS authors) in 2024 as an extension to handle large-scale environments. Prior methods for large scenes typically employed scene partitioning or multi-GPU training. H-3DGS addresses the memory bottlenecks of standard 3DGS by training chunks independently and merging them into a global LoD hierarchy. It is capable of rendering large scenes like Mont Saint-Michel interactively. The method introduces techniques such as varying level of detail noise to prevent overfitting and varying focal length adaptation to handle datasets with differing focal lengths. name: Octree-based 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Cluster-based 3DGS, Hierarchical 3DGS, Octree Gaussian Splatting, Octree-GS, Octree-based 3DGS, Towards Consistent Real-time Rendering with LOD-Structured 3D Gaussians
body:
Octree-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (Octree-GS) is a hierarchical Level-of-Detail (LoD) method that organizes Gaussian primitives into a sparse octree structure to enable consistent real-time rendering of large-scale scenes. It addresses the memory and computational bottlenecks of standard 3DGS by dynamically selecting an appropriate subset of Gaussians based on the camera's viewing distance and scene complexity, ensuring rendering stability irrespective of trajectory changes. Unlike sibling methods such as CityGaussian or Hierarchical-GS, Octree-GS employs an explicit octree with an accumulative LoD strategy and achieves these effects in a single end-to-end training round, avoiding the post-processing overhead and stroboscopic artifacts associated with distance-interval-based selection. Inputs: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud. Training images with known camera poses and intrinsics. Hyperparameters: base voxel size \delta, outlier discard ratio rd, visibility threshold 	auv, gradient threshold 	aug, growth difficulty factor  eta, bias increment \epsilon, and densification interval T. Outputs: An octree structure where each node (anchor) at level L contains a set of Gaussian primitives (either explicit or neural) and a learnable LoD bias \Delta Lj. A trained model capable of rendering novel views by selecting anchors based on distance. The core data structure is a sparse octree. Levels: The octree has K layers, indexed L \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}. LOD 0 is the coarsest level. Anchors: Each node in the octree is an "anchor." Anchors are positioned at the centers of sparse, uniform voxel grids. Voxel Size: The voxel size VL for anchors at level L is defined as VL = \delta / 2^L, where \delta is the base voxel size for LOD 0. Attributes: Each anchor j stores: Position \mathbf{p}j. Learnable LoD bias \Delta Lj. Associated Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients). The number of primitives per anchor is k. LoD Assignment: Each anchor is assigned a discrete LoD level Lj. The rendering strategy is cumulative: rendering at LoD K includes all primitives from levels 0 to K. 1. Calculate the distance d{ij} between each training camera center i and each SfM point j. 2. Determine d{max} and d{min} as the rd-th largest and smallest distances, respectively, to discard outliers. Typical rd = 0.999. 3. Calculate the number of octree layers K: K = \lfloor \log2(d{max}/d{min}) ceil + 1 where \lfloor \cdot ceil denotes the round operator. 4. Construct the octree-structured grids with K layers. 5. Initialize anchors at the voxel centers for each layer L with voxel size VL = \delta / 2^L. 6. Initialize anchor attributes (position, bias \Delta Lj = 0, and Gaussian primitives). For a given viewpoint i and anchor j: 1. Estimate the observation distance d{ij}. If camera intrinsics vary, apply a focal scale factor s to adjust the distance equivalently: d'{ij} = d{ij} \cdot s. 2. Calculate the fractional LOD level L^{ij}: L^{ij} = \log2(d{max} / d'{ij}) 3. Apply the learnable LoD bias \Delta Lj and clamp the result to [0, K-1] using a clamping function \Phi(\cdot): \hat{L}{ij} = \lfloor \Phi(L^{ij} + \Delta Lj) floor where \lfloor \cdot floor is the floor function. 4. Selection Criterion: An anchor j is selected if its assigned level Lj \le \hat{L}{ij}. 5. Opacity Blending for Smooth Transitions: To prevent artifacts at LoD boundaries, select "nearly satisfied" anchors where Lj = \hat{L}{ij} + 1. Scale the opacities of these nearly satisfied anchors by (L^{ij} - \hat{L}{ij}). Training is divided into phases to arrange Gaussians into appropriate LoD levels. Phase 1: Initial Densification 1. Run for T{prog} iterations (e.g., 10k) with a progress training weight \omega = 1.5. 2. Extend densification by an additional 10k iterations. Phase 2: Adaptive Control (Every T iterations, e.g., 100) 1. Anchor Growing: Calculate the average accumulated gradient 
abla g of spawned Gaussian primitives. If 
abla g > 	aug (default 0.0002), the primitive is significant. If the primitive is in an empty voxel, convert it to a new anchor. Next-Level Growth: To assign the LoD level L of the new anchor: Calculate thresholds: 	au{gL} = 	aug \cdot 2^{ eta L} (default  eta = 0.2). If 
abla g > 	au{g(L+1)}, promote the anchor to level L+1. If 	au{gL} < 
abla g < 	au{g(L+1)}, keep the anchor at level L. Bias Adjustment: Calculate the anchor gradient 
abla v (average gradient of spawned primitives for that anchor). If 
abla v > 	au{gL} \cdot 0.25, increase the anchor's LoD bias: \Delta Lj = \Delta Lj + \epsilon (default \epsilon = 0.01). 2. Anchor Pruning: Compute the average opacity of Gaussians generated over the last T iterations. Remove anchors with low average opacity. Calculate "view-frequency": the probability that an anchor is selected in training view frustums. Remove anchors with view-frequency below the visibility threshold 	auv (e.g., 0.7 for small scenes, 0.01 for large scenes). \delta: Base voxel size for LOD 0. rd: Outlier discard ratio (typical 0.999). 	aug: Gradient threshold for growing (default 0.0002).  eta: Growth difficulty factor (default 0.2). \epsilon: LoD bias increment (default 0.01). 	auv: Visibility threshold (0.7 small, 0.01 large, 0.2 multi-scale). T: Densification interval (default 100). \omega: Progress training weight (default 1.5). s: Focal scale factor for varying intrinsics. Varying Intrinsics: The observation distance must be scaled by s to ensure consistent footprint sizing across different camera resolutions. Stroboscopic Effects: Unlike methods using fixed distance intervals, Octree-GS uses cumulative LoD and opacity blending to avoid stroboscopic artifacts when switching levels. Floaters: Anchors with low view-frequency (invisible in most training views) can cause floaters and must be pruned. Performance: Octree-GS achieves up to 10x faster rendering than state-of-the-art methods in large-scale scenes. On the MatrixCity dataset, it achieves 32.0 FPS with 3.59M Gaussians, compared to 6.91 FPS with 20.8M Gaussians for Hierarchical-GS. Memory Efficiency: By dynamically selecting only relevant LoD levels, it significantly reduces the number of visible Gaussians (N{vis}) and storage overhead. It achieves a 99% reduction in visible primitives at far distances. Training Time: Due to single-stage LoD construction and fewer primitives to optimize, training time is reduced (e.g., 20-23 minutes vs 38-69 minutes on Mip-NeRF360). Quality: Achieves higher PSNR across all scales compared to baselines, effectively handling aliasing without erosion artifacts. Octree-GS was introduced to address the limitations of existing LoD methods in 3D Gaussian Splatting, such as the need for post-processing (Hierarchical-GS), manual threshold tuning (CityGaussian), or multi-resolution point cloud inputs (LetsGo). It builds upon the Scaffold-GS representation, extending it with an explicit octree structure and a cumulative LoD strategy. The method was developed to enable consistent real-time rendering for large-scale urban environments and complex scenes. The parent method that trains chunks independently and merges them into a global LoD hierarchy [10279-hierarchical-3d-gaussian-splatting-h-3dgs.md]. Octree-GS is a specific implementation within this family using an octree structure. Sibling methods that divide scenes into tiles, train per tile, and merge with overlap, using a LoD pyramid for streaming. They differ from Octree-GS by requiring manual distance threshold adjustments and lacking the explicit octree accumulative strategy. name: CityGaussian / VastGaussian / DoGaussian
head: City-Gaussian, CityGaussian / Hierarchical 3DGS, CityGaussian V2, DoGaussian, Vast 3D Gaussians
body: CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian are methods for large-scale urban reconstruction that partition scenes into overlapping blocks, train independent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models per block, and merge them at rendering time using a Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchy. They solve the memory and computational bottlenecks of standard 3DGS in city-scale scenes by enabling streaming and interactive exploration through spatial partitioning and distance-based detail selection. Unlike sibling methods like Octree-GS which use anchor-based neural decoders, or Iterative Gaussian Synopsis which compresses a global model, these methods rely on block-based training and merging with explicit LoD pyramids. Inputs: A set of calibrated images covering a large-scale scene (e.g., city-scale). Outputs: A set of block-specific 3DGS models and an LoD hierarchy for rendering. Data Structures: 1. Block Partition: The scene is divided into spatially overlapping or disjoint blocks (tiles). 2. Block Model: Each block contains a set of 3D Gaussians \{gi\} with parameters: position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for color. 3. LoD Pyramid: For each block, multiple detail levels are generated, typically by applying compression strategies (e.g., LightGaussian) to reduce point count, feature dimensions, and precision. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the scene into blocks. VastGaussian uses spatially disjoint regions with feathered overlap to handle varying lighting. CityGaussian uses overlapping tiles. 2. Independent Training: Train a separate 3DGS model for each block independently. DoGaussian extends this to distributed training across multiple nodes. 3. LoD Generation (Optional/Variant): Apply compression to create multiple detail levels per block. This involves reducing the number of Gaussians, lowering SH band, and quantizing parameters. 4. Rendering (Merge & Select): Distance Calculation: Calculate the distance from the camera to each block. LoD Selection: Select the appropriate detail level for each block based on the camera distance. Frustum Culling: Determine if a block intersects the camera frustum. Fusion: Concatenate Gaussians from selected blocks and detail levels for rasterization. Formulas: Block Bounds Estimation (CityGS): To avoid floaters, bounds \mathbf{p}{min}^j and \mathbf{p}{max}^j for block j are estimated using Median Absolute Deviation (MAD): MADj = \mathrm{median}\left( \left| \mathbf{p}k^j - \mathrm{median}\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right) \right| \right) \mathbf{p}{min}^j = \max\left( \min\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right), \mathrm{median}\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right) - n{MAD} \times MADj \right) \mathbf{p}{max}^j = \min\left( \max\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right), \mathrm{median}\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right) + n{MAD} \times MADj \right) where \mathbf{p}k^j are the positions of Gaussians in block j, and n{MAD} is a hyperparameter. LoD Selection: The detail level for a block is determined by the minimum distance from the block's eight corners to the camera center. Frustum Culling: Project block corners to screen space, create a bounding box, and calculate Intersection-over-Union (IoU) with the screen area. Include the block if IoU indicates intersection or if the camera is inside the block. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rendercitygaussian(camerapos, cameraproj, screenwidth, screenheight, sceneblocks, nMAD=3.0): """ Render a large-scale scene using block-based partitioning and LoD. Args: camerapos: 3D camera position array. cameraproj: 4x4 projection matrix. screenwidth, screenheight: Render resolution. sceneblocks: List of Block objects. Each Block has: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with.position attribute. lodlevels: List of compressed Gaussian sets (LOD 0, 1, 2...). lodthresholds: List of distance thresholds for LOD switching. nMAD: Hyperparameter for bound estimation. Returns: Image buffer (H, W, 3). """ image = np.zeros((screenheight, screenwidth, 3), dtype=np.float32) visiblegaussians = [] for block in sceneblocks: # 1. Estimate Block Bounds using MAD to filter floaters ppositions = np.array([g.position for g in block.gaussians]) medianpos = np.median(ppositions, axis=0) mad = np.median(np.abs(ppositions - medianpos), axis=0) pmin = np.maximum(np.min(ppositions, axis=0), medianpos - nMAD mad) pmax = np.minimum(np.max(ppositions, axis=0), medianpos + nMAD mad) # 2. Generate Box Corners corners = np.array([ [pmin[0], pmin[1], pmin[2]], [pmax[0], pmin[1], pmin[2]], [pmin[0], pmax[1], pmin[2]], [pmax[0], pmax[1], pmin[2]], [pmin[0], pmin[1], pmax[2]], [pmax[0], pmin[1], pmax[2]], [pmin[0], pmax[1], pmax[2]], [pmax[0], pmax[1], pmax[2]] ]) # 3. Frustum Culling via Screen-space IoU cornershomogeneous = np.hstack([corners, np.ones((8, 1))]) clipcoords = (cameraproj @ cornershomogeneous.T).T clipcoords = clipcoords[:,:3] / clipcoords[:, 3:4] screencoords = clipcoords[:,:2] minscreen = np.min(screencoords, axis=0) maxscreen = np.max(screencoords, axis=0) blockbbox = np.array([minscreen, maxscreen]) screenareabbox = np.array([[-1, -1], [1, 1]]) intermin = np.maximum(blockbbox[0], screenareabbox[0]) intermax = np.minimum(blockbbox[1], screenareabbox[1]) interarea = np.maximum(0, intermax - intermin).prod() blockarea = (blockbbox[1] - blockbbox[0]).prod() screenarea = 4.0 iou = interarea / (blockarea + screenarea - interarea) if (blockarea + screenarea - interarea) > 0 else 0.0 # Check if camera is inside block camerainside = np.all((camerapos >= pmin) & (camerapos <= pmax)) if iou > 0.0 or camerainside: # 4. LoD Selection based on min distance from corners to camera dists = np.linalg.norm(corners - camerapos, axis=1) mindist = np.min(dists) lodindex = 0 for i, threshold in enumerate(block.lodthresholds): if mindist > threshold: lodindex = i + 1 else: break lodindex = min(lodindex, len(block.lodlevels) - 1) visiblegaussians.extend(block.lodlevels[lodindex]) if not visiblegaussians: return image # 5. Rasterization (Standard 3DGS sorting and alpha blending) depths = np.linalg.norm([g.position for g in visiblegaussians] - camerapos, axis=1) sortedindices = np.argsort(depths) sortedgaussians = [visiblegaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] for g in sortedgaussians: # Standard 3DGS 2D projection and alpha compositing pass # Standard 3DGS rasterization step return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floaters: Outlier Gaussians (floaters) can distort block bounds. Using MAD for bound estimation mitigates this. Overlap Artifacts: Overlapping blocks may cause double rendering or seams. Feathered overlap or careful merging is required. Precision: Lower detail levels use compressed parameters with reduced precision, which may introduce visible artifacts if compression is too aggressive. Proxy-GS uses a coarse proxy mesh to guide Gaussian placement, significantly reducing the number of Gaussians required for background regions. It sets itself apart by leveraging geometric priors from a mesh to optimize Gaussian density, rather than relying solely on image-based optimization. CityGS Level-of-Detail (LoD) is a rendering optimization technique that generates multiple detail levels of Gaussians and selects them per block based on distance to the camera, reducing rasterizer load. It sets itself apart by using the LightGaussian compression strategy to create levels with different compression rates (r0, r1, r2), reducing points, feature dimensions, and precision. It is chosen for real-time rendering of very large scenes where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Time Complexity: Training is linear in the number of blocks and Gaussians per block, but parallelizable across blocks. Rendering complexity depends on the number of visible Gaussians, which is reduced by LoD selection. Memory Complexity: VRAM usage is proportional to the number of visible Gaussians at the selected LoD, significantly lower than loading all Gaussians. Measured Performance: CityGaussian enables interactive exploration of square-kilometer scenes. DoGaussian supports distributed training across nodes. Strengths: Scalability to city-scale scenes, parallelizable training, reduced VRAM usage. Limitations: Potential seams at block boundaries, complexity in managing overlapping blocks, dependency on block partitioning quality. When to use: Large-scale urban reconstruction, autonomous driving simulation, scenes with significant scale variation. When not to use: Small-scale scenes where standard 3DGS is sufficient, scenes with high dynamic content requiring global consistency (unless combined with methods like StreetGaussians). CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian originated from the need to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to city-scale environments. VastGaussian was introduced in CVPR'24, partitioning scenes into spatially-disjoint regions with decoupled appearance handling. CityGaussian and its V2 introduced hierarchical LoD across square kilometers with depth regularization and visibility-aware training. DoGaussian extended this to distributed training across nodes. These methods build on the principles of Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) [10279-hierarchical-3d-gaussian-splatting-h-3dgs.md] and address the memory bottlenecks of standard 3DGS in large scenes. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Neural Rendering — Technologies & Tricks, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeuralRenderingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03162, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) CityGaussian: Real-Time High-Quality Large-Scale Scene Rendering with Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72640-815, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: StreetGaussians
body: StreetGaussians is a method for reconstructing dynamic urban driving scenes by decomposing the environment into a static background and dynamic actors (vehicles, pedestrians). It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex, moving traffic in large-scale outdoor environments by associating each dynamic object with a separate 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) sub-model that can be transformed independently. It sets itself apart from monolithic 3DGS approaches by explicitly separating static and dynamic components, allowing for independent pose updates of actors without retraining the background. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view imagery of a driving scene and tracked trajectories/poses for dynamic objects (vehicles, pedestrians). Outputs: A static 3DGS representation of the background and a set of dynamic 3DGS sub-models, each associated with a specific actor and its time-varying pose. Data Structures: 1. Static 3DGS: Standard 3DGS representation for the background. 2. Dynamic Actor Sub-models: For each dynamic object i: A separate 3DGS representation. Standard 3DGS parameters (means, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients) apply to each sub-model. A tracked pose Ti(t) representing the object's transformation over time. Time-dependent SH coefficients c{lm,i}(t) to model appearance changes. Steps: 1. Incrementally optimize static 3D Gaussians for the background using input views. This process may be assisted by Segment Anything Model (SAM) masks and LiDAR depth data. 2. Identify dynamic objects (vehicles, pedestrians) using tracking or segmentation. 3. Train a separate 3DGS model for each dynamic object. The Gaussians are transformed by the tracked vehicle/actor poses Ti(t). 4. Approximate the appearance of dynamic objects using time-related spherical harmonic coefficients c{lm}(t). 5. Composite the static background and dynamic object renders to produce the final frame. Formulas: The position of a Gaussian g in object i's local frame is transformed to the world frame at time t via the tracked pose Ti(t). The final pixel color is computed by compositing the static background and all dynamic objects, where each dynamic object's contribution uses its transformed Gaussians and time-dependent SH coefficients. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Reconstructs dynamic driving data by compositing surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene. It aligns Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with tracked trajectories to model dynamic urban environments. It builds on StreetGaussians by adopting a similar static/dynamic separation strategy but focuses on composite reconstruction assisted by external priors. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently handles dynamic scenes by separating static and dynamic components; allows independent updates of dynamic actors; suitable for autonomous driving simulation. Limitations: Requires accurate tracking of dynamic objects to maintain pose alignment. When to use: Dynamic urban driving scenes with distinct, trackable vehicles and pedestrians. When not to use: Static scenes or scenes with untracked, highly dynamic elements. StreetGaussians was introduced to address the challenges of reconstructing dynamic urban environments for autonomous driving applications. It builds on the success of 3DGS but adapts it to handle motion by decomposing the scene into static and dynamic components. The method is part of a broader trend in 2026 towards per-actor 3DGS for AV simulation, allowing for the insertion of rare-event vehicles into any scene. It is related to other methods like DrivingGaussian, which composites surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene, assisted by external priors. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: DrivingGaussian
body: DrivingGaussian is a method for reconstructing dynamic driving data by compositing surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene. It specifically addresses the challenge of aligning the Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with their tracked trajectories to model dynamic urban environments. It builds on StreetGaussians by adopting a similar strategy of separating static and dynamic components, but focuses on the composite reconstruction process assisted by external priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-camera image sequences, input LiDAR depth data, and tracked trajectories for dynamic objects. Outputs: A single dynamic scene representation composed of static 3D Gaussians and dynamic object Gaussians aligned with trajectories. Data Structures: The method maintains two distinct sets of 3D Gaussians: 1. Static Gaussians: Representing the fixed urban background. 2. Dynamic Gaussians: Representing individual vehicles or pedestrians, each associated with a separate 3DGS sub-model. Steps: 1. Incrementally optimize the static 3D Gaussians. 2. Compose the static scene with dynamic objects' 3D Gaussians. 3. Align the Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with their tracked trajectories. 4. Assist the reconstruction process using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and input LiDAR depth data. Parameters: Tracked Trajectories: Required for each dynamic object to define its motion and pose over time. LiDAR Depth: Used as a geometric prior for depth estimation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Segmentation and Alignment: Accurate separation of dynamic objects from the static background and precise trajectory tracking are required for correct Gaussian placement. Specific failure modes or quantitative error bounds are not given in the sources. A method for urban scene data that makes Gaussians' mean and opacity values time-dependent functions centered at the corresponding Gaussian's life peak. The Life peak is defined as the maximum prominence over time. This approach allows for modeling the temporal evolution of dynamic objects within the scene. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables reconstruction of complex dynamic driving scenes by separating static and dynamic elements, leveraging external priors (LiDAR, SAM) for robustness. Limitations: Requires multi-camera setups, tracked trajectories, and external models (SAM, LiDAR), which may not be available in all scenarios. When to use: For dynamic urban driving scene reconstruction with available trajectory and LiDAR data. DrivingGaussian was introduced as a method to reconstruct dynamic driving data by compositing surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene. It aligns the Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with their tracked trajectories, building upon the concepts of modeling dynamic urban environments with separate sub-models for each vehicle or pedestrian. The method is assisted by the Segment Anything Model and input LiDAR depth data to improve reconstruction quality. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: UrbanGIRAFFE
head: UrbanGIRAFFE
body: UrbanGIRAFFE is a method for generating high-resolution, semantically controllable urban scene images by extending the GIRAFFE architecture with coarse panoptic priors. It addresses the challenge of maintaining 3D controllability and generating images exceeding 512×512 resolution under substantial camera viewpoint changes. It distinguishes itself from standard GIRAFFE by integrating semantic voxel grids and object layouts to enhance controllability for semantic layouts and large viewpoint shifts. UrbanGIRAFFE builds on the StyleGAN2-based architecture of GIRAFFE. The method extends the base concept by incorporating coarse panoptic priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Latent variables for scene generation; coarse panoptic priors consisting of semantic voxel grids and object layouts. Outputs: High-resolution images (exceeding 512×512) of urban scenes. Data Structures: Semantic Voxel Grids: A 3D grid representing semantic information of the scene. Object Layouts: Data structures defining the position and type of objects within the scene. Steps: 1. Initialize the StyleGAN2-based generator architecture as used in GIRAFFE. 2. Incorporate coarse panoptic priors into the generation process. These priors are defined as semantic voxel grids and object layouts. 3. Use these priors to guide the generation of the image, enhancing controllability for substantial camera viewpoint changes and semantic layouts. Parameters: Resolution: Exceeds 512×512. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. HiGS is a rendering architecture for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples spatial partitioning from rasterization granularity using a two-scale hierarchy. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Enhances controllability for substantial camera viewpoint changes and semantic layouts compared to standard GIRAFFE. When to use: When high-resolution (512×512+) generation with strong semantic and viewpoint controllability is required. When not: When 3D controllability is not the primary focus or when lower resolution is acceptable. UrbanGIRAFFE was introduced in [261] (cited in). It follows the footsteps of FFE HD [255] and work by Chan et al. [19], which aimed to retain the 3D controllability of GIRAFFE while generating higher quality and resolution images using StyleGAN2 [95]. UrbanGIRAFFE specifically extends this by using coarse panoptic priors. name: HiGS (Hierarchically Tiled Gaussian Splatting)
head: Hierarchical Rendering Architecture for Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: HiGS is a rendering architecture for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples spatial partitioning from rasterization granularity using a two-scale hierarchy. It solves the tile-size trade-off inherent in standard 3DGS, where large tiles reduce binning overhead but increase rasterization waste, and small tiles do the opposite. Unlike its siblings in the Pyramid, LOD, Downsampling family which often rely on model compression or hardware-specific optimizations, HiGS retains the standard exact-alpha compositing model on commodity GPUs by grouping render tiles into macro-tiles for sorting and splitting those macro-tiles into fixed-size Gaussian batches for load-balanced rasterization. HiGS operates by restructuring the pipeline into coarse partitioning/sorting and fine rasterization stages, utilizing a density-proportional work decomposition to eliminate the "rasterizer tail effect". Input: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, covariance (or conic parameters), opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Output: A 2D image frame. The implementation relies on preallocated buffers to avoid dynamic allocation stalls. 1. Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes. 2. Macro-tile List: A contiguous array of depth keys and Gaussian IDs, segmented by macro-tile. 3. Work Queue: A shared atomic queue for render tiles within a macro-tile. 4. Scheduling Buffer: Per-worker buffer to absorb variability in visible Gaussian counts. 5. Partial Blending Buffer: Per-batch buffer storing intermediate alpha/composite results. Render Tile Size: 8 \times 8 pixels. Macro-tile Size: 8 \times 4 render tiles (64 \times 32 pixels). Gaussian Batch Size: B = 1,024 Gaussians per processing unit. Partitioning Batch Size: P = 8,192 Gaussians per binning work group. 1. Binning (Coarse Partitioning): Gaussians are processed in partitioning batches of P Gaussians, each handled cooperatively by one work group. A conservative per-row ellipse-contour scan determines macro-tile overlap for each Gaussian. Overlapping Gaussians are assigned to the corresponding macro-tile's range in the output list. The output is a segmented structure containing per-macro-tile lists of depth keys and Gaussian IDs. 2. Segmented Depth Sort: A fully asynchronous on-device segmented sort is performed on the macro-tile lists. This runs as a cascade of tier-classified per-segment block sorts. Oversized segments are handled by a device-built merge tree consumed by a persistent kernel, scaling across orders of magnitude of segment sizes without host involvement. The result is a depth-sorted list of Gaussians for each macro-tile. 3. Work Decomposition: Each macro-tile's sorted Gaussian list is split into fixed-size batches of B=1,024 Gaussians. Each pair (\text{Macro-tile}, \text{Batch}) becomes an independent processing unit. A macro-tile with N Gaussians spawns \lceil N/B \rceil processing units. 4. Rasterization Dispatch: Within each processing unit, worker groups dynamically claim active render tiles from a shared tile work queue. This ensures dense macro-tiles spawn proportionally more work units, balancing load based on Gaussian density rather than screen area. 5. Visibility and Data Loading: For each claimed render tile, the worker group determines per-tile visibility masks inline. Gaussians are loaded from global memory into local storage once per macro-tile and reused across all member render tiles within that macro-tile. 6. Rasterization (Fine Granularity): Each worker group rasterizes its assigned 8 \times 8 pixel tile via front-to-back alpha blending. A per-worker scheduling buffer absorbs the per-tile variability in visible Gaussian count, allowing the blending pipeline to run at a fixed rate. All data is read from local storage. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from collections import deque RENDERTILEW = 8 RENDERTILEH = 8 MACROTILEWRT = 8 MACROTILEHRT = 4 BATCHSIZE = 1024 PARTITIONBATCHSIZE = 8192 def higgsrender(gaussians, camera, framewidth, frameheight): # 1. Binning: Group gaussians into macro-tiles macrotilelists = {} for i in range(0, len(gaussians), PARTITIONBATCHSIZE): batch = gaussians[i: i + PARTITIONBATCHSIZE] for g in batch: # Conservative per-row ellipse-contour scan determines overlap overlappingmacrotiles = getoverlappingmacrotiles(g, camera) for mtid in overlappingmacrotiles: if mtid not in macrotilelists: macrotilelists[mtid] = [] macrotilelists[mtid].append((g.depth, g.id)) # 2. Segmented Depth Sort: Sort each macro-tile list by depth for mtid in macrotilelists: macrotilelists[mtid].sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # 3. Prepare Processing Units: Split into batches processingunits = [] for mtid, sortedgaussians in macrotilelists.items(): for i in range(0, len(sortedgaussians), BATCHSIZE): batch = sortedgaussians[i: i + BATCHSIZE] processingunits.append((mtid, batch)) # 4. Rasterization: Process units frame = [[0.0] 3 for in range(frameheight framewidth)] for mtid, batch in processingunits: # Load macro-tile Gaussians into local storage localgaussians = [g for, g in batch] # Determine active render tiles in this macro-tile activetiles = [mtid 32 + t for t in range(32)] tilequeue = deque(activetiles) # Worker groups claim tiles dynamically while tilequeue: tileid = tilequeue.popleft() if tileid is None: break # Get tile coordinates rtid = tileid % 32 rtx = rtid % 8 rty = rtid // 8 tx, ty = rtx RENDERTILEW, rty RENDERTILEH # Determine visibility mask inline visiblegaussians = [] for g in localgaussians: # Check if gaussian overlaps the 8x8 tile if checkgaussiantileoverlap(g, tx, ty, RENDERTILEW, RENDERTILEH): visiblegaussians.append(g) # Sort visible gaussians by depth (preserved from global sort) visiblegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) # Rasterize tile via front-to-back alpha blending result = rasterizetilefronttoback(visiblegaussians, tx, ty, camera) # Write to frame for dy in range(RENDERTILEH): for dx in range(RENDERTILEW): px, py = tx + dx, ty + dy if 0 <= px < framewidth and 0 <= py < frameheight: idx = py framewidth + px frame[idx] = result return frame def getoverlappingmacrotiles(gaussian, camera): # Returns list of macro-tile IDs overlapping the gaussian # Uses conservative per-row ellipse-contour scan at macro-tile granularity return [0] def checkgaussiantileoverlap(gaussian, tx, ty, tw, th): # Standard axis-aligned bounding box or ellipse intersection check return True def rasterizetilefronttoback(gaussians, tx, ty, camera): color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 for g in gaussians: # Evaluate Gaussian at tile pixels # Stabilized half-precision using Cholesky factors of conics contribution = evaluategaussian(g, tx, ty, camera) color[0] += contribution.color[0] contribution.alpha (1.0 - alpha) color[1] += contribution.color[1] contribution.alpha (1.0 - alpha) color[2] += contribution.color[2] contribution.alpha (1.0 - alpha) alpha += contribution.alpha (1.0 - alpha) if alpha > 0.99: break return color def evaluategaussian(gaussian, tx, ty, camera): # Computes color and alpha contribution for the tile class Contribution: def init(self, c, a): self.color = c self.alpha = a return Contribution([0.5, 0.5, 0.5], 0.1) Precision: The data path uses half-precision (fp16) stabilized by Cholesky factors of conics. This converts the Mahalanobis quadratic into a sum of squares, preventing fp16 cancellation errors. Oversized Segments: During sorting, segments may vary greatly in size. The system uses a device-built merge tree consumed by a persistent kernel to handle this without host involvement. Memory Preallocation: To avoid producer-consumer stalls, per-macro-tile Gaussian lists, per-batch partition histograms, and per-batch partial blending buffers are preallocated up front. Performance: HiGS renders a 5.8M Gaussian scene at 1,124 FPS at 1080p resolution. It renders up to ~15.8x faster than the original 3DGS across tested scenes. Pair Count Reduction: At 1080p, mean tile-Gaussian pair counts drop from 10.1M (gsplat) to 1.51M (HiGS), an 85% reduction. At 4K, they drop from 29.3M to 2.21M, a 92% reduction. Load Balancing: In dense scenes, the peak per-work-unit load drops from 2,485 (gsplat) to ~340 (HiGS). Complexity: Time complexity is dominated by the segmented sort and rasterization. The work decomposition scales with Gaussian density rather than screen area, eliminating the tail effect. Memory: Memory footprint scales with the number of macro-tile Gaussian batches in the frame, roughly linearly with scene density at fixed resolution. Strengths: Eliminates the rasterizer tail effect, retains exact alpha compositing, works on commodity GPUs, and significantly reduces pair counts. Limitations: Requires preallocation of buffers which may increase peak memory usage compared to dynamic allocation approaches. The complexity of the segmented sort and hierarchical dispatch is higher than standard 3DGS. HiGS was introduced by Dawid Pająk, Martin Bisson, and Rodolfo Lima from NVIDIA. It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS tile-based rendering, where partitioning and rasterization costs are tied to a single tile size. Prior acceleration work like FlashGS, Splatshop, and TC-GS either fused stages, swapped compositing models, or moved to alternative hardware. HiGS differs from pair reduction methods like StopThePop and Speedy-Splat by reducing pair counts through coarser-than-render-tile partitioning rather than refining per-tile assignment. It builds on the AccuTile family's ellipse-contour intersection tests but applies them at a macro-tile level. name: Momentum-GS
head: Momentum Self-Distillation for 3DGS, Block-wise Momentum-GS
body: Momentum-GS is a block-wise training method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a momentum-updated teacher model to provide global self-distillation guidance to local block students. It decouples the block count from the GPU count and restores cross-block spatial consistency, addressing geometric inaccuracies and floaters caused by independent block training. Unlike CityGaussian, which relies on a static coarse prior and spatial contraction, Momentum-GS dynamically updates the teacher via exponential moving average (EMA) of student parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A large-scale scene dataset (images, poses), a block partitioning strategy, and hyperparameters for momentum decay (\beta), learning rate (\eta), and block weighting. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians optimized for the entire scene, with improved geometric consistency and reduced artifacts compared to independent block training. Data Structures: 1. Student Gaussians (Gs): The set of Gaussian parameters (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients C) for the current block being trained. 2. Teacher Gaussians (Gt): A global set of Gaussian parameters, updated via EMA to guide student optimization. 3. Block Weights (wb): A scalar value per block, calculated based on reconstruction accuracy. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Teacher Gaussians Gt using a coarse global prior or single-pass training, and initialize Student Gaussians Gs for each block. 2. Block Partitioning: Divide the scene into non-overlapping or overlapping blocks. 3. Training Loop (per block b): a. Forward Pass: Render the current block's Student Gaussians Gs^b to generate images. b. Distillation Loss: Compute a distillation loss between the rendered output of Gs^b and the rendered output of the global Teacher Gaussians Gt. c. Reconstruction Loss: Compute the photometric reconstruction loss between rendered images and ground truth images. d. Total Loss: Combine losses: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{rec}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{distill}}, where \lambda is a weighting factor. e. Optimization: Update Gs^b using gradient descent. f. Block Weighting: Calculate the reconstruction accuracy for block b and update its weight wb. 4. Teacher Update (EMA): After each optimization step or epoch, update the Teacher Gaussians Gt using the exponential moving average of the Student Gaussians Gs: Gt \leftarrow \beta Gt + (1 - \beta) Gs where \beta is the momentum coefficient. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-4 for all blocks until convergence. Parameters: Momentum Coefficient (\beta): Controls the decay rate of the EMA. Distillation Weight (\lambda): Balances reconstruction and distillation losses. Block Size: Determines the granularity of the partitioning. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: EMA updates can suffer from numerical instability if \beta is too close to 1 or if gradients are noisy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def momentumgs(scenedata, blockpartitions, beta, lambdadistill, lr, epochs): # Initialize teacher Gaussians from a coarse global prior teacherparams = initializegaussians(scenedata) # Initialize student Gaussians for each block studentparams = {b: initializegaussians(block.sceneregion) for b, block in enumerate(blockpartitions)} blockweights = [1.0] len(blockpartitions) for epoch in range(epochs): for b, block in enumerate(blockpartitions): # Render student and teacher Gaussians for block cameras studentrender = projectandrasterize(studentparams[b], block.cameras) teacherrender = projectandrasterize(teacherparams, block.cameras) # Compute photometric reconstruction loss against ground truth lossrec = meansquarederror(studentrender, block.gtimages) # Compute distillation loss between student and teacher renders lossdistill = meansquarederror(studentrender, teacherrender) # Total loss and gradient descent update loss = lossrec + lambdadistill lossdistill studentparams[b] = studentparams[b] - lr gradient(loss, studentparams[b]) # Update block weight based on reconstruction accuracy blockweights[b] = 1.0 / (1.0 + lossrec) # Update teacher Gaussians via exponential moving average for b in range(len(blockpartitions)): teacherparams = beta teacherparams + (1 - beta) studentparams[b] return studentparams, teacherparams def initializegaussians(region): return region.gaussianparameters def projectandrasterize(params, cameras): return renderimage(params, cameras) def meansquarederror(rendered, gt): return sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, gt)) / len(gt) def gradient(loss, params): return computegradients(loss, params) CityGS is a divide-and-conquer training method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a coarse global prior to enable parallel block-wise finetuning and a Level-of-Detail (LoD) strategy for real-time rendering. It solves the geometric inaccuracies and floaters caused by independent block training by initializing each block with a globally consistent Gaussian set, ensuring seamless fusion without complex alignment. Unlike Momentum-GS, which uses a momentum-updated teacher for self-distillation, CityGS relies on a static coarse prior and spatial contraction for data assignment. name: CityGS Training Pipeline
head: Block-wise Parallel Training with Global Prior, CityGaussian, CityGaussian Training
body: CityGS is a divide-and-conquer training method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a coarse global prior to enable parallel block-wise finetuning and a Level-of-Detail (LoD) strategy for real-time rendering. It solves the geometric inaccuracies and floaters caused by independent block training by initializing each block with a globally consistent Gaussian set, ensuring seamless fusion without complex alignment. Unlike Momentum-GS, which uses a momentum-updated teacher for self-distillation, CityGS relies on a static coarse prior and spatial contraction for data assignment. Inputs: A set of input images with known intrinsics \kappa and poses \taui. Initial sparse point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP). Hyperparameters: global training iterations (N{\text{global}}=30,000), SSIM threshold \epsilon, block bounds [b{j,\min}, b{j,\max}], and LoD compression rates r0, r1, r2. Outputs: A fused set of 3D Gaussians G{\text{final}} organized into detail levels for rendering. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gk contains: Position pk \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphak \in [0, 1]. Covariance defined by scaling and rotation. Spherical Harmonics (SH) features f^k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 16} for view-dependent color ck \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Generate Global Prior: Train the initial COLMAP points using all input images for 30,000 iterations with standard 3DGS densification/pruning to produce a coarse global Gaussian set GK = \{Gk | k = 1,..., K\}. 2. Contract Global Prior: Normalize the positions of GK to [-1, 1] using the min/max corners p{\min}, p{\max} of the scene bounds to get \hat{p}k. Apply non-linear contraction to handle positions with infinity norm > 1: \text{contract}(\hat{p}k) = \begin{cases} \hat{p}k & \text{if } \|\hat{p}k\|\infty \le 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\hat{p}k\|\infty}\right) \frac{\hat{p}k}{\|\hat{p}k\|\infty} & \text{if } \|\hat{p}k\|\infty > 1 \end{cases} where \|\cdot\|\infty is the infinity norm. 3. Partition Space: Divide the contracted cubic space evenly into blocks. For each block j, identify the subset of Gaussians G{Kj} contained within the block bounds [b{j,\min}, b{j,\max}] in the contracted space. 4. Handle Empty Blocks: If a block j has too few Gaussians (Kj below a threshold), enlarge its bounds b{j,\min} and b{j,\max} until the threshold is met. This adjustment is used only for data assignment to ensure sufficient training data, not for filtering final Gaussians. 5. Assign Training Data: For each block j and image pose \taui, determine if the image should be used for training block j using two criteria combined via sum: Visibility Criterion (B1): Calculate the SSIM loss between the image rendered by the global prior I{GK}(\taui) and the image rendered by the block's contribution I{GK \setminus G{Kj}}(\taui). If L{\text{SSIM}}(I{GK}(\taui), I{GK \setminus G{Kj}}(\taui)) > \epsilon, then B1(\taui, G{Kj}) = 1, else 0. Spatial Criterion (B2): Check if the camera pose position \hat{p}{\taui} (in world coordinates, contracted) falls within the block bounds: B2(\taui, G{Kj}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } b{j,\min} \le \text{contract}(\hat{p}{\taui}) < b{j,\max} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Final Assignment: B(\taui, G{Kj}) = B1(\taui, G{Kj}) + B2(\taui, G{Kj}). If B(\taui, G{Kj}) > 0, the image is assigned to block j. 6. Parallel Finetuning: Train each block j in parallel. Initialize the block's Gaussians with the corresponding subset G{Kj} from the global prior. Train in the original uncontracted space using the assigned images. The loss is the weighted sum of L1 and SSIM losses. 7. Post-processing: After training, filter the finetuned Gaussians of block j to keep only those physically located within the block's original spatial bounds (in uncontracted space). Concatenate all filtered blocks to form the final dense model. 8. Level-of-Detail (LoD) Generation: Compress the fused Gaussians into multiple detail levels using compression rates r0, r1, r2. 9. Rendering: For a given view, dynamically select the appropriate LoD level based on camera distance or resolution requirements. Splat the selected Gaussians to screen space, sort by depth, and render via alpha blending: ci(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^K \alphak \mathbf{c}k Gk^{2D}(\mathbf{x}) \prod{t=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphat Gt^{2D}(\mathbf{x})) where Gk^{2D} = \text{proj}(Gk, \kappa, \taui) is the projected 2D Gaussian distribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Compute SSIM loss between two images return 0.0 def citygstrainingpipeline(images, poses, initialpoints, epsilon, threshold, rates): # Step 1: Generate Global Prior # Train COLMAP points with all observations for 30,000 iterations globalgaussians = train3dgs(initialpoints, images, poses, iterations=30000) # Step 2: Contract Global Prior pmin = [min(g.position[d] for g in globalgaussians) for d in range(3)] pmax = [max(g.position[d] for g in globalgaussians) for d in range(3)] contractedgaussians = [] for g in globalgaussians: phat = [(g.position[d] - pmin[d]) / (pmax[d] - pmin[d]) 2.0 - 1.0 for d in range(3)] contractedpos = contractposition(phat) contractedgaussians.append(Gaussian(contractedpos, g.opacity, g.covscale, g.covrot, g.shfeatures)) # Step 3: Partition Space # Divide contracted cubic space evenly into blocks blocks = createevenpartitions(contractedgaussians, pmin, pmax) # Step 4 & 5: Assign Data and Handle Empty Blocks blockdataassignments = {} for j, block in enumerate(blocks): gkj = [g for g in contractedgaussians if isinbounds(g.position, block.min, block.max)] # Step 4: Handle Empty Blocks if len(gkj) < threshold: # Enlarge bounds until threshold met while len(gkj) < threshold: block.min = [block.min[d] - 0.1 for d in range(3)] block.max = [block.max[d] + 0.1 for d in range(3)] gkj = [g for g in contractedgaussians if isinbounds(g.position, block.min, block.max)] assignedimages = [] for i, (img, pose) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # Step 5: Assign Training Data imgglobal = render(globalgaussians, pose) imgblockcontrib = render(gkj, pose) ssimloss = computessimloss(imgglobal, imgblockcontrib) b1 = 1 if ssimloss > epsilon else 0 poseposcontracted = contractposition([(pose.position[d] - pmin[d]) / (pmax[d] - pmin[d]) 2.0 - 1.0 for d in range(3)]) b2 = 1 if isinbounds(poseposcontracted, block.min, block.max) else 0 if b1 + b2 > 0: assignedimages.append(img) blockdataassignments[j] = (gkj, assignedimages) # Step 6: Parallel Finetuning finetunedblocks = [] for j, (gkj, assignedimages) in blockdataassignments.items(): # Initialize with subset from global prior blockgaussians = [Gaussian(g.position, g.opacity, g.covscale, g.covrot, g.shfeatures) for g in gkj] # Train in original uncontracted space using assigned images blockgaussians = finetune(blockgaussians, assignedimages, loss='l1+ssim') # Step 7: Post-processing # Filter to keep only those within block spatial bounds (uncontracted) filteredgaussians = [g for g in blockgaussians if isinbounds(g.position, block.worldmin, block.worldmax)] finetunedblocks.append(filteredgaussians) finalgaussians = [] for blockgs in finetunedblocks: finalgaussians.extend(blockgs) # Step 8: LoD Generation lodlevels = generatelod(finalgaussians, rates) return lodlevels def train3dgs(points, images, poses, iterations): # Standard 3DGS training loop with densification/pruning gaussians = [Gaussian(p, 0.5, [1.0]3, [0,0,0,1], [0]48) for p in points] for in range(iterations): for img, pose in zip(images, poses): rendered = render(gaussians, pose) loss = computeloss(rendered, img) updategaussians(gaussians, loss) gaussians = densifyandprune(gaussians) return gaussians def createevenpartitions(gaussians, pmin, pmax): # Divide contracted space into uniform grid blocks # Returns list of Block objects with min, max, worldmin, worldmax # Implementation details for grid generation are standard return [] def render(gaussians, pose): # Project, splat, sort, alpha blend # Implementation details follow standard 3DGS rendering return [] def finetune(gaussians, images, loss): # Gradient descent with L1+SSIM loss for img in images: rendered = render(gaussians, img.pose) l1 = computel1(rendered, img) ssim = computessim(rendered, img) updategaussians(gaussians, 0.8 l1 + 0.2 ssim) return gaussians def generatelod(gaussians, rates): # Compress Gaussians at different rates # Implementation details for compression are standard return [] def computeloss(rendered, img): return 0.0 def updategaussians(gaussians, loss): pass def densifyandprune(gaussians): return gaussians def computel1(rendered, img): return 0.0 def computessim(rendered, img): return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Blocks: Extremely uneven Gaussian distributions may result in blocks with no Gaussians. The algorithm explicitly enlarges block bounds to ensure a minimum number of Gaussians, preventing overfitting due to lack of training data. Contraction Boundary: The contraction function is continuous but non-linear. Positions with infinity norm exactly 1 are unaffected. SSIM Threshold: The choice of \epsilon affects data assignment. Too high, and blocks may lack training data; too low, and blocks may train on irrelevant views. Time Complexity: Training is parallelized across blocks, reducing wall-clock time compared to single-process global training. The global prior generation takes 30,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the global prior and all block data. Performance: Achieves real-time rendering on large-scale scenes using LoD. Strengths: Eliminates floaters and geometric inaccuracies at block boundaries; enables parallel training; simple fusion via concatenation. Limitations: Requires a high-quality global prior; performance depends on the effectiveness of the contraction and partitioning. CityGaussian (CityGS) was introduced to address the challenges of training and rendering large-scale 3DGS in real-time. It builds on the 3DGS method and introduces a divide-and-conquer strategy with a global prior and LoD. name: Gaussian-JEPA Pretraining
head: Gaussian Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, Gaussian-JEPA, Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for 3D Gaussian Splats
body: Gaussian-JEPA is a self-supervised pretraining method for 3D Gaussian assets that predicts latent features of masked target blocks from shared context, using joint-embedding predictive learning to avoid raw-attribute reconstruction. It sets itself apart from Gaussian-MAE by predicting latent representations instead of reconstructing Gaussian parameters, and from contrastive methods by explicitly supervising missing spatial content through latent prediction of held-out blocks. It builds on Momentum-GS by providing a robust, object-level feature representation that is consistent across stochastic resampling, which serves as a foundation for downstream tasks like shape completion and segmentation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian asset X represented as a set of anisotropic primitives with 14 parameters each: centroids C (3), opacity O (1), scales S (3), rotation quaternions R (4), and DC spherical-harmonic coefficients SH (3). Output: Frozen feature representations of Gaussian tokens that capture geometric and appearance information, optimized via a joint-embedding predictive objective. Data Structures and Layout: 1. Gaussian Primitive Vector: 14-dimensional vector per primitive. 2. Token Group: A set of k=32 primitives centered around a Farthest Point Sampling (FPS)-selected centroid. 3. Token Sequence: T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times D}, where n=64 is the number of token groups and D=384 is the feature dimension. 4. Context: TC \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-nt) \times D}, the tokens not assigned to any target block. 5. Target Blocks: \{Bm\}{m=1}^M, non-overlapping sets of token indices. Preprocessing: 1. Sample p=1,024 distinct primitives from an 8,192-entry buffer with replacement. 2. Center centroids and divide by maximum radius to fit in a unit sphere. 3. Map opacity logits through sigmoid to [-1, 1]. 4. Exponentiate log-scales, center, and normalize in 3D attribute space. 5. Normalize rotation quaternions to unit length and sign-canonicalize by the first component. 6. Multiply DC coefficients by spherical-harmonic constant, clip to [-0.5, 0.5], and scale by \sqrt{2/3}. Tokenization: 1. Compute centroids C' of the sampled primitives. 2. Select n=64 centers U using Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) on C'. 3. For each center ui, gather k=32 neighbors Ii using hard KNN based on centroid distance. 4. Express neighborhood centroids relative to the group center ui. 5. Apply tokenizer \psi: Pointwise MLP: 14 \to 128 \to 256 with BatchNorm and ReLU. Max pooling over the k primitives to get a group descriptor. Concatenate descriptor with each local feature. Pointwise MLP: 512 \to 512 \to 384 with BatchNorm and ReLU. Max pooling to produce one 384-D token ti per group. 6. Assemble T = [t1, \dots, tn]. 7. Embed centers U using MLP \rho (3 \to 128 \to 384) for positional embeddings. Multi-Scale Target Sampling: 1. Define schedule s = [s1, \dots, sM] with s1 \ge \dots \ge sM and total budget nt = \sum sm. Default: M=4, s=[11, 9, 7, 5]. 2. Initialize available indices A0 = \{1, \dots, n\}. 3. For m = 1 to M: Select anchor am uniformly from A{m-1}. Select sm nearest available centers Bm to am. Update Am = A{m-1} \setminus Bm. 4. Context indices C = AM. Pitfall: Non-overlap applies only to token-center indices. Because KNN neighborhoods are formed independently around different centers, context and target tokens may share underlying Gaussian primitives; the construction does not impose primitive-level disjointness. Training Loop: 1. Online Encoder: Process context TC with online encoder f\theta to get ZC = f\theta(TC, \rho(UC)) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times (n-nt) \times D}. 2. EMA Encoder: For each block m, process full token field T with EMA encoder f\xi to get Hm^\xi = f\xi(T, \rho(U)) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times D}. 3. Target Selection: Select target features Zm^\xi = Hm^\xi[Bm] \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times sm \times D}. 4. Context Projection: Map ZC to predictor width Dp=192: ZC' = Wp ZC. 5. Prediction: Create learned query q \in \mathbb{R}^{Dp}, repeat sm times: Qm = \mathbf{1}{sm} q^T. Concatenate context and queries: [ZC'; Qm]. Embed positions: \Pim = [\rho\phi(UC); \rho\phi(U{Bm})] where \rho\phi is 3 \to 128 \to 192 MLP. Pass through 4-layer Transformer predictor h\phi (width 192, 6 heads). Retain final sm query outputs Vm \in \mathbb{R}^{sm \times Dp}. Apply linear heads rb (192 \to 384) for b \in \{\text{geo, app}\} to get predictions \hat{Z}m^b \in \mathbb{R}^{sm \times D}. 6. Target Projections: For each Zm^\xi, apply two independent MLP projectors gb (384 \to 384 \to 384, GELU) to get Ym^b. Detach and normalize: Zm^b = \text{LN}(\text{sg}(Ym^b)). 7. Loss Computation: Prediction Loss: L{\text{pred}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M \sum{b \in \{\text{geo, app}\}} \text{SmoothL1}(\hat{Z}m^b, Zm^b). Grounding Loss: Concatenate all Y^b across batch and blocks to Y^b \in \mathbb{R}^{Lt \times D}. Compute regularization R{\text{vis}}(Y^b): Centering: R{\text{center}} = \frac{1}{D} \|\mub\|^2, where \mub = \frac{1}{Lt} \sumi Yi^b. Scaling: R{\text{scale}} = \frac{1}{D} \sumj (\sigma{jb} - 1)^2, where \sigma{jb} = \frac{\|Y{:,j}^b\|2}{\sqrt{Lt + \epsilon}}. Sliced-Wasserstein: R{\text{shape}} = \frac{1}{Lt K} \sumt \sumk (P{ik}^t - qi)^2, where K=256 random directions, qi = \Phi^{-1}(i/(Lt+1)), and P{ik}^t are sorted projections. R{\text{vis}}(Y^b) = R{\text{center}} + R{\text{scale}} + R{\text{shape}}. Cross-covariance: Ye^b = Y^b - \text{mean}(Y^b), \Gamma = \frac{1}{D} (Ye^{\text{geo}})^T Ye^{\text{app}}, L{\text{cross}} = \|\Gamma\|F^2 / D. L{\text{ground}} = R{\text{vis}}(Y^{\text{geo}}) + R{\text{vis}}(Y^{\text{app}}) + L{\text{cross}}. Total Loss: L = L{\text{pred}} + \lambda L{\text{ground}} with \lambda = 0.1. 8. Update: Update online encoder, predictor, heads, and projectors using L. Update EMA encoder: \xi \leftarrow \tau \xi + (1-\tau) \theta. Parameters: n=64 token centers, k=32 neighbors, p=1,024 sampled Gaussians. M=4 target blocks, schedule s=[11, 9, 7, 5], effective mask ratio 0.5. Encoders: 12 layers, width 384, 6 heads, drop path 0.1. Predictor: 4 layers, width 192, 6 heads. Optimizer: AdamW, LR 10^{-3}, weight decay 0.05. Schedule: 300 epochs, 10 warm-up, batch size 256. EMA momentum: 0.996 to 0.9999. SWD projections: K=256, loss weight \lambda=0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns (B, ncenters) indices.""" B, P, = points.shape centroids = torch.zeros(B, ncenters, device=points.device, dtype=torch.long) dist = torch.ones(B, P, device=points.device) 1e10 randidx = torch.randint(P, (B,), device=points.device) centroids[:, 0] = randidx for i in range(1, ncenters): p = points[torch.arange(B), centroids[:, i-1]] disti = torch.norm(points - p.unsqueeze(1), dim=2) dist = torch.minimum(dist, disti) centroids[:, i] = torch.argmax(dist, dim=1) return centroids def knn(points, centers, k): """Hard KNN. points: (P, 3), centers: (N, 3). Returns (N, k) indices.""" dist = torch.cdist(centers, points), idx = torch.topk(dist, k, dim=1, largest=False) return idx class Encoder(nn.Module): def init(self, depth, width, heads): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(dmodel=width, nhead=heads, batchfirst=True) for in range(depth) ]) def forward(self, x, pos): x = x + pos for layer in self.layers: x = layer(x) return x class TransformerPredictor(nn.Module): def init(self, depth, width, heads): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(dmodel=width, nhead=heads, batchfirst=True) for in range(depth) ]) def forward(self, x, pos): x = x + pos for layer in self.layers: x = layer(x) return x class GaussianJEPA: def init(self, n=64, k=32, p=1024, M=4, s=[11, 9, 7, 5], D=384, Dp=192): self.n, self.k, self.p = n, k, p self.M, self.s = M, s self.D, self.Dp = D, Dp self.nt = sum(s) self.onlineencoder = Encoder(12, D, 6) self.emaencoder = Encoder(12, D, 6) self.emamomentum = 0.996 self.contextproj = nn.Linear(D, Dp) self.posembedcenters = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, Dp)) self.predictor = TransformerPredictor(4, Dp, 6) self.headgeo = nn.Linear(Dp, D) self.headapp = nn.Linear(Dp, D) self.projgeo = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(D, D), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(D, D)) self.projapp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(D, D), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(D, D)) self.query = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, 1, Dp)) self.tokenizermlp1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(14, 128), nn.BatchNorm1d(128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 256)) self.tokenizermlp2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.BatchNorm1d(512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, D)) def preprocess(self, X): centroids = X[:,:3] maxr = torch.norm(centroids, dim=1).max() centroids = (centroids - centroids.mean(dim=0)) / maxr X[:,:3] = centroids X[:, 3:4] = torch.sigmoid(X[:, 3:4]) 2 - 1 scales = torch.exp(X[:, 4:7]) scales = (scales - scales.mean(dim=0)) / (scales.norm(dim=0) + 1e-6) X[:, 4:7] = scales quats = X[:, 7:11] quats = quats / quats.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) quats = torch.where(quats[:, 0:1] < 0, -quats, quats) X[:, 7:11] = quats dc = torch.clamp(X[:, 11:14], -0.5, 0.5) torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2.0/3.0)) X[:, 11:14] = dc return X def tokenize(self, X): centroids = X[:,:3] centersidx = farthestpointsample(centroids.unsqueeze(0), self.n).squeeze(0) centers = centroids[centersidx] neighboridx = knn(centroids, centers, self.k) tokens, posembeds = [], [] for i in range(self.n): idx = neighboridx[i] group = X[idx] relcent = group[:,:3] - centers[i] local = torch.cat([relcent, group[:, 3:]], dim=1) h = F.relu(self.tokenizermlp1(local)) desc = h.max(dim=0, keepdim=True)[0] h = torch.cat([h, desc.expand(self.k, -1)], dim=1) h = F.relu(self.tokenizermlp2(h)) tokens.append(h.max(dim=0)[0]) posembeds.append(self.posembedcenters(centers[i])) return torch.stack(tokens), torch.stack(posembeds) def computervis(self, Y): D, Lt = Y.shape[1], Y.shape[0] eps = 1e-6 mu = Y.mean(dim=0) Rcenter = (1.0 / D) mu.norm()2 Yc = Y - mu sigma = Yc.norm(dim=0) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(Lt + eps)) Rscale = (1.0 / D) ((sigma - 1)2).sum() K = 256 dirs = torch.randn(K, D, device=Y.device) dirs = dirs / dirs.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) proj = Y @ dirs.t() sortedproj, = torch.sort(proj, dim=0) i = torch.arange(1, Lt + 1, device=Y.device).float() q = torch.erfinv(2 (i / (Lt + 1)) - P[anchor], dim=1), top = torch.topk(dists, self.s[m], largest=False) sel = [available[i] for i in top] targetindices.append(sel) for idx in sel: available.remove(idx) contextindices = available ZC = self.onlineencoder(T[contextindices], self.posembedcenters(centers=contextindices)) Zfullema = self.emaencoder(T, P) ZCproj = self.contextproj(ZC) losses = [] allYgeo, allYapp = [], [] for m in range(self.M): sm = self.s[m] idxm = targetindices[m] Zmema = Zfullema[:, idxm,:] Qm = self.query.expand(B, sm, -1) PC = self.posembedcenters(centers=contextindices) Pm = self.posembedcenters(centers=idxm) Pim = torch.cat([PC, Pm], dim=0) seq = torch.cat([ZCproj, Qm], dim=1) Vm = self.predictor(seq, Pim)[:, -sm:,:] Zhatgeo = self.headgeo(Vm) Zhatapp = self.headapp(Vm) Ygeo = self.projgeo(Zmema) Yapp = self.projapp(Zmema) Zgeo = F.layernorm(torch.detach(Ygeo), [self.D]) Zapp = F.layernorm(torch.detach(Yapp), [self.D]) losses.append(F.smoothl1loss(Zhatgeo, Zgeo) + F.smoothl1loss(Zhatapp, Zapp)) allYgeo.append(Ygeo) allYapp.append(Yapp) Lpred = sum(losses) / self.M Ygeocat = torch.cat(allYgeo, dim=1).view(-1, self.D) Yappcat = torch.cat(allYapp, dim=1).view(-1, self.D) Rgeo = self.computervis(Ygeocat) Rapp = self.computervis(Yappcat) Ygeoc = Ygeocat -
