name: CityGS-X
head: Anchor-Based Octree 3D Gaussian Splatting (Baseline), CityGS-X backbone, UrbanGS
body: CityGS-X is a large-scale urban reconstruction method that extends block-based partitioning with a geometry-aware architecture, refining block boundaries according to building footprints to achieve high accuracy. It builds on parent methods like CityGaussian and VastGaussian by replacing fixed grids with an anchor-based octree where visible anchors generate "Neural Gaussians" via shared MLPs. Inputs: Sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: Rasterized image; optimized anchor features and Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: 1. Octree: Branching factor b. Levels l \in \{0, 1, \dots, L{max}\}, where l=0 is the coarsest resolution. Voxel side length at level l is vl = v0 / b^l, where v0 is determined by the scene scale. 2. Anchors: Each non-empty voxel at every level instantiates one anchor at its center, yielding N anchors organized into L{max} + 1 levels. Layout per anchor ai: fi \in \mathbb{R}^d: Learnable feature vector. pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position at voxel center. li: Level index. \{\delta^ki\}{k=1}^K: Set of K learnable offset vectors. Per-anchor scaling, rotation, and opacity parameters (base attributes). Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction: Build an octree with branching factor b over the scene bounding volume from a sparse point cloud obtained from Structure-from-Motion. 2. Anchor Instantiation: Instantiate an anchor at the center of each non-empty voxel at every level, yielding N anchors organized into L{max} + 1 levels indexed by l \in \{0, 1, \dots, L{max}\}. 3. Visibility Filtering: Apply Level-of-detail filtering: retain anchor at level li only if li \leq \hat{l}(pi, c), where c is the current training camera and \hat{l} depends on anchor-to-camera distance and a scene-dependent reference distance. Apply view-frustum culling to remove anchors outside the camera frustum, resulting in visible anchor set V. 4. Neural Gaussian Generation: For each visible anchor, generate k Neural Gaussians whose attributes are decoded by three shared MLPs (MLP{op}, MLP{cov}, MLP{col}) from the anchor feature fi, viewing direction di, and camera-relative distance. 5. Rasterization: Rasterize the resulting Gaussians via differentiable tile-based splatting to produce the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def citygsxrender(anchors, camera, mlpop, mlpcov, mlpcol): """ anchors: List of Anchor objects. camera: Camera object with pose and intrinsics. mlpop, mlpcov, mlpcol: Shared MLPs. """ visibleanchors = [] # Step 3: Visibility Filtering for anchor in anchors: # Standard LoD threshold calculation based on distance and reference distance. lodthreshold = computelodthreshold(anchor.pos, camera, scenerefdist) if anchor.level > lodthreshold: continue # Standard view frustum culling test. if not isinfrustum(anchor.pos, camera): continue visibleanchors.append(anchor) gaussians = [] # Step 4: Neural Gaussian Generation for anchor in visibleanchors: # Compute viewing direction and camera-relative distance viewdir = normalize(anchor.pos - camera.pos) reldist = distance(anchor.pos, camera.pos) # Decode base attributes from shared MLPs baseopacity = mlpop(anchor.feature, viewdir, reldist) basecov = mlpcov(anchor.feature, viewdir, reldist) basecolor = mlpcol(anchor.feature, viewdir, reldist) # Generate K Neural Gaussians using offsets for k in range(anchor.numoffsets): offset = anchor.offsets[k] # Specific offset modulation formula not provided; assuming additive. finalcov = basecov + offset finalopacity = baseopacity + offset finalcolor = basecolor + offset gaussians.append({ 'pos': anchor.pos, 'cov': finalcov, 'opacity': finalopacity, 'color': finalcolor }) # Step 5: Rasterization # Standard differentiable tile-based splatting rasterizer. image = tilebasedsplatting(gaussians, camera) return image def computelodthreshold(pos, camera, refdist): # Formula not provided in sources; returns max level based on distance. return 0 def isinfrustum(pos, camera): # Standard view frustum culling test. return True def tilebasedsplatting(gaussians, camera): # Standard differentiable tile-based splatting rasterizer. return camera.render(gaussians) Parameters: b: Octree branching factor. Not given in the sources. L{max}: Maximum octree depth. Not given in the sources. v0: Initial voxel side length. Determined by scene scale. K: Number of Neural Gaussians per anchor. Not given in the sources. d: Dimension of anchor feature vector fi. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Empty Voxels: Anchors are only instantiated in non-empty voxels, reducing memory overhead. Far-away Anchors: LoD filtering prevents rendering sub-pixel Gaussians for distant anchors, improving performance. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of visible anchors |V| and the number of Neural Gaussians K per anchor, scaling as O(|V| \cdot K). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the total number of anchors N and the feature dimension d, scaling as O(N \cdot d). Strengths: High accuracy in urban reconstruction due to geometry-aware block refinement and efficient rendering via LoD and frustum culling. Limitations: Relies on SfM sparse point cloud for initialization, which may be sparse in textureless urban areas. Independent optimization of features across levels may lead to inconsistencies. When to use: Large-scale urban scenes with distinct building facades and road surfaces. When not to use: Not given in the sources. CityGS-X originates from the need to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to city-scale environments. It builds on block-based partitioning methods like VastGaussian and CityGaussian, which divide scenes into overlapping tiles. CityGS-X extends this by incorporating a geometry-aware architecture to refine block boundaries according to building footprints. It serves as the baseline for "Anchor-Based Octree 3D Gaussian Splatting" methods, where anchors in an octree generate Gaussians via neural networks. Semantic segmentation for facade and road allocation is attributed to the sibling method UrbanGS, not CityGS-X. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) TopoGS: Topology-Aware Anchor Feature Aggregation for Large-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27868, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Budgeted-GS
head: Factoring LOD
body: Budgeted-GS is a post-hoc method that converts any trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model into a multi-resolution hierarchy of moment-matched aggregates, enabling real-time rendering of city-scale scenes on consumer GPUs by selecting the level of detail that fits the target device's memory. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption in large-scale 3DGS by introducing a "capacity floor" derived from optimal transport in phase space, which determines the minimum number of primitives required for a given error budget, allowing the same model to serve GPUs with widely different memory capacities. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes a fixed set of primitives, Budgeted-GS separates the representation into a hierarchy where a single quality parameter selects the appropriate level of detail per view, ensuring that redundant primitives are merged or dropped based on a pixel-footprint scheduler. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained 3DGS model consisting of a flat set of raw planks (Gaussian primitives) defined by their spatial cells, opacity weights, and value models. Output: A rendered image stream emitted to any standard splatting rasterizer, where the stream consists of selected primitives from the factoring tree based on the current view and memory budget. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Factoring Tree, an octree of scale bands. Nodes: Each node corresponds to a leaf in the spatial octree and a specific scale band. Content: Nodes contain "moment-matched equivalent planks," which are pre-computed aggregates of raw planks that preserve the first and second moments (mean and covariance) of the original primitives within that spatial and scale region. Layout: The tree is structured as leaf × scale-band. Raw planks are stored at the finest scale bands, while coarser bands store aggregated planks. Steps: 1. Construction: Convert the trained model (flat set of raw planks) into the factoring tree of leaf × scale-band nodes containing moment-matched equivalent planks. This construction pass takes a few seconds. 2. Scheduling: For each view, determine the level of detail using a one-parameter pixel-footprint scheduler. 3. Selection: Select raw, fine, or aggregate content based on the threshold t. If the pixel footprint of a primitive is smaller than t, use aggregated content; otherwise, use raw or fine content. 4. Rendering: Emit the selected stream of primitives to a standard splatting rasterizer. Formulas: The selection threshold t is calculated as: t = c \cdot \frac{d}{f} Where: t: The pixel-footprint threshold. c: A constant parameter. d: Distance from the camera to the primitive. f: Focal length of the camera. The capacity floor, which dictates the minimum number of primitives N^ per tile j, is given by: N^j \propto \frac{Kj sj}{dj} Where: Kj: A constant related to the tile. sj: Scale of the primitives in tile j. dj: Distance to tile j. Parameters: c: Constant in the pixel-footprint threshold formula. Typical value not given in the sources. t: Threshold for LOD selection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on moment-matching, which may introduce approximation errors when aggregating primitives. The sources mention "bounded volumetric loss" but do not specify the error bounds. Boundaries: The octree structure handles spatial boundaries, but the scale bands must be carefully defined to ensure smooth transitions between LOD levels. Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a trained 3DGS model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def distance(p1, p2): """Euclidean distance between two 3D points.""" return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def computefootprint(plank, cameraposition, camerafocallength): """Compute pixel footprint by projecting Gaussian covariance to screen space.""" # Standard implementation: transform covariance to camera space, # project to 2D Jacobian, compute bounding box area in pixels. # For this article, we assume the primitive provides its projected radius. return plank.getscreenradius() 2.0 def budgetedgsselectprimitives(cameraposition, camerafocallength, tree, constantc): """ Selects primitives from the factoring tree based on the pixel-footprint threshold. Args: cameraposition: 3D coordinates of the camera. camerafocallength: Focal length f. tree: List of nodes, each containing 'center', 'scaleband', 'rawplanks', 'aggregateplanks'. constantc: Constant c for threshold calculation. Returns: List of selected primitive objects to be passed to a rasterizer. """ selected = [] for node in tree: d = distance(cameraposition, node.center) t = constantc (d / camerafocallength) # Select raw/fine or aggregate based on footprint threshold for plank in node.rawplanks: footprint = computefootprint(plank, cameraposition, camerafocallength) if footprint < t: # Use aggregate if available, else raw if node.aggregateplanks: selected.extend(node.aggregateplanks) else: selected.append(plank) else: selected.append(plank) # Add aggregate planks for regions where they are selected if node.aggregateplanks: for aggplank in node.aggregateplanks: footprint = computefootprint(aggplank, cameraposition, camerafocallength) if footprint < t: selected.append(aggplank) return selected def rendersplats(primitives, camera): """Standard splatting rasterization step.""" # Implementation details for rasterizing Gaussian splats are standard and external to this method. # This function accumulates screen-space contributions per pixel. return [] A quality modeling approach that classifies 3DGS videos into four tiers of models with varying qualities using a binary Gaussian mask based on significance distribution, considering both opacity and ellipsoid size to filter out less significant primitives. It identifies and filters out Gaussian primitives with lower transparency and smaller ellipsoid sizes, as they have minimal impact on rendering quality. Three distinct masking thresholds are established to classify the 3DGS videos within each Group of Frames (GoF) into four tiers of models with varying qualities. Thresholds are determined by referencing previously obtained saliency distribution maps and adjusting thresholds based on saliency weights within different tiles; for high-saliency regions, as many Gaussian primitives as possible are retained, while for less visually significant regions, thresholds are increased to exclude unnecessary primitives. All tiles of different quality levels are encoded to facilitate subsequent delivery from server to client. Time Complexity: The construction pass takes a few seconds. Rendering time depends on the number of selected primitives, which is dynamically adjusted by the scheduler. Memory Complexity: The method reduces memory usage by aggregating primitives, allowing city-scale scenes to fit on consumer GPUs. The exact memory savings depend on the scene and the chosen quality parameter. Measured Performance: Validated on 13 public scenes under a preregistered protocol, demonstrating real-time rendering of city-scale scenes. Scaling: The method scales to large scenes by using a multi-resolution hierarchy. The capacity floor provides a theoretical limit on the number of primitives needed. Strengths: Enables real-time rendering of large-scale scenes on consumer hardware; flexible quality adjustment via a single parameter; avoids wasted optimization effort in training. Limitations: Requires a post-hoc construction pass; relies on the accuracy of the moment-matching approximation; performance depends on the scene's complexity and the chosen quality parameter. When to use: When rendering large-scale, city-scale scenes on hardware with limited memory. When not to use: For small-scale scenes where standard 3DGS fits in memory; when training time is a critical constraint and budget-centered training is not used. Budgeted-GS was introduced in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It is grounded in a measurable capacity floor derived from optimal transport in phase space, which answers how many primitives a scene actually needs and how many can safely be given up. The method builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting Parent but extends it to handle large-scale scenes by introducing a multi-resolution hierarchy and a budget-centered training approach. name: Gaussian Hierarchies
head: H-3DGS hierarchy
body: Gaussian Hierarchies enable real-time rendering of ultra-large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting datasets by organizing Gaussians into a recursive tree structure. It solves the memory and bandwidth bottlenecks of flat Gaussian representations by providing a view-adaptive Level of Detail (LoD) mechanism, allowing the renderer to select a sparse subset of nodes that approximate the scene geometry at varying distances. It differs from flat splatting by introducing spatial hierarchy and from sibling methods like Budgeted-GS by relying on a strict tree-based cut condition rather than global budget optimization. Inputs: A set of original 3D Gaussians (leaves), camera position \mathbf{p}{\text{cam}}, and a global LoD threshold T. Outputs: A cut set of nodes to render. Data Structures: The structure is a tree where: Leaves: Correspond to the original optimized Gaussians. Non-leaf nodes: Approximate their children. Each node i has a mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i and a scale metric si^j. Tree Layout: Implicit or explicit parent-child pointers. Algorithm: The sources describe a Breadth-First Search (BFS) traversal to determine the cut set. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the logic: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecutset(root, camerapos, threshold): cutset = [] queue = [root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) mui = node.mean si = node.scalecomponents md = threshold / max(si) dist = math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(mui, camerapos))) if dist >= md: cutset.append(node) else: queue.extend(node.children) return cutset The algorithm initializes an empty cut set \mathcal{C}. It performs a Breadth-First Search (BFS) starting from the root node. For each node i visited, it evaluates the cut condition c{\text{hier}}(i, \text{cam}). If true, it adds node i to \mathcal{C} and skips processing all children of node i. If false, it continues BFS to process children of node i. It returns \mathcal{C}. Formulas: The cut condition used in H-3DGS is a simple cut-off according to camera distance: c{\text{hier}}(i, \text{cam}) = \left\| \boldsymbol{\mu}i - \mathbf{p}{\text{cam}} \right\|2 \geq md(i) where: \boldsymbol{\mu}i is the mean position of node i. \mathbf{p}{\text{cam}} is the camera position. md(i) is the distance threshold for node i, calculated as: md(i) = \frac{T}{\maxj si^j} T is a global LoD threshold parameter. si^j represents the scale components of node i. Parameters: T: Global LoD threshold. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it controls the granularity of the hierarchy. Edge Cases: Precision: Distance calculations must handle floating-point precision near the threshold boundary. Boundaries: The cut set must be proper, meaning no parent or child of an included node is also included. Degenerate Input: If a node has no children (leaf), the condition is evaluated against the leaf's properties. A dynamic memory management and Level of Detail (LoD) strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that maintains a hierarchical structure based on primitive screen size to handle large scenes with limited GPU memory. Unlike static hierarchies, this method is view-adaptive, triggering merges and retrievals based on the current viewpoint's projection of the Gaussians. It should be chosen when VRAM exhaustion during online optimization is a concern, as it merges sub-pixel Gaussians into coarser parents and offloads them to CPU RAM while retrieving finer details when the camera zooms in. Adaptive Gaussian Merging and Retrieval A graph-based method introducing a tree-structured hierarchical representation for 3D scenes. It assigns explicit attributes (e.g., position, opacity) to leaf nodes, while implicit attributes (e.g., covariance matrix, view-dependent color) are shared across hierarchical levels. Additionally, GaussianForest employs adaptive growth and pruning, dynamically adjusting the representation to scene complexities. Time Complexity: The BFS traversal is linear with respect to the number of nodes in the hierarchy. The cut condition evaluation is constant time per node. Memory Complexity: The hierarchy structure adds overhead for parent-child pointers and aggregated node properties, but allows for significant reduction in the number of Gaussians rendered per frame by skipping distant subtrees. Performance: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting limits typical training to roughly 500,000 Gaussians per GB of GPU memory, imposing strict constraints on the detail and extent of reconstructions. Gaussian Hierarchies overcome this limitation by enabling view-adaptive culling, making ultra-large scale reconstructions feasible. Strengths: View-adaptive LoD, efficient memory usage for large scenes. Limitations: Requires hierarchical construction; performance depends on the quality of the cut condition and tree balance. Gaussian Hierarchies were introduced in H-3DGS by Kerbl et al. in 2024. The method addresses the memory limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which typically supports only ~500,000 Gaussians per GB of GPU memory. It enables real-time rendering of ultra-large-scale reconstructions by leveraging external memory and hierarchical culling. name: Adaptive Gaussian Merging and Retrieval
head: Adaptive Merging, Screen-size based Merging
body: Adaptive Gaussian Merging and Retrieval is a dynamic memory management and Level of Detail (LoD) strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that maintains a hierarchical structure based on primitive screen size to handle large scenes with limited GPU memory. It solves the problem of VRAM exhaustion during online optimization by merging sub-pixel Gaussians into coarser parents and offloading them to CPU RAM, while retrieving finer details when the camera zooms in. Unlike static hierarchies, this method is view-adaptive, triggering merges and retrievals based on the current viewpoint's projection of the Gaussians. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives Gi organized in a hierarchy; the current camera viewpoint (projection matrix and intrinsics); a merging threshold \taul; a retrieval threshold \tauh. Outputs: An updated active set of Gaussian primitives (leaves and intermediate nodes) optimized for rendering; updated parent-child links in the hierarchy. The hierarchy consists of nodes. Each node stores: 1. Gaussian Parameters: Position \mathbf{p}, opacity \alpha, rotation \mathbf{q} (quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}, and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. 2. Topology: IDs of parent node(s) and child node(s). 3. Status: Flags indicating if the node is currently in the active set (on GPU) or offloaded (on CPU). \taul = 0.5 pixels: The screen size threshold below which a Gaussian is considered sub-pixel and eligible for merging. \tauh = 1 pixel: The screen size threshold above which a merged node triggers retrieval of its finer children. Merge Trigger Threshold: Merging is only triggered if more than 20% of the Gaussians satisfy Si < \taul. 1. Compute Screen Sizes: For every Gaussian Gi in the current active set, compute its screen size Si from the current viewpoint. 2. Check Merge Condition: Count the number of Gaussians where Si < \taul. If this count exceeds 20% of the total active Gaussians, proceed to merge; otherwise, skip merging for this frame. 3. Select Candidates: Identify the set of Gaussians C{\text{merge}} = \{Gi \mid Si < \taul\}. 4. Grouping via KNN: For each candidate Gi \in C{\text{merge}}, find the 4 closest Gaussians using a fast K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) search. 5. Deduplication: Remove duplicate entries in the grouping list to ensure a Gaussian primitive does not have multiple parents in the same merge operation. 6. Merge Operation: Perform merging on groups of 4 Gaussians using KL-divergence based merging. This creates a new parent Gaussian G{\text{parent}} that approximates the children. 7. Update Hierarchy: Remove the sub-pixel children from the active set. Add G{\text{parent}} to the active set. Establish child-parent links between G{\text{parent}} and its children. Optimization: If a Gaussian already has a parent, check if all its children are being merged. If so, "pull" the existing parent from the hierarchy (promote it to active) instead of creating a new node. 8. Offloading: Move small footprint leaf Gaussian primitives that are not in the active set to CPU RAM to free VRAM. 9. Retrieval (Navigation): When navigating, for any merged node G{\text{parent}} in the active set, compute its screen size S{\text{parent}}. If S{\text{parent}} > \tauh: Reload the finer child Gaussians from CPU RAM to GPU. Update the coarse parent nodes with the new children's parameters. Remove G{\text{parent}} from the active set. Add the children to the active set. 10. Loop Closure Handling: When loop closure is detected, move all hierarchy nodes following the transform of the keyframe most used to spawn its children asynchronously to avoid latency. Unverified code. name: Hierarchy Cut Selection and Level Switching
head: Granularity-based Cut Selection, Smooth Level Switching
body: This method selects a specific cut through a hierarchical tree of 3D Gaussians to maximize rendering performance while maintaining visual quality, based on the projected screen size of nodes. It enables smooth transitions between hierarchy levels by interpolating Gaussian attributes rather than abruptly swapping nodes, ensuring visual continuity during level-of-detail changes. It differs from sibling methods by using a granularity-based threshold on the largest dimension of the projected bounding box to determine the cut, and by explicitly handling orientation mismatches during hierarchy generation to prevent interpolation artifacts. Inputs: A hierarchical tree of 3D Gaussians, where each node n contains a set of leaf Gaussians and stores the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of its contained leaf Gaussians. A camera view V. A target granularity parameter \tau\epsilon (e.g., 1 pixel). Outputs: A set of nodes forming the "cut" through the hierarchy to be rendered. Interpolation weights tn for nodes undergoing transition. Node Structure: Each node n in the hierarchy stores: children: List of child nodes. parent: Reference to parent node. leafgaussians: List of 3D Gaussian primitives contained directly in this node. aabb: Axis-aligned bounding box encompassing all leaf Gaussians contained within the subtree of n, pre-computed during hierarchy generation. granularity: The projected screen size \epsilon(n), computed once per view. 1. Compute Granularity: For each node n in the hierarchy, compute its granularity \epsilon(n) for the current view V. Retrieve the AABB of node n. Identify the largest dimension of this bounding box, denoted as L{max}(n). Project L{max}(n) onto the screen plane using the camera projection matrix for view V. Let the resulting screen-space length be \epsilon(n). 2. Select Cut: Identify the nodes to include in the rendering cut. Iterate through all nodes n in the hierarchy. A node n is included in the cut if: 1. \epsilon(n) < \tau\epsilon (the node's projected size is smaller than the target granularity). 2. \epsilon(parent(n)) \ge \tau\epsilon (the parent's projected size is not smaller than the target granularity). This logic ensures that for any branch, either all children are selected (if the parent is too large) or the parent is selected (if all children are small enough), but never a mix that violates the hierarchy structure. Due to the hierarchy generation properties, the AABB of a parent can never appear smaller than one of its children in screen space, guaranteeing a valid cut. 3. Calculate Interpolation Weights: For nodes n that are in a transition state, calculate the interpolation weight tn. If node n is in the cut and its parent p is not (or vice versa), compute: tn = \frac{\tau\epsilon - \epsilon(n)}{\epsilon(p) - \epsilon(n)} Clamp tn to [0, 1]. If tn = 0, use the parent's attributes. If tn = 1, use the child's attributes. Intermediate values blend the attributes. 4. Interpolate Gaussian Attributes: For each Gaussian in the cut (or blending between parent and child), interpolate its properties. Position, Color, Spherical Harmonics: Interpolate linearly using tn. Covariance: Do not interpolate the covariance matrix directly. Instead: 1. Decompose the covariance into scale and rotation components for both parent and child. 2. Interpolate the scale linearly. 3. Interpolate the rotation linearly (not using slerp). 4. Reconstruct the covariance from the interpolated scale and rotation. Opacity (\alpha): Interpolate opacity carefully to maintain color consistency. At the start of the transition, the children share the parent's attributes initially. To ensure the blended color of the children equals the parent's color at the start of the transition, modify the child's opacity \alpha' using the parent's opacity \alphap. For two children, solve for \alpha' in the equation: \alphap cp = \alpha' cp + (1 - \alpha') \alpha' cp This yields: \alpha' = \frac{1}{1 - (1 - \alphap) \frac{1}{2}} Use this \alpha' to blend \alpha from the parent to the children using the same linear interpolation scheme as other attributes. 5. Orientation Matching (Pre-computation): During hierarchy generation (not per-frame), perform orientation matching to prevent interpolation artifacts. Starting from the root, recursively reinterpret the axes of orientation for each child Gaussian. The goal is to minimize the relative rotation between the child node and its parent. This is done via exhaustive search over possible axis permutations/rotations. This step prevents undesired rotations when interpolating Gaussians with the same shape (covariance) but different rotation/scaling orientations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projecttoscreen(length3d, cameraview): """Projects a 3D length onto the screen plane in pixels.""" # Standard perspective projection: screenpixels = (focallength length3d) / depth # Assuming cameraview provides focallength and depth along the view direction focallength = cameraview.focallength depth = cameraview.depth if depth == 0: depth = 1e-6 # Guard against division by zero return (focallength length3d) / depth def computegranularity(node, cameraview): """Computes the projected screen size of the largest dimension of the node's AABB.""" aabbmin = node.aabb.min aabbmax = node.aabb.max maxdim = max(aabbmax.x - aabbmin.x, aabbmax.y - aabbmin.y, aabbmax.z - aabbmin.z) return projecttoscreen(maxdim, cameraview) def selectcut(hierarchyroot, targetgranularity, cameraview): """Selects the cut through the hierarchy based on granularity.""" cutnodes = [] transitionnodes = [] # Pre-compute granularity for all nodes for node in hierarchyroot.traverseall(): node.granularity = computegranularity(node, cameraview) # Find the cut for node in hierarchyroot.traverseall(): if node.parent is None: continue parent = node.parent childgran = node.granularity parentgran = parent.granularity # Condition: Child is smaller than threshold, Parent is not if childgran < targetgranularity and parentgran >= targetgranularity: cutnodes.append(node) # Calculate interpolation weight denominator = parentgran - childgran if denominator == 0: tn = 1.0 # Guard for degenerate case else: tn = (targetgranularity - childgran) / denominator tn = max(0.0, min(1.0, tn)) # Clamp to [0, 1] transitionnodes.append((node, parent, tn)) return cutnodes, transitionnodes def interpolategaussianattributes(parentgauss, childgauss, t, alphap): """Interpolates Gaussian attributes between parent and child.""" resultpos = parentgauss.position + t (childgauss.position - parentgauss.position) resultcolor = parentgauss.color + t (childgauss.color - parentgauss.color) resultsh = parentgauss.shcoeffs + t (childgauss.shcoeffs - parentgauss.shcoeffs) # Covariance: Interpolate scale and rotation separately parentscale, parentrot = decomposecovariance(parentgauss.covariance) childscale, childrot = decomposecovariance(childgauss.covariance) interpscale = parentscale + t (childscale - parentscale) interprot = parentrot + t (childrot - parentrot) # Linear interpolation, not slerp resultcov = composecovariance(interpscale, interprot) # Opacity: Special handling for transition start # For two children, compute adjusted child opacity alphaprime alphaprime = 1.0 / (1.0 - (1.0 - alphap) 0.5) # Blend opacity using the same linear scheme resultalpha = alphap + t (alphaprime - alphap) return Gaussian(resultpos, resultcolor, resultsh, resultcov, resultalpha) def decomposecovariance(cov): """Decomposes covariance matrix into scale (vector) and rotation (quaternion).""" # Eigen decomposition or Cholesky decomposition # Returns scale vector and rotation quaternion pass def composecovariance(scale, rot): """Recomposes covariance matrix from scale and rotation.""" # Cov = R diag(scale^2) R^T pass def lerprotation(rot1, rot2, t): """Linear interpolation of rotation components.""" return rot1 + t (rot2 - rot1) # Component-wise lerp \tau\epsilon: Target granularity. Typical value: 1 pixel. \alphap: Parent opacity. Direct Covariance Interpolation: Interpolating the covariance matrix directly causes undesired rotation artifacts when Gaussians have the same shape but different rotation/scaling orientations. This is mitigated by interpolating scale and rotation separately. Orientation Mismatch: Without orientation matching during hierarchy generation, interpolating Gaussians with the same covariance but different axes leads to visual disturbances. Exhaustive search is used to minimize relative rotation between parent and child axes. Opacity Blending: Incorrect opacity blending can cause color inconsistencies during transitions. The specific formula for \alpha' ensures that the blended color of the children matches the parent's color at the start of the transition. Division by Zero: If \epsilon(p) = \epsilon(n), the interpolation weight calculation involves division by zero. A guard value is applied in implementation. Time Complexity: The cut can be found in linear time O(N) with respect to the number of nodes, or in constant time per node in a massively parallel setting. Performance: Maximizes rendering performance by selecting the coarsest possible nodes that still meet the visual quality threshold (granularity). Visual Quality: Maintains visual quality by ensuring smooth transitions between levels of detail through attribute interpolation. Strengths: Linear time cut selection, smooth transitions, handles orientation mismatches. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of orientation matching during hierarchy generation. Linear interpolation of rotations may not be as accurate as slerp, but is faster and deemed sufficient. Origin: This method is described in the paper "A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets" by Bernhard Kerbl, Andreas Meuleman, Georgios Kopanas, Michael Wimmer, Alexandre Lanvin, and George Drettakis. History: The method is part of the broader development of hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques for real-time rendering of large-scale scenes. Usage: Used in CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian for streaming and rendering large-scale 3D Gaussian representations. name: Octree-GS
head: LOD-Structured 3D Gaussians
body: Octree-GS is a level-of-detail (LOD) structured 3D Gaussian splatting method designed to enable consistent real-time rendering in large, complex scenes by decomposing scene representation into hierarchical LOD levels. Unlike conventional 3D-GS methods that treat all Gaussians equally, Octree-GS assigns anchor Gaussians to specific octree levels, allowing the renderer to adaptively fetch higher-detail anchors based on the camera's distance to occupied voxels, thereby addressing aliasing issues and rendering bottlenecks inherent in standard 3D-GS and Scaffold-GS. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse point cloud representing the scene geometry. Output: A rendered image from a novel view, utilizing a hierarchical set of 3D Gaussians organized in an octree structure. Data Structures: 1. Octree: A spatial data structure constructed over the bounded 3D space of the scene. Each node represents a voxel. 2. Anchor Gaussians: A set of 3D Gaussians assigned to specific octree levels. Each anchor Gaussian is associated with a specific LOD level \ell. 3. LOD Bias: A learnable scalar parameter associated with each anchor Gaussian, acting as a residual to the LOD level. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction: Starting from the input sparse point cloud, construct an octree for the bounded 3D space. 2. Anchor Gaussian Assignment: Assign a set of anchor Gaussians to each octree level. Each level \ell provides a set of anchor Gaussians assigned to the corresponding LOD level. The training process is progressive, guiding coarse-to-fine reconstruction to avoid overlapping between different LOD levels. 3. LOD Level Determination (Rendering): For each occupied anchor voxel in the octree, determine the required LOD level \ell based on the distance from the observation center (camera). Closer voxels require higher LOD levels (more detail), while distant voxels use lower LOD levels. 4. Gaussian Invocation: Invoke all anchor Gaussians up to the determined level \ell for final rendering. This is done in an accumulation manner, gradually fetching anchors from higher LODs as needed. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using the invoked set of Gaussians. The LOD bias parameter supplements high-frequency regions with more consistent details during inference. Formulas and Parameters: LOD Level Selection: The level \ell for a voxel is determined by the distance d from the camera. The specific function mapping d \to \ell is not explicitly defined in the sources, but the principle is that \ell increases as d decreases. LOD Bias: A learnable parameter bi for each anchor Gaussian i. It acts as a residual to the LOD level, effectively shifting the effective LOD of the Gaussian to better capture high-frequency details like sharp edges. Training Loss: Standard image reconstruction loss plus additional regularization loss following the practice of Scaffold-GS. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderoctreegs(cameraposition, octree, anchorgaussians, lodbiases): """ Renders a scene using Octree-GS. Args: cameraposition: 3D vector, position of the camera. octree: Octree structure containing voxel occupancy info. anchorgaussians: List of Gaussians, each with an associated LOD level. lodbiases: List of scalar biases corresponding to each anchor Gaussian. Returns: Rendered image. """ # 1. Determine active Gaussians based on LOD activegaussians = [] for voxel in octree.occupiedvoxels(): # Calculate distance from camera to voxel center distance = vectornorm(cameraposition - voxel.center) # Determine required LOD level based on distance # Note: Exact mapping function is not specified in sources # Typically, closer distance -> higher LOD level requiredlod = determinelodlevel(distance) # 2. Invoke all anchor Gaussians up to the determined level # This implies an accumulation: if level 2 is needed, levels 0, 1, 2 are used for gaussian in anchorgaussians: if gaussian.lodlevel <= requiredlod: # Apply LOD bias to adjust effective contribution # The bias acts as a residual to the LOD level effectivegaussian = applylodbias(gaussian, lodbiases[gaussian.id]) activegaussians.append(effectivegaussian) # 3. Render using standard 3D Gaussian Splatting accumulation # This step assumes standard 3D-GS rasterization is used on the active set image = standard3dgsrasterize(activegaussians, cameraposition) return image def determinelodlevel(distance): """ Determines the LOD level based on distance. Not fully specified in sources. Placeholder for implementation detail. """ # Example heuristic: # If distance < threshold1: return maxlod # If distance < threshold2: return maxlod - 1 #... # This function must be implemented based on the specific octree depth and distance thresholds # defined in the original implementation, which are not provided in the text. pass def applylodbias(gaussian, bias): """ Applies the LOD bias to the Gaussian. The bias supplements high-frequency regions with more consistent details. The exact mathematical operation (e.g., scaling, opacity adjustment) is not specified. """ # Placeholder: The bias likely modifies the Gaussian's properties # such as scale or opacity to better fit high-frequency details. # Implementation detail not provided in sources. return gaussian Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Octree-GS effectively addresses aliasing issues inherent to 3D-GS and Scaffold-GS by adaptively handling changed footprint sizes. Overlapping: Progressive training is used to avoid overlapping between different LOD levels, which reduces the number of rendered Gaussians and improves rendering accuracy of coarser LOD levels. High-Frequency Details: LOD bias is crucial for supplementing high-frequency regions (e.g., sharp edges) with consistent details. Performance: Octree-GS guarantees continuous real-time rendering in large scenes. It shows significant advantages over SOTA methods when rendering high-altitude views. Visual Quality: It successfully captures very fine details, particularly for objects with thin structures such as trees, light-bulbs, and decorative texts. Scalability: By using an octree structure and LOD decomposition, it manages the excessive number of Gaussians that cause rendering bottlenecks in standard 3D-GS for large scenes. Limitations: The specific computational complexity (time/memory) is not quantified in the sources. The method relies on the effectiveness of the LOD level determination function, which is not explicitly defined. Origin: Introduced by Kerui Ren, Lihan Jiang, Tao Lu, Mulin Yu, Linning Xu, Zhangkai Ni, and Bo Dai from Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Tongji University, University of Science and Technology of China, and The Chinese University of Hong Kong. Context: Developed to address the rendering bottlenecks of 3D Gaussian splatting (3D-GS) in large scenes with complex details, where the excessive number of Gaussians leads to performance issues. It builds upon the concept of hierarchical representations, similar to Scaffold-GS, but introduces a specific LOD-structured approach with anchor Gaussians and LOD bias. name: Hierarchical LOD for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS Hierarchy, 3DGS LOD, Hierarchical LOD for 3D Gaussian Splitting
body: Hierarchical LOD for 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) is a method that constructs a tree-based hierarchy of 3D Gaussian primitives to enable real-time rendering of large-scale scenes by providing Level-of-Detail (LOD) solutions. It differs from flat rasterization by merging child Gaussians into intermediate nodes that retain the full attribute set of a primitive (mean, covariance, SH coefficients, and a modified opacity/falloff), allowing the renderer to swap high-resolution leaf nodes for lower-resolution interior nodes based on screen-space granularity. Inputs: A set of optimized 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}, where each gi has mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, spherical harmonic coefficients SHi, and opacity oi. A camera view V defined by projection matrices. Outputs: A Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree where every node (leaf or interior) is associated with a 3D Gaussian. A set of active nodes (the "cut") for the current view V. Node Structure: Each node in the hierarchy stores the attributes of a single 3D Gaussian: mean: 3D vector \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. covariance: 3x3 symmetric matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. shcoeffs: Spherical Harmonic coefficients. falloff: A scalar value replacing standard opacity for interior nodes. children: List of child nodes (empty for leaves). aabb: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box enclosing the node's spatial extent. Leaf Nodes: Correspond directly to the original optimized Gaussians from the training process. falloff equals the original opacity oi. Interior Nodes: Created by merging children. falloff is computed as \frac{\sum w'i}{Sp}, where Sp is the surface area of the parent's ellipsoid. This value may exceed 1. 1. Hierarchy Generation (BVH Construction): 1. Compute the initial root AABB enclosing all primitives. The extent is calculated as 3 times the stored size of the Gaussians to capture their projected cutoff. 2. Recursively split nodes using a binary median split: Identify the longest axis of the current node's AABB. Project the means \mui of all Gaussians in the node onto this axis. Partition the primitives into two groups based on the median of these projections. 3. Repeat until leaf nodes contain a minimal number of primitives (implementation detail: typically 1 or a small constant, though exact leaf count threshold is not specified in sources). 2. Merging Attributes (Bottom-Up): For each interior node, compute its Gaussian attributes from its children i=1 \dots N starting from the leaves. 2.1. Compute Unnormalized Weights: Calculate the contribution weight w'i for each child. The sources derive this from the integral of the projected 2D Gaussian, assuming isotropy and low overlap: w'i = oi \sqrt{|\Sigma'i|} where \Sigma'i is the projected 2D covariance matrix. In practice, the surface area Si of the 3D ellipsoid is used instead of \sqrt{|\Sigma'i|}: w'i = oi Si 2.2. Normalize Weights: wi = \frac{w'i}{\sum{j=1}^N w'j} 2.3. Merge Mean: \mu^{(parent)} = \sum{i=1}^N wi \mui^{(child)} 2.4. Merge Covariance: \Sigma^{(parent)} = \sum{i=1}^N wi \left( \Sigmai^{(child)} + (\mui^{(child)} - \mu^{(parent)})(\mui^{(child)} - \mu^{(parent)})^T \right) 2.5. Merge SH Coefficients: SH^{(parent)} = \sum{i=1}^N wi SHi^{(child)} 2.6. Compute Falloff: Calculate the surface area Sp of the parent's merged ellipsoid (derived from \Sigma^{(parent)}). \text{falloff} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N w'i}{Sp} 3. Hierarchy Cut Selection: Given a view V, select a set of nodes to render such that screen-space detail is preserved while minimizing draw calls. 3.1. Define Granularity: For a node n, compute its projected screen-space bounding box. The granularity \epsilon(n) is defined as the largest dimension (length) of this projected bounding box. 3.2. Select Cut: Identify all nodes n such that \epsilon(n) \le \tau\epsilon, where \tau\epsilon is the target granularity threshold (typically 1 pixel or less). If a node satisfies the condition, it is included in the cut. If a node does not satisfy the condition, its children are evaluated. The cut is the set of nodes that satisfy the condition but whose parents do not (or are not included). 4. Smooth Transition (Interpolation): To avoid popping artifacts when switching between LOD levels, interpolate between the selected node n and its parent p (or children). 4.1. Calculate Interpolation Weight: Evaluate \epsilon(n) and \epsilon(p). The interpolation weight tn is derived from the ratio of these granularities. (Exact formula for tn is not fully explicit in the provided text snippets, but it depends on \epsilon(n) and \epsilon(p)). 4.2. Handle Rotation Ambiguity: When interpolating, directly interpolating rotation matrices can cause undesired rotations. The method renders the two children with the same parameters as the parent and progressively interpolates towards their separate values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeellipsoidsurface(covmatrix): """ Computes the surface area of a 3D ellipsoid defined by covariance matrix Sigma. Approximation using the determinant for isotropic case or standard formula. Note: Exact surface area of an ellipsoid has no closed form, but sources indicate using sqrt(det(Sigma)) or surface Si is proportional to it. We use the determinant-based metric as per source derivation w'i = oi sqrt(|Sigma'|). For 3D, we approximate surface Si proportional to det(Sigma)^(1/2) or similar. Source states: "square root of the determinant of a Gaussian's 2D covariance is proportional to the (projected) surface of the corresponding 3D ellipsoid". We will use det(Sigma)^(1/2) as the proxy for surface area Si. """ det = np.linalg.det(covmatrix) # Clamp to avoid negative determinants due to numerical error det = max(det, 1e-10) return np.sqrt(det) def mergegaussians(children): """ Merges a list of child Gaussians into a single parent Gaussian. Returns: (mean, cov, shcoeffs, falloff) """ if not children: return None, None, None, 0.0 # 1. Compute unnormalized weights w'i # w'i = oi Si unnormalizedweights = [] for child in children: Si = computeellipsoidsurface(child['cov']) wprimei = child['opacity'] Si unnormalizedweights.append(wprimei) sumwprime = sum(unnormalizedweights) if sumwprime == 0: # Fallback if all weights are zero return children[0]['mean'], children[0]['cov'], children[0]['sh'], 0.0 # 2. Normalize weights wi weights = [w / sumwprime for w in unnormalizedweights] # 3. Merge Mean # muparent = sum(wi mui) mergedmean = np.zeros(3) for i, child in enumerate(children): mergedmean += weights[i] child['mean'] # 4. Merge Covariance # Sigmaparent = sum(wi (Sigmai + (mui - muparent)(mui - muparent)^T)) mergedcov = np.zeros((3, 3)) for i, child in enumerate(children): diff = child['mean'] - mergedmean outerprod = np.outer(diff, diff) mergedcov += weights[i] (child['cov'] + outerprod) # 5. Merge SH Coefficients # SHparent = sum(wi SHi) # Assuming SH is a flat array or list of coefficients mergedsh = np.zeroslike(children[0]['sh']) for i, child in enumerate(children): mergedsh += weights[i] child['sh'] # 6. Compute Falloff # falloff = (sum(w'i)) / Sp # Sp is the surface of the parent ellipsoid Sp = computeellipsoidsurface(mergedcov) if Sp == 0: falloff = 0.0 else: falloff = sumwprime / Sp return mergedmean, mergedcov, mergedsh, falloff def buildbvh(gaussians, maxdepth=None): """ Builds a BVH hierarchy top-down. """ # 1. Create Root # AABB enclosing all primitives, 3x stored size # Assuming gaussians have 'aabb' or we compute it from means and covs # For simplicity, we assume a function to get AABB from a list of gaussians rootaabb = computeglobalaabb(gaussians) root = Node(aabb=rootaabb, children=[]) # 2. Recursive Split splitnode(root, gaussians) return root def splitnode(node, gaussians): """ Recursively splits a node. """ # Base case: if leaf condition met (e.g., 1 gaussian or max depth) if len(gaussians) <= 1: # Or some threshold node.isleaf = True node.gaussian = gaussians[0] if gaussians else None return # 1. Project means onto longest axis of AABB longestaxis = getlongestaxis(node.aabb) projections = [projectontoaxis(g['mean'], longestaxis) for g in gaussians] # 2. Find median medianval = np.median(projections) # 3. Partition leftgaussians = [] rightgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): if projections[i] < medianval: leftgaussians.append(g) else: rightgaussians.append(g) # 4. Create Children leftchild = Node(aabb=computeaabb(leftgaussians), children=[]) rightchild = Node(aabb=computeaabb(rightgaussians), children=[]) node.children = [leftchild, rightchild] # 5. Recurse splitnode(leftchild, leftgaussians) splitnode(rightchild, rightgaussians) # 6. Merge Attributes (Bottom-Up) # This must be done after children are fully built leftg = leftchild.gaussian if leftchild.isleaf else mergegaussiansfromnode(leftchild) rightg = rightchild.gaussian if rightchild.isleaf else mergegaussiansfromnode(rightchild) # If children are not leaves, we need to get their merged gaussians # This implies a post-order traversal or storing the merged gaussian in the node # For pseudocode clarity, we assume mergegaussiansfromnode retrieves the # pre-computed merged gaussian from children if leftchild.isleaf and rightchild.isleaf: mergedmean, mergedcov, mergedsh, falloff = mergegaussians([leftchild.gaussian, rightchild.gaussian]) else: # Get merged gaussians from children leftmerged = leftchild.gaussian # Assuming this is populated after recursion rightmerged = rightchild.gaussian mergedmean, mergedcov, mergedsh, falloff = mergegaussians([leftmerged, rightmerged]) node.gaussian = { 'mean': mergedmean, 'cov': mergedcov, 'sh': mergedsh, 'opacity': falloff # Falloff replaces opacity } def gethierarchycut(root, camera, targetgranularity=1.0): """ Selects the cut for the current view. Returns a list of nodes to render. """ activenodes = [] traverseforcut(root, camera, targetgranularity, activenodes) return activenodes def traverseforcut(node, camera, targetgranularity, activenodes): """ Recursively determines if a node should be included in the cut. """ # 1. Compute projected bounding box of the node projectedbbox = projectaabbtoscreen(node.aabb, camera) # 2. Compute granularity epsilon(n) # Largest dimension of the projected bounding box width = projectedbbox.maxx - projectedbbox.minx height = projectedbbox.maxy - projectedbbox.miny epsilonn = max(width, height) # 3. Check condition if epsilonn <= targetgranularity: # Node is small enough, include it activenodes.append(node) # Do not traverse children return else: # Node is too large, traverse children if node.children: for child in node.children: traverseforcut(child, camera, targetgranularity, activenodes) else: # Leaf node but still too large? # This implies the leaf itself is larger than target granularity. # In this case, we must render the leaf. activenodes.append(node) def rendernode(node, camera): """ Renders a single Gaussian node. """ g = node.gaussian # Standard 3DGS rasterization # Note: g['opacity'] is actually 'falloff' for interior nodes # Alpha blending clamps alpha to 1 if falloff > 1 alpha = rasterizegaussian(g, camera) alpha = min(alpha, 1.0) # Clamp alpha to 1 return alpha Bounding Box Expansion Factor: 3x the stored size of Gaussians. Target Granularity (\tau\epsilon): Threshold for projected AABB axis lengths, typically 1 pixel or less. Falloff > 1: The calculated falloff value for intermediate nodes can exceed 1. This is handled by clamping the resulting \alpha values to 1 during \alpha-blending. Rotation Ambiguity: Interpolating between nodes with different rotation axes can cause undesired rotations. The method handles this by rendering the two children with the same parameters as the parent and progressively interpolating towards their separate values. Isotropy Assumption: The weight derivation assumes Gaussians are nearly isotropic with little overlap and low perspective distortion. Typical scenes may violate this, requiring additional measures (not detailed in the provided snippets) to improve quality at higher LOD levels. Time Complexity: Hierarchy construction is O(N \log N) for N Gaussians due to the BVH build. Cut selection is linear time or constant time per node in a massively parallel setting. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full hierarchy tree. Each node stores a full Gaussian, so memory usage increases compared to flat 3DGS, proportional to the number of nodes in the hierarchy. Performance: Enables real-time rendering of very large scenes by reducing the number of primitives rendered at a distance. Strengths: Maintains visual quality at high LODs by accurately merging attributes; supports smooth transitions. Limitations: Increased memory overhead; potential artifacts if isotropy assumption is violated. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets". History: It builds upon the original 3D Gaussian Splatting method [Kerbl et al. 2023] by adding a hierarchical structure to handle large-scale scenes. Usage: Used for real-time rendering of large-scale 3D scenes, particularly in the context of CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian. name: Iterative Gaussian Synopsis
head: Iterative Gaussian Synopsis Framework, Iterative Gaussian Synopsis Unfolding, Top-Down Unfolding
body: Iterative Gaussian Synopsis is a top-down strategy for constructing a Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchy for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It begins with a full-fidelity model and progressively derives coarser levels through learnable anchor pruning and hierarchical grid downsampling. It sets itself apart from bottom-up approaches (e.g., LapisGS) by avoiding error accumulation and optimization conflicts, and from independent static models (e.g., Scaffold-GS variants) by sharing a foundational codebook and MLPs to minimize storage redundancy. Inputs: SfM point clouds, training images, target LoD count (L{max}), grid levels (Lg), codebook size (Nc). Outputs: A set of LoD representations \{L0, \dots, L{L{max}-1}\}. Data Structures: 1. Anchors: N anchors. Each anchor j has: Position \mathbf{x}a \in \mathbb{R}^3. Base scale \mathbf{l}a \in \mathbb{R}^3. K learnable offsets \mathbf{O}a \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 3}. Soft-index vector \mathbf{v}j \in \mathbb{R}^{Nc}. Mask parameters \mathbf{m}j \in \mathbb{R}^K. 2. Hierarchical Grids: Lg levels of multiresolution hash grids \{Gg\}{g=1}^{Lg}. Each grid level Gg stores features. Feature dimension per level is 4. 3. Anchor Codebook: \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nc \times Dc} (typically Dc=32). 4. MLPs: \text{MLP}{\text{fuse}}: Fuses hierarchical and local features. \text{MLP}{\text{attr}}: Predicts Gaussian attributes (\alpha, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}). Level-specific variants \text{MLP}^{(\ell)} and \mathbf{C}^{(\ell)} are created during unfolding. Formulas: Hierarchical Feature: \mathbf{f}{\text{hier}}(\mathbf{x}a) = [\text{Interpolate}(Gg, \mathbf{x}a)]{g=1}^{Lg}, where \text{Interpolate} is multi-linear interpolation. Local Feature (Training): \mathbf{w}j = \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{v}j) \mathbf{f}{\text{loc},j} = [\text{Onehot}(\text{argmax}(\mathbf{w}j^T)) + \mathbf{w}j^T - \text{sg}(\mathbf{w}j^T)] \cdot \mathbf{C} where \text{sg}(\cdot) is stop-gradient. Local Feature (Inference): \text{idx}j = \text{argmax}(\mathbf{v}j), \mathbf{f}{\text{loc},j} = \mathbf{C}[\text{idx}j]. Fused Feature: \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}a) = \text{MLP}{\text{fuse}}(\mathbf{f}{\text{hier}}(\mathbf{x}a) \oplus \mathbf{f}{\text{loc}}). Gaussian Prediction: \{\alpha^i, \mathbf{c}^i, \mathbf{s}^i, \mathbf{r}^i\}{i=0}^k = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}a), \sigmac, \vec{d}c), where \mathcal{F} comprises four MLPs (\mathcal{F}\alpha, \mathcal{F}c, \mathcal{F}s, \mathcal{F}r). Viewing Context: \sigmac = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}c\|2, \vec{d}c = \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}c}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}c\|2}, where \mathbf{x} is anchor position and \mathbf{x}c is camera position. Mask Computation: M{j,i} = \text{sg}(\mathbf{1}[\sigma(m{j,i}) > \epsilon] - \sigma(m{j,i})) + \sigma(m{j,i}) where \sigma(\cdot) is sigmoid, \mathbf{1}[\cdot] is indicator, \epsilon is threshold. Pruned Attributes: \hat{\alpha}{j,i} = M{j,i} \cdot \alpha{j,i}, \hat{\mathbf{s}}{j,i} = M{j,i} \cdot \mathbf{s}{j,i}. Anchor Pruning Condition: Anchor j is inactive if \sum{i=1}^K M{j,i} = 0. Loss Functions: Full-fidelity: \mathcal{L}{\text{full}} = (1 - \lambda{\text{SSIM}})\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{SSIM}}\mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} + \lambda{\text{vol}}\mathcal{L}{\text{vol}}. Masking Sparsity: \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} = \frac{1}{NK} \sumj \sum{i=1}^K \sigma(m{j,i}). Volume Regularization: \mathcal{L}{\text{vol}} = \mathbb{E}i [\prod{d} si^d] (product of scale entries). Parameters: L{max}: Number of LODs (typically 4, L0 to L3). Lg: Hierarchical grid levels (typically 12). Nc: Codebook size (typically 256). T{\text{full}}: Full-fidelity training iterations (typically 30,000). T{\text{unfold}}: Unfolding iterations per step (typically 10,000). \lambda{\text{SSIM}}: SSIM loss weight (typically 0.2). \epsilon: Mask threshold. Learning rate for masks during unfolding: 0.01. Codebook initialization: Normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Grid initialization: Not given in the sources. Grid retention per LOD: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativegaussiansynopsis(SfMpoints, images, Lmax, Lg, Nc): # 1. Initialization anchors = initializefromSfM(SfMpoints) # voxelization for anchor in anchors: anchor.offsets = learnableoffsets(K, 3) anchor.scales = learnablescales(3) anchor.vj = learnablesoftindex(Nc) anchor.mj = learnablemaskparams(K) grids = initializehierarchicalgrids(Lg, dim=4) codebook = initializecodebook(Nc, Dc=32) # N(0,1) MLPfuse, MLPattr = initializeMLPs() # 2. Full-fidelity training for t in range(Tfull): view = sampleview(images) render(view, anchors, grids, codebook, MLPfuse, MLPattr) Lfull = computeloss(view, anchors) # L1 + D-SSIM + vol updateallparameters(Lfull) # 3. Unfolding loop for anchor in anchors: anchor.idxj = argmax(anchor.vj) # discrete index for LOD Lmax-1 for l in range(Lmax - 1, 0, -1): # Grid restriction restrictgridstoLOD(l - 1) # Copy state M = oneslike(anchor.mj) C^(l-1) = copy(codebook) MLP^(l-1) = copy(MLPattr) # Adaptation modules (LAD/CBM) are integrated here # Pruning optimization for t in range(Tunfold): for anchor in anchors: for i in range(K): sigmaval = sigmoid(anchor.mj[i]) indicator = 1 if sigmaval > epsilon else 0 anchor.Mj[i] = stopgradient(indicator - sigmaval) + sigmaval anchor.alphahat = anchor.Mj anchor.alpha anchor.shat = anchor.Mj anchor.s renderatresolution(LOD=l-1) LLOD = computeLODloss(anchors, Lmask, Lgroup) updatemasksandadaptations(LLOD, C^(l-1), MLP^(l-1)) freezeanchorproperties() # positions, offsets, scales, grids return {L0,..., L{Lmax-1}} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: The discrete nature of the hierarchy can introduce mild visual "popping" artifacts as new anchors activate during LOD transitions. Optimization Conflicts: Bottom-up approaches suffer from accumulated errors; this top-down method avoids this by deriving coarser levels from the full-fidelity model. Level-aware Decoding (LAD) is a module within the Iterative Gaussian Synopsis framework that enables efficient, level-specific interpretation of modulated features for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of maintaining high visual fidelity across different Levels of Detail (LOD) without storing explicit, redundant Gaussian attributes for every level. By introducing level-specific fusion and attribute-prediction Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), LAD adapts a compact, function-based predictor to each LOD's objective, ensuring structural flexibility and strict model compactness. It sets itself apart from static attribute storage by dynamically fine-tuning the decoding network for each resolution level during the unfolding process. Complexity: Introduces additional training complexity compared to baseline methods due to the iterative unfolding and pruning optimization steps. Performance: Evaluated on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. The Full Model consistently achieves the best performance across all LODs. Storage: Significantly less storage than independent baseline models (e.g., independent Scaffold-GS) because it shares a foundational codebook and grids, extracting all LODs from a single optimization. Strengths: Coherent simplification, improved inter-layer consistency, compactness, and high-fidelity rendering across all LODs. Limitations: Limited to static scenes; potential for mild visual "popping" artifacts during LOD transitions. Usage: Designed for progressive streaming, real-time 3DGS deployment, and balancing compactness with high-fidelity rendering. Iterative Gaussian Synopsis was introduced in the paper "Unfolding 3D Gaussian Splatting via Iterative Gaussian Synopsis". It addresses the challenges of deploying large-scale 3DGS models for progressive and adaptive rendering by proposing a top-down unfolding strategy, contrasting with conventional bottom-up approaches like LapisGS. name: Level-aware Decoding
head: LAD
body: Level-aware Decoding (LAD) is a module within the Iterative Gaussian Synopsis framework that enables efficient, level-specific interpretation of modulated features for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of maintaining high visual fidelity across different Levels of Detail (LOD) without storing explicit, redundant Gaussian attributes for every level. By introducing level-specific fusion and attribute-prediction Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), LAD adapts a compact, function-based predictor to each LOD's objective, ensuring structural flexibility and strict model compactness. It sets itself apart from static attribute storage by dynamically fine-tuning the decoding network for each resolution level during the unfolding process. Inputs: Downsampled hierarchical grids for the target LOD \ell. Modulated local features associated with the anchors at LOD \ell. Level index \ell. Outputs: Predicted Gaussian attributes (opacity, covariance, color) for the primitives at LOD \ell. Data Structures: MLP Fusion (MLP^{(\ell)}{fuse}): A neural network specific to LOD \ell that fuses the modulated local features with the hierarchical grid features. MLP Attribute Prediction (MLP^{(\ell)}{attr}): A neural network specific to LOD \ell that predicts Gaussian properties from the fused features. Level Information: An explicit parameter or embedding representing the current LOD level, incorporated into the feature processing. Steps: 1. Initialize Level-Specific MLPs: During the unfolding step for LOD \ell, copy the weights of the fusion and attribute-prediction MLPs from the trained foundational codebook (or the previous level's foundational counterparts). This preserves coherence of the shared basis. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract features for each visible anchor point based on the LOD mask. 3. Level Incorporation: Incorporate the level index \ell into the feature processing pipeline via the addlevel parameter. This allows the networks to learn level-specific representations. 4. Fusion: Apply MLP^{(\ell)}{fuse} to the modulated local features and the downsampled hierarchical grid features. 5. Attribute Prediction: Apply MLP^{(\ell)}{attr} to the fused features to predict the Gaussian properties (opacity, covariance, color). 6. Fine-Tuning: Fine-tune the level-specific MLPs (MLP^{(\ell)}{fuse} and MLP^{(\ell)}{attr}) using the LLOD loss until the anchors condense to the next coarser level or the target LOD is reached. Parameters: Learning rate for fusion MLP updates during unfolding: 0.005. Learning rate for opacity MLP updates during unfolding: 0.002. Learning rate for color MLP updates during unfolding: 0.008. Learning rate for covariance MLP updates during unfolding: 0.004. addlevel: A boolean or configuration parameter that explicitly incorporates level information into the neural networks. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def levelawaredecoding(anchorpoints, hierarchicalgrids, levelindex, foundationalmlpfuse, foundationalmlpattr): """ Performs level-aware decoding for a specific LOD level. Args: anchorpoints: List of visible anchor points for the current LOD. hierarchicalgrids: Downsampled hierarchical grids for the current LOD. levelindex: The integer index of the current LOD (e.g., 0, 1, 2, 3). foundationalmlpfuse: The foundational fusion MLP weights. foundationalmlpattr: The foundational attribute prediction MLP weights. Returns: gaussianattributes: Predicted properties (opacity, covariance, color) for the Gaussians. """ # Step 1: Initialize level-specific MLPs from foundational counterparts # This preserves coherence of the shared basis mlpfuse = copyweights(foundationalmlpfuse) mlpattr = copyweights(foundationalmlpattr) # Step 2: Extract features for each anchor point # Select visible anchor points based on the LOD mask visibleanchors = selectvisibleanchors(anchorpoints, levelindex) features = extractfeatures(visibleanchors, hierarchicalgrids) # Step 3: Incorporate level information # Explicitly incorporate level information into feature processing levelembedding = getlevelembedding(levelindex) featureswithlevel = combinefeatures(features, levelembedding) # Step 4: Fusion # Apply level-specific fusion MLP fusedfeatures = mlpfuse(featureswithlevel) # Step 5: Attribute Prediction # Apply level-specific attribute prediction MLP gaussianattributes = mlpattr(fusedfeatures) # Step 6: Fine-Tuning (performed during the unfolding optimization loop) # The MLPs are fine-tuned under LLOD loss # Typical learning rates: # fusion: 0.005 # opacity: 0.002 # color: 0.008 # covariance: 0.004 return gaussianattributes A rendering pipeline stage where neural networks predict Gaussian properties (color, opacity, covariance) using features extracted from anchor points, explicitly incorporating level information to learn level-specific representations. It differs from standard generation by using the addlevel parameter to inject LOD context into the feature processing, allowing the MLPs (Feature Bank, Opacity, Covariance, Color) to adapt their predictions based on the current resolution level. Choose this when you need to dynamically adjust the number of Gaussians and their properties based on viewing distance or LOD mask. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory usage is lower than non-LOD approaches because only level-dependent data is loaded. The total model size is measured in megabytes (MB), including the Compressed Delta Size for transitions between LODs. Rendering time is consistent and bounded by level selection, as opposed to being inconsistent and dependent on the full scene complexity. Measured Performance: Evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Framework generates a hierarchy of 4 LODs (L0 to L3). Uses a multi-resolution hash grid with 12 levels and a feature dimension of 4. Global Anchor Codebook size Nc is 256 with feature dimension Dc = 32. Group sparsity loss weight \lambda{group} is 0.01. Models are trained for 30,000 iterations at full fidelity before unfolding. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High fidelity and structural flexibility while maintaining strict model compactness. Enables streaming suitability by quantifying incremental network payload. Limitations: Requires iterative unfolding and fine-tuning of MLPs for each level, which adds complexity to the training pipeline. When to Use: Use when deploying 3D Gaussian Splatting for streaming or real-time applications where bandwidth and memory are constrained. Use when a hierarchy of LODs is required to adapt rendering quality to viewing distance. Level-aware Decoding is part of the "Unfolding 3D Gaussian Splatting via Iterative Gaussian Synopsis" framework. It was introduced to address the need for efficient LOD management in 3D Gaussian Splatting, building on the iterative synopsis method that constructs a hierarchy from full fidelity down to coarse levels. The method leverages the concept of a foundational codebook and modulated features to avoid storing explicit attributes for every LOD. name: Sequential Point Trees (SPTs)
body: Sequential Point Trees (SPTs) are a hierarchical data structure originally developed for point cloud rendering, adapted here for efficient, view-dependent Level-of-Detail (LoD) selection in 3D Gaussian Splatting without requiring full tree traversal. Unlike sibling methods that rely on static spatial partitioning or post-training hierarchy construction, SPTs enable dynamic LoD hierarchies that evolve continuously during optimization. They are primarily used within the Hierarchical SPT (HSPT) framework to compute the correct LoD cut efficiently for individual views and camera paths. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Gaussian hierarchy \mathcal{H} (structured as a tree) and a specific cut condition, such as a distance threshold d^j for a single SPT. Output: A set of nodes representing the "cut" at the specified condition, which determines which Gaussians are included in the rendering for a given view or LoD level. Data Structures: The SPT is a binary tree hierarchy where each node represents a group of Gaussians. Each node stores bounding information (e.g., minimum distance to the camera) and references to left and right children. The structure supports efficient traversal and cutting. Algorithm Steps: 1. The CPU performs an initial efficient pre-culling to provide a large chunk of points. 2. The GPU performs fine-granularity culling in a simple vertex program, reporting a percentage of culled points going from 10% to 40%. 3. Back-face culling is performed by splitting the initial SPT list into an array of point lists with equal quantized normals, using 128 quantized normals. 4. For large complex scenes, normal clustering is replaced with position clustering to perform more accurate high-level view frustum and occlusion culling using a small bounding box hierarchy instead of a single large bounding box per object. 5. The SPT is cut at a particular distance d^j by finding the highest index where the minimum distance is less than the cut distance. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode implements the BFS Hierarchy Cut, adapted from the source for cutting a single SPT at a distance d^j. The condition evaluates whether a node's minimum distance is within the threshold. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cuthierarchy(hierarchyroot, condition): cut = [] queue = [hierarchyroot] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) if condition(node): cut.append(node) else: if node.left is not None: queue.append(node.left) if node.right is not None: queue.append(node.right) return cut Parameters: d^j: The cut distance threshold for the j-th view or LoD level. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hierarchy Updates: The SPT must remain robust to hierarchy updates during training, as the LoD structure evolves continuously. Precision: Efficient computation is critical for large models; full tree traversal is avoided to maintain performance. A hybrid data structure adapting SPTs to Gaussian splatting. It enables efficient, parallelizable LoD selection while remaining robust to hierarchy updates during training. It is chosen when dynamic, view-dependent LoD is required for ultra-large scenes without spatial partitioning. An algorithm to cut a single SPT at a particular distance d^j by finding the highest index where the minimum distance is less than the cut distance. It is used to determine the specific subset of Gaussians to render for a given view-dependent LoD level. Time Complexity: Efficient, avoiding full tree traversal. The BFS cut allows for parallelizable selection. Memory Complexity: Supports out-of-core memory usage, enabling training and rendering of city-scale scenes on a single consumer GPU. Strengths: Seamless, non-partitioned training of ultra-large Gaussian scenes; dynamic LoD evolution during optimization; reduced CPU-GPU data transfer via caching. Limitations: When used with a pure high-quality point-based rendering system, SPT is inefficient because much unnecessary data is processed by complex vertex programs. When to use: For ultra-large scale reconstruction (e.g., city-scale) where view-dependent LoD is critical and spatial partitioning is undesirable. When used with Deferred Splatting, it becomes very efficient because it is only used during pass 2 with a very simple vertex program. Sequential Point Trees were originally developed for point cloud rendering by Dachsbacher et al. in 2003. They have been adapted for 3D Gaussian Splatting in the context of "A LoD of Gaussians" (2025) to support stable and progressive refinement in ultra-large scenes. The adaptation addresses the challenge of efficient view-dependent selection when the hierarchy structure changes during optimization. name: Splat List (SVL) Generation with Multi-Level Downsampling
head: LOD Splatting, Sparse Voxel List
body: This method generates a Sparse Voxel List (SVL) of splat geometry across multiple levels of detail (LOD) by iteratively downsampling a voxel occupancy mask and extracting representative splat primitives for each level. Inputs: A voxel chunk containing an occupancy mask (array of Voxel types, where Voxel is uint8t) and metadata defining the chunk's spatial bounds and resolution. Outputs: A contiguous SVL buffer (uint16t) containing geometry items for all LOD levels, and a GeometrySVL structure describing the buffer's layout. Data Structures: The core output structure is struct GeometrySVL: lod: uint8t, the level of detail index. vao: uint32t, vertex array object identifier. vbo: uint32t, vertex buffer object identifier. vboitems: uint32t, number of items in the buffer. The chunk metadata is stored in struct ChunkMD, which includes: svl: uint16t, pointer to the SVL buffer. svlitems[MAXLODLEVEL]: uint32t, count of items per LOD level. svlitemstotal: uint32t, total item count across all LODs. svldirty: volatile uint8t, flag indicating the SVL needs regeneration. nogeometry: volatile uint8t, flag set if the chunk contains no geometry. mutexwrite: pthreadmutext, protects chunk access during meshing. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each chunk c, check if c->svldirty is set or if c->meshdirty is set. 2. Mask Generation: Generate the initial voxel occupancy mask for the chunk using chunkmakemask. 3. Iterative Downsampling and Extraction: Loop through LOD levels i from 0 to MAXLODLEVEL - 1: a. Splat Extraction: Extract splat primitives from the current occupancy mask for level i. b. Accumulation: Add the number of generated geometry items for this level to a running total geomitems. c. Downsampling: If i is not the final LOD level, downsample the current mask into a work buffer for level i+1 using chunkmaskdownsample. 4. Buffer Allocation: Allocate a contiguous SVL buffer of size geomitems sizeof(uint16t). 5. Data Copy: Copy the accumulated geometry data from the mesher buffer into the allocated SVL buffer. 6. Metadata Update: Update c->svlitems with the counts per level and c->svlitemstotal with the total count. 7. Empty Chunk Handling: If geomitems is zero, free any existing SVL buffer, zero out c->svlitems, set c->svlitemstotal to 0, set c->nogeometry to 1, and mark c->svldirty as 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatesvl(chunk, set, maxlodlevel=5): # Check dirty flags; skip if SVL or mesh needs regeneration if chunk.svldirty or chunk.meshdirty: return geomitems = 0 svlitemsperlevel = [0] maxlodlevel mask = chunkmakemask(chunk) # Generate initial voxel occupancy mask workbuffer = [0] len(mask) # Work buffer for downsampled masks for i in range(maxlodlevel): # Extract splat primitives from current mask for level i items = extractsplatsfrommask(mask, level=i) count = len(items) svlitemsperlevel[i] = count geomitems += count # Downsample current mask into work buffer for level i+1 if i < maxlodlevel - 1: chunkmaskdownsample(mask, workbuffer) mask = workbuffer # Handle empty chunk case if geomitems == 0: if chunk.svl is not None: memfree(chunk.svl) chunk.svl = None chunk.svlitems = [0] maxlodlevel chunk.svlitemstotal = 0 chunk.nogeometry = 1 chunk.svldirty = 1 return # Allocate and copy SVL buffer buffersize = geomitems 2 # sizeof(uint16t) svlbuffer = memalloc(buffersize) copygeometrytosvl(mesherbuffer, svlbuffer, geomitems) chunk.svl = svlbuffer chunk.svlitems = svlitemsperlevel chunk.svlitemstotal = geomitems chunk.svldirty = 0 Parameters: MAXLODLEVEL: Constant defining the number of splat LOD levels. Set to 5. Voxel: Type alias for uint8t. Coordinate/Iterator types: Chunk/voxel locations use uint16t, worldspace vectors use uint32t, iterators use uint32t. Edge Cases: Empty Chunk: If no geometry is generated (geomitems == 0), the SVL buffer is freed, and flags are reset to indicate no geometry. Concurrency: The method uses mutexwrite to protect chunk access during meshing.
