name: Octree-based Hierarchy
body: Octree-based Hierarchy is a family of hierarchical decomposition methods for volume rendering that organizes data into an octree structure to enable adaptive, multi-resolution rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Multi-Resolution and Level of Detail (Pyramid, LOD, Downsampling) by using a 3D spatial subdivision (octree) rather than a 2D image-space pyramid, allowing for precise culling of homogeneous 3D regions based on stored error metrics. The methods in this family share the mechanism of hierarchical decomposition and error-driven or distance-driven primitive selection, building on Splatting. 1. Hierarchical Decomposition: The input data (volume, point cloud, or Gaussian set) is organized into an octree structure where each node represents a spatial region. Each node stores aggregate properties derived from its children. 2. Error Metric Computation: For each internal node, a local error metric E is computed to quantify the approximation cost of representing the node's children with the node's aggregate properties. 3. Adaptive Traversal and Selection: During rendering, the hierarchy is traversed from the root to the leaves. A node is selected as a leaf (and thus rendered as a single primitive) if its error E is below a user-defined threshold \epsilon. If the error exceeds the threshold, the algorithm recurses to the children. 4. Primitive Aggregation: When a node is selected, its children are merged into a single representative primitive. The primitive's attributes are computed as weighted averages or sums of the children's attributes. 5. Multi-Resolution Rendering: The final image is composed of primitives from various levels of the hierarchy, allowing for efficient culling of distant or homogeneous regions while maintaining fidelity in foreground or complex areas. An object-order interactive volume rendering technique that approximates volume contributions using an octree hierarchy and geometric splats. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by adapting the resolution of rendered primitives based on a user-defined error tolerance, trading visual fidelity for speed. Choose it when real-time interaction on dense volumes is required. A hierarchical object-order rendering technique designed for Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly handling the conversion of irregular AMR block structures into a k-d-tree framework for domain subdivision, augmented with octrees to manage isovalue ranges. Choose it for efficiently rendering non-uniform, multi-resolution scalar fields. A hierarchical object-order volume rendering technique that renders non-leaf octree nodes as single primitives. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by actively utilizing internal tree nodes as renderable kernels rather than restricting them to occlusion culling, thereby reducing draw calls and traversal overhead. Choose it for accelerating the visualization of dense volumetric data. A topology-aware anchor feature aggregation framework designed to address feature isolation in octree-based 3D Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the octree's topological structure during feature aggregation rather than relying solely on spatial proximity or error metrics for primitive selection. Choose it when optimizing cross-level information flow and reducing redundancy in 3DGS representations. Splats are culled prior to sorting and rendering using a custom octree to optimize performance. The technique is utilized in real-time viewers and web-based splat rendering to optimize performance by culling splats prior to sorting and rendering using a custom octree. It supports progressive loading of.ply and.splat files, though converting scenes to the optimized.ksplat format results in the fastest loading times since the format matches the internal format for splat data. The rendering pipeline also incorporates WASM splat sort implemented in C++ using WASM SIMD instructions, alongside partially GPU accelerated splat sort using transform feedback to pre-calculate splat distances. mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, https://github.com/mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree-based Splatting
head: Laur and Hanrahan Splatting
body: Octree-based Splatting is an object-order interactive volume rendering technique that accelerates rendering by approximating volume contributions using an octree hierarchy and geometric splats. It solves the performance bottleneck of processing every voxel by culling homogeneous regions and distant details, allowing for real-time interaction. Unlike standard splatting, this method adapts the resolution of the rendered primitives based on a user-defined error tolerance, trading visual fidelity for speed. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset organized into an octree; an error tolerance threshold \epsilon. Output: A 2D image composed of splatted primitives. Data Structures The volume is organized into an octree. Each parent node in the octree stores: 1. Approximate Scalar Value (V{approx}): A representative scalar value for the region covered by the node. 2. Error Value (E): A metric indicating the deviation of the child nodes' scalar values from V{approx}. Algorithm Steps 1. Preprocessing (Octree Construction): The volume is decomposed into an octree. For each internal node, V{approx} is computed as a representative value of its children, and E is calculated to quantify the approximation error. The exact formula for E is not detailed in the sources, but it represents the deviation of child scalar values from the parent's approximate value. 2. Traversal and Selection: The algorithm traverses the octree starting from the root. At each node, check if the stored error value E is less than the given error tolerance \epsilon. If E < \epsilon: Stop descending. The node is selected as a leaf. The region of the volume represented by this node is approximated by rendering a single geometric primitive (splat). If E \ge \epsilon: Recurse to the children nodes. 3. Splat Rendering: When a node is selected as a leaf, a splat is rendered to approximate the contribution of that volume region. The size of the splat is changed based upon the cell it represents in the octree representation. The splat is composited into the image using standard splatting techniques (e.g., texture-mapped polygons). Parameters Error Tolerance (\epsilon): A threshold value for the error stored in octree nodes. Increasing \epsilon decreases rendering time by allowing larger regions to be approximated at higher levels in the octree. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The accuracy of the error metric E directly impacts the traversal path. The sources do not specify behavior for degenerate nodes or zero-error regions. Scaling: The size of the splat must be scaled to the octree cell size to maintain correct spatial correspondence. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderoctreesplat(rootnode, epsilon, camera): """Recursively traverse the octree and render splats for leaf nodes.""" traverse(rootnode, epsilon, camera) def traverse(node, epsilon, camera): """Traverse a single octree node.""" if node.error < epsilon: # Node is a leaf for rendering purposes rendersplat(node, camera) else: # Node is not a leaf, recurse to children for child in node.children: traverse(child, epsilon, camera) def rendersplat(node, camera): """Render a single splat for an octree node.""" # Determine splat size based on the octree cell the node represents # states size changes based on the octree cell cellextent = node.boundingbox.sidelength distance = abs(node.center.z - camera.position.z) screensize = cellextent camera.focallength / distance # Project node center to screen space clipcoords = camera.projectionmatrix @ (camera.viewmatrix @ node.center) screenpos = (clipcoords.x / clipcoords.w, clipcoords.y / clipcoords.w) # Rasterize the splat primitive rasterizesplat(screenpos, screensize, node.approximatescalarvalue) def rasterizesplat(position, size, value): # Standard splatting rasterization: draw a textured polygon or circle # with radius proportional to size, blending into the image buffer # pass The general class of methods using tree structures for adaptive resolution. Octree-based Splatting is a specific implementation using octrees. The base method that processes every voxel. Octree-based Splatting builds on this by adding hierarchical culling. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of leaf nodes selected by the error tolerance. Higher error tolerance \epsilon leads to fewer leaf nodes and faster rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storing an approximate scalar value and an error value in each parent node. Strengths: Decreases rendering time by allowing larger regions to be approximated at higher levels in the octree. Enables interactive frame rates. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: When interactive performance is required for large volume datasets and some loss of fidelity is acceptable. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Octree-based Splatting was introduced by Laur in 1991. It is also referred to as Laur and Hanrahan Splatting. The method was developed to address the dependency of rendering speed on the number of voxels in the dataset. It builds on earlier splatting techniques and uses octree structures to cull voxels. name: Splatting-Based AMR Volume Rendering
head: Hierarchical Splatting for AMR, Hierarchical Splatting with k-d-tree and Octree, Park et al. method, Park, Bajaj & Siddavanahalli (2002) method, k-d-tree/octree hierarchical splatting
body: Splatting-Based AMR Volume Rendering is a hierarchical object-order rendering technique designed for Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering non-uniform, multi-resolution scalar fields by converting the irregular AMR hierarchy into a structured k-d-tree of constant-resolution blocks, augmented with octrees to manage isovalue ranges. Unlike standard splatting which treats primitives uniformly, this method uses the hierarchical structure to cull regions outside a specified isovalue range and transfer function, rendering only relevant data back-to-front. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Octree-based Splatting by explicitly handling the conversion of AMR block structures into a k-d-tree framework for domain subdivision. Inputs: AMR scalar field data, a specified isovalue range, and a transfer function mapping scalar values to optical properties (color, opacity). Outputs: A rendered 2D image. Data Structures: 1. K-d-tree: Represents the spatial domain by converting the AMR hierarchy into blocks of constant resolution. 2. Augmented Octree: Each node in the k-d-tree is augmented with an octree structure. 3. Node Metadata: Both k-d-tree and octree nodes contain a 32-bit field where each bit represents a continuous range of isovalues. This allows for rapid identification of nodes containing values within the user-specified isovalue range. Algorithm Steps: 1. Convert the input AMR hierarchy into a k-d-tree structure where each leaf node represents a block of constant resolution. 2. Augment each node of the constructed k-d-tree with an octree. 3. Populate a 32-bit field in each k-d-tree and octree node, where each bit corresponds to a specific continuous isovalue range. 4. Traverse the k-d-tree and octree structures to identify regions (nodes) that contain scalar values within the specified isovalue range, as determined by the 32-bit metadata fields. 5. Render the identified regions back-to-front using hierarchical splatting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderamrvolume(AMRdata, isovaluerange, transferfunction): # Step 1: Convert AMR hierarchy to a k-d-tree structure of constant-resolution blocks # The sources do not specify the exact conversion algorithm. kdtreeroot = None # Conversion procedure not specified # Step 2: Augment each node of the k-d-tree with an octree # The sources do not specify the exact augmentation procedure. for node in kdtreeroot: node.octree = None # Augmentation procedure not specified # Step 3: Populate a 32-bit field in each node where each bit represents a continuous range of isovalues for node in kdtreeroot: node.isovaluemask = 0 for i in range(32): if node.containsvaluerange(i): node.isovaluemask |= (1 << i) # Step 4: Identify regions containing values within the specified isovalue range targetmask = 0 for i in range(32): if isovaluerange.containsrange(i): targetmask |= (1 << i) relevantnodes = [] for node in kdtreeroot: if node.isovaluemask & targetmask: relevantnodes.append(node) # Step 5: Render identified regions back-to-front using hierarchical splatting relevantnodes.sort(key=lambda n: n.cameradistance, reverse=True) image = compositebacktofront(relevantnodes, transferfunction) return image Parameters: Isovalue Range: The range of scalar values to visualize. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity. Bit Field Size: Fixed at 32 bits per node. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The 32-bit field limits the granularity of isovalue range identification to 32 continuous ranges. AMR Conversion: The conversion from AMR to k-d-tree must handle irregular block sizes and refinement levels correctly. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves rendering quality considerably compared to slicing-based approaches. Supports a more complex light model with wavelength-dependent absorption. Strengths: Efficient culling of irrelevant data via isovalue range identification; handles AMR data structure naturally through k-d-tree conversion. Limitations: Limited to scalar fields with specified isovalue ranges; 32-bit field constraint on isovalue granularity. When to use: When rendering AMR data with specific isovalue ranges and requiring high-quality volume rendering with complex lighting. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced by Park, Bajaj & Siddavanahalli in 2002. It builds on the hierarchical splatting approach by Laur & Hanrahan (1991). name: Octree Splatting
body: Octree Splatting is a hierarchical object-order volume rendering technique that renders non-leaf octree nodes as single primitives to accelerate the visualization of dense volumetric data. It distinguishes itself from standard splatting by actively utilizing internal tree nodes as renderable kernels, rather than restricting them to occlusion culling. Inputs: A volume dataset organized into an octree structure. Outputs: A 2D image composed of splatted primitives. Data Structures: Each octree node stores the children's average value \mu and an error metric \sigma based on the standard deviation of the children's values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Tree Construction: Build the octree from the input volume. For each internal node, compute \mu as the average of its children's values and \sigma as the standard deviation of those values. 2. Node Selection: Traverse the octree from the root. For each node, compare its pre-computed error metric \sigma against a user-defined pre-set threshold \epsilon. If \sigma \leq \epsilon, the node is selected as a leaf for rendering. Otherwise, recurse to its children. 3. Primitive Approximation: When a non-leaf node is selected, it is approximated by a single kernel (splat). The footprint radius R of the splat is set to twice the radius of the kernels of its immediate children (R{child}), i.e., R = 2 \times R{child}. 4. Compositing: Render the selected splats using standard alpha blending or accumulation techniques. Parameters: \epsilon: Pre-set error threshold for node selection. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A rendering method for non-uniform volumetric data that uses a hierarchical structure (octree or adaptive tree) to select levels of detail (LOD) based on a screen-space error metric, allowing for interactive navigation and progressive refinement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the octree structure plus the average and error metric for each node. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Laur and Hanrahan. It is based on the idea that non-leaf nodes in an octree can be approximated by kernels with a radius twice that of their children, providing a magnified footprint that represents the aggregate data of the subtree. This approach contrasts with other hierarchical methods that use internal nodes only for occlusion culling. name: Adaptive Hierarchical Splatting with View-Dependent LOD
head: View-Dependent Multiresolution Splatting
body: A rendering method for non-uniform volumetric data that uses a hierarchical structure (octree or adaptive tree) to select levels of detail (LOD) based on a screen-space error metric, allowing for interactive navigation and progressive refinement. It sets itself apart from standard octree splatting by using a fixed linear footprint for conservative LOD culling and non-uniform elliptical splats for leaf nodes to preserve local data distribution details. Inputs: Non-uniform volumetric data points. Camera parameters (position, orientation, projection matrix). Screen-space error metric threshold (E{screen}) in pixels. Scalar value error metric threshold (E{scalar}) for progressive refinement. Outputs: A rasterized image of the volume. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchy Node: Lx, Ly, Lz: Rectilinear cell dimensions (floats). children: Array of pointers to child nodes (internal nodes only). datapoints: List of non-uniform data points (leaf nodes only). avgscalar: Average scalar value of the node (for E{scalar} calculation). rmsdeviation: RMS deviation of scalar values from average (for E{scalar} calculation). 2. Splat: center: 3D position (sample point). scale: Derived from Voronoi cell. orientation: Derived from Voronoi cell. texture: Color/opacity mapping derived from scalar value. Hierarchy Construction: The hierarchy is built based on data dimensions Nx=2^m, Ny=2^n, Nz=2^p where m > n > p. 1. Create p levels with 8 children (8-fold branching). 2. Create n-p levels with 4 children (4-fold branching). 3. Create m-n levels with 2 children (2-fold branching). 4. Determine bin size for leaf nodes based on the minimum spacing of underlying data points, ensuring no more than two points per bin. 5. Fill bins with data points. Only filled bins are stored and accumulated into the tree. 6. For each node, calculate the fixed linear footprint size conservatively set to the maximum possible diagonal: F{linear} = \sqrt{Lx^2 + Ly^2 + Lz^2}. Rendering Steps: 1. Culling: Cull volume elements not in the view frustum as the viewpoint changes. 2. Traversal: Traverse the hierarchy from the root to the leaves. 3. LOD Selection: For each node, perspective project the linear footprint F{linear} onto the screen and convert to pixels (P{pixels}). If P{pixels} > E{screen}, traverse to children. If P{pixels} \le E{screen}, stop traversal at this node and render it. 4. Leaf Rendering: For leaf nodes containing non-uniform data points: Construct elliptical splats centered at sample points. Determine scale and orientation of each splat based on the Voronoi cell of the point to provide uniform coverage over neighbors. Combine closest splats to generate Levels of Detail (LODs). 5. Internal Node Rendering: For internal nodes selected by LOD, render a single splat representing the node's cell dimensions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Splat: def init(self, center, scale, orientation, value): self.center = center self.scale = scale self.orientation = orientation self.value = value def projecttoscreenpixels(linearsize, camera): # Perspective projection: pixels = (linearsize focallength) / distance # Uses camera distance to node center for projection scale return (linearsize camera.focallength) / camera.distancetocenter def rendersplat(splat, framebuffer): # Rasterize elliptical splat onto frame buffer with color/opacity from value pass def rendervolume(rootnode, camera, Escreen, framebuffer): splats = [] traverse(rootnode, camera, Escreen, splats) for s in splats: rendersplat(s, framebuffer) def traverse(node, camera, Escreen, splats): # Calculate fixed linear footprint footprintlinear = math.sqrt(node.Lx2 + node.Ly2 + node.Lz2) # Perspective project to screen pixels footprintpixels = projecttoscreenpixels(footprintlinear, camera) # Check screen space error metric if footprintpixels > Escreen: # If node has children, traverse them if node.children: for child in node.children: traverse(child, camera, Escreen, splats) else: # Leaf node too large: render as single splat covering cell rendersplat(Splat(center=node.center, scale=footprintlinear, orientation=(1,0,0), value=node.avgscalar), framebuffer) else: # Footprint is small enough, render this node if node.isleaf(): for point in node.datapoints: # Sources do not provide the exact Voronoi cell computation algorithm; standard computational geometry is used voronoicell = computevoronoicell(point, node.datapoints) scale = voronoicell.size orientation = voronoicell.orientation splats.append(Splat(center=point.position, scale=scale, orientation=orientation, value=point.scalarvalue)) else: rendersplat(Splat(center=node.center, scale=footprintlinear, orientation=(1,0,0), value=node.avgscalar), framebuffer) Parameters: Screen space error metric (E{screen}): Threshold in pixels for the projected footprint. Typical values tested: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 pixels. A value of 1 pixel results in an image barely distinguishable from high resolution. Scalar value error metric (E{scalar}): Derived from RMS deviation of scalar values in a node from their average. Used for progressive refinement when pausing for inspection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Using a view-dependent metric \ge 1 pixel removes aliasing (in the sense of Swan et al.) but reduces splat count. Error is confined to 1 pixel or less if metric \le 1 pixel. Non-uniform coverage: A single elliptical splat cannot provide uniform coverage for all neighbors in a non-uniform cell (e.g., overlapping some, missing others). Solved by using multiple splats oriented by Voronoi cells. Overestimation: Using a fixed linear footprint (diagonal) instead of precise orientation-dependent footprint saves computation but accepts a slight overestimation of splat count. This method organizes multiresolution splats of 3D non-uniform data into a hierarchical structure capable of handling different data types and large spatial magnitude differences between overviews and details. It is specifically designed for earth-based environments, such as atmospheric data, where the domain is a thin layer relative to the planetary ellipsoid. It sets itself apart from standard octree splatting by using a lat/lon quadtree for the global overview and switching to an embedded volume tree only when local dimensions become comparable, allowing for efficient view-dependent LOD selection as described in Adaptive Hierarchical Splatting with View-Dependent LOD. Time Complexity: Depends on the screen-space error metric. Larger metrics result in fewer splats and faster rendering. Memory Complexity: Depends on the hierarchy depth and number of data points. Only filled bins are stored. Measured Performance: Hardware: SGI 195MHz R1000 with Infinite Reality 2. Resolution: 800x600 pixels. Altitude: 2667km. Max rendering time (before culling): 1.7 seconds. Rendering times for screen-space metrics of 4, 8, 16, 32 pixels: 1.26s, 0.328s, 0.063s, 0.014s respectively. Strengths: Interactive navigation, progressive refinement, handles non-uniform data, culling efficiency. Limitations: Fixed footprint overestimation, computation per splat for non-uniform leaf nodes. When to use: Interactive visualization of large-scale non-uniform volumetric data (e.g., earth-based environments). When not to use: When precise orientation-dependent footprint is required for minimal splat count, or when data is uniformly distributed (standard octree may be simpler). Origin: Jang, Ribarsky, Shaw, and Faust (2002). History: Developed for interactive navigation of large-scale non-uniform volumetric data, specifically earth-based environments like atmospheric data. Usage: Demonstrated with NEXRAD Doppler Radar data. View-Dependent Multiresolution Splatting of Non-Uniform Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/vissym02/125-132, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Embedded, Adaptive Volume Tree Structure
head: Global earth-based hierarchy, Lat/lon quadtree with volume tree leaves
body: This method organizes multiresolution splats of 3D non-uniform data into a hierarchical structure capable of handling different data types and large spatial magnitude differences between overviews and details. It is specifically designed for earth-based environments, such as atmospheric data, where the domain is a thin layer relative to the planetary ellipsoid. It sets itself apart from standard octree splatting by using a lat/lon quadtree for the global overview and switching to an embedded volume tree only when local dimensions become comparable, allowing for efficient view-dependent LOD selection as described in Adaptive Hierarchical Splatting with View-Dependent LOD. Inputs: Non-uniform 3D data points (e.g., atmospheric measurements) defined by longitude, latitude, and altitude coordinates, along with scalar field values. Outputs: A hierarchical tree structure consisting of a top-level forest of quadtrees, mid-level volume trees, and leaf nodes containing the data points, along with aggregated metadata for each node. Data Structures: 1. Quadtree Node: Represents a region of the earth's surface. Contains pointers to child quadtree nodes or a volume tree root. 2. Volume Tree Node: Represents a 3D bin or aggregated region. Fields: totalrawelements: Integer count of raw volumetric data elements in children. totalfilledbins: Integer count of non-empty bins in children. avgscalar: Float, average scalar field value of children. varscalar: Float, variance of scalar field values of children. children: Array of pointers to child nodes. points: Array of data points (retained in bins for full resolution rendering if needed). Dimensions: Node dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz) are not stored explicitly but calculated on-the-fly based on the tree level and bin counts. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construct Top-Level Hierarchy: Create a forest of lat/lon quadtrees covering the entire domain (e.g., Earth). This structure is appropriate because the atmosphere is a thin layer relative to the Earth's ellipsoid. 2. Determine Switch Point: Traverse the quadtree. When a quadtree node's lat/lon dimensions are of the same order of magnitude as its altitude dimension, switch from the quadtree structure to a volume tree structure for that region. 3. Define Bin Grid: For each region requiring a volume tree, divide the space into Nx \times Ny \times Nz bins, where x, y, z correspond to longitude, latitude, and altitude directions, respectively. Constraint: Nx, Ny, Nz must be powers of 2 (Nx = 2^m, Ny = 2^n, Nz = 2^p) to permit straightforward binary hierarchy construction. 4. Bin Sort Data: Sort the non-uniform data points into the defined bins. Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of data points. Note: Bins are not rectilinear in Cartesian space due to Earth's curvature. This effect is ignored during volume rendering as curvature is small for rendered bins, except at high latitudes where lat/lon quadcells are nearly rectilinear. Bin widths may be non-uniform to accommodate data density variations (e.g., higher concentration near the ground). 5. Construct Volume Hierarchy: Build the hierarchy levels based on the exponents m, n, p. The number of children at a node is determined by the dimensions: If m > n > p: p levels with 8-fold branching (each parent has 8 children), n - p levels with 4-fold branching, and m - n levels with 2-fold branching. If two exponents are equal, there are only 8-fold and 4-fold levels. The placement of these branching factors depends on the specific data distribution. 6. Aggregate Properties: Accumulate bins to form parent nodes. Derive parent properties from weighted averages of child properties. totalrawelements = Sum of totalrawelements of children. totalfilledbins = Sum of totalfilledbins of children. avgscalar and varscalar are computed as weighted averages of children's scalar statistics. 7. Store Leaf Data: Store the specific data element positions in the leaf bins. This allows for full-resolution rendering if needed, while the hierarchy enables memory savings by retrieving coordinates only for viewable bins at the appropriate LOD. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class QuadTreeNode: def init(self, minlon, maxlon, minlat, maxlat, minalt, maxalt): self.minlon, self.maxlon = minlon, maxlon self.minlat, self.maxlat = minlat, maxlat self.minalt, self.maxalt = minalt, maxalt self.children = [] self.volumetreeroot = None class VolumeTreeNode: def init(self, children=None): self.children = children if children else [] self.totalrawelements = 0 self.totalfilledbins = 0 self.avgscalar = 0.0 self.varscalar = 0.0 self.points = [] def buildembeddedadaptivevolumetree(datapoints, domainbounds, maxquaddepth=4): # Step 1: Construct Top-Level Lat/Lon Quadtree # Standard lat/lon quadtree construction covering the domain quadtreeroot = buildquadtree(domainbounds.minlon, domainbounds.maxlon, domainbounds.minlat, domainbounds.maxlat, domainbounds.minalt, domainbounds.maxalt, maxquaddepth) # Step 2 & 3: Traverse and Switch to Volume Trees for quadnode in getallnodes(quadtreeroot): lonwidth = quadnode.maxlon - quadnode.minlon latwidth = quadnode.maxlat - quadnode.minlat altheight = quadnode.maxalt - quadnode.minalt # Switch when lat/lon dims are same order of magnitude as altitude if issameordermagnitude(lonwidth, altheight) or issameordermagnitude(latwidth, altheight): # Define bin dimensions as powers of 2 Nx = 2 nextpowerof2(lonwidth) Ny = 2 nextpowerof2(latwidth) Nz = 2 nextpowerof2(altheight) # Step 4: Bin Sort Data bins = createbins(Nx, Ny, Nz) for point in datapoints: if pointinbounds(point, quadnode): xidx = int((point.lon - quadnode.minlon) / (quadnode.maxlon - quadnode.minlon) Nx) yidx = int((point.lat - quadnode.minlat) / (quadnode.maxlat - quadnode.minlat) Ny) zidx = int((point.alt - quadnode.minalt) / (quadnode.maxalt - quadnode.minalt) Nz) xidx = min(xidx, Nx - 1) yidx = min(yidx, Ny - 1) zidx = min(zidx, Nz - 1) idx = (xidx Ny + yidx) Nz + zidx bins[idx].points.append(point) # Step 5 & 6: Construct Hierarchy and Aggregate m = int(math.log2(Nx)) n = int(math.log2(Ny)) p = int(math.log2(Nz)) volumetreeroot = buildvolumehierarchy(bins, m, n, p) quadnode.volumetreeroot = volumetreeroot return quadtreeroot def buildvolumehierarchy(bins, m, n, p): # Aggregate bins into a hierarchy based on exponents # Placement of branching factors depends on data distribution currentlevel = bins for in range(p): currentlevel = aggregate8fold(currentlevel) for in range(n - p): currentlevel = aggregate4fold(currentlevel) for in range(m - n): currentlevel = aggregate2fold(currentlevel) return currentlevel[0] def aggregate8fold(bins): parents = [] for i in range(0, len(bins), 8): children = bins[i:i+8] parent = VolumeTreeNode(children) parent.totalrawelements = sum(c.totalrawelements for c in children) parent.totalfilledbins = sum(c.totalfilledbins for c in children) parent.avgscalar = weightedavg([c.avgscalar for c in children], [c.totalrawelements for c in children]) parent.varscalar = computevariance(children) parents.append(parent) return parents def aggregate4fold(bins): parents = [] for i in range(0, len(bins), 4): children = bins[i:i+4] parent = VolumeTreeNode(children) parent.totalrawelements = sum(c.totalrawelements for c in children) parent.totalfilledbins = sum(c.totalfilledbins for c in children) parent.avgscalar = weightedavg([c.avgscalar for c in children], [c.totalrawelements for c in children]) parent.varscalar = computevariance(children) parents.append(parent) return parents def aggregate2fold(bins): parents = [] for i in range(0, len(bins), 2): children = bins[i:i+2] parent = VolumeTreeNode(children) parent.totalrawelements = sum(c.totalrawelements for c in children) parent.totalfilledbins = sum(c.totalfilledbins for c in children) parent.avgscalar = weightedavg([c.avgscalar for c in children], [c.totalrawelements for c in children]) parent.varscalar = computevariance(children) parents.append(parent) return parents def weightedavg(values, weights): totalw = sum(weights) if totalw == 0: return 0.0 return sum(v w for v, w in zip(values, weights)) / totalw def computevariance(children): # Variance of scalar field values across children if not children: return 0.0 n = len(children) mean = sum(c.avgscalar for c in children) / n return sum((c.avgscalar - mean) 2 for c in children) / n def buildquadtree(minlon, maxlon, minlat, maxlat, minalt, maxalt, depth): node = QuadTreeNode(minlon, maxlon, minlat, maxlat, minalt, maxalt) if depth == 0: return node midlon, midlat, midalt = (minlon+maxlon)/2, (minlat+maxlat)/2, (minalt+maxalt)/2 for i in range(4): node.children.append(buildquadtree( minlon if i < 2 else midlon, maxlon if i < 2 else maxlon, minlat if i % 2 == 0 else midlat, maxlat if i % 2 == 0 else maxlat, minalt, maxalt, depth - 1)) return node def getallnodes(root): nodes = [root] for node in nodes: nodes.extend(node.children) return nodes def issameordermagnitude(a, b): return abs(math.log10(a) - math.log10(b)) <= 1.0 def nextpowerof2(val): return int(math.ceil(math.log2(val))) if val > 0 else 0 def createbins(Nx, Ny, Nz): return [VolumeTreeNode() for in range(Nx Ny Nz)] def pointinbounds(point, node): return node.minlon <= point.lon <= node.maxlon and \ node.minlat <= point.lat <= node.maxlat and \ node.minalt <= point.alt <= node.maxalt Parameters: Nx, Ny, Nz: Bin dimensions in longitude, latitude, and altitude directions. Must be powers of 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Curvature: Bins are not rectilinear in Cartesian space. The method ignores this effect during volume rendering because Earth's curvature is small for rendered bins, and lat/lon quadcells are nearly rectilinear except at high latitudes. Dynamic Data: The bin structure and volume hierarchy are static in space. The method can be applied to moving volumetric elements only if the range of local spatial densities and the volume of the data do not change much over time. Time Complexity: The bin sort of non-uniform data points is O(n), where n is the number of points. Memory Complexity: The hierarchy provides significant savings in memory space and retrieval cost since only data element coordinates for viewable bins at the appropriate LOD are retrieved. Strengths: Efficiently supports different data types and spatial magnitudes. The bin sort is fast, and the hierarchy enables quick aggregation for detail management and view frustum culling. Limitations: The structure is static in space, limiting applicability to highly dynamic data distributions. The approximation of ignoring Earth's curvature may introduce errors at high latitudes or for very high-resolution rendering of small bins. This method was presented by Jang, Ribarsky, Shaw, and Faust in 2002 as part of their work on View-Dependent Multiresolution Splatting. It particularizes to earth-based data, specifically atmospheric data and whole earth environments, where the atmosphere is a thin layer relative to the Earth's ellipsoid. The approach builds on the need for automatic generation of volume tree structures in environments with different data organizations and spatial magnitudes. name: TopoGS
head: Topology-Aware Anchor Feature Aggregation for Large-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: TopoGS is a topology-aware anchor feature aggregation framework designed to address the feature isolation problem in octree-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations. It solves the issue where anchor features at different octree levels are optimized in isolation, leading to high cross-level similarity and poor information flow. Unlike standard uniform mean pooling which treats all adjacent-level anchors equally, TopoGS distinguishes anchors participating in valid parent/child containment relations from isolated anchors, establishing bidirectional cross-level gradient pathways. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Octree-based Splatting by explicitly modeling the octree's topological structure during feature aggregation rather than relying solely on spatial proximity or error metrics for primitive selection. TopoGS operates as a lightweight module situated between the backbone and the decoder of an octree-anchor 3DGS pipeline, leaving the octree structure and rasterization pipeline untouched. It consists of two complementary components: Hierarchical Anchor Coupling (HAC) and Structure-Aware Containment Aggregation (SACA). Input: Anchor features for all levels of the octree hierarchy. Specifically, for a target level L, it requires the mean features of level L, its adjacent parent level L-1, and its adjacent child level L+1. It also requires the spatial coordinates of anchors to determine containment relations. Output: Refined anchor features that incorporate bidirectional cross-level context and structure-aware weighting. Anchor Features: A tensor containing the learned feature vector for each Gaussian anchor. Octree Hierarchy: Implicitly defined by the parent-child relationships of the octree nodes. Hash Map: Used in SACA to map anchor coordinates to their containment relations efficiently. HAC establishes bidirectional cross-level gradient pathways by fusing context from adjacent levels. 1. Context Triplet Construction: For a target octree level L, organize the mean features of the level itself (FL), its adjacent parent level (F{L-1}), and its adjacent child level (F{L+1}) into a context triplet. 2. Feature Fusion: Fuse the context triplet through a shared lightweight residual MLP (\mathcal{M}) to obtain a level-wise feature increment \Delta FL. \Delta FL = \mathcal{M}(F{L-1}, FL, F{L+1}) Note: The specific architecture of \mathcal{M} is described as a "lightweight residual MLP" but exact layer counts or hidden units are not provided in the sources. 3. Residual Injection: Inject the level-wise feature increment residually into every anchor at the target level L. If fi is the original feature of an anchor i at level L, the updated feature f'i is: f'i = fi + \Delta FL SACA modulates aggregation through octree containment, distinguishing valid parent/child relations from isolated anchors. 1. Hash Lookup: For each query anchor, perform a logarithmic-time hash lookup to identify anchors participating in cross-level containment relations. The overall cost for constructing the containment mask is O(N \log N), where N is the number of anchors. 2. Soft Weighting: Apply a continuous soft-weighting scheme that interpolates between strict containment and uniform pooling. This accommodates varying topological sparsity across scenes and levels. Let wi be the weight for anchor i. The exact mathematical formulation of the soft-weighting scheme is not provided in the sources. The weights are applied to aggregate features from parent and child anchors based on their containment status. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def topogsaggregate(anchors, levelanchorsmap, containmenthash, mlp): """ Performs TopoGS feature aggregation. Args: anchors: List of anchor objects, each with attributes: feature: Tensor (anchor feature vector) position: Vector3 (spatial position) id: int (unique identifier) levelanchorsmap: Dict mapping level index to list of anchors at that level. containmenthash: Dict mapping anchor id to list of ids of anchors in valid containment relations. mlp: Lightweight residual MLP module. Returns: Updated list of anchors with refined features. """ # 1. Hierarchical Anchor Coupling (HAC) for levelidx, levelanchors in levelanchorsmap.items(): # Compute mean features for current level meancurrent = sum(a.feature for a in levelanchors) / len(levelanchors) # Compute mean features for parent level parentanchors = levelanchorsmap.get(levelidx - 1, []) meanparent = sum(a.feature for a in parentanchors) / len(parentanchors) if parentanchors else None # Compute mean features for child level childanchors = levelanchorsmap.get(levelidx + 1, []) meanchild = sum(a.feature for a in childanchors) / len(childanchors) if childanchors else None # Context triplet construction and fusion contexttriplet = (meanparent, meancurrent, meanchild) levelincrement = mlp(contexttriplet) # Residual injection into every anchor at target level for anchor in levelanchors: anchor.feature = anchor.feature + levelincrement # 2. Structure-Aware Containment Aggregation (SACA) # Containment mask construction is O(N log N) via hash lookup # Soft weighting scheme interpolates between strict containment and uniform pooling # Exact weighting formula and aggregation update rule are not provided in the sources. for anchor in anchors: neighbors = containmenthash.get(anchor.id, []) if not neighbors: continue # Compute soft weights (exact scheme not specified in sources) weights = [1.0 / len(neighbors)] len(neighbors) # Aggregate features from neighbors aggregated = sum(w neighbor.feature for w, neighbor in zip(weights, neighbors)) # Update anchor feature (exact combination rule not specified in sources) anchor.feature = anchor.feature + aggregated return anchors HAC MLP: A lightweight residual MLP. The specific architecture (layers, hidden units) is not detailed in the sources. Soft Weighting Scheme: A continuous scheme interpolating between strict containment and uniform pooling. The exact interpolation parameter or function is not provided. Sparse Topology: In regions with varying topological sparsity, the soft weighting scheme must adapt to avoid over-aggregating isolated anchors. Boundary Conditions: Levels at the root or leaf of the octree may lack parent or child levels, respectively. The pseudocode handles this by checking for empty neighbor lists. Precision: The hash lookup for containment relations must be robust to floating-point precision issues in anchor positions. A module that establishes bidirectional cross-level gradient pathways through per-level context triplets fused by a lightweight residual MLP. Choose this when you need to address feature isolation between adjacent octree levels without altering the topology. See TopoGS. A module that modulates aggregation through octree containment, distinguishing anchors participating in valid parent/child relations from isolated anchors via hash-based matching and applying a soft weighting scheme. Choose this when you need to handle varying topological sparsity across scenes and levels. See TopoGS. Time Complexity: The SACA mask construction complexity is O(N \log N), where N is the number of anchors. The HAC module operates at negligible cost. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On aerial scenes (Mill19), TopoGS achieves an average PSNR gain of +2.13 dB over the strongest reported PSNR baseline. On ground-level scenes (UrbanScene3D), TopoGS achieves an average PSNR gain of +1.78 dB over the strongest reported PSNR baseline. On synthetic-cartographic scenes (WHU), TopoGS achieves an average PSNR gain of +0.29 dB over the strongest reported PSNR baseline. On Tanks & Temples-Train, TopoGS improves PSNR by +1.82 dB compared to Geo-GS. On Mill19-Building, TopoGS improves PSNR by +2.67 dB compared to CityGS-X. TopoGS reduces the off-diagonal mean cosine similarity of anchor features across levels from 0.866 to 0.108. Strengths: Renders faster and uses lower memory compared to baselines. Compatible with Octree-GS and Proxy-GS backbones. Limitations: Requires hash-based lookup for containment relations, which may add overhead in highly dynamic scenes. When to use: When using octree-based 3DGS representations for large-scale scenes and experiencing feature isolation or redundancy across levels. When not to use: When the octree structure is not used or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of hash lookups is prohibitive. TopoGS was proposed in the paper "TopoGS: Topology-Aware Anchor Feature Aggregation for Large-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the open question of how to respect the octree's topological structure in 3DGS representations. The method was evaluated on ten scenes across five public benchmarks: Mill19, UrbanScene3D, Tanks & Temples, MatrixCity, and WHU. The code is available at https://github.com/WZ-CS/TopoGS. TopoGS: Topology-Aware Anchor Feature Aggregation for Large-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27868, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: LinearMask-GS
head: Linear increment activation, LinearMask
body: LinearMask-GS is a learned-mask pruning framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the Gumbel-Sigmoid activation with a linear increment activation to keep mask values in a mid-confidence regime, producing a stable unimodal distribution for reliable importance ranking. It solves the instability of prior learned-mask methods where mask values saturate to 0 or 1 before the importance ranking stabilizes, resulting in a bimodal distribution where the ranking reflects early optimization artifacts rather than true importance. Unlike its siblings which may use summation-based aggregation or different activation functions, LinearMask-GS combines max-pooling importance scoring with a linear activation to mitigate view-count inflation and ensure deterministic pruning decisions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}{i=1}^N optimized via a standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline (e.g., 3DGS, 2DGS, DropGaussian, OctreeGS, or FastGS) for an initial geometric warm-up phase. Output: A pruned set of K = \rho N Gaussians, where \rho is the minimum-survival ratio, and the optimized scene parameters for these remaining primitives. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive i: Contains mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai (decomposed into rotation Ri and scaling Si), opacity logit oi, and spherical harmonic coefficients ci. Learnable Mask Parameter mi: A scalar parameter for each Gaussian, initialized to 1. Importance Score Si: A scalar value computed per Gaussian using max-pooling over training views. Soft Mask Value \psii: A scalar in [0, 1] computed as \psii = f{LI}(mi \cdot Si; \tau). Parameters: \tau: Slope hyperparameter for the linear activation. Default value is 0.1. Grid search values include \{0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5\}. \rho: Minimum-survival ratio. Default value is 0.30. \lambdam: Mask sparsity loss weight. Value is 5 \times 10^{-4}. \lambdaD: Photometric loss weight. Value is 0.2. Learning rate for mi: 5 \times 10^{-2} using AdamW optimizer. Numbered Steps: 1. Geometric Warm-up: Run the standard Gaussian Splatting optimization pipeline for 19,500 iterations to ensure geometric convergence. 2. Compute Importance Scores: For each Gaussian i, compute the max-pooled importance score Si over all training views k \in \{1, \dots, K\} and pixels p: Si = \max{k} \max{p} w{k,p}^i where w{k,p}^i is the contribution weight of Gaussian i to pixel p in view k. Recompute Si every 20 iterations during the mask training phase. 3. Initialize Mask Parameters: Initialize learnable scalar parameters mi = 1 for all i=1, \dots, N. 4. Mask Training (Iterations 19,500–20,000): a. Compute the soft mask value for each Gaussian: \psii = f{LI}(mi \cdot Si; \tau) = \text{clip}(\tau \cdot (mi \cdot Si - 0.5) + 0.5, 0, 1) where f{LI} is the linear increment activation. b. Modulate the opacity of each Gaussian during rendering: \tilde{\alpha}{i,k,p} = \psii \cdot \alpha{i,k,p} where \alpha{i,k,p} is the original opacity. c. Compute the total training loss: L{total} = (1 - \lambdaD) L1 + \lambdaD (1 - \text{SSIM}) + \lambdam L{mask} where L1 is the pixel-wise L1 loss, SSIM is structural similarity, and L{mask} is the sparsity term. d. Compute the mask sparsity loss: L{mask} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} |mi| This encourages mi to shrink, reducing \psii. e. Update scene parameters and mask parameters \{mi\} using their respective optimizers. 5. Hard Pruning (Iteration 20,000): a. Rank all N Gaussians by their final soft mask values \psii in descending order. b. Select the top-\rho N Gaussians to retain: K = \text{top-}\rho N \text{ Gaussians ranked by } \psii c. Permanently prune the remaining N - K Gaussians. 6. Fine-tuning: Fine-tune the remaining K primitives without the mask loss term for the remainder of the training (up to 30,000 iterations total). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.optim as optim def linearincrementactivation(x, tau): """Linear increment activation: clip(tau (x - 0.5) + 0.5, 0, 1)""" return torch.clamp(tau (x - 0.5) + 0.5, min=0.0, max=1.0) def computemaxpoolimportance(gaussians, views): """Compute max-pooled importance score Si for each Gaussian over all views.""" N = len(gaussians) S = torch.zeros(N, device=gaussians[0].position.device) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): maxval = -float('inf') for view in views: # Project Gaussian to view and compute per-pixel contribution weights weights = projectgaussiantoview(g, view) viewmax = torch.max(weights) if viewmax > maxval: maxval = viewmax S[i] = maxval return S def projectgaussiantoview(gaussian, view): """Standard 3DGS rasterization: projects 3D Gaussian to 2D, computes coverage weights per pixel.""" # Returns a 1D tensor of weights for all pixels in the view return torch.rand(view.resolution[0] view.resolution[1]) def renderscene(gaussians, views, maskvalues=None): """Front-to-back alpha compositing: C = sumi ci alphai prod{j<i} (1 - alphaj).""" # Returns rendered image tensor return torch.zeros(views[0].height, views[0].width, 3) def gettargetimage(views): """Returns ground-truth image tensor for the current view.""" return torch.zeros(views[0].height, views[0].width, 3) def computel1loss(rendered, target): """Pixel-wise L1 loss.""" return torch.mean(torch.abs(rendered - target)) def computessimloss(rendered, target): """Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) computed via sliding window correlation. Returns 1 - SSIM.""" return 1.0 - torchvision.ops.ssim(rendered.unsqueeze(0), target.unsqueeze(0), windowsize=11, sizeaverage=True) def trainlinearmaskgs(gaussians, views, totaliterations=30000, warmupiterations=19500, maskiterations=500, rho=0.30, tau=0.1, lambdam=5e-4, lambdaD=0.2): N = len(gaussians) m = torch.ones(N, requiresgrad=True, device=gaussians[0].position.device) sceneoptimizer = optim.AdamW(gaussians.parameters(), lr=1.6e-4) maskoptimizer = optim.AdamW([m], lr=5e-2) # Step 1: Geometric Warm-up for iteration in range(warmupiterations): rendered = renderscene(gaussians, views) target = gettargetimage(views) loss = (1 - lambdaD) computel1loss(rendered, target) + lambdaD (1.0 - computessimloss(rendered, target)) sceneoptimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() sceneoptimizer.step() # Step 2: Mask Training importanceupdatefreq = 20 S = computemaxpoolimportance(gaussians, views) for iteration in range(warmupiterations, warmupiterations + maskiterations): if (iteration - warmupiterations) % importanceupdatefreq == 0: S = computemaxpoolimportance(gaussians, views) inputtoactivation = m S psi = linearincrementactivation(inputtoactivation, tau) rendered = renderscene(gaussians, views, maskvalues=psi) target = gettargetimage(views) photometricloss = (1 - lambdaD) computel1loss(rendered, target) + lambdaD (1.0 - computessimloss(rendered, target)) maskloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(m)) totalloss = photometricloss + lambdam maskloss sceneoptimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward(retaingraph=True) sceneoptimizer.step() maskoptimizer.zerograd() maskoptimizer.step() # Step 3: Hard Pruning, indices = torch.sort(psi, descending=True) K = int(rho N) keepindices = indices[:K] prunedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in keepindices] # Step 4: Fine-tuning for iteration in range(warmupiterations + maskiterations, totaliterations): rendered = renderscene(prunedgaussians, views) target = gettargetimage(views) loss = (1 - lambdaD) computel1loss(rendered, target) + lambdaD (1.0 - computessimloss(rendered, target)) sceneoptimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() sceneoptimizer.step() return prunedgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Saturation: Using Gumbel-Sigmoid activation causes mask values to saturate to 0 or 1 before importance ranking stabilizes, resulting in a bimodal distribution where the ranking reflects early optimization artifacts rather than true importance. View-Count Inflation: Summation-based aggregation introduces view-count inflation that dominates the activation choice and obscures the stability benefit of the linear mask. Max-pooling is used to mitigate this. Survival Ratio: Setting \rho too low (e.g., 0.20) removes too many primitives, degrading quality (-0.28 dB). Setting \rho too high (e.g., 0.40) retains 34% more Gaussians for only +0.03 dB gain. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Reduces Gaussian count significantly. On Mip-NeRF 360, it reduces Gaussian count from 3.36M (vanilla 3DGS) to 0.94M (3.6x reduction). For outdoor scenes, it yields a 1.6x reduction (from 2.18M to 1.36M Gaussians). Time: On the 3DGS backbone, LinearMask-GS is 2.12 minutes faster than its learned-mask parent LP-3DGS while reaching a more compact final model. On the FastGS backbone, LinearMask-GS⋆ reduces training time (1.93 to 1.81 minutes). Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF 360 (3DGS backbone): Reduces Gaussian count from 3.36M to 0.94M (3.6x reduction) while improving PSNR from 27.21 to 27.70 dB. Mip-NeRF 360 (vs LP-3DGS): Surpasses LP-3DGS by 0.23 dB PSNR and 0.0135 SSIM with 1.6x fewer Gaussians. Outdoor Scenes: Yields a 1.6x reduction (from 2.18M to 1.36M Gaussians) with PSNR gain of +0.38 dB, SSIM gain of +0.025, and LPIPS reduction of -0.029. 2DGS Backbone: Reduces count from 1.06M to 0.36M (2.9x), PSNR +0.22 dB, SSIM +0.009, LPIPS +0.008. DropGaussian Backbone: Improves PSNR by +0.31 to +0.52 dB over the unpruned backbone, while retaining 41% fewer primitives than the Gumbel variant. Octree-GS Backbone: Anchors reduced from 1.09M to 0.38M (2.9x), PSNR +0.12 dB. FastGS Backbone: 0.38M Gaussians, PSNR 27.69 dB, SSIM 0.8029, LPIPS 0.2227, Storage 94.89 MB, Training time 1.81 min. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Stable unimodal mask distribution, deterministic ranking, high compression ratios with minimal quality loss, compatible with various backbones (3DGS, 2DGS, DropGaussian, OctreeGS, FastGS) without architectural modifications. Limitations: The slope \tau and ratio \rho are tuned on a held-out set and fixed across scenes. The brief mask window can leave specular or transparent regions under-discriminated. The global \rho sets an overall rather than per-region budget. The method inherits the static-scene assumption of its backbones. LinearMask-GS was proposed by Ryu and Lee. It addresses the limitations of learned-mask pruning methods like LP-3DGS, which use Gumbel-Sigmoid activation. The authors identified that the steep slope of Gumbel-Sigmoid drives mask values to the extremes within the short mask-training window, before the importance ranking has stabilized, producing a sharply bimodal distribution from which that ranking can no longer be reliably recovered. LinearMask-GS replaces this with a linear increment activation to keep mask values in a mid-confidence regime, producing a stable, unimodal mask distribution whose ranking tracks importance. It is used for compact 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly for resource-constrained devices where storage overhead is a concern. LinearMask-GS: Stable-Mask Importance Pruning for Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10095, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 2^n-Tree Hierarchical Representation
head: 2^n-tree splatting, Generalized object space splatting, Hierarchical Multiresolution Splatting, Multiresolution Splatting
body: The 2^n-tree hierarchical representation is a data structure and rendering algorithm designed for the efficient visualization of high-dimensional (n-dimensional) datasets, such as hyper-volumes. It generalizes the octree-based acceleration of 3D splatting to arbitrary dimensions by organizing data into a hierarchy where groups of 2^n adjacent voxels are merged. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly addressing the storage and computational scaling challenges of n > 3 dimensions, leveraging the fact that the relative storage overhead of the full hierarchy decreases exponentially as the dimension n increases. Inputs: An n-dimensional scalar field sampled on a regular grid with k samples per dimension, resulting in M = k^n total samples. A user-specified error bound \epsilon. Outputs: A set of splat primitives rendered to the image, selected based on the error bound. Data Structures: The hierarchy is stored as a complete array representing the full 2^n-tree. Node: Represents a group of 2^n adjacent cells from the previous level. Attributes: Each node stores the averaged function value of its children and a precomputed error bound. Layout: The hierarchy is built bottom-up. Level 0 contains the original k^n voxels. Level i contains nodes formed by merging 2^n nodes from Level i-1. The number of nodes at level i is \frac{k^n}{(2^n)^i}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Build Hierarchy: Start with the leaf level (Level 0) containing the raw grid data. For each level i from 1 to h (where k=2^h): Group the nodes from Level i-1 into sets of 2^n adjacent nodes. Compute the parent node's value as the average of the 2^n children's values. Compute the error bound for the parent node based on the variance or difference between children and the average. Store the parent node in the array structure for Level i. 2. Display Stage (Traversal): Perform a Depth First Traversal (DFT) starting from the coarsest level (Level h, the root). For each node visited: Check if the node's error bound is less than or equal to the user-specified error bound \epsilon. If E{node} \le \epsilon: Select this node as a leaf. Render the node as a single generalized splat primitive using texture-mapped graphics hardware acceleration. Do not recurse to its children. If E{node} > \epsilon: Recursively visit the 2^n children of this node. Formulas: Total Samples: For a grid with k samples per direction in n dimensions, total samples M = k^n. Hierarchy Storage: Let m = k = 2^h. The total storage M^ for the complete 2^n-tree is: M^ = \sum{i=0}^h \frac{(2^h)^n}{(2^n)^i} = \sum{i=0}^h (2^n)^{h-i} = \sum{j=0}^h (2^n)^j Relative Storage Overhead: \frac{M^ - M}{M} < \frac{1}{(2^n - 1)} Parameters: Dimension n: The dimension of the embedding space. Typical values for visualization are n \ge 4. Error Bound \epsilon: A threshold controlling the trade-off between accuracy and speed. Set by the user via a UI slider. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grid Size: The derivation assumes m = 2^h for some integer h. If the grid dimensions are not powers of 2, padding or truncation may be required. High Dimensionality: While storage overhead decreases with n, the number of children 2^n grows exponentially. For very large n, the branching factor becomes large, potentially impacting traversal efficiency despite the storage benefits. Error Metric: The specific formula for the error bound is not detailed in the sources, only that it is precomputed and used for comparison. Pseudocode: Unverified code. # Actually, grouping 2^n adjacent cells reduces count by 2^n total. # If we group in a hyper-cube manner, side length reduces by 2^(i-1)? # The source says: "number of cells is reduced at each level by a factor of 2^n" # So if level i-1 has N cells, level i has N / 2^n cells. # Let's assume a regular grid structure where we merge 2^n neighbors. # For simplicity, assume k is a power of 2 and we merge 2x2x...x2 blocks. newshape = tuple(s // 2 for s in currentdata.shape) newdata = np.zeros(newshape) # Compute averages and errors # This requires iterating over the grid and grouping 2^n neighbors # For n dimensions, we iterate over the new shape and aggregate 2^n values # Placeholder for aggregation logic as specific implementation details # of the error metric and averaging kernel are not fully specified in sources. # Standard averaging: sum of 2^n children / 2^n. for indices in np.ndindex(newshape): # Generate indices of the 2^n children in currentdata childrenindices = generatechildrenindices(indices, currentdata.shape) childrenvalues = currentdata[childrenindices] avgvalue = np.mean(childrenvalues) error = computeerror(childrenvalues, avgvalue) # Placeholder for error metric newdata[indices] = (avgvalue, error) levels.append(newdata) currentdata = newdata return levels def render(levels, n, epsilon): """ Renders the 2^n-tree using depth-first traversal. levels: list of arrays, levels[i] is the data at depth i n: dimension epsilon: user-specified error bound """ h = len(levels) - 1 # Start from the root (coarsest level) rendernode(levels, h, (0,) n, epsilon) def rendernode(levels, levelidx, coords, epsilon): """ Recursively render a node. """ if levelidx == 0: # Leaf node (original voxel) value, error = levels[0][coords] # Render splat for this voxel drawsplat(coords, value) return value, error = levels[levelidx][coords] if error <= epsilon: # Select this node as a leaf drawsplat(coords, value) else: # Recurse to children # Children are at levelidx - 1 # There are 2^n children childrencoords = getchildrencoords(coords, levels[levelidx-1].shape) for childcoord in childrencoords: rendernode(levels, levelidx - 1, childcoord, epsilon) def generatechildrenindices(parentcoords, currentshape): """ Returns the indices of the 2^n children in the current level data that correspond to the parent node at parentcoords in the next level. """ # Similar logic to generatechildrenindices but for traversal children = [] for i in range(2n): childidx = integertondindex(i, n) scaledidx = tuple(c 2 + d for c, d in zip(parentcoords, childidx)) children.append(scaledidx) return children The 3D special case (n=3) of this method, using an octree structure. It is chosen when the data is strictly 3D and standard octree implementations are preferred. Link Uses Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) grids rather than a fixed 2^n-tree. It is chosen when the data has irregular refinement patterns that do not align with a regular hyper-cube hierarchy. It is chosen for 3D Gaussian Splatting applications where topological consistency is important. Link A method for Gaussian Splatting using linear masks. It is chosen for efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. The rendering phase depends on the error bound \epsilon; in the worst case (all leaves selected), it is O(M), but typically much faster due to culling. Memory Complexity: The storage overhead is bounded by \frac{1}{2^n - 1} relative to the raw data size. This overhead decreases exponentially as n increases, making the method highly memory-efficient for high-dimensional data compared to storing the full grid or other hierarchical structures. Measured Performance: For a 6-dimensional grid with 64 samples per direction (64^6 \approx 68 billion samples), the method enables efficient visualization that would otherwise be infeasible. Strengths: Scalability to high dimensions (n > 3). Low storage overhead for high n. User-controlled trade-off between accuracy and speed via \epsilon. Limitations: Requires regular grid data. Large branching factor (2^n) for high n may complicate traversal implementation. Not suitable for irregular or unstructured data without preprocessing. When to Use: When visualizing high-dimensional datasets (e.g., 4D, 6D) on regular grids where memory efficiency and interactive performance are critical. When Not to Use: For irregular data, or when n is very small (e.g., n=2) where the overhead of the hierarchy might not be justified compared to simpler methods. The method was introduced by Laur and Hanrahan, who accelerated 3D splatting by adopting an octree hierarchical representation. This work generalized that approach to arbitrary n dimensions, showing how the relative storage overhead of the full 2^n-tree hierarchy decreases as the dimension of the embedding space increases. It is used in hyper-volume visualization systems to handle large n-dimensional datasets, such as those arising in scientific computing and configuration space analysis. name: Hierarchical Point Cloud Rendering
head: out-of-core hierarchical traversal, view-dependent LOD selection
body: Hierarchical Point Cloud Rendering efficiently displays massive point clouds by organizing data into a spatial hierarchy (typically a uniform grid or octree) and dynamically selecting the Level of Detail (LOD) for each cell based on the viewer's distance. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering hundreds of millions of points by allowing aggressive pruning in distant or uniform regions while maintaining high fidelity in the foreground. It distinguishes itself from Multi Resolution Alpha Blending, Octree-based Hierarchy, and Multi-Resolution and Level of Detail (Pyramid, LOD, Downsampling) by using distance-driven LOD selection on a uniform grid rather than error metrics or pyramid downsampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A massive point cloud dataset (e.g., 150 million points) stored out-of-core, organized into a hierarchical structure (uniform grid cells or octree nodes). Output: A rendered image composed of textured splats, where each splat represents a subset of points from a selected LOD level of a spatial cell. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Index: A tree structure (uniform grid or octree) held in memory. Each node represents a spatial region. 2. LOD Levels: For each cell/node, multiple simplified versions of the point data are pre-computed. In the uniform grid approach, points are decimated by a factor of 10 for each decreasing LOD level. 3. Point Representation: Points are rendered as textured splats. The texture includes an alpha channel to preserve the original silhouette, allowing larger splats to be trimmed effectively. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Generate a discretization of the scene using a uniform grid (or octree). Store the bulk of the point data out-of-core (on disk or network). For each cell, produce multiple simplified point sets by decimating the original points. A common strategy is reducing the point count by a factor of 10 for each subsequent LOD level. Keep the coarser LOD levels in main memory for fast access, while the finest level (original points) may remain out-of-core. Compute or store scaling factors for the textured splats at each LOD level to ensure visual consistency. 2. Rendering Loop (Per Frame): Frustum Culling: Identify cells overlapping the view frustum. Front-to-Back Traversal: Traverse the selected cells in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. This order enables early depth culling and correct alpha blending. LOD Selection: For each cell, calculate the distance d from the cell center to the viewpoint. Dynamically select the most appropriate LOD level based on d. Closer cells use higher LODs (more points); distant cells use lower LODs (fewer points). Splat Rendering: For each selected cell at its chosen LOD, render the points as textured splats. The scaling factor for the splat is adjusted according to the LOD level to maintain visual density. Refinement (Optional): If the viewpoint is static for a duration (e.g., a few seconds), asynchronously load the finest LOD (original points) for visible cells from disk and update the display. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def distance(a, b): """Euclidean distance between two 3D points.""" return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) 2 for x, y in zip(a, b))) def project(pointpos, cameraviewproj): """Standard perspective projection to normalized device coordinates.""" vec = [pointpos[0], pointpos[1], pointpos[2], 1.0] res = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): res[i] += cameraviewproj[i][j] vec[j] if res[3] <= 0.0: return None return (res[0] / res[3], res[1] / res[3], res[2] / res[3]) def selectlodbydistance(dist, lodthresholds): """Selects LOD index based on distance thresholds. lodthresholds is sorted ascending.""" for i, threshold in enumerate(lodthresholds): if dist <= threshold: return i return len(lodthresholds) - 1 def isviewpointstatic(camerahistory, threshold=0.001, frames=150): """Returns True if camera movement delta is below threshold for N frames.""" if len(camerahistory) < frames: return False recent = camerahistory[-frames:] return all(math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a,b in zip(recent[i], recent[i+1]))) < threshold for i in range(len(recent)-1)) def renderhierarchicalpointcloud(viewpoint, frustum, hierarchy, lodcache, diskloader, camerahistory, cameraviewproj): """ viewpoint: Camera position (3D vector) frustum: View frustum object with overlap test method hierarchy: List of cells/nodes, each containing: center: 3D vector lodlevels: List of point sets [L0, L1,...] where L0 is finest scalingfactors: List of float scalars for each LOD lodthresholds: List of distance thresholds for LOD selection boundingbox: AABB for frustum culling lodcache: Dictionary mapping cellid -> currentlodindex diskloader: Function to load finest LOD points from disk for a cellid camerahistory: List of recent camera positions cameraviewproj: 4x4 view-projection matrix """ # 1. Identify visible cells visiblecells = [cell for cell in hierarchy if frustum.overlaps(cell.boundingbox)] # 2. Sort front-to-back based on distance to viewpoint visiblecells.sort(key=lambda c: distance(c.center, viewpoint)) # 3. Traverse and render for cell in visiblecells: # Calculate distance for LOD selection dist = distance(cell.center, viewpoint) # Select LOD index based on distance lodindex = selectlodbydistance(dist, cell.lodthresholds) # Retrieve points for this LOD # LOD levels are pre-decimated by factor of 10 points = cell.lodlevels[lodindex] scale = cell.scalingfactors[lodindex] # Render textured splats for point in points: # Project point to screen screenpos = project(point.position, cameraviewproj) if screenpos is not None: # Rasterize billboard at screenpos with scale, applying texture and alpha mask # Implementation depends on graphics API; standard splat draw call pass # 4. Background refinement (if static) if isviewpointstatic(camerahistory): for cell in visiblecells: # Load finest LOD from disk if not in cache if cell.id not in lodcache or lodcache[cell.id] != 0: finestpoints = diskloader.load(cell.id, lodlevel=0) cell.lodlevels[0] = finestpoints lodcache[cell.id] = 0 Parameters and Typical Values: Decimation Factor: 10 points per LOD level reduction. Performance: On an Intel Core i7-4790K and GeForce GTX 970, rendering ~150 million points achieved 600 fps for far-away views and 300-600 fps for closer views. Pruning Aggressiveness: Quality remains good even with 1 point out of 100 retained in areas with uniform sampling density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static View Latency: Loading the finest LOD from disk can take several seconds, causing a delay in high-fidelity display. Visual Consistency: Scaling factors for splats must be manually tuned per LOD level to avoid visual artifacts or density mismatches. Uniform Density Assumption: Aggressive pruning works best in areas with uniform sampling density; non-uniform areas may require finer LOD granularity. A variant where the dataset exceeds RAM capacity. The octree index is kept in RAM, while point data is streamed from disk or network on demand using a paging system. Nodes are loaded asynchronously to prevent render thread blocking, and evicted when they drift out of view. It relies on a streamable layout (e.g., COPC, Potree) that allows fetching a single node with a single byte-range HTTP request. Prefetching based on camera trajectory is critical to avoid pop-in latency. Time Complexity: Rendering time scales with the number of visible splats after frustum culling and LOD selection. Memory Complexity: Main memory usage is dominated by the in-memory LOD levels (coarser levels) and the hierarchy index. Out-of-core variants use a paging system to stream nodes from disk or network, evicting those that drift out of view. Performance: High frame rates (300-600 fps) are achievable for massive datasets (150M points) on mid-range hardware. Strengths: Handles datasets far larger than RAM; maintains visual quality in foreground; efficient culling. Limitations: Requires pre-processing to generate LODs; static view refinement has latency; scaling factors may need manual tuning. When to Use: Massive point clouds (hundreds of millions of points) where interactive frame rates are required. When Not to Use: Small datasets where overhead of hierarchy management is unjustified; scenes with highly non-uniform density requiring complex error metrics not covered by distance-based LOD. The method was presented in the paper "View-dependent Hierarchical Rendering of Massive Point Clouds through Textured Splats" (2019). It extends standard textured splatting by integrating a uniform grid hierarchy and distance-based LOD selection. The out-of-core streaming variant is discussed in later educational materials on point cloud level of detail, referencing formats like Potree and COPC.
