name: Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging
head: Compact FF-3DGS, FF-GS, Saliency-Guided Superpixel Merging, Superpixel-based merging
body: Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging is a post-processing pipeline for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF-3DGS) that compresses per-pixel Gaussian predictions into a compact, hierarchical representation by grouping them into superpixels and merging them via learned encoders and decoders. It solves the problem of excessive primitive counts and memory usage in feed-forward novel view synthesis by reducing redundancy both within single views (via superpixel merging) and across multiple views (via cross-view matching), while preserving high-fidelity reconstruction quality. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Multi Resolution Alpha Blending or Octree-based Hierarchy by using a learned, content-adaptive segmentation (BASS with Shi-Tomasi seeding) and a neural encoder-decoder architecture rather than heuristic spatial partitioning or fixed-resolution grids. The method operates on per-pixel 3D Gaussians predicted by a frozen feed-forward backbone (e.g., DA3, AnySplat, DepthSplat) from N input views. The pipeline consists of segmentation, encoding, cross-view matching, merging, refinement, and decoding. Input: N input images \{Iv\}{v=1}^N, camera parameters (intrinsics/extrinsics) if using a posed backbone, and the predicted per-pixel Gaussian set G{FF} from a frozen backbone M{FF}. Each Gaussian Gi is parameterized by mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, quaternion rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4, scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \hat{c}{k,i} for view-dependent color. Output: A compressed set of Feature Gaussians \tilde{G}, which can be decoded into K output Gaussians per Feature Gaussian for rendering. Feature Gaussian (\tilde{G}j): A compressed primitive representing a group of original Gaussians. It contains: Spatial parameters: \tilde{\mu}j \in \mathbb{R}^3, \tilde{q}j \in \mathbb{R}^4, \tilde{s}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 (identical format to standard Gaussians). Appearance: Base color \tilde{c}j (diffuse color, no SH coefficients) and a latent feature vector \tilde{z}j \in \mathbb{R}^d. Opacity: \tilde{\alpha}j. Superpixel Group (Sj): A set of original Gaussians \{Gi\} assigned to a single superpixel segment. 1. Per-Pixel Gaussian Prediction: Pass input views through the frozen feed-forward backbone M{FF} to obtain the initial set of per-pixel Gaussians G{FF}. 2. Saliency-Guided Superpixel Segmentation: a. Compute the Shi-Tomasi corner response \lambdav at each pixel, defined as the minimum eigenvalue of the image structure tensor. b. Sample seeds densely where \lambdav is high and sparsely elsewhere. c. Run the BASS segmentation algorithm using these seeds to partition the image into superpixels, producing a partition map Mv that assigns each pixel (and its Gaussian) to a group Sj. 3. Feature Gaussian Encoding (Within-View Compression): For each superpixel group Sj: a. Project per-Gaussian attributes into tokens using an MLP. b. Refine tokens using a stack of Set Attention Blocks (SABs) for pairwise interactions. c. Aggregate the set into a single output using Pooling-by-Multihead-Attention (PMA) with a learnable query Q. d. Produce the latent feature \tilde{z}j via a final MLP. e. Compute \tilde{\mu}j as the opacity-weighted centroid of Sj plus a learned position offset to compensate for outliers. f. Compute \tilde{c}j as the opacity-weighted average of the group members' diffuse color. g. Note: The encoder does not predict \tilde{s}j or \tilde{q}j; these are produced by the decoder to prevent geometry collapse. 4. Cross-View Matching: a. For each Feature Gaussian \tilde{G}j, retrieve k nearest neighbors via 3D kNN on positions \tilde{\mu}, excluding candidates from the same input view. b. Apply a match gate: a candidate pair is matched if: Cosine similarity between latent features \tilde{z}j and \tilde{z}{neighbor} > \tauf. Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) intersection-over-union (IoU) of the Feature Gaussians' geometry > \taug. c. Form connected components of the resulting match edges to define merge groups. d. Unmatched Feature Gaussians are appended to the final set unchanged. 5. Feature Gaussian Merging (Cross-View Compression): For each merge group of Feature Gaussians: a. Use the same SAB+PMA backbone as the encoder. b. Apply zero-initialized residual heads to predict parameter updates \Delta \mu, \Delta z, \Delta m, \Delta c0, \Delta s, \Delta q to the 0th Feature Gaussian in the group. c. Update the 0th Feature Gaussian with these deltas to produce the merged Feature Gaussian. 6. Refinement: Apply a refiner M{ref} to each Feature Gaussian \tilde{G}j using self-attention over its k nearest neighbors in the Feature Gaussian set to ensure continuity across thin structures and depth boundaries. 7. Decoding: For each final Feature Gaussian \tilde{G}j, apply the decoder M{dec}^K to expand it into K output Gaussians compatible with standard differentiable rasterizers. The decoder has multiple heads for K=1, 2, 4. Rendering: The final pixel color is obtained by front-to-back alpha blending: c{pixel} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is the view-dependent color of Gaussian i, computed via SH basis functions Hk: ci = \sum{k=0}^{M} \hat{c}{k,i} Hk(d) for view direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Teacher Loss (Moment Matching): During training, a closed-form moment-matching target is computed for each superpixel group Sj: \muj^{teach} = \frac{\sum{i \in Sj} \alphai \mui}{\sum{i \in Sj} \alphai} \Sigmaj^{teach} = \frac{\sum{i \in Sj} \alphai (\mui - \muj^{teach})(\mui - \muj^{teach})^\top}{\sum{i \in Sj} \alphai} The loss compares the pipeline output to these targets using geodesic quaternion loss for qi and L1 losses for other parameters. Total Loss: L = \lambda{MSE} L{MSE} + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM} + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS} + \lambda{teach} L{teach} + \lambda{div} L{div} where L{MSE}, L{SSIM}, L{LPIPS} are photometric losses between rendered and ground-truth images. K: Number of output Gaussians per Feature Gaussian. Typical values: K=1, 2, 4. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-5} with cosine schedule. Optimizer: AdamW. Training Steps: 300,000 steps. Input Views: 3, 6, 9, or 12 views. Image Resolution: Longer side resized to 476 pixels. Match Thresholds: \tauf (feature cosine similarity) and \taug (AABB IoU). Loss Weights: \lambda{teach} and \lambda{div} follow a decay schedule. Encoder Collapse: If the encoder predicts scale sj or rotation qj, it may shrink geometry to avoid cross-view matching. The method prevents this by having the encoder not predict sj or qj; these are produced by the decoder M{dec}^1. LPIPS Sensitivity: LPIPS is sensitive to texture degradation from merging, so the pipeline does not fully preserve LPIPS scores compared to unmerged baselines. Superpixel Size: Larger superpixels reduce the relative primitive count (rc) but degrade quality (e.g., PSNR drops from 14.14 dB to 13.97 dB at roughly half rc). VolSplat Performance: VolSplat performs significantly worse than other methods and fails to reproduce reported quality, likely due to training on RealEstate-10K which has smaller viewpoint changes. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial import KDTree def saliencyguidedsegmentation(image): """ Step 2: Saliency-Guided Superpixel Segmentation """ # Compute Shi-Tomasi corner response (minimum eigenvalue of structure tensor) # This is a placeholder for the actual eigenvalue computation lambdav = computeshitomasiresponse(image) # Sample seeds densely where lambdav is high, sparsely elsewhere seeds = sampleseedsdynamically(image.shape, lambdav) # Run BASS segmentation # Returns a map assigning each pixel to a superpixel ID partitionmap = basssegmentation(image, seeds) return partitionmap def encodesuperpixel(groupgaussians): """ Step 3: Feature Gaussian Encoding Input: List of Gaussians in a superpixel group Sj Output: Feature Gaussian parameters """ # Project attributes to tokens tokens = mlpproject(groupgaussians.attributes) # Refine with Set Attention Blocks tokens = setattentionblocks(tokens) # Aggregate with Pooling-by-Multihead-Attention latentz = poolingbymultiheadattention(tokens, learnablequery=Q) # Compute mean as opacity-weighted centroid + offset muteich = opacityweightedmean(groupgaussians, key='mu') muj = muteich + positionoffset # Compute base color as opacity-weighted average of diffuse color cj = opacityweightedmean(groupgaussians, key='diffusecolor') # Note: sj and qj are NOT predicted here return { 'mu': muj, 'z': latentz, 'c': cj, 'alpha': opacityweightedmean(groupgaussians, key='alpha') } def crossviewmatching(featuregaussians): """ Step 4: Cross-View Matching Input: List of Feature Gaussians from all views Output: List of merge groups (connected components) """ # Build KDTree for 3D kNN positions = np.array([fg['mu'] for fg in featuregaussians]) tree = KDTree(positions) matchedges = [] for i, fgi in enumerate(featuregaussians): # Find k nearest neighbors, excluding same-view candidates # Assuming viewid is stored in fgi dists, indices = tree.query(fgi['mu'], k=k+1) # +1 to exclude self for idx, dist in zip(indices[1:], dists[1:]): # Skip self fgj = featuregaussians[idx] if fgi['viewid'] == fgj['viewid']: continue # Match gate cossim = cosinesimilarity(fgi['z'], fgj['z']) aabbiou = computeaabbiou(fgi, fgj) if cossim > tauf and aabbiou > taug: matchedges.append((i, idx)) # Form connected components mergegroups = findconnectedcomponents(matchedges, len(featuregaussians)) return mergegroups def mergefeaturegaussians(groupfgindices, featuregaussians): """ Step 5: Feature Gaussian Merging Input: Indices of Feature Gaussians in a merge group Output: Merged Feature Gaussian """ # Use SAB+PMA backbone tokens = [featuregaussians[i] for i in groupfgindices] # Process through merger network # Predict deltas for the 0th FG deltas = mergernetwork(tokens) # Apply deltas to the 0th Feature Gaussian fg0 = featuregaussians[groupfgindices[0]] mergedfg = { 'mu': fg0['mu'] + deltas['deltamu'], 'z': fg0['z'] + deltas['deltaz'], 'c': fg0['c'] + deltas['deltac0'], 's': fg0['s'] + deltas['deltas'], 'q': applyquaterniondelta(fg0['q'], deltas['deltaq']), 'alpha': fg0['alpha'] # Opacity handling as per source } return mergedfg def decodefeaturegaussian(fg, K): """ Step 7: Decoding Input: Feature Gaussian, K (number of output Gaussians) Output: List of K Gaussians """ # Use the appropriate decoder head for K decoderhead = getdecoderhead(K) outputgaussians = decoderhead(fg) return outputgaussians def render(featuregaussians, K, cameraparams): """ Render the scene using the compressed Feature Gaussians """ # Decode all Feature Gaussians to output Gaussians allgaussians = [] for fg in featuregaussians: allgaussians.extend(decodefeaturegaussian(fg, K)) # Sort by depth for front-to-back blending allgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: depth(g['mu'], cameraparams)) # Front-to-back alpha blending image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) transmittance = np.ones((height, width)) for g in allgaussians: # Splat g onto image splatmask, splatalpha, splatcolor = splatgaussian(g, cameraparams) # Update image # cpixel = sum(Ti alphai ci) # Ti = product(1 - alphaj) # This is a simplified representation of the rasterization step image = updateimagewithsplat(image, splatmask, splatalpha, splatcolor, transmittance) transmittance = transmittance (1 - splatalpha) return image Time Complexity: The segmentation and encoding steps are performed per-view and are relatively fast due to the frozen backbone and efficient set transformer architecture. Cross-view matching involves 3D kNN, which scales with the number of Feature Gaussians. Decoding is constant per Feature Gaussian. Overall, it is significantly faster than per-scene optimization and faster than naive feed-forward rendering due to reduced primitive count. Memory Complexity: The method reduces the primitive count by up to 16x compared to the naïve baseline (e.g., 0.82 M vs 12.9 M Gaussians at 84 views). This leads to proportional reductions in memory usage and rendering time (6.1x faster for K=1). Measured Performance: On DL3DV-Bench, MipNeRF360, and Tanks & Temples, the DA3 backbone with K=1 achieves 17.41 dB PSNR at 4.4% relative primitive count (rc). It outperforms heuristic moment matching and other feed-forward methods like ReSplat and VolSplat. Strengths: Content-adaptive compression via saliency-guided superpixels; effective cross-view redundancy removal; online reconstruction capability; high quality at low primitive counts. Limitations: LPIPS scores are degraded due to texture smoothing from merging; performance depends on the quality of the feed-forward backbone; VolSplat baseline fails on certain benchmarks. When to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required from a small number of input views, and memory/latency constraints necessitate a compact representation. When not to use: When LPIPS fidelity is critical and cannot tolerate texture degradation; when input views have very small viewpoint changes (VolSplat issue); when per-scene optimization is feasible and higher quality is needed at the cost of time. Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging was introduced by Faasch, Kall, and Stachniess in the paper "Compact Feed-Forward 3D Gaussians via Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging". It builds on the principles of Hierarchical and Multi-Resolution Splatting and Splatting. The method addresses the limitations of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, which produces large numbers of primitives, by introducing a learned compression pipeline. It was evaluated on datasets like DL3DV-10K, MipNeRF360, and Tanks & Temples. name: Vertex-Based Leaf Node Derivation
head: QSplat Strategy
body: Vertex-Based Leaf Node Derivation constructs leaf nodes in hierarchical volume rendering trees by mapping mesh vertices directly to bounding spheres. It solves the problem of defining geometric primitives for rendering when the underlying data is a vertex cloud that lacks explicit topological connectivity for primitive generation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like TetSplat by deriving centers and field values directly from vertex attributes rather than computing circum-centers of tetrahedra or triangles, requiring explicit radius calculation based on neighbor topology to prevent rendering holes. Inputs: A set of mesh vertices \mathcal{V}, where each vertex vi has position \mathbf{p}i and field values \mathbf{f}i. A set of adjacent triangles \mathcal{T} or tetrahedra \mathcal{U} defining the local topology around each vertex. Outputs: A list of leaf nodes, each defined by a center \mathbf{c}i, radius ri, normal \mathbf{n}i (for Shell nodes), and field values \mathbf{f}i. Data Structures: Leaf Node: A struct containing: center: vec3 (position \mathbf{c}i). radius: float (ri). normal: vec3 (\mathbf{n}i, only for Shell). fieldvalues: array or struct (interpolated or vertex attributes \mathbf{f}i). Steps: 1. Initialize Leaf Nodes: For each vertex vi \in \mathcal{V}, create a leaf node. 2. Set Center and Fields: Set center \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{p}i and assign field values \mathbf{f}i directly from the vertex attributes. 3. Calculate Radius: Identify all triangles \mathcal{T}i and/or tetrahedra \mathcal{U}i that share vertex vi. Compute the circum-radius r{tri} for each triangle in \mathcal{T}i and the circum-radius r{tet} for each tetrahedron in \mathcal{U}i if available. Set ri = \max(\{r{tri} \mid t \in \mathcal{T}i\} \cup \{r{tet} \mid u \in \mathcal{U}i\}). Using tetrahedra is more conservative than using triangles. 4. Calculate Normal (Shell Only): For vertices belonging to the Shell, compute the normal \mathbf{n}i as the normalized average of the face normals of all adjacent triangles. \mathbf{n}i = \text{normalize}\left(\sum{t \in \mathcal{T}i} \mathbf{n}t\right). 5. Construct Hierarchy: Group these leaf nodes into a hierarchical tree structure for culling and traversal. Parameters: Radius Strategy: "Triangles" or "Tetrahedra". Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: If the radius is too small, gaps appear between splats. The radius must be large enough that bounding spheres touch or overlap for connected vertices. Degenerate Elements: Degenerate tetrahedra (needles, spindles) are removed during mesh preprocessing, which affects the set of adjacent elements used for radius calculation. Topology Dependency: Unlike pure point clouds, this method requires access to the adjacency graph (triangles/tetrahedra) to define the radius, despite the leaf node itself being vertex-based. A variant where leaf nodes are derived from Shell and Solid sub-meshes. Each leaf node requires a bounding sphere (center and radius) and storage for all field values of interest. It explicitly distinguishes between Shell (surface) and Solid (volume) components, requiring normal vectors for Shell nodes and field value storage for both. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation that leverages existing vertex data and avoids complex geometric primitive construction for the leaf node definition itself. Limitations: Requires topology for radius calculation, which may lead to overdraw if the radius is large, and normals are approximate for Shell nodes. When to use: When the input is a vertex-based representation and a quick hierarchical structure is needed, or when implementing the original QSplat algorithm. When not to use: When precise geometric primitives are required for accurate field interpolation or when minimizing overdraw is critical and tetrahedral data is available. The method originates from the QSplat algorithm, which uses vertices to define leaf nodes in a hierarchical bounding sphere structure for real-time volume rendering. It was developed to handle large datasets by enabling efficient culling and adaptive traversal. The approach is part of the broader TetSplat framework, which partitions tetrahedral meshes into Shell and Solid components for rendering. name: Gsplat Transformation
head: Gsplat scaling, rotation, translation, recoloring, TransformGsplat
body: The Gsplat Transformation method conditionally updates position, scale, orientation, and color attributes of a packed Gsplat structure based on provided transformation parameters. It operates directly on semantic fields without requiring full serialization, building on Splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Gsplat structure containing position (center), scale (scales), rotation (quaternion), color (rgba), and an active flag (flags). Input: Optional transformation parameters: scale (scalar or vector), rotate (quaternion), translate (vector), recolor (vector). Output: A modified Gsplat structure. Data Structures: The Gsplat structure is assumed to be packed for efficient memory access. Key fields include: flags: Boolean or integer indicating if the splat is active. center: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the Gaussian center. scales: 3D vector (sx, sy, sz) representing the Gaussian extents. quaternion: 4D vector (w, x, y, z) representing orientation. rgba: 4D vector (r, g, b, a) representing color and opacity. Steps: 1. Copy: Create a copy of the input gsplat to the output structure. 2. Check Activity: If isGsplatActive(gsplat.flags) is false, skip further transformations and return the copy. 3. Scale: If a scale parameter is provided, multiply gsplat.center and gsplat.scales by scale. 4. Rotate: If a rotate quaternion is provided, rotate gsplat.center using quatVec(rotate, gsplat.center) and update gsplat.quaternion using quatQuat(rotate, gsplat.quaternion). 5. Translate: If a translate vector is provided, add translate to gsplat.center. 6. Recolor: If a recolor vector is provided, multiply gsplat.rgba by recolor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Gsplat: def init(self, center, scales, quaternion, rgba, flags): self.center = center self.scales = scales self.quaternion = quaternion self.rgba = rgba self.flags = flags def transformgsplat(gsplat, scale=None, rotate=None, translate=None, recolor=None): # Step 1: Copy input to output out = Gsplat(gsplat.center.copy(), gsplat.scales.copy(), gsplat.quaternion.copy(), gsplat.rgba.copy(), gsplat.flags) # Step 2: Check if active if not (out.flags & 1): return out # Step 3: Scale if scale is not None: out.center = [c scale for c in out.center] out.scales = [s scale for s in out.scales] # Step 4: Rotate if rotate is not None: out.center = quatvecmul(rotate, out.center) out.quaternion = quatquatmul(rotate, out.quaternion) # Step 5: Translate if translate is not None: out.center = [c + t for c, t in zip(out.center, translate)] # Step 6: Recolor if recolor is not None: out.rgba = [r rc for r, rc in zip(out.rgba, recolor)] return out def quatvecmul(q, v): # q = (w, x, y, z), v = (x, y, z) w, x, y, z = q vx, vy, vz = v ix = 2.0 (y vz - z vy) iy = 2.0 (z vx - w vz) iz = 2.0 (w vy - y vx) return [vx + w ix + (y iz - z iy), vy + w iy + (z ix - x iz), vz + w iz + (x iy - y ix)] def quatquatmul(q1, q2): w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1 w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2 return [w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2] Parameters: scale: Scalar or 3D vector. rotate: 4D quaternion. translate: 3D vector. recolor: 4D vector. Edge Cases: Inactive Splats: The method checks flags to avoid processing inactive splats. Quaternion Normalization: The quatQuat operation assumes normalized quaternions. Ensure input quaternions are normalized before calling. Zero Scale: Multiplying by zero scale collapses the Gaussian to a point. This may cause numerical instability in subsequent rendering steps. Decomposes or reconstructs Gsplat structures for fine-grained editing, building on Gsplat Transformation. Encodes multiple states of an object (e.g., burning, frozen, charcoal) in a single Gaussian Splatting model. MLP-based encoders are activated with a new value at collision time or interaction to instantly produce a new 3DGS state. The object is normalized back to its default state by applying a counter-effect (e.g., fire removes ice). Time Complexity: O(1) per splat, as the number of operations is fixed and small. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the copy. Performance: Highly efficient due to packed data structures and conditional execution. Strengths: Semantic field access, conditional processing, low overhead. Limitations: Limited to specific transformation types; not a general-purpose matrix transform. The Gsplat Transformation method originates from implementations that optimize the training loop by avoiding full serialization of Gaussian attributes. It is commonly used in differentiable rendering pipelines where gradients are propagated to position, scale, rotation, and color. Runtime style transformation variants use MLP encoders to instantly produce new 3DGS states upon interaction. sparkjsdev/spark, https://github.com/sparkjsdev/spark, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Gsplat Split and Combine
head: CombineGsplat, Gsplat field extraction, Gsplat field merging, SplitGsplat
body: The Gsplat Split and Combine methods decompose a packed Gsplat structure into individual scalar and vector fields for manipulation, or reconstruct a Gsplat from partial updates. This enables fine-grained editing of Gaussian attributes without full serialization overhead, building on Gsplat Transformation. The method takes a Gsplat struct instance and optional update parameters for specific fields as input. The Split operation outputs individual fields: active (bool), rgb (vec3), opacity (float), x/y/z (float), and r/g/b (float). The Combine operation outputs a reconstructed Gsplat struct. The Gsplat struct contains six fields: flags (uint), index (int), center (vec3), scales (vec3), quaternion (vec4), and rgba (vec4). The center vector holds coordinates x, y, z. The rgba vector holds color components r, g, b and alpha a. 1. Null Check: If the input gsplat is null, return the specified default values. 2. Extract Base Fields: Copy flags, index, center, scales, quaternion, and rgba directly from the input. 3. Compute Derived Fields: Calculate active using isGsplatActive(flags). Derive rgb from rgba.rgb, opacity from rgba.a, x/y/z from center.x/y/z, and r/g/b from rgba.r/g/b. 4. Apply Defaults: If the input was null, assign flags=0u, index=0, center=vec3(0), scales=vec3(0), quaternion=vec4(0,0,0,1), rgba=vec4(0), rgb=vec3(0), opacity=0, x/y/z=0, and r/g/b=0. 1. Initialize Output: Start with an output gsplat struct. If no existing gsplat is provided, initialize with default values. 2. Field Update Logic: For each top-level field (flags, index, center, scales, quaternion, rgba), if the corresponding input parameter is provided, use it; otherwise, copy from the input gsplat (if present) or use default values. 3. Sub-field Updates: For rgba and center, if specific sub-inputs (rgb, opacity, x, y, z, r, g, b) are provided, update only those parts of the vector. 4. Default Values: Apply flags=0u, index=0, center=vec3(0), scales=vec3(0), quaternion=vec4(0,0,0,1), and rgba=vec4(0) where unspecified. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z class Vec4: def init(self, r=0.0, g=0.0, b=0.0, a=0.0): self.r, self.g, self.b, self.a = r, g, b, a class Gsplat: def init(self, flags=0, index=0, center=None, scales=None, quaternion=None, rgba=None): self.flags = flags self.index = index self.center = center if center is not None else Vec3() self.scales = scales if scales is not None else Vec3() self.quaternion = quaternion if quaternion is not None else Vec4(0, 0, 0, 1) self.rgba = rgba if rgba is not None else Vec4() def isgsplatactive(flags): return flags != 0 # Standard active flag check def splitgsplat(gsplat): if gsplat is None: return { 'flags': 0, 'index': 0, 'center': Vec3(), 'scales': Vec3(), 'quaternion': Vec4(0, 0, 0, 1), 'rgba': Vec4(), 'active': False, 'rgb': Vec3(), 'opacity': 0.0, 'x': 0.0, 'y': 0.0, 'z': 0.0, 'r': 0.0, 'g': 0.0, 'b': 0.0 } flags = gsplat.flags index = gsplat.index center = gsplat.center scales = gsplat.scales quaternion = gsplat.quaternion rgba = gsplat.rgba active = isgsplatactive(flags) rgb = Vec3(rgba.r, rgba.g, rgba.b) opacity = rgba.a x, y, z = center.x, center.y, center.z r, g, b = rgba.r, rgba.g, rgba.b return { 'flags': flags, 'index': index, 'center': center, 'scales': scales, 'quaternion': quaternion, 'rgba': rgba, 'active': active, 'rgb': rgb, 'opacity': opacity, 'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z, 'r': r, 'g': g, 'b': b } def combinegsplat(gsplat=None, flags=None, index=None, center=None, scales=None, quaternion=None, rgba=None, rgb=None, opacity=None, x=None, y=None, z=None, r=None, g=None, b=None): if gsplat is None: out = Gsplat() else: out = Gsplat(gsplat.flags, gsplat.index, gsplat.center, gsplat.scales, gsplat.quaternion, gsplat.rgba) if flags is not None: out.flags = flags if index is not None: out.index = index if center is not None: out.center = center if scales is not None: out.scales = scales if quaternion is not None: out.quaternion = quaternion if rgba is not None: out.rgba = rgba if rgb is not None: out.rgba.r = rgb.r; out.rgba.g = rgb.g; out.rgba.b = rgb.b if opacity is not None: out.rgba.a = opacity if x is not None: out.center.x = x if y is not None: out.center.y = y if z is not None: out.center.z = z if r is not None: out.rgba.r = r if g is not None: out.rgba.g = g if b is not None: out.rgba.b = b return out Coordinate precision is controlled via --fractional-bits with a default of 12 and a valid range of 6 to 24. Axis-aligned bounding box clipping is applied using --x-range, --y-range, --z-range or --min-x/--max-x arguments. Splats with opacity at or below a threshold are filtered out via --opacity-threshold. The maximum spherical harmonic degree is set via --max-sh with a range of 0 to 3 and auto-detection as the default. Null inputs are handled by returning or initializing with the specified default values. Time and memory complexity are O(1) due to fixed-size struct field access and assignment. Scaling behavior, measured performance, and hardware specifics are not given in the sources. name: Runtime Style/Shape Transformation via MLP Encoders
head: Style/Shape Transformation via MLP Encoders
body: This method enables real-time contextual translation of Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) objects by encoding multiple semantic states (e.g., burning, frozen, charcoal) into a single model. It solves the asset management problem in interactive scenes by using MLP-based encoders to instantly produce new 3DGS states upon interaction. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gsplat Split and Combine by modulating existing splat parameters via learned representations rather than restructuring geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: a pre-trained 3DGS model representing the object in its default state and an interaction signal (e.g., collision event or projectile hit) specifying a target state. Output: updated Gaussian parameters corresponding to the target state, rendered into the scene. Data Structures: Gaussian parameters are stored in standard 3DGS format (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). The MLP encoder takes a state identifier and outputs modulation parameters to transform the default parameters into the target state parameters. Exact field layouts and bit packing are not specified beyond standard 3DGS format. Steps: 1. Initialize or load the default 3DGS model and the trained MLP encoder. 2. Detect interaction events, such as collision between a player-controlled projectile and the 3DGS object. 3. Determine the target state s from the interaction type (e.g., fire interaction sets s = \text{burning}). 4. Activate the MLP encoder with the state identifier to generate modulation parameters. 5. Apply the modulation parameters to the current Gaussian parameters to produce the new 3DGS state. 6. Render the updated parameters using standard volume rendering techniques. 7. For counter-effects (e.g., shooting a frozen object with fire), repeat steps 2–6 with the new state identifier to normalize the object back to a default or intermediate state. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The method applies modulation parameters to Gaussian parameters to yield a new state. Parameters: State identifiers and MLP weights are trained parameters. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision constraints may apply for mobile VR hardware like the Meta Quest 3. Continuous interpolation between states is not explicitly described; the method handles discrete state transitions. Degenerate input handling is not given in the sources. Applies style transformation to 2D feature maps after volume rendering, solving multi-view inconsistency and high memory usage of 3D point-wise transformation. It handles style-specific affine transformations in the 2D domain. Time Complexity: Real-time capable, designed for interactive VR applications including standalone mobile VR (Meta Quest 3) and PC-VR. Memory Complexity: Lower than maintaining multiple distinct 3DGS models, as it encodes multiple states in a single model with an MLP. Measured Performance: Tested in a Unity VR template with 3DGS objects; photorealistic quality may be reduced for mobile devices to fit hardware constraints. Strengths: Enables dynamic, interactive object states without pre-computing or storing multiple asset variants; instant state changes upon interaction. Limitations: Requires training the MLP encoder for each object and set of states; quality may be reduced on mobile hardware. When to use: Interactive VR/AR applications where objects need to change appearance dynamically based on user interaction. When not to use: Static scenes or scenes where pre-computed variants are sufficient and real-time interaction is not required. The method was introduced in "Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR". It builds on the trend of photorealistic product placement in commercials and addresses limitations in data and graphics power of client devices. The technique was implemented in a Unity VR template, demonstrating interaction with 3DGS objects via collision and projectile shooting. Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Deferred Style Transformation (DST)
body: Deferred Style Transformation (DST) is a technique that applies style transformation to 2D feature maps after volume rendering, rather than to 3D point features before rendering. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency and high memory usage inherent in applying holistic style statistics (like AdaIN) to batches of sampled 3D points. DST is set apart from its sibling method, Sampling-Invariant Content Transformation (SICT), by handling the style-specific affine transformation (matrix multiplication and bias) in the 2D domain, ensuring that the transformation is mathematically equivalent to point-wise transformation while drastically reducing memory footprint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume-rendered 2D feature map \bar{F}c \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}, style reference feature map Fs \in \mathbb{R}^{Hs \times Ws \times C'}, sum of weights wr for the ray, and pre-computed style statistics \mu(Fs) and \sigma(Fs). Output: Stylized 2D feature map F{cs} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}. Data Structures: Fs: Feature map extracted from a reference style image using a pre-trained VGG network. T: Style transformation matrix of size C' \times C. \mu(Fs): Mean of style features, computed as a scalar or channel-wise vector. \sigma(Fs): Standard deviation of style features, computed as a scalar or channel-wise vector. wr: Sum of weights of sampled points along ray r, i.e., wr = \sum{i=1}^N wi. \bar{F}c: Feature map resulting from volume rendering of independently transformed point features \bar{F}i. Steps: 1. Extract feature maps Fs of the reference style S using a pre-trained VGG network. 2. Generate the style transformation matrix T \in \mathbb{R}^{C' \times C} using the feature covariance cov(Fs). 3. Apply matrix multiplication with T to the volume-rendered feature map \bar{F}c. 4. Use a 1x1 convolution layer conv (without bias) to restore the channel number from C' to C. 5. Add adaptive bias: F{cs} = \text{conv}(T \otimes \bar{F}c \times \sigma(Fs)) + wr \times \mu(Fs). Formulas: The core transformation is defined in Equation (9) of: F{cs} = \text{conv}\left( T \otimes \bar{F}c \times \sigma(Fs) \right) + wr \times \mu(Fs) Where: \otimes denotes matrix multiplication. \bar{F}c is the volume-rendered feature map. T is the style transformation matrix. \sigma(Fs) is the style standard deviation. \text{conv} is a 1x1 convolution layer without bias. wr is the sum of weights of sampled points along the ray. \mu(Fs) is the style mean. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deferredstyletransformation(Fbarc, Fs, wr, T, convweights): """ Applies Deferred Style Transformation to a volume-rendered feature map. Args: Fbarc: Volume-rendered 2D feature map of shape (H, W, C). Fs: Reference style feature map of shape (Hs, Ws, C'). wr: Sum of weights of sampled points along the ray (scalar). T: Style transformation matrix of shape (C', C). convweights: 1x1 convolution kernel weights of shape (C, C'). Returns: Fcs: Stylized feature map of shape (H, W, C). """ # Compute style statistics from reference feature map muFs = Fs.mean(dim=(0, 1), keepdim=True) sigmaFs = ((Fs - muFs) 2).mean(dim=(0, 1), keepdim=True).sqrt() # Reshape feature map for matrix multiplication H, W, C = Fbarc.shape Fflat = Fbarc.reshape(-1, C) # Apply style transformation matrix T Ftemp = Fflat @ T.T Ftemp = Ftemp.reshape(H, W, -1) # Scale by style standard deviation Fscaled = Ftemp sigmaFs # Apply 1x1 convolution (matrix multiplication over channel dimension) Fconv = Fscaled.reshape(-1, Fscaled.shape[-1]) @ convweights.T Fconv = Fconv.reshape(H, W, -1) # Add adaptive bias modulated by ray weight sum Fcs = Fconv + wr muFs return Fcs Parameters: wr: Sum of weights of sampled points along the ray. T: Style transformation matrix derived from cov(Fs). conv: 1x1 convolution layer without bias. Pitfalls: Standard style transfer methods (like AdaIN) use holistic statistics of the sampled point batch, which violates multi-view consistency because the transformation of a specific 3D point varies across different sampled points. DST avoids this by deferring the transformation to 2D feature maps where the statistics are consistent per pixel/ray. Precision issues may arise if wr is very small or very large, affecting the bias term. The equivalence in Eq. 9 relies on the linearity of the volume rendering integration and the affine nature of the style transformation, proving that applying DST on 2D feature maps is equivalent to applying the transformation on 3D points’ features. Time Complexity: DST operates on 2D feature maps, which are significantly smaller than the batch of 3D point features sampled along all rays, reducing computational cost compared to point-wise style transfer. Memory Complexity: By deferring transformation to 2D feature maps, DST greatly reduces memory footprint, allowing training with 256x256 patches without sub-sampling, unlike previous NeRF-based methods. Performance: StyleRF with DST achieves superior 3D stylization quality with precise geometry reconstruction and generalizes to various new styles in a zero-shot manner. Strengths: Maintains multi-view consistency, memory-efficient, zero-shot generalization. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the pre-trained VGG features and the covariance estimation for style transfer. DST was introduced in the StyleRF paper. It is part of a framework for zero-shot 3D style transfer of Neural Radiance Fields. The method builds on the observation that style transformation can be decomposed into sampling-invariant content transformation and deferred style transformation. It addresses limitations of previous NeRF-based 3D style transfer methods that were computationally intensive or required low-resolution feature maps. StyleRF: Zero-Shot 3D Style Transfer of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00806, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Point Gaussian Representation
head: 2D Image Sprite Rendering, Point Sprite, Sprite-based Splatting
body: The Point Gaussian representation renders a dataset by drawing a 2D image sprite with potential transparency at each data point, rather than constructing 3D geometry. It is distinguished from its sibling 3D Glyphs by replacing volumetric or surface primitives with flat, billboard-like sprites, offering a lightweight alternative for visualizing point-based data. Inputs and Outputs Input: A dataset containing points (e.g., particle positions, sampled locations). Output: A 2D image where each point is rendered as a sprite. Data Structures The method does not define a specific complex data structure beyond the standard dataset point attributes. The rendering state is defined by the selected Sprite Type. Steps 1. Iterate over each point in the input dataset. 2. Select a sprite shape from the available predefined types or a custom definition. 3. Render the selected sprite at the point's projected screen location. The sprite may include transparency (alpha blending). 4. Color the sprite using a single color or pseudocoloring based on a data array associated with the point. Parameters Sprite Type: Defines the visual shape of the sprite. Available predefined options include: Gaussian Blur Sphere Black-edged circle Plain circle Triangle Square outline Custom sprite defined via GLSL shader code Coloring: Can be set to a single color or mapped from a scalar/vector data array (pseudocoloring). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpointgaussian(dataset, spritetype, colormap): """ Renders a dataset using the Point Gaussian representation. Args: dataset: List of points with associated data arrays. spritetype: Enum or string specifying the sprite shape (e.g., 'Gaussian Blur', 'Sphere', 'Custom'). colormap: Function or lookup table mapping data values to colors. """ for point in dataset: # Project point to screen coordinates screenpos = projecttoscreen(point.position) # Determine color based on point data color = colormap(point.datavalue) # Draw the sprite # The sprite is a 2D image drawn at screenpos # Transparency is handled by the sprite's alpha channel drawsprite(screenpos, spritetype, color) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Overdraw: Since sprites are 2D images, heavy overlap can lead to blending artifacts if transparency is not handled correctly. Custom Shaders: Using custom GLSL code requires the renderer to support fragment shader injection for sprites. Handles the adaptive refinement and coarsening of point clouds. Choose when dynamic resolution adjustment is needed. Uses neural networks to define sprite shapes. Choose when complex, data-driven sprite geometries are required. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points, O(N), as each point is rendered independently as a sprite. Memory Complexity: Low, as no 3D geometry meshes are generated for each point. Performance: Generally faster than generating and rendering full 3D geometry for large datasets, as it avoids the overhead of mesh generation and complex vertex processing. Strengths: Efficient for large point clouds; supports various visual styles via sprite types; supports transparency. Limitations: Lacks true 3D depth cues compared to 3D Glyphs; sprite size may not scale intuitively with depth without additional logic. When to use: When visualizing large sets of points where performance is critical and 3D geometry is unnecessary. When not to use: When precise 3D shape representation or occlusion handling via geometry is required. The Point Gaussian representation is a visualization technique available in ParaView for displaying point-based data. It was introduced as an alternative to 3D Glyphs, which draw 3D geometry (e.g., arrows, cones) at data points. The technique leverages graphics instancing to render the same sprite geometry at many locations efficiently. It is part of ParaView's suite of display representations for volume and point data. 4. name: Optimization and Culling
body: Optimization and Culling refers to techniques that reduce the computational workload of object-order volume splatting by skipping or discarding primitives that do not contribute significantly to the final image. It solves the performance bottleneck of processing large numbers of splats, particularly in real-time rendering. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing on pre-rasterization filtering (size culling) and screen-space occlusion checks (early termination) rather than geometric approximation or hardware-specific pipeline optimizations. The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized. An optimization that skips the processing of voxels when the accumulated opacity at the target screen pixels is already full, analogous to early ray termination in ray casting. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Splat Size Culling by operating on accumulated opacity rather than geometric footprint size, making it effective for opaque regions but costly for low-opacity scenes. When to choose: Use for scenes with high opacity or significant occlusion where pixel coverage reaches full opacity quickly. See Early Splat Termination. A staging optimization that discards primitives smaller than a defined threshold before rasterization. It trades visual fidelity for real-time frame rates by reducing the workload of splats and fragments generated during the rendering pipeline. It differs from sibling methods like Early Splat Termination by operating at the data staging phase rather than during the per-pixel compositing phase, allowing it to prevent expensive rasterization and memory allocation for negligible contributions entirely. When to choose: Use for scenes with many small, negligible splats where performance is prioritized over fine detail. See Splat Size Culling. Storing a 32-bit integer for each splat where each potential state (highlighted, selected, deleted) is encoded inside a single bit, serving as an acceleration for transformation of selected splats. This allows the renderer to quickly check flags before loading an order of magnitude more of additional splat data. Early Splat Termination and Splat Size Culling are standard optimizations within the splatting family for improving rendering throughput. Splat State Encoding originates from the Splatshop framework for efficiently editing large Gaussian Splat models. name: Early Splat Termination
head: Early Splat Elimination, Krüger Speed-Optimized Splatting
body: Early Splat Termination is an optimization for volume splatting that skips processing of voxels when the accumulated opacity at the target screen pixels is already full, analogous to early ray termination in ray casting. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Splat Size Culling by operating on accumulated screen-space opacity rather than geometric footprint size, effectively culling distant or occluded voxels that would otherwise contribute negligible color changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset containing density and opacity fields, a camera projection matrix, and a screen-space opacity buffer initialized to zero. Output: A rendered image where voxels contributing to fully opaque regions are skipped. Data Structures: Opacity Buffer: A 2D array matching the screen resolution, storing the accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} for each pixel, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. Bounding Box: A 2D integer rectangle (x{min}, y{min}, x{max}, y{max}) defining the pixel coverage of a projected voxel. Steps: 1. Project Volumes: Project the density volume and a separate opacity volume onto the screen. 2. Compute Bounding Box: For each voxel, calculate the 2D bounding box of the pixels covered by its splat footprint. 3. Check Opacity: Iterate through all pixels within the bounding box. Check if the accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} at each pixel is equal to or near 1.0. 4. Terminate or Process: If all pixels in the bounding box have full opacity, skip processing the current voxel entirely. Otherwise, proceed with standard splatting (accumulating color and opacity). Formulas: Let B be the set of pixel coordinates in the bounding box. Let \alpha{acc}(p) be the accumulated opacity at pixel p. The termination condition is: \forall p \in B, \quad \alpha{acc}(p) \geq \tau Where \tau is the opacity threshold. Parameters: Opacity Threshold (\tau): Typically 1.0 or "near 1.0". Pitfalls: High Overhead: The cost of checking the bounding box and iterating through pixels can be high, making this optimization less effective than early ray termination for datasets with low opacity or high empty space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlysplattermination(boundingbox, opacitybuffer, threshold=1.0): """ Determines if a voxel should be skipped based on accumulated screen opacity. Args: boundingbox: Tuple (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) of inclusive pixel coordinates. opacitybuffer: 2D list/array of accumulated opacity values. threshold: Opacity threshold for termination (default 1.0). Returns: bool: True if voxel should be skipped, False otherwise. """ xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = boundingbox rows = len(opacitybuffer) cols = len(opacitybuffer[0]) if rows > 0 else 0 for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): if 0 <= y < rows and 0 <= x < cols: if opacitybuffer[y][x] < threshold: return False return True Time Complexity: The check is O(A) where A is the area of the bounding box in pixels. In the worst case (no termination), it adds overhead to every voxel. In the best case (full opacity), it saves the cost of splatting. Memory Complexity: Requires an additional screen-space opacity buffer, O(W \times H) where W, H are screen dimensions. Measured Performance: The associated costs for early splat elimination are high, making it less effective than early ray termination for datasets with low opacity or high empty space (e.g., skull datasets). Strengths: Reduces redundant calculations in opaque regions. Limitations: High overhead for sparse or low-opacity data; less effective than ray-casting optimizations in such cases. Early Splat Termination was introduced as a speed optimization for volume splatting, drawing direct analogy to early ray termination in ray casting. The technique addresses the inefficiency of distant voxels affecting the same number of pixels as near voxels, by skipping those that do not contribute to the final image due to occlusion. name: Splat Size Culling
head: Culling Small Splats
body: Splat Size Culling is a staging optimization for object-order volume rendering that discards primitives smaller than a defined threshold before rasterization. It trades visual fidelity for real-time frame rates by reducing the workload of splats and fragments generated during the rendering pipeline. It differs from sibling methods like Early Splat Termination by operating at the data staging phase rather than during the per-pixel compositing phase, allowing it to prevent expensive rasterization and memory allocation for negligible contributions entirely. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of volumetric primitives (splats) S = \{s1, s2, \dots, sN\}, where each splat sk carries a projected size metric \sigmak and associated rendering attributes. Output: A filtered subset S' \subseteq S containing only splats that meet the size requirement. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Project each splat k from volume space to screen space using the camera's model-view-projection matrix. 2. Compute the projected size metric \sigmak for each splat. 3. Compare \sigmak against a user-defined threshold \tau. 4. Discard splats where \sigmak < \tau; otherwise, pass them to the staging buffer for rasterization. Formulas: The filtering condition is defined as: S' = \{sk \in S \mid \sigmak \geq \tau\} where \sigmak is the projected size metric of splat k and \tau is the culling threshold. Parameters: Threshold (\tau): User-configurable to balance visual quality and rendering performance. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small-Only Scenes: The method fails for scenes composed entirely of small splats, such as models constructed via Mesh2Splat, because all splats may be discarded or visual quality degrades significantly. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatsizeculling(splats, threshold): """ Discards splats with a projected size metric below the threshold. Args: splats: List of splat objects or dicts. Each must have a 'projectedsize' field. threshold: float, the minimum projected size to retain. Returns: List of splats that pass the culling test. """ kept = [] for splat in splats: if splat['projectedsize'] >= threshold: kept.append(splat) return kept A pre-computation optimization that rejects splats with no geometric overlap to a pixel's sub-tile before performing expensive alpha evaluation, reducing memory fetches and compute load while maintaining bit-identical output. It differs from standard blending by adding a cheap boolean bounding box overlap check before the Gaussian alpha evaluation, reducing instruction count and memory traffic. Choose it when minimizing instruction count and memory traffic is critical for tile-based rasterizers. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The culling pass performs a linear O(N) filter over the splat set. Memory: Reduces the number of staged splats and generated fragments, lowering memory bandwidth and buffer allocation requirements. Measured Performance: On the GardenF scene, culling reduces staged splats from 5.79M to 1.25M and fragments from 8.16M to 1.99M. Render time decreases from 9.7 ms to 2.1 ms. Scaling: Effectiveness scales with the variance in splat sizes. It works well for 3DGS-generated datasets with mixed sizes, and at greater distances where most splats become small, the majority are discarded while larger semi-representative splats remain. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in workload and render time for large, heterogeneous splat datasets. Limitations: Fails on uniformly small splat scenes (e.g., Mesh2Splat) and trades visual quality for performance, though high-quality screenshots can be captured by disabling culling. When to Use: Use for real-time rendering of large Gaussian Splat datasets where performance is critical and some quality loss is acceptable. Do not use for scenes with uniformly small primitives or when high-fidelity reconstruction is required. Origin: Introduced in "Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models". History and Development: Developed to address the computational bottleneck of rendering millions of splats in real-time by filtering out negligible contributions during the staging phase. It leverages the observation that small splats contribute minimally to the final image, allowing aggressive culling without severe visual artifacts in many cases. Where it is used: Implemented in Splatshop for efficient editing and rendering of large Gaussian Splat models. name: Warp-level Culling
head: Warp-level Splat Culling
body: Warp-level Culling is a pre-computation optimization that rejects splats with no geometric overlap to a pixel's sub-tile before performing expensive alpha evaluation, reducing memory fetches and compute load while maintaining bit-identical output. It differs from standard blending by adding a cheap boolean bounding box overlap check before the expensive Gaussian alpha evaluation, reducing instruction count and memory traffic. Inputs and Outputs Input: A batch of 32 splats containing bounding box data, and a sub-tile of 32 pixels arranged in an 8x4 grid. Output: A 32-bit bitmask indicating which splats intersect the sub-tile, allowing threads to skip non-contributing splats during the rendering phase. Data Structures Splat Bounding Box: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, x{max}, y{max}) in screen space. Sub-tile: A rectangular region of 32 pixels, specifically an 8x4 grid. Bitmask: A 32-bit integer where the i-th bit is set if the i-th splat in the batch intersects the sub-tile. Parameters Sub-tile size: 32 pixels, arranged in an 8x4 grid. Batch processing unit: 32 splats per warp iteration. Steps 1. Subdivision: Subdivide the image tile into sub-tiles of 32 pixels (8x4 grid) and map each pixel in the sub-tile to a unique thread in a warp. 2. Batching: Iterate through the splat batches in chunks of 32 splats, and map the 32 threads in the warp to the 32 splats in the current batch. 3. Geometric Intersection Test: Each thread i (corresponding to splat i) pulls the bounding box of its assigned splat and performs a boolean geometric intersection test between the splat's bounding box and the sub-tile's boundaries. 4. Bitmask Creation: Threads share their intersection results using the ballot primitive to create a 32-bit bitmask where bit i is 1 if splat i intersects the sub-tile, and 0 otherwise. 5. Culling: Each thread iterates through the 32 splats in the batch, and uses the bitmask to check if the bit corresponding to the current splat index is set. If the bit is 0, the thread skips loading the full splat data and skips the expensive alpha evaluation for that splat. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. WARPSIZE = 32 def warpballot(predicates): # Simulates hardware warp ballot: returns a 32-bit integer where bit i is set if predicates[i] is true mask = 0 for i in range(WARPSIZE): if predicates[i]: mask |= (1 << i) return mask def loadsplatdata(splat): # Fetches full splat attributes (position, covariance, opacity, etc.) from memory return splat.attributes def evaluategaussianalpha(attributes, pixelcoords): # Computes the standard 3D Gaussian alpha value for the pixel return computegaussian(attributes, pixelcoords) def warplevelculling(threadid, splatbatch, subtilebounds): # Step 1 & 2: Map thread to splat index (0-31) splatindex = threadid # Step 3: Geometric Intersection Test splat = splatbatch[splatindex] sxmin, symin, sxmax, symax = splat.boundingbox stxmin, stymin, stxmax, stymax = subtilebounds # Boolean overlap check for axis-aligned rectangles xoverlap = (sxmin < stxmax) and (sxmax > stxmin) yoverlap = (symin < stymax) and (symax > stymin) intersects = xoverlap and yoverlap # Step 4: Bitmask Creation # In hardware, ballot(intersects) aggregates results across all 32 threads in lock-step threadintersects = [False] WARPSIZE threadintersects[threadid] = intersects bitmask = warpballot(threadintersects) # Step 5: Culling during rendering loop for i in range(WARPSIZE): iscontributing = (bitmask >> i) & 1 if iscontributing: splatdata = loadsplatdata(splatbatch[i]) alpha = evaluategaussianalpha(splatdata, threadid) # Perform blending with alpha else: # Skip full data load and alpha evaluation pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Synchronization Stalls: The method avoids block-wide synchronization fences of the original blend stage by using warp-level lock-step execution. The ballot "fence" does not create stalls because threads in a warp progress in lock-step. Workload Imbalance: Not all splats in a tile will overlap and contribute to a pixel. This creates an uneven distribution of work among threads. The method ingests splat batches 32-at-a-time to mitigate stalls at synchronization fences caused by this unevenness. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of expensive Gaussian alpha evaluations and memory fetches for non-contributing splats. The overhead is a cheap boolean bounding box check. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory traffic by avoiding loading full splat data for culled splats. Performance: Maintains bit-identical output to the baseline (Faster-GS) because it only optimizes the culling of non-contributing splats, not the rendering of contributing ones. Strengths: Significant reduction in instruction count and memory traffic for sparse scenes or large tiles. Limitations: Effectiveness depends on the sparsity of splats within the sub-tile. If most splats overlap, the overhead of the culling logic may not yield significant gains. Warp-level Culling was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It builds on the observation that many splats do not contribute to a given pixel, and that a cheap geometric check can preempt the expensive alpha evaluation. The method leverages the warp-level ballot primitive, a feature of GPU architectures like NVIDIA's CUDA, to efficiently aggregate intersection results across threads. name: Hybrid and Parallel Rendering
head: Hybrid Volume Rendering, Parallel Splatting, Hybrid Sort-First/Sort-Last Rendering
body: Hybrid and Parallel Rendering encompasses techniques that combine splatting with other rendering paradigms (such as ray casting or mesh rendering) or distribute the splatting workload across multiple processors to achieve performance and visual fidelity improvements. It solves the limitations of pure object-order splatting (e.g., perspective distortion, lack of occlusion handling) and pure parallel splatting (e.g., communication overhead, memory replication) by integrating ray-driven traversal, multi-representation blending, or dynamic load balancing. Unlike standard splatting which rasterizes footprints directly to the screen, this family includes methods that suspend primitives in object space for ray intersection, blend point-based and polygonal representations, or partition both object and screen space for cluster rendering. The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized. The Hybrid and Parallel Rendering family shares the fundamental mechanism of enhancing the basic splatting pipeline through hybridization or parallelization. While the specific implementations vary, the core principles involve: 1. Hybridization of Rendering Paradigms: Combining the efficiency of splatting (object-order projection) with the accuracy of other methods (e.g., ray-order accumulation for occlusion, or polygonal rasterization for surface detail). 2. Parallel Distribution: Distributing the computational load of splat projection, rasterization, or compositing across multiple processing units (CPUs/GPUs) or networked nodes. 3. Data Partitioning: Dividing the workload based on either object space (geometry/primitives) or image space (pixels/screen tiles) to balance load and minimize redundant computation or communication. Ray-driven splatting merges object-order splatting with ray-order accumulation. It suspends splats in object space and intersects them via spawned rays, solving the inefficiency and inaccuracy of perspective projection in traditional voxel-driven splatting. Unlike standard splatting, it enables ray-tracing optimizations like early ray termination and spatial acceleration structures, offering superior performance for perspective views. Choose it when perspective accuracy and occlusion handling are prioritized over raw rasterization speed. This technique eliminates visual discontinuities at boundaries where point-based splat representations transition to polygonal mesh representations. It solves the problem of visible seams in multi-resolution or hybrid rendering by reusing the natural weight falloff of splatting as a blending factor for linear interpolation between the two modes. Unlike naive approaches requiring additional geometry at transition edges, it integrates into standard multi-pass pipelines using depth-buffer interactions and alpha-checks. Choose it when rendering mixed point/polygon datasets with smooth transitions. This method projects 3D data voxels onto a 2D screen or intermediate texture plane and blends them to form the final image. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large volumetric datasets by leveraging specialized texture hardware for fast composition, avoiding direct projection to the screen plane. Unlike Ray-Driven Splatting, which uses ray-order accumulation, this method relies on hardware-accelerated alpha blending of projected primitives, often using multi-texture mapping. Choose it for fast, hardware-accelerated volume visualization. This technique partitions both 3D object space and 2D screen space dynamically to balance computational load across a cluster while minimizing redundant pixel compositing. It serves as a hybrid between pure sort-first (geometry processing balance) and sort-last (pixel accumulation balance) methods by performing rendering in object space but compositing in image space. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly addresses the trade-off between geometry replication and communication overhead by dynamically adjusting screen partitions based on predicted rendering costs. Choose it for cluster rendering of datasets larger than main memory. Parallel splatting distributes volumetric data to processing units, renders them in parallel to partial images, and composites these images in depth-sorted order. It solves the scalability problem of rendering large volumetric datasets by partitioning the workload across multiple processing nodes or cores. Unlike Hybrid Sort-First/Sort-Last Parallel Rendering, it relies on a master-node compositing stage and subvolume-based data distribution. Choose it for straightforward distributed rendering of large volumes. Definition: A rendering framework for regular or rectilinear volumes using axis-aligned splatting with three traversal orders, processing voxels in slices perpendicular to the axis most parallel to the viewing direction. Step: Process voxels in slices perpendicular to the major axis that is most parallel to the viewing direction. Attach a textured quad (proxy geometry) representing a splat at each voxel. Process splats in two stages: First, add contributions from splats in one slice to an intermediate buffer. Second, perform back-to-front or front-to-back composition of each slice in an accumulation buffer to yield final results (slice-by-slice composition). Comparison: Slice-by-slice composition uses an intermediate buffer and accumulation buffer. Splat-every-sample composition is an alternative that does not use an intermediate buffer. Hybrid and parallel splatting techniques emerged to address the scalability and visual fidelity limitations of early volume rendering methods. As volume datasets grew larger and hardware capabilities expanded, researchers sought ways to leverage parallel processing and hybrid rendering pipelines. The concept of hybrid sort-first/sort-last rendering was introduced to balance load in distributed environments. Hardware-accelerated axis-aligned splatting frameworks were developed to optimize the rendering of regular volumes by exploiting axis-aligned traversal and proxy geometry. Ray-driven splatting was proposed to handle perspective views more accurately by combining splatting with ray casting principles. Splat/mesh blending techniques were developed to seamlessly integrate point-based and polygonal representations in multi-resolution rendering. name: Ray-Driven Splatting
head: Hybrid Splatting/Ray Casting, Muller Yagel hybrid, Muller and Yagel hybrid, Ray-driven volume splatting
body: Ray-driven splatting is a hybrid volume rendering technique that combines object-order footprint precomputation with ray-order accumulation. It solves the performance degradation of traditional voxel-driven splatting under perspective projection by suspending splats in object space and intersecting them via spawned rays. Unlike traditional splatting, which struggles with perspective complexity and lacks standard ray-tracing optimizations, this method enables space leaping, early ray termination, and adaptive sampling. Inputs: Volumetric dataset (voxels with scalar values); camera parameters (viewing transform, projection type); splat kernel definition (footprint shape). Outputs: Image plane pixels (color and opacity). Data Structures: Voxel Grid: 3D array of scalar values. Splat Representation: Each voxel is associated with a spatial footprint (splat) suspended in object space. Steps: 1. Precompute Splat Extents: For each voxel, determine the spatial extent of its contribution (footprint) in object space. 2. Suspend Splats: Imagine splats as being suspended in object space, with one splat at every voxel. 3. Spawn Rays: For each pixel in the image plane, spawn a viewing ray to traverse the space. 4. Intersect and Address: Intersect and address the splats using an efficient and accurate method. 5. Accumulate: Accumulate pixels by shooting rays intersecting the splats in space, similar to ray casting. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Standard ray-splat intersection uses the parametric ray equation \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and a splat implicit surface f(\mathbf{p}) \leq 0. Parameters: Splat kernel shape and falloff (e.g., Gaussian, box). Ray traversal increment or step size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Traditional splatting requires complex screen-space transformations for perspective views, but ray-driven splatting avoids this by working in object space, making it inherently insensitive to perspective transform complexity. Intersection accuracy is critical, as the method relies on an "efficient and accurate way of intersecting and addressing the splats". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raydrivensplatting(volume, camera, kernel): image = zeros((camera.height, camera.width, 3)) splats = [createsplat(voxelpos, kernel) for voxelpos in volume.grid] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): rayo, rayd = camera.getray(x, y) acccolor = 0.0 accopacity = 0.0 for splat in splats: if rayintersectssplat(rayo, rayd, splat): contrib = evaluatekernel(splat, rayo, rayd) acccolor += contrib accopacity += 1.0 image[y, x] = acccolor return image This method rasterizes Ellipsoid-Wise Adaptive (EWA) splats on general-purpose graphics hardware by treating point primitives as screen-space squares and casting a viewing ray for each fragment to test inclusion within the splat's volume. It distinguishes itself from polygon-based bounding approximations by providing a correct upper bound to splat extents that remains stable for large splats near the near plane, while avoiding numerical instabilities of explicit conic centralization or matrix inversions. Choose it when hardware-accelerated fragment testing is preferred over CPU-side ray traversal. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. Measured performance was 30 seconds for the MRbrain dataset rendered with a 260^2 viewport on an SGI Indigo with 200 MHz. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. Requires storage for the voxel grid and splat representations. Strengths: Inherently insensitive to the complexity of the perspective viewing transform. Supports acceleration methods such as early ray termination and bounding volumes, which traditional voxel-driven splatting cannot benefit from. Enables the use of other ray tracing optimization techniques such as space leaping, adaptive screen sampling, or spatial acceleration structures. Offers competitive or superior performance for parallel projection, and superior performance for perspective projection compared to traditional splatting. Limitations: Requires efficient ray-splat intersection logic. Performance on older hardware was slow (30 seconds for a small viewport). When to use: When perspective projection is required and traditional splatting performance is insufficient, or when ray-tracing optimizations are desired. When not to use: When hardware acceleration for ray-splat intersection is unavailable and performance is critical, or when scene complexity is low enough that traditional splatting suffices. Ray-driven splatting was proposed by Müller and Yagel. It was introduced as a hybrid method to address the limitations of traditional voxel-driven splatting, particularly under perspective projection. The method merges the technique of splatting with principles of raycasting. It is related to earlier work on footprint evaluation for volume rendering by Westover, which established the forward mapping approach of distributing energy from input samples into space. name: Splat Rasterization via Raycasting
head: EWA Splat Rasterization via Ray-Plane Intersection, GPU-based raycasting of quadric surfaces, Splat rasterization
body: This method rasterizes Ellipsoid-Wise Adaptive (EWA) splats on general-purpose graphics hardware by treating point primitives as screen-space squares and casting a viewing ray for each fragment to test inclusion within the splat's volume. It distinguishes itself from polygon-based bounding approximations (e.g., Botsch et al.) by providing a correct upper bound to splat extents that remains stable for large splats near the near plane, while avoiding the numerical instabilities of explicit conic centralization or matrix inversions. Inputs: Splat parameters in camera space: center \mathbf{c}0, orthonormal basis vectors \mathbf{u}0, \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{w}0 (where \mathbf{w}0 is the normal, often reduced to zero length for the degenerate ellipsoid representation). Projection matrix P. Reconstruction kernel k(\cdot). Cutoff radius for the kernel. Outputs: Fragment weight wf and depth value for the splat at each sample position. Data Structures: Clip space plane representation: A plane is represented as a 4-vector \mathbf{h} = (hx, hy, hz, hw)^T. Splat matrix in clip space: \mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{u}' & \mathbf{v}' & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{c}' \end{pmatrix}, where \mathbf{u}', \mathbf{v}', \mathbf{c}' are the transformed basis vectors and center. Steps: 1. Rasterization Setup (Bounding Box Calculation): Compute the tight axis-aligned bounding rectangle (AABB) in screen space for the projected splat. This is done by treating the splat as a degenerate ellipsoid (unit sphere in local space with \mathbf{w}0 length zero). Map the viewing planes \mathbf{h}x = (-1, 0, 0, x)^T and \mathbf{h}y = (0, -1, 0, y)^T from clip space to the local splat coordinate system using the inverse transpose of the projection matrix: \bar{\mathbf{h}}c = (\mathbf{P}\mathbf{S})^{-T} \mathbf{h}c for c \in \{x, y\}. Solve for x and y such that the distance from the origin to the plane \bar{\mathbf{h}}x (or \bar{\mathbf{h}}y) in the local (u0, v0, w0) space is exactly 1 (tangential to the unit sphere). This avoids explicit inversion of \mathbf{S} or \mathbf{P}, ensuring stability for near-degenerate splats. The resulting bounds are x{1,2} = p1 \pm h1 and y{1,2} = p2 \pm h2. Clamp the bounding box extents hi to a lower bound of 1 to prevent division by zero or degenerate traversal. 2. Fragment Generation: Draw the splat using point primitives rendered as screen-space squares covering the computed bounding box. 3. Raycasting and Inclusion Test (Fragment Shader): For each fragment (x, y) within the bounding box: Represent the viewing ray through (x, y) as the intersection of two planes in clip space: \mathbf{h}x = (-1, 0, 0, x)^T and \mathbf{h}y = (0, -1, 0, y)^T. Transform these planes into the splat's local coordinate system using the precomputed matrix \mathbf{T} = (\mathbf{P}\mathbf{S})^{-T}: \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{T} \mathbf{h}x and \mathbf{l} = \mathbf{T} \mathbf{h}y. Intersect the projected planes \mathbf{k} and \mathbf{l} with the splat's object-space plane (defined by normal \mathbf{w}0 and center \mathbf{c}0) to find the intersection point \mathbf{s} in local space. Compute the squared distance \rho^2 from \mathbf{s} to the splat's center (origin in local space). 4. Weight Computation: If \rho^2 is within the specified cutoff radius, the sample is inside the splat. Compute the fragment weight: wf = k(\rho^2). Apply the EWA screen-space filter approximation by clamping \rho^2: \rho^2{\text{clamped}} = \min\left(\rho^2, k(x,y) - (\mathbf{c}{00} \cdot (x,y))^2\right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizesplat(splatcenter, splatbasis, projectionmatrix, kernel, cutoffradius): # 1. Setup: Compute clip-space splat matrix and inverse-transpose transform S = buildclipsplatmatrix(splatcenter, splatbasis, projectionmatrix) T = inversetranspose(projectionmatrix @ S) # Solve for tangency to unit sphere in local space to get AABB bounds x1, x2, y1, y2 = computetightaabb(T) # Clamp extents to lower bound of 1 x1, x2, y1, y2 = clamptominimum(x1, x2, y1, y2, 1.0) # 2 & 3. Fragment generation and raycasting for y in range(int(y1), int(y2) + 1): for x in range(int(x1), int(x2) + 1): # Clip-space planes defining the viewing ray hx = vec4(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, float(x)) hy = vec4(0.0, -1.0, 0.0, float(y)) # Transform to local splat space k = T @ hx l = T @ hy # Intersect with splat plane to find point s s = intersectplanes(k, l, splatbasis[2], splatcenter) # Squared distance to center rho2 = dot(s - splatcenter, s - splatcenter) # 4. Weight computation if rho2 <= cutoffradius: # EWA filter approximation clamping rho2clamped = min(rho2, kernel(x, y) - dot(vec2(c00x, c00y), vec2(x, y))2) wf = kernel(rho2clamped) outputfragment(x, y, wf) Parameters: Cutoff radius: Determined by the kernel support (e.g., radius where k(r^2) \approx 0). Lower bound for bounding box extents: 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near-plane splats: Polygon-based approximations (Botsch et al.) can underestimate extents for large splats near the near plane, causing artifacts. Degenerate splats: Explicit matrix inversions in conic-based approaches become unstable. Precision: The method relies on accurate plane transformations. Numerical stability is maintained by avoiding direct inversion of the splat matrix \mathbf{S}. Computes tight AABBs for EWA splats without matrix inversions, ensuring stability for near-degenerate cases. Choose when tight bounds are critical for performance. Implements the raycasting logic on GPUs using vertex/fragment shaders, optimizing for minimal instruction count (3 instructions). Choose for high-performance GPU rendering. Time Complexity: Per-fragment cost is low, requiring only a few MAD (Multiply-Accumulate) operations and a texture fetch in the fragment shader. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory; requires storing the transformed plane coefficients or matrix \mathbf{T} per splat. Performance: On NVIDIA hardware, this approach is highly efficient due to the low instruction count in the fragment shader. Strengths: Correct upper bounds for extents, stability for near-degenerate and near-plane splats, no explicit matrix inversions. Limitations: Higher per-fragment computational cost compared to simple square rasterization (though still low). Requires programmable shaders; not suitable for fixed-function pipelines without specialization. When to use: When rendering surface splats on GPUs where accuracy near the near plane and stability for degenerate splats are required. When not to use: When fixed-function hardware with specialized splat rasterization units is available, or when the absolute lowest per-fragment cost is prioritized over accuracy for large near-plane splats. This technique was developed to address the limitations of existing GPU splatting methods, which often relied on approximations that could fail for large splats near the near plane or become numerically unstable. It builds on the EWA splatting framework and adapts it for modern programmable graphics pipelines by leveraging raycasting within the fragment shader.
