name: LSD Block Sorting (Radix Sort)
head: LSD counting sort
body: LSD Block Sorting is a CPU-based radix sort that orders 32-bit integers by processing them in 8-bit blocks from least to most significant. It solves the depth-ordering requirement for volume rendering splatting by achieving linear time complexity through sequential counting sort passes, differing from distance-based bucketing methods by relying on exact integer comparison. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of N 32-bit unsigned integers representing face centroids or keys. Output: The array sorted in ascending order. Auxiliary: An auxiliary array of size N used to store intermediate results. Data Structures: input: Array of N 32-bit integers. output: Array of N 32-bit integers. counts: Array of 256 integers to store frequency for each 8-bit block value (0–255). Steps: 1. Count Pass: Traverse the input array once to count occurrences of all four 8-bit blocks (bits 0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31) for every element. 2. Sort Pass 1 (Bits 0–7): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 0–7 of the input array, writing the results to the auxiliary array. 3. Sort Pass 2 (Bits 8–15): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 8–15 of the auxiliary array (input), writing the results back to the original input array. 4. Sort Pass 3 (Bits 16–23): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 16–23 of the input array, writing the results to the auxiliary array. 5. Sort Pass 4 (Bits 24–31): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 24–31 of the auxiliary array (input), writing the final sorted results back to the original input array. Counting Sort Logic (per pass): For each pass, extract the relevant 8-bit block from each number using bitwise operations: key = (value >> shift) & 0xFF. Use these values as indices to accumulate frequencies in counts. Compute cumulative sums over counts to determine final positions in the target array. Place elements into the target array in reverse order to maintain stability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lsdblocksort(inputarray, n): outputarray = [0] n counts = [0] 256 # Pass 1: Count occurrences for all 4 blocks for i in range(n): val = inputarray[i] counts[(val >> 0) & 0xFF] += 1 counts[(val >> 8) & 0xFF] += 1 counts[(val >> 16) & 0xFF] += 1 counts[(val >> 24) & 0xFF] += 1 # Pass 2: Sort bits 0-7, write to outputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (inputarray[i] >> 0) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (inputarray[i] >> 0) & 0xFF outputarray[counts[key]-1] = inputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 # Pass 3: Sort bits 8-15, write to inputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (outputarray[i] >> 8) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (outputarray[i] >> 8) & 0xFF inputarray[counts[key]-1] = outputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 # Pass 4: Sort bits 16-23, write to outputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (inputarray[i] >> 16) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (inputarray[i] >> 16) & 0xFF outputarray[counts[key]-1] = inputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 # Pass 5: Sort bits 24-31, write to inputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (outputarray[i] >> 24) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (outputarray[i] >> 24) & 0xFF inputarray[counts[key]-1] = outputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 return inputarray Parameters: Block size: 8 bits. Number of passes: 5 total (1 counting pass + 4 sorting passes). Bit shifts: 0, 8, 16, 24. Edge Cases: Empty array (N=0): Return immediately. Precision: Uses 32-bit unsigned integers, avoiding floating-point precision issues. Degenerate input: Handles duplicate keys correctly due to stable counting sort implementation. A CPU-based sorting algorithm for volume rendering voxels that orders them back-to-front relative to the camera position. It solves the depth-sorting requirement for alpha blending or depth peeling by mapping voxel distances into fixed logarithmic buckets. It differs from Morton-order-based splat sorting (e.g., SVRaster) by relying solely on radial distance rather than ray-direction-dependent spatial locality, making it robust for arbitrary camera orientations but potentially less cache-friendly for static scenes. Time Complexity: Linear O(N), established by the constant five passes through the array. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the auxiliary array. Performance: A C++ implementation sorts upwards of 15 million faces per second. Strengths: Linear time complexity, simple implementation without machine-level optimizations, deterministic ordering. Limitations: Requires auxiliary memory, not in-place, performance can be improved with hardware-specific optimizations. The algorithm is described in Steve Callahan's MS thesis, "THE K-BUFFER AND ITS APPLICATIONS TO VOLUME RENDERING". It serves as a CPU fallback sort path for ordering face centroids in volume rendering applications, specifically within the k-buffer algorithm framework. name: Logarithmic Distance Bucket Sort
head: Back-to-Front Voxel Sorting, DistanceSorter
body: Logarithmic Distance Bucket Sort is a CPU-based sorting algorithm for volume rendering voxels that orders them back-to-front relative to the camera position. It solves the depth-sorting requirement for alpha blending or depth peeling by mapping voxel distances into fixed logarithmic buckets. It differs from Morton-order-based splat sorting (e.g., SVRaster) by relying solely on radial distance rather than ray-direction-dependent spatial locality. Inputs: positions: Float32Array of voxel centers, interleaved as [x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2,...]. cameraPosition: [number, number, number] representing the camera origin. outIndices: Optional pre-allocated Uint32Array for output. Outputs: Uint32Array of indices into positions, sorted such that voxels with larger distances from the camera appear first (back-to-front). Data Structures: The implementation maintains static state to avoid reallocation between frames: counts: Uint32Array of size BUCKETCOUNT (65536). Stores bucket occupancy during the first pass. starts: Uint32Array of size BUCKETCOUNT. Allocated for potential reuse, though the algorithm computes bucket positions in a local array during execution. lastCameraPosition: [number, number, number] or null. Stores the previous camera position for early-exit optimization. Parameters: BUCKETCOUNT: 65536 (256 \times 256). Formulas: Logarithmic distance: Li = \log(d^2), where d^2 = (x - cx)^2 + (y - cy)^2 + (z - cz)^2. Inverse scale factor: S = \frac{\text{BUCKET\COUNT} - 1}{\text{logRange} \parallel 1}, where \text{logRange} = \max(L) - \min(L). Bucket index: bi = \min(\text{BUCKET\COUNT} - 1, \lfloor (Li - \min(L)) \times S \rfloor). Algorithm Steps: 1. Early Exit Check: If lastCameraPosition exists, outIndices is provided, and outIndices.length equals numVoxels, calculate the dot product of lastCameraPosition and cameraPosition, compute their squared lengths, and evaluate \cos \theta = \frac{\mathbf{c}{last} \cdot \mathbf{c}{curr}}{\|\mathbf{c}{last}\| \|\mathbf{c}{curr}\|}. If | \cos \theta - 1 | < 0.01, return outIndices immediately. 2. Initialization: Determine numVoxels as positions.length / 3. Allocate or reuse indices array of size numVoxels. If counts or starts are null or have incorrect length, allocate them as Uint32Array of size BUCKETCOUNT; otherwise, clear counts by filling with zeros. 3. Log Distance Calculation: Initialize minDist to \infty and maxDist to -\infty. For each voxel i, extract coordinates (x, y, z), compute squared Euclidean distance d^2, compute logarithmic distance Li = \log(d^2), store it in a temporary logDistances array, and update minDist and maxDist. 4. Bucket Scaling: Calculate logRange = maxDist - minDist. Compute inverse scale factor S using the formula above. 5. First Pass (Counting): For each voxel i, calculate bucket index bi and increment counts[bi]. 6. Calculate Bucket Starts: Initialize position = 0. Iterate j from BUCKETCOUNT - 1 down to 0: set bucketStarts[j] = position and update position += counts[j]. This ensures back-to-front ordering. 7. Reset Counts: Clear counts array by filling with zeros. 8. Second Pass (Distribution): For each voxel i, calculate bucket index bi using the same formula as Step 5. Calculate output position p = \text{bucketStarts}[bi] + \text{counts}[bi], set indices[p] = i, and increment counts[bi]. 9. State Update: Store cameraPosition in lastCameraPosition for the next frame. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If logRange is 0 (all voxels at the same distance), the denominator in the scale factor defaults to 1 to prevent division by zero, effectively mapping all voxels to bucket 0. The early-exit condition assumes sort order remains valid if the camera direction has not changed significantly, but does not account for camera translation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math BUCKETCOUNT = 65536 counts = None starts = None lastcameraposition = None def sortvoxels(positions, cameraposition, outindices=None): global counts, starts, lastcameraposition numvoxels = len(positions) // 3 # Early exit optimization if (lastcameraposition is not None and outindices is not None and len(outindices) == numvoxels): lx, ly, lz = lastcameraposition cx, cy, cz = cameraposition dot = lx cx + ly cy + lz cz lensq1 = lx lx + ly ly + lz lz lensq2 = cx cx + cy cy + cz cz costheta = dot / math.sqrt(lensq1 lensq2) if abs(costheta - 1.0) < 0.01: return outindices # Initialize output if outindices is not None and len(outindices) == numvoxels: indices = outindices else: indices = [0] numvoxels # Represents Uint32Array # Initialize static arrays if counts is None or starts is None or len(counts) != BUCKETCOUNT: counts = [0] BUCKETCOUNT starts = [0] BUCKETCOUNT else: for i in range(BUCKETCOUNT): counts[i] = 0 # Calculate log distances logdistances = [0.0] numvoxels mindist = float('inf') maxdist = float('-inf') cx, cy, cz = cameraposition for i in range(numvoxels): x = positions[i 3] y = positions[i 3 + 1] z = positions[i 3 + 2] dx = x - cx dy = y - cy dz = z - cz distsq = dx dx + dy dy + dz dz logdist = math.log(distsq) logdistances[i] = logdist if logdist < mindist: mindist = logdist if logdist > maxdist: maxdist = logdist # Calculate scaling logrange = maxdist - mindist if logrange == 0: logrange = 1 distinv = (BUCKETCOUNT - 1) / logrange # First pass: Count for i in range(numvoxels): bucketidx = math.floor((logdistances[i] - mindist) distinv) if bucketidx >= BUCKETCOUNT: bucketidx = BUCKETCOUNT - 1 counts[bucketidx] += 1 # Calculate bucket starts (back-to-front) position = 0 bucketstarts = [0] BUCKETCOUNT for i in range(BUCKETCOUNT - 1, -1, -1): bucketstarts[i] = position position += counts[i] # Reset counts for second pass for i in range(BUCKETCOUNT): counts[i] = 0 # Second pass: Distribute for i in range(numvoxels): bucketidx = math.floor((logdistances[i] - mindist) distinv) if bucketidx >= BUCKETCOUNT: bucketidx = BUCKETCOUNT - 1 pos = bucketstarts[bucketidx] + counts[bucketidx] indices[pos] = i counts[bucketidx] += 1 # Update last camera position lastcameraposition = [cx, cy, cz] return indices Time Complexity: O(N + B), where N is the number of voxels and B is BUCKETCOUNT (65536). Memory Complexity: O(N + B). Performance: The use of logarithmic distance mapping compresses the dynamic range of distances, allowing a fixed number of buckets to provide reasonable depth resolution across varying scene scales. The early-exit optimization significantly reduces cost when the camera is static or moving very slightly. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory overhead compared to full radix sorts, effective early-exit for static scenes. Limitations: Does not account for spatial locality (unlike Morton/Z-order sorting), which may result in poorer cache performance during the subsequent splatting/composition phase compared to spatially coherent sorts. Sorting is strictly based on distance, so voxels at the same distance are not ordered relative to each other. This method is implemented in the unofficial WebGL port of Nvidia's SVRaster paper, specifically in the DistanceSorter class. It is designed as a CPU fallback or primary sorter for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering in WebGL contexts where GPU-based sorting might be complex or unavailable. It contrasts with the SVRaster paper's primary suggestion of using ray direction-dependent Morton ordering. Gaussian Splatting Alternative: WebGL Implementation of Nvidia's SVRaster, https://github.com/samuelm2/svraster-webgl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Cascaded 2-way Merge for Global Splat Sorting
body: Cascaded 2-way Merge is a GPU-based algorithm that merges pre-sorted splat lists from multiple independent renderers into a single globally depth-sorted order buffer using a cascaded binary merge tree. It solves the problem of incorrect depth ordering and excessive overdraw when rendering multiple active Gaussian Splat scenes in a unified viewport. Unlike per-renderer rendering, where each renderer handles its own depth sorting and draw calls independently, this method delegates sorting execution to a global sorter and rendering to a global renderer. The method operates on K active renderers, each providing a list of splats sorted by depth. The goal is to produce a single list of N = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \text{cnt}k splats sorted by depth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: K renderers. Renderer k has RemainingCount (\text{cnt}k) splats. Outputs: mglobalOrderBuffer containing the final sorted global order indices. Data Structures: The algorithm uses four scratch buffers and one global output buffer, all of size mtotalSplatCount: 1. mpackScratchOrders: GraphicsBuffer of type uint, name 'Gsplat.PackScratchOrders'. 2. mpackScratchDepths: GraphicsBuffer of type float, name 'Gsplat.PackScratchDepths'. 3. mmergeScratchOrders: GraphicsBuffer of type uint, name 'Gsplat.MergeScratchOrders'. 4. mmergeScratchDepths: GraphicsBuffer of type float, name 'Gsplat.MergeScratchDepths'. 5. mglobalOrderBuffer: GraphicsBuffer holding the final sorted global order, bound via kglobalOrderBuffer property. Parameters: krendererIdx: Index of the current renderer being packed. ksrcCount: Number of splats in the current renderer's range. kdstOffset: Offset in the destination scratch buffer for the current renderer's packed data. koffsetA: Offset of Source A (merged result) in the destination buffer. koffsetB: Offset of Source B (current renderer) in the destination buffer. kcountA: Number of elements in Source A. kcountB: Number of elements in Source B. Algorithm Steps: 1. Packing Phase: For each renderer k from 0 to K-1, if \text{cnt}k > 0, dispatch mkernelPackOrders with parameters krendererIdx = k, ksrcCount = cntk, kdstOffset = offk. The kernel reads raw orders/depths from res.OrderBuffer/res.InputKeys and writes to mpackScratchOrders/mpackScratchDepths at offset offk. 2. Initialization: Set mergedCount = activeGsplats[0].RemainingCount, mergedOffset = 0, mergedInPack = true. 3. Cascaded Merge Loop: Iterate k from 1 to K-1. Calculate total = mergedCount + cntk. Select Source A: if mergedInPack is true, use mpackScratchOrders/Depths; otherwise use mmergeScratchOrders/Depths. Select Source B: always mpackScratchOrders/Depths at offset offk. Select Destination: if k == K-1 (final pass), use mglobalOrderBuffer with dstDepths = null; otherwise use the buffer not currently holding the merged result. Dispatch merge kernel: use mkernelMergeTwo if final, otherwise mkernelMergeTwoWithDepth. Set parameters koffsetA = mergedOffset, koffsetB = offk, kcountA = mergedCount, kcountB = cntk, koutputOffset = 0. Bind sources and destination. Dispatch with thread count \lceil \text{total} / 256 \rceil. 4. Finalization: After the loop, set mtotalRemainingCount = mergedCount. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cascaded2waymerge(activegsplats, mtotalsplatcount, mglobalorderbuffer): K = len(activegsplats) if K < 2 or mglobalorderbuffer is None: return # Scratch buffers packorders = [0] mtotalsplatcount packdepths = [0.0] mtotalsplatcount mergeorders = [0] mtotalsplatcount mergedepths = [0.0] mtotalsplatcount # Step 1: Packing Phase offset = 0 for k in range(K): cntk = activegsplats[k].RemainingCount if cntk == 0: continue # Dispatch mkernelPackOrders: reads raw orders/depths from res.OrderBuffer/res.InputKeys # writes to mpackScratchOrders/mpackScratchDepths at offset off for i in range(cntk): packorders[offset + i] = activegsplats[k].OrderBuffer[i] packdepths[offset + i] = activegsplats[k].InputKeys[i] offset += cntk # Step 2: Initialization mergedcount = activegsplats[0].RemainingCount mergedoffset = 0 mergedinpack = True # Step 3: Cascaded Merge Loop for k in range(1, K): cntk = activegsplats[k].RemainingCount if cntk == 0: continue total = mergedcount + cntk isfinal = (k == K - 1) # Select Source A (current merged result) if mergedinpack: srcaorders, srcadepths = packorders, packdepths else: srcaorders, srcadepths = mergeorders, mergedepths # Select Source B (renderer k's data) srcboffset = offset - cntk srcborders, srcbdepths = packorders, packdepths # Select Destination if isfinal: dstorders = mglobalorderbuffer dstdepths = None else: if mergedinpack: dstorders, dstdepths = mergeorders, mergedepths else: dstorders, dstdepths = packorders, packdepths # Dispatch merge kernel koffseta = mergedoffset koffsetb = srcboffset kcounta = mergedcount kcountb = cntk koutputoffset = 0 threadcount = (total + 255) // 256 if isfinal: # Dispatch mkernelMergeTwo (final pass, no depth output) pass # Sources do not provide kernel internals else: # Dispatch mkernelMergeTwoWithDepth (intermediate passes, outputs depths) pass # Sources do not provide kernel internals # Update State mergedcount = total mergedoffset = 0 mergedinpack = not mergedinpack # Step 4: Finalization mtotalremainingcount = mergedcount Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If K < 2 or mglobalOrderBuffer is null, the merge process returns immediately without performing any merges. If a renderer's count is 0, it is skipped during the packing phase. The algorithm requires GPU subgroups/wave operations, which are only available in D3D12, Metal, or Vulkan graphics APIs. WebGPU supports subgroups but Unity has not implemented it for this feature. Global sort is all-or-nothing: presence of any uncompressed renderer forces fallback to per-renderer sorting. Global Splat Merge and Rendering is a technique that merges multiple independent Gaussian Splat renderers into a single global draw call by packing their splat data, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and depth/order information into shared global buffers, then performing a cascaded merge of depth-sorted orders. It merges two or more active Gaussian splat renderers into a single globally depth-sorted draw call to reduce overdraw and improve sorting accuracy across scenes. Unlike per-renderer rendering, where each renderer handles its own depth sorting and draw calls independently, this method delegates sorting execution to a global sorter and rendering to a global renderer, triggered when camera movement exceeds thresholds or refresh rate dictates. Global Depth Sorting for 3DGS sorts Gaussians across multiple renderers globally using GPU subgroups/waves to maintain correct depth ordering in a unified scene. It is activated by the EnableGlobalSort boolean setting, which requires all active renderers to use compressed assets. A key pitfall is that global sort is all-or-nothing: the presence of any uncompressed renderer forces a fallback to per-renderer sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the GPU's subgroup/wave support. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces overdraw, improves sorting accuracy across scenes, enables unified rendering of multiple scenes. Limitations: Requires compressed assets for all renderers, limited to specific graphics APIs, all-or-nothing activation. When to use: When rendering multiple Gaussian Splat scenes in a single viewport with overlapping depth ranges. When not to use: When renderers use uncompressed assets, or when the target platform does not support GPU subgroups (e.g., older APIs, WebGPU in Unity). The method originates from the wuyize25/gsplat-unity project. It builds on the b0nes164/GPUSorting library for GPU-based sorting primitives. The technique was developed to address the limitations of per-renderer sorting in multi-scene environments, providing a more efficient and accurate way to composite multiple Gaussian Splat scenes. wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Global Splat Merge and Rendering
head: Global Splat Sort & Merge, GsplatGlobalRenderer, Merged Draw
body: Global Splat Merge and Rendering is a technique that merges multiple independent Gaussian Splat renderers into a single global draw call by packing their splat data, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and depth/order information into shared global buffers, then performing a cascaded merge of depth-sorted orders. It merges two or more active Gaussian splat renderers into a single globally depth-sorted draw call to reduce overdraw and improve sorting accuracy across scenes. Unlike per-renderer rendering, where each renderer handles its own depth sorting and draw calls independently, this method delegates sorting execution to a global sorter and rendering to a global renderer, triggered when camera movement exceeds thresholds or refresh rate dictates. Inputs: A set of active Gaussian Splat renderers, each providing packed splat data, SH coefficients, and local depth-sorted order buffers. Camera state (translation and rotation) to determine if sorting needs refresh. Configuration parameters: EnableGlobalSort, MaxRenderOrder, CameraTranslationRefreshTreshold, CameraRotationRefreshTreshold. Outputs: A single globally depth-sorted order buffer. A single draw call rendering all active splats with correct depth ordering. The method relies on several global buffers allocated based on the total number of splats and the maximum SH bands among all active renderers. RendererParams struct (16-byte stride per renderer): Brightness: float (4 bytes) ScaleFactor: float (4 bytes) GammaToLinear: uint (4 bytes) SHDegree: uint (4 bytes). Global Buffers: mglobalPackedBuffer: uint[4] per splat. Stores packed splat data (center xyz, scale, rgba, quaternion). mglobalOrderBuffer: uint per splat. Stores the global render order. mrendererOffsetsBuffer: uint per active renderer. Stores the starting index in the global buffers for each renderer. mrendererTransformsBuffer: float[16] per renderer. Stores the 4x4 transformation matrix for each renderer. mrendererParamsBuffer: 16 bytes per renderer. Stores RendererParams. mglobalSH1Buffer: uint[2] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 1). mglobalSH2Buffer: uint[4] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 2). mglobalSH3Buffer: uint[4] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 3). mglobalSH4Buffer: uint[4] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 4). Scratch Buffers: mpackScratchOrders: Used during order packing. mpackScratchDepths: Used during depth packing. mmergeScratchOrders: Used during cascaded merge. mmergeScratchDepths: Used during cascaded merge. 1. Initialize Kernels: Find kernel indices for PackRendererOrders, MergeTwo, MergeTwoWithDepth in MergeShader, and CopyUint4, CopyUint2 in CopyBufferShader. 2. Check Dirty State: If mglobalBuffersDirty is true or ActiveSplatCountsChanged is true, proceed to rebuild global buffers. 3. Calculate Totals: Compute mtotalSplatCount as the sum of splat counts from all active renderers. Compute mrendererOffsets for each active renderer k as the cumulative sum of splat counts of previous renderers. Determine mglobalSHBands as the maximum SH bands among all active splats. 4. Allocate Global Buffers: Create GraphicsBuffers for mglobalPackedBuffer, mglobalOrderBuffer, mrendererOffsetsBuffer, mrendererTransformsBuffer, mrendererParamsBuffer, and SH buffers (mglobalSH1Buffer to mglobalSH4Buffer) based on mglobalSHBands. Set mrendererOffsetsBuffer data. 5. Copy Per-Renderer Data: For each active renderer k, copy its packed splat data, SH coefficients, and order data into the global buffer sub-ranges starting at mrendererOffsets[k]. 6. Dispatch Merge Passes: Use PackRendererOrders to pack orders/depths, then MergeTwo or MergeTwoWithDepth for cascaded merging of orders across renderers using scratch buffers (mpackScratchOrders, mpackScratchDepths, mmergeScratchOrders, mmergeScratchDepths). 7. Render: Delegate rendering to GsplatGlobalRenderer using the globally sorted order buffer. EnableGlobalSort: Boolean flag that activates the global merge pipeline. MaxRenderOrder: Maximum depth sorting layers allowed; range 1 to 20. CameraTranslationRefreshTreshold: Distance threshold in world units that forces recomputation of sorting and cutouts regardless of refresh rate; range 0.05 to 1.0, default 0.2. CameraRotationRefreshTreshold: Rotation threshold in degrees that forces recomputation of sorting and cutouts regardless of refresh rate; range 0.2 to 30.0, default 10. kmergePassName: String constant "Gsplat.MergeKWay" used for GPU profiling samples. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocatebuffer(size): return [0] size def dispatchcomputeshader(kernelfunc, numgroups, args): kernelfunc(numgroups, args) def CameraMovedSignificantly(camerastate, transthreshold, rotthreshold): return camerastate.translationdelta > transthreshold or camerastate.rotationdeltadeg > rotthreshold def PackRendererOrders(numgroups, packedbuffer, orderbuffer, depthbuffer, rendereroffsets, renderercounts): # GPU kernel: packs local orders/depths into scratch buffers pass def MergeTwo(numgroups, src1orders, src1depths, src2orders, src2depths, dstorders, dstdepths): # GPU kernel: merges two sorted lists pass def GsplatGlobalRendererDraw(packedbuffer, orderbuffer, transformsbuffer, paramsbuffer, shbuffers): # GPU kernel: renders all splats in global order pass def GlobalSplatMergeAndRender(activerenderers, camerastate, settings): if not settings.EnableGlobalSort: for renderer in activerenderers: renderer.Render() return if settings.mglobalBuffersDirty or settings.ActiveSplatCountsChanged: mtotalSplatCount = sum(r.SplatCount for r in activerenderers) mrendererOffsets = [] offset = 0 for r in activerenderers: mrendererOffsets.append(offset) offset += r.SplatCount mglobalSHBands = max((r.GsplatAsset.SHBands if r.GsplatAsset else 0) for r in activerenderers) mglobalPackedBuffer = allocatebuffer(mtotalSplatCount 4) mglobalOrderBuffer = allocatebuffer(mtotalSplatCount) mrendererOffsetsBuffer = allocatebuffer(len(activerenderers)) mrendererTransformsBuffer = allocatebuffer(len(activerenderers) 16) mrendererParamsBuffer = allocatebuffer(len(activerenderers) 16) mglobalSH1Buffer = allocatebuffer(mtotalSplatCount 2) if mglobalSHBands >= 1 else None mglobalSH2Buffer = allocatebuffer(mtotalSplatCount 4) if mglobalSHBands >= 2 else None mglobalSH3Buffer = allocatebuffer(mtotalSplatCount 4) if mglobalSHBands >= 3 else None mglobalSH4Buffer = allocatebuffer(mtotalSplatCount 4) if mglobalSHBands >= 4 else None mrendererOffsetsBuffer[:] = mrendererOffsets for k, renderer in enumerate(activerenderers): startidx = mrendererOffsets[k] count = renderer.SplatCount mglobalPackedBuffer[startidx 4: (startidx + count) 4] = renderer.PackedSplatsBuffer[:] if renderer.GsplatAsset.SHBands >= 1 and mglobalSH1Buffer is not None: mglobalSH1Buffer[startidx 2: (startidx + count) 2] = renderer.PackedSH1Buffer[:] if renderer.GsplatAsset.SHBands >= 2 and mglobalSH2Buffer is not None: mglobalSH2Buffer[startidx 4: (startidx + count) 4] = renderer.PackedSH2Buffer[:] if renderer.GsplatAsset.SHBands >= 3 and mglobalSH3Buffer is not None: mglobalSH3Buffer[startidx 4: (startidx + count) 4] = renderer.PackedSH3Buffer[:] if renderer.GsplatAsset.SHBands >= 4 and mglobalSH4Buffer is not None: mglobalSH4Buffer[startidx 4: (startidx + count) 4] = renderer.PackedSH4Buffer[:] mrendererTransformsBuffer[k 16: (k + 1) 16] = renderer.TransformMatrix[:] params = [renderer.Brightness, renderer.ScaleFactor, renderer.GammaToLinear, renderer.SHDegree] mrendererParamsBuffer[k 16: (k + 1) 16] = params settings.mglobalBuffersDirty = False settings.ActiveSplatCountsChanged = False if CameraMovedSignificantly(camerastate, settings.CameraTranslationRefreshTreshold, settings.CameraRotationRefreshTreshold): dispatchcomputeshader(PackRendererOrders, (mtotalSplatCount + 255) // 256, mglobalPackedBuffer, mglobalOrderBuffer, settings.mpackScratchDepths, mrendererOffsets, [r.SplatCount for r in activerenderers]) # Cascaded binary merge tree (log2(K) passes) numrenderers = len(activerenderers) currentorders = [mglobalOrderBuffer[i count: (i + 1) count] for i, count in enumerate([r.SplatCount for r in activerenderers])] currentdepths = [settings.mpackScratchDepths[i count: (i + 1) count] for i, count in enumerate([r.SplatCount for r in activerenderers])] while numrenderers > 1: nextorders = [] nextdepths = [] for i in range(0, numrenderers, 2): if i + 1 < numrenderers: mergedorder = allocatebuffer(len(currentorders[i]) + len(currentorders[i+1])) mergeddepth = allocatebuffer(len(currentdepths[i]) + len(currentdepths[i+1])) dispatchcomputeshader(MergeTwo, (len(mergedorder) + 255) // 256, currentorders[i], currentdepths[i], currentorders[i+1], currentdepths[i+1], mergedorder, mergeddepth) nextorders.append(mergedorder) nextdepths.append(mergeddepth) else: nextorders.append(currentorders[i]) nextdepths.append(currentdepths[i]) currentorders = nextorders currentdepths = nextdepths numrenderers = len(currentorders) finalorder = currentorders[0] GsplatGlobalRendererDraw(mglobalPackedBuffer, finalorder, mrendererTransformsBuffer, mrendererParamsBuffer, [mglobalSH1Buffer, mglobalSH2Buffer, mglobalSH3Buffer, mglobalSH4Buffer]) Async Upload Growth: If a renderer uses AsyncUpload and its SplatCount grows frame-to-frame, the global buffers must be rebuilt when the count changes. Otherwise, the global sub-ranges only contain splats present at the first build, leaving the merge to read stale/under-sized buffers. Uncompressed Assets: If any active renderer uses an uncompressed asset, the whole scene falls back to per-renderer rendering, even if EnableGlobalSort is true. Time Complexity: Dominated by the cascaded merge pass, which is O(N \log K) where N is the total number of splats and K is the number of active renderers. The merge is performed on the GPU using compute shaders. Memory Complexity: O(N) for global buffers, where N is the total number of splats. Additional memory for scratch buffers during merge is required. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of active renderers and total splat count. The cascaded merge tree depth increases logarithmically with the number of renderers. Strengths: Reduces overdraw by globally sorting splats across multiple renderers. Improves sorting accuracy across scenes. Limitations: Requires all active renderers to use compressed assets. Rebuilding global buffers can be expensive if splat counts change frequently. When to Use: When rendering multiple Gaussian Splat scenes in a single frame and global depth sorting is desired. When Not to Use: When renderers use uncompressed assets, or when the number of active renderers is small and per-renderer sorting is sufficient. The method is part of the Gsplat-Unity project, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unity. It builds on Cascaded 2-way Merge for Global Splat Sorting to handle cross-renderer depth ordering. The project is maintained by Yize Wu and Arthur Aillet. wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Half-Angle Slicing with Odd-Even Merge Sort
head: Half angle slicing technique
body: Half-angle slicing is a GPU-based volume rendering technique for particle systems that sorts particles along a view-dependent axis (the half-angle between the light and view directions) using an odd-even merge sort, then renders them in slices to handle transparency and shadows correctly. It sets itself apart from standard front-to-back splatting by decoupling the sorting axis from the view direction, allowing for efficient accumulation of opacity from the light's perspective to compute accurate volumetric shadows in a single pass. Unlike Bitonic Sort which sorts strictly by depth, this method sorts by a projected coordinate that aligns with the light transport, enabling the "slicing" strategy where particles are rendered in batches to build a light-space opacity texture. The method operates in three main phases: simulation, GPU-based sorting, and slice-based rendering with opacity accumulation. Inputs: Particle positions, velocities, lifetimes, and spawn data; camera view/projection matrices; light view/projection matrices; time delta. Outputs: Final composited image with volumetric shadows; opacity texture for light-space accumulation. The implementation relies on specific Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) and textures, typically stored in a grid layout for efficient GPU access. 1. Simulation FBOs (Ping-Pong): Two FBOs, mSimulationFbo[0] and mSimulationFbo[1]. Size: PARTICLES x PARTICLES (256x256). Internal Format: GLRGBA32F. Data Type: GLFLOAT. Purpose: Store particle state (position, velocity, etc.) for simulation updates. No depth buffer. 2. Particle Data Texture: Size: PARTICLES x PARTICLES (256x256). Format: GLRGBA32F. Layout: Each texel vec4 contains position.x, position.y, position.z, and lifetime (or spawn data). 3. Opacity FBO: One FBO. Size: OPACITYTEXTURERESOLUTION x OPACITYTEXTURERESOLUTION (1024x1024). Internal Format: GLRGBA. Data Type: GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. Purpose: Accumulate opacity from the light's perspective. No depth buffer. PARTICLES: Square root of total particle count. Default: 256. mMaxParticleCount: Total particles = PARTICLES PARTICLES. Default: 65536. SLICES: Number of depth slices for rendering. Default: 128. OPACITYTEXTURERESOLUTION: Resolution of the light-space opacity texture. Default: 1024. 1. Calculate Half-Vector for Sorting: Determine the sorting axis based on the angle between the view direction (\mathbf{v}) and the light direction (\mathbf{l}). If \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{l} > 0.0: \mathbf{halfVector} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}) mFlipped = \text{false} Else: \mathbf{halfVector} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{v}) mFlipped = \text{true} 2. Simulate Particle Movement: Bind the previous frame's position texture (mSimulationFbo[1 - mCurrent]) to texture unit 0. Bind the spawn data texture to texture unit 1. Execute the simulation shader for 1 frame (or BASELIFETIME / PRESIMULATIONDELTATIME frames on the first frame to initialize). Update mCurrent to swap ping-pong buffers. 3. Execute Odd-Even Merge Sort: Sort the particles based on their projection onto the \mathbf{halfVector}. Calculate total sort steps: m{\text{TotalSortSteps}} = \frac{\log2(m{\text{MaxParticleCount}}) \cdot (\log2(m{\text{MaxParticleCount}}) + 1)}{2} Loop mTotalSortSteps times: Swap read/write FBOs: mCurrent = 1 - mCurrent. Decrement mSortPass. If mSortPass < 0: Increment mSortStage. Set mSortPass = mSortStage. Bind source texture to unit 0. Pass uniforms to sort shader: uPass = float(1 << mSortPass) uStage = float(1 << mSortStage). Decrement mSortStepsLeft. If it reaches 0, reset counters (mSortPass, mSortStage, mSortStepsLeft). 4. Render Slices (View Pass): Loop i from 0 to SLICES - 1. Determine particle range: startIndex = i (mMaxParticleCount / SLICES) count = mMaxParticleCount / SLICES. Set camera matrices to view space. Bind opacity texture to unit 1. Set blend mode: If mFlipped is true: GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE Else: GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA. Draw the current slice of particles using point sprites. 5. Opacity Pass (Light View): Bind the opacity FBO. Set matrices to light camera (light view/projection). Draw the same particle slice with blend mode GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA to accumulate opacity into the opacity texture. 6. Final Composite: Draw the floor and fullscreen quad. Bind the accumulated opacity texture (from step 5) to unit 2. Use the light view projection matrix to sample the opacity texture for shadow calculation. Blend mode: GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math GLONE = 1 GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA = 771 GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA = 774 def bindtexture(unit, tex): textureunit[unit] = tex def setblend(srcfactor, dstfactor): blendsrc = srcfactor blenddst = dstfactor def drawparticles(startindex, count): for idx in range(startindex, startindex + count): rasterizeparticle(idx) def bindframebuffer(fbo): currentfbo = fbo def setcameramatrices(viewmat, projmat): activeviewmatrix = viewmat activeprojmatrix = projmat def drawfloorandquad(): rasterizefloor() rasterizefullscreenquad() def halfangleslicing(viewdir, lightdir, dt, time): # 1. Calculate Half-Vector dotval = math.dot(math.normalize(viewdir), math.normalize(lightdir)) if dotval > 0.0: halfvec = math.normalize(lightdir + viewdir) flipped = False else: halfvec = math.normalize(lightdir - viewdir) flipped = True # 2. Simulation bindtexture(0, simfbo[1 - current]) bindtexture(1, spawndatatex) runsimulationshader(1) # or BASELIFETIME / PRESIMULATIONDELTATIME on first frame current = 1 - current # 3. Odd-Even Merge Sort totalsteps = (math.log2(maxparticles) (math.log2(maxparticles) + 1)) / 2 sortpass = 0 sortstage = 0 sortstepsleft = totalsteps for in range(totalsteps): current = 1 - current sortpass -= 1 if sortpass < 0: sortstage += 1 sortpass = sortstage bindtexture(0, simfbo[current]) passuniforms(upass=1 << sortpass, ustage=1 << sortstage) runsortshader() sortstepsleft -= 1 if sortstepsleft == 0: sortpass = 0 sortstage = 0 sortstepsleft = totalsteps # 4. Render Slices & 5. Opacity Accumulation for i in range(slices): startidx = i (maxparticles // slices) count = maxparticles // slices # View Pass setcameramatrices(viewmatrix, projmatrix) bindtexture(1, opacitytex) if flipped: setblend(GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE) else: setblend(GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA) drawparticles(startidx, count) # Light View Pass (Opacity Accumulation) bindframebuffer(opacityfbo) setcameramatrices(lightviewmatrix, lightprojmatrix) setblend(GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA) drawparticles(startidx, count) bindframebuffer(defaultfbo) # 6. Final Composite setcameramatrices(viewmatrix, projmatrix) bindtexture(2, opacitytex) setblend(GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE) drawfloorandquad() Precision: The sorting relies on floating-point comparisons. Boundaries: When sampling the opacity texture in the final composite, check for coordinates outside [0, 1] to avoid wrapping artifacts. Degenerate Input: If particles are exactly on the sorting plane, the sort stability depends on the implementation of the odd-even merge sort shader. This variant extends the half-angle slicing technique to handle the gradual angular spreading of light during multiple scattering events, which is essential for capturing fine angularly dependent effects with large forward-scattering particles. It models the angular dispersion of light experiencing its first few scattering events for efficient single-pass rendering on programmable graphics hardware. A key pitfall in this approximation is the presence of the light term L\lambda on both sides of the governing equation (Equation 7 in the source), requiring separation of intensity and distribution to solve iteratively or approximately. Time Complexity: The sorting phase uses odd-even merge sort, which requires O(\log^2 N) steps for N particles. The rendering phase loops over SLICES batches. Memory Complexity: Requires O(N) storage for particle data and O(R^2) for the opacity texture, where R is the opacity texture resolution. Performance: The method is designed for GPU acceleration, leveraging parallel sorting and rasterization. Strengths: Handles volumetric shadows efficiently; works well with particle systems. Limitations: Sorting is view-dependent and must be recomputed if the camera or light moves significantly; limited to particle-based volumes. The half-angle slicing technique was originally described by Kniss et al. [KPHE02] for rendering volumetric effects. The specific implementation using GPU-based odd-even merge sort and ping-pong FBOs for particle shadows is based on a webGL implementation by David Li, which in turn was ported from a NVIDIA article on smoke particles. The technique is used in real-time volume rendering, particularly for atmospheric phenomena and particle systems where shadows are required. name: Bitonic Sort
head: ABisort, Bitonic Sort for GPGPU, Govindaraju et al. Bitonic Sort, Particle Sorting (Bitonic Sort)
body: Bitonic Sort is a data-independent network sorting algorithm used on the GPU to achieve exact depth ordering of splatted voxels for every frame. It is chosen over partial-ordering methods like Odd-Even Merge Sort because volume rendering requires strict front-to-back or back-to-front ordering per frame to correctly composite transparency. It is preferred over Adaptive Bitonic Sort (ABisort) in some implementations due to library accessibility and ease of adaptation, despite ABisort having potentially better theoretical complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of view-transformed voxels already resident in GPU memory, typically stored in a texture (View Transformed Voxels Texture). Each voxel is represented as a <key, value> pair, where the key is the depth value b and the value is the voxel index. Output: A sorted array of voxels stored in a texture (Depth-Sorted Voxels Texture), ordered by depth. Data Structures: The algorithm uses the Multiple Render Target (MRT) extension to store keys and values in separate render targets. A one-to-one correspondence exists between the key texture and the value texture. To optimize memory, four <key, value> instances can be packed into a single RGBA texel. Parameters: uPass: Current pass number in the sort algorithm. uStage: Current stage number within the pass. uHalfVector: The half-angle vector used for sorting particles. N: Total number of particles/voxels to sort. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: If the sorting direction needs to be reversed (e.g., due to camera movement), reset pass and stage counters. 2. Ping-Pong Buffering: Use two framebuffers (current and previous) to swap read/write roles between passes. 3. Comparison Logic: For each element at index i, determine the comparison direction and partner index based on the current pass and stage. 4. Fetch and Compare: Fetch the partner data and perform a comparison using the depth key and the half-vector. 5. Write Result: Write the sorted result to the appropriate render target. 6. Finalization: After all passes, a fragment shader fills the final Depth-Sorted Voxels Texture from the sorted render targets. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode describes the fragment shader logic for a single comparison step in the Bitonic Sort network. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bitonicsortstep(i, uPass, uStage, uHalfVector, prevPositions): # 1. Determine comparison direction and partner offset # The direction depends on the stage and pass in the bitonic network compare = determinecomparedirection(uPass, uStage, i) # 2. Calculate partner address # uPass represents the distance to the partner in the bitonic sequence adr = i + compare uPass # 3. Fetch data from previous render target # Fetch key (depth) and value (index) for self and partner selfdata = prevPositions.sample(i) partnerdata = prevPositions.sample(adr) selfkey = selfdata.key # Depth value b selfval = selfdata.value # Voxel index partnerkey = partnerdata.key partnerval = partnerdata.value # 4. Perform comparison using dot product with half vector # This logic implements the bitonic merge step # If selfProjectedLength compare < partnerProjectedLength compare, keep self # Note: 'compare' acts as a sign multiplier for the direction lhs = selfkey compare rhs = partnerkey compare if lhs < rhs: # Self is "smaller" (or in correct order relative to direction) outputkey = selfkey outputval = selfval else: # Partner is "smaller" outputkey = partnerkey outputval = partnerval return outputkey, outputval def determinecomparedirection(uPass, uStage, i): # Standard Bitonic Sort logic for determining swap direction # This is a placeholder for the specific bitonic network index logic # which depends on the binary representation of i relative to stage/pass # In standard bitonic sort, direction is determined by the bit at position uStage # within the block defined by uPass. # Standard bitonic sort uses the bit at index uStage of i to determine direction. # If the bit is 0, compare with lower; if 1, compare with higher. # The 'compare' variable here likely represents +1 or -1. if (i >> uStage) & 1: return -1 # Compare with higher index else: return 1 # Compare with lower index Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Independence: Unlike Quicksort, Bitonic Sort does not branch on data values, making it suitable for GPU SIMD/SIMT architectures but potentially slower for small datasets due to fixed work. Exact Ordering: Requires all passes to complete for exact ordering; partial results are insufficient for correct compositing. Memory Packing: Packing four values per texel requires careful handling of texture coordinates and swizzling to ensure correct key/value alignment. Time Complexity: O(N \log^2 N) comparisons and swaps. Adaptive Bitonic Sort (ABisort) claims O((N \log N)/P) complexity, where P is the number of stream processors. Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce 7800, Govindaraju's Bitonic Sort was approximately twice as fast as the best CPU QuickSort implementation at the time of the source. Strengths: Provides exact ordering every frame; highly parallelizable; cache-efficient memory access patterns in optimized implementations. Limitations: Fixed number of operations regardless of data distribution; not suitable for dynamic datasets where partial ordering is acceptable (Odd-Even Merge Sort is preferred there). When to Use: When exact depth sorting is required for every frame in volume splatting. When Not to Use: When partial ordering is sufficient (e.g., particle systems spread over multiple frames) or when adaptive sorting performance is critical and library access permits. Bitonic Sort was originally developed as a network sorting algorithm. In the context of GPU volume rendering, Govindaraju et al. [GRHM05] improved early implementations [KW05] by introducing cache-efficient memory accesses, leading to high performance on GPUs like the NVIDIA GeForce 7800. Gress and Zachmann [GZ06] later designed Adaptive Bitonic Sort (ABisort) with optimal complexity. In the specific implementation described in the sources, Govindaraju's method was chosen over ABisort due to the accessibility and adaptability of the library. name: Index Sorting
head: Key-index pair sorting
body: Index sorting is a sorting variant that produces a permutation of indices rather than reordering data values, allowing related information to be traced back to the original array. It solves the problem of determining related information from the sorted index, which is required because sorting values alone is insufficient for real applications. Unlike methods that pack keys and indices into a single register to save memory, index sorting keeps key counting independent from index values, preserving full precision and index range (up to 4 billion pairs on 32-bit hardware). Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of keys K of size n, and an initial index array I of size n. Output: A sorted permutation array P (indices). Data Structures: K: Array of keys, typically 32-bit integers or floats. I: Array of indices, initialized as I[i] = i for 0 \le i < n. P: Permutation array, same size as K, storing the sorted indices. Steps: 1. Initialize Index Array: Generate a companion index array I where I[i] = i. This indicates the original position of each value in K. 2. Perform Key Sorting: Execute a radix sort algorithm on the key array K to generate a permutation array P. The sorting logic operates independently on the keys; the indices in I are not involved in the comparison or counting phases. 3. Shuffle Indices: Apply the permutation P to the index array I to produce the final sorted index array. This step rearranges the indices according to the sorted order of the keys. Formula: I{sorted}[j] = I[P[j]] for 0 \le j < n. 4. Access Data: To retrieve the original data associated with the j-th sorted element, use the value I{sorted}[j] as an offset into the original data arrays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def indexsort(keys, n): # Step 1: Initialize index array indices = [i for i in range(n)] # Step 2: Sort keys to get permutation # Standard radix sort permutation generation. # The sources do not provide the internal kernel, so this step is marked as a standard operation. # In a full implementation, this would use counting sort passes to compute # prefix sums and place indices into the permutation array based on key digits. permutation = [0] n #... radix sort logic to fill permutation... # Step 3: Shuffle indices with the permutation sortedindices = [0] n for j in range(n): sortedindices[j] = indices[permutation[j]] return sortedindices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Misses: Index sorting exacerbates cache misses compared to value sorting because the shuffling step involves non-coalesced memory access patterns when applying the permutation to the indices. Memory Bandwidth: The additional shuffle step increases memory bandwidth requirements. Precision: Combining keys and indices into a single register reduces precision and index range. Index sorting avoids this by keeping them separate, allowing full 32-bit index ranges. Distance-aware index sorting optimizes sorting by computing distance data once and using an auxiliary structure to avoid redundant calculations during comparison. It computes the distance squared from the origin and the index for all blocks, sorts the auxiliary structure, and maps the sorted indices back to the original blocks. The auxiliary structure is a DistanceIndexPair containing a float mdistanceSquaredFromOrigin and an int mindex. Radix sort is asymptotically faster and not comparison-based, potentially replacing a custom BlockDistanceComparator. Time Complexity: Typically 1.5 to 1.8 times slower than value sorting due to non-coalesced shuffling. Optimization: Using a coalesced radix index sorting scheme reduces the performance penalty to a negligible factor of about 1.1. Memory: Requires storage for both the key array and the index array, doubling the memory footprint compared to sorting keys alone if the original data is not needed in place. Strengths: Preserves full precision and index range; simple to implement on top of existing radix sort kernels. Limitations: Higher memory bandwidth usage; potential for cache thrashing during the shuffle phase if not optimized. Index sorting was discussed in the context of GPU-based parallel sorting, specifically highlighting its application in scenarios where data association is crucial. The method was analyzed on NVIDIA GTX 280 hardware, demonstrating that while naive index sorting suffers from performance penalties, optimized coalesced approaches mitigate these issues. name: Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS)
head: FLAS, Fast Linear Assignment Sorting, PLAS (Fast Linear Assignment Sorting), PLAS sorting, Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids sorting
body: Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS) is a highly parallel 2D sorting algorithm designed to organize millions of high-dimensional Gaussian splat attributes into a 2D grid layout. It solves the problem of spatial correlation for compression by reordering Gaussian attribute vectors such that similar positions and colors share similar values in other attributes, leveraging the rendering invariance to sequential ordering. Unlike traditional grid-sorting algorithms like Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) or Linear Assignment Sorting (LAS) which are inadequate for millions of items, PLAS adapts these methods to enable continuous sorting during training without inflating duration. It sets itself apart by using a block-wise linear assignment approach with random block shifting to avoid local minima and ensure border coverage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussian splats, each defined by 59 attributes: 3D position (x,y,z), scale (sx,sy,sz), rotation (w,qx,qy,qz), opacity (\alpha), SH-DC coefficients (f{dc}, 3 values), and SH-AC coefficients (f{ac}, 45 values). Output: A permutation index array that reorders the splats into a square 2D grid of size n{sidelen} \times n{sidelen}, where n{sidelen} = \lceil \sqrt{N} \rceil. If N is not a perfect square, Gaussians with the lowest opacity are pruned to fit the largest square grid. Data Structures: 1. Attributes Grid: A 3D tensor of shape (n{sidelen}, n{sidelen}, 59) storing the sorted attributes. 2. Target Grid: A smoothed version of the current grid used as the assignment target. 3. Keys for Sorting: A subset of attributes used to compute the distance metric. Typically, this includes the 3D position and SH-DC coefficients (6 dimensions). Other implementations may use all attributes except SH-AC or all attributes. Parameters: \phi: The radius of the Gaussian blur applied to compute the target grid. Initial value \phi = w^2 - 1, where w is the grid width. \beta: Block size, set as \beta = \phi + 1. Minimum \beta = 16 to ensure efficient parallelization. improvementbreak: Threshold for early stopping if improvement is below this value. Default 10^{-4}. Convergence threshold: 0.01\% improvement in mean L2 distance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine grid side length n{sidelen} = \text{int}(N^{0.5}). Assert n{sidelen}^2 == N (prune low-opacity Gaussians if necessary). Normalize all Gaussian attributes independently to [0, 1] and scale with individual weights. Use activated values (e.g., exponentially activated scale) as seen by the renderer. Concatenate all parameter tensors (reshaped to (N, -1)) along the last dimension to form paramstosort. Generate a random permutation shuffledindices using torch.randperm(N). Map Gaussians to random positions in the grid to avoid local minima. 2. Target Construction: Perform low-pass filtering (Gaussian blur with radius \phi) on the current grid to construct an idealized target grid. 3. Block-wise Linear Assignment (Iterative): Shift all blocks by a random \Delta y and \Delta x to sort across block borders and cover all grid borders when not aligned at multiples of the current block size. Divide the grid into non-overlapping blocks of size \beta \times \beta. For each block, split elements into randomly assigned, non-overlapping groups of 4. Iterate through all 24 possible permutations for each group of 4. Calculate the total L2 distance between the permuted elements and the target grid values. Select the permutation with the lowest total distance. Apply the selected permutations to update the grid. 4. Convergence Check: Measure the mean L2 distance between the sorted grid and the target grid. If the improvement is less than 0.01\% compared to the previous value, restart the block shifting with new random \Delta x, \Delta y. If the assignment with new block positions does not improve the distance further (using the same threshold), reduce the radius: \phi = 0.95 \phi. 5. Termination: Finish when \phi < 1 and sorting has converged. Alternatively, stop if improvement is below improvementbreak. 6. Final Permutation Application: The sorting is based on a 6D vector (3D position + SH-DC). Uniformly apply the final permutation to all 59 attribute grids. Reshape paramstosort into (n{sidelen}, n{sidelen}, -1). Map sorted indices back to original space: sortedindices = shuffledindices[sortedindices]. Reorder all splat parameters in the splats dict according to sortedindices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def plassort(splatsdict, ngs, improvementbreak=1e-4, verbose=False): """ Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: splatsdict: Dictionary containing splat attributes. ngs: Number of Gaussians. improvementbreak: Threshold for early stopping. verbose: Print progress. Returns: splatsdict: Reordered splats. """ # 1. Initialization nsidelen = int(ngs0.5) assert nsidelen2 == ngs, "Grid must be a perfect square. Prune low-opacity Gaussians if necessary." # Normalize and scale attributes # Assume splatsdict contains tensors for each attribute # Normalize to [0, 1] and scale with weights # Use activated values (e.g., exp(scale)) # Concatenate parameters for sorting # Keys to sort: all except 'shN' (SH-AC) keystosort = [k for k in splatsdict.keys() if k != 'shN'] paramstosort = torch.cat([splatsdict[k].reshape(ngs, -1) for k in keystosort], dim=-1) # Random permutation for shuffling shuffledindices = torch.randperm(ngs) paramstosort = paramstosort[shuffledindices] # Initialize grid grid = paramstosort.reshape(nsidelen, nsidelen, -1) # Initial radius w = nsidelen phi = w2 - 1 prevdist = float('inf') # 2. Iterative Sorting while phi >= 1: # Shift blocks randomly deltax = torch.randint(0, nsidelen, (1,)).item() deltay = torch.randint(0, nsidelen, (1,)).item() # Circular shift grid grid = torch.roll(grid, shifts=(deltay, deltax), dims=(0, 1)) blocksize = phi + 1 if blocksize < 16: blocksize = 16 # Construct target grid via low-pass filtering # Use Gaussian blur with radius phi targetgrid = gaussianblur(grid, radius=phi) # Block-wise Linear Assignment # Process blocks in parallel newgrid = torch.zeroslike(grid) for y in range(0, nsidelen, blocksize): for x in range(0, nsidelen, blocksize): # Extract block block = grid[y:y+blocksize, x:x+blocksize,:] targetblock = targetgrid[y:y+blocksize, x:x+blocksize,:] # Split into groups of 4 # Flatten block to list of elements elements = block.reshape(-1, block.shape[-1]) nelements = elements.shape[0] # Random permutation of indices for grouping permindices = torch.randperm(nelements) elements = elements[permindices] # Process groups of 4 ngroups = nelements // 4 for i in range(ngroups): group = elements[i4:(i+1)4,:] targetgroup = targetblock.reshape(-1, block.shape[-1])[i4:(i+1)4,:] # Find best permutation bestperm = None bestdist = float('inf') # 24 permutations of 4 elements perms = torch.tensor(list(itertools.permutations([0, 1, 2, 3]))) for p in perms: permutedgroup = group[p,:] dist = torch.sum((permutedgroup - targetgroup)2) if dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestperm = p # Apply best permutation elements[i4:(i+1)4,:] = group[bestperm,:] # Reshape back to block and inverse permutation sortedblock = elements.reshape(block.shape) sortedblock = sortedblock[torch.argsort(permindices),:,:] newgrid[y:y+blocksize, x:x+blocksize,:] = sortedblock grid = newgrid # Convergence Check currentdist = torch.mean((grid - targetgrid)2).item() if prevdist != float('inf'): improvement = (prevdist - currentdist) / prevdist if improvement < 0.0001: # 0.01% # Try new random block position (already done by shifting) # If no improvement after shift, reduce radius pass else: prevdist = currentdist continue # Continue with same phi # Reduce radius phi = 0.95 phi if verbose: print(f"Phi: {phi}, Dist: {currentdist}") # 3. Final Permutation Application # Flatten grid to 1D indices sortedindicesflat = torch.arange(ngs) # Reshape to grid and get indices gridindices = torch.arange(ngs).reshape(nsidelen, nsidelen) # Apply roll inverse to get final order # Note: The pseudocode above modifies grid values. To get indices, we track indices instead. # Simplified: The final permutation is derived from the grid layout. # Map back to original space # sortedindices = shuffledindices[sortedindices] # Reorder splats for k in splatsdict.keys(): splatsdict[k] = splatsdict[k][sortedindices] return splatsdict Time Complexity: The algorithm is highly parallel on the GPU, sorting millions of Gaussians in seconds. The complexity is dominated by the block-wise assignment, which is O(N \cdot \beta^2 \cdot 24) per iteration, where \beta is the block size. The number of iterations depends on the decay of \phi. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 2D grid of attributes, which is O(N \cdot D), where D is the number of attributes. Performance: Reduces storage size by a factor of 17x to 42x while maintaining high visual quality. Strengths: Efficient for large-scale scenes (millions of Gaussians), enables continuous sorting during training, improves compression efficiency by increasing spatial correlation. Limitations: Requires perfect square grid size (pruning may be needed), attribute channels cannot be sorted individually. When to use: When compressing 3DGS models or requiring cache-coherent rendering of large Gaussian splat sets. When not to use: When real-time sorting is not required and standard rasterization order is sufficient, or when the number of Gaussians is small (thousands) where traditional sorting methods like LAS are adequate. Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS) was introduced by Morgenstern et al. in 2024 in the paper "Compact 3D Scene Representation via Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids". It is an adaptation of Linear Assignment Sorting (LAS) [2] and Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS) [2], which were previously used for non-parallel computations. PLAS extends these methods to handle millions of items on the GPU, addressing the inefficiency of traditional grid-sorting algorithms like SOM and Self-Sorting Map for large data volumes. It is primarily used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) compression, where it reorders Gaussian attributes to improve the efficiency of subsequent compression techniques like HEVC or VQ. name: AMR Splatting with FFT
head: Data projection on a Cartesian grid, splatting technique
body: AMR Splatting with FFT is a volume rendering technique for Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data that converts cells into size-weighted points, projects them to a 2D plane, and convolves them with a Gaussian kernel using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to produce a summation plot. It produces images close to Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) maps with adaptive Gaussian blur. It is primarily used for semi-interactive exploration of large AMR datasets where speed is prioritized over exact ray-traced precision. The method operates by decomposing the AMR hierarchy into leaf nodes relevant to the current view, converting them into 2D splats, and accumulating their contributions via frequency-domain convolution. Inputs: AMR dataset (hierarchical grid structure). Camera parameters (view direction, projection plane definition). Scalar physical values associated with each cell. Outputs: A 2D image (summation plot) representing the volume projection. AMR Cell: Defined by its center position, physical value (density/scalar), and size (resolution level). Projection Map: A 2D Cartesian grid (image buffer) initialized to zero, where contributions from all levels are accumulated. Gaussian Kernel: A 2D Gaussian function used for smoothing. Bit Packing: Not given in the sources. 1. Leaf Node Identification: Determine the maximum resolution level involved in the camera-defined image. Only cells ranked at this maximum level of resolution are considered as leaves. This ensures that reading every cell of the dataset is never required, optimizing performance. 2. Point Conversion: Convert each AMR leaf cell into a point with additional size information. The size of the point is determined by the AMR cell size. 3. Projection: Project the center points of the AMR cells onto the 2D projection plane. 4. Histogram Computation: For every pixel of the image, compute a 2D histogram weighted with the scalar physical value observed from the projected points. 5. Gaussian Convolution via FFT: Transform the projected points into 2D disks by convolving with a 2D Gaussian kernel. This is performed using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), as multiplication in Fourier space corresponds to a convolution product in spatial space. The implementation described uses Numpy's FFT module on the CPU. 6. Accumulation: Add all maps obtained for every AMR level to produce the final image. The core operation is a 2D convolution in the frequency domain: I{\text{level}}(x,y) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathcal{F}\{H(x,y)\} \cdot \mathcal{F}\{K(x,y)\} \right\} where H(x,y) is the 2D histogram of projected cell values, K(x,y) is the 2D Gaussian kernel, \mathcal{F} denotes the 2D FFT, and \mathcal{F}^{-1} denotes the inverse 2D FFT. The final image is the sum over all levels: I{\text{final}} = \sum{\text{level}} I{\text{level}}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def amrsplattingfft(amrdata, imageshape): """ Render AMR data using splatting with FFT convolution. Args: amrdata: Object containing AMR cells grouped by level. imageshape: Tuple (height, width) of the output image. Returns: numpy.ndarray: 2D image buffer. """ finalimage = np.zeros(imageshape, dtype=np.float32) #: A different map is computed for every AMR level involved. for level in amrdata.levels: levelcells = [c for c in amrdata if c.level == level] histogram = np.zeros(imageshape, dtype=np.float32) for cell in levelcells: # Standard model-view-projection to convert 3D center to 2D pixel coordinates (u, v). u, v = cell.center.x, cell.center.y if 0 <= u < imageshape[1] and 0 <= v < imageshape[0]: #: 2D histogram is computed for every pixel of the image, weighted with the scalar physical value. histogram[int(v), int(u)] += cell.value #: Transform projected points into 2D disks by doing a convolution product with a 2D Gaussian kernel. #: This step is done using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). maxradius = max(cell.size for cell in levelcells) kernelradius = int(maxradius) kernelsize = 2 kernelradius + 1 y, x = np.ogrid[-kernelradius:kernelradius+1, -kernelradius:kernelradius+1] kernel = np.exp(-(xx + yy) / (2.0 (kernelradius/2.0)2)) kernel /= kernel.sum() ffthistogram = np.fft.fft2(histogram) fftkernel = np.fft.fft2(kernel, s=histogram.shape) levelresult = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(ffthistogram fftkernel)) #: Finally all maps obtained for every level are added. finalimage += levelresult return finalimage Gaussian Kernel Width: Must be large enough to cover the splatted disk size. If points are not large enough to fill the image, the underlying grid structure may become visible. FFT Grid Size: Not given in the sources. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Grid Alignment Artifacts: Grid alignment may appear on resulting images due to the discrete nature of the projection and FFT. Mitigation: Increase splatted disk/point sizes or add a random shift to point positions. Note that these solutions lead to lower image quality. Memory and Compute Cost: Projecting data to a Cartesian grid incurs high memory cost and computing time, limiting its use for very high-resolution octrees. Resolution Mismatch: If the splat size is too small relative to the pixel grid, aliasing or grid visibility occurs. Handles AMR data by processing different resolution levels separately. Not given in the sources what sets it apart from its siblings or when to choose it. [8126-splat-sorting-and-composition.md] Identifies which voxels or cells contribute significantly to the final image, allowing for culling of empty or low-value cells. Not given in the sources what sets it apart from its siblings or when to choose it. [9025-significant-voxel-extraction.md] Time Complexity: Dominated by the FFT operation, which is O(N \log N) where N is the number of pixels in the image, plus the cost of projecting M cells (O(M)). This is generally faster than ray casting for dense views but slower than simple rasterization for very sparse data. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 2D image buffer and the FFT workspace, proportional to the image resolution. High-resolution octrees can lead to high memory costs due to the Cartesian grid projection. Performance: Produces semi-interactive visualization speeds. Implementation on CPU using Numpy's FFT module is described. Parallel projection and FFT processes can speed up the process. Strengths: Easy processing of complex AMR structures; produces images close to ray-traced MIP maps; semi-interactive speed. Limitations: High memory and compute cost for high-resolution octrees; grid alignment artifacts; lower image quality if mitigations (random shift, larger splats) are used. When to Use: Quick exploration of large AMR datasets; generating MIP-like visualizations. When Not to Use: When exact ray-traced transparency is required; when memory is severely constrained; when high-resolution static images are needed without artifacts. The technique is described in the context of the PYMSES project for visualizing AMR simulations, particularly from the RAMSES code. It builds on the splatting technique described by Westover (1990). The use of FFT for convolution is attributed to Thomas Jansen (2004). The implementation was developed by Chapon (2011) as part of a Ph.D. thesis at Universite Paris 7. It is used in the amrviewer GUI of PYMSES for semi-interactive exploration of astrophysical data. name: Silhouette Splatting
body: Silhouette Splatting is a volume rendering technique that projects irregular grid cells by triangulating their convex hulls and rendering them as geometric primitives. Unlike standard splatting which treats data as point samples, this method operates on the cells between sample points. It was developed for rendering irregular grids but was ultimately abandoned due to visual artifacts and lack of performance gain over simpler methods. Inputs: Irregular grid cells defined by their 3D vertices and associated scalar values at those vertices. Outputs: A 2D rendered image. Data Structures: Cell: A collection of N vertices \mathbf{v}i in 3D space with associated scalar values si. Convex Hull: The subset of cell vertices that form the outer boundary polygon when projected onto the view plane. Centroid: The geometric center of the cell, calculated as the arithmetic mean of its vertices. Steps: 1. Identify Convex Hull: Determine which vertices of the current cell lie on the convex hull relative to the current view direction. 2. Form Polygon: Connect the convex hull vertices to form a closed polygon. 3. Compute Centroid: Calculate the centroid \mathbf{c} of the cell. \mathbf{c} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{v}i 4. Estimate Properties: Determine the depth zc and the estimated scalar value Vc (e.g., average of vertex values) for the centroid. 5. Triangulate: Create a set of triangles by connecting the centroid \mathbf{c} to each edge of the convex hull polygon. 6. Project and Render: Transform the vertices of these triangles into screen space and rasterize them. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def silhouettesplatting(cellvertices, cellvalues, viewdirection, projectionmatrix): # 1. Project vertices to 2D plane perpendicular to view direction projected2d = [v - (v @ viewdirection) viewdirection for v in cellvertices] # 2. Compute convex hull of projected points hullindices = convexhull2d(projected2d) hullvertices = [cellvertices[i] for i in hullindices] # 3. Compute centroid centroid = sum(cellvertices) / len(cellvertices) # 4. Estimate depth and value at centroid depth = centroid @ viewdirection value = sum(cellvalues) / len(cellvalues) # 5. Triangulate by connecting centroid to hull edges triangles = [] for i in range(len(hullvertices)): v1 = hullvertices[i] v2 = hullvertices[(i + 1) % len(hullvertices)] triangles.append((centroid, v1, v2)) # 6. Rasterize triangles to screen for tri in triangles: rasterizetriangle(tri, depth, value, projectionmatrix) def convexhull2d(points): # Standard 2D convex hull algorithm (e.g., Graham scan) # Returns list of indices forming the convex hull n = len(points) if n <= 2: return list(range(n)) sortedpts = sorted(enumerate(points), key=lambda p: p[1][0]) hull = [] for p in sortedpts: while len(hull) >= 2 and cross(hull[-2][1], hull[-1][1], p[1]) <= 0: hull.pop() hull.append(p) lower = hull hull = [] for p in reversed(sortedpts): while len(hull) >= 2 and cross(hull[-2][1], hull[-1][1], p[1]) <= 0: hull.pop() hull.append(p) return [idx for idx, in lower[:-1] + hull[:-1]] def cross(o, a, b): return (a[0] - o[0]) (b[1] - o[1]) - (a[1] - o[1]) (b[0] - o[0]) def rasterizetriangle(tri, depth, value, projmat): # Standard GPU rasterization step: transforms vertices, clips, and writes depth/value to framebuffer pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blotchiness: Images produced are very blotchy from oblique angles on irregular grids. Performance: The method was not significantly faster than simpler projection methods like Cell Face Projection with Depth. Overlap: Unlike standard splatting, where overlapping splats can reduce blotchiness, this method's rigid triangulation does not easily allow for overlapping primitives without significant additional calculation (e.g., moving the convex hull away from the centroid). Time Complexity: Dominated by convex hull computation and triangulation per cell. The method was not significantly faster than cell face projection. Memory Complexity: Low, as it processes cells individually without complex data structures. Visual Quality: Poor on irregular grids, especially at oblique angles, resulting in blotchy images. Strengths: Simple to implement; conceptually similar to standard splatting but applied to cells. Limitations: Visual artifacts; no substantial performance benefit over alternatives; abandoned in favor of other methods. When to use: Not recommended. The method was abandoned due to poor results. Silhouette Splatting was proposed in the context of rapid exploration of irregular grids using direct volume rendering. It was mentioned primarily to document that the approach was tried and found unsuccessful, saving others from repeating the effort. It is distinct from standard splatting (e.g., Splatting) because it operates on cells rather than sample points.
