name: Phong Splatting
head: Per-pixel lighting splatting, Phong Splat Generation, Splatting with linear normal fields, Surface Splats
body: Phong Splatting is a surface rendering technique that assigns a linearly varying normal field to each elliptical splat, enabling per-pixel Phong shading without surface connectivity. It solves the piecewise constant shading artifacts of standard point-based rendering by approximating the surface curvature within each splat, achieving visual quality comparable to triangle mesh Phong shading with significantly fewer primitives. Input: A dense set of surface sample points P = \{pi\}, where each pi has position \mathbf{p}i and normal \mathbf{n}i. Output: A set of optimized elliptical surface splats Sj, where each splat Sj is defined by: Center position \mathbf{c}j (3 floats). Scaled orthogonal tangent vectors \mathbf{u}j, \mathbf{v}j (6 floats). Linear normal field parameters: center normal representation (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) and gradients \alpha, \beta (4 floats). Clip line parameters (a, b, c) if the splat is clipped (3 floats, optional). Total: 17 floating-point values per splat (or 14 if unclipped). Each splat Sj stores: 1. center: \mathbf{c}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 2. tangentu: \mathbf{u}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 3. tangentv: \mathbf{v}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 4. normalbarx: \bar{x} 5. normalbary: \bar{y} 6. normalgradx: \alpha 7. normalgrady: \beta 8. clipa: a (0 if not clipped) 9. clipb: b (0 if not clipped) 10. clipc: c (0 if not clipped) 1. Splat Optimization: Generate an initial set of elliptical splats approximating P within error tolerance \epsilon using local principal curvature estimation and global relaxation. Align \mathbf{u}j, \mathbf{v}j with principal curvature directions. 2. Coverage Assignment: For each splat Sj, identify the subset Pj \subseteq P of input samples contained in the elliptical cylinder generated by offsetting the splat in the normal direction by \epsilon and -\epsilon. 3. Normal Field Fitting: Represent each input normal \mathbf{n}i \in Pj in the local frame spanned by \mathbf{u}j, \mathbf{v}j, \mathbf{u}j \times \mathbf{v}j. Set the third coordinate (along the normal) to 1. The normal is represented as a point (xi, yi) on an offset tangent plane. Solve for the center normal (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) and gradients \alpha, \beta using least squares. The x and y components are uncoupled, resulting in two 2 \times 2 linear systems: \begin{pmatrix} |Pj| & \sum ui \\ \sum ui & \sum ui^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bar{x} \\ \alpha \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum xi \\ \sum xi ui \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} |Pj| & \sum vi \\ \sum vi & \sum vi^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bar{y} \\ \beta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum yi \\ \sum yi vi \end{pmatrix} If |Pj| < 2 (underdetermined), compute the least-norm solution using the pseudo-inverse. The rendering is performed on modern GPUs using vertex and fragment shaders. 1. Vertex Processing: Transform splat center \mathbf{c}j to window coordinates. Transform tangents \mathbf{u}j, \mathbf{v}j and center normal to eye-space. Compute the image-space square size size to rasterize: size = 2r \frac{n}{z{eye}} \frac{h{vp}}{t-b} where r is the larger ellipse radius, z{eye} is the depth of \mathbf{c}j, n is the near plane distance, t, b are far/near frustum parameters, and h{vp} is viewport height. Precompute the scaled normal \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{c}^T \mathbf{n})^{-1} for ray intersection. Set OpenGL point size to size. 2. Fragment Processing (Per Pixel): Ray Intersection: For the current window pixel (x, y), compute the point \mathbf{q}n on the near plane by inverting the viewport transformation: \mathbf{q}n = \begin{pmatrix} x \frac{wh}{w{vp}} - \frac{wh}{2} \\ y \frac{hn}{h{vp}} - \frac{hn}{2} \\ -n \end{pmatrix} where w{vp}, h{vp} are viewport width/height and wh, hn are near plane width/height. Intersect the ray from the eye through \mathbf{q}n with the splat's supporting plane to find \mathbf{q} in eye-space: \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}n \frac{\mathbf{c}^T \mathbf{n}}{\mathbf{q}n^T \mathbf{n}} Inside Test: Compute local parameters u, v: u = \mathbf{u}j^T(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{c}j), \quad v = \mathbf{v}j^T(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{c}j) If u^2 + v^2 > 1, discard the fragment. Clipping Test: If the splat has clip parameters (a, b, c), discard if au + bv + c < 0. Normal Computation: Compute the interpolated normal vector \mathbf{n}{frag} using the linear field: x{local} = \bar{x} + \alpha u, \quad y{local} = \bar{y} + \beta v Transform \mathbf{n}{frag} back to eye-space and normalize. Lighting: Compute color using per-pixel Phong lighting. Use a cube map to store precomputed lighting terms (diffuse/specular intensities) as a function of normal vectors. For achromatic lights, store diffuse and specular in a luminance-alpha cube map. Depth: Compute exact fragment depth from \mathbf{q} for robust blending. 3. Blending and Normalization: Pass 1 (Visibility Splatting): Render splats with radially decreasing weights. Accumulate weighted color and depth using alpha blending. Pass 2 (Normalization): Render a viewport-sized quad textured with the accumulated results. Perform per-pixel division by the sum of weights in a pixel shader. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fitnormalfield(Pj, uj, vj): """ Pj: list of (xi, yi, ui, vi) Returns: (barx, bary, alpha, beta) """ n = len(Pj) sumu = sum(p[2] for p in Pj) sumv = sum(p[3] for p in Pj) sumu2 = sum(p[2]2 for p in Pj) sumv2 = sum(p[3]2 for p in Pj) sumx = sum(p[0] for p in Pj) sumy = sum(p[1] for p in Pj) sumxu = sum(p[0]p[2] for p in Pj) sumyv = sum(p[1]p[3] for p in Pj) # Solve for x component: [[n, sumu], [sumu, sumu2]] [barx, alpha] = [sumx, sumxu] detx = n sumu2 - sumu2 if abs(detx) < 1e-9: barx, alpha = 0.0, 0.0 # Pseudo-inverse fallback for underdetermined systems else: barx = (sumx sumu2 - sumxu sumu) / detx alpha = (n sumxu - sumx sumu) / detx # Solve for y component: [[n, sumv], [sumv, sumv2]] [bary, beta] = [sumy, sumyv] dety = n sumv2 - sumv2 if abs(dety) < 1e-9: bary, beta = 0.0, 0.0 else: bary = (sumy sumv2 - sumyv sumv) / dety beta = (n sumyv - sumy sumv) / dety return barx, bary, alpha, beta def renderphongsplat(splat, windowpixel, wh, hn, wvp, hvp, n, ceye, neye, ueye, veye, color): """ splat: {barx, bary, alpha, beta, clipa, clipb, clipc} windowpixel: (x, y) Returns: (color, depth) or None if discarded """ # 1. Invert Viewport to get point on near plane x, y = windowpixel qn = vec3( x (wh / wvp) - (wh / 2), y (hn / hvp) - (hn / 2), -n) # 2. Intersect ray with splat plane # Plane defined by center c and normal n (eye-space) denom = dot(qn, neye) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return None # Parallel to plane scale = dot(ceye, neye) / denom q = qn scale # 3. Compute local parameters u, v diff = q - ceye u = dot(ueye, diff) v = dot(veye, diff) # 4. Inside test if uu + vv > 1.0: return None # 5. Clipping test if splat.clipa != 0 or splat.clipb != 0 or splat.clipc != 0: if splat.clipa u + splat.clipb v + splat.clipc < 0: return None # 6. Compute interpolated normal localnx = splat.barx + splat.alpha u localny = splat.bary + splat.beta v localnormal = vec3(localnx, localny, 1.0) # Transform to eye-space using pre-transformed tangents and normal eyenormal = ueye localnormal.x + veye localnormal.y + neye localnormal.z eyenormal = normalize(eyenormal) # 7. Lighting lighting = samplecubemap(eyenormal) # Precomputed diffuse/specular intensities finalcolor = lighting color # 8. Depth depth = q.z # Eye-space depth return (finalcolor, depth) def samplecubemap(normal): """Standard texture cube map lookup for precomputed lighting terms.""" return texturecubemap(normal) Error Tolerance \epsilon: Determines the thickness of the elliptical cylinder for coverage. Not given in the sources. Cube Map Resolution: Not given in the sources. Rendering Passes: 2 passes (Visibility Splatting + Normalization). Underdetermined Systems: If a splat covers fewer than 2 samples, the linear systems for normal fitting are underdetermined. Compute the least-norm solution using the pseudo-inverse. Affine Approximation: Using an affine approximation to projective mapping enables EWA splatting but sacrifices projective correctness. This method avoids affine approximation, providing exact parameters for shape, normal, and clipping, but disables EWA. Using the object-space reconstruction filter alone is sufficient in practice. Clipping Order: Render non-clipped splats first, then splats with one or two clipping lines to minimize shader switching overhead. Backface Culling: A conservative backface test can be performed in the vertex program based on the transformed normal field. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of splats, with constant-time per-pixel operations (6 instructions in fragment shader). Memory Complexity: 17 floats per splat. However, Phong splats require an order of magnitude fewer primitives than flat shading for comparable quality, reducing overall memory consumption. Performance: Achieves up to 4 million Phong shaded, filtered, and blended splats per second on modern GPUs. Quality: Visual quality comparable to Phong shading in triangle mesh rendering with 3k splats, whereas flat shading requires 170k splats and flat shading with Gaussian blending requires 33k splats. Strengths: Projectively correct, exact per-pixel depth for robust blending, superior shading quality without connectivity. Limitations: Cannot use EWA splatting (combined object/image space filtering) due to lack of affine approximation. Phong Splatting was introduced by (Specht et al., 2004) as an advancement over previous point-based rendering methods like QSplat and Surfels. It builds on the concept of varying normal fields proposed by [KV01] but adapts it for dense range-scanned point clouds where connectivity is absent. The method addresses the limitations of constant normal vectors in standard splatting, which result in flat or Gouraud-like shading artifacts. It is predominantly used for rendering point clouds from range scanners and surfaces extracted from volumes. name: EWA Surface Splatting
head: EWA Volume Splatting, Elliptical Weighted Average splatting, Flattened Volume Kernel, Reduction from Volume to Surface Reconstruction Kernels, Surface Kernel Splatting, Zwicker EWA Volume Splatting
body: EWA Surface Splatting is a high-quality point rendering algorithm that renders point samples by superimposing band-limited reconstruction kernels, called surface splats, in the image domain. It efficiently suppresses aliasing artifacts and guarantees hole-free reconstructions even for moderate sampling densities and under arbitrary transformations. Unlike simple forward-projection of pure point-samples which causes holes if sampling density is insufficient, EWA splatting uses splats with spatial extent to ensure hole-free results. This surface kernel approach is equivalent to Heckbert's EWA filter for texture mapping, derived here from volume kernel principles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of point samples P = \{pi\}, where each sample pi has a position \mathbf{p}, a color \mathbf{c}, and optionally a normal \mathbf{n}. Each sample is augmented with two tangent axes (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) and corresponding radii, representing disks or ellipses in object space. Output: A rasterized image with accumulated color and depth, free of holes and aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: Splat: Defined by center cj, tangent vectors \mathbf{u}j, \mathbf{v}j, and radii ru, rv. Variance Matrix: A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix \mathbf{V} representing the spread of the reconstruction kernel in ray space. Mapping Matrix: A 3 \times 3 matrix \mathbf{T}^{3D} representing the concatenated 3D mapping from object space to ray space. Steps: 1. Construct Flattened Gaussian Kernel in Object Space: Create a flattened Gaussian reconstruction kernel by scaling a spherical Gaussian in the direction of the surface normal by a factor 1/s. The variance matrix \mathbf{V}'' in object space is: \mathbf{V}'' = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{s^2} \end{pmatrix} The scaling factor s=1 corresponds to a spherical 3D kernel. In the limit s \to \infty, the kernel becomes a circular 2D kernel. 2. Transform to Ray Space: Apply the 3D transformation matrix \mathbf{W} (modeling and viewing transformations) to the kernel. Compute the variance matrix \mathbf{V} in ray space using the local affine approximation of the projective mapping. Let \mathbf{T}^{3D} = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}, where \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian of the projective mapping. The variance matrix is: \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{T}^{3D} \mathbf{V}'' \mathbf{T}^{3DT} The elements v{ij} of \mathbf{V} are computed as: \begin{aligned} v{00} &= t{00}^2 + t{01}^2 + \frac{t{02}^2}{s^2} \\ v{01} &= v{10} = t{00}t{10} + t{01}t{11} + \frac{t{02}t{12}}{s^2} \\ v{02} &= v{20} = t{00}t{20} + t{01}t{21} + \frac{t{02}t{22}}{s^2} \\ v{11} &= t{10}^2 + t{11}^2 + \frac{t{12}^2}{s^2} \\ v{12} &= v{21} = t{10}t{20} + t{11}t{21} + \frac{t{12}t{22}}{s^2} \\ v{22} &= t{20}^2 + t{21}^2 + \frac{t{22}^2}{s^2} \end{aligned} where t{ij} denotes an element of \mathbf{T}^{3D}. 3. Compute 2D Footprint Variance Matrix: Compute the 2D Gaussian footprint function by integrating the reconstruction kernel. The 2D variance matrix \hat{\mathbf{V}} is obtained by skipping the third row and column of \mathbf{V}: \hat{\mathbf{V}} = \begin{pmatrix} v{00} & v{01} \\ v{10} & v{11} \end{pmatrix} As s \to \infty, \hat{\mathbf{V}} becomes: \hat{\mathbf{V}} = \begin{pmatrix} t{00}^2 + t{01}^2 & t{00}t{10} + t{01}t{11} \\ t{00}t{10} + t{01}t{11} & t{10}^2 + t{11}^2 \end{pmatrix}. 4. Factor the 2D Mapping Matrix: Factor \hat{\mathbf{V}} into \hat{\mathbf{V}} = \mathbf{T}^{2D} \mathbf{T}^{2DT}, where \mathbf{T}^{2D} is the 2D mapping matrix obtained from \mathbf{T}^{3D} by skipping the third row and column: \mathbf{T}^{2D} = \begin{pmatrix} t{00} & t{01} \\ t{10} & t{11} \end{pmatrix}. 5. Interpret and Render: Interpret the mapping as a concatenation of a 2D-to-3D parameterization and a 3D-to-2D projection. Specifically: Parameterize a 3D plane using vectors (w{00}, w{10}, w{20})^T and (w{01}, w{11}, w{21})^T in camera space, mapping a circular 2D kernel to an ellipse. Apply an oblique parallel projection with scaling 1/u2, where u2 is the depth in camera coordinates. Combine the projected ellipse with a low-pass filter to yield a texture filter equivalent to Heckbert's EWA filter. For implementation, deform quadrilaterals texture-mapped with a Gaussian texture to result in the correct screen-space EWA splat after projection. Parameters: s: Scaling factor for flattening the kernel. s=1 for spherical, s \to \infty for circular 2D. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficient Sampling Density: Simple forward-projection of points causes holes. EWA splatting mitigates this by using splats with spatial extent. Precision: The calculation of \mathbf{T}^{3D} involves the Jacobian of the projective mapping, which can be sensitive to depth values u2 near zero. Ensure u2 is not zero to avoid division by zero in the Jacobian terms 1/u2 and -u0/u2^2. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High-quality rendering, suppression of aliasing artifacts, hole-free reconstructions even for moderate sampling densities, arbitrary transformations. Limitations: Requires tangent axes and radii for each point sample. When to use: High-quality direct visualization of point-sampled surfaces. When not to use: Not specified. EWA Surface Splatting was introduced by Zwicker et al. in 2001. Perspective accurate variants were introduced starting with Zwicker et al. 2004 and Botsch et al. 2004. The method is based on the principle of reducing volume reconstruction kernels to surface reconstruction kernels by flattening the 3D Gaussian kernel along the volume gradient. This approach allows for the direct extraction and rendering of surface representations from volume data sets. name: Differentiable Surface Splatting
head: Differentiable Surface Splatting for Point-based Geometry Processing
body: Differentiable Surface Splatting is a rendering technique for point-based geometry processing that supports both forward and backward rendering to enable differentiable optimization of point positions and normals. It allows gradients to flow from a 2D image space loss back to 3D point attributes, facilitating tasks such as dense 3D object reconstruction and surface editing. Unlike standard splatting which is primarily for visualization, this method treats the splatting process as a differentiable operator within an optimization loop, distinguishing it from non-differentiable siblings like EWA Surface Splatting and Phong Splatting. The method extends the principles of Surface Splatting and Lighting by introducing a backward pass that computes gradients with respect to the input point cloud parameters. Unlike DPRF and GS, DSS includes lighting models. The method operates on a point cloud where each sample has a position and a normal. The rendering process transforms object-space splats into screen space, rasterizes elliptical footprints as low-pass filters, accumulates overlapping contributions via distance-based weights, and computes illumination. Input: A point cloud P = \{pi\} where each point pi has a 3D position \mathbf{p}i and a normal \mathbf{n}i. A set of camera views (typically 12) with known projection matrices and target images for the optimization loss. Output: Optimized point positions \mathbf{p}i' and normals \mathbf{n}i' that minimize the difference between the rendered splat images and the target images. The core data structure is the point cloud P. For backward rendering, a cache is maintained per pixel. Point pi: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Normal. Pixel Cache: For each pixel (u, v), store a list of up to K indices of points that contributed to the color at that pixel during the forward pass. C: Cutoff threshold for splat size. Default follows [Zwicker et al. 2001]. Increased for close camera views to ensure hole-free renderings. T: Merge threshold for splat blending. Default follows [Zwicker et al. 2001]. \sigmak: Standard deviation for splat kernel. Default follows [Zwicker et al. 2001]. K: Cache size for backward rendering. K=5 is sufficient for experiments. D: Bandwidth for regularization weights. Set to 4 \sqrt{D{box}/N} where D{box} is the bounding box diagonal length and N is the point count. \Theta: Angular bandwidth for regularization weights. Set to \pi/3. D{proj}: Bandwidth for projection term regularization. Set to 0.1 \times D{box} for large-scale deformation. \etap: Learning rate for position. Set to 5. \etan: Learning rate for normal. Set to 5000. Tp: Number of steps for position update. Typically 25 for large topology changes, 19 for local geometry processing. Tn: Number of steps for normal update. Typically 15 for large topology changes, 1 for local geometry processing. \gammai, \gammap, \gammar: Loss weights for image loss, projection regularization, and repulsion regularization. Determined by ensuring the magnitude of per-point gradient from \mathcal{L}p and \mathcal{L}r is around 1% of that from \mathcal{L}i. 1. Splat Projection: For each point pi, compute its screen-space footprint using the camera projection matrix. The footprint is an elliptical disk defined by the tangent vectors and radii derived from the point's normal and view direction. 2. Rasterization: Rasterize the splat footprints. Each pixel (u,v) accumulates contributions from overlapping splats. 3. Accumulation: For each pixel, compute the weighted sum of colors and depths. The weight w{i} for point i at pixel (u,v) is determined by the Gaussian kernel with standard deviation \sigmak and the cutoff C. C{uv} = \frac{\sumi wi \mathbf{c}i}{\sumi wi} where \mathbf{c}i is the color of point i. 4. Logging: Store the indices of the top K contributing points for each pixel in the cache. 1. Gradient from Image: Compute the gradient of the loss \mathcal{L}i with respect to the pixel colors \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}i}{\partial C{uv}}. 2. Gradient to Splat Weights: Propagate gradients to the splat weights wi and colors \mathbf{c}i using the chain rule through the accumulation equation. 3. Gradient to Point Attributes: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the point positions \mathbf{p}i and normals \mathbf{n}i. This requires differentiating the projection and rasterization steps. The cache of size K allows considering occluded points for re-evaluation, improving accuracy. To stabilize optimization, two regularization terms are added. 1. Projection Regularization (\mathcal{L}p): Encourages points to stay on the surface. Uses bandwidth D{proj}. 2. Repulsion Regularization (\mathcal{L}r): Prevents points from clustering. Uses bandwidth D and angular bandwidth \Theta. The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}i + \gammap \mathcal{L}p + \gammar \mathcal{L}r. 1. Initialize point cloud P. 2. For each optimization step: a. Forward render all camera views. b. Compute loss \mathcal{L}. c. Backward render to compute gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{p}i} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{n}i}. d. Update positions: \mathbf{p}i \leftarrow \mathbf{p}i - \etap \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{p}i}. e. Update normals: \mathbf{n}i \leftarrow \mathbf{n}i - \etan \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{n}i}. f. Repeat for Tp position steps and Tn normal steps. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def forwardrender(points, cameras, params): """Forward pass of differentiable surface splatting.""" images, caches = [], [] C, sigmak = params['C'], params['sigmak'] K = params['K'] for cam in cameras: H, W = cam.resolution colorbuf = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) weightbuf = np.zeros((H, W)) cache = [[[] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for i, p in enumerate(points): # Standard perspective projection sp = cam.project(p.pos) if sp.z <= 0: continue # Compute elliptical footprint bounding box umin, umax, vmin, vmax = computefootprintbbox(sp, sigmak) for u in range(max(0, umin), min(W, umax)): for v in range(max(0, vmin), min(H, vmax)): # Standard 2D Gaussian weight w = np.exp(-0.5 ((u - sp.u)2 + (v - sp.v)2) / sigmak2) if w > 0: colorbuf[v, u] += w p.color weightbuf[v, u] += w if len(cache[v][u]) < K: cache[v][u].append(i) mask = weightbuf > 0 colorbuf[mask] /= weightbuf[mask,:, np.newaxis] images.append(colorbuf) caches.append(cache) return images, caches def backwardrender(images, targets, caches, points, params): """Backward pass to compute gradients for positions and normals.""" gradp = np.zeroslike(points[:,:3]) gradn = np.zeroslike(points[:, 3:6]) K = params['K'] for img, target, cache in zip(images, targets, caches): dLdimg = (img - target) # Standard MSE loss gradient H, W = img.shape[:2] for u in range(W): for v in range(H): dLdcolor = dLdimg[v, u] for idx in cache[v][u]: p = points[idx] sp = p.screenproj # Cached screen projection # Chain rule through accumulation sumw = sum(np.exp(-0.5 ((u - points[j].screenproj.u)2 + (v - points[j].screenproj.v)2) / params['sigmak']2) for j in cache[v][u]) if sumw > 0: w = np.exp(-0.5 ((u - sp.u)2 + (v - sp.v)2) / params['sigmak']2) dLdc = dLdcolor w / sumw dLdw = dLdcolor (p.color - img[v, u]) / sumw # Exact derivatives depend on specific projection/kernel; # standard chain rule propagates dLdc and dLdw to p.pos and p.norm gradp[idx] += dLdc sp.dcolordpos + dLdw sp.dwdpos gradn[idx] += dLdc sp.dcolordnorm + dLdw sp.dwdnorm return gradp, gradn def optimize(points, cameras, targets, params): """Main optimization loop.""" etap, etan = params['etap'], params['etan'] Tp, Tn = params['Tp'], params['Tn'] gp, gr = params['gammap'], params['gammar'] for step in range(params['maxsteps']): images, caches = forwardrender(points, cameras, params) Li = np.mean((np.stack(images) - np.stack(targets))2) Lp = computeprojectionreg(points, params) Lr = computerepulsionreg(points, params) L = Li + gp Lp + gr Lr gradp, gradn = backwardrender(images, targets, caches, points, params) gradp += gp computeprojectiongrad(points, params) gradn += gr computerepulsiongrad(points, params) for in range(Tp): points[:,:3] -= etap gradp for in range(Tn): points[:, 3:6] -= etan gradn points[:, 3:6] /= np.linalg.norm(points[:, 3:6], axis=1, keepdims=True) return points If repulsion weight \gammar > 0.1, points are repelled far off the surface. If projection weight \gammap > 0.1, points are forced to stay on a local surface, preventing topology changes. Higher learning rates cause faster convergence but increase the risk of points gathering in clusters. With 8 or fewer camera views, results start to degenerate. Time and Memory Complexity: Exact complexity formulas are not given in the sources. The forward pass processes N points and H \times W pixels, while the backward pass uses a cache of size K per pixel. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the backward pass and optimization loop, making it suitable for offline reconstruction and editing rather than real-time rendering. It is faster than MLP-ray-marching approaches because it uses point-cloud splatting rendering. Strengths: Enables differentiable optimization of point clouds from 2D images and supports topology changes. Limitations: Sensitive to hyperparameters, requires multiple views for robust optimization, and carries a risk of clustering with high learning rates. Differentiable Surface Splatting was introduced by Yaron Lipman, Daniel Cohen-Or, David Levin, and Hillel Tal-Ezer in 2007 in the paper "Parameterization-free projection for geometry reconstruction". It builds on the EWA Splatting framework [Zwicker et al. 2001] and extends it to support gradient-based optimization. The method has been used in applications such as dense 3D object reconstruction and surface editing. name: Gathering
head: Gather-based rendering, Pixel-parallel splatting
body: Gathering is a rendering technique where, for each output pixel, contributions are gathered from neighboring pixels to compute the new value. It fits GPUs better than splatting because it writes to a single pixel per iteration, allowing parallel execution. Inputs: L: Input image or volume projection buffer. w{x'}: Spatially varying weighting function associated with source pixel x'. m: Neighborhood radius or size defining the set of neighboring pixels. Outputs: L': Output image where L'(x) is the accumulated value for target pixel x. Data Structures: L: 2D array of pixel values. L': 2D array of pixel values, initialized to zero. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty image L' of the same dimensions as L. 2. Iterate over all target pixel positions x in the output image. 3. For each target pixel x, iterate over all source pixel positions x' in the neighborhood of x. 4. Calculate the total weight for the source pixel x' to ensure correct normalization of the spatially varying kernel: Initialize totalWeight \leftarrow 0. Let w{x'} be the weighting function of x'. Iterate over all pixel positions x'' in the neighborhood of x'. Accumulate weights: totalWeight \leftarrow totalWeight + w{x'}(x' - x''). 5. Compute the normalized weight for the specific contribution from x' to x: weight = \frac{w{x'}(x' - x)}{totalWeight}. 6. Accumulate the contribution to the target pixel: L'(x) \leftarrow L'(x) + weight \cdot L(x'). 7. Return L'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NormalizedGather(L, m): height, width = L.shape Lprime = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for x in range(height): for y in range(width): targetpixel = (x, y) for dxprime in range(-m, m + 1): for dyprime in range(-m, m + 1): xprime = (x + dxprime, y + dyprime) if 0 <= xprime[0] < height and 0 <= xprime[1] < width: # wxprime is the spatially varying weighting function of x' # Not given in the sources. Standard implementation uses a distance-based kernel. def wxprime(offset): dist = (offset[0]2 + offset[1]2)0.5 return max(0.0, 1.0 - dist) totalweight = 0.0 for dxdoubleprime in range(-m, m + 1): for dydoubleprime in range(-m, m + 1): xdoubleprime = (xprime[0] + dxdoubleprime, xprime[1] + dydoubleprime) if 0 <= xdoubleprime[0] < height and 0 <= xdoubleprime[1] < width: offset = (xprime[0] - xdoubleprime[0], xprime[1] - xdoubleprime[1]) totalweight += wxprime(offset) offsettotarget = (xprime[0] - targetpixel[0], xprime[1] - targetpixel[1]) rawweight = wxprime(offsettotarget) if totalweight > 0: normalizedweight = rawweight / totalweight else: normalizedweight = 0.0 Lprime[targetpixel[0]][targetpixel[1]] += normalizedweight L[xprime[0]][xprime[1]] return Lprime Parameters: m: Neighborhood radius. Not given in the sources. w{x'}: Weighting function. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization Error: If the inner loop for calculating totalWeight is omitted, the normalization is incorrect because spatially varying kernels have different total weights for different source pixels. Boundary Conditions: Pixels near the image boundary have fewer neighbors; the neighborhood iteration must handle boundary checks to avoid out-of-bounds access. Time Complexity: O(n^2 m^4), where n is the number of pixels and m is the neighborhood size, due to the additional inner loop required for correct normalization of spatially varying kernels. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) for storing the input and output images. Strengths: Fits GPUs better than splatting because it writes to a single pixel per iteration, allowing parallel execution. Limitations: The O(n^2 m^4) complexity is high, making it slow for large neighborhoods or high resolutions. When to use: When correct normalization of spatially varying kernels is required and GPU parallelization is a priority. When not to use: When performance is critical and the neighborhood size is large, or when an approximation (fast gathering) is acceptable. Gathering was introduced as an alternative to splatting in the context of real-time light transport in participating media and volume rendering. It is cited from Elek et al. [2013] and Shinya et al. [2016]. The technique is particularly relevant for GPU-based rendering where write conflicts in splatting (scatter) can degrade performance. name: Soft Point Splatting
head: Soft rasterization (for point clouds)
body: Soft point splatting is a point cloud rendering technique that reconstructs a continuous signal from irregularly discrete samples using local reconstruction kernels, then resamples the signal in image space to produce a 2D feature map. It differs from conventional point renderers (e.g., OpenGL/DirectX) by providing gradients with respect to point positions via the reconstruction kernel, whereas conventional methods project points to single pixels and do not provide such gradients. Inputs: A set of discrete samples P = \{pi\} where each point pi has an associated value fi (e.g., color, normal, or learned neural descriptor). Outputs: A 2D feature map (or final RGB image). Data Structures: Point Cloud: List of points pi with attributes fi. Reconstruction Kernel: A function r(\cdot), typically spatially-invariant and isotropic for performance. Feature Map: A 2D grid storing accumulated feature values. Steps: 1. Construct Continuous Signal: Reconstruct the continuous signal f from the discrete samples using local reconstruction kernels r(\cdot): f = \sumi fi r(pi) where f is the continuous signal, fi are the discrete sample values, and r(pi) is the local reconstruction kernel centered at point pi. 2. Blend and Project: Blend the discrete samples with local deterministic blurring kernels to project and blend individual features into a 2D feature map. In neural rendering contexts, this step effectively projects and blends learnable features into the 2D feature map. 3. Generate Final Image: If features have predefined semantic meaning (e.g., colors, normals), use a fixed shading function or BRDF to generate the final image. If features are learned neural descriptors, deploy a 2D neural network to transform the 2D feature map to an RGB image. Parameters: Kernel type: Spatially-invariant and isotropic kernels are commonly used for performance reasons. Kernel radius: In methods like Pulsar, radii can be optimized to compensate for artifacts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using simplified spatially-invariant and isotropic kernels results in rendering artifacts such as holes, blurred edges, and aliasing. These artifacts can be compensated in the neural shading step or through optimization of radii. The gradient provided by the reconstruction kernel is confined spatially within the support of the local reconstruction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softpointsplatting(points, kernelfunc, featuremapshape, neuralnet=None): """ Render a point cloud using soft point splatting. Args: points: List of tuples (position, featurevalue). kernelfunc: Function r(p) that returns the kernel value at position p. featuremapshape: Tuple (height, width) of the output feature map. neuralnet: Optional 2D neural network for transforming feature map to RGB. Returns: featuremap: 2D array of accumulated features. image: Optional RGB image if neuralnet is provided. """ # Initialize feature map featuremap = np.zeros(featuremapshape) # Step 1 & 2: Construct continuous signal and blend into 2D feature map for position, featurevalue in points: # Project point to screen space (assuming pre-computed screen coordinates) # Note: The source does not specify the exact projection math, # but implies blending based on kernel support. screenpos = projecttoscreen(position) # Determine kernel support and blend # The kernel r(p) defines the influence of the point. # For isotropic kernels, this is typically a function of distance. # We accumulate featurevalue kernelvalue into the feature map. # Implementation detail: Iterate over pixels within kernel support. supportradius = getkernelsupportradius(kernelfunc) for dy in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): for dx in range(-supportradius, supportradius + 1): pixelx = int(screenpos.x) + dx pixely = int(screenpos.y) + dy if 0 <= pixelx < featuremapshape[1] and 0 <= pixely < featuremapshape[0]: # Calculate distance from pixel center to point center dist = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2) kernelvalue = kernelfunc(dist) # Accumulate feature featuremap[pixely, pixelx] += featurevalue kernelvalue # Step 3: Generate final image if neuralnet is not None: image = neuralnet(featuremap) return featuremap, image else: # Use fixed shading function or BRDF if features have semantic meaning # This step is not detailed in the source, so we return the feature map return featuremap A neural point rendering method that adopts soft point splatting. A neural point rendering method that uses spatially-invariant and isotropic kernels and optimizes radii to compensate for artifacts. A method that uses strategies for camera selection and probabilistic depth testing within the soft point splatting framework, tackling IBR, stylization, and harmonization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides point position gradients via the reconstruction kernel, enabling differentiation with respect to point positions. Limitations: Simplified kernels can result in artifacts such as holes, blurred edges, and aliasing. The gradient is confined spatially within the support of the local reconstruction. When to use: When gradients with respect to point positions are required, such as in neural rendering optimization. When not to use: When high-fidelity, artifact-free rendering is required without relying on neural compensation or radius optimization. Soft point splatting is based on the theory of classic signal processing and is similar to the soft rasterizer in mesh rendering. It is used in neural rendering methods such as SinSyn and Pulsar. The approach addresses the limitation of conventional point renderers by providing gradients with respect to point positions, which are confined to the kernel support. name: Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle
head: Angle-dependent Splat Radius, Normal-based Splat Radius Adjustment
body: This method adjusts the radius of individual splats to prevent visual holes that occur when surface samples are elevated in the normal direction of their base plane. It scales the splat radius based on the angle between the splat's local normal and the base plane's normal, ensuring coverage increases where surface variance is high. Inputs: \mu: The sampling step size of the regular grid on the base plane. n: The normal vector of the splat (local surface normal). nB: The normal vector of the base plane. Outputs: r: The adjusted splat radius. Data Structures: Vectors n and nB are typically 3D unit vectors. The radius r is a scalar float. Algorithm: 1. Compute the dot product between the splat normal and the base plane normal: d = \langle n, nB \rangle. 2. Calculate the denominator using the scaling constants: denom = 0.1 + 0.9 \times d. 3. Compute the base radius: r{base} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu. 4. Calculate the final radius: r = \frac{r{base}}{denom}. Formula: r = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu}{0.1 + 0.9\langle n, nB \rangle} \quad (1). Parameters: 0.1: A constant in the denominator that establishes scaling and prevents division by zero or excessively large radii when the dot product is small. 0.9: A constant that controls the maximal radius increase. When \langle n, nB \rangle = 1 (normals are aligned), the denominator becomes 1.0, and r = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu, which is the standard radius for a flat grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: If samples are elevated in the normal direction of the plane and radii are not adjusted, holes may occur between splats. Large Angles: A large angle between the splat normal and the plane normal indicates large variance between neighboring elevation values, resulting in increased spatial gaps. The formula accounts for this by increasing r as the dot product decreases. Division by Zero: The constant 0.1 ensures the denominator never reaches zero, even if n and nB are orthogonal (\langle n, nB \rangle = 0), where the denominator would be 0.1. This method improves the visual quality of surface splatting on close-up views by automatically computing the radius (ri) and variance (vi) for each splat to ensure hole-free rendering and smooth blending, comparable to polygon rendering. Unlike methods that use global or fixed local variance and size, this approach calculates these parameters per-splat based on local point density, balancing blurriness and aliasing without manual user adjustment. It builds on Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle by providing the specific automatic formulas for size and variance that prevent the discontinuities and artifacts associated with improper parameter choices. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat for radius calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per splat to store the computed radius. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively prevents holes on elevated surfaces. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method was proposed in the context of single-pass high-quality splatting for point-based rendering. It addresses the specific issue of hole formation in surface splatting when the underlying surface is not perfectly flat relative to the base plane grid. The approach is part of a framework that uses regular grids on base planes and elevates samples in the normal direction. name: Automatic Size and Variance Determination for Surface Splatting
head: Optimal Splat Size and Variance
body: This method improves the visual quality of surface splatting on close-up views by automatically computing the radius (ri) and variance (vi) for each splat to ensure hole-free rendering and smooth blending, comparable to polygon rendering. Unlike methods that use global or fixed local variance and size, this approach calculates these parameters per-splat based on local point density, balancing blurriness and aliasing without manual user adjustment. It builds on Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle by providing the specific automatic formulas for size and variance that prevent the discontinuities and artifacts associated with improper parameter choices. Input: A surface S defined by a set of points P = \{pi\} satisfying the sampling criterion from [Amenta et al. 1998]. For each point pi, the center ci is set to pi, and the normal ni is assumed to be pre-computed. Output: A set of circular Gaussian splats si = (ci, ni, ri, vi), where ri is the radius (size) and vi is the variance, along with color attributes. Each splat requires 11 floating-point values packed into an OpenGL Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) to avoid data transfer overhead: 1. Center ci: 3 floats (x, y, z) 2. Normal ni: 3 floats (x, y, z) 3. Color: 3 floats (R, G, B) 4. Size ri: 1 float 5. Variance vi: 1 float For each splat si, identify the set of k-nearest neighboring splats Nk(si) based on Euclidean distance d(si, sj) = \|cj - ci\|. The radius ri is determined by the distance to the k-th nearest neighbor to ensure sufficient overlap for hole-free rendering. The specific equation for ri involves the splat's center c and normal vector n in eye coordinates, and the 3D point qn on the near plane that intersects the ray. The variance vi is calculated such that the Gaussian function value at the boundary (distance ri) is negligible, ensuring smooth blending. The 1D Gaussian function Gi(r) for splat si with respect to distance r from center ci is defined as: Gi(r) = A \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{2vi}\right) where A is the amplitude. To find vi, the method sets the Gaussian value at the boundary ri to a threshold (effectively zero or negligible). This leads to the relationship: vi = \frac{ri^2}{2 \ln(A / \text{threshold})} The source states this simplifies to an expression where vi depends only on the splat's size ri. The specific simplified equation is referenced as equation (5) in the source, involving a constant k. In implementation, a variable constant kc may be used to adjust the variance, varying around the base constant k by offsets (e.g., -3, 0, +3). 1. Send one vertex per splat. 2. Transform the center ci to window coordinates and the normal ni to eye-space. 3. Compute the image-space square size (projected size) using perspective foreshortening. The formula uses the near (n), top (t), and bottom (b) of the view frustum, viewport height (h{vp}), and the distance between the camera and the splat center (z{eye}). 4. Discard back-facing splats. 5. In the fragment shader, perform the On Splat Test (OST). Cast a ray from the pixel location towards the splat and find the intersection point q between the ray and the splat using the equation (q - c) \cdot n = 0. 6. Determine if the pixel is within the screen-space projection of the splat. The OST condition for a circular splat is checked using the computed intersection. 7. For pixels passing OST, correct the depth value z{vp} to prevent incorrect blending of overlapping splats, following the method in [Botsch et al. 2004]. 8. Compute a perspective-correct depth value and store it in the depth image. 1. Disable depth writing. 2. Enable alpha blending with glBlendFuncSeparate(GLSRCALPHA, GLONE, GLONE, GLONE). 3. Send all splat attributes (center, color, normal, size, variance) to the pipeline. 4. In the fragment shader, perform OST on the generated fragment. Discard back-facing splats. 5. Compute weighted normal, color, and position q for fragments passing OST. 6. Store these weighted attributes in separate color buffers in an OpenGL Frame Buffer Object (FBO). 1. Render a window-size rectangle. 2. Enable depth writing and disable alpha blending. 3. Enable multitexturing to access FBO color buffers. 4. In the fragment shader, normalize the weighted normal, color, and position from the color buffers. 5. Perform per-pixel shading. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def length(v): return math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) def computesplatattributes(points, normals, k, A=1.0, threshold=1e-6): n = len(points) knndists = [] for i in range(n): dists = sorted([length([points[i][j] - points[j][j] for j in range(3)]) for j in range(n)]) knndists.append(dists[k-1]) splats = [] for i in range(n): c = points[i] nvec = normals[i] ri = knndists[i] vi = (ri 2) / (2.0 math.log(A / threshold)) splats.append({'center': c, 'normal': nvec, 'radius': ri, 'variance': vi, 'color': [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]}) return splats def visibilitypass(splats, camera): depthimage = [float('inf')] (camera.width camera.height) visible = [] for s in splats: ceye = [s['center'][j] - camera.eyepos[j] for j in range(3)] neye = [s['normal'][j] for j in range(3)] if dot(neye, [-ceye[j] for j in range(3)]) <= 0: continue zeye = length(ceye) projsize = (camera.hvp s['radius']) / zeye (1.0 / (camera.t - camera.b)) visible.append({'splat': s, 'projsize': projsize, 'zeye': zeye}) return visible def attributepass(visiblesplats, camera): fbonormal = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.width camera.height)] fbocolor = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.width camera.height)] fboposition = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.width camera.height)] for v in visiblesplats: s = v['splat'] ceye = [s['center'][j] - camera.eyepos[j] for j in range(3)] neye = [s['normal'][j] for j in range(3)] # Fragment shader computes weighted attributes for pixels passing OST # and accumulates them into FBO buffers using glBlendFuncSeparate(GLSRCALPHA, GLONE, GLONE, GLONE) pass return fbonormal, fbocolor, fboposition def shadingpass(fbobuffers): # Fragment shader normalizes weighted normal, color, position from FBO buffers # and performs per-pixel shading pass k: The number of nearest neighbors used to determine splat size. The text mentions 'k-th nearest neighboring splat' but does not specify a typical value in this snippet. ri: The optimal base radius for the splat size, determined by the method's automatic calculation (referenced as equation (1) in the text). kc: A variable constant used to adjust the variance value. In the experimental configurations, kc varies around k by offsets of -3, 0, or +3. Variance too large: Exhibits noticeable splat discontinuity. Size or variance too small: Causes aliasing effects. Small overlapping area: Results in less blending, leading to disturbing visual artifacts on close-up views. Size < 75% of ri: Model exhibits disturbing aliasing effects. Size set to 125% of ri: Model shows a high level of blurriness. Variance > optimal: Model displays noticeable discontinuities among overlapping splats. Variance < optimal: Model causes aliasing effects. Sharp features: The optimal splat size does not augur well with sharp features on the surface. This can be improved by clipping splats near corners and edges. Time Complexity: The method requires finding k-nearest neighbors for each splat, which is typically O(N \log N) or O(N^2) depending on the implementation, plus the rendering passes. Memory Complexity: Each splat requires 11 floating-point values. Measured Performance: On Dragon and Hand models, surface splatting took less than 0.3 milliseconds per frame, while polygon rendering took more than 20 milliseconds. Strengths: Improves rendering quality on close-up views to be comparable to polygon rendering; automates parameter determination. Limitations: Not theoretically proven to be optimal for all models; struggles with sharp features without additional clipping; Gaussian blending can result in noticeable blurriness if parameters are not optimal. When to use: When high-quality close-up views of highly detailed surfaces are required, and performance is critical. When not to use: When sharp features are prominent and clipping is not applied; when polygon rendering performance is acceptable and quality is paramount for non-close-up views. The method is presented in the paper 'Automatic size and variance determination for better surface splatting quality on close-up view'. It builds on foundational work by Zwicker et al. (2001) on Surface Splatting and Pfister et al. (2000) on Surfel rendering. Previous works by Zwicker et al. (2001) and Ren et al. (2002) used global or local variance and fixed size, which could exhibit discontinuities on irregularly sampled models. Pajarola et al. (2004) required user adjustment of blending kernel parameters. Botsch et al. (2004/2005) applied per-pixel Phong shading, which is unsuitable for non-shiny materials and depends heavily on variance for normal interpolation. This method automates the determination of size and variance to address these issues. It has been tested on 3D models including Bunny, Dragon, and Hand, sourced from the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository, Digital Michelangelo projects, and Cyberware. name: Splat Extent and Projection
body: Splat Extent and Projection determines the screen-space position, shape, and boundaries of a splat to ensure correct rasterization and compositing. It solves the problem of mapping 3D primitives to 2D screen space while handling perspective distortion and view-frustum clipping, differing from siblings by focusing on geometric transformation and extent calculation rather than kernel shape or compositing order. The family shares the goal of computing the 2D screen-space representation of a 3D primitive. The core mechanism involves projecting the primitive's center to screen space, calculating the affected image region (extent), and handling view-frustum or clipping plane intersections to prevent artifacts. This method renders point clouds as splats with size attenuation based on perspective projection. It sets itself apart by computing the point size directly in the vertex shader using the projection matrix and view-space depth, ensuring visual size consistency with world-space radius. Choose this for point-based rendering where hardware point sprites are used. Footprint Evaluation is a forward-mapping algorithm that projects each voxel onto the 2D image plane, distributing its contribution as a "splat" or footprint. It sets itself apart by pre-integrating the 3D kernel into a 2D footprint table to avoid on-the-fly integration. Choose this for efficient volume rendering where cache coherency is prioritized. The Centralized Conics Approach is an efficient approximation method for computing the screen-space position and extents of a splat. It sets itself apart by using the inverse of a 2D-to-2D projective mapping from the splat's parameter space to screen space. Choose this when computational speed is critical and extreme perspective distortion is not a primary concern. Exact Half-Space Clipping computes the exact retained ray integral of a 3D Gaussian primitive when intersected by a clipping plane. It sets itself apart by providing a closed-form backward pass for clip-aware training without auxiliary networks, avoiding the aliasing and popping artifacts of binary culling. Choose this for differentiable rendering and training of Gaussian splats with clipping planes. Mueller's Splatting Approach is an object-order direct volume rendering technique that aligns sheet buffers parallel to the image plane. It sets itself apart by eliminating "popping" artifacts inherent in axis-aligned sheet approaches. Choose this for direct volume rendering of gray-scale volumes where sharp boundary preservation is less critical than speed. A method to compute screen-space position and extents of a splat by bounding it with a polygon in parameter space, transforming to clip space, clipping against the view-frustum, and performing perspective division. 1. Bound the splat by a polygon in its parameter space. 2. Transform the polygon to clip space. 3. Clip the polygon by the view-frustum using the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm. 4. Perform perspective division on each vertex to yield the clipped polygon in screen-space. 5. Compute desired quantities (position/extents) from the screen-space polygon. The method is not exact but produces a correct upper bound. Refines splatting by using precomputed footprint tables that adapt to view orientation and projection type, allowing precise control over kernel spread. Kernel spread can be set to e.g., 1.6 times the voxel spacing to balance hole filling and sharpness without excessive computation. The specific technique of bounding a splat by a polygon in parameter space and clipping it in clip space was devised by Sebastian Lippner as part of his surface splatting implementation. This approach addresses the limitations of previous methods that produced artifacts, particularly for large splats near the near plane. The method is implemented in the sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting repository. sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, https://github.com/sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) volume rendering, https://grokipedia.com/page/Volumerendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Perspective-Correct Point Splatting Vertex Shader
head: Point Splatting with Perspective Correction, Point Sprite Sizing
body: This method renders 3D point clouds as 2D splats in a vertex shader, ensuring that the visual size of the points attenuates correctly according to perspective projection. It solves the problem of points appearing unnaturally large or small at different depths by scaling the point size inversely with the depth coordinate. It differs from siblings like Centralized Conics Approach by relying on standard vertex shader outputs rather than computing complex screen-space conics in the fragment shader, and from Exact Half-Space Clipping by using hardware-accelerated point primitives rather than explicit geometry clipping. Inputs: inposition: 3D world-space or view-space position of the point center. particleradius: World-space radius of the point splat. incolor: Color data for the point. viewprojmatrix: Combined view and projection matrix. fovy: Vertical field of view in radians. viewportsize: Viewport dimensions, specifically height. Outputs: glPosition: Clip-space position. glPointSize: Screen-space point diameter in pixels. VertOut: Struct passing particleradius and incolor to the fragment shader. Data Structures: VertOut: radius: float representing the world-space radius. color: vec3 or vec4 representing the fragment color. Steps: 1. Transform inposition to clip space using viewprojmatrix and assign to glPosition. 2. Calculate the perspective-correct point size using the formula below. 3. Pass particleradius and incolor to the fragment shader via VertOut. Formula: The standard perspective-correct point size is calculated as: gl\PointSize = viewport\size[1] \times \left(\frac{1}{\tan(\frac{fov\y}{2})}\right) \times \frac{particle\radius}{gl\Position.w} Where: viewport\size[1] is the viewport height in pixels. fov\y is the vertical field of view in radians. particle\radius is the world-space radius of the point. gl\Position.w is the clip-space depth component, which corresponds to view-space depth for perspective projections. Alternative Formulations: Some implementations compute the projected corner components explicitly to derive the size: gl\PointSize = uScreenWidth \times 0.5 \times \frac{projectedCornerX}{projectedCornerW} \times 2.0 \times smoothstep(0., 1., \frac{data.a}{4.}) Or using a power function for opacity-based sizing: gl\PointSize = uScreenWidth \times 0.5 \times \frac{projectedCornerX}{projectedCornerW} \times 2.0 \times pow(\frac{data.a}{4.}, 0.1) Parameters: fovy: Vertical field of view in radians. viewportsize: Viewport dimensions, specifically height (viewportsize[1]). particleradius: World-space radius of the point splat. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by gl\Position.w causes numerical instability if points approach the near clipping plane. Ensure points are clipped before the near plane to avoid division by zero or extreme scaling. Boundary: Points partially outside the view frustum are handled by the graphics pipeline's built-in clipping routines. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def perspectivecorrectpointsplat(inposition, particleradius, incolor, viewprojmatrix, fovy, viewportheight): # 1. Transform to clip space and extract w-component # Compute clip-space w from the fourth row of the projection matrix clipw = (viewprojmatrix[3][0] inposition[0] + viewprojmatrix[3][1] inposition[1] + viewprojmatrix[3][2] inposition[2] + viewprojmatrix[3][3]) glPositionw = clipw # 2. Calculate perspective-correct point size cotfovhalf = 1.0 / math.tan(fovy / 2.0) pointsize = viewportheight cotfovhalf particleradius / glPositionw # 3. Prepare output struct for fragment shader vertout = {"color": incolor, "radius": particleradius} return {"glPosition": (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, glPositionw), "glPointSize": pointsize, "VertOut": vertout} Particle Sprite Rendering displays 3D data points as members of a particle system without surface fitting or interpolation, using animation for depth cues. It differs from surface rendering by not mapping data points onto a surface, avoiding surface fitting overhead and interpolation bias. A technique to scale points automatically according to distance from the eye point using the OpenGL point parameter extension, overcoming the limitation of standard glPointSize which does not support perspective scaling. Definition: Uses glPointParameter to scale points based on distance d from the eye. Formula: The conservative point diameter D as a function of distance d is: D = \frac{H}{2 \sqrt{2} d k \tan(\frac{\theta}{2})} Where k = (1 + 2 \tan^2(\frac{\theta}{2}))^{-1}. The OpenGL point size formula is: D = D0 \sqrt{\frac{1}{a + b d + c d^2}} Where D0 is user-defined diameter, and a, b, c are constants. Parameters: To match the derived diameter D, set D0 = 1, a = 0, b = 0, and c = \frac{2 k \tan^2(\frac{\theta}{2})}{H^2}. Pitfall: The point parameter extension scales according to distance d, not the z-coordinate. Using a lower bound for z ensures the point size is never smaller than the true size, preventing holes. Not given in the sources. Originating from early point cloud rendering techniques, this method leverages OpenGL's point sprite capabilities to render 3D data as 2D projections. It was developed to address the visual artifacts caused by naive point sizing in perspective views. name: Particle Sprite Rendering
head: Billboard Rendering, Point Sprite Rendering, Particle System Renderer
body: Particle Sprite Rendering displays 3D data points as members of a particle system without surface fitting or interpolation, using animation for depth cues. It differs from surface rendering by not mapping data points onto a surface, avoiding surface fitting overhead and interpolation bias. Inputs and Outputs Input: Radar Cross Section (RCS) data points containing phi, theta, radial distance, return strength, and polarity. Output: A sequence of frames stored in Utah Raster Toolkit (RLE) format. Data Structures Particle List: A dynamic linked list storing particles and their respective centroid. Centroid: Defined by a user-specified origin in world coordinates and a shape (e.g., spherical). View Volume: Defined by Viewer Position (PRP), Camera Looking Direction (CW), View Plane Normal (VPN), and View Up Vector (VUP). Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: All particles start at the same time. The starting position is determined by the centroid shape and coordinate system (spherical or cartesian). For RCS data, particles start at a sphere around the centroid with radius zero. 2. Time Step Loop: 1. Check for Spawning: Iterate through the particle list for new particles. If spawning, generate the new system and add it to the linked list. 2. Check for Death: If a particle is dead, mark it and ignore it in subsequent steps. 3. Move Particle: Update particle position based on velocity. Velocity is determined by the strength of the RCS return. 4. Render Particles: Render the current state of the particle system. 5. Increment Time Step: Advance the simulation time. Formulas Particle Position: Derived from RCS data phi and theta, with radial distance starting at zero. Particle Alpha: \alpha = \text{clamp}(1.0 - \text{distanceFromCenter} \times 2.0, 0.0, 1.0) \times uParticleAlpha, where distanceFromCenter is the distance from the center of the point sprite. Particle Color (Modulated by Shadow Opacity): \text{color} = (1.0 - vOpacity \times 0.75) \times uParticleColor, where vOpacity is the shadow opacity and uParticleColor is the base color. Output Premultiplied Alpha Color: \text{FragColor} = \text{vec4}(\text{color} \times \alpha, \alpha). Parameters Centroid Shape: Spherical (chosen for RCS to represent the center of a spherical coordinate system). Coordinate System: Spherical or Cartesian. Clipping: World limits including front and back. Memory Requirement: At least 16 megabytes. Filtering (Polarity Specific): W Polarity: Low pass filter at 20 dBsm, High pass filter at 65 dBsm. Particle color: Red. HH Polarity: High pass and low pass filter limits set to 0. Particle color: Blue. HV and VH Polarity: High pass and low pass filter limits set to 0. Particle color: Green. Multi-Polarity: Low pass filter set to 0, High pass filter set to 70. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Particle: def init(self, position, velocity, color): self.position = position self.velocity = velocity self.color = color self.alive = True def particlesystemloop(datapoints, centroidorigin, coordinatesystem, timestep): particles = [] # Dynamic linked list for dp in datapoints: # 1. Check for spawning if coordinatesystem == 'spherical': phi, theta = dp.phi, dp.theta r = 0.0 pos = ( centroidorigin[0] + r math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi), centroidorigin[1] + r math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi), centroidorigin[2] + r math.cos(theta)) else: pos = centroidorigin velocity = dp.strength color = getcolorbypolarity(dp.polarity) particles.append(Particle(pos, velocity, color)) # 2. Check for death for p in particles: if not p.alive: continue # 3. Move particle p.position = ( p.position[0] + p.velocity timestep, p.position[1], p.position[2]) # 4. Render particles renderparticle(p) # 5. Increment time step return particles def getcolorbypolarity(polarity): if polarity == 'W': return (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) if polarity == 'HH': return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) if polarity in ('HV', 'VH'): return (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) def renderparticle(p): # Wu antialiased line rendering: increment one pixel at a time along major axis. # For each increment, two pixels are drawn bracketing the axis. # Intensity determined by distance from actual line. # Fragment shader alpha: alpha = clamp(1.0 - distanceFromCenter 2.0, 0.0, 1.0) uParticleAlpha # Fragment shader color: color = (1.0 - vOpacity 0.75) uParticleColor # Output: FragColor = vec4(color alpha, alpha) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Random Placement: Random particle placement is not used for RCS data because data is mapped to specific locations. Static Images: Static images lack sufficient cues for the volumetric nature of the data. This is addressed by animating the development over time and allowing view rotation while growing. Resolution Loss: Significant loss of resolution occurs when transferring images to tape and displaying on NTSC monitors, causing blurring. Lack of standard aspect ratios in NTSC monitors alters the look of data, potentially hiding areas or falsely indicating large returns. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in sources. Rendering time was approximately 95 seconds per frame for the final data set. Memory Complexity: At least 16 megabytes of memory required. Measured Performance: Rendering a final data set required 10 minutes to load data files. The final video tape lasted 3 minutes, took 1900 separate images, and required 6 hours to record. Strengths: Minimal filtering and data manipulation; no surface fitting overhead; no interpolation bias; animation provides additional 3D cues. Limitations: Not designed for interactive display; significant resolution loss on NTSC monitors; aspect ratio sensitivity. When to Use: When displaying robust, vectorized data sets (like RCS) where volumetric nature needs to be conveyed through animation and minimal data manipulation is desired. Origin: Based on the description by Reeves [Ree 83]. History: The code was written in AT&T C++ version 2.1. The system was designed with portability and flexibility as primary considerations. It was used for viewing Radar Cross Section (RCS) data in three dimensions. Usage: Used for generating frame-by-frame depictions of environments for video recording and playback, providing additional 3D cues for data analysis. name: Footprint Evaluation
head: Footprint Mapping, Splatting (Westover), Westover 1990, Westover Splatting, Westover's Footprint Evaluation, Westover's Splatting
body: Footprint Evaluation is an object-order direct volume rendering algorithm that projects each voxel from the volume grid onto the 2D image plane as a "splat" (footprint) and accumulates these contributions to form the final image. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering volumetric data by distributing each sample's energy across a region on the screen using a pre-integrated reconstruction kernel, rather than casting rays per pixel. It sets itself apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives by using a forward-mapping scheme where the footprint is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view ray, allowing for pre-computation and fast rasterization, whereas Perspective-Correct Point Splatting Vertex Shader and Centralized Conics Approach focus on geometric projection accuracy, and Exact Half-Space Clipping focuses on boundary handling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume grid of voxels with values f(vk), a viewing direction (orthographic or perspective), a reconstruction kernel w, and a compositing order (front-to-back or back-to-front). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity from all overlapping splats. Data Structures: 1. Volume Grid: Array of voxels. Each voxel has a position (i,j,k) and a value f(vk) (density/color). 2. Footprint Table: A 2D lookup table storing the pre-integrated values of the reconstruction kernel. It represents the integration of the 3D spherically symmetric kernel along one axis (typically the view ray). Layout: A 2D array of floating-point values. The center of the table corresponds to the projected voxel center. The size of the table determines the support of the footprint. Generic vs. View-Transformed: For orthographic projection with uniform grid spacing and symmetric kernels, a single generic footprint table is used for all voxels. For perspective projection or non-uniform spacing, a view-transformed table is computed per view (or per voxel) to account for elliptical distortion. 3. Compositing Buffer: The final image buffer storing accumulated color and opacity. 4. Sheet Buffer (Optional): In the sheet-buffer method, splats are accumulated in intermediate buffers aligned with the volume face most parallel to the image plane before being composited into the final buffer. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Footprint Table Generation): Select a 3D reconstruction kernel w(x,y,z), typically a Gaussian. Compute the 2D footprint function F(x,y) by integrating the 3D kernel along the view ray (z-axis): F(x,y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} w(x,y,z) \, dz Sample F(x,y) on a 2D grid to create the Footprint Table. The resolution of this table should be high enough to avoid aliasing but low enough to fit in memory. For perspective projection, compute the orientation and scale of the elliptical footprint for the current view. 2. Voxel Traversal and Projection: Determine the traversal order of voxels. This is typically done by sorting voxels based on their depth along the view ray. Common strategies include: Back-to-front: Guarantees correct visibility. Front-to-back: Faster because compositing can stop when pixels are fully opaque. Sheet-based: Group voxels into slabs parallel to the image plane to optimize cache usage and compositing. For each voxel vk at position (xk, yk, zk) with value f(vk): Project the voxel center to the image plane coordinates (xs, ys) using the view and projection matrices. Determine the screen-space extent of the footprint. For orthographic projection, this is a circle (if the kernel is isotropic). For perspective projection, it is an ellipse. If using a view-transformed table, map the elliptical extent to the generic circular table extent using a transformation T^{-1}. 3. Rasterization (Splatting): Identify all pixels (x,y) that lie within the footprint's extent. For each pixel in the extent: Calculate the displacement (dx, dy) = (x - xs, y - ys) from the projected voxel center. Look up the weight w(x,y)s from the Footprint Table. If the footprint is elliptical, interpolate from the view-transformed table or map the coordinates to the generic table. Compute the contribution: C = f(vk) \times w(x,y)s. Composite this contribution into the Compositing Buffer (and/or Sheet Buffer) using the chosen compositing operator (e.g., front-to-back alpha blending). 4. Final Compositing (if using Sheet Buffer): If the sheet-buffer method is used, composite the accumulated sheet buffers into the final Compositing Buffer in front-to-back order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def footprintevaluation(volume, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, kernelwidth, footprinttablesize): # 1. Preprocessing: Generate Footprint Table footprinttable = generatefootprinttable(kernelwidth, footprinttablesize) # Initialize Compositing Buffer (Color and Opacity) height, width = volume.shape[1], volume.shape[2] compositingbuffer = [[(0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # 2. Determine Traversal Order voxels = [] for k in range(volume.shape[0]): for j in range(volume.shape[1]): for i in range(volume.shape[2]): if volume[k, j, i] != 0.0: voxels.append({'pos': (i, j, k), 'val': volume[k, j, i]}) # Sort voxels by depth along the view ray (simplified) voxels.sort(key=lambda v: v['pos'][0] + v['pos'][1] + v['pos'][2], reverse=True) # 3. Project and Splat for voxel in voxels: xs, ys, = voxel['pos'] # Project voxel center to screen space (simplified orthographic) screenx, screeny = xs, ys # Determine footprint extent in screen space extentradius = int(kernelwidth) for dy in range(-extentradius, extentradius + 1): for dx in range(-extentradius, extentradius + 1): x = int(screenx + dx) y = int(screeny + dy) if not (0 <= x < width and 0 <= y < height): continue tablex = (dx + extentradius) / (2 extentradius) tabley = (dy + extentradius) / (2 extentradius) weight = lookupfootprint(footprinttable, tablex, tabley) contribution = voxel['val'] weight cin, ain = compositingbuffer[y][x] cout = cin + contribution (1.0 - ain) aout = ain + contribution (1.0 - ain) compositingbuffer[y][x] = (cout, aout) return compositingbuffer def generatefootprinttable(kernelwidth, tablesize): table = [[0.0] tablesize for in range(tablesize)] sigma = kernelwidth / 2.0 center = tablesize // 2 for i in range(tablesize): for j in range(tablesize): x = (i - center) / tablesize y = (j - center) / tablesize table[i][j] = math.exp(-(x2 + y2) / (2 sigma2)) return table def lookupfootprint(table, tx, ty): h, w = len(table), len(table[0]) i = int(tx (w - 1)) j = int(ty (h - 1)) i = max(0, min(i, w - 2)) j = max(0, min(j, h - 2)) dx = tx (w - 1) - i dy = ty (h - 1) - j return (table[j][i] (1 - dx) (1 - dy) + table[j][i+1] dx (1 - dy) + table[j+1][i] (1 - dx) dy + table[j+1][i+1] dx dy) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Standard splatting suffers from aliasing when the volume sampling rate is higher than the image sampling rate (e.g., high-resolution volumes or perspective views). This is caused by the discrete evaluation of the splatting equation. Solutions include Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment [1288-antialiased-splatting-with-footprint-alignment.md] or EWA filters. Overlapping Splats: When splats overlap, the compositing order affects the result. Front-to-back compositing is faster but may produce incorrect results if the traversal order is not perfectly sorted. Back-to-front guarantees correct visibility, while front-to-back is faster because compositing can stop when pixels are fully opaque. Perspective Projection: The footprint becomes elliptical, requiring additional computation for orientation and scaling. Sheet Buffer Popping: In the sheet-buffer method, sudden changes in the orientation of the compositing sheets can cause popping artifacts. Kernel Size: Large footprints increase blurring; small footprints generate gaps. The footprint size must be tuned for the pixel-to-voxel ratio. Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment is a forward-mapping volume rendering technique that prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views by dynamically scaling splat sizes and attenuating splat energy for voxels beyond a critical distance. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by varying the kernel size and energy as a function of depth to match the diverging integration grid rays, ensuring the integration grid sampling frequency remains above twice the maximum volume raster frequency. The Separable Footprint (SF) projector is a forward mapping algorithm for X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT) that calculates line integrals through a voxelized volume by explicitly modeling the finite width of both detector pixels and volume voxels. Unlike Siddon or Joseph methods, which treat voxels and pixels as infinitesimal lines, SF provides higher quantitative accuracy and avoids specific artifacts, at the cost of increased computational complexity. The Footprint Function Mechanism implements 3D spherically symmetric splatting kernels in volume rendering by reducing computational dimensionality from 3D to 2D. It projects volumetric data onto a 2D image plane by pre-computing the integration of the 3D kernel along one axis and storing the result as a 2D lookup table. This approach avoids per-pixel 3D kernel evaluations by relying on 2D table lookups and interpolation, as detailed in Footprint Evaluation. Time Complexity: O(k^2 n^3), where n^3 is the number of voxels and k is the kernel size (footprint radius). This is faster than ray-casting's O(k^3 n^3) because the convolution is precomputed and each voxel is splatted exactly once. Memory Complexity: Depends on the footprint table size and the number of voxels. Measured Performance: Splatting is inherently faster than ray-casting for moderate screen sizes and specific datasets, but good quality results may require as much CPU time as ray-casting. It is efficient for real-time rendering on older hardware due to its simplicity and parallelizability. Strengths: Fast due to pre-integrated kernels and object-order processing. Simple static parallel decomposition. Easy to implement and parallelize. Supports scattered data (e.g., SPH) with sorting. Limitations: Poor quality without anti-aliasing techniques (aliasing artifacts). Blurry images for zoomed views due to Gaussian kernel properties. High fill-rate for zoomed splats. Incorrect compositing when splats overlap, especially with changing traversal orders. Not well-suited for perspective projection without additional transformations. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where speed is prioritized over perfect accuracy, or for orthographic projections of moderate-resolution volumes. When Not to Use: High-quality offline rendering, perspective views with high dynamic range, or when strict anti-aliasing is required without additional techniques. Footprint Evaluation, also known as Westover Splatting, was first described by L. Westover in 1990 in the paper "Footprint evaluation for volume rendering". It was introduced as a forward mapping algorithm for rendering regular grids on a CPU. The method was developed to address the computational cost of ray-casting by pre-computing the integration of the reconstruction kernel. It has since been extended to support perspective projection and anti-aliasing.
