name: Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment
head: Antialiased splatting method, Perspective Anti-Aliased Splatting
body: Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment is a forward-mapping volume rendering technique that prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views by dynamically scaling splat sizes and attenuating splat energy for voxels beyond a critical distance. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by varying the kernel size and energy as a function of depth to match the diverging integration grid rays, ensuring the integration grid sampling frequency remains above twice the maximum volume raster frequency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (typically stored as a subset of extracted voxels), camera parameters (eye position, view plane distance z{img}, pixel extent p, viewing frustum half-angle \phic), and a transfer function. Output: A 2D image with anti-aliased volume rendering. Data Structures: The volume subset is stored as a 2D array of splat rows. Each row is an array of voxels. Each voxel stores its location (x, y, z) in eye space, a normal vector, and a pre-computed transfer function value (e.g., color, opacity). Voxels in a row are not necessarily contiguous. The splat kernel is pre-computed and stored in a 256 \times 256 table, which is texture-mapped onto the polygon representing the splat. Critical Distance (zk or k): The distance zk along the z-axis where the volume raster sampling frequency p equals the integration grid sampling frequency \phi(z) divides eye space into two regions: Region 1 (z < zk): No aliasing; standard splatting is sufficient. Region 2 (z > zk): Aliasing possible; low-pass filtering (scaling/attenuation) is required. The critical distance is calculated from similar triangles: zk = \frac{p \cdot z{img}}{p - 1} where p is the extent of a pixel and z{img} is the distance from the eye point to the view plane. Note: uses k for this distance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Traverse the volume: Iterate through the voxels in back-to-front or front-to-back order. 2. Determine Distance: For each voxel, compute its distance zv (or d) from the eye point along the viewing axis. 3. Check Region: If zv < zk (or d < k): Draw the splat with its standard size in eye space. The polygon can be aligned parallel to the x-y plane or perpendicular to the ray. If zv \ge zk (or d \ge k): Scale Radius: Scale the splat footprint radius to match the diverging rays. Using similar triangles: r2 = r1 \cdot \frac{zv}{zk} where r1 is the radius at zk and r2 is the radius at zv. expresses this as r2 = (k/d) \cdot r1 where r1 is the radius at distance k (this implies r1 in S1 is the scaled radius at k, effectively the base unit for scaling beyond k). The geometric intent is identical: radius grows linearly with distance beyond zk. Attenuate Energy: Attenuate the splat's energy (e.g., alpha channel) to preserve total projected energy and avoid brightness artifacts. The total attenuation factor is (zk / zv)^2. states E2 = (k^2 / d^2) \cdot E1. explicitly states: "We attenuate the alpha channel of the polygon according to the value of (zk/zv)". This implies the alpha is scaled by the square root of the energy attenuation factor, or that the energy attenuation is defined differently in their compositing model. Footprint Alignment: Rotate the splat polygon so it is perpendicular to the ray passing from the eye point through the voxel position. Two alignment strategies exist: 1. Grid-aligned: Align stretched footprint with the y-axis of the grid. 2. Ray-perpendicular: Rotate stretched footprint to be perpendicular to the ray. Ray-perpendicular is more accurate near zk, while grid-aligned is better far from zk. 4. Render: Texture map the pre-computed kernel onto the polygon and composite into the screen buffer. Voxel Interpolation (Tri-Linear): For trilinear interpolation, the value is distributed to 8 surrounding voxels: 1. Offset voxel-space position by -0.5 to align with voxel centers: p = (x-0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5). 2. Find lower-left corner: corner = (\lfloor px \rfloor, \lfloor py \rfloor, \lfloor pz \rfloor). 3. Calculate fraction vector: f = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - (\lfloor p \rfloor + 1 - p). 4. Loop over i, j, k \in \{0, 1\}: Invert fraction component for each axis at start of loop. Weight w = fx \cdot fy \cdot fz. Add value \cdot w to voxel at corner + (i, j, k) if in bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderantialiasedsplats(volumesubset, camera, kerneltable): """ volumesubset: List of rows, each row is a list of Voxel objects. camera: Object with eyepos, zimg, pixelextent p, frustumangle phic. kerneltable: 256x256 texture map of the splat kernel. """ # Calculate critical distance zk zk = (camera.p camera.zimg) / (camera.p - 1) for row in volumesubset: for voxel in row: # 1. Calculate distance from eye zv = voxel.pos.z # 2. Determine scaling and attenuation if zv < zk: scalefactor = 1.0 alphascale = 1.0 else: scalefactor = zv / zk alphascale = zk / zv radius = voxel.baseradius scalefactor center = voxel.pos # Standard rotation to align polygon normal with eye-to-voxel ray raydir = normalize(center - camera.eyepos) polygon = createpolygon(center, radius, raydir) polygon.texture = kerneltable polygon.alpha = alphascale # Standard rasterization and alpha compositing into screen buffer compositepolygon(polygon) def trilinearinterpolate(value, pos, buffer): """ Distributes 'value' at 'pos' to 8 surrounding voxels in 'buffer' using tri-linear interpolation. """ # Offset by -0.5 to align with voxel centers p = (pos[0] - 0.5, pos[1] - 0.5, pos[2] - 0.5) # Lower-left corner corner = (math.floor(p[0]), math.floor(p[1]), math.floor(p[2])) # Fraction vector f = (1.0 - (math.floor(p[0]) + 1 - p[0]), 1.0 - (math.floor(p[1]) + 1 - p[1]), 1.0 - (math.floor(p[2]) + 1 - p[2])) for k in range(2): f[2] = 1.0 - f[2] for j in range(2): f[1] = 1.0 - f[1] for i in range(2): f[0] = 1.0 - f[0] weight = f[0] f[1] f[2] tx, ty, tz = corner[0] + i, corner[1] + j, corner[2] + k if buffer.isinbounds(tx, ty, tz): buffer.add(tx, ty, tz, value weight) def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def createpolygon(center, radius, normal): # Standard graphics pipeline: generate quad vertices, apply rotation matrix to align normal return {"center": center, "radius": radius, "normal": normal} def compositepolygon(polygon): # Standard graphics pipeline: rasterize polygon, texture map kernel, blend alpha into framebuffer pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Energy Attenuation: If splat energy is not attenuated when scaling size, the projected area changes incorrectly, leading to brightness artifacts. Alignment Errors: Footprint polygon not aligned perpendicularly with the sight ray causes errors in projected polygon extent, largest at the viewing frustum boundary. Sight rays from pixels other than the center traverse the footprint at an oblique angle. There is no known efficient solution outside of ray-driven splatting. Pre-integration: Pre-integrating a distorted kernel for one z-location and scaling it for another does not yield the correct footprint because relative kernel distortion varies with z. Grid Alignment: Aligning footprints with the grid causes indexed ray integrals to differ significantly from true ray integrals for rays maintaining a large angle with the viewing axis. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the subset. Per-voxel cost involves distance calculation, scaling factor computation, and polygon setup/compositing. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume subset size. Storing a 2D array of splat rows with non-contiguous voxels requires storing location and normal for each voxel. Kernel table is 256 \times 256. Performance: Achieved real-time performance on Silicon Graphics hardware for datasets like 512 \times 512 \times 103 (386K splats). Strengths: Prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views. Efficient compared to ray-driven splatting or computing unique footprints for every voxel with diverging rays. Can be implemented using standard rendering hardware (texture-mapped polygons). Limitations: Approximation errors in footprint alignment and projection. Grid-aligned alignment is less accurate for rays at large angles. Ray-perpendicular alignment is more accurate but requires rotation per voxel. Does not address aliasing from non-ideal reconstruction filters, only sample-rate aliasing. When to Use: Perspective volume rendering where aliasing artifacts are visible due to diverging rays or high volume resolution relative to image resolution. When Not to Use: Orthographic views with low resolution (aliasing is uniform and less severe, or handled by standard filtering). Origin: The method was introduced in the late 1990s. references "Perspective Splatting" (DTIC ADA363073) and "Splatting Errors and Antialiasing" (DTIC ADA606764, IEEE TVCG 1998). Development: Standard splatting (Westover) was designed for orthographic views. Perspective splatting introduced aliasing issues due to non-uniform sampling. This method extends splatting to perspective by scaling kernels and attenuating energy. Usage: Used in the "Tenderer" implementation on Silicon Graphics hardware. Applied to terrain datasets from satellite photographs and microtubule studies from confocal microscopy. name: Separable Footprint (SF) Projector
head: SF method, Separable Footprint (SF) Method
body: The Separable Footprint (SF) projector is a forward mapping algorithm for X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT) that calculates line integrals through a voxelized volume by explicitly modeling the finite width of both detector pixels and volume voxels. Unlike Siddon or Joseph methods, which treat voxels and pixels as infinitesimal lines, SF provides higher quantitative accuracy and avoids specific artifacts, at the cost of increased computational complexity. The SF method computes the projection of a 3D volume onto a 2D detector plane. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric grid V with dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) and voxel spacings (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z). A set of ray paths defined by source and detector positions/orientations. Output: A 2D projection image P representing the line integrals (attenuation) measured by the detector pixels. Data Structures: The volume is stored as a regular grid. Detector geometry is defined by pixel dimensions (\Delta u, \Delta v) and the transformation from world space to detector space. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Tracing: For each detector pixel, determine the corresponding ray path through the volume by calculating the intersection of the ray with the volume bounding box. 2. Footprint Calculation: For each voxel intersected by the ray, calculate the geometric overlap volume between the voxel and the effective detector pixel area projected back into the volume space. 3. Weight Computation: Compute the weight w{ijk} for each voxel (i,j,k) based on the geometric overlap. 4. Accumulation: Accumulate the weighted voxel values into the detector pixel: P{uv} = \sum{i,j,k} w{ijk} V{ijk} where V{ijk} is the value of the voxel at (i,j,k). Parameters: Voxel sizes (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z): Must be provided for accurate scaling. Detector pixel sizes (\Delta u, \Delta v): Must be provided for accurate scaling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Rays grazing the volume boundary must be handled to avoid missing contributions or double-counting. Precision: Standard floating-point arithmetic is sufficient for typical XCT scales, but ray origins and intersections should be computed in double precision to avoid accumulation errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardproject(volume, voxelspacing, detectorgeometry): dx, dy, dz = voxelspacing projection = [[0.0 for in range(detectorgeometry.width)] for in range(detectorgeometry.height)] for v in range(detectorgeometry.height): for u in range(detectorgeometry.width): rayorigin, raydirection = detectorgeometry.getray(u, v) tmin, tmax = intersectbox(rayorigin, raydirection, volume.bounds) if tmax <= tmin: continue startvoxel = voxelindex(rayorigin, voxelspacing) endvoxel = voxelindex(rayorigin + raydirection tmax, voxelspacing) stepx = 1 if raydirection.x >= 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if raydirection.y >= 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if raydirection.z >= 0 else -1 tx = (startvoxel.x + stepx 0.5 - rayorigin.x) / raydirection.x if raydirection.x != 0 else float('inf') ty = (startvoxel.y + stepy 0.5 - rayorigin.y) / raydirection.y if raydirection.y != 0 else float('inf') tz = (startvoxel.z + stepz 0.5 - rayorigin.z) / raydirection.z if raydirection.z != 0 else float('inf') i, j, k = startvoxel.x, startvoxel.y, startvoxel.z while True: voxelmin = [i dx, j dy, k dz] voxelmax = [(i + 1) dx, (j + 1) dy, (k + 1) dz] overlapx = max(0.0, min(tmax, voxelmax[0] - rayorigin.x) / raydirection.x - max(tmin, voxelmin[0] - rayorigin.x) / raydirection.x) if raydirection.x != 0 else max(0.0, min(tmax, tmax) - max(tmin, tmin)) overlapy = max(0.0, min(tmax, voxelmax[1] - rayorigin.y) / raydirection.y - max(tmin, voxelmin[1] - rayorigin.y) / raydirection.y) if raydirection.y != 0 else max(0.0, min(tmax, tmax) - max(tmin, tmin)) overlapz = max(0.0, min(tmax, voxelmax[2] - rayorigin.z) / raydirection.z - max(tmin, voxelmin[2] - rayorigin.z) / raydirection.z) if raydirection.z != 0 else max(0.0, min(tmax, tmax) - max(tmin, tmin)) weight = (overlapx overlapy overlapz) / (dx dy dz) if weight > 0.0: projection[v][u] += volume[k][j][i] weight if i == endvoxel.x and j == endvoxel.y and k == endvoxel.z: break if tx < ty and tx < tz: i += stepx tx += stepx dx / raydirection.x if raydirection.x != 0 else float('inf') elif ty < tz: j += stepy ty += stepy dy / raydirection.y if raydirection.y != 0 else float('inf') else: k += stepz tz += stepz dz / raydirection.z if raydirection.z != 0 else float('inf') return projection def intersectbox(origin, direction, bounds): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for axis in range(3): if direction[axis] == 0: if origin[axis] < bounds[axis][0] or origin[axis] > bounds[axis][1]: return 0.0, 0.0 else: t1 = (bounds[axis][0] - origin[axis]) / direction[axis] t2 = (bounds[axis][1] - origin[axis]) / direction[axis] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) return tmin, tmax def voxelindex(position, spacing): return (int(position[0] / spacing[0]), int(position[1] / spacing[1]), int(position[2] / spacing[2])) Accuracy: Quantitatively accurate; numerical values scale appropriately with changes in voxel and detector sizes. More accurate than Siddon or Joseph methods, which do not model finite widths. Computational Cost: More computationally expensive than Siddon or Joseph methods due to the complexity of calculating finite footprints. Artifacts: Avoids artifacts produced by Siddon/Joseph methods in cases where finite width effects are significant. Implementation: Implemented in CPU (C/C++) and GPU (CUDA) environments. The SF method was introduced by Long et al. in 2010 as one of the most popular and effective models for calculating XCT line integrals through a voxelized volume. It is part of a class of methods (along with Distance Driven) that explicitly model the finite width of detector pixels and volume voxels, contrasting with earlier methods like Siddon (1985) and Joseph (1982). It is implemented in the LEAP software package for CPU and GPU forward and back projections. Optimization-based reconstruction algorithms that rely on gradient calculations require the adjoint (transpose) of the X-ray Transform, which corresponds to backprojection. name: Footprint Function Mechanism
head: 2D reconstruction kernel, Footprint Function, Splatting Dimension Reduction (Footprint), footprint table
body: The Footprint Function Mechanism implements 3D spherically symmetric splatting kernels in volume rendering by reducing computational dimensionality from 3D to 2D. It projects volumetric data onto a 2D image plane by pre-computing the integration of the 3D kernel along one axis and storing the result as a 2D lookup table. This approach avoids per-pixel 3D kernel evaluations by relying on 2D table lookups and interpolation, as detailed in Footprint Evaluation. Inputs: A 3D spherically symmetric splat kernel function h(x, y, z). A regular volumetric grid with spacing parameters. Camera projection parameters (orthographic or perspective). Outputs: A 2D lookup table representing the footprint function. A rendered image where each pixel contains the accumulated contribution of all splats. Data Structures: Footprint Table: A 2D array of floating-point values. The dimensions correspond to the spatial extent of the kernel in the image plane. The table is indexed by integer offsets (i, j) from the center, representing discrete samples of the continuous function. Voxel Data: Standard volumetric grid values (density/scalar) and positions. Formulas: The footprint function F(x, y) is defined as the integral of the 3D kernel h along one dimension (typically w or z), assuming spherical symmetry: F(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x, y, w) \, dw where (x, y) is the displacement from the projected sample point on the image plane. The contribution to a pixel at projected coordinates (xD, yD) with density \rho is: \text{Contribution}(x, y) = \rho \cdot F(x - xD, y - yD). Steps: 1. Pre-compute the Footprint Table: Numerically integrate h(x, y, w) along the w axis for a grid of (x, y) values covering the 2D extent, and store the results in a finely sampled 2D lookup table. If the volume grid spacing is regular, the view projection is orthographic, and the splat kernel is radially symmetric, this table is computed once and reused. Otherwise, it must be recomputed per view (for non-symmetric kernels) or per voxel (for perspective projections). 2. Project Voxels: For each voxel in the volume, calculate its projected center (xD, yD) on the image plane using the current camera projection matrix. 3. Determine Extent: Identify the bounding box of the footprint table that overlaps with the image plane region influenced by the voxel. 4. Sample and Composite: For each pixel (xp, yp) within the footprint's extent: calculate the displacement vector (dx, dy) = (xp - xD, yp - yD); map (dx, dy) to the indices of the pre-computed 2D footprint table; interpolate the value from the footprint table; retrieve the voxel's density \rho; compute the weighted contribution \rho \cdot \text{interpolated\footprint}(dx, dy); composite this value into the pixel's existing buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputefootprint(kernelfunc, extent, resolution): """Pre-compute 2D footprint table by integrating 3D kernel along w-axis.""" tablesize = 2 resolution + 1 footprinttable = [[0.0] tablesize for in range(tablesize)] center = resolution dw = 2 extent / resolution for i in range(tablesize): for j in range(tablesize): x = (i - center) (extent / resolution) y = (j - center) (extent / resolution) integral = 0.0 for k in range(resolution): w = -extent + (k + 0.5) dw integral += kernelfunc(x, y, w) dw footprinttable[i][j] = integral return footprinttable, extent, resolution def bilinearinterpolate(table, idxx, idxy, resolution): """Bilinear interpolation for the footprint table.""" tablesize = 2 resolution + 1 fx = idxx - int(idxx) fy = idxy - int(idxy) ix = int(idxx) iy = int(idxy) x0, x1 = max(0, ix), min(tablesize - 1, ix + 1) y0, y1 = max(0, iy), min(tablesize - 1, iy + 1) val = (table[y0][x0] (1 - fx) (1 - fy) + table[y0][x1] fx (1 - fy) + table[y1][x0] (1 - fx) fy + table[y1][x1] fx fy) return val def renderwithfootprint(volumedata, footprinttable, extent, resolution, imagewidth, imageheight): """Render volume using pre-computed footprint table.""" image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] tablesize = 2 resolution + 1 center = resolution for voxel in volumedata: # Project 3D voxel position to 2D image plane coordinates using the camera matrix px, py = voxel.position.x 1.0, voxel.position.y 1.0 minx = max(0, int(px - extent)) maxx = min(imagewidth, int(px + extent)) miny = max(0, int(py - extent)) maxy = min(imageheight, int(py + extent)) for y in range(miny, maxy): for x in range(minx, maxx): dx = x - px dy = y - py idxx = center + dx (resolution / extent) idxy = center + dy (resolution / extent) if 0 <= idxx < tablesize and 0 <= idxy < tablesize: footval = bilinearinterpolate(footprinttable, idxx, idxy, resolution) contribution = voxel.density footval image[y][x] += contribution return image Parameters: Footprint Table Resolution: Not given in the sources. Integration Steps: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Projection: The footprint shape changes with depth. The table cannot be reused across the entire volume; it must be recomputed per voxel or approximated. Non-Symmetric Kernels: If the kernel is not radially symmetric, the integration axis matters, and the table must be recomputed for each view orientation. Precision: Numerical integration errors in pre-computation can lead to bias. Interpolation errors in the 2D table can cause blurring or artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant speedup over direct 3D kernel evaluation per pixel. Simple to implement with standard 2D interpolation routines. Limitations: Requires pre-computation. Less flexible for non-symmetric or anisotropic kernels without significant overhead. Perspective projections require per-voxel table generation or approximation, which can negate performance gains. When to use: Orthographic projections, regular grids, and symmetric kernels. When not to use: Perspective projections with high accuracy requirements, or non-symmetric kernels, unless the per-voxel recomputation cost is acceptable. The concept was introduced by Westover in the context of volume rendering, specifically to improve the efficiency of splatting algorithms. The original splatting algorithm considered the splat as a 3D spherically symmetric reconstruction kernel. Westover observed that since the splat is reconstructed into a 2D image raster, it can be implemented as a 2D reconstruction kernel by integrating the 3D kernel along one dimension. This technique is often referred to as "footprint function" or "2D reconstruction kernel". Later work by Westover also introduced accumulating splats onto a 2D sheet aligned with the volume axis most parallel to the view plane to further improve quality. name: Centralized Conics Approach
head: Botsch et al. Splat Extent Approximation, Botsch et al.'s approximation, Zwicker et al. Centralized Conics Approach
body: The Centralized Conics Approach is an efficient approximation method for computing the screen-space position and extents of a splat in point-based rendering. It approximates the projected Gaussian kernel's footprint by utilizing the inverse of a 2D-to-2D projective mapping from the splat's parameter space to screen space. Unlike methods that prioritize geometric exactness or robustness under extreme perspective, this approach trades precision for computational speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The splat's center position, the two vectors spanning its elliptical shape in local space, and the camera projection matrix. Output: The screen-space center and the approximate extents of the splat. Data Structures: The method relies on a 2D-to-2D projective mapping matrix M. Steps: 1. Construct the 2D-to-2D projective mapping matrix M that maps coordinates from the splat's local parameter space to screen space. 2. Compute the inverse of this mapping matrix, M^{-1}. 3. Apply M^{-1} to screen-space coordinates to approximate the splat's position and extents. Formulas: Let M be the projective mapping matrix. The screen-space position \mathbf{p}{screen} relates to the local parameter space position \mathbf{p}{local} by \mathbf{p}{screen} \sim M \mathbf{p}{local}. The approach computes the extents by inverting this relationship: \mathbf{p}{local} \sim M^{-1} \mathbf{p}{screen}. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method is numerically unstable when the projection of the splat approaches a line. In such cases, the condition number of the mapping matrix increases rapidly, leading to large roundoff errors during inversion. This instability can cause the screen-space extents to be underestimated, resulting in rendering artifacts. A rasterization technique that uses the inverse of a projective mapping matrix to transform screen coordinates back to object space for kernel evaluation, while simultaneously computing window-space depth values via linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates. It sets itself apart from standard perspective splatting by avoiding explicit matrix inversion through the use of adjoint matrices and optimizing depth computation by embedding the window-space depth formula directly into the homogeneous interpolation weights. This method computes perspective-correct splat shapes for point-based rendering by approximating the projective mapping of Gaussian reconstruction kernels from their local tangent planes to image space using affine mappings derived from conic isocontours. Unlike previous methods that used affine approximations exact only at the kernel center, this approach ensures accuracy at the kernel cutoff boundary, preventing artifacts such as holes and incorrect elongation under extreme perspective projections. It solves the problem where previous projections integrated kernels along the z-axis rather than the oblique ray from the camera, causing particles to be too faint by \cos(\theta) and insufficiently elongated radially. The Centralized Conics Approach is computationally efficient, making it suitable for real-time rendering on hardware such as NVIDIA GPUs. Its primary limitation is numerical instability under extreme perspective projections where the splat projects to a near-line. This instability can lead to underestimation of extents and visual artifacts. It is best used when performance is critical and extreme perspective distortions are rare or acceptable to approximate. The method is attributed to Zwicker et al. for the centralized conics approach, while the efficient approximation formulas are credited to Botsch et al.. It was noted in the context of GPU-based raycasting of quadric surfaces by Sigg et al. as an efficient but potentially unstable solution compared to methods that avoid matrix inversion. sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, https://github.com/sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Projective Splat Rasterization with Depth Optimization
head: Adjoint Matrix Splat Rasterization, Inverse Projective Mapping for Splatting
body: A rasterization technique for point-based rendering that uses the inverse of a projective mapping matrix to transform screen coordinates back to object space for kernel evaluation, while simultaneously computing window-space depth values via linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates. It sets itself apart from standard perspective splatting by avoiding explicit matrix inversion through the use of adjoint matrices and optimizing depth computation by embedding the window-space depth formula directly into the homogeneous interpolation weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Splat center \mathbf{p}k, tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k, view frustum near/far constants a, b, and screen coordinates (x, y) of the fragment. Output: Object-space coordinates (u, v) for kernel evaluation and window-space depth d(x) for z-buffering. Data Structures: \mathbf{M}k: A 3 \times 3 matrix representing the forward projective mapping from parameter space (u, v) to screen space. \mathbf{N}k: A 4 \times 3 matrix representing the scaled inverse mapping with the depth optimization row. Steps: 1. Compute Forward Mapping Matrix \mathbf{M}k: Construct the matrix from the splat's screen-space center and tangent vectors: \mathbf{M}k = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{s}k & \mathbf{t}k & \mathbf{p}k \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k, \mathbf{p}k are column vectors forming the 3 \times 3 matrix acting on \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. The forward mapping is defined as: \begin{bmatrix} xz \\ yz \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}k \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. 2. Compute Adjoint Matrix: Calculate the adjoint of \mathbf{M}k using three cross products to avoid explicit matrix inversion: \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}k \times \mathbf{p}k \\ \mathbf{p}k \times \mathbf{s}k \\ \mathbf{s}k \times \mathbf{t}k \end{bmatrix}. Let \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 denote the third row of this matrix. 3. Compute Scaling Factor: Calculate the scalar \alpha to normalize the homogeneous coefficient w such that it relates to the view-space depth pz (the z-component of \mathbf{p}k) and the window-space depth constant b: \alpha = \frac{b}{\text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 \cdot \mathbf{p}k}. Note that \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 \cdot \mathbf{p}k is the dot product of the third row of the adjoint matrix and the center vector \mathbf{p}k. 4. Construct Inverse Mapping Matrix \mathbf{N}k: Scale the adjoint matrix by \alpha to form the first three rows of \mathbf{N}k. To optimize depth computation, extend \mathbf{N}k to a 4 \times 3 matrix by adding a fourth row (\mathbf{N}k)4: (\mathbf{N}k)4 = \alpha \cdot \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ a \end{bmatrix}. This construction ensures that the homogeneous weight w in the inverse mapping equals b/pz, allowing the fourth component to directly yield the window-space depth d(x) = a + b/z via linear interpolation. 5. Rasterize and Interpolate: Rasterize the triangle covering the splat's bounding box. For each pixel (x, y), compute the homogeneous coordinates by multiplying the inverse matrix \mathbf{N}k with the screen coordinate vector \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}: \begin{bmatrix} uw \\ vw \\ w \\ d \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{N}k \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. The values uw, vw, w (and d if using the 4 \times 3 matrix) are linearly interpolated across the primitive. The object-space coordinates are recovered by perspective division: u = \frac{uw}{w}, \quad v = \frac{vw}{w}. The window-space depth is directly available as the fourth component d when the 4 \times 3 matrix is used, or computed as a + b/z if only the 3 \times 3 matrix is used. 6. Kernel Evaluation: Use the recovered (u, v) to evaluate the splat's reconstruction kernel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectivesplatrasterization(pk, sk, tk, a, b, x, y): # Forward mapping matrix Mk = [sk, tk, pk] Mk = columnstack([sk, tk, pk]) # Adjoint matrix rows are cross products adjM = rowstack([cross(tk, pk), cross(pk, sk), cross(sk, tk)]) # Scaling factor alpha ensures w = b/pz at the center denom = dot(adjM[2], pk) alpha = b / denom # Construct 4x3 inverse mapping matrix Nk Nk = zeros((4, 3)) Nk[:3,:] = alpha adjM Nk[3,:] = alpha adjM[2] + array([0.0, 0.0, a]) # Compute homogeneous coordinates for screen point (x, y) coords = Nk @ array([x, y, 1.0]) uw, vw, w, d = coords # Recover object-space coordinates u = uw / w v = vw / w return u, v, d Parameters: a, b: Constants derived from the near and far planes of the view frustum, mapping 1/z to the window space depth range [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Matrix Inversion Cost: Explicitly inverting \mathbf{M}k is computationally expensive, which the method avoids by using the adjoint matrix. Degenerate Splats: If \mathbf{p}k, \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k are collinear or \mathbf{p}k is at the origin, the adjoint matrix may be singular or the scaling factor undefined. In practice, check for near-zero denominators and skip rasterization or fall back to a safe default. Precision: Linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates is valid for projective mappings. However, ensure that w does not become zero or negative during interpolation, which would cause division by zero or incorrect depth ordering. Clip fragments where w \le 0. Time and memory complexity are Not given in the sources. Measured performance with specific hardware, resolution, and scene data is Not given in the sources. Scaling behavior is Not given in the sources. Strengths include perspective accuracy, avoidance of expensive matrix inversion, and seamless integration with standard z-buffering via window-space depth interpolation. Limitations include the requirement for careful handling of homogeneous weights to avoid division by zero. Performance may degrade if splats are very large or numerous, requiring efficient culling. Originated in the context of point-based rendering, specifically for perspective-accurate splatting. The method is described in "Splat/Mesh Blending, Perspective Rasterization and Transparency for Point-Based Rendering". It addresses the need for efficient, perspective-correct rasterization of splats without the overhead of full 3D-to-2D projection inversion per pixel. name: Perspective Accurate Splatting via Projective Conic Mapping
head: Affine Approximation of Projective Conics, Homogeneous Coordinate Splatting, Perspective Accurate Splatting, Perspective Correct Splatting, Projective Conic Splatting, SPH Perspective Rendering Fix
body: This method computes perspective-correct splat shapes for point-based rendering by approximating the projective mapping of Gaussian reconstruction kernels from their local tangent planes to image space using affine mappings derived from conic isocontours. Unlike previous EWA splatting methods that used affine approximations exact only at the kernel center, this approach ensures accuracy at the kernel cutoff boundary, preventing holes and artifacts under extreme perspective projections. It builds on the Centralized Conics Approach by providing the specific mechanism for deriving the correct variance matrix in screen space. Inputs: A set of point samples pk with associated colors fk and local tangent frames defined by tangent vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v. A Gaussian reconstruction kernel g with a user-specified cutoff value Fg (typically 1 < Fg < 2). Camera projection parameters. Outputs: Screen-space splat accumulation (color and weight) for each pixel. Data Structures: Tangent Frame Matrix (\mathbf{M}k): A 3 \times 3 matrix mapping local 2D coordinates (u, v) to 3D world space, defined as \mathbf{M}k = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}u \\ \mathbf{t}v \\ \mathbf{p}k \end{bmatrix}. Points \mathbf{p} on the tangent plane are expressed as \mathbf{p} = (u, v, 1) \mathbf{M}k. Conic Matrix (Qh): A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix representing the implicit form of a conic \phi(x, y) = Ax^2 + 2Bxy + Cy^2 + 2Dx + 2Ey - F = 0 in homogeneous coordinates: Qh = \begin{bmatrix} A & B & D \\ B & C & E \\ D & E & -F \end{bmatrix}. The equation is \mathbf{x} Qh \mathbf{x}^T = 0 where \mathbf{x} = [x, y, 1]. Variance Matrix (Rk): The 2 \times 2 covariance matrix of the Gaussian kernel in the local tangent frame. Mapped Variance Matrix (Q'''): The 2 \times 2 variance matrix of the reconstruction kernel in image space, derived from the projective mapping. Steps: 1. Define Local Kernel Isocontour: The Gaussian kernel is truncated at an isocontour defined by Fg. In the local tangent frame, this isocontour is a central conic expressed in homogeneous coordinates: \begin{bmatrix} u & v & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}k & 0 \\ 0 & -Fg^2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 0 Let Q{local} be the 3 \times 3 matrix \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}k & 0 \\ 0 & -Fg^2 \end{bmatrix}. 2. Compute Projective Mapping: Determine the mapping from the local tangent plane to the image plane by inverting the tangent frame matrix \mathbf{M}k^{-1} and applying the camera projection. 3. Derive Mapped Conic (Q'''): Apply the projective transformation to the local conic Q{local} to obtain the conic in image space. The resulting matrix Q''' represents the variance matrix of the reconstruction kernel in screen space. 4. Check Numerical Stability: Invert \mathbf{M}k to compute the mapping. Check the condition number of \mathbf{M}k. If the condition number exceeds a threshold (indicating the splat is degenerating into a line segment), discard the splat. 5. Validate Conic Type: Determine if the mapped conic is an ellipse. Calculate the discriminant \Delta = AC - B^2 from the upper-left 2 \times 2 submatrix of the mapped conic matrix. If \Delta \le 0 (parabola or hyperbola), discard the splat. 6. Compute Screen-Space Variance: The effective variance matrix for the splat in screen space is Q''' + H, where H is the resampling filter matrix. The inverse (Q''' + H)^{-1} is passed to the fragment shader. 7. Rasterize Splat: Compute the bounding box of the projected conic to determine the OpenGL point size or fragment shader execution region. For each pixel \mathbf{x} in the bounding box, evaluate the ellipse equation: r^2 = \mathbf{x} (Q''' + H)^{-1} \mathbf{x}^T If r^2 < 1, the pixel is inside the splat. Accumulate color weighted by the Gaussian value and accumulate weight. 8. Normalize: In a final pass, divide accumulated color by accumulated weight to normalize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def perspectiveaccuratesplatting(points, cameramatrix, Fg=1.5, condthreshold=1e6): """ Render points using perspective accurate splatting via projective conic mapping. """ imageheight, imagewidth = 1024, 1024 coloraccum = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) weightaccum = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for pt in points: pk = np.array(pt['p']) tu = np.array(pt['tu']) tv = np.array(pt['tv']) color = np.array(pt['color']) # 1. Construct Tangent Frame Matrix Mk Mk = np.vstack([tu, tv, pk]) # 2. Check Condition Number of Mk if np.linalg.cond(Mk) > condthreshold: continue # 3. Invert Mk try: Mkinv = np.linalg.inv(Mk) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue # 4. Define Local Conic Matrix Qlocal Rk = np.eye(2) # Assumed isotropic variance for simplicity Qlocal = np.zeros((3, 3)) Qlocal[:2,:2] = Rk Qlocal[2, 2] = -Fg2 # 5. Compute Homography from tangent plane to image plane # Hproj maps homogeneous (u,v,1) to homogeneous (x,y,1) in screen space Hproj = np.zeros((3, 3)) for i in range(3): for j in range(3): Hproj[i, j] = cameramatrix[i, j] Mkinv[j, 0] + cameramatrix[i, j+1] Mkinv[j, 1] + cameramatrix[i, j+2] Mkinv[j, 2] Hproj /= Hproj[2, 2] # 6. Project Conic to Image Space Qimage = Hproj.T @ Qlocal @ Hproj Qprime = Qimage[:2,:2] # 7. Check if Conic is Ellipse A, B, C = Qprime[0, 0], Qprime[0, 1], Qprime[1, 1] Delta = A C - B2 if Delta <= 0: continue # 8. Compute Resampling Filter Variance Hfilter = np.eye(2) # Identity resampling filter Variance = Qprime + Hfilter # 9. Invert Variance for Fragment Shader try: Varianceinv = np.linalg.inv(Variance) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue # 10. Compute Bounding Box eigenvalues, = np.linalg.eigh(Varianceinv) a = 1.0 / np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) b = 1.0 / np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) width, height = 2 a, 2 b cx, cy = Qimage[0, 2] / Qimage[2, 2], Qimage[1, 2] / Qimage[2, 2] ymin, ymax = int(cy - height), int(cy + height) xmin, xmax = int(cx - width), int(cx + width) # 11. Rasterize for y in range(max(0, ymin), min(imageheight, ymax)): for x in range(max(0, xmin), min(imagewidth, xmax)): offset = np.array([x - cx, y - cy]) rsq = offset @ Varianceinv @ offset if rsq < 1.0: weight = np.exp(-0.5 rsq) coloraccum[y, x] += color weight weightaccum[y, x] += weight # Pass 3: Normalization for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if weightaccum[y, x] > 1e-6: coloraccum[y, x] /= weightaccum[y, x] return coloraccum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioned Mapping: If the splat degenerates into a line segment, \mathbf{M}k becomes ill-conditioned. Check the condition number and discard if too high. Non-Elliptical Conics: Projective mapping can result in hyperbolas or parabolas. Check the discriminant \Delta and discard if \Delta \le 0. Precision: Perspective geometry should be computed in double precision to improve accuracy. SPH Specifics: For SPH particles, the kernel is evaluated at the impact parameter (perpendicular to the ray) rather than the offset in the particle plane. Pixels are placed at the depth of the slicing plane, not the particle depth. A texture mapping technique for point cloud color data that maintains uniform sample density across the unit sphere, addressing distortion and sampling efficiency issues in color atlases. It complements the geometric accuracy of this splatting method by ensuring high-quality attribute rendering. Time Complexity: Dominated by the vertex shader computation for each point (matrix inversions, conic mapping) and the fragment shader evaluation for each pixel in the bounding box. The bounding box size depends on the perspective distortion and kernel cutoff. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of points and pixels covered by splats. Requires storage for depth buffer, color buffer, and weight buffer. Performance: Implemented on modern GPUs using vertex and fragment programs. The three-pass approach (depth, accumulation, normalization) is efficient. The method avoids holes and artifacts, improving visual quality at the cost of slightly more complex vertex shader computations compared to affine approximations. Strengths: Perspective-correct splat shapes, no holes under extreme perspective, high image quality with anisotropic filtering. Limitations: More complex than affine methods, requires careful handling of degenerate cases and numerical stability. This method was introduced by Jussi Räsanen, Mario Botsch, Carsten Dachsbacher, and Mark Pauly. It addresses the limitations of previous EWA splatting methods by Heckbert and Zwicker, which used affine approximations exact only at the kernel center. The method was implemented in a point rendering algorithm using GPU vertex and fragment programs. It is also referenced in the context of SPH particle rendering fixes in the pynbody library. name: Stretch-invariant polar capped color map
head: Stretch-invariant polar capped map, plane-chart cylindrical projection with azimuthal equidistant polar caps, polar capped color map, polar capped map, spherical representation P
body: The stretch-invariant polar capped color map is a texture mapping technique that encodes point cloud color data onto a 2D image while maintaining uniform sample density across the unit sphere, solving the non-uniform density flaw of standard cylindrical plane-chart projections. It generates one texture map per scan location to store color information for textured splats while preserving occlusion equivalence with the original point cloud. The method maps texture coordinates (s, t) to a 3D direction vector (x, y, z) on the unit sphere using a hybrid projection: a plane-chart cylindrical projection for the equatorial band and azimuthal equidistant projections for the polar caps. Texture coordinates (s, t) are assumed to lie in [0, 1]. The geometry (point positions) is stored separately as regular (x, y, z) data to avoid precision loss from encoding depth in image formats like PNG, while the texture map stores only color data. Inputs: Forward: Texture coordinates (s, t). Inverse: Normalized direction vector (\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z}) from scan location sk to point p. Outputs: Forward: Unit direction vector (x, y, z). Inverse: Texture coordinates (s, t). Formulas and Steps: The sphere is divided into three regions based on the latitude angle \psi. 1. Bottom Cap (\psi \in -\pi/2, -\pi/4)): Corresponds to texture coordinate s \le 1/6. [Forward Mapping (Texel to Direction): Let ub = 6s - 0.5, vb = t - 0.5, and rb = ub^2 + vb^2. \begin{aligned} x &= \frac{ub}{rb} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rb}{2}\right) \\ y &= \frac{vb}{rb} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rb}{2}\right) \\ z &= -\cos\left(\frac{\pi rb}{2}\right) \end{aligned} Inverse Mapping (Direction to Texel): Let r = 2\pi \arccos(\bar{z}). \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{\frac{\bar{x} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 0.5}{6} \\ t &= \frac{\frac{\bar{y} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 0.5}{6} \end{aligned} 2. Top Cap (\psi \in (\pi/4, \pi/2]): Corresponds to texture coordinate 1/6 < s \le 2/6. Forward Mapping (Texel to Direction): Let ut = 6s - 1.5, vt = t - 0.5, and rt = \sqrt{ut^2 + vt^2}. \begin{aligned} x &= \frac{ut}{rt} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rt}{2}\right) \\ y &= \frac{vt}{rt} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rt}{2}\right) \\ z &= \cos\left(\frac{\pi rt}{2}\right) \end{aligned} Inverse Mapping (Direction to Texel): Let r = 2\pi \arccos(\bar{z}). \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{\frac{\bar{x} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 1.5}{6} \\ t &= \frac{\frac{\bar{y} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 0.5}{6} \end{aligned} 3. Equatorial Band (\psi \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]): Corresponds to texture coordinate s > 2/6. Forward Mapping (Texel to Direction): Let \psi = t \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} and \theta = (1.5s - 0.5)2\pi. \begin{aligned} x &= \cos(\psi) \cos(\theta) \\ y &= \cos(\psi) \sin(\theta) \\ z &= \sin(\psi) \end{aligned} Inverse Mapping (Direction to Texel): Let \psi = \arcsin(\bar{z}) and \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\bar{y}, \bar{x}). \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{\frac{\theta}{2\pi} + 0.5}{1.5} \\ t &= \frac{\psi + \frac{\pi}{4}}{2\pi} \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def forwardmap(s: float, t: float) -> tuple: """Maps texture coordinates (s, t) to a 3D direction vector (x, y, z).""" if s <= 1.0 / 6.0: # Bottom Cap ub = 6.0 s - 0.5 vb = t - 0.5 rb = ub ub + vb vb # Guard against division by zero at exact pole center if rb == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, -1.0) sinval = math.sin(math.pi rb / 2.0) x = (ub / rb) sinval y = (vb / rb) sinval z = -math.cos(math.pi rb / 2.0) return (x, y, z) elif s <= 2.0 / 6.0: # Top Cap ut = 6.0 s - 1.5 vt = t - 0.5 rt = math.sqrt(ut ut + vt vt) # Guard against division by zero at exact pole center if rt == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) sinval = math.sin(math.pi rt / 2.0) x = (ut / rt) sinval y = (vt / rt) sinval z = math.cos(math.pi rt / 2.0) return (x, y, z) else: # Equatorial Band psi = t (math.pi / 2.0) - (math.pi / 4.0) theta = (1.5 s - 0.5) 2.0 math.pi x = math.cos(psi) math.cos(theta) y = math.cos(psi) math.sin(theta) z = math.sin(psi) return (x, y, z) def inversemap(xbar: float, ybar: float, zbar: float) -> tuple: """Maps a normalized direction vector (xbar, ybar, zbar) to texture coordinates (s, t).""" # Normalize input to handle unnormalized vectors length = math.sqrt(xbar2 + ybar2 + zbar2) if length == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0) xbar /= length ybar /= length zbar /= length psi = math.asin(zbar) if psi <= -math.pi / 4.0: # Bottom Cap r = 2.0 math.pi math.acos(zbar) sinval = math.sin(math.pi r / 2.0) # Guard against division by zero at exact poles if sinval == 0.0: return (0.5 / 6.0, 0.5 / 6.0) s = ((xbar r / sinval) + 0.5) / 6.0 t = ((ybar r / sinval) + 0.5) / 6.0 return (s, t) elif psi > math.pi / 4.0: # Top Cap r = 2.0 math.pi math.acos(zbar) sinval = math.sin(math.pi r / 2.0) if sinval == 0.0: return (1.5 / 6.0, 0.5 / 6.0) s = ((xbar r / sinval) + 1.5) / 6.0 t = ((ybar r / sinval) + 0.5) / 6.0 return (s, t) else: # Equatorial Band theta = math.atan2(ybar, xbar) s = (theta / (2.0 math.pi) + 0.5) / 1.5 t = (psi + math.pi / 4.0) / (2.0 math.pi) return (s, t) Parameters: s, t: Texture coordinates, typically in [0, 1]. \psi: Latitude angle, range [-\pi/2, \pi/2]. \theta: Longitude angle, range [-\pi, \pi]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs in the cap formulas when rb=0 or rt=0 (exact pole centers) or when \sin(\pi r / 2) = 0 (poles). The pseudocode handles these centers explicitly. Precision loss is avoided by storing geometry as (x,y,z) rather than encoding depth in the texture, as noted in the source. The equatorial band formula for s involves division by 1.5; numerical error may push s slightly outside [2/6, 1], requiring standard clamping or wrapping in practice. Time Complexity: The mapping operations are O(1) per point/texel, involving basic trigonometric functions and arithmetic. Memory Complexity: Requires one texture map per scan location sk. Using texture maps for color data greatly reduces disk memory footprint compared to storing all color data in point structures, and allows for lossy image compression. Strengths: Minimizes distortion across every region of the unit sphere and achieves more uniform sample density compared to standard cylindrical plane-chart projections. Maintains occlusion equivalence with the original point cloud. When to use: When rendering point clouds with textured splats and uniform sampling density across the sphere is critical for visual quality or algorithmic consistency. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by M. Comino, A. Chica, and C. Andujar in 2019. It addresses a flaw in the cylindrical plane-chart projection used by Comino et al. in 2017, which resulted in non-uniform sample density across the unit sphere. The approach follows Snyder et al. for the mathematical formulation of the stretch-invariant projection. It is used in the context of view-dependent hierarchical rendering of massive point clouds through textured splats. View-dependent Hierarchical Rendering of Massive Point Clouds through Textured Splats, https://doi.org/10.2312/ceig.20191203, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Exact Half-Space Clipping
head: Exact Clipping, Ours, XClipGS (eXact Clipping), XClipGS Exact Half-Space Clipping
body: Exact Half-Space Clipping (implemented as XClipGS) is a differentiable operator for interactive volume rendering that computes the exact retained ray integral of a 3D Gaussian primitive when intersected by a clipping plane. It solves the problem of binary keep/drop decisions (Hard Cull) and approximate moment-matching, which cause aliasing, popping artifacts, and silhouette errors when clipping planes expose hidden anatomy. It sets itself apart from ClipGS by avoiding learned binary decisions and MLP deformations, and from RaRa by providing a closed-form backward pass for clip-aware training, all without auxiliary networks. Inputs: Primitive parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (positive definite), opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Camera parameters: projected center \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} \in \mathbb{R}^2, projection Jacobian \mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}, world-to-camera rotation \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Clipping plane: unit normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3, offset \tau \in \mathbb{R}. Pixel coordinate: \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Outputs: Clipped contribution: C{\text{clip}}(\mathbf{p}) = \alpha KG(\boldsymbol{\delta}; \mathbf{A}) \Phi(\mathbf{k}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta} + h), where KG is the Gaussian kernel, \Phi is the standard normal CDF, and \boldsymbol{\delta} = \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} - \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Primitive: Stores \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha. Precomputed Clip Coefficients (for straddling primitives): \mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{R}^2, h \in \mathbb{R}. Transient Buffer: 16 bytes per primitive per view to store clip coefficients. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Culling): Compute the variance along the plane normal and the standardized signed distance: \sigman^2 = \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{n} a = \frac{\tau - \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\sigman} If \Phi(a) \le 10^{-6}, discard the primitive. 2. Affine Projection Setup: Compute the screen-space covariance matrix \mathbf{A} and the projection matrix \mathbf{M}: \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{M}^\top Compute the cross-covariance vector \mathbf{b}: \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{n} 3. Clip Coefficient Calculation (for straddling primitives): Compute the conditional variance s^2 (Schur complement): s^2 = \sigman^2 - \mathbf{b}^\top \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{b} Apply variance floor to avoid division by zero: s^2{\text{impl}} = \max(s^2, 10^{-8}) Compute the affine coefficients \mathbf{k} and h: \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{b} / s{\text{impl}} h = (\tau - \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}) / s{\text{impl}} Store \mathbf{k} and h in the transient buffer. 4. Rasterization (Forward Pass): For each pixel \mathbf{p} covered by the primitive's footprint: Compute the unclipped Gaussian weight: KG(\boldsymbol{\delta}; \mathbf{A}) = \exp(-\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top \mathbf{A}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\delta}) Compute the clipping factor using the precomputed coefficients: \text{clip\factor} = \Phi(\mathbf{k}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta} + h) Compute the final contribution: C{\text{clip}}(\mathbf{p}) = \alpha \cdot KG(\boldsymbol{\delta}; \mathbf{A}) \cdot \text{clip\factor} Composite front-to-back. 5. Backward Pass (Training): Compute gradients for \mathbf{k} and h from the CDF derivative. Chain gradients through \mathbf{k} and h to \mathbf{A}^{-1}, \mathbf{b}, \sigman^2, and \tau. Chain through \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{b} to \boldsymbol{\Sigma} and \mathbf{M}. Chain through \mathbf{M} to \boldsymbol{\mu} (via \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}) and camera parameters. If s^2{\text{impl}} is active (i.e., s^2 < 10^{-8}), set the derivative through s^2 to zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def standardnormalcdf(x): """Standard normal CDF using the error function.""" return 0.5 (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0))) def standardnormalpdf(x): """Standard normal PDF.""" return math.exp(-0.5 x2) / math.sqrt(2 math.pi) def exacthalfspaceclippingforward(mu, Sigma, alpha, phat, J, W, n, tau, p): """ Computes the clipped contribution of a Gaussian primitive to a pixel. """ # 1. Preprocessing: Check retained mass sigmansq = float(n.T @ Sigma @ n) a = (tau - n.T @ mu) / math.sqrt(max(sigmansq, 1e-12)) if standardnormalcdf(a) <= 1e-6: return 0.0 # 2. Affine Projection Setup M = J @ W A = M @ Sigma @ M.T detA = A[0, 0] A[1, 1] - A[0, 1] A[1, 0] Ainv = np.array([[A[1, 1] / detA, -A[0, 1] / detA], [-A[1, 0] / detA, A[0, 0] / detA]]) b = M @ Sigma @ n # 3. Clip Coefficients ssq = sigmansq - b.T @ Ainv @ b ssqimpl = max(ssq, 1e-8) simpl = math.sqrt(ssqimpl) k = (Ainv @ b) / simpl h = (tau - n.T @ mu) / simpl # 4. Rasterization delta = phat - p KG = math.exp(-delta.T @ Ainv @ delta) clipfactor = standardnormalcdf(k.T @ delta + h) return alpha KG clipfactor def exacthalfspaceclippingbackward(dLdclip, k, h, delta, Ainv, b, sigmansq, tau, mu, Sigma, phat, J, W, n, ssqimpl, simpl): """ Computes gradients for the backward pass as described in the source. """ # Gradient of CDF: d/dx Phi(x) = phi(x) phival = standardnormalpdf(k.T @ delta + h) dLdphi = dLdclip math.exp(-delta.T @ Ainv @ delta) phival # Chain through k and h to Ainv, b, sigman^2, tau dLdk = dLdphi delta dLdh = dLdphi # Chain through Ainv and b to Sigma and M # Chain through M to mu (via phat) and camera parameters # When variance floor is active, set derivative through s^2 to zero pass Parameters: Retained-mass cutoff: \Phi(a) \le 10^{-6}. Variance floor: 10^{-8}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Case (s^2 = 0): Occurs when the clip coordinate is an affine function of the pixel coordinate (plane contains the viewing-ray direction). The conditional law collapses to a point mass. The implementation uses a variance floor of 10^{-8} and sets the derivative through s^2 to zero when the floor is active. Precision: The CDF is evaluated in fp32. The finite-precision rasterizer's active clipping branch is named "straddling". A technique to render sharp features (edges, corners) in point-sampled surfaces by explicitly representing features as clip lines in local tangent planes. It sets itself apart by discarding parts of reconstruction kernels to prevent blurring, rather than integrating restricted densities. It is chosen when rendering point-sampled objects like cubes to avoid geometric artifacts. It uses clip lines defined by two homogeneous points ch, dh in the local tangent plane, projected to image space as c', d'. A direction vector v perpendicular to the line is computed. The kernel is evaluated at x if (x - c') \cdot v > 0. Parameter: Fg (cutoff value, e.g., 0.5). Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Requires one transient 16-byte per-view buffer per primitive. Time: Adds one scalar fp32 CDF evaluation per straddling sample. Measured Performance: On an A100 at 800x800 with 300k Gaussians and active oblique clip, the forward-backward step reduces from 5.47 ms to 3.50 ms (1.6x speedup) relative to legacy per-pixel backward. Renders at over 650 FPS, versus 278 FPS for ClipGS. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exact closed-form operator; no learned clipping parameters or auxiliary networks; differentiable for training; high PSNR (33.56 dB vs 32.34 dB for ClipGS) and SSIM (0.860 vs 0.809) on medical volumes; 41x less leakage than ClipGS. Limitations: Relies on the local affine approximation of EWA splatting; global image metrics may dilute errors near the clipping plane (addressed by paired clipped/unclipped cut-face protocol). When to Use: Interactive volume rendering of medical scans where clipping planes expose hidden anatomy. Training scenarios requiring clip-aware supervision. When Not to Use: When binary keep/drop is sufficient and performance is critical (Hard Cull is faster). When sharp feature rendering via clip lines is the primary goal (use Sharp Feature Rendering via Clip Lines). XClipGS was introduced by Gao et al.. It is built on the N-DGS backbone. It addresses the limitations of prior clipping methods like ClipGS (which uses trainable binary decisions and MLP deformations) and RaRa (which lacks a backward pass for clip-aware training). The method is used for interactive rendering of volumetric medical scans, enabling users to inspect hidden anatomy via clipping planes without retraining. XClipGS: Exact Half-Space Clipping for Medical Volume Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2608.07760, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Perspective Accurate Splatting, http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/149345, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Camera-independent geometric cut error (CErr3D)
head: Geometric Cut Error
body: CErr3D is a closed-form diagnostic metric that quantifies the error introduced by approximate half-space clipping operators in Gaussian Splatting by computing the misplaced opacity mass directly from primitive geometry and plane parameters, independent of camera projection or rendering pipeline. It sets itself apart from image-space metrics by evaluating the operator's geometric fidelity against the exact analytic solution, allowing for hardware-agnostic comparison of clipping strategies without the noise of reconstruction artifacts or renderer mismatches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians (primitives) and a clipping plane defined by normal \mathbf{n} and offset \tau. Each primitive i is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, full covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, and opacity \alphai. Outputs: A scalar value \text{CErr}{3\text{D}} \in [0, 1] representing the ratio of total misplaced mass to total kept mass. Data Structures: Primitive i: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Full covariance matrix (rotated, including Mip-Splatting filter effects). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Plane: \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Unit normal vector. \tau \in \mathbb{R}: Offset. Steps: 1. For each primitive i, compute the normalized distance ti to the plane: ti = \frac{\tau - \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}i}{\sqrt{\mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \mathbf{n}}} 2. Compute the exact kept opacity mass ei for primitive i using the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF) \Phi: ei = \alphai \Phi(ti) 3. Compute the misplaced mass \epsiloni for primitive i based on the specific clipping operator being evaluated: XClipGS (Exact): \epsiloni^{\text{XClip}} = 0 (by analytic definition). Hard Cut (HC): \epsiloni^{\text{HC}} = |\alphai \mathbf{1}[ti \geq 0] - ei|. Mixture Model (MM): \epsiloni^{\text{MM}} = ei \Phi \left( -\frac{ti + \lambda(ti)}{\sqrt{v(ti)}} \right). 4. Sum the misplaced masses and kept masses over all primitives: \text{CErr}{3\text{D}} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} \epsiloni}{\sum{i=1}^{N} ei} Parameters: \Phi(\cdot): Standard normal CDF. \mathbf{1}[\cdot]: Indicator function. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i: Must be the full rotated covariance, not a diagonal approximation, to account for anisotropy and filtering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The metric is computed in closed form, but finite-precision arithmetic in the evaluation path (e.g., CUDA) can introduce minor deviations from the analytic ideal. Degenerate Input: If \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \mathbf{n} \leq 0, the denominator in ti is zero or imaginary. This implies a degenerate covariance (zero variance in the plane normal direction), which should be handled by clamping or skipping the primitive. Boundary: If \sum ei = 0 (all primitives are fully culled), the metric is undefined. In practice, this case should return NaN or a specific error code. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def standardnormalcdf(x): """Approximation of the standard normal CDF.""" return 0.5 (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0))) def computecerr3d(primitives, planenormal, planeoffset, operatortype): """ Compute Camera-independent geometric cut error. Args: primitives: List of dicts with keys 'mu' (3,), 'Sigma' (3,3), 'alpha' (float). planenormal: Array-like (3,) unit normal vector n. planeoffset: Float tau. operatortype: String, one of 'XClip', 'HC', 'MM'. Returns: float: CErr3D value. """ totalkeptmass = 0.0 totalmisplacedmass = 0.0 for prim in primitives: mu = prim['mu'] Sigma = prim['Sigma'] alpha = prim['alpha'] # Compute ti nSigman = planenormal @ (Sigma @ planenormal) # Handle degenerate covariance if nSigman <= 0: # Skip primitives with zero variance along the plane normal continue t = (planeoffset - planenormal @ mu) / math.sqrt(nSigman) # Exact kept mass ei = alpha standardnormalcdf(t) totalkeptmass += ei # Misplaced mass based on operator if operatortype == 'XClip': epsiloni = 0.0 elif operatortype == 'HC': # Hard Cut: 1 if t >= 0, else 0 indicator = 1.0 if t >= 0 else 0.0 epsiloni = abs(alpha indicator - ei) elif operatortype == 'MM': # Mixture Model: Formula requires lambda(t) and v(t) # Note: lambda(t) and v(t) are not defined in the provided sources. # Standard MM formulations typically use truncated normal parameters, # but exact definitions are omitted here. lambdat = 0.0 # Placeholder per source omission rule vt = 1.0 # Placeholder per source omission rule if vt <= 0: epsiloni = 0.0 else: epsiloni = ei standardnormalcdf(-(t + lambdat) / math.sqrt(vt)) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown operator type: {operatortype}") totalmisplacedmass += epsiloni if totalkeptmass == 0: return float('nan') return totalmisplacedmass / totalkeptmass A region symmetric difference metric that measures under-removal and over-removal errors, normalized by the reference affected region. It differs from CErr3D by operating in image space and using differencing to cancel reconstruction floor bias. To compute CDE: 1. Render full and clipped versions for both the method (R) and reference (G). 2. Compute luminance difference maps DR = Y(R{\text{full}}) - Y(R{\text{clip}}) and DG = Y(G{\text{full}}) - Y(G{\text{clip}}). 3. Threshold at \theta = 0.04 to obtain binary masks AR = \{|DR| > \theta\} and AG = \{|DG| > \theta\}. 4. Intersect with a band \mathcal{B} (whole frame for CDEp, \pm 12-pixel strip for CDEg) and compute the symmetric difference: \text{CDE} = \frac{\sumv |(AG \setminus AR) \cap \mathcal{B}| + \sumv |(AR \setminus AG) \cap \mathcal{B}|}{\sumv |AG \cap \mathcal{B}|}. Pitfall: Direct clipped-vs-reference comparison carries reconstruction floor bias; differencing against unclipped companions cancels this. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The metric is camera-independent, allowing for offline analysis of clipping operators without rendering. It provides a ground-truth geometric error metric that isolates clipping logic from renderer artifacts. Limitations: It does not account for image-space perceptual quality or reconstruction errors from the splatting process itself. It requires access to the full primitive geometry and covariance. When to use: It is used when comparing the geometric fidelity of different half-space clipping algorithms (e.g., XClipGS vs. HC vs. MM) in a controlled, renderer-agnostic manner. When not to use: It should not be used when image-space perceptual quality is the primary concern; use CDE or Sb in that case. CErr3D was introduced in the context of "XClipGS: Exact Half-Space Clipping for Medical Volume Gaussian Splatting". The paper proposes an exact half-space clipping operator that avoids the approximation errors of binary keep/drop projections by using a conditional Gaussian CDF. CErr3D serves as a diagnostic tool to validate the geometric correctness of this and other approximate operators (HC, MM) by quantifying the mass misplaced across the clipping plane. name: N-Dimensional Slice Membership and Geometry Resolution
head: Hidden Dimension Attenuation, nD Slab Clipping
body: N-Dimensional Slice Membership and Geometry Resolution renders N-dimensional data by intersecting primitives with a 3D display hyperplane, allowing users to navigate non-displayed dimensions via sliders or toggles. It solves the problem of visualizing higher-dimensional spatial data by computing the geometric intersection and attribute attenuation of primitives relative to the slice, differing from standard 3D rendering by handling the hidden dimensions explicitly rather than ignoring them. The method processes different geometry types by determining their membership in the display hyperplane or their intersection with the N-dimensional slab defined by the slice thickness. Inputs: Primitive geometry type: point, Gaussian splat, line segment, or triangle. Display hyperplane definition: normal vector \mathbf{n} and distance d0 from origin. Primitive parameters: center \mathbf{c}, radius r, covariance \Sigma, vertices \mathbf{v}i. Outputs: Clipped or attenuated primitive geometry ready for rasterization. Zero or null if the primitive is completely outside the slice. Data Structures: Points: Center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^N, radius r. Gaussian Splats: Center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^N, covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}, opacity \alpha. Line Segments: Endpoints \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2 \in \mathbb{R}^N, attributes \mathbf{a}1, \mathbf{a}2. Triangles: Vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 \in \mathbb{R}^N. Steps: 1. Point Clouds: Calculate the Euclidean distance d from the point center \mathbf{c} to the display hyperplane. If d > r, discard the point. Otherwise, compute the effective radius r{eff} = \sqrt{r^2 - d^2} and render the point with this radius. 2. Gaussian Splats: Compute the Mahalanobis distance from the splat center \mathbf{c} to the display hyperplane. Attenuate the splat's opacity and scale based on the marginal density along the hidden dimensions, modeled as a shifted Gaussian in the Mahalanobis distance. 3. Line Segments: Clip the line segment against the N-dimensional slab defined by the slice. Determine the intersection parameters where the line enters and exits the slab. If no intersection exists, discard the segment. Otherwise, interpolate every attribute at the clip parameter to form the clipped segment. 4. Triangles: Perform a slab membership test for each of the three vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. If all three vertices pass the test (i.e., are within the slab), draw the triangle. If any vertex fails, discard the triangle entirely, as this method acts as a whole-triangle cull instead of performing N-dimensional polygon clipping. Parameters: Slice thickness: Not given in the sources. Reference nominal primitive size: 4 px for points and splats, 1.5 px for lines. Edge Cases: d = r: Effective radius becomes 0. Degenerate triangles: Handled by standard rasterization. Precision: Floating point errors in distance calculations may cause incorrect culling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nDslicemembership(primitive, hyperplanenormal, hyperplanedist, slicethickness): # Assume hyperplanenormal is unit length def disttohyperplane(p): return abs(sum(p[i] hyperplanenormal[i] for i in range(len(p))) - hyperplanedist) if primitive['type'] == 'point': c = primitive['center'] r = primitive['radius'] d = disttohyperplane(c) if d > r: return None reff = (r2 - d2)0.5 return {'type': 'point', 'center': c, 'radius': reff} elif primitive['type'] == 'splat': c = primitive['center'] alpha = primitive['opacity'] # Attenuate by marginal density along hidden dimensions: shifted Gaussian in Mahalanobis distance from splat centre to slice d = disttohyperplane(c) attenuation = exp(-0.5 d2) return {'type': 'splat', 'center': c, 'opacity': alpha attenuation} elif primitive['type'] == 'line': p1 = primitive['p1'] p2 = primitive['p2'] attrs = primitive['attrs'] # Project endpoints onto the hyperplane normal to find slab intersection parameters val1 = sum(p1[i] hyperplanenormal[i] for i in range(len(p1))) - hyperplanedist val2 = sum(p2[i] hyperplanenormal[i] for i in range(len(p2))) - hyperplanedist halfthick = slicethickness / 2.0 tmin, tmax = 0.0, 1.0 if abs(val2 - val1) > 1e-9: t1 = (-halfthick - val1) / (val2 - val1) t2 = (halfthick - val1) / (val2 - val1) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None # Interpolate geometry and attributes at clip parameters newp1 = [p1[i] + tmin (p2[i] - p1[i]) for i in range(len(p1))] newp2 = [p1[i] + tmax (p2[i] - p1[i]) for i in range(len(p1))] # Interpolate each attribute channel linearly between endpoints newattrs = [attrs[i] + tmin (attrs[i] - attrs[i]) for i in range(len(attrs))] return {'type': 'line', 'p1': newp1, 'p2': newp2, 'attrs': newattrs} elif primitive['type'] == 'triangle': v1, v2, v3 = primitive['v1'], primitive['v2'], primitive['v3'] def inslab(v): return disttohyperplane(v) <= slicethickness / 2.0 if inslab(v1) and inslab(v2) and inslab(v3): return primitive else: return None Renders a 3D cross-section of a 4D voxel world by intersecting 4D primitives with a 3D hyperplane. It differs by treating blocks as 4D primitives (4-balls or 4-boxes) and generating accurate polygonal meshes for the resulting 3D volumes, allowing shape changes (e.g., rectangle to hexagon) as the hyperplane moves. Time Complexity: Depends on primitive type. Point and splat tests are O(N). Line clipping is O(N). Triangle culling is O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) per primitive. Performance: Frame rate is held at the cost of sharpness. Measurement window is 3 s at reference nominal primitive size (4 px for points, 1.5 px for lines). Strengths: Allows interactive navigation of N-dimensional data. Simple culling for triangles avoids complex polygon clipping. Limitations: Triangle culling may lose detail if triangles are partially inside the slab. Sharpness is reduced for points near the edge of the slice. When to use: Interactive visualization of multidimensional scientific data where navigation speed is critical. When not to use: When high-fidelity rendering of partial primitives is required. The method enables viewers to display three spatial dimensions and navigate non-displayed dimensions via sliders (continuous) or toggles (categorical/boolean). name: 4D Block Geometry Slicing
head: 4D cross-section rendering, Hyperplane block intersection
body: 4D Block Geometry Slicing renders a three-dimensional cross-section of a four-dimensional voxel world by intersecting 4D primitives with a 3D hyperplane. It builds on N-Dimensional Slice Membership and Geometry Resolution by treating blocks as 4D primitives (4-balls or 4-boxes) rather than 3D cubes, allowing the slice geometry to change shape as the hyperplane rotates or translates through the fourth dimension. Inputs: A 4D voxel world defined as a lattice of 4D primitives. A 3D hyperplane defined by its orientation (rotation angles \theta, \phi) and position (distance w along the fourth axis). A rendering mode flag P (boolean). Outputs: A 3D mesh representing the visible cross-section of the world. Data Structures: 4D Primitive: Defined by its center coordinates (x, y, z, w), dimensions (for 4-boxes), and radius (for 4-balls). 3D Hyperplane: Defined by normal vector and offset. The camera is fixed in 3D space; the hyperplane moves or rotates relative to the static world. Steps: 1. Identify the primitive type for each voxel (4-ball or 4-box). 2. Compute the intersection of each primitive with the 3D hyperplane to generate the visible cross-section geometry. 3. Apply the rendering mode flag P to determine whether to output exact polygonal meshes or cubic approximations. 4. Perform greedy meshing to merge adjacent faces where convexity is preserved. Formulas: r{3D} = \sqrt{r^2 - d^2}: Radius of the 3D spherical cross-section for a 4-ball, where r is the 4D radius and d is the distance from the 4D center to the hyperplane. Visibility condition: A 4-ball is visible only if d \le r. Parameters: P: Toggles between rendering blocks as exact 4D cross-sections (polygons) or as cubes (approximation). CLIPTIMEOFDAY: Controls the time of day for capture clips. Default behavior cycles naturally; specific values pin the time. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss in Translation: Translation along the fourth axis (w) is not round-trip invariant due to floating-point precision. Traveling from w=0 to w=9 and back to w=0 results in a difference of 9.77/255 compared to the original frame. Rotation, however, is byte-identical on round-trip. Degenerate Intersections: If d > r for a 4-ball, the block is empty. For 4-boxes, if the hyperplane misses the box entirely, no geometry is generated. Polygon Complexity: If the hyperplane rotation involves two planes (compound turn), cells become pentagons or hexagons. These cannot be rendered as cubes and require accurate polygonal geometry. A representation where the world is a four-dimensional lattice. The visible scene is a three-dimensional cross-section defined by a hyperplane. The camera is fixed in 3D space; changing the view involves rotating or translating the hyperplane through the 4D world. It is chosen when the goal is to visualize higher-dimensional spatial relationships without moving the observer. A key pitfall is that translation along the fourth axis (w) is not round-trip invariant due to floating-point precision, whereas rotation is byte-identical on round-trip. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Greedy meshing is complicated by varying polygon angles, though convex set properties allow merging. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated in a C++20 and OpenGL 4.1 voxel engine with live toggling of the P parameter and hyperplane rotation via scroll wheel. Scaling: Polygon complexity increases with compound rotations; cubic approximation (P false) reduces rendering cost but sacrifices geometric accuracy. Strengths: Provides exact geometric representation of 4D objects in 3D space; allows visualization of a fourth dimension as spatial traversal. Limitations: Floating-point precision errors in w-axis translation; complex polygon generation for compound rotations; greedy meshing is non-trivial due to non-aligned faces. When to use: When visualizing 4D data or simulating higher-dimensional spatial relationships. When not to use: When performance is critical and approximate cubic rendering is sufficient, or when round-trip precision in w-axis translation is required. Originating from a solo C++20 and OpenGL 4.1 voxel engine project by DanielWLiu07, this method demonstrates rendering a 3D cross-section of a 4D world. It challenges the assumption that greedy meshing is impossible for such geometry, leveraging convex set properties. The method highlights the difference between rotational and translational round-trip invariance in 4D slicing, noting that translation along the fourth axis is not round-trip invariant while rotation is byte-identical on round-trip. DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, https://github.com/DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
