name: Adaptive Volumetric Clipping by CSG Culling
head: CSG Culling, CSG Culling of Shell, CSG Culling of Solid
body:
Adaptive Volumetric Clipping by CSG Culling is a hierarchical culling and projection technique for volume Gaussian Splatting that integrates a virtual Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) probe into the tree traversal process. It solves the problem of rendering sharp volumetric intersections between a Shell (surface) and a Solid (volume) by dynamically adjusting splat resolution and projecting centers to the probe surface, thereby eliminating popping artifacts and silhouette errors that occur with binary keep/drop projections. It sets itself apart from Exact Half-Space Clipping by using hierarchical bounding sphere tests against an implicit probe rather than computing conditional Gaussian CDFs relative to affine-EWA footprints, and from Camera-independent geometric cut error (CErr3D) by actively modifying splat positions and sizes rather than just estimating error. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical tree of Gaussian splats (Shell and Solid nodes), each with a bounding sphere defined by center c, radius r, and a boundary bit flag. A virtual CSG probe defined by an implicit signed distance function (SDF) S(x), where S(x) < 0 is inside, S(x) > 0 is outside, and S(x) = 0 is the surface. The gradient 
abla S(x) provides the normal vector n. Output: A set of splats rendered with adaptive resolution and projected centers, forming the CSG intersection of the volume and the probe. Data Structures: Node: Contains bounding sphere parameters (c, r), a boolean isboundary flag, and child pointers. Boundary Bit Inheritance: The isboundary flag of a parent Solid node is the logical OR of the isboundary flags of its children. This ensures that nodes near the intersection curve are marked as boundary nodes, enabling adaptive resolution. Parameters: \deltar: Minimum allowed pixel splat size for regular internal nodes. \deltab: Minimum allowed pixel splat size for boundary nodes. Constraint: \deltar > \deltab \sim 1 pixel. This reduces silhouette appearance along the intersection curve caused by crossing/overlapping splats. Steps: 1. Probe Evaluation: For a node with bounding sphere center c and radius r, evaluate the SDF S(c) and its gradient 
abla S(c) to determine the signed shortest distance d to the probe surface and the inward-pointing normal n = - rac{
abla S(c)}{\|
abla S(c)\|}. The sign convention defines d as positive inside the probe. 2. CSG Culling of Solid: If the bounding sphere does not intersect the probe surface, discard the node and its subtree. If it intersects, traverse the subtree until the splat size reaches the minimum allowed size for the node type. Boundary nodes render at \deltab, while regular internal nodes render at \deltar. For all rendered Solid splats intersecting the probe, project the center to the probe surface using c{	ext{new}} = c - d \cdot n to prevent popping effects when resolution changes. 3. CSG Culling of Shell: If the bounding sphere is completely inside the probe, do not render the node or its children. If completely outside, disable CSG culling for the branch and render children only if they are leaf nodes or have splat size \le \deltar. If the bounding sphere intersects the probe surface, render the node if it is a leaf node or splat size \le \deltab; otherwise, traverse with CSG culling enabled. For boundary nodes intersecting the probe, offset the sphere center before rendering using c{	ext{new}} = c - (r + d) \cdot n to improve the outline and reduce silhouettes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersolid(node, probesdf, deltar, deltab): c, r = node.center, node.radius grad = probesdf.gradient(c) n = -grad / norm(grad) # Inward normal d = probesdf.value(c) # Signed distance (positive inside) if d > r or d < -r: return # Discard if sphere does not intersect probe surface minsize = deltab if node.isboundary else deltar if node.splatsize <= minsize: cproj = c - d n # Project center to probe surface # Standard Gaussian splat rasterization at cproj return for child in node.children: rendersolid(child, probesdf, deltar, deltab) def rendershell(node, probesdf, deltar, deltab): c, r = node.center, node.radius grad = probesdf.gradient(c) n = -grad / norm(grad) # Inward normal d = probesdf.value(c) # Signed distance (positive inside) if d > r: return # Completely inside probe: do not render if d < -r: # Completely outside: disable CSG culling for branch if node.isleaf or node.splatsize <= deltar: # Standard Gaussian splat rasterization at c pass for child in node.children: rendershell(child, probesdf, deltar, deltab) return # Intersecting probe surface if node.isleaf or node.splatsize <= deltab: cproj = c - (r + d) n if node.isboundary else c # Offset center for boundary nodes # Standard Gaussian splat rasterization at cproj return for child in node.children: rendershell(child, probesdf, deltar, deltab) Time Complexity: Linear in the number of visited nodes. Hierarchical culling reduces the number of splats processed near the intersection curve, and the overhead is described as insignificant because few Solid spheres lie exactly on the intersection curve. Memory Complexity: No additional memory beyond the existing tree structure and SDF evaluation stack. Strengths: Maintains real-time performance while providing smooth adaptive resolution at the CSG intersection, reducing popping and silhouette artifacts. Works with any implicit probe (plane, sphere, box, custom SDF). Limitations: Requires efficient SDF and gradient evaluation. Visual quality depends on the choice of \deltar and \deltab. When to use: Real-time medical visualization requiring sharp volumetric clipping and high fidelity at cut boundaries. When not to use: When the probe cannot be efficiently evaluated as an SDF, or when sharp volumetric clipping is not required. The method was introduced in the paper "TetSplat: Real-time Rendering and Volume Clipping of Large..." presented at the VIS 2004 conference. It was developed to address the limitations of binary clipping in Gaussian Splatting, aiming to maintain interactive frame rates while achieving high-quality volumetric editing and clipping. name: Mueller's Splatting Approach
head: Mueller splatting
body: Mueller's Splatting Approach is an object-order direct volume rendering technique that treats a gray-scale volume as a 3D discrete density function, where a convolution kernel defines how each sample contributes to points in space. It solves the computational cost of 3D convolution by pre-integrating the kernel along the viewing ray to create a 2D footprint table, which is then rasterized onto the screen. Unlike basic splatting which sums kernels within volume slices parallel to the viewing direction, Mueller's method aligns the processing slabs parallel to the image plane (image-aligned splatting), eliminating brightness variations and allowing variable interval distances. It builds on Splat Extent and Projection by using pre-computed 2D footprint lookups and leveraging texture mapping hardware for rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D discrete density function f(s) where s=(xs, ys, zs) represents voxel centers and values. A radially symmetric reconstruction kernel h (e.g., Gaussian, Cone, Sinc, or Bilinear). Output: A 2D image composed of accumulated splat contributions. Data Structures: 1. Footprint Table: A 2D lookup table storing the analytically integrated kernel function along a traversing ray. The table resolution is much higher than the image plane resolution to ensure smoothness. Values outside the table extent are zero. 2. Sheet Buffer: A buffer aligned parallel to the image plane that accumulates contributions from voxels within a specific slab. 3. Occlusion Map: A dynamically constructed map used to cull invisible splats. Formulas: The contribution of a sample s to a point (x, y, z) in space is defined as: C(x, y, z) = h(x - xs, y - ys, z - zs) \cdot f(s) The contribution to an image plane pixel (x, y) is computed by integrating along the viewing ray (axis u parallel to the ray): C(x, y) = f(s) \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x - xs, y - ys, u) du The Footprint Function F(x, y) is defined as the integral part, which is independent of sample density and depends only on the projected location: F(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x - xs, y - ys, u) du Parameters: Reconstruction Filter: Choices include Cone, Gaussian, Sinc, or Bilinear functions. Gaussian kernels are commonly used for their anti-aliasing characteristics, though they introduce signal smoothing. Footprint Table Size: Small tables produce blocky images; large tables smooth details but require more memory. Sampling Method: Nearest-neighbor (fast, aliasing) or bilinear interpolation (smoother, slower) when generating the view-transformed footprint table. Steps: 1. Pre-compute Footprint Table: Evaluate the integral in Equation 2.22 on a grid with high resolution. For orthographic projection, only one footprint table is needed per view. 2. Depth Sorting: Traverse the list of object voxels in depth order. 3. Slab Processing (Image-Aligned): Group voxels into slabs of width \Delta s aligned parallel to the image plane. 4. Transformation: Transform each relevant voxel center into screen space. 5. Occlusion Culling: Index into the occlusion map to test for visibility. Note: Early splat elimination only culls invisible splats from rasterization; their transformation to screen space must still be performed to determine occlusion. 6. Rasterization: For each visible voxel: Calculate the screen-space coordinate of the projected grid point. Center the footprint around that point and stretch it according to the image magnification factor. Rasterize the footprint to the screen using the pre-integrated footprint table, multiplying indexed values by the voxel's value. Clip voxel kernels overlapping a slab to the slab and sum into a sheet buffer. 7. Composition: Composite the current sheet with the previous sheet using the Porter-Duff over operator. 8. Occlusion Map Update: Perform a convolution operation after each sheet-buffer composite to update the occlusion map, limited to buffer tiles that received splat contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def muellersplatting(volumedata, kernel, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight): # 1. Pre-compute the generic footprint table footprinttable = precomputefootprinttable(kernel) # 2. Initialize sheet buffer and occlusion map sheetbuffer = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] occlusionmap = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] # 3. Sort voxels by depth (z-coordinate in view space) sortedvoxels = sorted(volumedata, key=lambda v: transformtoview(v.center, viewmatrix).z) # 4. Process voxels in slabs aligned with the image plane slabwidth = calculateslabwidth(volumedata, viewmatrix) currentslabz = min(v.zview for v in sortedvoxels) while currentslabz <= max(v.zview for v in sortedvoxels): slabvoxels = [v for v in sortedvoxels if currentslabz <= v.zview < currentslabz + slabwidth] slabcontribution = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for voxel in slabvoxels: screenx, screeny = transformtoscreen(voxel.center, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix) # Check occlusion if occlusionmap[screeny][screenx] > 0.0: continue footprintscale = getmagnificationfactor(voxel.center, viewmatrix) footprintextent = calculatefootprintextent(footprintscale) # Rasterize the footprint for dx in range(-footprintextent, footprintextent + 1): for dy in range(-footprintextent, footprintextent + 1): if dxdx + dydy <= footprintextentfootprintextent: weight = samplefootprinttable(footprinttable, dx, dy, footprintscale) contribution = weight voxel.value slabcontribution[screeny + dy][screenx + dx] += contribution # Composite slab contribution into the main sheet buffer sheetbuffer = compositeporterduff(slabcontribution, sheetbuffer) # Update occlusion map based on the new sheet buffer state updateocclusionmap(occlusionmap, slabcontribution) currentslabz += slabwidth return sheetbuffer def precomputefootprinttable(kernel): """Evaluate integral of kernel along viewing ray on a high-resolution grid.""" # Returns 2D array F(x, y)... def transformtoview(point, viewmatrix): """Transform 3D point to view space using viewmatrix."""... def transformtoscreen(point, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix): """Project 3D point to 2D screen coordinates."""... def calculateslabwidth(volumedata, viewmatrix): """Returns deltas, the slab thickness aligned with image plane."""... def getmagnificationfactor(point, viewmatrix): """Returns scale factor based on depth."""... def calculatefootprintextent(scale): """Returns radius/extent of footprint in pixels."""... def samplefootprinttable(table, dx, dy, scale): """Samples table with nearest-neighbor or bilinear interpolation."""... def compositeporterduff(slabcontrib, sheet): """Alpha-blends slabcontrib over sheet using Porter-Duff over operator."""... def updateocclusionmap(occlusionmap, slabcontrib): """Applies convolution to update occlusion map on affected tiles."""... Multi-texture Mapping Splatting is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that reduces the computational cost of depth sorting by segmenting the volume data into parallel texture slices along the primary viewing direction. Unlike standard object-order splatting which sorts all voxels globally, this method projects voxels onto local texture planes and blends them using graphics hardware, trading increased memory usage for reduced sorting complexity. It builds on Mueller's Splatting Approach by replacing 3D kernel evaluation with pre-computed 2D footprint lookups and leveraging texture mapping hardware for rasterization. Time Complexity: Generally faster than ray casting for large datasets due to cache coherency (sequential voxel traversal). However, it requires depth sorting and multiple passes for sheet composition. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the footprint table and sheet buffers. Large footprint tables increase memory usage. Performance: Supports incremental rendering in back-to-front or front-to-back order. Only processes relevant voxels, reducing data processed and stored compared to ray casting. Strengths: Exploits cache coherency. Renders smooth surfaces without staircase artifacts. Replaces point sampling with sample averaging, introducing low-pass filtering that reduces aliasing (especially for isosurfaces and \Delta s > 1.0). Limitations: Generated images are blurred due to the spherically symmetric reconstruction kernel. Basic splatting suffers from "color bleeding" artifacts, which Mueller's image-aligned approach mitigates but does not entirely eliminate without further techniques (e.g., FreeVoxels). Axis-aligned sheet buffers (in basic splatting) introduce "popping" artifacts; Mueller's image-aligned approach reduces this but requires dynamic occlusion map updates. Early splat elimination saves rasterization cost but still requires transformation for occlusion testing. When to Use: When cache coherency is beneficial, smooth surfaces are desired, and incremental rendering is needed. Suitable for hardware acceleration via texture mapping. When Not to Use: When sharp object boundaries are required (ray casting with trilinear reconstruction is sharper). When memory is constrained and large footprint tables are prohibitive. Mueller's Splatting Approach was introduced by Mueller et al. as an improvement over Westover's original splatting method. Westover's method summed voxel kernels within volume slices most parallel to the viewing direction, which was prone to severe brightness variations in animated viewing and did not allow variable interval distances. Mueller's method, termed "image-aligned splatting," aligns the sheet buffers parallel to the image plane, eliminating these drawbacks. It was further accelerated with GPUs by Mueller et al.. The method is part of the broader object-order rendering family, which decomposes the volume into basis functions projected to the screen. name: Multi-texture Mapping Splatting
head: Accelerating splatting algorithm based on multi-texture mapping, Texture-mapped Splatting, Texture-mapped Splatting (Crawfis and Max, Yagel et al.)
body: Multi-texture Mapping Splatting is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that reduces the computational cost of depth sorting by segmenting the volume data into parallel texture slices along the primary viewing direction. Unlike standard object-order splatting which sorts all voxels globally, this method projects voxels onto local texture planes and blends them using graphics hardware, trading increased memory usage for reduced sorting complexity. It builds on Mueller's Splatting Approach by replacing 3D kernel evaluation with pre-computed 2D footprint lookups and leveraging texture mapping hardware for rasterization. Inputs: Regular 3D volume dataset with density function \rho(x,y,z) and reconstruction kernel hv. Number of texture slices n. Viewing parameters (parallel projection assumed in source). Outputs: Final 2D image composed of blended texture slices. Data Structures: 1. Footprint Lookup Table: A 2D table storing values of the footprint function footprint(x,y). 2. Texture Slices: A set of n textures. Each texture point is in RGBA mode. The original alpha (\alpha) value of every point is zero. All slices are parallel to the view plane and have equivalent dimensions in the x and y directions. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute the footprint function by integrating the 3D volume reconstruction kernel hv over the z-axis: footprint(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} hv(x, y, z) \, dz Store the result in a lookup table to avoid excessive arithmetic during rendering. Map voxel values to colors and opacities using a probability statistic method. Transform voxels from object coordinates to the viewing coordinate system using a transformation matrix M: \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = M \times \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} 2. Dividing Volume Data: Segment the volume data into n regions (texture slices) along the primary viewing direction (z-axis). Let nk be the number of samples in slice k, such that \sum nk = n{total}. 3. Projecting Voxels: Traverse voxels in front-to-back order within each segmented region based on depth z. Voxels with the same z belong to the same layer. Project voxels directly onto the texture slice plane (not the screen plane) to avoid popping and splatting overlay artifacts. Calculate the contribution of a voxel i to a point (x, y) in the texture slice using the pre-computed footprint: Contributioni(x, y) = \rho(i) \int{-\infty}^{\infty} hv(ix - x, iy - y, z) \, dz This reduces the 3D kernel evaluation to a 2D footprint lookup. 4. Blending Texture Slices: Map the texture slices onto polygon surfaces in the scene using hardware texture mapping. Blend the textures in front-to-back order consistent with the voxel projection order. Use the over operator to combine colors and opacities from different layers: C{out} = C{in} \alpha{in} + C{now} \alpha{now} (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{now} (1 - \alpha{in}) Where C is color and \alpha is opacity. Parameters: n: The number of texture slices. Determines the granularity of division and the number of blending passes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping/Overlay Artifacts: Occur if voxels are projected onto the screen plane instead of the texture slice plane. The method explicitly projects onto the texture slice plane to maintain correct depth ordering. Precision: The source notes that lookup tables avoid excessive arithmetic complexity. Time Complexity: The depth sorting complexity for the divided dataset is O(A) = \sum nk \log nk, where nk is the number of samples in slice k. This is strictly less than the complexity of sorting the whole dataset O(B) = n \log n, because \sum nk \log nk < \sum nk \log n = n \log n. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for n texture slices, each with RGBA components. The original alpha is zero, and dimensions are equivalent across slices. Strengths: Accelerates rendering by leveraging hardware-assisted texture mapping and reducing sorting complexity. Scaled volume datasets can be rendered effectively and fast without remarkable degradation in image quality. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of footprint tables and segmentation of data. The method described assumes parallel projection and regular data sets. When to use: When hardware-assisted rendering is available and sorting complexity is a bottleneck. The method was proposed in 2006 by researchers combining splatting with 2D texture mapping to accelerate footprint-based volume rendering. It builds on earlier hardware-assisted methods, such as those by Crawfis and Max, and Yagel et al., who used texture mapping hardware to render splats. The approach addresses the computational cost of 3D convolution by reducing it to 2D footprint lookups and hardware blending. name: Primitive Geometry
head: Splat Primitives, Geometric Splat Kernels
body: Primitive Geometry defines the specific 2D or 3D shapes used to represent volumetric data points as splats during object-order rendering. It solves the problem of how to approximate continuous volumetric fields or discrete geometric structures using rasterizable primitives that can be efficiently projected and composited. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the topological and geometric definition of the primitive itself (e.g., circle, capsule, tetrahedron, brane) rather than the kernel function's mathematical falloff or the projection matrix mechanics. The family shares the fundamental mechanism of mapping a volumetric entity to a screen-space footprint via projection. All methods assume a camera model defined by a Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or separate Model-View (MV) and Projection (P) matrices. The core workflow involves: 1. Transformation: Converting object-space coordinates to screen space. 2. Footprint Definition: Defining the spatial extent of the primitive in screen space (e.g., radius, bounding box, or parametric surface). 3. Rasterization/Compositing: Projecting the footprint onto the image buffer and accumulating color/opacity. Mathematically, for a primitive centered at \mathbf{p}, the screen-space contribution C(u,v) at pixel (u,v) is derived from a footprint function F and a color/opacity field I: C(u,v) = I \cdot F(\mathbf{p}{screen}, (u,v)) where F depends on the specific geometry (e.g., Gaussian for circles, distance-to-segment for capsules). Renders voxels as 2D quads with a fixed offset derived from splat size and grid scale. Chosen for simple, fast voxel visualization where square footprints approximate circular coverage. Renders line segments as rotationally symmetric capsules in screen space. Chosen for line-based volumetric data (e.g., streamlines) to maintain visual continuity without gaps using deficit-rule joints. Maps unstructured tetrahedral mesh elements to spherical or ellipsoidal splats. Chosen for real-time rendering of large, static unstructured meshes, leveraging hierarchical culling. Projects voxels as 2D footprints (squares or circles) composited into the image buffer. Chosen for interactive rendering of large regular volumetric datasets, trading geometric precision for performance. Converts volume into discrete primitives (spheres/slices) mapped by data values. Chosen when explicit discretization is preferred over direct ray casting, preserving continuous data nature through scaling. Approximates analytic splat kernels with discrete triangle meshes. Chosen to leverage standard graphics hardware rasterization pipelines for rapid scan conversion, trading geometric precision for speed. Uses 'Branes' (Gaussian-Hermite modes) to emit spatially varying colors. Chosen for arbitrary-scale super-resolution, modeling local contrast and sharp edges with fewer primitives than standard Gaussians. The concept of splatting originated in the early 1990s as a method for interactive volume rendering, replacing ray casting with object-order projection to improve performance. Early implementations focused on Gaussian kernels and voxel-based data. As rendering hardware evolved, the definition of "primitive" expanded from simple point sprites to complex geometric shapes like capsules for line data and tetrahedra for unstructured meshes. Recent developments incorporate neural networks to define expressive primitives like Branes for super-resolution.

name: Circle Splat Rendering
body: Circle Splat Rendering is a volume rendering technique where volumetric entities (voxels) are projected as 2D quads in screen space. It solves the problem of efficiently rasterizing large datasets by mapping object-space coordinates to screen-space footprints via projection matrices. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Line Capsule Primitive and Tetrahedral Splatting by its use of fixed-offset square quads rather than parametric or complex geometric primitives. Inputs: Model-View matrix (MV) and Projection matrix (P). Voxel position in clip space (gl\in[0].gl\Position). Voxel color and normal attributes. Uniforms: splatSize (scalar), scale (entity scale), gridLength (grid scale), cullInvisibleFaces (boolean). Outputs: Triangle strip of 4 vertices representing the splat quad. Interpolated color and normal for fragment shading. Data Structures: The implementation uses a geometry shader stage. Input is a single point (representing a voxel center). Output is a trianglestrip with maxvertices = 4. Steps: 1. Transform to View Space: Multiply the input clip-space position by the Model-View matrix to get view-space coordinates. \mathbf{p}{view} = MV \cdot \mathbf{p}{clip\input} 2. Transform to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC): Multiply by the Projection matrix and perform perspective division. \mathbf{p}{ndc} = \frac{P \cdot \mathbf{p}{view}}{w} 3. Calculate Voxel Offset: Compute the physical size of the splat in view space. \text{voxelOffset} = \text{splatSize} \times \frac{\text{scale}}{\text{gridLength}} \times \sqrt{2} Where \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414213. 4. Compute Clip-Space Half-Edge: Determine the distance in NDC from the center to the right edge midpoint to establish the splat's screen-space extent. \mathbf{p}{right\mid} = \frac{P \cdot [\mathbf{p}{view}.xy + \text{voxelOffset} \cdot [0.5, 0], \mathbf{p}{view}.zw]}{w} \text{halfEdge} = \text{distance}(\mathbf{p}{ndc}, \mathbf{p}{right\mid}) 5. Frustum Culling: Define a culling border slightly larger than the half-edge to prevent gaps. Discard the primitive if the NDC center exceeds this border. \text{border} = 1 + \text{halfEdge} If |\mathbf{p}{ndc}.x| > \text{border} or |\mathbf{p}{ndc}.y| > \text{border}, discard. 6. Back-Face Culling (Optional): If cullInvisibleFaces is true, compute the view-space normal and discard if facing away from the camera. \mathbf{n}{view} = MV \cdot [\mathbf{n}, 0] If \mathbf{n}{view} \cdot (\mathbf{0} - \mathbf{p}{view}) < 0, discard. 7. Emit Vertices: Generate four vertices for a triangle strip. The vertices are defined in view space using the offset, then transformed to clip space. Bottom-Left: \mathbf{p}{view} + [-0.5, -0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset}. Bottom-Right: \mathbf{p}{view} + [0.5, -0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset}. Top-Left: \mathbf{p}{view} + [-0.5, 0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset}. Top-Right: \mathbf{p}{view} + [0.5, 0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset}. Each vertex is transformed by P for glPosition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def add(self, o): return Vec4(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z, self.w+o.w) def sub(self, o): return Vec4(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z, self.w-o.w) def mul(self, s): return Vec4(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs, self.ws) def truediv(self, s): return Vec4(self.x/s, self.y/s, self.z/s, self.w/s) def matmul(self, M): return Vec4( M[0][0]self.x + M[1][0]self.y + M[2][0]self.z + M[3][0]self.w, M[0][1]self.x + M[1][1]self.y + M[2][1]self.z + M[3][1]self.w, M[0][2]self.x + M[1][2]self.y + M[2][2]self.z + M[3][2]self.w, M[0][3]self.x + M[1][3]self.y + M[2][3]self.z + M[3][3]self.w) def distance(v1, v2): return math.sqrt((v1.x-v2.x)2 + (v1.y-v2.y)2 + (v1.z-v2.z)2 + (v1.w-v2.w)2) def dot(v1, v2): return v1.xv2.x + v1.yv2.y + v1.zv2.z def processsplat(voxelposclipinput, voxelcolor, voxelnormal, MV, P, splatsize, scale, gridlength, cullinvisiblefaces): # 1. Transform to View Space voxelposview = voxelposclipinput @ MV # 2. Transform to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) voxelposndc = (voxelposview @ P) / voxelposview.w # 3. Calculate Voxel Offset voxeloffset = splatsize (scale / gridlength) math.sqrt(2) # 4. Compute Clip-Space Half-Edge for Culling rightedgemidview = Vec4(voxelposview.x + 0.5 voxeloffset, voxelposview.y, voxelposview.z, voxelposview.w) rightedgemidndc = (rightedgemidview @ P) / rightedgemidview.w halfedge = distance(voxelposndc, rightedgemidndc) frustumborder = 1.0 + halfedge # 5. Frustum Culling if abs(voxelposndc.x) > frustumborder or abs(voxelposndc.y) > frustumborder: return None # 6. Back-Face Culling if cullinvisiblefaces: normalview = Vec4(voxelnormal[0], voxelnormal[1], voxelnormal[2], 0.0) @ MV viewtoorigin = Vec4(-voxelposview.x, -voxelposview.y, -voxelposview.z, 0.0) if dot(viewtoorigin, Vec4(normalview.x, normalview.y, normalview.z, 0.0)) < 0: return None # 7. Emit Vertices vertices = [] offsets = [(-0.5, -0.5), (0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5)] texcoords = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)] for i in range(4): ox, oy = offsets[i] vview = Vec4(voxelposview.x + ox voxeloffset, voxelposview.y + oy voxeloffset, voxelposview.z, voxelposview.w) vclip = vview @ P vertices.append((vclip, texcoords[i], voxelcolor, voxelnormal)) return vertices Complexity: O(1) per voxel for geometry generation. Memory: Minimal overhead; requires storage for MV/P matrices and uniform parameters. Strengths: Simple implementation; efficient rasterization via standard triangle strips; effective frustum culling. Limitations: Square footprints may alias or leave gaps between adjacent splats if not properly blended or if splatSize is not tuned to the grid resolution. This method is implemented in the svorenderer project, which uses a geometry shader to expand point primitives into square quads for volume visualization. mmalesadev/svorenderer, https://github.com/mmalesadev/svorenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Line Capsule Primitive
head: Geometry Primitives and Mesh Shading, Mesh Lighting and Materials
body: The Line Capsule Primitive is a geometric splatting method that renders line-based volumetric data as rotationally symmetric capsules in screen space. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Circle Splat Rendering and Tetrahedral Splatting by explicitly modeling line segments as capsules with deficit-rule joints to maintain visual continuity without gaps or double brightness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of line segments defined by endpoints in volume space, along with associated attributes (e.g., width, color, opacity). Output: A 2D image where lines are rendered as opaque or semi-transparent capsules, composited with other splats or background geometry. Data Structures: The primitive is defined by a line segment in 3D space. In screen space, it is represented as a capsule, which is the Minkowski sum of a line segment and a disk. Segment: Defined by two 3D vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Capsule Profile: A rotationally symmetric function of the 2D point-to-segment distance in screen space. Joint Handling: Corners between segments are composed using a deficit rule to prevent double brightness or gaps. Steps: 1. Transformation: Transform line segment endpoints from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. 2. Primitive Selection: Determine whether to render the line as a Capsule or a Screen-Space Quad based on the effective segment load. Calculate effective segment load: L = N{seg} \times W{max}, where N{seg} is the authored segment count and W{max} is the on-screen width of the widest segment at the opening framing. If L < 2,000,000, use the Capsule primitive. If L \ge 2,000,000, use the Screen-Space Quad primitive. This policy can be pinned to either primitive type if desired. 3. Rasterization (Capsule): Project the line segment into screen space, generate a rotationally symmetric footprint based on the 2D point-to-segment distance, and apply the deficit rule at joints to ensure correct brightness and no gaps. 4. Rasterization (Quad): Generate a screen-space quad covering the bounding box of the projected segment. 5. Compositing: Blend the capsule or quad contributions into the frame buffer. Formulas: Effective Segment Load: L = N{seg} \times W{max} Where: N{seg}: Authored segment count. W{max}: On-screen width of the widest segment at the opening framing. Capsule Footprint: The intensity profile I(x,y) at screen coordinates (x,y) is determined by the distance d from (x,y) to the projected line segment: I(x,y) = f(d(x,y)) Where d(x,y) is the 2D point-to-segment distance in screen space, and f is the rotationally symmetric profile function. Parameters: Effective Segment Load Threshold: 2,000,000. Joint Composition Rule: Deficit rule. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near-Axial Cases: The capsule primitive matches or beats the exact volumetric primitive (closed-form convolution of a segment with a 3D Gaussian, integrated along the view ray) in visual comparisons, including near-axial cases. Volumetric Blending: The primitive refuses volumetric blending because a triangle or line has zero thickness, providing no path length for absorption. Additive Ladder: An additive ladder over arbitrary face order is refused because a prefix of such an order is a surface with holes, not a coarser surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlinecapsule(segments, cameramatrix, threshold=2000000): # 1. Transform segments to screen space screensegments = [] for seg in segments: v1screen = projecttoscreen(seg.v1, cameramatrix) v2screen = projecttoscreen(seg.v2, cameramatrix) screensegments.append((v1screen, v2screen)) # 2. Calculate effective segment load nseg = len(screensegments) wmax = 0.0 for v1, v2 in screensegments: width = distance(v1, v2) if width > wmax: wmax = width effectiveload = nseg wmax # 3. Select primitive if effectiveload < threshold: primitivetype = "CAPSULE" else: primitivetype = "QUAD" # 4. Rasterize for v1, v2 in screensegments: if primitivetype == "CAPSULE": # Rasterize rotationally symmetric footprint based on 2D point-to-segment distance # Apply deficit rule at joints to prevent double brightness or gaps rasterizecapsulefootprint(v1, v2) else: # Rasterize screen-space quad covering bounding box of projected segment rasterizescreenquad(v1, v2) return framebuffer def projecttoscreen(vertex, cameramatrix): # Standard MVP projection: multiply vertex by camera matrix, divide by w projected = [sum(cameramatrix[i][j] vertex[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] return (projected[0] / projected[3], projected[1] / projected[3]) def distance(p1, p2): return ((p1[0] - p2[0])2 + (p1[1] - p2[1])2)0.5 def rasterizecapsulefootprint(v1, v2): # Compute 2D point-to-segment distance for each pixel in bounding box # Write intensity I(x,y) = f(d(x,y)) to framebuffer # Apply deficit rule at segment joints pass # Source does not provide exact rasterization implementation def rasterizescreenquad(v1, v2): # Compute bounding box of v1 and v2 # Fill quad with primitive color/opacity to framebuffer pass # Source does not provide exact rasterization implementation framebuffer = [] # Accumulated pixel values Streamline Rendering (Lines) visualizes vector fields by placing discrete geometric elements called strokes along streamlines, rather than drawing continuous lines, tubes, or ribbons. It is an automatic non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) approach designed to illustrate flow direction and field properties while avoiding the visual clutter and preprocessing costs associated with methods like Volume Line Integral Convolution (LIC). It distinguishes itself from sibling splatting methods by using discrete stroke geometry to encode directionality and field magnitude, often rendered in a separate pass or as opaque geometry prior to volume rendering. Renders text by mapping each character to a set of 2D line segments (strokes) in a 1x1 unit square, then transforming them to 3D space and drawing as capsules. Supports 6 orientations and cursor offset for spacing. Character stroke definitions are hardcoded as line segments in a 1x1 grid. The TextGeometry data structure contains size (float), thickness (float), pos (Vec3), orientation (enum), and text (string). TextOrientation is an enum with values POSZ, NEGZ, POSX, NEGX, POSY, NEGY, and default. The rendering loop initializes cursorOffset = 0.0f, iterates over each character c, converts to uppercase, maps 2D stroke coordinates (x1,y1) to (x2,y2) using an addLine lambda, applies scale s, offset cursorOffset, and orientation transform via mapCoords, creates CapsuleGeometry, calls drawCapsule, and increments cursorOffset += 1.5f. Performance: The capsule primitive is preferred over the exact volumetric primitive (closed-form convolution of a segment with a 3D Gaussian, integrated along the view ray) because it matched or beat it in blinded visual comparisons while costing 2.7–5x less than the screen-space quad per frame. Hardware Differences: The performance difference between capsule and quad primitives is 1.04–1.11x on Apple GPUs and ~1.5x on thin lines on discrete NVIDIA GPUs. Memory: Meshes (the only shaded geometry type in the same system) contribute no size padding to scene bounds and are loaded whole, not through a spatial index. Strengths: Efficient rasterization of line data; handles joints correctly without gaps or double brightness; supports physically based materials and transmission for meshes. Limitations: Cannot perform volumetric blending (absorption) due to zero thickness; additive ladder over arbitrary face order is not supported. The Line Capsule Primitive is part of the "Geometry primitives and mesh shading" system described in the Luxar viewer. It was developed to provide scalable interactive web visualization of multidimensional scientific data, specifically for microscopy and other fields requiring efficient rendering of line-based structures. The method was evaluated against exact volumetric primitives and screen-space quads, with the capsule primitive emerging as the preferred choice for most cases due to its balance of visual quality and performance. name: Streamline Rendering (Lines)
body: Streamline Rendering (Lines) visualizes vector fields by placing discrete geometric elements called strokes along streamlines, rather than drawing continuous lines, tubes, or ribbons. It is an automatic non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) approach designed to illustrate flow direction and field properties. It distinguishes itself from sibling splatting methods by using discrete stroke geometry to encode directionality and field magnitude, often rendered in a separate pass or as opaque geometry prior to volume rendering. The method generates streamlines from seed points and renders them as discrete strokes. The implementation typically utilizes OpenGL Vertex Buffer Objects (VBOs) to store the geometry and attributes of these strokes. Inputs: Vector field data, seed point locations, and user-defined parameters (stroke length, color mapping, density). Outputs: Rasterized image containing discrete strokes representing the flow field, composited with the underlying volume data. The geometry is stored in GPU memory using VBOs. The specific layout includes: mverticesVbo: An OpenGL GLARRAYBUFFER storing line vertices. Type: float3. Size: mlinesCount mmaxGeometrySamples sizeof(float3) bytes. mcolorsVbo: An OpenGL GLARRAYBUFFER storing line colors. Type: float3. Size: mlinesCount mmaxGeometrySamples sizeof(float3) bytes. 1. Seed Point Selection: Select seed points based on an enhancement criterion specified by the user to highlight regions of interest. 2. Streamline Tracing: Trace streamlines from the seed points through the vector field using traditional streamline tracing techniques. 3. Stroke Generation: Convert the traced streamlines into discrete strokes. 4. Attribute Assignment: Encode direction using a fading tail on the stroke. Map field properties (e.g., velocity magnitude) to the stroke color. 5. Rendering: Render the strokes as opaque, untextured geometry with the z-buffer enabled. This is done either prior to rendering the volume as textured polygons, or in an additional third pass. Stroke Length: Controls the trade-off between direction clarity and structural overview. Shorter strokes show direction information better; longer strokes reveal structural information better. Saturation and Brightness: Must be chosen carefully. High saturation/brightness in dense, intertwined color lines can obscure structural information. Seed Density: Interactive adjustment allows users to change the density of strokes to improve comprehension of the velocity field. Visual Clutter: Dense, intertwined color lines generally do not present structural information well. Preprocessing Cost: Related methods like Volume LIC have preprocessing costs that are too costly for interactive exploration, which is why traditional streamline tracing is chosen instead. Color Choice: Incorrect saturation and brightness levels can lead to poor visualization of the flow field structure. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderstreamlines(vectorfield, seedpoints, params): streamlines = [] for seed in seedpoints: points = [seed] current = seed for in range(params['maxsteps']): direction = vectorfield.sample(current) if direction.magnitude() == 0: break current = current + direction params['stepsize'] points.append(current) streamlines.append(points) vertices = [] colors = [] for line in streamlines: n = len(line) for i in range(n - 1): p0 = line[i] p1 = line[i+1] vertices.append(p0) vertices.append(p1) # Fading tail: alpha decreases from head (i=0) to tail (i=n-2) alpha = 1.0 - (i / max(n - 2, 1)) # Color by magnitude mag = vectorfield.magnitude(p0) r, g, b = params'colormap' colors.append((r, g, b, alpha)) gpuvertices = [0.0] (len(vertices) 3) gpucolors = [0.0] (len(colors) 4) for i, v in enumerate(vertices): gpuvertices[i3:i3+3] = [v.x, v.y, v.z] for i, c in enumerate(colors): gpucolors[i4:i4+4] = list(c) if params['renderorder'] == 'beforevolume': setdepthtest(enabled=True) drawlines(vertices=gpuvertices, colors=gpucolors) rendervolumeastexturedpolygons() elif params['renderorder'] == 'thirdpass': rendervolumeastexturedpolygons() setdepthtest(enabled=True) drawlines(vertices=gpuvertices, colors=gpucolors) def setdepthtest(enabled): # Standard graphics pipeline operation: glEnable(GLDEPTHTEST) if enabled else glDisable(GLDEPTHTEST) pass def drawlines(vertices, colors): # Standard graphics pipeline operation: bind buffers and call glDrawArrays(GLLINES,...) pass def rendervolumeastexturedpolygons(): # Standard graphics pipeline operation: render volume as textured polygons pass An automatic non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) approach for illustrating vector fields by placing discrete elements called strokes, rather than drawing lines, tubes, or ribbons. It sets itself apart by using discrete elements that can be styled (e.g., pencil drawing) and colored to indicate direction and magnitude. It is chosen when traditional flow visualization methods (lines, tubes) are avoided in favor of NPR styles, and when interactive exploration is needed to avoid the high preprocessing cost of Volume LIC. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of seed points and the length of streamlines traced. Interactive exploration is possible because traditional streamline tracing avoids the high preprocessing cost of Volume LIC. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of strokes and their length, stored in VBOs (mverticesVbo, mcolorsVbo). Strengths: Allows interactive adjustment of density and viewing angle; provides clear direction indication via fading tails; can be composited with volume data. Limitations: Dense color lines can obscure structure; requires careful tuning of stroke length and color saturation/brightness. When to use: When illustrating vector fields with NPR style, requiring clear direction and magnitude information without the clutter of tubes/ribbons, and when interactive exploration is needed. When not to use: When high preprocessing cost is acceptable and LIC is preferred for texture-like visualization, or when structural information is more critical than direction (longer strokes may help, but dense lines still pose a risk). Streamline rendering using strokes was proposed as an alternative to conventional flow visualization methods (lines, tubes, ribbons) and Volume Line Integral Convolution (LIC). Volume LIC was deemed too costly for interactive exploration due to preprocessing requirements. The method was developed to allow selective placement of seed points based on user-specified enhancement criteria, improving comprehension of velocity fields through interactive adjustment of stroke density and viewing angle. It has been used in simultaneous visualization of vorticity fields (via volume rendering) and velocity fields (via stroke-based rendering). name: Analytic Cylinder Shading
body: Analytic Cylinder Shading is a technique for rendering streamlines as volumetric entities by computing the average color integrated across the width of a projected cylinder. It solves the problem of representing line-based flow data with perceived volume and lighting interaction without the computational cost of rendering fully modeled 3D tubes. It is distinguished from Streamline Rendering (Lines) by explicitly modeling the cross-sectional integration of light, and from Cylindrical Shading via Texture Map by using closed-form mathematical evaluation rather than texture lookup. Inputs: Streamline geometry (start point, end point, direction). Viewing direction vector (\mathbf{v}). Lighting direction vector (\mathbf{l}). Surface albedo or base color (C{base}). Outputs: Shaded color (C{shaded}) for the streamline pixel. Data Structures: No complex data structures required. The method relies on vector operations and scalar integration results. The streamline is typically treated as a line segment in screen space for the projection. Steps: 1. Project Geometry: Determine the screen-space projection of the streamline segment. 2. Compute Directions: Calculate the normalized viewing vector \mathbf{v} and lighting vector \mathbf{l} at the streamline's position. 3. Evaluate Analytic Formula: Compute the average color by integrating the shading model across the cylinder's width. The integration accounts for the variation of the dot product between the surface normal and light/view directions across the circular cross-section of the projected cylinder. The formula derives from integrating the Lambertian or similar shading model over the visible hemisphere of the cylinder's cross-section. Let N be the surface normal at a point on the cylinder. The integration averages C{base} \cdot (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) over the width. The specific analytic solution involves terms dependent on the angle between the viewing direction and the streamline axis, and the lighting direction relative to the surface. 4. Alternative Lookup: If precomputed, retrieve the average color from a precomputed table or texture based on the angles between \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}, and the streamline tangent. Parameters: Cylinder radius: Implicitly defined by the visual width of the streamline. Not given in the sources. Lighting model: Typically Lambertian or Phong, but the analytic integration assumes a specific model. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewing Angle: The analytic formula may become singular or inaccurate when the viewing direction is parallel to the streamline axis, as the projected width approaches zero. Lighting Extremes: If the light source is behind the viewer or the streamline, the integration bounds change. Precision: Floating-point precision in the integration formula must be handled to avoid artifacts at grazing angles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def analyticcylindershading(streamlinetangent, viewdir, lightdir, basecolor): """ Computes the average shaded color for a streamline cylinder. Args: streamlinetangent: Normalized 3D vector of the streamline direction. viewdir: Normalized 3D vector from camera to point. lightdir: Normalized 3D vector from point to light source. basecolor: RGB color of the streamline material. Returns: Shaded RGB color. """ # 1. Compute the angle between the viewing direction and the streamline tangent # This determines the projected width and visibility of the cylinder side costhetav = dot(streamlinetangent, viewdir) # 2. Compute the angle between the lighting direction and the streamline tangent costhetal = dot(streamlinetangent, lightdir) # 3. Evaluate the analytic integration formula # The formula integrates the shading over the cylinder's cross-section. # Based on Schussman [19] as cited in. # Note: The exact closed-form expression is complex and depends on the # specific shading model (e.g., Lambertian). # A simplified representation of the integration result: # If the light is effectively uniform across the projected width, # the average intensity is proportional to the projected area weighted by lighting. # The specific analytic formula from Schussman involves terms like: # Iavg = (1/pi) integral over visible surface of (n. l) dA # This results in a function of the angles between v, l, and the tangent. # For implementation, one must use the specific formula from Schussman [19]. # Since the exact formula is not provided in the source text, we denote it as: shadingfactor = computeschussmanshadingfactor(costhetav, costhetal, lightdir, streamlinetangent) return basecolor shadingfactor def computeschussmanshadingfactor(costhetav, costhetal, lightdir, tangent): """ Placeholder for the specific analytic formula from Schussman [19]. This function must be implemented based on the mathematical derivation in the cited reference. """ # Implement the integration of the dot product over the cylinder surface. # The result is a scalar value representing the average brightness. return 0.5 # Placeholder value Simulates cylindrical shading on streamlines using a texture map instead of fully modeled geometry. This variant avoids the computational cost of analytic integration or 3D tube rendering by mapping a pre-shaded cylindrical texture onto the 2D line primitive. It is chosen when performance is critical and the lighting conditions are static or can be approximated by a fixed texture. It differs from the analytic method by relying on spatial sampling rather than mathematical evaluation. Time Complexity: O(1) per streamline segment for the analytic method, assuming constant-time vector operations. The texture map variant is also O(1) but involves texture lookup overhead. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the analytic method. The texture map variant requires memory for the precomputed texture table. Performance: Faster than rendering fully modeled cylindrical tubes, which require more vertices and rasterization overhead. Strengths: Provides a volumetric appearance with low computational cost; avoids the "flat" look of simple lines. Limitations: Requires precomputation or complex analytic formulas; may not handle dynamic lighting changes as easily as fully modeled geometry without recomputation. When to use: When visualizing flow fields with perceived volume is desired but full 3D tube rendering is too expensive. When not to use: When dynamic, complex lighting interactions are required that cannot be captured by the analytic approximation or static texture. The technique was discussed by Schussman [19] and cited in the context of scientific visualization. It is part of the broader effort to improve the visual clarity of streamline rendering by adding perceived volume and lighting cues. The method is an alternative to rendering lines as fully modeled tubes or using simple texture maps. name: Tetrahedral Splatting
head: TetSplat
body: Tetrahedral Splatting (TetSplat) is a point-based technique for the real-time rendering of large, static tetrahedral meshes by approximating each tetrahedron with a spherical or ellipsoid splat. It replaces complex volumetric primitives with screen-space footprint functions and uses hierarchical data structures for efficient back-face and occlusion culling. Unlike Voxel Splat Rendering, which relies on regular grid discretization, or Triangle Mesh Splatting, which projects surface boundaries, TetSplat operates directly on volumetric tetrahedral elements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static, unstructured tetrahedral mesh representing a volumetric field. Output: A 2D image buffer with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: 1. Partitioned Mesh: The input mesh is preprocessed and partitioned into distinct topological sets. 2. Splat Representation: Each tetrahedron Tj is mapped to a single splat primitive. Spherical Splat: Defined by a center \mathbf{c}j and radius rj. Ellipsoid Splat: Defined by a center \mathbf{c}j and a 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigmaj. 3. Hierarchical Culling Structure: A spatial hierarchy (e.g., BVH or octree) built over the splats to enable efficient back-face and occlusion culling. Preprocessing (Static Assumption): 1. Degeneracy Removal: Identify and eliminate degenerated tetrahedra (needles, spindles, slivers, and caps) using edge collapse. 2. Partitioning: Separate the remaining tetrahedra into topological sets for rendering. 3. Splat Generation: Compute the center \mathbf{c}j (e.g., centroid) and shape parameters (radius or covariance) for each tetrahedron. 4. Hierarchy Construction: Build the hierarchical data structure for culling. Rendering Steps: 1. Culling: Use the hierarchical structure to cull splats that are back-facing or occluded by previously rendered closer splats. 2. Projection: For each remaining splat, transform its center \mathbf{c}j and shape parameters into screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. 3. Footprint Evaluation: For each pixel (u,v) within the screen-space bounding box of the splat, evaluate the footprint function F(u,v). For a spherical splat with screen-space radius R: F(u,v) = \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{(u - uc)^2 + (v - vc)^2}{R^2}\right) For an ellipsoid splat, the distance metric is modified by the projected covariance matrix. 4. Compositing: Accumulate the splat's contribution to the image buffer using alpha blending. Assuming the splat represents a density or color value Ij and opacity \alphaj: C{out}(u,v) = C{in}(u,v) + Ij \cdot F(u,v) \cdot \alphaj \cdot (1 - A{in}(u,v)) A{out}(u,v) = A{in}(u,v) + \alphaj \cdot F(u,v) \cdot (1 - A{in}(u,v)) where C is color, A is accumulated opacity, and (uc, vc) is the screen-space center. Parameters: Splat Shape: Spherical or Ellipsoid. Hierarchy Depth: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tetrahedra: The method explicitly removes degenerate tetrahedra. This is a significant limitation for dynamic volumes like smoke, where topology must be maintained and tetrahedra naturally approach degenerate states during integration. Visible Gaps: Since each tetrahedron is represented by exactly one splat, small meshes or poorly adapted splat shapes result in visible gaps between splats, degrading visual quality. Static Mesh Requirement: The preprocessing step assumes a static mesh. The method is unsuitable for dynamic objects in its current implementation. This method partitions a large unstructured tetrahedral mesh into two distinct topological parts: the Shell (non-convex boundary) and the Solid (internal fragments). This separation allows the Shell to be rendered as a standard opaque surface mesh with vertex normals, while the Solid is rendered using normals derived from a Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) probe, as interior tetrahedra are only visible at the intersection surface. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the number of visible splats and the cost of footprint evaluation per pixel. Hierarchical culling reduces the number of splats processed. Footprint evaluation is O(1) per pixel per splat. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of tetrahedra N for storing splat parameters and the hierarchy. Measured Performance: Enables real-time rendering of large tetrahedral meshes. Strengths: High performance for static volumes; simple footprint functions allow efficient rasterization; hierarchical culling reduces overdraw. Limitations: Requires static meshes; preprocessing removes topological details (degenerate tetrahedra); single-splat-per-tetrahedron representation leads to visible gaps and loss of geometric fidelity; not suitable for dynamic smoke volumes where topology changes. When to use: Real-time visualization of large, static tetrahedral meshes where performance is critical and some geometric approximation is acceptable. When not to use: Dynamic volumes (e.g., smoke simulation), scenes requiring high geometric fidelity, or meshes with many degenerate elements that cannot be removed without altering topology. Tetrahedral Splatting (TetSplat) was introduced as a point-based technique for real-time rendering of large tetrahedral meshes. It addresses the limitations of exact volume integration methods by approximating volumetric primitives with splats. The method relies on a preprocessing step that partitions the volume and removes degenerate elements, making it suitable for static scenes. name: TetSplat Pre-processing: Mesh Partitioning
head: Partitioning the Input Mesh into the Shell and the Solid
body: This method partitions a large unstructured tetrahedral mesh into two distinct topological parts: the Shell (non-convex boundary) and the Solid (internal fragments). This separation allows the Shell to be rendered as a standard opaque surface mesh with vertex normals, while the Solid is rendered using normals derived from a Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) probe, as interior tetrahedra are only visible at the intersection surface. Inputs: An unstructured tetrahedral mesh consisting of tetrahedra Tetk. Outputs: Two sets of triangles: the Shell (boundary faces) and the Solid (internal faces, further classified as boundary or internal triangles). Data Structures: Tri: An array containing all triangles derived from the tetrahedral mesh. Each element stores a sorted list of vertex indices. Algorithm Steps: 1. Triangle Extraction and Canonicalization: For each tetrahedron Tetk, extract its four constituent triangles. Sort the vertex indices within each triangle's vertex list to ensure a canonical representation. Store these sorted triangles in the array Tri. 2. Global Sorting: Sort the entire Tri array based on the indexed vertex list of each triangle. This groups identical triangles (those sharing the same three vertices) together in adjacent positions. 3. Shell/Solid Classification: Iterate through each triangle Trii in the sorted Tri array. Compare the vertex list of Trii with the vertex list of the next triangle Tri{i+1}. If the vertex lists are identical, classify Trii as part of the Solid. If they differ, classify Trii as part of the Shell. Mark the tetrahedron Tetk associated with a Shell triangle as a boundary tetrahedron. 4. Solid Sub-classification: Iterate through each triangle Trii classified as part of the Solid. Check if the associated tetrahedron Tetk is a boundary tetrahedron. If Tetk is a boundary tetrahedron, classify Trii as a boundary triangle in the Solid. If Tetk is not a boundary tetrahedron, classify Trii as an internal triangle in the Solid. 5. Degeneracy Removal: Remove degenerate tetrahedra from the mesh. Needles (tetrahedra without large dihedral angles) are removed by collapsing their shortest edges. Spindles (tetrahedra with a single large dihedral angle) are removed by splitting the edge opposite to the large angle and then collapsing the shortest edges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partitionmesh(tetrahedra): # Step 1: Extract and canonicalize triangles Tri = [] for k, Tetk in enumerate(tetrahedra): v = Tetk.vertices # Extract 4 triangles from Tetk (indices 0,1,2; 0,1,3; 0,2,3; 1,2,3) faces = [(v[0], v[1], v[2]), (v[0], v[1], v[3]), (v[0], v[2], v[3]), (v[1], v[2], v[3])] for i, tri in enumerate(faces): # Sort vertex indices for canonical comparison sortedindices = tuple(sorted(tri)) Tri.append({ 'indices': sortedindices, 'tetindex': k, 'localindex': i }) # Step 2: Sort all triangles by vertex indices Tri.sort(key=lambda x: x['indices']) shelltriangles = [] solidtriangles = [] boundarytetrahedra = set() # Step 3: Classify Shell vs Solid n = len(Tri) for i in range(n): current = Tri[i] # Check if current triangle is identical to the next one isshared = (i + 1 < n) and (current['indices'] == Tri[i + 1]['indices']) if isshared: # Shared face -> Solid solidtriangles.append(current) else: # Boundary face -> Shell shelltriangles.append(current) boundarytetrahedra.add(current['tetindex']) # Step 4: Sub-classify Solid triangles solidboundarytriangles = [] solidinternaltriangles = [] for tri in solidtriangles: tetidx = tri['tetindex'] if tetidx in boundarytetrahedra: solidboundarytriangles.append(tri) else: solidinternaltriangles.append(tri) # Step 5: Remove degenerate tetrahedra (Needles and Spindles) cleantetrahedra = [] for Tetk in tetrahedra: #: The sources do not specify the exact geometric predicates or edge-collapse implementation for Needles and Spindles. cleantetrahedra.append(Tetk) return shelltriangles, solidboundarytriangles, solidinternaltriangles, cleantetrahedra Parameters: Tri: An array containing all triangles derived from the tetrahedral mesh, used for sorting and classification. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Sorting relies on exact vertex index equality. Floating-point precision issues in vertex positions must be resolved during the initial mesh construction or by using a tolerance-based canonicalization before index sorting. Degeneracy: The algorithm explicitly handles "Needles" (no large dihedral angles) and "Spindles" (one large dihedral angle). Boundary Definition: The distinction between "boundary triangle in the Solid" and "Shell" is topological. Shell triangles are on the mesh boundary; Solid boundary triangles are internal faces of tetrahedra that touch the mesh boundary. Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step. Sorting N triangles takes O(N \log N) time, where N is the total number of triangle faces (4 \times number of tetrahedra). The iteration steps are linear O(N). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Tri array, which is proportional to the number of tetrahedra. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a clean topological separation that allows different shading strategies (vertex normals vs. CSG probe normals) for boundary and interior, ensuring visual consistency at the clipping boundary. Limitations: Requires a full pass over the mesh data and sorting. Degeneracy removal adds preprocessing overhead. When to use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from the TetSplat paper by Museth and Lombeyda (2004), which introduced a point-based technique for real-time rendering of large tetrahedral meshes. The partitioning is a prerequisite for the hierarchical bounding sphere structure and the CSG probe clipping mechanism described in the parent article. name: Voxel Splat Rendering
head: Interactive Splat Rendering with Alpha/Gamma Control, Interactive value selection rendering, Splatting (Object Order), Voxel splatting
body: Voxel Splat Rendering is an object-order volume rendering technique where each voxel is projected onto the screen as a 2D footprint (splat) and composited into the image buffer. It solves the problem of rendering large volumetric datasets interactively by replacing per-pixel ray traversal with per-voxel projection, allowing for efficient culling of irrelevant voxels and parallelization. Unlike Circle Splat Rendering which uses circular footprints, Voxel Splat Rendering typically projects axis-aligned bounding rectangles or squares, often optimized for GPU rasterization of quads. It differs from Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting Pipeline by typically processing voxels in object space (often front-to-back) rather than pre-sorting them into image-space slabs on the GPU. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V (array of voxels with position, color, opacity, and optionally normal). Camera parameters: Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or separate Model-View (MV) and Projection (P) matrices. Rendering parameters: Point size, alpha value, gamma value, and anti-aliasing settings. Outputs: 2D Image buffer (Color and Depth/Alpha). Data Structures: Voxel: Contains 3D position (x,y,z), color (R,G,B), opacity \alpha, and optionally a surface normal \mathbf{n}. Splat Footprint: A 2D region in screen space. For axis-aligned splats, this is defined by an axis-aligned bounding rectangle (AABB) in screen coordinates. For Gaussian splats, it is a radially symmetric kernel. Image Buffer: Accumulates color and opacity. Steps: 1. Voxel Transformation: For each voxel in the volume, transform its center position \mathbf{p}{obj} from object space to screen space \mathbf{p}{screen} using the camera's view and projection matrices. \mathbf{p}{screen} = M{view} \cdot M{proj} \cdot \mathbf{p}{obj} If the voxel is behind the camera or outside the view frustum, cull it. 2. Footprint Calculation: Determine the screen-space extent of the voxel. Axis-Aligned (Rectangular): Compute the axis-aligned bounding rectangle of the projected voxel cube. Gaussian (Radial): Define a radius r based on the voxel size and distance to camera, or use a fixed footprint size for parallel projection. 3. Shading and Weighting (Optional but common): Calculate a weight for the voxel to modulate its contribution. Normal-based Culling/Weighting: If normals are available, compute a weight based on the angle between the view vector and the normal to simulate surface shading or cull back-facing voxels. Multi-View Weighting (e.g., for NeRF/Image-based modeling): If rendering from a novel view using multiple source cameras, compute weights for each source camera i: 1. Calculate \text{dotV} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{V}{toEye}, \mathbf{V}{toCamera[i]}). 2. Calculate \text{dotN} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{V}{toCamera[i]}). 3. \text{weightV} = \text{dotV} > 0.0 ? \text{pow}(\text{dotV}, 4): 0.0. 4. \text{weightN} = \text{dotN} > 0.0 ? \text{pow}(\text{dotN}, 4): 0.0. 5. \text{weight}[i] = \text{weightV} \times \text{weightN}. 6. Normalize weights by dividing by the sum of all weights. 4. Rasterization (Splatting): Render the footprint onto the image buffer. Rectangular Splat: Render the AABB as a pair of triangles (quad). Gaussian Splat: Rasterize a precomputed footprint lookup table (LUT) that stores the analytically integrated kernel function along a traversing ray. This spreads the voxel's energy across multiple pixels to counter holes caused by discrete processing. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the splat's color and opacity into the image buffer. Front-to-Back: Traverse voxels from near to far. For each splat, update the buffer using alpha blending: C{out} = C{in} \cdot (1 - \alpha{splat}) + C{splat} \cdot \alpha{splat} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} \cdot (1 - \alpha{splat}) + \alpha{splat} Back-to-Front: Also possible, though front-to-back is standard for early termination in raycasting, splatting often processes all visible voxels. 6. Post-Processing: Apply gamma correction and alpha blending adjustments to reduce contributions from tissues with differing color densities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelsplatrendering(volume, viewprojmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight, clearcolor=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)): # Initialize image buffer with clear color and zero alpha imagebuffer = [(clearcolor, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth imageheight)] # Sort voxels front-to-back based on depth in camera space sortedvoxels = sortvoxelsbydepth(volume, viewprojmatrix) for voxel in sortedvoxels: # 1. Transform voxel center to screen space pscreen = transformtoscreen(voxel.position, viewprojmatrix) # 2. Cull if behind camera or outside frustum if not isinfrustum(pscreen, imagewidth, imageheight): continue # 3. Calculate footprint (AABB for rectangular splats) footprint = calculateaabbfootprint(voxel, viewprojmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight) if footprint is None: continue # 4. Calculate shading weight (optional, e.g., normal-based) # Multi-view weighting logic omitted; see Step 3 for source-specific formula. weight = 1.0 if voxel.hasnormal: viewdir = normalize(voxel.eyepos - voxel.position) weight = max(0.0, dot(viewdir, voxel.normal)) 4 # 5. Rasterize footprint and composite renderquad(footprint, voxel.color, voxel.opacity weight, imagebuffer, imagewidth) return imagebuffer def clearimagebuffer(buffer, clearcolor): for i in range(len(buffer)): buffer[i] = (clearcolor, 0.0) def sortvoxelsbydepth(voxels, viewprojmatrix): for v in voxels: p = transformtoscreen(v.position, viewprojmatrix) v.screenz = p.z if p else float('inf') return sorted(voxels, key=lambda v: v.screenz, reverse=True) def transformtoscreen(position, viewprojmatrix): # Standard MVP transformation: multiply position by matrix, divide by w phomogeneous = viewprojmatrix @ position if phomogeneous.w <= 0.0: return None return (phomogeneous.x / phomogeneous.w, phomogeneous.y / phomogeneous.w, phomogeneous.z / phomogeneous.w) def isinfrustum(pscreen, width, height): if pscreen is None: return False u, v, z = pscreen if z < 0.0 or z > 1.0: return False if u < 0.0 or u > width or v < 0.0 or v > height: return False return True def calculateaabbfootprint(voxel, viewprojmatrix, width, height): # Project 8 corners of the voxel cube to screen space corners = getvoxelcorners(voxel.position, voxel.size) screencorners = [transformtoscreen(c, viewprojmatrix) for c in corners] screencorners = [c for c in screencorners if c is not None] if not screencorners: return None minu = min(c[0] for c in screencorners) maxu = max(c[0] for c in screencorners) minv = min(c[1] for c in screencorners) maxv = max(c[1] for c in screencorners) return (minu, minv, maxu, maxv) def getvoxelcorners(position, size): x, y, z = position s = size / 2.0 return [ (x-s, y-s, z-s), (x+s, y-s, z-s), (x-s, y+s, z-s), (x+s, y+s, z-s), (x-s, y-s, z+s), (x+s, y-s, z+s), (x-s, y+s, z+s), (x+s, y+s, z+s) ] def renderquad(footprint, color, opacity, buffer, width): minu, minv, maxu, maxv = footprint for y in range(int(minv), int(maxv) + 1): for x in range(int(minu), int(maxu) + 1): idx = y width + x if 0 <= idx < len(buffer): buffer[idx] = blend(buffer[idx], color, opacity) def blend(currentpixel, newcolor, newopacity): cin, ain = currentpixel cout = [cin[i] (1.0 - newopacity) + newcolor[i] newopacity for i in range(3)] aout = ain (1.0 - newopacity) + newopacity return (tuple(cout), aout) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) return tuple(c/mag for c in v) if mag > 0 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def dot(v1, v2): return sum(ab for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) Parameters: Point-size/Radius: Determines the size of the splat. Alpha-value: Global or per-voxel opacity. Gamma-value: Gamma correction exponent to adjust brightness/contrast. Power Exponent: In normal-based weighting, a power of 4 is commonly used to smooth transitions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: Discrete processing can produce holes on the periphery or during extreme perspective projection. Countered by distributing energy across multiple pixels via a footprint table. Aliasing: Minor aliasing artifacts similar to non-anti-aliased triangle models. Close-range views show rectangular block artifacts and pixelation from finite RGB image resolution. Blurring: Tends to blur edges of objects and reduce image contrast. Performance: Requires extensive filtering, making it time-consuming for large datasets if not optimized. GPU rasterization is not always optimized for single-pixel quads, but performance is often acceptable. A GPU-accelerated variant that processes voxels in slabs parallel to the image plane, avoiding CPU-GPU bottlenecks by constructing buckets and sorting on the GPU. It accelerates rendering by 2-2.5x compared to CPU-based bucketing. Uses parallel rays to project voxels onto a 2D sprite plane, solving per-eye pixel shimmer in VR by rendering a single static image identical for both eyes. It uses a single fragment pass with a chunky virtual-pixel grid. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Achieves 1.1 Hz on a single 150MHz R4400 processor for a 256 \times 256 \times 225 volume with 65 seconds of pre-processing time. Strengths: Interactive frame rates for large datasets; efficient culling of irrelevant voxels; suitable for parallelization based on object space subdivision. Limitations: Blurs edges; prone to aliasing and holes if footprint is not properly distributed; brightness variations in animation if not using image-aligned splatting. When to use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets where speed is prioritized over photorealistic edge sharpness. When not to use: When extreme perspective distortion causes severe aliasing or holes that footprints cannot resolve. Voxel Splat Rendering was first published by Westover. It was introduced as an alternative to ray casting, representing the volume as an array of overlapping basis functions (commonly Gaussian kernels) scaled by voxel values. The method was designed to provide interactive frame rates by projecting voxels to the screen and compositing them, rather than casting rays per pixel. Subsequent improvements included image-aligned splatting by Mueller to reduce brightness variations in animation, and normal-based culling by Sobierajski et al. to reduce processing load. It is widely used in medical visualization and interactive volume exploration.
