name: Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting Pipeline
head: GPU ISBS, GPU-based ISSB Splatting, GPU-based Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting, ISSB Splatting on the GPU, Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting on the GPU
body: Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting on the GPU (GPU ISBS) is a volume rendering technique that processes voxels in slabs parallel to the image plane, performing all bucket construction, voxel transformation, and depth sorting entirely on the GPU to avoid CPU-GPU memory transfer bottlenecks. Unlike the CPU-based approach where buckets contain all voxels intersecting a slab, the GPU method defines a bucket as the subset of depth-sorted voxels whose center falls inside a specific slab, allowing each voxel to belong to exactly one bucket while still being splatted for all intersecting slabs. This method accelerates rendering by a factor of 2 to 2.5 compared to implementations that compute buckets on the CPU. The pipeline processes voxels through texture-based stages: loading, viewing transform, GPGPU sorting, bucket size computation, and rendering. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of selected non-empty voxels, each defined by 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and a property value v (e.g., density or opacity). Output: A composited 2D image buffer. Data Structures 1. Voxels Texture: A 2D texture storing the input voxels. Each voxel is encoded in a texel using FP32RGBA format (32-bit floating point per channel). The RGB channels store the voxel coordinates (x, y, z), and the Alpha channel stores the property value v. 2. View Transformed Voxels Texture: A 2D texture storing the result of the viewing transform. Each texel stores the 2D raster projection coordinates in the R and G channels, the depth value in the viewing coordinate system in the B channel, and the voxel property value in the Alpha channel, denoted as (i, j, b, v). 3. Depth-Sorted Voxels Texture (Z-Sorted Voxels Texture): A 2D texture containing the voxels from the View Transformed Voxels Texture sorted by depth b. 4. Buckets Texture: A 2D texture storing the position (index) of the last voxel of each bucket (bucket boundary voxel). 5. Auxiliary Texture: Used during bucket size computation to mark boundary voxels. It stores bucket coordinates in R and G, an arbitrary z-value inside the viewing frustum for boundary voxels (outside otherwise) in B, and the bucket index in Alpha. Parameters Voxel Kernel Radius: Determines the number of previous and following buckets that affect a single slab in addition to its own bucket. Texture Memory Limit: The method assumes a maximum texture size of 4096 \times 4096, allowing up to 16 million selected voxels. Steps 1. Load Voxels: Load the selected non-empty voxels into the Voxels Texture on the GPU. Each voxel is encoded as <x, y, z, v> in FP32RGBA format. 2. Viewing Transform: Compute the View Transformed Voxels Texture using a fragment shader. For each texel in the Voxels Texture, transform the voxel coordinates (RGB) using the viewing matrix. Store the 2D raster projection coordinates in R and G, the depth value in B, and the voxel property value in Alpha. 3. GPGPU Sorting: Sort the View Transformed Voxels Texture by depth using a GPU Bitonic Sort. The sorting key is the depth value (B channel). The sort uses Multiple Render Targets (MRT) to store keys and values in separate textures, allowing four <key, value> instances per RGBA texel. The key is the depth value, and the value is the voxel index in the texture. After sorting, a fragment shader fills the Depth-Sorted Voxels Texture from the sorted render targets. This sorting creates an implicit representation of buckets, where slabs correspond to overlapping sorted subsequences of voxels in the texture. 4. Bucket Size Computation: Compute the Buckets Texture in two steps: Step 4a: Use a fragment shader to identify bucket boundary voxels. Render the Depth-Sorted Voxels Texture into an Auxiliary Texture. For each voxel, determine if it is a boundary voxel (i.e., its center falls inside a slab but the next voxel in the sorted texture does not). If it is a boundary voxel, store its bucket coordinates in R and G, an arbitrary z-value inside the viewing frustum in B, and the bucket index in Alpha. Step 4b: Use a vertex shader to construct the Buckets Texture from the Auxiliary Texture. The vertex shader renders the boundary voxels (identified by the z-value in B) to write the position of the last voxel of each bucket into the Buckets Texture. 5. Transfer Bucket Data: Transfer the small Buckets Texture to the CPU to determine bucket distribution. This is a low-cost operation because the texture size is small (number of buckets/slabs). 6. Rendering: Process slabs sequentially. For each slab i, retrieve its bucket from the Buckets Texture. The radius of the voxel kernel determines that a slab is affected by its own bucket plus previous and following buckets (from bucket{i-radius} to bucket{i+radius}). Use the Render to Vertex Buffer (R2VB) technique to create a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) containing all voxels from the relevant buckets. Render slabs by splatting voxels from the relevant buckets using DrawArrays. Project voxels from the current bucket onto a sheet buffer according to a preintegrated kernel slice. Composite the sheet buffer with the image buffer. No sorting is required inside the buckets as splats are simply added. Use the glPoint primitive with the Point Sprites extension to create automatic quads for splats. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. VoxelsTexture = create2dtexture(numvoxels, 1, format="FP32RGBA") for i, v in enumerate(voxels): VoxelsTexture[i] = (v.x, v.y, v.z, v.value) ViewTransformedTexture = create2dtexture(numvoxels, 1, format="FP32RGBA") for i in range(numvoxels): pos = VoxelsTexture[i].rgb val = VoxelsTexture[i].a # Transform 3D coordinates using viewing matrix proj = transform3dto2ddepth(pos, viewingmatrix) ViewTransformedTexture[i] = (proj.xy, proj.z, val) DepthSortedTexture = bitonicsortbydepth(ViewTransformedTexture) AuxiliaryTexture = create2dtexture(numvoxels, 1, format="FP32RGBA") for i in range(numvoxels - 1): currslab = getslabindex(DepthSortedTexture[i].b) nextslab = getslabindex(DepthSortedTexture[i+1].b) if currslab != nextslab: # Boundary voxel: store slab index in A, arbitrary z inside frustum in B AuxiliaryTexture[i] = (0.0, ZINSIDEFRUSTUM, currslab) else: AuxiliaryTexture[i] = (0.0, ZOUTSIDEFRUSTUM, 0.0) AuxiliaryTexture[numvoxels-1] = (0.0, ZINSIDEFRUSTUM, getslabindex(DepthSortedTexture[-1].b)) BucketsTexture = create2dtexture(numslabs, 1, format="FP32RGBA") for i in range(numvoxels): if AuxiliaryTexture[i].b == ZINSIDEFRUSTUM: slabidx = AuxiliaryTexture[i].a BucketsTexture[slabidx] = i bucketdistribution = readback(BucketsTexture) for slabi in range(numslabs): startb = max(0, slabi - kernelradius) endb = min(numslabs - 1, slabi + kernelradius) indices = [] for b in range(startb, endb + 1): endidx = BucketsTexture[b].a startidx = BucketsTexture[b-1].a if b > 0 else 0 indices.extend(range(startidx, endidx + 1)) # Create VBO from indices using R2VB vbo = createvbofromindices(indices, DepthSortedTexture) # Render using DrawArrays with Point Sprites drawarrays(vbo, primitive="POINTS") # Composite sheet buffer with image buffer compositesheetbuffer() This method defines the final rendering stage of the Image-Space Sheet-Buffered (ISSB) splatting pipeline, where depth-sorted voxels are rasterized using glPoint primitives and the Point Sprites extension. It distinguishes itself from prior ISSB implementations by computing and storing distinct kernel footprints for each voxel across all intersecting slabs, rather than storing a single footprint modulated by a slab coefficient. This approach provides finer tuning of the splat appearance at the cost of increased texture memory for footprint storage. Time Complexity: The most expensive stage of the pipeline is sorting, which uses data-independent network sorting strategies like Bitonic Sort. Memory Complexity: The method is limited by texture memory size. A 4096 \times 4096 texture allows up to 16 million selected voxels. For larger models, the volume is subdivided into bricks, each stored as a 2D texture. Measured Performance: On a Pentium Dual Core 3.2 GHz with 3.2 GB memory and an NVIDIA GeForce 7900 GTX with 512 MB memory, the method accelerates rendering by a factor of 2 to 2.5 compared to an implementation that computes buckets on the CPU. For the "Lobster" dataset (324x301x56, 233K effective voxels), CPU FPS was 13.2 and GPU FPS was 35.4. For the "Engine" dataset (256x128, 1.3M effective voxels), CPU FPS was 2.4 and GPU FPS was 5.6. Strengths: Avoids CPU-GPU memory transfer bottlenecks by performing all data management on the GPU. Simplifies bucket structure by assigning each voxel to exactly one bucket. Limitations: Scattering (random writes) is inefficient on GPUs, necessitating the use of sorting and implicit bucket representation. Determining bucket boundaries in a vertex shader is expensive due to inefficient texture fetches, requiring a two-step computation. The bottleneck is the computation of the buckets. When to use: When GPU computational resources are available and CPU-GPU memory transfer is a bottleneck. Suitable for static cameras where only the transfer function changes (only the render stage needs to be redone) or moving cameras where the full pipeline is executed. When not to use: When the number of voxels exceeds the texture memory limit and bricking is not feasible or desirable. Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting was originally proposed as a feed-forward algorithm for voxel-based volume datasets. It processes the volume by slabs parallel to the image plane. The GPU-based implementation was proposed to address the memory transfer bottleneck between CPU buckets and GPU slices present in earlier implementations by Neophitou and Mueller. The method uses GPGPU sorting and OpenGL Depth Test to manage buckets on the GPU. name: ISSB Rendering with Point Sprites and Dynamic Footprints
head: GPU Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting Rendering
body: This method defines the final rendering stage of the Image-Space Sheet-Buffered (ISSB) splatting pipeline, where depth-sorted voxels are rasterized using glPoint primitives and the Point Sprites extension. It distinguishes itself from prior ISSB implementations by computing and storing distinct kernel footprints for each voxel across all intersecting slabs, rather than storing a single footprint modulated by a slab coefficient. This approach provides finer tuning of the splat appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Bucket Texture (2D texture containing bucket sizes and distribution), a VBO (Vertex Buffer Object) containing all depth-sorted voxels, and a Footprint Texture (2D texture storing pre-computed kernel footprints). Output: The final rendered image on the GPU framebuffer. Data Structures: 1. Bucket Texture: A small 2D texture where each texel represents a bucket (slab). The transfer from GPU to CPU is low-cost due to this small size. 2. VBO: Created using the R2VB (Render to Vertex Buffer) extension, containing all voxels processed by the preceding ISSB stages. 3. Footprint Texture: A 2D texture storing multiple kernel footprints, where each voxel may have a different footprint depending on the slab it intersects. Parameters: Kernel Radius (r): The radius of the voxel's kernel. It determines the range of buckets that must be processed for each slab. Algorithm Steps: 1. Transfer Bucket Data: Transfer the Bucket Texture from GPU to CPU to obtain bucket sizes and distribution. 2. Create VBO: Use the R2VB extension to create a VBO containing all voxels from the depth-sorted data. 3. Compute Footprints: For each voxel, compute all different kernel footprints across all intersecting slabs and store them in the Footprint Texture. 4. Render Slabs: For each slab i, determine the range of buckets to process: from bucket{i-r} to bucket{i+r}, where r is the kernel radius. 5. Draw Buckets: For each bucket in this range, render all voxels using DrawArrays with the first voxel's position and the number of voxels in the bucket. 6. Vertex Shader Processing (Point Sprites): Use glPoint primitives with the Point Sprites extension to create automatic quads, reducing vertex instances from four to one. 7. Texture Coordinates: Since Point Sprites compute texture coordinates automatically, compute the correct texture coordinates manually in the vertex shader. 8. Footprint Indexing: Compute an index to the specific footprint based on the slab intersection and use it to determine the coordinates of the sub-texture containing the corresponding footprint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderissbpointsprites(bucketsizes, voxelstarts, footprinttexture, kernelradius): # Step 1: Bucket sizes are on CPU after transfer # Step 2: VBO contains all voxels; voxelstarts maps bucket index to first voxel position # Step 3: Footprints are pre-computed and stored in footprinttexture numslabs = len(bucketsizes) for slabi in range(numslabs): # Step 4: Determine bucket range based on kernel radius startbucket = max(0, slabi - kernelradius) endbucket = min(numslabs - 1, slabi + kernelradius) for bucketidx in range(startbucket, endbucket + 1): count = bucketsizes[bucketidx] if count == 0: continue firstvoxel = voxelstarts[bucketidx] # Step 4b: Render voxels using glDrawArrays with glPoint primitive for v in range(firstvoxel, firstvoxel + count): # Step 5: Point Sprites automatically generate a quad, reducing vertices from four to one # Compute correct texture coordinates manually in vertex shader footprintindex = computefootprintindex(slabi) uv = footprintindextouv(footprintindex, footprinttexture) rasterizepoint(v, uv) def computefootprintindex(slabindex): # Maps the current slab index to a unique footprint slot in the texture return slabindex % footprinttexture.height def footprintindextouv(index, texture): # Converts footprint index to normalized texture coordinates cols = texture.width return (index % cols, index // cols) def rasterizepoint(voxelindex, uv): # Rasterizes a single point sprite at the computed UV coordinates pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Size Limitations: The method's limitations can arise from texture size limits, which may not fit an entire volume. Automatic Texture Coordinates: With Point Sprites, texture coordinates are computed automatically. Failing to compute the correct coordinates in the vertex shader will result in incorrect footprint sampling. Bucket Boundary Rejection: Non-bucket boundary voxels may be rejected if their z-value does not align with the bucket boundary in the auxiliary texture (e.g., a bucket boundary voxel has a 0.5 z value, while a non-boundary voxel is rejected). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The bucket range processed per slab spans 2r+1 buckets, where r is the kernel radius. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Bucket Texture (small), VBO (all voxels), and Footprint Texture (multiple footprints per voxel). Strengths: Reduces vertex instances from four to one using Point Sprites, improving rendering efficiency. Dynamic footprints allow for better tuning of splats compared to single footprint modulation. Limitations: Texture size limitations may restrict volume size. The need to compute and store multiple footprints increases memory usage. The manual computation of texture coordinates in the vertex shader adds complexity. When to Use: Suitable for GPU-based volume visualization where rendering efficiency is critical and sufficient texture memory is available. When Not to Use: Not suitable if texture memory is severely constrained or if the overhead of computing and storing multiple footprints is prohibitive. This method is part of the Image-Space Sheet-Buffered (ISSB) splatting pipeline. It builds on previous GPU implementations of ISSB Splatting. The approach of storing a single footprint and modulating it with a slab coefficient was proposed by Neophytou and Mueller [14], but this method improves upon it by computing and storing all different kernel footprints for better tuning. name: Orthographic Voxel Sprite Rendering
head: Flat Billboard Voxel Rendering, Volumetric Ortho-Sprite Preview, VoxelOrthoSprite
body: Orthographic Voxel Sprite Rendering projects a 3D voxel model onto a 2D sprite plane using parallel rays to create a flat billboard appearance. It solves the problem of per-eye pixel shimmer in VR by ensuring both eyes march identical rays, rendering the model as a single static image that appears identical from both eyes. Unlike Image-Space Sheet-Buffered Splatting Pipeline, which uses complex sheet buffers, this method uses a single fragment pass with a chunky virtual-pixel grid and outline detection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Model bounding box (boxcenter, boxsize), sigma, quadsize, raydirlocal, spriteuplocal, lightdir, voxel texture sampler, getmaterialcolor, marchbox. Output: Fragment color (ALBEDO) with palette color, per-face lighting, and a one-pixel black outline on misses. Data Structures: Bounding Box: Defined by boxcenter (vec3) and boxsize (vec3) in voxel units. Virtual Pixel Grid: Defined by sigma (pixels per voxel). Coordinate Space: Godot Y-up voxel space (one unit per voxel), matching the local space of the VoxelOrthoSprite node and the DDA in voxelstorage.gdshaderinc. Parameters: sigma: Virtual pixels per voxel. Default: 4.0. Higher values produce finer resolution; a value of 1 makes every voxel one chunky pixel. quadsize: Size of the proxy quad in voxel units. The quad is centred on the model's bounding box centre. Default: vec2(1.0). lightdir: Unit vector from the model towards the light, in voxel space. Default: vec3(0.57735). Steps: 1. Quad Rasterization: Rasterize a camera-facing QuadMesh sized to the model's orthographic footprint plus a margin for the outline. Each fragment knows its position on the quad (quaduv), which represents the position on the unit quad (-0.5..0.5 on each axis), interpolated perspective-correctly. 2. Coordinate Conversion and Snapping: Convert fragment position to voxel units. Calculate deltapx as 1.0 / sigma, representing the width of one virtual pixel in voxel units. Snap the quaduv offset to the nearest virtual pixel centre: offset = \text{round}\left(\frac{quad\uv \times quad\size}{delta\px}\right) \times delta\px. 3. Ray Marching: Start a ray with the shared direction raydirlocal at the snapped position and march through the voxels using marchbox. Calculate spriteright as cross(raydirlocal, spriteuplocal). Calculate boxmin as boxcenter - boxsize 0.5 and boxmax as boxcenter + boxsize 0.5. Calculate maxdim as max(max(boxsize.x, boxsize.y), boxsize.z). Calculate origin as boxcenter + offset.x spriteright + offset.y spriteuplocal - 2.0 maxdim raydirlocal. Call marchbox(origin, raydirlocal, boxmin, boxmax, normal, hitpos). 4. Lighting and Color: If material > 0u, calculate lighting as max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) 0.7 + 0.3. Set ALBEDO to getmaterialcolor(material) lighting. 5. Outline Detection: If the march results in a miss, test the four cardinal neighbour pixels. Trace rays at offset - vec2(deltapx, 0.0), offset + vec2(deltapx, 0.0), offset + vec2(0.0, deltapx), and offset - vec2(0.0, deltapx). If any hit (material > 0u), set ALBEDO to vec3(0.0). Otherwise, discard the fragment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderorthographicvoxelsprite(quaduv, quadsize, sigma, boxcenter, boxsize, raydirlocal, spriteuplocal, lightdir, getmaterialcolor, marchbox): # 1. Calculate virtual pixel parameters deltapx = 1.0 / sigma # 2. Snap quaduv to virtual pixel grid # quaduv is in range [-0.5, 0.5] offset = round((quaduv quadsize) / deltapx) deltapx # 3. Calculate ray origin and boundaries spriteright = cross(raydirlocal, spriteuplocal) boxmin = boxcenter - boxsize 0.5 boxmax = boxcenter + boxsize 0.5 maxdim = max(max(boxsize.x, boxsize.y), boxsize.z) origin = boxcenter + offset.x spriteright + offset.y spriteuplocal - 2.0 maxdim raydirlocal # marchbox and getmaterialcolor are provided by the voxel storage system normal, hitpos, material = marchbox(origin, raydirlocal, boxmin, boxmax) # 4. Handle hit if material > 0: lighting = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) 0.7 + 0.3 albedo = getmaterialcolor(material) lighting return albedo # 5. Handle miss: Outline detection neighbors = [ offset - vec2(deltapx, 0.0), offset + vec2(deltapx, 0.0), offset + vec2(0.0, deltapx), offset - vec2(0.0, deltapx) ] for neighboroffset in neighbors: neighbororigin = boxcenter + neighboroffset.x spriteright + neighboroffset.y spriteuplocal - 2.0 maxdim raydirlocal,, neighbormaterial = marchbox(neighbororigin, raydirlocal, boxmin, boxmax) if neighbormaterial > 0: return vec3(0.0) # Black outline return None # Discard fragment Edge cases and pitfalls: Using screen position for the grid causes per-eye pixel shimmer in VR because each eye sees the same card from a slightly different place. The ray direction and quad orientation come from the HEAD position (midpoint between eyes), not the per-eye position, so both eyes march identical rays, ensuring the sprite reads as a flat billboard. Square-based voxel rendering is a technique for small voxel sets that maps 3D voxels to 2D squares (tiles) on the screen to achieve real-time performance with visual compromises, avoiding the GPU load of dense polygon sets while maintaining voxel destructibility. It differs from its parent, Orthographic Voxel Sprite Rendering, by projecting the voxel as a flat 2D square rather than a full 3D sprite billboard, sacrificing volumetric depth cues for rendering speed and simplicity. Performance: Single fragment pass makes it efficient for preview purposes. Scaling: Performance scales with sigma (higher values produce finer resolution) and voxel density. Limitations: Outline detection adds up to 4 additional ray marches per miss. When to use: VR previews, low-poly voxel art, performance-critical applications where visual fidelity is secondary to consistency. When not to use: High-resolution rendering, perspective-correct detailed views, scenes with complex lighting requirements beyond simple diffuse. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Origin: Developed for Godot engine-based voxel editors and viewers as the VoxelOrthoSprite node, utilizing voxelstorage.gdshaderinc for DDA raymarching. name: Square-based voxel rendering
head: 2D square mapping, Simplified voxel rendering
body: Square-based voxel rendering is a technique for small voxel sets that maps 3D voxels to 2D squares (tiles) on the screen to achieve real-time performance with visual compromises, avoiding the GPU load of dense polygon sets while maintaining voxel destructibility. It differs from its parent, Orthographic Voxel Sprite Rendering, by projecting the voxel as a flat 2D square rather than a full 3D sprite billboard, sacrificing volumetric depth cues for rendering speed and simplicity. Inputs and outputs: Input: A list of voxels, each defined by spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and a color value. Input: Screen dimensions (framebufferwidth, framebufferheight) and center offsets (halfscreenwidth, halfscreenheight). Input: An empirical parameter SIZEFACTOR (square size). Input: A depth buffer (zBuffer) initialized to maximum depth or infinity. Output: A 2D framebuffer (frameBuffer) containing the final pixel colors. Data structures: voxel: A struct or object with fields x, y, z (floats), and color (e.g., RGBA or integer). frameBuffer: A 1D array of size framebufferwidth framebufferheight. zBuffer: A 1D array of size framebufferwidth framebufferheight, storing depth values. Parameters: SIZEFACTOR: An empirical constant controlling the mapped square size. It is usually constant per frame. If the model is far, use a smaller number to prevent overlap; if close, use a larger number to prevent gaps. Steps: 1. For each voxel in the input set: a. Calculate the inverse depth: per\z = 1.0 / voxel.z. b. Determine the 2D screen coordinates of the square's corners using the projection formulas: xs1 = ((voxel.y - SIZE\FACTOR) \times per\z) + half\screen\width ys1 = -((voxel.x - SIZE\FACTOR) \times per\z) + half\screen\height xs2 = ((voxel.y + SIZE\FACTOR) \times per\z) + half\screen\width ys2 = -((voxel.x + SIZE\FACTOR) \times per\z) + half\screen\height Where xs1, ys1 is the top-left corner and xs2, ys2 is the bottom-right corner. c. Rasterize the square defined by [xs1, xs2] and [ys1, ys2]: i. Iterate i from \lfloor xs1 \rfloor to \lceil xs2 \rceil. ii. Iterate j from \lfloor ys1 \rfloor to \lceil ys2 \rceil. iii. Calculate the framebuffer index: index = i \times frame\buffer\width + j. iv. Skip the pixel if it is out of bounds: if j > frame\buffer\width or i > frame\buffer\height or j < 0 or i < 0, continue to the next iteration. v. Perform depth testing: if voxel.z < zBuffer[index], update the buffers: zBuffer[index] = voxel.z frameBuffer[index] = voxel.color Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersquarebasedvoxels(voxels, framebufferwidth, framebufferheight, halfscreenwidth, halfscreenheight, sizefactor): # Initialize buffers zbuffer = [float('inf')] (framebufferwidth framebufferheight) framebuffer = [None] (framebufferwidth framebufferheight) for voxel in voxels: # Guard against division by zero if voxel.z == 0: continue # 1. Calculate inverse depth perz = 1.0 / voxel.z # 2. Calculate square corners xs1 = ((voxel.y - sizefactor) perz) + halfscreenwidth ys1 = -((voxel.x - sizefactor) perz) + halfscreenheight xs2 = ((voxel.y + sizefactor) perz) + halfscreenwidth ys2 = -((voxel.x + sizefactor) perz) + halfscreenheight # 3. Rasterize the square xstart = int(xs1) xend = int(xs2) + 1 ystart = int(ys1) yend = int(ys2) + 1 for i in range(xstart, xend): for j in range(ystart, yend): # Boundary check if j < 0 or i < 0 or j >= framebufferwidth or i >= framebufferheight: continue index = i framebufferwidth + j # Depth test and update if voxel.z < zbuffer[index]: zbuffer[index] = voxel.z framebuffer[index] = voxel.color return framebuffer Edge cases and pitfalls: Gaps and Overlap: If the model is close to the view plane and SIZEFACTOR is too small, gaps appear between mapped voxels. If the model is far and SIZEFACTOR is too large, squares overlap excessively. Back-to-Front Rendering: If voxels are rendered back-to-front, the z-buffer cannot reject non-visible pixels, causing significant overdraw and performance drops. Division by Zero: If a voxel has z=0, the calculation of per\z results in infinity. The source does not specify a guard for this, but it is a necessary implementation detail. Time Complexity: The double iteration loop makes the method computationally intensive. Memory Complexity: Two arrays of size framebufferwidth framebufferheight are required for the framebuffer and z-buffer. Performance: On a horse model (49,152 voxels), performance was 355 FPS. On a medkit model (1,548,288 voxels), performance dropped to 63 FPS without optimization. Strengths: Real-time performance for small voxel sets; maintains voxel destructibility; avoids GPU load of dense polygons. Limitations: Visual compromises (reduced shading/shadows); significant performance degradation with large voxel counts or back-to-front rendering order; requires careful tuning of SIZEFACTOR. When to use: 2D computer games where 3D voxel units rotate or animate, requiring a 2D characteristic on screen but stored in 3D format. Square-based voxel rendering was introduced by Péter Mileff and Judit Dudra in their paper "Simplified voxel based visualization". The method was developed to address the limitations of existing voxel rendering techniques in the context of 2D computer games that feature 3D voxel units. The authors noted that while cube-based approaches could work, very small cubes would create dense sets that were computationally expensive, and larger cubes would not fit the desired 2D aesthetic. The simplified square-based approach was proposed as a solution to efficiently render small models in real-time, particularly for interactive elements like pickable items or animated units. name: Decomposition
body: Decomposition is an image-order volume rendering technique that converts a volumetric dataset into a collection of geometric primitives, such as spheres or slices, which are placed, scaled, and colored based on a data mapping. It treats the volume as a set of distinct geometric objects suitable for further processing or manipulation. Inputs: A volumetric dataset (scalar field V) and a mapping function. Outputs: A 2D image buffer. Data Structures: The dataset is decomposed into a list of primitives \mathcal{P} = \{p1, p2, \dots, pn\}. Each primitive pi stores its geometric parameters (position \mathbf{c}i, radius ri for spheres, or dimensions for slices) and visual attributes (color \mathbf{c}i, opacity \alphai). Steps: 1. Decomposition: Iterate through the volumetric dataset to generate a corresponding geometric primitive for each voxel or region. Spheres: Each voxel or cluster of voxels becomes a sphere. The radius ri and position \mathbf{c}i are determined by the voxel location and potentially the local density or gradient. Slices: The volume is sliced along a specific axis (e.g., axial, coronal, sagittal). Each slice becomes a 2D texture or height map. 2. Mapping: Apply the transfer function to determine the visual attributes (\mathbf{c}i, \alphai) for each primitive based on its underlying scalar value si. 3. Placement: Transform the primitives from object space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix as defined in Primitive Geometry. 4. Rasterization: Render the primitives to the image buffer. Slices are rendered as pseudo-colored textures or height maps. Spheres are rasterized as circles with appropriate shading or opacity blending. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the contributions of all primitives. For transparent primitives, standard front-to-back alpha compositing is used: C{out} = C{in} + \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alphai \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) where C{in} and \alpha{in} are the accumulated color and opacity from previously processed primitives. Parameters: Primitive Type: Sphere vs. Slice. Slices are commonly used for further processing like segmentation. Mapping Function: The specific transfer function defining color/opacity vs. scalar value. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Occlusion: Overlapping primitives must be sorted or handled via depth buffering to ensure correct compositing order. Artifacting: Spherical primitives may introduce "stair-step" artifacts if the voxel-to-sphere mapping is not carefully tuned. Represents a volume as a 1D skeleton to enable interactive manipulation. Unlike direct volume deformation, it separates geometric abstraction from rendering by decomposing the volume into bounding cuboids along the skeleton, allowing independent transformation and rendering of segments. Choose it when fast, minimum-geometric-processing manipulation (bend, move, re-pose) is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Curve-Skeleton Decomposition
head: Centerline, Centerline decomposition, Curve-skeleton, Skeleton-based block decomposition
body: Curve-Skeleton Decomposition is a proxy geometry technique that represents a volumetric object as a 1D line-like structure (skeleton or centerline) to enable bend, move, re-pose, and sweep transformations. It solves the problem of interactive manipulation of volumetric data by decomposing the volume into bounding cuboids along the skeleton, allowing independent transformation and rendering of segments. Unlike direct volume deformation, this method separates the geometric abstraction from the rendering, enabling fast, minimum-geometric-processing manipulation. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V. Extracted curve-skeleton S. Joint locations on S defining bending regions. Transfer function for color/opacity mapping. Outputs: Volume-rendered image of the deformed volume. Data Structures: 1. Skeleton S: A sequence of vertices and edges capturing the object's topology. 2. Distance Field D: Computed from V, storing distances to the volume boundary, used to determine cuboid widths. 3. Bounding Cuboids: One per skeletal segment between joints, with width derived from D. 4. Sliced Polygons: Planar slices of each cuboid, texture-mapped to the original volume data. 5. Depth Index: A data structure indexing polygons by their depth coordinate for sorting. Steps: 1. Extract the skeleton from the volumetric object. 2. Choose joints on the skeleton to define areas where bending can occur. 3. Define bounding cuboids for each skeletal segment between joints, determining the width from the distance field computed on the volume. 4. For interactive manipulation, transform cuboids about the joint. 5. Slice each cuboid along the viewport. 6. Map the slices back to the original texture to determine the appropriate color value. 7. Interpolate between the two end planes of adjoining bounding boxes to cover the joint area with a stretched volume. 8. Sort the sliced polygons along the view direction from back to front using a two-pass rendering algorithm and a data structure that indexes polygons with respect to their depth coordinate. 9. Composite the texture-mapped polygons back-to-front to volume render the deformed volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def curveskeletondecomposition(volume, skeleton, joints, transferfunction, viewmatrix): # Source does not specify distance field computation distancefield = computedistancefield(volume) cuboids = [] for i in range(len(joints) - 1): segpoints = skeleton[joints[i]:joints[i+1]+1] # Determine width from distance field widths = [distancefield[pointtogridindex(p)] for p in segpoints] avgwidth = sum(widths) / len(widths) # Create bounding cuboid around segment minpt = [min(p[d] for p in segpoints) for d in range(3)] maxpt = [max(p[d] for p in segpoints) for d in range(3)] cuboids.append({'min': minpt, 'max': maxpt, 'width': avgwidth}) transformedcuboids = [] for i, cuboid in enumerate(cuboids): jointpos = skeleton[joints[i]] # Source does not specify transformation application transformedcuboid = applytransformation(cuboid, jointpos, viewmatrix) transformedcuboids.append(transformedcuboid) slicedpolygons = [] for cuboid in transformedcuboids: # Source does not specify view plane intersection vertices = intersectcuboidviewplane(cuboid, viewmatrix) # Source does not specify texture mapping colors = [samplevolumetexture(v, volume, transferfunction) for v in vertices] slicedpolygons.append({'vertices': vertices, 'colors': colors, 'depth': meanz(vertices)}) # Source does not specify joint interpolation jointpolygons = interpolatejointregions(transformedcuboids, transferfunction) slicedpolygons.extend(jointpolygons) # Source does not specify depth indexing/sorting sortedpolygons = sorted(slicedpolygons, key=lambda p: p['depth'], reverse=True) # Source does not specify compositing image = alphablendbacktofront(sortedpolygons) return image def computedistancefield(vol): pass def applytransformation(cuboid, jointpos, viewmatrix): pass def intersectcuboidviewplane(cuboid, viewmatrix): pass def samplevolumetexture(v, volume, tf): pass def interpolatejointregions(cuboids, tf): pass def alphablendbacktofront(polygons): pass def pointtogridindex(p): pass def meanz(vertices): pass Parameters: Joint Density: Determines granularity of bending. Not given in the sources. Cuboid Width: Derived from the distance field. Not given in the sources. Slice Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the volume is rotated, the underlying geometry must be re-sliced and composited. Precision issues may arise in joint interpolation if the distance field is noisy. Degenerate skeletons (e.g., single point) require special handling. Derives the 1D curve-skeleton from the volume. Sets apart by preserving the object's essential topology. Choose when topological accuracy is critical. Link Identifies locations on the skeleton to define bending regions. Sets apart by enabling localized deformation of specific segments. Choose when specific parts need independent manipulation. Link Creates bounding volumes around skeletal segments. Sets apart by using a distance field to determine accurate width. Choose when accurate volume representation is needed. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Requires minimum geometric processing and is therefore very fast. Scaling: Scales with the complexity of the skeleton and the number of joints. Strengths: Fast, supports interactive manipulation, enables selective rendering and sweeps. Limitations: Requires re-slicing on rotation, may lose fine details if cuboids are too large. When to Use: Virtual colonoscopy, navigation along paths, selective rendering. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity detail is required without decomposition. Curve-Skeleton Decomposition was introduced in the context of illustrative focus+context approaches in interactive volume visualization. It builds on the traditional use of skeletons for specifying motion in computer graphics, extending motion capture techniques to volumetric data. The method is commonly used in medical illustration and virtual colonoscopy. name: Triangle Mesh Splatting
head: Laur and Hanrahan splatting
body: Triangle Mesh Splatting is an object-order rendering technique that approximates volumetric splats with triangle meshes to leverage graphics hardware for rapid scan conversion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of splats, each defined by a center position, orientation, shape parameters (e.g., covariance matrix), color, and opacity. Output: A 2D image buffer with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Splat Representation: Center position \mathbf{p}, orientation, covariance matrix \Sigma, color C, opacity \alpha. Triangle Mesh: List of vertices and indices defining triangles that approximate the splat's screen-space footprint. Steps: 1. Transformation: Transform the splat center from object space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. 2. Footprint Approximation: Approximate the splat's footprint (e.g., an ellipse) with a triangle mesh. 3. Rasterization: Rasterize the triangle mesh to determine covered pixels (fragments). 4. Fragment Processing: Evaluate the splat kernel function at each fragment's screen-space coordinates to compute weight. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the fragment's color and opacity into the image buffer using alpha compositing, ordered by depth. Formulas: Screen-space position: \mathbf{p}{screen} = P \cdot V \cdot M \cdot \mathbf{p}{object} Splat kernel value: K(\mathbf{u}) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{u}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{u}), where \mathbf{u} is the vector from the splat center to the fragment, and \Sigma is the covariance matrix Color contribution: C{frag} = C{splat} \cdot K(\mathbf{u}) \cdot \alpha{splat} Parameters: Triangle mesh resolution: The number of triangles used to approximate the footprint. Splat kernel width: Controls the spread of the splat. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when transforming coordinates, especially for large scenes. Boundaries: Ensure that the triangle mesh fully covers the splat's footprint to avoid artifacts. Degenerate Input: Handle splats with zero size or invalid orientations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trianglemeshsplatting(splats, imagewidth, imageheight, mvpmatrix): image = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] alphabuffer = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] def computeboundingbox(tri, w, h): xs = [max(0, min(w - 1, int(v[0]))) for v in tri] ys = [max(0, min(h - 1, int(v[1]))) for v in tri] return min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys) def pointintriangle(px, py, tri): x1, y1 = tri[0] x2, y2 = tri[1] x3, y3 = tri[2] denom = (y2 - y3) (x1 - x3) + (x3 - x2) (y1 - y3) if denom == 0: return False u = ((y2 - y3) (px - x3) + (x3 - x2) (py - y3)) / denom v = ((y3 - y1) (px - x3) + (x1 - x3) (py - y3)) / denom return 0 <= u <= 1 and 0 <= v <= 1 and u + v <= 1 for splat in splats: pobj = [splat.center[0], splat.center[1], splat.center[2], 1.0] pscreen = matmul(mvpmatrix, pobj) if pscreen[3] <= 0: continue pscreen[0] /= pscreen[3] pscreen[1] /= pscreen[3] # Sources do not specify mesh generation; standard polygonization of the footprint is used. triangles = [] for tri in triangles: bbox = computeboundingbox(tri, imagewidth, imageheight) for y in range(bbox[1], bbox[3] + 1): for x in range(bbox[0], bbox[2] + 1): if pointintriangle(x, y, tri): u = [x - pscreen[0], y - pscreen[1]] covinv = inverse(splat.covariance) k = exp(-0.5 dot(u, matmul(covinv, u))) if k > 0.01: cfrag = [c k for c in splat.color] afrag = splat.opacity k oldalpha = alphabuffer[y][x] newalpha = afrag (1.0 - oldalpha) alphabuffer[y][x] = oldalpha + newalpha for i in range(3): image[y][x][i] = image[y][x][i] oldalpha + cfrag[i] newalpha Differentiable Triangle Splatting is a real-time differentiable renderer that represents a scene as a soup of unstructured, disconnected 3D triangles and optimizes them via end-to-end gradients by rendering each triangle as a differentiable splat in screen space. It merges the adaptability of Gaussian splatting with the efficiency of triangle primitives, surpassing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), and 3D Convex Splatting (3DCS) in visual fidelity, training speed, and rendering throughput. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of splats and the resolution of the triangle mesh approximation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of splats and the size of the triangle meshes. Performance: Fast rendering due to hardware acceleration. Performance scales well with the number of splats. Strengths: Efficient use of graphics hardware, flexible footprint shapes. Limitations: Approximation errors from triangle mesh representation, potential artifacts at low mesh resolutions. When to Use: When real-time rendering of complex splat shapes is required and hardware acceleration is available. When Not to Use: When high precision is required and approximation errors are unacceptable. Triangle Mesh Splatting was introduced by Laur and Hanrahan as a method to improve rendering speed by approximating splats with triangle meshes and using graphics hardware for scan conversion. name: Differentiable Triangle Splatting
head: Triangle Splatting
body: Differentiable Triangle Splatting is a real-time differentiable renderer that represents a scene as a soup of unstructured, disconnected 3D triangles and optimizes them via end-to-end gradients by rendering each triangle as a differentiable splat in screen space. It merges the adaptability of Gaussian splatting with the efficiency of triangle primitives, surpassing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), and 3D Convex Splatting (3DCS) in visual fidelity, training speed, and rendering throughput. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D triangles T{3D}, each defined by three vertices vi \in \mathbb{R}^3, a color c, a smoothness parameter \sigma, and an opacity o. Camera parameters: intrinsic matrix K, rotation R, and translation t. Output: A rendered image and gradients for optimizing triangle vertices, colors, \sigma, and o. Data Structures: Each triangle primitive stores: vertices: Array of 3 vectors, each size 3 (float32). color: Vector of size 3 (float32). sigma: Scalar (float32). opacity: Scalar (float32). Steps: 1. Projection: Project each 3D vertex vi to the 2D image plane using the pinhole camera model: qi = K(R vi + t) where qi \in \mathbb{R}^2 forms the projected 2D triangle T{2D}. 2. Signed Distance Field (SDF) Computation: For each pixel p within the bounding box of T{2D}, compute the SDF \phi(p): \phi(\mathbf{p}) = \max{i \in \{1,2,3\}} Li(\mathbf{p}) where Li(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{p} + di. The \mathbf{n}i are unit normals of the triangle edges pointing outward, and di are offsets defining the zero-level set. \phi(\mathbf{p}) is positive outside the triangle, negative inside, and zero on the boundary. 3. Incenter Calculation: Find the incenter \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^2 of T{2D}, defined as the point within the triangle where \phi(\mathbf{p}) is minimum. 4. Window Function Evaluation: Compute the window function I(\mathbf{p}) for pixel p: I(\mathbf{p}) = \text{ReLU}\left(\frac{\phi(\mathbf{p})}{\phi(\mathbf{s})}\right)^\sigma At the incenter \mathbf{s}, I(\mathbf{s})=1; at the boundary where \phi(\mathbf{p})=0, I(\mathbf{p})=0; outside the triangle where \phi(\mathbf{p})>0, I(\mathbf{p})=0. 5. Accumulation: Accumulate the color of each image pixel p by summing contributions from all overlapping triangles in depth order, using I(\mathbf{p}) as the opacity weight for each triangle's color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computewindowfunction(p, trianglevertices, sigma): """Computes I(p) for pixel p relative to a projected triangle.""" # Step 2: Compute SDF components edges = [] for i in range(3): v1 = trianglevertices[i] v2 = trianglevertices[(i + 1) % 3] ex = v2[0] - v1[0] ey = v2[1] - v1[1] # Candidate outward normals (rotate edge 90 degrees) nx1, ny1 = ey, -ex nx2, ny2 = -ey, ex # Centroid to determine inside direction cx = sum(v[0] for v in trianglevertices) / 3.0 cy = sum(v[1] for v in trianglevertices) / 3.0 mx, my = (v1[0] + v2[0]) / 2.0, (v1[1] + v2[1]) / 2.0 dxc, dyc = cx - mx, cy - my # Select normal pointing away from centroid if nx1 dxc + ny1 dyc > 0: nx, ny = nx2, ny2 else: nx, ny = nx1, ny1 # Normalize length = math.sqrt(nxnx + nyny) if length == 0: return 0.0 nx /= length ny /= length # Offset d for line equation n. p + d = 0 d = -(nx v1[0] + ny v1[1]) edges.append((nx, ny, d)) # Compute Li(p) for each edge livalues = [nx p[0] + ny p[1] + d for nx, ny, d in edges] phip = max(livalues) # Step 3: Find incenter s (minimum phi inside triangle) a = math.hypot(trianglevertices[1][0]-trianglevertices[2][0], trianglevertices[1][1]-trianglevertices[2][1]) b = math.hypot(trianglevertices[0][0]-trianglevertices[2][0], trianglevertices[0][1]-trianglevertices[2][1]) c = math.hypot(trianglevertices[0][0]-trianglevertices[1][0], trianglevertices[0][1]-trianglevertices[1][1]) sx = (a trianglevertices[0][0] + b trianglevertices[1][0] + c trianglevertices[2][0]) / (a + b + c) sy = (a trianglevertices[0][1] + b trianglevertices[1][1] + c trianglevertices[2][1]) / (a + b + c) s = (sx, sy) # Compute phi(s) livaluess = [nx s[0] + ny s[1] + d for nx, ny, d in edges] phis = max(livaluess) # Step 4: Window function if phis == 0: return 0.0 ratio = phip / phis return max(0.0, ratio) sigma def rendertrianglesoup(triangles, cameraK, cameraR, camerat, imagewidth, imageheight): """Renders a soup of triangles using differentiable splatting.""" image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] projectedtriangles = [] for tri in triangles: verts3d = tri['vertices'] verts2d = [] avgz = 0.0 for v in verts3d: # Apply rotation and translation rx = cameraR[0][0]v[0] + cameraR[0][1]v[1] + cameraR[0][2]v[2] + camerat[0] ry = cameraR[1][0]v[0] + cameraR[1][1]v[1] + cameraR[1][2]v[2] + camerat[1] rz = cameraR[2][0]v[0] + cameraR[2][1]v[1] + cameraR[2][2]v[2] + camerat[2] if rz <= 0: continue # Apply intrinsic matrix K qx = cameraK[0][0] (rx / rz) + cameraK[0][2] qy = cameraK[1][1] (ry / rz) + cameraK[1][2] verts2d.append((qx, qy)) avgz += rz avgz /= 3.0 if len(verts2d) == 3: projectedtriangles.append({ 'verts': verts2d, 'color': tri['color'], 'sigma': tri['sigma'], 'opacity': tri['opacity'], 'depth': avgz }) # Sort by depth (near to far for standard alpha blending) projectedtriangles.sort(key=lambda t: t['depth']) for tri in projectedtriangles: verts = tri['verts'] sigma = tri['sigma'] color = tri['color'] opacity = tri['opacity'] minx = max(0, int(min(v[0] for v in verts))) maxx = min(imagewidth, int(max(v[0] for v in verts)) + 1) miny = max(0, int(min(v[1] for v in verts))) maxy = min(imageheight, int(max(v[1] for v in verts)) + 1) for y in range(miny, maxy): for x in range(minx, maxx): w = computewindowfunction((x, y), verts, sigma) if w < 1e-6: continue alphablend = w opacity curr = image[y][x] image[y][x] = ( curr[0] (1 - alphablend) + color[0] alphablend, curr[1] (1 - alphablend) + color[1] alphablend, curr[2] (1 - alphablend) + color[2] alphablend) return image Parameters: \sigma (smoothness parameter): Controls the falloff of the window function. As \sigma decreases, the function approximates a hard triangle boundary; as \sigma increases, the support exceeds the triangle footprint, becoming globally supported with value 0.5 everywhere in the limit. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \sigma is too large, the window function support exceeds the triangle footprint, causing every triangle to contribute to every pixel (globally supported with value 0.5), which is unsuitable for rasterization. Precision issues may arise when computing the incenter or SDF for degenerate triangles (zero area). This property ensures that the spatial influence of a triangle splat remains consistent regardless of its depth or projected scale, allowing a single smoothness parameter \sigma to be used for all triangles in the scene. It distinguishes Triangle Splatting from methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting, which require complex depth-dependent covariance adjustments to maintain consistent visual appearance across different distances. MeshSplatting extends Triangle Splatting by optimizing fully opaque, connected triangles, jointly refining geometry and appearance through differentiable rendering to produce coherent surfaces. The method produces coherent surfaces that integrate seamlessly with real-time rendering engines, enabling applications such as augmented and virtual reality without any postprocessing. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved, with reported throughput of over 2,400 FPS at 1280×720 resolution for the optimized triangle soup. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Surpasses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), and 3D Convex Splatting (3DCS) in visual fidelity, training speed, and rendering throughput. Strengths: Direct compatibility with standard mesh-based renderers and game engines; leverages decades of GPU-accelerated triangle processing. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \sigma to avoid global support artifacts. When to use: When high visual fidelity and real-time performance are required, and integration with existing graphics pipelines is desired. When not to use: When \sigma cannot be tuned appropriately, leading to performance degradation due to global contributions. Triangle Splatting was introduced in "Triangle Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering". It represents a step toward mesh-aware neural rendering, bridging classical computer graphics with modern differentiable frameworks. MeshSplatting, an extension, is described in the thesis "Bridging neural rendering and classical computer graphics". name: Depth-dependent scaling in Triangle Splatting
head: Triangle Splatting influence function scaling invariance
body: This property ensures that the spatial influence of a triangle splat remains consistent regardless of its depth or projected scale, allowing a single smoothness parameter \sigma to be used for all triangles in the scene. It distinguishes Triangle Splatting from other splatting methods by relying on a normalized signed distance field ratio rather than depth-dependent covariance adjustments. Input: A pixel coordinate \mathbf{p} in screen space, the triangle's three vertices, and the smoothness parameter \sigma > 0. Output: The influence value I(\mathbf{p}) \in [0, 1]. The signed distance field \phi(\mathbf{p}) is computed as the maximum of the signed distances to the three edges: \phi(\mathbf{p}) = \max{i=1,2,3} di(\mathbf{p}). Here, di(\mathbf{p}) is the signed distance from \mathbf{p} to the i-th edge, defined as negative inside the triangle and positive outside. \min \phi is the minimum value of \phi(\mathbf{p}) over the triangle interior, occurring at the incenter. 1. Compute Signed Distances: For a query pixel \mathbf{p}, calculate the signed distance di(\mathbf{p}) to each of the three triangle edges. 2. Compute SDF: Calculate \phi(\mathbf{p}) = \max(d1(\mathbf{p}), d2(\mathbf{p}), d3(\mathbf{p})). 3. Determine Minimum SDF: Retrieve \min \phi, the most negative value of \phi within the triangle (at the incenter). 4. Normalize: Compute the ratio r(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{\phi(\mathbf{p})}{\min \phi}. 5. Apply ReLU and Exponent: Compute the influence: I(\mathbf{p}) = \text{ReLU}(r(\mathbf{p}))^\sigma. The influence function is defined as: I(\mathbf{p}) = \text{ReLU}\left(\frac{\phi(\mathbf{p})}{\min \phi}\right)^\sigma such that I(\mathbf{p}) = 1 at the triangle incenter, 0 at the triangle boundary, and 0 outside the triangle. Scaling Invariance Proof: If the triangle is projected and scaled by a factor a > 0, the vertex coordinates and pixel coordinates transform as \mathbf{v}i \to a\mathbf{v}i and \mathbf{p} \to a\mathbf{p}. The signed distance to each edge scales linearly: d'i(\mathbf{p}') = a di(\mathbf{p}). Consequently: \phi'(\mathbf{p}') = \maxi d'i(\mathbf{p}') = a \maxi di(\mathbf{p}) = a \phi(\mathbf{p}) \min \phi' = a \min \phi The ratio remains constant: \frac{\phi'(\mathbf{p}')}{\min \phi'} = \frac{a \phi(\mathbf{p})}{a \min \phi} = \frac{\phi(\mathbf{p})}{\min \phi} Thus, I'(\mathbf{p}') = I(\mathbf{p}). \sigma (sigma): A scalar parameter \sigma > 0 controlling the smoothness of the window function. \sigma \to 0: The function converges to the hard triangle shape. \sigma \to \infty: The function converges to a delta function at the incenter. Typical values: Not specified in the sources, but must be >0. Small Triangles: Using LogSumExp to approximate the max in the SDF definition causes poor shape for small triangles, where only one vertex influences the shape; the actual max function must be used. Boundary Precision: The function is exactly 0 at the boundary and outside; care must be taken with floating-point precision near the boundary to avoid artifacts. Incenter Calculation: \min \phi is the value at the incenter; for implementation, this can be precomputed per triangle or approximated via the inradius. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetriangleinfluence(p, vertices, sigma): """ Computes the influence I(p) for a pixel p given a triangle. Args: p: (x, y) pixel coordinate. vertices: List of 3 (x, y) tuples representing triangle vertices (CCW winding). sigma: Smoothness parameter > 0. Returns: Influence value in [0, 1]. """ # Step 1: Compute signed distances to edges (negative inside, positive outside) distances = [] for i in range(3): v1 = vertices[i] v2 = vertices[(i + 1) % 3] # Edge vector ex, ey = v2[0] - v1[0], v2[1] - v1[1] # Vector from v1 to p px, py = p[0] - v1[0], p[1] - v1[1] # Length of edge length = math.hypot(ex, ey) if length == 0: distances.append(0.0) continue # Signed distance: negative inside for CCW winding dist = (ey px - ex py) / length distances.append(dist) # Step 2: Compute SDF phi(p) = max(di) phip = max(distances) # Step 3: Determine minphi (at incenter) # Compute inradius r = Area / s, where s is semi-perimeter x1, y1 = vertices[0] x2, y2 = vertices[1] x3, y3 = vertices[2] area = 0.5 abs(x1(y2-y3) + x2(y3-y1) + x3(y1-y2)) a = math.hypot(x2-x1, y2-y1) b = math.hypot(x3-x2, y3-y2) c = math.hypot(x1-x3, y1-y2) s = (a + b + c) / 2.0 inradius = area / s if s > 0 else 0.0 minphi = -inradius # Step 4: Normalize if minphi == 0: return 0.0 ratio = phip / minphi # Step 5: Apply ReLU and Exponent if ratio <= 0: return 0.0 return ratio sigma The Triangle Window Function is the specific implementation of the influence function I(\mathbf{p}) described above. It ensures maximum value (1) at the incenter, zero at the boundary, and zero outside. It solves the problem of defining a smooth, compact support for triangle splatting that converges to the triangle shape (\sigma \to 0) or a delta function (\sigma \to \infty) based on the parameter \sigma. Unlike sigmoid-based window functions (I = \text{sigmoid}(-\sigma^{-1} \phi(\mathbf{p}))) which fail to have max=1 and have support larger than the triangle, this formulation ensures tight support and correct maximum. Time Complexity: Computing the influence for a pixel involves constant-time operations (3 edge distance calculations, max, division, power). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the triangle vertices and precomputed \min \phi (inradius) per triangle. Strengths: Depth-independent scaling allows a single \sigma parameter for all triangles, simplifying optimization and rendering. Tight support reduces unnecessary computation outside the triangle. Limitations: The actual max function for SDF is not smooth everywhere, which may affect gradient-based optimization in some contexts, though it is preferred for shape accuracy. When to use: When rendering triangle-based representations where consistent appearance across depths is required without per-triangle depth scaling parameters. This property is a key component of Triangle Splatting, a method for real-time radiance field rendering. It addresses the limitations of other splatting methods by providing a depth-consistent influence function through normalization. The scaling invariance allows for simpler parameterization and efficient rendering.
