name: Resonant Brane Splatting
head: Brane, Brane Primitive, Brane Splatting, Resonant Brane
body: Resonant Brane Splatting (RBS) is a feedforward Arbitrary-Scale Super-Resolution (ASR) framework that replaces flat, single-color 2D Gaussians with 'Branes'. Branes are expressive primitives that emit spatially varying colors by augmenting a Gaussian envelope with internal Gaussian-Hermite modes, allowing a single primitive to model local contrast, sharp edges, and complex textures without requiring dense overlapping splats. Unlike 2DGH, which uses Hermite functions to modulate spatial opacity while keeping color constant, RBS assigns an RGB-valued coefficient to each Hermite mode, making the emitted color vary spatially within the primitive footprint. Inputs: Low-resolution input image I{LR} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, target scale factor s \in \mathbb{R}^+, and neural backbone parameters. Outputs: Super-resolved image I{SR} \in \mathbb{R}^{H{SR} \times W{SR} \times 3}, where H{SR} = \lfloor Hs \rfloor and W{SR} = \lfloor Ws \rfloor. Data Structures: Each Brane primitive k is defined by a state vector \Phik predicted from a feature vector fk. The layout is: \Phik = [\Delta xk, \Delta yk, \sigma{x,k}, \sigma{y,k}, \rhok, \alphak, \mathbf{C}{0,0,k}, \dots, \mathbf{C}{N,M,k}] Fields: \Delta xk, \Delta yk: Anchoring offsets (normalized). \sigma{x,k}, \sigma{y,k}: Anisotropic scale factors. \rhok: Rotation angle. \alphak: Opacity. \mathbf{C}{n,m,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color coefficients for each mode (n,m). Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction and Upsampling: A neural backbone extracts a dense feature map \hat{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{\hat{H} \times \hat{W} \times C} from I{LR}. This map is optionally upsampled by factor u to F \in \mathbb{R}^{H' \times W' \times C}, where H' = u\hat{H} and W' = u\hat{W}. The number of primitives is K = H'W'. 2. Prediction of Brane State: For each feature vector fk in F, an MLP head predicts the full Brane state \Phik. Anchoring: The k-th Brane is initially anchored at the center of its feature grid cell (xk^{\text{ref}}, yk^{\text{ref}}) = (\frac{j + 0.5}{W'}, \frac{i + 0.5}{H'}). An MLP head predicts continuous offsets \Delta xk, \Delta yk for sub-pixel adaptation. The final center is computed as xk = xk^{\text{ref}} + \frac{\Delta xk}{W'}, \quad yk = yk^{\text{ref}} + \frac{\Delta yk}{H'}. Footprint and Opacity: Additional heads predict anisotropic scales, rotation, and opacity: (\sigma{x,k}, \sigma{y,k}) = \text{sigmoid}(\text{MLP}{\theta3}(fk)), \rhok = \pi \tanh(\text{MLP}{\theta4}(fk)), \alphak = \text{sigmoid}(\text{MLP}{\theta5}(fk)). Mode Colors: Given maximum degrees N and M, each Brane has L = (N + 1)(M + 1) modes. A dedicated head predicts raw mode colors \tilde{\mathbf{C}}k = \text{MLP}{\theta2}(fk) \in \mathbb{R}^{3L}. Reshape into L coefficients \tilde{\mathbf{c}}k^{n,m} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Constrain base color to positive range and residuals to signed values: \mathbf{c}k^{n,m} = \text{sigmoid}(\tilde{\mathbf{c}}k^{n,m}) if n=0, m=0; else \tanh(\tilde{\mathbf{c}}k^{n,m}). 3. Rasterization: For each target pixel (u, v) in I{SR}: Project to normalized coordinates: (u{\text{norm}}, v{\text{norm}}) = (\frac{u + 0.5}{W{SR}}, \frac{v + 0.5}{H{SR}}). Compute displacement from Brane center: (\delta xk, \delta yk) = (u{\text{norm}} - xk, v{\text{norm}} - yk). Map to local canonical coordinates via inverse rotation and scaling: \begin{pmatrix} x'k \\ y'k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sigma{x,k}} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma{y,k} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \cos \rhok & \sin \rhok \\ -\sin \rhok & \cos \rhok \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \delta xk \\ \delta yk \end{pmatrix}. Evaluate Brane emission function \mathcal{B}k(x'k, y'k): \mathcal{B}k(x'k, y'k) = \alphak E(x'k, y'k) \sum{n=0}^N \sum{m=0}^M \mathbf{c}{n,m,k} \bar{H}n(x'k) \bar{H}m(y'k). Accumulate color: \mathbf{C}(u, v) = \sum{k=1}^K \mathcal{B}k(x'k, y'k). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrbs(branes, HSR, WSR, dmax, nmax, N, M): R2max = 2 nmax + 1 image = zeros(HSR, WSR, 3) for k in range(len(branes)): phi = branes[k] dx, dy = phi.anchoringoffsets sx, sy = phi.scales rho = phi.rotation alpha = phi.opacity cnm = phi.modecolors # shape (N+1, M+1, 3) # Compute center from reference grid and offsets xref = (j + 0.5) / Wprime yref = (i + 0.5) / Hprime xk = xref + dx / Wprime yk = yref + dy / Hprime for u in range(WSR): for v in range(HSR): unorm = (u + 0.5) / WSR vnorm = (v + 0.5) / HSR deltax = unorm - xk deltay = vnorm - yk if abs(deltax) < dmax and abs(deltay) < dmax: cosr, sinr = cos(rho), sin(rho) xprime = (1/sx) (cosr deltax + sinr deltay) yprime = sy (-sinr deltax + cosr deltay) if xprime2 + yprime2 <= R2max: contribution = zeros(3) for n in range(N + 1): for m in range(M + 1): if abs(cnm[n, m]).max() < 1e-4: continue Hn = normalizedhermite(n, xprime) Hm = normalizedhermite(m, yprime) contribution += cnm[n, m] Hn Hm gaussianenv = exp(-(xprime2 + yprime2) / 2) image[v, u] += alpha gaussianenv contribution return image Formulas: Normalized Hermite Polynomial: \bar{H}n(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n n!}} Hn(z). Physicist's Hermite Polynomial (Recursive): H0(z) = 1, H1(z) = 2z, Hn(z) = 2z H{n-1}(z) - 2(n-1) H{n-2}(z) for n > 1. 2D Mode: \Psi{n,m}(x,y) = \bar{H}n(x)\bar{H}m(y). Parameters: N, M: Maximum degrees of Gaussian-Hermite modes in x and y directions. Typical value: N = M = 3. u: Upsampling factor. Tested values: \{1, 2, 4\}. d{max}: Bounding box fraction in normalized space for culling candidate Branes. R{max}: Canonical space boundary radius for culling, R{max} = \sqrt{2n{max} + 1} where n{max} = \max(N, M). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Higher-order Hermite polynomials Hn(z) grow rapidly. Using normalized Hermite polynomials \bar{H}n(z) removes dominant degree-dependent growth. Aliasing: Training strictly on scales s \in U(1, 4) fails to suppress oscillations in smooth regions at higher scales, causing aliasing artifacts. Culling: Branes with x'k^2 + y'k^2 > R{max}^2 are discarded as their visual impact is negligible. A rasterization optimization that skips the evaluation of Hermite basis functions and color accumulation for Branes whose high-order mode coefficients are negligible, reducing computational load without affecting visual quality. For each Brane, iterate through predicted Hermite coefficients \mathbf{c}{n,m,k}. If the magnitude of an RGB coefficient for mode (n, m) is less than 10^{-4}, skip the Hermite polynomial evaluation and color accumulation for that mode. This exploits sparsity induced by fine-tuning or sparsity loss, where unneeded coefficients are driven to zero. An explicit regularization term added to the training objective to enforce sparsity in the Hermite mode coefficients, preventing excessive vibration (aliasing) in smooth regions. During training, compute the L1 norm of all Hermite coefficients where n+m > 0. Multiply the sum by sparsity weight \lambda{sparse} and 1/K (where K is number of channels, RGB): L{sparse} = \lambda{sparse} \cdot \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \sum{n+m>0} \|\mathbf{c}{n,m,k}\|1 A tuned value of \lambda{sparse} = 0.0005 yields results virtually identical to fine-tuning; an aggressive value of 0.1 stifles details. A training strategy to mitigate aliasing artifacts in smooth regions at large scales by fine-tuning the model on a wider range of scales, allowing it to naturally dampen high-order coefficients. Fine-tune the model using a scale distribution s \in U(1, 8) instead of the initial training range. The model learns to dampen coefficients \mathbf{c}{n,m} to 0 for n+m > 0 in flat/smooth areas, recovering performance. This achieves the same 'energy awareness' as explicit sparsity loss but implicitly through exposure to smoother targets. Time Complexity: Naive evaluation requires O(K H{SR} W{SR}) operations. Optimized via CUDA rasterizer with dual culling (bounding box d{max} and quantum turning point R{max}). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rmax culling accelerates rendering up to 65% without quality loss. RBS improves reconstruction quality over implicit and GS baselines, while achieving superior speed-quality trade-off than prior GS methods. Strengths: Models high frequencies internally, reducing overlap and rasterization bottlenecks. Single primitive can model local contrast, edges, and multi-colored textures. Limitations: Predicting excessive modes (e.g., N=M=7) in a single pass hampers generalization and causes smooth-region artifacts if not regularized. When to use: Arbitrary-Scale Super-Resolution where high-frequency detail reconstruction is critical and computational efficiency is desired. When not to use: When primitive sparsity is not an issue or when hardware lacks support for efficient CUDA rasterization with custom culling. Resonant Brane Splatting (RBS) is a feedforward ASR framework. It builds on the expressive Gaussian-Hermite primitive but differs in appearance representation from 2DGH by assigning RGB-valued coefficients to each Hermite mode. It is used in ASR benchmarks, compared against implicit (Meta-SR, LIIF) and explicit (GaussianSR, GSASR) methods. Resonant Brane Splatting for Arbitrary-Scale Super-Resolution, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.29453, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Brick Map Geometric Primitive
head: BKM geometric primitive, brickmap geometry
body: The Brick Map Geometric Primitive (BKM) is a method for rendering volumetric or surface data stored in a hierarchical brick map structure as a geometric primitive, treating each voxel as a splatted disk. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large-scale point clouds, surfaces, and volumes by leveraging on-demand loading and level-of-detail (LOD) selection based on screen coverage. It differs from standard voxel splatting by integrating directly into the Reyes rendering architecture as a first-class geometric primitive, supporting features like motion blur, displacement, and ray tracing alongside rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A brick map file (.bkm) containing hierarchical data bricks. Data attributes may include Position (P), Normal (N), Color (Cs), and Opacity (Os). Output: A rendered image where each brick voxel contributes a disk-shaped footprint to the screen buffer. Data Structures: The brick map is a hierarchical structure of "bricks" (sub-volumes). The specific binary layout of the.bkm file is not defined in the sources. The hierarchy allows selection of the appropriate resolution level based on the primitive's screen size. Parameters: ShadingRate: Controls the granularity of rendering. Higher values reveal the disk nature of voxels; lower values provide smoother thin geometry representation at the cost of larger file sizes and more voxels. Filename: Path to the brick map file. Steps: 1. Selection: Determine the appropriate LOD level in the brick map based on the screen size of the primitive and the current shading rate. For ray tracing, select the level based on ray differential size. 2. Loading: Read the selected bricks on demand and cache them in a brick cache. 3. Voxel Processing: For each voxel in the loaded bricks: a. Geometry Definition: If P and N data are baked into the brick map, use them to define the disk's position and orientation. If P and N are absent, center the disk at the voxel's geometric center and orient it to face the camera. b. Attribute Retrieval: If Cs (color) data exists in the brick map, use it; otherwise, use the global Color attribute. If Os (opacity) data exists in the brick map, use it; otherwise, use the global Opacity attribute [G: Default opacity is 1.0 if not specified]. c. Rasterization (Surface): Render the voxel as a disk. d. Compositing (Volume): If the brick map represents volume data (sem-transparent voxels), alpha-composite the voxel's color and opacity into the buffer. 4. Ray Tracing (Alternative Path): If ray traced, march through semitransparent brick voxels along the ray, composing colors and opacities sequentially. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbrickmapgeometricprimitive(filename, shadingrate, camera): # 1. Determine LOD based on screen size and shading rate # [G: Implementation detail of LOD selection is not provided in sources] level = selectlod(filename, shadingrate, camera) # 2. Load bricks on demand bricks = loadbricks(filename, level) # 3. Process each voxel in the bricks for voxel in bricks: # Determine geometry if voxel.haspositionandnormal(): pos = voxel.position normal = voxel.normal else: pos = voxel.center normal = camera.viewdirection # Face camera # Determine attributes if voxel.hascolor(): color = voxel.color else: color = getglobalattribute("Color") if voxel.hasopacity(): opacity = voxel.opacity else: opacity = 1.0 # Default opacity # Render as disk # [G: Specific disk rasterization algorithm is not provided] renderdisk(pos, normal, color, opacity, shadingrate) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Silhouette Bloat: Without baked P and N data, silhouettes are bloated because disks are centered at voxel centers and face the camera. Thin Geometry: For long, thin geometry (e.g., cylinders), points along the length are far apart. To cover gaps, disk radii must be large, causing significant silhouette bloat. The workaround is to reduce the ShadingRate during baking and rendering to create smaller brick voxels, increasing file size. Motion Blur: Deformation motion blur is not supported in PRMan 13.0.4. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of visible bricks and the selected LOD level. On-demand loading reduces memory pressure but adds I/O overhead. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of loaded bricks in the cache. Strengths: Integrates with Reyes algorithm; supports motion blur, displacement, and ray tracing; efficient LOD management. Limitations: Silhouette quality degrades without baked normals; thin geometry requires high-resolution (small voxel) maps, increasing file size; deformation motion blur unsupported in early versions. The brick map was introduced as a 3D data structure for textures in PRMan 12.0. In PRMan 13.0, it was extended to function as a geometric primitive on equal footing with quadrics, polygon meshes, NURBS patches, and subdivision surfaces. It is rendered using the Reyes algorithm, ray traced, motion blurred, shaded, and displacement mapped. The Brick Map Geometric Primitive, https://smartcg.com/tech/cg/refs/man/RMS1.0/rman/prmantechnicalrendering/AppNotes/brickmapgprim.html, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Edge-Preserving Splatting with Compression/Stretching
head: C1 Continuous Splatting, Edge-Enhanced Splatting
body: Edge-Preserving Splatting with Compression/Stretching is a volume rendering technique that sharpens discontinuities in low-resolution or undersampled data by applying non-linear transformations to the standard splatting kernel footprint. Unlike conventional splatting which produces smooth, blurred curves, this method ensures C1 continuity (continuous first derivative) across splat boundaries while producing much sharper decreasing regions and distinct edges. It sets itself apart from siblings like EWA Splatting by explicitly modeling edge direction and strength to drive view-dependent footprint selection, rather than relying solely on spatial covariance or fixed kernel shapes. Inputs: Volume dataset V. Contour value (threshold) T used for edge detection. Viewing direction vector \mathbf{v}. Precomputed texture memory containing splat footprints for various edge positions and strengths. Outputs: Rendered image with enhanced edge sharpness. The method requires storing specific geometric attributes per voxel or splat to facilitate view-dependent processing: 1. Edge Direction: A normalized vector \mathbf{d} representing the gradient direction at the edge. 2. Edge Position/Distance: A scalar value representing the distance from the voxel center to the iso-surface contour. 3. Edge Strength: Derived from the projected edge length onto the viewing plane. 4. Splat Classification: Each splat is classified as either a Primary or Secondary kernel based on whether its data value is larger or lower than the edge threshold T. This classification determines the direction of the compression/stretching application. To enable interactive rendering, the method precomputes splat footprints for a range of edge positions and strengths. 1. Gradient Estimation: Compute gradients using central differences. 2. Edge Position Estimation: Estimate the distance to the contour using trilinear interpolation of the voxel values and the gradient. The distance d is calculated as: d = \frac{|V(x) - T|}{\|\nabla V(x)\|} where V(x) is the voxel value, T is the threshold, and \nabla V(x) is the gradient. 3. Footprint Table: Generate a table of 2D footprint functions corresponding to different combinations of edge position and strength. These footprints are loaded into texture memory. 1. Edge Detection and Attribute Extraction: For each voxel, determine if it lies near an edge (within a certain distance of the threshold T). If so, estimate the gradient using central differences and the edge position using trilinear interpolation. Store the normalized edge direction separately from the edge distance or position. 2. View-Dependent Projection: Project the 3D edge direction \mathbf{d} onto the 2D viewing plane perpendicular to the viewing direction \mathbf{v}. If \mathbf{d} is parallel to \mathbf{v}, the edge is imperceptible; treat as a standard splat. If \mathbf{d} is perpendicular to \mathbf{v}, use the standard 2D edge reconstruction logic. Otherwise, use the projected length to select the appropriate edge strength for footprint lookup. 3. Footprint Selection: Based on the projected edge position and strength, select the corresponding precomputed footprint from the texture memory. The method uses four different footprints for the four consecutive voxels involved in the reconstruction along the direction most perpendicular to the edge. 4. Kernel Application (Compression/Stretching): Apply the selected footprint to the splat. The core of the method is the mapping function map(x) which modifies the standard kernel g(x) to preserve C1 continuity. The mapping function map(x) is defined such that its first derivative is 1 at the boundaries x=0 and x=1. This ensures that the derivative of the resulting profile h(x) matches the derivative of the original kernel g(x) at the boundaries, preserving C1 continuity: hx'(rmap(x)) = gx'(rmap(x)) \cdot rmap'(x) Since rmap'(x) = 1 at x=0, 1: hx'(rmap(x)) = gx'(rmap(x)) The specific application depends on the splat classification (Primary/Secondary) and data value relative to the threshold: Primary Kernel (Data Value > Threshold): h(x, y) = \begin{cases} g(map(1+x)-1, y) & \text{if } -1 \le x \le 0 \\ g(x, y) & \text{else} \end{cases} Secondary Kernel (Data Value < Threshold): h(x, y) = \begin{cases} g(map(2+x)-2, y) & \text{if } x \le -1 \\ g(x, y) & \text{else} \end{cases} Note: The definition of "Primary" vs "Secondary" is consistent as long as it is applied uniformly based on whether the data value is larger or lower than the threshold. 5. Shading: Apply view-dependent light source shading only to voxels labeled as primary or secondary edge splats, regardless of whether an edge-enhanced footprint is used. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderedgepreserving(volume, threshold, viewdirection, precomputedfootprints): """ Renders volume with edge-preserving splatting. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values. threshold: Scalar value for edge detection. viewdirection: 3D tuple (normalized). precomputedfootprints: Dictionary mapping (edgeposition, edgestrength) to footprint functions. Returns: Image buffer (2D list of floats). """ # Standard image buffer initialization width, height = 512, 512 image = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] # Precompute gradients and edge attributes for all voxels edgeattributes = [] for x, y, z in volume.indices(): val = volume[x, y, z] # Estimate gradient using central differences grad = computecentraldifferencegradient(volume, x, y, z) gradnorm = normalize(grad) # Estimate distance to contour # d = |V - T| / ||grad|| dist = abs(val - threshold) / (norm(grad) + 1e-6) # Store attributes if near edge if dist < 1.0: # Threshold for edge proximity edgeattributes.append({ 'pos': (x, y, z), 'val': val, 'gradnorm': gradnorm, 'dist': dist, 'isedge': True }) else: edgeattributes.append({ 'pos': (x, y, z), 'val': val, 'gradnorm': None, 'dist': None, 'isedge': False }) # Render each splat for attr in edgeattributes: pos = attr['pos'] val = attr['val'] if not attr['isedge']: # Standard kernel evaluation for non-edge voxels footprint = standardkernel applysplat(image, pos, footprint, val) continue gradnorm = attr['gradnorm'] # Project edge direction onto viewing plane # If parallel to view, no special treatment if isparallel(gradnorm, viewdirection): footprint = standardkernel applysplat(image, pos, footprint, val) continue projectededge = projectvectorontoplane(gradnorm, viewdirection) edgestrength = norm(projectededge) edgeposition = attr['dist'] # Select footprint from precomputed table footprint = precomputedfootprints.lookup(edgeposition, edgestrength) # Determine classification isprimary = val > threshold # Apply shading if it's an edge splat shade = isprimary or (not isprimary) # Always true for edge splats, but logic applies to lighting applysplat(image, pos, footprint, val, shade=shade) return image def computecentraldifferencegradient(volume, x, y, z): # Standard central difference implementation dx = (volume[x+1, y, z] - volume[x-1, y, z]) / 2.0 dy = (volume[x, y+1, z] - volume[x, y-1, z]) / 2.0 dz = (volume[x, y, z+1] - volume[x, y, z-1]) / 2.0 return (dx, dy, dz) def projectvectorontoplane(vector, planenormal): # Project vector onto plane perpendicular to planenormal # proj = v - (v. n) n dotval = dotproduct(vector, planenormal) return (vector[0] - planenormal[0] dotval, vector[1] - planenormal[1] dotval, vector[2] - planenormal[2] dotval) def computeedgestrength(projectededge): # Magnitude of the projected edge vector serves as strength indicator return norm(projectededge) def standardkernel(x, y): # Standard Gaussian or box kernel for conventional splatting return max(0.0, 1.0 - (xx + yy)) def applysplat(image, pos, footprint, value, shade=False): # Standard rasterization accumulation step px, py, pz = pos for dy in range(-2, 3): for dx in range(-2, 3): fx, fy = dx, dy weight = footprint(fx, fy) if weight > 0: ix, iy = int(px + fx), int(py + fy) if 0 <= ix < len(image[0]) and 0 <= iy < len(image): image[iy][ix] += weight value (1.0 if shade else 0.5) def dotproduct(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def norm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def normalize(v): n = norm(v) return (v[0]/n, v[1]/n, v[2]/n) if n > 0 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def isparallel(v1, v2): # Check if vectors are parallel using cross product magnitude crossx = v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1] crossy = v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2] crossz = v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0] return norm((crossx, crossy, crossz)) < 1e-6 Threshold (T): The iso-contour value used for edge detection. Typical values depend on the dataset normalization (e.g., 128 for 8-bit data, 0.0017 and 0.5 for Hipip dataset). Edge Detection Accuracy: Requires fairly good accuracy. Iso-contouring produces sharp discontinuities allowing good estimates of edge direction and contour distance. Gradient Estimation: Central differences. Edge Position Estimation: Trilinear interpolation. Parallel Viewing Direction: If the viewing direction is parallel to the edge direction, the edge is imperceptible and no special treatment is needed. Undersampled Structures: Small structures protruding into cavities are often undersampled due to high-frequency components in digitized data, making edge preservation challenging. Edge Detection Accuracy: The method requires accurate edge detection. For experimental or acquired data (CT/MRI), advanced techniques like model extraction or segmentation may be indispensable. Precomputation: Requires precomputing splats for various edge positions and strengths, which adds an initial offline cost. Rendering: Interactive rendering is achieved by loading precomputed splats into texture memory and using textured polygons, allowing for efficient on-the-fly rendering. Memory: Requires additional memory to store the precomputed footprint table and edge attributes (direction, position, strength) per voxel. The method was tested on a 12x12x12 synthesized dataset and real-world datasets like the Sinus Cavity (Visible Human) and Hipip. It produces much sharper edges and better contrast in low-resolution or undersampled data compared to conventional splatting. Details on sidewalls and coarse resolution cross-sections are considerably enhanced. Strengths: Preserves sharp edges in low-resolution data; C1 continuity prevents visual artifacts at splat boundaries; view-dependent processing enhances realism. Limitations: Requires accurate edge detection; struggles with undersampled high-frequency structures; more complex than standard splatting due to the need for edge attributes and precomputed tables. Use when rendering low-resolution or undersampled volume data where edge sharpness is critical (e.g., medical imaging of small structures). Use when interactive rendering is required and precomputation is feasible. Avoid when the viewing direction is frequently parallel to edge directions, as the benefit is minimal. Avoid if the data lacks clear iso-contours or if edge detection accuracy is poor. The method was introduced in the paper "Edge Preservation in Volume Rendering Using Splatting". It builds upon the principles of Splatting and Splat Kernels and Footprints. The technique was applied to the Sinus Cavity dataset (derived from the Visible Human dataset) and the Hipip (HIgh Potential Iron Protein) dataset. It addresses the limitations of conventional splatting in preserving details in coarse resolution data. Sinus Cavity Dataset: Used for virtual navigation to enhance sidewall details and coarse resolution cross-sections. Hipip Dataset: Used to enhance details in protein structure data. Edge Preservation in Volume Rendering Using Splatting, https://web.eecs.utk.edu/~huangj/papers/edgesplat.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Polynomial and Spline Kernels
body: Polynomial and Spline Kernels replace the standard Gaussian radial basis function in splatting with piecewise polynomial or spline functions to achieve compact support, specific decay properties, or tunable shape parameters. This family solves the problem of visual artifacts (such as Mach bands or infinite support tails) and performance bottlenecks associated with Gaussian kernels by providing finite extent and analytical derivatives. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the reliance on algebraic polynomial segments (quadratic, cubic, parabolic) or special functions (Beta, Dirichlet) rather than exponential decay or geometric projection adjustments alone. The family shares the following mechanism and mathematical structure: 1. Compact Support: Unlike Gaussian kernels which have infinite support, polynomial and spline kernels are defined to be zero outside a finite radius R. This allows for exact bounding box culling during rasterization. 2. Piecewise Definition: Most kernels in this family are defined piecewise, with different polynomial expressions for the inner region (near the center) and the outer region (near the boundary), ensuring continuity of value and derivatives at the transition point. 3. Radial Symmetry: The kernel value W depends only on the radial distance r (or squared Mahalanobis distance dM^2) from the splat center. 4. Normalization: Kernels are scaled such that the integral over the support equals the voxel density/weight, or the maximum value is normalized to 1. 5. body: Quadratic Spline Splatting replaces the standard Gaussian reconstruction kernel with a piecewise quadratic spline function to improve rendering accuracy under perspective projection. It belongs to the polynomial and spline kernel family, sharing compact support for exact bounding-box culling and piecewise continuity properties. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (voxel values and positions), camera parameters (view and projection matrices), and kernel parameters. Output: A 2D rasterized image. Data Structures: Splat Kernel: A radial function W(r) defined by a quadratic polynomial within a finite support radius R. Footprint: An elliptical region in screen space determined by the projected 2D covariance (conic) matrix. Method: 1. Covariance Transformation: For each voxel, compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma and transform it into a 2D conic matrix \mathbf{C} in screen space to define the elliptical footprint. 2. Footprint Culling: Calculate the bounding box of the elliptical footprint and cull voxels whose footprints do not contribute to the final image. 3. Rasterization: For each pixel within the footprint, compute the squared Mahalanobis distance dM^2 from the splat center using the conic matrix. 4. Kernel Evaluation: Evaluate the quadratic spline kernel W(dM) based on the computed distance. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the weighted voxel values into the pixel buffer using alpha blending or similar compositing techniques. Formulas: The quadratic spline kernel W(r) is defined piecewise: W(r) = \begin{cases} P1(r) & \text{if } r < R{\text{inner}} \\ P2(r) & \text{if } R{\text{inner}} \le r < R \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where P1 and P2 are quadratic polynomials optimized for certain conditions to ensure continuity and proper normalization. Parameters: Support Radius (R): The radius beyond which the kernel value is zero. Inner Radius (R{\text{inner}}): The transition point between the two quadratic pieces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Distortion: The kernel is optimized for perspective projection, requiring accurate covariance transformation to avoid artifacts. Discretization: Aliasing may occur if the footprint is undersampled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Smoothness Splines
body: Smoothness Splines (SS) is a scattered data approximation method for recovering volume rendered images from sparse pixel measurements by finding a smooth solution in a shift-invariant spline space. It minimizes a least-squares norm that penalizes non-smooth solutions using the second-order Beppo-Levi seminorm, distinguishing it from compressed sensing methods that rely on sparsity in wavelet or gradient domains. SS is more resilient to missing information and computationally less expensive than compressed sensing pursuit strategies. Inputs: y \in \mathbb{R}^M: Vector of measured pixel values at locations k1, \dots, kM. N: Total number of pixels in the image grid. j1, \dots, jN: Pixel locations corresponding to the full image grid (used for the basis functions). Outputs: x \in \mathbb{R}^N: Recovered image coefficients, which correspond to pixel values since the kernel is interpolating. Data Structures: Measurement Mask / Sampling Matrix: A boolean array or list of indices indicating which of the N grid locations jn correspond to the measured values ym. Let S be the M \times N sampling matrix where S{m,n} = 1 if jn = km and 0 otherwise. Kernel: The bivariate kernel \phi(t1, t2) = \betaI^3(t1)\betaI^3(t2), where \betaI^3 is the optimal interpolating cubic B-spline. Parameters: \lambda: Regularization parameter. Typical value: 10^{-2}. Steps: 1. Define the Kernel: Use the optimal interpolating cubic B-spline kernel. The univariate kernel is defined as: \betaI^3(t):= \beta^3(t) - \frac{1}{6} \frac{d^2}{dt^2} \beta^3(t) where \beta^3(t) is the univariate uniform centered cubic B-spline. The bivariate kernel is the tensor product \phi(t1, t2) = \betaI^3(t1)\betaI^3(t2). 2. Formulate the Optimization Problem: The goal is to find coefficients c such that f(t) = \sum{n=1}^N cn \phi(t - jn) fits the data while minimizing smoothness energy. Because \betaI^3 is interpolating, c = x. The problem is formulated as: \minx \|Sx - y\|2^2 + \lambda x^T H x where H is an N \times N matrix with entries: H{p,q} = \langle \phi(\cdot - jp), \phi(\cdot - jq) \rangle{BL2} 3. Define the Beppo-Levi Inner Product: The smoothness penalty uses the second-order Beppo-Levi inner product: \langle g, h \rangle{BL2}:= \langle \partial{t1 t1} g, \partial{t1 t1} h \rangle + 2 \langle \partial{t1 t2} g, \partial{t1 t2} h \rangle + \langle \partial{t2 t2} g, \partial{t2 t2} h \rangle where \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle is the standard L^2 inner product. 4. Derive the Linear System: Differentiating the objective function with respect to x yields the normal equations: (S^T S + \lambda H) x = S^T y The matrix S^T S + \lambda H is symmetric and positive definite. 5. Solve the System: Solve for x using the Conjugate Gradient (CG) method. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Matrix Storage: The matrix H does not need to be explicitly computed or stored; its action on a vector x is equivalent to a filtering operation where filter weights are obtained via the BL2 inner product definition. Implementers must implement the matrix-vector product Hx as a convolution/filtering step rather than forming H. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The BL2 inner product in 1D reduces to the integral of the product of second derivatives. This is a standard numerical integration step. """ tvals = np.linspace(-4, 4, 2000) d2phi = d2cubicbspline(tvals) weights = [] for k in range(-4, 5): d2phishifted = d2cubicbspline(tvals - k) w = np.trapz(d2phi d2phishifted, tvals) weights.append(w) return np.array(weights) def applyhfilter(x2d, weights1d): """ Applies the H operator to a 2D image x2d via separable convolution. Hx is equivalent to convolving with the BL2 inner product weights. This implements the filtering operation mentioned in the sources. """ paddedrows = np.pad(x2d, 2, mode='edge') convrows = np.zeroslike(paddedrows) for i in range(paddedrows.shape[0]): convrows[i,:] = np.convolve(paddedrows[i,:], weights1d, mode='same') paddedcols = np.pad(convrows, ((2, 2), (0, 0)), mode='edge') convcols = np.zeroslike(paddedcols) for j in range(paddedcols.shape[1]): convcols[:, j] = np.convolve(paddedcols[:, j], weights1d, mode='same') return convcols[2:-2, 2:-2] def solvesmoothnesssplines(y, measurementindices, N): """ Solves (S^T S + lambda H) x = S^T y using Conjugate Gradient. """ lambdareg = 1e-2 Sy = np.zeros(N) Sy[measurementindices] = y weights1d = computebl2filterweights() def matvecmult(v): vmasked = np.zeros(N) vmasked[measurementindices] = v[measurementindices] Hv = applyhfilter(v.reshape((int(np.sqrt(N)), int(np.sqrt(N)))), weights1d).flatten() return vmasked + lambdareg Hv x = np.zeros(N) b = Sy tol = 1e-6 maxiter = 1000 r = b - matvecmult(x) p = r.copy() rsold = np.dot(r, r) for i in range(maxiter): Ap = matvecmult(p) pAp = np.dot(p, Ap) if pAp == 0: break alpha = rsold / pAp x = x + alpha p r = r - alpha Ap rsnew = np.dot(r, r) if np.sqrt(rsnew) < tol: break p = r + (rsnew / rsold) p rsold = rsnew return x Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: More resilient to missing information than compressed sensing methods. Can achieve high quality recovery with as little as 20% of pixels distributed uniformly. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Smoothness Splines was proposed by Xu et al. [XAE12] and applied to volume rendering by Liu and Alim. It is based on the theory of scattered data approximation using shift-invariant spline spaces. The method uses the optimal interpolating cubic B-spline kernel proposed by Blu et al. [BTU01]. It is categorized as a smoothness-based recovery method, contrasting with compressed sensing methods that exploit sparsity in wavelet or gradient domains. head: Beta distribution splatting, Beta footprint
body: The Beta Function Splatting Kernel is a 2D kernel function used in volume rendering that replaces the standard Normal (Gaussian) distribution with a Beta function to control the footprint shape. It solves the problem of tuning visual parameters (opacity, zoom, shading) by offering smaller footprints that maintain equivalent visual quality while reducing rendering time. It sets itself apart from Gaussian splats by allowing independent control over the curve's openness, height, and width, resulting in more compact support and faster execution. Inputs: x: Normalized radial distance from the splat center, mapped to the range [0, 1]. a, b: Shape parameters controlling the curve profile. k{scale}: Scaling factor for the kernel height. Outputs: W: The kernel weight/value at distance x. Data Structures: The kernel is defined by the scalar parameters a, b, k{scale}. The footprint radius is fixed by the domain of x \in [0, 1]. Formula: The kernel value W is calculated as: W(x) = k{scale} \cdot x^a \cdot (1 - x)^b where x \in [0, 1]. Parameters: a, b: Shape parameters. Identical values (a=b) produce symmetric curves. Lower values produce "more opened" (wider/flatter) curves. k{scale}: Scaling factor applied to adjust the range/height of the curve. Steps: 1. Calculate the normalized distance x from the splat center to the sample point, ensuring x \in [0, 1]. 2. Compute the base Beta function value: x^a (1 - x)^b. 3. Multiply by the scaling factor k{scale} to obtain the final weight W. 4. If x < 0 or x > 1, the weight is 0 (compact support). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes at Boundaries: Holes may appear when voxel opacity decreases. This requires dynamic changes in footprint size to maintain continuity between neighbor voxels, especially at feature boundaries in tagged volumes. Precision: For very small a or b, numerical stability near x=0 or x=1 should be considered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns: float: Kernel weight W. """ if x < 0.0 or x > 1.0: return 0.0 # Compute x^a (1-x)^b # Note: 0^0 is treated as 1.0 in this context for continuity if a,b > 0 term1 = x a term2 = (1.0 - x) b return kscale term1 term2 Deformable Beta Splatting replaces standard Gaussian kernels with an adaptive, bounded Beta function kernel. It sets itself apart from fixed-shape siblings by allowing the kernel's profile to deform during training, enabling better modeling of diverse geometric structures such as solid geometry with sharp boundaries or high-frequency details. Choose this variant when rendering tagged volumes or features with sharp boundaries that require adaptive footprint shaping. Universal Beta Splatting is an N-dimensional splatting kernel that replaces the Gaussian distribution with a Beta function to enable independent per-dimension shape control. It sets itself apart from coupled Gaussian siblings by allowing each dimension to adopt fundamentally different profiles independently, addressing the limitations of methods like 6DGS and 7DGS. Choose this variant when per-dimension shape flexibility is required beyond radial symmetry. Performance: Beta footprints are smaller than Normal distribution footprints while providing equivalent visual quality, resulting in faster execution (e.g., twice as fast in tested examples). Tuning: Easier to tune visual parameters like opacity and zoom compared to Gaussian kernels. Limitations: Requires careful management of footprint size to avoid holes when opacity varies, particularly at feature boundaries. It was introduced to improve rendering performance by using smaller footprints that are easier to tune under visual changes, such as zooming and shading functions. name: Deformable Beta Splatting
head: DBS, Liu et al, 2025a
body: Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS) replaces standard Gaussian kernels with an adaptive, bounded Beta function kernel. It solves the limitation of fixed-shape primitives by allowing the kernel's profile to deform during training, enabling better modeling of diverse geometric structures such as solid geometry with sharp boundaries or high-frequency details. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N primitives with mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity oi, color ci, and learnable shape parameter bi. Output: Pixel color C(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Each primitive i stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color. bi \in \mathbb{R}: Learnable Beta shape parameter. Kernel Definition: Density is defined as \sigmai(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, bi) \cdot oi. The Beta kernel is: \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, b) = (1 - r(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta(b)} where the exponent is \beta(b) = 4 \exp(b). r(\mathbf{x}) is the normalized squared Mahalanobis distance, constrained to 0, 1). Rendering Steps: 1. Project \boldsymbol{\mu}i and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i to 2D screen space. 2. Cull primitives outside the pixel/tile bounding box. 3. Sort primitives front-to-back by depth. 4. Evaluate \sigmai(\mathbf{x}) for each pixel. 5. Composite color: C(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N ci \sigmai(\mathbf{x}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj(\mathbf{x})). Parameters: bi \in \mathbb{R} controls shape. Negative b produces flatter profiles with sharper boundaries for solid geometry; positive b yields sharper peaks for high-frequency details. Initialization approximates a scaled Gaussian. Pitfalls: Clamp r(\mathbf{x}) to [0, 1) to prevent NaNs in the power operation. Optimize b via gradient descent alongside other attributes. A unified framework that generalizes 3D [Gaussian Splatting to N-dimensional anisotropic Beta kernels. It sets itself apart by natively incorporating view and temporal dimensions into the kernel's query space, achieving parameter efficiency without auxiliary color encodings. Choose it when modeling view-dependent appearance and scene dynamics is required. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Adaptive kernel shapes model diverse geometries more effectively than fixed Gaussian kernels. Limitations: Requires optimization of the additional parameter b. When to use: When scene geometry varies significantly in sharpness or when Gaussian kernels fail to capture high-frequency details or sharp boundaries efficiently. Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS) was introduced by Liu et al. in 2025. It builds on the Beta Function Splatting Kernel, which uses the Beta function to control footprint shape. name: Universal Beta Splatting
head: UBS, UBS-6D, UBS-7D, Universal Beta Splatting 6D, Universal Beta Splatting 7D
body: Universal Beta Splatting (UBS) is a unified framework for explicit radiance field rendering that generalizes 3D Gaussian Splatting to N-dimensional anisotropic Beta kernels. It solves the problem of modeling complex light transport, view-dependent appearance, and scene dynamics simultaneously without requiring auxiliary color encodings (such as spherical harmonics) or separate networks. Unlike its siblings, UBS natively incorporates view and temporal dimensions into the kernel's query space, allowing the primitive's mean and covariance to adapt to these conditions via Beta-modulated conditional slicing. This approach achieves significant parameter efficiency (e.g., a 41% reduction over 3DGS for static scenes) while maintaining backward compatibility with Gaussian splatting as a special case. Inputs: Camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics). Query vector \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{N-3}, where N is the total dimensionality. For static view-dependent rendering, N=6 (UBS-6D) and \mathbf{q} encodes view direction. For dynamic rendering, N=7 (UBS-7D) and \mathbf{q} encodes view direction and time. A set of primitives, each defined by the parameters below. Outputs: Pixel color and depth via volume rendering of the conditioned 3D Beta kernel density. Each primitive stores parameters partitioned into spatial (x) and query (q) components. The total parameter count depends on the dimensionality N: UBS-6D (Static/View-Dependent): Total: 35 parameters per primitive. Geometry (32 params): Position \boldsymbol{\mu}x: 3 floats. Direction \boldsymbol{\mu}q (view mean): 3 floats. Spatial-Orthogonal Covariance: 21 floats (see Layout). Beta Shapes: 4 floats (spatial bx and angular \mathbf{b}q). Opacity o: 1 float. Color: 3 floats (direct RGB). UBS-7D (Dynamic): Total: 44 parameters per primitive. Geometry (41 params): Position \boldsymbol{\mu}x: 3 floats. Time \mu{t}: 1 float. Direction \boldsymbol{\mu}q (view mean): 3 floats. Spatial-Orthogonal Covariance: 28 floats (see Layout). Beta Shapes: 5 floats (spatial bx, angular \mathbf{b}q, temporal bt). Opacity o: 1 float. Color: 3 floats (direct RGB). The N-dimensional space is partitioned into spatial components (x \in \mathbb{R}^3) and query components (q \in \mathbb{R}^{N-3}): \boldsymbol{\mu} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}x \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}q \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}x & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{xq} \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qx} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}q \end{pmatrix} The covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is parameterized using Spatial-Orthogonal Cholesky to preserve orthonormal spatial structure while enabling cross-dimensional correlations. For N = 3 + C dimensions, the lower triangular Cholesky factor \mathbf{L} is constructed as: \mathbf{L} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{R}x \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{L}{qx} & \mathbf{L}q \end{pmatrix} Where: \mathbf{R}x \in SO(3) is the spatial rotation, computed via a first-order Taylor approximation of the matrix exponential: \mathbf{R}x \approx \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}x, where \mathbf{A}x is a skew-symmetric matrix derived from 3 learnable parameters. \mathbf{s}x are the spatial scales (3 parameters). \mathbf{L}{qx} encodes cross-correlations between spatial and query dimensions. \mathbf{L}q is the Cholesky factor for the non-spatial dimensions. 1. Compute Modulated Opacity: Calculate the per-dimension contribution to opacity based on the query vector \mathbf{q}: di^{\text{raw}} = (\hat{\mathbf{L}}q^{-1}(\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}q))i^2 di = \tanh(di^{\text{raw}}) \in [0, 1) o(\mathbf{q}) = o \prod{i=1}^C (1 - di)^{4\beta{qi}} Where \hat{\mathbf{L}}q is the Cholesky factor of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}q, and \beta{qi} = 4 \exp(b{qi}) are the positive Beta exponents derived from the learnable shape parameters b. 2. Compute Beta-Modulated Conditional Mean: Adjust the spatial mean based on the query: \boldsymbol{\mu}{x|q} = \boldsymbol{\mu}x + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{xq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}q^{-1} \operatorname{diag}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}q) (\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}q) Where \operatorname{diag}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}q) applies dimension-specific Beta modulation. 3. Compute Beta-Modulated Conditional Covariance: Adjust the spatial covariance based on the query: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{x|q} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{x'} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{xq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{q'}^{-1} \operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{q'}) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qx} Where \operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}{q'}) = \operatorname{diag}([\beta{q1}, \dots, \beta{qC}]{\le 1}) ensures modulation values are capped at 1, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{x'}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{q'} refer to the base covariance blocks \boldsymbol{\Sigma}x and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}q. 4. Evaluate Density: Compute the final conditioned 3D Beta kernel density: \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{q}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}{x|q}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{x|q}, bx) \cdot o(\mathbf{q}) Where \mathcal{B} is the Beta function density with spatial shape parameter bx. 5. Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering (e.g., alpha compositing) using the computed density \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{q}) and direct RGB color. 6. Optimization: Optimization minimizes a composite loss function: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda{\text{SSIM}})\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{SSIM}}\mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} + \lambdao \sumi |oi| + \lambda\Sigma \sumi \|\mathbf{s}i\|1 Spatial noise injection promotes exploration: \boldsymbol{\mu}x \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\mu}x - \lambda{lr}\nabla{\boldsymbol{\mu}} \mathcal{L} + \lambda\epsilon \boldsymbol{\epsilon}. Primitive management (densification/culling) uses the kernel-agnostic MCMC optimization from Deformable Beta Splatting. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeubsplatdensity(x, q, mux, muq, Lqx, Lq, sx, bx, bq, o): # 1. Reconstruct base covariance blocks from Cholesky factor L # L = [[Rx diag(sx), 0], [Lqx, Lq]] # Sigmax = Rx diag(sx) @ Rx diag(sx)^T # Sigmaq = Lq @ Lq^T # Sigmaxq = Rx diag(sx) @ Lqx^T # Sigmaqx = Sigmaxq^T # (Implementation details for Rx from skew-symmetric Ax omitted for brevity) # 2. Compute modulated opacity Lqinv = np.linalg.inv(Lq) draw = np.sum((Lqinv @ (q - muq))2, axis=0) # Per-dimension squared Mahalanobis distance d = np.tanh(draw) betaq = 4.0 np.exp(bq) oq = o np.prod((1.0 - d)(4.0 betaq)) # 3. Compute conditional mean Sigmaqinv = np.linalg.inv(Sigmaq) betahatq = betaq # diag(betahatq) applies modulation mucond = mux + (Sigmaxq @ Sigmaqinv) @ (np.diag(betahatq) @ (q - muq)) # 4. Compute conditional covariance betatildeq = np.minimum(betaq, 1.0) Sigmacond = Sigmax - (Sigmaxq @ Sigmaqinv @ np.diag(betatildeq) @ Sigmaqx) # 5. Evaluate Beta density (simplified 3D Beta kernel evaluation) # B(x; mu, Sigma, b) typically involves multivariate Beta function normalization # and exponent terms based on bx. Exact normalization constant not given in sources. density = evaluatebetakernel(x, mucond, Sigmacond, bx) return density oq Beta Parameters (b): Control the shape of the kernel. When b=0, the kernel approximates a Gaussian, recovering 3DGS, 6DGS, or 7DGS depending on dimensionality. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Typical values for similar splatting methods are \lambda{\text{SSIM}} \approx 0.2, but these are not confirmed in the UBS source. Precision: The first-order Taylor approximation for \mathbf{R}x is used to reduce computation; higher-order approximations may be needed for extreme rotations, though the source claims nearly identical fidelity. Boundaries: The \tanh function in opacity calculation bounds di to 0, 1), ensuring valid inputs for the Beta kernel. Degenerate Input: If \boldsymbol{\Sigma}q is singular, inversion in the conditional mean/covariance steps will fail. The Cholesky parameterization helps maintain positive semi-definiteness, but numerical stability checks are required. Time Complexity: Real-time performance is achieved via a fully accelerated CUDA implementation. Memory Complexity: Significant parameter reduction compared to baselines. UBS-6D uses 59% of the parameters of 3DGS (35 vs 59 per primitive). UBS-7D uses 27% of the parameters of 4DGS (44 vs 161 per primitive). Measured Performance: Static ([NeRF Synthetic/Mip-NeRF): UBS-6D averages 345.7 FPS, 300.0K primitives, 40.1 MB memory, and 8.7 minutes training time. Static (6DGS-PBR): UBS-6D averages 290.2 FPS, 300.0K primitives, 40.1 MB memory, and 27.7 minutes training time. Dynamic (7DGS-PBR/D-NeRF): UBS-7D averages 359.6 FPS, 234.3K primitives, 39.4 MB memory, and 59.9 minutes training time. Quality: Improves PSNR by up to +8.27 dB on static scenes and +2.78 dB on dynamic scenes compared to Gaussian baselines. Strengths: Eliminates auxiliary color encodings (SH), enables native view/temporal dependency modeling, and provides interpretable scene decomposition where spatial/angular/temporal Beta parameters separate geometry/texture/diffuse/specular/static/dynamic. Limitations: Requires CUDA acceleration for real-time performance and involves complex conditional slicing logic compared to simple Gaussian projection. Universal Beta Splatting was introduced in. It builds on Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS) and extends the Beta kernel concept to N dimensions. It addresses limitations in 3DGS, 6DGS, and 4DGS which rely on fixed Gaussian profiles and auxiliary encodings for view-dependent and temporal effects. name: Beta Decomposition
head: Geometry Decomposition, Lighting Decomposition
body: Beta Decomposition is a post-training analysis technique that separates a Deformable Beta Splatting scene into distinct geometric frequency bands and diffuse/specular lighting components by leveraging the Beta Kernel's parameterization. It enables the isolation of low-frequency solid geometry from high-frequency textures, and the separation of static diffuse color from view-dependent specular highlights, capabilities not available in standard Gaussian Splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained Deformable Beta Splatting scene consisting of a set of primitives \mathcal{P}. Each primitive i is defined by its position, orientation, scale, opacity, and the Beta Kernel parameters \alphai, \betai. It also includes Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Output: Two decomposed scenes: one containing only the geometric structure (geometry decomposition) and one containing only the lighting effects (lighting decomposition). Data Structures: The primitive data structure includes: \alphai, \betai: Beta Kernel shape parameters. \betai controls the frequency of the geometry representation. \mathbf{c}{i,0}: Zero-degree SH coefficient (base color/diffuse). \mathbf{c}{i,k}: Non-zero degree SH coefficients (specular/view-dependent details). Steps: 1. Geometry Decomposition: Calculate the mean \beta value across all primitives: \bar{\beta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \betai. Define a threshold \tau = \bar{\beta}. Split primitives into two sets: Low-frequency (Geometry): P{geo} = \{ i \mid \betai < \tau \}. These primitives represent fundamental geometric structures. High-frequency (Texture): P{tex} = \{ i \mid \betai \ge \tau \}. These primitives represent fine surface variations and textures. To render the geometry-only view, render only primitives in P{geo} using their original parameters but ignoring view-dependent lighting variations (or using only diffuse color). 2. Lighting Decomposition: Diffuse Component: Extract the base color \mathbf{c}{i,0} for all primitives. Render the scene using only these zero-degree SH coefficients, effectively removing view-dependent effects. Specular Component: Isolate the specular term. This is achieved by using only the non-zero degree SH coefficients (\mathbf{c}{i,k} for k > 0) for rendering. The base color \mathbf{c}{i,0} is set to zero or ignored. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def betadecomposition(primitives): """ Decomposes a Deformable Beta Splatting scene into geometry and lighting components. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects, each with attributes: beta: float, the Beta Kernel parameter controlling geometry frequency. c0: float, zero-degree SH coefficient (diffuse base color). csh: list, higher-degree SH coefficients (specular/view-dependent). Returns: geoprimitives: List of primitives for geometry-only rendering. specprimitives: List of primitives for specular-only rendering. """ # Step 1: Geometry Decomposition # Calculate mean beta to determine threshold totalbeta = sum(p.beta for p in primitives) meanbeta = totalbeta / len(primitives) geoprimitives = [] for p in primitives: if p.beta < meanbeta: # Keep primitive for geometry # Use original beta, but typically only diffuse color is used for pure geometry # or the full primitive is kept but lighting is stripped in rendering pass geoprimitives.append(p) # Step 2: Lighting Decomposition specprimitives = [] for p in primitives: # Create a modified primitive for specular rendering specp = copyprimitive(p) # Zero out diffuse component (zero-degree SH) specp.c0 = 0.0 # Keep higher-degree SH coefficients for specular/view-dependent effects # Note: The rendering engine must interpret non-zero SH as specular specprimitives.append(specp) return geoprimitives, specprimitives Parameters: Threshold (\tau): The mean \beta value is the default threshold. Other thresholds (e.g., median) may be used but are not specified in the source. SH Degree: Zero-degree for diffuse, non-zero for specular. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mirror-like Reflections: Spherical Beta Functions struggle to accurately model mirror-like reflections and anisotropic specular highlights. Distant Backgrounds: The frustum model can cause Beta Kernels to incorrectly optimize flat geometries for distant backgrounds, distorting the overall \beta geometry distribution. Popping Artifacts: Rasterization-based depth approximation during sorting can cause popping artifacts. Time Complexity: Post-processing is O(N) where N is the number of primitives, as it involves a single pass to calculate the mean \beta and another pass to split primitives. Memory Complexity: O(N), as it requires storing the original primitives and potentially copies or flags for the decomposed sets. Strengths: Enables artistic control and analysis of scene components (geometry vs. texture, diffuse vs. specular) which is difficult with standard Gaussian Splatting. Limitations: The decomposition relies on the quality of the Beta Kernel parameterization. If the training process does not adequately separate frequency bands via \beta, the decomposition may be imperfect. The method is specific to Deformable Beta Splatting and does not apply to other splatting methods. Beta Decomposition was introduced as part of the Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS) framework. DBS advances real-time radiance field rendering by using deformable Beta Kernels for adaptive geometry representation and Spherical Betas for view-dependent color. The decomposition capability arises from the dual role of the Beta Kernel in encoding both volumetric splatting and view-dependent color information. Deformable Beta Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3721238.3730716, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Universal Beta Splatting (UBS)
head: Beta kernel, N-dimensional Beta Kernel, Universal Beta Splatting (UBS) / N-dimensional Beta Kernel
body: Universal Beta Splatting (UBS) is an N-dimensional splatting kernel that replaces the Gaussian distribution with a Beta function to enable independent per-dimension shape control. Unlike Gaussian kernels where all dimensions are coupled through a joint distribution, UBS allows each dimension to adopt fundamentally different profiles (e.g., flat vs. peaked) independently, addressing the limitations of methods like 6DGS and 7DGS. Inputs and Outputs Input: A point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N, mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, and shape parameters \mathbf{b} = [b1, \dots, bN]. Output: A scalar kernel value \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1]. Data Structures \mathbf{b}: An array of N floating-point values representing the shape parameters for each dimension. di(\mathbf{x}): The bounded distance for dimension i, computed from the coordinates relative to the mean. Formulas The N-dimensional Beta kernel is defined as a gated product: \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \mathbf{b}) = \prod{i=1}^N (1 - di(\mathbf{x}))^{\betai} where di \in [0, 1) is the bounded distance and \betai is the shape exponent. The explicit per-dimension shape control formula is: \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}) = \prod{i=1}^N (1 - di(\mathbf{x}))^{4 \exp(bi)} where bi is the shape parameter for dimension i. The bounded distance di(\mathbf{x}) is defined differently based on the dimension index: 1. For the first three dimensions (i = 1, 2, 3), di is defined by ri in Equation [1] of the source. 2. For the remaining dimensions (i = 4, \dots, N), di is defined by Equation 11 of the source. Parameters bi: Shape parameter controlling the kernel profile. Typical practical range is bi \in [-5, 5]. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Flat Kernel: When bi < 0, the kernel profile becomes flatter with broader support (\betai < 4). Specifically, when bi = -5, \betai \approx 0.027 and the kernel becomes nearly constant ( (1-di)^{0.027} \approx 1). Peaked Kernel: When bi > 0, the kernel profile becomes more peaked with sharper localization (\betai > 4). Specifically, when bi = 5, \betai \approx 594. Gaussian Approximation: When bi = 0, \betai = 4, and the Beta kernel approximates a Gaussian via the relation (1 - d)^4 \approx \exp(-4.5d^2) for d \in [0, 1). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def universalbetasplatting(x, mu, sigma, b): """ Computes the Universal Beta Splatting kernel value. Args: x: Input point (N-dimensional vector). mu: Mean vector (N-dimensional). sigma: Covariance matrix (N x N). b: Shape parameters vector (N-dimensional). Returns: Kernel value. """ N = len(x) kernelvalue = 1.0 for i in range(N): # The sources do not provide the exact formulas for di; # a standard clamped normalized distance is used here. diff = x[i] - mu[i] var = sigma[i][i] if len(sigma) > i else 1.0 di = abs(diff) / math.sqrt(max(var, 1e-8)) di = max(0.0, min(di, 0.999999)) # Compute shape exponent betai betai = 4.0 math.exp(b[i]) # Multiply kernel component kernelvalue = (1.0 - di) betai return kernelvalue An extension that modifies the Beta kernel to adapt to complex geometries. Details on how it sets itself apart from UBS and when to choose it are not given in the sources. Link Complexity: The kernel evaluation is O(N) where N is the number of dimensions, due to the product form. Strengths: Enables independent modeling of spatial, angular, and temporal properties. A single primitive can represent static spatial surfaces with view-dependent reflectance, which Gaussian methods require multiple coupled primitives to approximate. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of bi parameters. Extreme values of bi can lead to numerical instability or overly flat/peaked kernels that may not represent the data well. Performance: Not given in the sources. UBS was introduced to address the inherent dimensional coupling limitations in 6DGS and 7DGS, where changes in view direction or time affect all dimensions simultaneously. The method uses the Beta function to replace the Normal distribution to enable easier tuning for visual parameters like shape and profile. name: Raised Cosine Splatting
head: 3DRCS, Modified Raised Cosine
body: Raised Cosine Splatting is a volume rendering technique that replaces the standard Gaussian radial basis function with a compactly supported raised cosine kernel to improve the reconstruction of fine geometric details. It differs from standard Gaussian splatting by using a trigonometric decay that provides sharper transitions and better preservation of high-frequency features like edges and small objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian splat defined by a mean position \mu, a 3D covariance matrix \Sigma, and a weight w. The splat is projected to 2D to yield a 2D conic matrix \mathbf{C} (inverse covariance) and a projected weight w{2D} (denoted as cono.w in implementation). Output: A 2D alpha value \alpha for each pixel within the splat's support, and gradients for backpropagation. Data Structures: The 2D conic matrix \mathbf{C} is stored as a symmetric 2 \times 2 matrix with elements a, b, c corresponding to cono.x, cono.y, cono.z in the quadratic form ax^2 + 2bxy + cy^2. Parameters: correctionFactor: A scalar multiplier applied to the 2D covariance matrix before conic computation. Value: 0.655. \xi: The scaling factor for the cosine argument, defined as \xi = \frac{5}{2\pi}. \alpha{max}: The maximum alpha value. Value: 0.99. Algorithm Steps: 1. Covariance Correction: Multiply the 2D covariance matrix by the correctionFactor before computing the conic matrix. \mathbf{C}{corrected} = \mathbf{C} \times 0.655 2. Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance (dM^2): For a pixel at position \mathbf{x} relative to the splat center \boldsymbol{\mu}', compute the distance metric using the corrected conic matrix elements a, b, c and displacement vector \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}': ellipse = a \cdot dx^2 + c \cdot dy^2 + 2b \cdot dx \cdot dy 3. Boundary Check: If ellipse < 0 or ellipse > 6.25, the pixel is outside the valid support (one pulse) and the splat contribution is skipped. 4. Compute Kernel Value: Calculate the square root of the ellipse metric: dM = \sqrt{ellipse} Calculate the scaled argument: ellipseFactor = \frac{\pi \cdot dM}{2.5} Compute the base cosine weight: Cosine = 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot \cos(ellipseFactor) 5. Compute Alpha: \alpha = \min(0.99, w{2D} \cdot Cosine) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raisedcosinesplatting(conicmatrix, weight, pixelpos, splatcenter): """ Computes the alpha value for a raised cosine splat at a specific pixel. Args: conicmatrix: Tuple (a, b, c) representing the 2x2 symmetric conic matrix [a, b; b, c]. weight: The projected 2D weight (cono.w). pixelpos: Tuple (x, y) of the pixel coordinates. splatcenter: Tuple (mux, muy) of the splat center. Returns: alpha: The computed alpha value, or None if outside support. """ # 1. Covariance Correction correctionfactor = 0.655 a = conicmatrix[0] correctionfactor b = conicmatrix[1] correctionfactor c = conicmatrix[2] correctionfactor # 2. Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance (ellipse) dx = pixelpos[0] - splatcenter[0] dy = pixelpos[1] - splatcenter[1] ellipse = a (dx 2) + c (dy 2) + 2.0 b dx dy # 3. Boundary Check if ellipse < 0 or ellipse > 6.25: return None # 4. Compute Kernel Value ellipseroot = math.sqrt(ellipse) ellipsefactor = math.pi ellipseroot / 2.5 cosineval = 0.5 + 0.5 math.cos(ellipsefactor) # 5. Compute Alpha alpha = min(0.99, weight cosineval) return alpha def raisedcosinegradient(conicmatrix, dLdconic): """ Computes gradients of the loss w.r.t. covariance matrix elements from conic matrix gradients. Args: conicmatrix: Tuple (a, b, c) representing the corrected 2x2 symmetric conic matrix. dLdconic: Tuple (dLdaconic, dLdbconic, dLdcconic) gradients w.r.t conic elements. Returns: dLda, dLdb, dLdc: Gradients w.r.t. covariance matrix elements. """ correctionfactor = 0.655 a = conicmatrix[0] correctionfactor b = conicmatrix[1] correctionfactor c = conicmatrix[2] correctionfactor denom = a c - b b denom2inv = 1.0 / denom # Gradients derived from chain rule and inverse covariance transformation dLda = correctionfactor denom2inv (-c c dLdconic[0] + 2 b c dLdconic[1] + (denom - a c) dLdconic[2]) dLdc = correctionfactor denom2inv (-a a dLdconic[2] + 2 a b dLdconic[1] + (denom - a c) dLdconic[0]) dLdb = correctionfactor denom2inv 2 (b c dLdconic[0] - (a c + b b) dLdconic[1] + a b dLdconic[2]) return dLda, dLdb, dLdc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The boundary check ellipse > 6.25 is critical. Values exceeding this result in negative cosine arguments beyond the first lobe, which are discarded. Normalization: The kernel is not normalized to integrate to 1 in the standard sense; instead, it is scaled by the weight w and capped at \alpha=0.99. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel within the support. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per splat. Support: The support is bounded by ellipse \le 6.25, which corresponds to a radius of 2.5 in Mahalanobis distance units. Performance: In 1D simulation reconstruction error (MSE) with N=10 components, Modified Raised Cosine achieved 0.00004, outperforming Gaussian (0.0001). With N=8 components, it achieved better reconstruction than Gaussians with N=10. Strengths: Provides modestly improved visual quality compared to Gaussians, particularly for fine details like buttons, marks, strings, and pot edges. Limitations: The compact support requires careful handling of the boundary check to avoid artifacts. Raised Cosine Splatting was introduced in the DARB-Splatting paper as a generalization of splatting using decaying anisotropic radial basis functions. It was developed to address the limitations of Gaussian kernels in reconstructing high-frequency details in 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Ideal Reconstruction Function for 3D Splatting
head: Optimized 3D splat filter, Splatting with optimized 3D reconstruction filter, Tri-cubic reconstruction kernel, Westover splatting
body: The Ideal Reconstruction Function for 3D Splatting is a rotationally symmetric, compact-support kernel designed to reconstruct 3D volume data via splatting with minimal visible artifacts. It solves the problem of "Mach bands" and visible individual splat boundaries that occur when approximating smooth volume data with polygon collections or non-optimized kernels. Unlike Gaussian splats, this kernel has a well-defined finite overlap extent and goes to zero in a minimum extent, providing high-quality smooth overlap from any viewing direction at the cost of higher performance penalties for large screen-space splats. It is distinct from its siblings by being mathematically optimized to minimize the relative variance of a constant cube reconstruction in 3D, rather than relying on standard spline continuity constraints alone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid with intensity values; a viewing direction; a splat center (0,0,0) in local coordinates. Output: A 3D reconstruction kernel function h(x,y,z) and its 2D projected footprint f(x,y) for rasterization. Data Structures: The kernel is defined by two scalar parameters s and t, and two cubic polynomial coefficient sets. t: Support radius (outer boundary). s: Transition radius (inner boundary). g(r): Radial function dependent on r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}. Parameters: Support radius t = 1.556228. Transition radius s = 0.889392. Inner polynomial coefficients (derived from optimization): a=0.557526, b=-1.157743, c=0.671033. Outer polynomial coefficients (derived from optimization): d=0.067599, e=-0.282474. Numbered Steps: 1. Calculate the radial distance r from the splat center for any point (x,y,z): r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} 2. Evaluate the kernel value h(x,y,z) using the radial function g(r): If 0 < r \le s: g(r) = 0.557526 - 1.157743 r^2 + 0.671033 r^3 If s < r \le t: g(r) = 0.067599 (r - t)^2 - 0.282474 (r - t)^3 If r > t: g(r) = 0 The kernel is C^1 continuous at the origin and at the transition point s. 3. To rasterize, compute the 2D footprint f(x,y) by integrating the 3D kernel along the view direction (z-axis): f(x,y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x,y,z) \, dz This integral has a closed-form solution because h is composed of low-degree polynomials in r^2+z^2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mach Bands: Using polygon approximations (15-21 triangles) for splats causes visible Mach bands and individual splat visibility because they do not overlap smoothly. This kernel eliminates this by providing smooth, analytic overlap. Precision: The maximum relative deviation from the mean for a constant cube reconstruction is small (0.00534), but intensities may need scaling to maintain accuracy in 8-bit color buffers. Viewing Direction: The kernel is rotationally symmetric, ensuring accuracy from any viewing direction, unlike axis-aligned approximations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def idealreconstructionkernel(x, y, z): """ Computes the value of the ideal 3D reconstruction kernel at (x, y, z). Parameters are fixed constants from the optimization in. """ t = 1.556228 s = 0.889392 rsq = xx + yy + zz r = rsq 0.5 if r > t: return 0.0 elif r == 0.0: return 0.557526 elif r <= s: return 0.557526 - 1.157743 rsq + 0.671033 (rsq r) else: diff = r - t return 0.067599 (diff diff) - 0.282474 (diff diff diff) def computefootprint(x, y): """ Computes the 2D footprint f(x,y) by integrating h(x,y,z) over z. The closed-form integral of the piecewise cubic radial function is required. Not given in the sources. """ # Not given in the sources. pass Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Higher performance penalty for large screen-space splats compared to Gaussian splats due to the finite support and complex footprint calculation. Quality: Minimizes relative variance of constant cube reconstruction to 0.00119. Maximum projected footprint deviation is approximately 1/256 of the mean, fitting within 8-bit color accuracy. When to use: When high-quality, artifact-free volume rendering is required and polygon-based splatting is insufficient. When not to use: When performance is critical and large screen-space splats are common, or when infinite support (Gaussian) is acceptable for smoother falloff. The method was developed by Laur and Hanrahan, building on Max's 2D ideal reconstruction function [Max92]. While Max's function was designed for 2D image reconstruction, Laur and Hanrahan extended it to 3D signals to replace polygon approximations of splats in volume rendering. The optimization minimizes the relative variance of a constant cube reconstruction, ensuring smooth overlap from any viewing direction. It was implemented using the fast compositing hardware of the SGI VGX. name: SPH Kernel Implementation
head: SPH Kernels
body: The SPH Kernel Implementation provides a polymorphic interface for evaluating Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) kernels on CPU and GPU architectures. It is distinguished from general splatting methods by its focus on particle-based simulation data, providing closed-form 3D expressions for both kernel values and spatial derivatives. It builds on the shared principles of compact support and radial symmetry defined in Polynomial and Spline Kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Particle position \mathbf{x}i, smoothing length h, particle mass m, and a kernel type identifier. Output: Kernel value W(\mathbf{x}) and its spatial derivative \nabla W(\mathbf{x}) at a query point, typically a voxel center. Data Structures: The module uses a polymorphic interface class structure where concrete implementations store kernel parameters and evaluation methods. A kd-tree is employed to calculate particle radii and perform neighbor searches for density estimation. Supported Kernels: The implementation supports the following families, each with closed-form 3D expressions for value and derivative: 1. Cubic B-spline 2. Quintic B-spline 3. Wendland C2 4. Wendland C4 5. Wendland C6 6. Wendland C8 Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute the Euclidean distance r = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\| between the query point and particle center. 2. Normalize the distance to q = r / h. 3. Check compact support: if q > 1, return zero value and gradient. 4. Evaluate the closed-form polynomial for W(q) and its derivative dW/dq based on the selected kernel type. 5. Compute the gradient \nabla W = (dW/dq \cdot 1/h) \cdot \mathbf{u}, where \mathbf{u} is the unit vector from the particle to the query point. 6. Apply density bias correction using the particle mass and smoothing length if computing volumetric density. Formulas: The sources confirm that closed-form 3D expressions exist for all supported kernels, but exact polynomial coefficients are not provided in the documentation. The evaluation relies on the normalized radial distance q = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\| / h and the compact support condition q \leq 1. Parameters: Smoothing Length (h): Controls the support radius of the kernel. Particle Mass (m): Used for density bias correction during voxelization. Kernel Type: Enumerated selector for the B-spline or Wendland variant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class SPHKernel: """Polymorphic base interface for SPH kernel evaluation.""" def evaluate(self, querypos, particlepos, smoothinglength): raise NotImplementedError class CubicBSplineKernel(SPHKernel): """Concrete implementation for the cubic B-spline kernel.""" def evaluate(self, querypos, particlepos, smoothinglength): # 1. Distance calculation diff = [querypos[i] - particlepos[i] for i in range(3)] r = math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in diff)) q = r / smoothinglength # 2. Compact support check if q > 1.0: return 0.0, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 3. Closed-form value and derivative (standard 1D radial form) val = (1.0 - q2)3 dWdq = -6.0 q (1.0 - q2)2 # 4. Gradient computation if r > 1e-9: grad = [dWdq / smoothinglength (diff[i] / r) for i in range(3)] else: grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return val, grad An extension that replaces the spherical support domain with an ellipsoidal one defined by an anisotropy matrix, designed to reduce artifacts in fluid surface rendering [18763-anisotropic-sph-kernel.md]. It differs from the isotropic parent by introducing directional dependence in the footprint to better capture surface geometry [18763-anisotropic-sph-kernel.md]. Choose this variant when rendering fluid interfaces where isotropic kernels produce visible smoothing artifacts. The provided sources do not detail its algorithmic implementation. Time Complexity: O(1) per kernel evaluation; neighbor search via kd-tree typically requires O(\log N). Memory Complexity: Low, as kernels are stateless functions; the kd-tree requires O(N) auxiliary space. Strengths: Closed-form derivatives enable efficient gradient-based operations for density calculation and voxelization. Support for multiple kernel families allows tuning for different simulation characteristics. Limitations: Voxelization requires extending the base algorithm to 3D grids. Exact polynomial coefficients for all supported kernels are not documented. When to use: Visualizing particle-based astrophysical or fluid simulations where accurate density estimation and smooth voxelization are required. The method originates from a C++ module defined in [Bös25] that provides a polymorphic interface for SPH kernels. The voxelization pipeline extends the algorithm described in [Pri07] to support 3D voxels. It is used in astrophysical simulation visualization pipelines to bridge particle data with volume rendering formats.
