name: Anisotropic Screen-Space Fluid Rendering
head: Anisotropic Point Sprite Fluid Rendering, Anisotropic Screen Space Transformation, Anisotropic screen space rendering for particle-based fluid simulation, Elliptical Point Sprite Rendering, Homogeneous Anisotropic Transformation, WPCA-based Anisotropic Fluid Rendering
body: Anisotropic Screen-Space Fluid Rendering is a real-time technique that converts discrete particle data (e.g., from SPH simulations) into a continuous fluid volume by applying anisotropic transformations to point sprites before screen-space filtering. It solves the problem of jagged, uneven surfaces and over-smoothing inherent in standard isotropic point sprite rendering by stretching particles along the principal axes of local particle distribution. Unlike standard methods that use spherical sprites and simple Gaussian filters, this method uses elliptical sprites derived from Weighted Principal Components Analysis (WPCA) to preserve sharp high-frequency details while smoothing discontinuities. The method extends the Screen-Space Fluid Rendering Pipeline by modifying the depth buffer generation step. Instead of rendering isotropic spheres, it renders anisotropic ellipsoids in parameter space, which are then projected to screen space. Inputs: Particle positions \mathbf{x}j, particle densities \rhoj, particle volumes mj, camera projection matrix P, model matrix M, camera position, and viewport dimensions. Outputs: Depth buffer, thickness buffer, reconstructed normal buffer, and final shaded fluid image. 1. Particle Data: Array of particles, each containing position \mathbf{x}j \in \mathbb{R}^3, density \rhoj, and volume mj. 2. Anisotropy Matrix B: A 3 \times 3 matrix derived from WPCA for each particle or local neighborhood. 3. Homogeneous Anisotropic Transformation Matrix C{r,h}: A 4 \times 4 matrix used to transform the sphere to an ellipsoid in parameter space. Layout: C{r,h} = \begin{bmatrix} Cr & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0}^T & 1 \end{bmatrix} Where Cr is the 3 \times 3 regularized covariance matrix from WPCA. 4. Scaling Matrix T: A 4 \times 4 diagonal scaling matrix. Layout: T = \begin{bmatrix} rc & 0 & 0 & xo \\ 0 & rc & 0 & yo \\ 0 & 0 & rc & zo \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} rc: Sphere radius in clip space. (xo, yo, zo): Particle position in object space. \sigmai: Standard deviation for Gaussian filter, determined by depth zi. h: Support radius of the kernel function. Beyond h, the kernel value is 0. \beta: Scaling factor in the anisotropic kernel function. rc: Radius of the sphere in clip space, measured from the bias between the sphere center and a point on the surface. k: Attenuation coefficient vector of the fluid. I0: Light intensity value. 1. Calculate Particle Anisotropy (WPCA): For each particle i, determine the local anisotropy matrix B using Weighted Principal Components Analysis on neighboring particles j. Compute weights \omega{ij} based on particle proximity (standard SPH weighting). Construct the weighted covariance matrix from the relative positions of neighbors. Perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the covariance matrix to obtain eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Construct B such that it stretches the kernel along the tangential directions of the fluid surface. 2. Construct Transformation Matrices: For each particle j at object position \mathbf{x}j = (xo, yo, zo): Define the scaling matrix T using the clip-space radius rc and object position: T = \begin{bmatrix} rc & 0 & 0 & xo \\ 0 & rc & 0 & yo \\ 0 & 0 & rc & zo \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Define the homogeneous anisotropic transformation matrix C{r,h} using the regularized covariance matrix Cr derived from WPCA: C{r,h} = \begin{bmatrix} Cr & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} 3. Render Anisotropic Point Sprites (Depth & Thickness): Transform the particle to screen space. Instead of rendering a sphere, render an elliptical point sprite. The shape is defined by applying C{r,h} in parameter space before projection. To determine the projected ellipse size in clip space, trace the boundary back to parameter space. For a point \mathbf{x}c inside the sprite in clip space, the condition \mathbf{n}c^T \mathbf{x}c \le 0 must hold, where \mathbf{n}c = (1, 0, 0, bx)^T. Trace bx back to parameter space using the inverse transformation: \mathbf{n}p = (P \cdot M \cdot T \cdot C{r,h})^T \mathbf{n}c where \mathbf{n}p is the normal vector in parameter space. Render these ellipses to extract depth values zi and thickness information into the depth buffer. Note that points on the resulting surface may not lie on the projected plane (x{c,z} \neq x{ani,c,z}). 4. Calculate Thickness Buffer: Compute the thickness T(\mathbf{p}i) at each screen pixel \mathbf{p}i by summing the contributions of all fluid particles j using a Gaussian kernel: T(\mathbf{p}i) = \sum{j=0}^{n} G(\mathbf{p}i - \hat{\mathbf{x}}j) where \hat{\mathbf{x}}j is the projection position of particle j in screen space, and G is the Gaussian function. 5. Smooth Depth Information: Apply screen-space filters to the depth buffer to resolve jagged edges. Gaussian Filter: G(\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{p}j, \sigmai) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigmai^2} e^{-\frac{\|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}j\|^2}{\sigmai}} where \mathbf{p}j is a neighbor pixel, and \sigmai is determined by the depth zi. Anisotropic Smoothing Kernel (Optional/Alternative): Use the anisotropic kernel W(\mathbf{r}, B) for smoothing: W(\mathbf{r}, B) = \beta \det(B) P(|\mathbf{r}B|) where \mathbf{r} is the relative position, B is the anisotropy matrix, \beta is a scaling factor, and P is a symmetric decaying spline with finite support. Combine with curvature flow or narrow-range filters to preserve sharp details. 6. Reconstruct Normals: Calculate partial derivatives of the smoothed depth image using finite differences to reconstruct the surface normal at each pixel. 7. Surface Shading: Render the fluid surface using the reconstructed normals and thickness information. Calculate transmittance using the Beer-Lambert law: I(d) = I0 d^{-kd} where d is the thickness, I0 is light intensity, and k is the attenuation coefficient. Apply Blinn-Phong illumination and refraction effects. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def anisotropicscreenspacefluidrendering(particles, camera, viewport): """ particles: List of Particle objects with pos (x,y,z), density, volume camera: Camera object with projection matrix P, model matrix M, position viewport: Viewport dimensions """ # 1. Pre-compute Anisotropy for each particle for particle in particles: # Get neighbors within support radius h neighbors = getneighbors(particle, particles, h=particle.supportradius) # Compute Weighted Covariance Matrix covmatrix = zeros((3, 3)) totalweight = 0 for neighbor in neighbors: r = neighbor.pos - particle.pos w = computeweight(particle, neighbor) # e.g., Gaussian weight based on distance covmatrix += w outerproduct(r, r) totalweight += w # Regularize and Decompose covmatrix += epsilon identity(3) # Regularization eigenvalues, eigenvectors = svd(covmatrix) # Construct Cr (Regularized Covariance Matrix for transformation) # Note: Source defines Cr as the regularized covariance matrix from WPCA Cr = covmatrix # Construct Homogeneous Anisotropic Transformation Matrix Cr,h particle.Crh = matrix4x4([ [Cr[0,0], Cr[0,1], Cr[0,2], 0], [Cr[1,0], Cr[1,1], Cr[1,2], 0], [Cr[2,0], Cr[2,1], Cr[2,2], 0], [0, 0, 0, 1] ]) # Construct Scaling Matrix T # rc is clip-space radius, determined by particle size and camera distance rc = computeclipradius(particle.pos, camera) particle.T = matrix4x4([ [rc, 0, 0, particle.pos.x], [0, rc, 0, particle.pos.y], [0, 0, rc, particle.pos.z], [0, 0, 0, 1] ]) # 2. Render Depth and Thickness Buffers depthbuffer = initializebuffer(viewport) thicknessbuffer = initializebuffer(viewport) for particle in particles: # Transform particle to clip space using anisotropic matrix # The sprite is an ellipsoid defined by Cr,h in parameter space cliptransform = camera.P camera.M particle.T particle.Crh # Determine ellipse boundary in clip space # For a point xc inside sprite, nc^T xc <= 0, nc = (1, 0, 0, bx)^T # Trace bx back to parameter space: np = (P M T Cr,h)^T nc # This defines the extent of the ellipse to rasterize rasterizeellipse(particle, cliptransform, depthbuffer, thicknessbuffer) # 3. Smooth Depth Buffer smootheddepth = applygaussianfilter(depthbuffer) # Alternatively, apply anisotropic kernel W(r, B) if B is available per pixel # 4. Reconstruct Normals normals = reconstructnormals(smootheddepth) # 5. Shade finalimage = zeros(viewport) for y in range(viewport.height): for x in range(viewport.width): d = thicknessbuffer[y, x] if d > 0: # Beer-Lambert Law # I(d) = I0 d^(-kd) # Note: Source formula I(d) = I0 d^(-kd) implies exponent is -kd intensity = camera.lightintensity (d (-camera.attenuationcoeff d)) normal = normals[y, x] finalimage[y, x] = applyblinnphong(intensity, normal, camera) return finalimage def computeclipradius(pos, camera): """ Helper to estimate rc. Source states rc is measured from bias between sphere center and surface point in clip coords. Typically rc = particleradius projectionscale. """ # Simplified estimation dist = length(camera.pos - pos) return 1.0 / dist # Placeholder for actual projection math Uneven Surfaces: Directly using spherical point sprites produces uneven fluid surfaces. Over-smoothing: Simple Gaussian filters cause over-smoothing and loss of edges. Bilateral Filter Artifacts: Bilateral Gaussian filters are not separable; approximate separation results in visual artifacts. Ellipse Boundary Derivation: The boundary of the resulting ellipse in clip space cannot be derived using traditional methods because points on the resulting surface may not lie on the projected plane (x{c,z} \neq x{ani,c,z}). Performance: Increasing simulation resolution for smoother edges requires complex computations that affect real-time performance. Time Complexity: Dominated by the WPCA calculation for each particle (neighbor search and SVD) and the screen-space filtering. The anisotropic transformation adds overhead to the rasterization step compared to simple spheres. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for depth, thickness, and normal buffers, plus particle data. Performance: Designed for real-time applications (video games, VR). Experiments on AMD Ryzen 7 5800H and NVIDIA RTX 3060 show efficient performance. Strengths: Preserves sharp high-frequency details while smoothing jagged edges; avoids over-smoothing of simple Gaussian filters and excessive flattening of bilateral filters. WPCA handles non-uniform particle distributions better than traditional PCA. Limitations: Sensitive to the choice of smoothing kernel parameters; complex boundary derivation for ellipses. Origin: Proposed in 2022 by Ban and Wang. History: Builds on screen-space fluid rendering techniques by Müller et al. [2] and improvements by Truong and Yuksel [16] and Oliveira and Paiva [17]. It addresses the limitations of isotropic point sprites and standard filters in real-time fluid visualization. Usage: Real-time graphics applications such as video games and virtual reality. name: Particle-Based Fire
head: Fuzzy Object Simulation, Primitive Particle Emitter Systems
body: Particle-based fire is a real-time rendering technique that decomposes fire into a set of discrete graphical primitives (particles) regulated by an emitter system. It solves the problem of rendering fuzzy, emissive phenomena efficiently on modern GPU hardware, serving as the standard alternative to prohibitively expensive volumetric rendering. It builds on Particle and Fluid Simulation and is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on discrete particle physics and splatting rather than continuous volume fields or screen-space approximations. Particle-based fire represents the fire medium as a collection of particles Pi, each carrying physical properties (position, velocity) and visual attributes (radius, color, opacity). The simulation updates these particles using physics-based rules, and the rendering projects them onto the 2D image plane for compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Particle emitter parameters, initial particle states (position \mathbf{p}i, velocity \mathbf{v}i, radius ri, color \mathbf{c}i, opacity \alphai), and simulation time step \Delta t. Output: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Each particle i is stored with the following fields: \mathbf{p}i: 3D position vector (x, y, z) \mathbf{v}i: 3D velocity vector (vx, vy, vz) ri: Scalar radius \mathbf{c}i: Color vector (RGB) \alphai: Scalar opacity Steps: 1. Emission: Generate new particles at the emitter source with initial positions and velocities based on turbulence or wind parameters. 2. Simulation: Update particle positions and properties over time \Delta t using physics-based rules such as buoyancy and drag. 3. Projection: Transform particle positions from world space to screen space using the view and projection matrices. 4. Splatting: Project each particle onto the 2D image plane and calculate its screen footprint. 5. Compositing: Accumulate particle contributions to the frame buffer using standard alpha blending for transparency. Parameters: Radius ri: Often enlarged to mitigate atomistic appearance. Particle count: Reduced to improve visual continuity and mitigate atomistic appearance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomistic Appearance: Standard particle fire suffers from appearing "atomistic" and lacking the natural holistic look of fire. Mitigation: Enlarge particle size and reduce particle count to improve visual continuity. A contemporary real-time fire model used in Half-Life 2: Episode 1. It uses a flat view-aligned plane with alpha-blending of colors into a pseudo-random fire pattern to simulate emissive lighting. It achieves fire animation with fewer particles than standard systems by using textured splats based on simple and local dynamics. Wei et al. combined this with the Lattice Boltzmann Model for real-time rendering, displaying around 100 texture splats and rendering the entire image in 15ms. It is chosen for performance-critical scenarios where a holistic look is less critical than speed. Pitfalls include poor scaling of fire size due to the flat geometry, inability to view-align along the y-axis (revealing perspective flaws), and a 5-second repeating texture cycle that limits dynamic change and LOD adjustment. A sophisticated fire model from F.E.A.R. consisting of at least two subsystems: a shader-based flame system and a particle smoke system. External detail helps conceal core flaws. It is chosen for high-quality cinematic effects where multiple layers of complexity are acceptable. Pitfalls include the core fire system being a rigid surface shader that does not evolve in shape over time. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Texture splat variants can render ~100 splats in 15ms. Strengths: Efficient and well-understood for real-time rendering of fuzzy phenomena. Limitations: Can appear atomistic; flat-geometry variants have poor perspective scaling and repetitive animations. When to use: Real-time applications where volumetric rendering is too expensive. When not to use: When a holistic, physically accurate fire appearance is required and performance allows for volumetric methods. Particle-based fire is one of the most efficient and well-understood ways to render fuzzy phenomena in real-time. It emerged as a practical alternative to volumetric rendering, which was considered prohibitively expensive for real-time applications. The technique has been used in numerous games including World of Warcraft, Company of Heroes, Guild Wars, and F.E.A.R.. Research by King et al. and Wei et al. explored textured splats and Lattice Boltzmann models to reduce computational complexity. Realistic Real-Time Rendering of Fire in a Production System, https://clas.iusb.edu/math-compsci/prior-proposals/YVanzineProposal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Particle System Renderer
body: The Particle System Renderer (PSR) is a general-purpose, object-order rendering system that converts discrete, time-evolving particles into rasterized images by managing explicit particle lifecycles and projecting them onto a defined viewport. It solves the visualization problem for Radar Cross Section (RCS) data and other discrete distributions by procedurally generating particles from centroids and accumulating their contributions via a CPU-based linked-list architecture. Unlike Billboards and particles, which rely on fixed 2D quads, or Screen-Space Fluid Rendering Pipeline, which uses GPU-accelerated screen-space techniques, PSR explicitly tracks spawn/die states and supports procedural centroid-based generation on the CPU. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A data file defining particle systems (centroids, shapes, velocities, lifetimes) and a control file defining the environment (viewport, world limits, camera view, time steps). Output: RLE (Run-Length Encoded) image files, one per frame, generated using the Utah Raster Toolkit. Data Structures: Particles and centroids are stored in a dynamic linked list. Particle Node: Contains position, velocity, color, tail length, time of death, time of spawn, spawn source flag, and a dead flag. Centroid Node: Defines the origin and shape (spherical or Cartesian) from which particles are procedurally generated. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Parse the control file to set the viewport, world limits, camera view (position, center of interest, view plane normal, view up vector), and time increment parameters. Initialize the linked list of particles and centroids. 2. Time Step Loop: For each time step: a. Spawn Check: Iterate through the linked list to identify particles marked for spawning based on the time of spawn attribute. Generate new particle systems at the current position of the spawning particle. b. Update Physics: Update particle positions based on velocity using linear movement. c. Death Check: Iterate through the list to identify particles whose current age exceeds their time of death. Mark these particles as dead so they are no longer displayed. d. Rendering: Project the active (non-dead) particles onto the 2D image plane defined by the viewport and camera view. e. Cleanup: Remove or mark dead particles so they are no longer displayed in subsequent frames. 3. View Change (Optional): If a view change is specified in the control file, interpolate the View Plane Normal (VPN) and View Up (VUP) vectors from the start values (svpn, svup) to the finish values (fvpn, fvup) over the specified duration or step count. If the freeze token is present, particle growth is halted during this transition. 4. Output: Write the accumulated pixel data to an RLE file, appending the current frame number to the output filename. Formulas and Parameters: Viewport: Defined by two min/max integer pairs (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}). The range is inclusive. Width W = x{max} - x{min} + 1. World Limits: Defined by min/max integer pairs for clipping, plus front and back clipping planes. View Definition: Requires camera position \mathbf{p}{cam}, center of interest \mathbf{c}{oi}, view plane normal \mathbf{n}{vpn}, and view up vector \mathbf{v}{vup}. Particle Origin (Spherical): Defined by \phi, \theta, r relative to the centroid. Particle Origin (Cartesian): Defined by XYZ coordinates relative to the centroid. Tail Length: A float value specifying the maximum length of the particle's tail. Default is -1, which disables the feature. Time Increment: User-specified step size (seconds) and duration (seconds or number of steps). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Particle: pos: tuple vel: tuple color: tuple taillen: float deathtime: float spawntime: float spawnfrom: str isdead: bool age: float class Centroid: shape: str origin: tuple diameter: float color: tuple class Environment: viewport: tuple worldlimits: tuple clipfront: float clipback: float campos: tuple coi: tuple vpn: tuple vup: tuple stepsize: float durationseconds: float durationsteps: int viewchangeactive: bool svpn: tuple svup: tuple fvpn: tuple fvup: tuple freezegrowth: bool def lerp(a, b, t): return tuple(a[i] + (b[i] - a[i]) t for i in range(len(a))) def projectworldtoscreen(pos, campos, vpn, vup, viewport): # Standard view-space to screen-space projection return (int((pos[0] - viewport[0]) / (viewport[1] - viewport[0] + 1) (viewport[1] - viewport[0] + 1)), int((pos[1] - viewport[2]) / (viewport[3] - viewport[2] + 1) (viewport[3] - viewport[2] + 1))) def isclipped(pos, worldlimits, clipfront, clipback): # Axis-aligned bounding box and depth clipping return not (worldlimits[0] <= pos[0] <= worldlimits[1] and worldlimits[2] <= pos[1] <= worldlimits[3] and clipfront <= pos[2] <= clipback) def generatespawnedparticles(spawnpos, spawnfrom): # Procedural generation from centroid based on spawn parameters return [] def saverle(image, filename): # Write image to RLE file using Utah Raster Toolkit pass def rendersystem(particles, centroids, env): currenttime = 0.0 stepcount = 0 while currenttime < env.durationseconds or stepcount < env.durationsteps: # 1. Spawn Check newparticles = [] for p in particles: if not p.isdead and p.spawntime > 0 and p.age >= p.spawntime: spawned = generatespawnedparticles(p.pos, p.spawnfrom) newparticles.extend(spawned) p.spawntime = -1.0 particles.extend(newparticles) # 2. Update Physics for p in particles: if not p.isdead: p.pos = tuple(p.pos[i] + p.vel[i] env.stepsize for i in range(3)) p.age += env.stepsize # 3. Death Check for p in particles: if not p.isdead and p.deathtime > 0 and p.age >= p.deathtime: p.isdead = True # 4. View Change if env.viewchangeactive: t = stepcount / env.durationsteps if env.durationsteps > 0 else 0.0 env.vpn = lerp(env.svpn, env.fvpn, t) env.vup = lerp(env.svup, env.fvup, t) if env.freezegrowth: pass # System growth halted during view change # 5. Render width = env.viewport[1] - env.viewport[0] + 1 height = env.viewport[3] - env.viewport[2] + 1 image = [[None] width for in range(height)] for p in particles: if not p.isdead: screen = projectworldtoscreen(p.pos, env.campos, env.vpn, env.vup, env.viewport) if not isclipped(p.pos, env.worldlimits, env.clipfront, env.clipback): if 0 <= screen[0] < width and 0 <= screen[1] < height: image[screen[1]][screen[0]] = p.color # 6. Output saverle(image, f"outputframe{stepcount}") currenttime += env.stepsize stepcount += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fade Time: The feature to fade out particle tails after death is defined as a hook but is not implemented. Direction Attribute: The direction attribute, originally intended to work with velocity, is obsolete. Spawn From: The from token for spawning systems currently only supports the generate token (random generation). The read token (from file) is not supported. Viewport Inclusion: The viewport is inclusive; a range of 0 to 10 is 11 pixels wide, not 10. Tail Length: A negative tail length disables the tail feature; it does not imply an infinite tail. Uses 2D textured quads to represent particles; simpler than PSR's explicit linked-list management but lacks the procedural generation features [9045-billboards-and-particles.md]. A GPU-based approach for fluid rendering using screen-space techniques; PSR is a CPU-based, offline renderer [14414-screen-space-fluid-rendering-pipeline.md]. Specialized for fire effects with specific emission and turbulence models; PSR is a general-purpose system [14658-particle-based-fire.md]. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active particles N per time step, as it iterates through a linked list for spawning, updating, and rendering. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of particles, as each particle is stored in a dynamic linked list node. Performance: Performance is limited by CPU processing speed and the overhead of linked list traversal. The system requires the Utah Raster Toolkit for output, which may add I/O overhead. Strengths: Flexible utility for generating particle systems from centroids; supports procedural generation and explicit lifecycle management (spawn, die). Limitations: No GPU acceleration; limited to linear velocity; no implemented tail fading; spawn from file not supported; obsolete features (direction) remain in the syntax. When to use: For legacy RCS data visualization or when explicit control over particle lifecycle and procedural generation from centroids is required on a CPU-only system. When not to use: For real-time rendering, large-scale particle systems requiring GPU acceleration, or when advanced visual effects like tail fading are needed. The Particle System Renderer (PSR) was developed as part of research into methods for viewing Radar Cross Section (RCS) data in three dimensions. It was designed to be a general-purpose system for generating particle systems, with features added to support RCS data rendering while remaining a flexible utility. The system relies on the Utah Raster Toolkit version 3.0 for generating RLE output files. DTIC ADA258905: Methods for Viewing Radar Cross Section Data in Three Dimensions, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA258905, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Particle Systems
head: Steam rendering via particles
body: Particle systems model natural phenomena by generating thousands of discrete particles to simulate change over time, rather than displaying the entire volumetric dataset. Unlike volume or surface generation techniques that render all data, this method represents objects as clouds of primitive particles occupying their volumes, allowing for the simulation of dynamic effects like advection and diffusion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: User-defined particle characteristics (color, initial velocity, lifetime). Outputs: A sequence of rendered frames depicting the dynamic phenomenon. Data Structures: Each particle i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i Velocity \mathbf{v}i Optical properties (color \mathbf{c}i, opacity \alphai, radius ri). Lifetime ti. Steps: 1. Initialization: The user defines inherent characteristics of the particle, such as color, initial velocity, and lifetime. 2. Generation: The algorithm uses these characteristics to generate thousands of particles. 3. Simulation: Particle positions and properties are updated over time to simulate the change of natural phenomena. For steam, this involves simulating advection and diffusion. 4. Rendering: Each 3D model or phenomenon component is represented as a particle with its own position, velocity, and optical properties. These particles are rendered to form the visual output. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def particlesystemsimulation(initialconditions, dt, maxsteps): particles = [] for in range(initialconditions['count']): particles.append({ 'position': list(initialconditions['initialposition']), 'velocity': list(initialconditions['initialvelocity']), 'color': initialconditions['color'], 'lifetime': initialconditions['lifetime'], 'age': 0.0 }) for step in range(maxsteps): for p in particles: # Update position using Euler integration p['position'][0] += p['velocity'][0] dt p['position'][1] += p['velocity'][1] dt p['position'][2] += p['velocity'][2] dt # Update age and handle lifetime p['age'] += dt if p['age'] > p['lifetime']: # Respawn particle at initial conditions p['position'] = list(initialconditions['initialposition']) p['velocity'] = list(initialconditions['initialvelocity']) p['age'] = 0.0 # Rendering is application-specific per source # render(particles) Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point precision may affect particle accumulation over long lifetimes. Performance: Rendering thousands of particles requires efficient culling and batching. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of particles N for simulation and rendering O(N). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of particles O(N). Strengths: Efficient for simulating dynamic, transient phenomena like fire, smoke, and steam. Limitations: The renderer is normally application specific. When to use: When simulating natural phenomena like steam, fire, or terrain features where individual particle dynamics are important. When not to use: When precise volumetric data representation is required for the entire dataset. Particle systems were introduced as a technique to model pieces of natural phenomena by generating thousands of particles to simulate change over time. Early applications include stochastic modeling for terrain by Fournier, Fussell, and Carpenter, and probabilistic algorithms for trees and grass by Reeves and Blau in The Adventures of Andre and Wally B.. Reeves and Blau also used these techniques to model dynamic environments like fire in Star Trek II. The method has been applied to volumetric RCS data rendering and steam rendering via particle systems. DTIC ADA259586: Scientific Visualization of Volumetric Radar Cross Section Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA259586, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChatGPT version of Ct Volume Rendering, https://www.flyriver.com/s/ct-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: gsplat
head: gsplat API
body: gsplat is a unified, high-performance API that continuously integrates low-level scheduling optimizations for constrained environments. It primarily improves the rasterization and training backend rather than changing the scene representation itself. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position \mathbf{p}k, covariance \Sigmak, opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Output: A rasterized 2D image (color and depth) and gradients for training. Data Structures: The method relies on a structured layout of Gaussian attributes to facilitate efficient matrix operations. The core computation uses a matrix multiplication C = AB, where A contains the Gaussian attributes and B contains the pixel-wise accumulation weights. Steps: 1. Attribute Loading: Load Gaussian attributes from global memory. For constrained environments, only Gaussians visible in the current view frustum are loaded from flash storage using quantized integer representations. 2. Projection: Transform 3D Gaussian centers to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. Compute the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} using the Jacobian of the projection transformation. 3. Splat Rasterization: For each tile, determine the contribution of overlapping Gaussians by computing the 2D Gaussian footprint and accumulating weights. 4. Matrix Multiplication: Perform C = AB to compute the final color and depth values, leveraging GPU tensor cores or optimized shader instructions. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the contributions using alpha blending to handle transparency. Parameters: Tile Size: The screen is partitioned into finer tiles to optimize cache locality and multi-GPU scheduling. Quantization: Positions and colors may be quantized to lower precision (e.g., integers) for memory-constrained deployments. Edge Cases: Precision: Mobile-GS performs blending in a lower-precision shader. Visibility: Culling Gaussians outside the view frustum is critical for performance in constrained environments. An optimization technique using warp-level reductions in CUDA to efficiently accumulate gradients during training. Implemented in a custom CUDA kernel, it is applied to improve training efficiency in custom multi-view regularization kernels. Performance: Enables real-time rendering on GPUs and mobile devices. Performance depends on visibility, projected footprint, memory access, and rasterizer implementation rather than Gaussian count alone. Quantized integer representations and lower-precision shaders reduce memory bandwidth pressure. Storage: Internal compression mechanisms like vector quantization (replacing Gaussian attributes with codebook entries) can reduce model size from 75.50 to 5.54 MiB (92.66% reduction) while retaining 25.08 dB PSNR. Scaling: Smaller representations do not automatically imply faster rendering; a pruned model with one-tenth the Gaussians may yield lower frame rates (155.15 versus 193.46 rFPS) due to memory access patterns. Strengths: Unified API, low-level scheduling optimizations, supports constrained environments, accelerates training. Limitations: Frame rate is sensitive to memory access and rasterizer implementation; aggressive pruning can degrade performance despite reduced Gaussian counts. gsplat continuously integrates low-level scheduling optimizations into a unified high-performance API. It underpins variants such as FlashGS, which accelerates forward processing by partitioning the screen into finer tiles for multi-GPU pipelines, and Mobile-GS, which targets smartphone deployment with memory-centric rendering. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting for real-time scene reconstruction: Methods, systems, and trade-offs, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2026.115120, fetched 2026-10-26 Geometry-Grounded Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17835v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Error-aware Streaming Fusion
body: Error-aware Streaming Fusion is a temporal stabilization technique for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that mitigates artifacts caused by warping inaccuracies and appearance variations. It operates by adaptively weighting the fusion of historical splats against current frame predictions based on per-pixel rendering error. Unlike standard streaming methods that may accumulate warping errors or flicker, this method explicitly suppresses unreliable historical contributions and erroneous current-frame predictions to ensure temporal consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of current-frame splats \mathcal{S}t predicted by a multi-view transformer, a set of historical splats \mathcal{S}{t-1} from past keyframes, and the camera parameters for input views. Outputs: A fused set of splats \mathcal{S}{fused} with updated weights and attributes for rendering. Data Structures: Keyframe Buffer: Maintains primitives from a set of past keyframes. In practice, two keyframes are maintained, placed 5 frames apart, each lasting 10 frames. Splat Attributes: Position, covariance/scale, rotation, opacity, and color follow the parent article Splatting. Steps: 1. Render Current Frame: Render the current frame splats \mathcal{S}t to the input views to obtain a reference depth map D{\text{ref}} and color image I{\text{ref}}. 2. Project Historical Splats: For each historical splat sh \in \mathcal{S}{t-1}, project it onto the input views. 3. Render Historical Splats: Render each historical splat sh to the input views to obtain I{\text{hist}} and D{\text{hist}}. 4. Error & Depth Assessment: For each input view, compute the per-pixel error between I{\text{hist}} and I{\text{ref}}, and check if D{\text{hist}} < D{\text{ref}} (historical splat appears in front). 5. Count Unreliable Views: Count the number of input views where sh produces increased rendering error and appears in front of the current frame depth. 6. Weight Historical Splats: If the error increases in more than half of the input views, set the fusion weight of sh to zero (wh = 0). 7. Weight Current Splats: Evaluate current frame splats sc \in \mathcal{S}t predicted by the transformer; if a current splat increases rendering error, assign it zero weight (wc = 0). 8. Identify Static Areas: During the Splat-to-voxel transfer process, identify static areas. 9. Mark Motion Regions: Historical splats undergoing deformation mark their neighboring voxels as regions of motion. 10. Blend Static Attributes: In static areas, retain 50% of the voxel attributes from the past keyframe to enhance temporal continuity. 11. Smooth Transition: Smoothly adjust contributions as older keyframes are replaced by newer ones to ensure seamless temporal transitions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errorawarestreamingfusion(currentsplats, historicalsplats, cameraparams, views, errorthreshold=0.0): """ Fuses current and historical splats based on per-pixel rendering error. errorthreshold: Per-pixel error threshold. Not given in the sources. """ fusedsplats = [] # Step 1: Render current frame to get reference refcolor, refdepth = projectandrasterize(currentsplats, cameraparams, views) # Step 2-6: Assess and weight historical splats for sh in historicalsplats: histcolor, histdepth = projectandrasterize([sh], cameraparams, views) errorviewcount = 0 for view in views: # Per-pixel error calculation (L2 norm of color difference) pixelerror = sum((c1 - c2)2 for c1, c2 in zip(histcolor[view], refcolor[view])) # Check if historical splat is in front of current depth isinfront = all(h < r for h, r in zip(histdepth[view], refdepth[view])) # If error exceeds threshold AND it occludes current frame, count it if pixelerror > errorthreshold and isinfront: errorviewcount += 1 # Step 6: Weight Adjustment if errorviewcount > len(views) / 2: sh.weight = 0.0 else: sh.weight = 1.0 fusedsplats.append(sh) # Step 7: Weight Adjustment for Current Splats for sc in currentsplats: # Evaluate if current splat increases error against reference currenterror = sum((sc.color - refcolor[view]).norm() for view in views) if currenterror > errorthreshold: sc.weight = 0.0 else: sc.weight = 1.0 fusedsplats.append(sc) # Step 8-10: Static Area Identification and Blending staticvoxels = identifystaticvoxels(historicalsplats, currentsplats) for s in fusedsplats: if s.position in staticvoxels: # Retain 50% of voxel attributes from past keyframe pastattrs = getpastkeyframeattributes(s.position) if pastattrs is not None: s.attributes = 0.5 s.attributes + 0.5 pastattrs return fusedsplats def projectandrasterize(splats, cameraparams, views): """Projects splats to screen space and rasterizes to color/depth buffers. """ # Follows standard MVP transformation and rasterization from Splatting colors = {v: [] for v in views} depths = {v: [] for v in views} for s in splats: screenpos = transformtoscreen(s.position, cameraparams) for v in views: colors[v].append(s.color) depths[v].append(s.depth) return colors, depths def identifystaticvoxels(historicalsplats, currentsplats): """Identifies static voxels by marking neighbors of deforming historical splats as motion. """ motionvoxels = set() for sh in historicalsplats: if hasdeformed(sh): for neighbor in getvoxelneighbors(sh.position): motionvoxels.add(neighbor) allvoxels = {s.position for s in currentsplats} | {s.position for s in historicalsplats} return allvoxels - motionvoxels def hasdeformed(splat): """Checks if a splat has undergone deformation. """ return splat.scalechange > 0.0 or splat.rotationchange > 0.0 def getvoxelneighbors(position): """Returns adjacent voxel coordinates. """ return [(position.x + dx, position.y + dy, position.z + dz) for dx in (-1, 0, 1) for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dz in (-1, 0, 1) if not (dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0)] def getpastkeyframeattributes(position): """Retrieves stored attributes from the past keyframe buffer. """ return cachedattributes.get(position, None) Parameters: Keyframe Interval: 5 frames apart. Keyframe Duration: 10 frames each. Static Blend Factor: 50% (0.5) of voxel attributes from the past keyframe. Error Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warping Inaccuracies: The method specifically targets artifacts from warping errors, appearance variation, and new objects. Motion Regions: Historical splats undergoing deformation mark neighboring voxels as motion, preventing incorrect static blending in dynamic areas. Transformer Errors: Current frame splats predicted by the multi-view transformer can be erroneous; the error check prevents these from corrupting the scene. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for rendering historical splats and current splats to assess error. The cost depends on the number of historical splats and views. Memory Complexity: Maintains primitives from a set of past keyframes. In practice, two keyframes are stored. Strengths: Mitigates warping inaccuracies, reduces temporal flickering, and improves reconstruction quality in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Requires rendering multiple passes for error assessment, which increases computational cost. Relies on the accuracy of the multi-view transformer for current frame prediction. When to Use: Dynamic scenes where temporal stability is critical and warping artifacts are prevalent. When Not to Use: Static scenes where temporal fusion is unnecessary, or real-time performance is severely constrained. Origin: Introduced in "Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". History: Developed to address temporal flickering and artifacts in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for video. It extends static-scene-trained models to video by merging historical and current frame information. Usage: Used in history-aware streaming reconstruction for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting. Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: History-Aware Streaming Reconstruction
head: Dynamic Scene Fusion
body: History-Aware Streaming Reconstruction is a zero-shot extension for dynamic scenes that uses historical information to fuse primitives across time, avoiding error accumulation and redundant primitives. It generalizes static-scene-trained feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting models to video by merging previous and current frame information to model occluded regions and improve temporal stability. Unlike per-frame reconstruction methods prone to flickering, this method merges history to provide a consistent set of primitives. The method operates in a streaming fashion, maintaining a set of past keyframes and fusing their information with the current frame. Inputs: Current frame input views and previous keyframe primitives. Outputs: Refined Gaussian primitives for the current frame. Data Structures: Splat-Voxel Representation: A hybrid structure where splat features are deposited onto a coarse-to-fine voxel grid. Keyframe Buffer: Maintains primitives from a set of past keyframes, with two keyframes placed 5 frames apart, each lasting 10 frames. Steps: 1. Scene Flow Estimation and Deformation: Compute triangulated scene flow from input views to estimate motion between the current frame and past keyframes. Triangulation: Solve for the closest point to N camera rays originating from 2D projections pi^t. This depends on depth-based visibility, determined by comparing the projected depth of a splat with the depth map obtained by rendering all splats to a given view using alpha blending. If the projected depth is smaller, the splat is unoccluded. Deformation: Use an Embedded Deformation Graph (EDG) based on optical flow to identify regions of significant movement. Select keypoints and compute deformations. Let \deltap be the deformation displacement. If the distance to anchors is greater than \lambda \bar{d} (where \bar{d} is the mean distance between anchor points and \lambda \in [0.2, 0.5]), set \deltap to zero. Apply these deformations to the previous keyframe primitives to warp them to the current frame. 2. Warping and Filtering: Warp primitives from the past frame to the current frame using the computed scene flow. Filter out primitives with large warping errors. 3. Splat Fusion (Deposit): Deposit primitives from both the warped past frame and the current frame onto the Splat-Voxel representation. Extract input image features using a multi-view transformer, outputting pixel-aligned Gaussian splats with associated features. Deposit splat features onto the coarse-to-fine voxel grid using the decoded position. 4. Fuse-and-Refine: Process the combined voxel representation through a secondary sparse voxel transformer to output final Gaussian parameters. Let \mathbf{G}j be the initial Gaussian rendering attributes on voxels obtained through Splat Fusion. Let \mathbf{E}j be the fused splat feature. Compute the refinement offset \Delta \mathbf{G}j using a fine-level MLP: \Delta \mathbf{G}j = \text{MLP}{fine}([\mathbf{O}j, \mathbf{E}j]) where \mathbf{O}j represents the voxel features. Update the Gaussian parameters: \mathbf{G}'j = \mathbf{G}j + \Delta \mathbf{G}j \tag{12} 5. Output: The resulting refined primitives \mathbf{G}'j are used for rendering. Parameters: \lambda: Hyperparameter controlling the motion graph's extent, typically between 0.2 and 0.5. Keyframe spacing: Two keyframes placed 5 frames apart, each lasting 10 frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Depth-based visibility checks are required during triangulation to correctly identify unoccluded splats. Motion Extent: Large motions beyond the deformation graph's extent (\lambda \bar{d}) are treated as zero displacement. Performance: Runs at 15 fps with a 350ms delay on a single H100 GPU. Resolution: Tested with two view inputs of resolution 320 \times 240. Capacity: The model processes around 200k primitives within 15ms for the refinement step. Strengths: Improves temporal stability, handles occlusions, and avoids redundant primitives compared to per-frame methods. Limitations: Requires maintaining a buffer of past keyframes; performance depends on the efficiency of scene flow estimation and deformation. This method was introduced in "Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods, which are typically trained on static scenes and struggle with dynamic scenes due to flickering and lack of temporal coherence. By leveraging historical information, it extends these models to dynamic scenes without additional training. name: Fuse-and-Refine Integration into DepthSplat
head: DepthSplat + Ours
body: This method integrates the "Fuse-and-Refine" module into the DepthSplat framework to improve feed-forward novel view synthesis. It addresses the limitation of standard DepthSplat by enhancing feature aggregation and refinement, resulting in higher fidelity 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstructions from sparse input views. It distinguishes itself from the base DepthSplat implementation by adding a specific fusion and refinement stage that boosts metrics like PSNR and LPIPS, and from sibling methods like 4DGS and GS-LRM by offering superior performance when evaluated under identical sparse-view constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images (typically N=2 for training, N=4 for evaluation) and their corresponding camera poses. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) suitable for rasterization via DepthSplat. Data Structures: The method builds upon the DepthSplat architecture. The core addition is the Fuse-and-Refine module. Specific internal tensor layouts for this module are not detailed in the provided sources, other than the output resolution being compatible with the downstream DepthSplat pipeline. Steps: 1. Base Feature Extraction: The input images are processed by the DepthSplat backbone to extract initial features. 2. Fuse-and-Refine Integration: The Fuse-and-Refine module is inserted into the DepthSplat pipeline. This module aggregates and refines the extracted features to produce a more robust representation for Gaussian parameter prediction. The exact internal mechanism of the Fuse-and-Refine module (e.g., attention heads, convolutional layers) is not specified in the provided notes, but it is described as a distinct module that improves upon the baseline. 3. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: The refined features are used to predict the 3D Gaussian parameters (mean, covariance, opacity, color). 4. Rasterization: The predicted Gaussians are rasterized using the DepthSplat renderer to generate novel views. Parameters: Training Resolution: 128 \times 192 pixels. Training Data: Subset of the DL3DV dataset, consisting of 1,000 scenes. Input Views (Training): 2 views per scene. Input Views (Evaluation): 4 views per scene. Test Scenes: 10 scenes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution: The method was evaluated at a reduced resolution (128 \times 192). Performance at higher resolutions is not given in the sources. Generalization: The method is evaluated on generalization from 2 input views to 4 input views. Performance on other view counts is not given. The Multi-View Feature Extraction Pipeline aggregates geometry-aware features from multiple input views to produce a unified low-resolution feature tensor. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the DL3DV dataset (10 test scenes, 4 input views) after retraining on a subset (1,000 scenes, 2 input views) at 128 \times 192 resolution. The integration of the Fuse-and-Refine module into DepthSplat yields the following improvements over the baseline DepthSplat: PSNR: Increases from 16.57 to 17.66. LPIPS: Decreases from 0.4272 to 0.4019. LPIS: Increases from 0.4108 to 0.4426. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly outperforms baselines like 4DGS and GS-LRM in feed-forward novel view synthesis tasks. Limitations: The provided evaluation is limited to a specific dataset (DL3DV), resolution (128 \times 192), and view configuration (2 to 4 views). Performance on other datasets or resolutions is not given. The Fuse-and-Refine module was proposed in the paper "Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". The authors validated the generalization capability of this module by integrating it into the publicly available DepthSplat implementation. The method is designed for feed-forward novel view synthesis, aiming to improve the quality of 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions from sparse input views. name: Multi-View Feature Extraction Pipeline
head: Cross-View U-Net Fusion, Multi-View Branch
body: The Multi-View Feature Extraction Pipeline aggregates geometry-aware features from multiple input views to produce a unified low-resolution feature tensor. It distinguishes itself by combining multi-view transformer features, monocular depth priors, and cost-volume matching evidence, outputting a fixed H/4 \times W/4 resolution tensor suitable for downstream compression or rendering. Inputs: N input views with images, camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics), and near/far depth ranges. Monocular depth prior model (DepthAnything V2). Outputs: Fused feature tensor F1 \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}}, where N is the number of views, C is the feature dimension, and H, W are the input image dimensions. Data Structures: Multi-view features (F{mv}): Tensor of shape N \times C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}. Monocular features (F{mono}): Tensor of shape N \times C{mono} \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}. Cost volumes (V{cv}): Tensor of shape N \times D \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}, where D is the number of depth candidates. Fused features (F1): Tensor of shape N \times C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}. Steps: 1. Per-View Feature Extraction: Extract per-view features using a lightweight ResNet-style backbone. 2. Multi-View Transformer Aggregation: Process the per-view features with a multi-view Transformer composed of alternating self-attention and cross-view attention layers. For N > 2 views, restrict cross-view interaction to nearby source views to maintain computational efficiency. Resize the resulting features to a common spatial resolution of \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}, yielding F{mv} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}}. 3. Cost-Volume Construction: Construct per-view cost volumes using plane-sweep stereo. For each reference view, sample depth candidates within the near–far range. Warp source view features to the reference camera at each candidate depth using known camera parameters. Compute correlations between warped source features and reference features. Aggregate correlations from selected neighboring views. Dataset-Specific Handling: For RealEstate10K and ACID: Construct the cost volume directly from the \frac{1}{4}-resolution multi-view features. For DL3DV: Due to high computational overhead from large resolution and many views, bilinearly downsample the multi-view features to a lower resolution, compute the cost volume, then bilinearly upsample the result back to \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}. 4. Monocular Geometric Prior Extraction: Extract per-view geometric priors independently using a monocular depth branch initialized from DepthAnything V2. Resize these features to \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}. 5. Cross-View U-Net Fusion: Fuse monocular geometric features, multi-view matching features, and cost-volume information using a cross-view U-Net. Retain the low-resolution U-Net representation at \frac{1}{4} input resolution as the final output F1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiviewfeatureextractionpipeline(images, cameras, nearfarranges, datasetname): """ Extracts and fuses multi-view features. Args: images: List of N images, shape (H, W, 3). cameras: List of N camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics). nearfarranges: List of N tuples (near, far). datasetname: String, one of 'RealEstate10K', 'ACID', 'DL3DV'. Returns: F1: Fused feature tensor, shape (N, C, H/4, W/4). """ N = len(images) # Step 1: Per-View Feature Extraction # ResNet-style backbone perviewfeatures = [] for img in images: # Backbone returns features at original resolution feat = resnetbackbone(img) perviewfeatures.append(feat) # Step 2: Multi-View Transformer Aggregation # Transformer with alternating self- and cross-view attention # Cross-view interaction restricted to nearby views if N > 2 mvtransformer = MultiViewTransformer() Fmvraw = mvtransformer(perviewfeatures, cameras) # Resize to H/4 x W/4 Fmv = resizebilinear(Fmvraw, targetsize=(images[0].shape[0] // 4, images[0].shape[1] // 4)) # Step 3: Cost-Volume Construction costvolumes = [] for i in range(N): reffeat = Fmv[i] refcam = cameras[i] near, far = nearfarranges[i] # Sample depth candidates depthcandidates = sampledepthcandidates(near, far) # Warp source features and compute correlations # Select neighboring views based on dataset or proximity sourceindices = getneighboringviews(i, N) cv = planesweepstereo( reffeat=reffeat, sourcefeats=[Fmv[j] for j in sourceindices], sourcecams=[cameras[j] for j in sourceindices], refcam=refcam, depthcandidates=depthcandidates) # Dataset-specific resolution handling if datasetname == 'DL3DV': # Downsample before computation, upsample after # Note: Fmv is already at 1/4 resolution. # The source says "bilinearly downsample the multi-view features # to a lower spatial resolution for cost-volume computation". # We assume a further downsampling factor 'k' for DL3DV. # Since 'k' is not specified, we note the operation. cvlowres = resizebilinear(cv, targetsize=(cv.shape[2] // 2, cv.shape[3] // 2)) # Placeholder factor # Recompute or interpolate? Source says "compute cost volume" at lower res. # This implies warping and correlation at lower res. # For implementation clarity, we assume the warping/correlation # is performed on the downsampled features. cvlowres = planesweepstereo( reffeat=resizebilinear(reffeat, targetsize=(reffeat.shape[2] // 2, reffeat.shape[3] // 2)), sourcefeats=[resizebilinear(Fmv[j], targetsize=(Fmv[j].shape[2] // 2, Fmv[j].shape[3] // 2)) for j in sourceindices], sourcecams=[cameras[j] for j in sourceindices], refcam=refcam, depthcandidates=depthcandidates) cv = resizebilinear(cvlowres, targetsize=(reffeat.shape[2], reffeat.shape[3])) else: # RealEstate10K and ACID: Direct construction from 1/4 resolution pass costvolumes.append(cv) # Step 4: Monocular Geometric Prior Extraction monocularbranch = DepthAnythingV2() Fmonoraw = [] for img in images: # Extract geometric priors independently monofeat = monocularbranch(img) Fmonoraw.append(monofeat) # Resize to H/4 x W/4 Fmono = [resizebilinear(f, targetsize=(images[0].shape[0] // 4, images[0].shape[1] // 4)) for f in Fmonoraw] # Step 5: Cross-View U-Net Fusion # Fuse Fmv, Fmono, and costvolumes crossviewunet = CrossViewUNet() F1 = crossviewunet(Fmv, Fmono, costvolumes) return F1 Parameters: Spatial resolution scaling factor: 1/4 of the input resolution. Feature dimension C: Not given in the sources. Number of depth candidates D: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: DL3DV Overhead: Large spatial resolution and many input views cause high computational and memory overhead during cost-volume construction. Mitigated by temporary bilinear downsampling before computation and upsampling back to 1/4 resolution. Near/Far Range: Incorrect near/far ranges will lead to incorrect depth sampling and warped features. Time Complexity: Dominated by the multi-view transformer and cost-volume construction. Cost-volume construction is O(N \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W) per view, where D is the number of depth candidates. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the cost volumes, which require storing correlations for each depth candidate. Strengths: Combines explicit geometric matching (cost volume) with learned features (transformer) and monocular priors. Limitations: High memory usage for high-resolution inputs or many views (mitigated for DL3DV). When to use: When geometry-aware multi-view feature fusion is required for downstream tasks like compression or rendering. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and monocular features alone are sufficient. The method is part of the FeCoSplat framework, which builds on DepthSplat. It was introduced in "FeCoSplat: Feedback-Guided Compression for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". name: Data Structure and Storage
body: This family defines the memory layouts, loading interfaces, and indexing strategies required to store volumetric primitives (splats) for efficient GPU rasterization. It solves the problem of transferring large-scale point-cloud or Gaussian data from CPU memory to GPU textures while maintaining fast access for rendering and picking. It differs from sibling articles by focusing on the storage and loading mechanics rather than the rendering pipeline, anti-aliasing, or sorting algorithms. The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized. All methods in this family store primitive data in GPU-accessible buffers or textures, load them asynchronously to prevent main-thread blocking, and maintain separate indexing structures to decouple source data from display parameters. Rendering transformations and compositing are handled by the parent Splatting. Generates initial splat primitives from volumetric data using gradient-based and uniform grid sampling to balance high-frequency detail capture with smooth region coverage. Chosen when an optimal, sparse set of splat positions is required without excessive redundancy. Defines the mechanism for storing and accessing splat primitive data within GPU-accessible 3D textures, enabling efficient hardware-accelerated rasterization. Sets itself apart by organizing per-primitive data into structured texture records that leverage GPU hardware filtering and caching. An abstract interface designed for the asynchronous loading of 3D Gaussian Splat data, returning a structured LoadResult upon completion. Distinguished by its non-blocking callback mechanism and specific handling of spherical harmonic coefficient packing for GPU consumption. Constructs a hierarchical level-of-detail (HLOD) octree for Gaussian splats aligned to world axes, grouping splats into leaves with bounded counts and ordering them by importance. Differs from standard splatting by pre-computing a spatial hierarchy and bounding volumes to prevent false resident culls and optimize memory access. An abstract class extending Splats that provides fixed packed storage with a visible-index contract for rendering and CPU reads, separating source opacity from display fade. IndexedSplatsOptions: capacity (number), layerSize (number), numSh (number), blockBits (number), packedOpacityGroups (boolean, optional). IndexedSplats fields: layerSize (readonly), numSh (readonly 0-4), opacities (SplatOpacityTable), sourceIndices (Uint32Array), visibleIndices (Uint32Array), sourceArrays, sourceCenters, sourceTextures, indexTexture, blockBits (readonly), disposed, uploadQueue (PendingUploads), spatialChunks, spatialBoundsBytes. IndexedSplats differs from Splats by maintaining separate sourceIndices and visibleIndices arrays, allowing opacity fading for display without altering source data used in picking. The data structures and loading interfaces described here originate from the Gaussian-Splat-Lite repository, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimized for web-based rendering environments. The architecture was developed to address performance bottlenecks in loading and storing large Gaussian splat clouds in JavaScript, leveraging Web Workers for asynchronous I/O and WebGL textures for GPU storage. name: Seed Generation for Initial Splats
head: Gradient and Uniform Grid Seeding, Initial Splat Position Generation
body: This method generates the initial set of splat primitives for volume rendering by combining gradient-based edge detection with uniform grid sampling. It solves the problem of sparse or uneven primitive distribution, ensuring that high-frequency details are captured by gradient-weighted sampling while smooth regions are covered by a uniform grid. It differs from sibling methods like World-aligned lattice octree bake by using a fixed budget split rather than hierarchical spatial partitioning, and from Splat Data Structure (ISplatSource) by focusing on the creation of positions rather than their storage. Inputs: Volume data V with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz (total voxels N{vox}). Target seed count N{target}. Gradient threshold \tau = 0.1. Exclusion radius r = 2 voxels. Grid coverage share S{grid} = 0.4 (40%). Outputs: A list of initial splat positions P = \{p1, p2,..., pk\} where k \le N{target}. Data Structures: GradientMap: 3D array of normalized gradient magnitudes, same size as V. CandidateList: List of voxel coordinates (x,y,z) passing the gradient threshold. PoissonDiskSampler: Maintains a spatial hash grid of exclusion zones to enforce minimum distance r. Steps: 1. Compute Gradients: Calculate Sobel gradients in all three dimensions for every voxel. Compute the normalized gradient magnitude g(x,y,z) for each voxel. 2. Filter Candidates: Identify voxels where g(x,y,z) > 0.1. Store these in CandidateList. 3. Poisson-Disk Sampling: Apply gradient-weighted Poisson-disk sampling on CandidateList with exclusion radius r=2. This selects a subset of high-gradient voxels, ensuring they are spatially separated. Let this set be P{edge}. 4. Calculate Grid Spacing: Determine the number of grid seeds N{grid} required to fill the remaining budget (40\% of N{target}). The grid spacing s is calculated such that the volume is tiled: s = \left(\frac{N{vox}}{N{grid}}\right)^{1/D} where D is the dimensionality (typically 3). 5. Generate Uniform Seeds: Create a uniform grid with spacing s across the volume bounds. Let this set be P{grid}. 6. Combine and Cap: Merge P{edge} and P{grid}. The default seeder enforces a 60/40 split, capping P{edge} at 60% of N{target} and P{grid} at 40% of N{target}. 7. GPU Execution: Run the seeding process on GPU (CUDA/MPS) if available. Parameters: Seed Target (N{target}): N{target} = \min\left(10000, \max\left(100, \left\lfloor \frac{N{vox}}{2^{1/D}} \right\rfloor\right)\right) Gradient Threshold: 0.1. Exclusion Radius: 2 voxels. Grid Share: 40\% of the seed budget. Edge Cases: If N{vox} / 2^{1/D} < 100, N{target} defaults to 100. Grid spacing is clamped to a minimum of 2 voxels to prevent overly dense uniform sampling in small volumes. The final retained count may be lower than N{target} due to post-fit culling (see Dynamic operations). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generateseeds(nx, ny, nz, data, D=3): # data is a flat list of length nxnynz def idx(x, y, z): return x ny nz + y nz + z # 1. Compute gradient magnitudes mag = [0.0] (nx ny nz) maxm = 0.0 for x in range(nx): for y in range(ny): for z in range(nz): gx = data[idx(min(x+1, nx-1), y, z)] - data[idx(max(x-1, 0), y, z)] gy = data[idx(x, min(y+1, ny-1), z)] - data[idx(x, max(y-1, 0), z)] gz = data[idx(x, y, min(z+1, nz-1))] - data[idx(x, y, max(z-1, 0))] m = math.sqrt(gx2 + gy2 + gz2) mag[idx(x, y, z)] = m if m > maxm: maxm = m normmag = [m / maxm if maxm > 0 else m for m in mag] # 2. Filter candidates candidates = [] for i, m in enumerate(normmag): if m > 0.1: x, rem = divmod(i, ny nz) y, z = divmod(rem, nz) candidates.append((x, y, z)) # 3. Poisson-disk sampling edgeseeds = [] r = 2 cellsize = r / math.sqrt(D) grid = {} def dist(a, b): return math.sqrt((a[0]-b[0])2 + (a[1]-b[1])2 + (a[2]-b[2])2) for p in candidates: gx, gy, gz = math.floor(p[0]/cellsize), math.floor(p[1]/cellsize), math.floor(p[2]/cellsize) valid = True for dx in range(-2, 3): for dy in range(-2, 3): for dz in range(-2, 3): key = (gx+dx, gy+dy, gz+dz) if key in grid: for existing in grid[key]: if dist(p, existing) < r: valid = False; break if not valid: break if not valid: break if not valid: break if valid: edgeseeds.append(p) grid[(gx, gy, gz)] = grid.get((gx, gy, gz), []) + [p] # 4. Calculate targets rawtarget = max(100, math.floor(nx ny nz / (2 (1/D)))) Ntarget = min(10000, rawtarget) Nedge = math.floor(0.6 Ntarget) Ngrid = math.floor(0.4 Ntarget) # 5. Cap edge seeds edgeseeds = edgeseeds[:Nedge] # 6. Generate uniform grid seeds spacing = max(2, math.floor((nx ny nz / Ngrid) (1/D))) gridseeds = [] for x in range(0, nx, spacing): for y in range(0, ny, spacing): for z in range(0, nz, spacing): gridseeds.append((x, y, z)) # 7. Cap grid seeds and combine gridseeds = gridseeds[:Ngrid] allseeds = edgeseeds + gridseeds return allseeds A technique that provides a preview of the selected seeds during the seed selecting process. This is part of an enhanced isosurface rendering approach involving voxel selecting and selection-based coloring. Time Complexity: O(N{vox}) for gradient computation and candidate filtering; Poisson-disk sampling scales with the number of candidates and spatial hash lookups. Memory Complexity: O(N{vox}) for gradient storage and candidate lists. Execution: Runs on GPU (CUDA/MPS) when available to prevent main-thread blocking. Strengths: Ensures coverage of smooth regions (via grid) and edges (via gradient). Limitations: The final retained count may be lower than requested due to post-fit culling. The method is described in the context of "Luxar," a Gaussian splatting framework for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualization of multidimensional scientific data. The specific seed generation strategy (60% gradient, 40% uniform) is the default "auto" seeder used in single-pass fitting reported in the source. The concept of seed preview is associated with enhanced isosurface rendering techniques. name: Splat Texture Layout & Mapping
head: Splat Data Texture Mapping
body: This method defines the GPU-accessible memory layout for volumetric splat primitives, mapping discrete splat data into two 3D textures backed by Uint32Array buffers to enable efficient attribute fetching during rasterization. It standardizes the storage structure so each splat occupies two 16-byte texture records. Inputs: Initial splat capacity and primitive data. Outputs: Two 3D textures backed by Uint32Array buffers, containing the mapped splat data. Data Structures: Each splat corresponds to two 16-byte texture records within the 3D textures. The total capacity is determined by getTextureSize(inputCapacity).maxSplats. Steps: 1. Calculate the maximum splat capacity using getTextureSize(inputCapacity).maxSplats. 2. If the input capacity differs from maxSplats, allocate new Uint32Array buffers of size maxSplats 4 and copy the original data. 3. Compute the layer bits and source layer mask for coordinate mapping. 4. Map each splat index to a 3D texture coordinate (ivec3). Formulas: The layer index within the 3D texture is derived from the splat's height and the texture width bits: \text{layerBits} = \text{SPLAT\TEX\WIDTH\BITS} + \lceil \log2(\text{height}) \rceil \text{sourceLayerMask} = 2^{\text{layerBits}} - 1 Parameters: SPLATTEXWIDTHBITS: Not given in the sources. height: The height dimension used in the layer bits calculation. Edge Cases: Capacity Mismatch: If the input capacity does not match the texture's maximum splat capacity, reallocation and copying are required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mapsplatdata(inputcapacity, inputdata): # 1. Calculate maximum splat capacity maxsplats = gettexturesize(inputcapacity).maxsplats # 2. Allocate and copy if capacity differs if inputcapacity != maxsplats: buffersize = maxsplats 4 texturebuffers = [[0] buffersize for in range(2)] texturebuffers[0][:len(inputdata)] = inputdata texturebuffers[1][:len(inputdata)] = inputdata else: texturebuffers = [[0] (inputcapacity 4) for in range(2)] texturebuffers[0][:len(inputdata)] = inputdata texturebuffers[1][:len(inputdata)] = inputdata return texturebuffers def calculatelayerbits(height, splattexwidthbits): # 3. Compute layer bits and mask layerbits = splattexwidthbits + math.ceil(math.log2(height)) sourcelayermask = (1 << layerbits) - 1 return layerbits, sourcelayermask def calculatesplatcoordinate(splatindex, layerbits, sourcelayermask): # 4. Map splat index to 3D texture coordinate (ivec3) # The exact bit-packing for x, y, z coordinates is not specified in the sources. # Standard practice decomposes the linear index into 3D coordinates. return (0, 0, 0) This variant organizes per-primitive texture data into large 2D atlas textures to leverage GPU hardware filtering and caching, avoiding multiple texture bindings and software-based sampling overhead. It builds on Splat Texture Layout & Mapping by consolidating individual primitive textures into a unified structure for efficient, filtered attribute fetching during rendering. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to maxSplats 4 for the Uint32Array backing plus texture storage overhead. Access time depends on texture sampling hardware efficiency. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Leverages GPU hardware filtering and caching; avoids multiple texture bindings and software-based sampling overhead. Limitations: Requires careful management of texture dimensions and capacity limits. When to Use: Use when efficient attribute fetching via hardware filtering is required and the scene size fits within texture volume constraints. The method is used in GPU-accelerated splatting implementations to manage primitive data storage. It is referenced in the gaussian-splat-lite library for streaming large scenes. name: Hardware Accelerated Texture Atlases
head: Indirect Texture Sampling for Splatting, Texture Atlas Splatting
body: Hardware Accelerated Texture Atlases organize per-primitive texture data into large 2D atlas textures to leverage GPU hardware filtering and caching, thereby avoiding multiple texture bindings and software-based sampling overhead. This method builds on Splat Texture Layout & Mapping by consolidating individual primitive textures into a unified structure that enables efficient, filtered attribute fetching during rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: P splats, each associated with a small fixed-resolution texture of size T \times T texels; C total attribute channels across all splats; GPU maximum texture dimensions. Outputs: One or more large 2D atlas textures; an indirection buffer mapping primitive IDs to atlas coordinates. Data Structures: 1. Atlas Texture(s): Large 2D textures containing packed T \times T charts. The layout is determined by GPU capabilities. If the total channels C exceed the maximum supported by a single CUDA texture object (typically 4), multiple atlases are created. For example, one atlas may store Albedo (RGB) and Roughness (A), while another stores Tangent Normals (RGB) and Metallic (A). 2. Indirection Buffer: A buffer storing the top-left corner coordinates (chart\idx\x, chart\idx\y) for each primitive's texture chart within the atlas. This maps primitive IDs to their specific location in the atlas grid. Parameters: T: Fixed resolution of each primitive's small texture, typically a power of 2. N{chartsx}, N{chartsy}: Total number of charts along the width and height of the atlas, respectively. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Atlas Dimensions: Calculate the maximum atlas dimensions supported by the GPU. Determine how many T \times T textures fit along each dimension (N{chartsx}, N{chartsy}). 2. Calculate Atlas Count: Compute the total number of textures per atlas based on channel constraints (e.g., max 4 channels per CUDA texture object). Determine the total number of atlases needed to store all P \times C textures. 3. Construct Atlases: Pack the P \times C \times T \times T texel data into the atlas textures. Assign each primitive's texture to a specific chart position within the atlas. 4. Build Indirection Buffer: For each primitive k, store the top-left chart coordinates (chart\idx\xk, chart\idx\yk) in the indirection buffer. Rendering (Hardware Accelerated Texture Sampling): For a given primitive k and local coordinates (u, v): 1. Normalize Coordinates: Map local coordinates to normalized texture coordinates (s, t) \in [0, 1] \times [0, 1]. 2. Retrieve Chart Coordinates: Look up (chart\idx\x, chart\idx\y) for primitive k from the indirection buffer. 3. Compute Atlas Coordinates: Calculate the normalized coordinates within the atlas texture using the following formulas: s{atlas} = \frac{chart\idx\x \cdot T + s \cdot T}{N{chartsx} \cdot T} t{atlas} = \frac{chart\idx\y \cdot T + t \cdot T}{N{chartsy} \cdot T} 4. Sample: Perform hardware-accelerated bilinear filtering using the CUDA tex2D() intrinsic: ak(x, y) = \text{BilinearFilter}(atlas, s{atlas}, t{atlas}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def bilinearfilter(texarray, s, t): """Standard bilinear interpolation for a 2D texture array.""" h, w = texarray.shape s0 = int(math.floor(s (w - 1))) s1 = min(s0 + 1, w - 1) t0 = int(math.floor(t (h - 1))) t1 = min(t0 + 1, h - 1) ws = s (w - 1) - s0 wt = t (h - 1) - t0 return (texarray[t0, s0] (1 - ws) (1 - wt) + texarray[t0, s1] ws (1 - wt) + texarray[t1, s0] (1 - ws) wt + texarray[t1, s1] ws wt) def constructatlas(primitives, T, maxatlaswidth, maxatlasheight, maxchannelsperatlas): chartsperatlasx = maxatlaswidth // T chartsperatlasy = maxatlasheight // T chartsperatlas = chartsperatlasx chartsperatlasy C = primitives[0].channels texturesperprimitive = math.ceil(C / maxchannelsperatlas) totaltextures = len(primitives) texturesperprimitive numatlases = math.ceil(totaltextures / chartsperatlas) atlases = [None] numatlases indirectionbuffer = [] currentatlasidx = 0 currentchartidx = 0 for pidx, primitive in enumerate(primitives): atlasidx = currentatlasidx chartidx = currentchartidx chartx = chartidx % chartsperatlasx charty = chartidx // chartsperatlasx indirectionbuffer.append({ 'primitiveid': pidx, 'atlasidx': atlasidx, 'chartidxx': chartx, 'chartidxy': charty }) if atlases[atlasidx] is None: atlases[atlasidx] = [[0.0] maxatlaswidth for in range(maxatlasheight)] # Pack T x T x C data into atlas at (chartx T, charty T) currentchartidx += 1 if currentchartidx >= chartsperatlas: currentchartidx = 0 currentatlasidx += 1 return atlases, indirectionbuffer def sampletexture(primitiveidx, u, v, atlases, indirectionbuffer, T, Nchartsx, Nchartsy): s = u t = v info = indirectionbuffer[primitiveidx] chartx = info['chartidxx'] charty = info['chartidxy'] atlasidx = info['atlasidx'] # Formula from source: (chartidx T + s T) / (Ncharts T) satlas = (chartx + s) / Nchartsx tatlas = (charty + t) / Nchartsy atlas = atlases[atlasidx] color = bilinearfilter(atlas, satlas, tatlas) return color A rendering technique where texture sampling is performed using GPU hardware filtering (e.g., CUDA tex2D()) rather than software interpolation. It maps primitive local coordinates to normalized atlas coordinates and retrieves values via bilinear filtering, leveraging dedicated texture caching for significant performance gains over manual global memory access. A process applied after shape/location refinement to generate a single texture atlas per splat by blending color information from multiple cameras. Unlike Yang et al. [2006] which uses view-dependent dynamic texture selection, or Sibbing et al. [2013] which uses a single texture per splat with three-pass rendering, this method blends multiple images into one atlas per splat to reduce inaccuracies from misalignments or irregular lighting. It works for splats even when they partially occlude each other, producing seamless transitions across surfaces. Performance: Significantly faster than software-based sampling approaches due to the use of dedicated texture caching and filtering hardware. Improves performance by avoiding multiple texture bindings during rendering, reducing API overhead. Memory: Requires large 2D atlas textures. The number of atlases depends on GPU texture object channel limits (typically 4) and total attribute channels. Limitations: CUDA texture objects typically support up to 4 channels; exceeding this requires splitting attributes across multiple atlases, which increases complexity. Use Cases: Suitable for non-specular scenes where high-quality material and normal texture splatting is required, capable of reaching performance levels comparable to vanilla 3DGS on NeRF Synthetic datasets. The technique is detailed in "TextureSplat: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the concept of Ewa splatting [Gross 2002]. The multi-texturing aspect is derived from work on textured splat-based point clouds for handheld devices, which itself references Pagés et al. [2015] for the blending approach.
