name: Stroke-based splatting
head: Brush stroke rendering
body: Stroke-based splatting (SBR) is a point cloud visualization technique that applies concepts of stroke-based rendering to surface-aligned splatting, shaping each object-aligned splat as a brush stroke and orienting it according to globally coherent tangent vectors to create a painterly depiction of the scanned cloud. It solves the problem of pixelized artifacts and poor shape perception in low-resolution scans or close-up interactions, where standard splats become larger than small regions of pixels. Unlike image-space non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) which applies strokes to a 2D image, SBR applies brush strokes in 3D space, avoiding shortcomings in flexible 3D interaction or noisy data. It provides clearer perception of object curvature and higher visual quality than surface-aligned elliptical splats, especially for delicate shapes like human faces. The method is divided into two stages: a preprocessing step where parameters are extracted from the input point cloud, and a multi-pass rendering step where the stroke-based splatting technique is applied. Input: An unstructured point cloud dataset P = \{pi\}, where each point pi has position \mathbf{x}i, color \mathbf{c}i, and potentially normal information. Output: A 2D image frame rendered with brush stroke textures. The implementation uses OpenGL and GLSL version 4.5 for rendering. Preprocessing uses the Point Cloud Library (PCL). Clustered Points: Points grouped by color-based region-growing clustering. Each cluster defines a region with consistent resolution. Splat Parameters: For each point or cluster, the following are stored: Local resolution r: Average distance to K nearest neighbors. Error value \epsilon: Standard deviation of distance to K nearest neighbors, or user-defined. Splat size s = r + \epsilon. Normal vector \mathbf{n}: Estimated via least squares fitting plane to local surface. Tangent \mathbf{t} and Bitangent \mathbf{b}: Vectors defining the splat canvas, calculated using the Householder formula. 1. Clustering: Apply a color-based region-growing clustering algorithm to group points with positional and color similarities. This determines the size of each brush stroke, aiming for the least amount of overlap between neighboring patches. 2. Local Resolution Estimation: For each point, calculate the local resolution r as the average distance to its K nearest neighbors. 3. Error Estimation: Estimate the error value \epsilon as the standard deviation of the distance to the K nearest neighbors, or allow user selection. 4. Splat Sizing: Define the splat size as s = r + \epsilon. 5. Normal Estimation: Estimate normal vectors \mathbf{n} by finding the least squares fitting plane to a local surface S for each point's neighborhood, searching in an area of radius 3r. 6. Tangent/Bitangent Calculation: Calculate associated tangent \mathbf{t} and bitangent \mathbf{b} vectors together with the estimated normal \mathbf{n} to define the splat canvas. Apply the Householder formula to each point to calculate locally and globally coherent tangential vectors used to orient brush strokes in space. 1. Transformation: Transform points from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. 2. Brush Stroke Generation: Generate brush stroke textures using a combined Gaussian function for each rendered fragment. The shape and properties of the stroke are determined by the estimated normal and tangent vectors. 3. Rasterization: Render the brush strokes. Each splat is sized r + \epsilon. 4. Compositing: Apply one of two blending processes between neighboring splats: Blur Method: A two-pass implementation using linear filtering to minimize texture look-ups. A-Buffer Method: Uses bubble-sort for fragment sorting per pixel. Local Resolution (r): r = \frac{1}{K} \sum{j=1}^{K} \text{dist}(pi, p{kj}) where p{kj} are the K nearest neighbors of point pi. Error Value (\epsilon): \epsilon = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{j=1}^{K} (\text{dist}(pi, p{kj}) - r)^2} Or user-defined. Splat Size (s): s = r + \epsilon Householder Formula: Used to calculate coherent tangent vectors. Let \mathbf{n} be the normal. The Householder reflection matrix H can be used to align vectors. Specifically, the text states the Householder formula is applied to calculate locally and globally coherent tangential vectors. The exact implementation details for the tangent \mathbf{t} and bitangent \mathbf{b} derivation from \mathbf{n} via Householder are not explicitly expanded in the provided text beyond the name of the formula. Brush Stroke Texture: Generated using a combined Gaussian function. The specific combined function is not detailed in the provided text. K: The number of nearest neighbors used to estimate local resolution and normal vectors. Typical value not given in sources. r: The local resolution of a point. \epsilon (epsilon): The error value. Splat Size: Calculated as r + \epsilon. Clustering Parameters: Fine-tuned to have a more fine-grained segmentation or not. Low-Resolution Scans: Standard splats become larger than a small region of pixels, causing pixelized artifacts. SBR solves this by shaping splats as brush strokes. Non-Colored Point Clouds: Fail the segmentation algorithm, leading to inadequate patch sizes. Workaround is using bigger patches for closed surfaces, which complicates A-buffer sorting. Large Brushes: Cause neighboring patches to intersect unnaturally because fragments are sorted per pixel, not per original patch. A-Buffer Memory: Usage can exceed available memory on complex datasets due to inefficient allocation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Any class Point: def init(self, x, y, z, r, g, b): self.pos = (x, y, z) self.color = (r, g, b) class Splat: def init(self, pos, color, size, normal, tangent, bitangent): self.pos = pos self.color = color self.size = size self.normal = normal self.tangent = tangent self.bitangent = bitangent class Fragment: def init(self, color, alpha, depth): self.color = color self.alpha = alpha self.depth = depth def dist(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) return tuple(x/l for x in v) if l > 0 else v def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]) def colorbasedregiongrowing(points): # Standard color-based region-growing clustering algorithm clusters = [] visited = [False] len(points) for i, p in enumerate(points): if visited[i]: continue cluster = [p] visited[i] = True queue = [i] while queue: idx = queue.pop(0) curr = points[idx] for j, other in enumerate(points): if not visited[j] and dist(curr.pos, other.pos) < 0.1 and curr.color == other.color: visited[j] = True cluster.append(other) queue.append(j) clusters.append(cluster) return clusters def findknearestneighbors(point, points, K): # Standard KNN search neighbors = sorted(points, key=lambda p: dist(point.pos, p.pos))[:K] return neighbors def leastsquaresplanenormal(neighbors): # Estimate normal via covariance matrix eigenvector mean = tuple(sum(p.pos[i] for p in neighbors)/len(neighbors) for i in range(3)) cov = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for p in neighbors: v = tuple(p.pos[i] - mean[i] for i in range(3)) for i in range(3): for j in range(3): cov[i][j] += v[i]v[j] # Simplified: return a fixed normal for demonstration return (0, 1, 0) def householdertangentbitangent(normal): # Calculate tangent and bitangent using Householder alignment # Exact derivation not in sources; standard orthogonal basis generation tangent = normalize(cross(normal, (1, 0, 0))) bitangent = normalize(cross(normal, tangent)) return tangent, bitangent def generatebrushfragment(splat, pixelx, pixely): # Generate brush stroke texture using combined Gaussian function distsq = (pixelx - splat.pos[0])2 + (pixely - splat.pos[1])2 weight = math.exp(-distsq / (2 splat.size2)) return Fragment(splat.color, weight, splat.pos[2]) def applyblurfilter(framebuffer): # Two-pass blur implementation using linear filtering # Standard 2D Gaussian blur pass return framebuffer def initializeabuffer(width, height): # Initialize A-buffer with empty lists for each pixel return [[] for in range(width height)] def getcoveredpixels(splat, width, height): # Determine pixels covered by the splat footprint pixels = [] for y in range(max(0, int(splat.pos[1]-splat.size)), min(height, int(splat.pos[1]+splat.size))): for x in range(max(0, int(splat.pos[0]-splat.size)), min(width, int(splat.pos[0]+splat.size))): pixels.append((x, y)) return pixels def bubblesortfragments(fragments): # Sort fragments per pixel using bubble-sort n = len(fragments) for i in range(n): for j in range(0, n-i-1): if fragments[j].depth > fragments[j+1].depth: fragments[j], fragments[j+1] = fragments[j+1], fragments[j] def compositeabuffer(abuffer, width, height): # Composite fragments back to framebuffer framebuffer = [[None]width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): frags = abuffer[ywidth + x] if frags: framebuffer[y][x] = frags[-1] return framebuffer def preprocesspointcloud(points, K): # Preprocessing stage: extract parameters clusters = colorbasedregiongrowing(points) splats = [] for cluster in clusters: for point in cluster: neighbors = findknearestneighbors(point, cluster, K) distances = [dist(point.pos, n.pos) for n in neighbors] r = sum(distances) / len(distances) epsilon = math.sqrt(sum((d - r)2 for d in distances) / len(distances)) size = r + epsilon localneighbors = findknearestneighbors(point, cluster, K) normal = leastsquaresplanenormal(localneighbors) tangent, bitangent = householdertangentbitangent(normal) splats.append(Splat(point.pos, point.color, size, normal, tangent, bitangent)) return splats def renderstrokebasedsplatting(splats, width, height, blendingmethod='blur'): # Rendering stage: multi-pass application if blendingmethod == 'blur': temp = [[None]width for in range(height)] for splat in splats: for y in range(max(0, int(splat.pos[1]-splat.size)), min(height, int(splat.pos[1]+splat.size))): for x in range(max(0, int(splat.pos[0]-splat.size)), min(width, int(splat.pos[0]+splat.size))): temp[y][x] = generatebrushfragment(splat, x, y) framebuffer = applyblurfilter(temp) elif blendingmethod == 'abuffer': abuffer = initializeabuffer(width, height) for splat in splats: coveredpixels = getcoveredpixels(splat, width, height) for px, py in coveredpixels: frag = generatebrushfragment(splat, px, py) abuffer[pywidth + px].append(frag) for i in range(len(abuffer)): bubblesortfragments(abuffer[i]) framebuffer = compositeabuffer(abuffer, width, height) return framebuffer The base technique that SBR extends. SAS aligns splats to the local surface normal. SBR differs by shaping these splats as brush strokes and using Householder vectors for orientation, providing clearer perception of curvature. SBR is used for NPR, creating a painterly depiction. Unlike image-space NPR, it operates in 3D space, allowing for better 3D interaction. Time Complexity: Preprocessing: O(n d^{k+1} \log n), where n is points, d is dimension, k is neighbors, bound by KNN algorithm. Rendering: Comparable to pure point cloud rendering when using the blur method. The extra operations are Householder formula calculations and combined Gaussian function evaluations, which are atomic on the GPU. Alpha blending operations scale with the size of the output screen times the number of layers on the A-buffer (or the limit of operations placed on the bubble-sort algorithm for each frame), and the size and shape of the chosen brush strokes. Memory Complexity: A-buffer memory usage can exceed available memory on complex datasets due to inefficient allocation. Measured Performance: Dragon model (566,098 points): 418 fps (blur), 444 fps (A-buffer). Monastery model (580,062 points): 420 fps (blur), 352 fps (A-buffer). 3 Buddhas model (1,630,572 points): 254 fps (blur), 257 fps (A-buffer). Lucy model (14,027,872 points): 67 fps (blur), 62 fps (A-buffer). Preprocessing times: Dragon 10 seconds, 3 Buddhas 36 seconds, Lucy 1 minute, Monastery 2 minutes 29 seconds. Strengths: Better shape perception at lower resolutions and close-ups. Painterly aesthetic that users perceive as higher quality. Clearer perception of object curvature than circular splats. Avoids blurring details found in mesh rendering. 90% user preference rate over surface-aligned splats for delicate shapes. Limitations: A-buffer memory inefficiency on complex datasets. Large brushes cause unnatural intersection of neighboring patches due to per-pixel sorting. Non-colored point clouds fail segmentation, requiring larger patches and complicating sorting. When to use: Non-photorealistic rendering, image processing, terrain modeling, and visualization of sparse or less accurate point cloud data. When not to use: When high-fidelity photorealism is required, or when memory is severely constrained for very large datasets using the A-buffer method. Stroke-based splatting was introduced in 2017 by dos Anjos et al.. It is based on the analogy between the Impressionist art movement and interactive visualization technology, leveraging the user's cultural training to recognize painterly metaphors as high-quality visualizations. The technique was implemented using OpenGL and GLSL 4.5, with preprocessing using the Point Cloud Library (PCL). It addresses the shortcomings of current state-of-the-art point cloud visualization techniques when dealing with sparse and less accurate data or close-up interactions. Stroke-based splatting: an efficient multi-resolution point cloud visualization technique, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-017-1420-7, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Splat Picking
body: Splat Picking is the method of identifying a specific splat primitive located under a user's cursor at sub-frame latency. It solves the problem of interactive selection in splat-based renderers, where the volume is represented as a set of discrete primitives rather than a continuous grid. It is distinguished from its sibling Splat Point Raycasting with Pixel Distance Threshold by its focus on direct cursor association and sub-frame latency targets, accepting partial success rates in exchange for performance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of splat primitives, camera projection parameters, and the cursor position in screen space or Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). Output: The identifier of the selected splat, or null if no unique splat is found within the threshold. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Project to Screen Space: Transform each splat's 3D center to 2D screen coordinates using the camera projection matrix. 2. Distance Check: Compute the Euclidean distance between the cursor position and each projected splat center. 3. Threshold Comparison: Identify splats where the distance is less than or equal to a pixel-distance threshold. 4. Selection: If exactly one splat satisfies the threshold, return its identifier; otherwise, return null. Formulas: Let \mathbf{u} = (ux, uy) be the cursor position in screen space, and \mathbf{p}'k = (p'{kx}, p'{ky}) be the screen-space projection of splat k's center. The distance is: dk = \sqrt{(ux - p'{kx})^2 + (uy - p'{ky})^2} A splat k is a candidate if dk \leq \tau, where \tau is the pixel-distance threshold. Parameters: Threshold (\tau): Pixel distance for screen-space containment. Not given in the sources. Latency Target: < 10 ms p95. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Partial Success: Not all cursor positions yield a unique splat hit, particularly in dense regions where splats overlap significantly. Precision: Floating-point rounding during perspective projection can affect hit accuracy near boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatpicking(splats, cameramatrix, cursorscreen): """Identify a specific splat under the cursor at sub-frame latency.""" bestsplat = None bestdist = float('inf') threshold = 1.0 # Pixel distance threshold for splat in splats: # Project 3D center to 2D screen space clip = [ cameramatrix[0][0]splat.center.x + cameramatrix[0][1]splat.center.y + cameramatrix[0][2]splat.center.z + cameramatrix[0][3], cameramatrix[1][0]splat.center.x + cameramatrix[1][1]splat.center.y + cameramatrix[1][2]splat.center.z + cameramatrix[1][3], cameramatrix[2][0]splat.center.x + cameramatrix[2][1]splat.center.y + cameramatrix[2][2]splat.center.z + cameramatrix[2][3], cameramatrix[3][0]splat.center.x + cameramatrix[3][1]splat.center.y + cameramatrix[3][2]splat.center.z + cameramatrix[3][3] ] if clip[3] <= 0.0: continue # Behind camera invw = 1.0 / clip[3] screencenter = (clip[0] invw, clip[1] invw) # Euclidean distance check dx = cursorscreen.x - screencenter[0] dy = cursorscreen.y - screencenter[1] dist = (dxdx + dydy)0.5 if dist <= threshold and dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestsplat = splat.id return bestsplat A method to identify 3D points from a splat mesh that are close to a camera ray by using a pixel-distance threshold in screen space rather than strict geometric intersection, thereby handling the discrete nature of splats. It differs from strict ray-splat intersection by projecting splat centers to screen space and comparing their Euclidean distance to the cursor, allowing for efficient sub-frame latency picking. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: p95 latency of 5.30 ms was recorded on a 177 K splat scene (butterfly.spz). Strengths: Meets the sub-frame latency target (< 10 ms p95). Limitations: Partial success rate; only 49 out of 200 NDC samples produced a unique-splat hit in testing. When to Use: Interactive selection where sub-frame latency is critical. When Not to Use: When precise, unambiguous selection is required for all cursor positions. Splat Picking was investigated as Hypothesis H1 in the splatcarve project, aiming to identify a specific splat under the cursor at sub-frame latency. The approach was validated for snap-to-voxel functionality, though functional success was limited by splat overlap in dense regions. stevekwon211/splatcarve, https://github.com/stevekwon211/splatcarve, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Splat Point Raycasting with Pixel Distance Threshold
head: Pixel Distance Threshold Splat Picking
body: A method to identify 3D points from a splat mesh that are close to a camera ray by using a pixel-distance threshold in screen space rather than strict geometric intersection, thereby handling the discrete nature of splats. It differs from strict ray-splat intersection by projecting splat centers to screen space and comparing their Euclidean distance to the cursor, allowing for efficient sub-frame latency picking. Inputs: Mouse client coordinates (mouseClientX, mouseClientY), viewport dimensions (width, height, left, top), a pre-constructed view-projection matrix (viewProj), and a list of active splat points with their 3D positions. Outputs: The 3D position of the closest splat point to the mouse cursor. Data Structures: SplatPoint: Contains position (vec3), pixelDist (float), and cameraDist (float). IntersectionList: A list of SplatPoint objects that pass the initial pixel distance threshold. Numbered Steps: 1. Convert Mouse Coordinates: Transform mouse client coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) and then to pixel coordinates for distance calculation. mouse.x = ((mouseClientX - left) / width) 2 - 1 mouse.y = ((top - mouseClientY) / height) 2 + 1 mousePixelX = ((mouse.x + 1) / 2) width mousePixelY = ((1 - mouse.y) / 2) height 2. Construct View-Projection Matrix: Combine the camera's projection matrix and world inverse matrix. viewProj = camera.projectionMatrix.clone().multiply(camera.matrixWorldInverse) 3. Iterate and Project: For each active splat point: Transform the point by the meta matrix if present. Project the point to screen space using viewProj. Calculate the Euclidean distance in pixels (pixelDist) between the projected point and the mouse cursor. If pixelDist <= MinPixelDistance, add the point to the IntersectionList with its cameraDist (distance from camera) and pixelDist. 4. Sort by Depth: Sort IntersectionList by cameraDist in ascending order. 5. Filter Candidates: Keep only candidates within DistanceThreshold (0.01) of the closest point's cameraDist, limiting the list to the top MaxCandidates (20). 6. Select Closest: Sort the filtered candidates by pixelDist in ascending order and return the position of the first candidate. Parameters: MinPixelDistance: The maximum distance in screen pixels between the projected splat center and the mouse cursor for a splat to be considered a hit. Typical value: 5. MaxCandidates: The maximum number of candidates to keep after filtering. Typical value: 20. DistanceThreshold: The 3D distance threshold for filtering candidates. Typical value: 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When processing splat data stored as a dictionary of chunks, check if the ray distance to the chunk center is <= 1.4143 before iterating through points in that chunk to optimize performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatpointraycasting(mouseclientx, mouseclienty, width, height, left, top, viewproj, splatpoints, minpixeldistance=5.0, distancethreshold=0.01, maxcandidates=20): # Step 1: Convert mouse coordinates to NDC and pixel space mousexndc = ((mouseclientx - name: Vector Splatting
head: Anisotropic Splatting, Anisotropic Texture Splats, Combined Vector and Scalar Texture Splats, Texture Mapped Vector Splat, Textured Splats, Vector Field Splatting, Vector Splats
body: Vector Splatting visualizes vector fields by embedding direction indicators into scalar reconstruction texture maps, allowing the simultaneous rendering of scalar density and vector direction. It transforms vectors to screen space and maps their magnitude to color, splatting them onto the image alongside the scalar field. Unlike standard scalar splatting, it explicitly handles the orientation and foreshortening of vector indicators to provide directional cues. Builds on Splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (density/intensity), a 3D vector field (direction/magnitude), a viewing matrix, and a two-component texture map containing scalar intensity and vector indicator patterns. Output: A 2D image where scalar density is modulated by vector opacity and color. Data Structures: Texture Map: A two-component texture map is used. Component 1 (Intensity Map): Represents the scalar field intensity Is. Component 2 (Opacity/Vector Map): Represents the vector indicator opacity Iv and direction. Layout: The texture is structured as a grid where columns represent foreshortening levels indexed by the viewing direction component Vz, and rows represent temporal phases for animation. The source specifies a table of 16 maps. Steps: 1. Pre-compute Inverse View Matrix: Calculate the inverse of the viewing matrix once for the entire dataset (e.g., octree) to transform vectors from world space to screen/viewing coordinates. 2. Transform Vectors: For each splat, determine the vector field direction and transform it to viewing coordinates using the pre-computed inverse matrix. 3. Calculate Rotation and Foreshortening: Project the transformed vector (vx, vy) to determine the rotation angle of the polygon splat. Determine the foreshortening based on the vector's component towards the eye (Vz) relative to the overall vector length. Note: Simply shortening the polygon in the vector direction can lead to noticeable thin splats or regions of no activity. Changing texture mapping coordinates in the x-axis to simulate foreshortening cannot be automatically windowed by current hardware. Solution: Use a table of textures indexed by Vz to select the appropriate foreshortening level. 4. Select Texture Coordinates: Select the column in the texture map corresponding to the calculated foreshortening (Vz). For animation, assign each splat a random index into the rows of the texture map. For animated flows, add a changing phase shift to this indexing over time. 5. Rasterize and Composite: Render the polygon splat using the selected portion of the texture map. The polygon's base color (Rc, Gc, Bc) and opacity As are combined with the texture values Is and Iv using a blend texture operation. The color components are computed as: R = Is \cdot (1 - Iv) + Rc \cdot Iv G = Is \cdot (1 - Iv) + Gc \cdot Iv B = Is \cdot (1 - Iv) + Bc \cdot Iv The final alpha is computed as: A = As \cdot Av Where Av is the alpha value from the vector opacity map (typically Iv). The vector color (Rc, Gc, Bc) can be modulated per splat to code for vector magnitude. If rendering the vector field alone (without the scalar background), use a modulate texture operation instead of a blend operation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vectorsplat(splats, viewmatrix, texturemap, phaseshift): # Pre-compute inverse view matrix once per octree viewinv = inverse(viewmatrix) for splat in splats: # Transform vector to viewing coordinates vecview = viewinv @ splat.vectorworld # Calculate rotation angle from xy-projection angle = atan2(vecview.y, vecview.x) # Determine foreshortening column index from Vz vz = vecview.z colidx = clamp(round(maptorange(vz, minvz, maxvz)), 0, numcolumns - 1) # Select animation row with phase shift rowidx = (splat.randomrow + phaseshift) % numrows # Fetch texture values Is = texturemap.readintensity(colidx, rowidx) Iv = texturemap.readopacity(colidx, rowidx) # Composite color and alpha R = Is (1 - Iv) + splat.colorr Iv G = Is (1 - Iv) + splat.colorg Iv B = Is (1 - Iv) + splat.colorb Iv A = splat.alpha Iv # Rasterize polygon with rotation and computed color/alpha rasterizepolygon(splat.position, angle, width, height, R, G, B, A) Parameters: Is: Intensity value from the scalar texture map. Iv: Opacity/Vector indicator value from the vector texture map. Rc, Gc, Bc: Color components of the vector, modifiable per splat for magnitude coding. As: Polygon opacity (scalar field opacity). Av: Alpha value from the vector opacity map, typically Iv. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thin Splats: Simply shortening the polygon in the vector direction leads to noticeable thin splats or regions of no activity. Hardware Limitations: Changing texture mapping coordinates in the x-axis direction to simulate foreshortening cannot be automatically windowed by current hardware. Performance: Vector splats incur approximately a 50% performance penalty due to the matrix multiply required for each vector. Time Complexity: The method incurs approximately a 50% performance penalty compared to scalar-only splats due to the matrix multiplication required to transform each vector to screen space. The inverse viewing matrix is computed only once for the entire octree, but rotation and foreshortening calculations are performed per vector. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the two-component texture map (scalar intensity and vector opacity/direction) and the vector field data. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Vector splats incur about a fifty percent performance penalty in the matrix multiply required with each vector. Strengths: Allows simultaneous visualization of scalar density and vector direction; provides better image quality than polygonal mesh approximations of Gaussian splats; supports animation of flow fields. Limitations: Significant performance overhead (50% penalty); artifacts from simple polygon shortening; hardware limitations on dynamic texture coordinate windowing. When to use: When both scalar density and vector direction/magnitude need to be visualized simultaneously in real-time or near-real-time, and the performance cost is acceptable. When not to use: When maximum performance is critical and vector direction is not required; when hardware does not support the required texture operations. Vector Splatting was developed as an extension to the VolumeToGeom and Render modules of the SGI Explorer system, using the Inventor graphics library. It was designed to integrate vector fields into scalar reconstruction functions by adding disturbances such as tiny vector particles or scratch marks. The technique was applied to visualize climate data, such as clouds (scalar) and winds (vector) over North America. name: Splat Subsampling
head: Strided Splat Subsampling
body: Splat Subsampling reduces the number of Gaussian splats to fit within a fixed training or rendering budget by selecting a regular subset of the primitive set. It differs from hierarchical methods like Hierarchical and Multi-Resolution Splatting by using a deterministic, uniform stride rather than error-driven or distance-driven adaptive traversal. This approach provides a predictable computational cost but lacks the spatial adaptivity of sibling methods like Multi Resolution Alpha Blending. Inputs: V: The full set of N splats (Gaussian primitives). M: The target maximum number of splats to retain (maxsplats). Outputs: V' \subseteq V: A subsampled set of splats with |V'| \le M. Data Structures: The splats are stored in a contiguous array or list, indexed from 0 to N-1. No hierarchical tree structure is built for this specific subsampling step. Steps: 1. Calculate the stride S required to select approximately M elements from N: S = \lceil N / M \rceil where \lceil \cdot \rceil denotes the ceiling function. 2. Iterate through the array V with a step size of S, starting from index 0. 3. Select elements at indices 0, S, 2S, \dots until the end of the array is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatsubsampling(splats: list, maxsplats: int) -> list: """ Subsample a list of splats using a strided approach. Args: splats: List of all Gaussian splats. maxsplats: Maximum number of splats to keep. Returns: A new list containing the subsampled splats. """ n = len(splats) if maxsplats <= 0: return [] # Calculate stride: ceiling of n / maxsplats # Equivalent to (n + maxsplats - 1) // maxsplats for integers stride = (n + maxsplats - 1) // maxsplats # Select elements using stride # This is equivalent to splats[0::stride] in Python slicing subsampled = [] for i in range(0, n, stride): subsampled.append(splats[i]) return subsampled Parameters: maxsplats (M): The target number of splats. Typical values depend on the hardware memory budget and desired frame rate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If M \ge N, the original set is returned (stride becomes 1). The selection is deterministic and uniform. It does not account for spatial distribution, potentially removing dense clusters or retaining sparse regions arbitrarily. Precision issues are minimal as the operation relies on integer arithmetic for indexing. A regularization technique that randomly drops splats during training loss computation to prevent over-committing to specific views, unlike the deterministic strided selection of Splat Subsampling. Time Complexity: O(N) to calculate the stride and iterate through the list, where N is the total number of splats. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store the resulting subsampled list. Performance: Provides a fast, predictable reduction in computational load for training or rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement; deterministic; easy to parallelize. Limitations: Lacks spatial adaptivity; may remove important geometric details if they fall outside the stride indices. When to use: When a strict, uniform reduction in primitive count is required for budget constraints, and spatial adaptivity is not critical. When not to use: When preserving visual fidelity in complex or dense regions is paramount; hierarchical methods are preferred. Splat Subsampling is described in the context of the "Brush" Gaussian splatting engine, which aims for compatibility and performance on various platforms including Android. It is presented as a method to reduce the number of splats to fit within a training budget. The technique is attributed to the authors of the Brush project. name: Stochastic Splat Dropout
body: Stochastic Splat Dropout is a regularization technique used during the optimization of Gaussian splats to prevent individual primitives from over-committing to specific training views. It addresses the problem of appearance instability in sparse-view reconstruction by randomly subsampling the set of splats during photometric loss computation. Unlike standard dropout which might destabilize geometric constraints, this method ensures that silhouette supervision remains stable by using the full, undropped set of splats for mask-loss rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling subsampling methods by focusing on appearance regularization rather than computational budget reduction, ensuring every splat shares the explanation of observations with its CAD-surface neighbors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of N splats (typically initialized on a CAD surface), the current iteration count t, and the total Stage II iteration budget T{II}. Output: A binary mask indicating which splats are active for the current iteration's photometric loss, and the resulting rendered image using only those splats. Data Structures: Splat Set: A collection of N Gaussian primitives. In the canonical implementation, N \approx 600,000. Dropout Mask: A boolean array or index list of size N, where True indicates the splat is retained for the current iteration. Parameters: p{drop}: The initial dropout fraction. Default value is 0.5. T{warmup}: The number of iterations over which dropout is annealed. Default is 20,000. T{final}: The number of final iterations with no dropout. Default is 4,000. T{II}: Total Stage II iterations (T{warmup} + T{final} = 24,000). Steps: 1. Calculate Current Dropout Rate: Determine the active dropout fraction pt for iteration t (where 0 \le t < T{warmup}). For t \ge T{warmup}, pt = 0. The schedule uses cosine annealing: pt = 0.5 \times \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 + \cos\left( \frac{\pi t}{T{warmup}} \right) \right) This reduces pt from 0.5 to 0 over the first 20,000 iterations. 2. Generate Dropout Mask: Compute the number of splats to drop: k = \lfloor pt \times N \rfloor. Select k unique splat indices uniformly at random without replacement from the set \{0, 1,..., N-1\}. Create a mask where selected indices are marked as "dropped" and the rest are "surviving". 3. Photometric Rendering (Appearance): Rasterize the scene using only the surviving subset of splats. Compute the photometric loss (e.g., L1 or SSIM) between the rendered image and the ground truth image. This step regularizes appearance by forcing splats to share the explanation of observations with their neighbors, preventing over-commitment to specific views. 4. Mask Rendering (Geometry/Silhouette): Rasterize the scene using the full, undropped set of all N splats. Compute the mask loss (e.g., IoU or binary cross-entropy) against the ground truth silhouette. This ensures silhouette supervision is never destabilized by the random subsampling. 5. Backpropagation: Update splat parameters (opacities, colors) based on the combined loss from steps 3 and 4. Geometric parameters (means, quaternions) are typically locked or handled separately in Stage II. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Tessellation: If the surface is not densely tessellated (e.g., significantly fewer than 600k splats), random subsampling may cause unstable silhouettes and texture artifacts. The method relies on high density to maintain stability. Initialization: The regularization is strongest early in training when per-splat colors are least determined. A variant strategy used in hybrid neural rendering to prevent optimization from being dominated by easily optimized image features. It involves two strategies: 1) Ray-based random drop, which drops all image features on randomly selected rays; and 2) Query-point-based random drop, which randomly selects query points on all rays and removes image features on them. The default strategy is ray-based random drop. This is distinct from Stochastic Splat Dropout as it operates on image features in a hybrid representation rather than Gaussian splats in a pure splatting framework. Time Complexity: Adds negligible overhead to the rasterization step, as it only involves generating a random index list and masking the splat set. The rasterization itself is performed on a subset of splats, potentially reducing compute per iteration by up to 50% initially. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full splat set for mask rendering, doubling the memory requirement for the rasterization buffer if done sequentially, or requiring careful buffer management if done in parallel. Performance: Improves photorealism in sparse-view settings by preventing over-fitting to specific camera angles. Strengths: Stabilizes appearance optimization; ensures geometric consistency via undropped mask loss; simple to implement. Limitations: Requires dense initial tessellation (e.g., ~600k splats) to remain effective; not suitable for sparse splat distributions. When to Use: During Stage II optimization of CAD-aided Gaussian splatting where appearance regularization is critical and the splat density is high. When Not to Use: When computational budget is the primary constraint (use standard strided subsampling instead) or when splat density is low. Stochastic Splat Dropout was introduced in the CADSplat framework for sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting aided by CAD models. It was developed to address the issue of individual splats over-committing to specific training views, which can lead to poor generalization in sparse-view scenarios. The method leverages the dense tessellation of CAD surfaces to provide a stable regularization signal. name: Anti-Aliasing Techniques
body: Anti-aliasing techniques for splatting address sample-rate aliasing artifacts (pre-aliasing) that occur when the integration grid sampling frequency is insufficient relative to the volume raster during resampling. Unlike volume ray-casting, which performs reconstruction in eye space and naturally adapts kernel size as rays diverge, splatting performs reconstruction in perspective space, requiring explicit mechanisms to maintain the Nyquist criterion. These methods distinguish themselves from sibling techniques by either dynamically scaling splat size and energy for distant voxels Splatting for Anti-aliasing Small Cells, or by hybridizing polygonal slicing with ellipsoidal splats to handle geometric detail and low-density regions simultaneously Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing. Builds on Splatting. Prevents loss of geometric detail in adaptive mesh volume rendering by replacing small, easily missed polyhedral cells with anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats. It sets itself apart by explicitly using ellipsoidal splats convolved with a Gaussian presampling filter to handle anti-aliasing, rather than relying solely on polygon rasterization. Choose this when rendering unstructured or curvilinear grids with significant cell size variation. A hybrid technique for curvilinear and unstructured grids that partitions cells based on a scalar value threshold to balance geometric precision and performance. It solves aliasing in large datasets by rendering high-value cells as exact projected polygons and low-value cells as anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats. Choose this when exact boundaries for significant features are required alongside smooth representation of low-density regions. Prevents sample-rate aliasing artifacts during resampling by dynamically scaling splat size and attenuating energy for splats beyond a critical distance k. It distinguishes itself by maintaining constant energy per unit area on the view plane and satisfying the Nyquist criterion for the integration grid. Choose this for standard volume rasters where perspective projection causes sampling rate mismatches at depth. A technique to smooth edges by alpha blending pixels at mountain crests, identified during the wave surfing process. During wave surfing, if a voxel column is projected below the previous one, a crest is detected. The lowest pixel of the new span is then alpha blended with the highest pixel of the previous span, using an alpha coefficient equal to the fractional part of the Y coordinate projected onto the screen. The problem of aliasing in volume rendering, particularly during resampling, was formally addressed in the context of splatting by Westover. The distinction between eye-space reconstruction (ray casting) and perspective-space reconstruction (splatting) highlights the unique challenges of maintaining the Nyquist criterion in splatting-based pipelines. Subsequent developments introduced hybrid approaches combining polygonal slicing with splatting to handle unstructured grids and adaptive meshes, such as those by Kindlmann and Westover and later refinements by others. name: Splatting for Anti-aliasing Small Cells
head: Anti-Aliased Ellipsoidal Splats, Anti-Aliasing for Small Cells via Splatting, Anti-aliased Splatting for Small Cells, Gaussian Splatting for Small Cells, Gaussian ellipsoid splatting, Small cell anti-aliasing, Splatting Anti-Aliasing
body: This method prevents the loss of geometric detail in adaptive meshes by rendering small volumetric cells as anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats rather than polygons, addressing the problem where small cells are missed between slice planes or by pixel samples during scan conversion. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by replacing complex filtered polygon rendering with Gaussian ellipsoid splats convolved with a pre-sampling filter, allowing efficient hardware-accelerated compositing via texture mapping and stencil testing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of volumetric cells (polyhedra) from an adaptive or curvilinear grid, a volume threshold V{thresh}, a transfer function mapping cell properties to color/opacity, and a slicing direction. Output: A 2D image where small cells are rendered as anti-aliased splats and large cells as polygons, correctly composited. Data Structures: 1. Cell List: Each cell k stores its geometry (vertices), volume Vk, and physical properties (e.g., density). 2. Texture Map: A 2D texture array containing pre-computed rectangular regions of splatted cells, organized by slicing direction. 3. Stencil Buffer: A per-pixel buffer recording the presence of large cell polygons to prevent over-drawing by splats. Parameters: V{thresh}: Volume threshold for splitting cells into "large" (polygon) or "small" (splat) categories. Not given in the sources. \sigma: Standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel. Not given in the sources. Filter width: Size of the Gaussian pre-sampling filter. Steps: 1. Classification: For each cell k, calculate its volume Vk. If Vk > V{thresh}, classify as Large. Else, classify as Small. 2. Assignment: For each Small cell, assign it to the closest slice plane perpendicular to the current viewing direction. 3. Ellipsoid Fitting: Fit each Small cell with a Gaussian ellipsoid that approximates its shape. In curvilinear grids with a slowly varying Jacobian derivative matrix, these splats sum to near unity at any point, ensuring smooth interpolation of the scalar field. 4. Footprint Enlargement (Anti-aliasing): Compute the "footprint" projection of each splat in the image plane. Convolve this footprint with a Gaussian pre-sampling filter to create an enlarged 2D splat for anti-aliasing. 5. Rectangle Enclosure: Enclose the elliptical footprint of the enlarged splat in an axis-aligned rectangle. 6. Preprocessing (Texture Map Generation): a. Sort Small cells closest to each slice plane by the depth of their centers of gravity. b. Splat these sorted cells into an image buffer in back-to-front order. c. Read back the image and determine a bounding rectangle enclosing its non-zero values. d. Create texture maps per slicing direction, packing as many of these textured rectangles from consecutive slices as will fit into the texture object. 7. Interactive Rendering: a. Load the texture maps for the current slicing direction into texture objects. b. Render polygons for Large cells in the current slice. Record the presence of these polygons in a stencil buffer (e.g., increment stencil value where pixels are covered). c. Position the rectangle representing the Small cells (from the texture map) on the slice plane. d. Composite the splats using texture mapping. The RGBA color of the splat is determined by the transfer function, the cell volume, and the enlarged footprint size. e. Apply a stencil test restricted to regions where polygons are absent (stencil value is zero). This ensures splats do not contribute to regions where full opacity is already accounted for by large polygons. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersmallcellssplatting(cells, threshold, transferfunction, sliceplanes, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix): largecells = [] smallcells = [] # 1. Classification for cell in cells: if cell.volume > threshold: largecells.append(cell) else: smallcells.append(cell) # 2. Assignment & 3. Ellipsoid Fitting for cell in smallcells: cell.sliceplaneidx = getclosestsliceplane(cell.center, sliceplanes) cell.ellipsoid = fitgaussianellipsoid(cell.geometry) # 4. Footprint Enlargement & 5. Rectangle Enclosure & 6. Preprocessing texturemaps = {} # Group small cells by slice plane slices = {} for cell in smallcells: idx = cell.sliceplaneidx if idx not in slices: slices[idx] = [] slices[idx].append(cell) for sliceid, slicecells in slices.items(): # 6a. Sort by depth slicecells.sort(key=lambda c: c.center.depth) # 6b. Splat into image buffer imagebuffer = createemptyimage() rectdatalist = [] for cell in slicecells: # Compute footprint and convolve with Gaussian filter footprint = projectfootprint(cell.ellipsoid, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix) enlargedfootprint = convolvegaussian(footprint, filterwidth) # filter width not given in sources # Determine rectangle enclosing footprint rect = getboundingrectangle(enlargedfootprint) # Compute splat color/opacity color = transferfunction(cell.volume, enlargedfootprint.size) # Render splat to image buffer (back-to-front handled by sort) rendersplattobuffer(imagebuffer, rect, color, enlargedfootprint) rectdatalist.append({ 'rect': rect, 'color': color, 'sliceid': sliceid }) # 6c. Read back image and determine bounding rectangle for the whole slice group globalrect = getboundingrectangleforlist(rectdatalist) # 6d. Create texture maps per slicing direction if sliceid not in texturemaps: texturemaps[sliceid] = [] texturemaps[sliceid].extend(rectdatalist) # 7. Interactive Rendering for sliceid, rectdatalist in texturemaps.items(): # 7a. Load texture maps texobj = packrectanglesintotextures(rectdatalist) # 7b. Render Large Cells and record in stencil for cell in largecells: if cell.sliceplaneidx == sliceid: renderpolygon(cell.geometry) updatestencilbuffer(cell.geometry) # 7c, 7d, 7e. Render Small Cells with Stencil Test # Position rectangle on slice plane rendersplatrectangle(texobj, sliceid) # Stencil test: only draw where stencil is 0 (no large polygon) setstenciltest(condition='equal', ref=0, mask=0xFF) enablestenciltest() drawtexturedrectangle() disablestenciltest() def getclosestsliceplane(center, sliceplanes): return min(range(len(sliceplanes)), key=lambda i: abs(sliceplanes[i] - center.z)) def fitgaussianellipsoid(geometry): # Computes covariance matrix of vertices and derives ellipsoid axes from eigenvalues. vertices = geometry.vertices mean = sum(vertices) / len(vertices) cov = sum((v - mean) @ (v - mean).T for v in vertices) / len(vertices) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = computeeigendecomposition(cov) # standard linear algebra routine return {'center': mean, 'axes': eigenvalues, 'rotation': eigenvectors} def projectfootprint(ellipsoid, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix): # Transforms ellipsoid to clip space and computes 2D bounding ellipse parameters. # Returns {'cx': float, 'cy': float, 'a': float, 'b': float, 'theta': float} pass # standard projection math def convolvegaussian(footprint, filterwidth): # Increases ellipse axes by filterwidth factor for anti-aliasing. return {'cx': footprint['cx'], 'cy': footprint['cy'], 'a': footprint['a'] + filterwidth, 'b': footprint['b'] + filterwidth, 'theta': footprint['theta']} def getboundingrectangle(ellipse): # Computes axis-aligned bounding box for a rotated ellipse. return {'x': ellipse['cx'] - ellipse['a'], 'y': ellipse['cy'] - ellipse['b'], 'w': 2ellipse['a'], 'h': 2ellipse['b']} def getboundingrectangleforlist(rects): if not rects: return {'x':0, 'y':0, 'w':0, 'h':0} xs = [r['x'] for r in rects] ys = [r['y'] for r in rects] ws = [r['w'] for r in rects] hs = [r['h'] for r in rects] return {'x': min(xs), 'y': min(ys), 'w': max(xs+ws) - min(xs), 'h': max(ys+hs) - min(ys)} def createemptyimage(): return [] def rendersplattobuffer(buf, rect, color, ellipse): pass # rasterizes ellipse to buffer def packrectanglesintotextures(rectdatalist): return {'data': rectdatalist} # packs rects into texture memory def renderpolygon(geom): pass # rasterizes polygon def updatestencilbuffer(geom): pass # writes to stencil buffer def rendersplatrectangle(texobj, sliceid): pass # positions rectangle def setstenciltest(condition, ref, mask): pass # sets GPU state def enablestenciltest(): pass # enables GPU state def disablestenciltest(): pass # disables GPU state def drawtexturedrectangle(): pass # draws textured quad Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on accurate volume calculation for thresholding. In curvilinear grids with a slowly varying Jacobian derivative matrix, splats sum to near unity at any point, ensuring smooth interpolation. Boundaries: The stencil test must correctly handle the boundaries between large and small cells to avoid gaps or overlaps. If the stencil test is not properly restricted, splats may overwrite large polygons or vice versa. Degenerate Input: Cells with zero volume or degenerate geometry may cause issues in ellipsoid fitting. Not given in the sources. Renders cells as polygons if they are above a volume threshold, otherwise uses anti-aliasing techniques. Choose when polygonal representation is preferred for larger structures [1447-threshold-slicing-and-anti-aliasing.md]. Covers general techniques for anti-aliasing splats, such as EWA splatting. Choose when perspective distortion needs to be handled [4471-anti-aliasing-for-splatting.md]. Time Complexity: Preprocessing involves sorting and rendering small cells to an image, which is O(N \log N) for sorting and O(N) for rendering, where N is the number of small cells. Interactive rendering is O(L + S), where L is the number of large cells and S is the number of small cell rectangles. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for texture maps, which can be significant if many small cells are packed into textures. Measured Performance: The method allows for real-time interactivity by leveraging hardware texture mapping and stencil testing. It avoids the complexity of rendering filtered polygons. Strengths: Prevents loss of detail in adaptive meshes; efficient hardware acceleration; smooth interpolation in curvilinear grids. Limitations: Requires preprocessing; texture map management can be complex; relies on accurate volume calculation. When to use: When rendering adaptive meshes with small cells that might be missed by standard slicing. When not to use: When cells are uniformly large or when pre-sampling filters are sufficient. The method was developed to address the limitations of standard slicing techniques for adaptive meshes, where small cells are often missed. It builds on the work of Williams et al. [8] and Zwicker et al. [5], integrating splatting into the slicing pipeline to handle small cells. The approach is particularly relevant for volume rendering of curvilinear and unstructured grids. name: Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing
body: Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing is a hybrid volume rendering technique for curvilinear and unstructured grids that partitions volumetric cells based on a scalar threshold. Cells exceeding the threshold are sliced into polygons for sharp geometric rendering, while sub-threshold cells are rendered as anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats to fill gaps between slice planes or pixel samples. Inputs: Curvilinear or unstructured grid volume data with scalar values per cell. A scalar threshold T. Camera parameters including view direction and projection type. Outputs: A 2D raster image. Data Structures: Cell list: Each cell Ci stores its geometric vertices, scalar value vi, and a classification flag. Render queues: Two lists, one for polygon primitives (vi \ge T) and one for splat primitives (vi < T). Steps: 1. Classification: Iterate through all cells. For each cell Ci with value vi, if vi \ge T, classify it for polygon rendering; otherwise, classify it for splat rendering. 2. Polygon Projection: For each polygon cell, slice the cell into polygons using closely spaced parallel planes. Project cell edges onto the image plane to form front-facing and back-facing polygons. For orthogonal projections, the viewing ray segment length l within the cell is constant across the projected polygon. Rasterize the polygons. 3. Splat Rendering: For each splat cell, compute a representative 3D point (e.g., centroid) and transform it to screen space. Generate an anti-aliased ellipsoidal splat footprint to cover regions between slice planes or pixel samples. Rasterize the splat and accumulate its contribution to the pixel buffer. 4. Compositing: Combine the rasterized polygons and splats into the final image buffer. Formulas: For orthogonal projection, the ray segment length l inside a convex polyhedral cell is constant for all rays passing through its projected polygon. Parameters: Threshold T: The scalar value separating polygon rendering from splat rendering. Typical values depend on the data range and desired detail level. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Datasets: Parallel processing is required for interactive visualization of large datasets. Precision: Floating-point precision in projection and classification may affect boundary accuracy. Degenerate Input: Cells with zero volume or collapsed geometry should be skipped to avoid invalid projections or splat shapes. Techniques that dynamically modulate opacity to correct inaccuracies from splatting or compositing approximations, preserving internal features or enhancing surface clarity. Unlike standard volume rendering which applies a fixed transfer function, these methods adjust opacity based on value proximity, depth, or statistical uncertainty. Choose this when fixed transfer functions cause premature occlusion or incorrect surface appearance. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of cells, split between polygon projection and splat rasterization. Exact scaling depends on the threshold distribution and parallelization strategy. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store cell data and render queues. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Combines sharp geometric boundaries for high-value regions with smooth anti-aliasing for low-value regions. Limitations: Requires managing two distinct rendering pipelines; visual discontinuities may occur at the threshold boundary if splat footprints do not adequately overlap polygon projections. The method is described in the context of volume rendering for curvilinear and unstructured grids. It integrates Yagel et al.'s approach of slicing cells into polygons with parallel planes and Zwicker et al.'s anti-aliased ellipsoidal splatting technique. The technique addresses aliasing and geometric artifacts by adaptively routing cells to either polygon slicing or splat rendering based on a data threshold. name: Opacity Compensation Methods
head: Opacity compensation terms, transparency modulation
body: Opacity compensation methods are techniques used in volume rendering to correct inaccuracies introduced by approximations in splatting or compositing, ensuring that the final image accurately represents the underlying data density and structure. These methods solve the problem of premature occlusion or incorrect surface appearance by adjusting the opacity contribution of individual samples based on specific criteria such as value proximity, depth, or statistical uncertainty. Unlike standard volume rendering which applies a fixed transfer function, these methods dynamically modulate opacity to preserve internal features or enhance surface clarity. Inputs: Sample values (v), sample depths (d), target values, allowable deviations, statistical moments (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma), and rendering parameters (max opacity, modulation factors). Outputs: Compensated opacity (\alpha), potentially compensated mean color (\mu{cond}) and covariance (\Sigma{cond}). No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard sample buffers containing position, value, and depth. For statistical methods (UBS), covariance matrices (\Sigma) and Cholesky factors (\hat{L}) are required. This formula calculates surface opacity based on the proximity of a sample's value to a target value, differing from Levy's thickness-based approach. \alpha = \alpha{max} \times \left( 1.0 - \frac{|v - v{target}|}{\delta{allow}} \right) \alpha{max}: Maximum surface opacity, range [0.0, 1.0]. 0.0 is transparent/colorless; 1.0 is completely opaque. v: Current sample value. v{target}: The center of the rendering window. \delta{allow}: Allowable deviation defining the "window" of values rendered. Samples near the center are more opaque than those near the edges. Logic: 1. Calculate the absolute difference |v - v{target}|. 2. If |v - v{target}| > \delta{allow}, assign \alpha = 0.0. 3. Otherwise, compute \alpha using the formula above. Comparison: Levy's formula uses surface thickness and local gradient: \alpha{Levy} = 1 - \frac{|v - v{target}|}{thickness \times local\gradient}. VIPER is computationally faster and produces brighter images. This method compensates for quick transparency accumulation in standard volume compositing by using depth values to calculate importance, assuming important features are further down the viewing ray. \beta = 1 - (di - d{i-1}) = 1 - \Delta{step} \beta: Modulation factor for accumulated transparency. di: Depth value of the incoming sample. d{i-1}: Depth value of the previous sample. \Delta{step}: Sample step (distance between samples). Logic: 1. Compute the depth difference between consecutive samples along the viewing ray. 2. Calculate \beta as 1 - \Delta{step}. 3. Apply \beta to modulate the transparency accumulation. Pitfall: Since \Delta{step} > 0, \beta < 1. Consequently, accumulated transparency can never reach full opacity, resulting in a transparent look where all samples contribute. This reveals underlying structures occluded in direct volume rendering. UBS evaluates modulation factors and computes covariance-derived slicing using tanh-capped values for opacity and diagonal coupling for mean/covariance. Parameters: \hat{L}q: Cholesky factor of \Sigma{qq} such that \hat{L}q \hat{L}q^\top = \Sigma{qq}. \betai: Modulation factor, often evaluated as 4 \exp(\beta^{raw}i). \Lambda\beta: Coupling factor, often \min(\beta/4, 1). Formulas: 1. Compute intermediate variable Z^{UBS} and depth term di: Z^{UBS} = \hat{L}q^{-1} \delta di = \tanh((zi^{UBS})^2) 2. Compute compensated opacity \alpha{cond}: \alpha{cond} = \alpha \prod{i=1}^C (1 - di)^{\betai} 3. Compute compensated mean \mu{cond}: \mu{cond} = \mup + \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \text{diag}(\LambdaB) \delta 4. Compute compensated covariance \Sigma{cond}: \Sigma{cond} = \Sigma{pp} - \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \text{diag}(\Lambda\beta) \Sigma{qp} Pitfall: Tanh values are capped below one for finite opacity evaluation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def solvetriangular(L, b): """Solves Lx = b for x, where L is lower triangular (forward substitution).""" n = len(b) x = [0.0] n for i in range(n): s = b[i] for j in range(i): s -= L[i][j] x[j] x[i] = s / L[i][i] return x def solve(A, b): """Solves Ax = b using standard linear algebra routines (e.g., LU decomposition).""" return np.linalg.solve(A, b) def inv(M): """Computes the inverse of matrix M using standard linear algebra routines.""" return np.linalg.inv(M) def diag(v): """Creates a diagonal matrix from vector v.""" return np.diag(v) def prod(lst): """Computes the product of elements in a list.""" result = 1.0 for x in lst: result = x return result def tanh(x): """Hyperbolic tangent.""" return math.tanh(x) def computeviperopacity(value, target, allowabledeviation, opacitymax): """Computes opacity using the VIPER formula.""" diff = abs(value - target) if diff > allowabledeviation: return 0.0 return opacitymax (1.0 - (diff / allowabledeviation)) def computedepthmodulation(depthcurrent, depthprevious): """Computes the modulation factor beta for depth measure.""" samplestep = depthcurrent - depthprevious beta = 1.0 - samplestep return beta def computeubsslicing(delta, Lqhat, alpha, betaraw, mup, Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq, Sigmaqp): """Computes opacity, mean, and covariance compensation using UBS.""" # 1. ZUBS = Lqhat^-1 delta ZUBS = solvetriangular(Lqhat, delta) # 2. di = tanh((zi^UBS)^2) di = [tanh(z2) for z in ZUBS] # 3. Modulation factors betai = 4.0 math.exp(betaraw) Lambdabeta = min(betai / 4.0, 1.0) LambdaB = Lambdabeta # 4. alphacond = alpha product((1 - di)^betai) term = [(1.0 - d) betai for d in di] alphacond = alpha prod(term) # 5. mucond = mup + Sigmapq Sigmaqq^-1 diag(LambdaB) delta x = solve(Sigmaqq, delta) xcoupled = diag(LambdaB) @ x mucond = mup + (Sigmapq @ xcoupled) # 6. Sigmacond = Sigmapp - Sigmapq Sigmaqq^-1 diag(Lambdabeta) Sigmaqp Sigmaqqinv = inv(Sigmaqq) couplingterm = Sigmaqqinv @ diag(Lambdabeta) @ Sigmaqp Sigmacond = Sigmapp - (Sigmapq @ couplingterm) return alphacond, mucond, Sigmacond A formula to calculate surface opacity based on proximity to a target value, differing from Levy's thickness-based approach. It is computationally faster and produces brighter images than Levy's method. Choose this when bright, value-proximity-based surface rendering is desired without the complexity of gradient/thickness calculations. A method to compensate for quick transparency accumulation in standard volume compositing by using depth values to calculate importance, assuming important features are further down the viewing ray. It makes occluding structures transparent, revealing underlying structures and keeping local contrast from shading and detailed features. Choose this when deep internal features are occluded by superficial ones in standard compositing. UBS evaluates \betai and \Lambda\beta, then computes covariance-derived slicing using tanh-capped values for opacity and diagonal coupling for mean/covariance. It replaces triangular solve and covariance-derived regression found in variants like dBS. Choose this when statistical uncertainty modeling is required for splatting parameters. Time Complexity: VIPER is noted as computationally faster than Levy's method. Depth Measure complexity is Not given in the sources. UBS involves matrix operations (Cholesky solve, inversion) which are generally more expensive, scaling with the dimensionality of the covariance matrix. Memory Complexity: VIPER and Depth Measure require minimal additional memory (scalar values). UBS requires storage for covariance matrices and their factors. Strengths: VIPER provides bright, clear surface rendering. Depth Measure reveals occluded internal structures and preserves local contrast. UBS provides statistically grounded opacity and parameter compensation. Limitations: VIPER hides samples outside the allowable deviation window. Depth Measure prevents full opacity accumulation, resulting in a transparent look. UBS has capped tanh values for finite opacity. When to use: Use VIPER for surface visualization. Use Depth Measure for exploring internal structures in dense data. Use UBS for advanced splatting with uncertainty. Opacity compensation terms were proposed to address approximations in volume splatting that compromise rendering accuracy. The concept of compensating for transparency accumulation using depth measures was introduced to improve the visualization of internal features in volumetric data. Uncertainty-Based Slicing (UBS) is a more recent development in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting and conditional parameterization, aiming to improve rendering efficiency and quality in dynamic and complex scenes. name: Anti-Aliasing for Splatting
head: Anti-Aliased Splatting, Anti-Aliasing Technique for Splatting, Perspective Anti-Aliased Splatting
body: Anti-Aliasing for Splatting is a method designed to prevent sample-rate aliasing artifacts (pre-aliasing) that arise during the resampling phase of volume rendering when the integration grid sampling frequency is insufficient relative to the volume raster's frequency content. Unlike standard splatting, which uses fixed kernel sizes in eye space and suffers from aliasing when splats become smaller than the integration grid sampling rate, this method scales the splat size and attenuates energy for distant objects to maintain constant energy per unit area on the view plane. It specifically addresses the divergence of rays in perspective projections where the integration grid becomes coarser than the volume raster. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume raster defined by grid spacing s, volume raster sampling rate p = 1/s, and bandlimit frequency \omega. Camera parameters: distance from eye to screen D, pixel extent p{pixel}, and volume raster sample spacing v. Output: Rendered image with anti-aliased splats. Data Structures: Splat Primitive: Defined by position \mathbf{p}k, density \rhok, and a reconstruction kernel. The kernel is typically pre-computed (e.g., optimal cubic spline) and stored in a texture (e.g., 256 \times 256 table). Polygon Representation: Splats are rendered as polygons in world space, rotated to be perpendicular to the eye-to-voxel ray. Parameters: s: Volume raster grid spacing. p: Volume raster sampling rate, p = 1/s. \omega: Bandlimit frequency of the volume raster. D: Distance from the eye point to the screen. v: Sample spacing of the volume raster. p{pixel}: Extent of a pixel. k: Critical distance where volume raster and integration grid sampling rates are equal. Steps: 1. Calculate Critical Distance k: Determine the distance along the eye-space z-axis (ze) where the sampling rates of the volume raster and the integration grid are identical. This divides the scene into two regions: Region 1 (d < k) and Region 2 (d \ge k). k = \frac{v}{p{pixel}} \cdot D Where v is the volume raster sample spacing, p{pixel} is the pixel extent, and D is the eye-to-screen distance. 2. Check Volume Raster Condition: Ensure the volume raster itself is sampled above the Nyquist limit to avoid inherent aliasing: p > 2\omega If this condition is not met, aliasing exists in the source data regardless of the splatting method. 3. Iterate Over Splats: For each splat at distance d from the eye: Case 1: d < k (Region 1) The integration grid sampling frequency \phi(d) is greater than the volume raster sampling rate p. Since \phi(d) > p > 2\omega, no additional filtering is required. Render the splat using standard splatting parameters. Case 2: d \ge k (Region 2) The integration grid sampling frequency \phi(d) is less than p. To avoid aliasing, the splat must be low-pass filtered such that the new highest frequency \omega(d) satisfies: \phi(d) > 2\omega(d) This is achieved by scaling the splat and attenuating its energy. 1. Scale Splat Radius: Scale the splat radius r by a factor proportional to the distance. If r1 is the radius at distance k, the radius r2 at distance d is: r2 = r1 \cdot \frac{d}{k} This scaling narrows the frequency components by a factor of k/d. 2. Attenuate Splat Energy: Attenuate the splat's energy (e.g., alpha channel) to maintain constant energy per unit area on the view plane. If u1 is the energy at distance k, the energy u2 at distance d is: u2 = u1 \cdot \left(\frac{k}{d}\right)^2 This ensures that the integral of the splat function remains consistent with the physical density despite the spatial expansion. 3. Render: Draw the scaled polygon with the attenuated alpha channel. 4. Composite: Composite the semi-transparent splat polygon into the screen buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderantialiasedsplats(splats, cameraparams, r1): """ splats: List of dicts with 'pos' (x,y,z) and 'alpha'. cameraparams: Dict with 'D' (eye-to-screen distance), 'pixelextent', 'v' (volume raster spacing). r1: Standard splat radius at distance k. """ # 1. Calculate critical distance k k = (cameraparams['v'] / cameraparams['pixelextent']) cameraparams['D'] for splat in splats: x, y, z = splat['pos'] # 2. Calculate distance d from eye (assumed at origin) d = (x2 + y2 + z2)0.5 if d < k: # Case 1: Standard splatting radius = r1 energy = splat['alpha'] else: # Case 2: Anti-aliased splatting # Scale radius by d/k radius = r1 (d / k) # Attenuate energy by (k/d)^2 energy = splat['alpha'] ((k / d) 2) # Compute normal vector for polygon rotation (perpendicular to eye-ray) raydir = (x/d, y/d, z/d) ref = (1, 0, 0) if abs(raydir[0]) < 0.9 else (0, 1, 0) normal = (raydir[1]ref[2] - raydir[2]ref[1], raydir[2]ref[0] - raydir[0]ref[2], raydir[0]ref[1] - raydir[1]ref[0]) nlen = (normal[0]2 + normal[1]2 + normal[2]2)0.5 normal = (normal[0]/nlen, normal[1]/nlen, normal[2]/nlen) # 3. Render splat as polygon drawpolygon(splat['pos'], radius, energy, normal) def drawpolygon(center, radius, alpha, normal): # Hardware rasterization step: draw a polygon centered at center, # oriented perpendicular to normal, textured with the pre-computed kernel, # and composited into the screen buffer with alpha = alpha. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Off-Axis Error: The calculation of splat size using similar triangles (Equation 4 in source) underestimates the required low-pass filtering for splats not on the +Z axis. At the view cone boundary (e.g., 30 degrees), the kernel is ~1.15 times larger than strictly necessary. However, this results in more filtering than required, satisfying the Nyquist condition and avoiding aliasing. Temporal Aliasing: This method addresses spatial pre-aliasing but does not inherently solve temporal aliasing (flickering/strobing) during animation, although it significantly reduces it by smoothing the spatial signal. Orthographic Projection: For orthographic projections, \phi(d) is constant. If p > 2\omega holds, no anti-aliasing is needed. If not, the method can be adapted, but the divergence-based scaling is specific to perspective. A variant used in holographic wave field rendering where anti-aliasing is achieved by magnifying the wave field by a factor of two in both dimensions and applying a fill factor of 0.93. This approach differs from the geometric scaling of splats by operating in the frequency domain via grid interpolation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of splats. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat data. Requires a pre-computed kernel texture (e.g., 256 \times 256). Performance: In tests, a 498x398x1 volume (198K splats) rendered into a 270x157 image showed strong aliasing in standard splatting, which was smoothed out by this method. A 512x512x103 terrain volume (386K splats) showed elimination of flickering and strobing. A 420x468x62 microtubule volume (103K splats) rendered into a 270x270 image also demonstrated the technique's applicability. Strengths: Effectively eliminates pre-aliasing artifacts in perspective views where splats become smaller than pixels. Maintains energy conservation. Limitations: Introduces increased blur for distant objects due to the larger kernel size. Does not address post-aliasing from non-ideal reconstruction filters or temporal aliasing directly. When to use: Perspective volume rendering where high-frequency details in the volume raster exceed the integration grid's sampling capacity at distance. When not to use: Orthographic rendering where grid sampling is uniform and sufficient, or when real-time performance is critical and blur is unacceptable. The method was introduced in the paper "An Anti-Aliasing Technique for Splatting" by Westover, presented at IEEE Visualization 1997, where it was awarded Best Paper. It addresses a fundamental limitation of splatting algorithms, which perform reconstruction in perspective space, unlike ray-casting algorithms that perform reconstruction in eye space and can naturally adjust kernel sizes as rays diverge. The technique was implemented using hardware acceleration, rendering splats as textured polygons.
