name: Differentiable Rendering
head: Differentiable Splatting, Gradient-Based Rendering
body: Differentiable rendering treats the image formation process as a differentiable function, enabling the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (geometry, appearance, pose) via backpropagation. This allows for gradient-based optimization of 3D representations directly from 2D image observations. It sets itself apart from standard rendering by exposing internal state gradients to upstream optimizers, facilitating tasks like pose estimation, shape reconstruction, and sequential affordance reasoning for robotic planning. It builds on Splatting by differentiating the rasterization and compositing steps. Solves the "many-to-one" mapping issue in temporal deformation by fusing source voxel values into a target grid using trilinear kernel weights, addressing density collisions during contraction. Focuses on optimizing primitive parameters and network weights through differentiable rendering pipelines to learn 3D representations from 2D images. Integrates kinematics-aware deformation with 3D Gaussian Splatting using Implicit Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) to provide accurate gradients for robotic control and planning. Performs sequential affordance reasoning on the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation, where rendered feature fields encode interaction probabilities over time, allowing robots to plan actions in the rendered 3D scene. For Fourier splatting, the forward pass implements a tile-based rasterizer in polar coordinates. For each pixel j with polar coordinates (\rhoj, \thetaj) in the tangent plane of primitive si, the signed distance to the boundary is computed as \varphij = \rhoj - ri(\thetaj). Points with \varphij \ge 0 are discarded. The per-pixel opacity is calculated as \alpha{i,j} = oi \cdot \max\left(0, \frac{ri(\thetaj) - \rhoj}{ri(\thetaj)}\right)^{\sigmai}. Colors are accumulated via front-to-back compositing. Differentiable rendering has evolved from volume rendering techniques to support modern neural graphics. Early work focused on volume rendering equations, where opacity \alpha is computed by integrating density along the ray: \alphai = 1 - \exp\left(-\int Gi(x) dx\right). Recent advancements integrate these principles with Gaussian Splatting, enabling applications like robot learning and 3D reconstruction. Fourier Splatting extends this by using generalized Fourier encoded primitives, adapting power window functions to polar coordinates for scalable radiance fields. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fourier Splatting: Generalized Fourier encoded primitives for scalable radiance fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.19834, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Differentiable Forward Warping with Average Splatting
head: Average Splatting, Forward Warping
body: Differentiable Forward Warping with Average Splatting synthesizes dynamic scenes by warping a canonical volumetric representation (e.g., a voxel grid or radiance field) from a reference time step to a target time step using estimated deformation flows. It solves the "many-to-one" mapping issue inherent in forward warping—where multiple source voxels map to the same target location, such as when an object shrinks—by fusing these contributions using a weighted average via a trilinear kernel. Unlike standard forward warping which may leave holes in the "one-to-many" case (expansion), this method specifically addresses the density accumulation conflict, often paired with an inpaint network for missing regions. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Differentiable Robot Rendering by focusing on temporal deformation of canonical fields rather than static multi-view consistency or specific robotic sensor models. Inputs: Source voxel grid \Vgrid{}{S} (e.g., canonical radiance field). Deformation flow field f{\text{S}\rightarrow\text{T}} mapping source positions to target positions. Outputs: Target voxel grid \Vgrid{}{T} with values fused from the source. Data Structures: \Vgrid{}{S} and \Vgrid{}{T}: 3D arrays indexed by integer coordinates (x, y, z). f{\text{S}\rightarrow\text{T}}[\mathbf{q}]: A vector field where each entry at source index \mathbf{q} is a 3D displacement vector \in \mathbb{R}^3. Algorithm: The warping function \Vgrid{}{T} = \text{Fwarp}(\Vgrid{}{S}, f{\text{S}\rightarrow\text{T}}) is computed as follows: 1. Initialize \Vgrid{}{T} with zeros (or appropriate background). 2. For each voxel \mathbf{q} in the source grid \Vgrid{}{S}: a. Calculate the deformed position: \mathbf{q}' = \mathbf{q} + f{\text{S}\rightarrow\text{T}}[\mathbf{q}]. b. Determine the integer target indices \mathbf{p} that fall within the support of the reconstruction kernel centered at \mathbf{q}'. c. For each target voxel \mathbf{p} in the support: i. Compute the fractional offset vector \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{q}' - \mathbf{p}. ii. Compute the trilinear kernel weight b[\mathbf{u}]. iii. Accumulate the weighted source value into the numerator and the weight into the denominator of \Vgrid{}{T}[\mathbf{p}]. 3. Normalize \Vgrid{}{T}[\mathbf{p}] by dividing the accumulated numerator by the accumulated denominator for all \mathbf{p}. Formulas: The value of a target voxel \mathbf{p} is given by: \Vgrid{}{T}[\mathbf{p}] = \frac {\sum {\forall \mathbf {q}\in \Vgrid {}{S}}b[\mathbf {u}]\cdot \Vgrid {}{S}[\mathbf {q}]}{\sum {\forall \mathbf {q}\in \Vgrid {}{S}}^{}b[\mathbf {u}]} where the trilinear kernel weight b[\mathbf{u}] is defined as: b[\mathbf {u}] = \prod {i \in \{x,y,z\}} \text {max}(0, 1\!-\!\left |\mathbf {u}i \right |) and the offset vector \mathbf{u} is: \mathbf {u} = (\mathbf {q}+f{\text {S}\rightarrow \text {T}}[\mathbf {q}]) - \mathbf {p} Here, \mathbf{q} is the integer coordinate of a source voxel, f{\text{S}\rightarrow\text{T}}[\mathbf{q}] is the deformation flow vector at \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p} is the integer coordinate of a target voxel, and \mathbf{u}i is the i-th component of \mathbf{u}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def forwardwarpaveragesplatting(sourcegrid, flowfield, targetshape): """ Warps sourcegrid to targetgrid using average splatting. Args: sourcegrid: 3D list of values indexed as [d][h][w]. flowfield: 3D list of 3-tuples (dx, dy, dz) indexed as [d][h][w]. targetshape: Tuple (D, H, W) defining the output grid dimensions. Returns: targetgrid: 3D list with warped values. """ # Initialize accumulators numerator = [[[0.0 for in range(targetshape[2])] for in range(targetshape[1])] for in range(targetshape[0])] denominator = [[[0.0 for in range(targetshape[2])] for in range(targetshape[1])] for in range(targetshape[0])] # Iterate over all source voxels for qd in range(len(sourcegrid)): for qh in range(len(sourcegrid[0])): for qw in range(len(sourcegrid[0][0])): val = sourcegrid[qd][qh][qw] flow = flowfield[qd][qh][qw] # Calculate deformed position deformedpos = (qd + flow[0], qh + flow[1], qw + flow[2]) # Determine bounding box of the kernel support # Trilinear kernel is non-zero when |ui| < 1 pmin = [int(math.floor(deformedpos[i] - 1.0)) for i in range(3)] pmax = [int(math.floor(deformedpos[i] + 1.0)) for i in range(3)] # Clip to target grid boundaries for i in range(3): pmin[i] = max(0, min(pmin[i], targetshape[i] - 1)) pmax[i] = max(0, min(pmax[i], targetshape[i] - 1)) # Iterate over target voxels in the support for pd in range(pmin[0], pmax[0] + 1): for ph in range(pmin[1], pmax[1] + 1): for pw in range(pmin[2], pmax[2] + 1): # Calculate fractional offset u u = (deformedpos[0] - pd, deformedpos[1] - ph, deformedpos[2] - pw) # Calculate trilinear weight b[u] weight = 1.0 for i in range(3): weight = max(0.0, 1.0 - abs(u[i])) # Accumulate numerator[pd][ph][pw] += weight val denominator[pd][ph][pw] += weight # Normalize targetgrid = [[[0.0 for in range(targetshape[2])] for in range(targetshape[1])] for in range(targetshape[0])] for d in range(targetshape[0]): for h in range(targetshape[1]): for w in range(targetshape[2]): denom = denominator[d][h][w] targetgrid[d][h][w] = numerator[d][h][w] / denom if denom != 0.0 else 0.0 return targetgrid Parameters: Kernel support: Trilinear (support size 2x2x2 in terms of integer grid steps, covering the immediate 8 neighbors). Flow estimation: The flow f{\text{S}\rightarrow\text{T}} is typically estimated to be smooth and continuous along the timeline. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Many-to-One: When multiple source voxels map to the same target voxel (e.g., object shrinking), average splatting correctly fuses them. One-to-Many: When one source voxel maps to multiple target voxels (e.g., object expanding), holes may appear in the target grid; the source notes indicate an inpaint network is used to handle this. Boundary Conditions: Source voxels near the boundary may warp outside the target grid bounds; the implementation must clip coordinates to valid grid indices. A variant used in multi-view warping contexts (e.g., Depth Peeling) to handle warping seams caused by source texel enlargement in the novel view. It uses four subpixel samples (subpixel offsets) to avoid seams, as no simpler solution is known. It also extends the field of view for Depth Peeling by scaling the screen dimension by a constant factor (1.2) to handle corrupt periphery due to large view displacements and lack of source pixels at image boundaries. Complexity: The complexity is proportional to the number of source voxels multiplied by the kernel support size (constant, 8 for trilinear). O(N \cdot K) where N is the number of source voxels and K is the kernel footprint. Performance: The method is differentiable, allowing gradients to flow back through the warping operation to the flow field and source grid, enabling end-to-end training. Strengths: Handles the many-to-one problem naturally without leaving artifacts or requiring complex conflict resolution logic beyond weighting. Ensures smooth flows by assuming continuous deformation. Limitations: Does not inherently solve the one-to-many problem (holes); requires additional inpainting or sampling strategies. Performance may degrade if the deformation field is highly discontinuous or if the kernel support is large. The method was introduced in the context of novel view synthesis for dynamic scenes, specifically in the paper "Forward Flow for Novel View Synthesis of Dynamic Scenes". It builds on the concept of forward warping, which estimates deformation from a canonical time to another time step. The specific "average splatting" technique was proposed to address the many-to-one mapping issue in forward warping of voxel grids. name: Learning and Training Methods
body: This family covers methods for learning and training 3D Gaussian splatting representations from 2D images. It focuses on optimizing primitive parameters (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) and network weights through differentiable rendering pipelines. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Splatting Without the Blur by its reliance on gradient-based learning rather than purely analytical initialization, and from Rendering Pipelines and Passes by its focus on the training loop rather than inference rasterization. All methods in this family rely on differentiable rendering to compute gradients from the rendered image to the Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) and/or network weights. The rendering process remains differentiable with respect to the scene representation. Loss functions typically combine photometric reconstruction error, such as \mathcal{L}{L1} or \mathcal{L}{MSE}, with perceptual or structural metrics like \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} or \mathcal{L}{LPIPS}. Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction refers to a family of methods that reconstruct animatable, photorealistic 3D human or head avatars by representing them as collections of 3D Gaussians [1575-gaussian-avatar-reconstruction.md]. Unlike static scene reconstruction, these methods must handle non-rigid deformation, ensuring that the Gaussian primitives move and deform consistently with the underlying subject's pose and expression [1575-gaussian-avatar-reconstruction.md]. The family is distinguished from static Gaussian Splatting [946-gaussian-splatting.md] by its integration of parametric body models (e.g., SMPL, FLAME) or deformation fields to constrain and drive the Gaussian positions, and from neural radiance field (NeRF) avatars by its explicit, rasterizable representation that enables real-time rendering speeds [1575-gaussian-avatar-reconstruction.md]. A core principle is the anchoring of Gaussians to a geometric prior. Most methods initialize Gaussians on the surface of a parametric mesh (e.g., SMPL for full body, FLAME for heads) in a canonical rest pose [1575-gaussian-avatar-reconstruction.md]. During training, these Gaussians are deformed to match the target pose using rigid transformations (e.g., Linear Blend Skinning) and/or non-rigid deformation fields [1575-gaussian-avatar-reconstruction.md]. This ensures that the avatar can be animated to novel poses while maintaining structural integrity [1575-gaussian-avatar-reconstruction.md]. This family encompasses methods that reconstruct 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes directly from input images without iterative per-scene optimization or reliance on pre-computed Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines [6500-pose-free-and-feed-forward-training.md]. Unlike traditional 3DGS which requires minutes to hours of per-scene optimization using known camera poses, these methods use feed-forward neural networks or geometry priors to generate primitives and camera parameters in seconds [6500-pose-free-and-feed-forward-training.md]. They are distinguished from sibling methods like Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction by their focus on generalizable scene reconstruction from static, unposed image collections rather than animatable human models [6500-pose-free-and-feed-forward-training.md]. VS-Splat integrated with the GenDen add-on model. On CO3D dataset, VS-Splat + GenDen yields PSNR 22.09, SSIM 0.865, LPIPS 0.208. Not given in the sources. VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.12343, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction
body: Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction is a family of methods that reconstruct photorealistic, animatable 3D human or head avatars from video data by representing them as collections of 3D Gaussians. It solves the challenge of maintaining topological consistency and rigging capabilities in dynamic reconstruction, which is difficult for implicit neural radiance fields (NeRFs) or unstructured Gaussian Splatting. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which treats primitives as independent entities, this family anchors Gaussians to parametric mesh priors (such as SMPL for bodies or FLAME for heads) to ensure structural integrity during animation. It sets itself apart from siblings like Pose-free and Feed-forward Training by explicitly binding geometry to a parametric model, and from Point-Based Neural Renderer Architecture by using explicit Gaussian primitives optimized directly from images. The family shares the following mechanisms, terms, and math, building on the splatting principles of primitive representation, transformation, rasterization, and compositing. Parametric Anchoring: Gaussians are initialized on the surface of a parametric mesh (e.g., SMPL, FLAME) in a canonical rest pose [S1, 1477-gaussian-avatars.md, 1482-relightable-gaussian-codec-avatars.md, unofficial]. Each Gaussian i is associated with a specific triangle t or vertex of the mesh. Deformation Pipeline: To animate the avatar, Gaussians are deformed from the canonical pose to a target pose \theta and expression \beta [S1, 8385-smpl-based-rigid-non-rigid-deformation.md, unofficial]. 1. Rigid Deformation: The canonical position \mathbf{p}i is transformed using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS): \mathbf{p}{rigid} = \sum{j=1}^{N{bones}} w{i,j} \mathbf{T}j(\theta) \mathbf{p}i where w{i,j} are skinning weights and \mathbf{T}j(\theta) are bone transformation matrices. 2. Non-Rigid Deformation: A residual offset \Delta \mathbf{p} is predicted by a deformation network (e.g., MLP) conditioned on pose and/or canonical position. The final position is: \mathbf{p}'i = \mathbf{p}{rigid} + \Delta \mathbf{p} Some methods predict parameters directly via a feedforward network, implicitly handling deformation. 3. Covariance Update: The covariance matrix \Sigmai is transformed using the Jacobian J of the deformation map with respect to the canonical position: \Sigma'i = J \Sigmai J^T + \sigma^2 I where \sigma^2 I is a small regularization term to ensure positive definiteness. The Jacobian J includes contributions from both LBS and the non-rigid deformation network. Differentiable Rendering: The deformed Gaussians are rendered using differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. Gradients are computed from the rendered image to the Gaussian parameters and network weights. Loss Function: Training minimizes a combination of photometric and perceptual losses: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 loss between rendered and ground truth images, and \mathcal{L}{MS-SSIM} is the multi-scale structural similarity loss. The foundational method for 3D scene representation using anisotropic 3D Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of NeRFs by replacing ray marching with tile-based rasterization. Choose this as the base rendering engine for all avatar methods. Enriches Gaussians with physical material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, normals) to enable specular and reflective rendering. Choose this when photorealistic material appearance is required beyond simple color. Improves robustness in casual captures by detecting and ignoring transient distractors in a pre-trained feature space. Choose this when training data contains significant noise or moving occluders. Reconstructs animatable head avatars by anchoring Gaussians to a FLAME mesh. It solves topological consistency by constraining Gaussians to mesh triangles. Choose this for high-fidelity head avatars with explicit rigging. Supports dynamic relighting under novel illumination by decoupling geometry and appearance into a FLAME-rigged Gaussian representation and a relightable BRDF. Choose this when interactive relighting is required. Eliminates the requirement for known camera poses by anchoring representation to a canonical system and using intrinsics token embeddings. Choose this when camera poses are unknown or unreliable. Provides the underlying deformation mechanism (rigid LBS + non-rigid offsets) for full-body avatars. Choose this as the deformation backbone for body avatars. Reconstructs animatable human avatars using drivable 3D Gaussians. It addresses the limitation of standard rigid deformation by leveraging two distinct MLPs to predict large motions and employing SE(3) fields to model pose-dependent effects. Choose this for detailed geometry and appearance reconstruction in full-body avatars. A production-grade GS-based head model for volumetric telepresence by Meta. A holistic scene reconstruction method including humans, vehicles, and static background. A representation for real-time 4D head avatar rendering targeting photorealism and efficiency on commodity devices. Introduces a learned manifold closely aligned with the head surface. Extracts layered mesh proxies from the manifold to approximate volumetric rendering while enabling fast rasterization. Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction emerged as a solution to the limitations of NeRF-based avatars, which suffer from slow rendering speeds and lack of explicit rigging. The field leverages the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting and adapts it to parametric human models like SMPL [S1, 8385-smpl-based-rigid-non-rigid-deformation.md, unofficial] and FLAME. Early works like Gaussian Avatars demonstrated the feasibility of anchoring Gaussians to mesh triangles for head avatars. Subsequent developments introduced relighting [S1, 1482-relightable-gaussian-codec-avatars.md, unofficial], robustness to noise, and full-body deformation [S1, 8385-smpl-based-rigid-non-rigid-deformation.md, unofficial]. The method is used in virtual production and telepresence applications. Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Gaussian Splatting
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), 3D GS
body: Gaussian Splatting is a method for 3D scene representation and novel view synthesis that models a scene as a collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color. It solves the computational bottleneck of implicit neural radiance fields (NeRFs) by replacing ray marching with a differentiable, tile-based rasterization pipeline. Unlike NeRFs, which query dense volumes along rays, Gaussian Splatting projects 3D ellipsoids to 2D screen-space footprints (splats) and composites them via alpha blending, enabling real-time rendering speeds. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using explicit, learnable Gaussian primitives optimized directly from images, rather than implicit neural networks or fixed geometric meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed input images \{Ii\} and a sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud providing initial camera poses and 3D points. Outputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N, where each gi is parameterized by a mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, an opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}i for color. The method also outputs rendered novel views. Data Structures: Each Gaussian gi stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i: 3D position (mean). \mathbf{q}i: A quaternion (4 floats) representing rotation, from which the rotation matrix \mathbf{R}i is derived. \mathbf{s}i: A 3D vector representing scale, from which the scaling matrix \mathbf{S}i = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}i) is derived. \alphai: Opacity (1 float). \mathbf{c}{i, l}: SH coefficients for band l (view-dependent color). For band 3, this is 48 floats (3 RGB channels \times 16 coefficients). The covariance matrix is reconstructed as \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^T \mathbf{R}i^T. This parameterization ensures \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i remains positive semi-definite during optimization. Rendering Pipeline: The rendering process consists of four main stages: Initialization, Projection, Sorting, and Compositing. 1. Initialization: Gaussians are initialized at the 3D points of the SfM cloud. The mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i is set to the point position. The initial scale \mathbf{s}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, and opacity \alphai are set to small constants or identity, as standard practice. Color \mathbf{c}i is initialized by averaging or median-filtering pixel colors from the input images where the point is visible. 2. Projection (Splatting): Each 3D Gaussian is projected to the 2D image plane. Coordinate Transformation: The 3D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i is transformed to camera coordinates: \boldsymbol{\mu}i^c = \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\mu}i, where \mathbf{W} is the world-to-camera transformation matrix. 2D Mean: The projected 2D mean is computed via perspective projection \phi{\mathbf{K}} (using camera intrinsics \mathbf{K}): \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i = \phi{\mathbf{K}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i^c). 2D Covariance: The perspective projection is non-affine. It is approximated by a local affine transformation using the Jacobian \mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} of the projection at \boldsymbol{\mu}i^c. The 2D covariance matrix \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i is computed as: \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T Note: \mathbf{W} in the covariance formula refers to the rotational component of the world-to-camera transform if \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i is defined in world space, or the full linearization if defined in camera space. Conic Matrix: To avoid matrix inversion in the fragment shader, the inverse 2D covariance is computed as the conic matrix \mathbf{C}i = \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i^{-1}. 3. Sorting: Frustum Culling: Gaussians outside the camera frustum are discarded. Tile Assignment: The image is divided into non-overlapping tiles (typically 16 \times 16 pixels). For each Gaussian, an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) is computed in screen space. The Gaussian is assigned to all tiles it intersects. Depth Sorting: Within each tile, the assigned Gaussians are sorted by depth (distance from camera center to \boldsymbol{\mu}i) in back-to-front order. This is typically done using a GPU-optimized radix sort on a packed key of (tile ID, depth). 4. Compositing (Alpha Blending): For each pixel in a tile, the sorted list of overlapping Gaussians is traversed front-to-back (or back-to-front depending on implementation, but standard is front-to-back accumulation of transmittance). 2D Gaussian Evaluation: For a pixel at screen coordinate \mathbf{x}, the value of the projected 2D Gaussian is: \mathcal{G}i^{2D}(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i)^T \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i)\right) In practice, this is computed using the conic matrix \mathbf{C}i = [C{00}, C{01}, C{11}] and local coordinates (x, y) = \mathbf{x} - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}i: \text{power} = -0.5 (C{00} x^2 + C{11} y^2) - C{01} xy \mathcal{G}i^{2D}(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(\text{power}). Effective Opacity: The effective opacity \alpha'i contributed by the Gaussian at the pixel is the product of the learned opacity \alphai and the 2D Gaussian value: \alpha'i = \alphai \mathcal{G}i^{2D}(\mathbf{x}). Color Retrieval: The color \mathbf{c}i is retrieved by evaluating the spherical harmonics at the viewing direction \mathbf{v} (from camera center to \boldsymbol{\mu}i). Accumulation: The pixel color \mathbf{C} is computed via alpha compositing: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{c}i \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where \mathcal{N} is the set of sorted Gaussians for the pixel, and the product term represents the accumulated transmittance Ti. Training Loop: Loss Function: The rendered image \tilde{C} is compared to the ground truth image C using a weighted combination of L1 loss and D-SSIM (Difference SSIM): \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \lambda is a hyperparameter. Optimization: Parameters \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{q}i, \mathbf{s}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i are updated via stochastic gradient descent. Adaptive Density Control: To manage the number of Gaussians, the method periodically (e.g., every 100 iterations) performs: 1. Clone: Small Gaussians with large position gradients are cloned to under-reconstructed regions. 2. Split: Large Gaussians with large position gradients are split into two smaller Gaussians to over-reconstructed regions. 3. Prune: Gaussians with opacity below a threshold \tau or screen-space size exceeding a limit are removed. 4. Opacity Reset: Opacities are periodically reset to a small value to prune redundancies. 2yy - 2zz, 2xy - 2zw, 2xz + 2yw], [2xy + 2zw, 1 - 2xx - 2zz, 2yz - 2xw], [2xz - 2yw, 2yz + 2xw, 1 - 2xx - 2yy] ]) def diagmatrix(s): return np.diag(s) def inverse2x2(M): det = M[0,0]M[1,1] - M[0,1]M[1,0] return np.array([[M[1,1]/det, -M[0,1]/det], [-M[1,0]/det, M[0,0]/det]]) def computeboundingbox(mu2d, Sigma2d): eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2d) stddevs = 2.0 np.sqrt(eigenvalues) dx = stddevs[0] + stddevs[1] dy = stddevs[0] + stddevs[1] return (mu2d[0] - 0.31539156525252005 basis[13] = 0.5462742152960396 np.sin(theta) np.cos(phi) basis[14] = 0.5462742152960396 np.sin(theta) np.sin(phi) basis[15] = 0.10578554698323738 (5np.cos(theta)2 - 3) return basis def evaluatesh(shcoeffs, viewdir): theta = np.arccos(np.clip(viewdir[2], -1.0, 1.0)) phi = np.arctan2(viewdir[1], viewdir[0]) shbasis = evaluateshbasis(theta, phi, degree=3) color = np.zeros(3) for c in range(3): color[c] = np.dot(shcoeffs[c], shbasis) return np.clip(color, 0, 1) def computejacobian(mucam, K): x, y, z = mucam fx, fy = K[0, 0], K[1, 1] cx, cy = K[0, 2], K[1, 2] J = np.zeros((2, 3)) J[0, 0] = fx / z J[0, 2] = -fx x / (z2) J[1, 1] = fy / z J[1, 2] = -fy y / (z2) return J def projectpoint(mucam, K): x, y, z = mucam fx, fy = K[0, 0], K[1, 1] cx, cy = K[0, 2], K[1, 2] u = fx x / z + cx v = fy y / z + cy return np.array([u, v]) def rendergaussians(gaussians, camerapose, intrinsics, imagewidth, imageheight): processedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(g.q) S = diagmatrix(g.s) Sigma = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T mucam = camerapose[:3,:3] @ g.mu + camerapose[:3, 3] J = computejacobian(mucam, intrinsics) Wrot = camerapose[:3,:3] Sigma2d = J @ Wrot @ Sigma @ Wrot.T @ J.T mu2d = projectpoint(mucam, intrinsics) Sigma2dinv = inverse2x2(Sigma2d) bbox = computeboundingbox(mu2d, Sigma2d) processedgaussians.append({ 'mu2d': mu2d, 'conic': Sigma2dinv, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'shcoeffs': g.shcoeffs, 'bbox': bbox, 'depth': mucam[2] }) tilesize = 16 tiles = createtiles(imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize) image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for tile in tiles: tilegaussians = [g for g in processedgaussians if intersectsbbox(g['bbox'], tile)] tilegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['depth'], reverse=True) for y in range(tile.ystart, min(tile.yend, imageheight)): for x in range(tile.xstart, min(tile.xend, imagewidth)): pixelcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) transmittance = 1.0 for g in tilegaussians: dx = x - g['mu2d'][0] dy = y - g['mu2d'][1] C00, C01, C11 = g['conic'] power = -0.5 (C00 dx2 + C11 dy2 + 2 C01 dx dy) power = max(power, -2.0) gaussianval = np.exp(power) alphaeff = g['alpha'] gaussianval viewdir = np.array([g['mu2d'][0], g['mu2d'][1], 1.0]) viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) color = evaluatesh(g['shcoeffs'], viewdir) pixelcolor += color alphaeff transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - alphaeff) if transmittance < 1e-4: break image[y, x] = pixelcolor return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential function in the 2D Gaussian evaluation can underflow to zero for distant pixels. Clamping the power term to a minimum value (e.g., -2.0) prevents numerical instability. Boundaries: Gaussians near the camera plane can cause division by zero in the Jacobian computation. A small epsilon should be added to the depth z in the Jacobian calculation. Degenerate Input: If the SfM point cloud is sparse or noisy, initialization may fail. Random initialization can be used but converges slower. Covariance Stability: Directly optimizing the covariance matrix can lead to non-positive semi-definite matrices. Using quaternion and scale parameterization ensures validity. The Unnormalized 3D Gaussian Function is a Gaussian representation used in 3D Gaussian Splatting where the amplitude a at the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} equals the opacity, representing the peak capacity to block or emit light. It differs from the Normalized 3D Gaussian Function by parameterizing the function via its peak value rather than its integral, making a the intensity at the center rather than the total light capacity. Row-constant hoisting is an optimization for the inner pixel loop of a Gaussian splatting rasterizer that hoists row-constant terms outside the inner (column) loop to minimize arithmetic operations per pixel. It reduces the computational cost of evaluating the 2D Gaussian exponent by precomputing terms dependent only on the row coordinate, allowing the inner loop to perform fewer multiplications and additions per column. This method is a specific implementation detail within the broader Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, distinct from higher-level optimizations like Contribution-based ordering or RoofGS Dual-Pixel Incremental Evaluation. This method projects a 3D Gaussian primitive, defined by a mean and a covariance matrix in world space, into a 2D elliptical footprint (splat) on the image plane for rasterization. It solves the problem of rendering millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians in real-time by avoiding ray marching; instead, it approximates the non-linear perspective projection with a local affine transformation, preserving the Gaussian form in 2D. It sets itself apart from Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection by using a fixed image plane rather than a per-Gaussian tangent plane, and from 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling by adding a constant epsilon to the diagonal for positive definiteness rather than rescaling the determinant. Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) is a novel view synthesis method for unconstrained image collections that explicitly separates scene appearance into intrinsic material properties and dynamic environmental factors (such as illumination and weather) per 3D Gaussian point. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeRF-based methods by avoiding global latent embeddings, which allows it to capture local high-frequency changes without blurring intrinsic textures with dynamic variations. The method employs adaptive sampling from image features and 2D visibility maps to mitigate transient occlusions and photometric variations. 3DGUT is a Gaussian projection technique that employs an unscented transform to improve the affine approximation of the projection operator, providing more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane. It replaces the standard first-order Taylor expansion used in Gaussian Splatting with a non-linear propagation of statistical samples to reduce projection approximation errors. Transformer-based Reconstruction methods replace the iterative optimization loop of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a feed-forward neural network that directly predicts Gaussian parameters from input images. This approach solves the computational bottleneck of per-scene optimization, enabling real-time reconstruction from single or sparse views. It differs from iterative siblings by eliminating the need for gradient descent on scene parameters, instead relying on learned priors within the transformer architecture to generalize across scenes. 3D Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering (VoGE) is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents scenes as a sum of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids and computes image synthesis via ray tracing rather than rasterization. It solves the occlusion ambiguity inherent in distance-based blending by accumulating volume density distributions along viewing rays, enabling realistic interaction between overlapping objects. Unlike its sibling Gaussian Splatting, which approximates volume rendering through 2D rasterization of projected splats, VoGE replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture exact volume density distributions for blending. Stochastic Gaussian Splatting (SGS) refers to two distinct methodological extensions of 3D Gaussian Splatting that replace deterministic rasterization with probabilistic sampling. The first variant, often termed Bayesian SGS, treats Gaussian parameters as random variables to enable uncertainty estimation alongside novel view synthesis. The second variant, Gaussian Point Splatting, eliminates the per-tile radix sort and tile-based rendering bottlenecks by sampling opaque points from Gaussians and compositing them via atomic operations, enabling the interactive rendering of hundreds of millions of Gaussians. Both methods rely on Variational Inference or stochastic transparency to approximate the volume rendering integral without explicit depth sorting. Rendering Implementation defines the computational pipeline that transforms a set of 3D Gaussian primitives into a 2D image via screen-space rasterization and alpha compositing. It solves the real-time rendering bottleneck of volumetric methods by replacing ray marching with a differentiable rasterization pipeline, allowing gradients to flow from the rendered image back to Gaussian parameters. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on full 3D covariance projection and tile-based depth sorting to handle arbitrary 3D geometry and occlusion. Contribution-based ordering is a post-training method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that sorts primitives by their visual importance to enable progressive rendering. It solves the problem of inefficient data streaming by ensuring high-impact splats are transmitted and rendered first. Unlike EAGLES which uses this metric during training to prune splats, this method operates on the fully trained model to select impactful splats for independent streaming. 3D Convex Splatting is a neural rendering method that replaces standard 3D Gaussian primitives with smooth convex shapes to represent scenes. It solves the limitation of Gaussians in accurately modeling flat surfaces and sharp edges, offering greater geometric flexibility and requiring fewer primitives for equivalent fidelity. Unlike its parent Gaussian Splatting, which relies on elliptical distributions, this method introduces non-elliptical convex boundaries to better approximate complex geometry. Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting is a method that predicts a complete 3D Gaussian representation of a scene directly from a sparse set of input images, bypassing the iterative optimization required by standard Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of slow reconstruction by using a multi-view Transformer to map image features to Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass. It differs from iterative methods by trading per-scene training time for inference latency, and from other feed-forward approaches by explicitly predicting the full set of Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color) via a linear projection of transformer latents. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N \cdot T), where N is the number of Gaussians and T is the number of tiles, but effectively O(P \cdot K) per pixel, where P is the number of pixels and K is the average number of overlapping Gaussians per tile. Sorting is O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: O(N), storing parameters for each Gaussian. Typical scenes require millions of Gaussians, leading to high memory usage. Measured Performance: Real-time rendering (60+ FPS) is achievable on modern GPUs for scenes with hundreds of thousands to millions of Gaussians. Training time is significantly faster than NeRFs (hours vs. days) but slower than feed-forward methods. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high visual fidelity, explicit representation allows for easy editing and integration with graphics pipelines. Limitations: High memory consumption and potential for popping artifacts due to depth sorting approximations. When to Use: Real-time novel view synthesis, interactive applications, and scenarios requiring high-quality rendering from sparse inputs. When Not to Use: Memory-constrained environments, scenes requiring precise volumetric effects (e.g., smoke, fire) without extensions, or real-time applications on low-end hardware. Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It builds on earlier work in volume splatting, particularly Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) splatting, and point-based rendering methods. The method was developed to address the computational limitations of NeRFs, offering a hybrid approach that combines the optimization benefits of neural networks with the efficiency of explicit rasterization. It has since become a dominant paradigm in 3D scene representation and novel view synthesis. name: Normalized 3D Gaussian Function
head: Normal Distribution Helper, Normalized Gaussian, Probability Density Function Gaussian
body: The Normalized 3D Gaussian Function is a probability density function (PDF) scaled by a weight parameter to model the extinction coefficient in volume rendering. It serves as the fundamental building block for EWA splatting and Gaussian mixture models, ensuring that the total integrated capacity of a primitive to block or emit light is explicitly controlled by its weight w rather than its peak amplitude. Unlike the Unnormalized 3D Gaussian Function, where the amplitude at the mean equals opacity, the normalized variant separates the shape normalization from the intensity scaling, making it suitable for accurate volumetric integration where the integral of the density field must equal a specific physical quantity. Inputs: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D position vector at which to evaluate the function. w \in \mathbb{R}: The weight parameter, representing the total capacity to block/emit light, equivalent to the unbounded integral of the function. \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The mean position (center) of the Gaussian. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The covariance matrix defining the shape and orientation of the Gaussian. Outputs: g \in \mathbb{R}: The value of the normalized 3D Gaussian function at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: Exact storage layouts and parameterization schemes are Not given in the sources. Formulas: The normalized 3D Gaussian function \mathcal{G}3^n is defined as the product of the weight w and the standard multivariate normal PDF \mathcal{N}3: \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathbf{x}, w, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = w \mathcal{N}3(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) where the PDF \mathcal{N}3 is: \mathcal{N}3(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}3(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} The normalization factor \mathcal{I}3(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) ensures that \mathcal{N}3 integrates to one over \mathbb{R}^3: \mathcal{I}3(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} Consequently, the weight w is equivalent to the unbounded integral of the function: \int{\mathbb{R}^3} \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathbf{x}, w, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \, d\mathbf{x} = w Steps: 1. Compute the difference vector \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}. 2. Compute the inverse covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}. If \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is singular or near-singular, add a small epsilon to the diagonal or use a pseudo-inverse. 3. Compute the quadratic form Q = \mathbf{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{d}. 4. Compute the determinant \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}). 5. Compute the normalization constant Z = \sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}. 6. Compute the exponential term E = \exp(-0.5 \cdot Q). 7. Compute the PDF value P = E / Z. 8. Return the result g = w \cdot P. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalized3dgaussian(x, w, mu, Sigma): """ Evaluates the normalized 3D Gaussian function. Args: x: list/tuple of 3 floats, position vector. w: float, weight parameter (total integral). mu: list/tuple of 3 floats, mean vector. Sigma: list of lists, 3x3 covariance matrix. Returns: float: Value of the normalized Gaussian at x. """ # 1. Difference vector d = [x[i] - mu[i] for i in range(3)] # 2. Inverse covariance matrix (3x3 cofactor method) a, b, c = Sigma[0][0], Sigma[0][1], Sigma[0][2] ds, e, f = Sigma[1][0], Sigma[1][1], Sigma[1][2] g, h, ival = Sigma[2][0], Sigma[2][1], Sigma[2][2] det = a(eival - fh) - b(dsival - fg) + c(dsh - eg) if det == 0: return 0.0 # Singular matrix fallback invdet = 1.0 / det inv = [ [(eival - fh)invdet, (ch - bival)invdet, (bf - ce)invdet], [(fg - dsival)invdet, (aival - cg)invdet, (cds - af)invdet], [(dsh - eg)invdet, (bg - ah)invdet, (ae - bds)invdet] ] # 3. Quadratic form: d^T inv d Q = 0.0 for k in range(3): for l in range(3): Q += d[k] inv[k][l] d[l] # 4. Normalization constant: sqrt((2pi)^3 det) normfactor = math.sqrt((2 math.pi)3 det) if normfactor == 0: return 0.0 # 5. Exponential term E = math.exp(-0.5 Q) # 6. PDF value and weighted result pdfval = E / normfactor return w pdfval Parameters: w: Typical values depend on the scene's lighting and opacity. In EWA splatting, w represents the total capacity to block and emit light. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Covariance: If \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = 0, the normalization factor is zero, leading to division by zero. This occurs if the Gaussian is degenerate (e.g., flattened to a plane or line in 3D). Regularization is required. Numerical Stability: For very large quadratic forms Q, \exp(-0.5 Q) underflows to 0, which is acceptable as the contribution is negligible. For very small determinants, the normalization factor becomes tiny, potentially causing overflow if not handled. Positive Definiteness: The inverse and determinant operations assume \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is positive-definite. If the matrix is not SPD (e.g., due to numerical drift in optimization), the quadratic form may yield negative values, resulting in \exp(\text{positive}) which explodes. This variant models the extinction function f(\mathbf{x}) as a mixture of normalized 3D Gaussians, allowing for view-dependent radiance ci(\mathcal{R}) per Gaussian. It is distinguished by its use in exact volumetric integration solutions for complex scenes, where the density field is explicitly defined as a sum of normalized primitives rather than a single blob. Definition: The extinction function is a sum of normalized 3D Gaussians: \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^N \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathbf{x}, wi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) Formula: The radiance along a ray \mathcal{R} at distance t is: c(\mathcal{R}, t) = \sum{i=0}^N ci(\mathcal{R}) \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), wi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) where ci(\mathcal{R}) is the radiance for ray \mathcal{R} from the i-th Gaussian. The final pixel intensity I(\mathbf{p}) is computed via exact volumetric integration: I(\mathbf{p}) = \int0^\infty \left( \sum{i=0}^N ci(\mathcal{R}) \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), wi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) \right) e^{-\int0^t \sum{i=0}^N \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(\tau), wi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) \, d\tau} \, dt This formulation explicitly models emission and attenuation using the normalized Gaussian mixture. Time Complexity: Evaluation of a single Gaussian is O(1) since matrix inverse and determinant operate on constant-size 3 \times 3 matrices. For a mixture of N Gaussians, evaluation is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, w, ci) for N Gaussians. Performance: The normalization factor requires computing a determinant and inverse, which is more expensive than the unnormalized variant where these terms cancel each other out. However, it provides physically meaningful weights for integration. Strengths: Ensures the total integral of the density is exactly w, which is crucial for accurate volumetric rendering and extinction modeling. It is the standard building block for EWA splatting and Gaussian mixture models. Limitations: More computationally intensive than unnormalized Gaussians due to the normalization factor calculation. Requires careful handling of singular covariance matrices. When to use: When accurate volumetric integration is required, or when the total mass/optical depth of a primitive must be explicitly controlled independent of its shape. When not to use: When performance is critical and approximate rendering is acceptable, or when using methods like standard 3DGS that prefer the unnormalized variant because the normalization factors cancel out during evaluation. The normalized 3D Gaussian function originates from the field of volume rendering and splatting, specifically as a building block for EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) splatting. It is formally defined in the context of Gaussian data models for volume rendering, where it is paired with a weight parameter to model extinction. The concept is rooted in the probability density function of the multivariate normal distribution, adapted for computer graphics to represent particle densities or extinction coefficients. It is used in EWA splatting [ZPVBG02] and is a fundamental component in the theoretical underpinnings of 3D Gaussian Splatting [KKLD23], although 3DGS often employs the unnormalized variant for efficiency. name: Gaussian Interpolation
head: Gaussian Filter
body: Gaussian interpolation is a volumetric reconstruction method that uses a Gaussian function as an interpolation kernel to estimate field values at arbitrary points from discrete samples. It solves the problem of reconstructing a continuous volume from a grid or point set while providing smooth, band-limited results. It is distinguished from its parent, the Normalized 3D Gaussian Function, by its specific role as a separable, rotationally symmetric interpolation filter rather than a primitive shape definition. Unlike the 2D Gaussian Probability Density (Standard), it is explicitly designed for multi-dimensional spatial reconstruction in volume rendering contexts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of discrete sample values V at grid points or positions, and a query position \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z). Output: The interpolated scalar value f(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: The kernel is defined by a width parameter \sigma (or a) and a scale factor b. In 3D, the kernel is often implemented via separability, storing 1D kernel weights or computing them on the fly. Formulas: The 1D Gaussian kernel is defined as: f{\text{Gaussian}}(z) = e^{-\frac{z^2}{2\sigma^2}} where \sigma controls the width of the filter. In the context of grid-based interpolation described in, the kernel is parameterized by a (width) and b (scale factor). The 3D Gaussian kernel is given by: h(u, v, w) = b \cdot e^{-a(u^2 + v^2 + w^2)} where u, v, w are the distances of the sample point from the lower, left, rear voxel in the containing cell. Note: also erroneously cites a linear interpolation formula f(x,y,z) = (1-w)f(u,v,0) + wf(u,v,1) as Gaussian in the same paragraph, but explicitly identifies the exponential form above as the Gaussian. When sources disagree on the exponent coefficient, uses a^2 while uses a. Parameters: \sigma (or a): Determines the width of the filter. Larger values result in more smoothing. b: A scale factor. Steps: 1. For a query point \mathbf{x}, identify the surrounding grid cells or sample points. 2. Compute the distance d from \mathbf{x} to each sample point. 3. Evaluate the Gaussian kernel weight w = e^{-\frac{d^2}{2\sigma^2}} for each sample. 4. Sum the weighted sample values and normalize if necessary (depending on whether the kernel is normalized to integrate to one or used as a raw filter). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ripple Artifact: The Gaussian introduces a slight ripple (about 0.1%) into an interpolated uniform function. Blurring: The filter distorts the passband by attenuating high frequencies, causing blurring in the output. Infinite Support: The Gaussian has infinite extent in spatial and frequency domains. It must be truncated for practical implementation, though it falls to zero quickly, minimizing ringing. Uniform Signal Interpolation: A Gaussian filter does not yield f(x,y,z) = V(x,y,z) at grid points and does not interpolate a uniform f(x,y,z) everywhere for uniform grid signals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gaussiankernel1d(dist, sigma): """Evaluates the 1D Gaussian kernel e^(-dist^2 / (2sigma^2)).""" return math.exp(-(dist 2) / (2 sigma 2)) def gaussianinterpolate1d(samples, querypos, sigma, truncationradius=None): """ Interpolate a value at querypos using a 1D Gaussian kernel. samples: list of (position, value) tuples. querypos: float, the position to interpolate at. sigma: float, the width parameter. truncationradius: float, optional cutoff distance for infinite support. """ totalweight = 0.0 totalvalue = 0.0 for pos, val in samples: dist = querypos - pos if truncationradius is not None and abs(dist) > truncationradius: continue weight = gaussiankernel1d(dist, sigma) totalweight += weight totalvalue += val weight if totalweight == 0: return 0.0 return totalvalue / totalweight def gaussianinterpolate3dseparable(grid, querypos, sigma, truncationradius=None): """ Interpolate using separable 1D Gaussians along x, y, z axes. grid: 3D array of values. querypos: tuple (x, y, z) of floats. sigma: float, the width parameter. truncationradius: float, optional cutoff distance for infinite support. """ totalweight = 0.0 totalvalue = 0.0 for i in range(len(grid)): for j in range(len(grid[0])): for k in range(len(grid[0][0])): dx = i - querypos[0] dy = j - querypos[1] dz = k - querypos[2] distsq = dx2 + dy2 + dz2 if truncationradius is not None and distsq > truncationradius2: continue weight = gaussiankernel1d(dx, sigma) gaussiankernel1d(dy, sigma) gaussiankernel1d(dz, sigma) totalweight += weight totalvalue += grid[i][j][k] weight if totalweight == 0: return 0.0 return totalvalue / totalweight The Gaussian Reconstruction Filter is a spatial weighting function applied to jittered samples to improve edge quality and stability in volumetric rendering, specifically replacing box filters in froxel-based temporal anti-aliasing. It is also used in A-buffer methods to compute data weights based on distance from a node. It sets itself apart from its sibling, the Gaussian Kernel Volumetric Primitive, by acting as a post-sampling reconstruction filter for discrete jittered points rather than defining the primitive's shape itself. Gaussian Kernel Volumetric Primitive represents a 3D scene as a collection of volumetric primitives, where each primitive is a 3D Gaussian distribution parameterized by mean, covariance, and color. Unlike standard splatting methods that project Gaussians to 2D ellipses for rasterization, this method treats the Gaussian as a continuous density field in 3D space, enabling physically-based volume rendering (e.g., scattering, emission) via ray tracing. It solves the problem of efficiently simulating 3D structure details and volumetric effects without requiring explicit meshing or expensive neural network evaluations. It is distinguished from its parent Gaussian Interpolation by its explicit use of the 3D Gaussian PDF as a volumetric density function rather than just an interpolation kernel, and from Gaussian Reconstruction Filter by its focus on forward volumetric rendering and ray-marching integration. A variant used in differentiable path tracing to handle shadow boundaries and reduce plateau artifacts. To compute the CDF, it integrates the PDF, treating each halfspace separately and normalizing the PDF on the positive halfspace to integrate to 0.5. The kernel derivative with respect to parameters is given by \frac{\partial \kernel}{\partial \parameters}(\offset) = \frac{-\offset}{\bandwidth^3\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(\frac{-\offset^2}{2\bandwidth^2}\right), which is a translated version of the main text's Eq. 11, simplified by treating offset relative to parameters. Time and Memory Complexity: The Gaussian kernel has infinite support, requiring truncation for practical implementation. The number of samples contributing to a query depends on the truncation radius and \sigma. Separability allows 3D reconstruction to be performed as three 1D passes, reducing computational complexity compared to full 3D convolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of samples within the truncation radius. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: It is the only filter that is both separable and rotationally symmetric. It provides smooth interpolation with infinite continuity in the derivative. It is widely used in point-tossing approaches like splatting because it allows integrating one dimension out, performing 2D reconstruction instead of 3D. Limitations: It introduces a slight ripple (0.1%) in uniform functions. It attenuates high frequencies, causing blurring. It does not preserve uniform values exactly. Interpolation cannot restore sharp edges that existed in the original function prior to sampling. When to Use: When a radially symmetric interpolation kernel is needed. For grids that assume the frequency spectrum is radially bandlimited. In splatting methods where separability and rotational symmetry are beneficial. When Not to Use: When sharp edge preservation is critical, as interpolation inherently smooths the signal and requires non-linear filtering to restore edges. When exact interpolation of uniform data is required. Gaussian interpolation is cited in the context of volume rendering overviews and parallel volume rendering algorithms. It is also used in modern differentiable rendering techniques, such as plateau-reduced differentiable path tracing. The method is often compared with box, linear, cubic, and cardinal spline filters. name: Gaussian Reconstruction Filter
head: Gaussian fit to Blackman-Harris 3.3, Gaussian Weighting Filter
body: The Gaussian Reconstruction Filter is a spatial weighting function applied to jittered sub-froxel samples to improve edge quality and stability compared to a box filter, based on distance from the froxel center. It is also used in A-buffer methods to compute data weights based on the Euclidean distance from a node to a data point. Inputs: Sample positions relative to the filter center (frocel center or grid node). Filter radius r (for the variant in). Standard deviation multiplier n (for the variant in). Radius multiplier m (for the variant in). Outputs: Normalized weight W(x) or w for each sample. Data Structures: Not specified. The filter operates on scalar distances. Steps: 1. Calculate the distance x (or d) from the sample to the center of the froxel (or node). 2. Compute the weight using the appropriate formula based on the specific variant being implemented. 3. Apply the weight to the sample's contribution during accumulation. Formulas: Variant 1: Gaussian fit to Blackman-Harris 3.3 W(x) = e^{-2.29x^2} Where: W(x) is the sample weight. x is the distance from the center of the froxel. Variant 2: Gaussian Weighting Filter First, calculate the variance term: 2\sigma^2 = 2 \left(\frac{r \cdot m}{n}\right)^2 Then, compute the weight: w = e^{-\frac{d^2}{2\sigma^2}} Where: w is the weight. d is the Euclidean distance from the node to the data point. r is the filter radius. m is the radius multiplier. n is the number of standard deviations the radius represents (standard deviation multiplier). Parameters: Blackman-Harris variant: The coefficient 2.29 is fixed. Gaussian Weighting variant: n (standard deviation multiplier): User-specified number of standard deviations the filter radius represents. r (filter radius): Defines the spatial extent. m (radius multiplier): Used in variance calculation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: In the variant, the weight is normalized to the filter radius to guarantee values between 0 and 1, preventing arithmetic overflow or underflow. Distance Calculation: d must be the Euclidean distance. Degenerate Input: If n=0, the variance calculation in would be undefined; however, n represents a user-specified multiplier for standard deviations, implying n > 0. A filtering function for the A-buffer method that computes weights based on the squared distance error or Gaussian distribution. Choose this when explicit control over the Gaussian spread relative to a defined filter radius is required, or when implementing A-buffer density weighting. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The Blackman-Harris fit provides better edge quality and stability under motion compared to a spatiotemporal box filter. The Gaussian Weighting Filter avoids arithmetic overflow/underflow through normalization. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Improved edge quality over box filters; stable under motion; prevents overflow/underflow. Limitations: Requires distance calculation. The variant requires user tuning of n and m. When to Use: Use the Blackman-Harris variant for froxel-based TAA to replace box filters. Use the Gaussian Weighting variant for A-buffer methods where parabolic or Gaussian falloff is desired. The Gaussian fit to Blackman-Harris 3.3 was introduced by Karis in the context of temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering to address the poor edge quality and instability of box filters. The Gaussian Weighting Filter was developed for sampling scattered data onto rectangular grids for volume visualization, offering an alternative to density weighting based on squared distance error. name: Gaussian Kernel Volumetric Primitive
head: 3D Gaussian PDF for Volume Rendering, 3D Gaussian Splatting (Method), Normalized Gaussian Kernel
body: Gaussian Kernel Volumetric Primitive represents a 3D scene as a collection of volumetric primitives, where each primitive is a 3D Gaussian distribution parameterized by mean, covariance, and color. Unlike standard splatting methods that project Gaussians to 2D ellipses for rasterization, this method treats the Gaussian as a continuous density field in 3D space, enabling physically-based volume rendering (e.g., scattering, emission) via ray tracing. It solves the problem of efficiently simulating 3D structure details and volumetric effects without requiring explicit meshing or expensive neural network evaluations. It is distinguished from its parent Gaussian Interpolation by its explicit use of the 3D Gaussian PDF as a volumetric density function rather than just an interpolation kernel, and from Gaussian Reconstruction Filter by its focus on forward volumetric rendering and ray-marching integration. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives. Camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics). Ray definition (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Outputs: Pixel color C and depth/transmittance. Each Gaussian primitive i is stored with: Mean (\mathbf{c}i): 3D position vector (x, y, z). Covariance (\Sigmai): 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix defining shape and orientation. Often parameterized via a rotation matrix R and scaling matrix S such that \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. Color (\mathbf{c}i): RGB color value. Opacity/Alpha (\alphai): Scalar controlling the strength of the primitive. The normalized 3D Gaussian kernel function gi(\mathbf{x}) at a point \mathbf{x} is defined as: gi(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2} |\Sigmai|^{1/2}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}i)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}i)} where: \mathbf{c}i is the center (mean) of the Gaussian. \Sigmai is the covariance matrix. |\Sigmai| is the determinant of \Sigmai. The density \rhoi(\mathbf{x}) along a ray is derived from this kernel. For rendering, the transmittance T(t) along a ray segment from t{near} to t{far} is computed by integrating the density. A closed-form solution using the error function (\text{erf}) is employed for efficiency. The transmittance T(t) is calculated as: T(t) = \exp\left( -\int{t{near}}^{t} \rhoi(\mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}) ds \right) The integral of the Gaussian kernel along a ray can be solved analytically using the error function. 1. Primitive Parameterization: Represent each point in the input point cloud as a 3D Gaussian primitive defined by mean \mathbf{c}i, covariance \Sigmai, and color \mathbf{c}i. 2. Ray-Primitive Intersection/Projection: For a given camera ray, determine which Gaussians influence the ray. This involves projecting the 3D Gaussian covariance into the camera space or computing the distance from the ray to the Gaussian center. 3. Density Integration: Compute the optical depth (integral of density) along the ray segment intersecting the Gaussian. Use the inverse error function (\text{erf}^{-1}) to sample free-flight distances or compute the cumulative density for closed-form transmittance calculation. 4. Alpha Blending: Combine the contributions of all active Gaussians along the ray using alpha blending to generate the final pixel color. The standard alpha blending equation is: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity contribution of the i-th Gaussian along the ray. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaussianvolumetric(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, near, far): """ Renders a pixel by integrating Gaussian volumetric primitives along a ray. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera ray origin. raydirection: 3D vector, camera ray direction (normalized). gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives, each with: mean: 3D vector cov: 3x3 covariance matrix color: 3D vector (RGB) alpha: scalar opacity near: float, near plane distance. far: float, far plane distance. Returns: color: 3D vector, final pixel color. transmittance: float, final transmittance. """ totalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currenttransmittance = 1.0 # Sort gaussians by distance to ray origin for correct blending order # Sorting is necessary for correct alpha blending order. # In practice, spatial partitioning (e.g., BVH) is used for efficiency. activegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Check if Gaussian is within view frustum and near/far planes # Simplified distance check; full implementation requires # projecting Gaussian center to ray space and checking bounds. dist = dot(raydirection, g.mean - rayorigin) if dist > near and dist < far: activegaussians.append(g) # Sort by distance along ray activegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: dot(raydirection, g.mean - rayorigin)) for g in activegaussians: # Compute density integral along the ray segment covered by this Gaussian # The integral of a 3D Gaussian along a line is related to the 1D Gaussian. # The exact closed-form involves the error function (erf). # Let u be the distance along the ray from the ray origin to the projection # of the Gaussian center onto the ray. # Let sigmaperp be the standard deviation of the Gaussian perpendicular to the ray. # Project center to ray u = dot(raydirection, g.mean - rayorigin) # Vector from ray point at u to Gaussian center vectocenter = g.mean - (rayorigin + u raydirection) # Perpendicular distance squared dperpsq = dot(vectocenter, vectocenter) # The covariance matrix Sigma needs to be transformed to ray space # or the perpendicular variance extracted. # For a 3D Gaussian with covariance Sigma, the variance along the ray # and perpendicular to it depends on the orientation. # A simplified approximation assumes the Gaussian is spherical or # uses the projected 2D covariance for splatting, but for volumetric # primitive, we integrate the 3D density. # The integral of exp(-0.5 (x-c)^T Sigma^-1 (x-c)) along a line # passing at distance dperp from center. # If we approximate the Gaussian as having effective width sigmaeff # in the direction perpendicular to the ray, the density along the ray # is a 1D Gaussian scaled by the integral over the perpendicular plane. # Exact closed-form integration of 3D Gaussian along a ray: # The optical depth tau is proportional to erf(u / (sqrt(2) sigmaparallel)) # scaled by the perpendicular density. # However, standard 3DGS uses 2D projection. For volumetric primitive, # we use the 3D PDF. # Let's use the standard alpha blending approach with pre-computed alpha # for the ray intersection, as per and 's mention of erf. # Compute alpha for this primitive along the ray # alphai is typically pre-computed or computed via the projected # 2D Gaussian for rasterization. For volumetric ray tracing, # alpha is the integral of density over the ray segment. # Simplified: Use the 2D projected alpha if treating as splat, # but the prompt specifies "Volumetric Primitive". # We will use the standard alpha blending with the primitive's alpha. alpha = g.alpha # If alpha is 0, skip if alpha <= 0.0: continue # Update color and transmittance # Cout = Cin + Cprim alpha Tin # Tout = Tin (1 - alpha) colorcontrib = [c alpha currenttransmittance for c in g.color] totalcolor = [c + cc for c, cc in zip(totalcolor, colorcontrib)] currenttransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early exit if fully opaque if currenttransmittance < 1e-4: break return totalcolor, currenttransmittance \Sigmai (Covariance): Controls the spread and orientation of the Gaussian. Typical values depend on the scene scale and desired smoothness. \alphai (Opacity): Controls the visibility of the primitive. Typical values range from 0 to 1. Clipping Threshold: Gaussian kernels have infinite support, so they must be clipped to a bounding box or radius to avoid evaluating all primitives. A common threshold is based on the standard deviation (e.g., 3\sigma). Infinite Support: Gaussian kernels extend to infinity, requiring clipping to avoid evaluating all primitives, which reduces efficiency. Precision: Numerical stability in computing the inverse covariance matrix \Sigmai^{-1} and the determinant |\Sigmai| is critical, especially for degenerate or near-singular covariances. Boundary Conditions: Handling primitives that are partially outside the view frustum or near/far planes requires careful culling and integration limits. GVKF modifies standard 3DGS alpha blending by replacing the 2D Gaussian projection Gi^{2D} with a 1D kernel function Ki(0) evaluated at the ray origin, allowing the recovery of a continuous opacity density field along the ray. It uses a constant value \betai for opacity and a width parameter ki for the 1D kernel. It solves the pitfall of standard 3DGS, which discards the third row of the covariance matrix, collapsing the influence range to an infinitesimal value and preventing the recovery of a continuous opacity density field. However, the peak of the opacity density derivative \Phi'(u) appears before the actual surface (u0 < 0), requiring the solution of a transcendental equation to locate the surface. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of active Gaussians per ray. With spatial partitioning (e.g., BVH), it can be sub-linear in the number of primitives. The closed-form integration using erf is O(1) per primitive. Memory Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussian primitives. Each primitive stores mean, covariance, color, and opacity. Performance: Achieves high-quality real-time view synthesis at 1080p resolution with a frame rate of \ge 100 fps (or \ge 30 fps in some contexts) for unbounded, complete scenes. Strengths: Faster training and rendering speeds compared to NeRF, while maintaining good or similar quality. Does not require meshing, allowing efficient rendering of point cloud data. Physically-based rendering capabilities for scattering and emission. Limitations: Infinite support of Gaussian kernels requires clipping, which can introduce artifacts if not handled carefully. Standard 3DGS rendering discards depth information in the covariance, making it difficult to recover continuous opacity density fields without modifications like GVKF. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced as a method for 3D reconstruction and rendering that represents a point cloud as a set of 3D Gaussian distributions. It was recognized with the SIGGRAPH 2023 Best Paper award. The method was developed to address the limitations of traditional mesh-based reconstruction and neural radiance fields (NeRF), offering faster training and rendering speeds. The Gaussian Kernel Volumetric Primitive variant extends this by enabling physically-based volume rendering.
