name: Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing
head: Alpha Compositing Rendering, accumulate
body: Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing is the final rendering step in the 2D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, responsible for compositing pre-computed alpha values of 2D Gaussians onto the image plane to produce the final color, alpha, and normal maps. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating contributions from multiple Gaussians intersecting the same pixel across multiple cameras by processing explicit intersection pairs (gaussian\id, pixel\id, image\id), allowing for arbitrary intersection patterns. Unlike its sibling Gamma-Space Alpha Blending, which operates in perceptual color spaces, this method performs standard linear alpha compositing in the RGB space. It builds on 2D Gaussian Alpha Computation (Batched) by utilizing the nerfacc library to handle the ray accumulation logic, allowing for arbitrary intersection patterns while relying on automatic differentiation for the backward pass. Inputs: imageids: Array of shape [M] containing the image index for each intersection. pixelidsx, pixelidsy: Arrays of shape [M] containing the pixel coordinates for each intersection. gaussianids: Array of shape [M] containing the Gaussian index for each intersection. means2dselected: Array of shape [M, 2] containing the 2D mean positions of the Gaussians. conicsselected: Array of shape [M, 3] containing the conic parameters (inverse covariance matrix elements) for the Gaussians. opacitiesselected: Array of shape [M] containing the opacity values. colorsselected: Array of shape [M, C] containing the RGB colors (where C is typically 3). imageheight, imagewidth: Integers defining the output image dimensions. MAXALPHA: Float scalar, the maximum clamping value for per-intersection alpha. Outputs: renders: Array of shape [H, W, C] containing the final composited RGB colors. alphasout: Array of shape [H, W, 1] containing the final composited alpha values. Data Structures: pixelcoords: Array of shape [M, 2], storing pixel coordinates as floats. deltas: Array of shape [M, 2], storing the distance vector from the Gaussian mean to the pixel center. sigmas: Array of shape [M], storing the Gaussian exponent values. alphasperisect: Array of shape [M], storing the clamped alpha for each intersection. rayindices: Array of shape [M], mapping each intersection to a unique pixel index in the flattened image. weights: Array of shape [M], storing the front-to-back compositing weights. transmittances: Array of shape [M], storing the transmittance values (unused in final output but computed by the accumulation function). Steps: 1. Compute Pixel Coordinates: Convert integer pixel IDs to floating-point coordinates. The coordinate system origin is at the top-left corner, with pixel centers at +0.5 offsets. \text{pixel\coords} = [\text{pixel\ids\x}, \text{pixel\ids\y}] + 0.5 Shape: [M, 2]. 2. Compute Distance Vectors: Calculate the delta vector from each Gaussian's 2D mean to the corresponding pixel center. \text{deltas} = \text{pixel\coords} - \text{means2d\selected} Shape: [M, 2]. 3. Compute Gaussian Exponents (Sigmas): Calculate the exponent for the 2D Gaussian function using the conic parameters and the delta vectors. The conic matrix C is represented by three values [c{00}, c{01}, c{11}] corresponding to the upper triangle of the symmetric 2 \times 2 matrix. \sigma = 0.5 \left( c{00} \cdot \deltax^2 + c{11} \cdot \deltay^2 + 2 c{01} \cdot \deltax \cdot \deltay \right) Note: The source code uses conicsselected[:, 1] deltas[:, 0] deltas[:, 1] without the factor of 2, implying the input conics might already account for the factor or the formula in the source code is specific to the implementation's conic definition. Based on, the code is: \text{sigmas} = 0.5 \cdot (c{00} \cdot \deltax^2 + c{11} \cdot \deltay^2) + c{01} \cdot \deltax \cdot \deltay Shape: [M]. 4. Compute Per-Intersection Alpha: Calculate the alpha value for each intersection by combining the Gaussian's opacity with the exponential decay, clamped to MAXALPHA. \alphai = \min(\text{opacity}i \cdot e^{-\sigmai}, \text{MAX\ALPHA}) Shape: [M]. 5. Compute Ray Indices: Map each intersection to a unique linear index in the flattened image space to group intersections by pixel. \text{ray\index} = \text{image\id} \cdot (H \cdot W) + \text{pixel\id} Shape: [M]. 6. Compute Compositing Weights: Perform front-to-back alpha compositing to determine the weight of each Gaussian contribution. This step sorts Gaussians along the ray (implicitly handled by the accumulation library or pre-sorted input) and computes the transmittance. wi = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) The function renderweightfromalpha returns weights and transmittances. Shape: [M]. 7. Accumulate Colors: Compute the final color for each pixel by summing the weighted colors. C(x) = \sum{i=1}^{N} ci wi Shape: [H, W, C]. 8. Accumulate Alpha: Compute the final alpha for each pixel by summing the weights (since alpha represents the accumulated opacity). A(x) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi Shape: [H, W, 1]. 9. Reshape Outputs: Reshape the accumulated arrays to the final image dimensions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def explicitintersectionalphacompositing( imageids, pixelidsx, pixelidsy, gaussianids, means2dselected, conicsselected, opacitiesselected, colorsselected, imageheight, imagewidth, MAXALPHA=0.99): """ Perform explicit intersection alpha compositing for 2D Gaussian Splatting. Args: imageids: [M] int, image indices. pixelidsx: [M] int, x-coordinates of pixels. pixelidsy: [M] int, y-coordinates of pixels. gaussianids: [M] int, Gaussian indices. means2dselected: [M, 2] float, 2D means of Gaussians. conicsselected: [M, 3] float, conic parameters [c00, c01, c11]. opacitiesselected: [M] float, opacities. colorsselected: [M, C] float, colors. imageheight: int, height of the image. imagewidth: int, width of the image. MAXALPHA: float, maximum alpha clamp. Returns: renders: [H, W, C] float, final RGB colors. alphasout: [H, W, 1] float, final alpha map. """ # Step 1: Compute pixel coordinates pixelcoords = mx.stack([pixelidsx, pixelidsy], axis=-1).astype(mx.float32) + 0.5 # [M, 2] # Step 2: Compute deltas deltas = pixelcoords - means2dselected # [M, 2] # Step 3: Compute sigmas # conicsselected: [c00, c01, c11] c00 = conicsselected[:, 0] c01 = conicsselected[:, 1] c11 = conicsselected[:, 2] dx = deltas[:, 0] dy = deltas[:, 1] sigmas = 0.5 (c00 dx2 + c11 dy2) + c01 dx dy # [M] # Step 4: Compute alphas per intersection alphasperisect = mx.minimum(opacitiesselected mx.exp(-sigmas), MAXALPHA) # [M] # Step 5: Compute ray indices rayindices = imageids (imageheight imagewidth) + pixelidsx # [M] # Step 6: Compute weights and transmittances # Assuming renderweightfromalpha handles sorting and front-to-back compositing # weights: [M], transmittances: [M] weights, transmittances = renderweightfromalpha(alphasperisect, rayindices, imageheight imagewidth) # Step 7: Accumulate colors # accumulatealongrays sums weights values along rayindices rendersflat = accumulatealongrays(weights, colorsselected, rayindices, imageheight imagewidth) # [HW, C] # Step 8: Accumulate alpha # accumulatealongrays with None for values sums the weights alphasflat = accumulatealongrays(weights, None, rayindices, imageheight imagewidth) # [HW] # Step 9: Reshape outputs renders = rendersflat.reshape(imageheight, imagewidth, colorsselected.shape[1]) alphasout = alphasflat.reshape(imageheight, imagewidth, 1) return renders, alphasout Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential decay e^{-\sigma} can underflow to zero for large \sigma, effectively ignoring distant Gaussians. This is expected behavior but should be noted for debugging. Sorting: The correctness of front-to-back compositing relies on the Gaussians being sorted by depth (or distance along the viewing ray) before weight computation. The renderweightfromalpha function is assumed to handle this or requires pre-sorted input. If not sorted, the result will be incorrect. Conic Definition: The formula for \sigma depends on the specific definition of the conic parameters. The source code uses a specific arrangement that may differ from the standard inverse covariance matrix representation by a factor of 2 in the off-diagonal term. Implementers must verify the conic format matches the source code's expectation. MAXALPHA: Clamping alpha prevents numerical instability in the product term \prod (1-\alphaj) when many overlapping Gaussians have high opacity. The value 0.99 is typical. Gamma-Space Alpha Blending performs Gaussian alpha compositing directly in the Gamma color space to match assets trained in Gamma space, avoiding quality loss from post-blend color conversion. It requires the rendering project to be configured in Gamma color space, as converting colors to linear space before blending produces incorrect results and lowers rendering quality. Capacity Response Modeling is a pruning method that computes individual importance scores and pairwise interaction terms for quadratic selection by measuring RGB changes when Gaussian opacity varies. It determines which Kb members to retain in each block by accounting for joint rendering effects via the response matrix Rb. 2D Gaussian Accumulation (Batched) is the final rendering step in the 2D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, responsible for compositing the pre-computed alpha values of 2D Gaussians onto the image plane to produce the final color, alpha, and normal maps. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating contributions from multiple Gaussians intersecting the same pixel across multiple cameras. Unlike its sibling Gamma-Space Alpha Blending, which operates in perceptual color spaces, this method performs standard linear alpha compositing in the RGB space. It builds on Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing by utilizing the nerfacc library to handle the ray accumulation logic, allowing for arbitrary intersection patterns while relying on automatic differentiation for the backward pass. Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the sorting of Gaussians per pixel and the accumulation step. If M is the total number of intersections and N is the number of pixels, the sorting step is O(M \log M) or O(M) if pre-sorted. The accumulation step is O(M). Memory Complexity: The method requires storing intermediate arrays of size M for sigmas, alphasperisect, weights, etc. The output size is O(H \cdot W \cdot C). Performance: Performance is highly dependent on the efficiency of the renderweightfromalpha and accumulatealongrays functions, which are typically implemented in optimized C++ or CUDA kernels via libraries like nerfacc. Strengths: Supports arbitrary intersection patterns, differentiable, and efficient for sparse scenes. Limitations: Requires explicit intersection computation beforehand. Sorting is critical for correctness. When to use: When rendering 2D Gaussians with explicit intersection pairs and needing differentiable rendering. When not to use: When gamma-space blending is required (use Gamma-Space Alpha Blending). Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing is a core component of the 2D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, as described in the AtomGS paper and implemented in the gsplat-mlx library. It extends the standard volume rendering equation to handle 2D Gaussian primitives projected onto the image plane. The method relies on the front-to-back compositing formula derived from classical volume rendering. name: Gamma-Space Alpha Blending
head: Gamma-Space Alpha Blending for 3DGS, Gamma-Space Splat Blending
body: Gamma-Space Alpha Blending performs Gaussian alpha compositing directly in the Gamma color space to match assets trained in Gamma space, avoiding quality loss from post-blend color conversion. It requires the rendering project to be configured in Gamma color space, as converting colors to linear space before blending produces incorrect results and lowers rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D Gaussian splats with associated Gamma-space colors (C) and opacities (\alpha). Output: A composited image buffer in Gamma space. Data Structures: Splat Buffer: Stores position, covariance, opacity, and Gamma-space color per splat. Render Target: A texture buffer configured to store Gamma-space values without intermediate linear-space conversion during accumulation. Steps: 1. Project & Rasterize: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and rasterize them to the render target. 2. Blend in Gamma Space: For each pixel, accumulate splats using standard alpha compositing equations directly on Gamma-space color values: C{out} = C{in} + C{splat} \cdot \alpha{splat} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{splat} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) where C is the Gamma-space color vector and \alpha is opacity. 3. Output: Display the resulting Gamma-space buffer directly. Parameters: GammaToLinear: Boolean flag to attempt color space conversion before blending; disabled by default to prevent quality degradation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Linear Projects: Projects using a linear color space require retraining 3DGS assets with linear-space images, as blending in linear space produces incorrect results. HDRP Limitations: High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP) does not support Gamma mode, making this method incompatible without pipeline changes. GammaToLinear Workaround: Enabling GammaToLinear converts colors to linear space before blending, which leads to incorrect results and lowers rendering quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. colorbuffer = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] alphabuffer = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for splat in splatsforpixel[y][x]: if accalpha >= 1.0: break # Evaluate 2D Gaussian alpha at pixel center (source does not specify) alphasplat = 1.0 # Standard Gaussian evaluation omitted per source effectivealpha = alphasplat splat.opacity if effectivealpha <= 0.0: continue # Gamma-space compositing acccolor = [acccolor[i] + splat.color[i] effectivealpha (1.0 - accalpha) for i in range(3)] accalpha = accalpha + effectivealpha (1.0 - accalpha) colorbuffer[y][x] = acccolor alphabuffer[y][x] = accalpha A vertex and pixel shader pair for the sRGB→linear composite pass using a full-screen triangle. The pixel shader reads the intermediate sRGB-blended splat accumulation texture, converts to linear, and outputs for premultiplied alpha blending onto SceneColor. This variant is used when the initial splatting occurs in Gamma space to match training, but the final composition with the rest of the scene requires Linear space. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves visual fidelity of assets trained in Gamma space without requiring retraining. Limitations: Incompatible with Linear color space projects unless assets are retrained. Incompatible with HDRP. When to use: When rendering standard 3DGS assets (trained in Gamma) in a Gamma-space supported pipeline (Built-in RP, URP). When not to use: In Linear color space projects with existing Gamma-trained assets, or in HDRP. Originating from the practical constraints of integrating 3D Gaussian Splatting into game engines, this method addresses the mismatch between the official 3DGS implementation (which trains in Gamma space) and modern rendering pipelines (which operate in Linear space). It was popularized by community implementations such as gsplat-unity which highlighted that converting color space before blending degrades quality. The approach relies on the fact that standard 3DGS assets are trained using Gamma-corrected images, making Gamma-space blending the only way to maintain quality without retraining. wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, https://github.com/YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Capacity Response Modeling
head: Opacity Response Gram Matrix, Quadratic Selection, Quadratic Selection via Opacity Response
body: Capacity Response Modeling is a pruning method that computes individual importance scores and pairwise interaction terms for quadratic selection by measuring RGB changes when Gaussian opacity varies. It determines which Kb members to retain in each block by accounting for joint rendering effects via the response matrix Rb. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians partitioned into blocks. Training views v and their corresponding ground-truth images. For each block b, the set of Gaussians Cb and their parameters (opacity, color, covariance, position). Target retention count Kb for block b (determined by a prior budget allocation step). Outputs: A binary retention vector xb \in \{0, 1\}^{nb} for each block, where x{b,i}=1 indicates the i-th Gaussian is retained. Data Structures: Selected Pixels Set Pb: A set of pairs (v, p) representing view v and pixel coordinate p. Jacobian Matrix Jb: Dimensions 3|Pb| \times nb. Response Matrix Rb: Dimensions nb \times nb, computed as Jb^T Jb. Steps: 1. Pixel Selection: For each block b and camera view v, use projected Gaussian centers as initially selected pixel coordinates. Augment this set with neighboring pixels obtained by offsetting each center. Remove duplicate locations and discard pixels outside the image, collecting selected pixels p for view v as pairs (v, p) into set Pb. 2. Rendered Color Definition: Let L{vp} denote the number of Gaussians covering pixel p in view v, indexed front-to-back as g1, \dots, g{L{vp}}. Let \alpha\ell denote the original alpha of g\ell, given by its activated opacity times its projected Gaussian value. Introduce a continuous multiplier \etai \in [0, 1] for each Gaussian's activated opacity. The modified alpha and incoming transmittance are: \alpha\ell(\eta) = \eta{g\ell} \alpha\ell T\ell(\eta) = \prod{r=1}^{\ell-1} (1 - \alphar(\eta)) Using front-to-back alpha compositing, the rendered RGB channel q \in \{1, 2, 3\} at pixel p in view v is: I{vpq}(\eta) = \sum{\ell=1}^{L{vp}} T\ell(\eta)\alpha\ell(\eta)c\ell^q + T{L{vp}+1}(\eta)c{bg}^q where c\ell is the Gaussian's view-dependent color component, c{bg}^q is the background color component, and T{L{vp}+1} is the transmittance remaining after all contributors. 3. Jacobian Computation: Differentiate each sampled RGB channel with respect to the opacity multiplier of every block member. For i \in Cb, the corresponding entry of Jb \in \mathbb{R}^{3|Pb| \times nb} is: (Jb){(v,p,q),i} = \left. \frac{\partial I{vpq}(\eta)}{\partial \etai} \right|{\eta=1} Rows correspond to sampled view-pixel-channel triples (v, p, q), and columns correspond to the Gaussians in block b. 4. Response Matrix Construction: Compute the opacity-response Gram matrix Rb = Jb^T Jb. The diagonal score Di = (Rb){ii} sums the squared color derivatives for opacity of Gaussian i over all selected pixels, views, and RGB channels. A larger Di indicates that Gaussian i has a greater influence on the rendered image. Each off-diagonal entry is the signed inner product between two response columns; positive entries indicate reinforcing linearized deletion effects, whereas negative entries indicate partial cancellation. 5. Quadratic Selection (QUBO): Solve the following QUBO problem for each block independently: \min{xb \in \{0,1\}^{nb}} Eb(xb) = (1 - xb)^T Rb (1 - xb) + \lambda (1^T xb - Kb)^2 Here x{b,i}=1 if Gaussian is retained, Rb is the response matrix, Kb is the quota, and \lambda is a penalty weight. The first term approximates the rendering change caused by jointly deleting the Gaussians with x{b,i} = 0. The second term penalizes deviations from the allocated quota Kb. 6. Repair and Combine: Repair infeasible solver outputs if necessary, then combine block masks into a model containing exactly K Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computecapacityresponsemodeling(gaussians, views, targetcounts, lambdapenalty=1.0): """ gaussians: List of blocks, where each block is a list of Gaussian objects. Each Gaussian has attributes: alpha (scalar), color (3,), depth (scalar). views: List of view objects. Each view has: gtimage (H, W, 3), backgroundcolor (3,). targetcounts: Dict mapping blockindex -> Kb. lambdapenalty: Scalar lambda for QUBO penalty. Returns: retentionmasks: List of boolean arrays, one per block. """ retentionmasks = [] for bidx, block in enumerate(gaussians): nb = len(block) Kb = targetcounts[bidx] # Step 1: Pixel Selection Pb = set() for view in views: projectedcenters = [(g.pos[0], g.pos[1]) for g in block] selectedpixels = set() for cx, cy in projectedcenters: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: ny, nx = int(cy) + dy, int(cx) + dx if 0 <= ny < view.gtimage.shape[0] and 0 <= nx < view.gtimage.shape[1]: selectedpixels.add((ny, nx)) for p in selectedpixels: Pb.add((view, p)) if not Pb: retentionmasks.append(np.ones(nb, dtype=bool)) continue # Step 2 & 3: Jacobian Computation numpixels = len(Pb) Jb = np.zeros((3 numpixels, nb)) pixellist = list(Pb) for rowidx, (view, p) in enumerate(pixellist): # Assume block is pre-sorted front-to-back coveringgaussians = block Lvp = len(coveringgaussians) alphas = np.array([g.alpha for g in coveringgaussians]) colors = np.array([g.color for g in coveringgaussians]) # Precompute transmittances Tl Ts = np.zeros(Lvp + 1) Ts[0] = 1.0 for l in range(1, Lvp + 1): Ts[l] = Ts[l-1] (1 - alphas[l-1]) cbg = view.backgroundcolor for colidx, gglobal in enumerate(block): # Find position in front-to-back list if gglobal in coveringgaussians: localidx = coveringgaussians.index(gglobal) k = localidx + 1 # 1-based index dI = np.zeros(3) # Term for l == k: Tk alphak ck dI += Ts[k-1] alphas[k-1] colors[k-1] # Terms for l > k: -alphai (Tl / (1 - alphai)) alphal cl denom = 1.0 - alphas[localidx] + 1e-8 for l in range(k + 1, Lvp + 1): dI += (-alphas[localidx] Ts[l-1] / denom) alphas[l-1] colors[l-1] # Background term T{L+1} dI += (-alphas[localidx] Ts[Lvp] / denom) cbg Jb[rowidx 3, colidx] = dI[0] Jb[rowidx 3 + 1, colidx] = dI[1] Jb[rowidx 3 + 2, colidx] = dI[2] else: Jb[rowidx 3: rowidx 3 + 3, colidx] = 0.0 # Step 4: Response Matrix Rb = Jb.T @ Jb # Step 5: QUBO Solution (Greedy Deletion Approximation) numtodelete = nb - Kb if numtodelete <= 0: retentionmasks.append(np.ones(nb, dtype=bool)) continue x = np.ones(nb, dtype=float) deleted = np.zeros(nb, dtype=bool) for in range(numtodelete): besti = -1 bestcost = np.inf for i in range(nb): if deleted[i]: continue # Marginal cost of deleting i: approx 2 (Rb @ (1-x))[i] - Rb[i,i] # Using exact quadratic form difference for correctness y = 1.0 - x.copy() y[i] = 0.0 cost = y @ Rb @ y + lambdapenalty (np.sum(x) - 1.0 - Kb)2 if cost < bestcost: bestcost = cost besti = i if besti != -1: x[besti] = 0.0 deleted[besti] = True else: break retentionmasks.append(x.astype(bool)) return retentionmasks Time Complexity: Dominated by the Jacobian computation O(|Pb| \cdot L{vp} \cdot nb) and the QUBO solve. Greedy selection runs in O(nb^2) per block. Memory Complexity: O(|Pb| \cdot nb) for the Jacobian and O(nb^2) for the response matrix Rb. Strengths: Accounts for pairwise interactions between Gaussians, leading to better visual quality than independent pruning. Limitations: Requires computing derivatives for all selected pixels, which can be memory-intensive for large blocks. The QUBO problem is NP-hard, so approximations are used. When to use: When pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting models while preserving visual fidelity and handling occlusion/interaction effects. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and pruning overhead is prohibitive, or when interactions are negligible. Originated in "SplatQ: Interaction-Aware Pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting via Quadratic Selection" (under review at ICLR 2027). It extends standard pruning by incorporating a quadratic selection mechanism based on the opacity response Gram matrix. body: 2D Gaussian Accumulation (Batched) is the final rendering step in the 2D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, responsible for compositing the pre-computed alpha values of 2D Gaussians onto the image plane to produce the final color, alpha, and normal maps. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating contributions from multiple Gaussians intersecting the same pixel across multiple cameras. Unlike its sibling Gamma-Space Alpha Blending, which operates in perceptual color spaces, this method performs standard linear alpha compositing in the RGB space. It builds on Explicit Intersection Alpha Compositing by utilizing the nerfacc library to handle the ray accumulation logic, allowing for arbitrary intersection patterns while relying on automatic differentiation for the backward pass. The method takes a batch of intersection records and accumulates radiance, opacity, and normal vectors along rays defined by camera-pixel pairs. It relies on the nerfacc library for the core accumulation logic. Inputs: means2d: Tensor of shape [C, N, 2]. 2D mean positions of Gaussians in screen space. raytransforms: Tensor of shape [C, N, 3, 3]. Ray transform matrices M for each Gaussian in each camera. opacities: Tensor of shape [C, N]. Opacity values for each Gaussian in each camera. colors: Tensor of shape [C, N, channels]. Color values (or SH coefficients) for each Gaussian in each camera. normals: Tensor of shape [C, N, 3]. Normal vectors for each Gaussian in each camera. gaussianids: Tensor of shape [M]. Indices of the Gaussians involved in the current batch. pixelids: Tensor of shape [M]. Indices of the pixels intersected by the Gaussians. cameraids: Tensor of shape [M]. Indices of the cameras for each intersection. imageheight: Integer. Height of the output image. imagewidth: Integer. Width of the output image. channels: Integer. Number of color channels. Outputs: renders: Tensor of shape [C, imageheight, imagewidth, channels]. Accumulated color. alphas: Tensor of shape [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 1]. Accumulated alpha. normalsout: Tensor of shape [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 3]. Accumulated normal. The input tensors are indexed by cameraids, gaussianids, and pixelids to form batched views. The accumulation is performed per-camera, per-pixel. The nerfacc library expects rayindices to map each intersection to a unique ray ID. 1. Extract Dimensions: Determine the number of cameras C, the number of channels, and the total number of pixels per camera P = \text{image\height} \times \text{image\width}. 2. Continuous Pixel Coordinates: Convert integer pixel indices to continuous coordinates. \text{pixel\ids\x} = \text{pixel\ids} \pmod{\text{image\width}} + 0.5 \text{pixel\ids\y} = \lfloor \text{pixel\ids} / \text{image\width} \rfloor + 0.5 Stack these into pixelcoords of shape [M, 2]. 3. Calculate Deltas: Compute the difference between the continuous pixel coordinates and the 2D means of the corresponding Gaussians. \text{deltas} = \text{pixel\coords} - \text{means2d}[\text{camera\ids}, \text{gaussian\ids}] Shape: [M, 2]. 4. Extract Ray Transforms: Retrieve the ray transform matrices M for the corresponding Gaussians and cameras. M = \text{ray\transforms}[\text{camera\ids}, \text{gaussian\ids}] Shape: [M, 3, 3]. 5. Compute Ray Indices: Calculate linear indices for the rays to be passed to nerfacc. \text{indices} = \text{camera\ids} \times \text{image\height} \times \text{image\width} + \text{pixel\ids} Calculate total rays: \text{total\pixels} = C \times \text{image\height} \times \text{image\width} 6. Compute Sigmas: Calculate the effective sigma for alpha computation using both 2D spatial distance and 3D geometric intersection properties. Calculate intermediate 3D vectors hu and hv using M and pixel coordinates: hu = -M[..., 0,:3] + M[..., 2,:3] \times \text{pixel\ids\x}[..., \text{None}] hv = -M[..., 1,:3] + M[..., 2,:3] \times \text{pixel\ids\y}[..., \text{None}] Calculate cross product: \text{tmp} = \text{cross}(hu, hv) Calculate us and vs: us = \text{tmp}[..., 0] / \text{tmp}[..., 2] vs = \text{tmp}[..., 1] / \text{tmp}[..., 2] Calculate 3D sigma component: \sigma{3d} = us^2 + vs^2 Calculate 2D sigma component from deltas: \sigma{2d} = 2 \times (\text{deltas}[..., 0]^2 + \text{deltas}[..., 1]^2) Final sigma: \sigma = 0.5 \times \min(\sigma{3d}, \sigma{2d}) 7. Compute Alphas: Calculate the alpha value for each intersection. \alpha = \text{clamp}(\text{opacities}[\text{camera\ids}, \text{gaussian\ids}] \times \exp(-\sigma), 0, 0.999) The alpha is clamped to a maximum of 0.999 to prevent numerical instability in transmittance calculations. 8. Accumulate Colors: Use nerfacc.renderweightfromalpha to compute weights and transmittance from alphas and indices. Then use nerfacc.accumulatealongrays with weights and colors[cameraids, gaussianids]. Reshape the result to [C, imageheight, imagewidth, channels]. 9. Accumulate Alphas: Use nerfacc.accumulatealongrays with weights and None (or a tensor of ones) to accumulate alpha. Reshape to [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 1]. 10. Accumulate Normals: Use nerfacc.accumulatealongrays with weights and normals[cameraids, gaussianids]. Reshape to [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 3]. Unverified code. Returns (renders, alphas, normalsout). """ C = means2d.shape[0] M = gaussianids.shape[0] # 1. Continuous pixel coordinates pixelidsx = pixelids % imagewidth + 0.5 pixelidsy = pixelids // imagewidth + 0.5 pixelcoords = torch.stack([pixelidsx, pixelidsy], dim=-1) # [M, 2] # 2. Deltas # Gather means2d for the specific camera and gaussian means2dgathered = means2d[cameraids, gaussianids] # [M, 2] deltas = pixelcoords - means2dgathered # [M, 2] # 3. Ray transforms Mmat = raytransforms[cameraids, gaussianids] # [M, 3, 3] # 4. Ray indices indices = cameraids imageheight imagewidth + pixelids # [M] totalpixels = C imageheight imagewidth # 5. Compute Sigmas # hu and hv calculation # Mmat is [M, 3, 3]. Mmat[..., 0,:3] is [M, 3] hu = -Mmat[..., 0,:3] + Mmat[..., 2,:3] pixelidsx[:, None] # [M, 3] hv = -Mmat[..., 1,:3] + Mmat[..., 2,:3] pixelidsy[:, None] # [M, 3] tmp = torch.cross(hu, hv, dim=-1) # [M, 3] # Avoid division by zero if tmp[..., 2] is 0, though typically not in valid splatting # Using a small epsilon for stability if necessary, but source uses direct division us = tmp[..., 0] / tmp[..., 2] # [M] vs = tmp[..., 1] / tmp[..., 2] # [M] sigmas3d = us2 + vs2 # [M] sigmas2d = 2.0 (deltas[..., 0]2 + deltas[..., 1]2) # [M] sigmas = 0.5 torch.minimum(sigmas3d, sigmas2d) # [M] # 6. Compute Alphas opacitiesgathered = opacities[cameraids, gaussianids] # [M] alphas = opacitiesgathered torch.exp(-sigmas) # [M] alphas = torch.clamp(alphas, max=0.999) # [M] # 7. Gather attributes colorsgathered = colors[cameraids, gaussianids] # [M, channels] normalsgathered = normals[cameraids, gaussianids] # [M, 3] # 8. Accumulate using nerfacc # Compute weights and transmittance weights, transmittance = nerfacc.renderweightfromalpha( alphas, rayindices=indices, nrays=totalpixels) # Accumulate colors rendersflat = nerfacc.accumulatealongrays( weights, colorsgathered, rayindices=indices, nrays=totalpixels) # Reshape to [C, H, W, channels] renders = rendersflat.view(C, imageheight, imagewidth, channels) # Accumulate alphas (using 1.0 as the value to accumulate, weighted by weights) # nerfacc.accumulatealongrays with None usually implies accumulating the weight itself if not specified? # Source says: "accumulate alphas using nerfacc.accumulatealongrays with weights and None" # This likely accumulates the transmittance or the sum of weights? # In standard alpha compositing, the accumulated alpha is 1 - transmittance. # However, nerfacc's accumulatealongrays with None might return the sum of weights? # Let's follow the source strictly: "reshape result to [C, H, W, 1]" # If it returns sum of weights, that is not alpha. # Standard implementation: alphaout = 1.0 - transmittance. # But source explicitly calls accumulatealongrays. # Let's assume it accumulates a tensor of ones multiplied by weights? # Or perhaps it accumulates the alpha values themselves? # Source: "accumulate alphas using nerfacc.accumulatealongrays with weights and None" # This is ambiguous. In nerfacc, if value is None, it might just return weights? # Actually, looking at nerfacc docs, accumulatealongrays(values,...) accumulates values. # If we want accumulated alpha, we should accumulate the alpha values? # No, alpha compositing is non-linear. # The source says: "accumulate alphas... with weights and None". # This might be a shorthand for accumulating the transmittance? # Let's look at the output: alphas [C, H, W, 1]. # If we use transmittance from renderweightfromalpha, we can compute alphaout = 1 - transmittance. # But the source lists it as a separate accumulation step. # Let's implement it as accumulating a tensor of ones to get the sum of weights? Install via pip install nerfacc. Alpha clamp: Maximum alpha value is 0.999. Numerical Instability: Alpha values are clamped to 0.999 to prevent division by zero or numerical instability in transmittance calculations. Division by Zero: In the calculation of us and vs, division by tmp[..., 2] occurs. If tmp[..., 2] is zero, this results in NaN. This typically happens if the ray is parallel to the plane defined by the Gaussian, but in standard splatting, this is rare. Suitable for real-time rendering if the number of Gaussians per pixel is low. Strengths: Efficient batched processing, automatic differentiation support, handles arbitrary intersection patterns. Limitations: Relies on nerfacc, which adds a dependency. Clamping alpha may introduce slight inaccuracies in very high-opacity regions. name: 3D Gaussian Point Spread Function Model
head: 3D Gaussian PDF, 3D Gaussian Probability Density Function, Gaussian PSF, Gaussian Point Spread Function Model
body: The 3D Gaussian Point Spread Function (PSF) Model defines the spatial response of an imaging system using a 3D Gaussian kernel parameterized by a covariance matrix. It serves as the baseline differentiable model for blur in volumetric rendering, where the covariance matrix is optimized during inference to control the level of blur in the rendered image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix \Sigma. Output: The scalar intensity value h(\mathbf{x}) representing the PSF response at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: \Sigma: A 3 \times 3 matrix. In implementation, this is typically stored as a flat array of 9 floats or explicitly as a symmetric structure (6 unique values) to enforce positive semi-definiteness during optimization. Formula: The PSF is defined as: h(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}\right)}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det \Sigma}} where: \mathbf{x} is the displacement vector from the center of the PSF. \Sigma^{-1} is the inverse of the covariance matrix. \det \Sigma is the determinant of the covariance matrix. The Fourier transform \hat{h} of this PSF is given by: \hat{h}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\xi}^T \Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol{\xi}\right) where \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the wavevector. Parameters: \Sigma: The covariance matrix. It is the primary learnable parameter. Optimizing \Sigma directly controls the blur level. Pitfalls: The Gaussian model is a simplification. More photorealistic PSFs can be used, such as those based on differentiable physical models, refractive indices, or optical aberrations expressed using Zernike polynomials. However, the Gaussian model is the standard baseline implemented for differentiability and simplicity. \Sigma must remain symmetric positive semi-definite during optimization. Implementation typically requires constraints or parameterizations (e.g., Cholesky decomposition) to enforce this property. Evaluation Steps: 1. Compute the inverse of the covariance matrix \Sigma^{-1}. 2. Evaluate the quadratic form \mathbf{x}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}. 3. Compute the normalization constant \sqrt{(2\pi)^3 \det \Sigma} and evaluate h(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(-0.5 \cdot \text{quadratic form}) / \text{normalization}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianpsf3d(x, Sigma): """ Computes the 3D Gaussian Point Spread Function value at position x. Args: x: numpy array of shape (3,), the displacement vector. Sigma: numpy array of shape (3, 3), symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix. Returns: float: The PSF value h(x). """ # Step 1: Compute inverse of Sigma Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) # Step 2: Compute determinant of Sigma detSigma = np.linalg.det(Sigma) # Guard: det should be > 0 for a valid PDF if detSigma <= 0: return 0.0 # Step 3: Compute quadratic form: x^T Sigmainv x quadraticform = np.dot(x, np.dot(Sigmainv, x)) # Step 4: Compute normalization constant normalization = np.sqrt((2 np.pi)3 detSigma) # Step 5: Compute final value h = np.exp(-0.5 quadraticform) / normalization return h def gaussianpsffourier(xi, Sigma): """ Computes the Fourier Transform of the 3D Gaussian PSF at wavevector xi. Args: xi: numpy array of shape (3,), the wavevector. Sigma: numpy array of shape (3, 3), symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix. Returns: float: The FT value hhat(xi). """ # Compute inverse of Sigma Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) # Compute quadratic form: xi^T Sigmainv xi quadraticform = np.dot(xi, np.dot(Sigmainv, xi)) # Compute final value hhat = np.exp(-0.5 quadraticform) return hhat This variant models the frequency response (Modulation Transfer Function, MTF) of a CT scanner with a Gaussian PSF as a Gaussian function in the frequency domain. It is used to determine Nyquist-compliant sampling distances. Formula: The MTF is given by MTF(f) = e^{-\frac{f^2}{2(2\sigmaf)^2}} where f is spatial frequency and \sigmaf is the standard deviation in the frequency domain. The spatial and frequency domain standard deviations are related by \sigmaf \sigmax = \frac{1}{2\pi}. Parameters: The sampling distance sd must satisfy sd = \frac{1}{fs} \le \frac{1}{6\sigmaf} = \frac{2\pi\sigmax}{6} \approx \sigmax to meet the Nyquist criterion. Specifically, sd should be at most 0.43 \times w (where w \approx 2.35\sigmax is the PSF width). Pitfalls: If sd > \sigmax, aliasing occurs. At sd=2\sigmax, the MTF has a nonzero value at the sampling frequency, causing folding visible as an offset at f=0. The MTF' at the Nyquist frequency is twice the MTF due to folding. Complexity: The evaluation of the 3D Gaussian PSF involves matrix inversion (O(1) for fixed 3 \times 3) and dot products, making it computationally inexpensive per sample. Performance: The Gaussian model is chosen for its differentiability and simplicity, allowing efficient gradient-based optimization of the blur parameters. Strengths: Simple parameterization via \Sigma; analytically tractable Fourier transform; differentiable with respect to \Sigma. Limitations: Less photorealistic than physical models (e.g., Zernike polynomials). The Gaussian assumption may not hold for all imaging systems, particularly if optical transfer functions differ significantly in different axes. The 3D Gaussian PSF model is used in differentiable rendering for 3D fluorescence microscopy. It provides a parameterized prior for the shape representation and topology of biological objects, such as cell membranes, by optimizing the covariance matrix \Sigma to match observed data. The connection to the Modulation Transfer Function in CT imaging highlights its broader application in medical imaging for determining sampling criteria. name: RoofGS Range-Aware Fast Exponential Evaluation
head: RoofGS fast exp, Schraudolph approximation for Gaussian Splatting
body: This method replaces the transcendental exponential function in the Gaussian blending loop with a range-aware bit-level approximation, leveraging the bounded exponent range resulting from opacity culling. It reduces special-function-unit (SFU) pressure and arithmetic overhead, achieving significant throughput gains with negligible visual quality loss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The pre-folded exponent value P(x, y) for a specific Gaussian-pixel pair. Output: The clamped opacity value \alpha(x, y) for alpha blending. Data Structures: P(x, y): A single-precision floating-point number. I(P): A 32-bit integer representing the bit pattern of the approximated exponential. Parameters: Mantissa scale: 2^{23}. Single-precision exponent bias: 127. Calibration constant: \sigma = 0.045677. Clamping threshold: 0.99. Exponent Range: Opacity culling restricts the exponent to the range P(x, y) \in [-\ln 255, 0] \approx [-5.541, 0]. Steps: 1. Compute the pre-folded exponent P(x, y) = p(x, y) + \log o, where p(x, y) is the quadratic form from the 2D Gaussian and o is the learned opacity. 2. Construct the 32-bit integer approximation I(P) using Schraudolph's method: I(P) = \lfloor P \cdot 2^{23} \cdot \log2(e) + 2^{23} \cdot (127 - \sigma) \rfloor where \log2(e) \approx 1.442695. 3. Reinterpret the integer bits as a single-precision floating-point number to get the unclamped approximation: \widehat{\exp}(P) = \text{reinterpret}{\text{float}}(I(P)). 4. Clamp the result to prevent over-saturation: \alpha(x, y) = \min(0.99, \widehat{\exp}(P)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import math def roofgsfastexp(P: float) -> float: """ Computes the range-aware fast exponential approximation for P in [-5.541, 0]. P: Pre-folded exponent (float32) Returns: Clamped opacity (float32) """ # Constants LOG2E = 1.4426950408889634 # log2(e) SIGMA = 0.045677 BIAS = 127.0 MANTISSASCALE = 223 CLAMPMAX = 0.99 # Step 2: Compute the bit pattern value val = P MANTISSASCALE LOG2E + MANTISSASCALE (BIAS - SIGMA) # Step 3: Bitwise reinterpretation (float -> int32 -> float) # struct.pack/unpack simulates the IEEE 754 bitcast intbits = struct.unpack('>I', struct.pack('>f', val))[0] approxexp = struct.unpack('>f', struct.pack('>I', intbits))[0] # Step 4: Clamp return min(CLAMPMAX, approxexp) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The approximation is only valid for P \in [-\ln 255, 0]. A technique that replaces the standard exponential operation with a bit-level approximation tailored to the bounded exponent range after opacity culling, reducing arithmetic and special-function-unit (SFU) pressure. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian-pixel pair, replacing a transcendental function with basic arithmetic and bitwise operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional memory required. Measured Performance: RoofGS achieves a 10.1× end-to-end speedup over 3DGS at 4K resolution on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, increasing throughput from 61 to 616 FPS. Accuracy: The relative error of the approximation is at most \epsilon{max} \approx 0.03 over the bounded range. This leads to a per-pixel color error bounded by |\Delta C|\infty \leq 0.03 in continuous color space, independent of the number of blended Gaussians. The PSNR loss is reported as 0.028 dB. Originated in the RoofGS paper by Yang Luo, Yan Gong, Yongsheng Gao, and Jie Zhao from the State Key Laboratory of Robotics and Systems, Harbin Institute of Technology. The method leverages Schraudolph's bit-level approximation of the exponential function. It was developed to address the computational bottleneck of the Gaussian blending loop in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically targeting the compute-bound rasterizer stage. RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15785, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Row-constant hoisting for Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
head: row-constant optimization, inner-loop hoisting
body: Row-constant hoisting is an optimization for the inner pixel loop of a Gaussian splatting rasterizer that hoists row-constant terms outside the inner (column) loop to minimize arithmetic operations per pixel. It reduces the computational cost of evaluating the 2D Gaussian exponent by precomputing terms dependent only on the row coordinate, allowing the inner loop to perform fewer multiplications and additions per column. This method is a specific implementation detail within the broader Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, distinct from higher-level optimizations like Contribution-based ordering or RoofGS Dual-Pixel Incremental Evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A projected 2D Gaussian primitive p with screen-space center (sx, sy), inverse covariance matrix elements a, b, d (where a = \Sigma^{-1}{00}, b = \Sigma^{-1}{01} = \Sigma^{-1}{10}, d = \Sigma^{-1}{11}), opacity \alphap, and color \mathbf{c}p. The bounding box of the splat [x0, y0, x1, y1] is precomputed. Input: A framebuffer fb of width w, where each cell stores an accumulated color \mathbf{C} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Input: Parameters saturation (max accumulated opacity) and alphathreshold (min alpha for contribution). Output: Updated framebuffer cells within the splat's bounding box. Data Structures: Framebuffer Cell: A tuple (\mathbf{Vec3}, f32) storing accumulated color and opacity. Projected Gaussian: Contains screen position, bounding box, inverse covariance components, opacity, and color. Steps: 1. Extract inverse covariance elements a, b, d from the projected Gaussian's inverse covariance matrix. 2. Compute coefficients for the quadratic form of the Gaussian exponent: dx{coeff} = -0.5 \cdot a dy{coeff} = -0.5 \cdot d cross{coeff} = -b (derived from -0.5 \cdot 2b) 3. Initialize loop bounds y from y0 to y1 inclusive. 4. For each row py in the outer loop: Compute dy = py - sy. Precompute row-constant terms: row{base} = dy{coeff} \cdot dy^2 row{slope} = cross{coeff} \cdot dy row{offset} = py \cdot w (for framebuffer indexing) 5. For each column px in the inner loop (from x0 to x1): Calculate framebuffer index idx = row{offset} + px. Check saturation: if fb[idx].\alpha{acc} \ge saturation, skip to next pixel. Compute dx = px - sx. Calculate the Gaussian exponent power using hoisted coefficients: power = dx{coeff} \cdot dx^2 + row{slope} \cdot dx + row{base} If power > 0.0, skip the pixel (exponential would exceed valid range). Compute alpha: \alpha = (\alphap \cdot e^{power}).\min(0.999). If \alpha < alpha{threshold}, skip the pixel. Compute contribution: t = 1.0 - fb[idx].\alpha{acc}, contrib = t \cdot \alpha. Update framebuffer: fb[idx].\mathbf{C} \leftarrow fb[idx].\mathbf{C} + contrib \cdot \mathbf{c}p fb[idx].\alpha{acc} \leftarrow fb[idx].\alpha{acc} + contrib Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositesplat(p: Projected, fb: List[Tuple[Vec3, float]], w: int, params: RenderParams): """ Composite a single 2D Gaussian splat into the framebuffer using row-constant hoisting. Args: p: Projected Gaussian with attributes: bbox: [x0, y0, x1, y1] (integers) cov2dinv: Inverse covariance matrix elements xaxis.x: a (Sigma^-100) xaxis.y: b (Sigma^-101) yaxis.y: d (Sigma^-111) screen: (sx, sy) (floats) opacity: alphap (float) color: cp (Vec3) fb: Framebuffer list of (color: Vec3, alpha: float) tuples w: Framebuffer width params: Render parameters including saturation and alphathreshold """ # Extract bounding box x0, y0, x1, y1 = p.bbox # Extract inverse covariance elements a = p.cov2dinv.xaxis.x b = p.cov2dinv.xaxis.y d = p.cov2dinv.yaxis.y # Precompute coefficients for the quadratic form dxcoeff = -0.5 a dycoeff = -0.5 d crosscoeff = -b # Equivalent to -0.5 2 b # Extract parameters saturation = params.saturation alphathreshold = params.alphathreshold opacity = p.opacity color = p.color sx = p.screen.x sy = p.screen.y # Outer loop over rows for py in range(y0, y1 + 1): # Compute row-constant terms dy = py - sy rowbase = dycoeff dy dy rowslope = crosscoeff dy rowoffset = py w # Inner loop over columns for px in range(x0, x1 + 1): idx = rowoffset + px cell = fb[idx] # Check saturation if cell[1] >= saturation: continue # Compute column offset dx = px - sx # Calculate power using hoisted row constants power = dxcoeff dx dx + rowslope dx + rowbase # Skip if power is positive (exponential > 1) if power > 0.0: continue # Compute alpha with clamping alpha = min(opacity fastexp(power), 0.999) # Skip if alpha is below threshold if alpha < alphathreshold: continue # Compute contribution t = 1.0 - cell[1] contrib = t alpha # Update framebuffer fb[idx] = ( cell[0] + contrib color, cell[1] + contrib) Parameters: saturation: Maximum accumulated opacity value in the framebuffer cell. If reached, further splats are skipped. alphathreshold: Minimum alpha value for a splat to contribute. Splats with alpha below this are skipped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the computed power is positive, the exponential term would exceed 1 (or be invalid for the Gaussian model), so the splat is skipped. Alpha is clamped to 0.999 to prevent numerical issues when blending. An optimization that exploits spatial coherence between vertically adjacent pixels by assigning each thread to process two pixels, (x, y) and (x, y+1), allowing reuse of shared-memory attribute loads and incremental exponent calculation. Time and Memory Complexity: The optimization reduces the number of arithmetic operations per pixel in the inner loop by hoisting row-constant calculations. Specifically, it moves the computation of dy{coeff} \cdot dy^2 and cross{coeff} \cdot dy outside the inner loop. Memory complexity is unchanged, as it operates on the same framebuffer structure. Limitations: Requires precomputing row-constant terms for each row, adding a small overhead to the outer loop. name: RoofGS Dual-Pixel Incremental Evaluation
head: RoofGS dual-pixel formulation, RoofGS vertical coherence optimization
body: An optimization that exploits spatial coherence between vertically adjacent pixels by assigning each thread to process two pixels, (x, y) and (x, y+1), allowing reuse of shared-memory attribute loads and incremental exponent calculation. It sets itself apart from standard single-pixel rasterization by halving shared-memory traffic and replacing the second pixel's full exponent evaluation with a lightweight incremental update. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The folded exponent P(x, y) for the first pixel (x, y), the Gaussian coefficients C2, C3, C5, and the pixel coordinates x, y. Output: The folded exponent P(x, y+1) for the second pixel (x, y+1). Data Structures: Registers: Store the pre-folded Gaussian coefficients C2, C3, C5 and register-resident coordinate terms. Shared Memory: Stores Gaussian attributes loaded once per tile. Numbered Steps: 1. Thread Assignment: Assign each thread to process two vertically adjacent pixels: (x, y) and (x, y+1). Both pixels traverse the same Gaussian sequence within a tile. 2. Attribute Load Reuse: Load Gaussian attributes from shared memory once. This single load serves both vertically adjacent pixels, halving per-pixel shared-memory traffic. 3. First Pixel Exponent: Compute the exponent P(x, y) for the first pixel using the regular FMA path (Eq. 16 from the parent article). 4. Incremental Update: Compute the exponent P(x, y+1) for the second pixel using the incremental formula derived from P(x, y). Formulas: Let P(x, y) be the folded exponent for pixel (x, y). The exponent for the adjacent pixel (x, y+1) is calculated as: P(x, y + 1) = P(x, y) + C2x + C3(2y + 1) + C5 Where: C2, C3, C5 are pre-folded Gaussian coefficients. x, y are the coordinates of the first pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def roofgsdualpixeleval(Pxy, C2, C3, C5, x, y): """ Computes the exponent for the second pixel (x, y+1) given the first pixel's exponent. Args: Pxy (float): The folded exponent P(x, y) for the first pixel. C2 (float): Coefficient C2. C3 (float): Coefficient C3. C5 (float): Coefficient C5. x (int): X-coordinate of the first pixel. y (int): Y-coordinate of the first pixel. Returns: float: The folded exponent P(x, y+1) for the second pixel. """ # Incremental update formula: P(x, y+1) = P(x, y) + C2x + C3(2y + 1) + C5 Pxy1 = Pxy + C2 x + C3 (2 y + 1) + C5 return Pxy1 Parameters: Tile Size: Not given in the sources. Resolution: Evaluated at 4K resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If y is the last row of the tile, the second pixel (x, y+1) may be out of bounds. Precision: The incremental update involves additions of potentially different magnitudes. A rasterization optimization that evaluates two adjacent pixels to improve instruction-level parallelism. It is chosen when vertical coherence can be exploited to reduce memory bandwidth and arithmetic operations. Time Complexity: Reduces arithmetic operations per pixel by avoiding re-evaluation of the full dot product for the second pixel. Memory Complexity: Halves per-pixel shared-memory traffic by reusing attribute loads for vertically adjacent pixels. Measured Performance: At 4K resolution on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, RoofGS increases average rendering throughput. Strengths: Reduces redundant arithmetic instructions and on-chip memory accesses in the innermost blending loop. Improves instruction scheduling and instruction-level parallelism (ILP) within the rasterization core. Limitations: Requires vertical coherence between pixels. When to Use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes on GPUs where shared-memory bandwidth and arithmetic throughput are bottlenecks. When Not to Use: When the overhead of managing dual-pixel threads outweighs the benefits, or on hardware with very high shared-memory bandwidth relative to arithmetic throughput. Originated in the paper "RoofGS: Roofline-Guided End-to-End Acceleration of 3D Gaussian Splatting" by Yang Luo, Yan Gong, Yongsheng Gao, and Jie Zhao. The work was supported by the National Science and Technology Major Project and the National Outstanding Youth Science Fund of the National Natural Science Foundation of China. It is used in the context of accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization by optimizing the inner pixel loop. name: 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization
head: 2D Gaussian Projection, 3D Gaussian Projection, 3D to 2D Projection in Gaussian Splatting, EWA Projection, Elliptical Weighted Average projection, Gaussian Projection, Linearized 2D Gaussian Projection, Splat Projection
body: 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization is the core rasterization primitive of 3D Gaussian Splatting that maps an anisotropic 3D Gaussian volume primitive into a 2D elliptical footprint (splat) on the image plane. It solves the problem of rendering millions of 3D probability distributions efficiently by approximating the non-linear perspective projection with a local affine transformation, thereby preserving the Gaussian form in screen space. It explicitly computes the screen-space covariance matrix to handle shape and spread, unlike point-sprite methods. The method stabilizes the projection by adding a small epsilon to the diagonal of the 2D covariance matrix to guarantee positive definiteness and numerical stability. Inputs: M 3D Gaussians, each defined by: Mean position in world space \muw \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized). Scale vector s \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-scale parameters). Opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients h for view-dependent color. Camera parameters: View matrix V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} (world-to-camera). Projection matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} (perspective). Image dimensions W, H (width, height in pixels). Principal point (cx, cy) (often center of image). Outputs: A list of projected 2D Gaussians, each containing: Screen-space mean \mu{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. Inverse covariance (conic) matrix \Sigma{2D}^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. Depth zc (for sorting). Bounding box (AABB) in screen coordinates. Color and opacity attributes. Data Structures: The projected Gaussian is stored in a struct with the following fields: screen: Vec2 (pixel center sx, sy). depth: f32 (zc, positive in front of camera). cov2dinv: Mat2 (inverse 2D covariance). bbox: [i32; 4] (inclusive x0, y0, x1, y1). color: Vec3 (RGB). opacity: f32 ([0, 1]). Steps: 1. Reconstruct 3D Covariance Matrix: Compute the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma from the quaternion q and scale s. R = \text{QuaternionToMatrix}(q) S = \text{diag}(\exp(s0), \exp(s1), \exp(s2)) \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top Note: \Sigma is symmetric positive semi-definite. 2. Transform to Camera Space: Transform the mean and covariance to camera space using the view matrix V. \muc = V{3 \times 3} \muw + V{3 \times 1} \Sigmac = V{3 \times 3} \Sigma V{3 \times 3}^\top Here, V{3 \times 3} is the upper-left 3 \times 3 rotation block of the view matrix. Translation is ignored for covariance as it describes spread around the centroid. 3. Compute Projection Jacobian: Linearize the perspective projection at \muc = (xc, yc, zc) using the Jacobian J. The perspective projection maps (x, y, z) to (u, v): u = fx \frac{x}{z} + cx, \quad v = fy \frac{y}{z} + cy The Jacobian J \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} evaluated at \muc is: J = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx}{zc} & 0 & -\frac{fx xc}{zc^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{zc} & -\frac{fy yc}{zc^2} \end{pmatrix} Focal lengths fx, fy are derived from the projection matrix or camera intrinsics. 4. Project Covariance to 2D: Compute the screen-space covariance \Sigma{2D} by applying the Jacobian to the camera-space covariance: \Sigma{2D} = J \Sigmac J^\top This results in a 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix. 5. Covariance Stabilization (Low-Pass Filter): Add a small epsilon \epsilon{2d} to the diagonal of \Sigma{2D} to ensure positive definiteness and numerical stability. \Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}} = \Sigma{2D} + \epsilon{2d} I Typical value for \epsilon{2d} is 0.3. Some implementations use 0.01. This ensures each Gaussian spans at least the width of a single pixel. 6. Compute Screen-Space Mean: Project the camera-space mean \muc to screen coordinates: \mu{2D} = \left( fx \frac{xc}{zc} + cx, \quad fy \frac{yc}{zc} + cy \right) 7. Compute Inverse Covariance (Conic): Compute the inverse of the stabilized covariance matrix \Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}} for efficient evaluation in the fragment shader. For a symmetric matrix \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{bmatrix}: \det = ad - b^2 If \det \le 0, cull the splat. \Sigma{2D}^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -b & a \end{bmatrix} 8. Compute Bounding Box: Determine the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for the splat to optimize rasterization. Compute eigenvalues \lambda{1,2} of \Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}}: \lambda{1,2} = \frac{\text{tr}(\Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}})}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{\text{tr}(\Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}})^2}{4} - \det(\Sigma{2D}^{\text{stab}})} Compute unit eigenvectors e1, e2. Define half-axes b1 = 3\sqrt{\lambda1}e1 and b2 = 3\sqrt{\lambda2}e2 (using 3\sigma cutoff). The bounding box is the AABB of the parallelogram spanned by b1 and b2 centered at \mu{2D}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Converts a normalized quaternion (w, x, y, z) to a 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - zw), 2(xz + yw)], [2(xy + zw), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - xw)], [2(xz - yw), 2(yz + xw), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) def projectgaussian(gaussian, camera): """ Projects a single 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space. Args: gaussian: dict with keys 'pos' (3,), 'rot' (4,), 'scale' (3,), 'opacity' (float) camera: dict with keys 'viewmatrix' (4x4), 'projmatrix' (4x4), 'fx', 'fy', 'cx', 'cy', 'width', 'height' Returns: dict with keys 'mu2d', 'cov2dinv', 'depth', 'bbox', 'color', 'opacity' or None if culled. """ # 1. Reconstruct 3D Covariance R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(gaussian['rot']) S = np.diag(np.exp(gaussian['scale'])) Sigma3d = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # 2. Transform to Camera Space V = camera['viewmatrix'] Vrot = V[:3,:3] Vtrans = V[:3, 3] muc = Vrot @ gaussian['pos'] + Vtrans Sigmac = Vrot @ Sigma3d @ Vrot.T xc, yc, zc = muc # Cull if behind camera if zc <= 0.0: return None # 3. Compute Jacobian fx = camera['fx'] fy = camera['fy'] J = np.array([ [fx / zc, 0, -fx xc / (zc2)], [0, fy / zc, -fy yc / (zc2)] ]) # 4. Project Covariance Sigma2d = J @ Sigmac @ J.T # 5. Stabilize Covariance eps2d = 0.3 # Default stabilization factor Sigma2dstab = Sigma2d + eps2d np.eye(2) # 6. Compute Screen Mean mu2d = np.array([ fx (xc / zc) + camera['cx'], fy (yc / zc) + camera['cy'] ]) # 7. Compute Inverse Covariance det = Sigma2dstab[0,0] Sigma2dstab[1,1] - Sigma2dstab[0,1]2 if det <= 0.0: return None # Cull singular covariance invdet = 1.0 / det cov2dinv = np.array([ [Sigma2dstab[1,1] invdet, -Sigma2dstab[0,1] invdet], [-Sigma2dstab[0,1] invdet, Sigma2dstab[0,0] invdet] ]) # 8. Compute Bounding Box (3-sigma) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2dstab) # eigenvalues are sorted ascending, so lambda1 is smallest lambda1, lambda2 = eigenvalues[0], eigenvalues[1] e1, e2 = eigenvectors[:, 0], eigenvectors[:, 1] b1 = 3.0 np.sqrt(lambda1) e1 b2 = 3.0 np.sqrt(lambda2) e2 # Bounding box corners corners = [ mu2d - b1 - b2, mu2d + b1 - b2, mu2d + b1 + b2, mu2d - b1 + b2 ] corners = np.array(corners) bbox = np.array([ np.floor(np.min(corners[:, 0])), np.floor(np.min(corners[:, 1])), np.ceil(np.max(corners[:, 0])), np.ceil(np.max(corners[:, 1])) ]) # Clip bbox to image bounds bbox[0] = max(0, bbox[0]) bbox[1] = max(0, bbox[1]) bbox[2] = min(camera['width'] - 1, bbox[2]) bbox[3] = min(camera['height'] - 1, bbox[3]) if bbox[0] > bbox[2] or bbox[1] > bbox[3]: return None # SH color evaluation not given in sources color = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) return { 'mu2d': mu2d, 'cov2dinv': cov2dinv, 'depth': zc, 'bbox': bbox, 'color': color, 'opacity': gaussian['opacity'] } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Divide Non-Linearity: The projection is non-linear. The affine approximation is valid only locally around the centroid. For very large Gaussians or extreme FOV, this approximation may introduce geometric warping artifacts. Singular Covariance: If the determinant of the 2D covariance is zero or negative, the inverse is undefined. This can happen if the Gaussian is viewed edge-on or if numerical errors accumulate. Stabilization (\epsilon{2d}) mitigates this. Depth Sorting: Gaussians must be sorted by depth (zc) before compositing to ensure correct alpha blending. Aliasing: Without stabilization, small Gaussians can cause high-frequency aliasing. The low-pass filter ensures minimum pixel coverage. Computes a tight, axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for a 2D Gaussian splat based on an opacity threshold, replacing the loose circular bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from siblings by explicitly integrating the splat's opacity and a configurable threshold to prune negligible contributions, thereby reducing false-positive tile intersections during rasterization. Render Means is the simplest possible rendering mode for 3D Gaussian Splatting, where each Gaussian is represented by a single pixel at the location where its 3D mean projects onto the 2D image plane. It demonstrates the basic camera transformation pipeline (world → camera → image) and frustum culling without any rasterization complexity. Unlike its sibling 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization, which computes screen-space covariance matrices for elliptical splatting, Render Means ignores shape and spread, treating Gaussians as point sprites. Optimal Gaussian Splatting Projection is a rendering method that minimizes projection error by projecting each 3D Gaussian onto a plane tangent to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than a fixed image plane. It sets itself apart from standard 3D-GS by using a unique tangent plane for each Gaussian based on its position relative to the camera, significantly reducing artifacts like blurriness and needle-like structures, particularly in wide-field-of-view or short focal length scenarios. Computes the 2 \times 3 Jacobian matrix of the perspective projection function with respect to 3D coordinates, used for linearizing the projection of 3D Gaussians into screen space. It transforms the 3D covariance structure into 2D screen-space covariance, enabling accurate Gaussian splatting. Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Gaussian Splatting assigns material properties as texture maps in the splat's local coordinate system rather than single attribute values per primitive, enabling higher-frequency spatial detail without increasing primitive count. It decouples geometry from appearance, allowing complex visual features and detailed normal maps to be captured within the existing Gaussian representation. This method differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by treating alpha-blending as a smoothing filter in a deferred rendering pipeline, which stabilizes the optimization of texture-sampled features and produces more cohesive results compared to shading directly on Gaussians. 3D Ellipsoid Projection is a Gaussian selection method used to identify candidate 3D Gaussians for rendering specific image slices in volume rendering pipelines. It approximates the spatial extent of a 3D Gaussian ellipsoid as a sphere to compute a uniform 2D bounding box, which is then projected orthogonally onto every image slice. Unlike sibling methods that adapt bounding boxes per slice or use complex covariance corrections, this approach prioritizes simplicity by treating the Gaussian's range as isotropic, though this leads to redundant computation for off-center slices. Time Complexity: O(M) for projection of M Gaussians, where each projection involves constant-time matrix operations (3 \times 3 and 2 \times 2). Sorting takes O(M \log M). Rasterization is O(P) where P is the number of pixels, but optimized by tile-based binning to only process relevant splats. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store the projected splats. Measured Performance: The method enables real-time rendering of millions of Gaussians. For example, on the Mip-NeRF360 benchmark, 3DGS reaches 27.21 dB PSNR and 0.214 LPIPS at 134 fps. An accelerator implementation achieved 129 FPS at Full HD (1080p). Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Performance is heavily dependent on the efficiency of the sorting and tile-based rasterization stages. Strengths: Closed-form projection allows for differentiable rendering, enabling gradient-based optimization of scene parameters. High rendering speed due to efficient rasterization. Limitations: The affine approximation of perspective projection can introduce artifacts for very large Gaussians or extreme viewpoints. Requires careful handling of numerical stability (covariance stabilization). When to use: When real-time or differentiable rendering of large-scale 3D scenes is required. When not to use: When high geometric accuracy for very large primitives is critical, or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained and M is extremely large. The method was originally described by Zwicker et al. in 2002 for anti-aliased splatting of volume data. It was later reused by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for the closed-form projection of 3D Gaussians, enabling real-time rendering of photorealistic scenes. name: Adaptive Bounding Box Computation
head: Tsplat bounding box
body: Computes a tight, axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for a 2D Gaussian splat based on a specific opacity threshold, replacing the loose circular bounding box used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). This method significantly reduces false-positive tile intersections and the resulting number of duplicated splat fragments during rasterization. Inputs: sx, sy: Screen-space center coordinates of the 2D Gaussian splat (float). cov2d00, cov2d11: Diagonal elements of the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma (float). opacity: The scalar opacity of the splat (float). alphathreshold: The minimum opacity threshold \tau for a pixel to be considered visible (float). maxk2: The maximum allowed squared Mahalanobis distance to prevent overflow or excessive box sizes (float). wi, hi: Framebuffer width and height in pixels (uint). Outputs: A bounding box defined by integer coordinates (x0, y0, x1, y1), or None if the splat is effectively invisible or has negligible size. Formula: The Gaussian opacity at screen-space displacement \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy) is \alpha = \text{opacity} \cdot \exp(-\tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{d}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{d}). Setting the visibility condition \alpha \ge \tau and rearranging yields \mathbf{d}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{d} \le 2 \ln(\frac{\text{opacity}}{\tau}) = k^2. For a diagonal covariance matrix, this bounds the displacement to |dx| \le \sqrt{k^2 \cdot cov2d{00}} and |dy| \le \sqrt{k^2 \cdot cov2d{11}}. Steps: 1. Opacity Check: If opacity \le alphathreshold, return None. 2. Compute Squared Mahalanobis Distance Limit (k^2): Calculate the squared distance in the normalized space corresponding to the opacity threshold: k^2 = \min\left(2.0 \cdot \ln\left(\frac{\text{opacity}}{\text{alpha\threshold}}\right), \text{max\k2}\right) If k^2 \le 0.0, return None. 3. Compute Half-Widths: Calculate the half-extents of the bounding box along the x and y axes: rxf = \sqrt{k^2 \cdot cov2d{00}} ryf = \sqrt{k^2 \cdot cov2d{11}} If rxf or ryf is not finite or is less than 1.0, return None. 4. Compute Integer Bounding Box: Determine the pixel coordinates of the bounding box corners: x0 = \lfloor sx - rxf \rfloor y0 = \lfloor sy - ryf \rfloor x1 = \lceil sx + rxf \rceil y1 = \lceil sy + ryf \rceil 5. Clip to Framebuffer: Clamp the coordinates to the valid framebuffer range: x0 = \max(0, x0) y0 = \max(0, y0) x1 = \min(wi - 1, x1) y1 = \min(hi - 1, y1) If x0 > x1 or y0 > y1, return None. 6. Return: Return the tuple (x0, y0, x1, y1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeadaptiveboundingbox(sx, sy, cov2d00, cov2d11, opacity, alphathreshold, maxk2, wi, hi): # Step 1: Opacity Check if opacity <= alphathreshold: return None # Step 2: Compute k^2 k2 = 2.0 math.log(opacity / alphathreshold) if k2 > maxk2: k2 = maxk2 if k2 <= 0.0: return None # Step 3: Compute half-widths rxf = math.sqrt(k2 cov2d00) ryf = math.sqrt(k2 cov2d11) if not math.isfinite(rxf) or rxf < 1.0: return None if not math.isfinite(ryf) or ryf < 1.0: return None # Step 4: Compute integer bounding box x0 = math.floor(sx - rxf) y0 = math.floor(sy - ryf) x1 = math.ceil(sx + rxf) y1 = math.ceil(sy + ryf) # Step 5: Clip to framebuffer x0 = max(0, x0) y0 = max(0, y0) x1 = min(wi - 1, x1) y1 = min(hi - 1, y1) # Step 6: Validity Check if x0 > x1 or y0 > y1: return None # Step 7: Return return (x0, y0, x1, y1) Parameters: maxk2: Caps the squared Mahalanobis distance to prevent overflow or excessive bounding box sizes. alphathreshold: Defines the visibility cutoff \tau for the Gaussian opacity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The calculation of k^2 involves logarithms and square roots; the check k^2 \le 0.0 handles cases where numerical noise might otherwise produce negative values under the square root. Boundaries: The clipping step ensures the bounding box stays within the framebuffer; if the splat is entirely outside the framebuffer, the clipping will result in an invalid box (x0 > x1), which is correctly handled. Degenerate Input: If cov2d00 or cov2d11 is zero or negative, the half-widths will be zero or NaN; the check for < 1.0 and isfinite filters these degenerate cases. Determines which image tiles a 2D Gaussian splat intersects by computing a tight, non-square AABB around the ellipse defined by the splat's covariance at a specific opacity threshold. It sets itself apart from the original 3DGS circular bounding box by tightly fitting the actual elliptical shape, significantly reducing false-positive tile intersections. Choose it when precise tile culling is required to minimize duplicated splat fragments in differentiable rendering pipelines. Computes the tight AABB of a projected 2D Gaussian ellipse in constant time to determine the rectangular tile extent for rasterization. It sets itself apart from iterative exact intersection methods like AccuTile by providing a static geometric bound suitable for initial culling and spatial indexing. Choose it for fast initial culling where iterative exact intersection methods are too slow. Computes a tight, axis-aligned rectangular bounding box for a 2D Gaussian splat based on its projected opacity and covariance, replacing the original 3DGS square bounding box derived from a fixed confidence radius. It sets itself apart from fixed-radius square boxes by accounting for the Gaussian's actual opacity and non-square shape. Choose it when splat aspect ratios vary significantly across views to reduce false positives in per-tile splat lists. Allows the axis-aligned bounding box of a projected 2D Gaussian to have different width and height dimensions, rather than forcing a square shape. On the Bicycle scene at native resolution with 16x16 tiles, non-square boxes reduced duplicated Gaussians from 55,648,264 (square) to 18,466,556. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat, as the computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations, logarithms, and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1) per splat, with no additional memory allocated for the bounding box computation itself. Measured Performance: On the Bicycle scene at native resolution, the combination of opacity-aware bounding boxes and other improvements decreased render time by a factor of 3.77 and GPU memory usage by a factor of 2.11. The reduction in duplicated Gaussians from 55,648,264 (square) to 18,466,556 (non-square) on the same scene highlights the efficiency gain in rasterization. Strengths: Significantly reduces false-positive tile intersections, leading to fewer splat duplications and lower memory bandwidth usage during rasterization. It is computationally inexpensive. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method addresses the inefficiencies of the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper's circular bounding box approach. It is implemented in the Tsplat project and discussed in the context of fast 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering improvements.
