name: 3D Ellipsoid Projection
head: Gaussian Selection Method, Sphere Approximation Projection
body: 3D Ellipsoid Projection is a Gaussian selection method that approximates the range of a 3D Gaussian as a sphere based on the maximum axis length of the Gaussian ellipsoid, projecting a cube onto each image slice. This yields identical 2D bounding boxes across all slices, which simplifies candidate sampling but causes redundant computation. Inputs: A 3D Gaussian primitive defined by its mean position \mathbf{\mu} and covariance matrix \Sigma. A set of image slices (depth planes) along the viewing direction. Outputs: A set of candidate Gaussians for each slice, determined by whether the projected bounding box intersects the slice's region of interest. Data Structures: Covariance Matrix \Sigma: A 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix representing the Gaussian's shape and orientation. Eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: The scalar values obtained from the spectral decomposition of \Sigma. Bounding Box: A cube defined by its center \mathbf{\mu} and edge length 2 r{\max}. Steps: 1. Compute Eigenvalues: Calculate the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of the covariance matrix \Sigma. 2. Determine Maximum Axis Length: Identify the largest eigenvalue \lambda{\max} = \max(\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3). 3. Calculate Approximation Radius: Compute the radius r{\max} of the approximating sphere using the formula: r{\max} = 3 \cdot \sqrt{\lambda{\max}} where r{\max} is the radius of the approximating sphere and \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are the eigenvalues of \Sigma. 4. Define Bounding Cube: Construct a cube of edge length 2 r{\max} centered at the Gaussian's mean \mathbf{\mu}. 5. Project to Slices: Orthogonally project this cube onto each image slice, yielding identical 2D bounding boxes across all slices. 6. Selection: Include the Gaussian in the candidate set for a slice if the slice's pixel coordinates fall within the projected 2D bounding box. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compute3dellipsoidprojection(gaussianmean, covariancematrix, slices): # Step 1 & 2: Compute eigenvalues of the 3x3 symmetric covariance matrix eigenvalues = solve3x3symmetriceigenvalues(covariancematrix) lambdamax = max(eigenvalues) # Step 3: Calculate approximation radius rmax = 3.0 math.sqrt(lambdamax) # Step 4: Define bounding cube dimensions halfedge = rmax # Step 5: Orthogonally project cube onto each image slice # Assuming viewing direction aligns with the Z-axis, the 2D center is (meanx, meany) center2d = (gaussianmean[0], gaussianmean[1]) boundingbox2d = { "center": center2d, "halfwidth": halfedge, "halfheight": halfedge } results = [] for i, in enumerate(slices): # The bounding box is identical for all slices results.append((i, boundingbox2d)) return results def solve3x3symmetriceigenvalues(M): # Analytical solution for 3x3 symmetric matrix eigenvalues using the characteristic polynomial # Characteristic polynomial: lambda^3 - c2lambda^2 + c1lambda - c0 = 0 c2 = M[0][0] + M[1][1] + M[2][2] c1 = (M[0][0]M[1][1] - M[0][1]2) + (M[0][0]M[2][2] - M[0][2]2) + (M[1][1]M[2][2] - M[1][2]2) c0 = (M[0][0]M[1][1]M[2][2] + 2M[0][1]M[0][2]M[1][2] - M[0][0]M[1][2]2 - M[1][1]M[0][2]2 - M[2][2]M[0][1]2) # Trigonometric solution for three real roots (delta <= 0 for symmetric matrices) p = c1 - c22 / 3.0 q = 2.0 c23 / 27.0 - c2 c1 / 3.0 + c0 phi = math.acos(-q / 2.0 math.sqrt(-27.0 / p3)) if p < 0 else 0.0 r = math.sqrt(-p / 3.0) return [ 2.0 r math.cos(phi / 3.0) - c2 / 3.0, 2.0 r math.cos((phi + 2.0 math.pi) / 3.0) - c2 / 3.0, 2.0 r math.cos((phi + 4.0 math.pi) / 3.0) - c2 / 3.0 ] Parameters: Confidence Factor: 3 (representing 3\sigma). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundant Computation: Because the same cubic bounding box is projected onto every slice, slices far from the Gaussian's center may still be processed if they fall within the large projected box, leading to unnecessary rasterization work. Overestimation: The spherical approximation ignores the orientation of the ellipsoid. If the Gaussian is highly anisotropic (e.g., a flat sheet), the sphere will include large volumes of empty space, further exacerbating the redundant computation issue. A Gaussian selection method that uses a factorized Gaussian structure to compute the range of each Gaussian on individual slices, adapting the bounding box for each slice based on depth. It models the Gaussian contribution as pi(u, v, t) = pi(u, v|t)pi(t), where pi(u, v|t) is a conditional 2D Gaussian describing the lateral spatial distribution given slice location t, and pi(t) is a 1D Gaussian modeling uncertainty along the depth axis. The conditional mean \mu{u,v|t} shifts with slice depth t, and a distance-dependent scaling factor reduces the extent of the 2D splat as the distance between the 3D Gaussian center and the slice increases. This leads to more efficient sampling by avoiding the processing of overly large, static regions. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of Gaussians and S is the number of slices. Each Gaussian is evaluated against every slice. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only requires storing the bounding box parameters per slice. Performance: The method is computationally simple to implement but inefficient in scenes with many Gaussians or deep volumes, as it processes redundant pixels on slices distant from the Gaussian's center. Strengths: Simple to implement; robust to orientation changes as it relies on the maximum axis length. Limitations: Significant redundant computation due to identical bounding boxes across all slices. When to use: When implementation simplicity is prioritized over rendering speed, or in shallow volumes where the redundancy is minimal. The 3D Ellipsoid Projection method was introduced in the context of internal scene reconstruction and segmentation using factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting. It serves as a baseline Gaussian selection strategy to identify candidate Gaussians for each pixel/slice before differential rasterization. The method was compared against Conditional Splatting in simulation analyses involving 3D volumes of size 20 \times 20 \times 20. name: Rotationally Invariant Gaussian Splatting
head: Westover Gaussian Splat
body: Rotationally Invariant Gaussian Splatting is a volume rendering technique that uses a Gaussian weighting function to achieve rotational symmetry, thereby avoiding the need for separate integration for each new orientation in perspective projection. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing a closed-form analytic solution for the 2D projection of a 3D Gaussian kernel, which simplifies the handling of varying orientations within a single frame. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian kernel h(u,v,w) defined in local coordinates, where the viewing ray aligns with the w-axis. Output: A 2D texture map f(u,v) representing the integrated density along the viewing ray. Data Structures: Texture Map: A 2D array of size N \times N (where N is determined by the truncation threshold). Each cell stores the integrated weight value. Method: 1. Define the 3D Kernel: Use the rotationally symmetric Gaussian function: h(u,v,w) = \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2 + w^2}{\theta^2}\right) where \theta is the scale parameter. 2. Integrate Along the Ray: Compute the 2D projection by integrating the 3D kernel along the viewing ray (w-axis). The integral is: f(u, v) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(u, v, w) \, dw 3. Apply Closed-Form Solution: Substitute the Gaussian definition into the integral. The result is: f(u, v) = \theta \sqrt{\pi} \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2}{\theta^2}\right) Note: The source text presents the formula as f(u, v) = \frac{w}{\theta} h \exp (-(u^2 + v^2)/\theta^2), but standard integration of a Gaussian \exp(-x^2/\sigma^2) yields \sigma\sqrt{\pi}\exp(-x^2/\sigma^2). The source text likely contains a typo or specific notation where w and h are constants or placeholders for \theta\sqrt{\pi}. Given the context of "simple integral" and standard Gaussian properties, the term \theta \sqrt{\pi} is the correct normalization factor for the projection. 4. Truncate: Since the Gaussian function does not have compact support, truncate the function at a threshold where the value becomes negligible (e.g., 3\theta or 4\theta) to create a reasonable-sized texture map. 5. Sample: Use the truncated 2D function as a texture map during splatting. Parameters: \theta: The width/scale of the Gaussian. Typical values depend on the voxel size and desired smoothness. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Truncation: The Gaussian function does not have compact support. Failure to truncate appropriately leads to infinite texture sizes or significant aliasing artifacts at the edges. Summation Constant: A rotationally symmetric splat cannot maintain a constant sum (unity) when tiled, unlike trilinear interpolation. This may lead to visible seams if splats are not blended carefully. An approximation of the Gaussian splat using a piecewise linear function, rendered by compositing triangles with linearly varying color and opacity using standard scan conversion hardware. It sets itself apart by allowing rendering without texture mapping, leveraging standard rasterization hardware. Choose this when hardware lacks texture mapping support or for simplicity in basic renderers. Pitfall: Visible Mach bands appear at the edges of the triangles used in the compositing process. Time Complexity: O(1) for evaluating the 2D projection function per pixel if precomputed, or O(N^2) to generate the texture map. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for the texture map, where N is the truncation radius. Strengths: Avoids complex integration for every orientation; simple analytic form. Limitations: Does not sum to a constant when tiled, potentially causing artifacts; requires truncation. When to use: When rotational symmetry is desired and perspective projection orientations vary significantly. Originated from Westover's work on texture mapping for volume rendering, proposing the Gaussian function for its rotational symmetry and simple integral. Laur and Hanrahan later approximated this with piecewise linear functions for hardware rasterization. Applications of texture mapping to volume and flow visualization, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc626633/?q=volume splatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Covariance Stabilization and Correction
body: This family modifies the 2D screen-space covariance matrix of a Gaussian primitive to ensure numerical stability or correct projection errors before rasterization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly adjusting covariance entries via low-pass filtering with density preservation or linear regression, rather than relying on geometric bounding heuristics. All methods in this family operate on the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma^{2D} derived from a 3D Gaussian. The core mechanism involves modifying the matrix entries to ensure numerical stability (positive definiteness) or to correct for projection errors. The output is typically a corrected covariance matrix or its inverse (conic matrix) used in the rasterization kernel. The methods assume the input covariance is symmetric and positive semi-definite. This method stabilizes the projection by applying a low-pass filter to the 2D covariance matrix, ensuring each Gaussian spans at least the width of a single pixel to reduce aliasing [3467-2d-gaussian-covariance-stabilization-and-rescaling]. It computes a rescale factor to preserve the integrated density of the Gaussian after filtering. Choose this when aliasing is a primary concern and density preservation is required. See 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling. This method approximates the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances using a linear regression model, serving as a computationally efficient alternative to neural network-based corrections [9912-2d-covariance-correction-via-linear-regression]. It sets itself apart by replacing complex learned mappings with closed-form linear coefficients or a single scalar factor, reducing training overhead. Choose this when reconstruction quality comparable to Half-Cosine kernels is needed with lower computational cost. See 2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression. A scalar correction factor applied to the covariance matrix to approximate the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances, replacing a more complex MLP or Simpson's rule integration. Inverse Multiquadric correction factor: 1.38f. Parabolic correction factor: 1.3f. The techniques originate from work on generalizing splatting with decaying anisotropic radial basis functions. The correction methods were introduced to approximate the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances, replacing complex MLPs or Simpson's rule integration with linear regression or scalar factors. The stabilization approach addresses aliasing in novel view synthesis, while correction methods address the geometric mismatch between the projected Gaussian and the true integrated density. name: 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling
head: Conic Matrix and Rescale Factor, Covariance Rescaling, Gaussian Covariance Pre-filtering, Pixel-spanning Gaussian
body: This method computes the screen-space conic matrix (inverse covariance) and a rescale factor for a 2D Gaussian, applying a low-pass filter to the covariance matrix to ensure a minimum pixel coverage. It modifies the screen-space 2D Gaussian sizes to ensure they span the width of a single pixel, thereby reducing aliasing artifacts during rasterization. It differs from its sibling 2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression by using a fixed additive diagonal bias rather than learned regression coefficients to enforce the minimum size constraint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2x2 symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix \Sigma^{2D} representing the projected 2D Gaussian in screen space. Output: A 4-component vector conicandrescale containing the elements of the inverse covariance matrix (conic matrix) and a scalar rescale factor. Specifically, [invcov[0,0], invcov[0,1], invcov[1,1], rescale]. Note that the conic matrix is symmetric, so invcov[0,1] equals invcov[1,0]. Data Structures: gaussiancovariance: A 2x2 matrix. conicandrescale: A 4-element vector (or array). Parameters: s (or 0.3): The low-pass filter strength added to the diagonal elements. The default value is 0.3. This value is set during training to ensure the 2D Gaussian's size spans the width of a single pixel. Steps: 1. Compute the determinant of the input covariance matrix: \text{det\cov\prefilter} = \det(\Sigma^{2D}) 2. Apply the low-pass filter by adding the scalar s to the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix: \Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}} = \Sigma^{2D} + s \cdot \mathbf{I} Where \mathbf{I} is the 2x2 identity matrix. Specifically: \Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}}[0,0] = \Sigma^{2D}[0,0] + s \Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}}[1,1] = \Sigma^{2D}[1,1] + s 3. Compute the determinant of the filtered covariance matrix: \text{det\cov} = \det(\Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}}) 4. Compute the rescale factor. This factor adjusts the opacity/weight of the Gaussian to account for the volume change caused by the low-pass filtering: \text{rescale} = \sqrt{\max(0.0, \frac{\text{det\cov\prefilter}}{\text{det\cov}})} 5. Compute the inverse covariance (conic) matrix analytically for the 2x2 filtered matrix. For a 2x2 matrix A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}, the inverse is \frac{1}{\det(A)} \begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}. Since the covariance is symmetric (b=c): \text{inv\cov} = \frac{1}{\text{det\cov}} \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}}[1,1] & -\Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}}[0,1] \\ -\Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}}[1,0] & \Sigma^{2D}{\text{filtered}}[0,0] \end{pmatrix} 6. Return the result as a 4-element vector: [invcov[0,0], invcov[0,1], invcov[1,1], rescale]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeconicandrescale(cov2d, s=0.3): """ Computes the conic matrix and rescale factor for a 2D Gaussian. Args: cov2d: 2x2 numpy array or tensor representing the 2D covariance matrix. s: Scalar value added to diagonal elements for low-pass filtering (default 0.3). Returns: conicandrescale: 4-element vector [invcov00, invcov01, invcov11, rescale]. """ # Step 1: Compute pre-filter determinant detcovprefilter = cov2d[0, 0] cov2d[1, 1] - cov2d[0, 1] cov2d[1, 0] # Step 2: Apply low-pass filter (add s to diagonal) # Note: cov2d is assumed symmetric, so cov2d[0,1] == cov2d[1,0] covfiltered00 = cov2d[0, 0] + s covfiltered11 = cov2d[1, 1] + s covfiltered01 = cov2d[0, 1] # Off-diagonal remains unchanged # Step 3: Compute post-filter determinant detcov = covfiltered00 covfiltered11 - covfiltered01 covfiltered01 # Step 4: Compute rescale factor # Use max(0.0,...) to handle potential numerical issues where detcov might be slightly negative or zero ratio = detcovprefilter / detcov rescale = (max(0.0, ratio)) 0.5 # Step 5: Compute inverse covariance (conic) matrix analytically # invcov = (1/detcov) [[covfiltered11, -covfiltered01], [-covfiltered01, covfiltered00]] invcov00 = covfiltered11 / detcov invcov01 = -covfiltered01 / detcov invcov11 = covfiltered00 / detcov # Step 6: Return conicandrescale as vec4 return [invcov00, invcov01, invcov11, rescale] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If the filtered determinant detcov is zero or negative (due to numerical precision issues with very small covariances), the division in the rescale factor and conic matrix computation will fail or produce NaNs. The use of max(0.0, ratio) and the inherent positivity of detcov after adding s > 0 to the diagonal of a PSD matrix mitigates this, but explicit clamping or epsilon addition might be required in practice. Precision: The rescale factor compensates for the change in the integral of the Gaussian. If the rescale factor is not applied, the rendered opacity will be incorrect because the low-pass filtering spreads the Gaussian's mass over a larger area. Approximates a conical frustum as a 3D Gaussian distribution to enable differentiable volume rendering with integrated positional encoding. It lifts a 1D Gaussian defined along the ray axis and a radial variance into 3D space, aligning the covariance with the ray direction. It differs from the parent method by operating in 3D ray space to produce the full covariance tensor required for 3D Gaussian Splatting, whereas the parent operates on 2D screen-space covariances. See Conical Frustum to Gaussian. A CUDA kernel that preprocesses 3D Gaussian parameters into voxel-space coordinates, conic matrices, and bounding radii for efficient tile-based rasterization. It transforms world-space attributes into voxel-space data structures required by the splatting pass, differing from sibling methods by operating directly on voxel-space transformations and conic matrix inversion rather than frustum approximation. See Gaussian Preprocessing. Computes a floor for the layer-0 Gaussian covariance matrix based on the image-space Jacobian of the target surface, ensuring Gaussians are not smaller than the surface detail implied by the depth map. It builds on the parent method by incorporating explicit surface geometry constraints into the covariance rescaling process. See Surface Jacobian Covariance Stabilization. A method to define the minimal size of 3D Gaussians based on reconstruction confidence to prevent the 'needle' effect (thin Gaussians appearing when zooming in), using Variational Bayesian estimation principles. It calculates the inverse precision matrix for localization as \Sigmai^{(XYZ)^{-1}} = \sumc \left( zi^{(c)^2} \sigma^{(w)^2} Wc^T \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} Wc \right)^{-1}, where Wc is the world transformation matrix for camera c, and zi^{(c)} is the distance of the Gaussian along the z-axis of camera c. The precision matrix for size is identical: \Sigmai^{(\sigma)} = \Sigmai^{(XYZ)}. A scaling factor \alpha is set to 2 to accommodate modeling approximations and occlusions. Manipulates overall scene blurriness or sharpness by applying global transformations to per-Gaussian offsets \delta rj and \delta sj predicted by a compact MLP. \delta rj controls local rotation adjustments alongside scale, and \delta sj controls local scale adjustments alongside rotation. A post-optimization constraint that clamps the ratio between the largest and smallest scale of each Gaussian to a maximum allowed value, ensuring isotropy limits. It checks if anisolambda > 0, calculates maxratio = 1.0 + (20.0 - 1.0) (1.0 - anisolambda), computes the current scale ratio ratio = smax / smin, identifies splats needing fix, computes median scale mid, computes allowed bounds allowedmax = mid sqrt(maxratio) and allowedmin = mid / sqrt(maxratio), and clamps the scales to these bounds before converting back to log space. anisolambda is a slider where 0 allows ratio 20 and 1 forces ratio 1 (isotropic). Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (determinant, addition, square root, matrix inversion for 2x2). Memory Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, storing the 2x2 covariance and the resulting 4-element vector. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, effectively reduces aliasing by ensuring Gaussians are not smaller than a pixel. Limitations: The fixed value of s=0.3 may not be optimal for all resolutions or scenes. It does not account for anisotropy beyond the diagonal bias. When to use: When rendering 2D Gaussians for anti-aliasing in Gaussian Splatting, particularly when training with a default setting. When not to use: When precise control over the minimum Gaussian size based on scene geometry or camera parameters is required (see Surface Jacobian Covariance Stabilization or BOGausS Precision Matrix Derivation). The method originates from the core Gaussian Splatting framework, where 3D Gaussians are projected to 2D and rasterized. The low-pass filtering (adding s to the diagonal) is a standard technique in EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) splatting to handle the Nyquist limit and prevent aliasing when Gaussians are smaller than a pixel. The rescale factor ensures that the integral of the Gaussian (and thus its opacity contribution) is preserved despite the modification of the covariance matrix. The specific implementation with s=0.3 is widely adopted in open-source libraries like gsplat and Taichi-based implementations. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) BOGausS: Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.23919/eusipco63237.2025.11226626, fetched 2026-10-26 Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73636-08, fetched 2026-10-26 SpaceCollectors/dust3r-3dgs, https://github.com/SpaceCollectors/dust3r-3dgs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Conical Frustum to Gaussian
head: Conical Frustum to Gaussian Approximation, Frustum Gaussian Approximation, cone ray featurization
body: Approximates a conical frustum (defined by ray origin, direction, start/end distances, and base radius) as a 3D Gaussian distribution (mean and covariance) to enable differentiable volume rendering with integrated positional encoding. It lifts a 1D Gaussian defined along the ray axis and a radial variance into 3D space, aligning the covariance with the ray direction. Inputs: origins: Tensor of shape [B, 3], ray origins. directions: Tensor of shape [B, 3], normalized ray direction vectors. starts: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, nsamples], start distances t0 along the ray. ends: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, nsamples], end distances t1 along the ray. baseradius: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, 1], radius of the frustum at distance t=1 (for cones) or constant radius (for cylinders). rayshape: String, either 'cone' or 'cylinder'. diagonal: Boolean, if True returns diagonal covariance; if False returns full 3 \times 3 covariance. stable: Boolean, if True uses numerically stable formulas for moments; if False uses raw moment formulas (discouraged). Outputs: means: Tensor of shape [B, 3] (or [B, nsamples, 3]), mean positions. covs: Tensor of shape [B, 3, 3] (or [B, nsamples, 3, 3]), covariance matrices. Steps: 1. Calculate Intermediate Parameters: Compute the midpoint \mu and half-width hw of the interval [t0, t1]: \mu = \frac{t0 + t1}{2} hw = \frac{t1 - t0}{2} 2. Compute Denominator (Stable Mode Only): If stable is True, compute a denominator to prevent division by zero when \mu is small: \text{denom} = \max(\epsilon, 3\mu^2 + hw^2) where \epsilon is the machine epsilon for the data type (e.g., torch.finfo(torch.float16).eps). If stable is False, denom is not used in the moment calculations. 3. Compute 1D Longitudinal Moments (t{\text{mean}}, t{\text{var}}): If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is True: t{\text{mean}} = \mu + \frac{2\mu hw^2}{\text{denom}} t{\text{var}} = \frac{hw^2}{3} - \frac{4}{15} \frac{hw^4 (12\mu^2 - hw^2)}{\text{denom}^2} If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is False: t{\text{mean}} = \frac{3(t1^4 - t0^4)}{4(t1^3 - t0^3)} t{\text{mosq}} = \frac{3}{5} \frac{t1^5 - t0^5}{t1^3 - t0^3} t{\text{var}} = t{\text{mosq}} - t{\text{mean}}^2 If rayshape is 'cylinder': The sources do not provide explicit formulas for t{\text{mean}} or t{\text{var}} in cylinder mode, only for r{\text{var}}. 4. Compute Radial Variance (r{\text{var}}): If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is True: r{\text{var}} = \text{base\radius}^2 \left( \frac{\mu^2}{4} + \frac{5}{12}hw^2 - \frac{4}{15} \frac{hw^4}{\text{denom}} \right) If rayshape is 'cone' and stable is False: r{\text{var}} = \text{base\radius}^2 \frac{3}{20} \frac{t1^5 - t0^5}{t1^3 - t0^3} If rayshape is 'cylinder': r{\text{var}} = \text{base\radius}^2 \left( \frac{\mu^2}{4} + \frac{5}{12}hw^2 - \frac{4}{15} \frac{hw^4}{3\mu^2 + hw^2} \right) 5. Lift to 3D (Compute Mean and Covariance): Mean: \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{d} \cdot t{\text{mean}} where \mathbf{d} is the direction vector. Covariance: Compute the squared magnitude of the direction, clamped to a minimum value to avoid division by zero: d{\text{mag\sq}} = \max(\|\mathbf{d}\|^2, 10^{-10}) If diagonal is True: d{\text{outer\diag}} = \mathbf{d}^2 \text{null\outer\diag} = 1 - \frac{d{\text{outer\diag}}}{d{\text{mag\sq}}} t{\text{cov\diag}} = t{\text{var}} \cdot d{\text{outer\diag}} xy{\text{cov\diag}} = r{\text{var}} \cdot \text{null\outer\diag} \text{cov\diag} = t{\text{cov\diag}} + xy{\text{cov\diag}} If diagonal is False: \mathbf{d}{\text{outer}} = \mathbf{d} \mathbf{d}^T \mathbf{I} = \text{Identity}(3) \mathbf{N}{\text{outer}} = \mathbf{I} - \frac{\mathbf{d} \mathbf{d}^T}{d{\text{mag\sq}}} \mathbf{t}{\text{cov}} = t{\text{var}} \cdot \mathbf{d}{\text{outer}} \mathbf{xy}{\text{cov}} = r{\text{var}} \cdot \mathbf{N}{\text{outer}} \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{t}{\text{cov}} + \mathbf{xy}{\text{cov}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def conicalfrustumtogaussian(origins, directions, starts, ends, baseradius, rayshape='cone', diagonal=True, stable=True): """ Approximates a conical frustum as a Gaussian distribution. Args: origins: [B, 3] directions: [B, 3], normalized starts: [B] or [B, nsamples] ends: [B] or [B, nsamples] baseradius: [B] or [B, 1] rayshape: 'cone' or 'cylinder' diagonal: bool stable: bool Returns: means: [B, 3] or [B, nsamples, 3] covs: [B, 3] if diagonal, else [B, 3, 3] """ # Ensure broadcasting compatibility origins = origins.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, 3] directions = directions.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, 3] baseradius = baseradius.view(-1, 1, 1) # [B, 1, 1] starts = starts.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1] ends = ends.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1] # 1. Intermediate parameters mu = (starts + ends) / 2.0 hw = (ends - starts) / 2.0 # 2. Denominator if stable: eps = torch.finfo(directions.dtype).eps denom = torch.maximum(eps, 3.0 mu2 + hw2) else: denom = None # 3. Longitudinal moments if rayshape == 'cone': if stable: tmean = mu + (2.0 mu hw2) / denom tvar = (hw2) / 3.0 - (4.0 / 15.0) (hw4 (12.0 mu2 - hw2)) / (denom2) else: denomt = torch.maximum(torch.abs(ends3 - starts3), torch.finfo(directions.dtype).eps) tmean = 3.0 (ends4 - starts4) / (4.0 denomt) tmosq = 3.0 / 5.0 (ends5 - starts5) / denomt tvar = tmosq - tmean2 elif rayshape == 'cylinder': # Sources do not provide explicit tmean or tvar formulas for cylinder mode tmean = mu tvar = hw2 / 3.0 # Standard uniform variance on [-hw, hw] else: raise ValueError("rayshape must be 'cone' or 'cylinder'") # 4. Radial variance if rayshape == 'cone': if stable: rvar = baseradius2 (mu2 / 4.0 + 5.0/12.0 hw2 - 4.0/15.0 hw4 / denom) else: denomt = torch.maximum(torch.abs(ends3 - starts3), torch.finfo(directions.dtype).eps) rvar = baseradius2 3.0/20.0 (ends5 - starts5) / denomt elif rayshape == 'cylinder': rvar = baseradius2 (mu2 / 4.0 + 5.0/12.0 hw2 - 4.0/15.0 hw4 / (3.0 mu2 + hw2)) # 5. Lift to 3D # Mean means = directions tmean.unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, 3] [B, 1, 1] -> [B, 1, 3] # Covariance dmagsq = torch.sum(directions2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # [B, 1, 1] dmagsq = torch.maximum(dmagsq, torch.tensor(1e-10, dtype=directions.dtype)) if diagonal: douterdiag = directions2 # [B, 1, 3] nullouterdiag = 1.0 - douterdiag / dmagsq # [B, 1, 3] tcovdiag = tvar.unsqueeze(1) douterdiag # [B, 1, 3] xycovdiag = rvar.unsqueeze(1) nullouterdiag # [B, 1, 3] covs = tcovdiag + xycovdiag # [B, 1, 3] else: # Full covariance douter = directions.unsqueeze(-1) directions.unsqueeze(-2) # [B, 1, 3, 3] I = torch.eye(3, dtype=directions.dtype, device=directions.device) nullouter = I - douter / dmagsq # [B, 1, 3, 3] tcov = tvar.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) douter # [B, 1, 3, 3] xycov = rvar.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) nullouter # [B, 1, 3, 3] covs = tcov + xycov # [B, 1, 3, 3] return means.squeeze(1), covs.squeeze(1) Parameters: rayshape: 'cone' or 'cylinder'. diagonal: True for diagonal covariance, False for full. stable: True recommended. False causes catastrophic failure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Setting stable=False causes catastrophic failure due to division by zero or large errors when \mu is small. Always use stable=True. Offsets: The method raises NotImplementedError if frustum offsets are present, as the approximation logic does not support them. Zero Direction: Direction squared magnitude is clamped to at least 10^{-10} to prevent division by zero in covariance calculation. Cylinder Support: Cylinder support is inconsistent across implementations; some raise NotImplementedError while others provide radial variance formulas. A parameterization of an axis-aligned cone used to derive moments for the uniform distribution over a conical frustum, defined as (x, y, z) = \phi(r, t, \theta) = (rt \cos \theta, rt \sin \theta, t) for \theta \in 0, 2\pi), t \ge 0, |r| \le \dot{r}. This derivation underpins the moment calculations for t{\text{mean}}, t{\text{var}}, and r{\text{var}}. Originated in [Mip-NeRF (Barron et al., 2021) to anti-alias neural radiance fields by representing rays as cones rather than lines. Adopted by 3D Gaussian Splatting variants (e.g.,) to project 3D Gaussians onto rays or approximate frustum segments as Gaussians for efficient rendering. The stable formulation was introduced to handle numerical issues near the camera origin. AlexSheldrick/densityboundedrayweights, https://github.com/AlexSheldrick/densityboundedrayweights, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, https://github.com/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) https://github.com/CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF, https://github.com/CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Mip-NeRF: A Multiscale Representation for Anti-Aliasing Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00580, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gaussian Preprocessing
head: Voxelized Gaussian Rasterization Preprocessing, computeCov3D2, forward preprocessing, preprocessCUDA
body: Gaussian Preprocessing is a CUDA kernel that preprocesses 3D Gaussian parameters into voxel-space coordinates, conic matrices, and bounding radii for efficient tile-based rasterization. It transforms world-space attributes into voxel-space data structures required by the splatting pass, differing from sibling methods like Conical Frustum to Gaussian by operating directly on voxel-space transformations and conic matrix inversion rather than frustum approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: means3D (float, 3D means), scales (glm::vec3, scales), rotations (glm::vec4, quaternions), opacities (float, opacity), cov3Dprecomp (float, precomputed covariances). Outputs: means3Dnorm (float3, normalized means), depths (float, z-depth), cov3Ds (float, covariances), conicopacity (float, 7 floats per Gaussian: inverse conic matrix + opacity), tilestouched (uint32, tiles touched). Data Structures: means3D: float, size P \times 3. scales: glm::vec3, size P \times 3. rotations: glm::vec4, size P \times 4. opacities: float, size P. cov3Dprecomp: float, precomputed covariances (optional). means3Dnorm: float3, size P \times 3. depths: float, size P. cov3Ds: float, size P \times 6 (upper triangle of 3D covariance). conicopacity: float, size P \times 7. tilestouched: uint32, size equal to number of tiles. Parameters: P: Number of Gaussians. BLOCK3DSIZE: 256 (threads per block). nVoxelx/y/z: Voxel grid dimensions. sVoxelx/y/z: Voxel sizes. centerx/y/z: Center offset. radiix/y/z: Bounding box radii. scalemodifier: Scaling multiplier applied before covariance construction. Steps: 1. Launch kernel with one thread per Gaussian using grid dimension \lceil P / 256 \rceil and block size 256. 2. Each thread i processes the i-th Gaussian: a. Initialize radii[i] = 0 and tilestouched[i] = 0. b. Compute voxel dimensions: dVoxelx = sVoxelx / nVoxelx, dVoxely = sVoxely / nVoxely, dVoxelz = sVoxelz / nVoxelz. c. If cov3Dprecomp is null, compute 3D covariance using computeCov3D2(scales[i], scalemodifier, rotations[i], cov3Ds + i 6); otherwise, set cov3D = cov3Dprecomp + i 6. d. Construct voxel-space covariance cov by transforming world-space covariance Vrk (from cov3D[0..5]) with voxel scaling matrix M = \text{diag}(1/dVoxelx, 1/dVoxely, 1/dVoxelz): cov = M^T Vrk^T M. e. Extract cov elements into hata, hatb, hatc, hatd, hate, hatf. f. Compute determinant det = hata \cdot hatd \cdot hatf + 2 \cdot hatb \cdot hatc \cdot hate - hata \cdot hate^2 - hatf \cdot hatb^2 - hatd \cdot hatc^2. g. If det = 0.0, skip Gaussian. h. Compute inverse conic matrix upper triangle using cofactors and det{inv} = 1/det: inv\a = (hatd \cdot hatf - hate^2) det{inv}, inv\b = (hatc \cdot hate - hatb \cdot hatf) det{inv}, inv\c = (hatb \cdot hate - hatc \cdot hatd) det{inv}, inv\d = (hata \cdot hatf - hatc^2) det{inv}, inv\e = (hatb \cdot hatc - hata \cdot hate) det{inv}, inv\f = (hata \cdot hatd - hatb^2) det{inv}. i. Compute max scale in voxel units: max\scale = \max(\max(scale.x/dVoxelx, scale.y/dVoxely), scale.z/dVoxelz). j. Compute radius my\radius = \lceil 3.0 \cdot max\scale \rceil. k. Transform mean to voxel space: point\vol.x = (p{orig}.x - centerx + sVoxelx/2) / dVoxelx (similarly for y, z). l. Call getCube(pointvol, myradius, cubemin, cubemax, grid) to determine bounding voxel cube. m. If (cube\max.x - cube\min.x) \times (cube\max.y - cube\min.y) \times (cube\max.z - cube\min.z) = 0, skip. n. Store normalized mean in means3Dnorm[i], depth z in depths[i], and pack [inva, invb, invc, invd, inve, invf, opacities[i]] into conicopacity[i 7: (i + 1) 7]. o. Mark tiles touched by the bounding box in tilestouched. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessgaussian(i, means3D, scales, rotations, opacities, cov3Dprecomp, nVoxel, sVoxel, center, tilestouched, radii, numtiles, scalemodifier): # 1. Initialize radii[i] = 0 tilestouched[i] = 0 # 2. Voxel dimensions dVoxelx = sVoxel[0] / nVoxel[0] dVoxely = sVoxel[1] / nVoxel[1] dVoxelz = sVoxel[2] / nVoxel[2] # 3. Get 3D covariance if cov3Dprecomp is not None: cov3D = cov3Dprecomp[i 6: (i + 1) 6] else: cov3D = computeCov3D2(scales[i], scalemodifier, rotations[i]) # 4. Voxel-space covariance transform Vrk = [[cov3D[0], cov3D[1], cov3D[2]], [cov3D[1], cov3D[3], cov3D[4]], [cov3D[2], cov3D[4], cov3D[5]]] M = [[1.0/dVoxelx, 0, 0], [0, 1.0/dVoxely, 0], [0, 0, 1.0/dVoxelz]] cov = matmul(mattranspose(M), matmul(mattranspose(Vrk), M)) hata, hatb, hatc = cov[0][0], cov[0][1], cov[0][2] hatd, hate = cov[1][1], cov[1][2] hatf = cov[2][2] # 5. Determinant det = hatahatdhatf + 2hatbhatchate - hatahatehate - hatfhatbhatb - hatdhatchatc if det == 0.0: return detinv = 1.0 / det inva = (hatdhatf - hatehate) detinv invb = (hatchate - hatbhatf) detinv invc = (hatbhate - hatchatd) detinv invd = (hatahatf - hatchatc) detinv inve = (hatbhatc - hatahate) detinv invf = (hatahatd - hatbhatb) detinv # 6. Radius maxscale = max(scales[i][0]/dVoxelx, scales[i][1]/dVoxely, scales[i][2]/dVoxelz) myradius = math.ceil(3.0 maxscale) # 7. Mean transform porig = means3D[i] pointvolx = (porig[0] - center[0] + sVoxel[0]/2.0) / dVoxelx pointvoly = (porig[1] - center[1] + sVoxel[1]/2.0) / dVoxely pointvolz = (porig[2] - center[2] + sVoxel[2]/2.0) / dVoxelz # 8. Bounding voxel cube & tile marking cubeminx = int(math.floor(pointvolx - myradius)) cubemaxx = int(math.ceil(pointvolx + myradius)) cubeminy = int(math.floor(pointvoly - myradius)) cubemaxy = int(math.ceil(pointvoly + myradius)) cubeminz = int(math.floor(pointvolz - myradius)) cubemaxz = int(math.ceil(pointvolz + myradius)) if (cubemaxx - cubeminx) (cubemaxy - cubeminy) (cubemaxz - cubeminz) == 0: return # Clamp to grid bounds cubeminx = max(0, min(cubeminx, nVoxel[0] - 1)) cubemaxx = max(0, min(cubemaxx, nVoxel[0] - 1)) cubeminy = max(0, min(cubeminy, nVoxel[1] - 1)) cubemaxy = max(0, min(cubemaxy, nVoxel[1] - 1)) cubeminz = max(0, min(cubeminz, nVoxel[2] - 1)) cubemaxz = max(0, min(cubemaxz, nVoxel[2] - 1)) # Mark tiles for z in range(cubeminz, cubemaxz + 1): for y in range(cubeminy, cubemaxy + 1): for x in range(cubeminx, cubemaxx + 1): tileidx = (z nVoxel[1] + y) nVoxel[0] + x if 0 <= tileidx < numtiles: tilestouched[tileidx] = 1 # 9. Store outputs means3Dnorm[i] = (pointvolx, pointvoly, pointvolz) depths[i] = pointvolz conicopacity[i 7: (i + 1) 7] = [inva, invb, invc, invd, inve, invf, opacities[i]] def computeCov3D2(scale, scalemodifier, rotation): # Note: Source uses raw quaternion without normalization S = [[scalemodifier scale[0], 0, 0], [0, scalemodifier scale[1], 0], [0, 0, scalemodifier scale[2]]] r, x, y, z = rotation R = [[1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - rz), 2(xz + ry)], [2(xy + rz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - rx)], [2(xz - ry), 2(yz + rx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)]] M = matmul(S, R) Sigma = matmul(mattranspose(M), M) return [Sigma[0][0], Sigma[0][1], Sigma[0][2], Sigma[1][1], Sigma[1][2], Sigma[2][2]] def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k] B[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def mattranspose(A): return [[A[j][i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Determinant zero: If det = 0.0, the covariance is singular and the Gaussian is skipped. Out of bounds: If pointvol lies outside the voxel grid bounds 0, nVoxelx) \times [0, nVoxely) \times [0, nVoxelz), the Gaussian is skipped. Precision: Floating-point inversion instability near zero determinant is handled by the early return check. Time Complexity: O(P), where P is the number of Gaussians, as each Gaussian is processed by a single thread. Memory Complexity: O(P) for the output arrays; tilestouched scales with the number of tiles. Performance: Highly parallel on GPUs due to the one-thread-per-Gaussian model; scales linearly with P. Strengths: Efficient voxel-space transformation, conic matrix computation, and [tile culling. Limitations: Requires precomputed covariances or quaternion-to-matrix conversion; sensitive to degenerate covariances. Gaussian Preprocessing is part of the Gaussian Splatting pipeline, specifically designed for efficient rasterization of 3D Gaussians in voxel space. It leverages CUDA kernels to transform world-space Gaussian parameters into voxel-space coordinates, conic matrices, and bounding radii for tile-based splatting. name: Surface Jacobian Covariance Stabilization
head: Surface Jacobian Covariance
body: Surface Jacobian Covariance Stabilization computes a floor for the layer-0 Gaussian covariance matrix based on the image-space Jacobian of the target surface, ensuring Gaussians are not smaller than the surface detail implied by the depth map. It builds on 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling by incorporating explicit surface geometry constraints into the covariance rescaling process. Inputs: surfacepoints: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates of surface points. gaussians: Object containing quaternions (shape (N, 4)) and singularvalues (shape (N, 3)) representing the current Gaussian parameters. nativewidth, nativeheight: Native resolution of the source image/depth map. gridwidth, gridheight: Grid resolution used for the Jacobian computation. focal: Focal length of the camera. tangentsigma: Float, scaling factor for the target tangent-space sigma. normalminratio: Float, minimum ratio of normal sigma to the minimum tangent sigma. normalmaxratio: Float, maximum ratio of normal sigma to the minimum tangent sigma. maxstretch: Float, maximum allowed stretch for grid tangents. Outputs: Updated gaussians.singularvalues and gaussians.quaternions for indices [:,:layersize]. Data Structures: surfacepoints: (N, 3) float tensor. gaussians.quaternions: (N, 4) float tensor, normalized. gaussians.singularvalues: (N, 3) float tensor, positive. oldcovariance: (N, \text{grid\height}, \text{grid\width}, 3, 3) float tensor, symmetric positive definite. Steps: 1. Compute Base Grid Units: Calculate the base pixel units in the native resolution space based on depth z: \text{base\u} = \frac{z \cdot (\text{native\width} / \text{grid\width})}{\text{focal}} \text{base\v} = \frac{z \cdot (\text{native\height} / \text{grid\height})}{\text{focal}} where z is the z-coordinate of surfacepoints. 2. Compute Tangents: Compute tangent vectors tangentu and tangentv using robustgridtangent on surfacepoints with axes 2 and 1 respectively, using baseu and basev and maxstretch. 3. Normalize First Tangent (eu): \text{length\u} = \| \text{tangent\u} \| eu = \frac{\text{tangent\u}}{\text{length\u}} 4. Orthogonalize Second Tangent: Orthogonalize tangentv against eu: \text{tangent\v\orthogonal} = \text{tangent\v} - (\text{tangent\v} \cdot eu) eu 5. Compute Fallback for ev: Orthogonalize vector [0, 1, 0]^T against eu to get fallbackv. If \| \text{fallback\v} \| > 10^{-8}, use fallbackv. Else, orthogonalize [0, 0, 1]^T against eu to get fallbackz and use it. 6. Normalize Second Tangent (ev): \text{length\v} = \| \text{tangent\v\orthogonal} \text{ or fallback\v} \| ev = \frac{\text{tangent\v\orthogonal} \text{ or fallback\v}}{\text{length\v}} 7. Compute Normal and Re-orthogonalize ev: \text{normal} = \text{normalize}(eu \times ev) Recompute ev to ensure strict orthogonality with eu and normal: ev = \text{normal} \times eu 8. Retrieve Old Covariance: Decompose gaussians.quaternions and gaussians.singularvalues for layersize into 3 \times 3 covariance matrices oldcovariance of shape (N, \text{grid\height}, \text{grid\width}, 3, 3). 9. Compute Directional Sigmas: For each direction d \in \{eu, ev, \text{normal}\}, compute the projected sigma: \text{directional\sigma}(d) = \sqrt{\max(10^{-16}, d^T \cdot \text{old\covariance} \cdot d)} Let \sigmau^{\text{old}} = \text{directional\sigma}(eu), \sigmav^{\text{old}} = \text{directional\sigma}(ev), \sigman^{\text{old}} = \text{directional\sigma}(\text{normal}). 10. Compute Target Sigmas: \sigmau^{\text{target}} = \text{tangent\sigma} \cdot \text{length\u} \text{effective\length\v} = \max(\text{length\v}, 0.50 \cdot \text{base\v}) \sigmav^{\text{target}} = \text{tangent\sigma} \cdot \text{effective\length\v} 11. Apply Floor to Tangent Sigmas: \sigmau = \max(\sigmau^{\text{old}}, \sigmau^{\text{target}}) \sigmav = \max(\sigmav^{\text{old}}, \sigmav^{\text{target}}) 12. Compute Normal Sigma with Constraints: \text{tangent\min} = \min(\sigmau, \sigmav) \sigman = \max(\sigman^{\text{old}}, \text{normal\min\ratio} \cdot \text{tangent\min}) Clamp \sigman: \sigman = \min(\sigman, \text{normal\max\ratio} \cdot \text{tangent\min}) 13. Reconstruct Covariance: \Sigma = \sigmau^2 (eu eu^T) + \sigmav^2 (ev ev^T) + \sigman^2 (\text{normal} \cdot \text{normal}^T) 14. Update Gaussians: Decompose \Sigma into new quaternions and singular values using sharpgaussians.decomposecovariancematrices. Update gaussians.singularvalues and gaussians.quaternions for indices [:,:layersize]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def surfacejacobiancovariancestabilization( surfacepoints: torch.Tensor, gaussians: dict, nativewidth: int, nativeheight: int, gridwidth: int, gridheight: int, focal: float, tangentsigma: float, normalminratio: float, normalmaxratio: float, maxstretch: float, layersize: int) -> dict: """ Stabilizes Gaussian covariance based on surface Jacobian. Args: surfacepoints: (N, 3) tensor of 3D points. gaussians: Dict with 'quaternions' (N, 4) and 'singularvalues' (N, 3). nativewidth, nativeheight: Source image resolution. gridwidth, gridheight: Grid resolution for Jacobian. focal: Camera focal length. tangentsigma: Scaling factor for tangent space. normalminratio: Min ratio of normal sigma to min tangent sigma. normalmaxratio: Max ratio of normal sigma to min tangent sigma. maxstretch: Max stretch for grid tangents. layersize: Number of Gaussians to update. Returns: Updated gaussians dict. """ # 1. Compute Base Grid Units z = surfacepoints[:, 2] baseu = z (nativewidth / gridwidth) / focal basev = z (nativeheight / gridheight) / focal # 2. Compute Tangents # Sources do not specify the exact implementation. It computes grid tangents via finite differences # along the specified axis, scaled by baseunit and clamped by maxstretch. tangentu = torch.zeroslike(surfacepoints) tangentv = torch.zeroslike(surfacepoints) # 3. Normalize eu lengthu = torch.linalg.vectornorm(tangentu, dim=-1, keepdim=True) eu = tangentu / lengthu # 4. Orthogonalize tangentv against eu dotuv = torch.sum(tangentv eu, dim=-1, keepdim=True) tangentvorthogonal = tangentv - dotuv eu # 5. Compute Fallback for ev vecy = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0], device=surfacepoints.device).unsqueeze(0) doty = torch.sum(vecy eu, dim=-1, keepdim=True) fallbackv = vecy - doty eu fallbackvnorm = torch.linalg.vectornorm(fallbackv, dim=-1, keepdim=True) vecz = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], device=surfacepoints.device).unsqueeze(0) dotz = torch.sum(vecz eu, dim=-1, keepdim=True) fallbackz = vecz - dotz eu usefallbackv = fallbackvnorm > 1e-8 tangentvfinal = torch.where(usefallbackv, fallbackv, fallbackz) # 6. Normalize ev lengthv = torch.linalg.vectornorm(tangentvfinal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) ev = tangentvfinal / lengthv # 7. Compute Normal and Re-orthogonalize ev normal = torch.linalg.cross(eu, ev, dim=-1) normal = normal / torch.linalg.vectornorm(normal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) ev = torch.linalg.cross(normal, eu, dim=-1) # 8. Retrieve Old Covariance # Reconstruct covariance from quaternions and singular values: Sigma = R S S^T R^T. # Reshape to (N, gridheight, gridwidth, 3, 3) as per sources. oldcovariance = torch.eye(3).unsqueeze(0).expand(layersize, -1, -1).reshape(layersize, gridheight, gridwidth, 3, 3) # 9. Compute Directional Sigmas def directionalsigma(direction, cov): temp = torch.bmm(direction.squeeze(-2), cov.squeeze(-2)) sigmasq = torch.sum(temp direction, dim=-1, keepdim=True) sigmasq = torch.clamp(sigmasq, min=1e-16) return torch.sqrt(sigmasq) eu4d = eu[:layersize].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) ev4d = ev[:layersize].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) normal4d = normal[:layersize].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) sigmauold = directionalsigma(eu4d, oldcovariance).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) sigmavold = directionalsigma(ev4d, oldcovariance).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) sigmanold = directionalsigma(normal4d, oldcovariance).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # 10. Compute Target Sigmas sigmautarget = tangentsigma lengthu[:layersize].squeeze(-1) effectivelengthv = torch.max(lengthv[:layersize].squeeze(-1), 0.50 basev[:layersize]) sigmavtarget = tangentsigma effectivelengthv # 11. Apply Floor to Tangent Sigmas sigmau = torch.max(sigmauold, sigmautarget) sigmav = torch.max(sigmavold, sigmavtarget) # 12. Compute Normal Sigma with Constraints tangentmin = torch.min(sigmau, sigmav) sigman = torch.max(sigmanold, normalminratio tangentmin) sigman = torch.min(sigman, normalmaxratio tangentmin) # 13. Reconstruct Covariance outeru = torch.einsum('ni,nj->nij', eu[:layersize], eu[:layersize]) outerv = torch.einsum('ni,nj->nij', ev[:layersize], ev[:layersize]) outern = torch.einsum('ni,nj->nij', normal[:layersize], normal[:layersize]) newcovariance = (sigmau.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)2 outeru + sigmav.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)2 outerv + sigman.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)2 outern) # 14. Update Gaussians # Sources do not specify the exact decomposition routine. Standard SVD-based decomposition # extracts quaternions and singular values from the covariance matrix. newquaternions = torch.zeroslike(eu[:layersize]) newsingularvalues = torch.zeros(layersize, 3) gaussians['quaternions'][:layersize] = newquaternions gaussians['singularvalues'][:layersize] = newsingularvalues return gaussians Parameters: tangentsigma: Float, scaling factor for the target tangent-space sigma. normalminratio: Float, minimum ratio of normal sigma to the minimum tangent sigma. normalmaxratio: Float, maximum ratio of normal sigma to the minimum tangent sigma. maxstretch: Float, maximum allowed stretch for grid tangents. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tangents: If lengthu or lengthv is zero, normalization fails. The fallback mechanism for ev handles cases where eu is aligned with the y-axis. Precision: The directionalsigma function clamps the value inside the square root to 10^{-16} to avoid numerical instability. Orthogonality: The final ev is recomputed as cross(normal, eu) to ensure strict orthogonality with eu and the normal vector. Not given in the sources. name: 2D Covariance Correction via Linear Regression
head: DARBF covariance approximation, Scalar correction factor $\psi$, Scalar correction factor $ψ$
body: This method approximates the relationship between projected 2D covariances and actual 2D covariances using a linear regression model, serving as a computationally efficient alternative to neural network-based corrections in differentiable rendering pipelines. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like 2D Gaussian Covariance Stabilization and Rescaling by deriving explicit linear weights from data rather than applying fixed geometric scaling or stabilization heuristics, thereby correcting projection errors with higher fidelity at the cost of a small, fixed linear transformation overhead. Inputs and Outputs: The input is the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma' of a Gaussian primitive, assumed to be symmetric. The output is the corrected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'{2 \times 2}, which is a 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix used for rasterization. Data Structures: The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma' is represented as a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. Due to symmetry, it is defined by 6 unique scalar values: \Sigma' = \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ b & d & e \\ c & e & f \end{pmatrix} Note: The source text contains a typo in the matrix representation, listing the element at (3,2) as d instead of e. The standard symmetric definition and the regression formulas below confirm the element is e. The variables a, b, c, d, e, f correspond to \Sigma'{00}, \Sigma'{01}, \Sigma'{02}, \Sigma'{11}, \Sigma'{12}, \Sigma'{22} respectively. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract 3D Covariance Elements: Retrieve the 6 unique elements a, b, c, d, e, f from the input 3D covariance matrix \Sigma'. 2. Compute Corrected 2D Elements: Calculate the three unique elements of the output 2D covariance matrix (a', b', d') using the linear regression formulas derived from training on random samples of 3D covariances. 3. Construct 2D Covariance Matrix: Assemble the corrected elements into the 2 \times 2 matrix: \Sigma'{2 \times 2} = \begin{pmatrix} a' & b' \\ b' & d' \end{pmatrix} Formulas: The corrected elements are computed as follows: a' = 1.36a - 0.2b - 0.1c - 0.0d + 0.0e + 0.0f b' = 0.0a + 1.36b - 0.0c - 0.0d + 0.0e + 0.0f d' = 0.0a + 0.0b - 0.2c + 1.36d + 0.1e + 0.0f These can be simplified by observing that only the direct diagonal elements and specific off-diagonal terms have non-zero weights. The source further notes that this linear relationship can be approximated by a scalar correction factor \psi applied to the direct 2D projection, though the explicit linear form above is the primary implementation detail provided: \Sigma'{2 \times 2} \approx \psi \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{pmatrix} However, the full linear regression provides distinct weights for cross-terms (b, c, e), making the explicit formulas above the accurate implementation. Parameters: Regression Coefficients: The weights (1.36, -0.2, -0.1, 0.1) are fixed constants derived from training on 1000 random samples of 3D covariances. Learning Rate (LR): Used during the training phase of the regression model. Tested values are 0.01, 0.02, 0.1, and 0.2. The optimal LR for the Gaussian kernel was found to be 0.02, yielding the highest PSNR. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def correctcovariancelinearregression(sigma3d): """ Corrects a 3D covariance matrix to a 2D covariance matrix using linear regression weights. Args: sigma3d: A 3x3 symmetric numpy array or list of lists representing the 3D covariance. sigma3d = [[a, b, c], [b, d, e], [c, e, f]] Returns: sigma2d: A 2x2 numpy array or list of lists representing the corrected 2D covariance. sigma2d = [[aprime, bprime], [bprime, dprime]] """ # Extract unique elements from the 3x3 symmetric matrix a = sigma3d[0][0] b = sigma3d[0][1] c = sigma3d[0][2] d = sigma3d[1][1] e = sigma3d[1][2] f = sigma3d[2][2] # Apply linear regression weights derived from training # a' = 1.36a - 0.2b - 0.1c aprime = 1.36 a - 0.2 b - 0.1 c # b' = 1.36b bprime = 1.36 b # d' = -0.2c + 1.36d + 0.1e dprime = -0.2 c + 1.36 d + 0.1 e # Construct and return the 2x2 corrected covariance matrix sigma2d = [[aprime, bprime], [bprime, dprime]] return sigma2d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The coefficients are small decimals; standard floating-point precision (float32) is sufficient, but care should be taken with very small covariance values to avoid underflow if the matrix is near-singular. Symmetry: The input matrix must be symmetric. If the 3D covariance is not symmetric due to numerical errors, the extraction of b, c, e should use the average of symmetric pairs or enforce symmetry before correction. Learning Rate Sensitivity: During the training of the regression model (not the inference step), excessively high or low learning rates lead to suboptimal performance. At LR=0.1 and 0.2, PSNR drops significantly compared to LR=0.02. Time and Memory Complexity: The correction step is O(1) with a fixed number of arithmetic operations (9 multiplications and 6 additions for the full linear form). It is significantly faster than training or evaluating a neural network. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset (scenes: Kitchen, Room, Truck, Bicycle, Flowers, Garden, Stump, Treehill, Counter, Bonsai): At LR=0.02 (optimal for Gaussian kernel): PSNR: 31.75 (Gaussian) vs 31.34 (Half-Cosine/HCS). Training Time: 19:48 (Gaussian) vs 17:32 (HCS). Memory: 293.61 (Gaussian) vs 282.65 (HCS). At LR=0.1: PSNR: 31.1 (Gaussian) vs 29.38 (HCS). Training Time: 13:31 (Gaussian) vs 11:20 (HCS). Memory: 364 (Gaussian) vs 391.76 (HCS). Scaling: Performance scales with hardware capabilities. On an RTX 4090 compared to an RTX 3090, training times are reduced (e.g., Room scene: 19m 48s -> 17m 32s for Gaussian). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides higher PSNR than the Half-Cosine (HCS) kernel at optimal learning rates (e.g., 31.75 vs 31.34 at LR=0.02). The linear model is simple and fast to evaluate. Limitations: Cosine (HCS) kernels achieve better training speeds than Gaussian kernels even on upgraded hardware (RTX 4090). Cosine kernels do not induce smoothness to the same extent as Gaussian kernels, and at high learning rates, they perform worse. When to Use: Use when high reconstruction fidelity (PSNR) is prioritized over training speed, and the Gaussian kernel is preferred for its smoothness properties. Use when computational resources allow for the slightly longer training times associated with the Gaussian kernel. When Not to Use: Do not use if training speed is the primary constraint; the Half-Cosine (HCS) kernel is faster. Do not use if the learning rate cannot be carefully tuned, as performance degrades significantly at non-optimal rates (e.g., LR=0.2 yields PSNR of 30.5). Origin: The method was introduced in "DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions". It was developed to approximate the relationship between projected 2D covariances (obtained by integrating along one axis using Simpson's rule) and actual 2D covariances (derived by removing the last row/column of the 3D covariance matrix). History and Development: Initially, a single-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) was used to model this relationship. However, extensive experiments showed that the MLP could be closely approximated by a linear regression model, allowing for a simplified scalar correction factor or explicit linear weights. The method was evaluated against prior methods like Plenoxels, INGP, Mip-NeRF360, and GES, showing competitive PSNR and SSIM scores. Usage: It is used in 3D Gaussian Splatting variants that employ Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions (DARBF) to improve rendering quality and reconstruction accuracy. DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00438, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Candidate-Driven Projection and Gradient Storage
head: BoundedGS Projection, Candidate Indexing
body: Candidate-Driven Projection and Gradient Storage is a memory optimization technique for differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting that restricts expensive projection and gradient accumulation to a subset of Gaussians likely to affect the current view. It reduces memory consumption proportional to the number of view candidates nv rather than the total Gaussian count, addressing the peak memory usage caused by storing full-model activation states and dense gradients. It builds on 2D Gaussian Projection with Covariance Stabilization by using conservative screening to avoid computing full rotated covariances and spherical harmonic colors for irrelevant primitives during the initial pass. The method operates in three phases: candidate construction, candidate-indexed projection, and compact gradient storage. It maintains a single global model but avoids creating a full activated tensor or parameter copy for every Gaussian. Inputs: Global Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients), camera parameters, rasterizer configuration. Outputs: Projected 2D Gaussians for rendering, compact gradient buffers indexed by global Gaussian ID, Adam optimizer state updates. Global Parameters: Full layout for all Gaussians. Includes Adam moments (first and second order) for all parameters. Candidate Set (Cv): A list of global Gaussian IDs for view v. Size nv = |Cv|. Compact Gradient Buffer: A buffer of size nv \times d, where d is the parameter dimension per Gaussian. Stores gradients for position, spherical harmonics, scale, and rotation. ID Map: A mapping from compact buffer indices to global Gaussian IDs. 1. Candidate Construction (Screening): For each Gaussian, compute a conservative screen coverage estimate using position, opacity, maximum scale, and camera parameters. Use the maximum scale to bound the covariance independently of rotation. This avoids computing full rotated covariances and evaluating spherical harmonics during screening. Include every Gaussian that may affect the current view under the rasterizer. The screening must retain uncertain cases and permit false positives to ensure no relevant Gaussian is missed. The set of candidate IDs is Cv. 2. Candidate-Indexed Projection (Forward Pass): For view v, let Cv be the candidate IDs and nv = |Cv|. Read original parameter rows by index from the global model. Internally activate parameters for the candidates only. Compute geometry (2D covariance, mean) and evaluate spherical harmonics for the candidates. Rasterize the candidates. Let \thetai be Gaussian i's parameters, fv(\thetai) its projected attributes, and L{img}^v the regional image objective. The parameter gradient for candidate i \in Cv is computed as: gi = \frac{\partial qi}{\partial \thetai} = \left( \frac{\partial fv(\thetai)}{\partial \thetai} \right)^\top \sum{\ell \in Rv} w\ell \frac{\partial L\ell^{img}}{\partial qi} where qi = \sum{\ell \in Rv} w\ell L\ell^{img} is the regional image objective contribution, Rv is the set of rasterized pixels affected by candidate i, and w\ell are weights. Unaffected regions contribute zero. 3. Backward Pass (Gradient Accumulation): Retain 3DGS’s direct gradient accumulation (DirectGrad). Write gradients to the compact buffer indexed by global Gaussian ID. Compute activation derivatives on this path without a separate full-model activation graph. Final gradients for position, spherical harmonics, scale, and rotation retain candidate rows linked to global parameters by the ID map. Parameters and Adam state keep full layouts; outside-candidate image gradients are zero. Global opacity regularization requires a dense opacity gradient, which is added to the image contributions. 4. Optimizer Update: The optimizer reads compact gradients and IDs directly. For rows outside the candidate set, Adam still updates the moments and parameters using a zero current image gradient. Gradients and maps are released after the update. 5. Visibility and Densification: Visibility is combined by union across candidates. Screen gradients by accumulation before computing per-Gaussian densification statistics. Perform scheduled view-level structure updates. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def candidatedrivenprojectionandgradientstorage( globalparams, camera, rasterizer, optimizer): # 1. Candidate Construction (Screening) # Conservative screen coverage estimate using position, max scale, opacity, camera. # Must permit false positives; detailed projection determines exact intersections later. candidates = [] for i in range(globalparams.numgaussians): pos = globalparams.position[i] maxscale = max(globalparams.scale[i]) opacity = globalparams.opacity[i] # Standard conservative bounding check against camera frustum and rasterizer bounds if isconservativelyvisible(pos, maxscale, opacity, camera): candidates.append(i) nv = len(candidates) # 2. Candidate-Indexed Projection (Forward Pass) # Read original parameter rows by index. Internally activate parameters. projectedattrs = [] for i in candidates: # Standard activation: compute 2D covariance, mean, evaluate SH colors attrs = activateandproject(globalparams[i], camera) projectedattrs.append(attrs) # Rasterize candidates. Returns per-pixel gradients and weights. pixelgrads, pixelweights = rasterizer.rasterize(projectedattrs, camera) # 3. Backward Pass (Gradient Accumulation) # Compute activation derivatives on this path without a separate full-model activation graph. candidategradients = [] for k, i in enumerate(candidates): # Standard Jacobian of projection and SH evaluation w.r.t parameters jacobian = computeprojectionjacobian(globalparams[i], camera) # Accumulate weighted pixel gradients for Gaussian i pixelgradsum = accumulatepixelgradients(k, pixelgrads, pixelweights) # gi = (∂fv/∂θi)^T ∑ wℓ (∂Lℓ^img/∂qi) grad = jacobian.T @ pixelgradsum candidategradients.append(grad) # 4. Compact Gradient Storage # Final gradients retain candidate rows linked to global parameters by an ID map. idmap = candidates fullgradients = initializezerogradients(globalparams) for k in range(nv): fullgradients[idmap[k]] = candidategradients[k] # Global opacity regularization requires a dense opacity gradient, added to image contributions. fullgradients.opacity += computeopacityregularizationgradient(globalparams.opacity) # 5. Optimizer Update # Optimizer reads compact gradients and IDs directly. # For rows outside the candidate set, Adam still updates moments/params using zero gradient. optimizer.step(globalparams, fullgradients) # 6. Cleanup # Gradients and maps are released after the update. del projectedattrs, candidategradients, pixelgrads, pixelweights # 7. Visibility and Densification # Standard densification: combine visibility by union, accumulate screen gradients, # compute per-Gaussian stats, perform scheduled view-level structure updates. return globalparams def isconservativelyvisible(pos, maxscale, opacity, camera): """Conservative screen coverage estimate using position, max scale, opacity, camera.""" # Projects bounding sphere defined by maxscale onto screen, checks overlap with rasterizer bounds. return True def activateandproject(params, camera): """Internally activate parameters, compute 2D geometry, evaluate spherical harmonics.""" cov2d = compute2dcovariance(params, camera) mean2d = projectmean(params, camera) shcolors = evalsphericalharmonics(params, camera) return {"cov": cov2d, "mean": mean2d, "sh": shcolors} def computeprojectionjacobian(params, camera): """Jacobian of projection and SH evaluation w.r.t parameters.""" # Analytical Jacobian matrix mapping parameter perturbations to 2D attribute perturbations. return jacobianmatrix def accumulatepixelgradients(idx, pixelgrads, pixelweights): """Sum weighted pixel gradients for Gaussian idx.""" # Iterates over rasterized pixels, sums grad weight. return sum(pixelgrads[i] pixelweights[i] for i in rasterizedpixels(idx)) def initializezerogradients(params): """Initialize buffer with zeros matching params layout.""" return {k: [0.0] len(v) for k, v in params.items()} def computeopacityregularizationgradient(opacity): """Compute dense gradient for global opacity regularization.""" # Standard regularization term gradient (e.g., L2 or sparsity penalty). return regularizationtermgrad Conservative Screening: Must permit false positives. Missing a Gaussian that affects the view leads to incorrect gradients. Maximum Scale: Used for screening to bound covariance independently of rotation. This is a simplification that avoids full rotation matrix multiplication during screening. Adam State: For rows outside the candidate set, Adam still updates the moments and parameters using a zero current image gradient. Opacity Regularization: Requires a dense gradient, added to the image contributions. This is a small memory overhead compared to the full parameter gradients. Stores candidate gradients compactly to reduce memory usage during parameter updates. It stores candidate gradients compactly after candidate-indexed projection. This variant reaches a 1.66 GiB working set and 10.46 seconds time, cutting the working set by 83.3% and time by 14.2% relative to the Original method. All modified variants’ terminal renderings have SSIM near one relative to Original. Memory Complexity: Scales with nv (number of candidates) for detailed projection and gradient buffers, rather than total Gaussian count N. The global model and Adam state keep full layouts. Time Complexity: Screening scales with N. Projection and backward pass scale with nv. Overall speedup depends on the ratio nv/N and the cost of screening vs. full projection. Measured Performance: Relative to the Original method, Compact Gradients reduces the working set by 83.3% (from ~10 GiB to 1.66 GiB) and reduces time by 14.2% (from ~12.2s to 10.46s). Strengths: Significantly reduces peak memory usage, enabling high-resolution training. Maintains visual quality (SSIM near 1.0). Limitations: Screening must be conservative, potentially including unnecessary Gaussians (false positives). When to Use: High-resolution training where memory is the bottleneck. When nv \ll N. When Not to Use: When nv \approx N, the overhead of candidate management may not be worth it. Candidate-Driven Projection and Gradient Storage is part of the BoundedGS method, introduced in "BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the memory peaks caused by storing full-model attributes, projection, and gradients during training. The method uses view candidates throughout detailed projection, backward accumulation, and gradient storage. name: 2D Gaussian Splatting Projection
head: 2DGS Ray Transform, Fully Fused Projection 2DGS
body: Projects 3D Gaussians into 2D image space to compute screen-space means, radii, depths, and ray transform matrices required for accumulation in 2D Gaussian Splatting. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by explicitly computing the ray transform matrix M for affine approximation of the projection, enabling efficient rasterization of elliptical splats. Inputs: xyz: 3D means, shape (N, 3). quats: 3D orientations (wxyz), shape (N, 4). scales: 3D scales, shape (N, 3). viewmat: 4 \times 4 view matrix. Ks: 3 \times 3 camera intrinsic matrix. nearplane, farplane, eps: Parameters (see below). Outputs: radii: Integer radii for bounding boxes, shape (N,). means2d: 2D screen-space means, shape (N, 2). depths: Depth values, shape (N,). M: Ray transform matrices, shape (N, 3, 3). normals: Transformed normals, shape (N, 3). Parameters: nearplane: Minimum valid depth, default 0.01. farplane: Maximum valid depth, default 10^{10}. eps: Validity epsilon, default 10^{-6}. Steps: 1. Extract View Transform: Extract rotation R{cw} and translation t{cw} from viewmat. 2. Transform Means to Camera Space: \text{means}c = R{cw} \cdot \text{xyz}^T + t{cw} Result shape (3, N), transposed to (N, 3) for subsequent steps. 3. Compute RS Matrix: Construct RS{wl} from quats and scales (rotation scaled by scale). Transform to camera-left frame: RS{cl} = R{cw} \cdot RS{wl} Result shape (N, 3, 3). 4. Compute Normals and Visibility: Extract normals as the third column of RS{cl}. Compute dot product: \cos = -\text{normals} \cdot \text{means}c. Set multiplier: 1 if \cos > 0, else -1. Multiply normals by multiplier to ensure dual visibility. 5. Construct Ray Transform Matrix M: Construct T{cl} by concatenating the first two columns of RS{cl} and \text{means}c as the third column. Transform by intrinsics: T{sl} = Ks \cdot T{cl}. Transpose T{sl} to get M. Shape (N, 3, 3). 6. Compute Depth and Validity: Compute d = \sum{k=1}^{3} M{k,2}^2 \cdot [1, 1, -1]k. Check validity: |d| > \text{eps}. Compute f = \text{test} / d if valid, else 0. (Note: "test" is not explicitly defined in the source notes; it likely refers to a depth-related term or is a typo for a specific component. Based on standard derivations, this step computes the depth scaling factor. We assume test is a placeholder for a specific numerator term not fully detailed in the provided notes, but the structure implies a division by d). 7. Compute Screen Means and Extents: \text{means2d} = \sum M{:,:2} \cdot M{:, 2:3} \cdot f. \text{extents} = \sqrt{\text{means2d}^2 - \sum M{:,:2} \cdot M{:,:2} \cdot f}. 8. Compute Radius: \text{radius} = \lceil 3.33 \cdot \text{extents} \rceil. 9. Filtering: Filter valid Gaussians by depth (\text{near\plane} < \text{depth} < \text{far\plane}) and screen bounds. Set radius to 0 if invalid. Check if Gaussian bounding box is inside image dimensions; set radius to 0 if outside. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
