name: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W)
head: GS-W, Intrinsic and Dynamic Appearance Fusion
body: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) is a novel view synthesis method for unconstrained image collections that explicitly separates scene appearance into intrinsic material properties and dynamic environmental factors (such as illumination and weather) per 3D Gaussian point. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeRF-based methods by avoiding global latent embeddings, which allows it to capture local high-frequency changes without blurring intrinsic textures with dynamic variations. The method employs adaptive sampling from image features and 2D visibility maps to mitigate transient occlusions and photometric variations. Inputs: A set of unconstrained 2D images with known camera poses (extrinsics and intrinsics). Outputs: A rendered image from a novel viewpoint, and implicitly, the optimized 3D Gaussian scene representation. The scene is represented as a collection of M 3D Gaussian points GP. Each Gaussian point i stores the following attributes: 1. Position Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: The center of the Gaussian. 2. Covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Modeled via a scaling matrix S and rotation matrix R (stored as quaternion q) to ensure positive semi-definiteness during optimization. \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = R S S^T R^T. 3. Intrinsic Appearance Feature s{f}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d: A learnable vector representing the static material properties of the point. 4. Dynamic Appearance Feature d{f}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d: A feature vector sampled from image features, representing dynamic environmental factors. 5. Opacity \alphai: Controls transparency. 6. View-dependent Color: Derived from the fused appearance feature and view direction via an MLP. 1. Projection: Each 3D Gaussian i is projected onto the 2D image plane. The 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i is transformed into the 2D screen space covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i using the affine approximation of the projective transformation J and the view matrix W: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i = J W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i W^T J^T The 2D Gaussian function is defined as: G(x - X, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-X)^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(x-X)} where x is a point in space (or pixel coordinates) and X is the Gaussian center. 2. Sorting: Gaussian points are sorted by depth for each tile on the image plane. The image plane is divided into a grid of 16 \times 16 tiles. 3. Alpha Blending: For each pixel px', the color C(px') is aggregated from the sorted Gaussian points GP{px'} using alpha blending: \sigmai = G(px' - Xi, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'i) C(px') = \sum{i \in GP{px'}} ci \sigmai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj) where ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian point. The core innovation of GS-W is the separation and fusion of appearance features. 1. Feature Extraction: Image features are extracted from a reference image using a U-Net model. These features are reshaped into K feature maps and one projection feature map. 2. Dynamic Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian point GPi, dynamic appearance features d{f}^i are sampled from the extracted feature maps using an adaptive sampling strategy. This strategy allows each point to focus on local and detailed information more effectively. 3. Fusion: The intrinsic appearance feature s{f}^i (learnable per point) and the sampled dynamic appearance feature d{f}^i are fused with the position Xi using a fusion network Mf. The network Mf is composed of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a{f}^i = Mf(s{f}^i, d{f}^i, Xi) where a{f}^i is the holistic appearance feature. 4. Color Decoding: The fused appearance feature a{f}^i and the view direction \phi are decoded by another MLP Mc to obtain the final color ci of the Gaussian point: ci = Mc(a{f}^i, \phi) 1. Initialization: 3D Gaussian points GP are initialized with positions X extracted from a point cloud generated via Structure-from-Motion (SfM) from the input image set. 2. Loss Calculation: The loss is computed between the rendered image Ir and the ground truth reference image I{gt}. To mitigate the impact of transient occluders (e.g., moving people, vehicles), a 2D visibility map VM \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times H \times W} is employed. This map is obtained from a U-Net model and facilitates segmentation between transient and static objects. The loss is weighted by this visibility map. 3. Optimization: All Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, intrinsic features sf^i) are jointly optimized. The method employs point growth and pruning strategies based on gradients and opacity to manage the number of Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class Gaussian: def init(self, pos, cov, opacity, intrinsicfeat): self.pos = pos # (3,) self.cov = cov # (3, 3) self.opacity = opacity # scalar self.intrinsicfeat = intrinsicfeat # (d,) self.dynamicfeat = None # (d,) self.color = None # (3,) def initializegaussians(pointcloud): """Create Gaussian objects from SfM point cloud.""" gaussians = [] for p in pointcloud: gaussians.append(Gaussian( pos=np.array(p[:3]), cov=np.eye(3), opacity=1.0, intrinsicfeat=np.zeros(64))) return gaussians def learnablevector(dim=64): """Return a learnable parameter vector.""" return np.zeros(dim) def reshapefeatures(imgfeatures, K=4): """Split extracted features into K maps and 1 projection map.""" # imgfeatures shape: (H, W, C) # Reshape into K spatial feature maps and 1 projection map return np.split(imgfeatures, K + 1, axis=-1) def adaptivesample(featuremaps, pos): """Sample dynamic features adaptively based on Gaussian position.""" # Standard bilinear/trilinear sampling from feature maps # Returns dynamic appearance feature vector return np.mean(featuremaps, axis=(0, 1)) # Placeholder for adaptive sampling logic def fusionnetwork(intrinsic, dynamic, pos): """Two-MLP fusion network Mf.""" # Concatenate and pass through two MLP layers combined = np.concatenate([intrinsic, dynamic, pos]) return np.tanh(combined) # Simplified MLP forward pass def colornetwork(holistic, viewdir): """MLP Mc for color decoding.""" combined = np.concatenate([holistic, viewdir]) return np.tanh(combined) # Simplified MLP forward pass def projectcovariance(cov, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """Transform 3D covariance to 2D screen space using affine approximation.""" # J: affine approximation of projective transformation # W: view matrix # Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T return projmatrix @ viewmatrix @ cov @ viewmatrix.T @ projmatrix.T def projectpoint(pos, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """Project 3D point to 2D pixel coordinates.""" homogenous = np.append(pos, 1.0) clip = projmatrix @ viewmatrix @ homogenous return clip[:2] / clip[2] def normalize(vec): return vec / (np.linalg.norm(vec) + 1e-8) def tilerasterize(projectedgaussians, width, height): """Tile-based alpha blending rasterizer.""" image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Group by 16x16 tiles tilesize = 16 for ty in range(0, height, tilesize): for tx in range(0, width, tilesize): tilegaussians = [g for g in projectedgaussians if tx <= g['pos'][0] < tx + tilesize and ty <= g['pos'][1] < ty + tilesize] tilegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['depth']) for px in range(tx, min(tx + tilesize, width)): for py in range(ty, min(ty + tilesize, height)): accumalpha = 0.0 color = np.zeros(3) for g in tilegaussians: sigma = math.exp(-0.5 (g['pos'] - np.array([px, py])).T @ np.linalg.inv(g['cov']) @ (g['pos'] - np.array([px, py]))) sigma = min(sigma, 0.99) color += g['color'] sigma (1 - accumalpha) accumalpha += sigma (1 - accumalpha) image[py, px] = color return image def weightedmseloss(rendered, groundtruth, visibilitymap): """Compute loss weighted by visibility map.""" return np.mean((rendered - groundtruth) 2 visibilitymap) def pruneandgrowgaussians(gaussians, gradients, opacitythreshold): """Manage Gaussian count based on gradients and opacity.""" # Prune low opacity and high gradient Gaussians gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g.opacity > opacitythreshold] # Grow new Gaussians in high-gradient regions (standard 3DGS strategy) return gaussians def gswrender(referenceimages, cameraposes, initialpointcloud): """Main pipeline for Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W).""" gaussians = initializegaussians(initialpointcloud) # Initialize learnable intrinsic appearance features for each Gaussian for g in gaussians: g.intrinsicfeat = learnablevector() # Initialize networks fusionnet = fusionnetwork colornet = colornetwork featureextractor = lambda img: np.random.rand(img.shape[0], img.shape[1], 64) # U-Net placeholder numepochs = 1000 imagewidth, imageheight = 512, 512 for epoch in range(numepochs): for refimg, campose in zip(referenceimages, cameraposes): # A. Feature Extraction imgfeatures = featureextractor(refimg) featuremaps = reshapefeatures(imgfeatures) visibilitymap = np.ones((imageheight, imagewidth)) # U-Net visibility map placeholder # B. Dynamic Feature Sampling for g in gaussians: g.dynamicfeat = adaptivesample(featuremaps, g.pos) # C. Appearance Fusion and Color Prediction for g in gaussians: holisticfeat = fusionnet(g.intrinsicfeat, g.dynamicfeat, g.pos) viewdirection = normalize(campose.cameracenter - g.pos) g.color = colornet(holisticfeat, viewdirection) # D. Rasterization projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.cov, campose.viewmatrix, campose.projmatrix) projectedgaussians.append({ 'position': projectpoint(g.pos, campose.viewmatrix, campose.projmatrix), 'covariance': sigma2d, 'color': g.color, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'depth': g.pos[2] }) projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) renderedimage = tilerasterize(projectedgaussians, imagewidth, imageheight) # E. Loss Computation loss = weightedmseloss(renderedimage, refimg, visibilitymap) # F. Optimization Step # loss.backward() and optimizer.step() would follow in a deep learning framework pass # G. Point Management gaussians = pruneandgrowgaussians(gaussians, np.zeroslike(gaussians[0].pos), 0.01) return gaussians Transient Occluders: Without the 2D visibility map, moving objects (people, cars) cause artifacts like floating points or ghosting because the model attempts to reconstruct their geometry and appearance as static. Dynamic Variations: Failing to separate intrinsic and dynamic features leads to blurring of material textures when lighting or weather changes, as the model conflates static properties with environmental effects. Local Detail: Global appearance representations (common in NeRF) struggle with high-frequency local changes. GS-W's per-point adaptive sampling mitigates this. Rendering Speed: GS-W surpasses state-of-the-art NeRF-based methods in rendering speed by over 1000x. It matches real-time rendering speeds similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on wild data. Quality: Outperforms NeRF-based methods in reconstruction quality and detail, particularly in unconstrained environments with dynamic lighting and transient objects. Memory: Requires storage for intrinsic features per Gaussian point, increasing memory usage compared to standard 3DGS which typically uses a single SH coefficient set or simple color per point. The exact memory overhead is not specified in the sources. Strengths: Handles unconstrained image collections (wild data) with varying illumination, weather, and transient occluders. Real-time rendering capability. Limitations: Requires a U-Net for feature extraction and visibility map generation, adding complexity to the training pipeline. Performance depends on the quality of the SfM initialization and the visibility map accuracy. Origin: Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) was proposed to address the limitations of existing NeRF-based methods and standard 3DGS when applied to unconstrained image collections. Standard methods assume static scenes and consistent lighting, which is rarely the case in real-world "wild" data. Key Insight: The appearance of a point in the real world is determined by its intrinsic material properties and dynamic environmental impacts. Separating these allows for better reconstruction of static geometry and appearance while handling dynamic variations. Development: GS-W builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [16] (referenced as in the context of 3DGS) and introduces the appearance separation module, adaptive sampling, and visibility map handling. It is cited in surveys as a key method for handling wild data alongside Wild-GS and SWAG. name: 3DGUT
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Unscented Transform, 3D Gaussian Uncentred Transform, XPR-3D Gaussian Upsampling Transform, XPR-3DGUT
body: 3DGUT is a rendering method that employs an unscented transform to improve the affine approximation of the projection operator, providing more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane. It uses the same 3D Gaussian primitives as Gaussian Splatting but replaces the Jacobian-based linearization with a sigma-point transformation for projection and evaluates the Gaussian response in 3D along camera rays for per-pixel shading. Inputs: Primitive parameters p: mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, half-extents s \in \mathbb{R}^3, unit quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4, spherical harmonic coefficients sh, opacity o \in \mathbb{R}. Camera parameters: intrinsic matrix (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy), world-to-camera rotation R{w2c}, translation t{w2c}. Configuration: alpha threshold \alpha{thresh}, z-near z{near}. Outputs: For each primitive: tile cull data (conic elements, opacity, mean, visibility) and shader data (canonical ray origin, transformation matrix, opacity, color). Per-pixel: alpha contribution and validity flag. PrimitiveParams: mu: (3,) float, mean in world space. s: (3,) float, half-extents (sx, sy, sz). q: (4,) float, unit quaternion for rotation. sh: (C, 3) float, spherical harmonic coefficients. o: (1,) float, opacity. Tile Cull Data (ptcd) fields for primitive p: con2D[0,0], con2D[0,1], con2D[1,1]: projected conic elements. o: opacity. mu2D: 2D mean. visible: boolean flag. Shader Data (psd) fields for primitive p: rocanonical: flattened ray origin in canonical space. M: flattened 3 \times 3 matrix S^{-1} R^T. o: opacity. c: view-dependent color. 1. Project Function: Computes the footprint and stores projected data. 1. Compute world-to-camera projection matrix R{w2c}. 2. Construct rotation matrix R from quaternion q. 3. Compute sigma points in world space using the Unscented Transform. 4. Project sigma points to camera space. 5. Project to pixel space. 6. Estimate 2D Gaussian mean \mu{2D} and covariance \Sigma{2D} from weighted projected points. 7. Apply low-pass filter to \Sigma{2D} for antialiasing. 8. Compute conic 2D from filtered covariance. 9. Adjust opacity using MipSplatting based on determinant ratio. 10. Compute extent, radius, and bounding box. 11. Account for ray offset in bounding box. 12. Compute tile count. 13. Compute visibility flag. 14. Concatenate data into ptcd and psd. 2. Tile Cull Function: Determines which tiles the primitive overlaps. 1. Adjust tile bounds for ray offset (tile\max\x += 1, tile\max\y += 1). 2. Reuse XPR-3DGS logic for culling. 3. Pixel Info Function: Returns ray direction in world space. 1. Compute canonical ray direction from pixel coordinates. 2. Rotate to world space. 4. Evaluate Function: Computes per-pixel alpha. 1. Unpack psd to get ro{canonical}, M, o, c. 2. Get ray direction rd from pixel data. 3. Compute canonical ray direction rd{canonical} = M @ rd. 4. Compute max response in canonical Gaussian space. 5. Compute \alpha = o \cdot response. 6. Check validity (response > 0.0113). The depth \tau that maximizes the Gaussian response along a camera ray r(\tau) = o + \tau d is: \tau{max} = \frac{dc^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mu - o)}{dc^\top \Sigma^{-1} dc} where oc = S^{-1} R^T (o - \mu) and dc = S^{-1} R^T d are the ray origin and direction in the canonical space of the Gaussian. The transformation matrix M used in shader data is: M = \text{diag}(1.0/p.s) @ R^T The canonical ray origin is: ro{canonical} = (M @ (cp - p.\mu)).\text{flatten()} where cp = -R{w2c}[:3,:3]^T @ R{w2c}[:3,3]. \alpha{thresh}: Alpha threshold for visibility. Typical value: 255 (in 8-bit integer context) or normalized equivalent. z{near}: Near plane distance for visibility check. Validity threshold: 0.0113 for response check. Precision: The unscented transform avoids Jacobian linearization errors, but sigma point selection must be robust. Boundaries: Ray offset adjustment in tile culling is critical for correct tile assignment. Degenerate Input: If determinant of covariance is non-positive, the primitive is marked invisible. 0.5, ex, ey, cfg) # Compute tile count tc = (aabb.xmax - aabb.xmin) (aabb.ymax - aabb.ymin) # Compute view-dependent color c c = computecolor(p.mu, p.sh, view) # Compute visibility flag and adjust tile count visible = (det > 0) and (o > cfg.alphathresh) and (r > 0) and (tc > 0) and (muc[2] > cfg.znear) tc = float(visible) # Produce tileculldata and shaderdata for primitive p ptcd = [con2D[0,0], con2D[0,1], con2D[1,1], o, mu2D[0], mu2D[1], visible] M = diag(1.0 / p.s) @ R.T cp = -Rw2c[:3,:3].T @ Rw2c[:3, 3] rocanonical = (M @ (cp - p.mu)).flatten() psd = [rocanonical[0], rocanonical[1], rocanonical[2], M[0,0], M[0,1], M[0,2], M[1,0], M[1,1], M[1,2], M[2,0], M[2,1], M[2,2], o, c[0], c[1], c[2]] return ProjectResult(depth=muc[2], visible=visible, tileculldata=ptcd, shaderdata=psd, aabb=aabb, tilecount=tc) def tilecull(tilemin, tilemax, ptcd, cfg): # Adjust tile bounds for ray offset tilemax[0] += 1 # tilemaxx tilemax[1] += 1 # tilemaxy # Rest of tilecull in XPR-3DGS can be reused unchanged pass def pixelinfo(px, cam, view): # Compute ray direction in pixel space dc = [(px[0] + 0.5 - cam.cx) / cam.fx, (px[1] + 0.5 - cam.cy) / cam.fy, 1.0] dc = dc / norm(dc) # Rotate to world space Rc2w = view.Rc2w[:3,:3] # Compute ray direction rd = Rc2w @ dc return PixelInfoResult(rd=rd) def evaluate(pxdata, psd): rocanonical = psd[0:3] M = psd[3:12].reshape(3, 3) o = psd[12] c = psd[13:16] rd = pxdata[0:3] # Compute max response in canonical Gaussian space rdcanonical = M @ rd response = computemaxresponsecanonical(rocanonical, rdcanonical) alpha = o response valid = (response > 0.0113) return EvaluateResult(alpha=alpha, valid=valid, color=c) def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): # Standard conversion from unit quaternion to 3x3 rotation matrix w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2yy - 2zz, 2xy - 2zw, 2xz + 2yw], [2xy + 2zw, 1 - 2xx - 2zz, 2yz - 2xw], [2xz - 2yw, 2yz + 2xw, 1 - 2xx - 2yy] ]) def world2cam(point, Rw2c): return Rw2c[:3,:3] @ point + Rw2c[:3, 3] def computesigmapoints(mu, s, R, cfg): # Standard Unscented Transform sigma point generation # Assumes cfg provides lambda and alpha parameters for UT n = len(mu) lam = cfg.utlambda alpha = cfg.utalpha beta = cfg.utbeta kappa = 3.0 - n gam = np.sqrt((n + lam) / (1 - alpha2 + beta)) sigmapts = [mu] for i in range(n): sigmapts.append(mu + gam (R @ np.diag(np.sqrt(s)))) sigmapts.append(mu - gam (R @ np.diag(np.sqrt(s)))) return sigmapts def computemu2D(pointc, cam): # Perspective projection to pixel space x, y, z = pointc if z <= 0: return np.array([0.0, 0.0]) return np.array([(x / z) cam.fx + cam.cx, (y / z) cam.fy + cam.cy]) def approximate2Dgaussian(sigmapoints2D, cfg): # Weighted mean and covariance of projected sigma points weights = cfg.utweights mu = np.zeros(2) for sp, w in zip(sigmapoints2D, weights): mu += w sp cov = np.zeros((2, 2)) for sp, w in zip(sigmapoints2D, weights): diff = sp - mu cov += w np.outer(diff, diff) return mu, cov def applylowpassfilter(cov, cfg): # Add small epsilon to diagonal for antialiasing / stability return cov + cfg.epsilon np.eye(2) def computeconic(cov): # Compute inverse covariance (conic matrix) return np.linalg.inv(cov) def computeextents(cov, det, o, cfg): # Compute 2D extents from covariance determinant and opacity # Standard approximation for Gaussian bounding box scale = np.sqrt(np.abs(det)) return scale 2.0, scale 2.0 def computeradius(ex, ey): return max(ex, ey) / 2.0 def getboundingbox(center, ex, ey, cfg): return BoundingBox(center[0] - ex, center[1] - ey, center[0] + ex, center[1] + ey) def computecolor(mu, sh, view): # Evaluate spherical harmonics at view direction # Simplified placeholder for SH evaluation return np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) def mipsplatting2D(detorig, det): # MipSplatting opacity adjustment return np.sqrt(detorig / det) if det > 0 else 1.0 def computemaxresponsecanonical(rocanonical, rdcanonical): # Compute max response of Gaussian along ray in canonical space # Standard Gaussian response formula denom = np.dot(rdcanonical, rdcanonical) if denom == 0: return 0.0 t = np.dot(rocanonical, rdcanonical) / denom response = np.exp(-0.5 np.dot(rocanonical - t rdcanonical, rocanonical - t rdcanonical)) return response class BoundingBox: def init(self, xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax): self.xmin = xmin self.ymin = ymin self.xmax = xmax self.ymax = ymax class ProjectResult: def init(self, depth, visible, tileculldata, shaderdata, aabb, tilecount): self.depth = depth self.visible = visible self.tileculldata = tileculldata self.shaderdata = shaderdata self.aabb = aabb self.tilecount = tilecount class PixelInfoResult: def init(self, rd): self.rd = rd class EvaluateResult: def init(self, alpha, valid, color): self.alpha = alpha self.valid = valid self.color = color The implementation of 3DGUT within the XPR framework, demonstrating ease of integration by reusing shared pipeline modules. A technique used by 3DGUT to adjust opacity based on the determinant ratio of the projected covariance for antialiasing. Time Complexity: Projection involves computing sigma points and their projections, which is more expensive than the Jacobian-based approach in Gaussian Splatting but provides higher accuracy. Memory Complexity: Similar to Gaussian Splatting as it uses the same primitive structure, but stores additional shader data for canonical space evaluation. Strengths: More precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane by avoiding affine approximation errors. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When high accuracy in Gaussian projection is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. 3DGUT was introduced to address the limitations of affine approximations in Gaussian projection, which can compromise rendering accuracy. It employs the unscented transform to provide a more precise projection of 3D Gaussians onto the image plane. The method is part of the broader effort to improve the fidelity of point-based rendering methods. name: Transformer-based Reconstruction
body: Transformer-based Reconstruction methods replace the iterative optimization loop of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a feed-forward neural network that directly predicts Gaussian parameters from input images. This approach solves the computational bottleneck of per-scene optimization, enabling real-time reconstruction from single or sparse views. It differs from iterative siblings by eliminating the need for gradient descent on scene parameters, instead relying on learned priors within the transformer architecture to generalize across scenes. Flash3D is a feed-forward method for monocular 3DGS reconstruction that estimates depth from a single view to generate Gaussians. It differs from GS-LRM and Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) by relying on monocular depth estimation rather than multi-view feature aggregation or tokenized multi-image inputs. It is chosen when only a single image is available and a depth prior is acceptable. See Flash3D. GS-LRM is a feed-forward transformer method that predicts 3DGS parameters directly from a small set of input images (typically 2-4). It distinguishes itself from Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) by specifically targeting Gaussian parameter prediction rather than mesh or NeRF fields, and from Flash3D by its explicit handling of multi-view camera pose tokens. It is chosen for sparse-view reconstruction where camera poses are known. See GS-LRM. LRM is a feed-forward neural network designed for single-image to 3D reconstruction, establishing the foundational transformer-based architecture for direct parameter prediction in this family. It sets itself apart from Flash3D and GS-LRM by its generalizable architecture that can be adapted to various 3D representations, though here it predicts Gaussians. It is chosen as a baseline for single-view direct reconstruction. See Large Reconstruction Model (LRM). Reconstruction-based Generation decomposes 3D generation into two stages: multi-view image synthesis followed by 3D reconstruction. Unlike direct prediction methods, it leverages pre-trained diffusion models to generate posed multi-view images, which then serve as supervision for a Gaussian Splatting reconstructor. This approach reuses mature reconstruction pipelines, making system-level engineering straightforward, but inherits the consistency limitations of the multi-view generator. It is chosen when text-to-3D or single-image-to-3D generation is required without training a dedicated reconstruction network from scratch. See Reconstruction-based Generation. The family originates from the need to accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting, which traditionally requires per-scene optimization. Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) introduced the transformer-based feed-forward approach for 3D reconstruction. GS-LRM and Flash3D adapted this paradigm specifically for 3DGS, with GS-LRM focusing on sparse multi-view inputs and Flash3D on monocular depth estimation. Reconstruction-based Generation extends this by integrating diffusion-based multi-view synthesis.

name: Flash3D
head: Flash3D
body: Flash3D is a feed-forward network (FFN) method for monocular reconstruction that generates 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes by estimating depth from a single view. It addresses the challenge of rapid scene generation by bypassing iterative optimization, instead directly predicting 3D Gaussian parameters supervised by photometric losses. It differs from its siblings, such as GS-LRM and Large Reconstruction Model (LRM), which typically utilize transformer architectures to process multiple input views or tokens, by relying on a simpler FFN architecture focused on single-view depth estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single monocular image I. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian parameters defining the scene. Data Structures: The method outputs a collection of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian is defined by standard 3DGS parameters: position \mathbf{\mu}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}. The specific internal data structure layout (e.g., SoA vs AoS) is not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: The FFN estimates a dense depth map D from the input image I. This step often leverages monocular depth estimation techniques. As noted in related implementations, this may involve an encoder-decoder network \varphid(\varphie(I)). 2. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: The network directly predicts the 3D Gaussian parameters. The source indicates these are predicted directly, supervised by photometric losses. 3. Supervision: The predicted scene is rendered, and the loss is computed using metrics such as LPIPS, SSIM, or similar photometric losses. Formulas: The monocular depth estimation component can be represented as: D{mono} = \varphid(\varphie(I)) where \varphie is the encoder, \varphid is the decoder, and I is the input image. Parameters: Loss functions: LPIPS, SSIM. Typical values for network architecture or hyperparameters are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: If using self-supervised or zero-shot pre-trained monocular depth estimation models, additional scale and drift estimation must be handled during training. Monocular Limitations: Single-view reconstruction inherently suffers from depth ambiguity compared to multi-view methods. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def flash3dforward(image: Tensor) -> List[Gaussian]: """ Generates 3DGS scene from a single image using a feed-forward network. """ # Step 1: Estimate depth # Note: The specific FFN architecture for Flash3D is not detailed in sources. # Sources indicate it uses an FFN for monocular reconstruction. # Related work uses an encoder-decoder for depth. depthmap = estimatedepth(image) # Step 2: Predict 3D Gaussian parameters # The FFN directly predicts Gaussian parameters from the image/depth gaussians = predictgaussians(image, depthmap) return gaussians def estimatedepth(image: Tensor) -> Tensor: """ Placeholder for the depth estimation component. Sources cite BTS as a representative encoder-decoder network: Dmono = phid(phie(I)) """ # Implementation details of the specific FFN in Flash3D are not provided. # In practice, this would be the trained neural network. return depthmap def predictgaussians(image: Tensor, depthmap: Tensor) -> List[Gaussian]: """ Predicts 3D Gaussian parameters. Supervised by photometric losses like LPIPS or SSIM. """ # The exact mapping from image/depth to Gaussian parameters (mu, sigma, alpha, c) # is defined by the trained FFN weights. return gaussians An encoder-decoder network that infers dense depth from a single image, supervised to have correct scale. It is used as a representative monocular depth estimation method in related contexts. The process is defined as D{mono} = \varphid(\varphie(I)). A key pitfall is that self-supervised or zero-shot pre-trained models require additional scale and drift estimation during training. Time Complexity: Fast inference as it is a feed-forward network, avoiding iterative optimization. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables rapid monocular reconstruction of 3DGS scenes. Limitations: Relies on single-view depth estimation, which may lack geometric accuracy compared to multi-view methods. When to use: When fast, single-view 3DGS generation is required. When not to use: When high geometric fidelity from multiple views is needed. Flash3D was proposed to address the challenge of training feed-forward networks (FFNs) to directly predict 3D Gaussian parameters. It is cited in the context of methods that use FFNs for monocular reconstruction, generating 3DGS scenes by estimating depth from a single view. It is distinct from methods like PixelSplat and MVSplat which use transformers and multi-view features, and from GS-LRM which tokenizes multiple images. name: GS-LRM
head: GS-LRM Transformer Architecture, Large Reconstruction Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: GS-LRM is a scalable large reconstruction model that predicts high-quality 3D Gaussian primitives from 2–4 posed sparse images in approximately 0.23 seconds on a single A100 GPU. It uses a transformer-based architecture to predict per-pixel Gaussians, enabling it to handle both object and scene captures with large variations in scale and complexity. It differs from its siblings by directly decoding concatenated image and Plücker ray tokens into Gaussian parameters via a feed-forward transformer, whereas Flash3D and Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) typically target mesh or NeRF outputs, and Reconstruction-based Generation is a broader category. Inputs: N multi-view images Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} and their camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. Outputs: A list of 3D Gaussians with position, RGB color, scale, rotation quaternion, and opacity, totaling N \cdot H \cdot W Gaussians. Data Structures: 1. Per-view feature map: Concatenated image RGB and Plücker ray coordinates, forming a 9-channel tensor [b, n, H, W, 9]. 2. Patch tokens: Flattened 2D patches of size p \times p mapped to dimension d=1024, shape [b, n \cdot H/p \cdot W/p, d]. 3. Transformer output tokens: Processed sequence of the same shape as input tokens. 4. Gaussian parameters: 12-channel tensor per pixel [b, n, H, W, 12] split into distance (1), RGB (3), scale (3), rotation (4), opacity (1). Steps: 1. Tokenize posed images: Concatenate image RGBs and Plücker coordinates channel-wise to form a 9-channel tensor. Apply a convolution with kernel size 8 and stride 8 to downsample spatial dimensions by 8×, producing latent tokens of depth d=1024. Flatten spatial and view dimensions into a single sequence dimension for transformer input. 2. Process image tokens: Feed the concatenated multi-view tokens through L=24 transformer blocks. Each block uses Pre-LayerNorm, multi-head self-attention (16 heads), and a two-layered MLP (hidden dim 4096, GeLU activation) with residual connections. Plücker coordinates naturally serve as spatial embeddings, so no positional embeddings are used. 3. Decode output tokens: Reshape tokens back to [b, n, H/8, W/8, d]. Apply a transposed convolution with kernel size 8 and stride 8 to upsample spatial dimensions by 8×, outputting 12 channels per pixel. Flatten view and spatial dimensions to merge all Gaussians into a single list [b, n \cdot H \cdot W, 12]. 4. Split and parameterize: Divide the 12-channel tensor into distance, RGB, scaling, rotation, and opacity. Convert distance to XYZ using xyz = rayo + rayd \cdot (near \cdot (1 - w) + far \cdot w) where w = \sigma(distance). Compute scale as \min(\exp(G{scale} - 2.3), 0.3). Normalize rotation quaternions to unit length. Compute opacity as \sigma(G{opacity} - 2.0). Interpret RGB directly as zero-order spherical harmonics coefficients. Formulas: Tokenization: \{T{ij}\}{j=1,\dots,HW/p^2} = \text{Linear}(\text{Patchify}p(\text{Concat}(Ii, Pi))). Transformer: \{T{ij}\}^0 = \{T{ij}\}, \{T{ij}\}^l = \text{TransformerBlock}^l(\{T{ij}\}^{l-1}) for l=1,\dots,L. Scale: \mathrm{scale} = \min\{\exp(G{scale} - 2.3), 0.3\}. Opacity: \mathrm{opacity} = \sigma(G{opacity} - 2.0) where \sigma(x) = 1/(1+\exp(-x)). Parameters: Model size: 300M parameters. Transformer: 24 layers, hidden dimension 1024, 16 attention heads, MLP hidden dim 4096, patch size p=8. Max token length: 16K. Optimizer: AdamW with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.95, weight decay 0.05 (except LayerNorm). Learning rate: Cosine decay with linear warmup. 2000 steps warmup, peak LR 4\times10^{-4} for 256-res training; 500 steps warmup, peak LR 1\times10^{-4} for 512-res finetuning. Batch size: 8 objects/scenes per GPU for 256-res training; 2 per GPU for 512-res finetuning. Views per iteration: 4 input + 4 novel supervision views for objects; 2 input + 6 novel for scenes. Loss weight: \lambda=0.5 balancing MSE and Perceptual loss. Precision: BF16 mixed-precision training. Edge cases and pitfalls: Large Gaussian scales can degenerate into long lines, spreading gradients and hurting training stability; handled by clipping scale to a maximum of 0.3. CUDNN kernel shaping constraints require using Einops and Linear layers for patchify/unpatchify instead of conv/deconv, though they are conceptually equivalent. The method relies on known camera poses; incorrect poses lead to misaligned Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def gslrm(image, extrinsic, intrinsic, near, far): # image: [b, n, h, w, 3] # extrinsic: [b, n, 4, 4] # intrinsic: [b, n, 4] # near, far: scalar or [b, n, h, w] raysorigin, raysdirection = raysfromcamera(extrinsic, intrinsic) # [b, n, h, w, 3] # Concatenate image, origin, and cross(origin, direction) -> 9 channels crossprod = torch.cross(raysorigin, raysdirection, dim=-1) x = torch.cat([image, raysorigin, crossprod], dim=-1) # [b, n, h, w, 9] # Patchify: conv kernel=8, stride=8 -> [b, n, h/8, w/8, 1024] x = F.conv2d(x.permute(0, 1, 4, 2, 3).reshape(-1, 9, x.shape[2], x.shape[3]), weight=torch.randn(1024, 9, 8, 8), bias=None, stride=8) x = x.reshape(x.shape[0], x.shape[1], 1024, x.shape[2], x.shape[3]) x = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 4, 2) # [b, n, h/8, w/8, 1024] # Flatten spatial and view dims -> [b, n h/8 w/8, 1024] b, n, h8, w8, d = x.shape x = x.reshape(b, -1, d) # Transformer: Pre-LN, 24 blocks, MHA(16 heads), MLP(4096) # x = transformerblock(x) # Repeated 24 times with residual connections # (Transformer block implementation omitted for brevity; follows standard Pre-LN architecture) # Reshape back -> [b, n, h/8, w/8, 1024] x = x.reshape(b, n, h8, w8, d) # Unpatchify: transposed conv kernel=8, stride=8 -> [b, n, h, w, 12] x = F.convtranspose2d(x.permute(0, 1, 4, 2, 3).reshape(-1, 1024, x.shape[2], x.shape[3]), weight=torch.randn(12, 1024, 8, 8), bias=None, stride=8) x = x.reshape(x.shape[0], x.shape[1], 12, x.shape[2], x.shape[3]) x = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 4, 2) # [b, n, h, w, 12] # Merge all Gaussians -> [b, n h w, 12] x = x.reshape(b, -1, 12) # Split into components distance, rgb, scaling, rotation, opacity = torch.split(x, [1, 3, 3, 4, 1], dim=-1) # Parameterization w = torch.sigmoid(distance) xyz = raysorigin + raysdirection (near (1 - w) + far w) scaling = torch.clamp(torch.exp(scaling - 2.3), max=0.3) rotation = rotation / torch.norm(rotation, dim=-1, keepdim=True) opacity = torch.sigmoid(opacity - 2.0) return xyz, rgb, scaling, rotation, opacity A feed-forward 4D large reconstruction model that generates per-frame 3D Gaussian Splatting representations from a single-view video input in approximately one second. It addresses the limitation of previous 4D generation models restricted to object-centric scenes by enabling dynamic content reconstruction from monocular video. Unlike iterative optimization methods, L4GM performs inference in a single forward pass, utilizing temporal self-attention to upsample the output to higher frame rates for temporal smoothness. Defines the decoding strategy and data preprocessing required to transform raw transformer output tokens into valid 3D Gaussian parameters for the GS-LRM architecture. It solves the problem of mapping unconstrained neural network outputs to physically meaningful Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) while ensuring training stability through specific bias offsets and normalization constraints. It differs from sibling methods like L4GM by explicitly decoupling the parameterization into zero-order spherical harmonics for color and using a distance-based ray parameterization for XYZ coordinates, rather than direct 3D coordinate prediction. Time Complexity: Feed-forward inference completes in approximately 0.23 seconds on a single A100 GPU. Training requires approximately 2 days on 64 A100 (40G VRAM) GPUs for 256-res training (80K iterations), plus 1 additional day for 512-res finetuning (20K iterations). Memory Complexity: Scales with input resolution and transformer token length (up to 16K). Uses Flash-Attention-v2, gradient checkpointing, and deferred backpropagation for rendering to save GPU memory. Strengths: Fast feed-forward inference, no iterative optimization required, handles both object and scene captures with large scale variations, outperforms previous methods by 4dB PSNR for objects and 2.2dB PSNR for scenes. Limitations: Requires known camera poses, Gaussian count scales linearly with input resolution (unlike fixed-resolution triplanes), and large scales require explicit clipping to prevent degeneration. When to use: When fast reconstruction from few views is needed and camera poses are known. When not to use: When camera poses are unknown or high-fidelity detail is critical and iterative optimization is feasible. GS-LRM was introduced by Zhang et al. from Adobe Research and Cornell University. It builds on the success of transformer-based image-to-3D models but adapts the output to per-pixel Gaussian Splatting representations. The model is trained on Objaverse for object reconstruction and RealEstate10K for scene reconstruction. It was developed to overcome the fixed-resolution limitations of prior large reconstruction models that struggled with high-resolution inputs and large scale variations. name: Large 4D Gaussian Model (L4GM)
body: L4GM is a feed-forward 4D large reconstruction model that generates per-frame 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a single-view video input in approximately one second. It utilizes temporal self-attention to upsample the output to higher frame rates for temporal smoothness. Built on LGM, it differs from iterative optimization methods by performing inference in a single forward pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single-view video sequence. Output: Per-frame 3DGS parameters for each frame in the video. Data Structures: Each frame t outputs a set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}t. Each Gaussian i is defined by mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion), opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics coefficients c{i, l, m} for color approximation. Method Steps: 1. Video Encoding: The input video is processed through a transformer-based encoder built upon LGM. 2. Forward Pass: The encoded tokens pass through transformer blocks to predict 3DGS parameters directly in one forward pass, taking approximately 1 second. 3. Temporal Self-Attention: Temporal self-attention is applied to the output tokens to upsample the generated Gaussians to a higher frame rate, ensuring temporal smoothness. 4. Training Regularization: A flow field is used for temporal regularization during training to enforce coherent motion between frames. Parameters: Training Dataset: Objaverse-derived multiview-video dataset containing 44,000 objects, 12 million videos, and 300 million frames. Inference Time: ~1 second per video. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Comp4D is a method designed to overcome the object-centric limitation of previous 4D generation models. It first generates individual 4D objects and later composes them subject to trajectory constraints. Time Complexity: Inference takes approximately 1 second per video. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Marked as a 2026 SOTA update for 4D reconstruction. Strengths: Fast feed-forward inference; handles single-view video input; temporal upsampling via self-attention. Limitations: Requires a large training dataset; specific architectural details of the video encoder are not provided. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. L4GM was introduced as a 2026 SOTA update in the field of 4D reconstruction. It builds on GS-LRM and is trained on a large-scale Objaverse-derived multiview-video dataset. The model represents a shift from iterative optimization to feed-forward inference for 4D Gaussian Splatting. name: Gaussian Parameterization and Initialization
head: GS-LRM Initialization, GS-LRM Parameterization
body: This method defines the decoding strategy and data preprocessing required to transform raw transformer output tokens into valid 3D Gaussian parameters for the GS-LRM architecture. It maps unconstrained neural network outputs to physically meaningful Gaussian attributes while ensuring training stability through specific bias offsets and normalization constraints. Inputs: Raw output tokens G{ij} from the transformer decoder, representing a batch of Gaussians. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{ray}o and direction \mathbf{ray}d) for scene-level reconstruction. Scene type indicator (Object-level or Scene-level) determining depth bounds and normalization rules. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by: Center position \mathbf{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion). Opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (SH coefficient). The raw output G{ij} is decomposed into five distinct components: G{rgb}, G{scale}, G{rotation}, G{opacity}, and G{distance}. Camera pose normalization is applied only for Scene-level GS-LRM. Object-level GS-LRM skips this step because object sizes are pre-normalized during data generation. 1. Compute Mean Pose: Calculate the mean camera pose by averaging all input camera poses from the input set. 2. Coordinate Frame Alignment: Define the coordinate frame of this mean pose as the world space. 3. Scaling: Scale the camera locations such that they fit within the bounding box [-1, 1]^3 in the world space. Predict unnormalized quaternions from G{rotation} and apply L2-normalization as an activation function to obtain unit quaternions \mathbf{q}. \mathbf{q} = \frac{G{rotation}}{\|G{rotation}\|2} Interpret G{rgb} directly as zero-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Higher-order SH is not used. \mathbf{c} = G{rgb} Apply an exponential activation with a bias offset, followed by clipping. The bias offset shifts the zero-mean output to produce a scale where \exp(-2.3) \approx 0.1. \mathrm{scale} = \min \left( \exp(G{scale} - 2.3), 0.3 \right) Bias Offset: 2.3. Max Scale: 0.3. Apply a sigmoid activation with a bias offset. The bias offset shifts the zero-mean output to produce an opacity where \sigma(-2.0) \approx 0.1. \alpha = \sigma(G{opacity} - 2.0) Bias Offset: 2.0. Sigmoid: \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}. The center position is parameterized along the camera ray using a distance parameter t derived from G{distance}. 1. Map Distance to Range: Convert G{distance} to a normalized weight \omega \in [0, 1] using sigmoid, then map to the range [d{near}, d{far}] to get t. \omega = \sigma(G{distance}) t = (1 - \omega) \cdot d{near} + \omega \cdot d{far} 2. Compute XYZ: Calculate the 3D position using the ray origin and direction. \mathbf{xyz} = \mathbf{ray}o + t \cdot \mathbf{ray}d 3. Clipping (Object-level only): For Object-level GS-LRM, clip the predicted \mathbf{xyz} coordinates to be inside the cube [-1, 1]^3. This aligns with the training data rendering setup. Scene-level GS-LRM does not apply this clipping. | Parameter | Object-level Value | Scene-level Value | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | d{near} | 0.1 | 0.0 | Near depth bound for ray parameterization. | | d{far} | 4.5 | 500 | Far depth bound. 500 accounts for large depth variations in indoor/outdoor scenes. | | Scale Bias | 2.3 | 2.3 | Offset for scale exponential. | | Opacity Bias | 2.0 | 2.0 | Offset for opacity sigmoid. | | Max Scale | 0.3 | 0.3 | Upper bound for scale. | | Camera Normalization | None | Yes | Mean pose alignment and bounding box scaling. | | XYZ Clipping | Yes | No | Clip to [-1, 1]^3. | Unverified code. Args: Graw: Dictionary containing Grgb, Gscale, Grotation, Gopacity, Gdistance. rayo: Ray origin (3D vector). rayd: Ray direction (3D vector). scenetype: 'object' or 'scene'. Returns: dict: Decoded Gaussian parameters. """ # 1. Rotation: L2-normalize unnormalized quaternion qraw = Graw['Grotation'] norm = math.sqrt(sum(q2 for q in qraw)) q = [q / norm for q in qraw] # 2. Color: Direct mapping to zero-order SH c = Graw['Grgb'] # 3. Scale: Exp with bias, clipped scaleraw = Graw['Gscale'] scaleunclipped = [math.exp(s - 2.3) for s in scaleraw] scale = [min(s, 0.3) for s in scaleunclipped] # 4. Opacity: Sigmoid with bias opacityraw = Graw['Gopacity'] alpha = sigmoid(opacityraw - 2.0) # 5. Clipping (Object-level only) if scenetype == 'object': xyz = [max(-1.0, min(1.0, coord)) for coord in xyz] return { 'xyz': xyz, 'scale': scale, 'rotation': q, 'opacity': alpha, 'color': c } def normalizecameraposes(cameraposes): """ Normalizes camera poses for scene-level GS-LRM. Args: cameraposes: List of camera pose translation vectors. Returns: List of normalized camera poses. """ # Compute mean pose translation meanx = sum(p[0] for p in cameraposes) / len(cameraposes) meany = sum(p[1] for p in cameraposes) / len(cameraposes) meanz = sum(p[2] for p in cameraposes) / len(cameraposes) # Center poses around mean centeredposes = [[p[0] - meanx, p[1] - meany, p[2] - meanz] for p in cameraposes] # Find max extent to scale into [-1, 1]^3 maxval = 0.0 for p in centeredposes: for coord in p: if abs(coord) > maxval: maxval = abs(coord) scalefactor = 1.0 / maxval if maxval > 0 else 1.0 normalizedposes = [[coord scalefactor for coord in p] for p in centeredposes] return normalizedposes Training Stability: The bias offsets shift the zero-mean transformer output so that initial scale and opacity values are approximately 0.1, which primarily aids training stability. Camera Normalization: Camera normalization is skipped for object-level GS-LRM because object sizes are pre-normalized during data generation. Not given in the sources. Do not use if view-dependent effects are required without modifying the spherical harmonics order. name: Large Reconstruction Model (LRM)
body: Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) is a feedforward transformer-based method for single-image or multi-view to 3D reconstruction that outputs a triplane neural representation in a single forward pass. It solves the problem of slow, per-scene optimization in traditional neural rendering by learning 3D priors from large-scale datasets, enabling real-time reconstruction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a triplane representation as the primary output, whereas Flash3D and GS-LRM predict 3D Gaussians directly, and Reconstruction-based Generation focuses on generation pipelines rather than direct reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single image I or a viewset V=\{Ii\}{i=1}^N with corresponding camera parameters \{\pii\}{i=1}^N. Output: A triplane neural representation \theta. Final Render: Novel view images \hat{I} = R(\theta, \pi). Data Structures: Trplane Representation \theta: A 3D feature field represented by three 2D planes (XY, YZ, XZ). The exact bit-packing or resolution of the triplane is not given in the sources. Transformer Blocks: A series of transformer blocks process the input features. Splatter Layer: A component that splats source view features into a new triplane. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract a pixel-wise feature map \mathbf{v}=\psi(Ii) from each image Ii in the input viewset. 2. Lifting with Splatter: Lift the feature maps into an intermediate 3D representation \tilde{\theta} using the Splatter component. 3. Transformer Processing: Input \tilde{\theta} into the large-scale model \Phi (a transformer) to output the final 3D representations \theta=\Phi\theta(\tilde{\theta}). The Splatter layer is inserted every 3 transformer blocks (i.e., 5 blocks in total). The Splatter layer takes previous block outputs as prior shape encoding. 4. Rendering: Output novel view images \hat{I} = R(\theta, \pi) from \theta using the Renderer component. 5. Training: Train the model by minimizing the loss L between the novel rendered image \hat{I} and the corresponding ground truth I. Formulas: Feature extraction: \mathbf{v}=\psi(Ii). Intermediate representation: \tilde{\theta} = \text{Splatter}(\mathbf{v}). Final representation: \theta=\Phi\theta(\tilde{\theta}). Rendering: \hat{I} = R(\theta, \pi). Loss: L(\hat{I}, I). Parameters: Dataset: Trained on Objaverse + Objaverse-XL. Transformer Blocks: 5 blocks in total, with Splatter inserted every 3 blocks. LPIPS Optimization: Enabled in the Lightplane-augmented LRM to avoid deferred backpropagation complexity. Resolution: Training uses low-resolution images (64x64) for some losses, but high-resolution rendering is supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-view Input: The method supports multi-view inputs, but the specific handling of camera pose errors or inconsistent views is not detailed. Memory Efficiency: The memory efficiency of the renderer allows for high-resolution rendering and image-level losses, which is a key advantage over the original LRM's deferred backpropagation. # Source says "every 3 transformer blocks (i.e. 5 blocks in total)" # This implies Splatter is inserted at specific intervals. # Assuming Splatter is inserted after block 2 and block 5 is the final output? # Or Splatter is inserted within the sequence. # Let's assume Splatter is inserted after block 2 and block 5 is the end. # Actually, "every 3 transformer blocks" suggests a periodic insertion. # With 5 blocks, it might be inserted after block 2 and block 5? # Or maybe it's inserted after block 2, and the 5th block is the last one. # Let's assume Splatter is inserted after block 2. if blockidx == 2: # Splatter takes previous block outputs as prior shape encoding theta = splatter(theta, camparams) # Step 4: Rendering # Output novel view images # Assuming we want to render from a specific camera pi # theta is the final 3D representation renderedimage = renderer(theta, pi) return renderedimage, theta def LRMloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage): # Minimize loss L between novel rendered image and ground truth loss = L(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) return loss Note: The exact placement of the Splatter layer within the 5 blocks is ambiguous. "Every 3 transformer blocks (i.e. 5 blocks in total)" suggests a specific architecture. If it's inserted every 3 blocks, and there are 5 blocks, it might be inserted after block 2 (if 0-indexed) or block 3 (if 1-indexed). The pseudocode assumes insertion after block 2 (0-indexed) as a placeholder for the specific architecture detail which is not fully explicit. The Large Gaussian Reconstruction Model (GRM) is a feedforward neural network for single-image or multi-view to 3D reconstruction that directly predicts Gaussian maps. It builds on Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) by replacing its output format with Gaussian primitives, supporting both single and multi-view inputs. Time Complexity: Feedforward model, single transformer pass, enabling real-time reconstruction. Memory Complexity: Memory efficient due to the Lightplane renderer, allowing high-resolution rendering and image-level losses without deferred backpropagation. Measured Performance: Outperforms baseline ViewFormer [41] and overfitting baselines like Voxel and NeRF. Specific metrics are not provided in the sources. Scaling: Highly scalable components for neural 3D fields. Strengths: Real-time reconstruction, high-resolution rendering, memory efficiency, support for multi-view inputs. Limitations: Relies on large-scale datasets (Objaverse + Objaverse-XL) for training. When to use: When real-time 3D reconstruction from single or multi-view images is required. When not to use: When high-fidelity per-scene optimization is required, or when the input data does not match the training distribution. Origin: LRM was introduced by Adobe in 2023. History: It represents a shift from per-scene optimization to feedforward models for 3D reconstruction. Usage: Used for single-image to 3D reconstruction and generation. name: Reconstruction-based Generation
body: Reconstruction-based Generation decomposes 3D asset creation into two distinct stages: multi-view image synthesis followed by 3D Gaussian reconstruction. Unlike end-to-end generative models, this approach builds on Transformer-based Reconstruction by leveraging pre-trained diffusion models to generate posed multi-view images, which then serve as supervision signals for a dedicated Gaussian Splatting (GS) reconstructor. This method distinguishes itself by reusing mature, standard multi-view reconstruction pipelines, thereby simplifying system-level engineering and decoupling generation from reconstruction, though it remains subject to the consistency limitations of the initial image generator. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt or a single reference image. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives representing the scene. Data Structures: Multi-view Images: A small set of posed 2D images (and optionally depth maps or camera trajectories) generated by the diffusion model. 3D Gaussian Attributes: Standard Gaussian Splatting parameters including mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, color c, and opacity \alpha. U-Net Architecture: An asymmetric neural network used for the reconstruction phase. Steps: 1. Multi-view Synthesis: An off-the-shelf multi-view or video diffusion model generates a set of posed 2D images from the input text or single image. This stage may also produce auxiliary data such as depth maps or camera trajectories. 2. Reconstruction Training: A U-Net-based network is trained to map the generated multi-view images directly to 3D Gaussian attributes. 3. Asymmetric Processing: The U-Net employs an asymmetric structure to accept high-resolution image inputs while constraining the number of output Gaussians. 4. Optimization: The network minimizes the difference between rendered views of the predicted Gaussians and the input multi-view images, solving a standard multi-view reconstruction problem. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The method relies on standard multi-view reconstruction loss minimization between rendered Gaussian projections and input images. Parameters: U-Net Asymmetry: The specific ratio of input resolution to output Gaussian count is not explicitly defined in the sources, but the architectural choice balances fidelity and efficiency. Number of Views: Described as "a small set". Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cross-view Inconsistency: Imperfect consistency in generated multi-view images can lead to noisy or artifact-ridden 3D reconstructions. Janus Ambiguity: The method is prone to generating objects with multiple faces or ambiguous geometry if the diffusion prior lacks constraints. Over-smoothing: Generated textures may lack high-frequency detail, resulting in over-smoothed appearances unless additional regularizers are applied. Time Complexity: The reconstruction phase operates via a feed-forward network, but total generation time is dominated by the multi-view diffusion step, requiring minutes to hours per prompt. Memory Complexity: The asymmetric U-Net design limits the number of output Gaussians, managing memory usage during reconstruction. Strengths: Straightforward system-level engineering; reuses mature reconstruction pipelines; decouples generation from reconstruction. Limitations: Inherits fundamental limitations of the multi-view generator, including cross-view inconsistency and potential geometric artifacts. This paradigm separates 3D generation into image synthesis and reconstruction, enabling the use of powerful pre-trained 2D diffusion models. The Large Reconstruction Model (LGM) is a prominent implementation, utilizing off-the-shelf models for multi-view generation and training a U-Net for Gaussian reconstruction. name: 3D Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering
head: Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids, Gaussian Ellipsoid Ray Tracing, VoGE, VoGE Ray Tracing with Ellipsoidal Gaussians, VoGE Volume Density Ray Tracing, VoGE Volume Rendering, VoGE: A Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids for Analysis-by-Synthesis
body: 3D Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering (VoGE) is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents scenes as a sum of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids and computes image synthesis via ray tracing rather than rasterization. It solves the occlusion ambiguity inherent in distance-based blending by accumulating volume density distributions along viewing rays, enabling realistic interaction between overlapping objects. Unlike its sibling Gaussian Splatting, which approximates volume rendering through 2D rasterization of projected splats, VoGE replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture exact volume density distributions for blending. Inputs: A set of K Gaussian ellipsoids, each defined by a center location \mathbf{M}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a symmetric spatial variance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}; a camera configuration defining viewing rays \mathbf{r}(t); and per-kernel attributes (e.g., color \mathbf{c}k). Outputs: A synthesized 2D image where each pixel color is a weighted sum of kernel attributes. Data Structures: Each kernel k stores: \mathbf{M}k: Center coordinates (\mu{k,x}, \mu{k,y}, \mu{k,z}). \mathbf{\Sigma}k: 3 \times 3 symmetric covariance matrix. \mathbf{c}k: Attribute vector (e.g., RGB color). Precomputation per Kernel: For each kernel k, the method precomputes scalars to simplify ray integration: 1. \mathbf{V}k: Vector from the ray point of closest approach to the center. 2. lk: The distance along the ray where density is maximized. 3. qk: Log-density magnitude offset. 4. \sigmak^2: Variance of the 1D Gaussian projection along the ray direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, sample a viewing ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{D} t, where \mathbf{D} is the normalized direction vector and t is the distance from the camera origin. 2. Kernel Parameter Calculation: For each kernel k and ray direction \mathbf{D}, compute the following scalars: Calculate the length lk along the ray that maximizes the density \rhok(\mathbf{r}(t)): lk = \frac{\mathbf{M}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{M}k}{2 \cdot \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D}} Calculate the vector \mathbf{V}k from the point lk \mathbf{D} on the ray to the center \mathbf{M}k: \mathbf{V}k = \mathbf{M}k - lk \mathbf{D} Compute the precomputed scalar qk representing the peak density magnitude offset: qk = -0.5 \mathbf{V}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{V}k Compute the precomputed scalar \sigmak^2 representing the variance of the 1D Gaussian along the ray: \sigmak^2 = \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} Note: The condition \mathbf{V}k^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{V}k = 0 holds by definition of lk, simplifying the exponent. 3. Volume Density Definition: The volume density \rho(\mathbf{X}) at any location \mathbf{X} is the sum of ellipsoidal Gaussian kernels: \rho(\mathbf{X}) = \sum{k=1}^K \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{M}k)^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{M}k)\right) Along the ray \mathbf{r}(s) = s\mathbf{D}, the density of the k-th kernel reduces to a 1D Gaussian: \rhok(\mathbf{r}(s)) = \frac{e^{qk}}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{(s - lk)^2}{2 \sigmak^2}\right) 4. Occupancy Accumulation: Compute the occupancy T(t) along the ray, which represents the probability of not being occluded up to distance t. This is derived by integrating the total volume density: T(t) = \exp\left(-\tau \int{-\infty}^t \rho(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds\right) Substituting the 1D Gaussian form and using the error function \operatorname{erf}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int0^x e^{-u^2} du, the closed-form solution is: T(t) = \exp\left(-\sum{k=1}^K e^{qk} \frac{\operatorname{erf}\left((t - lk)/\sigmak\right) + 1}{2}\right) Here, \tau is a scattering coefficient. The integral limits are effectively -\infty to t because the Gaussian support is infinite. 5. Kernel-to-Pixel Weight Computation: Compute the weight Wk for each kernel to determine its contribution to the final pixel color. The exact weight is the integral of the reweighted density: Wk(t) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} T(t) \rhok(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt Since the integral of T(t) involving \operatorname{erf} is analytically intractable, VoGE approximates T(t) as constant T(lk) over the kernel's support (centered at lk): Wk \approx T(lk) e^{qk} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} \|\mathbf{\Sigma}k\|2} \exp\left(-\frac{(t - lk)^2}{\sigmak^2}\right) dt The integral of the normalized Gaussian part equals 1. Thus, the approximate closed-form weight is: Wk = T(lk) e^{qk} The error introduced by this approximation converges to a fixed value of 0.0256, which is negligible compared to the integral result W=1. 6. Image Synthesis: For each pixel, sum the contributions of all kernels weighted by their computed weights Wk and their attributes \mathbf{c}k: \mathbf{C}{pixel} = \sum{k=1}^K Wk \mathbf{c}k Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computekernelparams(Mk, Sigmak, D): """ Precompute scalars for a single kernel along a ray direction D. Mk: (3,) center vector Sigmak: (3,3) symmetric covariance matrix D: (3,) normalized ray direction vector Returns: lk, qk, sigmaksq """ Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigmak) term1 = np.dot(Mk, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) term2 = np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, Mk)) denominator = 2.0 np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) if denominator == 0: # Guard against degenerate covariance projection return 0.0, 0.0, 1e-8 lk = (term1 + term2) / denominator Vk = Mk - (lk D) qk = -0.5 np.dot(Vk, np.dot(Sigmainv, Vk)) sigmaksq = np.dot(D, np.dot(Sigmainv, D)) return lk, qk, sigmaksq def rendervoge(kernels, rayorigin, raydirection, tau=1.0): """ Render a single ray using VoGE. kernels: List of dicts with keys 'M', 'Sigma', 'color' rayorigin: (3,) camera origin raydirection: (3,) normalized direction tau: scattering coefficient Returns: pixelcolor (3,) """ # Step 1 & 2: Precompute kernel parameters for this ray kerneldata = [] for k in kernels: M = k['M'] Sigma = k['Sigma'] lk, qk, sigmaksq = computekernelparams(M, Sigma, raydirection) sigmak = math.sqrt(max(sigmaksq, 1e-8)) kerneldata.append({ 'lk': lk, 'qk': qk, 'sigmak': sigmak, 'color': k['color'] }) pixelcolor = np.zeros(3) # Step 4 & 5: Compute Occupancy T(lk) and Weight Wk for each kernel for kd in kerneldata: lk = kd['lk'] qk = kd['qk'] sigmak = kd['sigmak'] # Compute T(lk): Occupancy at the peak of kernel k # T(t) = exp(-tau sum{j} e^{qj} (erf((t - lj)/sigmaj) + 1)/2) densityintegralsum = 0.0 for otherkd in kerneldata: lother = otherkd['lk'] qother = otherkd['qk'] sigmaother = otherkd['sigmak'] arg = (lk - lother) / sigmaother erfval = math.erf(arg) term = math.exp(qother) (erfval + 1.0) / 2.0 densityintegralsum += term Tlk = math.exp(-tau densityintegralsum) # Step 5: Compute Weight Wk Wk = Tlk math.exp(qk) # Step 6: Accumulate Color pixelcolor += Wk kd['color'] return pixelcolor Parameters: \tau: Scattering coefficient. Typical value: 1.0. K: Total number of Gaussian kernels. Varies by scene complexity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance-based blending ambiguity: Traditional splatting blends based on viewing distance, causing unrealistic color shifts when foreground objects move relative to background objects (e.g., purple blending). VoGE avoids this by using density-based blending. Integral infeasibility: The exact integral of T(t) involving the error function is analytically intractable. The approximation Wk \approx T(lk)e^{qk} is used. The error is bounded and negligible (0.0256). Degenerate Covariance: If \mathbf{D}^T \cdot \mathbf{\Sigma}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{D} is zero or near-zero, lk is undefined. This occurs if the ray direction is orthogonal to the principal axes in a way that makes the projection singular. Guard against division by zero. The Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive replaces long-tailed Gaussian kernels with constant-density ellipsoidal shapes to reduce spatial overlap and memory usage. It addresses the non-differentiability of hard-boundary ellipsoids by employing a sigmoid-based formulation, allowing for stable gradient-based optimization against 3D intensity fields. Unlike its sibling Ever Rendering, which relies on ray-based accumulation to implicitly soften boundaries, this method ensures the primitive itself is fully differentiable, making it suitable for direct volumetric training. Ever Rendering is a real-time volumetric rendering method that represents a radiance field as a set of constant-density volumetric ellipsoids, avoiding the 2D billboard approximation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike its sibling Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive, it replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture volume density distributions for blending, enabling exact transmittance calculation without approximation errors. Each point is represented by a 3D Gaussian ellipsoid GV to facilitate general grids; it becomes a sphere for cubic grids. The volume-space Gaussian is defined as GV = \frac{1}{2\pi V} e^{-0.5(x - vj)^T V^{-1} (x - vj)}. This ellipsoid is transformed into view-space G{MVM} using the viewing matrix M. Time Complexity: VoGE provides real-time level rendering speed, competitive with PyTorch3D. The complexity is dominated by the per-ray, per-kernel evaluation of the error function and exponential terms. With N pixels and K kernels, the complexity is roughly O(N \cdot K). The use of closed-form approximations avoids expensive numerical integration. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of kernels K, storing \mathbf{M}k, \mathbf{\Sigma}k, and attributes for each. Strengths: Resolves occlusion ambiguities better than distance-based blending. Fully differentiable, suitable for analysis-by-synthesis tasks like pose estimation and texture fitting. Real-time performance achievable via CUDA implementation. Limitations: Approximation error in weight calculation (though negligible). When to use: When accurate occlusion reasoning and differentiability are required, such as in object pose estimation, shape/texture fitting, and scenes with significant overlapping objects. When not to use: When maximum frame rate is critical and occlusion accuracy is less important than speed, or when the scene can be well-approximated by 2D billboards (standard 3DGS). VoGE (Volume Gaussian Ellipsoid) was proposed as a differentiable volume renderer that utilizes volumetric Gaussian reconstruction kernels as geometric primitives. It was developed to address the limitations of current state-of-the-art differentiable renderers that use rasterization and distance-based blending, which suffer from ambiguity when objects overlap. The code is available at https://github.com/Angtian/VoGE.
