name: Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive
head: Sigmoid-based ellipsoidal primitive
body: The Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive is a geometric representation used in volume rendering that replaces long-tailed Gaussian kernels with constant-density ellipsoidal shapes to reduce spatial overlap and memory usage. It addresses the non-differentiability of hard-boundary ellipsoids by employing a sigmoid-based formulation, allowing for stable gradient-based optimization against 3D intensity fields. Unlike its sibling Ever Rendering, which relies on ray-based accumulation to implicitly soften boundaries, this method ensures the primitive itself is fully differentiable, making it suitable for direct volumetric training. The method defines a primitive using a center intensity, a mean position, and a covariance matrix, modulated by a sharpness parameter. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Primitive parameters \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 (center), \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (covariance), I \in \mathbb{R} (center intensity), and k \in \mathbb{R} (sharpness). Query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Scalar intensity value \tilde{P}(x). Data Structures: Each primitive stores: 1. \mu: 3D vector. 2. \Sigma: 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix. 3. I: Scalar intensity. 4. k: Scalar sharpness (typically fixed). Formulas: Let d = x - \mu be the displacement vector from the center. The unnormalized primitive profile is defined as: P(x) = I \cdot \sigma(k \cdot (1 - d^T \Sigma^{-1} d)) where \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} is the sigmoid function. To decouple peak intensity from the sharpness parameter k, the primitive is normalized: \tilde{P}(x) = \frac{P(x)}{P(\mu)} = I \cdot \frac{\sigma(k \cdot (1 - d^T \Sigma^{-1} d))}{\sigma(k)} This normalization ensures that the peak intensity at the center (d=0) remains exactly I, regardless of k. Parameters: k: Controls boundary sharpness. A fixed hyperparameter is used in practice for efficiency. Typical values: Lower values cause peak intensity reduction in the unnormalized case; higher values increase boundary sharpness. Steps: 1. Compute displacement d = x - \mu. 2. Compute quadratic form q = d^T \Sigma^{-1} d. 3. Compute unnormalized sigmoid value s = \sigma(k \cdot (1 - q)). 4. Compute normalization factor n = \sigma(k). 5. Return \tilde{P}(x) = I \cdot (s / n). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Peak Intensity Deviation: If k is small and the primitive is not normalized, the peak intensity at the center decreases, deviating from the desired unit response. Truncation Artifacts: When using a fixed cutoff for rendering or voxelization, the spatial support varies with k. The cutoff region must be adjusted according to k to avoid truncation artifacts. Non-differentiability of Hard Boundaries: Using the indicator function form (as in EVER) results in vanishing gradients during optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(z): """Standard sigmoid function.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-z)) def differentiableellipsoidprimitive(x, mu, Sigmainv, I, k): """ Computes the normalized intensity of a differentiable ellipsoid primitive at point x. Args: x: Query point (3,) mu: Primitive center (3,) Sigmainv: Inverse covariance matrix (3x3) I: Center intensity (scalar) k: Sharpness parameter (scalar) Returns: Normalized intensity value (scalar) """ # 1. Compute displacement d = x - mu # 2. Compute quadratic form d^T Sigma^{-1} d q = d @ Sigmainv @ d # 3. Compute unnormalized sigmoid argument arg = k (1.0 - q) # 4. Compute unnormalized value sunnorm = sigmoid(arg) # 5. Compute normalization factor sigma(k) normfactor = sigmoid(k) # 6. Return normalized intensity return I (sunnorm / normfactor) A training stage that optimizes ellipsoidal primitive parameters to fit a volumetric intensity field, storing center intensity I and geometric parameters (\mu, \Sigma). It differs from view-dependent color learning (e.g., 3DGS) by directly modeling the per-voxel scalar value of the original volume. Definition: Optimizes primitives to predict voxel intensity \hat{V}(x) by summing normalized primitive profiles. Formula: The predicted voxel intensity is \hat{V}(x) = \sum{i \in N} \tilde{P}i(x) = \sum{i \in N} Ii \frac{\sigma(k(1 - di^\top \Sigmai^{-1} di))}{\sigma(k)}, where N is the set of primitives contributing at x. Steps: 1. Subsample a ground truth subvolume V{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times s \times s} from the GT volume at each iteration. 2. Align primitive coordinates to the GT volume coordinates. 3. Voxelize only the overlapping region to obtain the prediction subvolume \hat{V}. 4. Compute loss L{\text{rec}} = \beta L1 + (1 - \beta) L{\text{D-SSIM}} with \beta \in [0, 1]. When to choose: Use when training against a known 3D intensity field (e.g., medical volumes, scientific data) rather than multi-view images. Time Complexity: Rendering/voxelization depends on the number of primitives N and the spatial support. The ellipsoidal shape reduces spatial footprint by up to 9\times compared to Gaussian 3\sigma support, reducing overlap and computational cost. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory usage due to smaller spatial overlap and constant-density representation. Performance: Using k as a fixed hyperparameter improves efficiency. Making k learnable per primitive improves quality but adds overhead and reduces speed. Strengths: Fully differentiable primitive enables stable training against 3D intensity fields; reduced spatial overlap compared to Gaussians. Limitations: Requires careful adjustment of cutoff regions to avoid truncation artifacts; fixed k may limit adaptability compared to learnable k. When to use: Scalable learning on volumes exceeding GPU memory; scenarios requiring direct volumetric optimization. When not to use: When ray-based accumulation is preferred (see Ever Rendering); when extreme adaptability of boundary sharpness is required and speed is not a concern. The method originates from the ESVR (3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering) framework. It was developed to address the excessive spatial overlap and high memory usage caused by long-tailed Gaussian primitives in volume rendering. The approach is inspired by EVER [29], which uses indicator functions for ellipsoidal boundaries, but adapts it for differentiable volumetric optimization by replacing the hard boundary with a sigmoid function. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ever Rendering
head: Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering
body: Ever Rendering is a real-time volumetric rendering method that represents a radiance field as a set of constant-density volumetric ellipsoids, avoiding the 2D billboard approximation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike its sibling Differentiable Ellipsoid Primitive, it replaces rasterization with ray tracing to capture volume density distributions for blending, enabling exact transmittance calculation without approximation errors. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian ellipsoids, each defined by a center position \mathbf{t}k, a rotation matrix \mathbf{R}k, and a scaling vector \mathbf{s}k = [s{kx}, s{ky}, s{kz}]^T. An optimized scalar parameter \alphak \in [0, 1] representing the peak opacity along the shortest axis. Color \mathbf{c}k for each ellipsoid, stored as spherical harmonics coefficients for the first two degrees to model view-dependence. Camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics). Target images for optimization. Outputs: A rendered image with color and depth. Gradients for optimization via adjoint rendering, which recomputes function values during the backwards pass instead of storing them. The scene representation consists of a list of ellipsoids. Each ellipsoid k stores: \mathbf{t}k \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{R}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix (orthonormal). \mathbf{s}k \in \mathbb{R}^3: Axis scaling factors. \alphak \in \mathbb{R}: Optimized opacity parameter. \mathbf{c}k \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color. AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box computed from \mathbf{t}k, \mathbf{R}k, \mathbf{s}k for BVH acceleration. The acceleration structure is a Binary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) built using NVIDIA OptiX, where each leaf node contains an ellipsoid's AABB and intersection logic. Density Calculation: To ensure non-zero gradients even when opacity approaches 1, the method optimizes \alphak and maps it to density \sigma(\alphak) using the minimum axis scale: \sigma(\alphak) = -\frac{\log(1 - 0.99 \cdot \alphak)}{\min(s{kx}, s{ky}, s{kz})} This ensures that a primitive viewed along its shortest axis has a peak opacity equal to \alphak. Transmittance: The volume rendering transmittance is calculated as: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \Delta tj) This is identical to the quadrature rule derived by Max [30] using piecewise-constant approximation. In Ever Rendering, this is an intentional design decision with no approximation errors. Splitting Condition: A splitting condition detects vanished gradients when opacity is near 1 across the entire primitive along the major axis: 0.99 < 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\alphak) \cdot \max(s{kx}, s{ky}, s{kz})) If this inequality holds, the primitive is a candidate for splitting. Regularizer Loss: To discourage overly anisotropic primitives (which cause large AABBs and slow BVH traversal), a regularizer is applied only to visible primitives: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \text{stopgrad}(1 - \alpha) \cdot (\max(sx, sy, sz) - \min(sx, sy, sz)) where \alpha \in [0, 1] is the opacity and s \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the ellipsoid axis scaling vector. Splitting Threshold: 2.5 \times 10^{-7} (modified from 3DGS due to smaller spatial gradients). Cloning Threshold: 0.1. Density Division: When splitting, the density of the new primitives is divided in half. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def rayellipsoidintersect(rayo, rayd, ellt, ellR, ells): """ Computes near and far intersection distances along the ray. Transforms ray to ellipsoid local space and solves quadratic for unit sphere. """ invs = 1.0 / ells localo = (ellR.T @ (rayo - ellt)) invs locald = (ellR.T @ rayd) invs a = torch.dot(locald, locald) b = 2.0 torch.dot(localo, locald) c = torch.dot(localo, localo) - 1.0 disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return None, None sqrtdisc = torch.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 return t1, t2 def computedensity(alphak, sk): """Maps optimized opacity parameter alphak to density sigma.""" minscale = torch.min(sk) term = torch.clamp(1.0 - 0.99 alphak, min=1e-7) return -torch.log(term) / minscale def renderray(rayo, rayd, ellipsoids): """ Renders a single ray using Ever Rendering's front/back event decoupling. """ events = [] # List of (t, deltasigma, deltapremultipliedcolor) for ell in ellipsoids: tnear, tfar = rayellipsoidintersect(rayo, rayd, ell.t, ell.R, ell.s) if tnear is None: continue sigma = computedensity(ell.alpha, ell.s) # Front surface: add density and premultiplied color events.append((tnear, sigma, sigma ell.c)) # Back surface: subtract density and premultiplied color events.append((tfar, -sigma, -sigma ell.c)) # Sort events by distance along the ray events.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) runningsigma = 0.0 runningpremultc = torch.zeros(3) totaltransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = torch.zeros(3) prevt = events[0][0] if events else 0.0 for t, dsigma, dpremultc in events: deltat = t - prevt if deltat > 0 and runningsigma > 0: intervalcolor = runningpremultc / runningsigma intervalcontrib = intervalcolor (1.0 - torch.exp(-runningsigma deltat)) accumulatedcolor += totaltransmittance intervalcontrib totaltransmittance = torch.exp(-runningsigma deltat) if totaltransmittance < 1e-4: break prevt = t runningsigma += dsigma runningpremultc += dpremultc return accumulatedcolor def optimizestep(ellipsoids, images, targets, bvh): """ One step of optimization with adjoint rendering and ADC. """ renderedimages = [] for ray in rays: color = renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction, ellipsoids) renderedimages.append(color) loss = torch.mean((torch.stack(renderedimages) - targets) 2) # Add Regularizer Loss regloss = torch.tensor(0.0) for ell in visibleellipsoids: alphadetached = ell.alpha.detach() anisotropy = torch.max(ell.s) - torch.min(ell.s) regloss += (1.0 - alphadetached) anisotropy loss += regloss # Backward pass (adjoint rendering recomputes forward values) loss.backward() # Adaptive Density Control (ADC) for ell in ellipsoids: sigma = computedensity(ell.alpha, ell.s) maxscale = torch.max(ell.s) opacitymajor = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma maxscale) if opacitymajor > 0.99: splitellipsoid(ell) elif spatialgradient(ell) > 2.5e-7: splitellipsoid(ell) elif spatialgradient(ell) > 0.1: cloneellipsoid(ell) return loss def splitellipsoid(ell): """ Splits an ellipsoid: reduces size, perturbs position, halves density. """ newscale = ell.s 0.5 perturbation = torch.randn(3) 0.01 newt = ell.t + perturbation # Density is halved by adjusting alpha or scale; here we keep alpha and halve contribution newalpha = ell.alpha newc = ell.c / 2.0 # Create two new primitives with these parameters return [Ellipsoid(newt, ell.R, newscale, newalpha, newc), Ellipsoid(newt, ell.R, newscale, newalpha, newc)] def cloneellipsoid(ell): """ Clones an ellipsoid to add detail. """ perturbation = torch.randn(3) 0.01 newt = ell.t + perturbation return Ellipsoid(newt, ell.R, ell.s, ell.alpha, ell.c) def computespatialgradients(ellipsoids, renderedimages, targets): """ Accumulates xy gradients per primitive from the loss backward pass. Standard operation: maps per-pixel gradients to intersected primitives. """ for ell in ellipsoids: ell.grad = torch.zeros(3) # Placeholder for accumulated gradient magnitude return ell.grad Vanishing Gradients: If opacity approaches 1, gradients vanish. The mapping \sigma(\alphak) ensures non-zero gradients by anchoring \alphak to the shortest axis view. Anisotropy: Highly anisotropic primitives create large AABBs, slowing BVH traversal. The regularizer loss discourages this. Precision: The log term in density calculation must handle \alphak close to 1. The factor 0.99 prevents \log(0). BVH Rebuild: The BVH is rebuilt at every training step, taking tens of milliseconds. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved, with performance on Mip-NeRF360 reaching 36 FPS. Memory Complexity: 1134 MB on Mip-NeRF360. Performance: On Mip-NeRF360, EVER achieves PSNR 27.51, SSIM 0.825, LPIPS 0.194. Scaling: The method scales to larger scenes (Zip-NeRF) with improved sharpness. Strengths: Real-time performance, consistent 3D radiance field, no approximation errors in transmittance, improved blending and sharpness compared to 3DGS. Limitations: BVH rebuild overhead during training (tens of ms per step). Ever Rendering was introduced in the paper "EVER: Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering for Real-Time View Synthesis". It builds on the optimization framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) but replaces rasterization with ray tracing using NVIDIA OptiX and Slang for automatic differentiation. The method addresses the 2D billboard limitation of 3DGS by using 3D Gaussian ellipsoids that blend into a proper 3D radiance field. It is used for real-time 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis, specifically enabling effects like defocus blur and fish-eye camera distortion. EVER: Exact Volumetric Ellipsoid Rendering for Real-Time View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.00469, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Stochastic Gaussian Splatting
head: Bayesian Gaussian Splatting, Gaussian Point Splatting, Stochastic 3DGS Rendering, StochasticSplats, VI-based Gaussian Splatting
body: Stochastic Gaussian Splatting (SGS) refers to two distinct methodological extensions of 3D Gaussian Splatting that replace deterministic rasterization with probabilistic sampling. The first variant, often termed Bayesian SGS, treats Gaussian parameters as random variables to enable uncertainty estimation alongside novel view synthesis. The second variant, Gaussian Point Splatting, eliminates the per-tile radix sort and tile-based rendering bottlenecks by sampling opaque points from Gaussians and compositing them via atomic operations, enabling the interactive rendering of hundreds of millions of Gaussians. Both methods rely on Variational Inference or stochastic transparency to approximate the volume rendering integral without explicit depth sorting. The implementation details diverge significantly between the two primary SGS variants. The following sections describe the Bayesian approach for uncertainty estimation and the Point Splatting approach for massive scene rendering. This method extends the deterministic GS pipeline by learning a parametric distribution over Gaussian kernels using Variational Inference (VI). Inputs and Outputs Input: A dataset of posed images D = \{(oi, di, yi)\}, where (oi, di) are pixel coordinates and viewing directions, and yi is the observed color. Output: A synthesized image I(o, d) and an uncertainty map \sigma(o, d) representing the standard deviation of pixel color. Data Structures The scene is modeled as a collection of K Gaussian kernels Gk. Unlike deterministic GS, each kernel Gk is defined by a posterior distribution q{\thetak}(Gk) rather than fixed parameters. The learnable parameters \theta include the means and covariances of these distributions: \mu^k \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean of the Gaussian position. \Gamma^k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance of the Gaussian position. \alpha^k \in \mathbb{R}: Parameter for opacity distribution. \Pi^k \in \mathbb{R}: Variance parameter for opacity. c^{klm}, \Xi^{klm}: Mean and variance parameters for spherical harmonic coefficients. Prior Initialization Directly optimizing KL divergence with random initialization causes convergence issues by fixing Gaussians in random positions. SGS uses an Empirical Bayes approach: 1. Phase 1 (Standard GS): Run standard 3DGS for 2500 iterations. Spherical Harmonics degree: 1. Densification: Applied until iteration 1000. Center Learning Rate: Fixed at 10^{-2}. 2. Phase 2 (Bayesian SGS): At iteration 2500, fix the current GS parameters as the prior \hat{G}. Initialize prior covariance matrices \hat{\Sigma} as 10^{-2} I (identity matrix). Posterior Learning Rate: 10^{-4} for all learnable parameters. Training continues until iteration 10000. Rendering Formula The image is rendered using alpha blending (EWA Volume Splatting), treating parameters as samples from their distributions: I(o, d) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \alphak e^{zk(o,d)} ck(d) \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj e^{zj(o,d)}) where zk(o, d) is the splatting coefficient derived from the projected 2D Gaussian. The elliptical 3D Gaussian kernel \phi is defined as: \phi(x; \muk, \Sigmak) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (x - \muk)^T \Sigmak^{-1} (x - \muk)\right) where \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the mean and \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the covariance matrix. Optimization Objective The method minimizes the KL divergence between the approximate posterior q\theta(G) and the true posterior P(G|D). Using Bayes' theorem and assuming independence among kernels, the loss function is: L = L{rec} + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM} + \lambda{KL} L{KL} + \lambda{AUSE} L{AUSE} Reconstruction Loss (L{rec}): Typically the \ell1 norm between observed yi and rendered I(oi, di), though the probabilistic formulation models the conditional probability P(yi | (oi, di), G) as a normal distribution, leading to a log-likelihood term proportional to the squared error (yi - I(oi, di))^2. KL Loss (L{KL}): Sum of KL divergences between prior (hat variables) and posterior (starred variables) for all parameters: L{KL} = \sum{k=1}^{K} \left[ KL(\mathcal{N}{\hat{\mu}k, \hat{\Gamma}k} || \mathcal{N}{\mu^k, \Gamma^k}) + KL(\mathcal{N}{\hat{\alpha}k, \hat{\Pi}k} || \mathcal{N}{\alpha^k, \Pi^k}) + KL(\mathcal{N}{\hat{c}{klm}, \hat{\Xi}{klm}} || \mathcal{N}{c^{klm}, \Xi^{klm}}) \right] The closed-form KL divergence between two multivariate normals \mathcal{N}{\mu0, \Sigma0} and \mathcal{N}{\mu1, \Sigma1} is: KL = -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \text{Tr}(\Sigma1^{-1} \Sigma0) + \frac{1}{2} (\mu1 - \mu0)^T \Sigma1^{-1} (\mu1 - \mu0) + \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{\det \Sigma1}{\det \Sigma0}\right) AUSE Loss (L{AUSE}): Optimizes the Area Under the Sparsification Error. Inference Uncertainty is estimated via Monte Carlo sampling. The posterior is sampled 8 times during both training and testing to compute the variance of pixel colors. This method removes sorting by sampling opaque points and using atomics. Inputs and Outputs Input: A list of M 3D Gaussians (from a standard 3DGS model). Output: A rendered image. Data Structures Point Count List: For each Gaussian k, compute the number of points Nk to splat. This depends on the Gaussian's opacity and size in view, ranging from 1 to millions. Thread Workload Map: A parallel mapping from GPU thread IDs to the list of Gaussian IDs to splat, ensuring perfect workload distribution. Algorithm Steps 1. Sample Points: For each Gaussian k in view, sample Nk pixel-sized opaque points independently and identically from the Gaussian distribution. 2. Opacity Correction: Direct sampling leads to underestimation of true opacity due to collisions (multiple points hitting the same pixel). The effective opacity \alpha{eff} is derived such that the probability of splatting no points to a pixel is exactly 1 - \alpha{true}, where \alpha{true} is the true opacity of the Gaussian at that pixel. 3. Atomic Splatting: Splat the sampled points using 64-bit atomic operations to update the color and opacity buffers. 4. Stochastic Transparency: Apply stochastic transparency to the accumulated results. Parameters Samples Per Pixel (SPP): The number of points sampled per pixel. A typical value is 4, which produces a faithful approximation enabling real-time rendering. Pseudocode (Gaussian Point Splatting) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def gaussianpointsplatting(gaussians, camera, width, height, spp): # Initialize buffers colorbuffer = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height width)] alphabuffer = [0.0] (height width) # 1. Compute point counts per Gaussian pointcounts = [] for k in gaussians: # Compute projected area and opacity at pixel center # Nk depends on Gaussian k's opacity and size in view # Count ranges from 1 to millions projectedarea = 1.0 # Source does not specify exact projected area formula alphatrue = 0.5 # Source does not specify exact opacity evaluation formula nk = max(1, int(spp projectedarea)) pointcounts.append(nk) # 2. Map threads to Gaussian IDs gaussianidstosplat = [] for k, nk in enumerate(pointcounts): gaussianidstosplat.extend([k] nk) # 3. Parallel Splatting # In practice, this runs on GPU with 64-bit atomics for gid in gaussianidstosplat: k = gaussians[gid] # Sample a point from the Gaussian distribution # Standard multivariate normal sampling point = [k.mu[0] + random.gauss(0, 1), k.mu[1] + random.gauss(0, 1), k.mu[2] + random.gauss(0, 1)] # Project point to screen # Standard perspective projection screenx, screeny = int(point[0] width), int(point[1] height) # Check bounds if not (0 <= screenx < width and 0 <= screeny < height): continue # Compute true opacity at pixel alphatrue = math.exp(-0.5 ((screenx - k.mu[0])2 + (screeny - k.mu[1])2)) # Simplified Nk = pointcounts[gid] # Opacity Correction: alphap ensures P(no hit) = 1 - alphatrue alphap = 1.0 - (1.0 - alphatrue) (1.0 / Nk) # Splat using atomic operations # 64-bit atomic add to color and alpha buffers idx = screeny width + screenx atomicaddalpha(alphabuffer, idx, alphap) atomicaddcolor(colorbuffer, idx, alphap k.color) return colorbuffer, alphabuffer def atomicaddalpha(buffer, idx, val): # Simulates 64-bit atomic add buffer[idx] += val def atomicaddcolor(buffer, idx, val): # Simulates 64-bit atomic add for i in range(3): buffer[idx][i] += val[i] Bayesian SGS: Performance: Real-time rendering (\ge 30 fps at 1080p). Quality: On the LLFF dataset (504x378), it achieves PSNR 24.20, SSIM 0.842, LPIPS 0.121. Uncertainty: Provides AUSE RMSE 0.0147 and AUSE MAE 0.0092. Limitations: Requires 8 Monte Carlo samples per pixel for uncertainty, increasing compute cost compared to deterministic GS. Direct optimization of reconstruction loss alone underestimates pixel variance. Gaussian Point Splatting: Performance: Renders scenes with 425M Gaussians interactively on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti SUPER with 4 SPP. Scaling: Eliminates tile-based rendering and sorting bottlenecks, allowing linear scaling with the number of Gaussians. Quality: Faithful approximation of 3DGS; noise is unbiased and can be mitigated with temporal accumulation. Limitations: Introduces noise at low SPP (e.g., 4 SPP). Bayesian SGS: Introduced by Savant, Valsesia, and Magli in 2024 (arXiv:2403.18476) as the first framework for uncertainty estimation in Gaussian Splatting using Variational Inference. It addresses the lack of confidence metrics in GS compared to NeRF-based methods like S-NeRF. Gaussian Point Splatting: Introduced by Rijsdijk, Peters, Weinmann, and Marroquim in 2026 (ACM TOG) as a method for rendering massive 3DGS scenes. It addresses the latency of per-tile radix sort in standard 3DGS rasterization. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Modeling Uncertainty for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/tnnls.2025.3553582, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Point Splatting – a stochastic method for rendering 3DGS scenes, https://jorisar.nl/gaussianpointsplatting/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Rendering Implementation
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization Pipeline, 3DGS Rendering
body: Rendering Implementation defines the computational pipeline that transforms a set of 3D Gaussian primitives into a 2D image. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the volume rendering equation for explicit, particle-based scene representations by leveraging hardware-accelerated rasterization. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing the foundational mechanisms—specifically the projection from 3D covariance to 2D screen-space conics and the alpha compositing logic—that enable both the high-performance GPU rasterization of 3D Gaussian Splatting and the display-only CPU-sorted instancing of 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced). All rendering implementations for 3D Gaussians share the following mathematical and procedural core, as defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting and 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced): 1. Parameter Activation: Raw training parameters are transformed into geometric primitives [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]: Rotation q is normalized: q{\text{norm}} = q / \|q\| [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Scale s is exponentiated to ensure positivity: s{\text{eff}} = \exp(s) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Opacity \alpha is sigmoided: \alpha{\text{eff}} = \sigma(\alpha) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. The 3D covariance matrix is constructed as \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} is the rotation matrix derived from q{\text{norm}} and \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(s{\text{eff}}) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 2. Camera Space Transformation: The mean position is transformed to camera space: \boldsymbol{\mu}' = \mathbf{V} \boldsymbol{\mu} [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. The covariance is transformed using the upper-left 3 \times 3 submatrix of the view matrix \mathbf{V}: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{V}{1:3, 1:3} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} \mathbf{V}{1:3, 1:3}^T [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 3. Screen-Space Projection: The Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projective projection at \boldsymbol{\mu}' is computed: \mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx}{\mu'z} & 0 & -\frac{fx \mu'x}{\mu'z^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{\mu'z} & -\frac{fy \mu'y}{\mu'z^2} \end{pmatrix} [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. The 2D screen-space covariance is: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} = \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}^T [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. The 2D mean is: \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx \mu'x}{\mu'z} + cx \\ \frac{fy \mu'y}{\mu'z} + cy \end{pmatrix} [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 4. Alpha Compositing: Gaussians are sorted by depth (camera-space z) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. For each pixel, color C and transmittance T are accumulated: C \leftarrow C + T \cdot \alpha{\text{pixel}} \cdot \mathbf{c} T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{pixel}}) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Early termination occurs when T drops below a threshold (e.g., 0.05) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. A display-only technique that projects Gaussians to 2D quads, sorts them by depth on the CPU, and renders them via hardware-instanced drawing with standard alpha blending. It avoids GPU tile-based complexity by relying on CPU sorting. The primary real-time rendering method using GPU-based global depth sorting and tile-based rasterization. It computes 2D conics for efficient pixel-wise alpha evaluation and supports view-dependent color via spherical harmonics. The rendering pipeline originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework, which introduced explicit Gaussian primitives to replace volumetric ray marching for real-time novel view synthesis. The method was developed to overcome the computational cost of NeRFs while maintaining high visual fidelity. The specific projection and rasterization techniques described here are standard implementations of the 3DGS rendering equation.

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced)
head: 3DGS Weekend Renderer, Gaussian Splatting Instanced Draw, RViz Splat Cloud, SplatCloud Instanced Rendering
body: This method renders trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by projecting 3D Gaussian primitives into 2D screen-space quads, sorting them by camera-space depth on the CPU, and drawing them using hardware-instanced rendering with standard alpha blending. It solves the problem of visualizing large-scale, photorealistic 3D scenes on client-side hardware (such as mobile devices or web browsers) without requiring neural network inference or server-side ray tracing. It sets itself apart from its sibling Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by moving the sorting and blending logic entirely to the CPU and using standard fixed-function alpha blending rather than tile-based GPU accumulation, and from Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) by explicitly defining the instanced draw call structure and texture-based attribute fetching required for large splat counts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians defined by mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}, rotation q, scale s, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Output: A 2D image with color C and alpha \alpha. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Primitive: Defined by parameters transformed into effective values [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]: Rotation: q{\text{norm}} = q / \|q\| [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Scale: s{\text{eff}} = \exp(s) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Opacity: \alpha{\text{eff}} = \sigma(\alpha) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 3D Covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} is derived from q{\text{norm}} and \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(s{\text{eff}}) [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 2. GPU Buffers (Instanced Rendering): Quad VBO: Static buffer containing 4 vertices of a unit quad with corners at (-1,-1), (1,-1), (-1,1), (1,1). Index Buffer (IBO): 6 indices forming two triangles. Per-Instance VBO: A dynamic buffer of size N \times \text{sizeof(float)} containing sorted indices 0 \dots N-1. Step rate is 1. Texture Buffer Objects (TBOs) / Data Textures: splatPositionScale (or TBO Base): Stores per-splat centroid (xyz) and scale (w) in RGBA16F format. Size: N \times 32 bytes if packed as UI, or N texels. splatColorOpacity (or TBO SH): Stores SH coefficients (RGB) and opacity (A) in RGBA16F format. Size: N \times \text{sh\coeffs\per\splat} \times 8 bytes. Sampling mode: NEAREST filtering and CLAMPTOEDGE wrapping. Numbered Steps: 1. Parameter Activation: Transform raw training parameters into geometric primitives [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 2. Camera Space Transformation: Transform mean to camera space: \boldsymbol{\mu}' = \mathbf{V} \boldsymbol{\mu} [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Transform covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{V}{1:3, 1:3} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} \mathbf{V}{1:3, 1:3}^T [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 3. Screen-Space Projection: Compute Jacobian \mathbf{J} at \boldsymbol{\mu}': \mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx}{\mu'z} & 0 & -\frac{fx \mu'x}{\mu'z^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{\mu'z} & -\frac{fy \mu'y}{\mu'z^2} \end{pmatrix} [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Compute 2D covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} = \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}^T [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. Compute 2D mean: \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{fx \mu'x}{\mu'z} + cx \\ \frac{fy \mu'y}{\mu'z} + cy \end{pmatrix} [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md][2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md]. 4. Frustum Culling (Optional but Recommended): Remove Gaussians outside image bounds and near/far planes (e.g., with a FOV margin ratio of 0.3). 5. CPU Sorting: Compute depth for each splat i: zi = \boldsymbol{\mu}'i \cdot \mathbf{v}{\text{forward}} (camera-space Z). Sort splats by increasing camera-space Z (far-to-near order, assuming camera looks down negative Z). Reorder Gaussian and SH data based on sorted indices. Optimization: Re-sort only when camera direction delta exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1% of bounding radius) to avoid redundant computation. 6. Upload Sorted Data: Update the Per-Instance VBO with sorted indices. Update TBOs/Data Textures with sorted centroid, scale, color, and opacity data. If N > 65535 (16-bit index limit), split into multiple batches. 7. Rendering Setup: Disable depth test: glDisable(GLDEPTHTEST). Enable alpha blending: glEnable(GLBLEND) and glBlendFunc(GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). 8. Instanced Draw Call: Issue glDrawArraysInstanced(GLTRIANGLESTRIP, 0, 4, N) (or per batch). Vertex Shader computes clip position and quad expansion based on 2D covariance eigenvalues. Fragment Shader computes Gaussian falloff and outputs premultiplied color/alpha. Note: This pseudocode simulates the data preparation and sorting steps. Actual rendering requires a graphics API (OpenGL/Vulkan/WebGPU). """ # 1. Parameter Activation (from parent article) # qnorm, seff, alphaeff, Sigma3D computed as per [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] # 2. Prepare Instance Data (Simulating VBO/TBO upload) # In reality, this data is uploaded to GPU buffers instanceindices = np.arange(N, dtype=np.float32) # 7. Rendering Loop (Simulating the draw call and fragment shader) # Since we are simulating the "Instanced" logic in CPU for verification, # we iterate through splats and composite. # In the actual GPU method, this loop is implicit in the rasterizer. outputcolor = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3), dtype=np.float32) outputalpha = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(N): # Skip low opacity if gsopacities[i] < 0.05: continue # Get projected mean and covariance (from step 3) # For simulation, we assume we have umean, vmean, Sigma2D umean, vmean = meanscam[i, 0] / meanscam[i, 2], meanscam[i, 1] / meanscam[i, 2] # Compute bounding box (3-sigma) # Eigen-decomposition of Sigma2D a = Sigma2D[i, 0, 0] + 0.3 b = Sigma2D[i, 1, 0] d = Sigma2D[i, 1, 1] + 0.3 det = a d - b b mid = 0.5 (a + d) radius = np.sqrt(max(mid mid - det, 0.0)) lam1 = max(mid + radius, 0.01) lam2 = max(mid - radius, 0.01) # 3-sigma axes # e1, e2 computation... # b1 = 3.0 sqrt(lam1) e1 # b2 = 3.0 sqrt(lam2) e2 # Bounding box umin = int(np.floor(umean - 3 np.sqrt(lam1))) umax = int(np.ceil(umean + 3 np.sqrt(lam1))) vmin = int(np.floor(vmean - 3 np.sqrt(lam2))) vmax = int(np.ceil(vmean + 3 np.sqrt(lam2))) # Clip to image bounds umin = max(0, umin) umax = min(imagewidth, umax) vmin = max(0, vmin) vmax = min(imageheight, vmax) # Evaluate SH Color # direction = camera.viewdirectioncamtomeanworld(...) # shcolor = evalsphericalharmonics(gsshcoeffs[i], direction) shcolor = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) # Placeholder # Alpha compositing (Painter's Algorithm) # In GPU, this is done per-pixel by the fragment shader # Here we simulate the accumulation for verification for u in range(umin, umax): for v in range(vmin, vmax): # Pixel centering du = u + 0.5 - umean dv = v + 0.5 - vmean # Gaussian value at fragment # G(px, py) = exp(-4.5(px^2 + py^2)) where px, py are normalized quad coords # px = du / (3sqrt(lam1)), py = dv / (3sqrt(lam2)) px = du / (3.0 np.sqrt(lam1)) py = dv / (3.0 np.sqrt(lam2)) power = -4.5 (px2 + py2) if power < -9.0: continue alphabase = gsopacities[i] alphapixel = min(0.99, alphabase np.exp(power)) if alphapixel < 0.001: continue # Premultiplied alpha blending # Cout = Cin (1 - alpha) + Csplat alpha # Tout = Tin (1 - alpha) # Current transmittance T = 1.0 - outputalpha[v, u] if T < 0.05: # Early termination continue outputcolor[v, u] = outputcolor[v, u] (1 - alphapixel) + shcolor alphapixel outputalpha[v, u] = outputalpha[v, u] + alphapixel T return outputcolor Parameters: Jitter: 0.3 added to 2D covariance diagonal elements (covariance2D[0][0] and [1][1]) to prevent singularity. Minimum Eigenvalue: 0.01 clamp on lam1 and lam2. Alpha Clamp: Maximum alpha 0.99. Alpha Discard: Fragments with alpha < 0.001 are discarded. Power Discard: Fragments with power < -9.0 are discarded. Sort Re-trigger Threshold: Camera movement must exceed 1% of bounding radius to re-sort. Max Instances per Batch: 65535 (due to 16-bit index buffer). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use NEAREST filtering and CLAMPTOEDGE wrapping for data textures to avoid blending adjacent splat attributes. Bit Flips: Implement a Support Guard to clamp parameters to valid ranges to prevent catastrophic rendering errors from SEUs [17686-support-guard.md]. Large Scenes: If N > 65535, split into multiple batches and use glInstanceID offset to index into textures. Web Runtime ABI: Ensure material compilation matches the runtime version (e.g., Filament.js 1.70.2 vs Android 1.71.5). GPU-accelerated, tile-based parallel processing. Choose for real-time performance on high-end GPUs. Display-only, CPU-side sorting. Choose for client-side visualization without complex GPU shaders. Preprocessing step to reduce sorting overhead. Choose when fragment count is high. VR/AR focused, background CPU sorting. Choose for mobile XR hardware. Order-independent transparency approximation. Choose when sorting latency is prohibitive. Unity engine optimized. Choose for mobile avatar rendering in Unity. Pure CPU, JIT-compiled. Choose for fast preview generation. Fault mitigation for SEUs. Choose for spaceborne/robotic hardware. CPU-based, non-differentiable. Choose for debugging or no-GPU environments. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N \log N) on the CPU. Rendering is O(N \cdot A) where A is average splat area in pixels, but offloaded to GPU rasterizer. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat data in textures/VBOs. SH0 splats require ~28 bytes/splat in RGBA16F textures. Measured Performance: CPU radix sort of ~500k depth keys takes a few milliseconds on a worker thread. Mobile-GS reports up to 127 FPS on modern mobile GPUs using this instanced approach with OIT. Strengths: Simple implementation, works on standard graphics APIs (OpenGL/Vulkan/WebGPU) without compute shaders, suitable for mobile and web. Limitations: Less efficient than tile-based GPU sorting for very large scenes, sorting latency on CPU can cause frame drops if not throttled. When to Use: Mid-range mobile devices, web browsers, or environments lacking compute shader support. When Not to Use: High-end desktop rendering where tile-based GPU rasterization offers better performance. name: Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, Tile-based Gaussian Rasterization, Tiled Rendering of 3DGS, 3DGS Rasterization, Gaussian Rasterization (GPU)
body: Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization is a GPU-optimized, differentiable rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that partitions the image plane into macro-tiles to enable parallel, memory-efficient alpha blending. It solves the performance bottleneck of sorting millions of splats globally by assigning each tile to a CUDA thread block, which cooperatively fetches depth-sorted Gaussians and composites them per-pixel. It sets itself apart from its parent 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) by moving the sorting and blending entirely to the GPU, enabling real-time frame rates for training and inference. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (means \mathbf{x}, opacities \alpha, scales \mathbf{s}, rotations \mathbf{r}), spherical harmonics coefficients (or precomputed colors), camera matrices (view V, projection P), image dimensions (W, H), and field-of-view tangents (\tan \phix, \tan \phiy). Outputs: Rendered RGB image, auxiliary maps (depth, normals, opacity), and gradients for training. Data Structures: The method relies on three primary state buffers allocated on the GPU: 1. GeometryState: Per-Gaussian buffers. depths: float, size P (number of Gaussians). means2D: float2, size P (screen-space centers). cov3D: float, size P \times 6 (symmetric 3D covariance). conicopacity: float4, size P (inverse 2D covariance + opacity). rgb: float, size P \times 3 (projected colors). tilestouched: uint32t, size P (count of tiles intersected). pointoffsets: uint32t, size P (start index in flattened tile list). 2. BinningState: Sorting buffers. pointlistkeys: uint64t, size P (encoded tile ID + depth). pointlist: uint32t, size P (Gaussian indices). 3. ImageState: Per-pixel/tile buffers. accumalpha: float, size W \times H. ranges: uint2, size N{tiles} (start/end indices for each tile in the sorted list). Steps: 1. Preprocessing & Projection: For each Gaussian i: Transform mean \mathbf{x}i to camera space: \mathbf{x}'i = V \mathbf{x}i. Compute 3D covariance \Sigmai from scales and rotations. Project to 2D screen space using the Jacobian of the projection matrix J and camera intrinsics K: \Sigma'i = J \begin{bmatrix} V & \mathbf{x}'i \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \Sigmai \begin{bmatrix} V & \mathbf{x}'i \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T J^T (Simplified: \Sigma'{2D} = J \Sigma{3D} J^T restricted to the top-left 2 \times 2 block after perspective division). Compute the 2D conic matrix (inverse covariance) \mathbf{C}i = (\Sigma'{2D})^{-1}. Calculate the bounding radius ri = \lceil 3 \sqrt{\lambda{\max}} \rceil where \lambda{\max} is the largest eigenvalue of \Sigma'{2D}. Compute screen-space color \mathbf{c}i by evaluating Spherical Harmonics at the view direction. 2. Tile Binning: Determine the tile grid: N{tiles} = \lceil W / Tx \rceil \times \lceil H / Ty \rceil, where Tx, Ty are tile dimensions (typically 16x16 or 32x32). For each Gaussian, compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in tile coordinates. Assign the Gaussian to all overlapping tiles. Generate a 64-bit key for each Gaussian-tile pair: key = (tileid << 32) | depthid, where depthid is the view-space depth zi. Store pairs in pointlistkeys and pointlist. 3. Sorting: Perform a device-side radix sort on pointlistkeys to group Gaussians by tile and sort them front-to-back (increasing depth). Compute inclusive prefix sums on tilestouched to determine pointoffsets, which mark the start of each tile's Gaussian list in the sorted array. Scan the sorted keys to populate ranges in ImageState, storing the start and end indices for each tile. 4. Rasterization (Alpha Blending): Launch a CUDA kernel where each thread block (bx, by) is assigned to one tile. Each thread i in the block corresponds to a pixel (u, v) within the tile. Threads cooperatively iterate through the sorted Gaussian list for their tile (using ranges to bound the loop). For each Gaussian j overlapping pixel (u, v), compute the squared Mahalanobis distance: dist\sq = \mathbf{d}^T \mathbf{C}j \mathbf{d} = a \cdot du^2 + 2b \cdot du \cdot dv + c \cdot dv^2 where \mathbf{d} = [u - uj, v - vj]^T and \mathbf{C}j = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}. Compute opacity contribution: \alphaj = \sigma(oj) \exp(-\frac{1}{2} dist\sq) where \sigma is the sigmoid function and oj is the log-opacity. Accumulate color using alpha blending: C(u, v) = \sum{j=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}j \alphaj \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak). Early termination: If the accumulated transmittance \prod (1-\alphak) drops below a threshold (e.g., 1/255), stop processing further Gaussians for that pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def tiledgaussianrasterization( means3D: torch.Tensor, # [P, 3] opacities: torch.Tensor, # [P] scales: torch.Tensor, # [P, 3] rotations: torch.Tensor, # [P, 4] (quaternion) shs: torch.Tensor, # [P, K, 3] or None viewmatrix: torch.Tensor, # [4, 4] projmatrix: torch.Tensor, # [4, 4] focalx: float, focaly: float, tanfovx: float, tanfovy: float, imageheight: int, imagewidth: int, tilesize: int = 16, bgcolor: torch.Tensor = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0])): P = means3D.shape[0] device = means3D.device # 1. Precompute 2D Covariance and Conics # Transform means to camera space meanscam = (viewmatrix[:3,:3] @ means3D.T + viewmatrix[:3, 3:4]).T # Compute 3D Covariance from scales and rotations # (Simplified: assume cov3Dprecomp is available or computed via rotation matrix R) # R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(rotations) # S = diag(exp(scales)) # Sigma3D = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T # Project to 2D # J = d(proj) / d(campos) # Sigma2D = J @ Sigma3D @ J.T # Conic C = inv(Sigma2D) # 2. Binning # Compute bounding boxes in tile coordinates # Assign Gaussians to tiles # Generate keys: (tileid << 32) | depth # 3. Sorting # Sort keys and values (Gaussian indices) # Compute ranges for each tile # 4. Rasterization Kernel Launch # Block: (tilesize, tilesize) # Grid: (ceil(W/tilesize), ceil(H/tilesize)) # Inside Kernel: # tileid = blockIdx.x + blockIdx.y gridDim.x # pixelu = threadIdx.x + blockIdx.x tilesize # pixelv = threadIdx.y + blockIdx.y tilesize # if pixelu >= W or pixelv >= H: return # startidx = ranges[tileid].x # endidx = ranges[tileid].y # accalpha = 1.0 # acccolor = bgcolor[:, pixelv, pixelu] # for k in range(startidx, endidx): # gidx = sortedgaussianindices[k] # if gidx is invalid: break # # # Check if pixel is inside Gaussian bounding box (optional optimization) # # Compute distsq # alpha = sigmoid(opacities[gidx]) exp(-0.5 distsq) # # if alpha < 1e-4: continue # # color = shs[gidx] # or precomputed # acccolor += color alpha accalpha # accalpha = (1.0 - alpha) # # if accalpha < 1e-4: break # # outimage[:, pixelv, pixelu] = acccolor # outalpha[:, pixelv, pixelu] = 1.0 - accalpha return outimage, outalpha A rasterization method that iterates over Gaussians rather than tiles, using axis-aligned bounding boxes to limit pixel iteration and transmittance-based early ray termination for performance optimization. It produces visually identical results to tiled rasterization in most cases but is significantly faster due to early stopping and better culling. A GPU compute shader pass that projects 3D Gaussian splats into 2D screen space, culls invisible splats, computes view-dependent lighting, and prepares data for tile-based sorting. It differs from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by handling the geometric projection, visibility culling, and sorting key generation, whereas the parent handles the actual pixel-level rasterization within tiles. It differs from Gaussian Splat View Data Calculation by focusing on the projection and sorting preparation rather than the evaluation of appearance (SH) and 4D state resolution, although both may coexist in different pipeline implementations. The Spirula Renderer is a GPU-accelerated Gaussian Splatting renderer implemented as a native Vulkan bridge (librosplatspirula.so) called via Python's ctypes. It handles tile sorting, Gaussian rasterization, and rendering to Vulkan textures. It explicitly excludes CUDA, PyTorch, gsplat, or OpenGL renderer paths. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by performing the tile sorting and rasterization internally during the render call. Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity is a specialized rendering pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting that produces clean depth maps by forcing all Gaussians to have uniform opacity and color. Unlike standard alpha-blending which weights depth by Gaussian opacity and transmittance, this method ensures that depth accumulation is driven purely by geometric distance and rasterization order, eliminating shading artifacts and opacity-induced depth bias. It is distinct from Depth Rendering with Variable Opacity, which respects the learned alpha values of the Gaussians. Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort is a GPU-parallel rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that divides the image into tiles to manage memory and processing load, assigning Gaussians to tiles based on their projected 2D splats Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-pixel sorting by using a single global radix sort to achieve per-tile depth ordering, enabling real-time performance for millions of splats Tile-based Rasteriser. Unlike sibling methods that may perform redundant depth sorting or evaluate splats against irrelevant pixels, this method ensures that each tile is processed by one GPU thread block walking a single sorted list Tile-based Rasteriser. This method modifies the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline to allow the camera pose to be overridden by an external tensor during rendering, rather than using the stored viewpoint parameters. It solves the problem of rendering a pre-trained Gaussian model from arbitrary or dynamically computed camera positions (e.g., from a SLAM system or a differentiable reconstruction loop) without retraining the model. It sets apart from standard rendering by injecting a custom world-to-camera transformation (relw2c) and quaternion rotation into the projection and covariance computation steps, enabling differentiable rendering with respect to the camera pose. A strategy to address uneven computational load across pixel threads in Gaussian rasterization by reducing the number of Gaussians rendered for heavy-load pixels and increasing it for light-load pixels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by explicitly optimizing the count of splats per pixel to balance GPU thread utilization, rather than just spatially partitioning the image. Half-cosine Squared Splatting is a radial basis function technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the standard Gaussian decay with a half-cosine squared function. It solves the problem of slow convergence and high memory usage in standard splatting by providing higher opacity values per primitive, allowing fewer primitives to achieve the same accumulated opacity. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by using a bounded decay profile that accelerates training and reduces memory footprint. This method optimizes the HSPT cut and Gaussian loading by storing SPT properties in a continuous GPU buffer and transferring Gaussians via a single copy operation, reorganizing them on the GPU into a Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout. It reduces PCIe bus traffic and kernel launch overhead inherent in hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. This method renders 3D Gaussians as tightly fitted, non-axis-aligned quads to minimize overdraw and improve rendering performance, particularly on mobile hardware. It differs from standard axis-aligned bounding box approaches by computing a rotated rectangle that incorporates the splat's alpha value, ensuring only relevant pixels are processed. DP-GES is a sort-free rendering method that combines 2D surfels with semi-transparent boundaries and 3D Gaussians to achieve high-fidelity novel view synthesis, eliminating aliasing and popping artifacts while enabling correct transmittance modulation. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization and sibling Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling by introducing a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 uses z-buffer-based depth peeling to extract the nearest three layers of depth, color, and opacity from surfels, and Stage 2 splats 3D Gaussians without sorting, modulating their weights by the transmittance from the peeled surfel layers. Unlike Gaussian-Enhanced Surfels (GES), which uses fully opaque surfels, DP-GES uses semi-transparent boundaries to mitigate aliasing from depth testing and allow differentiable joint optimization. Per-fragment Voxel-Cell Mask Injection is a technique for carving cube-shaped holes in 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by injecting a Signed Distance Field (SDF) evaluation into the fragment shader at runtime. It solves the visual artifacts caused by deleting whole splats (the "H2" baseline) by operating at the fragment level, producing clean, sharp cube edges without forking the underlying renderer. Unlike its sibling Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling which manages opacity globally, this method uses a 3D texture lookup to discard specific fragments, leaving neighboring voxels untouched. Thread-efficient partial rendering is a GPU rasterization optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to reduce the computational overhead of multi-view training. It solves the problem of low GPU utilization caused by naive binary masking in tiled rendering, where idle threads wait for active threads to finish. Unlike naive multi-view training which renders all pixels for all views, or naive partial rendering with masks which leaves most threads in a block idle, this method maintains the same number of training pixels as single-view training while maximizing parallelization by assigning multiple GPU blocks to a single tile. A differentiable rasterization method for 3D Gaussians that sorts Gaussians by tile and depth to perform alpha blending in parallel per tile. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of 3D Gaussian splats to a 2D screen while maintaining exact gradients for all Gaussian parameters (means, opacities, scales, rotations, spherical harmonics) via a CUDA backend. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by implementing the specific sorting, binning, and tile-based parallel rendering kernels required for the standard 3DGS forward and backward passes, often exposed as a torch.autograd.Function. vtkPointGaussianMapper renders point clouds as simple points or anisotropic 3D Gaussian splats without requiring vertex cells, supporting per-point scale, rotation, opacity, and emissive properties. It differs from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by operating in object-order on the CPU-side data structure and projecting Gaussians via a vertex shader rather than GPU-parallel tile-based rasterization, and from Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling by lacking transmittance culling and relying on standard OpenGL blending. Feature 3DGS is a method for rendering high-dimensional semantic feature maps alongside RGB images using 3D Gaussians, enabling the distillation of knowledge from 2D foundation models (such as SAM or LSeg) into an explicit 3D scene representation. It sets itself apart from NeRF-based feature field methods by using an explicit representation that avoids interference between the radiance and feature fields, allowing for equal-weighted joint optimization without the sensitivity to hyperparameters required by implicit neural networks. This method defines the rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian splats stored in glTF assets via the KHRgaussiansplatting extension, treating splats as point primitives with specific geometric and color attributes. It differs from general rasterization implementations by enforcing a strict data layout and transformation constraints defined by the glTF standard, ensuring interoperability and fallback to sparse point cloud rendering if the extension is unsupported. Softmax-GS is a rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that employs a softmax-based competition mechanism to handle overlapping Gaussians, aiming to provide order-invariance and smooth transitions at Gaussian boundaries. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which suffers from popping artifacts due to sorting dependencies, or StopThePop, which exhibits abrupt color changes, Softmax-GS produces flicker-free, smooth transitions by treating overlapping splats as a competitive blending process rather than a strict depth-sorted accumulation. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by replacing the standard alpha blending step with this differentiable, order-invariant softmax competition. XPR-3DGS is a point-based differentiable rendering method that implements 3D Gaussian Splatting within the XPR framework. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, culls tiles based on conic bounds, and evaluates alpha blending per pixel. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing a high-level, Python-based implementation that requires significantly fewer lines of code than traditional C++/CUDA implementations, while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering (SSVR) is a volume rendering technique used as an alternative to vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rasterization to improve geometric fidelity, particularly for depth and surface reconstruction. It produces RGB images nearly identical to standard 3DGS rasterization under suitable conditions but offers geometric advantages by reducing holes and blurred boundaries in depth maps. It is equivalent to 3DGS rasterization when an appropriate vacancy function is applied. The Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline is a differentiable GPU-based rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates view-dependent scaling (mip-splatting) to handle aliasing and resolution changes. It extends the tiled rasterization approach by using a kernelsize parameter to adjust the Gaussian projection scale, ensuring consistent visual quality across different camera distances and resolutions. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by adding specific preprocessing for mip-levels and a robust binning/sorting mechanism for tile-based rendering. SimpleRenderer is a CPU-based rendering method for 3D Gaussian point clouds that approximates Gaussian Splatting using a painter's algorithm. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen ellipses and composites them to generate an RGB image, suitable for visualization and small-scale point clouds where GPU acceleration is unavailable. Unlike standard 3DD Gaussian Splatting which relies on CUDA-based tile-based rasterization for performance and differentiability, SimpleRenderer uses a simplified 2D ellipse approximation and non-differentiable alpha blending. This method casts geometrically consistent shadows in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by comparing elevation renders from a satellite camera and a "sun camera," avoiding ray marching which is incompatible with the splatting primitive. It differs from NeRF-based shadowing (e.g., EO-NeRF) by relying solely on rasterization and elevation comparison rather than volumetric ray marching. Bounded Execution of Rasterization (BoundedGS) is a memory-constrained rasterization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that partitions the image into non-overlapping leaves to bound peak memory usage. It solves the problem of high memory peaks during training by processing leaves sequentially, releasing local state after each leaf, and accumulating gradients into a shared buffer. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by explicitly separating the rasterization and projection backward passes, ensuring that rasterization caches do not coexist with projection gradients, thereby reducing the mean working set significantly. CoherentRaster is a GPU-parallel rasterization pipeline designed for efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting on light field displays (LFDs), synthesizing interlaced light field images by separating view-dependent attributes from cluster-shared ones. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [13469-3d-gaussian-splatting-gpu.md] and tiled variants [2061-tiled-2d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md] by employing Cross-view Coherent Attribute Reuse to eliminate redundant projection computations and View-coherent Remapping to enable coalesced memory accesses during alpha blending. A method to compute a spatially varying depth within the projected 2D Gaussian, rather than using a constant depth per Gaussian splat, to capture shape details. Standard Gaussian Splatting evaluates the depth of each 2D Gaussian by its center to sort them for alpha blending; this constant depth cannot capture shape details. This method derives a rasterized formula for efficient evaluation of spatially varying depths within a projected Gaussian. Time Complexity: O(P \log P) for sorting, where P is the number of Gaussians. Rasterization is O(T \cdot N{avg}), where T is the number of tiles and N{avg} is the average number of Gaussians per tile. Memory Complexity: O(P + W \cdot H) for storing geometry, binning, and image buffers. Performance: Enables real-time rendering (60+ FPS) for scenes with millions of Gaussians on modern GPUs. Strengths: High parallelism, differentiable, efficient memory usage via tiling. Limitations: Restricted to pinhole cameras; sorting overhead can be significant for very sparse scenes; memory usage scales with image resolution. Originated with the 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). It was developed to enable real-time differentiable rendering of 3D Gaussian primitives, overcoming the slowness of volume rendering and the lack of differentiability in standard rasterization.
