name: Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling
body: A rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that iterates over Gaussians rather than tiles, using axis-aligned bounding boxes to limit pixel iteration and transmittance-based early ray termination for performance optimization. It produces visually identical results to tiled rasterization in most cases but is significantly faster due to early stopping and better culling. Inputs: gs: List of N Gaussians, each with 3D mean, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. camera: Camera object containing intrinsic parameters (fx, fy, cx, cy), image dimensions (W, H), and extrinsic rotation/translation. sigmamultiplier: Scaling factor for the 2D covariance approximation (default 3.33). Outputs: renderedimage: An H \times W \times 3 image tensor in uint8 format. Data Structures: umean, vmean: Projected 2D mean coordinates in pixel space. opacitygaussian: Scalar opacity value. shcolor: 3-channel color vector derived from SH evaluation. a, b, c: Elements of the inverse 2D covariance matrix (conics). umin, vmin, umax, vmax: Axis-aligned bounding box coordinates in pixel space. color, alpha: H \times W tensors initialized to zeros, accumulating final color and alpha per pixel. Steps: 1. Initialize color and alpha tensors to zeros. 2. Perform background initialization, projection, and sorting identical to rendersplats: transform means to camera space, project to image plane, frustum cull with fovmarginratio=0.3, sort Gaussians back-to-front, rotate covariances to camera space, approximate 2D covariances with eps2d=0.3, compute conics (a, b, c), evaluate SH colors, and compute AABBs. 3. Iterate over each Gaussian index i from 0 to len(gs). 4. Retrieve properties: umean, vmean, opacitygaussian, shcolor, a, b, c, umin, vmin, umax, vmax. 5. If opacitygaussian < 0.01, skip the Gaussian. 6. Iterate over pixels upix from umin to umax and vpix from vmin to vmax. 7. Check if pixel is within image bounds: if 0 <= upix < W and 0 <= vpix < H. 8. Read current pixel alpha. If alphapixel >= 0.99, skip the Gaussian for this pixel (early termination). 9. Compute squared Mahalanobis distance with half-pixel offset: du = u\pix + 0.5 - u\mean, dv = v\pix + 0.5 - v\mean, dist\sq = a \cdot du^2 + 2 \cdot b \cdot du \cdot dv + c \cdot dv^2. 10. Calculate Gaussian alpha \alphag = \exp(-0.5 \cdot dist\sq) \cdot opacity\gaussian and update pixel alpha and color using standard alpha blending. 11. After processing all Gaussians, add background and clamp/convert to uint8 as in rendersplats. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendersplatsfovculltransmittance(gs, camera, sigmamultiplier=3.33): W, H = camera.width, camera.height # Initialize color and alpha buffers color = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] alpha = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] # Preprocessing (projection, sorting, conics, AABBs) is identical to rendersplats. # Assume gs[i] now contains: umean, vmean, opacity, shcolor, conics (a,b,c), aabb (umin,vmin,umax,vmax) for i in range(len(gs)): umean, vmean = gs[i].umean, gs[i].vmean opacitygaussian = gs[i].opacity shcolor = gs[i].shcolor a, b, c = gs[i].conics umin, vmin, umax, vmax = gs[i].aabb if opacitygaussian < 0.01: continue for upix in range(umin, umax + 1): for vpix in range(vmin, vmax + 1): if 0 <= upix < W and 0 <= vpix < H: if alpha[vpix][upix] >= 0.99: continue du = upix + 0.5 - umean dv = vpix + 0.5 - vmean distsq = a du2 + 2 b du dv + c dv2 alphag = math.exp(-0.5 distsq) opacitygaussian currentalpha = alpha[vpix][upix] alphanew = currentalpha + alphag (1.0 - currentalpha) colornew = [ color[vpix][upix][0] + shcolor[0] alphag (1.0 - currentalpha), color[vpix][upix][1] + shcolor[1] alphag (1.0 - currentalpha), color[vpix][upix][2] + shcolor[2] alphag (1.0 - currentalpha) ] alpha[vpix][upix] = alphanew color[vpix][upix] = colornew # Add background color and clamp/convert to uint8 bgcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for v in range(H): for u in range(W): for c in range(3): color[v][u][c] = color[v][u][c] + bgcolor[c] (1.0 - alpha[v][u]) color[v][u][c] = max(0.0, min(1.0, color[v][u][c])) return [[int(c 255) for c in row] for row in color] Edge cases and pitfalls: Low-opacity Gaussians (opacitygaussian < 0.01) are skipped entirely to save computation. Fully opaque pixels (alphapixel >= 0.99) trigger early termination for subsequent Gaussians, preventing redundant blending. The half-pixel offset in the Mahalanobis distance calculation aligns the Gaussian center with pixel sampling coordinates. Bounding box iteration must be clamped to image dimensions to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Performance: Significantly faster than tiled rasterization due to early stopping and better culling, while producing visually identical results in most cases. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Use when Gaussian-order iteration with transmittance culling yields better performance than tile-based rasterization, particularly for scenes where early termination is effective. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method is part of the splaty library, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting. sascha-kirch/splaty, https://github.com/sascha-kirch/splaty, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Projection and Sorting
head: Staging Splats
body: Gaussian Splat Projection and Sorting is a GPU compute shader pass that projects 3D Gaussian splats into 2D screen space, culls invisible splats, computes view-dependent lighting, and prepares data for tile-based sorting. It differs from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by handling the geometric projection, visibility culling, and sorting key generation, whereas the parent handles the actual pixel-level rasterization within tiles. It differs from Gaussian Splat View Data Calculation by focusing on the projection and sorting preparation rather than the evaluation of appearance (SH) and 4D state resolution, although both may coexist in different pipeline implementations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: SplatsBuffer: Array of Splat structs (std430). SplatInstanceIdsBuffer: Array of uvec2 where x is the unique instance ID and y is the index into SplatsBuffer. InstanceTransformsBuffer: Array of mat4 model matrices. Uniforms: camerapos (vec3), time (float), dims (ivec2, texture size), pointcount (int), lightcount (int). LightRigBuffer: Array of vec4 lights. InstanceRelightBuffer: Array of vec4 per instance. SplatLightingBuffer: Array of uint per splat (packed normals/AO). Outputs: CulledBuffer: Array of RasterizeData structs containing projected data for visible splats. SortKeysBuffer: Array of uint keys for radix sort. SortValuesBuffer: Array of uint values (original splat indices). Histograms: sortbuffersize (atomic counter) and histogram data. Data Structures: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Splat { vec3 position; float time; float covariance[6]; // Top triangle of symmetric 3x3 matrix float opacity; float pad; float shcoefficients[163]; // SH coefficients, degree 3 }; struct RasterizeData { vec2 imagepos; vec2 posxy; vec3 conic; // Inverse 2D covariance: (covz, -covxy, covx) / det float posz; vec4 color; // RGB + opacity vec4 depthdata; // z-depth info }; Constants: TILESIZE: 16. SHC0 to SHC36: Spherical harmonic constants. DECODECOVARIANCE(c): Reconstructs mat3 from 6 floats: mat3(c[0], c[1], c[2], c[1], c[3], c[4], c[2], c[4], c[5]). Steps: 1. Initialization: Get glGlobalInvocationID.x. If id >= pointcount, return. 2. Barrier: Synchronize workgroup. 3. Instance Data: Retrieve instanceid = splatinstancedata[id].x and uniquesplatindex = splatinstancedata[id].y. 4. Load Data: Load splat = splatbuffer[uniquesplatindex] and modelmatrix = instancemodelmatrices[instanceid]. 5. Visibility Check: If modelmatrix[0][3] < 0.5, return. Set modelmatrix[0][3] = 0.0. 6. Frustum Culling: Compute worldcovariance = objectlinear DECODECOVARIANCE(splat.covariance) transpose(objectlinear). Compute worldpos = modelmatrix vec4(splat.position, 1.0). Compute viewpos = viewmatrix worldpos. Compute clippos = projectionmatrix viewpos. Set viewbounds = clippos.w 1.2. If any(clippos.xyz < vec3(-viewbounds, -viewbounds, 0.0)) or any(clippos.xyz > vec3(viewbounds, viewbounds, clippos.w)), return. 7. Time Animation: Compute splattime = time - splat.time. Compute timefactor = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime, 0, 1)). Compute timefactorlate = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime - 0.35, 0, 1)). Compute splatopacity = splat.opacity timefactorlate timefactorlate. Compute splatscale = mix(2.0, 1.0, timefactorlate). easeoutcubic(x) = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - x, 3.0). 8. Project Covariance: Compute cov3d = worldcovariance splatscale^2. Compute tanfovinv = vec2(projectionmatrix[0][0], projectionmatrix[1][1]). Compute focal = (dims - 1) 0.5 tanfovinv (-1.0 / viewpos.z). Clamp mean.xy = clamp(viewpos.xy (-1.0 / viewpos.z), -tanfov 1.3, tanfov 1.3). Compute jacobian = mat3(focal.x, 0, 0, 0, focal.y, 0, focal.x mean.x, focal.y mean.y, 0). Compute screentransform = jacobian viewmatrix[:3,:3]. Compute cov2d = screentransform cov3d transpose(screentransform). Result: vec3(cov2d[0][0] + 0.3, cov2d[0][1], cov2d[1][1] + 0.3). 9. Determinant Check: det = covariance.x covariance.z - covariance.y covariance.y. If det == 0.0, return. 10. Eigenvalues: mid = 0.5 (covariance.x + covariance.z). eigenvalues = mid + vec2(1, -1) sqrt(max(0.1, mid mid - det)). If any(eigenvalues < 0), return. 11. Image Position: ndcpos = clippos.xyz / clippos.w. imagepos = ((ndcpos.xy + 1.0) 0.5 - vec2(1, 0.75) (1.0 - timefactor)) (dims - 1). 12. Radius: radius = pow(splatopacity, 0.2) 2.5 sqrt(max(eigenvalues.x, eigenvalues.y)). 13. Tile Bounds: gridsize = (dims + TILESIZE - 1) / TILESIZE. rectbounds = getrect(imagepos, radius, gridsize). getrect returns uvec4(clamp((imagepos - radius) / TILESIZE, vec2(0), gridsize), clamp(ceil((imagepos + radius) / TILESIZE), vec2(0), gridsize)). 14. Tile Count: numtilestouched = (rectbounds.z - rectbounds.x) (rectbounds.w - rectbounds.y). If numtilestouched == 0, return. 15. Atomic Sort Buffer: buffersize = atomicAdd(sortbuffersize, numtilestouched). sortbufferoffset = buffersize. 16. View Direction: viewdir = normalize(inverse(objectlinear) (worldpos.xyz - camerapos)). 17. Base Color: basecolor = getcolor(viewdir, splat.shcoefficients). Evaluates SH up to degree 3. 18. Relighting: If instancerelight[instanceid 2].w > 0.5: If instancerelight[instanceid 2].z > 0.5, basecolor = max(0.0, 0.5 + splat.shcoefficients[0..2] SHC0). Else, basecolor = relightfactor(uniquesplatindex, worldpos.xyz, objectlinear, relight.x, relight.y, instancerelight[instanceid2+1].rgb). 19. Fill RasterizeData: data.imagepos = imagepos. data.conic = vec3(covariance.z, -covariance.y, covariance.x) / det. data.color = vec4(basecolor, splatopacity). data.posxy = worldpos.xy. data.posz = worldpos.z. data.depthdata = vec4(-viewpos.z, 0, 0, 0). Write to culledbuffer[id]. 20. Sorting Keys: viewdepth = max(0.0, clippos.w). depth01 = viewdepth / (1.0 + viewdepth). depth = uint(depth01 65535.0) & 0xFFFF. Loop y from rectbounds.y to rectbounds.w, x from rectbounds.x to rectbounds.z: tileid = y gridsize.x + x. key = (tileid << 16) | depth. sortkeys[sortbufferoffset] = key. sortvalues[sortbufferoffset] = id. sortbufferoffset++. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. TILESIZE = 16 SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 def gaussiansplatprojectionandsorting(id, pointcount, splatbuffer, instancedata, modelmatrices, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, camerapos, time, dims, lightrig, instancerelight, splatlighting, sortbuffersize, sortkeys, sortvalues, culledbuffer, griddims, tanfov): if id >= pointcount: return instanceid = instancedata[id].x uniquesplatindex = instancedata[id].y splat = splatbuffer[uniquesplatindex] modelmatrix = modelmatrices[instanceid] # Visibility check if modelmatrix[0][3] < 0.5: return modelmatrix[0][3] = 0.0 # Frustum culling objectlinear = modelmatrix[:3,:3] worldcovariance = objectlinear @ decodecovariance(splat.covariance) @ objectlinear.T worldpos = modelmatrix @ vec4(splat.position, 1.0) viewpos = viewmatrix @ worldpos clippos = projectionmatrix @ viewpos viewbounds = clippos.w 1.2 if any(clippos.xyz < vec3(-viewbounds, -viewbounds, 0.0)) or any(clippos.xyz > vec3(viewbounds, viewbounds, clippos.w)): return # Time animation splattime = time - splat.time timefactor = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime, 0, 1)) timefactorlate = easeoutcubic(clamp(splattime - 0.35, 0, 1)) splatopacity = splat.opacity timefactorlate timefactorlate splatscale = mix(2.0, 1.0, timefactorlate) # Project covariance cov3d = worldcovariance (splatscale 2) tanfovinv = vec2(projectionmatrix[0][0], projectionmatrix[1][1]) focal = (dims - 1) 0.5 tanfovinv (-1.0 / viewpos.z) meanxy = clamp(viewpos.xy (-1.0 / viewpos.z), -tanfov 1.3, tanfov 1.3) jacobian = mat3(focal.x, 0, 0, 0, focal.y, 0, focal.x meanxy.x, focal.y meanxy.y, 0) screentransform = jacobian @ viewmatrix[:3,:3] cov2d = screentransform @ cov3d @ screentransform.T covariance = vec3(cov2d[0][0] + 0.3, cov2d[0][1], cov2d[1][1] + 0.3) # Determinant and eigenvalues det = covariance.x covariance.z - covariance.y 2 if det == 0.0: return mid = 0.5 (covariance.x + covariance.z) eigenvalues = mid + vec2(1, -1) sqrt(max(0.1, mid 2 - det)) if any(eigenvalues < 0): return # Image position ndcpos = clippos.xyz / clippos.w imagepos = ((ndcpos.xy + 1.0) 0.5 - vec2(1, 0.75) (1.0 - timefactor)) (dims - 1) # Radius radius = (splatopacity 0.2) 2.5 sqrt(max(eigenvalues.x, eigenvalues.y)) # Tile bounds gridsize = (dims + TILESIZE - 1) / TILESIZE rectbounds = getrect(imagepos, radius, gridsize) numtilestouched = (rectbounds.z - rectbounds.x) (rectbounds.w - rectbounds.y) if numtilestouched == 0: return # Atomic sort buffer buffersize = atomicadd(sortbuffersize, numtilestouched) sortbufferoffset = buffersize # View direction and color viewdir = normalize(inverse(objectlinear) @ (worldpos.xyz - camerapos)) basecolor = getcolor(viewdir, splat.shcoefficients) # Relighting if instancerelight[instanceid 2].w > 0.5: if instancerelight[instanceid 2].z > 0.5: basecolor = max(0.0, 0.5 + splat.shcoefficients[0:3] SHC0) else: basecolor = relightfactor(uniquesplatindex, worldpos.xyz, objectlinear, instancerelight[instanceid 2].xyz) # Fill RasterizeData data = RasterizeData() data.imagepos = imagepos data.conic = vec3(covariance.z, -covariance.y, covariance.x) / det data.color = vec4(basecolor, splatopacity) data.posxy = worldpos.xy data.posz = worldpos.z data.depthdata = vec4(-viewpos.z, 0, 0, 0) culledbuffer[id] = data # Sorting keys viewdepth = max(0.0, clippos.w) depth01 = viewdepth / (1.0 + viewdepth) depth = int(depth01 65535.0) & 0xFFFF for y in range(rectbounds.y, rectbounds.w): for x in range(rectbounds.x, rectbounds.z): tileid = y gridsize.x + x key = (tileid << 16) | depth sortkeys[sortbufferoffset] = key sortvalues[sortbufferoffset] = id sortbufferoffset += 1 def decodecovariance(c): return mat3(c[0], c[1], c[2], c[1], c[3], c[4], c[2], c[4], c[5]) def easeoutcubic(x): return 1.0 - (1.0 - x) 3 def getrect(imagepos, radius, gridsize): minx = clamp((imagepos.x - radius) / TILESIZE, 0, gridsize.x) miny = clamp((imagepos.y - radius) / TILESIZE, 0, gridsize.y) maxx = clamp(ceil((imagepos.x + radius) / TILESIZE), 0, gridsize.x) maxy = clamp(ceil((imagepos.y + radius) / TILESIZE), 0, gridsize.y) return uvec4(minx, miny, maxx, maxy) def getcolor(viewdir, shcoeffs): # Evaluates SH up to degree 3 using constants SHC0..SHC36 and coefficients from splat.shcoefficients # Standard SH evaluation implementation omitted for brevity return vec3(0.0) def relightfactor(uniquesplatindex, worldpos, objectlinear, relightparams): # Not given in the sources return 1.0 class RasterizeData: def init(self): self.imagepos = vec2(0, 0) self.posxy = vec2(0, 0) self.conic = vec3(0, 0, 0) self.posz = 0.0 self.color = vec4(0, 0, 0, 0) self.depthdata = vec4(0, 0, 0, 0) Parameters: TILESIZE: 16. SHC0 to SHC36: Spherical harmonic constants. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use float for covariance and depth calculations. Clamp values to avoid NaNs. Boundaries: Handle edge cases where det is zero or eigenvalues are negative. Degenerate Input: If numtilestouched is zero, skip the splat. Time Complexity: O(N) for N splats, with additional O(T) for tile sorting preparation, where T is the number of tiles touched. Memory Complexity: O(N) for CulledBuffer, O(T) for SortKeysBuffer and SortValuesBuffer. Performance: Efficient for large numbers of splats due to parallel compute shader execution. Strengths: Handles complex transformations, lighting, and sorting in a single pass. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of parameters like TILESIZE and viewbounds. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines, specifically in implementations like and. It is used to prepare splats for efficient tile-based rasterization. name: Gaussian Splat View Data Calculation
head: FGaussianSplatCalcViewDataCS
body: A GPU compute shader that transforms Gaussian splats to screen space, evaluates view-dependent spherical harmonics, and handles 4D temporal or native 4D transformations per frame. It serves as the final preparation step before sorting and rasterization, handling complex 4D temporal variations (keyframe interpolation, temporal marginalization, or native 4D primitives) and advanced culling mechanisms (cluster-based, LOD, and distance-based). It differs from its parent Gaussian Splat Projection and Sorting by focusing specifically on the evaluation of appearance (SH), 4D state resolution, and the population of the ViewDataBuffer with screen-space attributes required for the subsequent tiled rasterization pass. Inputs: Splat Data: PackedSplatBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 16 bytes/splat. Contains position, rotation (quaternion), scale, and opacity. SHBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer. Stores spherical harmonic coefficients. TemporalBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 16 bytes/splat. Used for temporal marginalization (velocity/motion). KeyframeBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 64 bytes/splat/frame. Stores baked splat data for keyframe-based 4D rendering. Native4DBuffer: ByteAddressBuffer, 80 bytes/splat. Stores dual-quaternion rotations and spherindrical harmonic coefficients for native 4D primitives. Culling/Visibility Data: SplatClusterIndexBuffer: StructuredBuffer<uint>. Maps splat indices to clusters. ClusterVisibilityBitmap: StructuredBuffer<uint>. Bitmask of visible clusters. LODClusterSelectedBitmap: StructuredBuffer<uint>. Bitmask for LOD cluster visibility. SelectedClusterBuffer: StructuredBuffer<uint>. List of selected cluster indices. CompactedSplatIndices: StructuredBuffer<uint>. List of visible splat indices (used if compaction is enabled). Transform Matrices: LocalToWorld: FMatrix44f. WorldToPLY: FMatrix44f. Transforms world directions to PLY/SH space for SH evaluation. WorldToClip: FMatrix44f. WorldToView: FMatrix44f. Camera/Scene Parameters: CameraPosition: FVector3f. ScreenSize: FVector2f. FocalLength: FVector2f. PreViewTranslation: FVector3f. Used for velocity calculation; TranslatedWorld = World + PreViewTranslation. Control Flags & Counts: SplatCount: Total splats to process. UseKeyframes, UseTemporal, UseNative4D: Boolean flags (uint32) enabling specific 4D modes. KeyframeSplatCount (M), KeyframeFrameCount (N), KeyframeFrameTime. Native4DSplatCount. TimeDuration (l). SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs, SHBufferCoeffs. UseSHRendering, OpacityScale, SplatScale. MaxDrawDistance, FadeOutStartDistance. UseClusterCulling, UseLODRendering, UseCompaction, UseGlobalCompactionPath. VisibleSplatCount, OriginalSplatCount, MaxRenderBudget. GlobalBaseOffset, ProxyIndex. TimeWeightMinAlpha. Outputs: ViewDataBuffer: RWStructuredBuffer<FGaussianSplatViewData>. Contains screen-space position, covariance, color (evaluated SH), opacity, and depth/visibility flags for each active splat. The output structure FGaussianSplatViewData is not explicitly defined in the source notes. Based on standard Gaussian Splatting rasterization requirements, it contains at least: float3 or float4 screen-space position (x, y, z/w); float3x3 or float4x4 2D covariance matrix (or its Cholesky decomposition/affine parameters); float3 or float4 color (RGB/RGBA); float opacity; uint or float depth/z-value; uint cluster index or visibility flags. Parameters are passed as shader constants or buffers. THREADGROUPSIZE is defined as 256 during shader compilation. SHOrder determines the spherical harmonic order, with NumSHCoeffs derived as (L+1)^2 for order L (commonly 4, 9, or 16). SHBufferCoeffs indicates the number of coefficients actually stored per splat based on asset SHBands. MaxDrawDistance sets the distance-based visibility range, where 0 means unlimited. FadeOutStartDistance defines the distance at which splats begin to fade out. MaxRenderBudget caps the write index, where 0 means no cap. UseKeyframes, UseTemporal, and UseNative4D are uint32 flags enabling keyframe-based 4D rendering, 4D temporal marginalization, and Fudan native 4D (dual-quaternion rotation + spherindrical harmonics), respectively. KeyframeSplatCount (M), KeyframeFrameCount (N), and KeyframeFrameTime control keyframe interpolation. Native4DSplatCount specifies the number of splats covered by the Native4DBuffer. TimeDuration (l) is the time duration (TimeEnd - TimeStart) for native 4D SH evaluation. UseSHRendering, OpacityScale, and SplatScale control appearance rendering and scaling. UseClusterCulling, UseLODRendering, UseCompaction, and UseGlobalCompactionPath enable cluster culling, LOD rendering, compaction processing, and global base offset reading, respectively. VisibleSplatCount and OriginalSplatCount track visible splats and the boundary where LOD splats start. GlobalBaseOffset and ProxyIndex manage buffer offsets for the non-compaction and global compaction paths. PreViewTranslation is used for velocity calculation (TranslatedWorld = World + PreViewTranslation). CameraPosition, ScreenSize, and FocalLength define the camera state. TimeWeightMinAlpha sets the minimum alpha threshold for temporal weighting. 1. Dispatch Setup: The shader is dispatched with THREADGROUPSIZE = 256. The thread group count is derived from SplatCount or VisibleSplatCount. 2. Splat Index Resolution: If UseCompaction is true, the thread ID maps to CompactedSplatIndices to retrieve the original splat index. If UseGlobalCompactionPath is true, the base offset is read from GlobalBaseOffsetsBuffer[ProxyIndex]; otherwise, GlobalBaseOffset is used directly. 3. 4D State Evaluation: The active 4D mode is selected by priority: UseNative4D > UseKeyframes > UseTemporal. Native 4D reads dual-quaternion rotations and spherindrical SH from Native4DBuffer, interpolating based on CurrentTime and TimeDuration (l). Keyframe mode interpolates between KeyframeFrameTime and adjacent frames using KeyframeBuffer, applying slerp for rotation. Temporal marginalization reads velocity/motion from TemporalBuffer, extrapolates position using CurrentTime and PreViewTranslation, and adjusts covariance for temporal variance. Static mode reads directly from PackedSplatBuffer. 4. Visibility Culling: Distance culling checks CameraPosition against MaxDrawDistance (0 disables it) and applies a fade-out factor if distance exceeds FadeOutStartDistance. Cluster culling (UseClusterCulling) checks SplatClusterIndexBuffer against ClusterVisibilityBitmap and LODClusterSelectedBitmap (if UseLODRendering). LOD rendering filters splats with index \ge OriginalSplatCount. 5. Projection to Screen Space: The splat center is transformed to clip space via WorldToClip, then projected to screen coordinates using ScreenSize and FocalLength. The 2D covariance is computed by transforming the 3D covariance with the projection Jacobian. 6. Spherical Harmonics Evaluation: If UseSHRendering is true, the view direction is transformed to PLY/SH space via WorldToPLY, and SH coefficients from SHBuffer (or Native4DBuffer) are evaluated. OpacityScale and SplatScale are applied to the result. 7. Write View Data: Computed attributes are written to ViewDataBuffer at baseoffset + globalidx. Writes are skipped if MaxRenderBudget is set and the index \ge MaxRenderBudget. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. THREADGROUPSIZE = 256 def evaluatesh(viewdirply, shcoeffs, shorder, numcoeffs): """Evaluates spherical harmonics for a given view direction.""" # Standard SH evaluation: sum over l, m of Yl^m(theta, phi) cl^m color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Standard implementation iterates through coefficients and applies basis functions for i in range(numcoeffs): # Basis function evaluation depends on shorder and viewdirply # color[0] += shcoeffs[i 3] basis[i] # color[1] += shcoeffs[i 3 + 1] basis[i] # color[2] += shcoeffs[i 3 + 2] basis[i] pass return color def slerp(q1, q2, t): """Spherical linear interpolation of quaternions.""" # Standard slerp: normalize(q1 (1-t) + q2 t) or dot-product based return q1 def interpolatedualquaternion(dq1, dq2, t): """Interpolates dual quaternions for native 4D.""" # Standard dual quaternion interpolation: slerp for rotation, lerp for translation return dq1 def main(threadidx, UseCompaction, CompactedSplatIndices, SplatCount, UseGlobalCompactionPath, GlobalBaseOffsetsBuffer, ProxyIndex, GlobalBaseOffset, UseNative4D, Native4DBuffer, CurrentTime, TimeDuration, UseKeyframes, KeyframeFrameTime, KeyframeBuffer, UseTemporal, TemporalBuffer, PreViewTranslation, PackedSplatBuffer, SplatScale, OpacityScale, MaxDrawDistance, FadeOutStartDistance, CameraPosition, UseClusterCulling, SplatClusterIndexBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmap, UseLODRendering, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, OriginalSplatCount, WorldToClip, ScreenSize, FocalLength, WorldToPLY, UseSHRendering, SHBuffer, Native4DSplatCount, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs, SHBufferCoeffs, MaxRenderBudget, GlobalBaseOffset): globalidx = threadidx splatidx = CompactedSplatIndices[globalidx] if UseCompaction else globalidx if splatidx >= SplatCount: return baseoffset = GlobalBaseOffsetsBuffer[ProxyIndex] if UseGlobalCompactionPath else GlobalBaseOffset pos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] rot = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] scale = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] opacity = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if UseNative4D: # Native 4D interpolation logic not detailed in sources pos = Native4DBuffer[splatidx].pos rot = interpolatedualquaternion(Native4DBuffer[splatidx].dq1, Native4DBuffer[splatidx].dq2, CurrentTime / TimeDuration) scale = Native4DBuffer[splatidx].scale opacity = Native4DBuffer[splatidx].opacity viewdir = [CameraPosition[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)] viewdirply = [sum(WorldToPLY[i][j] viewdir[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] color = evaluatesh(viewdirply, Native4DBuffer[splatidx].shcoeffs, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs) elif UseKeyframes: # Keyframe interpolation logic not detailed in sources pos = KeyframeBuffer[splatidx].pos rot = slerp(KeyframeBuffer[splatidx].rot1, KeyframeBuffer[splatidx].rot2, KeyframeFrameTime) scale = KeyframeBuffer[splatidx].scale opacity = KeyframeBuffer[splatidx].opacity viewdir = [CameraPosition[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)] viewdirply = [sum(WorldToPLY[i][j] viewdir[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] color = evaluatesh(viewdirply, SHBuffer[splatidx].shcoeffs, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs) elif UseTemporal: # Temporal marginalization logic not detailed in sources pos = [TemporalBuffer[splatidx].pos[i] + PreViewTranslation[i] CurrentTime for i in range(3)] rot = TemporalBuffer[splatidx].rot scale = TemporalBuffer[splatidx].scale opacity = TemporalBuffer[splatidx].opacity viewdir = [CameraPosition[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)] viewdirply = [sum(WorldToPLY[i][j] viewdir[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] color = evaluatesh(viewdirply, SHBuffer[splatidx].shcoeffs, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs) else: pos = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].pos rot = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].rot scale = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].scale opacity = PackedSplatBuffer[splatidx].opacity viewdir = [CameraPosition[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)] viewdirply = [sum(WorldToPLY[i][j] viewdir[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] color = evaluatesh(viewdirply, SHBuffer[splatidx].shcoeffs, SHOrder, NumSHCoeffs) scale = [s SplatScale for s in scale] opacity = OpacityScale dist = sum((pos[i] - CameraPosition[i])2 for i in range(3))0.5 if MaxDrawDistance > 0.0 and dist > MaxDrawDistance: return if dist > FadeOutStartDistance: fade = (dist - FadeOutStartDistance) / (MaxDrawDistance - FadeOutStartDistance) if MaxDrawDistance > FadeOutStartDistance else 0.0 opacity = max(0.0, 1.0 - min(1.0, fade)) if UseClusterCulling: clusteridx = SplatClusterIndexBuffer[splatidx] if not (ClusterVisibilityBitmap[clusteridx // 32] & (1 << (clusteridx % 32))): return if UseLODRendering and splatidx >= OriginalSplatCount: if not (LODClusterSelectedBitmap[clusteridx // 32] & (1 << (clusteridx % 32))): return clipposw = sum(WorldToClip[3][j] (pos[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) screenpos = [(sum(WorldToClip[i][j] (pos[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) / clipposw) ScreenSize[i] for i in range(2)] depth = (sum(WorldToClip[2][j] (pos[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) / clipposw) writeidx = baseoffset + globalidx if MaxRenderBudget == 0 or writeidx < MaxRenderBudget: # ViewDataBuffer write operation pass Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise during 4D interpolation, especially for large time durations or extreme scales. Boundaries: Ensure SplatCount and VisibleSplatCount are correctly synchronized with the input buffers. Degenerate Input: If MaxDrawDistance is 0, distance culling is disabled. If SHOrder is 0, SH evaluation simplifies to a constant color. Buffer Overflows: MaxRenderBudget is critical to prevent writing beyond the allocated ViewDataBuffer size. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of splats, as each splat is processed independently in parallel. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the ViewDataBuffer, with input buffers being read-only. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of splats and 4D evaluation complexity, with native 4D being more expensive than keyframe or temporal modes. Strengths: Handles complex 4D variations efficiently on the GPU and supports advanced culling mechanisms. Limitations: Requires DirectX 12 / Shader Model 6, crashes on non-ASCII paths, and has limited support for proprietary 4D formats. When to Use: Real-time rendering of 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting scenes in Unreal Engine 5. When Not to Use: Offline rendering, non-UE5 environments, or unsupported proprietary 4D formats. The method is part of the OpenSplat4D plugin for Unreal Engine 5, developed by YuanBaoSMadLab. It supports various 4D Gaussian Splatting techniques, including Spacetime Gaussians (STG), Fudan 4DGS, and keyframe-based 4DGS. The plugin aims to provide real-time rendering capabilities for 4D Gaussian Splatting in game engines. name: Spirula Renderer
head: Spirula Bridge, Spirula Renderer API, Spirula Vulkan bridge
body: The Spirula Renderer is a GPU-accelerated Gaussian Splatting renderer implemented as a native Vulkan bridge (librosplatspirula.so) called via Python's ctypes. It handles tile sorting, Gaussian rasterization, and rendering to Vulkan textures. It explicitly excludes CUDA, PyTorch, gsplat, or OpenGL renderer paths. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by performing the tile sorting and rasterization internally during the render call. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Contiguous numpy arrays for Gaussian properties (means, quaternions, log-scales, opacity logits, SH coefficients), camera parameters (view/projection matrices or intrinsics), and render options. Outputs: A caller-owned uint8t buffer (RGBA8, Depth, or Opacity) populated by the renderer. Data Structures: The renderer manages a device-resident scene. The C API exposes the following structures for device enumeration: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. typedef struct { char name[256]; uint64t vrambytes; int usable; } RosplatSpirulaDeviceInfo; The output mode is defined by: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. typedef enum { ROSPLATSPIRULAOUTPUTCOLOR = 0, ROSPLATSPIRULAOUTPUTDEPTH = 1, ROSPLATSPIRULAOUTPUTOPACITY = 2 } RosplatSpirulaOutputMode; Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the native library from candidate paths: environment variable ROSPLATSPIRULALIBRARY, build directories, or /opt/rosplat-native/lib/rosplat/. Count available Vulkan devices and select device 0, verifying it is usable. 2. Scene Reset: Call rosplatspirularesetscene(degree, reserve). degree: Spherical Harmonics (SH) degree (0-4). reserve: Number of Gaussians to pre-allocate. Constraint: The SH dimension must be divisible by 3. The number of coefficients (dim/3) must be a perfect square. The resulting degree (\sqrt{coefficients} - 1) must be between 0 and 4 inclusive. Streaming scenes cannot change SH degree after initialization. 3. Data Preparation: Convert Gaussian data into contiguous numpy arrays. means: float32 array of shape [count, 3] (xyz positions). quats: float32 array of shape [count, 4] (rotations, wxyz). logscales: float32 array of shape [count, 3]. Computed as \log(\text{scale} \times \text{scale\modifier}). The scalemodifier is a float multiplier applied to Gaussian scales before conversion to log space (default 1.0, must be positive). Values are clipped to a minimum of 10^{-12}. opacitylogits: float32 array of shape [count, 1]. Computed as \text{logit}(\text{opacity}). Opacity values are clipped to [10^{-6}, 1-10^{-6}] before computing logits to avoid singularities. dc: float32 array of shape [count, 3] (DC component of SH, first coefficient). higher: float32 array of shape [count, coefficients-1, 3] (higher-order SH coefficients), or None if only DC components are used. 4. Appending Gaussians: Call rosplatspirulaappend(count, meansptr, quatsptr, logscalesptr, opacitylogitsptr, dcptr, higherptr) to add Gaussians to the scene. Pointers must reference contiguous memory. The SH degree cannot change during streaming. 5. Camera Update: Call rosplatspirulasetcamera(width, height, viewmatrixptr, projmatrixptr) or equivalent intrinsics setter. The renderer marks cameradirty when the model matrix or resolution changes. Camera Convention: OpenCV (+Z forward, +Y down, row-major world-to-camera). OpenGL Conversion: If using OpenGL view matrices, convert to OpenCV convention using gl\to\cv = \text{diag}([1.0, -1.0, -1.0, 1.0]) and compute view{cv} = gl\to\cv \times view{gl} \times model\matrix. Intrinsics: If using focal length and field of view, calculate focal length as f = h / (2.0 \times \tan(fovy / 2.0)). The intrinsics array is [f, f, w/2.0, h/2.0]. 6. Render Options: Call rosplatspirulasetrenderoptions(mode, activeshdegree). mode: Output buffer mode (COLOR=0, DEPTH=1, OPACITY=2). activeshdegree: Active SH degree for rendering (-1 for scene maximum, or 0-4). 7. Rendering: Call rosplatspirularenderrgba8(outputbufferptr, buffersize). Renders top-to-bottom. Tile sorting and radix sorting are performed internally every render. outputbufferptr: Pointer to caller-owned uint8t buffer. buffersize: Size of the buffer in bytes. 8. Shutdown: Call rosplatspirulashutdown() to release resources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import ctypes import os import numpy as np class RosplatSpirulaDeviceInfo(ctypes.Structure): fields = [("name", ctypes.cchar 256), ("vrambytes", ctypes.cuint64), ("usable", ctypes.cint)] class SpirulaRenderer: def init(self, width, height, shdegree=1, reserve=0): libpath = os.environ.get('ROSPLATSPIRULALIBRARY', '/opt/rosplat-native/lib/rosplat/librosplatspirula.so') self.lib = ctypes.CDLL(libpath) # Count devices, select device 0, and verify it is usable self.lib.rosplatspirularesetscene(shdegree, reserve) self.width = width self.height = height def appendgaussians(self, means, quats, scales, opacity, shdc, shhigher=None): scalemodifier = 1.0 logscales = np.log(np.clip(scales scalemodifier, 1e-12, np.inf)) opacityclipped = np.clip(opacity, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6) opacitylogits = np.log(opacityclipped / (1 - opacityclipped)) means = np.ascontiguousarray(means, dtype=np.float32) quats = np.ascontiguousarray(quats, dtype=np.float32) logscales = np.ascontiguousarray(logscales, dtype=np.float32) opacitylogits = np.ascontiguousarray(opacitylogits, dtype=np.float32) shdc = np.ascontiguousarray(shdc, dtype=np.float32) higherptr = None if shhigher is not None: shhigher = np.ascontiguousarray(shhigher, dtype=np.float32) higherptr = shhigher.ctypes.data count = len(means) self.lib.rosplatspirulaappend( count, means.ctypes.data, quats.ctypes.data, logscales.ctypes.data, opacitylogits.ctypes.data, shdc.ctypes.data, higherptr) def setcamera(self, viewmatrix, projmatrix): viewcv = np.ascontiguousarray(viewmatrix, dtype=np.float32) projcv = np.ascontiguousarray(projmatrix, dtype=np.float32) self.lib.rosplatspirulasetcamera( self.width, self.height, viewcv.ctypes.data, projcv.ctypes.data) def setrenderoptions(self, mode, shdegree): self.lib.rosplatspirulasetrenderoptions(mode, shdegree) def render(self): buffersize = self.width self.height 4 outputbuffer = (ctypes.cuint8 buffersize)() self.lib.rosplatspirularenderrgba8( outputbuffer, buffersize) return np.ctypeslib.asarray(outputbuffer, shape=(self.height, self.width, 4)) def shutdown(self): self.lib.rosplatspirulashutdown() Hardware Requirements: Requires a Vulkan 1.2-capable GPU. Specifically requires Vulkan buffer device addresses and timeline semaphores. Performance: Tile sorting and radix sorting are performed internally every render call. The renderer is optimized for streaming Gaussian data via ROS2 messages, handling batched appends efficiently. Limitations: Explicitly excludes CUDA, PyTorch, gsplat, or OpenGL renderer paths. It relies on the wgpu-py Vulkan backend for UI rendering. Memory: Scene capacity is managed via reserve during reset. Subsequent appends may trigger internal reallocation if capacity is exceeded, though the exact growth strategy is not detailed in the sources. The Spirula Renderer is part of the ROSplat project, which integrates Gaussian Splatting with ROS2. It was developed to provide a portable Vulkan rendering backend for Gaussian Splatting, avoiding dependencies on CUDA or PyTorch. The project acknowledges influence from the original Gaussian Splatting implementation by graphdeco-inria and the GaussianSplattingViewer repository by limacv. It is designed to run on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS with ROS 2 Lyrical. Gaussian Splatting Meets ROS2, https://github.com/shadygm/ROSplat, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity
head: Depth-Only Rendering Mode
body: Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity is a specialized rendering pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting that produces clean depth maps by forcing all Gaussians to have uniform opacity and color. Unlike standard alpha-blending which weights depth by Gaussian opacity and transmittance, this method ensures that depth accumulation is driven purely by geometric distance and rasterization order, eliminating shading artifacts and opacity-induced depth bias. It is distinct from Depth Rendering with Variable Opacity, which respects the learned alpha values of the Gaussians. The method modifies the standard Gaussian rasterization pipeline to strip away appearance information (color and variable opacity) and gradient information related to scale and rotation, leaving only the geometric position and a constant alpha value to drive the depth accumulation. Inputs: pc: Gaussian model object providing getxyz, getscaling, getrotation, getcovariance, and activeshdegree. viewpointcamera: Camera object providing FoVx, FoVy, imagewidth, imageheight, worldviewtransform, fullprojtransform, and cameracenter. value: Constant opacity multiplier for all Gaussians (default 0.95). pipe: Pipeline configuration object containing computecov3Dpython and debug flags. background: Background color tensor, typically [1, 1, 1] or [0, 0, 0]. Outputs: render: Rendered image tensor (uniform due to constant color input). depth: Accumulated depth buffer in NDC coordinates. alpha: Accumulated opacity buffer. viewspacepoints: Tensor of 2D screen-space points initialized for gradient tracking. visibilityfilter: Boolean mask indicating visible Gaussians (radii > 0). radii: Screen-space bounding box radii for each Gaussian. screenspacepoints: Tensor of shape (numgaussians, 3) initialized to zeros with requiresgrad=True and retaingrad() enabled to allow gradient flow to 2D mean positions during optimization, even though forward depth computation does not use these gradients. opacity: Tensor of shape (numgaussians, 1) filled with the constant value. colorsprecomp: Tensor of shape (numgaussians, 3) filled with ones to strip color information. scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp: Set to None or detached tensors within a no-gradient context to prevent gradient leakage into depth estimation. 1. Initialize screenspacepoints with zeros and enable gradient retention: screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz, dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") + 0; apply screenspacepoints.retaingrad() if supported. 2. Compute tangent field of view values from the viewpoint camera: tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) and tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5). 3. Configure GaussianRasterizationSettings with image dimensions, tanfovx, tanfovy, background color, scalemodifier, view/projection matrices, shdegree, cameraposition, prefiltered=False, and debug flag. 4. Default is 0.95. Gradient Leakage: Failing to detach scales and rotations or set them to None inside torch.nograd() allows gradients to flow into the depth estimation process, corrupting optimization. Coordinate System: Depth values are returned in NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates); downstream consumers must convert to metric depth if required. Uniform Opacity Accumulation: Setting opacity to a constant value (e.g., 0.95) means final accumulated opacity depends on the number of overlapping Gaussians and their rasterization order, which can saturate alpha values in dense regions. Step 7: Return results visibilityfilter = radii > 0 return { "render": renderedimage, "depth": rendereddepth, "alpha": renderedalpha, "viewspacepoints": screenspacepoints, "visibilityfilter": visibilityfilter, "radii": radii } Computes a depth map by dividing the accumulated depth buffer by the accumulated opacity buffer to correct for transparency artifacts in Gaussian splatting renders. Computes a depth map by calculating a weighted average of Gaussian depths along a ray, where weights are determined by the alpha-compositing process. name: Normalized Depth Rendering
head: Depth Normalized by Opacity, Normalized Depth Map
body:
Normalized Depth Rendering computes a depth map by dividing the accumulated depth buffer by the accumulated opacity buffer to correct for transparency artifacts in Gaussian splatting renders. Inputs: renderdepth: Accumulated depth buffer from the rasterizer. renderacc: Accumulated alpha/opacity buffer from the rasterizer. znear: Near plane distance of the camera frustum. zfar: Far plane distance of the camera frustum. Outputs: rendereddepthnorm: Normalized depth map. rendereddispnorm: Displayable disparity map. Data Structures: renderdepth: 2D array of floats, shape (H, W). renderacc: 2D array of floats, shape (H, W). Steps: 1. Normalize Depth: Divide the accumulated depth buffer by the accumulated opacity buffer at each pixel (x, y) to produce the normalized depth map. 	ext{rendered\depth
orm}{x,y} =  rac{	ext{render\depth}{x,y}}{	ext{render\acc}{x,y}} 2. Convert to Disparity: Map the normalized depth to a displayable disparity range using the camera frustum bounds. 	ext{rendered\disp
orm}{x,y} = 1 -  rac{	ext{rendered\depth
orm}{x,y} - z{	ext{near}}}{z{	ext{far}} - z{	ext{near}}} Parameters: znear, zfar: Camera frustum bounds. Typical values depend on the scene scale and are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs when renderacc is exactly 0 (no Gaussians cover the pixel), yielding undefined results. Clamp the denominator to a small positive epsilon or mask these pixels to a default value like zfar or NaN. Precision loss may occur in low-opacity regions where the denominator approaches the epsilon floor, amplifying noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizeddepthrendering(renderdepth, renderacc, znear, zfar): epsilon = 1e-6 H, W = len(renderdepth), len(renderdepth[0]) # Step 1: Normalize depth, handling zero-opacity pixels safeacc = [[max(renderacc[i][j], epsilon) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] normalizeddepth = [[renderdepth[i][j] / safeacc[i][j] for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] # Step 2: Convert to disparity disparity = [[1.0 - (normalizeddepth[i][j] - znear) / (zfar - znear) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] return normalizeddepth, disparity A CUDA-based post-processing step that maps raw 3DGS depth outputs to the 0, 1.0) range to ensure compatibility with underwater visualization pipelines. It applies a logistic transformation to all raw depth values during the [rasterization pipeline. The normalized depth is computed as z{	ext{norm}} =  rac{2}{1 + e^{-0.1 \cdot z{	ext{raw}}}} - 1, where z{	ext{raw}} is the initial depth output from 3DGS manipulation. Time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory complexity is not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces geometrically accurate depth maps in transparent or semi-transparent regions where standard depth accumulation fails. Limitations: Sensitive to noise in low-opacity regions due to division by small values; requires robust handling of zero-opacity pixels. When to use: When accurate depth estimation is needed for scenes with varying opacity. When not to use: When simple geometric depth is sufficient and opacity is uniform, or when performance constraints prohibit the extra division step. Normalized Depth Rendering is a post-processing technique used in Gaussian Splatting pipelines to improve depth map quality. It leverages the existing alpha compositing infrastructure of Gaussian Splatting to derive a transparency-corrected depth value. brownvc/gftorf, https://github.com/brownvc/gftorf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-56917-4, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Depth Rendering with Variable Opacity
head: Gaussian Splatting Depth Output, Nearest Depth Rendering, Per-pixel Depth Buffer
body: This method extends Gaussian Splatting rasterization to produce a per-pixel depth buffer (NDC depth, +\infty where no surface is visible) while respecting the variable opacity of the Gaussians. Unlike Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity, which forces uniform opacity to drive depth accumulation by geometric distance, this method computes depth based on the actual alpha-weighted contribution of the splats. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity \alpha, color), camera projection matrices, and a configuration flag GsplatConfig::outputDepth set to true. Outputs: A color image (unchanged from standard rendering) and a per-pixel depth buffer storing NDC depth values. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: A texture or buffer of size W \times H (image resolution) storing floating-point NDC depth values. Raster Backend Auxiliary: An order-preserving unsigned integer encoding of depth, used for atomic operations in the fragment shader and decoded by a subsequent compute pass. Steps: 1. Configuration: Enable GsplatConfig::outputDepth to activate depth buffer writing. Ensure the device feature fragmentStoresAndAtomics is enabled if using the raster backend, as it requires atomic operations. 2. Projection Correction: Apply cropProjection() if rendering an off-centre view or crop. This centers the Gaussian projection guard band on the view rather than the optical axis to prevent distortion of Gaussians elongated along the view direction. 3. Sorting: Sort Gaussians by depth relative to the camera. 4. Rasterization and Compositing: Compute Backend: Blend Gaussians front-to-back. For each pixel, track the accumulated transmittance Tn. Record the depth zn of the Gaussian at which the transmittance first falls to 0.5 (median depth). Raster Backend: Blend Gaussians back-to-front. For each pixel, use atomicMin on an order-preserving uint encoding of depth to keep the nearest depth of a single splat that alone covers the pixel with an opacity of at least 0.5. After the render pass, a compute pass decodes this uint encoding into the final depth buffer. 5. Expected Depth Calculation: If expected depth is required instead of median/nearest, compute the alpha-weighted average depth using the formula below. Formulas: The accumulated transparency Tn for the n-th Gaussian at pixel (x, y) is: Tn = \prod{j=1}^{Q-1} (1 - \alphaj) where Q is the number of Gaussians covering the pixel, and \alphaj is the opacity of the j-th Gaussian in depth-sorted order. The Expected Depth d{x,y}^{exp} is: d{x,y}^{exp} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^N zn \cdot \alphan \cdot Tn}{\sum{n=1}^N \alphan \cdot Tn} where zn is the Z-depth of the n-th Gaussian. The Accumulated Depth d{x,y}^{acc} (numerator for expected depth) is: d{x,y}^{acc} = \sum{n=1}^N zn \cdot \alphan \cdot Tn Parameters: GsplatConfig::outputDepth: Boolean flag to enable depth output. Opacity threshold: 0.5 is used for median depth crossing (Compute) and nearest splat coverage (Raster). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Off-centre Projection Distortion: If the guard band is not centered on the view (e.g., in cropped renders), Gaussians away from the optical axis are incorrectly clamped, distorting their footprints. Use cropProjection() to fix this. Backend Disagreement: The Compute backend (median depth) and Raster backend (nearest splat with \alpha \ge 0.5) use different definitions. They agree on opaque surfaces with a median difference of 0.4% on the lantern scene, but may differ in semi-transparent regions. Hardware Support: The Raster backend requires fragmentStoresAndAtomics support on the GPU. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearencodedepth(z, minz, maxz): return int(((z - minz) / (maxz - minz)) 0xFFFFFFFF) def lineardecodedepth(encodedz, minz, maxz): return (encodedz / 0xFFFFFFFF) (maxz - minz) + minz def computedepthbuffer(gaussians, camera, width, height, minz, maxz): depthbuffer = [float('inf')] (width height) sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depthat(camera)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): pixelidx = y width + x transmittance = 1.0 mediandepth = float('inf') for gaussian in sortedgaussians: # Standard rasterization coverage check if not gaussian.intersectspixel(x, y): continue alpha = gaussian.opacityat(x, y) z = gaussian.depthat(x, y) # Update transmittance before checking crossing transmittance = (1 - alpha) # Check for median depth crossing (transmittance <= 0.5) if transmittance <= 0.5 and mediandepth == float('inf'): mediandepth = z depthbuffer[pixelidx] = mediandepth return depthbuffer def rasterdepthbuffer(gaussians, camera, width, height, minz, maxz): # Requires atomicMin support depthuintbuffer = [0xFFFFFFFF] (width height) sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depthat(camera), reverse=True) for gaussian in sortedgaussians: # Iterate over pixels covered by this Gaussian for x, y in gaussian.coveredpixels(): pixelidx = y width + x alpha = gaussian.opacityat(x, y) z = gaussian.depthat(x, y) # Encode depth into order-preserving uint encodedz = linearencodedepth(z, minz, maxz) # Atomic minimum to keep nearest depth # Only update if this splat covers the pixel with alpha >= 0.5 if alpha >= 0.5: if encodedz < depthuintbuffer[pixelidx]: depthuintbuffer[pixelidx] = encodedz # Decode uint buffer in a separate compute pass depthbuffer = [lineardecodedepth(z, minz, maxz) for z in depthuintbuffer] return depthbuffer Time Complexity: Same as standard Gaussian Splatting rasterization, O(N) for sorting and O(P \cdot G) for rasterization where P is pixels and G is Gaussians per pixel. The additional depth calculation is negligible per pixel. Memory Complexity: Adds one W \times H depth buffer. The Raster backend uses an order-preserving unsigned integer encoding for atomic operations, decoded by a compute pass after rendering. Performance: The Compute backend may be slower on some hardware due to lack of parallel atomic optimizations compared to the Raster backend, but offers more consistent depth definitions (median). The Raster backend requires fragmentStoresAndAtomics support. Strengths: Enables compositing of other geometry into the splat scene. Handles variable opacity naturally. Limitations: Two different depth definitions (median vs. nearest) lead to slight discrepancies between backends in semi-transparent regions. Off-centre projections require special handling to avoid distortion. This feature was introduced in the klartraum project by fortmeier and others in October 2026 to enable depth output for both Gaussian splatting backends (Compute and Raster). It addresses the need to composite other geometry into a splat scene, which was previously not possible as the splats would always render over other geometry. The implementation also fixed a bug related to off-centre projection guard bands. The expected depth formula is derived from the gsplat library documentation. feat: depth output for the Gaussian splatting backends, https://github.com/fortmeier/klartraum/pull/46, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Depth Rendering with Weighted Average
head: Alpha-blending Depth Rendering, Depth Map Rendering, Weighted Depth Accumulation, standard alpha-blending
body: Depth Rendering with Weighted Average computes a depth map for 3D Gaussian Splatting by calculating a weighted average of Gaussian depths along a ray, where the weights are determined by the alpha-compositing process. It differs from Depth Rendering with Constant Opacity by allowing opacity to influence the depth accumulation, which can lead to depth ambiguity at sharp edges or with misplaced "floaters". It is distinct from Normalized Depth Rendering and Depth Rendering with Variable Opacity in its reliance on standard alpha-blending mechanics rather than normalization or variable opacity constraints. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{c}i, covariance matrix \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i^{color}. Camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, intrinsics). Image resolution (W, H). Outputs: A depth map D of size W \times H, where each pixel (x, y) contains a single depth value d{x,y}. Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of structs containing fields: position (vec3), scale (vec3), rotation (quat), opacity (float), shcoeffs (array). Rasterization Buffer: For each pixel, store accumulated transmittance T (float, initialized to 1.0) and accumulated depth D{acc} (float, initialized to 0.0). Steps: 1. Projection and Sorting: Project each Gaussian's center to screen space. Sort Gaussians front-to-back relative to the camera for each tile or pixel to ensure correct alpha-compositing order. 2. Rasterization: For each pixel (x, y), iterate through the sorted Gaussians that overlap the pixel. 3. Weight Calculation: For the i-th Gaussian, calculate the alpha-compositing weight \alphai. This is typically derived from the Gaussian's 2D covariance and opacity. 4. Transmittance Update: Update the accumulated transmittance Ti for the current Gaussian: Ti = T{i-1} \cdot (1 - \alphai) where T0 = 1.0. 5. Depth Contribution: Calculate the depth contribution of the i-th Gaussian. Let di be the depth of the Gaussian center projected along the ray. The weighted depth contribution is Ti \cdot \alphai \cdot di. 6. Accumulation: Add the contribution to the accumulated depth D{acc} for the pixel: D{acc} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \cdot \alphai \cdot di. 7. Final Depth: The final depth d{x,y} is the accumulated depth D{acc}. Note: In some implementations, if the accumulated opacity is very low, the depth might be set to a default value (e.g., far plane) to handle background. Formula: The alpha-blending depth at pixel (x, y), denoted as d{x,y}^{alpha}, is calculated as: d{x,y}^{alpha} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai di where: N is the number of Gaussians overlapping the pixel. Ti is the accumulated transmittance for the i-th Gaussian, defined as Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). \alphai is the alpha-compositing weight of the i-th Gaussian. di is the depth of the i-th Gaussian. Alternatively, some implementations normalize the accumulation to compute a true weighted average: d = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} z^ci \omegai}{\sum{i=1}^{N} \omegai} where \omegai = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the blending weight, and z^ci is the depth of the i-th Gaussian in camera coordinates. The camera coordinates are obtained by transforming the world position [xi, yi, zi]^T using extrinsics [W, t] as [x^ci, y^ci, z^ci]^T = W[xi, yi, zi]^T + t. Parameters: \alphai: Typically derived from the Gaussian's opacity and the 2D projection. Not given in the sources. di: Depth of the Gaussian center. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floaters: Misplaced Gaussians (floaters) can significantly influence the depth value, leading to inaccurate depth maps. Precision: Accumulating many small contributions can lead to floating-point precision issues. Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Gaussians at the edge of the image or with large covariances may require careful handling to avoid artifacts. Not given in the sources. Unbiased Depth Rendering is a technique for estimating precise depth maps and normal maps from 3D Gaussian Splatting by approximating the underlying surface geometry. It sets itself apart from weighted average depth methods by flattening 3D Gaussian ellipsoids into planes, allowing depth to be calculated via ray-plane intersections rather than simple accumulation. This approach aims to reduce depth ambiguity at sharp edges and better reflect actual surface geometry. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of Gaussians and R is the number of rays (pixels). Sorting adds O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: O(N + W \cdot H) for storing Gaussian data and rasterization buffers. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of Gaussians and image resolution. Strengths: Simple to implement; widely used in NeRFs and adapted for 3DGS. Limitations: Susceptible to depth ambiguity caused by floaters and overlapping Gaussians with different opacities. When to Use: When a quick depth estimate is needed and the scene does not have significant floaters or complex transparency. When Not to Use: When high-precision depth is required, especially in scenes with sharp edges or many floaters. Consider Unbiased Depth Rendering (PGSR) for better geometric accuracy. Alpha-blending is a widely used technique in NeRFs. It has been adapted for 3D Gaussian Splatting to render depth maps. The method calculates the depth value of a pixel by weighting the depth of each Gaussian by its contribution to the final color, as determined by the alpha-compositing process. name: Unbiased Depth Rendering (PGSR)
head: Flattened Gaussian Plane Depth, PGSR depth rendering
body: Unbiased Depth Rendering is a technique for estimating precise depth maps and normal maps from 3D Gaussian Splatting by approximating the underlying surface geometry. It sets itself apart from weighted average depth methods by flattening 3D Gaussian ellipsoids into planes, allowing depth to be calculated via ray-plane intersections rather than simple accumulation. This approach aims to reduce depth ambiguity at sharp edges and better reflect actual surface geometry. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by mean position \mui, normal vector ni, and opacity \alphai. Camera parameters: intrinsic matrix K, camera center TC, and world-to-camera rotation matrix Rc. Image pixel coordinates \tilde{p}. Outputs: Depth map D(p) for each pixel p. Normal map N(p) for each pixel p. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: For each Gaussian i, store \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, normal vector ni \in \mathbb{R}^3, and opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Camera Matrices: K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, Rc \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, TC \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Flatten Gaussians to Planes: For each 3D Gaussian i, approximate its ellipsoidal shape as a plane and calculate the distance di from the camera center to this flattened plane. di = (Rc^T (\mui - TC))^T Rc^T ni Here, \mui - TC is the vector from the camera center to the Gaussian mean, and Rc^T transforms this vector and the normal ni into the camera coordinate system. The dot product of the transformed position and the transformed normal yields the signed distance from the camera center to the plane. 2. Render Normal Map via Alpha-Blending: Compute the accumulated normal vector N(p) at each pixel p by alpha-blending the rotated normals of all Gaussians i \in M that project onto the pixel. N(p) = \sum{i \in M} Rc ni \alphai Ti Where Rc ni is the normal vector of the i-th Gaussian rotated into the camera coordinate system, \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian, and Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance up to Gaussian i. 3. Render Distance Map via Alpha-Blending: Compute the accumulated distance D(p) at each pixel p by alpha-blending the distances di of the flattened planes. D(p) = \sum{i \in M} di \alphai Ti Where di is the distance from the camera center to the i-th Gaussian plane as calculated in Step 1. 4. Calculate Final Depth Map: Convert the accumulated distance and normal information into a standard depth map D(p) using ray-plane intersection logic. D(p) = \frac{D}{N(p)} K^{-1} \tilde{p} Where D is the accumulated distance from Step 3, N(p) is the accumulated normal vector, K^{-1} \tilde{p} is the ray direction in camera coordinates, and the source notation implies a dot product in the denominator to yield a scalar depth value consistent with ray-plane intersection. Pitfalls: Normal Ambiguity: Normal vectors exhibit ambiguity at edges where depth changes are sharp. The method handles this by using the alpha-blended normal map N(p), which aggregates contributions from all Gaussians passing through the ray. Precision: The calculation of di involves matrix multiplications and dot products. Degenerate Input: If the denominator in Step 4 approaches zero (ray parallel to the plane), the depth will explode. Not given in the sources. Unbiased Depth Rendering was proposed by Chen et al. (2024) as part of the PGSR framework. It is inspired by 2DGS (Huang et al., 2024a) and SuGaR (Guédon and Lepetit, 2024). The method approximates true surfaces by flattening 3D Gaussian ellipsoids into planes via minimizing aligned scale factors. PG-SAG: Parallel Gaussian Splatting for Fine-Grained Large-Scale Urban Buildings Reconstruction via Semantic-Aware Grouping, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41064-025-00343-0, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort
body: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort is a GPU-parallel rasterization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that divides the image into tiles to manage memory and processing load, assigning Gaussians to tiles based on their projected 2D splats Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-pixel sorting by using a single global radix sort to achieve per-tile depth ordering, enabling real-time performance for millions of splats Tile-based Rasteriser. The method operates on a list of N projected 2D Gaussian splats, each defined by center (xi, yi), 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i, color ci, opacity \alphai, and depth Zc Tile-based Rasteriser. The image is divided into a grid of tiles with dimensions Tw \times Th (typically 16 \times 16 pixels) Tile-based Rasteriser. The core mechanism involves three phases: 1. Tile Assignment: Each Gaussian is assigned to every tile its projected 2D splat touches. If a splat straddles tile boundaries, it is duplicated into each relevant tile Tile-based Rasteriser. This creates one work item per (Gaussian, tile) pair Tile-based Rasteriser. 2. Key Packing: For each (splat, tile) pair, a 64-bit integer sort key is constructed. The tile ID is packed into the high bits, and the splat's depth Zc is packed into the low bits Tile-based Rasteriser. Specifically, the key is formed as: \text{key} = (\text{tile\id} \ll 32) \mid (\text{uint32\t})Zc where tileid is the 1D tile index (y \times \text{grid\width} + x) and Zc is cast to a 32-bit unsigned integer Tile-based Rasteriser. 3. Global Radix Sort: A single GPU radix sort is performed over all (splat, tile) pairs Tile-based Rasteriser. This simultaneously bins splats by tile ID (ensuring contiguity) and sorts them by depth within each tile Tile-based Rasteriser. After sorting, each tile is processed by one GPU thread block that walks the sorted list Tile-based Rasteriser. For each pixel in a tile, front-to-back compositing is performed using the tile's sorted list of splats, evaluating per-pixel alpha \alphai(\mathbf{x}) and breaking early when transmittance T < \epsilon Tile-based Rasteriser. The same sorted lists are reused for backpropagation, allowing gradients to flow to position, shape, opacity, and color without additional sorting Tile-based Rasteriser. Unverified code. name: Opacity-Thresholded Tile Intersection Filtering
head: Alpha-threshold Gaussian Filtering, Synergistic Filtering with Tile Intersections
body: This method filters out 3D Gaussians during the tile intersection phase of tiled rasterization if their opacity \tau falls below a specified alpha-threshold \epsilon, treating their axis-aligned bounding box as effectively empty. It reduces the number of Gaussians requiring sorting and shading, addressing performance bottlenecks caused by large, mostly transparent Gaussians that intersect many tiles but contribute negligible color. It builds on Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of projected 2D Gaussians, each with screen-space opacity \tau and its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Output: A filtered list of (Gaussian, tile) pairs, excluding those with \tau < \epsilon. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores its screen-space opacity \taui. Tile Grid: The image is divided into a grid of tiles (typically 16 \times 16 pixels per parent article). Each tile maintains a list of candidate Gaussians. Parameters: Alpha-threshold (\epsilon): The minimum opacity required for a Gaussian to be considered visible. Gaussians with \tau < \epsilon are discarded. Typical values are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute the screen-space AABB for each Gaussian. 2. For each tile, identify Gaussians whose AABB intersects the tile's bounds. 3. During the intersection check, evaluate the Gaussian's opacity \tau. 4. If \tau < \epsilon, discard the Gaussian for this tile; its AABB is considered empty. 5. If \tau \ge \epsilon, add the Gaussian to the tile's candidate list for subsequent sorting and shading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def opacitythresholdedtileintersection(gaussians, tiles, epsilon): """ Filter Gaussians based on opacity during tile intersection. Args: gaussians: List of dicts/objects with keys: 'opacity': float, screen-space opacity tau. 'bbox': tuple (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in screen space. tiles: List of dicts/objects with keys: 'bbox': tuple (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in screen space. 'candidates': list to store filtered Gaussians. epsilon (float): Alpha-threshold for filtering. Returns: Updated tiles with filtered candidate lists. """ for tile in tiles: tile['candidates'] = [] for g in gaussians: # AABB intersection check if (g['bbox'][0] <= tile['bbox'][2] and g['bbox'][2] >= tile['bbox'][0] and g['bbox'][1] <= tile['bbox'][3] and g['bbox'][3] >= tile['bbox'][1]): # Opacity threshold filter if g['opacity'] >= epsilon: tile['candidates'].append(g) # Else: Gaussian is filtered out (opacity too low) return tiles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Backend-specific threshold application semantics vary; preserving non-empty support is not a method-wide invariant. An all-one policy (thresholds set to maximum) does not guarantee reproduction of every backend's native pair list solely from multiplier values due to differing cap and subtraction rules. Describes how exported absolute thresholds mg \tau0 are applied to Gaussian opacities \alphag during tile enumeration, determining whether a primitive participates in rendering. The default Speedy-Splat path compares the threshold directly to \alphag; if threshold \ge \alphag, it yields zero tile pairs. The 2DGS and Scaffold-GS ports reject primitives whose opacity cannot exceed the selected threshold. The FastGS port applies \min(mg \tau0, 0.95\alphag) as the effective threshold cap; if the cap binds (i.e., 0.95\alphag < mg \tau0), it subtracts 10^{-6} from the capped value before constructing the backend-specific extent. Preserving non-empty support is not a method-wide invariant, and an all-one policy should not be assumed to reproduce every backend's native pair list merely from its multiplier values. Time and Memory Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussians processed in subsequent sorting and shading steps, lowering both compute time and GPU memory usage. Measured Performance: Combining this modification with others decreased rendering time on the Bicycle scene at native resolution by a factor of 3.77 and GPU memory usage by a factor of 2.11 compared to the reference implementation. Scaling: Performance gains are greatest at higher resolutions, as there are more duplicated Gaussians and hence \alpha-computations. Render times are more consistent, particularly on the Bicycle scene at native resolution, because large transparent Gaussians no longer affect a significant number of tiles. Strengths and Limitations: Highly effective for scenes with many transparent or low-opacity Gaussians. At low resolutions, increasing tile size (e.g., 16 \times 32) increases the average render time to 9.77 ms, illustrating why tile size is only increased at higher resolutions. When to Use: Use when rendering scenes with many transparent Gaussians, particularly at high resolutions. Avoid increasing tile dimensions at low resolutions due to overhead. This method is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering that leverages the observation that many Gaussians have low opacity and contribute little to the final image, allowing them to be safely discarded early in the rendering pipeline.
