name: Tile-Based Culling
head: StopThePop Tile-Based Culling
body: Tile-Based Culling computes a precise Gaussian-to-Tile mapping to cull irrelevant tiles during rasterization. It replaces the overly conservative bounding box intersection of standard 3D-GS with a tight, opacity-aware bounding box and iterative tile examination. It sets itself apart from siblings like SnugBox by using a simpler control flow with warp-level load balancing, and from AccuTile by iterating over all candidate tiles within the bounding box rather than using a non-iterative precise algorithm. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of N projected 2D Gaussians, each defined by center (xi, yi), 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i, color ci, opacity \alphai, and depth Zc. Output: A filtered list of (Gaussian, Tile) pairs, where only tiles strictly intersecting the Gaussian's significant footprint are included. This list is then used for key packing and sorting as described in Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. Data Structures: Tile Grid: The image is divided into a grid of tiles with dimensions Tw \times Th (typically 16 \times 16 pixels). Bounding Box: An axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in screen space for each Gaussian, computed based on an opacity threshold. Tile List: A dynamic list of tile IDs that the Gaussian overlaps. Parameters: Alpha Threshold (\alpha{thresh}): A threshold used to determine the extent of the Gaussian's footprint. The sources note that a "padded alpha threshold" is required to accurately compute bounding boxes and prevent undercounting. The exact value is not provided in the ablation study. Steps: 1. Culling: Eliminate Gaussians entirely outside the camera’s view frustum or in extreme positions where contribution is negligible. 2. Projection: Project remaining 3D Gaussians to the 2D image plane using ScreenspaceGaussians(M,S,V) to get 2D position and footprint. 3. Bounding Box Computation: Compute a tight, opacity-aware bounding box per Gaussian. The box is derived from the Gaussian's 2D covariance and the alpha threshold. Pitfall: If thresholds are used improperly, not all bounding boxes are tight. Without a padded alpha threshold, the method undercounts Gaussian-to-Tile mappings, artificially improving downstream performance (Radix Sort, Identify Tile Ranges, Render) due to fewer elements to process. 4. Tile Examination: Iteratively examine each tile touching the bounding box to determine if it should be included in the final Gaussian-to-Tile mapping. For each tile inside the bounding rectangle, compute the point where the value of the Gaussian is maximal. Check if this maximal point satisfies the opacity threshold condition. Optimization: Use warp-level load balancing to accelerate the tile examination process. This approach is selected for its simpler control flow and load balancing compared to computing first/last tile indices per row/column. 5. Duplication: Duplicate Gaussians for every tile they overlap and assign a key combining depth and tile ID using DuplicateWithKeys(M', T). 6. Sorting: Sort Gaussians globally by depth and tile ID using GPU Radix Sort to ensure front-to-back blending within each tile. 7. Range Identification: Identify start and end indices for each tile in the sorted list using IdentifyTileRanges(T, K). 8. Rendering: Process each tile in parallel on the GPU; for each pixel, fetch the range of Gaussians, traverse the sorted list, and compute contribution using color and opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tilebasedculling(gaussians, imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize=16, alphathreshold=0.001): """ Computes precise Gaussian-to-Tile mapping using Tile-Based Culling. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: center: (x, y) in screen space cov2d: 2x2 covariance matrix [[a, b], [b, d]] alpha: opacity depth: Zc imagewidth: Width of the image in pixels imageheight: Height of the image in pixels tilesize: Size of each tile (default 16) alphathreshold: Threshold for determining Gaussian footprint extent Returns: List of (gaussianindex, tileid) pairs """ numtilesx = (imagewidth + tilesize - 1) // tilesize outputpairs = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Step 1: Frustum culling (simplified boundary check) if g.center[0] < 0 or g.center[0] >= imagewidth or g.center[1] < 0 or g.center[1] >= imageheight: continue # Step 2: Projection (assumed precomputed as g.center, g.cov2d, g.alpha, g.depth) # Step 3: Compute tight, opacity-aware bounding box # Extent at alphathreshold: sqrt(-2 ln(alpha) eigenvalues) eigenvalues = computeeigenvalues(g.cov2d) extentx = math.sqrt(-2 math.log(alphathreshold) eigenvalues[0]) extenty = math.sqrt(-2 math.log(alphathreshold) eigenvalues[1]) minx = max(0, g.center[0] - extentx) maxx = min(imagewidth, g.center[0] + extentx) miny = max(0, g.center[1] - extenty) maxy = min(imageheight, g.center[1] + extenty) tileminx = int(minx // tilesize) tilemaxx = int(maxx // tilesize) tileminy = int(miny // tilesize) tilemaxy = int(maxy // tilesize) # Step 4: Iteratively examine each tile touching the bounding box for ty in range(tileminy, tilemaxy + 1): for tx in range(tileminx, tilemaxx + 1): tileid = ty numtilesx + tx # Compute maximal Gaussian value within this tile tileminxpx = tx tilesize tilemaxxpx = (tx + 1) tilesize tileminypx = ty tilesize tilemaxypx = (ty + 1) tilesize # Closest point on tile to Gaussian center closestx = max(tileminxpx, min(g.center[0], tilemaxxpx)) closesty = max(tileminypx, min(g.center[1], tilemaxypx)) # Evaluate Gaussian at closest point diffx = closestx - g.center[0] diffy = closesty - g.center[1] invcov = invertmatrix(g.cov2d) distsq = diffx invcov[0][0] diffx + 2 diffx invcov[0][1] diffy + diffy invcov[1][1] diffy maxval = g.alpha math.exp(-0.5 distsq) if maxval >= alphathreshold: outputpairs.append((i, tileid)) return outputpairs def computeeigenvalues(cov2d): """Standard 2x2 symmetric eigenvalue computation.""" a, b = cov2d[0][0], cov2d[0][1] d = cov2d[1][1] trace = a + d det = a d - b b disc = math.sqrt(max(0, trace trace - 4 det)) return [(trace + disc) / 2, (trace - disc) / 2] def invertmatrix(m): """Standard 2x2 matrix inversion.""" det = m[0][0] m[1][1] - m[0][1] m[1][0] return [[m[1][1]/det, -m[0][1]/det], [-m[1][0]/det, m[0][0]/det]] SnugBox is a precise algorithm for computing Gaussian-to-tile bounding box intersections in 3D Gaussian Splatting, replacing the overly conservative tile assignment of standard 3D-GS to reduce the number of pixels processed per Gaussian. It computes a tight axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) around each Gaussian's elliptical extent in image space, assigning the Gaussian only to tiles that strictly intersect this box. Unlike the standard method which inscribes a circle and uses a square bounding box, SnugBox derives the box directly from the conic equation of the projected Gaussian, providing numerical stability under edge-on tilts. It serves as a lossless optimization that reduces the number of Gaussian-tile pairs, contributing to an average inference speed-up of 1.82×. Nearest alternatives include Warp-Level Culling and TileSkipper. A method to compute exact intersections between screen-space Gaussian ellipses and rendering tiles, eliminating the false-positive and false-negative errors inherent in distance-based, bounding-box, or compact box culling approaches. It sets itself apart by providing a branchless, closed-form solution that precisely determines tile overlap without the memory overhead of separate culling passes. An optimization for the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) alpha blending stage that uses warp-level collaboration to subdivide image tiles and cull splats with no geometric overlap, avoiding expensive alpha evaluation. It improves rendering speed without changing the rendered output, implemented in the existing CUDA differentiable pipeline. Unlike SnugBox, which focuses on tighter bounding boxes, this method focuses on geometric culling within the blending kernel to reduce the number of blending operations. TileSkipper is a post-training systems adapter for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that replaces a single scene-wide contribution cutoff with a static per-Gaussian cutoff policy to reduce tile-pair enumeration work without retraining the checkpoint. It differs from its siblings by using a region-adaptive search based on isolated-deletion distortion proxies and held-out validation, whereas SnugBox focuses on tight bounding boxes and Warp-Level Culling for Efficient Blending in 3D Gaussian Splatting operates at the warp level for blending efficiency. Time Complexity: The method iterates over all candidate tiles within the bounding box for each Gaussian, resulting in higher runtime cost for the preprocessing and key duplication stages compared to non-iterative methods like AccuTile, even with warp-level load balancing. Memory Complexity: The number of (Gaussian, Tile) pairs is reduced compared to standard 3D-GS, leading to lower memory usage for the sort buffer and reduced work for downstream stages (Radix Sort, Identify Tile Ranges, Render). Measured Performance: In ablation studies, AccuTile significantly outperforms Tile-Based Culling in Preprocess and Duplicate with Keys. Tile-Based Culling slightly outperforms AccuTile in downstream functions (Radix Sort, Identify Tile Ranges, Render) due to undercounting of Gaussian-to-Tile mappings when no padded alpha threshold is used. Strengths: Simpler control flow and better load balancing than row/column-based bounding box approaches. Limitations: Iterative tile examination can be costly if bounding boxes are not tight. Requires careful tuning of alpha thresholds to avoid undercounting. When to use: When a balance between precision and implementation simplicity is desired, and warp-level load balancing is available. When not to use: When maximum performance is required and non-iterative precise culling (like AccuTile) is feasible. Tile-Based Culling was introduced by Radl et al. in the StopThePop paper. It is part of the StopThePop framework, which aims to optimize 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. The method was selected for its simpler control flow and load balancing compared to other bounding box approaches. It is used in the StopThePop codebase and has been integrated into various 3DGS implementations. name: SnugBox
head: FastGS Optimizations, Rasterization Optimizations, Speedy-Splat Optimizations
body: SnugBox is a precise algorithm for computing Gaussian-to-tile bounding box intersections in 3D Gaussian Splatting, replacing the overly conservative tile assignment of standard 3D-GS to reduce the number of pixels processed per Gaussian. It computes a tight axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) around each Gaussian's elliptical extent in image space, assigning the Gaussian only to tiles that strictly intersect this box. Unlike the standard method which inscribes a circle and uses a square bounding box, SnugBox derives the box directly from the conic equation of the projected Gaussian, providing numerical stability under edge-on tilts. It serves as a lossless optimization that reduces the number of Gaussian-tile pairs, contributing to an average inference speed-up of 1.82×. Nearest alternatives include Warp-Level Culling and TileSkipper. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \mu{i3D}, scale si, rotation ri), camera parameters (view matrix W, projection matrix), tile size T, image dimensions. Output: A set of tile indices (tx, ty) that the Gaussian intersects. Data Structures: \Sigma{i3D}: 3 \times 3 3D covariance matrix. \Sigma{i2D}: 2 \times 2 2D projected covariance matrix. \Sigma{i2D}^{-1}: Inverse of the 2D covariance matrix, represented as \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix}. \mu{i2D}: 2D mean position (\mux, \muy). t: Threshold value for the ellipse equation. Steps: 1. Project 3D Covariance to 2D: Compute the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{i2D} from the 3D covariance \Sigma{i3D} using the Jacobian J of the perspective projection: \hat{\Sigma}{i3D} = J W \Sigma{i3D} W^T J^T Drop the last row and column of \hat{\Sigma}{i3D} to obtain \Sigma{i2D}. 2. Compute Inverse Covariance and Threshold: Compute the inverse of the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{i2D}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix}. Calculate the threshold t based on the Gaussian's opacity \sigmai: t = 2 \log(255 \sigmai) 3. Compute Extrema in X: Find the values of xd (where xd = px - \mux) where the derivative \partial yd / \partial xd = 0: x{d{args}} = \pm \sqrt{\frac{-b^2 t}{(b^2 - ac)a}} 4. Compute Extrema in Y: Substitute x{d{args}} into the rearranged ellipse equation to find the corresponding yd values. The equation for yd is: yd = \frac{-bxd \pm \sqrt{(b^2 - ac)xd^2 + tc}}{c} Calculate y{min} and y{max} by evaluating this for both x{d{args}} values and taking the minimum and maximum results. Add \muy to get the absolute y bounds: y{min} = \min(yd) + \muy, \quad y{max} = \max(yd) + \muy 5. Compute Extrema in X (Absolute): Due to the symmetry of the ellipse equation, find x{min} and x{max} by swapping yd and xd and constants a and c in the equations above. x{min} = \min(xd) + \mux, \quad x{max} = \max(xd) + \mux 6. Convert to Tile Indices: Convert the bounding box edges (x{min}, y{min}, x{max}, y{max}) to tile indices by dividing by the tile size T, rounding, and clipping to the image boundaries. tx^{start} = \max(0, \lfloor x{min} / T \rfloor), \quad tx^{end} = \min(\lceil W{img}/T \rceil - 1, \lceil x{max} / T \rceil) ty^{start} = \max(0, \lfloor y{min} / T \rfloor), \quad ty^{end} = \min(\lceil H{img}/T \rceil - 1, \lceil y{max} / T \rceil) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computesnugboxtileindices(gaussianmean2d, covinv2d, opacity, tilesize, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Computes the tile indices intersected by a Gaussian using SnugBox. Args: gaussianmean2d: Tuple (mux, muy) covinv2d: Tuple (a, b, c) representing [[a, b], [b, c]] opacity: Float sigmai tilesize: Float T imagewidth: Int Wimg imageheight: Int Himg Returns: Tuple (txstart, tystart, txend, tyend) """ mux, muy = gaussianmean2d a, b, c = covinv2d # Step 2: Compute threshold t if opacity <= 0: return (0, 0, 0, 0) t = 2.0 math.log(255.0 opacity) # Step 3: Compute xd extrema (xdargs) # xdargs = +/- sqrt( (-b^2 t) / ((b^2 - ac) a)) denomx = (b2 - ac) a if denomx == 0: return (0, 0, 0, 0) sqrttermx = math.sqrt((-b2 t) / denomx) xdargs = [sqrttermx, -sqrttermx] # Step 4: Compute yd extrema # yd = (-bxd +/- sqrt((b^2 - ac)xd^2 + tc)) / c ydvalues = [] det = b2 - ac for xd in xdargs: # Calculate discriminant for yd disc = det (xd2) + t c if disc < 0: # Numerical noise might cause slight negative values disc = 0.0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) # Guard against c=0 if c == 0: continue yd1 = (-b xd + sqrtdisc) / c yd2 = (-b xd - sqrtdisc) / c ydvalues.append(yd1) ydvalues.append(yd2) if not ydvalues: return (0, 0, 0, 0) ymind = min(ydvalues) ymaxd = max(ydvalues) ymin = ymind + muy ymax = ymaxd + muy # Step 5: Compute xd extrema (symmetric to y) # Swap a and c, and xd and yd logic. # We need to find ydargs (extrema in y) to get xd bounds. # The formula for xd given yd is: # xd = (-byd +/- sqrt((b^2 - ac)yd^2 + ta)) / a # Find ydargs: where dxd/dyd = 0 # ydargs = +/- sqrt( (-b^2 t) / ((b^2 - ac) c)) denomy = (b2 - ac) c if denomy == 0: return (0, 0, 0, 0) sqrttermy = math.sqrt((-b2 t) / denomy) ydargs = [sqrttermy, -sqrttermy] xdvalues = [] for yd in ydargs: disc = det (yd2) + t a if disc < 0: disc = 0.0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) if a == 0: continue xd1 = (-b yd + sqrtdisc) / a xd2 = (-b yd - sqrtdisc) / a xdvalues.append(xd1) xdvalues.append(xd2) if not xdvalues: return (0, 0, 0, 0) xmind = min(xdvalues) xmaxd = max(xdvalues) xmin = xmind + mux xmax = xmaxd + mux # Step 6: Convert to tile indices txstart = max(0, math.floor(xmin / tilesize)) txend = min(math.ceil(imagewidth / tilesize) - 1, math.ceil(xmax / tilesize)) tystart = max(0, math.floor(ymin / tilesize)) tyend = min(math.ceil(imageheight / tilesize) - 1, math.ceil(ymax / tilesize)) return (txstart, tystart, txend, tyend) Parameters: \sigmai: Gaussian opacity. The threshold t is computed as t = 2 \log(255 \sigmai). Tile Size T: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Covariance: If a=0 or c=0, the inverse covariance is singular or the ellipse is axis-aligned in a way that makes the derivative zero at infinity. The pseudocode handles this by returning empty bounds or skipping, which effectively culls the Gaussian or requires a fallback. Numerical Stability: Under edge-on tilts, the projected covariance can become ill-conditioned. SnugBox is noted to provide numerical stability in these cases compared to simpler bounding circles. Negative Discriminant: Due to floating-point errors, the term inside the square root for yd or xd might be slightly negative. It should be clamped to 0. Compact Box (CB) is a preprocessing optimization that tightens the effective support region of 2D Gaussians to eliminate negligible tile intersections. It sets itself apart from SnugBox by introducing a scaling factor \beta into the alpha blending equation, further shrinking the footprint. Choose it when maximum tile culling is required at the cost of modified blending weights. Compact Box (CB) A technique to reduce invalid Gaussian evaluations by using tighter intersection tests between Gaussians and tiles/pixels. AdR-Gaussian uses tight axis-aligned bounding boxes, while FlashGS refines Gaussian–tile intersection; both reduce associations, shrinking sorting input, traversal, and intermediate list traffic. Time Complexity: Constant number of operations per Gaussian (O(1)). It is called twice in the rendering pipeline: once to count Gaussians in the preprocess step and once to populate the Gaussian-to-tile arrays in duplicateWithKeys. Memory Complexity: No additional significant memory overhead compared to standard 3D-GS, as it only computes bounds. Performance: Produces an average overall inference speed-up of 1.82× on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets compared to baseline 3D-GS. When combined with AccuTile, it contributes to a 2× FPS boost. Strengths: Lossless (does not change rendered image), precise tile assignment reduces overestimation, numerically stable. Limitations: Requires computation of inverse covariance and eigenvalues/square roots, which is more expensive per Gaussian than the simple circle radius check in standard 3D-GS, but the reduction in tile processing offsets this. SnugBox was introduced in the "Speedy-Splat" paper by Hanson et al. (2025). It addresses the inefficiency of the standard 3D-GS tile assignment, which uses a square bounding box inscribing a circle with radius 3\sqrt{\lambda{max}}, leading to overly conservative tile assignments. SnugBox is one of several contributions in the Speedy-Splat suite, alongside AccuTile and pruning methods, designed to maximize rendering speed while maintaining visual fidelity. It builds on the concept of using the elliptical extent of the Gaussian for more precise culling. name: Compact Box (CB)
body: Compact Box (CB) is a preprocessing optimization for rasterization that reduces the number of Gaussian-tile pairs by tightening the effective support region of 2D Gaussians, eliminating unnecessary pairs where the Gaussian has negligible impact on pixels within a tile. It builds upon the precise tile-intersection strategy of Speedy-Splat to further reduce the effective 2D Gaussian region and eliminate redundant pairs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D Gaussian parameters (opacity \sigmai, 2D mean \mu{i2D}, 2D covariance \Sigma{i2D}), tile grid configuration, and scaling factor \beta. Output: A pruned set of relevant Gaussian-tile pairs for rasterization. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard 2D Gaussian representation used in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The covariance matrix \Sigma{i2D} is decomposed into rotation and scaling components, but for the CB calculation, the inverse covariance \Sigma{i2D}^{-1} is used directly in the Mahalanobis distance calculation. Steps: 1. Calculate Modified Alpha: For a given pixel p and the i-th Gaussian, compute the alpha value using the modified equation that incorporates the scaling factor \beta: \alphai(p) = \sigmai \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\beta}{2} (p - \mu{i2D})^\top \Sigma{i2D}^{-1} (p - \mu{i2D})\right) where \sigmai is the opacity, \mu{i2D} is the 2D mean position, \Sigma{i2D} is the 2D covariance matrix, and \beta is the scaling factor. The term (p - \mu{i2D})^\top \Sigma{i2D}^{-1} (p - \mu{i2D}) represents the squared Mahalanobis distance. 2. Determine Effective Support: Use the modified alpha equation to define the effective support region of the 2D Gaussian. A smaller \beta yields a tighter ellipse around the mean \mu{i2D}, reducing the spatial extent and limiting the number of pixels influenced by the Gaussian. 3. Integrate with SnugBox: Integrate the modified alpha equation into the SnugBox implementation. The parameter \beta further reduces the 2D Gaussian footprint and shrinks its intersection region with tiles. 4. Prune Gaussian-Tile Pairs: Use the reduced footprint to determine which Gaussian-tile pairs are relevant. Pairs where the Gaussian has negligible impact on pixels within a tile are eliminated. This is typically done using the accutile method from Speedy-Splat, which performs precise tile intersection based on the compacted region. Parameters: \beta: A scaling factor that flexibly controls the effective support region of each 2D Gaussian. A smaller \beta yields a tighter ellipse around the mean, reducing spatial extent and limiting pixels influenced by the Gaussian. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The calculation involves matrix inversion (\Sigma{i2D}^{-1}) and exponential functions. Numerical stability should be ensured for degenerate covariances. Boundary Conditions: The method relies on the precise tile intersection logic of SnugBox. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def compactboxrasterization(gaussians, tiles, beta): """ Rasterization with Compact Box optimization. Args: gaussians: list of dicts with keys 'sigma', 'mu2d' (2,), 'Sigma2d' (2,2) tiles: list of dicts with keys 'id', 'min' (2,), 'max' (2,) beta: float scaling factor Returns: list of (gaussianindex, tileindex) pairs """ relevantpairs = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Compute inverse covariance for Mahalanobis distance try: Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(g['Sigma2d']) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue # Skip degenerate covariance # Compute compacted support region # Smaller beta tightens the ellipse, reducing spatial extent # We approximate the compacted bounding box for tile culling eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(g['Sigma2d']) radii = np.sqrt(eigenvalues / beta) minpt = g['mu2d'] - radii maxpt = g['mu2d'] + radii # Precise tile intersection is handled by Speedy-Splat's accutile method # Here we perform a basic axis-aligned bounding box intersection check for j, t in enumerate(tiles): if minpt[0] <= t['max'][0] and maxpt[0] >= t['min'][0] and \ minpt[1] <= t['max'][1] and maxpt[1] >= t['min'][1]: relevantpairs.append((i, j)) return relevantpairs A precise algorithm for computing Gaussian-tile bounding box intersections, replacing the overly conservative tile assignment in standard 3D-GS to reduce the number of pixels processed per Gaussian. Choose when you need precise tile intersection without the additional support region tightening of CB. SnugBox Time Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussian-tile pairs, leading to faster rasterization. The exact complexity reduction depends on the scene and the value of \beta. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory usage associated with storing and processing Gaussian-tile pairs. Measured Performance: The sources do not provide specific performance metrics for CB alone, but FastGS (which integrates CB) achieves an average training time of around 100 seconds per scene. Strengths: Further reduces computational redundancy compared to vanilla 3DGS and Speedy-Splat by eliminating Gaussians with negligible impact on tiles. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \beta to balance between pruning efficiency and rendering quality. Typical values are not given in the sources. When to Use: Use when rendering efficiency is critical and the scene contains many Gaussians with negligible impact on certain tiles. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Compact Box (CB) was introduced in the paper "FastGS: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting in 100 Seconds". It builds upon the precise tile-intersection strategy of Speedy-Splat to further reduce the effective 2D Gaussian region and eliminate unnecessary Gaussian-tile pairs. The method addresses the computational redundancy introduced by the 3-sigma rule in vanilla 3DGS and the remaining negligible Gaussians in Speedy-Splat. name: Complete tile culling using scan-line intersection
head: Exact scan-line intersection culling, Closed-form ellipse-tile intersection
body: A method to compute exact intersections between screen-space Gaussian ellipses and rendering tiles, eliminating the false-positive and false-negative errors inherent in distance-based, bounding-box, or compact box culling approaches. It sets itself apart by providing a branchless, closed-form solution that precisely determines tile overlap without the memory overhead of separate culling passes. Inputs: Screen-space Gaussian parameters (center, covariance-derived ellipse coefficients a, b, c, opacity threshold \tau), tile grid dimensions, and tile boundaries. Outputs: A list of intersecting tile indices for each Gaussian, or a visibility mask for warp-level culling. Data Structures: Gaussian Ellipse Coefficients: Derived from the projected covariance matrix. The screen-space ellipse equation is a\tilde{x}^2 + 2b\tilde{x}\tilde{y} + c\tilde{y}^2 = \tau, where \tilde{x}, \tilde{y} are coordinates relative to the Gaussian center. Tile Buffer: Stores tile-depth pairs or tile indices. In the projection-forward pass, the number of intersecting tiles is computed per Gaussian. A separate pass fills the buffer with these pairs. Steps: 1. Select Shorter Dimension: Pick the shorter dimension of the screen-space Gaussian ellipse (e.g., vertical) to minimize the number of rows/columns to process. 2. Compute Global Extremes: Determine the global extreme points of the ellipse along the selected axis. For the vertical axis, this involves finding the maximum vertical radius dy: dy = \sqrt{\frac{a\tau}{ac - b^2}} This assumes the conic matrix is positive-definite (a > 0). 3. Determine Vertical Span: Calculate the continuous vertical span [y{min}, y{max}] of the ellipse. If the ellipse is rotated, the peak vertex location depends on the horizontal clipping interval [\tilde{x}0, \tilde{x}1] relative to the tile column. Case A (Peak Inside): If the peak vertex falls within the horizontal bounds, the max displacement is derived from the quadratic profile. Case B (Peak Outside): If the peak is outside, the maximum displacement occurs at the boundary closest to the peak. 4. Intersect with Tile Boundary: For each row (or column) of tiles, intersect the continuous vertical span [y{min}, y{max}] with the tile's vertical boundary [y{tile\min}, y{tile\max}] to yield the valid range [y{start}, y{end}]: y{start} = \max(y{tile\min}, \lceil y{min} \rceil) y{end} = \min(y{tile\max}, \lfloor y{max} \rfloor) 5. Discretize and Count: If y{start} \le y{end}, the Gaussian intersects the tile row. Round down the minimum coordinate and round up the maximum coordinate toward the tile boundary to efficiently count or iterate through tiles. For warp-level culling, map the span to discrete warp indices using bitwise right shifts (since each warp covers 2 pixel rows): w{start} = (y{start} - y{tile\min}) \gg 1 w{end} = (y{end} - y{tile\min}) \gg 1 6. Construct Visibility Mask: Create an 8-bit unsigned integer mask Mi where each bit represents the visibility of a 16x2 warp sub-region: Mi = ((1 \ll (w{end} - w{start} + 1)) - 1) \ll w{start} If y{start} > y{end}, then Mi = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetileintersection(gaussian, tilegrid): """ Computes exact tile intersections for a Gaussian using scan-line intersection. gaussian: object with attributes.a,.b,.c,.tau,.centerx,.centery tilegrid: object with attributes.width,.height,.tilewidth,.tileheight """ # 1. Compute ellipse coefficients and extremes # Note: a, b, c are derived from projected covariance. # For simplicity, assume they are pre-computed as per. discriminant = gaussian.a gaussian.c - gaussian.b 2 # 2. Compute vertical radius dy dy = math.sqrt((gaussian.a gaussian.tau) / discriminant) # 3. Determine global vertical span [ymin, ymax] # Assuming axis-aligned for simplicity or using peak vertex logic from ymin = gaussian.centery - dy ymax = gaussian.centery + dy intersectingtiles = [] # 4. Iterate over tile rows (shorter dimension assumed vertical) for tilerow in range(tilegrid.height // tilegrid.tileheight): ytilemin = tilerow tilegrid.tileheight ytilemax = (tilerow + 1) tilegrid.tileheight # 5. Intersect with tile boundary ystart = max(ytilemin, math.ceil(ymin)) yend = min(ytilemax, math.floor(ymax)) if ystart <= yend: # 6. Discretize to tile indices # Round down min, round up max toward tile boundary tileidxstart = math.floor(ystart / tilegrid.tileheight) tileidxend = math.ceil(yend / tilegrid.tileheight) - 1 for tidx in range(tileidxstart, tileidxend + 1): intersectingtiles.append(tidx) return intersectingtiles def constructwarpmask(ystart, yend, ytilemin): """ Constructs 8-bit visibility mask for warp-level culling. """ if ystart > yend: return 0 # Map span to discrete warp indices (2 pixels per warp row) wstart = (ystart - ytilemin) >> 1 wend = (yend - ytilemin) >> 1 # Construct mask if wend < wstart: return 0 mask = ((1 << (wend - wstart + 1)) - 1) << wstart return mask Parameters: Opacity Threshold (\tau): Determines the extent of the ellipse. Typical values depend on the rendering engine's opacity cutoff. Subgroup Size: Used to round up the batch size S to balance performance and hardware occupancy, capped at 128. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Ellipses: If ac - b^2 \le 0, the ellipse is degenerate or invalid. The method assumes a positive-definite conic matrix (a > 0). Precision: Rounding operations (\lceil \cdot \rceil, \lfloor \cdot \rfloor) must be handled carefully to avoid off-by-one errors at tile boundaries. False Positives/Negatives: Prior methods using bounding boxes suffer from these; this method eliminates them by using the exact ellipse equation. A technique to convert continuous geometric clipping of a Gaussian primitive against a tile column into a hardware-friendly 8-bit discrete warp mask, where each bit represents the visibility of a 16x2 warp sub-region. It serves as a front-end jump barrier to trigger hardware uniform branches, bypassing downstream instruction sequences for culled warps. Choose this when optimizing for GPU warp scheduler efficiency and reducing pipeline bubbles. See Warp-Level Culling for Efficient Blending in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Time Complexity: The intersection computation is O(1) per Gaussian per tile row, as it uses closed-form solutions. The overall rasterization latency is proportional to the product of the number of batches and Gaussians traversed per batch, minimized by a batch size S \approx \sqrt{NP}. Memory Complexity: Requires a separate buffer to store tile-depth pairs, introducing VRAM usage overhead compared to in-place culling. Performance: Eliminates false positives/negatives, improving rendering accuracy. The branchless implementation reduces instruction divergence. Warp-level culling mitigates pipeline bubbles by utilizing hardware uniform branches. Strengths: Exact intersection detection, high performance on modern GPUs due to branchless code and warp-level optimization. Limitations: Requires additional VRAM for the tile buffer. Computationally more intensive than simple bounding box checks, though still efficient due to closed-form nature. Originated in the context of high-performance 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, specifically addressing the limitations of prior culling methods that suffered from false positives or negatives. The scan-line approach was inspired by earlier works [HTL 25, LWC 25]. The warp-level mask construction was introduced in Local-GS to accelerate rendering via tile-local warp coherence. name: Warp-Level Culling for Efficient Blending in 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: An optimization for the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) alpha blending stage that uses warp-level collaboration to subdivide image tiles and cull splats with no geometric overlap, avoiding expensive alpha evaluation. It improves rendering speed without changing the rendered output, implemented in the existing CUDA differentiable pipeline. Unlike sibling methods that optimize bounding volumes, this method focuses on geometric culling within the blending kernel to reduce the number of blending operations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), camera parameters (view/projection matrices), image resolution, tile configuration (default 16×16 pixels). Output: Final 2D image (RGB + Alpha). Data Structures: Gaussian Batch: A contiguous array of Gaussian primitives processed in batches of 256 splats. Tile Data: A 2D grid of tiles covering the image, where each tile contains a list of assigned splats. Shared Memory: Used to store the current batch of splats and rearranged data for optimized shared memory access. Algorithm Steps: The rendering pipeline consists of four stages, with this method optimizing the fourth: 1. Preprocessing: The preprocesscu kernel selects relevant 3D Gaussians and projects them into screen space as 2D splats. 2. Depth Sorting: Splats are sorted by distance to the camera using CUB Device Radix Sort. 3. Instancing: The image is divided into tiles, and splats are duplicated into each tile they overlap. During this stage, a coarse culling is performed: the splat’s maximum opacity is computed in each assigned tile. If the opacity is below the minimum contribution threshold (8-bit RGB value of 1256), the splat is culled from that tile. 4. Blend (Warp-Level Culling): The blendcu kernel performs alpha-over compositing. Tile Subdivision: Each image tile (e.g., 16×16 pixels) is subdivided into sub-tiles. A GPU thread block is mapped to a tile, and warps within that block collaborate to process sub-tiles. Geometric Culling: For each sub-tile, the warp checks if any splats in the current batch have geometric overlap with the sub-tile's pixel region. Splats with no geometric overlap are culled, avoiding the expensive alpha evaluation and compositing for those pixels. Alpha-Over Compositing: For remaining splats, the standard alpha-over formula is applied: C{out} = C{in} (1 - \alpha{splat}) + C{splat} \alpha{splat} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} (1 - \alpha{splat}) + \alpha{splat} Batch Processing: Splat data is processed in batches of 256 splats. Each batch is processed in two synchronization-fenced stages: fetching from DRAM and rendering. Data Rearrangement: Splat data is rearranged into optimized structures for shared memory access to improve throughput. Parameters: Tile Size: 16 × 16 pixels (default in Faster-GS). Contribution Threshold: 1256 (minimum 8-bit RGB color value) used during instancing to cull low-opacity splats. Batch Size: 256 splats per batch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blendcukernel(tileid, splatbatches, threadid): TILEWIDTH = 16 TILEHEIGHT = 16 BATCHSIZE = 256 WARPSPERTILE = 8 SUBTILEW = TILEWIDTH // WARPSPERTILE SUBTILEH = TILEHEIGHT // WARPSPERTILE warpid = threadid // 32 subtilex = (warpid % WARPSPERTILE) SUBTILEW subtiley = (warpid // WARPSPERTILE) SUBTILEH tilecolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tilealpha = 0.0 for batch in splatbatches: # Stage 1: Fetch batch from DRAM into shared memory splatdata = batch # Array of 256 splats # Stage 2: Render with warp-level geometric culling for i in range(len(splatdata)): splat = splatdata[i] # Sources do not specify the exact geometric overlap formula; # standard implementation checks bounding box intersection. cx, cy = splat.center sx, sy = splat.scale if abs(cx - (subtilex + SUBTILEW / 2)) <= sx + SUBTILEW / 2 and \ abs(cy - (subtiley + SUBTILEH / 2)) <= sy + SUBTILEH / 2: a = splat.opacity c = splat.color tilecolor[0] = tilecolor[0] (1.0 - a) + c[0] a tilecolor[1] = tilecolor[1] (1.0 - a) + c[1] a tilecolor[2] = tilecolor[2] (1.0 - a) + c[2] a tilealpha = tilealpha (1.0 - a) + a writetiletoframebuffer(tileid, tilecolor, tilealpha) def writetiletoframebuffer(tileid, color, alpha): # Writes accumulated tile color and alpha to global framebuffer memory pass GEMM-GS is a rendering optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reformulates the opacity computation into a General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) compatible dot-product form to leverage GPU Tensor Cores. Unlike Warp-Level Culling for Efficient Blending in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which focuses on geometric culling to reduce the number of blending operations, GEMM-GS accelerates the remaining blending computations themselves. Choose it when Tensor Core utilization is the bottleneck rather than memory bandwidth or culling overhead. Performance: On NVIDIA RTX 4090, the method is up to 19% faster than Faster-GS. On NVIDIA RTX 2070 Super, the method is up to 32% faster. Across all tested GPUs (RTX 4090, RTX 3090, RTX 2070 Super), the changes reduce frame time over Faster-GS by 17% (+20% FPS) on average (geometric mean). On the RTX 2070 Super specifically, the frame time reduction is up to 24% (+32% FPS). Complexity: The baseline alpha-blending GPU kernel (Faster-GS) performs two to three times slower than the optimistic theoretical bound. This method reduces that gap by eliminating redundant computations. Strengths: Maintains identical visual fidelity and differentiability as the original 3DGS implementation. It stays within the CUDA differentiable framework, unlike methods such as PUP 3D-GS, Sort-Free Gaussians, or VKRayGS which sacrifice image quality or differentiability. Limitations: Requires modification of the standard CUDA pipeline. Performance gains are hardware-dependent (tested on NVIDIA RTX 4090, 3090, 2070 Super). 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] has become a dominant technique for novel view synthesis. Despite thousands of follow-up methods, there is still room for improvement in rendering speed. This method analyzes the state-of-the-art inference pipeline (Faster-GS) and improves it by focusing on the alpha blending stage, which is one of the longest-running stages in the pipeline. The code implementation can be used in the ICG Neural Radiance Fields and Novel View Synthesis Framework (NeRFICG) [Kappel et al. 2026]. name: GEMM-GS Blending
head: GEMM-compatible Blending, Intra-Tile Coordinate Transformation
body: GEMM-GS is a rendering optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reformulates the opacity computation into a General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) compatible dot-product form to leverage GPU Tensor Cores. It addresses the low compute efficiency of standard element-wise quadratic evaluations in the blending stage by exploiting intra-tile relative coordinates to transform quadratic power terms into linear dot products. Unlike Warp-Level Culling for Efficient Blending in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which focuses on geometric culling to reduce the number of blending operations, GEMM-GS accelerates the remaining blending computations themselves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of sorted 3D Gaussians overlapping with the current image tile, tile dimensions (16×16 pixels), and batch size (256 Gaussians). Output: Rendered color values for all pixels in the tile. Data Structures: Reference Pixel (pc): A fixed pixel within the tile, typically the center, with coordinates (xc, yc). Intra-tile Relative Coordinates (\bar{x}{pj}, \bar{y}{pj}): For any pixel pj in the tile, defined such that (x{pj}, y{pj}) = (xc - \bar{x}{pj}, yc - \bar{y}{pj}). These are constant for all tiles and precomputed offline. Gaussian Offset (\hat{x}{gi}, \hat{y}{gi}): The difference between the Gaussian's projected center and the reference pixel: \hat{x}{gi} = x{gi} - xc, \hat{y}{gi} = y{gi} - yc. Gaussian Vector (\hat{v}{gi}): A 6-dimensional vector per Gaussian. Pixel Vector (\hat{v}{pj}): A 6-dimensional vector per pixel. Matrix Mg: Dimensions B \times 6, where B is the batch size (e.g., 256). Rows are \hat{v}{gi}^T. Matrix Mp: Dimensions P \times 6, where P is the number of pixels in the tile (e.g., 256). Rows are \hat{v}{pj}^T. This matrix is identical across all tiles and stored in global memory for reuse. Matrix M{power}: Dimensions B \times P. Result of the dot-product computation between Mg and Mp. Formulas: The opacity \alpha{ij} for Gaussian gi at pixel pj is: \alpha{ij} = oi \times \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}{gi}^T \Sigmai^{-1} \mathbf{x}{gi}\right) where \mathbf{x}{gi} = [\Delta x{ij} \ \Delta y{ij}]^T is the vector from the Gaussian center to the pixel, and \Sigmai^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} Ai & Bi \\ Bi & Ci \end{bmatrix} is the inverse covariance matrix. The exponent term (power) is expanded as: power{ij} = -\frac{1}{2} Ai \Delta x{ij}^2 - Bi \Delta x{ij} \Delta y{ij} - \frac{1}{2} Ci \Delta y{ij}^2 By substituting \Delta x{ij} = \hat{x}{gi} + \bar{x}{pj} and \Delta y{ij} = \hat{y}{gi} + \bar{y}{pj}, the power term is transformed into a dot product: power{ij} = \hat{v}{gi} \cdot \hat{v}{pj} The components of \hat{v}{gi} are: \hat{v}{gi} = \left[ -\frac{1}{2}Ai, -\frac{1}{2}Ci, -Bi, -Ai\hat{x}{gi} - Bi\hat{y}{gi}, -Ci\hat{y}{gi} - Bi\hat{x}{gi}, -\frac{1}{2}Ai\hat{x}{gi}^2 - \frac{1}{2}Ci\hat{y}{gi}^2 - Bi\hat{x}{gi}\hat{y}{gi} \right] The components of \hat{v}{pj} are derived from the factorization of the quadratic form: \hat{v}{pj} = \left[ -\frac{1}{2}\bar{x}{pj}^2, -\frac{1}{2}\bar{y}{pj}^2, -\bar{x}{pj}\bar{y}{pj}, \bar{x}{pj}, \bar{y}{pj}, 1 \right]^T Parameters: Tile size: 16×16 pixels (256 pixels total). Batch size: 256 Gaussians. Thread block size: 256 threads (8 warps). Steps: 1. Precomputation: Offline, compute \hat{v}{pj} for all 256 pixels in a 16×16 tile relative to the center reference pixel. 2. Stage 1 (Load Indices): Load Gaussian indices for the current batch into shared memory. 3. Stage 2 (Fetch Attributes): Fetch Gaussian attributes (projected coordinates, covariance parameters Ai, Bi, Ci, opacity oi, color) from global memory. Compute \hat{x}{gi}, \hat{y}{gi} and construct \hat{v}{gi} for each Gaussian in the batch. 4. Stage 3 (GEMM and Rendering): Perform matrix multiplication M{power} = Mg \cdot Mp. Due to limited shared memory, use a mini-batch design. Execute this via four rounds of warp-level mma(m16n8k8) PTX instructions. Compute opacity: \alpha{ij} = oi \times \exp(M{power}[i][j]). Apply \alpha-skipping if \alpha{ij} \le 1/255. Perform alpha blending accumulation with early termination if transmittance Tj \le 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computepixelvectors(tilesize=16): """Precompute Mp for a tile. Returns a (256, 6) array.""" Mp = [] half = tilesize // 2 for dy in range(tilesize): for dx in range(tilesize): xbar = dx - half ybar = dy - half vp = [ -0.5 xbar2, -0.5 ybar2, -xbar ybar, xbar, ybar, 1.0 ] Mp.append(vp) return Mp def gemmgsblend(gaussianlist, tilerefcenter, Mpglobal): """ gaussianlist: List of sorted Gaussians overlapping the tile. tilerefcenter: (xc, yc) of the reference pixel. Mpglobal: Precomputed (256, 6) matrix of pixel vectors. """ xc, yc = tilerefcenter batchsize = 256 tilepixels = 256 # Stage 1: Load indices into shared memory (IBuffer) # Standard async memory copy from global to shared memory # Stage 2: Fetch attributes and construct Mg Mg = [] for i in range(batchsize): g = gaussianlist[i] xhat = g.xproj - xc yhat = g.yproj - yc vg = [ -0.5 g.A, -0.5 g.C, -g.B, -g.A xhat - g.B yhat, -g.C yhat - g.B xhat, -0.5 g.A xhat2 - 0.5 g.C yhat2 - g.B xhat yhat ] Mg.append(vg) # Stage 3: GEMM and Rendering # Mini-batch design due to shared memory limits # Multiply 16x8 submatrices of Mg with Mp using warp-level mma(m16n8k8) PTX instructions # A thread block of 8 warps makes 32 warp-level calls to complete m256n16k8 # Compute dot products explicitly to match Mpower[i][j] = vgi. vpj Mpower = [[sum(Mg[i][k] Mpglobal[j][k] for k in range(6)) for j in range(tilepixels)] for i in range(batchsize)] # Volume rendering per pixel for j in range(tilepixels): Tj = 1.0 Cj = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(batchsize): power = Mpower[i][j] alpha = gaussianlist[i].opacity math.exp(power) if alpha <= 1.0 / 255.0: continue Cj[0] += alpha Tj gaussianlist[i].color[0] Cj[1] += alpha Tj gaussianlist[i].color[1] Cj[2] += alpha Tj gaussianlist[i].color[2] Tj = (1.0 - alpha) if Tj <= 0.0: break # Store Cj to frame buffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shared Memory Limits: The mini-batch design (16×8 submatrices) is required due to limited shared memory. Boundary Conditions: Handling tiles at image boundaries requires padding or special handling not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The core blending operation is reduced to GEMM, which is highly optimized on Tensor Cores. The complexity is dominated by the matrix multiplication O(B \cdot P \cdot 6) per batch, where B is batch size and P is pixels per tile. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for Mp (256×6 floats) in global memory, plus shared memory for double-buffered indices, features, and Mg. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA A100, GEMM-GS achieves a 1.42× speedup over vanilla 3DGS. On H100, it achieves a 1.37× speedup. It provides an average 1.19× speedup over FlashGS, 1.42× over StopThePop, and 1.50× over SpeedySplat on A100. Strengths: High utilization of GPU Tensor Cores; efficient memory hierarchy usage via double buffering and warp-level synchronization. Limitations: Requires fixed tile and batch sizes for optimal performance; relies on specific PTX instructions for warp-level GEMM. When to use: When rendering 3DGS on modern NVIDIA GPUs with Tensor Cores and high throughput is required. When not to use: On hardware without Tensor Cores or warp-level MMA support. GEMM-GS was introduced in the paper "GEMM-GS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting on Tensor Cores with GEMM-Compatible Blending" by Haomin Li, Bowen Zhu, Fangxin Liu, et al., published in DAC ’26 (July 26–29, 2026, Long Beach, CA, USA). The work addresses the computational bottleneck of the blending stage in 3DGS, which traditionally uses element-wise quadratic calculations that do not map efficiently to GPU hardware. GEMM-GS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting on Tensor Cores with GEMM-Compatible Blending, https://doi.org/10.1145/3770743.3803899, fetched 2026-10-28

name: TileSkipper
head: Ours-Global, Ours-Regional, Region-Adaptive Tile Pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: TileSkipper is a post-training systems adapter for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces a single scene-wide contribution cutoff with a static per-Gaussian cutoff policy to reduce tile-pair enumeration work without retraining the checkpoint. It differs from AdaGScale by measuring candidate deletion residuals over calibration views using front transmittance and background color, allocating a discrete error budget across Gaussian groups, and rejecting policies via complete renders on disjoint training views, whereas AdaGScale derives a current-view peripheral score from local Gaussian contribution and depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A converged 3DGS checkpoint (frozen parameters), a tile rasterizer using a baseline scene-wide cutoff \tau0, and a set of calibration training views. Output: A compiled policy consisting of one uint8 byte per Gaussian (storing a multiplier index) and a threshold lookup table (LUT) of at most 256 thresholds. Data Structures: Gaussian Policy: An array of size N (number of Gaussians), where each element is a uint8 index into the LUT. Lookup Table (LUT): An array of at most 256 float values representing the actual cutoff thresholds \taug. Total size under 1 KB. Discrete Ladder (M): A fixed set of multipliers: \{1, 1.05, 1.1, 1.15, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}. Method Steps: 1. Geometric Support Definition: For a Gaussian g with peak opacity \alphag, the elliptical support boundary at threshold \tau is defined by the squared Mahalanobis radius: rg^2(\tau) = 2 \ln(\alphag / \tau) The support set is Sg(\tau) = \{x: \alphag(x) \ge \tau\}. 2. Runtime Rasterization (Inference): The rasterizer modifies only Stage 2 (Tile-Intersection) of the standard 3DGS pipeline: 1. Project: Project each visible Gaussian to screen space. 2. Enumerate Pairs: For each Gaussian g, read its policy byte to get index i, retrieve multiplier mg from the LUT, and compute \taug = mg \tau0. Create a (Gaussian, tile) pair if and only if the tile intersects the support Sg(\taug). 3. Sort: Sort each tile’s assigned Gaussians front-to-back. 4. Blend: Alpha-blend the sorted Gaussians per pixel. 3. Compilation (Offline Policy Search): The policy is compiled in five steps using calibration views: Step 1: Factorized Probes. For every Gaussian g and every multiplier m \in M (corresponding to ladder rung \ell): Perform a global render at threshold \tau = m \tau0. Measure pair savings s{g,\ell}: the exact change in enumerated pairs attributed to Gaussian g. Measure risk proxy \rho{g,\ell}: an isolated-deletion RGB-energy statistic computed via a custom backward pass that accumulates the squared contribution of removed pairs, holding others fixed: \rho{g,\ell} = \sum{v,x,c} \left( \alpha{g,v}(x) \frac{\partial C{v,c}(x)}{\partial \alpha{g,v}(x)} \right)^2 where the sum is over pixels x and channels c in pairs removed at rung \ell, and v denotes calibration views. Step 2: Risk Stratification. Bucket Gaussians into S=8 quantile strata based on the ratio of savings to risk at the most aggressive ladder rung. The sorting key is: \log\left(\frac{s{g,\ell} + \epsilon}{\rho{g,\ell} + \epsilon}\right) This groups Gaussians with similar "cheap-to-remove" characteristics. Step 3: Workload-Balanced Spatial Partition. Within each stratum, sort Gaussians by their Morton code (spatial locality). Cut the sorted list into contiguous blocks such that each block has equal measured tile-pair work. This produces K{reg} regions (default K{reg}=64). Step 4: Constrained Search. Aggregate savings and risk per region c: S{c,\ell} = \sum{g \in c} s{g,\ell} and R{c,\ell} = \sum{g \in c} \rho{g,\ell}. For 48 geometrically spaced penalty values \lambda, compute the optimal level \ell^ for each region by maximizing efficiency: \ell^c(\lambda) = \arg \max{\ell \in M} (S{c,\ell} - \lambda R{c,\ell}) Combine these regional proposals with uniform-level policies (where all Gaussians share one multiplier, K{reg}=1) to form the candidate set. Step 5: Held-out Selection. Render each candidate policy on a disjoint set of held-out training views. A candidate is feasible if: Minimum per-view Teacher PSNR \ge P{min}, and Maximum per-view p99 absolute residual \le E{max}. The Teacher PSNR is calculated against the unmodified renderer I0: P{teacher} = -10 \log{10} \text{mean}{x,c} (I(x,c) - I0(x,c))^2 The p99 residual is computed on a fixed 4x spatial subsample. Among feasible candidates, select the one with the greatest pair savings. Parameters: K{reg}: Number of regions. Default: 64. M: Discrete ladder of multipliers. Values: \{1, 1.05, 1.1, 1.15, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}. P{min}: Floor for teacher PSNR. E{max}: Cap for worst-view p99 absolute residual. \tau0: Baseline scene-wide cutoff (e.g., 1/255 in Speedy-Splat). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the threshold \taug reaches the Gaussian's opacity \alphag, the Gaussian produces no tile pairs but its checkpoint parameters are retained. The risk proxy \rho{g,\ell} omits cross terms when many contributions are removed jointly; it is a ranking proxy, not an exact prediction of joint image error. Compilation time averages 9.0 s per scene (max 14.0 s), requiring O(|M|V) rasterizer passes for probes. Time Complexity: Compilation is O(|M|V) rasterizer passes, where |M|=11 and V is the number of calibration views. Inference adds negligible overhead (one byte read and LUT lookup per Gaussian). Memory Complexity: Policy storage is 1 byte per Gaussian + <1 KB LUT. No additional memory for runtime inference. Performance: On 13 scenes from Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, TileSkipper provides dataset-macro speedups of 1.088\times at standard resolution and 1.238\times at 3840 pixels wide, with mean PSNR changes of -0.007 dB and -0.023 dB respectively. Strengths: Training-free, static policy, no per-frame inference, compatible with existing opacity-aware bounds. Limitations: Requires offline compilation; performance gain is modest compared to architectural changes; relies on calibration views for policy selection. TileSkipper addresses the limitation of fixed scene-wide cutoffs in tiled 3DGS rasterizers, which do not account for content sensitivity to support truncation. It builds on Tile-Based Culling by replacing the static cutoff with a compiled static policy. It is distinct from AdaGScale, which uses runtime view adaptation, by trading runtime adaptation for a scene-level, static one-byte policy. The authors and publication year are not given in the sources. TileSkipper: Region-Adaptive Tile Pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09343, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Tile-based Rasteriser
head: Tile-based Rasterizer
body: The tile-based rasteriser sorts projected 2D Gaussian splats once per frame to serve both forward rendering and backpropagation. It solves the depth-ordering problem for millions of splats by dividing the image into 16 \times 16 tiles and using a single global radix sort, eliminating sequential primitive processing steps. Unlike per-pixel sorting, which is too slow for real-time performance, this method achieves parallel depth resolution and compact per-tile lists, enabling the backward pass to reuse the same sorted lists for gradient computation without additional sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A list of N projected 2D Gaussian splats. Each splat i is defined by its center (xi, yi), 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i, color ci, opacity \alphai, and depth Zc. Outputs: A sorted list of (splat, tile) pairs, and the final rendered image with alpha-blended colors. Data Structures: Splat List: An array of N splats. Tile Grid: The image is divided into a grid of tiles with dimensions Tw \times Th. The standard tile size is 16 \times 16 pixels. Sort Key: A 64-bit integer key for each (splat, tile) pair. The key is constructed as: \text{key} = (\text{tile\id} \ll 32) \mid (\text{uint32\t})Zc where tileid is the 1D tile index (y \times \text{grid\width} + x) and Zc is cast to a 32-bit unsigned integer. The exact size of the tile index depends on the number of tiles fitting the current resolution. Steps: 1. Tile Assignment: Each Gaussian is assigned to every tile its projected 2D splat touches. If a splat straddles tile boundaries, it is duplicated into each relevant tile, creating one work item per (Gaussian, tile) pair. 2. Key Packing: For each (splat, tile) pair, a 64-bit integer sort key is constructed. The tile ID is packed into the high bits, and the splat's depth Zc is packed into the low bits. 3. Global Radix Sort: A single GPU radix sort is performed over all (splat, tile) pairs. This simultaneously bins splats by tile ID (ensuring contiguity) and sorts them by depth within each tile. 4. Range Identification: Per-tile ranges in the sorted array are identified by comparing the higher 32 bits of each element with its two neighbors using one thread per 64-bit element. This eliminates sequential primitive processing steps and produces more compact per-tile lists. 5. Rendering: Each tile is processed by one GPU thread block that walks the sorted list. For each pixel in a tile, front-to-back compositing is performed using the tile's sorted list of splats, evaluating per-pixel alpha \alphai(\mathbf{x}) and breaking early when transmittance T < \epsilon. 6. Backpropagation: The same sorted lists are reused for backpropagation, allowing gradients to flow to position, shape, opacity, and color without additional sorting. Parameters: Tile Size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Key Size: 64 bits (32 bits depth, 32 bits tile index). Alpha Clamping: Alpha is clamped with 0.99 from above. Blending Stop: Before including a Gaussian in the forward pass, the accumulated opacity if it were included is computed, and front-to-back blending stops before it can exceed 0.9999. Skip Threshold: Blending updates with \alpha < 1/255 are skipped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tilebasedrasterization(splats, imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize=16): """ Renders 3D Gaussian splats using tile-based rasterization. Args: splats: List of N splats, each with attributes: center: (x, y) in screen space cov2d: 2x2 covariance matrix Sigma' color: RGB color opacity: alpha value depth: Zc (view space depth) imagewidth: Width of the image in pixels imageheight: Height of the image in pixels tilesize: Size of each tile in pixels (default 16) Returns: renderedimage: Image buffer with final colors """ tilewidth = math.ceil(imagewidth / tilesize) tileheight = math.ceil(imageheight / tilesize) workitems = [] for i, splat in enumerate(splats): minx, maxx, miny, maxy = getsplattilebounds(splat.center, splat.cov2d, tilesize) mintx = math.floor(minx / tilesize) maxtx = math.floor(maxx / tilesize) minty = math.floor(miny / tilesize) maxty = math.floor(maxy / tilesize) for ty in range(max(0, minty), min(tileheight, maxty + 1)): for tx in range(max(0, mintx), min(tilewidth, maxtx + 1)): tileid = ty tilewidth + tx key = (tileid << 32) | (splat.depth & 0xFFFFFFFF) workitems.append((i, tileid, key)) # 2. Key Packing & 3. Global Radix Sort: Sort workitems by key using a GPU radix sort. # This bins by tileid and sorts by depth within each tile. workitems.sort(key=lambda item: item[2]) # 4. Range Identification tileranges = {} if not workitems: return emptyimage(imagewidth, imageheight) currenttile = workitems[0][1] startidx = 0 for idx, item in enumerate(workitems): tileid = item[1] if tileid != currenttile: tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, idx) currenttile = tileid startidx = idx tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, len(workitems)) # 5. Rendering renderedimage = emptyimage(imagewidth, imageheight) epsilon = 1e-4 for tileid, (start, end) in tileranges.items(): tilesplatindices = [workitems[i][0] for i in range(start, end)] ty = tileid // tilewidth tx = tileid % tilewidth for py in range(ty tilesize, min((ty + 1) tilesize, imageheight)): for px in range(tx tilesize, min((tx + 1) tilesize, imagewidth)): T = 1.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for splatidx in tilesplatindices: splat = splats[splatidx] alpha = evaluategaussianalpha(splat.center, splat.cov2d, px, py) if alpha < 1/255: continue alpha = min(alpha, 0.99) newalpha = 1.0 - T (1.0 - alpha) if newalpha > 0.9999: break color += splat.color alpha T T = (1.0 - alpha) if T < epsilon: break renderedimage[py, px] = color return renderedimage def evaluategaussianalpha(center, cov2d, px, py): dx = px - center[0] dy = py - center[1] invcov = invertmatrix(cov2d) exponent = -0.5 (dx invcov[0][0] dx + 2 dx invcov[0][1] dy + dy invcov[1][1] dy) return math.exp(exponent) def emptyimage(width, height): return [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] def getsplattilebounds(center, cov2d, tilesize): eigenvalues = computeeigenvalues(cov2d) sigmax = math.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) sigmay = math.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) minx = center[0] - 3 sigmax maxx = center[0] + 3 sigmax miny = center[1] - 3 sigmay maxy = center[1] + 3 sigmay return minx, maxx, miny, maxy def computeeigenvalues(matrix): a, b = matrix[0][0], matrix[0][1] c, d = matrix[1][0], matrix[1][1] trace = a + d det = a d - b c discriminant = trace trace - 4 det if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) eig1 = (trace + sqrtdisc) / 2 eig2 = (trace - sqrtdisc) / 2 return eig1, eig2 def invertmatrix(matrix): a, b = matrix[0][0], matrix[0][1] c, d = matrix[1][0], matrix[1][1] det = a d - b c if det == 0: return [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]] invdet = 1.0 / det return [[d invdet, -b invdet], [-c invdet, a invdet]] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: During the backward pass, reconstructing intermediate opacity values by dividing accumulated opacity by Gaussian opacity alpha is prone to numerical instabilities (e.g., division by 0). This is addressed by skipping blending updates with \alpha < 1/255 and clamping \alpha with 0.99 from above. Sorting Complexity: Sorting per pixel is too slow for millions of splats; tile-based sorting with a single global radix sort is required for real-time performance. Straddling Splats: A splat straddling tile boundaries is duplicated into each relevant tile. This results in a moderate increase in Gaussians to process, which is amortized by simpler control flow and high parallelism of optimized GPU Radix sort. Time Complexity: One O(n) radix sort over all (splat, tile) pairs replaces thousands of per-tile sorts. The sorting is performed once per frame. Memory Complexity: The number of work items increases due to splat duplication across tiles, but this is moderate and amortized by the efficiency of the radix sort. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 benchmark, the method reaches 27.21 dB PSNR and 0.214 LPIPS at 134 fps, surpassing the previous quality leader in perceptual similarity while trailing marginally in PSNR and rendering roughly three orders of magnitude faster. Strengths: Eliminates sequential primitive processing steps, produces more compact per-tile lists, and allows the backward pass to reuse the same sorted lists for training. Limitations: Numerical instability during the backward pass if not handled with clamping and thresholding. When to Use: When real-time rendering and training of 3D Gaussian Splatting are required, especially with millions of splats. The tile-based rasteriser was introduced in the paper "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering" by Kerbl et al.. It is a key component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, which also includes anisotropic 3D Gaussian projection, EWA projection, and adaptive density control. The method builds on the assumption of a high load of small splats and optimizes for this by sorting splats once for each frame using radix sort. It eliminates sequential primitive processing steps compared to previous methods like [Lassner and Zollhofer 2021]. An Architectural Review of the 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21739653, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079, fetched 2026-10-26 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering [pdf], https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/3dgaussiansplattinglow.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3DGS-101/textbook/05-alpha-compositing.md at main - GitHub, https://github.com/Chamud/3DGS-101/blob/main/textbook/05-alpha-compositing.md, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Rasterization Key Generation
head: Gaussian Tile Key Generation, Gaussian Tile Overlap Key Generation, Gaussian to Tile Mapping, Gaussian-to-Tile Key Generation, duplicateWithKeys, duplicateWithKeys kernel
body: This method generates key-value pairs for all Gaussians overlapping with tiles, enabling spatial sorting by tile ID and depth. It identifies which tiles each projected 2D Gaussian overlaps and constructs a 64-bit sort key combining the tile ID and the Gaussian's depth. This output serves as the direct input for the global radix sort performed by the parent method Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. It differs from sibling methods like Tile-Based Culling by explicitly generating the full set of overlaps for sorting rather than just filtering, and from Tile-based Depth Sorting by focusing on the key construction phase rather than the sorting algorithm itself. Inputs: pointsxy: Array of shape (N, 2) containing the 2D screen-space centers of N Gaussians. radii: Array of shape (N,) containing the radius of each Gaussian in pixels. depths: Array of shape (N,) containing the camera-space depth Zc for each Gaussian. gridwidth: Integer specifying the number of tiles in the x direction. gridheight: Integer specifying the number of tiles in the y direction. tilesize: Integer, typically 16 pixels Sibling: [Tile-based Rasteriser]. Outputs: gaussiankeysunsorted: Array of 64-bit integers (uint64t), one per generated overlap. gaussianvaluesunsorted: Array of 32-bit integers (uint32t), storing the original Gaussian index idx corresponding to each key. numoverlaps: Integer count of total key-value pairs generated. Data Structures: Keys are packed 64-bit integers. Bits [63:32] (Upper 32): 1D Tile ID, calculated as y{tile} \times W{tiles} + x{tile}. Bits [31:0] (Lower 32): Depth Zc, cast to uint32t. Values are 32-bit integers storing the source Gaussian index idx. Steps: 1. Initialize empty lists gaussiankeysunsorted and gaussianvaluesunsorted. 2. For each Gaussian index idx from 0 to N-1: a. If any radius component is \le 0, skip this Gaussian. b. Calculate the bounding rectangle in tile coordinates: x{min} = \lfloor (points\xy[idx, 0] - radii[idx]) / tile\size \rfloor. x{max} = \lceil (points\xy[idx, 0] + radii[idx]) / tile\size \rceil. y{min} = \lfloor (points\xy[idx, 1] - radii[idx]) / tile\size \rfloor. y{max} = \lceil (points\xy[idx, 1] + radii[idx]) / tile\size \rceil. c. Clamp x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max} to the valid tile grid boundaries [0, W{tiles}) and [0, H{tiles}). d. Iterate over tile rows y from y{min} to y{max} - 1: i. Iterate over tile columns x from x{min} to x{max} - 1: 1. Calculate 1D tile ID: tile\id = y \times W{tiles} + x. 2. Construct key: key = (tile\id \ll 32) \mid (\text{uint32\t})depths[idx]. 3. Append key to gaussiankeysunsorted and idx to gaussianvaluesunsorted. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generategaussianrasterizationkeys(pointsxy, radii, depths, gridwidth, gridheight, tilesize): """ Generates key-value pairs for Gaussian-tile overlaps. Args: pointsxy: (N, 2) array, screen space centers. radii: (N,) array, radii in pixels. depths: (N,) array, camera space depths. gridwidth: int, number of tiles horizontally. gridheight: int, number of tiles vertically. tilesize: int, pixels per tile. Returns: keys: List of uint64t sort keys. values: List of uint32t Gaussian indices. """ keys = [] values = [] N = len(pointsxy) for idx in range(N): r = radii[idx] if r <= 0: continue cx, cy = pointsxy[idx] # Calculate bounding rect in tile coordinates xmin = int(math.floor((cx - r) / tilesize)) xmax = int(math.ceil((cx + r) / tilesize)) ymin = int(math.floor((cy - r) / tilesize)) ymax = int(math.ceil((cy + r) / tilesize)) # Clamp to grid bounds xmin = max(0, xmin) xmax = min(gridwidth, xmax) ymin = max(0, ymin) ymax = min(gridheight, ymax) # Cast depth to uint32t depthuint = int(depths[idx]) & 0xFFFFFFFF for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): tileid = y gridwidth + x key = (tileid << 32) | depthuint keys.append(key) values.append(idx) return keys, values Parameters: tilesize: Typically 16 pixels [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. gridwidth: Determined by image width and tile size [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. Edge Cases: Zero Radius: Gaussians with radius \le 0 are skipped. Boundary Clamping: Tile coordinates must be clamped to the valid grid range to prevent out-of-bounds access. Depth Casting: Depth is cast to uint32t. Standard practice assumes positive depth within the 32-bit unsigned integer range. A CUDA-based preprocessing pipeline that culls invisible Gaussians, maps 3D Gaussian projections to tile-based intersection IDs, and sorts them. It generates key-value pairs for all Gaussian-tile overlaps to enable efficient tile-based rasterization. Unlike differentiable rendering steps, this mapping and sorting process is not differentiable to any input. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot A), where N is the number of Gaussians and A is the average number of tiles each Gaussian overlaps. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot A) for storing the keys and values arrays. Performance: This step is a simple parallel loop and is extremely fast compared to the subsequent radix sort. It scales linearly with the number of Gaussians and their spatial extent. Strengths: Simple logic, minimal memory overhead, highly parallelizable. Limitations: Generates duplicate entries for Gaussians spanning multiple tiles, increasing the workload for the subsequent sort. This method is part of the rendering implementation pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the CPU-sorted or tile-based rasterization variants [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. It was introduced in the context of efficient rasterization for Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction and Learning Methods [Sibling: Tile-based Rasteriser]. The specific implementation details (key packing, tile iteration) are derived from open-source implementations of Gaussian Splatting rasterizers. name: Gaussian-to-Intersect Mapping and Sorting
head: Gaussian rasterization preprocessing, Gaussian to Intersects Mapping, Tile-Based Gaussian Visibility Culling and Sorting, tile-key sorting
body: Gaussian-to-Intersect Mapping and Sorting is a CUDA-based preprocessing pipeline that culls invisible Gaussians, maps 2D Gaussian projections to tile-based intersection IDs, sorts them for depth ordering, and computes tile bins to enable efficient tile-based rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently organizing variable-length lists of Gaussian-tile overlaps for rasterization without resorting to a global composite-key sort, which is required by methods like Kerbl et al.'s original Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from its siblings by generating contiguous tile ranges in a depth-sorted Gaussian list, allowing downstream tile-based rasterizers to process Gaussians in spatially coherent batches. The method consists of a sequence of CUDA kernels and tensor operations that transform 3D Gaussian parameters into a sorted, tile-indexed format suitable for rasterization. Inputs: numpoints: Number of Gaussians. xys: Tensor of shape (batch, 2) containing x,y locations of 2D Gaussian projections. depths: Tensor of shape (batch, 1) containing z depth of Gaussians. radii: Tensor of shape (batch,) containing the 2D radii of Gaussians. cov2d: Tensor of shape (batch, 3) containing the upper triangular 2D covariance values. tilebounds: Tuple of (tilewidth, tileheight, numtiles) or (tiles.x, tiles.y, 1). blocksize: Integer block size for CUDA kernel. Outputs: isectids: Tensor of shape (cumtileshit, 1) containing unique IDs for each Gaussian in the form (tile | depth id). gaussianids: Tensor of shape (cumtileshit, 1) that maps isectids back to cumtileshit. tilebins: Tensor of shape (numintersects, 2) where each row represents the range of Gaussian IDs hit per tile. conic: Conic parameters derived from cov2d. radii: Computed radii derived from cov2d. It solves the parallel write-conflict problem of building variable-length lists without resorting to a global composite-key sort, which is required by methods like Kerbl et al.'s original Gaussian Splatting. name: Gaussian Partitioning (Count-Then-Fill Binning)
head: Count-Then-Fill Binning, HiGS Binning, Two-pass CUDA binning for Gaussians
body: Gaussian Partitioning is a two-pass CUDA binning algorithm that assigns 3D Gaussians to macro-tiles by constructing per-macro-tile, depth-keyed lists during the binning pass itself. It solves the parallel write-conflict problem of building variable-length lists without resorting to a global composite-key sort, which is required by methods like Kerbl et al.'s original Gaussian Splatting. By using batch-local atomics and hierarchical prefix scans, it eliminates the need for global sorting, leaving only in-segment ordering for downstream processing. Inputs: A batch of Bp = 8,192 Gaussians. Per-warp visibility bitmask from the projection front-end, used to cull invisible Gaussians before intersection tests. Macro-tile geometry (64×32 pixels) and frame dimensions. Outputs: A segmented structure of per-macro-tile lists containing (depth, gaussian-id) pairs, ready for in-segment sorting. Data Structures: 1. Histogram Matrix: An N{batch} \times N{macro} matrix stored in DRAM as packed uint16 pairs (two cells per 32-bit word). Size: 2 N{batch} N{macro} bytes. N{batch} = \lceil N{gs} / Bp \rceil N{macro}: Number of macro-tiles in the frame (~1,000 at 1080p, ~4,000 at 4K). 2. Output Pair List: Occupies 8 N{macro} bytes per batch. Each entry is a 4-byte depth key + 4-byte gaussian-id. 3. Local Histogram: Private shared memory in the CUDA work group, with one counter per macro-tile. Steps: 1. Batch Processing: The Gaussian set is divided into fixed-size batches of Bp = 8,192 Gaussians. Each batch is processed cooperatively by one CUDA work group (CTA). 2. Count Pass (Local Histogramming): The work group initializes a private shared-memory histogram with zeros, one counter per macro-tile. For each Gaussian in the batch: Check the per-warp visibility bitmask. If culled, skip. Perform a conservative per-row ellipse-contour intersection test against macro-tiles using Cholesky factors of the inverse covariance (AccuTile-style, but at macro-tile granularity). For each intersected macro-tile, increment the corresponding counter in the local histogram using local atomics. Flush the local histogram to DRAM as packed uint16 pairs into the Histogram Matrix. 3. Prefix Sum (Offset Calculation): Perform a two-level hierarchical prefix scan over the DRAM Histogram Matrix. Level 1: Aggregate batch-local counts to compute per-macro-tile total counts (widening 16-bit to 32-bit). Level 2: Compute global write offsets for each batch, determining the starting write position for each macro-tile's list in the output buffer. 4. Fill Pass: Replay the per-batch intersection logic (same visibility check and AccuTile intersection test). For each intersected macro-tile: Use the precomputed global write offset for that macro-tile and batch. Write a record consisting of a 4-byte depth key and a 4-byte gaussian-id to the output buffer. The depth key is stored as raw IEEE 754 float bits reinterpreted as int32 to exploit unsigned integer comparison sorting properties. Increment the write offset for that macro-tile (using local atomics or atomic add on the output buffer if necessary, though the hierarchical scan ensures disjoint ranges per batch if implemented correctly; the source implies direct writing into precomputed ranges). Histogram Matrix: Nbatch x Nmacro, stored as packed uint16 # Flattened to 1D array for simplicity in pseudocode histogram = [0] (Nbatch Nmacro) # --- Count Pass --- for batchidx in range(Nbatch): start = batchidx Bp end = min(start + Bp, Ngs) # Local histogram for this batch localhist = [0] Nmacro for i in range(start, end): g = gaussians[i] # Check visibility if not isvisible(g, visibilitymasks): continue # Intersection test intersectedtiles = accutileintersection(g, macrotilebounds) # Accumulate to local histogram for tileid in intersectedtiles: localhist[tileid] += 1 # Flush local histogram to DRAM for tileid in range(Nmacro): histogram[batchidx Nmacro + tileid] = localhist[tileid] # --- Prefix Sum --- # Compute global offsets for each batch-tile pair # This produces the starting write index for each macro-tile in each batch's segment offsets = computehierarchicalprefixsum(histogram, Nbatch, Nmacro) # --- Fill Pass --- for batchidx in range(Nbatch): start = batchidx Bp end = min(start + Bp, Ngs) # Current write pointer for each macro-tile within this batch's segment # Initialized to the base offset for this batch currentwriteptrs = [offsets[batchidx Nmacro + t] for t in range(Nmacro)] for i in range(start, end): g = gaussians[i] # Check visibility if not isvisible(g, visibilitymasks): continue # Intersection test intersectedtiles = accutileintersection(g, macrotilebounds) # Write to output buffer for tileid in intersectedtiles: depthkey = floattoint32bits(g.depth) record = (depthkey, i) outputbuffer[currentwriteptrs[tileid]] = record currentwriteptrs[tileid] += 1 return outputbuffer def floattoint32bits(f): """Reinterpret IEEE 754 float bits as int32 for sorting.""" import struct return struct.unpack('i', struct.pack('f', f))[0] def isvisible(g, masks): """Check if Gaussian is visible based on precomputed bitmask.""" # Implementation depends on specific warp mask layout return True # Placeholder for actual bitmask check def accutileintersection(g, bounds): """ Conservative per-row ellipse-contour intersection test. Returns list of intersected macro-tile IDs. """ # Uses Cholesky factors of inverse covariance # Returns tile IDs where the Gaussian overlaps return [] # Placeholder for actual intersection logic Parameters: Bp: Partition batch size, set to 8,192 Gaussians. Macro-tile size: 64×32 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Storage Capacity: A render-tile histogram would require 30,000–130,000 entries at 1080p/4K, exceeding commodity GPU local storage. Macro-tile histograms (~1,000 at 1080p, ~4,000 at 4K) fit comfortably. Depth Sorting: Depth must be stored as raw IEEE 754 float bits reinterpreted as int32 to ensure correct unsigned integer comparison sorting. Time Complexity: Dominated by the two passes over the Gaussian set and the hierarchical prefix scan. The prefix scan is O(N{batch} \cdot N{macro}). Memory Complexity: Histogram matrix size is 2 N{batch} N{macro} bytes. Output buffer size is proportional to the number of tile-Gaussian pairs. Performance: Reduces tile-Gaussian pair counts by 85–94% compared to gsplat (opacity-aware AABB) and AccuTile at render-tile granularity. 1080p: 10.1M pairs (gsplat) -> 1.51M pairs (HiGS). 4K: 29.3M pairs (gsplat) -> 2.21M pairs (HiGS). Strengths: Eliminates global composite-key sort; reduces data movement; fits in local storage. Limitations: Requires hierarchical prefix scan; dependent on AccuTile intersection accuracy. Origin: HiGS (Hierarchical Rendering Architecture for Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting). History: Developed as an alternative to Kerbl et al.'s global sort approach, addressing the scalability issues of global composite-key sorts for large Gaussian scenes. Usage: Used in real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines, particularly for CPU-sorted, instanced rendering and tiled rasterization.
