name: Tile Range Identification
head: identifyTileRanges, identifyTileRanges kernel
body: Tile Range Identification is a CUDA kernel that determines the contiguous start and end indices of each tile's Gaussian splats within a globally sorted list of projected 2D Gaussian keys. It solves the problem of mapping the flat, sorted array of (tile, depth) pairs back to per-tile ranges so that subsequent rasterization thread blocks can efficiently iterate only over the splats relevant to their assigned tile. Inputs and Outputs: Input: pointlistkeys, a 1D array of L 64-bit unsigned integers representing the sorted (splat, tile) pairs. Each key is constructed as (\text{tile\id} \ll 32) \mid (\text{uint32\t})Zc, where tileid is the 1D tile index and Zc is the depth. Output: ranges, a 1D array of uint2 structures of size N{tiles}. Each entry ranges[t] contains {start, end} indices into pointlistkeys for tile t. Data Structures: pointlistkeys: uint64t array of length L. ranges: uint2 array of length N{tiles}, where ranges[t].x is the start index and ranges[t].y is the end index (exclusive) for tile t. Algorithm Steps: The kernel launches one thread per entry in the sorted list L. Each thread idx performs the following logic to identify range boundaries: 1. Bounds Check: If idx >= L, terminate immediately. 2. Current Tile Extraction: Extract the tile ID from the current key by shifting right by 32 bits: \text{currtile} = \text{point\list\keys}[idx] \gg 32 3. First Element Handling: If idx == 0, set the start of the current tile's range to 0: \text{ranges}[\text{currtile}].x = 0 4. Boundary Detection: If idx > 0: Extract the previous tile ID: \text{prevtile} = \text{point\list\keys}[idx - 1] \gg 32 If \text{currtile} \neq \text{prevtile}, a tile boundary exists between idx - 1 and idx. Set the end of the previous tile's range to the current index and the start of the current tile's range to the current index: \text{ranges}[\text{prevtile}].y = idx \text{ranges}[\text{currtile}].x = idx 5. Last Element Handling: If idx == L - 1, set the end of the current tile's range to L: \text{ranges}[\text{currtile}].y = L Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def identifytilerangeskernel(pointlistkeys, ranges, L, threadid): idx = threadid if idx >= L: return currtile = pointlistkeys[idx] >> 32 if idx == 0: ranges[currtile].x = 0 if idx > 0: prevtile = pointlistkeys[idx - 1] >> 32 if currtile != prevtile: ranges[prevtile].y = idx ranges[currtile].x = idx if idx == L - 1: ranges[currtile].y = L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Tiles: If a tile has no splats, its range will remain at its default initialization value (typically {0, 0} or {L, L} depending on initialization strategy). The rasterizer must check if start >= end to skip empty tiles. Concurrent Writes: Multiple threads may write to the same ranges entry (e.g., thread idx and idx+1 both write to ranges[currtile].x if they are in the same tile, or thread idx writes ranges[prevtile].y while thread idx-1 wrote ranges[prevtile].x). Since these writes are idempotent for the start index (always setting to the first occurrence) and the end index (always setting to the last occurrence + 1), atomic operations are not strictly required if the logic is correct, but race conditions on the same field from different threads in the same tile are benign only if they write the same value. Specifically, ranges[currtile].x is written by the first thread in that tile, and ranges[prevtile].y is written by the last thread in that tile. There is no conflict for a single field from multiple threads unless the logic is flawed. However, ranges[currtile].x is written by thread idx where currtile is first seen. If multiple threads map to the same tile, only the first one (lowest idx) sets the start, while the others see currtile == prevtile and do not write. Thus, no atomics are needed. Initialization: The ranges array must be initialized to a safe default (e.g., {0, 0}) before kernel launch to handle tiles with no splats, or the rasterizer must handle uninitialized ranges. Time Complexity: O(L), where L is the number of (splat, tile) pairs after assignment, as each element is processed exactly once by one thread. Memory Complexity: O(N{tiles}) for the output ranges array. Performance: This kernel is extremely lightweight and typically completes in negligible time compared to the sorting and rasterization phases. It is memory-bandwidth bound due to reading pointlistkeys and writing ranges, but the working set is small. Strengths: Simple parallel logic, no synchronization barriers required between threads, and minimal overhead. Limitations: Requires the list to be fully sorted by tile ID before execution, and does not handle unsorted input. Tile Range Identification is a standard component in tile-based rasterization pipelines for Gaussian Splatting, introduced alongside the tiled 2D Gaussian rasterization method. It builds on the global radix sort performed in Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort to enable efficient per-tile processing. name: FlashGS
body: FlashGS is a multi-GPU rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that accelerates the forward pass by partitioning the screen into finer tiles and scheduling them across a multi-GPU pipeline. FlashGS builds on Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort by distributing the rasterization workload across multiple GPUs. Inputs: N projected 2D Gaussians, image resolution, tile grid dimensions, available GPU devices. Outputs: Rendered image buffer, per-Gaussian gradients. Data structures: Global list of (\text{splat}, \text{tile}) pairs; 64-bit sort keys; per-GPU tile assignment queues; per-tile sorted splat lists. Steps: 1. Finer Tile Partitioning: The screen is divided into a grid of tiles with higher granularity than standard single-GPU implementations. 2. Multi-GPU Scheduling: The partitioned tiles are distributed and scheduled across available GPUs for parallel execution. 3. Local Rasterization: Each GPU processes its assigned tiles using the standard tile-based rasterization pipeline Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. This covers projecting Gaussians, assigning them to tiles, packing 64-bit sort keys, performing a global radix sort, and executing front-to-back compositing per tile. 4. Gradient Computation: The same sorted lists are reused for backpropagation to compute gradients for position, shape, opacity, and color without additional sorting. Formulas: Sort key packing follows the parent method: \text{key} = (\text{tile\id} \ll 32) \mid (\text{uint32\t})Zc, where \text{tile\id} is the 1D tile index (y \times \text{grid\width} + x) and Zc is the splat depth cast to a 32-bit unsigned integer Sibling: [Tile-based Rasteriser]. Parameters: Tile dimensions are finer than the standard 16 \times 16 pixels, though exact values are not given in the sources. Edge cases: GPU memory limits may require dynamic tile redistribution; synchronization overhead between GPUs must be minimized to maintain throughput. It assigns Gaussians via index parity and distributes cameras, eliminating boundary waste and merge steps. Choose this for city-scale scenes with hundreds of millions of primitives where model size exceeds single-GPU memory. FlashGS focuses on screen partitioning for rendering acceleration. FlashGS accelerates the forward process by leveraging multiple GPUs. Specific time and memory complexity figures are not given in the sources. It is designed for high-performance rendering on multi-GPU setups. FlashGS was introduced in the context of surveying 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization techniques. It is cited alongside other optimization methods like gsplat and Mobile-GS. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: System Level Primitive Sharding
head: BlitzGS sharding, Distributed rendering, Index parity sharding, Primitive Sharding
body: System Level Primitive Sharding is a distributed rendering and training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that partitions a global Gaussian model across M GPUs to handle city-scale scenes with hundreds of millions of primitives. It ensures that both storage and per-step compute scale linearly with the GPU count by assigning Gaussians via index parity and distributing rendered tiles across the GPU cluster. Unlike spatial block partitioning, which incurs boundary waste, duplicate camera assignments, and merge steps, primitive sharding assigns every camera exactly once and eliminates the need for a final merge. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A global set of 3D Gaussians G with associated parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), optimizer states, camera parameters, and the number of GPUs M. Output: Rendered images for assigned tiles, updated Gaussian parameters, and distributed optimizer states. Data Structures: Shard G^{(m)}: A subset of the global Gaussian set G assigned to GPU rank m (0 \le m < M), containing approximately |G|/M Gaussians. Optimizer State: Per-Gaussian optimization buffers (e.g., momentum, variance) stored locally on the owning GPU. Tile Assignment: A mapping of image tiles to GPU ranks, determined by a cost-aware partitioning algorithm to balance rasterization load. Steps: 1. Initial Sharding: Partition the global Gaussian set G into M shards G^{(m)} based on index parity (i \bmod M). 2. Tile Partitioning: Divide the rendered image into tiles and assign each tile to a specific GPU rank using cost-aware partitioning to even out rasterization load. 3. Projection: Each GPU projects only the Gaussians in its local shard G^{(m)} into camera space. 4. All-to-All Communication: Perform a single all-to-all communication step to route every projected Gaussian to the GPUs owning the tiles it covers. 5. Compositing: Each GPU composites its assigned tiles using the received Gaussians. 6. Rebalancing: Apply index-parity redistribution to rebalance shard sizes if per-GPU skew exceeds a threshold. Formulas: Shard Size: |G^{(m)}| \approx \frac{|G|}{M}. Memory Scaling: Per-rank peak memory decreases as M increases. For the Rubble scene, memory drops from 17.2 GB at M=1 to 2.9 GB at M=8. Parameters: M: The number of GPUs across which the model is sharded. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def systemlevelprimitivesharding(G, M, rebalancethreshold): # Step 1: Initial Sharding by Index Parity shards = [[] for in range(M)] optimizerstates = [[] for in range(M)] for i, gaussian in enumerate(G): m = i % M shards[m].append(gaussian) optimizerstates[m].append(gaussian.optimizerstate) # Step 2: Tile Partitioning # Cost-aware tile partitioning to balance rasterization load # The exact algorithm is not specified in the sources. numtiles = 100 # Not given in the sources. tiletogpu = [t % M for t in range(numtiles)] # Step 3: Projection # Each GPU projects only the Gaussians in its local shard projectedgaussians = [] for m in range(M): projectedgaussians.append([project3dto2d(g) for g in shards[m]]) # Standard projection # Step 4: All-to-All Communication # Route every projected Gaussian to the GPUs owning the tiles it covers localgaussians = [[] for in range(M)] for m in range(M): for g in projectedgaussians[m]: coveredtiles = [t for t in range(numtiles) if gaussianoverlapstile(g, t)] # Standard coverage for t in coveredtiles: target = tiletogpu[t] if target == m: localgaussians[m].append(g) else: sendtorank(target, g) # Standard MPI all-to-all for m in range(M): localgaussians[m] += receivefromrank(m) # Standard MPI all-to-all # Step 5: Compositing # Each GPU composites its assigned tiles using the received Gaussians for m in range(M): assignedtiles = [t for t, gpu in enumerate(tiletogpu) if gpu == m] rendertiles(assignedtiles, localgaussians[m]) # Standard splatting rasterization # Step 6: Rebalancing # Apply index-parity redistribution to rebalance shard sizes if per-GPU skew exceeds a threshold if computeskew(shards) > rebalancethreshold: shards = redistributebyindexparity(shards) optimizerstates = redistributeoptimizerstates(optimizerstates) return shards, optimizerstates Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Skew: Non-uniform Gaussian distribution may cause imbalanced shards; index-parity redistribution mitigates this. Communication Overhead: The all-to-all step can become a bottleneck if the number of Gaussians or tiles is very large, though sources indicate manageable scaling. Boundary Issues: Unlike spatial partitioning, there are no spatial boundaries to handle, eliminating duplicate camera assignments and merge steps. Fixed Overhead: Per-rank data loading, optimizer, and bookkeeping remain constant at 15–20 ms and dominate shrinking iterations. Time Complexity: Per-iteration cost scales near-linearly with GPU count for compute-heavy stages like the backward pass. On the Residence scene with A800 80 GB GPUs, total per-iteration cost drops from 186.9 ms (1 GPU) to 68.6 ms (8 GPUs). Memory Complexity: Per-rank peak memory scales inversely with M. On the Rubble scene, it drops from 17.2 GB (1 GPU) to 2.9 GB (8 GPUs). The binding limit is the aggregate capacity across all GPUs. Strengths: Eliminates boundary waste and merge steps inherent in spatial block partitioning. Assigns every camera exactly once, preventing duplicate processing. Scales storage and compute linearly with GPU count. Limitations: Requires efficient all-to-all communication. Residual overhead from data loading and optimizer bookkeeping becomes significant as iteration time shrinks. When to Use: Suitable for city-scale scenes with hundreds of millions of primitives that exceed single GPU memory. System Level Primitive Sharding, also known as BlitzGS sharding, was introduced in "BlitzGS: City-Scale Gaussian Splatting at Lightning Speed". It addresses spatial block partitioning limitations, including cross-block visibility waste, imbalanced shards, and the need for a final merge step. The method is inspired by prior work on distributed rendering. It is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale scene reconstruction and rendering. name: Tile-based Depth Sorting
head: STP
body: Tile-based Depth Sorting is a rasterization strategy designed to mitigate "popping" artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by replacing per-ray depth sorting with tile-based sorting. It ensures a consistent depth ordering within a local region, addressing the sensitivity of alpha-blending order to viewpoint rotation. Inputs: List of N projected 2D Gaussian splats, each with center (xi, yi), 2D covariance \Sigma'i, color ci, opacity \alphai, and depth Zc. Outputs: A dictionary mapping each tile ID to a list of splats sorted front-to-back by depth. Data structures: A flat list of work items, each containing a 64-bit sort key, a 1D tile ID, and a splat index Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. The output is a tile-indexed array of splat lists. Numbered steps: 1. Tile Assignment: Each Gaussian is assigned to every tile its projected 2D splat bounding box touches Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. If a splat straddles tile boundaries, it is duplicated into each relevant tile, creating one work item per (splat, tile) pair Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. 2. Key Packing: For each work item, a 64-bit integer sort key is constructed by packing the tile ID into the high 32 bits and the splat's depth Zc into the low 32 bits Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. 3. Global Radix Sort: A single GPU radix sort is performed over all work items Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. This simultaneously bins splats by tile ID and sorts them by depth within each tile Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. 4. Tile Processing: Each tile is processed by one GPU thread block that walks the sorted list, performing front-to-back compositing and breaking early when transmittance T < \epsilon Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. Formulas: The sort key is formed as \text{key} = (\text{tile\id} \ll 32) \mid (\text{uint32\t})Zc, where \text{tile\id} = y \times \text{grid\width} + x and Zc is cast to a 32-bit unsigned integer Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. Parameters: Tile dimensions Tw \times Th, typically 16 \times 16 pixels Sibling: Tile-based Rasterization with Radix Sort. Edge cases and pitfalls: Per-ray depth sorting causes inconsistent ordering when viewpoints rotate, leading to "popping" artifacts and less faithful view-dependent effects. Tile-based sorting ensures consistent local ordering but may introduce slight depth inaccuracies at tile boundaries if splats are large. Precision loss can occur when casting Zc to uint32t if depth values exceed 2^{32} units. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilebaseddepthsorting(splats, imagew, imageh, tilesize=16): gridw = (imagew + tilesize - 1) // tilesize gridh = (imageh + tilesize - 1) // tilesize tilesplats = {} # 1. Tile Assignment & Key Packing workitems = [] for i, s in enumerate(splats): mintx = max(0, int((s['x'] - s['radius']) // tilesize)) maxtx = min(gridw - 1, int((s['x'] + s['radius']) // tilesize)) minty = max(0, int((s['y'] - s['radius']) // tilesize)) maxty = min(gridh - 1, int((s['y'] + s['radius']) // tilesize)) for ty in range(minty, maxty + 1): for tx in range(mintx, maxtx + 1): tileid = ty gridw + tx key = (tileid << 32) | (s['Zc'] & 0xFFFFFFFF) workitems.append((key, tileid, i)) # 2. Global Radix Sort workitems.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # 3. Group sorted splats by tile for key, tileid, idx in workitems: if tileid not in tilesplats: tilesplats[tileid] = [] tilesplats[tileid].append(splats[idx]) return tilesplats Per-tile sorting and per-pixel resorting is a rasterization strategy designed to mitigate "popping" artifacts in surface-based volumetric representations (such as 2DGS and QGS) where Gaussian distributions are concentrated on surfaces. It addresses the sensitivity of alpha-blending order by replacing inconsistent per-ray depth sorting with a two-stage approach: coarse global ordering via per-tile depth approximation and fine local ordering via per-pixel resorting. This method sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enforcing strict consistency between forward rendering and backward gradient computation traversal orders, thereby eliminating streak-like and blocky artifacts introduced by single-ray approximations. Not given in the sources. StopThePop identifies that standard 3D Gaussian Splatting cheats view-dependent effects by popping Gaussians due to per-ray depth sorting, yielding less faithful results upon viewpoint rotation. To mitigate this, StopThePop replaces per-ray sorting with tile-based sorting to enforce consistent depth ordering within local regions. name: Per-tile Sorting and Per-pixel Resorting
head: StopThePop's per-tile sorting and per-pixel resorting
body: Per-tile sorting and per-pixel resorting is a rasterization strategy designed to mitigate "popping" artifacts in surface-based volumetric representations (such as 2DGS and QGS) where Gaussian distributions are concentrated on surfaces. It addresses the sensitivity of alpha-blending order by replacing inconsistent per-ray depth sorting with a two-stage approach: coarse global ordering via per-tile depth approximation and fine local ordering via per-pixel resorting. This method sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enforcing strict consistency between forward rendering and backward gradient computation traversal orders, thereby eliminating streak-like and blocky artifacts introduced by single-ray approximations. The method operates on a tile-based rasterization pipeline, building on Tile-based Depth Sorting. It assumes a tile size of 16 \times 16 pixels, resulting in 256 pixels per tile. Inputs: Camera parameters (origin \hat{\mathbf{o}}, ray direction \hat{\mathbf{r}}). Set of projected 3D Gaussians (or quadric primitives) covering the current tile. Gaussian properties: opacity \alpha, scale, rotation, color, normal, curvature, etc.. Outputs: Final rendered color, depth, normal, and other volumetric maps \hat{X} for each pixel. Gradients for optimization. 1. Tile Depth Buffer: A single depth value d{tile} per 16 \times 16 tile. 2. Gaussian Property Buffer: An array of size 8 used to store intermediate Gaussian properties (depth, normal, etc.) for a specific pixel before blending. This buffer acts as a local staging area. 3. Sorted Gaussian List: A list of Gaussians covering the tile, sorted by the tile depth d{tile}. 1. Tile Depth Approximation: For each 16 \times 16 pixel tile, identify the pixel closest to the projected vertex of the underlying quadric surface. Compute the intersection depth d{tile} along the ray from this specific pixel. Apply this single depth value d{tile} to all 256 pixels in the tile. Use d{tile} to perform global sorting of all Gaussians covering the tile. This removes streak-like inconsistencies but may introduce blocky artifacts due to the single-ray approximation. 2. Per-Pixel Local Resorting: For each pixel within the tile: Retrieve the globally sorted list of Gaussians. Filter and reorder the Gaussians based on the actual per-ray depth for that specific pixel. This step eliminates the blocky artifacts introduced in Step 1. Store the calculated properties (depth, normal, opacity \alpha, etc.) of the Gaussians in the 8-length buffer array. Do not blend immediately. Once the buffer is full (or when processing the final Gaussian), select the closest Gaussian (front-most) for alpha-blending. This ensures a strict near-to-far traversal order. 3. Volumetric Rendering: Perform alpha-blending in the near-to-far order established by the resorting. The color \hat{X} (where X can be color, depth, normal, or curvature) is computed as: \hat{X} = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \bar{\alpha}i Ti Xi where: N is the number of Gaussians along the ray. \bar{\alpha}i = \alphai gi is the effective opacity (product of Gaussian opacity \alphai and visibility factor gi). Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \bar{\alpha}j) is the accumulated transmittance before Gaussian i. Xi represents the property value of the i-th Gaussian. 4. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients in the same near-to-far order as the forward pass to ensure consistency. The gradient of the rendered value \hat{X} with respect to the effective opacity \bar{\alpha}i is: \frac{\partial \hat{X}}{\partial \bar{\alpha}i} = \left( Xi - \frac{\hat{X} - \sum{j=0}^i Xj \bar{\alpha}j Tj}{T{i+1}} \right) Ti This front-to-back form ensures the backward computation follows the same order as the forward computation. Note that the distortion loss gradient does not require modification as its computation order is unaffected. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertile(tilepixels, gaussians, tilesize=16): """ Renders a single tile using per-tile sorting and per-pixel resorting. tilepixels: List of (x, y) pixel coordinates in the tile. gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives covering the tile. """ # Step 1: Tile Depth Approximation # Find the pixel closest to the projected vertex of the quadric surface refpixel = min(tilepixels, key=lambda p: distancetoprojectedvertex(p)) refray = computerayforpixel(refpixel) # Compute intersection depth for the reference ray tiledepth = computeintersectiondepth(refray, gaussians) # Global sort: Sort all gaussians by tiledepth sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.tiledepth if hasattr(g, 'tiledepth') else tiledepth) # Initialize output buffers for the tile tilecolor = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(tilesize tilesize)] tiledepthmap = [0.0] (tilesize tilesize) for idx, pixel in enumerate(tilepixels): # Step 2: Per-Pixel Local Resorting raypixel = computerayforpixel(pixel) # Re-sort gaussians based on actual per-pixel depth localsorted = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: computeintersectiondepth(raypixel, [g])) # Buffer for local processing (size 8) buffer = [] T = 1.0 acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accdepth = 0.0 # Step 3: Volumetric Rendering (Near-to-Far) for gaussian in localsorted: alpha = gaussian.opacity gaussian.visibility if alpha <= 0.0: continue # Store in buffer buffer.append(gaussian) # Once buffer is full, select closest Gaussian for alpha-blending if len(buffer) >= 8: closest = buffer.pop(0) effalpha = closest.opacity closest.visibility acccolor = [c + effalpha T closest.color[c] for c in range(3)] accdepth += effalpha T closest.depth T = (1.0 - effalpha) if T <= 1e-6: break # Flush remaining buffer for gaussian in buffer: effalpha = gaussian.opacity gaussian.visibility acccolor = [c + effalpha T gaussian.color[c] for c in range(3)] accdepth += effalpha T gaussian.depth T = (1.0 - effalpha) tilecolor[idx] = acccolor tiledepthmap[idx] = accdepth # Step 4: Gradient Computation (Backward Pass) # Compute gradients in near-to-far order to ensure consistency # Gradient formula: dX/dalphai = (Xi - (Xhat - sum{j=0}^i Xj alphaj Tj) / T{i+1}) Ti # Not given in the sources how to implement this efficiently in code, so we compute it directly. for i, gaussian in enumerate(localsorted): effalpha = gaussian.opacity gaussian.visibility Ti = prod(1.0 - g.opacity g.visibility for g in localsorted[:i]) Ti1 = prod(1.0 - g.opacity g.visibility for g in localsorted[:i+1]) sumterm = sum(g.color[c] g.opacity g.visibility prod(1.0 - gk.opacity gk.visibility for gk in localsorted[:j+1]) for j, g in enumerate(localsorted[:i+1])) grad = [gaussian.color[c] - (acccolor[c] - sumterm) / Ti1 for c in range(3)] gaussian.gradalpha = [g Ti for g in grad] return tilecolor, tiledepthmap Tile Size: Fixed at 16 \times 16 pixels in the source. Buffer Size: 8 elements. This likely refers to a hardware register or cache line constraint for local sorting, ensuring that the closest 8 Gaussians are readily accessible for blending. Precision: The method relies on accurate depth intersection. Degenerate cases where the ray is parallel to the surface or the intersection is undefined should be handled by falling back to a default depth or skipping the Gaussian. Consistency: The critical pitfall is the mismatch between forward and backward traversal orders. If the backward pass uses a different order (e.g., far-to-near) than the forward pass (near-to-far), the gradients will be incorrect, leading to training instability. The rewritten gradient formula ensures alignment. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard tile-based sorting with radix sort is O(N) per tile, and per-pixel resorting adds a local sorting cost proportional to the number of Gaussians per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the tile depth buffer and the per-pixel property buffer. The 8-length buffer is constant space per pixel. Strengths: Effectively removes streak-like and blocky artifacts in surface-based representations. Ensures gradient consistency. Limitations: Introduces overhead due to per-pixel resorting. The single-ray approximation for tile depth can still cause minor blocky artifacts if not corrected by the per-pixel step. When to Use: Recommended for surface-based Gaussian splatting (2DGS, QGS) where popping artifacts are prominent. Not necessary for standard 3DGS where Gaussians are volumetric and less sensitive to order. This method originates from the "StopThePop" paper, which addresses the popping artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting when applied to surface-based representations. The core insight is that alpha-blending order sensitivity is higher for surface-concentrated Gaussians. The method was introduced to improve the visual quality of reconstructed surfaces by ensuring consistent depth ordering during both rendering and gradient computation. name: CUDA Voxelizer Pipeline
head: CudaVoxelizer Forward/Backward Pass, Tile-based 3D Gaussian Voxelization
body: The CUDA Voxelizer Pipeline is a GPU-accelerated rendering and gradient computation method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that voxelizes 3D Gaussians into a 3D grid, sorts them per tile using radix sort, and renders/backpropagates gradients via tile-based blending. It differs from standard tile-based rasterization by explicitly constructing a 3D voxel grid to manage Gaussian spatial distribution and using a dedicated preprocessing phase to compute norms, depths, and conic opacities before binning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: P: Number of 3D Gaussians to process. Gaussian parameters: means, scales, rotations, opacities, 3D covariance matrices (\Sigma{3D}). Voxel grid parameters: dimensions (nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz), physical spacing (sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz), and world-space center (centerx, centery, centerz). Flags: scalemodifier (multiplicative factor applied to Gaussian scales during preprocessing), prefiltered (boolean flag passed to the preprocessing kernel to skip or apply pre-filtering logic). Outputs: Rendered volume/image. Gradients for 3D mean position, conic matrix, opacity, scale, and rotation. Data Structures: GeometryState: depths[P], internalradiix[P], internalradiiy[P], internalradiiz[P], means3Dnorm[P], cov3D[P6], conicopacity[P7], tilestouched[P], scanningspace[dynamic], scansize[dynamic], pointoffsets[P]. ImageState: ncontrib[N], ranges[N] where N = nVoxelx \times nVoxely \times nVoxelz. BinningState: pointlist[P], pointlistunsorted[P], pointlistkeys[P], pointlistkeysunsorted[P], listsortingspace[dynamic], sortingsize[dynamic]. Steps: 1. Allocate geometry buffers and call FORWARD::preprocess with Gaussian parameters (means, scales, rotations, opacities, cov3D), voxel grid parameters, and output buffers for norms, depths, cov3D, conicopacity, tilegrid, and tilestouched. 2. Compute an inclusive prefix sum over the full list of touched tile counts (tilestouched) to generate pointoffsets, which indicate cumulative counts per tile. 3. Retrieve the total number of Gaussian instances to render by copying the last element of pointoffsets to host: num\rendered = point\offsets[P - 1]. 4. Allocate binning buffers sized for num\rendered and reconstruct BinningState. 5. Launch duplicateWithKeys kernel with \lceil (P + 255) / 256 \rceil blocks of 256 threads. It generates [tile | depth] keys and duplicates Gaussian indices based on radii and tile grid. 6. Calculate the number of radix bits needed: bit = \text{getHigherMsb}(tile\grid.x \times tile\grid.y \times tile\grid.z). 7. Sort the duplicated Gaussian indices by their generated keys using CUB radix sort over range [0, 32 + bit). 8. Zero-initialize the ranges buffer for all tiles in the image state. 9. If num\rendered > 0, launch identifyTileRanges kernel with \lceil (num\rendered + 255) / 256 \rceil blocks of 256 threads to compute start/end indices per tile from the sorted keys. 10. Launch FORWARD::render kernel with tilegrid, block, ranges, pointlist, voxel dimensions, means3Dnorm, conicopacity, ncontrib, and outvolume to blend Gaussians per tile. 11. Backward pass reconstructs GeometryState, BinningState, and ImageState from provided buffers. 12. Launch BACKWARD::render kernel to compute loss gradients w.r.t. 3D mean position, conic matrix, and opacity. 13. Select cov3D pointer: use cov3Dprecomp if not null, otherwise fall back to geomState.cov3D. 14. Launch BACKWARD::preprocess kernel to compute gradients for mean3D, cov3D, scale, and rotation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Dict, Any def cudavoxelizerpipeline(P: int, voxelparams: Dict[str, Any], gaussians: Dict[str, Any], geometrystate: Dict[str, List], binningstate: Dict[str, List], imagestate: Dict[str, List]) -> None: # Parameters nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz = voxelparams['dimensions'] sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz = voxelparams['spacing'] centerx, centery, centerz = voxelparams['center'] scalemodifier = voxelparams['scalemodifier'] prefiltered = voxelparams['prefiltered'] tilegrid = voxelparams['tilegrid'] # Step 1: Preprocessing geometrystate['depths'] = [0.0] P geometrystate['internalradiix'] = [0.0] P geometrystate['internalradiiy'] = [0.0] P geometrystate['internalradiiz'] = [0.0] P geometrystate['means3Dnorm'] = [0.0] P geometrystate['cov3D'] = [0.0] (P 6) geometrystate['conicopacity'] = [0.0] (P 7) geometrystate['tilestouched'] = [0] P # # FORWARD::preprocess kernel launch # preprocesskernel(...) # Step 2: Prefix Sum pointoffsets = inclusiveprefixsum(geometrystate['tilestouched']) numrendered = pointoffsets[P - 1] # Step 3: Binning Buffer Allocation binningstate['pointlist'] = [0] numrendered binningstate['pointlistunsorted'] = [0] numrendered binningstate['pointlistkeys'] = [0] numrendered binningstate['pointlistkeysunsorted'] = [0] numrendered binningstate['listsortingspace'] = [] binningstate['sortingsize'] = 0 # Step 4: Key Generation and Duplication numblocks = (P + 255) // 256 threadsperblock = 256 # # duplicateWithKeys kernel launch # duplicatewithkeyskernel(...) # Step 5: Radix Sort tilegridvolume = tilegrid['x'] tilegrid['y'] tilegrid['z'] bit = gethighermsb(tilegridvolume) # # CUB radix sort over range [0, 32 + bit) # cubradixsort(...) # Step 6: Tile Range Identification N = tilegrid['x'] tilegrid['y'] tilegrid['z'] imagestate['ranges'] = [0] N if numrendered > 0: numblocks = (numrendered + 255) // 256 threadsperblock = 256 # # identifyTileRanges kernel launch # identifytilerangeskernel(...) # Step 7: Forward Rendering # # FORWARD::render kernel launch # forwardrenderkernel(...) # Step 8: Backward Pass # # BACKWARD::render kernel launch # backwardrenderkernel(...) cov3Dptr = gaussians['cov3Dprecomp'] if gaussians['cov3Dprecomp'] is not None else geometrystate['cov3D'] # # BACKWARD::preprocess kernel launch # backwardpreprocesskernel(...) def inclusiveprefixsum(arr: List[int]) -> List[int]: result = [0] len(arr) acc = 0 for i, val in enumerate(arr): acc += val result[i] = acc return result def gethighermsb(n: int) -> int: return n.bitlength() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If radiix/y/z pointers are null, the pipeline falls back to internalradii buffers to avoid segmentation faults during kernel launches. The identifyTileRanges kernel is guarded by a num\rendered > 0 check to prevent launching with zero threads or invalid memory ranges. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Gaussian Splatting Rendering with Camera Pose Override
head: render function with rel_w2c transform
body: This method modifies the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline to allow the camera pose to be overridden by an external tensor during rendering, rather than using the stored viewpoint parameters. It solves the problem of rendering a pre-trained Gaussian model from arbitrary or dynamically computed camera positions (e.g., from a SLAM system or a differentiable reconstruction loop) without retraining the model. It sets apart from standard rendering by injecting a custom world-to-camera transformation (relw2c) and quaternion rotation into the projection and covariance computation steps, enabling differentiable rendering with respect to the camera pose. Inputs: pc: The Gaussian Point Cloud object containing 3D means (xyz), rotations (quaternions), scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. camerapose: A tensor representing the override camera pose. Format depends on implementation, typically a 4x4 matrix or a quaternion + translation vector. In the reference implementation, it is used to construct a relative world-to-camera matrix. viewpointcamera: The original viewpoint object containing intrinsic parameters (FoVx, FoVy, projection matrix) and resolution. pipe: A pipeline configuration object with boolean flags computecov3Dpython and convertSHspython. overridecolor: Optional tensor to replace SH-based color computation. Outputs: renderimage: The rendered RGB image. viewspacepoints: Screen-space points with gradient tracking enabled. visibilityfilter: A boolean mask indicating which Gaussians have non-zero radii (are visible). radii: The screen-space radii of the Gaussians. Data Structures: screenspacepoints: A tensor of shape (N, 3) (where N is the number of Gaussians), initialized to zeros, with requiresgrad=True and retaingrad() called to allow backpropagation to 2D means. gaussiansxyztrans: Transformed 3D means in the camera frame. gaussiansrottrans: Transformed rotations (quaternions) in the camera frame. Steps: 1. Initialize Screen-Space Points: Create a zero tensor for screen-space points with gradient tracking enabled. This allows the rasterizer to update these points during forward pass, which are then used for backpropagation. \text{screenspace\points} = \text{zeros}(\text{pc.get\xyz.shape}, \text{dtype}=\text{pc.get\xyz.dtype}, \text{requires\grad}=\text{True}) \text{screenspace\points.retain\grad()} 2. Compute Field of View Tangents: Calculate the tangents of half the field of view angles from the viewpointcamera intrinsics. \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx} \times 0.5) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy} \times 0.5) 3. Construct Relative World-to-Camera Matrix: The method constructs a relative world-to-camera matrix (relw2c) from the camerapose input. In the reference implementation, this involves extracting the rotation and translation from the pose tensor. \text{rel\w2c} = \text{get\camera\from\tensor}(\text{camera\pose}) Note: In some variants, if no override is needed, w2c is set to identity and combined with the viewpoint's projection matrix. However, with override, relw2c is derived directly from the pose tensor. 4. Transform Gaussian Means: Transform the 3D Gaussian means from world space to the camera space using the relative world-to-camera matrix. Homogeneous coordinates are used for the transformation. \text{xyz\homo} = [\text{pc.get\xyz}, \mathbf{1}]^T \text{gaussians\xyz\trans} = (\text{rel\w2c} @ \text{xyz\homo}.T).T[:,:3] 5. Transform Gaussian Rotations: Transform the Gaussian rotations (stored as quaternions) from world space to the camera space. This is done by applying the rotation component of the camerapose to the stored Gaussian rotations using quaternion multiplication. \text{gaussians\rot\trans} = \text{quadmultiply}(\text{camera\pose}[:4], \text{gaussians\rot}) Where quadmultiply performs the rotation of one quaternion by another. 6. Determine Covariance Representation: Check the pipe.computecov3Dpython flag. If True: Compute the 3D covariance matrix (cov3Dprecomp) in Python using pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier). If False: Pass the scales and the transformed rotations (gaussiansrottrans) separately to the rasterizer, which computes the covariance on the GPU. 7. Determine Color Representation: Check the overridecolor and pipe.convertSHspython flags. If overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython is True: Convert Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients to RGB in Python. This involves evaluating the SH function at the direction vectors from the camera to the Gaussian centers (dirppnormalized) and clamping the result to [0, 1]. Otherwise: Pass the SH coefficients directly to the rasterizer or use the overridecolor tensor if provided. 8. Rasterize: Call the GaussianRasterizer with the transformed means (means3D), screen-space points (means2D), colors/SHs, opacities, and scales/rotations/covariances. The rasterizer returns the rendered image and the radii of the Gaussians. 9. Return Results: Return the rendered image, viewspace points, visibility filter (where radii > 0), and radii. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderwithcameraposeoverride(pc, camerapose, viewpointcamera, pipe, overridecolor=None): # 1. Initialize screen-space points for gradient tracking screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz, dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device='cuda') + 0 screenspacepoints.retaingrad() # 2. Compute FOV tangents tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # 3. Construct relative world-to-camera matrix from pose tensor # getcamerafromtensor extracts the 4x4 transformation matrix from the camerapose tensor relw2c = getcamerafromtensor(camerapose) # 4. Transform 3D means to camera space # xyzhomo is (N, 4) with 1s in the last column xyzhomo = torch.cat([pc.getxyz, torch.ones(pc.getxyz.shape[0], 1, device='cuda')], dim=1) gaussiansxyztrans = (relw2c @ xyzhomo.T).T[:,:3] # 5. Transform rotations (quaternions) to camera space # camerapose[:4] contains the quaternion [w, x, y, z] or [x, y, z, w] depending on convention # quadmultiply applies the rotation of camerapose to the Gaussian's rotation gaussiansrottrans = quadmultiply(camerapose[:4], pc.getrotations()) # 6. Determine covariance representation if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier=1.0) # scalingmodifier default else: cov3Dprecomp = None # Pass scales and rotations separately # 7. Determine color representation if overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython: # Compute directions from camera to Gaussian centers in camera space # Note: dirppnormalized should be normalized direction vectors dirpp = gaussiansxyztrans - relw2c.inverse()[3,:3] # Camera position in world space transformed? # Actually, in camera space, camera is at origin. So direction is just gaussiansxyztrans normalized dirppnormalized = torch.nn.functional.normalize(gaussiansxyztrans, dim=1) # Evaluate SHs shsview = pc.getSHs() # Shape (N, K, 3) shdegree = pc.activeshdegree colorsprecomp = evalsh(shdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized) colorsprecomp = torch.clamp(colorsprecomp, 0.0, 1.0) else: colorsprecomp = overridecolor if overridecolor is not None else pc.getSHs() # 8. Rasterize # GaussianRasterizer expects specific arguments based on pipe settings rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer( rastersettings={ 'tanfovx': tanfovx, 'tanfovy': tanfovy, 'imageheight': viewpointcamera.imageheight, 'imagewidth': viewpointcamera.imagewidth, 'shdegree': pc.activeshdegree, 'near': viewpointcamera.near, 'far': viewpointcamera.far }) renderedimage, radii = rasterizer( means3D=gaussiansxyztrans, means2D=screenspacepoints, shs=colorsprecomp if not pipe.convertSHspython else None, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp if pipe.convertSHspython else None, opacities=pc.getopacities(), scales=pc.getscales() if not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, rotations=gaussiansrottrans if not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp if pipe.computecov3Dpython else None) # 9. Return results visibilityfilter = radii > 0 return renderedimage, screenspacepoints, visibilityfilter, radii Parameters: camerapose: The override pose. Must be compatible with getcamerafromtensor. pipe.computecov3Dpython: Boolean. If true, covariance is computed in Python; otherwise, on GPU. pipe.convertSHspython: Boolean. If true, SH to RGB conversion is done in Python; otherwise, on GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Flow: screenspacepoints must have requiresgrad=True and retaingrad() called to ensure gradients can flow back to the 2D means during backpropagation. Rotation Convention: quadmultiply must handle the specific quaternion convention (wxyz vs xyzw) used by the Gaussian storage and the camerapose tensor. Direction Vectors: When computing SH colors in Python, the direction vectors must be normalized and computed in the correct coordinate system (camera space). This variant integrates a mask confidence score m{gi} as a new attribute for each 3D Gaussian gi, initialized to zero. The Gaussian is wholly assigned to either the segmentation target or the background. The mask rendering process uses the differentiable rasterization algorithm: M(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{|Gr|} \omega{gi} m{gi} where \omega{gi} is the weight of the Gaussian and m{gi} is its mask confidence score. This approach is more memory-efficient than using voxel grids (10 million Gaussians vs 32.77 million entries for a 320^3 grid) and has lower computation as no additional querying is needed. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(N) for N Gaussians, but depends on the number of visible Gaussians per tile. The overhead of transforming means and rotations is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian attributes. The mask representation adds O(N) memory for the mask confidence score. Strengths: Allows rendering from arbitrary camera poses without retraining. The mask representation is memory-efficient and computationally lightweight compared to grid-based methods. Limitations: Requires careful handling of coordinate transformations and quaternion rotations. The Python-based SH and covariance computations (if enabled) may be slower than GPU-based equivalents. This method is based on the implementation in NVlabs/InstantSplat, which provides a rendering function that overrides the camera pose. The concept of integrating mask attributes into 3D Gaussians for segmentation is described in "Segment Anything in 3D with Radiance Fields". name: Load Balancing for Pixel-parallel Splatting
head: Load balancing algorithm, Load balancing loss
body: A strategy to address uneven computational load across pixel threads in Gaussian rasterization by reducing the number of Gaussians rendered for heavy-load pixels and increasing it for light-load pixels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by explicitly optimizing the count of splats per pixel to balance GPU thread utilization, rather than just spatially partitioning the image. Inputs: Set of N 3D Gaussians. Camera parameters (view/projection matrices). Image resolution (width W, height H). Threshold for opacity contribution (implicit in the indicator function). Outputs: Modified set of Gaussians to be rendered per pixel, or a loss value guiding training to achieve this distribution. Data Structures: Gaussian: Standard 3DGS representation (mean, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). PixelLoad: Integer count of Gaussians contributing to a specific pixel. Steps: 1. Compute Pixel Loads: For each pixel i in the image, determine the number of Gaussians \elli that contribute to it. A Gaussian j contributes to pixel i if it projects within the pixel's bounds and its opacity is significant. \elli = \sum{j \in N} \mathbb{1}{Gj, pi} where \mathbb{1}{Gj, pi} is an indicator function equal to 1 if Gaussian j contributes to pixel i, and 0 otherwise. 2. Identify Load Imbalance: Calculate the standard deviation of \elli across all pixels. High standard deviation indicates uneven load, causing GPU thread waiting. 3. Apply Load Balancing Strategy: For heavy-load pixels (where \elli is high), reduce the number of Gaussians rendered. This can be done by culling Gaussians with low opacity or small contribution to the pixel's color/transmittance. For light-load pixels (where \elli is low), increase the number of Gaussians rendered. This may involve relaxing culling thresholds or including Gaussians that were previously discarded. 4. Training Integration (Load Balancing Loss): During training, a loss term \lambda{load} is added to the optimization objective to encourage this balanced distribution. The weight \lambda{load} is typically set to 0.45, while the sum of weights for remaining losses (e.g., L1, SSIM) is reduced to 0.55. Parameters: \lambda{load}: Weight for the load balancing loss term. Typical value: 0.45. \lambda{remaining}: Sum of weights for other loss terms (L1, SSIM). Typical value: 0.55. Opacity threshold: Used to determine if a Gaussian contributes to a pixel. Higher values accelerate rendering but may reduce quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quality Degradation: Aggressively reducing Gaussians for heavy-load pixels can lead to visible artifacts or loss of detail. Overhead: Computing exact pixel loads for every Gaussian can be expensive. Approximations or hierarchical methods may be needed for large scenes. Thread Divergence: If load balancing is not effective, GPU threads may still diverge, reducing efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computepixelloads(gaussians, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Computes the number of Gaussians contributing to each pixel. Returns a 2D array of loads. """ loads = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth), dtype=np.int32) for g in gaussians: # Project Gaussian center to screen space center2d = projecttoscreen(g.mean, g.viewmatrix, g.projmatrix) # Determine bounding box of Gaussian in screen space bbox = getgaussianbbox(center2d, g.covariance) # Iterate over pixels in bounding box for y in range(bbox.ymin, bbox.ymax): for x in range(bbox.xmin, bbox.xmax): if iswithinpixelbounds(center2d, g.covariance, x, y): # Check if opacity contribution is significant if getopacityatpixel(g, x, y) > THRESHOLD: loads[y, x] += 1 return loads def applyloadbalancing(gaussians, loads, lambdaload, lambdaremaining): """ Adjusts Gaussian rendering based on pixel loads. Returns modified Gaussians or loss value. """ # Calculate mean and standard deviation of loads meanload = np.mean(loads) stdload = np.std(loads) # Define heavy and light load thresholds heavythreshold = meanload + stdload lightthreshold = meanload - stdload # Identify heavy and light pixels heavypixels = np.where(loads > heavythreshold) lightpixels = np.where(loads < lightthreshold) # For heavy pixels, reduce Gaussian count (e.g., by increasing opacity threshold) # For light pixels, increase Gaussian count (e.g., by decreasing opacity threshold) # This part is typically handled during training via the loss function # Load Balancing Loss # Encourage uniform load distribution loadloss = stdload # Total Loss totalloss = lambdaload loadloss + lambdaremaining otherlosses return totalloss Gradient-Constrained Load Balancing Loss (LGC-load) is a regularization term used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting models to optimize computational efficiency by balancing the rendering workload across parallel pixel threads. It addresses the problem of uneven Gaussian distribution, where complex scene regions require more Gaussians for fidelity while simple regions do not, causing thread idle time in pixel-parallel rasterization. Unlike rigid load balancing that enforces uniform Gaussian counts, LGC-load adapts the allowed variance in Gaussian density per pixel based on local image gradients, thereby preserving reconstruction quality in intricate areas while reducing redundancy in simple areas. It builds on Load Balancing for Pixel-parallel Splatting. A workload distribution strategy to address severe imbalance in tile workloads, using early stopping depth prediction and Morton-order traversal to balance load across rasterization blocks. It involves preprocessing by discarding Gaussians beyond predicted early stopping depth, computing an ideal average workload W, and assigning tiles to blocks sequentially, deferring tiles if the cumulative Gaussian-tile pairs exceed (1 + 1/N)W. It employs Morton-order traversal to group spatially adjacent tiles, reducing memory access overhead, and sorts tiles within each block from light to heavy to prevent rasterization bubbles. A method that reuses image regions and schedules remaining tiles from predicted load. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N and image resolution W \times H. Computing pixel loads is O(N \cdot A) where A is the average area of a Gaussian in pixels. Load balancing adjustments are O(W \cdot H). Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for storing pixel loads. Performance: Improves rendering efficiency by reducing GPU thread waiting time due to load imbalance. Can lead to significant speedups in scenes with high variance in Gaussian density. Strengths: Simple to implement, directly addresses GPU thread divergence. Limitations: May reduce rendering quality if not carefully tuned. Requires accurate estimation of pixel loads. When to Use: In scenes with highly uneven Gaussian distribution, where some pixels are much more complex than others. When Not to Use: In scenes with uniform Gaussian distribution, where load balancing provides little benefit. Originated from the need to improve the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering on GPUs, where thread divergence due to uneven workload is a major bottleneck. The method was proposed to balance the number of Gaussians rendered per pixel, ensuring that all GPU threads finish their work at approximately the same time. name: Gradient-Constrained Load Balancing Loss
head: LGC-load
body:
Gradient-Constrained Load Balancing Loss (LGC-load) is a regularization term used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting models to optimize computational efficiency by balancing the rendering workload across parallel pixel threads. It addresses the problem of uneven Gaussian distribution, where complex scene regions require more Gaussians for fidelity while simple regions do not, causing thread idle time in pixel-parallel rasterization. Unlike rigid load balancing that enforces uniform Gaussian counts, LGC-load adapts the allowed variance in Gaussian density per pixel based on local image gradients, thereby preserving reconstruction quality in intricate areas while reducing redundancy in simple areas. It builds on Load Balancing for Pixel-parallel Splatting. Inputs: H 	imes W: Resolution of the rendered image grid. gi: The number of 3D Gaussian spheres contributing to the color/alpha blending of pixel i during the forward rasterization pass. 
abla Ii: The gradient magnitude (or gradient-dependent weight) for pixel i. Outputs: L{GC-load}: A scalar loss value representing the normalized standard deviation of the Gaussian count per pixel, weighted by scene complexity. Data Structures: A 1D array or flattened 2D grid of size H 	imes W storing the ratio ri = gi / wi for each pixel. Steps: 1. Compute Gradient Weights: For each pixel i in the H 	imes W grid, determine the gradient-dependent weight wi. In the source context, this is defined as the gradient magnitude 
abla Ii. Higher gradients indicate complex scene details requiring higher Gaussian density for accurate \alpha-blending and reconstruction. 2. Count Gaussians: During the rasterization step, count the number of Gaussian spheres gi that contribute to the final color of each pixel i. 3. Calculate Ratios: For each pixel i, compute the ratio ri of the Gaussian count to the gradient weight: ri =  rac{gi}{wi} This ratio normalizes the computational load by the scene complexity; pixels with high gradients (high wi) are allowed to have higher Gaussian counts (gi) without increasing the loss significantly. 4. Compute Standard Deviation: Calculate the standard deviation (std) of the ratios ri across all pixels in the grid. This forms the loss value L{GC-load}. Formula: L{GC-load} = 	ext{std}{i \in HW} \left(  rac{gi}{wi} ight) Where: gi is the number of Gaussian spheres contributing to pixel i. wi is the gradient-dependent weight 
abla Ii for pixel i. 	ext{std} represents the standard deviation over all pixels in the H 	imes W grid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelgcload(gaussiansperpixel, gradientweights): """ Compute the Gradient-Constrained Load Balancing Loss. Args: gaussiansperpixel (list[float]): List of counts gi for each pixel i. gradientweights (list[float]): List of gradient magnitudes wi for each pixel i. Returns: float: The LGC-load loss value. """ npixels = len(gaussiansperpixel) ratios = [] for i in range(npixels): gi = gaussiansperpixel[i] wi = gradientweights[i] # If gradient is zero, the ratio becomes undefined. # The source does not specify a guard. Clamping to 1.0 prevents division by zero. if wi == 0: wi = 1.0 ratio = gi / wi ratios.append(ratio) # Calculate mean of ratios meanratio = sum(ratios) / npixels # Calculate population standard deviation variance = sum((r - meanratio) 2 for r in ratios) / npixels stddev = variance 0.5 return stddev Parameters: wi (Gradient Weight): Defined as the gradient magnitude 
abla Ii. No explicit scaling factor is mentioned in the source for wi itself, but it is used directly in the denominator. Loss Weighting: The source mentions L{GC-load} is part of the overall loss, but does not specify a scalar multiplier \lambda for L{GC-load} in the provided excerpt, unlike other losses (L{mvgeo}, L{rgb}) which use \lambda1, \lambda2, etc.. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradients: If wi = 0, the ratio gi/wi becomes undefined. The source does not specify a guard. An implementer must handle this, e.g., by clamping wi to a small positive value or treating zero-gradient pixels as having a fixed weight. Fidelity vs. Load Trade-off: Directly enforcing load balance (minimizing std(gi)) risks compromising reconstruction fidelity in intricate scenes because such scenes naturally require higher Gaussian density. The gradient constraint mitigates this by allowing higher variance in gi where gradients are high. Gradient Source: The source defines wi as 
abla I but does not specify if this is the gradient of the photometric loss, geometric loss, or image intensity. In the context of "gradient-dependent weight," it likely refers to the magnitude of the gradient of the loss with respect to the pixel color or the image intensity gradient itself. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The loss aims to expedite training by adapting the number of Gaussian spheres according to scene complexity, thereby reducing thread idle periods during parallel pixel rendering. Strengths: Preserves reconstruction quality in complex regions while reducing computational load in simple regions. It adapts to scene complexity dynamically. Limitations: Requires access to gradient information or Gaussian counts per pixel during training. When to Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models on large-scale or complex scenes where computational efficiency is a bottleneck, and uniform Gaussian distribution is not optimal for fidelity. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Gradient-Constrained Load Balancing Loss was proposed in the context of parallel Gaussian Splatting for fine-grained large-scale urban buildings reconstruction. It builds upon the concept of "balance-load loss" introduced by AdR-Gaussian (Wang et al., 2024b), which constrains the number of Gaussians per pixel to promote consistent workload distribution across threads. The authors of PG-SAG noted that directly enforcing such load balance risks compromising reconstruction fidelity in intricate scenes, which require higher Gaussian density for better \alpha-blending. To address this, they introduced the gradient-constrained variant, which accounts for scene complexity via gradient weighting. The method is used in the PG-SAG framework for urban building reconstruction, where it is combined with multi-view consistency geometric loss, photometric consistency loss, flattening 3D Gaussian loss, and boundary-aware normal loss.
