name: Half-cosine Squared Splatting
head: 3DHCS, Half Cosine Squared
body: Half-cosine Squared Splatting is a radial basis function technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the standard Gaussian decay with a half-cosine squared function. It solves the problem of slow convergence and high memory usage in standard splatting by providing higher opacity values per primitive, allowing fewer primitives to achieve the same accumulated opacity. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by using a bounded decay profile that accelerates training and reduces memory footprint. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \mu, 3D covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color C); camera projection matrix; image resolution. Outputs: Final pixel color and alpha. Data Structures: cov: 3x3 symmetric 3D covariance matrix. cov2D: 2x2 symmetric 2D covariance matrix (projected). conic: 2x2 symmetric conic matrix (inverse of cov2D), stored as 3 floats (a, b, c) for the upper triangle. muprime: 2D mean in screen space. ellipse: Scalar value representing the squared Mahalanobis distance scaled by the ellipse factor. Parameters: correctionFactor: 1.36. \beta: 2. \xi: 36. ellipseLimit: 9.0. alphaClip: 0.99. Steps: 1. Covariance Correction: Multiply the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma by correctionFactor before projection. \Sigma{corrected} = \Sigma \times 1.36 2. Projection: Project the 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space to obtain the 2D mean \mu' and the 2D covariance \Sigma'{2 \times 2}. 3. Conic Calculation: Compute the inverse of the 2D covariance to get the conic matrix J = (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1}. 4. Ellipse Factor Calculation: For a pixel at screen coordinate x, calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance term dM^2 (referred to as ellipse in code): dM^2 = (x - \mu')^T (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu') In the implementation, this is computed using the conic matrix components (a, b, c) where J = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}: dM^2 = a \cdot dx^2 + c \cdot dy^2 + 2 \cdot b \cdot dx \cdot dy where dx = x - \mu'x and dy = y - \mu'y. 5. Boundary Check: If dM^2 < 0 or dM^2 > 9, skip the splat for this pixel. This limits the 2D ellipse to restrict the half-cosine pulse. 6. Weight Calculation: Calculate the half-cosine squared weight w: ellipseFactor = \frac{2 \pi \cdot dM^2}{36} \approx 0.175 \cdot dM^2 w = \cos(ellipseFactor) The validity condition requires the cosine argument to be \leq \pi/2, which corresponds to dM^2 \leq 9. 7. Alpha Computation: Compute the final alpha \alpha: \alpha = \min(0.99, \alpha{primitive} \cdot w) where \alpha{primitive} is the primitive's base opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def halfcosinesquaredsplat(xscreen, muprime, conicmatrix, primitiveopacity): """ xscreen: tuple (x, y) muprime: tuple (mux, muy) conicmatrix: tuple (a, b, c) representing [[a, b], [b, c]] primitiveopacity: float """ dx = xscreen[0] - muprime[0] dy = xscreen[1] - muprime[1] a, b, c = conicmatrix # Calculate squared Mahalanobis distance (ellipse) ellipse = a dx dx + c dy dy + 2.0 b dx dy # Boundary check: skip if outside valid half-cosine pulse range if ellipse < 0.0 or ellipse > 9.0: return 0.0, 0.0 # Calculate ellipse factor using exact 2pi/36 scaling ellipsefactor = 2.0 math.pi ellipse / 36.0 # Calculate cosine weight cosineweight = math.cos(ellipsefactor) # Calculate final alpha with clip alpha = min(0.99, primitiveopacity cosineweight) return alpha, cosineweight Backpropagation Details: The derivatives required for training are: \frac{dw}{d(x - \mu')} = \frac{-2(\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu') \sin\left(\frac{(x - \mu')^T (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu')}{\xi}\right)}{\xi} \frac{dw}{d((\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1})} = \frac{-(x - \mu') (x - \mu')^T \sin\left(\frac{(x - \mu')^T (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} (x - \mu')}{\xi}\right)}{\xi} The gradient w.r.t. the conic matrix entries must account for the correctionFactor if the conic is derived from the corrected covariance. Time Complexity: Similar to standard Gaussian Splatting per primitive, but the cosine calculation is slightly more expensive than the exponential Gaussian decay. However, overall training time is reduced because fewer primitives are needed. Memory Usage: Reduced compared to standard Gaussian Splatting. Half-cosine primitives provide higher opacity values, requiring fewer primitives to achieve the same accumulated opacity coverage. Performance: Demonstrates superior performance in training loss curves and speed compared to Gaussians, despite similar final training loss. Strengths: Faster training, lower memory usage, higher opacity per primitive. Limitations: The bounded nature of the cosine function requires careful boundary checking (ellipse < 9) to avoid invalid values. The computation of trigonometric functions may be slower than simple exponentials on some hardware, though this is offset by the reduced primitive count. Half-cosine Squared Splatting was introduced in the DARB-Splatting paper as a generalization of splatting using decaying anisotropic radial basis functions. It was developed to address the limitations of exponentially decaying functions (like Gaussians) which require many primitives for accurate blending. The method uses \beta=2 and \xi=36 as key parameters for the half-cosine square function. DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00438, fetched 2026-10-30

name: HSPT Cut and Gaussian Loading Optimization
head: GPU Memory Buffer Optimization
body: This method optimizes the HSPT cut and Gaussian loading by storing SPT properties in a continuous GPU buffer and transferring Gaussians via a single copy operation, reorganizing them on the GPU into a Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout. It reduces PCIe bus traffic and kernel launch overhead inherent in hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. Inputs: CPU Gaussian properties stored in a single PyTorch tensor in RAM as an Array of Structures (AoS). SPT properties (\text{min}(i), \text{min}(\text{parent}(i)), \text{scale}(i)) stored in a continuous GPU memory buffer. Current camera pose and view frustum. Outputs: A contiguous GPU buffer containing Gaussian properties in SoA layout, ready for the tiled rasterizer. 1. SPT Properties Buffer (GPU): A single continuous GPU memory buffer storing hierarchical metadata. For each Gaussian i, it stores \text{min}(i), \text{min}(\text{parent}(i)), and \text{scale}(i). 2. Gaussian Properties (CPU): A single PyTorch tensor in RAM in AoS layout, where each Gaussian's properties are stored concurrently. 3. Render Set (GPU): The final SoA layout required by the rasterizer, formed by appending reorganized Gaussians. 1. SPT Cut Execution: The GPU performs the HSPT cut in parallel using optimized CUDA kernels to determine visible Gaussians based on the current view and hierarchical SPT properties. 2. Single Copy Operation: Transfer the properties of all required Gaussians from the CPU AoS tensor to the GPU via a single contiguous memory copy operation. 3. GPU Reorganization: Reorganize the transferred Gaussian properties on the GPU into the SoA layout required by the rasterizer. 4. Append to Render Set: Append the reorganized Gaussians to the current render set. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegaussianloading(sptbuffer, cpugaussiantensor, cameraparams): # Step 1: Determine visible Gaussians using SPT properties on GPU # The sources state this is performed in parallel using optimized CUDA kernels # on min(i), min(parent(i)), and scale(i) to cull invisible Gaussians. visibleindices = performhsptcut(sptbuffer, cameraparams) # Step 2: Extract required Gaussian properties from CPU AoS tensor requiredgaussians = cpugaussiantensor[visibleindices] # Step 3: Transfer to GPU via single copy operation gpurequiredgaussians = requiredgaussians.to(device='cuda', nonblocking=True) # Step 4: Reorganize from AoS to SoA on GPU # Reshape tensor from (K, D) AoS to (D, K) SoA layout for memory coalescing gpusoAdata = gpurequiredgaussians.t().contiguous() # Step 5: Append to the current render set # Concatenate along the first dimension to form the final render buffer gpurenderset = torch.cat([gpurenderset, gpusoAdata], dim=0) return gpurenderset Cache Flush Interval: When using SPT caching, the entire cache is flushed every 1,000 training iterations to prevent overfitting to persistent cache entries. Memory Thresholds: VRAM usage is bounded by an LRU writeback policy; when the threshold is exceeded, entries are written back to RAM. Precision: Ensure the PyTorch tensor dtype matches the expected GPU kernel input types to avoid implicit conversion overhead. Degenerate Input: If no Gaussians are visible (e.g., camera outside scene bounds), skip the copy and reorganization steps to avoid empty buffer overhead. This variant extends the basic loading optimization by caching SPT cuts in VRAM to avoid redundant RAM-to-GPU transfers for similar views. For each training view, visible Gaussians are assembled from the upper hierarchy, cached SPTs, and skybox Gaussians (which remain in VRAM). If the condition D{\min} \leq \frac{d^j}{\overline{d}^j} \leq D{\max} is met, the cached SPT cut is reused, where d^j is the current distance metric and \overline{d}^j is the average, defining the allowable range for coarser-than-optimal detail. Uncached SPTs are streamed from RAM. Newly loaded SPTs are added to the cache after each iteration. An LRU policy bounds VRAM usage; when the threshold is exceeded, entries are written back to RAM. The entire cache is flushed every 1,000 iterations to prevent overfitting. This stochasticity in Level-of-Detail variability improves training robustness by discouraging overfitting to fixed camera distances and promotes generalization across scales. View selection prioritizes spatial locality by sampling the next training view from the k-nearest neighbours of the current view in a precomputed Euclidean distance graph. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the RAM-to-GPU transfer, reduced to a single bulk operation per frame. The AoS-to-SoA reorganization is performed on the GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires continuous GPU buffers for SPT properties and the render set. In a 60-million-Gaussian hierarchy on MC-smaller-city+, SPT metadata occupies 680 MB of VRAM and the upper hierarchy occupies 24 MB of VRAM. Performance: On wide-angle aerial views, 2.2 million Gaussians are rendered directly and 2.4 million are retained in the cache, demonstrating effective reuse. The method achieves high reconstruction quality (e.g., 21.71 PSNR) with manageable VRAM usage (15.7 GB training, 17.2 GB inference) compared to competitors like OctreeGS (26.6 GB training). Strengths: Significantly reduces PCIe bandwidth pressure; improves training stability through cache-induced stochasticity. Limitations: Requires careful management of VRAM thresholds; cache misses in large-scale scenes can still incur latency if spatial locality is not maintained via view selection. This method originates from the work on "A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory". It addresses the scalability issues of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in large scenes, where the sheer number of Gaussians makes naive rendering and densification infeasible. The approach builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) by introducing hierarchical memory management and optimized data layout transitions. A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.01110, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Tight Quad Rasterization with Eigenvalue Decomposition
head: Eigenvalue-based Tight Quad Rasterization
body: This method renders 3D Gaussians as tightly fitted, non-axis-aligned quads to minimize overdraw and improve rendering performance, particularly on mobile hardware. It differs from standard axis-aligned bounding box approaches by computing a rotated rectangle that incorporates the splat's alpha value, ensuring only relevant pixels are processed. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \mathbf{\mu}, 3D covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color C); camera projection matrix P; clipping threshold \tau\lambda. Outputs: Rasterized image with alpha-blended Gaussians. Data Structures: Gaussian: Struct containing mean (vec3), covariance (mat3), opacity (float), color (vec3). Quad: Defined by center \mathbf{c}, two orthogonal basis vectors \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, and half-extents hu, hv. Steps: 1. Cull Negative Opacity: Discard Gaussians where \alpha < 0. 2. Project Covariance: Compute the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} using the Jacobian of the projection. Let J be the Jacobian of the projection transform at \mathbf{\mu}. Then \Sigma{2D} = J \Sigma{3D} J^T. 3. Eigen Decomposition: Compute eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 of \Sigma{2D}. 4. Compute Basis and Extents: The eigenvectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 define the orientation of the quad. The eigenvalues determine the scale. The half-extents are derived from the square roots of the eigenvalues, scaled by a factor that incorporates the alpha value to ensure a tight fit. Let k be a scaling factor (e.g., 3 for 3-sigma coverage). The half-extents are hu = k \sqrt{\lambda1} and hv = k \sqrt{\lambda2}. 5. Clipping Check: Calculate the maximum axis length L{max} = \max(hu, hv). If L{max} > \tau\lambda, discard the Gaussian. This prevents processing Gaussians with large splats that extend outside the view frustum but have means outside it. 6. Emit Quad: Construct a non-axis-aligned quad centered at the projected mean \mathbf{p}, with axes \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{e}1 and \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{e}2, and extents hu, hv. 7. Rasterize: Render the quad to the fragment shader. The fragment shader computes the alpha value based on the distance from the center in the eigenbasis and blends it into the frame buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertightquad(gaussian, projectionmatrix, taulambda): # 1. Cull negative opacity if gaussian.opacity < 0: return None # 2. Project 3D covariance to 2D # J is the Jacobian of the projection at gaussian.mean J = computeprojectionjacobian(gaussian.mean, projectionmatrix) Sigma2D = J @ gaussian.covariance @ J.T # 3. Eigen decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = torch.linalg.eigh(Sigma2D) # eigenvalues are sorted ascending by default in some libraries, ensure order lambda1, lambda2 = eigenvalues[1], eigenvalues[0] # Assuming largest first for clarity e1, e2 = eigenvectors[:, 1], eigenvectors[:, 0] # 4. Compute extents incorporating alpha # The source mentions incorporating alpha into the bound rectangle. # A common implementation uses a scaling factor k (e.g., 3) and potentially # a function of alpha to tighten the bound. k = 3.0 hu = k torch.sqrt(lambda1) hv = k torch.sqrt(lambda2) # 5. Clipping check maxaxis = max(hu, hv) if maxaxis > taulambda: return None # 6. Emit Quad projectedmean = projectpoint(gaussian.mean, projectionmatrix) quad = Quad( center=projectedmean, axisu=e1, axisv=e2, halfextentu=hu, halfextentv=hv) return quad A rasterization method for 3D Gaussians that projects the 3D covariance to 2D, computes eigenvalues and eigenvectors to determine basis vectors, and emits a quad per splat to the fragment shader for alpha-based blending. Time Complexity: Dominated by eigen decomposition per Gaussian, which is O(1) for 2x2 matrices but involves square roots and trigonometric operations. Memory Complexity: Minimal overhead per Gaussian for storing the quad parameters. Performance: Reduces overdraw compared to axis-aligned boxes, leading to faster fragment shading. The clipping threshold \tau\lambda significantly speeds up rendering on mobile hardware by culling large, distant splats. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \tau\lambda and the scaling factor for the alpha incorporation. Eigen decomposition can be numerically unstable if the covariance is near-singular. This method is described in "Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR". It builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline but optimizes the bounding volume for tighter fitting. It references EWA Splatting [60] and modern implementations like GSplat [54] as predecessors in using non-axis-aligned quads. Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Fast Gaussian Rasterization (Covariance Eigen-decomposition and Quad Emission)
head: dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization
body: A rasterization method for 3D Gaussians that projects the 3D covariance to 2D, computes eigenvalues and eigenvectors to determine basis vectors, and emits a quad per splat to the fragment shader for alpha-based blending. It differs from software-based splatting by offloading clipping, interpolation, and blending to the fixed-function OpenGL rasterizer via a vertex-geometry-fragment pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position, a 3D covariance matrix (or its decomposition), and color/opacity attributes. Output: A 2D image with alpha-blended colors. Data Structures: The method uses standard OpenGL shader inputs and outputs. Geometry Shader Inputs: in vec2 basisVector0[]: First basis vector scaled by \sqrt{8} standard deviations. in vec2 basisVector1[]: Second basis vector scaled by \sqrt{8} standard deviations. in vec4 gColor[]: Color and opacity of the splat. in float gDepth[]: Depth of the splat center. Geometry Shader Outputs: out vec2 vPosition: Normalized position within the quad. flat out vec4 vColor: Interpolated color and opacity. flat out float vDepth: Interpolated depth. Fragment Shader Uniforms: uniform bool useDepth: Flag for depth visualization mode. uniform bool solidMode: Flag for solid opacity mode. uniform bool edgeMode: Flag for edge visualization mode. uniform float eight: Constant value 8.0. uniform float minAlpha: Minimum opacity threshold for fragment discard (Default: 0.004). uniform float maxAlpha: Maximum opacity cap (Default: 0.99). uniform float edgeThreshold: Threshold for edge mode (Default: 0.025). Steps: 1. Project Covariance and Compute Eigenvalues: In the vertex shader or pre-processing step, extract the 2D covariance components from the projected covariance matrix cov2Dv: a = \text{cov2Dv}.x d = \text{cov2Dv}.z b = \text{cov2Dv}.y Compute the determinant D: D = a \cdot d - b^2 Compute the trace and the term for eigenvalue calculation: \text{trace} = a + d \text{traceOver2} = 0.5 \cdot \text{trace} \text{term2} = \sqrt{\max(0.1, \text{traceOver2}^2 - D)} Compute the eigenvalues \lambda0 and \lambda1 (where \lambda0 \ge \lambda1): \lambda0 = \text{traceOver2} + \text{term2} \lambda1 = \text{traceOver2} - \text{term2} 2. Compute Eigenvectors: Compute the first eigenvector \mathbf{e}0: \mathbf{e}0 = \text{normalize}(\text{vec2}(b, \lambda0 - a)) Derive the orthogonal second eigenvector \mathbf{e}1: \mathbf{e}1 = \text{vec2}(\mathbf{e}0.y, -\mathbf{e}0.x) 3. Compute Basis Vectors: Scale the eigenvectors by \sqrt{8} standard deviations, capped at maxScreenSpaceSplatSize: \text{basisVector0} = \mathbf{e}0 \cdot \min(\sqrt{8} \cdot \sqrt{\lambda0}, \text{maxScreenSpaceSplatSize}) \text{basisVector1} = \mathbf{e}1 \cdot \min(\sqrt{8} \cdot \sqrt{\lambda1}, \text{maxScreenSpaceSplatSize}) The factor \sqrt{8} is used instead of the more common 3 standard deviations to eliminate more of the splat with very low opacity. 4. Validate and Prune: Check for illegal covariance matrices or degenerate splats. If any of the following conditions are met, prune the splat by setting gColor.a = 0.0 and returning early: D \le 0.0 a \le 0.0 d \le 0.0 \lambda0 \le 0.01 \lambda1 \le 0.01 \lambda0 < \lambda1 Aspect ratio \frac{\lambda0}{\lambda1} > 10000.0 5. Emit Quad in Geometry Shader: For each of the 4 corners of the quad, defined by vPosition in \{-1, 1\} \times \{-1, 1\}: Discard Check: If gColor[0].a < discardAlpha (0.0001), return without emitting vertices. Compute NDC Offset: \text{ndcOffset} = (\text{vPosition}.x \cdot \text{basisVector0} + \text{vPosition}.y \cdot \text{basisVector1}) \cdot \text{basisViewport} \cdot 2.0 Set Position: \text{gl\Position} = \text{vec4}(\text{ndcCenter}.xy + \text{ndcOffset}, \text{ndcCenter}.z, 1.0) Pass Attributes: Scale vPosition by \sqrt{8} and pass through vColor (from gColor) and vDepth (from gDepth). 6. Apply Mode-Specific Overrides (Geometry Shader): If solidMode is true, set opacity = 1.0. If useDepth is true, set color = vec3(vDepth). If edgeMode is true and \exp(\text{power}) < \text{edgeThreshold}, set color = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) and opacity = 1.0. 7. Fragment Shader Processing: Alpha Clipping: If the interpolated alpha vColor.a < minAlpha (0.004), discard the fragment. Alpha Capping: If vColor.a > maxAlpha (0.99), cap it to maxAlpha. Blending: Perform standard alpha blending using the fragment's color and alpha against the existing framebuffer content. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeeigenandbasis(cov2Dv, maxScreenSpaceSplatSize): """ cov2Dv: tuple/list (x=a, y=b, z=d, w=unused) Returns: basisVector0, basisVector1, eigenValue0, eigenValue1 """ a = cov2Dv[0] b = cov2Dv[1] d = cov2Dv[2] # Determinant D = a d - b b # Eigenvalues trace = a + d traceOver2 = 0.5 trace # Use max(0.1,...) to avoid numerical instability for very small traces term2 = math.sqrt(max(0.1, traceOver2 traceOver2 - D)) eigenValue0 = traceOver2 + term2 eigenValue1 = traceOver2 - term2 # Eigenvectors # e0 = normalize(vec2(b, eigenValue0 - a)) norme0 = math.sqrt(bb + (eigenValue0 - a)2) if norme0 < 1e-6: eigenVector0 = (1.0, 0.0) else: eigenVector0 = (b / norme0, (eigenValue0 - a) / norme0) # e1 is orthogonal to e0 eigenVector1 = (eigenVector0[1], -eigenVector0[0]) # Basis vectors scaled by sqrt(8) sqrt8 = math.sqrt(8.0) scale0 = min(sqrt8 math.sqrt(eigenValue0), maxScreenSpaceSplatSize) scale1 = min(sqrt8 math.sqrt(eigenValue1), maxScreenSpaceSplatSize) basisVector0 = (eigenVector0[0] scale0, eigenVector0[1] scale0) basisVector1 = (eigenVector1[0] scale1, eigenVector1[1] scale1) return basisVector0, basisVector1, eigenValue0, eigenValue1 def emitquad(basisVector0, basisVector1, gColor, gDepth, ndcCenter, basisViewport, discardAlpha): """ Emits 4 vertices for the quad. Returns list of vertex attributes: (vPosition, vColor, vDepth) """ vertices = [] # Check for early discard if gColor[3] < discardAlpha: return vertices # Corners of the quad in local space {-1, 1} x {-1, 1} corners = [(-1, -1), (1, -1), (1, 1), (-1, 1)] sqrt8 = math.sqrt(8.0) for vx, vy in corners: # NDC Offset calculation offsetx = (vx basisVector0[0] + vy basisVector1[0]) basisViewport 2.0 offsety = (vx basisVector0[1] + vy basisVector1[1]) basisViewport 2.0 # Final NDC Position finalx = ndcCenter[0] + offsetx finaly = ndcCenter[1] + offsety # vPosition is scaled by sqrt(8) for fragment shader evaluation vPosition = (vx sqrt8, vy sqrt8) # Pass through color and depth vColor = gColor vDepth = gDepth vertices.append((vPosition, vColor, vDepth)) return vertices def fragmentshader(vPosition, vColor, vDepth, useDepth, solidMode, edgeMode, edgeThreshold, minAlpha, maxAlpha): """ Returns final color and alpha. Returns (None, None) to discard. """ color = list(vColor[:3]) alpha = vColor[3] # Mode overrides if solidMode: alpha = 1.0 elif useDepth: color = [vDepth, vDepth, vDepth] elif edgeMode: # power is squared distance from center power = vPosition[0]2 + vPosition[1]2 if math.exp(power) < edgeThreshold: color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 1.0 # Alpha capping if alpha > maxAlpha: alpha = maxAlpha # Alpha clipping if alpha < minAlpha: return None, None # discard fragment return color, alpha This method renders 3D Gaussian splats as screen-space quads by leveraging the fixed-function OpenGL rasterizer via a vertex-geometry-fragment shader pipeline, offloading clipping, interpolation, and blending from software to hardware. It differs from CUDA-based software rasterization by reducing CPU/GPU synchronization overhead and explicit sorting stalls, achieving 5-10x speedup over the original software CUDA rasterizer for high pixel-to-point ratios. Time Complexity: O(N) for N splats, dominated by the geometry shader emission and fragment shader blending. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat attributes and intermediate buffers. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Tight quad bounding box (\sqrt{8} std devs) reduces overdraw compared to larger bounding boxes. Simple eigen-decomposition avoids iterative solvers. Limitations: Pruning conditions (aspect ratio, eigenvalue thresholds) may discard valid splats in edge cases if thresholds are too aggressive. When to Use: Real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian Avatars where performance is critical and OpenGL is available. When Not to Use: When maximum compatibility with non-OpenGL APIs is required, or when the scene has extremely low pixel-to-point ratios where software sorting might be more efficient. Origin and development history are not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization repository. dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, https://github.com/dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Rasterization via OpenGL Geometry Shader
head: OpenGL Geometry Shader Rasterization for 3D Gaussians, dsplat pipeline, fast-gauss rasterization
body: This method renders 3D Gaussian splats as screen-space quads by leveraging the fixed-function OpenGL rasterizer via a vertex-geometry-fragment shader pipeline, offloading clipping, interpolation, and blending from software to hardware. It differs from CUDA-based software rasterization by reducing CPU/GPU synchronization overhead and explicit sorting stalls, achieving a 5-10x speedup over the original software CUDA rasterizer for high pixel-to-point ratios. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian attributes including position (mean), covariance matrix (or scales/rotations), and RGBA color/opacity. Outputs: A rendered image texture (framebuffer) with alpha blending. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer Object (VBO): Contains attributes per Gaussian point. The layout consists of 4 attributes with sizes [3, 3, 3, 4] floats per vertex, representing positions (3 floats), covariance matrix elements (6 floats, packed as two vec3s), and RGBA (4 floats). Attribute Data Type: gl.GLFLOAT or gl.GLHALFFLOAT, determined by the dtype parameter (torch.float or torch.half). Output Texture Format: gl.GLRGBA16F for half precision, gl.GLRGBA32F for float, or gl.GLRGBA8 for uint8, determined by texdtype. Numbered Steps: 1. Upload Attributes: Upload Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, RGBA) to a vertex buffer object (VBO) on the GPU. 2. Vertex Shader Processing: The vertex shader processes each Gaussian point, passing attributes to the geometry shader. 3. Geometry Shader Emission: The geometry shader emits a quad (4 vertices) per Gaussian. Crucially, it computes the 3D-to-2D covariance projection once per Gaussian rather than per vertex, optimizing performance. 4. Fragment Shader Shading: The fragment shader shades the emitted quad using the interpolated Gaussian alpha and color. 5. Fixed-Function Rasterization: The OpenGL rasterizer handles clipping, interpolation of vertex attributes across the quad, and alpha blending into the framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. GLPOINTS = 0 GLTRIANGLESTRIP = 4 def setuprastercontext(dtype, texdtype): # Initialize raster context with specified data and texture types return {"dtype": dtype, "texdtype": texdtype, "vbo": None, "fbo": None} def compileshaders(): # Vertex Shader: Passes position, covariance, and color to geometry shader vertexshadersource = """ #version 430 core layout(location = 0) in vec3 position; layout(location = 1) in vec3 cov1; layout(location = 2) in vec3 cov2; layout(location = 3) in vec4 color; out vec3 vcov1; out vec3 vcov2; out vec4 vcolor; void main() { vcov1 = cov1; vcov2 = cov2; vcolor = color; glPosition = vec4(position, 1.0); } """ # Geometry Shader: Emits quad, computes 2D covariance once geometryshadersource = """ #version 430 core layout(points) in; layout(trianglestrip, maxvertices = 4) out; in vec3 vcov1[]; in vec3 vcov2[]; in vec4 vcolor[]; out vec2 vuv; out vec4 vcolorout; out float vdepth; uniform mat4 projectionmatrix; uniform mat4 viewmatrix; void main() { // Compute 3D-to-2D covariance projection once per Gaussian // C2D = J C3D J^T, where J is the projection Jacobian // Compute basis vectors (u, v) and scale factors for the quad // Emit 4 vertices forming a quad in screen space glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(vposition, 1.0); vuv = vec2(0.0); vcolorout = vcolor[0]; EmitVertex(); glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(vposition + u - v, 1.0); vuv = vec2(0.0, 0.0); EmitVertex(); glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(vposition + u + v, 1.0); vuv = vec2(1.0, 0.0); EmitVertex(); glPosition = projectionmatrix viewmatrix vec4(vposition - u + v, 1.0); vuv = vec2(0.0, 1.0); EmitVertex(); EndPrimitive(); } """ # Fragment Shader: Shading with Gaussian alpha/color fragmentshadersource = """ #version 430 core in vec2 vuv; in vec4 vcolorout; out vec4 fragcolor; void main() { // Evaluate Gaussian PDF at UV coordinates // alpha = exp(-0.5 dot(vuv, vuv)) opacity // fragcolor = vec4(vcolorout.rgb alpha, alpha) fragcolor = vcolorout; } """ return vertexshadersource, geometryshadersource, fragmentshadersource def rendergaussians(gaussians, context): # 1. Upload Gaussian attributes to VBO vbo = allocatevbo(gaussians.attributes) # 2. Set up shader program vs, gs, fs = compileshaders() shaderprogram = createshaderprogram(vs, gs, fs) # 3. Bind VBO and execute draw call bindvbo(vbo) useshader(shaderprogram) # 4. Draw points which are expanded to quads by GS drawarrays(GLPOINTS, 0, gaussians.count) # 5. Read back or use framebuffer texture return getframebuffertexture() Parameters: dtype: Data type for attributes (torch.float or torch.half). texdtype: Output texture format (gl.GLRGBA16F, gl.GLRGBA32F, or gl.GLRGBA8). initbuffersize: Initial size for buffer allocation. inittexturesize: Initial size for texture allocation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Triangles: Modern graphics hardware rasterization pipelines are not well-optimized for small triangles, which can cause performance drops during high-resolution rendering with large Gaussians. Covariance Computation: The source notes that a fast 3D covariance computation (from scales and rotations) in the shader is not yet implemented; only a PyTorch implementation is available for precomputation. Caching persistent results (e.g., the 6 elements of the covariance matrix) is recommended for best performance. Backward Pass: No backward pass is supported yet. Performance: Can be 5-10x faster than the original software CUDA rasterizer (diff-gaussian-rasterization). Can be 2-3x faster if using offline rendering, though bottlenecked by copying rendered images. Scaling: Speedup is most visible with high pixel-to-point ratio (large Gaussians, small point count, high-res rendering). For extremely dense point clouds (> 1 million points), the CUDA implementation might be faster due to hardware rasterization inefficiencies with small triangles. Strengths: Offloads clipping, interpolation, and blending to the fixed-function OpenGL pipeline, reducing CPU/GPU synchronization overhead and explicit sorting stalls. Uses non-blocking data passing and GPU sorting to minimize stalls. Limitations: No backward pass support. Performance degrades with small triangles in high-resolution rendering. Requires precomputation of covariance in PyTorch as shader-side computation is not yet optimized. When to Use: Real-time and offline 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering where speed is critical and backward pass is not needed. Best for high pixel-to-point ratios. When Not to Use: Extremely dense point clouds (> 1 million points) where CUDA software rasterization may be faster. When backward pass is required. This method is part of the fastgauss library, developed by dendenxu, for real-time and offline 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It builds on the principles of differentiable rendering and Gaussian Splatting, aiming to optimize the rasterization step by leveraging standard graphics APIs instead of custom CUDA kernels. dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, https://github.com/dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: DP-GES Rendering
head: DP-GES depth peeling pass, Depth Peeling for Gaussian-Enhanced Surfels, Depth Peeling for High-Fidelity Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering, Depth Peeling for Surfel Rendering, Ours
body: DP-GES is a sort-free rendering method that combines 2D surfels with semi-transparent boundaries and 3D Gaussians to achieve high-fidelity novel view synthesis, eliminating aliasing and popping artifacts while enabling correct transmittance modulation. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization and sibling Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling by introducing a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 uses z-buffer-based depth peeling to extract the nearest three layers of depth, color, and opacity from surfels, and Stage 2 splats 3D Gaussians without sorting, modulating their weights by the transmittance from the peeled surfel layers. Unlike Gaussian-Enhanced Surfels (GES), which uses fully opaque surfels, DP-GES uses semi-transparent boundaries to mitigate aliasing from depth testing and allow differentiable joint optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D surfels S, a set of 3D Gaussians G, and camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics). Outputs: Final rendered image color C and weight W (normalized to produce color). Data Structures: Surfel Set S: S = \{pi, ri, si, Bi\}{i=1}^N. pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^2: Anisotropic scaling. Bi: Spherical Beta parameters for view-dependent color. Gaussian Set G: G = \{pi, \sigmai, ri, si, Bi\}{i=1}^M. pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \sigmai: Scale (implied from 3DGS context). ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^2: Scaling. Bi: Spherical Beta parameters. Texture Buffers: A four-channel texture storing peeled depth maps \{Di^s\}{i=1}^2 and transmittance maps \{Ti^s\}{i=1}^2. D3^s and T3^s are not stored because Gaussians beyond the third layer are culled by hardware depth testing. Depth and color/opacity buffers are allocated for the three intermediate peeling layers. Parameters: Number of depth peeling layers: 3. This balances quality and efficiency; 2 layers cause background leakage, and 4 layers drop FPS significantly due to memory bandwidth issues in OpenGL. Opacity modulation parameter w: Fixed constant shared by all surfels. Default value is 30. If w < 1, the surfel is fully translucent; if w = 255, it is completely opaque. Depth margin \epsilons: A tiny depth margin for culling and depth buffer updates. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Surfel Rasterization via Depth Peeling. Initialize depth buffer with far plane. For layer k = 1 to 3: Clear color and opacity buffers for layer k. Rasterize all surfels S. For each surfel fragment at pixel (x,y): Calculate local coordinates (x,y) on the surfel disc. Compute opacity \alphai(x,y) = \min(1, w \cdot G(x,y)), where G(x,y) = \exp(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}). Perform depth test against the current depth buffer. If the surfel depth di is greater than the stored depth d{stored} by a small margin, discard. To handle interleaved surfels correctly, surfel IDs are also written to the buffer to identify intersections. Write depth di, color Ci (from Bi), opacity \alphai, and surfel ID to the buffers for layer k. Update the depth buffer with di + \epsilons for subsequent layers. After rasterizing all surfels, the buffers contain the k-th peeled layer's depth Dk^s, color Ck^s, and opacity Ak^s. Post-processing (Surfel Compositing): Alpha-blend the 3 peeled layers using front-to-back compositing (same as 3DGS) to obtain final surfel color CS and transmittance maps \{Ti^s\}{i=0}^3: CS = \sum{i=1}^3 A{si} T{i-1} C{is} + T3^s Cb Ti^s = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i=0 \\ \prod{j=1}^i (1 - A{sj}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where Cb is the background color. Pack D1^s, D2^s, T1^s, T2^s into a four-channel texture. Note: T0^s = 1 is implicit. 2. Stage 2: Sort-Free Gaussian Splatting. Clear final color and weight accumulators. Enable depth testing, disable depth writing. For each pixel \hat{x} (or in parallel via fragment shader): Initialize CG(\hat{x}) = 0, WG(\hat{x}) = 0. For each Gaussian i covering pixel \hat{x}: Calculate Gaussian weight \alphai(\hat{x}) (standard 2D Gaussian projection). Determine Gaussian center depth di. Query transmittance ts(\hat{x}) based on di and peeled depths \{Dj^s\}: ts(\hat{x}) = \begin{cases} T0^s(\hat{x}) & \text{if } di < D1^s(\hat{x}) \\ T1^s(\hat{x}) & \text{if } D1^s(\hat{x}) \le di < D2^s(\hat{x}) \\ T2^s(\hat{x}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Perform depth culling: Calculate indicator 1{dt}(\hat{x}) = 1 if di < ds(\hat{x}) + \epsilons, else 0. ds(\hat{x}) is the depth of the nearest peeled layer i where Ti^s(\hat{x}) = 0. If all Ti^s > 0, ds(\hat{x}) = D3^s(\hat{x}). If 1{dt}(\hat{x}) == 1 and ts(\hat{x}) > 0: Get Gaussian color ci from Bi. Accumulate: CG(\hat{x}) \leftarrow CG(\hat{x}) + 1{dt}(\hat{x}) ci \alphai(\hat{x}) ts(\hat{x}) WG(\hat{x}) \leftarrow WG(\hat{x}) + 1{dt}(\hat{x}) \alphai(\hat{x}) ts(\hat{x}) Final Post-processing: Calculate total weight W{total} = WS + WG, where WS = \sum{i=1}^3 A{si} T{i-1} is the constant sum of surfel color weights. Normalize and output final color: C = \frac{CS + CG}{WS + WG}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderdpges(surfels, gaussians, width, height, farplane, epsilons): # Stage 1: Depth Peeling for Surfels # layerdepths[k][y][x], layercolors[k][y][x], layeropacities[k][y][x] for k=0,1,2 layerdepths = [[[0.0] width for in range(height)] for in range(3)] layercolors = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height) for in range(3)] layeropacities = [[[0.0] width for in range(height)] for in range(3)] currentdepthbuffer = [[farplane] width for in range(height)] for k in range(3): # Clear buffers for layer k for y in range(height): for x in range(width): layerdepths[k][y][x] = 0.0 layercolors[k][y][x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] layeropacities[k][y][x] = 0.0 for surfel in surfels: for y in range(max(0, surfel.screenymin), min(height, surfel.screenymax)): for x in range(max(0, surfel.screenxmin), min(width, surfel.screenxmax)): localx, localy = surfel.tolocal(x, y) alpha = min(1.0, surfel.w math.exp(-(localx2 + localy2) / 2.0)) if surfel.depth > currentdepthbuffer[y][x] + epsilons: continue layerdepths[k][y][x] = surfel.depth layercolors[k][y][x] = surfel.getcolor() layeropacities[k][y][x] = alpha currentdepthbuffer[y][x] = surfel.depth + epsilons # Post-processing: Alpha blend peeled layers T = [1.0] 4 CS = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for i in range(1, 4): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): A = layeropacities[i-1][y][x] T[i] = T[i-1] (1.0 - A) CS[y][x][0] += A T[i-1] layercolors[i-1][y][x][0] CS[y][x][1] += A T[i-1] layercolors[i-1][y][x][1] CS[y][x][2] += A T[i-1] layercolors[i-1][y][x][2] packedtexture = [[[layerdepths[0][y][x], layerdepths[1][y][x], T[1], T[2]] for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] # Stage 2: Sort-Free Gaussian Splatting CG = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] WG = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] cullingdepths = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ds = layerdepths[2][y][x] for i in range(3): if T[i+1] < 1e-6: ds = layerdepths[i][y][x] break cullingdepths[y][x] = ds for gaussian in gaussians: for y in range(max(0, gaussian.screenymin), min(height, gaussian.screenymax)): for x in range(max(0, gaussian.screenxmin), min(width, gaussian.screenxmax)): alpha = gaussian.weight(x, y) di = gaussian.depth if di < layerdepths[0][y][x]: ts = T[0] elif di < layerdepths[1][y][x]: ts = T[1] else: ts = T[2] if di < cullingdepths[y][x] + epsilons and ts > 0: c = gaussian.getcolor() CG[y][x][0] += c[0] alpha ts CG[y][x][1] += c[1] alpha ts CG[y][x][2] += c[2] alpha ts WG[y][x] += alpha ts # Final Normalization WS = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): for i in range(1, 4): WS[y][x] += layeropacities[i-1][y][x] T[i-1] TotalW = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] FinalColor = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): TotalW[y][x] = WS[y][x] + WG[y][x] if TotalW[y][x] < 1e-6: TotalW[y][x] = 1e-6 FinalColor[y][x][0] = (CS[y][x][0] + CG[y][x][0]) / TotalW[y][x] FinalColor[y][x][1] = (CS[y][x][1] + CG[y][x][1]) / TotalW[y][x] FinalColor[y][x][2] = (CS[y][x][2] + CG[y][x][2]) / TotalW[y][x] return FinalColor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interleaved Surfels: Two intersecting surfels might be peeled only once along their intersection line if IDs are not tracked. Solution: Write surfel ID into the buffer during rasterization to correctly identify and handle interleaved surfels. Background Color Leakage: If T3 is not zero, background color leaks through. The loss Lt encourages surfels to separate, driving T3 to zero. For pixels covered by fewer than 2 surfel layers, gradients for Lt are masked out. 4-Layer Peeling: Breaks 4-float alignment packing in OpenGL, increasing memory bandwidth usage and dropping FPS. Transparent Objects: Shows artifacts because surfels are mainly opaque. Time Complexity: The surfel rendering is O(Ns \cdot P) across 3 passes, where Ns is the number of surfels and P is pixels. Gaussian rendering is O(Ng \cdot P) but sort-free. Overall, it is faster than sorting-based methods. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for 3 layers of depth/color/opacity during peeling, plus the packed texture for Stage 2. Surfel count is typically <10% of Gaussian count, so peeling cost is negligible. Measured Performance: On RTX 4090 for Mip-NeRF360 dataset: >470 FPS at 1080p. 2.5x faster than vanilla 3DGS and 3x faster than DBS. Ablation FPS (1080p): Full 472, 2 layers 578, 4 layers 278. Strengths: Sort-free, high fidelity, eliminates popping and aliasing, differentiable joint optimization, integrable into existing engines (OpenGL). Limitations: Artifacts on transparent/semi-transparent objects (e.g., glass), slightly higher FLIP error than GES due to view-dependent effects, requires extra initialization and longer training time compared to 2DGS. DP-GES was proposed by Keyang Ye, Hongzhi Wu, and Kun Zhou from Zhejiang University and Hangzhou Research Institute of Holographic and AI Technology. It was published on arXiv in May 2026. It is an improved variant of Gaussian-Enhanced Surfels (GES) [42], addressing GES's limitations of aliasing artifacts and suboptimal reconstruction by introducing semi-transparent surfel boundaries and depth peeling. name: Per-fragment Voxel-Cell Mask Injection
head: Fragment SDF Shader Patch, H2′
body: Per-fragment Voxel-Cell Mask Injection is a technique for carving cube-shaped holes in 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by injecting a Signed Distance Field (SDF) evaluation into the fragment shader at runtime. It solves the visual artifacts caused by deleting whole splats (the "H2" baseline) by operating at the fragment level, producing clean, sharp cube edges without forking the underlying renderer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian Splatting scene rendered via a WebGL renderer (specifically tested with Spark.js/Three.js), a voxel grid defining the carving space, and a set of active carve cells. Output: A rendered image where fragments falling within active carve cells are discarded, creating a hole with the exact shape of the voxel grid cells. Data Structures: The core state is managed by a FragmentSdfShaderPatch class exposing the following uniforms to the shader: 1. uCarveMask: A Data3DTexture (sampler3D) with dimensions matching the voxel grid counts (Nx, Ny, Nz). Data type is Uint8Array, initialized to 0 (not carved). 2. uVoxelOrigin: A vec3 representing the origin of the voxel grid in world space. 3. uVoxelSizeInv: A float equal to 1 / \text{voxelSize}. 4. uVoxelCountsInv: A vec3 equal to 1 / (Nx, Ny, Nz). 5. uCarveBoundsMin / uCarveBoundsMax: vec3 uniforms defining the union Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of all active carve cells for early-out optimization. 6. uCarveCount: An integer uniform tracking the number of active carve cells. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a FragmentSdfShaderPatch instance with the voxel grid. 2. Texture Allocation: Allocate a Data3DTexture sized according to the voxel grid counts. 3. Texture Initialization: Initialize all texels to zero (not carved). 4. Shader Injection: Use the renderer's Material.onBeforeCompile hook to modify the compiled fragment shader source code. 5. Uniform Declaration: Insert the uniform declarations before the out vec4 fragColor; statement. 6. Logic Insertion: Insert the SDF discard logic block immediately before the main body opener void main() { vec4 rgba = vRgba;. Pseudocode: The injected GLSL logic, inserted at the start of the fragment shader's main() function: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. // Uniforms declared before main() uniform sampler3D uCarveMask; uniform vec3 uVoxelOrigin; uniform float uVoxelSizeInv; uniform vec3 uVoxelCountsInv; uniform vec3 uCarveBoundsMin; uniform vec3 uCarveBoundsMax; uniform int uCarveCount; in vec3 vWorldPos; void main() { // Inserted Logic Start if (uCarveCount > 0 && vWorldPos.x >= uCarveBoundsMin.x && vWorldPos.x <= uCarveBoundsMax.x && vWorldPos.y >= uCarveBoundsMin.y && vWorldPos.y <= uCarveBoundsMax.y && vWorldPos.z >= uCarveBoundsMin.z && vWorldPos.z <= uCarveBoundsMax.z) { vec3 coord = (vWorldPos - uVoxelOrigin) uVoxelSizeInv; vec3 texCoord = coord uVoxelCountsInv; if (texture(uCarveMask, texCoord).r > 0.5) discard; } // Inserted Logic End vec4 rgba = vRgba; // Remaining original shader code follows } Parameters: Voxel Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. Tile Size: Inherits from parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, default 32x32 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on vWorldPos being accurate. If world-space reconstruction is imprecise, the cube edges may appear jagged or misaligned. Boundary Conditions: The AABB early-out is critical for performance. If the union AABB is not updated correctly when adding/removing carves, fragments may be incorrectly discarded or not discarded. Texture Updates: The needsUpdate flag must be set on the Data3DTexture after modifying the Uint8Array to ensure the GPU receives the new data. No shader recompilation is required per carve; the texture's version bump is the only GPU-visible change. A variant that renders an axis-aligned box SDF with zero opacity to hide splats inside the box. It avoids thinning artifacts by operating per-sample rather than deleting whole splats. Choose this when you need to hide volumetric regions without affecting neighboring splats. Time Complexity: O(1) per-fragment cost via Data3DTexture lookup. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the voxel grid volume (Nx \times Ny \times Nz) bytes for the Uint8Array backing the Data3DTexture. Measured Performance: p95 latency of 9.6 ms for 256 carves on a scene with 177 K splats (butterfly.spz). Strengths: Produces sharp, clean cube-shaped edges; does not require forking the renderer; scales well with the number of carves (no per-splat sorting or deletion overhead). Limitations: Requires WebGL 2.0+ for Data3DTexture support; carving is limited to axis-aligned cubes defined by the voxel grid; performance depends on the cost of the 3D texture lookup. When to use: When precise, geometrically clean carving is required and the underlying renderer allows shader injection. When not to use: When non-cubic carving shapes are needed, or when the renderer does not support dynamic shader modification or 3D textures. Originating from the splatcarve project by Steve Kwon (2026), this method was developed to demonstrate that browser-based 3D Gaussian Splatting editors could perform complex volumetric edits without forking the rendering engine. It addresses the limitations of the "H2" baseline, which deleted whole splats grouped by voxel, resulting in rough, artifact-prone masks. The "H2′" breakthrough showed that injecting SDF evaluation via THREE.Material.onBeforeCompile could achieve interactive carving latencies with high visual fidelity. stevekwon211/splatcarve, https://github.com/stevekwon211/splatcarve, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF-based Voxel Carving
head: SplatEditCarve
body: SDF-based Voxel Carving is a technique for removing 3D Gaussian Splatting samples within a specific volumetric region by rendering an axis-aligned box Signed Distance Field (SDF) with zero opacity. It acts as a visual mask that hides splat samples inside the box while leaving samples outside unchanged, avoiding the thinning artifacts caused by deleting whole splats. Unlike packed-array opacity mutation which deletes whole splats (causing visible thinning in neighboring voxels for anisotropic splats), SDF mutation is per-sample. Inside the box, the sample becomes invisible; outside, it remains untouched, resulting in a hole with the exact shape of the box. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A SplatMesh containing the 3D Gaussian splats, a target voxel defined by localCenter and voxelSize, and a SplatEdit component instance. Output: A visual modification where splats intersecting the voxel volume are masked out (opacity zeroed) without modifying the underlying splat data structure. Data Structures: SplatEdit: A component attached to the SplatMesh that manages SDF masks. It maintains a map of active SDFs keyed by voxel identifier. SplatEditSdf: Represents a single carving primitive. type: Enum, set to BOX. invert: Boolean, set to false. opacity: Float, set to 0. position: Vector3, set to the voxel's local center. scale: Vector3, set to half the voxelSize in all dimensions to define the box extent. Parameters: rgbaBlendMode: Set to MULTIPLY. softEdge: Set to 0. sdfSmooth: Set to 0. voxelSize: The side length of the cubic voxel being carved. Steps: 1. Initialize the SplatEdit component with rgbaBlendMode set to MULTIPLY, softEdge set to 0, and sdfSmooth set to 0. 2. Attach the SplatEdit instance as a child of the SplatMesh so that its coordinate system aligns with the mesh's local frame. 3. To carve a voxel at localCenter with voxelSize: a. Create a new SplatEditSdf instance. b. Set type to BOX. c. Set invert to false. d. Set opacity to 0. e. Set the SDF position to the voxel's localCenter. f. Set the SDF scale to voxelSize / 2 in all dimensions. g. Add the SDF to the SplatEdit instance. h. Store the reference in a map keyed by the voxel identifier. 4. To uncarve: a. Remove the SDF from the SplatEdit instance. b. Delete the reference from the map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SplatEditSdf: def init(self, type, invert, opacity, position, scale): self.type = type self.invert = invert self.opacity = opacity self.position = position self.scale = scale class SplatEdit: def init(self): self.rgbaBlendMode = "MULTIPLY" self.softEdge = 0 self.sdfSmooth = 0 self.activesdfs = {} # Map: voxelid -> SplatEditSdf def addcarve(self, voxelid, localcenter, voxelsize): # Create SDF with type BOX, invert false, opacity 0 sdf = SplatEditSdf( type="BOX", invert=False, opacity=0, position=localcenter, scale=Vector3(voxelsize / 2, voxelsize / 2, voxelsize / 2)) self.activesdfs[voxelid] = sdf def removecarve(self, voxelid): if voxelid in self.activesdfs: del self.activesdfs[voxelid] splatedit = SplatEdit() voxelid = "voxel1" localcenter = Vector3(0, 0, 0) voxelsize = 1.0 splatedit.addcarve(voxelid, localcenter, voxelsize) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: This method is a visual mask only; the underlying splat data is unmodified. Hard deletes (e.g., for PLY export or multiplayer sync) require baking the SDFs back into packed-array opacity. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Avoids thinning artifacts in neighboring voxels that occur when deleting whole splats, particularly for anisotropic splats. Provides precise, box-shaped holes. Limitations: Does not remove data, only masks it. Requires additional processing (baking) for permanent removal. When to Use: Use when visual editing of a Gaussian Splatting scene is required without permanently altering the source data or causing visible artifacts from partial splat deletion. When Not to Use: Do not use when permanent data reduction is needed for export or network transmission without a subsequent baking step. Origin: The technique is part of the splatcarve project by stevekwon211. History and Development: The method is described in the context of a stack-based editing system for 3D Gaussian Splatting, where operations are recorded in a history stack. Where it is used: Used in real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting viewers/editors for non-destructive voxel carving. stevekwon211/splatcarve, https://github.com/stevekwon211/splatcarve, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Thread-efficient Partial Rendering
head: Multi-view Tiled Partial Rendering, Subsampled Tile Rendering
body: Thread-efficient partial rendering is a GPU rasterization optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to reduce the computational overhead of multi-view training. It solves the problem of low GPU utilization caused by naive binary masking in tiled rendering, where idle threads wait for active threads to finish. Unlike naive multi-view training which renders all pixels for all views, or naive partial rendering with masks which leaves most threads in a block idle, this method maintains the same number of training pixels as single-view training while maximizing parallelization by assigning multiple GPU blocks to a single tile. The method modifies the standard tiled rasterization loop by decoupling the number of threads per block from the tile size, allowing multiple blocks to cooperatively render a single tile for multiple viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: K: The number of participating viewpoints. N: The number of pixels (and standard threads) in a tile. DI: A sorted array of Gaussian primitives projected onto the image plane of viewpoint I. PA: An array mapping thread indices to specific pixel coordinates to render. A: An index array defining which pixels are subsampled for each viewpoint. Outputs: Final color and opacity values written to pixel locations PA[k,i]. Data Structures: Shared Memory (Shmemk): An array of size N/K shared across all threads i within block k. Validity Flag (isValid{k,i}): A boolean flag for each thread indicating if its assigned pixel is within image bounds. Intermediate Value (V{k,i}): A temporal variable storing the intermediate result of alpha blending for thread i in block k. Parameters: i: Index of a thread in a tile. k: Index of a GPU block, ranging from 1 to K. N/K: The number of threads per block, which must equal the number of subsampled pixels for the assigned viewpoint. Algorithm Steps: 1. Subsampling: For each viewpoint, subsample the pixels to be rendered within a tile. Pass these subsampled pixel indices as an index array to the rasterizer. 2. Block Assignment: Assign K GPU blocks to a single tile. The number of blocks equals the number of viewpoints K. 3. Thread Configuration: Ensure each block k has exactly N/K threads, matching the number of subsampled pixels for that viewpoint. 4. Viewpoint Allocation: Assign each block k to a specific viewpoint k. 5. Execution: For each block k from 1 to K, execute the following kernel logic: Initialize shared memory Shmemk of size N/K. For each thread i from 1 to N/K in block k: Set isValid{k,i} to true. If the pixel coordinate PA[k,i] is outside the image bounds, set isValid{k,i} to false. While there is unfetched data left in the sorted Gaussian array DI for the assigned viewpoint: Load data from DI at index offset (N/K) + i into Shmemk[i]. If isValid{k,i} is true, update V{k,i} by calling alphaBlending(Shmemk, V{k,i}). Synchronize all threads in block k using synchronize(). Increment offset by 1. Assign the final blended value V{k,i} to pixel PA[k,i]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def threadefficientpartialrenderingblock(k, Nsub, DI, PA): # Shared memory allocation (conceptual) Shmem = [None] Nsub # Thread index within the block i = getthreadindexinblock() # 1. Initialize validity flag isvalid = True # 2. Check image bounds pixelcoord = PA[k, i] if not iswithinimagebounds(pixelcoord): isvalid = False offset = 0 # 3. Process Gaussians while dataexistsinDI(DI, offset, Nsub, i): # Load Gaussian data into shared memory # Index calculation: offset (N/K) + i gaussiandata = getgaussianfromsortedarray(DI, offset Nsub + i) Shmem[i] = gaussiandata # 4. Alpha Blending if valid if isvalid: # Vk,i is stored in thread-local or shared memory depending on implementation # Assuming Vk,i is accumulated across iterations Vki = alphablending(Shmem, Vki) # 5. Synchronize threads in the block synchronizeblock() # 6. Increment offset offset += 1 # 7. Write final result if isvalid: writetopixel(pixelcoord, Vki) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Idle Threads: Naive partial rendering using a binary mask in 3DGS causes idle threads because GPU threads are allocated in blocks. If a tile is masked such that only one pixel is unmasked, all other threads in the block wait, leading to low GPU utilization. This method eliminates that by ensuring every thread in a block has a valid pixel to render. Block Size Alignment: While 3DGS typically aligns tile size with block size, this method requires decreasing the block size to allow multiple blocks to render a single tile. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The method reduces rasterizer overhead compared to naive multi-view training by rendering only a subset of pixels per view, while maintaining the same total number of training pixels as single-view training. Memory Complexity: Uses shared memory Shmemk of size N/K per block. Performance: Maximizes GPU utilization by eliminating idle threads that occur in naive binary masking approaches. Strengths: Effective parallelization for multi-view training; reduces overhead without sacrificing training pixel count. Limitations: Requires custom kernel implementation to handle multiple blocks per tile and dynamic subsampling indices. When to use: Multi-view training of 3D Gaussian Splatting where GPU utilization is critical. When not to use: Single-view training, where standard tiled rendering is sufficient. The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient multi-view training for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the inefficiencies of standard tiled rendering when applied to multi-view scenarios, specifically the problem of thread divergence and idle threads caused by binary masking. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (GPU)
head: 3DGS Rasterization, GSplat rasterizer, Gaussian Rasterization (GPU), Gaussian Splatting Rasterizer, GaussianRasterizer, diff-gaussian-rasterization
body: A differentiable rasterization method for 3D Gaussians that sorts Gaussians by tile and depth to perform alpha blending in parallel per tile. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of 3D Gaussian splats to a 2D screen while maintaining exact gradients for all Gaussian parameters (means, opacities, scales, rotations, spherical harmonics) via a CUDA backend. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by implementing the specific sorting, binning, and tile-based parallel rendering kernels required for the standard 3DGS forward and backward passes, often exposed as a torch.autograd.Function. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes P 3D Gaussians defined by 3D means \mathbf{\mu}{3D}, scales \mathbf{s}, rotations \mathbf{q} (quaternions), opacities \alpha, and color representations (Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{SH} or direct colors \mathbf{c}). Camera parameters include view matrix \mathbf{V}, projection matrix \mathbf{P}, and field of view tangents \tan \thetax, \tan \thetay. Outputs are the rendered RGB image \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, radii \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{Z}^P, and optionally depth/weight buffers. The backward pass returns gradients for all input parameters. Data Structures: The implementation relies on three main GPU buffers managed by the C++/CUDA backend: 1. GeometryState: Stores per-Gaussian precomputed data. depths: float[P] means2D: float2[P] (screen-space center) cov3D: float[P6] (upper triangle of 3x3 3D covariance) rgb: float[P3] (precomputed color) conicopacity: float4[P] (x,y,z=conic matrix components, w=opacity) internalradii: int[P] tilestouched: uint32t[P] pointoffsets: int[P] (prefix sum of tiles touched) 2. BinningState: Stores sorting keys and values. pointlistkeysunsorted: uint64t[P] (Key: high 32 bits = tile ID, low 32 bits = depth) pointlistunsorted: uint32t[P] (Value: Gaussian index) pointlistkeys: uint64t[P] (Sorted keys) pointlist: uint32t[P] (Sorted indices) 3. ImageState: Stores per-pixel state. accumalpha: float[HW] ncontrib: int[HW] ranges: uint2[HW] (start/end indices in sorted pointlist for each tile/pixel) Parameters: BLOCKX, BLOCKY: Tile dimensions in pixels. Typical value: 16x16. BLOCKSIZE: Threads per block. Typical value: 256. NUMCHANNELS: 3 (RGB). scalemodifier: Multiplier for scale components. Typical value: 1.0. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Projection & Conic Computation): For each Gaussian i: a. Frustum Culling: Keep only Gaussians with a 99% confidence interval intersecting the view frustum. b. 3D Covariance: Compute 3D covariance matrix \Sigma{3D} from scale \mathbf{s} and rotation \mathbf{q}. If precomputed, use it. Apply scalemodifier. c. Jacobian: Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the affine approximation of the projective transformation. Let \mathbf{W} be the rotation part of the view matrix. The transformation matrix is \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{J}. d. 2D Covariance: Compute screen-space covariance \Sigma{2D} = \mathbf{T} \Sigma{3D} \mathbf{T}^T. e. Low-Pass Filter: Add 0.3 to the diagonal elements of \Sigma{2D} to ensure minimum pixel width/height. f. Conic Matrix: Invert \Sigma{2D} to get the conic matrix \mathbf{C}{2D} = \Sigma{2D}^{-1}. Store as conicopacity where x=C{00}, y=C{01}, z=C{11}, w=\alpha. g. Radius: Compute eigenvalues \lambda{1,2} of \Sigma{2D}: \lambda{1,2} = 0.5 \left( (\Sigma{2D}){00} + (\Sigma{2D}){11} \right) \pm \sqrt{\max(0.1f, 0.25 \left( (\Sigma{2D}){00} - (\Sigma{2D}){11} \right)^2 + (\Sigma{2D}){01}^2)} Calculate radius r = \lceil 3 \sqrt{\max(\lambda1, \lambda2)} \rceil. h. Tile Bounding Box: Determine the tiles touched by the Gaussian's bounding box. i. Key Generation: For each touched tile, generate a 64-bit key: (tileid << 32) | depthpacked. Store Gaussian index as value. If r \le 0, skip. 2. Sorting and Binning: a. Prefix Sum: Compute an inclusive prefix sum over tilestouched to determine offsets for writing to the binning buffer. b. Radix Sort: Sort the generated key/value pairs using CUDA Radix Sort (cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs) to order Gaussians first by tile ID and then by depth. c. Range Calculation: Identify start and end indices in the sorted list for each tile by comparing tile IDs of consecutive keys. Store these ranges in ImageState.ranges. 3. Rasterization (Tile-Parallel Rendering): Each thread block handles one tile. a. Load Range: Load the range of points for the tile from the sorted pointlist. b. Batch Processing: Iterate over Gaussians in batches. Collectively fetch Gaussian data (ID, xy, conicopacity) from global to shared memory. c. Pixel Loop: For each pixel (u,v) in the tile: i. Initialize transmittance and color buffers. ii. For each Gaussian j in the tile's range: 1. Compute displacement \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{xy}j - \mathbf{pix}{uv}. 2. Compute power: \text{power} = -0.5 \left( C{00} dx^2 + C{11} dy^2 \right) - C{01} dx dy 3. If \text{power} > 0, continue (outside ellipse). 4. Compute alpha: \alphaj = \min(0.99, \alphaj^{\text{orig}} \cdot e^{\text{power}}). 5. If \alphaj < 1/255, continue. 6. Composite: C \leftarrow C + \alphaj \cdot \mathbf{color}j \cdot T T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphaj) 7. If T < 0.0001, mark done for this pixel. d. Write Output: Write final T, contribution count, and C to output buffers. 4. Backward Pass: The backward pass restores saved tensors from the forward pass (ctx.saveforbackward) and calls the C++ backward kernel C.rasterizegaussiansbackward. It computes gradients for means3D, means2D, dc, sh, opacities, scales, rotations, and cov3Dsprecomp. The exact gradient formulas are implemented in the CUDA kernel, utilizing the saved radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, and imgBuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def rasterizegaussiansforward(means3D, scales, rotations, opacities, shs, dc, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier, width, height, shdegree): """ Forward pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. """ P = means3D.shape[0] H, W = height, width # Step 1: Preprocessing (Projection & Conic Computation) # Compute 3D covariance from scales/rotations or use cov3Dsprecomp # Transform to 2D using Jacobian of projection # Compute conic matrix and radius # Store in GeometryState: means2D, depths, cov3D, rgb, conicopacity, internalradii, tilestouched # (CUDA kernel: preprocessCUDA) # Step 2: Generate Keys and Values # For each Gaussian, determine tiles touched based on radius # Create keys: (tileid << 32) | depthpacked # Create values: gaussianindex # Store in BinningState: pointlistkeysunsorted, pointlistunsorted # (CUDA kernel: duplicateWithKeys) # Step 3: Sort (cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs) # Sort keys and values to order Gaussians by tile ID then depth # (CUDA kernel: cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs) # Step 4: Compute Ranges (computeRangesKernel) # Identify start/end indices for each tile in sorted list # (CUDA kernel: computeRangesKernel) # Step 5: Render (renderCUDA kernel) # Launch tile-parallel kernel tilegridx = (W + 15) // 16 tilegridy = (H + 15) // 16 # renderCUDA<<<(tilegridx, tilegridy, 1), (16, 16, 1)>>>(...) # Returns color, radii, invdepths, accumweights return color, radii, invdepths, accumweights def rasterizegaussiansbackward(gradoutcolor, savedtensors): """ Backward pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. """ # Restore saved tensors means3D, scales, rotations, opacities, shs, dc, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = savedtensors # Call backward CUDA kernel # C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(...) # Returns gradients for all input parameters # The exact gradient computation is implemented in the C++/CUDA extension. gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, graddc, gradsh, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward( gradoutcolor, means3D, scales, rotations, opacities, shs, dc, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) return gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, graddc, gradsh, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations Multi-scale technique decomposing the image into a Laplacian pyramid of Gaussian splats for independent optimization and rendering at different resolutions. Validation and dispatch layer for MiniGS-specific rasterizer entry points, enabling auxiliary statistics for blur-aware splitting and depth back-sampling during training. Variant accepting camera rotation and translation deltas to render with pose perturbations, returning pixel coverage statistics. A torch.autograd.Function that bridges Python and a C++ rasterization kernel for 3D Gaussian Splatting, handling argument restructuring and buffer management. Renders 3D Gaussians by leveraging OpenGL's fixed-function point rendering pipeline via CUDA-OpenGL interop, offloading fragment processing to the GPU driver's OpenGL implementation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Highly optimized for GPU parallelism. Tile-based approach ensures memory coalescing and efficient use of shared memory. Typical tile size is 16x16 pixels. Strengths: Differentiable, fast, supports millions of Gaussians, exact gradients. Limitations: Requires significant VRAM for large scenes due to sorting buffers. Depth packing assumes depth fits in 32 bits. When to use: Standard 3DGS rendering and training. When not to use: If VRAM is extremely limited, consider Non-Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting with Transmittance Culling or other memory-efficient variants. name: FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering
head: Laplacian pyramid accumulation, multi-scale Gaussian rendering
body: FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering is a multi-scale rendering technique that decomposes the target image into a Laplacian pyramid of Gaussian splats. The coarsest level renders the base image, while subsequent levels render signed residuals that are upsampled and accumulated to reconstruct the final high-resolution image. It sets itself apart from standard single-scale rasterization by allowing independent optimization and rendering of detail at different resolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A list of Gaussian models (gaussianslist) organized from coarsest to finest, camera views, ground-truth images, a rasterization function (renderfn), and a pyramid processing module (pyramidfunc). Outputs: A rendered image tensor, intermediate buffers for accumulated predictions and ground-truth residuals, and metadata including visibility filters and radii. Data Structures: gaussianslist: List of Gaussian model objects containing 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients). gtgaussianpyrdict: Dictionary mapping camera IDs to lists of ground-truth Gaussian pyramid levels. predaccumulateddict: Dictionary mapping camera IDs to the accumulated prediction tensor at each stage. renderpkg: Dictionary returned by renderfn containing 'render' (torch.Tensor, image), 'viewspacepoints' (torch.Tensor, shape [N, 4], requires gradient), 'visibilityfilter' (torch.Tensor, indices where screen-space radii are greater than 0), 'radii' (torch.Tensor, screen-space radii of splats), and 'accummetriccounts' (torch.Tensor, metric accumulation buffer). Parameters: posandneg: Boolean flag controlling output range. When False, the rasterizer outputs values clamped to [0, 1]. When True, it outputs signed values in [-1.0, 1.0] to represent residuals. mult: Scalar multiplier passed to GaussianRasterizationSettings, likely controlling opacity or scale weighting during rasterization. rendersize: Target resolution for the current stage, derived from the ground-truth pyramid level shape gtgau.shape[-2:]. Numbered Steps: 1. Load Gaussian models from subfolders L0 to L{n-1} into gaussianslist. 2. For each view, compute the ground-truth Gaussian pyramid: gtgaussianpyrdict[viewpointcam.uid] = [pyrgpu[0]] + [lvl.detach().to(device) for lvl in pyrgpu[1:]], where pyrgpu = pyramidfunc.buildpyrgaussian(viewpointcam.originalimage.unsqueeze(0)). 3. Iterate istage from 0 to len(gaussianslist) - 1. 4. Retrieve gaussians = gaussianslist[-istage-1] and gtgau = gtgaussianpyrdict[viewpointcam.uid][-istage-1].squeeze(0). 5. If istage == 0: render with posandneg=False. Set predaccumulated = rendering and gt = gtgau. 6. If istage > 0: render with posandneg=True. Compute upsampled = pyramidfunc.getupsampled([rendering.unsqueeze(0), predaccumulated.unsqueeze(0)]). Update predaccumulated = rendering + upsampled. Normalize rendering to [0, 1] via (rendering + 1.0) / 2.0. Set gt = gtgau - upsampled, then normalize to [0, 1]. 7. After each stage (except the last), prepare Gaussians for the next stage using inheritance or densification logic based on pipe.inheritstate (e.g., "keepandadc", "onlyxyz", "withstate"). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def renderfastgsstage(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt, pyramidfunc, gtgau, predaccumulated, istage, renderfn): rendersize = gtgau.shape[-2:] if istage == 0: renderpkg = renderfn( view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt.mult, rendersize=rendersize, posandneg=False) rendering = renderpkg["render"] predaccumulated = rendering gt = gtgau else: renderpkg = renderfn( view, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt.mult, rendersize=rendersize, posandneg=True) rendering = renderpkg["render"] upsampled = pyramidfunc.getupsampled([ rendering.unsqueeze(0), predaccumulated.unsqueeze(0) ]).squeeze(0) predaccumulated = rendering + upsampled rendering = (rendering + 1.0) / 2.0 gt = (gtgau - upsampled + 1.0) / 2.0 return rendering, predaccumulated, gt def fastgsrenderloop(gaussianslist, viewpointcams, pipeline, background, opt, pyramidfunc, renderfn): device = viewpointcams[0].originalimage.device gtgaussianpyrdict = {} predaccumulateddict = {} for viewpointcam in viewpointcams: pyrgpu = pyramidfunc.buildpyrgaussian(viewpointcam.originalimage.unsqueeze(0)) gtgaussianpyrdict[viewpointcam.uid] = [pyrgpu[0]] + [lvl.detach().to(device) for lvl in pyrgpu[1:]] numstages = len(gaussianslist) for istage in range(numstages): gaussians = gaussianslist[-istage-1] for viewpointcam in viewpointcams: gtgau = gtgaussianpyrdict[viewpointcam.uid][-istage-1].squeeze(0) predaccumulated = predaccumulateddict.get(viewpointcam.uid, None) rendering, predaccumulated, gt = renderfastgsstage( viewpointcam, gaussians, pipeline, background, opt, pyramidfunc, gtgau, predaccumulated, istage, renderfn) predaccumulateddict[viewpointcam.uid] = predaccumulated if istage < numstages - 1: # Prepare Gaussians for next stage based on pipe.inheritstate pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: PyTorch Version Compatibility: The viewspacepoints tensor is initialized with requiresgrad=True, but retaingrad() may fail on older PyTorch versions. The code uses a try-except block to handle this gracefully. Resolution Mismatch: The rendersize must match the shape of the current ground-truth pyramid level gtgau.shape[-2:] to ensure correct upsampling and accumulation. Signed Values: When posandneg=True, the rasterizer outputs values in [-1.0, 1.0]. Failure to normalize these values to [0, 1] before loss computation will lead to incorrect gradients. name: MiniGS Auxiliary & Depth Rendering Interface
head: MiniGS depth rasterization, MiniGS rasterization auxiliary
body: The MiniGS Auxiliary & Depth Rendering Interface is a validation and dispatch layer for MiniGS-specific rasterizer entry points that return auxiliary statistics for blur-aware splitting and depth back-sampling. It distinguishes itself from standard rendering by enforcing strict preconditions on the input configuration and attribute tensors before dispatching to the appropriate rasterization kernel. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, and rastersettings. Outputs: The result of the dispatched rasterization function, which returns auxiliary statistics and depth data. Data Structures rastersettings: Contains inferenceonly (bool) and pixelweights (tensor). Numbered Steps 1. Check rastersettings.inferenceonly; it must be False. 2. Check rastersettings.pixelweights; it must be None or empty. 3. Validate that dc, shs, scales, and rotations are not None. 4. Dispatch to minigsrasterizegaussiansaux or minigsrasterizegaussiansdepth with means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, and rastersettings. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minigsauxiliarydepthinterface( means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings): # Step 1: Validate inference mode if rastersettings.inferenceonly: raise Exception("MiniGS auxiliary rendering does not support inferenceonly=True.") # Step 2: Validate pixel weights if rastersettings.pixelweights is not None and rastersettings.pixelweights.numel() > 0: raise Exception("MiniGS auxiliary rendering does not support pixelweights.") # Step 3: Validate attribute tensors if dc is None or shs is None or scales is None or rotations is None: raise ValueError("dc, shs, scales, and rotations must not be None.") # Step 4: Dispatch to auxiliary or depth rasterizer # Source does not specify the exact selection logic between the two kernels return minigsrasterizegaussiansaux( means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings) def minigsrasterizegaussiansaux(means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings): raise NotImplementedError("Implementation not provided in source ") def minigsrasterizegaussiansdepth(means3D, means2D, dc, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings): raise NotImplementedError("Implementation not provided in source ") Parameters inferenceonly: bool. Must be False. pixelweights: tensor. Must be None or empty. dc: tensor. Diffuse color. shs: tensor. Spherical harmonics coefficients. scales: tensor. Gaussian scales. rotations: tensor. Gaussian rotations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls The interface explicitly fails if inferenceonly=True. The interface explicitly fails if pixelweights are provided and non-empty. The method requires all five Gaussian attribute tensors (dc, shs, scales, rotations, opacities) to be present; failure to provide them results in errors. Not given in the sources. The interface is part of the MiniGS implementation and is integrated into the training loop of the Improved-GS project. It is specifically designed to support training-time operations such as blur-aware splitting and depth back-sampling.
