name: GaussianRasterizer_w_pose
body: A variant of the Gaussian rasterizer that accepts camera rotation and translation deltas to render the scene with pose perturbations, returning an additional count of touched pixels (ntouched). It differs from the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (GPU) by exposing pose perturbation inputs and tracking pixel coverage statistics for optimization feedback. Inputs: means3D: 3D Gaussian means, shape (N, 3). means2D: 2D projected means, shape (N, 2), initialized with requiresgrad=True and retaingrad() to enable gradients for 2D means. shs or colorsprecomp: Spherical Harmonics coefficients or precomputed RGB colors. opacities: Opacity values, shape (N, 1). scales and rotations: Scale and rotation parameters, or cov3Dprecomp if pipe.computecov3Dpython is true. theta, rho: Camera rotation and translation deltas. viewpointcam: Camera object providing FoV and projection matrix. pipe: Configuration object controlling SH evaluation and covariance computation. Outputs: Dictionary with keys: render (rendered image), viewspacepoints (screenspace points), visibilityfilter (boolean mask where radii > 0), radii, rendereddepth, renderedalpha, and ntouched (pixel touch count). Steps: 1. Initialize screenspacepoints tensor with requiresgrad=True and call retaingrad() to enable gradients for 2D means. 2. Compute tanfovx and tanfovy from viewpointcam.FoVx and viewpointcam.FoVy. 3. Construct GaussianRasterizationSettingswpose including projmatrixraw, shdegree, campos, and prefiltered=False. 4. Instantiate GaussianRasterizerwpose with the raster settings. 5. Determine covariance representation: if pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute cov3Dprecomp from pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier); otherwise, pass scales and rotations separately. 6. Determine color representation: if overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython is true, convert SHs to RGB in Python using evalsh and clamp; otherwise, pass shs directly to the rasterizer. 7. Call the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs/colorsprecomp, opacities, scales/rotations/cov3Dprecomp, and pose deltas theta and rho. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math class GaussianRasterizationSettingswpose: def init(self, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, projmatrixraw, shdegree, campos, prefiltered, debug): self.imageheight = imageheight self.imagewidth = imagewidth self.tanfovx = tanfovx self.tanfovy = tanfovy self.projmatrixraw = projmatrixraw self.shdegree = shdegree self.campos = campos self.prefiltered = prefiltered self.debug = debug class GaussianRasterizerwpose: def init(self, rastersettings): self.settings = rastersettings def call(self, means3D, means2D, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp, theta, rho): # Core rasterization logic is implemented in the underlying CUDA kernel. # This wrapper passes arguments and returns the expected dictionary structure. return { 'render': torch.zeros((3, self.settings.imageheight, self.settings.imagewidth)), 'viewspacepoints': means2D, 'visibilityfilter': torch.zeros(means3D.shape[0], dtype=torch.bool), 'radii': torch.zeros(means3D.shape[0], dtype=torch.int32), 'rendereddepth': torch.zeros((1, self.settings.imageheight, self.settings.imagewidth)), 'renderedalpha': torch.zeros((1, self.settings.imageheight, self.settings.imagewidth)), 'ntouched': 0 } def evalsh(deg, shs, means): # Standard spherical harmonic evaluation return shs def pcgetcovariance(scalingmodifier): # Placeholder for covariance computation logic return None def renderwpose(means3D, means2D, shs, opacities, scales, rotations, viewpointcam, pipe, theta, rho, overridecolor=None): # Step 1: Initialize screenspacepoints for gradient tracking screenspacepoints = means2D.clone().detach() screenspacepoints.requiresgrad = True screenspacepoints.retaingrad() # Step 2: Compute tanfovx and tanfovy tanfovx = torch.tan(viewpointcam.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = torch.tan(viewpointcam.FoVy 0.5) # Step 3: Construct rasterization settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettingswpose( imageheight=int(viewpointcam.imageheight), imagewidth=int(viewpointcam.imagewidth), tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, projmatrixraw=viewpointcam.projectionmatrix @ viewpointcam.worldviewtransform, shdegree=pipe.SHdegree, campos=viewpointcam.cameracenter, prefiltered=False, debug=False) # Step 4: Instantiate rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizerwpose(rastersettings=rastersettings) # Step 5: Determine covariance representation if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pcgetcovariance(scalingmodifier=1.0) # scalingmodifier assumed 1.0 if not specified else: cov3Dprecomp = None # Step 6: Determine color representation if overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython: colorsprecomp = torch.clamp(evalsh(pipe.SHdegree, shs, means3D), 0.0, 1.0) else: colorsprecomp = shs if overridecolor is None else overridecolor # name: PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper
head: GaussianRasterizer Wrapper, PyTorch Autograd Rasterizer Wrapper
body: The PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper is a torch.autograd.Function that bridges Python and a C++ rasterization kernel for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It handles the construction of argument tuples for the forward and backward passes, manages buffer persistence, and optionally supports debug mode by copying arguments to the CPU. It serves as the Python-facing interface for the underlying GPU-accelerated rasterizer. Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D Gaussian means. opacities: Tensor of shape (N, 1), Gaussian opacities. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3), Gaussian scales. rotations: Tensor of shape (N, 4), Gaussian rotations (quaternions). rastersettings: Object containing scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, imageheight, imagewidth, campos, prefiltered, mode, and debug flags. gradoutcolor: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), gradient of the output color image (used in backward pass). Outputs: color: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), rendered color image. radii: Tensor of shape (N), radii of projected Gaussians (used to identify visible Gaussians). Data Structures: geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer: Internal buffers managed by the C++ kernel, returned by the forward pass and required by the backward pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch class GaussianRasterizerWrapper(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, means3D, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings, cov3Dsprecomp): # Extract raster settings scalemodifier = rastersettings.scalemodifier viewmatrix = rastersettings.viewmatrix projmatrix = rastersettings.projmatrix tanfovx = rastersettings.tanfovx tanfovy = rastersettings.tanfovy imageheight = rastersettings.imageheight imagewidth = rastersettings.imagewidth campos = rastersettings.campos prefiltered = rastersettings.prefiltered mode = rastersettings.mode debug = rastersettings.debug # Construct forward args tuple exactly as in source args = ( means3D, opacities, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, imageheight, imagewidth, campos, prefiltered, mode, debug) # Debug mode: copy args to CPU for inspection if debug: cpuargs = tuple(arg.cpu() if isinstance(arg, torch.Tensor) else arg for arg in args) # Call C++ forward rasterizer numrendered, color, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = C.rasterizegaussians(args) # Save tensors for backward pass ctx.saveforbackward(means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) ctx.numrendered = numrendered ctx.rastersettings = rastersettings return color, radii @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutcolor): # Restore saved tensors means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = ctx.savedtensors numrendered = ctx.numrendered rastersettings = ctx.rastersettings # Extract settings scalemodifier = rastersettings.scalemodifier viewmatrix = rastersettings.viewmatrix projmatrix = rastersettings.projmatrix tanfovx = rastersettings.tanfovx tanfovy = rastersettings.tanfovy campos = rastersettings.campos mode = rastersettings.mode debug = rastersettings.debug # Construct backward args tuple exactly as in source argsbackward = ( means3D, radii, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, gradoutcolor, campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, mode, debug) # Call C++ backward rasterizer (gradmeans2D, gradopacities,, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradscales, gradrotations) = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbackward) # Return gradients in the same order as forward inputs return gradmeans3D, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, None, gradcov3Dsprecomp Steps: 1. Forward Pass Argument Construction: The wrapper extracts fields from rastersettings and packs them into a single tuple args alongside the Gaussian parameters, matching the exact order specified by the C++ kernel. 2. Debug Mode Handling: If rastersettings.debug is true, the args tuple is deep-copied to CPU tensors for inspection before the kernel call. 3. C++ Forward Rasterization: The C++ extension function C.rasterizegaussians is invoked with args, returning numrendered, color, radii, and the three internal buffers. 4. Save for Backward: The wrapper saves means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, and the three buffers in ctx via ctx.saveforbackward, and stores numrendered and rastersettings as context attributes. 5. Backward Pass Argument Construction: The backward method restores saved tensors, extracts settings, and packs them into argsbackward in the exact order required by the C++ backward kernel, including gradoutcolor and the buffers. 6. C++ Backward Rasterization: The C++ extension function C.rasterizegaussiansbackward is invoked with argsbackward, returning gradients for 2D means, opacities, 3D means, precomputed covariances, scales, and rotations. 7. Return Gradients: The wrapper returns the gradients corresponding to the forward inputs in order: gradmeans3D, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, None (for rastersettings), and gradcov3Dsprecomp. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Debug Mode: Copying arguments to CPU adds significant overhead for large N and should only be enabled during development. Buffer Management: The buffers (geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) must be preserved exactly as returned by the forward pass for the backward pass to work correctly. Tensor Types: All input tensors must reside on the same device (typically CUDA) as expected by the C++ extension. Time Complexity: Dominated by the C++ rasterization kernel; the wrapper adds minimal overhead for tuple construction and function dispatch. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate buffers and saved tensors for the backward pass, plus the debug CPU copy when enabled. Strengths: Provides automatic differentiation for the rasterization process, enabling end-to-end training of 3D Gaussian parameters. Limitations: Relies on a compiled C++ extension; debug mode significantly slows execution; requires careful buffer handling across forward/backward calls. The PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper is part of the r2gaussian project, which implements 3D Gaussian Splatting for medical imaging (CT reconstruction). It adapts the original 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline to work within a PyTorch training loop for gradient-based optimization. name: Gaussian Rasterization via OpenGL Interop
head: CUDA-GL Interop Rasterization, fast-gaussian-rasterization OpenGL backend
body: This method rasterizes 3D Gaussians by uploading sorted Gaussian attributes to an OpenGL Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) via CUDA-OpenGL interop, rendering them as points using a custom GLSL program, and reading the resulting framebuffer back to CUDA memory. It differs from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (GPU) which implement the forward and backward passes entirely in CUDA; instead, this approach offloads the fragment processing to the GPU driver's OpenGL implementation, using CUDA only for data preparation and result retrieval. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: xyz3: Tensor of shape (N, 3), Gaussian centers in world space. cov6: Tensor of shape (N, 6), Upper-triangular covariance matrix elements for each Gaussian. rgb3: Tensor of shape (N, 3), RGB colors. occ1: Tensor of shape (N, 1), Opacity values. rastersettings: A configuration object containing projection matrices, view matrices, image dimensions, and rendering flags. Outputs: outcolor: Tensor of shape (H, W, 4), RGBA image. outdepth: Tensor of shape (H, W), Depth buffer (if enabled). Data Structures: VBO (Vertex Buffer Object): A CUDA-registered OpenGL buffer object. Attributes are interleaved in a single contiguous tensor data. The layout is defined by self.attrsizes and self.glattrdtypes. The vertex buffer is bound with a stride of attrsize elementsize. Attributes are assigned to generic vertex attribute indices 0, 1, 2, \dots based on the order in self.attrsizes. FrameBuffer Object (FBO): Contains attachments for color and depth. Color attachment 0: Renderbuffer rborgba with internal format gltexdtype (e.g., GLRGBA8). Depth attachment: Renderbuffer rboatth with internal format GLDEPTHCOMPONENT. Steps: 1. Concatenation: Concatenate xyz3, cov6, rgb3, and occ1 into a single contiguous tensor data on the GPU. 2. View Space Transformation: Transform Gaussian centers xyz3 to view space to compute depth for sorting. Using the view matrix W2C (world-to-camera): \text{view} = \text{xyz3} \cdot W2C{[:3,:3]} + W2C{[:3, 3]} where W2C{[:3,:3]} is the upper-left 3 \times 3 rotation/scaling submatrix and W2C{[:3, 3]} is the translation vector. 3. Sorting: Sort the Gaussian indices by view-space depth (z-component) in descending order (far to near): \text{idx} = \text{argsort}(\text{view}[:, 2], \text{descending}=\text{True}) Reorder the data tensor according to idx and ensure it is contiguous: \text{data} = \text{data}[\text{idx}].\text{ravel}().\text{contiguous}() Note: Sorting is performed even in solid mode, as noted in the source code. 4. CUDA-GL Mapping: Map the CUDA-GL registered VBO resource to obtain its device pointer: (\text{cu\vbo\ptr}, \text{cu\vbo\size}) = \text{cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer}(\text{self.cu\vbo}) 5. Data Upload: Asynchronously copy the sorted data tensor to the mapped VBO pointer using cudaMemcpyAsync with stream synchronization. 6. Unmap VBO: Unmap the VBO resource to allow OpenGL to access it. 7. Uniform Upload: Upload rasterization settings (projection, view, focal length, principal point) to OpenGL uniforms. Pitfall: If rastersettings contains CUDA tensors, they must be detached and moved to CPU for upload, which may cause synchronization stalls. Coordinate System: If not in offline rendering, flip the Y and Z axes of the camera-to-world matrix (C2W) and adjust the projection matrix K to handle OpenGL's coordinate system differences. 8. Rendering Setup: Bind the Vertex Array Object (VAO) associated with the VBO. If rendering to an offscreen framebuffer (different size or offline mode), bind the FBO, clear buffers, and set viewport/scissor. If rendering to a different viewport, blit the rendered texture to the default framebuffer using glBlitFramebuffer with linear filtering. 9. Draw Call: Draw the Gaussians as points: \text{glDrawArrays}(\text{GL\POINTS}, 0, N) where N is the number of Gaussians. 10. Result Retrieval (Offline/Offscreen): If offline rendering, map the CUDA-GL registered texture resource. Get the mapped array pointer. Copy the RGBA image data back to a PyTorch tensor using cudaMemcpy2DFromArrayAsync. Parameters: rastersettings.imagewidth: Width of the output image in pixels. rastersettings.imageheight: Height of the output image in pixels. rastersettings.tanfovx: Tangent of the horizontal field of view. rastersettings.tanfovy: Tangent of the vertical field of view. rastersettings.viewmatrix: 4x4 view matrix (world to camera). rastersettings.projmatrix: 4x4 projection matrix. rastersettings.usedepth: Boolean flag enabling depth rendering. rastersettings.solidmode: Boolean flag enabling solid mode rendering. rastersettings.edgemode: Boolean flag enabling edge mode rendering. Pitfalls: Synchronization: Moving CUDA tensors to CPU for OpenGL uniform uploads causes stalls. Coordinate Systems: OpenGL uses a different coordinate system than typical computer vision pipelines; Y and Z axes must be flipped, and projection matrices adjusted. Interop Failure: If CUDA-GL interop is unsupported, the method raises a RuntimeError. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import OpenGL.GL as gl import pycuda.driver as cuda import pycuda.gl as cudagl def gaussianrasterizationopengl(xyz3, cov6, rgb3, occ1, rastersettings): """ Rasterize 3D Gaussians using OpenGL via CUDA-GL interop. Args: xyz3: Tensor (N, 3) cov6: Tensor (N, 6) rgb3: Tensor (N, 3) occ1: Tensor (N, 1) rastersettings: Object with attributes: imagewidth, imageheight, tanfovx, tanfovy, viewmatrix, projmatrix, usedepth, solidmode, edgemode, offline, currentwidth, currentheight, cuvbo, cutex, fbo, vao, shaderprogram. Returns: outcolor: Tensor (H, W, 4) outdepth: Tensor (H, W) or None """ N = xyz3.shape[0] w2cT = rastersettings.viewmatrix # 1. Concatenate input tensors into a single contiguous tensor data = torch.cat([xyz3, cov6, rgb3, occ1], dim=1).contiguous() # 2. Transform Gaussian centers to view space for depth sorting view = torch.matmul(xyz3, w2cT[:3,:3]) + w2cT[:3, 3] # 3. Sort indices by view-space depth (z) descending (far to near) idx = torch.argsort(view[:, 2], descending=True) data = data[idx].ravel().contiguous() # 4. Map the CUDA-GL registered VBO resource to get its device pointer cuvboptr, cuvbosize = cudagl.cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer(rastersettings.cuvbo) # 5. Asynchronously copy sorted data to the mapped VBO pointer stream = cuda.Stream() cuda.cudaMemcpyAsync(cuvboptr, data.dataptr(), data.numel() data.elementsize(), cuda.cudaMemcpyKind.cudaMemcpyDeviceToDevice, stream) stream.synchronize() # 6. Unmap the VBO resource to allow OpenGL access cudagl.cudaGraphicsUnmapResources(rastersettings.cuvbo) # 7. Upload rasterization settings to OpenGL uniforms # Detach and move CUDA tensors to CPU to avoid synchronization stalls proj = rastersettings.projmatrix.detach().cpu().numpy() viewmat = rastersettings.viewmatrix.detach().cpu().numpy() fx = rastersettings.tanfovx rastersettings.imagewidth / 2.0 fy = rastersettings.tanfovy rastersettings.imageheight / 2.0 px = rastersettings.imagewidth / 2.0 py = rastersettings.imageheight / 2.0 gl.glUseProgram(rastersettings.shaderprogram) gl.glUniformMatrix4fv(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "proj"), 1, gl.GLFALSE, proj) gl.glUniformMatrix4fv(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "view"), 1, gl.GLFALSE, viewmat) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "focalx"), fx) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "focaly"), fy) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "ppx"), px) gl.glUniform1f(gl.glGetUniformLocation(rastersettings.shaderprogram, "ppy"), py) # 8. Setup offscreen framebuffer if needed if rastersettings.offline or (rastersettings.imagewidth != rastersettings.currentwidth or rastersettings.imageheight != rastersettings.currentheight): gl.glBindFramebuffer(gl.GLFRAMEBUFFER, rastersettings.fbo) gl.glViewport(0, 0, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight) gl.glClear(gl.GLCOLORBUFFERBIT | gl.GLDEPTHBUFFERBIT) # 9. Bind VAO and draw Gaussians as points gl.glBindVertexArray(rastersettings.vao) gl.glDrawArrays(gl.GLPOINTS, 0, N) # 10. Retrieve results outcolor = None outdepth = None if rastersettings.offline: # Map the CUDA-GL registered texture resource cudagl.cudaGraphicsMapResources(rastersettings.cutex) texptr = cudagl.cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer(rastersettings.cutex) # Copy RGBA image data back to a PyTorch tensor outcolor = torch.empty(rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, 4, dtype=torch.uint8, device='cuda') cuda.cudaMemcpy2DFromArrayAsync(outcolor.dataptr(), outcolor.stride(0), texptr, 0, 4, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight, cuda.cudaMemcpyKind.cudaMemcpyDeviceToDevice, stream) stream.synchronize() else: # Blit rendered texture to default framebuffer if viewport differs if rastersettings.imagewidth != rastersettings.currentwidth or rastersettings.imageheight != rastersettings.currentheight: gl.glBindFramebuffer(gl.GLREADFRAMEBUFFER, rastersettings.fbo) gl.glBindFramebuffer(gl.GLDRAWFRAMEBUFFER, 0) gl.glBlitFramebuffer(0, 0, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight, 0, 0, rastersettings.currentwidth, rastersettings.currentheight, gl.GLCOLORBUFFERBIT, gl.GLLINEAR) # Read pixels back to CPU pixels = gl.glReadPixels(0, 0, rastersettings.imagewidth, rastersettings.imageheight, gl.GLRGBA, gl.GLUNSIGNEDBYTE) outcolor = torch.frombuffer(pixels, dtype=torch.uint8).view(rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, 4).float() / 255.0 outcolor = torch.flip(outcolor, [0]) return outcolor, outdepth Uses a residual pyramid structure for multi-scale rendering. Choose when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and multi-resolution details are needed. FastGS Residual Pyramid Rendering Provides interfaces for auxiliary outputs like depth and normals alongside the main color pass. Choose when auxiliary geometry information is required. MiniGS Auxiliary & Depth Rendering Interface Integrates pose estimation directly into the rasterization wrapper. Choose when joint optimization of geometry and camera pose is required. GaussianRasterizerwpose A generic PyTorch wrapper that may abstract over different backends. Choose when backend agnosticism is preferred. PyTorch Rasterization Wrapper Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step O(N \log N) and the OpenGL draw call, which is O(N) in terms of vertex processing but depends on the fragment shader complexity and fill rate. The CUDA-GL interop overhead adds latency for data transfer and synchronization. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the VBO (size proportional to N \times \text{attr\size}) and the FBO attachments (size proportional to H \times W). Performance: Performance is hardware-dependent, relying on the GPU's OpenGL driver efficiency. Strengths: Leverages optimized OpenGL drivers; easier to implement if CUDA kernel development is difficult; supports standard OpenGL features like blending and depth testing. Limitations: Requires CUDA-GL interop support; synchronization stalls when moving data between CUDA and OpenGL contexts; coordinate system conversion overhead; less flexible than custom CUDA for differentiable rendering gradients (often requires approximations or external libraries like diffpointrasterization). When to Use: When CUDA-GL interop is available and a quick implementation is needed; when leveraging existing OpenGL pipelines; when custom CUDA kernel development is not feasible. When Not to Use: When maximum performance is required and custom CUDA kernels can be optimized; when CUDA-GL interop is unsupported; when precise control over differentiable gradients is needed without approximation. This method is part of the "fast-gaussian-rasterization" project, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It was developed to provide an alternative to pure CUDA rasterization by utilizing OpenGL's point sprite capabilities, potentially simplifying the rendering pipeline for certain hardware configurations or software ecosystems. dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, https://github.com/dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: vtkPointGaussianMapper
head: PointGaussianMapper, vtkOpenGLPointGaussianMapper
body: vtkPointGaussianMapper renders point clouds as simple points or anisotropic 3D Gaussian splats without requiring verts cells, supporting per-point scale, rotation, opacity, and emissive properties. Unlike sibling methods that rely on GPU-parallel tile-based rasterization or transmittance culling, it operates in object-order using standard OpenGL blending and a vertex shader for EWA projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vtkPolyData object containing point positions. If verts cells are present, only points referenced by these cells are drawn; otherwise, all points are drawn. Output: A rendered image of points or Gaussian splats. Data Structures: Position Array: Float positions. If no shift/scale is applied to the VBO, these are uploaded directly. Color Array: RGBA byte colors. Per-Point Attributes: Arrays for scale, rotation, and opacity. These are shared between simple-point and splat modes. Buffers: Per-point buffers are uploaded only when their source data changes. Arrays that do not cover every drawn point are staged. Parameters: scaleFactor: Scalar multiplier for splat size. A value of 0 disables splatting and renders simple points. anisotropic: Boolean flag enabling anisotropic 3D Gaussian splats. rotationArray: Name of the array containing rotation data for anisotropic splats. lowpassMatrix: Matrix used for low-pass filtering in anisotropic splatting calculation. emissive: Boolean flag. When true, splats add their coverage to the alpha channel for correct compositing over transparent backgrounds. scaleArray, scaleArrayComponent, scaleFunction, scaleTableSize: Controls for scale mapping. opacityArray, opacityArrayComponent, scalarOpacityFunction, opacityTableSize: Controls for opacity mapping. splatShaderCode: Custom shader code for splat rendering. boundScale: Bound scale parameter. Steps: 1. Input Validation: Check if polyData contains verts cells. If yes, identify the subset of points referenced by these cells. If no, use all points. 2. Buffer Management: Identify compatible arrays: float positions without shift/scale, RGBA byte colors, and float scale/rotation/opacity arrays. Upload compatible arrays directly to GPU buffers without staging copies. For arrays that do not cover every drawn point or require staging, use staging buffers. Re-upload buffers only if their source data has changed. 3. Rendering Mode Selection: If scaleFactor is 0, render as simple points. If scaleFactor is non-zero, render as Gaussian splats. 4. Simple Point Rendering: Use gl.POINTS primitive type. Submit one vertex per point. 5. Gaussian Splat Rendering: Use a four-vertex triangle strip instance per point. The vertex shader projects each 3D Gaussian to a screen-space ellipse using EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) projection. The shader places the four corners of the triangle strip around the projected Gaussian center. Splat sizes do not apply VBO shift and scale, ensuring data far from the origin retains its splat size. Every splat maintains one consistent winding order to ensure face culling treats rotated splats consistently. 6. Blending: If emissive is true, add splat coverage to the alpha channel. If emissive is false and using default Gaussian falloff, render with translucent geometry so faded corners do not hide objects behind them. Apply opacity array regardless of scalar colors. If opacity is below 1, render translucent. 7. Selection: Hardware selection returns point IDs for simple points and verts cells for splats. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpointgaussianmapper(polydata, scaleFactor, anisotropic, rotationArray, lowpassMatrix, emissive): # 1. Determine points to render if polydata.hasvertscells(): pointstorender = [p for p in polydata.points if p in polydata.vertscells] else: pointstorender = polydata.points # 2. Buffer Management positionarray = polydata.getpositions() colorarray = polydata.getcolors() # RGBA bytes scalearray = polydata.getarray('scale') opacityarray = polydata.getarray('opacity') rotationarray = polydata.getarray(rotationArray) if anisotropic else None # Upload compatible arrays directly; others staged def uploadbuffer(arr, name): if arr is not None and iscompatiblearray(arr): gpubuffer = allocategpumemory(arr) else: stagingmemory = allocatecpumemory() copytostaging(stagingmemory, arr) gpubuffer = uploadstaged(stagingmemory) bindbuffer(name, gpubuffer) uploadbuffer(positionarray, 'position') uploadbuffer(colorarray, 'color') uploadbuffer(scalearray, 'scale') uploadbuffer(opacityarray, 'opacity') if rotationarray is not None: uploadbuffer(rotationarray, 'rotation') # 3. Render if scaleFactor == 0: # Simple Points drawarrays(primitivetype=POINTS, count=len(pointstorender)) else: # Gaussian Splats for point in pointstorender: scale = getscale(point, scalearray) opacity = getopacity(point, opacityarray) rotation = getrotation(point, rotationarray) if anisotropic else identitymatrix() # EWA Projection screencenter, screencovariance = ewaproject(point.position, rotation, scale, cameramatrix) # Generate 4 corners of triangle strip corners = generatesplatcorners(screencenter, screencovariance) # Set attributes and draw for corner in corners: setvertexposition(corner) setcolor(colorarray[point.index]) setopacity(opacity) setemissive(emissive) drawarrays(primitivetype=TRIANGLESTRIP, count=4) def iscompatiblearray(arr): # Compatible: float positions without shift/scale, RGBA byte colors, float scale/rotation/opacity if arr.dtype == 'float32' and arr.shape == (len(polydata.points), 3) and not hasvboshift: return True if arr.dtype == 'uint8' and arr.shape == (len(polydata.points), 4): return True if arr.dtype == 'float32' and arr.ndim == 1: return True return False def ewaproject(position, rotation, scale, cameramatrix): # Standard EWA projection for 3D Gaussian to screen-space ellipse # Returns screencenter (vec2) and screencovariance (2x2 matrix) pass def generatesplatcorners(center, covariance): # Compute bounding box of ellipse and return 4 corners for triangle strip pass def getscale(point, scalearray): return scalearray[point.index] def getopacity(point, opacityarray): return opacityarray[point.index] def getrotation(point, rotationarray): return rotationarray[point.index] def identitymatrix(): return [[1, 0], [0, 1]] def allocategpumemory(data): return creategpubuffer(data) def allocatecpumemory(): return createcpubuffer() def copytostaging(staging, data): staging.data = data.copy() def uploadstaged(staging): return creategpubufferfromstaging(staging) def bindbuffer(name, buffer): bindbuffertotarget(name, buffer) def drawarrays(primitivetype, count): renderprimitive(primitivetype, count) def setvertexposition(pos): vertexx, vertexy = pos def setcolor(rgb): colorr, colorg, colorb, colora = rgb def setopacity(val): opacityvalue = val def setemissive(val): emissiveflag = val Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Culling: Splats centered outside the view are drawn if their projection reaches into the view. The projection is linearized no further than 30% beyond the view bounds. Winding Order: Every splat maintains one winding order to ensure face culling treats rotated splats consistently. Splat Size Scaling: Splat sizes do not apply VBO shift and scale, ensuring data far from the origin retains its splat size. Opacity Application: The opacity array applies regardless of scalar colors. If opacity is below 1, the property is rendered translucent. Non-emissive Rendering: Non-emissive splats with default Gaussian falloff render with translucent geometry, allowing faded corners to not hide objects behind them. Scalar Colors: Scalar colors are always per-point and never switch to texture coloring, even if interpolateScalarsBeforeMapping is set. Cell Scalars: Cell scalars only color points that are drawn by verts cells. Composite Datasets: Composite datasets are not supported because vtk.js mappers require polydata input. A subclass of vtkPointGaussianMapper designed for dense point clouds, defaulting to opaque simple points. It adds controls for point size multiplier (e.g., for device pixel ratio), round points (which also select as discs), point sizes in model units that follow camera distance, and a draw limit for progressive loading (showing a prefix of points without uploading them again). The OpenGL mapper uses an extension point to determine the number of points each draw submission submits. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Renders point clouds without requiring verts cells; supports anisotropic 3D Gaussian splats; efficient buffer management by sharing buffers between simple-point and splat modes; correct compositing for emissive splats; consistent winding order for face culling. Limitations: Does not support composite datasets; scalar colors are always per-point; non-emissive splats with default Gaussian falloff render with translucent geometry (which may differ from VTK's opaque geometry behavior); splats centered outside the view but projecting into the view are drawn (linearized up to 30% beyond view bounds). When to Use: Use when rendering point clouds as simple points or Gaussian splats in vtk.js without needing complex cell structures, especially for dense point clouds where vtkPointSpriteMapper is preferred. When Not to Use: Do not use for composite datasets or when texture-based scalar coloring is required. vtkPointGaussianMapper was added to vtk.js by PaulHax in a pull request (PR #42) in September 2026, porting VTK's vtkPointGaussianMapper with its API and defaults. It addresses the lack of a counterpart in vtk.js for rendering point clouds as Gaussian splats or showing 3D Gaussian splatting data (scale and rotation per point) without requiring verts cells. vtkPointSpriteMapper was added in the same PR as a subclass for dense point clouds. feat(PointGaussianMapper): add vtkPointGaussianMapper, https://github.com/PaulHax/vtk-js/pull/42, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Feature 3DGS Rendering
head: Differentiable Volumetric Feature Rendering, Joint RGB and Feature Rasterization
body: Feature 3DGS is a method for rendering high-dimensional semantic feature maps alongside RGB images using 3D Gaussians, enabling the distillation of knowledge from 2D foundation models (such as SAM or LSeg) into an explicit 3D scene representation. It sets itself apart from NeRF-based feature field methods by using an explicit representation that avoids interference between the radiance and feature fields, allowing for equal-weighted joint optimization without the sensitivity to hyperparameters required by implicit neural networks. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with optimized parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity, SH coefficients, and feature vectors); camera parameters (view and projection matrices); image resolution H \times W. Outputs: A rendered RGB image \hat{I} and a rendered feature map Fs(\hat{I}) of resolution H \times W \times N (where N is the internal feature dimension, upsampled to M if necessary). Data Structures Each 3D Gaussian i stores the following fields: Center: x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation: Quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (representing rotation matrix R). Scaling: Factor s \in \mathbb{R}^3 (representing scaling matrix S). Opacity: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}. Appearance: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients up to 3rd order (4 bands). Semantic Feature: Vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^N. Algorithm Steps 1. Tiling and Culling: Divide the screen into 16 \times 16 tiles. For each tile, cull 3D Gaussians against the view frustum and the tile's axis-aligned bounding box. 2. Projection: For each remaining Gaussian, compute the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma' in camera coordinates to project the 3D Gaussian to 2D space: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^{T} J^{T} where W is the world-to-camera transformation matrix, J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projective transformation, and \Sigma is the 3D covariance matrix. Note: To ensure \Sigma remains positive semi-definite during optimization, it is decomposed into rotation R and scaling S such that \Sigma = R S S^{T} R^{T}. 3. Sorting: Sort the Gaussians overlapping each pixel by their depth (distance from camera). 4. Joint Rasterization: For each pixel, perform alpha blending over the sorted overlapping Gaussians i \in \mathcal{N} to compute both the color C and the feature Fs simultaneously: C = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai Ti F{s} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} fi \alphai Ti where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance, ci is the color derived from SH coefficients, and fi is the semantic feature vector. 5. Upsampling (Speed-up): If the target teacher feature dimension M (e.g., 512 for LSeg) is larger than the initialized Gaussian feature dimension N (N \ll M), apply a lightweight 1 \times 1 convolutional decoder to upsample Fs(\hat{I}) from H \times W \times N to H \times W \times M. 6. Interpolation: Apply bilinear interpolation to resize the rendered feature map Fs(\hat{I}) to match the exact resolution H \times W of the teacher feature map Ft(I). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderfeature3dgs(gaussians, camera, imageh, imagew, teacherencoder, decoder, N, M, epsilon=1e-4): # Initialize output buffers renderedrgb = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageh imagew)] renderedfeatureraw = [[0.0] N for in range(imageh imagew)] tilesize = 16 for ty in range(0, imageh, tilesize): for tx in range(0, imagew, tilesize): ymin, ymax = ty, min(ty + tilesize, imageh) xmin, xmax = tx, min(tx + tilesize, imagew) activegaussians = cullgaussians(gaussians, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, camera) for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): sortedgs = sortbydepth(activegaussians, camera) coloracc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] featureacc = [0.0] N transmittance = 1.0 for g in sortedgs: sigma2d = projectcovariance(g, camera) alphag = evaluategaussianalpha(g, x, y, sigma2d) if alphag < epsilon: continue ci = evaluatesh(g.shcoeffs, g.center, camera.viewdirection) weight = alphag transmittance for k in range(3): coloracc[k] += ci[k] weight for k in range(N): featureacc[k] += g.f[k] weight transmittance = (1.0 - alphag) if transmittance < epsilon: break idx = y imagew + x renderedrgb[idx] = coloracc renderedfeatureraw[idx] = featureacc # Reshape to H x W x C renderedrgb = [[renderedrgb[y imagew + x] for x in range(imagew)] for y in range(imageh)] renderedfeatureraw = [[[renderedfeatureraw[y imagew + x][k] for k in range(N)] for x in range(imagew)] for y in range(imageh)] # Upsampling renderedfeature = decoder(renderedfeatureraw) if N < M else renderedfeatureraw # Resize to match teacher resolution teacherres = teacherencoder.resolution renderedfeature = bilinearresize(renderedfeature, teacherres[0], teacherres[1]) return renderedrgb, renderedfeature def cullgaussians(gaussians, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, camera): return [g for g in gaussians if intersects(getscreenbbox(g, camera), xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) and isinfrustum(g, camera)] def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): x, y, z, w = q return [[1-2(yy+zz), 2(xy-zw), 2(xz+yw)], [2(xy+zw), 1-2(xx+zz), 2(yz-xw)], [2(xz-yw), 2(yz+xw), 1-2(xx+yy)]] def computejacobian(camera): return [[camera.fx, 0, camera.cx], [0, camera.fy, camera.cy]] def getscreenbbox(g, camera): return (g.center[0]-3.0, g.center[1]-3.0, g.center[0]+3.0, g.center[1]+3.0) def intersects(bbox, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax): return bbox[0] <= xmax and bbox[2] >= xmin and bbox[1] <= ymax and bbox[3] >= ymin def isinfrustum(g, camera): return g.center[2] > 0.0 def sortbydepth(gs, camera): return sorted(gs, key=lambda g: g.center[2]) def projectcovariance(gaussian, camera): W = camera.viewmatrix R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(gaussian.q) S = [[gaussian.s[0], 0, 0], [0, gaussian.s[1], 0], [0, 0, gaussian.s[2]]] Sigma3d = matmul(R, matmul(S, matmul(transpose(S), transpose(R)))) J = computejacobian(camera) return matmul(matmul(J, matmul(W, Sigma3d)), matmul(transpose(W), transpose(J))) def evaluategaussianalpha(g, x, y, sigma2d): dist = [x - g.center[0], y - g.center[1]] invsigma = inverse2x2(sigma2d) exponent = -0.5 (dist[0] (invsigma[0][0]dist[0] + invsigma[0][1]dist[1]) + dist[1] (invsigma[1][0]dist[0] + invsigma[1][1]dist[1])) return g.alpha math.exp(exponent) def evaluatesh(coeffs, center, viewdir): return [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] def bilinearresize(featuremap, targeth, targetw): return featuremap Parameters Tile Size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Feature Loss Weight (\gamma): 1.0. D-SSIM Weight (\lambda): 0.2. SH Optimization Schedule: Optimize zeroth-order SH (diffuse color) for the first 1000 iterations. Introduce 1 band every 1000 iterations until all 4 bands are represented. Edge Cases and Pitfalls High-Dimensional Rendering Cost: Rendering high-dimensional feature maps directly (e.g., M=512 for LSeg) is time-consuming. The solution is to initialize Gaussians with a lower-dimensional feature vector N \ll M and use a lightweight 1 \times 1 convolutional decoder to upsample the rendered features to dimension M. Positive Semi-Definite Covariance: The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma must remain positive semi-definite. This is enforced by parameterizing it via rotation R and scaling S rather than optimizing \Sigma directly. Resolution Mismatch: The rendered feature map Fs(\hat{I}) must be resized via bilinear interpolation to match the resolution H \times W of the teacher feature map Ft(I) before calculating the \mathcal{L}1 loss. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization step. The tile-based approach (16 \times 16) manages memory load and allows efficient culling. Rendering high-dimensional features (N or M) increases computational cost linearly with the feature dimension. The speed-up module (1x1 conv) mitigates this by allowing optimization in lower dimensions. Memory Complexity: Stores N-dimensional feature vectors per Gaussian. Using N \ll M reduces memory footprint during training compared to storing full M-dimensional features. Strengths: Explicit representation avoids the interference between radiance and feature fields common in NeRF-based methods, allowing equal-weighted joint optimization (\gamma=1.0) without adverse effects. It preserves per-pixel accuracy for features by using the same rasterization procedure as RGB. Limitations: Requires a teacher model (e.g., SAM, LSeg) for supervision. High-dimensional feature rendering can be slow without the upsampling decoder. When to use: When distilling semantic features from 2D foundation models into a 3D explicit representation for tasks like promptable segmentation or language-driven 3D understanding. Feature 3DGS was introduced to enable the distillation of 2D foundation models (such as Segment Anything [20] and LSeg [23]) into 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. Unlike NeRF-based approaches where feature and radiance fields share layers, leading to interference and sensitivity to the feature loss weight \gamma, Feature 3DGS uses an explicit representation that decouples these fields. This allows for robust joint optimization of RGB and semantic features, facilitating zero-shot and language-driven 3D computer vision tasks. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting (glTF KHR_gaussian_splatting)
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting in glTF, 3DGS, Ellipsoid Splatting, Gaussian Splatting Extension
body: This method defines the rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian splats stored in glTF assets via the KHRgaussiansplatting extension, treating splats as point primitives with specific geometric and color attributes. It differs from general rasterization implementations by enforcing a strict data layout and transformation constraints defined by the glTF standard, ensuring interoperability and fallback to sparse point cloud rendering if the extension is unsupported. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A glTF scene containing a mesh primitive with mode POINTS (0) and attributes defined by the extension. The scene includes a camera with perspective projection. Output: A 2D image where each pixel is the result of alpha-blending projected Gaussian splats. Data Structures and Layout: The splat data is stored as attributes on a glTF mesh primitive. The primitive mode MUST be POINTS. The glTF material referenced by the primitive MUST be ignored for rendering. 1. POSITION (VEC3): The mean vector \mu in local space. Effective global mean is derived from this attribute and the node's global transformation matrix. 2. ROTATION (VEC4): Unit quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw) in glTF order. Values are guaranteed to be normalized. Supported component types: float32, snorm8, snorm16. 3. SCALE (VEC3): Linear spread (sx, sy, sz) along local principal axes. Values MUST be non-negative. Supported component types: float32, uint8, unorm8, uint16, unorm16. 4. OPACITY (SCALAR): Linear value \alpha \in [0.0, 1.0]. Out-of-range values are invalid. Supported types: float32, unorm8, unorm16. 5. Spherical Harmonics (SH): SHDEGREE0COEF0 (VEC3): Required. Degree 0 coefficients. SHDEGREElCOEFn (VEC3): Required if degree l is used. Degree 1 has 3 coefficients, Degree 2 has 5, Degree 3 has 7. Degrees must be fully defined; partial definitions are invalid. Coefficients are packed from lowest order m to highest. Total 45 coefficients for all 3 degrees. Node Transformation Constraints: The global transformation matrix of the node containing the splat primitive MUST satisfy: Last row is (0, 0, 0, 1). Lengths of the first three columns are finite positive numbers. The determinant of the upper-left 3x3 matrix (formed by dividing each element by its column's length) is close to +1. Non-decomposable matrices or negative scales are undefined. Rendering Steps: 1. Splat Reconstruction (Covariance Construction): Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma in global space. Let \mathbf{M} be the upper-left 3x3 submatrix of the node's global transformation matrix. Construct matrix \mathbf{C} from scale sx, sy, sz and quaternion qx, qy, qz, qw: \mathbf{C} = \begin{pmatrix} sx (1 - 2(qy^2 + qz^2)) & sy (2(qx qy - qw qz)) & sz (2(qx qz + qw qy)) \\ sx (2(qx qy + qw qz)) & sy (1 - 2(qx^2 + qz^2)) & sz (2(qy qz - qw qx)) \\ sx (2(qx qz - qw qy)) & sy (2(qy qz + qw qx)) & sz (1 - 2(qx^2 + qy^2)) \end{pmatrix} Compute \Sigma: \Sigma = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{C}^T \mathbf{M}^T 2. Splat Projection: Mean Vector: Project the global mean vector \mu onto the 2D image plane using standard perspective projection. 2D Covariance: Transform \Sigma to 2D covariance \Sigma' using affine approximation: \Sigma' = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \Sigma \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T Where \mathbf{W} is the 3x3 view-dependent transformation matrix from global to camera space (typically the upper-left 3x3 of the camera view matrix). Where \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian of the perspective projection. 3. Color Computation: Evaluate the spherical harmonics at the viewing direction to determine the RGB color. The color space is specified by the colorSpace property (srgbrec709display or linrec709display). 4. Sorting: Sort splats by distance to the camera origin. The default method is cameraDistance (vector length from splat to camera). 5. Rasterization and Blending: Project each splat onto the 2D plane. Assume a 3\sigma cut-off (Mahalanobis distance of 3 units) for the kernel shape. Alpha-blend the splats in sorted order. Intermediate rendering steps (including alpha blending) MUST be performed before any color gamut or transfer function conversions. Parameters: kernel: String, required. Currently only "ellipse" is defined. colorSpace: String, required. "srgbrec709display" or "linrec709display". projection: String, optional, default "perspective". Specifies projection method. sortingMethod: String, optional, default "cameraDistance". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computecmatrix(scale: np.ndarray, rotation: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: sx, sy, sz = scale qx, qy, qz, qw = rotation return np.array([ [sx (1 - 2 (qy2 + qz2)), sy (2 (qx qy - qw qz)), sz (2 (qx qz + qw qy))], [sx (2 (qx qy + qw qz)), sy (1 - 2 (qx2 + qz2)), sz (2 (qy qz - qw qx))], [sx (2 (qx qz - qw qy)), sy (2 (qy qz + qw qx)), sz (1 - 2 (qx2 + qy2))] ]) def evaluatesphericalharmonics(coeffs: list, direction: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: # The sources do not provide the spherical harmonic basis functions or evaluation algorithm. # Standard implementation evaluates SH basis functions at the viewing direction and dot-products with coefficients. if len(coeffs) == 0: return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) return coeffs[0] def lineartosrgb(linear: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: # Standard sRGB transfer function. return np.where(linear <= 0.0031308, 12.92 linear, 1.055 np.power(linear, 1/2.4) - 0.055) def rendergaussiansplats(splats: list, cameraviewmatrix: np.ndarray, cameraprojmatrix: np.ndarray, cameraworldpos: np.ndarray, imagewidth: int, imageheight: int, colorspace: str) -> np.ndarray: image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 4), dtype=np.float32) # 1. Sort splats by camera distance (near to far for front-to-back blending) sortedsplats = [] for splat in splats: nodemat = splat['nodetransform'] poslocal = np.array(splat['position']) poshomogeneous = np.append(poslocal, 1.0) posglobal = (nodemat @ poshomogeneous)[:3] dist = np.linalg.norm(posglobal - cameraworldpos) sortedsplats.append((dist, splat, posglobal)) sortedsplats.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=False) # 2. Render for dist, splat, posglobal in sortedsplats: scale = np.array(splat['scale']) rotation = np.array(splat['rotation']) opacity = splat['opacity'] shcoeffs = splat['shcoeffs'] # Compute Covariance Sigma C = computecmatrix(scale, rotation) M = splat['nodetransform'][:3,:3] Sigma = M @ C @ C.T @ M.T # Project Mean poshomogeneousglobal = np.append(posglobal, 1.0) posview = (cameraviewmatrix @ poshomogeneousglobal)[:3] z = posview[2] if z <= 0: continue posviewhomogeneous = np.append(posview, 1.0) posclip = cameraprojmatrix @ posviewhomogeneous if posclip[3] == 0: continue posndc = posclip[:3] / posclip[3] screenx = (posndc[0] + 1) 0.5 imagewidth screeny = (1 - posndc[1]) 0.5 imageheight # Project Covariance to 2D W = cameraviewmatrix[:3,:3] Sigmaview = W @ Sigma @ W.T # Jacobian for perspective projection (x/z, y/z) x, y = posview[0], posview[1] J = np.array([ [1/z, 0, -x/(z2)], [0, 1/z, -y/(z2)] ]) Sigma2d = J @ Sigmaview @ J.T # Scale to pixel coordinates scalex, scaley = imagewidth / 2, imageheight / 2 Sigma2dpixels = np.array([ [Sigma2d[0,0] scalex2, Sigma2d[0,1] scalex scaley], [Sigma2d[1,0] scalex scaley, Sigma2d[1,1] scaley2] ]) eigenvaluespx, = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2dpixels) sigmaxpx = math.sqrt(eigenvaluespx[0]) sigmaypx = math.sqrt(eigenvaluespx[1]) minx = max(0, int(math.floor(screenx - 3 sigmaxpx))) maxx = min(imagewidth, int(math.ceil(screenx + 3 sigmaxpx))) miny = max(0, int(math.floor(screeny - 3 sigmaypx))) maxy = min(imageheight, int(math.ceil(screeny + 3 sigmaypx))) # Color Computation camtosplat = posglobal - cameraworldpos camtosplat = camtosplat / np.linalg.norm(camtosplat) color = evaluatesphericalharmonics(shcoeffs, camtosplat) # Alpha Blending (front-to-back) invsigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2dpixels) for py in range(miny, maxy): for px in range(minx, maxx): dx = px - screenx dy = py - screeny posvec = np.array([dx, dy]) exponent = -0.5 posvec @ invsigma @ posvec weight = math.exp(max(exponent, -10)) alphasplat = opacity weight if alphasplat > 1e-6: currentalpha = image[py, px, 3] currentcolor = image[py, px,:3] newalpha = alphasplat + currentalpha (1 - alphasplat) if newalpha > 0: newcolor = (color alphasplat + currentcolor currentalpha (1 - alphasplat)) / newalpha else: newcolor = currentcolor image[py, px,:3] = newcolor image[py, px, 3] = newalpha if colorspace == "srgbrec709display": image = lineartosrgb(image) return image Renders 4D Gaussians (3D spatial + 1D temporal) into a 2D image for a specific viewpoint and timestamp. It extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting by handling time-dependent opacity, position offsets, and spherical harmonics evaluation in 4D. Unlike static splatting, it accounts for the motion and appearance of primitives over time, enabling the reconstruction of dynamic scenes. Choose this method when rendering time-varying scenes; otherwise, use the static 3D Gaussian Splatting method. Not given in the sources. The KHRgaussiansplatting extension was developed by Khronos Group to standardize the storage of 3D Gaussian splats in glTF assets. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering paper. The extension aims to establish a solid foundation for integrating 3D Gaussian splatting into glTF assets, enabling future enhancements. https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHRgaussiansplatting/README.md, https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHRgaussiansplatting/README.md, fetched 2026-10-30 KHRgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHRgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-30

name: 4D Gaussian Rasterization
head: 3D Gaussian Rasterization, 4D Gaussian Splatting Forward Pass, 4DGS Render, Gaussian Rasterization Rendering, Q1 Render
body: 4D Gaussian Rasterization renders a scene represented by 4D Gaussians (3D spatial + 1D temporal) into a 2D image for a specific viewpoint and timestamp. It extends the static 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline by handling time-dependent opacity, position offsets, and spherical harmonics evaluation in 4D. It differs from its parent method by supporting dynamic scenes through temporal attributes and 4D covariance transformations, while maintaining the differentiable rasterization core of 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced). Inputs: viewpointcamera: Object containing FoVx, FoVy, imageheight, imagewidth, worldviewtransform (4x4), fullprojtransform (4x4), cameracenter (3,), timestamp (float), timeduration (float). pc: GaussianModel object containing attributes: getxyz (N,3), getopacity (N,), getscaling (N,3 or N,1), getrotation (N,4), getfeatures (N, K), activeshdegree (int), activeshdegreet (int), rot4d (bool), gaussiandim (int, 3 or 4), forcesh3d (bool), timeduration (tuple/list), prefiltervar (float, optional). pipe: Configuration object containing computecov3Dpython (bool), convertSHspython (bool), envmapres (int, optional). bgcolor: torch.Tensor (3,), background color on GPU. scalingmodifier: float, default 1.0. Outputs: Dictionary with keys: render (C, H, W), viewspacepoints (N,2), visibilityfilter (N, bool), radii (N,), depth (H, W), alpha (H, W), flow (H, W, 2, optional), covscom (optional). Data Structures: GaussianRasterizationSettings: Struct holding image dimensions, FOV tangents, background, scale modifier, view/projection matrices, SH degrees, camera position, timestamp, time duration, 4D rotation flag, Gaussian dimension, and debug flags. GaussianRasterizer: CUDA kernel wrapper initialized with settings. screenspacepoints: Zero tensor on CUDA with requiresgrad=True, shape (N, 2), storing gradients of 2D screen-space means. Steps: 1. Initialization: If pc.getxyz.shape[0] == 0, return None. Initialize screenspacepoints as a zero tensor on CUDA with requiresgrad=True. 2. Camera Parameters: Compute tangent FOV values: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx} \times 0.5) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy} \times 0.5). 3. Rasterization Settings: Construct GaussianRasterizationSettings with: imageheight, imagewidth from viewpointcamera. tanfovx, tanfovy. bg: bgcolor if pipe.envmapres is not set, else torch.zeros(3, device="cuda"). scalemodifier: scalingmodifier. viewmatrix: viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform. projmatrix: viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform. shdegree: pc.activeshdegree. shdegreet: pc.activeshdegreet. campos: viewpointcamera.cameracenter. timestamp: viewpointcamera.timestamp. timeduration: pc.timeduration[1] - pc.timeduration[0]. rot4d: pc.rot4d. gaussiandim: pc.gaussiandim. forcesh3d: pc.forcesh3d. prefiltered: Boolean indicating if prefiltering is applied.. 4. Rasterizer Initialization: Initialize GaussianRasterizer with the configured settings. 5. Attribute Retrieval & Preprocessing: Retrieve means3D = pc.getxyz, opacity = pc.getopacity. If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true: Compute cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier). If pc.gaussiandim == 4, apply mean offset to means3D if pc.rot4d is true. If pc.gaussiandim == 4, multiply opacity by marginal time probability marginalt. Else (pipe.computecov3Dpython is false): Set cov3Dprecomp = None. Retrieve raw scales, rotations, and if pc.gaussiandim == 4, retrieve scalest, ts, and rotationsr if pc.rot4d is true. Retrieve prefiltervar if pc.prefiltervar > 0. If pc.getscaling.shape[-1] == 1, scales = pc.getscaling.repeat(1, 3), else scales = pc.getscaling. rotations = pc.getrotation. 6. Prefiltering (Optional): If pipe.computecov3Dpython and pc.gaussiandim == 4: Create boolean mask where marginalt[:, 0] > 0.05. Filter all relevant tensors (means2D, means3D, ts, shs, colorsprecomp, opacity, scales, scalest, rotations, rotationsr, cov3Dprecomp, flow2d) using this mask. 7. Color Computation: If pipe.convertSHspython is true: Extract SH features: shsview = pc.getfeatures.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 3, (pc.maxshdegree + 1)^2). Compute direction vectors dirpp = pc.getxyz - viewpointcamera.cameracenter.repeat(N, 1). Normalize: dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True). If pc.gaussiandim == 3 or forcesh3d: sh2rgb = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized). If pc.gaussiandim == 4: Compute temporal direction dirt. sh2rgb = evalshfs4d(spatialdir=dirppnormalized, temporaldir=dirt, sh=shsview, degree=pc.activeshdegree, degreet=pc.activeshdegreet, timestamp=viewpointcamera.timestamp, timeduration=timeduration). colorsprecomp = clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0). Else: shs = pc.getfeatures. colorsprecomp = None. 8. Rasterization Call: Call rasterizer with inputs: means3D, means2D (screenspacepoints), shs (if colorsprecomp is None), colorsprecomp (if shs is None), flows (if available), opacity, ts, scales, scalest, rotations, rotationsr, scalemodifier, cov3Dprecomp, prefiltervar, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, imageheight, imagewidth, sh (if colorsprecomp is None), degree, degreet, campos, timestamp, timeduration, rot4d, gaussiandim, forcesh3d, prefiltered, debug. Returns renderedimage, radii, depth, alpha, flow, covscom. 9. Post-Processing: If pipe.envmapres is set: Compute environment map background. Calculate ray intersection with sphere radius R=60 using rayso and raysd. Compute intersection parameter tinter and point xyzinter. Convert to spherical coordinates tu (theta) and tv (phi) normalized to [-1, 1]. Sample pc.envmap using F.gridsample. Add to renderedimage weighted by (1 - alpha). Construct radiiall: Zero-initialize tensor of size mask.shape (if prefiltered) or use original radii. If prefiltered, assign original radii to positions indicated by mask. Return dictionary: renderedimage, viewspacepoints (screenspacepoints), visibilityfilter (radiiall > 0), radiiall, depth, alpha, flow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math from torch.nn import functional as F def render4dgaussian(viewpointcamera, pc, pipe, bgcolor, scalingmodifier=1.0): # 1. Initialization if pc.getxyz.shape[0] == 0: return None screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz, dtype=pc.getxyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") + 0 try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except: pass # 2. Camera Parameters tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # 3. Rasterization Settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imageheight=int(viewpointcamera.imageheight), imagewidth=int(viewpointcamera.imagewidth), tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bg=bgcolor if not pipe.envmapres else torch.zeros(3, device="cuda"), scalemodifier=scalingmodifier, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, shdegreet=pc.activeshdegreet, campos=viewpointcamera.cameracenter, timestamp=viewpointcamera.timestamp, timeduration=pc.timeduration[1] - pc.timeduration[0], rot4d=pc.rot4d, gaussiandim=pc.gaussiandim, forcesh3d=pc.forcesh3d, prefiltered=False # Placeholder, determined in step 6) # 4. Rasterizer Initialization rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings=rastersettings) # 5. Attribute Retrieval & Preprocessing means3D = pc.getxyz opacity = pc.getopacity if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier) if pc.gaussiandim == 4 and pc.rot4d: # Apply mean offset to means3D # Note: Exact offset logic depends on pc implementation, assumed available means3D = means3D + pc.getmeanoffset() if pc.gaussiandim == 4: marginalt = computemarginaltimeprobability(pc, viewpointcamera.timestamp) opacity = opacity marginalt[:, 0] else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.getscaling if scales.shape[-1] == 1: scales = scales.repeat(1, 3) rotations = pc.getrotation if pc.gaussiandim == 4: scalest = pc.getscalest() ts = pc.getts() rotationsr = pc.getrotationsr() if pc.rot4d else None prefiltervar = pc.prefiltervar if hasattr(pc, 'prefiltervar') else 0.0 # 6. Prefiltering (Optional) mask = None if pipe.computecov3Dpython and pc.gaussiandim == 4: marginalt = computemarginaltimeprobability(pc, viewpointcamera.timestamp) mask = marginalt[:, 0] > 0.05 if mask is not None: means3D = means3D[mask] opacity = opacity[mask] cov3Dprecomp = cov3Dprecomp[mask] if cov3Dprecomp is not None else None # Filter other attributes if not precomputed if not pipe.computecov3Dpython: scales = scales[mask] rotations = rotations[mask] if pc.gaussiandim == 4: scalest = scalest[mask] ts = ts[mask] if pc.rot4d: rotationsr = rotationsr[mask] # 7. Color Computation if pipe.convertSHspython: shsview = pc.getfeatures.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 3, (pc.maxshdegree + 1)2) dirpp = pc.getxyz - viewpointcamera.cameracenter.repeat(pc.getxyz.shape[0], 1) dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) if pc.gaussiandim == 3 or pc.forcesh3d: sh2rgb = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized) elif pc.gaussiandim == 4: dirt = computetemporaldirection(pc, viewpointcamera.timestamp, rastersettings.timeduration) sh2rgb = evalshfs4d(dirppnormalized, dirt, shsview, pc.activeshdegree, pc.activeshdegreet, viewpointcamera.timestamp, rastersettings.timeduration) colorsprecomp = torch.clamp(sh2rgb + 0.5, min=0.0) shs = None else: shs = pc.getfeatures colorsprecomp = None # 8. Rasterization Call # Note: In 4DGS, the rasterizer kernel handles 4D covariance and SH evaluation internally if configured # The following arguments map to the CUDA kernel signature in renderedimage, radii, depth, alpha, flow, covscom = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=screenspacepoints, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, flows=None, # Placeholder if flow is not used opacity=opacity, ts=ts if pc.gaussiandim == 4 else None, scales=scales if not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, scalest=scalest if pc.gaussiandim == 4 and not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, rotations=rotations if not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, rotationsr=rotationsr if pc.gaussiandim == 4 and pc.rot4d and not pipe.computecov3Dpython else None, scalemodifier=scalingmodifier, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp, prefiltervar=prefiltervar if not pipe.computecov3Dpython else 0.0, viewmatrix=rastersettings.viewmatrix, projmatrix=rastersettings.projmatrix, tanfovx=rastersettings.tanfovx, tanfovy=rastersettings.tanfovy, imageheight=rastersettings.imageheight, imagewidth=rastersettings.imagewidth, degree=rastersettings.shdegree, degreet=rastersettings.shdegreet, campos=rastersettings.campos, timestamp=rastersettings.timestamp, timeduration=rastersettings.timeduration, rot4d=rastersettings.rot4d, gaussiandim=rastersettings.gaussiandim, forcesh3d=rastersettings.forcesh3d, prefiltered=mask is not None, debug=False) # 9. Post-Processing if pipe.envmapres: # Compute env map background # rayso, raysd derived from camera and pixel coordinates # tinter, xyzinter computed # tu, tv normalized # envbg = F.gridsample(pc.envmap,...) # renderedimage = renderedimage + envbg (1 - alpha) pass radiiall = radii.clone() if mask is not None: radiiallfull = torch.zeros(pc.getxyz.shape[0], device="cuda") radiiallfull[mask] = radii radiiall = radiiallfull visibilityfilter = radiiall > 0 return { 'render': renderedimage, 'viewspacepoints': screenspacepoints, 'visibilityfilter': visibilityfilter, 'radii': radiiall, 'depth': depth, 'alpha': alpha, 'flow': flow } def computemarginaltimeprobability(pc, timestamp): # Placeholder for marginal time probability calculation # Typically involves Gaussian PDF over time dimension return torch.oneslike(pc.getopacity) def computetemporaldirection(pc, timestamp, timeduration): # Placeholder for temporal direction vector return torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: 4D covariance computation can suffer from numerical instability if not handled via block matrix inversion. Boundaries: Timestamps outside timeduration range may require clamping or extrapolation. Degenerate Input: Zero Gaussians return None. 4D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the DreamGaussian4D method, generates dynamic 4D scenes from a single reference image or video. It differs from sibling methods like AYG by learning motion from a driving video generated by an image-to-video model rather than using a video diffusion prior directly on the scene. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) by extending the static representation to 4D using HexPlane deformations. The DOF Gaussian Rendering Interface is the entry point for rendering a scene with Depth-of-Field Gaussian Splatting, accepting camera, model, pipeline, and optical parameters. It extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by allowing the focal distance to be varied post-training, decoupling the rendered focus plane from the camera's optical center. It enables refocusing, defocus rendering, and blur removal by incorporating circle-of-confusion (CoC) alpha and depth-dependent scaling. 4D Gaussian Slicing is a method to calculate the 3D center position and 3D covariance of a 4D Gaussian at a specific time t by intercepting the 4D Gaussian with the t-plane. It enables the rendering of dynamic scenes represented by 4D Gaussians (3D spatial + 1D temporal) into a 2D image for a specific viewpoint and timestamp. It sets itself apart from static 3D Gaussian Splatting by handling time-dependent opacity, position offsets, and spherical harmonics evaluation in 4D, and from other 4D methods like 4D Gaussian Splatting (DreamGaussian4D) by explicitly deriving the 3D Gaussian parameters via block matrix inversion to avoid numerical instability. An extension to dynamic MRI data modeling temporal variations of anatomical structures from time-resolved MRI sequences using a static set of 3D Gaussians and a learned deformation field network. It initializes a static set of 3D Gaussians representing canonical anatomy, pretrained on slices from the first frame to provide a stable anatomical prior. A learned deformation field network (spatiotemporal encoder + lightweight MLP) predicts per-frame changes in position, covariance, color, and opacity. Baseline: Ground-truth image from the preceding timestamp (t-1) used as prediction for current test frame t. Simulates an oracle model memorizing prior structure. Wrist Motion MRI: 38 temporal frames, 12 wrist slice views per frame, resolution 64x64. 33 frames for training, every 8th frame held out for testing. 35^3 3D Gaussians initialized. Training time ~45 minutes. Wrist Motion MRI Performance: At Time=32, Ours SSIM=0.9224 vs Baseline 0.8909; PSNR=26.9297 vs Baseline 24.5761. At Time=16, Ours SSIM=0.9864 vs Baseline 0.9706; PSNR=39.0909 vs Baseline 34.4965. Retrieves the rendering pipeline and rasterizer settings via getrenderpip(option). Options include 'testoursfull' (using diffgaussianrasterizationch9), 'testourslite' (using forwardlite), 'testoursfullfused' (using forwardfull), 'testoursfullss' (using diffgaussianrasterizationch9), 'testoursfullssfused' (using forwardfull), and 'testourslitess' (using forwardlite). The output is a dictionary containing the rendered image at key 'render' with shape (C, H, W). Saves the rendered image as a PNG file with a zero-padded 5-digit index in the render path. rgbfunction: String specifying the RGB function. Default value is 'rgbv1'. loader: String specifying the data loader. Default value is 'colmap'. Directly converts 3D Gaussian into 4D Gaussian. Enhances the temporal continuity of SyncDreamer by fusing spatial volumes of adjacent timestamps. Achieves synchronization to generate better cross-time multi-view images for supervision. Limitations: Numerical instability in 4D covariance without proper handling. When to use: Dynamic view synthesis, 4D scene reconstruction. When not to use: Static scenes where 3DGS is sufficient. name: 4D Gaussian Splatting (DreamGaussian4D)
head: DreamGaussianHD
body: 4D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the DreamGaussian4D method, generates dynamic 4D scenes from a single reference image or video. It differs from sibling methods like AYG by learning motion from a driving video generated by an image-to-video model rather than using a video diffusion prior directly on the scene. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) by extending the static representation to 4D using HexPlane deformations. The method consists of three main phases: static initialization, dynamic generation, and optional refinement/export. Input: A single reference image or video. Output: A dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting representation, optionally exported as an animated mesh. 1. Static 3DGS: Generated via an improved version of DreamGaussian. Contains standard 3D Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). 2. Deformation Field Network: A network added to the static 3DGS to model temporal deformations. 3. HexPlane: Used to model Gaussian deformations for realistic motion. (Note: cites HexPlane [70] as the dynamic representation, while describes a "deformation network" optimized during dynamic generation. The exact internal structure of the HexPlane tensor is not detailed in the provided sources.) 1. Static Initialization: Generate a static 3DGS from the reference image using an improved DreamGaussian pipeline. 2. Driving Video Generation: Use an off-the-shelf Stable Diffusion Video model to generate a driving video from the reference image. 3. Dynamic Generation: Optimize the deformation field network added to the static 3DGS. Use the generated driving video as supervision. Apply a 3D SDS loss based on Zero-1-to-3 XL from sampled views to ensure cross-view consistency. Randomly select some frames to add image-based SDS to ensure generation quality. (Note: states motion is learned from the driving video generated by the image-to-video model, contrasting with AYG.) 4. Refinement (Optional): Perform video-to-video optimization pipeline to improve temporal coherence. 5. Export: Extract a mesh sequence and optimize its texture using an image-to-video diffusion model. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dreamgaussian4d(referenceimage): # Step 1: Static Initialization # Uses improved DreamGaussian static3dgs = dreamgaussianinit(referenceimage) # Step 2: Driving Video Generation # Uses off-the-shelf Stable Diffusion Video drivingvideo = stablediffusionvideogenerate(referenceimage) # Step 3: Dynamic Generation # Initialize deformation field network deformationnet = initializedeformationnetwork() # Optimization loop for epoch in range(numepochs): # Sample frames from driving video videoframes = sampleframes(drivingvideo) # Render dynamic 3DGS using deformation net # Note: Exact 4D rasterization details are in parent [13946-4d-gaussian-rasterization.md] renderedframes = render4dgaussians(static3dgs, deformationnet, videoframes) # Compute 3D SDS loss using Zero-1-to-3 XL # Sampled views are used for this loss views = sampleviews() sdsloss3d = compute3dsdsloss(renderedframes, views, zero1to3xl) # Compute image-based SDS loss for randomly selected frames selectedframes = randomsample(videoframes) sdslossimg = computeimagesdsloss(selectedframes) # Combine losses totalloss = sdsloss3d + sdslossimg # Update deformation network optimize(deformationnet, totalloss) # Step 4: Optional Refinement # Video-to-video optimization for temporal coherence refined3dgs = videotovideorefine(static3dgs, deformationnet) # Step 5: Export # Extract mesh sequence and optimize texture meshsequence = extractmeshsequence(refined3dgs) optimizedmesh = optimizemeshtexture(meshsequence, imagetovideodiffusion) return optimizedmesh Stable Diffusion Video: Off-the-shelf model used for driving video generation. Zero-1-to-3 XL: Used for 3D SDS loss. Temporal Coherence: Addressed via optional video-to-video refinement. Degenerate Input: Not specified in sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Generates dynamic 4D scenes from single image/video. Uses HexPlane for realistic motion. Can export as animated mesh. Limitations: Relies on off-the-shelf diffusion models (Stable Diffusion Video, Zero-1-to-3 XL) which may introduce artifacts. Temporal coherence may require additional refinement. When to use: When 4D generation from a single image is required. When not to use: When video diffusion prior is preferred over driving video. Origin: DreamGaussian4D [15] achieves 4D generation given a reference image. It is based on DreamGaussian [8, 128] for image-to-3D initialization. Development: It utilizes HexPlane [70] to model Gaussian deformations. It contrasts with AYG [48] by learning motion from a driving video generated by an image-to-video model. Usage: Used for dynamic 4D scene generation from single images or videos.
