name: DOF Gaussian Rendering Interface
body: The method serves as the entry point for rendering a scene with Depth-of-Field Gaussian Splatting, accepting camera, model, pipeline, and optical parameters. It extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by allowing the focal distance to be varied post-training, decoupling the rendered focus plane from the camera's optical center. It enables refocusing, defocus rendering, and blur removal by incorporating circle-of-confusion (CoC) alpha and depth-dependent scaling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A list of cameras (containing rotation R, translation T, and focal length), a Gaussian model object (with getxyz, getscaling, opacity, covarianceactivation), and a pipeline configuration. Parameters: focaldistance: Distance for depth-of-field focus (default None). Kapert: Aperture parameter (default None). kernelsize: Kernel size for blurring (default 0.1). bandlimit: Enable band limiting (default False). subpixeloffset: Subpixel shift (default None). scalingmodifier: Scale factor for Gaussians (default 1.0). Outputs: A rendered 2D image and associated depth/alpha buffers. Data Structures: cameras: List of objects. Each has R (3x3 rotation matrix, stored transposed due to 'glm' in CUDA code) and T (3x1 translation vector). model: Object containing getxyz, getscaling, opacity, covarianceactivation, and internal rotation/scale tensors. Steps: 1. Initialize Filter: Call compute3Dfilter(cameras) to determine valid points and distances. Initialize distance tensor of shape (N) with value 100000.0. Initialize validpoints boolean tensor of shape (N) to False. Iterate through each camera in cameras: Extract R and T from camera. Transform points to camera space (implementation detail: R is stored transposed). Calculate distance from camera center to each Gaussian center. Update distance and validpoints based on visibility and depth. 2. Compute Covariance: Call getcovariance(scalingmodifier). This calls model.covarianceactivation(model.getscaling, scalingmodifier, model.rotation). 3. Apply DOF Modifications: Use focaldistance and Kapert to compute Circle of Confusion (CoC) radii for each Gaussian based on its depth. Adjust Gaussian scales and opacities using the CoC values to simulate defocus blur. The opacity scaling factor is computed as \text{coef} = \sqrt{\det1 / \det2}, applied via \text{opacity} \leftarrow \text{opacity} \times \text{coef}[\dots, \text{None}]. If bandlimit is enabled, apply a band-limiting filter. If subpixeloffset is provided, shift Gaussian centers by the subpixel amount. 4. Rasterize: Pass the modified Gaussians to the underlying rasterizer to generate the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdof(cameras, model, pipeline, focaldistance=None, Kapert=None, kernelsize=0.1, bandlimit=False, subpixeloffset=None, scalingmodifier=1.0): xyz = model.getxyz # 1. Compute 3D filter and valid points distance = torch.ones((xyz.shape[0]), device=xyz.device) 100000.0 validpoints = torch.zeros((xyz.shape[0]), device=xyz.device, dtype=torch.bool) focallength = 0.0 for camera in cameras: R = torch.tensor(camera.R, device=xyz.device, dtype=torch.float32) T = torch.tensor(camera.T, device=xyz.device, dtype=torch.float32) # Transform xyz to camera space: xyzcam = (xyz - T) @ R # Update distance and validpoints based on depth pass # 2. Compute covariance covariances = model.covarianceactivation(model.getscaling, scalingmodifier, model.rotation) # 3. Apply DOF modifications opacity = model.opacity if focaldistance is not None and Kapert is not None: det1 = 1.0 # Source determinant det2 = 1.0 # Target determinant coef = torch.sqrt(det1 / det2) opacity = opacity coef[..., None] if bandlimit: # Apply frequency-domain low-pass filter to prevent aliasing pass if subpixeloffset is not None: xyz = xyz + subpixeloffset # 4. Rasterize to image using underlying tiled 2D splatting # Project covariances, compute 2D alpha, accumulate color/depth to image buffer return torch.zeros((pipeline.imageheight, pipeline.imagewidth, 3), device=xyz.device) DOF Gaussian Rasterization is a differentiable rendering method for 3D Gaussians that supports adjustable depth-of-field (DoF), enabling refocusing, defocus rendering, and blur removal by incorporating circle-of-confusion (CoC) alpha and depth-dependent scaling. It extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by allowing the focal distance to be varied post-training, decoupling the rendered focus plane from the camera's optical center. Not given in the sources. The method originates from an unofficial implementation of Depth-of-Field Gaussian Splatting. rongduo/DOFGSimplementation, https://github.com/rongduo/DOFGSimplementation, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DOF Gaussian Rasterization
head: Adjustable Depth-of-Field 3D Gaussian Splatting
body:
DOF Gaussian Rasterization is a differentiable CUDA-accelerated rasterization method for 3D Gaussians that supports adjustable depth-of-field, enabling refocusing, defocus rendering, and blur removal by incorporating circle-of-confusion (CoC) alpha and depth-dependent scaling. It builds on DOF Gaussian Rendering Interface and extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the rendered focus plane from the camera's optical center, allowing focal distance to be varied post-training. The method operates as a CUDA-accelerated rasterizer that processes a set of 3D Gaussians into a 2D image. It differs from standard splatting by computing a depth-dependent alpha mask (CoC alpha) that modulates the contribution of each Gaussian based on its distance from the specified focal plane. Inputs: Scene data: 3D means (\mu), precomputed colors (C), opacities (\alpha), scales (s), rotations (q), and spherical harmonics coefficients (SH) or precomputed colors. Camera parameters: View matrix (V), projection matrix (P), intrinsic matrix (K), focal length (F), camera position (c), image dimensions (H, W), and field of view tangents (	an 	hetax, 	an 	hetay). DoF parameters: Focal distance (df), circle-of-confusion coefficient (k{coc}), kernel size, and subpixel offset. Outputs: Forward pass: Rendered color image (I), depth map (D), 2D coordinates (xy), radii (r), radii derivatives (r{diff}), CoC alpha mask (\alpha{coc}), and buffers for backward pass (geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer). Backward pass: Gradients for means (

abla SH), and camera intrinsics (

Input Validation: Ensure exactly one of either SH coefficients or precomputed colors is provided. Ensure exactly one of either scale/rotation pairs or precomputed 3D covariances is provided. 2. Argument Restructuring (Forward): Pack the following arguments into a tuple for the C++/CUDA kernel: rastersettings.bg means3D colorsprecomp opacities scales rotations rastersettings.scalemodifier cov3Dsprecomp rastersettings.viewmatrix rastersettings.projmatrix F (Focal length) K (Intrinsics) rastersettings.vIdx rastersettings.tanfovx rastersettings.tanfovy rastersettings.kernelsize rastersettings.subpixeloffset rastersettings.imageheight rastersettings.imagewidth sh (Spherical Harmonics coefficients) rastersettings.shdegree rastersettings.campos rastersettings.prefiltered rastersettings.debug 3. Forward Rasterization: Invoke the C++/CUDA forward rasterization kernel C.rasterizegaussians(args). This computes the projected 2D Gaussians, sorts them by depth, and renders the image. It returns numrendered, color, depth, xy, radii, radiidiff, cocalpha, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, and imgBuffer. 4. Save Tensors: Store colorsprecomp, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, sh, F, K, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, and numrendered for use in the backward pass. 5. Argument Restructuring (Backward): Pack the following arguments for the backward kernel: rastersettings.bg means3D radii colorsprecomp scales rotations rastersettings.scalemodifier cov3Dsprecomp rastersettings.viewmatrix rastersettings.projmatrix F K rastersettings.coc2zcoeff rastersettings.vIdx rastersettings.tanfovx rastersettings.tanfovy rastersettings.kernelsize rastersettings.subpixeloffset gradoutcolor (Gradient from loss w.r.t. color) graddepth (Gradient from loss w.r.t. depth) gradxy (Gradient from loss w.r.t. 2D coordinates) sh rastersettings.shdegree rastersettings.campos geomBuffer numrendered binningBuffer imgBuffer rastersettings.debug 6. Backward Rasterization: Invoke the C++/CUDA backward rasterization kernel C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(args). This computes gradients for all input parameters, including specific gradients for camera intrinsics (K, F) enabled by the differentiable DoF formulation. The core innovation is the Circle-of-Confusion Alpha (\alpha{coc}). The forward pass computes a depth-dependent scaling factor that modulates the alpha contribution of each Gaussian based on its depth z relative to the focal depth zf. The exact forward formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided text, but it functions as a depth-dependent alpha mask. The parameter coc2zcoeff is used in the backward pass to convert \alpha{coc} gradients into depth gradients (
abla z). coc2zcoeff: A float parameter in rastersettings used in the backward pass to convert circle-of-confusion alpha to depth gradients. subpixeloffset: A torch.Tensor parameter in rastersettings, used for sub-pixel sampling or jittering during rasterization. kernelsize: Kernel size used additionally within the gaussian rasterizer. Input Validation: The method requires exactly one of either SHs or precomputed colors, and exactly one of either scale/rotation or precomputed 3D covariance. Debug Mode: If rastersettings.debug is true, tensors are copied to CPU before C++ invocation to allow saving a snapshot on exception. This significantly impacts performance and should be disabled in production. Unverified code. Save tensors for backward pass self.savedtensors = ( colorsprecomp, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, sh, F, K, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, numrendered) self.savedattrs = { 'bg': self.rastersettings.bg, 'scalemodifier': self.rastersettings.scalemodifier, 'viewmatrix': self.rastersettings.viewmatrix, 'projmatrix': self.rastersettings.projmatrix, 'vIdx': self.rastersettings.vIdx, 'tanfovx': self.rastersettings.tanfovx, 'tanfovy': self.rastersettings.tanfovy, 'kernelsize': self.rastersettings.kernelsize, 'subpixeloffset': self.rastersettings.subpixeloffset, 'imageheight': self.rastersettings.imageheight, 'imagewidth': self.rastersettings.imagewidth, 'shdegree': self.rastersettings.shdegree, 'campos': self.rastersettings.campos, 'prefiltered': self.rastersettings.prefiltered, 'debug': self.rastersettings.debug, 'coc2zcoeff': self.rastersettings.coc2zcoeff } return color, depth, xy, radii, radiidiff, cocalpha def backward(self, gradoutcolor, graddepth, gradxy): # Retrieve saved tensors (colorsprecomp, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, sh, F, K, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, numrendered) = self.savedtensors attrs = self.savedattrs # 5. Restructure args for backward C++ call args = ( attrs['bg'], means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, scales, rotations, attrs['scalemodifier'], cov3Dsprecomp, attrs['viewmatrix'], attrs['projmatrix'], F, K, attrs['coc2zcoeff'], attrs['vIdx'], attrs['tanfovx'], attrs['tanfovy'], attrs['kernelsize'], attrs['subpixeloffset'], gradoutcolor, graddepth, gradxy, sh, attrs['shdegree'], attrs['campos'], geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, attrs['debug']) # 6. Invoke C++/CUDA backward rasterization # Returns: gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, # gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations, # gradK, gradF gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, \ gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations, \ gradK, gradF = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(args) return gradmeans3D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradscales, \ gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradK, gradF Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables post-training refocusing and defocus effects without retraining. Differentiable with respect to camera intrinsics (K, F), allowing for joint optimization of scene and camera parameters. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of coc2zcoeff and kernelsize. Debug mode significantly slows down execution. The method relies on a C++/CUDA extension, which may have portability issues. DOF Gaussian Splatting (DOF-GS) was introduced by Yujie Wang, Praneeth Chakravarthula, and Baoquan Chen in a paper titled "DOF-GS: Adjustable Depth-of-Field 3D Gaussian Splatting for Refocusing, Defocus Rendering and Blur Removal" presented at CVPR 2025. The implementation is primarily based on the official codebase for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and draws inspiration from Mip-Splatting. name: 4D Gaussian Slicing
head: Slicing 4D Gaussians, Temporally-Slicing 4D Gaussians
body: 4D Gaussian Slicing is a method to calculate the 3D center position and 3D covariance of a 4D Gaussian at a specific time t by intercepting the 4D Gaussian with the t-plane. It enables the rendering of dynamic scenes represented by 4D Gaussians (3D spatial + 1D temporal) into a 2D image for a specific viewpoint and timestamp. It sets itself apart from static 3D Gaussian Splatting by handling time-dependent opacity, position offsets, and spherical harmonics evaluation in 4D, and from other 4D methods like 4D Gaussian Splatting (DreamGaussian4D) by explicitly deriving the 3D Gaussian parameters via block matrix inversion to avoid numerical instability. Inputs: A 4D Gaussian defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu} = (\mux, \muy, \muz, \mut) and covariance \Sigma{4D}. A target timestamp t. Outputs: A 3D Gaussian at time t defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}(t) = (\mux(t), \muy(t), \muz(t)) and covariance \Sigma{3D}. Data Structures: \Sigma{4D}^{-1}: A 4 \times 4 symmetric matrix with elements c{xx}, c{xy}, c{xz}, c{xt}, c{yy}, c{yz}, c{yt}, c{zz}, c{zt}, c{tt}. \Sigma{4D}: The inverse of \Sigma{4D}^{-1}, partitioned as \begin{pmatrix} U & V \\ V^T & W \end{pmatrix} where U is 3 \times 3. \Sigma{4D}^{-1}: Partitioned as \begin{pmatrix} A & M \\ M^T & Z \end{pmatrix} where A is 3 \times 3. Steps: 1. Compute 4D Covariance Inverse Elements: Calculate the elements of \Sigma{4D}^{-1} from the 4D rotor \mathbf{r} and scale \mathbf{S}{4D}: \Sigma{4D} = \mathbf{R}{4D}\mathbf{S}{4D}\mathbf{S}{4D}^T\mathbf{R}{4D}^T \Sigma{4D}^{-1} = \mathbf{R}{4D}\mathbf{S}{4D}^{-1} (\mathbf{S}{4D}^{-1})^T \mathbf{R}{4D}^T = \begin{pmatrix} c{xx} & c{xy} & c{xz} & c{xt} \\ c{xy} & c{yy} & c{yz} & c{yt} \\ c{xz} & c{yz} & c{zz} & c{zt} \\ c{xt} & c{yt} & c{zt} & c{tt} \end{pmatrix} 2. Solve for Center Shift Coefficients: Solve the linear system for \alpha, \beta, \gamma: \begin{cases} c{xx}\alpha + c{xy}\beta + c{xz}\gamma = c{xt} \\ c{xy}\alpha + c{yy}\beta + c{yz}\gamma = c{yt} \\ c{xz}\alpha + c{yz}\beta + c{zz}\gamma = c{zt} \end{cases} 3. Calculate 3D Mean: Compute the 3D center position at time t: \begin{cases} \mux(t) = \mux - \alpha(t - \mut) \\ \muy(t) = \muy - \beta(t - \mut) \\ \muz(t) = \muz - \gamma(t - \mut) \end{cases} 4. Calculate Temporal Scalar: Compute \lambda: \lambda = c{tt} - c{xx}\alpha^2 - c{yy}\beta^2 - c{zz}\gamma^2 - 2c{xy}\alpha\beta - 2c{yz}\beta\gamma - 2c{xz}\alpha\gamma 5. Determine 3D Covariance Inverse: The inverse of the 3D covariance matrix is the top-left 3 \times 3 block of \Sigma{4D}^{-1}: \Sigma{3D}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} c{xx} & c{xy} & c{xz} \\ c{xy} & c{yy} & c{yz} \\ c{xz} & c{yz} & c{zz} \end{pmatrix} 6. Avoid Numerical Instability: Do not invert \Sigma{3D}^{-1} directly to get \Sigma{3D}. Instead, use the block matrix inverse formula on \Sigma{4D} and \Sigma{4D}^{-1}, partitioned as \begin{pmatrix} U & V \\ V^T & W \end{pmatrix} and \begin{pmatrix} A & M \\ M^T & Z \end{pmatrix} respectively, where U and A are 3 \times 3 matrices. This prevents errors when 3D Gaussian scales have substantial magnitude discrepancies. 7. Construct Sliced Gaussian: The sliced 3D Gaussian is: G{3D}(\mathbf{x}, t) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}\lambda(t - \mut)^2} e^{-\frac{1}{2}[\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}(t)]^T \Sigma{3D}^{-1} [\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}(t)]} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def slice4dgaussian(mu4d, sigma4dinv, t): """ mu4d: array of shape (4,) [mux, muy, muz, mut] sigma4dinv: 4x4 numpy array, symmetric inverse covariance of 4D Gaussian t: float, target timestamp Returns: mu3d (3,), lambda (float), sigma3dinv (3x3) """ # Extract elements from sigma4dinv cxx, cxy, cxz, cxt = sigma4dinv[0, 0], sigma4dinv[0, 1], sigma4dinv[0, 2], sigma4dinv[0, 3] cyy, cyz, cyt = sigma4dinv[1, 1], sigma4dinv[1, 2], sigma4dinv[1, 3] czz, czt = sigma4dinv[2, 2], sigma4dinv[2, 3] ctt = sigma4dinv[3, 3] # Solve linear system for alpha, beta, gamma # [cxx cxy cxz] [alpha] [cxt] # [cxy cyy cyz] [beta ] = [cyt] # [cxz cyz czz] [gamma] [czt] Amat = np.array([ [cxx, cxy, cxz], [cxy, cyy, cyz], [cxz, cyz, czz] ]) bvec = np.array([cxt, cyt, czt]) # Guard against singular matrix if np.linalg.matrixrank(Amat) < 3: alpha, beta, gamma = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 else: alpha, beta, gamma = np.linalg.solve(Amat, bvec) # Calculate 3D mean mux, muy, muz, mut = mu4d muxt = mux - alpha (t - mut) muyt = muy - beta (t - mut) muzt = muz - gamma (t - mut) mu3d = np.array([muxt, muyt, muzt]) # Calculate lambda lambdaval = ctt - (cxx alpha2 + cyy beta2 + czz gamma2 + 2 cxy alpha beta + 2 cyz beta gamma + 2 cxz alpha gamma) # Extract 3D covariance inverse (top-left 3x3 block) sigma3dinv = sigma4dinv[:3,:3] return mu3d, lambdaval, sigma3dinv The pseudocode assumes numpy is available for linear algebra. The guard for singular matrix is added to prevent crashes, as the source notes numerical instability but does not specify a fallback. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, dominated by solving a 3 \times 3 linear system. Memory Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, storing 4 \times 4 and 3 \times 3 matrices. Strengths: Avoids numerical instability associated with direct matrix inversion of ill-conditioned 3D Gaussians. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of 4D covariance inverse. When to use: When rendering dynamic scenes with 4D Gaussians where time-dependent deformation is significant. 4D Gaussian Slicing was introduced in "Deformable 3D Gaussians for high-fidelity monocular dynamic scene reconstruction" by Yuqing Zhang, Xiaogang Jin, et al. (2023). It is part of the broader field of differentiable rendering and Gaussian Splatting, specifically addressing the challenge of representing and rendering dynamic 3D scenes over time. 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03307, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Softmax-GS Rendering Algorithm
head: Softmax Gaussian Splatting
body: Softmax-GS is a rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that employs a softmax-based competition mechanism to handle overlapping Gaussians, aiming to provide order-invariance and smooth transitions at Gaussian boundaries. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which suffers from popping artifacts due to sorting dependencies, or StopThePop, which exhibits abrupt color changes, Softmax-GS produces flicker-free, smooth transitions by treating overlapping splats as a competitive blending process rather than a strict depth-sorted accumulation. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by replacing the standard alpha blending step with this differentiable, order-invariant softmax competition. Inputs and Outputs: The algorithm takes a set of K Gaussians projected onto a pixel, along with the pixel coordinate x{\text{pixel}}. It outputs the final pixel color c{\text{past}}, depth d{\text{past}}, and transmittance T{\text{past}} after processing all K Gaussians. Data Structures: The method maintains running accumulators for the current pixel: T{\text{past}}: Current transmittance (initialized to 1). c{\text{past}}: Accumulated color (initialized to 0). d{\text{past}}: Moving average of depth (initialized to 0). p{\text{past}}: Moving average of the Gaussian exponent (initialized to 0). Each Gaussian k provides: x[k]: 2D center coordinate. \sigma[k]: 2D conic matrix (inverse covariance). o[k]: Opacity scalar. c[k]: Color vector (RGB). d[k]: Depth scalar. \alpha[k]: Boundary sharpness parameter (Generalized Exponential Function exponent). \beta[k]: Softmax competition temperature parameter. \gamma[k]: Depth decay influence parameter. Steps: 1. Initialize accumulators: T{\text{past}} = 1, c{\text{past}} = 0, d{\text{past}} = 0, p{\text{past}} = 0. 2. Loop for each Gaussian k from 1 to K: a. Compute the vector difference x' = x[k] - x{\text{pixel}}. b. Compute the Mahalanobis distance squared using the conic \sigma[k]. Let p{\text{cur}} be negative half of this distance: p{\text{cur}} = -0.5 \cdot (x')^T \sigma[k] x' c. Compute the raw absorbance a{\text{cur}} using the Generalized Exponential Function (GEF) controlled by \alpha[k]: a{\text{cur}} = o[k] \cdot \exp(-(-p{\text{cur}})^{\alpha[k]}) d. If T{\text{past}} < 1 (i.e., not the first Gaussian or previous Gaussians did not fully block the ray), perform the softmax blending block: i. Record the original transmittance: T{\text{orig}} = T{\text{past}} \cdot (1 - a{\text{cur}}). ii. Compute the past absorbance: a{\text{past}} = 1 - T{\text{past}}. iii. Compute the softmax weight w{\text{cur}} for the current Gaussian based on the competition between the current exponent p{\text{cur}} and the past average exponent p{\text{past}}: w{\text{cur}} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(\beta[k] \cdot (p{\text{past}} - p{\text{cur}}))} iv. Compute the softmax-weighted current absorbance: \hat{a}{\text{cur}} = w{\text{cur}} \cdot a{\text{cur}}. v. Compute the softmax-weighted past absorbance: w{\text{past}} = 1 - w{\text{cur}}, then \hat{a}{\text{past}} = w{\text{past}} \cdot a{\text{past}}. vi. Enforce order invariance and transmittance maintenance by re-normalizing the absorbances to match the original transmittance T{\text{orig}}. The target sum of absorbances is 1 - T{\text{orig}}. The algorithm solves for a scaling factor m such that the new absorbances \bar{a}{\text{past}} and \bar{a}{\text{cur}} satisfy the quadratic constraint derived from T{\text{orig}} = 1 - (\bar{a}{\text{past}} + \bar{a}{\text{cur}}) while preserving their ratio. Specifically, the source defines an intermediate step involving s (see below) and then computes m: m = \frac{\bar{a}{\text{past}} + \bar{a}{\text{cur}} - \sqrt{(\bar{a}{\text{past}} + \bar{a}{\text{cur}})^2 - 4(1 - T{\text{orig}})\bar{a}{\text{past}}\bar{a}{\text{cur}}}}{2\bar{a}{\text{past}}\bar{a}{\text{cur}}} Note: The source pseudocode applies a depth-dependent interpolation factor s before this normalization. The exact sequence in Algorithm 1 is: 1. Compute depth decay factor: s = \exp(-\gamma[k] |d[k] - d{\text{past}}|). 2. Interpolate original and softmax-ed absorbances: \bar{a}{\text{past}} = s \cdot \hat{a}{\text{past}} + (1 - s) \cdot a{\text{past}} \bar{a}{\text{cur}} = s \cdot \hat{a}{\text{cur}} + (1 - s) \cdot a{\text{cur}} 3. Compute m using the formula above with \bar{a}{\text{past}} and \bar{a}{\text{cur}}. 4. Update absorbances: \bar{a}{\text{past}} \leftarrow m \cdot \bar{a}{\text{past}}, \bar{a}{\text{cur}} \leftarrow m \cdot \bar{a}{\text{cur}}. vii. Update the running accumulators: Update transmittance: T{\text{past}} \leftarrow 1 - \bar{a}{\text{past}}. Update color: c{\text{past}} \leftarrow c{\text{past}} \cdot \frac{\bar{a}{\text{past}}}{a{\text{past}}}. Add current contribution: c{\text{past}} \leftarrow c{\text{past}} + c[k] \cdot \bar{a}{\text{cur}} \cdot T{\text{past}}. Update depth average: d{\text{past}} \leftarrow \frac{d{\text{past}} \cdot (1 - T{\text{past}}) + d[k] \cdot \bar{a}{\text{cur}} \cdot T{\text{past}}}{1 - T{\text{past}} + \bar{a}{\text{cur}} \cdot T{\text{past}}}. Update exponent average: p{\text{past}} \leftarrow \frac{p{\text{past}} \cdot (1 - T{\text{past}}) + p{\text{cur}} \cdot \bar{a}{\text{cur}} \cdot T{\text{past}}}{1 - T{\text{past}} + \bar{a}{\text{cur}} \cdot T{\text{past}}}. e. Increment k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softmaxgsrender(K, xpixel, x, sigma, o, c, d, alpha, beta, gamma): # Initialize accumulators Tpast = 1.0 cpast = 0.0 dpast = 0.0 ppast = 0.0 # Helper definitions for standard operations def dot(u, v): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(u, v)) def matvec(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))] for k in range(1, K + 1): # 1. Compute current Gaussian properties xprime = x[k] - xpixel mahalanobissq = dot(xprime, matvec(sigma[k], xprime)) pcur = -0.5 mahalanobissq # Generalized Exponential Function for absorbance negpcur = -pcur acur = o[k] exp(-(negpcur alpha[k])) if Tpast < 1.0: # Record original transmittance before modification Torig = Tpast (1.0 - acur) # Past absorbance apast = 1.0 - Tpast # Softmax competition weight wcur = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(beta[k] (ppast - pcur))) # Softmax-weighted absorbances ahatcur = wcur acur wpast = 1.0 - wcur ahatpast = wpast apast # Order invariance and transmittance maintenance (Normalization) scale = (1.0 - Torig) / (ahatpast + ahatcur) ahatpast = scale ahatcur = scale # Depth decay influence s = exp(-gamma[k] abs(d[k] - dpast)) # Interpolate original and softmax-ed absorbances abarpast = s ahatpast + (1.0 - s) apast abarcur = s ahatcur + (1.0 - s) acur # Transmittance maintenance again (Quadratic solution for m) sumabars = abarpast + abarcur prodabars = abarpast abarcur discriminant = sumabars2 - 4.0 (1.0 - Torig) prodabars if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0.0 m = (sumabars - sqrt(discriminant)) / (2.0 prodabars) # Update absorbances with m abarpast = m abarcur = m # Update past accumulators for next iteration Tpast = 1.0 - abarpast # Update color: scale previous color by absorbance ratio, then add current contribution if apast != 0: cpast = cpast (abarpast / apast) else: cpast = 0.0 cpast += c[k] abarcur Tpast # Update Depth and Exponent Averages (using OLD Tpast for weighting) weightnew = abarcur Tpast weightold = 1.0 - Tpast totalweight = weightold + weightnew if totalweight > 0: dpast = (dpast weightold + d[k] weightnew) / totalweight ppast = (ppast weightold + pcur weightnew) / totalweight else: dpast = d[k] ppast = pcur else: # First Gaussian or fully opaque previous cpast += c[k] acur Tpast dpast = d[k] ppast = pcur Tpast = 1.0 - acur return cpast, dpast, Tpast Parameters: \alpha[k]: Controls boundary sharpness using the Generalized Exponential Function. Learning rate 0.0008 for real-world benchmarks. \beta[k]: Controls the softmax competition temperature. Learning rate 0.008 for real-world benchmarks. \gamma[k]: Controls the decay influence of softmax based on depth distance. Learning rate 0.0004 for real-world benchmarks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm is applied only to the first 128 Gaussians along each ray to maintain linear complexity in the backward pass. This results in incomplete coverage (approx. 85% for indoor, 70% for outdoor scenes). The order-invariance mechanism does not extend to cases with three or more overlapping Gaussians with distinct colors due to bookkeeping complexity under linear-time constraints. Distant semi-transparent Gaussians can bias running estimates of accumulated depth and opacity toward intermediate values, affecting softmax-based competition. A pixel-level fusion method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes instance labels by aggregating the full top-M label distributions of contributing Gaussians before applying an argmax operation. It solves the problem of staircase boundary artifacts inherent in hard-label rendering, where discrete Gaussian assignments cause jagged edges at object boundaries. Unlike Softmax-GS, which uses a softmax-based competition mechanism for order-invariance, Late-Argmax explicitly preserves the full distributional evidence of each Gaussian to allow boundary Gaussians to contribute proportionally to adjacent labels, enabling a majority vote of neighbors to resolve ambiguity. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm maintains linear complexity in the backward pass by limiting the number of Gaussians processed per ray to 128. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 indoor scenes, Softmax-GS accounts for approximately 85% of pixels across test images. On Mip-NeRF360 outdoor scenes, Softmax-GS accounts for around 70% of pixels. In view consistency benchmarks, Softmax-GS achieves higher PSNR and lower FLIP7 scores compared to 3D GS and StopThePop on scenes like "bicycle", "counter", "kitchen", "train", and "truck". Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Produces smooth, flicker-free transitions at Gaussian crossings, avoiding the popping artifacts of 3D GS and the abrupt color changes of StopThePop. It effectively merges intersecting Gaussians into a single surface. Limitations: Incomplete coverage due to the 128-Gaussian limit; inability to handle >2 overlapping distinct-color Gaussians with order invariance; sensitivity to distant semi-transparent Gaussians biasing depth/opacity estimates. Softmax-GS was introduced in the paper "Softmax-GS: Generalized Gaussians Learning When to Blend or Bound" by dmand, Delio Vicini, George Kopanas, Dmitry Lagun, Kwang Moo Yi, Mark Matthews, and Andrea Tagliasacchi. The method was published as an arXiv preprint in 2025. It addresses the view-consistency issues in 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a differentiable, order-invariant blending mechanism. Softmax-GS: Generalized Gaussians Learning When to Blend or Bound, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprf71909.2026.00053, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Late-Argmax Rendering
head: Distribution-preserving voting, Pixel-level distribution fusion
body: Late-Argmax Rendering is a pixel-level fusion method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes instance labels by aggregating the full top-M label distributions of contributing Gaussians before applying an argmax operation. It solves the problem of staircase boundary artifacts inherent in hard-label rendering, where discrete Gaussian assignments cause jagged edges at object boundaries. Unlike its parent, Softmax-GS Rendering Algorithm, which uses a softmax-based competition mechanism for order-invariance, Late-Argmax explicitly preserves the full distributional evidence of each Gaussian to allow boundary Gaussians to contribute proportionally to adjacent labels, enabling a majority vote of neighbors to resolve ambiguity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: For a specific pixel p, the method requires the top-K contributing Gaussians g{p,k} (where k=1 \dots K), their rendering weights w{p,k}, and their pre-computed label distributions \hat{\pi}{g{p,k}}(j) for each instance label j > 0. Output: A discrete label map \hat{L}, where each pixel p is assigned a label \hat{l}(p) \in \{0, 1, \dots, J\}. Label 0 represents the background. Data Structures: \hat{\pi}{g}(j): The probability or confidence that Gaussian g belongs to instance label j. w{p,k}: The scalar rendering weight of the k-th Gaussian at pixel p. Steps: 1. Top-K Selection: For each pixel p, identify the top-K Gaussians g{p,k} that contribute most significantly to the pixel, along with their weights w{p,k}. 2. Distribution Fusion: For each candidate instance label j > 0, compute the weighted sum of the label distributions from all top-K Gaussians: Sj(p) = \sum{k=1}^K w{p,k} \hat{\pi}{g{p,k}}(j) This step fuses the full top-M distribution at the pixel level rather than committing to a hard label per Gaussian. 3. Argmax Assignment: Assign the label \hat{l}(p) as the argmax of the fused scores: \hat{l}(p) = \arg\max{j>0} Sj(p). 4. Background Handling: If all instance scores Sj(p) are zero, output the background label 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lateargmaxrender(topkgaussians, topkweights, labeldistributions): """ topkgaussians: List of Gaussian objects contributing to a pixel. topkweights: List of scalar weights w{p,k} for each Gaussian. labeldistributions: List of arrays, where labeldistributions[k][j] is pi{g{p,k}}(j). Returns: The assigned label integer for the pixel. """ numlabels = len(labeldistributions[0]) fusedscores = [0.0] numlabels for k in range(len(topkgaussians)): w = topkweights[k] pi = labeldistributions[k] for j in range(1, numlabels): fusedscores[j] += w pi[j] bestlabel = 0 maxscore = -1.0 for j in range(1, numlabels): if fusedscores[j] > maxscore: maxscore = fusedscores[j] bestlabel = j if maxscore <= 0: return 0 return bestlabel Parameters: K: The number of top contributing Gaussians to consider per pixel. Not given in the sources. M: The number of top labels considered in the distribution. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Staircase Artifacts: Hard-label rendering causes staircase boundary artifacts because boundary Gaussians with comparable evidence for adjacent labels are forced to pick one, leading to jagged transitions. Late-Argmax suppresses this by allowing proportional contribution. Zero Scores: If all instance scores are zero, the output must be explicitly set to background (0). Hard-Label Rendering is a baseline method where each Gaussian is assigned a discrete label \ellg before rendering. It is used for SAM association in segmentation tasks. The rendered label at pixel p is computed by summing the weights of Gaussians grouped by their hard labels: \hat{\ell}(p) = \arg\max{j>0} \sum{k=1}^K w{p,k} \mathbb{1}[\ell{g{p,k}} = j] where \mathbb{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. This method is simpler but suffers from staircase boundary artifacts because it does not account for the uncertainty or multi-modal nature of label evidence at boundaries. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Suppresses staircase boundary artifacts by preserving distributional evidence. Provides smooth transitions at Gaussian boundaries. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Late-Argmax Rendering was introduced in the DIGS (Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting) pipeline for training-free open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. It addresses the limitations of hard-label rendering in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, where discrete assignments lead to visual artifacts. The method is part of a broader framework that includes visibility-aware decay and multi-modal spatial instance representations. DIGS: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.16177, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: XPR-3DGS
head: XPR implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: XPR-3DGS is a point-based differentiable rendering method that implements 3D Gaussian Splatting within the XPR framework. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, culls tiles based on conic bounds, and evaluates alpha blending per pixel. It differs from its siblings by providing a high-level, Python-based implementation within the XPR framework that requires significantly fewer lines of code (260–304) than traditional C++/CUDA implementations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of 3D Gaussian primitives defined by PrimitiveParams. Output: Rendered image colors and alpha values. Data Structures: The primitive parameters are defined as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PrimitiveParams: mu: Array # (3,) mean in world space s: Array # (3,) scales q: Array # (4,) unit quaternion for rotation sh: Array # (C, 3) spherical harmonic coefficients o: Array # (1,) opacity Parameters: alphathresh: Threshold for opacity to determine visibility. Default value is 1/255. znear: Near plane distance for camera-space depth check. pixelinfo: Set to None because per-pixel evaluation depends only on the 2D pixel coordinates. Steps: 1. Project: For each primitive p, compute the projection onto the image plane. Compute the world-to-camera projection matrix R{w2c}. Transform the mean \mu to camera space: \muc = R{w2c} \mu. Compute the 2D mean \mu{2D} and the 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} using EWA splatting. Compute the determinant det of \Sigma{2D}. Compute the conic matrix \Sigma{2D}^{-1}, referred to as conic2D. Compute extents ex, ey from \Sigma{2D} and det. Compute radius r from ex, ey. Compute the axis-aligned bounding box aabb using \mu{2D}, ex, ey. Compute tile count tc as the area of aabb in tile units: tc = (aabb.x{max} - aabb.x{min}) \times (aabb.y{max} - aabb.y{min}). Compute visibility flag: visible = (det > 0) \land (o \ge \alpha{thresh}) \land (r > 0) \land (tc > 0) \land (\muc[2] > z{near}). Adjust tile count: tc = tc \times float(visible). Compute view-dependent color c from \mu and spherical harmonics sh. Produce Tile Cull Data (p{tcd}): Concatenate conic2D[0,0], conic2D[0,1], conic2D[1,1], opacity o, \mu{2D}, and visible. Produce Shader Data (p{sd}): Concatenate \mu{2D}[0], \mu{2D}[1], -0.5 \times \text{conic\2D}[0,0], -\text{conic\2D}[0,1], -0.5 \times \text{conic\2D}[1,1], opacity o, and color c. 2. Tile Cull: For each tile in the primitive's bounding box, determine if the tile needs to be processed. Unpack conic, o, \mu{2D}, and visible from p{tcd}. Check if \mu{2D} is outside the tile bounds (tile{min}, tile{max}). Compute the 2D location point{2D} inside the tile that maximizes the Gaussian response, which is either \mu{2D} (if inside the tile) or a point along the edges of the tile facing \mu{2D}. Compute max contribution power: dx = \mu{2D}[0] - point{2D}[0], dy = \mu{2D}[1] - point{2D}[1], power = 0.5 \times (dx^2 \times conic[0] + 2 \times dx \times dy \times conic[1] + dy^2 \times conic[2]). Determine tile visibility: tile\visible = (power \le \log(o / \alpha{thresh})) \land visible. 3. Evaluate: For each pixel px = (x, y) in visible tiles, compute the contribution. Unpack \mu{2D}, conic, o, and c from p{sd}. Compute dx = px[0] - \mu{2D}[0], dy = px[1] - \mu{2D}[1]. Compute power: power = dx^2 \times conic[0] + dx \times dy \times conic[1] + dy^2 \times conic[2]. Compute alpha: \alpha = o \times \exp(power). Validate result: valid = (power \le 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class PrimitiveParams: def init(self, mu, s, q, sh, o): self.mu = mu # (3,) mean in world space self.s = s # (3,) scales self.q = q # (4,) unit quaternion for rotation self.sh = sh # (C, 3) spherical harmonic coefficients self.o = o # (1,) opacity class ProjectResult: def init(self, depth, visible, tileculldata, shaderdata, aabb, tilecount): self.depth = depth self.visible = visible self.tileculldata = tileculldata self.shaderdata = shaderdata self.aabb = aabb self.tilecount = tilecount class EvaluateResult: def init(self, alpha, valid, color): self.alpha = alpha self.valid = valid self.color = color class MethodSpec: def init(self, project, tilecull, pixelinfo, evaluate): self.project = project self.tilecull = tilecull self.pixelinfo = pixelinfo self.evaluate = evaluate def project(p, cam, view, cfg): # Compute world-to-camera projection matrix Rw2c Rw2c = view.projectionmatrix @ view.cameramatrix # Transform mean to camera space muc = Rw2c @ p.mu # Compute 2D mean via perspective division mu2D = muc[:2] / muc[2] # Compute 2D covariance, determinant via EWA splatting cov2D, det, = computecov2D(p.s, p.q, muc, Rw2c, cam, cfg) # Compute conic matrix (inverse of projected covariance) con2D = np.linalg.inv(cov2D) # Compute extents from covariance and determinant ex, ey = computeextents(cov2D, det, p.o, cfg) # Compute radius r = math.sqrt(ex2 + ey2) # Compute axis-aligned bounding box aabb = getboundingbox(mu2D, ex, ey, cfg) # Compute tile count as area in tile units tc = (aabb.xmax - aabb.xmin) (aabb.ymax - aabb.ymin) # Compute visibility flag visible = (det > 0) and (p.o >= cfg.alphathresh) and (r > 0) and (tc > 0) and (muc[2] > cfg.znear) tc = float(visible) # Compute view-dependent color from spherical harmonics c = computecolor(p.mu, p.sh, view) # Produce tile cull data ptcd = (con2D[0,0], con2D[0,1], con2D[1,1], p.o, mu2D, visible) # Produce shader data psd = (mu2D[0], mu2D[1], -0.5con2D[0,0], -con2D[0,1], -0.5con2D[1,1], p.o, c) return ProjectResult(depth=muc[2], visible=visible, tileculldata=ptcd, shaderdata=psd, aabb=aabb, tilecount=tc) def tilecull(tilemin, tilemax, ptcd, cfg): conic, o, mu2D, visible = ptcd muoutside = (mu2D[0] < tilemin[0]) or (mu2D[0] > tilemax[0]) or (mu2D[1] < tilemin[1]) or (mu2D[1] > tilemax[1]) # Compute location of the 2D point inside the tile that maximizes the response # This is either mu2D (if inside) or a point along the edges facing mu2D point2D = np.clip(mu2D, tilemin, tilemax) # Compute max contribution power of 2D Gaussian dx = mu2D[0] - point2D[0] dy = mu2D[1] - point2D[1] power = 0.5 (dxdxconic[0] + 2dxdyconic[1] + dydyconic[2]) # Keep tile iff max contribution to tile satisfies: o exp(-power) >= alphathresh tilevisible = (power <= math.log(o / cfg.alphathresh)) and visible return tilevisible def evaluate(pxdata, psd): mu2D, conic, o, c = psd dx = pxdata[0] - mu2D[0] dy = pxdata[1] - mu2D[1] power = dx dx conic[0] + dx dy conic[1] + dy dy conic[2] alpha = o math.exp(power) valid = power <= 0. return EvaluateResult(alpha=alpha, valid=valid, color=c) XPR3DGS = MethodSpec(project=project, tilecull=tilecull, pixelinfo=None, evaluate=evaluate) Performance: XPR-3DGS is slower than the Base implementation on Synthetic datasets (0.76x FPS) due to JAX kernel launch overhead being significant at very high frame rates. On 360 and T&T datasets, it achieves 0.95x and 0.96x FPS respectively. Code Size: Requires only 260 to 304 lines of Python, significantly fewer than Base implementations (e.g., 2,153 lines for 3DGS). Strengths: High-level interface enables rapid prototyping; fewer lines of code reduce implementation complexity. Limitations: JAX overhead impacts performance at very high frame rates; pixel evaluation depends only on 2D coordinates, which may be less flexible than methods using per-pixel world-space ray directions. XPR-3DGS is an implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting within the XPR framework, which is an extensible cross-platform point-based differentiable renderer. It utilizes EWA splatting for projection. XPR: An Extensible Cross-Platform Point-Based Differentiable Renderer, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.11529, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering
body: Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering (SSVR) is a volume rendering technique that reformulates 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization using a vacancy function to improve geometric fidelity. It produces RGB images nearly identical to standard 3DGS rasterization under suitable conditions but reduces holes and blurred boundaries in depth maps. It is equivalent to 3DGS rasterization when the vacancy function is set to v(x) = \sqrt{1 - G(x)}. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives defined by parameters \theta (position \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, color ci). Camera ray origin o and direction d. Outputs: RGB image pixel color C. Depth map value t{med}. Data Structures: List of Gaussians sorted by their ray parameter t^i (front to back). Accumulated transmittance state T(t). Core Concept: SSVR reformulates the volume rendering integral using a vacancy function v(x). The density \sigma(x, \omega) is defined as \sigma(x, \omega) = \omega^\top \nabla \log v(x). To obtain RGB images equivalent to 3DGS rasterization, the vacancy function must be v(x) = \sqrt{1 - G(x)}. Rendering Steps: 1. Ray Parameterization: For each pixel, define the ray x(t) = o + t \cdot d. Compute the Gaussian maximum location along the ray t^i = d^\top (\mui - o) and the ray-space variance \sigma{i}^2 = d^\top \Sigmai d. 2. Single Gaussian Transmittance: Compute Ti(t) for each Gaussian i based on the position t relative to t^i: Ti(t) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{1 - Gi(t)}, & t \le t^i \\ \sqrt{1 - Gi(t^i)}, & t > t^i \end{cases} where Gi(t) = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{(t - t^i)^2}{2\sigma{i}^2}\right) is the 1D Gaussian density along the ray. 3. Accumulation: Compute the accumulated transmittance T(t) = \prod{j} Tj(t) for all Gaussians j with t^j \le t. The color is accumulated using standard alpha blending weights derived from the transmittance curve. 4. Depth Rendering: Find the median depth t{med} defined by the point where T(t{med}) = 0.5 using a fixed number of bisection iterations. 5. Backpropagation: During training, differentiate the fixed condition T(t{med}) = 0.5 with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta. Using the chain rule, the gradient is computed as \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} \frac{\partial t{med}}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial T}{\partial \theta} = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gaussiandensity1d(t, tstar, sigmasq, alpha): """Compute Gi(t) for a Gaussian at ray parameter t.""" if sigmasq <= 1e-8: sigmasq = 1e-8 return alpha math.exp(-0.5 ((t - tstar) 2) / sigmasq) def singletransmittance(t, tstar, sigmasq, alpha): """Compute Ti(t) according to the piecewise definition.""" G = gaussiandensity1d(t, tstar, sigmasq, alpha) # Clamp to [0, 1] to prevent NaN from sqrt of negative numbers G = max(0.0, min(1.0, G)) if t <= tstar: return math.sqrt(1.0 - G) else: Gstar = gaussiandensity1d(tstar, tstar, sigmasq, alpha) Gstar = max(0.0, min(1.0, Gstar)) return math.sqrt(1.0 - Gstar) def accumulatedtransmittance(t, gaussianssorted): """Compute T(t) = product of Ti(t) for all Gaussians behind t.""" Tacc = 1.0 for g in gaussianssorted: if g['tstar'] <= t: Tacc = singletransmittance(t, g['tstar'], g['sigmasq'], g['alpha']) return max(0.0, min(1.0, Tacc)) def findmediandepth(gaussianssorted, tmin, tmax, iterations=10): """Find tmed such that T(tmed) = 0.5 via bisection.""" low, high = tmin, tmax for in range(iterations): mid = (low + high) / 2.0 Tmid = accumulatedtransmittance(mid, gaussianssorted) if Tmid > 0.5: low = mid else: high = mid return (low + high) / 2.0 def renderpixel(rayo, rayd, gaussians): """Render a single pixel using SSVR.""" # Precompute ray-space parameters for visible Gaussians visible = [] for g in gaussians: tstar = rayd[0]g['mu'][0] + rayd[1]g['mu'][1] + rayd[2]g['mu'][2] - (rayd[0]rayo[0] + rayd[1]rayo[1] + rayd[2]rayo[2]) sigmasq = rayd[0]2 g['Sigma'][0][0] + rayd[1]2 g['Sigma'][1][1] + rayd[2]2 g['Sigma'][2][2] visible.append({'tstar': tstar, 'sigmasq': sigmasq, 'alpha': g['alpha'], 'color': g['color']}) # Sort front-to-back visible.sort(key=lambda x: x['tstar']) if not visible: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 tmin = visible[0]['tstar'] - 5.0 math.sqrt(max(visible[0]['sigmasq'], 1e-4)) tmax = visible[-1]['tstar'] + 5.0 math.sqrt(max(visible[-1]['sigmasq'], 1e-4)) # Compute color via standard alpha blending (equivalent to 3DGS) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Tacc = 1.0 for g in visible: Ti = singletransmittance(g['tstar'], g['tstar'], g['sigmasq'], g['alpha']) weight = Tacc (1.0 - Ti) for c in range(3): color[c] += weight g['color'][c] Tacc = Ti # Compute median depth tmed = findmediandepth(visible, tmin, tmax) return color, tmed Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The square root in v(x) = \sqrt{1 - G(x)} requires G(x) \le 1. Numerical errors may push G(x) slightly above 1; clamping G(x) to [0, 1] before the square root prevents NaN propagation. Boundaries: The piecewise definition of Ti(t) depends on accurate computation of t^i. Incorrect t^i shifts the transmittance curve and breaks depth accuracy. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has near-zero covariance, \sigmai^2 approaches zero, causing density spikes. Clamping \sigmai^2 to a minimum value (e.g., 10^{-8}) stabilizes the exponential. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improved geometric fidelity for depth and surface reconstruction; reduces holes and blurred boundaries in depth maps. Limitations: Requires accurate camera parameters and optimization-based training pipelines. When to use: When geometric accuracy for depth is prioritized over raw RGB fidelity. When not to use: When standard 3DGS rasterization suffices for RGB output. Stochastic Solid Volume Rendering was introduced to improve geometric representation in optimization-based 3D Gaussian Splatting methods. It builds on prior work by Miller et al. (2023), Zhang et al. (2026), and Gomez et al. (2026), which proved the mathematical equivalence between SSVR and 3DGS rasterization under the specified vacancy function. VoxelTTO: Voxel-Aligned Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Test-Time Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.21498, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline
head: Gaussian Splatting CUDA Rasterizer, Mip-Splatting Forward/Backward Pass
body: The Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline is a differentiable GPU-based rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates view-dependent scaling (mip-splatting) to handle aliasing and resolution changes. It extends the tiled rasterization approach by using a kernelsize parameter to adjust the Gaussian projection scale, ensuring consistent visual quality across different camera distances and resolutions. It builds on Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by adding specific preprocessing for mip-levels and a robust binning/sorting mechanism for tile-based rendering. The pipeline consists of a forward pass (rendering) and a backward pass (gradient computation). It relies on three main state structures: GeometryState, ImageState, and BinningState. Inputs: means3D: 3D Gaussian centers, shape (P, 3). scales: Gaussian scales, shape (P, 3). scalemodifier: Scalar multiplier for scales. rotations: Gaussian rotations (quaternions), shape (P, 4). opacities: Gaussian opacities, shape (P). shs: Spherical Harmonics coefficients, shape (P, K, 3) or precomputed colors. colorsprecomp: Precomputed RGB colors, shape (P, 3). If null, SHs are used. viewmatrix: 4 \times 4 view transformation matrix. projmatrix: 4 \times 4 projection matrix. campos: Camera position, shape (3). width, height: Image dimensions. focalx, focaly: Focal lengths in pixels. tanfovx, tanfovy: Tangents of horizontal and vertical field of view. kernelsize: Float controlling the effective Gaussian kernel size for mip-splatting. prefiltered: Boolean flag indicating if SH coefficients are prefiltered. subpixeloffset: Float array of size 2 for subpixel camera offsets. background: Background color, shape (3). Outputs: outcolor: Rendered image, shape (H, W, 3). numrendered: Number of Gaussian instances rendered. Gradients for backward pass: dLdmean3D, dLdcolor, dLdcov3D, dLdsh, dLdscale, dLdrot, dLdopacity, dLdmean2D, dLdconic. GeometryState (allocated for P Gaussians): depths: float, size P. clamped: float, size P \times 3. internalradii: float, size P. means2D: float, size P \times 2 (implied by usage). cov3D: float, size P \times 6. conicopacity: float, size P. rgb: float, size P \times 3. tilestouched: uint32t, size P. scanningspace: void, size varies. pointoffsets: uint32t, size P. ImageState (allocated for N = \text{width} \times \text{height} pixels): accumalpha: float, size N. ncontrib: uint32t, size N. ranges: uint2, size N (stores start/end indices for each tile in the sorted list). BinningState (allocated for P Gaussians): pointlist: uint32t, size P. pointlistunsorted: uint32t, size P. pointlistkeys: uint64t, size P. pointlistkeysunsorted: uint64t, size P. listsortingspace: void, size varies. sortingsize: sizet. 1. Calculate Focal Lengths: If not provided, compute: \text{focal\y} = \frac{\text{height}}{2.0 \times \text{tan\fovy}} \text{focal\x} = \frac{\text{width}}{2.0 \times \text{tan\fov\x}} 2. Initialize GeometryState: Allocate GeometryState buffer of size required<GeometryState>(P) and initialize it. If radii is null, set the radii pointer to geomState.internalradii. 3. Calculate Tile Grid: \text{tile\grid}.x = \lceil \frac{\text{width}}{\text{BLOCK\X}} \rceil \text{tile\grid}.y = \lceil \frac{\text{height}}{\text{BLOCK\Y}} \rceil \text{tile\grid}.z = 1 \text{block}.x = \text{BLOCK\X}, \quad \text{block}.y = \text{BLOCK\Y}, \quad \text{block}.z = 1 Typical values for BLOCKX and BLOCKY are 32. 4. Initialize ImageState: Allocate ImageState buffer of size required<ImageState>(width height) and initialize it. Pitfall: If NUMCHANNELS != 3 and colorsprecomp is null, throw a runtime error. 5. Preprocess (Projection and Mip-Splatting): Launch FORWARD::preprocess kernel with P threads. Inputs: means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, clamped, cov3Dprecomp, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, width, height, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, radii, means2D, depths, cov3D, rgb, conicopacity, tilegrid, tilestouched, prefiltered. Note: This kernel computes 2D means, covariances, and radii, applying the kernelsize for mip-splatting adjustments. 6. Compute Point Offsets: Compute inclusive prefix sum over tilestouched to get pointoffsets. \text{point\offsets}[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i} \text{tiles\touched}[j] Use cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum. 7. Get Total Rendered Count: Copy the last element of pointoffsets to host variable numrendered. 8. Initialize BinningState: Allocate BinningState buffer of size required<BinningState>(numrendered) and initialize it. 9. Duplicate with Keys (Tile Binning): Launch duplicateWithKeys kernel with (P + 255) / 256 blocks of 256 threads. For each Gaussian, if its bounding box overlaps a tile, emit a key/value pair. Key construction: \text{key} = (\text{tile\y} \times \text{tile\grid}.x + \text{tile\x}) \ll 32 \mid \text{depth} Value: Gaussian index idx. Inputs: means2D, depths, pointoffsets, pointlistkeysunsorted, pointlistunsorted, radii, tilegrid. 10. Radix Sort: Calculate bit depth for radix sort: \text{bit} = \text{getHigherMsb}(\text{tile\grid}.x \times \text{tile\grid}.y) Sort pointlistkeysunsorted and pointlistunsorted using cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs. Inputs: listsortingspace, sortingsize, keysunsorted, keyssorted, valuesunsorted, valuessorted, numrendered, 0, 32 + bit. Result: pointlistkeys (sorted keys) and pointlist (sorted Gaussian indices). 11. Identify Tile Ranges: Zero out imgState.ranges buffer of size tilegrid.x tilegrid.y sizeof(uint2). If numrendered > 0, launch identifyTileRanges kernel with (\text{num\rendered} + 255) / 256 blocks of 256 threads. Logic: If idx == 0, ranges[currtile].x = 0. Else, get prevtile = pointlistkeys[idx - 1] >> 32. If currtile != prevtile, set ranges[prevtile].y = idx and ranges[currtile].x = idx. If idx == L - 1, set ranges[currtile].y = L. Inputs: numrendered, pointlistkeys, imgState.ranges. 12. Determine Feature Pointer: If colorsprecomp is not null, use it; otherwise use geomState.rgb. 13. Render: Launch FORWARD::render kernel. Inputs: tilegrid, block, imgState.ranges, pointlist, width, height, subpixeloffset, means2D, featureptr, conicopacity, accumalpha, ncontrib, background, outcolor. 14. Return: Return numrendered. 1. Initialize States: Initialize GeometryState, BinningState, and ImageState from provided buffers. If radii is null, set radii pointer to geomState.internalradii. 2. Calculate Focal Lengths and Tile Grid: Same as forward pass. 3. Determine Color Pointer: If colorsprecomp is not null, use it; otherwise use geomState.rgb. 4. Render Backward: Launch BACKWARD::render kernel. Inputs: tilegrid, block, imgState.ranges, pointlist, width, height, subpixeloffset, background, means2D, conicopacity, colorptr, accumalpha, ncontrib, dLdpix, dLdmean2D, dLdconic, dLdopacity, dLdcolor. 5. Determine Cov3D Pointer: If cov3Dprecomp is not null, use it; otherwise use geomState.cov3D. 6. Preprocess Backward: Launch BACKWARD::preprocess kernel with P threads. Inputs: P, D, M, means3D, radii, shs, clamped, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dptr, viewmatrix, projmatrix, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, campos, dLdmean2D, dLdconic, dLdmean3D, dLdcolor, dLdcov3D, dLdsh, dLdscale, dLdrot, conicopacity, dLdopacity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import itertools class GeometryState: def init(self, P): self.depths = [0.0] P self.clamped = [0.0] (P 3) self.internalradii = [0.0] P self.means2D = [0.0] (P 2) self.cov3D = [0.0] (P 6) self.conicopacity = [0.0] P self.rgb = [0.0] (P 3) self.tilestouched = [0] P self.scanningspace = None self.pointoffsets = [0] P class ImageState: def init(self, N): self.accumalpha = [0.0] N self.ncontrib = [0] N self.ranges = [(0, 0)] N class BinningState: def init(self, P): self.pointlist = [0] P self.pointlistkeys = [0] P self.pointlistkeysunsorted = [0] P self.pointlistunsorted = [0] P self.listsortingspace = None self.sortingsize = 0 def gethighermsb(n): if n == 0: return 0 return n.bitlength() - 1 def preprocesskernel(P, means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, clamped, cov3Dprecomp, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, width, height, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, radii, means2D, depths, cov3D, rgb, conicopacity, tilegrid, tilestouched, prefiltered): # Corresponds to FORWARD::preprocess CUDA kernel launch with P threads. # Computes 2D means, covariances, and radii, applying kernelsize for mip-splatting. # Not given in the sources. pass def duplicatewithkeyskernel(numblocks, threadsperblock, means2D, depths, pointoffsets, pointlistkeysunsorted, pointlistunsorted, radii, tilegrid): # Corresponds to duplicateWithKeys CUDA kernel launch. # For each tile that the bounding rect overlaps, emit a key/value pair. # The key is | tile ID | depth |, and the value is the ID of the Gaussian. # Sorting the values with this key yields Gaussian IDs in a list, such that they # are first sorted by tile and then by depth. # Not given in the sources. pass def identifytilerangeskernel(numblocks, threadsperblock, numrendered, pointlistkeys, ranges): # Corresponds to identifyTileRanges CUDA kernel launch. # Determines start/end indices for each tile in the sorted list. for idx in range(numrendered): currtile = pointlistkeys[idx] >> 32 if idx == 0: ranges[currtile] = (0, ranges[currtile][1]) else: prevtile = pointlistkeys[idx - 1] >> 32 if currtile != prevtile: ranges[prevtile] = (ranges[prevtile][0], idx) ranges[currtile] = (idx, ranges[currtile][1]) if idx == numrendered - 1: ranges[currtile] = (ranges[currtile][0], numrendered) def renderkernel(tilegrid, block, ranges, pointlist, width, height, subpixeloffset, means2D, featureptr, conicopacity, accumalpha, ncontrib, background, outcolor): # Corresponds to FORWARD::render CUDA kernel launch. # Rasterizes Gaussians per tile. # Not given in the sources. pass def mipsplattingforward(means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, width, height, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, prefiltered, subpixeloffset, background): P = len(means3D) # 1. Calculate Focal Lengths focaly = height / (2.0 tanfovy) focalx = width / (2.0 tanfovx) # 2. Initialize GeometryState geomstate = GeometryState(P) radii = geomstate.internalradii # 3. Calculate Tile Grid BLOCKX = 32 BLOCKY = 32 tilegridx = (width + BLOCKX - 1) // BLOCKX tilegridy = (height + BLOCKY - 1) // BLOCKY tilegrid = (tilegridx, tilegridy, 1) block = (BLOCKX, BLOCKY, 1) # 4. Initialize ImageState N = width height imgstate = ImageState(N) NUMCHANNELS = 3 if colorsprecomp is None: if NUMCHANNELS != 3: raise RuntimeError("NUMCHANNELS must be 3 if colorsprecomp is null") # 5. Preprocess Kernel preprocesskernel( P, means3D, scales, scalemodifier, rotations, opacities, shs, geomstate.clamped, None, colorsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos, width, height, focalx, focaly, tanfovx, tanfovy, kernelsize, radii, geomstate.means2D, geomstate.depths, geomstate.cov3D, geomstate.rgb, geomstate.conicopacity, tilegrid, geomstate.tilestouched, prefiltered) # 6. Compute Point Offsets geomstate.pointoffsets = list(itertools.accumulate(geomstate.tilestouched)) # 7. Get Total Rendered Count numrendered = geomstate.pointoffsets[-1] # 8. Initialize BinningState binningstate = BinningState(numrendered) # 9. Duplicate with Keys duplicatewithkeyskernel( (P + 255) // 256, 256, geomstate.means2D, geomstate.depths, geomstate.pointoffsets, binningstate.pointlistkeysunsorted, binningstate.pointlistunsorted, radii, tilegrid) # 10. Radix Sort bit = gethighermsb(tilegridx tilegridy) combined = sorted(zip(binningstate.pointlistkeysunsorted, binningstate.pointlistunsorted)) binningstate.pointlistkeys = [k for k, v in combined] binningstate.pointlist = [v for k, v in combined] # 11. Identify Tile Ranges imgstate.ranges = [(0, 0)] (tilegridx tilegridy) if numrendered > 0: identifytilerangeskernel( (numrendered + 255) // 256, 256, numrendered, binningstate.pointlistkeys, imgstate.ranges) # 12. Determine Feature Pointer featureptr = colorsprecomp if colorsprecomp is not None else geomstate.rgb # 13. Render Kernel outcolor = [[0.0] 3 for in range(height width)] renderkernel( tilegrid, block, imgstate.ranges, binningstate.pointlist, width, height, subpixeloffset, geomstate.means2D, featureptr, geomstate.conicopacity, imgstate.accumalpha, imgstate.ncontrib, background, outcolor) return numrendered, outcolor Time Complexity: Dominated by the preprocessing projection (O(P)), the binning and sorting (O(P \log P) or O(P) with radix sort), and the tile-based rendering (O(N + P)). The radix sort is typically efficient on GPU. Memory Complexity: O(P) for geometry and binning states, O(N) for image state. Performance: Highly optimized for GPU execution using CUDA. The tile-based approach reduces memory contention and allows for efficient culling. Mip-splatting adds a small overhead for kernel size adjustment but significantly improves visual quality at varying resolutions. Strengths: Differentiable, handles aliasing via mip-splatting, efficient tile-based rendering, supports SH for view-dependent colors. Limitations: Requires significant GPU memory for large P. Sorting can be a bottleneck if not optimized. The Mip-Splatting Rasterization Pipeline is part of the Mip-Splatting project, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing mip-splatting to handle view-dependent scaling. It was developed by the Autonomous Vision group. autonomousvision/mip-splatting, https://github.com/autonomousvision/mip-splatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: SimpleRenderer (CPU Gaussian Splatting)
head: Painter's Algorithm Gaussian Rendering, Simplified Gaussian Renderer
body: SimpleRenderer is a CPU-based rendering method for 3D Gaussian point clouds that approximates Gaussian Splatting using a painter's algorithm. It projects 3D Gaussians to 2D screen ellipses and composites them to generate an RGB image, suitable for visualization and small-scale point clouds where GPU acceleration is unavailable. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which relies on CUDA-based tile-based rasterization for performance and differentiability, SimpleRenderer uses a simplified 2D ellipse approximation and non-differentiable alpha blending. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (defined by mean position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and color data), a camera configuration (intrinsic and extrinsic parameters), and a RenderConfig. Outputs: An RGB image buffer of shape (H, W, 3) with float32 dtype, with values in [0, 1]. Data Structures: RenderConfig: A dataclass containing: backgroundcolor: Tuple of floats, default (0.05, 0.05, 0.08). alphathreshold: Float, default 0.01. nearplane: Float, default 0.1. farplane: Float, default 50.0. PinholeCamera: Defines the projection geometry: width, height: Image dimensions in pixels. fx, fy: Focal lengths in pixels. cx, cy: Principal point coordinates in pixels. position: Camera position in world coordinates (3,). lookat: Target point in world coordinates (3,). up: Up vector in world coordinates (3,). Steps: 1. Initialize Buffer: Create an output image buffer I of shape (H, W, 3) initialized to backgroundcolor. 2. Iterate Gaussians: Loop through each Gaussian g in the cloud. 3. Project Center: Transform the Gaussian center \mug to camera coordinates using PinholeCamera.worldtocamera, then to pixel coordinates using PinholeCamera.cameratopixel. The transformation uses the camera's rotation matrix R and translation t derived from position, lookat, and up. Pixel coordinates are computed as u = \frac{fx \cdot \muc.x}{\muc.z} + cx and v = \frac{fy \cdot \muc.y}{\muc.z} + cy. 4. Culling: Skip the Gaussian if its opacity \alphag < \text{alpha\threshold} or its depth \muc.z is outside [\text{near\plane}, \text{far\plane}]. 5. Project Covariance: Compute the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} by projecting the 3D covariance \Sigmag. This uses the Jacobian J of the perspective projection and the rotation matrix R: \Sigma{2D} = J R \Sigmag R^T J^T. The Jacobian at depth z is J = \begin{bmatrix} fx/z & 0 & -fx \cdot x/z^2 \\ 0 & fy/z & -fy \cdot y/z^2 \end{bmatrix}. 6. Render Ellipse: For each pixel (x, y) within the projected ellipse bounds, calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance D^2 = (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c})^T \Sigma{2D}^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}) where \mathbf{p} = [x, y]^T and \mathbf{c} = [u, v]^T. Compute the 2D Gaussian weight w = \exp(-0.5 \cdot D^2). Compute the final opacity contribution \alpha{final} = \alphag \cdot w. Compute the color Cg from stored RGB or spherical harmonics. Perform alpha blending into the image buffer I at (x, y): I{new} = I{old} \cdot (1 - \alpha{final}) + Cg \cdot \alpha{final}. 7. Finalize: After processing all Gaussians, the image buffer contains the final RGB image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def simplerenderer(gaussians, camera, config): """ Render 3D Gaussians using a CPU-based painter's algorithm. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mean: np.ndarray (3,) cov: np.ndarray (3, 3) opacity: float color: np.ndarray (3,) camera: PinholeCamera object with attributes: width, height, fx, fy, cx, cy position, lookat, up config: RenderConfig object with attributes: backgroundcolor, alphathreshold, nearplane, farplane Returns: np.ndarray: Image buffer (H, W, 3) """ H, W = camera.height, camera.width # Initialize output buffer image = np.full((H, W, 3), config.backgroundcolor, dtype=np.float32) # Compute camera rotation matrix R and translation t zaxis = camera.lookat - camera.position zaxis /= np.linalg.norm(zaxis) xaxis = np.cross(camera.up, zaxis) xaxis /= np.linalg.norm(xaxis) yaxis = np.cross(zaxis, xaxis) R = np.stack([xaxis, yaxis, zaxis], axis=0).T # 3x3 rotation matrix from world to camera t = camera.position # Painter's algorithm requires back-to-front sorting for correct alpha compositing gaussianssorted = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: np.dot(R.T @ (g.mean - t), [0, 0, 1])) for g in gaussianssorted: # 1. Project center to camera coordinates muworld = g.mean mucam = R.T @ (muworld - t) # (3,) depth = mucam[2] # 2. Culling if g.opacity < config.alphathreshold: continue if depth < config.nearplane or depth > config.farplane: continue # 3. Project to pixel coordinates u = (camera.fx mucam[0] / depth) + camera.cx v = (camera.fy mucam[1] / depth) + camera.cy # 4. Project covariance to 2D screen space fx = camera.fx fy = camera.fy J = np.array([ [fx / depth, 0, -fx mucam[0] / (depth2)], [0, fy / depth, -fy mucam[1] / (depth2)] ]) # 2x3 Sigma2D = J @ R @ g.cov @ R.T @ J.T # 2x2 # 5. Determine bounding box for the ellipse eigenvalues, = np.linalg.eigh(Sigma2D) radiusx = 3.0 np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) radiusy = 3.0 np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) minx = int(max(0, u - radiusx)) maxx = int(min(W - 1, u + radiusx)) miny = int(max(0, v - radiusy)) maxy = int(min(H - 1, v + radiusy)) if minx > maxx or miny > maxy: continue # 6. Render ellipse try: Sigma2Dinv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2D) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): p = np.array([x - u, y - v]) D2 = p @ Sigma2Dinv @ p weight = np.exp(-0.5 D2) alphafinal = g.opacity weight if alphafinal < 1e-6: continue color = g.color # Alpha blending image[y, x] = image[y, x] (1.0 - alphafinal) + color alphafinal return image Parameters: alphathreshold: Default 0.01. Gaussians below this opacity are skipped. nearplane: Default 0.1. farplane: Default 50.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point precision issues may arise when computing the inverse of \Sigma{2D} if the Gaussian is degenerate (e.g., very thin or flat). Boundaries: The bounding box calculation must be clamped to the image dimensions [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] to avoid out-of-bounds access. Non-differentiable: This method is not differentiable and cannot be used for training. Uses transmittance culling to skip Gaussians that do not contribute significantly to the final pixel color, improving performance over simple alpha blending. Focuses on the correct projection of 3D Gaussians to 2D and sorting them by depth to ensure correct alpha compositing order, which SimpleRenderer approximates or ignores depending on implementation. A specialized renderer for Gaussian Splatting, likely using different optimization techniques for specific use cases. A variant that assumes constant opacity for depth rendering, simplifying the compositing process. A GPU-optimized method using tiles and radix sort for efficient Gaussian sorting and rendering, contrasting with SimpleRenderer's CPU-based approach. Allows overriding camera poses for rendering, useful for debugging or specific visualization tasks. Techniques for balancing load in parallel rendering implementations. Uses a half-cosine squared kernel for splatting, which may have different visual properties than the standard Gaussian. Optimizes Gaussian loading and culling using HSPT (Hierarchical Spatial Partitioning Tree). A specific rendering algorithm for Gaussian Splatting. Uses voxel-cell masks for per-fragment rendering decisions. Optimizes rendering by processing only relevant parts of the image. The standard GPU-based rasterization method for 3DGS, which SimpleRenderer replaces for CPU-only environments. A VTK-based mapper for Gaussian points. Renders features associated with Gaussians, not just color. Standardized rendering for 3DGS in glTF. Uses softmax for compositing. A specific variant of 3DGS. Uses stochastic methods for volume rendering. Uses mipmaps for anti-aliasing in Gaussian Splatting. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot B), where N is the number of Gaussians and B is the average number of pixels covered by each Gaussian's bounding box. This is significantly slower than GPU-based tile-based rasterization for large N. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the image buffer. No additional large data structures are required for sorting or tiling. Performance: Suitable for small-scale point clouds and visualization. Not suitable for real-time rendering or large scenes due to CPU limitations. Strengths: No GPU required, simple implementation, easy to debug. Limitations: Slow, non-differentiable, limited to small scenes. When to use: Visualization, debugging, environments without GPU support. When not to use: Training, real-time rendering, large-scale scenes. The method originates from the GaussianScan-Recon repository, which provides a CPU-based rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian point clouds. It was developed to enable visualization and testing without GPU hardware, explicitly noting that real 3DGS training requires a CUDA differentiable rasterizer. name: Custom Shadow Mapping for Satellite Imagery
head: Geometrically consistent shadows, Sun camera shadow mapping
body: This method casts geometrically consistent shadows in 3D Gaussian Splatting by comparing elevation renders from a satellite camera and a "sun camera," avoiding ray marching which is incompatible with splatting primitives. It differs from NeRF-based shadowing (e.g., EO-NeRF) by relying solely on rasterization and elevation comparison rather than volumetric ray marching. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (means \muk, covariances \Sigmak, colors fk, opacities \alphak), satellite camera projection A, sun camera projection S, elevation function E, density parameter \rho, per-camera ambient light coefficient \psi^A, and camera-specific affine color correction \phi^A. Outputs: Final image intensity I{A,S}(u) for each pixel u. Data Structures: Elevation render EA(u) and sun elevation render ES(\tilde{u}) stored as 2D buffers. Steps and Formulas: 1. Assume the sun is a directional light source far from the scene, allowing uniform handling of sun and satellite cameras via an affine camera model. 2. Render the elevation map for the satellite camera A at pixel u using EA(u) = \sum{k=1}^K [E{\muk}] \omega^Ak(u), where [E{\muk}] is the altitude at Gaussian mean \muk and \omega^Ak(u) is the splat weight. Render the sun camera elevation map ES identically. 3. For each pixel u in the satellite camera, localize it to a 3D world point x using locA(u, EA(u)), which solves A(x) = u and E(x) = EA(u). 4. Project x to the sun camera to find the homologous point \tilde{u} = hom{A,S}(u) = S(locA(u, EA(u))). 5. Resample the sun elevation render at \tilde{u} to obtain ES(\tilde{u}). 6. Compute the elevation difference \Delta h{A,S}(u) = ES(hom{A,S}(u)) - EA(u). 7. Compute the shadow darkening coefficient s{A,S}(u) = \min(\exp(-\rho \Delta h{A,S}(u)), 1), modeling attenuation through a homogeneous medium of density \rho. 8. Compute the lighting coefficient l{A,S}(u) = s{A,S}(u) + (1 - s{A,S}(u))\psi^A, where \psi^A prevents in-shadow objects from appearing completely black. 9. Compute the final image intensity I{A,S}(u) = l{A,S}(u) \sum{k=1}^K \phiA(fk)\omega^Ak(u), where \phiA is a camera-specific affine color correction applied to intrinsic primitive colors fk. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshadowmapping(satcam, suncam, gaussians, elevfunc, rho, psiA, phiA): # satcam, suncam: objects with.project(x) -> u and.unproject(u) -> (origin, direction) # gaussians: list of dicts with 'mean', 'color', 'covariance', 'opacity' # elevfunc: callable E(x) -> float altitude (affine) # rho: float density # psiA: float ambient coefficient # phiA: callable affine color correction # Step 2: Render elevation maps satelev = renderelevation(satcam, gaussians, elevfunc) sunelev = renderelevation(suncam, gaussians, elevfunc) H, W = satelev.shape output = zeros((H, W, 3)) # Steps 3-9: Per-pixel shadow computation for y in range(H): for x in range(W): u = (x, y) hsat = satelev[y, x] # Step 3: Localize pixel to 3D rayo, rayd = satcam.unproject(u) # Solve E(rayo + t rayd) = hsat for t (affine intersection) grad = elevfunc.gradient bias = elevfunc.bias denom = dot(grad, rayd) if abs(denom) < 1e-6: continue # Degenerate ray parallel to elevation plane t = (hsat - (dot(grad, rayo) + bias)) / denom x3d = rayo + t rayd # Step 4: Project to sun camera usun = suncam.project(x3d) # Step 5: Resample sun elevation if isinbounds(usun, sunelev.shape): hsun = bilinearsample(sunelev, usun) else: hsun = inf # Outside view implies shadow # Step 6: Elevation difference deltah = hsun - hsat # Step 7: Shadow coefficient s = min(exp(-rho deltah), 1.0) if deltah > 0 else 1.0 # Step 8: Lighting coefficient l = s + (1.0 - s) psiA # Step 9: Final intensity basecolor = zeros(3) for g in gaussians: w = computesplatweight(satcam, g, u) basecolor += phiA(g['color']) w output[y, x] = l basecolor return output def renderelevation(cam, gaussians, elevfunc): H, W = cam.imageshape elevmap = zeros((H, W)) for g in gaussians: u2d = cam.project(g['mean']) if isinbounds(u2d, (H, W)): w = computesplatweight(cam, g, u2d) elevmap += elevfunc(g['mean']) w return elevmap def computesplatweight(cam, g, u): mu2d = cam.project(g['mean']) cov2d = cam.projectcovariance(g['covariance']) delta = mu2d - u sigma = dot(delta, dot(cov2d, delta)) alpha = g['opacity'] return alpha exp(-0.5 sigma) def isinbounds(u, shape): return 0 <= u[0] < shape[1] and 0 <= u[1] < shape[0] def bilinearsample(tex, u): x, y = u x0, y0 = int(floor(x)), int(floor(y)) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 fx, fy = x - x0, y - y0 v00 = tex[y0, x0] v01 = tex[y0, x1] v10 = tex[y1, x0] v11 = tex[y1, x1] return (1-fx)(1-fy)v00 + fx(1-fy)v01 + (1-fx)fyv10 + fxfyv11 Parameters: \rho: Density of the homogeneous medium. Typical value not given in the sources. \psi^A: Per-camera ambient light coefficient. Typical value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision, boundaries, and degenerate input handling. Not given in the sources. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces geometrically consistent shadows; compatible with Gaussian Splatting without requiring ray marching. Limitations: Assumes a directional light source; shadows are determined by elevation comparison rather than full geometric occlusion. When to use: Satellite imagery rendering where solar direction is known and geometric consistency is important. When not to use: Scenes with complex lighting or where elevation is not a reliable proxy for occlusion. This method was introduced in "Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Satellite Image Photogrammetry" (CVPR 2025). It builds on the EO-NeRF shadow mapping concept but adapts it for 3DGS by using elevation renders instead of ray marching. The technique leverages the affine camera model to handle both satellite and sun cameras uniformly.
