name: Bounded Execution of Rasterization
head: BoundedGS Rasterization, Leaf-based Rasterization
body: Bounded Execution of Rasterization (BoundedGS) is a memory-constrained rasterization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that partitions the image into non-overlapping leaves to bound peak memory usage. It solves the problem of high memory peaks during training by processing leaves sequentially, releasing local state after each leaf, and accumulating gradients into a shared buffer. It sets itself apart from its parent Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by explicitly separating the rasterization and projection backward passes, ensuring that rasterization caches do not coexist with projection gradients, thereby reducing the mean working set significantly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients), camera view v, rasterization budget L{rast}, minimum leaf size (16x16 pixels). Outputs: Rendered image, accumulated projected gradients for optimizer update. Data Structures: Leaf Tree: A CPU-cached tree structure storing leaf boundaries per camera. Nodes represent regions of the image, subdivided based on measured Gaussian-tile intersection load estimates. Shared Projected-Gradient Buffer: A global buffer accumulating gradients from all leaves for a single view before the optimizer step. Local Leaf State: Per-leaf buffers for intersections, sorting, pixel compositing, checkpoints, output, and loss. These are allocated and released per leaf. Parameters: L{rast}: Rasterization budget. The maximum allowed memory for intersection, sorting, pixel, checkpoint, and output buffers for a single leaf. Regions exceeding this budget are split. Minimum leaf size: 16x16 pixels. Leaves are subdivided down to this size if they exceed the rasterization budget. Auto Leaf Budget: 384 MiB. A specific configuration for load-subdivided leaves to manage memory. Steps: 1. Leaf Partitioning (Pre-computation): 1. Count Gaussian-tile intersections for the current view. 2. Estimate rasterization allocations for potential leaf regions without materializing or sorting the intersection lists, combining intersection counts with pixel counts and buffer layout. 3. Identify regions where the estimated allocation exceeds L{rast}. 4. Split these regions along tile boundaries to form smaller leaves. 5. Subdivide until the estimated allocation fits within L{rast} or the minimum leaf size (16x16 pixels) is reached. 6. Cache the resulting CPU tree of leaf boundaries for the camera. On later visits, recount load, further split leaves above budget, and merge siblings if their combined and parent estimates pass a conservative test. 2. Sequential Leaf Processing: For each leaf \ell in the view v: 1. Generate Intersections: Identify Gaussians affecting the leaf's bounding box. 2. Sort: Sort the intersections for the leaf (e.g., by depth or opacity). 3. Composite: Compute pixel colors for the leaf's pixels using the sorted Gaussians. 4. Compute Loss and Backward: Compute the local loss for the leaf. Compute local backward contributions (gradients). Apply weight w\ell = P\ell / Pv to the additive L1 loss term, where P\ell is the number of pixels in leaf \ell and Pv is the total pixels in view v, to preserve the full-image pixel mean. Note: SSIM is computed using independent leaf windows, so its boundary treatment differs from full-image SSIM and changes with leaf layout. 5. Accumulate Gradients: Add the computed projected gradients to the shared projected-gradient buffer. 6. Release State: Release all local state for leaf \ell, including intersection, sorting, pixel, checkpoint, output, and loss buffers. 3. Optimizer Update: After all leaves in view v are processed: 1. Perform the projection backward pass using the accumulated projected gradients. 2. Execute one optimizer update using the accumulated gradients. Parameters remain fixed during the leaf processing phase. Formulas: Leaf Weight: w\ell = P\ell / Pv. Peak Rasterization/Loss State for View v: B^{leaf}v = \max{\ell \in Rv} B\ell, where Rv is the set of leaves for view v and B\ell is the peak state local to leaf \ell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundedexecutionrasterization(gaussians, camera, Lrast, minleafsize=16): # 1. Leaf Partitioning (Pre-computation) # Count Gaussian-tile intersections and estimate allocations without materializing lists # Split regions exceeding Lrast along tile boundaries down to minleafsize # Cache CPU tree of leaf boundaries per camera leaftree = buildleaftree(gaussians, camera, Lrast, minleafsize) # Constructs tree from intersection counts and buffer layout estimates # Shared projected-gradient buffer for the view sharedgradients = allocatesharedgradientbuffer() # Initializes zero buffer matching Gaussian attribute dimensions # 2. Sequential Leaf Processing for leaf in leaftree: # Generate intersections for Gaussians affecting leaf bounding box intersections = [g for g in gaussians if intersectsbbox(g, leaf.bbox)] # Standard AABB overlap check # Sort intersections (e.g., by depth or opacity) sortedintersections = sortintersections(intersections) # Standard depth/opacity sort # Composite pixels for the leaf leafpixels = compositepixels(sortedintersections, leaf.bbox, camera) # Alpha compositing loop over leaf pixels # Compute local loss and backward contributions localloss = computeloss(leafpixels, leaf.target) # L1/SSIM computation localgradients = computebackward(localloss, leafpixels, sortedintersections) # Backprop through compositing # Weight for L1 loss preservation: wl = Pl / Pv Pleaf = leaf.pixelcount Pview = camera.imagewidth camera.imageheight wleaf = Pleaf / Pview # Apply weight to L1 component if applicable # Note: SSIM uses independent leaf windows, boundary treatment differs from full-image SSIM # Accumulate gradients to shared buffer accumulategradients(sharedgradients, localgradients) # Element-wise addition to shared buffer # Release local state for leaf releaselocalstate(intersections, sortedintersections, leafpixels, localloss, localgradients) # Frees per-leaf memory # 3. Optimizer Update # Perform projection backward pass using accumulated projected gradients projectiongradients = computeprojectionbackward(sharedgradients) # Backprop through camera projection matrices # Execute one optimizer update using accumulated gradients optimizer.step(projectiongradients) # Standard parameter update (e.g., Adam) # Release shared buffer releasesharedbuffer(sharedgradients) # Frees shared memory return renderedimage # Final composited image def buildleaftree(gaussians, camera, Lrast, minleafsize): # Count intersections, estimate memory, split along tile boundaries, cache tree pass def allocatesharedgradientbuffer(): pass def intersectsbbox(g, bbox): return True # Standard check def sortintersections(intersections): return sorted(intersections) # Standard sort def compositepixels(intersections, bbox, camera): return [] # Alpha compositing def computeloss(pixels, target): return 0.0 # L1/SSIM def computebackward(loss, pixels, intersections): return {} # Backprop def accumulategradients(shared, local): pass # Add def releaselocalstate(args): pass # Free def computeprojectionbackward(shared): return {} # Backprop projection def releasesharedbuffer(buf): pass # Free A load-subdivided 384 MiB leaf structure that manages rasterization memory to expose subsequent memory peaks. It is added to the pipeline after stage separation. In the Bicycle 15K model, this variant reduces the mean working set to 5.05 GiB. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduces peak memory usage. By processing leaves sequentially and releasing state, the peak rasterization/loss state is bounded by the largest leaf's requirement (B^{leaf}v = \max{\ell \in Rv} B\ell). Measured Performance: In ablation studies on 5K outdoor scenes, the complete BoundedGS configuration (with 384 MiB Auto Leaf and compact gradients) reduced the mean working set from 9.98 GiB (Original) to 1.66 GiB, a reduction of 83.3%. Time decreased from 12.19s to 10.46s (14.2% reduction). Scaling: At higher resolutions, a fixed budget distributes added pixels and intersections among more sequential leaves, maintaining bounded principal raster allocations. Strengths: Enables high-resolution training by preventing memory overflow. Separates rasterization and projection peaks, allowing for better memory management. Limitations: SSIM boundary treatment differs from full-image SSIM due to independent leaf windows, though final quality is evaluated on complete images. Requires pre-computation of leaf trees, which may add overhead if Gaussians change frequently (though only layout is cached). When to Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models at high resolutions where memory is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When memory is not a constraint and the overhead of leaf management is undesirable, or when real-time inference with minimal latency is required (though this method is primarily for training). BoundedGS was introduced in the paper "BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of original rasterization methods where rasterization, projection, and parameter gradients coexist, leading to high memory peaks (e.g., 9.98 GiB). The method builds on the concept of tiled rasterization but introduces leaf-based partitioning and stage separation to bound memory usage. name: CoherentRaster Rasterization Pipeline
head: CoherentRaster, Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting for Light Field Displays
body: CoherentRaster is a GPU-parallel rasterization pipeline designed for efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting on light field displays (LFDs), synthesizing interlaced light field images by separating view-dependent attributes from cluster-shared ones. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [13469-3d-gaussian-splatting-gpu.md] and tiled variants [2061-tiled-2d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md] by employing Cross-view Coherent Attribute Reuse to eliminate redundant projection computations and View-coherent Remapping to enable coalesced memory accesses during alpha blending. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N 3D Gaussians (defined by 3D mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity oi, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color); a set of target viewpoints \mathcal{V} = \{vj\}{j=0}^{N-1}; a tile grid \mathcal{T} (default 32x32 pixels); cluster size |\mathcal{V}k|. Outputs: An interlaced light field image \mathbf{I}{LF} of resolution W \times H \times 3 (subpixels). Data Structures: Viewpoint Clusters: The viewpoints \mathcal{V} are uniformly partitioned into K disjoint clusters \{\mathcal{V}k\}{k=0}^{K-1}. Cameras are indexed sequentially along the viewing trajectory and grouped into contiguous clusters. If N is not divisible by cluster size, the final cluster is padded by duplicating the last camera v{N-1}. Sorting Key Buffer (\mathcal{P}): Stores tuples of <key, Gaussian Index i>. Sorted List (\mathcal{L}): The result of sorting \mathcal{P}, containing Gaussian indices ordered by key. Attribute Buffers: Per-view 2D means: \mu{i,j}^{2D} for each Gaussian i and view j. Cluster-shared attributes: 2D covariance \Sigma{i,k}^{2D}, depth d{i,k}, and color \mathbf{c}{i,k} for each Gaussian i and cluster k. Parameters: BitK: The number of bits required to represent the maximum Cluster ID K. Not explicitly given in sources, but implied by the key layout formula. Tile Size: Default 32x32 pixels, inherited from tiled rasterization [2061-tiled-2d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md]. Numbered Steps: 1. Viewpoint Clustering: Partition \mathcal{V} into K clusters \mathcal{V}k. Define the cluster center v'k as the viewpoint at index \lfloor |\mathcal{V}k|/2 \rfloor within the clustered sequence. 2. Stage 1: Projection with Cross-view Coherent Attribute Reuse: Initialize buffers for \mu{i,j}^{2D}, \Sigma{i,k}^{2D}, d{i,k}, and \mathbf{c}{i,k}. Per-view Means: Launch M \times N threads (where M is number of Gaussians, N is number of views). Thread r computes \mu{i,j}^{2D} = \Pi{\text{mean}}(vj; \mui), projecting the 3D mean to 2D screen space for view vj. Cluster-shared Attributes: Launch M \times K threads. Thread r computes \Sigma{i,k}^{2D}, d{i,k}, and \mathbf{c}{i,k} using the cluster center v'k: \Sigma{i,k}^{2D}, d{i,k}, \mathbf{c}{i,k} = \Pi{\text{cov,depth,SH}}(v'k; \Sigmai, \text{SH}i). These attributes are reused for all views j \in \mathcal{V}k. 3. Stage 2: Key Generation: Initialize empty buffer \mathcal{P}. Launch M \times K threads. Thread r retrieves Gaussian index i and cluster index k. Call GenerateKeys (see Subroutine below) to produce keys K{i,k} and save <key, i> to \mathcal{P}. 4. Sorting: Sort the buffer \mathcal{P} using the generated keys to produce the ordered list \mathcal{L}. 5. Stage 4: Alpha Blending with View-coherent Remapping: Initialize output image \mathbf{I}{LF}. Launch W \times H \times 3 pixel threads. Thread r obtains remapped coordinate \hat{x} = \Psi{\text{remap}}(r). Identify tile ID t from \hat{x}. Identify per-subpixel viewpoint index j = V[\hat{x}] and cluster ID k = \text{GetClusterID}(j). Identify Gaussian list range [S{t,k}, E{t,k}] for tile t and cluster k via IdentifyGaussianList on \mathcal{L}. Initialize accumulator p = 0. Loop e from S{t,k} to E{t,k} - 1: Retrieve Gaussian index i = \mathcal{L}[e]. Compute p = \text{BlendColor}(p, \hat{x}, \mu{i,j}^{2D}, \Sigma{i,k}^{2D}, \mathbf{c}{i,k}, oi). Set \mathbf{I}{LF}[\hat{x}] = p. Subroutines: GenerateKeys(\mu^{2D}, \Sigma^{2D}, d, \mathcal{T}, r): 1. i, k \leftarrow \text{GetIndex}(r) 2. \mathcal{T}{i,k} \leftarrow \emptyset // Merge tiles over all views in cluster \mathcal{V}k 3. For l from 0 to |\mathcal{V}k| - 1: a. j \leftarrow \text{GetViewpointIndex}(k, l) b. \text{region} \leftarrow \text{ComputeRegionAccuTile}(\mu{i,j}^{2D}, \Sigma{i,k}^{2D}) c. For each tile t \in \mathcal{T} overlapped by region: i. \mathcal{T}{i,k} \leftarrow \mathcal{T}{i,k} \cup \{t\} 4. \mathcal{K}{i,k} \leftarrow \emptyset 5. For each t \in \mathcal{T}{i,k}: a. \text{key} \leftarrow (t \ll (32 + \text{Bit}K)) \mid (k \ll 32) \mid \overline{d{i,k}} b. Append <key, i> to \mathcal{K}{i,k} 6. Return \mathcal{K}{i,k} Sorting Key Layout: The sorting key is constructed as: \text{key} = (t \ll (32 + \text{Bit}K)) \mid (k \ll 32) \mid \overline{d{i,k}} where t is Tile ID, k is Cluster ID, and \overline{d{i,k}} is the bitwise integer representation of depth d{i,k}. This layout sorts Gaussians primarily by spatial location (tile), then by cluster, and finally by depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Artifacts: Cross-view Coherent Attribute Reuse can introduce artifacts on highly specular surfaces due to angular deviation within clusters. This is mitigated in practice by high angular density sampling in commercial Light Field Displays and the natural attenuation of high-frequency specular components by spherical harmonics. Cluster Padding: If the number of viewpoints N is not perfectly divisible by the cluster size, the final cluster must be padded by duplicating the last camera v{N-1}. Time Complexity: The method reduces projection, key generation, and sorting times by eliminating redundant computations via attribute reuse. It decreases blending time by enabling coalesced memory accesses via view-coherent remapping. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduces VRAM usage compared to baselines without reuse/remapping by storing cluster-shared attributes once per cluster instead of per view. Measured Performance (RTX 3090, 6MB L2 Cache): Synthetic Blender 2K: 36 FPS, 3.01GB VRAM, 15.6M Gaussian-tile pairs, 4.45ms blending time. Synthetic Blender 4K: 23 FPS. Mip-NeRF 360 2K: 12 FPS. Mip-NeRF 360 4K: 6.0 FPS, 5.01GB VRAM, 129.7M Gaussian-tile pairs, 32.41ms blending time. Comparison: Outperforms 3DGS (batch=18) which achieves 8.5, 5.4, 3.1, and 1.7 FPS on the respective resolutions. Compared to 'Ours w/o Reuse w/o Remap' on Synthetic Blender 2K, it reduces VRAM from 4.22GB to 3.01GB and blending time from 15.73ms to 4.45ms. On Mip-NeRF 360 4K, it reduces VRAM from 18.12GB to 5.01GB and blending time from 67.43ms to 32.41ms. CoherentRaster was introduced in the paper "CoherentRaster: Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting for Light Field Displays". It addresses the computational bottleneck of rendering 3D Gaussian Splats for light field displays, which require synthesizing multiple viewpoints per pixel. The method builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer [13469-3d-gaussian-splatting-gpu.md] and tiled rasterization techniques [2061-tiled-2d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md]. CoherentRaster: Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting for Light Field Displays, https://doi.org/10.1145/3799902.3811217, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Rasterizing Depth for Gaussian Splats
head: RaDe-GS depth, Spatially varying depth
body: A method to compute a spatially varying depth within the projected 2D Gaussian, rather than using a constant depth per Gaussian splat, to capture shape details. Standard Gaussian Splatting evaluates the depth of each 2D Gaussian by its center to sort them for alpha blending; this constant depth cannot capture shape details. This method derives a rasterized formula for efficient evaluation of spatially varying depths within a projected Gaussian. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (center \mathbf{x}c, covariance \Sigma), camera parameters (center \mathbf{o}, extrinsics), pixel coordinates (u, v). Outputs: Depth d for the pixel (u, v) relative to the Gaussian splat. Data Structures: Ray Space Coordinates: A point \mathbf{u} = (u, v, t)^\top where (u, v) are image plane coordinates and t is the distance between the point and the uv-plane (t = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} in camera space, mapped to ray space). Transformed Center: \mathbf{u}c = (uc, vc, tc)^\top. Transformed Covariance: \Sigma', the covariance matrix transformed into ray space. Pre-computed Vectors: \hat{\mathbf{q}}: A 1 \times 3 vector defined as \hat{\mathbf{q}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}'^\top \Sigma'^{-1}}{\mathbf{v}'^\top \Sigma'^{-1}\mathbf{v}'}, where \mathbf{v}' = (0, 0, 1)^\top. \hat{\mathbf{p}}: A 1 \times 3 vector defined as \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \frac{zc}{tc} \hat{\mathbf{q}}, where zc is the z-coordinate of the Gaussian center in camera space. \mathbf{p}: A 1 \times 2 vector derived from \hat{\mathbf{p}} by skipping the third element. Steps: 1. Transform to Ray Space: Transform the Gaussian center \mathbf{x}c and covariance \Sigma from camera space to ray space, resulting in \mathbf{u}c = (uc, vc, tc)^\top and \Sigma'. In ray space, the light ray direction is normalized to \mathbf{v}' = (0, 0, 1)^\top. 2. Compute Pre-computed Vectors: Calculate \hat{\mathbf{q}} and \hat{\mathbf{p}} for the Gaussian splat. \hat{\mathbf{q}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}'^\top \Sigma'^{-1}}{\mathbf{v}'^\top \Sigma'^{-1}\mathbf{v}'} \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \frac{zc}{tc} \hat{\mathbf{q}} \mathbf{p} consists of the first two elements of \hat{\mathbf{p}}. 3. Calculate Relative Pixel Position: For a pixel (u, v), compute \Delta u = uc - u and \Delta v = vc - v. 4. Compute Depth: Use the rasterized depth formula: d = zc + \mathbf{p} \begin{pmatrix} \Delta u \\ \Delta v \end{pmatrix} Alternatively, using the full vector form: d = \hat{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{u}c - \mathbf{u}o) = \hat{\mathbf{p}} \begin{pmatrix} uc - u \\ vc - v \\ tc \end{pmatrix} where \mathbf{u}o = (u, v, 0)^\top. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizedepthgaussian(u, v, uc, vc, tc, zc, Sigmaprimeinv): """ Compute spatially varying depth for a pixel (u, v) covered by a Gaussian splat. Args: u, v: Pixel coordinates. uc, vc, tc: Ray space coordinates of the Gaussian center. zc: Z-coordinate of the Gaussian center in camera space. Sigmaprimeinv: Inverse of the transformed covariance matrix in ray space (3x3). Returns: d: Depth value. """ # Define ray direction in ray space vprime = [0, 0, 1] # Compute v'^T Sigma'^-1 vTSigmainv = [ sum(vprime[k] Sigmaprimeinv[k][0] for k in range(3)), sum(vprime[k] Sigmaprimeinv[k][1] for k in range(3)), sum(vprime[k] Sigmaprimeinv[k][2] for k in range(3)) ] # Compute v'^T Sigma'^-1 v' vTSigmainvv = sum(vTSigmainv[k] vprime[k] for k in range(3)) # Compute qhat (1x3 vector) # qhat = (v'^T Sigma'^-1) / (v'^T Sigma'^-1 v') qhat = [val / vTSigmainvv for val in vTSigmainv] # Compute phat (1x3 vector) # phat = (zc / tc) qhat phat = [val (zc / tc) for val in qhat] # Compute p (1x2 vector) by skipping the third element of phat p = [phat[0], phat[1]] # Compute relative pixel positions deltau = uc - u deltav = vc - v # Compute depth # d = zc + p [deltau, deltav]^T d = zc + p[0] deltau + p[1] deltav return d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The derivation assumes local affine projection. Boundaries: The method is valid for pixels (u, v) covered by the projected Gaussian. Degenerate Input: If tc = 0, the division by tc in \hat{\mathbf{p}} is undefined. This corresponds to the Gaussian center being in the camera plane, which is typically excluded or handled separately in rendering pipelines. Computes surface normal directions projected by a Gaussian splat by deriving the plane equation in ray space for the intersection points. The intersection points form a plane in ray space, and the plane's normal direction is taken as that of the projected Gaussian. The plane equation in ray space is given by (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}c) = \begin{pmatrix} -\Delta u \\ -\Delta v \\ (\Delta u - \Delta v) \mathbf{q}^\top \end{pmatrix}, where \mathbf{q} is the same as \hat{\mathbf{q}} skipping the last component. The normal vector is then transformed from ray space to camera space to compute the normal map. Not given in the sources. name: Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad)
body: Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) is a display-only rendering technique that projects 3D Gaussian distributions into 2D screen-space quads, sorts them by camera-space depth, and renders them using instanced drawing with standard alpha blending. It solves the problem of visualizing large-scale, photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed via Gaussian Splatting on client-side hardware without requiring neural network inference or server-side ray tracing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by utilizing a background worker or CPU-side depth sorting algorithm to resolve the non-commutative nature of alpha blending, whereas the parent 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced) describes the general projection and quad-drawing mechanism without specifying the sorting implementation. Unlike Tiled 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, this method relies on explicit per-splat sorting rather than tile-based accumulation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A depth-sorted index buffer (Uint32Array) mapping instance IDs to splat indices; view-space projection data (position, axes, color, opacity) stored in textures or buffers; camera matrices (Model-View, Projection); screen resolution parameters. Outputs: A composited color buffer with pre-multiplied alpha blending. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer: Contains 8 floats representing a unit quad: [-2, -2, 2, -2, 2, 2, -2, 2]. Index Buffer (Depth Index): A Uint32Array containing the depth-sorted splat indices, updated via worker messages. Splat Texture: Created with gl.RGBA32UI internal format, gl.RGBAINTEGER format, and gl.UNSIGNEDINT type, sized to the render data width and height. For animated or complex variants, additional textures (e.g., splatRotation as RGBA16F) may be used. View Data: Contains per-splat attributes including position, rotation (quaternion), scale, and color (SH degree 0). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the vertex buffer with quad coordinates and the index buffer for sorted splat indices. Initialize the scene, camera, and render data. 2. Sorting (Worker/CPU): Send initial sort data (positions, dummy transforms, transform indices) to a background worker. On each render frame, update the camera and send the view-projection matrix to the worker. The worker computes the depth-sorted order and returns the depthIndex buffer. 3. Setup Blending: Configure the graphics pipeline for alpha blending: gl.blendFuncSeparate(gl.ONEMINUSDSTALPHA, gl.ONE, gl.ONEMINUSDSTALPHA, gl.ONE). 4. Bind Attributes: Bind the index buffer using gl.vertexAttribIPointer with a divisor of 1 to enable instanced drawing. 5. Vertex Shader Execution: Map the instance ID to the splat index using the order buffer: instID = OrderBuffer[instID]. Load view data for the splat: SplatViewData view = SplatViewData[instID]. Check if the splat is behind the camera (centerClipPos.w <= 0). If so, output a NaN vertex (asfloat(0x7fc00000)) to discard the primitive. Transform the voxel position to view space: vec4 voxelPosViewSpace = MV glin[0].glPosition. Transform to clip space and normalize: vec4 voxelPosClipSpace = P voxelPosViewSpace; voxelPosClipSpace /= voxelPosClipSpace.w. Perform clip-space frustum culling. Calculate the voxel offset: voxelOffset = splatSize \times (scale/gridLength) \times \sqrt{2}. Calculate the half-edge length in clip space: voxelHalfEdgeLengthClipSpace = distance(voxelPosClipSpace, voxelRightEdgeMidPointClipSpace). Define the frustum culling border: voxelFrustumCullingBorder = 1 + voxelHalfEdgeLengthClipSpace. Discard if voxelPosClipSpace.x or y is outside [-voxelFrustumCullingBorder, voxelFrustumCullingBorder]. Calculate the quad position in clip space. For WebGL implementations, map instance ID to quad corners: quadPos = float2(idx&1, (idx>>1)&1) 2.0 - 1.0; quadPos = 2.0. Calculate screen delta: deltaScreenPos = (quadPos.x view.axis1 + quadPos.y view.axis2) 2 / ScreenParams.xy. Final vertex: o.vertex.xy += deltaScreenPos centerClipPos.w. (Optional) Handle selection bits if SplatBitsValid is true, marking selected splats with specific color values. 6. Fragment Shader Execution: Calculate the Gaussian falloff: power = -dot(i.pos, i.pos); alpha = exp(power). If not selected, saturate alpha: alpha = saturate(alpha i.col.a). If selected, apply magenta outline logic: if alpha > 7.0/255.0, set alpha = 1 and i.col.rgb = selectedColor if alpha < 10.0/255.0; otherwise alpha = saturate(alpha + 0.3) and tint i.col.rgb = lerp(i.col.rgb, selectedColor, 0.5). Discard fragment if alpha < 1.0/255.0. Output final color: res = half4(i.col.rgb alpha, alpha). 7. Draw Call: Call gl.drawArraysInstanced(gl.TRIANGLEFAN, 0, 4, vertexCount). Formulas: Voxel Offset: voxelOffset = splatSize \times \frac{scale}{gridLength} \times \sqrt{2}. Frustum Culling Border: voxelFrustumCullingBorder = 1 + distance(voxelPosClipSpace, voxelRightEdgeMidPointClipSpace). Gaussian Falloff: \alpha(u, v) = \alpha0 \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(u^2 + v^2)\right) where \alpha0 is the base opacity and (u, v) are normalized screen-space coordinates relative to the splat center. Parameters: ScreenParams.xy: Screen resolution in pixels, used to normalize the screen-space delta of the quad. ufocal: WebGLUniformLocation for camera focal lengths fx, fy. splatCount: The number of splats to render, coerced to the range 0..splatCloud.count. Defaults to the full cloud count. Used for LOD or reveal effects. utime: WebGLUniformLocation for animation time, typically set to Math.sin(Date.now() / 1000) / 2 + 1 / 2. uviewport: WebGLUniformLocation for canvas dimensions [canvas.width, canvas.height]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Behind Camera: Splats with clip-space w \le 0 must be discarded to prevent rendering artifacts. This is handled by outputting a NaN vertex in the vertex shader. Multiple Objects: Multiple Splatv objects are not supported in some implementations (e.g., gsplat.js), triggering a console warning. Worker Initialization: The background worker must be initialized before rendering; checks for renderer.renderProgram.worker === null and returns an error if null. Tone Mapping: The material cancels the View's tone mapping so colors are displayed as stored in the splat data (SH degree 0 only). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vertexshader(instanceid, quadcornerindex, orderbuffer, splatviewdata, mvmatrix, projectionmatrix, splatsize, gridlength, screenparams): # 1. Map instance to splat index splatindex = orderbuffer[instanceid] # 2. Load view data viewdata = splatviewdata[splatindex] # 3. Check behind camera centerclipw = viewdata.centerclippos.w if centerclipw <= 0: return float('nan') # Discard primitive # 4. Transform to view/clip space voxelposview = mvmatrix @ viewdata.position voxelposclip = projectionmatrix @ voxelposview voxelposclip = voxelposclip / voxelposclip.w # 5. Frustum Culling voxeloffset = splatsize (viewdata.scale / gridlength) math.sqrt(2) rightedgemid = projectionmatrix @ (voxelposview.xy + (0.5, 0) voxeloffset) rightedgemid = rightedgemid / rightedgemid.w halfedgelen = math.dist(voxelposclip, rightedgemid) cullingborder = 1.0 + halfedgelen if abs(voxelposclip.x) > cullingborder or abs(voxelposclip.y) > cullingborder: return float('nan') # Discard primitive # 6. Calculate Quad Position # Map quadcornerindex (0-3) to [-2, -2], [2, -2], [2, 2], [-2, 2] quadx = (quadcornerindex & 1) 2.0 - 1.0 quady = ((quadcornerindex >> 1) & 1) 2.0 - 1.0 quadpos = (quadx, quady) 2.0 # Screen delta calculation screendelta = (quadpos[0] viewdata.axis1[0] + quadpos[1] viewdata.axis2[0]) 2.0 / screenparams[0] finalvertex = (voxelposclip.x + screendelta[0], voxelposclip.y + screendelta[1]) return finalvertex def fragmentshader(interpolatedpos, interpolatedcolor, selectedcolor): # Calculate Gaussian falloff power = -sum(p p for p in interpolatedpos) alpha = math.exp(power) # Handle selection if interpolatedcolor.a < 0: # Selected if alpha > 7.0/255.0: if alpha < 10.0/255.0: alpha = 1.0 rgb = selectedcolor # Magenta else: alpha = min(alpha + 0.3, 1.0) rgb = tuple(lerp(a, b, 0.5) for a, b in zip(interpolatedcolor.rgb, selectedcolor)) else: return None # Discard fragment else: # Not selected alpha = min(alpha interpolatedcolor.a, 1.0) rgb = interpolatedcolor.rgb if alpha < 1.0/255.0: return None # Discard fragment return (rgb[0] alpha, rgb[1] alpha, rgb[2] alpha, alpha) WebGL Gaussian Splatting is a real-time rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) implemented in web browsers using WebGL 1.0, with variants utilizing the Three.js library or running without external dependencies. It solves the problem of displaying large-scale, photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed via Gaussian Splatting on client-side hardware without requiring neural network inference or server-side ray tracing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by utilizing a CPU-side depth sorting algorithm (often offloaded to a Web Worker) to resolve the non-commutative nature of alpha blending, whereas the parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) describes the general projection and quad-drawing mechanism without specifying the sorting implementation. Unlike Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering), this method typically omits spherical harmonics to reduce file size and memory footprint for web delivery. Debug Splat Point Rendering is a diagnostic visualization technique that renders individual 3D Gaussian splats as small screen-space quads centered at their projected positions. Unlike the production rendering path which draws full elliptical splats for opacity blending, this method isolates the center location and basic attributes of each splat, allowing developers to inspect splat distribution, density, and attribute correctness. It serves as a lightweight alternative to full splat rendering for verifying the correctness of the splat data pipeline and camera projection logic. This method configures the GPU render pass by populating a material property block (or uniform buffer) with splat count, spherical harmonic (SH) degree, brightness, scale, antialiasing settings, transform matrices, and optional skinning or volume lighting data. It solves the problem of efficiently passing per-renderer and global state to the fragment shader without causing state overwrites in multi-camera setups or shader compilation errors when optional features (like skinning) are disabled. It differs from standard mesh rendering by explicitly handling the decoupling of jittered projections and ensuring valid sampled resources even for unused features. Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering) is a GPU-accelerated rendering method for time-varying 3D Gaussian splats that computes time-dependent position, rotation, and scale deltas from packed texture data to enable smooth animation without per-frame CPU updates. It differs from static 3D Gaussian Splatting by evaluating polynomial motion deltas and applying temporal opacity decay in the vertex and fragment shaders, building on the screen-space quad rendering of Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad). Oriented Ellipse Splatting renders each Gaussian splat as an oriented ellipse in screen space, derived from its 3D rotation and 3-axis scale projected to a 2D covariance matrix, replacing the previous method of drawing round blobs sized by the largest axis. This approach improves visual fidelity by eliminating the "hazy" appearance of isotropic billboards and reduces overdraw, resulting in crisp edges and equal or better frame times. It differs from its parent Gaussian Splat Fragment Shader by explicitly computing the bounding quad from the covariance eigenvectors and evaluating the Gaussian kernel over the full anisotropic shape rather than a circular disc. The Gaussian Splat Vertex Shader transforms 3D Gaussian primitives into screen-space quads by computing their projected 2D covariance and conic parameters. It determines the bounding box of each splat in screen space and passes the necessary data to the fragment shader for alpha blending. It differs from sibling methods by handling the full projection pipeline (view-space to screen-space covariance) and degenerate case culling within the vertex stage, relying on the parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) for the quad assembly and transparency handling. A Unity Universal Render Pipeline (URP) ScriptableRendererFeature that renders pre-sorted 3D Gaussian splats into a temporary render target and composites the result onto the camera color buffer. It differs from raw shader implementations by integrating into the URP render graph, handling XR multipass separation, and managing the intermediate render target lifecycle automatically. Decoupled Appearance Modeling is a post-processing module that handles appearance variations, such as uneven illumination, by generating a per-pixel transformation map to adjust rendered images without modifying the underlying 3D Gaussian representation. It prevents the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) optimizer from creating "floaters" (spurious geometry) to compensate for photometric changes between training views. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex neural radiance fields or MLPs for appearance, this method uses a lightweight CNN to learn a residual appearance adjustment, allowing the 3D Gaussians to converge to a consistent average appearance and correct geometry. A rendering method for Gaussian splats that computes anisotropic covariance matrices to handle perspective distortion and view-dependent scaling, improving edge crispness and reducing haze compared to isotropic approximations. In the vertex shader, it computes the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma3 = R \cdot S^2 \cdot R^T, transforms it to view space, computes the perspective Jacobian J, applies a low-pass filter (+0.3 \text{ px}^2) to \Sigma2, and eigen-decomposes it to place quad corners at \text{centre} \pm 3\sqrt{\lambda}v. It requires a third RGBA16F texture (splatRotation) for quaternions. A rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting where each splat is rendered as an isotropic billboard (circle) using the maximum of the three axis scales, ignoring the rotation for the shape geometry. This results in a hazy, over-bright appearance (the 'P1 isotropic artefact'). It fetches per-splat data from two RGBA16F textures, determines billboard size using max axis scale, and renders as hardware-instanced camera-facing quads with batches of at most 65535 instances per draw call. Sorting complexity is O(n \log n) on the CPU. A rendering technique that projects 3D Gaussian ellipses onto the screen space by computing a 2x2 covariance matrix, allowing for accurate anisotropic rendering of splats as ellipses rather than circles. It computes \Sigma = R \cdot S \cdot S^T \cdot R^T, projects it using the view Jacobian, eigen-decomposes to find major/minor axes, and places quad corners on these axes. It differs from isotropic rendering by using the full covariance matrix, reducing overdraw and providing a sharper image. It requires a third RGBA16F texture for rotation/scale data. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(n \log n) on the CPU. Rendering is O(n) for the draw call, but fragment processing is proportional to the number of overlapping pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for splat data (positions, rotations, scales, colors) and the sorted index buffer. For 233k splats, sorting involves ~5.6 MB of texture re-upload per frame. Measured Performance: On mid-range phones, fill rate and overdraw dominate performance. Anisotropic ellipses reduce overdraw compared to max-axis discs, offering a performance win. The CPU sort is feasible up to ~300–500k splats; beyond that, LOD/pruning is needed. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard graphics APIs (WebGL, Unity URP); leverages existing instanced drawing capabilities; effective for real-time web and mobile visualization. Limitations: CPU sorting becomes a bottleneck at very high splat counts (>500k); isotropic variants suffer from visual artifacts (haze); multiple Splatv objects are not supported in some WebGL implementations. When to Use: Real-time visualization of Gaussian Splatting scenes in web browsers (WebGL) or Unity URP environments where background worker or CPU sorting is acceptable. When Not to Use: Scenes with millions of splats requiring real-time performance without LOD; platforms where CPU sorting is too slow or unavailable (e.g., pure GPU sorting required). Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) is a rendering technique identical in geometry generation to Circle Splat, used for Gaussian Splat visualization, projecting voxels as 2D quads. It is used in gsplat.js for real-time WebGL rendering of Gaussian splats. The method builds on the general 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, adapting it for screen-space quad rendering with background worker sorting. It is commonly used in web-based viewers (e.g., gsplat.js) and Unity URP implementations. mmalesadev/svorenderer, https://github.com/mmalesadev/svorenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, https://github.com/aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) huggingface/gsplat.js, https://github.com/huggingface/gsplat.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(sceneview): sort splats for the scene camera by default and add …, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/5f2a4dd1f683ddb444669be54b78ce7913b55b70, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Explore: Gaussian splatting, OpenUSD, AI world generation, volumetric video — study, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/issues/4023, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, https://github.com/YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) feat(sceneview): sort splats for the scene camera by default and add …, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/5f2a4dd1f683ddb444669be54b78ce7913b55b70, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Explore: Gaussian splatting, OpenUSD, AI world generation, volumetric video — study, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/issues/4023, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: WebGL Gaussian Splatting
head: Gaussian Splat Rendering Pipeline, Gaussian Splatting Web Rendering (Three.js), Gaussian Splatting WebGL, Three.js Gaussian Splatting, Web-based 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering, WebGL 1.0 Gaussian Splatting
body: WebGL Gaussian Splatting is a real-time rendering technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) implemented in web browsers using WebGL 1.0, with variants utilizing the Three.js library or running without external dependencies. It solves the problem of displaying large-scale, photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed via Gaussian Splatting on client-side hardware without requiring neural network inference or server-side ray tracing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by utilizing a CPU-side depth sorting algorithm (often offloaded to a Web Worker) to resolve the non-commutative nature of alpha blending, whereas the parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) describes the general projection and quad-drawing mechanism without specifying the sorting implementation. Unlike Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering), this method typically omits spherical harmonics to reduce file size and memory footprint for web delivery. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary.splat file containing N Gaussian primitives. Each primitive consists of a 3D center, 3D scale, a quaternion stored as 4 bytes (normalized by subtracting 128 and dividing by 128.0, with the z-component negated), and color/alpha data. Output: A 2D screen image rendered via WebGL 1.0 drawElements or drawArrays with instanced rendering, using custom vertex and fragment shaders. Data Structures: The implementation typically uses InstancedBufferGeometry in Three.js. The layout per vertex in the raw.splat file is 32 bytes: 1. center: 3 Float32 (12 bytes, offset 0). 2. scale: 3 Float32 (12 bytes, offset 12). 3. color/alpha: 4 Uint8 (R, G, B, A, offset 24). 4. quaternion: 4 Uint8 (x, y, z, w, offset 28). In the GPU buffers, these are unpacked into: splatColor: Float32Array of size 4N (RGBA, normalized to [0,1]). splatCenterCovariance: Float32Array of size 9N. The covariance matrix \mathbf{V}{rk} is stored as 3 vec3s: [0] is the center, [1] is (M{11}, M{12}, M{13}), [2] is (M{22}, M{23}, M{33}). position: Float32Array of size 18 (6 components for 4 vertices, including duplicates for triangle rendering) defining a quad with corners (2,2,0), (-2,2,0), (-2,-2,0), (2,-2,0). Numbered Steps: 1. Data Parsing and Matrix Construction: Parse the.splat file. For each vertex i: Extract center from fbuffer[8i+0..2], scale from fbuffer[8i+3+0..2], quaternion from ubuffer[32i+28..31] (normalized by subtracting 128 and dividing by 128.0, with z-component negated), and color/alpha from ubuffer[32i+24..27] (divided by 255). Construct a 4 \times 4 instance matrix \mathbf{M}i. Compute rotation matrix \mathbf{R} from q. Scale by scale vector. The matrix is constructed as \mathbf{M}i = \mathbf{R}^T \cdot \text{Scale} \cdot \mathbf{R} \cdot \text{Translate}(\text{center}). Encode color/alpha into matrix elements 3, 7, 11, 15. 2. Depth Sorting (CPU): Calculate depth for each splat using the view vector \mathbf{v}{view} (camera forward direction from camera.matrixWorld elements 2, 6, 10): \text{depth}i = \mathbf{v}{view}[0] \cdot \mathbf{M}i[12] - \mathbf{v}{view}[1] \cdot \mathbf{M}i[13] - \mathbf{v}{view}[2] \cdot \mathbf{M}i[14] Perform a 16-bit single-pass counting sort to reorder indices based on depth. Compute depthInv = (65535)/(maxDepth-minDepth), bin = ((depth-minDepth)depthInv)|0, count bins, compute starts, and place indices in depthIndex array. Reorder the instance matrices and attributes into sortedMatrices and sortedAttributes. This step is often offloaded to a Web Worker to prevent blocking the main thread. 3. Vertex Shader Execution: For each instance (splat) and each vertex of the quad: Frustum Culling: Compute clip-space position \mathbf{pos}{2d} = \text{realProjectionMatrix} \cdot \text{viewMatrix} \cdot \text{vec4}(\text{splatCenter}, 1). Let w = \mathbf{pos}{2d}.w. If \mathbf{pos}{2d}.z < -w or |\mathbf{pos}{2d}.x| > 1.2w or |\mathbf{pos}{2d}.y| > 1.2w, discard the primitive by setting glPosition to (0,0,2,1). Covariance Projection: Compute focal length: focal = \frac{\text{size}.y}{2.0 \cdot \tan(\frac{\text{camera.fov} \cdot \pi}{360.0})}. Compute Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projection at the splat center \mathbf{c} in camera space \mathbf{c}{cam}: \mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{fx}{cz} & 0 & -\frac{fx cx}{cz^2} \\ 0 & \frac{fy}{cz} & -\frac{fy cy}{cz^2} \end{bmatrix} Compute transformation \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{J}, where \mathbf{W} is the rotation part of the view matrix (transpose of the upper-left 3x3 of viewMatrix). Compute 2D covariance \mathbf{cov}{2D} = \mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{V}{rk} \mathbf{T}. Regularize: \mathbf{cov}{00} \leftarrow \mathbf{cov}{00} + 0.3, \mathbf{cov}{11} \leftarrow \mathbf{cov}{11} + 0.3. Eigenvalue Decomposition: diagonal1 = \mathbf{cov}{00}, diagonal2 = \mathbf{cov}{11}, offDiagonal = \mathbf{cov}{01}. mid = 0.5(diagonal1 + diagonal2). radius = \sqrt{(\frac{diagonal1 - diagonal2}{2})^2 + offDiagonal^2}. \lambda1 = mid + radius. \lambda2 = \max(mid - radius, 0.1). Basis Vectors: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(offDiagonal, \lambda1 - diagonal1). \mathbf{v}1 = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda1}, 1024.0) \cdot \mathbf{d}. \mathbf{v}2 = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda2}, 1024.0) \cdot \text{vec2}(\mathbf{d}.y, -\mathbf{d}.x). Position Output: \mathbf{v}{Center} = \frac{\mathbf{pos}{2d}}{w}. \mathbf{p}{screen} = \mathbf{v}{Center} + \frac{x \cdot \mathbf{v}2 + y \cdot \mathbf{v}1}{\text{viewport}} \cdot 2.0. glPosition = \text{vec4}(\mathbf{p}{screen}, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Fragment Shader Execution: Compute distance from fragment center to splat center in local quad space: A = -\mathbf{v}{Position} \cdot \mathbf{v}{Position}. If A < -4.0, discard fragment. Compute alpha: B = e^A \cdot v{Color}.a. Output color: \text{gl\FragColor} = \text{vec4}(B \cdot v{Color}.rgb, B). 5. Blending: Render with depthTest=false, depthWrite=false. Blending function: blendSrc=OneMinusDstAlphaFactor, blendDst=OneFactor, blendSrcAlpha=OneMinusDstAlphaFactor, blendDstAlpha=OneFactor. Parameters: WebGL Version: 1.0. Culling Bound: 1.2 \cdot w. Covariance Regularization: 0.3 added to diagonal elements. Minimum Eigenvalue: 0.1 for \lambda2. Maximum Axis Length: 1024.0 for \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Gaussian Cutoff: Discard if squared distance > 4.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting: Incorrect sorting order leads to visual artifacts due to non-commutative alpha blending. The sorting must be updated every frame as the camera moves. A simpler variant using isotropic point sprites with CPU-side back-to-front sorting to correct blending order, lacking anisotropic covariance and spherical harmonics. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N) with counting sort, but dominated by the constant factor of memory access and worker communication. Rendering is O(N) for draw calls. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing splat data and sorted indices. Performance: Real-time on modern desktop GPUs via WebGL 1.0. Performance scales with the number of splats N and viewport resolution. Strengths: No external dependencies beyond Three.js; works on standard web browsers; efficient on ordinary graphics hardware compared to NeRFs. Limitations: No view-dependent shading (spherical harmonics omitted for file size); limited to WebGL 1.0 features; sorting on CPU can block main thread if not offloaded. When to use: Web-based visualization of static or slowly moving 3DGS scenes. When not to use: High-fidelity view-dependent effects; scenes with extreme depth complexity requiring tile-based rasterization; mobile devices with poor WebGL 1.0 support. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a real-time radiance field rendering technique. WebGL implementations, such as the one by antimatter15, adapted this technique for the web using WebGL 1.0 and Three.js, focusing on efficient point-cloud-like rendering without neural network inference. The method was developed to allow interactive viewing of 3DGS models in browsers without heavy dependencies. antimatter15/splat, https://github.com/antimatter15/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Isotropic Gaussian Point-Sprite Rendering
head: Gaussian-opacity point sprites, Soft Gaussian primitives
body: A rendering technique using isotropic 3D point primitives with a Gaussian alpha falloff in screen space, rendered via custom GLSL shaders. It demonstrates soft Gaussian opacity and transparency but does not implement full 3D Gaussian Splatting (no anisotropic covariance, no spherical harmonics, no GPU tile-based rasterization). It sets itself apart from its sibling WebGL Gaussian Splatting by explicitly implementing a CPU-side back-to-front sort to correct the arbitrary alpha blending order inherent in THREE.Points, whereas the parent article describes the general bounding quad approach without detailing the specific sorting mechanism for isotropic sprites. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A THREE.Points object containing attributes: position (vec3), aColor (vec3), and aRadius (float). Uniforms: uScale (float), uPixelRatio (float), uPointMode (float, 0.0 for Gaussian, 1.0 for hard-edged), uOpacity (float). Output: Screen-space pixels with color and alpha, composited using standard source-over blending. Data Structures: THREE.BufferGeometry with Float32Array attributes for positions, colors, and radii. CPU-side index array for sorting. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Execution: For each point primitive: a. Compute the model-view position: mv = modelViewMatrix vec4(position, 1.0). b. Calculate screen-space radius in pixels: \text{radiusPixels} = \text{aRadius} \times \text{uScale} \times 220.0 \times \text{uPixelRatio} / \max(1.0, -\text{mv.z}). c. Set glPointSize by clamping the radius scaled by the point mode factor: \text{gl\PointSize} = \text{clamp}(\text{radiusPixels} \times \text{mix}(1.0, 0.22, \text{uPointMode}), 1.0, 150.0 \times \text{uPixelRatio}). d. Pass color to fragment shader: vColor = aColor. 2. Fragment Shader Execution: For each fragment covered by the point sprite: a. Compute normalized sprite coordinates: p = glPointCoord 2.0 - 1.0. b. Calculate squared distance from center: r2 = dot(p, p). c. Discard fragment if r2 > 1.0. d. Compute alpha: \alpha = \text{mix}(\exp(-4.5 \times r^2), 1.0, \text{uPointMode}) \times \text{uOpacity}. Where r = \sqrt{r2}. e. Discard fragment if \alpha < 0.008. f. Output glFragColor = vec4(vColor, alpha). 3. CPU-Side Back-to-Front Sorting: To ensure correct transparency compositing: a. Trigger sort when camera changes (dirtySort = true). b. Compute camera depth for each point i using the inverse world matrix M: zi = M{2}xi + M{6}yi + M{10}zi + M{14}. Where M is the 16-element array of camera.matrixWorldInverse.elements, and (xi, yi, zi) are the world-space coordinates of point i. c. Sort indices by zi ascending (more negative is farther). d. Reorder position, aColor, and aRadius arrays in the THREE.BufferGeometry attributes according to the sorted indices. e. Set needsUpdate = true on the attributes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def clamp(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(x, hi)) def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def vec4(x, y, z, w): return [x, y, z, w] def vertexshader(position, aColor, aRadius, modelViewMatrix, uScale, uPixelRatio, uPointMode): # position is vec3, aColor is vec3, aRadius is float mv = [sum(modelViewMatrix[r][c] (position[c] if c < 3 else 1.0) for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)] mvz = mv[2] vColor = aColor glPosition = [sum(mv[c] (projectionMatrix[c][r] if False else 0) for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)] radiuspixels = aRadius uScale 220.0 uPixelRatio / max(1.0, -mvz) scalefactor = mix(1.0, 0.22, uPointMode) glPointSize = clamp(radiuspixels scalefactor, 1.0, 150.0 uPixelRatio) return vColor, glPosition, glPointSize def fragmentshader(vColor, uOpacity, uPointMode, pointcoord): # pointcoord is vec2 in [0, 1] p = [pointcoord[0] 2.0 - 1.0, pointcoord[1] 2.0 - 1.0] r2 = dot(p, p) if r2 > 1.0: return None # discard gaussianalpha = math.exp(-4.5 r2) alpha = mix(gaussianalpha, 1.0, uPointMode) uOpacity if alpha < 0.008: return None # discard return [vColor[0], vColor[1], vColor[2], alpha] # glFragColor def sortbackfront(mflat, positions, colors, radii, count): indices = list(range(count)) def getdepth(idx): i3 = idx 3 return mflat[2]positions[i3] + mflat[6]positions[i3+1] + mflat[10]positions[i3+2] + mflat[14] indices.sort(key=getdepth) for attrname, attr in [("position", positions), ("aColor", colors), ("aRadius", radii)]: if attrname in ("position", "aColor"): newdata = [attr[i3 + k] for i in indices for k in range(3)] else: newdata = [attr[i] for i in indices] attr[:] = newdata needsUpdate = True Parameters: uOpacity: Peak opacity multiplier. Typical value: 1.0. uPointMode: Switch between Gaussian (0.0) and hard-edged (1.0). uScale: Global scale factor for point sizes. uPixelRatio: Device pixel ratio (e.g., 1.0 or 2.0). Sorting Cadence: Performed approximately every 150 ms while the camera is moving. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha Blending Order: Three.js does not automatically sort individual points inside a THREE.Points object. Without sorting, alpha blending order is arbitrary, leading to incorrect transparency. Depth Calculation: The depth zi is computed in view space using the inverse world matrix. More negative values indicate points farther from the camera. Precision: The alpha discard threshold is 0.008. Values below this are discarded to optimize rendering. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N \log N) where N is the number of points. This is performed on the CPU, causing overhead. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing positions, colors, radii, and the index array. Measured Performance: The CPU sort introduces latency, especially with large N. The approximate update cadence (150 ms) mitigates this but results in visual jitter if the camera moves rapidly. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard WebGL point sprites; visually demonstrates Gaussian opacity; works in browsers via Three.js. Limitations: No anisotropic covariance (sprites are always circular); no spherical harmonics (view-independent color); no GPU-based tile rasterization; CPU sorting bottleneck. When to use: Educational demos, simple browser-based visualizations where high performance is not critical. When not to use: Production 3DGS rendering, scenes with millions of points, or when anisotropic splats are required. Originating from an interactive browser-based experiment exploring Gaussian point-sprite rendering with Three.js and custom GLSL shaders. Built as an educational graphics demo to understand the basic visual effect of soft Gaussian primitives and transparency, not as a full 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) implementation. It references Kerbl et al. for the underlying 3DGS concept but explicitly states it does not reconstruct scenes from photos or implement production 3DGS.
