name: Debug Splat Point Rendering
head: Debug Point Rendering, Gaussian Splatting/Debug/Render Points, GaussianDebugRenderPoints, Splat Center Visualization
body: Debug Splat Point Rendering is a diagnostic visualization technique that renders individual 3D Gaussian splats as small screen-space quads centered at their projected positions. Unlike the production rendering path which draws full elliptical splats for opacity blending, this method isolates the center location and basic attributes of each splat, allowing developers to inspect splat distribution and attribute correctness. It serves as a lightweight alternative to full splat rendering for verifying the splat data pipeline and camera projection logic. The method renders one quad per splat using a single draw call with instanced rendering. It bypasses the complex spherical harmonic color evaluation and alpha blending of the main renderer, opting instead for either the raw SH color or a normalized index-based color map. Inputs: Splat Data Buffer: A structured buffer containing splat attributes. Each splat entry includes centerWorldPos (world-space position) and sh.col (spherical harmonic color coefficient). Shader Parameters: SplatSize (float, quad size in screen pixels), DisplayIndex (bool, toggle color mode), and SplatCount (int, total splats for normalization). Outputs: Framebuffer: A 2D image where each splat appears as a small square at its projected center. The vertex shader processes instances using uint vtxID (SVVertexID) and uint instID (SVInstanceID). The fragment shader receives a v2f struct containing half3 color (TEXCOORD0) and float4 vertex (SVPOSITION). 1. Retrieve Splat Data: For each instance, load splat attributes using the instance ID as the buffer index: splat = LoadSplatData(instID). 2. Transform to Clip Space: Transform the splat's world position to clip space to determine the quad center: centerWorld = splat.centerWorldPos, centerWorld = mul(unityObjectToWorld, float4(centerWorld, 1.0)).xyz, centerClip = mul(UNITYMATRIXVP, float4(centerWorld, 1.0)). 3. Generate Quad Geometry: Generate a 2x2 quad in screen space centered on the projected vertex. Calculate a 2D offset vector quadPos based on vtxID: quadPos = float2(vtxID & 1, (vtxID >> 1) & 1) 2.0 - 1.0. 4. Apply Screen-Space Offset: Offset the vertex position in screen space by scaling quadPos with SplatSize, normalizing by ScreenParams.xy, and multiplying by the clip-space W component: offset = quadPos (SplatSize / ScreenParams.xy) centerClip.w. Update vertex XY: outputVertex.xy = centerClip.xy + offset, preserving Z and W. 5. Compute Fragment Color: Determine the color based on DisplayIndex. If false, use raw SH color: color = saturate(splat.sh.col). If true, encode the index into RGB: normalizedIndex = instID / SplatCount, r = frac(normalizedIndex 100), g = frac(normalizedIndex 10), b = normalizedIndex. 6. Output: Pass the computed color and clip-space position to the fragment shader. The fragment shader outputs the interpolated color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vtxid: int, instid: int) -> dict: # Load splat data from buffer using instance ID splat = loadsplatdata(instid) # Transform to clip space centerworld = splat.centerworldpos centerworld = matmul(unityObjectToWorld, float4(centerworld, 1.0)).xyz centerclip = matmul(UNITYMATRIXVP, float4(centerworld, 1.0)) # Generate 2x2 quad offset based on vertex ID quadposx = (vtxid & 1) 2.0 - 1.0 quadposy = ((vtxid >> 1) & 1) 2.0 - 1.0 quadpos = float2(quadposx, quadposy) # Apply screen-space offset offset = quadpos (SplatSize / ScreenParams.xy) centerclip.w outputvertex = float4(centerclip.xy + offset, centerclip.z, centerclip.w) # Compute color based on display mode if DisplayIndex: normalizedindex = instid / SplatCount colorr = frac(normalizedindex 100.0) colorg = frac(normalizedindex 10.0) colorb = normalizedindex color = float3(colorr, colorg, colorb) else: color = saturate(splat.sh.col) return {"vertex": outputvertex, "color": color} def fragmentshader(inputdata: dict) -> float4: # Outputs interpolated color with full opacity return float4(inputdata["color"], 1.0) SplatSize: Float scalar defining the width/height of the debug quad in screen pixels. DisplayIndex: Boolean flag. If true, colors represent splat indices; if false, colors represent SH color. SplatCount: Integer scalar, the total number of splats, used for normalizing indices. Quad Generation Assumption: The method assumes a fixed 2x2 grid per splat (4 vertices). Division by Zero: If SplatCount is zero, division by zero occurs during index encoding. Precision: Using frac() for index encoding can lead to visual banding if SplatCount is very large, as floating-point precision limits distinct adjacent indices. A shader for rendering debug point clouds with configurable size, color, and alpha, using spatial rendering mode. Parameters include pointsize (float, default 10.0), color (vec3, default cyan vec3(0.0, 1.0, 1.0)), and alpha (float, default 0.1). The vertex shader sets POINTSIZE = pointsize, and the fragment shader outputs ALBEDO = color with ALPHA = alpha. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. Debug Splat Point Rendering is a specialized technique developed within real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations for Unity, utilizing unityObjectToWorld and UNITYMATRIXVP matrices. It emerged as a diagnostic tool for developers to inspect splat positions and attributes during pipeline development. The method is used for verifying that splat data has been correctly loaded, transformed, and projected. aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, https://github.com/aras-p/UnityGaussianSplatting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, https://github.com/nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) dsvalerian/better-procedural-terrain, https://github.com/dsvalerian/better-procedural-terrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Shader Property Configuration
head: Render property block setup, Splat instance property binding
body: This method configures the GPU render pass by populating a material property block with splat count, spherical harmonic (SH) degree, brightness, scale, antialiasing settings, transform matrices, and optional skinning or volume lighting data. It solves the problem of efficiently passing per-renderer and global state to the fragment shader without causing state overwrites in multi-camera setups or shader compilation errors when optional features (like skinning) are disabled. Inputs: Splat count (mtotalRemainingCount or SplatCount). SH degree (shDegree or SHBands). Brightness scaling factor (brightness, default 1.0). Scale factor (scaleFactor, default 1.0). Renderer-specific parameters (gamma, downscale). Global buffers: Order buffer, Packed buffer, SH buffers, Transform buffers. Optional: Skinning weights/bone indices if rigging is enabled. Outputs: A populated MaterialPropertyBlock (Unity) or uniform buffer structure containing all necessary shader constants and texture bindings. RendererParams: Brightness: float ScaleFactor: float GammaToLinear: uint (1 if true, 0 if false) SHDegree: uint GsplatRigWeight (for skinning support): BoneIndex0: uint Weight0: float Padding: Aligned to sizeof(uint) 4 + sizeof(float) 4 total size. 1. Check Global State: If mglobalBuffersDirty is true, mglobalOrderBuffer is null, or mtotalRemainingCount is 0, return early to prevent stale buffer usage. 2. Initialize Property Block: Clear or initialize mglobalPropertyBlock. 3. Bind Core Buffers: Bind the following to their respective shader properties: kglobalOrderBuffer, kglobalPackedBuffer, krendererOffsetsProp, krendererTransformsProp, krendererParamsProp. 4. Bind Integer Parameters: ktotalSplatCount = mtotalRemainingCount, ksplatInstanceSize = GsplatSettings.Instance.SplatInstanceSize. 5. Bind SH Buffers: Conditionally bind SH buffers based on mglobalSHBands: if mglobalSHBands >= 1, bind kglobalSH1Buffer; if >= 2, bind kglobalSH2Buffer; if >= 3, bind kglobalSH3Buffer; if >= 4, bind kglobalSH4Buffer. 6. Update Per-Renderer Parameters: For each active renderer k: if it is a GsplatRenderer, set Brightness = gs.Brightness, ScaleFactor = 1.0 - gs.SplatDownscaleFactor, GammaToLinear = 1 if gs.GammaToLinear else 0, SHDegree = min(gs.SHDegree, activeGsplats[k].SHBands). Else, set Brightness = 1.0, ScaleFactor = 1.0, GammaToLinear = 0, SHDegree = activeGsplats[k].SHBands. Set the cached RendererParams array into mrendererParamsBuffer. 7. Construct Render Params: Create RenderParams with the global material, world bounds (1e6 units), and the populated property block. 8. Compute Instance Count: instanceCount = ceil(mtotalRemainingCount / SplatInstanceSize). 9. Issue Draw Call: Use RenderMeshPrimitives with the instance mesh, instanceCount, and RenderParams. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class MaterialPropertyBlock: def init(self): self.props = {} def setbuffer(self, name, buf): self.props[name] = buf def setint(self, name, val): self.props[name] = val def settexture(self, name, tex): self.props[name] = tex def setbufferarray(self, name, arr): self.props[name] = arr def configuresplatshaderproperties(renderer, globalstate, splatasset): # Step 1: Check global state if globalstate.mglobalbuffersdirty or \ globalstate.mglobalorderbuffer is None or \ globalstate.mtotalremainingcount == 0: return # Step 2: Initialize Property Block propblock = MaterialPropertyBlock() # Step 3: Bind Core Buffers propblock.setbuffer("kglobalOrderBuffer", globalstate.kglobalorderbuffer) propblock.setbuffer("kglobalPackedBuffer", globalstate.kglobalpackedbuffer) propblock.setbuffer("krendererOffsetsProp", globalstate.krendereroffsetsprop) propblock.setbuffer("krendererTransformsProp", globalstate.krenderertransformsprop) propblock.setbuffer("krendererParamsProp", globalstate.krendererparamsprop) # Step 4: Bind Integer Parameters propblock.setint("ktotalSplatCount", globalstate.mtotalremainingcount) propblock.setint("ksplatInstanceSize", GsplatSettings.instance.splatinstancesize) # Step 5: Bind SH Buffers globalshbands = globalstate.mglobalshbands if globalshbands >= 1: propblock.settexture("kglobalSH1Buffer", globalstate.kglobalsh1buffer) if globalshbands >= 2: propblock.settexture("kglobalSH2Buffer", globalstate.kglobalsh2buffer) if globalshbands >= 3: propblock.settexture("kglobalSH3Buffer", globalstate.kglobalsh3buffer) if globalshbands >= 4: propblock.settexture("kglobalSH4Buffer", globalstate.kglobalsh4buffer) # Step 6: Update Per-Renderer Parameters rendererparamsarray = [] for k in range(renderer.activerenderercount): gs = renderer.activegsplats[k] if renderer.isgsplatrenderer(k): brightness = gs.brightness scalefactor = 1.0 - gs.splatdownscalefactor gammatolinear = 1 if gs.gammatolinear else 0 shdegree = min(gs.shdegree, gs.shbands) else: brightness = 1.0 scalefactor = 1.0 gammatolinear = 0 shdegree = gs.shbands rendererparamsarray.append({ "Brightness": brightness, "ScaleFactor": scalefactor, "GammaToLinear": gammatolinear, "SHDegree": shdegree }) propblock.setbufferarray("mrendererParamsBuffer", rendererparamsarray) # Step 7: Construct Render Params renderparams = { "material": splatasset.gsplatmaterial, "worldbounds": {"center": (0, 0, 0), "extents": (1e6, 1e6, 1e6)}, "propertyblock": propblock } # Step 8: Compute Instance Count instancecount = math.ceil(globalstate.mtotalremainingcount / GsplatSettings.instance.splatinstancesize) # Step 9: Issue Draw Call rendermeshprimitives( instancemesh=splatasset.instancemesh, instancecount=instancecount, renderparams=renderparams) shDegree: Order of SH coefficients used for rendering, capped by the asset's SHBands property. brightness: Brightness color scaling factor, default 1.0. scaleFactor: Splat UV scaling factor to reduce splat size while keeping visual fidelity, default 1.0. Portable Shader Variants: If skinning is disabled, valid sampled resources must still be bound. Binding null or uninitialized buffers causes shader compilation/runtime errors. Stale Buffers: Drawing is skipped if mglobalBuffersDirty is true. This is critical in URP where DrawAllIfEnabled may fire before DispatchSort. SH Degree Clamping: SHDegree must be clamped to the renderer's SHBands to prevent EvalSH from reading uninitialized data, as global buffers are sized to the max bands across all renderers. Integrates temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) jitter into the Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline to prevent splats from appearing "swimming" or bit-stable while surrounding meshes are correctly jittered [Brief]. It solves the problem where splats, previously rendered with an unjittered projection matrix, failed to accumulate temporal history correctly under TAA and temporal upscaling (e.g., FSR2), causing residual displacement and visual artifacts [Brief]. It differs from standard mesh rendering by explicitly excluding the engine's depth correction from the jittered projection, as the Gaussian pipeline relies on linear view-space depth [Brief]. Binds the two main splat textures to uniforms sourceSplats and sourceSplats2. Binds Spherical Harmonics block textures to uniforms shBlock0Texture through shBlock5Texture. If a specific block texture is missing, binds Splats.emptyTexture. Sets layer configuration uniforms: sourceLayerBits to layerBits, sourceLayerMask to 2 layerBits - 1, and sourceBlockBits to SPLATBLOCKSDISABLED. Disables advanced features by setting sourcePackedGroups to false, sourceBlocks/sourceOpacities/sourceIndices to Splats.emptyTexture, and sourceIndexed to false. Marks the splats object as needing no further updates by setting needsUpdate to false. Binds global splat data buffers to the rendering material using a MaterialPropertyBlock to support multi-camera setups without state overwrites. Returns early if mglobalBuffersDirty, mglobalOrderBuffer is null, or mtotalRemainingCount is 0. Initializes or clears mglobalPropertyBlock. Binds core buffers: kglobalOrderBuffer, kglobalPackedBuffer, krendererOffsetsProp, krendererTransformsProp, krendererParamsProp. Binds integer parameters: ktotalSplatCount (mtotalRemainingCount) and ksplatInstanceSize (GsplatSettings.Instance.SplatInstanceSize). Binds SH buffers conditionally based on mglobalSHBands: kglobalSH1Buffer (if >=1), kglobalSH2Buffer (if >=2), kglobalSH3Buffer (if >=3), kglobalSH4Buffer (if >=4). Drawing is skipped if mglobalBuffersDirty is true, preventing stale buffer usage, especially important in URP where DrawAllIfEnabled fires before DispatchSort. Updates per-renderer parameters including brightness, scale, gamma, and spherical harmonic degree, ensuring SH evaluation does not read uninitialized data. For each active renderer k, if it is a GsplatRenderer, sets Brightness=gs.Brightness, ScaleFactor=1.0f-gs.SplatDownscaleFactor, GammaToLinear=gs.GammaToLinear?1u:0u, SHDegree=min(gs.SHDegree, activeGsplats[k].SHBands). If the renderer is not a GsplatRenderer, sets Brightness=1.0f, ScaleFactor=1.0f, GammaToLinear=0u, SHDegree=activeGsplats[k].SHBands. Sets the cached RendererParams array into mrendererParamsBuffer. SHDegree is clamped to the renderer's SHBands to prevent EvalSH from reading slots not copied for that renderer, as global buffers are sized to max bands across all renderers. Binds renderer parameters buffer containing total splat count and instance size to krendererParamsProp. Conditionally binds spherical harmonic buffers for bands 1 through 4 based on mglobalSHBands. Constructs RenderParams with the appropriate global material, a world bounds covering 1e6 units in all directions, and the populated property block. Computes instance count by dividing remaining splat count by SplatInstanceSize, rounded up. Issues the draw call using RenderMeshPrimitives with the pre-built instance mesh, instance count, and render params. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently handles multi-camera setups without state overwrites. Prevents shader errors by ensuring valid resources for disabled features. Limitations: Requires careful management of buffer dirty flags to avoid stale data. SH degree clamping is necessary to prevent out-of-bounds reads. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated from the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting in real-time engines like Unity and WebGL. The method was developed to address the specific challenges of passing large amounts of per-splat and global state to the GPU efficiently. Key implementations include UnitySplats and Gaussian-Splat-Lite. The approach evolved to support multi-camera setups, TAA jitter integration, and efficient SH evaluation. arloopa/UnitySplats, https://github.com/arloopa/UnitySplats, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) WilliamLiu-1997/Gaussian-Splat-Lite, https://github.com/WilliamLiu-1997/Gaussian-Splat-Lite, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat TAA Jitter Integration
head: gaussian_splatting: render splats with the engine's TAA jitter
body: This method integrates temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) jitter into the Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline to prevent splats from appearing "swimming" or bit-stable while surrounding meshes are correctly jittered. It solves the problem where splats, previously rendered with an unjittered projection matrix, failed to accumulate temporal history correctly under TAA and temporal upscaling (e.g., FSR2), causing residual displacement and visual artifacts. It differs from standard mesh rendering by explicitly excluding the engine's depth correction from the jittered projection, as the Gaussian pipeline relies on linear view-space depth. Inputs: scenedata->camprojection: The base camera projection matrix. scenedata->flipy: Boolean indicating if the Y-axis of the projection needs flipping. scenedata->taajitter: A 2D vector representing the temporal jitter offset. scenedata->depthcorrection: The engine's standard depth correction matrix (ignored by this method). Outputs: renderprojection: The GPU projection matrix, including jitter, used for culling and rendering. Data Structures: Projection: A 4x4 matrix structure. Access via columns[row][col] or standard indexing. Vector2: A 2D vector with x and y components. Steps: 1. Initialize: Copy scenedata->camprojection into renderprojection. 2. Flip Y: If scenedata->flipy is true, negate the Y-axis scaling factor: \text{render\projection}[1][1] = -\text{render\projection}[1][1] 3. Check Jitter: If scenedata->taajitter is exactly (0,0), return renderprojection immediately. This short-circuits the non-temporal path, ensuring bit-identical results to the pre-jitter state. 4. Apply Jitter: If scenedata->taajitter is non-zero, apply an identity-plus-translation correction to renderprojection. This matches the engine's standard jitter application method (e.g., Projection::addjitteroffset()). The correction is a translation in the projection space corresponding to the jitter vector. Do not apply the engine's depth correction, as the Gaussian pipeline uses linear view-space depth and applying depth correction would distort the splat positions. 5. Return: Return the modified renderprojection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildrenderprojection(camprojection, flipy, taajitter): """ Builds the GPU projection matrix for Gaussian Splatting with TAA jitter. Args: camprojection (Matrix4x4): Base camera projection. flipy (bool): Whether to flip the Y-axis. taajitter (Vector2): Temporal jitter offset (0,0) if no temporal stage. Returns: Matrix4x4: The jittered projection matrix. """ # Step 1: Copy base projection renderprojection = camprojection.copy() # Step 2: Apply Y-flip if necessary if flipy: renderprojection[1][1] = -renderprojection[1][1] # Step 3: Check for zero jitter if taajitter.x == 0.0 and taajitter.y == 0.0: return renderprojection # Step 4: Apply TAA jitter (identity-plus-translation correction) # Adds the jitter vector to the translation components of the projection matrix. renderprojection[3][0] += taajitter.x renderprojection[3][1] += taajitter.y return renderprojection Parameters: scenedata->taajitter: A vector representing the temporal jitter offset. It is exactly (0,0) unless a temporal stage (TAA or temporal upscaling) is active. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Key: The render cache reuse key must include the jittered projection matrix. Previously, the key was the unjittered pinput.projection, causing static camera frames to re-compose frozen jitter phases every frame. The key must be the GPU projection carrying the jitter. Depth Correction: Do not apply the engine's depth correction to the projection. The Gaussian pipeline uses linear view-space depth, and applying depth correction would distort the splat positions. Zero Jitter: If taajitter is zero, the method must short-circuit and return the flipped matrix immediately without further modification to ensure bit-identical results to the pre-jitter state. Time Complexity: O(1) for matrix modification. The short-circuit for zero jitter ensures minimal overhead when no temporal stage is active. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the projection matrix. Measured Performance: TAA: Under TAA, splats previously had 0.0000 px displacement (bit-stable). After the fix, splats move by ~0.0156 px, matching the mesh order of magnitude (~0.0152 px). FSR2 @1.0: Splat displacement reduced from 0.2525 px to 0.0900 px (-64%). FSR2 @0.5: Splat displacement reduced from 0.3603 px to 0.0927 px (-74%). Strengths: Eliminates "swimming" artifacts under TAA and temporal upscaling. Matches mesh jitter behavior. Limitations: Residual displacement of ~0.09 px remains under FSR2 due to FSR2 not accumulating history on splat pixels (clamped to 0.9 destination alpha). This is not a defect of the jitter integration but a limitation of the composite feed. When to Use: Use when rendering Gaussian Splats in a scene with TAA or temporal upscaling to ensure visual consistency with meshes. When Not to Use: Not applicable; this is a necessary fix for correct temporal behavior. This method originated from a fix for the Gaussian Splat Renderer in Godot, where splats were not jittered, causing them to 'swim' under FSR2 and remain bit-stable (non-antialiased) under TAA, while meshes were correctly jittered. The fix was implemented in PR #929 and #1026 by klausi3D in the godotGS repository. The issue was identified as the projection uploaded to the splat GPU pipeline never carrying the engine's temporal jitter. The fix involved modifying GaussianSplatRenderer::buildrenderprojection() to apply the jitter and updating the render cache key to include the jittered projection. gaussiansplatting: render splats with the engine's TAA jitter, and key the render cache on the matrix that carries it (#929), https://github.com/klausi3D/godotGS/pull/1026, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering)
head: Splatv vertex shader, VideoRenderProgram
body: Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering) is a GPU-accelerated rendering method for time-varying 3D Gaussian splats that computes time-dependent position, rotation, and scale deltas from packed texture data to enable smooth animation without per-frame CPU updates. It differs from static 3D Gaussian Splatting by evaluating polynomial motion deltas and applying temporal opacity decay in the vertex and fragment shaders, building on the screen-space quad rendering of Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A packed 2D texture (utexture) containing static and motion data for N splats; camera matrices (View V, Projection P); camera intrinsics (focal vector (fx, fy)); current animation timestamp (time); viewport dimensions (viewport (W, H)); and the splat index i. Outputs: Screen-space quad vertices for each splat; final color and alpha per fragment. Data Structures: Splat data is packed into a 2D texture where each splat index i occupies 4 consecutive texels. Row Index: row = uint(i) >> 10 Column Index: col = ((uint(i) & 0x3ffu) << 2), where k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} is the texel offset within the splat's block. Texel Layout:.x: motion0.x.y: motion0.y.z: motion0.z.w: motion1.w (packed half-float pair) Static Data: static0 and static1 are fetched at offsets | 0 and | 1 respectively from the base index. Numbered Steps: 1. Fetch Motion Data: Unpack motion0 and motion1 from the texture using the row/column coordinates derived from the splat index i. 2. Compute Time Delta: Calculate dt = t - t{start}, where t is the uniform time and t{start} is unpacked from motion1.w as the x-component of a half-float pair. 3. Compute Motion Deltas: Calculate position delta \Delta p and rotation delta \Delta q as polynomials in dt: \Delta p = c{p1} dt + c{p2} dt^2 + c{p3} dt^3 \Delta q = c{q1} dt Coefficients c{p1..3} and c{q1} are unpacked from motion0 and motion1 as half-float pairs. 4. Transform Position: Add \Delta p to the static world position p{static} (converted from fixed-point or half-float representation) and transform to camera space: p{cam} = V \cdot (p{static} + \Delta p, 1)^T Then project to clip space: p{clip} = P \cdot p{cam} 5. Clip: Discard the splat if it is outside the extended view frustum: |p{clip}.x| > 1.2 p{clip}.w, \quad |p{clip}.y| > 1.2 p{clip}.w, \quad \text{or} \quad p{clip}.z < -1.2 p{clip}.w. 6. Reconstruct Rotation: Compute the normalized quaternion q by adding the rotation delta to the static quaternion components and normalizing: q = \text{normalize}(q{static} + \Delta q). 7. Compute World Covariance: Construct the scale matrix S = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz) and rotation matrix R from q. Compute the transformation matrix M = S R and the world covariance matrix: \Sigma{world} = 4 M^T M. 8. Compute 2D Covariance: Calculate the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} using the Jacobian J of the projection and the view rotation V{rot} (upper-left 3x3 of V): T = V{rot}^T J \Sigma{2D} = T^T \Sigma{world} T The Jacobian J is defined as: J = \begin{bmatrix} fx/z & 0 & -fx x/z^2 \\ 0 & -fy/z & fy y/z^2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} where (x,y,z) are the camera-space coordinates from p{cam}. 9. Eigenvalue Decomposition: Compute eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvector v of \Sigma{2D} analytically: \mu = \frac{\Sigma{2D}[0][0] + \Sigma{2D}[1][1]}{2} r = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\Sigma{2D}[0][0] - \Sigma{2D}[1][1]}{2}\right)^2 + \Sigma{2D}[0][1]^2} \lambda1 = \mu + r, \quad \lambda2 = \mu - r Discard the splat if \lambda2 < 0. 10. Compute Ellipse Axes: Determine the screen-space axes a and b: v = \text{normalize}([\Sigma{2D}[0][1], \lambda1 - \Sigma{2D}[0][0]]) a = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda1}, 1024) v b = \min(\sqrt{2\lambda2}, 1024) [vy, -vx] The maximum axis length is clamped to 1024 pixels to prevent overdraw. 11. Compute Screen Position: For each quad vertex with local position (u,v), compute the final screen position: p{screen} = \frac{p{clip}}{p{clip}.w} + u \frac{a}{W} + v \frac{b}{H} where (W,H) is the viewport size. 12. Fragment Evaluation: In the fragment shader, evaluate the Gaussian kernel based on the local position p{local} (relative to the quad center): A = -\|p{local}\|^2 Discard if A < -4. 13. Compute Final Color: Calculate the time-decayed opacity \alpha{time} and final color: \alpha{time} = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{dt}{\tau}\right)^2\right) where \tau is unpacked from motion1.w as the y-component of a half-float pair. C = \exp(A) \alpha{time} C{base} Apply depth fog factor \min(\frac{z}{w}+1, 1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Discard(Exception): pass def unpackhalf2(halfval): # Converts a packed half-float representation to a float vec2 return vec2(float(halfval.x), float(halfval.y)) def quaterniontomatrix(q): x, y, z, w = q.x, q.y, q.z, q.w return mat3( 1.0 - 2.0(yy + zz), 2.0(xy - zw), 2.0(xz + yw), 2.0(xy + zw), 1.0 - 2.0(xx + zz), 2.0(yz - xw), 2.0(xz - yw), 2.0(yz + xw), 1.0 - 2.0(xx + yy)) def rendersplatvertex(splatindex, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, focal, time, viewport, u, v): # 1. Fetch Data row = splatindex >> 10 col = (splatindex & 0x3ff) << 2 # Fetch 4 consecutive texels for motion data texels = [texture2d(utexture, row, col + k) for k in range(4)] motion0x = texels[0].x motion0y = texels[0].y motion0z = texels[0].z motion1w = texels[0].w # Static data fetch at offsets | 0 and | 1 static0 = texture2d(utexture, row, col) static1 = texture2d(utexture, row, col + 1) # 2. Time Delta motion1pair = unpackhalf2(motion1w) tstart = motion1pair.x tau = motion1pair.y dt = time - tstart # 3. Motion Deltas # Coefficients unpacked as vectors for each axis cp1, cp2, cp3 = vec3(motion0x), vec3(motion0y), vec3(motion0z) cq1 = motion1pair.y # Reused from motion1.w per source layout deltap = cp1 dt + cp2 (dt 2) + cp3 (dt 3) deltaq = vec4(cq1 dt, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 4. Transform Position pstatic = vec4(unpackhalf2(static0.x), unpackhalf2(static0.y), unpackhalf2(static0.z), 1.0) pcam = viewmatrix (pstatic + vec4(deltap, 0.0)) pclip = projectionmatrix pcam # 5. Clip if abs(pclip.x) > 1.2 pclip.w or abs(pclip.y) > 1.2 pclip.w or pclip.z < -1.2 pclip.w: raise Discard() # 6. Reconstruct Rotation qstatic = vec4(unpackhalf2(static1.x), unpackhalf2(static1.y), unpackhalf2(static1.z), unpackhalf2(static1.w)) q = normalize(qstatic + deltaq) R = quaterniontomatrix(q) # 7. World Covariance sx, sy, sz = unpackhalf2(static0.w), unpackhalf2(static1.x), unpackhalf2(static1.y) S = mat3(sx, 0, 0, 0, sy, 0, 0, 0, sz) M = S @ R Sigmaworld = 4.0 (M.transpose() @ M) # 8. 2D Covariance fx, fy = focal x, y, z = pcam.x, pcam.y, pcam.z J = mat3( fx / z, 0.0, -(fx x) / (z 2), 0.0, -fy / z, (fy y) / (z 2), 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Vrot = viewmatrix[0:3, 0:3] T = Vrot.transpose() @ J Sigma2D = T.transpose() @ Sigmaworld @ T # 9. Eigenvalues mu = (Sigma2D[0][0] + Sigma2D[1][1]) / 2.0 r = sqrt(((Sigma2D[0][0] - Sigma2D[1][1]) / 2.0) 2 + Sigma2D[0][1] 2) lambda1 = mu + r lambda2 = mu - r if lambda2 < 0: raise Discard() # 10. Axes vvec = normalize(vec2(Sigma2D[0][1], lambda1 - Sigma2D[0][0])) a = min(sqrt(2 lambda1), 1024.0) vvec b = min(sqrt(2 lambda2), 1024.0) vec2(vvec.y, -vvec.x) # 11. Screen Position W, H = viewport pscreen = pclip / pclip.w + u (a / W) + v (b / H) return pscreen, vcolor, vpositionlocal def rendersplatfragment(vpositionlocal, vcolor, time, tstart, tau): A = -dot(vpositionlocal, vpositionlocal) if A < -4.0: raise Discard() dt = time - tstart alphatime = exp(-((dt / tau) 2)) B = exp(A) alphatime fragcolor = vec4(B vcolor.rgb, B vcolor.a) return fragcolor Parameters: focal: Camera focal length vector (fx, fy). Typical value: derived from camera intrinsics. time: Current animation timestamp in seconds. Used to compute dt for motion interpolation. viewport: Canvas dimensions (W, H) in pixels. Used to scale ellipse axes to screen space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Eigenvalue: \lambda2 < 0 indicates a degenerate or flipped covariance matrix, often caused by extreme perspective or invalid transforms. The shader discards the splat to prevent rendering artifacts. Axis Clamping: Axis lengths are clamped to a maximum of 1024 pixels to prevent overdraw and performance degradation from excessively large splats. Time Complexity: O(N) for N splats, performed entirely on the GPU in the vertex and fragment shaders. No CPU sorting or per-frame update overhead for motion. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the packed texture storing static and motion data. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables smooth, real-time animation of Gaussian splats without CPU-side interpolation or sorting updates per frame. Limitations: Relies on pre-computed polynomial coefficients, limiting the complexity of motion to cubic polynomials for position and linear for rotation. When to Use: When rendering animated 3D Gaussian Avatars or dynamic scenes where motion is smooth and can be approximated by low-order polynomials. When Not to Use: For highly discontinuous or complex non-polynomial motion. Animated 3D Gaussian Splatting (Splatv rendering) is an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting designed for time-varying scenes. It was introduced in the context of GPU-accelerated web-based Gaussian Splatting implementations, specifically within the gsplat.js project. The method allows for the rendering of animated Gaussian splats by embedding motion parameters directly into the texture data and evaluating them in the shader pipeline. huggingface/gsplat.js, https://github.com/huggingface/gsplat.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Oriented Ellipse Splatting
head: Anisotropic Splat Rendering, Gaussian Ellipse Rendering, Screen-space 2D Covariance Rendering, not round blobs, oriented ellipses
body: Oriented Ellipse Splatting renders each Gaussian splat as an oriented ellipse in screen space, derived from its 3D rotation and 3-axis scale projected to a 2D covariance matrix, replacing the previous method of drawing round blobs sized by the largest axis. This approach improves visual fidelity by eliminating the "hazy" appearance of isotropic billboards and reduces overdraw, resulting in crisp edges and equal or better frame times. It differs from its parent Gaussian Splat Fragment Shader by explicitly computing the bounding quad from the covariance eigenvectors and evaluating the Gaussian kernel over the full anisotropic shape rather than a circular disc. Inputs: Splat attributes: center position, 3D rotation matrix R, 3-axis scale vector S, and color (SH degree 0 only). Camera matrices: View matrix and Projection matrix (or clip-from-view transformation). Low-pass filter constant: 0.3 \text{ px}^2. Extent scaling factor: 3 (standard deviations). Outputs: A screen-space quad for each splat, rendered with fragment shader evaluation of the Gaussian kernel. A 4-byte-per-splat order texture for re-sorting. Data Structures: Splat Instance: Contains position, rotation, scale, and color. The API provides a 4-texture overload for instance data; the previous 2-texture overload is deprecated. Order Texture: A 4-byte-per-splat texture storing the sorted indices, re-uploaded to the GPU on re-sort. Steps: 1. Compute 3D Covariance: Calculate the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma3 in view space using the rotation R and scale S: \Sigma3 = R \cdot S^2 \cdot R^T where S^2 is a diagonal matrix with elements Sx^2, Sy^2, Sz^2. 2. Project to Screen Space: Project \Sigma3 to screen space using the perspective Jacobian J (derived from the clip-from-view matrix focal terms): \Sigma2 = J \cdot \Sigma3 \cdot J^T Add a low-pass filter of 0.3 \text{ px}^2 to \Sigma2 to prevent aliasing and singularities. 3. Compute Eigen-decomposition: Calculate the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and corresponding eigenvectors v1, v2 of the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma2. 4. Determine Bounding Quad Corners: Calculate the corners of the quad in screen space using the center c, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and the scaling factor k=3: \text{corners} = c \pm 3 \cdot \sqrt{\lambdai} \cdot vi \quad \text{for } i \in \{1, 2\} Clamp the calculated corners to the valid quad bounds. 5. Render Quad: Render the splat as a screen-space quad defined by the calculated corners. 6. Fragment Shader Evaluation: For each fragment within the quad, calculate the distance vector d from the splat center to the fragment's interpolated screen coordinate. Evaluate the Gaussian kernel: \text{opacity} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} d^T \Sigma2^{-1} d\right) Multiply the splat's color by this opacity. Parameters: Scaling Factor: 3 standard deviations for bounding box calculation. Low-pass Filter: 0.3 \text{ px}^2 added to \Sigma2. Color Bandwidth: SH degree 0 only. Splat Count: Defaults to the full cloud count; can be lowered for LOD or reveal effects. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Camera Position: If a cameraPositionProvider is not supplied, the compositing order remains as loaded, causing visual popping when the camera orbits. Web Implementation: The web port (tracked in #4046) currently still uses isotropic billboards; anisotropic rendering is planned but not yet implemented in the web version. Tone Mapping: The material must cancel the View's tone mapping to ensure colors display as captured; otherwise, they may appear washed out. Batching: Clouds with more than 65535 splats are split into multiple draw calls or batches. Performance: Frame time is equal or better compared to the previous round-blob implementation, attributed to less overdraw. Memory: On re-sort, only a 4-byte-per-splat order texture is re-uploaded to the GPU. Visual Quality: Produces crisp edges and eliminates the haze associated with isotropic billboards. Limitations: Currently restricted to SH degree 0 color. The web implementation does not yet support this feature. Splats are composited using premultiplied-alpha blending. This method was introduced in the sceneview project to improve the rendering of Gaussian splats in AR and mobile contexts. It was implemented in commit e956f46 by Thomas Gorisse, addressing issues where previous isotropic billboards resulted in hazy scans. The change aligns the rendering with the reference 3DGS renderer's approach to anisotropic splats. It is part of a broader effort to support SPZ v4 and improve visual fidelity in "Your scan, in your room" AR demos. name: Gaussian Splat Vertex Shader
head: FGaussianSplatVS, OpenGL Gaussian Splat Renderer, SplatRenderer
body: The Gaussian Splat Vertex Shader renders Gaussian splats as screen-space quads. It computes the projected 2D covariance and conic parameters for each splat, determines the bounding box in screen space, and passes the necessary data to the fragment shader for alpha blending. It differs from sibling methods by handling the full projection pipeline (view-space to screen-space covariance) and degenerate case culling within the vertex stage, relying on the parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) for quad assembly and transparency handling. Inputs: gaussiandata (SSBO, binding=0): Packed float array containing splat attributes. gaussianorder (SSBO, binding=1): Integer array gi[] mapping instance ID to splat index. ViewDataBuffer (StructuredBuffer): Per-splat view data. SortKeysBuffer (StructuredBuffer<uint>): Pre-computed depth sort keys. Uniforms: SplatCount (uint32), DebugMode (uint32), EnableNanite (uint32), wh (viewport width/height). Matrices: W (view matrix), J (Jacobian of projection). Outputs: Clip-space position of the quad center. vQuadSize: Screen-space width and height. vConic: Conic matrix parameters (vec3) for the fragment shader. vAlpha: Base opacity. vColor: Color data. The gaussiandata SSBO layout per splat is a packed float array with the following offsets: POSIDX = 0: Position (3 floats: x, y, z). ROTIDX = 3: Rotation quaternion (4 floats: w, x, y, z). SCALEIDX = 7: Scale (3 floats: x, y, z). OPACITYIDX = 10: Opacity (1 float). SHIDX = 11: Spherical Harmonics coefficients (variable dimension, shdim). Total dimension per splat: 3 + 4 + 3 + 1 + \text{sh\dim}. 1. Retrieve Splat Data: Load position, rotation, scale, and opacity from gaussiandata using the index from gaussianorder. 2. Compute 3D Covariance: Construct the 3D covariance matrix M from scale S and rotation R (derived from quaternion q): M = S \cdot R; \Sigma{3D} = M^T M. 3. Project to Screen Space: Compute the 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} using the Jacobian J of the projection and view matrix W: T = W \cdot J; \Sigma{2D} = T^T \Sigma{3D}^T T. 4. Regularize Covariance: Add regularization to the diagonal of \Sigma{2D}: \Sigma{2D}[0][0] += 0.3f; \Sigma{2D}[1][1] += 0.3f. 5. Compute Conic Matrix: Calculate the inverse of the 2D covariance components: \text{det} = \Sigma{2D}[0][0] \cdot \Sigma{2D}[2][2] - \Sigma{2D}[0][2]^2; \text{det\inv} = 1.0 / \text{det}; \text{conic} = (\Sigma{2D}[2][2] \cdot \text{det\inv}, -\Sigma{2D}[0][2] \cdot \text{det\inv}, \Sigma{2D}[0][0] \cdot \text{det\inv}). 6. Determine Quad Size: Calculate screen-space width and height: \text{quadwh\scr} = (3.0 \cdot \sqrt{\Sigma{2D}[0][0]}, 3.0 \cdot \sqrt{\Sigma{2D}[2][2]}). 7. Clamp Quad Size: Prevent giant splats: \text{quadwh\scr} = \min(\text{quadwh\scr}, \text{wh} \cdot 0.5). 8. Cull Degenerate Splats: Discard if max scale > 1.0, anisotropy ratio > 50, or determinant \le 0. 9. Pass Data to Fragment Shader: Output vQuadSize, vConic, vAlpha, and vColor. If DebugMode is 1, color is set to cluster colors (Nanite-style debug). If EnableNanite is 1, Nanite LOD compaction may be applied. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k] B[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def transpose(M): return [[M[j][i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def quattorotmat(q): w, x, y, z = q return [ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ] def main(instanceid: int, gaussiandata: list, gaussianorder: list, shdim: int, W: list, J: list, wh: tuple, debugmode: int) -> dict: # 1. Retrieve Splat Index splatidx = gaussianorder[instanceid] # 2. Load Splat Data base = splatidx (3 + 4 + 3 + 1 + shdim) pos = gaussiandata[base: base+3] quat = gaussiandata[base+3: base+7] scale = gaussiandata[base+7: base+10] alpha = gaussiandata[base+10] shcoeffs = gaussiandata[base+11: base+11+shdim] # 3. Compute 3D Covariance R = quattorotmat(quat) M = [[scale[i] R[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] cov3d = matmul(transpose(M), M) # 4. Project to Screen Space T = matmul(W, J) cov2d = matmul(transpose(T), matmul(transpose(cov3d), T)) # 5. Regularize Covariance cov2d[0][0] += 0.3 cov2d[1][1] += 0.3 # 6. Compute Conic Matrix covx, covy, covz = cov2d[0][0], cov2d[0][1], cov2d[1][1] det = covx covz - covy covy if det <= 0.0: return {"discard": True} detinv = 1.0 / det conic = (covz detinv, -covy detinv, covx detinv) # 7. Determine Quad Size quadwhscr = (3.0 math.sqrt(covx), 3.0 math.sqrt(covz)) # 8. Clamp Quad Size quadwhscr = (min(quadwhscr[0], wh[0] 0.5), min(quadwhscr[1], wh[1] 0.5)) # 9. Cull Degenerate Splats maxscale = max(scale) minscale = min(scale) anisotropy = maxscale / minscale if minscale > 0 else float('inf') if maxscale > 1.0 or anisotropy > 50.0: return {"discard": True} # 10. Pass Data to Fragment Shader vQuadSize = quadwhscr vConic = conic vAlpha = alpha vColor = shcoeffs[:3] if shdim >= 3 else [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if debugmode == 1: vColor = [splatidx % 256 / 255.0, (splatidx 7) % 256 / 255.0, (splatidx 13) % 256 / 255.0] clippos = [pos[0], pos[1], pos[2], 1.0] return {"clippos": clippos, "vQuadSize": vQuadSize, "vConic": vConic, "vAlpha": vAlpha, "vColor": vColor} SHC0: 0.28209479177387814f. Regularization: 0.3f. Max Scale: 1.0. Max Anisotropy: 50. DebugMode: 0=off, 1=cluster colors (Nanite-style debug). EnableNanite: 1=Nanite enabled, 0=disabled. Degenerate Splats: Splats with zero determinant in 2D covariance or extreme anisotropy must be discarded to prevent rendering artifacts. Giant Splats: Quad size must be clamped to prevent splats from covering the entire screen. Numerical Stability: Regularization is added to the covariance diagonal to prevent division by zero or negative determinants. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the gaussiandata and gaussianorder buffers. Strengths: Efficient culling of degenerate splats, robust handling of projection and regularization. Limitations: Relies on pre-sorted order buffer from parent method. Performance depends on the efficiency of the Jacobian computation. When to Use: When rendering large numbers of Gaussian splats with high performance requirements. When Not to Use: When dynamic updates to splat attributes are frequent and require frequent buffer updates. The Gaussian Splat Vertex Shader is implemented in various open-source projects such as dust3r-3dgs and OpenSplat4D. It operates as a core component of the GPU rendering pipeline for differentiable Gaussian splatting, handling per-splat projection and culling before fragment shading. name: Gaussian Splat URP Render Pass
head: GSRenderPass, GaussianSplatURPFeature
body: A Unity Universal Render Pipeline (URP) ScriptableRendererFeature that renders Gaussian splats into a temporary render target and composites it onto the camera color target. Input: Camera data (CameraData), XR state, and a GaussianSplatSystem instance containing splat data and sorting logic. Output: The composited Gaussian splats appear in the final camera color target. The feature maintains a dictionary of render passes keyed by eye ID to support XR multipass rendering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. mPassPerEye = {} # Dictionary mapping eye ID to GSRenderPass instances mCmb = None # Command buffer for the current frame mRenderTarget = None # Temporary target for splat accumulation matComposite = None # Material for blitting splats to screen The temporary render target mRenderTarget is configured with: Format: R16G16B16A16SFloat. Dimensions: Tex2D. Depth buffer: None (depthBufferBits=0). MSAA: Disabled (msaaSamples=1). Name: "GaussianSplatRT". 1. Initialization: In OnCameraSetup, allocate mRenderTarget if needed using the descriptor above. Set it as a global texture. Configure the render pass to render to mRenderTarget and read from the camera depth buffer. Clear the target with Color(0,0,0,0). 2. Pass Creation: In GetOrCreatePass, determine the eyeId. If eyeId is not in mPassPerEye, create a new GSRenderPass with the specified renderPassEvent and a named CommandBuffer ('RenderGaussianSplats{eyeId}'). Store and return it. 3. Event Hooking: In OnCameraPreCull, if the camera is a Preview, return. Otherwise, call GetOrCreatePass for GetEyeId(cameraData). In AddRenderPasses, if Preview, return. Get eyeId, get/create the pass, set pass.mRenderer = renderer, and enqueue the pass. 4. Execution: In the pass's Execute method, if mCmb is null, return. Get the system and camera. Call system.GatherSplatsForCamera(cam). If it returns false, return. Clear mCmb. Call system.SortAndRenderSplats(cam, mCmb) to populate the command buffer and retrieve matComposite. If matComposite is null, return. Begin profiling sample sProfCompose. Blit mRenderTarget to cameraColorTargetHandle using matComposite pass 0. End profiling sample. Execute mCmb. 5. Eye ID Logic: GetEyeId returns cameraData.xr.multipassId if XR is enabled, otherwise cameraData.camera.GetInstanceID(). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GaussianSplatURPFeature: def init(self): self.mPassPerEye = {} self.mRenderTarget = None self.matComposite = None self.renderPassEvent = "BeforeRenderingTransparents" def OnCameraSetup(self, cameraData, renderTargetDescriptor): desc = { 'width': renderTargetDescriptor['width'], 'height': renderTargetDescriptor['height'], 'graphicsFormat': 'R16G16B16A16SFloat', 'dimension': 'Tex2D', 'volumeDepth': 1, 'vrUsage': None } if self.mRenderTarget is None or not self.mRenderTarget.iscreated(): self.mRenderTarget = createtexture(desc) self.mRenderTarget.name = 'GaussianSplatRT' setglobalshadertexture('GaussianSplatRT', self.mRenderTarget) configurerendertarget(self.mRenderTarget, cameraData.depthbuffer) clearrendertarget(self.mRenderTarget, color=(0, 0, 0, 0)) def GetEyeId(self, cameraData): if cameraData.xr.enabled: return cameraData.xr.multipassId return cameraData.camera.getinstanceid() def GetOrCreatePass(self, eyeId): if eyeId not in self.mPassPerEye: newpass = GSRenderPass() newpass.renderPassEvent = self.renderPassEvent newpass.commandBuffer = CommandBuffer() newpass.commandBuffer.name = f'RenderGaussianSplats{eyeId}' self.mPassPerEye[eyeId] = newpass return self.mPassPerEye[eyeId] def OnCameraPreCull(self, cameraData): if cameraData.cameraType == 'Preview': return self.GetOrCreatePass(self.GetEyeId(cameraData)) def AddRenderPasses(self, renderer, cameraData): if name: Decoupled Appearance Modeling
head: Appearance Adjustment CNN, Decoupled AM, Transformation Map Generator
body: Decoupled Appearance Modeling is a post-processing module that handles appearance variations, such as uneven illumination, by generating a per-pixel transformation map to adjust rendered images without modifying the underlying 3D Gaussian representation. It prevents the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) optimizer from creating "floaters" (spurious geometry) to compensate for photometric changes between training views. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex neural radiance fields or MLPs for appearance, this method uses a lightweight CNN to learn a residual appearance adjustment, allowing the 3D Gaussians to converge to a consistent average appearance and correct geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A rendered image I{ir} of resolution H \times W \times 3 from the parent Gaussian Splat Rendering (Screen-Space Quad) method, and an optimizable appearance embedding vector \elli of length m. Output: An appearance-variant image I{ia} of resolution H \times W \times 3, and a transformation map Mi of resolution H \times W \times C (where C is the number of channels in the transformation, typically 3). Data Structures: Appearance Embedding (\elli): A learnable vector of length m. Typical value: m=64. Feature Map (Di): A 2D tensor of shape \frac{H}{32} \times \frac{W}{32} \times (3 + m). Transformation Map (Mi): A 2D tensor of shape H \times W \times C. For simple pixel-wise multiplication, C=3. Numbered Steps: 1. Downsample: Downsample the rendered image I{ir} by a factor of 32 to obtain an image of resolution \frac{H}{32} \times \frac{W}{32} \times 3. This prevents the network from learning high-frequency details and reduces computation/memory. 2. Concatenate Embedding: Concatenate the appearance embedding \elli (length m) to every pixel of the downsampled image. This creates the input feature map Di with shape \frac{H}{32} \times \frac{W}{32} \times (3 + m). 3. Initial Convolution: Pass Di through a 3 \times 3 convolutional layer to increase the channel depth to 256. The output shape is \frac{H}{32} \times \frac{W}{32} \times 256. 4. Upsampling Blocks: Process the feature map through 4 upsampling blocks. Each block consists of: A 4 \times pixel shuffle layer (increasing resolution by 2 \times in each dimension, reducing channels by a factor of 4). A 3 \times 3 convolutional layer. A ReLU activation. Each block doubles the feature map resolution and halves its channel depth. After 4 blocks, the resolution becomes H \times W and the channel depth becomes 16. 5. Bilinear Interpolation: Upsample the feature map to H \times W via bilinear interpolation. The pixel shuffle blocks restore resolution to H/2 \times W/2; the bilinear layer completes the upscaling to full resolution. 6. Final Convolution: Apply two 3 \times 3 convolutional layers with a ReLU activation between them to produce the transformation map Mi of shape H \times W \times 3. 7. Transformation: Apply the pixel-wise transformation T using Mi to the original rendered image I{ir} to get I{ia}. Formulas: The appearance-variant image is computed as: I{ia} = T(I{ir}; Mi) where T is a pixel-wise transformation. For the default configuration, T is simple pixel-wise multiplication: I{ia}(x,y) = I{ir}(x,y) \odot Mi(x,y) where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The loss function combines a structural loss on the raw rendering and an appearance loss on the adjusted rendering: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1(I{ia}, Ii) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM}(I{ir}, Ii) where Ii is the ground truth image, \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss, and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss. The parameter \lambda balances the two terms. Parameters: Downsampling factor: 32. Appearance embedding length (m): 64. Initial conv output channels: 256. Number of upsampling blocks: 4. Transformation channels: 3 (default, for multiplication). Alternative configurations use 6 channels (multiplication + addition) or 4 channels (multiplication + Gamma correction). Learning rate: 0.001 for both appearance embeddings and CNN. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visualization: Transformation maps are 3-channel tensors. For visualization purposes, they must be converted to grayscale, as noted in the supplementary material. Complexity: Extending to affine transformations (multiplication + addition) or Gamma correction yields only marginal improvements in quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) on the tested datasets, suggesting simple multiplication is sufficient. Training vs. Inference: The CNN and embeddings are optimized during training but must be discarded after training to maintain real-time rendering speed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DecoupledAppearanceModeling(nn.Module): def init(self, m=64): super().init() self.m = m # Step 3: Initial Conv self.convinit = nn.Conv2d(3 + m, 256, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Step 4: 4 Upsampling Blocks # Each block: PixelShuffle(2) -> Conv2d(in/4, in/2, 3, padding=1) -> ReLU # Block 1: 256 -> 128 # Block 2: 128 -> 64 # Block 3: 64 -> 32 # Block 4: 32 -> 16 self.upsampleblocks = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Sequential( nn.PixelShuffle(2), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernelsize=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()), nn.Sequential( nn.PixelShuffle(2), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()), nn.Sequential( nn.PixelShuffle(2), nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()), nn.Sequential( nn.PixelShuffle(2), nn.Conv2d(8, 16, kernelsize=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()) ]) # Step 6: Final Convs self.convfinal1 = nn.Conv2d(16, 16, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.convfinal2 = nn.Conv2d(16, 3, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # Output 3 channels for multiplication def forward(self, renderedimage, appearanceembedding): """ renderedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) appearanceembedding: Tensor of shape (m,) Returns: Iia: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) Mi: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) """ H, W, = renderedimage.shape # Step 1: Downsample by 32 downsampled = F.avgpool2d(renderedimage.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), kernelsize=32, stride=32) downsampled = downsampled.squeeze(0).permute(1, 2, 0) # Shape: H/32, W/32, 3 # Step 2: Concatenate appearance embedding embgrid = appearanceembedding.repeat(downsampled.shape[0], downsampled.shape[1], 1) Di = torch.cat([downsampled, embgrid], dim=-1) # Shape: H/32, W/32, 3+m # Permute to (N, C, H, W) for Conv2d Di = Di.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) # Shape: 1, 3+m, H/32, W/32 # Step 3: Initial Conv x = self.convinit(Di) # Shape: 1, 256, H/32, W/32 # Step 4: Upsampling Blocks for block in self.upsampleblocks: x = block(x) # After 4 blocks, x is Shape: 1, 16, H/2, W/2 # Step 5: Bilinear Interpolation x = F.interpolate(x, size=(H, W), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) # Step 6: Final Convs x = F.relu(self.convfinal1(x)) Mi = self.convfinal2(x) # Shape: 1, 3, H, W # Permute back to (H, W, 3) Mi = Mi.squeeze(0).permute(1, 2, 0) # Step 7: Transformation Iia = renderedimage Mi return Iia, Mi A rendering implementation targeting web browsers that adapts Gaussian splatting for browser-based hardware constraints. Link A visualization method for debugging individual splat points without appearance adjustment logic. Link The low-level shader implementation for rendering splats, which can be modified to incorporate the transformation map if integrated differently. Link Configuration of shader properties that may include passing the transformation map to the shader if integrated differently. Link A method for animating Gaussians that may require separate appearance modeling for temporal consistency. Link An alternative rendering primitive that projects Gaussians as oriented ellipses rather than axis-aligned quads. Link The vertex-level implementation for transforming 3D Gaussians to screen space, which may be adapted for appearance-aware rendering. Link An implementation within Unity's Universal Render Pipeline that handles Gaussian splatting and appearance adjustments within Unity's rendering architecture. Link Time Complexity: The CNN processing is lightweight. On the Sci-Art scene, adding decoupled AM increases training time from 1h25m to 1h33m, a less than 10% increase. Memory Complexity: VRAM usage increases from 10.23G to 11.18G, a less than 10% increase. Performance: Improves quality metrics significantly: SSIM from 0.858 to 0.885, PSNR from 25.08 to 26.81, and LPIPS from 0.148 to 0.121 on the Sci-Art scene. Strengths: Prevents floaters caused by photometric inconsistencies; allows 3D Gaussians to learn consistent geometry; minimal impact on training time and memory; discards overhead at inference time for real-time rendering. Limitations: Requires additional training time and memory (though small); the CNN must be discarded after training; simple multiplication is sufficient, limiting the complexity of appearance adjustments that can be learned. When to use: When training views have significant appearance variations (e.g., lighting changes) that cause floaters in standard 3DGS. When not to use: When real-time inference speed is critical and the overhead of the CNN cannot be avoided (though it is discarded, the training overhead remains); when appearance variations are minimal. Decoupled Appearance Modeling was introduced in the paper "VastGaussian: Vast 3D Gaussians for Large Scene Reconstruction". It addresses the issue where 3D Gaussian Splatting tries to compensate for photometric changes between training views by creating spurious geometry (floaters). By decoupling appearance adjustment from the 3D Gaussian representation, the method allows the Gaussians to converge to a consistent average appearance and correct geometry. The method was evaluated on large-scale scenes from the Mill-19 and UrbanScene3D datasets. VastGaussian: Vast 3D Gaussians for Large Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00494, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Depth-First Splat Sorting
head: Pre-fragment depth sort, Sorting visible splats by depth
body: Depth-First Splat Sorting is a preprocessing step for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering that sorts visible Gaussian splats by camera-space depth before they are expanded into per-tile fragments. It solves the problem of high sorting overhead inherent in the original 3DGS pipeline, where fragments (one per tile a splat touches) are sorted using a combined 48-bit key. By sorting the smaller set of visible splats first, this method reduces the number of items to sort by a factor of 1.5 to 4, significantly lowering computational cost while maintaining correct depth ordering for subsequent rasterization. The method operates on a list of "staged splats" (visible 3D Gaussians projected into screen space). The goal is to produce a list of tile fragments that preserves the depth order of the original splats, allowing for efficient grouping by tile ID later. Inputs: splatlist: An array of N visible splats. Each splat i contains: depth: Camera-space depth value (zi). tileids: A list of tile IDs touched by the splat. tilecount: The number of tiles touched (ki = \text{len}(tile\ids)). index: The original index in the unsorted list (used as the sort value). Outputs: fragmentlist: An array of tile fragments. The total size is \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ki. Fragments are stored such that fragments from splat i occupy a contiguous block in the array, and these blocks are ordered by the depth of splat i. Data Structures: Splat Item: Contains depth (float32), tileids (array of integers), tilecount (integer), index (integer). Fragment Item: Contains tileid (integer), splatindex (integer, referencing the original splat), and attributes copied from the splat (e.g., position, covariance, color). The exact layout depends on the downstream rasterizer but must include tileid for grouping. Steps: 1. Sort Splats by Depth: Perform a stable 32-bit radix sort on the splatlist using depth as the key and index as the value. This produces a permutation of splats ordered from nearest to farthest. 2. Compute Exclusive Prefix Sum: Calculate the exclusive prefix sum of the tilecounts from the sorted splats to determine storage offsets for fragments. Let ki be the number of tiles touched by the i-th splat in the sorted list. Let Oi be the offset for the i-th splat's fragments. O0 = 0 Oi = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} kj \quad \text{for } i > 0 3. Create Fragments: Iterate through the sorted splats and their corresponding offsets. For each splat i: Let Oi be the computed offset. For each tile ID t in splat.tileids at index j: Create a fragment object. Set fragment.tileid = t. Set fragment.splatindex = splat.index. Copy necessary attributes from the splat to the fragment. Store the fragment at fragmentlist[Oi + j]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth values must be compared consistently. Using 32-bit floats is standard, but ensure the radix sort handles the bit representation correctly for depth comparison. Empty Splats: If a splat touches no tiles (e.g., outside the screen), it should be filtered out before sorting or handled with a tile count of 0. Stability: The sort must be stable to preserve the relative order of splats with identical depths, which the prefix sum approach relies on to maintain depth ordering during fragment creation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthfirstsplatsort(splatlist): # Step 1: Stable 32-bit radix sort by depth, using original index as value sortedsplats = sorted(splatlist, key=lambda s: s['depth']) # Step 2: Compute exclusive prefix sum of tile counts offsets = [] currentoffset = 0 for splat in sortedsplats: offsets.append(currentoffset) currentoffset += splat['tilecount'] totalfragments = currentoffset fragmentlist = [None] totalfragments # Step 3: Create fragments for i, splat in enumerate(sortedsplats): offset = offsets[i] tileids = splat['tileids'] splatindex = splat['index'] for j, tileid in enumerate(tileids): fragindex = offset + j fragmentlist[fragindex] = { 'tileid': tileid, 'splatindex': splatindex, 'depth': splat['depth'] } # Copy attributes (position, covariance, color) from splat to fragment return fragmentlist This variant emphasizes the use of an exclusive prefix sum to determine fragment storage offsets. It ensures that fragments from each splat are stored contiguously in the output array, inheriting the depth-sorted order of the splats. This allows for a subsequent stable sort by tile ID to group fragments per tile without breaking the depth order within each tile. The key advantage is that the initial depth sort is performed on N splats rather than M fragments (M > N), reducing sorting complexity. Time Complexity: Sorting N splats takes O(N) with a 32-bit radix sort. Prefix sum and fragment creation take O(M), where M is the total number of fragments. Since M \approx 1.5-4N, the dominant cost is the initial sort on N items, which is significantly cheaper than sorting M fragments. Memory Complexity: Requires O(N) for the sorted splats and O(M) for the fragment list. The prefix sum array requires O(N). Performance: Reduces sorting overhead by a factor of 1.5 to 4 compared to the original 3DGS approach. This is particularly beneficial for scenes with high overlap where splats touch many tiles. Strengths: Lower sorting cost, simpler key generation (32-bit vs 48-bit), and easier implementation on CPU. Limitations: Requires a subsequent stable sort by tile ID to group fragments per tile for rendering. The fragment list is not yet grouped by tile immediately after this step. This method is described in the Splatshop paper as an optimization for the rendering pipeline that sorts splats by depth before creating fragments to reduce sorting costs. It addresses the inefficiency of the original 3DGS rendering pipeline, which sorts fragments after splitting splats into tiles. By sorting splats first, it reduces the number of items to sort, leveraging the fact that the number of fragments is typically 1.5 to 4 times the number of visible splats. Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Splatapult Gaussian Splat Renderer
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (SplatNode pipeline), Gaussian Splatting radiance-field cloud render, SplatNode pipeline, SplatNode render
body: A renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) files that supports VR, camera navigation, and optional spherical harmonic (SH) rendering, using either a C++ radix sort or a GPU-based multi-radix sort for depth sorting. It decodes a 3D Gaussian Splat radiance-field cloud from a PLY file and renders it as hardware-instanced, camera-facing quads on-device. It supports both desktop and mobile XR environments, with configurable sorting backends (CPU vs GPU) and optional sRGB framebuffer conversion to reduce color banding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary PLY file containing 3D Gaussian parameters (positions, covariances, spherical harmonics, opacity). Output: A rendered image with correct alpha blending order (back-to-front). Data Structures: PLY Layout: INRIA binarylittleendian 1.0 format with properties in order: x, y, z, fdc0, fdc1, fdc2, opacity, scale0, scale1, scale2, rot0, rot1, rot2, rot3. Buffers: posBuffer: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores posVec (Gaussian positions x,y,z,1.0). keyBuffer, keyBuffer2: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores depth keys (depthVec). valBuffer, valBuffer2: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores indices (indexVec). histogramBuffer: GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, stores histogram data (histogramVec). atomicCounterBuffer: GLATOMICCOUNTERBUFFER, stores atomicCounterVec. Parameters: NUMBLOCKSPERWORKGROUP: Constant set to 1024. splatCount: Controls the number of splats drawn (0..count), used for LOD or reveal hooks. Defaults to the full cloud count. isFramebufferSRGBEnabled: Boolean flag enabling sRGB framebuffer conversion to reduce color banding; triggers the #define FRAMEBUFFERSRGB in shaders. gaussianCloud->HasFullSH(): Boolean flag indicating if full spherical harmonics are loaded; triggers the #define FULLSH in shaders to enable full SH rendering. useRgcSortOverride: Boolean flag; if true, forces the use of the CPU-based rgc::radixsort instead of the GPU-based multiradixsort even if hardware supports it. cameraPositionProvider: A callback returning the live camera world position, fed to the node's painter's sort each frame. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load vertex, geometry, and fragment shaders (splatvert.glsl, splatgeom.glsl, splatfrag.glsl) with defines for SRGB and Full SH. Load pre-sort compute shader (presortcompute.glsl). If GLEWKHRshadersubgroup is present and useRgcSortOverride is false, load multi-radix sort shaders (multiradixsort.glsl, multiradixsorthistograms.glsl). Reserve posVec and fill it with Gaussian positions (x,y,z,1.0). Build Vertex Array Object (VAO). Resize depthVec. If using multi-radix sort, allocate keyBuffer, keyBuffer2, histogramBuffer, valBuffer, valBuffer2, posBuffer. If not, allocate keyBuffer, valBuffer, posBuffer and create rgc::radixsort::sorter. 2. Decode PLY: Decode the bundled.ply asset off the main thread using SplatParser.fromPly(bytes) to produce a SplatCloud object. Handle null SplatCloud during loading. 3. Pre-sort (Compute Shader): Bind preSortProg. Set uniforms: modelViewProj (projMat modelViewMat), nearFar, keyMax (std::numericlimits<uint32t>::max). Reset atomicCounterBuffer to 0. Bind buffers: slot 0 posBuffer (readonly), slot 1 keyBuffer (writeonly), slot 2 valBuffer (writeonly), slot 4 atomicCounterBuffer. Dispatch compute with LOCALSIZE=256 threads per group: glDispatchCompute(((numPoints + 255) / 256), 1, 1). Barrier: GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT | GLATOMICCOUNTERBARRIERBIT. 4. Get Count: Read atomicCounterBuffer into atomicCounterVec. Set sortCount = atomicCounterVec[0]. Assert sortCount <= numPoints. 5. Sort: Multi-Radix Sort (if enabled): Set NUMELEMENTS = sortCount, NUMWORKGROUPS = (NUMELEMENTS + 1023) / 1024. Loop i from 0 to 3 (NUMBYTES=4): 1. Bind histogramProg, set gshift = 8i. 2. Bind keyBuffer or keyBuffer2 to slot 0, histogramBuffer to slot 1. 3. Dispatch compute NUMWORKGROUPS. 4. Barrier. 5. Bind sortProg, set gshift = 8i. 6. Bind buffers based on parity of i: If even: slot 0=keyBuffer, 1=keyBuffer2, 2=valBuffer, 3=valBuffer2, 4=histogramBuffer. If odd: slot 0=keyBuffer2, 1=keyBuffer, 2=valBuffer2, 3=valBuffer, 4=histogramBuffer. 7. Dispatch compute NUMWORKGROUPS. 8. Barrier. CPU Radix Sort (if multi-radix disabled): Call sorter->sort(keyBuffer->GetObj(), valBuffer->GetObj(), sortCount). 6. Copy Sorted: If using multi-radix sort and NUMBYTES is odd, bind valBuffer2 to GLCOPYREADBUFFER, else bind valBuffer. Bind splatVao->GetElementBuffer() to GLCOPYWRITEBUFFER. Perform glCopyBufferSubData to transfer sorted indices to the VAO element buffer for rendering. 7. Render: On each frame, read the live camera world position and pass it to the node's painter's sort via a cameraPositionProvider callback. The node re-sorts the splats back-to-front based on the camera position so the far side composites correctly behind the near side. Render using hardware-instanced, camera-facing quads. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatapultrender(plybytes, cameraposition, projmat, modelviewmat, usegpusort=True): # Helper definitions for OpenGL-like operations def allocatestoragebuffer(size): return [0] size def allocateatomiccounterbuffer(): return [0] def loadshader(name): return {"name": name} def bindshader(prog): pass def setuniform(prog, name, value): pass def resetatomiccounter(buf): buf[0] = 0 def bindbuffer(prog, slot, buf, readonly=False): pass def dispatchcompute(x, y, z): pass def barrier(flags): pass def readatomiccounter(buf): return buf def rgcradixsortcreatesorter(): return type('Sorter', (), {'sort': lambda s, k, v, c: k.sort(v, key=lambda x: x)})() def glcopybuffersubdata(src, dst, srcoff, dstoff, size): pass def renderinstancedquads(vao, count): pass # 1. Decode PLY splatcloud = SplatParser.fromPly(plybytes) if splatcloud is None: return None # Handle null case during loading numpoints = splatcloud.count posvec = splatcloud.positions # x,y,z,1.0 # 2. Initialize Buffers if usegpusort: keybuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) keybuffer2 = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) histogrambuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) valbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) valbuffer2 = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) posbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) atomiccounterbuffer = allocateatomiccounterbuffer() presortprog = loadshader("presortcompute.glsl") histogramprog = loadshader("multiradixsorthistograms.glsl") sortprog = loadshader("multiradixsort.glsl") else: keybuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) valbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) posbuffer = allocatestoragebuffer(numpoints) atomiccounterbuffer = allocateatomiccounterbuffer() sorter = rgcradixsortcreatesorter() # 3. Pre-sort Compute bindshader(presortprog) setuniform(presortprog, "modelViewProj", projmat @ modelviewmat) setuniform(presortprog, "nearFar", nearfar) setuniform(presortprog, "keyMax", 0xFFFFFFFF) resetatomiccounter(atomiccounterbuffer) bindbuffer(presortprog, 0, posbuffer, readonly=True) bindbuffer(presortprog, 1, keybuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(presortprog, 2, valbuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(presortprog, 4, atomiccounterbuffer, readonly=False) dispatchcompute(((numpoints + 255) // 256), 1, 1) barrier(GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT | GLATOMICCOUNTERBARRIERBIT) # 4. Get Count atomiccountervec = readatomiccounter(atomiccounterbuffer) sortcount = atomiccountervec[0] assert sortcount <= numpoints # 5. Sort if usegpusort: numelements = sortcount numworkgroups = (numelements + 1023) // 1024 for i in range(4): # NUMBYTES=4 # Histogram Step bindshader(histogramprog) setuniform(histogramprog, "gshift", 8 i) keysrc = keybuffer if i % 2 == 0 else keybuffer2 bindbuffer(histogramprog, 0, keysrc, readonly=True) bindbuffer(histogramprog, 1, histogrambuffer, readonly=False) dispatchcompute(numworkgroups, 1, 1) barrier() # Sort Step bindshader(sortprog) setuniform(sortprog, "gshift", 8 i) if i % 2 == 0: bindbuffer(sortprog, 0, keybuffer, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 1, keybuffer2, readonly=False) bindbuffer(sortprog, 2, valbuffer, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 3, valbuffer2, readonly=False) else: bindbuffer(sortprog, 0, keybuffer2, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 1, keybuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(sortprog, 2, valbuffer2, readonly=True) bindbuffer(sortprog, 3, valbuffer, readonly=False) bindbuffer(sortprog, 4, histogrambuffer, readonly=True) dispatchcompute(numworkgroups, 1, 1) barrier() else: sorter.sort(keybuffer, valbuffer, sortcount) # 6. Copy Sorted if usegpusort: if 4 % 2 != 0: readbuf = valbuffer2 else: readbuf = valbuffer writebuf = splatvao.elementbuffer glcopybuffersubdata(readbuf, writebuf, 0, 0, sortcount 4) else: writebuf = splatvao.elementbuffer glcopybuffersubdata(valbuffer, writebuf, 0, 0, sortcount 4) # 7. Render renderinstancedquads(splatvao, splatcount=numpoints) SplatXR is a Unity-based renderer designed to display 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assets directly on Extended Reality (XR) headsets, supporting both in-editor previews and on-headset execution with automatic camera switching. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose GPU-sorted renderers by offloading the depth-sorting of splats to a background CPU thread at a configurable rate, allowing the GPU shader to focus solely on rasterization and alpha-blending. This approach trades off sorting latency for reduced GPU overhead, making it suitable for mobile XR hardware where computational budgets are shared with other system tasks. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the radix sort implementation (GPU multi-radix or CPU radix). Rendering is O(N) for instanced drawing. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing positions, keys, values, and histograms. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces GPU overhead by offloading sorting to CPU, suitable for mobile XR hardware. Stable within-batch alpha-blend order prevents splat popping during slow camera orbits. Limitations: 24-bit radix sort has artifacts on some datasets, so 32-bit sort is used by default. When to use: Mobile XR hardware, real-time on-device rendering. When not to use: When GPU sorting is preferred or hardware does not support CPU offloading. Origin: Splatapult is a program to display 3D Gaussian Splatting files. History: Developed by Anthony J. Thibault. Usage: Used in Android, Apple, Web, Flutter, and React Native SDKs for real-time on-device Gaussian Splatting rendering.
