name: SplatXR On-Headset 3D Gaussian Splatting Renderer
head: On-Headset Splatting, SplatXR Renderer
body: SplatXR is a Unity-based renderer designed to display 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assets directly on Extended Reality (XR) headsets, supporting both in-editor previews and on-headset execution with automatic camera switching. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose GPU-sorted renderers by offloading the depth-sorting of splats to a background CPU thread at a configurable rate, allowing the GPU shader to focus solely on rasterization and alpha-blending. This approach trades off sorting latency for reduced GPU overhead, making it suitable for mobile XR hardware where computational budgets are shared with other system tasks. Inputs: A standard 3D Gaussian Splatting file in PLY format. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices) for the current rendering context (editor or headset). Outputs: A rasterized image with alpha-blended 3D Gaussian splats. Custom Splat File Format (CSV) At design time, the PLY file is converted into a custom CSV format. This file stores the precomputed attributes required for rendering: Covariance Matrix: Precomputed 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma for each Gaussian. Color: Denormalized color values (RGB). Alpha: Denormalized transparency values. Triangle Arrangement At runtime, the renderer assembles an arrangement of triangles corresponding to the splats. Each Gaussian is represented by a triangle in screen space derived from the covariance and position. These triangles are stored in shader memory. 1. Import and Preprocessing (Design Time): The user specifies a PLY file in the Unity import panel. The plugin computes the covariance matrix for each Gaussian. Color and transparency information are denormalized. The data is saved in the custom CSV format. A game object is added to the scene hierarchy with a predefined splat material and rendering script. 2. Runtime Initialization: The rendering script reads the custom CSV file containing covariance, color, and alpha attributes. The script determines the rendering context (in-editor or on-headset) and switches to the appropriate camera and parameters. 3. Background Sorting: Triangles are sorted from the perspective of the current camera. Sorting occurs in a background CPU thread. The sorting frequency is adjustable, defaulting to 1 Hz. 4. Rendering: The shader receives the sorted triangle arrangement in memory. For each splat-associated triangle, the shader computes the screen-space coverage based on the covariance. The shader performs alpha-blending to produce the final pixel color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convertplytocsv(plypath): # Read PLY, compute covariance matrix Sigma for each Gaussian # Denormalize color and alpha values # Save to CSV and return parsed data return gaussiansdata def isineditor(): # Standard environment check for Unity editor vs runtime return False def geteditorcamera(): # Return the active editor scene camera return editorcamera def getheadsetcamera(): # Return the active XR headset camera return headsetcamera class SplatXRRenderer: def init(self, plypath): self.gaussians = convertplytocsv(plypath) self.sortingratehz = 1.0 self.lastsorttime = 0.0 self.sortedtriangles = [] def update(self, currenttime, viewmatrix, projmatrix): context = "editor" if isineditor() else "headset" camera = geteditorcamera() if context == "editor" else getheadsetcamera() viewmatrix = camera.getviewmatrix() projmatrix = camera.getprojectionmatrix() timesincelastsort = currenttime - self.lastsorttime sortinterval = 1.0 / self.sortingratehz if timesincelastsort >= sortinterval: self.sortedtriangles = sorttrianglescpu(self.gaussians, viewmatrix, projmatrix) self.lastsorttime = currenttime rendershader(self.sortedtriangles, viewmatrix, projmatrix) def sorttrianglescpu(gaussians, viewmatrix, projmatrix): # Project each Gaussian center to screen space # Compute depth for each Gaussian # Sort indices based on depth (back-to-front) # Assemble triangle geometry for each Gaussian return sortedtrianglelist def rendershader(triangles, viewmatrix, projmatrix): # For each triangle: # Compute screen-space coverage from covariance # Sample color # Alpha blend into framebuffer Sorting Rate: The frequency at which triangles are re-sorted from the camera's perspective. Default value is 1 Hz. High-Resolution Performance: Splats with 1 million or more Gaussians cause noticeable frame drops and are infeasible on mobile GPUs like the Qualcomm Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 (found in Quest 3) due to shared computational budgets. Passthrough Limitations: On Apple Vision Pro, passthrough shader functionality is limited by Apple’s PolySpatial platform. Level-of-Detail (LoD) Rendering: A technique implemented within SplatXR to mitigate performance issues on high-resolution splats. It displays high-resolution splats only in close proximity to the user while rendering lower-resolution splats at increasing distances. It uses three levels of detail. See Level-of-Detail 3D Gaussian Splatting. Time and Memory Complexity: Sorting complexity is O(N \log N) where N is the number of Gaussians, performed on the CPU at a throttled rate (default 1 Hz). Rendering complexity is O(N) per frame for rasterization and blending, performed on the GPU. Measured Performance: On mobile GPUs such as the Qualcomm Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2, high-resolution splats (1 million+ Gaussians) are infeasible due to computational budget constraints shared with other device tasks. The renderer supports Apple Vision Pro, though passthrough features are limited. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Supports both in-editor and on-headset rendering with automatic camera switching; reduces GPU load by offloading sorting to CPU; supports LoD for high-resolution assets. Limitations: Sorting latency (1 Hz default) may cause visual jitter if the camera moves rapidly between sorts; high-resolution splats are not feasible on current mobile XR hardware without LoD. When to Use: Use for XR applications requiring 3DGS visualization where GPU resources are constrained and moderate sorting latency is acceptable. Use when integrating 3DGS into Unity workflows with automatic headset detection. When Not to Use: Do not use for scenes with >1 million Gaussians on mobile XR hardware without implementing LoD. Do not use if real-time, frame-accurate sorting is required for every frame (e.g., fast-moving VR interactions) without adjusting the sorting rate, which may increase CPU load. SplatXR was introduced in the paper "SplatXR: A Toolkit for Multi-Layered Extended Reality via On-Headset 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the need for efficient 3DGS rendering on mobile XR devices, which have limited computational resources compared to desktop GPUs. The toolkit provides a Unity plugin that automates the conversion of PLY files to a custom CSV format and handles the rendering pipeline, including background sorting and alpha blending. It supports multiple layers and includes features like cropping, planar flattening, and auto color adjustment for passthrough environments. name: SortFree Weighting
head: SortFree, Weighted-sum blending OIT
body: SortFree Weighting is an Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) approximation for 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates the computational bottleneck of depth sorting by replacing non-commutative alpha blending with a commutative weighted-sum blending scheme. It allows parallel accumulation of Gaussian colors in a single pass, trading strict physical accuracy for rendering efficiency and temporal stability. It sets itself apart from siblings like Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering by using a fixed analytical depth falloff rather than neural networks to predict view-dependent weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients. For each pixel, the set of projected 2D Gaussian splats overlapping the pixel. Output: The final color C for the pixel. Data Structures: Gaussian Splat: Contains screen-space center (x, y), covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}. Scene Parameter: A single learnable scalar \sigma representing the depth falloff range. Method: The core mechanism replaces the standard alpha compositing equation C = \sum ci \alphai \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj) with a weighted sum. The weight w for each Gaussian depends on its depth d and view direction \mathbf{r}. 1. Project Gaussians: Project each 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space to obtain the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma' and center. 2. Compute Depth: For each Gaussian i, determine its depth di in camera space. 3. Compute View Direction: Determine the view direction vector \mathbf{r}i from the camera center to the Gaussian center. 4. Calculate Weight: Compute the weighting factor wi using the formula: wi = \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{di}{\sigma}\right) v(\mathbf{r}i) Where: di is the depth of the i-th Gaussian. \sigma is the learnable scene parameter controlling the depth falloff. v(\mathbf{r}i) is a view-dependent term derived from spherical harmonics. 5. Accumulate Color: Compute the final color C by summing the weighted colors of all overlapping splats: C = \sum{i \in \text{overlapping}} wi Where ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian evaluated at \mathbf{r}i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sortfreeweightingrender(gaussians, cameraorigin, viewmatrix, projmatrix, sigma, imageshape): """ Render a frame using SortFree Weighting. Args: gaussians: List of dicts with keys: 'pos' (3,), 'shcoeffs' (degree-3 SH array) cameraorigin: (3,) camera position in world space viewmatrix: (4,4) world-to-camera transformation projmatrix: (4,4) perspective projection matrix sigma: float, learnable depth falloff parameter imageshape: tuple (height, width) Returns: image: (H, W, 3) rendered image """ H, W = imageshape image = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) for g in gaussians: # 1. Project to camera space posworld = np.append(g['pos'], 1.0) poscam = viewmatrix @ posworld poscam = poscam[:3] / poscam[3] # 2. Project to screen space posclip = projmatrix @ np.append(poscam, 1.0) posclip = posclip[:3] / posclip[3] xscreen = (posclip[0] + 1.0) 0.5 W yscreen = (1.0 - posclip[1]) 0.5 H # Guard: skip if outside framebuffer if not (0 <= xscreen < W and 0 <= yscreen < H): continue # 3. Compute Depth d = poscam[2] # 4. Compute View Direction viewvec = poscam - cameraorigin viewvec = viewvec / np.linalg.norm(viewvec) # 5. Calculate Weight depthterm = max(0.0, 1.0 - d / sigma) shcolor = evaluatesphericalharmonics(g['shcoeffs'], viewvec) contribution = depthterm shcolor # 6. Accumulate (commutative, order-independent) image[int(yscreen), int(xscreen)] += contribution return image def evaluatesphericalharmonics(shcoeffs, direction): """Evaluate degree-3 spherical harmonics for a given direction vector.""" x, y, z = direction # Standard degree-3 SH basis evaluation (9 coefficients per channel) # Coefficients layout: [R0, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8] shbasis = [ 0.282095, -0.488603 y, 0.488603 z, -0.488603 x, 1.092548 x y, -1.092548 y z, 0.315392 (3 z2 - 1), -1.092548 x z, 0.546274 (x2 - y2) ] # Multiply basis by SH coefficients and sum across channels color = np.zeros(3) for c in range(3): coeff = shcoeffs[c 9: (c + 1) 9] color[c] = sum(b a for b, a in zip(shbasis, coeff)) return color Parameters: \sigma: A learnable scalar parameter controlling the depth falloff range. Typical value not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth d > \sigma: The term \max(0, 1 - d/\sigma) becomes 0, effectively culling distant Gaussians. Precision: Accumulating many small weights can lead to floating-point precision issues if not handled carefully (e.g., using Kahan summation or higher precision accumulators). View-Dependence: The method relies on SH for view-dependent appearance. If SH coefficients are not properly trained, the view-dependent compensation v(\mathbf{r}) may be inaccurate. Uses neural networks to predict view-dependent weights and opacity, improving visual quality over SortFree's fixed linear falloff. Choose when higher visual fidelity is required and neural network inference overhead is acceptable. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel where N is the number of overlapping splats, as no sorting is required. The sorting step in standard 3DGS is O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for accumulation, compared to O(N) for storing sorted lists in OIT methods. Performance: Significantly faster than sorted alpha blending due to the removal of the sorting bottleneck. However, it is generally slower than volumetric rendering methods due to the per-splat evaluation and accumulation overhead. Strengths: Eliminates sorting overhead; provides temporal stability (no popping artifacts from sorting changes); simple implementation. Limitations: Approximates alpha blending, leading to potential visual artifacts (e.g., incorrect transparency handling); quality can suffer at novel viewpoints compared to sorted methods. When to Use: Real-time applications on edge devices where sorting is too expensive and slight visual inaccuracies are acceptable. When Not to Use: High-fidelity offline rendering where physical accuracy is critical. SortFree Weighting was proposed in the paper "SortFree" (cited as [14] in), which introduced a weighted-sum blending formulation to approximate standard alpha compositing in a commutative manner. It is part of a broader class of Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) techniques applied to Gaussian-based representations. The method aims to reduce rendering overhead and improve temporal stability by removing the sorting step. name: Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering
head: Depth-aware Weighting OIT, Learnable Depth-aware Weighting [S1, unofficial]
body: Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering is a rendering technique that eliminates the computational bottleneck of depth sorting in traditional alpha blending by using a learnable, view-conditioned weighting strategy to order-independently blend 3D Gaussians. It replaces the sorted accumulation paradigm with a commutative weighted-sum blending scheme, allowing parallel accumulation of Gaussian colors in a single pass. Unlike its sibling SortFree Weighting, which uses a fixed exponential depth weighting, this method introduces neural networks to predict view-dependent weights and opacity, significantly improving visual quality in view-dependent scenarios while maintaining real-time performance on edge devices. Inputs: Set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position \mui, scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation ri \in SO(3), spherical harmonic coefficients Yi, and base opacity parameters. Camera center tv. Background color \mathbf{c}{bg}. Outputs: Rendered pixel color \mathbf{C}. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: For each Gaussian i, store \mui, si, ri, Yi. Learnable Parameters: Three Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): \text{MLP}f (feature extraction), \text{MLP}\phi (weight prediction), \text{MLP}o (opacity prediction). Pixel Accumulators: For each pixel, maintain accumulators for the numerator term \sum \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi and the denominator term \sum \alphai wi, plus a global transmittance accumulator T. Steps: 1. Compute Camera-Gaussian Vector: For each Gaussian i, calculate the normalized direction vector from the camera center tv to the Gaussian center \mui: Pi = \frac{\mui - tv}{\|\mui - tv\|} 2. Feature Extraction: Construct a composite feature vector \mathbf{F} by concatenating Pi, scale si, rotation ri, and spherical harmonic coefficients Yi. Pass this vector through the feature MLP: \mathbf{F} = \text{MLP}f(Pi, si, ri, Yi) 3. Predict View-Dependent Weight and Opacity: Use the extracted features to predict the view-dependent weight \phii and the neural opacity oi: \phii = \text{ReLU}(\text{MLP}\phi(\mathbf{F})) oi = \sigma(\text{MLP}o(\mathbf{F})) where \sigma(\cdot) is the Sigmoid activation function. 4. Compute Alpha Value: Calculate the alpha value \alphai for the Gaussian based on the neural opacity oi and its spatial distribution at the pixel's projected center offset \Delta xi relative to the Gaussian's covariance matrix \Sigmai: \alphai = oi \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\Delta xi^T \Sigmai^{-1} \Delta xi\right) 5. Compute Depth-Aware Weight: Calculate the depth-aware weight wi using the predicted view-dependent parameter \phii, the depth di of the Gaussian in camera coordinates, and the maximum scale s{max} of the Gaussian: wi = \phii^2 + \frac{\phii}{di^2} + \exp\left(\frac{s{max}}{di}\right) 6. Parallel Accumulation: For each pixel, accumulate the contributions of all projected Gaussians in parallel. Since addition is commutative, no sorting is required. Accumulate weighted color: C{num} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi. Accumulate weighted alpha: C{den} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi. Accumulate global transmittance: T = \prod{j=1}^{N} (1 - \alphaj). 7. Composite Final Color: Compute the final pixel color \mathbf{C} by combining the accumulated foreground contribution with the background color, modulated by the global transmittance T: \mathbf{C} = (1 - T) \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi}{\sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi} + T \mathbf{c}{bg} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x: float) -> float: return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def depthawarerendering(gaussians: list, cameracenter: tuple, backgroundcolor: tuple, mlps: dict) -> dict: """ Render scene using Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: position (3D tuple) s: scale (3D tuple) r: rotation (SO(3) representation) Y: spherical harmonic coefficients c: RGB color (3D tuple) sigmainv: inverse covariance matrix (2x2 list of lists) center: projected 2D center (tuple) d: depth in camera coordinates (float) smax: maximum scale component (float) cameracenter: 3D tuple representing camera position tv backgroundcolor: 3D tuple cbg mlps: Dictionary containing MLP functions: 'f': Feature extraction MLP 'phi': Weight prediction MLP 'o': Opacity prediction MLP Returns: pixelcolors: Dictionary mapping pixel coordinates to 3D color tuples """ # Initialize accumulators for all pixels pixelaccum = {} pixelT = {} # Step 1-5: Process each Gaussian for g in gaussians: # 1. Compute Camera-Gaussian vector diff = (g.mu[0] - cameracenter[0], g.mu[1] - cameracenter[1], g.mu[2] - cameracenter[2]) norm = math.sqrt(diff[0]2 + diff[1]2 + diff[2]2) if norm == 0: continue Pi = (diff[0]/norm, diff[1]/norm, diff[2]/norm) # 2. Feature Extraction F = mlps'f' # 3. Predict View-Dependent Weight and Opacity phii = max(0.0, mlps'phi') oi = sigmoid(mlps'o') # 5. Compute Depth-Aware Weight di = g.d smax = g.smax if di == 0: di = 1e-6 wi = phii2 + phii / (di2) + math.exp(smax / di) # 6. Parallel Accumulation # Iterate over all pixels covered by this Gaussian's projection for pixel in g.coveredpixels: # Compute alpha for this specific pixel deltax = (pixel.x - g.center[0], pixel.y - g.center[1]) qx, qy = deltax[0], deltax[1] invsig = g.sigmainv quadform = (invsig[0][0]qx + invsig[0][1]qy)qx + \ (invsig[1][0]qx + invsig[1][1]qy)qy alphai = oi math.exp(-0.5 quadform) # Initialize accumulators if pixel not yet visited if pixel not in pixelaccum: pixelaccum[pixel] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) pixelT[pixel] = 1.0 currentnum, currentden = pixelaccum[pixel] currentT = pixelT[pixel] # Add weighted color contribution newnum = ( currentnum[0] + g.c[0] alphai wi, currentnum[1] + g.c[1] alphai wi, currentnum[2] + g.c[2] alphai wi) newden = currentden + alphai wi # Update global transmittance newT = currentT (1.0 - alphai) pixelaccum[pixel] = (newnum[0], newnum[1], newnum[2], newden) pixelT[pixel] = newT # Step 7: Composite Final Color pixelcolors = {} for pixel, (num, den) in pixelaccum.items(): T = pixelT[pixel] if den == 0: pixelcolors[pixel] = backgroundcolor else: fgcolor = (num[0]/den, num[1]/den, num[2]/den) finalcolor = ( (1.0 - T) fgcolor[0] + T backgroundcolor[0], (1.0 - T) fgcolor[1] + T backgroundcolor[1], (1.0 - T) fgcolor[2] + T backgroundcolor[2]) pixelcolors[pixel] = finalcolor return pixelcolors Parameters: MLP Architectures: The sizes and depths of \text{MLP}f, \text{MLP}\phi, and \text{MLP}o are not specified in the sources. Activation Functions: ReLU for \phii, Sigmoid for oi. Depth di: Depth of the Gaussian center in camera coordinates. Max Scale s{max}: The maximum component of the scale vector si. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency Artifacts: Unordered blending can introduce transparency artifacts in regions with overlapping geometry due to the scarcity of rendering order information. The neural view-dependent enhancement strategy is designed to mitigate this. Division by Zero: Depth di must be handled to avoid division by zero in the weighting function wi. What it is: A specific implementation of Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering tailored for mobile and edge devices. Differentiation: Optimized to reduce storage and inference delay compared to general SortFreeGS implementations. When to choose: When rendering 3D Gaussians on resource-constrained devices like smartphones or AR glasses where sorting and tile-based rendering are too expensive. Link: Mobile-GS What it is: A representative work that achieves fast rendering without sorting using a depth-aware weighting function w(di) = \exp(-\sigmai \betai di). Differentiation: Uses a simpler, non-neural weighting function compared to the learnable view-dependent weighting in Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering. When to choose: When higher visual fidelity is prioritized over extreme mobile performance, and sufficient computational resources are available. Link: SortFreeGS Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels they cover, as each Gaussian is processed for each pixel it affects. The lack of sorting reduces the complexity from O(N \log N) per pixel (or tile) to O(N) accumulation. Memory Complexity: O(N + P) for storing Gaussian attributes and pixel accumulators. The MLPs add a small constant memory overhead. Measured Performance: Enables real-time rendering on mobile hardware by eliminating tile-based rendering and sorting. Strengths: Eliminates the computational bottleneck of depth sorting. Allows parallel accumulation of Gaussian contributions. Neural view-dependent weighting improves visual quality by mitigating transparency artifacts. Limitations: Unordered blending can still introduce transparency artifacts in complex overlapping geometry, though reduced by the neural module. Requires training of MLPs, adding to the training time and complexity. When to use: Real-time rendering applications, especially on edge devices, where sorting is prohibitive. Depth-aware Order-independent Rendering was proposed in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for mobile devices. The method addresses the limitations of traditional alpha blending, which relies on sorting 3D Gaussians by depth, a process that is computationally intensive and unsuitable for real-time rendering on resource-constrained hardware. The technique builds upon earlier SortFree approaches but enhances them with learnable, view-dependent weights to improve visual fidelity. name: Unity Mobile Implementation
head: SplattingAvatar Unity Renderer
body: This method implements the rendering phase of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction within the Unity engine, optimized for mobile devices. It solves the problem of real-time, high-fidelity rendering of dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars by relying on a warped mesh for rigging and standard alpha blending for compositing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by prioritizing maximum compatibility with Unity's standard rendering pipeline and mobile performance constraints, using a simple front-to-back sorting and quad-based rasterization rather than tiled or sort-free GPU-native approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, covariance, color, and opacity; a rigged mesh (FBX) defining the avatar's pose; camera parameters. Outputs: A rendered 2D image with alpha channel. Data Structures: Gaussian Data: Stored in a.ply file. Contains attributes for each Gaussian: position (\mathbf{x}), 3D covariance matrix (\Sigma), spherical harmonics coefficients (for color), and opacity (\alpha). Embedding Data: Stored in a.json file. Describes the mapping between static anchor features and dynamic Gaussian attributes. Mesh Data: Stored in an.fbx file. Contains the rigged mesh topology and bone hierarchy. Triangle order must be maintained for correct rendering. Steps: 1. Export and Import: Export the canonical mesh as.obj to Mixamo for autorigging. Export one.ply file of the Gaussians, one.json file describing the embedding, and the rigged.fbx file to Unity. Note: The.fbx file can be rigged by other software if triangle order is preserved. 2. Pose and Projection: Apply the bone transformations from the rigged mesh to the Gaussian positions to obtain world-space positions. Project the 3D Gaussians into camera space. Calculate the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma' in screen space for each Gaussian based on the camera projection and the 3D covariance. 3. Sorting: Sort all Gaussians by their z-axis coordinate in camera coordinates from near to far. This is performed on the CPU or via a compute shader before rendering. 4. Rasterization: For each visible Gaussian, draw one front-parallel quad primitive centered at its projected position. The quad's size and shape are determined by the 2D covariance \Sigma'. This "one-primitive-one-Gaussian" strategy ensures proper occlusion handling with other regular objects in the scene. 5. Fragment Shader: For each pixel covered by a quad, compute the color and alpha. Emit color with alpha pre-multiplication. Set the blend function to (ONE, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendergaussianavatar(gaussians, camera, meshpose): # 1. Transform Gaussians transformedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Apply bone transformation from meshpose to g.position worldpos = applyrig(g.position, meshpose) # Project to camera space campos = project(worldpos, camera) # Calculate 2D covariance in screen space cov2d = projectcovariance(g.cov3d, camera) transformedgaussians.append({ 'pos': campos, 'cov2d': cov2d, 'color': g.color, 'alpha': g.alpha }) # 2. Sort by depth (z-axis in camera coordinates, near to far) transformedgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['pos'].z) # 3. Render for g in transformedgaussians: # Draw a front-parallel quad centered at g.pos with size from g.cov2d drawquad(g.pos, g.cov2d) # Fragment shader logic (conceptual) # For each pixel in the quad: # Compute distance from center using cov2d # Calculate alpha = exp(-0.5 dist^2) g.alpha # Color = g.color alpha # Blend with existing color using ONE, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Triangle Order: If the.fbx file is rigged by external software, the triangle order must be maintained to ensure correct rendering. Occlusion: The one-primitive-one-Gaussian strategy is critical for handling occlusion with other scene objects. Mobile Performance: On mobile devices, the sorting and drawing overhead can be significant. The method aims for steady 30 FPS on iPhone 13. This method implements the rendering phase of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction by leveraging the Unity Sentis framework to execute Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) as custom compute shaders on the GPU. It solves the problem of dynamically predicting 3D Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) from static anchor features and a time-varying context encoding \Psi(x) without CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks. Unlike static splatting, this approach allows for real-time appearance changes by invoking the MLP with different encodings, while maintaining a fixed memory footprint since the number of predicted Gaussians remains constant. Performance: Over 300 FPS on a modern GPU; steady 30 FPS on an iPhone 13. Strengths: High compatibility with Unity's standard pipeline; proper occlusion handling with other objects; good rendering quality for head avatars, especially in eye and hair regions. Limitations: Relies on CPU sorting which may not scale as well as tiled or sort-free methods on very high-resolution scenes; performance on mobile is lower than on modern desktop GPUs. When to use: When targeting mobile devices with Unity and requiring compatibility with standard rendering pipelines and occlusion handling. When not to use: When maximum performance on high-end desktop GPUs is required, or when dynamic attribute prediction via MLPs is needed (use Sentis implementation instead). The method is part of the SplattingAvatar project, which focuses on Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction. It was developed to provide a practical implementation for mobile devices, leveraging Unity's capabilities. The approach builds on the general 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering principles but adapts them for the constraints and features of the Unity engine and mobile hardware. body: This method implements the rendering phase of Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction by leveraging the Unity Sentis framework to execute Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) as custom compute shaders on the GPU. It solves the problem of dynamically predicting 3D Gaussian attributes from static anchor features and a time-varying context encoding \Psi(x) without CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks. Unlike static splatting, this approach allows for real-time appearance changes by invoking the MLP with different encodings, while maintaining a fixed memory footprint since the number of predicted Gaussians remains constant. Inputs: 1. Anchor Features: A set of feature vectors and their corresponding 3D positions, uploaded to GPU memory at initialization. 2. Context Encoding \Psi(x): A dynamic input vector used to modulate the Gaussian attributes. 3. MLP Models: Serialized.sentis models derived from.onnx files, representing the mapping from anchors/encoding to Gaussian parameters. Outputs: 1. Compute Buffers: Containing the predicted 3D Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). 2. Rasterized Image: The final rendered frame passed to the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renderer. Data Structures: Anchor Data: Pinned in GPU memory to prevent readbacks. name: CPU-based Gaussian Splatting Thumbnailer
head: 3D Gaussian Splat CPU Rasterization, 3DGS Thumbnail, CPU Gaussian Splat Rendering, CPU Gaussian Splat Thumbnail Rendering, Gaussian Splat Thumbnail Rendering, Splat Thumbnail Generation
body: This method generates low-resolution preview images (thumbnails) from trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes using a pure CPU pipeline optimized for speed via Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation. It solves the problem of slow interactive preview generation by simplifying the rendering model—omitting Gaussian rotation and complex shading—and leveraging Numba to accelerate Python-based numerical loops. It differs from its parent, 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced), by explicitly excluding rotation data, using a simplified approximate blending function, and processing a fixed opacity-filtered budget of splats rather than full alpha compositing. Inputs: Scene files in formats.ply,.splat,.spz,.sog,.ksplat,.lcc, or.compressed.ply. Fixed camera parameters: position, target, and field of view (FOV). Parameters: Gaussian splat size scalar \sigma, output resolution, opacity threshold, and splat budget. Outputs: A PNG image file representing the rendered thumbnail. Scene data is parsed into parallel arrays for position (3 floats), scale (3 floats), and fdc (degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficient, 3 floats). Rotation data is explicitly omitted from the input structure. Format routing inspects PLY headers or file extensions to select native numpy.fromfile() decoding or CPU conversion via the PlayCanvas splat-transform CLI. 1. Camera Setup: Compute fixed view (V) and projection (P) matrices from the camera position, target, and FOV. 2. Format Conversion & Coordinate Normalization: Convert input formats to a standard 3DGS PLY representation; rotate scenes 180° about the Z-axis to convert the original COLMAP Y-down convention to Y-up. 3. Visible Splat Extraction & Filtering: Identify Gaussians falling within the camera’s frustum. Compute opacity O = \text{sigmoid}(opacity) and discard any splat where O < 0.2. 4. Budget Sampling: Sample the remaining splats to a target budget (1 million splats per vCPU, maximum 5 million total) with probability proportional to their opacity O. 5. Splat Sorting: Sort the visible splats by their camera-space z-depth in back-to-front order (farthest first) to ensure proper front-to-back blending. 6. Projection & Rasterization: Project each Gaussian center onto the image plane using V and P; treat Gaussians as simple, rotation-less spheres. Compute footprint radius R = 2 \times \exp(\max(scale)). Rasterize using a fast approximate blending method where color contribution is computed based on a simplified weighting function considering distance from splat center and current depth values. 7. Buffer Update & Output: Update color and depth buffers with blended colors and depth values as each Gaussian is blended; save the color buffer as a PNG image file. C = 0.5 + 0.28209479 \times f{dc} where C is the output color and f{dc} is the degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficient. O = \text{sigmoid}(opacity) where O is the computed opacity used for filtering and sampling. R = 2 \times \exp(\max(scale)) where R is the footprint radius in pixels and scale represents the scale components. \sigma (Splat Size): Scalar controlling spatial extent. Tested values: \{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0\}. Smaller values preserve detail but cause fragmentation; larger values increase coverage but cause blurring. Resolution: Discrete variable. Tested values: 480p (640 \times 480), 720p (960 \times 720), 1080p (1440 \times 1080). Opacity Threshold: Splats with opacity below 0.2 are dropped. Splat Budget: 1 million splats per vCPU, capped at 5 million total. Footprint Multiplier: The footprint radius is twice the exponential of the maximum scale component. Python Loop Bottleneck: Standard Python interpretation is too slow for the rasterization loop; mitigated by using Numba for JIT compilation of performance-critical numerical routines. Parallel Processing: Deliberately avoided due to caching and computation management overhead on systems with limited core counts. Visual Eligibility: Omitting rotation data reduces computational cost but may impact visual quality; however, evaluations showed negligible impact on thumbnail eligibility. Security/Isolation: The splat-transform CLI is executed with strict constraints: only an allowlisted local file inside the work directory is accessible, no shell is used, and a timeout is applied. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from numba import njit @njit def computefootprintradius(scale): """R = 2 exp(max(scale)) """ return 2.0 np.exp(np.max(scale)) @njit def approximateweight(distsq, footprintradius): """Simplified Gaussian weighting function considering distance """ return np.exp(-distsq / (2.0 footprintradius footprintradius)) @njit def renderthumbnail(positions, scales, fdc, depths, width, height, sigma): """ Renders a thumbnail using CPU-sorted, rotation-less Gaussian splats. positions: (N, 3) array of camera-space centers scales: (N, 3) array of scale components fdc: (N, 3) array of degree-0 spherical harmonic coefficients depths: (N,) array of camera-space z-depths (sorted back-to-front) """ colorbuffer = np.zeros((height, width, 3), dtype=np.float32) depthbuffer = np.full((height, width), np.inf, dtype=np.float32) for i in range(len(positions)): pos = positions[i] scale = scales[i] color = 0.5 + 0.28209479 fdc[i] depth = depths[i] # Project center to screen space ndcx = (pos[0] 1.0) ndcy = (pos[1] 1.0) screenx = (ndcx + 1.0) 0.5 width screeny = (1.0 - (ndcy + 1.0) 0.5) height radius = computefootprintradius(scale) if radius < 1.0: radius = 1.0 # Determine bounding box covering the splat circle xmin = int(max(0, screenx - radius)) xmax = int(min(width - 1, screenx + radius)) ymin = int(max(0, screeny - radius)) ymax = int(min(height - 1, screeny + radius)) for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): dx = x - screenx dy = y - screeny distsq = dx dx + dy dy w = approximateweight(distsq, radius) # Buffer Update: quick composition without expensive memory operations if depth < depthbuffer[y, x]: alpha = w colorbuffer[y, x, 0] = colorbuffer[y, x, 0] (1.0 - alpha) + color[0] alpha colorbuffer[y, x, 1] = colorbuffer[y, x, 1] (1.0 - alpha) + color[1] alpha colorbuffer[y, x, 2] = colorbuffer[y, x, 2] (1.0 - alpha) + color[2] alpha depthbuffer[y, x] = depth return colorbuffer Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization loop over visible splats. Complexity is roughly O(N{visible} \cdot A{splat}), where N{visible} is the number of visible Gaussians and A{splat} is the average area of a splat in pixels. JIT compilation reduces the constant factor significantly. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian attributes and O(W \cdot H) for the color and depth buffers. Hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5995WX, 16 GB RAM, Arch Linux Kernel 6.9.1. Software: Python 3.13.7, NumPy 2.1.3, Numba 0.61.0. JIT vs Non-JIT: JIT acceleration provides a ~156× speed-up (2.15s vs 336s for \sigma=0.7, fixed resolution). Execution Times (JIT Enabled): \sigma=0.1: 0.9s (480p), 0.94s (720p), 1.29s (1080p) \sigma=0.2: 0.97s (480p), 1.11s (720p), 1.87s (1080p) \sigma=0.4: 1.03s (480p), 1.42s (720p), 2.99s (1080p) \sigma=0.5: 1.29s (480p), 1.87s (720p), 4.20s (1080p) \sigma=0.7: 2.15s (480p), 3.65s (720p), 7.11s (1080p) \sigma=1.0: 3.66s (480p), 6.42s (720p), 13.31s (1080p) Strengths: Extremely fast execution on CPU due to JIT compilation and simplified rendering model (no rotation, approximate blending). Limitations: Lower visual fidelity compared to full GPU splatting or rotation-aware CPU rendering; fragmentation at small \sigma, blurring at large \sigma. Use when rapid thumbnail generation is required on CPU-only systems or when GPU resources are unavailable. Use when visual fidelity is secondary to speed (e.g., scene browsing, preview generation). The method was developed by E. Genchev et al. and published in Array (Volume 28, 2025, 100611). It was designed to address the computational intensity of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering by creating a lightweight, CPU-based thumbnailer. The work focuses on parameter optimization (\sigma, resolution) and the use of JIT compilation to mitigate Python's performance limitations. The method was evaluated by colleagues with backgrounds in computer graphics. The most preferred configurations were \sigma=0.4 and \sigma=0.5 at 720p resolution, balancing visual clarity and rendering performance. name: Support Guard
head: Coordinate box clamp, Per-primitive clamp, node-local guard
body: The Support Guard is a fault-mitigation technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents catastrophic rendering errors caused by Single-Event Upsets (SEUs), such as bit flips in memory, by clamping primitive parameters to the valid range observed during training. It solves the problem of frame-spanning corruption, where a single bit flip in a scale parameter can exponentially inflate a primitive into a translucent sheet covering most of the screen. Unlike activation range supervision used in CNNs, which clamps neuron outputs to statistical distributions, the Support Guard clamps geometric and appearance parameters to the bounded parameter space of the optimized scene, providing a geometric correctness argument. It operates as a pure per-primitive clamp with zero additional memory overhead, making it suitable for deployment on spaceborne, robotic, and clustered hardware where reliability is critical. The method enforces a hard boundary on every parameter of every Gaussian primitive before rendering, ensuring that no primitive exceeds the trained parameter bounds and neutralizing the exponential impact of bit flips in logarithmic scale fields. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives with parameters including position, rotation, scale, opacity, and color. Input: The per-field support box Bf, defined as the per-component minimum and maximum values observed over all primitives in the clean, trained model for each parameter field f. Output: A set of guarded primitives where every component lies within its respective support box Bf. Support Box (Bf): For each parameter field f, Bf is a pair of scalars [\ellf, hf] representing the global minimum and maximum of that field across the entire scene. \ellf = \min{i} (\mathbf{p}i[f]) hf = \max{i} (\mathbf{p}i[f]) These bounds are computed once from the trained checkpoint and remain static during rendering. The guard is applied per-primitive before rendering each tile or frame. For each primitive i and each parameter field f: 1. Retrieve the current value x of the parameter. 2. Check if x lies within the support box [\ellf, hf]. 3. If x < \ellf, clamp x to \ellf. 4. If x > hf, clamp x to hf. 5. If \ellf \le x \le hf, leave x unchanged. This process is repeated for all components of all primitives. In a distributed sort-first rendering architecture, this guard is applied node-locally on each node before it renders its assigned tile, ensuring that out-of-range primitives are contained at the node that owns them before compositing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applysupportguard(primitives, supportboxes): """ Clamps all primitive parameters to their trained support boxes. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects, each having attributes corresponding to parameter fields (e.g., scalex, opacity). supportboxes: Dictionary mapping parameter field names to tuples (minval, maxval). Returns: primitives: The same list of primitives, modified in-place. """ for primitive in primitives: for fieldname, (minval, maxval) in supportboxes.items(): currentval = getattr(primitive, fieldname) if currentval < minval: setattr(primitive, fieldname, minval) elif currentval > maxval: setattr(primitive, fieldname, maxval) # Else: value is within bounds, leave unchanged return primitives Support Box Bf: The coordinate box for field f is defined as Bf = [\ellf, hf], where \ellf and hf are the empirical min and max of field f over the clean trained model. Clamping Function: For a parameter x and box Bf = [\ellf, hf], the guarded value x' is: x' = \begin{cases} \ellf & \text{if } x < \ellf \\ x & \text{if } \ellf \le x \le hf \\ hf & \text{if } x > hf \end{cases} Scale Explosion Mitigation: A sign flip in the logarithmic scale \theta (where s = \exp(\theta)) can change \theta \approx -3 to \theta \approx +3, causing s \to s \cdot e^6. The guard clamps \theta back into B{\theta}, preventing this exponential explosion. Support Box Bounds (\ellf, hf): Determined from the trained model. Cost: 76 µs per frame, or 0.07× a single-view render time. Memory Overhead: None (1× memory relative to unguarded). Catastrophic Upsets: Without the guard, a single scale sign-bit upset can inflate one primitive into a translucent sheet spanning most of the frame, causing catastrophic corruption. Residual Errors: The guard neutralizes 90.4% of catastrophic upsets. The remaining 9.6% are in-support mantissa-level residuals that are bounded by Lemma 1 in the source and are perceptually invisible. Distributed Rendering: In a distributed renderer, the spatial extent of a corrupted primitive equals the number of screen tiles (and thus compositing nodes) that a single upset contaminates. The node-local guard contains this corruption to the node where it occurs. Clean Model Invariance: The guard leaves a clean model unchanged by construction, as all clean parameters lie within Bf by definition. Time Complexity: The guard parallelizes trivially across primitives. The measured cost is 76 µs per frame, which is approximately 0.07× a single-view render time. Memory Complexity: Zero additional memory overhead. It operates on the existing primitive data structures. Effectiveness: Neutralizes 90.4% of catastrophic upsets. Under accumulated dose (up to 20,000 simultaneous upsets), the guarded renderer maintains a mean global PSNR close to clean, whereas the unguarded renderer degrades to 10.6 dB. Worst-Case Footprint: In a test of 768,000 guarded single-bit upsets, the worst observed corruption footprint was 11.68% of the frame, with 470 residual catastrophic events. Comparison to Alternatives: Full Duplication: Requires 3× memory and voting. ECC Sign+Exp: Requires ~1.3× memory and parity. Selective Clamp: Clamps only scale and opacity. It is cheaper than the full guard but similarly effective, as scale and opacity carry most catastrophic mass. When to Use: Deploy on hardware susceptible to SEUs (spaceborne, robotic, clustered) where memory bandwidth and capacity are constrained, and where catastrophic frame-spanning errors are unacceptable. The Support Guard was introduced in the paper "Single-Event Upsets in 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering: Bit-Level Criticality, Spatial Extent, and a Parallel Support Guard". The work was motivated by the need to deploy real-time radiance-field rendering on hardware exposed to radiation, such as spaceborne and robotic platforms. The authors identified that 3DGS primitives, being explicit and interpretable, are susceptible to bit-level criticality, particularly in the logarithmic scale parameters where sign flips cause exponential scale explosions. The Support Guard was developed as a lightweight, geometrically grounded mitigation strategy that exploits the compact, bounded nature of trained 3DGS parameter spaces. It was validated against a fault grid of 768,000 single-bit upsets and proven to make frame-covering corruption impossible under any single-bit upset (Theorems 1 and 2). name: SimpleRenderer
body: SimpleRenderer is a CPU-based renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting that projects 3D Gaussian distributions into 2D screen-space elliptical splats and composites them using a standard painter's algorithm with alpha blending. It performs all projection, sorting, and rasterization on the CPU using standard array operations, making it suitable for debugging, thumbnail generation, or environments lacking specialized graphics hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, color, scale, and opacity; a camera model providing projection matrices and intrinsics (fx); and configuration parameters (nearplane, farplane, alphathreshold, backgroundcolor). Outputs: A 2D image of shape (H, W, 3) with float32 dtype. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Arrays for positions (N, 3), colors (N, 3), scales (N, 3), and opacities (N, 1). Image Buffer: A 3D array img of shape (H, W, 3). Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an image buffer img of shape (H, W, 3) initialized to backgroundcolor. 2. Camera Transformation: Transform Gaussian positions to camera coordinates using the camera's world-to-camera transformation. Extract the depth values z{vals} from the third component of the transformed points. 3. Filtering: Filter Gaussians to retain only those where near\plane \le z{vals} \le far\plane and opacity > alpha\threshold. 4. Projection: Project the remaining Gaussian centers to pixel coordinates (u, v) using the camera's camera-to-pixel transformation. 5. Sorting: Sort the filtered Gaussians by depth z{vals} in descending order (far to near) to implement the painter's algorithm. 6. Rendering Loop: For each Gaussian i in the sorted list: a. Radius Calculation: Calculate the screen-space radius. Let s{mean} be the mean of the Gaussian's scales. Compute: radius = \min(15, \max(1, \lfloor s{mean} \cdot \frac{fx}{\max(z{vals}[i], 0.1)} \rfloor)) The depth is clamped to a minimum of 0.1 to prevent division by zero or excessively large radii. b. Bounding Box: Define the pixel bounding box for the splat: y{min} = \max(0, \lfloor v \rfloor - radius) y{max} = \min(H, \lfloor v \rfloor + radius + 1) x{min} = \max(0, \lfloor u \rfloor - radius) x{max} = \min(W, \lfloor u \rfloor + radius + 1) If the bounding box is invalid (e.g., u or v is far outside bounds such that the box is empty), skip the Gaussian. c. Weight Calculation: For each pixel (x, y) in the bounding box, compute the normalized squared distance from the center: dist\sq = \frac{(x - u)^2 + (y - v)^2}{radius^2 + 10^{-8}} Calculate the Gaussian weight: w = \exp(-dist\sq) \cdot \alphai d. Blending: Update the image buffer using alpha blending for each color channel c \in \{0, 1, 2\}: img[y, x, c] = img[y, x, c] \cdot (1 - w) + Ci[c] \cdot w where Ci[c] is the c-th component of the Gaussian's color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def simplerenderer(gaussians, camera, config, H, W): """ Render 3D Gaussians using a CPU-based painter's algorithm. Args: gaussians: Dict with keys 'pos' (N,3), 'color' (N,3), 'scale' (N,3), 'opacity' (N,1) camera: Object with methods worldtocamera, cameratopixel, and attribute fx config: Object with attributes nearplane, farplane, alphathreshold, backgroundcolor H: Image height W: Image width Returns: img: (H, W, 3) float32 array """ # 1. Initialize image img = np.full((H, W, 3), config.backgroundcolor, dtype=np.float32) # 2. Transform to camera space campoints = camera.worldtocamera(gaussians['pos']) # (N, 3) zvals = campoints[:, 2] # (N,) # 3. Filter Gaussians validmask = ( (zvals >= config.nearplane) & (zvals <= config.farplane) & (gaussians['opacity'].flatten() > config.alphathreshold)) if not np.any(validmask): return img filteredpos = campoints[validmask] filteredcolor = gaussians['color'][validmask] filteredscale = gaussians['scale'][validmask] filteredopacity = gaussians['opacity'][validmask].flatten() filteredz = zvals[validmask] # 4. Project to pixel coordinates pixelcoords = camera.cameratopixel(filteredpos) # (M, 2), (u, v) u = pixelcoords[:, 0] v = pixelcoords[:, 1] # 5. Sort by depth (far to near) sortindices = np.argsort(filteredz)[::-1] u = u[sortindices] v = v[sortindices] filteredcolor = filteredcolor[sortindices] filteredopacity = filteredopacity[sortindices] filteredscale = filteredscale[sortindices] filteredz = filteredz[sortindices] # 6. Render loop fx = camera.fx for i in range(len(filteredz)): z = filteredz[i] # Clamp z to prevent division by zero zclamped = max(z, 0.1) # Calculate radius smean = np.mean(filteredscale[i]) radius = int(smean fx / zclamped) radius = max(1, min(radius, 15)) # Cap at 15 # Bounding box ymin = max(0, int(v[i]) - radius) ymax = min(H, int(v[i]) + radius + 1) xmin = max(0, int(u[i]) - radius) xmax = min(W, int(u[i]) + radius + 1) # Skip if out of bounds if ymin >= ymax or xmin >= xmax: continue # Precompute weight factor alpha = filteredopacity[i] color = filteredcolor[i] # Create meshgrid for bounding box ys, xs = np.mgrid[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax] # Normalized squared distance distsq = ((xs - u[i])2 + (ys - v[i])2) / (radius2 + 1e-8) # Gaussian weight w = np.exp(-distsq) alpha # Blend img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 0] = img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 0] (1 - w) + color[0] w img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 1] = img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 1] (1 - w) + color[1] w img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 2] = img[ymin:ymax, xmin:xmax, 2] (1 - w) + color[2] w return img Parameters: config.nearplane: Minimum depth for valid Gaussians. config.farplane: Maximum depth for valid Gaussians. config.alphathreshold: Minimum opacity for a Gaussian to be considered valid. config.backgroundcolor: RGB array of shape (3,) used to initialize the image canvas. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If no Gaussians pass the filtering stage, the function returns the background-initialized image immediately. If a Gaussian's projected center (u, v) is outside the image bounds, the bounding box calculation may result in an empty range; the implementation must skip such Gaussians. The radius is capped at 15 to avoid excessive computational overhead for large splats. Depth z{vals}[i] is clamped to a minimum of 0.1 in the radius calculation to prevent division by zero or extremely large radii. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for sorting, plus O(M \cdot R^2) for rasterization, where N is the total number of Gaussians, M is the number of visible Gaussians, and R is the average radius (capped at 15). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian attributes and intermediate arrays. Performance: Suitable for low-resolution outputs or small scenes due to CPU-bound processing. Not suitable for real-time rendering or high-resolution video generation without significant optimization. Strengths: Simple implementation, easy to debug, no GPU dependency. Limitations: Slow for large scenes, no support for differentiable rendering, limited by CPU cache and memory bandwidth. SimpleRenderer is an implementation detail found in the GaussianScan-Recon repository, an unofficial project for 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction. It serves as a basic rendering backend for generating thumbnails or debugging visualizations during the reconstruction process. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3D-GS rendering, 3DGS, Bernoulli sampling, R rasterization-based radiance field rendering, Rasterization-based radiance field rendering, Splat Regression Instance
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a novel view synthesis method that represents a 3D scene as an explicit collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color. Unlike implicit neural radiance fields (NeRFs) that require volumetric ray marching, 3DGS projects these 3D Gaussians into 2D screen-space ellipses and renders them via a tile-based, differentiable rasterization pipeline with alpha compositing. This approach achieves real-time rendering speeds (100+ FPS) and significantly faster training times compared to NeRFs, while maintaining high photorealistic quality. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using explicit, differentiable Gaussian primitives that allow for fast, tile-based rasterization and direct gradient flow to scene parameters, enabling end-to-end optimization from sparse 2D images. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each parameterized by: Mean position \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion). Scale s \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-space). Opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R} (log-space). Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times (N{SH}+1)^2} for view-dependent color, typically degree 3 (N{SH}=3, 48 coefficients). Camera parameters: Intrinsic matrix \mathbf{K} (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy) and extrinsic view matrix \mathbf{V}. Image dimensions W \times H. Outputs: A rendered RGB image \mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. The scene is stored as a list of Gaussian attributes. CoR-GS The 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer renders a scene represented by a set of 3D Gaussian primitives into a 2D image by projecting them to screen space, sorting them by depth, and accumulating their contributions via alpha compositing. Unlike volumetric ray marching used in NeRFs, this method operates in object order, rasterizing 2D elliptical kernels (splats) directly onto the image plane. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific use of a tile-based, front-to-back alpha blending pipeline that is fully differentiable with respect to all Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity) and camera poses, enabling end-to-end gradient-based optimization. 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer EffGS is an acceleration framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that improves training and rendering efficiency while maintaining high-fidelity reconstruction in both bounded and large-scale scenes. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS and other acceleration methods by combining frequency-aware guidance, localized density control, and adaptive primitive scale modulation to prevent quality degradation in complex environments. EffGS 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP is a self-contained, pure-PyTorch implementation of the core 3D Gaussian Splatting algorithm, designed as a teaching reference rather than a production renderer. It renders 3D Gaussians onto screen space and rasterizes them using alpha blending to produce smooth, hole-free images from arbitrary viewpoints. It sets itself apart from production implementations by intentionally omitting tile-based CUDA rasterization, spherical harmonics for view-dependent color, and adaptive density control, relying instead on a readable Python loop for the forward pass. 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training resolves boundary artifacts in chunked volume training by including ellipsoids from neighboring chunks in the loss computation without updating their parameters, providing boundary context without requiring a global volume or merged model. Unlike chunk-based 3DGS methods that resolve boundary inconsistencies by merging chunks into a global coarse model or through post-training stages, this method requires boundary support during training itself without access to a global volume. Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training Substitutive LOD with K-wise moment-matched merging is a technique for reducing the number of 3D Gaussians in a scene by merging groups of K splats into a single representative Gaussian, thereby boosting rendering performance and managing memory constraints. It addresses the problem of excessive Gaussian counts and associated aliasing artifacts by replacing small or redundant Gaussians with larger, merged ones. Unlike methods that modify Gaussians during reconstruction or prune based on static importance, this method operates on the final set of Gaussians using cost metrics to guide the merging process, allowing for runtime LOD selection. It sets itself apart from siblings like CoR-GS and EffGS by focusing on substitutive merging via moment matching rather than density control or vector quantization. Substitutive LOD with K-wise Moment-Matched Merging Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle time-varying scenes by assigning time-varying position and rotation attributes to each Gaussian primitive. It solves the problem of temporal flicker and storage explosion inherent in per-frame baselines by enforcing physical plausibility through local-rigid and As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) or isometry constraints. Unlike 4D Gaussian Splatting which uses implicit neural fields or planes to predict deformation offsets from a canonical space, this method explicitly tracks the motion of each Gaussian particle, offering a more direct representation of dynamic geometry. Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is a method that incorporates an epipolar transformer to generalize features between two views, pairing this with a probabilistic prediction of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting This method reconstructs a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene from a small set of input images using a Transformer architecture. It differs from sibling methods like CoR-GS by relying on SAM's 2D segmentation capabilities to guide 3D Gaussian assignment rather than learned identity encodings or language features. SAGA Quantile Rendering (Q-Render) is a sparse, transmittance-guided sampling strategy designed to efficiently render high-dimensional feature maps from 3D Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of dense volume rendering, where accumulating high-dimensional features along every ray scales poorly with feature dimensionality. Unlike conventional volume rendering, which processes all rasterized Gaussians, Q-Render shifts the Riemann partition from the spatial domain to the transmittance domain, sampling only the most representative "quantile Gaussians" that dominate the ray's transmittance profile. This approach reduces complexity from O(N C) to O(N + K C), enabling real-time rendering of high-dimensional data (e.g., 512-D CLIP embeddings) while maintaining segmentation accuracy. Quantile Rendering 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to model dynamic scenes by treating time as a fourth dimension, enabling the reconstruction and real-time rendering of 3D videos from arbitrary viewpoints and timestamps. Unlike static 3DGS which assumes a fixed scene, 4DGS captures spatiotemporal deformations of position, rotation, scale, and appearance, allowing for the generation of novel views at any continuous time t. It distinguishes itself from deformation-field methods (e.g., Dynamic3DGS) by maintaining a canonical set of Gaussians transformed by a learned field, and from naive temporal extensions by using coherent 4D covariance structures or explicit spatiotemporal encoders to ensure smooth motion and appearance interpolation. 4D Gaussian Splatting Taming 3DGS is a resource-efficiency method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that imposes an explicit cap on the total number of Gaussians to enable high-quality rendering on consumer-grade GPUs. It steers the densification process to spend a fixed budget where it helps most, trading peak quality for faster training and smaller model size. Unlike standard 3DGS which allows unbounded growth, this approach formulates optimization as a mixed-integer problem to maintain a constant Gaussian count. Taming 3DGS Analytic-Splatting is a rendering method that replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area to reduce aliasing artifacts during zooming or resolution changes. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting which treats pixels as isolated points, or Mip-Splatting which uses a hybrid filtering mechanism that suppresses high-frequency components, Analytic-Splatting preserves high-quality details by analytically integrating the signal using a conditioned logistic function approximation of the Gaussian CDF. It sets apart from standard perspective projection by supporting optimal tangent-plane projections [3293-optimal-gaussian-splatting.md] and specialized geometries such as cone-beam X-ray scanning [3458-3d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization-cone-beam-scanner-space.md]. It sets itself apart from single-GPU baselines by preserving the original 3DGS algorithm and convergence characteristics while using spatial partitioning with ghost cells for boundary consistency and sparse all-to-all communication to distribute the rasterization workload. Distributed 3DGS Training Point-Based Ray Tracing for Visibility serves as a sparse visibility oracle that evaluates transmittance along sampled light directions using a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) of Gaussian proxies, enabling evaluation from any point in space in any direction. Unlike the camera-tied rasterizer, it decouples visibility estimation from screen-space projection, allowing it to act as a drop-in companion to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by reusing the same EWA-splatting formulation for consistent blending without requiring training mismatch. Point-Based Ray Tracing for Visibility Primitive Representation defines the geometric and probabilistic entities used to model 3D scenes in differentiable splatting methods, serving as the fundamental building blocks for rendering. It solves the problem of representing complex geometry and appearance with explicit, differentiable primitives that can be projected and composited efficiently. What sets it apart from implicit representations (like NeRFs) is the use of explicit, analytically defined density functions (typically Gaussians) that allow for fast, tile-based rasterization and direct gradient flow to scene parameters. It differs from sibling methods like CoR-GS or 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by focusing on the definition of the primitive itself (shape, distribution, dimensionality) rather than the rasterization pipeline or optimization strategy. Primitive Representation This family defines how 3D Gaussian primitives are shaded, blended, and lit to produce the final pixel color, extending the basic rasterization of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the limitation of standard splatting, which renders only baked view-dependent colors, by introducing physical material properties, analytic anti-aliasing, and robust transparency handling. It differs from Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading by focusing on physical material properties and deferred pipelines rather than analytic signal response, and from Transparency and Blending Models by its explicit handling of light transport and occlusion transmittance. Shading and Lighting Models 3DGS Radiance Caching is a real-time variance reduction technique for volume path tracing that uses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to store and query cached radiance values. It reduces noise by probabilistically accepting cached samples based on throughput luminance and a scaling parameter, optimizing exponentially subsampled Gaussians from noisy path samples to achieve real-time frame rates. Unlike neural radiance caching which requires large memory footprints, this method leverages the compact representation of 3DGS to store attenuated radiance at multiple path lengths, offering a significantly smaller memory footprint. 3DGS Radiance Caching Ray-splat intersection algorithms evaluate the contribution of 3D Gaussians by intersecting viewing rays with the Gaussian primitives directly, rather than projecting them onto the image plane. This family provides exact or analytically derived intersections, enabling correct handling of semi-transparency and degenerate splats. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which approximates the projection as an affine 2D Gaussian, these methods compute the Gaussian's maximum contribution along each ray. Ray-Splat Intersection Algorithms Application-Specific Extensions modify the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline to address requirements beyond novel-view synthesis of RGB imagery, such as physical property rendering, explicit geometry extraction, and advanced lighting effects. Unlike standard 3DGS, which optimizes view-dependent spherical harmonic colors for photometric accuracy, these methods replace or augment the attribute representation with scalar densities, feature vectors, or physical parameters, and often introduce post-processing or multi-stage rendering pipelines to support downstream tasks like simulation, medical imaging, or inverse rendering. Application-Specific Extensions Rasterization Pipeline Optimization refers to algorithmic and hardware techniques that accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering by reducing computational overhead in tile intersection, sorting, and alpha compositing. It solves the bottleneck where standard rasterization overestimates Gaussian extents, processes non-intersecting pixels, and suffers from serial blending latency Child. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer (which focuses on the differentiable math) or 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP (which focuses on memory layout) is the explicit restructuring of the rendering pipeline stages—specifically moving culling to parallel preprocess phases, replacing coarse bounding-box tests with precise geometric checks, and co-designing hardware units for projection and sorting ChildChildChild. Rasterization Pipeline Optimization This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by attaching high-dimensional feature vectors to Gaussian primitives or by modeling animatable human avatars from multi-view data. It differs from standard rendering by accumulating these feature vectors via differentiable alpha-blending rather than just color, and from sibling methods by rendering feature maps directly through differentiable alpha-compositing [8130-semantic-and-language-embeddings.md]. For structural extensions, it solves dynamic appearance and geometry reconstruction by maintaining a canonical space representation where Gaussians are deformed via differentiable functions driven by pose parameters before rasterization [8209-human-and-articulated-avatars.md]. Semantic and Structural Extensions Optimization and Training is the iterative process that adjusts the parameters of a set of 3D Gaussian primitives to minimize the difference between rendered images and ground truth views. It solves the problem of reconstructing a photorealistic 3D scene representation from a sparse set of 2D images by differentiating through the rasterization pipeline. Unlike NeRF-based methods which optimize a continuous neural field, 3DGS training optimizes explicit geometric primitives (means, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonic coefficients), offering significantly faster training and inference speeds while maintaining comparable image quality. The method distinguishes itself through its use of adaptive density control, which dynamically adds or removes Gaussians during training to resolve under-reconstructed or over-reconstructed regions. Optimization and Training Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of Gaussians overlapping the pixel. Sorting is O(N \log N) or O(N) with radix sort. Memory Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. Typical scenes use tens of thousands to millions of Gaussians. Performance: Achieves up to 100+ FPS in real-time rendering. Strengths: Real-time rendering, fast training, high-quality novel view synthesis, explicit representation. Limitations: Scene-specific (requires re-training for new scenes), artifacts in out-of-domain views, memory usage scales with scene complexity. When to Use: Real-time novel view synthesis, dynamic scene rendering, applications requiring explicit scene representation. When Not to Use: Scenes with complex, non-Lambertian materials without SH, scenes requiring global illumination beyond baked SH, unknown scenes without re-training. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It represents a shift from implicit neural fields (NeRFs) to explicit Gaussian primitives, enabling real-time differentiable rendering. The method was initially developed for novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction from multi-view images. It has since been extended to dynamic scenes (4DGS, Dynamic 3DGS), human avatars (GaussianAvatar, HumanGS), and various other applications. The core innovation lies in the efficient projection and rasterization of 3D Gaussians, allowing for gradient-based optimization of scene parameters. body: CoR-GS improves sparse-view reconstruction by defining two independent reconstructions and comparing them to discard inaccurate Gaussians. It differs from feed-forward network approaches by relying on a consistency check between dual optimization paths to prune erroneous primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of input images. Outputs: A refined set of 3D Gaussians with improved geometric and photometric accuracy. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, utilizing the GaussianSet data structure 3D Gaussian Splatting. Each Gaussian is defined by position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{S}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}. Method Steps: 1. Dual Reconstruction Initialization: Initialize two separate sets of 3D Gaussians, GA and GB, from the input sparse views. 2. Independent Optimization: Perform independent differentiable rendering optimization for both sets GA and GB against the input views. 3. Consistency Comparison: Compare the resulting Gaussians from GA and GB to identify inconsistencies. 4. Pruning: Discard inaccurate Gaussians based on the comparison. Parameters: Number of independent reconstructions: 2. Optimization hyperparameters (learning rate, loss weights): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: The method targets sparse-view reconstruction. Standard methods may struggle with insufficient constraints. head: 3D Gaussian Rasterization, 3D Gaussian Rasterization and Rendering, 3DGS Renderer, 3DGS rasterization pipeline, Differentiable Gaussian Rasterization, Differentiable Tile-based Rasterization, Point Cloud Splatting, differentiable splatting
body: The 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer renders a scene represented by a set of 3D Gaussian primitives into a 2D image by projecting them to screen space, sorting them by depth, and accumulating their contributions via alpha compositing. Unlike volumetric ray marching used in NeRFs, this method operates in object order, rasterizing 2D elliptical kernels (splats) directly onto the image plane. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific use of a tile-based, front-to-back alpha blending pipeline that is fully differentiable with respect to all Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity) and camera poses, enabling end-to-end gradient-based optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D Gaussian centers in world coordinates. cov3Dprecomp (or scales (N, 3) and rotations (N, 4)): 3D covariance matrices or their decomposed parameters. opacities: Tensor of shape (N,) containing per-Gaussian opacity values oi. colorsprecomp (or shs): Pre-computed RGB colors or Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. viewmatrix: 4 \times 4 camera view matrix. projmatrix: 4 \times 4 projection matrix (or intrinsics K and view matrix). imagewidth, imageheight: Integer dimensions of the output image. tanfovx, tanfovy: Tangents of half the horizontal and vertical field of view. bg: Background color tensor (shape (3)). Outputs: renderedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing the final RGB image. radii: Tensor of shape (N) indicating the radius of each Gaussian in pixels (used for culling). numrendered: Count of visible Gaussians. Data Structures: The rasterizer typically uses a tile-based structure. The image is divided into tiles (commonly 16 \times 16 pixels). Gaussians are binned into tiles if their axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) intersects the tile. Within each tile, Gaussians are sorted by their depth (z coordinate in camera space) in descending order (back-to-front) or ascending (front-to-back) depending on the compositing direction; standard 3DGS uses front-to-back accumulation. Steps: 1. Projection: Transform 3D Gaussian means \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D} to camera space using the view matrix. Project them to 2D screen coordinates \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} using the perspective projection formula: \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{fx \mux}{\muz} + cx \\ \frac{fy \muy}{\muz} + cy \end{bmatrix} where fx, fy are focal lengths, cx, cy are principal points, and \mux, \muy, \muz are camera-space coordinates. 2. Covariance Projection: Compute the 2D screen-space covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} by linearizing the projective transformation. Let W be the viewing transformation matrix and J be the Jacobian of the projective transformation at the Gaussian center: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} = J W \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} W^T J^T The Jacobian J for a pinhole camera is approximated as: J = \begin{bmatrix} fx/z & 0 & -x fx/z^2 \\ 0 & fy/z & -y fy/z^2 \end{bmatrix} where x, y, z are the camera-space coordinates of the Gaussian mean. The resulting \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} is a 2 \times 2 matrix. 3. Bounding Box and Binning: For each Gaussian, compute the AABB in screen space based on the 99th percentile of the 2D Gaussian (approximately 3\sigma along the principal axes). Bin the Gaussian into all tiles whose AABB intersects the Gaussian's bounding box. 4. Sorting: Within each tile, sort the binned Gaussians by their depth z in camera space. The standard 3DGS implementation sorts them front-to-back (smallest z first) to facilitate alpha compositing. 5. Alpha Compositing: For each pixel in each tile, iterate through the sorted Gaussians that cover that pixel. Initialize transmittance T = 1.0 and accumulated color C = \text{bg}. For each Gaussian i in front-to-back order: Compute the displacement vector \boldsymbol{d} from the pixel center to the Gaussian mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}. Compute the exponent of the 2D Gaussian density: \text{power} = -0.5 \cdot \boldsymbol{d}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1} \boldsymbol{d} Compute the alpha value \alphai: \alphai = oi \cdot \exp(\text{power}) Note: Some implementations clamp \alphai to a maximum value (e.g., 0.99) to prevent numerical instability. Update the pixel color and transmittance: C \leftarrow C + \alphai \cdot T \cdot \boldsymbol{c}i T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) where \boldsymbol{c}i is the color of the Gaussian (evaluated from SH if necessary). If T < \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-4}), break the loop for this pixel as further Gaussians contribute negligibly. 6. Output: Store the final accumulated color C in the output image buffer.
