name: Restricting Gaussian Kernel Support
head: Adaptive Alpha Clamping for 3DGS, Generalized Gaussian Kernel
body: Restricting Gaussian Kernel Support is a rendering optimization technique that reduces the spatial footprint of Gaussian primitives to minimize superfluous ray-Gaussian intersections and accelerate volume rendering. It achieves this by replacing the standard Gaussian kernel with a generalized exponent form and applying adaptive alpha clamping to zero out contributions below a specific threshold. Unlike standard splatting which uses fixed bounding boxes or infinite support approximations, this method dynamically adjusts the effective radius based on the kernel's shape parameters and opacity. It is a core component of the GaussianRasterizationSettings in differentiable rendering pipelines, building on GaussianRasterizationSettings. The method combines two distinct mathematical modifications to the standard Gaussian splatting formulation. Inputs: \mu: The mean position of the Gaussian in 3D space. \Sigma: The 3 \times 3 covariance matrix of the Gaussian. \alpha: The base opacity scalar of the Gaussian. n{\text{expo}}: The exponent parameter controlling the kernel's bulkiness (typically 2). \epsilon: The minimum contribution threshold for clamping (typically 0.01). \vec{k}W: The whitened frequency vector (used in Gabor variants, 0 for standard Gaussians). Outputs: A modified rendering kernel that yields zero contribution outside a calculated adaptive extent E{\text{adaptive}}. A clamped alpha value for rasterization. No new persistent data structures are required. The method modifies the evaluation logic of the Gaussian primitive during the forward pass. The covariance matrix \Sigma and its determinant |\Sigma| are accessed directly from the primitive's state. 1. Generalized Gaussian Kernel Definition The standard Gaussian kernel is replaced by a generalized form to control the "bulkiness" of the primitive. The contribution C(x) at a point x is defined as: C(x) = \alpha \cdot \exp \left[ -\frac{1}{2n{\text{expo}}} \left( (x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu) \right)^{n{\text{expo}}} \right] Where: n{\text{expo}} is the exponent. Increasing n{\text{expo}} makes the Gaussian bulkier (slower decay in the center, sharper cutoff at the edges). The term (x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu) is the squared Mahalanobis distance. 2. Adaptive Extent Calculation To restrict the support, the method calculates the maximum extent E{\text{adaptive}} from the mean \mu beyond which the contribution is considered negligible. This is derived by solving for the eccentricity E where the contribution drops below \epsilon. For a standard Gaussian primitive (f0 = 0, implying \vec{k}W = 0), the extent is: E{\text{adaptive}} = \sqrt{-2 \ln \left( 2\pi \cdot \epsilon \sqrt{|\Sigma|} \right)} For Gabor kernels (non-zero frequency), the extent includes a frequency-induced decay term: E{\text{adaptive}} = \sqrt{-2 \ln \left( 2\pi \cdot \epsilon \sqrt{|\Sigma|} \right) - \vec{k}W^2} Where: |\Sigma| is the determinant of the covariance matrix. \epsilon is the minimum contribution threshold. \vec{k}W is the whitened frequency vector. 3. Alpha Clamping During rasterization, for each pixel or sample point, the calculated alpha value is compared against the threshold derived from the extent. If the distance from the center exceeds E{\text{adaptive}}, the alpha is set to 0. Alternatively, the alpha is explicitly clamped: if \alpha{\text{calc}} < \epsilon, set \alpha{\text{final}} = 0. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the evaluation and clamping logic for a single Gaussian primitive. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def evaluategaussiankernel(x, mu, Sigma, alpha, nexpo=2.0, epsilon=0.01, kW=0.0): """ Evaluates the contribution of a Gaussian primitive at point x, applying generalized kernel and adaptive support restriction. Args: x: numpy array, shape (3,), point in 3D space. mu: numpy array, shape (3,), Gaussian mean. Sigma: numpy array, shape (3,3), Gaussian covariance matrix. alpha: float, base opacity. nexpo: float, exponent for generalized kernel (default 2.0). epsilon: float, minimum contribution threshold (default 0.01). kW: float, whitened frequency magnitude (default 0.0 for standard Gaussians). Returns: float: Clamped alpha contribution. """ # 1. Calculate Mahalanobis distance squared diff = x - mu # Solve Sigma invdiff = diff for invdiff, then dot product # More stable: invdiff = np.linalg.solve(Sigma, diff) # Mahalanobissq = diff @ invdiff # Using inverse directly for clarity if Sigma is small/positive definite Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) mahalanobissq = diff @ (Sigmainv @ diff) # 2. Apply Generalized Kernel Exponent # Formula: exp[ -1/(2nexpo) (mahalanobissq)^nexpo ] exponentterm = (mahalanobissq nexpo) kernelvalue = math.exp(-0.5 exponentterm / nexpo) # 3. Calculate Adaptive Extent Threshold # Determine if the point is within the adaptive support # Eadaptive^2 = -2 ln(2 pi epsilon sqrt(|Sigma|)) - kW^2 detSigma = np.linalg.det(Sigma) # Guard against numerical issues with log of non-positive numbers if detSigma <= 0: return 0.0 logarg = 2.0 math.pi epsilon math.sqrt(detSigma) # If logarg >= 1, the log is non-positive, meaning the extent is imaginary or zero. # This implies the threshold is so high that even the center might be clamped, # or the Gaussian is too small to matter. if logarg >= 1.0: return 0.0 eadaptivesq = -2.0 math.log(logarg) - (kW 2) # If eadaptivesq is negative, the support is effectively zero if eadaptivesq < 0: return 0.0 # Check if point is within adaptive extent if mahalanobissq > eadaptivesq: return 0.0 # 4. Final Alpha finalalpha = alpha kernelvalue # Explicit clamping as per 3DGRT description: zero out if below epsilon # Note: The extent check above is equivalent to this for the radial profile, # but explicit clamping ensures strict adherence to the threshold. if finalalpha < epsilon: return 0.0 return finalalpha n{\text{expo}}: 2.0. \epsilon: 0.01. Minimum spatial extent: 3\sigma. Clamping below this threshold creates visible artifacts such as clipped primitives with obvious boundaries. 1. Denominator Discrepancy: There is a known implementation difference regarding the denominator in the generalized kernel exponent. 3DGRT uses 4.5 \cdot 2^{n{\text{expo}}} in the denominator, whereas GRay uses 1 \cdot 2^{n{\text{expo}}}. The latter makes initialization less sensitive to n{\text{expo}} and results in smaller initial Gaussians. The formula above uses the standard generalized form; implementers must choose the denominator scaling factor based on the target compatibility (3DGRT vs. GRay). 2. Large Gaussian Artifacts: Dynamic clamping can cause visible artifacts for very large Gaussians. However, in Differentiable Integration (DI) contexts, most Gaussians remain small, making these artifacts less apparent. 3. Determinant Stability: Calculating \sqrt{|\Sigma|} can be numerically unstable if the Gaussian is degenerate (determinant near zero or negative due to noise). A guard clause is required. A variant specifically tailored for Gabor kernels, which are orientation-selective. It calculates the spatial extent E{\text{adaptive}} based on frequency and opacity to reduce ray-intersection queries while maintaining low error. It is chosen when rendering volumetric data with spectral/angular decomposition, such as in Gabor Fields. The key distinction is the inclusion of the \vec{k}W^2 term in the extent calculation, allowing higher-frequency Gabors to have smaller extents. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of ray-Gaussian intersections and overlap processing steps, leading to faster rendering. The cost of calculating the adaptive extent is negligible compared to the savings in rasterization. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead; it modifies the evaluation logic. Strengths: Significantly reduces superfluous computations for large or low-opacity Gaussians. Maintains high visual quality when hyperparameters are tuned correctly. Limitations: Can introduce visible artifacts if the clamping threshold \epsilon is too high or if Gaussians are extremely large. The choice of denominator scaling (4.5 vs 1) affects initialization sensitivity and final scale. When to use: Recommended for standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines to improve performance, especially when using differentiable integration or high Gaussian counts. The technique originated with 3DGRT (3D Gaussian Ray Tracing), which proposed reducing Gaussian footprints using generalized kernels and adaptive alpha clamping to decrease superfluous ray-Gaussian intersections. It was later adopted and refined in GRay, which adjusted the denominator scaling for better initialization stability. The adaptive extent formulation for Gabor kernels was further developed in "Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering". GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804496, fetched 2026-10-29 Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05081, fetched 2026-10-27

head: GaussianRasterizationSettings Initialization, Rasterization Settings Setup
body: This method initializes the GaussianRasterizationSettings configuration object and prepares auxiliary state tensors required to invoke the differentiable Gaussian rasterizer. It translates high-level camera parameters and scene constraints into the numerical formats expected by the rendering kernel. Inputs: viewpointcamera: Object containing FoVx, FoVy, and worldviewtransform. pc: Object providing getxyz() to determine tensor device and data type. imageheight, imagewidth: Target render dimensions. bgcolor: Background color tensor. scalemodifier: Multiplier for Gaussian scales. returndepth: Boolean flag for depth output. Outputs: settings: Initialized configuration object. screenspacepoints: Zero-initialized tensor for gradient accumulation. Data Structures: 1. GaussianRasterizationSettings: Holds imageheight (int), imagewidth (int), tanfovx (float), tanfovy (float), bgcolor (tensor), scalemodifier (float), worldviewtransform (tensor), and returndepth (bool). 2. screenspacepoints: Tensor matching the shape, dtype, and device of pc.getxyz(), initialized to zeros, with requiresgrad=True. Steps: 1. Compute the tangent of half the horizontal and vertical fields of view: \text{tanfovx} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{FoV}x}{2}\right) \text{tanfovy} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{FoV}y}{2}\right) 2. Cast imageheight and imagewidth to integers. 3. Initialize the GaussianRasterizationSettings object with the computed tangents, dimensions, background color, scale modifier, and world view transform. 4. Retrieve the device and data type from the Gaussian positions via pc.getxyz(). 5. Create a screenspacepoints tensor of zeros with the same shape, dtype, and device. 6. Set requiresgrad=True on screenspacepoints. 7. Attempt to call screenspacepoints.retaingrad(). If unavailable (e.g., older PyTorch versions), pass silently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch class GaussianRasterizationSettings: def init(self, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bgcolor, scalemodifier, worldviewtransform, returndepth=False): self.imageheight = int(imageheight) self.imagewidth = int(imagewidth) self.tanfovx = tanfovx self.tanfovy = tanfovy self.bgcolor = bgcolor self.scalemodifier = scalemodifier self.worldviewtransform = worldviewtransform self.returndepth = returndepth def setupgaussianrasterization(viewpointcamera, pc, imageheight, imagewidth, bgcolor, scalemodifier=1.0, returndepth=False): # 1. Compute tan(fov/2) tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # 2. Initialize Settings Object settings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imageheight=imageheight, imagewidth=imagewidth, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bgcolor=bgcolor, scalemodifier=scalemodifier, worldviewtransform=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform, returndepth=returndepth) # 3. Prepare screenspacepoints tensor xyz = pc.getxyz() screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(xyz, dtype=xyz.dtype, device=xyz.device, requiresgrad=True) # 4. Retain gradients for backward pass try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except AttributeError: pass return settings, screenspacepoints Parameters: scalemodifier: Multiplier applied to Gaussian scales during rasterization. Default value is 1.0. returndepth: Boolean flag controlling whether depth information is returned alongside the color render. Edge Cases: PyTorch Version Compatibility: retaingrad() may not be available in older PyTorch versions; a try-except fallback handles this. Device Mismatch: Ensure bgcolor and other tensors are on the same device as the Gaussian positions to avoid CUDA errors. body: This step prepares the scene data and computational buffers required to invoke the differentiable Gaussian rasterizer. It initializes tensors for gradient accumulation and constructs the configuration object that defines the camera parameters and rendering constraints. It differs from the rasterizer itself by handling the setup of state and memory layout rather than the pixel-wise projection and blending logic. Inputs: pc: The Gaussian point cloud object containing attributes (e.g., xyz, scales, rotations, SH coefficients). viewpointcamera: The current camera object containing field of view (FoV) and position. imagewidth, imageheight: The resolution of the target image. background: The background color tensor. Outputs: GaussianRasterizationSettings: An object containing all camera and rendering parameters. screenspacepoints: A tensor initialized to zero, used to store gradients for 2D screen-space means. GaussianRasterizationSettings The settings object aggregates the following fields: imagewidth, imageheight, tanfovx, tanfovy, bgcolor, scalemodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree, campos, and implementation-specific parameters. screenspacepoints Shape: Matches the number of Gaussians. Dtype: Same as pc.getxyz.dtype. Device: Same as pc.getxyz.device. Requires Grad: True. 1. Initialize Gradient Tensor: Create a zero tensor screenspacepoints with the same dtype and device as pc.getxyz, requiring gradients. 2. Enable Gradient Retention: Call retaingrad() on screenspacepoints to allow gradient access during the backward pass. 3. Calculate FOV Tangents: Compute the tangent of half the field of view for the x and y axes: \text{tanfovx} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx}}{2}\right) and \text{tanfovy} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy}}{2}\right). 4. Construct Settings Object: Instantiate GaussianRasterizationSettings with the calculated FOV tangents, image dimensions, background color, scale modifier, view/projection matrices, SH degree, camera position, and other settings. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch class GaussianRasterizationSettings: """Aggregates camera and rendering parameters for the rasterization kernel.""" def init(self, imagewidth, imageheight, tanfovx, tanfovy, bgcolor, scalemodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree, campos): self.imagewidth = imagewidth self.imageheight = imageheight self.tanfovx = tanfovx self.tanfovy = tanfovy self.bgcolor = bgcolor self.scalemodifier = scalemodifier self.viewmatrix = viewmatrix self.projmatrix = projmatrix self.shdegree = shdegree self.campos = campos def setupgaussianrasterization(pc, viewpointcamera, imagewidth, imageheight, background): """ Prepares tensors and settings for Gaussian rasterization. Args: pc: Gaussian point cloud object with getxyz property. viewpointcamera: Camera object with FoVx, FoVy, viewmatrix, projmatrix, campos. imagewidth: int, width of the output image. imageheight: int, height of the output image. background: Tensor, background color on GPU. Returns: settings: GaussianRasterizationSettings object. screenspacepoints: Tensor for 2D mean gradients. """ # Step 1: Initialize screenspacepoints tensor # Must match dtype and device of 3D positions xyz = pc.getxyz screenspacepoints = torch.zeros(xyz.shape[0], device=xyz.device, dtype=xyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True) # Step 2: Retain gradients for screenspacepoints # This allows gradient access during backward pass screenspacepoints.retaingrad() # Step 3: Calculate FOV tangents tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # Step 4: Construct GaussianRasterizationSettings settings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imagewidth=imagewidth, imageheight=imageheight, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bgcolor=background, scalemodifier=1.0, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.viewmatrix, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.projmatrix, shdegree=pc.shdegree, campos=viewpointcamera.campos) return settings, screenspacepoints scalemodifier: Multiplier for the Gaussian scale. Default is 1.0. bgcolor: Background color tensor, must be on GPU. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. body: A differentiable rasterization method that projects 3D Gaussians onto a 2D image plane to produce a rendered image and per-Gaussian screen-space radii, supporting both precomputed 3D covariances and scale/rotation parameterizations. It differs from standard rasterization by handling continuous volumetric primitives via alpha blending, enabling gradient flow through the rendering process for optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: means3D: (N, 3) tensor of 3D Gaussian centers. colorsprecomp: (N, 3) or (N, C) tensor of precomputed colors. opacities: (N,) tensor of per-Gaussian opacities. scales: (N, 3) tensor of log-scale factors (optional if cov3Dprecomp is provided). rotations: (N, 4) tensor of unit quaternions (optional if cov3Dprecomp is provided). cov3Dprecomp: (N, 6) tensor of precomputed 3D covariance matrix elements (optional if scales/rotations are provided). rastersettings: A GaussianRasterizationSettings object containing camera and rendering parameters. sh: Spherical Harmonics coefficients (optional, used if colorsprecomp is not provided). shdegree: Degree of SH. Outputs: color: (H, W, 3) or (H, W, C) rendered image tensor. radii: (N,) tensor of screen-space radii for visible Gaussians (used for backward pass and culling). Data Structures: GaussianRasterizationSettings: A NamedTuple or struct containing: imageheight: int imagewidth: int tanfovx: float (tangent of half horizontal FOV) tanfovy: float (tangent of half vertical FOV) scalemodifier: float viewmatrix: torch.Tensor (4, 4) projmatrix: torch.Tensor (4, 4) campos: torch.Tensor (3,) camera position prefiltered: bool mode: int (controls FOV calculation) debug: bool GeometryState: Contains depths (float, size P), clamped (float, size P \times 3), internalradii (float, size P), means2D (float2, size P), cov3D (float, size P \times 6), conicopacity (float4, size P), rgb (float, size P \times 3), semanticfeature (float, size P \times \text{NUM\SEMANTIC\CHANNELS}), tilestouched (uint32t, size P), scanningspace (temporary for scan), pointoffsets (uint32t, size P). ImageState: Contains accumalpha (float, size N=H \times W), ncontrib (uint32t, size N), ranges (uint2, size N). BinningState: Contains pointlist (uint32t, size P), pointlistunsorted (uint32t, size P), pointlistkeys (uint32t, size P), pointlistkeysunsorted (uint32t, size P), listsortingspace (temporary for sort). Initialize missing optional inputs (shs, colorsprecomp, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp) to empty PyTorch tensors if they are None. 2. Backend Invocation: Invoke the C++/CUDA rasterization routine C.rasterizegaussians with the restructured arguments. 4. Gradient Saving: Save relevant tensors for the backward pass using ctx.saveforbackward: colorsprecomp, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, sh, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer. 5. Return: Return the rendered color image and radii of visible Gaussians. 6. Internal CUDA Pipeline (executed inside C.rasterizegaussians): Allocate GeometryState, ImageState, and BinningState buffers via callbacks. Compute tile grid dimensions: tilegrid.x = (width + BLOCKX - 1) / BLOCKX, tilegrid.y = (height + BLOCKY - 1) / BLOCKY. Call FORWARD::preprocess to transform Gaussians, compute 2D means, depths, covariances, colors, conic matrices, and radii. Compute inclusive prefix sum over tilestouched to get pointoffsets using geomState.scanningspace. Retrieve numrendered from the last element of pointoffsets (pointoffsets[P-1]). Allocate BinningState buffers with size numrendered. Launch duplicateWithKeys kernel to create sorting keys and duplicated Gaussian indices from means2D, depths, pointoffsets, radii, and tilegrid. Calculate bit depth for radix sort: bit = getHigherMsb(tilegrid.x tilegrid.y). Sort pairs using cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs over range 0 to 32+bit. Zero out imgState.ranges array. If numrendered > 0, launch identifyTileRanges kernel to compute start/end indices in the sorted pointlist for each tile. name: GSCache DiffRasterizer Interface
head: DiffRasterizer
body: The GSCache DiffRasterizer Interface is a C++ class interface for differentiable rasterization that manages camera state, frame buffers, and forward/backward passes for Gaussian splatting. It distinguishes itself by providing a unified interface that handles rendering alongside optimization integration (densification, pruning) and direct data access for Gaussian model parameters. It builds on GaussianRasterizationSettings and sits within the 3D Gaussian Splatting differentiable rasterizer pipeline. The interface accepts camera parameters (intrinsic and extrinsic via mviewmatrix, mprojectionmatrix, mfovy, mfovx, maspectratio, mposition, mcenter, mup), Gaussian model parameters (mxyz, mfeatures, mscaling, mrotation, mopacity), and loss gradients for the backward pass. It outputs a rendered image (RGB via mrgb), intermediate buffers (radii, geometrybuffer, binningbuffer, imagebuffer), and gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters (dxyz, dconic, dopacity, dcolor, dmean2D, dcov3D, dsh, dscale, drotation). The interface relies on specific structs to manage state and results. Camera Struct Fields: mfovy (float), mfovx (float), maspectratio (float), mposition (glm::vec3), mcenter (glm::vec3), mup (glm::vec3), mviewmatrix (torch::Tensor), mprojectionmatrix (torch::Tensor), mpositiontensor (torch::Tensor). FrameBuffer Struct Fields: mdirtycpu (bool), mdirtygpu (bool), msize (glm::ivec2), mrgb (torch::Tensor), mrgbrwcpu (torch::Tensor), mrgbrwgpu (torch::Tensor). DiffRasterizerForwardResult Fields: nrendered (int), framebuffer (FrameBuffer), radii (torch::Tensor), geometrybuffer (torch::Tensor), binningbuffer (torch::Tensor), imagebuffer (torch::Tensor). DiffRasterizerBackwardResult Fields: radii (torch::Tensor), dxyz (torch::Tensor), dconic (torch::Tensor), dopacity (torch::Tensor), dcolor (torch::Tensor), dmean2D (torch::Tensor), dcov3D (torch::Tensor), dsh (torch::Tensor), dscale (torch::Tensor), drotation (torch::Tensor). 1. Initialization: The rasterizer initializes with Gaussian model parameters (mxyz, mfeatures, mscaling, mrotation, mopacity) and camera settings. It allocates internal buffers for rendering and gradient accumulation (mxyzgradientaccum, mdenom). 2. Visibility Culling: Call markVisible or setVisible to determine which Gaussians are within the camera frustum and have non-zero radii, updating the mvisible tensor. 3. Forward Pass: Call forward with the current camera state. This performs projection of 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorting by depth, and rasterization onto the frame buffer, returning a DiffRasterizerForwardResult. 4. Backward Pass: Call backward with a loss gradient tensor. This computes gradients for all Gaussian parameters based on the forward pass results and the input loss gradient, returning a DiffRasterizerBackwardResult. 5. Optimization Step: The interface provides optimize() to trigger parameter updates using an internal optimizer (moptimizer). 6. Densification and Pruning: Periodically, densifyAndPrune is called with thresholds (gradientthreshold, opacitythreshold, extent, sizethreshold) to split or clone Gaussians with high gradients or remove those with low opacity or large extent. Gaussian parameters # Updates mxyzgradientaccum and mdenom # Returns DiffRasterizerBackwardResult pass def optimize(self): self.moptimizer.step() def densifyandprune(self, gradientthreshold, opacitythreshold, extent, sizethreshold): # Calls densifyAndClone, densifyAndSplit, prunePoints internally # Implementation details not provided in source def getxyz(self): return self.mxyz def getfeatures(self): return self.mfeatures def getscaling(self): return self.mscaling def getrotation(self): return self.mrotation def getopacity(self): return self.mopacity def getvisible(self): return self.mvisible def getmaxradii2d(self): return self.mmaxradii2d def getxyzgradientaccum(self): return self.mxyzgradientaccum def getdenom(self): return self.mdenom def getmaxshdegree(self): return self.mmaxshdegree def getactiveshdegree(self): return self.mactiveshdegree def saveply(self, filename): pass def loadply(self, filename): pass gradientthreshold (float), opacitythreshold (float), extent (float), and sizethreshold (int) control densification and pruning thresholds. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting
head: High Fidelity Point Cloud Rendering via Feature Splatting, PFGS (Point Cloud Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting)
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline to handle high-dimensional semantic feature tensors alongside RGB color, enabling high-fidelity point cloud rendering where both appearance and semantic information are preserved. It differs from standard 3DGS by modifying the rasterization kernel to accumulate and differentiate multi-channel feature maps in addition to color, allowing for downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation or feature-based reconstruction. It builds on GaussianRasterizationSettings and Gaussian Rasterization (Forward). Inputs: means3D: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D Gaussian centers. colorsprecomp: Tensor of shape (N, 3), RGB colors. semanticfeature: Tensor of shape (N, C), C-dimensional semantic features per Gaussian. opacities: Tensor of shape (N, 1), per-Gaussian opacities. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3), Gaussian scales. rotations: Tensor of shape (N, 4), Gaussian rotations (quaternions). cov3Dsprecomp: Tensor of shape (N, 6), precomputed covariances (optional if scales/rotations provided). rastersettings: Configuration object containing camera parameters and image dimensions. Outputs: color: Rendered RGB image tensor of shape (3, H, W). featuremap: Rendered semantic feature tensor of shape (C, H, W). radii: Tensor of shape (N), radius of each Gaussian in pixel space for visibility culling. GaussianRasterizationSettings A named tuple or struct containing: imageheight (int): Height of the output image. imagewidth (int): Width of the output image. tanfovx (float): Tangent of horizontal field of view. tanfovy (float): Tangent of vertical field of view. bg (torch.Tensor): Background color tensor. scalemodifier (float): Global scale modifier for Gaussian sizes. viewmatrix (torch.Tensor): 4 \times 4 view transformation matrix. projmatrix (torch.Tensor): 4 \times 4 projection matrix. shdegree (int): Degree of spherical harmonics (0 for precomputed colors). campos (torch.Tensor): Camera position. prefiltered (bool): Whether SH coefficients are prefiltered. debug (bool): Enable debug mode. CUDA Rasterizer Configuration The underlying CUDA kernel requires NUMSEMANTICCHANNELS to be defined in submodules/diff-gaussian-rasterization/cudarasterizer/config.h at compile time to determine the dimensionality C of the feature map. 1. Input Validation and Preparation: Check that exactly one of the covariance representations is provided: either (scales, rotations) or cov3Dsprecomp. If scales is None, set to an empty tensor. If rotations is None, set to an empty tensor. If cov3Dsprecomp is None, set to an empty tensor. Ensure semanticfeature is a valid tensor of shape (N, C). 2. Forward Pass Argument Restructuring: The argument tuple is ordered as follows: python args = ( rastersettings.bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.debug) 3. Forward Rasterization Execution: Invoke the C++/CUDA rasterizer via C.rasterizegaussians(args). The kernel projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorts them by depth, and performs alpha blending. The function returns (numrendered, color, featuremap, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer). Return (color, featuremap, radii). 4. Backward Pass Input: The backward function receives gradoutcolor and gradoutfeature (in addition to the unused). The gradoutfeature is the gradient of the loss with respect to the featuremap output. 5. Backward Pass Argument Restructuring: The argument tuple is ordered as follows: python argsbackward = ( rastersettings.bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutfeature, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rastersettings.debug) 6. Backward Rasterization Execution: Invoke the C++/CUDA backward rasterizer via C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbackward). It returns gradients for: gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations. 7. Backward Pass Return: The gradients are returned in the order corresponding to the forward inputs: (gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, None). The last None corresponds to the rastersettings argument which does not require a gradient. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class RasterizeGaussians(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings, sh): """ Forward pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting. Args: means3D: (N, 3) Tensor of 3D Gaussian centers. colorsprecomp: (N, 3) Tensor of RGB colors. semanticfeature: (N, C) Tensor of semantic features. opacities: (N, 1) Tensor of opacities. scales: (N, 3) Tensor of scales. rotations: (N, 4) Tensor of rotations (quaternions). cov3Dsprecomp: (N, 6) Tensor of precomputed covariances. rastersettings: Configuration object. sh: Spherical harmonics coefficients. Returns: color: (3, H, W) Rendered RGB image. featuremap: (C, H, W) Rendered semantic feature map. radii: (N,) Tensor of radii for visible Gaussians. """ # 1. Validation if scales is None: scales = torch.empty(0) if rotations is None: rotations = torch.empty(0) if cov3Dsprecomp is None: cov3Dsprecomp = torch.empty(0) # Check that exactly one covariance representation is provided hasscalesrot = (len(scales) > 0 and len(rotations) > 0) hascov = len(cov3Dsprecomp) > 0 if not (hasscalesrot ^ hascov): raise ValueError("Exactly one of (scales, rotations) or cov3Dsprecomp must be provided.") # 2. Construct Args for Forward rs = rastersettings argsforward = ( rs.bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, rs.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rs.viewmatrix, rs.projmatrix, rs.tanfovx, rs.tanfovy, rs.imageheight, rs.imagewidth, sh, rs.shdegree, rs.campos, rs.prefiltered, rs.debug) # 3. Execute Forward Rasterization # C.rasterizegaussians returns: numrendered, color, featuremap, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer numrendered, color, featuremap, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = C.rasterizegaussians(argsforward) # 4. Save for Backward ctx.saveforbackward( means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) ctx.rastersettings = rs return color, featuremap, radii @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutcolor, gradoutfeature): """ Backward pass for 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting. Args: gradoutcolor: (3, H, W) Gradient of loss w.r.t. color. gradoutfeature: (C, H, W) Gradient of loss w.r.t. feature map. Returns: Gradients for all input tensors. """ # Retrieve saved tensors means3D, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer = ctx.savedtensors rs = ctx.rastersettings # 5. Construct Args for Backward argsbackward = ( rs.bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, semanticfeature, scales, rotations, rs.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rs.viewmatrix, rs.projmatrix, rs.tanfovx, rs.tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutfeature, None, # sh rs.shdegree, rs.campos, geomBuffer, None, # numrendered binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rs.debug) # 6. Execute Backward Rasterization # Returns: gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbackward) # 7. Return Gradients in Forward Input Order return ( gradmeans3D, None, # means2D not in forward inputs gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradsemanticfeature, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, None, # rastersettings does not require gradient None # sh) NUMSEMANTICCHANNELS: Must be defined at compile time in submodules/diff-gaussian-rasterization/cudarasterizer/config.h. This determines the channel dimension C of the semanticfeature and featuremap tensors. Visibility Marking: The markVisible method uses C.markvisible(positions, viewmatrix, projmatrix) to return a boolean tensor of points within the camera frustum. Precision: Standard 3DGS precision issues (e.g., depth sorting stability) apply. The addition of feature channels does not change the depth sorting logic but increases memory bandwidth usage during the blending step. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tested on RTX 3090 with PyTorch 1.13.0 and CUDA 11.7. Specific FPS numbers are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Enables semantic-aware rendering and reconstruction from point clouds. Limitations: Requires recompilation of the CUDA rasterizer for different feature dimensions. Not given in the sources: specific scalability limits for very large C. Origin: PFGS (Point Cloud Gaussian Splatting with Feature Splatting) was introduced by Jiaxu Wang, Ziyi Zhang, Junhao He, and Renjing Xu in 2024. Paper: "PFGS: High Fidelity Point Cloud Rendering via Feature Splatting," ECCV 2024. Development: The rasterization kernel is based on Feature-3DGS but with minor differences and bug fixes. It extends the original 3DGS rasterizer to support high-dimensional features. Usage: Used for high-fidelity rendering of point clouds with semantic information, demonstrated on datasets like ScanNet, DTU, and THuman2. name: DOFGS Rendering Pipeline
head: DOFGS render function, Depth of Field Gaussian Splatting Render
body: The DOFGS (Depth of Field Gaussian Splatting) rendering pipeline extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing differentiable depth-of-field (DoF) effects, allowing for the simulation of camera defocus blur during rasterization. It solves the problem of realistic optical blur in neural radiance fields by treating focal distance and aperture size as learnable parameters, enabling joint optimization of scene geometry and camera optics. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting by computing a Circle of Confusion (CoC) alpha channel and applying a spatially varying blur kernel based on depth, rather than a uniform opacity mask. The pipeline prepares Gaussian attributes, computes depth-dependent defocus parameters, and invokes a differentiable rasterizer that blends Gaussians with a DoF-aware kernel. Inputs: pc: Point cloud object containing parameters (xyz, rotation, scaling, opacity, featuresdc, featuresrest, Fs, Ks). viewpointcamera: Camera object with fields FoVx, FoVy, imageheight, imagewidth, cameracenter, focalx. pipe: Configuration object with flags bandlimit, convertSHspython, tonemap. tonemap: Optional function or string ('gamma', 'learn') for post-processing. Outputs: renderedimage: Tensor of shape (3, H, W). rendereddepth: Tensor of shape (1, H, W). cocalpha: Tensor of shape (1, H, W) representing the Circle of Confusion alpha. xy: Screenspace points tensor. radii, radiidiff: Visibility and gradient radii tensors. The point cloud pc maintains the following learnable parameters (all on CUDA): xyz: (N, 3) float32, 3D positions. rotation: (N, 4) float32, unit quaternions. scaling: (N, 3) float32, log-scale factors. opacity: (N, 1) float32, inverse-sigmoided opacity. featuresdc: (N, 1, 3) float32, DC spherical harmonic coefficients. featuresrest: (N, 15, 3) float32, higher-order SH coefficients (assuming max degree 3). Fs: (Nview, 1) float32, learnable focal distance scaling factors. Ks: (Nview, 1) float32, learnable aperture kernel scaling factors. The GaussianRasterizationSettings (inherited from parent) includes: tanfovx, tanfovy: Tangent half-angles of view. kernelsize: Float, size of the splatting kernel. subpixeloffset: (H, W, 2) float32, subpixel shifts. bg: GPU tensor, background color. coc2zcoeff: Float, coefficient for CoC to depth conversion (default 0.0). 1. Initialize Screenspace Points: Create a tensor for screenspace points with gradient tracking enabled. python screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.xyz, dtype=pc.xyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") + 0 screenspacepoints.retaingrad() 2. Compute Tangent FOV: python tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) 3. Initialize Subpixel Offset: If not provided, initialize to zero. python subpixeloffset = torch.zeros((int(viewpointcamera.imageheight), int(viewpointcamera.imagewidth), 2), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda") 4. Select Opacity Source: If pipe.bandlimit is true, use pc.getopacitywith3Dfilter. Else, use pc.getopacity. 5. Compute Defocus Parameters: If focaldistance and Kapert are not explicitly provided as inputs, compute them from the learnable parameters Fs and Ks. python focaldistance = torch.clamp(pc.Fs, 0.01, 1000) 10.0 Kapert = torch.clamp(pc.Ks, 0.01, 200) 100.0 + 100.0 Note: Fs and Ks are typically initialized based on scene depth statistics (median depth for focal distance, depth range for aperture). 6. Select Scales and Covariance: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier). Else if pipe.bandlimit is true, use pc.getscalingwith3Dfilter. Else, use pc.getscaling. Rotations are always pc.getrotation. 7. DOFGS (Depth of Field Gaussian Splatting) is an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting that incorporates optical defocus models. It was introduced by Rongduo et al. in an unofficial implementation. name: Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, Gaussian Splatting Rasterization Pipeline Setup, Gaussian Splatting Rasterization and Rendering Pipeline
body: The Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline orchestrates the differentiable rasterization of a scene represented as a set of 3D Gaussians into a 2D image for a specific camera viewpoint. It solves the problem of efficiently projecting millions of adaptive volumetric primitives onto a screen while preserving differentiability for gradient-based optimization. Unlike standard polygon rasterization, it computes 2D covariances via Jacobian approximation and composites Gaussians front-to-back using alpha blending. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly handling the conversion of 3D shape parameters (quaternions, scales) into screen-space covariances and managing view-dependent color evaluation via Spherical Harmonics (SH) within the same pipeline flow. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: pc: Gaussian model object containing attributes: getxyz (means, [N, 3]), getopacity (opacities, [N]), getscaling (scales, [N, 3]), getrotation (quaternions, [N, 4]), getfeatures (SH coefficients, [N, K, 3]), getcovariance (precomputed 3D covariance, optional), activeshdegree (int), maxshdegree (int). viewpointcamera: Camera object containing FoVx, FoVy (field of view in radians), worldviewtransform (4 \times 4 view matrix V), fullprojtransform (4 \times 4 projection matrix P), cameracenter ([3]), imagewidth, imageheight. pipe: Pipeline configuration object containing flags: computecov3Dpython (bool), convertSHspython (bool), depthratio (float), debug (bool). bgcolor: Background color tensor [3]. overridecolor: Optional precomputed RGB colors [N, 3] to bypass SH evaluation. Outputs: render: Rendered image tensor [H, W, 3] (or other channels based on mode). viewspacepoints: Tensor of 2D screen-space means [N, 2] with gradients enabled. visibilityfilter: Boolean tensor [N] indicating visible Gaussians (radii > 0). radii: Integer tensor [N] of screen-space radii. renderdepth (optional): Depth map if requested. Data Structures: GaussianRasterizationSettings: Struct holding imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier (default 1.0), viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree, campos, prefiltered (default False), debug. screenspacepoints: Zero-initialized tensor [N, 2] on the target device (e.g., CUDA) with requiresgrad=True to capture 2D mean gradients. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Gradient Container: Create screenspacepoints as a zero tensor with the same dtype and device as pc.getxyz, setting requiresgrad=True. Attempt to call retaingrad() to ensure gradients are retained for this tensor during backpropagation. 2. Compute Camera Parameters: Calculate half-field-of-view tangents: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx} \times 0.5) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy} \times 0.5) Extract camera position campos from the view matrix V = [R | t; 0 \ 1] as \text{campos} = -R^T t. 3. Configure Rasterization Settings: Construct GaussianRasterizationSettings with: imageheight, imagewidth from viewpointcamera. tanfovx, tanfovy from Step 2. bg from bgcolor. scalemodifier (default 1.0). viewmatrix from viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform. projmatrix from viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform. shdegree from pc.activeshdegree. campos from Step 2. prefiltered=False, debug from pipe.debug. 4. Assign Basic Attributes: means3D = pc.getxyz ([N, 3]). means2D = screenspacepoints ([N, 2]). opacity = pc.getopacity ([N]). 5. Select Covariance Representation: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is True: Compute cov3Dprecomp by calling pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier). Else: Set cov3Dprecomp to None. Set scales = pc.getscaling ([N, 3]). Set rotations = pc.getrotation ([N, 4]). 6. Evaluate Color (SH or Direct): If overridecolor is not None: Set colorsprecomp = overridecolor ([N, 3]). Else if pipe.convertSHspython is True: Extract SH coefficients: shsview = pc.getfeatures.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 3, (\text{pc.max\sh\degree}+1)^2). Compute view directions: dirpp = pc.getxyz - viewpointcamera.cameracenter.repeat(N, 1). Normalize: dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True). Evaluate SH: sh2rgb = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized). Clamp: colorsprecomp = torch.clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0). Else: Set shs = pc.getfeatures ([N, K, 3]). Set colorsprecomp = None. 7. Invoke Rasterizer: Instantiate GaussianRasterizer with GaussianRasterizationSettings. Call rasterizer with arguments: means3D means2D shs (if colorsprecomp is None) colorsprecomp (if shs is None) opacity scales (if cov3Dprecomp is None) rotations (if cov3Dprecomp is None) cov3Dprecomp (if scales/rotations are None) Return renderedimage and radii. 8. Construct Return Dictionary: Return { 'render': renderedimage, 'viewspacepoints': screenspacepoints, 'visibilityfilter': radii > 0, 'radii': radii }. Optional Depth Rendering: If returndepth is True: 1. Extract view direction projvect1 (first 3 elements of worldviewtransform[:,2]) and offset projvect2 (last element). 2. Compute depth values: means3Ddepth = dot(means3D, projvect1) + projvect2. Repeat 3 times for RGB channels. 3. Rasterize again with shs=None, colorsprecomp=means3Ddepth, and other attributes same as above. 4. Average resulting depth image over channels: renderdepth = renderdepth.mean(dim=0). 5. Add renderdepth to return dictionary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def renderpipeline(viewpointcamera, pc, pipe, bgcolor, overridecolor=None): # Step 1: Initialize screenspacepoints for gradients screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(pc.getxyz, dtype=torch.float32, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") try: screenspacepoints.retaingrad() except RuntimeError: pass # retaingrad may not be supported in all environments # Step 2: Compute camera parameters tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) # Extract camera position from view matrix V = [R|t; 0 1] # campos = -R^T @ t R = viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform[:3,:3] t = viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform[:3, 3] campos = -R.T @ t # Step 3: Configure Rasterization Settings rastersettings = GaussianRasterizationSettings( imageheight=viewpointcamera.imageheight, imagewidth=viewpointcamera.imagewidth, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bg=bgcolor, scalemodifier=1.0, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=campos, prefiltered=False, debug=pipe.debug) # Step 4: Assign basic attributes means3D = pc.getxyz means2D = screenspacepoints opacity = pc.getopacity # Step 5: Select covariance representation if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier=1.0) scales = None rotations = None else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.getscaling rotations = pc.getrotation # Step 6: Evaluate color shs = None colorsprecomp = None if overridecolor is not None: colorsprecomp = overridecolor else: if pipe.convertSHspython: # Extract SH coefficients: shape [N, 3, (maxshdegree+1)^2] shsview = pc.getfeatures.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 3, (pc.maxshdegree + 1)2) # Compute view directions dirpp = pc.getxyz - viewpointcamera.cameracenter.repeat(pc.getfeatures.shape[0], 1) dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) # Evaluate SH sh2rgb = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized) # Clamp to [0, 1] colorsprecomp = torch.clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0) else: shs = pc.getfeatures # Step 7: Invoke Rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings=rastersettings) renderedimage, radii = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, opacity=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp) # Step 8: Construct return dictionary result = { 'render': renderedimage, 'viewspacepoints': screenspacepoints, 'visibilityfilter': radii > 0, 'radii': radii } return result The Neural Gaussian Rasterization Pipeline replaces the standard exponential opacity formulation of 3D Gaussian Splatting with direct neural network outputs for per-Gaussian opacity and color, while retaining the standard 2D Gaussian rasterizer for compositing. It computes view-dependent color and density (\sigma) for each Gaussian center, maps \sigma directly to opacity, and composites the result using standard alpha blending. Octree-GS Rendering integrates an octree structure into the Gaussian Splatting pipeline. It initializes a GaussianModel with dataset parameters including feature dimensions, offsets, and level mappings. It applies a compatibility patch to gaussianrenderer.generateneuralgaussians to replace apecode[0] with apecode. It sets an anchor mask for the current view using gaussians.setanchormask based on camera center and resolution scale. It prefilters voxels to determine visibility using prefiltervoxel. It renders the scene using render with a visible mask and apecode argument (default 10). It clamps the rendered image to [0.0, 1.0] and saves it, recording the number of visible Gaussians per view. The Unity 3DGS Rendering Pipeline Integration adapts the rasterization for the Unity engine. It inserts an additional sorting pass into each camera's command buffer. It inserts draw calls for 3DGS objects into the existing rendering queue for transparent meshes based on their bounding boxes. It differs from separate render texture approaches by avoiding an intermediate texture and color space conversion pass after alpha blending. Per-pixel Depth Comparison for Transparency is a technique to resolve popping artifacts (temporal instability) caused by depth-sorting swaps. It replaces global sorting with per-pixel depth comparison or ray-tracing. Popping artifacts arise from the depth-sorting step, where overlapping Gaussians may swap their sort order as the camera moves, causing a sudden discontinuity in the alpha-blending accumulation. Near-plane Culling is a culling method using axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABB) to check depth and remove Gaussian points that are behind the camera near-plane, reducing unnecessary computations and memory accesses. It filters out Gaussian points that lie behind or too close to the near clipping plane before they enter the rendering pipeline. It checks each Gaussian's position relative to the camera near plane, discarding points that fail the test before projection. The culling condition is z{\max} < z{\text{near}}, where z is the Gaussian center depth in camera coordinates, \Delta z \ge 0 is the half-extent of the AABB along the camera z-axis, z{\min} = z - \Delta z, z{\max} = z + \Delta z, and z{\text{near}} is the camera near-plane depth. It operates with a single MAC unit, latency of 4 cycles, processing inputs (x, y, \text{depth}) and view matrix row [3:0], using D flip-flops for timing stability at 800 MHz FP16. It achieves a 56% culling rate on the compressed model, saving 56% of unnecessary Gaussian point computations and memory accesses. It increases throughput from 15.81% to 35.94% (2.27× gain), raising FPS from 20.4 to 46.4 at 1080p. Radiance Field Reconstruction from Gaussians reconstructs a radiance field representation by rendering RGB, depth, alpha, and normal maps from a set of Gaussian splats for a given set of viewpoints. It initializes a background color tensor. For each viewpoint, it calls the render function renderpkg = self.render(viewpointcam, self.gaussians). It extracts RGB from renderpkg['render']. It extracts alpha from renderpkg['rendalpha']. It computes surface normal by normalizing the rendered normal: normal = torch.nn.functional.normalize(renderpkg['rendnormal'], dim=0). It extracts depth from renderpkg['depth']. It extracts surface normal from depth: depthnormal = renderpkg['surfnormal']. It appends CPU tensors of RGB and depth to respective lists. After processing all viewpoints, it estimates the bounding sphere of the scene. Time Complexity: The pipeline is dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(N) for N Gaussians, but optimized via tiling. Tile intersection and sorting are integer operations performed on the CPU or specialized hardware. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N Gaussians with attributes (position, covariance/rotation/scale, opacity, SH coefficients). Scenes with millions of Gaussians require several gigabytes of VRAM. Measured Performance: On Apple Silicon (M1-M4) using gsplat-mlx, the full pipeline (forward pass) for 100K Gaussians at 256x256 resolution takes approximately 62.6ms for projection and 29.8ms for covariance computation, with total forward+backward times scaling accordingly. On hardware accelerators, near-plane culling can increase FPS from 20.4 to 46.4 at 1080p. Scaling: Scales well with resolution and Gaussian count due to tile-based rasterization. The tile size is typically 16 pixels. Strengths: Real-time performance on high-end GPUs; differentiable; handles millions of Gaussians. Limitations: High memory usage for large scenes; not seamlessly integrable into standard VR/AR pipelines without adaptation; requires CUDA or equivalent GPU acceleration (though MLX ports exist). When to use: Novel view synthesis, training of 3D Gaussian scenes, real-time rendering on modern GPUs. When not to use: Low-end devices with limited VRAM without compression; integration with hardware rasterization of polygon models in VR/AR without specific adaptation. The Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting method introduced by Kerbl et al. [13] (cited in). It builds upon EWA volume splatting [34] to efficiently compute the projection of 3D Gaussians to 2D. The method models a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians with shape and appearance parameters, optimized via differentiable rendering to match recorded images. It was developed to address the limitations of NeRF-style approaches, which require exhaustive sampling, by providing a sparse adaptive scene representation that can be rendered at high speed. The pipeline has been ported to various platforms, including Apple Silicon via gsplat-mlx, Unity via gsplat-unity, and Jittor via gaussian-splatting-jittor. name: Neural Gaussian Rasterization Pipeline
head: DNGaussian rendering, Neural opacity/color rasterization
body: The Neural Gaussian Rasterization Pipeline replaces the standard exponential opacity formulation of 3D Gaussian Splatting with direct neural network outputs for per-Gaussian opacity and color, while retaining the standard 2D Gaussian rasterizer for compositing. It computes view-dependent color and density (\sigma) for each Gaussian center, maps \sigma directly to opacity, and composites the result using standard alpha blending. The pipeline integrates a neural density network into the Gaussian Splatting rendering loop. Inputs: viewpointcamera: Camera parameters including cameracenter, FoVx, FoVy, projection matrix, and view matrix. pc (GaussianModel): The set of 3D Gaussians containing xyz (3D positions), scalingmodifier, and a neuralrenderer. background: A tensor representing the background color. pipe: A configuration object containing computecov3Dpython, scalemodifier, and other rasterization settings. Outputs: renderedimage: Tensor containing the final RGB image. radii: Tensor indicating which Gaussians are visible (radius > 0). rendereddepth: Tensor containing the accumulated depth. renderedalpha: Tensor containing the accumulated alpha. GaussianModel (pc): xyz: Tensor of 3D positions of N Gaussians. neuralrenderer: A neural network that takes (3,) position and (3,) direction as input and outputs (1,) sigma and (3,) color. getcovariance(scalingmodifier): Method to compute the 3D covariance matrix. getopacity(): Method to retrieve standard learned opacity if neural mode is disabled. GaussianRasterizationSettings: imagewidth, imageheight: Integer dimensions of the output image. tanfovx, tanfovy: Tangent of half horizontal and vertical field of view. background: Background color tensor. scalemodifier: Float multiplier for Gaussian sizes. viewmatrix, projmatrix: Camera transformation matrices. shdegree: Spherical Harmonics degree. cameraposition: Camera center vector. prefiltered: Boolean, typically False for neural variants. 1. Compute Direction Vectors: Calculate the vector from the camera center to each Gaussian center. \mathbf{dir}{pp} = \mathbf{p}c - \mathbf{c}{cam} where \mathbf{p}c is the tensor of Gaussian positions (N, 3) and \mathbf{c}{cam} is the camera center (3,). 2. Normalize Directions: Normalize \mathbf{dir}{pp} along the batch dimension. \mathbf{dir}{pp\normalized} = \frac{\mathbf{dir}{pp}}{\|\mathbf{dir}{pp}\|2} 3. Neural Query: Pass the 3D positions and normalized directions to the neuralrenderer to obtain density (\sigma) and color (\mathbf{c}). \sigma, \mathbf{c} = \text{neural\renderer}(\mathbf{p}c, \mathbf{dir}{pp\normalized}) 4. Opacity Assignment: Assign opacity directly from \sigma without the standard 1 - e^{-\sigma} transformation. \alpha{neural} = \sigma Note: In inference mode, the standard pc.getopacity() may override this. 5. Initialize Screenspace Points: Prepare the 2D mean positions (means2D) for rasterization. These must be initialized with requiresgrad=True to enable gradient flow back to 2D means during rasterization. 6. Configure Rasterization Settings: Compute tangent FOV: \text{tanfovx} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{FoVx}}{2}\right), \quad \text{tanfovy} = \tan\left(\frac{\text{FoVy}}{2}\right) Set scalemodifier (default 1.0). Select covariance computation: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute cov3Dprecomp via pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier); otherwise, use precomputed scales and rotations. 7. Rasterize: Execute the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales/rotations or cov3Dprecomp, returning renderedimage, radii, rendereddepth, renderedalpha. 8. Filter Visibility: Check radii > 0 to exclude frustum-culled or zero-radius Gaussians from further processing (e.g., splitting criteria). Unverified code. Select covariance computation mode if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(pipe.scalemodifier) scales = None rotations = None else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.getscaling rotations = pc.getrotation # 9. Initialize screenspace points (means2D) # Projection logic not given in sources; typically involves perspective projection using viewmatrix and projmatrix. means2D = preparemeans2D(pc.getxyz, rastersettings) # 10. Execute rasterizer rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings) renderedimage, radii, rendereddepth, renderedalpha = rasterizer( means3D=pc.getxyz, means2D=means2D, colorsprecomp=color, opacities=finalopacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp) # 11. Filter visibility (for downstream tasks like splitting) visiblemask = radii > 0 return { 'render': renderedimage, 'radii': radii, 'depth': rendereddepth, 'alpha': renderedalpha, 'visiblemask': visiblemask } def preparemeans2D(means3D, rastersettings): # Projection logic not given in sources; typically involves perspective projection using viewmatrix and projmatrix. raise NotImplementedError(" Projection logic not given in sources.") scalingmodifier: Scales the Gaussian covariance/sizes before rasterization. Default value is 1.0. inference: Boolean flag. When true, overrides neural opacity with pc.getopacity() instead of the neural output. value: Constant opacity multiplier used in depth-only rendering mode. Default value is 0.95. Precision: The neural renderer outputs \sigma directly as opacity. The standard 1 - e^{-\sigma} transformation is omitted, which simplifies the gradient flow but requires careful initialization of the neural network to prevent exploding opacities. Boundaries: Frustum culling is handled by the rasterizer's radii output. Gaussians with radii == 0 are excluded from splitting criteria. Degenerate Input: If dirpp is zero (Gaussian at camera center), normalization fails. A small epsilon should be added to the denominator during normalization to prevent NaN gradients. A rendering pass that isolates opacity computation by using fixed colors and detaching 3D parameters, useful for debugging or training opacity networks. It detaches means3D from the computation graph to freeze 3D positions during the pass, and uses the model's stored opacity values directly instead of neural outputs. Time Complexity: Dominated by the neural network inference for each Gaussian (O(N \cdot D{MLP})) and the rasterization step (O(N \cdot P) where P is pixels). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the neural network weights and the output tensors for \sigma and color for all Gaussians. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of Gaussians N and the complexity of the neural network. Strengths: Allows for view-dependent appearance and complex material representation without explicit spherical harmonics or texture maps. Limitations: Slower rendering due to per-Gaussian neural queries. Requires careful tuning of the neural network architecture and training. When to use: When high-fidelity view-dependent effects are required and rendering speed is secondary to quality. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring high frame rates with large numbers of Gaussians. This pipeline is implemented in the DNGaussian repository. It extends the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by integrating a neural density network to handle opacity and color, aiming to improve reconstruction quality for complex scenes. name: Unified Gaussian Splatting Renderer Dispatch
head: Gaussian Splatting Renderer Dispatch, render function dispatch, vggt Gaussian Renderer
body: The Unified Gaussian Splatting Renderer Dispatch is a routing mechanism that selects and invokes the appropriate differentiable Gaussian rasterization backend (3DGS, 2DGS, or GGGS) based on the model's geometric configuration or explicit mode flags. It abstracts the heterogeneity of Gaussian splatting variants by handling the preparation of input tensors (means, opacities, spherical harmonics, covariances) and the post-processing of rasterizer outputs (depth, normals, alpha) into a unified interface. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by acting as the central dispatcher that validates inputs and routes execution, rather than performing the rasterization itself. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A Gaussian point cloud object pc containing learned parameters (means, opacities, scales, rotations, spherical harmonics); a viewpointcamera object containing projection matrices and field of view; a pipe configuration object controlling computation modes; and an optional gsmode string. Outputs: Rendered color image, alpha mask, depth map, and optionally normals, depending on the selected backend and post-processing steps. Data Structures: pc: Contains tensors for means (3D coordinates), opacities (scalar opacity per Gaussian), scales (scaling factors), rotations (quaternions), and harmonics or features (spherical harmonic coefficients). viewpointcamera: Contains FoVx, FoVy (field of view angles), viewmatrix (world-to-camera), projmatrix (camera-to-clip), campos (camera position). GaussianRasterizationSettings: A configuration object passed to the rasterizer constructor, containing image dimensions, FOV tangents, background color, scaling modifier, view/projection matrices, SH degree, and camera position. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract Batch-Specific Attributes: Identify the active Gaussians for the current batch index batchidx. Extract 3D means xyz and unsqueeze opacities to shape (-1, 1). python xyz = pc.means[batchidx] opacity = pc.opacities[batchidx].unsqueeze(-1) 2. Initialize Screen-Space Points: Create a zero-initialized tensor for screen-space points to capture gradients during the backward pass. This tensor must require gradients and reside on the CUDA device. python screenspacepoints = torch.zeroslike(xyz, dtype=xyz.dtype, requiresgrad=True, device="cuda") 3. Compute Tangent Field of View: Calculate the tangent of half the horizontal and vertical field of view angles from the viewpointcamera. python tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx 0.5) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy 0.5) 4. Determine Render Mode: Select the rasterization backend mode. If gsmode is explicitly provided, use it. Otherwise, infer the mode from the scale dimensions of the point cloud: if the second dimension of pc.scales[batchidx] is 2, select "2DGS"; otherwise, default to "3DGS". 5. Select Rasterizer Classes: Map the determined requestedrendermode to the corresponding GaussianRasterizationSettings and GaussianRasterizer classes from the appropriate library: "2DGS": diffsurfelrasterization "3DGS": diffgaussianrasterization "GGGS": gggsdiffgaussianrasterization 6. Construct GaussianRasterizationSettings: Instantiate the settings object with common parameters: imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg (background color), scalingmodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree, campos, prefiltered=False, and debug. For GGGS, additionally pass kernelsize, sgdegree=0, and requiredepth. 7. Prepare Covariance: If pipe.computecov3Dpython is true: Compute cov3Dprecomp by transforming the world-space covariance to pixel space using ndc2pix and world2pix matrices. Reshape the result to (-1, 9) in column-major order. Otherwise: Extract scales and rotations directly from pc. 8. Prepare Colors: If overridecolor is None and pipe.convertSHspython is true: 1. Extract spherical harmonic features: shsview = pc.getfeatures.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 3, (pc.maxshdegree+1)2). 2. Compute normalized viewing directions: dirppnormalized = dirpp / dirpp.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True). 3. Evaluate SHs to RGB: sh2rgb = evalsh(pc.activeshdegree, shsview, dirppnormalized). 4. Clamp and offset: colorsprecomp = torch.clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0). Else: Set shs from pc.harmonics[batchidx].permute(0, 2, 1). 9. Execute Rasterizer: Call the selected rasterizer with the prepared arguments: means3D, means2D, shs, colorsprecomp, opacity, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp. For GGGS, additionally pass sgaxis, sgsharpness, and sgcolor. 10. Post-Process 2DGS Outputs: If the mode is 2DGS, extract the multi-channel output allmap: renderalpha = allmap[1:2] rendernormal = allmap[2:5] (transformed to world space) renderdepthmedian = allmap[5:6] renderdepthexpected = allmap[0:1] / renderalpha renderdist = allmap[6:7] Compute the final surface depth and normal: python surfdepth = renderdepthexpected (1 - pipe.depthratio) + pipe.depthratio renderdepthmedian surfnormal = depthtonormal(viewpointcamera, surfdepth) renderalpha.detach() 11. Post-Process 3DGS Outputs: If the mode is 3DGS, compute the depth from the inverse depth output invdepth: python depth = 1.0 / invdepth.clamp(min=1e-6) 12. Post-Process GGGS Outputs: If the mode is GGGS, retrieve optional attributes sgaxis, sgsharpness, sgcolor from pc (handling defaults and tensor dimensions). Return renderedmediandepth, renderedalpha, and renderednormal. Parameters with Typical Values: prefiltered: False. sgdegree (GGGS): 0. mindepth (clamp): 1e-6. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Inverse depth calculation requires clamping to 1e-6 to avoid division by zero or numerical instability. Dimensions: Ensure opacity is unsqueezed to (-1, 1) to match rasterizer expectations. Mode Inference: The fallback logic for gsmode relies on the shape of pc.scales. If the scale tensor dimension is ambiguous, explicit gsmode should be provided. Constructs the specific tensor dictionaries required by differentiable Gaussian rasterization kernels, transforming raw learned parameters into the formats expected by the CUDA/C++ backend. It filters active Gaussians by temporal validity, normalizes geometric attributes, and computes derived values such as opacities and 2D means, ensuring the rasterizer receives consistent, normalized inputs for forward and backward passes. A visualization technique that renders a filtered Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) voxel band as a continuous surface using isotropic Gaussian splats, where one Gaussian is generated per surface voxel. It differs from mesh-based extraction (e.g., marching cubes) by providing a differentiable, continuous representation suitable for real-time interactive visualization, and from raw voxel rendering by smoothing discrete grid artifacts into a coherent surface. Time Complexity: Dominated by the CUDA rasterization kernel execution, which is generally O(N) with respect to the number of Gaussians N, though overhead from Python-side tensor preparation (SH evaluation, covariance transformation) adds constant factors. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for input tensors (means, SHs, covariances) and output buffers (color, depth, alpha, normals). The screenspacepoints tensor adds O(N) memory for gradient storage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of active Gaussians and image resolution. The dispatch overhead is negligible compared to the rasterization cost. Strengths: Unified interface for multiple Gaussian variants (3DGS, 2DGS, GGGS); automatic handling of data preparation and post-processing; supports differentiable rendering for training. Limitations: Relies on specific CUDA backends (diffgaussianrasterization, etc.); Python-side SH evaluation can be a bottleneck if not optimized; mode inference logic may fail if scale dimensions are non-standard. When to use: When training or rendering scenes using different Gaussian splatting variants (3D, 2D, or GGGS) and needing a consistent API. When not to use: When using a fixed, single variant without need for dispatch abstraction, or when hardware does not support the required CUDA kernels. The Unified Gaussian Splatting Renderer Dispatch originates from the VGGT (Video Gaussian Gaussian Transformer) project, specifically within the rendering pipeline of the VGVGGT repository. It was developed to support the integration of various Gaussian splatting techniques (3DGS, 2DGS, GGGS) into a single coherent framework for video-based 3D reconstruction and rendering tasks. The method is part of the broader effort to make Gaussian splatting differentiable and trainable for dynamic scene modeling.
