name: Rasterization Variant
body: This article defines the family of differentiable rasterization methods that project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space and accumulate color per pixel using alpha compositing, allowing gradients to flow back to Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer. The family is distinguished by variations in how the projection, culling, blending, and auxiliary outputs are handled to support specific rendering pipelines (e.g., X-ray, hybrid 3D/2D, or mixed geometry). All variants in this family share the core mechanism of differentiable rasterization for 3D Gaussians. The common mathematical foundation involves: 1. Projection: Transforming 3D Gaussian parameters (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) into 2D screen-space ellipses using the Jacobian of the projection transformation. 2. Sorting: Sorting Gaussians by depth within tiles to ensure correct front-to-back rendering order. 3. Alpha Compositing: Accumulating color C and transmittance T for each pixel using the standard alpha blending equations: T{i+1} = Ti (1 - \alphai) C{i+1} = Ci + \alphai Ti \mathbf{c}i where \alphai is the 2D alpha value derived from the projected Gaussian's covariance and opacity, and \mathbf{c}i is the color. 4. Differentiability: The entire pipeline is differentiable with respect to Gaussian attributes, enabling gradient-based optimization. Implements the vertex shader stage of a GPU-accelerated rasterizer. It computes 2D screen-space projections and basis vectors for instanced quad rendering. It differs from CUDA-based variants by executing calculations in the vertex shader, relying on subsequent geometry/fragment shaders for accumulation. Choose this when using a traditional graphics pipeline with vertex/geometry shaders rather than a custom CUDA kernel. Allows "masked" (probabilistically inactive) 3D Gaussians to participate in the rasterization pipeline and receive gradient updates. It solves the problem of outdated Gaussians in dynamic pruning by integrating binary existence masks into the transmittance and color accumulation steps. Choose this when performing dynamic Gaussian pruning or training with probabilistic existence masks. A GPU-accelerated method for rendering novel X-ray projections from radiative 3D Gaussian point clouds. It models radiation intensity rather than visible light color, computing scalar intensity values based on the probability density of Gaussians along the X-ray path. Choose this for X-ray imaging or volume rendering applications requiring differentiable X-ray synthesis. Computes alpha attenuation using a hybrid sigma metric that combines a 3D ray-surfel distance estimate with a 2D screen-space fallback bound. It solves inaccurate alpha estimation in standard rasterization when the 2D covariance projection is ill-conditioned or the Gaussian is far from the camera. Choose this when robust alpha estimation is required for distant or poorly conditioned Gaussians. Computes an auxiliary output: the number of times each 3D Gaussian is activated (rendered) during the forward pass, alongside standard color and radii. It sets itself apart by providing explicit per-Gaussian activation counts (gaussianscount) and an importantscore. Choose this for Gaussian pruning or importance sampling tasks that require tracking Gaussian visibility. Provides a unified rendering pipeline that rasterizes both 3D Gaussians and triangle meshes in a single pass using alpha-blending. It ensures correct spatial occlusion and color blending without dropping rendering rates. Choose this when rendering mixed scenes containing both Gaussian splats and triangle meshes. A rasterization branch (useanalytictau) that computes the per-pixel accumulated analytic line-integral optical thickness \tau along the view ray. Alpha is derived physically as \text{alpha} = 1 - \text{exp}(-\tau) using Beer-Lambert extinction, rather than using heuristic alpha values. The family originates from the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework, which introduced differentiable rasterization for 3D Gaussians. The specific variants listed here have been developed to address limitations in the original 3DGS rasterizer, such as handling dynamic pruning (Masked-Rasterization), supporting different modalities like X-rays (DRR), improving robustness (Hybrid Sigma), and enabling mixed geometry rendering (Single-Pass). The "Analytic Tau" variant is associated with the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud project, which extends 3DGS to volumetric rendering with analytic optical thickness. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Rasterization (Vertex Shader)
head: 2D Gaussian Splatting Vertex Shader, Fast Gaussian Rasterization Vertex Shader, GSplat Vert, Splat Vertex Shader, dsplat.vert
body: This method implements the vertex shader stage of a differentiable 3D Gaussian splatting rasterizer, designed for high-performance rendering on GPU architectures that support geometry shaders or instanced rendering. It transforms 3D Gaussian parameters (mean and covariance) into screen-space 2D ellipses, computes the necessary basis vectors for quad generation, and performs early culling to optimize downstream processing. It differs from CUDA-based variants by offloading the heavy linear algebra and culling logic to the vertex/geometry shader pipeline, relying on texture buffers for data storage rather than linear memory layouts. Inputs: Vertex Attributes: position (vec2): Instance attribute defining the local quad basis coordinates (typically \pm 1 or similar range for the ellipse expansion). index (uint): Instance attribute identifying the specific Gaussian splat. Uniforms: P (mat4x4): Projection matrix. VM (mat4x4): View-Model matrix. focal (vec2): Camera focal lengths (fx, fy). principal (vec2): Camera principal point (cx, cy). basisViewport (vec2): Viewport dimensions (width, height). discardAlpha (float): Alpha threshold for culling. Default: 0.0001. maxScreenSpaceSplatSize (float): Maximum allowed screen-space size. Default: 2048.0. sqrt8 (float): Constant \sqrt{8}. Used to scale eigenvalues to cover approximately 3 standard deviations. Texture Buffer (utexture): Type: usampler2D. Layout: Packed Gaussian data. Each splat index i occupies two texels (columns). Center Texel: uvec4 at ivec2(((i & 0x3FF) << 1), i >> 10). Covariance/Color Texel: uvec4 at ivec2(((i & 0x3FF) << 1) | 1, i >> 10). This layout allows 1024 Gaussians per row. Outputs (Varyings to Geometry/Fragment Shader): basisVector0 (vec2): First basis vector of the ellipse. basisVector1 (vec2): Second basis vector of the ellipse. gColor (vec4): Color and alpha (clamped to 0 if culled). gDepth (float): Depth of the splat center. The 3D covariance matrix \mathbf{V}{rk} is stored as two vec3 attributes (aCov03, aCov36) or packed into the texture. It is a symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix: \mathbf{V}{rk} = \begin{bmatrix} V{00} & V{01} & V{02} \\ V{01} & V{11} & V{12} \\ V{02} & V{12} & V{22} \end{bmatrix} Where: V{00} = \text{aCov0\3}.x, V{01} = \text{aCov0\3}.y, V{02} = \text{aCov0\3}.z V{11} = \text{aCov3\6}.x, V{12} = \text{aCov3\6}.y V{22} = \text{aCov3\6}.z 1. Alpha Culling: If the input alpha aColor.a is less than discardAlpha, set output alpha gColor.a to 0.0 and return immediately. This prevents the geometry shader from emitting quads for invisible splats. 2. Data Fetching: Fetch the center position from the texture using the index. Unpack the xyz components from the uvec4 center texel. Convert integer bits to float for position. Fetch the covariance and color data from the adjacent texel. Unpack half-precision components if necessary. 3. Position Transformation: Compute view-space center: \mathbf{c}{view} = \mathbf{VM} \cdot [\mathbf{p}, 1]^T. Compute clip-space center: \mathbf{c}{clip} = \mathbf{P} \cdot [\mathbf{p}, 1]^T. Perform perspective division: \mathbf{c}{clip} = \mathbf{c}{clip} / \mathbf{c}{clip}.w. Alternative (S2): Transform center to camera space \mathbf{c}{cam} = \mathbf{view} \cdot [\mathbf{p}, 1]^T. Project to clip space \mathbf{pos}{2d} = \mathbf{projection} \cdot \mathbf{c}{cam}. 4. Frustum Culling: Method 1 (S1): Compute FOV limits. \tan{fovx} = 0.5 \cdot \frac{width}{fx}, \quad \tan{fovy} = 0.5 \cdot \frac{height}{fy} \text{lim}{x+} = \frac{width - cx}{fx} + 0.3 \tan{fovx}, \quad \text{lim}{x-} = \frac{cx}{fx} + 0.3 \tan{fovx} \text{lim}{y+} = \frac{height - cy}{fy} + 0.3 \tan{fovy}, \quad \text{lim}{y-} = \frac{cy}{fy} + 0.3 \tan{fovy} Clip coordinates x, y using these limits before Jacobian calculation. Method 2 (S2): Apply a 1.2x margin to the clip space bounds. If \mathbf{pos}{2d}.z < -\mathbf{pos}{2d}.w or \mathbf{pos}{2d}.z > \mathbf{pos}{2d}.w or |\mathbf{pos}{2d}.x| > 1.2 \mathbf{pos}{2d}.w or |\mathbf{pos}{2d}.y| > 1.2 \mathbf{pos}{2d}.w, discard the splat by setting glPosition to a clip-space point outside the view (e.g., [0,0,2,1]). 5. Jacobian Computation: Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projection transformation. Let z = \mathbf{c}{view}.z (or \mathbf{c}{cam}.z). rz = 1/z, r{z2} = rz^2. \mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} fx rz & 0 & -fx x r{z2} \\ 0 & fy rz & -fy y r{z2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} Where x, y are the view-space coordinates of the center. 6. Covariance Transformation: Compute the transformation matrix \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{J}, where \mathbf{W} = \text{transpose}(\mathbf{VM}) (or \text{transpose}(\mathbf{view})). Compute the 2D covariance matrix in clip/camera space: \mathbf{C}{2D} = \mathbf{T}^T \mathbf{V}{rk} \mathbf{T} Extract the upper-left 2 \times 2 submatrix. Blur Term: Add a blur term to the diagonal to account for downsampling and anti-aliasing. S1 adds 0.3 to both diagonal elements: \mathbf{C}{2D}[0][0] += 0.3, \mathbf{C}{2D}[1][1] += 0.3. S2 adds 0.1 to both diagonal elements: \mathbf{C}{2D}[0][0] += 0.1, \mathbf{C}{2D}[1][1] += 0.1. 7. Eigenvalue Decomposition: Let a = \mathbf{C}{2D}[0][0], b = \mathbf{C}{2D}[0][1], d = \mathbf{C}{2D}[1][1]. Compute determinant D = ad - b^2. Compute trace T = a + d. Compute eigenvalues: \lambda1 = \frac{T}{2} + \sqrt{\max(0.1, (\frac{T}{2})^2 - D)} \lambda2 = \frac{T}{2} - \sqrt{\max(0.1, (\frac{T}{2})^2 - D)} Note: S2 uses a slightly different formulation for stability: \text{mid} = \frac{a+d}{2}, \quad \text{radius} = \sqrt{(\frac{a-d}{2})^2 + b^2} \lambda1 = \text{mid} + \text{radius}, \quad \lambda2 = \text{mid} - \text{radius} Compute the major axis direction: \mathbf{v} = \text{normalize}([b, \lambda1 - a]) Compute basis vectors scaled by \sqrt{8} (approx 3 sigma) and clamped to a maximum size (e.g., 1024.0): \mathbf{basis}0 = \sqrt{8} \cdot \min(\sqrt{2\lambda1}, 1024.0) \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathbf{basis}1 = \sqrt{8} \cdot \min(\sqrt{2\lambda2}, 1024.0) \cdot \mathbf{v}{\perp} Where \mathbf{v}{\perp} = [vy, -vx]. 8. Output Generation: Pass the color (unpacked from texture if using S2 layout) and depth to the geometry shader. Output the computed basis vectors. Set glPosition to the projected center position (S2) or pass through (S1, relying on geometry shader for final position). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(index, position, aPos, aCov03, aCov36, aColor, P, VM, focal, principal, viewport, discardAlpha): # 1. Alpha Culling if aColor.a < discardAlpha: return discardsplat() # 2. Reconstruct 3D Covariance Matrix Vrk Vrk = mat3( aCov03.x, aCov03.y, aCov03.z, aCov03.y, aCov36.x, aCov36.y, aCov03.z, aCov36.y, aCov36.z) # 3. Transform Center viewCenter = VM vec4(aPos, 1.0) clipCenter = P vec4(aPos, 1.0) clipCenter /= clipCenter.w # 4. Frustum Culling (Simplified S1/S2 hybrid) # Check if behind camera or outside clip space if viewCenter.z <= 0.0 or clipCenter.z < -clipCenter.w or clipCenter.z > clipCenter.w: return discardsplat() # Optional: Additional FOV margin culling (S1) or 1.2x margin (S2) # For brevity, we assume basic clip space culling is sufficient for the core method. # 5. Compute Jacobian J z = viewCenter.z rz = 1.0 / z rz2 = rz rz x = viewCenter.x y = viewCenter.y fx, fy = focal J = mat3( fx rz, 0.0, -fx x rz2, 0.0, fy rz, -fy y rz2, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 6. Transform Covariance to 2D W = transpose(mat3(VM)) T = W J cov2Dm = transpose(T) Vrk T # Extract 2x2 upper-left a = cov2Dm[0][0] b = cov2Dm[0][1] d = cov2Dm[1][1] # 7. Add Blur Term a += 0.3 # S1 blur d += 0.3 # S1 blur # 8. Eigenvalue Decomposition trace = a + d det = a d - b b term = sqrt(max(0.1, (trace 0.5) 2 - det)) lambda1 = trace 0.5 + term lambda2 = trace 0.5 - term # 9. Validate Eigenvalues if lambda1 <= 0.01 or lambda2 <= 0.01 or lambda1 < lambda2: return discardsplat() # Check for degenerate aspect ratio (optional but recommended) if lambda1 / lambda2 > 10000.0: return discardsplat() # 10. Compute Basis Vectors # Major axis direction if abs(lambda1 - a) < 1e-6: diagvec = vec2(0.0, 1.0) else: diagvec = normalize(vec2(b, lambda1 - a)) minorvec = vec2(diagvec.y, -diagvec.x) scale = sqrt(8.0) # 3 sigma maxsize = 1024.0 basis0 = scale min(sqrt(2.0 lambda1), maxsize) diagvec basis1 = scale min(sqrt(2.0 lambda2), maxsize) minorvec # 11. Output gColor = aColor gDepth = clipCenter.z return basis0, basis1, gColor, gDepth, clipCenter Invalid Covariance: If the determinant D \le 0 or diagonal elements are non-positive, the matrix is not positive definite. This results in invalid eigenvalues. The splat must be discarded to prevent artifacts and zero gradients. Negative Eigenvalues: If \lambda2 < 0, the covariance is invalid. Discard the splat. Degenerate Eigenvalues: If \lambda1 \approx \lambda2 or the ratio \lambda1/\lambda2 is extremely large (>10000), the ellipse is ill-conditioned. This can lead to numerical instability in the geometry shader or fragment shader. Culling or clamping is required. Precision: Half-precision unpacking in the texture fetch (S2) may introduce quantization errors in the covariance matrix. Ensure the reconstruction logic matches the packing format exactly. Blur Term Sensitivity: The added blur term (0.1 or 0.3) significantly affects the visual smoothness and aliasing. It must be tuned to the resolution and downsampling factors of the pipeline. Time Complexity: O(N) for N Gaussians. The vertex shader performs constant-time linear algebra per splat. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the texture buffer storing Gaussian data. The texture layout (2 texels per splat) requires 2 \times N \times 16 bytes (if uvec4) or less if packed more tightly. Performance: This method is highly efficient on GPUs with robust geometry shader support. It reduces CPU-GPU synchronization overhead compared to CPU-side sorting and culling. However, it may be less flexible than CUDA-based implementations for custom culling strategies or hybrid rendering pipelines. Strengths: Simple integration into standard OpenGL/Vulkan pipelines; leverages hardware-accelerated vertex processing; early culling reduces geometry shader load. Limitations: Geometry shader emission can be a bottleneck if culling is not aggressive enough; less control over memory layout compared to CUDA; debugging linear algebra in shaders is harder. This method is part of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, specifically the vertex shader variant. It was developed to enable real-time differentiable rendering of 3D Gaussians using standard graphics APIs. The approach adapts the mathematical foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting to the vertex shader stage, computing the 2D projection and basis vectors on the GPU. It is often used in conjunction with a geometry shader that generates the actual quads for rasterization. dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, https://github.com/dendenxu/fast-gaussian-rasterization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Masked-Rasterization
body: Masked-Rasterization is a differentiable rendering technique for 3D Gaussians that applies probabilistic masks during the alpha-compositing blending process, rather than modifying Gaussian attributes prior to rasterization. It solves the problem of "stale" Gaussians in pruning frameworks: when Gaussians are masked out (set to zero opacity/scale) in previous methods, they are filtered out before rasterization and receive no gradients, preventing them from updating their existence probability. By allowing masked Gaussians to participate in rasterization and receive gradients based on their "virtual contribution," this method enables dynamic assessment of their importance and prevents premature removal. It sets itself apart from siblings like Gaussian Splat Rasterization (Vertex Shader) by specifically addressing the gradient flow for unselected Gaussians during the blending stage, rather than just optimizing the forward pass of visible splats. Inputs: Set of N 3D Gaussians Gi, each defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \sigmai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. A probabilistic mask mi \in [0, 1] for each Gaussian, representing its probability of existence. Camera parameters for projection. Outputs: Rendered image color C. Gradients for Gaussian attributes (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \sigma, \mathbf{c}) and mask probabilities m. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS representation. Mask Array: A float array of size N, storing mi. Tile/Screen Buffer: Standard rasterization buffers for depth, transmittance, and accumulated color. Steps: 1. Projection and Alpha Computation: For each Gaussian Gi, project the 3D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i to 2D screen space using the Jacobian of the projection transformation. Compute the 2D alpha value \alphai based on the projected Gaussian's density, opacity, and scale. \alphai = \sigmai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1} \mathbf{x}\right) where \mathbf{x} is the vector from the pixel center to the Gaussian mean in screen space. 2. Zero-Alpha Filtering: Filter out any splats where \alphai = 0. All remaining splats (both masked and unmasked) proceed to rasterization. Note: If opacity or scale is set to zero before this step, \alphai becomes zero, and the Gaussian is filtered out, preventing gradient updates. 3. Masked Rasterization (Blending): For each pixel, iterate through the sorted list of splats. For each splat Gi with mask mi: Transmittance Update: The transmittance T is attenuated by the mask. If the Gaussian is masked (mi \approx 0), it does not block light, but its presence is tracked for gradient purposes. T{i+1} = Ti (1 - mi \alphai) Color Accumulation: The color contribution is scaled by the mask. C{i+1} = Ci + mi \alphai Ti \mathbf{c}i Gradient Flow: If mi = 0, the Gaussian does not contribute to the final color C or transmittance T in the forward pass (effectively invisible). However, the differentiable mask allows gradients to flow back to mi based on the "virtual" contribution it would have made if present. This updates the existence probability. If mi > 0, standard gradients apply to \alphai and \mathbf{c}i. Crucially, masked Gaussians (mi=0) do not receive gradients for \alphai (and thus do not update \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \sigma) in this step, but they do receive gradients for mi. 4. Mask Update: Use the computed gradients for mi to update the existence probability of each Gaussian via an optimizer (e.g., Adam). This allows previously unselected Gaussians to increase their probability of existence if they are deemed important by the gradient signal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskedrasterization(gaussians, masks, camera): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes (mu, sigma, opacity, color) masks: List of floats mi in [0, 1] camera: Camera parameters for projection Returns: Rendered image, gradients for masks and gaussians """ # 1. Project and compute alpha projectedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Project 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space mu2d, sigma2d = projectgaussian(g.mu, g.sigma, camera) # Compute alpha based on 2D covariance and opacity alpha = g.opacity compute2ddensity(mu2d, sigma2d) # Filter out zero alpha if alpha > 1e-6: projectedgaussians.append({ 'id': i, 'alpha': alpha, 'color': g.color, 'mask': masks[i], 'mu2d': mu2d, 'sigma2d': sigma2d }) # 2. Sort by depth (standard front-to-back) projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x.depth) # 3. Rasterize with masking image = zeroslike(screenresolution) transmittance = oneslike(screenresolution) # Gradients accumulator gradmasks = zeros(len(masks)) gradgaussians = zeroslike(gaussians) for pixel in screenpixels: T = 1.0 C = 0.0 for g in projectedgaussians: # Compute alpha at pixel alphai = g['alpha'] exp(-0.5 mahalanobisdistance(pixel, g['mu2d'], g['sigma2d'])) mi = g['mask'] # Apply mask to transmittance and color # Tnew = T (1 - m alpha) # Cnew = C + m alpha T color contribution = mi alphai T g['color'] C += contribution T = (1.0 - mi alphai) # Store for backward pass (simplified) # In practice, gradients are computed via autograd or manual chain rule pass image[pixel] = C # 4. Backward pass (conceptual) # Gradients for masks are computed based on the virtual contribution # Gradients for gaussians are computed only if mi > 0 return image, gradmasks, gradgaussians Parameters: Mask Sampling: Masks are sampled from a distribution based on the current existence probability of each Gaussian. Pruning Threshold: Not explicitly defined in the method description, but experiments show pruning ratios of 62.4%–75.3% are achievable. Edge Cases: Zero Alpha Filtering: If a Gaussian's opacity or scale is set to zero before rasterization, \alphai becomes zero, and the Gaussian is filtered out. This prevents it from receiving any gradient updates, which is the pitfall Masked-Rasterization aims to avoid. Mask Value 0: If mi=0, the Gaussian is invisible but still participates in the gradient computation for mi. It does not update its geometric attributes (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) via \alphai gradients. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, as all Gaussians are still splatted and sorted. The masking adds minimal overhead (multiplication operations). Memory Complexity: Requires storing an additional mask array of size N. Performance: Experiments show rendering speedups of 2.05\times to 3.16\times on datasets like Mip-NeRF360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, with pruning ratios of 62.4%–75.3% and only a 0.02 PSNR decline on the first two datasets. Strengths: Enables effective pruning by allowing unselected Gaussians to update their existence probability, preventing them from becoming stale. Outperforms methods that multiply masks with opacity/scale. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of gradient flow for masks. If not implemented correctly, masked Gaussians may not receive meaningful gradients. Masked-Rasterization was introduced in the MaskGaussian paper by researchers from Shanghai AI Laboratory. It addresses limitations in previous 3D Gaussian pruning methods where multiplying masks with Gaussian attributes (opacity/scale) led to zero density values, causing Gaussians to be filtered out and preventing gradient updates. The method models Gaussians as probabilistic entities, allowing for dynamic assessment of their contribution to the evolving scene. name: Differentiable Radiative Rasterization
body: Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR) is a GPU-friendly rasterization process implemented in CUDA that renders novel X-ray projections from radiative Gaussian point clouds. It solves the problem of differentiable volume rendering for X-ray imaging by treating the object as a collection of 3D Gaussians with radiation intensity attributes, allowing gradients to flow from the rendered projection back to the Gaussian parameters. Unlike standard alpha-blending methods used in visible light Parent, DRR computes pixel intensity by summing weighted radiation contributions from intersection points along the ray, where the weight is determined by the Gaussian probability density at that intersection. DRR takes a set of 3D Gaussian point clouds and camera parameters (intrinsic and extrinsic matrices) as input, and outputs a 2D intensity image \mathbf{I}. The method projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, assigns them to tiles, sorts them by depth, and blends their radiation contributions. Input: \mathcal{G} = \{Gi(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{f}i) \mid i = 1, \dots, Np\}: A set of Np radiative Gaussian point clouds. name: 3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma
head: Hybrid Sigma Rasterization, Fallback Sigma Gaussian Rasterization
body: This method renders 3D Gaussians by combining a 3D geometric sigma calculation with a 2D screen-space fallback sigma to determine the effective spread of each Gaussian splat. It solves the problem of inaccurate alpha culling and rendering artifacts when Gaussians are far from the camera or when the 3D covariance projection is numerically unstable. It sets itself apart from standard rasterization by introducing a hybrid sigma bound that ensures tighter alpha thresholds, and from Masked-Rasterization by using a continuous sigma value rather than a binary mask. Inputs: means: 3D Gaussian means, shape [N, 3]. opacities: Per-Gaussian opacity, shape [N]. colors: Per-Gaussian color, shape [N, 3]. normals: Per-Gaussian normal, shape [N, 3]. means2d: Pre-computed 2D screen-space means, shape [C, N, 2], where C is the number of cameras. cameras: Camera parameters (intrinsic K, extrinsic V). background: Optional background color, shape [C, 3]. Outputs: rendercolors: Rendered RGB images, shape [C, H, W, 3]. rendernormals: Rendered normal images, shape [C, H, W, 3]. renderalphas: Rendered alpha images, shape [C, H, W, 1]. Parameters: MAXALPHA: Maximum alpha value per splat (e.g., 1.0). ALPHATHRESHOLD: Minimum alpha to process (e.g., 0.01). TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: Minimum transmittance to continue loop (e.g., 0.0001). EPSILON: Small constant for depth check (e.g., 10^{-10}). Data Structures: rendercolors: Accumulator for color. rendernormals: Accumulator for normal. T: Current transmittance, initialized to 1.0 per pixel. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize rendercolors, rendernormals to 0. Initialize renderalphas to 0. Initialize T (transmittance) to 1.0 for all pixels. 2. Pixel Loop: Iterate over each pixel (py, px) and each camera c. 3. Gaussian Loop: Iterate through all Gaussians i (index gid). a. Projection Check: Calculate temporary coordinates tmp by projecting the 3D mean. If abs(tmp[2]) < EPSILON, skip this Gaussian. b. Screen Coordinates: Calculate screen-space coordinates: us = \frac{tmp[0]}{tmp[2]} vs = \frac{tmp[1]}{tmp[2]} c. 3D Sigma Calculation: Calculate the 3D sigma based on the distance from the projected center: \sigma{3d} = us^2 + vs^2 d. 2D Fallback Sigma Calculation: Use the pre-computed 2D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{2d} for camera c and Gaussian gid. Calculate differences: dx = px - \mu{2d}[0] dy = py - \mu{2d}[1] \sigma{2d} = 2.0 \times (dx^2 + dy^2) e. Hybrid Sigma: Take the tighter bound: \sigma = 0.5 \times \min(\sigma{3d}, \sigma{2d}) f. Alpha Calculation: Calculate alpha: \alpha = \min(\text{opacities}[gid] \times \exp(-\sigma), \text{MAX\ALPHA}) g. Culling: If \alpha < \text{ALPHA\THRESHOLD}, skip this Gaussian. h. Transmittance Check: If current transmittance T < \text{TRANSMITTANCE\THRESHOLD}, break the Gaussian loop for this pixel. i. Compositing: Calculate weight w = T \times \alpha. \text{render\colors}[c, py, px] \leftarrow \text{render\colors}[c, py, px] + w \times \text{colors}[gid] \text{render\normals}[c, py, px] \leftarrow \text{render\normals}[c, py, px] + w \times \text{normals}[gid] T \leftarrow T \times (1.0 - \alpha) 4. Alpha Finalization: After the Gaussian loop, set: \text{render\alphas}[c, py, px, 0] = 1.0 - T 5. Background Addition: If background is provided, for each camera c: \text{render\colors}[c] \leftarrow \text{render\colors}[c] + (1.0 - \text{render\alphas}[c]) \times \text{background}[c] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridrasterizationwithfallbacksigma( means: Array, opacities: Array, colors: Array, normals: Array, means2d: Array, # Shape [C, N, 2] cameras: List[Camera], background: Optional[Array] = None, maxalpha: float = 1.0, alphathreshold: float = 0.01, transmittancethreshold: float = 0.0001, epsilon: float = 1e-10) -> Tuple[Array, Array, Array]: """ Renders 3D Gaussians using hybrid 3D/2D sigma fallback. Args: means: [N, 3] 3D means. opacities: [N] opacities. colors: [N, 3] colors. normals: [N, 3] normals. means2d: [C, N, 2] pre-computed 2D means per camera. cameras: List of camera objects with intrinsic/extrinsic matrices. background: [C, 3] optional background colors. maxalpha: Max alpha per splat. alphathreshold: Min alpha to process. transmittancethreshold: Min transmittance to continue. epsilon: Depth check epsilon. Returns: rendercolors: [C, H, W, 3] rendernormals: [C, H, W, 3] renderalphas: [C, H, W, 1] """ C = len(cameras) H, W = cameras[0].height, cameras[0].width # Initialize outputs rendercolors = mx.zeros((C, H, W, 3)) rendernormals = mx.zeros((C, H, W, 3)) renderalphas = mx.zeros((C, H, W, 1)) for c in range(C): cam = cameras[c] # Project all means to screen space for this camera # This step is assumed to be done externally or via a helper # to get tmp coordinates and depth projectedmeans = projectgaussians(means, cam) # Returns [N, 3] in clip space for py in range(H): for px in range(W): T = 1.0 for gid in range(len(means)): tmp = projectedmeans[gid] # Check depth if abs(tmp[2]) < epsilon: continue # Screen coordinates us = tmp[0] / tmp[2] vs = tmp[1] / tmp[2] # 3D Sigma sigma3d = us us + vs vs # 2D Fallback Sigma mu2d = means2d[c, gid] dx = px - mu2d[0] dy = py - mu2d[1] sigma2d = 2.0 (dx dx + dy dy) # Hybrid Sigma sigma = 0.5 min(sigma3d, sigma2d) # Alpha alpha = min(opacities[gid] mx.exp(-sigma), maxalpha) # Culling if alpha < alphathreshold: continue # Transmittance check if T < transmittancethreshold: break # Compositing weight = T alpha rendercolors[c, py, px] += weight colors[gid] rendernormals[c, py, px] += weight normals[gid] T = (1.0 - alpha) renderalphas[c, py, px, 0] = 1.0 - T # Background addition if background is not None: for c in range(C): rendercolors[c] += (1.0 - renderalphas[c,:,:, 0]) background[c] return rendercolors, rendernormals, renderalphas Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Zero: If tmp[2] is near zero, division by zero occurs. The check abs(tmp[2]) < EPSILON handles this. Negative Sigma: Although unlikely with squared terms, a check if sigma < 0.0 is included as a safeguard. Numerical Stability: The hybrid sigma ensures that even if the 3D projection is inaccurate, the 2D fallback provides a reasonable bound. Computes gradients for training. Adds color residuals. Adds language feature channels. Time Complexity: O(C \times H \times W \times N) in the worst case, where C is cameras, H,W resolution, N Gaussians. Culling reduces this significantly. Memory Complexity: O(C \times H \times W) for output buffers. O(C \times N) for means2d. Strengths: Robust to projection errors; tighter alpha culling improves performance. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of means2d; hybrid sigma calculation adds overhead per pixel. When to Use: When standard rasterization suffers from artifacts due to inaccurate sigma estimation or when culling efficiency is critical. This method is part of the gsplat-mlx library, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for the MLX framework. It introduces the hybrid sigma approach to improve robustness and culling. head: Backward Pass of Gaussian Rasterizer, Gaussian Rasterization (Backward), ToF Gaussian Rasterization Backward Pass

It enables end-to-end differentiable training by propagating loss gradients from the rendered image back to the 3D scene representation. It builds on 3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma by providing the necessary gradient flow for the hybrid rasterization variant. The backward pass is implemented as a Python wrapper around a C++/CUDA kernel. It retrieves cached tensors from the forward pass context, restructures arguments to match the kernel's expected layout, invokes the native routine, and returns a tuple of gradients matching the forward pass input order. Inputs: 1. Gradients from downstream loss: gradoutcolor, gradoutphasor, gradoutdepth, gradoutnormal, gradoutacc, gradentropy, graddepthdistortion, gradampdistortion. 2. Forward Pass Context (Saved Tensors): means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, colorsprecomp, phasorsprecomp, sh, shp, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, numrendered, phaseoffset, dcoffset. 3. Raster Settings: bg, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, campos, scalemodifier, shdegree, useviewdependentphase, debug, nearn, farn, depthrange. Outputs: A tuple of gradients corresponding to the forward pass inputs: gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradshp, gradcolorsprecomp, gradphasorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradphaseoffset (or None), graddcoffset (or None), and None for rastersettings. Argument Order for the Backward Kernel: bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, phasorsprecomp, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutphasor, gradoutdepth, gradoutnormal, gradoutacc, gradentropy, graddepthdistortion, gradampdistortion, sh, shp, shdegree, campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, debug, nearn, farn, depthrange, useviewdependentphase, phaseoffset, dcoffset. 1. Restore Context: Retrieve all saved tensors and settings from the forward pass context. 2. Restructure Arguments: Pack the inputs into the tuple order defined above. 3. Invoke Kernel: Call the native backward rasterization function C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(args). 4. Construct Return Tuple: Create a tuple of gradients in the order expected by the autograd engine, matching the forward pass input signature. If optimizephaseoffset is false, gradphaseoffset is None. Gradient Order: The order of gradients returned by the kernel must exactly match the forward pass input signature to ensure correct autograd integration. Non-Optimized Parameters: If phaseoffset or dcoffset are not optimized, their gradients are returned as None to prevent PyTorch from updating non-trainable parameters. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fully differentiable rasterization enabling gradient propagation. Limitations: Requires saving forward pass context tensors for gradient computation. When to Use: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting models requiring gradient computation. When Not to Use: Inference-only applications where gradients are not needed. The backward pass implementation is provided in the EGGS repository and extended in gftorf to support Time-of-Flight rendering and additional modalities. It is a critical component for optimizing the 3D scene representation from 2D images during differentiable training. name: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting (IBGS)
head: IBGS: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting
body: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting (IBGS) is a novel view synthesis method that augments standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by predicting a color residual from neighboring training images to capture high-frequency details and view-dependent effects that low-degree spherical harmonics cannot represent. Unlike methods that attach per-Gaussian texture maps (high storage) or global texture maps (poor complex scene handling), IBGS uses a lightweight neural network to learn the difference between the base 3DGS rendering and the actual pixel colors observed in source views, maintaining the original storage footprint while significantly improving rendering quality. IBGS decomposes the final pixel color into a base color rendered via standard 3DGS volume rendering and a learned residual derived from multi-view features. The method involves feature extraction from source views, residual prediction via a convolutional decoder, and optional exposure correction. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (centers \mui, covariances \Sigmai, opacities oi, spherical harmonics coefficients hi, and normal vectors ni). Camera poses and intrinsics for the target view and M neighboring source views. Source images C^m{real} for m \in \{1, \dots, M\}. Outputs: Final rendered image C{final} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores center \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}, SH coefficients hi (degree l=2), and normal vector ni \in \mathbb{R}^3. Feature Map: F \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 32}, containing aggregated multi-view features per pixel. Base Image: C \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, the result of standard 3DGS rasterization. Ray Direction Map: D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, containing camera ray directions for each pixel. Residual Map: \Delta C \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, predicted by the decoder. l: Spherical Harmonics degree. Value: 2. K: Number of median intersection points used for feature extraction. Value: 4. M: Number of visible source views used as input. Value: 3. S: Number of candidate source views (closest views) before visibility filtering. Value: 4. \tau: Depth error threshold for visibility check. Value: 0.001. \beta: Weight for L1 vs SSIM in loss. Value: 0.8. \gamma: Weight balancing base image loss vs final image loss. Initial: 1, decreased to 0.5 in last 20,000 iterations. \lambda1, \lambda2: Loss weights for photometric and normal consistency. Value: 0 for first 7,000 iterations, then 0.3 and 0.03 respectively. Opacity prune threshold: 0.05. 1. Base Color Rendering: Compute the base color c(p) for each pixel p using standard 3DGS volume rendering: c(p) = \sum{i} wi ci where wi = \alphai Ti, Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \alphai = oi G{2D}^i(p), and ci = \Psil(hi, vi) is the color of Gaussian i evaluated at ray direction vi using SH degree l. 2. Median Intersection Selection: To filter out floating Gaussians, select K intersection points \{xk(p)\}{k=1}^K where the accumulated transmittance Ti is closest to 0.5. 3. Warping to Source Views: For each selected intersection point xk(p) and each candidate source view m: Project xk(p) to the source view image plane using projection function \pim: \text{coord}{m} = \pim(xk(p)) Bilinearly interpolate the color from the source image C^m{real}: c^{warp}{k,m}(p) = B(\text{coord}{m}, C^m{real}) where B(\cdot) is bilinear interpolation. 4. Visibility Filtering: Select the M visible source views from the S candidates based on depth consistency (threshold \tau). 5. Per-Pixel Feature Extraction: For each visible source view m \in \{1, \dots, M\}: Compute the weighted average warped color: c^{warp}m(p) = \frac{\sum{k=1}^K wk c^{warp}{k,m}(p)}{\sum{k=1}^K wk} Compute the appearance feature deviation: \Delta cm(p) = c^{warp}m(p) - c(p) Define the camera feature \Delta dm(p) \in \mathbb{R}^4 (derived from source view pose/direction). Process features through encoder E (two linear layers, 32 output dim, ReLU): fm(p) = E(\Delta cm(p), \Delta dm(p)) Apply max-pooling across all M views to get aggregated feature \bar{f}(p) \in \mathbb{R}^{32}. Assemble feature map F \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 32}. 6. Exposure Correction (Optional): If applied (e.g., on Tanks and Temples), estimate an affine transformation A^ from the nearest source view and correct the base color: c^{expo}(p) = A^ c(p) If used, replace c(p) with c^{expo}(p) in subsequent steps. 7. Residual Prediction: Feed the base image C (or C^{expo}), ray direction map D, and feature map F into a nine-layer convolutional decoder D(\cdot) with 3 \times 3 kernels to predict the residual map \Delta C: \Delta C = D(C, D, F). 8. Final Rendering: Add the residual to the base image: C{final} = C + \Delta C. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projecttoimageplane(intersections, viewpose, viewintrinsics): """Project 3D intersection points to 2D image coordinates of a source view.""" # Transform to camera space: Xc = R (Xw - t) Xc = viewpose.R @ intersections.T + viewpose.t # Project: u = K Xc / Z coords = viewintrinsics.K @ Xc coords = coords[:2,:] / coords[2,:] return coords.T # Shape: (N, 2) def bilinearinterpolate(image, coords): """Bilinearly sample color from image at given (H, W, 2) coordinates.""" h, w, = image.shape u = np.clip(coords[:, 0], 0, w - 1) v = np.clip(coords[:, 1], 0, h - 1) u0, v0 = np.floor(u).astype(int), np.floor(v).astype(int) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 wu, wv = u - u0, v - v0 # Interpolate val = (1 - wu) (1 - wv) image[v0, u0] + \ wu (1 - wv) image[v0, u1] + \ (1 - wu) wv image[v1, u0] + \ wu wv image[v1, u1] return val # Shape: (N, 3) def selectmedianindices(transmittance, K): """Select K indices per pixel where transmittance is closest to 0.5.""" # transmittance shape: (H, W, N) diff = np.abs(transmittance - 0.5) # Get indices of K smallest differences indices = np.argpartition(diff, K, axis=-1)[:,:,:K] return indices # Shape: (H, W, K) def filtervisibility(candidateviews, gaussians, camera, tau): """Filter S candidate views to M visible views based on depth threshold tau.""" # Compute depth error for each candidate view against target view geometry # Keep views where max depth error < tau visible = [] for m in candidateviews: deptherr = computedeptherror(gaussians, camera, m) if deptherr.max() < tau: visible.append(m) return visible[:3] # M=3 def computecamerafeature(viewidx, raydirs): """Compute 4D camera feature from view pose and ray directions.""" # Placeholder for view-specific pose encoding; returns dummy 4D feature per evidence return np.zeroslike(raydirs)[:,:,:4] def applyexposure(image, Astar): """Apply affine exposure correction matrix A to image.""" # Astar is 3x3 or 4x4 affine matrix; apply to each pixel return (Astar[:3,:3] @ image.reshape(-1, 3).T + Astar[:3, 3]).T.reshape(image.shape) class IBGS: def init(self, K=4, M=3, S=4, tau=0.001, l=2): self.K = K self.M = M self.S = S self.tau = tau self.l = l # Encoder: 2 linear layers, 32 output dim, ReLU self.encoderW1 = np.random.randn(7, 32) self.encoderb1 = np.zeros(32) self.encoderW2 = np.random.randn(32, 32) self.encoderb2 = np.zeros(32) # Decoder: 9-layer CNN, 3x3 kernels, input channels: 38, output: 3 self.decoderweights = [np.random.randn(32, 38, 3, 3) if i == 0 else np.random.randn(32, 32, 3, 3) for i in range(9)] self.decoderbias = [np.zeros(32) for in range(9)] self.decoderoutW = np.random.randn(3, 32, 3, 3) self.decoderoutb = np.zeros(3) def encoderforward(self, x): # x: (H, W, 7) x = np.tanh(x @ self.encoderW1 + self.encoderb1) x = np.tanh(x @ self.encoderW2 + self.encoderb2) return x # (H, W, 32) def decoderforward(self, x): # x: (H, W, 38) -> (H, 38, W, H) for conv x = np.transpose(x, (0, 2, 1)) for i in range(9): x = np.tanh(np.conv2d(x, self.decoderweights[i], padding=1) + self.decoderbias[i]) x = np.conv2d(x, self.decoderoutW, padding=1) + self.decoderoutb x = np.transpose(x, (0, 2, 3, 1)) return x # (H, W, 3) def render(self, gaussians, camera, sourceviews): # 1. Base render (standard 3DGS rasterization assumed from parent article) C, transmittance, weights, raydirs = standard3dgsrasterize(gaussians, camera, self.l) # 2. Median intersection selection medianindices = selectmedianindices(transmittance, self.K) # 3. Warp to source views candidateviews = selectclosestviews(camera, sourceviews, self.S) visibleviews = filtervisibility(candidateviews, gaussians, camera, self.tau) warpedcolors = [] for m in visibleviews: coords = projecttoimageplane(gaussians[medianindices], sourceviews[m].pose, sourceviews[m].intrinsics) colors = bilinearinterpolate(sourceviews[m].image, coords) warpedcolors.append(colors) warpedcolors = np.stack(warpedcolors, axis=2) # (H, W, M, K, 3) # 4. Feature extraction features = [] for m in range(self.M): avgwarped = np.sum(warpedcolors[:,:, m,:,:] weights[:, medianindices].reshape(weights.shape[0], weights.shape[1], self.K, 1), axis=3) / \ np.sum(weights[:, medianindices], axis=3).reshape(weights.shape[0], weights.shape[1], 1) deltac = avgwarped - C deltad = computecamerafeature(m, raydirs) fm = self.encoderforward(np.concatenate([deltac, deltad], axis=-1)) features.append(fm) F = np.max(np.stack(features, axis=2), axis=2) # (H, W, 32) # 5. Exposure correction (optional) if exposurecorrectionenabled: Astar = estimateexposure(camera, sourceviews) C = applyexposure(C, Astar) # 6. Residual prediction Dmap = raydirs inputtensor = np.concatenate([C, Dmap, F], axis=-1) deltaC = self.decoderforward(inputtensor) # 7. Final rendering Cfinal = C + deltaC return Cfinal, C, deltaC Time Complexity: Dominated by the standard 3DGS rasterization and the lightweight 9-layer CNN decoder. The feature extraction involves projecting K points to M views, which is negligible compared to rasterization for typical K=4, M=3. Memory Complexity: Storage footprint is identical to standard 3DGS (Gaussians + SH coefficients). The neural network weights are small and not stored per-Gaussian. Performance: Significantly outperforms prior Gaussian Splatting approaches in rendering quality (PSNR, SSIM) on benchmarks like Tanks and Temples, Deep Blending, and Mip-NeRF360, without increasing storage. Strengths: Captures high-frequency details and view-dependent effects (specular highlights, reflections) that low-degree SH (l \le 3) misses, without the storage overhead of per-Gaussian textures. Limitations: Requires access to neighboring training images for feature extraction. Performance depends on the quality of multi-view correspondences. Auto-exposure settings in cameras can cause inconsistent brightness across views, introducing noise into Gaussian optimization if uncorrected. When to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required, especially for scenes with complex lighting or fine textures, and storage is constrained. When not to use: If source views are not available or have poor overlap/visibility with the target view. IBGS was proposed by Hoang Chuong Nguyen, Wei Mao, Jose M. Alvarez, and Miaomiao Liu from the Australian National University and NVIDIA. It was published on arXiv in November 2025. The method addresses the limitations of 3DGS, which uses low-degree spherical harmonics to model view-dependent color, limiting its ability to capture spatially varying color and effects like specular highlights. Previous attempts to augment Gaussians with texture maps either struggled with complex scenes (global maps) or introduced high storage overhead (per-Gaussian maps). IBGS leverages image-based rendering principles to "borrow" pixels from source views, modeling the residual color to supplement the base 3DGS rendering. IBGS: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14357v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering with Language Features
head: LangSplat Rendering, Language Feature Rasterization
body: This method extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer to simultaneously render a language feature image alongside the RGB image by passing precomputed per-Gaussian language features to the rasterization backend. It differs from standard 3DGS rendering by adding a parallel feature channel output and normalizing features per Gaussian before rasterization to prevent magnitude bias. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: pc (Gaussian primitive container), opt (configuration with includefeature flag), pipe (pipeline configuration with computecov3Dpython, convertSHspython, and scalingmodifier), bgcolor (background color tensor of shape [3] on GPU). Outputs: renderedimage (RGB tensor), languagefeatureimage (feature tensor), radii (screen-space radii tensor), and a dictionary containing "render", "languagefeatureimage", "viewspacepoints", "visibilityfilter", and "radii". Data Structures: Per-Gaussian Language Features: A tensor retrieved from pc via pc.getlanguagefeature(). The dimensionality depends on the feature level (e.g., 3D or higher), but the rasterization backend expects a feature tensor per Gaussian. GaussianRasterizationSettings: Configuration object passed to the rasterizer backend, specifically setting includefeature=opt.includefeature. Steps: 1. Check the opt.includefeature flag to decide whether to compute and return language features. 2. If opt.includefeature is true, retrieve per-Gaussian language features via pc.getlanguagefeature(). 3. L2-normalize the language features per Gaussian to prevent magnitude bias during blending by dividing by the L2 norm along the last dimension plus a small epsilon. The normalization formula is: \mathbf{f}{norm} = \frac{\mathbf{f}}{\|\mathbf{f}\|2 + \epsilon} where \mathbf{f} is the feature vector, \|\mathbf{f}\|2 is the L2 norm along the last dimension, and \epsilon = 10^{-9}. 4. If opt.includefeature is false, set languagefeatureprecomp to a dummy tensor of shape (1,) matching the dtype and device of opacity. 5. Configure GaussianRasterizationSettings with includefeature=opt.includefeature. 6. Prepare covariance and color data based on pipe settings: if pipe.computecov3Dpython is true, compute 3D covariance in Python via pc.getcovariance(scalingmodifier); otherwise, pass scales and rotations to the rasterizer. If pipe.convertSHspython is true, evaluate spherical harmonics in Python using evalsh; otherwise, pass raw SH coefficients (shs) or precomputed colors (colorsprecomp). 7. Call the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs/colorsprecomp, languagefeatureprecomp, opacity, and scales/rotations/cov3Dprecomp. 8. The rasterizer returns renderedimage, languagefeatureimage, and radii. Return a dictionary containing "render", "languagefeatureimage", "viewspacepoints", "visibilityfilter" (radii > 0), and "radii". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def renderlanguagefeatures(pc, opt, pipe, bgcolor, imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree): # Step 1-4: Prepare language features if opt.includefeature: languagefeatureprecomp = pc.getlanguagefeature() # L2-normalize to prevent magnitude bias during blending languagefeatureprecomp = languagefeatureprecomp / ( languagefeatureprecomp.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-9) else: # Dummy tensor matching dtype and device of opacity languagefeatureprecomp = torch.zeros(1, dtype=pc.opacity.dtype, device=pc.opacity.device) # Step 6: Prepare covariance and colors if pipe.computecov3Dpython: cov3Dprecomp = pc.getcovariance(pipe.scalingmodifier) scales = None rotations = None else: cov3Dprecomp = None scales = pc.scales rotations = pc.rotations if pipe.convertSHspython: # Evaluate spherical harmonics in Python colorsprecomp = pc.getshcolors() shs = None else: colorsprecomp = None shs = pc.shs # Step 5: Configure rasterization settings rasterizationsettings = { "imageheight": imageheight, "imagewidth": imagewidth, "tanfovx": tanfovx, "tanfovy": tanfovy, "bg": bgcolor, "scalemodifier": pipe.scalingmodifier, "viewmatrix": viewmatrix, "projmatrix": projmatrix, "shdegree": shdegree, "includefeature": opt.includefeature } # Step 7-8: Call rasterizer backend and return results renderedimage, languagefeatureimage, radii = rasterize( means3D=pc.means3D, means2D=pc.means2D, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=colorsprecomp, languagefeatureprecomp=languagefeatureprecomp, opacities=pc.opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp, settings=rasterizationsettings) visibilityfilter = radii > 0 return { "render": renderedimage, "languagefeatureimage": languagefeatureimage, "viewspacepoints": pc.means2D, "visibilityfilter": visibilityfilter, "radii": radii } def rasterize(means3D, means2D, shs, colorsprecomp, languagefeatureprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp, settings): # Invokes the CUDA rasterization backend # Returns rendered RGB image, language feature image, and screen-space radii return torch.zeros(1, 3, settings["imageheight"], settings["imagewidth"]), \ torch.zeros(1, 3, settings["imageheight"], settings["imagewidth"]), \ torch.zeros(means3D.shape[0], dtype=torch.int32) Parameters: opt.includefeature (bool): Flag to enable/disable language feature rendering and computation. scalingmodifier (float, default 1.0): Multiplier applied to Gaussian scales during rasterization. pipe.computecov3Dpython (bool): If true, computes 3D covariance in Python; otherwise passes scales and rotations. pipe.convertSHspython (bool): If true, evaluates spherical harmonics in Python; otherwise passes raw SH coefficients. bgcolor (torch.Tensor, shape [3]): Background color tensor on GPU, set to [1,1,1] for white background or [0,0,0] for black. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Magnitude Bias: Failure to L2-normalize language features can lead to magnitude bias during blending, causing incorrect feature interpolation. Feature Dimensionality: The decoder elevates features from 3 dimensions to 512 dimensions for further operations, implying the rasterized language feature image may be low-dimensional (e.g., 3D) and requires post-processing for high-dimensional tasks. Dummy Tensor: When features are disabled, a dummy tensor of shape (1,) must be passed to maintain tensor shape consistency in the rasterizer call. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables simultaneous rendering of semantic/language information alongside geometry and appearance, facilitating tasks like 3D object localization and semantic segmentation. Limitations: Requires precomputed language features and an additional normalization step. The output language feature image is low-dimensional (3D) and requires a decoder for high-dimensional applications. Origin: LangSplat was introduced by Minghan Qin, Wanhua Li, Jiawei Zhou, Haoqian Wang, and Hanspeter Pfister in the paper "LangSplat: 3D Language Gaussian Splatting" (CVPR 2024). History: The method extends the original 3D Gaussian Splatting framework to include language features, allowing for 3D language understanding and interaction. It builds upon the differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians. Usage: Used for 3D object localization on LERF and 3D semantic segmentation on LERF, leveraging preprocessed datasets like 3D-OVS with language features. minghanqin/LangSplat, https://github.com/minghanqin/LangSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
