name: Gaussian Rasterization with F-Count
head: LightGaussian rasterization
body: Gaussian Rasterization with F-Count is a variant of the 3D Gaussian Splatting differentiable rasterizer that computes an additional output: the number of times each Gaussian is activated (rendered) during the forward pass, alongside the standard color and radii outputs. It sets itself apart from the standard rasterizer by exposing per-Gaussian rendering statistics, which are used in downstream optimization pipelines (such as LightGaussian) for importance scoring and pruning, whereas the standard variant only returns pixel colors and hit radii. The method modifies the standard 3D Gaussian rasterization pipeline by introducing a boolean flag fcount in the rasterization settings. When enabled, the Python dispatcher invokes a specialized C++/CUDA backend function (C.countgaussians) instead of the standard C.rasterizegaussians. This backend function performs the standard projection, sorting, and alpha compositing steps defined in the parent Rasterization Variant but additionally accumulates a count of active Gaussians per pixel or per Gaussian instance, depending on the internal implementation details of the specific fork. Inputs: The forward pass accepts a tuple of arguments constructed in a specific order. The inputs are: 1. rastersettings.bg: Background color tensor. 2. means3D: 3D Gaussian means tensor. 3. colorsprecomp: Precomputed colors tensor (or None if SHs are used). 4. opacities: Gaussian opacities tensor. 5. scales: Gaussian scales tensor (or None if cov3Ds are used). 6. rotations: Gaussian rotations tensor (or None if cov3Ds are used). 7. rastersettings.scalemodifier: Scale modifier float. 8. cov3Dsprecomp: Precomputed 3D covariances tensor (or None if scales/rotations are used). 9. rastersettings.viewmatrix: View matrix tensor. 10. rastersettings.projmatrix: Projection matrix tensor. 11. rastersettings.tanfovx: Tangent of horizontal field of view. 12. rastersettings.tanfovy: Tangent of vertical field of view. 13. rastersettings.imageheight: Image height integer. 14. rastersettings.imagewidth: Image width integer. 15. sh: Spherical Harmonics coefficients tensor (or None if colorsprecomp are used). 16. rastersettings.shdegree: SH degree integer. 17. rastersettings.campos: Camera position tensor. 18. rastersettings.prefiltered: Prefiltered boolean. 19. rastersettings.debug: Debug boolean. 20. rastersettings.fcount: Boolean flag enabling F-Count mode. Outputs: If fcount is true, the forward pass returns a tuple: 1. gaussianscount: Tensor containing the count of activated Gaussians. 2. importantscore: Tensor containing importance scores derived from the counts. 3. color: Rendered color image tensor. 4. radii: Hit radii tensor. If fcount is false, it returns the standard tuple: (color, radii). GaussianRasterizationSettings: A NamedTuple containing the following fields: imageheight: int imagewidth: int tanfovx: float tanfovy: float bg: torch.Tensor scalemodifier: float viewmatrix: torch.Tensor projmatrix: torch.Tensor shdegree: int campos: torch.Tensor prefiltered: bool debug: bool fcount: bool 1. Input Validation: Verify that exactly one of shs or colorsprecomp is provided. If both are None or both are not None, raise an exception. Verify that exactly one of the following pairs is provided: scales and rotations (both not None). cov3Dprecomp (not None). If (scales is None or rotations is None) AND cov3Dprecomp is None, raise an exception. If (scales is not None or rotations is not None) AND cov3Dprecomp is not None, raise an exception. 2. Argument Construction: Construct the args tuple for the C++ backend in the specific order listed in "Inputs and Outputs" above. Ensure rastersettings.fcount is the 20th element of this tuple. 3. Dispatch: Check the value of rastersettings.fcount. If True, call C.countgaussians(args). If False, call C.rasterizegaussians(args). 4. Execution and Return: The C++ backend performs the standard rasterization steps (projection, sorting, compositing) as defined in the parent article [17388-rasterization-variant.md]. If fcount is true, the backend additionally computes gaussianscount and importantscore. Return the appropriate tuple based on the mode. 5. Backward Pass: Construct the backward args tuple in this specific order: 1. rastersettings.bg 2. means3D 3. radii 4. colorsprecomp 5. scales 6. rotations 7. rastersettings.scalemodifier 8. cov3Dsprecomp 9. rastersettings.viewmatrix 10. rastersettings.projmatrix 11. rastersettings.tanfovx 12. rastersettings.tanfovy 13. gradoutcolor 14. sh 15. rastersettings.shdegree 16. rastersettings.campos 17. geomBuffer 18. numrendered 19. binningBuffer 20. imgBuffer 21. rastersettings.debug Call C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(args). The backward function returns: (gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations). Return the gradients corresponding to the forward inputs: (gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, None). The last None corresponds to the non-differentiable rastersettings argument. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import copy def gaussianrasterizationwithfcount( means3D: torch.Tensor, colorsprecomp: torch.Tensor, opacities: torch.Tensor, scales: torch.Tensor, rotations: torch.Tensor, cov3Dsprecomp: torch.Tensor, sh: torch.Tensor, rastersettings: GaussianRasterizationSettings) -> tuple: """ Differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians with optional F-Count output. Args: means3D: Tensor of 3D Gaussian means. colorsprecomp: Tensor of precomputed colors (or None). opacities: Tensor of Gaussian opacities. scales: Tensor of Gaussian scales (or None). rotations: Tensor of Gaussian rotations (or None). cov3Dsprecomp: Tensor of precomputed 3D covariances (or None). sh: Tensor of Spherical Harmonics coefficients (or None). rastersettings: GaussianRasterizationSettings NamedTuple. Returns: Tuple of tensors: (gaussianscount, importantscore, color, radii) if fcount is True. Tuple of tensors: (color, radii) if fcount is False. """ # Input Validation if colorsprecomp is None and sh is None: raise ValueError("Either colorsprecomp or sh must be provided.") if colorsprecomp is not None and sh is not None: raise ValueError("Only one of colorsprecomp or sh can be provided.") if (scales is None or rotations is None) and cov3Dsprecomp is None: raise ValueError("Either (scales and rotations) or cov3Dsprecomp must be provided.") if (scales is not None or rotations is not None) and cov3Dsprecomp is not None: raise ValueError("Only one of (scales and rotations) or cov3Dsprecomp can be provided.") # Construct Forward Arguments # Order: bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, # cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, imageheight, imagewidth, # sh, shdegree, campos, prefiltered, debug, fcount args = ( rastersettings.bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.debug, rastersettings.fcount) try: if rastersettings.fcount: # Call specialized count function # Returns: (gaussianscount, importantscore, numrendered, color, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) forwardoutput = C.countgaussians(args) # Extract relevant outputs gaussianscount = forwardoutput[0] importantscore = forwardoutput[1] color = forwardoutput[3] radii = forwardoutput[4] return (gaussianscount, importantscore, color, radii) else: # Call standard rasterization function # Returns: (numrendered, importantscore/None, numrendered, color, radii, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) forwardoutput = C.rasterizegaussians(args) color = forwardoutput[3] radii = forwardoutput[4] return (color, radii) except Exception as e: if rastersettings.debug: # Deep copy args to CPU and save for debugging argscpu = copy.deepcopy(args) torch.save(argscpu, 'snapshotfw.dump') raise e def gaussianrasterizationwithfcountbackward( gradoutcolor: torch.Tensor, means3D: torch.Tensor, radii: torch.Tensor, colorsprecomp: torch.Tensor, scales: torch.Tensor, rotations: torch.Tensor, cov3Dsprecomp: torch.Tensor, sh: torch.Tensor, rastersettings: GaussianRasterizationSettings, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) -> tuple: """ Backward pass for Gaussian rasterization with F-Count. Args: gradoutcolor: Gradient of the loss with respect to the output color. means3D: 3D Gaussian means. radii: Hit radii from forward pass. colorsprecomp: Precomputed colors. scales: Gaussian scales. rotations: Gaussian rotations. cov3Dsprecomp: Precomputed 3D covariances. sh: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. rastersettings: GaussianRasterizationSettings NamedTuple. geomBuffer: Geometry buffer from forward pass. numrendered: Number of rendered Gaussians from forward pass. binningBuffer: Binning buffer from forward pass. imgBuffer: Image buffer from forward pass. Returns: Tuple of gradients: (gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, None) """ # Construct Backward Arguments # Order: bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, # cov3Dsprecomp, viewmatrix, projmatrix, tanfovx, tanfovy, gradoutcolor, # sh, shdegree, campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, debug argsbw = ( rastersettings.bg, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, gradoutcolor, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rastersettings.debug) try: # Call backward function # Returns: (gradmeans2D, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradmeans3D, # gradcov3Dsprecomp, gradsh, gradscales, gradrotations) gradoutput = C.rasterizegaussiansbackward(argsbw) gradmeans2D = gradoutput[0] gradcolorsprecomp = gradoutput[1] gradopacities = gradoutput[2] gradmeans3D = gradoutput[3] gradcov3Dsprecomp = gradoutput[4] gradsh = gradoutput[5] gradscales = gradoutput[6] gradrotations = gradoutput[7] # Return gradients in the order expected by the autograd engine for the forward inputs # Forward inputs: means3D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, sh, rastersettings return ( gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, None) except Exception as e: if rastersettings.debug: argsbwcpu = copy.deepcopy(argsbw) torch.save(argsbwcpu, 'snapshotbw.dump') raise e fcount: A boolean flag in GaussianRasterizationSettings. When True, the rasterizer invokes C.countgaussians and returns gaussianscount and importantscore. When False, it invokes C.rasterizegaussians and returns only color and radii. Input Validation: The forward pass raises an exception if both shs and colorsprecomp are None, or if both are not None. It must receive exactly one of either. Covariance Input: The forward pass raises an exception if (scales is None or rotations is None) AND cov3Dprecomp is None, OR if (scales is not None or rotations is not None) AND cov3Dprecomp is not None. It must receive exactly one of either scale/rotation pair or precomputed 3D covariance. Debugging Snapshots: If an exception occurs during the forward pass and rastersettings.debug is True, the arguments are deep-copied to CPU and saved to snapshotfw.dump before re-raising the exception. Similarly, backward pass exceptions save to snapshotbw.dump. Time Complexity: The time complexity is dominated by the standard 3D Gaussian rasterization steps (projection, sorting, compositing) as defined in the parent article [17388-rasterization-variant.md]. The additional computation for fcount is minimal, involving simple increment operations during the compositing loop. Memory Complexity: The memory complexity is similar to the standard rasterizer, with the addition of storing the gaussianscount and importantscore tensors. The buffers (geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer) are reused from the forward pass. Performance: The specific performance impact of fcount is not quantified in the sources beyond the fact that it is a lightweight addition to the forward pass. Strengths: Enables importance scoring and pruning strategies (e.g., in LightGaussian) by providing per-Gaussian rendering statistics. Limitations: Only available in specific forks/implementations (e.g., Fov-3DGS) and not part of the core 3DGS standard. This variant is associated with the "LightGaussian" approach and is implemented in the Fov-3DGS repository by Horizon Research. It is used in training pipelines where Gaussian pruning or importance-based optimization is required, allowing the system to track how often each Gaussian contributes to the final image. horizon-research/Fov-3DGS, https://github.com/horizon-research/Fov-3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Single-Pass Rasterization with Alpha-Blending
head: Single-Pass Anti-Aliased Rasterization, Unified Rasterization
body: This method provides a unified rendering pipeline that rasterizes both 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives and triangle meshes in a single pass using alpha-blending, ensuring correct spatial occlusion and color blending without dropping rendering rates. It solves the problem of integrating mesh-based deformation or proxy geometry with 3DGS by treating depth-adjacent triangles as a single entity for transmittance calculation, thereby avoiding color overflow artifacts that occur when Gaussians are present between triangles. Unlike standard 3DGS rasterization which only handles splats, or standard rasterization which only handles triangles, this variant unifies them by applying Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) logic to triangle fragments while maintaining the standard front-to-back alpha compositing for Gaussians. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian fragments, each defined by color \mathbf{c}i, opacity \alphai, and depth. A set of triangle fragments, each defined by color \mathbf{c}i, opacity \alphai (typically 1.0 for opaque triangles, but treated as alpha for blending), and depth. A background color \mathbf{C}{bg} and background opacity \alpha{bg}. Initial transmittance T{in} (typically 1.0). Number of sub-pixels M for MSAA (typically 4). Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{pixel}. Data Structures: Fragments are sorted by depth (front-to-back) within each tile/pixel. For triangles, sub-pixel coverage is tracked. Let o{ji} \in \{0, 1\} be a boolean indicating whether the i-th triangle fragment covers the j-th sub-pixel. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial transmittance T{in} = 1.0. 2. Process Gaussian Fragments: For each Gaussian fragment i (in depth order): Compute transmittance Ti representing the visibility of the fragment: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where T1 = T{in}. Accumulate Gaussian color contribution \mathbf{C}{gs}: \mathbf{C}{gs} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where N is the number of overlapping fragments. 3. Process Triangle Fragments: For each triangle fragment i (in depth order): Sub-pixel Transmittance: Calculate the transmittance at the sub-pixel level t{ji} for each sub-pixel j \in \{1, \dots, M\}: t{ji} = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - o{jk} \alphak) with t{j1} = 1.0. Pixel Coverage: Compute the effective coverage Oi of the triangle at the pixel level by averaging sub-pixel coverages weighted by sub-pixel transmittance: Oi = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} o{ji} t{ji} where o{ji} is the geometric coverage of fragment i on sub-pixel j. Triangle Color Accumulation: Compute the color contribution \mathbf{C}{tris} for the current group of depth-adjacent triangles. The method treats depth-adjacent triangles as a single entity to ensure correct transmittance decay for subsequent blending: \mathbf{C}{tris} = T{in} \sum{i=1}^{N} Oi \alphai \mathbf{c}i Note: The pixel-level transmittance Ti is updated using Oi for subsequent blending, but is not used in the summation for \mathbf{C}{tris} itself. Update Pixel Transmittance: Update the pixel-level transmittance Ti for the next fragment: Ti = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - Ok \alphak) This Ti is used for the final pixel color calculation and for blending subsequent fragments, ensuring that transmittance decay accounts for both Gaussians and triangles. 4. Final Color Calculation: Combine the triangle contribution, Gaussian contribution (if applicable in the same pass, though the source describes them as separate accumulation paths merged at the end or via the unified transmittance), and background: \mathbf{C}{pixel} = \mathbf{C}{tris} + T{bg} \mathbf{C}{bg} where T{bg} = TN (1 - \alpha{bg}) and TN is the final transmittance after all fragments. Parameters: M: Number of sub-pixels for MSAA. Typical value: 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Overflow: If all triangles overlapping a pixel are treated as a single entity when Gaussians are present between them, the transmittance for deeper triangles does not account for decay from Gaussians. This results in color overflow, manifesting as white artifacts. To avoid this, only depth-adjacent triangles are treated as a single entity for the \mathbf{C}{tris} calculation. Sub-pixel Logic: The transmittance calculation for triangles must be performed at the sub-pixel level to accommodate MSAA, differing from the pixel-level transmittance used for Gaussians. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of fragments (Gaussians and triangles) per pixel. The sub-pixel averaging for triangles adds a constant factor of M (typically 4) to the triangle processing cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing sub-pixel coverage data for triangles, increasing memory usage compared to standard rasterization. Strengths: Enables unified rendering of 3DGS and meshes in a single pass, maintaining high rendering rates while providing correct spatial occlusion and anti-aliasing for both primitives. Limitations: Requires careful handling of depth-adjacent triangles to avoid artifacts when mixed with Gaussians. This method was proposed in "UniMGS: Unifying Mesh and 3D Gaussian Splatting with Single-Pass Rasterization and Proxy-Based Deformation". It addresses the limitations of proxy-based 3DGS deformation, which is sensitive to mesh topology quality, by providing a robust rasterization pipeline that links trained 3DGS to proxy meshes with minimal artifacts. UniMGS: Unifying Mesh and 3D Gaussian Splatting with Single-Pass Rasterization and Proxy-Based Deformation, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.19233, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Camera Pose Gradient Computation
head: Camera pose gradient derivation, Gradient computation for camera pose optimization, Jacobian of Gaussians w.r.t. Camera Poses
body: This method computes the gradient of the rendering loss \mathcal{L} with respect to virtual camera poses \mathbf{T}i to enable joint optimization of 3D Gaussian parameters and camera trajectories. It differs from standard differentiable rasterization by explicitly deriving the analytical Jacobian of the Gaussian mean transformation with respect to the camera pose, allowing gradients to flow from the image loss back to the pose parameters. This extends the backpropagation path of the parent method 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer to include extrinsic camera parameters. The method computes the gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} for a virtual camera pose \mathbf{T}i \in SE(3) associated with the i-th virtual sharp image \mathbf{C}i. The computation relies on the chain rule, decomposing the gradient into terms involving the loss, the rendered image, the Gaussian parameters, and the camera pose. Inputs: \mathcal{L}: The scalar rendering loss. \mathbf{T}i: The virtual camera pose for the i-th view, represented as an element of SE(3). \boldsymbol{\mu}: The 3D mean position of a Gaussian in world coordinates. \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}: The rotation matrix and translation vector components of \mathbf{T}i. \mathbf{C}i: The virtual sharp camera pose for the i-th view. \mathbf{B}k: The blurred image pixels. Outputs: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}: The gradient of the loss with respect to the camera pose parameters. Pose \mathbf{T}i: Represented as an SE(3) transformation, parameterized by control knots optimized in the Lie algebra se(3). Gaussian Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}: A 3D vector \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera Coordinate Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}c: A 3D vector \in \mathbb{R}^3. 1. Compute Loss Gradients: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the blurred image pixels \mathbf{B}k and the sharp poses \mathbf{C}i using automatic differentiation. 2. Decompose Gaussian Parameter Gradients: The gradient with respect to the Gaussian parameters \theta is defined as: \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \left[ \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}, \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}, \frac{\partial c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}, \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} \right] where \boldsymbol{\mu}' is the transformed mean, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' is the transformed covariance, c is color, and \rho is opacity. 3. Apply Efficiency Approximations: Color c and opacity \rho are independent of the virtual camera pose \mathbf{T}i, so their gradients are zero. For efficiency, the gradient of the transformed covariance \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} is ignored. Consequently, only \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} needs to be computed analytically. 4. Compute Mean Transformation Gradient: Decompose \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} using the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} where \boldsymbol{\mu}c = \mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{t} is the mean transformed into the camera's coordinate space. 5. Evaluate Chain Rule Terms: Rasterization Jacobian: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}. This is the Jacobian of the rendered image with respect to the Gaussian mean in world coordinates, computed in the CUDA backend. Inverse Rotation: \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c} = \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\partial \mathbf{R} \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{t}} = \mathbf{R}^T. Pose Jacobian: \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \mathbf{I}3 \otimes [\boldsymbol{\mu}^\top \mathbf{I}] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}, where \otimes is the Kronecker operator and \mathbf{I}3 is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. 6. Pose Interpolation Jacobian: The virtual camera pose \mathbf{T}i is interpolated from SE(3) control knots (e.g., \mathbf{T}{start}, \mathbf{T}{end} for linear, or \mathbf{T}1, \mathbf{T}2, \mathbf{T}3, \mathbf{T}4 for cubic B-spline). The Jacobian of \mathbf{T}i with respect to pose adjustments (e.g., \varepsilon \in se(3)) is computed using PyPose and PyTorch auto-differentiation. The complete gradient computation is given by: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{T}i}:= \left( \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{B}k} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} \left( \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}k}{\partial \mathbf{C}i} \right) \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \theta} \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} where: K is the number of pixels. n is the number of virtual cameras. \theta represents the Gaussian parameters. The specific term for the mean transformation is: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} \mathbf{R}^T \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computecameraposegradient( gradLB: torch.Tensor, # Sum of dL/dBk over pixels, shape (numcameras, H, W, C) gradBC: torch.Tensor, # 1/n Sum of dBk/dCi over cameras, shape (numcameras, H, W, C) gradCmu: torch.Tensor, # dCi/dmu from CUDA backend, shape (numcameras, H, W, C, numgaussians, 3) R: torch.Tensor, # Rotation matrices, shape (numcameras, 3, 3) posejacobian: torch.Tensor # dTi/depsilon from PyPose, shape (numcameras, 6)): # 1. Combine loss and blur gradients (auto-diff terms) gradLC = gradLB gradBC # 2. Compute inverse rotation R^T RT = R.transpose(1, 2) # 3. Apply inverse rotation to rasterization Jacobian # gradCmu[...,:3] corresponds to the 3D spatial gradient gradCmurotated = torch.matmul(gradCmu, RT.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1)) # 4. Contract with pose Jacobian dmuc / dTi # posejacobian is precomputed via PyPose/PyTorch auto-diff # The Jacobian maps the 3D gradient to the 6D pose adjustment space gradpergaussian = torch.einsum('niklm,ni->nkm', gradCmurotated, posejacobian) # 5. Scale by loss gradient and return gradLCexpanded = gradLC.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) return gradLCexpanded gradpergaussian Efficiency vs. Accuracy: Ignoring \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} improves efficiency but omits its contribution to the gradient. Pose Interpolation: The method relies on PyPose for SE(3) interpolation. Incorrect implementation of the interpolation or its Jacobian can lead to incorrect gradients. Dimensionality: The source specifies \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}c}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}, which implies a specific vectorization or flattening convention for the gradient with respect to the pose parameters. Strengths: Enables joint optimization of 3D Gaussians and camera poses, which is crucial for tasks like Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting. Limitations: The approximation of ignoring \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'}{\partial \mathbf{T}i} simplifies computation but discards covariance-related pose gradients. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the supplementary materials of "BAD-Gaussians: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussian Splatting and extends it to support camera pose optimization, similar to approaches in GS-SLAM. The analytical derivation of the Jacobian w.r.t. camera poses allows for efficient gradient computation without relying solely on numerical differentiation or full auto-diff through the projection matrix, although the implementation still uses auto-diff for the interpolation part. BAD-Gaussians: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72698-914, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering
head: stochastic solids
body: Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering is a technique that treats Gaussian primitives as continuous stochastic solids, replacing standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rasterization to improve geometric accuracy and depth synthesis quality. It solves the problem of floating-depth artifacts caused by vanilla 3DGS alpha-blending, which blends foreground and background depths, by allowing transmittance to vary continuously along each ray. Unlike sibling methods such as 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform (3DGUT) which use fixed median-depth selection, this method provides a differentiable, continuous formulation for depth and normal rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} (or viewing direction \omega), and a set of N 3D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \mathbf{I}{pix}, depth map d, and normal map \mathbf{n}. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Defined by 3D position \mu, 3x3 covariance matrix \Sigma (or quaternion scale/rotation), scalar opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Ray: Parametrized as \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where t is the depth along the ray. Formulas: 1. Vacancy Formulation: The per-pixel opacity \alpha is interpreted as the maximum value of the Gaussian primitive along the pixel ray. The vacancy v is defined as: v = \sqrt{1 - G(t^)} where t^ is the location of the maximum Gaussian response along the ray, and G(t^) is the Gaussian response at that location. This converts the 3D Gaussian distribution into a Gaussian primitive suitable for volume rendering. 2. Attenuation Coefficient: For a stochastic solid with vacancy v, the attenuation coefficient \sigma is defined as: \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \omega) = |\omega \cdot \nabla \log(v(\mathbf{x}))| = \frac{|\omega \cdot \nabla v(\mathbf{x})|}{v(\mathbf{x})} where \mathbf{x} is the 3D spatial position and \omega is the viewing direction. 3. Volume Rendering Integral: The rendered color \mathbf{I}{pix} is computed by integrating along the ray from near plane tn to far plane tf: \mathbf{I}{pix} = \int{tn}^{tf} p(t) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}(t), \omega) dt = \mathbf{c} \left( 1 - v(t)^2 \right) where the density p(t) and accumulated transmittance T(t) are: p(t) = T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{x}(t), \omega) T(t) = \exp \left( - \int{tn}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{x}(s), \omega) ds \right) Here, \mathbf{v} denotes the vacancy of the solid. 4. Depth Rendering (Median Depth): The depth map is defined as the median depth, i.e., the location d where accumulated transmittance reaches 0.5. The accumulated transmittance of multiple Gaussian primitives is computed by multiplicative composition. 5. Normal Rendering: Normal maps are rendered directly from Gaussian primitives using the same volume rendering formulation as RGB rendering. For each primitive, the tangent-plane normal of the density surface is computed at the ray intersection under the current viewing direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera origin through the pixel center. 2. Primitive Sorting: Sort all Gaussian primitives intersecting the ray's bounding volume by their distance to the camera (or along the ray parameter t). 3. Vacancy Calculation: For each primitive, determine the maximum Gaussian response G(t^) along the ray segment covered by the primitive. Compute the vacancy v = \sqrt{1 - G(t^)}. 4. Transmittance Integration: Compute the accumulated transmittance T(t) along the ray by integrating the attenuation coefficient \sigma derived from the vacancy v. This is done by multiplicative composition of transmittance contributions from each primitive. 5. Color Computation: Compute the final pixel color \mathbf{I}{pix} using the volume rendering integral, which simplifies to \mathbf{c}(1 - v(t)^2) at the point of maximum response. 6. Depth Solving: Solve for the median depth d where T(d) = 0.5. This is achieved using a fixed number of bisection iterations. 7. Normal Computation: Compute the tangent-plane normal of the density surface at the ray intersection for each primitive. Accumulate these normals using the same volume rendering formulation to produce the final normal map. 8. Backpropagation: Propagate gradients with the closed-form derivative of depth with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta: \frac{\partial d}{\partial \theta} = - \frac{\partial T(d; \theta) / \partial \theta}{\partial T(d; \theta) / \partial d} where d is the median depth location and \theta are the Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderstochasticsolid(rayorigin, raydir, gaussians): # Sort primitives by distance along ray sortedgaussians = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: dot(g.mean - rayorigin, raydir)) T = 1.0 color = vec3(0.0) for g in sortedgaussians: # Find t for maximum Gaussian response tstar = findmaxresponse(g, rayorigin, raydir) Gtstar = evaluategaussian(g, tstar) v = sqrt(1.0 - Gtstar) # Compute attenuation coefficient gradv = computegradientv(g, v) sigma = abs(dot(raydir, gradv)) / v # Update transmittance via multiplicative composition dt = computestepsize(g) T = T exp(-sigma dt) # Accumulate color alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma dt) color = color (1.0 - alpha) + g.color alpha # Solve median depth where T(d) = 0.5 d = bisectionsolve(lambda t: computetransmittance(t) - 0.5) # Render normal directly normal = rendernormaldirect(gaussians, rayorigin, raydir) return color, d, normal Parameters: Bisection Iterations: A fixed number of iterations is used to solve for the median depth. Optimizer: AdamW optimizer is used for training. Learning Rate: Initial learning rate 3 \times 10^{-6}, decayed to 1 \times 10^{-8} using cosine annealing. Iterations: 420K iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating-Depth Artifacts: Vanilla 3DGS alpha-blending blends foreground and background depths, producing artifacts. This method avoids this by using continuous transmittance. Discontinuities: Fixed median-depth selection (used in 2DGS) can introduce discontinuities in boundary regions. This method's continuous formulation mitigates this. Gradient Flow: Median-depth rendering affects only a single median Gaussian primitive during backpropagation, which is unfavorable for optimizing generalizable foundation models. This method allows gradients to flow through the continuous volume rendering formulation. Stochastic Depth Rendering is a method for computing depth maps from 3D Gaussian primitives by modeling them as continuous stochastic solids. It solves the problem of noisy, inconsistent depth estimates in standard Gaussian Splatting by defining depth as the median transmittance crossing (T=0.5) rather than an opacity-weighted average. Unlike alpha-averaged expected depth, which blurs silhouettes and suffers from view-dependent floater bias, this approach provides sharper boundary transitions and superior multi-view consistency. It builds on Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering by applying the stochastic solid attenuation model specifically to depth estimation. Time Complexity: The method requires sorting primitives and integrating transmittance along rays, which is comparable to standard rasterization but involves additional bisection iterations for depth solving. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Gaussian parameters and intermediate transmittance values along the ray. Strengths: Improves geometric accuracy and depth synthesis quality by avoiding floating-depth artifacts. Provides smoother depth maps compared to rasterization-based median depth. Decouples normal supervision from depth rendering, allowing direct normal rendering from primitives. Limitations: More complex than standard rasterization due to the volume rendering formulation and bisection iterations. When to Use: When accurate scene geometry and depth maps are critical, such as in visual geometry grounded transformers or generalizable foundation models. When Not to Use: When computational efficiency is the primary concern and geometric accuracy is less critical, standard 3DGS rasterization may be preferred. Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering was introduced in the paper \text{VG}^2GT: Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer. It builds upon the concept of treating Gaussian primitives as continuous stochastic solids, as proposed in [52] (cited in). The method addresses limitations of existing 3DGS variants, such as 2DGS, which use fixed median-depth selection and suffer from discontinuities and limited gradient flow. It is used in the context of feed-forward Gaussian primitives for visual geometry tasks. \text{VG}^2GT: Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.01573, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stochastic Depth Rendering
head: Depth from Stochastic Solids, Depth-Rendering via Stochastic Theory, Median Depth via Stochastic Solids, Stochastic Solid Depth Rendering, Volumetric Depth Formulation
body: Stochastic Depth Rendering is a method for computing depth maps from 3D Gaussian primitives by modeling them as continuous stochastic solids. It solves the problem of noisy, inconsistent depth estimates in standard Gaussian Splatting by defining depth as the median transmittance crossing (T=0.5) rather than an opacity-weighted average. Unlike alpha-averaged expected depth, which blurs silhouettes and suffers from view-dependent floater bias, this approach provides sharper boundary transitions and superior multi-view consistency. It builds on Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering by applying the stochastic solid attenuation model specifically to depth estimation. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}, each defined by position, covariance, opacity, and color; a camera ray r defined by origin o and direction d. Outputs: A scalar median depth value t{med} for the ray. The method operates on the parameters of the Gaussian primitives projected onto the ray. For each Gaussian i, the following values are computed along the ray parameter t: ti^: The location of the Gaussian's maximum density along the ray (the center of the Gaussian projected onto the ray axis). vi(t): The continuous attenuation profile (vacancy) of the i-th Gaussian at distance t. This is derived from the Gaussian's covariance and position. 1. Compute Individual Transmittance: For a given ray parameter t, calculate the transmittance Ti(t) for each Gaussian i using the stochastic solid attenuation function: Ti(t) = \begin{cases} vi(t), & t \leq ti^ \\ \frac{vi(ti^)^2}{vi(t)}, & t > ti^ \end{cases} Here, vi(t) represents the probability that the ray has not been "absorbed" or blocked by the Gaussian up to point t. The term vi(ti^)^2/vi(t) for t > ti^ ensures the attenuation profile is symmetric and continuous at the peak ti^. 2. Compute Overall Transmittance: Assuming statistical independence of ray intersections with different Gaussians, compute the total transmittance T(t) as the product of individual transmittances: T(t) = \prod{i=1}^{N} Ti(t) The product is taken over all Gaussians intersecting the ray. 3. Find Median Depth: The median depth t{med} is defined as the inverse transmittance at 0.5: t{med} = T^{-1}(0.5) Since T(t) is monotonically decreasing along the ray (as transmittance decreases with distance), a binary search is used to find t{med} such that T(t{med}) = 0.5. Binary Search: Initialize an interval [t{min}, t{max}] covering the scene depth. Iteratively narrow the interval by evaluating T(t{mid}) and updating bounds until convergence. Gradient Computation: During backpropagation, the iterative search is bypassed. The gradient of the median depth with respect to Gaussian parameters \theta is computed using the implicit function theorem: \frac{\partial t{med}}{\partial \theta} = -\frac{\frac{\partial T(t{med}; \theta)}{\partial \theta}}{\frac{\partial T(t; \theta)}{\partial t} \Big|{t=t{med}}} This allows gradients to be distributed to all contributing Gaussians along the ray. The stochastic-solid formulation models attenuation continuously, yielding a smooth transmittance function and reducing staircasing. Precision: The binary search relies on the monotonicity of transmittance. If the ray does not intersect any Gaussians, T(t)=1 everywhere, and no solution exists. Guard against empty intersections. Runtime: The method is computationally more expensive than standard rasterization due to the binary search and the evaluation of the product of transmittances for all Gaussians along the ray. Outperforms PGSR and RaDe-GS in multi-view consistency and floater suppression. Limitations: Higher runtime than standard rasterization methods. Requires careful initialization of the binary search interval. When to Use: When geometric accuracy, multi-view consistency, and sharp depth boundaries are critical, such as in Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction or high-fidelity shape reconstruction. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is the primary constraint and geometric consistency is less important than raw rendering speed. History: The method addresses limitations in prior Gaussian Splatting depth rendering, such as view-dependent depth planes [Yu et al. 2024c; Zhang et al. 2024] and opacity-weighted ray averaging [Chen et al. 2024], which suffer from blurred silhouettes and floater bias. It builds on the concept of treating Gaussians as stochastic solids to align volume rendering with rasterization-based rendering. Usage: Used in Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction and geometric regularization tasks to improve cross-view consistency and reduce reprojection error. name: Differentiable Gaussian Rasterization with Plane/Depth Output

body: This method extends the standard differentiable Gaussian rasterizer to simultaneously output color, depth, and geometric auxiliary maps per pixel. It solves the problem of extracting dense geometric information from 3D Gaussian splats by treating depth and geometric attributes as additional channels in the alpha-compositing accumulation, allowing gradients to flow back to the 3D Gaussian parameters for geometry-aware training. It differs from standard color-only rasterization by maintaining and backpropagating through additional output tensors (outallmap, outplanedepth) alongside the color buffer. The method operates in two phases: a forward pass that projects 3D Gaussians and accumulates color, depth, and geometric maps, and a backward pass that computes gradients for all Gaussian parameters. Forward Inputs: rastersettings.bg, means3D, colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, allmaps, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.rendergeo, rastersettings.debug. Forward Outputs: color, radii, outobserve, outallmap, outplanedepth. Backward Inputs: rastersettings.bg, allmappixels, means3D, radii, colorsprecomp, allmaps, scales, rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, gradoutcolor, gradoutallmap, gradoutplanedepth, sh, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, geomBuffer, numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, rastersettings.rendergeo, rastersettings.debug. name: EffGS
body: EffGS is an acceleration framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that improves training and rendering efficiency while maintaining high-fidelity reconstruction in both bounded and large-scale scenes. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS and other acceleration methods by combining frequency-aware guidance, localized density control, and adaptive primitive scale modulation to prevent quality degradation in complex environments. EffGS modifies the standard 3DGS optimization loop [1795-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] by introducing three key components: Frequency-Aware Optimization, Localized Density Control (LDP), and Adaptive Primitive Compactness. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses; a set of 3D Gaussians \{Gk\} initialized from the parent method. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, opacity, rotation, base-scale, spherical harmonic coefficients) and a unified supervision signal for density control. The method operates on the standard 3DGS Gaussian representation: Position \mathbf{p}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity ok \in \mathbb{R} Rotation Rk \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} Base-scale \mathbf{s}k = [s{xk}, s{yk}, s{zk}]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3 Spherical Harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}k EffGS introduces a learnable scalar \gammak per Gaussian to modulate scale. 1. Frequency Mask Generation: For each training image: a. Convert the ground-truth image to grayscale and downsample to obtain I{\text{down}}. b. Compute the difference-of-Gaussians response H: H = I{\text{down}} \mathcal{G}{\sigma1} - I{\text{down}} \mathcal{G}{\sigma2} where \mathcal{G}\sigma is a normalized Gaussian kernel with standard deviation \sigma, and \sigma2 = 2\sigma1. c. Determine the bandwidth schedule parameter f(t) based on the current training iteration t and total iterations T{\text{total}}: f(t) = 100 \frac{t}{T{\text{total}}} d. Set \sigma1 according to the piecewise schedule controlled by f(t). e. Upsample H to the original image resolution and normalize. f. Threshold the response to create the frequency-aware mask M{\text{freq}}: If f(t) < 50, threshold the complemented response (1 - H). If f(t) \ge 50, threshold the direct response (H). 2. Unified Supervision Signal: a. Compute the pixel-wise reconstruction error between the rendered image I{\text{rend}} and ground-truth I{\text{gt}}. b. Fuse the error-aware mask with M{\text{freq}} to create a unified 2D supervision signal. 3. Importance Scoring and Localized Density Control (LDP): a. Project visible Gaussians to 2D using the projected covariance: \Sigmak^{2D} = JW\Sigmak W^\top J^\top where W \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3} is the rotational part of the world-to-camera transform, J is the projection Jacobian evaluated at \mathbf{p}k, and \Sigmak = Rk Sk Sk^\top Rk^\top. b. Accumulate importance scores from the unified supervision signal for each Gaussian based on its projected footprint. c. Restrict densification (cloning/splitting) and pruning operations only to Gaussians with valid projected footprints in the sampled views, excluding primitives outside the current active set. 4. Adaptive Primitive Compactness: a. Introduce a learnable scalar \gammak for each Gaussian. b. Modulate the base-scale components during optimization: \mathbf{s}k^{\text{eff}} = \gammak \cdot [s{xk}, s{yk}, s{zk}]^\top c. Jointly optimize \gammak and the base scales to adapt the effective primitive extent while retaining the Compact Box rasterization rule. 5. Rendering and Loss: a. Render the image using front-to-back alpha compositing: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{u}) = \sumk \mathbf{c}k \alphak(\mathbf{u}) \prod{\ell < k} (1 - \alpha\ell(\mathbf{u})) where \mathbf{u} is the image-plane coordinate. b. Compute the Gaussian alpha value: \alphak(\mathbf{u}) = ok \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{p}k^{2D})^\top (\Sigmak^{2D})^{-1}(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{p}k^{2D})\right) where \mathbf{p}k^{2D} is the projected Gaussian center. c. Calculate the standard 3DGS objective: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda{\text{dssim}})\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{dssim}}(1 - \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}) with \lambda{\text{dssim}} = 0.2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def effgsoptimizationstep(gaussians, trainingimages, cameraposes, t, Ttotal, optimizer): """ One optimization step for EffGS. """ # 1. Frequency Mask Generation Mfreqlist = [] for img, pose in zip(trainingimages, cameraposes): gt = img Idown = downsample(grayscale(gt), scale=0.5) ft = 100 t / Ttotal # Sources do not specify the exact piecewise schedule for sigma1 sigma1 = getsigmafromschedule(ft) sigma2 = 2 sigma1 H = convolve(Idown, gaussiankernel(sigma1)) - convolve(Idown, gaussiankernel(sigma2)) Hup = upsample(H, targetsize=gt.shape[:2]) Hnorm = normalize(Hup) if ft < 50: Mfreq = threshold(1 - Hnorm, threshold=0.5) # Threshold value not specified else: Mfreq = threshold(Hnorm, threshold=0.5) Mfreqlist.append(Mfreq) # 2. Rendering & Loss projected = [] for g in gaussians: # Adaptive Primitive Compactness: modulate base scales with gammak effs = g.gamma g.s Sigma3D = g.R @ diag(effs) @ g.R.T W = pose.R J = computeprojectionjacobian(g.p, pose) Sigma2D = J @ W @ Sigma3D @ W.T @ J.T projected.append({'g': g, 'Sigma2D': Sigma2D, 'p2D': g.p2D}) projected.sort(key=lambda x: x['g'].depth) renderedcolor = zeroslike(gt) accumulatedalpha = zeroslike(gt[..., 0]) for pg in projected: g = pg['g'] for u in pixelsinfootprint(pg['Sigma2D']): dist = (u - pg['p2D']).T @ inv(pg['Sigma2D']) @ (u - pg['p2D']) alpha = g.o exp(-0.5 dist) weight = alpha (1 - accumulatedalpha[u]) renderedcolor[u] += g.c weight accumulatedalpha[u] += weight L1 = l1loss(renderedcolor, gt) SSIM = ssimloss(renderedcolor, gt) lambdadssim = 0.2 loss = (1 - lambdadssim) L1 + lambdadssim (1 - SSIM) errormask = abs(renderedcolor - gt) unifiedsupervision = fusemasks(errormask, Mfreq) loss.backward() # 3. Density Control (LDP) importancescores = zeros(len(gaussians)) for pg in projected: g = pg['g'] if hasvalidfootprint(g, trainingimages): importancescores[g.id] += sum(unifiedsupervision[footprintpixels(g)]) # Standard densification/pruning logic based on importance scores gaussians = applydensitycontrol(gaussians, importancescores, threshold=0.01) optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return loss def downsample(img, scale): return img[::int(1/scale),::int(1/scale)] def grayscale(img): return mean(img, axis=-1) def getsigmafromschedule(ft): return 1.0 if ft < 50 else 0.5 # Piecewise schedule per def gaussiankernel(sigma): return exp(-x2/(2sigma2)) / (sigmasqrt(2pi)) def convolve(img, kernel): return correlate(img, kernel) def upsample(img, targetsize): return resize(img, targetsize, interpolation='bilinear') def normalize(H): return (H - min(H)) / (max(H) - min(H)) def threshold(mask, threshold): return mask > threshold def computeprojectionjacobian(p, pose): return pose.projmatrix @ diag([1, 1, 1/p.z]) def pixelsinfootprint(Sigma2D): return boundingboxpixels(Sigma2D) def l1loss(pred, gt): return mean(abs(pred - gt)) def ssimloss(pred, gt): return 1 - structuralsimilarity(pred, gt) def fusemasks(m1, m2): return m1 m2 def hasvalidfootprint(g, views): return any(projectedinview(g, v) for v in views) def footprintpixels(g): return boundingboxpixels(g.Sigma2D) def applydensitycontrol(gaussians, scores, threshold): return [g for g in gaussians if scores[g.id] > threshold] \lambda{\text{dssim}} = 0.2: Weight for the SSIM term in the loss function. f(t) = 100t/T{\text{total}}: Bandwidth schedule parameter controlling the piecewise schedule for \sigma1. Thresholds for M{\text{freq}}: Applied at f(t) = 50. Precision: The difference-of-Gaussians computation requires careful handling of convolution boundaries and normalization to avoid artifacts in M{\text{freq}}. Boundaries: LDP excludes primitives outside the current active set, which may lead to orphaned Gaussians if not handled by the densification strategy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments on bounded and urban-scale datasets show that EffGS combines high reconstruction quality with efficient training and real-time rendering. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves quality–efficiency tradeoff; retains Compact Box rasterization rule; effective in large-scale scenes. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction is required in complex, large-scale scenes with efficient training and rendering. When not: Not given in the sources. EffGS was proposed to address the severe rendering quality degradation suffered by existing general-purpose acceleration methods when extended to more complex, large-scale scenes. It builds on the core principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting [1795-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] and introduces frequency-aware guidance, localized density control, and adaptive primitive scale modulation. EffGS: Efficient and High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39553, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP
head: 3DGS MVP, Adaptive Surface Splatting Using Elliptical Gaussians, Differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting, pure PyTorch 3DGS
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP is a self-contained, pure-PyTorch implementation of the core 3D Gaussian Splatting algorithm, designed as a teaching reference rather than a production renderer. It renders 3D Gaussians onto screen space and rasterizes them using alpha blending to produce smooth, hole-free images from arbitrary viewpoints. It sets itself apart from production implementations by intentionally omitting tile-based CUDA rasterization, spherical harmonics for view-dependent color, and adaptive density control, relying instead on a readable Python loop for the forward pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians defined by their parameters; a pinhole camera model (lookat, OpenCV/COLMAP convention). Outputs: A rendered RGB image of resolution H \times W. Data Structures: Each Gaussian k is parameterized by 11 values: 1. Mean: \mathbf{p}k = (x, y, z) in world space. 2. Scale: \mathbf{s}k = (\sigmax, \sigmay, \sigmaz) stored in log-space. 3. Rotation: \mathbf{q}k = (qw, qx, qy, qz) as a unit quaternion. 4. Color: \mathbf{c}k = (r, g, b) per-Gaussian RGB. 5. Opacity: ok (scalar). The covariance matrix \Sigmak is constructed from scale and rotation to ensure it is symmetric positive semi-definite (PSD): \Sigmak = R S S^T R^T where R is the rotation matrix derived from \mathbf{q}k, and S = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}k). Algorithm Steps: 1. World-to-Camera Transformation: Transform the Gaussian mean \mathbf{p}k from world space to camera space using the viewing transformation W. The viewing transformation W is defined by camera rotation T and translation t: W = \begin{bmatrix} T & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Let \mathbf{p}'k be the transformed mean in camera space. 2. 3D Covariance Transformation: Transform the 3D covariance matrix \Sigmak into the camera frame: \Sigma'k = W{3\times3} \Sigmak W{3\times3}^T where W{3\times3} is the upper-left 3\times3 rotation submatrix of W. 3. 2D Screen-Space Projection: Project \Sigma'k to 2D screen space using the EWA / Zwicker-style projection Jacobian J. The screen-space covariance \Sigmak^{(s)} is approximated as: \Sigmak^{(s)} = J \Sigma'k J^T where J is the Jacobian of the perspective projection. For a point with camera-space coordinates (x, y, z) and focal lengths fx, fy, J is given by: J = \begin{bmatrix} fx/z & 0 & -fx x / z^2 \\ 0 & fy/z & -fy y / z^2 \end{bmatrix} A small isotropic dilation/blur is added to \Sigmak^{(s)} for numerical stability. 4. Splat Boundary Determination: Determine the bounding box for each splat in screen space. A threshold of three times the standard deviation of the Gaussian is used to define the boundaries. 5. Depth Sorting: Sort the set of splats U covering the image by depth (the z coordinate in camera space) in front-to-back order. Note: The implementation uses argsort, which is non-differentiable across order changes; gradients flow through the values given the fixed ordering. 6. Per-Pixel Alpha Compositing: For each pixel \mathbf{x}, identify the set of splats U = \{ \langle G(\mathbf{p}'k + \deltak, \Sigmak^{(s)}), ok, \mathbf{c}k \rangle \mid k=1,\dots,K \} that cover the pixel. Calculate the opacity \alphak of the k-th splat at pixel \mathbf{x} by evaluating the 2D Gaussian density, weighted by the estimated opacity ok: \alphak = ok \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{d}k^T (\Sigmak^{(s)})^{-1} \mathbf{d}k} where \mathbf{d}k is the distance vector between the pixel center and the projected Gaussian center in screen space. Compute the final color C(\mathbf{x}) using front-to-back alpha blending: C(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k where Tk = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance. Args: gaussians: Dict with keys 'mean' (N,3), 'scale' (N,3), 'rot' (N,4), 'color' (N,3), 'opacity' (N,1). All in world space. cameraparams: Dict with 'Rcam' (3,3), 'Tcam' (3,). Defines world-to-camera transformation. imageh, imagew: Output image dimensions. Returns: renderedimage: (H, W, 3) tensor. """ N = gaussians['mean'].shape[0] # 1. World-to-Camera Transformation # pcam = Rcam @ pworld + Tcam meanscam = (cameraparams['Rcam'] @ gaussians['mean'].T).T + cameraparams['Tcam'] # 2. Construct 3D Covariance Matrices # Sigma = R S S^T R^T # R from quaternion Rs = [] for i in range(N): q = gaussians['rot'][i] # qw, qx, qy, qz R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) Rs.append(R) Rs = torch.stack(Rs) # (N, 3, 3) # S from log-scale scales = torch.exp(gaussians['scale']) # (N, 3) S = torch.zeros(N, 3, 3) for i in range(N): S[i] = torch.diag(scales[i]) # Sigma3d = R S S^T R^T Sigma3d = torch.bmm(torch.bmm(Rs, S), torch.bmm(S, Rs.transpose(1, 2))) # 3. Transform Covariance to Camera Frame # Sigmacam = Rcam @ Sigma3d @ Rcam^T Sigmacam = torch.bmm(torch.bmm(cameraparams['Rcam'].unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1, -1), Sigma3d), cameraparams['Rcam'].unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1, -1).transpose(1, 2)) # 4. Project to Screen Space # Jacobian J depends on camera-space coordinates (x, y, z) and focal lengths # Assume focal lengths fx, fy are part of cameraparams or derived from FOV fx = cameraparams.get('fx', 1.0) fy = cameraparams.get('fy', 1.0) xs = meanscam[:, 0] ys = meanscam[:, 1] zs = meanscam[:, 2] # J matrix construction # J = [[fx/z, 0, -fxx/z^2], # [0, fy/z, -fyy/z^2]] J = torch.zeros(N, 2, 3) J[:, 0, 0] = fx / zs J[:, 0, 2] = -fx xs / (zs2) J[:, 1, 1] = fy / zs J[:, 1, 2] = -fy ys / (zs2) # Sigma2d = J @ Sigmacam @ J^T Sigma2d = torch.bmm(torch.bmm(J, Sigmacam), J.transpose(1, 2)) # Add small isotropic blur for stability Sigma2d[:, 0, 0] += 0.3 Sigma2d[:, 1, 1] += 0.3 # 5. Depth Sorting # Sort by z-coordinate (meanscam[:, 2]) depths = meanscam[:, 2] sortindices = torch.argsort(depths, dim=0) # Gather sorted parameters sortedmeans = meanscam[sortindices] sortedSigma2d = Sigma2d[sortindices] sortedcolors = gaussians['color'][sortindices] sortedopacities = gaussians['opacity'][sortindices] # 6. Rasterization # Initialize output image image = torch.zeros(imageh, imagew, 3, device=gaussians['mean'].device) transmittance = torch.ones(imageh, imagew, 1, device=gaussians['mean'].device) # Iterate over Gaussians (front to back) for k in range(N): meank = sortedmeans[k] sigmak = sortedSigma2d[k] colork = sortedcolors[k] opack = sortedopacities[k] # Determine bounding box for this splat # Threshold: 3 stddev. Eigenvalues of Sigma2d give variances. eigvals = torch.linalg.eigvals(sigmak) stdx = torch.sqrt(torch.max(eigvals.real[0], torch.tensor(1e-6))) stdy = torch.sqrt(torch.max(eigvals.real[1], torch.tensor(1e-6))) # Project mean to screen space # Assuming standard pinhole projection: xscreen = fx Xcam / Zcam # This part requires mapping camera coords to pixel coords. # For MVP, we assume a simple projection or that the Jacobian logic # implicitly handles the coordinate mapping for the density evaluation. # To be precise, we need the pixel coordinates of the center. # Let's assume cameraparams includes projection matrix or we compute pixel coords. # px = fx X / Z + cx # py = fy Y / Z + cy cx = cameraparams.get('cx', imagew / 2) cy = cameraparams.get('cy', imageh / 2) px = fx meank[0] / meank[2] + cx py = fy meank[1] / meank[2] + cy # Define bounding box in pixels minx = int(max(0, px - 3 stdx)) maxx = int(min(imagew, px + 3 stdx)) miny = int(max(0, py - 3 stdy)) maxy = int(min(imageh, py + 3 stdy)) if minx >= maxx or miny >= maxy: continue # Create grid for bounding box ycoords, xcoords = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(miny, maxy), torch.arange(minx, maxx), indexing='ij') ycoords = ycoords.to(gaussians['mean'].device) xcoords = xcoords.to(gaussians['mean'].device) # Distance vector dk from pixel to center in screen space # Note: Sigma2d is in pixel units if J was constructed with pixel units? # The formula for J uses fx, fy. If fx is in pixels, Sigma2d is in pixels^2. # dk should be in the same units as Sigma2d. dx = xcoords - px dy = ycoords - py # Stack dk dk = torch.stack([dx, dy], dim=-1) # (H', W', 2) # Compute exponent: -0.5 d^T Sigma^{-1} d # Sigmainv = inverse of Sigma2d Sigmainv = torch.linalg.inv(sigmak) # (2, 2) # d^T Sigmainv d # For each pixel: sumi sumj di Sigmainvij dj # Using einsum for efficiency exponent = -0.5 torch.einsum('...i,ij,...j->...', dk, Sigmainv, dk) # Alpha alpha = opack torch.exp(exponent) # Update image and transmittance # Tk = product(1 - alphaj) for j < k # Current transmittance is Tk # New color contribution: Tk alpha color # New transmittance: Tk (1 - alpha) alphaclamped = torch.clamp(alpha, 0, 1) # Update image contribution = transmittance[:,:, 0] alphaclamped colork image[miny:maxy, minx:maxx] += contribution # Update transmittance transmittance[miny:maxy, minx:maxx, 0] = (1 - alphaclamped) return image def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Converts a quaternion (w, x, y, z) to a 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q.unbind(dim=-1) N = w2 + x2 + y2 + z2 w, x, y, z = w/torch.sqrt(N), x/torch.sqrt(N), y/torch.sqrt(N), z/torch.sqrt(N) return torch.stack([ 1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy), 2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx), 2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2) ], dim=-1).reshape(3, 3) Parameters: Camera Model: Pinhole camera with lookat function using OpenCV/COLMAP convention. Splat Threshold: 3 times the standard deviation of the Gaussian. Stability Blur: Small isotropic dilation added to screen-space covariance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiable Sort: The depth sort uses argsort, which is non-differentiable across order changes. Gradients flow through the values given the ordering, which is accepted for the fit-from-scratch demo. Performance: The implementation uses a Python loop over Gaussians rather than vectorizing over all (H, W, N) at once for readability. End-to-end run takes ~30 seconds on CPU for a 64x64 image. Omissions: The MVP intentionally skips tile-based CUDA rasterizer, spherical-harmonics view-dependent color, adaptive density control, real captures, and SSIM losses. Relightable 3DGS extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle complex appearances such as reflections, transparency, and glossy materials, which standard rasterization approximates poorly. It embeds physically-based material properties into each Gaussian for deferred shading, decomposing outgoing radiance into a BRDF integration that respects material parameters. This approach enables relighting the entire scene under novel illumination conditions while preserving real-time performance during view synthesis. HiFi4G is a 3D Gaussian Splatting variant designed for high-fidelity reconstruction of dynamic humans from monocular video. It combines standard 3D Gaussian Splatting with a dual-graph mechanism to enable non-rigid tracking, ensuring spatial-temporal consistency while maintaining a compact representation. It distinguishes itself from static 3DGS by explicitly modeling temporal deformation and from other dynamic methods by its specific dual-graph topology for tracking. PRoGS is a post-training technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that approximates each Gaussian's contribution to the final scene to construct a prioritization order, enabling progressive rendering or streaming by dynamically selecting splats to display or transmit. Unlike existing web-viewers that require full scene retrieval before rendering, PRoGS loads a representative subset early, significantly reducing time-to-first-paint while maintaining perceptual quality. It is designed for on-device rendering applications constrained by memory and streaming applications requiring minimal bandwidth. This article describes the OpenGL-based rendering pipeline for visualizing 3D Gaussian Splatting data within the ROS RViz environment. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of 2D-projected Gaussian splats as a single instanced draw call while handling depth sorting and view-dependent shading. It differs from pure software implementations by leveraging GPU-based sorting and texture buffer objects (TBOs) for data storage, and from other RViz plugins by supporting both exact back-to-front sorting and Order-Independent Transparency (WBOIT) approximations. This method provides a lightweight, CPU-only pipeline for generating rapid visual thumbnails from 3D Gaussian Splatting datasets, prioritizing responsiveness and portability over high-fidelity rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard GPU-accelerated splatting by omitting rotation parameters, approximating Gaussians as spheres, and leveraging Python's Numba JIT compiler to achieve near-real-time performance on constrained hardware. OmniGS is a method for fast radiance field reconstruction and real-time omnidirectional novel view synthesis using calibrated monocular 360-degree images and sparse SfM point clouds. It replaces the standard perspective camera model with an omnidirectional equirectangular projection model, allowing 3D Gaussians to be splatted directly onto the equirectangular screen space. Unlike sibling methods such as 360-GS, which rely on tangent-plane approximations and two-stage projection, OmniGS uses direct screen-space splatting without requiring scene assumptions or deep networks. TR-Gaussians is a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based representation designed for the high-fidelity, real-time rendering of planar transmission and reflection effects, such as those found in indoor glass panes. Unlike vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting, which overfits training images by mixing transmission and reflection into low-opacity artifacts, TR-Gaussians explicitly decomposes the scene into real geometry (transmission) and virtual geometry (reflection) using a learnable reflection plane. This separation prevents the entanglement of real scene geometry with virtual reflections, ensuring that reflections remain coherent and artifact-free in novel views where the real scene is occluded or unobserved. DOF-GS is a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that incorporates a finite-aperture camera model to explicitly model and render depth-of-field (DOF) effects, enabling post-capture control of aperture and focal distance. Unlike previous NeRF-based techniques that simulate defocus via expensive per-ray blur kernels or recent 3DGS methods that use black-box neural networks for shape offsets, DOF-GS blurs individual Gaussians based on learnable Circle-of-Confusion (CoC) cues before compositing, allowing efficient, differentiable, and intuitive DOF adjustment. Temporal Gaussian Splatting (TemporalGS) is a training-free, plug-and-play acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that leverages temporal priors from previous frames to reduce computational redundancy in Gaussian preprocessing, sorting, and rasterization. It solves the challenge of high FPS and low latency rendering by culling unnecessary Gaussians and approximating static regions via warped buffers, achieving up to 1.48× acceleration over vanilla 3DGS while maintaining competitive quality. Unlike sibling methods that may require post-training compression or hardware-specific optimizations, TemporalGS operates as a software rasterization plugin that interleaves dynamic culling and selective rendering intervals. This family of methods adapts the volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to better handle geometric constraints, sparse inputs, or surface-oriented rendering tasks. While standard 3DGS relies on dense multi-view photometric consistency to implicitly define geometry, these variants introduce explicit geometric supervision, surface parameterizations, or thickness regularization to resolve ambiguities inherent in sparse or deformable scenarios. They differ from standard 3DGS by decoupling or constraining the spatial distribution of Gaussians to align with known geometric priors (meshes, depth maps, or height fields) rather than relying solely on appearance optimization. A method that utilizes vector clustering to encode color and geometric attributes into two codebooks, using a sensitivity-aware KMeans method. For disk data storage, SASCGS utilizes the entropy encoding method DEFLATE, which combines the LZ77 algorithm and Huffman coding, to compress the data. On the MipNeRF360 dataset, SASCGS achieves SSIM 0.801, PSNR 26.98, LPIPS 0.238, and a size of 28.80 MB. Enforces that alpha blending exactly satisfies the front-to-back absorption-emission model by deriving discrete compositing as an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of the continuous integral. Introduces a continuous density field along the ray to resolve artifacts in scenes with semi-transparent objects. Volumetric alpha computation: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\int Gi(x) dx), accumulating density along the ray in accordance with volume rendering equation. A modified alpha-blending function designed to perform image rendering over re-sketched Gaussian lines and Gaussian triangles. Render the re-sketched primitives using the modified alpha-blending function in a similar manner as original Gaussian ellipses. A method to compute accurate depth \hat{D} for a pixel by treating it as a linear interpolation of distances from 3D Gaussians to the image plane, avoiding the floating problem and disc aliasing associated with peak selection in forward mapping splatting. For each pixel, render the view using 3D Gaussians to obtain Ti, \alphai, di, and ni for all contributing Gaussians i. Formula: \hat{D} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \hat{w}i di, where \hat{w}i = \frac{Ti \alphai}{\sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai}, di is the distance from the i-th Gaussian to the image plane, Ti is accumulated transmittance, and \alphai is opacity. Time Complexity: The MVP implementation uses a Python loop over Gaussians, making it significantly slower than the tile-based CUDA rasterizer used in production 3DGS. End-to-end run takes ~30 seconds on CPU for a 64x64 image. Memory Complexity: Stores N Gaussians with 11 parameters each. No additional large buffers for tile-based sorting or hierarchical binning are used. Strengths: High readability and ease of implementation; suitable for educational purposes and prototyping; pure PyTorch allows for easy integration with standard deep learning workflows without custom CUDA kernels. Limitations: Lacks performance optimizations (tile-based rasterization, vectorization); does not support view-dependent color (spherical harmonics); lacks adaptive density control (splitting/merging Gaussians); not suitable for real-time rendering or large-scale scenes. When to use: Teaching, understanding the mathematical foundations of 3DGS, or small-scale experiments where performance is not critical. When not to use: Production rendering, real-time applications, or large-scale scene reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP is based on the core algorithm of 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., SIGGRAPH 2023). It was introduced as a self-contained Jupyter notebook implementation in pure PyTorch, intended as a teaching reference to "grind on the math" without the complexity of custom CUDA kernels. The implementation demonstrates the forward rasterization pipeline, including covariance construction, projection, sorting, and alpha compositing, using a simple pinhole camera model.
