name: Relightable 3DGS
head: Handling Challenging Objects (Reflections/Transparency), Relightable 3D GS, Specular 3D GS
body: Relightable 3DGS extends standard 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle complex appearances such as reflections, transparency, and glossy materials, which standard rasterization approximates poorly. It embeds physically-based material properties into each Gaussian for deferred shading, decomposing outgoing radiance into a BRDF integration that respects material parameters. This approach enables relighting the entire scene under novel illumination conditions while preserving real-time performance during view synthesis. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, where each Gaussian i is defined by position \mathbf{p}i, covariance matrix \Sigmai (or rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color coefficients (typically spherical harmonics). Material properties per Gaussian: diffuse albedo fd, specular BRDF parameters (roughness r), normal \mathbf{n}i, and potentially metallic/roughness maps. Lighting environment: Defined by incident radiance Li(\omegai) for various directions \omegai. Outputs: Pixel color C(x,y) for the rendered image. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian stores standard 3DGS attributes plus: \mathbf{n}i: Surface normal vector (unit length). ri: Roughness parameter (scalar, typically [0, 1]). f{d,i}: Diffuse albedo color (RGB). f{s,i}: Specular BRDF parameters (encoded in ri and potentially Fresnel base reflectivity). Lighting Data: A set of light sources or an environment map providing Li(\omegai). Steps: 1. Rasterization: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space. Compute 2D covariance \Sigma' and mean \mathbf{m} for each Gaussian. Sort Gaussians by depth for alpha blending. 2. Per-Pixel Shading: For each pixel (x,y), iterate through sorted Gaussians i that contribute to the pixel. 3. BRDF Evaluation: For each contributing Gaussian i, compute the specular BRDF fs(\omega0, \omegai) using the Cook-Torrance model: fs(\omega0, \omegai) = \frac{D(h; ri) \cdot F(\omega0, h) \cdot G(\omegai, \omega0, h; ri)}{(\mathbf{n}i \cdot \omegai) \cdot (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \omega0)} where: \omega0 is the view direction from the camera to the Gaussian. \omegai is the incident lighting direction from the light source to the Gaussian. \mathbf{h} = \frac{\omegai + \omega0}{\|\omegai + \omega0\|} is the half vector. D(h; ri) is the Normal Distribution Function (NDF), e.g., GGX, parameterized by roughness ri. F(\omega0, h) is the Fresnel term, typically using Schlick's approximation. G(\omegai, \omega0, h; ri) is the Geometry term (shadowing/masking), e.g., Smith's method. \mathbf{n}i is the normal of the Gaussian. 4. Direct Illumination: Compute the contribution of direct lights. For point sources, trace secondary rays from the Gaussian to the light to evaluate shadow maps. Calculate the incident radiance Li(\omegai) at the Gaussian's position. 5. PBR Color Calculation: Compute the outgoing radiance c'(\omega0) for the Gaussian by integrating the BRDF over the incident lighting directions: c'(\omega0) = \sum{j=0}^{Ns} (f{d,i} + fs(\omega0, \omega{i,j})) L{i,j}(\omega{i,j}) (\omega{i,j} \cdot \mathbf{n}i) \Delta \omega{i,j} where: Ns is the number of sampled light directions. L{i,j}(\omega{i,j}) is the incident radiance from direction j. \Delta \omega{i,j} is the solid angle associated with the sampled incident direction j. Note: The diffuse term f{d,i} is typically a constant albedo, while fs is view-dependent. 6. Alpha Blending: Blend the computed color c'(\omega0) with the accumulated background color using the Gaussian's opacity \alphai and the standard alpha blending equation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrelightable3dgs(gaussians, camera, lights): # 1. Project Gaussians to 2D projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Compute 2D mean and covariance from 3D parameters m2d, sigma2d = projectgaussian2d(g, camera) projectedgaussians.append({ 'mean': m2d, 'cov': sigma2d, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'normal': g.normal, 'roughness': g.roughness, 'albedo': g.albedo, 'depth': g.depth }) # 2. Sort by depth projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['depth']) # 3. Rasterize and Shade image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for g in projectedgaussians: # Check if pixel is within Gaussian support if not isinsidesupport(g['mean'], g['cov'], x, y): continue # Compute 2D Gaussian weight weight = computegaussianweight(g['mean'], g['cov'], x, y) # View direction viewdir = computeviewdirection(camera, g['mean']) # Compute PBR color pbrcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) for light in lights: lightdir = computelightdirection(light, g['mean']) halfvec = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) # BRDF components D = computendf(halfvec, g['roughness']) F = computefresnel(viewdir, halfvec) G = computegeometry(lightdir, viewdir, halfvec, g['roughness']) # Specular BRDF denom = max(dot(g['normal'], lightdir) dot(g['normal'], viewdir), 1e-6) fs = (D F G) / denom # Direct illumination with shadowing shadow = evaluateshadow(g['mean'], light) Li = light.intensity shadow # PBR contribution pbrcolor += (g['albedo'] / pi + fs) Li max(dot(g['normal'], lightdir), 0) # Alpha blending a = g['alpha'] weight accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor (1 - a) + pbrcolor a accumulatedalpha += a (1 - accumulatedalpha) if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break image[y, x] = accumulatedcolor return image Parameters: Ns: Number of light samples. Not given in the sources. Roughness r: Range [0, 1]. Typical values depend on material. Edge Cases: Shadow Ray Tracing: Tracing secondary rays from each Gaussian to the light can be computationally expensive. Optimization strategies like shadow maps are used. Degenerate Normals: If the normal \mathbf{n}i is not well-defined (e.g., at boundaries), the BRDF evaluation may produce artifacts. Precision: The denominator in the BRDF formula can approach zero if the view or light direction is tangent to the surface, requiring clamping. Deferred Shading with Alpha-Blended Feature Maps is a rendering approach where material properties (albedo, metallic, roughness, normal) are aggregated into pixel-level feature maps via alpha-blending of 2D Gaussians, and the rendering equation is applied in a deferred shading pass. This method treats alpha-blending as a smoothing filter to stabilize optimization and produce cohesive results, unlike shading directly on Gaussians before blending. It differs from per-Gaussian shading by performing complex shading calculations on a per-pixel basis rather than a per-Gaussian basis, which significantly enhances rendering quality and performance for complex materials. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the rasterization of Gaussians and the per-pixel BRDF evaluation. The addition of secondary ray tracing for shadows increases complexity compared to standard 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional material properties (normal, roughness, albedo) per Gaussian. Strengths: Handles complex appearances like reflections, transparency, and glossy materials better than standard 3DGS. Enables relighting under novel illumination. Limitations: More complex to implement and train than standard 3DGS. Performance may be lower due to BRDF calculations and shadow ray tracing. Robust reconstruction of reflective and transparent objects in general scenes remains challenging. When to use: When realistic rendering of complex materials and dynamic lighting is required. When not to use: When real-time performance on simple scenes is the primary concern, or when hardware does not support the required shading operations efficiently. Relightable 3DGS was introduced to address the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in handling complex appearances. Standard 3DGS uses a view-dependent spherical harmonics color model, which fails to represent specular reflections, glossy materials, and global illumination. Relightable 3DGS represents a major paradigm shift by embedding physically-based material properties into each Gaussian for deferred shading. It decomposes the outgoing radiance into a BRDF integration that respects material parameters. This approach allows for relighting the entire scene under novel illumination conditions while preserving real-time performance during view synthesis. Related works include GaussianShader, which simplifies the BRDF to a neural shader, and GS-IR, which performs inverse rendering. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3807511, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Deferred Shading with Alpha-Blended Feature Maps
head: Deferred Shading (Gaussian Splatting), Deferred Shading with Aggregated Feature Maps, G-buffer shading, deferred pipeline
body: Deferred Shading with Alpha-Blended Feature Maps is a rendering approach where material properties (albedo, metallic, roughness, normal) are aggregated into pixel-level feature maps via alpha-blending of 2D Gaussians, and the rendering equation is applied in a deferred shading pass. This method treats alpha-blending as a smoothing filter to stabilize optimization and produce cohesive results, unlike shading directly on Gaussians before blending. It differs from per-Gaussian shading by performing complex shading calculations on a per-pixel basis rather than a per-Gaussian basis, which significantly enhances rendering quality and performance for complex materials. The method operates in two distinct passes: a Geometry Pass to populate G-buffers and a Shading Pass to compute final radiance. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance, opacity \alphai, and material attributes: albedo \lambdai \in [0, 1]^3, metallic mi \in [0, 1], roughness ri \in [0, 1], and tangential vectors t{u,i}, t{v,i}. Outputs: Final screen-space RGB image I{RGB}. Data Structures 1. G-Buffer (Feature Maps): A set of 2D screen-space buffers storing aggregated attributes. \mathbf{X} = [\Lambda, M, R, N]^T \Lambda: Albedo map (3 channels, float) M: Metallic map (1 channel, float) R: Roughness map (1 channel, float) N: Normal map (3 channels, float, normalized) 2. Lookup Textures: 2D texture map for the first term of the split-sum approximation (dependent on \omegai \cdot N and roughness R). Series of cubemaps for the second term of the split-sum approximation (incident radiance). Step 1: Compute Per-Gaussian Normals For each Gaussian i, derive the normal vector \mathbf{n}i from its tangential vectors t{u,i} and t{v,i} using the cross product: \mathbf{n}i = t{u,i} \times t{v,i} Normalize \mathbf{n}i to unit length. Step 2: Geometry Pass (Rasterization) Rasterize the scene attributes of the nearest surface into the G-buffers. For each pixel p in the screen space, compute the aggregated feature map \mathbf{X}p by alpha-blending the per-Gaussian features \mathbf{x}i projected onto that pixel. The aggregation follows the standard alpha-blending order (front-to-back): \mathbf{X}p = \sum{i=1}^{Np} \mathbf{x}{i,p} \alpha{i,p} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{j,p}) Where: Np is the number of Gaussians covering pixel p. \mathbf{x}{i,p} = [\lambda{i,p}, m{i,p}, r{i,p}, \mathbf{n}{i,p}]^T are the per-Gaussian values interpolated or sampled at the pixel location. \alpha{i,p} is the projected opacity of Gaussian i at pixel p. The product term \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{j,p}) represents the accumulated transparency from previous (front) Gaussians. The resulting \mathbf{X}p contains the aggregated albedo \Lambdap, metallic Mp, roughness Rp, and normal Np for the pixel. Step 3: Shading Pass (Per-Pixel Lighting) Execute a per-pixel shading program that reads the G-buffers to compute the final color. The outgoing radiance L(\omegao) is calculated using the rendering equation: L(\omegao) = \int{\Omega} Li(\omegai) f(\omegai, \omegao) (\omegai \cdot \mathbf{N}p) \, d\omegai Where: Li(\omegai) is the incident radiance from direction \omegai. f(\omegai, \omegao) is the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF). \mathbf{N}p is the aggregated normal from the G-buffer. \Omega is the hemisphere of incident directions. Step 4: Split-Sum Approximation for Specular Term To compute the specular component efficiently, the split-sum approximation is adopted: Ls(\omegao) \approx \left( \int{\Omega} fs(\omegai, \omegao) (\omegai \cdot \mathbf{N}p) d\omegai \right) \cdot \left( \int{\Omega} Li(\omegai) D(\omegai, \omegao) (\omegai \cdot \mathbf{N}p) d\omegai \right) Where fs is the specular BRDF term defined by the GGX model: fs(\omegai, \omegao) = \frac{D G F}{4(\omegao \cdot \mathbf{N}p)(\omegai \cdot \mathbf{N}p)} D: GGX normal distribution function. F: Fresnel term. G: Shadowing-masking term. Step 5: Precomputation and Lookup 1. First Term (BRDF Integral): The first term depends solely on (\omegai \cdot N) and roughness Rp. It is precomputed and stored in a 2D lookup texture map. During rendering, this term is queried using the roughness Rp and the dot product. 2. Second Term (Environment Map): The second term represents the integral of incident radiance over the specular lobe. It is pre-integrated at the beginning of each training iteration for different roughness levels. This is represented by a series of cubemaps. During rendering, trilinear interpolation is performed using the reflected direction and the roughness Rp as parameters to sample the appropriate cubemap. Step 6: Diffuse Term The diffuse term is computed by querying a pre-integrated environment map using the normal Np and multiplying by the material terms (albedo \Lambdap, metallic Mp, roughness Rp). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computenormal(tu, tv): """Compute normal from tangential vectors.""" return np.cross(tu, tv) def alphablendfeatures(gaussianscoveringpixel): """ Aggregate per-Gaussian features into a single pixel feature vector X. gaussianscoveringpixel: List of dicts with keys: 'lambda': albedo (3,), 'm': metallic (1,), 'r': roughness (1,), 'n': normal (3,), 'alpha': opacity (1,) Returns: X = [Lambda, M, R, N] """ X = np.zeros(8) # [3 albedo, 1 metal, 1 rough, 3 normal] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 # Sort gaussians by depth (front-to-back) if not already sorted # Implementation detail: Depth sorting is required for correct alpha blending for g in gaussianscoveringpixel: alpha = g['alpha'] # Contribution: xi alphai product(1 - alphaj) for j < i # product(1 - alphaj) is equivalent to (1 - accumulatedalpha) weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) X[0:3] += g['lambda'] weight X[3] += g['m'] weight X[4] += g['r'] weight X[5:8] += g['n'] weight accumulatedalpha += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) # Note: standard alpha blending accumulates alpha differently, # but the formula in uses the product term explicitly. # Standard alpha blend: Cout = Cin + (Cnew - Cin) alphanew (1 - alphaaccum) # The formula in is a direct weighted sum. # To strictly follow: X = sum(xi alphai prod{j<i}(1-alphaj)) # We must track the product term explicitly. # Correction to strictly follow formula structure: # Re-implementing with explicit product tracking X = np.zeros(8) prodterm = 1.0 for g in gaussianscoveringpixel: alpha = g['alpha'] contribution = g['featurevector'] alpha prodterm X += contribution prodterm = (1.0 - alpha) # Normalize normal vector X[5:8] /= np.linalg.norm(X[5:8]) return X def splitsumspecular(N, R, roughnesslevels, envcubemaps): """ Compute specular radiance using split-sum approximation. N: Normal vector R: Roughness value roughnesslevels: Array of roughness values for precomputed textures envcubemaps: List of cubemaps for different roughness levels """ # First term: BRDF integral (precomputed 2D lookup) # Implementation detail: Query 2D texture with (N dot V, R) brdfterm = querybrdflookup(N, R) # Second term: Environment integral (precomputed cubemaps) # Implementation detail: Reflect view vector V around N to get Rdir # Sample cubemap at Rdir with interpolation based on R reflecteddir = reflect(-viewdir, N) envterm = samplecubemapseries(envcubemaps, reflecteddir, R) return brdfterm envterm def renderdeferred(gaussians, camera, envlight, brdflookup, cubemaps): """ Main rendering loop. """ # Initialize G-buffers width, height = camera.resolution gbuffer = np.zeros((height, width, 8)) # [Lambda(3), M(1), R(1), N(3)] # Pass 1: Geometry Pass for pixel in screenpixels: coveringgaussians = getgaussianscoveringpixel(pixel, gaussians, camera) if coveringgaussians: # Compute normals for each gaussian if not precomputed for g in coveringgaussians: if 'n' not in g: g['n'] = computenormal(g['tu'], g['tv']) g['featurevector'] = np.concatenate([g['lambda'], [g['m']], [g['r']], g['n']]) # Aggregate features X = alphablendfeatures(coveringgaussians) gbuffer[pixel.y, pixel.x] = X # Pass 2: Shading Pass finalimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for pixel in screenpixels: X = gbuffer[pixel.y, pixel.x] Lambda = X[0:3] M = X[3] R = X[4] N = X[5:8] # Compute Diffuse # Implementation detail: Query pre-integrated env map for diffuse diffuse = querydiffuseenvmap(N, Lambda, M, R) # Compute Specular specular = splitsumspecular(N, R, roughnesslevels, cubemaps) finalimage[pixel.y, pixel.x] = diffuse + specular return finalimage A post-training optimization step that switches from forward shading to deferred shading to refine appearance by optimizing 3DGS attributes (displacement, scales, rotations, opacities). It renders per-Gaussian attributes into screen-space maps (I\mu, In, Ia, I\rho, Im) and computes the final RGB image in screen space via PBR. Optimization is performed with a learning rate of 0.001 for 100 steps (~1 minute), unlocking geometry constraints to allow modification of positions, scales, rotations, normals, and opacities. On the TensoIR Synthetic Dataset, average L1 differences after optimization are: positions 0.0014, scales 0.0003, rotations 0.0148, opacities 0.0131, normals 0.0146. A method that observes that geometry attributes of 3D Gaussians like opacity overfit to the input lighting condition and exhibit blending artifacts when they are relit. It distills geometry attributes of a signed distance function to 3D Gaussians and introduces the deferred shading technique into the rendering of 3D Gaussians to avoid blending artifacts caused by multiple shading calculations. Time Complexity: The geometry pass is O(N \cdot A) where N is the number of Gaussians and A is the average number of Gaussians per pixel (rasterization cost). The shading pass is O(W \cdot H) where W, H are screen dimensions, as shading is per-pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for G-buffers (albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, depth) proportional to screen resolution W \times H. Additional memory for precomputed lookup textures and cubemaps. Performance: Significantly enhances rendering quality and performance for complex materials compared to per-Gaussian shading. The split-sum approximation allows real-time rendering by avoiding expensive Monte Carlo sampling. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization of features by treating alpha-blending as a smoothing filter. Efficiently renders high-frequency, view-dependent effects. Avoids blending artifacts caused by multiple shading calculations. Limitations: Requires precomputation of lookup textures and cubemaps, which may increase training time or memory usage. The transition from forward to deferred shading may introduce artifacts if not optimized. Deferred shading is a two-pass rendering technique that decouples geometry processing from lighting and material computations. It has been successfully adapted to Gaussian Splatting to efficiently render high-frequency, view-dependent effects. The specific application to 3D Gaussian Splatting with alpha-blended feature maps was introduced in "Reflective Gaussian Splatting". Variants like GeoSplatting and DeferredGS have further refined this approach for inverse rendering and artifact reduction. name: HiFi4G
body: HiFi4G is a 3D Gaussian Splatting method that combines 3DGS with a dual-graph mechanism for non-rigid tracking to achieve high-fidelity rendering. It successfully preserves spatial-temporal consistency in a more compact manner than standard 3DGS. Inputs: Monocular video sequence (typically 50–100 frames). Outputs: High-fidelity rendered frames with preserved spatial-temporal consistency. Data Structures: Tri-plane Representation: Factorizes the canonical space to reconstruct the person and scene. Dual-Graph Mechanism: Provides non-rigid tracking for the Gaussians across frames. Steps: 1. Factorize the canonical space using a tri-plane representation. 2. Combine 3D Gaussian Splatting with the dual-graph mechanism for non-rigid tracking. 3. Reconstruct the person and scene from the monocular video input. 4. Render frames while preserving spatial-temporal consistency in a compact manner. Parameters: Video length: 50–100 frames. Reconstruction time: ~30 minutes. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Speed: Reconstruction takes approximately 30 minutes for 50–100 frames. Compactness: Preserves spatial-temporal consistency in a more compact manner than standard 3DGS. Consistency: Successfully preserves spatial-temporal consistency. Hardware: Not given in the sources. HiFi4G was introduced in reference [208]. It addresses the reconstruction of dynamic humans from monocular video by leveraging 3D Gaussian Splatting and a dual-graph tracking mechanism. It is discussed alongside other 3DGS advancements such as GPS-Gaussian and GART. name: PRoGS
head: PRoGS (Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats), contribution-based prioritization method, importance-based sampling method
body: PRoGS is a post-training technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that approximates each Gaussian's contribution to the final scene to construct a prioritization order, enabling progressive rendering or streaming by dynamically selecting splats to display or transmit. Unlike existing web-viewers that require full scene retrieval before rendering, PRoGS loads a representative subset early, significantly reducing time-to-first-paint while maintaining perceptual quality. It is designed for on-device rendering applications constrained by memory and streaming applications requiring minimal bandwidth. Inputs: A trained set of 3D Gaussians (positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a set of training views (camera poses and intrinsics). Outputs: A static global ordering of splats based on contribution, and a dynamic rendering pipeline that selects splats based on this order and viewport context. Data Structures: 1. Training Views: A list of camera parameters and image dimensions. 2. Contribution Map: A global aggregation structure storing the count of times each Gaussian index appears in the top-k contributors for any pixel in any training view. 3. Splat Order: A sorted list of Gaussian indices, sorted descending by their total contribution count. Parameters: k: Number of contributing splats to return per pixel per training image during the contribution calculation phase. Typical value: 20. p: Progression percentage, the fraction of the total splats used for initial rendering or streaming chunks. Typical values tested: 0.2%, 0.5%, 1.0%, 10.0%. Steps: 1. Render Training Views: For each training view, render the scene using all 3D Gaussians to compute per-pixel contributions. 2. Aggregate Contributions: Initialize a global counter array C of size N (total number of Gaussians) to zero. For every occurrence of a Gaussian i in the top-k lists from Step 1, increment C[i]. 3. Create Ordering: Sort all Gaussian indices i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\} based on the values in C in descending order. 4. Dynamic Selection: To render or stream a scene, select the first M = \lfloor p \times N \rfloor splats from the sorted order. 5. Viewport Integration: Integrate the static ordering with real-time viewport context to prioritize relevant content during rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecontributionorder(gaussians, trainingviews, k=20): """ Computes a global ordering of splats based on their contribution to training views. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with properties (position, covariance, opacity, etc.) trainingviews: List of camera parameters and image dimensions k: Number of top contributing splats per pixel to track Returns: orderedindices: List of Gaussian indices sorted by contribution (descending) """ ngaussians = len(gaussians) contributioncounts = [0] ngaussians # Step 1 & 2: Render and Aggregate for view in trainingviews: # Standard 3DGS rasterization: project Gaussians to 2D, sort by depth, # accumulate per-pixel color/alpha, and collect top-k contributing indices pixeltopkindices = rasterizeandcollecttopk(gaussians, view, k) for rowindices in pixeltopkindices: for idx in rowindices: contributioncounts[idx] += 1 # Step 3: Create Ordering # Sort indices by contribution count descending orderedindices = sorted(range(ngaussians), key=lambda i: contributioncounts[i], reverse=True) return orderedindices def rasterizeandcollecttopk(gaussians, view, k): """ Performs standard 3DGS rasterization and returns top-k contributing Gaussian indices per pixel. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects view: Camera parameters and image dimensions k: Number of top contributors per pixel Returns: pixeltopkindices: 2D list of lists, shape (height, width), containing top-k indices per pixel """ pixeltopkindices = [] for y in range(view.height): row = [] for x in range(view.width): topk = collecttopkgaussiansforpixel(gaussians, view, x, y, k) row.append(topk) pixeltopkindices.append(row) return pixeltopkindices def collecttopkgaussiansforpixel(gaussians, view, x, y, k): """ Standard 3DGS splatting contribution calculation for a single pixel. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects view: Camera parameters x, y: Pixel coordinates k: Number of top contributors to return Returns: List of Gaussian indices sorted by contribution weight descending """ covering = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Standard 3DGS projection check if standard3dgsprojectioncoverspixel(g, view, x, y): # Standard 3DGS splatting contribution weight calculation weight = standard3dgscontributionweight(g, view, x, y) covering.append((weight, i)) covering.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0], reverse=True) return [idx for, idx in covering[:k]] def standard3dgsprojectioncoverspixel(g, view, x, y): """Standard 2D Gaussian projection check.""" return True def standard3dgscontributionweight(g, view, x, y): """Standard 3DGS splatting contribution weight calculation.""" return 1.0 def progressiverender(gaussians, orderedindices, view, progressionpercentage=0.01): """ Renders a view using a subset of splats determined by the precomputed order. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects orderedindices: Precomputed global ordering of Gaussian indices view: Current camera parameters progressionpercentage: Fraction of total splats to use (e.g., 0.01 for 1%) Returns: image: Rendered image """ ngaussians = len(gaussians) numsplatstorender = int(progressionpercentage ngaussians) # Select top splats from the global order selectedindices = orderedindices[:numsplatstorender] selectedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in selectedindices] # Render using only the selected splats via standard 3DGS rasterization image = standard3dgsrasterize(selectedgaussians, view) return image def standard3dgsrasterize(gaussians, view): """Standard 3DGS rasterization returning final image.""" return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If training views do not cover the entire scene, Gaussians outside the training view frustums may have zero contribution and be placed at the end of the order. Ensure training views are representative of the final intended viewing angles. Precision: Contribution counts are integers. For very large scenes, use 64-bit integers to avoid overflow. Boundaries: The method assumes a fixed set of training views. Changing the training set requires recomputing the order. Time Complexity: The pre-processing step (contribution calculation) requires rendering all training views with all Gaussians. The rendering step itself is proportional to the number of splats rendered. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the contribution counts (O(N)) and the ordered indices (O(N)). The rendering memory is proportional to the number of splats currently being rendered. Measured Performance: At 0.2% of splats, PRoGS loads a basic level of the scene (e.g., a truck) while alternative approaches show it as completely missing. It significantly reduces time-to-first-paint compared to loading the full scene. Strengths: Reduces initial load time and bandwidth usage. Works with existing compression methods. Applicable to both complete scenes and individual objects. Limitations: Requires a post-training pass over all training views. The initial quality is an approximation; fine details may be missing until more splats are loaded. When to use: On-device rendering with memory constraints, streaming applications with bandwidth limits, web-based viewers requiring fast initial paint. When not to use: When full fidelity is required immediately without progressive refinement. PRoGS was introduced by Zoomers et al. in September 2024 as the first academic work to bring progressive rendering of 3DGS to an academic context. It addresses the substantial storage requirements of 3DGS, where each splat's individual data must be stored, and the limitation of compression techniques that still necessitate retrieving the entire scene before any part can be rendered. The method establishes a foundation for making remotely hosted 3DGS content more quickly accessible to end-users in over-the-top consumption scenarios. PRoGS: Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00308, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline (RViz Plugin)
head: SplatCloud rendering
body: This article describes the OpenGL-based rendering pipeline for visualizing 3D Gaussian Splatting data within the ROS RViz environment. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering millions of 2D-projected Gaussian splats as a single instanced draw call while handling depth sorting and view-dependent shading. It differs from pure software implementations by leveraging GPU-based sorting and texture buffer objects (TBOs) for data storage, and from other RViz plugins by supporting both exact back-to-front sorting and Order-Independent Transparency (WBOIT) approximations. The pipeline renders a cloud of 3D Gaussians by projecting them into 2D screen space, sorting them by depth, and accumulating their colors with transparency. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians defined by position, orientation (quaternion), scale, opacity, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Output: A 2D image frame rendered by the RViz viewport. The plugin uses specific GPU memory layouts to minimize bandwidth and decouple sorting from rendering. 1. Base Splat Data (TBO): Stored in a Texture Buffer Object (TBO) bound to texture unit 0 immediately before the draw call via the notifyRenderSingleObject callback. Layout: 2 uvec4 texels per splat. Size: 32 bytes per splat. Content: Packed SplatGPU data including position, covariance/rotation, scale, and opacity. 2. Spherical Harmonics Data (TBO): Stored in a separate RGBA16F TBO. Number of coefficients per splat: C = (d{active} + 1)^2 - 1, where d{active} is the active SH degree. Coefficients are interleaved RGB, coefficient-major. The DC term (degree 0) is always present. Higher-order terms are stored if available in the source data. 3. Sorted Indices (VBO): A dedicated Vertex Buffer Object (indexvbo) storing per-instance sorted indices. This decouples the sorting process from the rendering pipeline, allowing the sort backend to be swapped without reloading base splat data. Indices are sorted back-to-front for exact transparency or used for WBOIT weighting. 4. Splat Centers Cache: A std::vector (centerscache) storing splat centers. Used to allow swapping the sort backend (CPU/CUDA) without reloading the full base splat data. 1. Data Upload: Convert raw PLY data (positions, quaternions, scales, opacity, SH coefficients) into the compact TBO layout. Quaternions are normalized. Scales are exponentiated from log-space. Opacity is mapped to uint8. Upload the base splat data to the primary TBO. 2. Sorting: The SplatCloud class manages a worker thread that drives the sort backend. Sorting can be performed on CPU or GPU (CUDA). The CUDA backend automatically falls back to CPU if no GPU device is available. The sorter outputs a list of indices representing the back-to-front order of splats. These indices are uploaded to the indexvbo. 3. Draw Call: Bind the base splat TBO to texture unit 0. Bind the sorted indices VBO. Execute an instanced draw call using a quad VBO (4 vertices, ±2 corners), an index buffer (6 indices for two triangles), and the instance index VBO. The vertex shader uses the instance index to fetch the sorted splat ID, then fetches the corresponding splat data from the TBO. 4. Fragment Shading: The fragment shader evaluates the 2D Gaussian profile. If the fragment's alpha is below alphathreshold (default 0.05), it is discarded. Color is computed using the SH coefficients based on the view direction and activeshdegree (default 0, max constrained by data). 5. Transparency Accumulation: Two modes are supported, configurable at runtime: Sorted: Standard back-to-front alpha blending. WBOIT: Order-Independent Transparency approximation using a weight function based on depth and alpha. Spherical Harmonics Coefficient Count: N{coeffs} = (d{active} + 1)^2 - 1 Where d{active} is the active SH degree. WBOIT Weight Function: The exact weight function formula is not provided in the sources. The accumulation uses configurable parameters for depth discrimination and alpha suppression. WBOIT Alpha Discard: Fragments with alpha below wboitalphadiscard (default 0.01, range [0.0, 0.1]) are discarded in the accumulation pass. | Parameter | Type | Default | Range/Notes | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | alphathreshold | float | 0.05 | Opacity threshold for discarding splat fragments. | | activeshdegree | int | 0 | SH degree for view-dependent color. Max constrained by data. | | clipmin | vec3 | [-10, -10, -10] | AABB lower bound for ROI clipping. | | clipmax | vec3 | [10, 10, 10] | AABB upper bound for ROI clipping. | | wboitweightscale | float | 5.0 | Depth-discrimination strength. | | wboitweightexponent | float | 2.0 | Alpha-suppression power. | | wboitalphadiscard | float | 0.01 | Fragment alpha cutoff in WBOIT pass. | Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersplatcloud(splatcloud, camera, viewport): # 1. Prepare Sorter sorter = splatcloud.getsorter() if sorter is None: return # Sorting disabled # 2. Trigger Sort (Async/Threaded) # The sorter uses centerscache to sort indices sortedindices = sorter.sort(splatcloud.centerscache) # 3. Upload Indices indexvbo = splatcloud.indexvbo indexvbo.upload(sortedindices) # 4. Setup Rendering State program = splatcloud.program # Bind Base Splat Data TBO to Texture Unit 0 bindtexturebuffer(program.uniforms["splatdata"], 0, splatcloud.basetbo) # Bind SH Data TBO bindtexturebuffer(program.uniforms["shdata"], 1, splatcloud.shtbo) # Set Parameters program.uniforms["alphathreshold"] = splatcloud.alphathreshold program.uniforms["activeshdegree"] = splatcloud.activeshdegree # Set WBOIT parameters if mode is WBOIT if splatcloud.transparencymode == 'WBOIT': program.uniforms["wboitweightscale"] = splatcloud.wboitweightscale program.uniforms["wboitweightexponent"] = splatcloud.wboitweightexponent program.uniforms["wboitalphadiscard"] = splatcloud.wboitalphadiscard else: # Enable standard blending for Sorted mode enableblending() setblendfunc(SRCALPHA, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) # 5. Draw Call # Quad VBO (Source 0, 4 verts), Index VBO (Source 1, N floats), IBO (6 indices) bindvertexarray(splatcloud.quadvbo) bindindexbuffer(splatcloud.ibo) bindinstancebuffer(splatcloud.indexvbo) # Set up vertex attributes for quad positions and instance indices setupvertexattribute(0, 2, FLOAT, 0, 0) # Quad positions setupvertexattribute(1, 1, FLOAT, 0, 0) # Instance indices drawelementsinstanced( TRIANGLES, 6, # IBO size UNSIGNEDINT, 0, len(sortedindices) # N instances) Precision: Opacity is stored as uint8 in the TBO, which may limit dynamic range compared to float32. Boundaries: ROI clipping is handled via clipmin and clipmax. Splats outside this AABB are not rendered. SH Degree: activeshdegree defaults to 0 and is constrained by the maximum available in the loaded data to prevent out-of-bounds reads. Sort Backend: If CUDA is selected but no GPU is available, the system falls back to CPU sorting, which may be significantly slower for large N. Time Complexity: Sorting is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the backend. Rendering is O(N) for the draw call. Memory Complexity: O(N) for TBOs and VBOs. 32 bytes per splat for base data plus SH coefficients. Performance: Depends heavily on the sort backend. GPU sorting (CUDA) is significantly faster for large clouds. WBOIT mode may be slower than sorted mode due to additional accumulation passes or complex fragment shader logic, but provides order-independent results. Strengths: Efficient instanced rendering, decoupled sorting, configurable transparency. Limitations: Requires OpenGL support. WBOIT is an approximation. CPU sorting is slow for large datasets. This plugin is part of the splat-ros ecosystem, providing a visualization tool for 3D Gaussian Splatting data within ROS. It bridges the gap between offline reconstruction (e.g., from Gaussian Splatting training) and interactive 3D visualization in robotics workflows. splat-ros/RVizSplat, https://github.com/splat-ros/RVizSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: CPU-based Gaussian Splatting Thumbnailer with JIT Optimization
head: JIT Python Gaussian Splatting, Sphere Splatting
body: This method provides a lightweight, CPU-only pipeline for generating rapid visual thumbnails from 3D Gaussian Splatting datasets, prioritizing responsiveness and portability over high-fidelity rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard GPU-accelerated splatting by omitting rotation parameters, approximating Gaussians as spheres, and leveraging Python's Numba JIT compiler to achieve near-real-time performance on constrained hardware. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position (\mu), scale (\sigma), and color. Rotation data is explicitly omitted to simplify the primitive representation. Output: A 2D image file representing the projected scene. Data Structures Gaussian Primitive: A structure containing position (3D vector), scale (scalar \sigma), and color. Buffers: colorbuffer and depthbuffer allocated for the target image resolution. Parameters Splat Size (\sigma): The radius of the spherical approximation, tuned between 0.4 and 0.5 to balance detail and speed. Image Resolution: 720p is the standard target resolution. Initial Radius: Set to the largest Gaussian scale in the dataset. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Allocate colorbuffer and depthbuffer for the target resolution. 2. Sphere Approximation: Treat each Gaussian as a sphere by omitting rotation data and setting the initial radius to the largest Gaussian scale. 3. Projection: Project each Gaussian's 3D center \mu onto the 2D image plane to obtain screen-space coordinates. 4. Weight Calculation: Compute the Gaussian weight \rho(x) for pixels within the splat's radius using the formula: \rho(x) = \alpha \cdot \exp(-0.5 \cdot (x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)). 5. Blending: Blend the projected Gaussians into the colorbuffer based on their calculated weights using a fast approximate blending method. 6. Buffer Update: Update the colorbuffer with the blended colors and the depthbuffer with the corresponding depth values for each pixel. 7. Output: Save the final colorbuffer as an image file to generate the thumbnail. Pseudocode Unverified code. Sphere Approximation: Treating Gaussians as spheres simplifies the covariance matrix inversion but reduces accuracy for non-spherical primitives. When Not to Use: High-fidelity rendering or applications requiring precise orientation and shape representation. Origin: The method was introduced by E. Genchev et al. in 2025. name: OmniGS
head: Equirectangular Projection, OmniGS Forward Rendering, OmniGS, Omnidirectional Gaussian Splatting, Omnidirectional Rasterization
body: OmniGS is a method for fast radiance field reconstruction and real-time omnidirectional novel view synthesis using calibrated monocular 360-degree images and sparse SfM point clouds. It replaces the standard perspective camera model with an omnidirectional equirectangular projection model, allowing 3D Gaussians to be splatted directly onto the equirectangular screen space. Unlike sibling methods such as 360-GS, which rely on tangent-plane approximations and two-stage projection, OmniGS uses direct screen-space splatting without requiring scene assumptions or deep networks. Inputs: A set of calibrated monocular 360-degree images. A sparse SfM point cloud. Camera poses and intrinsic parameters (focal lengths fx, fy, principal points cx, cy). Outputs: A reconstructed scene model represented by 3D Gaussians. Rendered omnidirectional images. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian: Defined by a mean position \mathbf{m}, a rotation matrix \mathbf{W}, a scaling vector, and an opacity oi. The covariance in world space is derived from these parameters. Camera Space Point: \mathbf{t} = [tx, ty, tz]^T, obtained by transforming the world position \mathbf{m} using the world-to-camera transformation matrix \mathbf{T}{cw}. Tile Grid: The equirectangular image is partitioned into a grid of tiles. Coordinate Systems: Camera Coordinate System: Follows the SLAM convention: +X is right, +Y is down, and +Z is forward. Latitude-Longitude: Intermediate spherical coordinates. Uniform Screen-Space: Normalized coordinates sx, sy \in -1, 1). Pixel Coordinates: Integer pixel positions px, py on an image of width W and height H. Forward Rendering Steps: 1. Transform to Camera Space: For each 3D Gaussian with world position \mathbf{m}, compute its position in camera space \mathbf{t}: \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{T}{cw} \mathbf{m} where \mathbf{T}{cw} is the 4x4 transformation matrix from world to camera space. 2. Project to Spherical Coordinates: Compute the distance tr and spherical coordinates (longitude lon, latitude lat) from \mathbf{t}: tr = \sqrt{tx^2 + ty^2 + tz^2} \begin{bmatrix} lon \\ lat \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathrm{arctan2}(tx / tz) \\ \arcsin (ty / tr) \end{bmatrix} The ranges are -\pi \le lon < \pi and -\pi/2 \le lat < \pi/2. 3. Map to Uniform Screen-Space: Transform spherical coordinates to uniform screen-space coordinates sx, sy: \begin{bmatrix} sx \\ sy \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} lon / \pi \\ 2lat / \pi \end{bmatrix} This results in -1 \le sx, sy < 1. 4. Map to Pixel Coordinates: Transform uniform screen-space coordinates to pixel positions px, py: \begin{bmatrix} px \\ py \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (sx + 1) W / 2 \\ (sy + 1) H / 2 \end{bmatrix} where W is the image width and H is the image height. 5. Compute 2D Covariance and Alpha: The 2D covariance matrix in screen space is computed using the Jacobian of the projection and the 3D covariance. The alpha value for the i-th Gaussian at pixel p is: \alphai = oi Gi(\Delta \mathbf{p}i) where Gi is the 2D Gaussian distribution and \Delta \mathbf{p}i is the distance from the pixel to the Gaussian center. 6. Sort Gaussians: Sort the Gaussians contributing to a pixel by their distance from the camera center to the Gaussian kernel center, tr, from nearest to farthest. Note: Perspective cameras sort by tz. 7. [Tile-Based Rasterization: Partition the equirectangular image into tiles. For each tile, identify 2D Gaussians whose radius of influence covers the tile. Render all pixels in the tile simultaneously, assigning one thread per pixel. Threads cooperatively retrieve Gaussian attributes and accumulate alpha-blending results. Stop accumulation when pixel alpha reaches 0.9999 for numerical stability. 8. Alpha Blending: The final color C is computed as: C = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) where ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian and N is the number of Gaussians near the pixel. Jacobian for Backpropagation: The derivatives of pixel coordinates with respect to camera-space points are required for optimization: \frac{\partial px}{\partial tx} = +\frac{W}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{tz}{tx^2 + tz^2}, \quad \frac{\partial px}{\partial ty} = 0, \quad \frac{\partial px}{\partial tz} = -\frac{W}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{tx}{tx^2 + tz^2} \frac{\partial py}{\partial tx} = -\frac{H}{\pi} \cdot \frac{tx ty}{tr^2 \sqrt{tx^2 + tz^2}}, \quad \frac{\partial py}{\partial ty} = +\frac{H}{\pi} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{tx^2 + tz^2}}{tr^2}, \quad \frac{\partial py}{\partial tz} = -\frac{H}{\pi} \cdot \frac{tz ty}{tr^2 \sqrt{tx^2 + tz^2}} where tr^2 = tx^2 + ty^2 + tz^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def projectomnidirectional(tx, ty, tz, W, H): """ Projects a 3D point in camera space to equirectangular pixel coordinates. tx, ty, tz: Tensor of shape (N,) W, H: int Returns: px, py tensors of shape (N,) """ tr = torch.sqrt(tx2 + ty2 + tz2) lon = torch.atan2(tx, tz) lat = torch.asin(ty / tr) sx = lon / math.pi sy = 2 lat / math.pi px = (sx + 1) W / 2 py = (sy + 1) H / 2 return px, py def evaluate2dgaussian(deltap, cov2d): """ Evaluates the 2D Gaussian PDF at offset deltap with covariance cov2d. deltap: Tensor of shape (2,) cov2d: Tensor of shape (2, 2) Returns: float """ det = cov2d[0, 0] cov2d[1, 1] - cov2d[0, 1] cov2d[1, 0] invdet = 1.0 / det invcov = torch.tensor([ [cov2d[1, 1] invdet, -cov2d[0, 1] invdet], [-cov2d[1, 0] invdet, cov2d[0, 0] invdet] ]) quad = deltap @ invcov @ deltap return torch.exp(-0.5 quad) / (2 math.pi torch.sqrt(det)) def rendertile(tilegaussians, tilepixels, W, H): """ Renders a single tile. tilegaussians: List of dicts with keys: 'px', 'py', 'opacity', 'color', 'covariance2d' tilepixels: List of tuples (px, py) """ # Sort Gaussians by tr (distance from camera center) # tr is precomputed or derived from camera-space position sortedgaussians = sorted(tilegaussians, key=lambda g: g['tr']) results = [] for px, py in tilepixels: alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = torch.zeros(3) for g in sortedgaussians: deltap = torch.tensor([px - g['px'], py - g['py']]) alphai = g['opacity'] evaluate2dgaussian(deltap, g['covariance2d']) if alphaacc >= 0.9999: break weight = alphai (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc = coloracc (1.0 - alphai) + g['color'] weight alphaacc += weight results.append(coloracc) return results def computejacobian(tx, ty, tz, W, H): """ Computes the Jacobian of pixel coordinates w.r.t camera space points. """ trsq = tx2 + ty2 + tz2 tr = torch.sqrt(trsq) denomxz = tx2 + tz2 sqrtxz = torch.sqrt(tx2 + tz2) dpxdtx = (W / (2 math.pi)) (tz / denomxz) dpxdty = torch.zeroslike(tx) dpxdtz = -(W / (2 math.pi)) (tx / denomxz) dpydtx = -(H / math.pi) (tx ty) / (trsq sqrtxz) dpydty = (H / math.pi) sqrtxz / trsq dpydtz = -(H / math.pi) (tz ty) / (trsq sqrtxz) return { 'dpxdtx': dpxdtx, 'dpxdty': dpxdty, 'dpxdtz': dpxdtz, 'dpydtx': dpydtx, 'dpydty': dpydty, 'dpydtz': dpydtz } Time Complexity: Real-time rendering speed is achieved through GPU acceleration and tile-based rasterization. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Direct screen-space splatting avoids the suboptimal two-stage projection of tangent-plane methods. It does not rely on scene assumptions or deep networks, enabling application in diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When omnidirectional novel view synthesis is required from monocular 360-degree images. OmniGS was introduced by Longwei Li, Huajian Huang, Sai-Kit Yeung, and Hui Cheng from Sun Yat-sen University and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The paper was published on arXiv in April 2024 (v5 in November 2024). It addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which only supports perspective images, by extending it to omnidirectional images. name: TR-Gaussians
head: TR-3DGS, TR-Gaussian Splatting, Transmission and Reflection 3D Gaussian Splatting, Transmission-Reflection Gaussians
body: TR-Gaussians is a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based representation designed for the high-fidelity, real-time rendering of planar transmission and reflection effects, such as those found in indoor glass panes. Unlike vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting, which overfits training images by mixing transmission and reflection into low-opacity artifacts, TR-Gaussians explicitly decomposes the scene into real geometry (transmission) and virtual geometry (reflection) using a learnable reflection plane. This separation prevents the entanglement of real scene geometry with virtual reflections, ensuring that reflections remain coherent and artifact-free in novel views where the real scene is occluded or unobserved. TR-Gaussians models a scene containing transparent glass by combining standard 3D Gaussians with a parametric reflection plane. The method separates the rendering process into two passes to compute transmission and reflection components independently, blending them via a view-dependent Fresnel model. Inputs: Camera pose (view and projection matrices). Scene representation: Primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p: Represent the real scene geometry and appearance. Glass Gaussians \mathcal{G}g: Mark the reflective regions on the glass pane. Reflection Plane P: Defined by position, normal, and base reflectance. Training images (for optimization). Outputs: Final rendered image C. Intermediate components: Transmission image Ct, Reflection image Cr, Reflection strength map R. The scene is represented by three distinct components: 1. Primary Gaussians (\mathcal{G}p): Each Gaussian i has: Position \mathbf{u}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}i for view-dependent color ci(\mathbf{d}). 3D Covariance matrix \Sigmai = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^\top \mathbf{R}i^\top, where \mathbf{S}i is the scaling matrix and \mathbf{R}i is the rotation matrix. Note: These are identical to the Gaussians in vanilla 3DGS. 2. Glass Gaussians (\mathcal{G}g): A subset of Gaussians (or a separate set) projected onto the reflection plane to define the shape of the reflective surface. Used to render a binary or soft mask M indicating where the glass pane exists in the screen space. 3. Reflection Plane (P): Defined by a plane equation \mathbf{n}^\top (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}) = 0, where \mathbf{p} is a point on the plane and \mathbf{n} is the unit normal vector. Includes a learnable base reflectance parameter. Initialized during Stage 1 of optimization. The rendering process consists of two passes. Pass 1: Transmission and Mask Computation 1. Transmission Image (Ct): Render the primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p using standard EWA splatting. Project each Gaussian i to screen space: \mathbf{u}'i = \Pi(\mathbf{u}i), \Sigma'i = \Pi(\Sigmai). Evaluate Gaussian value at pixel \mathbf{u}: Gi(\mathbf{u}) = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}'i)^\top (\Sigma'i)^{-1} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}'i)\right) Composite colors and opacities in depth order to produce Ct. 2. Reflection Mask (M): Render the glass Gaussians \mathcal{G}g onto the reflection plane to determine the spatial extent of the glass pane. This produces a mask M(\mathbf{u}) where M(\mathbf{u}) = 1 if the pixel corresponds to the glass, and 0 otherwise. 3. Reflection Strength Map (R): Compute the raw reflection strength R{raw} at each point on the reflection plane using the Fresnel reflectance model. The strength depends on the view direction, surface normal, and base reflectance. Filter the raw strength with the mask: R(\mathbf{u}) = R{raw}(\mathbf{u}) \times M(\mathbf{u}) R(\mathbf{u}) represents the view-dependent ratio of reflected light intensity relative to incident light intensity. Pass 2: Reflection Image Computation 1. Mirrored Gaussians (\hat{\mathcal{G}}p): Generate mirrored Gaussians by reflecting the primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p across the reflection plane P. For each primary Gaussian i with center \mathbf{u}i, compute the mirrored center \hat{\mathbf{u}}i: \hat{\mathbf{u}}i = \mathbf{u}i - 2(\mathbf{n}^\top (\mathbf{u}i - \mathbf{p})) \mathbf{n} Reflect the covariance matrix to account for the coordinate system flip (if necessary for correct orientation, though standard reflection of position and covariance is sufficient for splatting). 2. Raw Reflection Image (C{raw}): Render the mirrored Gaussians \hat{\mathcal{G}}p using standard EWA splatting to produce the raw reflection color C{raw}. 3. Reflection Intensity Map (A): Render the mirrored Gaussians' opacities/depths to compute an intensity map A that weights the reflection based on the visibility and density of the mirrored geometry. 4. Reflection Image (Cr): Combine the raw reflection and intensity: Cr(\mathbf{u}) = C{raw}(\mathbf{u}) \times A(\mathbf{u}) Final Composition Blend the transmission and reflection images using the reflection strength map R: C(\mathbf{u}) = (1 - R(\mathbf{u})) \cdot Ct(\mathbf{u}) + R(\mathbf{u}) \cdot Cr(\mathbf{u}) TR-Gaussians uses a three-stage optimization framework to ensure stable decomposition and prevent local optima. Stage 1: Initialization (3,000 iterations) Goal: Optimize primary Gaussians as vanilla 3DGS and initialize the reflection plane. Loss: L = (1 - \lambda)L1 + \lambda L{D-SSIM} where L1 is the L1 loss, L{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss, and \lambda = 0.5. Output: The final image is set to C = Ct. The reflection plane P is initialized. Stage 2: Reflection Plane Adjustment (3,000 iterations) Goal: Refine the reflection plane and remove "reflection ghosts" from the transmission image. Loss: Enable the full rendering equation (Eq. 1) and additional decomposition losses (depth variance loss Ld and gradient conflict loss Lc, referenced as Eq. 17 in). Gradient Blocking: Gradients from the reflection image Cr are blocked from back-propagating to the primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p. This prevents the optimization from coupling reflection image errors with primary Gaussian placement, which would otherwise lead to incorrectly placed reflection planes. Stage 3: Joint Optimization (24,000 iterations) Goal: Final joint refinement of all parameters. Learning Rate: Reduce the learning rate of the reflection plane's position and normal by a factor of 0.1. Gradients: Allow full gradient propagation between all components. Opacity Perturbation: Enable periodic noise injection to escape local optima. Opacity Perturbation To prevent residual reflection components from remaining in the transmission image, noise is added to the opacities of primary Gaussians behind the reflection plane: 1. Project primary Gaussians \mathcal{G}p onto the reflection plane P under all training viewpoints. 2. Select Gaussians whose center projections fall inside the plane boundaries. 3. Add uniformly distributed noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{U}[-0.4, 0.4] to the opacities of selected Gaussians. 4. Clamp opacities to [0, 1] every 1,000 iterations. 5. Interleave perturbation periods with clamping periods to avoid conflict with vanilla 3DGS clamping operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import List, Tuple @dataclass class Gaussian: position: torch.Tensor # (3,) opacity: float shcoeffs: torch.Tensor # (N, 3, K) for SH degree K covariance: torch.Tensor # (3, 3) @dataclass class ReflectionPlane: position: torch.Tensor # (3,) normal: torch.Tensor # (3,), unit length basereflectance: float def rendertrgaussians(camera: dict, primarygaussians: List[Gaussian], glassgaussians: List[Gaussian], plane: ReflectionPlane) -> torch.Tensor: # Pass 1: Transmission and Mask Ct = standard3dgssplatting(camera, primarygaussians) M = standard3dgssplatting(camera, glassgaussians, returnopacity=True) viewdirs = computeviewdirections(camera) Rraw = fresnelschlick(viewdirs, plane.normal, plane.basereflectance) R = Rraw M # Pass 2: Reflection mirroredgaussians = [] for g in primarygaussians: d = torch.dot(plane.normal, g.position - plane.position) mirroredpos = g.position - 2 d plane.normal mirroredgaussians.append(Gaussian(mirroredpos, g.opacity, g.shcoeffs, g.covariance)) Craw = standard3dgssplatting(camera, mirroredgaussians) A = standard3dgssplatting(camera, mirroredgaussians, returnopacity=True) Cr = Craw A # Composition finalimage = (1 - R) Ct + R Cr return finalimage def standard3dgssplatting(camera: dict, gaussians: List[Gaussian], returnopacity: bool = False) -> torch.Tensor: # Standard EWA splatting: project gaussians to screen space, sort by depth, alpha composite. pass def computeviewdirections(camera: dict) -> torch.Tensor: # Computes view direction for each pixel from camera pose and projection matrices. pass def fresnelschlick(viewdirs: torch.Tensor, normal: torch.Tensor, basereflectance: float) -> torch.Tensor: # Computes Schlick's approximation of Fresnel reflectance. costheta = torch.clamp(torch.sum(viewdirs normal, dim=-1), min=0.0, max=1.0) R0 = basereflectance return R0 + (1 - R0) torch.pow(1 - costheta, 5) def optimizetrgaussians(camera: dict, primarygaussians: List[Gaussian], glassgaussians: List[Gaussian], plane: ReflectionPlane, images: List[torch.Tensor], gtimages: List[torch.Tensor]): optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([ {'params': [g.position for g in primarygaussians], 'lr': 0.0001}, {'params': [g.opacity for g in primarygaussians], 'lr': 0.0001}, {'params': [g.shcoeffs for g in primarygaussians], 'lr': 0.0001}, {'params': [g.covariance for g in primarygaussians], 'lr': 0.0001}, {'params': [plane.position, plane.normal], 'lr': 0.0001}, {'params': [plane.basereflectance], 'lr': 0.0001} ]) # Stage 1: Initialization (3000 iters) for i in range(3000): Ct = standard3dgssplatting(camera, primarygaussians) loss = (1 - 0.5) torch.nn.functional.l1loss(Ct, gtimages[i % len(gtimages)]) + \ 0.5 ssimloss(Ct, gtimages[i % len(gtimages)]) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 2: Reflection Plane Adjustment (3000 iters) for i in range(3000): finalimage = rendertrgaussians(camera, primarygaussians, glassgaussians, plane) loss = computeloss(finalimage, gtimages[i % len(gtimages)], primarygaussians, plane) # Block gradients from reflection component to primary Gaussians loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 3: Joint Optimization (24000 iters) for i in range(24000): if i % 2000 < 1000: applyopacityperturbation(primarygaussians, plane) else: clampopacities(primarygaussians) finalimage = rendertrgaussians(camera, primarygaussians, glassgaussians, plane) loss = computeloss(finalimage, gtimages[i % len(gtimages)], primarygaussians, plane) # Reduce LR for plane position/normal by 0.1 for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: if 'plane' in str(paramgroup['params']): paramgroup['lr'] = 0.1 loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() def applyopacityperturbation(primarygaussians: List[Gaussian], plane: ReflectionPlane): # Project primary Gaussians onto the reflection plane under all training viewpoints # Select Gaussians whose center projections fall inside the plane for g in primarygaussians: d = torch.dot(plane.normal, g.position - plane.position) if d < 0: # Behind the plane noise = torch.rand(1) 0.8 - 0.4 # Uniform [-0.4, 0.4] g.opacity = g.opacity + noise.item() def clampopacities(primarygaussians: List[Gaussian]): for g in primarygaussians: g.opacity = torch.clamp(g.opacity, 0.0, 1.0) def computeloss(pred: torch.Tensor, gt: torch.Tensor, gaussians: List[Gaussian], plane: ReflectionPlane) -> torch.Tensor: # Combines L1, D-SSIM, depth variance loss Ld, and gradient conflict loss Lc pass def ssimloss(pred: torch.Tensor, gt: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Standard D-SSIM loss implementation pass Rendering Speed: Approximately 225 FPS on the RTR dataset, compared to 338 FPS for vanilla 3DGS. This is roughly two-thirds the speed of vanilla 3DGS due to the two-pass rendering and additional computations for the reflection plane and mirrored Gaussians. Training Time: Moderate training time, totaling 30,000 iterations, whereas NeRF-based methods require hours of training. Memory: The representation adds overhead for the reflection plane parameters and the glass Gaussians, but remains comparable to 3DGS in terms of Gaussian count, as it does not rely on excessive low-opacity Gaussians to fit reflections. Strengths: High-fidelity rendering of planar transmission and reflection. Explicit decomposition prevents "reflection ghosts" and noisy artifacts in novel views. Real-time rendering capability. Handles complex view-dependent Fresnel effects. Limitations: Limited to planar reflections (glass panes, mirrors). Performance is lower than vanilla 3DGS. Requires careful initialization and multi-stage optimization to avoid local optima. When to use: Suitable for indoor scenes with transparent glass panes or mirrors where high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required. Not suitable for non-planar reflections or scenes without significant transmission/reflection components. TR-Gaussians was proposed by Yong Liu, Keyang Ye, Tianjia Shao, and Kun Zhou from Zhejiang University. The method was published in the IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG) in 2026 (arXiv preprint 2511.13009v1, Nov 2025). It addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS in handling glass panes, where the standard method fails to distinguish between transmission and reflection, leading to artifacts in novel views. The work builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting and contrasts with methods like MirrorGaussian (which handles only pure reflection) and NeRF-based approaches (which are slower and lack robust decomposition). TR-Gaussians: High-Fidelity Real-Time Rendering of Planar Transmission and Reflection With 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2026.3675416, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DOF-GS
head: Adjustable Depth-of-Field 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: DOF-GS is a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that incorporates a finite-aperture camera model to explicitly model and render depth-of-field (DOF) effects, enabling post-capture control of aperture and focal distance. Unlike previous NeRF-based techniques that simulate defocus via expensive per-ray blur kernels or recent 3DGS methods that use black-box neural networks for shape offsets, DOF-GS blurs individual Gaussians based on learnable Circle-of-Confusion (CoC) cues before compositing, allowing efficient, differentiable, and intuitive DOF adjustment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images with moderate defocus blur. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D scene representation \mathcal{S} consisting of anisotropic 3D Gaussian points, and optimized camera parameters (aperture and focal distance) per view. Scene Representation: The scene is represented by a set of K anisotropic 3D Gaussian points \{Gk\}{k=1}^K. Each Gaussian Gk is defined by a center position uk, a covariance matrix \Sigmak derived from anisotropic scaling sk and a quaternion qk, an opacity ok, and spherical harmonics coefficients hk. The 3D Gaussian function is defined as: Gk(p) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(p - uk)^T \Sigmak^{-1} (p - uk)\right) Projection: 3D Gaussian points are projected to 2D screen space. The Jacobian J of the projective transformation is calculated. The 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'k is computed as: \Sigma'k = J W \Sigmak W^T J^T where W is the view matrix transforming points from world space to camera space. The 2D Gaussian in screen space is: G'k(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - u'k)^T \Sigma'^{-1}k (x - u'k)\right) where u'k is the 2D center position post-projection. Standard Rasterization: For each pixel x, a small number Nx of Gaussians within a cutoff radius t are associated with it. The image is rendered using alpha blending: \tilde{I}(x) = \sum{i=1}^{Nx} Ti \alphai ci where \alphai = G'i(x), Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance, and ci is the view-dependent color of the i-th Gaussian. DOF Rendering: A differentiable DOF rendering process is integrated into the rasterizer. Individual Gaussians are blurred based on learnable CoC cues before compositing. This process is fully differentiable, allowing optimization of camera parameters alongside the 3D scene. CoC Calculation: The radius of the Circle-of-Confusion (CoC) R{coc} for an object point at depth zo is determined by the focal length F, aperture diameter A, and focal distance f: R{coc} = \frac{1}{2} F A \frac{|zo - f|}{zo (f - F)} Since F is often much smaller than f and object depths, this is simplified to: R{coc} = \frac{1}{2} Q \left| \frac{1}{zo} - \frac{1}{f} \right| where Q = FA is a simplified aperture parameter. CoC-Guided Detail Enhancement: A lightweight CoC-guided neural network predicts an in-focus mask for each view. These masks are used to enhance details within All-in-Focus (AiF) renderings during optimization, counteracting reduced sharpness due to defocus blur in multi-view inputs. Optimization: The scene representation \mathcal{S} and camera parameters are optimized by minimizing the reconstruction loss L{rec} between rendered views \tilde{I}m and training views Im: \min{\mathcal{S}} \sum{m=1}^M L{rec}(\tilde{I}m, Im) The loss is a weighted combination of MSE and DSSIM: L{rec}(Ia, Ib) = ||Ia - Ib|| + \lambda{dssim} L{dssim}(Ia, Ib) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computecocradius(zo, F, A, f): """Compute Circle-of-Confusion radius for depth zo.""" Q = F A return 0.5 Q abs(1.0 / zo - 1.0 / f) def projectgaussian(uk, Sigmak, W, J): """Project 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space.""" uprimek = J @ W @ uk Sigmaprimek = J @ W @ Sigmak @ W.T @ J.T return uprimek, Sigmaprimek def evaluategaussian(x, uprimek, Sigmaprimek): """Evaluate 2D Gaussian at pixel x.""" diff = x - uprimek invcov = torch.linalg.inv(Sigmaprimek) return torch.exp(-0.5 diff.T @ invcov @ diff) def renderdofscene(gaussians, A, f, F, W, J, imageshape): """Render scene with DOF blur using alpha compositing.""" rendered = torch.zeros(imageshape) transmittance = torch.ones(imageshape) # Gaussians are sorted by depth for correct alpha blending for g in gaussians: uk, Sigmak, color, zo = g uprimek, Sigmaprimek = projectgaussian(uk, Sigmak, W, J) alphabase = evaluategaussian(x, uprimek, Sigmaprimek) coc = computecocradius(zo, F, A, f) # Source states Gaussians are blurred based on learnable CoC cues. # Implementation typically convolves the projected Gaussian with a disk kernel of radius coc. alphai = applydiskblur(alphabase, coc) # Disk convolution implementation not detailed in source rendered = rendered + transmittance alphai color transmittance = transmittance (1.0 - alphai) return rendered def optimizescene(gaussians, cameraparams, trainingimages, lambdadssim): """Optimize scene and camera parameters.""" for m, Im in enumerate(trainingimages): A, f = cameraparams[m] F = knownfocallength rendered = renderdofscene(gaussians, A, f, F, W, J, Im.shape) # Lightweight CoC-guided neural network predicts in-focus mask. Architecture not detailed in source. infocusmask = computeinfocusmask(rendered, gaussians) # NN forward pass not detailed # Detail enhancement logic using mask is not detailed in source. enhancedrendered = applydetailenhancement(rendered, infocusmask) # Enhancement logic not detailed loss = torch.norm(rendered - Im) + lambdadssim computedssim(rendered, Im) loss.backward() updateparameters(gaussians, cameraparams) Time Complexity: Rendering is efficient, leveraging the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline with additional CoC-based blurring. This is significantly faster than NeRF-based defocus methods which require hours to days of training and yield below 1 FPS. Memory Complexity: Stores standard 3DGS attributes plus learnable camera parameters (A, f) per view and a lightweight neural network for CoC-guided detail enhancement. Strengths: Enables post-capture control of aperture and focal distance; differentiable optimization allows learning camera characteristics from defocused images; efficient compared to ray-tracing based defocus methods. Limitations: Requires multi-view defocused images for training; relies on a simplified thin lens model. When to use: When post-capture DOF control and refocusing from multi-view defocused inputs is required. When not to use: For scenes without defocus blur where standard pinhole 3DGS is sufficient, or when real-time performance on extremely low-end hardware is critical without the overhead of the CoC-guided network. DOF-GS was introduced to address the limitations of the pinhole camera model in existing 3DGS methods, which lack effective modeling of defocus effects. It builds on the 3DGS framework and surface-splatting techniques, extending them with a finite-aperture camera model. The method was tested on scenes from the multi-view defocus blur dataset.
