name: Temporal Gaussian Splatting
head: TemporalGS
body: Temporal Gaussian Splatting (TemporalGS) is a training-free, plug-and-play acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that leverages temporal priors from previous frames to reduce computational redundancy in Gaussian preprocessing, sorting, and rasterization. It solves the challenge of high FPS and low latency rendering by culling unnecessary Gaussians and approximating static regions via warped buffers, achieving up to 1.48× acceleration over vanilla 3DGS while maintaining competitive quality. Unlike sibling methods that may require post-training compression or hardware-specific optimizations, TemporalGS operates as a software rasterization plugin that interleaves dynamic culling and selective rendering intervals. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, camera poses Wt (reference) and W{t+i} (target), intrinsic matrix K, and temporal priors from reference frame It (TGB, TAB, Temporal Gaussian Buffer). Outputs: Rendered frame \bar{I}{t+i} for intermediate frames i \in [1, \lambda-1]. Data Structures: 1. Temporal Geometry Buffer (TGB): Stores per-pixel depth Dt(x,y) and depth standard deviation \sigmat(x,y) for the reference frame. Dt(x,y) = \frac{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y) di}{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y)} \sigmat(x,y) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y) (di - Dt(x,y))^2}{\sum{Gi \in Tk} wi(x,y)}} Where Tk is the tile containing pixel (x,y), wi is the Gaussian weight, and di is the Gaussian depth. 2. Temporal Appearance Buffer (TAB): The color image of the reference frame It. 3. Temporal Gaussian Buffer (G{rendered}): The subset of Gaussians that contributed to the reference frame. G{rendered} = \{Gi \mid \max{(x,y) \in It} wi(x,y) > 0\} Parameters: \lambda: Interval between reference frames. Accelerates \lambda-1 frames between It and I{t+\lambda}. \lambda{TDC}: Interval for Temporal Dynamic Culling. Typical value: 50. \lambda{SR}: Interval for Selective Rendering. Typical value: 5. \eta: Threshold percentage of selected tiles triggering a pseudo reference frame. Typical value: 40%. \lambda1, \lambda2: Variance range parameters for surface modeling in TGB. Typical values: \lambda1=3, \lambda2=0. \epsilon: Small constant for depth initialization. Value: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Reference Frame Rendering: Render reference frame It using standard 3DGS. Construct TGB (Dt, \sigmat), TAB (It), and G{rendered}. 2. Initialization: For the target frame t+i, initialize warped depth D'{min} to z{far} + \epsilon and warped standard deviation \sigma'{max} to 0. 3. Forward Warping: Map pixels from It to t+i using camera matrices Wt, W{t+i} and intrinsic K: (x', y') \approx K W{t+i} Wt^{-1} Dt(x,y) K^{-1} [x, y, 1]^T Clip to nearest pixel. If multiple source pixels map to the same destination, preserve the geometry closer to the camera and the maximum depth standard deviation to obtain high recall. Update D'{min} and \sigma'{max} at the destination pixels. 4. Surface Modeling: Define the visible surface range at t+i as [D'{min} - \lambda1 \sigma'{max}, D'{min} + \lambda2 \sigma'{max}]. 5. Temporal Dynamic Culling (TDC): Performed every \lambda{TDC} frames. Adaptive Frustum Culling (AFC): After near-plane culling, keep only Gaussians Gi where F{min} \leq ndci \leq F{max}. ndci = \text{Pix2NDC}(\mu'i), where \mu'i is the 2D mean of Gi in screen space. F{min} = \min{Gj \in G{rendered}} (ndcj), F{max} = \max{Gj \in G{rendered}} (ndcj). Temporal Occlusion Culling (TOC): Remove Gaussians Gi whose 2D means are in screen space AND whose depth di > D'{min}(\bar{\mu}i) + \lambda2 \sigma'{max}(\bar{\mu}i), where \bar{\mu}i is the nearest screen pixel to Gi's mean. Pixels with no warped geometry retain z{far} + \epsilon depth, allowing new closer surfaces to be included. 6. Selective Rendering (SR): Performed every \lambda{SR} frames. Depth Repair: Identify "no-hit" pixels in warped depth map (where D'{min} == z{far} + \epsilon). If all 3x3 neighbors are valid, fill the pixel with the average of neighbors. Denote repaired depth as D'{min}'. Tile Selection: Perform backward warping (inverse of forward warping) on D'{min}' to query correspondence in reference frame. Mark tile Tk as T{unselected} if any pixel in Tk fails to find correspondence. Combine Selection: T{selected} = T{oc\selected} \cup T{unselected}, where T{oc\selected} are tiles intersecting Gaussians that passed TOC. 7. Rendering: Sort Gaussians intersecting T{selected} by depth. Render T{selected} tiles using standard alpha blending. For tiles T \setminus T{selected}, use the warped TAB \bar{I}{t \to t+i} obtained via backward warping of It using D'{min}' and bilinear interpolation. Stitch rendered tiles and warped TAB to form \bar{I}{t+i}. 8. Adaptive Reference Frame Insertion: If the number of selected tiles at t+i exceeds \eta\% of total tiles, force t+i+1 to be a pseudo reference frame (rendered with AFC). 9. Loop: Interleave TDC and SR steps for intermediate frames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def temporalgaussiansplatting(Gaussians, Wref, Wtarget, K, TGBdepth, TGBsigma, TAB, Grendered, lambdaval, lambdaTDC, lambdaSR, eta, lambda1, lambda2, zfar, epsilon, framecount): """ Render intermediate frame between reference and target using TemporalGS. Gaussians: list of dicts with keys 'mean', 'depth', 'covariance', 'opacity', 'sh' TGBdepth, TGBsigma: 2D numpy arrays (H, W) TAB: 2D numpy array (H, W, 3) """ H, W = TGBdepth.shape # 1. Forward Warping warpeddepth = np.full((H, W), zfar + epsilon) warpedsigmamax = np.zeros((H, W)) # Iterate over reference frame pixels ys, xs = np.where(TGBdepth < zfar + epsilon) for y, x in zip(ys, xs): depthz = TGBdepth[y, x] # Unproject to 3D: p3d = Wref^-1 K^-1 [x, y, 1, 1]^T depthz p3dref = unproject(x, y, depthz, K, Wref) # Project to target view: p2d = K Wtarget p3d p2dtarget = project(p3dref, K, Wtarget) tx, ty = cliptopixel(p2dtarget) # Bounds check if 0 <= ty < H and 0 <= tx < W: sigma = TGBsigma[y, x] # Preserve max sigma and min depth if sigma > warpedsigmamax[ty, tx]: warpedsigmamax[ty, tx] = sigma if depthz < warpeddepth[ty, tx]: warpeddepth[ty, tx] = depthz Dmin = warpeddepth Sigmamax = warpedsigmamax # 2. Temporal Dynamic Culling (TDC) if framecount % lambdaTDC == 0: # Adaptive Frustum Culling (AFC) ndcvals = [pix2ndc(g['mean'], K) for g in Grendered] ndcmin = min(ndcvals) ndcmax = max(ndcvals) filteredGaussians = [] for g in Grendered: # Near-plane culling if g['depth'] < 0.1: # Standard near-plane threshold continue ndc = pix2ndc(g['mean'], K) if ndcmin <= ndc <= ndcmax: # Temporal Occlusion Culling (TOC) mubar = nearestscreenpixel(g['mean'], K, Wtarget) dminbuf = Dmin[mubar.y, mubar.x] sigmamaxbuf = Sigmamax[mubar.y, mubar.x] # Cull if behind warped surface if g['depth'] > dminbuf + lambda2 sigmamaxbuf: continue filteredGaussians.append(g) Gactive = filteredGaussians else: Gactive = Grendered # 3. Selective Rendering (SR) Tselected = set() # Depth Repair Dminrepaired = Dmin.copy() nohitmask = (Dmin == zfar + epsilon) for y, x in zip(np.where(nohitmask)): neighbors = get3x3neighbors(Dmin, y, x) if allvalid(neighbors): Dminrepaired[y, x] = mean(neighbors) # Tile Selection # Tumselected: tiles with unmatched pixels for tiley in range(0, H, 16): # Assuming 16x16 tiles for tilex in range(0, W, 16): hasunmatched = False for py in range(tiley, min(tiley+16, H)): for px in range(tilex, min(tilex+16, W)): if Dminrepaired[py, px] >= zfar + epsilon: hasunmatched = True break if hasunmatched: break if hasunmatched: Tselected.add((tilex, tiley)) # Tocselected: tiles intersecting surviving Gaussians for g in Gactive: mubar = nearestscreenpixel(g['mean'], K, Wtarget) tilex = (mubar.x // 16) 16 tiley = (mubar.y // 16) 16 Tselected.add((tilex, tiley)) # 4. Render Image = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) # Render selected tiles for tx, ty in Tselected: Gtile = [g for g in Gactive if intersects(g, (tx, ty), K, Wtarget)] Gtile.sort(key=lambda g: g['depth']) Image[ty:ty+16, tx:tx+16] = rasterize(Gtile, (tx, ty), K, Wtarget) # Warp TAB for non-selected tiles if len(Tselected) < (HW)/(1616): Iwarped = backwardwarp(TAB, Dminrepaired, K, Wref, Wtarget) for tiley in range(0, H, 16): for tilex in range(0, W, 16): if (tilex, tiley) not in Tselected: Image[tiley:tiley+16, tilex:tilex+16] = Iwarped[tiley:tiley+16, tilex:tilex+16] # Adaptive Reference Frame Insertion totaltiles = (H W) / (16 16) if len(Tselected) > (eta / 100.0) totaltiles: return Image, True # Signal pseudo reference frame insertion return Image, False def unproject(x, y, z, K, W): invK = np.linalg.inv(K) invW = np.linalg.inv(W) pcam = invK @ np.array([x, y, 1.0]) z pworld = invW @ np.append(pcam, 1.0) return pworld[:3] def project(p3d, K, W): pcam = W @ np.append(p3d, 1.0) p2d = K @ pcam[:3] return p2d[:2] / p2d[2] def cliptopixel(p2d): return int(round(p2d[0])), int(round(p2d[1])) def pix2ndc(mean2d, K): # Simplified NDC conversion from screen coordinates return (mean2d[0] / K[0, 0]) - 1.0 # Approximation for standard FOV def nearestscreenpixel(mean3d, K, W): pcam = W @ np.append(mean3d, 1.0) p2d = K @ pcam[:3] x, y = p2d[:2] / p2d[2] return type('Pixel', (), {'x': int(round(x)), 'y': int(round(y))})() def get3x3neighbors(depthmap, y, x): neighbors = [] for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < depthmap.shape[0] and 0 <= nx < depthmap.shape[1]: neighbors.append(depthmap[ny, nx]) return neighbors def allvalid(depths, zfar, epsilon): return all(d < zfar + epsilon for d in depths) def mean(depths): return sum(depths) / len(depths) def backwardwarp(TAB, depthmap, K, Wref, Wtarget): H, W, = TAB.shape warpedtab = np.zeroslike(TAB) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): if depthmap[y, x] < zfar + epsilon: # Inverse of forward warp: target -> ref p3dref = unproject(x, y, depthmap[y, x], K, Wref) p2dtarget = project(p3dref, K, Wtarget) tx, ty = cliptopixel(p2dtarget) if 0 <= ty < H and 0 <= tx < W: warpedtab[y, x] = TAB[ty, tx] # Bilinear interpolation omitted for brevity return warpedtab def intersects(g, tile, K, W): mubar = nearestscreenpixel(g['mean'], K, W) return tile[0] <= mubar.x < tile[0] + 16 and tile[1] <= mubar.y < tile[1] + 16 def rasterize(Gtile, tile, K, W): # Standard alpha-blending rasterization for the tile # Returns 3-channel image patch return np.zeros((16, 16, 3)) # Placeholder for standard 3DGS rasterizer Time Complexity: Reduces sorting and rasterization cost by culling Gaussians (TDC) and rendering only a subset of tiles (SR). The acceleration factor is up to 1.48× compared to vanilla 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for TGB (depth + sigma), TAB (color), and G{rendered} (Gaussian indices). TGB can be downscaled by a factor of 2 on large-scale scenes. Strengths: Training-free, plug-and-play, works with software and hardware rasterization, maintains high quality. Limitations: Rendering quality degrades with significant camera motion or inaccurate 3DGS surface representation. When to use: Stream rendering, video playback, or applications requiring high FPS with moderate camera motion. When not to use: Scenes with rapid, large-scale changes where \eta threshold is frequently exceeded, causing frequent reference frame resets. TemporalGS was introduced as the first training-free, plug-and-play algorithmic approach to accelerate 3DGS rendering using temporal priors. It addresses the computational bottleneck of sorting and rasterization in 3DGS by leveraging temporal coherence between consecutive frames. TemporalGS: Training-Free Plug-and-Play Acceleration for 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering via Temporal Priors, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2607.03390, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Geometry and Representation Adaptation
head: Geometry-aware 3DGS, Surface-constrained Gaussian Splatting
body: This family of methods adapts the volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to better handle geometric constraints, sparse inputs, or surface-oriented rendering tasks. While standard 3DGS relies on dense multi-view photometric consistency to implicitly define geometry, these variants introduce explicit geometric supervision, surface parameterizations, or thickness regularization to resolve ambiguities inherent in sparse or deformable scenarios. They differ from standard 3DGS by decoupling or constraining the spatial distribution of Gaussians to align with known geometric priors (meshes, depth maps, or height fields) rather than relying solely on appearance optimization. All methods in this family retain the core differentiable rasterization pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting [3410-3d-gaussian-splatting-mvp.md] but modify the optimization objective or data representation to incorporate geometric information. 1. Geometric Supervision: Methods introduce loss terms that enforce consistency between rendered outputs and external geometric signals (depth maps, mesh surfaces, or TSDF fields). This is often combined with standard photometric losses (\mathcal{L}{color}). 2. Representation Modification: The standard set of independent 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} is either: Constrained to lie on a surface (Height-Field). Projected onto a 2D texture atlas (UV Parameterization). Dynamically expanded from sparse seeds (Unpooling). 3. Differentiable Geometry: All geometric constraints are differentiable with respect to Gaussian parameters to allow gradient-based optimization. What it is: A method for Few-Shot Gaussian Splatting (FSGS) that reconstructs scenes from sparse views (N < 10). Distinction: Unlike dense-view baselines, it initializes Gaussians from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points and uses "Gaussian unpooling" to expand the representation. It incorporates external geometric supervision via monocular depth estimation to resolve ambiguity. When to choose: Use when input views are extremely sparse and standard 3DGS fails due to under-constrained geometry. What it is: A method for real-time animated human reconstruction that projects Gaussian attributes into a 2D UV texture space. Distinction: Decouples spatial appearance from 3D coordinates, enabling efficient pose-dependent deformation via mesh topology. It differs from volumetric methods by storing attributes in a 2D atlas. When to choose: Use for animatable human avatars where pose-dependent deformation and detailed clothing capture are required. What it is: A method that converts volumetric 3DGS into a thin, deformable cortical surface using curved height-field Gaussians initialized on a TSDF zero level set. Distinction: Solves depth ambiguity and volumetric thickness issues (common in medical imaging) by enforcing a surface-oriented representation. It uses a three-stage pipeline: photometric bootstrap, ray-wise density concentration, and TSDF-guided conversion. When to choose: Use for medical imaging or scenarios with limited view coverage where a sharp, thin surface is preferred over a volumetric blob. 3D Gaussian Splatting [3410-3d-gaussian-splatting-mvp.md] was originally designed for dense multi-view reconstruction. However, applications such as few-shot learning, animated avatars, and medical imaging revealed limitations in handling sparse data, deformation, and surface sharpness. These adaptations emerged to extend 3DGS capabilities to these specific domains by integrating geometric priors.

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Gaussian Unpooling
head: FSGS
body: FSGS (First Sparse Gaussian Splatting) is a method for reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse view inputs, addressing the challenge of limited camera poses where standard 3D Gaussian Splatting fails due to insufficient geometric constraints. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting with Mesh UV Parameterization and H-2DGS (Height-Field 2D Gaussian Splatting) by dynamically expanding the Gaussian representation via unpooling from sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) seeds, rather than relying on static surface parameterizations or height fields. Inputs: Sparse set of input images with known camera poses (typically derived from SfM). A pre-trained 2D monocular depth estimation network. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} optimized to represent the scene geometry and appearance. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: A list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation Ri and scale Si), opacity \alphai \in [0,1], and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. SfM Points: A sparse set of 3D points \{Pj\} with associated image observations, serving as the initialization seeds. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian set using the sparse 3D points obtained from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) on the input images. These points serve as the initial means \mui and provide initial covariance estimates based on local point cloud density or fixed small scales. 2. Gaussian Unpooling: Identify and expand the sparse Gaussians to cover the scene volume. This involves "unpooling" existing Gaussians, which typically entails duplicating or splitting Gaussians in regions where the initial sparse representation is insufficient to capture fine details or occluded surfaces. The exact mathematical operation for unpooling is not detailed in the provided sources, but it serves to densify the representation from the sparse SfM seeds. 3. Depth Supervision: Render depth images from the current Gaussian set using differentiable volume rendering. Pass the input images through the pre-trained 2D depth estimation network to obtain predicted depth maps. Compute a loss between the rendered depth and the predicted depth. 4. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, colors) using a combined loss function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{depth} where \mathcal{L}{color} is the standard photometric loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS) between rendered and input images, and \mathcal{L}{depth} is the consistency loss between rendered and predicted depth maps. The parameter \lambda balances the two terms. 5. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with incorrect depth values or low opacity to maintain efficiency and reduce noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainfsgs(inputimages, cameraposes, depthnet): # Step 1: Initialize from SfM sfmpoints = runsfm(inputimages, cameraposes) gaussians = initializegaussiansfromsfm(sfmpoints) # Step 2 & 4: Optimization Loop for step in range(numsteps): # Sample a random input image imgidx = randomchoice(len(inputimages)) img = inputimages[imgidx] cam = cameraposes[imgidx] # Render current Gaussians renderedimg, rendereddepth = render(gaussians, cam) # Get predicted depth from pre-trained network predicteddepth = depthnet(img) # Compute losses losscolor = computecolorloss(renderedimg, img) lossdepth = computedepthloss(rendereddepth, predicteddepth) # Combined loss loss = losscolor + lambdadepth lossdepth # Backpropagate and update Gaussians updategaussians(gaussians, loss) # Step 5: Prune invalid Gaussians gaussians = prunegaussians(gaussians, rendereddepth, predicteddepth) # Step 2: Unpool if necessary (implementation detail not specified) if shouldunpool(gaussians): gaussians = unpoolgaussians(gaussians) return gaussians Parameters: \lambda: Weight for depth loss. Not given in the sources. numsteps: Number of optimization iterations. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Sparse Input: If the SfM reconstruction is too sparse or fails, initialization may be poor. The method relies on the robustness of the pre-trained depth network to fill gaps. Depth Ambiguity: Monocular depth estimation can be ambiguous for textureless or reflective surfaces. The depth loss may introduce artifacts if not balanced correctly with photometric loss. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and optimization steps. Unpooling increases the number of Gaussians, potentially increasing rendering and optimization time compared to standard 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of Gaussians. Unpooling increases memory usage. Strengths: Enables high-quality reconstruction from very few views (sparse input) where standard 3DGS fails. Leverages strong priors from pre-trained 2D depth networks. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the pre-trained depth network. Performance may degrade if the depth predictions are significantly incorrect. Unpooling strategy is critical and not fully detailed, potentially leading to over-smoothing or noise if not tuned. When to use: Sparse-view reconstruction scenarios. When not to use: Dense-view scenarios where standard 3DGS is sufficient and faster. FSGS was introduced as the first method to explore reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse view input using Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the core differentiable rasterization pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting [3410-3d-gaussian-splatting-mvp.md] but modifies the representation to handle sparse data by initializing from SfM and using depth supervision. It is part of a family of methods including SparseGS, CoherentGS, and DNGaussian that target sparse-view reconstruction. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Mesh UV Parameterization
head: ASH
body: This method adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time, high-quality animated human reconstruction by projecting the 3D Gaussian parameters into a 2D texture space using mesh UV parameterization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gaussian Unpooling and H-2DGS by explicitly leveraging a template mesh's UV coordinates to bind appearance and geometry, enabling efficient pose-dependent deformation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A template mesh (typically a canonical human body mesh) with UV coordinates; a set of posed training images; the initial 3D Gaussian parameters defined in the canonical space. Outputs: A 2D texture atlas storing Gaussian attributes (opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients for color, and potentially scale/rotation); a deformation field or pose-dependent transformation mechanism that maps canonical Gaussians to posed space for rendering. Data Structures: 1. UV Texture Atlas: A 2D image buffer where each texel corresponds to a region on the template mesh. Fields: Opacity (\alpha), Spherical Harmonics coefficients (c{lm}), and potentially base scale/rotation. Layout: Standard RGBA or custom packed format. The resolution is determined by the desired detail level (Not given in the sources). 2. Canonical Gaussians: A set of Gaussians \{Gi\} defined in the canonical space, associated with specific UV coordinates (ui, vi) on the template mesh. Numbered Steps: 1. Canonical Initialization: Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians in the canonical space of the template mesh. Each Gaussian i is associated with a specific UV coordinate (ui, vi) on the mesh surface. 2. UV Parameterization: Map the 3D Gaussian attributes to the 2D texture space. For each Gaussian i, its attributes (opacity, color SH coefficients) are stored in the texel corresponding to its UV coordinate (ui, vi). 3. Pose Projection: Given a target pose, apply a deformation function (e.g., linear blend skinning or a learned deformation field) to transform the canonical Gaussian positions and orientations to the posed space. The UV coordinates remain fixed to the mesh topology, allowing the texture atlas to serve as a compact representation of the appearance. 4. Differentiable Rasterization: Render the posed Gaussians using the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting differentiable rasterizer. The gradients flow back through the rasterization process to the Gaussian attributes in the texture atlas and the deformation parameters. 5. Optimization: Minimize a loss function combining photometric loss (\mathcal{L}{color}) between rendered and ground-truth images. Geometric regularization may be applied to ensure consistency with the template mesh. Formulas: Texture Lookup: The attribute Ai of Gaussian i is retrieved from the texture atlas T using its UV coordinate (ui, vi): Ai = T(ui, vi) Deformation: The position pi^{posed} of a Gaussian in the posed space is derived from its canonical position pi^{can} and the pose P: pi^{posed} = \text{Deform}(pi^{can}, P) (Specific deformation function not given in the sources.) Parameters: Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Spherical Harmonics Degree: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: UV Overlap: If the template mesh has overlapping UV islands, Gaussians from different body parts may map to the same texel, causing artifacts. Ensure UV layout is non-overlapping. Boundary Artifacts: Gaussians near the edge of UV islands may suffer from interpolation artifacts if not handled carefully. Use clamping or specific boundary handling in texture lookup. Pose Extrapolation: Performance may degrade for poses significantly outside the training distribution if the deformation field is not robust. Regularize deformation to prevent unrealistic stretching. Combines CNN-based generators with 3DGS for virtual humans with sophisticated details like clothing. Choose when high-frequency detail is critical and computational resources allow for CNN inference. Uses a shallow MLP instead of SH for color and regularizes deformation with geometry priors. Choose when pose-dependent cloth deformation generalization is required. Leverages physically-based priors to regularize Gaussians in canonical space for monocular video. Choose when reconstructing from monocular video to avoid dynamic cloth artifacts. Redesigns the prune/split/clone operations of original 3DGS. Choose when optimizing for dynamic human reconstruction efficiency. Time Complexity: Rendering is real-time, comparable to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, as the rasterization step remains unchanged. Training time depends on the complexity of the deformation field and texture resolution. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to storing independent Gaussians for every frame, as attributes are stored in a 2D texture atlas. Strengths: Real-time performance, high-quality animated humans, compact representation. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the template mesh and UV parameterization; may struggle with non-rigid deformations not captured by the template. When to Use: Real-time animated human avatars from posed data. When Not to Use: Scenes with complex, non-human geometry or where a template mesh is not available. The method was introduced as part of the ASH (Avatar Shell) approach for reconstructing virtual humans. It builds on the core differentiable rasterization pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting [3410-3d-gaussian-splatting-mvp.md] and incorporates geometric supervision via UV parameterization. It is primarily used for dynamic digital human modeling and virtual try-on applications. name: H-2DGS (Height-Field 2D Gaussian Splatting)
head: Height-Field Gaussian Splatting
body: H-2DGS converts a volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction into a thin, geometrically sharp, and deformable cortical surface using curved height-field Gaussian primitives initialized on a shared Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) zero level set. It solves the problem of depth ambiguity and thick, geometrically inconsistent opacity bands in standard 3DGS, particularly in medical imaging where explicit surface geometry is required for navigation and analysis. Unlike its siblings, which either expand from sparse seeds or parameterize onto a UV atlas, H-2DGS explicitly constructs a continuous surface representation by concentrating volumetric density into a TSDF and then mapping curved 2D Gaussians to that surface. H-2DGS operates as a three-stage pipeline: photometric bootstrap, ray-wise density concentration, and TSDF-guided surface conversion. Inputs: Multi-view images Iv from training cameras. Camera poses and intrinsics. (Optional) Postoperative MRI-derived depth geometry for deformation. Outputs: A set of curved height-field Gaussian primitives \{Gj\} representing the surface. Each primitive contains height, color, and opacity bases. Height-Field Primitive: Unlike standard 3D Gaussians defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics c, H-2DGS primitives are defined on a 2D manifold (the TSDF zero level set). Position: 3D coordinates on the TSDF surface. Orientation: Normal vector derived from the TSDF gradient. Bases: Separate parameters for height (geometry deviation from the TSDF), color (appearance), and opacity. Stage I: Photometric Bootstrap 1. Train a conventional 3DGS model using adaptive densification. 2. Optimize using the standard photometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} to establish appearance and scene support without surface constraints. \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = (1 - \lambda) \|\hat{I}v - Iv\|1 + \lambda(1 - \text{SSIM}(\hat{I}v, Iv)) where \lambda = 0.2, \hat{I}v is the rendered image, and Iv is the input image. Stage II: Ray-wise Density Concentration 1. Initialize with the Stage I model after a 5,000 iteration warm start. 2. Optimize for 1,000 iterations using a combined loss \mathcal{L}{\text{stage2}} to concentrate density along rays. 3. For each camera ray r(t) = o + td, compute 1D Gaussian contributions: \sigmai(t) = \betai \exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}ai(t - mi)^2\right] where \betai is amplitude, ai is inverse variance, and mi is mean position along the ray. 4. Compute normalized density pm and cumulative distribution Fm at sample tm: pm = \frac{\sigma(tm)}{\sumn \sigma(tn) + \epsilon}, \quad Fm = \sum{n=1}^m pn 5. Approximate quantile q using differentiable quantile approximation: wm(q) = \frac{\exp(-\tauq|Fm - q|)}{\sumn \exp(-\tauq|Fn - q|)}, \quad tq = \summ wm(q)tm where \tauq is the temperature parameter. 6. Calculate effective thickness \Delta t = t{q{\text{high}}} - t{q{\text{low}}} with q{\text{low}} = 0.01 and q{\text{high}} = 0.99. 7. Compute thickness loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{thick}}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\max(0, \Delta t - \Delta t^)}{E} where \Delta t^ is the target thickness (set to zero normalized thickness) and E is the scene extent. 8. Total loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{stage2}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{thick}} \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{r}}[\mathcal{L}{\text{thick}}] where \lambda{\text{thick}} = 5.0. Stage III: TSDF-Guided Surface Conversion 1. Render depth maps from all training cameras using the Stage II model. 2. Fuse these depth observations into a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF). 3. For a voxel center \mathbf{x} and view v, compute the signed distance observation: \phiv(\mathbf{x}) = \text{clip}\left(\frac{\hat{D}v(\piv(\mathbf{x})) - dv(\mathbf{x})}{\mu}, -1, 1\right) where \hat{D}v is the rendered depth, dv(\mathbf{x}) is the projected depth, and \mu is the truncation margin. 4. Fuse observations into the global TSDF \Phi(\mathbf{x}) using view weights wv(\mathbf{x}). 5. Initialize curved height-field primitives on the TSDF zero level set \Phi(\mathbf{x}) = 0. 6. Apply neighbor-transition optimization to coordinate overlapping patches and ensure locally continuous geometry. Postoperative Deformation (Optional) 1. Deform the explicit height-field surface toward postoperative MRI-derived depth geometry. 2. Use tracked-color supervision and alternating geometry-appearance updates to preserve photorealistic texture. \lambda (SSIM weight): 0.2. \lambda{\text{thick}} (Thickness loss weight): 5.0. q{\text{low}}: 0.01. q{\text{high}}: 0.99. \Delta t^ (Target thickness): Zero normalized thickness. Stage II iterations: 1,000. Warm start iterations: 5,000. Depth Ambiguity: Standard 3DGS may distribute opacity through a thick band under limited view coverage; Stage II is required to resolve this. Floating Density: Stage II may leave residual floating density; TSDF fusion in Stage III aggregates evidence to create a clean surface. Postoperative Changes: Brain motion and tissue removal alter anatomy; the deformation stage must preserve texture while aligning to new geometry. Representation Size: Compact, achieving 7.97 MB across five real neurosurgical cases. Performance: Interactive rendering at 29–42 ms per frame. Strengths: Produces sharp, geometrically consistent surfaces; supports postoperative deformation; integrates with tractography and MRI anatomy. Limitations: Requires multi-stage training; dependent on TSDF fusion quality; specific to surface reconstruction tasks. H-2DGS was introduced to address the limitations of conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting in neurosurgical visualization, where explicit surface geometry is critical for navigation and analysis. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating geometric supervision and representation modification [21351-geometry-and-representation-adaptation.md]. The method was developed for real neurosurgical cases to provide low multi-view depth inconsistency and a compact representation. name: Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training
head: Ghost cell techniques adapted for unstructured primitives
body: Ghost Ellipsoids for Chunked Training resolves boundary artifacts in chunked volume training by including ellipsoids from neighboring chunks in the loss computation without updating their parameters, providing boundary context without requiring a global volume or merged model. Unlike chunk-based 3DGS methods that resolve boundary inconsistencies by merging chunks into a global coarse model or through post-training stages, this method requires boundary support during training itself without access to a global volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D ellipsoids partitioned into spatial chunks, each with a defined spatial extent and normalized coordinate space. Output: Updated parameters for the current chunk's ellipsoids, with boundary context provided by ghost ellipsoids from neighbors. Data Structures: Chunk: A spatial subdivision of the volume. Ellipsoid Primitive: Defined by position \mathbf{p}, rotation matrix R, scale matrix S, and covariance \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. Positions are stored with a per-chunk spatial offset mapping them to the shared world coordinate system. Ghost Region: A boundary region around each chunk, defined by the chunk boundary offset, used to identify neighboring ellipsoids that influence the current chunk's loss. Steps: 1. Chunk Partitioning: Divide the volume into chunks. Each chunk is trained in its own normalized coordinate space scaled to its spatial extent (e.g., [-0.5, 0.5]^3 for a volume split into 2 \times 2 \times 2 chunks). 2. Ghost Ellipsoid Identification: For each chunk, identify boundary ellipsoids from all neighboring chunks (face-, edge-, and vertex-adjacent) by selecting those whose centers fall within the ghost region of the current chunk. 3. Voxelization and Loss Computation: Voxelize the ghost ellipsoids together with the current chunk's ellipsoids during the loss computation step. 4. Gradient Update: Ensure that ghost ellipsoids receive no gradient updates. Only the parameters of the ellipsoids belonging to the current chunk are updated. 5. Training Mode Selection: Sequential Mode (Single-GPU): Chunks are trained one at a time using ghost ellipsoids from completed neighbors. Parallel Mode (Multi-GPU): All chunks are trained simultaneously with ghost ellipsoids periodically synchronized across GPUs. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Coordinate Space Rescaling: Training all chunks in a shared [-1, 1]^3 space and applying post-hoc rescaling is computationally impractical. It requires computing \Sigma' = K \Sigma K^T = K R S S^T R^T K^T for each primitive, where K is a chunk-dependent anisotropic scale matrix. Since K and R do not generally commute, this cannot be simplified by scaling S alone. Correctly decomposing \Sigma' back into rotation and scale parameters requires a QR decomposition per primitive. Merging: The per-chunk primitive sets resulting from this method can be merged through simple concatenation without additional alignment, avoiding the need for global model merging. A training scheme for large volumes that partitions the volume into spatially non-overlapping chunks and uses ghost ellipsoids to provide boundary context. Ghost ellipsoids are used to provide boundary context across neighboring chunks during optimization, enabling scalable learning on volumes exceeding GPU memory. Training chunks separately introduces boundary artifacts because ellipsoids near chunk borders lack support from neighboring regions. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates boundary artifacts without requiring a global volume or merged model. Avoids computationally expensive QR decompositions associated with post-hoc rescaling. Limitations: Requires identification of neighboring ellipsoids and synchronization (in parallel mode). When to use: When training large volumes on limited GPU memory by chunking, and boundary consistency is critical. When not to use: When a global model can be afforded or when post-training merging is acceptable. The technique is inspired by ghost cell techniques [45], but adapted for unstructured primitives. Classical ghost cells copy boundary values from adjacent regular grid cells, but this method cannot rely on grid adjacency since the primitives are spatially unstructured. The method addresses the incompatibility of standard 3DGS screenspace rasterization with accurate TF mapping in volumetric settings. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Substitutive LOD with K-wise Moment-Matched Merging
head: Cost-aware merging, Cost-increment relocation, Gaussian Hierarchy, Greedy hierarchical LOD, Joint relaxation LOD, Level of Detail (LOD) via Gaussian Merging, Merged Gaussian LOD
body: Substitutive LOD with K-wise moment-matched merging is a technique for reducing the number of 3D Gaussians in a scene by merging groups of K splats into a single representative Gaussian, thereby boosting rendering performance and managing memory constraints. It addresses the problem of excessive Gaussian counts and associated aliasing artifacts by replacing small or redundant Gaussians with larger, merged ones. Unlike methods that modify Gaussians during reconstruction or prune based on static importance, this method operates on the final set of Gaussians using cost metrics to guide the merging process, allowing for runtime LOD selection. It sets itself apart from siblings like CoR-GS and EffGS by focusing on substitutive merging via moment matching rather than density control or vector quantization. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each Gaussian gi is defined by its mean \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai (or Cholesky factor Ri), and opacity/amplitude \alphai. Outputs: A reduced set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with N' < N Gaussians, where each output Gaussian is a moment-matched merge of K input Gaussians. Data Structures: The implementation relies on a spatial partitioning structure (e.g., grid or octree) to identify candidate groups of K Gaussians for merging. Each Gaussian is stored with its parameters: \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (symmetric positive definite). \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity or amplitude. Optional: Color coefficients (not detailed in sources for the merging math). Parameters: K: The number of Gaussians to merge into one. Compression factors of four and above are used in experiments. Cost Metric: One of L2, Cauchy–Schwarz, gKL, W2, MMD, or L∞. Partitioning Algorithm: One of Greedy Hierarchical, Cost-Increment Relocation, or Joint Relaxation. Steps: 1. Spatial Partitioning: Divide the scene into spatial bins or tiles to group nearby Gaussians. 2. Group Selection: Identify groups of K Gaussians within each bin that are candidates for merging. The selection is guided by the chosen cost metric and partitioning algorithm. 3. Merging: For each group of K Gaussians, compute a single merged Gaussian using moment matching. The merged mean \mu' and covariance \Sigma' are computed as the weighted average of the input means and covariances, weighted by their amplitudes \alphai. The merged amplitude \alpha' is optimized to minimize the L2 error between the merged Gaussian and the sum of the original Gaussians. 4. Replacement: Replace the K input Gaussians with the single merged Gaussian in the scene representation. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–4 until the desired compression factor is reached or no further beneficial merges can be found. Formulas: Merged mean: \mu' = \frac{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai \mui}{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai}. Merged covariance: \Sigma' = \frac{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai (\Sigmai + (\mui - \mu')(\mui - \mu')^T)}{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai}. L2-optimal amplitude: \alpha' = \frac{\sum{i=1}^K \alphai \mathcal{N}(\mu'; \mui, \Sigmai + \Sigma')}{\mathcal{N}(\mu'; \mu', 2\Sigma')}, where \mathcal{N}(\mua; \mub, \Sigma{sum}) is the Gaussian PDF evaluated at \mua with mean \mub and covariance \Sigma{sum}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mergegaussians(group): """Merges a group of K Gaussians into one using moment matching.""" totalalpha = sum(g.alpha for g in group) muprime = [sum(g.alpha g.mu[j] for g in group) / totalalpha for j in range(3)] sigmaprime = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for g in group: diff = [g.mu[j] - muprime[j] for j in range(3)] for r in range(3): for c in range(3): sigmaprime[r][c] += g.alpha (g.sigma[r][c] + diff[r] diff[c]) for r in range(3): for c in range(3): sigmaprime[r][c] /= totalalpha numerator = 0.0 for g in group: sumcov = [[g.sigma[r][c] + sigmaprime[r][c] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] numerator += g.alpha gaussianpdf(muprime, sumcov) denomcov = [[2 sigmaprime[r][c] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] denominator = gaussianpdf(muprime, denomcov) alphaprime = numerator / denominator return (muprime, sigmaprime, alphaprime) def gaussianpdf(mu, sigma): diff = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] inv = invert3x3(sigma) det = det3x3(sigma) exponent = -0.5 sum(diff[j] sum(inv[j][k] diff[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)) return (1.0 / ((2 3.14159265358979) 1.5 (det 0.5))) (2.718281828459045 exponent) def invert3x3(M): d = det3x3(M) return [[(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])/d, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])/d, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])/d], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])/d, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])/d, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])/d], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])/d, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])/d, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])/d]] def det3x3(M): return M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0]) def substitutivelod(gaussians, K, metric, algorithm): """Performs substitutive LOD by merging Gaussians.""" bins = {} for g in gaussians: binkey = spatialhash(g.mu) bins.setdefault(binkey, []).append(g) mergedgaussians = [] for binkey, bingaussians in bins.items(): if len(bingaussians) >= K: groups = selectgroupsfrombin(bingaussians, K, metric, algorithm) for group in groups: mergedg = mergegaussians(group) mergedgaussians.append(mergedg) remaining = bingaussians[len(groups)K:] for g in remaining: mergedgaussians.append(g) else: mergedgaussians.extend(bingaussians) return mergedgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral lower bounds have explicit limits and counterexamples where they fail to accurately predict merging quality. Precision issues may arise when computing the L2-optimal amplitude, especially for very small or very large Gaussians. Boundary effects in spatial partitioning may lead to suboptimal merging if Gaussians near bin boundaries are not considered. A partitioning algorithm that merges Gaussians hierarchically, similar to the Runnalls algorithm. A partitioning algorithm that relocates Gaussians to minimize the cost increment of merging. It matches greedy merging within 5.5% at compression factors of four and above. A partitioning algorithm that relaxes the merging constraints to find a globally optimal solution. Time Complexity: Depends on the partitioning algorithm and the cost metric. Memory Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussians by a factor of K, thus reducing memory usage by approximately 1/K. Measured Performance: Cost-increment relocation matches greedy merging within 5.5% at compression factors of four and above. Cost-aware merging beats mass-ranked culling with and without amplitude refit on full fits, while culling wins in the median on sparse subsamples. Strengths: Effective at reducing aliasing and managing memory footprint, especially on mobile devices. Limitations: Spectral lower bounds may fail to predict merging quality accurately. When to Use: When memory constraints are tight or rendering performance needs to be boosted without modifying the reconstruction process. When Not to Use: When high fidelity is required and compression artifacts are unacceptable. The method was introduced in the context of Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualization. It builds on earlier work by Yan et al. [24] who combined Gaussians to solve aliasing problems, and Kerbl et al. [18] who introduced a hierarchy of Gaussians. The technique is part of the broader effort to make 3D Gaussian Splatting more efficient and scalable, particularly for mobile and web-based applications. name: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: 3DGS with temporal constraints, DG-Mesh, Li et al
body: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle time-varying scenes by assigning time-varying position and rotation attributes to each Gaussian primitive. It solves the problem of temporal flicker and storage explosion inherent in per-frame baselines by enforcing physical plausibility through local-rigid and As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) or isometry constraints. Unlike 4D Gaussian Splatting which uses implicit neural fields or planes to predict deformation offsets from a canonical space, this method explicitly tracks the motion of each Gaussian particle, offering a more direct representation of dynamic geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of T images \{It\}{t=1}^T with known camera poses \{Ct\}{t=1}^T. Outputs: A set of N dynamic 3D Gaussians, where each Gaussian i is defined by a time-varying position \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t), rotation qi(t), scale \mathbf{s}i (static), opacity \alphai(t), and color representation. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3: Time-varying center position. qi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^4: Time-varying unit quaternion for rotation. \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Static scale vector. \alphai(t) \in \mathbb{R}: Time-varying opacity. Color features: Base color \mathbf{c}{base}, view-related feature \mathbf{f}{view}, time-related feature \mathbf{f}{time}. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians from the first frame or via structure-from-motion, similar to static 3DGS. 2. Temporal Parameterization: Position and Rotation: Model \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) and qi(t) using a polynomial function. Other variants use local-rigid constraints or ARAP/isometry constraints to ensure physically plausible deformation. Opacity: Model \alphai(t) using a temporal radial basis function (RBF) to handle appearance and disappearance of content. Color: Replace spherical harmonics with a feature-based approach. The final color \mathbf{c}i(t, \mathbf{v}) is computed as: \mathbf{c}i(t, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{c}{base} + \text{MLP}(\mathbf{f}{view}, \mathbf{f}{time}) where \mathbf{c}{base} is the base color, and the MLP outputs a residual color based on view direction \mathbf{v} and time t. 3. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between rendered images and ground truth images. Apply Temporal Smoothness Loss: Encourages smooth motion trajectories over time. Apply kNN Rigid Loss: Enforces local rigidity by comparing the motion of neighboring Gaussians. Densification: During optimization, sample new 3D Gaussians at under-optimized positions based on training error and coarse depth estimates to capture new details or dynamic regions. 4. Rendering: For a given time t and camera pose Ct: Compute \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) and qi(t) for all Gaussians. Project the Gaussians to 2D using the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline. Render using the time-varying opacity and color features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class DynamicGaussian: def init(self, mu0, q0, s, cbase, fview, ftime, polypos, polyrot, rbfcenters, rbfweights): self.mu0 = mu0 self.q0 = q0 self.s = s self.cbase = cbase self.fview = fview self.ftime = ftime self.polypos = polypos self.polyrot = polyrot self.rbfcenters = rbfcenters self.rbfweights = rbfweights def evaluatepolynomial(coeffs, t): """Evaluates polynomial given coefficients [c0, c1,...] at time t.""" dim = len(coeffs[0]) result = [0.0] dim for k, c in enumerate(coeffs): for d in range(dim): result[d] += c[d] (t k) return result def normalizequaternion(q): norm = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in q)) return [x / norm for x in q] if norm > 1e-8 else q def computeattributes(g, t): mut = evaluatepolynomial(g.polypos, t) qt = normalizequaternion(evaluatepolynomial(g.polyrot, t)) alphat = 0.0 for center, weight in zip(g.rbfcenters, g.rbfweights): alphat += weight math.exp(-((t - center) 2)) alphat = max(0.0, min(1.0, alphat)) residual = [sum(ab for a, b in zip(g.fview, g.ftime)) / len(g.fview)] 3 color = [g.cbase[i] + residual[i] for i in range(3)] return mut, qt, alphat, color def renderframe(gaussians, camera, t): framegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: mut, qt, alphat, color = computeattributes(g, t) framegaussians.append({'pos': mut, 'rot': qt, 'scale': g.s, 'opacity': alphat, 'color': color}) projected = [] for g in framegaussians: depth = g['pos'][2] projected.append({'depth': depth, 'opacity': g['opacity'], 'color': g['color']}) projected.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) image = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for g in projected: alpha = g['opacity'] for c in range(3): image[c] = image[c] (1 - alpha) + g['color'][c] alpha return image Parameters: Polynomial degree for position/rotation: Not given in the sources. RBF centers and widths: Not given in the sources. MLP architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vanishing Content: The RBF opacity model handles appearance and disappearance of content over time. GaussianFlow is a point-based differentiable rendering approach for dynamic 3D scene reconstruction that models a 4D scene as a set of deformable 3D Gaussian particles advected by an explicit 3D velocity field. It solves the problem of efficient dynamic scene reconstruction by introducing a Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM) that explicitly models attribute deformations (position, rotation, radiance) in both time and frequency domains, eliminating the need for implicit neural fields or per-frame optimization. Unlike Dynamic 3D Gaussians which tracks motion via persistent view synthesis and local constraints, GaussianFlow uses a global flow-based deformation model, achieving 5× faster training than per-frame 3DGS while preserving real-time rendering speeds. Dynamic 3D Gaussians performs tracking by persistent dynamic view synthesis, linking the motion of each Gaussian to the movement of a corresponding 3D point in the scene. It extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle dynamic scenes by explicitly defining a tracking mechanism that differs from its parent Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting and from GaussianFlow by relying on persistent synthesis rather than flow-based deformation fields. SWAGS is a dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting method that addresses the challenge of modeling complex, non-rigid motion in dynamic scenes by partitioning the temporal sequence into distinct windows based on motion intensity. Unlike sibling methods that track a single global deformation field or flow across the entire sequence, SWAGS trains separate dynamic 3DGS models for each window, each with its own canonical space and deformation field, thereby isolating local motion characteristics. This approach improves reconstruction fidelity for highly dynamic segments while maintaining temporal consistency through fine-tuning on overlapping frames. SpeeDe3DGS is a method that accelerates deformable 3DGS by applying temporal pruning. It identifies static and active Gaussians and groups the dynamic parts by motion similarity to reduce the number of deformation queries. This variant constructs an opacity offset table to model changes in digital subtraction angiography. This method leverages a diffusion prior to enhance dynamic scene reconstruction and proposes a neural bone transformation module for reconstructing animatable objects from monocular video. DynMF assumes that each dynamic scene is composed of a finite, fixed number of motion trajectories represented in a learned basis, generated by a small temporal MLP. All motion trajectories in the scene can be linearly represented in this learned basis, with regularization, sparsity, and local rigidity terms introduced during optimization. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to per-frame baselines due to explicit deformation modeling, but depends on the complexity of the temporal functions (polynomial/RBF) and the MLP for color. GaussianFlow claims 5× faster training than per-frame 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Storage is linear in the number of Gaussians N and the size of the temporal parameters (polynomial coefficients, RBF weights, MLP weights). It is more compact than storing a full 3DGS per frame but potentially larger than implicit deformation fields if the number of Gaussians is high. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Large-scale scenes stress the rasterizer through primitive count and memory bandwidth, similar to static 3DGS. Strengths: Real-time rendering of dynamic scenes; explicit representation allows for easy editing and manipulation; avoids overfitting associated with implicit neural fields. Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Luiten et al. in 3DV'24. It emerged as a response to the limitations of per-frame 3DGS training, which suffers from storage explosion and temporal flicker. The method builds on the explicit nature of 3D Gaussian Splatting, extending it to 4D by parameterizing the Gaussian attributes over time. It is part of a broader family of dynamic 3DGS methods, including 4D Gaussian Splatting and Deformable 3DGS, which explore different approaches to modeling temporal dynamics. name: GaussianFlow
head: DDDM
body: GaussianFlow is a point-based differentiable rendering method for dynamic 3D scene reconstruction that models a 4D scene as a set of deformable 3D Gaussian particles advected by a 3D velocity field. It solves the problem of efficient, high-fidelity reconstruction from monocular or multi-view video by replacing implicit neural deformation fields with an explicit Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM). Unlike its sibling Dynamic 3D Gaussians, which tracks time-varying attributes via local-rigid and ARAP constraints, GaussianFlow explicitly models attribute deformations in both time and frequency domains to capture complex motions without neural networks. It differs from Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade, which applies optical flow directly to rendered primitives for alignment, by using an explicit flow field for temporal regularization of the underlying Gaussian parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of images (monocular or multi-view) with known camera poses (or estimated poses) and timestamps t. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gj\} where each Gaussian j has time-varying attributes: position \boldsymbol{\mu}j(t), rotation qj(t), scale \mathbf{s}j(t), and color \mathbf{c}j(t). Data Structures: Each Gaussian j stores canonical (static) attributes and deformation coefficients for the DDDM. Canonical Position: \boldsymbol{\mu}j^0 \in \mathbb{R}^3 Canonical Rotation: qj^0 \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) Canonical Scale: \mathbf{s}j^0 \in \mathbb{R}^3 Canonical Color: \mathbf{c}j^0 \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or SH coefficients) Deformation Coefficients: Stored per attribute, representing polynomial and Fourier coefficients. Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM): The DDDM models the time-dependent residual for each deformable attribute (position, rotation, scale, color) by combining polynomial fitting in the time domain and Fourier approximation in the frequency domain. For a generic attribute A (e.g., position component x), the value at time t is: Aj(t) = Aj^0 + \Delta Aj^{\text{poly}}(t) + \Delta Aj^{\text{fourier}}(t) 1. Time Domain (Polynomial): Captures smooth, low-frequency motion. \Delta Aj^{\text{poly}}(t) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \alpha{j,k}^A t^k where \alpha{j,k}^A are learned polynomial coefficients and K is the polynomial order. 2. Frequency Domain (Fourier): Captures high-frequency, "violent" motions or oscillations. \Delta Aj^{\text{fourier}}(t) = \sum{m=1}^{M} \left( \beta{j,m}^A \cos(2\pi m t) + \gamma{j,m}^A \sin(2\pi m t) \right) where \beta{j,m}^A, \gamma{j,m}^A are learned Fourier coefficients and M is the number of harmonics. Adaptive Timestep Scaling: To prevent optimization problems caused by uniform time division (e.g., overfitting to frames with violent motion), adaptive timestep scaling is applied. The time t is normalized or scaled based on the temporal distribution of the input frames, ensuring that the polynomial and Fourier bases are well-conditioned across the video duration. Optimization Loop: The training iterates between static optimization and dynamic optimization. 1. Static Optimization: Optimizes canonical attributes \boldsymbol{\mu}j^0, qj^0, \mathbf{s}j^0, \mathbf{c}j^0 while keeping deformation coefficients fixed or zero-initialized. 2. Dynamic Optimization: Optimizes the deformation coefficients (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) and potentially refines canonical attributes. Loss Functions: Image Loss: Standard photometric loss between rendered and input images. Bidirectional Optical Flow Loss: 2D flow estimation results are introduced into training to support deformation modeling between neighboring frames. Temporal Smoothness Loss: Encourages smooth variation of attributes over time. KNN Rigid Loss: Regularizes the motion trajectory by applying KNN-based rigid constraints, ensuring that neighboring Gaussians move coherently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializegaussians(images, timestamps): """ Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians from static 3DGS initialization. Returns list of Gaussian objects with canonical attributes and zero deformation coeffs. """ # Standard 3DGS initialization from SfM points or random seeding gaussians = [] for i in range(numgaussians): g = Gaussian() g.mu0 = canonicalposition[i] g.q0 = canonicalrotation[i] g.s0 = canonicalscale[i] g.c0 = canonicalcolor[i] # Initialize deformation coefficients to zero g.alphapoly = np.zeros(K) g.betafourier = np.zeros(M) g.gammafourier = np.zeros(M) gaussians.append(g) return gaussians def computedeformation(g, t): """ Compute time-varying attributes for Gaussian g at time t using DDDM. """ # Polynomial part polypos = sum(g.alphapoly[k] (t (k+1)) for k in range(K)) # Fourier part fourierpos = sum( g.betafourier[m] np.cos(2 np.pi (m+1) t) + g.gammafourier[m] np.sin(2 np.pi (m+1) t) for m in range(M)) # Total deformation residual deltapos = polypos + fourierpos # Apply to canonical position mut = g.mu0 + deltapos # Repeat for rotation, scale, color (using respective coefficients) # Rotation requires quaternion integration; scale/color are additive/multiplicative return mut, qt, st, ct def adaptivetimescaling(timestamps): """ Scale timestamps to prevent optimization issues from uniform division. """ # Normalize timestamps to [0, 1] or use a non-linear mapping based on frame density tmin = min(timestamps) tmax = max(timestamps) scaledts = [(t - tmin) / (tmax - tmin) for t in timestamps] return scaledts def traingaussianflow(images, timestamps, numiterations): gaussians = initializegaussians(images, timestamps) scaledtimestamps = adaptivetimescaling(timestamps) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Alternate between static and dynamic optimization if iteration % 2 == 0: # Static Optimization optimizecanonicalattributes(gaussians, images, scaledtimestamps) else: # Dynamic Optimization optimizedeformationcoeffs(gaussians, images, scaledtimestamps) # Compute losses imgloss = computeimageloss(gaussians, images, scaledtimestamps) flowloss = computebidirectionalflowloss(gaussians, images, scaledtimestamps) smoothloss = computetemporalsmoothnessloss(gaussians, scaledtimestamps) rigidloss = computeknnrigidloss(gaussians, scaledtimestamps) totalloss = imgloss + flowloss + smoothloss + rigidloss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return gaussians Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade is a method that directly applies optical flow estimation to the rendered Gaussians, using the flow to align dynamic objects across frames and improve temporal consistency. It distinguishes itself from parent method GaussianFlow, which uses an explicit flow field for temporal regularization, by operating directly on the rendered Gaussian primitives rather than an explicit geometric point cloud or a separate flow MLP. MotionGS is a dynamic representation method that adds explicit motion supervision to the deformation field by decomposing optical flow into camera and object motion components. It uses the formula F^M{t\to t+1} = F{t\to t+1} - F^C{t\to t+1}, where F^M{t\to t+1} is the object motion flow, F{t\to t+1} is the total optical flow, and F^C{t\to t+1} is the camera-induced flow. The flow loss is defined as L{\text{flow}} = \| sg(F^M{t\to t+1}) - F^G{t\to t+1} \|1, where sg is the stop-gradient operator and F^G{t\to t+1} is the projected Gaussian flow. A known pitfall is that MotionGS exhausted 80 GB GPU memory at iteration 7,600 on the DyNeRF flamesteak sequence and did not complete. Training Speed: Achieves 5× faster training speed compared with per-frame 3DGS modeling. Rendering Speed: Preserves ultra-fast rendering speed comparable to original 3DGS, enabling real-time rendering. Memory: More memory-efficient than implicit neural field methods and per-frame 3DGS, as it stores a single set of Gaussians with deformation coefficients rather than duplicating geometry per frame. Strengths: Handles complex scene deformations across long video footage; supports both multi-view and monocular videos; explicit deformation modeling avoids the slow training/rendering of NeRF-based approaches. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of polynomial order K and Fourier harmonics M; adaptive timestep scaling is necessary to avoid overfitting to violent motions. When to Use: Dynamic scene reconstruction and real-time rendering from monocular or multi-view videos where training speed and rendering fidelity are critical. When Not to Use: If the scene has extremely sparse temporal sampling or if the motion is highly non-smooth and cannot be captured by low-order polynomials and Fourier series. GaussianFlow was introduced by Yao et al. in 2024. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for static scenes and addresses the limitations of NeRF-based dynamic reconstruction methods, which suffer from slow training and rendering speeds. The method was developed to enable fast dynamic scene reconstruction and real-time rendering from both multi-view and monocular videos. It is used in applications requiring high-fidelity 4D reconstruction and real-time rendering, such as virtual reality and digital twins. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian-Flow: 4D Reconstruction with Dynamic 3D Gaussian Particle, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01997, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting for real-time scene reconstruction: Methods, systems, and trade-offs, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2026.115120, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade
body: Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade directly applies optical flow estimation to rendered Gaussians to align dynamic objects across frames and improve temporal consistency. It distinguishes itself from its parent method GaussianFlow, which uses an explicit flow field for temporal regularization, by operating directly on the rendered Gaussian primitives rather than an explicit geometric point cloud or a separate flow MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of 2D image frames and a set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene. Output: Temporally consistent 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) aligned across frames. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: A collection of N Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{p}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. Optical Flow Field: A 2D vector field \mathbf{u}(x, y) representing pixel displacement between frames. Steps: 1. Render: Render the current frame using the current set of 3D Gaussians via differentiable rasterization. 2. Estimate Flow: Compute the optical flow \mathbf{u}(x, y) between the rendered frame and the target frame using a standard Lucas-Kanade optical flow algorithm or a learned equivalent. 3. Align Gaussians: Map the 2D optical flow to 3D space by determining each Gaussian's projected 2D center \mathbf{c}i and applying the flow vector \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{c}i) to update the Gaussian's position or adjust its parameters to minimize photometric error. 4. Update: Update the Gaussian parameters based on the flow alignment, which may involve translating Gaussian centers or adjusting covariances to account for motion blur or deformation. 5. Iterate: Repeat for subsequent frames to maintain temporal consistency. Formulas: Lucas-Kanade Optical Flow: Solves for \mathbf{u} by minimizing \sum{i \in W} \left( I1(xi + ux, yi + uy) - I0(xi, yi) \right)^2, where I0, I1 are image intensities, W is a window around the pixel, and \mathbf{u} = (ux, uy). Gaussian Update: The position \mathbf{p}i is updated by \Delta \mathbf{p}i derived from the flow. Parameters: Window Size: For Lucas-Kanade, typically 5 \times 5 or 7 \times 7 pixels. Regularization: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Large Motions: Standard Lucas-Kanade assumes small motions; large displacements may require pyramidal approaches. Degenerate Input: Low-texture regions may yield unreliable flow. Occlusions: Flow estimation may fail in occluded regions. Scene Flow Prior enhances the temporal consistency of 4D spatio-temporal representations by incorporating a flow Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for motion estimation. It maps spatio-temporal coordinates from \mathbb{R}^4 to motion fields in \mathbb{R}^3, predicting displacement only between adjacent frames to avoid the difficulty of establishing long-term correspondences in deformable scenes. Unlike its parent method, Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade, which applies optical flow to rendered Gaussians, this method operates on explicit geometric point clouds derived from LiDAR data to impose a motion prior and geometric supervision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Direct application to Gaussians; improves temporal consistency. Limitations: Relies on accurate optical flow; may struggle with large motions or occlusions. When to Use: Dynamic scenes requiring temporal consistency in Gaussian Splatting. When Not to Use: Scenes with large, unstructured motions or significant occlusions where flow estimation is unreliable. Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade is a method that directly applies optical flow estimation to the rendered Gaussians, using the flow to align dynamic objects across frames and improve temporal consistency. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and optical flow estimation. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Scene Flow Prior
head: Flow MLP for motion estimation
body: Scene Flow Prior enhances the temporal consistency of 4D spatio-temporal representations by incorporating a flow Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for motion estimation. It maps spatio-temporal coordinates from \mathbb{R}^4 to motion fields in \mathbb{R}^3, predicting displacement only between adjacent frames to avoid the difficulty of establishing long-term correspondences in deformable scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Spatio-temporal coordinates (\mathbf{x}, t) where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and t is the time index; LiDAR point clouds Si for frame i. Outputs: Predicted scene flow displacement \Delta \mathbf{x}; transformed point cloud \mathbf{x}'. Data Structures: Flow MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that processes position-encoded inputs. Positional Encoding: \gamma(\mathbf{x}, t) applies element-wise sine and cosine functions across L frequency bands to the concatenated coordinate and time vector. Point Clouds: Sets of 3D points S and \hat{S} representing two adjacent frames, each containing K points. Parameters: L: Number of frequency bands in positional encoding. K: Number of points in each point cloud set. n: Total number of frames in the sequence. Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Encode the input coordinate \mathbf{x} and time t using \gamma(\mathbf{x}, t). 2. Flow Prediction: Feed the encoded coordinates into the flow MLP to predict the displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x}: \Delta \mathbf{x} = \mathrm{MLP}\mathrm{flow}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}, t)) 3. Motion Application: Compute the transformed coordinate \mathbf{x}': \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x} 4. Geometric Loss Calculation: Supervise the motion prediction by calculating the Chamfer Distance (CD) between the predicted transformed point cloud and the ground truth point cloud of the adjacent frame. The flow loss \mathcal{L}\mathrm{flow} sums the CD over forward and backward adjacent frames: \mathcal{L}\mathrm{flow} = \sum{j \in \{-1, 1\}} \mathrm{CD}(Si + \mathrm{MLP}\mathrm{flow}(Si), S{i+j}) where i \in (0, n-1). 5. Chamfer Distance Definition: The Chamfer Distance between two point cloud sets S and \hat{S} is defined as: \mathrm{CD} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{\hat{p}i \in \hat{S}} \min{pi \in S} \|\hat{p}i - pi\|2^2 + \frac{1}{K} \sum{pi \in S} \min{\hat{p}i \in \hat{S}} \|pi - \hat{p}i\|2^2 where S and \hat{S} are two frames of point clouds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(coords, L): """Applies positional encoding to coordinates. coords: (N, D) array L: int, number of frequency bands Returns: (N, 2 D L) encoded vector """ frequencies = 2.0 np.arange(L) encoded = [] for freq in frequencies: encoded.append(np.sin(coords freq)) encoded.append(np.cos(coords freq)) return np.concatenate(encoded, axis=1) def mlpforward(x, weights): """Standard MLP forward pass. x: (N, Din) weights: list of (W, b) tuples Returns: (N, Dout) """ for W, b in weights: x = x @ W + b x = np.maximum(0, x) # ReLU activation return x def chamferdistance(S, Shat): """Computes Chamfer Distance between two point clouds. S: (K, 3), Shat: (K, 3) Returns: float """ K = S.shape[0] # Pairwise squared Euclidean distances dists = np.sum((S[:, np.newaxis,:] - Shat[np.newaxis,:,:]) 2, axis=2) # Minimum distances for each point in Shat to S minShattoS = np.min(dists, axis=1) # Minimum distances for each point in S to Shat minStoShat = np.min(dists, axis=0) cd = (1.0 / K) np.sum(minShattoS) + (1.0 / K) np.sum(minStoShat) return cd def computeflowloss(Si, Sadj, flowmlpweights, L, ti): """Computes flow loss for a frame and its adjacent frame. Si: (K, 3) point cloud of frame i Sadj: (K, 3) point cloud of frame i+j flowmlpweights: weights for the flow MLP L: positional encoding bands ti: time index of Si Returns: float, CD value """ # Concatenate coordinates and time for encoding coordswithtime = np.concatenate([Si, np.full((Si.shape[0], 1), ti)], axis=1) encoded = positionalencoding(coordswithtime, L) # Predict displacement deltax = mlpforward(encoded, flowmlpweights) # Transform point cloud Sitransformed = Si + deltax # Compute Chamfer Distance return chamferdistance(Sitransformed, Sadj) def totalflowloss(Sall, flowmlpweights, L): """Computes total flow loss over all frames. Sall: list of (K, 3) arrays for frames 0 to n-1 Returns: float, total Lflow """ n = len(Sall) totalloss = 0.0 for i in range(n): for j in [-1, 1]: targetidx = i + j if 0 <= targetidx < n: # Boundary guard totalloss += computeflowloss(Sall[i], Sall[targetidx], flowmlpweights, L, ti=i) return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Long-term Correspondences: The method explicitly avoids long-term correspondences to canonical space because vehicle motion range may span a long distance in autonomous driving scenarios, making such correspondences hard to establish. Precision: The Chamfer Distance uses squared Euclidean norms, which penalize large errors quadratically. Boundary Conditions: The index i ranges over valid frame indices where adjacent frames exist, and the summation over j \in \{-1, 1\} naturally skips out-of-bounds targets. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enhances temporal consistency by leveraging explicit geometric constraints from LiDAR point clouds and imposes a motion prior that helps in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Relies on the availability of LiDAR point clouds, and predicting motion only between adjacent frames may require proper aggregation to maintain consistency over long sequences. When to Use: Suitable for dynamic scene reconstruction in autonomous driving scenarios where LiDAR data is available and temporal consistency is critical. The Scene Flow Prior method is part of the LiDAR4D framework, introduced in the paper "LiDAR4D: Dynamic Neural Fields for Novel Space-Time View LiDAR Synthesis". It was developed to address the challenges of reconstructing dynamic scenes from LiDAR data, specifically focusing on temporal consistency and geometric accuracy. The method builds on the idea of using flow MLPs for motion estimation, as seen in prior works cited in the source.
