name: Dynamic 3D Gaussians
head: Persistent Dynamic View Synthesis, Tracking by Persistent Dynamic View Synthesis
body: Dynamic 3D Gaussians is a method for dynamic scene novel-view synthesis and 6-DOF tracking that models a scene as a collection of 3D Gaussians which move and rotate over time while maintaining persistent color, opacity, and size. It performs tracking by persistent dynamic view synthesis, linking the motion of each Gaussian to the movement of a corresponding 3D point in the scene. Unlike Eulerian representations or canonical-space deformation fields, this method uses a Lagrangian particle-based representation where Gaussians move through space, enabling natural long-term correspondence without explicit flow or canonical warping. It sets itself apart from siblings like GaussianFlow and SWAGS by fixing geometric attributes (scale, color, opacity) after the first timestep and optimizing only motion parameters with physical regularization losses. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Synchronized multi-view video frames I{t,c} for timesteps t=0 \dots T and cameras c. Camera intrinsics Kc and extrinsics E{t,c}. Optional sparse depth samples for initialization. Outputs: A sequence of scene representations St, each consisting of a set of Dynamic 3D Gaussians with time-varying positions \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t} and rotations q{i,t}, and static attributes (scale Si, color ci, opacity oi, background logit bgi). Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: Position: \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (optimized per timestep) Rotation: q{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion, optimized per timestep) Scale: Si = \text{diag}(s{xi}, s{yi}, s{zi}) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (fixed after t=0) Color: ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 (fixed after t=0) Opacity logit: oi \in \mathbb{R} (fixed after t=0) Background logit: bgi \in \mathbb{R} (fixed after t=0) Total parameters per Gaussian: 7 parameters per timestep (3 position + 4 rotation) + 8 static parameters. Number of Gaussians: 200,000–300,000 per scene. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (t=0): Initialize a sparse point cloud using available depth samples. Optimize all Gaussian properties (\boldsymbol{\mu}{i,0}, q{i,0}, Si, ci, oi, bgi) using gradient-based optimization with a differentiable renderer \mathcal{R} for 10,000 iterations. Apply densification (from 3D Gaussian Splatting) to increase density. Compute initial neighbor weights w{i,j} based on distance at t=0 (see Formula 3). 2. Subsequent Timesteps (t > 0): Initialization: Estimate initial position and rotation for timestep t using forward velocity from t-1: \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t}^{init} = \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t-1} + v{i,t-1} q{i,t}^{init} = \text{normalize}(q{i,t-1} \otimes \Delta q) where v{i,t-1} = \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t-1} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t-2} (or similar velocity estimate) and \Delta q is the normalized quaternion difference. Reset Optimizer: Reset Adam optimizer first and second order momentum parameters. Optimization: Optimize only \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t} and q{i,t} for 2,000 iterations. Fix Si, ci, oi, bgi. Rendering: Render scene St into each training camera c: \hat{I}{t,c} = \mathcal{R}(St, Kc, E{t,c}) \quad \text{[Formula 1]} Loss Calculation: Compute losses (see Formulas 2-6) and update parameters via automatic differentiation. Formulas: 1. Rendering: \hat{I}{t,c} = \mathcal{R}(St, Kc, E{t,c}) where \mathcal{R} is the differentiable renderer, St is the scene representation, Kc is intrinsic matrix, E{t,c} is extrinsic matrix. 2. 3D Gaussian Influence: f{i,t}(p) = \text{sigm}(oi) \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (p - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t})^T \Sigma{i,t}^{-1} (p - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t}) \right) where \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t} is the center, \Sigma{i,t} is the covariance, oi is opacity logit. 3. Covariance Construction: \Sigma{i,t} = R{i,t} Si Si^T R{i,t}^T where Si = \text{diag}(s{xi}, s{yi}, s{zi}) and R{i,t} is the rotation matrix derived from quaternion q{i,t}. 4. 2D Splatting (Center): \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} = K ((E\boldsymbol{\mu})/(E\boldsymbol{\mu})z) where K is intrinsic matrix, E is extrinsic matrix, \boldsymbol{\mu} is 3D center, (E\boldsymbol{\mu})z is the z-component of the transformed center. 5. 2D Splatting (Covariance): \Sigma{2D} = J E \Sigma E^T J^T where J is the Jacobian of the point projection formula (\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D} / \partial \boldsymbol{\mu}). 6. Volume Rendering: C{pix} = \sum{i \in S} ci f{2D}^{i,pix} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - f{2D}^{j,pix}) where ci is color, f{2D}^{i,pix} is 2D influence, sorted by depth. 7. Local Rigidity Loss: L{rigid}^{i,j} = w{i,j} \| (\boldsymbol{\mu}{j,t-1} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t-1}) - R{i,t-1} R{i,t}^{-1} (\boldsymbol{\mu}{j,t} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t}) \|^2 Enforces rigid body transform consistency between neighbors i and j. 8. Total Local Rigidity Loss: L{rigid} = \frac{1}{k|S|} \sum{i \in S} \sum{j \in knn{i;k}} L{rigid}^{i,j} where k=20 nearest neighbors. 9. Local Rotation Similarity Loss: L{rot} = \frac{1}{k|S|} \sum{i \in S} \sum{j \in knn{i;k}} w{i,j} \| \hat{q}{j,t} \hat{q}{j,t-1}^{-1} - \hat{q}{i,t} \hat{q}{i,t-1}^{-1} \|^2 where \hat{q} is normalized quaternion. 10. Long-term Local Isometry Loss: L{iso} = \frac{1}{k|S|} \sum{i \in S} \sum{j \in knn{i;k}} w{i,j} | \| \boldsymbol{\mu}{j,0} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,0} \|^2 - \| \boldsymbol{\mu}{j,t} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,t} \|^2 | Enforces constant distance between neighbors over time. 11. Neighbor Weighting: w{i,j} = \exp(-\lambdaw \| \boldsymbol{\mu}{j,0} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,0} \|^22) with \lambdaw = 2000 (std dev ~2.2cm). Parameters: Number of Gaussians: 200,000–300,000. Training cameras: 27. Optimization iterations: 10,000 for t=0; 2,000 for t>0. Rigidity weight \lambdaw: 2000. Spherical harmonics: Off. Densification: Only at t=0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Requires synchronized multi-view video; does not support monocular video. Mis-tracking occurs for foreground objects with colors similar to background (e.g., grey shirt vs grey background). Gaussians may move freely in uniform color areas without physical regularization. Drift of scene elements over long time horizons due to short-term loss enforcement. Background points should not move or rotate; losses are restricted to foreground points to avoid enforcing rigidity between foreground and static floor. A method to estimate the 3D position of a Gaussian primitive at a current frame t from its position at a previous frame t' using 2D point tracking and triangulation. It computes 2D projections across N input views, runs 2D point tracking to obtain corresponding 2D pixel positions, and recovers 3D position by finding the closest point to the N camera rays. Motion is propagated from sparse anchor points (selected via farthest point sampling) to the entire scene using an embedded deformation graph, connecting each splat to its K nearest anchor points with blend weights based on spatial distances. It maintains primitives only from a set of past keyframes, smoothly adjusting contributions as older keyframes are replaced. Time Complexity: Optimization is performed per timestep. First timestep takes ~4 minutes (10,000 iterations); subsequent timesteps take ~50 seconds (2,000 iterations). Total training time: 2 hours for 150 timesteps on a single RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Stores 15 parameters per Gaussian. 200,000–300,000 Gaussians per scene. Measured Performance: Renders at 850 FPS. Achieves 28.7 PSNR on dynamic novel view rendering. Average L2 error of 2.21cm in 3D tracking over 150 timesteps. Scaling: Rendering speed is high due to graphics/CUDA optimizations. Strengths: Real-time rendering, accurate 6-DOF tracking, persistent color/opacity/size, Lagrangian representation avoids canonical warping. Limitations: Requires multi-view input, sensitive to color similarity between foreground/background, potential drift over long horizons. When to use: Dynamic scene reconstruction with synchronized multi-view video where persistent tracking and real-time rendering are needed. When not to use: Monocular video input, scenes with significant textureless uniform regions without physical priors. Dynamic 3D Gaussians was introduced in the paper "Dynamic 3D Gaussians: Tracking by Persistent Dynamic View Synthesis". It follows an analysis-by-synthesis framework, inspired by 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method falls into the category of Lagrangian representations, where an observer follows a particular particle through space and time, contrasting with Eulerian representations that track motion at fixed grid locations. It was evaluated on the CMU Panoptic Studio dataset. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Dynamic 3D Gaussians: Tracking by Persistent Dynamic View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00044, fetched 2026-10-26 Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: SWAGS
body: SWAGS is a dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting method that partitions a dynamic sequence into distinct windows based on motion amount. It trains separate dynamic 3DGS models for each window, each with its own canonical space and deformation field. The deformation field employs a tunable MLP that focuses on modeling the dynamic part of the scene. Temporal consistency across windows is ensured through fine-tuning on overlapping frames. Inputs and outputs: Input is a sequence of frames with timestamps and a motion partitioning criterion. Output is a set of window-specific models, each containing canonical Gaussians, a tunable MLP deformation field, and 4D rendering parameters. Data structures: Each window maintains a canonical space (reference geometry), a tunable MLP deformation field, and a set of 3D Gaussians. Time-varying parameters are computed at render time. The 4D scaling matrix is diagonal, formed by appending a time-dimension scaling factor to the 3D scaling matrix diagonal. View-dependent color uses a 4D spherical harmonics extension, combining 3D SH with 1D time basis functions. Numbered steps: 1. Partition the dynamic sequence into windows based on motion amount. 2. For each window, initialize a canonical space and a tunable MLP deformation field. 3. Train a separate dynamic 3DGS model per window, optimizing canonical Gaussians and MLP parameters. 4. Identify overlapping frames between adjacent windows. 5. Fine-tune the models using overlapping frames to enforce temporal consistency. During this phase, freeze the MLP parameters and optimize only the canonical representation. Formulas: 4D scaling matrix: S{4D} = \text{diag}(S{3D}, st), where st is the time-dimension scaling factor. 4D spherical harmonics: SH{4D}(\omega, t) = SH{3D}(\omega) \otimes B1(t), combining 3D SH with 1D time basis functions B1(t). Parameters: Motion threshold for window partitioning (typical values not given in the sources). Edge cases and pitfalls: Insufficient overlap between windows or inadequate fine-tuning iterations may cause temporal discontinuities at window boundaries. Precision in time-dimension scaling and basis function evaluation must be maintained to avoid artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def swagstrain(sequenceframes, motionthreshold): # Step 1: Divide sequence into windows based on motion amount windows = [] currentwindow = [] for frame in sequenceframes: currentwindow.append(frame) if len(currentwindow) >= motionthreshold: windows.append(currentwindow) currentwindow = [] if currentwindow: windows.append(currentwindow) trainedmodels = [] for windowframes in windows: # Step 2: Initialize canonical space and tunable MLP deformation field canonicalgaussians = initializecanonicalgaussians(windowframes) # Standard 3DGS initialization deformationmlp = TunableMLP() model = Dynamic3DGSModel(canonicalgaussians, deformationmlp, windowframes) # Step 3: Train separate dynamic 3DGS model per window model.train() trainedmodels.append(model) # Step 4 & 5: Fine-tune for temporal consistency using overlapping frames for i in range(len(trainedmodels) - 1): overlapframes = findoverlapframes(trainedmodels[i].frames, trainedmodels[i+1].frames) if overlapframes: trainedmodels[i].freezemlp() trainedmodels[i+1].freezemlp() trainedmodels[i].optimizecanonical(overlapframes) trainedmodels[i+1].optimizecanonical(overlapframes) return trainedmodels class TunableMLP: def init(self): self.weights = initializeweights() # Standard weight initialization def forward(self, canonicalpos, timet): return applymlp(self.weights, canonicalpos, timet) # Standard MLP forward pass class Dynamic3DGSModel: def init(self, canonicalgaussians, deformationmlp, frames): self.canonicalgaussians = canonicalgaussians self.deformationmlp = deformationmlp self.frames = frames self.mlpfrozen = False def freezemlp(self): self.mlpfrozen = True def train(self): for frame in self.frames: rendered = renderframe(self.canonicalgaussians, self.deformationmlp, frame) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, frame.image) updateparameters(loss, self.canonicalgaussians, self.deformationmlp) def optimizecanonical(self, overlapframes): for frame in overlapframes: rendered = renderframe(self.canonicalgaussians, self.deformationmlp, frame) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, frame.image) updateparameters(loss, self.canonicalgaussians, frozenmlp=self.deformationmlp) def renderframe(self, canonicalgaussians, deformationmlp, frame): worldgaussians = [] for g in canonicalgaussians: tmu = g.position + deformationmlp.forward(g.position, frame.time) S4d = construct4dscalingmatrix(g.scale, frame.time) sh4d = compute4dsh(g.sh3d, frame.time) worldgaussians.append(Gaussian(tmu, g.rotation, S4d, g.opacity, sh4d)) return rasterizegaussians(worldgaussians, frame.camerapose) def construct4dscalingmatrix(scale3d, timet): return diagonalmatrix(scale3d + [timescalingfactor(timet)]) def compute4dsh(sh3d, timet): return combineshbasis(sh3d, timebasis(timet)) Complexity: Memory and compute scale linearly with the number of windows and the size of each window's Gaussian set. Exact complexity bounds are not given in the sources. Strengths: Isolating motion into windows allows effective handling of scenes with varying motion intensities. The MLP's focus on dynamic parts enables efficient motion representation. Limitations: Requires careful motion-based window partitioning. Temporal consistency depends on sufficient overlap and fine-tuning; poor overlap or insufficient iterations can cause discontinuities. Performance: Not given in the sources. SWAGS is introduced as a window-based dynamic 3DGS method. It has been applied to medical fields, including markerless motion reconstruction for infants and neonates, utilizing additional mask and depth supervisions. name: Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is a method that incorporates an epipolar transformer to generalize features between two views, pairing this with a probabilistic prediction of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two or more input images and their camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color coefficients). Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: A list of objects containing position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4, opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and color coefficients \mathbf{c}. Feature Tokens: Concatenated sequence of image and camera parameter embeddings processed by the transformer. Steps: 1. Tokenization: Tokenize the input images and camera parameters, then concatenate the tokens from all views. 2. Feature Generalization: Pass the concatenated tokens through a transformer block to generalize features between the views. 3. Probabilistic Prediction: Decode the transformer output tokens into Gaussian parameters, predicting a probabilistic distribution of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays. 4. Rendering: Render the predicted Gaussians using differentiable rasterization to produce the output image. 5. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian parameters (and encoder weights if trained end-to-end) by minimizing photometric losses such as LPIPS or SSIM against the input views. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Specific hyperparameters such as transformer depth, heads, and loss weights are not detailed in the source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pose Requirement: Standard implementation requires known camera poses, though variants like NoPoSplat eliminate this need. Depth Ambiguity: Probabilistic prediction along rays may produce multiple Gaussians per ray; standard sorting and alpha blending must handle this correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def epipolar3dgs(images, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics): # 1. Tokenization: Embed image patches and concatenate with camera pose embeddings tokens = [] for img, intr, extr in zip(images, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics): # Standard vision transformer patch embedding and positional encoding tokens.append(embedandconcat(img, intr, extr)) combinedtokens = torch.cat(tokens, dim=1) # 2. Feature Generalization: Process tokens through a transformer block # Epipolar transformer generalizes features between views # Exact architectural details (layers, heads, dimensions) are not specified transformeroutput = transformerforward(combinedtokens) # 3. Probabilistic Prediction: Decode tokens into Gaussian parameters # Predicts Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays # MLP decoder outputs position, scale, rotation, opacity, color gaussians = decodetogaussians(transformeroutput) # 4. Rendering: Differentiable rasterization # Project 3D Gaussians to 2D, sort by depth, alpha blend renderedimage = rasterizegaussians(gaussians, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics) return renderedimage, gaussians Pose-Aware Projection (PAP) is a feature aggregation technique used in differentiable volume rendering to extract multi-view contextual information for specific 3D locations (voxels or skeletal Gaussians) by projecting their positions onto 2D feature maps from multiple camera views. It solves the problem of ambiguous feature assignment inherent in global backprojection methods, which ignore actual surface geometry and assume features map reliably to voxel centers via camera rays, leading to errors in occluded or background regions. What sets PAP apart from its parent Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is its focus on aggregating features based on camera distance for selected skeletal primitives rather than generalizing features via an epipolar transformer for all pixels. It differs from its sibling Geometry Aware Feature Extraction by using explicit inverse-distance weighting of projected features rather than cross-view attention guided by geometric constraints. Scaling: Scales with the number of input views and image resolution. Strengths: Leverages epipolar geometry for robust feature generalization; probabilistic prediction allows for flexible Gaussian placement. Limitations: Requires known camera poses in standard formulations, though pose-agnostic variants exist. When to use: When reconstructing 3DGS from limited multi-view inputs with known poses. When not to use: When camera poses are unknown (use NoPoSplat) or when transformer overhead is prohibitive. Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is part of the broader trend of integrating neural rendering techniques with 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds upon methods like PixelSplat, which uses an epipolar transformer for feature generalization between two views. MVSplat extends this to multi-view settings using transformers and cost volumes. GS-LRM tokenizes multiple images and camera parameters for transformer-based decoding. NoPoSplat addresses critical limitations by eliminating the need for known camera poses. The method is supervised by photometric losses such as LPIPS, SSIM, or similar metrics. name: Pose-Aware Projection (PAP)
head: Pose-Aware Projection at selected voxels
body: Pose-Aware Projection (PAP) is a feature aggregation technique used in differentiable volume rendering to extract multi-view contextual information for specific 3D locations (voxels or skeletal Gaussians) by projecting their positions onto 2D feature maps from multiple camera views. It solves the problem of ambiguous feature assignment inherent in global backprojection methods, which ignore actual surface geometry and assume features map reliably to voxel centers via camera rays, leading to errors in occluded or background regions. What sets PAP apart from its parent Epipolar 3D Gaussian Splatting is its focus on aggregating features based on camera distance for selected skeletal primitives rather than generalizing features via an epipolar transformer for all pixels. It differs from its sibling Geometry Aware Feature Extraction by using explicit inverse-distance weighting of projected features rather than cross-view attention guided by geometric constraints. Inputs: 1. A set of selected skeletal Gaussian positions \{\mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d}: (h, w, d) \in \mathcal{I}\}, where \mathcal{I} is the index set of selected voxels/primitives. 2. A set of N pose-aware 2D feature maps \{fn: n = 1, \dots, N\}, obtained from a coarse stage, corresponding to N input camera views. Outputs: 1. A set of PAP-derived feature volumes \{\bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}: (h, w, d) \in \mathcal{I}\} for each view n, containing features sampled at the projected locations. 2. A final aggregated feature volume \hat{v}{h,w,d} for each selected voxel/primitive. Data Structures: \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d}: 3D position vector (x, y, z) of the skeletal Gaussian at voxel indices (h, w, d). fn: 2D feature map for view n, a tensor of shape (Hn, Wn, C), where Hn, Wn are height/width and C is channel depth. \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}: Feature vector of size C for voxel (h,w,d) from view n. \hat{v}{h,w,d}: Final aggregated feature vector of size C. Steps: 1. Projection & Sampling: For each selected skeletal Gaussian position \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} and for each view n \in \{1, \dots, N\}: a. Project the 3D position \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} onto the 2D image plane of view n using standard camera projection. Let the resulting 2D coordinates be (un, vn). b. Sample the feature map fn at coordinates (un, vn) using bilinear interpolation. Let the sampled feature be \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}. 2. Distance Calculation: For each selected voxel (h,w,d) and each view n, calculate the Euclidean distance z{(h,w,d),n} between the skeletal Gaussian position \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} and the camera position of view n. 3. Aggregation: For each selected voxel (h,w,d), aggregate the PAP-derived features \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n} from all N views using inverse distance weighting: \hat{v}{h,w,d} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^N z{(h,w,d),n}^{-1} \cdot \bar{v}{(h,w,d),n}}{\sum{n'=1}^N z{(h,w,d),n'}^{-1}} where z{(h,w,d),n} is the distance between \mu^{\text{crs}}{h,w,d} and the n-th view camera position. Parameters: N: Number of input camera views used for projection and aggregation. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-bounds projection: If the projected 2D coordinates (un, vn) fall outside the image boundaries of fn, sampling is undefined. Implementation must handle this, e.g., by clamping or using a default value. Zero distance: If z{(h,w,d),n} = 0 (camera at the same position as the Gaussian), the inverse distance becomes undefined. This is unlikely in practice but should be guarded against. Occlusion: PAP assumes that projecting to the 2D feature map provides relevant context. In occluded regions, the projected feature might come from a different surface, leading to ambiguity. PAP mitigates this by focusing on selected voxels likely to belong to the object, but residual errors may persist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def poseawareprojection(skeletalgaussians, featuremaps, camerapositions, N): """ skeletalgaussians: dict mapping (h, w, d) to 3D position tuple (x, y, z) featuremaps: list of N 2D arrays of shape (Hn, Wn, C) camerapositions: list of N 3D position tuples (cx, cy, cz) N: int Returns: dict mapping (h, w, d) to aggregated feature vector """ C = featuremaps[0].shape[-1] aggregated = {} for (h, w, d), mu in skeletalgaussians.items(): weightedsum = [0.0] C invdistsum = 0.0 for n in range(N): u, v = project2d(mu, featuremaps[n].shape) vbar = sample2d(featuremaps[n], u, v) cam = camerapositions[n] dx, dy, dz = mu[0] - cam[0], mu[1] - cam[1], mu[2] - cam[2] z = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 if z == 0.0: continue invz = 1.0 / z for c in range(C): weightedsum[c] += invz vbar[c] invdistsum += invz if invdistsum > 0.0: for c in range(C): weightedsum[c] /= invdistsum else: weightedsum = [0.0] C aggregated[(h, w, d)] = weightedsum return aggregated def project2d(pos, shape): # Standard pinhole projection assumed return pos[0] / pos[2], pos[1] / pos[2] def sample2d(map2d, u, v): # Bilinear interpolation assumed h, w, c = map2d.shape u = max(0, min(w - 1, u)) v = max(0, min(h - 1, v)) return map2d[int(v), int(u)] Enhances source view features using cross-view attention and geometric constraints (ray projection) to resolve ambiguous feature assignment. It builds on PAP by providing geometrically enhanced features for robust generalization in synthetic-to-real scenarios. Aligns features from neighboring training views with a novel rendered view by explicitly reprojecting 3D coordinates into the novel view and validating via depth-based visibility testing. It differs from PAP by relying on explicit geometric reprojection rather than implicit geometric awareness via distance weighting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Resolves ambiguous feature assignment from global backprojection by aligning selected 3D skeletal primitives with 2D feature maps from different camera views, allowing association with rich, pose-aligned features for accurate fine-grained rendering. Limitations: Still relies on the assumption that 2D features can be reliably mapped to the selected 3D position via projection, which may be inaccurate in highly occluded or textureless regions. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Pose-Aware Projection (PAP) was introduced in the paper "VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views". It is part of the fine stage of the VS-Splat method, following the coarse stage and voxel selection. The method was developed to address limitations of global backprojection in voxel-based feature volumes, specifically the discarding of sub-voxel geometric precision and ambiguous feature assignment in occluded regions. name: Geometry Aware Feature Extraction
head: Geometrically Enhanced Feature Aggregation
body: Geometry Aware Feature Extraction is a module that enhances source view features by aggregating information from other source views using geometric constraints (ray projection) and cross-view attention. It sets itself apart from siblings like 3D Alignment via Reprojection by explicitly modeling the 3D ray structure to guide feature aggregation, rather than relying solely on 2D reprojection alignment. Inputs: Set of N source views \{Ii, Ki, Ei\}{i=1}^N, where Ii is the image, Ki is the camera intrinsic matrix, and Ei = [Ri, ti] contains the rotation matrix Ri and translation vector ti for the i-th view. Number of sample points per ray, Ns. Outputs: Geometrically enhanced features \{F'i\}{i=1}^N. Data Structures: Fi: Feature map extracted from Ii by a shared CNN. fi: Local feature vector at 2D coordinate ui in Fi. g{js}: Local feature vector at projected coordinate v{js} in Fj. P(s): Position embedding for the s-th sample point along the ray. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each source view i, use a shared Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract feature map Fi from image Ii. 2. Ray Definition: For each 2D coordinate ui = [u, v]^\top on the i-th source view, compute the corresponding ray R in world coordinates parametrized by \delta: R(\delta) = ti + \delta Ri Ki^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} ui \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where Ki is the intrinsic matrix and [Ri, ti] are the extrinsic parameters of the i-th source view. 3. Ray Sampling and Projection: Sample a sequence of points ps = R(\deltas) along the ray R for s = 1, \dots, Ns. Project each point ps to the j-th source view to obtain 2D coordinates v{js} and depth d{sj}: d{sj} \begin{bmatrix} v{js}^\top \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = Kj Rj^{-1} (ps - tj) where v{js} is the 2D coordinate in the j-th source view and d{sj} is the corresponding depth. This yields a collection of projections \{v{js}\}{s=1}^{Ns} for the j-th source view. 4. Stage 1: Intra-View Aggregation: For a target view i and a neighbor view j, let fi be the local feature of Fi at ui, and g{js} be the local feature of Fj at v{js}. Aggregate features from the projection points within the j-th source view using Multi-Head Attention (MHA): gj = \text{MHA}(fi, \{g{js} + P(s)\}{s=1}^{Ns}) Here, fi is the query, \{g{js} + P(s)\}{s=1}^{Ns} serve as the keys and values, and P(s) is the position embedding of the sample index s. 5. Stage 2: Cross-View Aggregation: Aggregate features from other source views. Compute the enhanced feature f'i using MHA: f'i = \text{MHA}(fi, \{gj\}{j=1, j \neq i}^{N}) Here, fi is the query and \{gj\}{j=1, j \neq i}^{N} are the keys and values. 6. Iteration: Apply the above process for all source views to obtain the final geometrically enhanced features \{F'i\}{i=1}^N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryawarefeatureextraction(sourceviews, Ns): """ sourceviews: List of dicts with keys 'image', 'K', 'R', 't'. Ns: Number of sample points per ray. Returns: List of enhanced feature maps Fprime. """ N = len(sourceviews) # Step 1: Feature extraction with shared CNN F = [sharedcnn(view['image']) for view in sourceviews] Fprime = [None] N for i in range(N): Fprimei = createzeroslike(F[i]) for ui in allpixelindices(F[i]): fi = F[i][ui] # Step 2: Ray definition homu = [ui[0], ui[1], 1.0] invKi = matrixinverse(sourceviews[i]['K']) dirvec = matrixvectormul(sourceviews[i]['R'], matrixvectormul(invKi, homu)) # Step 3: Ray sampling deltas = linspace(0.1, 10.0, Ns) pslist = [vectoradd(sourceviews[i]['t'], scalarmul(dirvec, d)) for d in deltas] viewglist = [] for j in range(N): if i == j: continue gjs = [] for s, ps in enumerate(pslist): invKj = matrixinverse(sourceviews[j]['K']) invRj = matrixinverse(sourceviews[j]['R']) rhs = matrixvectormul(sourceviews[j]['K'], matrixvectormul(invRj, vectorsub(ps, sourceviews[j]['t']))) dsj = rhs[2] vjs = [rhs[0] / dsj, rhs[1] / dsj] # Step 3: Projection feature sampling gjs.append(bilinearsample(F[j], vjs)) # Step 4: Stage 1 aggregation keysvals = [vectoradd(gjs[s], positionembedding(s)) for s in range(Ns)] gj = multiheadattention(query=fi, keys=keysvals, values=keysvals) viewglist.append(gj) # Step 5: Stage 2 aggregation fprimei = multiheadattention(query=fi, keys=viewglist, values=viewglist) Fprimei[ui] = fprimei Fprime[i] = Fprimei return Fprime def sharedcnn(image):... def createzeroslike(tensor):... def allpixelindices(tensor):... def matrixinverse(M):... def matrixvectormul(M, v):... def linspace(a, b, n):... def vectoradd(a, b):... def scalarmul(v, s):... def vectorsub(a, b):... def bilinearsample(tensor, coords):... def positionembedding(s):... def multiheadattention(query, keys, values):... Parameters: Ns: Number of sample points along the ray. Not given in the sources. Position Embedding P(s): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray projection may fall outside the image boundaries of source views j. The source does not specify handling for out-of-bounds projections. Standard practice is to clamp or ignore such samples. Depth ambiguity: The parametrization \delta requires a range. The source does not specify how \deltas are chosen (e.g., uniform, learned). Implementers must define a depth range [\delta{min}, \delta{max}]. Cross-Reprojection Attention (CRA) is a two-stage attention mechanism that approximates dense semantic connections in 3D space by reprojecting query rays to source views and aggregating features, solving the insufficiency of single-point feature extraction for semantic prediction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves N views, Ns samples per ray, and Multi-Head Attention operations, suggesting complexity related to O(N^2 \cdot Ns). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Approximates dense semantic connections in 3D space by reprojecting query rays to source views and aggregating features. Reduces computational cost and GPU memory usage compared to dense multi-view attention while maintaining comparable semantic segmentation performance. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera parameters and geometry. May fail if the geometry prediction is inaccurate, leading to artifacts. When to use: Synthetic-to-real generalization of NeRF where semantic consistency across views is critical. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and Ns or N are large, as the attention mechanism adds overhead. Originated in the paper "ContraNeRF: Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields for Synthetic-to-real Novel View Synthesis via Contrastive Learning". The method was introduced to address the problem where existing NeRF models may fail to accurately predict scene geometry, resulting in serious artifacts in rendered images, particularly in synthetic-to-real generalization scenarios. It is used in the context of training NeRF models on synthetic data to generalize to real data. name: Cross-Reprojection Attention
head: CRA Module, Cross-Reprojection Attention (CRA) Module
body: Cross-Reprojection Attention (CRA) is a two-stage attention mechanism that approximates dense semantic connections in 3D space by reprojecting query rays to source views and aggregating features, solving the insufficiency of single-point feature extraction for semantic prediction. It replaces dense multi-view attention to reduce computational cost and GPU memory usage while maintaining comparable semantic segmentation performance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A query ray r(z) defined by two points pi, pj in the query view; camera poses (R, t) for m source views; camera calibration matrix K; N sample points \{zk\}{k=1}^N along the ray; feature dimension C; number of attention heads H. Outputs: A refined semantic ray feature s and rendered semantic logits \hat{S}(r). Data Structures: 3D Contextual Space (M): A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{m \times N \times C}. It is structured as M = [F1, \dots, Fm]^T, where Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C} contains the features extracted from the i-th source view along the reprojected ray. Attention Projections: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices of shape \mathbb{R}^{N \times dk}, where dk = C/H. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Warping and Feature Extraction: For each source view j \in \{1, \dots, m\} with pose (Rj, tj): a. Define the query ray in the query view coordinate system: r(z) = pi + z \frac{pj - pi}{\|pj - pi\|}, \quad z \in \mathbb{R}. b. Reproject the ray to the source view plane using the warping function w: r^(z) = w(r(z), Rj, tj) = K \pi(Rj \cdot r(z) + tj) where \pi(u) = [ux/uz, uy/uz] is the perspective projection function. c. Extract features Fj(r^(z)) at the N sampled points along r^(z) using a shared U-Net-based CNN. This yields Fj \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}. d. Assemble M = [F1, \dots, Fm]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times N \times C}. 2. Intra-View Radial Attention: Refine the contextual space M to M' by processing each view Fi independently. For each i \in \{1, \dots, m\}: a. Compute projections: QR = Fi Wq, \quad KR = Fi Wk, \quad VR = Fi Wv where Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C} are learnable projection matrices. b. Compute attention heads for h = 1, \dots, H: A^{(h)} = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QR^{(h)} (KR^{(h)})^T}{\sqrt{dk}}\right) VR^{(h)} where dk = C/H. c. Concatenate heads and project: F'i = \text{Concat}(A^{(1)}, \dots, A^{(H)}) Wo. d. Update M' such that M' = [F'1, \dots, F'm]^T. 3. Cross-View Sparse Attention: Decompose M' across views to form semantic rays. For each sample point k \in \{1, \dots, N\}: a. Extract the cross-view feature vector: F'{r^(k)} = [F'1(r^(zk)), \dots, F'm(r^(zk))]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times C}. b. Compute view weights w \in \mathbb{R}^m using a Semantic-aware Weight Network subject to constraints: w \in \mathcal{C}(\tau):= \left\{ w: 0 < wi < \frac{\tau}{m}, \sum{i=1}^m wi = 1 \right\} where \tau > 0 is a hyperparameter bounding deviation from uniform distribution. c. Construct the semantic ray feature s(zk): s(zk) = \sum{i=1}^m wi F'i(r^(zk)). 4. Semantic Field Rendering: Render the final semantic logits \hat{S}(r) using volume rendering along the query ray: \hat{S}(r) = \sum{k=1}^N T(zk) \{1 - \exp(-\sigma(zk)\deltak)\} s(zk) where: \sigma(zk) is the predicted density from a Geometry-aware Network. \deltak = z{k+1} - zk is the interval between sampled points. T(zk) = \exp\left(-\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(z{k'})\delta{k'}\right) is the accumulated transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns: semanticlogits (Csemantic,) """ m = len(sourceposes) # 1. Ray Definition direction = (querypointsj - querypointsi) / torch.norm(querypointsj - querypointsi) # Standard NeRF stratified sampling is used in practice. zsamples = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples, device=querypointsi.device) # 2. Build 3D Contextual Space M M = torch.zeros(m, numsamples, featuredim, device=querypointsi.device) for i, (R, t) in enumerate(sourceposes): direxp = direction.unsqueeze(0).expand(numsamples, -1) piexp = querypointsi.unsqueeze(0).expand(numsamples, -1) # r(z) = pi + z direction rz = piexp + zsamples.unsqueeze(1) direxp # (N, 3) # Warping: r(z) = K pi(R r(z) + t) rtransformed = torch.einsum('ij,nj->ni', R, rz) + t # (N, 3) rproj = torch.einsum('ij,nj->ni', K, rtransformed) # (N, 3) rpixel = rproj[:,:2] / (rproj[:, 2:] + 1e-6) # (N, 2) # Normalize to [-1, 1] for grid sampling rpixelnorm = (rpixel / K[:2, 2].unsqueeze(0)) 2.0 - 1.0 # Extract features using shared U-Net-based CNN # Sources do not specify exact architecture; standard grid-sampling U-Net is used. Fi = cnnextractor(sourceimages[i], rpixelnorm) # (N, C) M[i] = Fi # 3. Intra-View Radial Attention Mprime = torch.zeroslike(M) Wq = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) Wk = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) Wv = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) Wo = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, featuredim)) for i in range(m): Fi = M[i] # (N, C) Q = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', Fi, Wq) Katt = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', Fi, Wk) V = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', Fi, Wv) dk = featuredim // numheads Qheads = Q.view(numsamples, numheads, dk).transpose(0, 1) Kheads = Katt.view(numsamples, numheads, dk).transpose(0, 1) Vheads = V.view(numsamples, numheads, dk).transpose(0, 1) scores = torch.matmul(Qheads, Kheads.transpose(1, 2)) / (dk 0.5) attnweights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) outheads = torch.matmul(attnweights, Vheads) out = outheads.transpose(0, 1).contiguous().view(numsamples, featuredim) Fiprime = torch.einsum('nc,cd->nd', out, Wo) Mprime[i] = Fiprime # 4. Cross-View Sparse Attention & Semantic Ray Construction # Compute weights w subject to 0 < wi < tau/m and sum(w)=1 # Sources do not specify exact optimization; standard projection is used. rawscores = torch.randn(m, device=Mprime.device) wbase = F.softmax(rawscores, dim=0) w = torch.clamp(wbase, min=1e-6, max=tau / m) w = w / w.sum() # Aggregate features: s(zk) = sumi wi F'i(r(zk)) s = torch.einsum('i,nci->nc', w, Mprime) # (N, C) # 5. Semantic Field Rendering # Predict density sigma from Geometry-aware Network sigma = geometrynetwork(s) # (N,) deltas = torch.diff(zsamples, dim=0) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltas[-1]]) # (N,) alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) # (N,) # T(zk) = exp(- sum{k'=1}^{k-1} sigma(z{k'}) delta{k'}) Tprev = 1.0 - alphas[:-1] T = torch.cat([torch.tensor([1.0], device=sigma.device), torch.cumprod(Tprev, dim=0)]) # Render: Shat(r) = sum T(zk) alphak s(zk) weightsrender = T alphas semanticlogits = torch.einsum('n,nc->c', weightsrender, s) return semanticlogits Parameters: \tau: Hyperparameter for weight distribution deviation bound. Constraint: 0 < wi < \tau/m. Keeps semantic consistency instead of bias across views. \tau=1 corresponds to mean aggregation. dk: Dimension of each attention head. Calculated as dk = C/H, where C is feature dimension and H is number of heads. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projection function \pi(u) involves division by uz. Ensure uz is not zero (ray parallel to image plane) to avoid division by zero. Add a small epsilon. Boundaries: The reprojection r^(z) may fall outside the image boundaries of source views. The CNN extractor should handle out-of-bounds coordinates (e.g., via padding or clamping). Degenerate Input: If source views are too close or too far, the reprojection may be inaccurate. The method assumes known camera poses (R, t) and calibration K. Time and Memory Complexity: CRA improves performance by 47.3% in FLOPs and 76.5% in GPU memory compared to dense attention. Measured Performance: On real data (ScanNet), with an input of 1024 \times 64 \times 8 \times 32, the full CRA module achieves 76.30% mIoU and 91.08% Total Accuracy with 5.40 GFLOPs, compared to 10.25 GFLOPs for Dense Attention. Strengths: Captures dense and global contextual information with computational efficiency; avoids heavy computational costs of dense attention. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera poses and calibration; performance depends on the quality of the shared CNN feature extractor. When to use: When generalizable semantic rendering is required with limited computational resources (GPU memory/FLOPs). Origin: Proposed in the S-Ray method. History: Developed to address the insufficiency of single-point feature extraction for semantic prediction in NeRF-based generalization rendering methods. Usage: Used in the S-Ray method for generalizable semantic rendering, compared against MVSNeRF, NeuRay, and Semantic-NeRF. It is designed to work without positional encoding engineering, unlike GPNR. name: 3D Alignment via Reprojection
head: Feature Reprojection Alignment
body: 3D Alignment via Reprojection is a technique in differentiable volume rendering that aligns features from neighboring training views with a novel rendered view by compensating for pose and geometry discrepancies. It solves the problem of leveraging relevant multi-view contextual information when camera orientations and positions differ significantly. Unlike its parent Pose-Aware Projection (PAP), which aggregates features based on camera distance to resolve ambiguous assignments, this method explicitly reprojects 3D coordinates into the novel view using the pinhole camera model and validates them via depth-based visibility testing. It differs from sibling Geometry Aware Feature Extraction by relying on explicit geometric reprojection rather than implicit geometric awareness. Inputs: Novel view image Ik and its camera pose Ck and intrinsic matrix Kk. Set of n neighboring training images \{Hi\}{i=1}^n with poses Ci and intrinsics Ki. NeRF depth map zi for the novel view, used for visibility checking. Leniency threshold l (typical value: 0.25). Outputs: Reprojected feature map H^f{i \rightarrow k} aligned with the novel view coordinates. Data Structures: Image features I^fk and H^fi: Dense tensors of spatial dimensions matching the input images, with a channel depth of 64. 3D coordinates \bm{x}k: Represented as homogeneous vectors [\bm{x}k, 1] where \bm{x}k = (xk, yk, zk), with (xk, yk) being pixel coordinates and zk the depth. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract 64-dimensional image features from the novel view Ik and each neighboring image Hi using separate small convolutional encoder blocks: I^fk = \text{conv}I(Ik) \{H^fi\}{i=1}^n = \text{conv}H(\{Hi\}{i=1}^n) 2. Coordinate Reprojection: For each pixel in the novel view with 3D coordinate \bm{x}k = (xk, yk, zk), reproject the coordinate into the neighboring camera view i using the pinhole camera model: \bm{x}{k \rightarrow i} = Ki Ci Ck^{-1} Kk^{-1} [\bm{x}k, 1] Here, \bm{x}{k \rightarrow i} = (x{k \rightarrow i}, y{k \rightarrow i}, z{k \rightarrow i}, 1) is the resulting homogeneous coordinate in camera i's space. Ki is the intrinsic matrix of camera i, and Ci is the pose matrix of camera i. 3. Visibility Testing: Calculate a visibility score visi to ensure geometric consistency by comparing the reprojected depth z{k \rightarrow i} with the NeRF-computed depth zi: visi = \mathcal{H}\left(1 - \frac{z{k \rightarrow i}}{zi} + l\right) Where \mathcal{H} is the Heaviside function and l is the leniency threshold (0.25). 4. Feature Copying: Form the reprojected feature map by copying values from the neighbor's feature map H^fi at the projected coordinates \bm{x}{k \rightarrow i} to the original coordinates \bm{x}k, weighted by the visibility score: H^f{i \rightarrow k} \langle \phi(\bm{x}k) \rangle = visi \times H^fi \langle \phi(\bm{x}{k \rightarrow i}) \rangle Where \phi(\bm{x}k) = (xk/zk, yk/zk) represents the 2D normalized coordinates, and \langle \rangle denotes 2D coordinate indexing (sampling). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ConvBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, inch, outch=64): super().init() self.conv = nn.Conv2d(inch, outch, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): return F.relu(self.conv(x)) def reprojectfeatures(novelimg, neighborimgs, novelpose, neighborposes, novelK, neighborKs, nerfdepth, l=0.25): """ Aligns neighbor features to the novel view via 3D reprojection. Args: novelimg: Tensor (B, 3, H, W) neighborimgs: List of Tensors [(B, 3, H, W)] novelpose: Tensor (4, 4) Camera pose matrix Ck neighborposes: List of Tensors [(4, 4)] Camera pose matrices Ci novelK: Tensor (3, 3) Intrinsic matrix Kk neighborKs: List of Tensors [(3, 3)] Intrinsic matrices Ki nerfdepth: Tensor (B, 1, H, W) Depth map zi from NeRF for novel view leniencythreshold: Float l Returns: reprojectedfeatures: Tensor (B, 64, H, W) Aligned features """ convI = ConvBlock(3) convH = ConvBlock(3) novelfeat = convI(novelimg) neighborfeats = [convH(img) for img in neighborimgs] B,, H, W = novelfeat.shape u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='xy') u = u.float().to(novelimg.device).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) v = v.float().to(novelimg.device).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) z = nerfdepth # Homogeneous coordinate [xk, 1] as defined in source Xkhom = torch.cat([u, v, z, torch.oneslike(z)], dim=1) totalfeat = torch.zeroslike(novelfeat) for feati, posei, Ki in zip(neighborfeats, neighborposes, neighborKs): # Reprojection: x{k->i} = Ki Ci Ck^{-1} Kk^{-1} [xk, 1] Xkflat = Xkhom.permute(0, 1, 3, 2).contiguous().view(B, 4, -1) Xray = torch.matmul(torch.inverse(novelK), Xkflat) Xworld = torch.matmul(torch.inverse(novelpose), torch.cat([Xray, torch.ones(B, 1, Xray.shape[2]).to(novelimg.device)], dim=1)) Xcami = torch.matmul(posei, Xworld) Xproj = torch.matmul(Ki, Xcami[:3,:,:]) Xproj = Xproj.view(B, 3, H, W) xproj, yproj, zproj = Xproj[:, 0], Xproj[:, 1], Xproj[:, 2] # Visibility test vis = (1.0 - zproj / (z + 1e-6) + l) > 0.0 vis = vis.float() # Feature sampling at phi(x{k->i}) = (xproj/zproj, yproj/zproj) # Normalize to [-1, 1] for gridsample xnorm = (xproj / (Ki[0, 0] W) 2 - 1) ynorm = (yproj / (Ki[1, 1] H) 2 - 1) grid = torch.stack([xnorm, ynorm], dim=-1) sampled = F.gridsample(feati, grid, aligncorners=False) totalfeat += vis sampled return totalfeat Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Inconsistency: Errors in camera pose estimation (e.g., from COLMAP) or NeRF geometry lead to imperfect correspondences. Depth Ambiguity: The visibility test relies on the accuracy of the NeRF depth map. Out-of-Bounds: Reprojected coordinates may fall outside the neighbor image boundaries. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of neighbors n. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and neighbors, as features for all neighbors are processed. Performance: Evaluated on LLFF, 360v2, and DTU datasets. Uses 5 neighbors for LLFF/360v2 and 2 for DTU. Strengths: Leverages relevant information from neighbors despite pose differences. Limitations: Dependent on the accuracy of camera poses and NeRF geometry. Originated in RoGUENeRF: A Robust Geometry-Consistent Universal Enhancer for NeRF. It is used to enhance NeRF renderings by aligning features from neighboring training views. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Transformer-based Parameterization
head: GS-LRM
body: This method reconstructs a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene from a small set of input images using a Transformer architecture. It tokenizes input views and camera parameters, processes them through a Transformer block, and directly decodes the resulting tokens into 3D Gaussian parameters. Inputs: N input images (I1, \dots, IN) and their corresponding camera parameters (C1, \dots, CN), where N is typically 2 to 4. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity, and color). Data Structures: 1. Input Tokens: A concatenated sequence of image features and camera parameter embeddings. 2. Latent Tokens: The output sequence from the Transformer block. 3. Gaussian Parameters: The decoded primitive attributes. Steps: 1. Tokenization: The N input images and their camera parameters are tokenized and concatenated into a single sequence T{\text{in}}. 2. Transformer Processing: The sequence T{\text{in}} is passed through a Transformer block to produce latent tokens T{\text{out}}. 3. Decoding: The latent tokens T{\text{out}} are decoded into the final 3D Gaussian parameters G. Formulas: T{\text{in}} = \text{Concat}(\text{Tokenize}(I1, \dots, IN), \text{Tokenize}(C1, \dots, CN)) T{\text{out}} = \text{Transformer}(T{\text{in}}) G = \text{Decoder}(T{\text{out}}) where T{\text{in}} is the concatenated input token sequence, \text{Tokenize} converts images and camera parameters into embeddings, \text{Transformer} is the processing block, T{\text{out}} is the latent token sequence, \text{Decoder} maps latent tokens to Gaussian attributes, and G is the output parameter set. Parameters: Number of input views: Typically 2 to 4. Transformer depth and width: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Scale Ambiguity: If camera intrinsics are not properly encoded, scale ambiguity may arise; NoPoSplat addresses this by introducing intrinsics token embeddings, while the base method assumes known poses. Replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a voxel-aligned strategy, aggregating multi-view features into a shared 3D voxel grid to decouple feature fusion from camera frustums and enable adaptive density control. Choose when multi-view consistency and scene complexity adaptation are prioritized over pixel-aligned methods. Estimates Gaussian attributes from tri-plane features in a fixed order rather than in parallel, creating dependencies that allow specialized decoding and reduce high degrees of freedom. Choose when joint attribute prediction causes instability. Maps learned scene tokens to freely placed 3D Gaussians, decoupling center prediction from fixed ray intersections to allow variable spatial extent. Choose when flexible placement outside camera rays is needed. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is referred to as GS-LRM in the literature. It builds upon earlier feed-forward networks like MVSplat and PixelSplat. GS-LRM specifically tokenizes images and camera parameters, processes them with a Transformer, and decodes them into Gaussian parameters, representing a shift from pixel-aligned to token-aligned Gaussian prediction. NoPoSplat is a related variant that removes the need for known camera poses. From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting: Theory and Applications, https://doi.org/10.1109/sibgrapi67909.2025.11223276, fetched 2026-10-26

name: VolSplat
head: Differentiable Multi-scale Voxel Module, Rethinking Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Voxel-Aligned Prediction, Voxel-aligned Feed-forward 3DGS
body: VolSplat is a multi-view feed-forward framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that replaces pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction with voxel-aligned prediction. It directly regresses 3D Gaussian primitives from a predicted 3D voxel grid, overcoming the alignment errors and view-biased density distributions inherent in pixel-aligned methods. By aggregating multi-view features into a shared 3D voxel container, it decouples feature fusion from camera view frustums, enabling adaptive density control based on scene complexity and robust multi-view consistency. VolSplat operates in two main phases: 3D feature construction via voxelization and Gaussian parameter regression from refined voxel features. A variant, \text{VG}^2GT, introduces a coarse-to-fine multi-scale voxel strategy. Inputs: N input images I = \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Corresponding camera poses P = \{Pi\}{i=1}^N (for VolSplat) or unposed images (for \text{VG}^2GT). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians G = \{(\mug, \Sigmag, \alphag, cg)\}{g=1}^M, where M is the number of occupied voxels. In \text{VG}^2GT, additionally predicted camera parameters \{Ci\}{i=1}^N. 1. Image Patch Features (F{Pi}): Extracted from a Transformer-based backbone for each input image Ii. Shape: \mathbb{R}^{Hp \times Wp \times C}, where Hp, Wp are patch dimensions. 2. Global Point Cloud (\Omegam): A set of 3D points obtained by unprojecting pixels using estimated depth maps and camera parameters. 3. Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid containing features. Coarse Voxel Features (fm^v): Computed for coarse voxels. Fine Voxel Features (fm^{dv}): Computed for fine voxels (in \text{VG}^2GT). 4. Gaussian Parameters: Center \mug \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale sg \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation rg \in \mathbb{R}^4 (Quaternion) Opacity \sigmag \in \mathbb{R} Color cg (Spherical Harmonics coefficients). 1. Extract 2D image features for each input image Ii using a Transformer-based network (e.g., ViT backbone) to obtain patch features F{Pi}. 2. Construct per-view cost volumes using plane sweeping. 3. Estimate a depth map Di for each view using a Depth Prediction Module. Note: In \text{VG}^2GT, camera parameters Ci are also predicted by a head. 1. Unprojection: Unproject the 2D features into 3D space using the estimated depth maps Di and camera poses Pi to form a dense global point cloud \Omegam. For each pixel p in image i, compute 3D point xp = Pi^{-1}(p, Di(p)). 2. Voxel Feature Aggregation: For each voxel m in the grid, compute the voxel feature fm^v as a confidence-weighted average of features from all 3D points \Omegam falling inside the voxel: fm^v = \frac{\sum{p \in \Omegam} n(p) f(p)}{\sum{p \in \Omegam} n(p)} where n(p) is the depth confidence of point p, defined as the minimum point confidence within the voxel: nm = \min{p \in \Omegam} n(p). Note: VolSplat aggregates features directly into the voxel grid without explicit point-cloud downsampling in the description, while \text{VG}^2GT explicitly mentions point-cloud downsampling and interpolation. VolSplat Path: 1. Refine the 3D voxel features using a sparse 3D decoder (3D U-Net). 2. The 3D U-Net predicts residual features \Delta fm for each voxel. 3. Add the predicted residual features to the original voxel features: fm^{refined} = fm^v + \Delta fm. \text{VG}^2GT Path (Coarse-to-Fine): 1. Coarse Enhancement: Serialize the sparse voxel grid into a 1D feature sequence with operator S. Enhance the sequence with PointTransformerV3 (\gamma\psi). Deserialize back to voxel space with S^{-1}: \hat{f}m^v = S^{-1} \circ \gamma\psi \circ S (fm^v) 2. Feature Mapping: Map enhanced voxel features back to 3D points in \Omegam. For each point p, find its 16 nearest voxel centers with KNN. Interpolate enhanced voxel features back to the point by distance-weighted aggregation. 3. Fusion: Fuse these enhanced features into backbone patch features using zero convolution, then decode depth maps and camera parameters again. 4. Fine-Level Construction: Repeat the aggregation in Step 2 to obtain fine voxel features fm^{dv} from enhanced image patches. Use a DPT head to upsample image features and align them with the global point cloud, without downsampling the global point cloud. 5. Fine Enhancement: Enhance fine voxel features using PointMLP (\mathcal{M}\phi) instead of PTv3 for memory efficiency: \hat{f}m^{dv} = S^{-1} \circ \mathcal{M}\phi \circ S (fm^{dv}) For each occupied voxel m with center xm and refined feature fm^{refined} (or \hat{f}m^{dv}): 1. Initialization: Initial Gaussian center \mu{g,0} = xm (voxel center). Initial color c{g,0} is a weighted average of image colors. Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients above order 0 are initialized to 0. 2. Residual Prediction: Predict residual offsets for Gaussian center \Delta \mug and color \Delta cg using an MLP. Final center: \mug = \mu{g,0} + \Delta \mug. 3. Scale Prediction: Predict scale sg by applying a sigmoid activation with an upper bound of twice the voxel size. 4. Rotation and Opacity: Regress rotation quaternion rg and opacity \sigmag directly by MLPs. 5. Self-Splitting (Optional, \text{VG}^2GT): Each voxel feature regresses multiple sets of Gaussian primitive parameters to improve fine-grained accuracy. Render novel views from the predicted 3D Gaussians using differentiable volume rendering. In \text{VG}^2GT, Continuous Stochastic Solids Volume Rendering is used, where the color at pixel pix is determined by the maximum Gaussian response along the ray t^: I{pix} = cG(t^) Input Images: N views, resolution H \times W. Voxel Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. KNN Neighbors: 16 (in \text{VG}^2GT). Scale Upper Bound: 2 \times voxel size. Alignment Errors: Pixel-aligned methods suffer from alignment errors when source views contain occlusions or low texture, leading to floaters and view-dependent inconsistency. VolSplat mitigates this by volumetric aggregation. Density Control: Pixel-aligned methods enforce a uniform density distribution, causing redundant primitives in simple regions and failure to capture fine-grained structures. VolSplat enables adaptive density control based on 3D scene complexity. Memory Usage: PointTransformerV3 has substantially higher memory consumption when processing million-point-scale point clouds, potentially leading to GPU out-of-memory errors. PointMLP is used in the fine level to mitigate this. VS-Splat is a feed-forward framework for 3D object reconstruction from sparse-view 2D images that employs a coarse-to-fine (C2F) strategy to predict 3D Gaussian primitives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like LaRa and GenDen by performing voxel-level selection before generating fine primitives, rather than selecting existing primitives for refinement. This ensures that the coarse representation determines the spatial location for new fine primitives, enabling adaptive density control without auxiliary supervision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources, though PointMLP is noted as more memory efficient than PointTransformerV3 for large-scale point clouds. Measured Performance: Evaluated on RealEstate10K, ScanNet, and ACID benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Strengths: Robust multi-view consistency, cleaner occlusion handling, adaptive density control, reduced floaters. Limitations: Voxel sparsity limits recoverable scene detail. When to use: When multi-view alignment is challenging due to occlusions or low texture, and adaptive density control is required. When not to use: When high-frequency details are critical and voxel sparsity is a bottleneck, or when computational resources are extremely limited for large-scale point cloud processing. VolSplat was introduced to rethink the widely adopted pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction paradigm in feed-forward 3DGS. It addresses the limitations of 2D feature matching and rigid pixel-to-Gaussian association. The method is evaluated on large-scale benchmarks such as RealEstate10K, ScanNet, and ACID. A related method, \text{VG}^2GT, extends this concept with a multi-scale voxel module and joint camera parameter prediction. name: VS-Splat
head: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting [S1, unofficial]
body: VS-Splat is a feed-forward framework for 3D object reconstruction from sparse-view 2D images that employs a coarse-to-fine (C2F) strategy to predict 3D Gaussian primitives. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like LaRa and GenDen by performing voxel-level selection before generating fine primitives, rather than selecting existing primitives for refinement. This ensures that the coarse representation determines the spatial location for new fine primitives, enabling adaptive density control without auxiliary supervision. Inputs: N 2D images \{in: n = 1, \dots, N\} and corresponding camera pose parameters. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gk\} aligned to selected voxels. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Predefined in normalized 3D space [-0.5, 0.5]^3, centered at the origin, using the center-coordinate system. Dimensions are H \times W \times D. All views share this grid. 3D Gaussian Primitive Gk: Parameterized by: Mean vector \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position). Covariance matrix \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, decomposed into scale vector sk \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation quaternion rk \in \mathbb{R}^4. Opacity ok \in [0, 1]. Spherical harmonics coefficients hk \in \mathbb{R}^{3S} (view-dependent color, S basis functions per channel). Algorithm Steps: 1. View-Specific Volumetric Feature Extraction: Extract 2D feature maps from each input image in using a shared feature extractor. Modulate each feature map using Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) with a Plücker embedding map pn derived from camera pose parameters. Backproject the modulated feature maps into the predefined voxel grid to produce view-specific feature volumes vn \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times C} for n=1, \dots, N. 2. Multi-View Feature Aggregation and Compression: Form an initial unified feature volume v0 by concatenating the voxel-wise mean and variance of the view-specific volumes: v0 = \text{Mean}(v1, \dots, vN) \oplus \text{Var}(v1, \dots, vN) where \oplus denotes channel-wise concatenation, and \text{Mean}(\cdot) and \text{Var}(\cdot) are voxel-wise operators across views. Compress v0 using a 3D convolutional compressor \mathcal{C}: v{\text{comp}} = \mathcal{C}(v0), \quad \mathcal{C}: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times 2C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times \tilde{C}} where \tilde{C} \ll 2C. Transform the compressed volume using a lightweight 3D U-Net variant \mathcal{U}{\text{light}} (with one encoding and one decoding block) to obtain the unified volumetric representation \tilde{v}: \tilde{v} = \mathcal{U}{\text{light}}(v{\text{comp}}) \tilde{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times \tilde{C}}. 3. Coarse Stage (Primitive Prediction): Decode features from \tilde{v} into coarse Gaussian primitives. For each voxel (h, w, d), use a fully-connected decoder \mathcal{D}{\text{crs}} to predict parameters \{\mu{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, s{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, r{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, o{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}, h{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}\}. Position Prediction: Predict a positional offset \Deltak \in [-r, r]^3 for the k-th voxel, where r > 0 is the maximum displacement. Compute the final mean: \muk = \text{voxel\center}k + \Deltak This ensures the primitive remains within its voxel. 4. Voxel Selection Stage: Predict voxel-wise confidence scores \sigma \in [0, 1]^{H \times W \times D} using a fully-connected predictor \mathcal{P}: \mathbb{R}^{\tilde{C}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} and a Gumbel-Sigmoid operator. For each feature vector \tilde{v}{h,w,d}, compute the confidence logit \mathcal{P}(\tilde{v}{h,w,d}). Apply Gumbel-Sigmoid to obtain the score \sigma{h,w,d}: \sigma{h,w,d} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\frac{\mathcal{P}(\tilde{v}{h,w,d}) + g0 - g1}{\tau}\right)} where g0, g1 \sim \text{Gumbel}(0, 1) are i.i.d. samples, and \tau is the temperature. Opacity Refinement: Multiply the coarse opacity by the confidence score to refine it: \tilde{o}{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}} = \sigma{h,w,d} \cdot o{h,w,d}^{\text{crs}}. Selection: Define the set of selected indices I where confidence exceeds 0.5: I = \{(h, w, d): \sigma{h,w,d} > 0.5\} The coarse primitives at these indices are termed "skeletal" Gaussian primitives. 5. Fine Stage: Predict multiple fine-grained Gaussian primitives near each "skeletal" primitive at selected voxels (h, w, d) \in I. Use a selective feature refinement module to refine coarse global features by integrating fine local geometric features. Note: The specific architecture of the fine stage decoder is not detailed in the provided sources. 6. Training: Use 2D supervision (rendering loss) on both coarse and fine renderings. The selection module is trained end-to-end solely through the rendering objective, without pseudo-labels or auxiliary supervision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Sequential Gaussian Attribute Decoding
head: Iterative Attribute Decoding, Sequential Decoder
body: Sequential Gaussian Attribute Decoding estimates 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes (color, opacity, rotation, scale, position offset) from tri-plane features by processing them in a fixed order rather than in parallel. It solves the problem of high degrees of freedom in joint attribute prediction by creating dependencies between attributes, allowing each decoder to specialize based on prior information. It differs from parallel decoders (e.g., HUGS [21]) which compute all attributes simultaneously. Inputs: Tri-plane features representing the 3D scene. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position offset, scale, rotation, opacity, and color. Data Structures: The method uses a series of fully connected neural network decoders. Each decoder Di corresponds to one attribute in the sequence. Decoder Architecture: Hidden layers: 3 layers. Neurons per layer: 128. Activation: GELU for hidden layers. Output activation: None for all attributes except scale. Scale output activation: Inverted Softplus. Numbered Steps: 1. Color Decoding: Forward the tri-plane features into the first decoder D{color} to estimate the color attribute C. 2. Opacity Decoding: Concatenate the estimated color C with the original tri-plane features. Feed this combined input into the second decoder D{opacity} to estimate opacity \alpha. 3. Rotation Decoding: Concatenate the estimated rotation R, the previously estimated opacity \alpha, and the tri-plane features. Feed this into the third decoder D{rotation} to estimate rotation R. 4. Scale Decoding: Concatenate the estimated scale S, the previously estimated rotation R, opacity \alpha, and the tri-plane features. Feed this into the fourth decoder D{scale} to estimate scale S. The output layer applies an inverted Softplus activation to prevent excessive Gaussian sizes. 5. Position Offset Decoding: Concatenate the estimated position offset \Delta P, the previously estimated scale S, rotation R, opacity \alpha, and the tri-plane features. Feed this into the final decoder D{pos} to estimate the position offset \Delta P. Formulas: Let T be the tri-plane features. Let Ai be the attribute decoded at step i. The input to decoder Di is: Input(Di) = [T, A1, A2,..., A{i-1}] where A1 = \text{Color}, A2 = \text{Opacity}, A3 = \text{Rotation}, A4 = \text{Scale}, A5 = \text{PositionOffset}. Parameters: Hidden layers: 3. Neurons per hidden layer: 128. Activation function: GELU. Scale output activation: Inverted Softplus. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Memory Usage: Without the inverted Softplus activation on the scale decoder, Gaussians may become excessively large, leading to excessive GPU memory usage during rasterization. Dependency Order: The method relies on the specific order (Color \rightarrow Opacity \rightarrow Rotation \rightarrow Scale \rightarrow Position Offset) to reduce degrees of freedom for each subsequent decoder. A decoder variant that spawns exactly kn Gaussian tokens per anchor n based on an allocation k, refining them via local cross-attention to produce B final Gaussians with computational cost linear in B. It differs from standard sequential decoding by introducing a hierarchical neighbor search and token spawning mechanism. Choose this when exact Gaussian count allocation and linear computational cost with respect to the number of Gaussians are required. Steps: 1. Token Spawning: For each anchor an, instantiate kn distinct Gaussian tokens tb using a TokenGen function conditioned on the slot index: \{tb\}{b=1}^B = \text{TokenGen}(\{(an, kn)\}{n=1}^N). 2. Initial Prediction: Predict an initial Gaussian g{b0} = \text{Head}(tb) for each token, including its initial center \mu{b0}. 3. Anchor Centroid Calculation: For each anchor n with kn > 0, compute the centroid of its initial Gaussians: \bar{\mu}n = \frac{1}{kn} \sum{b: nb=n} \mu{b0}. 4. Hierarchical Neighbor Search: Find K{anc} nearest anchors to \bar{\mu}n among anchors with km > 0: N{anc}(n) = \text{KNN}{K{anc}}(\bar{\mu}n; \{\bar{\mu}m: km > 0\}). Find K{gs} nearest Gaussian tokens to \mu{b0} only among Gaussians belonging to the local anchors N{anc}(nb): N{gs}(b) = \text{KNN}{K{gs}}(\mu{b0}; \{\mu{j0}: nj \in N{anc}(nb)\}). 5. Refinement: Refine token tb over L layers of cross-attention with neighbors N{gs}(b), followed by a feed-forward layer: tb \leftarrow tb + \text{CrossAttn}(tb, \{tj\}{j \in N{gs}(b)}). 6. Final Prediction: Predict a correction \Delta gb from the refined token tb using a residual head, yielding the final Gaussian gb = g{b0} + \Delta gb. Parameters: K{anc}: Number of nearest anchors to search for hierarchical neighbor search. K{gs}: Number of nearest Gaussian tokens to search within local anchors. L: Number of cross-attention layers for refinement. Regularizers (to ensure validity of hierarchical search): Voronoi Loss: Keeps each Gaussian closer to its own parent anchor’s centroid \bar{\mu}{nb} than to any neighboring anchor’s centroid \bar{\mu}m: L{vor} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{b=1}^B \max{m \in N{anc}(nb)} \left( 0, \|\mu{b0} - \bar{\mu}{nb}\| - \|\mu{b0} - \bar{\mu}m\| \right). Offset Loss: Constrains the residual correction \Delta \mub to limit Gaussian drift: L{offset} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{b=1}^B \max \left( 0, \frac{\|\Delta \mub\|}{d{nb}} - \delta \right)^2 where dn is the local anchor spacing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces high degrees of freedom for each decoder, allowing for easier specialization of the network for specific attributes. The inverted Softplus activation prevents excessive GPU memory usage during rasterization. Limitations: The fixed sequential dependency order restricts simultaneous attribute estimation. When to use: When using a decoder network to estimate Gaussian Splatting attributes from tri-plane features and specialization per attribute is desired. When not to use: When parallel computation of all attributes is preferred. Sequential Gaussian Attribute Decoding was introduced in the context of Gaussian Splatting Decoders for 3D-aware Generative Adversarial Networks. It contrasts with parallel decoders like HUGS [21] and transformer-based models [50] by calculating attributes sequentially. The Resource-Linear variant was introduced in RLSplat to provide exact Gaussian count allocation and linear computational cost.
