name: Gaussian Decoding from Scene Tokens
head: Scene Token Fusion and Gaussian Decoding, Scene Token Gaussian Decoding
body: Gaussian Decoding from Scene Tokens is a method that maps learned scene tokens into a set of freely placed 3D Gaussian primitives, allowing each token to represent a surface region with variable spatial extent and complexity. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by decoupling Gaussian center prediction from fixed ray intersections, enabling the decoder to place Gaussians anywhere in 3D space rather than anchoring them to specific rays. This approach builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting with Transformer-based Parameterization by introducing a fusion stage that integrates geometry and appearance information before decoding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene tokens \stokk (derived from fused geometry and visual features), color embeddings, and camera parameters. Outputs: A set of G 3D Gaussians per scene token, each defined by 23 parameters. Data Structures: Scene Token (\stokk): A vector representation for the k-th scene region. Geometry Tokens: Derived from backbone features, serving as keys in cross-attention. Visual Tokens: Layer-specific features serving as values in cross-attention. Color Embedding: Appearance information used in the final residual cross-attention. Gaussian Parameters: Each Gaussian j in token k has: \gmean{kj} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center. \gscale{kj} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale. \grot{kj} \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (unit quaternion). \gopac{kj} \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \gcolor{kj}: Color represented by degree-1 spherical harmonics. Numbered Steps: 1. Token Initialization: Scene tokens start from a shared template with a forward bias of z=0.5 in the reference frame. 2. Fusion: Perform fusion using three blocks. Each block consists of: Cross-Attention: Queries are scene tokens; keys are geometry tokens; values are visual tokens from one backbone layer (deepest first). Self-Attention: Among scene tokens. Parameters: 24 attention heads, MLP ratio 4, GELU activation, residual gates initialized to 0.01. 3. Appearance Injection: Apply a final residual cross-attention with the color embedding as values to add appearance information to the scene tokens. 4. Decoding: Decode each scene token into G Gaussians using a two-layer MLP. 5. Parameter Constraints: Apply squared-hinge penalties to keep scales in [10^{-6}, 0.1], opacities above 0.01, and positions within a radius of 10. Formula: The set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}k for token k is decoded as: \mathcal {G}k = \left \{ \left ( \gmean {kj}, \gscale {kj}, \grot {kj}, \gopac {kj}, \gcolor {kj} \right) \right \}{j=1}^{\ngs } = D(\stok k) where D is the MLP decoder, \ngs = G is the number of Gaussians per token, and the full scene is assembled from all K tokens. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiandecodefromscenetokens(scenetokens, geometrytokens, visualtokenslayers, colorembedding): """ Decodes scene tokens into 3D Gaussians. Args: scenetokens: Tensor of shape (K, Dtoken) geometrytokens: Tensor of shape (Ngeo, Dgeo) visualtokenslayers: List of Tensors, one per layer, deepest first. Each shape (Nvis, Dvis) colorembedding: Tensor of shape (Ncolor, Dcolor) Returns: gaussians: List of K lists, each containing G Gaussian parameter sets. """ K, Dtoken = scenetokens.shape G = 32 # Number of Gaussians per token # Step 1: Fusion Blocks currenttokens = scenetokens for i in range(3): # Cross-Attention: Queries=currenttokens, Keys=geometrytokens, Values=visualtokenslayers[i] # Using 24 heads, MLP ratio 4, GELU, residual gates init 0.01 crossattnout = crossattention( query=currenttokens, key=geometrytokens, value=visualtokenslayers[i], numheads=24, mlpratio=4, activation='gelu', residualgateinit=0.01) currenttokens = currenttokens + crossattnout # Residual connection # Self-Attention among scene tokens selfattnout = selfattention( query=currenttokens, key=currenttokens, value=currenttokens, numheads=24, mlpratio=4, activation='gelu', residualgateinit=0.01) currenttokens = currenttokens + selfattnout # Residual connection # Step 2: Appearance Injection # Final residual cross-attention with color embedding as values appearanceattnout = crossattention( query=currenttokens, key=geometrytokens, # Or geometry tokens as per standard practice, source says "residual cross-attention with color embedding as values" value=colorembedding, numheads=24, mlpratio=4, activation='gelu', residualgateinit=0.01) currenttokens = currenttokens + appearanceattnout # Step 3: Decode to Gaussians gaussians = [] # Two-layer MLP decoder D decoder = TwoLayerMLP(inputdim=Dtoken, outputdim=G 23) for k in range(K): token = currenttokens[k] params = decoder(token) # Shape (G 23,) tokengaussians = [] for j in range(G): # Extract 23 parameters offset = j 23 gmean = params[offset: offset+3] gscale = params[offset+3: offset+6] grot = params[offset+6: offset+10] gopac = params[offset+10] gcolor = params[offset+11: offset+23] # Degree-1 SH # Apply constraints # Squared-hinge penalties are applied during training loss, # but for inference, we assume valid parameters. # If implementing training, apply penalties to gradients. tokengaussians.append({ 'mean': gmean, 'scale': gscale, 'rot': grot, 'opacity': gopac, 'color': gcolor }) gaussians.append(tokengaussians) return gaussians Parameters: G=32: Number of Gaussians per scene token. Degree-1 spherical harmonics: Used for color representation. Cross-attention: 24 heads, MLP ratio 4, GELU activation, residual gates initialized to 0.01. Reference frame: All geometry is expressed in the coordinate frame of the first input camera. Scene scale: Normalized so that the median distance of input depth points to the origin is one. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Free Placement: Nothing constrains decoded Gaussians to stay near their source patch; the decoder can place them anywhere in 3D. This requires auxiliary losses (e.g., Cone loss) to ground Gaussians in their source patch. Precision: Scales are constrained to [10^{-6}, 0.1] and opacities above 0.01 to prevent numerical instability. Boundaries: Positions are constrained within a radius of 10. A variant that predicts depth from features to map pixel-aligned predictions to 3D space, decoupling Gaussian center prediction from fixed ray intersections. It differs by inferring geometry directly from latent features without relying on encoder-side depth maps. Choose this when explicit 3D geometry reconstruction from feature streams is required without external depth inputs. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On DL3DV at 6 views, G=32 gains 0.34 to 0.36 dB PSNR over G=8, while G=64 adds at most 0.08 dB at twice the Gaussians. Scaling: The number of Gaussians per token can be varied (G=8, 16, 32, 64), with diminishing returns for higher G. Strengths: Allows tokens to spread Gaussians over observed regions with variable complexity; free placement offers flexibility. Limitations: Requires auxiliary losses (Cone loss) to prevent Gaussians from drifting away from their source patch; no guarantee of association between token and observation. When to Use: When flexible, region-based Gaussian representation is needed and computational budget allows for transformer-based fusion. When Not to Use: When strict ray-anchored Gaussian placement is required or when auxiliary losses cannot be applied. Originated in ZipSplat (Lin et al., 2026), which builds on DA3-Giant. The method uses features from three backbone layers merged into geometry tokens, fused into scene tokens, and decoded into Gaussians. It is trained on RealEstate10K and DL3DV datasets. name: Depth and Gaussian Decoding
head: Depth-guided Gaussian Decoding, Inverse-depth Gaussian Decoding
body: Depth and Gaussian decoding is a method for reconstructing explicit 3D Gaussian primitives from encoded feature streams by predicting depth from the features and mapping pixel-aligned predictions to 3D space. It solves the problem of generating 3D geometry without relying on encoder-side depth maps or original context images, instead inferring geometry directly from the latent feature representation. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the Gaussian center prediction from fixed ray intersections, using a learned depth head to establish the third dimension. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reconstructed feature maps \hat{F}{c,i} for each context view i \in \{1, \dots, N\}; camera intrinsics Ki and extrinsics Ti; near and far depth bounds ni and fi for each view. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \hat{G}. Data Structures: Feature Map: \hat{F}{c,i} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} (or similar layout depending on implementation). Depth Map: Si \in [0, 1]^{H \times W}, representing normalized inverse depth. Gaussian Attributes: \hat{\Theta}i \in \mathbb{R}^{A \times H \times W}, where A is the number of attributes (e.g., opacity, scale, rotation, color). Parameters: ni, fi: Near and far depth bounds for context view i. These are stored in the bitstream and define the valid scene range. \sigma: Sigmoid activation function. Steps: 1. Predict Normalized Inverse-Depth Map: Apply a depth head network to the reconstructed feature map \hat{F}{c,i} and pass the output through a sigmoid function to constrain values to [0, 1]: Si = \sigma(\text{DepthHead}(\hat{F}{c,i})) where Si \in [0, 1]^{H \times W}. 2. Convert to Metric Depth: Convert the normalized inverse-depth value Si(p) at pixel p to metric depth \hat{D}i(p) using the near and far bounds: \hat{D}i(p) = \left( fi^{-1} + Si(p) (ni^{-1} - fi^{-1}) \right)^{-1} This parameterization ensures that Si(p)=0 corresponds to the far bound fi and Si(p)=1 corresponds to the near bound ni, constraining decoded depth to the valid scene range. 3. Predict Pixel-Aligned Gaussian Attributes: Apply a Gaussian head network to the post-codec refined features F{dec,i} and the decoded metric depth \hat{D}i to predict attributes: \hat{\Theta}i = \text{GSHead}(F{dec,i}, \hat{D}i). 4. Map to 3D Primitives: Use the decoded depth \hat{D}i, predicted attributes \hat{\Theta}i, and camera parameters Ki, Ti to instantiate 3D Gaussians: \hat{G} = \text{Map2D}\to3D(\{\hat{D}i, \hat{\Theta}i, Ki, Ti\}{i=1}^N) The \text{Map2D}\to3D function uses the depth and camera parameters to determine Gaussian centers and assigns the pixel-aligned attributes to the corresponding primitives. Pitfalls: Inverse-Depth Parameterization: The mapping Si(p)=0 \to fi and Si(p)=1 \to ni is critical. If the sigmoid output is not properly bounded or if the inverse calculation encounters division by zero (e.g., if ni or fi is zero), the depth will be invalid. Precision: The conversion involves inverse operations (^{-1}). Care must be taken with floating-point precision near the bounds, especially if ni \approx fi. A decoder that transforms geometry-guided features into per-Gaussian updates using an image-space dual-branch mixer followed by per-attribute heads. It differs from the standard depth-and-Gaussian decoding by operating iteratively to refine existing Gaussians rather than generating them from scratch. Choose this variant when pose-free refinement or iterative optimization is required. Steps: 1. Dual-Branch Mixer: Coarse Branch: Rearrange input from H \times W \times C to H/2 \times W/2 \times 4C via pixel-unshuffle (lossless space-to-depth reshaping), then apply dilated convolutions at half resolution. Detail Branch: Stay at full H \times W resolution and apply lightweight convolutions to preserve high-frequency residual signal. Fuse: Add the outputs of the two branches into a single feature map. 2. Per-Attribute Head: Each Gaussian samples the fused feature map at its projected mean in each context view. Aggregate per-view samples by averaging weighted by the Gaussian's rasterizer blending weights. Concatenate the aggregated feature with the Gaussian's current parameters and decode into the update using three parallel MLPs (one per attribute: position, opacity, color). Parameters: All output layers are zero-initialized so that refinement starts exactly at \Delta = 0. Pitfalls: Numerical Scale: Position, opacity, and color updates differ substantially in numerical scale. Using a single shared MLP lets the largest signal dominate others; hence, three parallel MLPs are required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Constrains decoded depth to a valid scene range using inverse-depth parameterization; does not require encoder-side depth or original context images. Limitations: Requires accurate camera parameters (Ki, Ti) and depth bounds (ni, fi). When to use: When reconstructing 3D Gaussians from latent features without access to ground-truth depth maps. When not to use: When iterative refinement of existing Gaussians is preferred over initial generation. Originated in CodecSplat, which introduces ultra-compact latent coding for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method separates optimization into two stages: a codec-free stage for stable Gaussian generation and a codec-aware stage for rate-distortion performance. The Delta Decoder variant was introduced in DeltaSplat for pose-free feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, focusing on iterative refinement. CodecSplat: Ultra-Compact Latent Coding for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25563, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) DeltaSplat: Iterative Gaussian Refinement for Pose-Free Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09853, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: SAGA
head: OmniSeg3D-GS, SegAnyGaussians
body: SAGA is a 2D promptable segmentation method lifted to 3D, leveraging the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for efficient segmentation within 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It differs from sibling methods like CoR-GS by relying on SAM's 2D segmentation capabilities to guide 3D Gaussian assignment rather than learned identity encodings or language features. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussians reconstructed from images and 2D segmentation prompts (points, boxes, or masks). Outputs: A segmented 3D scene where Gaussians are classified into foreground/background or specific object instances based on the 2D prompts. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation. Layout details: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. SAM Integration: Leverage SAM to extract segmentation masks or features from input 2D views. 2. Prompt Lifting: Map 2D prompts to 3D space by associating 2D segmentation results with the corresponding 3D Gaussians. 3. Gaussian Assignment: Assign instance IDs or segmentation labels to individual 3D Gaussians based on their overlap with the 2D SAM-generated masks. 4. name: Quantile Rendering
head: Q-Render
body: Quantile Rendering (Q-Render) is a sparse, transmittance-guided sampling strategy designed to efficiently render high-dimensional feature maps from 3D Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of dense volume rendering, where accumulating high-dimensional features along every ray scales poorly with feature dimensionality. Unlike conventional volume rendering, which processes all rasterized Gaussians, Q-Render shifts the Riemann partition from the spatial domain to the transmittance domain, sampling only the most representative "quantile Gaussians" that dominate the ray's transmittance profile. This approach reduces complexity from O(N C) to O(N + K C), enabling real-time rendering of high-dimensional data (e.g., 512-D CLIP embeddings) while maintaining segmentation accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathcal{G}: Set of optimized 3D Gaussians, where each gi \in \mathcal{G} contains parameters \{\mui, si, ri, \alphai, \text{sph}i\}. \mathcal{F}: Predicted Gaussian features, where each fi \in \mathcal{F} is a vector in \mathbb{R}^C. K: Hyperparameter defining the number of quantile segments (and thus the number of sampled Gaussians). I: Indices of rasterized 3D Gaussians intersecting the target ray, sorted by depth. Output: \tilde{f}Q \in \mathbb{R}^C: The rendered feature vector for the ray. Data Structures: The algorithm iterates through the list of rasterized Gaussian indices I using standard accumulators for transmittance and feature vectors. Mathematical Background: Standard volume rendering integrates feature c(t) weighted by density \sigma(t) and transmittance T(t) over spatial distance t: C{vol} = \int0^\infty c(t) \sigma(t) T(t) dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int0^t \sigma(s) ds). By changing variables to transmittance u = T(t), where du = -\sigma(t)T(t)dt, the integral transforms to a Riemann integral over u \in [0, 1]: C{vol} = \int0^1 c(u) du Q-Render approximates this integral using a Right Riemann Sum by partitioning the transmittance domain [0, 1] into K+1 equal segments defined by boundaries 0 = u{K+1} < uK < \dots < u1 < u0 = 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulators: Set current transmittance T \leftarrow 1, accumulated feature fQ \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, and quantile counter k \leftarrow 0. 2. Iterate Rasterized Gaussians: For each Gaussian index i in I: a. Retrieve Gaussian gi and feature fi. b. Compute test transmittance after passing through gi: T{test} \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha'i), where \alpha'i is the effective alpha of the Gaussian. c. Quantile Boundary Check: Determine if the transmittance has crossed the next quantile boundary. The boundary for the (k+1)-th segment is 1 - \frac{k+1}{K+1}. If T{test} < 1 - \frac{k+1}{K+1}: i. Increment k to reflect crossing a boundary. ii. Sample Quantile Gaussian: The current Gaussian gi is selected as the representative for the quantile interval ending at the boundary. Compute its weight wQ \leftarrow T \cdot \alpha'i (using the incoming transmittance T for correct alpha-blending). iii. Alpha-Blend: Update accumulated feature: fQ \leftarrow fQ + wQ \cdot fi. iv. Handle Multiple Crossings: While T{test} < 1 - \frac{k+1}{K+1}, increment k again to account for cases where a single Gaussian causes the transmittance to drop across multiple quantile boundaries or due to precision issues. d. Termination Check: If T{test} < \frac{1}{K+1}, break the loop, as remaining transmittance is negligible for the quantile approximation. e. Update Transmittance: Set T \leftarrow T{test} for the next iteration. 3. Normalize Feature Vector: Divide the accumulated feature by the remaining transmittance to correct for the unblended portion: \tilde{f}Q \leftarrow fQ / (1 - T). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def QuantileRender(G, F, K, I): """ G: List of Gaussian objects with attribute alpha F: List of feature vectors corresponding to G, each of dimension C K: Number of quantile segments I: List of indices of rasterized Gaussians sorted by depth Returns: Rendered feature vector of dimension C """ T = 1.0 # Current transmittance fQ = [0.0] C # Accumulated feature vector k = 0 # Counter for quantile boundaries crossed for i in I: alpha = G[i].alpha f = F[i] # Transmittance after this Gaussian Ttest = T (1.0 - alpha) # Check if transmittance crossed the next quantile boundary boundary = 1.0 - (k + 1) / (K + 1) if Ttest < boundary: k += 1 # Weight uses current incoming transmittance T for correct blending wQ = T alpha for c in range(C): fQ[c] += wQ f[c] # Handle multiple boundary crossings for the same Gaussian while Ttest < 1.0 - (k + 1) / (K + 1): k += 1 # Termination check for negligible remaining transmittance if Ttest < 1.0 / (K + 1): break # Update transmittance for subsequent Gaussians T = Ttest # Normalize to account for residual transmittance denom = 1.0 - T if denom < 1e-6: return fQ fQnormalized = [val / denom for val in fQ] return fQnormalized Parameters: K: Number of quantile segments. Typical values are 10, 20, 40. K=40 yields best performance, but convergence is achieved at K \ge 10 (~50 mIoU). Using K < 10 causes significant performance drops due to transmittance profile discrepancy. C: Feature dimension (e.g., 512). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed K Sensitivity: The optimal K varies with the transmittance distribution of the ray. Using a fixed K=40 is a simplification. Inference with K \neq 40 (when trained with 40) causes significant performance drops, indicating a need for adaptive K selection. Normalization: The final normalization step corrects for residual transmittance T remaining after processing all K quantile Gaussians. Without this, the accumulated feature would be biased because the sum of weights would not equal 1. Precision: The while loop for boundary crossing handles precision issues where multiple boundaries might be crossed by a single Gaussian or due to floating-point errors. An adaptive variant of Q-Render that dynamically selects the number of quantiles K per input ray by predicting feature similarity. Definition: Instead of a fixed K, this method predicts the optimal K based on the ray's transmittance profile. Method: The model is trained with three candidate K values: \{10, 20, 40\}. A similarity-prediction head takes the transmittance profiles \{Tn\} as input and outputs predicted similarity scores for each candidate K. An additional loss computes the difference between predicted similarity scores and actual feature similarity. During inference, the model evaluates these scores and dynamically selects the K that yields the highest predicted similarity. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Reduces complexity from O(N C) in dense volume rendering to O(N + K C), where N is the number of rasterized Gaussians per pixel and C is the feature dimension. This is significantly faster than top-K sampling, which requires sorting and has complexity O(N \log K + K C). Memory: Requires storing the rasterized Gaussian indices and features, similar to standard 3DGS, but reduces the computational load during the accumulation phase. Measured Performance: Speed: On ScanNet scene000600 with 512-D feature maps, Q-Render achieves 28.42 FPS, a ~43.7× speedup over a modified baseline for-loop implementation (0.65 FPS). It is up to 1.5× faster than standard volume rendering (V-Render). Accuracy: On ScanNet, Q-Render with K=10 achieved 50.75 mIoU, comparable to V-Render's 49.02 mIoU, and superior to top-K (e.g., 45.70 mIoU at K=40). At K=40, mIoU reached 50.85. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables real-time rendering of high-dimensional features (e.g., for open-vocabulary segmentation); avoids sorting overhead of top-K; converges quickly with small K. Limitations: Sensitivity to the fixed K hyperparameter; performance drops if inference K differs from training K; theoretical approximation error converges at O(1/K). Quantile Rendering was introduced in the paper "Quantile Rendering: Efficiently Embedding High-dimensional Feature on 3D Gaussian Splatting". It was developed to address the computational cost of rendering high-dimensional features (such as CLIP embeddings) in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is critical for tasks like open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation. The method builds on the continuous volume rendering integral formulation, shifting the sampling domain from spatial distance to transmittance. It is used in architectures like GS-Mink and GS-PTv3 for generalizable 3D neural networks. name: 4D Gaussian Splatting
head: 4D Gaussian Representation, 4D-GS
body: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to model dynamic scenes by treating time as a fourth dimension, enabling the reconstruction and real-time rendering of 3D videos from arbitrary viewpoints and timestamps. Unlike static 3DGS which assumes a fixed scene, 4DGS captures spatiotemporal deformations of position, rotation, scale, and appearance, allowing for the generation of novel views at any continuous time t. It distinguishes itself from deformation-field methods (e.g., Dynamic3DGS) by maintaining a canonical set of Gaussians transformed by a learned field, and from naive temporal extensions by using coherent 4D covariance structures or explicit spatiotemporal encoders to ensure smooth motion and appearance interpolation. 4DGS methods generally follow one of two architectural paradigms: Native 4D Gaussian Slicing (Yang et al.) or Canonical Deformation Fields (Wu et al.). Both aim to render a 2D image \mathcal{I}(u,v,t) for a given camera pose and timestamp t. Inputs: Camera extrinsics/intrinsics M, timestamp t, ground truth images \mathcal{I}{gt}. Outputs: Rendered image \hat{\mathcal{I}}, deformed 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' (for deformation methods) or conditional 3D Gaussians (for slicing methods). The primitive is a Gaussian. In Native 4DGS, the Gaussian is a 4D entity. In Canonical Deformation methods, the Gaussian is stored in a canonical 3D space with associated feature vectors for deformation prediction. 1. Native 4D Gaussian (Yang et al.) Mean: \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (spatial \boldsymbol{\mu}{1:3}, temporal \mu4). Covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, symmetric positive definite. Rotation: Represented by two unit quaternions ql, qr \in \mathbb{R}^4 (left and right isoclinic rotations) forming a 4D rotation matrix R = L(ql)R(qr). Scale: S = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz, st). Appearance: 4D Spherindrical Harmonics (4DSH) coefficients. Basis: Z{nl}^m(t, \theta, \phi) = \cos(\frac{2\pi n}{T}t) Yl^m(\theta, \phi), combining Fourier series for time and 3D SH for space. 2. Canonical 3D Gaussian + Deformation Field (Wu et al.) Canonical Gaussians: \mathcal{G} = \{\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{S}, \alpha, \mathbf{c}\} in 3D space. Spatial-Temporal Structure Encoder \mathcal{H}: Uses 6 multi-resolution HexPlane/K-Plane modules Rl(i,j) for pairs (i,j) \in \{(x,y), (x,z), (y,z), (x,t), (y,t), (z,t)\} and a tiny MLP \phid. Feature query: fh = \bigcupl \prodl \text{interp}(Rl(i,j)) where \text{interp} is bilinear interpolation at grid vertices. Deformation Decoder: Predicts offsets \Delta \boldsymbol{\mu}, \Delta \mathbf{R}, \Delta \mathbf{S} based on canonical position and time t. 1. Initialization: Sample points in a 4D bounding box or use COLMAP points from the first frame. Initialize 4D means \boldsymbol{\mu}, temporal mean \mu4 (scene duration), and temporal scale st (initially half scene duration to leverage anisotropy). Initialize 4D rotation quaternions ql, qr to identity (1,0,0,0). 2. Rendering at time t: Compute marginal temporal probability: p(t) = \mathcal{N}(t; \mu4, \Sigma{4,4}). Compute conditional 3D mean: \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D|t} = \boldsymbol{\mu}{1:3} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{1:3,4} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4,4}^{-1} (t - \mu4). Compute conditional 3D covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D|t} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{1:3,1:3} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{1:3,4} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4,1:3}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4,1:3}. Project \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D|t} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D|t} to 2D image plane using standard 3DGS projection. Render using the standard alpha-blending equation, weighted by p(t): \mathcal{I}(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^N pi(t) pi(u, v|t) \alphai ci(d) \prod{j=1}^N (1 - pj(t) pj(u, v|t) \alphaj) where pi(u,v|t) is the 2D Gaussian probability. 3. Culling: Cull Gaussians if outside the view frustum OR if pi(t) is negligible (not present at timestamp t). 1. Initialization: Initialize canonical 3D Gaussians using SfM points. Warm-up: Optimize static 3DGS for 3000 iterations without deformation. 2. Deformation Prediction at time t: Encode spatial-temporal features for each Gaussian using \mathcal{H}(\mathcal{G}, t) via HexPlane queries. Decode offsets: (\Delta \boldsymbol{\mu}, \Delta \mathbf{R}, \Delta \mathbf{S}) = \phid(fh). Apply offsets to canonical Gaussians: \mathcal{G}' = \{\boldsymbol{\mu} + \Delta \boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{R} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{S} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{S}, \alpha, \mathbf{c}\}. 3. Rendering: Splat the deformed 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' using standard 3DGS rasterizer. 4. Optimization: Loss: \mathcal{L} = |\hat{\mathcal{I}} - \mathcal{I}| + \mathcal{L}{tv}, where \mathcal{L}{tv} is grid-based total variation loss. Train with batch sampling of timestamps to prevent temporal flickering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def render4dgs(gaussians, camera, timestamp): """ Render a frame for a specific timestamp using Native 4D Gaussian Slicing. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. Each has: mu: (4,) array [x, y, z, tmean] Sigma: (4, 4) covariance matrix alpha: float shcoeffs: 4D SH coefficients R4d: 4x4 rotation matrix (from quaternions) S4d: (4,) scale vector [sx, sy, sz, st] camera: Camera object with projection matrix P and view matrix V. timestamp: float, the time t to render. Returns: image: (H, W, 3) rendered image. """ # 1. Compute Marginal Temporal Probability p(t) # p(t) = N(t; mut, sigmatt) mut = gaussians.mu[:, 3] sigmatt = np.diag(gaussians.Sigma)[:, 3] # Assuming diagonal for simplicity or extract Sigma[3,3] # More precisely: Sigma4,4 is the element at index 3,3 of the 4x4 covariance sigma44 = gaussians.Sigma[:, 3, 3] # Shape (N,) pt = gaussianpdf(timestamp, mut, sigma44) # 2. Compute Conditional 3D Mean and Covariance # mu3D|t = mu1:3 + Sigma1:3,4 Sigma4,4^-1 (t - mu4) mu13 = gaussians.mu[:,:3] # Shape (N, 3) mu4 = gaussians.mu[:, 3] # Shape (N,) # Sigma1:3,4 is the first 3 rows, 4th column of Sigma sigma134 = gaussians.Sigma[:,:3, 3] # Shape (N, 3) # Delta t deltat = timestamp - mu4 # Shape (N,) # Conditional Mean # mu3D|t = mu13 + (sigma134 / sigma44) deltat # Note: sigma44 is scalar per Gaussian mucond = mu13 + (sigma134 / sigma44[:, np.newaxis]) deltat[:, np.newaxis] # Sigma3D|t = Sigma1:3,1:3 - Sigma1:3,4 Sigma4,4^-1 Sigma4,1:3 # Sigma4,1:3 is the 4th row, first 3 columns (transpose of sigma134) sigma1313 = gaussians.Sigma[:,:3,:3] # Shape (N, 3, 3) # Outer product: sigma134.T @ sigma134 is (3, N) @ (N, 3) -> (3, 3) per Gaussian? # Actually: Sigma1:3,4 is (N, 3). Sigma4,1:3 is (N, 3). # Term is Sigma1:3,4 (1/sigma44) Sigma4,1:3 # This results in a (N, 3, 3) matrix. correction = np.einsum('ni,ni->nij', sigma134, sigma134) / sigma44[:, np.newaxis, np.newaxis] sigmacond = sigma1313 - correction # 3. Project to 2D # Standard 3DGS projection: # mu2d = P V [mu3D; 1] # J = Jacobian of projection # Sigma2D = J Sigma3D J^T mu2d, J, validmask = projectto2d(mucond, sigmacond, camera) # 4. Rasterize # Filter by bounding box and p(t) threshold visible = validmask & (pt > 1e-5) # Sort by depth depths = mu2d[visible, 2] # Assuming z is depth indices = np.argsort(depths) # Alpha blending image = rasterizealphablending( mu2d[visible][indices], sigmacond[visible][indices], gaussians.alpha[visible][indices], pt[visible][indices], gaussians.shcoeffs[visible][indices], camera.resolution) return image def gaussianpdf(t, mu, sigmasq): """1D Gaussian PDF.""" return np.exp(-0.5 ((t - mu) 2) / sigmasq) / np.sqrt(2 np.pi sigmasq) Densification Threshold: 5e-5 for D-NeRF, 2e-4 for Plenoptic. Loss Weights (Native 4DGS): \lambda1=0.2 (L1), \lambda2=0.01 (Entropy), \lambda3=0.05 (4D Consistency). \lambda2=0 for Plenoptic. Initial Time Scale: Half of total scene duration. Training Steps: 20,000 (D-NeRF), 30,000 (Plenoptic). Temporal Culling: Points must be culled if they are not present at the requested timestamp, not just outside the frustum. Entropy Loss: Can cause PSNR degradation on Plenoptic dataset due to dense views and transparent objects; recommended only for opaque surfaces and sparse views. No-4DRot Variant: Disabling 4D rotation updates reduces temporal variance, impairing motion fitting and causing flicker/blur. Urban Scenes: Standard indoor bounding boxes fail for infinite-distance backgrounds; requires sky masks and sparse depth supervision. Spacetime Gaussians (STG) is a 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models dynamic scenes using native 4D primitives, enabling real-time rendering of any arbitrary time slice without per-frame optimization. It distinguishes itself from MLP-based deformation approaches like DGS by explicitly parameterizing temporal opacity envelopes and polynomial trajectories for each Gaussian, allowing for smooth interpolation of geometry and appearance between discrete keyframes. 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting (4DRotorGS) is a differentiable rendering method for dynamic scenes that lifts 3D Gaussians into 4D space (x, y, z, t) using a rotor-based rotation representation from Clifford algebra. Unlike sibling methods such as Real-time 4DGS which use dual-quaternions that entangle spatial and temporal rotations, 4DRotorGS provides a spatial-temporal separable and interpretable rotation representation. It avoids the numerical instability of directly inverting the 3D covariance matrix by leveraging block matrix inversion formulas on the 4D covariance to compute sliced 3D parameters. Real-time 4DGS is a rendering method that achieves interactive frame rates by fusing a static background with a small, fast-updating set of dynamic foreground Gaussians. It distinguishes itself from general 4D Gaussian Splatting by treating the time dimension equally with spatial dimensions, utilizing a 4D scaling matrix and isotropic rotations to represent 4D rotation, and conditioning the marginal distribution on time. Temporal Axis Resolution Adjustment reduces the temporal axis resolution of K-Planes feature grids by narrowing the time normalization range to [-0.8, 0.8]. This technique accommodates camera-specific time offsets in unsynchronized video data without degrading rendering performance. It is distinct from Initial Time Scaling, which adjusts Gaussian variance; this method adjusts the feature grid's temporal domain to prevent offset values from deviating outside the learned feature planes. A time-lapse rendering architecture where each timepoint's splats are fitted independently and stored contiguously, with time acting as a hard ordering barrier to prevent LOD rung blending across timepoints. It fits Gaussian splats per timepoint (e.g., 256K per frame), streams timepoints sequentially, and renders time-dependent elements by clipping polylines and fading splats based on their temporal extent. Training and rendering modifications for sparse, wide-baseline outdoor scenes to prevent overfitting and model infinite-distance backgrounds. It integrates sparse depth supervision from LiDAR using inverse L1 loss, adopts a cube map for the sky, and penalizes inverse depth in sky-masked regions. The temporal coefficient of 4DSH is deactivated (set to zero) to reduce overfitting. A variant that disables 4D rotation updates, resulting in less temporal variance and impaired motion fitting. Disabling 4D rotation causes flicker/blur in rendered videos and poor reconstruction of object rims compared to the Full variant. A method that achieves continuous-time 4D reconstruction by modeling the trajectories with a neural ODE solver, allowing frame rates to be arbitrarily adjusted at test time. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) per pixel, similar to 3DGS, but requires computing conditional Gaussians or deformation offsets per frame. Training is significantly faster than NeRF-based methods but slower than static 3DGS due to temporal consistency losses and deformation field updates. Memory Complexity: Native 4DGS: O(N) where N is the number of 4D Gaussians. Canonical Deformation (4D-GS): O(N + F), where F is the size of the deformation field network, avoiding the O(tN) storage of explicit timestamp tables. Performance: 4D-GS (Wu et al.): 82 FPS at 800x800 on RTX 3090 (synthetic); 30 FPS at 1352x1014 (real). PSNR 34.05 dB on synthetic. 4D-Rotor (Yang et al.): 277 FPS on RTX 3090 at 1352x1014; 583 FPS on RTX 4090. PSNR 34.26 dB on D-NeRF. Optimized 4DGS: 2.8x training speedup over reference implementation, VRAM reduced from 1.9GiB to 1.2GiB. Strengths: Real-time rendering of dynamic scenes; high-quality novel view synthesis; efficient storage compared to per-frame methods. Limitations: Struggles with highly complex, non-rigid deformations without sufficient Gaussian density; entropy loss can degrade quality on transparent/dense scenes; urban scenes require specific adaptations for infinite background. 4D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Wu et al. in CVPR'24 and Yang et al. in CVPR'24. It addresses the limitation of 3D-GS failing to capture the dynamic nature of scenes. Early methods stored explicit tables for each timestamp, leading to linear memory growth O(tN). 4DGS methods evolved to use either native 4D primitives (slicing) or canonical deformation fields to maintain efficiency. It is widely used in dynamic scene reconstruction, avatar creation, and video editing. name: Spacetime Gaussians (STG)
body: Spacetime Gaussians (STG) is a 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models dynamic scenes using explicit temporal primitives, enabling real-time rendering of any time slice from discrete inputs. It distinguishes itself from MLP-based deformation approaches (like DGS) and rotor-based methods (like 4D-Rotor GS) by using polynomial trajectories and explicit opacity envelopes rather than learned implicit fields or Clifford algebra. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} captured or reconstructed from video frames at discrete time steps tk. Output: A continuous 4D representation allowing real-time rendering of color and geometry at any arbitrary time t. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi is extended with temporal parameters: 1. Spatial State: Mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, Covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation R and scale S), Opacity \alpha. 2. Appearance: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients c{l,m} for each band l. 3. Temporal Trajectory: Polynomial coefficients for position p(t) and velocity v(t). 4. Temporal Opacity Envelope: Parameters defining birth, death, and peak times, or a function e(t) modulating opacity. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from static reconstruction or multi-view stereo at keyframes. 2. Trajectory Modeling: Fit a polynomial trajectory pi(t) = \sum{k=0}^{d} a{i,k} t^k for each Gaussian i, where a{i,k} are learned coefficients. 3. Opacity Envelope: Define a temporal opacity function ei(t) that controls when the Gaussian is visible (born/dies/peaks). This allows Gaussians to appear and disappear smoothly over time. 4. SH Interpolation: Interpolate SH coefficients ci(t) over time, either linearly or via learned interpolation, to handle temporal color changes. 5. Rendering: For a target time t: Compute current position pi(t) and covariance (if velocity/acceleration are modeled). Compute opacity \alphai(t) = \alphai \cdot ei(t). Compute SH color Ci(t) from interpolated coefficients. Project to 2D and splat as in standard 3DGS. Formulas: Position: pi(t) = \mui + vi t + \frac{1}{2} ai t^2 (if quadratic) or higher order polynomial. Opacity: \alphai(t) = \alphai \cdot \text{Envelope}(t; \text{birth}, \text{peak}, \text{death}). Parameters: Polynomial degree: Typically 1 or 2. SH bands: Same as static 3DGS (e.g., order 3). Edge Cases: Extrapolation: Performance degrades outside the training time range. Precision: Polynomial fitting can be sensitive to time normalization. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian is only visible in one frame, trajectory estimation is ill-posed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderstg(gaussians, timet, camera): """ Render a scene at timet using Spacetime Gaussians. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: (3,) initial mean v: (3,) velocity coefficient a: (3,) acceleration coefficient (if degree >= 2) alpha: (1,) base opacity envelopeparams: (3,) birth, peak, death times shcoeffs: (L,) spherical harmonic coefficients shinterpcoeffs: (L,) interpolation coefficients for time """ projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # 1. Compute temporal position pos = g.mu + g.v timet if hasattr(g, 'a'): pos += 0.5 g.a (timet 2) # 2. Compute temporal opacity envelope # Simple linear envelope for demonstration; sources mention "born/dies/peaks" birth, peak, death = g.envelopeparams if timet < birth or timet > death: alphat = 0.0 elif timet <= peak: alphat = g.alpha (timet - birth) / (peak - birth) else: alphat = g.alpha (death - timet) / (death - peak) # 3. Interpolate SH coefficients # Linear interpolation between base and time-varying coeffs sht = g.shcoeffs + g.shinterpcoeffs timet # 4. Project and splat (standard 3DGS projection) # Assume projectgaussian handles view matrix, projection, and covariance rotation projg = projectgaussian(pos, g.covariance, camera) projg.alpha = alphat projg.sh = sht projectedgaussians.append(projg) # Standard alpha blending return composite(projectedgaussians, camera) Spacetime is a method that adds a temporal dimension to the feature field of 3D Gaussians, enabling real-time interpolation of both color and geometry between discrete keyframes. Time Complexity: O(N) per frame, where N is the number of Gaussians. Real-time rendering is achieved as trajectory and envelope evaluations are cheap polynomial operations. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where D is the size of trajectory and envelope parameters. Slightly higher than static 3DGS due to temporal coefficients. Strengths: Real-time rendering of arbitrary time slices; explicit control over motion; no need for MLP inference at render time. Limitations: Polynomial trajectories may not capture complex, non-smooth motions; requires sufficient temporal sampling for accurate fitting. When to use: When real-time rendering of smooth, continuous dynamic scenes is required, and the motion can be approximated by polynomials. When not to use: For highly complex, non-smooth, or chaotic motion; when memory is extremely constrained. Spacetime Gaussians (STG) was introduced by Li et al. in CVPR'24. It addresses the limitations of MLP-based deformation networks (like DGS) by providing a more explicit and efficient representation for dynamic scenes. It is part of the broader family of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods, alongside 4D-Rotor GS and Real-time 4DGS. name: Spacetime
head: Spacetime feature interpolation, temporal feature field extension
body: Spacetime is a method that adds a temporal dimension to the feature field of 3D Gaussians, enabling real-time interpolation of both color and geometry between discrete keyframes. It addresses the problem of rendering smooth, continuous dynamic scenes from sparse or discrete temporal samples, distinguishing itself from methods that rely solely on explicit particle tracking or optical flow by embedding time directly into the feature representation. Unlike Spacetime Gaussians (STG), which uses explicit polynomial trajectories and opacity envelopes, Spacetime relies on learned feature fields conditioned on time. The method extends the static Gaussian feature representation by conditioning it on a time coordinate t. This allows the radiance field to reconstruct geometry and appearance for any time t within the training range, not just the keyframes used during optimization. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each with spatial parameters (position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}). A time feature \gamma(t) derived from the current time t. Camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, intrinsics). Outputs: Rendered image (color and depth) for the specified time t and camera pose. The core data structure is the Gaussian packet, which includes: getfeatures: The base feature vector (e.g., SH coefficients or MLP input features) associated with each Gaussian. uniquekfIDs: An integer array indicating which keyframe(s) each Gaussian was primarily associated with or trained on. dxyz: Deformation deltas, if applicable for the specific variant (e.g., in GToF). 1. Time Feature Generation: Compute the time feature \gamma(t) for the desired rendering time t. This is typically done using positional encoding or a learned embedding. 2. Feature Conditioning: Input the spatial position \mathbf{x}, the time feature \gamma(t), and potentially other attributes into the feature network (e.g., an MLP or grid-based field) to retrieve the color and deformation parameters for that specific time. 3. Deformation (Optional): If the scene is dynamic, compute the deformed position \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x}(t) using the learned deformation field. 4. Rendering: Rasterize the Gaussians using the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer, using the time-conditioned features for color and the deformed positions for geometry. The attenuated time feature \gamma{time}(t) used in some implementations to prevent overfitting to time in deforming regions is given by: \gamma{time}(t) = \gamma(t) e^{-\frac{\lambda}{2} \frac{L(\gamma(t))}{\Delta x}} Where: \gamma(t) is the original time feature. \Delta x is the norm of the deformation distance. \lambda is the attenuation strength hyperparameter. L(\gamma(t)) is a term related to the feature magnitude (exact formulation garbled in source, but conceptually scales with feature energy). Attenuation strength \lambda: Controls the degree of time feature attenuation. Set to 60 in experiments. Blend alpha \alpha: Used in conditional feature blending for visualization. Set to 0.1. Noisy Reconstructions: In monocular settings, relying solely on the time feature can cause the radiance field to overfit to time rather than learning correct geometry, leading to noisy novel view synthesis. The attenuation method mitigates this. Discrete Keyframe Artifacts: Without interpolation, rendering between keyframes may result in popping or discontinuities. Temporal interpolation of features or deformations is required. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderspacetime(gaussians, camera, timet, lambdaatten=60): """ Renders a scene at time t using spacetime feature conditioning. """ # 1. Generate time feature # gammat is the encoded time feature, e.g., via positional encoding gammat = encodetime(timet) # 2. Query deformation and features # This step depends on the specific implementation (MLP/Grid) # For GToF variant, we might interpolate deformation deltas if usegtofinterpolation: dxyz = interpolatedeformation(gaussians, timet) else: # Query deformation from network conditioned on time dxyz = deformationnetwork(gaussians.positions, gammat) # 3. Apply attenuation if deformation is large (Ced-NeRF style) # Calculate deformation distance norm deltaxnorm = torch.norm(dxyz, dim=-1) # Calculate attenuation factor # Note: L(gamma(t)) is approximated or retrieved from feature magnitude # Assuming L is a scalar or per-gaussian feature norm featurenorm = getfeaturenorm(gaussians) attenuationfactor = torch.exp(-0.5 lambdaatten featurenorm / (deltaxnorm + 1e-6)) # Attenuated time feature gammatime = gammat attenuationfactor # 4. Get final features and positions # In a full implementation, the feature network takes (x, gammatime) # and returns color and updated covariance/opacity finalpositions = gaussians.positions + dxyz finalfeatures = featurenetwork(finalpositions, gammatime) # 5. Rasterize # Standard 3DGS rasterization with finalpositions and finalfeatures image = rasterize(finalpositions, finalfeatures, camera) return image A variant used in the GToF (Gaussian Flow) context for the ToRF scene type. It ensures smooth motion between discrete keyframes by linearly interpolating deformation deltas (d\xyz) across time steps. It calculates current and next interpolation frame IDs based on view.frameid // 4 and blends the deltas if the frame is not a multiple of 4. This is chosen when discrete keyframe-based training is used but smooth temporal rendering is required. A technique introduced in Ced-NeRF to reduce the frequency of the time feature for deforming parts of the scene. It prevents the radiance field from relying solely on time features, which causes noisy novel view synthesis. It is chosen when using monocular cameras or when deformation is significant, as it forces the network to learn geometry from coordinates rather than just time. A visualization/debugging method that blends Gaussian features with a colormap based on keyframe IDs. It is controlled by a UI checkbox and uses a blend alpha of 0.1. It is not a rendering method for production but a tool for inspecting which keyframes influence which Gaussians. Time Complexity: Rendering time is similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, as the time conditioning is typically a lightweight lookup or small MLP evaluation per Gaussian. Interpolation adds minimal overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing time-conditioned features or a deformation network. If using explicit interpolation (GToF), no extra memory beyond deformation deltas is needed. If using a neural field (Ced-NeRF), the network weights add memory overhead. Measured Performance: Real-time frame rates are achievable, as demonstrated by the ability to interpolate between keyframes in real-time. Ced-NeRF reports efficient performance on a single RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Enables smooth, continuous rendering of dynamic scenes from sparse temporal data; real-time performance. Limitations: Can suffer from noisy reconstructions in novel views if not properly regularized (e.g., via attenuation). Relies on the quality of the time feature encoding. Spacetime feature extension was introduced as part of the broader evolution of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods. It is cited in the context of "Flow, Tracking, and Control" methods, distinguishing it from Gaussian-Flow (which uses velocity fields) and Gaussian Splatting Lucas-Kanade (which uses optical flow). The concept of adding a temporal dimension to feature fields has been explored in dynamic NeRFs (e.g., Ced-NeRF) and adapted for Gaussian Splatting to enable real-time interpolation. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) brownvc/gftorf, https://github.com/brownvc/gftorf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ced-NeRF: A Compact and Efficient Method for Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i4.28138, fetched 2026-10-26 muskie82/MonoGS, https://github.com/muskie82/MonoGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting
head: 4D-Rotor GS, Clifford Algebra 4DGS
body: 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting (4DRotorGS) is a differentiable rendering method for dynamic scenes that lifts 3D Gaussians into 4D space (x, y, z, t) using a rotor-based rotation representation from Clifford algebra. Unlike sibling methods such as Real-time 4DGS which use dual-quaternions that entangle spatial and temporal rotations, 4DRotorGS provides a spatial-temporal separable and interpretable rotation representation. It avoids the numerical instability of directly inverting the 3D covariance matrix by leveraging block matrix inversion formulas on the 4D covariance to compute sliced 3D parameters. Inputs: A set of N 4D Gaussians, each defined by a 4D center \boldsymbol{\mu}{4D}, a 4D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4D}, spherical harmonics coefficients (or RGB color), and opacity o. Camera parameters (extrinsics \mathbf{V}, intrinsics) and a specific timestamp t for the frame to render. Scene scales for normalizing 4D neighbor distances. Outputs: A 2D rendered image C and depth/alpha buffers. 4D Rotor \mathbf{r}: A 4D rotor consists of 8 components stored as a vector of size 8: [s, b{01}, b{02}, b{12}, b{03}, b{13}, b{23}, p]. These correspond to the Clifford algebra basis elements 1, \mathbf{e}{01}, \mathbf{e}{02}, \mathbf{e}{12}, \mathbf{e}{03}, \mathbf{e}{13}, \mathbf{e}{23}, \mathbf{e}{0123}, where \mathbf{e}{ij} = \mathbf{e}i \wedge \mathbf{e}j and \mathbf{e}{0123} = \mathbf{e}0 \wedge \mathbf{e}1 \wedge \mathbf{e}2 \wedge \mathbf{e}3. The axes 0,1,2,3 correspond to x,y,z,t. 4D Covariance Block Matrices: The 4D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4D} and its inverse \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4D}^{-1} are partitioned into symmetric block matrices: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4D} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{U} & \mathbf{V} \\ \mathbf{V}^T & \mathbf{W} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4D}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{M} \\ \mathbf{M}^T & \mathbf{Z} \end{pmatrix} where \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{A} are 3 \times 3 matrices, \mathbf{V} is 3 \times 1, and \mathbf{W}, \mathbf{Z} are scalars. 1. Spatial Position: Randomly sample positions within an axis-aligned bounding box (e.g., [-1.3, 1.3]^3 for D-NeRF, or SfM range for Plenoptic Video). 2. Time Mean: Uniformly sample \mut from [0, 1] for D-NeRF or [0, 10] for Plenoptic Video. 3. Time Scale: Initialize st to 0.1414 for D-NeRF or 1.414 for Plenoptic Video. 4. 3D Scales: Initialize sx, sy, sz. 5. Rotors: Initialize the 8 components of the rotor \mathbf{r} such that they satisfy the normalization conditions (see Normalization below). To ensure \mathbf{r} represents a valid rotation, two conditions must be met: 1. ps - b{01}b{23} + b{02}b{13} - b{03}b{12} = 0 2. b{01}^2 + b{02}^2 + b{03}^2 + b{12}^2 + b{13}^2 + b{23}^2 + p^2 + s^2 = 1 The normalization function \mathcal{F}{norm} corrects deviations using a gradient-based step: 1. Calculate squared norm l^2 = \sum \text{components}^2. 2. Calculate \Delta = b{01}b{23} - b{02}b{13} + b{03}b{12}. 3. Calculate \varepsilon = ps - \Delta. 4. Calculate gradient \nabla \varepsilon: \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial p} = s, \quad \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial s} = p \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial b{01}} = -b{23}, \quad \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial b{23}} = -b{01} \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial b{02}} = b{13}, \quad \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial b{13}} = b{02} \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial b{03}} = -b{12}, \quad \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial b{12}} = -b{03} 5. Calculate step size \delta = \frac{-l^2 + \sqrt{l^4 - 4\varepsilon^2}}{2\varepsilon}. 6. Update components: \mathbf{r} \leftarrow \mathbf{r} + \delta \nabla \varepsilon. The 4D rotation matrix \mathbf{R}{4D} is constructed from the normalized rotor components. 1. Unpack normalized rotor \mathbf{r} into s, b{01}, b{02}, b{12}, b{03}, b{13}, b{23}, p. 2. Construct matrix \mathbf{M}l from components s, b{01}, b{02}, b{03} (interpreted as quaternion-like vector \mathbf{q}l) using the pattern: \mathbf{M}l = \begin{pmatrix} s & -b{01} & -b{02} & -b{03} \\ b{01} & s & -b{03} & b{02} \\ b{02} & b{03} & s & -b{01} \\ b{03} & -b{02} & b{01} & s \end{pmatrix} (Note: Source describes a permutation and reshaping of [a,-b,-c,-d, b, a,-d, c, c, d, a,-b, d,-c, b, a]. The explicit matrix above is the standard left-multiplication matrix for a quaternion/vector in 4D Clifford algebra context derived from the basis order 1, \mathbf{e}{01}, \mathbf{e}{02}, \mathbf{e}{03}). 3. Construct matrix \mathbf{M}r from components b{12}, b{13}, b{23}, p (interpreted as quaternion-like vector \mathbf{q}r) using the pattern: \mathbf{M}r = \begin{pmatrix} p & b{12} & b{13} & b{23} \\ -b{12} & p & -b{23} & b{13} \\ -b{13} & b{23} & p & -b{12} \\ -b{23} & -b{13} & b{12} & p \end{pmatrix} (Note: Source describes a permutation and reshaping of [p, q, r, s, -q, p,-s, r, -r, s, p,-q, -s,-r, q, p]. The explicit matrix above corresponds to the right-multiplication structure for the remaining basis elements). 4. Compute \mathbf{R}{4D} = \mathbf{M}l \mathbf{M}r. 5. Flip the last two dimensions of \mathbf{R}{4D} to account for coordinate system conventions. At a given timestamp t, the 4D Gaussian is sliced into a 3D Gaussian. 1. Extract blocks \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W} from \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{4D}. 2. Compute the temporal decay parameter \lambda = \mathbf{W}^{-1}. 3. Compute the sliced 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} without inverting \mathbf{A} directly: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D} = \mathbf{U} - \frac{\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^T}{\mathbf{W}} 4. Compute the time-dependent 3D center \boldsymbol{\mu}(t): \boldsymbol{\mu}(t) = (\mux, \muy, \muz)^T + (t - \mut) \frac{\mathbf{V}}{\mathbf{W}} 5. The sliced 3D Gaussian density is: G{3D}(\mathbf{x}, t) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}\lambda(t-\mut)^2} e^{-\frac{1}{2}[\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}(t)]^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{3D}^{-1}[\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}(t)]} The term e^{-\frac{1}{2}\lambda(t-\mut)^2} acts as a temporal envelope, causing the Gaussian to appear, peak at t=\mut, and vanish as t moves away. 1. Project the sliced 3D Gaussians to the 2D image plane using the standard 3DGS projection \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^T\mathbf{J}^T. 2. Sort Gaussians by depth. 3. Perform alpha blending to compute pixel colors: C = \sum{i=1}^N ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) The method uses Adam optimizer with specific learning rates: Positions/Times: 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (exponential decay to 1.6 \times 10^{-6} at step 30,000). 3D Scales/Time Scales: 5 \times 10^{-3}. Rotation: 1 \times 10^{-3}. SH Low Degree: 2.5 \times 10^{-3}. SH High Degrees: 1.25 \times 10^{-4}. Opacity: 0.05. Loss Function: L = (1 - \lambda1)L1 + \lambda1 L{ssim} + \lambda2 L{\text{entropy}} + \lambda3 L{\text{consistent4D}} 1. L1 and SSIM: Standard image reconstruction losses. 2. Entropy Loss: Encourages opacity oi to approach 0 or 1, reducing floaters: L{\text{entropy}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N -oi \log(oi) 3. 4D Consistency Loss: Enforces similar motion among 4D neighbors: L{\text{consistent4D}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left\| \mathbf{s}i - \frac{1}{K} \sum{j \in \Omegai} \mathbf{s}j \right\|1 where \mathbf{s}i is the speed term derived from slicing (\mathbf{V}/\mathbf{W}), K is the number of neighbors, and \Omegai is the set of K nearest 4D neighbors. Neighbors are found using Euclidean distance in 4D, balanced by scene scales. Training Details: Densification every 100 steps (steps 500–15,000). Opacity reset every 3,000 steps. Pruning of near-zero opacity Gaussians. Constructs the 4D transformation matrix by combining scaling and rotation. Initializes a zero matrix \mathbf{L} of shape (N, 4, 4), sets diagonal elements to scaling factors sx, sy, sz, st, computes the rotation matrix \mathbf{R} using the rotor normalization and mapping steps, and returns \mathbf{R} \mathbf{L}. The specific numerical procedure to enforce the Clifford algebra constraints on the 8-component rotor vector. It calculates the squared norm l^2 and the constraint violation \varepsilon, then applies a gradient-based correction step \delta to satisfy both the unit norm and the pseudo-scalar constraint ps - \Delta = 0. Complexity: Rendering complexity is similar to 3DGS, O(N) per pixel for blending, with the overhead of computing the sliced 3D covariance and center at each timestamp. Performance: Achieves real-time rendering speeds comparable to 3DGS when implemented in CUDA. Strengths: Interpretable separation of spatial and temporal rotations; handles dynamic scenes with appearing/disappearing objects better than deformation-based methods; avoids numerical instability in covariance inversion. Limitations: Entropy loss does not improve PSNR for dense-view reconstruction (e.g., vanilla 3DGS garden scene) but helps in sparse-view. Requires careful initialization of time scales. Metrics: On D-NeRF dataset, full model PSNR is 33.06. Removing KNN reduces it to 31.91; removing Entropy to 32.11; removing Batch to 32.64. 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Li et al. in 2024. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al. 2023] by lifting Gaussians into 4D space. It contrasts with RealTime4DGS [Yang et al. 2024] by using Clifford algebra rotors instead of dual-quaternions for better interpretability and spatial-temporal separability. The method is used for dynamic scene reconstruction from multi-view videos, such as the D-NeRF and Plenoptic Video datasets. name: Real-time 4DGS
head: RealTime4DGS
body: Real-time 4DGS achieves interactive frame rates by building a specialized renderer that fuses static background Gaussians with a small, fast-updating set of dynamic foreground Gaussians. It distinguishes itself from general 4D Gaussian Splatting by being the first to reformulate 3D-GS into 4D-GS, treating the time dimension equally with spatial dimensions. Inputs: A set of 4D Gaussians representing the scene, where each Gaussian is defined in 4D space-time. Outputs: A rendered image frame for a specific timestamp t. Data Structures: The method separates Gaussians into two sets: 1. Static Background Gaussians: Stored in a standard 3D-GS tile-based rasterization structure. 2. Dynamic Foreground Gaussians: A smaller set of Gaussians that are updated frequently. Method Steps: 1. Reformulation: The method reformulates 3D-GS into 4D-GS, representing each Gaussian with a 4D scaling matrix and a pair of isotropic rotations to define 4D rotation. 2. Time Conditioning: The 4D Gaussians are conditioned on time t multiplied by the marginal distribution to render the dynamic scene. 3. Sampling: At the current rendering timestamp t, the 4D Gaussians are sampled into 3D Gaussians. 4. Rendering: The sampled 3D Gaussians from both the static background and the projected dynamic foreground are rasterized using the tile-based approach to produce the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrealtime4dgs(staticgaussians, dynamic4dgaussians, timestamp): # Step 1: Sample dynamic 4D Gaussians into 3D Gaussians at the current timestamp # Project 4D primitives to 3D spatial slice at time t using 4D scaling and rotation dynamic3dgaussians = [] for g in dynamic4dgaussians: mean3d = g.mean[:3] cov3d = evaluate4dgaussianslice(g, timestamp) dynamic3dgaussians.append({'mean': mean3d, 'cov': cov3d, 'color': g.color, 'opacity': g.opacity}) # Step 2: Combine static and dynamic sets allgaussians = staticgaussians + dynamic3dgaussians # Step 3: Rasterize using the tile-based approach # Standard tile-based rasterization: tile culling, depth sorting, alpha blending image = zeroslike(targetresolution) for tile in tiles: tilegaussians = [g for g in allgaussians if g.boundsoverlaptile(tile)] tilegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) for pixel in tile.pixels: color = zeros(3) alpha = 0.0 for g in tilegaussians: contribution = g.opacity gaussianpdf(pixel, g.mean, g.cov) color += contribution g.color alpha += contribution image[tile.y:tile.y+tile.height, tile.x:tile.x+tile.width] += color return image Parameters: Timestamp: The specific time instance for which the frame is rendered. Update Frequency: The rate at which dynamic foreground Gaussians are updated. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Extends 3D-GS by explicitly modeling spacetime covariance. Choose when global spacetime coherence is more critical than the specific static/dynamic split optimization. Spacetime Gaussians (STG) Uses 4D rotors for rotation representation and adds temporal decay. Choose when modeling complex, challenging dynamics with interpretable rotation is required. 4D-Rotor Gaussian Splatting Adjusts resolution along the temporal axis. Choose when temporal aliasing or high-frequency temporal changes need specific handling. Temporal Axis Resolution Adjustment Time Complexity: Interactive frame rates are achieved by limiting expensive 4D-to-3D sampling and updates to a small set of dynamic foreground Gaussians, while leveraging the optimized tile-based rasterizer for the static background. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High rendering speed (interactive); effective separation of static and dynamic content; leverages mature 3D-GS rasterization infrastructure. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Real-time applications requiring dynamic scenes with a dominant static background. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Real-time 4DGS is cited as the first method to reformulate 3D-GS into 4D-GS by treating time and space dimensions equally. It was developed to address the computational bottleneck of rendering dynamic scenes in Gaussian Splatting by introducing a specialized renderer that fuses static and dynamic components. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Dynamic Scene Reconstruction: Recent Advance in Real-time Rendering and Streaming, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2503.08166, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Temporal Axis Resolution Adjustment
head: Time Normalization Range Adjustment
body: Temporal Axis Resolution Adjustment reduces the temporal axis resolution of K-Planes feature grids by narrowing the time normalization range to [-0.8, 0.8]. This technique accommodates camera-specific time offsets in unsynchronized video data without degrading rendering performance. It is distinct from Initial Time Scaling, which adjusts Gaussian variance; this method adjusts the feature grid's temporal domain to prevent offset values from deviating outside the learned feature planes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A K-Planes feature grid initialized with a standard temporal normalization range (typically [-1.0, 1.0]). Input: Camera-specific time offsets \deltak for each camera k. Output: A modified K-Planes feature grid with adjusted temporal resolution and normalization range [-0.8, 0.8]. Data Structures: The K-Planes feature grid consists of 2D planes representing spatial and temporal dimensions. No explicit bit-packing or new data structures are introduced; the adjustment is a parameter change in the coordinate normalization function. Steps: 1. Identify the current temporal normalization range of the K-Planes feature grid. 2. Narrow the temporal normalization range to [-0.8, 0.8]. 3. When sampling coordinates for feature lookup, compute the normalized time coordinate t{norm} for a camera k at time t using the offset \deltak: tk = t + \deltak t{norm} = \text{normalize}(tk, \text{range}=[-0.8, 0.8]) where \text{normalize}(x, [a, b]) = \frac{x - a}{b - a} \times 2 - 1 maps x to [-1, 1] within the specified range. 4. Use t{norm} to index into the temporal axis of the K-Planes feature grid. Parameters: Time normalization range: [-0.8, 0.8]. Original range (for comparison): [-1.0, 1.0]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the time offset \deltak is large, the adjusted range [-0.8, 0.8] ensures that tk remains within the bounds of the feature grid, preventing out-of-bounds access or interpolation errors. Reducing the normalization range effectively reduces the temporal resolution of the feature grid. Experiments confirm that this reduction does not harm overall performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizetime(t, deltak, rangemin=-0.8, rangemax=0.8): """ Normalize time t with camera-specific offset deltak to the range [-0.8, 0.8] for K-Planes feature grid lookup. """ tk = t + deltak # Map tk from [rangemin, rangemax] to [-1, 1] tnorm = 2.0 (tk - rangemin) / (rangemax - rangemin) - 1.0 return tnorm Sync-K-Planes is a variant of K-Planes adapted for unsynchronized video by incorporating camera-specific time offsets and adjusted time normalization. It is chosen when dealing with imperfectly synchronized video data, such as the Plenoptic Video Dataset, where fast dynamic contents like flames show different visual appearances in the same frame. The training involves two versions: hybrid and explicit. The hybrid version is trained for 90K iterations, and the explicit version for 120K iterations. An ISG sampling strategy is applied for the first 50K iterations with time offset, followed by an IST sampling strategy for both versions. The time offset learning rate is set to 0.1\times the K-Planes backbone learning rate. The time normalization range is set to [-0.8, 0.8] to prevent camera-specific time tk = t + \deltak from deviating from the feature planes. On the flame salmon scene, the hybrid version renders in 15.2 min, trains in 2.0 hrs, and has 27.0 M parameters. The explicit version renders in 22.0 min, trains in 3.8 hrs, and has 50.7 M parameters. Time and Memory Complexity: The method introduces negligible or tolerable differences in rendering and training time compared to the baseline K-Planes.
