name: Taming 3DGS
head: Budget-constrained 3DGS, Explicit Gaussian Cap, High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources, Taming3DGS
body: Taming 3DGS is a resource-efficiency method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that imposes an explicit cap on the total number of Gaussians to enable high-quality rendering on consumer-grade GPUs. It steers the densification process to spend a fixed budget where it helps most, trading peak quality for faster training and smaller model size. Unlike standard 3DGS which allows unbounded growth, this approach formulates optimization as a mixed-integer problem to maintain a constant Gaussian count. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients), a target maximum count N{max}, and a training schedule or importance metric. Outputs: A pruned and densified set of Gaussians \{G'i\} where |\{G'i\}| \le N{max}. Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of size N{max} storing each Gaussian's attributes. Global Score: A scalar value per Gaussian, computed from four factors: gradient magnitude, pixel coverage, per-view saliency, and core attributes (opacity, depth, scale). Steps: 1. Initialize: Start with the standard 3DGS initialization. Set current count N = N{init}. 2. Iterative Optimization Loop: a. Perform standard differentiable rasterization and backpropagation to compute gradients. b. Score: Calculate the global score for each Gaussian using the four factors. c. Prune: Identify the least important Gaussians based on the global score. Remove them if N > N{max} or if they fall below a threshold. d. Densify: Identify the Gaussians with the top B scores, where B is the desired number of new Gaussians. Split or clone these Gaussians to increase local density. e. Budget Enforcement: Maintain N \le N{max} by pruning excess Gaussians after densification. 3. Schedule/Policy: Use either a predictable schedule (fixed pruning/densification intervals) or adaptive importance guidance to decide when to apply steps 2b–2e. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def taming3dgsstep(gaussians, Nmax, B): # 1. Compute global score per Gaussian scores = [] for g in gaussians: # Standard differentiable rasterization provides positional gradients grad = computegradientnorm(g) # Projected screen-space area coverage = computescreencoverage(g) # View-dependent saliency metric saliency = computesaliency(g) # Normalized opacity, depth, and scale core = computecoreattributes(g) scores.append(grad + coverage + saliency + core) # 2. Prune least important if over budget if len(gaussians) > Nmax: sortedindices = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: scores[i]) prunecount = len(gaussians) - Nmax removeindices = set(sortedindices[:prunecount]) gaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if i not in removeindices] scores = [s for i, s in enumerate(scores) if i not in removeindices] # 3. Densify top B Gaussians if len(gaussians) < Nmax: sortedindices = sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: scores[i], reverse=True) topindices = sortedindices[:B] newprimitives = [] newscores = [] for idx in topindices: g = gaussians[idx] # Standard 3DGS split/clone: generate child with perturbed position/scale child = clonewithperturbation(g, offset=0.01) newprimitives.append(child) newscores.append(0.0) gaussians.extend(newprimitives) scores.extend(newscores) return gaussians, scores Edge Cases: Boundaries: N{max} must be chosen carefully; too low causes quality loss, too high defeats the purpose. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced due to fewer Gaussians to rasterize and backpropagate through. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by O(N{max}), significantly lower than unconstrained 3DGS. Performance: Enables high-quality rendering on consumer-grade GPUs. Strengths: Faster training, smaller model size, predictable resource usage. Limitations: Slight quality loss compared to unconstrained 3DGS. When to use: When hardware resources are limited or training time is a constraint. When not to use: When peak visual fidelity is required regardless of cost. Taming 3DGS was introduced to address the resource intensity of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. It explores a spectrum of trade-offs from predictable schedules to adaptive importance guidance. The method is part of a broader trend of optimizing 3DGS for efficiency, alongside works like LightGaussian and RTGS. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Splats Part 2: From Photos to a Trained Model, https://alphapixeldev.com/gaussian-splats-part-2-creating-gaussian-splats/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Analytic-Splatting
head: Analytic Integration for 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: Analytic-Splatting is a rendering method that replaces the point-sampling of 2D Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an analytical approximation of the integral of the Gaussian signal over the pixel window area to reduce aliasing artifacts during zooming or resolution changes. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting which treats pixels as isolated points, or Mip-Splatting which uses a hybrid filtering mechanism that suppresses high-frequency components, Analytic-Splatting preserves high-quality details by analytically integrating the signal using a conditioned logistic function approximation of the Gaussian CDF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D mean \mathbf{m}, a 3D covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} (or its Cholesky factor), opacity \alpha, and color \mathbf{c}. A camera view (projection matrix) and pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} = [ux, uy]^\top. Output: The final color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) for each pixel. Data Structures: The method operates on the projected 2D Gaussian parameters derived from the 3D input. \hat{\bm{\mu}} \in \mathbb{R}^2: The projected 2D mean. \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times2}: The projected 2D covariance matrix. \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}: The inverse covariance matrix, decomposed into coefficients: a = \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{22}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|}, \quad b = -\frac{\hat{\Sigma}{12}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|}, \quad c = \frac{\hat{\Sigma}{11}}{|\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}|} \{\lambda1, \lambda2\}: Eigenvalues of \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}. \{\mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2\}: Corresponding eigenvectors, forming the matrix V = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}1 & \mathbf{v}2 \end{bmatrix}. \sigma1 = \sqrt{\lambda1}, \sigma2 = \sqrt{\lambda2}: Standard deviations along the principal axes. Numbered Steps: 1. Project 2D Gaussian: Compute the projected 2D mean \hat{\bm{\mu}} and covariance \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} from the 3D Gaussian parameters using the affine approximation of the perspective projection. Compute the inverse \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1} and its coefficients a, b, c. 2. Eigenvalue Decomposition: Perform eigenvalue decomposition on \hat{\bm{\Sigma}} to obtain eigenvalues \{\lambda1, \lambda2\} and eigenvectors \{\mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2\}. 3. Transform Pixel Center: Transform the pixel center \mathbf{u} into the diagonalized coordinate system defined by the eigenvectors. Let \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = [\tilde{u}x, \tilde{u}y]^\top be the transformed coordinates: \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = V^\top (\mathbf{u} - \hat{\bm{\mu}}) Component-wise: \tilde{u}x = v{1x} (ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{1y} (uy - \hat{\mu}y) \tilde{u}y = v{2x} (ux - \hat{\mu}x) + v{2y} (uy - \hat{\mu}y) 4. Compute 1D Logistic Approximation: Define the standard logistic approximation function S(x) for the Gaussian CDF: S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-1.6 \cdot x - 0.07 \cdot x^3)} Define the scaled logistic function for standard deviation \sigma: S\sigma(x) = S\left(\frac{x}{\sigma}\right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-1.6 \cdot \frac{x}{\sigma} - 0.07 \cdot \left(\frac{x}{\sigma}\right)^3\right)} Compute the 1D integral approximations for the x and y axes over the unit pixel window centered at \tilde{u}x and \tilde{u}y: \mathcal{I}{\sigma1} = \sigma1 \left[ S{\sigma1}\left(\tilde{u}x + \frac{1}{2}\right) - S{\sigma1}\left(\tilde{u}x - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right] \mathcal{I}{\sigma2} = \sigma2 \left[ S{\sigma2}\left(\tilde{u}y + \frac{1}{2}\right) - S{\sigma2}\left(\tilde{u}y - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right] 5. Compute 2D Intensity Integral: Calculate the analytically approximated 2D Gaussian integral \mathcal{I}g^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u}) by combining the 1D integrals: \mathcal{I}g^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u}) = 2\pi \mathcal{I}{\sigma1} \mathcal{I}{\sigma2} This replaces the point-sampled Gaussian value g^{2D}(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{u}-\hat{\bm{\mu}})^\top \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}-\hat{\bm{\mu}})\right). 6. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) using alpha blending, where the transmittance Ti and the contribution of each Gaussian i use the integral \mathcal{I}{g-i}^\text{2D} instead of the point sample: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) = \sum{i\in N} Ti \mathcal{I}{g-i}^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u} | \hat{\bm{\mu}}i, \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}i) \alphai \mathbf{c}i Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left(1 - \mathcal{I}{g-j}^\text{2D}(\mathbf{u} | \hat{\bm{\mu}}j, \hat{\bm{\Sigma}}j) \alphaj\right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def logisticcdfapprox(x): """ Approximates the CDF of a standard Gaussian using a logistic function. S(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-1.6x - 0.07x^3)) """ exponent = -1.6 x - 0.07 (x 3) return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(exponent)) def scaledlogisticcdfapprox(x, sigma): """ Approximates the CDF of a Gaussian with standard deviation sigma. Ssigma(x) = S(x / sigma) """ return logisticcdfapprox(x / sigma) def computeanalyticsplatintensity(ux, uy, mux, muy, v1x, v1y, v2x, v2y, lambda1, lambda2): """ Computes the 2D integral approximation Ig^2D for a single Gaussian. Args: ux, uy: Pixel center coordinates. mux, muy: Projected 2D mean of the Gaussian. v1x, v1y: Components of the first eigenvector. v2x, v2y: Components of the second eigenvector. lambda1, lambda2: Eigenvalues of the projected covariance matrix. Returns: The 2D intensity integral value. """ # Step 3: Transform pixel center to diagonalized coordinates # utilde = V^T (u - mu) deltax = ux - mux deltay = uy - muy utildex = v1x deltax + v1y deltay utildey = v2x deltax + v2y deltay # Step 2/4: Standard deviations sigma1 = math.sqrt(lambda1) sigma2 = math.sqrt(lambda2) # Step 4: Compute 1D integral approximations # Isigma = sigma [Ssigma(u + 0.5) - Ssigma(u - 0.5)] # X-axis integral s1plus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildex + 0.5, sigma1) s1minus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildex - 0.5, sigma1) isigma1 = sigma1 (s1plus - s1minus) # Y-axis integral s2plus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildey + 0.5, sigma2) s2minus = scaledlogisticcdfapprox(utildey - 0.5, sigma2) isigma2 = sigma2 (s2plus - s2minus) # Step 5: Compute 2D intensity integral # Ig^2D = 2 pi Isigma1 Isigma2 intensity = 2.0 math.pi isigma1 isigma2 return intensity def renderpixelanalytic(pixels, gaussians): """ Renders a single pixel using Analytic-Splatting. Args: pixels: List of pixel centers (ux, uy) to render. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. Each object must have: mux, muy (projected 2D mean) v1x, v1y, v2x, v2y (eigenvectors of projected covariance) lambda1, lambda2 (eigenvalues of projected covariance) alpha (opacity) cr, cg, cb (color components) Returns: Dictionary mapping pixel coordinates to final color (r, g, b). """ results = {} for (ux, uy) in pixels: # Assumes gaussians are pre-sorted by depth for correct alpha blending t = 1.0 # Transmittance colorr = 0.0 colorg = 0.0 colorb = 0.0 for g in gaussians: # Compute analytic intensity intensity = computeanalyticsplatintensity( ux, uy, g.mux, g.muy, g.v1x, g.v1y, g.v2x, g.v2y, g.lambda1, g.lambda2) # Contribution contributionr = t intensity g.alpha g.cr contributiong = t intensity g.alpha g.cg contributionb = t intensity g.alpha g.cb # Accumulate color colorr += contributionr colorg += contributiong colorb += contributionb # Update transmittance t = (1.0 - intensity g.alpha) # Early exit if transmittance is negligible if t < 1e-4: break results[(ux, uy)] = (colorr, colorg, colorb) return results Parameters: Logistic linear coefficient: 1.6. Logistic cubic coefficient: 0.07. Pixel window size: Assumed to be 1 \times 1 centered at the pixel coordinate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Correlation Term: The 2D integral of a Gaussian with a non-diagonal covariance matrix contains an intractable correlation term b(x-\hat{\mu}x)(y-\hat{\mu}y). Analytic-Splatting resolves this by diagonalizing the covariance matrix and rotating the integration domain to align with the eigenvectors, approximating the 2D integral as a product of two independent 1D integrals. Small Standard Deviation: Unlike Mip-Splatting which convolves with a Gaussian kernel (approximating the integral as g \circledast gw), Analytic-Splatting calculates the integral analytically. This avoids large gaps for high-frequency components (small \sigma) where convolution-based methods might fail. Precision: The logistic approximation is differentiable, allowing for gradient computation. However, extreme values of x/\sigma in the exponential function may lead to overflow or underflow; standard numerical stability techniques (e.g., clamping) should be applied. This method computes the exact gradient of the analytically integrated 2D Gaussian splat intensity with respect to the elements of the 2D covariance matrix (\hat{\Sigma}). It solves the problem of differentiating the analytic approximation used in Analytic-Splatting, which integrates the Gaussian density over the pixel area to reduce aliasing. Unlike point-sampling methods, this gradient accounts for the boundary effects of the pixel window by propagating derivatives through the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix. Time Complexity: The method replaces the exponential function evaluation in standard 3DGS with logistic function evaluations and eigen-decomposition. The logistic function involves exponentials and cubic terms, which are computationally more expensive than a single exponential but cheaper than Monte Carlo super-sampling. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the standard 3DGS parameters, as the integral is computed analytically on the fly. Performance: Analytic-Splatting provides better anti-aliasing capability than standard 3DGS and Mip-Splatting, preserving high-quality details and fidelity, especially during zooming or resolution changes. It avoids the over-smoothing caused by Mip-Splatting's low-pass filtering. Strengths: Analytical solution avoids sampling noise; handles varying resolutions effectively; preserves high-frequency details better than convolution-based methods. Limitations: The eigen-decomposition and logistic function evaluation add computational overhead compared to the simple point-sampling of 3DGS. Analytic-Splatting was introduced by Zhihao Liang et al. in the paper "Analytic-Splatting: Anti-Aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via Analytic Integration" (arXiv:2403.11056v2, 2024). It addresses the aliasing artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting caused by treating pixels as isolated points, which leads to severe blurring or jaggies when rendering at varying resolutions. The method uses a conditioned logistic function as an analytic approximation of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Gaussian signal. name: Analytic-Splatting Gradient Computation
head: Gradient of 2D Gaussian integral w.r.t covariance matrix, Gradient of Analytic 2D Gaussian Splat
body: This method computes the exact gradient of the analytically integrated 2D Gaussian splat intensity with respect to the elements of the 2D covariance matrix (\hat{\Sigma}). It propagates derivatives through the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix to account for the boundary effects of the pixel window. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The 2D covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, its eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, the projected mean \hat{\mu} = (\hat{\mu}x, \hat{\mu}y), the pixel center (ux, uy), the integrated intensity \mathcal{I}^{2D}g, and the intermediate integral terms \mathcal{I}{\sigma 1}, \mathcal{I}{\sigma 2}. Output: The gradient matrix \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}} with elements for \hat{\Sigma}{11}, \hat{\Sigma}{12}, \hat{\Sigma}{22}. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Eigen-decomposition: Decompose \hat{\Sigma} to obtain \lambda1, \lambda2 and \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. 2. Compute Eigenvector Gradients: Calculate the gradient of the intensity with respect to each eigenvector \mathbf{v}k (k \in \{1, 2\}). For \mathbf{v}2, the gradient is given by: \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \mathbf{v}2} = 2\pi \mathcal{I}{\sigma 1} \left( \frac{\partial S{\sigma2}(\tilde{u}y + 1/2)}{\partial \tilde{u}y} - \frac{\partial S{\sigma2}(\tilde{u}y - 1/2)}{\partial \tilde{u}y} \right) \begin{bmatrix} ux - \hat{\mu}x \\ uy - \hat{\mu}y \end{bmatrix} where S{\sigma2}(\cdot) denotes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a 1D Gaussian with standard deviation \sigma2. The gradient for \mathbf{v}1 follows a symmetric derivation involving \mathcal{I}{\sigma 2} and derivatives with respect to \tilde{u}x. 3. Compute Eigenvalue Gradients: Calculate \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda1} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda2} from the forward pass intensity derivatives. 4. Compute Covariance Element Gradients: For each element \hat{\Sigma}{ij} where (i,j) \in \{(1,1), (1,2), (2,2)\}, apply the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda1} \frac{\partial \lambda1}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} + \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \lambda2} \frac{\partial \lambda2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} + \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \mathbf{v}1}\right)^\top \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}1}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} + \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{I}^{2D}g}{\partial \mathbf{v}2}\right)^\top \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}2}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} The terms \frac{\partial \lambdak}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}k}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}{ij}} are standard derivatives from matrix calculus for symmetric matrices. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Eigenvalues: If \lambda1 \approx \lambda2, the eigenvectors are not unique and the gradient \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}k}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}} becomes unstable, requiring regularization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def analyticsplattinggradient( cov2d: np.ndarray, dIdlambda1: float, dIdlambda2: float, Isigma1: float, Isigma2: float, pixelcenter: np.ndarray, projectedmean: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Computes gradient of analytic 2D Gaussian intensity w.r.t covariance matrix. """ # 1. Eigen-decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov2d) # Sort descending for implementation stability idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] lambda1, lambda2 = eigenvalues v1, v2 = eigenvectors[:, 0], eigenvectors[:, 1] # 2. Compute eigenvector gradients # dSsigma/d(utilde) is the Gaussian PDF def gaussianpdf(x, sigma): return (1.0 / (np.sqrt(2 np.pi) sigma)) np.exp(-0.5 (x / sigma)2) # Transformed coordinates utildex = np.dot(pixelcenter - projectedmean, v1) utildey = np.dot(pixelcenter - projectedmean, v2) # Gradient w.r.t v2 pdf2plus = gaussianpdf(utildey + 0.5, np.sqrt(lambda2)) pdf2minus = gaussianpdf(utildey - 0.5, np.sqrt(lambda2)) dIdv2 = 2 np.pi Isigma1 (pdf2plus - pdf2minus) (pixelcenter - projectedmean) # Gradient w.r.t v1 (symmetric) pdf1plus = gaussianpdf(utildex + 0.5, np.sqrt(lambda1)) pdf1minus = gaussianpdf(utildex - 0.5, np.sqrt(lambda1)) dIdv1 = 2 np.pi Isigma2 (pdf1plus - pdf1minus) (pixelcenter - projectedmean) # 3. Chain rule for covariance gradient gradcov = np.zeros((2, 2)) # Eigenvalue contributions: d(lambdak)/d(cov) = vk vk^T gradcov += dIdlambda1 np.outer(v1, v1) gradcov += dIdlambda2 np.outer(v2, v2) # Eigenvector contributions: d(vk)/d(cov) # For symmetric matrices, the gradient contribution is: # sum{k} (dI/dvk). (dvk/dcov) # Using standard result: dvk/dcov applied to gk yields # sum{m != k} (gk. vm) / (lambdak - lambdam) (vk vm^T + vm vk^T) if np.abs(lambda1 - lambda2) > 1e-8: # Contribution from v1 coeff1 = np.dot(dIdv1, v2) / (lambda1 - lambda2) gradcov += coeff1 (np.outer(v1, v2) + np.outer(v2, v1)) # Contribution from v2 coeff2 = np.dot(dIdv2, v1) / (lambda2 - lambda1) gradcov += coeff2 (np.outer(v2, v1) + np.outer(v1, v2)) else: # Degenerate case: eigenvectors are not unique. # Gradient is undefined without regularization. pass return gradcov Computes the exact gradient of a scalar loss L with respect to the input 3D Gaussian parameters (color c, opacity o, mean \mu, scale s, rotation q) by propagating pixel gradients backward through the alpha-compositing rasterizer. It enables differentiable training of Gaussian splat parameters by providing gradients for all learnable variables required for optimization. Unlike the forward pass which composites colors front-to-back, this method propagates gradients back-to-front to correctly account for occlusion and transparency. Gaussian Triangle Rendering is a surface reconstruction technique that represents primitives as "Gaussian triangles"—composed of three 2D Gaussian ellipses connected by common tangent lines—to achieve better surface continuity than single ellipses. It solves the problem of representing non-elliptical shapes in Gaussian Splatting by decomposing the triangle into its vertices, splatting them, and then re-sketching the triangle on the image plane with a modified fading parameter \gamma that handles inner, vertex, and edge regions separately. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which uses only ellipses, this method uses triangles and lines to better represent surfaces. Not given in the sources. The method originates from the paper "Analytic-Splatting: Anti-Aliased 3D Gaussian Splatting via Analytic Integration". It computes gradients by referring to standard matrix calculus results for eigenvalue and eigenvector derivatives. name: Backward Pass for Gaussian Gradients
head: Gaussian Splatting Backpropagation, Gradient Computation for Gaussian Parameters, Gaussian Rasterization Backward Pass, Splatter Backpropagation, Splatter backward pass
body: Computes the gradients of a scalar loss with respect to the input 3D Gaussian parameters (color, opacity, mean, scale, rotation) by propagating pixel-level loss gradients backward through the differentiable rasterization process. It enables end-to-end training of Gaussian Splatting models by providing exact analytic gradients for the 2D covariance matrix, 2D means, and 3D attributes via the chain rule. Unlike parent methods that focus on forward projection, this method specifically handles the reverse accumulation of gradients through the alpha-compositing and projection steps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gradient of the loss \mathcal{L} with respect to the rendered pixel colors \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial Ci} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each pixel i. Saved tensors from the forward pass: colorsprecomp, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, dc, sh, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, sampleBuffer. Output: A tuple of gradients: gradmeans3D, gradmeans2D, graddc, gradsh, gradcolorsprecomp, gradopacities, gradscales, gradrotations, gradcov3Dsprecomp, and three None values. Data Structures: The backward pass operates on the same Gaussian attributes as the forward pass. Key intermediate values saved from the forward pass include the transmittance Tn and the accumulated color contribution Sn for each Gaussian n contributing to a pixel. Gradient tensors are allocated with exact layouts: dLdconic is a float32 tensor of shape [P, 2, 2] storing the 2D conic matrix gradients, and dLdrotations is a float32 tensor of shape [P, 4] storing quaternion gradient components. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Restore numrendered, numbuckets, rastersettings, and the saved tensors from the forward pass. Pack arguments for the backward kernel call. Extract P = \text{means3D.size}(0) and M = \text{sh.size}(1) if \text{sh.size}(0) \neq 0 else 0. Allocate gradient tensors: dLdmeans2D [P, 3], dLdcolors [P, 3], dLdopacity [P, 1], dLdmeans3D [P, 3], dLdcov3D [P, 6], dLdsh [P, M, 3], dLdscales [P, 3], dLdrotations [P, 4], dLdconic [P, 2, 2]. 2. Null Pointer Handling: Nullify radiip, colorsp, and cov3Dprecompp if their respective shape0 dimensions are zero. 3. Focal Length Calculation: Calculate focal lengths: \text{focal\y} = \text{height} / (2.0 \times \text{tan\fovy}) and \text{focal\x} = \text{width} / (2.0 \times \text{tan\fov\x}). 4. Pixel to Gaussian Gradient Propagation (Back-to-Front): Iterate through the Gaussians contributing to each pixel in reverse order (back to front). Transmittance Update: Compute T{n-1} from the saved Tn using: T{n-1} = \frac{Tn}{1 - \alpha{n-1}} \quad (23) where \alphan is the opacity of Gaussian n at the pixel. Accumulated Color Update: Compute S{n-1} iteratively: SN(k) = 0 S{n-1}(k) = cn(k)\alphan Tn + Sn(k) \quad (25) where cn(k) is the color of Gaussian n in channel k. Color Gradient: Compute \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial cn(k)}: \frac{\partial Ci(k)}{\partial cn(k)} = \alphan \cdot Tn \quad (22) Opacity Gradient: Compute \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphan}: \frac{\partial Ci(k)}{\partial \alphan} = cn(k) \cdot Tn - \frac{Sn(k)}{1 - \alphan} \quad (24) Opacity Parameter Gradient: Compute \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial on} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \sigman} (where \sigman is the exponent term in the Gaussian PDF): \frac{\partial \alphan}{\partial on} = \exp(-\sigman) \frac{\partial \alphan}{\partial \sigman} = -on \exp(-\sigman) \quad (26) 5. 2D Covariance Gradient: Compute the gradient of \sigman with respect to the inverse 2D covariance matrix \mathbf{Y} = (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n)^{-1}: \frac{\partial \sigman}{\partial \mathbf{Y}} = \frac{1}{2} \Deltan \Deltan^\top \quad (28) where \Deltan = \mathbf{p}{(x,y)} - \boldsymbol{\mu}'n is the vector from the 2D mean to the pixel center. Using the identity \frac{\partial \mathbf{Y}}{\partial x} = -\mathbf{Y} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n}{\partial x} \mathbf{Y}, compute the gradient with respect to \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n: \frac{\partial \sigman}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n} = -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n^{-1} \Deltan \Deltan^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n^{-1} \quad (31) 6. 2D Mean Gradient: Compute the gradient of \sigman with respect to the 2D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}'n: \frac{\partial \sigman}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'n} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n^{-1} \Deltan \quad (27) 7. Projection Gradient (3D to 2D): Propagate gradients from 2D space (\boldsymbol{\mu}', \boldsymbol{\Sigma}') to 3D camera coordinates \mathbf{t} and view matrix \mathbf{T}{cw}. 2D Mean Contribution to \mathbf{t}: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}{\mu'}}{\partial \mathbf{t}} = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{P}^\top \begin{bmatrix} w/tw & 0 & 0 & -w \cdot tx / tw^2 \\ 0 & h/tw & 0 & -w \cdot ty / tw^2 \end{bmatrix}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}'} \quad (33) where \mathbf{P} is the projection matrix, w, h are image dimensions, and tw is the homogeneous coordinate. 2D Covariance Contribution to \mathbf{t}: Compute Jacobians of the projection matrix \mathbf{J} with respect to camera coordinates tx, ty, tz, tu (Equations 37, 38 in) and aggregate with \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'}. View Matrix and 3D Mean: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{T}{cw}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{t}} \mathbf{q}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} = \mathbf{R}{cw}^\top \left[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial tx} \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ty} \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial tz} \right]^\top \quad (40) where \mathbf{q} = [\boldsymbol{\mu}, 1]^\top and \mathbf{R}{cw} is the rotation component of \mathbf{T}{cw}. 8. Scale and Rotation Gradients: Decompose the 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{M}^\top into rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{S}. Compute gradients with respect to \mathbf{R} and \mathbf{S} using: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{R}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{M}} \mathbf{S}^\top, \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{S}} = \mathbf{R}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{M}} \quad (44) Compute Jacobians of \mathbf{R} with respect to quaternion components w, x, y, z (Equations 45, 46 in) to get gradients for rotations. 9. Execution: Call the CUDA backward kernel C.rasterizegaussiansbackward with the unpacked arguments to compute gradients for all Gaussian parameters. Return the tuple of computed gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backwardpass(dLdpix, savedtensors): # 1. Restore state and allocate gradient tensors P = savedtensors['means3D'].shape[0] M = savedtensors['sh'].shape[1] if savedtensors['sh'].shape[0] != 0 else 0 dLdmeans2D = torch.zeros(P, 3) dLdcolors = torch.zeros(P, 3) dLdopacity = torch.zeros(P, 1) dLdmeans3D = torch.zeros(P, 3) dLdcov3D = torch.zeros(P, 6) dLdsh = torch.zeros(P, M, 3) dLdscales = torch.zeros(P, 3) dLdrotations = torch.zeros(P, 4) dLdconic = torch.zeros(P, 2, 2) # 2. Handle null pointers for precomputed attributes if savedtensors['radii'].shape[0] == 0: savedtensors['radii'] = None if savedtensors['colorsprecomp'].shape[0] == 0: savedtensors['colorsprecomp'] = None if savedtensors['cov3Dsprecomp'].shape[0] == 0: savedtensors['cov3Dsprecomp'] = None # 3. Compute focal lengths focaly = savedtensors['height'] / (2.0 savedtensors['tanfovy']) focalx = savedtensors['width'] / (2.0 savedtensors['tanfovx']) # 4. Iterate pixels and back-to-front Gaussians for pixelidx in range(savedtensors['height'] savedtensors['width']): dLdpixpixel = dLdpix[pixelidx] gaussians = savedtensors['geomBuffer'].pixelgaussians[pixelidx] Tn = 1.0 Sn = torch.zeros(3) for n in reversed(gaussians): alphan = savedtensors['conicopacity'][n, 0] cn = savedtensors['colorsprecomp'][n] if savedtensors['colorsprecomp'] is not None else savedtensors['geomState'].rgb[n] # Transmittance and Accumulation updates Tn1 = Tn / (1.0 - alphan) Sn = cn alphan Tn + Sn # Color gradient dLdcn = dLdpixpixel alphan Tn dLdcolors[n] += dLdcn # Opacity gradient dLdalphan = dLdpixpixel (cn Tn - Sn / (1.0 - alphan)) dLdopacity[n] += dLdalphan # 2D Mean and Covariance gradients delta = savedtensors['means2D'][n] - pixelcoords sigmagrad = -0.5 torch.inverse(savedtensors['cov2D'][n]) @ delta @ delta.T @ torch.inverse(savedtensors['cov2D'][n]) dLdconic[n] += sigmagrad dLdmeans2D[n] += torch.inverse(savedtensors['cov2D'][n]) @ delta Tn = Tn1 # 5. Project 2D gradients to 3D space # Compute Jacobians for projection matrix J w.r.t camera coordinates t # Aggregate gradients for tx, ty, tz # Compute view matrix and 3D mean gradients # Compute scale and rotation gradients via SVD of 3D covariance #... (standard chain rule steps) # 6. Return tuple of gradients return (dLdmeans3D, dLdmeans2D, dLdcolors[:,:3], dLdsh, dLdcolors[:, 3:], dLdopacity, dLdscales, dLdrotations, dLdcov3D, None, None, None) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The computation involves matrix inverses (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'n^{-1}) and divisions by (1-\alphan), which can be numerically unstable if \alphan \approx 1. Boundaries: Gradients for Gaussians outside the viewing frustum or with zero radius are typically zero or undefined, requiring careful handling in the kernel. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has a singular covariance matrix, the inverse in Equation (31) fails. An optional extension that skips parameter updates for Gaussians that are not visible in the current view during the backward pass, based on the idea by Mallick et al.. It identifies invisible Gaussians and omits their parameter update computation. This speeds up training and reduces VRAM usage but slightly degrades quality and can cause inconsistencies and performance regressions compared to the original 3DGS implementation. On Mip-NeRF360 outdoor scenes (RTX 4090), it reduces training time from 5m31s to 3m03s, VRAM from 6.0GiB to 5.1GiB, and Gaussian count from 3.87M to 3.34M, while PSNR drops from 24.72 to 24.59. Analytical derivation of gradients for Gaussian attributes (e.g., mean \boldsymbol{\mu}) during rendering, accounting for the multiplicative effect of the selection mask and 2D projection coefficients. It computes the gradient for \mui using the derived formula, substituting the respective attribute for other parameters. The effective opacity is \hat{o}i = oi \cdot \hat{M}i. The loss is Ls = |I{es} - I{GT}|. The gradient is: \frac{\partial Ls}{\partial \mui} = G2 \cdot \left( \frac{\partial Ls}{\partial \hat{o}i} \cdot oi \cdot \hat{M}i \right) + oi \cdot \hat{M}i \cdot \left( \frac{\partial Ls}{\partial G2} \cdot \frac{\partial G2}{\partial \mui} \right) where G2(i, p) is the effect coefficient of the 2D projection of Gaussian i onto pixel p. A technique to prevent numerical instabilities during gradient computation by reconstructing intermediate opacity values and clamping/skipping low-opacity Gaussians. In both forward and backward passes, skip blending updates for any Gaussian where opacity \alpha < \epsilon. Clamp opacity \alpha from above with 0.99. Before including a Gaussian in the forward rasterization pass, compute the accumulated opacity if it were included; stop front-to-back blending before it exceeds 0.9999. Naïvely reconstructing intermediate opacity by dividing accumulated opacity by Gaussian \alpha is prone to numerical instabilities, such as division by zero. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians and pixels, dominated by the C++ kernel execution. Memory Complexity: Requires saving forward pass intermediates (transmittance, accumulated color) for each Gaussian-pixel interaction, increasing VRAM usage. Measured Performance: On an RTX 4090, the standard backward pass is the bottleneck for training speed. Skipping invisible Gaussians reduces training time by ~45% and VRAM by ~15%. Strengths: Provides exact analytic gradients, enabling stable and efficient optimization of Gaussian parameters. Limitations: High VRAM usage due to saved tensors; potential numerical instability near \alpha=1. Skipping updates can degrade quality. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models and gradients are needed for optimization. When not to use: When memory is severely constrained and quality degradation from skipping updates is unacceptable. Originated with the 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023), which introduced the differentiable rasterization pipeline. The backward pass implementation was detailed in the appendix of the gsplat library documentation and subsequent analyses. It is a core component of the training loop for Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction and other 3DGS-based methods. name: Gaussian Triangle Rendering
head: Gaussian Triangle Splatting, Mixed primitive rendering, Triangle-centered primitive splatting
body: Gaussian Triangle Rendering is a surface reconstruction technique that represents primitives as "Gaussian triangles"—composed of three 2D Gaussian ellipses connected by common tangent lines—to achieve better surface continuity than single ellipses. It solves the problem of representing non-elliptical shapes in Gaussian Splatting by decomposing the triangle into its vertices, splatting them, and then re-sketching the triangle on the image plane with a modified fading parameter \gamma that handles inner, vertex, and edge regions separately. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which uses only ellipses, this method uses triangles and lines to better represent surfaces. Inputs: A 3D Gaussian triangle primitive defined by three 3D vertices. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices) to project vertices to 2D. For each projected vertex i \in \{1, 2, 3\}: 2D mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^i. 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2D} (shared for the triangle structure). Opacity \alpha. Color c (derived from SH coefficients, independent of shape). Outputs: For each pixel p covered by the triangle: Fading parameter \gamma(p). Color c (same for all pixels in the primitive). Data Structures: Vertices: List of 3 points \{\boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^1, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^2, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^3\}. Tangency Points: List of 6 points \{t{1,2}, t{2,1,2}, t{1,3}, t{3,1,3}, t{2,3}, t{3,2,3}\}. t{i,j} is the tangency point on the i-th ellipse for the common tangent line connecting ellipse i and j. Quadrangles: Three quadrangles \square{1,2}, \square{1,3}, \square{2,3}. \square{1,2} vertices: \{\boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^1, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^2, t{2,1,2}, t{1,1,2}\}. \square{1,3} vertices: \{\boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^1, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^3, t{3,1,3}, t{1,1,3}\}. \square{2,3} vertices: \{\boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^2, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^3, t{3,2,3}, t{2,2,3}\}. Steps: 1. Vertex Splatting: Project the three 3D vertices of the Gaussian triangle to the image plane to obtain \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^1, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^2, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^3. Splat these points using standard point-based splatting to generate three boundary ellipses. 2. Boundary Construction (Dual Ellipse Intersection): For every pair of boundary ellipses (e.g., 1 and 2), solve the system of their dual boundary ellipse equations to find intersection points (xs, ys). The dual boundary ellipse equation gi^{dual} for ellipse i is a binary quadratic function: \begin{aligned} gi^{dual} &= \left( -\frac{1}{4}(di)^2 + ai fi \right) x^2 + \left( -ci di + \frac{1}{2} bi ei \right) x \\ &+ \left( -\frac{1}{4}(di)^2 + ai fi \right) y^2 + \left( \frac{1}{2} bi ei - ai ei \right) y - \frac{1}{4}(bi)^2 + ai ci = 0 \end{aligned} where ai, bi, ci, di, ei, fi are the coefficients of the implicit ellipse equation aix^2 + bixy + ciy^2 + dix + eiy + fi = 0. Solve the system: \begin{cases} g1^{dual} = 0 \\ g2^{dual} = 0 \end{cases} \quad (8) This system of two binary quadratic functions has closed-form solutions for intersection points (xs, ys). 3. Tangency Points: Common Tangent Line: For each intersection point (xs, ys) from Step 2, derive a common tangent line using the duality property: xs \times x + ys \times y + 1 = 0 \quad (9) Since Eq. 8 yields multiple solutions, select the common tangent line that is farthest from the third vertex of the triangle. Let the chosen line be xs^c x + ys^c y + 1 = 0. Tangency Calculation: Solve for the unique point of tangency t{1,2} between the chosen line and the first boundary ellipse g1^{ct}=0: \begin{cases} xs^c \times x + ys^c \times y + 1 = 0 \\ g1^{ct} = 0 \end{cases} \quad (10) Repeat for the second ellipse to get t{2,1,2}. Repeat this process for all three pairs of ellipses to acquire all tangency points t{i,j}. 4. Rendering Setup: Define the triangle \triangle formed by \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^1, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^2, \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^3. Define the three quadrangles \square{1,2}, \square{1,3}, \square{2,3} using the vertices and their corresponding tangency points. 5. Fading Parameter Calculation: For a pixel p, determine its location relative to \triangle and the quadrangles to compute \gamma(p): Case (i) Inner: If p is inside \triangle, set \gamma = \alpha. Case (ii) Vertex: If p is outside \triangle and outside all quadrangles, identify the nearest vertex \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^j. Set: \gamma = \alpha e^{-\frac{1}{2}(p-\boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^j)^T(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2D})^{-1}(p-\boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^j)} \quad (11) Case (iii) Edge: If p is inside a quadrangle (e.g., \square{1,2}), find points p{e1} on edge e1 (connecting \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^1 and t{1,1,2}) and p{e2} on edge e2 (connecting \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}^2 and t{2,1,2}) such that p lies on the segment p{e1}p{e2}. Calculate \eta using the Gaussian formula for both points (they should be equal) and set \gamma = \eta: \eta = \alpha e^{-\frac{1}{2}(p{e1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}1^{2D})^T(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2D})^{-1}(p{e1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}1^{2D})} = \alpha e^{-\frac{1}{2}(p{e2}-\boldsymbol{\mu}2^{2D})^T(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{2D})^{-1}(p{e2}-\boldsymbol{\mu}2^{2D})} \quad (17) The color c is calculated independently using SH coefficients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def conicfromsigma(sigma2d): """Map 2D covariance matrix to implicit conic coefficients [a, b, c, d, e, f].""" invsigma = np.linalg.inv(sigma2d) a, b = invsigma[0, 0], invsigma[0, 1] c, d = invsigma[1, 1], 0.0 e, f = 0.0, -2.0 return np.array([a, b, c, d, e, f]) def solvedualintersection(coeffs1, coeffs2): """Solve system of two dual conics g1dual=0 and g2dual=0.""" # Form conic matrices C1, C2 from coefficients def tomatrix(c): return np.array([[c[0], c[1]/2, c[3]/2], [c[1]/2, c[2], c[4]/2], [c[3]/2, c[4]/2, c[5]]]) C1, C2 = tomatrix(coeffs1), tomatrix(coeffs2) # Find lambda where det(C1 + lambdaC2) = 0 coeffsdet = np.polyder(np.poly(np.linalg.eigvals(np.linalg.inv(C2) @ C1))) lambdas = np.roots(coeffsdet) intersections = [] for lam in lambdas: Cdeg = C1 + lam C2 # Solve degenerate conic for intersection points # Use SVD to find null space direction, then intersect with original conic U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Cdeg) if np.allclose(S[:2], 0, atol=1e-6): v = Vt[2] # Intersect line v^T x = 0 with C1 # Substitute x = t u + s v into C1, solve quadratic # Simplified: use standard conic intersection fallback pass # Fallback to numerical root finding for robustness from scipy.optimize import root def equations(vars): x, y = vars def g(c, x, y): return c[0]x2 + c[1]xy + c[2]y2 + c[3]x + c[4]y + c[5] return [g(coeffs1, x, y), g(coeffs2, x, y)] sols = [] for x0 in np.linspace(-10, 10, 5): for y0 in np.linspace(-10, 10, 5): res = root(equations, [x0, y0]) if res.success and np.allclose(equations(res.x), 0, atol=1e-4): sols.append(res.x) return list(set([tuple(np.round(s, 4)) for s in sols])) def gettangencypoint(linecoeffs, ellipsecoeffs): """Solve for unique tangency point between line and ellipse.""" xs, ys = linecoeffs # Line: xsx + ysy + 1 = 0 => y = (-1 - xsx)/ys (if ys != 0) # Substitute into ellipse: ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 + dx + ey + f = 0 a, b, c, d, e, f = ellipsecoeffs if abs(ys) < 1e-6: x = -1.0 / xs y = 0.0 else: # Quadratic in x: Ax^2 + Bx + C = 0 A = a + b(-xs/ys) + c(xs/ys)2 B = b(-1/ys) + 2c(-xs/ys)(-1/ys) + d + e(-xs/ys) C = c(1/ys)2 + e(-1/ys) + f # Tangency implies discriminant ~ 0, solve directly x = -B / (2A) y = (-1 - xsx) / ys return np.array([x, y]) def pointintriangle(p, v1, v2, v3): """Barycentric coordinate check.""" v0 = v3 - v1 v1vec = v2 - v1 v2vec = p - v1 dot00 = np.dot(v0, v0) dot01 = np.dot(v0, v1vec) dot02 = np.dot(v0, v2vec) dot11 = np.dot(v1vec, v1vec) dot12 = np.dot(v1vec, v2vec) invdenom = 1 / (dot00 dot11 - dot01 dot01) u = (dot11 dot02 - dot01 dot12) invdenom v = (dot00 dot12 - dot01 dot02) invdenom return (u >= 0) and (v >= 0) and (u + v <= 1) def pointinquadrangle(p, q1, q2, q3, q4): """Split quad into two triangles and check.""" return pointintriangle(p, q1, q2, q3) or pointintriangle(p, q1, q3, q4) def gaussianfade(p, mu, sigmainv, alpha): """Calculate Gaussian fading parameter.""" diff = p - mu exponent = -0.5 diff @ sigmainv @ diff return alpha np.exp(exponent) def lineintersection(p1, p2, p3, p4): """Find intersection of line p1-p2 and p3-p4.""" x1, y1 = p1; x2, y2 = p2 x3, y3 = p3; x4, y4 = p4 denom = (x1 - x2) (y3 - y4) - (y1 - y2) (x3 - x4) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: return None px = ((x1 y2 - y1 x2) (x3 - x4) - (x1 - x2) (x3 y4 - y3 x4)) / denom py = ((x1 y2 - y1 x2) (y3 - y4) - (y1 - y2) (x3 y4 - y3 x4)) / denom return np.array([px, py]) def rendergaussiantriangle(vertices3d, cameraparams, sigma2d, alpha, colorshcoeffs): """Renders a Gaussian Triangle.""" # Step 1: Project vertices def projectto2d(v, cam): # Standard perspective projection vhom = np.append(v, 1.0) vclip = cam @ vhom if vclip[2] <= 0: return None return vclip[:2] / vclip[2] vertices2d = [projectto2d(v, cameraparams) for v in vertices3d] if any(v is None for v in vertices2d): raise ValueError("Vertex behind camera plane") # Step 2 & 3: Boundary Construction and Tangency Points tangencypoints = {} sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(sigma2d) coeffs = conicfromsigma(sigma2d) for i in range(3): for j in range(i + 1, 3): intersections = solvedualintersection(coeffs, coeffs) k = 3 - i - j bestlinecoeffs = None maxdist = -1 for (xs, ys) in intersections: linecoeffs = np.array([xs, ys]) dist = abs(xs vertices2d[k][0] + ys vertices2d[k][1] + 1) / np.sqrt(xs2 + ys2) if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist bestlinecoeffs = linecoeffs tij = gettangencypoint(bestlinecoeffs, coeffs) tji = gettangencypoint(bestlinecoeffs, coeffs) tangencypoints[(i, j)] = (tij, tji) # Step 4: Define Regions v1, v2, v3 = vertices2d t112, t212 = tangencypoints[(0, 1)] t113, t313 = tangencypoints[(0, 2)] t223, t323 = tangencypoints[(1, 2)] q12 = [v1, v2, t212, t112] q13 = [v1, v3, t313, t113] q23 = [v2, v3, t323, t223] # Step 5: Render for each pixel def getgamma(p): if pointintriangle(p, v1, v2, v3): return alpha # Case (i) Inner if pointinquadrangle(p, q12): # Case (iii) Edge: find pe1, pe2 such that p lies on segment # Direction parallel to tangency edge dirvec = t112 - t212 pe1 = lineintersection(p, p + dirvec, v1, t112) pe2 = lineintersection(p, p + dirvec, v2, t212) if pe1 is not None and pe2 is not None: eta1 = gaussianfade(pe1, v1, sigmainv, alpha) eta2 = gaussianfade(pe2, v2, sigmainv, alpha) return eta1 # They should be equal per source if pointinquadrangle(p, q13): dirvec = t113 - t313 pe1 = lineintersection(p, p + dirvec, v1, t113) pe3 = lineintersection(p, p + dirvec, v3, t313) if pe1 is not None: return gaussianfade(pe1, v1, sigmainv, alpha) if pointinquadrangle(p, q23): dirvec = t223 - t323 pe2 = lineintersection(p, p + dirvec, v2, t223) if pe2 is not None: return gaussianfade(pe2, v2, sigmainv, alpha) # Case (ii) Vertex dists = [np.linalg.norm(p - v) for v in vertices2d] nearestidx = np.argmin(dists) return gaussianfade(p, vertices2d[nearestidx], sigmainv, alpha) return getgamma Complexity: The method requires solving systems of quadratic equations for each triangle per frame, which is more computationally intensive than standard ellipse splatting. The number of operations scales with the number of triangles and pixels covered. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Better surface continuity than single ellipses; handles inner, vertex, and edge regions separately for accurate fading. Limitations: More complex implementation due to dual ellipse intersection and tangency calculations; requires careful handling of degenerate cases (e.g., parallel tangents). When to use: When surface reconstruction quality is critical and the scene contains sharp features or planar surfaces that benefit from triangle-based representation. Gaussian Triangle Rendering is part of the Mixed-Primitive-based Gaussian Splatting (MP-GS) framework, introduced to enable the splatting of non-elliptical primitives like "Gaussian lines" and "Gaussian triangles". It was proposed to address the limitations of standard Gaussian Splatting, which uses only ellipses, by allowing for more accurate reconstruction of object surfaces. A Mixed-Primitive-based Gaussian Splatting Method for Surface Reconstruction, https://core.ac.uk/works/308836756, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Projection Geometry and Coordinate Systems
body: This family defines the mathematical framework for transforming 3D Gaussian primitives, defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, into 2D distributions suitable for rasterization. It sets apart from standard perspective projection by supporting optimal tangent-plane projections [3293-optimal-gaussian-splatting.md] and specialized geometries such as cone-beam X-ray scanning [3458-3d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization-cone-beam-scanner-space.md]. All methods in this family map a 3D Gaussian primitive to a 2D Gaussian distribution for rasterization. The shared pipeline involves: 1. World-to-Local Transformation: Transforming the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} from world space to a local coordinate system where the viewing direction aligns with a principal axis (typically the z-axis). 2. Projection: Mapping the 3D geometry to a 2D plane using a projection function \varphi. 3. Covariance Handling: Computing the 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} from the 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' in the local space using the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the projection function: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} \approx \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}^\top. 4. Rasterization: Evaluating the 2D Gaussian at pixel coordinates to determine opacity or density contribution. Reduces projection error by radially projecting each 3D Gaussian onto a unique tangent plane perpendicular to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than a single fixed plane z=1. Choose this when high-fidelity rendering of large or off-center Gaussians is required. Renders X-ray projections by integrating 3D Gaussians along cone-beam ray paths, summing 2D Gaussians instead of alpha-compositing. Choose this for medical imaging or CT reconstruction tasks where integration bias must be avoided. Adapts the rasterization projection for panoramic images by mapping pixel coordinates to the unit sphere. Definition: For a pixel (u, v) on a panoramic image of height H and width W, a ray is cast and mapped to the 2D coordinate vector \mathbf{x}{2D}. Formula: The projection maps to the unit sphere before applying the optimal projection function \varphip: \mathbf{x}{2D} = \varphip \left( \begin{bmatrix} \sin \left( \frac{\pi(-W+2u)}{W} \right) \cos \left( \frac{\pi(-\frac{H}{2}+v)}{H} \right) \\ \sin \left( \frac{\pi(-\frac{H}{2}+v)}{H} \right) \\ \cos \left( \frac{\pi(-\frac{H}{2}+v)}{H} \right) \cos \left( \frac{\pi(-W+2u)}{W} \right) \end{bmatrix} \right) Parameters: H is the image height, W is the image width. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting method uses a fixed perspective projection plane. Research has extended the projection model to support fisheye cameras, such as the equidistant projection model, and panoramic images. On the Error Analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting and an Optimal Projection Strategy, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72643-915, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Optimal Gaussian Splatting
head: Optimal Projection, Unit Sphere Based Rasterizer
body: Optimal Gaussian Splatting is a rendering method that reduces projection error by radially projecting each 3D Gaussian primitive onto a unique tangent plane perpendicular to the line connecting the Gaussian mean to the camera center, rather than projecting all Gaussians onto a single plane z=1. Unlike the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization which uses a fixed perspective plane, this method adapts the projection geometry per primitive to minimize the discrepancy between the 3D Gaussian density and its 2D rasterized approximation. It achieves higher-quality rendering with smaller projection errors compared to the original approach. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitive defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} in world coordinates. Camera extrinsic matrix (World-to-Camera transformation). Camera intrinsic parameters: principal point (cx, cy) and focal lengths (fx, fy). Pixel coordinates (u, v). Outputs: 2D Gaussian value G{2D}(\mathbf{x}{2D}) for alpha blending at pixel (u, v). Data Structures: \boldsymbol{\mu}': 3D mean in camera coordinates. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}': 3D covariance in camera coordinates. \mathbf{x}p: Projection point on the unit sphere (3D vector). \mathbf{J}p: 3 \times 3 Jacobian matrix of the optimal projection function. \mathbf{Q}: Invertible 3 \times 3 matrix used to handle rank deficiency in the covariance inverse. Steps: 1. Transform to Camera Space: Transform the Gaussian mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} from world coordinates to camera coordinates, resulting in \boldsymbol{\mu}' and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}'. 2. Compute Projection Point on Unit Sphere: Calculate the point \mathbf{x}p where the line from the camera center to the Gaussian mean intersects the unit sphere: \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{p}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}' \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}'^{\top} \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right)^{-1/2} This defines the normal of the tangent plane. 3. Define Optimal Projection Plane: The projection plane is tangent to the unit sphere at \mathbf{x}p. Its equation is: \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{p}}^T \cdot \left( \mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{p}} \right) = 0. 4. Compute Ray Direction and Project to Tangent Plane: For a pixel (u, v), construct the ray direction in camera space using pinhole intrinsics: \mathbf{d} = \begin{bmatrix} (u - cx) / fx \\ (v - cy) / fy \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. Project this ray direction onto the tangent plane defined by \mathbf{x}p using the optimal projection function \varphip: \varphip \left( \mathbf{x}' \right) = \mathbf{x}' \left( \mathbf{x}p^\top \mathbf{x}' \right)^{-1}. The resulting 2D coordinate on the tangent plane is: \mathbf{x}{2D} = \varphip \left( \mathbf{d} \right). Note that \mathbf{x}{2D} is a 3D vector lying on the tangent plane, but for the 2D Gaussian evaluation, it is treated as the coordinate relative to the projection of the mean. 5. Compute Jacobian Matrix \mathbf{J}p: Compute the Jacobian of the projection function \varphip evaluated at the mean \boldsymbol{\mu}': \mathbf{J}p = \frac{\partial \varphip}{\partial \mathbf{x}'} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right) = \mathbb{I} \left( \mathbf{x}p^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right)^{-1} - \boldsymbol{\mu}' \left( \mathbf{x}p^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}' \right)^{-1} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}'^\top \mathbf{x}p \right)^{-1} \mathbf{x}p^\top. Explicitly, for \boldsymbol{\mu}' = [\mux, \muy, \muz]^\top and N = \mux^2 + \muy^2 + \muz^2, the matrix elements are derived from the source. The source provides a specific form for \mathbf{J}p where the diagonal elements involve terms like \frac{\muy^2 + \muz^2}{N^{3/2}} and off-diagonals involve \frac{\mux \muy}{N^{3/2}}. 6. Handle Rank Deficiency with Matrix \mathbf{Q}: The Jacobian \mathbf{J}p has a rank of 2. The resulting matrix \mathbf{J}p \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}p^\top has non-zero third row and column entries, unlike the standard projection Jacobian \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}^\top where these are zero. To correctly invert the covariance for the 2D Gaussian, an invertible matrix \mathbf{Q} is introduced. The matrix \mathbf{Q} is defined as: \mathbf{Q} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \frac{\muz}{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muz^2}} \\ \frac{\mux \muy}{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muz^2} \sqrt{\mux^2 + \muy^2 + \muz^2}} \\ \frac{\mux}{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muz^2} + \muy^2 + \muz^2} \end{array} \right] \cdot \left[ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muz^2}}{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muy^2 + \muz^2}} - \frac{\mux}{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muz^2}} \\ \frac{\muy \muz}{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muz^2} \sqrt{\mux^2 + \muy^2 + \muz^2}} \\ \frac{\muz}{\sqrt{\mux^2 + \muy^2 + \muz^2}} \end{array} \right]. 7. Evaluate 2D Gaussian: Compute the 2D Gaussian value for alpha blending: G{2D}(\mathbf{x}{2D}) = \exp \left\{ -1/2 \left( \mathbf{x}{2D} - \varphip(\boldsymbol{\mu}') \right)^T \left( \mathbf{J}p \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}p^\top \right)^{-1} \left( \mathbf{x}{2D} - \varphip(\boldsymbol{\mu}') \right) \right\}. The inverse covariance matrix is obtained by skipping the third row and column of \mathbf{J}p \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}p^\top after applying the transformation involving \mathbf{Q} to ensure the equation holds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def optimalgaussiansplatting(muworld, sigmaworld, extrinsic, intrinsic, u, v): """ Computes the 2D Gaussian value for a single pixel and Gaussian primitive. Args: muworld: Tensor [3], Gaussian mean in world coordinates. sigmaworld: Tensor [3, 3], Gaussian covariance in world coordinates. extrinsic: Tensor [4, 4], World-to-Camera transformation matrix. intrinsic: Tuple (cx, cy, fx, fy), Camera intrinsics. u, v: Float, Pixel coordinates. Returns: Tensor [1], The 2D Gaussian value G2D. """ # 1. Transform to Camera Space R = extrinsic[:3,:3] t = extrinsic[:3, 3] mucam = (R @ muworld + t).squeeze() sigmacam = R @ sigmaworld @ R.T cx, cy, fx, fy = intrinsic # 2. Compute Projection Point on Unit Sphere (xp) munormsq = torch.dot(mucam, mucam) munorm = torch.sqrt(munormsq) xp = mucam / munorm # 3. Compute Ray Direction in Camera Space d = torch.tensor([(u - cx) / fx, (v - cy) / fy, 1.0]) # 4. Project Ray Direction to Tangent Plane (x2D) dotxpd = torch.dot(xp, d) x2D = d / dotxpd # Project Mean to Tangent Plane dotxpmu = torch.dot(xp, mucam) muproj = mucam / dotxpmu # 5. Compute Jacobian Jp # Jp = I (xp^T mu')^-1 - mu' (xp^T mu')^-1 (mu'^T xp)^-1 xp^T invdot = 1.0 / dotxpmu Jp = invdot torch.eye(3) - invdot invdot torch.outer(mucam, xp) # 6. Compute 2D Covariance and Inverse # Sigma2Draw = Jp @ Sigmacam @ Jp^T Sigma2Draw = Jp @ sigmacam @ Jp.T # Handle Rank Deficiency: Skip third row and column as per source # Note: The source's Equation 18 for matrix Q contains formatting inconsistencies. # The implementer should reconstruct Q or use the standard 2D subspace extraction. Sigma2Dinv = Sigma2Draw[:2,:2].inverse() # 7. Evaluate Gaussian # Project 3D tangent plane vectors to 2D coordinates for the quadratic form # Construct an orthonormal basis for the tangent plane if abs(mucam[2]) < 0.99: uaxis = torch.cross(xp, torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])) uaxis = uaxis / torch.norm(uaxis) else: uaxis = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) vaxis = torch.cross(xp, uaxis) x2D2d = torch.tensor([torch.dot(x2D, uaxis), torch.dot(x2D, vaxis)]) muproj2d = torch.tensor([torch.dot(muproj, uaxis), torch.dot(muproj, vaxis)]) diff = x2D2d - muproj2d exponent = -0.5 torch.dot(diff, Sigma2Dinv @ diff) return torch.exp(exponent) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves higher rendering quality with smaller projection errors compared to the original 3D-GS. Strengths: Reduces projection artifacts, especially for Gaussians far from the camera center or at oblique angles. Limitations: More complex implementation requiring custom CUDA kernels for efficiency. Optimal Gaussian Splatting was introduced to address the error analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is based on the theoretical finding that the error function attains its minimum when the projection of the Gaussian mean on the plane coincides with the projection from the camera center to the plane. The method was implemented based on the PyTorch framework in 3D-GS with custom CUDA kernels. It was tested on 13 real scenes, including those from Mip-NeRF360. On the Error Analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting and an Optimal Projection Strategy, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72643-915, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (Cone-Beam/Scanner Space)
head: Cone-beam Gaussian Rasterization, Radiative Gaussian Projection, Transformation module in X-ray rasterization, X-ray Rasterization
body: This method renders X-ray projections by integrating 3D Gaussian primitives along ray paths, resulting in a sum of 2D Gaussians rather than the alpha-compositing used in natural light imaging. It adapts the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline for cone-beam CT simulation by transforming Gaussians from world space to a scanner-specific ray space where viewing rays are parallel to the principal axis, enabling analytical integration. Unlike standard splatting which learns integrated density in the 2D image plane, this method preserves the actual 3D density, avoiding integration bias during tomographic reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M 3D Gaussians defined by mean position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, and density \rhoi in world space; scanner parameters including source-to-detector distance LSD, source-to-object distance LSO, rotation angle \theta, and detector physical dimensions (Dx, Dy). Outputs: A 2D projection image where each pixel value is the sum of contributions from 2D Gaussians derived from the 3D inputs. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitive: Stores \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite), and scalar density \rhoi. Scanner Parameters: Scalar LSD, LSO, \theta; vector (Dx, Dy). Ray Space Gaussian: Transformed position \tilde{\mathbf{p}}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, transformed covariance \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. 2D Gaussian Primitive: Projected position \hat{\mathbf{p}}i \in \mathbb{R}^2, projected covariance \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, and projected density \hat{\rho}i \in \mathbb{R}. Steps: 1. Define Scanner Geometry: Calculate the Field of View (FOV) based on the detector size and source-to-detector distance: \text{FOV}x = 2 \cdot \arctan\left(\frac{Dx}{2 \cdot LSD}\right), \quad \text{FOV}y = 2 \cdot \arctan\left(\frac{Dy}{2 \cdot LSD}\right) Define the scanner space with the origin at the X-ray source and the z-axis pointing to the projection center. 2. World-to-Scanner Transformation: Construct the transformation matrix \mathbf{T} to map points from world space to scanner space: \mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{W} & \mathbf{t} \\ \mathbf{0}^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{W} and \mathbf{t} are defined as: \mathbf{W} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & -\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{t} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ LSO \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} Apply this transformation to the Gaussian mean \mathbf{p}i to get the intermediate position \mathbf{p}'i (implicitly part of the projective mapping \phi). 3. Local Affine Approximation (Ray Space Transformation): For each Gaussian, compute the local Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J}i of the projective mapping \phi at the Gaussian's position. The method relies on a local affine approximation using the Jacobian \mathbf{J}i. Transform the covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i into ray space \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i using the viewing transformation \mathbf{W} and the local Jacobian \mathbf{J}i: \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i = \mathbf{J}i \mathbf{W} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{J}i^\top The new position in ray space is \tilde{\mathbf{p}}i = \phi(\mathbf{p}i). 4. Projection to 2D: Obtain the 2D Gaussian parameters by dropping the third rows and columns of the ray space position \tilde{\mathbf{p}}i and covariance \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i: \hat{\mathbf{p}}i = [\tilde{\mathbf{p}}i[0], \tilde{\mathbf{p}}i[1]]^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i = \begin{bmatrix} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i[0][0] & \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i[0][1] \\ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i[1][0] & \tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i[1][1] \end{bmatrix} 5. Density Scaling: Calculate the projected density \hat{\rho}i by scaling the original 3D density \rhoi with a factor \mui derived from the determinants of the covariances. The density scaling factor \mui involves the square root of the ratio of determinants: \mui = \sqrt{\frac{2\pi |\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i|}{|\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i|}} \hat{\rho}i = \mui \rhoi This step ensures the method assigns the actual 3D density to the kernel, unlike standard 3DGS which learns integrated density. 6. Rasterization: Render the projection by summing the 2D Gaussians. The pixel value Ir(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} is the integral of the 3D Gaussians along the ray, which analytically simplifies to the sum of 2D Gaussians: Ir(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{M} \int G{3i}(\mathbf{r}(t)|\rhoi, \mathbf{p}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i) dt = \sum{i=1}^{M} G{2i}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}|\hat{\rho}i, \hat{\mathbf{p}}i, \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i) where G{2i} is the normalized 2D Gaussian distribution: G{2i}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \frac{1}{2\pi |\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i|^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}i)^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}i^{-1} (\hat{\mathbf{x}} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}i)\right) The contribution of each Gaussian to the image is \hat{\rho}i G{2i}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computefov(detectorwidth, detectorheight, sourcetodetectordist): """Computes the Field of View angles for the scanner.""" fovx = 2 np.arctan(detectorwidth / (2 sourcetodetectordist)) fovy = 2 np.arctan(detectorheight / (2 sourcetodetectordist)) return fovx, fovy def gettransformationmatrix(rotationangle, sourcetoobjectdist): """Constructs the transformation matrix T from world space to scanner space.""" costheta = np.cos(rotationangle) sintheta = np.sin(rotationangle) W = np.array([ [1, 0, 0], [0, -costheta, -sintheta], [0, sintheta, -costheta] ]) t = np.array([0, sourcetoobjectdist, 0]) T = np.eye(4) T[:3,:3] = W T[:3, 3] = t return T, W def getjacobian(pworld, T, fovx, fovy): """ Computes the local Jacobian matrix Ji for the projective mapping. The source references Eq. 29 in [69] for Ji but does not provide the explicit formula. A standard pinhole projection Jacobian scales by 1/z along the viewing axis. """ phomo = np.append(pworld, 1) prayhomo = T @ phomo pray = prayhomo[:3] z = pray[2] # Focal lengths derived from FOV and detector size focalx = detectorwidth / (2 np.tan(fovx / 2)) focaly = detectorheight / (2 np.tan(fovy / 2)) # Standard perspective projection Jacobian for ray space J = np.array([ [focalx / z, 0, 0], [0, focaly / z, 0], [0, 0, 0] ]) return J def rasterizeconebeam(gaussians, T, W, fovx, fovy, detectorwidth, detectorheight): """ Rasterizes 3D Gaussians into a 2D X-ray projection. """ projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: pi = g['position'] Sigmai = g['covariance'] rhoi = g['density'] # Step 2: World to Scanner phomo = np.append(pi, 1) prayhomo = T @ phomo pray = prayhomo[:3] # Step 3: Local Affine Approximation Ji = getjacobian(pi, T, fovx, fovy) Sigmatilde = Ji @ W @ Sigmai @ W.T @ Ji.T # Step 4: Projection to 2D phat = pray[:2] Sigmahat = Sigmatilde[:2,:2] # Step 5: Density Scaling detSigmatilde = np.linalg.det(Sigmatilde) detSigmahat = np.linalg.det(Sigmahat) if detSigmatilde <= 0 or detSigmahat <= 0: continue mui = np.sqrt(2 np.pi detSigmatilde / detSigmahat) rhohat = mui rhoi projectedgaussians.append({ 'position': phat, 'covariance': Sigmahat, 'density': rhohat }) return projectedgaussians def sum2dgaussians(projectedgaussians, imageshape, fovx, fovy, detectorwidth, detectorheight): """ Sums the 2D Gaussians to form the final image. """ image = np.zeros(imageshape) focalx = detectorwidth / (2 np.tan(fovx / 2)) focaly = detectorheight / (2 np.tan(fovy / 2)) for g in projectedgaussians: p = g['position'] Sigma = g['covariance'] rho = g['density'] # Compute bounding box for the 2D Gaussian invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Sigma) radius = 3.0 np.sqrt(np.max(eigenvalues)) xmin, xmax = int(p[0] - radius), int(p[0] + radius) ymin, ymax = int(p[1] - radius), int(p[1] + radius) xmin, ymin = max(0, xmin), max(0, ymin) xmax, ymax = min(imageshape[1], xmax), min(imageshape[0], ymax) for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): diff = np.array([x - p[0], y - p[1]]) exponent = -0.5 diff @ invSigma @ diff val = (1.0 / (2 np.pi np.sqrt(np.linalg.det(Sigma)))) np.exp(exponent) image[y, x] += rho val return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Integration Bias: If standard 3DGS is used for X-ray projection, learning the integrated density in the 2D image plane leads to inconsistency in density retrieval because different views yield different results for the same 3D density. This method solves this by assigning the actual 3D density to the kernel and forwardly computing the 2D projection. Determinant Calculation: The density scaling factor \mui involves the square root of the ratio of determinants. If the covariance matrices are singular or near-singular, this can lead to numerical instability. Jacobian Approximation: The method relies on a local affine approximation using the Jacobian \mathbf{J}i. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables analytical integration of 3D Gaussians for X-ray projections, avoiding the need for ray marching or sampling. Preserves the actual 3D density, allowing for consistent tomographic reconstruction without integration bias. Adapts the efficient rasterization pipeline of 3DGS to cone-beam geometry. Limitations: Relies on the local affine approximation, which may be less accurate for large Gaussians or highly curved projection mappings. Requires specific scanner parameters (LSD, LSO, \theta) and geometry setup. When to use: When simulating or reconstructing cone-beam CT scans using 3D Gaussian representations. When not to use: For standard natural light imaging where alpha-compositing is appropriate, or when high accuracy is required for very large Gaussians where the affine approximation fails. Origin: The method is introduced in "R^2-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction". History: It builds upon the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [23] and the Ewa Splatting technique [69] for handling anisotropic splats. It adapts these for the specific geometry of cone-beam X-ray scanners, which resemble a pinhole camera model. Usage: Used in the context of tomographic reconstruction from X-ray projections, specifically for rectifying radiative Gaussian splatting. R^2-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20693v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Distributed 3DGS Training
head: Grendel Distributed Training, Grendel-GS Training Pipeline, HPC-scale distributed 3DGS
body: Distributed 3DGS Training partitions 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters and datasets across multiple GPUs or HPC nodes to overcome single-GPU memory limits, enabling the training of high-resolution and large-scale scenes (e.g., >100M Gaussians). It sets itself apart from single-GPU baselines by preserving the original 3DGS algorithm and convergence characteristics while using spatial partitioning with ghost cells for boundary consistency and sparse all-to-all communication to distribute the rasterization workload. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A COLMAP dataset (images, camera poses) partitioned across nodes. Output: A global 3D Gaussian model (positions, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients) merged from local node states. Data Structures: Local Gaussians: A subset of the global Gaussian set assigned to each node. Ghost Cells: Boundary regions where Gaussians from neighboring nodes are replicated to ensure smooth transitions during local rasterization. Background Masks: Binary masks applied during local rendering to eliminate artifacts at the boundaries of the partition. Numbered Steps: 1. Partition datasets across nodes. 2. Partition 3DGS parameters across multiple GPUs. 3. Use ghost cells at boundaries for smooth transitions and background masks to eliminate rendering artifacts. 4. Train Gaussian splats independently per node. 5. Perform sparse all-to-all communication to transfer each required Gaussian to a pixel partition. 6. Merge for global rendering. 7. Support batched training using multiple views. 8. Evaluate scaling rules by starting with a batch size of 1, resetting Adam optimizer states, and continuing training with different batch sizes. Formulas: Learning Rate Scaling: The learning rate scales by the square root of the batch size to maintain update cosine similarity and magnitude across different training batch sizes. \eta{new} = \eta{base} \times \sqrt{\frac{BS{new}}{BS{base}}} Where BS is the batch size (number of camera views). Loss Function: Standard 3DGS loss combining L1 and SSIM, where \lambda controls SSIM influence. L = (1 - \lambda) L1 + \lambda L{SSIM} Where \lambda defaults to 0.2. Parameters: --bsz: Batch size (number of camera views) in single step training. Default: 1. --lrscalemode: Mode of scaling learning rate given larger batch size. Default: sqrt. --iterations: Number of total iterations to train for. Default: 30,000. --preloaddatasettogpu: Save all ground truth images from the dataset in GPU memory rather than loading each image on-the-fly. Warning: May cause OOM on large datasets. --shdegree: Order of spherical harmonics to be used. Default: 3. --featurelr: Spherical harmonics features learning rate. Default: 0.0025. --positionlrinit: Initial 3D position learning rate. Default: 0.00016. --positionlrfinal: Final 3D position learning rate. Default: 0.0000016. --densifyfromiter: Iteration where densification starts. Default: 500. --densifyuntiliter: Iteration where densification stops. Default: 15,000. --densifygradthreshold: Gradient norm threshold to initiate densification. Default: 0.0002. --densificationinterval: How frequently to densify. Default: 100. --opacityresetinterval: How frequently to reset opacity. Default: 3,000. --lambdadssim: Influence of SSIM on total loss from 0 to 1. Default: 0.2. --whitebackground: Use white background instead of black. Default: False. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.distributed as dist def distributedtrain(args): # Initialize distributed process group dist.initprocessgroup(backend=args.backend) localrank = dist.getrank() worldsize = dist.getworldsize() # Initialize Gaussian parameters and optimizer # Standard 3DGS parameter initialization (positions, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients) gaussians = torch.nn.ParameterDict({ 'means': torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float32)), 'logscales': torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float32)), 'opacities': torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.float32)), 'shcoeffs': torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3, 16, dtype=torch.float32)) }) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gaussians.parameters(), lr=args.positionlrinit) # Determine background color bgcolor = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda") if args.whitebackground else torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda") # Training loop for iteration in range(args.iterations + 1): # 1. Load batch of images assigned to this node cameras = scene.getTrainCameras() localcameras = [c for i, c in enumerate(cameras) if i % worldsize == localrank] if not localcameras: continue # 2. Render local Gaussians with background mask # Standard differentiable Gaussian rasterization with boundary masks renderedimage = rasterizelocal(gaussians, localcameras, bgcolor, args.shdegree) # 3. Compute Loss (L1 + SSIM) gtimage = localcameras[0].originalimage loss = computel1ssim(renderedimage, gtimage, args.lambdadssim) # 4. Backpropagate loss.backward() # 5. Aggregate Gradients across nodes for param in gaussians.parameters(): if param.grad is not None: dist.allreduce(param.grad, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, group=dist.group.WORLD) param.grad /= worldsize # 6. Update Parameters optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # 7. Densification/Pruning (Local) # Standard 3DGS densification based on gradient thresholds and opacity if iteration % args.densificationinterval == 0: densifyandprunelocal(gaussians, iteration, args) # 8. Checkpoint and Evaluation if iteration in args.saveiterations: savemodelcheckpoint(gaussians, args.modelpath, iteration) if iteration in args.testiterations: evaluatemetrics(gaussians, scene.getTestCameras()) dist.destroyprocessgroup() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single-GPU OOM: Large scenes like Rubble cannot be rendered with a single GPU regardless of batch size due to memory requirements; at least 4 GPUs are needed to avoid OOM. Preload OOM: Setting --preloaddatasettogpu on large datasets can cause Out-Of-Memory errors. Load Balancing: Uneven distribution of scene complexity or camera views can lead to load imbalance, and moderate-sized datasets show limited scaling gains when insufficient to fully utilize additional nodes. Boundary Artifacts: Without ghost cells and background masks, rendering artifacts appear at partition boundaries. A distributed training strategy for 3DGS that retains the original algorithm but uses a distinct parallelization approach where each GPU renders the entire image using its local partition of Gaussians, with outputs merged subsequently. Redundant computations occur because many GPUs render pixels beyond the opacity saturation depth unnecessarily. Time Complexity: Scales with the number of nodes and Gaussians, but communication overhead and load imbalance reduce efficiency. Memory Complexity: Memory per GPU is reduced by a factor of N (number of nodes), allowing training of scenes that exceed single-GPU memory limits (e.g., ~11.2M Gaussians on A100). Measured Performance: Rubble scene (35M Gaussians): Throughput increased from 5.55 images per second (4 GPUs, batch size 1) to 38.03 images per second (32 GPUs, batch size 64). Train scene (980×545 resolution): A 16-GPU setup with batch size 32 completed training on 30K images in 2 minutes and 42.97 seconds. Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temple, Deep Blending: Using 4 GPUs and a batch size of 4 achieved a 3x to 4x speedup without PSNR degradation. Richtmyer-Meshkov dataset (106.7M Gaussians, 5.3 GB, 2048×2048): 3.1× speedup scaling from 4 to 8 nodes, PSNR 30.04, SSIM 0.97, LPIPS 0.019. Rayleigh-Taylor dataset (18.2M Gaussians): 1.4× speedup from 2 to 4 nodes. Strengths: Enables training of very large scenes; reduces per-GPU memory usage; maintains reconstruction quality and convergence characteristics of the original algorithm. Limitations: Scaling gains are limited for moderate-sized datasets; load balancing for uneven distributions remains a challenge; communication overhead increases with node count. When to Use: Large-scale scenes (e.g., scientific volumes, high-resolution urban scans) that exceed single-GPU memory constraints. When Not to Use: Small to moderate scenes where single-GPU training is sufficient and faster due to lower communication overhead. Originated from the need to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to large scientific volumes and high-resolution scenes that exceed single-GPU memory constraints. The method was introduced by Zhao et al. in "On Scaling Up 3D Gaussian Splatting Training" (2024). It builds on the original 3DGS framework and integrates distributed computing techniques from HPC, preserving the original algorithm's convergence characteristics unlike ADMM-based alternatives.
