name: Point-Based Ray Tracing for Visibility
head: VisibilitySplat Ray Tracing
body: Point-Based Ray Tracing for Visibility serves as a sparse visibility oracle that evaluates transmittance along sampled light directions using a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) of Gaussian proxies, enabling evaluation from any point in space in any direction. Unlike the camera-tied rasterizer, it decouples visibility estimation from screen-space projection, allowing it to act as a drop-in companion to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by reusing the same EWA-splatting formulation for consistent blending without requiring training mismatch. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity \alpha, color); a ray r(t) = o + td; an early-out threshold T{stop}; a minimum response threshold \epsilon. Output: The accumulated transmittance T along the ray. Data Structures Gaussian Proxy: For each Gaussian, a proxy mesh (e.g., a subdivided regular icosahedron) is constructed. The triangles of this proxy are inserted into a BVH for fast ray-triangle traversal. Proxy Scale: The proxy is scaled to tightly bound the region where the particle’s response exceeds \epsilon. The scale explicitly incorporates the particle’s opacity \alpha to apply "adaptive clamping," ensuring nearly transparent splats receive proportionally tighter bounds to reduce false-positive hits during traversal. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Query: For a given ray r(t) = o + td, query the BVH to gather the batch of intersected Gaussian proxies. 2. Virtual Camera Setup: To reuse the unmodified rasterizer for consistent blending, instantiate a one-pixel virtual camera at the ray origin o with the optical axis aligned to the ray direction d. 3. Splatting Evaluation: Splat exactly the Gaussians reported by the BVH for that ray into the center pixel of this virtual camera using the standard EWA-splatting formulation. This computes the per-hit attenuation \Delta ai from the Gaussian’s line integral along the ray segment covered by the proxy. 4. Transmittance Update: Update the accumulated transmittance T using the formula: T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \Delta ai) where \Delta ai is the attenuation of the i-th hit. 5. Ordering: For occlusion-only queries, hits do not need to be depth-sorted because multiplication commutes; they can be processed in arbitrary order while maintaining correctness for T. 6. Early Termination: If T \le T{stop}, terminate the traversal and return T. Parameters T{stop}: The early-out threshold for transmittance. It should match the early-out used by the rasterizer to keep consistency between visibility estimated by ray tracing and the screen-space renderer. \epsilon: A small minimum response threshold used to define the tight bounding region for the proxy. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatevisibility(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, bvh, tstop, epsilon): """ Evaluates transmittance along a ray using Gaussian proxies. Args: rayorigin (vec3): Origin of the ray o. raydirection (vec3): Direction of the ray d. gaussians (list): List of Gaussian objects with properties: position (vec3) covariance (mat3) opacity (float) proxymesh (mesh): Triangles bounding the Gaussian response > epsilon. bvh (BVH): Bounding Volume Hierarchy containing all proxymeshes. tstop (float): Early-out threshold for transmittance. epsilon (float): Minimum response threshold for proxy scaling. Returns: float: Accumulated transmittance T. """ T = 1.0 # 1. Query BVH for intersected proxies # The BVH contains proxies scaled by opacity (adaptive clamping) intersectedproxies = bvh.query(rayorigin, raydirection) # 2. Setup virtual camera frame # Local camera frame aligned with ray direction # This allows reusing the standard EWA-splatting logic camframe = createlocalcameraframe(rayorigin, raydirection) # 3. Process intersections # No depth sorting required for transmittance accumulation for proxy in intersectedproxies: # Find the corresponding Gaussian gaussian = proxy.parentgaussian # 4. Evaluate attenuation using EWA-splatting via virtual camera # Splat the Gaussian into the center pixel of the 1-pixel virtual camera # This computes the line integral along the ray segment covered by the proxy deltaa = splatgaussiantopixel(gaussian, camframe) # 5. Update transmittance T = T (1.0 - deltaa) # 6. Early termination if T <= tstop: break return T def createlocalcameraframe(origin, direction): """ Creates a camera frame where the optical axis is the ray direction. Returns a structure containing view matrix or projection parameters compatible with the standard rasterizer's splatting function. """ # Implementation detail: Construct a rotation matrix that aligns # the camera's Z-axis with 'direction'. # The resulting frame is passed to the rasterizer's splatting kernel. pass def splatgaussiantopixel(gaussian, camframe): """ Reuses the unmodified rasterizer's EWA-splatting formulation. Evaluates the Gaussian's contribution to the center pixel of the virtual camera defined by camframe. """ # This function encapsulates the standard 3DGS rasterization step # for a single Gaussian projected onto a 1x1 pixel buffer. # It returns the opacity/attenuation deltaa. pass Time Complexity: Depends on BVH traversal depth and the number of intersected proxies per ray. Early termination reduces average cost when transmittance drops below T{stop}. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the BVH of Gaussian proxies. The proxy scale incorporates opacity, which may increase memory slightly compared to minimal bounding spheres but reduces false positives. Strengths: Decouples visibility from camera projection; allows reuse of pretrained 3DGS point clouds and the existing rasterizer without training mismatch; consistent blending with the screen-space renderer. Limitations: Not a full renderer; serves only as a visibility oracle. Requires careful tuning of T{stop} to match the rasterizer's early-out behavior. When to use: When evaluating transmittance along arbitrary light directions for relighting or shadowing in 3DGS scenes. When not to use: For primary view synthesis where the tile-based rasterizer is more efficient. The method was introduced in "VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of the standard 3DGS rasterizer, which is tied to camera projection and ordered blending per tile, by providing a point-based ray tracer that evaluates Gaussian splatting from any point in space in any direction. It contrasts with alternative ray-based renderers like 3DGRT (which evaluates at max response and uses a k-buffer) and IRGS (which collapses to 2D disks) by strictly adhering to the EWA-splatting formulation. name: Primitive Representation
head: Gaussian Primitives, Splatting Kernels, Volumetric Primitives
body: Primitive Representation defines the geometric and probabilistic entities used to model 3D scenes in differentiable splatting methods, serving as the fundamental building blocks for rendering. It solves the problem of representing complex geometry and appearance with explicit, differentiable primitives that can be projected and composited efficiently. What sets it apart from implicit representations (like NeRFs) is the use of explicit, analytically defined density functions (typically Gaussians) that allow for fast, tile-based rasterization and direct gradient flow to scene parameters. It differs from sibling methods like CoR-GS or 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by focusing on the definition of the primitive itself (shape, distribution, dimensionality) rather than the rasterization pipeline or optimization strategy. All primitive representations in this family share the core mechanism of defining a 3D primitive with a position, orientation, scale, and appearance attributes. The standard 3D Gaussian primitive is defined by a mean \boldsymbol{\mu} for position, a covariance \Sigma for shape and orientation, and appearance attributes like Spherical Harmonics coefficients and opacity \alpha. Parameterized as \Sigma^w = R S S^T R^T in world space, where R is rotation and S is scaling. The rendering pipeline projects these 3D primitives to 2D screen space. The covariance transforms via the view matrix W and projection Jacobian J: \Sigma = J W \Sigma^w W^T J^T. The integral of the 3D density along the view direction yields the 2D splat density. The GaussianSet is a data structure representing a collection of 3D Gaussians, storing means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients, and computing covariance matrices. It solves the problem of efficiently organizing explicit volumetric primitives for GPU batch processing and differentiable rasterization. It sets itself apart from hierarchical scene representations by using a flat, contiguous array layout optimized for vectorized tensor operations. MaskGaussian is a differentiable pruning method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that models Gaussians as probabilistic entities rather than deterministically removing them based on static importance scores. It solves the problem of sub-optimal reconstruction caused by early pruning by introducing masked-rasterization, which allows gradients to flow to "masked-out" (inactive) Gaussians, enabling them to be re-evaluated and potentially reactivated as the scene evolves. Unlike sibling methods like Compact3DGS which use deterministic pruning or multiply masks with opacity/scale (blocking gradients), MaskGaussian applies masks during the alpha-blending stage, decoupling Gaussian existence from its geometric attributes. 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization is a differentiable rendering technique that represents scene geometry and radiance using semi-opaque 2D Gaussian primitives (surfels). It solves the problem of accurate ray-splat intersection and normal estimation by replacing 3D ellipsoids with 2D oriented planar disks, which allows for more precise surface reconstruction and view-consistent geometry. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, is the use of 2D Gaussians defined by tangential vectors and a zero depth scale, enabling direct normal extraction via the cross product of tangents and avoiding degenerate line projections through low-pass filtering. It builds on Primitive Representation by projecting these 2D primitives to screen space and accumulating color, alpha, depth, and normal maps via front-to-back alpha compositing. This method decomposes a 3D Gaussian probability density into a product of a marginal distribution along the depth axis and a conditional distribution over the 2D coordinates given the depth. It treats the unnormalized 4D Gaussian as a special probability distribution over spatial coordinates (u, v) and time t (or depth), enabling factorization into temporal and conditional spatial components. This factorized approach provides a computationally efficient way to model volumetric data for slice-based rendering or tomographic reconstruction compared to processing the full 3D density directly. This family defines the geometric primitives used to represent 3D scenes in differentiable splatting methods, extending the standard 3D Gaussian ellipsoid to alternative shapes, distributions, and dimensionalities. It addresses specific limitations of standard volumetric representations by introducing specialized primitives: planar disks for surface reconstruction 2D Gaussian Splatting, fat-tailed distributions for non-monotonic density modeling 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting, generalized exponential functions for high-frequency content Generalized Exponential Splatting, and transparent polyhedra for linear volumetric rendering [LinPrim Octahedron Representation]. It differs from sibling methods by varying the fundamental density function or geometric support of the primitive while maintaining the core splatting pipeline of projection and alpha compositing. 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting (3D-HGS) is a reconstruction kernel for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the standard full 3D Gaussian with a 3D Half-Gaussian to address shape and color discontinuities (Gibbs phenomenon) at object boundaries and texture-rich areas. It achieves higher rendering quality without compromising speed by allowing each half of the split Gaussian to have different opacity values while sharing geometric parameters. Unlike 2D-GS, which performs surface rendering, 3D-HGS retains volumetric rendering to preserve performance while enabling accurate modeling of discontinuous functions. Texture and Appearance Representation covers methods that extend 3D Gaussian primitives with appearance attributes to determine color during rendering. It solves the limitation of static color storage by enabling high-frequency details or view-dependent effects without excessively increasing the number of primitives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GaussianSet Data Structure by focusing on the semantic definition of color rather than memory layout, and from Primitive Geometry and Distribution by addressing radiance rather than shape. The Bézier Gaussian Triangle (BG-Triangle) is a hybrid 3D primitive representation that combines Bézier triangle surfaces for explicit geometry with 3D Gaussian sub-primitives for appearance, enabling differentiable rendering with sharp boundaries. It solves the problem of blurry or aliased edges common in pure Gaussian splatting by defining the object's silhouette and surface topology via parametric Bézier patches, while using Gaussians only for shading and color. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which relies on the overlap of many opaque Gaussians to form shapes, BG-Triangle maintains distinct, sharp boundaries between primitives, making it particularly suitable for vectorization and compact scene representation. Uses zero-thickness oriented surfels. A technique using negative density components in a mixture model to enhance representational power and parameter efficiency, allowing subtraction of color/density to capture complex topologies (e.g., holes) with fewer components. The rendering equation uses signed weights w \in \mathbb{R} (instead of w > 0) in the standard alpha-compositing sum: C(u) = \sum{i=1}^N ci oi Ti^{2D}(u) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj Tj^{2D}(u)), where oi is opacity and Ti^{2D} is the 2D component function. Opacity constraint: Opacity o is constrained by a tanh function during learning so that o \in [-1, 1], allowing positive and negative components to dynamically change signs while being bounded. Using squared negative components (Eq. 5: P(x) = (\sum wi Ti(x))^2) introduces pairwise interactions between all K components, increasing evaluation complexity to O(n^2), which is significantly slower. Therefore, the linear sum (Eq. 3) with signed weights is used instead. The concept of primitive representation in volume rendering has evolved from simple geometric primitives (points, lines, triangles) to probabilistic distributions (Gaussians, t-distributions) to enable differentiable rendering. The standard 3D Gaussian primitive, popularized by 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023), provides a balance between representational capacity and computational efficiency. Subsequent research has explored alternative distributions (e.g., Student's t, Half-Gaussians) and dimensionalities (2D surfels) to address specific limitations such as aliasing, surface reconstruction accuracy, and handling of discontinuities. The field continues to expand with hybrid representations (e.g., Bézier-Gaussian) and advanced data structures to optimize training and rendering performance. name: GaussianSet Data Structure
head: 3D Gaussian Representation, Gaussian Set
body: The GaussianSet is a data structure representing a collection of 3D Gaussians, storing means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients, and computing covariance matrices. It solves the problem of efficiently organizing explicit volumetric primitives for GPU batch processing and differentiable rasterization. It sets itself apart from hierarchical scene representations by using a flat, contiguous array layout optimized for vectorized tensor operations. Input: A set of N Gaussian primitives defined by their mean position, rotation, scale, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Output: A structured data object containing contiguous tensors for all attributes, ready for projection and rasterization. The GaussianSet consists of the following fields, typically implemented as contiguous column-major tensors: 1. means: Float32[N, 3] The 3D position \boldsymbol{\mu} of each Gaussian. 2. quats: Float32[N, 4] The orientation represented as unit quaternions q = (w, x, y, z). 3. scales: Float32[N, 3] The local scaling factors sx, sy, sz. 4. opacities: Float32[N] The scalar opacity \alpha for each Gaussian. 5. shcoefficients: Float32[N, S, 3] Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent color, where S is the number of SH bands. 6. covariances: Float32[N, 3, 3] The precomputed 3 \times 3 world-space covariance matrix \Sigma for each Gaussian. The covariances field is derived from quats and scales using the following steps: 1. Normalize Quaternions: Ensure q is a unit quaternion. q{norm} = \frac{q}{\|q\|2} 2. Convert Quaternion to Rotation Matrix: Construct the 3 \times 3 rotation matrix R from q{norm}. 3. Construct Local Covariance Matrix: Create the diagonal matrix S from the scales. S = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) 4. Compute World Covariance: Calculate the world-space covariance \Sigma. \Sigma = R S R^T The following Python-like pseudocode demonstrates the construction of the covariances field from the raw attributes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computecovariances(quats: torch.Tensor, scales: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the world-space covariance matrix for a set of Gaussians. Args: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4), quaternions (w, x, y, z). scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3), local scaling factors. Returns: covariances: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3), world-space covariance matrices. """ # 1. Normalize quaternions to ensure unit length quats = quats / torch.norm(quats, dim=1, keepdim=True) # 2. Convert quaternions to rotation matrices def quattorot(q): w, x, y, z = q[:, 0], q[:, 1], q[:, 2], q[:, 3] R = torch.zeros(q.shape[0], 3, 3, device=q.device) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (x2 + y2) return R R = quattorot(quats) # 3. Construct local covariance matrix S (diagonal) scalessq = scales 2 S = torch.zeroslike(R) S[:, 0, 0] = scalessq[:, 0] S[:, 1, 1] = scalessq[:, 1] S[:, 2, 2] = scalessq[:, 2] # 4. Compute world covariance: Cov = R S R^T covariances = torch.bmm(R, torch.bmm(S, R.transpose(1, 2))) return covariances Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized before conversion to rotation matrices to ensure valid rotation. Scale Exponentiation: Raw stored scales are exponentiated (torch.exp) to ensure they remain positive. The GaussianSet may store the exponentiated values directly or compute them on the fly. Opacity Sigmoid: Raw stored opacities are sigmoided (torch.sigmoid) to bound them between 0 and 1. SH Concatenation: Spherical harmonics coefficients from different degrees are concatenated along the band dimension. Precision: Using Float32 is standard, but Float64 may be used for high-precision training to avoid gradient instability. name: ECoNGS Optimization and Coding
head: ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats), Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats
body: ECoNGS (Efficient Compressive Neural Gaussian Splats) is a scene representation method that transforms time-consuming volume rendering into an efficient process by optimizing neural editable Gaussians and compressing their attributes via neural entropy coding. It solves the problem of large storage and computational costs in volume visualization by extracting multi-view images and point clouds, grouping geometrically similar scenes for joint learning, and compressing anchor attributes to exploit inter-scene redundancy. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which stores all attributes explicitly, ECoNGS uses a two-stage optimization process involving anchor attribute optimization and joint context model training, achieving compression with minimal distortion. ECoNGS operates on a set of basic scenes, each represented by a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives. The method involves data extraction, two-stage optimization, and entropy coding. Inputs: Multi-view images and corresponding point clouds for each basic scene. Hyperparameters: \lambdas = 0.001 (scaling regularization weight), K=10 (number of neural editable Gaussians per anchor), learning rates (0.01 for anchor feature, opacity, scaling, rotation, TF embeddings; 1\times 10^{-4} for palette color), training iterations (10,000 per stage), and \lambdae (trade-off hyperparameter for compression losses). Outputs: A compressed binary bitstream of anchor attributes encoded via arithmetic coding. MLP parameters stored as 32-bit floating-point values. A complete VolVis scene representation formed by compositing trained basic scenes. The method relies on the GaussianSet Data Structure, which stores means, orientations, scales, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. ECoNGS introduces: Anchor Points: A subset of Gaussians whose attributes are optimized and compressed. Neural Editable Gaussians: Derived from anchor points; K=10 editable Gaussians are generated per anchor. Context Model: A lightweight MLP used to estimate probabilities for entropy coding. Hash Grids: Used for inter-scene redundancy; M+ and M- denote the total numbers of +1 and -1 values in the hash grids. The 3D Gaussian function is defined as: C(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^s)^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^s)} where \mathbf{x} is an arbitrary 3D position, \mathbf{x}^s is the position attribute of the Gaussian point, and \mathbf{\Sigma} is the covariance matrix. The covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} is parameterized by a scaling factor s and a quaternion rotation vector q to ensure positive semi-definiteness. Rendering uses EWA volume splatting to transform 3D Gaussians G(\mathbf{x}) to 2D Gaussians G'(\mathbf{x}') on the image plane. Pixel color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}') is determined by \alpha-blending: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}') = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \quad \alphai = oi Gi(\mathbf{x}') where c is modeled by spherical harmonics (SH) parameters, oi is opacity, and N is the number of depth-sorted layered 2D Gaussians. Loss Functions: Stage 1 loss: L{\text{stage1}} = L{\text{rec}} + \lambdas \sum{j=1}^{N^s} \text{prod}(\mathbf{s}j) where L{\text{rec}} is the image reconstruction loss (L1 + SSIM), N^s is the number of predicted editable Gaussians, \text{prod}(\cdot) is the vector product of scaling factors, and \lambdas = 0.001. Stage 2 loss: L{\text{stage2}} = L{\text{stage1}} + \lambdae \frac{L{\text{entropy}} + L{\text{hash}}}{N^a \times dA} where N^a is the number of anchors, dA is the sum of all anchor attribute dimensions, and \lambdae is the trade-off hyperparameter. L{\text{entropy}} and L{\text{hash}} encourage distribution of values within anchor attributes and a more concentrated hash grid, reducing bit consumption. 1. Data Extraction: Extract multi-view images and corresponding point clouds from different basic scenes. 2. Scene Grouping: Group geometrically similar scenes for joint learning. 3. Stage 1 Optimization: Optimize only anchor point attributes and lightweight MLPs for 10,000 iterations using L{\text{stage1}}. Turn off uniform noise for the first 3,000 iterations to stabilize optimization. 4. Stage 2 Optimization: Update all parameters, including the context model, for the remaining 10,000 iterations using L{\text{stage2}}. Enable uniform noise after 3,000 iterations. 5. Encoding: Encode the context model first. Then, encode anchor attributes into a binary bitstream using an arithmetic encoder based on probabilities estimated by the context model. 6. Storage: Store MLP parameters as 32-bit floating-point values. 7. Compositing: Composite all trained basic scenes to form a complete VolVis scene representation. Unverified code. name: GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization
head: GaussianList
body: The GaussianList is a contiguous, column-major data structure that stores the attributes of a set of 3D Gaussians to enable batch processing during differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently managing geometric primitives (positions, scales, rotations, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients) and their derived covariance matrices for rasterization. It sets itself apart from hierarchical variants like Octree-GS / Scaffold-GS by using a flat array, and from GaussianProperty Loading by providing the specific memory layout and initialization logic required for the rendering pipeline. Inputs: A vector of Gaussian objects containing position, scale, rotation (quaternion), opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Outputs: A GaussianList struct populated with column-major matrices and vectors, with cov3d computed. The GaussianList struct stores attributes in column-major matrices for batch processing. The fields are: positions: na::Matrix4xX<f32>, 4 rows \times N columns. Stores 3D positions as homogeneous coordinates (x, y, z, 1.0). scales: na::Matrix3xX<f32>, 3 rows \times N columns. Stores scale components. opacities: na::DVector<f32>, 1D vector of size N. Stores opacity values. rotations: na::Matrix4xX<f32>, 4 rows \times N columns. Stores quaternion components. sh: Matrix48xX<f32>, 48 rows \times N columns. Stores SH coefficients. numgaussians: usize. The count of Gaussians N. cov3d: na::Matrix3xX<f32>, 3 rows \times N columns. Pre-allocated zeros, filled by computecov3d(). Spherical Harmonics Layout: The sh matrix columns store coefficients. Within a column, the layout is: C{0,R}, C{0,B}, C{0,G}, C{1,R}, C{1,B}, C{1,G}, \dots, corresponding to RGB channels for each SH degree/order. 1. Set numgaussians to the length of the input vector. 2. Construct positions: Iterate over gaussians, clone position components, and append 1.0 to make them 4D homogeneous coordinates. 3. Construct scales: Clone scale components into the 3xN matrix. 4. Construct opacities: Clone opacity values into the 1D vector. 5. Construct rotations: Clone quaternion components into the 4xN matrix. 6. Construct sh: Clone spherical harmonic coefficients into the 48xN matrix. 7. Initialize cov3d with zeros of size N \times 3 (3 rows, N columns). 8. Call computecov3d() to calculate covariance matrices. To center the Gaussian positions around the origin: 1. Initialize avgpos as a zero Vector3. 2. Iterate over all gaussians, adding each position to avgpos. 3. Divide avgpos by numgaussians to get the mean. 4. Iterate over all gaussians again, subtracting avgpos from each position. For each Gaussian i from 0 to numgaussians - 1: 1. Extract rotation quaternion from rotations column i. 2. Convert quaternion to UnitQuaternion, then to a 3x3 rotation matrix R. 3. Create a diagonal scale matrix S by squaring the scale components: S = \begin{bmatrix} sx^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz^2 \end{bmatrix} where sx, sy, sz are scales[(0,i)], scales[(1,i)], scales[(2,i)]. 4. Compute covariance \Sigma = R S R^T. 5. Copy the resulting 3x3 covariance matrix into cov3d at offset i \times 3 (column i). For a given Gaussian and camera: 1. Get Gaussian position p and view matrix V. 2. Convert position to homogeneous vector pw = (x, y, z, 1.0). 3. Transform to camera space: p{cam} = V \cdot pw. 4. Get focal length (fx, fy) and tangent of FOV (htanfovxy). 5. Compute tangent of Gaussian center: t{xz} = p{cam}.x / p{cam}.z, \quad t{yz} = p{cam}.y / p{cam}.z 6. Clamp tangents to limits: t.x = \text{clamp}(t{xz}, -1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{fov}x), 1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{fov}x)) \cdot p{cam}.z t.y = \text{clamp}(t{yz}, -1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{fov}y), 1.3 \cdot \tan(\text{fov}y)) \cdot p{cam}.z The multiplier 1.3 defines the FOV Clamping Limit. 7. Compute Jacobian J (3x3 matrix) using fx, fy, t.x, t.y, t.z. 8. Compute W as the transpose of the top-left 3x3 of the view matrix. 9. Compute T = W \cdot J. 10. Compute projected covariance: \Sigma{2D} = T^T \cdot \Sigma{3D} \cdot T 11. Extract the top-left 2x2 submatrix as cov2d. 12. Apply low-pass filter by adding 0.3 to cov2d[(0,0)] and cov2d[(1,1)]. 13. Return cov2d. 1. Pass the SH coefficients column for the given index, the SH dimension, and the viewing direction to evalsphericalharmonics. 2. Return the resulting color vector and the Gaussian's opacity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializegaussianlist(gaussians): """ Initialize GaussianList from a list of Gaussian objects. gaussians: list of objects with.position (3,),.scale (3,),.rotation (quat),.opacity (float),.sh (coeffs) """ N = len(gaussians) # 1. Positions: 4xN, homogeneous positions = np.zeros((4, N), dtype=np.float32) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): positions[:3, i] = g.position positions[3, i] = 1.0 # 2. Scales: 3xN scales = np.zeros((3, N), dtype=np.float32) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): scales[:, i] = g.scale # 3. Opacities: 1D vector opacities = np.array([g.opacity for g in gaussians], dtype=np.float32) # 4. Rotations: 4xN (quaternions) rotations = np.zeros((4, N), dtype=np.float32) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): rotations[:, i] = g.rotation # w, x, y, z or x, y, z, w depending on convention # 5. SH: 48xN sh = np.zeros((48, N), dtype=np.float32) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): sh[:, i] = g.sh # Layout: C0R, C0B, C0G, C1R... # 6. Cov3d: 3xN, initialized to zeros cov3d = np.zeros((3, N), dtype=np.float32) # Note: source says 3 rows x N cols # 7. Compute Cov3d computecov3d(positions, scales, rotations, cov3d) # 8. Center positions centerpositions(positions) return GaussianList(positions, scales, opacities, rotations, sh, N, cov3d) def computecov3d(positions, scales, rotations, cov3d): """ Compute 3D covariance matrices for all Gaussians. cov3d layout: 3 rows, N columns. """ N = positions.shape[1] for i in range(N): # Extract quaternion q = rotations[:, i] # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix R (3x3) R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) # Scale matrix S (diagonal) s = scales[:, i] S = np.diag(s2) # Covariance = R S R^T cov = R @ S @ R.T # Store in cov3d (column i) cov3d[:, i] = cov.flatten() # Or reshape if cov3d is 3xN def centerpositions(positions): """ Center Gaussian positions around the origin. positions: 4xN matrix. """ N = positions.shape[1] # Average position (ignore w=1) avgpos = np.mean(positions[:3,:], axis=1) # Subtract mean positions[:3,:] -= avgpos.reshape(3, 1) def projectcov3dtoscreen(cov3d, position, viewmatrix, focalx, focaly, fovx, fovy): """ Project 3D covariance to 2D screen space. cov3d: 3xN matrix, column i is the covariance for Gaussian i. position: 3D position of the Gaussian. viewmatrix: 4x4 view matrix. """ # Homogeneous position pw = np.array([position[0], position[1], position[3], 1.0]) # Note: source uses posw # Transform to camera space pcam = viewmatrix @ pw # Tangents tz = pcam[2] if tz == 0: tz = 1e-6 # Guard against division by zero tx = pcam[0] / tz ty = pcam[1] / tz # Clamp tangents limitx = 1.3 np.tan(fovx) limity = 1.3 np.tan(fovy) tx = np.clip(tx, -limitx, limitx) tz ty = np.clip(ty, -limity, limity) tz # Jacobian J (3x3) # J = [[fx, 0, tx], [0, fy, ty], [0, 0, 1]] ? # Source says "Compute Jacobian J (3x3 matrix) using focalx, focaly, t.x, t.y, t.z" # Standard projection Jacobian for perspective: # xproj = fx X/Z, yproj = fy Y/Z # d(xproj)/dX = fx/Z, d(xproj)/dY = 0, d(xproj)/dZ = -fxX/Z^2 # Let's assume standard derivation based on variables provided J = np.array([ [focalx / tz, 0, -focalx tx / (tztz)], [0, focaly / tz, -focaly ty / (tztz)], [0, 0, 0] # Depth derivative often ignored or handled separately ]) # W: transpose of top-left 3x3 of view matrix W = viewmatrix[:3,:3].T # T = W J T = W @ J # Cov2D = T^T Cov3D T cov2d = T.T @ cov3d @ T # Extract 2x2 cov2d2x2 = cov2d[:2,:2] # Low-pass filter cov2d2x2[0, 0] += 0.3 cov2d2x2[1, 1] += 0.3 return cov2d2x2 LinPrim Population Control manages the density of linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra) during differentiable volume rendering optimization by pruning, cloning, and splitting primitives to adapt to scene complexity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by redefining primitive size metrics to accommodate non-spherical kernels and adjusting sampling distributions to respect the anisotropic geometry of linear primitives. Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization is the process of constructing the initial set of 3D Gaussian primitives from input data, typically a sparse point cloud generated by Structure from Motion (SfM) or random sampling. It solves the problem of providing geometrically plausible starting positions, orientations, scales, and appearance attributes for the differentiable renderer, avoiding the poor convergence and artifacts associated with purely random initialization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Random Gaussian Generation by leveraging multi-view geometric constraints to anchor primitives to observed scene structure, and from Random Large-Variance Initialization by relying on deterministic feature matching rather than stochastic sampling. Octree-GS and Scaffold-GS are hierarchical rendering methods that replace the flat list of 3D Gaussians with a structured representation anchored to a sparse voxel grid or octree. Scaffold-GS initializes anchors from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, using a neural network to predict Gaussian attributes on the fly, while Octree-GS builds an octree where nodes summarize radiance and opacity of children. This approach reduces memory usage by approximately 5× compared to vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) at equivalent quality and naturally adapts to view distance by allocating primitives only in occupied regions. It builds on GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization by introducing spatial hierarchy and neural decoding. GaussianHair is a strand-aware hair rendering method that combines the Marschner Hair Model with Unreal Engine 4’s real-time hair rendering pipeline to create the Gaussian Hair Scattering Model. It uses a hybrid strand + Gaussian Splat (GS) representation to capture complex hair geometry and appearance, enabling fast rasterization and volumetric rendering. It is distinguished from general GS variants by its specific focus on hair topology and physically-based scattering, enabling applications such as editing and relighting. Random Gaussian Generation is the initialization procedure for creating a set of 3D Gaussians from scratch, typically to serve as the starting point for differentiable rendering optimization in methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting. It generates a fixed number of Gaussian primitives with random positions, scales, orientations, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. It differs from LinPrim Population Control which manages the density of existing Gaussians during training, and from Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization which may use structured or data-driven initialization strategies. This method provides a uniform, uninformative prior over the parameter space. Hierarchical Gaussian Generation with Densify is a method for constructing 3D Gaussian representations in a coarse-to-fine hierarchy, primarily designed to stabilize Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) training by regularizing the position and scale of synthesized primitives. It solves the problem of training instability and poor management of geometric parameters (position \mu and scale s) in generative models by enforcing locality constraints between adjacent hierarchy levels. Unlike flat initialization methods, it establishes a dependency where fine-level Gaussians are derived from coarse-level counterparts via residual updates, allowing the generator to model multi-scale details effectively. Uses per-image and per-Gaussian embeddings optimized via an MLP to model view-dependent appearance, illumination, and weather effects. Learning rate for the appearance MLP: 0.0005. Learning rate for per-image embeddings \mathbf{e}j: 0.001. Learning rate for per-Gaussian embeddings \mathbf{z}i: 0.005. Per-image embedding \mathbf{e}j \in \mathbb{R}^{de} with dimension de = 32. Per-Gaussian embedding \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^{dz} with dimension dz = 24, initialized using Fourier frequencies with 4 components. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) for copying attributes and O(N) for covariance computation. Projection is O(N) per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N) for flat storage. The column-major layout allows efficient batch processing but may have poor cache locality for scattered access compared to AoS. Strengths: Simple, contiguous memory layout suitable for GPU batch processing. Efficient for uniform scene densities. Limitations: No spatial hierarchy, leading to potential over-rendering in empty regions and under-rendering in complex areas. Memory usage scales linearly with N, which can be high for high-quality reconstructions. When to use: When scene complexity is uniform or when using hierarchical variants (like Octree-GS) that manage the list structure. When not to use: For very large scenes with high dynamic range of detail, where hierarchical methods are preferred. The GaussianList is a core data structure in 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations, particularly those using column-major matrices for batch processing. It originates from the need to efficiently store and process thousands of 3D Gaussians for real-time differentiable rendering. The specific initialization and covariance computation steps are derived from implementations like thomasantony/splat. thomasantony/splat, https://github.com/thomasantony/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DeSplat: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting for Distractor-Free Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.00076, fetched 2026-11-03

name: LinPrim Population Control
head: Adaptive Population Control, LinPrim-MCMC
body: LinPrim Population Control manages the density of linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra) during differentiable volume rendering optimization by pruning, cloning, and splitting primitives to adapt to scene complexity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by redefining primitive size metrics to accommodate non-spherical kernels and adjusting sampling distributions to respect the anisotropic geometry of linear primitives. Inputs: Current set of primitives \mathcal{P}, each with position \mathbf{p}, color \mathbf{c}, distances to corners \mathbf{d}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, view-space positional gradient \nabla{\mathbf{p}}, and opacity \alpha. Camera parameters for known views. Scene extent bounds. Outputs: Updated set of primitives \mathcal{P}' with modified count, positions, and sizes. Each primitive stores: position: 3D vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. color: 3D vector \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. distances: Array of distances to corner vertices. For octahedra, 3 values (along axes); for tetrahedra, 4 values (to vertices). rotation: Quaternion \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4. gradientmomentum: 3D vector for optimizer state. gradient: 3D view-space positional gradient vector. opacity: Scalar transparency value. type: Enum (OCTAHEDRON, TETRAHEDRON). Remove primitives that fail fidelity or efficiency criteria. Size Definition: For Octahedra: Size S{oct} = 2 \cdot \max(\mathbf{d}), where \mathbf{d} are the distances along the principal axes. For Tetrahedra: Size S{tet} \approx \sqrt{2} \cdot d{max}, where d{max} is the distance to the furthest corner vertex. Criteria: A primitive is pruned if: 1. Opacity is below a threshold. 2. Size exceeds a fraction of the scene extent. 3. Screen-space area exceeds a threshold. (Specific threshold values are not given in the sources.) Initialize primitives from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points: 1. For each SfM point \mathbf{p}i with color \mathbf{c}i: Find distance to closest SfM neighbor d{min}. Set initial distances \mathbf{d} = d{min} for all corners. Set rotation \mathbf{q} to a uniformly random quaternion. Set position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}i. Select primitives with large view-space positional gradients \|\nabla{\mathbf{p}}\|. (Gradient threshold is not given in the sources.) Cloning (for small primitives): 1. Create new primitive with identical features: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{c}{new} = \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d}{new} = \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{q}{new} = \mathbf{q}. 2. Reset gradient momentum to zero. Splitting (for large primitives): 1. Create two new primitives with smaller sizes. 2. Sample positions from a PDF based on the original primitive's geometry. Sampling Logic: Octahedra: Standard deviations \sigmai = di (corresponding distance for each axis). Sample offset \Delta \mathbf{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \text{diag}(\sigma^2)). Apply rotation afterwards to spread primitives along longer dimensions. Tetrahedra: Set \sigma = \frac{1}{2} \max(\mathbf{d}) for all dimensions. Sample offset \Delta \mathbf{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}). Apply rotation afterwards. Adapt GS-MCMC population control by treating primitives as equivalent Gaussians. 1. Scale octahedron distances: \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{d} / 2.6. 2. Use \mathbf{d}' as Gaussian standard deviations for MCMC sampling. 3. Perform MCMC steps to draw samples from the scene distribution, allowing precise control over final population size. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import copy as stdcopy def quattorotmat(q): """Convert quaternion [w, x, y, z] to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) def calculatescreenarea(prim, camera): """Estimate screen-space area from camera projection. Not given in the sources. Standard perspective projection used.""" # Placeholder for standard projection logic return 0.0 def cloneprimitive(prim): """Deep copy primitive fields and reset momentum.""" new = stdcopy.deepcopy(prim) new.gradientmomentum = np.zeros(3) return new def pruneprimitives(primitives, camera, sceneextent, opacitythresh, sizefrac, screenthresh): """Remove primitives based on opacity, size, and screen space.""" toremove = [] for i, prim in enumerate(primitives): if prim.opacity < opacitythresh: toremove.append(i) continue if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': size = 2.0 np.max(prim.distances) elif prim.type == 'TETRAHEDRON': size = np.sqrt(2.0) np.max(prim.distances) else: size = 0.0 if size > sizefrac sceneextent: toremove.append(i) continue if calculatescreenarea(prim, camera) > screenthresh: toremove.append(i) for i in reversed(toremove): primitives.pop(i) return primitives def cloneandsplit(primitives, gradthresh, sizethresh): """Clone small primitives with high gradients, split large ones.""" newprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(prim.gradient) if gradnorm > gradthresh: if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': size = 2.0 np.max(prim.distances) else: size = np.sqrt(2.0) np.max(prim.distances) if size < sizethresh: newprimitives.append(cloneprimitive(prim)) else: posa, posb = samplesplitpositions(prim) newa = cloneprimitive(prim) newa.position = posa newa.distances = [d 0.5 for d in prim.distances] newb = cloneprimitive(prim) newb.position = posb newb.distances = [d 0.5 for d in prim.distances] newprimitives.extend([newa, newb]) else: newprimitives.append(prim) return newprimitives def samplesplitpositions(prim): """Sample positions for splitting based on primitive type.""" R = quattorotmat(prim.rotation) if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': sigma = np.array(prim.distances) delta = np.random.normal(0, sigma) posoffset = R @ delta elif prim.type == 'TETRAHEDRON': maxd = np.max(prim.distances) sigma = 0.5 maxd delta = np.random.normal(0, sigma, 3) posoffset = R @ delta else: posoffset = np.zeros(3) posa = prim.position + posoffset posb = prim.position - posoffset return posa, posb def linprimmcmcstep(primitives, scalefactor=2.6): """Apply LinPrim-MCMC adjustments.""" for prim in primitives: if prim.type == 'OCTAHEDRON': prim.distancesscaled = [d / scalefactor for d in prim.distances] # MCMC sampling logic relies on external GS-MCMC implementation Opacity threshold: Not given in the sources. Screen-space area threshold: Not given in the sources. Scene extent fraction: Not given in the sources. Gradient threshold: Not given in the sources. scalefactor (LinPrim-MCMC): 2.6 sceneextent: Bounding box diagonal or max dimension of the scene Tetrahedron Splitting: Non-trivial to sample along principal axes due to lack of symmetry; use isotropic scaling with \sigma = \frac{1}{2} \max(\mathbf{d}). Octahedron Anisotropy: Must sample along local axes before rotating to spread along longer dimensions. Momentum Reset: Cloned primitives must reset gradient momentum to avoid biased updates. Magnitude Mismatch: Direct use of octahedron distances as Gaussian standard deviations is invalid; scaling by 2.6 is required for MCMC compatibility. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficiently adapts to scene detail; prevents over-rendering in uniform regions and under-rendering in complex areas. Strengths: Compatible with 3DGS advancements (e.g., MCMC); handles non-spherical primitives correctly. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of size thresholds. When to Use: When optimizing linear primitives for novel views or high-fidelity reconstruction where fixed initialization is insufficient. LinPrim Population Control originates from the LinPrim paper (2025), which adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques to linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra). It addresses the need for dynamic population management in differentiable volumetric rendering with non-Gaussian kernels. The method incorporates insights from GS-MCMC and Distribution Alignment to handle magnitude differences between linear primitive distances and Gaussian standard deviations. name: Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization
head: SfM Initialization, COLMAP Initialization, Structure from Motion Initialization
body: Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization constructs the initial set of 3D Gaussian primitives from input data, typically a sparse point cloud generated by Structure from Motion (SfM) or random sampling. It solves the problem of providing geometrically plausible starting positions, orientations, scales, and appearance attributes for the differentiable renderer, avoiding the poor convergence and artifacts associated with purely random initialization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Random Gaussian Generation by initializing directly from sparse Structure from Motion (SfM) points rather than random coordinates, and from Random Large-Variance Initialization by relying on deterministic feature matching rather than stochastic sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D images, camera poses (extrinsics and intrinsics), and a sparse 3D point cloud with RGB colors (typically from COLMAP). Alternatively, random coordinates and colors if SfM is unavailable. Output: A GaussianList data structure containing N learnable parameters: positions (\mathbf{x}), scales (\mathbf{s}), rotations (\mathbf{q}), opacities (\alpha), and spherical harmonic coefficients (\mathbf{f}). Data Structures: The parameters are stored as PyTorch nn.Parameter tensors on the GPU: xyz: Shape (N, 3), float32. featuresdc: Shape (N, 1, 3), float32. Stores the zero-order (DC) spherical harmonic coefficients. scaling: Shape (N, 3), float32. Stores the logarithm of the scale factors. rotation: Shape (N, 4), float32. Stores quaternions in [w, x, y, z] format. opacity: Shape (N, 1), float32. Stores the logit of the opacity. Numbered Steps: 1. SfM Reconstruction (if not pre-computed): Input 2D images. Estimate camera intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point) and extrinsic parameters (rotation \mathbf{R}{cam}, translation \mathbf{T}{cam}). Match feature points across images and back-project pixels to 3D space using the inverse projection matrix to generate a sparse 3D point cloud with associated RGB colors. Note: Using dense Multi-View Stereo (MVS) clouds is discouraged for standard initialization as it wastes time and bakes in MVS errors as starting bias; sparse SfM is sufficient because the optimizer creates detail during training. 2. Position Initialization: Copy the 3D coordinates (X, Y, Z) from the SfM point cloud directly to the xyz tensor. 3. Scale Initialization: Compute the distance to the k-nearest neighbors (KNN) for each point. Calculate the scale parameter as the logarithm of the distance. Method A (Fixed Base): Use a base distance d{base} = 0.1. Compute dist2 = \text{clamp}(d{base}, \min=10^{-7}). Set \mathbf{s} = \log(\sqrt{dist2}) repeated for x, y, z dimensions. Method B (KNN): Compute mean distance to k nearest neighbors. Apply log. Set \mathbf{s} = \log(\text{mean\dist}). Method C (Isotropic Flag): If isotropic is true, replicate the single scale value across all three dimensions. 4. Rotation Initialization: Set all quaternions to the identity rotation [1, 0, 0, 0]. Alternative (Normal-based): If surface normals are available (e.g., from depth maps), compute the quaternion that aligns the local z-axis with the estimated surface normal. 5. Opacity Initialization: Initialize the logit parameter opacity to a value that yields a sigmoid output close to, but less than, 1.0. Method A: Set pre-activation value to 8.0. \sigma(8.0) \approx 0.9997. Method B: Set target opacity to 0.1 or 0.5. Compute logit: \text{logit}(p) = \log(p / (1-p)). Clamp the resulting logit to [10^{-4}, 0.99] to prevent extreme values. 6. Color (Spherical Harmonics) Initialization: Normalize the SfM point's RGB color to the range [-0.5, 0.5]. Compute the DC coefficient \mathbf{f}{dc} by dividing the normalized RGB by the SH basis constant C0 = 0.28209479177387814. Initialize all higher-order AC coefficients (featuresrest) to zero. 7. Covariance Construction (Runtime/Forward Pass): Construct the diagonal scaling matrix \mathbf{S} from scaling: \mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{sx} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & e^{sy} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e^{sz} \end{bmatrix} Normalize the quaternion \mathbf{q} to unit length and convert to a rotation matrix \mathbf{R}. Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma: \Sigma = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T Note: This split into scale and rotation ensures \Sigma remains positive semi-definite during optimization. 8. 2D Projection Covariance (Runtime/Forward Pass): Transform 3D positions to camera coordinates: \mathbf{x}{cam} = \mathbf{R}{cam} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{T}{cam}. Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the perspective projection. With focal length f and depth z (clamped with 10^{-7} to prevent division by zero): \mathbf{J} = \begin{bmatrix} f/z & 0 & -fx/z^2 \\ 0 & f/z & -fy/z^2 \end{bmatrix} Compute the 2D covariance \Sigma': \Sigma' = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \Sigma \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T where \mathbf{W} is the world-to-camera rotation matrix. Add a numerical stability bias of 0.3 to the diagonal elements \Sigma'{0,0} and \Sigma'{1,1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 BASEDISTANCE = 0.1 NUMNEIGHBORS = 50 OPACITYLOGITINIT = 8.0 def initializegaussians(sfmpointsxyz, sfmpointsrgb, useknn=True): """ Initialize Gaussian parameters from SfM data. Args: sfmpointsxyz: Tensor of shape (N, 3) sfmpointsrgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3), values in [0, 1] useknn: Boolean flag to choose between KNN (default) or fixed base scaling. Returns: Dictionary of initialized parameters """ N = sfmpointsxyz.shape[0] device = sfmpointsxyz.device # 1. Positions xyz = sfmpointsxyz.clone() # 2. Scales if useknn: # Compute pairwise distances dists = torch.cdist(sfmpointsxyz, sfmpointsxyz) # Exclude self-distance by setting diagonal to infinity dists = dists + torch.eye(N, device=device) 1e9 # Get distances to k nearest neighbors knndists, = torch.topk(dists, k=NUMNEIGHBORS, largest=False, dim=1) meanknndist = torch.mean(knndists, dim=1, keepdim=True) scaling = torch.log(meanknndist) else: # Fixed base distance method dist2 = torch.clamp(torch.full((N, 1), BASEDISTANCE, device=device), min=1e-7) scaling = torch.log(torch.sqrt(dist2)).repeat(1, 3) # 3. Rotations (Identity) rotation = torch.zeros(N, 4, device=device) rotation[:, 0] = 1.0 # w=1, x=y=z=0 # 4. Opacity (Logit) opacity = torch.full((N, 1), OPACITYLOGITINIT, device=device) # 5. Colors (SH DC) rgbnorm = sfmpointsrgb - 0.5 # Normalize to [-0.5, 0.5] featuresdc = (rgbnorm / SHC0).unsqueeze(1) # Shape (N, 1, 3) featuresrest = torch.zeros(N, 12, 3, device=device) # Degree 1 SH AC coefficients return { 'xyz': xyz, 'scaling': scaling, 'rotation': rotation, 'opacity': opacity, 'featuresdc': featuresdc, 'featuresrest': featuresrest } def computecovariance(scaling, rotation): """ Compute 3D covariance matrix from scale and rotation parameters. """ scales = torch.exp(scaling) S = torch.zeros(scaling.shape[0], 3, 3, device=scaling.device) S[:, 0, 0] = scales[:, 0] S[:, 1, 1] = scales[:, 1] S[:, 2, 2] = scales[:, 2] qnorm = torch.nn.functional.normalize(rotation, p=2, dim=1) w, x, y, z = qnorm[:, 0], qnorm[:, 1], qnorm[:, 2], qnorm[:, 3] R = torch.stack([ 1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy), 2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx), 2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2) ], dim=1).reshape(-1, 3, 3) Sigma = R @ (S S) @ R.transpose(1, 2) return Sigma Parameters: C0: SH basis constant, 0.28209479177387814. Base Distance: 0.1 (used in fixed-scale initialization). Opacity Pre-activation: 8.0 (yields \sigma \approx 0.9997). Numerical Stability Bias: 0.3 added to 2D covariance diagonal. Max Scaling: 10.0 (clamped after exponential transformation). Learning Rates (Adam): Means: 0.00016, Scales: 0.005, Quats: 0.001, Features DC: 0.0025, Features Rest: 0.000125, Opacities: 0.05. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In Jacobian computation, depth z must be clamped with 10^{-7}. Singular Covariance: Adding 0.3 to the diagonal of the 2D covariance matrix prevents singular matrices during projection. Invalid Rotations: Quaternions must be normalized to unit length before converting to rotation matrices. Excessive Scale: Scaling values are clamped to a maximum of 10.0 after exponential transformation to prevent excessively large Gaussians. MVS Bias: Using dense MVS clouds for initialization is discouraged as it wastes time and bakes in MVS errors as starting bias. Random Large-Variance Initialization is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives that relaxes the assumption of using only Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud data. It addresses the problem of generating a geometrically plausible starting configuration when SfM data is sparse or absent by sampling Gaussians randomly with large variance. It sets itself apart from SfM-Based Triangle Initialization by relying on stochastic sampling rather than deterministic SfM-derived positions and local density scaling. This method reduces training time for dynamic video scenes by initializing the point cloud of the current frame using the learned model from the previous frame, leveraging temporal correlation between nearby frames. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by explicitly optimizing geometric alignment between consecutive frames via Chamfer distance minimization before refining radiance parameters. Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction is a method for initializing and refining the geometric attributes of 3D Gaussian primitives in a feed-forward manner, typically using a global volumetric representation rather than per-pixel alignment. It solves the problem of redundant, inconsistent, and ghosting artifacts that arise when accumulating locally predicted Gaussians from multiple views. Unlike sibling methods that rely on per-scene optimization or local cost volumes, this approach predicts a unified global scene representation by refining noisy depth-initialized points in 3D space, thereby improving global consistency and reducing floating artifacts. Background Hemisphere Initialization is a technique for handling unbounded scenes in 3D Gaussian Splatting by modeling the distant background as a separate, fixed-radius hemisphere of Gaussians. It solves the problem of representing distant regions (hundreds of meters away) that would otherwise require foreground Gaussians to extend to infinity, which degrades novel view synthesis quality. It sets itself apart from standard background models by explicitly disentangling the sky from the foreground geometry using a moving hemisphere that maintains a fixed relative distance to the target camera. ReSplat Initialization predicts an initial set of 3D Gaussians from a sparse point cloud by aggregating local and global 3D context to compensate for information loss incurred by downsampling the input point cloud by 16x. Unlike naive prediction methods that directly map point features to Gaussian parameters, this method uses a transformer-based encoder to enrich features with neighborhood context before decoding. It sets the stage for the subsequent Recurrent Gaussian Update by providing a structured initial state \mathcal{G}^0. This family of methods initializes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives using pre-existing 3D geometry (point clouds or meshes) rather than relying solely on sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) outputs. It solves the problem of initializing high-quality radiance fields when multi-view images are unavailable or when the user possesses dense, surface-aligned volumetric data (e.g., MPEG plenoptic point clouds or meshes) [16108-3dgs-custom-initialization-from-point-cloud-mesh.md]. It differs from Random Large-Variance Initialization by anchoring Gaussians to observed geometry, and from Gaussian Model Initialization by supporting dense mesh inputs and optional fixed-position constraints [16108-3dgs-custom-initialization-from-point-cloud-mesh.md]. Cone Scatter Initialization (CSI) is a technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enriches sparse point clouds (typically from COLMAP) by scattering new points within a predefined viewing frustum, specifically to address depth coverage issues in low-light or nighttime scenes where COLMAP fails to produce high-quality distant points. Unlike standard initialization which relies solely on existing sparse matches, CSI ensures Gaussians form at correct, deeper depths, preventing the generation of structures at incorrect depths and lack of fine details. A method to initialize the neural point cloud and their features for Point-NeRF using an external point cloud reconstruction (specifically COLMAP). It solves the problem of how to provide initial positions, variances, and feature vectors for the neural points. The variance parameter \gammai for each point pi is initialized to 0.3. To acquire the feature vector fi for a point pi, views where the point is occluded are ruled out, and the view where the camera is closest to the point is selected. The point is unprojected onto the feature maps extracted by the Image Feature Extraction 2D CNN (Gf) from the selected closest view to obtain fi. During optimization, the confidence score of valid points is pushed to 1. The hierarchy is a binary tree. Leaf nodes contain the full set of optimized Gaussian properties (base color, SH coefficients, position, covariance). Internal nodes store merged approximations of their two child nodes. Initializes a single ellipsoid from a set of 3D points using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to determine orientation, center, and radii. The minimum allowed radius r{\min} is typically 0.005 to avoid numerical problems. A scaling factor \alpha (typically 3) is used to ensure points are mostly covered. Aggregates filtered multiview depth maps from an MVS method into a unified 3D point cloud. An initial optimization phase prunes noisy Gaussians by freezing Gaussian centers and optimizing other parameters for N{prun} iterations, removing Gaussians with opacity \alphak < \tau. Afterward, all parameters are unfrozen for standard optimization with Adaptive Density Control. Initializes the base feature f{base} and directional feature f{dir} with the RGB color values of the corresponding SfM points. The temporal feature f{time} is initialized as a zero vector. The MVS point cloud is generated in the same coordinate system as the SfM reconstruction used to initialize 3DGS, allowing direct comparison with Gaussian centers. A dense MVS point cloud is generated from the wall image sequence using COLMAP, and a uniform scale factor is applied to both the MVS point cloud and the Gaussian centers. Initializes each image volume with 50,000 Gaussians. The background threshold is 0.05, and the intensity initialization coefficient ci is 0.15. This initialization yields performance comparable to fitting Gaussians to an FBP-reconstructed image but avoids extra computational overhead. Time Complexity: SfM initialization is significantly slower than random initialization due to the feature matching and triangulation steps. COLMAP initialization takes approximately 6 minutes compared to 0.1 seconds for random initialization. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of points N. The SfM point cloud size varies by scene but is typically sparse (e.g., 150,000 points for large scenes). Performance: SfM initialization yields higher quality results. On the Average-30K dataset, SfM initialization achieves a PSNR of 26.05, while random initialization drops to 20.42. In other benchmarks, COLMAP initialization achieves 35.201 PSNR, while random initialization yields 6.023 PSNR. Strengths: Provides geometrically accurate starting points, improving overall reconstruction quality and convergence speed. Limitations: Requires a successful SfM reconstruction; fails if image coverage is too thin or if there are insufficient feature matches. Random initialization is faster but results in poorer background quality and lower PSNR. When to Use: Use SfM initialization when 2D images are available and sufficient feature matches can be found. Use random initialization only when camera poses are known (e.g., synthetic datasets) or SfM fails. The method originates from the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper, which proposed initializing Gaussians from sparse Structure from Motion (SfM) points. SfM is a well-established computer vision technique used to reconstruct 3D structure and camera poses from 2D images. The use of COLMAP, a goto implementation for SfM, is standard in the community. The approach was shown to be superior to random initialization, which was previously used in some NeRF variants but led to slower convergence and lower quality. name: Random Large-Variance Initialization
head: RAIN-GS Initialization, Sparse-Large-Variance Init
body: Random Large-Variance Initialization is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives that relaxes the assumption of using only Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud data. It addresses the problem of generating a geometrically plausible starting configuration when SfM data is sparse or absent by sampling Gaussians randomly with large variance. It sets itself apart from SfM-Based Triangle Initialization by relying on stochastic sampling rather than deterministic SfM-derived positions and local density scaling. Inputs: A scene bounding box or volume definition; a target number of Gaussians N. Outputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians with initial parameters. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (parameterized via scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Spherical Harmonics coefficients c{i, l} for color features. Steps: 1. Define the spatial bounds of the scene (e.g., the bounding box of the available sparse point cloud or the camera frustum). 2. Sample N positions \mui uniformly at random within these bounds. 3. Initialize scales si to large values. The "large-variance" aspect implies that the initial Gaussians are significantly larger than the typical final converged size, covering a broad area of the scene to ensure coverage. 4. Initialize rotations qi to identity or random unit quaternions. 5. Initialize opacities \alphai to a small constant (e.g., 0.1) or derived from the initial coverage. 6. Initialize SH coefficients c{i, l} to zero or average color values if RGB is available. Parameters: N: Number of Gaussians. Not given in the sources. Scale magnitude: Large relative to the average inter-point distance in SfM data. Not given in the sources. Edge cases: If the scene bounds are undefined, the initialization may place Gaussians in empty space, wasting compute. Large initial variances may lead to slow convergence or require careful learning rate scheduling to avoid instability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def randomlargevarianceinit(numgaussians, scenebounds): """ Initialize Gaussians with random positions and large variances. Args: numgaussians (int): Number of Gaussians to create. scenebounds (tuple): (minxyz, maxxyz) defining the bounding box. Returns: dict: Dictionary containing initialized Gaussian parameters. """ minxyz, maxxyz = scenebounds boundssize = maxxyz - minxyz # Sample positions uniformly within bounds positions = np.random.uniform(minxyz, maxxyz, size=(numgaussians, 3)) # Initialize scales to large values # The exact magnitude of "large" is not specified in sources # A heuristic is to use a fraction of the scene diagonal or a fixed large value scalemagnitude = np.linalg.norm(boundssize) / 10.0 scales = np.full((numgaussians, 3), scalemagnitude) # Initialize rotations to identity (or random) # Using identity for simplicity, though random is also valid rotations = np.tile([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], (numgaussians, 1)) # Initialize opacities to a small value opacities = np.full(numgaussians, 0.1) # Initialize SH coefficients to zero # Assuming degree 0 for simplicity, or average color if available shcoeffs = np.zeros((numgaussians, 3)) return { 'positions': positions, 'scales': scales, 'rotations': rotations, 'opacities': opacities, 'shcoeffs': shcoeffs } Uses deterministic SfM data for position and local density for scale, rather than purely random sampling with large variance. Choose when high-quality SfM data is available and geometric accuracy is prioritized over robustness to sparse input. Time and memory complexity: O(N) for initialization, where N is the number of Gaussians. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Robust to sparse or missing SfM data; ensures broad coverage of the scene. Limitations: May require more optimization steps to converge to fine details compared to SfM-based initialization; initial Gaussians are large and may blur fine structures. When to use: When SfM data is sparse, noisy, or unavailable. When not: When high-precision geometric initialization is critical and dense SfM data is available. Origin: Introduced in the context of RAIN-GS, as cited in. History: It relaxes the traditional assumption that initialization must be strictly based on SfM point clouds, allowing for more flexible initialization strategies. Usage: Used in differentiable Gaussian splatting pipelines where robust initialization is needed. name: SfM-Based Triangle Initialization
head: Initialization and Training, SfM Triangle Init, Triangle Initialization
body: SfM-Based Triangle Initialization is a method for initializing 3D triangle primitives for differentiable rendering by leveraging Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds. It solves the problem of generating a geometrically plausible starting configuration for triangle splats, ensuring they are sized appropriately relative to local point density and randomly oriented to avoid bias. It sets apart from sibling methods like Random Large-Variance Initialization by using deterministic SfM data for position and local density for scale, rather than purely random sampling with large variance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points Q = \{q1,..., qN\} from an SfM reconstruction. Output: A set of N triangles, each defined by three vertices Vi = \{v{i,1}, v{i,2}, v{i,3}\}, along with initial parameters for sharpness \sigma, opacity o, and spherical harmonic color coefficients c. Data Structures: Each triangle i is stored as a list of three 3D vertices. Associated scalar/vector attributes (opacity, SH coefficients) are stored per triangle. Steps: 1. Point Sampling (Optional, per): If using the hybrid sampling strategy from, select 2/3 of the target points using Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) on the SfM points Q, and the remaining 1/3 uniformly at random. Let the selected subset be Q'. If not specified, use all Q. 2. Local Density Estimation: For each point q \in Q', find its three nearest neighbors in Q. Calculate d as the average Euclidean distance from q to these three neighbors. 3. Vertex Initialization: Sample three vertices \{u1, u2, u3\} uniformly at random from the unit sphere. Scale and translate these vertices to form the triangle around q: v{i,j} = q + k \cdot d \cdot uj, \quad j \in \{1, 2, 3\} where k is a scaling constant. describes this as creating an approximately equilateral, randomly oriented triangle with size proportional to d. specifies the radius (distance from center to vertex) is set to one quarter of the average nearest-neighbor distance, implying k \approx 0.25 in that context, though leaves k as a general constant. 4. Parameter Initialization: Initialize opacity o, sharpness \sigma, and spherical harmonic coefficients c to default values (e.g., opacity to 1.0, SH to white/neutral, sharpness to a standard value). mentions optimizing these; does not specify initial values for non-vertex parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializetriangles(sfmpoints, k=1.0, usefps=False, fpsratio=2/3): """ Initialize 3D triangles from SfM points. Args: sfmpoints: Array of shape (N, 3) containing SfM 3D points. k: Scaling constant for triangle size relative to neighbor distance. usefps: If True, sample points using FPS for 2/3 of points. fpsratio: Ratio of points to sample via FPS. Returns: vertices: Array of shape (N, 3, 3) containing 3 vertices per triangle. """ N = sfmpoints.shape[0] vertices = np.zeros((N, 3, 3)) # Step 1: Point Sampling if usefps: # Farthest Point Sampling implementation required # Select fpsratio N points via FPS, rest randomly # Note: Exact FPS algorithm not detailed in sources, assumed available indices = farthestpointsampling(sfmpoints, int(fpsratio N)) randomindices = np.random.choice(N, N - len(indices), replace=False) selectedindices = np.concatenate([indices, randomindices]) # Shuffle to maintain correspondence if needed, but order doesn't matter for set selectedpoints = sfmpoints[selectedindices] # Map back to original indices if tracking is needed, but here we just process selected # For simplicity, we assume we process the selected subset and map results back # However, the output should be N triangles. # Let's assume we initialize triangles for ALL points, but the 'target' points # for initialization logic are the sampled ones. # Re-reading: "sample two-thirds... and draw remaining one-third... # We then randomly initialize triangles around THESE sampled points". # This implies only sampled points get initialized? Or all points get initialized # but the distribution is biased? # implies initializing for "each SfM 3D point q". # says "initialize triangles around these sampled points". # Ambiguity: Does discard unsampled points? # Given "Extreme Radiance Field Simplification", it likely reduces primitives. # But the parent is "Gaussian Splatting Initialization", which usually keeps N. # Let's assume for SfM-Based Triangle Initialization (general), we use all points. # The FPS part is a variant detail from. pass # Use all points for the general method as per pointstoinit = sfmpoints # Step 2 & 3: For each point for i, q in enumerate(pointstoinit): # Find 3 nearest neighbors # Compute distances to all other points diffs = pointstoinit - q dists = np.linalg.norm(diffs, axis=1) # Exclude self (distance 0) dists[i] = np.inf nearestidx = np.argsort(dists)[:3] nearestpoints = pointstoinit[nearestidx] # Average distance d d = np.mean(np.linalg.norm(nearestpoints - q, axis=1)) # Sample 3 vertices from unit sphere u = np.random.randn(3, 3) u = u / np.linalg.norm(u, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Scale and center vertices[i] = q + k d u return vertices Parameters: k: Scaling constant. uses a general k. implies k=0.25 (radius is 1/4 of average NN distance). \lambda: Weight for L1 vs SSIM loss. Set to 0.8. Optimizers: VectorAdam for vertex positions, Adam for other parameters. Edge Cases: Sparse SfM points: d may be large, leading to oversized triangles. Dense clusters: d may be small, leading to tiny triangles. Degenerate triangles: Random sampling on unit sphere is unlikely to produce collinear points, but precision issues could arise. HDR-GS initialization and optimization is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives and training a Gaussian Splatting model for High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N \cdot K) where K is the number of points used for nearest neighbor search (typically small, e.g., 3-10). If FPS is used, it adds O(N^2) or O(N \log N) depending on implementation. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing vertices and attributes. Strengths: Geometrically aware initialization; adapts to local scene density; avoids the "blobby" artifacts of large-variance random init. Limitations: Requires high-quality SfM point cloud; sensitive to SfM noise/outliers; suggests it may require more iterations or specific loss terms for texture. Originated in the context of differentiable triangle splatting. (Triangle Splatting) proposes this initialization to replace Gaussian initialization with triangle primitives. (DiffSoup) adapts it for extreme simplification, using a hybrid sampling strategy. name: HDR-GS Initialization and Optimization
head: HDR-GS loss, HDR-GS training
body: HDR-GS initialization and optimization is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives and training a Gaussian Splatting model for High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis. It addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which relies on Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images and often lacks accurate Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization in HDR datasets. Unlike standard 3DGS which initializes from SfM points of LDR inputs, HDR-GS recalibrates camera parameters using SfM on LDR views captured at a single exposure time to generate initial 3D Gaussian positions, then optimizes the scene using a combined pixel-wise loss and a µ-law domain constraint loss. This approach establishes a robust data foundation for 3DGS-based algorithms in 3D HDR imaging. Inputs: A multi-view HDR dataset containing Nv viewpoints. For each viewpoint j, LDR images \hat{I}{lj}(ts) captured at a specific exposure time ts. Ground truth HDR images I{hj} (available for synthetic scenes, not for real scenes). Rendered LDR images \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj) and HDR images \hat{I}{hj} generated from the current Gaussian set G. Outputs: Recalibrated camera intrinsics M{int} and extrinsics \{Mj^{ext}\}{j=1}^{Nv}. Initial number of points Np and their 3D positions \{\mui\}{i=1}^{Np}. Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, features, opacity, scaling, rotation) and tone mapper network weights. The method initializes the Gaussian set G as described in GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization. Positions: Initialized from SfM output \{\mui\}. Other Parameters: Randomly initialized. 1. SfM Initialization: Select LDR images \{\hat{I}j(ts)\}{j=1}^{Nv} from the multi-view HDR dataset where all images share the same exposure time ts. This constraint is critical because SfM relies on multi-view feature detection and matching, and exposure changes degrade accuracy. Apply the SfM mapping function F{SfM} to obtain camera parameters and initial point cloud: M{int}, \{Mj^{ext}\}{j=1}^{Nv}, Np, \{\mui\}{i=1}^{Np} = F{SfM}(\{\hat{I}j(ts)\}{j=1}^{Nv}) where Nv is the number of viewpoints, M{int} is the intrinsic matrix (constant across viewpoints), and \{\mui\} are the initial 3D Gaussian positions. 2. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian set G with Np points at positions \{\mui\}. Randomly initialize all other learnable parameters of G (features, opacity, scaling, rotation). 3. Training Loop: For each training iteration (total 3 \times 10^4 iterations): a. Rendering: Render LDR images \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj) and HDR images \hat{I}{hj} for a batch of B viewpoints using the current Gaussian set G and camera poses \{Mj^{ext}\}. b. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L = Lp + \gamma \cdot Lc. c. Optimization: Update parameters using the Adam optimizer. Pixel-wise Loss (Lp): Combines L1 loss and D-SSIM loss on LDR images to ensure photometric consistency: Lp = \sum{j=1}^B L1(I{lj}(\Delta tj), \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj)) + \lambda \cdot L{D-SSIM}(I{lj}(\Delta tj), \hat{I}{lj}(\Delta tj)) where B is the batch size, I{lj} is the ground truth LDR image, \hat{I}{lj} is the rendered LDR image, and \lambda is a hyperparameter. µ-law Domain Constraint Loss (Lc): Enforces a constraint on the rendered HDR image in the µ-law LDR domain, primarily for synthetic scenes where ground truth HDR is available: Lc = \sum{j=1}^B \left( \frac{\log(1 + \mu \cdot norm(I{hj}))}{\log(1 + \mu)} - \frac{\log(1 + \mu \cdot norm(\hat{I}{hj}))}{\log(1 + \mu)} \right)^2 where I{hj} is the ground truth HDR image, \hat{I}{hj} is the rendered HDR image, \mu is the compression amount, and norm(\cdot) is min-max normalization. Total Loss: L = Lp + \gamma \cdot Lc where \gamma controls the relative importance of Lc. \mu (Compression): The amount of compression in the µ-law normalization. \gamma (Constraint Weight): Synthetic datasets: \gamma = 0.6. Real datasets: \gamma = 0 (since ground truth HDR images are unavailable). \lambda (D-SSIM Weight): Hyperparameter for the D-SSIM term in Lp. Optimizer: Adam. \beta1 = 0.9 \beta2 = 0.999 \epsilon = 1 \times 10^{-15} Learning Rates: Point cloud position: Initial 1.6 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially decaying to 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. Point feature: 2.5 \times 10^{-3}. Opacity: 5 \times 10^{-2}. Scaling: 5 \times 10^{-3}. Rotation: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Tone mapper network: Initial 5 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially decaying to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Training Iterations: 3 \times 10^4. Unverified code.
