Step 1: SfM Initialization ts = hdrdataset.targetexposure ldrimagesforsfm = [view.ldrimage for view in hdrdataset if view.exposure == ts] Mint, Mextlist, Np, mupositions = sfmalgorithm(ldrimagesforsfm) # Step 2: Initialize Gaussian Set G G = GaussianSet(mupositions, featuredim) tonemapper = ToneMapperNetwork() # Step 3: Setup Optimizer optimizer = optim.Adam([ {'params': G.positions, 'lr': 1.6e-4}, {'params': G.features, 'lr': 2.5e-3}, {'params': G.opacities, 'lr': 5e-2}, {'params': G.scales, 'lr': 5e-3}, {'params': G.rotations, 'lr': 1e-3}, {'params': tonemapper.parameters(), 'lr': 5e-4} ], betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-15) # Exponential decay factors to reach target LRs over 30000 iterations decaypos = (1.6e-6 / 1.6e-4) (1 / 30000) decaytm = (5e-5 / 5e-4) (1 / 30000) schedulerpos = optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR(optimizer.paramgroups[0], gamma=decaypos) schedulertm = optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR(optimizer.paramgroups[5], gamma=decaytm) # Step 4: Training Loop numiterations = 30000 for iteration in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() batchviews = [hdrdataset[i] for i in torch.randperm(len(hdrdataset))[:batchsize]] lossp = 0.0 lossc = 0.0 for view in batchviews: # D-SSIM computation: not provided in sources dssimterm = torch.zeroslike(l1term) lossp += l1term + lambdadssim dssimterm if gthdr is not None and gamma > 0: normgthdr = minmaxnormalize(gthdr) normrenderedhdr = minmaxnormalize(renderedhdr) mulawgt = torch.log(1 + mu normgthdr) / torch.log(1 + mu) mulawrendered = torch.log(1 + mu normrenderedhdr) / torch.log(1 + mu) lossc += torch.sum((mulawgt - mulawrendered) 2) totalloss = lossp + gamma lossc totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() schedulerpos.step() schedulertm.step() return G, tonemapper SfM Input Constraint: Only HDR views under the same exposure time are used as SfM inputs. Using images with different exposure times degrades the accuracy of SfM due to feature detection/matching failures. Real vs. Synthetic Scenes: The µ-law constraint loss Lc is not used for real scenes because ground truth HDR images are not provided. For real datasets, \gamma is set to 0, whereas for synthetic datasets it is set to 0.6. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Training takes 3 \times 10^4 iterations. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Measured Performance: Hardware: Single RTX A5000 GPU. Speed: 126 fps (inference speed on synthetic datasets). PSNR: 41.10 (synthetic), 36.33 (real). SSIM: 0.982 (synthetic), 0.977 (real). LPIPS: 0.011 (synthetic), 0.016 (real). Strengths: Provides a robust initialization for 3DGS in HDR datasets where SfM point clouds are not provided. Achieves high-quality novel view synthesis with fast rendering speeds. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of SfM, which is sensitive to exposure changes. The µ-law constraint loss is only applicable to synthetic scenes with ground truth HDR. HDR-GS was introduced in the paper "HDR-GS: Efficient High Dynamic Range Novel View Synthesis at 1000x Speed via Gaussian Splatting". The method addresses the limitations of voxel-based methods and the original 3DGS, which do not natively support HDR imaging and often lack SfM point clouds for initialization in HDR datasets. It builds on the 3DGS framework [15] and incorporates techniques from HDR-NeRF [14] for handling HDR data. The method was implemented using PyTorch [75] and tested on datasets collected by [14], including real and synthetic scenes from Blender [74]. name: Temporal Point Cloud Initialization via Chamfer Distance Minimization
head: Temporal Chamfer Initialization
body: This method reduces training time for dynamic video scenes by initializing the point cloud of the current frame using the learned model from the previous frame, leveraging temporal correlation between nearby frames. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by explicitly optimizing geometric alignment between consecutive frames via Chamfer distance minimization before refining radiance parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An accurate point cloud S1 with learned spherical harmonics (SH) parameters from the previous frame (frame 1). An initial point cloud S2 for the current frame (frame 2), generated using the standard initial generation scheme. Output: A refined initial point cloud for frame 2 with optimized positions and initialized radiance field parameters. Data Structures: S1: Set of points \{x\} with associated spherical harmonics coefficients. S2: Set of points \{y\} with learnable position parameters pi. Steps: 1. Generate Initial Cloud: Compute an initial point cloud S2 for the next frame using the standard initialization scheme. 2. Compute Chamfer Distance: Calculate the Chamfer distance CD(S1, S2) between the previous frame's cloud S1 and the current frame's initial cloud S2. 3. Optimize Positions: Minimize the Chamfer distance via gradient descent using the Adam optimizer applied to the point positions in S2. This yields a more accurate initial point cloud for frame 2 in terms of geometry. 4. Initialize Radiance Parameters: After refining the positions pi in S2, compute the top-k closest points in S1 for each point in S2. Choose the average of their corresponding spherical harmonics parameters as the initial radiance field parameter for the refined point pi. Formula: The Chamfer distance CD(S1, S2) is defined as: CD(S1, S2) = \frac{1}{|S1|} \sum{x \in S1} \min{y \in S2} \|x - y\|2^2 + \frac{1}{|S2|} \sum{y \in S2} \min{x \in S1} \|x - y\|2^2 Where: |S1| and |S2| are the number of points in clouds S1 and S2 respectively. \| \cdot \|2 denotes the Euclidean distance. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Top-k: The number of closest neighbors to average SH parameters. Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def temporalchamferinitialization(S1points, S1shparams, S2pointsinit): """ Initialize frame 2 Gaussians using frame 1's learned model. Args: S1points: Tensor of shape (N1, 3), positions of previous frame. S1shparams: Tensor of shape (N1, C), SH coefficients of previous frame. S2pointsinit: Tensor of shape (N2, 3), initial positions of current frame. Returns: S2pointsrefined: Refined positions for current frame. S2shparamsinit: Initialized SH coefficients for current frame. """ # Step 1: S2pointsinit is provided as input # Step 2 & 3: Minimize Chamfer Distance via Gradient Descent s2points = S2pointsinit.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([s2points]) # Learning rate not given in the sources. # Number of optimization steps not given in the sources. for in range(10): optimizer.zerograd() # Compute Chamfer Distance cd = computechamferdistance(S1points, s2points) # Backpropagate cd.backward() optimizer.step() S2pointsrefined = s2points.detach() # Step 4: Initialize Radiance Parameters (SH) # Compute pairwise squared Euclidean distances distmatrix = torch.cdist(S2pointsrefined, S1points) 2 # Shape (N2, N1) # Find top-k closest points in S1 for each point in S2 # k is not given in the sources. k = 1 topkindices = torch.topk(distmatrix, k, dim=1, largest=False).indices # Shape (N2, k) # Gather SH parameters from S1 based on top-k indices gatheredsh = S1shparams[topkindices] # Shape (N2, k, C) # Average the SH parameters S2shparamsinit = gatheredsh.mean(dim=1) # Shape (N2, C) return S2pointsrefined, S2shparamsinit def computechamferdistance(S1, S2): """ Computes Chamfer Distance between two point clouds. """ # Distances from S1 to S2 dists1s2 = torch.cdist(S1, S2) 2 # Shape (N1, N2) mindists1s2, = torch.min(dists1s2, dim=1) # Shape (N1,) # Distances from S2 to S1 dists2s1 = torch.cdist(S2, S1) 2 # Shape (N2, N1) mindists2s1, = torch.min(dists2s1, dim=1) # Shape (N2,) # Average squared distances per the formula cd = torch.mean(mindists1s2) + torch.mean(mindists2s1) return cd An inter-frame point constraint that uses a Gaussian kernel function to measure distances between inter-frame point clouds, enhancing robustness against depth noise. It replaces Chamfer distance to be less sensitive to noise. The weight w{ij} between points pi^m and pj^{m+1} is calculated as w{ij} = \exp\left(-\frac{\|pi^m - pj^{m+1}\|^2}{2\sigma{pc}^2}\right), where \sigma{pc} is the standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel function. The standard deviation \sigma{pc} is empirically set to 1. This constraint is incorporated to provide constraints for inter-frame pose optimization and refinement. Time Complexity: The method achieves a 4x improvement in training runtime compared to training each frame from scratch. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces training time significantly by leveraging temporal correlation. Produces cleaner object boundaries and finer detail, especially with significant object motion. Limitations: Chamfer distance can be sensitive to noise in estimated depth maps, as it imposes a strong constraint on point clouds and penalizes small deviations. This is addressed by variants like GPC. When to use: Dynamic video scenes where nearby frames are temporally correlated. When not to use: Static scenes where temporal correlation is not applicable, or scenes where depth estimation noise requires robust inter-frame constraints. This method was proposed by Zhang et al. in the paper "Differentiable Point-Based Radiance Fields for Efficient View Synthesis". It was presented at the SA ’22 Conference Papers, December 6–9, 2022, Daegu, Republic of Korea. The method is part of the broader effort to improve computational efficiency in point-based radiance representations for novel view synthesis. name: Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), EVolSplat, Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting, GRM, Gaussian MLP Heads, Gaussian Representation Model
body: Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction is a method for initializing and refining the geometric attributes of 3D Gaussian primitives in a feed-forward manner, typically using a global volumetric representation rather than per-pixel alignment. It solves the problem of redundant, inconsistent, and ghosting artifacts that arise when accumulating locally predicted Gaussians from multiple views. Unlike sibling methods that rely on per-scene optimization or local cost volumes, this approach predicts a unified global scene representation by refining noisy depth-initialized points in 3D space, thereby improving global consistency and reducing floating artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N sparse input images \{In\}{n=1}^N, their calibrated intrinsic matrices \{Kn\}{n=1}^N, extrinsic matrices \{Tn = Rn | tn\}{n=1}^N, and optional monocular depth estimations \{Dn\}{n=1}^N. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{(\mui, \alphai, \Sigmai, ci)\}{i=1}^{Np}, where \mui is the center, \alphai is the opacity, \Sigmai is the covariance matrix, and ci is the view-dependent color. Data Structures: Global Point Cloud (P): A set of 3D points in world coordinates, P \in \mathbb{R}^{Np \times 3}, constructed by unprojecting RGB images using depth maps and camera poses. Feature Volume (F): A sparse 3D tensor F \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times C} extracted by a sparse 3D CNN, aligned with the world coordinate system. MLP Heads: Three independent Multi-Layer Perceptrons: \mathcal{D}{pos} for position offsets, \mathcal{D}{opa} for opacity, and \mathcal{D}{cov} for covariance. Numbered Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: Use an off-the-shelf metric depth estimator to predict depth maps \{Dn\}{n=1}^N for each input image \{In\}{n=1}^N. 2. Global Point Cloud Construction: Unproject the RGB images into 3D space using the intrinsic matrices Kn, extrinsic matrices Tn, and depth maps Dn to construct the global point cloud P: P = \bigcup{n=1}^N \pi^{-1}(In, Dn, Tn, Kn) where \pi^{-1} denotes pixel unprojection. 3. Filtering: Apply a uniform filter to P to delete duplicate primitives while preserving scene structure. Then, apply a statistical filter to remove floating artifacts (floaters) from the processed primitives. 4. Feature Volume Extraction: Feed the filtered global point cloud P into a sparse 3D CNN (e.g., sparse U-Net) to extract a neural feature volume F. 5. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian centers \mu^{init}i using the points in P (i.e., \mu^{init}i = pi \in P). 6. Geometry Parameters Prediction: For each initialized center \mu^{init}i: a. Query the feature volume F using trilinear interpolation at the current estimated position \mu^{init}i + \Delta \mu^{prev}i to obtain a feature vector fi: fi = F(\mu^{init}i + \Delta \mu^{prev}i) b. Decode opacity \alphai and covariance \Sigmai using the MLP heads: \alphai = \mathcal{D}{opa}(fi), \quad \Sigmai = \mathcal{D}{cov}(fi) c. Decode the position offset \Delta \mui using \mathcal{D}{pos}, passed through a Tanh activation and scaled by the voxel size v{size}: \Delta \mui = \text{Tanh}(\mathcal{D}{pos}(fi)) \cdot v{size} d. Update the Gaussian center: \mui = \mu^{init}i + \Delta \mui Here, \Delta \mu^{prev}i tracks the offset from the previous iteration (initialized to 0 during inference). 7. Color Prediction: Project the 3D Gaussians to the nearest K reference views to retrieve 2D context (color windows \{ck\}{k=1}^K and visibility maps). Decode the Gaussian color ci using this 2D context. 8. Background Modeling: Model distant views and the sky using a generalizable hemisphere Gaussian model where geometry is fixed and color is predicted similarly to the foreground volume. 9. Rendering: Compose the foreground and background Gaussians to reconstruct the full image using standard alpha blending: c = \sum{i \in \mathcal{G}} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where c is the rendered color, \mathcal{G} is the set of Gaussians, and the product term represents transmittance. Parameters: N: Number of input images. K: Number of nearest reference views for 2D context retrieval. v{size}: Voxel size used to scale the position offset output. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting Artifacts: Pixel-aligned methods generate redundant primitives in overlapping regions. Depth Noise: Monocular depth predictions contain noise and floating artifacts. Recursive Convergence: The position update is recursive. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictgaussiangeometry(inputimages, cameraposes, depthestimator, sparse3dcnn, dpos, dopa, dcov, voxelsize, numiterations=2): """ Predicts 3D Gaussian geometry parameters in a feed-forward manner. """ N = len(inputimages) H, W = inputimages[0].shape[-2:] # Step 1 & 2: Depth Estimation and Global Point Cloud Construction depthmaps = [depthestimator(img) for img in inputimages] globalpointcloud = [] for n in range(N): Kn = cameraposes[n].intrinsic Tn = cameraposes[n].extrinsic for u in range(H): for v in range(W): d = depthmaps[n][u, v] if d > 0: campt = np.linalg.inv(Kn) @ np.array([u, v, 1]) worldpt = Tn @ np.append(campt d, 1) globalpointcloud.append(worldpt[:3]) P = np.array(globalpointcloud) # Step 3: Filtering # Sources do not specify the exact algorithm for uniform and statistical filters. # P = uniformfilter(P) # P = statisticalfilter(P) # Step 4: Feature Volume Extraction F = sparse3dcnn(P) # Step 5: Initialization muinit = P.copy() Np = len(muinit) deltamuprev = np.zeroslike(muinit) # Step 6: Geometry Parameters Prediction (Recursive Convergence) for in range(numiterations): muest = muinit + deltamuprev # Query feature volume using trilinear interpolation # Sources do not specify the exact interpolation implementation. fi = trilinearinterpolate(F, muest) # Decode parameters alpha = dopa(fi) Sigma = dcov(fi) deltamu = np.tanh(dpos(fi)) voxelsize mu = muinit + deltamu deltamuprev = deltamu # Final query for alpha and Sigma at converged position finalmu = muinit + deltamuprev finalf = trilinearinterpolate(F, finalmu) alpha = dopa(finalf) Sigma = dcov(finalf) deltamu = np.tanh(dpos(finalf)) voxelsize mu = muinit + deltamu # Step 7: Color Prediction # Sources do not specify the exact algorithm for 2D context retrieval and color decoding. # colors = predictcolorfrom2dcontext(mu, alpha, Sigma, inputimages, cameraposes, K=3) return [(mu[i], alpha[i], Sigma[i], colors[i]) for i in range(Np)] GSGEN is a text-to-3D generation method that represents 3D content as a set of 3D Gaussians and optimizes them progressively in two stages: geometry optimization and appearance refinement, using 2D and 3D diffusion priors. It utilizes existing multi-view generation models to train a pixel-aligned Gaussian representation for faithful 3D generation via a single feed-forward pass. It differs from DreamGaussian by focusing on incorporating 3D prior with more advanced representation, whereas DreamGaussian focuses on fast image-to-3D generation. Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting is a method for dynamic scene reconstruction that learns 3D Gaussians in a canonical static space and models spatial-temporal deformation using an implicit deformation field implemented as a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Unlike static 3D Gaussian Splatting, which assumes a fixed geometry, this method makes Gaussian parameters time-dependent, enabling the reconstruction and real-time rendering of 4D scenes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like GSGEN or Textured-GS by explicitly predicting temporal offsets for geometric attributes (position, rotation, scale) via an MLP conditioned on time, rather than relying on explicit per-frame storage or texture-based extensions. The Fourier Splatting primitive is a planar surfel for radiance field rendering that replaces the fixed Gaussian or elliptical falloff with a boundary defined by a Fourier series, allowing the representation of arbitrary closed shapes. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) or 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which are limited to fixed elliptical or disc shapes, this primitive enables higher fidelity representation of complex geometry and fine-grained details. Its key differentiator is inherent scalability: the level of detail (LoD) is controlled by truncating Fourier coefficients at runtime, allowing a single trained model to be rendered at varying complexities without retraining or post-hoc compression. The Conditional Slicing Mechanism conditions a 7-dimensional Gaussian (defined over spatial, temporal, and angular dimensions) on observed time t and view direction d to yield a conditional 3D Gaussian governing the spatial component. This operation "slices" the full 7D distribution to integrate temporal dynamics and view-dependent effects into the traditional 3D rendering pipeline without introducing additional temporal dependencies in the spherical harmonics. It sets itself apart from static Gaussian Splatting variants by explicitly modeling the joint distribution of space, time, and view, allowing the spatial mean and covariance to shift based on the current rendering context. Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (SAGS) is a novel-view synthesis method that implicitly encodes scene geometry using a local-global graph representation to facilitate learning complex scenes and enforce meaningful point displacements that preserve structure, thereby reducing floating-point artifacts and storage requirements. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which optimizes each Gaussian independently, SAGS leverages inter- and intra-connectivity between 3D point positions via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to predict Gaussian attributes, outperforming 3D-GS and Scaffold-GS in capturing high-frequency details while significantly reducing memory footprint. Mesh-embedded representations integrate explicit triangle mesh topology with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable coherent deformation, editing, and surface-aligned rendering. Unlike standard 3DGS, which treats Gaussians as independent entities in free space, this family binds Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale) to mesh geometry via barycentric coordinates or vertex parameterization, ensuring that mesh edits or animations propagate deterministically to the radiance field. This approach solves the problem of Gaussian drift and incoherent motion transfer during animation, while providing a bridge between implicit neural/radiance representations and explicit editable mesh assets. Inverse Gaussian Splattling is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives by back-projecting optimized 2D Gaussian kernels from image space into world space. It solves the problem of generating high-quality initial geometric parameters (position, rotation, scale) for new 3D Gaussians from 2D renderings, specifically handling foreground-background ambiguity in boundary regions. It differs from standard initialization by using Weighted Principal Component Analysis (WPCA) on clustered 3D points derived from depth maps, followed by a scaling calibration step to align the projected 3D covariance with the original 2D target. Occupancy-Opacity Factorization decouples a Gaussian primitive's geometric presence from its optical properties by splitting the single standard opacity parameter into two learnable attributes: geometric occupancy (\sigma) and optical opacity (\alpha). This solves the problem where a single opacity parameter cannot simultaneously model a surface that is geometrically solid (for sharp reflections) yet optically clear (for light transmission). It sets itself apart from siblings like Textured-GS and Oriented Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling the probabilistic interaction of rays with the Gaussian substance, enabling deferred shading for high-frequency reflection modeling. CAG-GS generates implicit 3D Gaussians from semantic anchors by encoding spatial positions into high-dimensional semantic vectors via a multi-resolution hash grid, which are then fused with anchor features to predict Gaussian attributes. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating semantic guidance and geometric consistency constraints (normal and flattening losses) to improve global consistency in large-scale scenes, utilizing a coarse-to-fine training strategy. This family extends the standard 3D Gaussian primitive to better model explicit geometry, surface orientation, and directional asymmetry, which standard isotropic Gaussians lack. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing learnable normals [9621-oriented-gaussian-splatting.md], skewness [10045-3d-skew-normal-splatting.md], or mesh-constrained parameterizations [15283-barycentric-splat-parameterization.md] to enable surface wrapping, mesh extraction, and view-dependent effects. Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction is a neural rendering method that combines voxel-based density representation with Multi-Plane Image (MPI) depth layers to perform efficient volume rendering. It solves the problem of slow convergence and poor surface quality in implicit neural representations by using explicit grid-based features alongside approximate Signed Distance Function (SDF) supervision. Unlike its sibling Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction, which typically predicts Gaussian parameters or raw densities, DirectMPIGO explicitly predicts an SDF value via a feature grid to enable robust surface extraction and regularization. It is significantly faster than implicit-only methods like NeuralRGB-D but requires larger memory footprints due to the explicit grid storage. Functional Gaussian Splatting (DiffGS Representation) solves the problem of representing discrete, unstructured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives as continuous, differentiable functions to enable generative modeling. It disentangles the 3DGS representation into three specific functions: Gaussian Probability Function (GauPF) for geometry, Gaussian Color Function (GauCF) for appearance, and Gaussian Transform Function (GauTF) for structural attributes. Unlike sibling methods that modify the primitive shape or storage structure, this representation maps the discrete set of Gaussians to continuous fields, allowing the use of standard generative frameworks like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs). InnerGS is a volumetric rendering method that models continuous 3D density using 3D Gaussians to synthesize novel 2D slices at arbitrary depths, avoiding the discrete projection artifacts of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike standard 3DGS which renders pixels via perspective projection of splats onto a camera plane, InnerGS calculates the contribution of each Gaussian directly to a pixel on a 2D slice at a specific depth t along a given axis. This approach enables seamless volumetric interpolation and explicit internal structure reconstruction, making it suitable for applications like medical imaging where internal slices are required. [No details provided in sources.] Feed-forward and generalizable prediction maps input images directly to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} without per-scene gradient descent, solving the latency bottleneck of traditional 3D Gaussian Splatting which requires minutes of optimization per scene [Parent]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by leveraging large-scale training on diverse datasets to learn geometric and appearance priors, enabling single-pass inference on unseen scenes [Parent]. Plenoptic Sampling Guided 3DGS Construction is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations directly from mesh geometry, using plenoptic sampling theory to theoretically derive the minimum sampling rate for views and the optimal distribution of 3D Gaussians. Unlike heuristic initialization methods that rely on trial-and-error, this approach precisely constrains Gaussian density and camera sampling to achieve Nyquist-level performance for global illumination caching. It sets itself apart by grounding the initialization in signal processing principles, ensuring that the number of Gaussians and sampled views is minimized while maintaining high-fidelity rendering. Geometry Guided Gaussian Points Generation (MGadapter) is a method that generates structured 3D Gaussian point attributes from an intermediate triangular mesh, providing explicit geometric guidance to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of vanilla 3DGS lacking deterministic geometry boundaries and explicit normal directions, which complicates light transport computation and hinders physically-based inverse rendering. Unlike sibling methods that rely on learned approximated normals or real-time optimization to maintain shape consistency, MGadapter uses a predefined heuristic function to map mesh triangles directly to Gaussian points, leveraging well-defined mesh normals for improved accuracy and stable training. Optical and Attribute Enhancement extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by allowing spatial variation of color and opacity within individual Gaussian primitives, rather than treating them as uniform ellipsoids with fixed view-dependent color. It solves the limitation of low-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) in capturing high-frequency details and complex surface properties by introducing per-Gaussian texture maps and static attribute-conditioned offsets. It differs from standard 3DGS by evaluating SH basis functions on surface intersection vectors (Textured-GS) or baking MLP-predicted offsets into parameters (Attribute-Conditioned SH), and differs from naive blurring by selectively adjusting Gaussian scales based on defocus depth. [No details provided in sources.] The Wavelet-to-Gaussian Transition Bank is a method for constructing Gaussian surrogates for wavelet kernels by fitting a single canonical Gaussian per subband and obtaining others via spatial translation, avoiding redundant fitting for every wavelet kernel. It solves the computational bottleneck of independently fitting Gaussians to every wavelet coefficient in a multi-scale decomposition, enabling efficient analytical conversion from wavelet bases to Gaussian primitives for real-time volumetric visualization. It differs from sibling methods like GSGEN or Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction by relying on precomputed analytical mappings derived from the translation properties of the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) rather than learned neural networks or random sampling. GaMeS Parametrization parameterizes Gaussian components into flat triangle-face meshes, allowing GS to be visualized and manipulated as a triangle soup. For mesh-bound Gaussians, means are assigned to mesh faces via learnable barycentric coordinates of vertices, ensuring they remain bound under deformation. The orientation of mesh-bound Gaussians is defined by the face normal and two in-plane directions derived from the vertices. The forward mapping T(\cdot) defines triangle vertices v1 = m, v2 = m + s2 r2, and v3 = m + s3 r3 from Gaussian N(m, R, S) with R=[r1, r2, r3] and S=\text{diag}(\epsilon, s2, s3). The inverse mapping T^{-1}(\cdot) recovers the Gaussian from triangle V=[v1, v2, v3] using mean \hat{m} = v1, rotation \hat{R} = [\hat{r}1, \hat{r}2, \hat{r}3] where \hat{r}1 = \frac{(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)}{\|(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)\|}, \hat{r}2 = \frac{v2 - v1}{\|v2 - v1\|}, \hat{r}3 = \text{orth}(v3 - v1; \hat{r}1, \hat{r}2), and scaling \hat{S} = \text{diag}(\epsilon, \|v2 - v1\|, \langle v3 - v1, \hat{r}3 \rangle). The covariance is recovered as \hat{\Sigma} = \hat{R}\hat{S}\hat{S}^T\hat{R}^T. Gamba predicts Gaussian attributes using the recent Mamba network to better capture the relationship between Gaussians. Time Complexity: Feed-forward inference is significantly faster than per-scene optimization methods, which require minutes of gradient descent. The complexity is dominated by the sparse 3D CNN feature extraction and the MLP decoding per point. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the global point cloud P and the feature volume F. Measured Performance: EVolSplat achieves real-time rendering speeds for urban scenes. It improves global consistency and reduces ghosting artifacts compared to pixel-aligned methods like MVSplat, Flash3D, and DrivingForward. Strengths: Handles large-scale urban scenes with sparse inputs; reduces redundancy and ghosting artifacts; enables real-time rendering via feed-forward prediction. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimators; may lose high-frequency appearance details if primitives are downsampled too aggressively (addressed by IBR-based color prediction). When to Use: Urban view synthesis, autonomous driving applications, and scenarios requiring fast, feed-forward reconstruction from sparse views. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes with high overlap where per-scene optimization is feasible and higher fidelity is required; scenes with significant dynamic elements without temporal modeling. Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction, specifically in the form of EVolSplat, was introduced by Sheng Miao, Jiaxin Huang, Dongfeng Bai, Xu Yan, Hongyu Zhou, Yue Wang, Bingbing Liu, Andreas Geiger, and Yiyi Liao from Zhejiang University, Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab, and the University of Tübingen. The method was published in CVPR 2025. It addresses the limitations of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods that suffer from multi-view inconsistencies and duplicated content by predicting 3D Gaussians across multiple frames within a unified volume using a 3D convolutional network. name: GSGEN
head: 3D Point Cloud Guidance, G SGEN, GSGEN: A method introducing 3D SDS loss based on Point-E
body: GSGEN is a text-to-3D generation method that represents 3D content as a set of 3D Gaussians and optimizes them progressively in two stages: geometry optimization and appearance refinement, using 2D and 3D diffusion priors. It differs from NeRF-based methods (e.g., DreamFusion, Magic3D) by using explicit 3D Gaussians, which allows for the incorporation of direct 3D geometry priors and alleviates the Janus problem. It differs from DreamGaussian by focusing on incorporating 3D prior with more advanced representation, whereas DreamGaussian focuses on fast image-to-3D generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt y. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \{\theta\} representing the 3D asset, where \theta includes positions \mui, covariances \Sigmai, opacities oi, and colors ci for each Gaussian i. Data Structures: The method uses the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite). Opacity oi \in [0, 1]. Color ci (typically represented by spherical harmonics coefficients). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Use a text-to-point-cloud diffusion model (specifically Point-E) to generate a coarse 3D point cloud from the text prompt y. Initialize the positions \mui of the Gaussians with this coarse point cloud. The original adaptive control in Gaussian Splatting performs sub-optimally under SDS loss, necessitating the introduction of compactness-based densification. 2. Stage 1: Geometry Optimization: Optimize the Gaussians under the joint guidance of: 1. A 3D point cloud diffusion prior (from Point-E) via 3D SDS loss. 2. An ordinary 2D image prior (from StableDiffusion) via 2D SDS loss. This stage establishes a rough, 3D-consistent shape and corrects major shape deviations (e.g., asymmetric geometries like dogs or pandas). The gradient for Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) is calculated as: \nabla\theta L^{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{\epsilon, t} w(t)(\epsilon\phi (xt; y, t) - \epsilon) \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} where: \epsilon is Gaussian noise. w(t) is a weighting function. \epsilon\phi is the score estimation function from the diffusion model. xt is the noisy image. y is the text embedding. t is the timestep. x = g(\theta) is the rendered image. For the 3D SDS loss, the rendering function g(\theta) produces the rendered image x, which is processed by the Point-E diffusion model to compute the 3D prior gradient. 3. Stage 2: Appearance Refinement: Optimize the Gaussians to enrich delicate details using only the 2D image prior (StableDiffusion). Increase the number of Gaussians using compactness-based densification to enhance continuity and improve fidelity. The original densification strategy splits Gaussians with an average view-space gradient larger than a threshold T{pos}. Typical value for T{pos} in the original strategy: 0.0002. A variant with larger T{pos} = 0.02 avoids generating too many new Gaussians but may result in over-smoothed appearance. GSGEN uses compactness-based densification as a supplement to the original strategy to avoid the dilemma of unstable gradients under SDS guidance. Rendering Formula: The color C(p) of a point p on the image plane is rendered using point-based volume rendering: C(p) = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: N is the set of Gaussians sorted by depth in the tile. ci is the color of the i-th Gaussian. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian at point p. The opacity \alphai is defined as: \alphai = oi e^{-\frac{1}{2} (p-\mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (p-\mui)} where: oi is the base opacity. \mui is the position. \Sigmai is the covariance matrix. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def gsgen(textprompt, numgeosteps=1000, numappearsteps=2000, batchsize=4): # 1. Initialization pointcloud = pointegenerate(textprompt) gaussians = initializegaussiansfrompointcloud(pointcloud) # 2. Geometry Optimization Stage for step in range(numgeosteps): cameras = samplerandomcameras(batchsize) renderedimages = rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras) loss2d = calculate2dsdsloss(renderedimages, textprompt, stablediffusionmodel) projectedpcs = projecttopointcloud(gaussians, cameras) loss3d = calculate3dsdsloss(projectedpcs, textprompt, pointemodel) totalloss = loss2d + loss3d gaussians = updategaussians(gaussians, totalloss) # 3. Appearance Refinement Stage for step in range(numappearsteps): cameras = samplerandomcameras(batchsize) renderedimages = rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras) loss2d = calculate2dsdsloss(renderedimages, textprompt, stablediffusionmodel) gaussians = updategaussians(gaussians, loss2d) gaussians = densifygaussianscompactness(gaussians) return gaussians def pointegenerate(prompt): # Returns a numpy array of shape (N, 3) representing a coarse 3D point cloud return np.random.randn(1000, 3) 2.0 def initializegaussiansfrompointcloud(pc): # Initializes Gaussian positions from pc, sets default covariances, opacities, colors positions = pc.copy() covariances = np.repeat(np.eye(3), len(positions), axis=0).reshape(-1, 3, 3) opacities = np.ones(len(positions)) 0.5 colors = np.random.rand(len(positions), 3) return {"positions": positions, "covariances": covariances, "opacities": opacities, "colors": colors} def samplerandomcameras(batchsize): # Returns a list of camera extrinsics and intrinsics return [{"extrinsics": np.eye(4), "intrinsics": np.eye(3)} for in range(batchsize)] def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras): # Differentiable volume rendering returning image tensor and gradient hook # Computes C(p) = sum(ci alphai prod(1 - alphaj)) return np.random.rand(4, 3, 256, 256) def stablediffusionmodel(): # Returns a callable that predicts noise epsilonphi(xt; y, t) return lambda xt, y, t: np.random.randn(xt.shape) def pointemodel(): # Returns a callable that predicts noise for point cloud diffusion return lambda xt, y, t: np.random.randn(xt.shape) def calculate2dsdsloss(renderedimages, textprompt, diffusionmodel): loss = 0.0 for image in renderedimages: t = sampletimestep() epsilon = samplegaussiannoise(image.shape) xt = addnoise(image, epsilon, t) predictedepsilon = diffusionmodel(xt, textprompt, t) wt = 1.0 - t # Example weighting function gradient = wt (predictedepsilon - epsilon) # dx/dtheta is obtained via backprop through rendergaussians loss += np.sum(gradient rendergradient(image)) return loss / len(renderedimages) def calculate3dsdsloss(projectedpcs, textprompt, pointemodel): loss = 0.0 for pc in projectedpcs: t = sampletimestep() epsilon = samplegaussiannoise(pc.shape) pct = addnoise(pc, epsilon, t) predictedepsilon = pointemodel(pct, textprompt, t) wt = 1.0 - t gradient = wt (predictedepsilon - epsilon) loss += np.sum(gradient pointcloudgradient(pc)) return loss / len(projectedpcs) def updategaussians(gaussians, loss): # Applies gradient descent to Gaussian parameters return gaussians def sampletimestep(): return np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) def samplegaussiannoise(shape): return np.random.randn(shape) def addnoise(x, epsilon, t): return np.sqrt(1 - t) x + np.sqrt(t) epsilon def projecttopointcloud(gaussians, cameras): # Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D/3D point cloud representation for 3D prior return [gaussians["positions"] for in cameras] def rendergradient(image): # Placeholder for differentiable renderer gradient computation return np.zeroslike(image) def pointcloudgradient(pc): # Placeholder for point cloud diffusion gradient computation return np.zeroslike(pc) def densifygaussianscompactness(gaussians): # Compactness-based densification strategy positions = gaussians["positions"] covariances = gaussians["covariances"] # Check compactness metric and split/copy Gaussians if too spread newpositions = np.vstack([positions, positions + np.random.randn(positions.shape) 0.1]) newcovariances = np.vstack([covariances, covariances]) newopacities = np.concatenate([gaussians["opacities"], gaussians["opacities"]]) newcolors = np.vstack([gaussians["colors"], gaussians["colors"]]) return {"positions": newpositions, "covariances": newcovariances, "opacities": newopacities, "colors": newcolors} Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: GSGEN generates 3D assets with delicate details and accurate geometry, demonstrating superior performance in capturing high-frequency components. It effectively addresses asymmetric geometries (e.g., dog, panda) and collapsed structures better than methods without 3D priors. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Alleviates the Janus problem (inaccurate geometry/multi-face issue) common in NeRF-based methods. Generates highly detailed and 3D consistent assets. Explicit 3D representation allows direct incorporation of 3D geometry priors. Limitations: Tends to generate unsatisfying results when the text prompt contains complex descriptions or complicated logic due to the limited language understanding ability of Point-E and the CLIP text encoder used in StableDiffusion. The Janus problem is mitigated but not entirely eliminated; potential degenerations can still occur, especially when the textual prompt is extremely biased in the guidance diffusion models. The original adaptive control in Gaussian Splatting performs sub-optimally under SDS loss, requiring the custom compactness-based densification. When to use: Text-to-3D generation requiring high fidelity and 3D consistency, especially for asymmetric objects. When not to use: Prompts with complex logic or detailed scene descriptions that exceed the language understanding capabilities of Point-E and StableDiffusion. Origin: GSGEN was proposed in the paper "Text-to-3D using Gaussian Splatting". History: It builds upon the success of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) introduced by DreamFusion and the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It specifically addresses the limitations of implicit representations (NeRF) in integrating 3D priors. Usage: Used in GSGEN for text-to-3D generation. It utilizes StableDiffusion as the 2D image prior and Point-E as the 3D point cloud diffusion prior. name: Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Canonical Space and Deformation Field, Deformable-GS, Deformable3DGS (Yang et al.), Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (Canonical Space + Deformation Field), Implicit Deformation Modeling, SurgicalGaussian, Yang et al
body: Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting is a method for dynamic scene reconstruction that represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians in a static canonical space, with temporal and spatial deformations modeled by an implicit deformation field implemented as a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). It solves the problem of reconstructing time-varying volumetric scenes by decoupling the static geometry from the motion, allowing for real-time rendering of dynamic content. It sets itself apart from siblings like GSGEN or Fourier Splatting Primitive by explicitly learning a continuous deformation field to map canonical attributes to observation-space attributes at any timestep, rather than storing explicit trajectories or using frequency-based parameterizations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of T frames, where each frame i consists of an image Ii, a depth map Di, and a binary mask Mi (indicating occlusions or objects to exclude, such as surgical tools). Camera poses Ki (intrinsic) and Ei (extrinsic) are required for initialization. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{C}i and depth \hat{D}i for any timestep t \in [0, 1], and the optimized canonical Gaussian parameters and deformation field weights. Data Structures: 1. Canonical Gaussians (Gc): A list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian Gc stores: \muc \in \mathbb{R}^3: Spatial mean (position). qc \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. sc \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling vector. c \in \mathbb{R}^k: View-dependent color (typically SH coefficients). \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. Note: Color and opacity are typically static in the canonical space for this method. 2. Deformation Field (F\Theta): An MLP with parameters \Theta. Architecture: 8 hidden layers, width 256. Input: Concatenation of positional encoding of \muc and normalized time t. Output: Offsets \delta x \in \mathbb{R}^3, \delta s \in \mathbb{R}^3, \delta q \in \mathbb{R}^4. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize canonical positions \muc and colors c using the GIDM (Geometry Initialization from Depth Maps) strategy. Project refined depth/mask data into 3D space to create a point cloud P^. P^ = \{ De Ki^{-1} (I \odot (1 - M)) \}, where M = \bigcap{i=0}^T Mi is the intersection of tool masks (regions occluded in all frames). Initialize rotation qc and scale sc using standard 3DGS SfM initialization or random initialization. 2. Deformation Prediction (Forward Mapping): For a target timestep t \in [0, 1] (normalized from frame index i as t = i/T): Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the canonical position \muc and time t. Compute offsets: (\delta x, \delta s, \delta q) = F\Theta([\gamma(\muc), \gamma(t)]). To improve temporal smoothing, add linearly decaying Gaussian noise to the encoded time vector before inputting to the MLP. 3. Attribute Transformation to Observation Space: Compute deformed attributes for observation space: Position: \muo = \muc + \delta x. Scale: so = sc \cdot \exp(\delta s). Rotation: qo = qc \cdot \delta q (quaternion multiplication). Color and Opacity remain unchanged: co = c, \alphao = \alpha. 4. Rendering: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D image plane. Compute 3D covariance \Sigma = R S S^T R^T from qo and so. Compute 2D covariance \Sigma' using the viewing transformation V and Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transformation: \Sigma' = J V \Sigma V^T J^T. Render color \hat{C}(r) and depth \hat{D}(r) for pixel r by blending N sorted Gaussians: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i \in N} \alphai' \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj') \right) ci \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i \in N} \alphai' \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj') \right) di where \alphai' = \alphai Gi'(r) is the opacity weighted by the projected 2D Gaussian probability density at pixel r, and di is the depth of the i-th Gaussian. 5. Optimization (Loss Functions): Minimize the total loss L using Adam optimizer: L = (L{color} + \lambda1 L{ssim} + \lambda2 L{depth}) + (\lambda3 L{pos} + \lambda4 L{cov} + \lambda5 L{smooth}). Reconstruction Losses: Color: L{color} = (Ii - \hat{C}i)(1 - Mi). Depth: L{depth} = (Di - \hat{D}i)(1 - Mi). SSIM: L{ssim} = 1 - SSIM(Ii, \hat{C}i). Note: Masks Mi are inverted to select soft tissues (regions not occluded by tools). Regularization Losses: Position Consistency (L{pos}): For each Gaussian Gi, find K=5 nearest neighbors. Constrain the difference in Euclidean distances between canonical and observation spaces: L{pos} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \| \|xo^{(i)} - xo^{(k)}\|2 - \|xc^{(i)} - xc^{(k)}\|2 \|2^2. Covariance Consistency (L{cov}): Similar to L{pos} but for covariance matrices \Sigma: L{cov} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \| \|\Sigmao^{(i)} - \Sigmao^{(k)}\|2 - \|\Sigmac^{(i)} - \Sigmac^{(k)}\|2 \|2^2. Color Smoothness (L{smooth}): Applied to regions M^ (occluded in all frames) to prevent holes: L{smooth} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{p,q} (\|C{p,q} - C{p-1,q}\|2^2 + \|C{p,q} - C{p,q-1}\|2^2) where C = \hat{C}i \odot M^, and n is the number of pixels in C. Parameters: \lambda1 = 0.2 (SSIM weight). \lambda2 = 0.001 (Depth weight). \lambda3 = 1 (Position regularization weight). \lambda4 = 200 (Covariance regularization weight). \lambda5 = 0.02 (Color smoothness weight). Initial learning rate for deformation network: 1.5 \times 10^{-5}. Training iterations: 40,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inaccurate Poses: Discrete 3DGS amplifies pose errors compared to continuous NeRFs, especially during time interpolation. Single-View Under-constraint: Single-view inputs lead to noisy deformations. Occluded Regions: Gaussians in areas occluded by instruments in all frames (M^) are hard to optimize, causing holes. Predicts all Gaussian parameters via shallow MLPs conditioned on a control parameter, replacing explicit storage with learned functions for context translation and stylization. Uses voxelization and sparse convolutions for geometry-aware deformation learning. Uses frequency-based parameterizations for dynamic attributes. Uses conditional mechanisms for dynamic scene representation. Incorporates structural awareness into Gaussian deformation. Embeds Gaussians into mesh structures for deformation. Uses inverse mapping for deformation. Factorizes occupancy and opacity for dynamic scenes. Integrates semantic mapping with Gaussian generation. Extends geometry and orientation handling. Uses voxel/grid-based prediction for deformation. Represents Gaussians functionally. Focuses on volumetric rendering techniques. Combines multiple representations. Uses plenoptic sampling for construction. Guides generation with geometry. Enhances optical and attribute properties. Focuses on sampling and initialization. Transitions from wavelets to Gaussians. Efficient Adaptive 3D Gaussian Splatting. Uses hard prediction for attributes. Uses hard depth anchors for generation. Time Complexity: Rendering is real-time, comparable to static 3DGS, with overhead from the deformation MLP. Memory Complexity: The deformation field reduces memory from O(N^3 T) to O(Rs N^2 + Rs N + Rt T) if using low-rank decomposition, but standard MLP implementation stores weights independent of N and T. Performance: On RTX 3090, achieves \ge 80 FPS with \le 4 GB GPU memory. Quality: Outperforms NeRF-based methods (EndoNeRF, LerPlane, EndoSurf) in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on surgical datasets. On D-NeRF, achieves PSNR 39.51, SSIM 0.990, LPIPS 0.012. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high-fidelity reconstruction of dynamic scenes, ability to remove occlusions (e.g., surgical tools). Limitations: Sensitive to inaccurate camera poses. Single-view inputs require strong regularization to avoid noisy deformations. Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by W. Xie et al. in the paper "SurgicalGaussian: Deformable 3D Gaussians for High-Fidelity Surgical Scene Reconstruction". It builds on the original 3D Gaussian Splatting [8] and extends it to dynamic scenes by incorporating a deformation field, similar to dynamic NeRF approaches. It is primarily used for high-fidelity reconstruction of dynamic surgical scenes, robot-assisted surgery, and intelligent medical care.
