name: Shape-Shifting Splats
head: Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting
body: Shape-Shifting Splats predicts all 3D Gaussian parameters via shallow, fully-connected MLPs conditioned on a control parameter, allowing all attributes to change at render time. It builds on Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting and Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization by replacing explicit storage of scale, rotation, offset, and opacity with learned functions, enabling context translation and stylization without retraining scene geometry. Inputs: Posed images (RGB, thermal, or stylized) and a sparse input point cloud derived via a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipeline such as COLMAP. Outputs: Rendered images via tile-based rasterization. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a set of anchors. For each anchor v: av \in \mathbb{R}^3: Anchor point position. fa \in \mathbb{R}^{32}: Anchor feature vector. MLP weights: Separate shallow, fully-connected MLPs for scale, rotation, offset, color, and opacity. Control encoding parameters: \sigma (standard deviation), s (sampling interval), d (embedding dimension). Voxel scaling lv \in \mathbb{R}^3 and k offsets o{kv} \in \mathbb{R}^3 are not stored; they are predicted by dedicated MLPs. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the scene with a sparse input point cloud derived via an SfM pipeline such as COLMAP. 2. Voxelization: Separate the scene into voxels. Each voxel is associated with one anchor point av, one feature vector fa, a voxel scaling parameter lv \in \mathbb{R}^3, and k offsets o{kv} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The feature-bank implementation of Scaffold-GS is omitted to avoid training instability. 3. Control Encoding: Define a control parameter x \in \mathbb{R} to encode the current modality or style (e.g., x=0 for RGB, x=1 for thermal). Map x to a higher-dimensional embedding space via a d-dimensional encoding \Psi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^d using a 1D Gaussian embedder: \psi(t, x) = \exp\left(-\frac{\|t - x\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \Psi(x) = [\psi(0, x), \psi(s, x), \dots, \psi((d - 1)s, x)]^\top where t is the sampling point, \sigma is the standard deviation, and s is the sampling interval. 4. Viewing Direction: For each anchor av and camera position xc, compute the viewing direction vector \delta{xc, av}: \delta{xc, av} = \frac{av - xc}{\|av - xc\|2}. 5. Parameter Prediction: Predict each Gaussian parameter using respective shallow, fully-connected MLPs. The inputs to the MLPs are the anchor features fa, the control encoding \Psi(x), and (for color only) the viewing direction \delta{xc, av}. Color: c = F{\text{color}}(fa \oplus \delta{xc, av} \oplus \Psi(x)), where F{\text{color}} is the color MLP and \oplus denotes concatenation. Position: \mu = av + o{kv} lv, where \mu is the Gaussian position, o{kv} is the offset, and lv is the voxel scaling parameter. Two additional shallow, fully-connected MLPs predict lv and o{kv}. Covariance: The covariance matrix \Sigma is parameterized by a scaling matrix S and a rotation matrix R: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. Opacity: Predicted by the opacity MLP. Each anchor feature fa predicts k Gaussians, with k=10 in the original Scaffold-GS implementation. 6. Rendering: Perform the standard 3DGS workflow. Render images via tile-based rasterization. The final color cp at pixel p is calculated by alpha-blending N sorted Gaussians in the view frustum: cp = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci and \alphai are the color and opacity of Gaussian i, and j < i. 7. Pruning: Prune anchors if Gaussians spawned by them do not contribute to the scene, using anchor-wise opacity and view thresholds. 8. Stylization (Optional): To change style, apply a stylization loss using CLIP features. Compute direction loss \Delta T from style source S (text prompt or image) and reference "A Photo": \Delta T = \Phi{\text{CLIP}}(S) - \Phi{\text{CLIP}}(\text{"A Photo"}). Compute image loss \Delta I from rendered image patch \hat{I}{Rn} and ground truth I{GT}: \Delta I = \Phi{\text{CLIP}}(R(\hat{I}{Rn})) - \Phi{\text{CLIP}}(I{GT}) where R(\cdot) denotes random cropping and perspective distortion. Calculate cosine distance pn = D(\Delta T, \Delta I) and loss L{\text{CLIP}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum pn. Pass a segmentation mask to exclude certain parts from stylization; loss is only calculated on pixels outside the mask. Apply background loss L{BG} (L1 distance between background pixels of rendered image and GT image) as additional regularization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianembedder(t, x, sigma): """1D Gaussian embedder psi(t, x).""" return np.exp(-np.square(t - x) / (2 sigma2)) def computecontrolencoding(x, d, s, sigma): """Compute d-dimensional control encoding Psi(x).""" tvalues = np.arange(d) s return np.array([gaussianembedder(t, x, sigma) for t in tvalues]) def computeviewingdirection(anchor, camerapos): """Compute viewing direction deltaxcav.""" diff = anchor - camerapos return diff / np.linalg.norm(diff) def predictgaussianparameters(anchorfeatures, controlencoding, viewingdirection, mlps): """Predict Gaussian parameters using MLPs.""" colorinput = np.concatenate([anchorfeatures, viewingdirection, controlencoding]) color = mlps'color' baseinput = np.concatenate([anchorfeatures, controlencoding]) scale = mlps'scale' rotation = mlps'rotation' offset = mlps'offset' opacity = mlps'opacity' return color, scale, rotation, offset, opacity def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameraparams, imageshape): """Render images via tile-based rasterization.""" projected = projectto2d(gaussians, cameraparams) sortedindices = sortbydepth(projected) alphablend = np.zeros(imageshape[:2]) for i in sortedindices: g = gaussians[i] alphablend = alphablend (1 - g.alpha) + g.color g.alpha return alphablend def computeregularization(opacities, scales, lambdaalpha, lambdaS): """Compute Lreg = (lambdaalpha/N) sum(|alphai|) + (lambdaS/N) sum(mean(|Si|)).""" N = len(opacities) term1 = (lambdaalpha / N) np.sum(np.abs(opacities)) term2 = (lambdaS / N) np.sum(np.mean(np.abs(scales), axis=1)) return term1 + term2 def computessim(rendered, groundtruth): """Compute SSIM similarity term.""" # Standard structural similarity calculation return 1.0 - ssim(rendered, groundtruth) def trainstep(images, gtimages, anchors, mlps, controlencoding, lossweights): """Training step including L3DGS, Lreg, and optional LCLIP.""" predictedgaussians = [] opacities = [] scales = [] for anchor in anchors: viewingdir = computeviewingdirection(anchor.pos, cameraparams.pos) c, s, r, o, alpha = predictgaussianparameters(anchor.features, controlencoding, viewingdir, mlps) predictedgaussians.append({'mu': anchor.pos + o anchor.scale, 'Sigma': r @ np.diag(s) @ r.T, 'alpha': alpha, 'color': c}) opacities.append(alpha) scales.append(s) renderedimages = rendergaussians(predictedgaussians, cameraparams, imageshape) l1loss = np.mean(np.abs(renderedimages - gtimages)) ssimloss = computessim(renderedimages, gtimages) l3dgs = lossweights['lambda3dgs'] l1loss + (1 - lossweights['lambda3dgs']) ssimloss lreg = computeregularization(opacities, scales, lossweights['lambdaalpha'], lossweights['lambdaS']) totalloss = l3dgs + lreg if stylizationrequired: deltaT = phiclip(stylesource) - phiclip("A Photo") deltaI = phiclip(randomcropperspective(renderedimages)) - phiclip(gtimages) pn = cosinedistance(deltaT, deltaI) lclip = np.mean(pn) totalloss += lclip return totalloss Parameters: k: Number of offsets per voxel, set to k = 10. \sigma: Standard deviation of the Gaussian embedder. s: Sampling interval of the Gaussian embedder. d: Dimensionality of the control encoding. \lambda{3DGS}: Weight for L1 loss in the 3DGS loss function. \lambda\alpha: Hyperparameter for opacity regularization. \lambdaS: Hyperparameter for scale regularization. \Phi{\text{CLIP}}: CLIP encoder. R(\cdot): Random cropping and perspective distortion applied to the rendered image. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Instability: The feature-bank implementation of Scaffold-GS is omitted because it introduced instability during training. Interpolation: Using 1D Gaussian embedders allows interpolation between encodings, avoiding the issue where encodings far apart in input space might be closer in embedded space (as seen in frequency encoding). Inference: During inference, only the forward flow is necessary. The color MLP must be re-evaluated whenever the viewing angle shifts, while other MLPs predict k parameters per anchor and do not require per-viewing-direction inference. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Memory requirements are significantly reduced compared to storing all Gaussian parameters explicitly, as only anchor positions, corresponding features, and MLP weights need to be stored. Performance: Demonstrated on VR devices such as Meta Quest 2, Meta Quest 3, and Apple Vision Pro, where computational limits are reached early. Strengths: Allows changing all attributes of 3D Gaussians at render time; reduces memory requirements; enables context translation and stylization. Limitations: Requires MLP inference for each Gaussian parameter at render time; color MLP must be re-evaluated for every viewing direction. When to use: When dynamic context translation (e.g., RGB to thermal) or stylization is required, and memory/compute constraints on devices like VR headsets are a concern. When not to use: When static scene representation is sufficient and MLP inference overhead is unacceptable. Shape-Shifting Splats builds on 3DGS and Scaffold-GS. It addresses the computational limits of VR devices by reducing resource usage while maintaining visual quality. Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Fourier Splatting Primitive
head: Fourier encoded primitive, Fourier surfel
body: The Fourier Splatting primitive is a planar surfel for radiance field rendering that replaces the fixed Gaussian or elliptical falloff with a boundary defined by a Fourier series, allowing the representation of arbitrary closed shapes. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) or 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which are limited to fixed elliptical or disc shapes, this primitive enables higher fidelity representation of complex geometry and fine-grained details. Its key differentiator is inherent scalability: the level of detail (LoD) is controlled by truncating Fourier coefficients at runtime, allowing a single trained model to be rendered at varying complexities without retraining or post-hoc compression. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera parameters (view/projection matrices), a set of primitives \{si\}, and a target resolution. Output: A rendered image with color and opacity per pixel. Data Structures Each primitive si is parameterized by the following fields: 1. Center: pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Rotation: qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion) defining the local tangent frame (tu, tv, tw). 3. Opacity: oi \in (0, 1). 4. Appearance: ci \in \mathbb{R}^{48} (Spherical Harmonics coefficients, degree 3). 5. Circumradius: Ri \in \mathbb{R}{>0}, bounding the primitive extent. 6. Fourier Amplitudes: \{r{i,k}\}{k=0}^{K-1} \in \mathbb{R}^K. 7. Fourier Phases: \{\phi{i,k}\}{k=0}^{K-1} \in \mathbb{R}. 8. Sharpness: \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}{>0}. Parameters K: Number of Fourier frequencies. Typical value: 6. K{\text{active}}: Number of active frequency components at the start of optimization. Typical value: 1. Formulas The boundary of the primitive in its local tangent plane is a closed curve ri(\theta). To ensure the boundary does not exceed the circumradius Ri, the raw amplitudes r{i,k} are normalized using squared-\ell1 normalization: \bar{r}{i,k} = \frac{r{i,k}^2}{\sum{k'=0}^{K-1} r{i,k'}^2} \quad \text{such that} \quad \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \bar{r}{i,k} = 1 This guarantees ri(\theta) \le Ri for all \theta. The boundary radius ri(\theta) is computed efficiently using Horner’s method to avoid transcendental calls for e^{ik\theta}. Let w = e^{i\theta} = (\cos \theta, \sin \theta). The complex coefficients c{i,k} are derived from the normalized amplitudes and phases as c{i,k} = \bar{r}{i,k} e^{i \phi{i,k}}. The recurrence is computed from k = K-1 down to 0: z{K-1} = c{i,K-1} z{k} = z{k+1} \cdot w + c{i,k} \quad \text{for } k = K-2, \dots, 0 The final radius is: ri(\theta) = Ri |z0| This requires K-1 complex multiply-adds. Numbered Steps 1. Ray-Plane Intersection: For each pixel, compute the intersection with the primitive's plane defined by pi and normal tw. Transform the intersection point into the local tangent frame (tu, tv) to obtain coordinates (uj, vj). 2. Polar Conversion: Compute the polar coordinates (\rhoj, \thetaj) in the tangent plane. \rhoj = \sqrt{uj^2 + vj^2} \cos \thetaj = uj / \rhoj \sin \thetaj = vj / \rhoj Handle \rhoj \approx 0 by setting \thetaj = 0 to avoid division by zero. 3. Boundary Evaluation: Compute ri(\thetaj) using the Horner’s method recurrence defined above. 4. Signed Distance: Compute the signed distance \varphij from the pixel to the boundary: \varphij = \rhoj - ri(\thetaj) 5. Alpha Compositing: Use a power window function (adapted from Triangle Splatting) based on \varphij and the sharpness parameter \sigmai to determine the alpha value for the primitive at this pixel. 6. Color Evaluation: Evaluate the spherical harmonics using the view direction to get the color contribution. 7. Rendering: Composite the primitives tile-by-tile using standard alpha blending. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Converts a unit quaternion (x, y, z, w) to a 3x3 rotation matrix.""" x, y, z, w = q return [ [1 - 2yy - 2zz, 2xy - 2zw, 2xz + 2yw], [2xy + 2zw, 1 - 2xx - 2zz, 2yz - 2xw], [2xz - 2yw, 2yz + 2xw, 1 - 2xx - 2yy] ] def evaluatesh(csh, viewdir): """Evaluates degree-3 Spherical Harmonics (48 coefficients) for a view direction.""" x, y, z = viewdir xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, yz, xz = xy, yz, xz x2 = xx - yy y2 = yy - zz z2 = 3zz - 1 r = 0.2820948csh[0] + 0.4886025(csh[1]y + csh[2]z + csh[3]x) + \ 1.0925484(csh[4]yz + csh[5]xz + csh[6]x2 + csh[7]xy + csh[8]0.5z2) g = 0.2820948csh[9] + 0.4886025(csh[10]y + csh[11]z + csh[12]x) + \ 1.0925484(csh[13]yz + csh[14]xz + csh[15]x2 + csh[16]xy + csh[17]0.5z2) b = 0.2820948csh[18] + 0.4886025(csh[19]y + csh[20]z + csh[21]x) + \ 1.0925484(csh[22]yz + csh[23]xz + csh[24]x2 + csh[25]xy + csh[26]0.5z2) return (r, g, b) def computeprimitivealphaandcolor(pi, qi, oi, csh, Ri, rraw, phiraw, sigmai, K, rayorigin, raydir, imgwidth, imgheight): """ Evaluates a single Fourier Splatting primitive over a pixel grid. Returns alpha and color contribution arrays. """ # Extract local frame Rmat = quaterniontorotationmatrix(qi) tu = Rmat[0] tv = Rmat[1] tw = Rmat[2] alphagrid = [0.0] (imgheight imgwidth) colorgrid = [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] (imgheight imgwidth) # Precompute normalization sumsq = sum(r2 for r in rraw) if sumsq == 0: return alphagrid, colorgrid rnorm = [r2 / sumsq for r in rraw] # Precompute complex coefficients c{i,k} = rnorm[k] exp(i phiraw[k]) creal = [rnorm[k] math.cos(phiraw[k]) for k in range(K)] cimag = [rnorm[k] math.sin(phiraw[k]) for k in range(K)] for y in range(imgheight): for x in range(imgwidth): # 1. Ray-Plane Intersection denom = tw[0]raydir[0] + tw[1]raydir[1] + tw[2]raydir[2] if abs(denom) < 1e-6: continue t = ((pi[0] - rayorigin[0])tw[0] + (pi[1] - rayorigin[1])tw[1] + (pi[2] - rayorigin[2])tw[2]) / denom if t < 0: continue ix = rayorigin[0] + t raydir[0] iy = rayorigin[1] + t raydir[1] iz = rayorigin[2] + t raydir[2] # 2. Local Tangent Coordinates vecx = ix - pi[0] vecy = iy - pi[1] vecz = iz - pi[2] uj = vecxtu[0] + vecytu[1] + vecztu[2] vj = vecxtv[0] + vecytv[1] + vecztv[2] # 3. Polar Conversion rhoj = math.sqrt(ujuj + vjvj) if rhoj < 1e-6: thetaj = 0.0 costheta = 1.0 sintheta = 0.0 else: thetaj = math.atan2(vj, uj) costheta = uj / rhoj sintheta = vj / rhoj # 4. Horner's Method for Boundary zreal = creal[K-1] zimag = cimag[K-1] for k in range(K-2, -1, -1): newreal = zreal costheta - zimag sintheta newimag = zreal sintheta + zimag costheta zreal = newreal + creal[k] zimag = newimag + cimag[k] rboundary = Ri math.sqrt(zrealzreal + zimagzimag) # 5. Signed Distance signeddist = rhoj - rboundary # 6. Alpha Calculation (Power Window) if signeddist > 0: alpha = 0.0 else: alpha = max(0.0, 1.0 - (signeddist / sigmai)2)2 if alpha < 1e-4: continue # 7. Color Evaluation viewdirlocal = ( tu[0]raydir[0] + tu[1]raydir[1] + tu[2]raydir[2], tv[0]raydir[0] + tv[1]raydir[1] + tv[2]raydir[2], tw[0]raydir[0] + tw[1]raydir[1] + tw[2]raydir[2]) color = evaluatesh(csh, viewdirlocal) idx = y imgwidth + x alphagrid[idx] += alpha oi colorgrid[idx] = ( colorgrid[idx][0] + color[0] alpha oi, colorgrid[idx][1] + color[1] alpha oi, colorgrid[idx][2] + color[2] alpha oi) return alphagrid, colorgrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls Ray-Plane Intersection: For each pixel, compute the intersection with the primitive's plane defined by pi and normal tw. Division by Zero: When computing \thetaj, if \rhoj \approx 0, \cos \thetaj and \sin \thetaj are undefined. Overshooting: Without squared-\ell1 normalization, amplitudes can sum to exceed Ri, causing the boundary to overshoot the circumscribed circle. Optimization Stability: The optimization process begins with K{\text{active}} = 1 to establish a stable global structure. Time Complexity: The boundary evaluation uses Horner’s method, requiring K-1 complex multiply-adds, which is O(K) per pixel per primitive. With K=6, this is constant and fast. Memory Complexity: Each primitive stores K amplitudes and K phases. With K=6 and degree 3 SH (48 coeffs), plus center, quaternion, opacity, and radius, the parameter count is 70 per primitive. Scalability: The method is inherently scalable. Rendering at lower LoD is achieved by truncating Fourier coefficients at runtime (e.g., using only k < K{\text{active}}) without retraining. Strengths: Arbitrary shape representation allows higher fidelity for complex geometry compared to 2D/3D Gaussians. Continuous LoD control. Limitations: Requires careful initialization (K{\text{active}}=1) to avoid optimization instability. The Fourier Splatting primitive was introduced in "Fourier Splatting: Generalized Fourier encoded primitives for scalable radiance fields". It addresses the limitation of existing methods where visual fidelity is tied strictly to the number of primitives, requiring pruning for quality downscaling. It builds on the concept of planar surfels (like 2DGS) but enhances expressiveness with Fourier-encoded boundaries. Fourier Splatting: Generalized Fourier encoded primitives for scalable radiance fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.19834, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Conditional Slicing Mechanism
body: The Conditional Slicing Mechanism conditions a 7-dimensional Gaussian on observed time t and view direction d to yield a conditional 3D Gaussian governing the spatial component. This operation "slices" the full 7D distribution to integrate temporal dynamics and view-dependent effects into the traditional 3D rendering pipeline without introducing additional temporal dependencies in the spherical harmonics. It sets itself apart from static Gaussian Splatting variants by explicitly modeling the joint distribution of space, time, and view, allowing the spatial mean and covariance to shift based on the current rendering context. Inputs: Base Gaussian parameters: spatial mean \mup, temporal mean \mut, directional mean \mud, base opacity \alpha, scaling factors \lambdat, \lambdad. Covariance structure: Lower-triangular matrix L such that \Sigma = LL^\top, or the partitioned blocks \Sigma{(t,d)}, \Sigma{p,(t,d)}, \Sigmap. Context variables: Observed time t, view direction d. Optional refinement features: Feature vector f (if adaptive refinement is applied). Outputs: Conditional spatial mean \mu{cond}. Conditional spatial covariance \Sigma{cond}. Conditional opacity \alpha{cond}. Optional: Scale S and Rotation R extracted from \Sigma{cond} for densification. Data Structures: The 7D Gaussian is represented by a mean vector \mu = [\mup, \mut, \mud] and a 7 \times 7 covariance matrix \Sigma. The matrix is partitioned into blocks corresponding to spatial (p), temporal (t), and directional (d) dimensions: \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \Sigmap & \Sigma{p,(t,d)}^\top \\ \Sigma{p,(t,d)} & \Sigma{(t,d)} \end{bmatrix} where \Sigma{(t,d)} is the 4 \times 4 block for time and direction: \Sigma{(t,d)} = \begin{bmatrix} \Sigmat & \Sigma{td} \\ \Sigma{td}^\top & \Sigmad \end{bmatrix} and \Sigma{p,(t,d)} = [\Sigma{pt} \quad \Sigma{pd}] links spatial dimensions with the combined temporal-directional space. Steps: 1. Adaptive Gaussian Refinement (Optional but standard in implementation): Compute a feature vector f by concatenating the means and a temporal encoding \gamma(t): f = \text{concat}(\mup, \mut, \mud, \gamma(t)) Apply refinement functions \phip, \phit, \phid, \phil to update the parameters: \hat{\mu}p = \mup + \phip(f), \quad \hat{\mu}t = \mut + \phit(f) \hat{\mu}d = \mud + \phid(f), \quad \hat{l} = l + \phil(f) Reconstruct the refined covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} = \hat{L}\hat{L}^\top. Note: If refinement is skipped, replace \hat{\mu} and \hat{\Sigma} with \mu and \Sigma. 2. Partition the Covariance: Partition \hat{\Sigma} into blocks \hat{\Sigma}p, \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}, and \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} as defined above. 3. Compute Conditional Mean: Calculate the conditional spatial mean \mu{cond} using the standard multivariate Gaussian conditioning formula: \mu{cond} = \hat{\mu}p + \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} t - \hat{\mu}t \\ d - \hat{\mu}d \end{bmatrix} The term \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}^{-1} acts as a correction that shifts the spatial mean according to deviations in time and view direction from their expected values. 4. Compute Conditional Covariance: Calculate the conditional spatial covariance \Sigma{cond}: \Sigma{cond} = \hat{\Sigma}p - \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)} \hat{\Sigma}{(t,d)}^{-1} \hat{\Sigma}{p,(t,d)}^\top This adjusts the spatial uncertainty by removing the variance explained by the temporal and directional components. 5. Compute Modulation Factors: Compute the temporal modulation factor f{temp}: f{temp} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \lambdat (t - \hat{\mu}t)^2 \hat{\Sigma}t^{-1}\right) Compute the directional modulation factor f{dir}: f{dir} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \lambdad (d - \hat{\mu}d)^\top \hat{\Sigma}d^{-1} (d - \hat{\mu}d)\right) Here, \lambdat and \lambdad are positive scalar parameters controlling sensitivity. 6. Compute Conditional Opacity: Combine the base opacity \alpha with the modulation factors: \alpha{cond} = \alpha \cdot f{temp} \cdot f{dir} This ensures Gaussians contribute less when the current time or view direction is far from their expected values. 7. Extract Scale and Rotation (Optional): For densification steps, perform SVD on \Sigma{cond} = U D U^\top. Extract scale S = \text{diag}(D) and rotation R = U. Adjust R to ensure \det(R) > 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gamma(t): # Standard positional encoding for time return np.array([np.sin(t), np.cos(t)]) def phip(f): return np.zeroslike(mup) # MLP from parent model def phit(f): return np.zeroslike(mut) # MLP from parent model def phid(f): return np.zeroslike(mud) # MLP from parent model def phil(f): return np.zeroslike(L) # MLP from parent model def conditionalslicing(mup, mut, mud, alpha, L, lambdat, lambdad, t, d, applyrefinement=True): """ Conditions a 7D Gaussian on time t and view direction d. Args: mup: Spatial mean (3,) mut: Temporal mean (scalar) mud: Directional mean (3,) alpha: Base opacity (scalar) L: Lower triangular matrix (7,7) such that Sigma = L @ L.T lambdat: Temporal sensitivity scalar lambdad: Directional sensitivity scalar t: Observed time (scalar) d: View direction (3,) applyrefinement: Boolean flag for adaptive refinement Returns: mucond: Conditional spatial mean (3,) Sigmacond: Conditional spatial covariance (3,3) alphacond: Conditional opacity (scalar) S: Scale (3,) - optional, for densification R: Rotation (3,3) - optional, for densification """ # Step 1: Adaptive Refinement (if enabled) if applyrefinement: # Compute feature vector f f = np.concatenate([mup, [mut], mud, gamma(t)]) # Apply refinement functions phi deltamup = phip(f) deltamut = phit(f) deltamud = phid(f) deltal = phil(f) mup = mup + deltamup mut = mut + deltamut mud = mud + deltamud L = L + deltal # Reconstruct Sigma from L Sigma = L @ L.T # Step 2: Partition Sigma # Dimensions: p=3, t=1, d=3. Total 7. Sigmap = Sigma[:3,:3] Sigmapt = Sigma[:3, 3:4] Sigmapd = Sigma[:3, 4:7] Sigmat = Sigma[3:4, 3:4] Sigmatd = Sigma[4:7, 3:4] Sigmad = Sigma[4:7, 4:7] # Construct blocks Sigmaptd = np.hstack([Sigmapt, Sigmapd]) # (3, 4) Sigmatdt = Sigmat # (1, 1) Sigmatdd = Sigmatd # (3, 1) Sigmadd = Sigmad # (3, 3) # Sigma(t,d) is (4,4) Sigmatdblock = np.block([ [Sigmatdt, Sigmatdd.T], [Sigmatdd, Sigmadd] ]) # Step 3: Compute Conditional Mean diff = np.array([t - mut, (d - mud)]) # (4,) x = np.linalg.solve(Sigmatdblock, diff.reshape(-1, 1)) correction = Sigmaptd @ x # (3, 1) mucond = mup + correction.flatten() # Step 4: Compute Conditional Covariance invSigmatd = np.linalg.inv(Sigmatdblock) Sigmacond = Sigmap - (Sigmaptd @ invSigmatd @ Sigmaptd.T) # Step 5: Compute Modulation Factors difft = t - mut ftemp = np.exp(-0.5 lambdat (difft2) (1.0 / Sigmat[0,0])) diffd = d - mud invSigmad = np.linalg.inv(Sigmad) quadraticform = diffd @ invSigmad @ diffd fdir = np.exp(-0.5 lambdad quadraticform) # Step 6: Conditional Opacity alphacond = alpha ftemp fdir # Step 7: Extract S and R (Optional) U, D, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Sigmacond) S = D R = U if np.linalg.det(R) < 0: R[:, 0] = -1 return mucond, Sigmacond, alphacond, S, R Parameters: \lambdat: Positive scalar controlling temporal modulation sensitivity. \lambdad: Positive scalar controlling directional modulation sensitivity. \phip, \phit, \phid, \phil: Refinement functions (typically small MLPs) mapping feature f to parameter deltas. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: \Sigma{(t,d)} or \Sigmad may be singular if correlations are perfect or data is insufficient. Use pseudo-inverse or add small jitter to diagonal if inversion fails. Degenerate Input: If t or d are NaN, the exponential terms become NaN. Guard against invalid inputs. Precision: The exponential decay can underflow to zero for large deviations, effectively culling the Gaussian. This is intended behavior but may cause artifacts if \lambda is too high. This is the core algorithmic procedure described in the main method. It refers to the specific implementation of partitioning the 7D covariance and computing the conditional 3D Gaussian statistics. It is chosen when one needs to render a specific frame at time t from direction d using the 7DGS representation. It is distinct from static slicing because it includes the adaptive refinement step before conditioning. Time Complexity: Dominated by matrix inversion of 4 \times 4 (\Sigma{(t,d)}) and 3 \times 3 (\Sigmad) matrices, which is O(1) constant time per Gaussian. The refinement step involves MLP evaluation, also O(1). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full 7D parameters (\mup, \mut, \mud, \Sigma) plus refinement network weights. Strengths: Efficiently integrates temporal and view-dependent effects into standard 3D rendering pipelines without modifying the core rasterizer. Limitations: The intrinsic shape of the Gaussian (covariance) remains static over time if refinement is not used, which may hinder representing complex non-rigid deformations. When to use: When rendering dynamic scenes with view-dependent appearance using Gaussian Splatting. The Conditional Slicing Mechanism was introduced in "7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting". It conditions a 7-dimensional Gaussian on observed time and view direction to yield a conditional 3D Gaussian governing the spatial component. The method leverages standard properties of multivariate Gaussian distributions to condition the spatial component on observed time and view direction. It builds on the Gaussian Geometry Parameters Prediction method [8442-gaussian-geometry-parameters-prediction.md] by providing a mechanism to interpret the 7D parameters during rendering. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (SAGS)
head: SAGS (Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting)
body: Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (SAGS) is a novel-view synthesis method that implicitly encodes scene geometry using a local-global graph representation to facilitate learning complex scenes and enforce meaningful point displacements that preserve structure, thereby reducing floating-point artifacts and storage requirements. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which optimizes each Gaussian independently, SAGS leverages inter- and intra-connectivity between 3D point positions via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to predict Gaussian attributes, outperforming 3D-GS and Scaffold-GS in capturing high-frequency details while significantly reducing memory footprint. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse point cloud P \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3} derived from COLMAP, a set of sparse input views with known camera parameters, and a global scene feature g. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean position \mu, color c, opacity \alpha, and covariance \Sigma, rendered into 2D images. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud Graph: A k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) graph where nodes are points pi \in P and edges connect points within a local region. 2. Feature Encoding: Each point pi has a feature vector fi. Positions are encoded using multi-resolution hash encoding [23] into a higher-dimensional space D via \gamma(\cdot). 3. Global Feature: A single vector g representing the global scene feature, calculated as the maximum of all point feature encodings: g = \maxi(fi). 4. Gaussian Attributes: Position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, Color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}^1, Covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} decomposed into scale S \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation R (quaternion). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using the sparse point cloud P from COLMAP. 2. Curvature Estimation: Estimate the Gaussian mean curvature of point cloud P using the local-PCA approach [25]. Identify a set of low-curvature points PL \subset P where curvature is below a threshold. 3. Curvature-Aware Densification: For under-represented areas, create a k-NN graph for points p \in PL. Generate midpoints pm for each p and its neighbor pj \in k\text{-NN}(p): pm = \frac{1}{2} (p + pj) 4. Graph Construction: Apply k-NN search to link points p within local regions to create a point set graph enabling point interaction. 5. Relative features fj - fi are used instead of raw features for efficiency and expressivity. 6. Attribute Decoding: Decode \Phi(pi, fi) to Gaussian attributes using four distinct small MLPs (hidden size 32): Position: Learn \mu in a camera-agnostic manner as a displacement from the initial point pi: \mui = pi + \Delta pi, \quad \Delta pi = \text{MLP}{\mu}(\Phi(pi, fi)) Color, Opacity, Covariance: Predict these attributes using view-dependent point positions. Calculate normalized view-dependent position p^ci: p^ci = \frac{pi - xc}{\|pi - xc\|2} where xc is the camera coordinate. Color: ci = \text{MLP}c(\Phi(pi, fi), p^ci) Opacity \alphai, Scale Si, Rotation Ri are predicted similarly using view-dependent positions. Covariance Decomposition: To ensure positive semi-definiteness, decompose \Sigma as: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T where R is represented by quaternions. 7. SAGS-Lite Midpoint Generation: For the lightweight variant, generate midpoints on-the-fly from initial key points. Interpolate features for midpoint m between keypoints i, j \in P: f'm = \frac{1}{2} (f'i + f'j) Feed interpolated features f'm and corresponding view-dependent interpolated positions to refinement networks to predict attributes. 8. Rendering: Render the 3D Gaussians using the 3D-GS Gaussian rasterizer [15]. The 2D pixel color C is calculated by blending N ordered Gaussians: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) ci 9. Optimization: Train the model for 30,000 iterations. Apply growing and pruning steps every 100 iterations, starting from iteration 1500 until iteration 15,000. The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = (1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda\mathcal{L}{SSIM} where \lambda = 0.2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. imagegt)) ssimloss = ssimlossfunction(imagepred, imagegt) loss = 0.8 l1loss + 0.2 ssimloss loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() def densifyandprune(self, iteration): # Standard 3D-GS growing and pruning logic applied to predicted Gaussians pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance Definiteness: The decomposition \Sigma = R S S^T R^T is critical to prevent non-positive semi-definite matrices during optimization. Relative Features: Using relative features fj - fi is essential for efficiency and expressivity. Curvature Threshold: The choice of threshold for low-curvature points PL determines which points undergo densification. Global Feature: The global feature g is shared across all points and computed as the maximum of point features. Time Complexity: Training runs for 30,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: SAGS achieves significant memory reduction. On benchmark datasets, SAGS uses 99 MB compared to 3D-GS's 414 MB. The lightweight SAGS-Lite version achieves up to 24× size reduction without compression, using only 43 MB. Limitations: Requires initial sparse point cloud from COLMAP. Structure-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (SAGS) was proposed by E. Ververas et al. to address the limitations of structure-agnostic optimization schemes in 3D Gaussian Splatting, which often result in floating points and artifacts due to independent Gaussian optimization. The method builds on the 3D-GS framework [15] and incorporates ideas from graph neural networks and curvature-aware densification. It was published in 2024. name: Mesh-embedded representation
body: Mesh-embedded representations parameterize 3D Gaussian primitives relative to an explicit canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} to disentangle motion from appearance and enable explicit mesh editing. This family solves the problem of coherent, large-scale deformation and geometric coherence in Gaussian Splatting by tying Gaussian position, rotation, and scale to mesh geometry via barycentric embeddings or vertex parameterization, avoiding the artifacts and rigidity of implicit MLP-based skinning fields. Unlike standard 3DGS, which treats Gaussians as independent entities in free space, this approach ensures that mesh edits or animations propagate deterministically to the radiance field. The core mechanism relies on parameterizing Gaussian attributes relative to a canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, normals n, and faces F. Embedding Definition: Each Gaussian i is defined by an embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\}: k: Integer index of the triangle k \in F in the canonical mesh. (u, v): Barycentric coordinates within triangle k, constrained such that u \ge 0, v \ge 0, u+v \le 1. d: Scalar normal displacement along the interpolated surface normal. Canonical Position and Normal: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via Phong interpolation on the canonical mesh: \mu{cano} = \mathcal{V}(k, u, v) = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 n{cano} = \mathcal{N}(k, u, v) = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 where Vj and nj are the vertices and per-vertex normals of triangle k. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed by an animation function \text{Deform}(\cdot), the posed position \mu{pose} is derived by applying the deformation to the displaced canonical position: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence: Rotation: Per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 are interpolated using barycentric weights to get \delta q, which is then combined with the canonical rotation \bar{q}: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, \quad \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Scale: Scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} where A{pose} and A{cano} are the areas of the triangle in the posed and canonical states, respectively. Cross-Triangle Handling: Barycentric coordinates are differentiable only within a single triangle. If optimization moves an embedding point across a boundary (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability. Failure to handle this causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeposedgaussian(gaussian, mesh, posetransform): """ Computes the posed position, rotation, and scale for a single Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Dict with keys 'k', 'u', 'v', 'd', 'qcanon', 'scanon'. mesh: Dict with 'faces' (list of dicts with 'vertices', 'vertexnormals', 'vertexquaternions'). posetransform: Function that applies deformation to mesh vertices. Returns: mupose: Posed mean position. qpose: Posed rotation quaternion. spose: Posed scale vector. """ k = gaussian['k'] u = gaussian['u'] v = gaussian['v'] d = gaussian['d'] face = mesh.faces[k] V1, V2, V3 = face['vertices'] n1, n2, n3 = face['vertexnormals'] # Canonical position and normal mucano = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 ncano = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 # Posed position displacedpos = mucano + d ncano mupose = posetransform(displacedpos) # Posed rotation q1, q2, q3 = face['vertexquaternions'] deltaq = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 qpose = deltaq gaussian['qcanon'] # Posed scale V1pose, V2pose, V3pose = posetransform(V1), posetransform(V2), posetransform(V3) Apose = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2pose - V1pose, V3pose - V1pose)) Acano = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2 - V1, V3 - V1)) spose = (Apose / Acano) gaussian['scanon'] return mupose, qpose, spose A hybrid representation that defines 3D Gaussians over an explicit canonical triangle mesh to enable large-scale, interactive deformations. It sets itself apart by explicitly controlling Gaussian pose through mesh warping, enabling compatibility with skeletal animation and direct mesh editing without relying on implicit MLP-based skinning fields. Choose when coherent motion transfer and explicit mesh editing are required. This method initializes and deforms 3D Gaussians by anchoring them to a canonical triangle mesh using barycentric coordinates and normal displacement. It sets itself apart by defining a local triangle space to ensure robust results even with inaccurate meshes, tracking Gaussians through mesh topology rather than direct vertex positions. Choose when maintaining geometric coherence during mesh deformation is needed. GaMeS integrates 3DGS with mesh-based parameterization, allowing Gaussian components to be modified and deformed in the same manner as a traditional triangle mesh. It sets itself apart by providing a direct, one-stage parameterization that supports real-time editing and animation, unlike methods relying on expensive pre-processing or SDF regularization. Choose for direct mesh editing and animation. SuGaR and Gaussian Frosting extract a canonical triangle mesh from an optimized 3DGS scene to enable explicit mesh editing while preserving high-fidelity rendering. They set themselves apart by combining the editing capabilities of explicit meshes with differentiable Gaussian splatting via an adaptive Gaussian layer with variable thickness. Choose when extracting editable meshes from optimized Gaussians is needed. Mesh to DRK Conversion is a training-free procedure that converts traditional triangle and polygon mesh faces into Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) primitives for seamless integration into radiance field scenes. It sets itself apart by providing a direct, deterministic mapping that eliminates the need for training data rendering or model optimization. Choose for converting traditional 3D assets to splatting representations. The Gaussian Extraction Algorithm extracts discrete 3D Gaussian primitives from continuous Gaussian Splatting Functions at arbitrary densities. It sets itself apart by using an octree-guided progressive sampling strategy to locate high-probability regions, followed by gradient-based optimization of proxy points, rather than fixed-grid voxelization or direct mesh embedding. Choose when converting continuous neural fields to discrete Gaussians is needed. GauMesh combines tracked textured meshes with canonical 3D Gaussians and a learnable deformation field for dynamic human head avatars. It sets itself apart by introducing a learnable deformation field rather than relying solely on rigid or skeletal mesh transforms. Choose for dynamic avatar synthesis from few views. MiraGe edits 2D images by temporarily interpreting selected regions as 3D objects via Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart by using the source image as a strict reference for explicit 3D reconstruction rather than synthesizing new content, and from Implicit Neural Representations by providing addressable Cartesian coordinates. Choose for intuitive 2D image editing with 3D manipulation. GauS is a render-then-fuse approach for high-fidelity mesh reconstruction from 3DGS inputs without fine-tuning. It uses volumetric fusion to convert 3D Gaussians into textured triangle meshes. It is a plug-and-play module compatible with various GS-based methods. Unlike NeRF-based re-training or further fine-tuning required for explicit surface modeling in other methods, GauS converts optimized Gaussians directly into textured meshes serving as a versatile plug-and-play solution. Choose for explicit surface modeling from 3DGS. This method transfers mesh deformation to 3D Gaussians by calculating vertex transformations using ACAP, interpolating them via barycentric coordinates, and averaging transformations across 8 bound faces. It sets itself apart by using Gaussian-centric binding and averaging operations for robust deformation transfer. Choose for transferring cage or box deformations to Gaussians. For each of the 8 BBX corners (index i) and 3 triangle vertices (index j), calculate offset \Delta{ji}, rotation R{ji}, and shear S{ji} using polar decomposition of transformation matrix D{ji}. Average the transformations (R, S, \Delta) across the 8 bound faces to get global transformation for the Gaussian. Formulas: \Deltai = u\Delta{1i} + v\Delta{2i} + w\Delta{3i} = u(V'{i1} - V{i1}) + v(V'{i2} - V{i2}) + w(V'{i3} - V{i3}), where u,v,w are barycentric coordinates. Ri = u \log(R{i1}) + v \log(R{i2}) + w \log(R{i3}), and Si = uS{i1} + vS{i2} + wS{i3}. R' = \exp(\frac{1}{8} \sum{i=1}^{8} Ri), S' = \frac{1}{8} \sum{i=1}^{8} Si, \Sigma' = R' S' \Sigma (R' S')^T, \mu' = \mu + \frac{1}{8} \sum{i=1}^{8} \Deltai. G'(x) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu')^T (\Sigma')^{-1} (x-\mu')), where G' is the updated Gaussian kernel. The concept of embedding Gaussian primitives onto explicit geometry emerged to address the limitations of free-space 3DGS in handling dynamic scenes and editable assets. Early works introduced barycentric parameterization to tie Gaussians to canonical meshes for animation. Subsequent developments refined this by aligning Gaussians to reconstructed surfaces or extracting meshes from optimized Gaussians, enabling hybrid rendering and editing. The family also includes training-free conversions and neural-to-discrete extraction methods, expanding the applicability of mesh-embedded concepts to broader radiance field representations. body: Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Splatting is a hybrid 3D representation that parameterizes 3D Gaussians relative to an explicit canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} to disentangle motion from appearance. It solves the problem of coherent, large-scale deformation in Gaussian Splatting by tying Gaussian position, rotation, and scale to mesh geometry via barycentric embeddings, avoiding the artifacts and rigidity of implicit MLP-based skinning fields. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on implicit deformation fields or separate optimization pipelines, this method explicitly controls Gaussian pose through mesh warping, enabling compatibility with skeletal animation, blend shapes, and direct mesh editing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, per-vertex normals n, and faces F; monocular video frames of the subject in various poses; initial Gaussian parameters. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by embedding tuples Ei, optimized Gaussian attributes (opacity, color, canonical rotation/scale), and a renderer capable of real-time synthesis. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is defined by an embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\}: k: Integer index of the triangle k \in F in the canonical mesh. (u, v): Barycentric coordinates within triangle k, constrained such that u \ge 0, v \ge 0, u+v \le 1. d: Scalar normal displacement along the interpolated surface normal. Additionally, each Gaussian stores pose-invariant attributes: canonical rotation \bar{q}, canonical scale \bar{s}, opacity o, and color c. Canonical Position and Normal: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via Phong interpolation on the canonical mesh: \mu{cano} = \mathcal{V}(k, u, v) = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 n{cano} = \mathcal{N}(k, u, v) = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 where Vj and nj are the vertices and per-vertex normals of triangle k. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed by an animation function \text{Deform}(\cdot), the posed position \mu{pose} is derived by applying the deformation to the displaced canonical position: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence: Rotation: Per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 are interpolated using barycentric weights to get \delta q, which is then combined with the canonical rotation \bar{q}: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, \quad \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Scale: Scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} where the ratio of the posed triangle area to the canonical triangle area scales the invariant canonical scale \bar{s}. Optimization and Adaptation: During training, Gaussian parameters and embedding parameters are updated simultaneously. The method adapts the clone and split scheme of 3D Gaussians to better suit the mesh-embedded representation. Cross-Triangle Handling: Barycentric coordinates are differentiable only within a single triangle. If optimization moves an embedding point across a boundary (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability. This is achieved via lifted optimization, where embedding points walk on the triangle mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeposedgaussian(gaussian, mesh, posetransform): """ Computes the posed position, rotation, and scale for a single Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Dict with keys 'k', 'u', 'v', 'd', 'qcanon', 'scanon'. mesh: Dict with 'faces' (list of dicts with 'vertices', 'vertexnormals', 'vertexquaternions'). posetransform: Function that applies deformation to mesh vertices. Returns: mupose: Posed mean position. qpose: Posed rotation quaternion. spose: Posed scale vector. """ k = gaussian['k'] u = gaussian['u'] v = gaussian['v'] d = gaussian['d'] face = mesh.faces[k] V1, V2, V3 = face['vertices'] n1, n2, n3 = face['vertexnormals'] # Canonical position and normal (Phong interpolation) mucano = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 ncano = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 # Posed position displacedpos = mucano + d ncano mupose = posetransform(displacedpos) # Posed rotation q1, q2, q3 = face['vertexquaternions'] deltaq = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 qpose = deltaq gaussian['qcanon'] # Posed scale V1pose, V2pose, V3pose = posetransform(V1), posetransform(V2), posetransform(V3) Apose = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2pose - V1pose, V3pose - V1pose)) Acano = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2 - V1, V3 - V1)) spose = (Apose / Acano) gaussian['scanon'] return mupose, qpose, spose def handlecrosstriangleupdate(embedding, mesh, gradientu, gradientv): """ Handles the case where barycentric update moves the point outside the current triangle. Re-expresses the embedding in the neighboring triangle. Args: embedding: Current E={k, u, v, d}. mesh: Mesh structure with adjacency info. gradientu, gradientv: Gradients of the loss w.r.t u and v. Returns: New embedding tuple. """ k = embedding['k'] u = embedding['u'] v = embedding['v'] # Check boundary conditions if u < 0 or v < 0 or u + v > 1: # Find neighboring triangle that contains the projected point or is adjacent # In lifted optimization, this involves walking to the adjacent face neighbork = mesh.getneighbor(k, u, v) # Re-express barycentric coordinates in the new triangle # Sources do not specify the exact barycentric remapping algorithm for lifted optimization. unew, vnew = mesh.remapbarycentric(k, neighbork, u, v) # Update embedding newembedding = { 'k': neighbork, 'u': unew, 'v': vnew, 'd': embedding['d'] } return newembedding else: return embedding Defines 3D Gaussians over an explicit triangle mesh for large-scale, interactive deformations driven by mesh editing. It sets itself apart by utilizing a reconstructed explicit mesh for initialization and employing specific face-split and normal-guidance strategies to handle large deformations without relying on implicit MLP-based skinning. Focuses on the initialization and deformation mechanics of mesh-embedded Gaussians. Introduces a hybrid "Gaussian Mesh Splatting" representation where each Gaussian is parameterized by the vertices of a mesh face, inducing coherent changes via classical mesh operations. A method for extracting Gaussian splats from meshes, focusing on the conversion process. Details the conversion of mesh data into a differentiable radiance kernel format. Algorithms for extracting Gaussian primitives from mesh-based representations. Performance: Achieves over 300 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU and 30 FPS on an iPhone 13. Strengths: Explicit motion control allows compatibility with various animation techniques including skeletal animation, blend shapes, and mesh editing. The mesh represents low-frequency motion while Gaussians capture high-frequency geometry and appearance. Limitations: Relies on accurate semantic labels or mesh proxies for initialization. Cross-triangle updates require careful handling to maintain differentiability. Usage: Ported to Unity for real-time rendering. Originating from the SplattingAvatar paper, this method was developed to create realistic, real-time human avatars from monocular videos. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Phong surfaces, addressing the limitations of MLP-based linear blend skinning fields for motion. The approach disentangles motion and appearance by embedding Gaussians on a canonical triangle mesh, allowing for explicit control via mesh deformation. body: GaussianMesh is a method that defines 3D Gaussians over an explicit triangle mesh to enable large-scale, interactive deformations driven by mesh editing. It solves the problem of coherent motion transfer in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by tying Gaussian parameters to mesh geometry via joint refinement, where GS rendering guides adaptive splitting and mesh constraints regularize Gaussian shapes. It sets itself apart from parent methods by utilizing a reconstructed explicit mesh from calibrated images for initialization and employing specific face-split and normal-guidance strategies to handle large deformations without relying on implicit MLP-based skinning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A reconstructed explicit triangle mesh derived from calibrated images; 3DGS rendering parameters. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians embedded on the mesh faces, supporting real-time deformation. Data Structures: Exact Layouts: Not given in the sources. Mesh: Explicit triangle mesh with vertices and faces. Gaussians: Each Gaussian is associated with a specific mesh face. Its position is determined by barycentric coordinates within that face, and its orientation/scale is influenced by the face's normal and local geometry. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using the reconstructed explicit mesh derived from calibrated images. 2. Adaptive Refinement: Employ face split and normal guidance strategies to guide Gaussian learning and adapt density. 3. Regularization: Introduce a regularization loss to preserve the shape of the Gaussians during optimization. 4. Deformation: Incorporate user-controlled mesh deformations. 5. Rendering: Achieve real-time deformation and rendering. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Faces: Exhibits artifacts when dealing with significant deformations in meshes with large faces, leading to inaccuracies. Proxy Errors: Relies on accurate semantic labels or mesh proxies; errors in segmentation or remeshing can easily produce artifacts. OMeGa is a joint representation framework that optimizes an explicit triangle mesh and 2D Gaussian splats simultaneously. It sets itself apart by decoupling geometric support from textural detail, allowing adaptive density control and free movement of splats within the face plane, unlike methods that allocate fixed splats or keep rotation/scale fixed. Choose it when accurate geometry in texture-less regions is needed and mesh geometry should guide splat optimization. Gaussian Splitting for Bent Shapes is a procedure to split bent Gaussians into multiple well-formed ellipsoids to approximate non-rigid warping shapes. It sets itself apart by preventing visual artifacts caused by a single transformed Gaussian failing to represent bent shapes. Choose it when non-rigid warping causes single-Gaussian representation failures. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports large, interactive deformations driven by mesh editing; enables real-time animation and scene editing. Limitations: Exhibits artifacts with significant deformations on meshes with large faces. Relies on accurate initial mesh proxies; errors in segmentation or remeshing cause artifacts. When to use: When large-scale, user-controlled mesh deformations are required for 3DGS avatars or scenes. When not to use: When the input mesh has large faces or when accurate semantic labels/proxies are unavailable. GaussianMesh (also known as Mesh-GS) was introduced to realize large-scale 3DGS deformation. It utilizes a reconstructed explicit mesh from calibrated images to initialize Gaussians, employing face split and normal guidance strategies, and introduces regularization loss to preserve Gaussian shape. It builds on the concept of embedding Gaussians on meshes to disentangle motion from appearance Parent. name: OMeGa Joint Representation
head: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats, OMeGa
body: OMeGa is an end-to-end framework that jointly optimizes an explicit triangle mesh and 2D Gaussian splats via a flexible binding strategy, where spatial attributes of Gaussian splats are expressed in the mesh frame and texture attributes are retained on the splats. Unlike methods that allocate a fixed number of splats uniformly to each face or keep rotation/scale fixed, OMeGa decouples geometric support from textural detail, allowing adaptive density control and free movement of splats within the face plane. This approach addresses inaccurate geometry in texture-less indoor regions and leverages mesh geometry to guide splat optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images and an initial mesh topology. Outputs: Optimized learnable vertex positions V, mesh faces F, Gaussian splat set G, and binding map B. Data Structures: 1. Mesh Parameters: V \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv \times 3}: Learnable vertex positions, where Nv is the number of vertices. F \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf \times 3}: Mesh faces, where Nf is the number of faces. Each face fj is defined by three vertices. 2. Gaussian Splat Set G: Each splat gi contains texture attributes (color, opacity) and spatial parameters derived from the mesh. Spatial parameters include barycentric coordinates (u, w), relative scale s{rel}, and in-plane rotation R{2d}. 3. Binding Map B: B: G \rightarrow F maps each splat gi to its supporting face fj. Stored as a list or hash map of pairs (gi, fj). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize mesh vertices V and faces F. Initialize Gaussian splats G with initial barycentric coordinates (u, w), relative scales s{rel}, and in-plane rotations R{2d}. Initialize binding map B mapping each splat to a face. 2. Spatial Attribute Derivation: For each splat gi bound to face fj, compute mean m, scale s, and rotation R using the formulas below. 3. Rasterization: Render the scene using the derived Gaussian splats (means, scales, rotations, colors, opacities). 4. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss from rasterized images and mesh regularization losses (mesh constraint, monocular normal supervision). 5. Optimization: Update learnable parameters (V, splat attributes) via gradient descent. 6. Adaptive Density Control (Splat Management): Cloning/Splitting: When a Gaussian gi bound to fj is cloned or split, create g{new}, bind it to fj, inherit gi's barycentric position with a small in-plane offset onto the face plane \Pi{fj}, and insert (g{new}, fj) into B. Removal: If a splat is pruned by the adaptive density controller, remove its entry from B. 7. Mesh Refinement (Topology Management): Subdivision: When face fj is subdivided into children \{f{jk}\}, reassign each splat previously bound to fj to the child whose domain contains its barycentric coordinates, preserving per-splat attributes. Removal: When face fj is removed, identify all splats mapped to fj and flag them for removal in subsequent steps. Formulas: 1. Splat Mean (Position): The mean m of a splat bound to face fj with vertices v1, v2, v3 is: m = u \cdot v1 + w \cdot v2 + (1 - u - w) \cdot v3 where u, w \in [0, 1] and u + w \le 1. 2. Splat Scale: The scale s is the element-wise product of a learnable relative scale s{rel} and a predefined base scale s0 derived from the mesh face: s = s{rel} \odot s0 where s{rel} = (s{rel,1}, s{rel,2}) \in [s{min}, s{max}] \times [s{min}, s{max}]. 3. Splat Rotation: The final rotation matrix R is computed from the face rotation Rs and an in-plane rotation parameter R{2d}: R = Rs \cdot R{2d} where Rs is the rotation matrix of the triangle face. Parameters: s{min}, s{max}: Lower and upper bounds for Gaussian Splat scale components to prevent discrepancies with triangular face scales. Typical values for s{min}, s{max}: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Discrepancy: Significant differences between Gaussian Splat scales and triangular face scales can occur. This is prevented by imposing upper and lower bounds on s{rel}. Barycentric Validity: Ensure u, w \in [0, 1] and u + w \le 1 to keep splats within the face boundaries. Topology Changes: When mesh topology changes (subdivision/removal), the binding map B must be updated consistently to maintain valid splat-face associations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: OMeGa achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging indoor scenes. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Decouples geometric support from textural detail; allows adaptive density control; enables free movement of splats within the face plane; regularizes geometry learning via mesh constraints and monocular normal supervision. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When accurate geometry in texture-less regions is required, and when joint optimization of mesh and splats is beneficial for scene-level surface reconstruction. When not to use: Not given in the sources. OMeGa was introduced in the paper "OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction". It addresses limitations of previous works, such as inaccurate geometry in texture-less indoor regions and the decoupling of mesh extraction from optimization. The method integrates mesh constraints and monocular normal supervision to regularize geometry learning and proposes a heuristic, iterative mesh-refinement strategy. OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00427, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Gaussian Splitting for Bent Shapes
head: Bent Gaussian Splitting
body: A procedure to split bent Gaussians into multiple well-formed ellipsoids to approximate non-rigid warping shapes that a single Gaussian cannot represent, preventing visual artifacts. It addresses the limitation where a single transformed Gaussian fails to properly represent bent shapes caused by non-rigid warping, which leads to visual artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each represented by a proxy point cloud APd after initial deformation (e.g., cage-based deformation). The proxy points include the deformed center c'd and deformed points on the principal axes (e.g., x'1, x'2 for the x-axis). Output: A refined set of Gaussians where bent primitives have been split into multiple smaller, well-formed ellipsoids, ready for MVC (Mean Value Coordinates) transformation. Data Structures: Proxy Point Cloud (APd): A set of points representing the Gaussian ellipsoid. For a Gaussian with semi-principal axes a, b, c, the proxy points typically include the center and points along the axes at distances proportional to the axis lengths. Gaussian Parameters: Mean position, covariance matrix (or semi-principal axes a, b, c and orientation), opacity, and color. Parameters: Splitting Threshold: 175^\circ. Splitting is required if the calculated angle falls below this value. Scaling Factor (k): 1/2. Although theoretically derived as (1/2)^{1/3}, setting k=1/2 produces marginally better results. Minimum Axis Length: 1e-2. Axes with lengths below this threshold are not split for numerical stability. Steps: 1. Identify Bent Gaussians: For each Gaussian, calculate the angle between vectors from the deformed center c'd to two deformed points x'1 and x'2 on the same axis (e.g., x-axis) in the deformed point cloud APd. Vector 1: \vec{v}1 = x'1 - c'd Vector 2: \vec{v}2 = x'2 - c'd Angle \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\vec{v}1 \cdot \vec{v}2}{\|\vec{v}1\| \|\vec{v}2\|}\right). If \theta < 175^\circ, the Gaussian is considered bent and requires splitting on this axis. 2. Split the Ellipsoid: Divide the pre-MVC Gaussian ellipsoid into two smaller ellipsoids along the chosen axis. Each new ellipsoid has axis lengths reduced by factor k. Both new ellipsoids are positioned to meet at the center of the original ellipsoid along the splitting axis. Specifically, if splitting along the x-axis with original semi-axis a, the new semi-axes are ka, b, c. The centers are shifted by \pm (a - ka)/2 along the x-axis relative to the original center. 3. Apply MVC Transformation: Apply the MVC transformation again to the resulting two smaller ellipsoids for further processing. 4. Repeat for All Axes: Run the identification and splitting process across all axes (x, y, z) to ensure Gaussians requiring splitting on multiple axes are split more than once. Formulas: Volume Preservation Constraint: The combined volume of two smaller ellipsoids approximates the original volume. LV = \frac{2}{3}\pi abc - 2 \cdot \frac{2}{3}\pi (k1 a)(k2 b)(k3 c) \approx 0 Simplified: k1 k2 k3 = 1/2. Shape Preservation Constraint: Each smaller ellipsoid maintains shape similar to original. \frac{k1}{a} \approx \frac{k2}{b} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{k1}{a} \approx \frac{k3}{c} (Constraints ensure shape similarity, leading to k1=k2=k3). Scaling Factor: k1 = k2 = k3 = \sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{2}} In practice, k = 1/2 is used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def splitbentgaussians(gaussians, threshold=175.0, k=0.5, minaxis=1e-2): """ Splits bent Gaussians into multiple well-formed ellipsoids. Args: gaussians: List of dicts with keys: 'center': list of 3 floats 'axes': list of 3 vectors (each list of 3 floats) representing semi-principal axes 'proxypoints': list of 3D vectors (center + 2 points per axis) threshold: Angle threshold in degrees for splitting (default 175) k: Scaling factor for splitting (default 0.5) minaxis: Minimum axis length to avoid splitting (default 1e-2) Returns: List of Gaussian dicts (split Gaussians replace originals) """ def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def norm(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def copygaussian(g): return { 'center': list(g['center']), 'axes': [list(a) for a in g['axes']], 'proxypoints': list(g['proxypoints']) } def getaxispoints(proxypoints, axisidx): # proxypoints[0] is center, proxypoints[1+2axisidx] and [2+2axisidx] are x1, x2 return proxypoints[1 + 2axisidx], proxypoints[2 + 2axisidx] newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: splitaxes = [] center = g['center'] for i in range(3): p1, p2 = getaxispoints(g['proxypoints'], i) if p1 is None or p2 is None: continue v1 = [p1[j] - center[j] for j in range(3)] v2 = [p2[j] - center[j] for j in range(3)] cosangle = dot(v1, v2) / (norm(v1) norm(v2)) cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosangle)) angle = math.degrees(math.acos(cosangle)) if angle < threshold: splitaxes.append(i) if not splitaxes: newgaussians.append(g) continue # Split sequentially per axis as described: "run across all axes to ensure... split more than once" currentbatch = [g] for axisidx in splitaxes: nextbatch = [] for curr in currentbatch: originalaxis = list(curr['axes'][axisidx]) axislen = norm(originalaxis) if axislen < minaxis: nextbatch.append(curr) continue # Scale axis by k newaxis = [originalaxis[j] k for j in range(3)] curr['axes'][axisidx] = newaxis # Shift centers to meet at the original center along the splitting axis # Shift magnitude is half the difference between original and new axis length shiftmag = (axislen - k axislen) / 2.0 shift = [originalaxis[j] (shiftmag / axislen) for j in range(3)] g1 = copygaussian(curr) g2 = copygaussian(curr) g1['center'] = [curr['center'][j] + shift[j] for j in range(3)] g2['center'] = [curr['center'][j] - shift[j] for j in range(3)] nextbatch.append(g1) nextbatch.append(g2) currentbatch = nextbatch newgaussians.extend(currentbatch) return newgaussians Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians and axes checked. Splitting increases the number of Gaussians, potentially doubling the count for heavily bent regions. Memory Complexity: Increases proportionally to the number of splits. Strengths: Prevents visual artifacts from non-rigid warping; no architectural changes or retraining needed; can work in real-time with caching. Limitations: Increases the number of primitives, which may impact rendering performance if many splits occur. When to use: When deforming 3DGS Gaussians using cage-based deformation or other methods that cause non-rigid warping, leading to bent Gaussians. When not to use: When deformation is rigid or minimal, as splitting adds unnecessary complexity. Originated in GSDeformer: Direct Cage-based Deformation for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method was developed to address artifacts in 3DGS deformation caused by non-rigid warping, where a single Gaussian cannot represent bent shapes. It operates directly on the primitives of 3DGS, allowing integration with other 3DGS variants without retraining. GSDeformer: Direct Cage-based Deformation for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.15491, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Mesh-Embedded Gaussian Initialization and Deformation
head: Gaussian Embedding, Triangle Embedding
body: This method initializes and deforms 3D Gaussians by anchoring them to a canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} using barycentric coordinates and normal displacement. It solves the problem of maintaining geometric coherence during mesh deformation by tracking Gaussians through mesh topology rather than direct vertex positions. It builds on Mesh-embedded representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, per-vertex normals n, and faces F; deformation function \text{Deform}(\cdot); number of Gaussians N (10,000). Output: Set of N Gaussians, each defined by embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\} and derived attributes (position, rotation, scale). Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores an embedding tuple Ei: k \in F: Index of the triangle in the canonical mesh. (u, v): Barycentric coordinates within triangle k, constrained such that u \ge 0, v \ge 0, u+v \le 1. d: Scalar normal displacement along the interpolated surface normal. Canonical Position and Normal: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via Phong interpolation on the canonical mesh: \mu{cano} = \mathcal{V}(k, u, v) = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 n{cano} = \mathcal{N}(k, u, v) = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 where Vj and nj are the vertices and per-vertex normals of triangle k. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed, the posed position \mu{pose} is derived by applying the mesh deformation function \text{Deform}(\cdot) to the displaced canonical position: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence: Rotation: Interpolate per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 using barycentric weights to get \delta q, then combine with canonical rotation \bar{q}: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, \quad \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Scale: Scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} where A{pose} and A{cano} are the areas of the triangle in the posed and canonical states, respectively. Initialization: 1. Randomly select 10,000 pairs of triangle indices k and barycentric coordinates (u, v) on the canonical mesh. 2. Initialize all displacements d to zero. 3. Set canonical rotation \bar{q} and scale \bar{s} for each Gaussian. 4. Spherical harmonics for color representation are turned off for simplicity. Cross-Triangle Handling: Barycentric coordinates are differentiable only within a single triangle. If optimization moves an embedding point across a boundary (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability. Failure to handle this causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quatmul(q1, q2): """Hamilton product of two quaternions [w, x, y, z].""" w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1 w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2 return np.array([ w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2 ]) def computeposedgaussian(gaussian, mesh, posetransform): """ Computes the posed position, rotation, and scale for a single Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Dict with keys 'k', 'u', 'v', 'd', 'qcanon', 'scanon'. mesh: Dict with 'faces' (list of dicts with 'vertices', 'vertexnormals', 'vertexquaternions'). posetransform: Function that applies deformation to mesh vertices. Returns: mupose: Posed mean position. qpose: Posed rotation quaternion. spose: Posed scale vector. """ k = gaussian['k'] u = gaussian['u'] v = gaussian['v'] d = gaussian['d'] face = mesh['faces'][k] V1, V2, V3 = face['vertices'] n1, n2, n3 = face['vertexnormals'] # Canonical position and normal mucano = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 ncano = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 # Posed position displacedpos = mucano + d ncano mupose = posetransform(displacedpos) # Posed rotation q1, q2, q3 = face['vertexquaternions'] deltaq = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 qpose = quatmul(deltaq, gaussian['qcanon']) # Posed scale V1pose, V2pose, V3pose = posetransform(V1), posetransform(V2), posetransform(V3) Apose = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2pose - V1pose, V3pose - V1pose)) Acano = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2 - V1, V3 - V1)) spose = (Apose / Acano) gaussian['scanon'] return mupose, qpose, spose Walking on Triangle is a constraint mechanism that binds 3D Gaussians to the surface of a triangle mesh, ensuring they remain within the boundaries of their corresponding triangles during optimization and deformation. It solves the problem of Gaussians drifting off-mesh or piling up at triangle edges when the underlying mesh is manipulated, animated, or deformed. Unlike methods that rely heavily on precise mesh accuracy, it defines a local triangle space to ensure robust results even with inaccurate meshes. A method that adapts mesh-based deformation to 3DGS by harnessing the priors of explicit representation. It uses surface properties like normals of the mesh, and gradients generated by explicit deformation methods. It learns the face split to optimize the parameters and number of Gaussians, which provides adequate topological information to 3DGS and improves the quality of both reconstruction and geometry editing results. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) where N is 10,000. Posed state computation is O(1) per Gaussian per frame. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the embedding tuples and derived attributes for each Gaussian. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Maintains geometric coherence during deformation. Limitations: Requires careful handling of cross-triangle boundaries to avoid piling up. When to use: When deforming a mesh-based representation with Gaussians. When not to use: When the mesh deformation is unknown or non-differentiable. Originated in SplattingAvatar. The method builds on the concept of mesh-embedded representations.
