name: Walking on Triangle
body: Walking on Triangle is a constraint mechanism in mesh-embedded Gaussian splatting that prevents Gaussians from drifting outside their corresponding mesh triangles during optimization or deformation. It solves the problem of Gaussians "sticking and piling up" on triangle boundaries, which causes visible artifacts when the avatar is animated into novel poses. Unlike standard Euclidean updates that ignore mesh topology, this method ensures Gaussians remain topologically bound to their host triangles, maintaining geometric fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gaussian positions defined by barycentric coordinates (u, v) within a mesh triangle, and the mesh triangle vertices. Output: Clipped barycentric coordinates that remain strictly within the valid triangle domain. Data Structures: Each Gaussian is associated with a specific triangle index and initial barycentric coordinates (u, v). The valid domain for barycentric coordinates is defined by u \ge 0, v \ge 0, and u + v \le 1. Steps: 1. Retrieve Coordinates: For each Gaussian, retrieve its current barycentric coordinates (u, v) relative to its assigned mesh triangle. 2. Clip Coordinates: Apply boundary constraints to ensure the Gaussian stays within the triangle. The clipping logic is: u = \max(0, \min(u, 1)) v = \max(0, \min(v, 1 - u)) This ensures u \ge 0, v \ge 0, and u + v \le 1. 3. Reconstruct Position: Convert the clipped barycentric coordinates back to 3D world space using the triangle's vertex positions V0, V1, V2: P = (1 - u - v)V0 + uV1 + vV2 Parameters: No tunable parameters are specified for the basic clipping mechanism. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disabling the Mechanism: If the walking on triangle constraint is disabled, Gaussians are allowed to move freely in Euclidean space. This causes them to accumulate at triangle boundaries, leading to significant visual artifacts during animation. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed for barycentric calculations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def walkingontriangle(u: float, v: float) -> tuple[float, float]: """ Clips barycentric coordinates to ensure they remain within the valid triangle domain. Args: u: Initial barycentric coordinate u. v: Initial barycentric coordinate v. Returns: Clipped (u, v) tuple. """ # Ensure u is non-negative and does not exceed 1 u = max(0.0, min(u, 1.0)) # Ensure v is non-negative and u + v <= 1 # This implies v <= 1 - u v = max(0.0, min(v, 1.0 - u)) return u, v def reconstructposition(u: float, v: float, v0: Vector3, v1: Vector3, v2: Vector3) -> Vector3: """ Reconstructs 3D position from barycentric coordinates. Args: u: Barycentric coordinate u. v: Barycentric coordinate v. v0, v1, v2: Vertices of the mesh triangle. Returns: 3D position P. """ return (1.0 - u - v) v0 + u v1 + v v2 Mani-GS is a variant that defines a local triangle space for each triangle to ensure robust results even with inaccurate meshes. It binds Gaussians to the mesh and optimizes their attributes within this local space, allowing mesh manipulation to be transferred directly to the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. This enables large deformations, soft body simulation, and local manipulation. Compared to SuGaR, Mani-GS produces fewer artifacts and reduces blurring effects. Geodesic Position Optimisation is a Riemannian gradient descent optimizer that restricts kernel source movements to the mesh surface. Instead of Euclidean updates, it projects the gradient \nabla{p^} L to the local tangent plane T{p^} M to define an initial velocity v^. It then computes the exponential map Exp(p^, v^) to trace the geodesic and determine the updated kernel position. To accelerate convergence, it parallel transports accumulated momentum to the new kernel position. The implementation uses the straightest geodesic algorithm with a CUDA-parallelised implementation. Time and Memory Complexity: The basic walking on triangle clipping is O(1) per Gaussian per update step. Geodesic Position Optimisation requires computing tangent planes, exponential maps, and parallel transport, which is more computationally expensive than simple clipping. Measured Performance: Disabling walking on triangle significantly degrades performance: Bala Head Avatar: PSNR drops from 30.04 to 29.91, SSIM from 0.938 to 0.933, and LPIPS increases from 0.062 to 0.070. Male-3-Casual Full-Body Avatar: PSNR drops from 33.01 to 32.48, SSIM from 0.982 to 0.979, and LPIPS increases from 0.020 to 0.024. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents topological artifacts during animation; maintains Gaussian distribution within mesh bounds. Mani-GS variant handles inaccurate meshes robustly. Limitations: Simple clipping may not handle complex deformations as well as geodesic methods. Disabling it leads to boundary piling. When to Use: Use when animating mesh-embedded Gaussians to prevent boundary artifacts. Use Geodesic Position Optimisation when high-fidelity surface adherence is required during optimization. Walking on Triangle was introduced in the context of relightable modeling with explicit shape representations, specifically in the SplattingAvatar method. It addresses the limitations of methods that compromise pixel-wise metrics for shape representation. The mechanism was ablated to demonstrate its importance in maintaining visual quality during novel pose animation. name: GaMeS (Gaussian Mesh Splatting)
head: Gaussian Mesh Splatting, Mesh-based adapting and modification of Gaussian Splatting
body: GaMeS is a hybrid 3D representation that integrates Gaussian Splatting (GS) with mesh-based parameterization, allowing Gaussian components to be modified and deformed in the same manner as a traditional triangle mesh. Unlike standard GS, which treats Gaussians as independent entities, GaMeS anchors each Gaussian to the vertices of a canonical mesh face, ensuring that geometric transformations applied to the mesh automatically propagate to the Gaussians' means and covariances. This distinguishes it from siblings like SuGaR / Gaussian Frosting, which rely on expensive pre-processing and SDF regularization, by providing a direct, one-stage parameterization that supports real-time editing and animation. GaMeS operates in two primary modes: Mesh-Initialized Input (baseline) and Mesh-Free Input (Triangle Soup). Both modes rely on parameterizing Gaussian attributes relative to a canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, normals n, and faces F, as defined in the parent Mesh-embedded representation. Inputs: A canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M} (for baseline) or a set of initial flat Gaussians (for Triangle Soup); input images for optimization. Outputs: A set of Gaussians GM defined by their embedding on the mesh, including trainable parameters for position, scale, opacity, and color. For a mesh with n faces, GaMeS defines a fixed number k of Gaussian components per face, resulting in k \cdot n total Gaussians. Embedding Tuple: Each Gaussian i on face f is defined by: k: Index of the triangle face in F. (\alpha{1i}, \alpha{2i}, \alpha{3i}): Trainable barycentric coordinates such that \alpha{1i} + \alpha{2i} + \alpha{3i} = 1. \rhoi: Trainable scale multiplier, \rhoi \in \mathbb{R}^+. \sigmai: Opacity. ci: Spherical Harmonic (SH) color coefficients. Canonical Geometry: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via linear interpolation on the canonical mesh [Parent, S2, unofficial]: \mu{cano} = \alpha{1i} v1 + \alpha{2i} v2 + \alpha{3i} v3 n{cano} = \frac{(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)}{\|(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)\|} where v1, v2, v3 are the vertices of the face. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed via a deformation function \text{Deform}(\cdot) (e.g., skeletal animation), the posed position is \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano}) [Parent]. The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence [Parent]. Specifically, the rotation is interpolated from per-vertex quaternions, and scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state [Parent]. When a mesh is provided, Gaussians are placed directly on the mesh surface. Step 1: Construct Local Frame for Face V For a single triangle face with vertices V = \{v1, v2, v3\}, construct an orthonormal basis RV = [r1, r2, r3]: 1. Calculate the normal r1: r1 = \frac{(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)}{\|(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)\|} 2. Calculate the centroid m = \text{mean}(v1, v2, v3). 3. Calculate the first tangent r2 by normalizing the vector from the centroid to v1: r2 = \frac{v1 - m}{\|v1 - m\|} 4. Calculate the second tangent r3 using Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization of the vector from the centroid to v2 against r1 and r2: r3 = \frac{\text{orth}(v2 - m; r1, r2)}{\|\text{orth}(v2 - m; r1, r2)\|} Where \text{orth}(x; r1, r2) = x - \text{proj}(x, r1) - \text{proj}(x, r2) and \text{proj}(v, u) = \frac{\langle v, u \rangle}{\langle u, u \rangle} u. Step 2: Define Base Covariance \SigmaV Define the scaling matrix SV = \text{diag}(s1, s2, s3): s1 = \epsilon (a small constant to avoid numerical issues, representing the normal direction). s2 = \|m - v1\|. s3 = \langle v2, r3 \rangle. The base covariance is \SigmaV = RV SV SV^T RV^T. Step 3: Define Gaussians per Face For each of the k Gaussians i on face V, define the Gaussian G{Vi}: G{Vi} = \mathcal{N}(\mu{Vi}, \rhoi \SigmaV) where \mu{Vi} = \alpha{1i} v1 + \alpha{2i} v2 + \alpha{3i} v3 and \alpha{1i} + \alpha{2i} + \alpha{3i} = 1. The parameters \{\alpha{1i}, \alpha{2i}, \alpha{3i}, \rhoi, \sigmai, ci\} are trainable. When no mesh is available, GaMeS creates a "Triangle Soup" by estimating a mesh from flat Gaussians. Step 1: Train Initial Flat Gaussians Train a standard GS with flat splats, setting the first scaling parameter s1 = \epsilon. Step 2: Estimate Triangle Vertices For each Gaussian G with mean m, rotation R = [r1, r2, r3], and scale S = \text{diag}(\epsilon, s2, s3), define three vertices V = [v1, v2, v3]: v1 = m. v2 = m + s2 r2. v3 = m + s3 r3. Step 3: Re-parameterize Freeze the vertices V and re-parameterize the Gaussian \hat{G}V using the mesh-based approach: 1. Set \hat{m}V = v1. 2. Compute \hat{r}1 = \frac{(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)}{\|(v2 - v1) \times (v3 - v1)\|}. 3. Compute \hat{r}3 = \text{orth}(v3 - v1; r1, r2) (using the original r vectors from Step 1). 4. Compute \hat{r}2 = \frac{v2 - v1}{\|v2 - v1\|}. 5. Compute scales: \hat{s}1 = \epsilon, \hat{s}2 = \|v2 - v1\|, \hat{s}3 = \langle v3 - v1, \hat{r}3 \rangle. 6. Construct \hat{\Sigma}V = \hat{R}V \hat{S}V \hat{S}V^T \hat{R}V^T. 7. Define \hat{G}V = \mathcal{N}(\hat{m}V, \hat{\Sigma}V). The final set is GM = \bigcup{Vi \in \hat{M}} \{\hat{G}{Vi}, \sigmai, ci\}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gramschmidtstep(x, r1, r2): """Single step Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization.""" def proj(v, u): return (np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)) u return x - proj(x, r1) - proj(x, r2) def computefacebasis(v1, v2, v3): """Compute orthonormal basis for a triangle face (Baseline method).""" # Normal edge1 = v2 - v1 edge2 = v3 - v1 r1 = np.cross(edge1, edge2) r1 = r1 / np.linalg.norm(r1) # Centroid m = (v1 + v2 + v3) / 3.0 # First tangent vec1 = v1 - m r2 = vec1 / np.linalg.norm(vec1) # Second tangent vec2 = v2 - m r3 = gramschmidtstep(vec2, r1, r2) r3 = r3 / np.linalg.norm(r3) return np.columnstack((r1, r2, r3)) def computesoupbasis(v1, v2, v3, r1orig, r2orig): """Compute orthonormal basis for Triangle Soup re-parameterization.""" # Normal edge1 = v2 - v1 edge2 = v3 - v1 r1 = np.cross(edge1, edge2) r1 = r1 / np.linalg.norm(r1) # Second tangent (from evidence) r2 = (v2 - v1) / np.linalg.norm(v2 - v1) # Third tangent r3 = gramschmidtstep(v3 - v1, r1orig, r2orig) r3 = r3 / np.linalg.norm(r3) return np.columnstack((r1, r2, r3)) def creategaussianmeshsplat(meshfaces, k, epsilon=1e-4): """ Initialize GaMeS Gaussians for a given mesh. Args: meshfaces: List of triangles, each triangle is (v1, v2, v3) where v are (3,) arrays. k: Number of Gaussians per face. epsilon: Small constant for normal scaling. Returns: Gaussians: List of Gaussian dictionaries. """ gaussians = [] for faceidx, (v1, v2, v3) in enumerate(meshfaces): # 1. Compute Face Basis RV = computefacebasis(v1, v2, v3) r1, r2, r3 = RV[:, 0], RV[:, 1], RV[:, 2] # 2. Compute Base Scaling m = (v1 + v2 + v3) / 3.0 s1 = epsilon s2 = np.linalg.norm(m - v1) s3 = np.dot(v2, r3) SV = np.diag([s1, s2, s3]) SigmaV = RV @ SV @ SV.T @ RV.T # 3. Create k Gaussians for this face for i in range(k): # Initialize barycentric coordinates alpha = np.random.dirichlet([1, 1, 1]) # Mean mu = alpha[0] v1 + alpha[1] v2 + alpha[2] v3 # Scale multiplier (trainable) rho = np.random.uniform(0.5, 1.5) # Covariance Sigma = rho SigmaV # Opacity and Color (trainable) sigma = np.random.uniform(0.1, 0.9) color = np.random.rand(3) gaussians.append({ 'faceidx': faceidx, 'alpha': alpha, 'rho': rho, 'mu': mu, 'Sigma': Sigma, 'sigma': sigma, 'color': color }) return gaussians def createtrianglesoupfromgs(gslist, epsilon=1e-4): """ Convert standard GS to GaMeS Triangle Soup. Args: gslist: List of standard GS objects with mean, rotation (3x3), scale (3,). epsilon: Small constant. Returns: GaMeS Gaussians (same structure as creategaussianmeshsplat). """ gaussians = [] for gs in gslist: m = gs.mean R = gs.rotation # 3x3 matrix [r1, r2, r3] s = gs.scale # [s1, s2, s3] r1, r2, r3 = R[:, 0], R[:, 1], R[:, 2] # Define vertices v1 = m v2 = m + s[1] r2 v3 = m + s[2] r3 # Re-parameterize # Compute new basis from vertices using Soup method Rhat = computesoupbasis(v1, v2, v3, r1, r2) rhat1, rhat2, rhat3 = Rhat[:, 0], Rhat[:, 1], Rhat[:, 2] # Compute new scales shat1 = epsilon shat2 = np.linalg.norm(v2 - v1) shat3 = np.dot(v3 - v1, rhat3) Shat = np.diag([shat1, shat2, shat3]) Sigmahat = Rhat @ Shat @ Shat.T @ Rhat.T # Create GaMeS Gaussian alpha = np.array([1/3, 1/3, 1/3]) mu = alpha[0]v1 + alpha[1]v2 + alpha[2]v3 gaussians.append({ 'faceidx': None, 'alpha': alpha, 'rho': 1.0, 'mu': mu, 'Sigma': Sigmahat, 'sigma': gs.opacity, 'color': gs.color }) return gaussians Face Size Variation: If mesh faces vary significantly in size, using a fixed number k of Gaussians per face leads to poor resolution on large faces and redundancy on small ones. The solution is to subdivide large faces into smaller parts before initialization. Numerical Stability: The normal scaling parameter s1 is set to \epsilon rather than 0 to avoid numerical problems in the covariance matrix inversion or decomposition. Cross-Triangle Handling: As noted in the parent Mesh-embedded representation, if optimization moves an embedding point across a triangle boundary, the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability [Parent, S2]. Failure to handle this causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up [Parent]. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(n \cdot k) where n is the number of faces and k is Gaussians per face. Rendering is O(N) where N = n \cdot k is the total number of Gaussians, identical to standard GS. Memory Complexity: O(N) for Gaussian attributes. The mesh storage is O(F) where F is the number of faces. Strengths: Enables real-time editing and deformation of Gaussians via mesh manipulation. Avoids expensive pre-processing stages required by methods like SuGaR. Supports both mesh-initialized and mesh-free inputs. Limitations: Requires a mesh (or estimated mesh) as input. Performance degrades if mesh faces are highly irregular in size without subdivision. When to use: When the goal is to edit, animate, or condition 3D Gaussians using mesh-based controls (e.g., facial expressions using FLAME). When not to use: When no mesh structure is desired or available and Triangle Soup estimation is insufficient; when high-frequency details require adaptive Gaussian density not tied to mesh topology. GaMeS was introduced in the paper "GaMeS: Mesh-based adapting and modification of Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting, which lacks a well-defined approach for conditioning hundreds of thousands of Gaussian components. The method was demonstrated on datasets including Mip-NeRF360 and synthetic objects, and specifically used for initializing human meshes using the FLAME framework to modify facial expressions. It differs from SuGaR by not requiring SDF regularization or two-stage training. name: SuGaR / Gaussian Frosting
head: SuGaR, Gaussian Frosting
body: SuGaR (Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting) and Gaussian Frosting are methods that extract a canonical triangle mesh from an optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene to enable explicit mesh editing while preserving high-fidelity rendering. SuGaR aligns Gaussians to a surface and extracts a base mesh via Poisson reconstruction, while Gaussian Frosting binds Gaussians to this mesh surface for hybrid rendering, introducing an adaptive Gaussian layer with variable thickness to enhance detail and volumetric effects. This approach combines the editing capabilities of explicit meshes with the rendering quality of differentiable Gaussian splatting. Inputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting scene (means \mu, covariances \Sigma, colors, opacities); optional user-defined mesh deformations. Outputs: Canonical triangle mesh \mathcal{M}; Gaussian parameters parameterized relative to \mathcal{M}; rendered images. Data Structures: 1. Canonical Mesh \mathcal{M}: Defined by vertices V, normals n, and faces F. 2. Gaussian Embeddings: Each Gaussian i is defined by an embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\}, where k is the triangle index, (u, v) are barycentric coordinates, and d is the normal displacement. 3. Adaptive Layer: Gaussian Frosting introduces a parameterization to constrain Gaussians within a layer of variable thickness around the base mesh. Steps: 1. Base Mesh Extraction: Extract a base mesh \mathcal{M} from the optimized 3DGS representation. SuGaR achieves this by aligning Gaussians to a surface and performing Poisson reconstruction. 2. Parameterization: Bind each Gaussian to the extracted mesh using the embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\}. This constrains the Gaussians to the surface geometry. 3. Adaptive Layer Introduction (Gaussian Frosting): Introduce an adaptive Gaussian layer with variable thickness around the base mesh to enhance fine details and volumetric effects. The Gaussians are parameterized to remain within this layer. 4. Deformation and Rendering: When the base mesh is manipulated (e.g., via skeletal animation or direct editing), the Gaussians are automatically adjusted. The posed position \mu{pose} is computed by deforming the canonical position \mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano} using the mesh deformation function \text{Deform}(\cdot). The rotation and scale are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence. 5. Cross-Triangle Handling: If optimization or deformation causes barycentric coordinates to move outside the current triangle (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability. Formulas: Canonical Position: \mu{cano} = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 Canonical Normal: n{cano} = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 Posed Position: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) Posed Rotation: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, where \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Posed Scale: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeposedgaussian(gaussian, mesh, posetransform): """ Computes the posed position, rotation, and scale for a single Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Dict with keys 'k', 'u', 'v', 'd', 'qcanon', 'scanon'. mesh: Dict with 'faces' (list of dicts with 'vertices', 'vertexnormals', 'vertexquaternions'). posetransform: Function that applies deformation to mesh vertices. Returns: mupose: Posed mean position. qpose: Posed rotation quaternion. spose: Posed scale vector. """ k = gaussian['k'] u = gaussian['u'] v = gaussian['v'] d = gaussian['d'] face = mesh.faces[k] V1, V2, V3 = face['vertices'] n1, n2, n3 = face['vertexnormals'] # Canonical position and normal mucano = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 ncano = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 # Posed position displacedpos = mucano + d ncano mupose = posetransform(displacedpos) # Posed rotation q1, q2, q3 = face['vertexquaternions'] deltaq = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 qpose = deltaq gaussian['qcanon'] # Posed scale V1pose, V2pose, V3pose = posetransform(V1), posetransform(V2), posetransform(V3) Apose = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2pose - V1pose, V3pose - V1pose)) Acano = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2 - V1, V3 - V1)) spose = (Apose / Acano) gaussian['scanon'] return mupose, qpose, spose Parameters: Poisson reconstruction depth/resolution: Not given in the sources. Adaptive layer thickness: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Boundary Crossing: Failure to handle barycentric coordinate boundaries causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up. Mesh Degeneracy: If the canonical triangle area A{cano} is zero or near-zero, the scale computation s{pose} becomes numerically unstable. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Enables real-time deformation when combined with mesh-based Gaussian splatting representation. Strengths: Combines mesh editing ability with 3DGS rendering quality. Enhances detail and volumetric effects via adaptive layer. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the extracted base mesh. SuGaR was introduced to address the lack of explicit geometry in 3D Gaussian Splatting, allowing for mesh extraction and editing. Gaussian Frosting extends this by introducing an adaptive layer for better detail preservation. These methods are used in applications requiring both high-fidelity rendering and explicit mesh manipulation, such as character animation and scene editing. name: Mesh to DRK Conversion
head: Mesh2DRK
body: Mesh to DRK Conversion is a training-free procedure that converts traditional triangle and polygon mesh faces into Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) primitives for seamless integration into radiance field scenes. Unlike existing splatting methods (2D-GS, 3D-GS, 3D-HGS, GES) which fail to integrate traditional assets seamlessly, this method provides a direct, training-free conversion pipeline. It bridges the gap between millions of traditional 3D assets and fast, high-quality reconstruction representations, enabling unified rendering, VR digital world creation, and AR scene enhancement. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A traditional 3D mesh \mathcal{M} defined by polygon faces (typically triangles). Output: A list of DRK primitives representing the mesh geometry. Data Structures: Each primitive is defined by its endpoints, sharpness parameters, and curvature parameters. The specific internal layout of a DRK primitive is not detailed in the sources, but the conversion logic maps mesh vertices directly to DRK endpoints. Steps: 1. Vertex Mapping: For each polygon face in the input mesh, place the DRK endpoints directly at the polygon's vertices. 2. Curvature Initialization: Set both the L1 and L2 curvature parameters for all generated DRK primitives to 1. 3. Sharpness Tuning: Adjust the parameters \tau and \eta to control the sharpness of the resulting DRK primitives. Parameters: \tau: Sharpness control parameter for DRK primitives. \eta: Sharpness control parameter for DRK primitives. L1 Curvature: Fixed value of 1. L2 Curvature: Fixed value of 1. Both \tau and \eta are tuned per asset; no fixed default is given. Pitfalls: The conversion process relies on fixed curvature values (L1=1, L2=1) that may not adapt to complex local geometry without manual tuning of \tau and \eta. While this avoids convergence issues associated with training-based methods, it requires manual adjustment for optimal results on complex assets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshtodrk(mesh): """ Converts a mesh into DRK primitives. Args: mesh: A mesh object with attributes 'faces' (list of dicts with 'vertexindices') and 'vertices' (list of 3D position arrays). Returns: drkprimitives: A list of DRK primitive dictionaries. """ drkprimitives = [] for face in mesh.faces: vertexindices = face['vertexindices'] vertices = [mesh.vertices[i] for i in vertexindices] primitive = { 'endpoints': vertices, 'tau': 1.0, 'eta': 1.0, 'l1curvature': 1.0, 'l2curvature': 1.0 } drkprimitives.append(primitive) return drkprimitives Time Complexity: The conversion is O(N) where N is the number of faces in the mesh, as it involves a direct mapping of vertices to primitives without iterative optimization. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is proportional to the number of primitives generated, which is directly related to the mesh resolution (number of faces/vertices). Strengths: The method is training-free, avoiding convergence issues and the need for training data rendering or model optimization. It allows for the effortless conversion of traditional assets into DRK scenes. Limitations: It relies on fixed curvature values (L1=1, L2=1) which may not adapt to complex local geometry without manual tuning of \tau and \eta. When to use: When integrating traditional 3D assets (e.g., flowers, leaves, detailed textures) into DRK scenes for unified rendering, VR, or AR applications. When not to use: When high-fidelity adaptation to complex local geometry is required without manual parameter tuning, or when the asset is already in a format compatible with other splatting methods that might offer better automatic adaptation. The method was introduced in the paper "Deformable Radial Kernel Splatting". It addresses the limitation of existing splatting methods (2D-GS, 3D-GS, 3D-HGS, GES) in seamlessly integrating with traditional 3D assets. The DRK framework provides a versatile representation that allows for this conversion, bridging the gap between traditional 3D assets and fast, high-quality reconstruction representations. Deformable Radial Kernel Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.02004, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Gaussian Extraction Algorithm
head: Discretization Algorithm, Octree-Guided Geometry Sampling, Optimizing Geometry with GauPF, Octree-guided Sampling
body: The Gaussian Extraction Algorithm extracts discrete 3D Gaussian primitives from continuous Gaussian Splatting Functions (GauPF) at arbitrary densities. It solves the problem of converting a continuous, neural-network-parameterized probability field into a finite set of splattable Gaussians, analogous to how Marching Cubes extracts meshes from Signed Distance Functions. Unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed initialization or mesh embedding constraints, this algorithm uses an octree-guided progressive sampling strategy to locate high-probability regions, followed by gradient-based optimization to refine those locations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained Gaussian Probability Function \psi{pf} (neural network), a Gaussian Color Function \psi{cf}, a Gaussian Transform Function \psi{tf}, a triplane representation t, and a target number of Gaussians N. Output: A set of N discrete 3D Gaussians \hat{G} = \{\hat{\sigma}i, \hat{c}i, \hat{r}i, \hat{s}i, \hat{o}i\}{i=1}^N, where \hat{\sigma}i is the center, \hat{c}i is the color, and \{\hat{r}i, \hat{s}i, \hat{o}i\} are rotation, scale, and opacity. Data Structures: Octree: A hierarchical 3D grid used to progressively subdivide space. The depth is limited to L layers. Proxy Points: A set of learnable 3D coordinates \{\rhoi\}{i=1}^N representing coarse initial locations of Gaussian centers. Triplane t: A set of feature planes used for attribute interpolation. Steps: 1. Octree Construction: Build an octree progressively over L layers. At each depth, identify 3D regions with large probabilities using \psi{pf} and subdivide only those regions. 2. Coarse Sampling: After L layers of subdivision, uniformly sample N 3D points within the leaf nodes of the octree. These points form the initial proxy points \{\rhoi\}{i=1}^N. 3. Geometry Optimization: Optimize the positions of the proxy points \rhoi to maximize the probability assigned by \psi{pf}. The positions \rhoi are treated as learnable parameters. 4. Attribute Extraction: Once the optimized centers \hat{\sigma}i are found, extract color and transform attributes using the triplane t and the respective predictor functions. Formulas: Geometry Loss: The proxy points are optimized to maximize the Gaussian probability. The loss function is defined as: L{Geo} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \psi{pf}(\rhoi) where \rhoi are the learnable positions of the proxy points. Color Extraction: The color \hat{c}i for the i-th Gaussian is extracted by interpolating the triplane t at the optimized center \hat{\sigma}i and passing it through the color predictor \psi{cf}: \hat{c}i = \psi{cf}(\text{interp}(t, \hat{\sigma}i)) Transform Extraction: The rotation \hat{r}i, scale \hat{s}i, and opacity \hat{o}i are extracted similarly: \{\hat{r}i, \hat{s}i, \hat{o}i\} = \psi{tf}(\text{interp}(t, \hat{\sigma}i)) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianextractionalgorithm(pfnet, cfnet, tfnet, triplane, N, L, bounds, lr, maxiter): """ Extracts N discrete Gaussians from continuous Gaussian Splatting Functions. Args: pfnet: Gaussian Probability Function network (psipf) cfnet: Gaussian Color Function network (psicf) tfnet: Gaussian Transform Function network (psitf) triplane: Feature planes t for attribute interpolation N: Number of target Gaussians L: Number of octree subdivision layers bounds: 3D bounding box [minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz] lr: Learning rate for optimization maxiter: Number of optimization iterations Returns: gaussians: List of N Gaussian dictionaries with sigma, c, r, s, o """ # Step 1 & 2: Octree-guided coarse sampling # Build octree over L layers, subdividing regions where pfnet probability is high octree = buildoctree(pfnet, bounds, L) # Uniformly sample N points from leaf nodes as initial proxy points rhoi proxypoints = sampleoctreeleaves(octree, N) # Step 3: Geometry Optimization # Proxy points are learnable parameters proxypoints.requiresgrad = True optimizer = Adam([proxypoints], lr=lr) for in range(maxiter): probabilities = pfnet(proxypoints) loss = -np.mean(probabilities) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() sigmahat = proxypoints.detach() # Step 4: Attribute Extraction gaussians = [] for i in range(N): center = sigmahat[i] features = interpolatetriplane(triplane, center) chat = cfnet(features) rhat, shat, ohat = tfnet(features) gaussians.append({'sigma': center, 'c': chat, 'r': rhat, 's': shat, 'o': ohat}) return gaussians def buildoctree(pfnet, bounds, maxdepth): """Recursively subdivide bounding box where pfnet probability exceeds threshold.""" def subdivide(nodebounds, depth): if depth >= maxdepth: return [nodebounds] mid = (nodebounds[:3] + nodebounds[3:]) / 2.0 children = [] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): childmin = np.array([nodebounds[i2] if i==0 else mid[i2], nodebounds[j2+1] if j==0 else mid[j2+1], nodebounds[k2+2] if k==0 else mid[k2+2]]) childmax = np.array([mid[0] if i==0 else nodebounds[3], mid[1] if j==0 else nodebounds[4], mid[2] if k==0 else nodebounds[5]]) childbounds = np.concatenate([childmin, childmax]) center = (childmin + childmax) / 2.0 if pfnet(center.reshape(1, -3)) > 0.5: children.extend(subdivide(childbounds, depth + 1)) return children if children else [nodebounds] return subdivide(bounds, 0) def sampleoctreeleaves(octree, N): """Uniformly sample N points from leaf node bounds.""" points = [] for bounds in octree: points.append(np.random.uniform(bounds[:3], bounds[3:])) points = np.array(points) if len(points) < N: points = np.vstack([points] (N // len(points) + 1)) return points[:N] def Adam(params, lr): """Minimal Adam optimizer implementation.""" state = {'m': [np.zeroslike(p) for p in params], 'v': [np.zeroslike(p) for p in params], 't': 0} def zerograd(): for p in params: p.grad = np.zeroslike(p) def step(): state['t'] += 1 beta1, beta2, eps = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8 for i, p in enumerate(params): state['m'][i] = beta1 state['m'][i] + (1 - beta1) p.grad state['v'][i] = beta2 state['v'][i] + (1 - beta2) p.grad2 mhat = state['m'][i] / (1 - beta1state['t']) vhat = state['v'][i] / (1 - beta2state['t']) p -= lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + eps) return type('Adam', (), {'zerograd': zerograd, 'step': step}) def interpolatetriplane(triplane, center): """Trilinear interpolation of triplane features at center.""" features = [] for plane in triplane: x, y, z = center u, v = np.clip((x - plane.minx) / plane.width, 0, 1), np.clip((y - plane.miny) / plane.height, 0, 1) features.append(plane.data[int(vplane.H), int(uplane.W)]) return np.concatenate(features) Parameters: N: The number of Gaussians to extract. The algorithm supports arbitrary numbers, enabling scalable generation. L: The number of octree subdivision layers. Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Max Iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Naive uniform sampling across the entire 3D space is computationally expensive and fails to accurately locate high-probability regions. The octree-guided approach mitigates this by focusing computation on relevant regions. Arbitrary Density: The method allows generating Gaussians at any density N, unlike fixed-grid methods. Precision: Gradient optimization of proxy points may converge to local maxima in the probability field; multiple restarts or adaptive thresholds are recommended. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The complexity depends on the octree depth L, the number of subdivisions, and the optimization iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the octree structure and the number of proxy points N. Measured Performance: Evaluated on ShapeNet airplane and chair classes using FID and KID metrics. Strengths: Scalability: Can generate Gaussian primitives at arbitrary numbers. Quality: Generates native 3DGS without voxelization, preserving unimpaired quality. Generality: Applicable to unconditional generation, text/image conditional generation, and point-to-gaussian generation. Limitations: Requires a trained continuous Gaussian Splatting Function (GauPF) as input. Optimization of proxy points requires iterative gradient descent, which adds time to the extraction process compared to direct sampling. When to use: When you need to convert a continuous, learned Gaussian Splatting Function into a discrete set of splats for rendering or further processing, especially when the number of splats needs to be flexible. When not to use: When real-time extraction is required without optimization overhead, or when the input is already discrete Gaussians. The Gaussian Extraction Algorithm was introduced in the DiffGS (Functional Gaussian Splatting Diffusion) paper. It was designed to complement the generation of continuous Gaussian Splatting Functions by a latent diffusion model, providing a way to discretize these functions into usable 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives. The approach is inspired by the Marching Cubes algorithm, which extracts meshes from Signed Distance Functions. name: GauMesh
head: GauMesh [S2, unofficial]
body: GauMesh is a hybrid representation for dynamic human head avatars that combines tracked textured triangle meshes with canonical 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of high-fidelity dynamic head reconstruction from few input views by jointly optimizing the mesh and Gaussians, using a learnable deformation field to handle temporal changes. It sets itself apart from pure Gaussian splatting methods by maintaining explicit geometric structure via the mesh, which aids in deformation coherence and texture tracking. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of input views (images), a template triangle mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices V, normals n, and faces F. Outputs: Posed 3D Gaussians (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, color c, opacity \alpha) and a deformed textured mesh for each frame. Data Structures: 1. Triangle Mesh \mathcal{M}: Stores vertex positions, per-vertex normals, and per-vertex quaternions q for rotation interpolation. 2. Gaussian Set: Each Gaussian i is defined by an embedding tuple Ei = \{k, u, v, d\}: k: Integer index of the triangle k \in F in the canonical mesh. (u, v): Barycentric coordinates within triangle k, constrained such that u \ge 0, v \ge 0, u+v \le 1. d: Scalar normal displacement along the interpolated surface normal. Additional attributes: Canonical rotation \bar{q}, canonical scale \bar{s}, color c, and opacity \alpha. Canonical Position and Normal: The canonical mean \mu{cano} and normal n{cano} are computed via Phong interpolation on the canonical mesh: \mu{cano} = \mathcal{V}(k, u, v) = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 n{cano} = \mathcal{N}(k, u, v) = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 where Vj and nj are the vertices and per-vertex normals of triangle k. Posed State Computation: When the mesh is deformed by an animation function \text{Deform}(\cdot), the posed position \mu{pose} is derived by applying the deformation to the displaced canonical position: \mu{pose} = \text{Deform}(\mu{cano} + d \cdot n{cano}) The posed rotation q{pose} and scale s{pose} are derived from mesh attributes to maintain coherence: Rotation: Per-vertex quaternions q1, q2, q3 are interpolated using barycentric weights to get \delta q, which is then combined with the canonical rotation \bar{q}: q{pose} = \delta q \bar{q}, \quad \delta q = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 Scale: Scale is proportional to the area change of the embedded triangle relative to the canonical state: s{pose} = \left( \frac{A{pose}}{A{cano}} \right) \bar{s} where A{pose} and A{cano} are the areas of the triangle in the posed and canonical states, respectively. Deformation Network: A multi-resolution Hexplane and a shallow MLP are used to get features for 3D Gaussians and deform each vertex in the mesh using a displacement vector to translate it to a new position. Cross-Triangle Handling: Barycentric coordinates are differentiable only within a single triangle. If optimization moves an embedding point across a boundary (u < 0, v < 0, or u+v > 1), the embedding must be re-expressed in the neighboring triangle to maintain differentiability. Failure to handle this causes Gaussians to stick to boundaries and pile up. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeposedgaussian(gaussian, mesh, posetransform): """ Computes the posed position, rotation, and scale for a single Gaussian. Args: gaussian: Dict with keys 'k', 'u', 'v', 'd', 'qcanon', 'scanon'. mesh: Dict with 'faces' (list of dicts with 'vertices', 'vertexnormals', 'vertexquaternions'). posetransform: Function that applies deformation to mesh vertices. Returns: mupose: Posed mean position. qpose: Posed rotation quaternion. spose: Posed scale vector. """ k = gaussian['k'] u = gaussian['u'] v = gaussian['v'] d = gaussian['d'] face = mesh.faces[k] V1, V2, V3 = face['vertices'] n1, n2, n3 = face['vertexnormals'] # Canonical position and normal mucano = u V1 + v V2 + (1 - u - v) V3 ncano = u n1 + v n2 + (1 - u - v) n3 # Posed position displacedpos = mucano + d ncano mupose = posetransform(displacedpos) # Posed rotation q1, q2, q3 = face['vertexquaternions'] deltaq = u q1 + v q2 + (1 - u - v) q3 qpose = deltaq gaussian['qcanon'] # Posed scale V1pose, V2pose, V3pose = posetransform(V1), posetransform(V2), posetransform(V3) Apose = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2pose - V1pose, V3pose - V1pose)) Acano = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(V2 - V1, V3 - V1)) spose = (Apose / Acano) gaussian['scanon'] return mupose, qpose, spose Constructs a graph during precomputation, determining k-nearest control points for Gaussian endpoints and sampled points. Applies the same graph deformation to both the Gaussian radiance field and the vertices of the original mesh. Precomputation overhead (graph construction, sampling, k-nearest determination) typically requires 1 to 3 seconds for most datasets. Updates logical coordinates w'i = wi + \Delta wi and vertex positions v'j = vj + \Delta vj. Computes new mean position \mu'i = f(w'i, v'{j1}, v'{j2}, v'{j3}) + w'{i3} n'j l'j, where n'j is the deformed normal and l'j is the deformed scaling factor. Updates covariance/scale \sigma'i = f(w'i, \Delta \sigma{j1}, \Delta \sigma{j2}, \Delta \sigma{j3}) \cdot \sigmai, color c'i = f(w'i, \Delta c{j1}, \Delta c{j2}, \Delta c{j3}) + ci, size s'i = \Delta lj \cdot f(w'i, \Delta s{j1}, \Delta s{j2}, \Delta s{j3}) \cdot si, and rotation q'i = \Delta nj \cdot f(w'i, \Delta q{j1}, \Delta q{j2}, \Delta q{j3}) \cdot qi. Scaling factor change is \Delta lj = l'j / lj. Not given in the sources. GauMesh was introduced as part of the recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting for dynamic scene reconstruction. It specifically targets high-fidelity head avatar learning from few input views. The method was cited in surveys on dynamic scene reconstruction and real-time rendering. name: MiraGe
head: Editable 2D Images using Gaussian Splatting
body: MiraGe is a method for editing 2D images by temporarily interpreting selected regions as 3D objects via Gaussian Splatting, allowing for intuitive manipulation and transformation before rendering back to 2D. It distinguishes itself from generative AI tools (e.g., ControlNet, Firefly) by using the source image as a strict reference for explicit 3D reconstruction rather than synthesizing new content, and from Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) like SIREN by providing addressable Cartesian coordinates. It builds on Mesh-embedded representation by utilizing Gaussian Mesh Splatting (GaMeS) to treat flat Gaussians as triangle soups. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D image and a user-defined selection region. Output: An edited 2D image. Data Structures: The method relies on the GaMeS parametrization where each flat Gaussian is represented as three points in a "triangle soup". This allows the Gaussian splats to be interpreted as traditional CGI meshes, subject to warping and modification. The system uses two opposing cameras positioned along the Y-axis, symmetrically aligned around the origin and directed towards one another. Steps: 1. Mirror Setup: Create a "mirror" image of the selection by horizontally flipping the image. Position two cameras along the Y-axis: Camera 1 reconstructs the original image, and Camera 2 models the mirror reflection. 2. 3D Interpretation: Use GaMeS parametrization to extract the selected area into a Gaussian/mesh representation. The 2D image is conceptualized as a translucent tracing paper sheet embedded in 3D space. 3. Deformation: Apply deformation to the 3D representation. MiraGe offers two approaches: Amorphous (directly utilizes GaMeS, allowing the extracted selection to move freely in 3D space) and Graphite (constrains Gaussians to 2D space during initialization and training). 4. Physics Simulation (Optional): The Gaussian Splat acts as a guiding proxy for an equivalent mesh version. The image is reconstructed using the Material Points Method (MPM) technique. 5. Rendering: Render the deformed 3D representation back to 2D. Parts of the image not influenced by the deformation are hidden from the user during the process to prevent visible context shifts until completion. Parameters: Deformation Mode: Amorphous or Graphite. Camera Alignment: Symmetric along Y-axis around origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tears/Rifts: The Amorphous approach may produce "tears" or rift artifacts where the edge of the deformation aligns with the unaffected portion of the image. Context Visibility: Unaffected parts of the image are not visible to the user during editing; failure to manage this visibility can lead to disorienting edits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def mirageedit(image, selectionmask): # 1. Mirror Setup: Create mirror image by horizontally flipping mirrorimage = image[:,::-1,:] # 2. Camera Setup: Two opposing cameras along Y-axis, symmetric around origin camoriginal = {'pos': np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]), 'target': np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0])} cammirror = {'pos': np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]), 'target': np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0])} # 3. 3D Interpretation: Extract selection into Gaussian/mesh representation # GaMeS parametrization converts the 2D selection into a triangle soup mesh mesh3d = gamesextract(image, selectionmask, camoriginal) meshmirror3d = gamesextract(mirrorimage, selectionmask, cammirror) # 4. Deformation: Apply transformation to the 3D representation # Amorphous mode allows free 3D movement; Graphite constrains to 2D deformedmesh = applydeformation(mesh3d, mode='amorphous') # Optional: Physics Simulation using Material Points Method (MPM) # deformedmesh = mpmsimulate(deformedmesh) # 5. Rendering: Render deformed 3D representation back to 2D # Unaffected image parts are hidden from the user during the process editedimage = renderbackto2d(deformedmesh, camoriginal) return editedimage def gamesextract(img, mask, cam): # Standard GaMeS extraction: projects image pixels onto triangle soup using camera intrinsics/extrinsics pass # GaMeS extraction logic not detailed in sources def applydeformation(mesh, mode): # Apply deformation to mesh vertices if mode == 'graphite': mesh.vertices[:, 2] = 0.0 # Constrain to 2D plane return mesh def renderbackto2d(mesh, cam): # Rasterize deformed mesh back to 2D image plane return np.zeroslike(mesh.vertices) Performance: Tests were conducted on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 laptop and NVIDIA RTX 2080 hardware. Quality: Outperforms prior frameworks (SIREN, WIRE, I-NGP, NeuRBF) on Kodak Lossless True Color Image Suite and DIV2K validation sets using SNR and MS-SIM metrics. Strengths: Explicit addressable coordinates; intuitive 3D manipulation of 2D content; high-fidelity reflections via mirror-camera setup. Limitations: Amorphous mode may cause tearing artifacts; requires external physics engines (e.g., Blender, TaichiElements) for advanced simulation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. MiraGe was introduced in the paper "MiraGe: Editable 2D Images using Gaussian Splatting" by researchers from Jagiellonian University and the University of Cambridge, published on October 3, 2024. It builds on GaMeS parametrization, developed by a group including two of the paper's authors. The Material Points Method (MPM) technique used for reconstruction was first outlined in a 2018 CSAIL paper. The concept of using GSplat in 2D space was prominently presented in the 2024 "GaussianImage" collaboration, which achieved 1000fps inference but has no implementation related to image editing. MiraGe can be integrated into Blender and uses external physics engines like those in Blender or TaichiElements. name: Inverse Gaussian Splattling
head: 2D to 3D Back-projection, Back-projection of 2D Gaussians, Geometric Back-projection, Inverse Gaussian Splattering, Inverse splatting
body: Inverse Gaussian Splattling is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian primitives by back-projecting optimized 2D Gaussian kernels from image space into world space. It solves the problem of generating high-quality initial geometric parameters (position, rotation, scale) for new 3D Gaussians from 2D renderings, specifically handling foreground-background ambiguity in boundary regions. It differs from standard initialization by using Weighted Principal Component Analysis (WPCA) on clustered 3D points derived from depth maps, followed by a scaling calibration step to align the projected 3D covariance with the original 2D target. Inputs: gaussian2d: A 2D Gaussian primitive with center (u, v), covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma}{2D}, and opacity/weight distribution. depthmap: A rendered depth map corresponding to the camera view. camera: Camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. Outputs: position: 3D world-space coordinates. rotation: 3D Gaussian rotation (quaternion). scaling: 3D Gaussian scaling factors. lobeorientation: Unit vector for opacity lobe orientation. T: Opacity lobe width parameter. beta: Opacity lobe sharpness parameter. color: Base color. opacity: Base opacity. shcoeffs: Higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients. Data Structures: pixelsworld: List of dictionaries containing 3D position, depth, and 2D Gaussian weight for each covered pixel. groups: List of clusters from hierarchical clustering. Parameters: threshold: Initial clustering distance threshold set to 5 \cdot \deltad, where \deltad is the world-space distance between adjacent pixels at the Gaussian center's depth. thresholdmultiplier: Factor by which to increase the clustering threshold if clustering fails. Value: 1.5. Steps: 1. Compute 3D Coordinates: For all pixels covered by the 2D Gaussian kernel, compute the 3D world coordinates using the depth map and camera parameters. Assign each point a weight equal to the 2D Gaussian distribution value at that pixel. 2. Foreground-Background Separation (Clustering): Initialize threshold to 5 \cdot \deltad. Perform hierarchical clustering using single-linkage merging on pixelsworld using threshold as the distance limit. Check if any cluster contains at least 3 points and covers the Gaussian center's pixel. If no such cluster exists, select the largest cluster with at least 3 points. If clustering fails to produce a valid cluster, increase threshold by multiplying by 1.5 and repeat clustering. 3. Weighted PCA (WPCA): Select the valid cluster from Step 2 as filteredpoints. Determine if the Gaussian center's pixel is included in filteredpoints (boolean INCLUDECENTER). Compute WPCA on filteredpoints using the 2D Gaussian weights. The principal axes form the rotation matrix R (converted to quaternion). The standard deviations \sigma1, \sigma2, \sigma3 from WPCA form the base scaling vector. 4. Position Determination: If INCLUDECENTER is true, sample the depth value d from the depthmap at the Gaussian center (u, v). If INCLUDECENTER is false, compute the weighted average depth \bar{d} of filteredpoints, where weights are the 2D Gaussian distribution values. Convert (u, v, d) to world space using the camera parameters to get position. 5. Scaling Calibration: Project the current 3D Gaussian (defined by position, rotation, and base scaling from WPCA) into the 2D image space to obtain the projected covariance matrix \Sigma{2D}. The relationship is given by: \Sigma{2D} = J W R S (J W R S)^T where J \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times3} is the Jacobian of the projective transformation, W is the world-to-view matrix, R is the rotation matrix, and S = \text{diag}(\sigma1, \sigma2, \sigma3) is the scaling diagonal matrix. Define Q = \Sigma{2D} / k^2, where k is the target scaling coefficient. Minimize the Frobenius norm between the projected covariance and the target 2D covariance \hat{\Sigma}{2D}: \mink ||\Sigma{2D} - \hat{\Sigma}{2D}||F The solution for k is: k = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{ij} Q{ij} \hat{\Sigma}{2D{ij}}}{||Q||F^2}} where ||Q||F is the Frobenius norm of Q. Update the scaling: S{final} = k \cdot \text{diag}(\sigma1, \sigma2, \sigma3). 6. Opacity Lobe and Color Initialization: Opacity Lobe Orientation: Set to the unit vector from the Gaussian centroid to the camera. Width T: Initialize as c \bar{\theta}i / \pi, where \bar{\theta}i is the minimum angle between the viewing vector and the lobe orientation for visible cameras Ci, and c is a constant. Sharpness \beta: Initialize to 0. Color/Opacity: Initialize base color and opacity to the 2D primitive counterparts. Zero-initialize higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inversesplatting(gaussian2d, depthmap, camera): # Step 1: Compute 3D coordinates for all pixels covered by the 2D Gaussian pixelsworld = [] for u, v in gaussian2d.supportpixels(): d = depthmap[u, v] if d > 0: pixelsworld.append({ 'pos': camera.unproject(u, v, d), 'depth': d, 'weight': gaussian2d.density(u, v) }) # Initial threshold: 5 world-space distance between adjacent pixels at center depth centerdepth = depthmap[gaussian2d.center] deltad = camera.pixeldistanceatdepth(centerdepth) threshold = 5.0 deltad groups = [] while True: groups = clusterpoints(pixelsworld, threshold) center3d = camera.unproject(gaussian2d.center[0], gaussian2d.center[1], centerdepth) validcluster = None # Priority: cluster with >=3 points covering center for cluster in groups: if len(cluster) >= 3 and any(dist(p['pos'], center3d) < 1e-6 for p in cluster): validcluster = cluster break if validcluster is None: # Fallback: largest cluster with >=3 points validclusters = [c for c in groups if len(c) >= 3] if validclusters: validcluster = max(validclusters, key=len) else: threshold = threshold 1.5 continue break filteredpoints = validcluster INCLUDECENTER = any(dist(p['pos'], center3d) < 1e-6 for p in filteredpoints) # Step 2: Weighted Principal Component Analysis (WPCA) rotation, scalingbase = WPCA(filteredpoints) # Step 3: Position determination if INCLUDECENTER: depth = centerdepth else: totalweight = sum(p['weight'] for p in filteredpoints) depth = sum(p['depth'] p['weight'] for p in filteredpoints) / totalweight position = camera.unproject(gaussian2d.center[0], gaussian2d.center[1], depth) # Step 4: Scaling calibration # Q = Sigma2D / k^2. Computing with base scaling (k=1) yields Q directly. Q = projectcovariance(rotation, scalingbase, position, camera) numerator = sum(Q[i][j] gaussian2d.cov[i][j] for i in range(2) for j in range(2)) denominator = frobeniusnorm(Q) 2 k = sqrt(numerator / denominator) scaling = k scalingbase # Step 5: Opacity Lobe and Color Initialization lobeorientation = normalize(camera.position - position) # T initialization: c minangle / pi visiblecameras = camera.getfrustumvisiblecameras() minangle = min(anglebetween(camera.viewvector(c), lobeorientation) for c in visiblecameras) T = c minangle / pi beta = 0.0 color = gaussian2d.color opacity = gaussian2d.opacity shcoeffs = [0.0] (gaussian2d.shdegree + 1) 2 return position, rotation, scaling, lobeorientation, T, beta, color, opacity, shcoeffs def clusterpoints(points, threshold): groups = [] for p in points: found = False for g in groups: if any(dist(p['pos'], q['pos']) <= threshold for q in g): g.append(p) found = True break if not found: groups.append([p]) return groups def WPCA(points): totalweight = sum(p['weight'] for p in points) centroid = sum(p['pos'] p['weight'] for p in points) / totalweight cov = sum((p['pos'] - centroid) @ (p['pos'] - centroid).T p['weight'] for p in points) / totalweight eigenvalues, eigenvectors = torch.linalg.eigh(cov) rotation = matrixtoquaternion(eigenvectors) scalingbase = sqrt(eigenvalues) return rotation, scalingbase def projectcovariance(rotation, scaling, position, camera): R = quaterniontomatrix(rotation) S = torch.diag(scaling) W = camera.extrinsics J = camera.jacobian(position) Sigma3D = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T Sigma2D = J @ W @ Sigma3D @ W.T @ J.T return Sigma2D[:2,:2] def frobeniusnorm(M): return sqrt(sum(M[i][j]2 for i in range(M.shape[0]) for j in range(M.shape[1]))) def dist(a, b): return sqrt(sum((a[i]-b[i])2 for i in range(3))) def normalize(v): return v / sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) def anglebetween(a, b): costheta = sum(a[i]b[i] for i in range(len(a))) / (sqrt(sum(x2 for x in a)) sqrt(sum(x2 for x in b))) return acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta))) Not given in the sources. Inverse Gaussian Splattling was introduced in "Augmented Radiance Field: A General Framework for Enhanced Gaussian Splatting" (ICLR 2026). It addresses the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting initialization by incorporating view-dependent opacity models (based on Phong shading) which require careful initialization of opacity lobes. The method back-projects 2D Gaussians optimized in image space to 3D space to serve as initializations for new 3D Gaussians, improving reconstruction fidelity, particularly in complex radiance distributions. During the final joint optimization stage, learning rates are configured as 0.000016 for position, 0.001 for diffuse color, 0.001/20 for higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients, 0.02 for opacity, 0.002 for scaling, 0.0005 for rotation, 0.001 for opacity lobe orientation, 0.0002 for opacity lobe width T, and 0.002 for sharpness \beta. name: Occupancy-Opacity Factorization
head: factorized opacity, sigma-alpha factorization
body: Occupancy-Opacity Factorization decouples a Gaussian primitive's geometric presence from its optical properties by splitting the single standard opacity parameter into two learnable attributes: geometric occupancy (\sigma) and optical opacity (\alpha). This solves the problem where a single opacity parameter cannot simultaneously model a surface that is geometrically solid (for sharp reflections) yet optically clear (for light transmission). It sets itself apart from siblings like Textured-GS and Oriented Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling the probabilistic interaction of rays with the Gaussian substance, enabling deferred shading for high-frequency reflection modeling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance (geometry), color, and the new parameters \sigma and \alpha. Output: Rendered color and surface attributes (e.g., normals, roughness) for each pixel. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \sigmai \in [0, 1]: Geometric occupancy. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Optical opacity. \mathcal{G}i: The standard Gaussian weight (spatial falloff). Formulas: The effective opacity used for volumetric compositing is the product: \alpha{\text{eff}, i} = \sigmai \alphai Optical attenuation only occurs where the Gaussian is geometrically present. The probability pi that the i-th Gaussian is the first surface element with which a ray interacts is: pi = \sigmai \mathcal{G}i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj \mathcal{G}j) Here, \mathcal{G}i represents the Gaussian weight. The expected value of a surface attribute \mathbf{a} (e.g., normal or roughness) for the first-hit surface is computed as: \mathbf{A} = \sumi pi \mathbf{a}i This formulation treats the collection of Gaussians as a unified, probabilistic representation of a single surface, justifying deferred shading. Steps: 1. For each ray, sort intersecting Gaussians by depth. 2. Initialize transmittance T = 1.0. 3. For each Gaussian i in sorted order: a. Compute interaction probability pi = \sigmai \mathcal{G}i T. b. Accumulate surface attributes: \mathbf{A} \leftarrow \mathbf{A} + pi \mathbf{a}i. c. Compute effective opacity \alpha{\text{eff}, i} = \sigmai \alphai. d. Composite color: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{c}i \alpha{\text{eff}, i} T. e. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T (1 - \sigmai \mathcal{G}i). 4. Apply transparent mask regularization to \alpha during optimization. Parameters: \sigma: Learnable, constrained to [0, 1]. \alpha: Learnable, constrained to [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gaussians with high geometric occupancy but near-zero optical opacity can exist anywhere in the scene without affecting the final rendered color, leading to unconstrained "ghost" geometries that corrupt the surface representation. This is resolved by a transparent mask regularization loss. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, as the compositing loop remains the same, but with an additional multiplication for \alpha{\text{eff}} and probability calculation for surface attributes. Memory Complexity: Increases by one scalar (\sigma) per Gaussian, as \alpha replaces the single opacity scalar. Strengths: Enables sharp specular reflections on transparent objects; physically grounded surface representation. Limitations: Requires additional regularization to prevent ghost geometries; optimization may be unstable in diffuse regions without strong specular cues. When to use: When rendering transparent objects with sharp reflections or when surface attributes (normals, roughness) are needed for deferred shading. When not to use: For purely opaque scenes where standard opacity suffices, or when computational budget is extremely tight. Originated in "RT-Splatting: Joint Reflection-Transmission Modeling with Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting where a single opacity parameter fails to model both solid geometry and optical transparency simultaneously. RT-Splatting: Joint Reflection-Transmission Modeling with Gaussian Splatting, https://github.com/WoojunePark/splatpapers/issues/71, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: CAG-GS Semantic Mapping and Gaussian Generation
head: CAG-GS
body: CAG-GS generates implicit 3D Gaussians from semantic anchors by encoding spatial positions into high-dimensional semantic vectors via a multi-resolution hash grid, which are then fused with anchor features to predict Gaussian attributes. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating semantic guidance and geometric consistency constraints (normal and flattening losses) to improve global consistency in large-scale scenes, utilizing a coarse-to-fine training strategy. Inputs: A set of semantic anchors, each with a pre-extracted feature vector fj \in \mathbb{R}^d. Spatial positions of the anchors pj \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera pose (R, t) for computing Gaussian distances to the camera center. Ground truth images \hat{I} and per-pixel semantic features \hat{F} extracted using SAM2. Outputs: A set of implicit 3D Gaussians, each defined by center \mui, opacity \sigmai, color ci, and covariance (derived from scaling si and rotation). Rendered images I, normal maps Nr, depth maps D, and semantic feature maps F. Semantic Mapping Module: Implemented as a compact multi-resolution hash grid. Uses fixed-size feature hash tables. Memory consumption is constant regardless of the number of anchors. Supports efficient queries via hash-based feature indexing and trilinear feature interpolation. Anchor Data: Each anchor j has: Position pj \in \mathbb{R}^3. Feature vector fj \in \mathbb{R}^d, where d=32. Gaussian Data (per anchor): Each anchor j generates K=10 Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has: Center \mui. Opacity \sigmai. Color ci. Scaling vector si \in \mathbb{R}^3. d: Feature dimensionality for each anchor, set to 32. K: Number of Gaussians constructed per anchor, set to 10. D: Output dimensionality of the semantic mapping module, matching the dimensionality of extracted SAM2 features. \lambda: Weighting coefficient for photometric loss, fixed to 0.2. \lambda1: Weighting coefficient for semantic feature alignment loss, set to 1.0. \lambda2: Weighting coefficient for flattening loss, set to 100.0. \lambda3: Weighting coefficient for normal consistency loss, set to 0.015. 1. Semantic Mapping: For each selected anchor j with position pj, encode the spatial position into a high-dimensional semantic vector using the semantic mapping module \gamma. The module \gamma: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^D is implemented as a multi-resolution hash grid. 2. Feature Fusion: Fuse the encoded semantic vector with the original anchor feature fj to obtain the enhanced feature \tilde{f}j: \tilde{f}j = W \cdot \gamma(pj) + fj where W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times D} is a learnable weight matrix. 3. Gaussian Prediction: Feed the enhanced semantic feature \tilde{f}j into MLP decoders to predict the opacities \sigmai, colors ci, and covariances (scaling si) of the K implicit 3D Gaussians associated with the anchor. 4. Center Determination: Determine the centers \mui of the K Gaussians by applying K learnable spatial offsets to the anchor position pj. 5. Geometric Normal and Depth Computation: Compute the Gaussian normal ni as the direction of its shortest axis (corresponding to \min(si)). Compute the distance to the camera center di = ni^T (\mui + Rt), where (R, t) is the world-to-camera transformation. Render the normal map Nr(x') and unbiased depth map D(x') following PGSR (Chen et al. 2024a). 6. Surface Normal Estimation: Backproject the unbiased depth map into 3D space to recover per-pixel 3D coordinates. Estimate the surface normal N(x') for each pixel from the 3D coordinates of its adjacent pixels. 7. Semantic Feature Map Synthesis: Feed the positions of the implicit Gaussians \mui into the semantic mapping module to obtain embedding vectors \gamma(\mui). Composite these embedding vectors into a feature map F(x') using the 3D-GS rasterizer: F(x') = \sum{i \in I(x')} \gamma(\mui) \alphai \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak) where \alphai = \sigmai G'i(x'), G'i is the 2D Gaussian kernel, and I(x') are the sorted indices of contributing Gaussians. Synthesize feature maps at a downscaled resolution while maintaining the original aspect ratio to reduce computational overhead. 8. Loss Computation: Photometric Loss: L{3DGS} = (1 - \lambda)L1(I, \hat{I}) + \lambda L{SSIM}(I, \hat{I}) where L1 and L{SSIM} are L1 and SSIM losses, and \lambda=0.2. Flattening Loss: Compress Gaussians along their shortest axis: L{flat} = \frac{1}{|I|} \sum{i \in I} \min(si) where I is the set of indices of all implicit Gaussians. Normal Consistency Loss: L{norm} = \frac{1}{|X|} \sum{x' \in X} w(x') \| N(x') - Nr(x') \|1 where w(x') = (1 - |\nabla \hat{I}|(x'))^2 and |\nabla \hat{I}| is the normalized image gradient magnitude scaled to [0, 1]. Semantic Feature Alignment Loss: L{feat} = \frac{1}{|X|} \sum{x' \in X} \| F(x') - \hat{F}(x') \|1 where \hat{F} represents per-pixel features extracted using SAM2. Overall Loss: L = L{3DGS} + \lambda1 L{feat} + \lambda2 L{flat} + \lambda3 L{norm} with \lambda1=1.0, \lambda2=100.0, \lambda3=0.015. 9. Optimization: Optimize the 3D Gaussians (and associated parameters) by minimizing the overall loss L. Unverified code. Fixed-size hash table def query(self, positions): """Hash-based feature indexing and trilinear interpolation.""" indices = torch.clamp((positions 100).long() % 1024, 0, 1023) return self.table[indices] class CAGGSGenerator(nn.Module): def init(self, d=32, K=10, D=256): super().init() self.d = d self.K = K self.D = D self.semanticmapping = HashGrid(D) self.W = nn.Linear(D, d) # W in R^{d x D} self.mlpopacity = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 1)) self.mlpcolor = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 3)) self.mlpscaling = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 3)) self.mlpoffsets = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 3 K)) self.offsets = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(K, 3)) # K learnable spatial offsets def forward(self, anchors): generated = [] for anchor in anchors: pj = anchor['position'] fj = anchor['feature'] gammapj = self.semanticmapping(pj.unsqueeze(0)).squeeze(0) ftilde = self.W(gammapj) + fj # ftildej = W gamma(pj) + fj sigma = torch.sigmoid(self.mlpopacity(ftilde)) color = torch.sigmoid(self.mlpcolor(ftilde)) scale = torch.exp(self.mlpscaling(ftilde)) offsetpred = self.mlpoffsets(ftilde).view(self.K, 3) centers = pj.unsqueeze(0) + self.offsets + offsetpred # Apply K offsets generated.append({'centers': centers, 'opacities': sigma, 'colors': color, 'scales': scale}) return generated def rendernormaldepth(gaussians, cameraparams): """Render normal map and unbiased depth map following PGSR.""" centers = torch.cat([g['centers'] for g in gaussians], dim=0) scales = torch.cat([g['scales'] for g in gaussians], dim=0) camcenters = centers @ cameraparams['R'].T + cameraparams['t'] depth = -camcenters[:, 2] minscaleidx = torch.argmin(scales, dim=1, keepdim=True) axes = torch.eye(3).to(scales.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(scales.shape[0], -1, -1) normalscam = axes[torch.arange(scales.shape[0]), minscaleidx.squeeze()] normalsworld = normalscam @ cameraparams['R'] return normalsworld, depth def backprojectdepth(depthmap, cameraparams): """Backproject depth map into 3D space to recover per-pixel 3D coordinates.""" H, W = depthmap.shape y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H), torch.arange(W), indexing='ij') fx, fy = cameraparams['fx'], cameraparams['fy'] cx, cy = cameraparams['cx'], cameraparams['cy'] X = (x - cx) depthmap / fx Y = (y - cy) depthmap / fy Z = depthmap coordscam = torch.stack([X, Y, Z], dim=-1) coordsworld = (coordscam - cameraparams['t']) @ cameraparams['R'] return coordsworld def estimatenormalfromcoords(coords3d): """Estimate surface normal from 3D coordinates of adjacent pixels.""" dy, dx = torch.gradient(coords3d[..., 0], coords3d[..., 1], dim=0, dim=1) normal = torch.cross(dy, dx, dim=-1) return F.normalize(normal, dim=-1) def compositeembeddings(gaussians, embeddings, cameraparams, imagesize): """Composite embedding vectors into feature map using 3D-GS rasterizer.""" H, W = imagesize centers = torch.cat([g['centers'] for g in gaussians], dim=0) opacities = torch.cat([g['opacities'] for g in gaussians], dim=0) camcenters = centers @ cameraparams['R'].T + cameraparams['t'] u = camcenters[:, 0] cameraparams['fx'] / camcenters[:, 2] + cameraparams['cx'] v = camcenters[:, 1] cameraparams['fy'] / camcenters[:, 2] + cameraparams['cy'] Fmap = torch.zeros(H, W, embeddings.shape[1]) for i in range(len(gaussians)): alphai = opacities[i] torch.exp(-0.5 ((u[i]-u)2 + (v[i]-v)2)) alphai = torch.clamp(alphai, 0, 1) Fmap += embeddings[i] alphai.unsqueeze(-1) torch.prod(1 - torch.clamp(Fmap.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True), 0, 1)) return Fmap def computenormalizedgradientmagnitude(image): """Compute normalized image gradient magnitude scaled to [0, 1].""" gradx = F.conv2d(image.unsqueeze(0), torch.tensor([[[[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]]]).float()) grady = F.conv2d(image.unsqueeze(0), torch.tensor([[[[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]]]]).float()) mag = torch.sqrt(gradx2 + grady2) return mag / mag.max() def ssimloss(img1, img2): """Standard SSIM loss.""" return F.mseloss(img1, img2) def getallscales(gaussians): return torch.cat([g['scales'] for g in gaussians], dim=0) def computelosses(renderedimage, gtimage, Nr, Nestimated, Fmap, gtsemanticfeatures, gaussians): lambdaphot = 0.2 L3DGS = (1 - lambdaphot) F.l1loss(renderedimage, gtimage) + lambdaphot ssimloss(renderedimage, gtimage) lambdanorm = 0.015 gradmag = computenormalizedgradientmagnitude(gtimage) w = (1 - gradmag) 2 Lnorm = torch.mean(w torch.abs(Nestimated - Nr)) lambdafeat = 1.0 Lfeat = F.l1loss(Fmap, gtsemanticfeatures) lambdaflat = 100.0 scales = getallscales(gaussians) minscales = torch.min(scales, dim=1)[0] Lflat = torch.mean(minscales) L = L3DGS + lambdafeat Lfeat + lambdaflat Lflat + lambdanorm Lnorm return L Precision: The hash grid implementation must handle hash collisions appropriately. Boundaries: During scene division, the threshold for importance score ratio \epsilon is set to 0.1. Anchors with importance scores below this threshold relative to the total may be excluded or handled differently in block-wise local fine-tuning. Degenerate Input: If an anchor has no contributing Gaussians to a pixel, it does not contribute to the feature map or image rendering for that pixel. The product term \prod (1-\alphak) handles the transparency correctly. A training approach consisting of coarse global model training, scene division, and block-wise local fine-tuning to improve global consistency. A method to balance workload and provide supervision by dividing the scene into blocks based on anchor importance scores, with additional views selected for blending. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The use of a multi-resolution hash grid allows for efficient queries, but the number of Gaussians per anchor (K=10) and the number of anchors affect the rendering cost. Memory Complexity: The semantic mapping module has constant memory consumption regardless of the number of anchors, due to fixed-size feature hash tables. Measured Performance: Experiments were conducted on 8 RTX 3090Ti GPUs. The coarse global model is optimized for 60,000 iterations, and each block is fine-tuned for another 60,000 iterations. Strengths: Improves global consistency in large-scale scenes through semantic guidance and geometric constraints. Efficient memory usage for semantic features. Limitations: Requires pre-extraction of semantic features using SAM2, which adds preprocessing overhead. The coarse-to-fine strategy adds complexity to the training pipeline. When to Use: Large-scale scene rendering where global consistency and semantic understanding are important. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes where the overhead of semantic feature extraction and coarse-to-fine training is not justified. Origin: CAG-GS was introduced in the paper "CAG-GS: Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting for Large-scale Scene Rendering". History: It incorporates a multi-resolution hash grid from Müller et al. (2022) and normal/depth rendering techniques from PGSR (Chen et al. 2024a). Usage: Used for large-scale scene rendering, leveraging semantic anchors and a divide-and-conquer strategy.
