name: Geometry and orientation extension
body: This family extends the standard 3D Gaussian primitive to better model explicit geometry, surface orientation, and directional asymmetry, which standard isotropic Gaussians lack. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing learnable normals [9621-oriented-gaussian-splatting.md], skewness [10045-3d-skew-normal-splatting.md], or mesh-constrained parameterizations [15283-barycentric-splat-parameterization.md] to enable surface wrapping, mesh extraction, and view-dependent effects. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting primitive is defined by a center \mui, a covariance matrix \Sigmai (parameterized by rotation Ri and scaling Si), opacity \alphai, and color ci. The covariance is typically \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top. The unnormalized probability density function is: Gi(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mui)\right) Extensions in this family modify the geometric or orientation parameters to address specific limitations: 1. Orientation: Adding a normal vector ni [9621-oriented-gaussian-splatting.md] or skewness parameter ki [10045-3d-skew-normal-splatting.md] to define directional attenuation or asymmetry. 2. Constraint: Constraining centers \mui to lie on a mesh surface using barycentric coordinates [15283-barycentric-splat-parameterization.md]. 3. Dimensionality: Extending the Gaussian to higher dimensions (e.g., 6D for space+direction) to model view-dependent effects. Augments the standard 3D Gaussian with a learnable normal vector ni to create a reciprocal attenuation model, enabling explicit geometric field derivation (normal and occupancy) via the Objects as Volumes (OaV) framework. It sets itself apart by restoring reciprocity (\sigma(x, w) = \sigma(x, -w)), which is broken by standard isotropic attenuation, thereby allowing for consistent surface wrapping and mesh extraction. Replaces the standard symmetric 3D Gaussian kernel with the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution to model directional asymmetry, sharp boundaries, and one-sided surfaces. It sets itself apart from Oriented Gaussian Splatting by using a continuous skewness parameter rather than a hard half-space truncation, allowing smooth interpolation between symmetric Gaussians and half-ellipsoids while preserving analytical tractability under affine transformations. Constrains 2D Gaussian Splat centers to lie on triangular mesh faces using barycentric coordinates, allowing splats to move freely on the face while preserving per-splat attributes. It differs from sibling methods by deriving Gaussian geometry directly from mesh topology via heuristic midpoint sampling rather than learning orientation vectors or skewness parameters. Allows 3D Gaussian primitives to scale anisotropically along the x, y, and z axes and rotate in 3D space, rather than remaining spherical, to better fit scene geometry. It solves the problem of geometric mismatch where isotropic primitives fail to represent elongated structures, resulting in blurry or rounded artifacts. It sets itself apart from the isotropic baseline by introducing 7 additional optimization variables per primitive (3 scales, 4 quaternion components) to model directional attenuation. An extension of 3DGS that models view-dependent effects by adding directional dimensions, representing scene elements as 6D Gaussians (space+direction). It parameterizes the full 6D covariance via Cholesky decomposition \Sigma = LL^\top with L lower-triangular and positive diagonal entries to guarantee positive definiteness. A parameterization for the orientation of Gaussian Splats on the face plane using an in-plane rotation parameter R{2d}, transformed into world space. The final rotation matrix is R = Rs \cdot R{2d}, where R is the final rotation matrix used for rasterization, Rs is the rotation matrix of the triangle faces, and R{2d} is the in-plane rotation parameter. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent] uses isotropic or anisotropic Gaussians for view synthesis but lacks explicit geometric primitives for surface reconstruction. Recent extensions have addressed limitations: 4D Gaussian Splatting incorporates temporal dynamics, while 6D Gaussian Splatting models view-dependent effects by adding directional dimensions. Oriented Gaussian Splatting introduces normals for surface wrapping [9621-oriented-gaussian-splatting.md]. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting uses skew-normal distributions for asymmetry [10045-3d-skew-normal-splatting.md]. Barycentric Splat Parameterization binds Gaussians to meshes using barycentric coordinates [15283-barycentric-splat-parameterization.md]. Anisotropic covariance allows 3D Gaussians to scale along x, y, and z axes and rotate in 3D space to better fit scene geometry [11879-anisotropic-covariance.md]. In-plane rotation is used in mesh-constrained frameworks like OMeGa. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26 OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00427, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Oriented Gaussian Splatting
head: Definition 2, Oriented Gaussian, Reciprocal Oriented Gaussian
body:
Oriented Gaussian Splatting is a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that assigns a learnable normal vector ni to each primitive to enforce a reciprocal attenuation model. This modification restores the reciprocity condition (\sigma(x, w) = \sigma(x, -w)) broken by standard Gaussian Splatting, enabling the application of the Objects as Volumes (OaV) framework to derive explicit geometric fields, such as normals and occupancy. Unlike 3D Skew-Normal Splatting which uses skewness for asymmetry, or Barycentric Splat Parameterization which constrains centers to a mesh, this method explicitly models surface wrapping via half-space attenuation to facilitate high-fidelity mesh extraction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N Gaussian primitives, each defined by center \mui, covariance \Sigmai (from rotation Ri and scaling Si), opacity \alphai, color ci, and a learnable oriented normal vector ni \in S^2. Training images, camera poses, and initial Gaussian parameters. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, ci, ni) and an explicit triangular mesh extracted from the resulting geometric fields. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. Ri \in SO(3): Rotation matrix (parameterized by quaternion or axis-angle). Si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling vector. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color (SH coefficients). ni \in S^2: Oriented normal vector (unit length). Method Steps: 1. Oriented Attenuation Definition: For a query point \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{w}, the oriented attenuation coefficient  ar{\sigma}i is defined as:  ar{\sigma}i(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{1}{ni^T(\mathbf{x}-\mui) \geq 0} |\mathbf{w} \cdot 
abla \log(1 - Gi(\mathbf{x}))| where Gi(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \exp\left(- rac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mui)^	op \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mui)ight) is the standard Gaussian density, and \mathbf{1} is the indicator function ensuring attenuation only occurs on the side of the center pointed to by ni. This formulation ensures reciprocity. 2. Geometric Field Derivation (OaV): Assuming the Gaussians properly wrap the scene geometry, the vacancy field v(\mathbf{x}) is approximated by iterating over all training camera rays \mathcal{T}c to find the maximum product of unobstructed transmittance: v(\mathbf{x}) = \max{(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}) \in \mathcal{T}c} \left\{ \prod{i=1}^N \left( 1 -  ar{G}{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}}^{(i)}(t) ight): \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{w}, t > 0 ight\} where  ar{G}{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}}^{(i)}(t) = Gi(\mathbf{o} + \min(t, t{Gi}^{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}})\mathbf{w}) and t{Gi}^{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}:= \arg \max{t \geq 0} Gi(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{w}). The Gaussian vector field V(\mathbf{x}) is the gradient of the log-vacancy, computed as the sum of gradients of the Gaussian components for those oriented towards the query point: V(\mathbf{x}):= 
abla \log v(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{1}{ni^T(\mathbf{x}-\mui) \geq 0} 
abla \log(1 - Gi(\mathbf{x})) The normal field is the normalized vector field: \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}):=  rac{V(\mathbf{x})}{\|V(\mathbf{x})\|} 3. Training Loss: The total loss combines photometric, depth-normal consistency, normal alignment, and multi-view losses: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{	ext{RGB}} + \lambda{	ext{DN}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{DN}} + \lambda{	ext{N}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{N}} + \mathcal{L}{	ext{MV}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{RGB}}: Standard photometric loss. \mathcal{L}{	ext{DN}}: Depth-normal consistency loss. \mathcal{L}{	ext{N}}: Normal alignment loss, enforcing surface wrapping by aligning rendered normals with depth gradients: \mathcal{L}N = \sump 1 - N(p) \cdot 
abla D(p) where N(p) is the rendered oriented normal at pixel p and 
abla D(p) is the image-space gradient of the rendered depth. \mathcal{L}{	ext{MV}}: Multi-view consistency loss. Parameters: \lambda{	ext{DN}} = 0.05, \lambda{	ext{N}} = 0.05, \lambda{	ext{pc}} = 0.6, \lambda{	ext{gc}} = 0.02. 4. Densification: Every K iterations, compute errors \mathcal{L}N(p) across all training views and propagate them to individual Gaussians via their blending weights. High-error Gaussians are cloned with flipped normals to close holes in the wrapping shell. 5. Mesh Extraction (Pivot-Based Marching Tetrahedra): 1. Spawn Pivots: For each Gaussian i, spawn two Delaunay pivots: the center \mui and \mui + 3si ni, where si = \|Si Ri^T ni\|2 is the ellipsoid scaling along ni. 2. Compute Occupancy: Calculate vacancy values at each pivot using the approximation in Step 2. 3. Marching Tetrahedra: Apply Marching Tetrahedra on the resulting Delaunay triangulation. 4. Refinement: Refine vertices to the 0.5-isosurface via binary search. Alternative: Primal Adaptive Meshing: 1. Initialization: Initialize vertices by sampling marching tetrahedra mesh faces, weighting each face inversely proportional to its distance from the nearest training camera. 2. Refinement: Project vertices onto the 0.5-isosurface of v via iterative Newton update: x{i+1} = xi +  rac{1}{2}(0.5 - v(xi))\mathcal{N}(xi) 3. Filtering: Remove vertices x with |0.5 - v(x)| > \epsilon. Iterate stages 1-3 until no points are removed. 4. Delaunay & Extraction: Compute Delaunay tetrahedralization of remaining vertices, classify tetrahedra as inside/outside based on vacancy of sampled interior points, and extract triangle faces separating inside and outside tetrahedra. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeorientedattenuation(x, w, mu, Sigmainv, alpha, n): """Computes the oriented attenuation coefficient for a single Gaussian.""" diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 diff @ Sigmainv @ diff G = alpha np.exp(exponent) if G >= 1.0: return 0.0 gradlog = (G / (1.0 - G)) (Sigmainv @ diff) directionalderiv = np.abs(w @ gradlog) if n @ diff >= 0: return directionalderiv return 0.0 def computevacancyfield(x, gaussians, trainingrays): """Computes the vacancy field v(x) by iterating over training rays.""" maxtransmittance = 0.0 for o, w in trainingrays: transmittance = 1.0 for g in gaussians: mu, Sigma, alpha, n = g['mu'], g['Sigma'], g['alpha'], g['n'] Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) A = w @ Sigmainv @ w B = w @ Sigmainv @ (o - mu) tG = -B / A if A != 0 else 0.0 tx = w @ (x - o) if tx <= 0: continue teval = max(0.0, min(tx, tG)) xeval = o + teval w diff = xeval - mu exponent = -0.5 diff @ Sigmainv @ diff Gval = alpha np.exp(exponent) transmittance = (1.0 - Gval) if transmittance > maxtransmittance: maxtransmittance = transmittance return maxtransmittance def computevectorfield(x, gaussians): """Computes V(x) = sum of gradients for oriented Gaussians.""" V = np.zeros(3) for g in gaussians: mu, Sigmainv, alpha, n = g['mu'], np.linalg.inv(g['Sigma']), g['alpha'], g['n'] diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 diff @ Sigmainv @ diff G = alpha np.exp(exponent) if G >= 1.0: continue gradlog = (G / (1.0 - G)) (Sigmainv @ diff) if n @ diff >= 0: V += gradlog return V def extractmeshpivotbased(gaussians, trainingrays): """Extracts mesh using Pivot-Based Marching Tetrahedra.""" pivots = [] pivotvalues = [] for g in gaussians: mu, n, S, R = g['mu'], g['n'], g['S'], g['R'] Smat = np.diag(S) si = np.linalg.norm(Smat @ (R.T @ n)) p1 = mu p2 = mu + 3 si n pivots.extend([p1, p2]) pivotvalues.extend([computevacancyfield(p1, gaussians, trainingrays), computevacancyfield(p2, gaussians, trainingrays)]) # Standard Delaunay triangulation and Marching Tetrahedra algorithms are applied here. # Not given in the sources. return pivots, pivotvalues def trainorientedgaussians(gaussians, images, cameras, gtdepths, iterations=30000, K=100, lr=0.01): """Main training loop with explicit loss and densification steps.""" lambdaDN = 0.05 lambdaN = 0.05 lambdapc = 0.6 lambdagc = 0.02 for i in range(iterations): # 1. Render: Composite Gaussians using a differentiable rasterizer renderedrgb, rendereddepth, renderednormals = [], [], [] for cam, img in zip(cameras, images): rgb = np.zeroslike(img) depth = 0.0 normal = np.zeros(3) totalalpha = 0.0 for g in gaussians: # Project Gaussian to 2D, compute screen-space contribution # (Implementation details of differentiable rasterization omitted; standard in 3DGS) pass renderedrgb.append(rgb) rendereddepth.append(depth) renderednormals.append(normal) # 2. Compute Losses LRGB = np.mean(np.array([np.mean((r - i)2) for r, i in zip(renderedrgb, images)])) LDN = np.mean(np.array([np.mean(np.abs(r - d)) for r, d in zip(rendereddepth, gtdepths)])) # Normal alignment loss: sump (1 - N(p). grad D(p)) LN = np.mean(np.array([np.mean(1 - np.sum(n np.gradient(d))) for n, d in zip(renderednormals, rendereddepth)])) LMV = lambdapc LRGB + lambdagc LRGB # Multi-view consistency approximation Ltotal = LRGB + lambdaDN LDN + lambdaN LN + LMV # 3. Update parameters via gradient descent for g in gaussians: g['mu'] -= lr np.gradient(Ltotal, g['mu']) g['n'] -= lr np.gradient(Ltotal, g['n']) # Other parameters (Sigma, alpha, c) updated similarly via backpropagation # 4. Densification if i % K == 0: # Compute per-pixel normal alignment errors pixelerrors = [np.mean(1 - np.sum(n np.gradient(d))) for n, d in zip(renderednormals, rendereddepth)] # Propagate errors to Gaussians via blending weights (standard alpha-weighted accumulation) gaussianerrors = [np.mean(e) for e in pixelerrors] # Clone high-error Gaussians and flip normals to close holes newgaussians = [] for g, err in zip(gaussians, gaussianerrors): newgaussians.append(g) if err > np.mean(gaussianerrors): flippedg = g.copy() flippedg['n'] = -flippedg['n'] newgaussians.append(flippedg) gaussians = newgaussians return gaussians Time Complexity: Rendering is similar to standard 3DGS, O(N) per pixel for splatting. Vacancy field computation for mesh extraction is O(N \cdot R) where R is the number of training rays, which is expensive and typically done offline or sparsely. Memory Complexity: Stores an additional normal vector ni per Gaussian, increasing memory by 3 	imes 4 bytes per Gaussian compared to standard 3DGS. Performance: Produces substantially lighter, fully watertight meshes compared to prior works requiring 9 pivots per Gaussian, without sacrificing surface fidelity. Strengths: Enables explicit geometric field derivation (normals, occupancy) via OaV; restores reciprocity; facilitates high-fidelity mesh extraction. Limitations: Requires Gaussians to properly "wrap" the scene geometry; consistency requirement that the region where transmittance is constant lies inside the object. Hidden Gaussians inside geometry can violate wrapping assumptions and produce artifacts if intersected. When to use: When explicit surface reconstruction (mesh) is required from a radiance field representation, particularly for scenes where standard 3DGS fails to provide clean normals or watertight meshes. When not to use: When only novel view synthesis is needed and mesh extraction is not required, as standard 3DGS is simpler and faster. Oriented Gaussian Splatting was introduced in "From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians". It addresses the lack of reciprocity in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting attenuation, which prevents the direct application of the Objects as Volumes (OaV) framework for deriving explicit geometric fields. The method builds on the OaV theory [39] and integrates with differentiable rasterizers [55, 56, 57]. From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37095-24, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 3D Skew-Normal Splatting
head: Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS)
body: 3D Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS) is a volume rendering method that replaces the standard symmetric 3D Gaussian kernel with the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution to model asymmetric structures, such as sharp boundaries and one-sided surfaces, while preserving analytical tractability under affine transformations. It sets apart from its siblings, such as Oriented Gaussian Splatting and Barycentric Splat Parameterization, by introducing a continuous, learnable skewness parameter that allows primitives to interpolate between symmetric Gaussians and half-ellipsoids, enabling the representation of directional asymmetry that symmetric or constrained primitives cannot capture. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Skew-Normal primitives, each defined by location \mui, scale matrix \Omegai, and skew parameter ki; camera parameters (view/projection matrices); and scene geometry. Output: A rendered 2D image where each pixel color C(u) is computed via alpha blending of projected 2D Skew-Normal kernels. Data Structures: Each primitive i stores: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Location parameter. Ri \in SO(3): Rotation matrix. Si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling vector (diagonal of scaling matrix). \Omegai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Scale matrix. ki \in \mathbb{R}^3: Latent skewness variable, factorized into magnitude m{k,i} \in \mathbb{R}+ and direction d{k,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (\|d{k,i}\|2 = 1). ci: Color (typically represented by Spherical Harmonics coefficients). oi \in [-1, 1]: Signed opacity. Parameters: Skew magnitude parameterization: mk = \frac{8}{1 + \exp(-\frac{x}{6})}, where x \in \mathbb{R} is a learnable scalar. Skew direction: dk = \frac{v}{\|v\|2 + \epsilon}, where v \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a learnable vector. Skew vector: k = mk dk. Formulas: The 3D Skew-Normal kernel is defined as: SN(x; \mu, \Omega, k) = G3(x - \mu; \Omega) \Phi \left( \alpha^\top \omega^{-1}(x - \mu) \right) where: G3(x - \mu; \Omega) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu)^\top \Omega^{-1} (x - \mu) \right) is the unnormalized Gaussian PDF. \Phi(\cdot) is the standard normal CDF. \omega = (\Omega \odot I3)^{1/2} is the diagonal matrix of standard deviations derived from \Omega using the Hadamard product \odot. \alpha = \omega R S^{-1} k is the slant parameter, decoupled from rotation and scale. The spatial mean of the distribution is shifted from the location parameter \mu: \mathbb{E}[X] = \mu + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{R S k}{\sqrt{1+k^\top k}} This offset is used to compute the bounding box center \mu{bbox} for rasterization: \mu{bbox} = \mu^{2D} + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{A R S k}{\sqrt{1+k^\top k}} where \mu^{2D} = A\mu is the projected location. Projection to 2D: The 3D primitive is projected onto the image plane using the affine transformation matrix A = JW \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} (Jacobian J and world-to-camera W). The resulting 2D Skew-Normal kernel is: SN^{2D}(u; \mu^{2D}, \Omega^{2D}, m^{2D}) = G2(u - \mu^{2D}; \Omega^{2D}) \Phi \left( (m^{2D})^\top (u - \mu^{2D}) \right) with parameters: \mu^{2D} = A\mu, \quad \Omega^{2D} = A\Omega A^\top m^{2D} = \frac{(\Omega^{2D})^{-1} A R S k}{\sqrt{1 + k^\top k} - (A R S k)^\top (\Omega^{2D})^{-1} A R S k} Rendering: Color aggregation uses signed opacity splatting to allow subtractive volumetric density: C(u) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci oi SNi^{2D}(u) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj SNj^{2D}(u)) where \mathcal{N} is the set of depth-sorted intersecting kernels. Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize primitives with standard 3DGS parameters. 2. Phase 1 (Global Structure): Jointly optimize all parameters (R, S, mk, dk) using the Adam optimizer to establish a global scene structure. 3. Phase 2 (Block Coordinate Descent): Use a cyclic alternating schedule to reduce parameter interference: Part 1: Update ellipsoidal base parameters (R, S) while freezing skew parameters (mk, dk). Part 2: Refine skew parameters (mk, dk) while holding (R, S) constant. 4. Positional Update: Update positional parameters \mu using Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC) to escape local minima. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def sortprimitivesbydepth(primitives, cameraz): """Sort primitives by their camera-space z-coordinate in descending order.""" indices = torch.argsort(cameraz, descending=True) return [primitives[i] for i in indices] def computeskewparameters(x, v): """Factorizes latent variables into magnitude and direction.""" mk = 8.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-x / 6.0)) dk = v / (torch.norm(v) + 1e-6) return mk, dk def computeslant(R, S, k): """Computes decoupled slant parameter alpha and diagonal omega.""" Omega = R @ torch.diag(S2) @ R.T omegadiag = torch.sqrt(torch.diag(Omega)) omega = torch.diag(omegadiag) Sinv = torch.diag(1.0 / S) alpha = omega @ R @ Sinv @ k return alpha, omega def project3dto2dskew(mu3d, Omega3d, R, S, k, A): """Projects 3D Skew-Normal to 2D image plane.""" mu2d = A @ mu3d Omega2d = A @ Omega3d @ A.T ARSk = A @ R @ torch.diag(S) @ k Omega2dinv = torch.inverse(Omega2d) numerator = Omega2dinv @ ARSk denominator = torch.sqrt(1.0 + torch.dot(k, k)) - (ARSk.T @ Omega2dinv @ ARSk) m2d = numerator / denominator return mu2d, Omega2d, m2d def renderpixel(u, primitives, Amatrix, cameraz): """Renders a single pixel u [2] given depth-sorted primitives.""" sortedprimitives = sortprimitivesbydepth(primitives, cameraz) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 color = torch.zeros(3) for prim in sortedprimitives: mu2d, Omega2d, m2d = project3dto2dskew( prim['mu3d'], prim['Omega3d'], prim['R'], prim['S'], prim['k'], Amatrix) diff = u - mu2d gaussval = torch.exp(-0.5 diff.T @ torch.inverse(Omega2d) @ diff) skewarg = m2d.T @ diff skewval = 0.5 (1.0 + torch.erf(skewarg / torch.sqrt(2.0))) sn2d = gaussval skewval o = prim['o'] c = prim['c'] contribution = c o sn2d weight = o sn2d (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) color += contribution accumulatedalpha += weight if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Tails: Without bounded skewness, asymmetric tails cause primitives to intersect excessive tiles, degrading tile-based rasterization performance and violating local affine approximation assumptions. The parameterization mk \in \mathbb{R}+ and bounded Mardia's skewness measure prevent this. Parameter Coupling: Strong coupling between scale, rotation, and skewness causes optimization instability. The decoupled parameterization \alpha = \omega R S^{-1} k and factorization of k into mk, dk resolve this. Mean vs Location: The location parameter \mu does not coincide with the spatial mean. Using \mu for bounding box localization leads to inaccurate coverage. The corrected center \mu{bbox} must be used. Computes the parameters of a 2D Skew-Normal distribution (SN2D) resulting from the linear projection of a 3D Skew-Normal kernel (SN3) onto the image plane. It sets apart from standard Gaussian splatting by preserving the asymmetry (skewness) of the 3D primitive during projection, allowing the 2D kernel to model one-sided surfaces and sharp boundaries that symmetric Gaussians cannot. Addresses the discrepancy between the location parameter \mu and the spatial mean \mathbb{E}[X] of the Skew-Normal distribution. It derives a deterministic spatial offset \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{RSk}{\sqrt{1+k^\top k}} to shift the bounding box center to the true spatial mean, ensuring accurate tile culling and rasterization. Time Complexity: Comparable to standard 3DGS and SSS, with overhead from computing the skew term (CDF evaluation) and additional parameter updates. Memory Complexity: Slightly higher than 3DGS due to the storage of skew parameters (k or mk, dk) and the need for more complex gradient computations. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, SNS achieves 30.17 PSNR, 0.895 SSIM, and 0.144 LPIPS, outperforming SSS (29.90 PSNR) and 3DGS (28.69 PSNR). On the drjohnson scene, SNS completes 30,000 iterations in 38m 4s (29.89 dB PSNR), comparable to SSS (38m 7s, 29.66 dB PSNR). Strengths: Continuous interpolation between symmetric and asymmetric shapes; analytical tractability under affine transformations; ability to model sharp boundaries and one-sided surfaces with fewer primitives. Limitations: Optimization instability due to parameter coupling requires complex decoupling strategies and block-wise updates; signed opacity requires careful handling to avoid artifacts. When to use: Scenes with sharp edges, flat surfaces, or one-sided structures where symmetric Gaussians require excessive overlap or fail to capture asymmetry. When not to use: Scenes with purely symmetric, smooth geometry where the added complexity of skewness provides negligible benefit and may hinder convergence. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting was proposed to address the limitations of symmetric Gaussian kernels in representing asymmetric structures. It builds on the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution, which provides directional asymmetry through a slant parameter. The method was introduced to enable continuous shape interpolation between symmetric Gaussians and half-ellipsoids, allowing for flexible modeling of sharp boundaries and interior regions while maintaining the efficiency of splat-based rendering. It is implemented in PyTorch, extending the 3DGS rasterization engine, and tested on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.15010, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 2D Skew-Normal Parameter Projection
head: 2D Kernel Parameter Projection, SN2D Projection, Skew-Normal 2D Parameter Computation
body: Computes the parameters of a 2D Skew-Normal distribution (SN2D) resulting from the linear projection of a 3D Skew-Normal kernel (SN3) onto the image plane. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Skew-Normal kernel parameters \mathcal{X} \sim \text{SN3}(\mu, \Omega, \alpha), where \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the mean, \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the covariance, and \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the skewness parameter. Input: Projection matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}. Output: 2D Skew-Normal parameters \mathcal{Y} \sim \text{SN2}(\muY, \OmegaY, \alphaY), where \muY \in \mathbb{R}^2, \OmegaY \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, and \alphaY \in \mathbb{R}^2. Data Structures: The 3D kernel is parameterized using a rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, a scale matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (diagonal), and a skewness vector k \in \mathbb{R}^3. The covariance is \Omega = R S S^\top R^\top. The skewness parameter is \alpha = \omega R S^{-1} k, where \omega = (1 + k^\top k)^{-1/2}. Steps: 1. Compute 2D Mean: \muY = A \mu 2. Compute 2D Covariance: \OmegaY = A \Omega A^\top 3. Compute Intermediate Vector v: Calculate the term \omega \delta from the 3D parameters: \omega \delta = \frac{R S k}{\sqrt{1 + k^\top k}} Let v = A (\omega \delta) = \frac{A R S k}{\sqrt{1 + k^\top k}}. 4. Compute 2D Skewness \alphaY: The skewness parameter is derived from the projected intermediate vector and the 2D covariance: \alphaY = \frac{\OmegaY^{-1} v}{\sqrt{1 - v^\top \OmegaY^{-1} v}} (Note: The source derivation includes a normalization factor \omegaY in the numerator, which is absorbed or set to unity during the direct projection step to avoid circular dependency.) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projectskewnormal3dto2d(mu3d: np.ndarray, R: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray, k: np.ndarray, A: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Projects a 3D Skew-Normal kernel to 2D. Args: mu3d: (3,) array, 3D mean. R: (3, 3) array, rotation matrix. S: (3,) array, scale vector (diagonal elements of S matrix). k: (3,) array, skewness vector. A: (2, 3) array, projection matrix. Returns: mu2d: (2,) array, 2D mean. Omega2d: (2, 2) array, 2D covariance. alpha2d: (2,) array, 2D skewness parameter. """ # 1. Compute 2D Mean mu2d = A @ mu3d # 2. Compute 3D Covariance Omega = R diag(S)^2 R^T Smat = np.diag(S) Omega3d = R @ (Smat @ Smat.T) @ R.T # 3. Compute 2D Covariance Omega2d = A @ Omega3d @ A.T # 4. Compute intermediate vector v = A (R S k / sqrt(1 + k^T k)) knormsq = np.dot(k, k) scalefactor = 1.0 / np.sqrt(1.0 + knormsq) # R @ (S @ k) RSk = R @ (S k) # v = A @ (scalefactor RSk) v = scalefactor (A @ RSk) # 5. Compute alpha2d Omega2dinv = np.linalg.inv(Omega2d) numerator = Omega2dinv @ v denominatorterm = v.T @ Omega2dinv @ v denominator = np.sqrt(1.0 - denominatorterm) alpha2d = numerator / denominator return mu2d, Omega2d, alpha2d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \OmegaY is singular (e.g., the kernel is viewed edge-on and collapses to a line), \OmegaY^{-1} does not exist. Regularization or culling is required. Domain Error: The term 1 - v^\top \OmegaY^{-1} v must be positive to prevent imaginary results in the square root. Evaluating the Skew-Normal distribution requires computing the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). The implementation uses the erf function for mathematical precision. Using the precise erf function incurs moderate penalties on rendering speed compared to faster analytic approximations. Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "3D Skew-Normal Splatting". The method extends the standard Gaussian Splatting framework by replacing the symmetric 3D Gaussian kernel with the Azzalini Skew-Normal distribution to model asymmetric structures. The 2D projection formula is derived from the properties of the Skew-Normal distribution under linear transformations. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.15010, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Anisotropic Covariance
head: Gaussian Scaling, Isotropic (baseline)
body: Anisotropic Covariance allows 3D Gaussian primitives to scale anisotropically along the x, y, and z axes and rotate in 3D space, rather than remaining spherical, to better fit scene geometry. It solves the problem of geometric mismatch where isotropic primitives fail to represent elongated structures, resulting in blurry or rounded artifacts. It sets itself apart from the isotropic baseline by introducing 7 additional optimization variables per primitive (3 scales, 4 quaternion components) to model directional attenuation, which is critical for high-fidelity reconstruction of non-spherical objects like tree trunks or leaves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial Gaussian parameters (center \mui, base scale, base rotation, opacity \alphai, color ci). Output: Optimized covariance matrix \Sigmai defined by anisotropic scales and rotation. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive i stores: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector [s{i,x}, s{i,y}, s{i,z}]. These are optimized parameters representing expansion along local axes. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion [w, x, y, z]. Normalized to unit length. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color (SH coefficients). Method Steps: 1. Parameterization: For each Gaussian i, initialize or optimize the scale vector si and quaternion qi. The isotropic variant fixes s{i,x} = s{i,y} = s{i,z} and qi = [1, 0, 0, 0] (identity), removing 7 variables per primitive. 2. Covariance Construction: Construct the covariance matrix \Sigmai using the scale and rotation parameters: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top Where: Si = \text{diag}(s{i,x}, s{i,y}, s{i,z}) is the diagonal scaling matrix. Ri is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion qi. 3. Rendering: Use \Sigmai in the Gaussian probability density function for splatting: Gi(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mui)\right) 4. Optimization: During training, gradients are backpropagated through the rendering process to update si and qi (along with \mui, \alphai, ci) to minimize the difference between rendered and ground truth images. Parameters: Scale Initialization: Not given in the sources. Quaternion Normalization: qi must be normalized after each update step to ensure valid rotation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Scales: If a scale parameter approaches zero, the Gaussian becomes needle-like, potentially causing numerical instability in \Sigmai^{-1} or rendering artifacts. This is monitored by metrics like GAI. Isotropic Limitation: Forcing isotropy (s{i,x}=s{i,y}=s{i,z}) results in "round dots" for elongated features, significantly degrading PSNR and visual quality. A primitive-level diagnostic metric measuring geometric anisotropy of 3D Gaussian primitives to detect structural degeneration (needle-like artifacts). It is used to monitor optimization drift in sparse-view settings. Definition: GAI is computed from the post-activation principal scales (s{i,x}, s{i,y}, s{i,z}) of each primitive. Formula: GAIi = f(s{i,x}, s{i,y}, s{i,z}) with \epsilon = 10^{-8} for numerical stability. The exact functional form f is defined in the main paper Eq. 3, but the inputs are the optimized scales. Parameters: \epsilon: Epsilon for stability. Value: 10^{-8}. \tau{GAI}: Threshold for classifying a primitive as needle-like. Default: 50. Usage: Compute R{needle}, the ratio of primitives where GAIi > \tau{GAI} to the total active primitives. Sensitivity: The relative ordering of methods is preserved across thresholds \tau{GAI} \in \{20, 30, 50, 80, 100\}, but the reduction factor increases monotonically. At \tau{GAI}=20, R{needle} for R2-GS is 17.12% vs LADES 4.49% (3.8x reduction). At \tau{GAI}=100, R2-GS is 3.48% vs LADES 0.15% (23.4x reduction). Complexity: The isotropic variant removes 7 variables per primitive, reducing learning cost compared to the anisotropic method. Performance: On the Average-30K dataset, the full anisotropic method achieves a PSNR of 26.05, while the isotropic variant achieves 25.23. Strengths: Significantly improves reconstruction quality for elongated or planar structures (e.g., tree trunks, leaves, vehicle bodies) by allowing non-spherical shapes. Limitations: Requires careful handling of scale parameters to avoid degenerate "needle" artifacts, which may require additional regularization or diagnostic monitoring (e.g., GAI). The concept of anisotropic scaling in 3D Gaussian Splatting is a core component of the original Gaussian Splatting method, as opposed to earlier isotropic variants. The original paper demonstrates that allowing Gaussians to scale along x, y, and z axes and rotate is essential for fitting scene geometry effectively. The isotropic variant serves as an ablation study baseline to prove the necessity of anisotropy. The Geometric Anisotropy Index (GAI) was later introduced as a diagnostic tool to analyze the structural properties of these anisotropic primitives in sparse-view tomography settings. GaussianSplatting論文のAblationについての解説・考察, https://qiita.com/kotauchisunsun/items/f1e89f28aa770b8d3b19, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence: Diagnosing and Controlling Optimization Drift in Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.22525, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Barycentric Splat Parameterization
head: GeoSplatting Face-Sampling, Heuristic Gaussian sampling from triangles, Mesh-Gaussian binding via midpoints, Splat center derivation from mesh faces
body: Barycentric Splat Parameterization constrains 2D Gaussian Splat centers to lie on triangular mesh faces using barycentric coordinates, allowing splats to move freely on the face while preserving per-splat attributes. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by deriving geometry directly from mesh topology rather than learning unconstrained centers, and from Oriented Gaussian Splatting by explicitly binding splat scales and orientations to local mesh edge vectors and face area. Inputs: Triangular mesh face Fi with vertices v1, v2, v3. Vertex attributes: Position \mathbf{P}i = (\mathbf{p}{i1}, \mathbf{p}{i2}, \mathbf{p}{i3}), Normal \mathbf{N}i = (\mathbf{n}{i1}, \mathbf{n}{i2}, \mathbf{n}{i3}). Barycentric coordinates u, w for the center, and u, v for midpoints. Hyperparameters: u=0.07, v=0.22, \alpha{jk}, \beta{jk}, \delta{jk}. Outputs: Gaussian parameters: center position \mathbf{c}, normal \mathbf{n}, scaling vector \mathbf{s}, rotation basis vectors \mathbf{r}x, \mathbf{r}y, \mathbf{r}z. Data Structures: Barycentric coordinates are scalars u, w, v \in [0, 1] satisfying u+w \le 1 for centers, and specific values for midpoints. Steps: 1. Define Barycentric Interpolation: For any attribute vector \mathbf{A}i = (\mathbf{a}{i1}, \mathbf{a}{i2}, \mathbf{a}{i3}) defined at triangle vertices and barycentric weights (q1, q2, q3), compute the interpolated value: \mathbf{A}i \odot (q1, q2, q3) = q1 \mathbf{a}{i1} + q2 \mathbf{a}{i2} + q3 \mathbf{a}{i3} 2. Compute Splat Center (General): If deriving a single center per face using general barycentric coordinates u, w: \mathbf{m} = u \cdot \mathbf{v}1 + w \cdot \mathbf{v}2 + (1 - u - w) \cdot \mathbf{v}3 where \mathbf{v}k are the vertex positions. 3. Compute Midpoints for Heuristic Sampling: Define six midpoints \mathbf{m}{jk} on the edges of the triangle using specific barycentric weights derived from hyperparameters u and v: Edge 1-2: \mathbf{m}{12} = (\frac{1-u}{2}, \frac{1-u}{2}, u) Edge 2-3: \mathbf{m}{23} = (\frac{1-u}{2}, \frac{1-u}{2}, u) Edge 3-1: \mathbf{m}{31} = (\frac{1-u}{2}, u, \frac{1-u}{2}) Edge 4-5 (Edge 1-2 variant): \mathbf{m}{45} = (\frac{1-v}{2}, \frac{1-v}{2}, v) Edge 5-6 (Edge 2-3 variant): \mathbf{m}{56} = (\frac{1-v}{2}, \frac{1-v}{2}, v) Edge 6-4 (Edge 3-1 variant): \mathbf{m}{64} = (\frac{1-v}{2}, v, \frac{1-v}{2}) The actual 3D position is obtained by interpolating vertex attributes with these weights: \mathbf{pos} = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot \mathbf{P}i. 4. Sample Gaussian Parameters for Each Midpoint \mathbf{m}{jk}: For each midpoint \mathbf{m}{jk}, calculate the Gaussian parameters: a. Center Position: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot \mathbf{P}i b. Normal: \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot \mathbf{N}i c. Edge Vector: Let \mathbf{b}k be the vertex index of the "end" of the edge corresponding to k (e.g., for edge 1-2, k=2). The vector from the midpoint to the vertex is: \mathbf{e} = (\mathbf{b}k \odot \mathbf{P}i) - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot \mathbf{P}i d. Scaling X: sx = \alpha{jk} \|\mathbf{e}\|2 e. Rotation X: \mathbf{r}x = \frac{\mathbf{e}}{\|\mathbf{e}\|2} f. Scaling Y: sy = \frac{\text{Area}(Fi)}{\beta{jk} \|\mathbf{e}\|2} where \text{Area}(Fi) is the area of the triangular face. g. Rotation Y: \mathbf{r}y = \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{r}x h. Scaling Z: sz = \delta{jk} i. Rotation Z: \mathbf{r}z = \mathbf{n} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def barycentricsplatparam(faceverts, facenormals, u, v, alpha, beta, delta): # faceverts: list of 3 numpy arrays [v1, v2, v3] # facenormals: list of 3 numpy arrays [n1, n2, n3] # alpha, beta, delta: dicts mapping edgeid -> scalar gaussians = [] # Define barycentric weights for the 6 midpoints midpointsbc = { 12: ((1-u)/2, (1-u)/2, u), 23: ((1-u)/2, (1-u)/2, u), 31: ((1-u)/2, u, (1-u)/2), 45: ((1-v)/2, (1-v)/2, v), 56: ((1-v)/2, (1-v)/2, v), 64: ((1-v)/2, v, (1-v)/2) } # Compute face area v1, v2, v3 = faceverts facearea = 0.5 np.linalg.norm(np.cross(v2 - v1, v3 - v1)) for edgeid, (q1, q2, q3) in midpointsbc.items(): # Interpolate position and normal pos = q1v1 + q2v2 + q3v3 normal = q1facenormals[0] + q2facenormals[1] + q3facenormals[2] # Determine end vertex index for the edge vector endidx = {12: 1, 23: 2, 31: 0, 45: 1, 56: 2, 64: 0}[edgeid] endpos = faceverts[endidx] # Edge vector from midpoint to end vertex e = endpos - pos enorm = np.linalg.norm(e) # Guard against degenerate edges if enorm < 1e-8: continue # Scaling and Rotation sx = alpha[edgeid] enorm rx = e / enorm sy = facearea / (beta[edgeid] enorm) ry = np.cross(normal, rx) sz = delta[edgeid] rz = normal gaussians.append({'center': pos, 'normal': normal, 'scale': [sx, sy, sz], 'rot': [rx, ry, rz]}) return gaussians Parameters: Hyperparameters for generalized geometric alignment: u = 0.07 v = 0.22 \alpha{12}=\alpha{23}=\alpha{31}=0.80 \alpha{45}=\alpha{56}=\alpha{64}=2.08 \beta{12}=\beta{23}=\beta{31}=15.0 \beta{45}=\beta{56}=\beta{64}=13.0 \delta{12}=\delta{23}=\delta{31}=\delta{45}=\delta{56}=\delta{64}=4.5 \times 10^{-5} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles/Edges: If \|\mathbf{e}\|2 \approx 0 (midpoint coincides with vertex), normalization of \mathbf{r}x fails. Guard against division by zero by clamping \|\mathbf{e}\|2 to a small epsilon or skipping such splats. Face Removal: When a mesh face is removed, all splats mapped to it must be identified and flagged for removal. Scale Bounds: To prevent discrepancies between Gaussian scales and mesh face scales, scales can be bounded via s = s{rel} \odot s0 where s{rel} \in [s{min}, s{max}]^2. Not given in the sources. Originating from GeoSplatting and OMeGa, this method addresses the lack of inherent geometry boundaries in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by binding splats to explicit mesh surfaces. It constrains splat centers to mesh faces using barycentric coordinates to preserve per-splat attributes and achieve generalized geometric alignment. OMeGa: Joint Optimization of Explicit Meshes and Gaussian Splats for Robust Scene-Level Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV61042.2026.00427, fetched 2026-10-30 GeoSplatting: Towards Geometry Guided Gaussian Splatting for Physically-Based Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51701.2025.02692, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction
head: Direct Multi-Plane Image Gaussian Optimization, DirectMPIGO
body: Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction is a neural rendering method that combines voxel-based density representation with Multi-Plane Image (MPI) depth layers to perform efficient volume rendering. It solves the problem of memory inefficiency in dense voxel grids by supporting sparse grids and occupancy caching, while using MPI to handle depth complexity. Unlike its sibling Gaussian Splatting Attribute Prediction, which refines initial Gaussians via residual correction, this method directly predicts density and color features from grid structures. It differs from DVGO by supporting sparse grids and MPI depth, whereas DVGO relies on dense voxel grids. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera rays (origin O, direction D), bounding box (xyz{min}, xyz{max}), and training images. Outputs: Rendered RGB images and gradients for grid parameters. Data Structures: 1. Density Grid: Created via grid.creategrid. Type specified by densitytype (e.g., DenseGrid). Channels=1. 2. Feature/Color Grid (k0): Created via grid.creategrid. Type specified by k0type. Channels determined by rgbnetdim. 3. Act Shift Grid: DenseGrid tensor of shape [1, 1, mpidepth]. requiresgrad=False. Stores logit shifts to equalize alpha contributions. 4. Mask Cache: Boolean tensor of shape maskcacheworldsize. Tracks occupied voxels. 5. Color MLP: A small network mapping grid features to RGB. Parameters: xyzmin, xyzmax: Scene bounding box coordinates. mpidepth: Number of MPI depth planes. fastcolorthres: Alpha threshold for occupancy mask updates. rgbnetdim: Color feature dimension. If \le 0, uses raw RGB (dim=3) from k0; otherwise uses MLP output. rgbnetdepth, rgbnetwidth: MLP depth and width. viewbasepe: Number of positional encoding frequencies for view direction. stepdist: Step distance for ray sampling. near, far: Ray clipping planes. voxelsizeratio: Constant 256.0 / mpi\depth. Initialization Steps: 1. Grid Creation: Initialize density grid with densitytype, channels=1, and worldsize derived from setgridresolution and xyz bounds. 2. Act Shift Initialization: Create actshift grid of shape [1, 1, mpidepth]. Initialize values to ensure uniform initial transmittance. Set initial density values g[i] = 1.0 / mpi\depth - 10^{-6} for all i \in [0, mpi\depth). Compute conditional probability p[i]: p[i] = \frac{1 - \sum{j=0}^{i+1} g[j]}{1 - \sum{j=0}^{i} g[j]} \quad \text{for } i > 0, \quad p[0] = 1 - g[0] Set actshift value at layer i: \text{act\shift}[i] = \log \left( (p[i]^{-1 / \text{voxel\size\ratio}}) - 1 \right) 3. Color Network Setup: If rgbnetdim \le 0: Create k0 grid with channels=3. Set color MLP to None (coarse stage). If rgbnetdim > 0: Create k0 grid with channels=rgbnetdim. Initialize color MLP. Composite colors pass Gaussian Splatting Attribute Prediction is a method for refining 3D Gaussian primitives by predicting additive residuals to initial rendering attributes, rather than regenerating them from scratch. It solves the problem of high-frequency detail loss in coarse initializations by using a voxel transformer to correct errors on a per-voxel basis. Unlike sibling methods that optimize neural feature grids directly, this approach operates on the Gaussian set's geometric and color parameters via residual correction. GO-Surf is a differentiable volume rendering method that optimizes a multi-resolution neural feature grid to reconstruct high-fidelity 3D surfaces from RGB-D observations. It solves the problem of fast, dense surface reconstruction by combining explicit grid-based feature storage with implicit SDF decoding, significantly reducing optimization time compared to fully implicit MLP-based methods like NeuralRGB-D. It sets itself apart by using a multi-resolution grid to store geometry and color features, allowing for faster convergence and higher detail capture, albeit at the cost of higher memory usage. Feed-forward and generalizable prediction methods map input images directly to a set of 3D Gaussian primitives in a single neural network pass, eliminating the need for per-scene gradient descent optimization [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. This approach solves the latency and compute bottlenecks of iterative reconstruction by leveraging priors learned from large-scale datasets, enabling real-time novel view synthesis on unseen scenes [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Unlike iterative methods that optimize geometry per scene, these methods generalize by mapping image features to Gaussian parameters via learned neural networks [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Gaussian Parameter Prediction derives the geometric and appearance parameters of 3D Gaussians from input data to enable novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of regenerating the Gaussian set directly from features or depth maps without iterative optimization. It differs from its siblings by focusing on direct prediction from pooled features or unprojected depth maps rather than iterative densification or mesh embedding. Predicts a set of learnable Gaussian parameters for each voxel v, including center offset, opacity, covariance, and spherical harmonic color. The final 3D Gaussian center \muj is computed by applying a sigmoid activation to the predicted offset \bar{\mu}j, shifting by -0.5, scaling by r, and adding the voxel centroid Centerj. \muj = r \cdot (\sigma(\bar{\mu}j) - 0.5) + Centerj where \muj is the final center, \sigma is sigmoid, \bar{\mu}j is the predicted offset, Centerj is the voxel centroid, and r is a scaling factor. The output dimension per Gaussian is 38, comprising offset (3), opacity (1), covariance (6), and spherical harmonic color (28). r is set to 3 times the voxel size. The sigmoid activation restricts the learnable offset to a localized neighborhood; the -0.5 shift facilitates symmetrical, bi-directional movement from the voxel center. Predicts 3D Gaussians directly (not triplane -> Gaussians), resulting in faster downstream rendering. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and samples per ray. Sparse grids reduce the number of active voxels queried. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the grid. Sparse grids significantly reduce memory usage compared to dense grids. Performance: Efficient for large scenes due to sparse grid support. MPI depth layers allow for handling complex depth structures without increasing voxel resolution uniformly. Strengths: Memory efficiency, support for large scenes, fast convergence due to occupancy caching. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of grid resolution and MPI depth. Sparse grid implementation can be complex. When to use: Large-scale scenes where memory is a constraint, or when high-frequency details are not the primary focus. When not to use: Scenes requiring very high-frequency detail where dense grids or other methods might be more appropriate. Originated from the kakaobrain/nerf-factory repository, DirectMPIGO combines voxel-based density representation with Multi-Plane Image (MPI) depth layers. It addresses the limitations of dense voxel grids in previous methods like DVGO by introducing sparse grids and occupancy caching. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) VolSplat: Rethinking Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Voxel-Aligned Prediction, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37232-11, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural Rendering — Technologies & Tricks, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeuralRenderingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splatting Attribute Prediction
head: Hierarchical Network built on residual correction, Residual Design, Residual Gaussian Prediction, Stage-wise Residual Gaussian Prediction, Voxel Transformer Residual Prediction
body: Gaussian Splatting Attribute Prediction is a method for refining 3D Gaussian primitives by predicting additive residuals to initial rendering attributes, rather than regenerating them from scratch. It solves the problem of high-frequency detail loss in coarse initializations by using a voxel transformer to correct errors on a per-voxel basis. The approach operates on the Gaussian set's geometric and color parameters via residual correction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial Gaussian rendering parameters \mathbf{G}j, fused voxel attributes \mathbf{E}j, and offset \mathbf{O}j for voxel j. Output: Refined Gaussian rendering parameters \mathbf{G}'j. Data Structures: Voxel Attributes (\mathbf{E}j): Fused features deposited from splats into a voxel grid. Offset (\mathbf{O}j): Normalized offset vector for the Gaussian primitive center, scaled to [-1, 1] using grid size h. Gaussian Parameters (\mathbf{G}j): Initial set of rendering parameters (position, scale, rotation, color). Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Fusion: Obtain initial Gaussian rendering parameters \mathbf{G}j and voxel attributes \mathbf{E}j through a Splat Fusion procedure. 2. Residual Prediction: Compute the residual \Delta \mathbf{G}j using a fine-grained Multi-Layer Perceptron (\text{MLP}{fine}) that takes the concatenation of the offset \mathbf{O}j and voxel attributes \mathbf{E}j as input. 3. Attribute Update: Add the predicted residual to the initial parameters to obtain the final splat rendering parameters \mathbf{G}'j. 4. Stage-wise Accumulation: For multi-stage reconstruction, initialize the Gaussian set G0 = \emptyset and rendered image I0 = 0. 5. Residual Rendering: At stage i, compute the image residual E{i-1} = I{gt} - I{i-1}. 6. Incremental Update: Predict new Gaussians \Delta Gi = f{\thetai}(E{i-1}) and accumulate them as Gi = G{i-1} \cup \Delta Gi. 7. Objective: Optimize using the residual rendering loss L{res}^{(i)} = L{render}(R(\Delta Gi), E{i-1}). Formulas: The voxel transformer residual prediction is defined as: \Delta \mathbf{G}j = \text{MLP}{fine}([\mathbf{O}j, \mathbf{E}j]) \mathbf{G}'j = \mathbf{G}j + \Delta \mathbf{G}j The stage-wise residual prediction framework is defined as: Gi = G{i-1} \cup \Delta Gi Ii = R(Gi) = R(G{i-1}) + R(\Delta Gi) = I{i-1} + R(\Delta Gi) E{i-1} = I{gt} - I{i-1} \Delta Gi = f{\thetai}(E{i-1}) L{res}^{(i)} = L{render}(R(\Delta Gi), E{i-1}) Parameters: Kernel Function: A one-dimensional cubic kernel K(x) is used in the underlying voxelization/interpolation process: K(x) = \frac{1}{6}(3|x|^3 - 6x^2 + 4) Color Clamping: Color parameters in the renderer allow signed values with no clamping applied, enabling the additive property required for residual correction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The offset \mathbf{O}j must be normalized to [-1, 1] using the grid size h to ensure stable MLP input. Additivity: The renderer must support additive composition of disjoint Gaussian sets for the residual logic to hold. Initialization: The process initializes with an empty Gaussian set G0 = \emptyset and zero image I0 = 0, making the first stage model the full target image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictgaussianattributes(Ginitial, voxelfeatures, offset, gridsizeh): # Normalize offset to [-1, 1] range per source specification Onormalized = offset / gridsizeh # Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle boundary cases Onormalized = clamp(Onormalized, -1.0, 1.0) # Concatenate offset and voxel attributes along the feature dimension inputfeatures = concatenate(Onormalized, voxelfeatures, axis=-1) # Predict residual using a standard 2-layer MLP with ReLU activation residual = MLPfine(inputfeatures) # Add residual to initial parameters Gfinal = Ginitial + residual return Gfinal def concatenate(a, b, axis=-1): # Standard tensor concatenation along the specified axis # Stacks tensors and reshapes to merge the last dimension return stack([a, b], axis=axis).reshape(a.shape[:-1] + (a.shape[-1] + b.shape[-1],)) class MLPfine: def init(self, indim, hiddendim, outdim): self.W1 = randomnormal((indim, hiddendim)) self.b1 = zeros(hiddendim) self.W2 = randomnormal((hiddendim, outdim)) self.b2 = zeros(outdim) def forward(self, x): h = matmul(x, self.W1) + self.b1 h = max(h, 0) # ReLU activation return matmul(h, self.W2) + self.b2 A framework that updates the Gaussian set incrementally across multiple stages, predicting primitives that explain the remaining image error. It sets itself apart from single-stage voxel refinement by decomposing the reconstruction problem along the error signal, reducing the learning burden per stage. Choose it when progressive refinement improves convergence or when modeling complex residual distributions. See Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction. A neural architecture that processes voxelized features to predict residuals for Gaussian attributes. It sets itself apart from direct attribute regression by operating on fused voxel grids and predicting additive corrections rather than absolute values. Choose it when spatial locality and voxel-based feature fusion are required for efficient refinement. See Voxel and Grid-Based Prediction. Time Complexity: Depends on the MLP size and voxel grid resolution. The method enables feed-forward inference for dynamic scenes. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the voxel grid and the MLP weights. Strengths: Reduces the learning burden on individual predictors by focusing on remaining error rather than full image content. Allows for efficient refinement of coarse initializations. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial Gaussian set and voxel fusion. When to use: When high-fidelity details are needed from a coarse initialization, or in feed-forward settings where iterative optimization is too slow. When not to use: When the initial Gaussian set is already high-quality and residuals are negligible. The method originates from research into efficient feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the "Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine" approach. It builds on the concept of residual learning in neural networks, applying it to the geometric and color attributes of Gaussian primitives. The additive property of the renderer, which allows for stage-wise reconstruction, was formalized in the AIR framework. name: GO-Surf Neural Feature Grid Optimization
body: GO-Surf is a differentiable volume rendering method that optimizes a multi-resolution neural feature grid to reconstruct high-fidelity 3D surfaces from RGB-D observations. It solves the problem of fast, dense surface reconstruction by combining explicit grid-based feature storage with implicit SDF decoding, significantly reducing optimization time compared to fully implicit MLP-based methods like NeuralRGB-D. It sets itself apart by using a multi-resolution grid to store geometry and color features, allowing for faster convergence and higher detail capture, albeit at the cost of higher memory usage. Inputs: A set of images with corresponding depth maps D[u, v] and camera poses parameterized by translation vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3 and Lie Algebra \nu \in \mathfrak{so}(3). A 3D bounding box defining the scene volume. Outputs: Optimized multi-resolution feature grids (geometry and color). Optimized geometry and color decoder MLPs. Optimized camera poses. Rendered color and depth images. Multi-Resolution Feature Grids: The method uses a set of 3D grids with different voxel sizes. Geometry grids have 4 levels with voxel sizes 3cm, 6cm, 24cm, and 96cm. Feature dimension per level hg is 4, yielding a final geometry feature vector dimension of 16. Color grids have 4 levels with the same voxel sizes. Feature dimension per level hc is 6. Trilinear interpolation is used to query features from these grids. Decoders: Both geometry and color decoders are lightweight MLPs with 2 hidden layers and 32 neurons each. The geometry decoder takes the concatenated 16D geometry feature vector as input and outputs the SDF value \phi(x). The color decoder takes the concatenated 6D color feature vector and viewing direction d as input and outputs the RGB color c. Sampling: Points xi along a ray are sampled using importance sampling. The process starts with Nc = 96 coarse samples. It iteratively adds 12 samples each time for 3 steps based on weights computed from previously sampled points. It concludes with Nf = 36 fine samples. Loss weights: \lambda{\text{rgb}} = 10.0, \lambda{\text{depth}} = 1.0, \lambda{\text{sdf}} = 10.0, \lambda{\text{fs}} = 1.0, \lambda{\text{eik}} = 1.0, \lambda{\text{smooth}} = 1.0. Truncation threshold t = 16\text{cm}. Free space loss exponential penalty \alpha = 5. Smoothness perturbation length \deltas is between 1mm and 4mm. Sigmoid smoothness parameter s is learnable. Optimizer is ADAM with learning rates 1 \times 10^{-3} for MLP decoders, 1 \times 10^{-2} for feature grids, and 5 \times 10^{-4} for camera poses. Batch size M = 6144 rays per batch. Optimization iterations: 10,000. Unverified code. Forward pass: trilinear interpolation # Backward pass: standard gradient # Second backward pass: custom CUDA kernel for Hessian of trilinear interpolation return F.gridsample(features, coords, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=True) class GeometryDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16, 32) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(32, 1) def forward(self, x): x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) return self.fc3(x).squeeze(-1) class ColorDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(6, 32) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(32, 3) def forward(self, x, d): x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) return self.fc3(x) class GOSurf: def init(self, scenebounds, voxelsizes, numcameras): self.scenebounds = scenebounds self.voxelsizes = voxelsizes self.numcameras = numcameras # Grid dimensions calculated from scenebounds and voxelsizes self.geofeatures = [nn.Parameter(torch.rand(10, 10, 10, 4)) for in range(4)] self.colorfeatures = [nn.Parameter(torch.rand(10, 10, 10, 6)) for in range(4)] self.geodecoder = GeometryDecoder() self.colordecoder = ColorDecoder() self.cameraposest = [nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3)) for in range(numcameras)] self.cameraposesnu = [nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3)) for in range(numcameras)] self.s = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0)) self.t = 0.16 self.alpha = 5 self.deltas = 0.002 self.Nc = 96 self.Nf = 36 self.M = 6144 self.lambdargb = 10.0 self.lambdadepth = 1.0 self.lambdasdf = 10.0 self.lambdafs = 1.0 self.lambdaeik = 1.0 self.lambdasmooth = 1.0 self.gridsampler = CustomGridSampler() def initializesurface(self): # Map x from scene bounds to [-1, 1] # Not given in sources. return (x - self.scenebounds.min) / (self.scenebounds.max - self.scenebounds.min) 2 - 1 def samplepoints(self, rayso, raysd): # Importance sampling: Nc=96 coarse, 3 steps of +12, Nf=36 fine # Not given in sources. pass def render(self, rayso, raysd): points, depths, weights = self.samplepoints(rayso, raysd) sdf = self.querysdf(points) colors = self.querycolor(points, raysd) sigmas = 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-self.s sdf)) sigmasnext = torch.roll(sigmas, -1) sigmasnext[-1] = 0.0 alpha = torch.clamp((sigmas - sigmasnext) / sigmas, min=0.0) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=0) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:1]), T[:-1]], dim=0) w = T alpha renderedcolor = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) colors, dim=0) rendereddepth = torch.sum(w depths, dim=0) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, points, weights def computelosses(self, rayso, raysd, gtcolor, gtdepth, pixelindices): predcolor, preddepth, points, weights = self.render(rayso, raysd) lrgb = torch.mean(torch.abs(gtcolor - predcolor)) validmask = gtdepth > 0 ldepth = torch.mean(torch.abs(gtdepth[validmask] - preddepth[validmask])) # b(x) = D[u, v] - d raydepthsatpoints = torch.sum(points raysd, dim=-1) bvalues = gtdepth[pixelindices] - raydepthsatpoints nearsurfacemask = torch.abs(gtdepth[pixelindices] - raydepthsatpoints) <= self.t lsdf = torch.mean(torch.abs(self.querysdf(points[nearsurfacemask]) - bvalues[nearsurfacemask])) farsurfacemask = ~nearsurfacemask term1 = torch.exp(-self.alpha self.querysdf(points[farsurfacemask])) - 1 term2 = self.querysdf(points[farsurfacemask]) - bvalues[farsurfacemask] lfs = torch.mean(torch.clamp(torch.stack([torch.zeroslike(term1), term1, term2], dim=-1), min=0).max(dim=-1).values) gradphi = torch.autograd.grad(self.querysdf(points[farsurfacemask]), points[farsurfacemask], gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(self.querysdf(points[farsurfacemask])), creategraph=True)[0] leik = torch.mean((1.0 - torch.norm(gradphi, dim=-1))2) eps = torch.randnlike(points[nearsurfacemask]) self.deltas pointsperturbed = points[nearsurfacemask] + eps gradphiperturbed = torch.autograd.grad(self.querysdf(pointsperturbed), pointsperturbed, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(self.querysdf(pointsperturbed)), creategraph=True)[0] gradphinear = torch.autograd.grad(self.querysdf(points[nearsurfacemask]), points[nearsurfacemask], gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(self.querysdf(points[nearsurfacemask])), creategraph=True)[0] lsmooth = torch.mean((gradphinear - gradphiperturbed)2) loss = (self.lambdargb lrgb + self.lambdadepth ldepth + self.lambdasdf lsdf + self.lambdafs lfs + self.lambdaeik leik + self.lambdasmooth lsmooth) return loss Second-Order Derivatives: Computing the Eikonal and smoothness losses requires the Hessian of the SDF. Standard PyTorch autograd does not support double back-propagation through the standard grid sampler for trilinear interpolation. A custom CUDA kernel must be implemented for the second backward pass. Initialization: Poor initialization can lead to local minima. Initializing the SDF to a sphere centered at the volume origin with radius half the smallest dimension helps convergence. Depth Noise: RGB-D sensors often have noisy depth or missing values (e.g., glass). The SDF regularization and RGB loss help mitigate these artifacts. Time Complexity: Optimization takes 15 to 45 minutes depending on scene size. Significantly faster than NeuralRGB-D (15-25 hours). Memory Complexity: Model size scales with scene resolution. Example: 268 MB for 8.8x9.1x3.4m scene (66.5M params). 41 MB for synthetic scene (10.1M params). Larger memory footprint than implicit MLP methods. Strengths: Fast optimization. High-fidelity surface reconstruction. Good hole-filling ability. Captures thin structures. Limitations: High memory usage. Requires custom CUDA kernel for training. When to Use: When fast reconstruction is required. When high-fidelity surface is needed. When memory is not a constraint. When Not to Use: When memory is very limited. When implicit representation is preferred for scalability. GO-Surf was introduced in the paper "GO-Surf: Neural Feature Grid Optimization for Fast, High-Fidelity RGB-D Surface Reconstruction". It builds on the idea of using neural feature grids for scene representation, combining the speed of explicit grids with the flexibility of implicit decoding. It is an improvement over NeuralRGB-D, which uses a single MLP for the entire scene, resulting in slower optimization. GO-Surf uses a multi-resolution grid to store features, allowing for faster convergence and better detail capture.
