name: Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction
head: GRM, Generalizable Reconstruction Method
body: Feed-forward and generalizable prediction methods map input images directly to a set of 3D Gaussian primitives in a single neural network pass, eliminating the need for per-scene gradient descent optimization [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. This approach solves the latency and compute bottlenecks of iterative reconstruction by leveraging priors learned from large-scale datasets, enabling real-time novel view synthesis on unseen scenes [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Unlike iterative methods that optimize geometry per scene, these methods generalize by mapping image features to Gaussian parameters via learned neural networks [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. All methods in this family share the core objective of mapping input image features to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 1. Input Representation: Inputs are typically one or more RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Some methods require known camera poses P, while others (e.g., Splatt3R, ZeroGS) predict poses or operate on uncalibrated inputs [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 2. Feature Encoding: A shared encoder (e.g., Vision Transformer, CNN) extracts multi-scale features from the input images. Cross-attention or cost volumes are often used to aggregate multi-view information [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 3. Primitive Prediction: A decoder head predicts Gaussian attributes. These attributes are usually: Mean (\mu): 3D position. Covariance (\Sigma): Defined by scale s and rotation r (quaternion or 6D). Opacity (\alpha): Scalar. Color (c): Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients or constant RGB [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 4. Differentiable Rendering: The predicted Gaussians are rendered into target views using differentiable rasterization to compute reconstruction losses (e.g., L1, SSIM, LPIPS) for training the network [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 5. Generalization: The network is trained on a large dataset of scenes to learn priors about geometry and appearance, allowing inference on unseen scenes [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. HFGaussian is a generalizable, feed-forward framework for real-time 3D human avatar reconstruction that simultaneously estimates novel views, 3D pose, and biomechanical features (such as dense pose and 3D keypoints) from sparse input images. Unlike sibling methods that rely on parametric body models (e.g., SMPL) or fail to integrate structural biomechanics, HFGaussian uses Gaussian splatting to represent the human subject and its associated features directly. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction by introducing a "feature splatting" mechanism that decouples human feature learning from the geometric Gaussian parameters, allowing different frequencies of features to be rendered efficiently without per-subject optimization. ZeroGS is a pipeline for training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from hundreds of unposed and unordered images without requiring Structure-from-Motion (SfM) tools like COLMAP. It differs from its siblings by leveraging a pretrained foundation model (Spann3R) as a neural scene representation and employing an incremental training buffer to progressively register images and refine poses. Unlike ACE0, which predicts sparse points using CNNs, ZeroGS predicts dense pointmaps and 3D Gaussians using transformers and optimizes the scene via rendering loss rather than reprojection error. The Deformation Field MLP is a coordinate-based neural network that predicts spatial offsets for 3D Gaussian primitives to model dynamic geometry or correct canonical shapes. It maps input coordinates (and optionally time) to deviations in position, rotation, and scale, serving as a smooth prior to prevent overfitting to sparse or noisy views. Unlike grid-based methods, it uses a compact MLP structure, making it suitable for dynamic scenes with high-rank variations where explicit point-based rendering exacerbates complexity. Shape Completion Training is a feed-forward method that predicts all 14 3D Gaussian attributes from partial inputs without requiring target coordinates or per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a fixed 2×2 folding grid to expand a small set of coarse primitives into a dense Gaussian set, enabling reconstruction of missing geometry in occluded or sparse scenes. Feed-forward generalizable reconstruction methods predict a set of 3D Gaussian primitives directly from input images in a single forward pass, eliminating the need for per-scene gradient descent optimization [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. This approach solves the latency and compute bottlenecks of iterative reconstruction by leveraging priors learned from large-scale datasets, enabling real-time novel view synthesis on unseen scenes [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Unlike iterative methods that optimize geometry per scene, these methods generalize by mapping image features to Gaussian parameters via learned neural networks [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Feature Uplifting via Forward Rendering is a method to estimate 3D language features f \in \mathbb{R}^d for 3D Gaussians from observed 2D features F{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^d by formulating the problem as a Maximum Likelihood (ML) or Maximum-a-Posteriori (MAP) estimation, assuming uniform prior and Gaussian noise. It differs from back-projection methods (e.g., conventional semantic feature learning) by leveraging the forward rendering process to establish precise correspondence, eliminating costly back-projection or iterative optimization. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction. Occam's LGS is a training-free method for lifting 2D language features to 3D Gaussian representations by applying Occam’s razor to the forward rendering process of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of expensive iterative optimization in feature space by computing weighted multi-view feature aggregation directly from the alpha blending weights of the standard color rendering pass. Unlike sibling methods that rely on scene-specific autoencoders, quantization, or costly semantic feature rendering, Occam's LGS supports arbitrary-dimensional uncompressed features without compromising training speed, achieving a two-order-of-magnitude speed-up while maintaining state-of-the-art performance for open-set vision-language tasks. Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression (FCGS) is an autoencoder-based compression method that encodes 3D Gaussian attributes into a latent space using hyperpriors and context models, addressing the fidelity drop caused by the non-invertibility of MLPs in geometry attributes. Unlike anchor-based quantization methods that modify Gaussian locations and require finetuning, FCGS creates context grids in a feed-forward manner without altering the original Gaussian positions. SHARE is a pose-free framework for generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting that estimates camera poses via predicted rays and uses anchor-aligned coarse-to-fine geometry estimation to predict 3D Gaussian parameters without ground-truth poses. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like PixelSplat and MVSplat by explicitly embedding pose awareness into multi-view cost volumes via Plücker rays, making it robust to pose inaccuracies where generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting methods are highly sensitive. HiGDiff is a feed-forward reconstruction method for computed tomography (CT) that predicts a set of 3D Gaussian primitives from degraded projections without per-scene optimization. It solves the problem of sparse-view, low-dose, or limited-angle CT reconstruction by using two explicit Gaussian banks (structure and detail) initialized from anatomical cues and refined via a sequential structure-to-detail diffusion hierarchy. It differs from single-bank Gaussian reconstruction by maintaining separate banks for global attenuation geometry and residual detail, and from dense voxel diffusion by operating on explicit Gaussian primitives with a sequential hierarchy. Amortized Image Reconstruction (AIR) is a self-supervised feed-forward framework that reconstructs a target image into a set of 2D Gaussian primitives in a single network pass, eliminating the costly per-image iterative optimization required by prior methods like GaussianImage. Unlike Instant-GI, which relies on handcrafted priors and pseudo-labels for initialization, AIR uses a stage-wise residual architecture to progressively predict Gaussian primitives from reconstruction residuals, achieving higher quality with encoding times of 160–300 ms. UniQueR is a feedforward framework for fast 3D reconstruction from unposed images using sparse learnable 3D queries. It predicts camera-to-world transforms and per-view local point maps, then uses queries to spawn Gaussians rendered via differentiable splatting for supervision. It sets itself apart from siblings like TokenGS by decoupling 3D Gaussian prediction from pixels with learnable implicit tokens, and avoids the quadratic complexity of full self-attention on concatenated tokens by using decoupled attention between image tokens and 3D queries. GS3 is an efficient self-supervised learning framework for learning point cloud representations by integrating fast 3D Gaussian Splatting into a rendering-based pretext task. It solves the problem of high computational cost and memory intensity inherent in existing volume rendering-based self-supervised methods. Unlike its sibling Ponder, which uses differentiable volume rendering with ray marching, GS3 employs a tile-based rasterizer to render 3D Gaussians, achieving significantly faster pre-training speeds and lower memory usage. DIF-Gaussian is a feed-forward neural network that reconstructs a 3D volume from multi-view 2D projections by predicting 3D Gaussian parameters at sampled points and decoding features via Gaussian interpolation. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the feature aggregation step as a differentiable Gaussian splatting operation, allowing the network to learn spatial priors directly in the Gaussian domain rather than through standard grid-based or point-based interpolation. Compact Feed-Forward 3D Gaussians via Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging is a post-processing pipeline that consolidates redundant, per-pixel 3D Gaussians produced by any feed-forward Gaussian predictor into a compact, content-adaptive set. It solves the inefficiency of per-pixel primitives by grouping spatially coherent Gaussians via saliency-guided superpixel segmentation, compressing them into latent representations, and merging them across views, retaining visual quality at approximately 1/20th of the original primitive count. Unlike uniform discretization or detection-based reduction methods, it is backbone-agnostic and operates as a plug-in module without retraining the underlying feed-forward network. A 3D-aware image synthesis generator that predicts color and density values on a sparse voxel grid, conditioned on camera pose. It uses a mapping network with 2 layers and 64 channels. The channel base is set to 4000 (reduced from StyleGAN2's 32768) to account for higher parameter count in 3D convolutions. It implements skip connections that add an upsampled version of the output grid of the previous layer to the input of the next layer. It conditions the generator on a camera pose represented by a rotation matrix and a translation vector, yielding a 12-dimensional input vector. It outputs coefficients of spherical harmonics for color, using degree 0 (single coefficient per color channel). It multiplies the network's density output by a factor of 30 to facilitate generating high density values for sharp surfaces. Parameters include: Channel base: 4000; Density multiplier: 30; Mapping network layers: 2; Mapping network channels: 64; Spherical harmonics degree: 0. A 3DGS-based human avatar modeling framework that reconstructs animatable and relightable human avatars from monocular video by decomposing geometry and appearance attributes and using dynamic skinning weights for pose-variant deformation. It encodes Gaussian attributes using the Gaussian Attributes Encoder DG, which consists of two sub-encoders Dg and Da. Both are multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) that take the Gaussian position x as input and output the corresponding geometric and appearance attributes, respectively. It articulates the human avatar by applying Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) transformations using the dynamic skinning weights W{\Thetat} to deform the 3D Gaussians from canonical space to posed space. It optimizes the RnD-Avatar through a Physically-Based Rendering (PBR) process to optimize geometric attributes (position and normal) and appearance attributes (albedo, roughness, and visibility). It renders photorealistic images given an environmental light by performing a PBR process on the optimized avatar. Starts from the same feed-forward scene initialization. It keeps the Gaussian centers fixed during all updates. It averages over N = 4, 8, 16 input views during evaluation. On ETH3D, learned refinement improves PSNR by 0.64 dB compared to the feed-forward baseline. It outperforms Direct Gradient Descent (Adam) on all four metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS) and yields stronger surface quality with fewer artifacts. Retrieves Gaussian attributes: xyz, opacity, scale, rot, and features (SHs). If computecov3Dpython is true, it computes pre-computed covariance: cov3Dprecomp = gaussianmodel.getcovariance(self.scalingmodifier). Otherwise, it keeps scales and rotations separate. If convertSHspython is true, it converts spherical harmonics to RGB: reshapes features to (-1, 3, (gaussianmodel.maxshdegree+1)2), computes view direction dirpp = (xyz - cameracenter), normalizes it, evaluates SHs using evalsh, and clamps result to [0.0, 1.0] via torch.clampmin(sh2rgb + 0.5, 0.0). If convertSHspython is false, it keeps SHs as raw features: shs = gaussianmodel.getfeatures. Parameters include: kernelsize: Default 0; scalingmodifier: Default 1; whitebackground: Default False; convertSHspython: Default False; computecov3Dpython: Default False. Neural fields used to predict the anisotropic shape and view-dependent color of 3D Gaussians within the HyRF framework. Predicts scene 3D Gaussian parameters from point cloud features in a point-aligned manner, allowing simultaneous optimization of multiple scenes without per-scene optimization. It uses a cost volume module or epipolar line transformer to perform cross-view feature encoding on input features F1, F2 to produce encoded features \hat{F}1, \hat{F}2. It passes encoded features \hat{F} through feed-forward network f\theta to predict Gaussian parameters. The mapping is defined as f\theta: \hat{F}i^{(H \times W)} \mapsto k \times \{ (\Delta \muj, \Sigmaj, \alphaj, cj) \}{j=1}^{(H \times W)} where f\theta is a feed-forward network, \hat{F}i are encoded point cloud features, k is the number of Gaussians per point, and parameters are mean offset \Delta \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and SH coefficients c. The mean is computed as \muj = pi + \Delta \muj where pi is the 3D coordinate of the j-th point and \Delta \muj is the offset between the point and the predicted Gaussian center \muj. The parameter k is the number of Gaussians predicted at each point. Value not explicitly fixed in text, but total Gaussians is k \times (H \times W) \times N. The concept of generalizable reconstruction using Gaussian Splatting emerged as a solution to the high computational cost of per-scene optimization in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. Early work, such as GRM (Generalizable Reconstruction Method), utilized existing multi-view generation models to train a pixel-aligned Gaussian representation for faithful 3D generation using a single feed-forward pass. This family of methods has since expanded to include pose-free frameworks, dynamic deformation modeling, and specialized applications in human avatar reconstruction and medical imaging. name: HFGaussian
head: Human Feature Gaussian
body: HFGaussian is a generalizable, feed-forward framework for real-time 3D human avatar reconstruction that simultaneously estimates novel views, 3D pose, and biomechanical features (such as dense pose and 3D keypoints) from sparse input images. Unlike sibling methods that rely on parametric body models (e.g., SMPL) or fail to integrate structural biomechanics, HFGaussian uses Gaussian splatting to represent the human subject and its associated features directly. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction by introducing a "feature splatting" mechanism that decouples human feature learning from the geometric Gaussian parameters, allowing different frequencies of features to be rendered efficiently without per-subject optimization. HFGaussian operates in two stages: depth estimation and joint Gaussian/pose/feature prediction. It uses two nearest source views to estimate depth, which informs the 3D position of Gaussians and provides point cloud data for pose regression. Inputs: Two RGB images Il, Ir \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} corresponding to the left and right nearest source views, and their known camera parameters. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{X, c, r, s, \alpha, f\}, where X is position, c is color, r is rotation, s is scaling, \alpha is opacity, and f is the human feature vector. Rendered novel view images. Estimated 3D pose (19 keypoints). Human features (continuous surface embeddings/dense pose). The scene is represented as a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color (RGB). ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. fi \in \mathbb{R}^d: Human feature vector (dimension d depends on the specific feature, e.g., dense pose embedding). 1. View Selection: Select the two nearest source views, Il and Ir, relative to the target view. 2. Image Encoding: Feed Il and Ir into a shared image encoder \epsilon{img} to generate multiscale image features f^ls and f^rs, where s is the feature scale. 3. Cost Volume & Depth Estimation: Generate a cost volume C by correlating the feature maps f^ls and f^rs. Use an iterative update mechanism on C to estimate depth maps Dl and Dr for the left and right views. 4. Gaussian Feature Generation: Encode the depth maps Dl, Dr using a depth encoder \epsilon{depth}. Combine the encoded depth features with the image features f{img} (concatenation \oplus) and pass them through a U-Net-like decoder \epsilon{params} to generate a Gaussian feature map \Gamma: \Gamma = \epsilon{params}(\epsilon{img}(I) \oplus \epsilon{depth}(I)) Apply four separate convolutional prediction heads to \Gamma to estimate parameter maps for rotation (Mr), scaling (Ms), opacity (M\alpha), and human features (Mf). The human feature map is defined as: Mf = \text{Sigmoid}(hf(\Gamma(x))) where hf is the feature head and x is the foreground pixel coordinate. 5. Gaussian Parameter Mapping: Map 2D pixel coordinates x to 3D positions X using the predicted depth and camera parameters via map Mp. Extract color c directly from the source images via map Mc. The full Gaussian set is \mathcal{G} = \{Mp(x), Mc(x), Mr(x), Ms(x), M\alpha(x), Mf(x)\}. 6. Pose Regression: Generate point clouds Pl, Pr from depth maps Dl, Dr and camera parameters. Extract human point clouds using 2D masks. Combine point clouds from both views into a single point cloud. Randomly sample 2048 points to form Pc. Input Pc into a pose regression network (based on DGCNN and PointNet) to estimate 3D pose (19 keypoints). 7. Feature Splatting (Rendering Features): Project Gaussians into 2D space using view transformation matrix W and Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transform. Calculate the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma': \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T where \Sigma is the 3D covariance matrix derived from r and s. Render human feature vectors fp by splatting Gaussian features fi in the image plane using alpha composition: fp = \sum{i \in N} fi \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where \alpha'i is the opacity \alphai multiplied by the 2D Gaussian value, and N is the set of splatted Gaussians. Decode the blended feature vectors fp using an MLP with two linear layers (ReLU activation) followed by a final sigmoid layer to render continuous surface embeddings. 8. Color Rendering: Render final pixel colors C using alpha blending: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) where ci is the learned color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def HFGaussianforward(Il, Ir, cameraparamsl, cameraparamsr, masksl, masksr): # 1. Image Encoding fl = sharedencoder(Il) fr = sharedencoder(Ir) # 2. Depth Estimation C = correlatecostvolume(fl, fr) Dl, Dr = iterativedepthupdate(C) # 3. Gaussian Parameter Estimation depthfeat = depthencoder(Dl) + depthencoder(Dr) imgfeat = sharedencoder(Il) + sharedencoder(Ir) Gamma = unetdecoder(depthfeat + imgfeat) Mr = convhead(Gamma, 4) Ms = convhead(Gamma, 3) Malpha = convhead(Gamma, 1) Mf = sigmoid(convhead(Gamma, 1)) # 4. Gaussian Construction Gaussians = [] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): if masksl[y, x] > 0.5: X = backproject(x, y, Dl[y, x], cameraparamsl) c = Il[y, x] r = Mr[y, x] s = Ms[y, x] alpha = Malpha[y, x] f = Mf[y, x] Gaussians.append({'X': X, 'c': c, 'r': r, 's': s, 'alpha': alpha, 'f': f}) # 5. Pose Regression Pl = backprojectall(Dl, cameraparamsl) Pr = backprojectall(Dr, cameraparamsr) Plhuman = [p for p in Pl if masksl[p.y, p.x] > 0.5] Prhuman = [p for p in Pr if masksr[p.y, p.x] > 0.5] Pcombined = Plhuman + Prhuman Psampled = randomsample(Pcombined, 2048) pose = posenetwork(Psampled) # 6. Rendering projected = project2d(Gaussians, cameraparamsl) projected.sort(key=lambda g: g['depth']) renderedcolor = alphablendcolor(projected) renderedfeatures = alphablendfeatures(projected) decodedfeatures = featuremlp(renderedfeatures) return renderedcolor, pose, decodedfeatures, Gaussians def sharedencoder(I): return VisionTransformer(I) # def correlatecostvolume(fl, fr): return crosscorrelation(fl, fr) # def iterativedepthupdate(C): return depthregression(C) # def depthencoder(D): return Conv3D(D) # def unetdecoder(F): return UNet(F) # def convhead(G, outch): return Conv2D(G, outch) # def sigmoid(x): return 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) # def backproject(x, y, depth, params): return depth unproject(x, y, params) # def backprojectall(D, params): return [backproject(x, y, D[y,x], params) for y, x in grid(D)] # def randomsample(P, n): return random.choices(P, k=n) # def posenetwork(P): return DGCNNPointNet(P) # def project2d(G, params): return [projectgaussian(g, params) for g in G] # def alphablendcolor(G): C = zeros(H, W, 3) accalpha = 0.0 for g in G: alphaprime = g['alpha'] gaussian2d(g) C = C + g['c'] alphaprime (1 - accalpha) accalpha += alphaprime return C def alphablendfeatures(G): F = zeros(H, W, d) accalpha = 0.0 for g in G: alphaprime = g['alpha'] gaussian2d(g) F = F + g['f'] alphaprime (1 - accalpha) accalpha += alphaprime return F def featuremlp(F): return Sigmoid(Linear(ReLU(Linear(F)))) # Human Feature Map: Mf = \text{Sigmoid}(hf(\Gamma(x))), where hf is the feature head and x is the foreground pixel coordinate. Feature Splatting: fp = \sum{i \in N} fi \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j), where fi is the Gaussian feature, \alpha'i is the resulting alpha from opacity \alphai and 2D Gaussian multiplication, and N is the set of splatted Gaussians. 2D Covariance: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T, where \Sigma is the 3D covariance matrix. Color Rendering: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j), where ci is learned color. Combined Loss: L = L{image} + L{depth} + L{pose} + L{feature}. Photometric Loss: L{image} = \beta L{mae} + \gamma L{ssim}, where \beta=1.6 and \gamma=0.4. Depth Loss: L{depth} = \sum{t=1}^T \mu^{T-t} \|d{gt} - dt\|1, where d is depth, \mu=0.9, and t is the iteration step. Pose Loss: L{pose} is the L2 loss between ground truth and estimated 3D keypoints. Feature Loss: L{feature} is the L1 loss between ground truth and predicted human features (continuous surface embeddings). Learning Rate: 2 \times 10^{-4}. Weight Decay: 1 \times 10^{-5}. Batch Size: 4. Dataset Resolution: 512 \times 512. Source Views: 8 images rendered in a circle at 45-degree intervals. Target Views: 3 random viewpoints. Keypoints: 19 (nose, neck, shoulders, elbows, wrists, pelvis, hips, knees, ankles, eyes, ears). Depth Estimator Training Iterations: 40,000. Joint Training Iterations: 100,000. Loss Weights: \beta=1.6 (MAE), \gamma=0.4 (SSIM) for photometric loss; \mu=0.9 for depth loss weighting. Feature Parameterization: Directly parameterizing 3D Gaussians with human features (opacity, scaling, rotation) yields suboptimal performance because these geometric parameters are not suitable for the different frequencies of human features. HFGaussian avoids this by optimizing separate feature parameters decoded after rendering. Point Cloud Sampling: The pose regression relies on a subset of Gaussians. Randomly sampling 2048 points is critical for the DGCNN/PointNet backbone to function effectively. Generalization: The method is designed to generalize to unseen data without fine-tuning, leveraging GPS-Gaussian as a backbone. Speed: Real-time rendering at 25 FPS. Performance: Achieves a PSNR of 32.43 on novel view synthesis, closely matching GPS-Gaussian's 32.55. Strengths: Simultaneously estimates RGB, 3D pose, and biomechanical features (dense pose) without per-subject optimization or parametric body models. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial depth estimation and the generalizability of the backbone encoder. Hardware: Implemented using PyTorch and AdamW optimizer. HFGaussian was introduced by Arnab Dey, Cheng-You Lu, Andrew I. Comport, Jean Martinet, Srinath Sridhar, and Chin-Teng Lin in arXiv:2411.03086v1 on 5 Nov 2024. It addresses the limitations of previous methods that either rely on substantial computational resources for parametric models (SMPL/STAR) or fail to incorporate biomechanical features essential for virtual interactions. It is used for 3D human avatar reconstruction, AR/VR, entertainment, and medical applications. HFGaussian: Learning Generalizable Gaussian Human with Integrated Human Features, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2411.03086, fetched 2026-10-26

name: ZeroGS
body: ZeroGS is a pipeline for training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from hundreds of unposed and unordered images without requiring Structure-from-Motion (SfM) tools like COLMAP. It differs from its siblings by leveraging a pretrained foundation model (Spann3R) as a neural scene representation and employing an incremental training buffer to progressively register images and refine poses. Unlike ACE0, which predicts sparse points using CNNs, ZeroGS predicts dense pointmaps and 3D Gaussians using transformers and optimizes the scene via rendering loss rather than reprojection error. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of unposed, unordered RGB images \{Ik\}. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} and camera poses for all registered images. Data Structures: Training Buffer: A collection of registered images and their associated poses and 3D Gaussians. Spatial Feature Memory: Used by the Spann3R backbone to store fused features for global coordinate regression. Method Steps: 1. Seed Initialization: Initialize the pipeline with a pretrained model (based on DUSt3R/Spann3R) and a single seed image I{seed}. Unlike incremental SfM which initializes from an image pair to fix gauge freedom, ZeroGS initializes from a pretrained model and a single seed image. 2. Batch Registration: Register a batch of unregistered images. For each image pair (Ii, Ij) where Ii is from the registered set (or seed) and Ij is from the unregistered set: a. Feature Encoding: Compute shared features using a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder V: f{ie}, f{je} = V(Ii, Ij) b. Decoder Processing: Pass features through reference and target transformer decoders D{ref} and D{tgt}: f{id} = D{ref}(f{ie}, f{je}), \quad f{jd} = D{tgt}(f{je}, f{ie}) c. Pointmap Prediction: Map decoder features to pointmaps using projection heads H{ref} and H{tgt}. Spann3R predicts pointmaps in a global coordinate frame X{k,g}: X{i,g}, X{j,g} = H{ref}(f{id}), H{tgt}(f{jd}) Note: X{i,j} denotes the pointmap of image j in camera i's coordinate frame in the base DUSt3R formulation, but ZeroGS uses Spann3R to regress directly into the global frame of the seed image without aligning pairwise dense pointmaps. d. Coarse Pose Estimation: Compute coarse camera poses for Ij using RANSAC and a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solver on 2D-3D correspondences between the predicted pointmaps and the known geometry. e. Pose Refinement: Refine the coarse poses by minimizing a point-to-camera ray consistency loss between the 3D points and camera centers across multiple views. f. Gaussian Prediction: Predict 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}k for the scene using the same network. 3. Rendering and Loss: Rasterize the predicted 3D Gaussians using the refined poses to render images. Compute an RGB reconstruction loss (e.g., L1) and back-propagate gradients to update the network. 4. Buffer Update: At the end of each training epoch, update the training buffer by registering new images that meet the registration criteria (using RANSAC and PnP). 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 until all images are registered or no more images can be registered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def ZeroGSpipeline(images, pretrainedmodel, seedimage): # Initialize training buffer with seed image buffer = {seedimage: {'pose': np.eye(4), 'gaussians': None}} unregistered = list(images - {seedimage}) # Initialize spatial feature memory for global frame regression memory = SpatialFeatureMemory(pretrainedmodel) while unregistered: # Select a batch of unregistered images batch = SelectBatch(unregistered, buffer) for refimg, tgtimg in batch: # 1. Feature Encoding frefe, ftgte = pretrainedmodel.encoder(refimg, tgtimg) # 2. Decoder and Pointmap Prediction (Spann3R) # Uses memory for global coordinate regression frefd = pretrainedmodel.decoderref(frefe, ftgte, memory) ftgtd = pretrainedmodel.decodertgt(ftgte, frefe, memory) # Predict pointmaps in global frame Xrefg = pretrainedmodel.headref(frefd) Xtgtg = pretrainedmodel.headtgt(ftgtd) # Predict 3D Gaussians G = pretrainedmodel.predictgaussians(Xtgtg) # 3. Coarse Pose Estimation # Use RANSAC + PnP on 2D-3D correspondences coarsepose = RANSACPnP(Xrefg, Xtgtg, buffer[refimg]['pose']) # 4. Pose Refinement # Minimize point-to-camera ray consistency loss refinedpose = RefinePose(coarsepose, Xtgtg, buffer[refimg]['pose']) # 5. Rendering Loss renderedimg = DifferentiableRasterize(G, refinedpose) loss = ComputeRGBLoss(renderedimg, tgtimg) # Backpropagate to update model and memory pretrainedmodel.backward(loss) memory.update(ftgtd) # Register image if successful if IsRegistered(refinedpose): buffer[tgtimg] = {'pose': refinedpose, 'gaussians': G} unregistered.remove(tgtimg) return buffer def SpatialFeatureMemory(model): # Initializes the spatial feature memory buffer for global coordinate regression return model.memoryencoder def SelectBatch(unregistered, buffer): # Selects a fixed-size chunk of unregistered images for parallel processing return unregistered[:min(8, len(unregistered))] def RANSACPnP(Xref, Xtgt, refpose): # Standard RANSAC + PnP: matches 2D pixels to 3D points, filters outliers, solves for camera pose # Implementation uses standard computer vision solvers; exact code omitted return np.eye(4) def RefinePose(coarsepose, Xtgt, refpose): # Minimizes point-to-camera ray consistency loss across multiple views # Implementation uses gradient descent on camera parameters; exact code omitted return coarsepose def DifferentiableRasterize(G, pose): # Rasterizes 3D Gaussians to image using differentiable splatting # Standard 3DGS rasterizer implementation; exact code omitted return np.zeroslike(G) def ComputeRGBLoss(rendered, target): # Computes L1 or SSIM reconstruction loss return np.mean(np.abs(rendered - target)) def IsRegistered(pose): # Checks if the estimated pose is geometrically valid and consistent return np.linalg.norm(pose - np.eye(4)) > 1e-6 Parameters: GPU Memory: Runs on a 24GB consumer-level GPU for hundreds of images. Batch Size: Images are registered in batches rather than individually. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: Aligning pairwise dense pointmaps to a global frame (as done in DUSt3R post-processing for >2 images) is time-consuming and can exceed GPU memory limits. ZeroGS avoids this by regressing in the global frame directly via Spann3R. Textureless Areas: 3DGS can struggle to identify Gaussians in textureless areas; the method relies on the pretrained model's geometric priors to mitigate this. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but incremental registration and batch processing are used to manage computational load. Memory Complexity: Fits within 24GB GPU memory for hundreds of images. Strengths: Handles hundreds of unposed/unordered images; recovers more accurate poses than state-of-the-art pose-free NeRF/3DGS methods; renders higher quality images than 3DGS with COLMAP poses. Limitations: Requires a large pretrained foundation model; finetuning is challenging as 3D foundation models are supervised by ground-truth 3D points difficult to obtain in unseen scenes. When to use: When COLMAP fails or is unavailable for large, unordered, or densely captured image sets. ZeroGS was proposed by researchers from Alibaba Group (AIBluefisher). It builds upon the DUSt3R and Spann3R architectures. The method addresses the limitation of traditional SfM (like COLMAP) which limits completeness and requires posed images. It differs from ACE0 by using transformers and dense predictions, and from InstantSplat and Splatt3R by regressing points in the global coordinate frame without aligning dense pointmaps. Evaluated on LLFF, MipNeRF360, and Tanks-and-Temples datasets. ZeroGS: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting from Unposed Images, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2411.15779, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Deformation Field MLP
head: Coordinate MLP
body: The Deformation Field MLP is a coordinate-based neural network that predicts spatial offsets for 3D Gaussian primitives to model dynamic geometry or correct canonical shapes. It maps input coordinates (and optionally time) to deviations in position, rotation, and scale, serving as a smooth prior to prevent overfitting to sparse or noisy views. Unlike grid-based methods, it uses a compact MLP structure, making it suitable for dynamic scenes with high-rank variations where explicit point-based rendering exacerbates complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Canonical 3D Gaussian position \mu. In dynamic variants, time t is concatenated with \mu. Output: Position offset \Delta\mu. In dynamic variants, offsets for position \deltax, rotation \deltar (or quaternion \deltaq), and scaling \deltas. Data Structures: Network Parameters (\theta): Weights and biases for an 8-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Hidden Dimension: 256 neurons per layer. Storage Overhead: Approximately 2 MB compared to standard 3D Gaussians. Algorithm: The network applies sinusoidal positional encoding to the input, processes it through two blocks of linear layers with a skip connection, and predicts the final offset. 1. Positional Encoding: Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the input coordinate \mu. For dynamic scenes, encode the concatenated vector (\mu, t). 2. Feature Extraction (Layers 1–4): Pass the encoded input through the first four of eight fully connected layers with ReLU activations and a hidden dimension of 256. 3. Skip Connection: Concatenate the positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) with the hidden feature vector output from Layer 4. 4. Feature Refinement (Layers 5–8): Pass the concatenated vector through four additional fully connected layers with ReLU activations and a hidden dimension of 256. 5. Offset Prediction: Pass the final feature vector through linear output head(s) without activation. Static/canonical correction uses a single linear layer to output \Delta\mu. Dynamic deformation uses three separate linear layers to output \deltax, \deltar, and \deltas. 6. Deformation Application: Static: Compute the deformed position \mu' = \mu + \Delta\mu. Dynamic: Apply offsets to canonical Gaussian parameters: xo = xc + \deltax, so = sc \cdot \exp(\deltas), qo = qc \cdot \deltaq. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class SinusoidalPositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, numbands=10): super().init() self.numbands = numbands def forward(self, x): # x shape: (..., D) where D=3 (pos) or D=4 (pos+time) # Standard NeRF-style PE freqbands = torch.exp(torch.linspace(0, math.log(10000), self.numbands) -math.log(10000)) freqbands = freqbands.view(1, 1, -1) x = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands pe = torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1) return pe class DeformationFieldMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=3, outputdim=3, hiddendim=256, numbands=10, isdynamic=False): super().init() self.pe = SinusoidalPositionalEncoding(numbands) self.isdynamic = isdynamic self.pedim = inputdim 2 numbands # Layers 1-4 self.layers14 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(self.pedim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU()) # Layers 5-8: Input dimension doubles due to skip connection concatenation self.layers58 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim + self.pedim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU()) # Output head if isdynamic: self.head = nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim 3) # pos, rot, scale else: self.head = nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim) # pos only def forward(self, x): # x: (..., inputdim) pe = self.pe(x) # Layers 1-4 h = self.layers14(pe) # Skip connection: concat input PE with hidden features h = torch.cat([h, pe], dim=-1) # Layers 5-8 h = self.layers58(h) # Output delta = self.head(h) return delta Parameters: MLP Depth: 8 layers. Hidden Width: 256 neurons. PE Frequency Bands: 10. Activation: ReLU for hidden layers, none for output layers. Deformation Learning Rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-5}. Loss Weight (\lambda): 0.2 for D-SSIM in L1+D-SSIM loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: The output head must be initialized such that \Delta\mu \approx 0 (identity) to prevent the network from absorbing pose errors at the start of training. Pose Accuracy: Inaccurate camera poses can lead to convergence failure, as the deformation field may struggle to correct for large geometric mismatches. Dynamic Rank: Grid/plane-based structures are avoided because dynamic scenes have higher rank than static scenes, and explicit point-based rendering exacerbates this. Memory: Adds approximately 2 MB of storage overhead compared to standard 3D Gaussians. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of Gaussians, as each Gaussian is processed independently through the MLP. Strengths: Injects a spatial smoothness prior, helping to avoid overfitting to sparse training views. Compact structure suitable for dynamic scenes. Limitations: Performance degrades with significantly inaccurate camera poses. May not outperform grid-based methods in static, low-rank scenes. When to Use: Dynamic scene reconstruction or sparse-view reconstruction aided by canonical CAD models. When Not to Use: Static scenes with high-quality dense input where grid-based methods may be more efficient. The Deformation Field MLP was introduced in the context of deformable 3D Gaussian splatting for dynamic scene reconstruction and later adapted for sparse-view reconstruction aided by CAD models. It draws inspiration from coordinate-based MLPs used in NeRF and other implicit representations. The method was developed to address the limitations of explicit point-based rendering in dynamic scenarios, where high-rank variations make grid-based approaches less effective. name: Shape Completion Training
head: Decoder-based Shape Completion, Folding Grid Expansion for Shape Completion
body: Shape Completion Training is a feed-forward method that predicts all 14 3D Gaussian attributes from partial inputs without requiring target coordinates or per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a fixed 2×2 folding grid to expand a small set of coarse primitives into a dense Gaussian set, enabling reconstruction of missing geometry in occluded or sparse scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Partial 3D data (e.g., point clouds or voxel grids) with missing regions. No target coordinates are provided during inference. Output: A set of 1,024 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, ci\}{i=1}^{1024}, where \mu is mean, \Sigma is covariance (defined by scale s and rotation q), \alpha is opacity, and c is color (DC spherical harmonic coefficients). Data Structures: 1. Coarse Primitives: A list of 256 entities. Each entity contains 14 attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color). 2. Folding Grid: A fixed 2 \times 2 grid structure used to spatially expand the coarse primitives. 3. Final Gaussians: A list of 1,024 entities with the same 14-attribute layout. Algorithm Steps: 1. Encoder Freezing: Initialize a pretrained feature encoder and freeze its weights. 2. Decoder Initialization: Initialize an identical decoder architecture to the encoder's output space. 3. Feature Processing: Pass the input features through four Transformer layers in the decoder (width 256, 8 attention heads) to predict 256 coarse primitive attributes. 4. Grid Expansion: Expand the 256 coarse primitives to 1,024 Gaussians using the fixed 2×2 folding grid. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of geometric and attribute losses: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{Chamfer}^{2} + \mathcal{L}{NN} + 0.1 \left( \mathcal{L}{L1}(\alpha, s, c) + \mathcal{L}{sign\text{-}inv}(q) \right) Where: \mathcal{L}{Chamfer}^{2} is the squared \ell2 Chamfer distance between predicted and target points. \mathcal{L}{NN} is the nearest-neighbor attribute matching loss. \mathcal{L}{L1} is the \ell1 loss applied to opacity \alpha, scale s, and DC color coefficients c. \mathcal{L}{sign\text{-}inv}(q) is the sign-invariant quaternion similarity loss for rotation q. The aggregate attribute term is scaled by a weight of 0.1. 6. Optimization: Optimize the decoder weights using AdamW for 80 epochs. Learning rate: 10^{-3}. Weight decay: 0.05. Warm-up: 5 epochs. Batch size: 64. Train three independent decoder seeds per frozen encoder. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class ShapeCompletionDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self, numcoarse=256, numfinal=1024, width=256, heads=8, layers=4): super().init() self.transformerblocks = nn.ModuleList([ nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(dmodel=width, nhead=heads) for in range(layers) ]) self.attrproj = nn.Linear(width, 14) self.numcoarse = numcoarse self.numfinal = numfinal self.expansionfactor = numfinal // numcoarse def forward(self, x): # x: [Batch, CoarsePrimitives, Width] for block in self.transformerblocks: x = block(x) coarseattrs = self.attrproj(x) # [Batch, 256, 14] finalattrs = self.expandfoldinggrid(coarseattrs) return finalattrs def expandfoldinggrid(self, coarseattrs): # coarseattrs: [B, 256, 14] expanded = coarseattrs.repeatinterleave(self.expansionfactor, dim=1) # [B, 1024, 14] # Fixed 2x2 grid offsets for position (first 3 dims) offsets = torch.tensor([ [-0.5, -0.5, 0], [0.5, -0.5, 0], [-0.5, 0.5, 0], [0.5, 0.5, 0] ], device=coarseattrs.device).float() pos = expanded[:,:,:3] others = expanded[:,:, 3:] gridindices = torch.arange(self.expansionfactor, device=coarseattrs.device) gridoffsets = offsets[gridindices] gridoffsets = gridoffsets.view(1, 1, 4, 3) posexpanded = pos.view(pos.shape[0], 256, 4, 3) posfinal = posexpanded + gridoffsets posfinal = posfinal.view(pos.shape[0], -1, 3) return torch.cat([posfinal, others], dim=-1) def computeloss(predattrs, targetattrs): # predattrs: [B, 1024, 14], targetattrs: [B, N, 14] predpos = predattrs[:,:,:3] targetpos = targetattrs[:,:,:3] dists = torch.cdist(predpos, targetpos, p=2) # [B, 1024, N] chamferpred = torch.min(dists, dim=2)[0].mean() chamfertarget = torch.min(dists, dim=1)[0].mean() chamferloss = (chamferpred + chamfertarget) / 2.0 nnindices = torch.argmin(dists, dim=2) targetnnattrs = torch.gather(targetattrs, 1, nnindices.unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, -1, 14)) nnloss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(predattrs, targetnnattrs) # Attribute losses: alpha (idx 10), scale (idx 3:6), color (idx 11:14) attrl1 = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(predattrs[:,:, 10], targetnnattrs[:,:, 10]) + \ torch.nn.functional.l1loss(predattrs[:,:, 3:6], targetnnattrs[:,:, 3:6]) + \ torch.nn.functional.l1loss(predattrs[:,:, 11:14], targetnnattrs[:,:, 11:14]) # Sign-invariant quaternion loss (idx 6:10) predrot = torch.nn.functional.normalize(predattrs[:,:, 6:10], p=2, dim=-1) targetrot = torch.nn.functional.normalize(targetnnattrs[:,:, 6:10], p=2, dim=-1) dotprod = torch.sum(predrot targetrot, dim=-1) signinvloss = torch.nn.functional.mseloss(dotprod, torch.oneslike(dotprod)) return chamferloss + nnloss + 0.1 (attrl1 + signinvloss) def trainshapecompletion(encoder, decoder, dataloader, epochs=80, lr=1e-3, weightdecay=0.05, warmupepochs=5, batchsize=64): optimizer = optim.AdamW(decoder.parameters(), lr=lr, weightdecay=weightdecay) scheduler = optim.lrscheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, Tmax=epochs) device = next(decoder.parameters()).device for epoch in range(epochs): if epoch < warmupepochs: for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = lr (epoch + 1) / warmupepochs for batch in dataloader: inputs, targets = batch inputs = inputs.to(device) targets = targets.to(device) with torch.nograd(): features = encoder(inputs) preds = decoder(features) loss = computeloss(preds, targets) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() scheduler.step() Time Complexity: Inference is feed-forward with no per-scene optimization state. Training requires 80 epochs per decoder seed. Memory Complexity: Low inference memory footprint as no per-scene optimization state is stored. Training memory depends on batch size (64) and the size of the feature maps. Performance: Evaluated on 520 held-out objects with visible ratios {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} and three crop seeds. Render metrics use the seed-0 decoder at 50% visibility and four fixed views per object. Strengths: No per-scene tuning required; handles severe occlusion; deterministic output structure. Limitations: Fixed expansion ratio (256 to 1,024) may not adapt to scene complexity; relies on the quality of the pretrained encoder. Shape Completion Training was introduced in the context of Gaussian-JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for 3D Gaussian Splats). It addresses the challenge of reconstructing 3D scenes from partial observations, a common issue in real-world scanning where occlusions and sensor noise lead to incomplete data. By freezing a pretrained encoder and training a decoder to complete the shape, it leverages learned priors from large-scale data to infer missing geometry without iterative optimization. Gaussian-JEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for 3D Gaussian Splats, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15651v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Feed-forward Generalizable Reconstruction
head: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS), Generalizable 3DGS
body: Feed-forward generalizable reconstruction methods predict a set of 3D Gaussian primitives directly from input images in a single forward pass, eliminating the need for per-scene gradient descent optimization [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. This approach solves the latency and compute bottlenecks of iterative reconstruction by leveraging priors learned from large-scale datasets, enabling real-time novel view synthesis on unseen scenes [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Unlike iterative methods that optimize geometry per scene, these methods generalize by mapping image features to Gaussian parameters via learned neural networks [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. All methods in this family share the core objective of mapping input image features to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 1. Input Representation: Inputs are typically one or more RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Some methods require known camera poses P, while others (e.g., Splatt3R, ZeroGS) predict poses or operate on uncalibrated inputs [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 2. Feature Encoding: A shared encoder (e.g., Vision Transformer, CNN) extracts multi-scale features from the input images. Cross-attention or cost volumes are often used to aggregate multi-view information [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 3. Primitive Prediction: A decoder head predicts Gaussian attributes. These attributes are usually: Mean (\mu): 3D position. Covariance (\Sigma): Defined by scale s and rotation r (quaternion or 6D). Opacity (\alpha): Scalar. Color (c): Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients or constant RGB [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 4. Differentiable Rendering: The predicted Gaussians are rendered into target views using differentiable rasterization to compute reconstruction losses (e.g., L1, SSIM, LPIPS) for training the network [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. 5. Generalization: The network is trained on a large dataset of scenes to learn priors about geometry and appearance, allowing inference on unseen scenes [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. AnySplat is a feed-forward, generalizable reconstruction method that predicts a set of 3D Gaussians directly from uncalibrated input images without per-scene optimization. It solves the problem of requiring known camera poses and per-scene training by jointly predicting Gaussian parameters, depth maps, and camera poses using a transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on fixed grids or specific calibration assumptions, AnySplat operates on unconstrained views and uses a differentiable voxelization module to handle the transition from pixel-wise predictions to a renderable 3D primitive set. Splatt3R is a feed-forward model that predicts 3D Gaussian Splat parameters directly from a pair of uncalibrated RGB images, without requiring camera intrinsics, extrinsics, or depth maps. It extends the MASt3R foundation model by adding a parallel "Gaussian head" to predict per-pixel Gaussian attributes, enabling novel view synthesis via differentiable rendering. Unlike sibling methods that typically supervise only interpolated views between input cameras, Splatt3R is designed to extrapolate to viewpoints outside the stereo baseline using a novel loss masking strategy. RLSplat is a resource-linear, budget-controllable feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) framework that generates exactly B Gaussians from uncalibrated input images, ensuring that inference latency and peak memory scale linearly with the requested Gaussian budget. Unlike prior budget-controllable methods that predict a dense set of candidates and subsequently prune them—resulting in nearly constant computational cost regardless of the target budget—RLSplat learns a discrete allocation policy to distribute the budget across local scene regions and refines the resulting Gaussians via a resource-linear decoder with hierarchical neighbor search. LGTM is a feed-forward framework that predicts compact 2D Gaussian primitives coupled with per-primitive texture maps to enable high-fidelity 4K novel view synthesis without per-scene optimization. It solves the quadratic growth in primitive count inherent to pixel-aligned feed-forward 3DGS methods, which makes high-resolution synthesis intractable due to memory and compute limits. Unlike standard 3DGS which couples appearance and geometry within each primitive, LGTM decouples them, allowing a compact set of geometric primitives to represent rich texture regions via per-primitive textures. InfiniSplat v2 is a feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction method for arbitrary input views that decouples geometry and attribute prediction, uses ground-truth (GT) camera poses for alignment during training, and employs large-angle target view supervision to improve rendering quality under large viewpoint changes. It differs from its sibling DA3-GS by freezing the geometry branch to prevent geometric degradation caused by joint optimization, and from other feed-forward methods by using GT poses for alignment to avoid pose errors that misguide the network under large-angle supervision. DepthSplat is a feed-forward method for 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction that connects multi-view depth estimation with Gaussian rendering by leveraging pre-trained monocular depth features to augment multi-view feature matching. It solves the problem of robust depth prediction in challenging scenarios (occlusions, low-texture, non-Lambertian surfaces) where standard multi-view stereo fails, and scale ambiguities where monocular estimation fails, by fusing both signals early in the pipeline. Unlike TranSplat, which uses monocular features to refine coarse depth (vulnerable to error propagation), DepthSplat combines cost volumes and monocular features early, and unlike GS-LRM, it relies on explicit feature matching rather than heavy data-driven priors, making it significantly cheaper to train. VG2GT is a feed-forward, non-pixel-aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction framework that directly regresses geometrically accurate Gaussian scenes and camera parameters from an arbitrary number of unposed and uncalibrated images. It solves the problem of uneven Gaussian distributions and cross-view inconsistencies inherent in pixel-aligned methods by introducing a multi-scale differentiable voxel module that aggregates point-cloud features into a structured representation. Unlike siblings such as AnySplat Pipeline, which first regresses pixel-aligned primitives and then aggregates them, VG2GT directly decodes Gaussian primitives from structured voxel features, avoiding the intermediate pixel-aligned representation. Direct Pixel-Wise Regression is a feed-forward method that predicts a set of 3D Gaussian primitives directly from input image patches, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between 2D pixels and 3D Gaussians. It differs from sibling methods like Triplane-LRM by avoiding fixed-resolution latent representations (e.g., triplanes), thereby enabling pixel-aligned prediction of per-Gaussian colors and scaling Gaussian count with input resolution to capture high-frequency details. WildSplat is a feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework designed for appearance-conditioned novel-view synthesis from sparse, unposed, in-the-wild images. It solves the problem of inconsistent photometric conditions (e.g., varying weather, lighting, or time of day) by explicitly decoupling geometry from appearance. Unlike sibling methods that assume photometric consistency or require precomputed poses, WildSplat jointly predicts camera poses, appearance-invariant 3D geometry, and reference-conditioned appearance attributes in a single forward pass. StereoGaussians is a feed-forward method that predicts a metric 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation from a single calibrated stereo pair, enabling nearby-view extrapolation without per-scene optimization. It sets itself apart from its siblings by reusing intermediate representations from frozen pretrained stereo networks to predict Gaussian attributes, while calibrated disparity anchors the geometry. Unlike methods that synthesize images directly (e.g., LVSM) or refine inverse depth through a composer (e.g., SHARP), StereoGaussians uses explicit feed-forward multi-view Gaussian prediction with a second Gaussian layer and an expanded image canvas to provide capacity for disoccluded and outside-field-of-view content. Latent Space Representation methods map input images to a compact, structured latent code (tokens, features, or distributions) which is subsequently decoded into explicit 3D Gaussian primitives, enabling generalizable reconstruction without per-scene optimization [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Unlike sibling methods that predict Gaussians directly from pixel-wise features or cost volumes, this family explicitly models the scene as a set of learnable latent entities (e.g., tokens or entropy-coded features) to enforce global consistency, reduce representation bloat, or handle ambiguity [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. Use sliding windows to process the sequence and construct a unified large-scale Gaussian scene. Successfully applied to a KITTI street sequence containing over 1,000 frames. Feed-forward generalizable reconstruction emerged as a response to the high computational cost of per-scene optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Early methods like SplatterImage utilized U-Net architectures to translate single-view images into Gaussian attributes, which could be extended to multi-view inputs via warping. Subsequent works integrated cost volumes (e.g., MVSplat) and foundation models (e.g., MASt3R, VGGT) to improve geometric consistency and generalization across diverse scenes. The field has since diversified into budget-controllable frameworks (RLSplat), texture-decoupled models (LGTM), and methods handling uncalibrated or wild inputs (WildSplat, AnySplat). name: AnySplat Pipeline
head: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting from Unconstrained Views
body: AnySplat is a feed-forward, generalizable reconstruction method that predicts a set of 3D Gaussians directly from uncalibrated input images, eliminating the need for per-scene optimization. It differs from iterative methods by using a transformer-based encoder-decoder to predict Gaussian parameters, depth, and camera poses in a single forward pass, leveraging pseudo-geometry priors from a pretrained Vision Transformer (VGGT) for supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of K uncalibrated RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times K \times 3 \times 448 \times 448}. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} (defined by mean \mu, scale s, rotation r, opacity \alpha, and color c) and predicted camera poses (extrinsic E and intrinsic K). Data Structures: The method constructs pixel-wise 3D Gaussians from the decoder outputs. These are then voxelized into "pre-voxel 3D Gaussians" using a Differentiable Voxelization module to handle density and rendering efficiency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: Input images are processed by a transformer-based geometry encoder to extract multi-scale features. 2. Parameter Prediction: Three decoder heads (FG, FD, FC) predict: FG: Gaussian parameters (\mu, \sigma, r, s, c). Note: \sigma typically denotes standard deviation related to scale, or the covariance components. FD: A depth map D. FC: Camera poses p (extrinsic and intrinsic matrices). 3. Gaussian Construction: The predicted parameters are used to construct a set of pixel-wise 3D Gaussians. 4. Differentiable Voxelization: The pixel-wise Gaussians are voxelized into pre-voxel 3D Gaussians. 5. Rendering: Multi-view images and depth maps are rendered from the voxelized Gaussians using differentiable rasterization. 6. Loss Computation: RGB Loss: Rendered images are compared against ground truth images using an RGB loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS). Geometry Loss: Rendered depth maps, decoded depth D, and predicted poses p are used to compute geometry losses. 7. Pseudo-Geometry Supervision: The geometry predictions are supervised by pseudo-geometry priors obtained from a pretrained VGGT model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Preprocess: Normalize images from [0, 1] to [-1, 1] if required by model, # or [0, 1] if model expects [0, 1]. The code snippet shows (images+1)0.5, # implying input might be [-1, 1] normalized, converting to [0, 1]. # However, standard image inputs are often [0, 1]. The snippet suggests: # imagesinput = (images + 1) 0.5 # This implies the 'images' passed to inference are in [-1, 1] range. # 2. Forward Pass # The model consists of a geometry encoder and three decoder heads (FG, FD, FC) gaussians, predcontextpose = model.inference(images) # 3. Extract Poses predallextrinsic = predcontextpose['extrinsic'] predallintrinsic = predcontextpose['intrinsic'] # 4. Voxelization (Internal to model or separate module) # The model internally voxelizes the pixel-wise Gaussians into pre-voxel 3D Gaussians # using a Differentiable Voxelization module. # 5. Rendering and Loss (During Training) # Rendered images and depth maps are generated from the voxelized Gaussians. # Losses are computed against GT images and VGGT pseudo-geometry priors. return gaussians, predcontextpose Parameters: Input resolution: 448 \times 448 pixels. Number of views K: Variable, typically small (e.g., 3-5) for unconstrained views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uncalibrated Inputs: The method must handle unknown camera poses, relying on the network to predict them and the VGGT priors for geometric consistency. Voxelization Artifacts: The Differentiable Voxelization step is critical for managing Gaussian density and preventing rendering artifacts. A high-resolution variant using a Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterizer to increase density from low-resolution features. A variant replacing fixed Gaussians with flexible planar kernels for better geometric fidelity with fewer primitives. Time Complexity: Inference is O(1) with respect to scene complexity, as it is a single forward pass through a neural network. Training time depends on the dataset size and VGGT prior computation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of predicted Gaussians and the voxel grid resolution. The voxelization step helps manage memory by aggregating nearby Gaussians. Strengths: Fast inference, handles uncalibrated views, generalizes to unseen scenes without per-scene optimization. Limitations: Quality depends on the generalization capability of the network and the accuracy of VGGT pseudo-geometry priors. May struggle with highly dynamic or out-of-distribution scenes. Hardware: Requires GPU for inference and training. PyTorch 2.2.0 and CUDA 12.1 recommended. AnySplat is part of the family of feed-forward generalizable reconstruction methods for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the principles of mapping input features to Gaussian parameters without per-scene optimization [16746-feed-forward-generalizable-reconstruction.md]. It specifically addresses the challenge of unconstrained views by predicting camera poses and leveraging pretrained vision models for geometric supervision. name: SubSplat
head: Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterization, Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterizer
body: SubSplat is a method for high-resolution novel-view synthesis that resolves the trade-off between network computational cost and rendering fidelity in pixel-aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of insufficient Gaussian density and artifacts when using low-resolution backbone inputs by introducing a Sub-pixel Gaussian Reparameterizer (SPGR). Unlike prior methods limited by fixed grids or image-space upsamplers, SubSplat subdivides each grid-anchored primary Gaussian into multiple fine-grained sub-pixel primitives, restoring structural density directly from low-resolution features while maintaining stable network latency. SubSplat builds on the AnySplat Pipeline by refining the Gaussian generation stage. It takes low-resolution multi-view features and primary Gaussian anchors as input, and outputs a set of sub-pixel Gaussians suitable for high-resolution rendering. Inputs: N primary Gaussians \mathcal{A} = \{\mathbf{a}p\}{p=1}^N, where \mathbf{a}p = [\boldsymbol{\mu}p, \mathbf{s}p, qp, \alphap] \in \mathbb{R}^{11}. Spherical Harmonic (SH) colors \mathcal{H} = \{\mathbf{h}p \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times D{\mathrm{sh}}}\}{p=1}^N. Default: C=3, D{\mathrm{sh}}=25 (degree-4 SH). Multi-view feature maps \mathcal{F} = \{\Phi{v,\ell}\}{v=1..V, \ell=1..L}, where \Phi{v,\ell} \in \mathbb{R}^{H\ell \times W\ell \times D\ell}. Fixed camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Outputs: K sub-pixel Gaussians per primary Gaussian, defined by position \boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k}, scale \mathbf{s}{p,k}, quaternion q{p,k}, opacity \alphak, and SH color \mathbf{h}{p,k} for k=1 \dots K. K is the squared ratio of target to input resolution (e.g., K=4 for 2x, K=16 for 4x). Primary Gaussian State: \mathbf{a}p contains world-space position \boldsymbol{\mu}p (3), per-axis scales \mathbf{s}p (3), unit quaternion qp (4), and opacity \alphap (1). Embeddings: Geometry and appearance queries are aligned to a shared embedding dimension E=128. Feature Maps: Multi-view features \Phi{v,\ell} are sampled via the deformable attention operator using bilinear weights g(a, b) = \max(0, 1-|a-b|). 1. Initialization: Define N primary Gaussians \mathcal{A} and SH colors \mathcal{H} from the backbone output. Camera metadata is kept separate. 2. Feature Aggregation: Geometry Query: Encode primary Gaussian attributes into a 128-dimensional embedding using per-attribute MLPs \phix, \phis, \phiq, \phi\alpha, then project with linear Wg: \mathbf{z}^gp = Wg(\phix(\boldsymbol{\mu}p) + \phis(\mathbf{s}p) + \phiq(qp) + \phi\alpha(\alphap)) Geometry Aggregation: Perform 3-stage deformable attention. Initialize \mathbf{f}^{g,0}p = \mathbf{0}. For t=0,1,2: \mathbf{f}^{g,t+1}p = \mathrm{DA}(\mathcal{F}; \mathbf{z}^gp, \mathbf{f}^{g,t}p, \mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol{\mu}p), \mathbf{a}p) Final geometry descriptor \mathbf{f}^gp = \mathbf{f}^{g,3}p. Appearance Query: Encode flattened SH coefficients \mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{h}p) into a 128-dimensional embedding: \mathbf{z}^ap = \phic(\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{h}p)) Appearance Aggregation: Perform 1-stage deformable attention conditioned on the geometry descriptor: \mathbf{f}^ap = \mathrm{DA}(\mathcal{F}; \mathbf{z}^ap, \mathbf{f}^gp, \mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol{\mu}p), \mathbf{a}p) 3. Primary View Selection: For each anchor \boldsymbol{\mu}p, project into all cameras. Select the primary view v^ with the smallest positive depth zv > 0. 4. Geometry Reparameterization: Predict offsets using geometry head g\theta: \mathbb{R}^E \to \mathbb{R}^{K \times 9}: [\Delta uk, \Delta vk, \Delta zk, \Delta \log \mathbf{s}k, \Delta \mathbf{r}k]{k=1}^K = g\theta(\mathbf{f}^gp) Position: Back-project sub-pixel offsets (\Delta uk, \Delta vk) using selected depth z{\mathrm{sel}} and focal lengths fx, fy. Bound depth residual via \tanh: \Delta \hat{z}k = \tanh(\Delta zk) \boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + R{c2w} \begin{bmatrix} z{\mathrm{sel}}\Delta uk / fx \\ z{\mathrm{sel}}\Delta vk / fy \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \Delta \hat{z}k R{c2w} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where R{c2w} is the camera-to-world rotation matrix. Scale: Refine scales element-wise: \mathbf{s}{p,k} = \mathbf{s}p \odot \exp(\Delta \log \mathbf{s}k) Rotation: Convert axis-angle residual \Delta \mathbf{r}k to quaternion q(\Delta \mathbf{r}k), compose, and normalize: q{p,k} = \mathrm{norm}(qp \otimes q(\Delta \mathbf{r}k)) Covariance: Compute covariance matrix: \Sigma{p,k} = R(q{p,k}) \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s}{p,k}^2) R(q{p,k})^\top 5. Appearance Reparameterization: Predict opacity logits \ellk and color gain \gammak using appearance head h\phi: \mathbb{R}^E \to \mathbb{R}^{K \times 2}: [\ellk, \gammak]{k=1}^K = h\phi(\mathbf{f}^ap) Projected Area: Compute pinhole Jacobian B at \boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k} in camera coordinates (where xc, yc, zc are camera-frame coords): B = \begin{bmatrix} fx/zc & 0 & -fx xc/zc^2 \\ 0 & fy/zc & -fy yc/zc^2 \end{bmatrix} Compute world-space projection Jacobian J{v^}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k}) = B R^{v^}{\mathrm{w2c}}. Estimate projected area: Ak \approx \sqrt{\det(J{v^}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k}) \Sigma{p,k} J{v^}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{p,k})^\top)} Opacity Allocation: Compute weights to preserve integrated opacity: wk = \mathrm{softmax}(\ellk), \quad \tilde{w}k = \frac{wk}{Ak + \varepsilon} \alphak = \alphap \cdot \frac{\tilde{w}k}{\sumj \tilde{w}j} Color Modulation: Scale SH coefficients: \mathbf{h}{p,k} = \gammak \mathbf{h}p Anti-aliasing: If Ak < A{\mathrm{min}}, adjust in-plane scales to ensure minimum area, preventing flickering. 6. Training: Minimize loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\ell2} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{LPIPS}} with \lambda = 0.05. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def axisangletoquaternion(axisangle): angle = torch.norm(axisangle, dim=-1, keepdim=True) axis = axisangle / (angle + 1e-8) halfangle = angle / 2 return torch.cat([torch.cos(halfangle), torch.sin(halfangle) axis], dim=-1) def quaternionmultiply(q1, q2): w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1[..., 0], q1[..., 1], q1[..., 2], q1[..., 3] w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2[..., 0], q2[..., 1], q2[..., 2], q2[..., 3] return torch.stack([w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2], dim=-1) def quaternionnormalize(q): return q / (torch.norm(q, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): w, x, y, z = q[..., 0], q[..., 1], q[..., 2], q[..., 3] R = torch.zeros(q.shape[:-1], 3, 3, device=q.device) R[..., 0, 0] = 1 - 2(y2 + z2) R[..., 0, 1] = 2(xy - wz) R[..., 0, 2] = 2(xz + wy) R[..., 1, 0] = 2(xy + wz) R[..., 1, 1] = 1 - 2(x2 + z2) R[..., 1, 2] = 2(yz - wx) R[..., 2, 0] = 2(xz - wy) R[..., 2, 1] = 2(yz + wx) R[..., 2, 2] = 1 - 2(x2 + y2) return R def computecovariance(s, q): R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) return R @ torch.diagembed(s2) @ R.transpose(-1, -2) def bilinearsample(features, coords): x, y = coords[..., 0], coords[..., 1] x0, y0 = torch.floor(x).long(), torch.floor(y).long() x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 # Triangular kernel g(a, b) = max(0, 1 - |a - b|) per evidence w00 = torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(x - x0), min=0) torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(y - y0), min=0) w10 = torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(x - x1), min=0) torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(y - y0), min=0) w01 = torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(x - x0), min=0) torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(y - y1), min=0) w11 = torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(x - x1), min=0) torch.clamp(1 - torch.abs(y - y1), min=0) return (w00.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) features[:,:, y0, x0] + w10.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) features[:,:, y0, x1] + w01.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) features[:,:, y1, x0] + w11.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) features[:,:, y1, x1]) class SubSplatSPGR: def init(self, E=128, C=3, Dsh=25, K=4): self.E = E self.K = K self.phix = nn.Linear(3, E) self.phis = nn.Linear(3, E) self.phiq = nn.Linear(4, E) self.phialpha = nn.Linear(1, E) self.Wg = nn.Linear(E, E) self.phic = nn.Linear(C Dsh, E) self.gtheta = nn.Linear(E, K 9) self.hphi = nn.Linear(E, K 2) def encodegeometry(self, mu, s, q, alpha): zsum = self.phix(mu) + self.phis(s) + self.phiq(q) + self.phialpha(alpha) return self.Wg(zsum) def encodeappearance(self, h): return self.phic(h.view(h.size(0), -1)) def deformableaggregation(self, features, zquery, fprev, mu, extrinsics, fx, fy, numstages): fcurr = fprev for in range(numstages): Rw2c = extrinsics[:,:3,:3] t = extrinsics[:,:3, 3] mucam = torch.bmm(Rw2c, (mu - t).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) x = mucam[..., 0] fx / mucam[..., 2] y = mucam[..., 1] fy / mucam[..., 2] phifeat = bilinearsample(features, torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1)) attn = torch.softmax((fcurr + zquery) phifeat, dim=-1) fcurr = (attn phifeat).sum(dim=-1) return fcurr def geometryreparam(self, fg, mu, s, q, zsel, fx, fy, Rc2w): offsets = self.gtheta(fg).view(-1, self.K, 9) du, dv, dz = offsets[:,:, 0], offsets[:,:, 1], offsets[:,:, 2] dlogs, dr = offsets[:,:, 3:6], offsets[:,:, 6:9] dzhat = torch.tanh(dz) dx = zsel du / fx dy = zsel dv / fy offsetvec = torch.stack([dx, dy, torch.zeroslike(dx)], dim=-1) offsetworld = torch.matmul(offsetvec, Rc2w.transpose(1, 2)) depthvec = torch.stack([torch.zeroslike(dzhat), torch.zeroslike(dzhat), dzhat], dim=-1) depthworld = torch.matmul(depthvec, Rc2w.transpose(1, 2)) mup = mu.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.K, -1) munew = mup + offsetworld + depthworld snew = s.unsqueeze(1) torch.exp(dlogs) qres = axisangletoquaternion(dr) qnew = quaternionnormalize(quaternionmultiply(q.unsqueeze(1), qres)) return munew, snew, qnew def appearancereparam(self, fa, mu, s, q, alpha, h, Rw2c, fx, fy): preds = self.hphi(fa).view(-1, self.K, 2) l, gamma = preds[:,:, 0], preds[:,:, 1] covsnew = computecovariance(s.unsqueeze(1), q.unsqueeze(1)) mucam = torch.bmm(Rw2c, (mu.unsqueeze(1) - 0).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) xc, yc, zc = mucam[..., 0], mucam[..., 1], mucam[..., 2] B = torch.stack([fx/zc, torch.zeroslike(zc), -fxxc/(zc2), torch.zeroslike(zc), fy/zc, -fyyc/(zc2)], dim=-1).view(-1, self.K, 2, 3) J = torch.matmul(B, Rw2c) areas = torch.sqrt(torch.det(J @ covsnew @ J.transpose(-1, -2)).clamp(min=1e-6)) w = torch.softmax(l, dim=-1) eps = 1e-6 wtilde = w / (areas + eps) alphanew = alpha.unsqueeze(1) (wtilde / wtilde.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)) hnew = gamma.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) h.unsqueeze(1) return alphanew, hnew def forward(self, mu, s, q, alpha, h, features, extrinsics, intrinsics): zg = self.encodegeometry(mu, s, q, alpha) za = self.encodeappearance(h) fx, fy = intrinsics[..., 0, 0], intrinsics[..., 1, 1] fg = self.deformableaggregation(features, zg, torch.zeroslike(zg), mu, extrinsics, fx, fy, 3) fa = self.deformableaggregation(features, za, fg, mu, extrinsics, fx, fy, 1) mucam = torch.bmm(extrinsics[:,:3,:3], (mu - extrinsics[:,:3, 3:4]).squeeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) depths = mucam[..., 2] validdepths = torch.where(depths > 0, depths, torch.inf) vstar = torch.argmin(validdepths, dim=-1) Bidx = torch.arange(mu.size(0)) Rc2w = extrinsics[Bidx, vstar,:3,:3] zsel = depths[Bidx, vstar] munew, snew, qnew = self.geometryreparam(fg, mu, s, q, zsel, fx, fy, Rc2w) alphanew, hnew = self.appearancereparam(fa, mu, s, q, alpha, h, Rc2w.transpose(1, 2), fx, fy) return munew, snew, qnew, alphanew, hnew K: Number of sub-pixel primitives per primary Gaussian. K = (\text{target\res} / \text{input\res})^2. Typical values: 4 (2x), 16 (4x). \lambda: LPIPS loss weight. Default: 0.05. C, D{\mathrm{sh}}: SH dimensions. Default: C=3, D{\mathrm{sh}}=25. E: Embedding dimension. Default: 128. Depth Instability: Unbounded depth residuals cause instability. Mitigated by bounding \Delta zk via \tanh. Aliasing/Flickering: Extremely small primitives (Ak < A{\mathrm{min}}) cause flickering. Mitigated by enforcing minimum area A{\mathrm{min}} and adjusting in-plane scales. Opacity Preservation: Sub-pixel primitives must sum to primary opacity. Mitigated by renormalization \alphak = \alphap \cdot (\tilde{w}k / \sumj \tilde{w}j). Time and Memory Complexity: SubSplat maintains stable backbone latency by using low-resolution inputs. The reparameterization stage adds negligible computational overhead compared to the backbone. It achieves over 3x latency reduction compared to full-resolution baselines. Measured Performance: Evaluated on RealEstate10K and ACID datasets, reconstructing from 256x256 input and rendering at 512x512 (2x) and 1024x1024 (4x). Strengths: High-fidelity reconstruction at extended scales; superior efficiency; content-aware density scaling; mitigates quadratic cost of high-resolution inputs. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the backbone features; requires deformable attention which can be complex to implement efficiently. When to use: When high-resolution output is required from sparse, low-resolution inputs, and inference latency is a constraint. When not to use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable and latency is not a concern, or when input resolution is already high enough to support direct high-res Gaussian prediction. SubSplat was proposed by Jiun Lee et al. in 2024. It addresses the limitations of pixel-aligned Gaussian methods that are constrained by fixed grids or suffer from high computational costs at high resolutions. It uses the same input structure as MVSplat and incorporates a deformable-attention operator following the formulation used in GaussianFormer and PixelGaussian. It is used for novel-view synthesis in computer vision, specifically for sparse-view reconstruction. name: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK)
head: DRK Splatting
body: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) Splatting is a 3D scene representation method that replaces the fixed radial symmetry of Gaussian primitives with a flexible planar kernel defined by multiple radial basis functions. It solves the overparameterization and geometric fidelity limitations of Gaussian Splatting by allowing adaptive stretching, rotation, and sharp boundary control, enabling high-fidelity rendering with significantly fewer primitives. Unlike standard 2D Gaussian Splatting, which relies on smooth, elliptical distributions, DRK supports straight edges and sharp corners through L1/L2 norm blending and piecewise edge sharpening. Inputs: Camera parameters: Ray origin \mathbf{r}o, ray direction \mathbf{r}d, view up vector \mathbf{R}z. Scene representation: A set of N DRK primitives. Each primitive i is defined by parameters \Thetai = \{\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{q}i, \{s{k,i}, \theta{k,i}\}{k=1}^K, \etai, \taui, oi, \mathbf{sh}i\}. Image resolution and tile configuration: 16 \times 16 tiles. Outputs: Final color image \mathbf{C} and depth buffer. Each DRK primitive i stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position in world space. \mathbf{q}i \in SO(3): Orientation quaternion, converted to rotation matrix \mathbf{R}i = [\mathbf{R}{x,i}, \mathbf{R}{y,i}, \mathbf{R}{z,i}]. \{s{k,i}, \theta{k,i}\}{k=1}^K: K radial basis lengths and polar angles, ordered 0 < \theta{1,i} < \dots < \theta{K,i} \le 2\pi. \etai \in (0, 1): Blending weight between L1 and L2 norms. \taui \in (-1, 1): Edge sharpening coefficient. oi \in (0, 1): Base opacity. \mathbf{sh}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent appearance.
