Project to Local Tangent Coordinates d = pixelworldpos - prim.mu u = dot(d, prim.Rx) v = dot(d, prim.Ry) # B. Compute Polar Coordinates r = sqrt(uu + vv) if r == 0: theta = 0.0 # Handle division by zero else: theta = arccos(u / r) if v < 0: theta = 2 pi - theta # Cover full 2pi range # C. Determine Radial Basis Interval k = findindex(prim.theta, theta) # Find k such that theta[k] < theta <= theta[k+1] # D. Compute Relative Angular Distance deltatheta = (theta - prim.theta[k]) pi / (prim.theta[k+1] - prim.theta[k]) # E. Compute L2 Norm Component sbarsq = (1 + cos(deltatheta)) / (2 prim.s[k]2) + \ (1 - cos(deltatheta)) / (2 prim.s[k+1]2) r2sq = r r # F. Compute L1 Norm Component # Maps diamond-shaped L1 unit ball to segment between adjacent endpoints r1 = 1.0 / (abs(u / (prim.s[k] cos(prim.theta[k]))) + \ abs(v / (prim.s[k] sin(prim.theta[k])))) # G. Blended Kernel Value g = exp(-(prim.eta r12 + (1 - prim.eta) r2sq / 2) / sbarsq) # H. Edge Sharpening alpha = prim.o psi(g, prim.tau) # I. Low-Pass Filtering deltapw = abs(pixel.u - prim.projectedu) deltaph = abs(pixel.v - prim.projectedv) viewscale = abs(dot(ray.direction, prim.Rz)) alphafiltered = max(alpha, prim.o exp(-0.5 (deltapw2 / sl2 + deltaph2 / (sl2 viewscale2)))) # J. Compositing colori = evalsh(prim.sh, ray.direction) coloraccum += alphafiltered colori (1 - alphaaccum) alphaaccum += alphafiltered (1 - alphaaccum) if alphaaccum >= 0.999: break image[pixel] = coloraccum K: Number of radial bases. Default/Typical: Not specified, but 2D-GS is a special case with K=4. \eta \in (0, 1): L1/L2 blend weight. \tau \in (-1, 1): Edge sharpness coefficient. sl: Filter radius. Not given in the sources. Division by Zero: When r=0 (kernel center), \theta is undefined. Set \theta=0. View Orthogonality: If \mathbf{r}d \cdot \mathbf{R}{z,i} \approx 0, the kernel is viewed edge-on. The low-pass filter denominator becomes small, increasing the filter size to prevent aliasing. Degenerate Input: If \thetak = \theta{k+1}, the sector is empty. Ensure \thetak are strictly increasing. Time Complexity: Rasterization is O(N \cdot T) where N is primitives and T is tiles, but optimized by cache sorting (length 8) and culling. Per-pixel cost is proportional to the number of overlapping primitives in the cache (max 8). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot K) to store radial basis parameters. Performance: DRK achieves superior rendering quality with significantly fewer primitives (e.g., 30 vs thousands for Gaussians) on detailed textures and sharp geometry. Strengths: Better representation of sharp edges and straight lines; reduced overparameterization. Limitations: More complex kernel evaluation than Gaussians; requires careful tuning of \eta and \tau. DRK Splatting was proposed by Yi-Hua Huang et al. in 2025 (arXiv:2412.11752v2). It extends 2D Gaussian Splatting by introducing deformable radial bases to overcome the smoothness and symmetry constraints of Gaussians. It is backwards-compatible, reducing to a Gaussian kernel when using two orthogonal bases with specific decay rates. name: Splatt3R
head: Splatt3R: Zero-Shot Gaussian Splatting from Uncalibrated Image Pairs
body: Splatt3R is a feed-forward method that predicts 3D Gaussian Splat primitives directly from a pair of uncalibrated natural images, without requiring camera intrinsics, extrinsics, or depth information. It extends the MASt3R foundation model by adding a Gaussian prediction head to output geometry and appearance parameters in a single forward pass. Unlike existing generalizable 3D-GS methods that are limited to interpolating viewpoints between input stereo views, Splatt3R supports extrapolation to wider baselines using a novel loss masking strategy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two uncalibrated RGB images I1, I2 \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} (typically 512 \times 512). Camera parameters are unknown. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and color c (or spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: The method predicts per-pixel Gaussians. For each pixel j in the input images, the network outputs: Base position xj \in \mathbb{R}^3 (in the coordinate frame of the first image). Position offset \Delta xj \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation quaternion qj \in \mathbb{R}^4. Scale sj \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphaj \in \mathbb{R}. Color cj: Constant view-independent color S \in \mathbb{R}^3 is used in experiments, with ablation for view-dependent spherical harmonics. Architecture: 1. Encoder: The two input images are encoded using a shared Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder and cross-attention transformers. This backbone is based on MASt3R and is frozen during training. 2. Point Cloud Head: The frozen MASt3R backbone predicts 3D point locations \hat{X}1, \hat{X}2 and confidence maps C1, C2 in the coordinate frame of the first image. 3. Gaussian Head: A parallel head (using DPT architecture) predicts the additional Gaussian attributes: offsets \Delta, rotations q, scales s, opacities \alpha, and spherical harmonics S for each pixel. 4. Primitive Construction: The final set of Gaussian primitives is the union of primitives predicted from both input images. Formulas: The mean position \muj of each Gaussian is calculated as the sum of the predicted base position xj and the offset \Delta xj: \muj = xj + \Delta xj The covariance matrix \Sigmaj is reparameterized using the rotation quaternion qj and scale sj to ensure positive semi-definiteness: \Sigmaj = R(qj) S(sj) S(sj)^T R(qj)^T where R(qj) is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion and S(sj) is the diagonal scale matrix. The total loss L is a weighted sum of masked Mean Squared Error (MSE) and LPIPS losses: L = \lambda{MSE} L{MSE}(M \odot \hat{I}, M \odot I) + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS}(M \odot \hat{I}, M \odot I) where \hat{I} is the rendered image, I is the ground truth target image, M is the loss mask, and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. Parameters: Activation Functions: Normalization for quaternions, exponential for scales and offsets, and sigmoid for opacities. Color: Constant view-independent color S \in \mathbb{R}^3 is used in the primary experiments. Overlap Thresholds: Hyperparameters \phi and \psi control the selection of context and target images during training. Typical values tested: Close (\phi=0.9, \psi=0.9), Medium (0.7, 0.7), Wide (0.5, 0.5), Very Wide (0.3, 0.3). Training Procedure: Training is performed in two stages: 1. Geometry Loss: The 3D point cloud's geometry is optimized using a confidence-based regression loss L{pts} and L{regr} from the MASt3R backbone. 2. Novel View Synthesis: The Gaussian head is trained to minimize the rendering loss on target views. Loss Masking: To prevent destructive updates from unseen parts of the scene, a loss mask M is calculated for each target image: 1. Unproject target image points to 3D. 2. Reproject these points onto the context images. 3. Check if the reprojected pixel is inside the frustum of at least one context view. 4. Check if the rendered depth matches the ground truth depth within a tolerance. 5. Pixels satisfying these conditions are marked as valid (mask M=1); others are masked out (M=0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatt3rforward(I1, I2, backbone, gaussianhead): """ Forward pass of Splatt3R. I1, I2: Input images (H, W, 3) backbone: Frozen MASt3R encoder (ViT + Cross-Attention) gaussianhead: DPT-based decoder for Gaussian parameters Returns: List of Gaussian primitives (mu, sigma, alpha, color) """ # 1. Encode images using frozen MASt3R backbone features = backbone.encode(I1, I2) # 2. Predict base 3D points and confidences (in I1's frame) # x1, x2 are base positions; c1, c2 are confidences x1, c1 = backbone.pointhead(features, view=1) x2, c2 = backbone.pointhead(features, view=2) # 3. Predict Gaussian attributes using the parallel Gaussian Head # Outputs: offsets (delta), rotations (q), scales (s), opacities (alpha), colors (S) delta1, q1, s1, alpha1, S1 = gaussianhead(features, view=1) delta2, q2, s2, alpha2, S2 = gaussianhead(features, view=2) # 4. Construct Gaussian primitives gaussians = [] # Process primitives from Image 1 for j in range(numpixels): mu = x1[j] + delta1[j] sigma = computecovariance(q1[j], s1[j]) alpha = alpha1[j] color = S1[j] gaussians.append(Gaussian(mu, sigma, alpha, color)) # Process primitives from Image 2 for j in range(numpixels): # Note: x2 is also in I1's frame according to MASt3R convention mu = x2[j] + delta2[j] sigma = computecovariance(q2[j], s2[j]) alpha = alpha2[j] color = S2[j] gaussians.append(Gaussian(mu, sigma, alpha, color)) return gaussians def computecovariance(q, s): """ Compute covariance matrix from quaternion q and scale s. q: (4,) quaternion s: (3,) scale Returns: (3, 3) covariance matrix """ R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) S = diag(s) return R @ S @ S.T @ R.T def calculatelossmask(targetdepth, targetpose, contextdepths, contextposes, tolerance=0.05): """ Calculate loss mask M for a target view. M[i,j] = 1 if pixel (i,j) is visible and consistent in context views. """ H, W = targetdepth.shape M = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=bool) # Unproject target pixels to 3D targetpoints3d = unproject(targetdepth, targetpose) for k in range(len(contextposes)): # Reproject onto context view k contextpoints2d, depths = reproject(targetpoints3d, contextposes[k], targetpose) # Check frustum and depth consistency validinfrustum = isinsidefrustum(contextpoints2d, contextposes[k]) depthmatch = np.abs(depths - contextdepths[k][contextpoints2d]) < tolerance # Combine conditions validpixels = validinfrustum & depthmatch & (contextdepths[k][contextpoints2d] > 0) # Update mask M[validpixels] = True return M Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unseen Regions: Supervising rendering loss for pixels not visible in context views (obscured or outside frustums) is counterproductive and can destroy model performance. This is addressed by the loss masking strategy. Local Minima: Directly supervising positions using ground-truth point clouds avoids the local minima present in training 3D Gaussian Splats from stereo views where camera rays are unknown. The foundation model for uncalibrated stereo reconstruction. It predicts 3D points and confidences without camera parameters. Splatt3R freezes this backbone and adds a Gaussian head. A technique to restrict training supervision to pixels that are feasibly reconstructed (visible and depth-consistent in context views), enabling extrapolation beyond the stereo baseline. Time Complexity: Single forward pass for inference. Construction/export runtime is approximately 1.10 seconds on ScanNet++ with 2 views. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On ScanNet++ test scenes with Close view overlap (\phi=0.9, \psi=0.9), Splatt3R achieves PSNR 19.66, SSIM 0.757, LPIPS 0.234. With 2 views, it achieves PSNR 23.30, SSIM 0.823, LPIPS 0.125. Strengths: Pose-free, works with uncalibrated images, supports extrapolation to wider baselines, fast inference. Limitations: Performance degrades with very wide baselines (e.g., PSNR drops to 18.56 for Very Wide overlap). Requires a large pre-trained backbone (MASt3R). Splatt3R was introduced in 2024 by Brandon, Zheng, Iro, and Victor from the University of Oxford. It builds upon the MASt3R foundation model for 3D geometry reconstruction. The method was trained on the ScanNet++ dataset. It addresses the limitation of existing generalizable 3D-GS methods that only supervise viewpoints between input stereo views, by enabling supervision of extrapolated viewpoints. Splatt3R: Zero-Shot Gaussian Splatting from Uncalibrated Image Pairs, https://splatt3r.active.vision/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting for real-time scene reconstruction: Methods, systems, and trade-offs, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2026.115120, fetched 2026-10-26

name: RLSplat
head: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: RLSplat is a resource-linear, budget-controllable feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) framework that generates exactly B Gaussians for a given input, ensuring that inference latency and peak memory scale linearly with the requested budget. Unlike prior budget-controllable methods that predict a dense set of candidates and prune them (resulting in constant high cost), RLSplat uses a learned allocation policy to distribute the budget across local scene regions and a resource-linear decoder that refines Gaussians via local cross-attention. It solves the problem of adapting to diverse resource constraints in real-world deployment (e.g., AR/VR, robotics) where both output size and inference speed must be controlled. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: V uncalibrated context images \{Ii\}{i=1}^V, and a target Gaussian budget B (integer). Outputs: A set of B 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gb\}{b=1}^B and camera parameters \{Pi\}{i=1}^V for the context views. Each Gaussian gb consists of a 3D center, opacity, scale, rotation, and color coefficients. Data Structures: 1. Anchor Tokens: A set of N tokens \{an\}{n=1}^N representing local 3D regions, extracted from the geometry backbone. 2. Allocation Vector: A discrete vector k \in \mathbb{Z}{\ge 0}^N where kn is the number of Gaussians assigned to anchor n, such that \sum{n=1}^N kn = B. 3. Gaussian Tokens: A sequence of B tokens, where anchor n spawns kn tokens. 4. Hierarchical Neighbor Search Structure: Used to find the K{gs} nearest Gaussian neighbors for each token efficiently. Parameters: B: Target Gaussian budget. Typical values: 2K (2,048), 8K, 64K. K{gs}: Number of nearest Gaussian neighbors for local refinement. Default ablation value: 16. Can be changed at inference without retraining. K{anc}: Number of anchor neighbors in hierarchical search. Fixed value in ablations: 16. C: Number of rollouts (candidate allocations) drawn per training step for GSPO optimization. Algorithm Steps: 1. Geometry Encoding: The geometry backbone encodes the V input images into N anchor tokens \{an\}{n=1}^N and predicts camera parameters \{Pi\}{i=1}^V. 2. Gaussian Allocation: The allocation policy \pi\psi assesses the local significance of each anchor based on image features (e.g., texture complexity) and predicts a discrete allocation k \in \mathbb{Z}{\ge 0}^N such that \sum{n=1}^N kn = B. This policy is trained using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO). 3. Token Spawning: Each anchor n spawns kn Gaussian tokens. The total number of Gaussian tokens is exactly B. 4. Resource-Linear Decoding: Initialization: The decoder instantiates initial Gaussian states (center, scale, rotation, opacity, color) from the B Gaussian tokens. Hierarchical Neighbor Search: For each Gaussian token, the system finds its K{gs} nearest neighbors among the other B-1 Gaussian tokens using a hierarchical neighbor search. This search operates over the anchor tokens first (using K{anc} neighbors) to narrow down the candidate Gaussian tokens, ensuring efficiency. Local Refinement: Each Gaussian token refines its state via local cross-attention with its K{gs} nearest Gaussian neighbors. This replaces global self-attention, reducing complexity from O(B^2) to O(B \cdot K{gs}). 5. Rendering: The final set of B Gaussians is rendered into target views using differentiable rasterization. Training (GSPO): To optimize the non-differentiable allocation policy \pi\psi: 1. Draw C candidate allocations k^{(c)} \sim \pi{\text{old}} = \text{Mult}(B, \text{sg}(p)), where p are the policy probabilities and \text{sg}(\cdot) stops gradients. 2. For each rollout c, generate the 3DGS representation \mathcal{G}^{(c)} and render an image \hat{I}^{(c)} at novel target views. 3. Compute reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} against ground-truth images I. 4. Use \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} as the reward signal to update the policy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch import torch.nn as nn from typing import List, Tuple class RLSplat: def init(self, geometrybackbone, allocationpolicy, decoder, numanchors: int): self.geometrybackbone = geometrybackbone self.allocationpolicy = allocationpolicy self.decoder = decoder self.numanchors = numanchors # Hierarchical neighbor search structure self.hierarchicalsearch = HierarchicalNeighborSearch() def forward(self, images: torch.Tensor, budget: int) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ Args: images: Tensor of shape (V, H, W, 3) or (V, 3, H, W) budget: Integer B, total number of Gaussians to generate Returns: gaussians: Tensor of shape (B, 14) or similar, containing Gaussian parameters cameras: Tensor of camera parameters for V views """ # Step 1: Geometry Encoding # Encodes images into N anchor tokens and predicts camera parameters anchortokens, cameras = self.geometrybackbone(images) # anchortokens shape: (N, Danchor) # Step 2: Gaussian Allocation # Predicts discrete allocation k summing to budget # Policy outputs probabilities p, sampled to get k # k is a tensor of shape (N,) with integer values >= 0 k = self.allocationpolicy(anchortokens, budget) # Step 3: Token Spawning # Create B Gaussian tokens. Each anchor n spawns k[n] tokens. # We need to expand anchor tokens to match the budget gaussiantokens = [] for n in range(self.numanchors): count = k[n].item() # Expand anchor token 'count' times # Add small noise or variation if needed, but source implies direct spawning expandedtokens = anchortokens[n].unsqueeze(0).expand(count, -1) gaussiantokens.append(expandedtokens) gaussiantokens = torch.cat(gaussiantokens, dim=0) # gaussiantokens shape: (B, Dgaussian) # Step 4: Resource-Linear Decoding # Initialize Gaussians from tokens initialgaussians = self.decoder.initialize(gaussiantokens) # Hierarchical Neighbor Search # Find Kgs nearest neighbors for each of the B Gaussians # This uses the hierarchical structure to avoid O(B^2) neighborindices = self.hierarchicalsearch.findneighbors( initialgaussians, kgs=self.decoder.kgs, kanc=self.decoder.kanc) # neighborindices shape: (B, Kgs) # Local Refinement via Cross-Attention finalgaussians = self.decoder.refine( initialgaussians, neighborindices) return finalgaussians, cameras class HierarchicalNeighborSearch: def init(self): # Implementation details of hierarchical search (e.g., KD-Tree or FAISS-like structure) # Source mentions it is 27x faster than exact search at 65,536 Gaussians pass def findneighbors(self, gaussians: torch.Tensor, kgs: int, kanc: int) -> torch.Tensor: """ Finds kgs nearest Gaussian neighbors for each Gaussian. Uses hierarchical search over anchors first. """ # Pseudocode for hierarchical search: # 1. Map each Gaussian to its parent anchor. # 2. For each Gaussian, find kanc nearest parent anchors. # 3. Collect all Gaussians belonging to those anchors. # 4. Compute distances to these candidate Gaussians. # 5. Select the kgs nearest ones. # Note: Exact implementation depends on the specific hierarchical structure used. # The source emphasizes efficiency: O(B Kgs) vs O(B^2). pass class AllocationPolicy(nn.Module): def init(self, numanchors: int): super().init() self.numanchors = numanchors # Policy network to output probabilities for allocation self.network = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(128, 256), # Example hidden size nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, numanchors)) def forward(self, anchortokens: torch.Tensor, budget: int) -> torch.Tensor: """ Predicts allocation k summing to budget. Uses GSPO during training. """ # Compute probabilities logits = self.network(anchortokens) probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1) # Sample discrete allocation # In training, this is sampled from Multinomial distribution # In inference, it might be deterministic or sampled # Source says "predicts a discrete allocation k" # We assume a sampling step here for the policy k = torch.multinomial(probs, numsamples=budget, replacement=True) # Count occurrences to get kn for each anchor # k is a list of anchor indices, length B # We need to count how many times each anchor index appears kcounts = torch.zeros(self.numanchors, dtype=torch.long) kcounts.scatteradd(0, k, torch.oneslike(k)) return kcounts Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The allocation policy produces discrete integers. Gradient estimation via GSPO is required for training. Boundaries: The hierarchical neighbor search must correctly handle boundary cases where fewer than K{gs} neighbors are available (though with B Gaussians and K{gs} \ll B, this is rare). Degenerate Input: If input images are uncalibrated, the geometry backbone must robustly predict camera parameters. The projection loss \mathcal{L}{proj} is critical to tie anchors to image regions; removing it causes training failure. A learned policy that distributes the Gaussian budget B across anchors based on local scene significance (texture complexity). It differs from uniform allocation by concentrating capacity on high-frequency structures (e.g., thin balusters) and smoothing low-frequency areas (e.g., walls). It is chosen when resource efficiency and high-fidelity reconstruction of complex details are required. A refinement module that uses local cross-attention with hierarchical neighbor search instead of global self-attention. It differs from global attention by reducing complexity from O(B^2) to O(B \cdot K{gs}). It is chosen when inference latency and memory must scale linearly with the output size. An efficient search structure to find K{gs} nearest neighbors among B Gaussians. It differs from exact search by being 27x faster at large budgets (e.g., 65,536 Gaussians). It is chosen to enable real-time or near-real-time decoding for large Gaussian sets. Time Complexity: Decoding cost is O(B \cdot K{gs}), scaling linearly with the Gaussian budget B. This is a significant improvement over global self-attention, which costs O(B^2). Memory Complexity: Peak memory usage scales linearly with B. At 2K Gaussians, RLSplat uses 9.6× less peak memory than F4 Splat. Measured Performance: ACID Dataset (B=8,192): PSNR 22.84 dB, SSIM 0.643, LPIPS 0.353. RE10K Dataset (B=8,000): Full-view PSNR 26.51 dB, compared to 23.42 dB for F4 Splat and 21.82 dB for EcoSplat. Speed: At 2K Gaussians, RLSplat runs 4.1× faster than F4 Splat. Quality vs. Budget: RLSplat achieves higher PSNR than F4 Splat at 2K Gaussians while using significantly less memory and time. Strengths: Linear scaling of inference cost with budget; high-quality reconstruction of thin, high-frequency structures; no need for per-scene optimization. Limitations: Requires training of the allocation policy and decoder; performance depends on the accuracy of the geometry backbone and camera prediction. When to Use: Applications requiring limited resource budgets, such as AR/VR, robotics, and digital content creation, where both output size and inference speed must be controlled. When Not to Use: When maximum possible quality is required regardless of resource constraints (e.g., offline rendering with unlimited memory/time), traditional 3DGS with per-scene optimization may be better. RLSplat was proposed by Bae, Park, and Kim from KAIST. The paper "RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting" was published on arXiv in October 2026. It addresses the limitations of prior budget-controllable FF3DGS methods like EcoSplat and F4 Splat, which predict dense sets of Gaussians and then prune them, resulting in constant inference latency and memory usage regardless of the target budget. RLSplat introduces a resource-linear approach by learning a Gaussian allocation policy and using a resource-linear decoder with local cross-attention. name: LGTM (Less Gaussians, Texture More)
head: Feed-Forward Prediction of Textured Gaussians, Feed-Forward Textured Splatting
body: LGTM is a feed-forward framework that predicts compact 2D Gaussian primitives coupled with per-primitive texture maps, decoupling geometric complexity from rendering resolution to enable high-fidelity 4K novel view synthesis without per-scene optimization. It solves the quadratic growth in primitive count as resolution increases in existing feed-forward 3DGS methods, which makes high-resolution synthesis intractable due to memory and compute limits. Unlike standard 3DGS which couples appearance and geometry within each primitive, LGTM decouples them, allowing a compact set of geometric primitives to represent rich texture regions via per-primitive textures. Inputs and Outputs: The network f takes a set of input images \{I^v\}{v=1}^N and their low-resolution counterparts \{I^v{low}\}{v=1}^N as input. It outputs a set of textured 2D Gaussians: f: (I^v, I^v{low}) \rightarrow \{\mui, si, ri, ci, T^ic, T^i\alpha\} where \mui is the mean, si and ri define the covariance (scale and rotation), ci are spherical harmonics coefficients, T^ic is the color texture map, and T^i\alpha is the alpha texture map for primitive i. Data Structures: Primitive Grid: The primitive network predicts a grid of size h \times w corresponding to the low-resolution input dimensions. Each cell contains 2DGS parameters: mean \mu, scale s, rotation r, base opacity o, and SH coefficients c. Per-Primitive Texture Maps: Each primitive i has two texture maps: Color texture: T^ic \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T \times 3} Alpha texture: T^i\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T} T is the texture resolution, a tunable parameter trading off primitive size and texture size. T^ic is zero-initialized. Rendering Formulas: For a ray-splat intersection point u on primitive i, the alpha and color are redefined using the texture maps: ai(u) = oi \cdot T^i\alpha[u] \hat{c}i(u, di) = T^ic[u] + SH(ci, di) where T[u] denotes bilinear sampling from the texture map at local coordinate u, oi is the base opacity, di is the view direction, and SH(ci, di) is the spherical harmonics evaluation. The alpha texture replaces the standard Gaussian falloff G(u) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2}(u^2 + v^2)), and the color texture adds high-frequency detail to the SH base color. The final pixel color C is computed by alpha-blending contributions from all primitives sorted by depth: C = \sumi ai(ui) \hat{c}i(di) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - aj(uj)) Algorithm Steps: The architecture consists of two submodules: a primitive network f{prim} and a texture network f{texture}. 1. Primitive Network (f{prim}): Input: Low-resolution image I^v{low} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times 3}. Process: Pass through a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder-decoder. Output: Predict primitive grid parameters \{\mui, si, ri, oi, ci\} and feature maps F^{v}{prim}. Note: The network is trained with high-resolution supervision (rendering at full resolution H \times W despite low-res input) to ensure anti-aliasing and robust geometry. 2. Texture Network (f{texture}): Input: High-resolution image I^v and primitive features F^{v}{prim}. Feature Extraction: Compute patch features F^{v}{patch} from I^v via image patchification and convolutions. Compute projective features F^{v}{proj} by mapping source image pixels back to primitive local coordinates using the inverse transformation M{i,v}^{-1}: T^{c,proj}i[u] = I^v[x] = I^v[M{i,v}^{-1}(u)] where M{i,v} is the 2D homography transformation mapping pixel coordinates to primitive local coordinates. Features are extracted from this projective prior texture. Aggregate F^{v}{prim}, F^{v}{patch}, and F^{v}{proj} to predict per-primitive texture maps T^i\alpha and T^ic. 3. Rendering: For each ray, find intersection u with primitives. Retrieve ai(u) and \hat{c}i(u, di) from texture maps using bilinear sampling. Composite using alpha-blending. Training Strategy: A staged two-stage strategy is used: 1. Stage 1: Pre-train the primitive network f{prim} in isolation to establish a robust geometric foundation. Loss: MSE + LPIPS between rendered and ground truth images. 2. Stage 2: Jointly train f{prim} and f{texture}. Freeze or reduce the learning rate of f{prim} by 0.1x to maintain geometric stability. The color texture Tc is zero-initialized. Loss: MSE + LPIPS. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lgtmforward(inputimages, lowresimages, cameraparams): """ inputimages: List of high-res RGB images [N, H, W, 3] lowresimages: List of low-res RGB images [N, h, w, 3] cameraparams: Camera poses and intrinsics for each view Returns: List of textured Gaussian primitives """ N = len(inputimages) allprimitives = [] # Stage 1: Primitive Network (Pre-trained) # fprim takes low-res images and predicts geometry for v in range(N): # Encode low-res image features = vitencoder(lowresimages[v]) # Decode to predict primitive grid primgrid = vitdecoder(features) # Extract primitive parameters # primgrid contains mu, s, r, o, c for hw primitives primitivesv = decodeprimitives(primgrid) # Store features for texture network Fprim = getprimitivefeatures(primgrid) # Stage 2: Texture Network # ftexture takes high-res image and primitive features # 1. Patchify high-res image Fpatch = extractpatchfeatures(inputimages[v]) # 2. Projective Mapping # Map primitive local coordinates to image pixels # Minv is inverse homography for each primitive Tproj = projectivetexturemapping(inputimages[v], primitivesv, cameraparams[v]) Fproj = extractprojectivefeatures(Tproj) # 3. Aggregate and Predict Textures # Combine Fprim, Fpatch, Fproj texturemaps = predicttextures(Fprim, Fpatch, Fproj) # Assign textures to primitives for i, prim in enumerate(primitivesv): prim.Tc = texturemaps['color'][i] prim.Talpha = texturemaps['alpha'][i] allprimitives.append(primitivesv) return allprimitives def rendertexturedgaussians(primitives, cameraparams): """ Render textured Gaussians using alpha blending """ # Initialize output image image = zeroslike(targetresolution) # Sort primitives by depth for current view sortedprims = sortbydepth(primitives, cameraparams) for prim in sortedprims: # Find ray-splat intersection u for each pixel # This is handled by the rasterizer u = getlocalcoordinates(prim, cameraparams) # Sample textures alpha = prim.o bilinearsample(prim.Talpha, u) color = bilinearsample(prim.Tc, u) + sphericalharmonics(prim.c, prim.viewdirection) # Alpha blend # C = sum(ai ci product(1 - aj)) image = compositepixel(image, alpha, color) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: Standard feed-forward methods fail at 2K+ resolutions due to memory limits (e.g., NoPoSplat requires >61 GB for 1024x576). LGTM uses <30 GB. Holes in Rendering: Without high-resolution supervision, predicted Gaussians may result in holes due to lack of anti-aliasing. High-res supervision forces the network to learn proper coverage. Geometric Stability: In Stage 2, the primitive network must be trained with a reduced learning rate (0.1x) to prevent destabilizing the geometry while learning textures. Memory: LGTM trains successfully at 2K and 4K resolutions using under 30 GB of memory. In contrast, NoPoSplat fails to train at 2K or higher due to memory constraints (OOM). Scalability: Scaling from 512 to 4K requires 64x more Gaussians in standard methods. LGTM scales efficiently at inference, adding only modest memory and time overhead for a 64x pixel increase. Performance: Enables high-fidelity 4K novel view synthesis, a capability previously out of reach for feed-forward methods. Strengths: Decouples geometry and appearance; enables high-resolution rendering with significantly fewer primitives; no per-scene optimization required; versatile input support (monocular, posed/unposed two-view, multi-view). Limitations: Requires a dual-network architecture; relies on high-resolution supervision during training to avoid holes; texture resolution T is a hyperparameter that trades off primitive count and texture detail. LGTM was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026 by Yixing Lao, Xuyang Bai, Xiaoyang Wu, Nuoyuan Yan, Zixin Luo, Jean-Daniel Nahmias, Yanghai Tsin, Shiwei Li, and Hengshuang Zhao from HKU and Apple. It addresses the limitations of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods which suffer from quadratic primitive growth and the per-scene optimization requirement of textured Gaussian methods. Less Gaussians, Texture More: 4K Feed-Forward Textured Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.25745, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: InfiniSplat v2
head: InfiniSplat
body: InfiniSplat v2 is a feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction method for arbitrary input views that decouples geometry and attribute prediction, uses ground-truth (GT) camera poses for alignment during training, and employs large-angle target view supervision to improve rendering quality under large viewpoint changes. It differs from its parent Feed-forward Generalizable Reconstruction and sibling DA3-GS by freezing the geometry branch to prevent geometric degradation caused by joint optimization, and by using GT poses to avoid pose errors that misguide the network under large-angle supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N input RGB images IC = \{Ii\}{i \in C} and optional pose conditions QC (camera intrinsics and poses). In the pose-free setting, QC = \emptyset. Outputs: A set of M 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{(\mum, \xim)\}{m=1}^M, where \mum \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the center and \xim = (\alpham, sm, qm, cm) contains opacity, three-axis scale, rotation (quaternion), and zeroth-order spherical-harmonic (SH) color. Data Structures: Gaussian Set: A list of M Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores \mum, \alpham, sm, qm, cm. Hidden State: A 16-dimensional vector per Gaussian, updated during Stage II refinement. KNN Graph: A global graph storing neighbor indices for each Gaussian, reused across refinement steps. Parameters: Voxel merging side length: 0.004 in the scale-normalized reconstruction frame. Opacity pruning threshold \tau\alpha: 0.01. Mask thresholds: \tau{abs} = 0.03, \tau{rel} = 0.01. Learning rates: Stage I: 10^{-6} (last 10 attribute blocks), 2 \times 10^{-4} (Gaussian head). Stage II: 2 \times 10^{-4}. AdamW: \beta = (0.9, 0.95), global batch size 16, L2 gradient clipping at 1.0. Algorithm: The method consists of two stages. Stage I initializes the scene using a dual-branch architecture. Stage II refines attributes using input-view feedback. 1. Feature Extraction: Initialize two branches, \Phi{geo} and \Phi{attr}, from pretrained DA3 weights. Freeze \Phi{geo}. Fine-tune only the last K=10 Transformer blocks of \Phi{attr} and the Gaussian head. Compute predicted depth \hat{D} and cameras \hat{\Pi}C using \Phi{geo}(IC; QC). Compute multi-layer patch features FC using \Phi{attr}(IC; QC). 2. Scale Alignment: Normalize predicted depths and translations by s{norm} > 0. Fit an Umeyama similarity transform from the GT trajectory to the normalized predicted trajectory using only input-camera center correspondences. Retain the scale factor sC. Align GT poses: R^\starv = Rv and t^\starv = sC tv. 3. Point Construction and Pruning: Construct initial Gaussian centers \mum from normalized predicted z-depth, GT intrinsics, and scale-aligned GT poses. Map FC to per-pixel attributes \xi using a DPT decoder. Merge Gaussians using voxel merging with side length 0.004. Prune Gaussians with opacity \alpham < \tau\alpha = 0.01. Let the initial scene be \mathcal{G}0 with M Gaussians. 4. Rendering and Loss: Render \mathcal{G}0 into input views C and target views T using aligned cameras \hat{\Pi}^\starv: \hat{I}{bv} = \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}0; \hat{\Pi}^\starv). Construct visibility masks Mv for target pixels: Retain if GT depth > 10^{-6} and passes validity mask. Retain if at least one input view places the point in front of the camera, within bounds, with valid sampled depth d{src}, and |z{proj} - d{src}| \le \max(\tau{abs}, \tau{rel} d{src}). Compute LPIPS spatial distance map dv = \text{LPIPS}{spatial}(Mv \odot \hat{I}{bv}, Mv \odot Iv), zeroing invalid regions before normalization. Compute Stage I loss \mathcal{L}I: \mathcal{L}I = \frac{\sum{v \in V} \sum{p} Mv(p) [ev(p) + dv(p)]}{\max(1, \sum{v \in V} \sum{p} Mv(p))} where ev(p) is the RGB-channel-averaged absolute error. Optimize \Phi{attr} and Gaussian head for 25,000 steps (2,000 warmup, cosine decay to 0.1 peak). 1. Architecture: Freeze \mathcal{G}0 and \Phi{attr} backbone. Train a DPT feature projection (1x1 conv to 8 channels) and a refiner. Refiner input: Concatenation of image features, current attributes, gradient feedback, neighbor distances, and 16-dim hidden state, projected to 64 dims. Process through four KNN Transformer blocks (single-head attention over 8 neighbors, LayerNorm, MLP, residual). Output: MLP predicts increments for attributes and hidden state. 2. Feedback and Updates: Render current scene into input views. Compute feedback loss \ell{fb} = 0.8 L1 + 0.2 L{DSSIM}, where L{DSSIM} = (1 - \text{SSIM})/2. Compute gradients w.r.t attributes, normalize, and detach. Update attributes: Scales: s{new} = s{old} \exp(\Delta \log s). Opacity-logit, local rotation-vector, RGB-logit: a \tanh(\text{raw}) with a = 0.1, 0.25, 1.0 respectively. Hidden state: 0.1 \tanh(\text{raw}). Clamp logit inputs to [10^{-6}, 1-10^{-6}]. Centers, counts, and correspondence remain fixed. 3. Multi-step Objective: Sample Kr \in \{1, 2, 3\} updates during training, use 3 at inference. First-order surrogate loss: Let xk be updated parameters. Compute rendering gradients on leaf copies zk = \text{sg}(xk) to form rk = \text{sg}(\nablaz \mathcal{L}{render}(zk)). Outer loss per view: \ell{out} = 0.8 L1 + 0.2 L{DSSIM} + 0.5 L{LPIPS}. Multi-step objective: \mathcal{L}{II} = \sum{k=1}^{Kr} 0.9^{Kr-k} \mathcal{L}k^{render} + 0.1 \mathcal{L}{opacity} where \mathcal{L}{opacity} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M [\text{logit}\epsilon(\alpha{m, Kr}) - \text{logit}\epsilon(\alpha{m, 0})]^2 with \epsilon=10^{-6}. 4. Chunked Execution: Reuse global KNN graph. Sort points along longest voxel-coordinate axis. Expand core sets of at most 200,000 points with four-hop neighborhoods. Recursively bisect chunks exceeding 300,000 points by point count along longest axes, recomputing neighborhoods. Retain only core-point outputs; use gradient checkpointing. Feature Extraction # If gtposes is None, use predicted poses for alignment, but GT for construction if gtposes is not None: # Use GT poses for construction to avoid pose errors predicteddepth, = self.phigeo(images, None) # QC is optional # Use GT poses for alignment calculation #... (Umeyama transform logic to get sC)... alignedposes = scalegtposes(gtposes, sC) else: # Pose-free: reference cameras only for eval frame predicteddepth, = self.phigeo(images, None) #... (scale alignment logic)... alignedposes = getreferenceposes() features = self.phiattr(images, None) # 2. Point Construction # Back-project depth to 3D points using aligned poses and intrinsics centers = backprojectdepth(predicteddepth, alignedposes, intrinsics) # Decode attributes rawattrs = self.gaussianhead(features) # 3. Voxel Merging and Pruning gaussians = mergevoxels(centers, rawattrs, sidelength=self.voxelside) gaussians = pruneopacity(gaussians, threshold=self.alphathresh) return gaussians def stageiloss(self, gaussians, images, targetimages, targetposes): # Render into input and target views inputviews = render(gaussians, inputposes) targetviews = render(gaussians, targetposes) # Construct masks masks = constructvisibilitymasks(targetimages, gaussians, targetposes, tauabs=self.tauabs, taurel=self.taurel) # Compute LPIPS lpipsmap = computelpipsspatial(masks inputviews, masks targetimages) # Compute L1 l1map = torch.abs(inputviews - targetimages) # Aggregate loss = aggregateloss(l1map, lpipsmap, masks) return loss def stageioptimize(self, images, targetimages, targetposes, optimizer, steps=25000): for step in range(steps): gaussians = self.stageiinit(images, targetposes) loss = self.stageiloss(gaussians, images, targetimages, targetposes) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() def stageirefine(self, gaussians, images, targetposes, optimizer, steps=5000): # Freeze gaussians and phiattr for in range(steps): # Render and compute feedback loss rendered = render(gaussians, inputposes) fbloss = computefeedbackloss(rendered, images) # 0.8 L1 + 0.2 LDSSIM # Compute gradients grads = torch.autograd.grad(fbloss, gaussians.attributes, retaingraph=True)[0] grads = normalizeanddetach(grads) # Update attributes gaussians = updateattributes(gaussians, grads) # Compute outer loss for supervision outerloss = computeouterloss(gaussians, images, targetimages, targetposes) outerloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() def stageirefinemultistep(self, gaussians, images, targetimages, targetposes, optimizer, steps=5000): for step in range(steps): # Sample Kr Kr = random.choice([1, 2, 3]) currentgaussians = gaussians totalloss = 0 for k in range(1, Kr + 1): # Render and compute feedback rendered = render(currentgaussians, inputposes) fbloss = computefeedbackloss(rendered, images) # Get gradients grads = torch.autograd.grad(fbloss, currentgaussians.attributes, retaingraph=True)[0] grads = normalizeanddetach(grads) # Update attributes currentgaussians = updateattributes(currentgaussians, grads) # Compute surrogate loss # First-order surrogate xk = currentgaussians.attributes zk = xk.detach() # sg(xk) rendergrads = torch.autograd.grad(render(zk, inputposes), zk, retaingraph=True)[0] rk = rendergrads.detach() # sg(grad) # Lproxy = sg(L) + <x - sg(x), r> # Gradient of Lproxy w.r.t trainable params theta (refiner) # dLproxy/dx = rk # So we pass rk to the refiner as gradient feedback # Compute outer loss outerloss = computeouterloss(currentgaussians, images, targetimages, targetposes) # Weighted sum weight = 0.9 (Kr - k) totalloss += weight outerloss # Opacity regularization opacityloss = computeopacityreg(gaussians, currentgaussians) totalloss += 0.1 opacityloss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Update main gaussians gaussians = currentgaussians def computefeedbackloss(rendered, target): l1 = torch.mean(torch.abs(rendered - target)) ssim = computessim(rendered, target) ldssim = (1 - ssim) / 2 return 0.8 l1 + 0.2 ldssim def computeouterloss(gaussians, images, targetimages, targetposes): rendered = render(gaussians, targetposes) l1 = torch.mean(torch.abs(rendered - targetimages)) ssim = computessim(rendered, targetimages) ldssim = (1 - ssim) / 2 lpips = computelpips(rendered, targetimages) return 0.8 l1 + 0.2 ldssim + 0.5 lpips def computeopacityreg(g0, gk): # logitepsilon(alpha) = log(alpha / (1 - alpha + eps)) alpha0 = g0.attributes.alpha alphak = gk.attributes.alpha logit0 = torch.log(alpha0 / (1 - alpha0 + 1e-6)) logitk = torch.log(alphak / (1 - alphak + 1e-6)) return torch.mean((logitk - logit0) 2) def updateattributes(gaussians, grads): # grads are normalized and detached # Scales: snew = sold exp(deltalogs) # deltalogs is derived from grads # Opacity, Rotation, RGB: a tanh(raw) # Hidden state: 0.1 tanh(raw) #... implementation details... pass Time Complexity: Stage I is dominated by the forward pass of the DA3 backbone and DPT decoder. Stage II involves iterative KNN queries and transformer blocks, with chunked execution to manage memory. The global KNN graph is reused. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians M. Chunked execution limits peak memory by processing subsets of points (core sets up to 200,000, chunks bisected if >300,000). Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS on six datasets in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, reduces LPIPS and DISTS by 25.8% and 32.9% respectively compared to the strongest baseline. Strengths: Decoupled geometry and attribute prediction prevents geometric degradation. GT pose alignment avoids pose errors under large-angle supervision. Large-angle target views constrain Gaussian shapes better than local views. Limitations: Requires GT camera poses for training alignment (though inference can be pose-free). Joint optimization of geometry and attributes is avoided, which may limit flexibility in some scenarios. InfiniSplat v2 was introduced by Lin et al. in 2026 as an improvement over DA3-GS and InfiniSplat. It addresses limitations in Gaussian attribute learning, specifically flying-point artifacts and pose errors under large viewpoint changes. name: DepthSplat
body: DepthSplat is a feed-forward method for 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction that integrates pre-trained monocular depth features into a multi-view cost volume framework to produce robust depth maps and Gaussian parameters. It solves the problem of inaccurate depth estimation in low-texture, occluded, or reflective regions where standard multi-view stereo fails, and scale ambiguities inherent in monocular estimation. Unlike sibling methods that either discard explicit feature matching (e.g., GS-LRM) or use monocular features only to refine coarse depth (e.g., TranSplat), DepthSplat concatenates monocular features with multi-view cost volumes early in the pipeline, enabling efficient training on limited hardware and high-quality generalizable reconstruction. Inputs: N RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known projection matrices \{Pi\}{i=1}^N (intrinsic and extrinsic). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\muj, \alphaj, \Sigmaj, cj\} for each pixel j in the reference views, and rendered novel views. Data Structures: Image Features: Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s} \times C}, extracted per view. Cost Volume: Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s} \times D}, representing correlation scores for depth candidates. Depth Map: Di \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}, predicted dense depth. Gaussian Parameters: \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3, \alphaj \in \mathbb{R}, \Sigmaj \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or parameterized as scale/rotation), cj (color/SH). Parameters: N: Number of input views. D: Number of depth candidates sampled uniformly between near and far planes. s: Downsampling factor for feature extraction. s=4 if two stride-2 convolutions are used; s=8 if three are used. K: Number of nearest neighbor views selected for cross-attention. K=2 is used when N > 2. Steps: 1. Monocular Feature Extraction: For each input image Ii, extract features Fi^{mono} using a pre-trained monocular depth encoder (e.g., ViT-based). 2. Multi-View Feature Extraction: Encode input images \{Ii\} into multi-view features Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s} \times C} using a backbone with stride-2 convolutions. 3. Cost Volume Construction: For each reference view i: a. Uniformly sample D depth candidates \{dm\}{m=1}^D from the near/far depth ranges. b. Identify the set of neighboring views. If N > 2, select the top-K (K=2) nearest neighboring views based on camera distance to view i. c. For each selected neighbor j and each depth candidate dm: i. Warp the feature map Fj of view j to the coordinate system of view i using Pi and depth dm to obtain warped features F{j \to i}^m. ii. Compute the dot-product correlation between Fi and F{j \to i}^m. d. Combine correlation values from the selected neighbors by averaging. e. Stack correlations for all D depth candidates to form the cost volume Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s} \times D}. 4. Multi-View Transformer: Process the features \{Fi\} using a Multi-View Transformer consisting of six stacked self- and cross-attention layers to obtain multi-view-aware features. 5. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the multi-view cost volumes Ci with the monocular features Fi^{mono} (upsampled or aligned as necessary). 6. Depth Regression: Pass the concatenated features through a 2D U-Net architecture followed by a softmax layer to predict the probability distribution over depth candidates, yielding the dense per-pixel depth map Di \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}. 7. Gaussian Center Unprojection: Unproject the predicted depth map Di to 3D space using the camera projection matrix Pi to obtain the Gaussian centers \muj for each pixel j. 8. Remaining Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Predict opacity \alphaj, covariance \Sigmaj, and color cj using an additional lightweight network head operating in parallel with the depth regression. 9. Rendering: Render novel views using the differentiable splatting operation with the predicted 3D Gaussians \{\muj, \alphaj, \Sigmaj, cj\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DepthSplat: def init(self, numdepthcandidates=64, downsamplingfactor=4, numneighborviews=2): self.D = numdepthcandidates self.s = downsamplingfactor self.K = numneighborviews # Placeholder for actual network components defined in source self.monocularencoder = MonocularDepthEncoder() # Pre-trained self.multiviewencoder = MultiViewEncoder() # Stride-2 convs self.multiviewtransformer = MultiViewTransformer(numlayers=6) self.depthhead = DepthRegressionHead() # 2D U-Net + Softmax self.gaussianhead = GaussianParameterHead() # Lightweight head def forward(self, images, projectionmatrices): """ images: List of N tensors, shape (H, W, 3) projectionmatrices: List of N matrices, shape (3, 4) Returns: List of Gaussian sets for each view """ N = len(images) H, W = images[0].shape[0], images[0].shape[1] # 1. Monocular Features monofeatures = [] for i in range(N): # Extract features from pre-trained monocular model feat = self.monocularencoder(images[i]) monofeatures.append(feat) # 2. Multi-View Features # Encode all images into multi-view features # Input: N images. Output: List of N feature maps mvfeatures = self.multiviewencoder(images) # 3. Multi-View Transformer # Exchange info across views mvfeaturesaware = self.multiviewtransformer(mvfeatures) gaussiansperview = [] for i in range(N): # 4. Cost Volume Construction # Select neighbors neighbors = self.selectneighbors(i, projectionmatrices, self.K) # Sample depth candidates depthcandidates = self.sampledepthcandidates(projectionmatrices[i]) costvolume = [] for d in depthcandidates: correlations = [] for j in neighbors: # Warp neighbor feature to reference view i at depth d warpedfeat = self.warpfeature(mvfeaturesaware[j], projectionmatrices[i], projectionmatrices[j], d) # Dot product correlation corr = torch.sum(mvfeaturesaware[i] warpedfeat, dim=-1) # Shape: (H/s, W/s) correlations.append(corr) # Average correlations from selected neighbors if len(correlations) > 0: avgcorr = torch.mean(torch.stack(correlations, dim=0), dim=0) costvolume.append(avgcorr.unsqueeze(-1)) # Stack to form Cost Volume: (H/s, W/s, D) costvolume = torch.cat(costvolume, dim=-1) # 5. Concatenate Monocular and Cost Volume # Note: Mono features might need resizing to match (H/s, W/s) monofeatresized = F.interpolate(monofeatures[i].unsqueeze(0), size=(H//self.s, W//self.s), mode='bilinear').squeeze(0) combinedfeatures = torch.cat([costvolume, monofeatresized], dim=-1) # 6. Depth Regression # 2D U-Net + Softmax depthprobs = self.depthhead(combinedfeatures) # Shape: (H/s, W/s, D) # Convert probabilities to depth values depthmap = self.computedepthfromprobs(depthprobs, depthcandidates) # Upsample depth map to original resolution if needed for unprojection depthmapfullres = F.interpolate(depthmap.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), size=(H, W), mode='bilinear').squeeze(0).squeeze(0) # 7. Unproject to 3D Gaussians # Get 2D pixel coordinates y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H), torch.arange(W), indexing='ij') coords = torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1).float() # Unproject using Pi and depth # This is a simplified representation; actual unprojection uses P^{-1} centers = self.unproject(coords, depthmapfullres, projectionmatrices[i]) # 8. Predict remaining parameters # Use a head that takes image features or depth features alpha, sigma, color = self.gaussianhead(mvfeaturesaware[i], depthmapfullres) gaussiansperview.append({ 'mu': centers, 'alpha': alpha, 'sigma': sigma, 'color': color }) return gaussiansperview def selectneighbors(self, refidx, projectionmatrices, K): # Compute camera distances between refidx and all other views # Select top K nearest views # Not given in sources: specific distance metric (e.g., translation norm) # Placeholder logic distances = [self.cameradistance(projectionmatrices[refidx], projectionmatrices[j]) for j in range(len(projectionmatrices)) if j != refidx] sortedindices = torch.argsort(torch.tensor(distances)) return [sortedindices[k] for k in range(K)] def sampledepthcandidates(self, projectionmatrix): # Uniformly sample D depth candidates from near/far ranges # Not given in sources: specific near/far values # Placeholder logic near, far = 0.1, 100.0 # Example values return torch.linspace(near, far, self.D) def warpfeature(self, featj, Pi, Pj, depthd): # Warp feature map from view j to view i using depth d # Not given in sources: specific warping implementation (e.g., gridsample) # Placeholder logic pass def computedepthfromprobs(self, probs, candidates): # Weighted sum of candidates based on softmax probabilities return torch.sum(probs candidates, dim=-1) def unproject(self, coords, depth, P): # Unproject 2D coords + depth to 3D using P # Not given in sources: specific unprojection math # Placeholder logic pass def cameradistance(self, P1, P2): # Compute distance between camera poses # Not given in sources pass A feed-forward method that models relations between Gaussian groups from different views using a Gaussian Graph structure to reduce artifacts and memory costs. It performs message passing at the Gaussian level, unlike DepthSplat which operates on pixel-aligned Gaussians derived from depth maps. Choose when inter-view consistency of individual Gaussians is critical and computational resources allow for graph-based aggregation. Time Complexity: The method is feed-forward, enabling fast inference. Reconstruction from 12 input views at 512x960 resolution takes 0.6 seconds. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of depth candidates D and the cost volume size \frac{H}{s} \times \frac{W}{s} \times D. Selecting only top-2 neighbors for N>2 views keeps memory usage tractable. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results on ScanNet, RealEstate10K, and DL3DV datasets for both depth estimation and Gaussian splatting. Training Efficiency: Trained on 4 GPUs for 2 days, significantly cheaper than methods like GS-LRM which require 64 A100 GPUs. Strengths: Robustness to low-texture, occluded, and reflective regions due to monocular feature augmentation; multi-view consistency maintained by using monocular features as augmentation rather than primary signal; efficient training. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained monocular depth model; multi-view depth estimation can still fail in extreme occlusions or non-Lambertian surfaces, though mitigated by monocular features. When to use: When generalizable, feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction is needed from sparse or multi-view inputs, especially in challenging scenes with low texture or reflections, and when training compute is limited. When not to use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher quality is required regardless of speed; when input images lack known camera poses (DepthSplat requires poses). DepthSplat was introduced to connect the fields of Gaussian splatting and depth estimation, leveraging their mutual benefits. It addresses the limitations of multi-view stereo (failure in low-texture/occluded areas) and monocular depth estimation (scale ambiguity) by combining pre-trained monocular depth features with multi-view cost volumes. The method was trained on large-scale datasets including TartanAir, ScanNet, RealEstate10K, and DL3DV. It also demonstrates that Gaussian splatting can serve as an unsupervised pre-training objective for learning depth models from large-scale multi-view posed datasets without ground truth depth supervision. name: Gaussian Graph Network
body: Gaussian Graph Network (GGN) is a feed-forward method that generates efficient and generalizable 3D Gaussian representations from multi-view images by modeling relations between Gaussian groups from different views using a Gaussian Graph structure. It solves the problem of artifacts and excessive memory costs caused by previous methods that simply combine pixel-aligned Gaussians from multiple views without capturing their inter-view relations. Unlike sibling methods that treat multi-view Gaussians as independent sets, GGN performs message passing and aggregation at the Gaussian level, allowing each Gaussian to benefit from connected groups in other views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images I = \{Ii\} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H \times W \times 3} and their corresponding camera parameters C = \{ci\}. Outputs: Gaussian parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c), where \mu is the mean position, \Sigma is the covariance matrix, \alpha is opacity, and c is color. Data Structures: Node vi: Represents a group of pixel-aligned Gaussians for view i. It consists of a mean position vector \mui \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times 3} and a feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^{HW \times D}. Edge Weight Matrix E{s \to k}: A matrix of size HW \times HW containing binary values (0 or 1) indicating pixel correspondence between Gaussians in group s and group k. Specifically, e{ij}^{s \to k} = 1 if \psi{proj}(\mu{s,i}, cs) = \psi{proj}(\mu{k,j}, cs), and 0 otherwise, where \psi{proj} projects the Gaussian center to the image plane. Adjacency Matrix A: A matrix of size N \times N where a{ij} = 1 if i=j, and a{ij} = \psi{overlap}(vi, vj) if i \neq j, where \psi{overlap} computes the overlap ratio between views. Degree Matrix D: A diagonal matrix where d{ii} = \sumj a{ij}. It improves rendering quality by 4.9dB on PSNR and reduces the number of Gaussians to nearly one-fourth compared to the model without it. It uses a similarity function \psi{similarity} and a merge function \psi{merge} controlled by a threshold \lambda. It computes aggregated features by summing transformed features of neighbors weighted by the scaled adjacency matrix and edge matrices. Performance improves with more input views, unlike previous methods. Strengths: Efficient and generalizable representations; reduces artifacts and floaters; benefits from more input views. Limitations: Computational complexity of graph operations; requires careful tuning of pruning and pooling parameters. Gaussian Graph Network (GGN) was proposed to address the limitations of previous methods that simply combine pixel-aligned Gaussians from multiple views without modeling relations. It was introduced in the paper "Gaussian Graph Network: Learning Efficient and Generalizable Gaussian Representations from Multi-view Images". The method builds on the concept of pixelSplat and MVSplat but extends them by introducing Gaussian Graphs and specific layers for message passing and pooling. name: VG2GT
head: VG^2GT, Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer
body: VG2GT is a feed-forward, non-pixel-aligned 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction framework that directly regresses geometrically accurate Gaussian scenes and camera parameters from an arbitrary number of unposed and uncalibrated images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like AnySplat by avoiding the intermediate step of regressing pixel-aligned primitives; instead, it decodes Gaussian primitives directly from structured voxel features, thereby mitigating the uneven distributions and cross-view inconsistencies inherent in pixel-aligned formulations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N unposed and uncalibrated RGB images \{\mathbf{I}i\}{i=1}^N. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and camera pose representations \mathbf{C}i. Data Structures: The method relies on the output of the frozen Visual Foundation Model (VGGT) and a multi-scale voxel module. 1. VGGT Outputs: For each image i, the backbone produces: Pixel-aligned point maps \mathbf{P}i \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Depth maps \mathbf{D}i \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 1}. Camera pose representations \mathbf{C}i \in \mathbb{R}^9. 2. Voxel Features: A structured 3D voxel grid containing refined geometric features, derived from point-cloud features via voxelization. 3. Gaussian Primitives: Defined by position \mathbf{x}, covariance matrix \Sigma (parameterized by rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps: 1. Joint Encoding: The frozen VGGT backbone \mathcal{F}\phi jointly encodes the input images to produce initial geometric cues: \mathcal{F}\phi (\{\mathbf{I}i\}{i=1}^N) = \{\mathbf{P}i, \mathbf{D}i, \mathbf{C}i\}{i=1}^N The backbone uses a ViT-based encoder (e.g., DINO) with alternating attention, where patch tokens are downsampled by a factor of 14. 2. Coarse-Scale Feature Enhancement: PointTransformer [47] and trilinear interpolation are used to compute complementary geometric features from the point maps \mathbf{P}i. These features are injected into the patch tokens of the VGGT backbone to enhance global scene understanding. 3. Fine-Scale Voxelization: A DPT head [28] extracts global point-cloud features from the enhanced tokens. These features are voxelized into a structured 3D voxel representation. 4. Voxel Refinement and Decoding: The voxel features are refined by a PointMLP network. A self-splitting Gaussian head decodes the refined voxel features to predict the parameters of the Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). 5. Rendering and Supervision: Standard 3DGS rasterization is replaced with stochastic solid volume rendering during training. This formulation models Gaussian primitives as continuous stochastic solids and renders them along camera rays, improving the quality of synthesized Gaussian depth maps and strengthening geometric reconstruction accuracy. The rendered images and depth maps are compared against ground truth (or pseudo-ground truth from the VGGT outputs) to compute loss. 6. Optimization: The original VGGT components (backbone, depth head, camera head) are kept fully frozen. Only the multi-scale voxel module (PointTransformer, DPT, PointMLP) and the Gaussian primitive decoding head are optimized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vg2gtforward(images, vggtbackbone, voxelmodule, gaussianhead): """ Forward pass of VG2GT. Args: images: List of N RGB images [H, W, 3]. vggtbackbone: Frozen VGGT model (ViT-based encoder + DPT heads). voxelmodule: Multi-scale differentiable voxel module (PointTransformer, PointMLP). gaussianhead: Self-splitting Gaussian head. Returns: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitive parameters. cameraposes: List of camera pose representations. """ # Step 1: Joint Encoding with Frozen VGGT # VGGT produces pixel-aligned point maps, depth maps, and camera poses pointmaps, depthmaps, cameraposes = vggtbackbone(images) # Step 2: Coarse-Scale Feature Enhancement # Compute geometric features using PointTransformer and trilinear interpolation # Inject into patch tokens to enhance global understanding # Note: VGGT backbone is frozen, so this likely involves external feature injection # or modifying the input to the frozen backbone's attention layers if supported. # Assuming the 'voxelmodule' handles the interaction with the frozen backbone's features. enhancedfeatures = voxelmodule.coarseenhance(pointmaps, depthmaps) # Step 3: Fine-Scale Voxelization # Extract global point-cloud features via DPT (part of VGGT or separate head?) # The source says "DPT head extracts... and voxelizes". # Since VGGT is frozen, we assume the DPT head used for feature extraction # is either part of the frozen VGGT or a separate frozen component, # but the voxelization and refinement are trainable. # Clarification from source: "Only the multi-scale voxel module and Gaussian primitive # decoding head are optimized." # Thus, the DPT head extracting features might be frozen or part of the VGGT output. # We assume pointmaps/depthmaps are sufficient or enhanced features are used. # Voxelize point-cloud features into structured representation voxelfeatures = voxelmodule.voxelize(pointmaps, enhancedfeatures) # Step 4: Refine and Decode # Refine voxel features with PointMLP refinedvoxelfeatures = voxelmodule.refine(voxelfeatures) # Decode Gaussian primitive parameters gaussians = gaussianhead.decode(refinedvoxelfeatures) return gaussians, cameraposes def vg2gtrender(gaussians, cameraposes, pixelcoords): """ Stochastic solid volume rendering. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. cameraposes: Camera poses for each view. pixelcoords: 2D pixel coordinates to render. Returns: renderedimage: Rendered RGB image. rendereddepth: Rendered depth map. """ # Replace standard 3DGS rasterization with stochastic solid volume rendering # This models Gaussians as continuous stochastic solids renderedimage = stochasticsolidvolumerender(gaussians, cameraposes, pixelcoords) rendereddepth = computedepthfromgaussians(gaussians, cameraposes, pixelcoords) return renderedimage, rendereddepth Parameters: VGGT Backbone: Uses a ViT-based encoder (e.g., DINO) with alternating attention. Patch tokens are downsampled by a factor of 14. Training: The VGGT backbone, depth head, and camera head are frozen. Only the voxel module and Gaussian head are trained. Pitfalls: Pixel-Aligned Artifacts: Pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives impose a one-to-one correspondence between 2D pixels and 3D points. In real multi-view observations, the same 3D point can be visible from multiple pixels and viewpoints. Aggregating these observations is essential for compact, coherent, and geometrically consistent scene representations. Pixel-aligned formulations tend to produce uneven Gaussian distributions and cross-view inconsistencies. VG2GT avoids this by using a non-pixel-aligned voxel-based approach. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, as a feed-forward method, it avoids the iterative optimization loop of standard 3DGS, implying significantly faster inference/training time compared to optimization-based methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The voxel module introduces additional memory overhead compared to direct pixel-aligned decoding, but the frozen VGGT backbone reduces the need for large trainable parameters. Measured Performance: VG2GT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DTU, Replica, TAT, and ScanNet datasets. Strengths: Feed-forward: No iterative optimization required. Non-pixel-aligned: Avoids uneven Gaussian distributions and cross-view inconsistencies. Frozen Backbone: Substantially reduces training cost and allows plugging into patch-feature-based VFMs. Geometric Accuracy: Stochastic solid volume rendering improves depth map quality and geometric reconstruction accuracy. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the frozen VGGT backbone. Not given in the sources. When to Use: When fast, geometrically accurate 3D reconstruction from unposed/uncalibrated images is required, and high multi-view consistency is critical. When Not to Use: When iterative optimization is acceptable and higher fidelity is needed for specific scenes, or when the VGGT backbone is not suitable for the domain. VG2GT was proposed by Zhao et al. in 2026 (preprint). It builds on the VGGT visual foundation model [36] and addresses the limitations of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods that use pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives. The method is designed to be plugged into patch-feature-based VFMs, reducing training cost and improving geometric reasoning through a multi-scale differentiable voxel module. \text{VG}^2GT: Voxel-Gaussian Splatting Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.01573, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Direct Pixel-Wise Regression
body: Direct Pixel-Wise Regression is a feed-forward method that predicts a set of 3D Gaussian primitives directly from input image patches, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between 2D pixels and 3D Gaussians. It differs from sibling methods like Triplane-LRM by avoiding fixed-resolution latent representations (e.g., triplanes), thereby enabling pixel-aligned prediction of per-Gaussian colors and scaling Gaussian count with input resolution to capture high-frequency details. See Feed-forward Generalizable Reconstruction for shared principles. FineSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that predicts a set of 3D Gaussians from N context views using a two-stage dual-grouping strategy to balance local detail preservation with global multi-view reasoning. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like YoNoSplat and ZipSplat by employing high-resolution 4x4 patch tokens instead of coarser 14x14 patches, combined with serialized attention for 3D spatial grouping to avoid the prohibitive cost of global multi-view attention. SparSplat is a generalizable, feed-forward model that maps a sparse set of input images to 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) parameters in a single forward pass to perform both 3D shape reconstruction and novel view synthesis. It differs from its sibling MVSGaussian by using 2D planar primitives instead of 3D volumetric primitives, which ensures multi-view depth consistency required for coherent TSDF mesh fusion. Unlike prior generalizable methods designed primarily for novel view synthesis, SparSplat is explicitly optimized for feed-forward surface reconstruction, offering inference speeds nearly two orders of magnitude faster than implicit volume rendering methods. Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting (GPS-Gaussian) is a feed-forward method for real-time novel view synthesis of humans from sparse camera views. It solves the problem of per-subject optimization latency in 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly regressing Gaussian parameters from source images without fine-tuning. Unlike sibling methods that recompute view-correlated modules for every target viewpoint, GPS-Gaussian performs source-view computation once and renders novel views instantly, allowing concurrent rendering of multiple views. GS-LRM predicts 3D Gaussians directly from image patches, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between 2D pixels and 3D Gaussians. The Gaussian center is calculated as xyz = rayo + t \cdot rayd, where t is the ray distance, rayo is the ray origin, and rayd is the ray direction. Each Gaussian is parameterized by q=12 values: 3-channel RGB, 3-channel scale, 4-channel rotation quaternion, 1-channel opacity, and 1-channel ray distance. The model uses a patch size of p=8 \times 8 for both patchifying and unpatchifying operations. The total output is N \cdot HW Gaussians for N input views, where H and W are image height and width, scaling with input resolution unlike fixed-resolution triplanes. This pixel-aligned scheme creates a shortcut for learning accurate per-Gaussian colors from input RGB images, unlike the non-pixel-aligned prediction of Triplane-LRM. The concept of direct pixel-wise regression for 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in GS-LRM (Large Reconstruction Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting). The method was developed to address the limitations of fixed-resolution latent representations in prior Large Reconstruction Models (LRM) like Triplane-LRM, which struggled with high-frequency details and per-pixel color accuracy. By predicting Gaussians directly from image patches, GS-LRM allows the number of primitives to scale with input resolution, facilitating better handling of large-scale scene captures and high-frequency details. name: FineSplat
head: Detailed Splats, Fine Patches, Local Groups
body: FineSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework that predicts a set of 3D Gaussians from N context views (with or without known poses) using a two-stage dual-grouping strategy to balance local detail preservation with global multi-view reasoning. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SparSplat and Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting by employing high-resolution 4 \times 4 patch tokens and serialized 3D spatial attention, avoiding the prohibitive cost of global multi-view attention while preserving fine-grained visual information. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N context views (images I \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H \times W \times 3}) and their camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). Poses may be known or predicted. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (centers, covariances, colors, opacities) representing the scene. Data Structures: Tokens: A set of M fine-grained tokens z \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d}, where M = N \cdot (H/p) \cdot (W/p) and p=4 is the patch size. Gaussians: K Gaussian primitives predicted per token. Parameters: p: Patch size, fixed at 4 \times 4 pixels. T: Number of iterative refinement steps in Stage 2, fixed at 4. K: Number of Gaussians per token (typically 4). s: Sub-patch stride, fixed at 2. S: Group size for serialized attention (number of consecutive points along the space-filling curve). N: Number of input context views. Training samples N \in \{6, 12, 24, 32\}. Algorithm: 1. Scene Normalization: To handle scale ambiguity in feed-forward reconstruction, normalize scene scale using context camera poses. Express poses in the mean context camera frame. Rescale translations so that all context camera centers lie within [-1, 1]^3. Apply the same transform to target poses. 2. Stage 1: View-Wise Token Grouping: a. Feature Extraction: Extract feature maps F^l for levels l \in \{1, 2, 3\} (finest to coarsest) from the input images using a backbone (e.g., MVP architecture). b. Token Initialization: Fuse features into M fine-grained tokens z^{(0)} using Equation (1): z^{(0)} = \text{fuse}(\text{up}(\text{fuse}(\text{up}(F^3) + F^2)) + F^1) where \text{up}(\cdot) is bilinear upsampling and \text{fuse}(\cdot) is a convolutional fusion block. M = N \cdot (H/p) \cdot (W/p). c. View-Wise Attention: Encode tokens using view-wise token grouping. Perform fine-grained attention within small view groups and exchange information across all views via coarser global tokens. This restricts attention scope to keep multi-view reasoning affordable. 3. Stage 2: 3D Spatial Token Grouping (Iterative Refinement for t = 1 \dots T): a. Gaussian Prediction: Decode tokens z^{(t-1)} into an initial set of Gaussians using a lightweight Gaussian head \mathcal{D} (linear decoder). For each token, predict K Gaussians. b. Patch-Aligned Sub-Pixel Reconstruction: i. Predict 4 Gaussians per 4 \times 4 token, assigning each to a non-overlapping 2 \times 2 sub-patch. ii. Learn a 2D image-space offset \Delta = (\Deltax, \Deltay) for each Gaussian. iii. Bound the offset to keep the Gaussian within its sub-patch: \deltax = 2s \tanh(\Deltax), \quad \deltay = 2s \tanh(\Deltay) where s=2 is the sub-patch stride. This ensures \deltax, \deltay \in [-s/2, s/2]. iv. Compute displaced coordinate (u, v) = (uc, vc) + \delta, where (uc, vc) is the sub-patch center. v. Ray Unprojection: Unproject (u, v) using predicted camera intrinsics. Transform and normalize direction using camera-to-world rotation, using camera translation as ray origin. c. Rendering: Render the predicted Gaussians into every context view to obtain rendered images \hat{I}n. d. Error Feature Computation: i. Compute signed error map En = \hat{I}n - In for each view n. ii. Compute feature-level difference \Delta \phin = \phi(\hat{I}n) - \phi(In) using a pretrained ResNet-18 encoder \phi(\cdot). iii. Combine with finest-scale features Fn^1 from Stage 1 via linear embeddings E{err} and E{feat}: Fn^{\text{err}} = [E{err}(En, \Delta \phin); E{\text{feat}}(Fn^1)] \in \mathbb{R}^{(H/p) \times (W/p) \times de} where [\cdot; \cdot] represents concatenation. e. Error Aggregation: i. For each token, gather two error signals: Self error feature e{\text{self}} from the patch where the token is predicted. Aggregated error feature e{\text{agg}} averaged over all context views where the token is visible (including views outside the Stage 1 view group). f. 3D Spatial Grouping: i. Lift tokens to 3D space using predicted Gaussian centers. ii. Order tokens along a space-filling curve and partition them into groups of S consecutive points. iii. Use four attention blocks, each using a different space-filling curve, so each token meets a different set of neighbors. iv. Apply serialized self-attention within each group to exchange error signals. v. Update tokens: \Delta zj^{(i)} = \text{Linear}(\text{SerialAttn}(hj^{(i)})) zj^{(i+1)} = zj^{(i)} + \Delta zj^{(i)} where hj^{(i)} are the features of the token in the 3D group. g. Repeat: Go to step 3a with updated tokens z^{(t)}. Pitfalls: Blind Spots: Fixed view grouping in Stage 1 leaves blind spots where fine-grained tokens in different groups cannot interact. Stage 2 3D spatial grouping connects tokens across view groups once lifted to 3D. Scale Ambiguity: Feed-forward reconstruction is scale-ambiguous. Must normalize scene scale using context camera poses as described in Step 1. Iteration Count: Quality improves with more Stage 2 steps, but going beyond T=4 yields no further gain. Time Complexity: FineSplat is faster than explicit k-nearest-neighbor search for 3D grouping and scales favorably with token count due to serialized attention. It is faster than SparSplat and Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting variants using larger patches (14 \times 14) for 6 and 12 input views, and remains efficient with 24 views. Memory Complexity: Uses a small primitive budget (e.g., 62K Gaussians for 6 views on DL3DV) compared to baselines like ZipSplat (1.5M Gaussians). Performance: DL3DV (6 views): 27.325 PSNR, 0.871 SSIM, 0.115 LPIPS (62K Gaussians). RE10K (6 views): 27.394 PSNR, 0.886 SSIM, 0.116 LPIPS (75K Gaussians). Mip-NeRF 360 (128 views): 23.463 PSNR, 0.706 SSIM, 0.214 LPIPS (1.6M Gaussians). Strengths: High quality with few Gaussians; efficient dual-grouping strategy; robust to varying numbers of input views. Limitations: Requires camera poses (known or predicted); performance on Mip-NeRF 360 (zero-shot) is lower than on DL3DV, likely due to domain shift and larger scene scale. FineSplat was introduced in 2026 by. It builds on Direct Pixel-Wise Regression and Feed-forward Generalizable Reconstruction principles. It is trained on the DL3DV dataset and evaluated on DL3DV, RealEstate10K, and Mip-NeRF 360 for novel view synthesis.
