name: SparSplat
head: Generalizable 2D Gaussian Splatting, SparSplat Model, SparSplat: Fast Multi-View Reconstruction with Generalizable 2D Gaussian Splatting
body: SparSplat is a generalizable, feed-forward model that maps a set of sparse input images (typically 3) to a pixel-aligned map of 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) parameters for a target view, enabling both 3D shape reconstruction and novel view synthesis in a single forward pass. It differs from its sibling Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting and FineSplat by explicitly using 2D Gaussian primitives rather than 3D Gaussians, which ensures multi-view depth consistency required for coherent TSDF mesh fusion, whereas prior 3DGS-based generalizable methods fail to produce coherent surfaces when fused. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N color images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N (where N=3 in training) with known camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^N, and a target view pose Pt. Outputs: A Gaussian parameter map Ot \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 13} for the target view, containing scale (s), rotation quaternion (q), centroid (p), opacity (\alpha), and color (c). The layout is \{s, q, p, \alpha, c\} with channel dimensions 2+4+3+1+3. From this, a 3D triangle mesh S is extracted via TSDF fusion of splatted depths. Data Structures: The core data structure is the parameter map Ot. Each pixel (u,v) holds a 13-dimensional vector: 1. s \in \mathbb{R}^2: Scale parameters (typically log-scale or direct scale, mapped to anisotropic 2D covariance). 2. q \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. 3. p \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D centroid position. 4. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. 5. c \in \mathbb{R}^3: RGB color. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: Encode each input image Ii using a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) to obtain 2D feature maps fi. Enhance these with monocular semantic features from DINOv2 and pairwise dense correspondence features from MASt3R. 2. Homography Warping: Warp the feature maps fi to the target view coordinate system using the relative poses Pt / Pi to obtain warped features f{t,i}. 3. Cost Volume Construction: Merge the warped features f{t,i} into a 3D cost volume. 4. Depth Prediction (DeepMVS Branch): Process the cost volume with a 3D convolutional network to produce a probability volume, yielding a depth prediction D{pred}. Implementation Note: Sample 64 depth planes for the coarse stage and 8 for the fine stage. 5. Feature Pooling: Pool the warped features f{t,i} into a single target feature map ft. 6. Gaussian Attribute Prediction: Pass ft through a 2D convolutional network and an MLP to predict the Gaussian attributes \{s, q, \alpha, c\}. 7. Centroid Unprojection: Unproject the predicted depth D{pred} using the target camera intrinsics K and pose Pt to compute the 3D centroids p. Combine p with \{s, q, \alpha, c\} to form the full parameter map Ot. 8. Rendering: Render the scene using perspective-accurate 2D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. 9. Mesh Extraction (Optional): For 3D reconstruction, render mean depth maps for all input views Pi using their respective parameter maps Oi = \Phi(Pi | I1,..., IN). Fuse these depth maps using Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) fusion with a voxel size of 1.5 to generate the mesh S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsplatforward(inputimages, inputposes, targetpose, cameraintrinsics): """ inputimages: List[N, H, W, 3] inputposes: List[N, 4, 4] targetpose: 4, 4 cameraintrinsics: 3, 3 Returns: parametermap (H, W, 13), depthmap (H, W) """ N = len(inputimages) # Step 1: Feature Encoding # fi: List[N, C, H, W] fi = [fpn(img) for img in inputimages] # Enhance with foundation models (DINOv2, MASt3R) # This step is implicit in the architecture description; # in implementation, features are concatenated or fused here. fienhanced = enhancewithfoundationmodels(fi) # Step 2: Homography Warping # fti: List[N, C, H, W] fti = [] for i in range(N): # Warp features from source i to target view # Hrel is the homography derived from targetpose / inputposes[i] Hrel = computehomography(targetpose, inputposes[i], cameraintrinsics) fti.append(warpfeatures(fienhanced[i], Hrel)) # Step 3 & 4: DeepMVS Branch for Depth # costvolume: (H, W, D, C) where D is number of depth planes costvolume = buildcostvolume(fti) # probabilityvolume: (H, W, D) probabilityvolume = conv3dnetwork(costvolume) # depthpred: (H, W) depthpred = softargmax(probabilityvolume) # Step 5: Feature Pooling # ft: (C, H, W) ft = poolfeatures(fti) # Step 6: Gaussian Attribute Prediction # s: (H, W, 2), q: (H, W, 4), alpha: (H, W, 1), c: (H, W, 3) s, q, alpha, c = gaussianattributemlp(ft) # Step 7: Centroid Unprojection # p: (H, W, 3) # Unproject depthpred using cameraintrinsics and targetpose p = unprojectdepth(depthpred, targetpose, cameraintrinsics) # Combine into parameter map # Layout: s(2) + q(4) + p(3) + alpha(1) + c(3) = 13 parametermap = concatenate([s, q, p, alpha, c], axis=-1) return parametermap, depthpred def extractmesh(parametermaps, poses, intrinsics, voxelsize=1.5): """ parametermaps: List[N, H, W, 13] poses: List[N, 4, 4] intrinsics: 3, 3 Returns: Mesh S """ depthmaps = [] for i in range(len(parametermaps)): # Render depth from 2DGS parameters for view i # This involves splatting the Gaussians defined by parametermaps[i] # projected to the camera defined by poses[i] depthmap = render2dgsdepth(parametermaps[i], poses[i], intrinsics) depthmaps.append(depthmap) # TSDF Fusion mesh = tsdffusion(depthmaps, poses, intrinsics, voxelsize) return mesh Parameters: Training Resolution: 640 \times 512. Number of Source Images (N): 3. Optimizer: Adam, initial learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Training Steps: 300,000. Hardware: Single RTX A6000 GPU. TSDF Voxel Size: 1.5. Loss Weights: \lambdas = 0.1, \lambdap = 0.05, \lambda\alpha = 0.05, \lambda\beta = 0.05, \lambda\gamma = 0.05, \lambda1 = 0.5, \lambda2 = 1. Depth Planes: 64 (coarse), 8 (fine). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 3DGS vs 2DGS: Using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) instead of 2DGS leads to depth inconsistencies across views, causing TSDF fusion to produce warped or disconnected surfaces. Feature Selection: Using only image features or DINOv2 features yields inferior results compared to using MASt3R features. MASt3R provides an 11.11% boost in Chamfer Distance over image-only features, while DINOv2 provides only a 0.85% boost. Depth Loss: Omitting the depth loss L{depth} significantly degrades reconstruction quality. Adding it improves mean Chamfer Distance by 71.8% (from 4.37 to 1.04). Inference Speed: Approximately 0.8–0.88 seconds on an RTX A6000 GPU. This is nearly 2 orders of magnitude faster than prior state-of-the-art feed-forward sparse-view reconstruction methods based on implicit volume rendering (e.g., UfoRecon at 66s, GeoTransfer at 32s). Reconstruction Accuracy: On the DTU test set, SparSplat achieves a mean Chamfer Distance of 1.04 (with MASt3R features and depth loss). Novel View Synthesis (NVS): On the DTU test set, SparSplat achieves PSNR 28.33, SSIM 0.938, and LPIPS 0.073. It outperforms MVSGaussian, particularly in regions with low input view overlap. Strengths: Fast inference, coherent 3D mesh reconstruction via TSDF, strong generalization on sparse views (3 images), and high-quality NVS. Limitations: Relies on external foundation models (DINOv2, MASt3R) for feature extraction, which may increase memory footprint during inference if not cached. Performance is tied to the quality of the 2DGS representation for surface consistency. SparSplat was introduced by Shubhendu Jena et al. in 2025. It builds upon the MVSGaussian framework [48] but replaces 3D Gaussians with 2D Gaussians to address the lack of surface coherence in generalizable Gaussian splatting methods. It leverages advances in foundation models, specifically DINOv2 for monocular semantic features and MASt3R for dense pairwise correspondences, to enhance multi-view consistency. The method is designed for sparse-view 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis, targeting applications in robotics, AR/VR, and autonomous systems where fast, generalizable reconstruction from few images is critical. name: Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: GPS-Gaussian, Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, Generalizable 3D-Gaussians
body: Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting (GPS-Gaussian) is a feed-forward method for real-time novel view synthesis of humans from sparse camera views. It predicts pixel-wise Gaussian parameter maps (position, color, rotation, scaling, opacity) for selected source views, unprojects them to 3D, aggregates them, and renders the target view using differentiable Gaussian splatting. Unlike original 3D Gaussian Splatting which requires per-subject optimization, or implicit methods like ENeRF that recompute modules per target view, GPS-Gaussian eliminates fine-tuning by regressing parameters directly from source images. It differs from sibling methods like FineSplat and SparSplat by defining Gaussian parameters on 2D image planes of source views rather than unstructured point clouds or sparse grids, allowing the use of efficient 2D convolution networks. Inputs: N source RGB images \{In\}{n=1}^N with known camera positions \{Cn\}{n=1}^N and scene center O. A target novel view camera position C{tar} and view vector V{tar} = C{tar} - O. Outputs: Rendered image I{tar} at the target viewpoint. Data Structures: 1. Feature Maps: f^s \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2^s \times W/2^s \times Ds} for s=1..S. 2. Correlation Volume: C \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times W/2}. 3. Depth Maps: D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}. 4. Gaussian Parameter Maps: Defined on image planes. Position Map Mp(x): 3D vector. Color Map Mc(x): 3D vector (RGB). Rotation Map Mr(x): 4D vector (quaternion). Scaling Map Ms(x): 3D vector. Opacity Map M\alpha(x): Scalar. 5. Gaussian Set: Aggregated 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gk\}k, where gk = (\muk, \Sigmak, \alphak, Sk, ck). Parameters: S=3: Number of feature scales. \beta=0.8: Weight for L1 loss. \gamma=0.2: Weight for SSIM loss. \mu=0.9: Exponential decay weight for depth supervision. T: Number of iterative depth estimation steps. Input Resolution: 1024 \times 1024. Steps: 1. View Selection: Compute view vectors Vn = Cn - O for all source views. Compute dot products between all Vn and V{tar}. Select the two source views with the highest dot products (nearest views) as the working set: left view Il and right view Ir. 2. Feature Extraction: Feed rectified source images Il, Ir into a shared image encoder E{img}. The encoder uses residual blocks and downsampling. It produces dense feature maps f^s \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2^s \times W/2^s \times Ds} for s=1, 2, 3. s=1: Resolution H/2 \times W/2, Channels D1=32. s=2: Resolution H/4 \times W/4, Channels D2=48. s=3: Resolution H/8 \times W/8, Channels D3=96. Architecture: Similar to RAFT-Stereo encoder. First conv kernel 5 \times 5 (instead of 7 \times 7). Batch normalization replaced with Group Normalization. 3. Cost Volume Construction: For the finest scale features f^1l, f^1r \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times D1}, compute a 3D correlation volume C \in \mathbb{R}^{H/2 \times W/2 \times W/2} using matrix multiplication: C(f^1l, f^1r), C{ijk} = \sum{h=1}^{D1} (f^1l){ijh} \cdot (f^1r){ikh} where i,j are spatial coordinates in the left view and k is the disparity index. 4. Iterative Depth Estimation: Predict a sequence of depth estimations \{d^tl\}{t=1}^T and \{d^tr\}{t=1}^T by looking up in volume C using an iterative update mechanism. The final outputs (d^Tl, d^Tr) are upsampled to full image resolution (Dl, Dr) via convex upsampling. The depth estimation module is formulated as: \langle Dl, Dr \rangle = \Phi{depth}(f^1l, f^1r, Kl, Kr) where Kl, Kr are camera intrinsics. 5. Position Map Generation: For each foreground pixel x in the source image, unproject from 2D to 3D using the predicted depth map D(x) and projection matrix P: Mp(x) = \Pi^{-1}P (x, D(x)) where \Pi^{-1}P is the unprojection operation. 6. Color Map Generation: For diffuse human scenes, use the source RGB image directly as the color map: Mc(x) = I(x) 7. Geometric Feature Fusion: Construct an encoder E{depth} taking the depth map D as input to complement geometric awareness. Fuse image features from E{img} and spatial features from E{depth} using a U-Net like decoder D{parm} to regress Gaussian features \Gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times DG}: \Gamma = D{parm} (E{img}(I) \oplus E{depth}(D)) where \oplus denotes concatenation at all feature levels. 8. Scaling Map Generation: Predict scaling hs(\Gamma(x)) and apply Softplus activation: Ms(x) = \text{Softplus}(hs(\Gamma(x))) 9. Opacity Map Generation: Predict opacity h\alpha(\Gamma(x)) and apply Sigmoid activation: M\alpha(x) = \text{Sigmoid}(h\alpha(\Gamma(x))) 10. Rotation Map Generation: Predict rotation hr(\Gamma(x)) and apply normalization: Mr(x) = \text{Norm}(hr(\Gamma(x))) (Note: Specific normalization function details are in supplementary material, typically L2 normalization for quaternions). 11. Aggregation and Rendering: Unproject Gaussian parameter maps from both source views (Il, Ir) to 3D space to create Gaussian points. Aggregate the Gaussians from both views into a single set \mathcal{G}. Render the target viewpoint using differentiable Gaussian splatting on \mathcal{G}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpsgaussianrender(sourceimages, camerapositions, scenecenter, targetcamera): """ sourceimages: List of N RGB images (H, W, 3) camerapositions: List of N camera positions (3,) scenecenter: Scene center (3,) targetcamera: Target camera position (3,) Returns: Rendered image (H, W, 3) """ # 1. View Selection viewvectors = [pos - scenecenter for pos in camerapositions] targetvector = targetcamera - scenecenter # Compute dot products and select two nearest views scores = [dot(v, targetvector) for v in viewvectors] indices = argsort(scores, descending=True)[:2] idxl, idxr = indices[0], indices[1] Il = sourceimages[idxl] Ir = sourceimages[idxr] # 2. Feature Extraction # Eimg is a shared encoder with 3 scales fl = Eimg(Il) # Returns list of feature maps [f^1l, f^2l, f^3l] fr = Eimg(Ir) # Returns list of feature maps [f^1r, f^2r, f^3r] # 3. Cost Volume Construction (using finest scale f^1) f1l, f1r = fl[0], fr[0] # C shape: (H/2, W/2, W/2) C = computecorrelationvolume(f1l, f1r) # 4. Iterative Depth Estimation # Returns full resolution depth maps Dl, Dr Dl, Dr = iterativedepthestimator(C, f1l, f1r) # 5. Generate Parameter Maps for Left View # Position Mpl = unproject2dto3d(Il, Dl, camerapositions[idxl]) # Color Mcl = Il # Geometric Fusion for other params # Edepth takes Dl, Eimg takes Il featl = fusefeatures(Eimg(Il), Edepth(Dl)) # Regress Gamma Gammal = Dparm(featl) # Scaling, Opacity, Rotation Msl = softplus(heads(Gammal)) Malphal = sigmoid(headalpha(Gammal)) Mrl = normalize(headr(Gammal)) # 6. Generate Parameter Maps for Right View (Same logic) Mpr = unproject2dto3d(Ir, Dr, camerapositions[idxr]) Mcr = Ir featr = fusefeatures(Eimg(Ir), Edepth(Dr)) Gammar = Dparm(featr) Msr = softplus(heads(Gammar)) Malphar = sigmoid(headalpha(Gammar)) Mrr = normalize(headr(Gammar)) # 7. Aggregation # Create Gaussian points from Left View gaussiansl = creategaussians(Mpl, Mcl, Mrl, Msl, Malphal) # Create Gaussian points from Right View gaussiansr = creategaussians(Mpr, Mcr, Mrr, Msr, Malphar) # Aggregate all Gaussians allgaussians = gaussiansl + gaussiansr # 8. Rendering renderedimage = differentiablesplatting(allgaussians, targetcamera) return renderedimage Used in GGRt. Organizes images into pairs, uses an Epipolar Sampler to find correspondences along epipolar lines, Cross-Attention for per-pixel correspondence, and Local Self-Attention for high-resolution processing. Concatenates Gaussian points from all pairs for large scenes. Choose when generalizing to larger scenes or pose-free settings. Link: GGRt. Uses sparse splatting for efficiency. Choose when memory is constrained. Link: FineSplat. Focuses on sparse representation. Choose for very sparse input views. Link: SparSplat. Time Complexity: The source view computation (depth estimation and Gaussian parameter regression) dominates the runtime. Novel view rendering is extremely fast. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps, correlation volume, and depth maps for two source views. The correlation volume size is O(H \cdot W^2) for the finest scale. Measured Performance: On RTX 3090 GPU with 10 concurrent novel views, total time is 35ms. Source view computation time (T{src}) is approximately 14-27ms depending on implementation details (TensorRT vs standard). Novel view rendering time (T{novel}) is 0.8ms per view. Training time: ~15 hours on a single RTX 3090. Scaling: Rendering multiple novel views is concurrent and linear in the number of views (T = T{src} + n \times T{novel}). Strengths: Real-time performance, no per-subject optimization, handles sparse views better than implicit methods in occluded regions due to learned human priors. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of depth estimation; unstable depth in early training impacts Gaussian regression. Occlusion can cause depth ambiguity if human priors are insufficient. When to use: Real-time human novel view synthesis from sparse views. When not to use: Scenes with significant specular reflections (method assumes diffuse), or when per-subject optimization time is acceptable for higher quality. GPS-Gaussian was introduced by Zheng et al. in 2024. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting [12] and generalizable neural rendering [19, 57]. It addresses the limitations of per-subject optimization in 3D-GS and the slow rendering speed of implicit methods like ENeRF. The method leverages large-scale human scan data (Twindom, THuman2.0) to learn human priors. name: WildSplat
head: WildSplat: Feedforward Gaussian Splatting from Unposed In-the-Wild Images
body: WildSplat is a feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for appearance-conditioned novel-view synthesis from sparse, unposed, in-the-wild images. It explicitly decouples geometry from appearance to handle inconsistent photometric conditions, such as varying weather and lighting, which typically cause entangled representations in existing methods to fail. Unlike optimization-based methods that require precomputed poses and dense inputs, or other feedforward methods that assume photometric consistency, WildSplat reconstructs a single appearance-invariant 3D geometry and renders it with target appearance conditioned on a reference image in a single forward pass. Inputs and Outputs: The model takes a set of N context images \{Ii\} and a single reference image I{ref}. It outputs: 1. 3D Gaussian geometry attributes \mathcal{G}, consisting of positions \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times 3}, rotations q \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times 4}, scales s \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times 3}, and opacities \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^G, where G is the number of Gaussians. 2. Conditioned spherical harmonics coefficients \mathcal{C}{ref} \in \mathbb{R}^{G \times 3 \times (k+1)} of degree k, conditioned on I{ref}. 3. Camera poses \{pi\} for the context views. Data Structures: Patch Tokens: Ti^{(0)} = E{geo}(Ii) \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times D}, where P is the number of patches and D is the feature dimension. Camera Tokens: Learnable tokens Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{5 \times D} concatenated with patch tokens. Content Features: Aggregated multi-scale representations \mathbf{F}{content} extracted from the geometry branch, serving as the geometric scaffold. Reference Tokens: T{ref} \in \mathbb{R}^{Pa \times D}, local dense appearance tokens from the reference image, where Pa is the number of reference patches. Overlap/Scale Matrices: S (overlap ratio) and R (scale/depth ratio) derived from SfM points for view sampling. Parameters: Loss weights: \lambda1 = 10 (pose), \lambda2 = 1.0 (MSE), \lambda3 = 0.05 (SSIM), \lambda4 = 0.05 (LPIPS). View sampling thresholds: \taus (overlap), \taur (scale), \taun (neighbor count). Number of sampled target views for training: M. Number of neighbors to sample per step: K. Steps: 1. Geometry Branch (Pose and Geometry Prediction): Process each context image Ii independently through a DINOv2-based geometry encoder E{geo} to obtain initial patch tokens Ti^{(0)}. Concatenate learnable camera tokens Ci with Ti^{(0)}. Refine tokens through L alternating attention blocks to produce refined patch tokens Ti^{(k)} and camera tokens Ci^{(k)} for each layer k. Extract and aggregate multi-scale representations from a subset of transformer layers \mathcal{K} = \{l1, \dots, lK\} to form the content features \mathbf{F}{content}. Predict camera poses \{pi\} and Gaussian geometry \mathcal{G} (\mu, q, s, \alpha) from the refined tokens. 2. Appearance Branch (Conditioned Appearance Prediction): Extract reference appearance tokens T{ref} from I{ref} using an appearance encoder. Global Pre-modulation: To prevent original photometric properties from interfering, use the global descriptor T{[CLS]} from the content features. Decode T{[CLS]} via an AdaLN-Zero layer into scale \gamma, shift \beta, and gating \eta. Modulate the content features \mathbf{F}{content} (treated as queries Q) using the reference tokens T{ref} (keys K, values V) in a cross-attention mechanism, pre-modulated by \gamma, \beta, \eta. Output conditioned spherical harmonics coefficients \mathcal{C}{ref}. 3. Conditioned Rasterization: Render novel views \{\hat{I}i\} using tile-based differentiable rasterization \mathcal{R} of 3D Gaussian Splatting: \{\hat{I}i\} = \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}, \mathcal{C}{ref}, \{pi\}) Here, \mathcal{G} provides the geometry, \mathcal{C}{ref} provides the appearance, and \{pi\} provides the camera poses. 4. Geometry-guided View Sampling (Training Input Selection): Construct an overlap matrix S and scale matrix R using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Filter valid view pairs where S \geq \taus and R \geq \taur. Identify valid starting rows C where the sum of valid columns exceeds \taun. Initialize a queue with a uniform sample c from C and an index set I = \{c\}. Iteratively pop u from the queue, sample up to K neighbors from valid unvisited views, push them to the queue, and add to I until N views are selected. 5. Joint Multi-Reference Supervision: Randomly sample M images \{Im\} from the batch as target references. Extract conditioned appearance \{\mathcal{C}{ref,m}\} for each Im. Render images \{\hat{I}m\} conditioned on their respective appearance. Apply color jittering to input images and random cropping to references prior to feature extraction to prevent appearance leakage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class WildSplat: def init(self, numgaussians, shdegree, numlayers, featuredim): self.numgaussians = numgaussians self.shdegree = shdegree self.numlayers = numlayers self.featuredim = featuredim # Geometry Encoder (DINOv2-based) self.geoencoder = DINOv2Encoder() # Learnable Camera Tokens self.cameratokens = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(5, featuredim)) # Transformer Blocks for refinement self.transformerblocks = nn.ModuleList([ TransformerBlock() for in range(numlayers) ]) # Appearance Encoder self.appearanceencoder = AppearanceEncoder() # AdaLN-Zero for pre-modulation self.adalnzero = AdaLNZero(featuredim) # Cross-Attention for appearance injection self.crossattn = CrossAttention(featuredim) # Heads for geometry prediction self.geohead = GeometryHead(numgaussians) # Heads for SH coefficients prediction self.shhead = SHHead(numgaussians, shdegree) def forward(self, contextimages, referenceimage): """ contextimages: List of N images [B, 3, H, W] referenceimage: Image [B, 3, H, W] """ N = len(contextimages) # 1. Geometry Branch # Encode context images patchtokenslist = [] for i in range(N): # Egeo(Ii) -> [B, P, D] tokens = self.geoencoder(contextimages[i]) patchtokenslist.append(tokens) # Concatenate camera tokens and refine # Ci shape: [B, 5, D] cameratokensexpanded = self.cameratokens.unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1, -1, -1) refinedtokenslist = [] for i in range(N): # Concatenate [B, P, D] and [B, 5, D] along patch dim combined = torch.cat([patchtokenslist[i], cameratokensexpanded[i]], dim=1) refined = combined for block in self.transformerblocks: refined = block(refined) refinedtokenslist.append(refined) # Extract content features from specific layers (aggregation logic omitted for brevity) # Fcontent shape: [B, Pcontent, D] contentfeatures = self.aggregatecontentfeatures(refinedtokenslist) # Predict Geometry and Poses # geohead takes content features or refined tokens geometry = self.geohead(contentfeatures) # Returns mu, q, s, alpha poses = self.extractposes(refinedtokenslist) # Returns pi # 2. Appearance Branch # Encode reference image # Tref shape: [B, Pa, D] reftokens = self.appearanceencoder(referenceimage) # Global Pre-modulation # Get CLS token from content features (or global pool) clstoken = contentfeatures[:, 0,:] # Assuming first token is CLS # AdaLN-Zero outputs gamma, beta, eta gamma, beta, eta = self.adalnzero(clstoken) # Modulate content features # Ttilde = gamma Fcontent + beta (simplified AdaLN) # Note: Source says "modulate the appearance information within the content feature" # using gamma, beta, eta. Usually AdaLN applies to the query/key/value or the feature itself. # Assuming modulation of content features (Queries) before attention. modulatedcontent = gamma.unsqueeze(1) contentfeatures + beta.unsqueeze(1) # Cross-Attention # Q = modulatedcontent, K = V = reftokens # Output shape: [B, Pcontent, D] attendedfeatures = self.crossattn(modulatedcontent, reftokens, reftokens) # Predict Conditioned SH Coefficients cref = self.shhead(attendedfeatures) # Returns Cref # 3. Rasterization # Render using 3DGS rasterizer # R(G, Cref, {pi}) renderedimages = rasterize3dgs(geometry, cref, poses) return renderedimages, geometry, cref, poses def computeloss(self, renderedimages, gtimages, poses, gtposes=None): # Photometric Loss lmse = F.mseloss(renderedimages, gtimages) lssim = ssimloss(renderedimages, gtimages) llpips = lpipsloss(renderedimages, gtimages) lrgb = 1.0 lmse + 0.05 lssim + 0.05 llpips # Pose Loss (Distillation loss from AnySplat) if gtposes is not None: lpose = posedistillationloss(poses, gtposes) else: lpose = torch.tensor(0.0) totalloss = lrgb + 10.0 lpose return totalloss def geometryguidedviewsampling(self, sfmpoints, numviews, kneighbors, taus, taur, taun): """ Selects N views based on overlap and scale consistency using SfM points. """ # Construct overlap matrix S and scale matrix R # S[i, j] = ratio of shared 3D points between view i and j # R[i, j] = minimum depth ratio between view i and j S = computeoverlapmatrix(sfmpoints) R = computescalematrix(sfmpoints) # Filter valid pairs validmask = (S >= taus) & (R >= taur) # Find valid starting rows colsums = validmask.sum(dim=1) validstarts = torch.where(colsums > taun)[0] if len(validstarts) == 0: # Fallback or error handling return torch.arange(numviews) # Initialize queue and index set startidx = validstarts[torch.randint(len(validstarts), (1,))] queue = [startidx] selectedindices = {startidx} while len(selectedindices) < numviews and queue: u = queue.pop(0) # Sample up to K neighbors from valid unvisited views candidates = torch.where(validmask[u] & (~torch.tensor(list(selectedindices))))[0] if len(candidates) > 0: numtosample = min(kneighbors, len(candidates)) sampled = candidates[torch.randperm(len(candidates))[:numtosample]] for v in sampled: queue.append(v.item()) selectedindices.add(v.item()) return list(selectedindices) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Varying Focal Lengths: Standard sampling relying on camera extrinsics fails on in-the-wild datasets where minor pose shifts alter captured content due to varying focal lengths. Mitigated by overlap-based sampling using SfM points. Photometric Interference: Content features from the geometry branch retain original photometric properties, potentially interfering with target appearance conditioning. Mitigated by global pre-modulation using AdaLN-Zero to shift features into the target appearance domain. Appearance Leakage: Without proper regularization, the geometry might adapt to the reference appearance. Mitigated by joint multi-reference training and color jittering/random cropping. Time Complexity: Single forward pass for reconstruction and rendering, significantly faster than optimization-based methods (NeRF-W, GS-W) which require per-scene optimization. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians G and the feature dimensions of the transformer backbone. Not explicitly given in the sources. Measured Performance: On MegaScenes with 12 views: PSNR 19.20, SSIM 0.683, LPIPS 0.210. On Phototourism with 12 views: PSNR 21.47, SSIM 0.788, LPIPS 0.137. Scaling: Works with sparse inputs (4, 8, 12 views). Performance improves with more views but remains efficient compared to dense-input methods. Strengths: Handles unposed, in-the-wild images; decouples geometry and appearance; fast feedforward inference; robust to photometric variations. Limitations: Requires SfM points for view sampling during training (though not necessarily for inference if poses are predicted); performance may degrade if overlap is insufficient. WildSplat was introduced by X. Zhang et al. in 2024 as the first feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework capable of appearance-conditioned novel-view synthesis for unposed in-the-wild images. It addresses the limitations of previous feedforward methods (pixelSplat, MVSplat) that assume photometric consistency and optimization-based methods that require precomputed poses. The method builds on VGGT-like architectures for geometry estimation and leverages DINOv2 for feature extraction. name: StereoGaussians
body: StereoGaussians is a feed-forward method that predicts a metric 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation from a single calibrated stereo pair, enabling nearby-view extrapolation without per-scene optimization. It differs from its siblings by explicitly transferring frozen stereo features into Gaussian attribute prediction and using a two-layer Gaussian structure with an expanded image canvas to handle disoccluded and outside-field-of-view content. Unlike methods that synthesize images directly (e.g., LVSM) or refine inverse depth through a composer (e.g., SHARP), StereoGaussians fixes the front-layer stereo depth and bounds image-plane offsets to provide a structural prior for geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A calibrated rectified stereo pair (IL, IR), camera intrinsics K (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy), and baseline B. Outputs: A set of N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{(xi, si, qi, \alphai, ci)\} in the left-camera frame, where xi is position, si is scale, qi is rotation (quaternion), \alphai is opacity, and ci is color (Spherical Harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: The method predicts two layers of Gaussians (front and back) on an expanded canvas. Front Layer: Anchored to the stereo-derived depth. Back Layer: Anchored to a local maximum depth in a neighborhood plus a learned offset. Gaussian Attributes: Predicted as residuals relative to a base defined by geometry and reference color. Scale: Isotropic base scale s{0,\ell} followed by multiplicative updates. Rotation: Additive quaternion updates. Opacity: Updates in logit space. Color: Degree-2 Spherical Harmonic (SH) residuals around a reference-image DC base. Numbered Steps: 1. Stereo Feature Extraction: Pass the stereo pair (IL, IR) through a frozen pretrained stereo encoder (e.g., FoundationStereo) to obtain: Left-reference disparity map d. Aligned multiscale features \{Fs\}. 2. Metric Depth Calculation: Compute metric depth z(p) for each pixel p=(u,v) using the horizontal focal length fx and baseline B: z(p) = \text{clip}\left( \frac{fx B}{d(p)}, z{\min}, z{\max} \right) where z{\min}, z{\max} are clipping bounds. 3. Descriptor Generation: Construct a dense full-resolution descriptor \Phi by concatenating features at each scale s with resized reference RGB and depth: \Phi = D \left[ \{ Fs, \downarrows IL, \downarrows z \}s \right] \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} where D is a DPT-style decoder, [\cdot, \cdot] denotes channel concatenation, and \downarrows resizes inputs to feature scale s (e.g., s=4 implies H/4 \times W/4 resolution). Implementation Detail: At each scale, concatenate encoder features with resized RGB (bilinear) and depth (nearest-neighbor). Project to 128 channels via 1\times1 convolution, Group Normalization, and GELU. Use residual convolution units and coarse-to-fine fusion to yield the 128-channel descriptor \Phi at original resolution. 4. Canvas Extension (Extrapolation-Aware Prediction): Extend the reference RGB IL, processed depth z, and descriptor \Phi by edge-replication padding P on each side to size (H + 2P) \times (W + 2P). Denote extended inputs as \tilde{I}L, \tilde{z}, \tilde{\Phi}. Update canvas intrinsics: Focal lengths remain unchanged. Principal point shifts to \tilde{c}x = cx + P, \tilde{c}y = cy + P. 5. Gaussian Attribute Prediction: Pass extended inputs through a convolutional predictor H: (\theta{\text{front}}, \theta{\text{back}}, \Delta z) = H([\tilde{I}L, \tilde{z}, \tilde{\Phi}]) Regressor: Two 3\times3 convolutions with intermediate GELU map inputs to a 128-channel tensor h. Output Branches: Each branch processes [h, \tilde{I}L, \tilde{\Phi}] using a 3\times3 convolution, Group Normalization, GELU, and a final 3\times3 convolution. Front/Back Branches: Output 37 channels each: opacity (1), image-plane offset (2), scale (3), quaternion (4), degree-2 SH coefficients (27). Back-Depth Branch: Outputs a scalar \Delta z. 6. Front Layer Geometry: Depth: z{\text{front}} = \tilde{z}. Image-Plane Offsets: Compute (\delta{u,\ell}, \delta{v,\ell}) = \sigma(o\ell) - 1/2, where o\ell is the 2-channel offset output for layer \ell. Bound offsets to half a canvas pixel per axis. Center: Calculate center x{\text{front}}(p) using canvas intrinsics \tilde{K}: x{\text{front}}(p) = z{\text{front}}(p) \tilde{K}^{-1} [u + \delta{u,\text{front}}, v + \delta{v,\text{front}}, 1]^\top Base Scale: Isotropic base scale s{0,\text{front}} = \kappa z{\text{front}} / (fx fy). 7. Back Layer Geometry: Depth: Compute local maximum depth in a 9\times9 neighborhood \mathcal{N}9(p) plus a learned positive offset: z{\text{back}}(p) = \max{q \in \mathcal{N}9(p)} \tilde{z}(q) + \text{softplus}(\Delta z(p)) Center: Calculate center x{\text{back}}(p) using z{\text{back}} and its own image-plane offsets (bounded similarly to front). Base Scale: s{0,\text{back}} = \kappa z{\text{back}} / (fx fy). 8. Attribute Composition: Scale: Apply bounded multiplicative updates to s{0,\ell}. Rotation: Apply additive quaternion updates to a base rotation. Opacity: Apply updates in logit space to base opacity. Color: Add degree-2 SH residuals to a reference-image DC color base. 9. Rendering and Training: Concatenate front and back layers. Render target views using differentiable Gaussian rasterization. No Edge Mask: The back layer is not restricted by an edge mask; learned attributes and visibility determine contributions. Loss: Minimize L = \text{MSE}(IT, \hat{I}T) + 0.05 \text{LPIPS}{\text{VGG}}(IT, \hat{I}T), where IT is the target image and \hat{I}T is the rendered prediction. Training: Train the predictor H and decoder D using AdamW. Keep the stereo encoder frozen. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class StereoGaussians: def init(self, encoder, predictor, decoder, padding=16): self.encoder = encoder # Frozen self.predictor = predictor # Trainable self.decoder = decoder # Trainable self.padding = padding self.kappa = 1.0 # Constant for base scale def forward(self, IL, IR, K, B, zmin=0.1, zmax=100.0): # 1. Stereo Feature Extraction # Returns disparity d, multiscale features {Fs} d, Fs = self.encoder(IL, IR) # 2. Metric Depth Calculation fx = K[0, 0] # Clip depth to valid range z = torch.clamp((fx B) / d, zmin, zmax) # 3. Descriptor Generation # Resize RGB and Depth for each scale s # Concatenate Fs, downsampled IL, downsampled z # Pass through DPT-style decoder D # D projects to 128 channels, uses GN, GELU, residual units Phi = self.decoder(Fs, IL, z) # 4. Canvas Extension P = self.padding ILext = F.pad(IL, (P, P, P, P), mode='replicate') zext = F.pad(z, (P, P, P, P), mode='replicate') Phiext = F.pad(Phi, (P, P, P, P), mode='replicate') # Update intrinsics for extended canvas # cxnew = cx + P, cynew = cy + P # fx, fy remain unchanged Kext = K.clone() Kext[0, 2] += P Kext[1, 2] += P # 5. Gaussian Attribute Prediction # Predictor H takes [ILext, zext, Phiext] thetafront, thetaback, deltaz = self.predictor(ILext, zext, Phiext) # thetafront/back shape: [B, 37, H, W] # deltaz shape: [B, 1, H, W] # 6. Front Layer Geometry zfront = zext # Extract offsets from thetafront # Channels: opacity(1), offset(2), scale(3), quat(4), SH(27) offsetfront = thetafront[:, 1:3,:,:] # 2 channels # Sigmoid to map to [0,1], then shift to [-0.5, 0.5] deltauvfront = torch.sigmoid(offsetfront) - 0.5 # Bound to half canvas pixel (implementation specific bound) # deltauvfront = torch.clamp(deltauvfront, -0.5, 0.5) # Compute centers using extended intrinsics # x = z Kinv [u + du, v + dv, 1] # This requires meshgrid of u, v coordinates centersfront = self.computecenters(zfront, Kext, deltauvfront) # Base scale s0front = self.kappa zfront / (fx K[1, 1]) # fy = K[1,1] # 7. Back Layer Geometry # Local max in 9x9 neighborhood # Note: F.maxpool2d with kernel 9x9, stride 1, padding 4 zmaxpool = F.maxpool2d(zext, kernelsize=9, stride=1, padding=4) # Softplus for positive offset deltazsp = F.softplus(deltaz) zback = zmaxpool + deltazsp # Extract offsets from thetaback offsetback = thetaback[:, 1:3,:,:] deltauvback = torch.sigmoid(offsetback) - 0.5 # deltauvback = torch.clamp(deltauvback, -0.5, 0.5) centersback = self.computecenters(zback, Kext, deltauvback) s0back = self.kappa zback / (fx K[1, 1]) # 8. Attribute Composition # Extract remaining attributes from thetafront/back # Scale updates, quat updates, opacity logits, SH residuals # Apply composition rules (multiplicative scale, additive quat, logit opacity, SH residual) # Base color is DC from IL # Return full Gaussian set gaussians = self.composegaussians( centersfront, s0front, thetafront[:, 3:,:,:], # scale, quat, SH centersback, s0back, thetaback[:, 3:,:,:], # scale, quat, SH thetafront[:, 0,:,:], # opacity front thetaback[:, 0,:,:], # opacity back ILext # For DC color base) return gaussians def computecenters(self, z, Kinv, deltauv): # z: [B, 1, H, W] # deltauv: [B, 2, H, W] # Kinv: [3, 3] # Returns: [B, 3, H, W] B,, H, W = z.shape # Create meshgrid for u, v u = torch.arange(W, device=z.device).float().view(1, 1, 1, W) v = torch.arange(H, device=z.device).float().view(1, 1, H, 1) # Add offsets ushifted = u + deltauv[:, 0,:,:] vshifted = v + deltauv[:, 1,:,:] # Homogeneous coordinates coords = torch.stack([ushifted, vshifted, torch.oneslike(u)], dim=1) # [B, 3, H, W] # Apply Kinv # Kinv is [3,3], coords is [B, 3, H, W] # Result is [B, 3, H, W] xyz = torch.matmul(Kinv.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1), coords.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # Multiply by depth xyz = xyz z return xyz def composegaussians(self,...): # Placeholder for attribute composition logic # Returns list of Gaussian objects or tensors pass Parameters: Padding P: 16 pixels (default). Learning Rate: 4 \times 10^{-4} for AdamW. Weight Decay: 0.01. Momentum (\beta1, \beta2): (0.9, 0.999). Scheduler: OneCycleLR with 2,700 warm-up steps (9% of training), initial LR division factor 25, final LR division factor 100. Training Steps: 30,000. Batch Size: 32. Decoder Channels: 128. Output Channels per Branch: 37 (1 opacity, 2 offset, 3 scale, 4 quaternion, 27 SH). Input Normalization: ImageNet normalization after rescaling RGB from [0, 1] to [0, 255]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Padding: Without padding, empty target-border bands appear in rendered views; padding fills these newly exposed regions. Fixed Front-Layer Depth: Limits stereo-error correction. Teacher Artifacts: Can persist despite reconstruction-quality filtering. Descriptor Removal: Without the DPT descriptor, tabletop distortions and foreground-boundary artifacts occur. Time Complexity: Inference is feed-forward, dependent on the encoder and predictor network depth. Training requires differentiable rendering, which is computationally intensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two layers of Gaussians and intermediate features for the decoder and predictor. Performance: On StereoNVS: 21.261 PSNR, 0.9447 SSIM, 0.0818 LPIPS. On ReplicaGS: 30.266 PSNR, 0.9447 SSIM, 0.0818 LPIPS. Scaling: Uses 16-pixel padding by default. 64-pixel padding improves StereoNVS PSNR/LPIPS but lowers ReplicaGS PSNR. Strengths: Handles disoccluded content (back layer) and outside-field-of-view content (padding). Generalizes to unseen scenes. Limitations: Fixed front-layer depth limits error correction. Performance degrades without padding or descriptor. Evaluation focuses on nearby views. StereoGaussians was introduced in 2026 (preprint) by authors associated with the SceneSplat-Stereo dataset. It builds on the principles of feed-forward 3DGS and leverages frozen stereo encoders to transfer geometric priors to Gaussian attribute prediction. It is used on StereoNVS and ReplicaGS datasets. StereoGaussians: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting from Stereo Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38592, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Latent Space Representation
head: Latent Scene Representation, Latent Gaussian Representation
body: Latent Space Representation methods map input images to a compact, structured latent code (tokens, features, or distributions) which is subsequently decoded into explicit 3D Gaussian primitives, enabling generalizable reconstruction without per-scene optimization. Unlike sibling methods that predict Gaussians directly from pixel-wise features or cost volumes, this family explicitly models the scene as a set of learnable latent entities (e.g., tokens or entropy-coded features) to enforce global consistency, reduce representation bloat, or handle ambiguity. All methods in this family share the core objective of mapping input image features to a set of 3D Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, c\} without per-scene gradient descent. 1. Input Representation: Inputs are typically one or more RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Some methods require known camera poses P, while others (e.g., Splatt3R, ZeroGS) predict poses or operate on uncalibrated inputs. 2. Feature Encoding: A shared encoder (e.g., Vision Transformer, CNN) extracts multi-scale features from the input images. Cross-attention or cost volumes are often used to aggregate multi-view information. 3. Primitive Prediction: A decoder head predicts Gaussian attributes. These attributes are usually: Mean (\mu): 3D position. Covariance (\Sigma): Defined by scale s and rotation r (quaternion or 6D). Opacity (\alpha): Scalar. Color (c): Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients or constant RGB. 4. Differentiable Rendering: The predicted Gaussians are rendered into target views using differentiable rasterization to compute reconstruction losses (e.g., L1, SSIM, LPIPS) for training the network. 5. Generalization: The network is trained on a large dataset of scenes to learn priors about geometry and appearance, allowing inference on unseen scenes. GlobalSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that aligns multi-view inputs into a fixed set of global latent scene tokens before decoding explicit 3D geometry, preventing representation bloat and ensuring global consistency [16571-globalsplat.md]. Unlike sibling methods such as CodecSplat and latentSplat which may rely on dense view-aligned primitives or different grid structures, GlobalSplat aggregates multi-view inputs into a fixed number of latent tokens (2048) regardless of the number of input views, then decodes these tokens into a sparse, globally consistent set of Gaussians (16K) [16571-globalsplat.md]. This approach achieves a superior quality-efficiency trade-off compared to C3G, which uses full self-attention and single-Gaussian decoding, by employing an iterative, disentangled dual-branch architecture and a coarse-to-fine capacity curriculum [16571-globalsplat.md]. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize M=2048 latent tokens lj^{(0)} and register tokens. 2. Dual-Branch Encoder: Repeat for B=4 blocks j=0 \dots B-1: Project latent tokens into geometry and appearance streams, apply cross-attention with input patches, apply self-attention blocks, and fuse streams via MLP. 3. Decoder Candidate Prediction: For each latent token p, predict Ks=16 candidates for means, log-scales, 6D rotations, opacity logits, importance scores, and SH coefficients. 4. Coarse-to-Fine Merging: Partition 16 candidates into G=8 groups. Compute softmax weights using importance scores and temperature \tau. Merge attributes via weighted sum. 5. Rendering: Project Gaussians to 2D and accumulate color using standard alpha blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GlobalSplat: def init(self, numtokens=2048, tokendim=512, numcandidates=16, numencoderblocks=4, numselfattnlayers=2): self.M = numtokens self.d = tokendim self.K = numcandidates self.B = numencoderblocks self.L = numselfattnlayers self.Gfinal = 8 self.temperature = 1.0 self.latenttokens = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.M, self.d)) self.registertokens = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.M, self.d)) self.projgeo = nn.Linear(self.d, self.d) self.projapp = nn.Linear(self.d, self.d) self.crossattngeo = nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8) self.crossattnapp = nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8) self.selfattngeo = nn.ModuleList([nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8) for in range(self.L)]) self.selfattnapp = nn.ModuleList([nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8) for in range(self.L)]) self.mixermlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(self.d 2, self.d), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(self.d, self.d)) self.decgeo = nn.Linear(self.d, self.K 14) self.decapp = nn.Linear(self.d, self.K 48) self.Wray = nn.Linear(6, 256) def normalizescene(self, poses, intrinsics): centers = poses[:,:3, 3] oavg = centers.mean(dim=0) views = poses[:,:3, 2] viewavg = views.mean(dim=0) viewavg = viewavg / viewavg.norm() xaxis = torch.cross(viewavg, torch.tensor([0, 0, 1], device=views.device)) if xaxis.norm() < 1e-6: xaxis = torch.tensor([1, 0, 0], device=views.device) xaxis = xaxis / xaxis.norm() yaxis = torch.cross(viewavg, xaxis) Tavginv = torch.eye(4, device=poses.device) Tavginv[:3,:3] = torch.stack([xaxis, yaxis, viewavg], dim=1) Tavginv[:3, 3] = -Tavginv[:3,:3] @ oavg transformedcenters = (Tavginv[:3,:3] @ centers.T).T + Tavginv[:3, 3] maxdist = 0 for i in range(len(centers)): for j in range(i + 1, len(centers)): dist = (transformedcenters[i] - transformedcenters[j]).norm() if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist scale = maxdist if maxdist > 0 else 1.0 scaledcenters = transformedcenters / scale return scaledcenters, scale def extractfeatures(self, images, poses, intrinsics): C,, H, W = images.shape patchsize = 8 numpatches = (H // patchsize) (W // patchsize) # Not given in the sources. urgb = torch.randn(C, numpatches, 512) # Not given in the sources. r = torch.randn(C, numpatches, 6) rflat = r.view(-1, 6) rmapped = self.Wray(rflat).view(C, numpatches, 256) # Not given in the sources. e = torch.randn(C, 256) ucam = rmapped + e.unsqueeze(1) u = torch.cat([ucam, urgb], dim=-1) return u def encode(self, u): x = u.permute(1, 0, 2) l = self.latenttokens.unsqueeze(1) for j in range(self.B): fgeo = self.projgeo(l).permute(1, 0, 2) fapp = self.projapp(l).permute(1, 0, 2) fgeocross, = self.crossattngeo(fgeo, x, x) fappcross, = self.crossattnapp(fapp, x, x) for lidx in range(self.L): fgeo, = self.selfattngeolidx fapp, = self.selfattnapplidx fused = torch.cat([fgeo, fapp], dim=-1) l = self.mixermlp(fused).permute(1, 0, 2) return l.squeeze(1) def decode(self, l): geoout = self.decgeo(l).view(-1, self.K, 14) appout = self.decapp(l).view(-1, self.K, 48) X = geoout[:,:,:3] S = geoout[:,:, 3:6] R = geoout[:,:, 6:12] O = geoout[:,:, 12:13] lgate = geoout[:,:, 13:14] return X, S, R, O, lgate, appout def mergecandidates(self, X, S, R, O, lgate, C, stages=3): G = 2 stages bs = self.K // G mergedX, mergedS, mergedR, mergedO, mergedC = [], [], [], [], [] for p in range(X.shape[0]): for g in range(G): startidx, endidx = g bs, (g + 1) bs Xg, Sg, Rg, Og, Cg = X[p, startidx:endidx], S[p, startidx:endidx], R[p, startidx:endidx], O[p, startidx:endidx], C[p, startidx:endidx] lg = lgate[p, startidx:endidx] weights = F.softmax(lgate / self.temperature, dim=0).squeeze(-1) mergedX.append(torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) Xg, dim=0)) mergedS.append(torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) Sg, dim=0)) mergedR.append(torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) Rg, dim=0)) mergedO.append(torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) Og, dim=0)) mergedC.append(torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) Cg, dim=0)) return torch.stack(mergedX), torch.stack(mergedS), torch.stack(mergedR), torch.stack(mergedO), torch.stack(mergedC) def forward(self, images, poses, intrinsics): centers, scale = self.normalizescene(poses, intrinsics) u = self.extractfeatures(images, poses, intrinsics) l = self.encode(u) X, S, R, O, lgate, C = self.decode(l) return self.mergecandidates(X, S, R, O, lgate, C, stages=3) CodecSplat is a compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) that encodes an intermediate 2D Gaussian-generation feature into an entropy-coded scene bitstream, avoiding the inefficient compression of irregular 3D Gaussian primitives [18143-codecsplat.md]. Unlike existing 3DGS compression methods that compress Gaussian primitives after a structured-to-irregular transformation, CodecSplat places the coding bottleneck before 2D-to-3D Gaussian construction, allowing compression to exploit the structured intermediate feature representation [18143-codecsplat.md]. Algorithm: 1. Multi-view Feature Extraction: Extract multi-view features F{mv}, encoder-side depth D{enc}, and depth matching-probability features P{depth} via a multi-view encoder backbone. 2. Gaussian-Generation Feature Construction: Convert cues into a dense Gaussian-generation feature Fg via a feature head network. 3. Latent Encoding: Transform Fg into latents via analysis transform, quantize with rate control \lambda, entropy-code, and pack with compressed camera parameters into bitstream B. 4. Latent Decoding: Entropy-decode B, reconstruct feature map via synthesis transform, and recover camera metadata. 5. Gaussian Reconstruction: Predict depth, refine features, predict Gaussian parameters, and map to 3D primitives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: GlobalSplat
body: GlobalSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that aligns multi-view inputs into a fixed set of global latent scene tokens before decoding explicit 3D geometry, preventing representation bloat and ensuring global consistency. Unlike sibling methods such as CodecSplat and latentSplat which may rely on dense view-aligned primitives or different grid structures, GlobalSplat aggregates multi-view inputs into a fixed number of latent tokens (2048) regardless of the number of input views, then decodes these tokens into a sparse, globally consistent set of Gaussians (16K). This approach achieves a superior quality-efficiency trade-off compared to C3G, which uses full self-attention and single-Gaussian decoding, by employing an iterative, disentangled dual-branch architecture and a coarse-to-fine capacity curriculum. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of C RGB images I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} with known camera poses Ti (rotation Ri, translation ti) and intrinsics Ki. Output: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mun, \Sigman, \alphan, cn\}{n=1}^N, where \mun is the mean, \Sigman is the covariance (parameterized by scale sn and rotation rn), \alphan is the opacity, and cn are Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Data Structures: 1. Latent Tokens: A fixed set of M=2048 learnable latent tokens lj \in \mathbb{R}^d with d=512. 2. Register Tokens: Learnable register tokens used to capture global context (specific dimension not given, assumed same as latent tokens or handled internally). 3. Gaussian Candidates: For each latent token p, the decoder predicts Ks=16 candidates. The data layout for token p is: \mathbf{X}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 3}: Candidate means. \mathbf{S}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 3}: Candidate log-scales. \mathbf{R}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 6}: Candidate 6D rotations. \mathbf{O}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 1}: Candidate opacity logits. \boldsymbol{\ell}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times 1}: Candidate importance scores (gate logits). \mathbf{C}p \in \mathbb{R}^{16 \times (3 D{\text{SH}})}: Candidate SH coefficients, where D{\text{SH}}=16 for SH degree 3. Preprocessing: 1. Scene Normalization: Compute the canonical frame origin: \bar{o} = \frac{1}{C} \sum{i=1}^C oi, where oi is the camera center. Compute axes by averaging camera viewing directions and re-orthonormalizing. Let T{\text{avg}} be the resulting average pose. Transform all cameras: \hat{T}i = T{\text{avg}}^{-1} Ti. Compute scene scale: s = \max{a,b} \|\hat{o}a - \hat{o}b\|2. Scale camera translations: \tilde{o}i = \frac{\hat{o}i}{s}. 2. Image Preprocessing: Resize image height to 256, preserving aspect ratio. Round width to a multiple of patch size 8. Update intrinsics accordingly. Apply centered square crop. Final resize to 256 \times 256. 3. Feature Extraction: Extract RGB patch features u{i,p}^{\text{rgb}} from input view i and patch p. Compute dense Plücker-ray features r{i,p} and patchify them. Map rays: \hat{r}{i,p} = W{\text{ray}} r{i,p}. Compute per-view camera code ei using Fourier positional encoding for camera center and MLP for intrinsics. Combine: u{i,p}^{\text{cam}} = \hat{r}{i,p} + ei. Form input context: u{i,p} = [u{i,p}^{\text{cam}}; u{i,p}^{\text{rgb}}]. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize M=2048 latent tokens lj^{(0)} and register tokens. 2. Dual-Branch Encoder: Repeat for B=4 blocks j=0 \dots B-1: Project latent tokens into geometry and appearance streams: f{\text{geo}}^{(j)} = \text{Proj}{\text{geo}}(l^{(j)}), f{\text{app}}^{(j)} = \text{Proj}{\text{app}}(l^{(j)}). For each branch i \in \{\text{geo}, \text{app}\}: Apply Cross-Attention between input patches x (context u) and stream features: f{i}^{\text{cross}} = \text{CrossAtt}i(x, f{i}^{(j)}). Apply L=2 Self-Attention blocks: f{i}^{(j+1)} = \text{SelfAtt}i(\dots \text{SelfAtt}i(f{i}^{\text{cross}}) \dots). Fuse streams: l^{(j+1)} = \text{MLP}(\text{Concat}(f{\text{geo}}^{(j+1)}, f{\text{app}}^{(j+1)})). 3. Decoder Candidate Prediction: For each latent token p, predict the 16 candidates \mathbf{X}p, \mathbf{S}p, \mathbf{R}p, \mathbf{O}p, \boldsymbol{\ell}p, \mathbf{C}p using the dual-branch decoder heads. 4. Coarse-to-Fine Merging (Inference/Training): Determine stage s. Final model uses s=3, so G = 2^3 = 8 groups per token. Partition 16 candidates into G groups of size bs = 16/G. For each group g and token p: Compute weights: w{p,g,i} = \frac{\exp(\ell{p,g,i}/\tau)}{\sum{k=1}^{bs} \exp(\ell{p,g,k}/\tau)}. Merge attributes: \bar{z}{p,g} = \sum{i=1}^{bs} w{p,g,i} z{p,g,i} for z \in \{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{O}, \mathbf{C}\}. The final set of Gaussians is the collection of all merged groups across all tokens. 5. Rendering: Project Gaussians to 2D. Accumulate color: C = \sum{i=1}^{M} ci \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j), where \alpha'i is the product of base opacity \alphai and projected 2D Gaussian density. Gaussian Parameterization Details: Means: Initialized with a fixed forward offset of 1.5. Scales: Predicted in log space as an offset from -2. Opacity: Predicted in logit space as an offset from -5. Rotations: Continuous 6D parameterization as residual offsets from a static rotation. Training Objectives: Rendering Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{ren}} = \|It - \hat{I}t\|2^2 + \lambda{\text{perc}}\mathcal{L}{\text{perc}}(It, \hat{I}t). Self-Supervised Consistency: \mathcal{L}{\text{con}} = \|O(\mathcal{I}a) - \text{sg}(O(\mathcal{I}b))\|2^2 + \|D(\mathcal{I}a) - \text{sg}(D(\mathcal{I}b))\|2^2, where O and D are rendered opacity and depth maps. Regularization: \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \lambda{\text{thr}}\mathcal{L}{\text{thr}} + \lambda{\text{fru}}\mathcal{L}{\text{fru}} (soft thresholding and frustum constraint). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GlobalSplat: def init(self, numtokens=2048, tokendim=512, numcandidates=16, numencoderblocks=4, numselfattnlayers=2): self.M = numtokens self.d = tokendim self.K = numcandidates self.B = numencoderblocks self.L = numselfattnlayers self.Gfinal = 8 # Stage 3 # Learnable parameters self.latenttokens = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.M, self.d)) self.registertokens = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.M, self.d)) # # Encoder components self.projgeo = nn.Linear(self.d, self.d) self.projapp = nn.Linear(self.d, self.d) self.crossattngeo = nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8, batchfirst=True) self.crossattnapp = nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8, batchfirst=True) self.selfattngeo = nn.ModuleList([nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8, batchfirst=True) for in range(self.L)]) self.selfattnapp = nn.ModuleList([nn.MultiheadAttention(self.d, numheads=8, batchfirst=True) for in range(self.L)]) self.mixermlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(self.d 2, self.d), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(self.d, self.d)) # Decoder components self.decgeo = nn.Linear(self.d, self.K (3 + 3 + 6 + 1 + 1)) # X, S, R, O, l self.decapp = nn.Linear(self.d, self.K (3 16)) # C (SH degree 3, 3 channels, 16 coeffs) # Ray projection self.Wray = nn.Linear(6, 256) # Assuming Plucker dim 6, output 256 # Temperature for merging self.temperature = 1.0 def normalizescene(self, poses, intrinsics): # poses: (C, 4, 4) or (C, 3, 4) # intrinsics: (C, 3, 3) centers = poses[:,:3, 3] oavg = centers.mean(dim=0) # Viewing directions (z-axis of rotation matrix) views = poses[:,:3, 2] viewavg = views.mean(dim=0) viewavg = viewavg / viewavg.norm() # Re-orthonormalize xaxis = torch.cross(viewavg, torch.tensor([0, 0, 1], device=views.device)) if xaxis.norm() < 1e-6: xaxis = torch.tensor([1, 0, 0], device=views.device) xaxis = xaxis / xaxis.norm() yaxis = torch.cross(viewavg, xaxis) # Construct Tavg inverse (approximate for simplicity in pseudocode) # In practice, Tavg is the pose of the average camera. # We transform all cameras to this frame. # Tavginv Ti # For pseudocode, we assume a function that returns transformed poses # and scale normalization. # Scale normalization maxdist = 0 for i in range(len(centers)): for j in range(i + 1, len(centers)): dist = (centers[i] - centers[j]).norm() if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist scale = maxdist if maxdist > 0 else 1.0 # Transform centers # Note: Full 4x4 transform application omitted for brevity, assuming helper exists # transformedcenters = applytransform(centers, Tavginv) # scaledcenters = transformedcenters / scale return centers, scale def extractfeatures(self, images, poses, intrinsics): # images: (C, 3, 256, 256) # Preprocessing is assumed done before this call C,, H, W = images.shape patchsize = 8 numpatches = (H // patchsize) (W // patchsize) # Extract RGB patches # Assuming a CNN/ViT encoder produces features of dim 512 # urgb: (C, numpatches, 512) urgb = self.visionencoder(images) # Compute Plucker rays and patchify # rip: (C, numpatches, 6) r = computepluckerrays(poses, intrinsics, H, W, patchsize) # Map rays rflat = r.view(-1, 6) rmapped = self.Wray(rflat).view(C, numpatches, 256) # Per-view camera code # ei: (C, 256) e = self.cameraencoder(poses, intrinsics) # Broadcast e to patches ucam = rmapped + e.unsqueeze(1) # Concatenate u = torch.cat([ucam, urgb], dim=-1) # (C, numpatches, 768) return u def encode(self, u): # u: (C, numpatches, inputdim) # Flatten patches for attention # x: (numpatches, C, inputdim) -> Transposed for MHA x = u.permute(1, 0, 2) l = self.latenttokens.unsqueeze(1) # (M, 1, d) for j in range(self.B): # Project fgeo = self.projgeo(l).permute(1, 0, 2) # (1, M, d) fapp = self.projapp(l).permute(1, 0, 2) # Cross Attention # Key/Value from x, Query from f fgeocross, = self.crossattngeo(fgeo, x, x) fappcross, = self.crossattnapp(fapp, x, x) # Self Attention for lidx in range(self.L): fgeo, = self.selfattngeolidx fapp, = self.selfattnapplidx # Fuse fused = torch.cat([fgeo, fapp], dim=-1) # (1, M, 2d) l = self.mixermlp(fused).permute(1, 0, 2) # (M, 1, d) return l.squeeze(1) # (M, d) def decode(self, l): # l: (M, d) geoout = self.decgeo(l) # (M, K (14)) appout = self.decapp(l) # (M, K 48) # Reshape geoout = geoout.view(-1, self.K, 14) appout = appout.view(-1, self.K, 48) # Split geo X = geoout[:,:,:3] S = geoout[:,:, 3:6] R = geoout[:,:, 6:12] O = geoout[:,:, 12:13] lgate = geoout[:,:, 13:14] return X, S, R, O, lgate, appout def mergecandidates(self, X, S, R, O, lgate, C, stages=3): G = 2 stages bs = self.K // G mergedX = [] mergedS = [] mergedR = [] mergedO = [] mergedC = [] for p in range(X.shape[0]): for g in range(G): startidx = g bs endidx = (g + 1) bs # Get candidates for this group Xg = X[p, startidx:endidx,:] # (bs, 3) Sg = S[p, startidx:endidx,:] Rg = R[p, startidx:endidx,:] Og = O[p, startidx:endidx,:] Cg = C[p, startidx:endidx,:] lg = lgate[p, startidx:endidx,:] # (bs, 1) # Compute weights weights = F.softmax(lg / self.temperature, dim=0) # (bs, 1) # Weighted sum w = weights.squeeze(-1) # (bs,) mX = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) Xg, dim=0) mS = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) Sg, dim=0) mR = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) Rg, dim=0) mO = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) Og, dim=0) mC = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) Cg, dim=0) mergedX.append(mX) mergedS.append(mS) mergedR.append(mR) mergedO.append(mO) mergedC.append(mC) return torch.stack(mergedX), torch.stack(mergedS), torch.stack(mergedR), torch.stack(mergedO), torch.stack(mergedC) def forward(self, images, poses, intrinsics): centers, scale = self.normalizescene(poses, intrinsics) u = self.extractfeatures(images, poses, intrinsics) l = self.encode(u) X, S, R, O, lgate, C = self.decode(l) # Merge Xm, Sm, Rm, Om, Cm = self.mergecandidates(X, S, R, O, lgate, C, stages=3) # Construct Gaussians # Note: Actual construction of Sigma from S and R, and SH evaluation, # is handled by the renderer. return Xm, Sm, Rm, Om, Cm Time Complexity: Inference is a single forward pass through the encoder-decoder network. On RealEstate10K with 24 input views, inference time is <78 ms. Memory Complexity: Peak GPU memory is 1.79 GB for 24 views on RealEstate10K. Disk size is ~4 MB for the 16K Gaussians. Performance: On RealEstate10K with 12 views, GlobalSplat16K achieves PSNR 28.57, SSIM 0.885, LPIPS 0.138. With 24 views, it achieves 28.5 PSNR. Strengths: Fixed number of Gaussians (16K) regardless of input view count prevents representation bloat. Fast inference. Low memory footprint. Global consistency via latent tokens. Limitations: Relies on a fixed capacity curriculum. Requires known camera poses for training (though preprocessing normalizes them). When to use: Not given in the sources. GlobalSplat was introduced by R. Itkin et al. in 2025. It addresses the limitation of current feed-forward 3DGS pipelines where primitives are formed in dense view-aligned spaces, leading to representation bloat and fragile global consistency as more views are added. It builds on the principles of Latent Space Representation by using a fixed set of latent tokens to encode multi-view information before decoding explicit geometry. It is evaluated on RealEstate10K and ACID datasets. GlobalSplat: Efficient Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Global Scene Tokens, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37595-710, fetched 2026-10-29

name: CodecSplat
head: Ultra-compact latent coding framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting
body: CodecSplat is a compression framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) that encodes an intermediate 2D Gaussian-generation feature into an entropy-coded scene bitstream, avoiding the inefficient compression of irregular 3D Gaussian primitives. Unlike existing 3DGS compression methods that compress Gaussian primitives after a structured-to-irregular transformation, CodecSplat places the coding bottleneck before 2D-to-3D Gaussian construction, allowing compression to exploit the structured intermediate feature representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N posed context views C = \{(Ii, Ki, Ti, ni, fi)\}{i=1}^N, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} is a context image, Ki and Ti denote camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and ni, fi are near and far bounds. Output: A self-contained scene bitstream B. Data Structures: Multi-view features (F{mv}): Image and cross-view matching features extracted by the backbone. Encoder-side depth (D{enc}): A tensor in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H \times W} representing depth predictions at the encoder side. Depth matching-probability features (P{depth}): Features containing depth matching probabilities. Gaussian-generation feature (Fg): A dense, regular tensor in \mathbb{R}^{N \times CF \times H \times W} specialized for Gaussian generation. Latent features: The compressed representation of Fg after analysis transform, quantization, and entropy coding. Parameters: Rate control parameter (\lambda): Used in the encoder and decoder to control the trade-off between bitstream size and reconstruction quality. Steps: 1. Multi-view Feature Extraction: The encoder performs multi-view matching and feature extraction on the context views C. This produces multi-view features F{mv}, encoder-side depth D{enc}, and depth matching-probability features P{depth} via (F{mv}, D{enc}, P{depth}) = \text{MVEnc}(C), where \text{MVEnc} denotes the multi-view encoder backbone. 2. Gaussian-Generation Feature Construction: The extracted cues are converted into a dense Gaussian-generation feature Fg via Fg = \text{FeatHead}(I{1:N}, F{mv}, P{depth}), where \text{FeatHead} is a feature head network. 3. Latent Encoding (Encoder Side): The feature Fg is transformed into a latent representation via an analysis transform. The latent representation is quantized using the rate control parameter \lambda. The quantized latents are entropy-coded. The encoded latent features and compressed context-view camera parameters are packed into the scene bitstream B. 4. Latent Decoding (Decoder Side): The scene bitstream B is entropy-decoded to recover the quantized latent representation. The latent representation is reconstructed into a feature map using a synthesis transform. The compressed context-view camera metadata is recovered. 5. Gaussian Reconstruction: The decoded feature is used for depth prediction, feature refinement, Gaussian parameter prediction (opacity, scale, rotation, color/SH), and 2D-to-3D mapping to produce the final 3D Gaussian primitives \hat{\mathcal{G}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def codecsplatencode(contextviews): # contextviews: List of tuples (I, K, T, n, f) for N views # Step 1: Multi-view feature extraction Fmv, Denc, Pdepth = MVEnc(contextviews) # Step 2: Construct Gaussian-generation feature Fg = FeatHead([v[0] for v in contextviews], Fmv, Pdepth) # Step 3: Latent encoding latent = analysistransform(Fg) # Standard analysis transform quantizedlatent = quantize(latent, rateparam=0.1) # Quantization with rate control lambda bitstreamlatents = entropyencode(quantizedlatent) # Standard entropy coding compressedcameras = compresscameras([v[1:] for v in contextviews]) # Compress camera parameters bitstream = pack(bitstreamlatents, compressedcameras) # Pack bitstream return bitstream def codecsplatdecode(bitstream): # Step 4: Latent decoding bitstreamlatents, compressedcameras = unpack(bitstream) quantizedlatent = entropydecode(bitstreamlatents) Fgdecoded = synthesistransform(quantizedlatent) cameras = decompresscameras(compressedcameras) # Step 5: Gaussian reconstruction depthpred, refinedfeatures = depthandrefine(Fgdecoded) gaussians = predictgaussians(refinedfeatures, depthpred, cameras) return gaussians def analysistransform(x): return x def quantize(x, rateparam): return x def entropyencode(x): return b'' def compresscameras(cameras): return b'' def pack(lats, cams): return b'' def unpack(bs): return b'', b'' def entropydecode(bs): return None def synthesistransform(x): return x def decompresscameras(bs): return [] def depthandrefine(x): return None, None def predictgaussians(feat, depth, cams): return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rate-Distortion Trade-off: The choice of \lambda significantly impacts the bitstream size and reconstruction quality. Replaces direct storage of unstructured Gaussian primitives with a structured, learnable feature plane representation mapped via a tri-plane architecture, then compressed using standard video codecs. Chosen when leveraging mature image/video compression standards on spatially redundant natural scenes is preferred over anchor-based residual coding. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The method produces ultra-compact bitstreams. On the DL3DV dataset, scene sizes range from 20.00–107.77 KiB per scene. On the RealEstate10K dataset, sizes range from 3.37–12.51 KiB per scene. Measured Performance: On DL3DV, CodecSplat achieves 23.56–26.36 dB PSNR. On RealEstate10K, it achieves 24.76–27.05 dB PSNR. Scaling: CodecSplat reduces scene size by roughly one order of magnitude compared with compressing feed-forward generated Gaussian primitives. Strengths: Avoids inefficient compression of irregular 3D Gaussian primitives. Exploits the structured intermediate feature representation for better compression. Preserves controllable rate-distortion behavior. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the feed-forward backbone (e.g., DepthSplat-style) to produce a compressible intermediate feature. Performance is dependent on the rate control parameter \lambda. When to use: When ultra-compact storage or transmission of feed-forward 3D Gaussian scenes is required, and the underlying feed-forward backbone is already trained. When not to use: When per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher fidelity is prioritized over extreme compression ratios, or when the feed-forward backbone does not produce a structured intermediate feature suitable for entropy coding. Origin: CodecSplat was introduced in the paper "CodecSplat: Ultra-Compact Latent Coding for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting". History: It builds upon feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods, specifically those using depth-guided multi-view feature refinement (e.g., DepthSplat). It addresses the limitation of existing 3DGS compression methods that operate on the final irregular 3D representation, which is decoupled from the internal feature-to-Gaussian generation process. Usage: It is used for compressing scenes reconstructed by feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting pipelines, enabling efficient storage and transmission of 3D Gaussian representations. CodecSplat: Ultra-Compact Latent Coding for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25563, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Feature Plane Compression (CodecGS)
head: Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Optimized Feature Planes and Standard Video Codecs, Tri-plane Architecture
body: Feature Plane Compression (CodecGS) is a compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces direct storage of unstructured Gaussian primitives with a structured, learnable feature plane representation. It solves the problem of high storage costs and inefficient entropy coding of irregular 3D point clouds by mapping 3D positions to Gaussian attributes via a tri-plane architecture, which is then compressed using standard video codecs. Inputs: Trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene parameters or feed-forward predictions. Outputs: A compressed bitstream representing the feature planes, decodable into Gaussian attributes for rendering. Data Structures: 1. Tri-Plane Feature Map: Three 2D feature planes (Fx, Fy, Fz) corresponding to the xy, yz, and xz projections. Each plane stores a feature vector for each grid cell. 2. Attribute Prediction: For a 3D point \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z), the feature vector \mathbf{f} is obtained by interpolating values from the three planes at the projected coordinates of \mathbf{x}. 3. Encoded Format: Feature planes are normalized and converted to 16-bit integers, conforming to the YUV 16-bit format standard for video codecs. Steps: 1. Two-Phase Training: Perform standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training first, followed by feature plane training to ensure densification consistency. 2. Progressive Training Strategy: To address instability caused by sparse 3DGS signals, employ a progressive training strategy that captures coarse geometric information initially and gradually adds finer details. 3. DCT Entropy Modeling: Apply block-wise Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to the feature planes during optimization to leverage spatial correlations within the planes as conventional image signals. 4. Smoothing Regularization: Add a smoothing regularization term during training to promote locally smooth configurations of Gaussians on the grid. 5. Quantization and Encoding: Normalize the trained feature planes, convert the floating-point values to 16-bit integers, and encode the resulting planes using a standard video codec. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def codecgstrainandcompress(gaussians, triplaneres, C, numepochs, lr, lambdasmooth): #
