name: latentSplat
head: Autoencoding Variational Gaussians for Fast Generalizable 3D Reconstruction
body: latentSplat is a method for generalizable 3D reconstruction from two reference views that predicts semantic 3D Gaussians in a latent space. It models uncertainty explicitly by storing distributions (mean and variance) of spherical harmonic coefficients for each Gaussian, allowing sampling of specific instances for rendering. Unlike regression-based methods such as pixelSplat which provide a single low-variance solution, latentSplat handles high-ambiguity regions and view extrapolation better, avoiding blurry reconstructions in unobserved areas. Compared to generative diffusion-based methods like GeNVS, it is orders of magnitude faster and scales to high resolutions by using efficient Gaussian splatting for rendering instead of volume rendering or iterative diffusion sampling. Inputs: Two reference views (RGB images) and their corresponding camera poses. Outputs: A synthesized RGB image for an arbitrary novel view. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a set of N variational Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{R}, o, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{h}\mu, \mathbf{h}\sigma)i\}{1 \leq i \leq N}. \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D location. \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (diagonal matrix elements). \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Rotation (normalized quaternion). o \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{Kc}: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. \mathbf{h}\mu \in \mathbb{R}^{Kh}: Mean of the Gaussian distribution for semantic feature SH coefficients. \mathbf{h}\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{Kh}: Standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution for semantic feature SH coefficients. The covariance matrix is \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^\top \mathbf{R}^\top. SH coefficients are computed up to degree 4 for RGB and degree 2 for semantic features (dimensionality 4). Parameters: N: Total number of variational Gaussians representing the scene. Token dimensionality in the epipolar transformer: 128. Input feature maps downscaled by a factor of 4 in each dimension for computational feasibility. Epipolar transformer processes 32 samples of each pixel's epipolar line. Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: Encode the two input views using a DINOv1 ViT-B/8 backbone. Upscale local patch tokens by repeating them to the original patch size. Add a linearly projected global class token to obtain a feature map at the original image resolution. Downscale the input feature maps by a factor of 4 in each dimension for computational feasibility. 2. Epipolar Aggregation: Process 32 samples of each pixel's epipolar line using an epipolar transformer. The transformer consists of two blocks with four-head attention. Token dimensionality is 128. Add a skip connection at the original resolution to prevent a bottleneck with low spatial dimensions in the epipolar transformer. 3. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Pass the aggregated features through a Gaussian sampling head. The head employs simple linear projections with specific activation functions: normalized quaternions for rotation \mathbf{R}, and scaled and shifted sigmoid for scale \mathbf{S} and opacity o. Predict \mathbf{h}\mu and \mathbf{h}\sigma for the semantic feature distributions. 4. Sampling: Sample a specific instance of semantic Gaussians from the variational distributions using the reparameterization trick. For each Gaussian i, sample feature coefficients \mathbf{h}i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{h}{\mu,i}, \mathbf{h}{\sigma,i}). 5. Rendering: Render the sampled instance of semantic Gaussians to the target novel view using efficient Gaussian splatting. This produces an auxiliary RGB rendering and feature maps. 6. Decoding: Decode the splatted features into pixel space using a lightweight generative decoder network (VAE-GAN decoder). The decoder is a fully convolutional architecture with four upsample blocks, each containing two residual blocks. Add 1x1 convolutions as skip connections to feed downscaled versions of the intermediate auxiliary RGB renderings and feature maps into each upsample block. Initialize the weights of these additional skip connection layers to zero to avoid noisy gradients. 7. Discrimination (Training Only): A discriminator (small CNN with three strided convolutions) predicts the likelihood of patches. It has no global receptive field. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class latentSplat: def init(self, N, tokendim=128): self.N = N # Encoder components self.vitbackbone = nn.Module() # DINOv1 ViT-B/8 self.epipolartransformer = EpipolarTransformer( numblocks=2, numheads=4, tokendim=tokendim) self.gaussianhead = GaussianSamplingHead() # Decoder components self.decoder = VAEGANDecoder() self.skipconnections = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Conv2d(tokendim, tokendim, 1) for in range(4) ]) # Initialize skip connection weights to zero to avoid noisy gradients for m in self.skipconnections: nn.init.zeros(m.weight) # Discriminator (for training) self.discriminator = Discriminator() def encode(self, refviews, poses): # 1. Feature Encoding vitfeatures = self.vitbackbone(refviews) # Upscale local patch tokens by repeating for original patch size # Add linearly projected global class token featmap = self.upscaleandaddclasstoken(vitfeatures) # Downscale by factor of 4 for computational feasibility featmapdown = F.interpolate(featmap, scalefactor=0.25, mode='bilinear') # 2. Epipolar Aggregation epipolarfeatures = self.epipolartransformer( featmapdown, poses, numsamples=32) # Skip connection at original resolution epipolarfeatures = self.mergeskipconnection(epipolarfeatures, featmap) # 3. Gaussian Parameter Prediction gaussians = self.gaussianhead(epipolarfeatures) return gaussians def samplegaussians(self, gaussians): hmu = gaussians['hmu'] hsigma = gaussians['hsigma'] # Reparameterization trick eps = torch.randnlike(hmu) hsampled = hmu + hsigma eps sampledgaussians = { 'x': gaussians['x'], 'S': gaussians['S'], 'R': gaussians['R'], 'o': gaussians['o'], 'c': gaussians['c'], 'h': hsampled } return sampledgaussians def render(self, gaussians, targetpose): # Standard differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians rgbrender, featrender = self.differentiablesplatting(gaussians, targetpose) return rgbrender, featrender def decode(self, rgbrender, featrender): skipinputs = [] for i in range(4): skipinputs.append(self.skipconnectionsi) output = self.decoder(featrender, skipinputs) return output def forward(self, refviews, poses, targetpose): gaussians = self.encode(refviews, poses) sampledgaussians = self.samplegaussians(gaussians) rgbrender, featrender = self.render(sampledgaussians, targetpose) output = self.decode(rgbrender, featrender) return output, rgbrender, featrender def upscaleandaddclasstoken(self, vitfeatures): # Repeat patch tokens to original size and add projected class token return vitfeatures def mergeskipconnection(self, epipolarfeatures, originalfeat): # Concatenate or add original resolution features to prevent bottleneck return epipolarfeatures def differentiablesplatting(self, gaussians, camerapose): """Standard 2D projection and alpha compositing for Gaussian splatting.""" # Project 3D centers to 2D screen space # Compute 2D covariance from 3D covariance and view matrix # Sort by depth, project to screen, and alpha blend return torch.zeros(1, 3, 256, 256), torch.zeros(1, 4, 256, 256) class EpipolarTransformer(nn.Module): def init(self, numblocks, numheads, tokendim): super().init() self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([ EpipolarAttentionBlock(numheads, tokendim) for in range(numblocks) ]) self.tokendim = tokendim def forward(self, featmap, poses, numsamples): # Process 32 samples of each pixel's epipolar line for block in self.blocks: featmap = block(featmap, poses, numsamples) return featmap class EpipolarAttentionBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, numheads, tokendim): super().init() self.numheads = numheads self.tokendim = tokendim def forward(self, featmap, poses, numsamples): # Standard multi-head attention over epipolar line samples return featmap class GaussianSamplingHead(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Linear projections with specific activations pass class VAEGANDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Fully convolutional architecture with 4 upsample blocks, each with 2 residual blocks pass class Discriminator(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Small CNN with 3 strided convolutions pass Time Complexity: Fast rendering due to Gaussian splatting, orders of magnitude faster than diffusion-based methods. Memory Complexity: Scales to high resolutions due to the efficient Gaussian representation. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art quality in two-view reconstruction, especially in challenging cases of wide-spread input views and view extrapolation. Strengths: Handles high-ambiguity regions, generalizes to interpolated and extrapolated views, purely trained on real video data without 3D supervision (depth/pose labels for target view). Limitations: Requires two reference views and their camera poses. When to use: When fast, generalizable 3D reconstruction from few views is needed, especially for extrapolation or ambiguous scenes. When not to use: When single-view reconstruction is required or when per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher fidelity is needed. latentSplat was introduced by C. Wewer et al. in 2024. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting [31] and addresses limitations of previous generalizable methods that either do not scale to large scenes or are limited to interpolation of close input views. It combines regression-based and generative approaches, using variational Gaussians to model uncertainty. latentSplat, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16292, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Feature Uplifting via Forward Rendering
head: Forward Feature Collection, LGS estimator, MAP estimator for LGS, Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation for LGS, Maximum Likelihood Feature Uplifting, Occam's LGS Feature Uplifting
body: Feature Uplifting via Forward Rendering is a method to estimate 3D language features f \in \mathbb{R}^d for 3D Gaussians from observed 2D features F{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^d by formulating the problem as a Maximum Likelihood (ML) or Maximum-a-Posteriori (MAP) estimation, assuming uniform prior and Gaussian noise. It differs from back-projection methods (e.g., conventional semantic feature learning) by leveraging the forward rendering process to establish precise correspondence, eliminating costly back-projection or iterative optimization. It builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction. Inputs: A set of training camera views S = \{s1, \dots, sn\}. A set of trained 3D Gaussians G = \{G1, \dots, Gm\}, where each Gaussian Gi has mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color ci. 2D language feature maps F = \{f^{s1}, \dots, f^{sn}\}, where each f^s \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times d} is extracted from the input images using a feature extractor (e.g., OpenCLIP ViT-B/16). Outputs: Uplifted 3D language features fi \in \mathbb{R}^d for each Gaussian Gi. A filtered set of semantic Gaussians G^s = \{G^si\}{i=1}^M where M \ll N, representing Gaussians that meaningfully contribute to the scene’s semantic representation. Data Structures: Gaussian: Stores \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or scale si and rotation ri), \alphai \in [0,1], ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, and accumulated feature fi \in \mathbb{R}^d and weight wi \in \mathbb{R}. 2D Feature Map: A tensor of shape H \times W \times d for each view. Formulas: The method assumes a uniform prior p(f) \propto \text{constant}, reducing the MAP estimation to maximizing the likelihood: \arg \maxf p(f | F{2D}) = \arg \maxf p(F{2D} | f) Assuming conditional independence of pixels given the surface representation and 3D features f, the likelihood is: p(F{2D} | f) = \prod{v=1}^V \prod{p \in Pv} p(f{p,v}^{2D} | f) The 2D feature at pixel p in view v is modeled as a weighted sum of 3D Gaussian features plus Gaussian noise: f{p,v}^{2D} = \sum{k=1}^R w{k,p,v} fk + \epsilon{p,v}, \quad \epsilon{p,v} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) where R is the number of Gaussians along the ray, and w{k,p,v} is the alpha blending weight for Gaussian k at pixel p in view v: w{i,p,v} = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) To maximize the likelihood, we transform to the log-likelihood domain: \log p(F{2D} | f) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum{v,p} \| f{p,v}^{2D} - \sum{k=1}^R w{k,p,v} fk \|^2 + \text{const} Taking the derivative with respect to the 3D language feature fi of Gaussian i and setting to zero yields: \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sum{v,p} w{i,p,v} (f{p,v}^{2D} - \sum{k=1}^R w{k,p,v} fk) = 0 The final closed-form solution for the 3D feature fi of Gaussian i is the weighted average of observed 2D features: fi = \frac{\sum{v=1}^V \sum{p \in Pv} w{i,p,v} f{p,v}^{2D}}{\sum{v=1}^V \sum{p \in Pv} w{i,p,v}} This formula interprets the optimal 3D feature as a weighted average of 2D features observed at pixels where the Gaussian has influence, with weights proportional to the Gaussian’s contribution. Practical Simplification: The method assumes sparse influence: for most views/pixels, one dominant Gaussian has weight close to 1, leading to negligible cross-talk where w{i,p,v} w{k,p,v} \approx 0 for i \neq k. This eliminates cross-Gaussian terms, allowing the closed-form solution above. Parameters: Feature Dimension (d): The dimensionality of the CLIP language features. Evaluated at 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 dimensions. Training Iterations: 30,000 iterations using common Gaussian Splatting parameters. Average Number of Gaussians: ~2,500,000 Gaussians for RGB representation across scenes. LERF Mask Threshold: 0.5 for computing relevancy scores. 3D-OVS Area Thresholds: Reject spurious masks with areas smaller than 0.005% or larger than 0.90% of the image. 3D-OVS Object Stability Threshold: 0.4. Algorithm: 1. Initialize accumulated features fi = 0 and weights wi = 0 for each Gaussian Gi. 2. For each camera view s \in S: a. Iterate through each Gaussian Gi in the view frustum. b. Render Gi to get the alpha blending weight w{i,s} and the projected pixel location \psii = \lfloor x'i \rfloor. c. Extract the 2D feature f{i,s} from the feature map for view s at pixel \psii. d. Update fi \leftarrow fi + w{i,s} f{i,s} and wi \leftarrow wi + w{i,s}. 3. For each Gaussian Gi: a. If wi > 0, normalize fi \leftarrow fi / wi. b. If wi = 0, filter out Gi (no contribution across all views). 4. Return the refined set of semantic Gaussians G^s with uplifted features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def featureuplifting(gaussians, views, featuremaps): """ Uplift 2D language features to 3D Gaussians using forward rendering. """ d = featuremaps[0].shape[2] # Initialize accumulated features and weights for g in gaussians: g['f'] = [0.0] d g['w'] = 0.0 for view in views: fm = view['featuremap'] # Standard view frustum culling visible = [g for g in gaussians if isinfrustum(g['mu'], view['pose'])] for g in visible: # Standard perspective projection xprime = project2d(g['mu'], view['pose']) psi = (int(xprime[0]), int(xprime[1])) # Standard alpha blending calculation along ray covering = [g2 for g2 in gaussians if coverspixel(g2, psi, view)] covering.sort(key=lambda g2: depth(g2['mu'], view['pose'])) try: idx = covering.index(g) except ValueError: continue weight = g['alpha'] for j in range(idx): weight = (1 - covering[j]['alpha']) wis = weight # Extract 2D feature at projected pixel fis = fm[psi[1], psi[0],:] # Update accumulated feature and weight for k in range(d): g['f'][k] += wis fis[k] g['w'] += wis semanticgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if g['w'] > 0: # Normalize feature for k in range(d): g['f'][k] /= g['w'] semanticgaussians.append(g) # Gaussians with wi = 0 are filtered out return semanticgaussians def isinfrustum(mu, pose): return True def project2d(mu, pose): return [mu[0], mu[1]] def coverspixel(g, pixel, view): return True def depth(mu, pose): return mu[2] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Dimensionality: High dimensionality (d \gg 3) prevents GPU from fitting all required data in the shader L1 cache, causing color blending issues in Equation 2. Localization Accuracy: Localization accuracy metric is prone to noise because it only measures the closest matching pixel, ignoring feature distribution and object shape. No Contribution: Gaussians with no contributions across all views are filtered out to reduce noise and the number of Gaussians significantly. Dynamic Thresholding: For 3D-OVS, dynamic thresholding is used. For each query, evaluate threshold values with step size 0.01. Create binary mask where relevancy score > threshold. Compute average relevancy score within masked area. Identify stable region: Find region where absolute gradient of average relevancy score (rate of change w.r.t threshold) is below a chosen stability threshold. Select the middle value from the stable range as the final threshold. Time Complexity: O(N \times V) for feature uplifting, where N is number of Gaussians and V is number of views, but optimized by tile-based rendering and frustum culling. Measured Performance: On LERF dataset, localization accuracy improves to 84.1 when feature dimension reduces to 32D. 64D features achieve 64.5% mIoU on LERF, outperforming LangSplat baseline by 13.1% mIoU. LERF mIoU improvement: 9.9% improvement over LangSplat under identical experimental settings. 3D-OVS mIoU improvement: 1.6% improvement over LangSplat. Speed: Uplifts features in 16.4 seconds (no setup) or 31.9 seconds (with setup) vs 60-67 minutes for others (LangSplat, GOI, 3DVLM). Hardware: Single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Strengths: Computationally efficient (single forward pass), handles occlusions via frustum culling, establishes precise correspondence, avoids iterative optimization. Limitations: High dimensionality causes cache issues, localization metric is noisy, requires pre-trained Gaussian Splat. When to use: When efficient, accurate 3D language feature lifting is needed from a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splat model. When not to use: When iterative optimization is acceptable and higher dimensional features are required without compression. Origin: The method is introduced in "Occam's LGS: An Efficient Approach for Language Gaussian Splatting". History: It builds on the principles of 3DGS and probabilistic modeling, formulating feature uplifting as a MAP estimation problem. It differs from conventional semantic feature learning methods that rely on back-projection. Usage: Used for open vocabulary semantic segmentation and 3D scene understanding, evaluated on LERF and 3D-OVS datasets. Occam's LGS: An Efficient Approach for Language Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01807v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Occam's LGS
head: Language Gaussian Splatting via weighted multi-view feature aggregation, Occam LGS
body: Occam's LGS is a training-free method for lifting 2D language features to 3D Gaussian representations by applying Occam’s razor to the forward rendering process of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of expensive iterative optimization in feature space by computing weighted multi-view feature aggregation directly from the alpha blending weights of the standard color rendering pass. Unlike sibling methods that rely on scene-specific autoencoders, quantization, or costly semantic feature rendering, Occam's LGS supports arbitrary-dimensional uncompressed features without compromising training speed, achieving a two-order-of-magnitude speed-up while maintaining state-of-the-art performance for open-set vision-language tasks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (providing geometry and appearance parameters) and a set of input images with known camera poses. The underlying encoder provides 2D semantic features f \in \mathbb{R}^d for each pixel. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian Gi is augmented with a high-dimensional semantic feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^d. Data Structures: The primitive Gaussian representation is defined as G = \{x, \Sigma, c, o\}, where: x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the 3D position. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{6} (or \mathbb{R}^{2\times2} when projected) is the covariance matrix. c is the color (or Spherical Harmonics parameters). o \in \mathbb{R} is the opacity. For language splatting, this is augmented to include the semantic feature fi. The rendering process uses a tile-based sorting strategy, partitioning the image into tiles typically spanning 16 \times 16 pixels. Mathematical Formulation: The standard color rendering for a pixel p along a ray with R Gaussians is: C(p) = \sum{i=1}^{R} \alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity contribution of the i-th Gaussian: \alphai = oi \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{2} (p-x'i)^\top \Sigma'^{-1} (p-x'i)} Here, x'i is the projected 2D center and \Sigma' is the projected 2D covariance matrix. The alpha blending weight for Gaussian i is defined as: wi = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) In explicit feature rendering, the semantic feature at pixel p would be: F(p) = \sum{i=1}^{R} wi fi However, explicit rendering is expensive because the high dimensionality d \gg 3 prevents fitting data in the GPU shader L1 cache. Occam's LGS avoids this by aggregating features per Gaussian during the forward pass. Algorithm Steps: For each Gaussian Gi in the scene: 1. Identify the set of views Si where Gi is visible (within the view frustum). 2. For each view s \in Si, determine the Gaussian’s center projected pixel location p{si} = \lfloor x'i \rfloor. 3. During the standard tile-based rendering pass, record the alpha blending weight w{si} and extract the 2D feature f{si} at pixel p{si} from the pre-computed feature map. 4. Compute the weighted average of the multi-view features to assign to Gi: fi = \frac{\sum{s \in Si} w{si} f{si}}{\sum{s \in Si} w{si}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def occamlgslift(gaussians, views, featuremaps): """ gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'x' (3,), 'o' (float), 'sigma2dinv' (2x2). views: List of dicts with keys 'Kinv' (3x3), 'H', 'W', 'featuremap' (H, W, d). featuremaps: List of numpy arrays matching views. """ for g in gaussians: g['semanticfeature'] = None visibleviews = [] totalweight = 0.0 weightedfeaturesum = np.zeros(1) # Placeholder for dimension d, updated dynamically for view, fmap in zip(views, featuremaps): # Step 1 & 2: Project 3D center to 2D pixel coordinates x3d = g['x'] x2dhom = view['Kinv'] @ np.append(x3d, 1.0) x2d = x2dhom[:2] / x2dhom[2] px, py = int(x2d[0]), int(x2d[1]) # Check frustum bounds (isinfrustum replacement) if not (0 <= px < view['W'] and 0 <= py < view['H']): continue # Step 3: Compute alpha blending weight wsi (computealpha replacement) diff = np.array([px - x2d[0], py - x2d[1]]) alpha = g['o'] np.exp(-0.5 diff @ g['sigma2dinv'] @ diff) wsi = alpha # Contribution weight for the center pixel # Extract 2D feature at projected pixel fsi = fmap[py, px] visibleviews.append((wsi, fsi)) # Step 4: Compute weighted average if visibleviews: for w, f in visibleviews: totalweight += w weightedfeaturesum += w f if totalweight > 0: g['semanticfeature'] = weightedfeaturesum / totalweight else: g['semanticfeature'] = np.zeros(f.shape[0]) else: g['semanticfeature'] = np.zeros(f.shape[0]) return gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory/Compute: Explicit rendering of semantics is expensive due to high dimensionality d \gg 3, causing cache misses in GPU shaders. Occam's LGS avoids this by aggregating in 3D space. Occlusion: View frustum culling and tile-based sorting naturally handle occluded Gaussians, ensuring only visible features are aggregated. Precision: Projecting 3D centers to 2D pixels involves rounding (\lfloor x'i \rfloor). This discretization may introduce minor alignment errors between the feature map and the Gaussian center. Time Complexity: The method is training-free and requires only a single forward pass through the views. It efficiently completes the lifting of 512-dimensional features to 3D in less than one minute. Memory Complexity: It does not require storing large intermediate feature volumes for explicit rendering, reducing memory overhead compared to methods that render features per pixel. Performance: Offers a speed-up of two orders of magnitude compared to existing methods that rely on cumbersome techniques like iterative optimization or quantization. Strengths: Supports arbitrary-dimensional uncompressed features; preserves semantic meaning without preprocessing; enables open-vocabulary generalization; allows for easy scene manipulation and editing. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the underlying 3D Gaussian model and the 2D feature extractor. It does not refine the features through optimization, so errors in the initial geometry or feature extraction are not corrected. Occam's LGS was introduced by Jan-Nico Zaech and Jiahuan Cheng from the INSPIRE Institute. The work is based on the arXiv preprint "Occam's LGS: An Efficient Approach for Language Gaussian Splatting" (arXiv:2412.01807v2), published in March 2025. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and Language Gaussian Splatting, applying Occam’s razor to simplify the pipeline by removing unnecessary optimization steps in feature space. name: Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression
body: Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression (FCGS) is an autoencoder-based compression method that projects 3D Gaussian attributes into a quantized latent space using hyperpriors and context models. It addresses the fidelity drop caused by MLP non-invertibility in geometry attributes by bypassing MLPs for geometry and using a mask for color attributes. Unlike anchor-based quantization methods that modify Gaussian locations and require finetuning, FCGS creates context grids in a feed-forward manner without altering original positions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians where each Gaussian i has geometry attributes f{geo} \in \mathbb{R}^8 (opacity \alpha, diagonal scaling S, quaternion rotation R) and color attributes f{col} \in \mathbb{R}^{48} (3-degree Spherical Harmonics coefficients). The concatenated attribute vector is f{gau} \in \mathbb{R}^{56}. Output: A compressed bitstream representing latent variables \hat{y} and hypervariables \hat{z}, which decode to reconstructed Gaussian attributes \hat{x}. Data Structures: Transform Networks: Analysis (ga) and Synthesis (gs) are 4-layer MLPs; Hyperprior Analysis (ha) and Synthesis (hs) are 3-layer MLPs. Context Models: Inter-Gaussian uses 3D and 2D grids storing features f{kv} from previously decoded Gaussians; Intra-Gaussian processes chunks of \hat{y}i sequentially. Probability Model: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) combining parameters from hyperprior, inter-context, and intra-context models. Parameters: Ns: Number of batches for inter-Gaussian context decoding. Typical value: 2. Nc: Number of chunks for intra-Gaussian context. Nc=4 for path m=1 (channel split), Nc=3 for path m=0 (RGB split). q: Quantization step size. q=1 if mi=1 (latent space), q is a trainable decimal parameter if mi=0 (bypass). \epsilonm: Hyperparameter threshold for binarizing the mask m. \lambdam: Explicitly NOT used in FCGS to avoid complicating Rate-Distortion trade-off. Algorithm Steps: 1. Attribute Partitioning: Separate Gaussian attributes into geometry f{geo} and color f{col}, then concatenate to form f{gau}. 2. Mask Generation (MEM): For each Gaussian i, compute a binary mask mi to determine if color attributes pass through the MLPs or bypass them: mi = \text{Sig}(\text{MLP}m(f{gau})) > \epsilonm, where \text{Sig} is the Sigmoid function. 3. Latent Encoding: For geometry attributes (f{geo}), bypass MLPs to ensure exact recovery by setting y = x. For color attributes (f{col}), compute the latent yi = Q(ga(xi)) if mi=1, or yi = Q(xi) if mi=0, where Q is quantization with step q. Compute hyperprior zi = ha(xi). 4. Inter-Gaussian Context Decoding: Split all Gaussians' latents \hat{y} into Ns batches and decode sequentially. For a Gaussian i in the current batch at \mu{gi}, identify voxels V{\mui}^g forming its minimum bounding box in the grid. Compute interpolated feature f{i\mu} = \sum{k: vk \in V{\mui}^g} wk f{kv} where wk are interpolation weights. Compute inter-context distribution parameters \mu{si}, \sigma{is}, \pi{is} = \text{MLP}s(\oplus [f{i\mu}, \text{emb}(\mu{gi})]), where \text{emb} is sincos positional embedding and \oplus is channel-wise concatenation. 5. Intra-Gaussian Context Decoding: Split \hat{y}i into Nc chunks. For path m=1, split along the channel dimension (Nc=4); for path m=0, split along the RGB axis (Nc=3). Compute intra-context parameters for chunk nc: \mu{i,nc}, \sigma{i,nc}, \pi{i,nc} = \text{MLP}c(\hat{y}{i,[0,nc-1]}). Aggregate parameters: \mu{ci}, \sigma{ic}, \pi{ic} = \oplus{nc=1}^{Nc} \{\mu{i,nc}, \sigma{i,nc}, \pi{i,nc}\}. 6. Hyperprior Context: Compute hyperprior parameters \mu{hi}, \sigma{ih}, \pi{ih} from \hat{z}i using hs. 7. Probability Estimation: Combine inter-context, intra-context, and hyperprior parameters using a GMM to estimate the probability of each latent value \hat{y}i. 8. Arithmetic Decoding: Use the estimated probabilities to decode the bitstream into \hat{y} and \hat{z}. 9. Reconstruction: Apply synthesis transform gs to \hat{y}i if mi=1, or use \hat{y}i directly if mi=0, to obtain \hat{x}i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SimpleMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, indim, outdim, layers=4): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(indim if i == 0 else outdim, outdim) for i in range(layers)]) def forward(self, x): for layer in self.layers: x = F.relu(layer(x)) return x class FCGSCompression: def init(self, numgaussians, numchannelsgeo=8, numchannelscol=48): self.numgaussians = numgaussians self.numchannelsgeo = numchannelsgeo self.numchannelscol = numchannelscol self.numchannelsgau = numchannelsgeo + numchannelscol # Transform Networks self.ga = SimpleMLP(self.numchannelsgau, 128, layers=4) self.gs = SimpleMLP(128, self.numchannelsgau, layers=4) self.ha = SimpleMLP(self.numchannelsgau, 64, layers=3) self.hs = SimpleMLP(64, 128, layers=3) # Context & Mask Models self.mlps = SimpleMLP(128 + 6, 128, layers=2) self.mlpc = SimpleMLP(128, 128, layers=2) self.mlpm = SimpleMLP(self.numchannelsgau, 1, layers=2) # Grids for Inter-Gaussian Context self.grid3d = None self.grid2d = None # Parameters self.Ns = 2 self.Nc = 4 self.epsilonm = 0.5 self.qtrainable = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(0.1)) def quantize(self, x, q): return torch.round(x / q) q def sincosposembed(self, pos): # Standard sincos positional embedding freqs = torch.arange(0, 6, dtype=torch.float32) / 6 torch.pi return torch.cat([torch.sin(pos.unsqueeze(1) freqs), torch.cos(pos.unsqueeze(1) freqs)], dim=-1) def interpolategrid(self, grid, pos): # Standard trilinear/bilinear grid interpolation return torch.zeros(128) def encode(self, xgeo, xcol): x = torch.cat([xgeo, xcol], dim=1) mask = (torch.sigmoid(self.mlpm(x)) > self.epsilonm).float() y = torch.zeroslike(x) for i in range(self.numgaussians): if mask[i] > 0.5: y[i] = self.quantize(self.ga(x[i]), q=1.0) else: y[i] = self.quantize(x[i], q=self.qtrainable) z = self.ha(x) zquantized = self.quantize(z, q=1.0) return y, zquantized, mask def decode(self, yhat, zhat, gridfeatures, gaussianpositions): xhat = torch.zeroslike(yhat) batchsize = self.numgaussians // self.Ns indices = torch.randperm(self.numgaussians) for ns in range(self.Ns): startidx = ns batchsize endidx = (ns + 1) batchsize currentindices = indices[startidx:endidx] for idx in currentindices: mugi = gaussianpositions[idx] fimu = self.interpolategrid(gridfeatures, mugi) posemb = self.sincosposembed(mugi) contextparamsinter = self.mlps(torch.cat([fimu, posemb], dim=-1)) yi = yhat[idx] chunks = torch.chunk(yi, self.Nc, dim=-1) contextparamsintra = [] for nc in range(len(chunks)): prevy = torch.cat(chunks[:nc], dim=-1) if nc > 0 else torch.zeroslike(chunks[0]) contextparamsintra.append(self.mlpc(prevy)) contextparamsintra = torch.cat(contextparamsintra, dim=-1) contextparamshyper = self.hs(zhat[idx]) # GMM probability estimation and arithmetic decoding would occur here # Reconstruction: xhat[idx] = self.gs(yhat[idx]) if (torch.rand(1) > 0.5) else yhat[idx] return xhat Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N for the feed-forward encoding/decoding steps, plus the cost of grid interpolation for context models. Memory Complexity: Depends on the grid size for inter-Gaussian context. Strengths: Feed-forward nature allows fast inference without per-scene optimization; avoids the fidelity drop associated with MLP non-invertibility by bypassing geometry attributes. Limitations: Requires training on a large dataset; grid creation and interpolation add computational overhead compared to simple quantization. FCGS was introduced in 2024 for the ICLR 2025 conference. It builds upon the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and image compression techniques, specifically autoencoders with hyperpriors and context models. It addresses the limitations of previous compression methods that suffered from fidelity drops due to the non-invertibility of MLPs in geometry attributes. name: SHARE
head: Pose-free 3D Gaussian splatting via shape-ray estimation
body: SHARE is a pose-free framework for generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting that estimates camera poses via predicted rays and uses anchor-aligned coarse-to-fine geometry estimation to predict 3D Gaussian parameters without ground-truth poses. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like PixelSplat and MVSplat by explicitly embedding pose awareness into multi-view cost volumes via Plücker rays, making it robust to pose inaccuracies where generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting methods are highly sensitive. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: M input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^M. For DTU, M=4 (3 context, 1 target); for RealEstate10K, M=5 (2 context, 3 targets). Input resolution is 256 \times 256. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mu, \alpha, \Sigma, c\} and estimated camera poses (implicitly via rays). Data Structures: Cost Volume Ci: For each viewpoint i, a cost volume of shape \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times D}, where D is the number of depth hypotheses. Spatial Weight Volume Wi: Shape \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4}, accounting for view-dependent effects (occlusion, lighting). Canonical Geometry Volume Vg: Shape \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times C}, fusing refined cost volumes. Canonical Feature Volume Vf: Shape \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}, constructed from upsampled multi-view features. Gaussian Primitives: K=3 offsets per anchor. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction and Cost Volume Construction: Extract features from input images. Construct initial cost volumes Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times D} for each viewpoint i using matching Transformer layers. The cost volume is computed as: Ci = \frac{1}{\sqrt{Ci}} \sum{j \neq i} F{j \to i} where F{j \to i} are warped features. 2. Pose-Aware Cost Aggregation: Refine cost volumes Ci through cost aggregation conditioned on predicted Plücker rays. Use patch-wise cross-attention to embed pose awareness into the cost volumes, introducing geometric bias. 3. Spatial Weight Estimation: Estimate a spatial weight volume Wi \in \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4} for each cost volume to account for view-dependent effects such as occlusion and lighting variations. 4. Canonical Volume Construction: Fuse refined cost volumes C'i and weights Wi into a canonical geometry volume Vg \in \mathbb{R}^{H/4 \times W/4 \times C}: Vg = \sum{i=1}^M Wi C'i + \phi \oplus C' where C' is the average of all cost volumes, \oplus denotes channel-wise concatenation, and \phi is a CNN layer for channel projection. A mean and variance-based volume is also added following previous MVS techniques. Similarly, construct the canonical feature volume Vf \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} using the same aggregation method with upsampled multi-view features. 5. Coarse Depth Estimation: Compute initial coarse depth z as the expected value over depth hypothesis planes D \in \mathbb{R}^D. The probability of each depth candidate is predicted using Vg through a lightweight MLP depth head fg followed by a softmax function: z = \sumd \text{softmax}(fg(Vg))d \cdot Dd The estimated 3D anchor position pi for pixel i is: pi = o + zi di where o is the ray origin and di is the ray direction. 6. Anchor-Aligned Offset Prediction: Estimate K offset vectors \Delta p{i,k} for each anchor using the canonical feature volume Vf. The offset prediction MLP head fo outputs: \Delta p{i,k} = fo(Vf) where k \in \{1, \dots, K\} and K=3. 7. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Define Gaussian means as \mu{i,k} = pi + \Delta p{i,k}. Predict remaining parameters (opacity \alpha, covariance \Sigma, color c) using an MLP head fp applied to the positional encoding of offsets and the feature volume: \{\alpha, \Sigma, c\}{i,k} = fp(\text{PE}(\Delta p{i,k}), Vf) where \text{PE}(\cdot) denotes positional encoding. 8. Rendering: Rasterize the predicted Gaussians into 2D space to render the target image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def shareforward(images, numdepthhypotheses, numoffsets=3): """ Forward pass for SHARE. images: List of M images, shape (M, 3, 256, 256) numdepthhypotheses: D, number of depth planes numoffsets: K, number of Gaussian offsets per anchor """ M = len(images) H, W = 256, 256 Cfeat, C = 64, 128 # Channel dimensions for feature and canonical volumes # 1. Feature Extraction and Cost Volume Construction features = extractfeatures(images) # Shape: (M, Cfeat, H//4, W//4) costvolumes = [] for i in range(M): # Fix: Use list comprehension instead of unparenthesized generator expression warped = [warpfeatures(features[j], features[i]) for j in range(M) if j != i] Ci = aggregatecost(warped, features[i]) costvolumes.append(Ci) # 2. Pose-Aware Cost Aggregation pluckerrays = predictpluckerrays(images) # Shape: (M, H//4, W//4, 6) refinedcostvolumes = [] for i in range(M): Crefined = patchcrossattention(costvolumes[i], pluckerrays[i]) refinedcostvolumes.append(Crefined) # 3. Spatial Weight Estimation weightvolumes = [predictspatialweights(refinedcostvolumes[i]) for i in range(M)] # 4. Canonical Volume Construction avgcost = np.mean(refinedcostvolumes, axis=0) Vg = np.zeros((H//4, W//4, C)) for i in range(M): term1 = weightvolumes[i] refinedcostvolumes[i] term2 = convproject(np.concatenate([refinedcostvolumes[i], avgcost], axis=-1)) Vg += term1 + term2 Vf = constructcanonicalfeaturevolume(images, features) # Shape: (H, W, C) # 5. Coarse Depth Estimation depthlogits = depthhead(Vg) # Shape: (H//4, W//4, D) depthprobs = np.exp(depthlogits) / np.sum(np.exp(depthlogits), axis=-1, keepdims=True) Dplanes = np.linspace(0.1, 10.0, numdepthhypotheses) z = np.sum(depthprobs Dplanes, axis=-1) # Shape: (H//4, W//4) rayorigins, raydirections = getrayinfo(pluckerrays) anchors = rayorigins + z[..., np.newaxis] raydirections # Shape: (H//4, W//4, 3) # 6. Anchor-Aligned Offset Prediction offsets = offsethead(Vf) # Shape: (H, W, numoffsets, 3) # 7. Gaussian Parameter Prediction anchorsupsampled = interpolate(anchors, targetsize=(H, W)) means = anchorsupsampled[..., np.newaxis,:] + offsets # Shape: (H, W, numoffsets, 3) peoffsets = positionalencoding(offsets) alphas, sigmas, colors = gaussianparamshead(peoffsets, Vf) # 8. Rendering renderedimage = rasterizegaussians(means, alphas, sigmas, colors, cameraintrinsics) return renderedimage, means, alphas, sigmas, colors Parameters: Context/Target Images: 3 context + 1 target for DTU; 2 context + 3 targets for RealEstate10K. Input Resolution: 256 \times 256. Number of Gaussian Primitives per Anchor (K): 3. Number of Depth Hypotheses (D): Not given in the sources. Training Iterations: 140K on DTU, 300K on RealEstate10K. Optimizer: Adam. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pose Uncertainty: SHARE is designed to be robust to pose inaccuracies, whereas generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting methods (e.g., PixelSplat, MVSplat) are highly sensitive to pose errors, with even minor Gaussian noise (\sigma = 0.01) causing significant degradation. Depth Discontinuities: Coarse depth estimation may lead to over-smooth geometry in regions with depth discontinuities or complex surfaces. The anchor-aligned coarse-to-fine estimation with offsets mitigates this. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DTU (Predicted Poses via DUSt3R): PSNR 19.36, SSIM 0.61, LPIPS 0.31. RealEstate10K (Predicted Poses via DUSt3R): PSNR 21.23, SSIM 0.64, LPIPS 0.26. Scaling: Demonstrates scalability to complex, large-scale scenes (RealEstate10K). Strengths: Robust to pose uncertainty; outperforms generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting under noisy pose conditions; achieves LPIPS/SSIM scores comparable to ground-truth poses. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: When ground-truth camera poses are unavailable or unreliable, and robust generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting is required. When Not to Use: When high-precision ground-truth poses are available and pose-free methods are not necessary. SHARE was introduced in the paper "Pose-free 3D Gaussian splatting via shape-ray estimation". It addresses the challenge of generalizable 3D Gaussian splatting without requiring ground-truth camera poses, which are often unavailable or inaccurate in real-world scenarios. The method builds on Feed-forward and Generalizable Prediction by incorporating pose estimation directly into the geometry prediction pipeline. name: Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion
head: HiGDiff, Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion
body: HiGDiff is a feed-forward reconstruction method for computed tomography (CT) that predicts a set of 3D Gaussian primitives from degraded projections without per-scene optimization. It solves the problem of sparse-view, low-dose, or limited-angle CT reconstruction by using two explicit Gaussian banks (structure and detail) initialized from anatomical cues and refined via a sequential structure-to-detail diffusion hierarchy. It differs from single-bank Gaussian reconstruction by maintaining separate banks for global attenuation geometry and residual detail, and from dense voxel diffusion by operating on explicit Gaussian primitives with a sequential hierarchy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Degraded projection data Y \in \mathbb{R}^{Nr}, where Nr is the number of rays. Each ray r has an observed count Yr and a mask Mr \in \{0, 1\} indicating if the ray is observed. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \mathcal{G}s \cup \mathcal{G}d, where \mathcal{G}s is the structure bank and \mathcal{G}d is the detail bank. Each Gaussian i in bank b is defined by mean m{b,i}, covariance \Sigma{b,i} (parameterized by scale and rotation), opacity a{b,i}, and color/attenuation attributes. The final output is the reconstructed attenuation field rendered from these Gaussians. Data Structures: Physics Features (F{phy}): A multi-scale feature pyramid extracted from the initial volume estimate. Anchors (K): A set of landmark-free anatomical anchor points predicted from F{phy}. Foreground Capacity Field (F{fg}): A continuous scalar field predicting the density/capacity for Gaussian placement. Gaussian Bank (\mathcal{G}b): A fixed-cardinality set of Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has attributes \xi{b,i} = [m{b,i}, \Sigma{b,i}, a{b,i}, \dots]. Diffusion State (\delta \xi{b,i}^t): The noise-corrupted Gaussian attributes at diffusion timestep t. Parameters: I0: Incident photon count. \bar{\alpha}{b,t}: Cumulative noise schedule coefficient for bank b at step t. \eta: DDIM inversion parameter (set to 0 for deterministic inversion). \lambda{kp}, \lambda{fg}, \lambdab: Loss weights for anchor consistency, capacity field, and diffusion loss respectively. w(q): Attention weighting function, w(q) = 0.15 + 0.85q. Steps: 1. Initialization: a. Compute estimated photon count for each ray: Ir = I0 \exp(-Yr). b. Compute normalized inverse-noise reliability Wr: Wr = \frac{\sqrt{\max(Ir, 1)}/Mr}{\sqrt{\max{l:Ml=1}\max(Il, 1)}} where Mr is the observation mask. c. Compute initial volume estimate V0 using filtered back-projection (FBP): V0 = \text{FBP}\theta(Y). d. Compute physics features F{phy} using a physics encoder E{phy} on V0 and the back-projected residual weighted by W: F{phy} = E{phy}(V0, \text{UBP}\theta(W \bullet [Y - \text{Proj}\theta(V0)])) where \text{UBP} is unweighted back-projection and \text{Proj} is forward projection. e. Predict anatomical anchors K and foreground capacity field F{fg}: K = E{kp}(F{phy}) F{fg} = E{fg}(F{phy}, K). f. Initialize the structure bank \mathcal{G}{s,0} and detail bank \mathcal{G}{d,0} using K and F{fg}. Positions are initialized in normalized scanner coordinates [-1, 1]^3. 2. Structure Gaussian Diffusion (Stage I): For each diffusion step t from T down to 1: a. For each structure primitive i: i. Sample physics features at current mean m{s,i}^t: f{s,i}^t = \text{Samp}(F{phy}, m{s,i}^t). ii. Compute context c{s,i}^t by concatenating initial token z{s,i}, sampled features f{s,i}^t, and inverse-standardized initial attributes \phis(g{s,i,0}), then passing through fusion MLP Ms and attention weighting w(q{s,i}^t): c{s,i}^t = w(q{s,i}^t) Ms [z{s,i}, f{s,i}^t, \phis(g{s,i,0})]. iii. Predict noise \hat{\epsilon}{s,i}^t using structure denoiser Ds: \hat{\epsilon}{s,i}^t = Ds(\delta \xi{s,i}^t, c{s,i}^t, t). b. Update state using DDIM inverse step (\eta=0): \delta \xi{s,i}^{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}{s,t}}} \left( \delta \xi{s,i}^t - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}{s,t}} \hat{\epsilon}{s,i}^t \right). c. Apply inverse standardization \phis^{-1} and add correction to \mathcal{G}{s,0}. Apply center clipping and positive numerical floors to ensure valid attributes (e.g., positive scales). 3. Detail Gaussian Diffusion (Stage I): a. Construct stopped conditions for detail diffusion using the refined structure bank. The detail bank is initialized based on the structure bank's output. b. For each diffusion step t from T down to 1: i. For each detail primitive i: Predict noise \hat{\epsilon}{d,i}^t using detail denoiser Dd conditioned on the structure bank and current detail state. ii. Update state using DDIM inverse step: \delta \xi{d,i}^{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}{d,t}}} \left( \delta \xi{d,i}^t - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}{d,t}} \hat{\epsilon}{d,i}^t \right). c. Apply inverse standardization \phid^{-1} and domain validity checks (center clipping, positive floors). 4. Refinement (Stage II): After freezing Stage I modules, a refinement network is trained to correct residual errors after dense voxelization, using stop-gradient to preserve the division between structure and detail. 5. Rendering: Render the attenuation field using the Gaussian renderer: \mathcal{R}G(\mathcal{G}b)(x) = \sum{i=1}^{Nb} a{b,i} \mathcal{G}G(x; m{b,i}, \Sigma{b,i}) where \mathcal{G}G(x; m, \Sigma) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2}(x-m)^\top \Sigma^{-1}(x-m)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def normalizedinversenoisereliability(Y, I0, M): """ Y: (Nr,) observed projections I0: float, incident photon count M: (Nr,) binary mask """ Ir = I0 torch.exp(-Y) maxIr = torch.clamp(Ir, min=1.0) numerator = torch.sqrt(maxIr) / M.clamp(min=1e-9) maxdenom = torch.sqrt(torch.max(torch.where(M == 1, maxIr, torch.tensor(0.0, device=Y.device)))) return numerator / maxdenom def initializebanks(Fphy, K, Ffg, Ns, Nd): """ Initialize structure and detail Gaussian banks from anchors and capacity field. Returns: Gs0, Gd0 """ # The exact anchor-to-Gaussian mapping and capacity sampling are not specified in the sources. # This function would deterministically place Ns structure Gaussians at K # and sample Nd detail Gaussians weighted by Ffg. Gs0 = torch.zeros(Ns, 10) Gd0 = torch.zeros(Nd, 10) return Gs0, Gd0 def structurediffusionstep(Gst, Fphy, Ds, alphabart, phis, phisinv, Gs0, t): """ One step of structure diffusion reverse process. """ ms = Gst[:,:3] fs = samplefeatures(Fphy, ms) # zs is the initial token for each primitive qs = computeattentionweight(ms) wq = 0.15 + 0.85 qs context = torch.cat([zs, fs, phis(Gst[:, 3:])], dim=-1) cs = wq.unsqueeze(-1) Ms(context) epshat = Ds(Gst, cs, t) deltaxitminus1 = (1.0 / math.sqrt(alphabart)) (Gst - math.sqrt(1 - alphabart) epshat) Gstminus1 = phisinv(deltaxitminus1) + Gs0 Gstminus1 = centerclip(Gstminus1) Gstminus1 = positivefloor(Gstminus1) return Gstminus1 def detaildiffusionstep(Gdt, Gs, Fphy, Dd, alphabart, phid, phidinv, Gd0, t): """ One step of detail diffusion reverse process. """ contextd = computedetailcontext(Gs, Gdt, Fphy) epshat = Dd(Gdt, contextd, t) deltaxitminus1 = (1.0 / math.sqrt(alphabart)) (Gdt - math.sqrt(1 - alphabart) epshat) Gdtminus1 = phidinv(deltaxitminus1) + Gd0 Gdtminus1 = centerclip(Gdtminus1) Gdtminus1 = positivefloor(Gdtminus1) return Gdtminus1 def rendergaussians(Gs, Gd): """ Render attenuation field from structure and detail banks. """ attenuation = renderbank(Gs) + renderbank(Gd) return attenuation def trainstageI(Y, Ns, Nd, Ds, Dd, Ephy, Ekp, Efg, Ms, phis, phid): """ Stage I: Alternating structure and detail updates. """ Wr = normalizedinversenoisereliability(Y, I0, M) V0 = FBP(Y) Fphy = Ephy(V0, UBP(Wr (Y - Proj(V0)))) K = Ekp(Fphy) Ffg = Efg(Fphy, K) Gs0, Gd0 = initializebanks(Fphy, K, Ffg, Ns, Nd) for t in range(T, 0, -1): Gst = addnoise(Gs0, t) Gstminus1 = structurediffusionstep(Gst, Fphy, Ds, alphabarst, phis, phisinv, Gs0, t) Gdt = addnoise(Gd0, t) Gdtminus1 = detaildiffusionstep(Gdt, Gstminus1, Fphy, Dd, alphabardt, phid, phidinv, Gd0, t) lossdiff = computediffusionloss(epshat, epstrue) lossaux = computeauxloss(K, Ffg, Gs, Gd) lossdiff.backward() lossaux.backward() def trainstageII(Gs, Gd, Y, RefinementNet): """ Stage II: Refinement network training. """ Attenuation = rendergaussians(Gs, Gd) Voxel = voxelize(Attenuation) RefinedVoxel = RefinementNet(Voxel) loss = L1(RefinedVoxel, ReferenceCT) loss.backward() Time Complexity: Inference is feed-forward, consisting of a single pass through the physics encoder, anchor/capacity predictors, and two diffusion hierarchies. The complexity is dominated by the diffusion steps (T) and the size of the Gaussian banks (Ns, Nd). Each diffusion step involves sampling features and passing through MLPs/denoisers. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the physics feature pyramid, the two Gaussian banks, and the diffusion states during inference. The fixed-cardinality banks make memory usage predictable. Performance: Designed for extreme CT reconstruction (sparse-view, low-dose, limited-angle). It outperforms single-bank Gaussian reconstruction and dense voxel diffusion in these challenging settings by separating structure and detail. Strengths: Handles degraded projections well; explicit Gaussian representation allows for efficient rendering; hierarchical diffusion improves detail recovery. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of diffusion schedules and loss weights; initialization from anchors may fail if anatomical cues are absent; two-stage training adds complexity. HiGDiff was proposed in "Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion for Extreme CT Reconstruction" (2026). It builds on the line of work using discretized Gaussian functions for continuous representation. It extends DiffGS, which demonstrated generative modeling of Gaussian attributes, and UltraGS, which adapted Gaussian attributes to medical image formation. HiGDiff integrates explicit Gaussian representation, spatially selective capacity allocation, and a feed-forward structure-to-detail diffusion hierarchy. name: Amortized Image Reconstruction (AIR)
head: Self-Supervised Feed-Forward 2D Gaussian Splatting
body: Amortized Image Reconstruction (AIR) is a self-supervised feed-forward framework that reconstructs a target image into a set of 2D Gaussian primitives in a single network pass, eliminating the costly per-image iterative optimization required by prior methods like GaussianImage. Unlike Instant-GI, which relies on handcrafted priors and pseudo-labels for initialization, AIR uses a stage-wise residual architecture to progressively predict Gaussian primitives from reconstruction residuals, achieving higher quality with encoding times of 160–300 ms. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target RGB image I{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Output: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{\mun, \Sigman, cn\}{n=1}^N, where N is the number of primitives. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive n is defined by: 1. Center: \mun \in \mathbb{R}^2, the 2D coordinates on the image plane. 2. Covariance: \Sigman \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, a symmetric positive-definite matrix. To ensure positive definiteness, it is parameterized by a rotation angle \thetan and scale factors s{n1}, s{n2}: \Sigman = (Rn Sn) (Rn Sn)^T where Rn is a 2D rotation matrix determined by \thetan, and Sn = \text{diag}(s{n1}, s{n2}). 3. Color: cn \in \mathbb{R}^3, the RGB color value. The source notes cn absorbs opacity in the baseline GaussianImage formulation. Rendering: The rendered image I{render} is computed via differentiable rasterization R(\cdot). For a pixel p, the color Cp is a weighted aggregation of all Gaussians n covering p: Cp = \frac{\sum{n \in \mathcal{N}(p)} cn \alpha{n,p}}{\sum{n \in \mathcal{N}(p)} \alpha{n,p}} where \mathcal{N}(p) is the set of Gaussians covering pixel p, and the weight \alpha{n,p} is: \alpha{n,p} = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} d{n,p}^T \Sigman^{-1} d{n,p} \right) where d{n,p} = p - \mun is the offset vector. Inference Algorithm: AIR reconstructs an image through stage-wise residual Gaussian prediction. 1. Initialization: Start with an empty Gaussian set \mathcal{G}0 = \emptyset and rendered image I0 = 0. 2. Stage-wise Prediction: For each stage k = 1, \dots, K: a. Compute the current reconstruction residual R{k-1} = I{gt} - I{k-1}, where I{k-1} = R(\mathcal{G}{k-1}). b. The feed-forward predictor network takes I{gt} and R{k-1} as input to predict a new set of Gaussian primitives \Delta \mathcal{G}k. c. Stage Control: An explicit mechanism activates new primitives only in under-reconstructed regions (where residual error is high) to ensure compactness. d. Update the accumulated set: \mathcal{G}k = \mathcal{G}{k-1} \cup \Delta \mathcal{G}k. e. Render the current accumulated set to get Ik = R(\mathcal{G}k). 3. Final Output: The final Gaussian set is \mathcal{G}K. Training Strategy (Predict–Optimize–Distill): Direct supervision with rendering loss is unstable due to the under-constrained mapping from image space to Gaussian space. AIR uses a distillation approach: 1. Predict: The predictor outputs \Delta \mathcal{G}k for the current stage. 2. Optimize: A detached copy of the accumulated Gaussian set \mathcal{G}{k-1} \cup \Delta \mathcal{G}k is refined using a few steps of differentiable rendering optimization (gradient descent on Gaussian parameters) to minimize L{render}(R(\mathcal{G}), I{gt}). Let the refined set be \mathcal{G}^{k}. 3. Distill: The refined set \mathcal{G}^{k} serves as a regression target in Gaussian space. The predictor is supervised by the difference between its output \Delta \mathcal{G}k and the increment required to reach \mathcal{G}^{k} from \mathcal{G}{k-1}. 4. Finetuning: After the POD training strategy stabilizes the multi-stage predictor, AIR is jointly finetuned across all stages with direct rendering supervision on the whole Gaussian set \mathcal{G}K. Quantization: An image-adaptive quantizer is applied to the predicted Gaussian parameters to enable compact Gaussian storage without per-image post-optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn from typing import List, Dict, Tuple def computecovariance(theta: torch.Tensor, s: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Compute Sigma = (RS)(RS)^T from angle theta and scale s.""" cost = torch.cos(theta) sint = torch.sin(theta) R = torch.stack([torch.stack([cost, -sint]), torch.stack([sint, cost])]) S = torch.diagembed(s) RS = torch.matmul(R, S) return torch.matmul(RS, RS.transpose(-2, -1)) def rendergaussians(gaussians: List[Dict], imgh: int, imgw: int) -> torch.Tensor: """Differentiable rasterization of 2D Gaussians. Returns rendered image (H, W, 3).""" outimg = torch.zeros((imgh, imgw, 3), device=gaussians[0]['mu'].device) for y in range(imgh): for x in range(imgw): pixelpos = torch.tensor([x, y], dtype=torch.float32, device=gaussians[0]['mu'].device) numerator = torch.zeros(3, device=gaussians[0]['mu'].device) denominator = torch.tensor(0.0, device=gaussians[0]['mu'].device) for g in gaussians: mu = g['mu'] cov = g['cov'] try: covinv = torch.inverse(cov) except RuntimeError: continue d = pixelpos - mu alpha = torch.exp(-0.5 torch.matmul(d.t(), torch.matmul(covinv, d))) if alpha < 1e-6: continue numerator += g['c'] alpha denominator += alpha if denominator > 0: outimg[y, x] = numerator / denominator return outimg def optimizegaussians(gaussians: List[Dict], target: torch.Tensor, steps: int) -> List[Dict]: """Refines a detached copy of Gaussians via gradient descent to match target image.""" # Standard Adam optimizer with L1 loss is assumed for this step. optgaussians = [dict(g) for g in gaussians] for in range(steps): rendered = rendergaussians(optgaussians, target.shape[0], target.shape[1]) loss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(rendered, target) loss.backward() # Optimizer step and zerograd omitted for brevity return optgaussians def computegaussianspaceloss(predictednew: List[Dict], optimizedtotal: List[Dict], accumulated: List[Dict]) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes regression loss between predicted increments and optimized increments in Gaussian parameter space.""" # Standard L1/L2 loss between predicted parameters and optimized parameters is assumed. loss = torch.tensor(0.0, device=predictednew[0]['mu'].device) for p, o in zip(predictednew, optimizedtotal[len(accumulated):]): loss += torch.nn.functional.l1loss(p['mu'], o['mu']) loss += torch.nn.functional.l1loss(p['theta'], o['theta']) loss += torch.nn.functional.l1loss(p['s'], o['s']) loss += torch.nn.functional.l1loss(p['c'], o['c']) return loss def stagecontrolmask(residual: torch.Tensor, threshold: float) -> torch.Tensor: """Returns binary mask activating primitives only in under-reconstructed regions.""" # Standard thresholding on residual magnitude is assumed. return (residual.abs().mean(dim=-1) > threshold).float() class AIRPredictor(nn.Module): """Feed-forward network predicting Gaussian primitives.""" def init(self): super().init() # Encoder-Decoder architecture details omitted as not specified in source self.encoder = nn.Identity() self.decoder = nn.Identity() def forward(self, image: torch.Tensor, residual: torch.Tensor) -> List[Dict]: """Predicts a list of Gaussian primitives given the input image and residual.""" # Implementation specific to the paper's architecture # Inputs: image (H, W, 3), residual (H, W, 3) # Output: List of dicts with keys 'mu', 'theta', 's', 'c' pass # Network forward pass implementation omitted def trainstepaire(imagegt: torch.Tensor, predictor: AIRPredictor, numstages: int = 3, threshold: float = 0.05): """Simplified training loop illustrating the POD strategy.""" gaussians = [] currentrendered = torch.zeroslike(imagegt) for k in range(numstages): residual = imagegt - currentrendered # Predict new primitives based on residual newprimitives = predictor(imagegt, residual) # Stage Control: filter predictions based on residual magnitude mask = stagecontrolmask(residual, threshold) # Masking logic applied to predicted primitives omitted # Optimize (Distillation Target Generation) tempgaussians = gaussians + newprimitives refinedgaussians = optimizegaussians(tempgaussians, imagegt, steps=5) # Distill distillloss = computegaussianspaceloss(newprimitives, refinedgaussians, gaussians) distillloss.backward() # Update accumulated set gaussians = refinedgaussians currentrendered = rendergaussians(gaussians, imagegt.shape[0], imagegt.shape[1]) return gaussians Parameters: Number of Stages (K): Not given in the sources, but described as "stage-wise". Encoding Time: 160–300 ms on Kodak and DIV2K datasets. Optimization Steps (POD): "A few" differentiable rendering optimization steps are used during the distillation phase. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Under-constrained Mapping: Direct supervision with rendering loss leads to unstable optimization. The POD strategy is required to stabilize training. Primitive Allocation: Without Stage Control, predicting primitives uniformly may lead to redundancy. The explicit Stage Control mechanism ensures new primitives are only activated in under-reconstructed regions. Compactness: The goal is to find the smallest Gaussian set G^ satisfying a fidelity target \epsilon: G^ \in \arg \minG |G| \text{ s.t. } L{render}(R(G), I{gt}) \le \epsilon. Time Complexity: Encoding time is 160–300 ms per image on standard datasets (Kodak, DIV2K), significantly faster than iterative methods like GaussianImage which require per-image optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses an image-adaptive quantizer for compact Gaussian storage, reducing memory footprint compared to unquantized representations. Strengths: Fully self-supervised and end-to-end; eliminates per-image test-time optimization; achieves better reconstruction quality than Instant-GI and GaussianImage; no reliance on handcrafted priors (e.g., PPM, dithering). Limitations: Relies on a trained feed-forward network, so it generalizes based on the training data distribution; the POD training strategy adds complexity to the training pipeline compared to direct supervised learning. When to Use: When fast, high-quality image reconstruction into 2D Gaussian splats is required without per-image optimization overhead. When Not to Use: When per-image iterative refinement is acceptable for higher fidelity, or when the input images are significantly out-of-distribution from the training set (Kodak/DIV2K). AIR was introduced by Yuesong Wang in a preprint titled "AIR: Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework for Self-Supervised Feed-Forward 2D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of existing 2D Gaussian image reconstruction methods, which either rely on costly per-image iterative optimization (GaussianImage, Image-GS) or handcrafted priors and pseudo-labels (Instant-GI). The method builds on the 2D Gaussian splatting formulation introduced in GaussianImage. name: UniQueR
body: UniQueR is a feedforward framework for fast 3D reconstruction from unposed images using sparse learnable 3D queries. It predicts camera-to-world transforms and per-view local point maps, then uses queries to spawn Gaussians rendered via differentiable splatting for supervision. It sets itself apart from siblings like TokenGS by decoupling 3D Gaussian prediction from pixels with learnable implicit tokens, and avoids the quadratic complexity of full self-attention on concatenated tokens by using decoupled attention between image tokens and 3D queries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N of the same scene, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Camera poses are not provided. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} and camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^N. Data Structures: Image Tokens: Ti \in \mathbb{R}^{(HW/p^2) \times d}, extracted from each image Ii. Queries: A fixed set of Q learnable queries \mathcal{Q} = \{qi\}{i=1}^Q. Each query qi has a latent embedding and an explicit 3D coordinate pi. Gaussian Set: \mathcal{G} = \bigcup{i=1}^Q \bigcup{k=1}^K (pi + \delta{qi} + \delta{g{ik}}, \Sigma{ik}, c{ik}, \alpha{ik}), where \Sigma{ik} is the covariance, c{ik} is the color, and \alpha{ik} is the opacity. Parameters: Q = 4096: Fixed budget of learnable 3D queries. K = 64: Number of Gaussians spawned per query. p: Patch size of the Vision Transformer backbone (typically 14). d: Token dimensionality of the backbone. \lambdad = 0.1: Weight for the scale-invariant rendered-depth loss. \lambdac = 0.2: Weight for the backbone camera loss. Total Gaussians: Q \times K = 262,144. Steps: 1. Image Tokenization: Extract per-frame visual tokens using a Vision Transformer backbone: Ti = \text{ViT}(Ii) \in \mathbb{R}^{(HW/p^2) \times d} where T = HW/p^2 is the number of tokens per image. 2. Cross-View Aggregation: Apply an alternating-attention (AA) transformer to aggregate tokens across N views: \{T^{l+1}i\} = \text{AA-Transformer}(\{T^li\}) where l is the layer index. This alternates between intra-frame and inter-frame attention operations. 3. Geometric Decoding: Decode the aggregated tokens into per-frame geometric annotations: \{Pi, Xi, Ci\} = \text{Decoder}(\{T^li\}) where Pi \in SE(3) is the camera-to-world transform, Xi \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W} is the local point map, and Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} is the confidence map. 4. Query Initialization: Initialize Q queries with hybrid coordinates: Half of the query coordinates are sampled from the predicted non-metric point maps Xi, providing geometric grounding on observed surfaces. The remaining queries are initialized uniformly in the normalized 3D scene range. Random-only initialization is unstable in dense reconstruction because only 2D rendered image losses are available, not ground-truth 3D boxes. 5. Positional Encoding: Convert predicted camera poses Pi into Plücker ray embeddings to serve as positional encodings for the image tokens. Each query qi uses its 3D coordinate pi as its positional embedding. 6. Query Refinement: Update queries using a 12-layer Query Transformer with decoupled attention. In each layer: Q = \text{Cross-Attn}(Q, T) Q = \text{Self-Attn}(Q) This decoupled design reduces complexity from O((Q + NT)^2) to O(QNT + Q^2), enabling scaling to high-resolution images. 7. Gaussian Spawning: For each query qi at location pi: Predict a deformation \delta{qi}. The cluster center becomes pi + \delta{qi}. An MLP decodes K local offsets \delta{g{ik}} for k=1 \dots K. Attribute heads predict opacity \alpha{ik}, scale, rotation, and color c{ik} for each spawned Gaussian. The final Gaussian set is defined as: \mathcal{G} = \bigcup{i=1}^Q \bigcup{k=1}^K (pi + \delta{qi} + \delta{g{ik}}, \Sigma{ik}, c{ik}, \alpha{ik}) 8. Rendering: Render the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} into RGB images \hat{I} and depth maps \hat{D} via differentiable splatting. 9. Supervision: Novel-View Supervision: Supervise renderings of a superset of input views (e.g., 6 renderings for 3 inputs). Held-out target views correct empty holes and discourage reproducing only input-view surfaces. Loss Function: The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}{depth} + \lambdac \mathcal{L}{cam} where \mathcal{L}{rgb} includes L1 and LPIPS in Stage 1, or only L1 in Stage 2. \mathcal{L}{depth} is the scale-invariant rendered-depth loss, and \mathcal{L}{cam} is the backbone camera loss. 10. Staged Training: Stage 1: Train at 224^2 resolution for 100 epochs. \mathcal{L}{rgb} includes L1 and LPIPS. Stage 2: Fine-tune at 448^2 resolution for 20 epochs. \mathcal{L}{rgb} uses only L1 because LPIPS substantially increases training time. The DINOv2 encoder, alternating-attention transformer, and point-map head are frozen. The camera head, Query Transformer, and GS heads are updated. 11. Post Optimization (TTO): Test-time optimization using predicted Gaussians and poses. Render back to input views, compute reconstruction losses, and backpropagate to refine Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class UniQueR: def init(self, Q=4096, K=64, patchsize=14, d=1024, numaalayers=7, numqtlayers=12): self.Q = Q self.K = K self.patchsize = patchsize self.d = d self.numaalayers = numaalayers self.numqtlayers = numqtlayers # Frozen backbone components self.dinov2 = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(3 patchsize patchsize, d) for in range(12)]) self.aatransformer = nn.ModuleList([nn.MultiheadAttention(d, 8) for in range(numaalayers)]) self.geometricdecoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(d, d), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(d, 3 H W + H W + 1)) # Trainable components self.camerahead = nn.Linear(d, 7) # SE(3) parameterization self.querytransformer = nn.ModuleList([ nn.ModuleDict({ 'crossattn': nn.MultiheadAttention(d, 8), 'selfattn': nn.MultiheadAttention(d, 8), 'ffn': nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, d 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(d 4, d)) }) for in range(numqtlayers) ]) self.gsmlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, d), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(d, K 3)) self.gsheads = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(d, 1 + 3 + 4 + 3) for in range(K)]) # alpha, scale, rot, color # Learnable query embeddings self.queryembeddings = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Q, d)) def forward(self, images): N = len(images) H, W = images[0].shape[1], images[0].shape[2] T = (H W) // (self.patchsize 2) # 1. Image Tokenization tokens = [] for img in images: patches = img.unfold(1, self.patchsize, self.patchsize).unfold(2, self.patchsize, self.patchsize) patches = patches.reshape(N, -1, 3 self.patchsize self.patchsize) ti = patches for layer in self.dinov2: ti = layer(ti) ti = ti + F.layernorm(ti, (ti.size(-1),)) tokens.append(ti) # 2. Cross-View Aggregation for layer in self.aatransformer: # Intra-frame attention tokens = [F.layernorm(layer(t, t, t)[0], (t.size(-1),)) for t in tokens] # Inter-frame attention (concatenate across views) stacked = torch.stack(tokens, dim=1) stacked = layer(stacked, stacked, stacked)[0] tokens = [stacked[:, i] for i in range(N)] # 3. Geometric Decoding poses = [] pointmaps = [] for t in tokens: out = self.geometricdecoder(t) # Decode to poses, point maps, confidence pi = self.camerahead(t.mean(dim=1)) xi = out[:,:3 H W].reshape(-1, 3, H, W) poses.append(pi) pointmaps.append(xi) # 4. Query Initialization # Sample half from point maps, half uniformly qcoords = torch.zeros(self.Q, 3) half = self.Q // 2 # Sample from transformed point maps (simplified gauge assumption) qcoords[:half] = pointmaps[0][:,:, torch.randint(0, H, (half,)), torch.randint(0, W, (half,))].T qcoords[half:] = torch.rand(half, 3) 2 - 1 # Uniform in [-1, 1]^3 qemb = self.queryembeddings.clone() # 5 & 6. Query Refinement (Decoupled Attention) for layer in self.querytransformer: # Cross-Attn: Queries attend to Image Tokens qemb = layer'crossattn', torch.stack(tokens, dim=1))[0] qemb = qemb + layer'ffn' # Self-Attn: Queries attend to Queries qemb = layer'selfattn'[0] qemb = qemb + layer'ffn' # 7. Gaussian Spawning deformations = self.gsmlp(qemb).reshape(self.Q, self.K, 3) querycenters = qcoords.unsqueeze(1) + deformations gaussians = [] for k in range(self.K): attr = self.gsheadsk alpha = torch.sigmoid(attr[:, 0]) scale = torch.exp(attr[:, 1:4]) rot = F.normalize(attr[:, 4:8], dim=1) color = torch.sigmoid(attr[:, 8:11]) gaussians.append((querycenters[:, k], scale, rot, color, alpha)) # 8. Rendering (Placeholder for standard differentiable splatting rasterizer) # renderedrgb, rendereddepth = splattingrasterize(gaussians, poses, H, W) # For self-containment, we return the structure ready for rasterization return gaussians, poses def computeloss(self, gaussians, poses, images, targetdepths, stage=1): # 8. Rendering renderedrgb, rendereddepth = splattingrasterize(gaussians, poses, images[0].shape[1], images[0].shape[2]) # 9. Supervision lrgb = F.l1loss(renderedrgb, images[0]) if stage == 1: lrgb = lrgb + lpipsloss(renderedrgb, images[0]) ldepth = scaleinvariantdepthloss(rendereddepth, targetdepths) lcam = cameraloss(poses) lambdad = 0.1 lambdac = 0.2 return lrgb + lambdad ldepth + lambdac lcam def splattingrasterize(gaussians, poses, H, W): # Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting differentiable rasterizer # Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorts by depth, alpha-blends pass def scaleinvariantdepthloss(pred, target): # Standard scale-invariant depth loss pass def cameraloss(poses): # Backbone camera supervision loss pass def lpipsloss(pred, target): # Perceptual loss pass Time Complexity: The decoupled attention design reduces the theoretical attention complexity from O((Q + NT)^2) to O(QNT + Q^2), where T = HW/p^2 is the number of tokens per image. This enables scaling to high-resolution images. Memory Complexity: Substantial memory savings compared to full self-attention, allowing the model to handle larger image sizes and more queries. Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 with 3 views, UniQueR achieves PSNR 22.70, SSIM 0.660, LPIPS 0.261, and inference time 0.416s on A100. On RealEstate10K with 2 input views, UniQueR achieves PSNR 20.50, SSIM 0.672, LPIPS 0.196. Model Size: UniQueR has 502.31M trainable parameters; the frozen backbone has 890.99M parameters (1.393B total). Strengths: Fast feedforward inference, handles unposed images, high-fidelity reconstruction with sparse inputs, and efficient attention mechanism. Limitations: Requires test-time optimization for best results, and LPIPS loss substantially increases training time in Stage 2. When to use: When fast, feedforward 3D reconstruction from unposed images is required, and computational resources for per-scene optimization are limited. UniQueR was proposed by C. Peng et al. in the paper "UniQueR: Unified Query-Based Feedforward 3D Reconstruction". It builds on the principles of feedforward reconstruction models like TokenGS but introduces sparse learnable 3D queries to decouple Gaussian prediction from pixels. The method leverages DINOv2 for feature extraction and alternating-attention transformers for cross-view aggregation, similar to VGGT and Pi3. It is trained on datasets including DL3DV-10K, ScanNet++, BlendedMVS, and Co3D.
