name: GS3
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based Self-Supervised framework
body: GS3 is an efficient self-supervised learning framework for learning point cloud representations by integrating fast 3D Gaussian Splatting into a rendering-based pretext task. It solves the problem of high computational cost and memory intensity inherent in existing volume rendering-based self-supervised methods. Unlike its sibling Ponder, which uses differentiable volume rendering with ray marching, GS3 employs a tile-based rasterizer to render 3D Gaussians, achieving significantly faster pre-training speeds and lower memory usage. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N sparse-view RGB-D images \{Ii, Di \mid Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, Di \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}\}{i=1}^N, camera intrinsic parameters \{Ki\}{i=1}^N, and camera poses \{Ti \mid Ti = [Ri | ti]\}{i=1}^N, where N is the number of views, and H, W are image dimensions. Outputs: A pre-trained point cloud encoder capable of extracting features from 3D point clouds, which can be fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as 3D semantic segmentation, 3D instance segmentation, 3D object detection, and 3D scene reconstruction. Data Structures: The method operates on a set of 3D points \mathcal{P} generated from the input RGB-D images. Each point p \in \mathcal{P} is associated with: Position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (RGB). Learned features \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^d (output of the point cloud encoder). From these features, 3D Gaussian primitives are predicted. Each Gaussian gj is defined by: Mean \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance \Sigmaj \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (parameterized by scale and rotation). Opacity \alphaj \in [0, 1]. Color cj (typically spherical harmonics coefficients or RGB). Steps: 1. Back-projection: For each input view i, back-project the RGB-D image into 3D space to generate a colored point cloud. For each pixel (u, v) with depth d, compute the 3D point \mathbf{x} = [x, y, z]^T in the world coordinate system using the camera intrinsic matrix Ki and pose Ti = [Ri | ti]: \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = Ri^{-1} \left( d \cdot Ki^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - ti \right) Append the RGB color of the pixel to the corresponding 3D point. 2. Feature Encoding: Input the generated point clouds into a point cloud encoder to extract point-wise features \mathbf{f} for each point. 3. Gaussian Parameter Prediction: Predict the 3D Gaussian primitive parameters (locations \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and color c) aligned with the input points based on the learned features \mathbf{f}. 4. Rendering: Employ a real-time tile-based rasterizer (based on 3D Gaussian Splatting) to render RGB images from the predicted 3D Gaussians given the specific camera intrinsic parameters and poses. 5. Training: Train the model by minimizing the difference between the rendered RGB images and the input real RGB images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def meshgrid(width, height): u = np.arange(width).reshape(1, -1) v = np.arange(height).reshape(-1, 1) return np.broadcastto(u, (height, width)), np.broadcastto(v, (height, width)) def computel1loss(rendered, target): return np.mean(np.abs(rendered - target)) def gs3pretraining(inputrgbds, inputposes, inputintrinsics, encoder, gaussianhead, renderer): """ inputrgbds: List of (H, W, 3) RGB images and (H, W) Depth maps inputposes: List of (4, 4) transformation matrices [R|t] inputintrinsics: List of (3, 3) intrinsic matrices K encoder: Point cloud feature extractor gaussianhead: Network predicting Gaussian params from features renderer: Tile-based 3D Gaussian rasterizer Returns: Pre-trained encoder weights """ points3dlist = [] # Step 1: Back-projection to generate colored point clouds for i in range(len(inputrgbds)): I, D = inputrgbds[i] K = inputintrinsics[i] T = inputposes[i] Rinv = np.linalg.inv(T[:3,:3]) t = T[:3, 3] # Get pixel coordinates (u, v) and depth d u, v = meshgrid(I.shape[1], I.shape[0]) d = D # Flatten arrays for vectorized operation uflat = u.flatten() vflat = v.flatten() dflat = d.flatten() # Homogeneous pixel coordinates pixelhomo = np.vstack([uflat, vflat, np.oneslike(uflat)]) # Back-projection formula: x = R^-1 (d K^-1 [u,v,1]^T - t) Kinv = np.linalg.inv(K) pixelhomoinv = Kinv @ pixelhomo scaled = dflat[:, None] pixelhomoinv shifted = scaled - t[:, None] xworld = (Rinv @ shifted.T).T # Shape: (Npixels, 3) # Get RGB colors colors = I.reshape(-1, 3) # Create point cloud: positions and colors points = np.hstack([xworld, colors]) points3dlist.append(points) # Step 2 & 3: Encode and Predict Gaussians # Concatenate all points from all views for batch processing allpoints = np.vstack(points3dlist) positions = allpoints[:,:3] # Extract features using encoder features = encoder(positions) # Predict Gaussian parameters from features gaussians = gaussianhead(features) # Step 4: Render renderedimages = [] for i in range(len(inputrgbds)): K = inputintrinsics[i] T = inputposes[i] # Render the full set of gaussians from this view img = renderer.render(gaussians, K, T) renderedimages.append(img) # Step 5: Compute Loss and Update totalloss = 0 for i in range(len(inputrgbds)): target = inputrgbds[i][0] # RGB image rendered = renderedimages[i] loss = computel1loss(rendered, target) totalloss += loss # Standard gradient descent update totalloss.backward() encoder.optimizer.step() gaussianhead.optimizer.step() encoder.zerograd() gaussianhead.zerograd() return encoder Parameters: Rendered Image Resolution: Pre-training time and memory usage are measured at 320 \times 240 resolution. Number of Views (N): Sparse views (exact number not specified, but typically small, e.g., 2-4). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Accuracy: The quality of the back-projected point cloud depends heavily on the accuracy of the input depth maps Di. Speed: GS3 achieves approximately 9\times pre-training speedup compared to the baseline method Ponder. Memory: GS3 uses less than 0.25\times the memory cost of Ponder during pre-training. Performance Context: Measurements were taken at a rendered image resolution of 320 \times 240. Strengths: High efficiency in pre-training due to the use of tile-based rasterization instead of ray marching. Enables generalizable pre-training for point cloud encoders. Limitations: Relies on the availability of RGB-D inputs for pre-training. Performance on downstream tasks depends on the quality of the pre-trained encoder. When to use: When pre-training a point cloud encoder for downstream 3D vision tasks (segmentation, detection) with limited annotations and computational resources. When not to use: When only RGB inputs are available without depth, or when per-scene optimization (not pre-training) is required. GS3 was proposed by Hao Liu, Minglin Chen, Yanni Ma, Haihong Xiao, and Ying He from Nanyang Technological University, Sun Yat-Sen University, and South China University of Technology. It was published on arXiv in November 2024. The method addresses the computational demands of existing rendering-based self-supervised frameworks like Ponder, which use differentiable volume rendering with dozens of point queries along each ray. GS3 is the first attempt to explore generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting for point cloud self-supervised learning. name: DIF-Gaussian
body: DIF-Gaussian is a feed-forward neural network that reconstructs a 3D volume from multi-view 2D projections by predicting 3D Gaussian parameters at sampled points and decoding features via Gaussian interpolation. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the feature aggregation step as a differentiable Gaussian splatting operation, allowing the network to learn spatial priors directly in the Gaussian domain rather than through standard grid-based or point-based interpolation. Inputs: Multi-view 2D projections. Outputs: Reconstructed 3D volume values at query points. Data Structures: The method outputs a dictionary gsparams containing the following fields with exact layouts: feats: Feature vectors, shape [B, C, K] where B is batch size, C is feature dimension, and K is the number of Gaussians. offsets: Gaussian mean offsets, shape [B, K, 3]. det: Determinant of the covariance matrix, shape [B, K]. inv: Inverse of the covariance matrix, shape [B, K, 3, 3]. Parameters: gsres: Grid resolution for point spacing. pdistscaling: Scaling factor for point distance. oscaling: Offset scaling factor. sscaling: Scaling factor for Gaussian size. t: Temperature/scale factor for Gaussian parameters, computed as t = 1.0 / \text{gs\cfg}.t. Steps: 1. Encoding: Encode multi-view projections using a U-Net to extract features. 2. Feature Query: Query view features at projected 3D points using max-pooling fusion to obtain pfeats. 3. MLP Processing: Pass fused features through gsfeatsmlp and gsparamsmlp. 4. Parameter Decoding: Decode Gaussian parameters (offsets, scaling, rotation) from MLP outputs. 5. Covariance Computation: Compute the covariance matrix, its determinant, and its inverse. 6. Inference/Rendering: Interpolate features at query points using Gaussian weights, concatenate with view features, and pass through a point decoder to predict volume values. Formulas: The point distance \text{p\dist} is computed as: \text{p\dist} = \frac{1}{\text{gs\res}} \times \text{p\dist\scaling}. The maximum offset distance is: \text{max\dist} = \text{p\dist} \times 0.5 \times \text{o\scaling}. The offsets are decoded from the MLP output offsetsraw as: \text{offsets} = (\sigma(\text{offsets\raw}) - 0.5) \times 2 \times \text{max\dist} where \sigma is the sigmoid function. The mean scale is: s{\text{mean}} = \sqrt{\text{p\dist}}. The scale s is decoded from sraw as: s = \sigma(s{\text{raw}}) \times 2 \times \text{s\scaling} \times s{\text{mean}} + (1 - \text{s\scaling}) \times s{\text{mean}}. This maps the sigmoid output (0, 1) to the range ((1-k)d, (1+k)d) where k = \text{s\scaling} and d = s{\text{mean}}. The rotation r is taken directly from the MLP output as a quaternion of shape [B, K, 4]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def buildrotation(q): """Converts quaternion [B, 4] (w, x, y, z) to rotation matrix [B, 3, 3].""" w, x, y, z = q[:, 0], q[:, 1], q[:, 2], q[:, 3] R = torch.zeros((q.size(0), 3, 3), dtype=torch.float, device=q.device) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (yy + zz) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (xx + zz) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (xx + yy) return R def buildcovariance(s, q): """Computes covariance matrix from scale [B, N, 3] and quaternion [B, N, 4].""" b, n = s.shape[:2] sflat = s.reshape(b n, 3) qflat = q.reshape(b n, 4) R = buildrotation(qflat) L = torch.zeros((b n, 3, 3), dtype=torch.float, device=s.device) L[:, 0, 0] = sflat[:, 0] L[:, 1, 1] = sflat[:, 1] L[:, 2, 2] = sflat[:, 2] L = R @ L Cov = L @ L.transpose(1, 2) return Cov.reshape(b, n, 3, 3) def querygs(querypoints, gscenters, gsparams): """Interpolates features at query points using Gaussian weights.""" feats = gsparams['feats'] # [B, C, K] inv = gsparams['inv'] # [B, K, 3, 3] det = gsparams['det'] # [B, K] centers = gscenters # [B, K, 3] diff = querypoints.unsqueeze(2) - centers.unsqueeze(1) # [B, P, K, 3] invdiff = torch.matmul(diff, inv) # [B, P, K, 3] dist = torch.sum(invdiff diff, dim=3) # [B, P, K] weights = torch.exp(-0.5 dist) / torch.sqrt(det) # [B, P, K] weights = weights / (weights.sum(dim=2, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) interpfeats = torch.matmul(feats.transpose(1, 2), weights.transpose(1, 2)) # [B, C, P] return interpfeats class PointDecoder(torch.nn.Module): """Point-wise prediction network with residual connections.""" def init(self, channels, residual=True, usebn=True): super().init() self.residual = residual self.mlps = torch.nn.ModuleList() for i in range(len(channels) - 1): modules = [] if i == 0 or not self.residual: modules.append(torch.nn.Conv1d(channels[i], channels[i + 1], kernelsize=1)) else: modules.append(torch.nn.Conv1d(channels[i] + channels[0], channels[i + 1], kernelsize=1)) if i != len(channels) - 1: if usebn: modules.append(torch.nn.BatchNorm1d(channels[i + 1])) modules.append(torch.nn.LeakyReLU(inplace=True)) self.mlps.append(torch.nn.Sequential(modules)) def forward(self, x): x = x for i, m in enumerate(self.mlps): if i != 0 and self.residual: x = torch.cat([x, x], dim=1) x = m(x) return x def difgaussianforward(gscfg, gsres, encoderoutput, pfeats, querypoints, querygspoints): """Main forward pass for DIF-Gaussian.""" # 1. Parameter Decoding gsparamsraw = encoderoutput['gsparamsraw'] t = 1.0 / gscfg.t gsparams = gsparamsraw / t pdist = 1.0 / gsres gscfg.pdistscaling maxdist = pdist 0.5 gscfg.oscaling smean = np.sqrt(pdist) offsetsraw = gsparams[:,:3,:].transpose(1, 2) # [B, K, 3] offsets = (torch.sigmoid(offsetsraw) - 0.5) 2 maxdist sraw = gsparams[:, 3:6,:].transpose(1, 2) # [B, K, 3] s = torch.sigmoid(sraw) 2 gscfg.sscaling smean + (1 - gscfg.sscaling) smean r = gsparams[:, 6:,:].transpose(1, 2) # [B, K, 4] Cov = buildcovariance(s, r) det = torch.linalg.det(Cov) inv = torch.linalg.inv(Cov) gsparamsdict = { 'feats': encoderoutput['feats'], 'offsets': offsets, 'det': det, 'inv': inv } # 2. Feature Interpolation interpfeats = querygs(querypoints, querygspoints, gsparamsdict) # 3. Point-wise Prediction pfeatsfinal = torch.cat([pfeats, interpfeats], dim=1) # Example channel configuration matching typical decoder stacks ppred = PointDecoder([pfeatsfinal.size(1)] + [64, 64, 1])(pfeatsfinal) return ppred, gsparamsdict Edge Cases and Pitfalls: U-Net Padding Mismatch: When using skip connections in the U-Net encoder, upsampling may cause dimension mismatches. This is handled by padding the upsampled feature map using F.pad with diffX // 2 and diffY // 2 to align with the skip connection features. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly models spatial feature aggregation using Gaussian splatting. Limitations: Relies on a fixed grid resolution (gsres) for point spacing. When to use: Suitable for 3D volume reconstruction from multi-view projections, such as in CBCT (Cone Beam Computed Tomography). When not to use: Not suitable for per-scene optimization or scenes where camera poses are unknown and uncalibrated [Parent]. The method builds on the principles of feed-forward generalizable reconstruction, extending them by incorporating Gaussian splatting for feature interpolation [Parent, S1, unofficial]. It is used for CBCT volume reconstruction. xmed-lab/DIF-Gaussian, https://github.com/xmed-lab/DIF-Gaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Compact Feed-Forward 3D Gaussians via Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging
head: Compact FF-3DGS
body: Compact Feed-Forward 3D Gaussians via Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging is a post-processing pipeline that consolidates redundant, per-pixel 3D Gaussians produced by any feed-forward Gaussian predictor into a compact, content-adaptive set. It solves the inefficiency of per-pixel primitives by grouping spatially coherent Gaussians via saliency-guided superpixel segmentation, compressing them into latent representations, and merging them across views, retaining visual quality at approximately 1/20th of the original primitive count. Unlike uniform discretization or detection-based reduction methods, it is backbone-agnostic and operates as a plug-in module without retraining the underlying feed-forward network. The method takes a set of per-pixel 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{FF} generated by a feed-forward backbone and outputs a compact set \mathcal{G}K with a controllable number of primitives K. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Per-pixel 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{FF} = \{G1, \dots, GN\} from a feed-forward method, where each Gi is defined by mean \mui, quaternion qi, scale si, opacity \alphai, and SH coefficients \hat{c}{0...M,i}. Input views Iv are also used for saliency estimation. Output: A compact set of K Gaussians \mathcal{G}K. Data Structures: Per-pixel Gaussian Gi: Defined by \Thetai = (\mui, qi, si, \alphai, \hat{c}{0...M,i}). Saliency Map \lambdav: A per-view map guiding segmentation granularity. Superpixel Segmentation Mv: A partition of pixels into clusters based on \lambdav. Latent Representation: A compressed vector encoding a cluster of Gaussians, produced by the encoder. Numbered Steps: 1. Per-view Preprocessing: Input views Iv are processed by a frozen feed-forward Gaussian Splatting (FF-GS) backbone to produce per-pixel 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{FF}. 2. Segmentation: A saliency map \lambdav is computed for each view. This map guides an adaptive superpixel segmentation Mv, which groups spatially coherent and perceptually similar per-pixel Gaussians into variable-size clusters. Textured regions receive fine segments; homogeneous areas receive coarse segments. 3. Encoding: A learned set-attention encoder M{enc} processes each cluster from Mv and compresses it into a compact latent representation. 4. Matching: The latent representations from different views are matched based on geometric overlap and feature similarity. 5. Merging: A learned merger M{mrg} consolidates the matched representations from multiple views into a unified set. 6. Refinement: A local self-attention module refines the merged representations to improve coherence. 7. Decoding: A level-of-detail decoder M{dec} produces the final Gaussians \mathcal{G}K at a controllable resolution K. Parameters: K: The controllable resolution or number of output Gaussians per cluster/scene. Typical values shown in the source are K=1, 2, 4. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compactff3dgs(inputviews, ffbackbone, encoder, merger, decoder, K): """ Consolidates per-pixel Gaussians into a compact set. Args: inputviews: List of input images Iv. ffbackbone: Frozen feed-forward network predicting per-pixel Gaussians. encoder: Set-attention encoder Menc. merger: Learned merger Mmrg. decoder: Level-of-detail decoder Mdec. K: Target number of output Gaussians. Returns: GK: Compact set of K Gaussians. """ # Step 1: Per-view Preprocessing # Generate per-pixel Gaussians GFF from the frozen backbone GFF = ffbackbone(inputviews) # Step 2: Segmentation # Compute saliency maps and perform adaptive superpixel segmentation superpixelclusters = [] for viewidx, Iv in enumerate(inputviews): lambdav = computesaliency(Iv) # Group spatially coherent Gaussians based on lambdav # This creates variable-size clusters: fine for textured, coarse for homogeneous clusters = adaptivesuperpixelsegmentation(GFF[viewidx], lambdav) superpixelclusters.append(clusters) # Step 3: Encoding # Compress each cluster into a latent representation latentrepresentations = [] for viewidx, clusters in enumerate(superpixelclusters): viewlatents = [] for cluster in clusters: # Encode the set of Gaussians in the cluster latent = encoder(cluster) viewlatents.append(latent) latentrepresentations.append(viewlatents) # Step 4: Matching # Match representations across views based on geometric overlap and feature similarity matchedgroups = matchacrossviews(latentrepresentations) # Step 5: Merging # Consolidate matched representations mergedlatents = [] for group in matchedgroups: # Merge the matched latent representations mergedlatent = merger(group) mergedlatents.append(mergedlatent) # Step 6: Refinement # Refine the result using local self-attention refinedlatents = localselfattentionrefinement(mergedlatents) # Step 7: Decoding # Produce final Gaussians at controllable resolution K GK = decoder(refinedlatents, K) return GK def computesaliency(Iv): # Computes a saliency map lambdav from the input view Iv # Uses standard edge and texture detection to guide segmentation granularity return edgeandtexturescore(Iv) def adaptivesuperpixelsegmentation(Gview, lambdav): # Groups spatially coherent and perceptually similar per-pixel Gaussians # into variable-size clusters based on the saliency map lambdav clusters = [] visited = set() for i, Gi in enumerate(Gview): if i in visited: continue cluster = [Gi] visited.add(i) for j, Gj in enumerate(Gview): if j in visited: continue if spatialdistance(Gi.mu, Gj.mu) < PROXIMITYTHRESHOLD and featuresimilarity(Gi, Gj) > lambdav: cluster.append(Gj) visited.add(j) clusters.append(cluster) return clusters def matchacrossviews(latentrepresentations): # Matches latent representations across views based on geometric overlap and feature similarity # Groups latents that correspond to the same 3D structure across different camera poses matchedgroups = {} for viewidx, viewlatents in enumerate(latentrepresentations): for idx, latent in enumerate(viewlatents): key = (viewidx, idx) matchedgroups[key] = latent # Consolidate into cross-view matched groups return list(matchedgroups.values()) def localselfattentionrefinement(mergedlatents): # Applies a local self-attention mechanism to refine merged representations # Improves coherence and resolves ambiguities from cross-view merging refined = [] for latent in mergedlatents: attentionweights = computeselfattention(latent) refined.append(applyattention(latent, attentionweights)) return refined Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the accuracy of the underlying feed-forward backbone. Errors in the initial per-pixel prediction propagate through the merging process. Boundaries: The adaptive segmentation must handle boundaries between distinct objects or textures correctly to avoid merging dissimilar Gaussians. Degenerate Input: The pipeline requires a functional feed-forward predictor to generate initial per-pixel Gaussians. Time and Memory Complexity: The method adds a post-processing overhead to the feed-forward inference. The complexity depends on the number of per-pixel Gaussians N and the number of clusters. The merging and decoding steps are designed to be efficient, resulting in a final representation with K \approx N/20. Measured Performance: Retains the bulk of novel view synthesis quality at just 1/20th of the Gaussians of a per-pixel method. This vastly increases rendering speed for downstream applications. Scaling: The controllable resolution K allows for a flexible quality-efficiency trade-off at inference. Strengths: Backbone-agnostic, robust quality in sparse-view settings, highly compact representation, efficient rendering. Limitations: Requires an initial feed-forward prediction; performance is dependent on the quality of the saliency map and segmentation. When to use: When using a feed-forward Gaussian predictor that produces redundant per-pixel primitives and a compact, efficient representation is needed for downstream applications. When not to use: When the underlying feed-forward backbone cannot produce accurate per-pixel Gaussians, as prediction errors propagate through the merging pipeline. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as a set of N anisotropic Gaussians G = \{G1, \dots, GN\}. Each Gaussian Gi is parameterized by a mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, with its evaluation at position x \in \mathbb{R}^3 given by Gi(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^\top \Sigmai^{-1}(x - \mui)\right). The 3D covariance is decomposed as \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri into rotation Ri and diagonal scale Si, parameterized by a quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector si \in \mathbb{R}^3. The view-dependent color ci is encoded via spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \hat{c}{0,i}, \dots, \hat{c}{M,i}, where ci = \sum{k=0}^M \hat{c}{k,i} Hk(d) for view direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. The final pixel color is obtained by front-to-back alpha blending: c{pixel} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai ci, where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance and \alphai is the opacity. Feed-forward variants of 3DGS provide fast reconstruction from sparse input views but often produce per-pixel primitives, leading to highly redundant and inefficient representations. Compact Feed-Forward 3D Gaussians via Saliency-Guided Primitive Merging was introduced to address this redundancy by consolidating these primitives into a compact, content-adaptive set. name: Gaussian Parameter Prediction
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Parameter Prediction
body: Gaussian Parameter Prediction derives the geometric and appearance parameters of 3D Gaussians from input data to enable novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of regenerating the Gaussian set directly from features or depth maps without iterative optimization. It differs from its siblings by focusing on direct prediction from pooled features or unprojected depth maps rather than iterative densification or mesh embedding. The method varies by source. predicts parameters from a single view using depth unprojection and a DPT head. predicts parameters from aggregated features of a Gaussian Graph. Inputs:: Input image Ii, per-pixel depth map, camera parameters ci, monocular features F{mono}.: Pooled features f from a Gaussian Graph aggregation. Outputs: Gaussian centers \muj. Covariance matrices \Sigmaj. Opacity \alphaj. Color cj. Gaussian Center: 3D vector \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance: 3x3 symmetric positive definite matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Rotation/Scale: Rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, Scale matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (diagonal). Features: Vector f \in \mathbb{R}^D. 1. Unproject Depth: Unproject per-pixel depth maps to 3D space using camera parameters to obtain Gaussian centers \muj. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract monocular features F{mono} using a pre-trained backbone (Depth Anything V2 [70], a ViT with patch size 14) and bilinearly interpolate the spatial resolution to match the input resolution. 3. Concatenation: Concatenate the original image, depth map, and monocular feature information. 4. Prediction: Pass the concatenated input through a DPT head [41] to predict remaining parameters: opacity \alphaj, covariance \Sigmaj, and color cj. 5. Rendering: Render novel views using the predicted 3D Gaussians with the Gaussian splatting operation [29]. 1. Feature Aggregation: Compute aggregated features f from the Gaussian Graph using a pooling operation \phi{pooling}. 2. Parameter Prediction: Map the pooled feature f to parameters using prediction heads \phiR, \phiS, \phi\alpha, \phic. 3. Covariance Construction: Compute the covariance matrix \Sigma using the predicted rotation and scale matrices. Covariance: \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top. Feature Aggregation: \hat{f}i = \sum{j=1}^{N} \tilde{a}{ij} E{j \to i} fj W \in \mathbb{R}^D, where \tilde{a}{ij} are normalized attention weights, E{j \to i} is an edge feature, and W is a weight matrix. Pooling: \phi{pooling}(G) = \bigcup{s=1}^{l} \phi{pooling}(Gs), where Gs are connected subgraphs. Prediction Heads: \phiR, \phiS, \phi\alpha, \phic are neural network layers mapping f to parameters. Monocular Backbone: ViT with patch size 14. Feature-less regions and reflective surfaces are handled by integrating pre-trained monocular depth features into the cost volume. Details on precision, boundaries, or degenerate input handling are not given in the sources. GSGAN is a generative model that synthesizes 3D Gaussian splats hierarchically to approximate complex 3D shapes and textures, building on the primitive representation defined in Gaussian Parameter Prediction. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by generating the Gaussian parameters via a deep neural network conditioned on pose and camera views, rather than optimizing them from static point clouds. This allows for the generation of novel 3D objects from 2D images. Choose this when hierarchical generative control over pose and view is required. See GSGAN Hierarchical Generation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: stores features per pixel. stores graph structures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: handles challenging scenes with monocular features. generalizes well across datasets. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. (DepthSplat) connects Gaussian Splatting with monocular depth estimation. (Gaussian Graph Network) introduces a graph-based representation for learning efficient and generalizable Gaussian representations. name: GSGAN Hierarchical Generation
head: GSGAN
body: GSGAN is a generative model that synthesizes 3D Gaussian splats hierarchically to approximate complex 3D shapes and textures, building on the primitive representation defined in Gaussian Parameter Prediction. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by generating the Gaussian parameters via a deep neural network conditioned on pose and camera views, rather than optimizing them from static point clouds. This allows for the generation of novel 3D objects from 2D images. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes an intermediate feature tensor xl at level l and a camera parameter vector \theta as input. It outputs a set of Gaussian parameters: opacity \hat{\alpha}, quaternion orientation \hat{q}, position \hat{\mu}, scale difference \hat{s}, and color \hat{c}. The final scale is derived from \hat{s} and a hierarchical constant \Delta s. Data Structures: The Gaussian set is organized hierarchically across L levels. Level l=0 starts with N=256 Gaussians. Each level upsamples by a ratio r=4. Total Gaussians are 87,000 for 256 \times 256 resolution (L=5) and 349,000 for 512 \times 512 resolution (L=6). Channel dimensions per level [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] are [512, 512, 256, 128, 128, 128]. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the bias of the linear layers to set the quaternion to an identity rotation matrix, the opacity to 0.1, and the scale to e^{\frac{\sqrt{\Delta s}}{N}}. 2. Feature Propagation: For each level l from 0 to L-1: a. Attention Mechanism: Compute attention scores between Gaussians to model interactions. For l=0, use general self-attention. For 0 < l \le 3, use local attention similar to EdgeConv, computing attention scores against K-nearest neighbors (K=16). For l > 3, model interactions between points generated from the identical parent point in level l-1, rather than computing actual K-NN. b. Parameter Synthesis (toGaus Layer): Apply 5 parallel linear layers to the intermediate feature xl to predict parameters. 3. Parameter Activation: Apply specific activation functions to the linear outputs. Position \hat{\mu} uses \tanh activation. Scale difference \hat{s} uses -\text{softplus} activation. Color \hat{c} is the linear output. Quaternion \hat{q} is normalized to unit length. Opacity \hat{\alpha} is initialized to 0.1. In the rendering process, an exponential activation function is applied to the scale parameters. 4. Hierarchical Scaling: Calculate the scale reduction constant \Delta s based on resolution and hierarchy depth. The final scale is derived from the predicted \hat{s} and \Delta s. Formulas: The output of the toGaus layer at level l is defined as: pl = \text{Lin}p(xl) \hat{\mu}l = \tanh(\text{Lin}{\hat{\mu}}(xl)) \hat{s}l = -\text{softplus}(\text{Lin}{\hat{s}}(xl)) \hat{c}l = \text{Lin}{\hat{c}}(xl, \theta) where p \in \{\hat{\alpha}, \hat{q}\} and \text{Lin}{(\cdot)} is a linear layer. The constant \Delta s is calculated as: \Delta s = -\log\left(\sqrt{\frac{H \times W}{L \times N}}\right) where H, W are image height and width, L is the total number of hierarchical levels, and N is the initial number of Gaussians at level l=0. Parameters: Upsampling ratio r = 4. Initial Gaussians N = 256. Hierarchical levels L = 5 for 256 \times 256 resolution, L = 6 for 512 \times 512 resolution. Objective function coefficients: \lambda = 1, \lambda{pose} = 1, \lambda{knn} = 10. \lambda{center} = 1 for FFHQ dataset, \lambda{center} = 10 for AFHQ-Cat dataset. Training duration: Discriminator sees 10–15 million images. AdaIN and adaptive layerscale are applied only to layers lower than level 3. Equalized learning rate is used for every layer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational cost of self-attention and KNN grows with the number of Gaussians. The method switches to parent-point interaction for l>3 to mitigate this. Modulation (AdaIN) on higher levels (l \ge 3) does not significantly affect rendering results and is omitted to save computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def initializebiases(numgaussians, deltas): qbias = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Identity quaternion [w, x, y, z] alphabias = math.log(0.1 / 0.9) # Inverse sigmoid for 0.1 sbias = math.exp(math.sqrt(deltas) / numgaussians) return qbias, alphabias, sbias def computeattention(xl, level, parentxl=None): n = len(xl) dim = len(xl[0]) if level == 0: # General self-attention: aggregate features from all Gaussians agg = [sum(xl[i][k] for i in range(n)) for k in range(dim)] return [agg for in range(n)] elif level <= 3: # Local attention similar to EdgeConv against KNN points (k=16) # KNN computation is a standard geometric operation agg = [sum(xl[i][k] for i in range(n)) for k in range(dim)] return [agg for in range(n)] else: # Parent-point interaction: aggregate features from identical parent points m = len(parentxl) agg = [sum(parentxl[j][k] for j in range(m)) for k in range(dim)] return [agg for in range(n)] def toGauslayer(xl, theta): dim = len(xl) # Linear projections (weights are learned during training) plin = xl mulin = xl slin = xl clin = [xl[k] + theta[k % len(theta)] for k in range(dim + len(theta))] qlin = xl # Activations per source formulas alphahat = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-plin)) muhat = [math.tanh(v) for v in mulin] shat = [-math.log(1.0 + math.exp(v)) for v in slin] chat = clin normq = math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in qlin)) qhat = [v / normq for v in qlin] return alphahat, qhat, muhat, shat, chat def generategaussians(imageresolution, numlevels, initialgaussians): H, W = imageresolution N = initialgaussians L = numlevels r = 4 deltas = -math.log(math.sqrt((H W) / (L N))) qbias, alphabias, sbias = initializebiases(N, deltas) xl = [[1.0] 512 for in range(N)] theta = [0.0] 128 allgaussians = [] for l in range(L): parentxl = allgaussians[-1] if l > 0 else None xl = computeattention(xl, l, parentxl) alphahat, qhat, muhat, shat, chat = toGauslayer(xl[0], theta) levelgaussians = [alphahat] + qhat + muhat + shat + chat allgaussians.append(levelgaussians) if l < L - 1: xl = [[v for v in xl[i]] for in range(r) for i in range(len(xl))] return allgaussians Time Complexity: Computational cost of self-attention and KNN grows with the number of Gaussians. Self-attention at level 0 is O(N^2). Local attention at levels 1-3 is O(N \cdot K) where K=16. Parent-point interaction at levels 4+ is O(N). The hierarchical structure keeps the total computational cost manageable compared to global self-attention on the full set. Memory Complexity: Stores Gaussian parameters for all levels simultaneously during generation. Total Gaussians: 87K (256^2) or 349K (512^2). Strengths: Generates high-fidelity 3D structures with hierarchical detail. Efficient attention mechanisms allow scaling to higher resolutions. Limitations: Requires significant training time (10-15M images for discriminator). Performance depends on the quality of the pose conditioning. When to use: When generating novel 3D objects from 2D images is required, and hierarchical detail is beneficial. When not to use: When real-time rendering of a fixed set of Gaussians is the only goal without generation capability. GSGAN was introduced in the paper "GSGAN: Adversarial Learning for Hierarchical Generation of 3D Gaussian Splats". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation and the StyleGAN2 architecture. The method was developed to enable the generation of 3D-aware images using Gaussian primitives, extending the capabilities of GANs to 3D space. name: Functional Gaussian Splatting Representation
head: DiffGS Representation, Functional Gaussian Splatting, GauCF, GauPF, GauTF, Gaussian Splatting Functions
body: Functional Gaussian Splatting (DiffGS Representation) solves the problem of representing discrete, unstructured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives as continuous, differentiable functions to enable generative modeling. It disentangles the 3DGS representation into three specific functions: Gaussian Probability Function (GauPF) for geometry, Gaussian Color Function (GauCF) for appearance, and Gaussian Transform Function (GauTF) for structural attributes. Unlike sibling methods that modify the primitive shape or storage structure, this representation maps the discrete set of Gaussians to continuous fields, allowing the use of standard generative frameworks like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs). Inputs and Outputs Input: A fitted set of N discrete 3D Gaussians G = \{gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian gi is defined by its center \sigmai, rotation ri, scale si, opacity oi, and color ci. Output: Three continuous functions: GauPF, GauCF, and GauTF. Data Structures The representation relies on a Feature Triplane t to encode the global latent features of the Gaussian set. Layout: t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C \times 3}. Components: Three orthogonal feature planes \{t{XY}, t{XZ}, t{YZ}\} aligned with the coordinate axes. Feature Extraction: For any 3D query location qj, the corresponding feature vector fj is obtained by projecting qj onto the three orthogonal planes and concatenating the interpolated features from each plane. Mathematical Formulation The geometry of the i-th Gaussian is parameterized by center \sigmai and covariance \Sigmai: gi(x) = \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (x - \sigmai)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \sigmai) \right) where the covariance matrix \Sigmai is factorized into rotation ri and scale si as: \Sigmai = ri si si^T ri^T Here, ri \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) and si \in \mathbb{R} (scale parameters). The appearance is controlled by opacity oi \in \mathbb{R} and color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. The Three Functions 1. Gaussian Probability Function (GauPF): Models the geometry by predicting the probability that a sampled 3D location qj is a Gaussian center. The ground truth probability pj for a query qj is defined based on the distance to the nearest Gaussian center: pj = \text{GauPF}(qj) = \tau \left( \lambda \left( \min{i \in [1,N]} ||qj - \sigmai||^2 \right) \right) where \lambda is a truncation function that filters extremely large distances, and \tau is a continuous function mapping distances to the range [0,1]. 2. Gaussian Color Function (GauCF): Predicts the color attribute ci given the Gaussian center \sigmai: \{ci\} = \text{GauCF}(\sigmai) 3. Gaussian Transform Function (GauTF): Predicts the rotation ri, scale si, and opacity oi given the Gaussian center \sigmai: \{ri, si, oi\} = \text{GauTF}(\sigmai) Prediction via Neural Predictors Given the feature triplane t and a query location qj, the system first extracts features fj = \text{interp}(t, qj). Then, neural predictors \psi{pf}, \psi{cf}, \psi{tf} predict the attributes: \{\hat{p}i\} = \psi{pf}(fj), \quad \{\hat{c}i\} = \psi{cf}(fj), \quad \{\hat{r}i, \hat{s}i, \hat{o}i\} = \psi{tf}(fj) where \hat{p}i, \hat{c}i, \hat{r}i, \hat{s}i, \hat{o}i are the predicted probability, color, rotation, scale, and opacity, respectively. Training Objectives The representation is typically trained within a Gaussian VAE framework. 1. VAE Loss: Combines an L1 reconstruction loss and a KL-divergence regularization term: L{VAE} = ||\{\hat{p}, \hat{c}, \hat{r}, \hat{s}, \hat{o}\} - \{p, c, r, s, o\}||1 + \beta (D{KL}(Q\phi(z|G) || P(z))) where Q\phi(z|G) is the inferred posterior distribution of the latent vector z, and P(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the standard normal prior. 2. LDM Loss: If a Latent Diffusion Model is used for generation, the loss follows the standard denoising objective: L{LDM} = \mathbb{E}{z0, t, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)} ||\epsilon - \epsilon\sigma(zt, \delta(y), t)||^2 where \epsilon\sigma is the noise predictor conditioned on time step t and condition embedding \delta(y) via cross-attention. Pseudocode: Feature Triplane Query and Attribute Prediction Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gettriplanefeature(triplanet, querypointq): """ Extracts features from the triplane for a 3D query point. triplanet: List of 3 tensors [tXY, tXZ, tYZ], each shape (H, W, C) querypointq: Tuple (x, y, z) Returns: Feature vector fj """ x, y, z = querypointq # Project onto XY, XZ, YZ planes. Coordinates assumed normalized to [0, 1]. fxy = interpolatebilinear(triplanet[0], x, y) fxz = interpolatebilinear(triplanet[1], x, z) fyz = interpolatebilinear(triplanet[2], y, z) return concatenatechannels([fxy, fxz, fyz]) def interpolatebilinear(plane, u, v): """Bilinear interpolation on a 2D feature plane of shape (H, W, C).""" H, W, C = plane.shape uidx = u (W - 1) vidx = v (H - 1) u0, v0 = int(floor(uidx)), int(floor(vidx)) u1, v1 = min(u0 + 1, W - 1), min(v0 + 1, H - 1) du, dv = uidx - u0, vidx - v0 c00 = plane[v0, u0,:] c01 = plane[v0, u1,:] c10 = plane[v1, u0,:] c11 = plane[v1, u1,:] top = c00 (1 - du) + c01 du bottom = c10 (1 - du) + c11 du return top (1 - dv) + bottom dv def concatenatechannels(features): """Concatenate a list of 1D feature vectors along the channel dimension.""" result = [] for f in features: result.extend(f) return result def predictgaussianattributes(fj): """ Predicts Gaussian attributes from the extracted feature vector. fj: Feature vector Returns: Predicted probability, color, rotation, scale, opacity """ # Neural predictors psipf, psicf, psitf. # Exact network architecture is not specified in the sources. # Represented here as standard function calls. phat = psipf(fj) chat = psicf(fj) rhat, shat, ohat = psitf(fj) return phat, chat, rhat, shat, ohat Edge Cases and Pitfalls Truncation: The GauPF relies on a truncation function \lambda to handle points far from any Gaussian center; failure to truncate can lead to numerical instability or incorrect probability mapping. Discretization: While the representation is continuous, the final output requires extracting discrete Gaussians. The source notes an "octree-guided sampling and optimization" algorithm for this extraction, implying that naive sampling from the continuous functions may not yield optimal discrete primitives without this post-processing step. Complexity: The representation itself is a continuous function evaluation, which is computationally lightweight during inference compared to managing large discrete lists. However, training requires encoding the entire Gaussian set into a latent vector and decoding to a triplane, adding overhead. Strengths: Enables the use of powerful generative models (VAEs, LDMs) on 3DGS data by solving the discreteness and unstructured nature of raw Gaussians. Allows for conditional generation (e.g., from text) and unconditional generation of Gaussians at arbitrary numbers. Limitations: Requires a discretization/extraction algorithm to convert the continuous functions back into renderable 3DGS primitives, which adds complexity to the pipeline. When to use: When the goal is to generate 3D Gaussian Splatting representations using diffusion models or to compress 3DGS into a latent space for efficient storage/transmission. Functional Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the paper "DiffGS: Functional Gaussian Splatting Diffusion". The method addresses the challenge that the discrete and unstructured nature of 3DGS prevents the direct application of well-studied generative frameworks. By disentangling the representation into GauPF, GauCF, and GauTF, the authors enable the training of a Gaussian VAE and a Latent Diffusion Model (based on the DALLE-2 architecture) to generate high-fidelity 3DGS. name: InnerGS Volumetric Rendering
head: Factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inner Scenes [S1, unofficial]
body: InnerGS is a volumetric rendering method that models continuous 3D density using 3D Gaussians to synthesize novel 2D slices at arbitrary depths, avoiding the discrete projection artifacts of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike standard 3DGS which renders pixels via perspective projection of splats onto a camera plane, InnerGS calculates the contribution of each Gaussian directly to a pixel on a 2D slice at a specific depth t along a given axis. This approach enables seamless volumetric interpolation and explicit internal structure reconstruction, making it suitable for applications like medical imaging where internal slices are required. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by position, covariance (geometry), opacity \alphai, and color ci. A target slice depth t and pixel coordinates (u, v). Outputs: The final color I(u, v, t) for the pixel on the slice at depth t. Data Structures The method operates on a list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i contains: \mathbf{\mu}i: 3D center position. \mathbf{\Sigma}i: 3D covariance matrix (defining shape/orientation). \alphai: Scalar opacity. ci: Color value (e.g., RGB or SH coefficients). Algorithm Steps 1. Candidate Selection: Identify candidate Gaussians for the target slice. The method sorts Gaussians based on the distance between their centers \mathbf{\mu}i and the slice plane at depth t. Two methods are described for bounding box adaptation: Method 1 projects a fixed cubic bounding box onto every slice. Method 2 computes an adapted bounding box for each slice. Method 2 is preferred for efficiency, reducing average bounding box area and false positives, though it introduces a small rate of false negatives. 2. Contribution Calculation: For each pixel (u, v) on the slice at depth t, calculate the scalar contribution pi(u, v, t) of each candidate Gaussian i. This value represents the volumetric density contribution of Gaussian i at that specific 2D location and depth. 3. Volumetric Accumulation: Compute the final color I(u, v, t) using alpha compositing, accounting for the transmittance of preceding Gaussians. Formulas The final color is computed as: I(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N} pi(u, v, t)\alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) Where: I(u, v, t): Final color of pixel (u, v) on the slice at depth t. N: Total number of Gaussians. pi(u, v, t): Contribution (density/weight) of Gaussian i at pixel (u, v) and depth t. \alphai: Opacity of Gaussian i. ci: Color of Gaussian i. The product term \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) represents the transmittance, ensuring Gaussians are composited in sorted order (typically by distance to the slice). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderinnerslice(gaussians, slicedeptht, pixelu, pixelv): """ Renders a single pixel on a 2D slice at depth t using InnerGS. Assumes the slice plane is perpendicular to the Z-axis at Z = slicedeptht. """ # Step 1: Filter and Sort Candidates candidates = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): dist = abs(g.center[2] - slicedeptht) candidates.append((dist, i)) candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Step 2: Volumetric Accumulation transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for, i in candidates: g = gaussians[i] pi = evaluategaussianpdf(g.center, g.cov, pixelu, pixelv, slicedeptht) if pi < 1e-6: continue alphacontribution = pi g.alpha for k in range(3): accumulatedcolor[k] += transmittance alphacontribution g.color[k] transmittance = (1.0 - alphacontribution) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return tuple(accumulatedcolor) def evaluategaussianpdf(center, cov, u, v, t): """ Computes the scalar contribution pi(u, v, t) by evaluating the 3D Gaussian PDF. """ d = [u - center[0], v - center[1], t - center[2]] # Standard multivariate Gaussian evaluation: exp(-0.5 d^T Sigma^-1 d) covinv = invertmatrix3x3(cov) quadform = sum(d[k] sum(covinv[k][m] d[m] for m in range(3)) for k in range(3)) return math.exp(-0.5 quadform) def invertmatrix3x3(M): # Standard 3x3 matrix inversion using cofactors/determinant det = (M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])) if det == 0: return [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] invdet = 1.0 / det return [ [(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])invdet], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])invdet], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])invdet] ] Parameters Density Threshold: 0.01. Used during simulation analysis to decide whether a Gaussian is considered "active" at a given pixel. Initial Positions: Uniform 3D grid of 423 points. Used as initialization for Gaussian centers in MRI reconstruction experiments. Training Iterations: Maximum 1,000 iterations or until absolute loss decrease over 100 iterations falls below 1 \times 10^{-4}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls False Negatives: Method 2 (adapted bounding boxes) introduces false negatives (0.126 per pixel) compared to Method 1, meaning some high-density Gaussians might be missed. Precision: The method relies on accurate distance calculations between Gaussian centers and the slice plane to ensure correct sorting and candidate selection. Time Complexity: Rendering time is reduced compared to standard projection methods. In simulation tests on a 20 \times 20 \times 20 volume with 50 Gaussians, Method 2 (InnerGS) took 0.10s per slice compared to 0.69s for Method 1 (3D Ellipsoid Projection). Memory/Processing: Method 2 processes fewer candidate Gaussians per pixel (2.62 vs 16.70) and has a smaller average bounding box area (63.09 vs 209.80). Strengths: Enables synthesis of novel slices at arbitrary depths without relying on projection; provides continuous volumetric interpolation; explicit and explainable representation suitable for medical imaging. Limitations: Introduces a small rate of false negatives in candidate selection; requires careful handling of the contribution function pi(u, v, t) which differs from standard 2D rasterization. Hardware: Experiments conducted on NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. InnerGS was introduced to address the limitation of standard 3DGS, which fails to capture continuous volumetric information between discrete slices, leading to incomplete internal representations. It combines the continuous nature of NeRF-like interpolation with the explicit efficiency of discrete Gaussian representations. The method was specifically designed for internal scene reconstruction and segmentation, with applications in medical imaging such as Brain MRI reconstruction. name: HO-Gaussian
head: Hybrid Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: HO-Gaussian is a point-free representation method for multi-camera urban scenes that combines a grid-based volume with the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline to eliminate dependency on Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point initialization. It solves the problem of rendering low-texture, sky, and distant areas in large-scale urban environments where standard 3DGS fails due to sparse or outlier-prone SfM data. Unlike standard 3DGS, which relies on well-initialized point clouds, HO-Gaussian learns Gaussian positions directly from a grid volume, uses Gaussian Directional Encoding to replace spherical harmonics for view-dependent color, and applies neural warping to ensure consistency across multiple camera viewpoints. Inputs: Multi-view RGB images from a multi-camera setup (e.g., autonomous driving rigs); no SfM point cloud or LiDAR data required. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians with optimized positions, opacities, and view-dependent colors; rendered novel views. Data Structures: 1. Grid-Based Volume: A 3D voxel grid storing features used for position prediction and directional encoding. The specific resolution and channel dimensions are not given in the sources. 2. Gaussian Set: A collection of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i: Learned from the grid volume, not initialized from points. Opacity \alphai: Standard scalar. Color \mathbf{c}i: Encoded via Gaussian Directional Encoding (GDE) from the grid volume, replacing spherical harmonics coefficients. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the grid-based volume and the Gaussian set without using SfM points or LiDAR, relying solely on supervised information from images. 2. Position Learning: Query the grid-based volume to predict the 3D position \mathbf{p}i for each Gaussian, facilitating the learning of geometric information in sky, distant, and low-texture areas. 3. Gaussian Directional Encoding (GDE): Compute view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i using the grid volume features instead of storing high-order spherical harmonic functions, which reduces disk space requirements from gigabytes to megabytes. 4. Neural Warping: Generate virtual viewpoints and warp features from observed cameras to these viewpoints to enhance consistent appearance and geometry across multiple cameras, reducing overfitting to specific viewpoints. 5. Hybrid Optimization: Iteratively optimize the grid-based volume and the Gaussian parameters (positions, opacities, GDE features) using gradient descent on the rendering loss between rendered images and ground truth RGB images. 6. Point Densification: At regular intervals during training, add new Gaussian positions to regions with high error, low texture, or distant areas, and fine-tune these positions via gradient descent in the Gaussian pipeline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hogaussiantraining(images, cameraposes, numiterations, densificationinterval): def initializegridvolume(): pass # Not given in sources def initializegaussians(): pass # Not given in sources def samplebatch(imgs, poses): return imgs[0], poses[0] # Not given in sources def querygrid(vol, pos): return pos # Not given in sources def querydirectionalencoding(vol, pos, cams): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Not given in sources def generatevirtualviews(cams): return cams # Not given in sources def warpfeatures(vol, cams, views): return [0.0] # Not given in sources def rasterizegaussians(gs, cams): return [0.0] # Not given in sources def computerenderingloss(rendered, gt): return 0.0 # Not given in sources def computewarpingloss(warped, gt): return 0.0 # Not given in sources def gradientdescent(vol, gs, loss): return vol, gs # Not given in sources def densifygaussians(gs, vol, errors): return gs # Not given in sources gridvolume = initializegridvolume() gaussians = initializegaussians() for iteration in range(numiterations): batchimages, batchcameras = samplebatch(images, cameraposes) for g in gaussians: g.position = querygrid(gridvolume, g.initialpos) for g in gaussians: g.color = querydirectionalencoding(gridvolume, g.position, batchcameras) virtualviews = generatevirtualviews(batchcameras) warpedfeatures = warpfeatures(gridvolume, batchcameras, virtualviews) renderedimages = rasterizegaussians(gaussians, batchcameras) loss = computerenderingloss(renderedimages, batchimages) loss += computewarpingloss(warpedfeatures, batchimages) gridvolume, gaussians = gradientdescent(gridvolume, gaussians, loss) if iteration % densificationinterval == 0: gaussians = densifygaussians(gaussians, gridvolume, renderingerrors) return gridvolume, gaussians Parameters: Densification Interval: Not given in the sources. Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. Spherical Harmonics Degree: Replaced by GDE; not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low-Texture Regions: Standard 3DGS treats these as outliers; HO-Gaussian uses grid volume learning and densification to address this. Distant/Sky Areas: SfM points are sparse here; HO-Gaussian learns positions from the grid volume to improve representation. Multi-Camera Consistency: Without neural warping, views from different cameras may conflict; warping ensures mutual learning. Disk Space: Standard 3DGS with spherical harmonics requires gigabytes for large scenes; HO-Gaussian reduces this to ~123MB for the evaluated scene. A technique replacing spherical harmonics with grid-based directional encoding to reduce disk space and model view-dependent color. It sets itself apart by eliminating the need to store high-order coefficients. Choose it when disk space is a constraint in large-scale scenes. Link is a sibling but focuses on textured primitives, not directional encoding. A scheme for multi-camera consistency by warping features to virtual viewpoints. It sets itself apart by enabling mutual learning between camera perspectives. Choose it for multi-camera urban scenes. Link is a sibling but focuses on deformation, not warping for consistency. Time Complexity: Training time is 76 minutes on the evaluated urban scene (Argoverse dataset). Memory Complexity: Model size is 123MB, significantly smaller than baseline 3DGS (557MB) and NeRF-based methods (e.g., LocalRF 3762MB). Measured Performance: On the Argoverse dataset, HO-Gaussian achieves PSNR 30.98, SSIM 0.9043, LPIPS 0.2287 with RGB input only. Rendering Speed: 71 FPS on the evaluated urban scene. Scaling: The method is designed for large-scale urban scenes and multi-camera systems. It scales by using grid-based volume for efficient position and color encoding, avoiding the O(N) storage of spherical harmonics per Gaussian. Strengths: Point-free initialization (no SfM/LiDAR needed), reduced disk space, real-time rendering, good performance in low-texture/distant areas, multi-camera consistency. Limitations: Relies on grid volume learning. When to use: Large-scale urban scene reconstruction from multi-camera RGB data where SfM points are sparse or unreliable. HO-Gaussian was proposed by Li et al. in the paper "HO-Gaussian: Hybrid Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Urban Scenes". It addresses limitations of previous 3DGS-based methods in urban scenes, specifically their reliance on SfM points and difficulties in rendering distant, sky, and low-texture areas. The method was evaluated on the Argoverse and Waymo datasets for autonomous driving scenarios. It builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline but introduces hybrid optimization with a grid-based volume, Gaussian Directional Encoding, and neural warping. name: Plenoptic Sampling Guided 3DGS Construction
head: White-Box 3DGS Construction
body: Plenoptic Sampling Guided 3DGS Construction is a method for initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations directly from mesh geometry, using plenoptic sampling theory to theoretically derive the minimum sampling rate for views and the optimal distribution of 3D Gaussians. Unlike heuristic initialization methods that rely on trial-and-error, this approach precisely constrains Gaussian density and camera sampling to achieve Nyquist-level performance for global illumination caching. It sets itself apart by grounding the initialization in signal processing principles, ensuring that the number of Gaussians and sampled views is minimized while maintaining high-fidelity rendering. The method constructs 3D Gaussians from a given scene mesh G by deriving sampling parameters from camera intrinsics and scene depth bounds. The process involves determining the camera sampling interval, computing the world-space Gaussian sampling interval, initializing Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity), and optimizing color attributes using an albedo-shading decomposition strategy. Inputs: Scene geometry: A mesh G representing the scene surfaces. Camera parameters: Focal length f, pixel size \Delta v (or resolution R and field of view \theta), minimum observation distance z{min}, and maximum observation distance z{max}. Light field properties: Highest spatial frequency in the continuous light field Bv. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} with initialized positions, scales, rotations, opacities, and colors. A neural illumination enhancement module (optional, for non-Lambertian effects). The core data structure is a list of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian gi contains: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D coordinates. Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Diagonal elements of the scaling matrix, typically rx, ry, rz. Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: A quaternion representing orientation. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]: Scalar opacity value. Color \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: RGB color value (optimized; initial value is derived or set to 0.5 opacity base). 1. Compute Maximum Camera Sampling Interval (\Delta t): Calculate the highest spatial frequency Kv and the maximum interval between sampled views: Kv = \min\left(Bv, \frac{1}{2\Delta v}\right) \Delta t = \frac{1}{Kv f \left(\frac{1}{z{min}} - \frac{1}{z{max}}\right)} If the scene is decomposed into D depth ranges, the interval increases by a factor of D: \Delta t = \frac{D}{Kv f \left(\frac{1}{z{min}} - \frac{1}{z{max}}\right)} 2. Sample Camera Views: Uniformly sample views from a spherical space around each object in the scene. Maintain a minimum observation distance of z{min} and ensure adequate coverage of all visible surfaces. The number of views nc is determined such that the sampling interval \Delta t is satisfied. 3. Compute World-Space Sampling Interval (\Delta w): Derive the sampling interval in world space from the image space sampling interval \Delta v: \Delta v = \frac{2f \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{R} \Delta w = \frac{z{min} \Delta v}{f} where \theta is the field of view angle and R is the camera resolution (e.g., width or height). 4. Initialize Gaussian Positions: Uniformly sample points on the mesh G according to the sampling interval \Delta w. For each point, calculate the downward offset d{off} from the surface to place the Gaussian just below the visible surface: d{off} = \frac{\Delta w^2 \sin\alpha}{2(z{min} + z{max})} where \alpha is the angle between the surface normal and the principal axis of the camera. The Gaussian position is set at this offset. 5. Initialize Gaussian Scales: Set the scale parameters based on \Delta w and z{min}: rx = ry = \Delta w rz = \frac{\Delta w^2}{4z{min}} 6. Initialize Gaussian Rotation: Align the rotation of each Gaussian with the surface normal at its position. This ensures the Gaussian ellipsoid is tangent to the surface. 7. Initialize Gaussian Opacity: Set the initial opacity for all Gaussians to 0.5. 8. Freeze Non-Color Attributes: Freeze all attributes of the 3D Gaussians except for the color values. This allows for efficient caching of global illumination in dynamic scenes. 9. Optimize Color Attributes (Albedo-Shading Decomposition): Decompose the scene into albedo Ia and shading Is. The Gaussian image is represented as the product Ig = Ia Is. Obtain the albedo image Ia from G-Buffers. Optimize the color attributes of the Gaussians to fit the shading image Is derived from path-traced renderings. Use noisy 1-spp path-traced renderings with an exponential moving average (EMA) strategy for real-time shared rendering applications. 10. Neural Illumination Enhancement (Optional): For non-Lambertian regions, introduce a neural residual In. The final rendered image I is the sum of the Gaussian image Ig and the neural residual In: I = Ig + In The neural module models view-dependent residuals, while explicit Gaussians handle the base appearance. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computecamerasamplinginterval(f, dv, zvmin, zvmax, Bv, D=1): Kv = min(Bv, 1.0 / (2.0 dv)) deltat = D / (Kv f (1.0/zvmin - 1.0/zvmax)) return deltat def computeworldsamplinginterval(f, dv, zvmin): deltaw = (zvmin dv) / f return deltaw def computepixelsize(f, fovtheta, R): dv = (2.0 f math.tan(fovtheta / 2.0)) / R return dv def initializegaussians(mesh, f, fovtheta, R, zvmin, zvmax, Bv, D=1): dv = computepixelsize(f, fovtheta, R) deltaw = computeworldsamplinginterval(f, dv, zvmin) # Standard mesh utility to uniformly sample points by area/interval sampledpoints = mesh.sampleuniformpoints(interval=deltaw) gaussians = [] for pos, normal in sampledpoints: # Compute alpha: angle between surface normal and camera principal axis # Standard vector math; viewdir is derived from the sampled camera pose viewdir = np.array([0, 0, -1]) cosalpha = np.dot(normal, viewdir) / (np.linalg.norm(normal) np.linalg.norm(viewdir)) sinalpha = math.sqrt(max(0, 1 - cosalpha2)) doff = (deltaw2 sinalpha) / (2.0 (zvmin + zvmax)) finalpos = pos - normal doff rx = deltaw ry = deltaw rz = (deltaw2) / (4.0 zvmin) scale = np.array([rx, ry, rz]) # Standard rotation to align z-axis with surface normal zaxis = np.array([0, 0, 1]) v = np.cross(zaxis, normal) s = np.linalg.norm(v) if s < 1e-6: rotation = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1]) if normal[2] > 0 else np.array([1, 0, 0, 0]) else: c = np.dot(zaxis, normal) q = np.array([v[0], v[1], v[2], 1 + c]) rotation = q / np.linalg.norm(q) opacity = 0.5 color = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]) gaussians.append({ 'position': finalpos, 'scale': scale, 'rotation': rotation, 'opacity': opacity, 'color': color }) return gaussians z{min}: Minimum observation distance. Not given in the sources. z{max}: Maximum observation distance. Not given in the sources. f: Camera focal length. Not given in the sources. \theta: Field of view angle. Not given in the sources. R: Camera resolution. Not given in the sources. Bv: Highest spatial frequency in the continuous light field. Not given in the sources. D: Number of depth ranges. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The initialization step is linear with respect to the number of sampled points on the mesh, which is determined by \Delta w. The optimization step involves path-traced renderings and EMA updates, which are computationally intensive but optimized for real-time shared rendering. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is proportional to the number of Gaussians, which is minimized by the plenoptic sampling theory. The method achieves Nyquist-level performance, meaning it uses the minimum necessary Gaussians for the given resolution and depth range. Measured Performance: The method surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both qualitative and quantitative metrics for global illumination rendering. Strengths: Theoretically grounded initialization reduces trial-and-error. Efficient caching of global illumination in dynamic scenes. Supports real-time shared rendering with noisy 1-spp path-traced renderings. Limitations: Requires mesh geometry as input. Limited in modeling non-Lambertian effects without the neural enhancement module. When to Use: When high-quality global illumination caching is required, and mesh geometry is available. Particularly suitable for real-time shared rendering applications. When Not to Use: When mesh geometry is not available, or when the scene is primarily non-Lambertian and the neural enhancement module is not desired. The method was introduced in the paper "Mesh2GS: White-Box 3DGS Construction via Plenoptic Sampling". It is based on plenoptic sampling theory, which derives the minimum sampling rate for light fields. The method addresses the limitations of heuristic 3DGS construction methods (e.g., SuGaR, GaussianMesh) by providing a rigorous formulation for Gaussian distribution and camera sampling density. It is used for high-quality global illumination rendering and real-time shared rendering applications. name: Geometry Guided Gaussian Points Generation
head: MGadapter, Mesh Sampler, generalized adapter, heuristic function T
body: Geometry Guided Gaussian Points Generation (MGadapter) generates structured 3D Gaussian point attributes from an intermediate triangular mesh to provide explicit geometric guidance to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem that vanilla 3DGS lacks deterministic geometry boundaries and explicit normal directions, which complicates light transport computation and hinders physically-based inverse rendering. Unlike sibling methods that rely on learned approximated normals or real-time optimization to maintain shape consistency, MGadapter uses a predefined heuristic function to map mesh triangles directly to Gaussian points, leveraging well-defined mesh normals for improved accuracy and stable training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular mesh M derived from a scalar field \zeta via differentiable isosurface extraction (e.g., FlexiCubes). Each triangle face Fi consists of three vertices Pi = (p{i1}, p{i2}, p{i3}) and corresponding vertex normals Ni = (n{i1}, n{i2}, n{i3}). Output: A set of K Gaussian point attributes \{(\mui, Si, Ri, ni) \mid i=1,\dots,K\} for each triangle P. Data Structures: Triangle Face Fi: Defined by vertex positions Pi and vertex normals Ni. Per-vertex Attributes Ai: Stored as tuples Ai = (a{i1}, a{i2}, a{i3}) corresponding to the three vertices of the triangle. Gaussian Point Attributes: Position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Normal ni \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scale Si (represented as S{ix}, S{iy}). Rotation Ri (represented as direction vector R{ix}). Opacity: Fixed to 1. Parameters: K: Number of Gaussian points per triangle. Empirically set to K=6. u, v: Scalar parameters defining barycentric coordinates for sampling points. Values are not specified in the sources. \alpha{jk}, \beta{jk}: Scaling factors for the Gaussian dimensions. Values are not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Mesh Generation: Obtain the intermediate triangular mesh M from the scalar field \zeta using a differentiable isosurface extraction technique such as FlexiCubes. 2. Iteration: For each triangle face Fi in mesh M, generate K=6 Gaussian points. 3. Barycentric Coordinate Definition: Define 6 barycentric coordinates \mathbf{b}j for j=1,\dots,6 using parameters u and v: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{b}1 &= (u, u, 1-2u) \\ \mathbf{b}2 &= (u, 1-2u, u) \\ \mathbf{b}3 &= (1-2u, u, u) \\ \mathbf{b}4 &= (v, v, 1-2v) \\ \mathbf{b}5 &= (v, 1-2v, v) \\ \mathbf{b}6 &= (1-2v, v, v) \end{aligned} 4. Midpoint Calculation: Compute 6 midpoints \mathbf{m}{jk} by averaging pairs of barycentric coordinates: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{m}{12} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}1 + \mathbf{b}2}{2} = \left(u, \frac{1-u}{2}, \frac{1-u}{2}\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{23} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}2 + \mathbf{b}3}{2} = \left(\frac{1-u}{2}, \frac{1-u}{2}, u\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{31} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}3 + \mathbf{b}1}{2} = \left(\frac{1-u}{2}, u, \frac{1-u}{2}\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{45} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}4 + \mathbf{b}5}{2} = \left(v, \frac{1-v}{2}, \frac{1-v}{2}\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{56} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}5 + \mathbf{b}6}{2} = \left(\frac{1-v}{2}, \frac{1-v}{2}, v\right) \\ \mathbf{m}{64} &= \frac{\mathbf{b}6 + \mathbf{b}4}{2} = \left(\frac{1-v}{2}, v, \frac{1-v}{2}\right) \end{aligned} 5. Barycentric Interpolation: For any attribute Ai = (a{i1}, a{i2}, a{i3}) defined at the triangle vertices and a barycentric coordinate (q1, q2, q3), compute the interpolated value as: (q1, q2, q3) \odot Ai = q1 a{i1} + q2 a{i2} + q3 a{i3} 6. Gaussian Point Attribute Assignment: For each midpoint \mathbf{m}{jk} (where jk \in \{12, 23, 31, 45, 56, 64\}), assign the Gaussian point attributes: Position: \mu = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi Normal: n = \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Ni Scale X: S{ix} = \alpha{jk} \| \mathbf{b}k \odot Pi - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi \|2. Rotation X: R{ix} = \frac{\mathbf{b}k \odot Pi - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi}{\| \mathbf{b}k \odot Pi - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi \|2}. Scale Y: S{iy} = \frac{\text{Area}(Fi)}{\beta{jk} \| \mathbf{b}j \odot Pi - \mathbf{m}{jk} \odot Pi \|2}. Opacity: Set to 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generategaussiansfromtriangle(vertices, normals, u, v, alpha, beta): """ Generates 6 Gaussian points from a single triangle face using MGadapter. Args: vertices: List of 3 vertex positions [p1, p2, p3], each (x,y,z). normals: List of 3 vertex normals [n1, n2, n3], each (x,y,z). u: Scalar parameter for first set of barycentric coordinates. v: Scalar parameter for second set of barycentric coordinates. alpha: List of 6 scaling factors for Sx [alpha12, alpha23,...]. beta: List of 6 scaling factors for Sy [beta12, beta23,...]. Returns: List of 6 Gaussian point dictionaries. """ # Barycentric coordinates for 6 sample points b = [ (u, u, 1 - 2u), (u, 1 - 2u, u), (1 - 2u, u, u), (v, v, 1 - 2v), (v, 1 - 2v, v), (1 - 2v, v, v) ] # Midpoint pairs indices: (1,2), (2,3), (3,1), (4,5), (5,6), (6,4) # Python 0-indexed: (0,1), (1,2), (2,0), (3,4), (4,5), (5,3) midpairs = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 3)] gaussians = [] for idx, (j, k) in enumerate(midpairs): # Midpoint barycentric coordinates m = ((b[j][0] + b[k][0]) / 2, (b[j][1] + b[k][1]) / 2, (b[j][2] + b[k][2]) / 2) # Barycentric interpolation helper def baryinterp(attrlist, coords): return (coords[0] attrlist[0][0] + coords[1] attrlist[1][0] + coords[2] attrlist[2][0], coords[0] attrlist[0][1] + coords[1] attrlist[1][1] + coords[2] attrlist[2][1], coords[0] attrlist[0][2] + coords[1] attrlist[1][2] + coords[2] attrlist[2][2]) # Position and Normal mu = baryinterp(vertices, m) n = baryinterp(normals, m) # Vector for Scale X and Rotation X (using bk) posk = baryinterp(vertices, b[k]) posm = baryinterp(vertices, m) veck = (posk[0] - posm[0], posk[1] - posm[1], posk[2] - posm[2]) normk = (veck[0]2 + veck[1]2 + veck[2]2)0.5 # Vector for Scale Y (using bj) posj = baryinterp(vertices, b[j]) vecj = (posj[0] - posm[0], posj[1] - posm[1], posj[2] - posm[2]) normj = (vecj[0]2 + vecj[1]2 + vecj[2]2)0.5 # Guard for degenerate triangles eps = 1e-8 if normk < eps: Sx, Rx = 0.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: Sx = alpha[idx] normk Rx = (veck[0]/normk, veck[1]/normk, veck[2]/normk) if normj < eps: Sy = 0.0 else: # Completed formula based on source pattern Sy = trianglearea(vertices) / (beta[idx] normj) # Rotation Y is not explicitly defined in the source excerpt Ry = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) gaussians.append({ 'mu': mu, 'n': n, 'Sx': Sx, 'Rx': Rx, 'Sy': Sy, 'Ry': Ry, 'opacity': 1.0 }) return gaussians def trianglearea(p1, p2, p3): v1 = (p2[0]-p1[0], p2[1]-p1[1], p2[2]-p1[2]) v2 = (p3[0]-p1[0], p3[1]-p1[1], p3[2]-p1[2]) cross = (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) return (cross[0]2 + cross[1]2 + cross[2]2)0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If the triangle area or edge length is zero, division by zero occurs in scale/rotation normalization.
