name: PhysGaussian
head: 3D Gaussian MPM Simulation, MPM over Gaussians
body: PhysGaussian is a physical simulation pipeline that treats reconstructed 3D Gaussian primitives as Material Point Method (MPM) particles to model the deformation and motion of soft tissue structures. It couples 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with continuum mechanics, allowing a single representation to serve for both high-fidelity rendering and physics-based simulation of dynamics such as deformation, fracture, and fluid-like behavior. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on geometric deformation or linear transformations, PhysGaussian assigns physical properties to each Gaussian, enabling the simulation of materials like cloth, jelly, sand, and snow within a unified framework. PhysGaussian integrates the static 3D Gaussian representation with a continuum mechanics solver. The method proceeds by initializing Gaussians from a reconstruction, mapping them to MPM particles, and evolving their state through physical simulation steps. Inputs: A set of static 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^N reconstructed from sparse-view projections (e.g., CT data). Material parameters: Young's modulus (E), Poisson's ratio (\nu), and density (\rho). Simulation environment settings (e.g., gravity, boundary conditions). Outputs: Deformed 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity) suitable for differentiable rendering. Visualizations of deformation and motion. The core data structure is the Gaussian, which is augmented with physical state variables required by the MPM solver. Each Gaussian gi stores: 1. Geometric State: Position \mathbf{x}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or rotation/scale), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. 2. Physical State: Mass mi, velocity \mathbf{v}i, and deformation gradient \mathbf{F}i. The Gaussians are treated as particles in the MPM grid. The particle distribution is voxelized to compute macroscopic motion and deformation fields. Typical values for a simplified "jelly" material model mimicking soft tissue are: Young's modulus (E): 2 \times 10^6. Poisson's ratio (\nu): 0.4. Density (\rho): 200. 1. Reconstruction: Reconstruct the target object (e.g., a coronary artery) from sparse-view projections to obtain a static set of 3D Gaussians. 2. Particle Initialization: Treat each Gaussian gi as an MPM particle. Initialize physical properties: Assign mass mi based on the Gaussian's volume and density \rho. Initialize velocity \mathbf{v}i = \mathbf{0} and deformation gradient \mathbf{F}i = \mathbf{I} (identity). 3. Voxelization: Map the particle positions to a background grid for the MPM solver. This allows the computation of overall motion and deformation fields. 4. Force Application: Apply external forces. In demonstrations, a transient impulsive force is applied in a zero-gravity environment to isolate the force effects. 5. Simulation Step: Run the MPM simulation loop: Transfer particle momentum and position to the grid. Solve the grid equations using the constitutive model (e.g., neo-Hookean for soft tissue). Transfer updated grid velocities back to particles. Update particle positions and deformation gradients. 6. Rendering: Use the updated Gaussian parameters (positions and covariances derived from deformation) to render the scene using standard 3DGS rasterization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def physgaussiansimulation(gaussians, materialparams, numframes): """ Simulate deformation of 3D Gaussians using MPM. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with pos, cov, opacity, etc. materialparams: Dict with 'E' (Young's modulus), 'nu' (Poisson's ratio), 'rho' (density). numframes: Number of simulation steps. """ # 1. Initialize Physical State for g in gaussians: # Estimate volume from covariance determinant volume = sqrt(det(g.cov)) g.mass = materialparams['rho'] volume g.velocity = Vector3(0, 0, 0) g.deformationgradient = Matrix3.identity() # 2. Setup MPM Grid grid = MPMGrid(gaussians) # 3. Simulation Loop for frame in range(numframes): # Apply external forces (e.g., transient impulse) applyexternalforces(gaussians, frame) # MPM Step: Particle-to-Grid grid.transferparticlestogrid(gaussians) # MPM Step: Grid Solve # Solve momentum equation with constitutive model (e.g., Neo-Hookean) grid.solve(materialparams) # MPM Step: Grid-to-Particle gaussians = grid.transfergridtoparticles(gaussians) # Update Gaussian Geometry from Particle State for g in gaussians: # Update position g.pos += g.velocity dt # Update covariance based on deformation gradient F # Sigmanew = F Sigmaold F^T g.cov = g.deformationgradient @ g.cov @ g.deformationgradient.transpose() # Normalize covariance to maintain stability if needed return gaussians Precision: The simulation requires consistent units for mass, density, and modulus to avoid numerical instability in the MPM solver. Boundaries: Zero-gravity environments are used in demonstrations to isolate force effects; gravity must be explicitly handled if added. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a valid initial reconstruction. Poor reconstruction quality (e.g., missing regions) will lead to inaccurate physical behavior. GASP is a pipeline that integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting with black-box physics engines by converting flat Gaussian components into triangle faces, simulating the vertices using the Material Point Method (MPM), and reconstructing Gaussians from the deformed triangles. It solves the problem of simulating deformable objects in Gaussian representations without requiring modifications to the physics engine or complex mesh extraction strategies like marching cubes. Unlike PhysGaussian, which approximates deformation via first-order linear transformations and requires adjustments to the physics engine, GASP operates directly on the geometry of flat Gaussians using the GaMeS parameterization, ensuring stable simulations and avoiding artifacts associated with treating points as discrete entities. The MPM Simulation Framework is a physics-based simulation method used within the PhysGaussian pipeline to model the large-deformation behavior of materials such as cloth, jelly, sand, and snow. It serves as the physical prior for soft-body control, allowing shape changes to be computed via physical simulation rather than purely geometric deformation. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as GASP, by its support for a wide variety of constitutive and plasticity models within a unified continuum mechanics framework. Time Complexity: The simulation cost scales with the number of particles (Gaussians) and the grid resolution. Performance on an RTX 3090 GPU with >50,000 particles over 100 frames is approximately 250 ms per frame. Memory Complexity: Peak GPU memory usage is reported at 18 GB for the aforementioned configuration. Strengths: Provides a single representation for both rendering and simulation, enabling real-time visualization of physical dynamics. Suitable for clinical applications like surgical planning and stent deployment prediction. Limitations: Requires a pre-reconstructed 3D Gaussian model. The physical simulation adds computational overhead compared to static rendering. The simplified material models may not capture all complex tissue behaviors accurately. When to use: When physical interaction and deformation of soft tissues or materials need to be visualized alongside high-fidelity rendering, particularly in medical or robotics simulation contexts. When not to use: For static scene rendering where physics is irrelevant, or for scenes with extremely high particle counts where the 250 ms/frame performance becomes a bottleneck. PhysGaussian was introduced in CVPR'24. It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by integrating the Material Point Method (MPM), a continuum mechanics technique widely used for simulating large deformations in materials like sand, snow, and soft tissues. The method was developed to address the need for physically plausible simulations in computer graphics and medical imaging, allowing for applications such as surgical planning, stent deployment prediction, and catheterization vessel compression analysis. 3DGR-CT: Sparse-view CT reconstruction with a 3D Gaussian representation, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2025.103585, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural Rendering — Technologies & Tricks, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeuralRenderingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GASP
head: GASP (Gaussian Splatting for Physic-Based Simulations), GASP pipeline
body: GASP is a pipeline that integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting with black-box physics engines by converting flat Gaussian components into triangle faces, simulating the vertices using the Material Point Method (MPM), and reconstructing Gaussians from the deformed triangles. It solves the problem of simulating deformable objects in Gaussian representations without requiring modifications to the physics engine or complex mesh extraction strategies like marching cubes. Unlike PhysGaussian, which approximates deformation via first-order linear transformations and requires adjustments to the physics engine, GASP operates directly on the geometry of flat Gaussians using the GaMeS parameterization, ensuring stable simulations and avoiding artifacts associated with treating points as discrete entities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A collection of flat Gaussians G = \{(N(mi, Ri, Si), \sigmai, ci)\}{i=1}^p, where mi is the mean, Ri is the rotation matrix, Si = \text{diag}(s{i1}, s{i2}, s{i3}) is the scaling matrix with s{i1} = \epsilon (making the Gaussian effectively 2D), \sigmai is opacity, and ci is color. Output: A time-evolved collection of Gaussians Gt = \{(N(m'i, R'i, S'i), \sigmai, ci)\}{i=1}^p reflecting the physics simulation. Data Structures: Gaussian: Defined by mean m \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, scaling S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (diagonal), opacity \sigma \in \mathbb{R}, and color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Triangle Face (GaMeS): A triplet of vertices V = [v1, v2, v3] representing a flat Gaussian. Triangle Soup: A collection of vertices V and edges E derived from the Gaussians. Parameters: \epsilon: A small constant such that s1 = \epsilon. \alpha: A hyperparameter for the correction algorithm, controlling the threshold for scaling correction. Steps: 1. Initialization (GaMeS Conversion): Convert each flat Gaussian N(m, R, S) into a triangle face V = [v1, v2, v3] using the mapping T(\cdot): v1 = m v2 = m + s2 r2 v3 = m + s3 r3 where r2 and r3 are the second and third columns of the rotation matrix R. This creates a triangle soup (V, E). 2. Physics Simulation: Apply the physics engine (e.g., MPM) to the vertices V individually to obtain deformed vertices Vt: Vt = \{\phi(v, t): v \in V\} where \phi(\cdot, t) is the deformation map provided by the black-box physics engine (such as Genesis, Blender, or Taichi Elements). The edges E are preserved to maintain the triangle structure. 3. Reconstruction (Inverse GaMeS): Recover the Gaussian parameters from the deformed triangle vertices Vt = [v'1, v'2, v'3] using the inverse mapping T^{-1}(\cdot): Mean: \hat{m} = v'1. Rotation Axis 1: \hat{r}1 = \frac{(v'2 - v'1) \times (v'3 - v'1)}{\|(v'2 - v'1) \times (v'3 - v'1)\|} (normalized face normal). Rotation Axis 2: \hat{r}2 = \frac{v'2 - v'1}{\|v'2 - v'1\|} (normalized edge vector). Rotation Axis 3: \hat{r}3 = \text{orth}(v'3 - v'1; \hat{r}1, \hat{r}2) (Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization). Scaling: \hat{s}1 = \epsilon \hat{s}2 = \|v'2 - v'1\| \hat{s}3 = \langle v'3 - v'1, \hat{r}3 \rangle The new rotation matrix is \hat{R} = [\hat{r}1, \hat{r}2, \hat{r}3] and scaling is \hat{S} = \text{diag}(\hat{s}1, \hat{s}2, \hat{s}3). 4. Correction Algorithm: To mitigate artifacts from independent vertex processing, check if the distance between transformed nodes exceeds a threshold relative to original nodes. For each Gaussian face with original vertices V = [v1, v2, v3] and deformed vertices Vt = [v'1, v'2, v'3]: If \|v'1 - v'i\| > \alpha \|v1 - vi\| for i \in \{2, 3\}, then correct the scaling parameter \hat{s}i to \alpha \cdot si (where si is the original scaling parameter before simulation). 5. Hierarchical Simulation (Optional): Use BIRCH clustering to group Gaussians into CoreGaussians and SubGaussians. Simulate only the CoreGaussians using the steps above. Transfer the movement pattern (deformation) from CoreGaussians to their associated SubGaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gasppipeline(gaussians, physicsengine, alpha=1.5): """ gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'm', 'R', 'S', 'sigma', 'c' physicsengine: Object with method 'simulate(points)' returning deformed points alpha: Hyperparameter for correction """ # Step 1: Convert Gaussians to Triangle Soup triangles = [] for g in gaussians: m = g['m'] R = g['R'] S = g['S'] s2 = S[1, 1] s3 = S[2, 2] r2 = R[:, 1] r3 = R[:, 2] v1 = m v2 = m + s2 r2 v3 = m + s3 r3 triangles.append({ 'v1': v1, 'v2': v2, 'v3': v3, 'origs2': s2, 'origs3': s3, 'sigma': g['sigma'], 'c': g['c'] }) # Collect all vertices for the point cloud pointcloud = [] for t in triangles: pointcloud.extend([t['v1'], t['v2'], t['v3']]) # Step 2: Physics Simulation # The black-box engine applies the deformation map phi(v, t) to each point deformedcloud = physicsengine.simulate(pointcloud) # Step 3 & 4: Reconstruct Gaussians and Apply Correction newgaussians = [] idx = 0 for t in triangles: v1 = deformedcloud[idx] v2 = deformedcloud[idx + 1] v3 = deformedcloud[idx + 2] idx += 3 # Inverse GaMeS: Mean mhat = v1 # Inverse GaMeS: Rotation edge1 = v2 - v1 edge2 = v3 - v1 r1hat = np.cross(edge1, edge2) normr1 = np.linalg.norm(r1hat) if normr1 < 1e-8: r1hat = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # Fallback for degenerate triangle else: r1hat /= normr1 r2hat = edge1 / np.linalg.norm(edge1) # Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization for r3 r3hat = edge2 - np.dot(edge2, r1hat) r1hat - np.dot(edge2, r2hat) r2hat normr3 = np.linalg.norm(r3hat) if normr3 < 1e-8: r3hat = np.cross(r1hat, r2hat) # Fallback else: r3hat /= normr3 Rhat = np.columnstack((r1hat, r2hat, r3hat)) # Inverse GaMeS: Scaling s1hat = 1e-6 # epsilon s2hat = np.linalg.norm(edge1) s3hat = np.dot(edge2, r3hat) # Correction Algorithm origv1 = t['v1'] origv2 = t['v2'] origv3 = t['v3'] origs2 = t['origs2'] origs3 = t['origs3'] distv1v2orig = np.linalg.norm(origv1 - origv2) distv1v3orig = np.linalg.norm(origv1 - origv3) distv1v2deform = np.linalg.norm(v1 - v2) distv1v3deform = np.linalg.norm(v1 - v3) if distv1v2deform > alpha distv1v2orig: s2hat = alpha origs2 if distv1v3deform > alpha distv1v3orig: s3hat = alpha origs3 newgaussians.append({ 'm': mhat, 'R': Rhat, 'S': np.diag([s1hat, s2hat, s3hat]), 'sigma': t['sigma'], 'c': t['c'] }) return newgaussians A parameterization of flat Gaussians as triangle faces by setting one scaling axis to \epsilon. It sets apart from other flat Gaussian representations like 2DGS by naturally fitting the triangle-based simulation setting, avoiding pointed artifacts and holes. It is chosen when stable, triangle-based physics simulation is required for Gaussian splats. Link A particle-based physics simulation method used in GASP to compute vertex trajectories. It sets apart as a black-box engine capable of handling large deformations and complex material behaviors like cloth, jelly, sand, and snow. It is chosen for its ability to process point clouds efficiently without requiring modifications to the simulation code. Link A method that adapts Newtonian dynamics to 3D Gaussians using a first-order approximation of deformation maps. It sets apart by operating directly on Gaussian distributions but requires adjustments to the physics engine to accommodate the linear transformations. It is chosen when direct Gaussian dynamics are preferred over mesh conversion, though it may produce artifacts compared to triangle-based approaches. Link Time Complexity: The conversion to triangles and back is linear with respect to the number of Gaussians p. The physics simulation cost depends on the engine. Hierarchical simulation reduces the number of points simulated, accelerating computation. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of Gaussians, storing vertices and edges for the triangle soup. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Compatible with any black-box physics engine (Genesis, Blender, Taichi). Avoids artifacts from discrete point processing. Avoids complex mesh extraction strategies like marching cubes. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the black-box physics engine. Artifacts can still occur if the correction threshold \alpha is not tuned. Hierarchical simulation requires clustering overhead. When to use: When simulating deformable objects (cloth, jelly, sand) with Gaussian Splatting and leveraging existing physics engines without modifying them. When not to use: When high-fidelity continuous deformation fields are required beyond the triangle approximation, or when the physics engine cannot handle point clouds efficiently. GASP was introduced in the paper "GASP: Gaussian Splatting for Physic-Based Simulations" by Waczja et al. (2024). It builds upon the GaMeS parameterization of flat Gaussians. The method was demonstrated using the Genesis engine, Blender software, and the Taichi Elements library. It addresses limitations in previous methods like PhysGaussian (which requires adjustments to the physics engine) and mesh-based approaches (which suffer from extraction artifacts). Internal forces are derived from the Cauchy stress tensor \mathbf{T}, which is defined by \mathbf{F} and the chosen constitutive model. For plastic materials, \mathbf{F} is constrained within an elastic region, and a return mapping Z is applied to project \mathbf{F} back onto the yield surface if it exceeds this region. It is distinguished from its siblings by its unified support for diverse constitutive and plasticity models within a single particle-based framework. Not given in the sources. name: Neo-Hookean Elasticity
head: Neo-Hookean Model
body:
Neo-Hookean elasticity is a hyperelastic constitutive model used to simulate the large-deformation behavior of incompressible or nearly incompressible materials, such as soft tissues and rubber. It defines the Cauchy stress tensor \mathbf{T} as a function of the deformation gradient \mathbf{F} and the material's Lamé parameters. In the context of Gaussian Splatting and implicit neural representations, it serves as the physical prior for soft-body control, allowing shape changes to be computed via physical simulation rather than purely geometric deformation. It is distinguished from linear elasticity by its ability to handle finite strains and from plasticity models by its reversible, energy-conserving nature. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Deformation gradient tensor \mathbf{F} (a 3 	imes 3 matrix); Lamé parameters \mu and \lambda; Identity tensor \mathbf{I}. Outputs: Cauchy stress tensor \mathbf{T} (a 3 	imes 3 matrix). Data Structures: \mathbf{F}: 3 	imes 3 matrix of floats. \mathbf{T}: 3 	imes 3 matrix of floats. \mathbf{I}: 3 	imes 3 identity matrix. J: Scalar float, determinant of \mathbf{F}. Parameters: \mu (Shear modulus): Derived from Young’s modulus E and Poisson’s ratio 
u. \lambda (First Lamé parameter): Derived from E and 
u. E: Young’s modulus (typical range depends on material, e.g., soft tissue vs. rubber). 
u: Poisson’s ratio (typically 0 < 
u < 0.5 for stable materials). Formulas: The Cauchy stress \mathbf{T} is calculated as: \mathbf{T} = \mu(\mathbf{F}\mathbf{F}^T) + (\lambda \log(J) - \mu)\mathbf{I} where: \mathbf{F}^T is the transpose of \mathbf{F}. J = \det(\mathbf{F}). \log(J) is the natural logarithm of the determinant. The Lamé parameters are derived from engineering constants: \mu =  rac{E}{2(1 + 
u)} \lambda =  rac{
u E}{(1 + 
u)(1 - 2
u)} Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute the determinant J = \det(\mathbf{F}). 2. Compute the right Cauchy-Green deformation tensor \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{F}^T. 3. Calculate the logarithmic term \lambda \log(J). 4. Compute the stress contribution from shear: \mu \mathbf{C}. 5. Compute the stress contribution from volumetric change: (\lambda \log(J) - \mu)\mathbf{I}. 6. Sum the contributions: \mathbf{T} = \mu \mathbf{C} + (\lambda \log(J) - \mu)\mathbf{I}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def neohookeanstress(F, E, nu): """ Computes Cauchy stress T for a Neo-Hookean material. Args: F: 3x3 numpy array, deformation gradient. E: float, Young's modulus. nu: float, Poisson's ratio. Returns: T: 3x3 numpy array, Cauchy stress tensor. """ # Calculate Lamé parameters mu = E / (2.0 (1.0 + nu)) lambdaparam = (nu E) / ((1.0 + nu) (1.0 - 2.0 nu)) # Calculate determinant J J = np.linalg.det(F) # Calculate F F^T FFt = F @ F.T # Calculate Identity matrix I = np.eye(3) # Compute Cauchy Stress T # T = mu (F F^T) + (lambda log(J) - mu) I T = mu FFt + (lambdaparam np.log(J) - mu) I return T Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If J \le 0, the material has inverted or collapsed, and \log(J) is undefined. This indicates a numerical instability or severe mesh distortion. A guard should clamp J to a small positive epsilon or trigger a reset. Incompressibility: As 
u 	o 0.5, \lambda 	o \infty. This leads to numerical stiffness. In practice, slightly compressible formulations or penalty methods are used. Precision: For large deformations, \mathbf{F} can become ill-conditioned. Double precision is recommended for J calculation if strains are large. A method that applies Neo-Hookean elasticity to implicit neural representations for soft-body manipulation. It disperses the object (e.g., a human face) into elastic units, constructs an implicit control signal field, and applies stress to each unit to calculate shape changes via physical simulation. This allows for physically plausible deformation driven by implicit signals rather than explicit keyframes. Time Complexity: O(1) per element evaluation, dominated by matrix multiplication and determinant calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) per element, storing \mathbf{F} and \mathbf{T}. Strengths: Handles large deformations better than linear models; computationally efficient for real-time simulation if \mathbf{F} is known; widely used in biomechanics and soft robotics. Limitations: Not suitable for plastic deformation or fracture; becomes numerically unstable for nearly incompressible materials (
u \approx 0.5) without special handling; assumes homogeneous, isotropic material properties. When to use: Simulating soft tissues, rubber-like materials, or implicit neural avatars requiring physical plausibility. When not to use: Plasticine, metals undergoing yielding, or fluids (use Newtonian or StVK models instead). The Neo-Hookean model is a foundational hyperelastic model derived from statistical mechanics of polymer chains. It is a special case of the Mooney-Rivlin model where one of the material constants is zero. In the context of differentiable rendering and neural fields, it has been adopted to provide physical priors for geometry optimization, particularly in physics-augmented neural radiance fields (PAC-NeRF) and implicit neural representations for human avatars. The specific formulation using Cauchy stress defined by \mathbf{F} and \log(J) is cited in recent works on learning physics with graph networks and physics-augmented neural fields. name: GaussianEditor
body: GaussianEditor is a text-driven local editing method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that leverages 2D image-editing models to drive updates of 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of localized appearance and geometry modification by repeatedly rendering views, applying 2D edits, and back-propagating differences to Gaussian parameters. It is distinguished by its use of Gaussian semantic tracing for local editing and hierarchical Gaussian splatting (HGS) for adaptive generative guidance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained 3DGS model, a text prompt describing the desired edit, and optionally a mask or region of interest (RoI). Outputs: An updated 3DGS model with modified Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS parameter set. It introduces a semantic tracing mechanism to map text prompts to specific 3D Gaussian subsets. Steps: 1. Region of Interest (RoI) Extraction: Extract the target region from text instructions. 2. Semantic Tracing: Align the text RoI with 3D Gaussians through the image space using Gaussian semantic tracing. This identifies which Gaussians correspond to the semantic region defined by the text. 3. 2D Edit Application: Render views of the current 3DGS. Apply a 2D image-editing model (e.g., diffusion-based editor) to the rendered images, guided by the traced RoI. Two specific guidance models are implemented: GaussianEditor-iN2N guided by IN2N, and GaussianEditor-DDS guided by DDS. GaussianEditor-iN2N achieves superior results. 4. Back-propagation: Compute the difference between the edited 2D image and the original rendered image. Back-propagate this difference to update the 3D Gaussian parameters. 5. Iterative Refinement: Repeat steps 3–4 to refine the edit and improve multi-view consistency. Parameters: Guidance Model: IN2N or DDS. Iteration Count: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unintended Deformations: Due to weak 3D geometry priors, the method can suffer from unintended deformations. Computational Cost: The pipeline is computationally heavy due to repeated rendering and back-propagation. A version guided by IN2N, achieving superior results compared to the DDS variant. A version guided by DDS. Time Complexity: Computationally heavy due to iterative rendering and back-propagation. Memory Complexity: Standard 3DGS memory usage plus overhead for semantic tracing and 2D model inference. Strengths: Intuitive, compatible with powerful 2D priors, enables text- or mask-driven appearance and geometry changes. Limitations: Can suffer from unintended deformations due to weak 3D geometry priors. When to use: When text-driven local editing is required and computational resources are available. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical or when strong 3D geometry consistency is required without iterative refinement. GaussianEditor was introduced by Chen et al. in CVPR'24. It belongs to the family of methods that leverage 2D image-editing models to drive updates of 3D Gaussians. Follow-up works have improved spatial localization and multi-view consistency via attention, view correspondence, or iterative refinement. name: Gaussian Asset Generation
head: Gaussian Splatting Asset Generation, PLY generation for SplatNode, Rainbow Sphere Splat Asset, Synthetic Gaussian Asset Generation
body:
Gaussian Asset Generation is a deterministic method for creating a reproducible 3D Gaussian Splatting PLY asset, specifically a dense "rainbow sphere" shell, without using randomness or external data. It solves the problem of needing a standardized, visually recognizable test asset for validating parsers and renderers (such as SceneView's PlyParser) by generating a synthetic point cloud with specific color, scale, opacity, and rotation parameters. It differs from other initialization methods like Gaussian Model Initialization or DreamGaussian by being purely synthetic and deterministic, rather than derived from input images or learned optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Number of Gaussians n (default 8000), output file path, radius R (default 0.5), target opacity p (default 0.80), target scale \sigma (default 0.012). Outputs: A binary PLY file (binarylittleendian 1.0) containing n vertices. Data Structures: The PLY header defines an element vertex with 14 float32 properties in this exact order: 1. x, y, z (position) 2. fdc0, fdc1, fdc2 (DC spherical harmonic coefficients) 3. opacity (logit-encoded) 4. scale0, scale1, scale2 (log-encoded) 5. rot0, rot1, rot2, rot3 (quaternion, scalar-first w,x,y,z) The binary record is packed using struct.Struct("<14f") (little-endian, 14 floats). Parameters: SH\C0 = 0.28209479177387814. Golden angle ga = \pi (3 - \sqrt{5}). Clamping bounds for opacity: [10^{-4}, 1 - 10^{-4}]. Steps: 1. Generate Positions: Distribute n points on a sphere of radius R using the Fibonacci sphere algorithm. For each i \in [0, n-1]: yi = 1.0 -  rac{i}{n-1} 	imes 2.0 ri = \sqrt{\max(0.0, 1.0 - yi^2)} 	hetai = ga 	imes i xi = \cos(	hetai) 	imes ri 	imes R zi = \sin(	hetai) 	imes ri 	imes R yi = yi 	imes R 2. Calculate Color (fdc): Compute azimuth: \phi = \operatorname{atan2}(zi, xi). Compute hue: h =  rac{\phi + \pi}{2\pi}. Compute elevation: e =  rac{yi}{R} (normalized to [-1, 1]). Compute value: v = 0.72 + 0.18 	imes e. Set saturation: s = 0.95. Convert HSV (h, s, v) to sRGB (cr, cg, cb) using standard colorsys.hsvtorgb. Convert sRGB to linear RGB (c{r,lin}, c{g,lin}, c{b,lin}) using the sRGB gamma function: c{lin} =  egin{cases}  rac{c}{12.92} & 	ext{if } c \le 0.04045 \ \left( rac{c + 0.055}{1.055}ight)^{2.4} & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} Encode to f\dc: f\dck =  rac{c{k,lin} - 0.5}{SH\C0} \quad 	ext{for } k \in \{r, g, b\} 3. Encode Opacity: Clamp target opacity p to [10^{-4}, 1 - 10^{-4}]. Compute logit: 	ext{opacity}{stored} = \ln\left( rac{p}{1 - p}ight) 4. Encode Scale: Compute natural log of target scale \sigma: 	ext{scale}{stored} = \ln(\sigma) Assign to all three axes: scale\0 = scale\1 = scale\2 = 	ext{scale}{stored}. 5. Encode Rotation: Set identity quaternion in scalar-first order: rot\0 = 1.0, rot\1 = 0.0, rot\2 = 0.0, rot\3 = 0.0. 6. Write PLY: Write header with ply, format binarylittleendian 1.0, element vertex n, and property definitions. Write binary body by packing the 14 floats for each vertex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import struct import colorsys SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 def srgbtolinear(c: float) -> float: if c <= 0.04045: return c / 12.92 return ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) 2.4 def logit(p: float) -> float: p = min(max(p, 1e-4), 1.0 - 1e-4) return math.log(p / (1.0 - p)) def generategaussianasset(n: int, outpath: str, radius: float = 0.5, sigma: float = 0.012, opacity: float = 0.80): if n < 2: raise ValueError("n must be at least 2 to avoid division by zero in Fibonacci sphere distribution") ga = math.pi (3.0 - math.sqrt(5.0)) lnsigma = math.log(sigma) logitopacity = logit(opacity) header = ( "ply
" "format binarylittleendian 1.0
" f"element vertex {n}
" "property float x
" "property float y
" "property float z
" "property float fdc0
" "property float fdc1
" "property float fdc2
" "property float opacity
" "property float scale0
" "property float scale1
" "property float scale2
" "property float rot0
" "property float rot1
" "property float rot2
" "property float rot3
" "endheader
") rec = struct.Struct("<14f") body = b"" for i in range(n): ynorm = 1.0 - (i / float(n - 1)) 2.0 rnorm = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - ynorm ynorm)) theta = ga i x = math.cos(theta) rnorm radius y = ynorm radius z = math.sin(theta) rnorm radius azimuth = math.atan2(z, x) hue = (azimuth + math.pi) / (2.0 math.pi) elevation = ynorm val = 0.72 + 0.18 elevation sat = 0.95 sr, sg, sb = colorsys.hsvtorgb(hue, sat, val) rlin = srgbtolinear(sr) glin = srgbtolinear(sg) blin = srgbtolinear(sb) fdc0 = (rlin - 0.5) / SHC0 fdc1 = (glin - 0.5) / SHC0 fdc2 = (blin - 0.5) / SHC0 body += rec.pack( x, y, z, fdc0, fdc1, fdc2, logitopacity, lnsigma, lnsigma, lnsigma, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) with open(outpath, "wb") as f: f.write(header.encode("ascii")) f.write(body) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Space: Colors must be converted from sRGB to linear RGB before encoding into f\dc because the renderer applies a linear-to-sRGB display transform. Activation Inversion: The parser expects inverted activations. Scales are stored as \ln(\sigma), f\dc as (c{lin}-0.5)/SH\C0, opacity as \logit(p), and rotation as scalar-first w,x,y,z. Division by Zero: The Fibonacci sphere formula uses n-1 in the denominator. If n=1, this causes a division by zero. The method assumes n > 1. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The generation is instantaneous for typical n (e.g., 8000 points) as it involves no optimization or external data loading. Strengths: Deterministic, reproducible, no external dependencies, small file size, easy to debug. Limitations: Only generates a synthetic sphere. When to use: For testing parsers, validating rendering pipelines, and creating demo assets. When not to use: For training or initializing models on real data. Gaussian Asset Generation was introduced as part of the SceneView project to provide a standardized synthetic asset for testing the SplatNode and PlyParser components. It was developed to ensure that the demo asset (rainbowsphere.ply) is fully reproducible and does not rely on random seeds or external image data. The method is specific to the INRIA binary PLY layout used by SceneView. feat(samples): splat-preview demo — first on-device SplatNode render ( #…, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/5682de62179014b063bdff5529bedb8638385f03, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Learning-based and Generative Initialization
body: Learning-based and Generative Initialization methods initialize 3D Gaussian primitives using learned priors, neural decoders, or generative models rather than relying on random point clouds or simple geometric heuristics. This family addresses the problem of slow convergence and poor structural alignment in sparse or unstructured initializations by providing spatially aligned covariance structures and semantic consistency before optimization begins. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI) and Mesh-based Initialization by leveraging data-driven latent spaces or volume gradients to seed anisotropic Gaussians, rather than using deterministic geometric distributions or surface mesh sampling. The core mechanism of this family involves replacing the initial random or heuristic placement of Gaussian parameters \Theta0 = \{\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i\} with outputs from a learned model or a structured prior. Common principles include: 1. Latent Space Mapping: Encoding input data (such as sparse point clouds or images) into a compact latent vector z, which is then decoded into Gaussian parameters. 2. Structural Priors: Using gradient fields from volume priors or spherical folding grids to align Gaussian covariances with local surface normals or geometric structures. 3. Generative Guidance: Utilizing pre-trained generative models (e.g., VAEs, diffusion models) to provide initial geometry and color, often followed by optimization to refine the fit. Volume Prior Initialization extracts structural gradients from a dense ground-truth volume prior \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}} to determine the locations and orientations of initial Gaussians. It sets itself apart from siblings like SF-VAE and GaussianCube by directly operating on voxelized volume gradients to seed anisotropic Gaussians, rather than using latent space folding or cube-based discretization. It is chosen when a dense volume representation (e.g., from a neural radiance field or voxel grid) is available and high-fidelity structural alignment is required from the start. SF-VAE is a learning-based initialization method that encodes 3D Gaussian parameters into a latent space and decodes them using a spherical folding grid to reconstruct geometry and color. It differs from Volume Prior Initialization by using a neural decoder with a specific spherical folding mechanism rather than direct volume grid sampling, and from GaussianCube by operating on a continuous latent space decoded via folding rather than discrete voxel-based representations. It is suitable for scenarios requiring structured, prior-driven initialization from sparse inputs. GaussianCube utilizes an unstructured, explicit set of 3D Gaussians initialized from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds, optimizing parameters via interleaved density control. It is distinct from its siblings, Volume Prior Initialization and SF-VAE, by explicitly optimizing the Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, SH) via interleaved density control rather than relying solely on latent space encoding or spherical folding priors for initialization. It is chosen for real-time, high-quality novel-view synthesis where efficient radiance field rendering is prioritized over generative priors. This variant initializes the Gaussian map by minimizing a cost function similar to RGB-D SLAM systems, incorporating both photometric and geometric losses. Step: Train the Gaussian map by minimizing the combined cost function. Formula: Find G{init} by minimizing: \mathcal{G}{init} = \arg \min{\mathcal{G}} \sum{\forall k \in \mathcal{W}} (\lambda{pho} E{pho}^k + (1 - \lambda{pho}) E{geo}^k) + \lambda{iso} E{iso} Parameters: Photometric loss weight \lambda{pho} = 0.9; Isotropic regularization weight \lambda{iso} = 10. This variant initializes the Gaussian map without depth supervision, relying solely on photometric loss and isotropic regularization while keeping camera poses fixed. Step: Train initial 3D Gaussian map G{init} without depth supervision. Randomly initialize 3D Gaussians' positions. Keep camera poses fixed during optimization. Formula: Find G{init} by minimizing: \mathcal{G}{init} = \arg \min{\mathcal{G}} \sum{\forall k \in \mathcal{W}} E{pho}^k + \lambda{iso} E{iso} Parameters: Training iterations: 30,000 iterations using training views. This method initializes Gaussians using pre-computed properties from a generalized Gaussian splatting model to alleviate quality decline when Gaussian shapes deviate from actual surface geometry, especially in scenarios with limited scene observations. Definition: Initializing Gaussians using pre-computed properties \theta from a generalized Gaussian splatting model to alleviate quality decline when Gaussian shapes deviate from actual surface geometry, especially in scenarios with limited scene observations. Parameters: Pre-computed properties \theta from a generalized Gaussian splatting model are used for initialization. This strategy initializes Gaussian colors using random values instead of pre-generated textures to avoid detrimental artifacts. Definition: An initialization strategy for Gaussian colors that uses random values instead of pre-generated textures, avoiding detrimental artifacts. Pitfall: Directly applying Point-E generated colors to the Gaussians produces detrimental visual effects and should be avoided. The concept of learning-based initialization in Gaussian Splatting emerged as a response to the limitations of random or SfM-based initialization, which often leads to slow convergence and poor structural alignment. Volume Prior Initialization and SF-VAE leverage neural networks to encode geometric priors, drawing from variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures. Generalized Gaussian Splatting Initialization addresses the issue of shape deviation by using pre-computed properties from broader Gaussian splatting models. Random Color Initialization was introduced in the context of text-to-3D generation (e.g., GSGEN) to prevent artifacts from generative models like Point-E. Convergence Basin Analysis Training methods are rooted in SLAM literature, adapting RGB-D SLAM cost functions to Gaussian map optimization. name: Volume Prior Initialization
head: Gradient-based Gaussian Initialization with Volume Prior
body: Volume Prior Initialization addresses the problem of initializing 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters when a ground-truth volumetric representation (such as a CT volume) is available, rather than relying on sparse point clouds or random initialization. It differs from sibling methods like SF-VAE and GaussianCube by directly extracting structural gradients from the ground-truth volume to seed the Gaussian primitives, providing a geometry-aware starting point that accelerates convergence in reconstruction tasks. Inputs: Ground-truth volume \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}}: A dense 3D voxel grid representing the target geometry and appearance. \alpha{\text{SSIM}}: Weight for the SSIM loss component. Outputs: Initial Gaussian parameters \Theta0: A set of Gaussians \{\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i\} initialized based on volume gradients. Data Structures: \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}}: 3D array of voxels. \mathbf{V}r: Voxelized representation of the current Gaussian set, used for loss evaluation. Steps: 1. Gradient Extraction: Compute gradients from the ground-truth volume \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}} to identify surface locations and orientations. This step serves as the initialization phase, placing Gaussians at high-gradient regions. 2. Initialization: Place initial Gaussians at the detected gradient locations. The specific parameterization (covariance, opacity, color) is derived from the local volume statistics at these locations. 3. Optimization Loop: For each training step: a. Voxelization: Render the current Gaussian representation \Theta into a 3D voxel grid \mathbf{V}r. This involves projecting or splatting the Gaussians into the voxel space. b. Loss Evaluation: Compute the total loss between the rendered volume \mathbf{V}r and the ground-truth volume \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}} using the following formula: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}1(\mathbf{V}r, \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}}) + \alpha{\text{SSIM}} \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}(\mathbf{V}r, \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}}) where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss and \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} is the 3D Structural Similarity Index Measure loss. c. Update: Perform gradient descent to update \Theta to minimize \mathcal{L}{\text{total}}. Parameters: \alpha{\text{SSIM}}: Weight for the 3D SSIM loss. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: The voxelization step at each iteration is computationally expensive due to the number of processed voxels, making a single optimization step slower than standard 2D rendering pipelines. Voxel Resolution: The accuracy of the gradient extraction and subsequent voxelization depends on the resolution of \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}} and the voxel grid used for \mathbf{V}r. Seeds anisotropic Gaussians by estimating local surface statistics from a dense prior, explicitly constructing disc-like covariance structures aligned to estimated normals. Time Complexity: Slower per step than standard 2D Gaussian Splatting due to the 3D voxelization required at each optimization step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the ground-truth volume \mathbf{V}{\text{gt}} and the intermediate voxelized representation \mathbf{V}r. Strengths: Provides a strong geometric prior when a ground-truth volume is available, leading to faster convergence in reconstruction tasks. Limitations: High computational cost per iteration; requires a ground-truth volume, limiting applicability to scenarios where such data is available (e.g., CT reconstruction). Originated in the context of Fast and Scalable CT Reconstruction with Gaussian Splatting (FaCT-GS). The method leverages the availability of ground-truth volumetric data in computed tomography to initialize Gaussians more effectively than random or point-cloud-based methods. name: Prior-Conditioned Parameterization (I)
head: I operator, Initialization Operator, Prior-Conditioned Gaussian Parameterization
body: Prior-Conditioned Parameterization (I) is an initialization method that seeds anisotropic Gaussians by estimating local surface statistics (normals and scales) from a dense prior P, front-loading structure discovery. It addresses the problem where standard 3D Gaussian Splatting initializes isotropic Gaussians from interpoint distances, leaving local surface scale and rotation to be recovered during optimization, which consumes available updates under short iteration horizons. By mapping the dense prior P to a surface-aligned anisotropic set \Theta0, it provides spatial support, scale, and rotation before optimization, supporting rapid early convergence. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly constructing disc-like covariance structures aligned to estimated normals, rather than relying on isotropic scaling or post-initialization densification to find surface geometry. Inputs and Outputs Input: A dense geometric prior point cloud P = \{\mathbf{p}i\}, constructed by the Geometry Operator (G). Output: An initialized Gaussian set \Theta0 = \{(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \mathbf{c}i, \alphai)\}, where \boldsymbol{\mu}i is the position, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i is the covariance, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and \alphai is the opacity. Data Structures The method operates on the GaussianList data structure. For each point \mathbf{p}i \in P: \boldsymbol{\mu}i = \mathbf{p}i (Position initialized to the prior point). \mathbf{q}i (Quaternion rotation): Initialized to align the Gaussian's local z-axis with the estimated surface normal \mathbf{n}i. \mathbf{s}i = [st, st, sn] (Scale vector): Optimized in log-space for positivity. \alphai: Opacity initialized to the logit of 0.1, i.e., \alphai = \log(0.1 / (1 - 0.1)). \mathbf{c}i: Color is typically copied from the prior or a default value; the source focuses on geometry parameterization. Parameters Kn = 16: Number of neighbors for normal estimation. A larger neighborhood suppresses sampling noise. Ks = 3: Number of neighbors for tangential scale estimation. Tracks local density to avoid over-smoothing thin structures. r{\text{normal}}: A constant factor for the normal-direction scale relative to the tangential scale. The exact numerical value is not specified in the source text. Steps 1. Estimate Local Surface Statistics: For each point \mathbf{p}i in the dense prior P: a. Identify Kn nearest neighbors \{\mathbf{p}{i,k}\}{k=1}^{Kn} and Ks nearest neighbors \{\mathbf{p}{i,k}\}{k=1}^{Ks} within P. b. Compute the centroid of the normal neighbors: \bar{\mathbf{p}}i = \frac{1}{Kn} \sum{k=1}^{Kn} \mathbf{p}{i,k}. c. Compute the local covariance matrix \mathbf{C}i: \mathbf{C}i = \frac{1}{Kn} \sum{k=1}^{Kn} (\mathbf{p}{i,k} - \bar{\mathbf{p}}i)(\mathbf{p}{i,k} - \bar{\mathbf{p}}i)^T d. Extract the local surface normal \mathbf{n}i as the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue of \mathbf{C}i. e. Compute the tangential scale st: st = \frac{1}{Ks} \sum{k=1}^{Ks} \|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}{i,k}\| f. Compute the normal-direction scale sn: sn = r{\text{normal}} st 2. Seed Gaussians: For each point \mathbf{p}i: a. Initialize position \boldsymbol{\mu}i = \mathbf{p}i. b. Initialize rotation \mathbf{q}i such that the Gaussian's local z-axis aligns with \mathbf{n}i. c. Initialize scale \mathbf{s}i = [st, st, sn]. The Gaussian is seeded as a thin disc-like ellipsoid tangent to the local surface. d. Initialize opacity \alphai = \text{logit}(0.1). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def priorconditionedparameterization(points: np.ndarray, Kn: int = 16, Ks: int = 3, rnormal: float = 0.1) -> dict: """ Seeds anisotropic Gaussians from a dense prior point cloud. Args: points: Array of shape (N, 3) containing the dense prior points P. Kn: Number of neighbors for normal estimation. Ks: Number of neighbors for tangential scale estimation. rnormal: Constant factor for normal-direction scale. Returns: A dictionary containing initialized Gaussian parameters: positions: (N, 3) scales: (N, 3) in linear space [st, st, sn] rotations: (N, 4) quaternions aligning z-axis with normals opacities: (N,) logit values """ N = points.shape[0] positions = points.copy() scales = np.zeros((N, 3)) rotations = np.zeros((N, 4)) opacities = np.log(0.1 / (1 - 0.1)) np.ones(N) # Precompute KNN indices for efficiency. # In a real implementation, use a KDTree or similar structure. # Here we assume a helper function getknnindices returns indices for all points. knnindicesn = getknnindices(points, Kn) knnindicess = getknnindices(points, Ks) for i in range(N): # 1. Estimate Normal neighborsn = points[knnindicesn[i]] centroidn = np.mean(neighborsn, axis=0) # Local covariance matrix diff = neighborsn - centroidn Ci = (diff.T @ diff) / Kn # Eigendecomposition to find smallest eigenvalue eigenvector eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(Ci) # eigenvectors are columns; smallest eigenvalue is at index 0 normal = eigenvectors[:, 0] # 2. Estimate Scales neighborss = points[knnindicess[i]] # Tangential scale: average distance to Ks nearest neighbors distances = np.linalg.norm(neighborss - points[i], axis=1) st = np.mean(distances) # Normal-direction scale sn = rnormal st # 3. Seed Gaussian scales[i] = [st, st, sn] # Initialize rotation to align z-axis (0,0,1) with normal # Using quaternion rotation from vector v1 to v2 rotations[i] = quaternionfromvectors(np.array([0, 0, 1]), normal) return { "positions": positions, "scales": scales, "rotations": rotations, "opacities": opacities } def getknnindices(points: np.ndarray, k: int) -> np.ndarray: """ Helper to get KNN indices. Note: In a production environment, this would use scipy.spatial.cKDTree or similar. This is a placeholder for the algorithmic step described in the source. """ # Implementation detail: Using a simple brute-force for clarity, # though the source notes the scheme is "embarrassingly parallel and memory-bounded". # A KDTree is recommended for performance. from scipy.spatial import cKDTree tree = cKDTree(points) distances, indices = tree.query(points, k=k+1) # +1 because the point itself is the nearest neighbor # Remove the point itself (index 0) if it's included in the query return indices[:, 1:] def quaternionfromvectors(v1: np.ndarray, v2: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Computes the quaternion representing the rotation from v1 to v2. """ v1 = v1 / np.linalg.norm(v1) v2 = v2 / np.linalg.norm(v2) cross = np.cross(v1, v2) w = np.sqrt((1 + np.dot(v1, v2)) 2) x, y, z = cross[0], cross[1], cross[2] return np.array([x/w, y/w, z/w, 0.5 w]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Normals as Initialization Only: Estimated normals are used only for initialization and never as training constraints. Scale Positivity: Scales are optimized in log-space to ensure positivity. Noise Sensitivity: The choice of Kn is critical; too small a neighborhood may lead to noisy normal estimates, while too large may smooth out fine details. Thin Structures: Ks is kept small (3) to track local density and avoid over-smoothing thin structures. Time Complexity: The normal estimation involves KNN queries and eigendecomposition for each point. With fixed Kn and Ks, this is O(N \cdot K \log N) or O(N \cdot K) depending on the KNN implementation, where N is the number of points. The source notes the scheme is "embarrassingly parallel and memory-bounded". Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Gaussian parameters. The KNN structures add O(N \cdot K) overhead. Performance: The method is designed for mobile devices, targeting strict runtime and memory constraints. It reduces reliance on in-loop densification by providing a geometry-informed warm start. Strengths: Rapid early convergence under short iteration horizons; reduces the need for scale and rotation correction during optimization; hardware-aligned for mobile GPUs. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the dense prior P; if P is noisy or incomplete, the initialization may be suboptimal. The exact value of r{\text{normal}} is not specified, requiring empirical tuning. Prior-Conditioned Parameterization (I) is part of the PocketGS pipeline, a high-fidelity on-device training method for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was introduced in the paper "PocketGS: High-Fidelity On-Device Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting". The method addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS initialization on resource-constrained devices by front-loading geometry discovery.
