name: Octree-GS / Scaffold-GS
head: Anchor-Based Structured Representation, Anchor-based Gaussian Splatting, Anchor-based Representations
body: Octree-GS and Scaffold-GS are hierarchical rendering methods that replace the flat list of 3D Gaussians with a structured representation anchored to a sparse voxel grid or octree. Scaffold-GS initializes anchors from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, using a neural network to predict Gaussian attributes on the fly, while Octree-GS builds an octree where nodes summarize radiance and opacity of children. This approach reduces memory usage by approximately 5× compared to vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) at equivalent quality and naturally adapts to view distance by allocating primitives only in occupied regions. It builds on GaussianList Data Structure and Initialization by introducing spatial hierarchy and neural decoding. Inputs: Sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); camera poses; training images. Outputs: Rendered RGB image; optimized anchor features and offsets. Data Structures: 1. Sparse Voxel Grid / Octree: A hierarchical spatial index. In Scaffold-GS, this is initialized from SfM points. Each active voxel center serves as an Anchor. 2. Anchor Attributes: For each anchor, the following learnable parameters are stored: Position \mathbf{p}a (fixed or learnable, typically voxel center). Context features \mathbf{f}a (learnable vector). Learnable scale sa. Learnable offsets \{\mathbf{O}k\}{k=1}^k for spawned Gaussians. 3. Neural Decoder: A small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) F\theta that takes anchor features and viewing direction as input to predict Gaussian attributes. Parameters: k: Number of Gaussians generated per visible anchor. Typical value k=4. \tau\alpha: Opacity threshold. Gaussians with predicted opacity \alpha < \tau\alpha are not rasterized. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Voxelize the initial SfM-derived point cloud. Place an anchor at the center of each occupied voxel. Assign each anchor a local context feature \mathbf{f}a, a scale sa, and k learnable offsets \{\mathbf{O}k\}. 2. Gaussian Generation (Per View): For each training view: a. Identify visible anchors within the view frustum. b. For each visible anchor a, generate k candidate Gaussians. The i-th Gaussian's position is \mathbf{p}{a,i} = \mathbf{p}a + \mathbf{O}{a,i}. c. Pass the anchor's context feature \mathbf{f}a and the viewing direction \mathbf{v} into the neural decoder F\theta. d. The decoder outputs the attributes for the k Gaussians: opacity \alpha{a,i}, color \mathbf{c}{a,i} (often via spherical harmonics coefficients or direct RGB), scale \mathbf{s}{a,i}, and rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}{a,i}. 3. Filtering: Discard any generated Gaussian where \alpha{a,i} < \tau\alpha. 4. Rasterization: Render the remaining significant Gaussians using standard alpha-blending (d\alpha-blending). 5. Optimization: Compute reconstruction loss (e.g., L1, SSIM, volumetric loss) between rendered and ground truth images. Backpropagate to update anchor context features \mathbf{f}a, offsets \mathbf{O}a, and MLP weights \theta. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class AnchorBasedRenderer: def init(self, sfmpoints, voxelsize, k=4, taualpha=0.01): """ Initialize Scaffold-GS / Anchor-based representation.:param sfmpoints: Nx3 array of initial SfM points:param voxelsize: Size of voxel grid cells:param k: Number of Gaussians per anchor:param taualpha: Opacity threshold for rasterization """ self.k = k self.taualpha = taualpha # 1. Initialize Sparse Voxel Grid from SfM # Map SfM points to voxel centers self.anchors = {} # Map: voxelindex -> AnchorData for point in sfmpoints: voxelidx = np.floor(point / voxelsize).astype(int) if voxelidx not in self.anchors: # Anchor Data: Context feature, Scale, Offsets # Context feature: learnable vector (e.g., dim 16) context = np.random.randn(16) # Scale: learnable scalar scale = 1.0 # Offsets: k x 3 array for k Gaussians offsets = np.zeros((k, 3)) self.anchors[voxelidx] = { 'voxelidx': voxelidx, 'pos': voxelidx voxelsize + voxelsize / 2, # Center 'context': context, 'scale': scale, 'offsets': offsets } # Neural Decoder MLP (simplified) # Input: Context (16) + ViewDir (3) -> Output: k (1 + 3 + 1 + 4) # Attributes: alpha (1), color (3), scale (1), quat (4) self.mlpweights = np.random.randn(24, k 9) # 24 inputs, 9k outputs self.mlpbias = np.zeros(k 9) def decodegaussians(self, anchor, viewdir): """ Predict Gaussian attributes from an anchor and view direction.:param anchor: Dict with 'context', 'pos', 'scale', 'offsets':param viewdir: Normalized view direction vector (3,):return: List of Gaussian attributes """ # Concatenate context and view direction inputvec = np.concatenate([anchor['context'], viewdir]) # Linear layer (simplified MLP step) logits = np.dot(inputvec, self.mlpweights) + self.mlpbias # Reshape to k Gaussians, each with [alpha, color(3), scale(1), quat(4)] # Note: Real implementation uses activation functions (ReLU, Softmax, etc.) # Here we assume raw logits are processed appropriately # alpha: sigmoid # color: tanh or direct # scale: exp # quat: normalize gaussians = [] for i in range(self.k): offset = anchor['offsets'][i] pos = anchor['pos'] + offset # Extract attributes from logits # Assuming logits layout: [alpha0, c00, c01, c02, s0, q00, q01, q02, q03,...] startidx = i 9 alpharaw = logits[startidx] colorraw = logits[startidx+1:startidx+4] scaleraw = logits[startidx+4] quatraw = logits[startidx+5:startidx+9] # Apply activations (standard assumptions for neural fields) alpha = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-alpharaw)) # Sigmoid color = np.tanh(colorraw) # Tanh for color range scale = np.exp(scaleraw) # Positive scale quat = quatraw / np.linalg.norm(quatraw) # Normalize quaternion gaussians.append({ 'pos': pos, 'alpha': alpha, 'color': color, 'scale': scale, 'quat': quat }) return gaussians def render(self, camera, anchors): """ Render scene using anchor-based Gaussians.:param camera: Camera object with projection matrix and view direction:param anchors: List of active anchors in view frustum:return: Rendered image """ # 1. Generate Gaussians for all visible anchors allgaussians = [] for anchor in anchors: # Get view direction for this anchor from camera viewdir =... # Calculate based on anchor pos and camera pos gaussians = self.decodegaussians(anchor, viewdir) allgaussians.extend(gaussians) # 2. Filter by opacity threshold significantgaussians = [g for g in allgaussians if g['alpha'] >= self.taualpha] # 3. Rasterize (Standard 3DGS Splatting) # Project to 2D, compute covariance, sort, blend image = standard3dgsrasterize(significantgaussians, camera) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The neural decoder introduces approximation errors. If the MLP is too small, it may fail to capture high-frequency details, leading to blurring. Boundaries: Voxelization resolution determines the minimum detail level. Too coarse a voxel size loses fine geometry; too fine increases memory overhead and reduces the benefit of anchoring. Degenerate Input: If SfM points are sparse, large empty voxels may be created. The method avoids allocating Gaussians in these regions, but the neural decoder must still handle queries for empty space gracefully (typically returning low opacity). Context-GS is a structured compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enhances representational capacity by explicitly modeling hierarchical relationships among anchor primitives. Unlike flat compression approaches, it employs a context-aware encoding scheme where higher-level anchors rely on context from coarser-level anchors for both encoding and decoding. It builds on anchor-based representations to predict attributes of dependent Gaussians, reducing redundancy and improving coding efficiency. Anchor-2D-GS and Anchor-3D-GS are modified variants of 2D-GS [15] and 3D-GS [5] that employ an anchor grid structure to organize Gaussian primitives more efficiently, reducing redundancy and storage overhead. They achieve competitive rendering quality with fewer file storage than original methods, demonstrating that the anchor design organizes primitives more efficiently. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is approximately 5× less than vanilla 3DGS at the same visual quality. This is achieved by storing only anchor features and offsets rather than full attributes for every Gaussian. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of visible anchors and the cost of the neural decoder. The MLP inference is fast but adds overhead compared to direct attribute lookup. Rasterization complexity is proportional to the number of significant Gaussians generated. Measured Performance: In large-scale scenes (e.g., CityGaussian), Scaffold-GS enables real-time rendering of massive datasets that would otherwise exceed memory limits. Strengths: High memory efficiency for large scenes. Natural Level-of-Detail (LoD) adaptation; distant views render fewer Gaussians. Better generalization to extrapolated views compared to flat representations. Limitations: Requires SfM initialization; performance degrades if SfM points are sparse or noisy. Neural decoding adds computational overhead per view compared to static attribute storage. May struggle with high-frequency details if the anchor density or MLP capacity is insufficient. When to Use: Large-scale urban reconstruction, huge scenes (CityGaussian), and scenarios requiring significant memory compression. When Not to Use: Small scenes where vanilla 3DGS fits in memory, or scenes with very sparse SfM data where voxelization is unreliable. Origin: Anchor-based representations were introduced to address the memory bottleneck of 3D Gaussian Splatting in large scenes. Scaffold-GS [34] (cited as [141] in, [34] in) pioneered the use of a sparse voxel grid with neural decoding. Octree-GS [142] (cited in) extended this with hierarchical octree structures for LoD. History: The method evolved from the need to scale 3DGS to city-scale environments. Early works like CityGaussian used tiling, while Scaffold-GS and Octree-GS introduced structured, hierarchical representations. Context-GS [50] (cited in) further refined this by adding hierarchical context prediction. Usage: Widely used in large-scale reconstruction pipelines, such as CityGaussian and VastGaussian, for streaming and rendering massive urban environments. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Compression in 3D Gaussian Splatting: A Survey of Methods, Trends, and Future Directions, https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSVT.2026.3676048, fetched 2026-10-26 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural Rendering — Technologies & Tricks, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeuralRenderingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Context-GS
head: Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting with Anchor Level Context Model, ContextGS
body: Context-GS is a structured compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enhances representational capacity by explicitly modeling hierarchical relationships among anchor primitives. Unlike flat compression approaches, it employs a context-aware encoding scheme where higher-level anchors rely on context from coarser-level anchors for both encoding and decoding. It builds on anchor-based representations to predict attributes of dependent Gaussians, reducing redundancy and improving coding efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} organized into a hierarchical anchor structure. Output: A compressed bitstream representing Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity) using entropy coding guided by the context model. Data Structures: The method employs a three-level hierarchical encoding scheme for anchors. 1. Coarse Level: Sparse anchor primitives that serve as reference points. 2. Intermediate/Fine Levels: Dependent Gaussians whose attributes are predicted based on the context of previously decoded anchors. Note: The exact bit-packing layout for entropy-coded residuals is not given in the sources. A low-dimensional quantized feature is introduced as a hyperprior for each anchor to improve entropy coding efficiency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Hierarchical Organization: Divide anchors into different levels based on their spatial positions. 2. Coarse-to-Fine Encoding: Hierarchically encode anchor attributes starting from the coarsest level to the finest level. 3. Contextual Prediction: For each uncoded anchor, predict its attributes based on already coded anchors in all coarser levels. Use earlier decoded anchors to guide the prediction of neighboring ones. 4. Residual Coding: Encode the difference between predicted and actual attributes using entropy coding. 5. Decoding: Reverse the process: decode coarse anchors first, use them to predict and decode finer anchors, reconstructing the full Gaussian set. Formulas: Let Ai be the attributes of the i-th anchor. The probability distribution P(Ai | \text{Context}i) is modeled using the context from previously decoded anchors. The context \text{Context}i includes attributes of coarser-level anchors and spatially neighboring decoded anchors. Specific mathematical formulations for the context model or prediction function are not provided in the sources. Parameters: Hierarchy Levels: Three levels are specified. name: Anchor-2D-GS / Anchor-3D-GS
head: Anchor-GS, modified versions of 2D-GS and 3D-GS
body: Anchor-2D-GS and Anchor-3D-GS are modified variants of 2D-GS [15] and 3D-GS [5] that employ an anchor grid structure to organize Gaussian primitives more efficiently, reducing redundancy and storage overhead. They achieve competitive rendering quality with fewer file storage than original methods, demonstrating that the anchor design organizes primitives more efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Output: A set of 2D or 3D Gaussians organized within an anchor grid structure. Data Structures: The method voxelize the input SfM points to create anchors. Each anchor is assigned 2D or 3D Gaussians. The exact layout of Gaussian attributes (fields, sizes, bit packing) is Not given in the sources, but follows the standard definitions of the parent method with spatial distribution constrained by the anchor grid. Numbered Steps: 1. Voxelize the input SfM points to generate the anchor grid. 2. Assign 2D or 3D Gaussians to each anchor. 3. Optimize the Gaussian parameters using the specified loss functions and densification strategy. Formulas: For Anchor-3D-GS, standard L1 and SSIM losses are used. For Anchor-2D-GS, the distortion loss is Ld = \sum{i,j} \omegai \omegaj |zi - zj| and the normal loss is Ln = \sumi \omegai (1 - \mathbf{n}i^T \mathbf{N}), where \omegai and \omegaj are opacities, zi and zj are depths, \mathbf{n}i is the predicted normal, and \mathbf{N} is the target normal. Parameters: Voxel size for the anchor grid is 0.001 for all scenes. Training runs for 40k iterations with densification concluding at 20k iterations for standard scenes, or 100k iterations with densification ending at 50k iterations for large-scale scenes. The densification interval is T = 100. The visibility threshold is \tauv = 0.7 for small-scale scenes. Loss weights are 0.8 (L1) and 0.2 (SSIM) for Anchor-3D-GS, and 0.01 (distortion) and 0.05 (normal) for Anchor-2D-GS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the input consists of SfM points. Not all layers are fully densified during progressive training, which may require extending densification by an additional 10k iterations. Anchor Gaussians are hypothesized to constrain and regularize parameters of coarser-level Gaussians, typically having larger scales than regular Gaussians. They do not have actual opacity for rendering; for visualization, their opacity is manually set to \text{sigmoid}(1). The average scale of anchors is e^{-5.08} across 100 randomly sampled scenes, while the average scale of Gaussians is e^{-7.12}. This size difference suggests that Gaussians adjust their scales to represent sharp details in real-world images, whereas anchor Gaussians serve a regularization role. The method achieves fewer file storage than original 2D-GS and 3D-GS methods. It delivers competitive rendering quality compared to original methods. The anchor design creates a more compact representation by reducing redundancy. While Anchor-2D/3D-GS reduce storage, Octree-GS delivers better visual performance and fewer Gaussian primitives due to its explicit, multi-level anchor design. Introduced in Octree-GS, the method modifies 2D-GS [15] and 3D-GS [5] by voxelizing input SfM points into an anchor grid and assigning Gaussians to each anchor, while adopting Scaffold-GS's densification strategy. name: Random Gaussian Generation
head: Gaussian Generation Dataset, Random Gaussian Cloud Generation, Random Gaussian Sampling
body: Random Gaussian Generation is the initialization procedure for creating a set of 3D Gaussians from scratch, typically to serve as the starting point for differentiable rendering optimization in methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting. It generates a fixed number of Gaussian primitives with random positions, scales, orientations, opacities, and spherical harmonics coefficients. It differs from LinPrim Population Control which manages the density of existing Gaussians during training, and from Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization which may use structured or data-driven initialization strategies. This method provides a uniform, uninformative prior over the parameter space. The method generates a set of N Gaussian objects. Each Gaussian is defined by a centroid, a scale vector, a rotation quaternion, an opacity scalar, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for color. Inputs: numsamples: Total number of Gaussians to generate. Default: 1000. numpoints: Number of points per Gaussian (used for internal representation or visualization, not stored in the final Gaussian object). Default: 144 (12 \times 12). minscale: Lower bound for the uniform distribution of scale components. Default: -12. maxscale: Upper bound for the uniform distribution of scale components. Default: -2. minopacity: Lower bound for the uniform distribution of opacity. Default: -5. maxopacity: Upper bound for the uniform distribution of opacity. Default: 10. shdegree: Maximum spherical harmonics degree to generate. Default: 3. returntype: Output format. Options: 'gaussian', 'param', or 'both'. Default: 'gaussian'. bounds: Tuple of 3 floats defining the spatial range [-b, b] for each dimension. Default: (2.0, 2.0, 2.0). Outputs: A list or tensor of Gaussian objects/parameters. If returntype is 'gaussian', returns full Gaussian objects. If 'param', returns raw parameter tensors. If 'both', returns both. Each Gaussian object contains: centroid: 3D vector representing the initial position. scale: 3D vector [sx, sy, sz]. rotation: Quaternion q derived from a rotation matrix. opacity: Scalar \alpha. featdc: 3D vector containing DC SH coefficients for R, G, B. featextra: Concatenated higher-order SH coefficients. 1. Initialize Position: Sample x, y, z independently from a uniform distribution over the bounding box defined by bounds. (Note: Some implementations fix the centroid at [0, 0, 0] and apply transformations later). 2. Initialize Scale: Sample sx, sy, sz independently from a uniform distribution U(\text{min\scale}, \text{max\scale}). (Alternative fixed distribution: s = |\mathcal{N}(0, 0.03) \times 0.03 + 0.04|). 3. Initialize Rotation: Generate a 3 \times 3 matrix M with entries drawn from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Compute the QR decomposition of M: M = QR. Take the Q factor as the rotation matrix R{mat}. Convert R{mat} to a quaternion q using a standard conversion function (e.g., rotmat2qvec). 4. Initialize Opacity: Sample opacity \alphai from a uniform distribution U(\text{min\opacity}, \text{max\opacity}). (Alternative clipped distribution: \alpha = \text{clip}(\mathcal{U}(0, 1) \times 0.5 + 0.5, 0, 1)). Note: The parameterized range [-5, 10] indicates logit space, requiring a sigmoid activation if interpreted as a probability. 5. Initialize Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: For each color channel (R, G, B) and each degree d from 0 to \text{sh\degree}: Calculate variance \sigmad^2 = \frac{1}{4^d}. Sample (2d+1) coefficients from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, \sigmad). If \text{sh\degree} < \text{max\SH\degree}, fill the remaining coefficients with normal noise \mathcal{N}(0, 0.05). The DC coefficients (d=0) for R, G, B form featdc. Higher-order coefficients (d > 0) are concatenated to form featextra. 6. Construct Gaussian Object: Assemble the components into a Gaussian object with centroid at [0,0,0], scale [sx, sy, sz], rotation q, opacity \alpha, featdc, and featextra. 7. Repeat: Steps 1-6 are repeated for N = \text{num\samples} Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generaterandomgaussians(numsamples=1000, minscale=-12, maxscale=-2, minopacity=-5, maxopacity=10, shdegree=3, bounds=(2.0, 2.0, 2.0), returntype='gaussian'): """ Generates a set of random 3D Gaussians for initialization. Follows parameterized generation from with bounds support from. """ gaussians = [] for in range(numsamples): # 1. Generate Position pos = (np.random.rand(3) - 0.5) 2.0 np.array(bounds) # 2. Generate Scale scale = np.random.uniform(minscale, maxscale, 3) # 3. Generate Rotation M = np.random.randn(3, 3) Q, = np.linalg.qr(M) # Ensure proper rotation matrix (handle reflection if det(Q) == -1) if np.linalg.det(Q) < 0: Q[:, 0] = -1 rotation = rotmat2qvec(Q) # 4. Generate Opacity opacity = np.random.uniform(minopacity, maxopacity) # 5. Generate Spherical Harmonics Coefficients featdc = [] featextra = [] for d in range(shdegree + 1): variance = 1.0 / (4 d) std = np.sqrt(variance) numcoeffs = 2 d + 1 # Sample coefficients for R, G, B coeffsr = np.random.normal(0, std, numcoeffs) coeffsg = np.random.normal(0, std, numcoeffs) coeffsb = np.random.normal(0, std, numcoeffs) if d == 0: featdc = [coeffsr[0], coeffsg[0], coeffsb[0]] else: featextra.extend(coeffsr) featextra.extend(coeffsg) featextra.extend(coeffsb) # Fill remaining coefficients if shdegree < max possible (assumed 3) maxshdegree = 3 if shdegree < maxshdegree: for d in range(shdegree + 1, maxshdegree + 1): numcoeffs = 2 d + 1 featextra.extend(np.random.normal(0, 0.05, numcoeffs)) featextra.extend(np.random.normal(0, 0.05, numcoeffs)) featextra.extend(np.random.normal(0, 0.05, numcoeffs)) # 6. Construct Gaussian Object gaussian = { 'centroid': pos, 'scale': scale, 'rotation': rotation, 'opacity': opacity, 'featdc': np.array(featdc), 'featextra': np.array(featextra) } gaussians.append(gaussian) return gaussians def rotmat2qvec(R): """ Converts a 3x3 rotation matrix to a quaternion [w, x, y, z]. Standard conversion algorithm. """ m00, m01, m02 = R[0, 0], R[0, 1], R[0, 2] m10, m11, m12 = R[1, 0], R[1, 1], R[1, 2] m20, m21, m22 = R[2, 0], R[2, 1], R[2, 2] trace = m00 + m11 + m22 if trace > 0: s = 0.5 / np.sqrt(trace + 1.0) w = 0.25 / s x = (m21 - m12) s y = (m02 - m20) s z = (m10 - m01) s elif (m00 > m11) and (m00 > m22): s = 2.0 np.sqrt(1.0 + m00 - m11 - m22) w = (m21 - m12) / s x = 0.25 s y = (m01 + m10) / s z = (m02 + m20) / s elif m11 > m22: s = 2.0 np.sqrt(1.0 + m11 - m00 - m22) w = (m02 - m20) / s x = (m01 + m10) / s y = 0.25 s z = (m12 + m21) / s else: s = 2.0 np.sqrt(1.0 + m22 - m00 - m11) w = (m10 - m01) / s x = (m02 + m20) / s y = (m12 + m21) / s z = 0.25 s return np.array([w, x, y, z]) Reflection in Rotation: The QR decomposition of a random normal matrix can produce a reflection (determinant -1) instead of a rotation. The pseudocode includes a check to flip the first column if det(Q) < 0 to ensure a proper rotation matrix. Opacity Range: The default opacity range [-5, 10] suggests logit space. If used directly as probability, it will cause numerical issues. It should be passed through a sigmoid function if interpreted as probability. SH Variance: The variance decreases exponentially with degree (1/4^d). This ensures higher-frequency details have smaller initial amplitudes, stabilizing optimization. Missing SH Coefficients: If shdegree is less than the maximum supported degree, remaining coefficients must be filled with noise to maintain tensor shape consistency. Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting (CAG-GS) is a large-scale scene rendering method that employs a divide-and-conquer strategy with semantic guidance to ensure global consistency across spatial blocks, thereby avoiding artifacts such as floaters and brightness inconsistencies. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Momentum-GS by directly incorporating consistent semantic information from a pre-trained segmentation model (SAM2) to guide feature learning, rather than relying solely on shared MLP decoders for regularization. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of samples and D is the number of SH coefficients. The QR decomposition is O(1) per Gaussian (fixed 3x3 matrix). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) to store the generated Gaussians. Performance: The method is fast and deterministic in its randomness. It does not depend on scene geometry, making it suitable for initial exploration or when no point cloud is available. Strengths: Simple to implement, no external data required, provides a diverse initial set of orientations and scales. Limitations: The Gaussians are not aligned with any scene structure, leading to slow convergence if the scene is complex. The random positions require subsequent transformation or optimization to match the scene. When to Use: When initializing a new scene with no prior geometric information, or as a baseline for comparison. When Not to Use: When a point cloud or mesh is available, structured initialization (e.g., Gaussian Splatting Initialization and Parameterization) is preferred for faster convergence and better initial quality. The method is described in the context of the gs-embedding project, which explores embedding-based representations for 3D Gaussians. The specific parameters and generation steps are derived from the implementation details provided in the source code and documentation of this project. The use of QR decomposition for random rotations is a standard technique in computer graphics for generating uniform random rotations. The exponential decay of SH variance is a common practice in neural rendering to stabilize training. name: Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting
head: CAG-GS
body: Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting (CAG-GS) is a large-scale scene rendering method that employs a divide-and-conquer strategy with semantic guidance to ensure global consistency across spatial blocks, thereby avoiding artifacts such as floaters and brightness inconsistencies. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Momentum-GS by directly incorporating consistent semantic information from a pre-trained segmentation model (SAM2) to guide feature learning, rather than relying solely on shared MLP decoders for regularization. Inputs: Sparse point cloud P from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); training views with ground truth images; pre-trained semantic segmentation model (SAM2). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by anchors, optimized for novel view synthesis. Anchor (Aj): Each anchor is defined by: Level-of-Detail (lj): Integer level in the hierarchy. Position (pj): 3D coordinate in space. Learnable Feature (fj): Vector in \mathbb{R}^d. Spatial Offsets (o{j,1}, \dots, o{j,K}): K learnable 3D offset vectors in \mathbb{R}^{3K} used to predict Gaussian positions. Implicit Gaussians: Generated per anchor. Each Gaussian i has: Position (\mui): Derived from anchor position and offsets. Color (ci): Predicted by MLP. Opacity (\sigmai): Predicted by MLP. Covariance (\Sigmai): Parameterized by scaling and rotation (standard 3D-GS definition). L: Number of Level-of-Detail (LoD) levels for voxelization. \delta: Base voxel size. d: Dimensionality of the anchor feature vector fj. K: Expected number of Gaussians generated per anchor. \lambda: Weighting coefficient for SSIM loss (standard 3D-GS parameter). 1. Scene Discretization (Anchor Generation): The sparse point cloud P is voxelized at L different resolutions to generate anchor points A. For each point p \in P and level l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}, the anchor position is calculated as: A = \left\{ \left\lfloor \frac{p}{\delta/2^l} \right\rceil \cdot \frac{\delta}{2^l} \mid p \in P, l = 0, \dots, L-1 \right\} where \lfloor \cdot \rceil denotes element-wise rounding and \delta is the base voxel size. 2. Coarse Global Training: A coarse global model is trained using all available training views to provide global priors. 3. Block Division: The scene is divided into multiple spatial blocks. 4. Semantic Mapping Module Initialization: A semantic mapping module \gamma: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^D is introduced. This module is trained to align its outputs with visual features extracted from the pre-trained SAM2 model. 5. Block-wise Fine-Tuning (Iterative per Block): For each block: a. View Assignment: Training views are assigned to the block according to blending weights computed during rendering. b. Anchor Selection: During rendering, visible anchors are selected based on their LoD levels and distance from the target viewpoint. c. Feature Fusion: For each selected anchor j with position pj and feature fj, a semantic vector is generated and fused: \tilde{f}j = W \cdot \gamma(pj) + fj where \gamma(pj) is the semantic vector encoded by the mapping module, and W is a learnable weight matrix. d. Gaussian Prediction: The enhanced feature \tilde{f}j is passed through MLP decoders to predict the attributes of K implicit Gaussians associated with the anchor. e. Rendering: The predicted 3D Gaussians are projected to 2D. They are sorted by depth and composited using alpha blending: C(x') = \sum{i \in I(x')} ci \alphai \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak) where x' is the queried pixel, I(x') is the set of indices of contributing Gaussians sorted by depth, and \alphai = \sigmai G'i(x') is the transmittance/opacity contribution of Gaussian i at pixel x'. f. Optimization: The Gaussians are optimized by minimizing the photometric loss: \mathcal{L}{3DGS} = (1 - \lambda)\mathcal{L}1(I, \hat{I}) + \lambda\mathcal{L}{SSIM}(I, \hat{I}) where I is the rendered image, \hat{I} is the ground truth, \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss, and \mathcal{L}{SSIM} is the SSIM loss. 6. Merging: The optimized blocks are cropped along their division boundaries and seamlessly merged to obtain the final reconstruction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class MLP: """Standard feedforward network for Gaussian attribute prediction.""" def init(self, indim, outdim): self.W = [[0.0]outdim for in range(indim)] def call(self, x): return [sum(self.W[i][j]x[i] for i in range(len(x))) for j in range(len(self.W[0]))] def roundelementwise(vec, scale): """Element-wise rounding to grid centers.""" return [round(v / scale) scale for v in vec] def generateanchors(pointcloud, delta, L, d, K): """Discretize point cloud into anchors at L levels of detail.""" anchors = [] for p in pointcloud: for l in range(L): gridsize = delta / (2 l) pos = roundelementwise(p, gridsize) anchors.append({ 'level': l, 'position': pos, 'feature': [0.0]d, 'offsets': [[0.0]3 for in range(K)] }) return anchors def semanticmapping(position, gammanet): """Encode 3D position into semantic vector via SAM2-aligned module.""" return gammanet(position) def fusefeatures(anchor, semanticvec, W): """Fuse semantic information with anchor's learnable feature.""" return [sum(W[i][j]semanticvec[i] for i in range(len(W))) + anchor['feature'][j] for j in range(len(anchor['feature']))] def predictgaussians(enhancedfeat, mlpdec): """Predict attributes for K Gaussians from enhanced feature.""" return mlpdec(enhancedfeat) def renderblock(anchors, viewpoint, gammanet, W, mlpdec, K): """Render a single block using selected anchors.""" visible = [a for a in anchors if math.dist(a['position'], viewpoint.campos) < viewpoint.maxdist] gaussians = [] for a in visible: semvec = semanticmapping(a['position'], gammanet) fused = fusefeatures(a, semvec, W) attrs = predictgaussians(fused, mlpdec) for k in range(K): gaussians.append({ 'pos': [a['position'][i]+a['offsets'][k][i] for i in range(3)], 'color': attrs[k4:k4+3], 'opacity': attrs[k4+3] }) gaussians.sort(key=lambda g: math.dist(g['pos'], viewpoint.campos)) img = [[0.0]3 for in range(viewheight)] for g in gaussians: alpha = g['opacity'] math.exp(-0.5 math.dist(g['pos'], viewpoint.pixelproj)) img = [[img[r][c](1-alpha) + g['color'][c]alpha for c in range(3)] for r in range(viewheight)] return img def traincaggs(pointcloud, views, gammanet, W, mlpdec, delta, L, K, d): """Main training loop with coarse-to-fine strategy.""" anchors = generateanchors(pointcloud, delta, L, d, K) # Coarse global training: optimize all anchors using all views for epoch in range(numepochscoarse): for v in views: img = renderblock(anchors, v, gammanet, W, mlpdec, K) loss = photometricloss(img, v.gtimage) updateparameters(loss) # Block division: partition anchors into spatial blocks blocks = dividescene(anchors) for block in blocks: # View assignment: assign views based on blending weights blockviews = assignviews(block, views) # Block-wise fine-tuning for epoch in range(numepochsfine): for v in blockviews: img = renderblock(block, v, gammanet, W, mlpdec, K) loss = photometricloss(img, v.gtimage) updateparameters(loss) # Merging: crop blocks at boundaries and merge finalscene = mergeblocks(blocks) return finalscene Precision: The rounding operation \lfloor \cdot \rceil in anchor generation must be handled carefully to ensure consistent anchor placement across different resolutions. Boundaries: When merging blocks, cropping along division boundaries is required to avoid double-counting or gaps, though the specific blending function for the merge is not detailed beyond "seamlessly merged". Global Priors: The coarse global model provides global priors during the initial training phase. Time Complexity: The method involves a coarse global training phase followed by block-wise fine-tuning. The complexity is dominated by the rendering and optimization steps per block. The use of LoD levels allows for efficient culling of distant anchors. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced compared to explicit 3D-GS by using implicit Gaussian prediction from anchors. The number of anchors is determined by the voxelization of the SfM point cloud. Strengths: Handles large-scale scenes efficiently; avoids floaters and brightness inconsistencies through semantic guidance; preserves global consistency via coarse-to-fine training. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained semantic segmentation model (SAM2); performance depends on the quality of the initial SfM point cloud. When to use: Large-scale scene rendering where global consistency is critical and explicit Gaussian storage is prohibitive. When not to use: Small-scale scenes where explicit 3D-GS is sufficient; scenes with poor SfM reconstruction. CAG-GS was proposed to address the computational and storage burdens of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) when applied to large-scale scenes. It builds on the implicit scene representation approach where anchors predict Gaussian attributes. The method was introduced to overcome the limitations of divide-and-conquer strategies that often lead to limited performance due to inconsistent lighting and floaters. The hierarchical representation follows OctreeGS. The method integrates semantic guidance from SAM2 to improve feature learning. name: Hierarchical Gaussian Generation with Densify
head: coarse-to-fine Gaussian hierarchy, densify operation
body: Hierarchical Gaussian Generation with Densify is a method for constructing 3D Gaussian representations in a coarse-to-fine hierarchy, primarily designed to stabilize Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) training by regularizing the position and scale of synthesized primitives. It solves the problem of training instability and poor management of geometric parameters (position \mu and scale s) in generative models by enforcing locality constraints between adjacent hierarchy levels. Unlike flat initialization methods, it establishes a dependency where fine-level Gaussians are derived from coarse-level counterparts via residual updates, allowing the generator to model multi-scale details effectively. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Latent code z, initial learnable positions const \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}, and hierarchy level index l. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian parameters Gl at level l, comprising position \mul, scale sl, rotation ql, opacity \alphal, and color cl. Data Structures: Each Gaussian G is defined by the tuple (\mu, s, q, \alpha, c). \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. s \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale. q \in \mathbb{R}^4: Unit quaternion representing rotation. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity scalar. c \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color vector. Intermediate residual parameters \hat{G}l contain (\hat{\mu}l, \hat{s}l, \hat{q}l, \hat{\alpha}l, \hat{c}l). Parameters: l: Hierarchy level index, integer, range \{0, \dots, L-1\}. N: Number of initial Gaussians at level l=0. r: Upsampling ratio, multiplier for the number of Gaussians at each finer level. Steps: 1. Level 0 Initialization: Input N learnable positions const and latent code z into generator block block0. Output high-dimensional features x0. Process each feature x{0i} through output layer toGaus0 to obtain initial Gaussian parameters G{0i} = \{\mu{0i}, s{0i}, q{0i}, \alpha{0i}, c{0i}\}. 2. Hierarchical Expansion (Level l > 0): For each Gaussian G{l-1,i} from the previous level, generate r new Gaussians at level l. The index mapping is j = r \cdot i + k, where k \in \{0, \dots, r-1\}. Compute features x{lj} using generator block blockl taking input from the parent feature x{l-1,i} and latent code z: x{lj} = blockl(x{l-1,i}, z) Generate intermediate residual parameters \hat{G}{lj} using output layer toGausl: \hat{G}{lj} = toGausl(x{lj}) Where \hat{G}{lj} = \{\hat{\mu}{lj}, \hat{s}{lj}, \hat{q}{lj}, \hat{\alpha}{lj}, \hat{c}{lj}\}. 3. Densify Operation: Combine the coarse Gaussian G{l-1,i} with the residual parameters \hat{G}{lj} to produce the fine-level Gaussian G{lj}. This operation is denoted as G{lj} = densify(G{l-1,i}, \hat{G}{lj}). Position Update: The position \mu{lj} is constrained to be local relative to the parent G{l-1,i}. The residual \hat{\mu}{lj} is defined in the coordinate system centered, rotated, and scaled by G{l-1,i}. \mu{lj} = \mu{l-1,i} + R{l-1,i} S{l-1,i} \hat{\mu}{lj} Where R{l-1,i} and S{l-1,i} are the rotation and scaling matrices derived from the quaternion q{l-1,i} and scale s{l-1,i} of the parent Gaussian G{l-1,i}. Residual Updates for Other Parameters: Opacity, rotation, and color are updated via simple addition of residuals: \alpha{lj} = \alpha{l-1,i} + \hat{\alpha}{lj} q{lj} = q{l-1,i} + \hat{q}{lj} c{lj} = c{l-1,i} + \hat{c}{lj} The source explicitly specifies this additive form for quaternions. 4. Rendering: Render the scene using all generated Gaussians from all levels l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}. Total number of Gaussians: N + rN + \dots + r^{L-1}N. Use a tile-based rasterizer following 3D Gaussian Splatting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """Converts a unit quaternion [w, x, y, z] to a 3x3 rotation matrix.""" w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ]) def densify(parentg, residualparams): """ Combines a parent Gaussian with residual parameters to create a child Gaussian. parentg: dict with keys 'mu', 's', 'q', 'alpha', 'c' residualparams: dict with keys 'muhat', 'shat', 'qhat', 'alphahat', 'chat' Returns: dict with keys 'mu', 's', 'q', 'alpha', 'c' """ R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(parentg['q']) S = np.diag(parentg['s']) # Position update (Eq. 3) muc = parentg['mu'] + R @ S @ residualparams['muhat'] # Opacity update (Eq. 4) alphac = parentg['alpha'] + residualparams['alphahat'] # Color update (Eq. 5) cc = parentg['c'] + residualparams['chat'] # Quaternion update (Eq. 5) qc = parentg['q'] + residualparams['qhat'] # Scale update: The source provides explicit formulas for mu, alpha, q, c # but does not explicitly define the update rule for scale s using shat. sc = parentg['s'] return {'mu': muc, 's': sc, 'q': qc, 'alpha': alphac, 'c': cc} def generatehierarchicalgaussians(N, r, L, z, const, blockfunc, toGausfunc): """ Generates hierarchical Gaussians following the densify method. N: Initial number of Gaussians at level 0 r: Upsampling ratio L: Number of levels (0 to L-1) z: Latent code const: Initial learnable positions [N, 3] blockfunc: blockl(xprev, z) -> xcurr toGausfunc: toGausl(x) -> paramsorresiduals """ alllevels = [] # Level 0 Initialization x0 = blockfunc(0, const, z) G0 = [toGausfunc(0, x) for x in x0] alllevels.append(G0) # Hierarchical Expansion for levels 1 to L-1 for l in range(1, L): Gprev = alllevels[-1] Gcurr = [] xprev = alllevels[l-2] if l > 1 else x0 # Features from previous level for i in range(len(Gprev)): for k in range(r): j = r i + k xlj = blockfunc(l, xprev[i], z) residual = toGausfunc(l, xlj) Glj = densify(Gprev[i], residual) Gcurr.append(Glj) alllevels.append(Gcurr) return alllevels Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Variance: The scale of Gaussians can become nearly zero along a specific axis, leading to excessively strong regularization on the position of finer-level Gaussians. Quaternion Normalization: The additive update q{lj} = q{l-1,i} + \hat{q}{lj} is explicitly defined in the source. Scale Update: The source provides explicit formulas for \mu, \alpha, q, c but does not explicitly define the update rule for scale s using \hat{s}l in equations 3-5, despite mentioning \hat{s}l as an intermediate parameter. An auxiliary set of Gaussians Al used only for regularization (input to densify) to prevent strong regularization issues (e.g., zero variance) when guiding finer-level Gaussians, without contributing to actual rendering. For level l=0, A{0i} = \hat{A}{0i} and G{0i} = densify(A{0i}, \hat{G}{0i}). Anchors relieve the effect of strong regularization caused by zero variance in the parent Gaussians. Complexity: The number of Gaussians grows exponentially with hierarchy depth L: N(1 + r + \dots + r^{L-1}). Performance: Rendering uses a tile-based rasterizer following 3D-GS. Strengths: Stabilizes GAN training by reducing the possible positions of Gaussians and encourages the use of various scales, boosting the capability to model both coarse and fine details. Limitations: Requires careful handling of scale parameters to avoid zero variance. Originated in GSGAN (Gaussian Splatting GAN), which proposes a generator architecture with hierarchical 3D Gaussians to handle unstructured 3D point cloud data. The method addresses training instability and failure to properly manage position and scale in generative models. name: Gaussian Property Loading
head: PLY Property Loading with Fallbacks, PLY Gaussian Loading, PLY Stream Parsing, PLY Parser
body: Gaussian Property Loading is the method for ingesting 3D Gaussian Splatting scene data from Polygon File Format (PLY) files and decoding raw vertex properties into the explicit mathematical parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) required by the rasterization pipeline. It solves the problem of converting the standardized, often compressed or logarithmically encoded PLY storage format into the structured GaussianSet representation. It differs from its siblings by focusing on the initial ingestion and decoding of the PLY file into the GaussianData structure, whereas Coordinate System Conversion for Gaussian Splats handles spatial alignment and INRIA V1 PLY Splat Parsing addresses specific legacy format variations. Inputs: A PLY file (ASCII or binary, little/big endian) containing vertex elements with properties for position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) or RGB color. Outputs: A contiguous array or list of Gaussian objects containing decoded means, normalized quaternions, exponential scales, sigmoid opacities, and SH coefficients. Data Structures: The packed Gaussian structure in memory typically consists of: 1. position: 3 floats (x, y, z). 2. logScale: 3 floats (log of scale factors). 3. rotQuat: 4 floats (quaternion components w, x, y, z). 4. opacityLogit: 1 float (logit of opacity). 5. shCoeffs: A static array of nShCoeffs groups of 3 floats (RGB coefficients for each SH degree). Numbered Steps: 1. File Ingestion: Read the PLY file into memory. For binary files, read as an ArrayBuffer or byte stream. For ASCII, parse line by line. Detect format (ASCII, binary little-endian, binary big-endian). 2. Header Parsing: Parse the PLY header to identify the vertex element count and property definitions. Map property names to their types (float, uchar, etc.). 3. Property Mapping & Fallbacks: Identify the specific property names used in the file. Apply fallback logic for compatibility: Scale: Try scale0, scale1, scale2. If not found, try scaling0, scaling1, scaling2. Rotation: Try rot0, rot1, rot2, rot3. If not found, try rotation0, rotation1, rotation2, rotation3. Color/SH: Try fdc0, fdc1, fdc2 for DC spherical harmonics. If not found, try red, green, blue for RGB. If neither, default to white. Opacity: Try opacity. If not found, default to full opacity (1.0). 4. Data Extraction: Extract the raw values for each vertex. Position: Map x, y, z to position components. Stack into shape (N, 3). Scale: Extract scale values. These are stored as log-scale values. Apply exponential activation: s = \exp(v). Rotation: Extract rot values. These form a quaternion. Normalize the quaternion to unit length: q{norm} = q / \|q\|. Opacity: Extract opacity value. This is stored as a logit. Apply sigmoid activation: \alpha = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-v}}. Spherical Harmonics: Determine the SH degree by counting properties starting with frest. Let n{rest} be this count. Calculate coefficients per color n{coeffs} = n{rest} / 3. The degree L is derived from n{coeffs} = (L+1)^2 - 1, so L = \sqrt{n{coeffs} + 1} - 1. Map fdc0, fdc1, fdc2 to the first 3 SH coefficients (DC term). Map frest properties to higher-order SH coefficients starting at index 3. Sort frest properties by their integer suffix to maintain order. 5. Coordinate System Conversion (Optional but Common): If the PLY was generated in a different coordinate system (e.g., Right-handed Down-Forward vs. Right-handed Up-Back), apply axis flips and rotations to positions and quaternions to align with the renderer's coordinate space. 6. DC Color Computation: Compute the base color from the DC SH coefficients. The DC coefficient c0 relates to color C by C = c0 \cdot C0 + 0.5, where C0 \approx 0.28209479177387814. The final color is often clamped: C{final} = \max(C \cdot C0 + 0.5, 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import struct def loadgaussiansfromply(filepath): """ Loads 3D Gaussian Splatting data from a PLY file. Returns a list of Gaussian dicts with keys: xyz, rot, scale, opacity, shs, dccolours. """ # 1. Read file content with open(filepath, 'rb') as f: content = f.read() # 2. Parse Header headerend = content.find(b'endheader') if headerend == -1: raise ValueError("Invalid PLY file: no endheader found") headertext = content[:headerend].decode('ascii') vertexcount = 0 properties = {} for line in headertext.split('\n'): if line.startswith('element vertex'): parts = line.split() vertexcount = int(parts[2]) elif line.startswith('property'): parts = line.split() # Format: property <type> <name> proptype = parts[1] propname = parts[2] properties[propname] = proptype # 3. Identify Property Names with Fallbacks posnames = ['x', 'y', 'z'] # Scale fallback: scale0/1/2 or scaling0/1/2 if 'scale0' in properties: scalenames = ['scale0', 'scale1', 'scale2'] elif 'scaling0' in properties: scalenames = ['scaling0', 'scaling1', 'scaling2'] else: raise ValueError("No scale properties found") # Rotation fallback: rot0..3 or rotation0..3 if 'rot0' in properties: rotnames = ['rot0', 'rot1', 'rot2', 'rot3'] elif 'rotation0' in properties: rotnames = ['rotation0', 'rotation1', 'rotation2', 'rotation3'] else: raise ValueError("No rotation properties found") # SH fallback: fdc0..2 or red/green/blue if 'fdc0' in properties: hassh = True shdcnames = ['fdc0', 'fdc1', 'fdc2'] # Count rest coefficients to determine degree restnames = [k for k in properties.keys() if k.startswith('frest')] restnames.sort(key=lambda x: int(x.split('')[1])) # Sort by suffix nrest = len(restnames) # nrest = 3 ((L+1)^2 - 1) # (L+1)^2 - 1 = nrest / 3 # (L+1)^2 = nrest / 3 + 1 # L = sqrt(nrest / 3 + 1) - 1 ncoeffspercolor = nrest / 3 shdegree = math.sqrt(ncoeffspercolor + 1) - 1 nshcoeffs = int((shdegree + 1)2) # Total coeffs per color (including DC) # Actually, shs array usually stores all coeffs. # DC is 3 coeffs (R,G,B). Rest is 3 ((L+1)^2 - 1). # Total floats for SH = 3 (L+1)^2 totalshfloats = 3 int((shdegree + 1)2) elif 'red' in properties: hassh = False shdcnames = ['red', 'green', 'blue'] totalshfloats = 3 # Just RGB else: hassh = False shdcnames = ['red', 'green', 'blue'] # Default to white if missing totalshfloats = 3 # Opacity fallback if 'opacity' in properties: opacityname = 'opacity' else: opacityname = None # Default to 1.0 # 4. Parse Data # Determine byte offset after header dataoffset = headerend + len(b'endheader\n') + 1 # +1 for newline # Determine endianness and type sizes from header or assume little-endian float # For simplicity, assuming little-endian floats for binary, or parsing ASCII # This pseudocode assumes binary little-endian for brevity, but handles ASCII logic conceptually gaussians = [] # Helper to read float def readfloat(data, offset): return struct.unpackfrom('<f', data, offset)[0] # Helper to read uchar (0-255) def readuchar(data, offset): return struct.unpackfrom('B', data, offset)[0] / 255.0 # Helper to read int/short etc if needed, but PLY GS usually uses float/uchar currentoffset = dataoffset for i in range(vertexcount): g = {} # Position x = readfloat(content, currentoffset) y = readfloat(content, currentoffset + 4) z = readfloat(content, currentoffset + 8) g['xyz'] = [x, y, z] currentoffset += 12 # Scale (Log scale) s0 = readfloat(content, currentoffset) s1 = readfloat(content, currentoffset + 4) s2 = readfloat(content, currentoffset + 8) # Apply exp() g['scale'] = [math.exp(s0), math.exp(s1), math.exp(s2)] currentoffset += 12 # Rotation (Quaternion) w = readfloat(content, currentoffset) xq = readfloat(content, currentoffset + 4) yq = readfloat(content, currentoffset + 8) zq = readfloat(content, currentoffset + 12) # Normalize norm = math.sqrt(ww + xqxq + yqyq + zqzq) if norm > 0: g['rot'] = [w/norm, xq/norm, yq/norm, zq/norm] else: g['rot'] = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentoffset += 16 # Opacity (Logit) if opacityname: oplogit = readfloat(content, currentoffset) # Apply sigmoid g['opacity'] = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-oplogit)) currentoffset += 4 else: g['opacity'] = 1.0 # SH / Color if hassh: shdata = [] # Read DC for name in shdcnames: # Find offset of this property in the vertex record # In a real parser, we'd map property names to offsets in the header # Here we assume contiguous reading based on header order or explicit offsets # For pseudocode, we assume we can find the offset for 'fdc0' etc. # This part is complex in raw binary parsing without a library. # We will assume a helper getpropertyoffset(name) exists. offset = getpropertyoffset(name, properties) val = readfloat(content, offset) # Simplified: assumes float type shdata.append(val) # Read Rest for name in restnames: offset = getpropertyoffset(name, properties) val = readfloat(content, offset) shdata.append(val) g['shs'] = shdata # Compute DC Colour # C0 constant C0 = 0.28209479177387814 # DC coeffs are the first 3 values in shdata (R, G, B) dcvals = shdata[:3] # Formula: dccolours = max(dcvals C0 + 0.5, 0) g['dccolours'] = [max(v C0 + 0.5, 0.0) for v in dcvals] else: # RGB Fallback r = readuchar(content, getpropertyoffset('red', properties)) gval = readuchar(content, getpropertyoffset('green', properties)) b = readuchar(content, getpropertyoffset('blue', properties)) g['shs'] = [r, gval, b] g['dccolours'] = [r, gval, b] gaussians.append(g) return gaussians def getpropertyoffset(propname, properties): """ Stub for finding the byte offset of a property in the binary record. In a real implementation, this parses the header to calculate offsets based on property types and order. """ # This is a placeholder. Real implementation requires parsing the # 'property <type> <name>' lines to build a layout map. return 0 # Placeholder Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: PLY files may use uchar for color/opacity. Ensure division by 255.0 is applied correctly. Endianness: Binary PLY files can be little-endian or big-endian. Detect and swap bytes if necessary. SH Degree: The SH degree is not always explicitly stated in the header. It must be inferred from the count of frest properties. Coordinate Systems: Different tools export PLYs in different coordinate systems (e.g., Z-up vs Y-up). Coordinate conversion may be required before or after loading. The Gaussian Splat PLY Loader parses 3D Gaussian Splatting scene data from a Polygon File Format (PLY) file, decoding raw vertex properties into a structured Gaussian representation suitable for rendering. It solves the problem of converting the standardized, often compressed or logarithmically encoded PLY storage format into the explicit mathematical parameters (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity) required by the rasterization pipeline. It differs from its siblings by focusing on the initial ingestion and decoding of the PLY file into the GaussianData structure, whereas Coordinate System Conversion for Gaussian Splats handles spatial alignment and INRIA V1 PLY Splat Parsing addresses specific legacy format variations. This method transforms Gaussian splat attributes (position, rotation, spherical harmonics) between different coordinate systems, such as converting from the Right-handed Up-Back (RUB) format used internally to the Right-handed Down-Forward (RDF) format used in PLY files. It sets apart from sibling loaders by handling the specific axis flips and rotations required for quaternion and spherical harmonic consistency, ensuring that the rendered output remains invariant under coordinate system changes. The INRIA V1 PLY Splat Parsing method decodes the text-based.ply files generated by the original INRIA 3D Gaussian Splatting implementation into an uncompressed, contiguous array of Gaussian properties suitable for rendering or further processing. It solves the problem of interpreting variable-length spherical harmonic (SH) fields and applying specific activation functions (sigmoid for opacity, exponential for scale) and coordinate system transformations required by downstream engines. Unlike the standard.splat binary format which uses fixed-width records, this method handles the PLY header's variable field counts to dynamically determine the SH degree (0, 1, or 2) and extract the corresponding coefficients. This method preprocesses a raw 3D Gaussian Splatting model stored in PLY format for use in Unreal Engine. It parses the PLY file, converts coordinate systems and property encodings to match the engine's internal representation, and partitions the Gaussians into a spatial grid for efficient culling and rendering. It differs from generic loaders by applying specific axis swaps, exponential scale decoding, and sigmoid opacity activation required by the target engine's shader pipeline. A method to read standard 3D Gaussian Splatting.ply files into Unreal Engine data structures, supporting both ASCII and binary (little/big endian) formats. The parser uses Miniply to load the file. It identifies the file type from constants: kFileTypes = {"ascii", "binarylittleendian", "binarybigendian"} and property types from kPropertyTypes = {"char", "uchar", "short", "ushort", "int", "uint", "float", "double"}. The output FGaussianSplatData struct contains: Positions (TArray<FVector>), Normals (TArray<FVector>), Orientations (TArray<FQuat>, stored as wxyz from PLY), Scales (TArray<FVector>), Opacity (TArray<float>), ZeroOrderHarmonicsCoefficients (TArray<FVector>), and HighOrderHarmonicsCoefficients (TArray<FHighOrderHarmonicsCoefficientsStruct> where FHighOrderHarmonicsCoefficientsStruct contains TArray<FVector> Values). The DC color conversion uses the constant C0 = 0.28209479177387814. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, as each vertex property is read and transformed once. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) where D is the dimensionality of the Gaussian properties (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients). Performance: Loading is generally fast, dominated by I/O and simple arithmetic operations (exp, sigmoid, normalization). Parsing binary PLY is faster than ASCII. Strengths: Standardized format (PLY) ensures compatibility across many 3D reconstruction tools. Fallbacks for property names increase robustness. Limitations: PLY files can be large, especially with high-degree SH. Loading time increases with file size. Coordinate system mismatches are a common source of visual errors if not handled. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The standard output format for trained 3DGS models is the PLY file. Various implementations (INRIA, WebGPU viewers, Unreal Engine plugins) have developed loaders to interpret these files, leading to the variants described in the Subtopics section. The method described here synthesizes the common practices found in these implementations.
