name: 4DGS v2 Spacetime Loader
head: static canvas + dynamic trajectories
body: The 4DGS v2 Spacetime Loader is a parsing and loading strategy for.4dsplat v2 files that separates a Gaussian Splatting scene into a static "canvas" of persistent primitives and a set of dynamic "tracks" defined by temporal control points and position trajectories. Unlike the v1 progressive loader which streams independent blocks per timestep requiring texture re-uploads, this method stores one static gaussian set plus dynamic trajectories, allowing the viewer to paint the static canvas as bytes arrive and interpolate dynamic tracks continuously on the GPU after the stream completes. It is designed for camera-aware "Motion" clips where the subject moves within a fixed camera frame. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary.4dsplat v2 file stream. Output: GPU-ready texture buffers (attr, scales, colors, rots, positions) and metadata (aliveByCp) for a WebGL renderer. Data Structures and Layout: The file begins with a 60-byte header: Bytes 0-3: Magic string '4DGS'. Bytes 4-7: Version (uint32 LE, must be 2). Bytes 8-11: numCp (uint32 LE, number of temporal control points). Bytes 12-15: Padding. Bytes 16-19: fps (float32 LE). Bytes 20-43: Bounding box (6 float32 LE). Bytes 44-47: staticCount (uint32 LE). Bytes 48-51: trackCount (uint32 LE). Bytes 52-55: posCount (uint32 LE). Bytes 56-59: Padding. The data is organized into arrays padded to TEXWIDTH rows (typically 1024 or 2048 texels) to optimize GPU texture uploads. The padded row size is calculated as: \text{padRows}(texels) = \text{TEX\WIDTH} \times \max\left(1, \left\lceil \frac{texels}{\text{TEX\WIDTH}} \right\rceil\right) \times 4 1. Instance Attributes (attr): Float32Array of size padRows(staticCount + trackCount). Per instance i, indices i \times 4 to i \times 4 + 3 store [posBase, birth, death, flags]. For static instances, posBase=i, birth=0, death=0, flags=0. 2. Scales (scales): Float32Array of size padRows(staticCount + trackCount). Per instance i, indices i \times 4 to i \times 4 + 2 store [sx, sy, sz]. Index i \times 4 + 3 is unused/padded. 3. Colors (colors): Uint8Array of size padRows(staticCount + trackCount). Per instance i, indices i \times 4 to i \times 4 + 3 store [r, g, b, a]. Opacity is stored as peak value; the shader applies the temporal envelope. 4. Rotations (rots): Uint8Array of size padRows(staticCount + trackCount). Per instance i, indices i \times 4 to i \times 4 + 3 store quaternion components encoded as (int8 + 128). Decoding formula: q = \frac{v - 128}{127}, where v is the raw uint8 value. 5. Positions (positions): Float32Array of size padRows(posTexels) \times 4, where posTexels = staticCount + posCount. Static positions are stored first (indices 0 to staticCount-1), followed by the position stream for tracks. 6. Track Position Texels: For a track instance i (where i \ge \text{staticCount}), the position data is stored in the positions array starting at index posBase (from attr[i]). The length is (death - birth + 1) 4 (stride 4 for xyz + padding). 7. Alive by Control Point (aliveByCp): An array of Uint32Arrays. aliveByCp[c] contains the instance IDs of track instances possibly visible at control point c. Parameters: TRACKFADEIN: Flag constant 1. TRACKFADEOUT: Flag constant 2. Steps: 1. Read and validate the 60-byte header. Extract staticCount, trackCount, posCount, numCp, and fps. 2. Calculate posTexels = staticCount + posCount and allocate positions array of size padRows(posTexels) 4. 3. Allocate attr, scales, colors, rots arrays of size padRows(staticCount + trackCount). 4. Decode static records: For static instances i from 0 to staticCount - 1: a. Read 32-byte record from byte stream at base + i 32. b. Extract positions (3 float32), scales (3 float32), colors (4 uint8), and rotations (4 uint8). c. Store positions in positions at index i \times 4. d. Store scales in scales at index i \times 4. e. Store colors in colors at index i \times 4. f. Decode rotations: For each component j \in \{0,1,2,3\}, read byte v at rec + 28 + j. Compute qj = \frac{v - 128}{127}. Store qj in rots at index i \times 4 + j. g. Set attr[i4] = i, attr[i4+1] = 0, attr[i4+2] = 0, attr[i4+3] = 0. 5. Decode dynamic tracks: For track instances i from 0 to trackCount - 1: a. Read 32-byte record from byte stream at base + (staticCount + i) 32. b. Extract posBase, birth, death, flags into attr[(staticCount+i)4] to attr[(staticCount+i)4+3]. c. Extract scales, colors, rotations similarly to static instances and store in respective arrays. d. Read position trajectory data for this track from the stream. The number of position vectors is death - birth + 1. Store these in positions starting at index posBase 4. 6. Construct aliveByCp array based on birth, death, and numCp. 7. Upload arrays to GPU textures. The static canvas is painted as bytes arrive; dynamic tracks activate when the stream completes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import math TEXWIDTH = 1024 # Example value, typically 1024 or 2048 def padrows(texels): return TEXWIDTH max(1, math.ceil(texels / TEXWIDTH)) 4 def decodequaternionbyte(v): return (v - 128) / 127 def load4dgsv2spacetime(filestream): # 1. Read Header headerdata = filestream.read(60) if len(headerdata) < 60: raise ValueError("Incomplete header") magic = headerdata[0:4] if magic != b'4DGS': raise ValueError("Invalid magic number") version = struct.unpackfrom('<I', headerdata, 4)[0] if version != 2: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported version {version}") numCp = struct.unpackfrom('<I', headerdata, 8)[0] fps = struct.unpackfrom('<f', headerdata, 16)[0] bbox = struct.unpackfrom('<6f', headerdata, 20) staticCount = struct.unpackfrom('<I', headerdata, 44)[0] trackCount = struct.unpackfrom('<I', headerdata, 48)[0] posCount = struct.unpackfrom('<I', headerdata, 52)[0] # 2. Allocate Arrays posTexels = staticCount + posCount positions = [0.0] (padrows(posTexels)) attr = [0.0] (padrows(staticCount + trackCount)) scales = [0.0] (padrows(staticCount + trackCount)) colors = [0] (padrows(staticCount + trackCount)) rots = [0.0] (padrows(staticCount + trackCount)) # 3. Decode Static Instances for i in range(staticCount): recoffset = 60 + i 32 rec = filestream.read(32) if len(rec) < 32: raise ValueError("Incomplete static record") # Positions (3 float32) pos = struct.unpackfrom('<3f', rec, 0) for k in range(3): positions[(i 4 + k)] = pos[k] # Scales (3 float32) sc = struct.unpackfrom('<3f', rec, 12) for k in range(3): scales[(i 4 + k)] = sc[k] # Colors (4 uint8) col = struct.unpackfrom('<4B', rec, 24) for k in range(4): colors[(i 4 + k)] = col[k] # Rotations (4 uint8) rotbytes = struct.unpackfrom('<4B', rec, 28) for k in range(4): rots[(i 4 + k)] = decodequaternionbyte(rotbytes[k]) # Attrs attr[i 4] = i attr[i 4 + 1] = 0 attr[i 4 + 2] = 0 attr[i 4 + 3] = 0 # 4. Decode Dynamic Tracks currentposbase = staticCount aliveByCp = [[] for in range(numCp)] for i in range(trackCount): instidx = staticCount + i recoffset = 60 + staticCount 32 + i 32 rec = filestream.read(32) if len(rec) < 32: raise ValueError("Incomplete track record") # Attrs: posBase, birth, death, flags # Note: The source says "read 32-byte records... Extract positions...". # Assuming the first 4 floats in the record are posBase, birth, death, flags? # Or is it packed differently? The source says "Extract positions (3 float32)...". # Let's assume the record layout is consistent with static: # 0-11: posBase (float? or int?), birth, death, flags? # The source says "Extract positions (3 float32)". This implies the first 12 bytes are positions? # But attr stores posBase. Let's look at "Decode static records... Extract positions...". # And "Instance attributes array... store [posBase, birth, death, flags]". # It is likely the 32-byte record contains: # 0-11: Position (for static) OR posBase/birth/death/flags (for track)? # The source says for static: "Extract positions... Store in respective arrays". # For track: "Track instance i... owns position texels... from posBase". # It is highly likely the 32-byte record for tracks contains: # 0-11: posBase (float32? or int32?), birth (float32?), death (float32?), flags (float32?) # Let's assume standard packing: 4 floats. attrs = struct.unpackfrom('<4f', rec, 0) posBase = int(attrs[0]) birth = attrs[1] death = attrs[2] flags = attrs[3] attr[instidx 4] = posBase attr[instidx 4 + 1] = birth attr[instidx 4 + 2] = death attr[instidx 4 + 3] = flags # Scales, Colors, Rotations (same as static) sc = struct.unpackfrom('<3f', rec, 12) for k in range(3): scales[(instidx 4 + k)] = sc[k] col = struct.unpackfrom('<4B', rec, 24) for k in range(4): colors[(instidx 4 + k)] = col[k] rotbytes = struct.unpackfrom('<4B', rec, 28) for k in range(4): rots[(instidx 4 + k)] = decodequaternionbyte(rotbytes[k]) # Read Position Trajectory numpos = int(death - birth + 1) # The source says "posCount" is in header. posCount is total position texels for tracks? # "posTexels = staticCount + posCount". So posCount is the number of position vectors for all tracks. # We need to read numpos vectors. # Each vector is 3 floats. posdata = filestream.read(numpos 12) if len(posdata) < numpos 12: raise ValueError("Incomplete track position data") posvecs = struct.unpackfrom(f'<{numpos 3}f', posdata, 0) for k in range(numpos): positions[(posBase 4 + k 3)] = posvecs[k 3] positions[(posBase 4 + k 3 + 1)] = posvecs[k 3 + 1] positions[(posBase 4 + k 3 + 2)] = posvecs[k 3 + 2] # Padding at k3+3 is 0.0 # Update aliveByCp # Determine which control points this track is alive for # Assuming control points are evenly spaced or indexed by integer timesteps # The source doesn't specify the mapping of birth/death to control points. # We assume birth and death are indices into the control point timeline. for c in range(numCp): if birth <= c <= death: aliveByCp[c].append(instidx) return { 'positions': positions, 'attr': attr, 'scales': scales, 'colors': colors, 'rots': rots, 'aliveByCp': aliveByCp, 'fps': fps, 'bbox': bbox } Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of static instances and track position texels. Parsing is CPU-bound but lightweight. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the file size. The padded arrays may introduce up to ~25% overhead depending on TEXWIDTH and instance count. Performance: Allows immediate rendering of the static canvas while dynamic data loads, improving perceived latency. Continuous GPU interpolation reduces CPU load during playback compared to v1's per-timestep re-uploads. Strengths: Efficient for long-duration videos with moving subjects; reduces bandwidth and GPU memory churn by separating static and dynamic data. Limitations: Requires complete track data for interpolation; degenerate tracks (birth > death) must be handled. Precision issues may arise if posBase exceeds integer limits for array indexing. The 4DGS v2 Spacetime Loader is part of the "4D" full-stack web app ecosystem, which transforms ordinary video into renderable Gaussian Splats. It was developed to support "Motion" clips where the camera is static and the subject moves, representing the scene as a spacetime gaussian model. It succeeds the v1 progressive loader, which was less efficient for continuous playback. devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, https://github.com/devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Model Preprocessing and Grid Partitioning
head: PLY Gaussian Loading with Fallbacks
body: This method preprocesses a raw 3D Gaussian Splatting model stored in PLY format for use in Unreal Engine. It parses the PLY file, converts coordinate systems and property encodings to match the engine's internal representation, and partitions the Gaussians into a spatial grid for efficient culling and rendering. It differs from generic loaders by applying specific axis swaps, exponential scale decoding, and sigmoid opacity activation required by the target engine's shader pipeline. Inputs: FilePath: Relative path to the PLY file within the project content directory. ProjectContentDir: Base directory path for the application's content. Outputs: GaussianData: A structured collection of Gaussian properties (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, Opacity, Harmonics) organized by spatial grid cells. GridMetadata: Bounding box (BoundsMin, BoundsMax) and grid resolution (CellsPerEdge). Data Structures: FLinearColor: A 4-component vector (R, G, B, A) used to pack multiple float properties. FQuat: A 4-component quaternion (X, Y, Z, W) for rotation. GridCell: A container holding lists of Gaussian properties for a specific 3D grid coordinate (i, j, k). Steps: 1. Path Construction and Validation: Construct the absolute file path: \text{AbsolutePath} = \text{ProjectContentDir} + \text{"Models/"} + \text{FilePath} Initialize a PLY reader with the absolute path and validate that it successfully opened the file. If invalid, abort. 2. Header Parsing and Element Identification: Iterate through the PLY header elements using reader.haselement() and reader.nextelement(). Identify the vertex element by checking if reader.elementis(miniply::kPLYVertexElement). 3. Data Extraction: Load the vertex data using reader.loadelement() and retrieve the number of vertices N = \text{reader.num\rows()}. For each property in the vertex element, allocate a float array of size N and extract the data into a map keyed by property name. Validate that the following required properties exist in the map: Position (x, y, z), Orientation (rot0..rot3), Scale (scale0..scale2), Opacity, Zero Order Harmonics (fdc0..fdc2), and optionally Higher Order Harmonics (frest0..frest44). 4. Bounding Box Calculation: Initialize BoundsMin and BoundsMax with the first vertex's position converted to Unreal coordinates: P{\text{unreal}} = 100.0 \times (x, -z, -y) Iterate through all N vertices to update BoundsMin and BoundsMax component-wise. Compute BoxEdgeLengths: L = \text{BoundsMax} - \text{BoundsMin} All values are scaled by 100.0. 5. Grid Resolution Determination: Determine CellsPerEdge based on N: If N \le 1,500,000, CellsPerEdge = 1. If 1,500,000 < N \le 3,500,000, CellsPerEdge = 2. If N > 3,500,000, CellsPerEdge = 4. 6. Directory Creation: Create necessary directories for the model and emitter data using a helper function CreateDirectory. 7. Gaussian Property Processing and Grid Assignment: Initialize an empty grid structure of size CellsPerEdge \times CellsPerEdge \times CellsPerEdge. Iterate through each vertex v from 0 to N-1: a. Position Conversion: Convert to Unreal coordinates and scale by 100.0. Pack into FLinearColor as (R=x, G=-z, B=-y, A=0). b. Scale Conversion: Apply exponential activation and axis swap: s'0 = \exp(\text{scale\0}v), s'1 = \exp(\text{scale\2}v), s'2 = \exp(\text{scale\1}v). Scale by 100.0 and pack into FLinearColor as (R=s'0, G=s'1, B=s'2, A=0). c. Rotation Conversion: Construct quaternion from PLY order (rot1, rot2, rot3, rot0), normalize it, and apply axis swap/sign flip: (X=q.x, Y=-q.z, Z=-q.y, W=q.w). Pack into FLinearColor. d. Color and Opacity Conversion: Extract Zero Order Harmonics as BaseColor. Apply sigmoid to opacity: \alphav = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\text{opacity}v)}. Clamp \alphav to [0, 1]. Pack into FLinearColor as (R=C{base}.x, G=C{base}.y, B=C{base}.z, A=\alphav). e. Higher Order Harmonics (L1): If frest properties exist, iterate y from 0 to 9 with step 3. Extract fresty, fresty+1, fresty+2 and pack into an FLinearColor. Append to harmonicsL1TextureData. f. Grid Indexing: Calculate the grid index for the current vertex's position: i = \left\lfloor \frac{P{\text{final}}.x - \text{BoundsMin}.x}{L.x} \times \text{CellsPerEdge} \right\rfloor j = \left\lfloor \frac{P{\text{final}}.y - \text{BoundsMin}.y}{L.y} \times \text{CellsPerEdge} \right\rfloor k = \left\lfloor \frac{P{\text{final}}.z - \text{BoundsMin}.z}{L.z} \times \text{CellsPerEdge} \right\rfloor Clamp i, j, k to [0, \text{CellsPerEdge}-1]. Store the processed properties in the grid cell (i, j, k). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def preprocessgaussians(filepath, projectcontentdir): # 1. Path & Reader absolutepath = projectcontentdir + "Models/" + filepath # Initialize PLY reader (implementation omitted) reader = PLYReader(absolutepath) if not reader.valid(): raise ValueError("PLY file invalid or missing") # 2. Header & Vertex numvertices = 0 vertexdata = {} for element in reader.elements(): if element.isvertex(): element.load() numvertices = reader.numrows() for propname in element.properties(): propidx = element.findproperty(propname) columndata = [0.0] numvertices reader.extractproperties([propidx], 1, PLYPropertyType.FLOAT, columndata) vertexdata[propname] = columndata # 3. Validate Required Properties required = ["x", "y", "z", "rot0", "rot1", "rot2", "rot3", "scale0", "scale1", "scale2", "opacity", "fdc0", "fdc1", "fdc2"] for req in required: if req not in vertexdata: raise ValueError(f"Missing required property: {req}") hasrest = "frest0" in vertexdata # 4. Bounding Box (Unreal coords: 100.0 (x, -z, -y)) boundsmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] boundsmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for v in range(numvertices): px = 100.0 vertexdata["x"][v] py = 100.0 -vertexdata["z"][v] pz = 100.0 -vertexdata["y"][v] if v == 0: boundsmin = [px, py, pz] boundsmax = [px, py, pz] else: boundsmin = [min(boundsmin[i], [px, py, pz][i]) for i in range(3)] boundsmax = [max(boundsmax[i], [px, py, pz][i]) for i in range(3)] boxedgelengths = [boundsmax[i] - boundsmin[i] for i in range(3)] # 5. Grid Resolution if numvertices <= 1500000: cellsperedge = 1 elif numvertices <= 3500000: cellsperedge = 2 else: cellsperedge = 4 # 6. Directories # CreateDirectory helper not detailed in sources # 7. Process & Grid Assign grid = [[[] for in range(cellsperedge)] for in range(cellsperedge)] harmonicsl1 = [] for v in range(numvertices): # Position pos = [100.0 vertexdata["x"][v], 100.0 -vertexdata["z"][v], 100.0 -vertexdata["y"][v]] poscolor = [pos[0], pos[1], pos[2], 0.0] # Scale s0 = math.exp(vertexdata["scale0"][v]) s1 = math.exp(vertexdata["scale2"][v]) s2 = math.exp(vertexdata["scale1"][v]) scalecolor = [100.0 s0, 100.0 s1, 100.0 s2, 0.0] # Rotation quat = normalizequat([vertexdata["rot1"][v], vertexdata["rot2"][v], vertexdata["rot3"][v], vertexdata["rot0"][v]]) rotcolor = [quat[0], -quat[2], -quat[1], quat[3]] # Color & Opacity basecolor = [vertexdata["fdc0"][v], vertexdata["fdc1"][v], vertexdata["fdc2"][v]] opacity = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-vertexdata["opacity"][v])) opacity = max(0.0, min(1.0, opacity)) coloralphacolor = [basecolor[0], basecolor[1], basecolor[2], opacity] # Higher Order Harmonics if hasrest: for y in range(0, 10, 3): h = [vertexdata[f"frest{y}"][v], vertexdata[f"frest{y+1}"][v], vertexdata[f"frest{y+2}"][v], 0.0] harmonicsl1.append(h) # Grid Index idx = getgridindex(pos, boundsmin, boxedgelengths, cellsperedge) grid[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]].append({ "pos": poscolor, "scale": scalecolor, "rot": rotcolor, "color": coloralphacolor }) return grid, harmonicsl1 def getgridindex(pos, boundsmin, edgelengths, cellsperedge): i = int(math.floor((pos[0] - boundsmin[0]) / edgelengths[0] cellsperedge)) j = int(math.floor((pos[1] - boundsmin[1]) / edgelengths[1] cellsperedge)) k = int(math.floor((pos[2] - boundsmin[2]) / edgelengths[2] cellsperedge)) return [max(0, min(cellsperedge - 1, idx)) for idx in [i, j, k]] def normalizequat(q): norm = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in q)) return [c/norm for c in q] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of FLinearColor (typically 32-bit floats per channel) for packed data may introduce quantization errors for properties like rotation or high-precision harmonics. Axis Swaps: The specific axis swaps (Y/Z swap for position, 1/2 swap for scale, X/Z/Y permutation for rotation) are critical. Incorrect mapping results in rotated or scaled splats. Harmonics Storage: Higher order harmonics are stored in a separate texture-like structure (harmonicsL1TextureData), not in the main grid cell properties. Time Complexity: O(N) for parsing, conversion, and grid assignment, where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Gaussian properties and the grid structure. The grid itself is O(C^3) where C is CellsPerEdge, but typically C^3 \ll N. Performance: The method is a one-time preprocessing step. The grid partitioning enables O(1) spatial queries during rendering. Limitations: The grid resolution is fixed based on vertex count thresholds, which may not be optimal for all scene densities. The coordinate system conversion is hardcoded for Unreal Engine's right-handed coordinate system. This method originates from the unreal-splat project, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unreal Engine. It adapts the standard PLY format (which uses a left-handed coordinate system and raw scale/opacity values) to Unreal's requirements (right-handed, exponential scale, sigmoid opacity). The grid partitioning strategy is a heuristic based on vertex count to balance memory usage and culling efficiency. name: 3D Covariance Computation
head: 3D Covariance Construction, Covariance Matrix Computation from Quaternions and Scales, Gaussian Splatting Covariance Computation, Gaussian covariance from quaternion and scale
body: 3D Covariance Computation calculates the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} for a set of 3D Gaussians from their stored rotation (quaternion) and scale parameters. It solves the problem of representing the spatial extent and orientation of each Gaussian in world coordinates, which is required for projecting the Gaussian to 2D screen space for rendering. It sets itself apart from direct optimization of covariance entries by explicitly decoupling rotation and scale into distinct learnable components, ensuring the resulting matrix is always positive semi-definite (PSD) and physically interpretable. Inputs: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing unit quaternions (w, x, y, z) representing orientations. scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing scale factors (sx, sy, sz) along each axis, representing standard deviations in 3D. Outputs: covariances: Float32 tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) containing the computed covariance matrices \boldsymbol{\Sigma} for each of the N Gaussians. Data Structures: The rotation matrix \mathbf{R} is a 3 \times 3 matrix derived from the quaternion. The local scale matrix \mathbf{S} is a 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix containing the squared scales (variances). Steps: 1. Normalize Quaternions: Ensure input quaternions are unit length. If q = (w, x, y, z), compute q{norm} = q / \|q\|. 2. Construct Rotation Matrix: Convert the normalized quaternion to a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix \mathbf{R}. 3. Construct Scale Matrix: Create a diagonal matrix \mathbf{S} where the diagonal elements are the squared scale values: S{ii} = si^2. 4. Compute Covariance: Calculate the world-space covariance matrix using the similarity transformation \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{R}^T. Alternatively, compute \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{R} \cdot \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}) and then \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{L}^T. Formulas: The covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is defined as: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{R}^T where: \mathbf{R} is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion. \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) is the local covariance matrix with variances along each axis. The rotation matrix \mathbf{R} from a unit quaternion q = w + xi + yj + zk is: \mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2(y^2 + z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \\ 2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \\ 2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2) \end{bmatrix} [Derived from standard quaternion-to-matrix conversion, consistent with ]. Parameters: quats: Input tensor of shape (N, 4). scales: Input tensor of shape (N, 3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-unit Quaternions: Quaternions must be normalized before conversion to ensure a valid rotation matrix. Isotropic Scales: If scales are isotropic (single scalar), the scale matrix is constructed from that scalar repeated on the diagonal. Numerical Stability: The decomposition \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{R}^T guarantees \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is positive semi-definite, avoiding numerical instability during gradient-based training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def computecov3d(quats: torch.Tensor, scales: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the 3D covariance matrix for a set of Gaussians. Args: quats: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing quaternions (w, x, y, z). scales: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing scale factors (sx, sy, sz). Returns: covariances: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) containing covariance matrices. """ # Step 1: Normalize quaternions quats = quats / torch.norm(quats, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Extract components w = quats[:, 0] x = quats[:, 1] y = quats[:, 2] z = quats[:, 3] # Step 2: Construct rotation matrix R # R is 3x3 for each Gaussian # Using batched operations R = torch.zeros(quats.shape[0], 3, 3, device=quats.device, dtype=quats.dtype) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (xy - wz) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (xz + wy) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (xy + wz) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (yz - wx) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (xz - wy) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (yz + wx) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (x2 + y2) # Step 3: Construct scale matrix S (diagonal) # S = diag(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2) scalessq = scales2 S = torch.zeros(quats.shape[0], 3, 3, device=quats.device, dtype=quats.dtype) S[:, 0, 0] = scalessq[:, 0] S[:, 1, 1] = scalessq[:, 1] S[:, 2, 2] = scalessq[:, 2] # Step 4: Compute covariance Sigma = R @ S @ R^T # Using einsum for efficiency: cov[i,j,k] = sumn summ R[i,j,n] S[n,m] R[k,m] # Or simply: L = R @ diag(s), then Cov = L @ L^T # Let's use the L @ L^T approach as it is numerically stable and common # L = R @ diag(s) # L[i,j,k] = sumn R[i,j,n] diag(s)[n,k] = R[i,j,k] s[k] (since diag(s) is diagonal) L = R scales.unsqueeze(1) # Broadcast scales (N,3) to (N,1,3) # Cov = L @ L^T covariances = torch.bmm(L, L.transpose(1, 2)) return covariances This method is a preprocessing step that converts raw Gaussian splat parameters (position, scale, rotation, color) into pre-computed 3 \times 3 covariance matrices and normalized float colors to accelerate rendering. It solves the problem of per-frame matrix multiplication and color decoding by computing these values once during load. Covariance Factorisation is the parameterization strategy used in 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} as a product of a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and a scaling matrix \mathbf{S}. It solves the problem that directly optimizing the entries of \boldsymbol{\Sigma} can result in non-positive semi-definite (PSD) matrices, which violates physical interpretation and causes numerical instability during gradient-based training. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats by explicitly decoupling rotation and scale into distinct learnable components, rather than relying on a triangular factorization to implicitly encode orientation. This method updates the parameters of 3D Gaussians when the underlying mesh vertices are transformed, ensuring that splats correctly reflect the new geometry without requiring manual recalculation of scaling factors. It sets itself apart from vanilla Gaussian Splatting modifications, which often require explicit matrix updates that can introduce holes or blurriness, by moving vertices directly in \mathbb{R}^3 and automatically deriving the new covariance and rotation parameters. To convert a Gsplat to a CovSplat: 1. Initialize covsplat.flags to 0u. 2. Check if isGsplatActive(gsplat.flags) is true. 3. If active, copy flags, index, rgba, and center from gsplat. 4. Compute rotation matrix m by calling scaleQuaternionToMatrix(gsplat.scales, gsplat.quaternion). 5. Compute the symmetric covariance matrix components: m = m transpose(m). 6. Extract diagonal elements into covsplat.xxyyzz = vec3(m[0][0], m[1][1], m[2][2]). 7. Extract off-diagonal elements into covsplat.xyxzyz = vec3(m[0][1], m[0][2], m[1][2]). If the input gsplat is null or inactive, the output covsplat.flags remains 0u, and other fields are not updated (or initialized to defaults in the JS wrapper). Vs Isotropic: Anisotropy significantly improves alignment with surfaces, allowing higher rendering quality while maintaining same point count. Isotropic optimization uses a single scalar value controlling radius on all three axes. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the resulting N covariance matrices. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of Gaussians. Strengths: Ensures PSD property, differentiable, efficient batched computation. Limitations: Requires quaternion normalization. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussians in world space. name: Pre-computed Covariance and Color Buffer Generation
head: Covariance and Color Pre-computation, Gaussian Parameter Pre-processing
body: This method is a preprocessing step that converts raw Gaussian splat parameters (position, scale, rotation, color) into pre-computed 3x3 covariance matrices and normalized float colors to accelerate rendering. It solves the problem of per-frame matrix multiplication and color decoding by computing these values once during load. Inputs: bufferData: A byte array containing interleaved Gaussian parameters. vertexCount: The total number of Gaussians. Outputs: covarianceArray: A Float32Array of size 6 vertexCount. Stores the 6 unique elements of the symmetric covariance matrix for each Gaussian. colorArray: A Float32Array of size 4 vertexCount. Stores normalized RGBA color values in the range [0.0, 1.0]. Data Structures and Layout: The input bufferData is organized in rows of 44 bytes per vertex. The layout per vertex is: Bytes 0–11: Position (XYZ), 3 Float32 values. Bytes 12–23: Scale (XYZ), 3 Float32 values. Bytes 24–39: Rotation (IJKW), 4 Float32 values. The source specifies the order IJKW corresponds to x, y, z, w components of the quaternion. Bytes 40–43: Color (RGBA), 4 Uint8 values. The output buffers are tightly packed arrays of Float32 values. Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Create covarianceBufferData with size CovarianceSizeBytes vertexCount and colorBufferData with size ColorSizeBytes vertexCount. Wrap these in Float32Array instances named covarianceArray and colorArray. 2. Iterate Over Vertices: For each vertex index i from 0 to vertexCount - 1: 2.1. Process Color: Calculate byte offset baseColor = 44 i + 40. Read 4 Uint8 values from bufferData at baseColor. Normalize each value by dividing by 255.0. Store the normalized floats in colorArray at indices 4i to 4i+3. 2.2. Extract Scale: Calculate float offset baseScale = 11 i + 3. Read 3 Float32 values from bufferData at baseScale. Construct a diagonal scale matrix S. 2.3. Extract Rotation: Calculate float offset rotationBase = 11 i + 7. Read 4 Float32 values from bufferData at rotationBase. Interpret these as quaternion components (qx, qy, qz, qw) corresponding to the I, J, K, W order. Construct a rotation matrix R. 2.4. Compute Transformation Matrix M: Compute M = R \times S. Let M{ij} be the element at row i and column j (0-indexed) of the 3 \times 3 matrix M. 2.5. Compute Covariance Elements: The symmetric covariance matrix C is computed as C = M M^T. The 6 unique elements are stored in covarianceArray at indices 6i to 6i+5: C{00} = M{00}^2 + M{01}^2 + M{02}^2 C{01} = M{00}M{10} + M{01}M{11} + M{02}M{12} C{02} = M{00}M{20} + M{01}M{21} + M{02}M{22} C{11} = M{10}^2 + M{11}^2 + M{12}^2 C{12} = M{10}M{20} + M{11}M{21} + M{12}M{22} C{22} = M{20}^2 + M{21}^2 + M{22}^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct def precomputecovarianceandcolor(bufferdata, vertexcount): """ Pre-computes covariance matrices and normalized colors from raw splat data. Args: bufferdata: bytes or bytearray containing interleaved Gaussian parameters. vertexcount: int, number of Gaussians. Returns: covariancearray: list of floats, length 6 vertexcount. colorarray: list of floats, length 4 vertexcount. """ covariancearray = [0.0] (6 vertexcount) colorarray = [0.0] (4 vertexcount) # Constants for layout SCALEOFFSETFLOATS = 3 ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS = 7 COLOROFFSETBYTES = 40 for i in range(vertexcount): basefloatoffset = i 11 basebyteoffset = i 44 # 1. Process Color r = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES] g = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 1] b = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 2] a = bufferdata[basebyteoffset + COLOROFFSETBYTES + 3] colorarray[4 i] = r / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 1] = g / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 2] = b / 255.0 colorarray[4 i + 3] = a / 255.0 # 2. Extract Scale sx = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS)[0] sy = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS + 1)[0] sz = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + SCALEOFFSETFLOATS + 2)[0] # 3. Extract Rotation qx = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS)[0] qy = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 1)[0] qz = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 2)[0] qw = struct.unpackfrom('<f', bufferdata, basefloatoffset + ROTATIONOFFSETFLOATS + 3)[0] # Compute Rotation Matrix R from Quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw) qx2, qy2, qz2, qw2 = qxqx, qyqy, qzqz, qwqw xy, xz, xw, yz, yw, zw = qxqy, qxqz, qxqw, qyqz, qyqw, qzqw r00 = 1 - 2 (qy2 + qz2) r01 = 2 (xy - zw) r02 = 2 (xz + yw) r10 = 2 (xy + zw) r11 = 1 - 2 (qx2 + qz2) r12 = 2 (yz - xw) r20 = 2 (xz - yw) r21 = 2 (yz + xw) r22 = 1 - 2 (qx2 + qy2) # 4. Compute M = R S # Since S is diagonal, Mij = Rij Sjj m00, m01, m02 = r00 sx, r01 sy, r02 sz m10, m11, m12 = r10 sx, r11 sy, r12 sz m20, m21, m22 = r20 sx, r21 sy, r22 sz # 5. Compute Covariance C = M M^T c00 = m00m00 + m01m01 + m02m02 c01 = m00m10 + m01m11 + m02m12 c02 = m00m20 + m01m21 + m02m22 c11 = m10m10 + m11m11 + m12m12 c12 = m10m20 + m11m21 + m12m22 c22 = m20m20 + m21m21 + m22m22 covariancearray[6 i] = c00 covariancearray[6 i + 1] = c01 covariancearray[6 i + 2] = c02 covariancearray[6 i + 3] = c11 covariancearray[6 i + 4] = c12 covariancearray[6 i + 5] = c22 return covariancearray, colorarray Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Order: The source explicitly notes that the rotation data is stored as IJKW (x, y, z, w). Standard libraries often expect WXYZ or XYZW. Misinterpreting this order will result in incorrect rotation matrices and thus incorrect covariance shapes. Matrix Multiplication Order: The covariance is derived from M = R \times S. Since S is diagonal, this scales the columns of R. If S were applied as S \times R, the rows would be scaled, which is incorrect for transforming a sphere into an ellipsoid defined by scale axes aligned with the rotation basis. Precision: The input color is Uint8. Normalization by 255.0 introduces floating-point representation errors, but this is standard for color data. The covariance elements are Float32, which may lose precision for very small or very large scales, potentially affecting rendering stability at extreme zoom levels. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of Gaussians. The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N). The output buffers require 10 \times N \times 4 bytes (6 floats for covariance + 4 floats for color). Performance: This preprocessing moves computation from the GPU fragment/vertex shader to the CPU (or a compute shader) during asset loading. This reduces the per-frame cost of rendering, as the shader only needs to sample the pre-computed covariance and color values. Strengths: Eliminates per-pixel or per-vertex matrix multiplication and quaternion-to-matrix conversion during rendering. Simplifies the shader logic. Limitations: Requires storing additional data (covariance matrix) in memory. If the Gaussians are dynamic (e.g., animated), this pre-computation must be repeated every frame or whenever parameters change, negating the benefit. This method is part of the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time web rendering, specifically within the context of Three.js and A-Frame viewers. It is based on the work of Mark Kellogg (GaussianSplats3D) and Kevin Kwok (WebGL implementation of Gaussian Splatting). The technique leverages the fact that the covariance matrix for a Gaussian splat is constant for a given set of scale and rotation parameters, allowing it to be pre-computed. akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Covariance Factorisation
head: Covariance Decomposition, RQ Decomposition for Covariance, Rotation and Scale Parameterization
body: Covariance Factorisation is the parameterization strategy used in 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} as a product of a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and a scaling matrix \mathbf{S}. It solves the problem that directly optimizing the entries of \boldsymbol{\Sigma} can result in non-positive semi-definite matrices, which violates physical interpretation and causes numerical instability during gradient-based training. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats by explicitly decoupling rotation and scale into distinct learnable components, rather than relying on a triangular factorization to implicitly encode orientation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unconstrained learnable parameters for rotation (typically a quaternion) and scale (a 3D vector). Output: The 3 \times 3 symmetric positive semi-definite covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}. Data Structures: The method does not store \boldsymbol{\Sigma} directly. Instead, it stores: 1. Rotation: A quaternion \mathbf{q} = (w, x, y, z) or equivalent representation, normalized to unit length. 2. Scale: A 3D vector \mathbf{s} = (sx, sy, sz) with si > 0. Steps: 1. Construct Rotation Matrix: Convert the learnable rotation parameter (e.g., quaternion \mathbf{q}) into a 3 \times 3 orthogonal rotation matrix \mathbf{R}. 2. Construct Scaling Matrix: Create a diagonal matrix \mathbf{S} from the scale vector \mathbf{s}: \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz). 3. Compute Covariance: Calculate \boldsymbol{\Sigma} using the factorization formula: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T. Since \mathbf{S} is diagonal, \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T = \mathbf{S}^2 = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2). Thus: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \begin{bmatrix} sx^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz^2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}^T. Formulas: \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}) Parameters: Scale vector \mathbf{s}: Values must be positive. Rotation \mathbf{R}: Derived from a unit quaternion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-PSD Matrices: If \mathbf{R} is not orthogonal or \mathbf{s} contains negative values, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} may not be PSD. Ensure \mathbf{R} is constructed from a normalized quaternion and \mathbf{s} is clamped to positive values or passed through an exponential activation function during optimization. Numerical Stability: Factorizing the covariance into rotation and scale ensures it remains positive semi-definite under unconstrained gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecovariance(quaternion: Tuple[float, float, float, float], scale: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> List[List[float]]: """ Computes the 3x3 covariance matrix from a quaternion and scale vector. Args: quaternion: (w, x, y, z) normalized quaternion. scale: (sx, sy, sz) positive scale factors. Returns: 3x3 covariance matrix as a list of lists. """ # Normalize quaternion to ensure valid rotation w, x, y, z = quaternion norm = (w2 + x2 + y2 + z2)0.5 w, x, y, z = w/norm, x/norm, y/norm, z/norm # Construct rotation matrix R from quaternion R = [ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ] # Construct scaling matrix S^2 (diagonal) sx, sy, sz = scale S2 = [ [sx2, 0, 0], [0, sy2, 0], [0, 0, sz2] ] # Compute R S2 RS2 = [ [R[0][0]S2[0][0], R[0][1]S2[1][1], R[0][2]S2[2][2]], [R[1][0]S2[0][0], R[1][1]S2[1][1], R[1][2]S2[2][2]], [R[2][0]S2[0][0], R[2][1]S2[1][1], R[2][2]S2[2][2]] ] # Compute R S2 R^T Rt = [ [R[0][0], R[1][0], R[2][0]], [R[0][1], R[1][1], R[2][1]], [R[0][2], R[1][2], R[2][2]] ] Sigma = [ [RS2[0][0]Rt[0][0] + RS2[0][1]Rt[1][0] + RS2[0][2]Rt[2][0], RS2[0][0]Rt[0][1] + RS2[0][1]Rt[1][1] + RS2[0][2]Rt[2][1], RS2[0][0]Rt[0][2] + RS2[0][1]Rt[1][2] + RS2[0][2]Rt[2][2]], [RS2[1][0]Rt[0][0] + RS2[1][1]Rt[1][0] + RS2[1][2]Rt[2][0], RS2[1][0]Rt[0][1] + RS2[1][1]Rt[1][1] + RS2[1][2]Rt[2][1], RS2[1][0]Rt[0][2] + RS2[1][1]Rt[1][2] + RS2[1][2]Rt[2][2]], [RS2[2][0]Rt[0][0] + RS2[2][1]Rt[1][0] + RS2[2][2]Rt[2][0], RS2[2][0]Rt[0][1] + RS2[2][1]Rt[1][1] + RS2[2][2]Rt[2][1], RS2[2][0]Rt[0][2] + RS2[2][1]Rt[1][2] + RS2[2][2]Rt[2][2]] ] return Sigma This method parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix using Cholesky decomposition to guarantee positive-definiteness by construction during gradient-based optimization. It stores D(D+1)/2 elements per splat (6 for 3D), ensuring the covariance matrix remains valid without requiring post-hoc projection or regularization. It differs from sibling methods like Quaternion-Scale Covariance Parameterization by avoiding explicit rotation parameterization, instead relying on the triangular structure of the Cholesky factor to encode orientation and scale implicitly. This method parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma using a quaternion q and a 3D scale vector s to ensure the matrix remains positive semi-definite during optimization. It solves the problem that directly optimizing the entries of \Sigma can result in non-positive semi-definite matrices, violating physical interpretation and causing numerical instability. Unlike siblings such as Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats, which uses a triangular factorization, this approach explicitly decouples rotation and scale, allowing for efficient gradient derivation and intuitive ellipsoid parameterization. Decomposes \boldsymbol{\Sigma} into rotation and scaling matrices to maintain practical physical significance. Limitations: Not given in the sources. name: Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats
head: Cholesky Decomposition for Covariance, Cholesky-based Covariance Parameterization
body: This method parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix using Cholesky decomposition to guarantee positive-definiteness by construction during gradient-based optimization. It stores D(D+1)/2 elements per splat (6 for 3D), ensuring the covariance matrix remains valid without requiring post-hoc projection or regularization. It differs from sibling methods like Quaternion-Scale Covariance Parameterization by avoiding explicit rotation parameterization, instead relying on the triangular structure of the Cholesky factor to encode orientation and scale implicitly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unconstrained optimization variables representing the Cholesky factor elements and amplitude parameters. Output: A valid, positive-definite 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma and a non-negative amplitude \alpha for each Gaussian splat. Data Structures: For a 3D Gaussian, the covariance matrix \Sigma is factorized as \Sigma = L L^T, where L is a lower triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries. The Cholesky parameterization stores the 6 unique elements of L: L = \begin{bmatrix} l{11} & 0 & 0 \\ l{21} & l{22} & 0 \\ l{31} & l{32} & l{33} \end{bmatrix} These 6 values are stored directly in the splat's attribute buffer. Steps: 1. Initialize Parameters: Store 6 unconstrained real numbers for the lower triangular Cholesky factor L. Store 1 unconstrained real number for the amplitude log-scale and 1 for the minimum standard deviation floor if not fixed. 2. Enforce Diagonal Positivity: The diagonal elements l{ii} must be positive to ensure \Sigma is positive-definite. This is achieved by parameterizing the diagonal as: l{ii} = \sigma{min} + \text{softplus}(zi) where zi is the learned unconstrained variable, \text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x), and \sigma{min} is a small constant. 3. Construct Covariance: Compute \Sigma = L L^T. This guarantees \Sigma is symmetric and positive-definite by construction. 4. Parameterize Amplitude: The amplitude \alpha is made non-negative using a softplus activation on a learned variable a: \alpha = \text{softplus}(a) Optionally, \alpha is upper-bounded by a configurable maximum a{max}: \alpha = \min(\alpha, a{max}). 5. Compute Density: Use the standard Gaussian density formula with the computed \Sigma and mean \mu for rendering. Formulas and Definitions: \Sigma = L L^T: Covariance matrix reconstruction. l{ii} = \sigma{min} + \text{softplus}(zi): Diagonal parameterization. \sigma{min} = 1/\sqrt{12} voxels: The minimum standard deviation floor, representing the standard deviation of a uniform voxel. This ensures no splat is narrower than a voxel’s own spread. \alpha = \min(\text{softplus}(a), a{max}): Amplitude parameterization with upper bound. Parameters: \sigma{min}: Minimum standard deviation floor. Typical value: 1/\sqrt{12} voxels. a{max}: Maximum amplitude bound. Configurable, not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The softplus function can suffer from overflow or underflow for large positive or negative inputs. Use numerically stable implementations (e.g., log1p(exp(x)) for softplus). Degenerate Input: If l{ii} becomes too small, the Gaussian becomes extremely narrow, potentially causing numerical instability in rasterization. The \sigma{min} floor prevents this. Boundary Conditions: The Cholesky factorization is undefined for non-positive-definite matrices. By construction, this method avoids this issue, but gradient updates must not violate the softplus constraint (which they won't if implemented correctly). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def choleskycovariancefromparams(Lelements, sigmamin=1.0/120.5): """ Reconstructs a 3x3 covariance matrix from 6 Cholesky elements. Args: Lelements: Tensor of shape (N, 6) containing [l11, l21, l22, l31, l32, l33] sigmamin: Minimum standard deviation floor (default: 1/sqrt(12)) Returns: Sigma: Tensor of shape (N, 3, 3) representing the covariance matrix """ # Reshape to (N, 3, 3) lower triangular L = torch.zeros(Lelements.shape[0], 3, 3, device=Lelements.device) # Extract elements l11 = Lelements[:, 0] l21 = Lelements[:, 1] l22 = Lelements[:, 2] l31 = Lelements[:, 3] l32 = Lelements[:, 4] l33 = Lelements[:, 5] # Apply softplus to diagonal elements and add sigmamin # Ensure diagonal is positive l11 = sigmamin + F.softplus(l11) l22 = sigmamin + F.softplus(l22) l33 = sigmamin + F.softplus(l33) # Fill lower triangular matrix L[:, 0, 0] = l11 L[:, 1, 0] = l21 L[:, 1, 1] = l22 L[:, 2, 0] = l31 L[:, 2, 1] = l32 L[:, 2, 2] = l33 # Compute Sigma = L @ L.T Sigma = torch.bmm(L, L.transpose(1, 2)) return Sigma def computeamplitude(amplitudelog, amax=None): """ Computes non-negative amplitude with optional upper bound. Args: amplitudelog: Tensor of shape (N,) containing log-amplitude amax: Optional maximum amplitude bound Returns: alpha: Tensor of shape (N,) representing the amplitude """ alpha = F.softplus(amplitudelog) if amax is not None: alpha = torch.min(alpha, torch.fulllike(alpha, amax)) return alpha Combines Cholesky factorization with skew-symmetric rotation matrices to preserve explicit 3D spatial interpretability. Used in Universal Beta Splatting (UBS) for cross-dimensional correlations. Optimizes rasterization for fp16 by using Cholesky factors to prevent numerical instability and overflow. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat for covariance reconstruction (constant number of multiplications for 3D). Memory Complexity: O(1) per splat, storing 6 floats for the Cholesky factor plus amplitude parameters. Strengths: Guarantees positive-definiteness by construction, simplifying optimization. No need for post-hoc projection or regularization. Limitations: Loses explicit spatial rotation structure compared to quaternion-based methods. The triangular structure may introduce correlations between scale and rotation parameters that are not immediately interpretable. When to Use: When positive-definiteness is critical and explicit rotation parameterization is not required. Suitable for general-purpose Gaussian splatting where simplicity and stability are prioritized. When Not to Use: When explicit control over rotation is needed, or when generalizing to dimensions beyond 3D where quaternion parameterization is more natural. This method is described in the Luxar paper, which applies Gaussian splatting to microscopy and multidimensional scientific data visualization. It leverages the mathematical property that Cholesky decomposition of a positive-definite matrix yields a unique lower triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries, ensuring the covariance matrix remains valid during optimization. name: Spatial-Orthogonal Cholesky Parameterization
head: Hybrid Cholesky-Skew-Symmetric parameterization, UBS covariance parameterization
body: Spatial-Orthogonal Cholesky Parameterization is a method for parameterizing the covariance matrix of N-dimensional Gaussian splats that combines Cholesky factorization with skew-symmetric rotation matrices to ensure positive semi-definiteness while preserving explicit 3D spatial interpretability. It solves the limitation of pure Cholesky parameterization, which loses explicit spatial rotation structure, and the limitation of quaternion parameterization, which does not generalize beyond 3D. It is used in Universal Beta Splatting (UBS) to enable flexible cross-dimensional correlations with non-spatial dimensions (e.g., view, time) while maintaining efficient optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Learnable parameters for a single splat: \boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Skew-symmetric rotation vector. \mathbf{s}x \in \mathbb{R}^3: Spatial scale vector. \mathbf{s}q \in \mathbb{R}^C: Non-spatial scale vector (for C additional dimensions). \mathbf{L}{qx} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times 3}: Cross-dimensional correlation matrix. \mathbf{L}q \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}: Lower-triangular matrix for non-spatial dimensions (Cholesky factor). Output: The N \times N covariance matrix \Sigma, where N = 3 + C. Data Structures: The covariance matrix \Sigma is constructed as \Sigma = L L^\top, where L is a structured lower-triangular matrix of size N \times N: L = \begin{pmatrix} Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) & \mathbf{0}{3 \times C} \\ \mathbf{L}{qx} & \mathbf{L}q \end{pmatrix} Here, Rx \in SO(3) is the spatial rotation matrix, \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) is a 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix of spatial scales, \mathbf{0}{3 \times C} is a zero matrix, \mathbf{L}{qx} encodes correlations between spatial and non-spatial dimensions, and \mathbf{L}q is a lower-triangular matrix for the non-spatial subspace. Steps: 1. Construct Skew-Symmetric Matrix: Create Ax \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} from \boldsymbol{\omega} = (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3)^\top: Ax = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\omega3 & \omega2 \\ \omega3 & 0 & -\omega1 \\ -\omega2 & \omega1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} 2. Compute Rotation Matrix: Approximate Rx using the first-order Taylor expansion of the matrix exponential: Rx \approx I + Ax This approximation maintains approximate orthogonality for small \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| and initializes with identity rotation (\boldsymbol{\omega} = \mathbf{0}). 3. Construct Spatial Block: Compute the spatial part of L: L{xx} = Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) 4. Assemble L: Combine blocks into the full lower-triangular matrix L: L = \begin{pmatrix} L{xx} & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{L}{qx} & \mathbf{L}q \end{pmatrix} 5. Compute Covariance: Calculate \Sigma = L L^\top. The expanded form is: \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x)^2 Rx^\top & Rx \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) \mathbf{L}{qx}^\top \\ \mathbf{L}{qx} \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}x) Rx^\top & \mathbf{L}{qx} \mathbf{L}{qx}^\top + \mathbf{L}q \mathbf{L}q^\top \end{pmatrix} Parameters: \boldsymbol{\omega}: Initialized to \mathbf{0}. \mathbf{s}x, \mathbf{s}q: Initialized to positive values (e.g., small constants or derived from initial splat size). \mathbf{L}{qx}: Initialized to \mathbf{0}. \mathbf{L}q: Initialized as a lower-triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The first-order Taylor approximation Rx \approx I + Ax is only valid for small \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\|. \mathbf{L}q must remain lower-triangular with positive diagonal entries to ensure \Sigma is positive semi-definite. Time Complexity: Efficient due to the first-order Taylor approximation for rotation, avoiding expensive matrix exponential computations. Memory Complexity: Stores 3 + 3 + C + 3C + C(C+1)/2 parameters per splat. For C=0 (pure 3D), this is 6 parameters, same as standard 3DGS. For C>0, it scales with C^2. Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 (UBS-3D), achieves 25.54 dB PSNR with 1 hour training time, outperforming Quaternion (25.50 dB, 3h26m), Cholesky (25.28 dB, 1h14m), and Cayley Transform (25.52 dB, 1h16m). Strengths: Generalizes to arbitrary N dimensions, preserves 3D spatial interpretability, enables cross-dimensional correlations, and is computationally efficient. Limitations: The first-order Taylor approximation may not capture large rotations accurately. Pure Cholesky loses spatial structure, and Quaternions do not generalize beyond 3D. When to Use: When rendering N-dimensional radiance fields (e.g., with view or time dimensions) and requiring explicit 3D spatial structure and cross-dimensional correlations. When Not to Use: When only 3D spatial rendering is needed and simplicity is preferred (standard 3DGS or Cholesky may suffice), or when large rotations are expected and higher-order rotation parameterizations are needed. Originated in Universal Beta Splatting (UBS). It addresses the challenge of parameterizing covariance matrices in N-dimensional radiance field rendering, combining the benefits of Cholesky factorization (PSD guarantee, generalization) and skew-symmetric rotation (spatial interpretability). Universal Beta Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2510.03312, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Half-Precision Rasterization with Cholesky Covariance and Local Coordinates
head: FP16 Rasterization with Cholesky and Local Coordinates
body: This method optimizes the rasterization stage of 3D Gaussian Splatting by executing the entire pipeline in half-precision (fp16) to maximize memory bandwidth and load/store throughput. It specifically addresses numerical instability in fp16 by replacing conic covariance representations with Cholesky factors and using local coordinates to prevent overflow. It builds on Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats to ensure positive-definiteness and avoids the arithmetic speedup benefits (negligible on commodity GPUs) in favor of memory efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{S}, each defined by a mean \mathbf{t}, a 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigma{3D} (parameterized via Cholesky), and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Camera parameters (view/projection matrices). Output: A rendered image with alpha compositing. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Stored in fp16. The inverse covariance \Sigma^{-1} is stored as its lower triangular Cholesky factor L such that \Sigma^{-1} = LL^\top. For 2D screen-space, this requires 3 elements (l0, l1, l2). SH Compression: Coefficients are packed into 32 bytes using YCoCg-R color-space conversion, square-root gamma quantization (6 bits luma, 4 bits chroma), and per-basis percentile scaling. This reduces bandwidth from 192 bytes (fp32) to 32 bytes. Coordinates: Positions are stored relative to the macro-tile center rather than absolute screen-space coordinates. Steps: 1. Global Projection and SH Evaluation: A single kernel processes each Gaussian end-to-end. Each thread handles one Gaussian: Transform \mathbf{t} to camera space. Project to screen space to get 2D mean \boldsymbol{\mu}. Compute the 2D screen-space covariance \Sigma{2D} via Jacobian projection of \Sigma{3D}. Compute the Cholesky decomposition of the inverse covariance \Sigma{2D}^{-1} = LL^\top. Compute the view direction inline. Evaluate degree-3 spherical harmonics for color. 2. Tile Rasterization: Gaussians are assigned to macro-tiles. Within a tile, positions are treated as relative to the macro-tile center to keep intermediate products within fp16 range. For each pixel (x, y) in the tile, compute the offset (dx, dy) = \mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}, where \mathbf{p} is the pixel position relative to the tile center. 3. Mahalanobis Distance Calculation: Compute q using the Cholesky factors to avoid cancellation: q = (l0 \cdot dx + l1 \cdot dy)^2 + (l2 \cdot dy)^2 Here, l0, l1, l2 are elements of L, and (dx, dy) are the local offsets. 4. Alpha Compositing: Use front-to-back blending. The scheduling buffer decouples variable-rate mask compaction from fixed-rate blending. 5. Decoding (SH): Use a pure fp16 SIMD pipeline with byte-permute instructions for bitfield extraction, avoiding integer-to-float conversions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizetile(tilecenter, gaussians, camera): """ Rasterize a single tile using half-precision arithmetic. tilecenter: (x, y) macro-tile center in screen space. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes in fp16. camera: Camera parameters for projection. """ # Shared memory / local storage for tile tilewidth = 16 # Example tile size tileheight = 16 image = zeros((tileheight, tilewidth, 3), dtype=fp16) alpha = zeros((tileheight, tilewidth), dtype=fp16) # Sort gaussians by depth within tile (simplified) tilegaussians = filtergaussiansintile(gaussians, tilecenter) tilegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) for g in tilegaussians: # 1. Project Gaussian mucam = camera.project(g.mean3d) # 2. Compute 2D Covariance and Cholesky Factor # J is Jacobian of projection at mucam Sigma2d = J @ g.Sigma3d @ J.T # Inverse Cholesky: Sigmainv = L @ L.T L = choleskylower(Sigma2d.inv()) # 3. Evaluate SH Color (compressed decode) color = decodeshcolor(g.shcoeffs, g.viewdir) # 4. Rasterize Gaussian to Tile Pixels for dy in range(tileheight): for dx in range(tilewidth): # Local coordinates relative to tile center pixelabs = (tilecenter.x + dx, tilecenter.y + dy) localoffset = (pixelabs.x - tilecenter.x, pixelabs.y - tilecenter.y) # Offset from Gaussian center (also local) dxrel = localoffset.x - (mucam.x - tilecenter.x) dyrel = localoffset.y - (mucam.y - tilecenter.y) # Mahalanobis distance in fp16 # q = (l0dx + l1dy)^2 + (l2dy)^2 term1 = fp16mul(L.l0, fp16add(fp16mul(L.l0, dxrel), fp16mul(L.l1, dyrel))) term2 = fp16mul(L.l2, dyrel) q = fp16add(fp16mul(term1, term1), fp16mul(fp16mul(term2, term2), term2)) # Note: term2 squared # Actually: q = (l0dx + l1dy)^2 + (l2dy)^2 inner = fp16add(fp16mul(L.l0, dxrel), fp16mul(L.l1, dyrel)) q = fp16add(fp16mul(inner, inner), fp16mul(fp16mul(L.l2, dyrel), L.l2)) alphaval = fp16exp(-0.5 q) g.opacity # Front-to-back blending # alphaout = alphain + alphag (1 - alphain) # colorout = (colorin alphain + colorg alphag (1 - alphain)) / alphaout # Simplified accumulation for single pass currentalpha = alpha[dy, dx] newalpha = fp16add(currentalpha, fp16mul(alphaval, fp16sub(1.0, currentalpha))) if newalpha > 0: blendedcolor = fp16add( fp16mul(color, alphaval), fp16mul(fp16sub(1.0, alphaval), fp16mul(image[dy, dx], currentalpha))) blendedcolor = fp16div(blendedcolor, newalpha) image[dy, dx] = blendedcolor alpha[dy, dx] = newalpha return image Note: The pseudocode above is a conceptual representation. The actual implementation uses a single kernel where each thread processes one Gaussian end-to-end, and a scheduling buffer decouples masking from blending. Parameters: SH Compression: 32-byte packed representation. Tile Size: Not given in the sources. Batch Size: Drain batch Bd = 64. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cancellation Hazard: Storing \Sigma^{-1} as conic coefficients (A, B, C) leads to catastrophic cancellation in fp16 due to mixed-sign cross terms. Using Cholesky factors eliminates this. Overflow Hazard: Absolute screen-space coordinates can cause lk \cdot dx to overflow fp16 range. Using local coordinates relative to the macro-tile center prevents this. A sibling method for parameterizing covariance. It differs in the specific constraints applied to the Cholesky factor to enforce spatial orthogonality. Choose when strict orthogonality is required. See Spatial-Orthogonal Cholesky Parameterization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Halves the footprint in DRAM and on-chip local storage compared to fp32, doubling effective load/store throughput. Performance: On commodity GPUs, packed half and single precision share math throughput, so the benefit is memory-bound, not compute-bound. Quality: HiGS reaches 67.0 dB PSNR without SH compression and 55.6 dB with 32-byte SH compression, with no observable image-quality loss compared to the gsplat baseline. Strengths: Reduced memory bandwidth, increased resident Gaussian count per processing unit, exact compositing algorithm. Limitations: Requires careful handling of fp16 precision hazards (addressed by Cholesky and local coords). This method is part of the HiGS (Hierarchical Rendering Architecture for Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting) pipeline, targeting NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. It addresses the memory bandwidth bottleneck in real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting by optimizing the numerical representation and rasterization pipeline for half-precision hardware. HiGS: A Hierarchical Rendering Architecture for Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.00352, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Quaternion-Scale Covariance Parameterization
head: Quaternion-Scale Covariance, Quaternion and Scale Parameterization, Covariance Parameterization via Quaternion and Scale, QS Covariance
body: This method parameterizes the 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma using a quaternion q and a 3D scale vector s to ensure the matrix remains positive semi-definite during optimization. It solves the problem that directly optimizing the entries of \Sigma can result in non-positive semi-definite matrices, violating physical interpretation and causing numerical instability. Unlike siblings such as Cholesky Parameterisation for Gaussian Splats, which uses a triangular factorization, this approach explicitly decouples rotation and scale, allowing for efficient gradient derivation and intuitive ellipsoid parameterization. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A quaternion q = [w, x, y, z]^T representing rotation, and a 3D scale vector s = [sx, sy, sz]^T representing anisotropic scaling. Outputs: The covariance matrix \Sigma or its inverse \Sigma^{-1}, used in the Gaussian density function. Data Structures Quaternion (q): A 4-element vector [w, x, y, z] representing orientation. The quaternion must be normalized to unit length to represent a valid rotation. Scale Vector (s): A 3-element vector [sx, sy, sz] defining the scaling along local axes. The scaling matrix S = \text{diag}(s) guarantees that the eigenvalues of \Sigma remain positive. Construction Steps 1. Construct Rotation Matrix (R): Convert the quaternion q into a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix R. The standard conversion from quaternion components w, x, y, z to R is: R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2(y^2 + z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \\ 2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \\ 2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2) \end{bmatrix}. Implementations may vary in convention (e.g., row-major vs column-major), but R must be orthogonal with determinant +1. 2. Construct Scale Matrix (S): Create a 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix from the scale vector s: S = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz) = \begin{bmatrix} sx & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz \end{bmatrix}. 3. Compute Covariance Matrix (\Sigma): The covariance matrix is reconstructed as: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T. Since S is diagonal, S S^T = S^2 = \text{diag}(sx^2, sy^2, sz^2), yielding: \Sigma = R \begin{bmatrix} sx^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz^2 \end{bmatrix} R^T. This construction ensures \Sigma is symmetric and positive semi-definite by design. 4. Compute Inverse Covariance (\Sigma^{-1}): For rendering, the inverse is required. Using matrix inversion properties: \Sigma^{-1} = (R S S^T R^T)^{-1} = R (S S^T)^{-1} R^T = R S^{-2} R^T where S^{-2} = \text{diag}(1/sx^2, 1/sy^2, 1/sz^2). Gradients Instead of relying on automatic differentiation through the complex graph q, s \rightarrow \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma^{-1} \rightarrow \alpha (where \alpha is opacity/density), gradients for q and s are derived analytically to avoid computational cost and potential numerical errors. The partial derivatives of the intermediate matrix M=RS with respect to the quaternion components and scale components are explicitly computed for efficient backpropagation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """ Converts a quaternion [w, x, y, z] to a 3x3 rotation matrix R. q: array-like of shape (4,) Returns: R, shape (3, 3) """ w, x, y, z = q[0], q[1], q[2], q[3] xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz R = np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) return R def computecovariance(q, s): """ Computes the covariance matrix Sigma from quaternion q and scale vector s. q: array-like of shape (4,), quaternion s: array-like of shape (3,), scale factors Returns: Sigma, shape (3, 3) """ q = q / np.linalg.norm(q) # Normalize quaternion R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) Ssquared = np.diag(s2) Sigma = R @ Ssquared @ R.T return Sigma def computeinversecovariance(q, s): """ Computes the inverse covariance matrix Sigmainv from quaternion q and scale vector s. q: array-like of shape (4,), quaternion s: array-like of shape (3,), scale factors (must be non-zero) Returns: Sigmainv, shape (3, 3) """ q = q / np.linalg.norm(q) # Normalize quaternion R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) ssqinv = 1.0 / (s2 + 1e-8) # Guard against division by zero Sinvsquared = np.diag(ssqinv) Sigmainv = R @ Sinvsquared @ R.T return Sigmainv Parameters Learning Rate: Applied to q and s during optimization. Not given in the sources. Clamping: Scale values s are often clamped to a minimum positive value to prevent numerical instability in \Sigma^{-1}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-Positive Semi-Definite Matrix: Directly optimizing \Sigma entries can lead to invalid matrices. This parameterization guarantees validity by construction. Quaternion Normalization: The quaternion must remain unit length during optimization. Scale Zero/Negative: If any scale component si is zero, \Sigma^{-1} becomes singular. Negative scales are mathematically valid since s^2 is positive, but the physical interpretation of ellipsoid axis direction becomes ambiguous. Notation Confusion: In probability theory, \Sigma often denotes standard deviation, while \Sigma^2 denotes variance. In this context, \Sigma is the covariance matrix (variance), and s represents scale factors analogous to standard deviation. Confusion here leads to errors in constructing S (using s vs s^2). Constructs the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma from stored rotation (quaternion) and scale parameters, then projects it into 2D screen space to determine the rendering footprint. It preserves full rotation and scaling information to maintain the correct ellipsoidal orientation and aspect ratio in screen space, unlike billboarding techniques that discard orientation. See Covariance Matrix from Scaling and Rotation. Computes the gradients of the rendering loss with respect to the rotation quaternion q and scaling vector s. It explicitly derives the partial derivatives of the intermediate matrix M=RS with respect to the quaternion and scale components, allowing for efficient, closed-form gradient computation without numerical differentiation. See Gradient Computation for 3D Gaussians. Time Complexity: Constructing R from q is O(1). Matrix multiplications for \Sigma and \Sigma^{-1} are O(1) for fixed 3 \times 3 size. Analytical gradient derivation is O(1). Memory Complexity: Stores 4 floats for q and 3 floats for s, totaling 7 floats per Gaussian. This is compared to 6 floats for the upper triangular \Sigma or 9 for full \Sigma. Strengths: Guarantees positive semi-definiteness; intuitive interpretation as an ellipsoid; efficient gradient computation via analytical derivatives; avoids complex automatic differentiation graphs. Limitations: Requires careful handling of quaternion normalization; scale parameters may need regularization to prevent degenerate Gaussians. When to Use: Standard for 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization where physical interpretability and stability are prioritized. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. The method draws from computer graphics traditions of parameterizing ellipsoids with scale and rotation, as well as probability theory's generalization of Gaussian PDFs using covariance matrices. It was introduced to address the instability of direct covariance optimization in differentiable rendering pipelines.
