name: Covariance Matrix from Scaling and Rotation
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting Covariance Computation, Covariance Matrix Construction from Quaternions and Scales, Gaussian Splatting Covariance Computation
body: This method constructs the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma of a 3D Gaussian primitive from its stored rotation (quaternion) and scale parameters, then projects it into 2D screen space to determine the rendering footprint. It solves the problem of defining the ellipsoidal shape of a Gaussian splat and accurately approximating its perspective-projected 2D covariance for rasterization. Unlike billboarding techniques that discard orientation by setting the model-view rotation to identity, this method preserves the full rotation and scaling information to maintain the correct ellipsoidal orientation and aspect ratio in screen space. Inputs: Rotation quaternion q = [qx, qy, qz, qw]. Scaling vector s = [sx, sy, sz]. Model-view matrix M{view} (4x4). Projection matrix P (4x4). Viewport dimensions: width W, height H, device pixel ratio dpr. Centroid position \mu (3D). Outputs: 2D covariance matrix components a, b, d (upper-left 2x2 of projected 3x3 covariance). 2D basis vectors for rendering quad construction. Data Structures: Matrices are stored in column-major order. The 3D covariance matrix \Sigma is 3x3. The projected covariance is extracted as a 2x2 matrix from the 3x3 result. Steps: 1. Construct Rotation Matrix R: Convert the quaternion q to a 3x3 rotation matrix R. R = \text{mat3\from\quat}(q) 2. Construct Scaling Matrix S: Create a 3x3 diagonal scaling matrix from s. S = \begin{bmatrix} sx & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz \end{bmatrix} 3. Compute Transformation Matrix T: Multiply rotation and scaling. T = R \cdot S 4. Compute 3D Covariance \Sigma: \Sigma = T \cdot T^\top 5. Extract Model-View Matrix W: Take the upper-left 3x3 corner of the 4x4 model-view matrix and transpose it. W = (\text{mat3\from\mat4}(M{view}))^\top Note: This preserves rotation and scaling, unlike billboarding which uses identity. 6. Compute Jacobian J for Perspective Projection: Perspective projection is non-affine and warps ellipsoids. We approximate it using a first-order Taylor expansion (Jacobian) assuming constant depth zp for sorting. a. Calculate focal lengths: fx = P{0,0} \cdot dpr \cdot W \cdot 0.5 fy = P{5,5} \cdot dpr \cdot H \cdot 0.5 b. Transform centroid to camera space: \mu{cam} = M{view} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \mux \\ \muy \\ \muz \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Let \mu{cam} = [xc, yc, zc, wc]^\top. The code uses zc directly from the transformed vector. c. Compute scaling factor sz: sz = \frac{1}{zc^2} d. Construct J (column-major): J = \begin{bmatrix} -\frac{fx}{zc} & 0 & fx \cdot xc \cdot sz \\ 0 & -\frac{fy}{zc} & fy \cdot yc \cdot sz \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} 7. Project Covariance to 2D: Combine W and J to get the total projection transformation T{proj}: T{proj} = W \cdot J Update the covariance matrix: \Sigma{proj} = T{proj}^\top \cdot \Sigma \cdot T{proj} 8. Extract 2D Covariance Components: Extract the upper-left 2x2 elements from \Sigma{proj} (indices 0, 1, 4 in column-major 3x3): a = \Sigma{proj}[0] b = \Sigma{proj}[1] d = \Sigma{proj}[4] 9. Compute Eigenvalues: Calculate the determinant D and trace: D = a \cdot d - b^2 \text{trace} = a + d \text{traceOver2} = 0.5 \cdot \text{trace} \text{term2} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{trace}^2}{4} - D} Eigenvalues: \lambda1 = \text{traceOver2} + \text{term2} \lambda2 = \max(\text{traceOver2} - \text{term2}, 0.00) Pitfall: Clamp \lambda2 to 0.00 to prevent negative eigenvalues due to numerical instability. 10. Compute Eigenvectors: First eigenvector: v1 = \text{normalize} \begin{bmatrix} b \\ \lambda1 - a \end{bmatrix} Second eigenvector (orthogonal to v1): v2 = \begin{bmatrix} v{1,y} \\ -v{1,x} \end{bmatrix} 11. Compute Basis Vectors for Rendering: Scale eigenvectors by the square root of their eigenvalues, capped at a maximum splat size (1024.0): \text{basis}1 = v1 \cdot \min(\sqrt{\lambda1} \cdot 4, 1024.0) \text{basis}2 = v2 \cdot \min(\sqrt{\lambda2} \cdot 4, 1024.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def quattomat3(q): """Convert quaternion [x, y, z, w] to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" x, y, z, w = q # Standard quaternion to rotation matrix conversion xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz return np.array([ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(xx + yy)] ]) def computecovarianceandbasis(q, s, mu, modelview, projection, width, height, dpr): """ Compute 2D covariance and basis vectors for a 3D Gaussian splat. Args: q: Quaternion [x, y, z, w] s: Scale vector [sx, sy, sz] mu: Centroid [x, y, z] modelview: 4x4 Model-View matrix (column-major) projection: 4x4 Projection matrix (column-major) width: Viewport width height: Viewport height dpr: Device pixel ratio Returns: a, b, d: 2D covariance components basis1, basis2: 2D basis vectors """ # 1. Construct Rotation Matrix R R = quattomat3(q) # 2. Construct Scaling Matrix S S = np.diag(s) # 3. Compute Transformation Matrix T = R S T = R @ S # 4. Compute 3D Covariance Sigma = T T^T Sigma = T @ T.T # 5. Extract Model-View Matrix W (upper-left 3x3 of modelview, transposed) # Note: modelview is 4x4. Take [:3,:3] then transpose. W = modelview[:3,:3].T # 6. Compute Jacobian J # Focal lengths fx = projection[0, 0] dpr width 0.5 fy = projection[1, 1] dpr height 0.5 # Transform centroid to camera space muhomogeneous = np.array([mu[0], mu[1], mu[2], 1.0]) mucam = modelview @ muhomogeneous xc, yc, zc = mucam[0], mucam[1], mucam[2] # Scaling factor sz = 1.0 / (zc zc) # Construct J (column-major representation, but we build row-by-row for clarity then transpose if needed) # The source defines J as: # [[-fx/zc, 0, fxxcsz], # [0, -fy/zc, fyycsz], # [0, 0, 0]] J = np.array([ [-fx / zc, 0.0, fx xc sz], [0.0, -fy / zc, fy yc sz], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] ]) # 7. Project Covariance Tproj = W @ J Sigmaproj = Tproj.T @ Sigma @ Tproj # 8. Extract 2D Covariance Components (upper-left 2x2) a = Sigmaproj[0, 0] b = Sigmaproj[0, 1] d = Sigmaproj[1, 1] # 9. Compute Eigenvalues detD = a d - b b trace = a + d traceover2 = 0.5 trace term2 = math.sqrt(trace trace / 4.0 - detD) lambda1 = traceover2 + term2 lambda2 = max(traceover2 - term2, 0.00) # 10. Compute Eigenvectors # v1 = normalize([b, lambda1 - a]) v1x = b v1y = lambda1 - a normv1 = math.sqrt(v1x2 + v1y2) if normv1 == 0: v1 = np.array([1.0, 0.0]) else: v1 = np.array([v1x / normv1, v1y / normv1]) # v2 = [v1.y, -v1.x] v2 = np.array([v1[1], -v1[0]]) # 11. Compute Basis Vectors maxsplatsize = 1024.0 scale1 = min(math.sqrt(lambda1) 4, maxsplatsize) scale2 = min(math.sqrt(lambda2) 4, maxsplatsize) basis1 = v1 scale1 basis2 = v2 scale2 return a, b, d, basis1, basis2 Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) per Gaussian primitive, involving a fixed number of matrix multiplications and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per primitive for intermediate matrices. Strengths: Accurately preserves orientation and scale during projection; handles perspective distortion via Jacobian approximation; robust against numerical instability via eigenvalue clamping. Limitations: The Jacobian approximation assumes constant depth within the Gaussian, which may introduce slight warping errors for very large or deep Gaussians. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian splats with arbitrary orientation and scale in a perspective camera. When not to use: For billboarding (where rotation is ignored) or orthographic projection (where Jacobian simplifies). This method is central to the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, specifically for converting learned or stored Gaussian parameters into screen-space primitives for rasterization. It was popularized by the 3D Gaussian Splatting paper (Kerbl et al., 2023), though the specific implementation details regarding the Jacobian approximation and eigen-decomposition for basis vector generation are documented in practical WebGPU tutorials. The approach ensures that the ellipsoidal shape of the Gaussian is correctly transformed from 3D world space to 2D screen space, allowing for efficient alpha-blended rendering. xmed-lab/DIF-Gaussian, https://github.com/xmed-lab/DIF-Gaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) WebGPU Unleashed: A Practical Tutorial, https://shi-yan.github.io/webgpuunleashed/Advanced/gaussiansplatting.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Gradient Computation for 3D Gaussians
head: Chain rule gradient for scale and rotation, Gradient of 3D Gaussian parameters
body: This method computes the gradients of the rendering loss with respect to the rotation quaternion q and scaling vector s of 3D Gaussians. It solves the problem of backpropagating errors through the non-linear parameterization of the covariance matrix \Sigma, which is defined as \Sigma = RSS^T R^T where R is the rotation matrix derived from q and S is the diagonal scaling matrix derived from s. It sets itself apart by explicitly deriving the partial derivatives of the intermediate matrix M=RS with respect to the quaternion components and scale components, allowing for efficient, closed-form gradient computation without numerical differentiation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: q: Unit quaternion with real part qr and imaginary parts qi, qj, qk. s: Scaling vector with components sX, sY, sZ. \frac{\partial Z}{\partial M}: Gradient of the loss Z with respect to the intermediate matrix M. Outputs: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial q}: Gradient of the loss with respect to the quaternion components. \frac{\partial Z}{\partial s}: Gradient of the loss with respect to the scale components. Data Structures: q: A 4-element vector [qr, qi, qj, qk]. s: A 3-element vector [sX, sY, sZ]. M: A 3 \times 3 matrix defined as M = RS. R(q): A 3 \times 3 rotation matrix derived from q. Mathematical Derivation: The covariance matrix is defined as \Sigma = MM^T where M = RS. The gradient of the loss Z with respect to M is given by the chain rule: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial M} = 2M^T \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \Sigma} Since \Sigma is symmetric, this compact form is used. The gradients for s and q are then computed via: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial Z}{\partial M} \frac{\partial M}{\partial s} \frac{\partial Z}{\partial q} = \frac{\partial Z}{\partial M} \frac{\partial M}{\partial q} Note: The source notation \frac{d\Sigma'}{ds} refers to the projected covariance \Sigma', but the core gradient derivation for the parameters s and q relies on the world/view space covariance \Sigma and the intermediate matrix M. Rotation Matrix R(q): The rotation matrix is computed from the unit quaternion q as: R(q) = 2 \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{2} - (qj^2 + qk^2) & (qi qj - qr qk) & (qi qk + qr qj) \\ (qi qj + qr qk) & \frac{1}{2} - (qi^2 + qk^2) & (qj qk - qr qi) \\ (qi qk - qr qj) & (qj qk + qr qi) & \frac{1}{2} - (qi^2 + qk^2) \end{pmatrix} Correction Note: The source text contains a typo in the (2,3) and (3,2) entries of the matrix provided in the notes vs the standard derivation. The source text explicitly lists: Row 2: (qi qj + qr qk), (\frac{1}{2} - (qi^2 + qk^2)), (qj qk - qr qi) Row 3: (qi qk - qr qj), (qj qk + qr qi), (\frac{1}{2} - (qi^2 + qk^2)) We use the explicit matrix provided in the source notes. Gradients for Scale s: The partial derivative of M with respect to the scale components is diagonal. Since M = RS, \frac{\partial M{ij}}{\partial sk} is non-zero only when i=j=k. Specifically: \frac{\partial M}{\partial sX} = \begin{pmatrix} R{11} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \frac{\partial M}{\partial sY} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & R{22} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \frac{\partial M}{\partial sZ} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & R{33} \end{pmatrix} The source does not explicitly write out the full matrix form for \frac{\partial M}{\partial sk} in the same detailed block as q, but implies it via M=RS. The gradient \frac{\partial Z}{\partial sk} is the dot product of \frac{\partial Z}{\partial M} and \frac{\partial M}{\partial sk}. Gradients for Quaternion q: The partial derivatives of M with respect to the quaternion components are given by: \frac{\partial M}{\partial qr} = 2 \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -sY qk & sZ qj \\ sX qk & 0 & -sZ qi \\ -sX qj & sY qi & 0 \end{pmatrix} \frac{\partial M}{\partial qi} = 2 \begin{pmatrix} 0 & sY qj & sZ qk \\ sX qk & -2sY qi & -sZ qr \\ sX qk & sY qr & -2sZ qj \end{pmatrix} \frac{\partial M}{\partial qj} = 2 \begin{pmatrix} -2sX qk & sY qj & sZ qr \\ sX qk & 0 & sZ qk \\ -sX qr & sY qk & -2sZ qj \end{pmatrix} \frac{\partial M}{\partial qk} = 2 \begin{pmatrix} -2sX qk & -sY qj & sZ qi \\ sX qk & -2sY qk & sZ qj \\ sX qi & sY qj & 0 \end{pmatrix} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradients(dZdM, q, s): """ Computes gradients of loss Z w.r.t. quaternion q and scale s. Args: dZdM: 3x3 matrix, gradient of loss w.r.t. M. q: 4-element vector [qr, qi, qj, qk]. s: 3-element vector [sX, sY, sZ]. Returns: dZdq: 4-element vector. dZds: 3-element vector. """ qr, qi, qj, qk = q sX, sY, sZ = s # Compute gradients for quaternion components # dZdqk = sum(dZdM dM/dqk) # dM/dqr dMdqr = 2 np.array([ [0, -sY qk, sZ qj], [sX qk, 0, -sZ qi], [-sX qj, sY qi, 0] ]) # dM/dqi dMdqi = 2 np.array([ [0, sY qj, sZ qk], [sX qk, -2 sY qi, -sZ qr], [sX qk, sY qr, -2 sZ qj] ]) # dM/dqj dMdqj = 2 np.array([ [-2 sX qk, sY qj, sZ qr], [sX qk, 0, sZ qk], [-sX qr, sY qk, -2 sZ qj] ]) # dM/dqk dMdqk = 2 np.array([ [-2 sX qk, -sY qj, sZ qi], [sX qk, -2 sY qk, sZ qj], [sX qi, sY qj, 0] ]) # Gradient is the Frobenius inner product: sum(dZdM dM/dqcomponent) dZdqr = np.sum(dZdM dMdqr) dZdqi = np.sum(dZdM dMdqi) dZdqj = np.sum(dZdM dMdqj) dZdqk = np.sum(dZdM dMdqk) dZdq = np.array([dZdqr, dZdqi, dZdqj, dZdqk]) # Compute gradients for scale components # M = R S, so dM/dsX has R11 at (0,0), etc. # dM/dsX = [[R00, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]] # dM/dsY = [[0, 0, 0], [0, R11, 0], [0, 0, 0]] # dM/dsZ = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, R22]] # We need R to compute these. R is computed from q. R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(q) dZdsX = dZdM[0, 0] R[0, 0] dZdsY = dZdM[1, 1] R[1, 1] dZdsZ = dZdM[2, 2] R[2, 2] dZds = np.array([dZdsX, dZdsY, dZdsZ]) return dZdq, dZds def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): """ Converts quaternion to rotation matrix R as defined in. """ qr, qi, qj, qk = q R = 2 np.array([ [0.5 - (qj2 + qk2), qiqj - qrqk, qiqk + qrqj], [qiqj + qrqk, 0.5 - (qi2 + qk2), qjqk - qrqi], [qiqk - qrqj, qjqk + qrqi, 0.5 - (qi2 + qk2)] ]) return R Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Normalization: The derivation assumes q is a unit quaternion. During optimization, q may drift from unit length. The source mentions that "Deriving gradients for quaternion normalization is straightforward," implying a projection step or normalization constraint is applied, but does not provide the explicit gradient for the normalization operation itself. Implementers must ensure q is normalized before computing R(q) or apply a normalization gradient. Symmetry: The covariance matrix \Sigma is symmetric. The gradient \frac{\partial Z}{\partial M} should be handled carefully to respect this symmetry if derived from \Sigma. Precision: The formulas involve products of quaternion components and scales. Small scales or near-zero quaternion components may lead to precision issues. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, as it involves fixed-size matrix multiplications and additions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, storing only the gradients for q (4 floats) and s (3 floats). Strengths: Closed-form gradients allow for efficient backpropagation during training. No numerical differentiation is required. Limitations: Requires the computation of the rotation matrix R from q to compute scale gradients. The quaternion normalization constraint is not explicitly handled in the gradient formulas provided. This method is part of the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for real-time radiance field rendering. It was introduced by Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, and Drettos in 2023. The derivation relies on the chain rule applied to the parameterization of the covariance matrix using quaternions and scaling vectors. 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Automatic covariance and rotation recalculation
head: Automatic parameter update for transformed Gaussians, Covariance update under mesh transformation
body: This method updates the parameters of 3D Gaussians when the underlying mesh vertices are transformed, ensuring that splats correctly reflect the new geometry without requiring manual recalculation of scaling factors. It sets itself apart from vanilla Gaussian Splatting modifications, which often require explicit matrix updates that can introduce holes or blurriness, by moving vertices directly in \mathbb{R}^3 and automatically deriving the new covariance and rotation parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original Gaussian parameters (rotation matrix R, scaling matrix S), and a vertex transformation matrix B \in SO(3) representing the movement or rotation of the mesh vertex in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Updated rotation matrix R' and updated covariance matrix \Sigma'. Data Structures: R: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix. S: 3 \times 3 diagonal scaling matrix. B: 3 \times 3 transformation matrix in SO(3). \Sigma: 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite covariance matrix. Steps: 1. Calculate the new rotation matrix R' by substituting the original rotation R with the transformation B: R' = B R 2. Calculate the new covariance matrix \Sigma' using the new rotation R' and the original scaling S: \Sigma' = R' S S^T R'^T 3. Substitute R' into the covariance equation to express \Sigma' in terms of the original parameters and the transformation B: \Sigma' = (B R) S S^T (B R)^T = B R S S^T R^T B^T Formulas: Original Covariance: \Sigma = R S S^T R^T Updated Covariance: \Sigma' = B R S S^T R^T B^T Parameters: B: The transformation matrix applied to the mesh vertex. Must be in SO(3) (rotation) or include translation if applied to means separately. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Manual Scaling Errors: Manually updating scaling factors via S' = AS (where A is a diagonal scaling matrix) is error-prone because exact scaling factors are not always apparent for intended modifications, especially when scales differ per Gaussian. Shear: If the transformation B introduces non-rigid warping or shear, the resulting covariance matrix may not correspond to a valid rotation and scaling decomposition directly compatible with standard rendering pipelines without further processing (see Covariance Re-fitting). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatecovariance(R, S, B): """ Updates Gaussian covariance and rotation after vertex transformation. Args: R (np.ndarray): Original 3x3 rotation matrix. S (np.ndarray): Original 3x3 diagonal scaling matrix. B (np.ndarray): 3x3 transformation matrix in SO(3). Returns: Rprime (np.ndarray): New rotation matrix. Sigmaprime (np.ndarray): New covariance matrix. """ # Step 1: Calculate new rotation Rprime = B @ R # Step 2: Calculate new covariance # Sigma = R S S^T R^T # Sigmaprime = Rprime S S^T Rprime^T # Equivalent to: B R S S^T R^T B^T # Compute S S^T (since S is diagonal, this is just element-wise square) SST = S @ S.T # Compute original covariance part: R S S^T R^T # This is equivalent to the original Sigma if needed, but we compute directly Sigmaprime = B @ (R @ SST @ R.T) @ B.T return Rprime, Sigmaprime A post-processing step applied to the transformed covariance matrix to recover rotation and scaling parameters compatible with 3DGS rendering, handling potential shear introduced by deformation. It is chosen when the transformation B is non-rigid (e.g., cage-based deformation) and introduces shear, which standard 3DGS rendering cannot handle directly. 1. Perform eigendecomposition on the deformed covariance matrix \Sigmad to obtain the orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors Rd and the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues \Lambdad, such that \Sigmad = Rd \Lambdad Rd^T. 2. Set the new rotation parameter to the orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors Rd. 3. Compute the new scaling parameters from the square roots of the eigenvalues in \Lambdad. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian, as it involves fixed-size matrix multiplications (3 \times 3). Memory Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian for storing the updated parameters. Strengths: Eliminates the need for manual scaling factor calculation, reducing user error and visual artifacts like holes or blurriness associated with naive updates. Allows direct manipulation of mesh vertices in \mathbb{R}^3. Limitations: If the transformation is non-rigid, the resulting covariance may require re-fitting (see Covariance Re-fitting) to remain compatible with the rendering pipeline. When to use: When modifying the geometry of a mesh represented by Gaussian splats and automatic parameter updates are desired. When not to use: When the transformation is complex and introduces significant shear, requiring additional re-fitting steps. This method originates from the GaMeS (Mesh-based adapting and modification of Gaussian Splatting) paper, which proposes moving vertices directly in \mathbb{R}^3 to update Gaussian parameters automatically. It addresses limitations in vanilla Gaussian Splatting where explicit matrix updates can lead to visual artifacts. The related Covariance Re-fitting technique is described in GSDeformer, which handles non-rigid cage-based deformations. GaMeS: Mesh-based adapting and modification of Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2026.114561, fetched 2026-10-29 GSDeformer: Direct Cage-based Deformation for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.15491, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Data Layout
head: 3DGS Parameter Storage, Gaussian Struct Definition, GaussianModel, GaussianPoint Data Structure
body: The 3D Gaussian Data Layout defines the in-memory representation of a single 3D Gaussian primitive for differentiable rendering. It stores the geometric parameters (position, scale, rotation), appearance parameters (opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), and often a precomputed covariance matrix. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly separating the logical primitive definition from the physical memory layout (e.g., Structure of Arrays vs. Array of Structures) to facilitate efficient GPU batch processing and dynamic resizing. Input: Raw parameters for a set of N Gaussians: positions \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}, colors or SH coefficients, scales \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}, rotations \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 4}, and opacities \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{N}. Output: A contiguous memory buffer (or data structure) containing the serialized fields required for rasterization. The layout varies by implementation language and optimization goal, but generally consists of the following fields per primitive: 1. Position: 3 floats (x, y, z). 2. Scale: 3 floats (sx, sy, sz). Often stored in log-space for optimization. 3. Rotation: 4 floats representing a unit quaternion (w, x, y, z). 4. Opacity: 1 float. Often stored as log-odds for optimization. 5. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Coefficients: 3 \times D floats, where D is the SH degree. Degree 0 (DC): 3 coefficients (RGB color). Degree 1: 12 coefficients. Degree 2: 27 coefficients. Degree 3: 48 coefficients. 6. Covariance: (Optional/Precomputed) 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix (6 floats) or derived on-the-fly from scale and rotation. Layout Variants: Structure of Arrays (SoA): Used in. Separate arrays for each attribute (e.g., positions[N][3], scales[N][3]). Facilitates vectorized GPU access. Array of Structures (AoS): Used in. A single struct per Gaussian containing all fields. Easier to manage logically but may have padding overhead. Packed Integer Layout: Used in [S3257-gaussian-data-packing.md]. Attributes packed into uint32 integers for serialization. Based on, the initialization of the GaussianModel involves: 1. Initialize Position: Store raw XYZ coordinates in a tensor xyz of shape (N, 3) with float32 dtype. 2. Initialize Color (DC SH): Store 0th-degree SH coefficients in featuresdc of shape (N, 1, 3). 3. Initialize Scale: Store log-scales in scaling of shape (N, 3). The linear scale is retrieved via torch.clamp(torch.exp(self.scaling), max=10.0). 4. Initialize Rotation: Store quaternions in rotation of shape (N, 4). Ensure they are normalized to unit length using torch.nn.functional.normalize(self.rotation). 5. Initialize Opacity: Store log-odds in opacity of shape (N, 1). The linear opacity is retrieved via torch.sigmoid(self.opacity). 6. Handle Missing Rotation: If rotation is not provided, default to identity quaternion [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]. 7. Clip Opacity: Ensure opacity values are within [0.0, 1.0] if stored directly. Linear Scale from Log-Scale: s{linear} = \min(\exp(s{log}), 10.0) Linear Opacity from Log-Odds: \alpha = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\alpha{log})} Unit Quaternion Normalization: \mathbf{q}{unit} = \frac{\mathbf{q}}{\|\mathbf{q}\|2} SH Degree (D): Determines the number of coefficients. D=0: 3 coeffs (RGB). D=1: 12 coeffs. D=2: 27 coeffs. D=3: 48 coeffs. Max Scale: Clamped to 10.0 during retrieval. Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized to represent valid rotations. Failure to normalize leads to scaling artifacts. Log-Space Clamping: Exponential of large log-scales can overflow. Clamping the result to a maximum value (e.g., 10.0) prevents numerical instability. Opacity Bounds: Opacity must be bounded between 0 and 1. Storing as log-odds allows unconstrained optimization, but the final value must be sigmoided. Memory Alignment: When packing into uint32 (as in [S3257-gaussian-data-packing.md]), ensure proper bit-packing to avoid alignment issues on GPU [S3257-gaussian-data-packing.md]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np class GaussianDataLayout: """ Represents the data layout for a single 3D Gaussian primitive. Implements the initialization and retrieval logic from. """ def init(self, positions, featuresdc, scaling, rotation, opacity): """ Initialize Gaussian data layout. Args: positions: np.ndarray or torch.Tensor of shape (N, 3), float32. featuresdc: np.ndarray or torch.Tensor of shape (N, 1, 3), float32. scaling: np.ndarray or torch.Tensor of shape (N, 3), float32 (log-space). rotation: np.ndarray or torch.Tensor of shape (N, 4), float32 (quaternions). opacity: np.ndarray or torch.Tensor of shape (N, 1), float32 (log-odds). """ self.xyz = torch.astensor(positions, dtype=torch.float32) self.featuresdc = torch.astensor(featuresdc, dtype=torch.float32) self.scaling = torch.astensor(scaling, dtype=torch.float32) self.rotation = torch.astensor(rotation, dtype=torch.float32) self.opacity = torch.astensor(opacity, dtype=torch.float32) # Normalize rotations to unit quaternions self.rotation = torch.nn.functional.normalize(self.rotation) def getscaling(self): """ Retrieve linear scale from log-space, clamped to max 10.0. Returns: torch.Tensor: Shape (N, 3), float32. """ return torch.clamp(torch.exp(self.scaling), max=10.0) def getrotation(self): """ Retrieve normalized rotation quaternion. Returns: torch.Tensor: Shape (N, 4), float32. """ return torch.nn.functional.normalize(self.rotation) def getopacity(self): """ Retrieve linear opacity from log-odds. Returns: torch.Tensor: Shape (N, 1), float32, values in [0, 1]. """ return torch.sigmoid(self.opacity) def getposition(self): """ Retrieve position. Returns: torch.Tensor: Shape (N, 3), float32. """ return self.xyz def getfeaturesdc(self): """ Retrieve 0th-degree SH coefficients (RGB color). Returns: torch.Tensor: Shape (N, 1, 3), float32. """ return self.featuresdc def tolist(self): """ Flatten all parameters into a single list/array for serialization. Order: centroid, scale, rotation, opacity, featdc, featextra. Note: featextra is empty for DC-only representation. Returns: torch.Tensor: Shape (N, 10 + 3D), float32. """ # Concatenate: xyz(3) + scale(3) + quat(4) + opacity(1) + dc(3) # For full SH, featextra would be appended. data = torch.cat([ self.xyz, self.scaling, self.rotation, self.opacity, self.featuresdc.squeeze(1) ], dim=1) return data @classmethod def fromlist(cls, data): """ Reconstruct Gaussian from flattened list. Args: data: torch.Tensor of shape (N, 10 + 3D). Returns: GaussianDataLayout instance. """ N = data.shape[0] # Extract fields based on fixed offsets xyz = data[:, 0:3] scale = data[:, 3:6] rotation = data[:, 6:10] opacity = data[:, 10:11] featdc = data[:, 11:14] # Reshape featdc to (N, 1, 3) featdc = featdc.unsqueeze(1) return cls(xyz, featdc, scale, rotation, opacity) The primary in-memory container organizing per-primitive attributes into column-major arrays for GPU batch processing. Choose this when you need efficient dynamic resizing and dense buffer management for real-time splatting. Serializes Gaussians into a compact uint32 binary layout for CPU-to-GPU transfer. Choose this when you need to serialize Gaussians for storage or network transmission. Allocates contiguous device memory for intermediate rendering states (projected coordinates, covariances). Choose this when you need to manage the memory buffers for the rasterizer itself, not the input primitives. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Retrieval of parameters is O(1) per primitive. Memory Complexity: O(N \times C) where C is the number of coefficients per Gaussian. For DC-only (RGB), C=10 (3+3+4+1). For Degree 3 SH, C=55 (3+3+4+1+45). Performance: SoA layout is generally faster for GPU rendering due to coalesced memory access. AoS layout is simpler to implement but may suffer from cache misses if not packed tightly. Strengths: Explicit separation of logical and physical layout allows for flexible optimization strategies (e.g., log-space parameters). Limitations: Requires careful handling of quaternion normalization and log-space conversions to avoid artifacts. The 3D Gaussian Data Layout is a core component of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It was introduced as part of the 3DGS pipeline to efficiently store and manipulate the parameters of millions of Gaussian primitives during differentiable rendering. The layout has been adapted in various open-source implementations, such as GaussianScan-Recon, splat, gs-embedding, and mini-splat, each with slight variations in field ordering and storage format. name: Gaussian Data Structure
head: GaussianList
body: The Gaussian Data Structure is the primary in-memory container for 3D Gaussian primitives in differentiable rendering pipelines, organizing per-primitive attributes into column-major arrays to enable efficient GPU batch processing and dynamic resizing. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly separating the logical primitive definition (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients, covariance) from the physical memory layout (SoA arrays), facilitating the dense buffer management required for real-time splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussian primitives with attributes defined in 3D Gaussian Data Layout. Output: A contiguous memory structure (typically GPU global memory) organized as Struct-of-Arrays (SoA) for batched rendering and optimization. Data Structures: The structure is implemented as a GaussianList (or GaussianSet) containing the following fields: 1. positions: Matrix4xN<f32> (or Vector3<f32>[N]). Stores (x, y, z) for each Gaussian. The 4th component is often unused or reserved for padding to 16-byte alignment. 2. scales: Matrix3xN<f32> (or Vector3<f32>[N]). Stores (sx, sy, sz) for each Gaussian. 3. opacities: DVector<f32> (or f32[N]). Stores scalar opacity \alphai for each Gaussian. 4. rotations: Matrix4xN<f32> (or Quaternion<f32>[N]). Stores (w, x, y, z) for each Gaussian. 5. sh: Matrix48xN<f32> (or f32[48][N]). Stores Spherical Harmonics coefficients. The layout is flat: C{0,R}, C{0,B}, C{0,G}, C{1,R}, \dots up to degree 3 (48 coefficients). 6. numgaussians: usize. The current count of active primitives N. 7. cov3d: Matrix3xN<f32> (or Matrix3<f32>[N]). Precomputed 3D covariance matrices \Sigmai for each Gaussian, derived from scale and rotation. Numbered Steps for Initialization and Update: 1. Allocation: Allocate contiguous memory for arrays of size N{max} (maximum capacity) for each field. 2. Population: For each primitive i \in [0, N): Set positions[:, i] to the 3D position. Set scales[:, i] to the scale vector. Set opacities[i] to the opacity scalar. Set rotations[:, i] to the quaternion. Set sh[:, i] to the SH coefficient vector. Compute and set cov3d[:, i] using the formula from 3D Gaussian Data Layout: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T. 3. Update: When primitives are added/removed (densification/pruning): Determine retained and new indices. Create host-side target arrays for parameters, Adam state, and density statistics. Move retained rows in chunks and append new rows. Release old device layout and upload target arrays to GPU. Formulas: Covariance Construction (from parent): \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T Where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from the quaternion, and Si is the diagonal scale matrix. SH Coefficient Layout: \text{sh}[k \cdot 3 + c, i] = \text{coeff}{k,c}^{(i)} Where k \in [0, 15] is the SH band/degree index, c \in \{R, G, B\} is the color channel, and i is the Gaussian index. Parameters: SH Degree: Typically 3, resulting in 48 coefficients per Gaussian. Data Type: f32 (32-bit float) for all attributes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use f32 for GPU compatibility; f64 may be used for CPU-side optimization but requires conversion. Boundaries: Ensure numgaussians does not exceed allocated array size; handle dynamic resizing via Dynamic Buffer Management. Degenerate Input: Handle Gaussians with zero scale or invalid quaternions by clamping or reinitializing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GaussianList: def init(self, maxcapacity: int): self.maxcapacity = maxcapacity self.numgaussians = 0 # Allocate arrays: N x 4 for positions/rotations, N x 3 for scales/cov3d, N for opacities, N x 48 for SH self.positions = [[0.0] 4 for in range(maxcapacity)] self.scales = [[0.0] 3 for in range(maxcapacity)] self.opacities = [0.0] maxcapacity self.rotations = [[0.0] 4 for in range(maxcapacity)] self.sh = [[0.0] 48 for in range(maxcapacity)] self.cov3d = [[0.0] 9 for in range(maxcapacity)] # Flattened 3x3 matrix def addgaussian(self, pos: list, scale: list, opacity: float, rot: list, sh: list): if self.numgaussians >= self.maxcapacity: raise Exception("GaussianList full") i = self.numgaussians self.positions[i] = pos + [0.0] # Pad to 4 self.scales[i] = scale self.opacities[i] = opacity self.rotations[i] = rot self.sh[i] = sh # Compute cov3d from scale and rotation self.cov3d[i] = self.computecov3d(scale, rot) self.numgaussians += 1 def computecov3d(self, scale: list, rot: list) -> list: # Simplified covariance computation # In practice, this involves quaternion-to-matrix conversion and matrix multiplication # Placeholder for actual math: R S S^T R^T return [0.0] 9 # Return placeholder def getbatchedarrays(self) -> dict: # Return numpy-like arrays for GPU upload return { "positions": self.positions[:self.numgaussians], "scales": self.scales[:self.numgaussians], "opacities": self.opacities[:self.numgaussians], "rotations": self.rotations[:self.numgaussians], "sh": self.sh[:self.numgaussians], "cov3d": self.cov3d[:self.numgaussians] } GSPull leverages neural distance functions (SDFs/UDFs) to recover detailed mesh structures from 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing the volumetric nature of standard splats by integrating distance-field supervision. It uses dense queries around the zero-level set to refine geometry conservatively, preventing error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions. Choose this when explicit surface geometry is required from a Gaussian representation. Link: GSPull. A density control mechanism using a frequency-aware mask and photometric loss to compute densification/pruning scores, reducing redundancy and improving fidelity over vanilla 3DGS. It integrates a frequency-aware mask to filter noise and weights pruning scores with image-level photometric loss, unlike siblings focusing on second-order sensitivity or Hessian approximations. Choose this for high-fidelity reconstruction with efficient primitive management. Link: Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring. The runtime strategy for resizing GPU memory buffers storing 3D Gaussian primitives during training/inference, solving unpredictable population sizes from densification/pruning. It grows/shrinks buffers on-the-fly, distinguishing it from static allocation and compression techniques by focusing on buffer expansion and data migration mechanics. Choose this for dynamic scenes with varying Gaussian counts. Link: Dynamic Buffer Management. The component of Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) predicting per-Gaussian appearance and visibility from reference images, replacing static color with learnable features sampled by viewpoint. It uses a U-Net encoder-decoder and fusion network for view-dependent appearance without explicit SH, unlike standard 3DGS. Choose this for unconstrained image collections with complex lighting. Link: GS-W Network Architecture. A large-scale 3DGS method partitioning scenes into spatially-disjoint regions for scalable training/rendering, solving memory/computational bottlenecks of global optimization. It uses visibility-aware iterative training and explicit appearance embeddings for lighting variations, distinguishing it from naive spatial splitting. Choose this for massive urban environments. Link: VastGaussian. Defines memory organization, serialization, and runtime management of 3DGS attributes for efficient GPU rendering and optimization. It focuses on raw memory layout and buffer management infrastructure, distinct from rendering algorithms, error-based densification, or network architectures. Choose this for cross-platform data transfer and cache-friendly batched processing. Link: Data Layout and Storage. Uses SH basis to represent view-dependent color of each Gaussian primitive, capturing appearance variations static RGB cannot. It adds view-dependent color and analytical Jacobian for gradient propagation, though incorrect SH modeling may worsen trajectory estimates. Choose this for view-dependent appearance modeling. Link: Spherical Harmonics Representation. A unified framework for real-time rendering of dynamic scenes with complex view-dependent effects, representing elements as 7D Gaussians (3D space, 1D time, 3D view direction). It jointly models spatial, temporal, and view-dependent dimensions in a single framework, using conditional slicing to transform 7D Gaussians into time/view-conditioned 3D Gaussians. Choose this for dynamic scenes with scattering/anisotropic reflections. Link: 7D Gaussian Splatting. Defines unconstrained learnable parameters for 3D Gaussian kernel attributes, ensuring valid physical ranges via specific activation functions. It introduces a three-step activation for basis angles to maintain angular separation and monotonicity, and configurable density control thresholds for sparse training. Choose this for constrained optimization of Gaussian attributes. Link: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) Parametrization. A method for 3DGS editing leveraging explicit primitives for direct parameter manipulation (position, rotation, scale, color) based on user commands. It enables local editing (3D inpainting, object removal, composition) with real-time fine-grained control, unlike implicit or global optimization methods. Choose this for user experience and real-time editing. Link: GaussianEditor (Local). Enhances 3DGS by incorporating identity encodings for 3D objects, enabling grouping splats by semantic identity. It solves precise object-level manipulation (removal, inpainting, recomposition) by rebuilding/segmenting objects under 2D mask and 3D consistency constraints. Compared to siblings, it reduces artifacts and avoids blurry backgrounds. Choose this for object-level manipulation. Link: Gaussian Grouping. A technique introducing a learnable per-Gaussian scalar factor \betai to reparameterize effective scales, providing an optimization pathway for adapting primitive extent while retaining tile-culling rules. It initializes \betai \in \mathbb{R} to zero, optimizes it with Adam, and scales covariance by \gammai^2 where \gammai = \text{sigmoid}(\betai). Unlike vanilla 3DGS, it changes overall extent while keeping anisotropic axis ratios from base scales. Choose this for compact representations with improved quality. Link: Learnable Scale Modulation for Primitive Compactness (Note: No dedicated article, cited under Subtopics). Replaces V{pq} \text{diag}(\Lambda) V{qq} with a free matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C}, removing spatial normalization and bounded coupling. It uses a matrix learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-6}, scaled by median primitive size. Unrestricted direct coordinates alone do not explain quality gains; structured parameterization performs better. Choose this for direct regression experiments. Link: Direct-Unrestricted (DU) Variant (Note: No dedicated article, cited under Subtopics). Stores control points of Bézier curves directly in 3D spatial coordinates using attribute c{\text{curve}}^{3D} \in \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 3} instead of 2D subspace. It omits the equation to acquire c{\text{curve}}^{3D} from c{\text{curve}} during rendering, as c{\text{curve}}^{3D} is a direct attribute. Choose this for discontinuity-aware rendering with 3D Bézier curves. Link: DisC-GS 3D Extension (Note: No dedicated article, cited under Subtopics). A Python-based container storing points in a list of GaussianPoint objects, providing methods to retrieve batched numpy arrays (positions, colors, scales, opacities, rotations). It serializes/deserializes via todict()/fromdict() with keys for positions (N,3), colors (N,3), scales (N,3), opacities (N,), rotations (N,4), numpoints (int). Default scale is [0.02, 0.02, 0.02] if None. Choose this for prototyping and compatibility with CloudCompare/MeshLab. Link: GaussianCloud Container (Note: No dedicated article, cited under Subtopics). A density-control event determines retained/new Gaussians, commits structural change in one target layout, and manages image supply. It creates host-side target arrays for parameters, Adam state, and density statistics, moves retained rows in chunks, appends new rows, releases old device layout, and uploads target arrays. Training images remain as compressed JPEG bytes on host, decoded in camera order through a queue of capacity K=16. Choose this for memory-efficient training with asynchronous image decoding. Link: Structure Updates and Image Supply (Note: No dedicated article, cited under Subtopics). Time Complexity: O(N) for rendering and updates, where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where D is the number of parameters per Gaussian (e.g., 59 for SH3). For SH3, approximately 0.685 GiB per million Gaussians. Measured Performance: On Deep Blending and Tanks & Temples, EffGS (using this structure) achieves PSNR 30.01 dB, SSIM 0.910, and LPIPS 0.238 with 0.25M Gaussians, outperforming EDGS and 3DGS-MCMC. Scaling: Scales linearly with N; efficient for large scenes with dynamic buffer management. Strengths: Efficient batched processing, dynamic resizing, compatibility with GPU rendering. Limitations: Memory-intensive for high-resolution scenes with many Gaussians; requires careful buffer management. When to Use: Real-time rendering, dynamic scenes, large-scale environments. When Not to Use: Memory-constrained environments without dynamic buffer management; static scenes with low N may not benefit from SoA layout. Originated in 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) for real-time differentiable rendering. Developed to address the inefficiencies of point-based rendering and neural radiance fields, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction and real-time visualization. name: GSPull
head: GSDF / GSPull
body: GSPull is a technique that leverages neural distance functions (SDFs or UDFs) to recover detailed mesh structures from 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which produces volumetric splats rather than explicit surfaces, by integrating distance-field supervision to refine geometry. Unlike methods that directly pull Gaussians to the zero-level set, GSPull uses dense queries around the zero-level set as strong geometric cues to refine the surface conservatively and gradually, preventing error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions. Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) initialized from standard 3DGS reconstruction. Multi-view images for supervision. A neural network parameterizing the distance field. Outputs: Refined 3D Gaussians with improved geometric alignment. A detailed mesh extracted from the converged distance field zero-level set. Data Structures: The Gaussian set follows the standard 3DGS layout containing position \mathbf{p}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients. The distance field is stored as a neural network mapping 3D coordinates to scalar distance values d(\mathbf{x}). Steps: 1. Initialize Gaussians using standard 3DGS and initialize the distance field network. 2. Jointly optimize the Gaussian parameters and distance field network parameters via gradient descent. 3. Query the distance field at dense points around the current Gaussian positions or surface estimates instead of pulling directly to the zero-level set d(\mathbf{x})=0. 4. Use the dense queries as geometric cues to update Gaussian positions and orientations, applying the refinement gradually. 5. Progressively finetune the Gaussian distribution and distance field representation over time. Formulas: The distance field d(\mathbf{x}) represents the signed or unsigned distance from point \mathbf{x} to the surface. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Ambiguous pulling directions can cause error accumulation if gradients are unclear; GSPull mitigates this by relying on dense queries rather than direct zero-level set pulling. Unlike methods that directly pull Gaussians to the UDF zero-level set, GSPull leverages dense queries around the zero-level set as strong geometric cues. It refines the surface in a conservative and gradual manner, effectively preventing error accumulation caused by ambiguous pulling directions. Time and Memory Complexity: Evaluating the neural distance field network for dense queries adds computational cost during optimization. Memory usage increases due to the storage of the distance field network parameters. Measured performance, hardware specifics, resolution scaling, and scene dependencies are Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: GSPull recovers more detailed mesh structures compared to standard 3DGS. It prevents error accumulation from ambiguous pulling directions. The method requires joint optimization of Gaussians and a neural network. When to Use: Use when explicit, high-quality mesh extraction is required. Use when standard zero-level pulling leads to geometric artifacts. GSPull was introduced as an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting to enable surface reconstruction. It was inspired by similar approaches used in NeRF-based methods. The technique is often cited alongside GSDF as a method that adopts neural distance functions for recovering detailed mesh structures. name: Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring
head: EffGS density control, Frequency-aware mask scoring
body: A density control mechanism that uses a frequency-aware mask and photometric loss to compute densification and pruning scores for Gaussian primitives, reducing redundancy and improving fidelity compared to vanilla 3DGS. It sets itself apart from its siblings by integrating a frequency-aware mask into the error computation to filter noise, and by weighting pruning scores with image-level photometric loss rather than raw pixel counts, whereas Efficient Pruning Score focuses on second-order sensitivity and Fisher Sensitivity Score uses Hessian approximations. Inputs: Set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}t at update step t. K distinct training views sampled uniformly without replacement. Rendered images I{\text{rend}}^j and ground-truth images I{\text{gt}}^j for each sampled view j. Frequency-aware mask M{\text{freq}}^j for each view j. Parameters: \tau \in (0, 1) (error threshold), \taup \in [0, 1) (pruning score threshold), \taud \ge 0 (densification score threshold), \taus > 0 (scale threshold), \rho \in [0, 1] (pruning sampling ratio), \lambda{\text{dssim}} (SSIM weight). Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}{t+1}. Data Structures: \mathcal{V}i: Set of view indices where Gaussian i has a valid projected footprint. \mathcal{A}t: Set of active primitives \{i \in \mathcal{G}t: |\mathcal{V}i| > 0\}. \Omegai^j: Set of pixels where Gaussian i contributes during compositing in view j. M{\text{err}}^j: Composite error mask for view j. Steps: 1. Identify Active Primitives: For each Gaussian i \in \mathcal{G}t and each sampled view j \in \{1, \dots, K\}: Get projected radius ri^j from the rasterizer. Determine visibility: \mathcal{V}i = \{j: ri^j > 0\}. Count visible views: |\mathcal{V}i| = \sum{j=1}^K \mathbb{I}[ri^j > 0]. Define active set: \mathcal{A}t = \{i \in \mathcal{G}t: |\mathcal{V}i| > 0\}. If \mathcal{A}t = \emptyset, skip density control. 2. Compute Composite Error Map: For each sampled view j: Compute raw per-pixel RGB reconstruction error: e^j(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{1}{3} \sum{c=1}^3 \left| I{\text{rend},c}^j(\mathbf{u}) - I{\text{gt},c}^j(\mathbf{u}) \right|. Normalize error over pixel grid \mathcal{P}j: \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) = \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{P}j}e^j where \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{P}j} is min-max normalization. If e^j is constant, map to zero. Compute composite error mask M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}): M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbb{I} \left[ \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) > \tau \vee \left( M{\text{freq}}^j(\mathbf{u}) = 1 \wedge \bar{e}^j(\mathbf{u}) > 0.5\tau \right) \right]. Note: The source text contains a typo M{\text{reeq}} which is corrected to M{\text{freq}} based on context. 3. Compute Densification Scores: For each i \in \mathcal{A}t: Compute weighted pixel count per view: ni^j = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \Omegai^j} M{\text{err}}^j(\mathbf{u}). Compute valid-view average count: Ci = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}i|} \sum{j \in \mathcal{V}i} ni^j. Compute densification score: sd^i(t) = \omega(t)Ci. where \omega(t) is a positive, nondecreasing clipped-linear schedule over the densification interval. 4. Compute Pruning Scores: For each i \in \mathcal{A}t: Compute image-level photometric loss for view j: E{\text{photo}}^j = (1 - \lambda{\text{dssim}}) \mathcal{L}1^j + \lambda{\text{dssim}} \left( 1 - \text{SSIM}(I{\text{rend}}^j, I{\text{gt}}^j) \right). where \mathcal{L}1^j = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}j|} \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}j} e^j(\mathbf{u}). Compute summed, loss-weighted count: Qi = \sum{j \in \mathcal{V}i} ni^j E{\text{photo}}^j. Normalize pruning score over active set: sp^i = \mathcal{N}{\mathcal{A}t}Q. 5. Execute Pruning: Identify mandatory removals: \mathcal{H}t = \{i \in \mathcal{A}t: oi < 0.1 \vee \gammai < 0.01\}. where oi is opacity and \gammai is the learnable scale-modulation factor. Identify candidates: \mathcal{P}t = \{i \in \mathcal{A}t \setminus \mathcal{H}t: sp^i > \taup\}. Sample bt = \lfloor \rho |\mathcal{P}t| \rfloor candidates without replacement using weights proportional to sp^i. Removal set: \mathcal{R}t = \mathcal{H}t \cup \text{sampled candidates}. Remove \mathcal{R}t from \mathcal{G}t. 6. Execute Densification: Select surviving active primitives with sd^i(t) > \taud. For each selected primitive i: If largest base-scale component < \taus: Clone and shift along positional gradient. Otherwise: Replace with two smaller Gaussians. New primitives inherit parent's unconstrained modulation parameter \betai \in \mathbb{R}, with \gammai = 2 \text{sigmoid}(\betai) \in (0, 2). Remaining attributes follow clone/split updates. Primitives outside \mathcal{A}t are unaffected. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When pruning and densification coincide, pruning must be applied first. New primitives are scored only at the next density update to avoid using post-update scores for pre-update decisions. Density control is skipped if \mathcal{A}t = \emptyset. A sensitivity-based metric that reparameterizes the Hessian approximation to reduce storage requirements by 36×, enabling soft pruning during training. It sets itself apart from the Composite Error Map by focusing on second-order sensitivity to spatial parameters rather than frequency-aware photometric error. A pruning metric that estimates the impact of each Gaussian on the L2 reconstruction loss using a block-diagonal Hessian approximation. It sets itself apart by evaluating geometric sensitivity through the log-determinant of parameter gradients, avoiding bias toward larger Gaussians. A technique for mapping 2D imagespace photometric errors back to 3D Gaussian primitives by aggregating alpha-weighted error metrics across multiple sampled views. It sets itself apart by ensuring only Gaussians with high visibility and significant contribution to reconstruction error are modified, avoiding overfitting to single-view occlusions. Not given in the sources. The method is described in EffGS (Efficient and High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting). It builds on Gaussian Data Structure and integrates frequency-aware masking to improve density control. name: Efficient Pruning Score
head: Pruning (Speedy-Splat), Speedy-Splat Pruning Score
body:
The Efficient Pruning Score is a sensitivity-based metric used to identify and remove redundant 3D Gaussian primitives during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and inefficient gradient flow associated with the original PUP 3D-GS pruning score by reparameterizing the Hessian approximation with respect to the 2D projected Gaussian value gi rather than the 3D spatial parameters. This reparameterization reduces storage requirements by 36×, enabling the score to be computed and applied during training (Soft Pruning) rather than only post-hoc. It sets itself apart from its parent method, the Composite Error Map, by focusing specifically on second-order sensitivity to spatial parameters to reduce Gaussian count, whereas the parent method uses frequency-aware masks and photometric loss for densification control. The method computes a pruning score for each Gaussian primitive to determine its contribution to the reconstruction error. It operates in two phases: Soft Pruning during the initial densification stage and Hard Pruning after densification is complete. Inputs: \mathcal{G}i: The set of N Gaussian primitives. \mathcal{P}{gt}: The set of all training camera poses. I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi): The rendered image for camera pose \phi. gi(\phi, p): The projected scalar value of Gaussian \mathcal{G}i at pixel p for pose \phi. 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi, p): The gradient of the rendered image with respect to the projected Gaussian value gi, computed during the standard backward pass of the 3DGS render kernel. Outputs: 	ilde{U}i: The pruning score for Gaussian \mathcal{G}i. A binary mask or list of indices for Gaussians to be pruned. Pruning Score Array: An array of size N (number of Gaussians) storing the scalar score 	ilde{U}i for each Gaussian. This replaces the N 	imes 36 matrix required by the original PUP 3D-GS score. The original PUP 3D-GS sensitivity score Ui is defined as the log determinant of the second-order approximation of the L2 reconstruction error with respect to the mean \mui and scaling si parameters: Ui = \log \left| 
abla{\mui,si}^2 L2 ight| = \log \left| \sum{\phi \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} 
abla{\mui,si} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) 
abla{\mui,si} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^T ight| where 
abla{\mui,si} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) is a vector of gradients with respect to the 3D parameters. The Efficient Pruning Score 	ilde{U}i reparameterizes this by computing the Hessian approximation with respect to the 2D projected value gi: 	ilde{U}i = \log \left| \sum{\phi \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi) 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^T ight| Since gi is a scalar at each pixel, the term inside the determinant is a scalar squared. Because the logarithm is monotonically increasing, the log determinant simplifies to the sum of squared gradients: 	ilde{U}i = \sum{\phi \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}(\phi)^2 In implementation, the gradient 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}} is accumulated per pixel during the backward pass. The final score is the sum of these squared gradients across all training views. Pruning Threshold: The sources do not specify a fixed constant threshold. The method identifies Gaussians with low scores for removal, achieving up to 90% reduction. Densification Iteration Limit: 15,000 iterations. Soft pruning occurs before this limit; Hard pruning occurs after. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeefficientpruningscore(gaussians, trainingposes, gradients): """ Computes the Efficient Pruning Score for all Gaussians. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. trainingposes: List of all training camera poses. gradients: 2D array of shape (N, P) containing gradient values dI/dgi for each Gaussian i and each training pose p. Returns: scores: Array of pruning scores for each Gaussian. """ ngaussians = len(gaussians) scores = [0.0] ngaussians for p in range(len(trainingposes)): for i in range(ngaussians): scores[i] += gradients[i][p] 2 return scores def applypruning(gaussians, scores, keepratio=0.1): """ Applies pruning based on the computed scores. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. scores: Array of pruning scores. keepratio: Fraction of Gaussians to retain. Set to 0.1 for ~90% reduction. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of Gaussians remaining after pruning. """ ngaussians = len(gaussians) numtokeep = int(ngaussians keepratio) sortedindices = sorted(range(ngaussians), key=lambda k: scores[k]) keepindices = set(sortedindices[-numtokeep:]) prunedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in keepindices] return prunedgaussians Gradient Availability: The method relies on 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}} being available from the standard backward pass. Precision: Squaring small gradients may lead to underflow or loss of precision if not handled with appropriate data types. Boundary Conditions: The simplification 	ilde{U}i = \sum (
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}})^2 assumes gi is a scalar. A scoring mechanism that selects a subset of Gaussians based solely on intrinsic 3D attributes, decoupling geometry from appearance to prevent high-dimensional spherical harmonics from dominating the selection. It avoids expensive ray-pixel intersections and is chosen when memory efficiency is critical and appearance details are less important than global structure. Time Complexity: The score computation requires iterating over all Gaussians and all training poses. However, since the gradients are already computed during the backward pass, the additional cost is primarily the summation of squared gradients, which is O(N \cdot |\mathcal{P}{gt}|). Memory Complexity: The storage requirement is proportional to N (one score per Gaussian), a 36× reduction compared to the N 	imes 36 storage required by the original PUP 3D-GS score. Measured Performance: The full method (including pruning) achieves 6.51× FPS, 10.6× compression, and 1.45× faster training compared to original 3D-GS. It reduces the total number of Gaussians by approximately 90%. Strengths: Enables training-time pruning, reducing memory footprint and accelerating training and rendering. It maintains high visual quality despite significant compression. Limitations: Requires the standard 3DGS backward pass to expose 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}}, which is natively available in the Speedy-Splat implementation. The Efficient Pruning Score was introduced in the Speedy-Splat paper by Zwicker et al. in 2025. It builds upon the PUP 3D-GS method, which demonstrated that post-hoc pruning could reduce Gaussian counts by ~90% but suffered from high memory overhead and inefficient gradient flow. The Speedy-Splat authors identified these drawbacks and proposed the reparameterization to enable efficient, training-time pruning. The method is part of the Speedy-Splat framework, which also includes sparse pixels and sparse primitives techniques. name: Geometry-Driven Pruning Score
body:
A scoring mechanism to select a subset of K Gaussians that preserves global structure and visual appearance using only intrinsic 3D attributes, avoiding expensive ray-pixel intersections. It balances geometric coverage and appearance contribution by weighting normalized opacity and volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by opacity \alphai, scale vector \mathbf{s}i = (s{xi}, s{yi}, s{zi}), and spherical harmonic coefficients. Output: Indices of the top K Gaussians with the highest scores. Data Structures: Gaussian attributes are stored in parallel arrays of size N. Steps: 1. Compute the raw volume Vi for each Gaussian i: Vi =  rac{4}{3} \pi s{xi} s{yi} s{zi} 2. Compute the z-score normalized opacity 
u(\alphai) and volume 
u(Vi) across all N Gaussians: 
u(x) =  rac{x - \mux}{\sigmax} where \mux and \sigmax are the mean and standard deviation of the respective attribute. 3. Compute the pruning score Si for each Gaussian i: Si = \lambda\alpha \cdot 
u(\alphai) + (1 - \lambda\alpha) \cdot 
u(Vi) 4. Select the top K Gaussians with the highest scores Si. Parameters: \lambda\alpha \in [0, 1]: Trade-off parameter controlling the balance between appearance (opacity) and spatial (volume) contribution. Typical value: 0.3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \sigma\alpha or \sigmaV is zero (all Gaussians have identical opacity or volume), z-score normalization is undefined. In this case, the normalized values are set to 0. The source does not specify handling for degenerate inputs or precision limits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def geometrydrivenpruningscore(gaussians, K, lambdaalpha=0.3): """ Select top K Gaussians based on geometry-driven pruning score. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: alpha: float, opacity scale: tuple (sx, sy, sz), scale vector K: int, number of Gaussians to select lambdaalpha: float, trade-off parameter (default 0.3) Returns: List of indices of the top K Gaussians """ N = len(gaussians) if N == 0: return [] # Extract attributes alphas = np.array([g.alpha for g in gaussians]) scales = np.array([g.scale for g in gaussians]) # Compute volumes volumes = (4.0 / 3.0) np.pi scales[:, 0] scales[:, 1] scales[:, 2] # Z-score normalization alphamean = np.mean(alphas) alphastd = np.std(alphas) if alphastd == 0: alphanorm = np.zeros(N) else: alphanorm = (alphas - alphamean) / alphastd volumemean = np.mean(volumes) volumestd = np.std(volumes) if volumestd == 0: volumenorm = np.zeros(N) else: volumenorm = (volumes - volumemean) / volumestd # Compute scores scores = lambdaalpha alphanorm + (1 - lambdaalpha) volumenorm # Select top K topkindices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:K] return topkindices.tolist() PointSplat is a geometry-driven prune-and-refine framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables high-quality reconstruction of compact Gaussian sets without requiring per-scene optimization at deployment. It bridges the gap between Gaussian pruning and transformer refinement by using intrinsic 3D attributes for pruning and a dual-branch encoder for refinement. Unlike image-driven pruning methods that rely on 2D images and per-scene optimization, PointSplat uses only 3D attributes for pruning. Unlike SplatFormer, which concatenates all Gaussian parameters into a single feature vector causing appearance dominance due to high-dimensional spherical harmonics, PointSplat decouples geometry and appearance. FFW computes an importance score for each Gaussian primitive using a combination of position, color, opacity, and transparency to selectively remove less important Gaussians while preserving visual quality. It is chosen when explicit multi-factor weighting is preferred over normalized z-score aggregation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient as it avoids ray-pixel intersections required by image-driven methods. Strengths: Preserves global structure and visual appearance using only intrinsic 3D attributes. Results remain stable across a range of \lambda\alpha values, demonstrating robustness. Limitations: Relies on z-score normalization, which may be sensitive to outliers in opacity or volume distributions. When to use: When pruning 3D Gaussians for compact representation without per-scene optimization, especially in transformer-based refinement frameworks like PointSplat. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Introduced in the PointSplat framework for efficient geometry-driven pruning and transformer refinement. It was developed to address the limitations of image-driven pruning methods that require expensive ray-pixel intersections and per-scene optimization. The method leverages intrinsic 3D attributes to enable efficient pruning for transformer-based refinement. name: PointSplat
body: PointSplat is a geometry-driven prune-and-refine framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reconstructs compact Gaussian sets without requiring per-scene optimization at deployment. It bridges Gaussian pruning and transformer refinement by ranking Gaussians using only intrinsic 3D attributes and refining them via a dual-branch encoder. Unlike image-driven pruning methods (e.g., LightGaussians, PUP-3DGS, Speedy-Splat) that require 2D images and per-scene optimization, PointSplat operates solely on 3D geometry. Unlike SplatFormer, which concatenates all parameters into a single vector causing appearance dominance from high-dimensional spherical harmonics, PointSplat decouples geometry and appearance to prevent feature imbalance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N from a trained 3DGS model. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonics coefficients \gamma^{(i)}. Output: A refined, compact subset of Gaussians with improved structural integrity and visual quality. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi retains its standard 3DGS parameters: \mui: Mean position (3 floats). \Sigmai: Covariance matrix, decomposed into rotation Ri (from quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4) and scaling Si (from vector si = [s{xi}, s{yi}, s{zi}]). \alphai: Opacity (1 float). \gamma^{(i)}: Spherical harmonics coefficients. For degree L=3, this results in up to 48 dimensions for appearance coefficients. Method Steps: 1. Geometry-Driven Pruning Score Calculation: Compute a pruning score for each Gaussian Gi based solely on intrinsic 3D attributes (opacity and volume/spatial coverage). The score balances spatial coverage and opacity to select a compact yet informative subset. This avoids complex image-ray interactions. Formula for Gaussian definition: Gi(x) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (x - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right) where \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T. Select the top K Gaussians with the highest scores. 2. Dual-Branch Encoder Initialization: Separate the geometric attributes (\mui, Ri, Si) and appearance attributes (\alphai, \gamma^{(i)}) of the retained Gaussians into two distinct branches. This explicit separation prevents feature imbalance where high-dimensional appearance features (e.g., 48D SH coefficients for L=3) dominate lower-dimensional geometric features. 3. Feature Reweighting with Positional Encoding: Reweight the separated geometric and appearance features using positional encoding. This step ensures balanced learning and prevents appearance dominance during transformer refinement. 4. Transformer Refinement: Process the reweighted features through a 3D transformer network (based on PointTransformerV3 architecture) to globally coordinate Gaussian parameters. This captures fine-grained structural details, addressing artifacts such as blurred textures and broken geometric edges that may result from pruning alone. The output is a set of compact, well-aligned ellipsoids. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from typing import List class Gaussian: def init(self, mu: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray, s: np.ndarray, alpha: float, shcoeffs: np.ndarray): self.mu = mu # (3,) mean position self.q = q # (4,) quaternion self.s = s # (3,) scaling vector self.alpha = alpha self.shcoeffs = shcoeffs # (D,) spherical harmonics coefficients def getcovariance(self) -> np.ndarray: R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(self.q) S = np.diag(self.s) return R @ S @ S.T @ R.T def computepruningscore(self) -> float: # Score based on intrinsic 3D attributes: opacity and volume volume = np.prod(self.s) return self.alpha volume def pointsplat(gaussians: List[Gaussian], k: int) -> List[Gaussian]: # Step 1: Geometry-Driven Pruning scores = [g.computepruningscore() for g in gaussians] sortedindices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k] retainedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] # Step 2 & 3: Dual-Branch Encoder and Feature Reweighting geometricfeatures = [] appearancefeatures = [] for g in retainedgaussians: geofeat = np.concatenate([g.mu, g.q, g.s]) geometricfeatures.append(geofeat) appfeat = np.concatenate([[g.alpha], g.shcoeffs]) appearancefeatures.append(appfeat) geometricfeatures = np.array(geometricfeatures) appearancefeatures = np.array(appearancefeatures) # Apply positional encoding and reweighting posencoding = positionalencoding(geometricfeatures[:,:3]) geometricfeatures = geometricfeatures + posencoding # Normalize features to prevent dominance geometricfeatures = geometricfeatures / (np.linalg.norm(geometricfeatures, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) appearancefeatures = appearancefeatures / (np.linalg.norm(appearancefeatures, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) # Step 4: Transformer Refinement # Note: The exact transformer architecture and forward pass are not specified in the sources combinedfeatures = np.concatenate([geometricfeatures, appearancefeatures], axis=1) # refinedfeatures = transformerrefine(combinedfeatures) # Extract refined parameters refinedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(retainedgaussians): # Note: Mapping refined features back to quaternion/scale/etc. is not specified in the sources # Assuming identity mapping for structural completeness refinedg = Gaussian( mu=geometricfeatures[i,:3], q=geometricfeatures[i, 3:7], s=geometricfeatures[i, 7:10], alpha=appearancefeatures[i, 0], shcoeffs=appearancefeatures[i, 1:]) refinedgaussians.append(refinedg) return refinedgaussians def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: w, x, y, z = q return np.array([ [1 - 2yy - 2zz, 2xy - 2zw, 2xz + 2yw], [2xy + 2zw, 1 - 2xx - 2zz, 2yz - 2xw], [2xz - 2yw, 2yz + 2xw, 1 - 2xx - 2yy] ]) def positionalencoding(features: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: # Standard positional encoding using sine/cosine functions scales = np.logspace(-1, 4, features.shape[1]) scaledfeatures = features[:, None,:] scales[None,:, None] return np.sin(scaledfeatures) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Imbalance: If geometry and appearance are not properly separated and reweighted, high-dimensional spherical harmonics coefficients (up to 48D for L=3) can dominate the learning process, leading to suboptimal refinement. Degenerate Input: Pruning based solely on opacity and volume may remove Gaussians critical for fine details if their opacity is low but they cover unique spatial regions. The transformer refinement helps mitigate this by globally coordinating parameters. Deployment Constraints: PointSplat is designed to eliminate reliance on per-scene optimization at deployment, so it trades absolute peak quality for rapid compression and inference efficiency. Time Complexity: Pruning is O(N) to compute scores and select top K. Transformer refinement depends on the transformer architecture but is generally efficient for compact sets. Memory Complexity: Reduced by pruning N to K Gaussians. No additional per-scene optimization memory overhead is incurred. Measured Performance: Experiments on ScanNet++ and Replica datasets demonstrate competitive rendering quality and superior efficiency across varying sparsity levels. Strengths: No reliance on 2D images for pruning. No per-scene optimization required. Avoids feature imbalance through dual-branch encoder. Limitations: May not achieve the same quality as methods with per-scene optimization. Relies on intrinsic attributes which may not capture all visual importance. When to Use: When efficient compression of 3DGS models is needed without per-scene optimization, and when feature imbalance is a concern. PointSplat was introduced in the paper "PointSplat: Efficient Geometry-Driven Pruning and Transformer Refinement for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses limitations in existing 3DGS compression methods, which either rely on image-driven pruning with per-scene optimization or suffer from feature imbalance in transformer-based refinement. The method builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and integrates concepts from point cloud processing refinements.
