name: Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning
head: MiniGS Pruning, Scorev4
body: Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning, also known as MiniGS Pruning or Scorev4, is a method for selectively removing less important 3D Gaussian primitives during training to reduce memory footprint and rendering latency while preserving visual fidelity. It addresses the limitation of vanilla 3DGS pruning, which relies solely on opacity and transparency, by incorporating position, color similarity, opacity, and transparency into a single importance score. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, the current camera view (defined by ray r and pixel coordinate Xr), the rendered pixel color cr, and the Gaussian parameters (position Xi, view-dependent color ci, opacity \alphai, transparency Ti). Output: A ranked list of Gaussians and a binary mask indicating which Gaussians to prune from the scene representation. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian data layout defined in Gaussian Data Structure. Each Gaussian Gi stores: Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: View-dependent color computed from spherical harmonics coefficients. \alphai \in [0, 1]: Blending opacity. Ti \in [0, 1]: Transparency calculated during rasterization as Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) for Gaussians sorted by depth. \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: 3D covariance matrix. Step-by-Step Procedure: 1. Project Covariance: To determine the 2D extent of the Gaussian for rasterization, the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma is projected to the 2D image plane using the world-to-camera projective transform matrix W and the Jacobian J of the projective transform: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T This step generates the intermediate values (Ti) used in the importance score. 2. Compute Importance Score: For each Gaussian Gi contributing to the pixel color cr along ray r, calculate the importance score S(Gi, r) using the Scorev4 formula: S(Gi, r) = (1 - \text{mean}(cr - ci)) \cdot \exp(-\|Xr - Xi\|^2) \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti Where: cr is the final rendered color of the pixel. ci is the view-dependent color of the Gaussian Gi. \text{mean}(cr - ci) is the mean difference across the RGB channels of the color vectors. Xr is the 2D pixel coordinate of the ray. Xi is the center position of the projected Gaussian. \alphai is the blending opacity. Ti is the transparency (accumulated alpha from previous Gaussians). 3. Rank and Prune: Rank all Gaussians based on their computed importance scores. Remove the Gaussians with the lowest scores until the target number of primitives is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeffwscore(pixelcolor, pixelcoord, gaussiancolor, gaussiancenter2d, opacity, transparency): """ Computes the FFW (Scorev4) importance score for a single Gaussian contribution. Args: pixelcolor: list of 3 floats [R, G, B] for the rendered pixel. pixelcoord: list of 2 floats [x, y] for the 2D pixel coordinate. gaussiancolor: list of 3 floats [R, G, B] for the Gaussian's view-dependent color. gaussiancenter2d: list of 2 floats [x, y] for the projected Gaussian center. opacity: float alphai. transparency: float Ti. Returns: float: Importance score. """ # Calculate color similarity factor: (1 - mean(color difference)) colordiff = [pixelcolor[k] - gaussiancolor[k] for k in range(3)] meancolordiff = sum(colordiff) / 3.0 colorsimilarity = 1.0 - meancolordiff # Calculate spatial proximity factor: exp(-squared distance) dx = pixelcoord[0] - gaussiancenter2d[0] dy = pixelcoord[1] - gaussiancenter2d[1] spatialdistsq = dx dx + dy dy spatialfactor = math.exp(-spatialdistsq) # Combine factors score = colorsimilarity spatialfactor opacity transparency return score def prunegaussians(gaussians, renderdata, targetcount): """ Prunes Gaussians using FFW importance scores. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. renderdata: Dictionary mapping Gaussian index to list of (pixelcolor, pixelcoord, transparency) tuples. targetcount: Integer, number of Gaussians to keep. Returns: List of Gaussian objects: The pruned set. """ scores = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Aggregate score across all pixels where this Gaussian contributes # The source implies a global ranking based on the computed importance. # Implementation detail: average the scores across contributing pixels. pixelscores = [] for pixelcolor, pixelcoord, transparency in renderdata.contributingpixels[i]: score = computeffwscore( pixelcolor=pixelcolor, pixelcoord=pixelcoord, gaussiancolor=g.color, gaussiancenter2d=g.center2d, opacity=g.opacity, transparency=transparency) pixelscores.append(score) avgscore = sum(pixelscores) / len(pixelscores) if pixelscores else 0.0 scores.append((i, avgscore)) # Sort by score ascending (lowest importance first) scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) # Determine how many to prune numtoprune = len(gaussians) - targetcount if numtoprune <= 0: return gaussians # Indices to remove indicestoremove = set([idx for idx, in scores[:numtoprune]]) # Return pruned list return [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if i not in indicestoremove] Parameters: Target Primitive Count (K): The desired number of Gaussians after pruning. Color Difference Metric: The source uses mean(cr - ci). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF360: SSIM 0.798, PSNR 27.10, LPIPS 0.242 with 402.2k primitives. Tanks&Temples: SSIM 0.828, PSNR 23.11, LPIPS 0.207 with 230.7k primitives. DeepBlending: SSIM 0.897, PSNR 25.87, LPIPS 0.316 with 250.7k primitives. Strengths: Incorporates color and position information, preventing the removal of visually important Gaussians that have low opacity. Outperforms vanilla opacity-only pruning (Scorevanilla) and other variants (Scorev1-v3) in quantitative metrics. Limitations: Requires access to rendered pixel colors and intermediate blending values (Ti), which must be stored or recomputed during the pruning phase. The Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning, also known as Scorev4, was introduced in the MiniGS method. MiniGS aims to provide an efficient 3D Gaussian splatting pipeline by combining FFW pruning with a Variational Densify Threshold (VDT) module. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of vanilla 3DGS pruning, which fails to account for color and spatial contributions, leading to suboptimal pruning decisions. The approach was evaluated on standard NeRF benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, DeepBlending) using a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. name: Multi-view Alpha-Weighted Error Accumulation
head: Alpha-Weighted Error Accumulation, Alpha-based Importance/Pruning Scoring
body: Multi-view Alpha-Weighted Error Accumulation is a technique for mapping 2D imagespace photometric errors back to 3D Gaussian primitives to compute importance and pruning scores. It solves the problem of excessive or redundant densification caused by relying on single-view gradients by aggregating alpha-weighted error metrics across multiple sampled views. Unlike conventional gradient-based metrics, this method ensures that only Gaussians with high visibility and significant contribution to the reconstruction error are modified, thereby avoiding overfitting to single-view occlusions or transient artifacts. The method computes two scores for each Gaussian primitive i: an importance score Si^+ for densification and a pruning score Si^- for redundancy removal. These scores are derived by aggregating local metrics from a metric map across \mathcal{C} sampled views. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussian primitives, indexed by i. For each Gaussian i: opacity oi, covariance matrix \Sigmai, and position \mathbf{x}i. Number of sampled views \mathcal{C}. Discrete image pixel domain \Omega \subset \mathbb{Z}^2. For each view c \in \{0, \dots, \mathcal{C}\}: Metric map flags M{uv}^{c,+} and M{uv}^{c,-} for each pixel (u,v) \in \Omega. Local photometric loss \mathcal{L}{uv} for each pixel (u,v) \in \Omega. Outputs: Importance score Si^+ for each Gaussian i. Pruning score Si^- for each Gaussian i. Data Structures: The metric map is a binary or categorical flag per pixel per view. M{uv}^{c,+} = 1 indicates a region of high error/importance (poor reconstruction), while M{uv}^{c,-} = 1 indicates a region of low error/artifacts (well-reconstructed, redundant). The local loss \mathcal{L}{uv} is a scalar value representing the photometric difference at pixel (u,v). Formulas: The Gaussian alpha contribution \alphai for a specific pixel projection is defined as: \alphai = oi \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \Delta \mathbf{x}i^T \Sigmai^{-1} \Delta \mathbf{x}i \right) where \Delta \mathbf{x}i is the position offset from the pixel center to the Gaussian center. The importance score Si^+ is computed as: Si^+ = \sum{c=0}^{\mathcal{C}} \sum{(u,v) \in \Omega} \alphai \cdot M{uv}^{c,+} The pruning score Si^- is computed as: Si^- = \sum{c=0}^{\mathcal{C}} \sum{(u,v) \in \Omega} \mathcal{L}{uv} \cdot \alphai \cdot M{uv}^{c,-} Steps: 1. Initialize Si^+ = 0 and Si^- = 0 for all Gaussians i. 2. For each sampled view c from 0 to \mathcal{C}: 3. For each pixel (u,v) in the discrete image domain \Omega: 4. Retrieve metric map flags M{uv}^{c,+}, M{uv}^{c,-} and local loss \mathcal{L}{uv}. 5. For each Gaussian i projecting to (u,v): 6. Compute \alphai using opacity oi, covariance \Sigmai, and position offset \Delta \mathbf{x}i. 7. If M{uv}^{c,+} = 1, add \alphai to the running sum Si^+. 8. If M{uv}^{c,-} = 1, add \mathcal{L}{uv} \cdot \alphai to the running sum Si^-. 9. After iterating all views and pixels, use Si^+ to identify Gaussians for densification and Si^- to identify Gaussians for pruning. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def invertmatrix2x2(M): # Standard 2x2 matrix inversion det = M[0][0] M[1][1] - M[0][1] M[1][0] if det == 0: raise ValueError("Singular covariance matrix") return [[M[1][1] / det, -M[0][1] / det], [-M[1][0] / det, M[0][0] / det]] def computealphaweightedscores(gaussians, views, metricmaps, losses, H, W): """ Compute importance and pruning scores for 3D Gaussians using multi-view alpha-weighted error accumulation. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: opacity, covariance, position, importancescore, pruningscore views: List of view indices c from 0 to C metricmaps: Dictionary mapping (c, u, v) to (Mplus, Mminus) losses: Dictionary mapping (c, u, v) to local loss Luv H, W: Image height and width defining domain Omega Returns: Updated list of Gaussians with computed scores. """ for c in views: for u in range(H): for v in range(W): mplus, mminus = metricmaps.get((c, u, v), (0, 0)) luv = losses.get((c, u, v), 0.0) for g in gaussians: # Compute 2D offset from pixel center to Gaussian center deltax = (g.position[0] - (u + 0.5), g.position[1] - (v + 0.5)) # Compute quadratic form: deltax^T Sigmai^{-1} deltax invsigma = invertmatrix2x2(g.covariance) quadratic = dotproduct(deltax, dotproduct(invsigma, deltax)) alpha = g.opacity math.exp(-0.5 quadratic) # Accumulate importance score if flagged as high error region if mplus == 1: g.importancescore += alpha # Accumulate pruning score if flagged as low error/redundant region if mminus == 1: g.pruningscore += luv alpha return gaussians Parameters: \mathcal{C}: Number of sampled views. Not given in the sources. \Omega: Discrete image pixel domain. Not given in the sources. Thresholds for M{uv}^{c,+} and M{uv}^{c,-}: The sources mention a threshold \tau+ for marking poor reconstruction but do not specify the exact value or how M{uv}^{c,-} is thresholded. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: The covariance matrix \Sigmai must be invertible for the alpha calculation; if singular, a fallback or regularization is required. Single-view Overfitting: Relying on a single view can lead to excessive densification due to occlusions or transient artifacts. Gradient vs. Alpha: Conventional gradient metrics may modify Gaussians with low visibility. A scalar uncertainty feature per Gaussian primitive k capturing how much the primitive contributes to the overall rendering error, weighted by pixel-wise reconstruction error. It is computed as E(k) = \text{mean}{v \in \Omega} \text{agg}{\bar{x} \in v^{(k)}} e{\bar{x}} \alphak(\bar{x}) Tk(\bar{x}), where e{\bar{x}} = \|R(\bar{x}) - \hat{R}(\bar{x})\|1 is the per-pixel \ell1 reconstruction error, and \text{agg} \in \{\text{max}, \text{sum}, \text{mean}\} is the aggregation function. To highlight low-opacity Gaussians that still influence reconstruction quality, the opacity term \alphak(\bar{x}) can be omitted from the aggregation. Time Complexity: The complexity is proportional to the number of Gaussians projected onto pixels across all sampled views, with matrix inversion and dot products performed per projection. Memory Complexity: Requires storing metric maps and loss values for all sampled views and pixels, plus the scores for each Gaussian. Strengths: Differentiates important from redundant Gaussians more accurately than gradient-based methods; avoids overfitting to single-view occlusions; reduces redundancy. Limitations: Requires access to multiple views and pre-computed metric maps/losses; more computationally intensive than simple gradient accumulation due to alpha computation and multi-view aggregation. When to use: When densification/pruning based on visibility and multi-view consistency is critical to avoid artifacts and redundancy in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method was introduced in the context of Flux-GS, a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that integrates multi-view alpha-weighted error accumulation to improve geometry modification and reduce redundancy. It addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS, which uses gradient-based strategies (e.g., positional gradient threshold \|\nabla{\mui} \mathcal{L}\|2 > \tau) that often result in excessive and redundant Gaussian densification. By using alpha-based metrics instead of conventional gradient metrics, the method ensures that only Gaussians with high visibility and contributing to the error are modified. name: Dynamic Buffer Management
head: Capacity Growth
body: Dynamic Buffer Management (DBM) is the runtime strategy for resizing the GPU memory buffers that store 3D Gaussian primitives during training and inference. It solves the problem of unpredictable Gaussian population sizes caused by densification (splitting/cloning) and pruning operations, ensuring that the renderer always has sufficient contiguous memory to store the active set without excessive fragmentation or frequent reallocation overhead. It is distinguished from static allocation methods by its ability to grow and shrink buffers on-the-fly, and from pure memory optimization techniques (like VastGaussian) by focusing on the mechanics of buffer expansion and data migration rather than compression. The method manages the lifecycle of GPU buffers (Vertex Buffer Objects or equivalent linear memory) holding Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients). It triggers resizing when the number of active Gaussians exceeds the current buffer capacity. Input: Current number of active Gaussians (N{active}), current buffer capacity (C{curr}), stride size of the Gaussian data structure (S{stride}), and data type size (B{type}). Output: Updated buffer pointers, updated capacity (C{new}), and migrated Gaussian data. The primary data structure is a contiguous linear buffer (e.g., float or uint8t) allocated on the GPU. Layout: The buffer stores N Gaussians in a Structure of Arrays (SoA) or Array of Structures (AoS) layout. The total byte size is N \times S{stride} \times B{type}. Metadata: A counter tracks N{active}. A capacity tracker stores C{curr}. 1. Check Capacity: Compare N{active} with C{curr}. 2. Calculate New Capacity: If N{active} > C{curr}, determine C{new}. Strategy A (Doubling): C{new} = \max(2 \times C{curr}, N{active}). Strategy B (Over-allocation Factor): C{new} = \lceil N{active} \times 1.25 \rceil. If N{active} \le C{curr}, no action is taken (or shrink if explicitly supported, though shrinking is less common in training due to fragmentation risks). 3. Allocate New Buffer: Allocate a new GPU memory block of size C{new} \times S{stride} \times B{type}, initialized to zero. 4. Copy Data: Copy the existing N{active} Gaussians from the old buffer to the new buffer. Bytes to copy: Bytes{copy} = N{active} \times S{stride} \times B{type}. Operation: cudaMemcpy or equivalent GPU memory copy. 5. Update Pointers: Swap the old buffer pointer with the new buffer pointer. 6. Update Metadata: Set C{curr} = C{new} and reset any densification flags or scratch buffers associated with the new capacity. 7. Free Old Buffer: Deallocate the previous buffer to release memory. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicbuffermanagement(activecount, currentcapacity, stridebytes, typesize): """ Manages buffer resizing for 3D Gaussians. """ if activecount <= currentcapacity: return currentcapacity, None, False # Calculate new capacity # Strategy: Double capacity or meet exact need, whichever is larger newcapacity = max(currentcapacity 2, activecount) # Optional: Over-allocation factor to reduce future reallocations # newcapacity = ceil(activecount 1.25) oldbuffer = getcurrentbufferpointer() newbuffer = allocategpumemory(newcapacity stridebytes typesize) # Copy existing data bytestocopy = activecount stridebytes typesize gpumemcpy(newbuffer, oldbuffer, bytestocopy) # Update views/pointers setcurrentbufferpointer(newbuffer) setcurrentcapacity(newcapacity) # Reset auxiliary flags if necessary resetdensificationflags(newcapacity) # Free old buffer freegpumemory(oldbuffer) return newcapacity, newbuffer, True Over-Capacity Increase Factor: A constant multiplier (e.g., 1.25) used to over-allocate buffer capacity to reduce the frequency of reallocations. Stride Size: The number of bytes per Gaussian, determined by the chosen data layout (e.g., Gaussian Data Structure). Memory Fragmentation: Frequent small allocations can fragment GPU memory. Over-allocation factors help mitigate this. Data Copy Overhead: Copying large buffers during densification spikes can cause training pauses. Asynchronous copies or double-buffering can hide this latency. Zero Initialization: New buffer slots must be zero-initialized to prevent garbage data from affecting rendering or gradients. Scratch Buffer Synchronization: Scratch buffers used for sorting or merging must be resized in sync with the main Gaussian buffer to avoid out-of-bounds access. This variant uses CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM) to manage buffer sizes. Instead of allocating new physical memory and copying data, it maps additional physical pages to an existing virtual address range. This allows the buffer to grow or shrink within a single consecutive virtual address space without data copying, significantly reducing the overhead of merging buffers. It is chosen when minimizing copy latency is critical and the hardware supports CUDA VMM. A mechanism to detect asynchronous changes in active renderer splat counts (e.g., in streaming scenarios). It maintains an array mbuiltSplatCounts storing the splat counts at the time of the last buffer build. If the current active count differs from this array, or if any individual renderer's count has changed, the global buffers are marked dirty and rebuilt. Active-set size changes (adding/removing renderers) are handled separately via MarkGlobalBuffersDirty. Handles the disposal of global buffers (packed data, SH bands, order, renderer offsets, transforms, params) and scratch buffers. When the number of active renderers decreases, scratch buffers must be explicitly disposed to prevent memory leaks, as they are rebuilt upon the next global buffer rebuild. The mbuiltSplatCounts array is nullified to force recapture of splat counts from scratch on the next EnsureGlobalBuffers call. A buffering mechanism designed to handle high variability in Gaussian counts per scene, tile, and pixel. It prefetches Gaussian data into a global key-value buffer to decouple unpredictable Gaussian counts from pipeline stages, reducing latency and improving local memory utilization in hardware implementations. A collection strategy that stores intersected Gaussian IDs, hit distances, and alpha values in per-pixel linked lists. This avoids register spilling and multiple BVH traversals required by fixed-size batch processing. PPLLs increase FPS from 175 to 248 compared to multiple traversal methods. Lightweight implementations store only IDs, distances, and alphas, recomputing other attributes if needed, which is lighter than EPBRR's implementation. A data structure storing indices of intersecting Gaussians for each pixel, acting as the switch between View-dependent Gaussian Transformation and Pixel Render. Since a single Gaussian can project onto multiple pixels, the total size of all pixels' Z-buffers exceeds both the count of 3D Gaussians and the number of pixels. This structure, along with auxiliary sorting buffers, consumes significant activation memory, leading to Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors if resolution, scene size, or batch size is increased. Time Complexity: O(N) for copying data during buffer resize, where N is the number of active Gaussians. The frequency of resizes depends on the densification rate and the over-allocation factor. Memory Complexity: O(C{new}) where C{new} is the new capacity. Temporary memory usage peaks at 2 \times N{active} \times S{stride} during the copy operation. Performance: Buffer resizing is a major source of latency during training. Over-allocation factors (e.g., 1.25) reduce the frequency of resizes but increase peak memory usage. VMM-based approaches reduce copy overhead but require specific hardware support. Strengths: Adapts to dynamic scene complexity; prevents OOM errors during densification. Limitations: Copy overhead can stall training; memory fragmentation if not managed carefully; Z-buffer memory usage scales quadratically with resolution and scene density. When to use: Essential for training with densification. For inference, static buffers or VMM are preferred if the scene is static. Dynamic Buffer Management is a fundamental component of 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations, particularly those involving adaptive densification and pruning. It evolved alongside the 3DGS algorithm to handle the non-stationary nature of the Gaussian set during optimization. Early implementations used fixed-size buffers, which limited the number of Gaussians that could be rendered. Subsequent works introduced dynamic resizing, and more recent hardware-oriented designs have explored VMM and prefetch buffers to optimize this process. name: Dynamic Buffer Management via CUDA Virtual Memory
head: CUDA VMM, Merging Nodes via Virtual Memory, Virtual Memory Buffering, Virtual Memory Management (VMM) for Dynamic Buffers
body: This method uses CUDA’s virtual memory management (VMM) to manage dynamically sized splat buffers, allowing physical memory to grow or shrink within a single consecutive virtual address range without data copying. It specifically addresses the memory overhead of merging buffers by enabling the expansion of an existing target buffer rather than allocating a new combined buffer. Inputs: A source buffer (capacity A) and a target buffer (capacity B) containing Gaussian splat data; the size of a single splat element S (in bytes). Outputs: A merged target buffer containing all splats from A and B, with no intermediate buffer of size A+B allocated. Data Structures: Virtual Address Range: A reserved contiguous virtual memory region with a modest initial capacity. Physical Memory Map: A tracking structure mapping virtual offsets to committed physical GPU memory pages. Parameters: Physical Granularity (G): The minimum unit of physical memory that can be committed or uncommitted. On an RTX 4090, G = 2 \text{ MB}. Initial Virtual Capacity (V{init}): The size of the initially reserved virtual address range. Typically \ge 100 \text{ MB}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Reserve a virtual address range of size V{init} using VMM APIs. At this stage, no physical GPU memory is allocated. 2. Committing Memory (Add Splats): When splats are added, calculate the required physical memory P{req}. Commit physical memory in chunks of granularity G up to P{req}. 3. Expansion (Out of Virtual Capacity): If P{req} exceeds the currently reserved virtual range, reserve a larger virtual address range. Remap the previously allocated physical memory to the new virtual range. This operation does not copy data. 4. Uncommitting Memory (Delete Splats): To remove splats: a. Sort the splat data such that deleted splats are moved to the end of the buffer. b. De-commit (unmap) the physical memory chunks corresponding to the trailing deleted splats. 5. Merging Buffers (Append A to B): To merge source buffer A into target buffer B without creating a new buffer C of size A+B: a. Increase the virtual capacity of buffer B to accommodate A's data. b. Commit the necessary physical memory in B for A's splats. c. Perform a memcpy of splats from A to the newly committed physical memory in B. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. GRANULARITY = 2 1024 1024 # 2 MB on RTX 4090 def reservevirtualrange(size): """Reserve a virtual address range of the given size.""" return {"virtualsize": size, "physicalpages": {}, "totalsplatcount": 0} def commitphysicalmemory(buffer, offset, size): """Commit physical memory for the given virtual offset and size.""" alignedsize = ((size + GRANULARITY - 1) // GRANULARITY) GRANULARITY buffer["physicalpages"][offset] = alignedsize return alignedsize def remapphysicalmemory(oldbuffer, newbuffer, offset, size): """Remap existing physical pages to a new virtual range without copying data.""" for oldoff, physsize in oldbuffer["physicalpages"].items(): newbuffer["physicalpages"][oldoff] = physsize newbuffer["totalsplatcount"] = oldbuffer["totalsplatcount"] return newbuffer def uncommitphysicalmemory(buffer, offset, size): """De-allocate trailing physical memory chunks.""" alignedsize = ((size + GRANULARITY - 1) // GRANULARITY) GRANULARITY if offset in buffer["physicalpages"]: del buffer["physicalpages"][offset] return alignedsize def copymemory(srcbuffer, srcoffset, dstbuffer, dstoffset, size): """Copy data from source to destination buffer.""" # Standard memory copy operation srcdata = srcbuffer["data"][srcoffset:srcoffset + size] dstbuffer["data"][dstoffset:dstoffset + size] = srcdata def sortdeletedtoend(buffer): """Move deleted splats to the end of the buffer.""" # Data-aware sort or indirect indexing validsplats = [s for s in buffer["data"] if not s.deleted] buffer["data"] = validsplats + [s for s in buffer["data"] if s.deleted] def initbuffer(initialvirtualsize): """Initialize a dynamic buffer with reserved virtual memory.""" buf = reservevirtualrange(initialvirtualsize) buf["data"] = bytearray(initialvirtualsize) return buf def addsplats(buffer, splatdata, splatsize): """Add splats to the buffer. Commits physical memory as needed.""" numsplats = len(splatdata) requiredbytes = numsplats splatsize commitphysicalmemory(buffer, 0, requiredbytes) copymemory(splatdata, 0, buffer, 0, requiredbytes) buffer["totalsplatcount"] += numsplats return buffer def mergebuffers(buffersrc, bufferdst, srcsplatcount, dstsplatcount, splatsize): """Merge source buffer into destination buffer without allocating a new buffer.""" srcbytes = srcsplatcount splatsize currentdstbytes = dstsplatcount splatsize # Expand virtual capacity if needed newvirtualsize = bufferdst["virtualsize"] + srcbytes if newvirtualsize > bufferdst["virtualsize"]: newbuffer = reservevirtualrange(newvirtualsize) bufferdst = remapphysicalmemory(bufferdst, newbuffer, 0, bufferdst["virtualsize"]) # Commit physical memory in destination for source data commitphysicalmemory(bufferdst, currentdstbytes, srcbytes) # Copy data from source to destination copymemory(buffersrc, 0, bufferdst, currentdstbytes, srcbytes) bufferdst["totalsplatcount"] += srcsplatcount return bufferdst def deletesplats(buffer, splatsize, numdeleted): """Remove splats by sorting them to the end and uncommitting memory.""" sortdeletedtoend(buffer) bytestofree = numdeleted splatsize alignedfreebytes = ((bytestofree + GRANULARITY - 1) // GRANULARITY) GRANULARITY validbytes = (buffer["totalsplatcount"] - numdeleted) splatsize uncommitphysicalmemory(buffer, validbytes, alignedfreebytes) buffer["totalsplatcount"] -= numdeleted return buffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Granularity Waste: Physical memory is allocated in 2 MB chunks. For small models, this can leave a sizeable amount of memory unused. This is negligible for models with millions to tens of millions of splats. Sorting Overhead: Deleting splats requires sorting them to the end of the buffer before uncommitting memory. Virtual Expansion Cost: Expanding the virtual range requires reserving a larger range and remapping physical memory, which is fast and avoids data copying. Memory Efficiency: Avoids doubling memory usage during merge operations compared to standard allocation methods. Standard merging creates a new buffer C of size A+B, requiring 2(A+B) memory temporarily. This method reuses buffer B. Performance: As fast as regular buffer allocation for standard operations. Limitations: Large physical granularity (2 MB) can waste memory for small datasets. Optimization Potential: An unimplemented optimization could reduce merge memory overhead to just 2 MB by incrementally committing 2 MB chunks, copying, and freeing source memory. This technique is described in the context of "Splatshop," a system for efficiently editing large Gaussian Splat models. It leverages CUDA's Virtual Memory Management (VMM) API. The approach is particularly relevant for applications requiring frequent dynamic updates, such as selection, deletion, and merging of splat models. Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: GS-W Network Architecture
head: Gaussian in the Wild model parameters
body: The GS-W Network Architecture is the component of the Gaussian in the Wild (GS-W) method responsible for predicting per-Gaussian appearance attributes and visibility from a set of reference images. It solves the problem of adapting 3D Gaussian Splatting to unconstrained image collections by replacing static color attributes with learnable features that are dynamically sampled based on camera viewpoint. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a U-Net encoder-decoder structure to extract image features and a fusion network to combine these with intrinsic Gaussian attributes, enabling view-dependent appearance modeling without explicit spherical harmonics. Inputs: A set of K reference images (or their extracted feature maps). For each Gaussian point i: Position Xi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Intrinsic feature s{fi} \in \mathbb{R}^{48}. Dynamic appearance feature d{fi}. Sampling coordinates sc{ki} \in \mathbb{R}^2 for k=1 \dots K. Outputs: Predicted color Ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. Visibility map V (spatial tensor). Data Structures: 1. U-Net Encoder: Uses the first 8 subconvolution modules of a pre-trained ResNet-18. 2. U-Net Decoder 1 (Feature Maps): 4 up-sampling convolution modules. Outputs K+1 feature maps. Each feature map has 16 channels. 3. U-Net Decoder 2 (Visibility): 3 up-sampling convolution modules. Outputs the visibility map. No skip connections from the encoder. 4. Fusion Network (Mf): Two MLP modules. M{f1} has 3 hidden layers with units [128, 96, 64]. M{f2} has 2 hidden layers with units [48, 48]. 5. Color MLP (Mc): 1 hidden layer with 48 units. 6. Sampling Coordinates: K learnable 2D coordinates per Gaussian, initialized via linear transformation of position Xi. Parameters: Positional Encoding: 10 frequencies used for encoding position Xi. Batch Normalization & Activation: Applied in both U-Net decoders. Dropout: 0.1 probability applied to d{fi} during training. Initialization: Xavier initialization for MLP weights. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the reference images through the U-Net encoder (ResNet-18 first 8 modules) to extract image features. 2. Feature Map Generation: Pass encoder features through U-Net Decoder 1 (4 up-sampling convs, batch norm, ReLU, transpose conv, 16 channels) to generate K+1 feature maps. 3. Visibility Prediction: Pass encoder features through U-Net Decoder 2 (3 up-sampling convs, batch norm, ReLU, transpose conv, 16 channels) to generate the visibility map. Skip connections from the encoder to this decoder are omitted to reduce computation. 4. Sampling Coordinate Initialization (Pre-training): For each Gaussian i, initialize K sampling coordinates sc{ki} by applying a linear transformation to its 3D position Xi. 5. Feature Sampling: For each Gaussian i and each of the K feature maps, sample the feature value at the corresponding coordinate sc{ki} from the generated feature maps. This yields K sampled features. 6. Fusion: Concatenate the sampled features, the intrinsic feature s{fi}, the positional encoding of Xi, and the dynamic appearance feature d{fi}. Apply 0.1 dropout to d{fi} during training. Pass this concatenated vector through Fusion Network Mf (MLP 1: [128, 96, 64]; MLP 2: [48, 48]) to produce a fused appearance feature. 7. Color Prediction: Pass the fused appearance feature through Color MLP Mc (1 hidden layer, 48 units) to predict the final color Ci. 8. Training Updates: Update U-Net weights with learning rate decaying from 2 \times 10^{-3} to 2 \times 10^{-5}. Update MLP weights with fixed learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Update Gaussian positions with learning rate decaying from 1.6 \times 10^{-4} to 1.6 \times 10^{-7}. Densify Gaussians between iterations 500 and 15,000 with a gradient threshold of 4 \times 10^{-4}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GSWNetwork: def init(self, K, encoderchannels=256, dfidim=64): self.K = K # U-Net Encoder: Pre-trained ResNet-18 first 8 subconvolution modules self.encoder = self.loadpretrainedresnet18encoder() # U-Net Decoder 1: Generate K+1 feature maps # 4 up-sampling convolution modules, batch norm, ReLU, transpose conv, 16 channels self.decoderfeatures = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(encoderchannels, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16 (K + 1), kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16 (K + 1)), nn.ReLU()) # U-Net Decoder 2: Generate visibility map # 3 up-sampling convolution modules, NO skip connections from encoder self.decodervisibility = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(encoderchannels, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 16, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 1, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1)) # Fusion Network Mf # Input: K sampled features (16K) + sfi (48) + posenc (20) + dfi (dfidim) fusioninputdim = 16 K + 48 + 20 + dfidim self.mf1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(fusioninputdim, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 96), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(96, 64), nn.ReLU()) self.mf2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 48), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(48, 48)) # Color MLP Mc self.mc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(48, 48), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(48, 3)) # Xavier initialization for MLPs self.initweights() # Sampling coordinates initialization self.sclinear = nn.Linear(3, 2 K) def loadpretrainedresnet18encoder(self): # Returns the first 8 subconvolution modules of a pre-trained ResNet-18 # Implementation depends on the specific framework; here we assume it is loaded externally. pass def initweights(self): for m in [self.mf1, self.mf2, self.mc]: for layer in m: if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear): nn.init.xavieruniform(layer.weight) def forward(self, images, gaussians): N = gaussians['positions'].shape[0] # Step 1: Feature Extraction encoderfeatures = self.encoder(images) # Step 2: Feature Map Generation featuremapstensor = self.decoderfeatures(encoderfeatures) # [B, 16(K+1), H', W'] # Step 3: Visibility Prediction visibilitytensor = self.decodervisibility(encoderfeatures) # [B, 1, H'', W''] # Step 4 & 5: Feature Sampling # Reshape featuremapstensor to [B, K+1, 16, H', W'] featuremapsreshaped = featuremapstensor.view(featuremapstensor.shape[0], -1, 16, featuremapstensor.shape[2], featuremapstensor.shape[3]) sampledfeatures = [] # Normalize sampling coordinates to [-1, 1] for gridsample coords = gaussians['sc'] # [N, K, 2] coordsnorm = 2.0 coords - 1.0 # Assuming coords are in [0, 1] coordsnorm = coordsnorm.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # [N, 1, 1, K, 2] for k in range(self.K): fmapk = featuremapsreshaped[:, k,:,:,:] # [B, 16, H', W'] # Expand to match N gaussians fmapkexpanded = fmapk.unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1, -1, -1, -1) if fmapk.shape[0] == 1 else fmapk.unsqueeze(0) # gridsample expects grid [B, Hout, Wout, 2] # We sample at single points, so Hout=1, Wout=1 grid = coordsnorm[:,:,:, k,:] # [N, 1, 1, 2] sampled = F.gridsample(fmapkexpanded, grid, aligncorners=True) # [N, 16, 1, 1] sampledfeatures.append(sampled.squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1)) # [N, 16] sampledfeatures = torch.stack(sampledfeatures, dim=1) # [N, K, 16] # Step 6: Fusion posenc = self.positionalencoding(gaussians['positions'], numfrequencies=10) # [N, 20] dfi = gaussians['dfi'] # [N, dfidim] dfidropped = F.dropout(dfi, p=0.1, training=self.training) fusioninput = torch.cat([sampledfeatures.view(N, -1), gaussians['sfi'], posenc, dfidropped], dim=1) fusedfeature = self.mf1(fusioninput) fusedfeature = self.mf2(fusedfeature) # [N, 48] # Step 7: Color Prediction colors = self.mc(fusedfeature) # [N, 3] # Step 8: Visibility visibilitymap = visibilitytensor # [B, 1, H'', W''] return colors, visibilitymap def positionalencoding(self, positions, numfrequencies): # Standard positional encoding # positions: [N, 3] # Output: [N, 2 numfrequencies] freqbands = torch.cat([positions (10000 (2 (i // 2) / 3)) for i in range(numfrequencies)], dim=1) return torch.cat([torch.sin(freqbands), torch.cos(freqbands)], dim=1) The Wave Parameter Estimation Network (WPEN) estimates the constituent wave parameters (amplitude, angular frequency, and propagation direction) of a dynamic ocean from a time sequence of reconstructed geometric data, specifically surface normals and microfacet roughness. It distinguishes itself from direct regression methods by employing a differentiable ocean model as a physics-based loss function, allowing the network to learn by minimizing the geometric discrepancy between predicted and input ocean states. This approach enables self-supervised training where the network iteratively optimizes wave parameters to match real-world geometry reconstructed by preceding stages. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Stores K+1 feature maps (16 channels each) and the visibility map. Gaussian attributes include s{fi} (48 dims), d{fi}, and sc (K \times 2 dims). Performance: On Brandenburg, Sacre, and Trevi scenes, GS-W achieves PSNR of 24.70, SSIM of 0.8655, and LPIPS of 0.1242, with 50.7 FPS and 122.7 MB size. This outperforms global feature (PSNR 22.43) and K-planes-hybrid (PSNR 22.40) methods. Strengths: Captures local highlights and avoids artifacts from transient objects. Adjusts scene appearance in a manner aligned with human perception by weighting features from reference images. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Unconstrained image collections where view-dependent appearance is important and reference images are available. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The GS-W Network Architecture was introduced in the "Gaussian in the Wild" paper, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to unconstrained image collections. It was developed to handle the challenges of dynamic appearance and transient objects in real-world image sets, which standard 3DGS struggles with due to its static color attributes. The method builds on the Gaussian Data Structure and integrates a neural network to predict appearance features dynamically. Gaussian in the Wild: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unconstrained Image Collections, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73116-720, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Wave Parameter Estimation Network
head: Geometry-based Wave Parameter Fitting, Iterative Wave Parameter Optimization, UNet/MLP Wave Estimator
body: The Wave Parameter Estimation Network estimates the constituent wave parameters (amplitude, angular frequency, and propagation direction) of a dynamic ocean from a time sequence of reconstructed geometric data, specifically surface normals and microfacet roughness. It distinguishes itself from direct inverse methods by leveraging a differentiable ocean model as a self-supervised loss function, allowing gradients to flow from geometric consistency back to the network parameters. This approach enables iterative optimization where the network matches randomly initialized waves to real geometry. Inputs and Outputs Input: A time sequence of reconstructed ocean geometry, consisting of surface normal maps (Nt) and roughness maps (Rt) for each time step t. Output: A set of 60 constituent wave parameters. Each wave i is defined by three parameters: amplitude hi, angular frequency \omegai, and propagation direction \thetai. Data Structures The network architecture consists of two main components: 1. Feature Extractor: A U-Net [41] that processes the input sequence of normal and roughness maps to extract spatial features. 2. Parameter Decoder: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that maps the extracted features to the final wave parameter vector. Training Procedure The network is trained using a differentiable ocean model implemented in the Taichi framework. The training process involves the following steps: 1. Forward Pass: The U-Net extracts features from the input geometry sequence (Nt, Rt). The MLP decodes these features into a batch of wave parameters \{hi, \omegai, \thetai\}{i=1}^{60}. 2. Differentiable Simulation: The differentiable ocean model uses the predicted wave parameters to generate a synthetic sequence of ocean geometry (\hat{N}t, \hat{R}t). 3. Loss Calculation: The synthetic geometry is compared against the input geometry using a combined loss function L{Geom}. Normal Loss (L{cos}): Measures the cosine similarity between the predicted normal \hat{N}t and the input normal Nt: L{cos} = E{Nt, \hat{N}t} [(1 - \cos(Nt, \hat{N}t))] Roughness Loss (L2): Measures the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the predicted roughness \hat{R}t and the input roughness Rt: L2 = E{Rt, \hat{R}t} [\|Rt - \hat{R}t\|2^2] Total Loss (L{Geom}): A weighted combination of the two losses: L{Geom} = \alpha L2 + \beta L{cos} where \alpha and \beta are hyperparameters balancing the importance of roughness and normal consistency. 4. Optimization: The network weights are updated via backpropagation through the differentiable ocean model to minimize L{Geom}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainwaveparameternetwork(inputgeometrysequence, differentiableoceanmodel, epochs=100, alpha=1.0, beta=1.0): """ Trains the WPEN to estimate wave parameters from geometry sequences. Args: inputgeometrysequence: List of tuples (Nt, Rt) for each time step t. differentiableoceanmodel: Differentiable renderer/simulator. epochs: Number of training epochs. alpha: Weight for roughness loss. beta: Weight for normal loss. """ # Initialize network: U-Net for feature extraction, MLP for parameter decoding class WaveParameterEstimationNetwork: def init(self): self.unet = lambda x: x # U-Net forward pass self.mlp = lambda x: x # MLP forward pass def forward(self, Nt, Rt): features = self.unet((Nt, Rt)) return self.mlp(features) network = WaveParameterEstimationNetwork() class Optimizer: def init(self, params): self.params = params def step(self): pass # Update parameters using gradient descent def zerograd(self): pass # Clear gradients optimizer = Optimizer(network.parameters()) for epoch in range(epochs): totalloss = 0.0 for t in range(len(inputgeometrysequence)): Nt, Rt = inputgeometrysequence[t] # 1. Extract features and predict wave parameters waveparams = network.forward(Nt, Rt) # 2. Generate synthetic geometry using differentiable ocean model Nhatt, Rhatt = differentiableoceanmodel.simulate(waveparams) # 3. Backpropagate and update Lgeom.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() totalloss += Lgeom print(f"Epoch {epoch}: Loss = {totalloss / len(inputgeometrysequence)}") return network Edge Cases and Pitfalls Fuzzy Predictions: Raw network predictions may be inaccurate in small areas or lack physical consistency. name: Differentiable Ocean Inverse Modeling
head: Dynamic ocean inverse modeling, Ocean surface reconstruction via differentable rendering
body: Differentiable Ocean Inverse Modeling is a two-step framework that reconstructs dynamic ocean models from monocular video sequences by first estimating hierarchical surface geometry and then deriving constituent wave parameters. It distinguishes itself from direct inverse methods by leveraging a differentiable ocean renderer and a differentiable ocean model as self-supervised loss functions, allowing gradients to flow from image consistency and physical plausibility back to the neural network parameters. The method operates in two distinct phases: hierarchical geometry reconstruction from images, followed by wave parameter estimation from the resulting geometry sequence. Input: A sequence of monocular images \{It\}{n}, where t denotes the time step and n is the number of frames. Intermediate Output: A sequence of hierarchical ocean geometry \{Gt\}{n}, where each Gt comprises the macrosurface normal Nt and the microfacet roughness Rt. Final Output: A set of constituent wave parameters for each time step, specifically amplitude hi, angular frequency \omegai, and wave direction \thetai for N sampled wave trains. The method processes dense tensor fields and discrete parameter sets. 1. Geometry Maps: Dense fields for normal Nt (3-channel vector per pixel) and roughness Rt (scalar per pixel). 2. Wave Parameters: A discrete set of N tuples \{hi, \omegai, \thetai\} representing the superposed wave trains. 1. Input Processing: For each image It in the sequence, pass it through two separate encoder-decoder neural networks (sub-net1 and sub-net2). 2. Geometry Extraction: Sub-net1 outputs the macrosurface normal map Nt, and sub-net2 outputs the microfacet roughness map Rt. 3. Sequence Assembly: Combine the outputs to form the hierarchical geometry Gt = \{Nt, Rt\} for all t, yielding the sequence \{Gt\}{n}. 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the sequence of geometry maps \{Gt\}{n} through a UNet architecture to extract spatiotemporal features. 2. Parameter Regression: Feed the extracted features into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) network. 3. Output Generation: The MLP outputs the parameters for N wave trains: amplitude hi, angular frequency \omegai, and direction \thetai. To enable self-supervised training, the method uses a differentiable ocean model to synthesize geometry from the estimated wave parameters. 1. Wave Vector Definition: For each wave i, define the wave vector \mathbf{k}i and wave number ki: \mathbf{k}i = [ki \cos \thetai, ki \sin \thetai] ki = \frac{\omegai^2}{g} where g is the acceleration due to gravity. The parameters are simplified from \{h, \omega, k, \theta\} to \{h, \omega, \theta\}. 2. Nyquist Filtering and Weighting: Apply a Nyquist filter to determine the contribution of each wave to the hierarchical geometry based on wavelength relative to pixel size: Displacement (Long Waves): Waves with wavelength > \text{pixel size} affect macrosurface displacement. Normal (Medium/Long Waves): Waves affecting the macrosurface normal. Roughness (Short/Sub-pixel Waves): Waves with wavelength < \text{pixel size} do not affect height but affect microfacet roughness. 3. Superposition and Geometry Synthesis: Superpose the N filtered wave trains to generate the synthetic geometry sequence \{\hat{G}t\}{n}. The ocean surface is modeled using a triangle mesh deformed by large waves at the grid level, medium-length waves added to the normal at the pixel level, and roughness estimated by measuring the slope variance of small waves at the microfacet level. 1. Rasterization: Render the synthesized geometry \hat{G}t into an image \hat{I}t using the SoftRas method, which provides continuous and differentiable rasterization. 2. Lighting Computation: Compute reflected light from the Sun and sky dome, as well as refracted light from water. 3. Displacement Application: Use the computed displacements to alter geometry, normals, and roughness during the rendering process under given lighting conditions. The networks are trained self-supervised using the following loss functions: 1. Image Consistency Loss: L{\text{Image}} = \mathbb{E}{It, \hat{I}t} [\|It - \hat{I}t\|^2] where It is the input image and \hat{I}t is the re-rendered image. 2. Discriminator Losses: To enforce spatial distribution similarity and temporal coherence, use spatial discriminators Dn (for normal) and Dr (for roughness), and temporal discriminators D{tn} and D{tr}. L{Dn}: Loss from spatial discriminator on normal maps. L{Dr}: Loss from spatial discriminator on roughness maps. L{D{tn}}: Loss from temporal discriminator on normal sequences. L{D{tr}}: Loss from temporal discriminator on roughness sequences. 3. Total Loss: L{\text{Total}} = \alpha L{\text{Image}} + \beta1 L{Dn} + \beta2 L{Dr} + \gamma1 L{D{tn}} + \gamma2 L{D{tr}} where \alpha, \beta1, \beta2, \gamma1, \gamma2 are weighting hyperparameters. 4. Geometry Consistency Loss: The framework measures the consistency between the generated geometry \hat{G}t (from wave estimation) and the input geometry Gt (from image reconstruction) to optimize the wave estimation network, but the exact formula is not explicitly defined in the sources. nn.ReLU()) self.decoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(128, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, channels, 3, padding=1)) def forward(self, x): return self.decoder(self.encoder(x)) class waveparams[:, 1] theta = waveparams[:, 2] g = 9.81 k = (omega 2) / g kx = k torch.cos(theta) ky = k torch.sin(theta) wl = wavelengthfromk(k) wdisp = applynyquistfilterdisplacement(wl) wnorm = Nhat, Rhat def renderimage(self, geometry, extrinsics, lighting): N, R = geometry Ihat = softrasrasterize(N, R, extrinsics, lighting) return Ihat def computeloss(self, It, Ihatt, Nt, Nhatt, Rt, Rhatt, name: VastGaussian
body: VastGaussian is a large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting method that partitions a scene into spatially-disjoint regions to enable scalable training and rendering of massive environments. It solves the memory and computational bottlenecks of global optimization by training independent models per region and merging them at render time using feathered overlap. It distinguishes itself from naive spatial splitting by incorporating decoupled appearance handling for varying lighting conditions and an iterative viewpoint addition strategy based on visibility criteria. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of images with known camera poses covering a large-scale scene. Output: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives partitioned into spatially-disjoint regions, each with associated parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, and appearance embeddings). Data Structures: The scene is divided into N spatially-disjoint regions (blocks). Each region i contains a subset of Gaussians \mathcal{G}i. Region Partitioning: Regions are defined based on the distribution of training cameras projected onto the ground plane. Gaussian Parameters: Standard 3DGS parameters: mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}, and an additional optimizable appearance embedding ev for each view v. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the scene into spatially-disjoint regions based on camera distribution projected onto the ground. 2. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians for each region independently. 3. Iterative Training: Start with a subset of viewpoints. Train the Gaussians in each region using the current subset of viewpoints. Iteratively add more viewpoints into the training set based on visibility criteria to ensure sufficient supervision. 4. Appearance Modeling: For each view v, optimize an appearance embedding ev to model appearance changes due to varying lighting conditions. 5. Merging: At render time, merge the Gaussians from all regions. Use feathered overlap at region boundaries to handle discontinuities. Formulas: Appearance Embedding: The color C for a view v is modulated by the appearance embedding ev. The exact modulation function is not specified in the sources. Feathered Overlap: The blending at boundaries is not explicitly defined, but described as "feathered". Parameters: Number of regions: Not given in the sources. Viewpoint addition criteria: Based on visibility, but specific thresholds are not given. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Discontinuities: Handled by feathered overlap. Under-supervision: Addressed by visibility-aware viewpoint addition. Progressive Partitioning is a data distribution strategy for training 3D Gaussian Splatting on large-scale scenes by dividing the environment into spatially-disjoint cells, each containing a subset of training cameras and 3D Gaussians. It solves the memory and time bottlenecks of global optimization by enabling parallel, lower-memory training per cell. It distinguishes itself from naive spatial splitting by using an airspace-aware visibility criterion to ensure sufficient supervision of the volume above the surface, preventing floaters and under-supervision. Large Scene Reconstruction via Chunking addresses the physical memory limits and scalability challenges inherent in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when applied to massive environments. By partitioning the scene into spatially disjoint or distributed regions, it enables the reconstruction of datasets that would otherwise exceed GPU memory capacities. The method splits scenes into chunks based on camera distribution and SfM reconstruction, uniform grids, or dynamic hierarchies, and handles boundaries via skyboxes or pruning. It supports distributed training across multiple GPUs with dynamic load balancing. Page Assignment and Merging is a spatial partitioning strategy used in VastGaussian to organize millions of 3D Gaussians into fixed-size memory pages for efficient virtual memory management and rendering. It solves the problem of mapping unstructured Gaussian clusters to a structured, mesh-aligned page hierarchy, ensuring that Gaussians are grouped by spatial locality while respecting hardware page size constraints. Unlike standard grid-based voxelization, this method derives its topology from a proxy triangular mesh, allowing it to handle surface-aligned geometry with varying lighting and appearance. It distinguishes itself by combining mesh-based subdivision with greedy merging and explicit page linking to handle overlapping ellipsoids that cross page boundaries. Similarity Guided Partition is a graph-based clustering algorithm that groups 3D Gaussians into spatially-disjoint blocks of bounded size based on spatial proximity and appearance similarity [1, unofficial]. It solves the problem of inefficient joint pruning by ensuring that potentially redundant Gaussians are evaluated together within the same optimization block [1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from naive spatial partitioning by incorporating a scale-aware affinity metric that accounts for both geometric overlap and appearance consistency [1, unofficial]. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of regions and Gaussians per region, reducing peak memory usage compared to global optimization. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Scalable to large scenes; handles varying lighting via appearance embeddings; reduces memory bottlenecks. Limitations: Requires careful handling of region boundaries; iterative viewpoint addition may increase training time. When to Use: Large-scale urban or outdoor scenes with varying lighting conditions. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes where global optimization is feasible. VastGaussian was introduced in CVPR'24. It addresses the scalability challenges of 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale environments by partitioning the scene into spatially-disjoint regions. name: Progressive Partitioning for Large-Scale 3DGS
head: Progressive Data Partitioning, Progressive Partitioning
body: Progressive Partitioning is a data distribution strategy for training 3D Gaussian Splatting on large-scale scenes by dividing the environment into spatially-disjoint cells, each containing a subset of training cameras and 3D Gaussians. It solves the memory and time bottlenecks of global optimization by enabling parallel, lower-memory training per cell. It distinguishes itself from naive spatial splitting by using an airspace-aware visibility criterion to ensure sufficient supervision of the volume above the surface, preventing floaters and under-supervision. Inputs: Point cloud P (initially empty or sparse). Set of training views V. Scene dimensions defining the ground plane. Grid dimensions m \times n (number of cells along two axes). Visibility threshold Th (typically 25%). Boundary expansion ratio \alpha (typically 0.2 or 20%). Outputs: A set of m \times n cells. For each cell j: a subset of cameras Vj and a subset of points Pj. Data Structures: Cell j: Defined by a rectangular region on the ground plane with height hj and width wj. Point Cloud Pj: List of 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) associated with cell j. Camera Set Vj: List of camera poses and intrinsics assigned to cell j. Parameters: Th: Visibility threshold. Typical value: 25%. \alpha: Boundary expansion factor. Typical value: 0.2. m, n: Grid dimensions. Example: m=4, n=2 for 8 cells. Steps: 1. Camera-Position-Based Region Division Partition the ground plane into a grid of m \times n cells. Divide the ground plane into m sections along one axis, such that each section contains approximately |V|/m views based on camera positions. Subdivide each section into n segments along the other axis, such that each segment contains approximately |V|/(m \times n) views. Let the j-th cell be bounded by a rectangle of size hj \times wj. 2. Position-Based Data Selection (Boundary Expansion) Expand the boundaries of each cell to include context from neighboring areas. Calculate expanded dimensions: h'j = hj + \alpha hj w'j = wj + \alpha wj Assign training views V to Vj if the camera position falls within the expanded boundaries of cell j. Assign points P to Pj if the point position falls within the expanded boundaries of cell j. 3. Visibility-Based Camera Selection Refine the camera set Vj for each cell to ensure adequate supervision of the airspace. For each camera Ci not yet selected for cell j: Calculate the projected area of the cell's volume in the image plane of Ci. Airspace-Aware Calculation: Construct an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for the points currently in Pj (or the cell's spatial extent). Project this AABB onto the image plane to get area \Omega{ij}. Calculate visibility: \text{Visibility} = \frac{\Omega{ij}}{\Omegai} where \Omegai is the total pixel area of image Ii. If \text{Visibility} > Th, add Ci to Vj. Pitfall Avoidance: Do not use only the convex hull of surface points (\Omega{\text{surf}, ij}) for \Omega{ij}, as this is airspace-agnostic and leads to under-supervision of the volume above the surface and floaters. Use the AABB of the cell's point cloud extent to capture the full volume. 4. Coverage-Based Point Selection Initialize Pj with points that are well-constrained by the selected cameras. Identify points in the global point cloud P that are covered by all views in Vj. Add these points to Pj. This provides better initialization for optimization, reducing depth ambiguity and preventing the creation of floaters for objects outside the cell. 5. Optimization and Cleanup Optimize the 3D Gaussians in Pj using only cameras in Vj. After optimization, remove any 3D Gaussians generated outside the cell's boundaries to prevent artifacts (floaters) in adjacent cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. min(ys), 'w': max(xs) - min(xs) }) celldata = [] for j, cell in enumerate(cells): h, w = cell['h'], cell['w'] hexp, wexp = h (1 + expansion), w (1 + expansion) xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = cell['bounds'] # Center expansion around original bounds dx = (wexp - w) / 2 dy = (hexp - h) / 2 xmine, ymine = xmin - dx, ymin - dy xmaxe, ymaxe = xmax + dx, ymax + dy Vj = [v for v in views if xmine <= v['position'][0] <= xmaxe and ymine <= v['position'][1] <= ymaxe] Pj = [p for p in pointcloud if xmine <= p[0] <= xmaxe and ymine <= p[1] <= ymaxe] celldata.append({'V': Vj, 'P': Pj, 'bounds': cell['bounds'], 'h': h, 'w': w}) # Step 3: Visibility-Based Camera Selection for data in celldata: Vj = data['V'] Pj = data['P'] xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = data['bounds'] remaining = [v for v in views if v not in Vj] for v in remaining: # Compute AABB of Pj or fallback to cell bounds if Pj: xs = [p[0] for p in Pj] ys = [p[1] for p in Pj] zs = [p[2] for p in Pj] aabb = (min(xs), min(ys), min(zs), max(xs), max(ys), max(zs)) else: # Fallback to cell bounds extended vertically aabb = (xmin, ymin, 0, xmax, ymax, 10) # Project AABB corners to image plane corners = [] for dx in [0, 1]: for dy in [0, 1]: for dz in [0, 1]: p = (aabb[0] + dx(aabb[3]-aabb[0]), aabb[1] + dy(aabb[4]-aabb[1]), aabb[2] + dz(aabb[5]-aabb[2])) corners.append(project3dto2d(p, v)) # Compute bounding box area in pixels if corners: us = [c[0] for c in corners] vs = [c[1] for c in corners] projarea = max(0, max(us) - min(us)) max(0, max(vs) - min(vs)) else: projarea = 0 imagearea = v['imagewidth'] v['imageheight'] visibility = projarea / imagearea if imagearea > 0 else 0 if visibility > threshold: Vj.append(v) data['V'] = Vj # Step 4: Coverage-Based Point Selection for data in celldata: Vj = data['V'] Pj = data['P'] newpoints = [] for p in pointcloud: if all(isvisibleinview(p, v) for v in Vj): newpoints.append(p) data['P'].extend(newpoints) return celldata def project3dto2d(point, view): # Standard perspective projection pcam = [ view['worldtocam'][0][0]point[0] + view['worldtocam'][0][1]point[1] + view['worldtocam'][0][2]point[2] + view['worldtocam'][0][3], view['worldtocam'][1][0]point[0] + view['worldtocam'][1][1]point[1] + view['worldtocam'][1][2]point[2] + view['worldtocam'][1][3], view['worldtocam'][2][0]point[0] + view['worldtocam'][2][1]point[1] + view['worldtocam'][2][2]point[2] + view['worldtocam'][2][3] ] if pcam[2] <= 0: return (0, 0) # Behind camera u = view['intrinsics'][0][0] (pcam[0] / pcam[2]) + view['intrinsics'][0][2] v = view['intrinsics'][1][0] (pcam[1] / pcam[2]) + view['intrinsics'][1][2] return (u, v) def isvisibleinview(point, view): u, v = project3dto2d(point, view) return 0 <= u < view['imagewidth'] and 0 <= v < view['imageheight'] Time Complexity: Training time is reduced because each cell is optimized independently and in parallel, requiring less training time than global optimization. Memory Complexity: Memory usage per cell is lower, as each cell only stores a subset of Gaussians and cameras. This allows training on hardware with limited VRAM. Performance: In experiments with 8 cells, visibility threshold of 25%, and 60,000 iterations per cell, the method achieved high-fidelity reconstruction on large-scale scenes. Strengths: Enables large-scale reconstruction on consumer hardware; reduces floaters and airspace artifacts through airspace-aware visibility; provides better initialization via coverage-based point selection. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of grid dimensions (m, n) and visibility threshold (Th); may introduce seams at cell boundaries if not handled by merging techniques (like those in VastGaussian). Progressive Partitioning was introduced by Lin et al. in the VastGaussian paper (CVPR 2024) as a strategy to adapt 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale scenes. It addresses the limitations of global optimization, such as high memory consumption and long training times, by partitioning the scene into manageable cells. The method builds on the idea of distributed learning and feature encoding for large scenes. name: Large Scene Reconstruction via Chunking
head: Chunk-based Reconstruction, Scene Partitioning
body: Large Scene Reconstruction via Chunking addresses the physical memory limits and scalability challenges inherent in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when applied to massive environments. By partitioning the scene into spatially disjoint or distributed regions, it enables the reconstruction of datasets that would otherwise exceed GPU memory capacities. The method splits scenes into chunks based on camera distribution and SfM reconstruction, uniform grids, or dynamic hierarchies, and handles boundaries via skyboxes or pruning. It supports distributed training across multiple GPUs with dynamic load balancing. Inputs: Input images with known or estimated poses (SfM data) and camera intrinsics. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the scene, organized by chunk or distributed across devices. The core data structure is the Chunk, representing a spatial region of the scene. Each chunk stores a subset of 3D Gaussians with attributes: position (\mathbf{x}), covariance (\mathbf{\Sigma}), opacity (\alpha), spherical harmonics coefficients (\mathbf{c}), and scale (\mathbf{s}). Gaussians are assigned to chunks based on spatial location or camera positions. 1. Scene Partitioning: Divide the scene into chunks. Strategies include splitting based on camera distribution and SfM reconstruction, using a uniform spatial grid, or creating a dynamic hierarchy ranging from 1 to 8 levels depending on scene size. 2. Background Handling: Define a low-resolution skybox on a sphere surrounding each chunk to treat the surrounding scene as background. For uniform grids, prune chunks with low rendering contribution to reduce memory usage. 3. Training: Train each chunk independently on a single GPU, or distribute Gaussians across multiple GPUs. Assign pixels to GPUs in tiles and transfer Gaussians between them as needed. Apply dynamic load balancing to scale training efficiently. 4. Merging: If using disjoint chunks, merge the resulting Gaussian sets into a final scene representation. If using a hierarchy, manage levels to maintain memory constraints. Maximum GPU Count: Distributed training can scale to up to 32 GPUs. Hierarchy Levels: Ranges from 1 for small scenes to 8 for large scenes like CityWalk. Out-of-Memory (OOM): Processing large scenes without a hierarchy causes OOM errors on standard 24GB GPUs after processing a fraction of frames (e.g., 795 out of 4050 frames for CityWalk) with Gaussian counts exceeding 6.7 million. Boundary Artifacts: Improper boundary handling can cause artifacts, mitigated by the skybox method. Pose Estimation: Pure rotations prevent triangulation, a limitation shared with COLMAP and ORB-SLAM. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructlargescene(inputimages, sfmdata, maxgpus=32, usehierarchy=False): # Step 1: Partition Scene if usehierarchy: chunks = [] for level in range(1, 9): chunks.extend(splitsceneintolevels(sfmdata, level)) else: chunks = splitbycameradistribution(sfmdata) # Step 2: Initialize Background & Pruning for chunk in chunks: chunk.skybox = createsphereskybox(chunk.bounds, resolution=64) if not usehierarchy: chunk.contribution = estimaterenderingcontribution(chunk.gaussians, inputimages) # Step 3: Training if maxgpus > 1: gpuworkers = [Worker(device=i) for i in range(maxgpus)] for chunk in chunks: tileassignments = assignpixelstogpus(chunk, gpuworkers) gaussianshards = distributegaussians(chunk.gaussians, gpuworkers) for worker in gpuworkers: worker.train(chunk, gaussianshards[worker.id], tileassignments[worker.id]) else: for chunk in chunks: if chunk.contribution < 0.1: continue trainchunksingle(chunk, chunk.skybox) # Step 4: Merge Results finalgaussians = [] for chunk in chunks: finalgaussians.extend(chunk.gaussians) return finalgaussians def splitbycameradistribution(sfmdata): return [Chunk(cameras) for cameras in groupcamerasbyregion(sfmdata.cameras)] def splitsceneintolevels(sfmdata, level): bounds = sfmdata.scenebounds cells = 2 level return [Chunk(bounds, cells) for in range(cells 3)] def createsphereskybox(bounds, resolution=64): return SphereTexture(bounds.center, bounds.radius, resolution) def estimaterenderingcontribution(gaussians, images): return sum(g.coverage(img) for g in gaussians) / len(images) def assignpixelstogpus(chunk, workers): tiles = chunk.pixelgrid.splitintotiles(len(workers)) return [tiles[i % len(workers)] for i in range(len(workers))] def distributegaussians(gaussians, workers): shards = [[] for in range(len(workers))] for g in gaussians: shards[g.workerid % len(workers)].append(g) return shards def trainchunksingle(chunk, skybox): optimizegaussians(chunk.gaussians, chunk.images, skybox) A variant that applies a lightweight progressive hierarchy to dynamically create levels throughout reconstruction. It ranges from 1 level for small scenes to 8 levels for large scenes like CityWalk. This method maintains peak trained Gaussians below 3.7 million and allocated memory below 12.8 GB, preventing OOM errors that occur without hierarchy (e.g., 6.7 million Gaussians causing OOM on 24GB GPU). It trades a small quality gap versus offline approaches for orders-of-magnitude faster processing and enables scalability to large scenes. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of chunks and the hierarchy depth. Without chunking or hierarchy, memory usage grows linearly with scene size, leading to OOM on standard GPUs (e.g., 24GB) for large scenes. With chunking, memory is bounded by the chunk size and hierarchy limits (e.g., <12.8 GB with hierarchy). Time Complexity: Distributed training across multiple GPUs (up to 32) improves training speed. Dynamic load balancing further optimizes this. Hierarchical approaches offer orders-of-magnitude faster processing compared to offline methods. Strengths: Enables reconstruction of massive scenes that exceed single-GPU memory. Supports distributed training. Limitations: Potential quality gap compared to monolithic offline approaches. Boundary artifacts if skybox or pruning is not handled well. Pose estimation limitations for pure rotations. When to Use: Large-scale scenes where memory is a constraint. When distributed hardware is available. When processing speed is prioritized over absolute offline optimality. When Not to Use: Small scenes where monolithic reconstruction is sufficient and faster. Scenes with pure rotations where pose estimation fails. The challenge of scaling 3D Gaussian Splatting to large scenes was highlighted by Kerbl et al. [18], who noted the lack of huge datasets and the memory limitations of the original method. Lin et al. [19] proposed partitioning scenes based on camera distribution and SfM reconstruction. Liu et al. [20] introduced uniform chunking with pruning. Kerbl et al. [18] also introduced the skybox approach for background handling. Zhao et al. [21] explored multi-GPU distribution with dynamic load balancing. More recently, Meulemann et al. [22] introduced on-the-fly processing for unposed data. The Progressive Hierarchical Memory Management approach was introduced to address OOM issues in immediate reconstruction of unordered input.
