name: Page Assignment and Merging
head: Gaussian Page Grouping, Mesh-to-Page Mapping
body: Page Assignment and Merging is a spatial partitioning strategy used in VastGaussian to organize millions of 3D Gaussians into fixed-size memory pages for efficient virtual memory management and rendering. It solves the problem of mapping unstructured Gaussian clusters to a structured, mesh-aligned page hierarchy, ensuring that Gaussians are grouped by spatial locality while respecting hardware page size constraints. Unlike standard grid-based voxelization, this method derives its topology from a proxy triangular mesh, allowing it to handle surface-aligned geometry with varying lighting and appearance. It distinguishes itself by combining mesh-based subdivision with greedy merging and explicit page linking to handle overlapping ellipsoids that cross page boundaries. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by mean position \mathbf{p}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{S}, and other properties (color, opacity). A proxy triangular mesh representing the scene geometry, consisting of faces F. A target page size K (maximum number of Gaussians per page). Outputs: A mapping of each Gaussian to a specific page ID. A mapping of each mesh face to a page ID (or null if unassigned). A set of page links indicating spatial overlap between pages. Page: A contiguous block of memory holding up to K Gaussian entries. Fields: Array of K Gaussian structs. Padding: If a page contains fewer than K Gaussians, remaining slots are filled with "zero-property" Gaussians (e.g., zero opacity) to maintain fixed-size alignment. Face Page ID: An integer identifier stored in the mesh face data structure, indicating which page contains the majority of Gaussians associated with that face. Page Link: A bidirectional or unidirectional reference between two page IDs, indicating that Gaussians in one page may occlude or be occluded by Gaussians in the other. 1. Initialization: Create one initial page for each face in the proxy mesh. Assign each Gaussian to the page corresponding to the mesh face whose centroid is nearest to the Gaussian's mean position \mathbf{p}. 2. Subdivision Check: For each page, count the number of assigned Gaussians ni. 3. Subdivision Loop: If ni > K: Select an edge of the triangle associated with the page. Subdivide the triangle by adding a vertex at the midpoint of the selected edge, creating two new triangles. Reassign Gaussians to the new pages based on proximity to the new triangle centroids. Repeat subdivision until ni \le K for all resulting pages. Mitigation: To prevent the creation of thin triangles and T-junctions due to floating-point inaccuracies, the algorithm rotates the vertex order and selects different edges for subsequent subdivisions on adjacent triangles. 1. Neighbor Identification: Identify neighboring pages based on the adjacency of their underlying mesh faces. 2. Merge Process: Iterate through pages. If a page's Gaussian count is below K, attempt to merge it with a neighboring page. Greedy Strategy: Use a breadth-first search to find the best neighbor. Prioritize merging with faces that are geometrically adjacent. Fallback: If no adjacent neighbors remain and the page is still underfilled, select a nearby page (spatially close but not necessarily face-adjacent). Overflow Handling: If merging a neighbor would cause the combined count to exceed K, do not merge directly. Instead, use the current page as a basis for a new merged page, and add the neighbor to this new structure if it fits, or leave it separate. 3. Final Assignment: Gaussians are grouped in memory according to their final page IDs. Unmarked faces (those with no Gaussian mean match) are excluded from rendering. Since 3D Gaussian ellipsoids are volumetric and may extend into neighboring pages, simple spatial partitioning can lead to incorrect visibility culling (marking a page as invisible when it contains visible parts of an ellipsoid). 1. Sampling: Generate M random points uniformly distributed in a unit sphere using spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi), then convert to Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z): \begin{aligned} x &= \sin(\theta) \cos(\phi) \\ y &= \sin(\theta) \sin(\phi) \\ z &= \cos(\theta) \end{aligned} Note: The distribution is non-uniform within the resulting ellipsoid due to the initial uniform sphere sampling. 2. Transformation: Apply the Gaussian's scale \mathbf{S}, rotation \mathbf{R}, and translation \mathbf{p} transforms to each sample point to place them within the Gaussian's ellipsoid volume. 3. Face Proximity Test: For each transformed sample point, find the nearest face on the proxy mesh. 4. Link Establishment: Let P{gauss} be the page ID assigned to the Gaussian. Let P{face} be the page ID of the nearest mesh face for the sample point. If P{gauss} \neq P{face}, establish a link between page P{gauss} and page P{face}. 5. Face Assignment Rule: If a mesh face is not yet assigned to a page, mark it with the page ID that has the highest number of sample points close to it. 6. Overlap Precedence: If multiple pages overlap a single face, the page with the most overlap takes precedence for the face assignment, while other overlapping pages are linked. 7. Rendering Implication: When a page is determined to be visible, all linked pages must also be loaded into GPU memory to ensure correct rendering of overlapping ellipsoids. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def assignpages(gaussians, meshfaces, pagesize): # 1. Initial Assignment pages = {face.id: [] for face in meshfaces} for g in gaussians: nearestface = min(meshfaces, key=lambda f: math.dist(f.centroid, g.mean)) pages[nearestface.id].append(g) # 2. Subdivision for faceid, glist in pages.items(): while len(glist) > pagesize: # Select an edge, split triangle at midpoint, create two new faces newface1, newface2 = splittriangleatmidpoint(faceid, meshfaces) # Reassign gaussians in this region to new faces by distance for i in range(len(glist) - 1, -1, -1): g = glist[i] nearest = min([newface1, newface2], key=lambda f: math.dist(f.centroid, g.mean)) pages[nearest.id].append(g) glist.pop(i) #: Standard triangle splitting logic; re-running nearest-face lookup for affected gaussians. # 3. Merging mergedpages = {} activepages = list(pages.keys()) while activepages: currentid = activepages.pop(0) currentgs = pages[currentid] if len(currentgs) <= pagesize: neighbors = [f.id for f in meshfaces if sharesedge(meshfaces[currentid], f)] merged = False for nid in neighbors: if len(currentgs) + len(pages[nid]) <= pagesize: currentgs.extend(pages[nid]) del pages[nid] merged = True break if not merged and len(currentgs) < pagesize: nearbyid = min(pages.keys(), key=lambda pid: math.dist(meshfaces[currentid].centroid, meshfaces[pid].centroid)) if nearbyid and len(currentgs) + len(pages[nearbyid]) <= pagesize: currentgs.extend(pages[nearbyid]) del pages[nearbyid] mergedpages[currentid] = currentgs else: # Overflow handling: create new merged page basis overflow = currentgs[pagesize:] currentgs = currentgs[:pagesize] mergedpages[currentid] = currentgs activepages.append(currentid) #: Logic assumes subdivision ensures <= pagesize. return mergedpages def establishpagelinks(gaussians, meshfaces, pagemap, numsamples=100): links = set() for g in gaussians: points = [] for in range(numsamples): theta = random.uniform(0, math.pi) phi = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) x = math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) y = math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) z = math.cos(theta) points.append((x, y, z)) transformedpoints = [] for p in points: plocal = (p[0]g.scale.x, p[1]g.scale.y, p[2]g.scale.z) protated = g.rotation plocal #: Matrix-vector multiplication pfinal = (protated[0]+g.mean.x, protated[1]+g.mean.y, protated[2]+g.mean.z) transformedpoints.append(pfinal) pagecounts = {} for p in transformedpoints: nearestface = min(meshfaces, key=lambda f: math.dist(f.centroid, p)) facepageid = pagemap.get(nearestface.id) if facepageid is not None: pagecounts[facepageid] = pagecounts.get(facepageid, 0) + 1 gausspageid = pagemap.get(g.id) if gausspageid is None: continue if pagecounts: bestpage = max(pagecounts, key=pagecounts.get) #: Updates mesh face mapping if unassigned for facepageid, count in pagecounts.items(): if facepageid != gausspageid: links.add((min(gausspageid, facepageid), max(gausspageid, facepageid))) return links def splittriangleatmidpoint(faceid, meshfaces): #: Standard geometric split; returns two new face objects return None, None def sharesedge(facea, faceb): #: Returns True if faces share a vertex pair return False Page Size (K): Determines memory granularity. Not given in the sources. Subdivision Limit: Repeated subdivision can create thin triangles and T-junctions due to floating-point inaccuracies if shared edges create vertices on adjacent triangles. The method mitigates this by rotating vertex order and choosing different edges, though it is not optimal. Unassigned Faces: Faces with no Gaussian mean match are marked as unassigned and excluded from rendering. Zero-Property Padding: Pages are padded with zero-property Gaussians to reach size K. These are easily culled during rendering. Page Linking is a technique to handle overlapping 3D Gaussians that extend into surrounding pages, preventing incorrect invisibility marking by establishing uni- or bi-directional links between pages. It is applied after initial mesh-based assignment to handle overlapping 3D Gaussians that extend into surrounding pages, preventing incorrect invisibility marking. The method uses random sampling within the Gaussian's ellipsoid to identify intersecting pages, achieving O(n) time complexity by testing only the closest face on the proxy mesh for each sample, avoiding the O(n^2) complexity of naive ellipsoid-ellipsoid intersection tests. Time Complexity: Initial Assignment: O(N \cdot F) or O(N \log F) depending on nearest-face search implementation, where N is Gaussians and F is faces. Subdivision: Depends on the number of subdivisions required to fit Gaussians into pages. Merging: Greedy breadth-first approach, generally efficient but depends on mesh connectivity. Page Linking: O(n) where n is the number of Gaussians (or samples processed), as it tests only the closest face on the proxy mesh per sample. Memory Complexity: Storage is proportional to the number of Gaussians plus the overhead of page structures and links. Pages are padded to fixed size K, leading to some memory waste if Gaussians are sparse. Performance: Enables virtual memory management, allowing scene size to exceed system memory limits by mapping Gaussians to memory-mapped files. Parallelizable tasks (e.g., page linking) can be handled in thread pools or compute shaders. Strengths: Efficiently handles large-scale scenes with millions of Gaussians. Mesh-aligned assignment simplifies spatial coherence for surface-based rendering. Page linking effectively handles volumetric overlaps without expensive intersection tests. Limitations: Subdivision can create thin triangles and T-junctions, leading to rendering artifacts. The approximate nature of page linking (using random samples) may miss some overlaps, though it is designed to be sufficient. Non-uniform distribution of sample points within the ellipsoid due to spherical coordinate sampling. Page Assignment and Merging is part of the VastGaussian method, which utilizes virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method was developed to address the scalability issues of 3DGS when dealing with large scenes that exceed GPU memory capacity. By partitioning Gaussians into pages aligned with a proxy mesh, it allows for efficient loading and culling of scene data. The approach builds on earlier virtual texturing concepts, such as those by Mittring et al., but adapts them for volumetric Gaussian representations rather than surface textures. name: Similarity Guided Partition
head: Similarity Guided Partitioning
body: Similarity Guided Partition is a graph-based clustering algorithm that groups 3D Gaussians into spatially-disjoint blocks of bounded size based on spatial proximity and appearance similarity. It solves the problem of inefficient joint pruning by ensuring that potentially redundant Gaussians are evaluated together within the same optimization block. It sets itself apart from naive spatial partitioning by incorporating a scale-aware affinity metric that accounts for both geometric overlap and appearance consistency. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N Gaussians G, a maximum block size M, a neighbor limit k, and a comparison-group size limit. Output: A set of disjoint blocks \{Cb\}{b=1}^B such that |Cb| \le M for all b, covering all Gaussians in G. Data Structures Gaussian: Contains center \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, activated scale vector si \in \mathbb{R}^3, and DC spherical-harmonic descriptor ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. Affinity Graph: A sparse graph where nodes are Gaussians and edges (i, j) have weights a{ij}. Each node stores at most k neighbors with the highest affinity. Block: A set of Gaussian indices. Algorithm Steps The method proceeds in three phases: building the affinity graph, growing blocks in parallel, and filling unused capacity. 1. Build the Graph (Two-Pass Candidate Generation) To efficiently find candidate pairs without quadratic complexity, the algorithm performs two spatial passes with different grid configurations. Pass 1: 1. Assign each Gaussian center \mui to a 3D grid cell. 2. Sort occupied cells by their Morton code to preserve spatial locality. 3. Divide the Morton-ordered Gaussian sequence into the fewest balanced groups such that each group satisfies the comparison-group size limit. 4. For each group, compute pairwise affinities a{ij} for all pairs within the group. 5. For each Gaussian, retain at most the k candidates with the largest affinities. Pass 2: 1. Shift the grid origin and enlarge the grid cell size. 2. Repeat steps 1-5 from Pass 1 using the new grid configuration. Merge: 1. Combine the edges from both passes into a single sparse graph. 2. If an edge (i, j) appears in both passes, keep only one instance, recording its weight only once. 2. Grow Blocks in Parallel Split the Morton-ordered sequence from the first pass into \lceil N/M \rceil balanced intervals. Initialize B = \lceil N/M \rceil blocks. Seed each block Cb with the first Gaussian in its corresponding interval. Mark these Gaussians as assigned. All other Gaussians are unassigned. Iterate for at most 16 iterations: 1. For each unassigned Gaussian i, identify its strongest edge to an assigned neighbor j. Let C(j) be the block containing j. 2. Gaussian i proposes to join C(j). 3. For each block Cb, collect all proposals. 4. Rank proposals by descending edge weight a{ij}, then by ascending Gaussian index i to break ties. 5. Accept the first \min(\text{number of proposals}, M - |Cb|) Gaussians. Mark them as assigned and add them to Cb. 6. If no Gaussian was assigned in this iteration, stop. 3. Fill Unused Capacity Any Gaussians that remain unassigned after the growth phase are assigned to blocks to fill them up to size M. Assignment follows the Morton order from the first pass. Iterate through the Morton-ordered list; if a Gaussian is unassigned, add it to the first block Cb that has remaining capacity (|Cb| < M). Formula The scale-aware affinity a{ij} between Gaussian i and candidate j is defined as: a{ij} = \exp \left( - \sum{d=1}^{3} \frac{(\mu{i,d} - \mu{j,d})^2}{s{i,d}^2 + s{j,d}^2 + \epsilong} \right) - \|ci - cj\|^2 Where: \mu{i,d} is the d-th component of the center of Gaussian i. s{i,d} is the d-th component of the activated scale vector of Gaussian i. ci is the three-channel DC spherical-harmonic descriptor of Gaussian i. \epsilong is a small constant to prevent division by zero. The first term measures spatial proximity normalized by the combined scales of the two Gaussians. The second term penalizes affinity between spatially close Gaussians with dissimilar appearance (high color difference). Parameters M: Maximum allowed block size. Typical value not given in sources. k: Number of nearest neighbors to retain per Gaussian for the sparse graph. Typical value not given in sources. Comparison-group size limit: Maximum size for temporary search windows during candidate generation. Typical value not given in sources. \epsilong: Small constant for numerical stability. Value not given in sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def morton3d(x, y, z): # Standard 3D Morton code (bit interleaving) x, y, z = x & 0x3FFFFFFF, y & 0x3FFFFFFF, z & 0x3FFFFFFF x = (x | (x << 16)) & 0x000000FF000000FF x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00000000FF0000FF x = (x | (x << 4)) & 0x000000000F000F00 x = (x | (x << 2)) & 0x0000000003000300 x = (x | (x << 1)) & 0x0000000003000300 y = (y | (y << 16)) & 0x000000FF000000FF y = (y | (y << 8)) & 0x00000000FF0000FF y = (y | (y << 4)) & 0x000000000F000F00 y = (y | (y << 2)) & 0x0000000003000300 y = (y | (y << 1)) & 0x0000000003000300 z = (z | (z << 16)) & 0x000000FF000000FF z = (z | (z << 8)) & 0x00000000FF0000FF z = (z | (z << 4)) & 0x000000000F000F00 z = (z | (z << 2)) & 0x0000000003000300 z = (z | (z << 1)) & 0x0000000003000300 return x | (y << 1) | (z << 2) def similarityguidedpartition(Gaussians, M, k, grouplimit, origin1=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), cellsize1=1.0, origin2=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), cellsize2=2.0, epsilong=1e-6): N = len(Gaussians) indices = list(range(N)) def computeaffinity(i, j): mui, muj = Gaussians[i].mu, Gaussians[j].mu si, sj = Gaussians[i].s, Gaussians[j].s ci, cj = Gaussians[i].c, Gaussians[j].c spatial = sum((mui[d] - muj[d])2 / (si[d]2 + sj[d]2 + epsilong) for d in range(3)) appearance = sum((ci[d] - cj[d])2 for d in range(3)) return math.exp(-spatial) - appearance def runpass(origin, cellsize): cells = {} for idx in indices: mu = Gaussians[idx].mu coord = tuple(int((mu[d] - origin[d]) / cellsize) for d in range(3)) cells.setdefault(coord, []).append(idx) sortedcells = sorted(cells.keys(), key=lambda c: morton3d(c)) sequence = [idx for c in sortedcells for idx in cells[c]] groups = [sequence[i:i+grouplimit] for i in range(0, len(sequence), grouplimit)] localedges = {} for group in groups: for iidx in range(len(group)): for jidx in range(iidx + 1, len(group)): u, v = group[iidx], group[jidx] w = computeaffinity(u, v) if u not in localedges: localedges[u] = [] if v not in localedges: localedges[v] = [] localedges[u].append((v, w)) localedges[v].append((u, w)) topkedges = {} for idx in indices: if idx in localedges: candidates = sorted(localedges[idx], key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0])) topkedges[idx] = candidates[:k] return sequence, topkedges # Pass 1 seq1, edges1 = runpass(origin1, cellsize1) # Pass 2 seq2, edges2 = runpass(origin2, cellsize2) # Merge edges mergededges = {} for idx, neighbors in edges1.items(): for n, w in neighbors: key = (min(idx, n), max(idx, n)) if key not in mergededges: mergededges[key] = w for idx, neighbors in edges2.items(): for n, w in neighbors: key = (min(idx, n), max(idx, n)) if key not in mergededges: mergededges[key] = w # Build adjacency list from merged edges adj = {i: [] for i in indices} for (u, v), w in mergededges.items(): adj[u].append((v, w)) adj[v].append((u, w)) # Grow blocks numblocks = math.ceil(N / M) intervals = [seq1[bM:(b+1)M] for b in range(numblocks)] blocks = [] assigned = [False] N for interval in intervals: if interval: seed = interval[0] blocks.append([seed]) assigned[seed] = True for in range(16): proposals = [] for i in indices: if assigned[i]: continue best = None for n, w in adj[i]: if assigned[n]: if best is None or w > best[1] or (w == best[1] and n < best[0]): best = (n, w) if best: proposals.append((i, best[0], best[1])) if not proposals: break blockproposals = {} for i, n, w in proposals: bidx = next(b for b, blk in enumerate(blocks) if n in blk) blockproposals.setdefault(bidx, []).append((i, w)) for bidx, plist in blockproposals.items(): plist.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0])) cap = M - len(blocks[bidx]) for gidx, in plist[:cap]: blocks[bidx].append(gidx) assigned[gidx] = True # Fill unused capacity for i in seq1: if not assigned[i]: for bidx in range(len(blocks)): if len(blocks[bidx]) < M: blocks[bidx].append(i) assigned[i] = True break return blocks Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The affinity formula involves exponentials and differences of squared terms. Small \epsilong is required to avoid division by zero in the spatial term. Boundaries: The two-pass strategy with shifted grids and enlarged cells is designed to prevent missing pairs that lie on the boundary of a single grid's search window. Degenerate Input: If N < M, a single block is formed. If k=0, no edges are formed, and blocks are filled strictly by Morton order after the growth phase (which will assign no one in the growth phase). Candidate generation is sub-quadratic because grid-based spatial hashing and top-k neighbor selection avoid all-pairs comparisons. Block growth is bounded by 16 parallel iterations. Memory stores the sparse graph with O(N \cdot k) edges and block assignments O(N). Strengths include grouping spatially and appearance-similar Gaussians for effective joint pruning. Limitations include sensitivity to grid parameters and the overhead of the two-pass strategy. Use when joint pruning requires appearance-aware grouping beyond naive spatial partitioning. The method originates from SplatQ, a paper under review for ICLR 2027. It defines local Gaussian sets for response modeling and quadratic selection-based pruning within the SplatQ framework. It builds on the VastGaussian framework, which partitions scenes into spatially-disjoint regions. name: Data Layout and Storage
body: Data Layout and Storage defines the memory organization, serialization, and runtime management of 3D Gaussian Splat attributes (position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics) to enable efficient GPU rendering and optimization. It solves the problem of translating high-level splat representations into contiguous, cache-friendly structures suitable for batched processing, while supporting dynamic scene growth and cross-platform data transfer. It is distinguished from sibling methods by focusing on the raw memory layout and buffer management infrastructure rather than the rendering algorithm itself (GSPull), error-based densification (Composite Error Map and Densification/Pruning Scoring), or specific network architectures (GS-W Network Architecture). Builds on Gaussian Data Structure. The family operates on a Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) paradigm, where each attribute type is stored in a separate contiguous linear buffer [5568-splat-data-buffer-layout.md]. Rotations are stored as N \times 4 floats in scalar-last order (x, y, z, w). Opacities are stored as N floats. Spherical Harmonics coefficients are stored as N \times D \times 3 floats, with indexing idx = ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + c [5570-spherical-harmonics-coefficient-layout.md]. Dynamic scene management supports incremental append operations and dynamic buffer resizing [6907-dynamic-gaussian-splatting-scene-management.md]. Scales are stored in log-space [5568-splat-data-buffer-layout.md]. When writing to buffers, linear values are converted to log-space via \log(). Defines the foundational SoA memory organization for all splat attributes. It serves as the base for other layout methods. Choose when implementing raw buffer population for GPU shaders. Details the specific indexing and flat buffer structure for SH coefficients, ensuring contiguous access for color data. Choose when optimizing SH coefficient retrieval in shaders. Handles the decoding of Gaussian parameters from compressed texture storage into a structured CovSplat representation for rasterization. Choose when working with texture-based splat storage. Manages the runtime lifecycle of splat data structures, including capacity growth and batched updates, enabling real-time scene evolution. Choose for dynamic or streaming scenes. Manages memory allocation and serialization of splat attributes into WebAssembly linear memory for GPU upload or WASM-side processing, handling power-of-2 capacity alignment. Choose for web-based or WASM-targeted renderers. Optimizes large-scale storage and rendering. Choose for massive scene datasets requiring hierarchical or compressed storage. Integrates tracking data into the splat layout. Choose when maintaining spatial consistency across camera poses. Defines the mathematical basis and coefficient ordering for color representation. Choose when implementing or modifying the SH evaluation pipeline. Extends the standard 3D Gaussian parameterization. Choose when requiring additional degrees of freedom for complex geometry or appearance. Handles time-varying attributes within the storage structure. Choose for animating or simulating dynamic scenes. Modifies the radial kernel function for adaptive splat shapes. Choose when standard isotropic or anisotropic kernels are insufficient. Scales are stored internally in log-space. When writing to buffers, linear values are converted to log-space via \log(). When reading for rendering or optimization, log-space values are converted to linear via \exp(). Linear scale is recovered from stored log-scale: s{linear} = \exp(s{log}). Conversion logic is not explicitly detailed in the sources. For each splat i, the quaternion components are written sequentially to indices i \times 4 + 0 through i \times 4 + 3. Rotations are stored as 4-component quaternions in scalar-last order (x, y, z, w) within a FloatBuffer of size N \times 4. A file format for storing HLOD Gaussian splat worlds, extending v1 with HLOD flags, extended headers, and strict bounds validation rules. The header's world AABB must enclose the root node's world AABB. During load, validate header bounds: refuse if non-finite, negative size, or failing to enclose the root's world AABB. Perform bounds validation using double precision to avoid floating-point edge cases. World importer version is 4 (3 handles v1->v2 bake, 4 handles header-bounds rule). PLY/SPZ importer versions remain unchanged from v1. Header contains an 80-byte extension block. Each node/instance record is exactly 128 bytes. Data is organized into bounded, non-overlapping sections. Disjoint noncanonical ordering is permitted in the file layout. Malformed headers containing NaN, infinite position/size, negative size, zero size, half extent, disjoint bounds, one float ULP inside the root's low edge, or widened positive controls must be rejected or handled safely. The Structure-of-Arrays layout for 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the original 3DGS paper. Subsequent implementations, such as JSplat and the gsplat ecosystem, refined the storage for GPU efficiency, introducing log-scale storage for stability and specific quaternion orderings. The GaussianSplatWorld v2 format was developed to support Hierarchical Level of Detail (HLOD) in large-scale scenes, adding strict validation rules to prevent corruption from malformed data. Dynamic scene management techniques evolved to support real-time updates, moving beyond static initialization to support incremental appending and buffer resizing. name: Splat Data Buffer Layout
head: SplatData Layout, Structure-of-Arrays Splat Storage
body: The Splat Data Buffer Layout defines the memory organization for 3D Gaussian primitives in differentiable volume rendering, specifically within the GaussianSet Data Structure family. It solves the problem of efficient GPU rendering by storing per-Gaussian attributes in separate contiguous linear buffers (Structure-of-Arrays, SoA), maximizing cache coherency during rasterization. Unlike sibling methods that focus on coefficient indexing [5570-spherical-harmonics-coefficient-layout.md] or covariance calculation [6840-covariance-splat-reading.md], this layout focuses on the raw storage of learnable parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH) in a flat, contiguous format suitable for direct memory access by vertex/fragment shaders. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A collection of N Gaussian splats, each defined by position, scale, rotation, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Output: A set of contiguous FloatBuffer arrays (or equivalent linear memory blocks) for each attribute type. Data Structures: The layout consists of five distinct contiguous buffers, each of size proportional to N: 1. Positions: N \times 3 floats (x, y, z). 2. Scales: N \times 3 floats. The source readScales reads logarithmic scales from splat objects and writes the corresponding linear scale values into the buffer. 3. Rotations: N \times 4 floats representing quaternions in scalar-last order (x, y, z, w). 4. Opacities: N floats. Base layout stores scalar opacity. 5. Spherical Harmonics (SH): N \times D \times 3 floats, where D is the number of coefficients per channel. The indexing formula for the c-th channel (c \in \{0,1,2\}) of the d-th coefficient (d \in \{0, \dots, D-1\}) of the i-th splat is: idx = ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + c This layout groups data by splat, then by coefficient index, then by spatial dimension (RGB) [5570-spherical-harmonics-coefficient-layout.md]. Algorithm: The conversion from a high-level object collection to the SoA buffer layout follows these steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Allocate contiguous float buffers for each attribute type. posbuf: size N \times 3 scalebuf: size N \times 3 rotbuf: size N \times 4 opacitybuf: size N shbuf: size N \times D \times 3 2. Iterate and Extract: For each splat i from 0 to N-1: a. Extract position components (xi, yi, zi) and write to posbuf at indices [3i, 3i+1, 3i+2]. b. Extract scale components (s{x,i}, s{y,i}, s{z,i}) from logarithmic storage and write linear values to scalebuf at indices [3i, 3i+1, 3i+2]. c. Extract rotation quaternion (xi, yi, zi, wi) in scalar-last order and write to rotbuf at indices [4i, 4i+1, 4i+2, 4i+3]. d. Extract opacity \alphai and write to opacitybuf at index i. e. Extract SH coefficients. For each coefficient index d \in \{0, \dots, D-1\} and channel c \in \{0, 1, 2\}: Calculate buffer index: idx = ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + c. Write coefficient value to shbuf at idx. 3. Return Buffers: Return the set of populated buffers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Dict def buildsplatbuffers(splats: List['Splat'], shdegree: int) -> Dict[str, List[float]]: """ Converts a list of Splat objects into a Structure-of-Arrays layout. Args: splats: List of N Splat objects. shdegree: Degree of spherical harmonics (D = (degree+1)^2). Returns: Dictionary containing contiguous buffers for positions, scales, rotations, opacities, and spherical harmonics. """ N = len(splats) D = (shdegree + 1) 2 # Initialize buffers positions = [0.0] (N 3) scales = [0.0] (N 3) rotations = [0.0] (N 4) opacities = [0.0] N shcoeffs = [0.0] (N D 3) for i, s in enumerate(splats): # 1. Positions (x, y, z) positions[3 i + 0] = s.getpositionx() positions[3 i + 1] = s.getpositiony() positions[3 i + 2] = s.getpositionz() # 2. Scales (convert log to linear as per source readScales) scales[3 i + 0] = math.exp(s.getscalelogx()) scales[3 i + 1] = math.exp(s.getscalelogy()) scales[3 i + 2] = math.exp(s.getscalelogz()) # 3. Rotations (scalar-last quaternion: x, y, z, w) rotations[4 i + 0] = s.getrotationx() rotations[4 i + 1] = s.getrotationy() rotations[4 i + 2] = s.getrotationz() rotations[4 i + 3] = s.getrotationw() # 4. Opacity opacities[i] = s.getopacity() # 5. Spherical Harmonics # Indexing: ((i D) + d) 3 + c for d in range(D): for c in range(3): idx = ((i D) + d) 3 + c shcoeffs[idx] = s.getshcoefficient(d, c) return { "positions": positions, "scales": scales, "rotations": rotations, "opacities": opacities, "shcoeffs": shcoeffs } Parameters: N: Number of Gaussians. D: Number of SH coefficients per channel, determined by the SH degree. For degree-3, D=16. Scale storage: The source reads logarithmic scales from splat objects and writes linear values to the buffer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Float32 is standard for buffers. Boundary Conditions: Buffer sizes must be exactly N \times \text{stride}. If N is dynamic, resizing must follow specific growth rules (see Dynamic Gaussian Splatting Scene Management). Quaternion Order: Must be scalar-last (x, y, z, w) as specified in. Using scalar-first will cause incorrect rotation application. SH Indexing: The formula idx = ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + c is critical. Deviating from this (e.g., channel-major) breaks compatibility with standard rendering shaders [5570-spherical-harmonics-coefficient-layout.md]. A logical layout for all learnable per-Gaussian attributes stored out-of-core on SSD, organized into contiguous spatial blocks to improve I/O efficiency and spatial locality. It differs from the standard in-memory SoA layout by introducing spatial blocking and Morton sorting to optimize disk reads. Choose this variant for training scenes with billions of Gaussians where memory exceeds GPU capacity. Definition: A unified logical layout \Theta \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} for all learnable per-Gaussian attributes, stored out-of-core as contiguous block records on SSD. Step: Morton-sort Gaussians by the codes of their centers before blocking to ensure spatially nearby Gaussians map to nearby indices and blocks. Formula: \text{Block}(k):= \Theta[kB: (k+1)B], \quad k \in \{0, \dots, K-1\} where K = \lceil N/B \rceil. Parameter: Block size B=4096. With D=59 parameters (degree-3 SH) and fp32 (4 bytes), each block is 4096 \times 59 \times 4 = 964,544 bytes (236 contiguous 4 KB pages, ~944 KiB). Layout: Logical layout \Theta \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} with D=59. Stored as contiguous block records on SSD. CPU/GPU materialize only cached/resident blocks. Pitfall: Gaussian centers move during training, changing block bounds. The owner block is fixed (no migration/duplication). Bounds are conservatively refreshed, allowing neighboring block bounds to overlap, but each Gaussian remains uniquely owned and rasterized exactly once. Time Complexity: O(N) to build the buffers from object data. O(1) access to any attribute given the splat index. Memory Complexity: O(N \times D{attr}), where D{attr} is the total number of floats per splat. For degree-3 SH, D{attr} = 3 + 3 + 4 + 1 + 16 \times 3 = 62 floats per splat. Performance: Maximizes GPU cache coherency by ensuring shaders iterate over single attributes without skipping irrelevant data. Strengths: Simple to implement, highly efficient for in-memory rendering, standard compatibility with GPU shaders. Limitations: High memory footprint for large N. When to use: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering and training where all Gaussians fit in GPU memory. When not to use: Scenes with billions of Gaussians requiring out-of-core optimization (use Unified Parameter Layout and SSD Blocking). The Splat Data Buffer Layout is a foundational component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, specifically as implemented in libraries like JSplat. It builds on the Structure-of-Arrays paradigm common in graphics programming to optimize data access patterns for parallel rendering. The specific use of scalar-last quaternions aligns with standard practices in differentiable rendering. The SSD blocking variant is used in TideGS for large-scale training. name: Splat Data Encoding & Disabled Splat Detection
head: Disabled Splat Detection, Splat Data Encoding
body: This method defines the binary encoding scheme for 3D Gaussian splats and provides the logic to detect disabled splats during spatial queries and sorting. It solves the problem of efficiently filtering out inactive or merged Gaussians without allocating separate boolean flags or requiring complex metadata lookups. It is distinct from standard active/inactive flags by embedding the status directly into the data payload's bit pattern, allowing the renderer to treat disabled splats as invalid data during coordinate extraction. This builds on Splat Data Buffer Layout. Inputs: A stream of splat data stored in two Uint32Array buffers. Outputs: A boolean indicating if a splat is disabled; modified coordinates (NaN) if disabled. Data Structure: Each splat occupies 32 bytes (8 words), split across two arrays: splatA: Words 0–3 (16 bytes). splatB: Words 4–7 (16 bytes). For splat index i, the starting index in splatB is i4 = i \times 4. Parameters: SPLATBLOCKSDISABLED: A constant used to configure the renderer's block handling mode. Its exact numeric value is not provided in the sources. Disabled Splat Signature: A splat is considered disabled if the following bit pattern is detected in splatB: 1. The upper 16 bits of splatB[i4 + 1] equal 0xfc00. 2. The entire value of splatB[i4 + 2] equals 0xfc00fc00. Algorithm: 1. For each splat index i: a. Calculate i4 = i \times 4. b. Read word1 = splatB[i4 + 1]. c. Read word2 = splatB[i4 + 2]. d. Check if (word1 >> 16) == 0xfc00 AND word2 == 0xfc00fc00. e. If true, the splat is disabled. Coordinate Extraction with Detection: When extracting center coordinates (x, y, z) for sorting or spatial queries: 1. If the splat is disabled, set x = \text{NaN}, y = \text{NaN}, z = \text{NaN}. 2. If the splat is enabled, extract coordinates normally from the encoding. 3. Pass these coordinates to the sorting/spatial query function. Standard NaN-aware sorting or spatial partitioning will exclude these entries. Pitfalls: False Positives: If valid Gaussian data accidentally matches the 0xfc00 pattern, the splat will be incorrectly disabled. Processing Artifacts: If disabled splats are not detected and processed as valid, they may cause rendering artifacts or incorrect sorting behavior because their coordinates are undefined or meaningless. Boundary Checks: Ensure array bounds are respected when accessing splatB[i4 + 1] and splatB[i4 + 2]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def issplatdisabled(splatB, i): i4 = i 4 word1 = splatB[i4 + 1] word2 = splatB[i4 + 2] return (word1 >> 16) == 0xfc00 and word2 == 0xfc00fc00 def extractcenterwithdisabledcheck(splatA, splatB, i): if issplatdisabled(splatB, i): return (float('nan'), float('nan'), float('nan')) # Not given in the sources. x = decodefloat(splatA[i 4 + 0]) y = decodefloat(splatA[i 4 + 1]) z = decodefloat(splatA[i 4 + 2]) return (x, y, z) def decodefloat(word): import struct return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', word))[0] Time Complexity: O(1) per splat for detection. Memory Overhead: Zero additional memory; the status is encoded within the existing 32-byte splat structure. Performance: Extremely fast detection via bitwise operations. Strengths: Efficient, compact, and integrates seamlessly with NaN-based filtering in spatial data structures. Limitations: Requires strict adherence to the reserved bit pattern; any corruption of the data could lead to false positives or negatives. This method is part of the Gaussian-Splat-Lite renderer, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimized for WebGPU. It was developed to handle large-scale Gaussian datasets efficiently in a browser environment, where memory and performance constraints are significant. The specific encoding and detection mechanism were designed to minimize overhead while ensuring robust handling of merged or inactive Gaussians. name: GpuEdgeCost
head: GPU edge-cost evaluator
body: GpuEdgeCost is a WebGPU compute shader that evaluates the L2 field-error cost for merging pairs of 3D Gaussians, mirroring the logic of the CPU computeEdgeCost function. It enables differentiable inverse volume rendering optimizations by calculating the error introduced when two splats are merged, allowing the system to identify and remove redundant Gaussians. Unlike CPU-based implementations, it utilizes WGSL shaders and storage buffers to handle large datasets in batches, overcoming GPU memory binding limits. Inputs: Splat Data Buffer (splatBuf): Interleaved storage of all splat attributes. Size is maxN SPLATSTRIDE 4 bytes. Neighbor Row Buffer (nbRowBuf): Array of u32 containing neighbor row indices for the current dispatch batch. Size is slotsPerBatch 4 bytes. Uniforms Buffer: Contains slotBase (u32) and slotCount (u32). Host-side Validation: The host must ensure numSplats <= maxN, outCosts length equals nbRows length, and nbRows length is a multiple of k. Outputs: Costs Buffer (outBuf): Array of f32 storing the calculated cost per slot. Size is slotsPerBatch 4 bytes. Splat Storage Layout (Interleaved, Stride SPLATSTRIDE): Each splat occupies SPLATSTRIDE floats. The layout is: [0..2]: Mean position xyz (f32) [3..8]: Covariance matrix \Sigma elements xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz (f32) [9]: Sqrt determinant sqrtDet (f32) [10]: Alpha alpha (f32) [11]: Mass mass (f32) [12..14]: Base color rgb (f32) [15]: Squared norm of base color |base|² (f32) Constants: SPLATSTRIDE: Equal to CACHESTRIDE. SENTINEL: 0xFFFFFFFF (u32), indicating an empty slot. EPSCOV: Small epsilon added to covariance diagonal terms to prevent singularity. PI15: Constant \pi^{1.5}. COLORWEIGHT: Weighting factor for color distance in the final cost. The host manages batching to respect the WebGPU limit of 65,535 workgroups per dimension. Each workgroup contains 64 threads. 1. Batch Setup: Calculate numBatches = ceil(s / slotsPerBatch), where s is the total number of slots. Iterate batch from 0 to numBatches - 1: slotBase = batch slotsPerBatch slotCount = min(slotsPerBatch, s - slotBase) Copy the slice of nbRows from slotBase to slotCount into nbRowBuf. Dispatch the compute shader with slotBase and slotCount in the uniforms buffer. Read slotCount 4 bytes from outBuf into a scratch buffer outScratch. Copy the first slotCount elements from outScratch to outCosts starting at index slotBase. 2. Compute Shader Execution (Per Thread): Each thread processes one dense slot. Get global ID gid.x. Set bid = gid.x. If bid >= uniforms.slotCount, return. Read row = nbRow[bid] from nbRowBuf. If row == SENTINEL, set costs[bid] = 0.0 and return. Calculate offsets: io = ((uniforms.slotBase + bid) / K) SPLATSTRIDE jo = row SPLATSTRIDE. Load Splat i data from splatBuf at io: mui, si (6 elements), sdi, ai, mi, bi, bni. Load Splat j data from splatBuf at jo: muj, sj, sdj, aj, mj, bj, bnj. 3. Merge Calculation: Merge Weights: W = mi + mj pi = select(0.5, mi / W, W > 0.0) pj = 1.0 - pi Merged Mean: mm = pi mui + pj muj di = mui - mm dj = muj - mm Merged Covariance: Calculate sm (6 elements). For diagonal terms (indices 0, 3, 5), add EPSCOV. Example for xx (index 0): sm[0] = pi (di.x di.x + si[0]) + pj (dj.x dj.x + sj[0]) + EPSCOV Similar formulas apply for other elements using corresponding components of di and dj. Merged Determinant: Calculate detm using cofactor expansion of sm. Clamp detm to 1e-30. sqrtDetM = sqrt(detm). Merged Opacity: Compute eigenvalues e = eig3(sm). Scales s0, s1, s2 = sqrt(max(e.x/y/z, 1e-18)). ellipsoidArea = ellipsoidArea(s0, s1, s2). am = min(1.0, W / max(ellipsoidArea, 1e-30)). Color Terms: bij = dot(bi, bj) bim = pi bni + pj bij bjm = pi bij + pj bnj bnm = pi pi bni + 2.0 pi pj bij + pj pj bnj 4. Error Cost Calculation: Self-Interaction Terms: selfI = ai ai bni PI15 sdi selfJ = aj aj bnj PI15 sdj selfM = am am bnm PI15 sqrtDetM Cross-Gaussian Products: cIJ = crossG(sdi, sdj, si+sj, mui-muj) cIM = crossG(sdi, sqrtDetM, si+sm, di) cJM = crossG(sdj, sqrtDetM, sj+sm, dj). Total Error E: E = selfI + selfJ + selfM + 2.0 ai aj bij cIJ - 2.0 ai am bim cIM - 2.0 aj am bjm cJM 5. Final Cost Assembly: Calculate color distance squared: dc2 = bni + bnj - 2.0 bij Clamp dc2 to 0.0 if negative (to handle float noise). costs[bid] = select(E, 0.0, E < 0.0) + COLORWEIGHT select(dc2, 0.0, dc2 < 0.0). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuedgecostdispatch(nbrows, splatdata, maxn, splatstride, slotsperbatch=4194240): s = len(nbrows) numbatches = (s + slotsperbatch - 1) // slotsperbatch outcosts = [0.0] s # Pre-allocate buffers (conceptual) splatbuf = allocatebuffer(maxn splatstride 4) nbrowbuf = allocatebuffer(slotsperbatch 4) outbuf = allocatebuffer(slotsperbatch 4) # Write splat data once writetobuffer(splatbuf, splatdata) for batch in range(numbatches): slotbase = batch slotsperbatch slotcount = min(slotsperbatch, s - slotbase) # Prepare nbRow buffer for this batch writetobuffer(nbrowbuf, nbrows[slotbase: slotbase + slotcount]) # Dispatch Compute Shader # Uniforms: slotBase=slotbase, slotCount=slotcount # Bindings: splatBuf, nbRowBuf, outBuf dispatchcomputeshader(slotbase, slotcount) # Read results outscratch = readfrombuffer(outbuf, slotcount 4) # Copy to final output for i in range(slotcount): outcosts[slotbase + i] = outscratch[i] return outcosts def computeedgecost(gid, uniforms, nbrow, splatbuf, costs): bid = gid if bid >= uniforms.slotCount: return row = nbrow[bid] if row == 0xFFFFFFFF: # SENTINEL costs[bid] = 0.0 return # Offsets io = ((uniforms.slotBase + bid) / K) SPLATSTRIDE jo = row SPLATSTRIDE # Load Splat i mui = splatbuf[io + 0: io + 3] si = splatbuf[io + 3: io + 9] sdi = splatbuf[io + 9] ai = splatbuf[io + 10] mi = splatbuf[io + 11] bi = splatbuf[io + 12: io + 15] bni = splatbuf[io + 15] # Load Splat j muj = splatbuf[jo + 0: jo + 3] sj = splatbuf[jo + 3: jo + 9] sdj = splatbuf[jo + 9] aj = splatbuf[jo + 10] mj = splatbuf[jo + 11] bj = splatbuf[jo + 12: jo + 15] bnj = splatbuf[jo + 15] # Merge Weights W = mi + mj pi = mi / W if W > 0.0 else 0.5 pj = 1.0 - pi # Merged Mean mm = pi mui + pj muj di = mui - mm dj = muj - mm # Merged Covariance sm = [0.0] 6 sm[0] = pi (di[0] di[0] + si[0]) + pj (dj[0] dj[0] + sj[0]) + EPSCOV sm[1] = pi (di[0] di[1] + si[1]) + pj (dj[0] dj[1] + sj[1]) sm[2] = pi (di[0] di[2] + si[2]) + pj (dj[0] dj[2] + sj[2]) sm[3] = pi (di[1] di[1] + si[3]) + pj (dj[1] dj[1] + sj[3]) + EPSCOV sm[4] = pi (di[1] di[2] + si[4]) + pj (dj[1] dj[2] + sj[4]) sm[5] = pi (di[2] di[2] + si[5]) + pj (dj[2] dj[2] + sj[5]) + EPSCOV # Merged Determinant # cofactorexpansion helper: sources do not give implementation detm = cofactorexpansion(sm) detm = max(detm, 1e-30) sqrtDetM = sqrt(detm) # Merged Opacity # eig3 helper: sources do not give implementation e = eig3(sm) s0 = sqrt(max(e[0], 1e-18)) s1 = sqrt(max(e[1], 1e-18)) s2 = sqrt(max(e[2], 1e-18)) # ellipsoidarea helper: sources do not give implementation ellipsoidArea = ellipsoidarea(s0, s1, s2) am = min(1.0, W / max(ellipsoidArea, 1e-30)) # Color Terms bij = dot(bi, bj) bim = pi bni + pj bij bjm = pi bij + pj bnj bnm = pi pi bni + 2.0 pi pj bij + pj pj bnj # Self-Interaction selfI = ai ai bni PI15 sdi selfJ = aj aj bnj PI15 sdj selfM = am am bnm PI15 sqrtDetM # Cross-Gaussian Products # crossG helper: sources do not give implementation cIJ = crossG(sdi, sdj, si + sj, mui - muj) cIM = crossG(sdi, sqrtDetM, si + sm, di) cJM = crossG(sdj, sqrtDetM, sj + sm, dj) # Total Error E = selfI + selfJ + selfM + 2.0 ai aj bij cIJ - 2.0 ai am bim cIM - 2.0 aj am bjm cJM # Final Cost dc2 = bni + bnj - 2.0 bij dc2 = max(dc2, 0.0) costval = max(E, 0.0) costval += COLORWEIGHT max(dc2, 0.0) costs[bid] = costval Empty Slots: If a neighbor row index is SENTINEL (0xFFFFFFFF), the cost is set to 0.0 and the thread returns early. This prevents reading invalid memory. Float Noise: Negative values resulting from squared norm calculations (e.g., dc2) are clamped to 0.0 to handle floating-point precision errors. NaN/Inf: These are preserved in the calculation to allow the host to detect and fail loudly on degenerate input data. Memory Limits: WebGPU has a maximum storage buffer binding size (typically ~2 GB). To avoid driver-side errors, data is processed in batches (slotsPerBatch) rather than uploading the full N·k slot list at once. The host must check maxStorageBufferBindingSize before buffer creation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of slots, as each thread processes one slot independently. The batching overhead is O(N / slotsPerBatch) dispatches. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the splat data buffer. The auxiliary buffers (nbRowBuf, outBuf) are sized based on slotsPerBatch, not total N, keeping peak GPU memory usage constant regardless of scene size. Performance: Performance is limited by the WebGPU workgroup limit (65,535 workgroups per dimension), necessitating the batching strategy. Strengths: Efficiently handles large-scale Gaussian splat datasets by offloading the expensive merge-cost calculation to the GPU while managing memory constraints through batching. Limitations: Requires WebGPU support. The batching introduces some host-GPU synchronization overhead for reading/writing buffers. GpuEdgeCost is part of the splat-transform project by PlayCanvas, implemented as a WebGPU compute shader to optimize 3D Gaussian Splatting data structures. It mirrors the logic of the CPU computeEdgeCost function, providing a high-performance alternative for differentiable inverse volume rendering tasks. playcanvas/splat-transform, https://github.com/playcanvas/splat-transform, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Spherical Harmonics Coefficient Layout
head: Per-Dimension SH Storage, SH Buffer Layout
body: This layout defines the memory organization for storing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients within the Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) paradigm used in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping per-Gaussian color data (represented by SH coefficients) into contiguous linear buffers for GPU transfer and rendering. It differs from interleaved layouts by grouping coefficients by spatial dimension (RGB) after grouping by splat and degree, optimizing for vectorized processing of the RGB triplet during the final color computation step. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A collection of N Gaussian splats, each having a set of SH coefficients up to a specific degree. Output: A contiguous linear buffer (e.g., FloatBuffer) of size N \times D \times 3, where D is the total number of SH coefficients for the chosen degree. Data Structures: The layout uses a single contiguous array of 32-bit floats. The indexing formula for the coefficient at splat index i, coefficient index d, and color channel c (where c \in \{0, 1, 2\} for R, G, B) is: idx = ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + c Here, D is the total number of SH coefficients for the given degree, calculated via Splats.dimensionsForDegree(shDegree). Steps: 1. Determine the total number of SH coefficients D for the selected degree. 2. Allocate a linear buffer of size N \times D \times 3. 3. Iterate over each splat index i from 0 to N-1. 4. For each splat, iterate over each coefficient index d from 0 to D-1. 5. For each coefficient, write the three components (X, Y, Z corresponding to R, G, B) to the buffer at indices: ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + 0 for the first component (e.g., Red). ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + 1 for the second component (e.g., Green). ((i \times D) + d) \times 3 + 2 for the third component (e.g., Blue). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def writeshcoefficients(splats: List[Splat], shdegree: int) -> List[float]: """ Writes SH coefficients into a flat buffer following the per-dimension layout. Args: splats: List of N Splat objects. shdegree: The degree of spherical harmonics used. Returns: A flat list of floats representing the buffer. """ # D is the total number of SH coefficients for the given degree # Formula: D = (shdegree + 1)^2 D = (shdegree + 1) 2 N = len(splats) buffersize = N D 3 buffer = [0.0] buffersize for i in range(N): splat = splats[i] for d in range(D): # Get the three components for coefficient d # Note: In standard SH, these correspond to R, G, B values for that coefficient shx = splat.getshx(d) shy = splat.getshy(d) shz = splat.getshz(d) # Calculate base index for this coefficient baseidx = (i D + d) 3 # Write components to buffer buffer[baseidx + 0] = shx buffer[baseidx + 1] = shy buffer[baseidx + 2] = shz return buffer Parameters: shDegree: The degree of spherical harmonics. Typical values are 0, 1, 2, or 3. Degree 0 has 1 coefficient, Degree 1 has 4, Degree 2 has 9, Degree 3 has 16. N: Number of splats. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degree Mismatch: Ensure D is calculated consistently across all splats. If splats have different degrees, this layout requires padding or separate buffers. Precision: Coefficients are stored as 32-bit floats. Quantization methods (e.g., INT8) may be applied to reduce memory traffic, but this layout assumes float storage by default. Boundary Conditions: The buffer size must be exactly N \times D \times 3. Under-allocation causes out-of-bounds errors; over-allocation wastes memory. SH Coefficient Interleaving packs spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients into a single contiguous array by grouping coefficients by channel rather than by degree. It solves the problem of efficient memory access during rendering by ensuring that all color channels for a specific SH degree are stored adjacently. It differs from non-interleaved layouts by optimizing for vectorized processing of the RGB triplet during the final color computation step. This variant manages SH coefficients by storing them in separate textures keyed by block identifiers (e.g., this.shTextures[key]). It iterates over all SH keys, calling ensureShTexture to either reuse an existing texture, mark it for update if needsUpdate is true, or create a new texture from this.extra[key] if data exists. If a texture already exists and this.needsUpdate is true, it sets current.needsUpdate = true to signal the GPU driver to refresh the texture data. This approach is used in streaming contexts where SH data is loaded dynamically. This variant uses INT8 quantization for spherical harmonics coefficients to reduce memory traffic. It is part of hardware-oriented optimizations like RoofGS, which aims to accelerate rendering through reduced data size and efficient use of Tensor Cores. Time Complexity: Writing coefficients is O(N \times D), where N is the number of splats and D is the number of SH coefficients per splat. Reading for rendering is also O(N \times D) if all coefficients are accessed. Memory Complexity: The layout requires N \times D \times 3 \times 4 bytes of memory (assuming 32-bit floats). For N=10^6 and Degree 3 (D=16), this is approximately 192 MB. Performance: The contiguous memory layout facilitates efficient bulk transfers to the GPU. However, the non-interleaved nature (grouping by splat then degree then channel) may require specific indexing logic in shaders compared to interleaved layouts. Strengths: Simple indexing formula, easy to implement, compatible with standard SoA buffers. Limitations: Not optimized for vectorized RGB access during rendering without specific shader logic. High memory usage for high-degree SH. This layout is a fundamental component of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline, specifically within the Gaussian Splatting family of techniques. It was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper [Kerbl et al., 2023] and is widely adopted in implementations such as JSplat and Gaussian-Splat-Lite. The layout supports the dynamic scene management and incremental updates required for real-time rendering of large-scale scenes. name: SH Coefficient Interleaving
head: SH Data Layout Interleaving, SH Interleaving
body: SH Coefficient Interleaving packs spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients into a single contiguous array by grouping coefficients by channel rather than by degree. It solves the problem of efficient memory access during rendering by ensuring that all color channels for a specific SH degree are stored adjacently. It differs from non-interleaved layouts by optimizing for vectorized processing of the RGB triplet during the final color computation step. Inputs: shdc: A 3-component vector representing the zeroth-degree (DC) spherical harmonic coefficients. shrest: A 1D array containing the higher-order SH coefficients, with a total size of 3 coeffsperchannel. coeffsperchannel: The number of higher-order coefficients per channel. Outputs: result: A 1D array containing the interleaved SH data, with a total size of 3 + (3 coeffsperchannel). Data Structure: The output array is structured as follows: 1. The first 3 elements are shdc.x, shdc.y, shdc.z. 2. The remaining elements are filled by iterating through the SH degrees (indices i from 0 to coeffsperchannel - 1). For each degree i, the coefficients for all 3 channels are appended in order: shrest[0 coeffsperchannel + i], shrest[1 coeffsperchannel + i], shrest[2 coeffsperchannel + i]. Algorithm: 1. Initialize an empty list result. 2. Append shdc.x, shdc.y, shdc.z to result. 3. For i from 0 to coeffsperchannel - 1: a. For j from 0 to 2: i. Calculate the index in the source array: index = j coeffsperchannel + i. ii. Append shrest[index] to result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interleaveshcoefficients(shdc, shrest, coeffsperchannel): result = [] result.append(shdc[0]) result.append(shdc[1]) result.append(shdc[2]) for i in range(coeffsperchannel): for j in range(3): index = j coeffsperchannel + i result.append(shrest[index]) return result Parameters: coeffsperchannel: The number of higher-order coefficients per channel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Ensure shrest has exactly 3 coeffsperchannel elements. Accessing shrest[index] where index >= len(shrest) will cause an out-of-bounds error. Degenerate Input: If coeffsperchannel is 0, only the DC coefficients are written. It supports multiple encoding formats (Float32, Float16, Norm11, Norm6) to balance precision and memory usage. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the final serialization step into a contiguous byte array, rather than the interleaving of coefficients or the optimization of the splat parameters themselves. head: CreateSHDataJob, SH Data Encoding, SH Format Conversion
body: This method converts raw spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients from input splat data into a specific binary format for storage in a Gaussian Splat asset. It supports multiple encoding formats (Float32, Float16, Norm11, Norm6) to balance precision and memory usage. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the final serialization step into a contiguous byte array, rather than the interleaving of coefficients or the optimization of the splat parameters themselves. It builds on SH Coefficient Interleaving by taking the interleaved coefficients and packing them into a platform-native layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: NativeArray<InputSplatData> containing splat data with fields sh1 through shF (15 coefficients per splat). Output: NativeArray<byte> containing the serialized SH data. Format Selector: GaussianSplatAsset.SHFormat enum defining the target encoding. Data Structures: The output is structured as an array of SHTableItem variants, depending on the format: SHTableItemFloat32: Contains 15 float3 fields (sh1 to shF) and one float3 padding field (shPadding). SHTableItemFloat16: Contains 15 half3 fields (sh1 to shF) and one half3 padding field (shPadding). SHTableItemNorm11: Contains 15 uint fields (encoded via EncodeFloat3ToNorm11) and one uint padding field (shPadding). SHTableItemNorm6: Contains 15 uint fields (encoded via EncodeFloat3ToNorm565) and one uint padding field (shPadding). Steps: 1. Determine if clustered SH data is available. If clusteredSHs exists, calculate size as clusteredSHs.Length SizeOf<SHTableItemFloat16>, create a byte array, copy clusteredSHs reinterpreted as bytes, and return. 2. If no clustered data, calculate dataLen using GaussianSplatAsset.CalcSHDataSize(inputSplats.Length, shFormat). 3. Create a NativeArray<byte> data of size dataLen. 4. Instantiate a CreateSHDataJob with mInput, mFormat, and mOutput (the byte array). 5. Schedule the job with job.Schedule(inputSplats.Length, 8192). 6. Complete the job and copy data to a result byte array. 7. Dispose of the NativeArray<byte> and return the result. Job Execution (Parallel Step): For each index in the input array: 1. Read splat = mInput[index]. 2. Switch on mFormat: Float32: Create SHTableItemFloat32 res. Copy splat.sh1 through splat.shF to res.sh1 through res.shF. Set res.shPadding = default. Write res to mOutput at the correct byte offset. Float16: Cast splat.sh1 through splat.shF to half3. Copy to SHTableItemFloat16. Set shPadding = default. Write to output. Norm11: Encode splat.sh1 through splat.shF using EncodeFloat3ToNorm11. Copy to SHTableItemNorm11. Write to output. Norm6: Encode splat.sh1 through splat.shF using EncodeFloat3ToNorm565. Copy to SHTableItemNorm6. Set shPadding = default. Write to output. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class float3: x: float; y: float; z: float class half3: x: float; y: float; z: float # half precision storage class uint: value: int class SHTableItemFloat32: sh1: float3; sh2: float3; sh3: float3; sh4: float3; sh5: float3; sh6: float3 sh7: float3; sh8: float3; sh9: float3; shA: float3; shB: float3; shC: float3 shD: float3; shE: float3; shF: float3; shPadding: float3 class SHTableItemFloat16: sh1: half3; sh2: half3; sh3: half3; sh4: half3; sh5: half3; sh6: half3 sh7: half3; sh8: half3; sh9: half3; shA: half3; shB: half3; shC: half3 shD: half3; shE: half3; shF: half3; shPadding: half3 class SHTableItemNorm11: sh1: uint; sh2: uint; sh3: uint; sh4: uint; sh5: uint; sh6: uint sh7: uint; sh8: uint; sh9: uint; shA: uint; shB: uint; shC: uint shD: uint; shE: uint; shF: uint; shPadding: uint class SHTableItemNorm6: sh1: uint; sh2: uint; sh3: uint; sh4: uint; sh5: uint; sh6: uint sh7: uint; sh8: uint; sh9: uint; shA: uint; shB: uint; shC: uint shD: uint; shE: uint; shF: uint; shPadding: uint def EncodeFloat3ToNorm11(v: float3) -> uint: # Standard 11-bit float quantization return uint(int(v.x 2047) & 0x7FF) # Simplified for illustration def EncodeFloat3ToNorm565(v: float3) -> uint: # Standard 5-6-5 RGB quantization r = int(v.x 31) & 0x1F g = int(v.y 63) & 0x3F b = int(v.z 31) & 0x1F return uint((r << 11) | (g << 5) | b) def sizeof(typename: str) -> int: # Returns byte size of the struct sizes = {"SHTableItemFloat32": 192, "SHTableItemFloat16": 96, body: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting Scene Management handles the runtime lifecycle of 3D Gaussian splats within a rendering engine, specifically addressing the need for continuous, batched updates in dynamic scenes. Unlike static loading methods that require full re-initialization, this method supports incremental append operations and dynamic buffer resizing, allowing the scene to grow or refresh without restarting the renderer. The method operates on a Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) paradigm, maintaining device-resident buffers for splat attributes and metadata. It manages the transition from host memory to device memory through a series of validated steps. Inputs: shdegree: Integer in [0, 4] determining spherical harmonic complexity. initialcapacity: Integer \ge 0 for the initial buffer size. batchcount: Number of splats to append. meansxyz: N \times 3 float array of positions. quaternionswxyz: N \times 4 float array of rotations in scalar-last order (x, y, z, w). logscalesxyz: N \times 3 float array of log-scales. opacitylogits: N float array of opacity logits. featuresdcrgb: N \times 3 float array of DC spherical harmonic coefficients. featuresshrgb: N \times D \times 3 float array of higher-order SH coefficients, where D = (sh\degree + 1)^2 - 1. cameraparams: Width, height, view matrix (4 \times 4), and intrinsics (fx, fy, cx, cy). scalemodifier: Positive finite float for global scale adjustment. Outputs: Rendered image buffers (RGBA8, Depth, or Opacity). Updated scene state (count, capacity, device buffers). The core state is held in DeviceScene and HostRender structures. DeviceScene (Device Memory): means: float3 pointer, size capacity \times 3. quats: float4 pointer, size capacity \times 4. scales: float3 pointer, size capacity \times 3. opacities: float pointer, size capacity. featuresdc: float3 pointer, size capacity \times 3. featuressh: float3 pointer, size capacity \times num\sh. count: int64t, current number of splats. capacity: int64t, current buffer capacity. shdegree: int, current SH degree. numsh: int, number of SH coefficients per splat. HostRender (Pinned Host Memory): rgb: float3 pointer, size rgb\pixels. scalar: float pointer, size scalar\pixels. rgbpixels: sizet. scalarpixels: sizet. 1. Initialize Renderer: Validate shdegree in [0, 4] and initialcapacity \ge 0. Reset engine state and release existing scene data. Set scene.shdegree to shdegree. Calculate scene.numsh as (sh\degree + 1)^2 - 1. Reserve memory for initialcapacity. Bind scene to engine. 2. Reserve Scene Capacity: If requestedcapacity > currentcapacity: Calculate nextcapacity as \max(requested, \max(4096, current\capacity \times 2)). Grow all device buffers (means, quats, scales, opacities, featuresdc) to nextcount. If numsh > 0, grow featuressh to nextcount numsh. Update scene.capacity and bind scene. 3. Bind Scene to Engine: Set state.curnumsplats to scene.count. Set state.maxnumsplats to scene.capacity. Set state.numsh to scene.numsh and state.shdegree to scene.shdegree. Create DeviceVector views for means, quats, scales, opacities, featuresdc with size capacity. If numsh > 0, create DeviceTensor2D view for featuressh with dimensions (capacity, numsh, 3); else empty tensor. Set state.world.initialized to true if capacity > 0. 4. Append Splats: Validate batchcount \ge 0 and input arrays are non-null. Check for integer overflow: if scene.count > numericlimits<int64t>::max() - batchcount, throw std::overflowerror. Calculate offset = scene.count. Reserve space for offset + batchcount (triggering capacity growth if needed). Copy means, quats, scales, opacities, featuresdc from host to device at offset. If numsh > 0, copy featuressh from host to device at offset numsh. Increment scene.count. 5. Set Camera: Validate width/height > 0 and viewmatrix/intrinsics non-null. Initialize distcoeffs[8] to zero internally. Call setcameraparams with width, height, "PINHOLE", "NONE", viewmatrix (1 \times 4 \times 4 float), and intrinsics (1 \times 4 float). Set width, height, and cameraready = true. 6. Set Scale Modifier: Validate modifier > 0 and finite. If modifier equals current scalemodifier, return. Calculate logdelta = \log(requested\modifier / scale\modifier). Calculate numel = scene.count \times 3. Allocate device scratch buffer of size maxchunk (1 \ll 20). Loop over numel in chunks: Copy logdelta to device chunk. Call floataddinto on scales chunk and device delta chunk. Free scratch buffer. Update scalemodifier. 7. Render Color: Validate output buffer size \ge pixelcount \times 4. If scene.count == 0, fill output with black (RGB 0,0,0) and alpha 255. Determine rendershdegree as \min(requested\sh\degree, scene.sh\degree) if requested \ge 0, else scene.shdegree. Call forward3dgs("3dgs", rendershdegree, true). Get RGB buffer from state.fwd.renders. Resize host.rgb if needed. Copy RGB from device to host. Write RGB to output buffer using writegrayorrgb. 8. Render Depth: Validate output. If scene.count == 0, fill black/alpha 255. Call forward3dgs. Get depth buffer from state.fwd.renders (index 1). Resize host.scalar if needed. Copy depth from device to host. Call writedepth(output, pixelcount). 9. Render Opacity: Validate output. If scene.count == 0, fill black/alpha 255. Call forward3dgs. Get transmittance buffer from state.fwd.renderTs. Resize host.scalar if needed. Copy transmittance from device to host. Loop over pixels to write opacity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class DynamicGaussianScene: def init(self, shdegree: int, initialcapacity: int): self.shdegree = shdegree self.numsh = (shdegree + 1) 2 - 1 self.count = 0 self.capacity = 0 self.scalemodifier = 1.0 # Device buffers (simulated as numpy arrays for clarity) self.means = None self.quats = None self.scales = None self.opacities = None self.featuresdc = None self.featuressh = None self.resize(initialcapacity) def resize(self, newcapacity: int): """Grow buffers to newcapacity following the doubling strategy.""" if newcapacity > self.capacity: nextcapacity = max(newcapacity, max(4096, self.capacity 2)) else: nextcapacity = self.capacity if nextcapacity == self.capacity: return # Grow buffers self.means = np.resize(self.means, (nextcapacity, 3)) self.quats = np.resize(self.quats, (nextcapacity, 4)) self.scales = np.resize(self.scales, (nextcapacity, 3)) self.opacities = np.resize(self.opacities, (nextcapacity,)) self.featuresdc = np.resize(self.featuresdc, (nextcapacity, 3)) if self.numsh > 0: self.featuressh = np.resize(self.featuressh, (nextcapacity, self.numsh, 3)) self.capacity = nextcapacity def append(self, count: int, means: np.ndarray, quats: np.ndarray, logscales: np.ndarray, opacities: np.ndarray, featuresdc: np.ndarray, featuressh: np.ndarray): """Append a batch of splats.""" if count < 0: raise ValueError("Batch count must be >= 0") # Overflow check if self.count > np.iinfo(np.int64).max - count: raise OverflowError("Scene count overflow") offset = self.count self.resize(offset + count) # Copy data to device (simulated by numpy slice assignment) end = offset + count self.means[offset:end] = means self.quats[offset:end] = quats self.scales[offset:end] = logscales self.opacities[offset:end] = opacities self.featuresdc[offset:end] = featuresdc if self.numsh > 0: self.featuressh[offset:end] = featuressh self.count = end def setscalemodifier(self, modifier: float): """Apply global scale modifier via log-space addition.""" if modifier <= 0 or not math.isfinite(modifier): raise ValueError("Modifier must be positive and finite") if modifier == self.scalemodifier: return logdelta = math.log(modifier / self.scalemodifier) self.scalemodifier = modifier # Apply to existing scales in log space using chunked scratch buffer simulation numel = self.count 3 maxchunk = 1 << 20 for i in range(0, numel, maxchunk): chunksize = min(maxchunk, numel - i) # Simulate floataddinto on scales chunk and devicedelta chunk self.scales[i // 3: (i + chunksize) // 3] += logdelta def render(self, width: int, height: int, viewmatrix: np.ndarray, intrinsics: np.ndarray, outputmode: int): """Render the scene.""" pixelcount = width height if self.count == 0: # Fill black/alpha 255 return np.zeros((pixelcount, 4), dtype=np.uint8) # Determine SH degree # In a real implementation, this calls forward3dgs # Here we simulate the result based on mode if outputmode == 0: # Color # Simulate RGB output return np.random.randint(0, 255, (pixelcount, 3), dtype=np.uint8) elif outputmode == 1: # Depth # Simulate Depth output return np.random.rand(pixelcount).astype(np.float32) elif outputmode == 2: # Opacity # Simulate Opacity output return np.random.rand(pixelcount).astype(np.float32) else: raise ValueError("Unknown output mode") shdegree: Integer, range [0, 4]. Determines spherical harmonic complexity. numsh is calculated as (sh\degree + 1)^2 - 1. scalemodifier: Float, must be positive and finite. Applied multiplicatively to splat scales via log-space addition to avoid precision issues and allow dynamic adjustment. Empty Scene: If scene.count == 0 during render, the renderer outputs a black image (RGB 0,0,0) with full alpha (255) instead of crashing or rendering nothing. Buffer Overflow: Append checks for integer overflow when adding batchcount to scene.count. Throws std::overflowerror if scene.count > numericlimits<int64t>::max() - batchcount. Precision: Scales are stored in log-space to ensure positivity during optimization. Linear scales are recovered via s{linear} = \exp(s{log}) for covariance calculation. Manages the dynamic lifecycle of 3D Gaussian splats within a ROS2-enabled rendering pipeline, bridging sensor or simulation data to the GPU renderer. It solves the problem of real-time scene updates by queuing incoming Gaussian batches and efficiently draining them to the renderer state. It differs from static loading by enabling continuous, batched updates via ROS2 communication, allowing the scene to grow or refresh without full re-initialization. Time Complexity: Append operations are O(N) for data copy, where N is the batch size. Capacity growth involves reallocation and copy, which is amortized O(1) per splat if the doubling strategy is used. Rendering is O(P \cdot N) where P is pixel count and N is splat count, typical for Gaussian Splatting. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot C) where N is capacity and C is the number of attributes per splat. The doubling strategy ensures memory usage is at most 2 \times the required capacity. Performance: The method uses pinned host memory for readback and device buffers for storage, optimizing data transfer. The use of log-space for scales and opacities avoids precision issues during optimization. Strengths: Supports dynamic scenes with incremental updates. Efficient buffer management with minimum capacity of 4096 and doubling strategy. Limitations: Requires careful management of buffer sizes to avoid excessive reallocation. Integer overflow checks are necessary for large scenes. The method originates from the ROSplat project, which integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting with ROS2 for dynamic scene management. It builds on the principles of Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) data layout for cache coherency. The specific implementation details, such as the buffer growth logic and log-space storage, are derived from the Spirula renderer bridge. It solves the problem of real-time scene updates by queuing incoming Gaussian batches and efficiently draining them to the renderer state. It differs from static loading by enabling continuous, batched updates without full re-initialization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: ROS2 messages (SingleGaussian, GaussianArray) containing Gaussian attributes; configuration parameters for scene capacity and rendering options. Output: Updated GPU device memory (DeviceScene) containing Gaussian attributes; rendered images (color, depth, opacity) based on current camera and scene state. Data Structures: The core state is held in DeviceScene and managed via TorchTensorView wrappers. DeviceScene layout: float3 means: Device pointer to position data. Size: capacity 3 floats. float4 quats: Device pointer to rotation quaternions. Size: capacity 4 floats. float3 scales: Device pointer to scale vectors. Size: capacity 3 floats. float opacities: Device pointer to opacity values. Size: capacity floats. float3 featuresdc: Device pointer to DC spherical harmonic coefficients. Size: capacity 3 floats. float3 featuressh: Device pointer to higher-order SH coefficients. Size: capacity numsh 3 floats (if numsh > 0). int64t count: Current number of active Gaussians. int64t capacity: Maximum allocated Gaussians. int shdegree: Active SH degree. int numsh: Number of SH coefficients per Gaussian. TorchTensorView layout: uint64t pointer: Raw device pointer address. int itemsize: Element size in bytes (always sizeof(float)). std::vector<int64t> shape: Dimensions of the tensor. Allocate arrays of shape (count, 3), (count, 4), (count, 3), (count, 1), (count, shdim). Fill arrays by iterating messages. Pack data into a batch structure compatible with appendgaussians. 2. Batch Queuing: Acquire pendinglock. If refresh flag is true: Clear pendingbatches, set gaussiancount to batchcount, and assign batch to gaussianset. Else (append mode): Calculate available = MAXGAUSSIANS - gaussiancount. If available <= 0, return (drop batch). If batchcount > available, truncate batch to available elements across all fields. Increment gaussiancount by batchcount. Append (batch, refresh) to pendingbatches. Set fullscenedirty = False and havenewgaussians = True. 3.
