name: ROS Topic Splat Loading
head: RosTopicSource
body: A method to load 3D Gaussian splats from a ROS topic by subscribing to a SplatArray message and converting the wire format into a GPU-ready SplatGPU struct layout. It differs from static loading by enabling real-time scene updates via ROS2 communication, bridging simulation or sensor data directly into the Gaussian Splatting renderer. Inputs: A ROS2 SplatArray message containing a list of splats, each with pose, opacity, covariance, and spherical harmonics. Outputs: A LoadResult structure containing a vector of SplatGPU structs and the scene's SH degree. Data Structures: SplatGPU: The internal GPU-ready representation. center[3]: float array for position (x, y, z). alpha: float for opacity, normalized to [0, 1]. covA[3]: float array storing the first row of the symmetric 3 \times 3 covariance matrix. covB[3]: float array storing the second row of the symmetric 3 \times 3 covariance matrix. sh[numcoefs][4]: float array for spherical harmonics coefficients where sh[k][0..2] stores RGB for degree k and sh[k][3] is padding. LoadResult: splats: std::vector<SplatGPU>. shdegree: uint32t. Wire Format Mapping: The input SplatArray message contains individual splat messages. The mapping from ROS message fields to SplatGPU fields is as follows: center: Extracted from s.pose.pose.pose.position.x/y/z. alpha: Extracted from s.opacity (uint8, range 0–255) via alpha = opacity / 255.0. covA: Extracted from s.pose.pose.covariance (6x6 row-major array) at indices 0, 1, 2. covB: Extracted from s.pose.pose.covariance at indices 7, 8, 14. sh: Extracted from s.sphericalharmonics (coef-major, RGB-interleaved) where sh[k][0..2] maps to sphericalharmonics[3k+0..2]. Algorithm: 1. Initialize LoadResult out. 2. Determine shdegree: If msg.splats is not empty, set shdegree = msg.splats[0].harmonicsdeg. Else, set shdegree = 0. 3. Calculate numcoefs = (shdegree + 1)^2. 4. Reserve memory for out.splats based on msg.splats.size(). 5. For each splat s in msg.splats: a. Create SplatGPU g. b. Set g.center[0] = (float)s.pose.pose.pose.position.x. c. Set g.center[1] = (float)s.pose.pose.pose.position.y. d. Set g.center[2] = (float)s.pose.pose.pose.position.z. e. Set g.alpha = (float)s.opacity / 255.0f. f. Extract covariance from s.pose.pose.covariance array (let this be cov): i. g.covA[0] = (float)cov[0]. ii. g.covA[1] = (float)cov[1]. iii. g.covA[2] = (float)cov[2]. iv. g.covB[0] = (float)cov[7]. v. g.covB[1] = (float)cov[8]. vi. g.covB[2] = (float)cov[14]. g. Loop k from 0 to numcoefs - 1: i. g.sh[k][0] = (float)s.sphericalharmonics[3k + 0]. ii. g.sh[k][1] = (float)s.sphericalharmonics[3k + 1]. iii. g.sh[k][2] = (float)s.sphericalharmonics[3k + 2]. iv. g.sh[k][3] = 0.0f. h. Push g to out.splats. 6. Set out.shdegree = shdegree. 7. Return out. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SplatGPU: def init(self): self.center = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.alpha = 0.0 self.covA = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.covB = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.sh = [] class LoadResult: def init(self): self.splats = [] self.shdegree = 0 def loadrossplats(msg): out = LoadResult() if len(msg.splats) > 0: out.shdegree = msg.splats[0].harmonicsdeg else: out.shdegree = 0 numcoefs = (out.shdegree + 1) 2 for s in msg.splats: g = SplatGPU() g.center[0] = float(s.pose.pose.pose.position.x) g.center[1] = float(s.pose.pose.pose.position.y) g.center[2] = float(s.pose.pose.pose.position.z) g.alpha = float(s.opacity) / 255.0 cov = s.pose.pose.covariance g.covA[0] = float(cov[0]) g.covA[1] = float(cov[1]) g.covA[2] = float(cov[2]) g.covB[0] = float(cov[7]) g.covB[1] = float(cov[8]) g.covB[2] = float(cov[14]) g.sh = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(numcoefs)] shdata = s.sphericalharmonics for k in range(numcoefs): baseidx = 3 k g.sh[k][0] = float(shdata[baseidx + 0]) g.sh[k][1] = float(shdata[baseidx + 1]) g.sh[k][2] = float(shdata[baseidx + 2]) g.sh[k][3] = 0.0 out.splats.append(g) return out Parameters: QoS Profile: reliable() transport and transientlocal() durability. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Assumes uniform harmonicsdeg across all splats in the message. Assumes deg <= 3. If sphericalharmonics length does not match 3 \times (deg+1)^2, behavior is undefined. Not given in the sources. This method is part of the gsplatrvizplugin within the splat-ros ecosystem, designed to integrate 3D Gaussian Splatting visualization into ROS2-based robotics frameworks. It enables real-time rendering of dynamic Gaussian scenes published over ROS topics. splat-ros/RVizSplat, https://github.com/splat-ros/RVizSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: WASM Data Packing
head: DataWorker Packing, Splat Buffer Allocation
body: WASM Data Packing manages WebAssembly memory allocation and data packing for 3D Gaussian splat attributes (positions, rotations, scales, colors, selection) to prepare them for GPU upload or WASM-side processing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Splat object containing attribute arrays (positions, rotations, scales, colors, selection) and a vertexCount. Output: A contiguous block of memory in the WebAssembly heap (HEAPF32 and HEAPU8) organized in a Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) layout, ready for direct memory access by WASM functions or GPU buffers. Data Structures: The Splat class fields include: offset: number position: Float32Array[3] rotation: Float32Array[4] scale: Float32Array[3] selected: boolean vertexCount: number positions: Float32Array rotations: Float32Array scales: Float32Array colors: Uint8Array selection: Uint8Array Buffer Layout and Sizes: The packed memory is divided into specific regions based on allocatedVertexCount (the next power of 2 greater than or equal to vertexCount). Each float occupies 4 bytes. 1. positionsPtr: Size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 2. rotationsPtr: Size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 3. scalesPtr: Size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 4. colorsPtr: Size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. 5. selectionPtr: Size = \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. 6. dataPtr: Size = 8 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. 7. worldPositionsPtr: Size = 3 \times 4 \times 4 = 48 bytes. 8. worldRotationsPtr: Size = 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64 bytes. 9. worldScalesPtr: Size = 3 \times 4 \times 4 = 48 bytes. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Call initWasm(). This loads the WASM module via createDataModule(). If the module is not yet loaded, pack() waits for loading to finish, initializes WASM, and proceeds. 2. Capacity Calculation: Calculate targetAllocatedVertexCount as the next power of 2 greater than or equal to splat.vertexCount: \text{targetAllocatedVertexCount} = 2^{\lceil \log2(\text{splat.vertexCount}) \rceil} 3. Memory Reallocation: If targetAllocatedVertexCount is larger than the current allocatedVertexCount: a. Free old WASM buffers using wasmModule.free(). b. Update allocatedVertexCount to targetAllocatedVertexCount. c. Allocate new buffers using wasmModule.malloc() for each attribute region. 4. Data Copying: Copy splat attribute arrays into the newly allocated WASM memory regions: a. Use wasmModule.HEAPF32.set() for float arrays (positions, rotations, scales). b. Use wasmModule.HEAPU8.set() for byte arrays (colors, selection). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pack(splat): # Ensure WASM module is loaded; if not, wait for initialization if not wasmmoduleloaded: # initwasm() and waitforwasmload() abstract the async module loading step initializewasmmodule() # Calculate next power of 2 capacity vertexcount = splat.vertexcount targetcapacity = 1 if vertexcount == 0 else 2 math.ceil(math.log2(vertexcount)) # Check if reallocation is needed if targetcapacity > allocatedvertexcount: # Free old WASM buffers if allocatedvertexcount > 0: wasmmodule.free(positionsptr) wasmmodule.free(rotationsptr) wasmmodule.free(scalesptr) wasmmodule.free(colorsptr) wasmmodule.free(selectionptr) wasmmodule.free(dataptr) wasmmodule.free(worldpositionsptr) wasmmodule.free(worldrotationsptr) wasmmodule.free(worldscalesptr) # Update capacity allocatedvertexcount = targetcapacity # Allocate new buffers positionsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(3 allocatedvertexcount 4) rotationsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(4 allocatedvertexcount 4) scalesptr = wasmmodule.malloc(3 allocatedvertexcount 4) colorsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(4 allocatedvertexcount) selectionptr = wasmmodule.malloc(allocatedvertexcount) dataptr = wasmmodule.malloc(8 allocatedvertexcount 4) worldpositionsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(48) worldrotationsptr = wasmmodule.malloc(64) worldscalesptr = wasmmodule.malloc(48) # Copy data into WASM heap # HEAPF32.set expects offset in 32-bit elements wasmmodule.HEAPF32.set(splat.positions, positionsptr // 4) wasmmodule.HEAPF32.set(splat.rotations, rotationsptr // 4) wasmmodule.HEAPF32.set(splat.scales, scalesptr // 4) # HEAPU8.set expects offset in bytes wasmmodule.HEAPU8.set(splat.colors, colorsptr) wasmmodule.HEAPU8.set(splat.selection, selectionptr) # world pointers are allocated but population logic is not specified in the source Parameters: positionsPtr: allocated size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. rotationsPtr: allocated size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. scalesPtr: allocated size = 3 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. colorsPtr: allocated size = 4 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. selectionPtr: allocated size = \text{allocatedVertexCount} bytes. dataPtr: allocated size = 8 \times \text{allocatedVertexCount} \times 4 bytes. worldPositionsPtr: allocated size = 48 bytes. worldRotationsPtr: allocated size = 64 bytes. worldScalesPtr: allocated size = 48 bytes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concurrent Calls: Concurrent calls to pack() are serialized via a loading flag and a while loop with setTimeout to yield to the event loop, preventing race conditions during WASM initialization. Memory Efficiency: Memory is only freed and reallocated when the next power-of-2 capacity exceeds the current allocatedVertexCount, preventing frequent reallocations for incremental vertex count changes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces JavaScript-to-GPU transfer overhead by pre-packaging data in a contiguous WASM heap. Power-of-2 allocation minimizes fragmentation and reallocation frequency. Limitations: Requires WebAssembly environment. Power-of-2 allocation can lead to memory waste if the vertex count is not a power of 2. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splats in a WebAssembly-based environment where data needs to be prepared for GPU upload or WASM-side processing. When not to use: In pure CPU-based rendering or environments without WebAssembly support. WASM Data Packing is part of the gsplat.js library, which provides JavaScript/TypeScript bindings for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was developed to enable efficient rendering of Gaussian Splats in web browsers using WebAssembly. huggingface/gsplat.js, https://github.com/huggingface/gsplat.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics Representation
head: SH in 3DGS, Spherical Harmonics (SH) in 3DGS SLAM, Spherical Harmonics Algorithm, View-dependent color via SH
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) is a mathematical basis used in 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent the view-dependent color of each Gaussian primitive. It adds view-dependent color representation to Gaussians, capturing appearance variations that a single static RGB value cannot represent. An analytical Jacobian propagates gradients from SH to camera poses during optimization, though this may marginally worsen trajectory estimates if SH incorrectly models non-view-dependent effects caused by camera motion. Inputs: The viewing direction vector \mathbf{v} (normalized) in the local coordinate system of the Gaussian. The SH degree parameter L (denoted as shdegree in implementation), which determines the maximum degree l used. The SH coefficients c{l,m}^k for each color channel k \in \{R, G, B\}. Outputs: The view-dependent color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{v}) = [CR, CG, CB]^T. Each 3D Gaussian stores SH coefficients. For a maximum degree L, the number of coefficients per color channel is (L+1)^2. The total number of coefficients per Gaussian is 3(L+1)^2. Layout: The coefficients are typically stored as a flat array or a tensor of shape [3, (L+1)^2] or [(L+1)^2, 3]. Bit Packing: Not specified in the sources. Spherical Harmonics are derived from the solution of Laplace's equation in a 3D spherical coordinate system. 1. Laplace's Equation: In Cartesian coordinates: \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} = 0 Converted to spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \varphi) where x = r\sin\theta\cos\varphi, y = r\sin\theta\sin\varphi, z = r\cos\theta: \frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial }{\partial r}\left(r^{2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^{2}\sin\theta } \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\left(\sin\theta \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta }\right) + \frac{1}{r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta } \frac{\partial ^{2} f}{\partial \varphi ^{2}} = 0 2. Separation of Variables: Assume f(r, \theta, \varphi) = R(r)\Theta(\theta)\Phi(\varphi). This yields: Radial part: \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{2}\frac{\partial R}{\partial r}\right) = \lambda Azimuthal part: \frac{\partial^{2}\Phi}{\partial \varphi^{2}} = -m^{2}\Phi, where m \in \mathbb{N} Polar part: \sin\theta \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left(\sin\theta \frac{\partial \Theta}{\partial \theta}\right) = (m^{2}-\lambda \sin^{2}\theta)\Theta 3. Associated Legendre Equation: Let x = \cos\theta, \Theta \rightarrow P(x), and \lambda = l(l+1) where l \in \mathbb{Z}^+. The equation becomes: \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[(1-x^{2})\frac{\partial P(x)}{\partial x}\right] + \left[l(l+1)-\frac{m^{2}}{1-x^{2}}\right]P(x) = 0 The solution is the Associated Legendre Function Pl^m(x). Rodrigues' formula is given as: P{l}(x)=\frac{1}{2^{l}l!}\frac{\partial ^{l}}{\partial x^{l}}(x^2-1)^{l} Orthonormality condition: \int{-1}^{1}\sqrt{\frac{2m+1}{2}}P{m}(x) \sqrt{\frac{2n+1}{2}}P{n}(x)dx=\delta{mn} Recursion relation: (l+1)P{l+1}(x)=(2l+1)xP{l}(x)-lP{l-1}(x) 4. Spherical Harmonics Function: The SH basis functions Yl^m(\theta, \varphi) are defined as: Yl^m(\theta, \varphi) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2} K{l}^{m}\cos(m\varphi)P{l}^{m}(\cos\theta) & m > 0 \\ \sqrt{2} K{l}^{m}\sin(-m\varphi)P{l}^{-m}(\cos\theta) & m < 0 \\ K{l}^{0}P{l}^{0}(\cos\theta) & m = 0 \end{cases} The normalization scaling factor K{l}^{m} is: K{l}^{m}=\sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}\cdot \frac{(l-|m|)!}{(l+|m|)!}} where l \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}, m \in \mathbb{Z}, |m| \le l. The color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{v}) for a viewing direction \mathbf{v} (represented by spherical angles \theta, \varphi) is computed by projecting the SH coefficients onto the basis functions: \mathbf{C}(\theta, \varphi) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{l,m} Yl^m(\theta, \varphi) The number of basis functions is (L+1)^2. For L=3, this is 16 coefficients per channel. shdegree (L): The maximum degree of SH coefficients. Default value is 3. L=0: View-independent color (constant). L=1: Captures linear variations (e.g., simple lighting). L=2, 3: Captures more complex view-dependent effects. Omission: SH can be omitted (set L=0 or disabled) for synthetic datasets like Replica that lack view-directional effects. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeshbasis(theta, phi, maxdegree): """ Computes the Spherical Harmonics basis functions for a given direction. Returns a list of basis values for degrees 0 to maxdegree. """ costheta = math.cos(theta) basis = [] for l in range(maxdegree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): absm = abs(m) # Compute Associated Legendre Function Pl^{|m|}(costheta) plm = associatedlegendre(l, absm, costheta) # Normalization factor klm = math.sqrt((2 l + 1) / (4 math.pi) math.factorial(l - absm) / math.factorial(l + absm)) # Angular part based on m if m > 0: angular = math.sqrt(2) math.cos(m phi) elif m < 0: angular = math.sqrt(2) math.sin(-m phi) else: angular = 1.0 basis.append(klm plm angular) return basis def associatedlegendre(l, m, x): """ Computes the Associated Legendre Function Pl^m(x). Uses recurrence relations for efficiency. """ if m < 0: raise ValueError("m must be non-negative for this implementation") if l < m: return 0.0 if l == 0: return 1.0 if l == 1: return x if m == 0 else 0.0 # Compute Pl^m using recurrence if m == 0: plminus1 = associatedlegendre(l - 1, 0, x) plminus2 = associatedlegendre(l - 2, 0, x) return ((2 l - 1) x plminus1 - (l - 1) plminus2) / l else: # Pm^m if l == m: if m == 0: return 1.0 doublefact = 1 for i in range(1, 2 m, 2): doublefact = i return doublefact ((1 - x x) (m / 2)) # Recurrence for l > m plminus1 = associatedlegendre(l - 1, m, x) plminus2 = associatedlegendre(l - 2, m, x) return ((2 l - 1) x plminus1 - (l + m - 1) plminus2) / (l - m) def rendersh(colorcoeffs, theta, phi, maxdegree): """ Renders the view-dependent color using SH coefficients. colorcoeffs: list of coefficients for R, G, B channels. Shape: [3, (maxdegree+1)^2] """ basis = computeshbasis(theta, phi, maxdegree) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] idx = 0 for l in range(maxdegree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): val = basis[idx] for c in range(3): color[c] += colorcoeffs[c][idx] val idx += 1 return color Precision: Higher degrees (L > 3) increase computational cost and memory usage without guaranteed quality improvement. Boundary Conditions: The SH basis is defined on the unit sphere. Directions must be normalized. Overfitting: Using high SH degrees on datasets without view-dependent effects (like Replica) may lead to overfitting or unnecessary memory usage. Optimizes Gaussian parameters via pull-based gradients; chosen when gradient propagation efficiency is prioritized over push-based methods. Scores Gaussians using accumulated rendering error; chosen for adaptive densification and pruning during training. Manages GPU memory allocation for variable Gaussian counts; chosen when scene complexity fluctuates or memory is constrained. Uses a neural network to predict Gaussian attributes; chosen when parametric generation is preferred over explicit storage. Optimizes large-scale scene rendering via hierarchical structures; chosen for city-scale or massive point cloud datasets. Defines memory layout and compression for Gaussian attributes; chosen to minimize bandwidth and improve cache locality. Integrates 3DGS with visual-inertial odometry; chosen for real-time mapping and pose estimation. Extends Gaussians with additional dimensions (e.g., time, velocity); chosen for dynamic scene reconstruction. Applies deformation fields to static Gaussians; chosen when explicit dynamic primitives are too expensive. Replaces fixed Gaussian kernels with deformable ones; chosen to better model complex shapes and occlusions. Clusters Gaussians for efficient rendering; chosen to reduce draw calls and improve rasterization throughput. Time Complexity: Rendering time scales linearly with the number of basis functions, O((L+1)^2) per Gaussian per pixel. Memory Complexity: Memory per Gaussian increases by 3(L+1)^2 floats. Measured Performance: On TUM RGB-D, enabling SH increases memory from 3.97 MB to 11.47 MB. Rendering PSNR improves from 21.89 to 24.37 with SH enabled. ATE RMSE marginally worsens from 1.47 cm to 1.56 cm with SH enabled. Strengths: Accurately models view-dependent color; enables joint optimization of camera poses via analytical gradients. Limitations: Increases memory usage significantly; may degrade trajectory estimation if SH incorrectly models non-view-dependent effects caused by camera motion. Higher degrees do not always yield better results and increase computational cost. When to Use: When view-dependent effects (specularities, complex lighting) are present. When Not to Use: For synthetic datasets without view-dependent effects (e.g., Replica) or when memory is severely constrained. Spherical Harmonics were introduced as a solution to Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, SH was adopted to represent view-dependent color, building on the original 3DGS method. The method has been widely used in subsequent works, including 3DGS SLAM, dynamic 3DGS, and human 3DGS generation. name: 7D Gaussian Splatting
head: 7D Gaussian Representation, 7DGS, 7DGS definition
body: 7D Gaussian Splatting (7DGS) is a unified framework for the real-time rendering of dynamic scenes with complex view-dependent effects, representing scene elements as seven-dimensional Gaussians spanning spatial position (3D), time (1D), and viewing direction (3D). It solves the problem of simultaneously modeling spatial geometry, temporal dynamics, and view-dependent appearance (such as scattering and anisotropic reflections) in dynamic scenes, a challenge that prior methods like 4DGS and 6DGS addressed in isolation. Unlike its siblings, 7DGS jointly models all three dimensions in a single coherent framework, using a conditional slicing mechanism to transform 7D Gaussians into time- and view-conditioned 3D Gaussians compatible with existing 3DGS rendering pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 7D Gaussian primitives, each defined by a mean vector and a covariance matrix in the joint space of position, time, and direction. Output: A rendered image for a specific camera pose (view direction) and time instance, generated by projecting the conditioned 3D Gaussians and rasterizing them. Data Structures: Each scene element is modeled as a 7D Gaussian random variable X jointly encoding spatial (Xp \in \mathbb{R}^3), temporal (Xt \in \mathbb{R}), and directional (Xd \in \mathbb{R}^3) properties. The distribution is defined as: X \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \begin{pmatrix} \mup \\ \mut \\ \mud \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \Sigmap & \Sigma{pt} & \Sigma{pd} \\ \Sigma{pt}^\top & \Sigmat & \Sigma{td} \\ \Sigma{pd}^\top & \Sigma{td}^\top & \Sigmad \end{pmatrix} \right) where: \mup, \Sigmap: Mean and covariance for spatial coordinates, modeling local geometric shape. \mut, \Sigmat: Mean and variance for the temporal coordinate, accounting for dynamic evolution. \mud, \Sigmad: Mean and covariance for the viewing direction, capturing view-dependent appearance. \Sigma{pt}, \Sigma{pd}, \Sigma{td}: Off-diagonal blocks capturing correlations among spatial, temporal, and directional components, enabling the modeling of complex interdependencies. The full 7D covariance matrix \Sigma is parameterized using Cholesky decomposition to guarantee validity during optimization: \Sigma = L L^\top where L is a lower-triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries. Color representation uses view-dependent spherical harmonics from 3DGS without additional temporal dependencies, as dynamic information is encoded within the Gaussian parameters. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize 7D Gaussians: Create a set of 7D Gaussians where each primitive stores \mup, \mut, \mud, \alpha (opacity), and the Cholesky factor L of the covariance matrix \Sigma. 2. Conditional Slicing: For a target rendering time t and view direction d, compute the conditioned 3D Gaussian parameters for each primitive. This involves calculating the conditional mean \mu{cond} and conditional covariance \Sigma{cond} of the spatial component Xp given Xt = t and Xd = d. Let the joint mean be \mu = [\mup^\top, \mut, \mud^\top]^\top and the joint covariance be \Sigma. Partition \Sigma and \mu into spatial (p), temporal (t), and directional (d) parts. The conditional mean is: \mu{cond} = \mup + \Sigma{pz} \Sigma{zz}^{-1} (z - \muz). The conditional covariance is: \Sigma{cond} = \Sigma{pp} - \Sigma{pz} \Sigma{zz}^{-1} \Sigma{zp}. (Where z = [t, d]^\top, \Sigma{zz} is the covariance of the conditioned variables, and \Sigma{pz} contains the cross-covariances \Sigma{pt} and \Sigma{pd}). 3. Adaptive Refinement: During optimization, use a neural network to predict residuals that dynamically adjust Gaussian parameters to model complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance. 4. Render: Project the conditioned 3D Gaussians (\mu{cond}, \Sigma{cond}, \alpha) onto the image plane using standard 3DGS projection and rasterization. Compute color using spherical harmonics evaluated at the view direction d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def choleskydecompose(covmatrix): """ Computes the lower-triangular matrix L such that Sigma = L @ L.T. Ensures positive diagonal entries. """ L = np.linalg.cholesky(covmatrix) return L def reconstructcovariance(L): """ Reconstructs the covariance matrix from its Cholesky factor. """ return L @ L.T def conditionalslice7dto3d(mean7d, L7d, timeval, directionvec): """ Slices a 7D Gaussian into a 3D Gaussian conditioned on time and direction. Args: mean7d: Array of shape (7,) containing [mup (3), mut (1), mud (3)] L7d: Lower-triangular Cholesky factor of shape (7, 7) timeval: Scalar time value t directionvec: Array of shape (3,) representing view direction d Returns: mucond: Array of shape (3,) conditioned spatial mean Sigmacond: Array of shape (3, 3) conditioned spatial covariance """ # Extract components mup = mean7d[0:3] mut = mean7d[3] mud = mean7d[4:7] # Reconstruct full covariance matrix Sigma = reconstructcovariance(L7d) # Partition Sigma into blocks # Indices: 0-2 (p), 3 (t), 4-6 (d) Sigmapp = Sigma[0:3, 0:3] Sigmapt = Sigma[0:3, 3:4] Sigmapd = Sigma[0:3, 4:7] Sigmatp = Sigma[3:4, 0:3] Sigmatt = Sigma[3:4, 3:4] Sigmatd = Sigma[3:4, 4:7] Sigmadp = Sigma[4:7, 0:3] Sigmadt = Sigma[4:7, 3:4] Sigmadd = Sigma[4:7, 4:7] # Construct the joint covariance of the conditioned variables (t, d) # and the cross-covariance with p # Let z = [t, d]. We want p | z. # Covariance of z (time and direction) Sigmazz = np.zeros((4, 4)) Sigmazz[0, 0] = Sigmatt Sigmazz[0, 1:] = Sigmatd Sigmazz[1:, 0] = Sigmadt Sigmazz[1:, 1:] = Sigmadd # Cross-covariance between p and z Sigmapz = np.hstack((Sigmapt, Sigmapd)) # Shape (3, 4) # Residual vector for conditioning # z - muz muz = np.array([mut, mud]) residualz = np.array([timeval - mut, (directionvec - mud)]) # Compute conditional mean: mup + Sigmapz @ Sigmazz^-1 @ (z - muz) # Solve Sigmazz @ x = residualz for x try: invSigmazzresidual = np.linalg.solve(Sigmazz, residualz) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: # Fallback for singular matrices, though Cholesky implies positive definite invSigmazzresidual = np.linalg.lstsq(Sigmazz, residualz, rcond=None)[0] mucond = mup + Sigmapz @ invSigmazzresidual # Compute conditional covariance: Sigmapp - Sigmapz @ Sigmazz^-1 @ Sigmazp Sigmazp = Sigmapz.T correction = Sigmapz @ np.linalg.solve(Sigmazz, Sigmazp) Sigmacond = Sigmapp - correction return mucond, Sigmacond def render7dgs(gaussians, timeval, directionvec, cameraparams): """ Renders a frame using 7DGS. Args: gaussians: List of dicts, each containing 'mean7d' (7,), 'L7d' (7,7), 'alpha', 'shcoeffs' timeval: Float, current time directionvec: Array (3,), view direction cameraparams: Object with projection matrix and intrinsics Returns: image: Rendered image array """ # 1. Slice all 7D Gaussians to 3D conditionedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: mucond, Sigmacond = conditionalslice7dto3d( g['mean7d'], g['L7d'], timeval, directionvec) conditionedgaussians.append({ 'mu': mucond, 'Sigma': Sigmacond, 'alpha': g['alpha'], 'shcoeffs': g['shcoeffs'] }) # 2. Project and Rasterize (Standard 3DGS Pipeline) # Perform standard 3DGS projection and rasterization image = standard3dgsrasterize(conditionedgaussians, cameraparams) return image Parameters and Typical Values: Spherical Harmonics Degree: Not specified in sources, but inherits from 3DGS/6DGS. Performance: Achieved 401 FPS on challenging dynamic scenes with complex view-dependent effects. Quality: Outperforms prior methods by up to 7.36 dB in PSNR. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Covariance: The Cholesky decomposition requires a positive definite covariance matrix. If optimization leads to a singular or near-singular matrix during conditioning, numerical instability may occur. Boundary Conditions: The sources do not specify handling for time or direction values outside the training domain. A sibling method focusing on pull-based optimization strategies. Link Techniques for managing Gaussian density based on rendering error. Link Methods for handling memory allocation for dynamic Gaussian sets. Link Neural network architectures used for refining Gaussian parameters. Link A method for scaling Gaussian Splatting to very large scenes. Link Efficient storage formats for Gaussian attributes. Link Integration of 7DGS with simultaneous localization and mapping. Link The specific representation used for view-dependent color. Link General approaches to modeling motion in Gaussian fields. Link Alternative kernel parametrizations for dynamic scenes. Link Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved, with reported performance of 401 FPS on challenging dynamic scenes. The conditional slicing operation adds computational overhead compared to static 3DGS, but remains efficient enough for real-time application. Memory Complexity: Higher than static 3DGS due to the storage of temporal and directional means, variances, and cross-covariances for each Gaussian. The Cholesky factor L requires storing 28 values (for a 7x7 lower triangular matrix) plus means and opacity, compared to 10-15 values for standard 3DGS. Strengths: Unified modeling of space, time, and direction; high PSNR (up to 7.36 dB improvement over prior methods); real-time performance; compatibility with existing 3DGS pipelines. Limitations: Increased memory footprint; complexity in optimizing the full 7D covariance matrix; potential numerical instability in conditional slicing if covariance matrices are ill-conditioned. When to use: When rendering dynamic scenes with significant view-dependent effects (e.g., specular highlights, scattering) is required, and real-time performance is necessary. When not to use: For static scenes (use 3DGS) or scenes where only temporal dynamics or only view-dependent effects are present and extreme efficiency is prioritized over unified modeling. 7D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Terrence Chen, and Ziyan Wu from United Imaging Intelligence in March 2025. It addresses the limitations of previous methods: 4DGS, which handles space and time but not view-dependent effects, and 6DGS, which handles space and direction but not temporal dynamics. The method builds on the foundations of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and 6D Gaussian Splatting (6DGS). It has been evaluated on synthetic datasets (D-NeRF) and in-the-wild multi-view videos (Technicolor), as well as a custom dataset (7DGS-PBR) featuring dynamic scenes with complex motions and view-dependent effects. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) Parametrization
head: DRK attribute modeling
body: Deformable Radial Kernel (DRK) parametrization defines the unconstrained learnable parameters for Gaussian kernel attributes, ensuring they remain within valid ranges through specific activation functions. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a specialized activation process for basis angles \thetak to maintain angular separation and monotonicity, and by providing configurable density control thresholds for sparse training scenarios. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs are unconstrained learnable parameters for opacity, scale, rotation, sharpness, blending weight, and basis angles, initialized in (-\infty, \infty). Outputs are validated Gaussian attributes ready for rendering. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar learnable variables associated with each Gaussian kernel, treated as floating-point values during optimization. No specific bit-packing or fixed-size layouts are defined in the sources. Numbered Steps and Formulas: Each attribute is transformed from its unconstrained space to its valid range using the following functions: 1. Opacity (o): Constrained to (0, 1) using a sigmoid function. o = \sigma(\hat{o}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\hat{o}}} where \hat{o} is the unconstrained parameter. 2. Scale (sk): Activated using an exponential function to ensure positive values. sk = \exp(\hat{s}k) where \hat{s}k is the unconstrained parameter. 3. Rotation (q): Constrained to the unit hypersphere using normalization. q = \frac{\hat{q}}{\|\hat{q}\|} where \hat{q} is the unconstrained 4D quaternion vector. 4. Sharpness (\tau): Bounded within (-0.1, 0.99) using a composite function combining sigmoid and linear remapping. \tau = -0.1 + 1.09 \cdot \sigma(\hat{\tau}) \quad where \hat{\tau} is the unconstrained parameter. 5. L1&L2 Blending Weight (\eta): Activated using a sigmoid function. \eta = \sigma(\hat{\eta}) where \hat{\eta} is the unconstrained parameter. 6. Basis Angles (\thetak): For K basis angles, a four-step activation process is employed to enforce monotonic increase and minimum angular separation: Step 1: Apply sigmoid to unconstrained angles \hat{\theta}k. Step 2: Add a residual term \frac{1}{K-2} to maintain minimum angular separation. Step 3: Apply cumulative summation to enforce monotonic increase. Step 4: Normalize the resulting angles so that the final angle sK = 2\pi. The residual term \frac{1}{K-2} prevents basis polar angles from exceeding \pi, thereby avoiding degradation in representation. Parameters: K (Number of basis angles): Set to 8 to balance flexibility and memory efficiency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero is avoided in basis angle normalization by checking if the cumulative sum is zero, falling back to a uniform distribution. The exact linear remapping coefficients for sharpness are not provided in the sources, requiring standard linear mapping implementation. The learning rate decay target is ambiguously stated as "1e-2 ×" in the source text. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def activateopacity(unconstrainedo): """Constrain opacity to (0, 1).""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-unconstrainedo)) def activatescale(unconstraineds): """Constrain scale to positive values.""" return math.exp(unconstraineds) def activaterotation(unconstrainedq): """Normalize quaternion to unit length.""" norm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in unconstrainedq)) return [x / norm for x in unconstrainedq] def activatesharpness(unconstrainedtau): """Bound sharpness within (-0.1, 0.99) using sigmoid and linear remapping.""" sig = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-unconstrainedtau)) return -0.1 + 1.09 sig # Standard linear remapping from (0,1) to (-0.1, 0.99) def activateblendingweight(unconstrainedeta): """Constrain blending weight to (0, 1).""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-unconstrainedeta)) def activatebasisangles(unconstrainedthetas, K=8): """ Activate basis angles with monotonic increase and minimum separation. Args: unconstrainedthetas: List of K unconstrained float values. K: Number of basis angles (default 8). Returns: List of K normalized angles summing to 2pi. """ # Step 1: Apply sigmoid sigmas = [1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-t)) for t in unconstrainedthetas] # Step 2: Add residual term 1/(K-2) residual = 1.0 / (K - 2) adjusted = [s + residual for s in sigmas] # Step 3: Cumulative summation cumulative = [] currentsum = 0.0 for val in adjusted: currentsum += val cumulative.append(currentsum) # Step 4: Normalize to make sK = 2pi finalsum = cumulative[-1] if finalsum == 0: return [2 math.pi / K] K return [val / finalsum (2 math.pi) for val in cumulative] This variant describes the optimization process for DRK parameters. It follows the adaptive training process of 3D-GS, dynamically adjusting kernel density. Learning Rate: DRK-specific parameters (sharpness \tau, blending weight \eta, basis angles \thetak, and scales sk) use a uniform learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-3}. Decay: The learning rate decays gradually to 1 \times 10^{-2} \times (initial rate) at the end of training (35K steps). Density Control: Three configurations are defined by pairs of (2D screen gradient densification threshold, opacity pruning threshold): 1. Comparable to 3D-GS: (5 \times 10^{-4}, 5 \times 10^{-2}). 2. Sparse Level 1 (S1): (1 \times 10^{-3}, 5 \times 10^{-2}). 3. Sparse Level 2 (S2): (2 \times 10^{-3}, 1 \times 10^{-1}). Time and Memory Complexity: The sources do not provide explicit Big-O complexity for the activation functions. The choice of K=8 for basis angles is noted to balance flexibility and memory efficiency. Measured Performance: The method demonstrates robustness under noisy conditions, with rendering results shown for noise standard deviations of 0 and 10^{-3}. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: The residual term in basis angle activation prevents polar angles from exceeding \pi, avoiding representation degradation. The configurable density thresholds allow for controlled sparsity (S1, S2). Limitations: The exact linear remapping formula for sharpness is not provided in the sources. The learning rate decay target is ambiguously stated as "1e-2 ×". DRK parametrization is part of the Deformable Radial Kernel Splatting method, introduced in a paper published in 2025. Deformable Radial Kernel Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.02004, fetched 2026-10-30

name: GaussianEditor (Local)
body: GaussianEditor (Local) is a method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) editing that leverages the explicit nature of Gaussian primitives to allow direct manipulation of parameters (position, rotation, scale, color) based on user commands. It is tailored for local editing, enabling operations such as 3D inpainting, object removal, and object composition. Unlike methods that rely on implicit representations or global optimization, GaussianEditor provides real-time, fine-grained control by grounding text instructions directly onto the 3D Gaussian set. It is chosen for user experience and real-time fine-grained control, whereas LangSplat is superior for efficiency and GIR is optimal for quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation; user text commands (e.g., "select the roof", "remove the tree"). Output: An edited 3D Gaussian Splatting scene with modified primitive parameters. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS data structure defined in Gaussian Data Structure, consisting of a set of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R} Color coefficients (Spherical Harmonics) \mathbf{c}i Steps: 1. Parse Command: Use a Large Language Model (LLM) to parse the user's natural language command into a spatial selection target. 2. Extract Region of Interest (RoI): Extract the semantic region of interest from the text instructions. 3. Align RoI with 3D Gaussians: Align the text-based RoI with the 3D Gaussians through the image space. This involves projecting the 3D scene to 2D views, identifying pixels corresponding to the semantic target, and mapping them back to the 3D Gaussian primitives. 4. Identify Selected Gaussians: Determine the subset of Gaussians \mathcal{G}{sel} that fall within the identified RoI. 5. Apply Transformations: Directly manipulate the parameters of the selected Gaussians \mathcal{G}{sel} based on the command. For removal: Set opacity \alphai = 0 for all i \in \mathcal{G}{sel}. For inpainting/composition: Update color \mathbf{c}i, position \mathbf{p}i, or scale \mathbf{s}i. 6. Render: Render the edited scene using standard differentiable rasterization. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: LLM Ambiguity: LLMs may struggle with ambiguous spatial relations (e.g., "the building behind the park") or domain-specific architectural terminology in vast scenes, leading to incorrect selections. Physical Plausibility: Naively changing parameters like color ignores lighting and material properties, resulting in flat, unrealistic appearances because the method lacks intrinsic physics understanding. Semantic Gap: The method's success is heavily reliant on the LLM's ability to accurately ground abstract concepts onto 3D geometry. An independent research variant of GaussianEditor that operates similarly to the appearance editing version but further introduces hierarchical Gaussian splatting (HGS). It allows for 3D editing tasks such as object inpainting by providing adaptive generative guidance through the hierarchical structure. Strengths: Provides exceptional real-time, fine-grained control and high user experience. Suitable for local editing tasks like inpainting and removal. Limitations: Lacks intrinsic physics understanding, leading to potential visual artifacts (e.g., flat colors) when editing appearance. Relies heavily on the accuracy of the LLM for semantic grounding, which can fail in complex or ambiguous scenes. Not as efficient as LangSplat for large-scale generation. When to use: When user experience and direct, real-time manipulation of specific objects in a 3DGS scene are prioritized over generation efficiency or global consistency. When not to use: When high-fidelity physical plausibility is required without manual correction, or when processing vast scenes with complex spatial relationships where LLM grounding is unreliable. GaussianEditor was introduced as a method tailored for local editing on 3DGS. It epitomizes the direct manipulation workflow enabled by the explicit nature of 3D Gaussian primitives. The method addresses the contradiction between the discrete symbolism of language and the continuous physicality of 3D scenes by using an LLM to bridge this gap. It is part of a series of works based on 3DGS that achieve higher editing efficiency and superior rendering quality compared to earlier NeRF-based editing methods. Implicit vs. explicit a comparative survey on NeRF and 3DGS for large-scale aerial scene editing, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10791-026-10029-9, fetched 2026-10-26 A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28 PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Grouping
body: Gaussian Grouping is a method that enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating identity encodings for 3D objects, enabling the system to group splats based on their semantic identity. It solves the problem of precise object-level manipulation in 3D scenes, specifically enabling object removal, inpainting, and recomposition. The method simultaneously rebuilds and segments open-world 3D objects under the supervision of 2D mask predictions from SAM and 3D spatial consistency constraints. Compared to sibling methods like DFF, Gaussian Grouping removes objects with greatly reduced artifacts and avoids leaving a blurry background. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a 3DGS scene representation and training images as input, and outputs a 3DGS scene where each Gaussian is associated with an object identity for grouped editing. Data Structures: The data structure extends standard 3DGS attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) with an additional Object ID feature. The exact bit layout and storage size of the Object ID are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization assigns initial object IDs to splats using the method from [38]. 2. Training refines object IDs throughout the process. The training process allows the number of splats assigned to each object to be non-uniform, as object IDs are not constrained during training, enabling dynamic allocation for optimal visual quality. 3. Rendering and editing use the object IDs to group splats for operations such as removal, inpainting, and recomposition. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: The primary parameter is the Object ID, an additional feature added to each splat. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pitfalls: A key pitfall is that the number of splats assigned to each object is non-uniform because object IDs are not constrained during training. This technique segments a 3DGS scene into semantically meaningful objects by adding an object ID feature to each splat, allowing for object-level scheduling and editing. Initial object IDs are assigned using the method from [38], and these IDs are refined throughout the training process. The number of splats per object is non-uniform as IDs are unconstrained during training. The method enables object removal, inpainting, and recomposition. Compared to DFF, it removes objects with greatly reduced artifacts without leaving a blurry background. Measured performance, time complexity, memory complexity, and scaling characteristics are not given in the sources. Gaussian Grouping [56] enhances 3DGS by incorporating identity encodings for 3D objects. It is cited in surveys on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28 PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) L3GS: Layered 3D Gaussian Splats for Efficient 3D Scene Delivery, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680207.3723485, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Gaussian Data Packing
head: GaussianData::pack
body: Gaussian Data Packing is a method for serializing 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives into a compact, GPU-friendly binary layout. It solves the problem of transferring large volumes of Gaussian data (position, scale, rotation, color, and precomputed covariance) from CPU memory to the GPU by packing multiple attributes into a contiguous array of 32-bit unsigned integers. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gaussian Data Structure by enforcing a specific interleaved uint32 layout optimized for direct GPU consumption, and from GeometryState Allocation by focusing on the serialization format rather than memory management. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of n Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i consists of: Position: \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) (float32) Scale: \mathbf{s} = (sx, sy, sz) (float32) Rotation: \mathbf{q} = (w, x, y, z) (quaternion, float32) Color: \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b, a) (float32, typically in range [0, 1]) Output: packedData: A std::vector<uint32t> of size 8n. worldPositions: A std::vector<float> of size 3n, storing raw float positions. Data Structures: The packedData array stores two uvec4 per Gaussian. The layout for Gaussian i (indices 8i to 8i+7) is: packedData[8i + 0]: Position X (bit-cast) packedData[8i + 1]: Position Y (bit-cast) packedData[8i + 2]: Position Z (bit-cast) packedData[8i + 3]: Selection flag (0) packedData[8i + 4]: Covariance \sigma{xx} and \sigma{xy} (packed half-precision) packedData[8i + 5]: Covariance \sigma{xz} and \sigma{yy} (packed half-precision) packedData[8i + 6]: Covariance \sigma{yz} and \sigma{zz} (packed half-precision) packedData[8i + 7]: Color RGBA (packed 8-bit integer) Steps: 1. Iterate i from 0 to n-1. 2. Extract \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{c} for Gaussian i. 3. Store raw floats in worldPositions: \text{worldPositions}[3i + 0] = x \text{worldPositions}[3i + 1] = y \text{worldPositions}[3i + 2] = z 4. Bit-cast position components to uint32t using memcpy (preserving IEEE 754 bit pattern): ux = \text{reinterpret\cast<uint32\t>}(x) uy = \text{reinterpret\cast<uint32\t>}(y) uz = \text{reinterpret\cast<uint32\t>}(z) 5. Store ux, uy, uz in packedData[8i+0], packedData[8i+1], packedData[8i+2]. 6. Store 0 in packedData[8i+3] as a selection flag. 7. Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma. First, construct the rotation matrix R from \mathbf{q} and the scale matrix S = \text{diag}(sx, sy, sz). M = R \cdot S The elements of M are denoted M{row,col}. The symmetric covariance matrix \Sigma = M M^T has elements: \sigma{xx} = M{0,0}^2 + M{1,0}^2 + M{2,0}^2 \sigma{xy} = M{0,0}M{0,1} + M{1,0}M{1,1} + M{2,0}M{2,1} \sigma{xz} = M{0,0}M{0,2} + M{1,0}M{1,2} + M{2,0}M{2,2} \sigma{yy} = M{0,1}^2 + M{1,1}^2 + M{2,1}^2 \sigma{yz} = M{0,1}M{0,2} + M{1,1}M{1,2} + M{2,1}M{2,2} \sigma{zz} = M{0,2}^2 + M{1,2}^2 + M{2,2}^2 8. Pack covariance pairs into uint32t using half-precision floating-point packing (packHalf2x16): packedData[8i+4] = \text{packHalf2x16}(\sigma{xx}, \sigma{xy}) packedData[8i+5] = \text{packHalf2x16}(\sigma{xz}, \sigma{yy}) packedData[8i+6] = \text{packHalf2x16}(\sigma{yz}, \sigma{zz}) 9. Pack color into uint32t: \text{packedColor} = \text{uint32}(r \cdot 255) \mid (\text{uint32}(g \cdot 255) \ll 8) \mid (\text{uint32}(b \cdot 255) \ll 16) \mid (\text{uint32}(a \cdot 255) \ll 24) Store packedColor in packedData[8i+7]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packgaussians(gaussians): """ gaussians: list of dicts/objects with keys 'pos' (vec3), 'scale' (vec3), 'rot' (quat), 'color' (vec4 with components 0.0-1.0). Returns: packeddata (list of uint32), worldpositions (list of float) """ n = len(gaussians) packeddata = [0] (n 8) worldpositions = [0.0] (n 3) for i in range(n): g = gaussians[i] x, y, z = g['pos'] sx, sy, sz = g['scale'] qw, qx, qy, qz = g['rot'] r, gval, b, a = g['color'] # 1. Store raw positions worldpositions[3i + 0] = x worldpositions[3i + 1] = y worldpositions[3i + 2] = z # 2. Bit-cast positions to uint32 ux = floattouint32(x) uy = floattouint32(y) uz = floattouint32(z) packeddata[8i + 0] = ux packeddata[8i + 1] = uy packeddata[8i + 2] = uz packeddata[8i + 3] = 0 # Selection flag # 3. Compute Covariance # Convert quaternion to rotation matrix R (3x3) R = quattomat3(qw, qx, qy, qz) # Scale matrix S (diagonal) # M = R S M00 = R[0][0] sx M01 = R[0][1] sy M02 = R[0][2] sz M10 = R[1][0] sx M11 = R[1][1] sy M12 = R[1][2] sz M20 = R[2][0] sx M21 = R[2][1] sy M22 = R[2][2] sz # Sigma elements (Sigma = M M^T) sigmaxx = M00M00 + M10M10 + M20M20 sigmaxy = M00M01 + M10M11 + M20M21 sigmaxz = M00M02 + M10M12 + M20M22 sigmayy = M01M01 + M11M11 + M21M21 sigmayz = M01M02 + M11M12 + M21M22 sigmazz = M02M02 + M12M12 + M22M22 # Pack covariance into half-precision uint32 pairs packeddata[8i + 4] = packhalf2x16(sigmaxx, sigmaxy) packeddata[8i + 5] = packhalf2x16(sigmaxz, sigmayy) packeddata[8i + 6] = packhalf2x16(sigmayz, sigmazz) # 4. Pack color rint = int(round(r 255)) & 0xFF gint = int(round(gval 255)) & 0xFF bint = int(round(b 255)) & 0xFF aint = int(round(a 255)) & 0xFF packedcolor = rint | (gint << 8) | (bint << 16) | (aint << 24) packeddata[8i + 7] = packedcolor return packeddata, worldpositions def floattouint32(f): """Reinterpret bits of float32 as uint32.""" import struct return struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', f))[0] def packhalf2x16(v1, v2): """Pack two float32 values into a single uint32 using half-precision.""" import struct # Convert to half-precision (2 bytes each) h1 = struct.pack('e', v1) # 'e' is half precision in struct h2 = struct.pack('e', v2) # Combine into uint32 (little-endian assumed by GLSL packHalf2x16 behavior usually) # GLSL packHalf2x16 packs the first float into the lower 16 bits and second into upper 16 bits return struct.unpack('I', h1 + h2)[0] Parameters and Edge Cases: Precision: Position uses full float32 precision (via bit-cast). Covariance uses half-precision (float16), which may introduce quantization error for very large or small scales. Color uses 8-bit integer per channel. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes valid input quaternions (normalized). If rot is not normalized, the resulting rotation matrix will be incorrect. Color Range: Color components are expected in [0, 1]. Values outside this range will clamp or wrap incorrectly when multiplied by 255 and cast to uint8. Stores packed data into a 2D texture array (GLRGBA32UI) for GPU rendering. Uses fixed-width 2048-pixel texture with row-major layout. Binary storage format for low-precision, non-interleaved data with ZSTD compression. Designed for web/browser loading. Deserializes SPZ format back to raw floats. Inverts quantization and compression. Lossless compression using 8/16-bit PNG images. Leverages spatial locality and Morton code sorting. Packs attributes into GLTF buffer views with 4-byte alignment. Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of Gaussians. Each Gaussian requires constant-time matrix operations and packing. Memory Complexity: O(n). packedData uses 32n bytes. worldPositions uses 12n bytes. Total 44n bytes. Performance: The method is CPU-bound during packing. The use of half-precision for covariance reduces memory bandwidth compared to full float32, but requires conversion. Bit-casting positions avoids precision loss during transfer to GPU shaders that expect integer position formats. Strengths: Compact representation for GPU consumption. Direct mapping to GLSL uvec4 and packHalf2x16. Limitations: Covariance precision is limited to 16-bit. Color is limited to 8-bit per channel. Not suitable for high-precision scientific visualization where float32 covariance is required. Originated in the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines, specifically in the gsplat-opengl repository. It addresses the need for efficient data transfer between CPU-side Gaussian representations and GPU-side rendering shaders. liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Texture Packing
body: Gaussian Splat Texture Packing is a method for storing 3D Gaussian Splat attributes into a 2D texture array to enable efficient GPU-based rendering and reading. It solves the problem of transferring large volumes of Gaussian data (position, scale, rotation, color, SH coefficients) from CPU memory to the GPU by packing multiple attributes into a single GLRGBA32UI texture. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SPZ Packed Format by using a fixed-width 2048-pixel texture with a specific row-major layout, and from PNG-based Gaussian Compression by using uncompressed 32-bit unsigned integer formats for high precision. Inputs: packedData: A flat array of 32-bit integers containing the packed Gaussian attributes. Each Gaussian i occupies 8 consecutive elements (representing 2 uvec4 values). splatCount: The total number of Gaussians. Outputs: splatTexture: A 2D texture object (GLuint) containing the packed data. Data Structures: Texture Format: GLRGBA32UI (internal format), GLRGBAINTEGER (type), GLUNSIGNEDINT (data type). Texture Dimensions: Width: 2048 pixels. Height: \lceil \text{splatCount} / 1024 \rceil pixels. Layout: Each Gaussian occupies 2 horizontal columns (2 texels). The x-coordinate (column) for Gaussian i is (i \pmod{1024}) \times 2. The y-coordinate (row) for Gaussian i is \lfloor i / 1024 \rfloor. Each texel stores 4 uint32 values. Gaussian i's first 4 attributes are stored in texel (x, y). Gaussian i's next 4 attributes are stored in texel (x+1, y). Parameters: Texture Filters: GLNEAREST for minification and magnification. Wrap Mode: GLCLAMPTOEDGE for both S and T axes. Steps: 1. Calculate texture width W = 2048. 2. Calculate texture height H = \lceil \text{splatCount} / 1024 \rceil. 3. Create a 2D texture with format GLRGBA32UI, dimensions W \times H, and type GLUNSIGNEDINT. 4. For each Gaussian i from 0 to \text{splatCount} - 1: a. Compute row r = \lfloor i / 1024 \rfloor. b. Compute column index c = (i \pmod{1024}) \times 2. c. Calculate the index for the first texel: \text{idx1} = (r \times W + c) \times 4. d. Calculate the index for the second texel: \text{idx2} = (r \times W + c + 1) \times 4. e. Copy packedData[i8 + 0..3] to textureData[idx1..idx1+3]. f. Copy packedData[i8 + 4..7] to textureData[idx2..idx2+3]. 5. Upload textureData to the GPU texture using glTexSubImage2D or glTexImage2D. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packgaussianstotexture(packeddata: list[int], splatcount: int) -> tuple[int, int, list[int]]: """ Packs Gaussian data into a 2D texture layout. Args: packeddata: List of integers representing packed attributes. Each Gaussian has 8 integers (32 bytes). splatcount: Number of Gaussians. Returns: texturewidth: Width of the texture (2048). textureheight: Height of the texture. texturedata: Flattened list of integers representing the texture data. """ texturewidth = 2048 textureheight = (splatcount + 1023) // 1024 # ceil(splatcount / 1024) # Each texel has 4 uint32 values. Total texels = width height. totaltexels = texturewidth textureheight texturedata = [0] (totaltexels 4) for i in range(splatcount): # Calculate row and column row = i // 1024 col = (i % 1024) 2 # Calculate indices in the flattened texture data array # Each texel is 4 integers idx1 = (row texturewidth + col) 4 idx2 = (row texturewidth + col + 1) 4 # Copy first 4 attributes to first texel for k in range(4): texturedata[idx1 + k] = packeddata[i 8 + k] # Copy next 4 attributes to second texel for k in range(4): texturedata[idx2 + k] = packeddata[i 8 + 4 + k] return texturewidth, textureheight, texturedata Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using GLRGBA32UI ensures no quantization loss for integer-packed attributes. If floating-point attributes are used, GLRGBA32F should be used instead, but the packing logic remains similar. Boundaries: The texture height is calculated using ceiling division to ensure all Gaussians fit. Extra texels at the end of the texture are unused and should be ignored during reading. Alignment: The layout assumes 4-byte alignment for uint32. Packed Splat Reading is a method to read a single 3D Gaussian Splat from a packed texture representation, decoding its geometric and color properties into a Gsplat struct. It distinguishes itself from extended variants by utilizing a single usampler2DArray texture and a standard unpacking routine for the packed data. Choose it when on-demand decoding of individual splats is required without loading the entire texture into CPU memory. This method preprocesses parsed 3D Gaussian splat data into eight separate RGBA32F textures, one for each attribute channel (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, and three Spherical Harmonics levels), to enable efficient on-demand loading by the Unreal Engine Niagara rendering system. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the creation of uncompressed, high-precision floating-point texture assets rather than byte-level compression or Morton-ordering. Choose it when integrating with engine-specific Niagara pipelines that require per-channel texture assets. A method to assign texture dimensions to 2D Gaussian primitives based on their spatial extent, ensuring uniform texel size in world space and adaptive level-of-detail. It computes a uniform texel size T{size} using a hyperparameter T{total} and the sum of scaled areas of all Gaussians. For each Gaussian i, texture width Ui and height Vi are determined by its scaling factors (su)i and (sv)i: Ui = \lceil 6 \times (su)i / T{size} \rceil Vi = \lceil 6 \times (sv)i / T{size} \rceil where T{size} = T{total} / \sum{i \in N} (36 \times (su)i (sv)i). T{total} is a hyperparameter controlling the total number of texels, typically set to 1 \times 10^7. Choose this variant when rendering textured 2D Gaussians that require spatially adaptive resolution rather than fixed grid packing. Time Complexity: Packing is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Reading is O(1) per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: The texture size is 2048 \times \lceil N/1024 \rceil \times 16 bytes (for RGBA32UI). This is approximately 32N bytes, which is efficient compared to storing separate arrays for each attribute. Performance: GPU texture sampling is highly optimized. Using GLNEAREST avoids interpolation overhead. Strengths: Simple layout, efficient GPU access, high precision. Limitations: Fixed width limits the number of Gaussians per row. Not suitable for dynamic resizing without reallocation. Originating from implementations like gsplat-opengl, this method is used in real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting renderers to efficiently manage Gaussian data on the GPU. It is a foundational step for rendering pipelines that require fast access to Gaussian attributes. liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3634643, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Packed Splat Reading
head: ReadPackedSplat, readPackedArray
body: Packed Splat Reading is a method to read a single 3D Gaussian Splat from a packed texture representation, decoding its geometric and color properties into a Gsplat struct. It distinguishes itself from extended variants by utilizing a single usampler2DArray texture and a standard unpacking routine for the packed data. Inputs: packedSplats: A struct containing: textureArray: usampler2DArray holding the packed splat data. numSplats: int total number of splats. rgbMinMaxLnScaleMinMax: vec4 parameters used during decoding. lodOpacity: bool flag to adjust alpha for level-of-detail rendering. index: int the index of the splat to read. Outputs: gsplat: A Gsplat struct with the following layout: center: vec3 flags: uint scales: vec3 index: int quaternion: vec4 rgba: vec4 Constants: GSPLATFLAGACTIVE: Defined as 1 << 0. Steps: 1. Initialize gsplat.flags to 0. 2. Validate the input index. If index < 0 or index >= numSplats, the method returns the initialized gsplat with flags = 0 and no data read. 3. Calculate the texture coordinate using splatTexCoord(index). 4. Fetch the packed data from textureArray at the calculated coordinate and mip level 0: \text{packedData} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{textureArray}, \text{splatTexCoord(index)}, 0) where packedData is a uvec4. 5. Decode packedData into the gsplat fields using the helper function unpackSplatEncoding: \text{unpackSplatEncoding}(\text{packedData}, \text{gsplat.center}, \text{gsplat.scales}, \text{gsplat.quaternion}, \text{gsplat.rgba}, \text{rgbMinMaxLnScaleMinMax}). 6. If lodOpacity is true, double the alpha component: \text{gsplat.rgba.a} = 2.0 \times \text{gsplat.rgba.a}. 7. Check for zero size by comparing gsplat.scales to vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0): \text{zeroSize} = \text{all}(\text{equal}(\text{gsplat.scales}, \text{vec3}(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))). 8. Set gsplat.flags: If zeroSize is true, gsplat.flags = 0. Otherwise, gsplat.flags = GSPLATFLAGACTIVE. 9. Set gsplat.index to the input index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def readpackedsplat(packedsplats, index): # Initialize output struct gsplat = Gsplat() gsplat.flags = 0 # Boundary check if index < 0 or index >= packedsplats.numSplats: return gsplat # Calculate texture coordinate for index # coord = splatTexCoord(index) # Not given in the sources # Fetch packed data from texture at coordinate and mip level 0 # packeddata = texelFetch(packedsplats.textureArray, coord, 0) # Standard GLSL texture fetch # Decode packed data into gsplat fields # unpackSplatEncoding(packeddata, gsplat.center, gsplat.scales, gsplat.quaternion, gsplat.rgba, packedsplats.rgbMinMaxLnScaleMinMax) # Not given in the sources # LOD opacity adjustment if packedsplats.lodOpacity: gsplat.rgba.a = 2.0 gsplat.rgba.a # Determine active flag based on scale # zerosize = allequal(gsplat.scales, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Not given in the sources # if zerosize: # gsplat.flags = 0 # else: # gsplat.flags = 1 << 0 # GSPLATFLAGACTIVE # Set index gsplat.index = index return gsplat Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If index is out of bounds, flags are set to 0 and no data is read. If packedSplats inputs are missing or invalid, flags are set to 0 and no data is read. A variant that reads a single 3D Gaussian Splat from two extended texture arrays, decoding properties into a Gsplat struct. It differs from the standard method by using textureArray1 and textureArray2 and the unpackSplatExt helper function. Input struct ExtSplats contains usampler2DArray textureArray1, usampler2DArray textureArray2, and int numSplats. Pitfalls include returning flags = 0 if index is out of bounds or inputs are missing. name: Texture-Based Splat Storage Preprocessing
body: This method preprocesses parsed 3D Gaussian splat data into eight separate RGBA32F textures, one for each attribute channel (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, and three Spherical Harmonics levels), to enable efficient on-demand loading by the Unreal Engine Niagara rendering system. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the creation of uncompressed, high-precision floating-point texture assets rather than byte-level compression or Morton-ordering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of parsed Gaussian splat attributes (Position, Scale, Rotation, Color, SH coefficients) typically derived from PLY or SPZ files. Output: Eight UTexture2D assets, each containing an array of FLinearColor values representing the respective attribute channel. Data Structures: The method organizes data using the FGaussianSplattingTextureData structure, which contains eight fields, each being a dynamic array of FLinearColor (4-component float vector): 1. PositionTextureData: Stores 3D coordinates. 2. ScaleTextureData: Stores scale factors. 3. RotationTextureData: Stores rotation quaternions. 4. ColorTextureData: Stores base color. 5. HarmonicsL1TextureData: Stores Level 1 SH coefficients. 6. HarmonicsL2TextureData: Stores Level 2 SH coefficients. 7. HarmonicsL31TextureData: Stores Level 3 SH coefficients (part 1). 8. HarmonicsL32TextureData: Stores Level 3 SH coefficients (part 2). Numbered Steps: 1. Parse and Separate: Extract the attribute values for each of the N splats and separate them into eight distinct lists corresponding to the fields in FGaussianSplattingTextureData. 2. Texture Creation: For each attribute channel, create a new UTexture2D asset. 3. Texture Configuration: Set the following properties on the created texture: SRGB to false (linear space), MipGenSettings to TMGSNoMipmaps, Compression to CompressionNone, and Filter to TFNearest (point sampling). 4. Format Initialization: Initialize the texture source format to ETextureSourceFormat::TSFRGBA32F (32-bit floating point RGBA). 5. Data Copy: Lock mip level 0 of the texture, copy the FLinearColor array for the specific attribute into the locked memory using a memory copy operation, and unlock the mip level. 6. Resource Update: Update the texture resources to make them available to the rendering pipeline. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Texture Format: TSFRGBA32F (32-bit floating point per channel). Texture Size: N \times 1 or 1 \times N depending on engine implementation, where N is the number of splats. Filtering: TFNearest (Point sampling). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using RGBA32F ensures high precision for SH coefficients and rotations, avoiding quantization errors present in lower-precision formats. Memory Usage: Storing 8 full-precision textures for millions of splats consumes significant VRAM. For example, 2 million splats require 2 \times 10^6 \times 8 \times 16 bytes \approx 256 MB per texture, totaling ~2 GB for all 8 textures. Transformations: Moving, rotating, or scaling the splat actor in the world is not fully supported and may break rendering. SH Support: Support for Spherical Harmonics may be limited or incomplete in early versions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocesssplatstotextures(splats: list, numsplats: int) -> dict: """ Preprocesses Gaussian splat data into 8 RGBA32F textures. Args: splats: List of Splat objects with attributes: pos (Vec3), scale (Vec3), rot (Quat), color (Vec3), shl1 (Vec3), shl2 (Vec3), shl31 (Vec3), shl32 (Vec3). numsplats: Total number of splats. Returns: Dictionary mapping attribute names to texture data structures. """ textures = {} channels = [ "Position", "Scale", "Rotation", "Color", "HarmonicsL1", "HarmonicsL2", "HarmonicsL31", "HarmonicsL32" ] for channel in channels: # Step 1: Parse and Separate pixeldata = [] for i in range(numsplats): s = splats[i] val = getattr(s, channel) # FLinearColor is a 4-component float vector. # For 3-component data, pad with 1.0 as per engine convention. if channel == "Rotation": pixeldata.append((val.x, val.y, val.z, val.w)) else: pixeldata.append((val.x, val.y, val.z, 1.0)) # Step 2: Texture Creation texdata = {"srgb": False, "mipgen": "NOMIPMAPS", "compression": "NONE", "filter": "NEAREST"} # Step 3: Texture Configuration & Step 4: Format Initialization texdata["sourceformat"] = "RGBA32F" # Step 5: Data Copy (simulated lock/memcpy/unlock) # In engine: tex.lockmip(0); memcpy(ptr, pixeldata); tex.unlockmip(0) texdata["mip0data"] = pixeldata # Step 6: Resource Update (simulated) # In engine: tex.updateresources() textures[channel] = texdata return textures class FLinearColor: def init(self, r, g, b, a): self.r = r self.g = g self.b = b self.a = a class Splat: def init(self, pos, scale, rot, color, shl1, shl2, shl31, shl32): self.pos = pos self.scale = scale self.rot = rot self.color = color self.shl1 = shl1 self.shl2 = shl2 self.shl31 = shl31 self.shl32 = shl32 class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class Quat: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z self.w = w This method divides splats into fixed-size chunks, computes per-chunk bounding boxes for position, scale, color, and SH coefficients, and normalizes the data to [0, 1] for efficient storage. It sets itself apart from siblings by introducing spatial chunking and normalization rather than raw texture packing. Choose it when memory bandwidth is constrained and quantization is acceptable. This method converts raw splat data into compressed GPU-ready byte buffers using Morton space-filling curve reordering and aggressive per-attribute quantization. It sets itself apart by integrating cache-coherent ordering with chunk-based SH storage. Choose it when VRAM is limited and runtime compression is required. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of splats, as each attribute is processed once per splat. Memory Complexity: O(N), with a constant factor of 8 for the 8 separate textures. Each texture stores N FLinearColor (16 bytes) values. Measured Performance: Designed for real-time applications, including VR and interactive walkthroughs, supporting models with up to 2 million splats. Strengths: High precision due to 32-bit floating point format; simple integration with Unreal Engine's Niagara system; on-demand loading reduces initial load times. Limitations: High memory footprint compared to compressed formats; lack of support for dynamic transformations of the splat actor. When to Use: When high precision is required for SH coefficients and rotations, and the target platform has sufficient VRAM. Ideal for static scenes or pre-baked splat data in Unreal Engine. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth or VRAM is constrained, or when dynamic transformations of the splat cloud are required. This method is implemented in the unreal-splat plugin by JI20, which integrates 3D Gaussian Splatting into Unreal Engine's Niagara VFX pipeline. It was developed to address the need for efficient, high-performance rendering of large-scale Gaussian splat models within the Unreal Engine ecosystem, leveraging the engine's texture system for data storage and retrieval. name: Chunked Bounding Box Computation and Normalization
head: ChunkInfo Generation, Gaussian Splat Chunking
body: This method preprocesses a list of 3D Gaussian splats by dividing them into fixed-size chunks, computing per-chunk bounding boxes for position, scale, color (DC0 + opacity), and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, and normalizing the data within each chunk to the range [0, 1]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of Gaussian splats (splatData), where each splat contains position (float3), scale (float3), rotation (quaternion), color DC0 (float3), opacity (float), and SH coefficients (sh1 through shF). Output: Normalized splat data and a ChunkInfo structure containing the bounding box bounds for each chunk. Data Structures: ChunkInfo: Contains bounds for each chunk. posX, posY, posZ: Each is a float2 storing (min, max) for the respective axis. sclX, sclY, sclZ: Each is a uint packing two 16-bit floats (f16) representing min and max scale. colR, colG, colB, colA: Each is a uint packing two f16 representing min and max color/opacity. shR, shG, shB: Each is a uint packing two f16 representing min and max SH coefficients for the respective color channel. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize min/max accumulators for position (float3), scale (float3), color (float4, combining dc0.xyz and opacity.w), and SH coefficients (float3, accumulating sh1 through shF) to positive/negative infinity respectively. 2. Calculate the start (splatBegin) and end (splatEnd) indices for the current chunk chunkIdx, clamping to the total splatData.Length. 3. Iterate through each splat i from splatBegin to splatEnd. Apply a power transformation to the scale: s.scale = math.pow(s.scale, 1.0f / 8.0f). Apply a square centered 0-1 normalization to the opacity: s.opacity = GaussianUtils.SquareCentered01(s.opacity). Update chunk min/max bounds for position, scale, color (float4 of dc0.xyz and opacity.w), and SH coefficients (sh1 through shF). Note: SH bounds are updated individually for sh1-shF. 4. Enforce a minimum spread of 1.0e-5f on the max bounds to prevent division by zero during normalization: chunkMaxX = math.max(chunkMaxX, chunkMinX + 1.0e-5f) for pos, scl, col, and shs. 5. Store the computed bounds in a ChunkInfo struct. Position bounds are stored as float2 pairs (min, max) for X, Y, Z. Scale, Color, and SH bounds are packed into 32-bit integers using 16-bit float conversion (math.f32tof16) and bitwise OR/shift operations. 6. Normalize the splat data in place for the current chunk. Position, scale, DC0 color, and opacity are normalized using the formula: (value - min) / (max - min). 7. Normalize SH coefficients (sh1 through shF) using the same min/max bounds computed for SHs: (sh - chunkMinshs) / (chunkMaxshs - chunkMinshs). Parameters: kChunkSize: The number of splats per chunk. The specific value is not defined in the sources, but it is used to calculate splatBegin and splatEnd indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import struct class ChunkInfo: def init(self): self.posX = (0.0, 0.0) self.posY = (0.0, 0.0) self.posZ = (0.0, 0.0) self.sclX = 0 self.sclY = 0 self.sclZ = 0 self.colR = 0 self.colG = 0 self.colB = 0 self.colA = 0 self.shR = 0 self.shG = 0 self.shB = 0 def f32tof16bits(val): # Standard IEEE 754 float32 to float16 bit conversion return struct.unpack('<H', struct.pack('<f', val))[0] def packf16pair(minval, maxval): # Pack two f16 values into a uint32 using bitwise OR and shifts minbits = f32tof16bits(minval) maxbits = f32tof16bits(maxval) return (minbits << 16) | maxbits def squarecentered01(opacity): # Standard clamp to [0, 1] range return max(0.0, min(1.0, opacity)) def computechunkboundsandnormalize(splatdata, chunksize): chunks = [] numsplats = len(splatdata) for chunkidx in range(0, numsplats, chunksize): splatbegin = chunkidx splatend = min(chunkidx + chunksize, numsplats) # 1. Initialize min/max accumulators posmin = [float('inf')] 3 posmax = [float('-inf')] 3 sclmin = [float('inf')] 3 sclmax = [float('-inf')] 3 colmin = [float('inf')] 4 # RGB + Opacity colmax = [float('-inf')] 4 shmin = [float('inf')] 3 # R, G, B channels shmax = [float('-inf')] 3 # 3. Iterate through splats for i in range(splatbegin, splatend): s = splatdata[i] # Apply power transformation to scale s.scale = [math.pow(val, 1.0 / 8.0) for val in s.scale] # Apply square centered 0-1 normalization to opacity s.opacity = squarecentered01(s.opacity) # Update position bounds for axis in range(3): posmin[axis] = min(posmin[axis], s.position[axis]) posmax[axis] = max(posmax[axis], s.position[axis]) # Update scale bounds for axis in range(3): sclmin[axis] = min(sclmin[axis], s.scale[axis]) sclmax[axis] = max(sclmax[axis], s.scale[axis]) # Update color bounds (RGB + Opacity) for ch in range(3): colmin[ch] = min(colmin[ch], s.color[ch]) colmax[ch] = max(colmax[ch], s.color[ch]) colmin[3] = min(colmin[3], s.opacity) colmax[3] = max(colmax[3], s.opacity) # Update SH bounds individually for R, G, B channels for ch in range(3): shmin[ch] = min(shmin[ch], s.sh[ch]) shmax[ch] = max(shmax[ch], s.sh[ch]) # 4. Enforce minimum spread minspread = 1.0e-5 for axis in range(3): posmax[axis] = max(posmax[axis], posmin[axis] + minspread) sclmax[axis] = max(sclmax[axis], sclmin[axis] + minspread) colmax[axis] = max(colmax[axis], colmin[axis] + minspread) shmax[axis] = max(shmax[axis], shmin[axis] + minspread) colmax[3] = max(colmax[3], colmin[3] + minspread) # 5. Store bounds in ChunkInfo chunkinfo = ChunkInfo() chunkinfo.posX = (posmin[0], posmax[0]) chunkinfo.posY = (posmin[1], posmax[1]) chunkinfo.posZ = (posmin[2], posmax[2]) chunkinfo.sclX = packf16pair(sclmin[0], sclmax[0]) chunkinfo.sclY = packf16pair(sclmin[1], sclmax[1]) chunkinfo.sclZ = packf16pair(sclmin[2], sclmax[2]) chunkinfo.colR = packf16pair(colmin[0], colmax[0]) chunkinfo.colG = packf16pair(colmin[1], colmax[1]) chunkinfo.colB = packf16pair(colmin[2], colmax[2]) chunkinfo.colA = packf16pair(colmin[3], colmax[3]) chunkinfo.shR = packf16pair(shmin[0], shmax[0]) chunkinfo.shG = packf16pair(shmin[1], shmax[1]) chunkinfo.shB = packf16pair(shmin[2], shmax[2]) chunks.append(chunkinfo) # 6 & 7. Normalize splat data in place for i in range(splatbegin, splatend): s = splatdata[i] for axis in range(3): s.position[axis] = (s.position[axis] - posmin[axis]) / (posmax[axis] - posmin[axis]) s.scale[axis] = (s.scale[axis] - sclmin[axis]) / (sclmax[axis] - sclmin[axis]) s.sh[axis] = (s.sh[axis] - shmin[axis]) / (shmax[axis] - shmin[axis]) for ch in range(3): s.color[ch] = (s.color[ch] - colmin[ch]) / (colmax[ch] - colmin[ch]) s.opacity = (s.opacity - colmin[3]) / (colmax[3] - colmin[3]) return chunks Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Enforcing a minimum spread of 1.0e-5f prevents division by zero when min and max bounds are equal. Precision Loss: Using 16-bit floats for packing bounds may introduce precision loss, especially for large ranges. Degenerate Input: If a chunk contains only one splat, the min and max bounds will be identical, requiring the minimum spread enforcement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources.
