name: Gaussian Splat Data Packing and Compression
head: Gaussian Splat Encoding, Runtime Splat Processing, SPZ Processing
body: This method converts raw InputSplatData arrays (from SPZ or PLY files) into compressed GPU-ready byte buffers stored in RuntimeSplatData. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by integrating Morton space-filling curve reordering for cache coherence with aggressive per-attribute quantization and chunk-based storage for spherical harmonics. Inputs: Raw splat data array (NativeArray<InputSplatData>), containing position, scale, rotation, color, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Format specifications for each attribute: posFormat, scaleFormat, colorFormat, shFormat. Outputs: Compressed GPU-ready byte buffers stored in RuntimeSplatData. Reordered splat indices based on Morton codes. Data Structures: 1. InputSplatData: The raw input structure. 2. GaussianSplatAsset.ChunkInfo: Used when SH data is not stored in full float32. 3. ReorderMortonJob: A job struct for parallel Morton reordering. const float kScaler = (1<<21)-1 float3 mBoundsMin float3 mInvBoundsSize ReadOnly NativeArray<InputSplatData> mSplatData NativeArray<(ulong, int)> mOrder (stores Morton code and original index) 4. CalcChunkDataJob: A job struct for computing SH chunks. NativeArray<InputSplatData> splatData NativeArray<GaussianSplatAsset.ChunkInfo> chunks Parameters (Defaults): posFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.VectorFormat.Norm11 scaleFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.VectorFormat.Norm11 colorFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.ColorFormat.Norm8x4 shFormat: GaussianSplatAsset.SHFormat.Norm6 Steps: 1. Input Validation: Check if the input splat array is empty. If empty, throw ArgumentException. 2. Scene Bounds Calculation: Iterate through all splats to find the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Initialize bMin to positive infinity and bMax to negative infinity. For each splat position p: bMin = min(bMin, p) and bMax = max(bMax, p). 3. Morton Reordering: Calculate inverse bounds size: invSize = 1.0f / (bMax - bMin). Normalize position to [0, 1] and scale: pos = ((inputpos - boundsMin) invSize) kScaler. Cast to integer: ipos = casttouint3(pos). Generate Morton code: code = MortonEncode3(ipos). Sort splats by code and reorder the InputSplatData array accordingly. 4. Chunk Data Creation (Conditional): If any format is not full float32 (posFormat != Float32 OR scaleFormat != Float32 OR colorFormat != Float32x4 OR shFormat != Float32), call CreateChunkData. Ensure chunk bounds are clamped to splatData.Length to avoid out-of-bounds access. 5. Position Encoding: Call CreatePositionsData with the reordered splats and posFormat. Apply Norm11 or Norm16 encoding formulas. 6. Scale and SH Index Encoding: Call CreateOtherData with splats, scaleFormat, and splatSHIndices. 7. Color Encoding: Call CreateColorData with splats. 8. SH Data Encoding: Call CreateSHData with splats, shFormat, and clusteredSHs. Formulas: Position normalization for Morton encoding: pos = ((input\pos - boundsMin) \times (1.0f / (boundsMax - boundsMin))) \times kScaler, where kScaler = (1 \ll 21) - 1. Morton code generation: code = MortonEncode3(ipos), where ipos is the normalized position cast to uint3. Float3 to Norm16 encoding: enc = (v.x \times 65535.5f) \mid (v.y \times 65535.5f \ll 16) \mid (v.z \times 65535.5f \ll 32), stored as 4 bytes uint + 2 bytes ushort. Float3 to Norm11 encoding: enc = (v.x \times 2047.5f) \mid (v.y \times 1023.5f \ll 11) \mid (v.z \times 2047.5f \ll 21), stored as 4 bytes uint. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty input arrays throw ArgumentException. Chunk bounds must be explicitly clamped to splatData.Length to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Quantization reduces precision; Norm11 and Norm16 formats trade accuracy for memory savings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Standard 21-bit Morton code interleaving (7 bits per axis) x, y, z = v.x, v.y, v.z x = (x | (x << 16)) & 0x0000007F0000FF x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00007F00007F007F x = (x | (x << 4)) & 0x00000F000F000F000F x = (x | (x << 2)) & 0x000000000F000F000F y = (y | (y << 16)) & 0x0000007F0000FF y = (y | (y << 8)) & 0x00007F00007F007F y = (y | (y << 4)) & 0x00000F000F000F000F y = (y | (y << 2)) & 0x000000000F000F000F z = (z | (z << 16)) & 0x0000007F0000FF z = (z | (z << 8)) & 0x00007F00007F007F z = (z | (z << 4)) & 0x00000F000F000F000F z = (z | (z << 2)) & 0x000000000F000F000F return (x << 0) | (y << 1) | (z << 2) def packgaussiansplats(splatdata: List[Splat], posformat: str = "Norm11", scaleformat: str = "Norm11", colorformat: str = "Norm8x4", shformat: str = "Norm6") -> RuntimeSplatData: if not splatdata: raise ArgumentException("Input splat array is empty") bmin = float3(float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')) bmax = float3(float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')) for splat in splatdata: bmin = bmin.min(splat.position) bmax = bmax.max(splat.position) invboundssize = float3(1.0 / (bmax.x - bmin.x), 1.0 / (bmax.y - bmin.y), 1.0 / (bmax.z - bmin.z)) kscaler = (1 << 21) - 1 indexedsplats = [] for i, splat in enumerate(splatdata): posnorm = (splat.position - bmin) invboundssize ipos = uint3(int(posnorm.x kscaler), int(posnorm.y kscaler), int(posnorm.z kscaler)) mortoncode = mortonencode3(ipos) indexedsplats.append((mortoncode, i)) indexedsplats.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) reorderedsplatdata = [splatdata[idx] for, idx in indexedsplats] needschunks = (posformat != "Float32" or scaleformat != "Float32" or colorformat != "Float32x4" or shformat != "Float32") chunks = [] if needschunks: # Sources do not specify CreateChunkData implementation. # Placeholder for chunk generation logic. chunks = [] # Clamp chunk bounds to splatData.Length to avoid out-of-bounds access for chunk in chunks: chunk.end = min(chunk.end, len(reorderedsplatdata)) posbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: if posformat == "Norm11": enc = int((splat.position.x 2047.5) | (splat.position.y 1023.5 << 11) | (splat.position.z 2047.5 << 21)) posbuffer += enc.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') elif posformat == "Norm16": enc = int((splat.position.x 65535.5) | (splat.position.y 65535.5 << 16) | (splat.position.z 65535.5 << 32)) posbuffer += (enc & 0xFFFFFFFF).tobytes(4, byteorder='little') posbuffer += ((enc >> 32) & 0xFFFF).tobytes(2, byteorder='little') scalebuffer = bytearray() shindicesbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: if scaleformat == "Norm11": enc = int((splat.scale.x 2047.5) | (splat.scale.y 1023.5 << 11) | (splat.scale.z 2047.5 << 21)) scalebuffer += enc.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') shindicesbuffer += splat.shindex.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') colorbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: if colorformat == "Norm8x4": # Standard 8-bit per channel quantization r = int(splat.color[0] 255) g = int(splat.color[1] 255) b = int(splat.color[2] 255) a = int(splat.color[3] 255) colorbuffer += bytes([r, g, b, a]) shbuffer = bytearray() for splat in reorderedsplatdata: if shformat == "Norm6": # Standard 6-bit SH quantization for coeff in splat.shcoefficients: q = int(coeff 31.5) shbuffer += q.tobytes(1, byteorder='little') return RuntimeSplatData(posbuffer, scalebuffer, shindicesbuffer, colorbuffer, shbuffer, chunks) Time Complexity: Dominated by the Morton sort, which is O(N \log N) where N is the number of splats. Bounds calculation is O(N). Encoding is O(N). Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to raw float32 storage. Position and scale drop from 12 bytes each to 4 bytes (Norm11) or 6 bytes (Norm16). Color drops from 16 bytes to 4 bytes (Norm8x4). SH data is heavily compressed via quantization and chunking. Performance: The method is designed for runtime execution using Burst compilation, ensuring zero Editor dependencies and safe usage in builds. Strengths: High compression ratio, cache-friendly ordering via Morton codes, runtime-safe. Limitations: Quantization introduces precision loss. Morton reordering requires sorting, which can be costly for very large datasets if not parallelized effectively. Empty input arrays cause exceptions. This method is part of the WorldLabs Unity integration package, specifically designed for processing SPZ (Splat Zone) files generated by WorldLabs' AI world generation API. It enables efficient runtime rendering of Gaussian Splat scenes in Unity, particularly for VR and mobile platforms. The approach reflects the broader trend in 3D Gaussian Splatting towards optimizing data layouts for real-time rendering engines. nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, https://github.com/nigelhartman/worldlabsunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

body: SPZ Packed Format is a binary storage format for 3D Gaussian splats designed for low-precision, non-interleaved data storage with ZSTD compression. It solves the problem of efficiently loading high-fidelity Gaussian splat captures in environments lacking native system-level decompression libraries, such as web browsers. It is distinguished from earlier SPZ versions (1–3) by using per-attribute ZSTD compression instead of a single gzip stream, and from generic PLY parsers by its specific handling of quantized fields and coordinate system transformations. Inputs: A binary stream containing the SPZ file data. Outputs: A GaussianCloud structure containing unpacked positions, rotations, scales, alphas, colors, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Data Structures: The format uses a header followed by parallel attribute buffers. 1. Header (PackedGaussians): version (uint32t): Format version. Default is LATESTSPZHEADERVERSION (4). numPoints (int32t): Number of Gaussian primitives. shDegree (int32t): Degree of spherical harmonics (0–4). fractionalBits (int32t): Precision bits for position/scale quantization. antialiased (bool): Flag indicating antialiasing support. usesQuaternionSmallestThree (bool): Default true. hadSkippedExtensions (bool): Flag for unknown extensions. Note: Data is stored in separate std::vector<uint8t> buffers for positions, scales, rotations, alphas, colors, and SH. 2. Single Point View (PackedGaussian): Represents a single Gaussian for indexing purposes (92 bytes for SH degree 4): position: std::array<uint8t, 9> (3 floats, 3 bytes each). rotation: std::array<uint8t, 4> (4 bytes). scale: std::array<uint8t, 3> (3 bytes). color: std::array<uint8t, 3> (3 bytes). alpha: uint8t. shR, shG, shB: std::array<uint8t, 24> each (24 coefficients for degree 4). Parameters: SHMAXCOEFFS: 24 (for degree 4). DEFAULTSH1BITS: 5 (bits for first SH coefficient). DEFAULTSHRESTBITS: 4 (bits for remaining SH coefficients). LATESTSPZHEADERVERSION: 4. MINZSTDSPZHEADERVERSION: 4 (minimum version supporting ZSTD). MINSMALLESTTHREEQUATERNIONSVERSION: 3 (minimum version using SmallestThree encoding). Steps: 1. Read Header: Read the 8-byte magic number 0x5053474e ("NGSP"). Read the header fields. If version < MINZSTDSPZHEADERVERSION, decompression must be handled differently (e.g., gzip). 2. Decompress Buffers: Decompress each attribute buffer (positions, rotations, etc.) using ZSTD. The compression is applied per attribute, not to the entire file as a single stream. 3. Decode Positions: Each position is 9 bytes (3 floats). Unquantize using fractionalBits. 4. Decode Rotations: Depending on version and usesQuaternionSmallestThree: If version >= MINSMALLESTTHREEQUATERNIONSVERSION and usesQuaternionSmallestThree is true, use SmallestThree decoding. Otherwise, use FirstThree decoding. 5. Decode Scales: Unquantize from uint8 to float. 6. Decode Colors: Unquantize from uint8 to float. Apply base color scale factor C{base} = C{raw} \times 0.15. 7. Decode Alphas: Unquantize from uint8 to float. 8. Decode SH Coefficients: Unquantize uint8 values to float using v = \frac{x - 128.0}{128.0}. 9. Apply Extensions: If hadSkippedExtensions is true, parse optional extension blocks (e.g., CoordinateSystemAdobe, SafeOrbitCameraAdobe). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import zstd import math def decodespz(data: bytes): """ Decodes an SPZ packed file into a GaussianCloud structure. """ # 1. Read Header magic = struct.unpack('<I', data[0:4])[0] if magic != 0x5053474e: raise ValueError("Invalid SPZ magic number") version = struct.unpack('<I', data[4:8])[0] numpoints = struct.unpack('<i', data[8:12])[0] shdegree = struct.unpack('<i', data[12:16])[0] fractionalbits = struct.unpack('<i', data[16:20])[0] antialiased = struct.unpack('<?', data[20:21])[0] usessmallestthree = struct.unpack('<?', data[21:22])[0] hadskippedextensions = struct.unpack('<?', data[22:23])[0] # Calculate buffer offsets (simplified: assume contiguous after header for this example) # In reality, offsets are stored or calculated based on compressed sizes. # For implementation, one must read the compressed chunk sizes for each attribute. # Here we assume a helper readattributebuffer exists which handles ZSTD decompression. positionsraw = readattributebuffer(data, "positions") rotationsraw = readattributebuffer(data, "rotations") scalesraw = readattributebuffer(data, "scales") colorsraw = readattributebuffer(data, "colors") alphasraw = readattributebuffer(data, "alphas") shraw = readattributebuffer(data, "sh") # Interleaved R,G,B or separate? Source implies separate vectors. # 2. Decode Attributes positions = decodepositions(positionsraw, fractionalbits) rotations = decoderotations(rotationsraw, version, usessmallestthree) scales = decodescales(scalesraw, fractionalbits) colors = decodecolors(colorsraw) alphas = decodealphas(alphasraw) shcoeffs = decodesh(shraw, shdegree) return { "numpoints": numpoints, "positions": positions, "rotations": rotations, "scales": scales, "colors": colors, "alphas": alphas, "shcoeffs": shcoeffs } def decodepositions(rawbytes, fractionalbits): """ Decodes 9 bytes per position (3 floats, 3 bytes each). """ positions = [] for i in range(0, len(rawbytes), 9): x = decodefloatfrombytes(rawbytes[i:i+3], fractionalbits) y = decodefloatfrombytes(rawbytes[i+3:i+6], fractionalbits) z = decodefloatfrombytes(rawbytes[i+6:i+9], fractionalbits) positions.append((x, y, z)) return positions def decoderotations(rawbytes, version, usessmallestthree): """ Decodes quaternion rotations. """ rotations = [] if version >= 3 and usessmallestthree: # SmallestThree: 4 bytes per quaternion for i in range(0, len(rawbytes), 4): comp = struct.unpack('<I', rawbytes[i:i+4])[0] ilargest = comp >> 30 rotation = [0.0] 4 sumsquares = 0.0 tempcomp = comp # Extract 3 components for j in range(3, -1, -1): if j != ilargest: mag = tempcomp & 0x1FF negbit = (tempcomp >> 9) & 1 tempcomp >>= 10 val = math.sqrt(0.5) mag / 511.0 if negbit: val = -val rotation[j] = val sumsquares += val val # Calculate largest component rotation[ilargest] = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - sumsquares)) # Flip Q if necessary (coordinate system adjustment) # Note: c.flipQ is typically -1 or 1 depending on coordinate system # Assuming standard right-handed to left-handed or similar flip # The source mentions c.flipQ applied to first 3 components. # We assume a global flipQ factor is available or defaults to 1. # Default flipQ is 1.0 if not specified by extension. flipq = 1.0 rotation[0] = flipq rotation[1] = flipq rotation[2] = flipq rotations.append(rotation) else: # FirstThree: 3 bytes per quaternion (8-bit fixed point) for i in range(0, len(rawbytes), 3): x = (rawbytes[i] / 127.5) - 1.0 y = (rawbytes[i+1] / 127.5) - 1.0 z = (rawbytes[i+2] / 127.5) - 1.0 # flipQ applied to xyz flipq = 1.0 x = flipq y = flipq z = flipq w = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - (xx + yy + zz))) rotations.append([x, y, z, w]) return rotations def decodecolors(rawbytes): """ Decodes colors. Base scale factor is 0.15. """ colors = [] for i in range(0, len(rawbytes), 3): r = rawbytes[i] 0.15 g = rawbytes[i+1] 0.15 b = rawbytes[i+2] 0.15 colors.append((r, g, b)) return colors def decodesh(rawbytes, shdegree): """ Decodes Spherical Harmonics coefficients. """ # SHMAXCOEFFS is 24 for degree 4 # Each coefficient is 1 byte (uint8) # Formula: v = (x - 128.0) / 128.0 coeffs = [] for byteval in rawbytes: v = (byteval - 128.0) / 128.0 coeffs.append(v) return coeffs def readattributebuffer(data, attrname): """ Placeholder for ZSTD decompression of specific attribute chunks. In the actual SPZ format, the file structure includes offsets and lengths for each compressed attribute buffer. """ # Implementation detail: The SPZ format stores compressed chunks for each attribute. # This function would parse the chunk header, decompress using zstd.decompress(), # and return the raw bytes. pass def decodefloatfrombytes(bytes3, fractionalbits): """ Decodes a 3-byte float with given fractional bits. """ # The exact quantization scheme for 3-byte floats is not fully detailed in the notes. # Typically, it involves interpreting the 3 bytes as a fixed-point integer and scaling. # Assuming a standard fixed-point interpretation: val = (bytes3[0] << 16) | (bytes3[1] << 8) | bytes3[2] # Handle signedness if necessary (source doesn't specify signed/unsigned for pos) # Assuming unsigned 24-bit integer, then scaling. # The source mentions fractionalBits. # v = val / (2^fractionalBits) ? Or similar. # Without exact formula, we leave this as a placeholder for the implementer to fill # based on the specific quantization logic in the source code. return val / (1 << fractionalbits) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Reconstruction: If numerical error causes 1 - \sum{i=0}^{2} ri^2 < 0, use std::max(0.0f,...) to ensure the sqrt argument is non-negative. WASM Memory View: In JavaScript/WebAssembly environments, the typed memory view must be consumed immediately because it detaches if any subsequent WASM allocation grows the heap. Coordinate Systems: Extensions like CoordinateSystemAdobe may require flipping quaternion components or axes. Check hadSkippedExtensions and parse extensions if present. SPZ v4 format parsing is the method for decoding binary SPZ v4 files containing compressed 3D Gaussian splat data into a usable SplatCloud structure. It solves the problem of loading high-fidelity Gaussian splat captures in environments lacking native system-level decompression libraries, such as web browsers. It is distinguished from earlier SPZ versions (1–3) by using ZSTD compression per attribute instead of a single gzip stream, and from generic PLY parsers by its specific handling of quantized fields and coordinate system transformations. Time Complexity: Decompression is linear with respect to the number of bytes, O(N), where N is the file size. Decoding is also O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the decompressed cloud. Performance: ZSTD compression provides high compression ratios for quantized data, reducing file size significantly compared to uncompressed PLY. Strengths: Efficient storage, fast decompression, browser-friendly (via WASM ZSTD), supports high-degree SH. Limitations: Requires ZSTD library for decompression. Non-interleaved layout may complicate certain GPU upload strategies compared to interleaved formats. When to Use: When storage efficiency and fast loading are critical, especially in web or mobile environments. When Not to Use: When random access to individual Gaussian attributes is required without decompressing the entire file, or when ZSTD is not available. The SPZ format was developed by Niantic Labs. It is an evolution of earlier Gaussian Splatting storage formats, designed to address the limitations of PLY files in terms of size and loading speed. Version 4 introduced ZSTD compression and SmallestThree quaternion encoding. nianticlabs/spz, https://github.com/nianticlabs/spz, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

body: SPZ v4 format parsing is the method for decoding binary.spz files containing compressed 3D Gaussian splat data into a SplatCloud structure. It solves the problem of loading high-fidelity Gaussian splat captures in environments lacking native system-level decompression libraries, such as web browsers, by using a built-in ZSTD decoder instead of native gzip. It is distinguished from earlier SPZ versions (1–3) by using one ZSTD stream per attribute instead of a single gzip stream, and from generic PLY parsers by its specific handling of quantized fields and coordinate system transformations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary file with the.spz extension. Output: A SplatCloud object containing decoded Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics up to degree 4). The output coordinate system is either the file's native Right-Up-Back (RUB) or a requested Right-Down-Front (RDF) compatible with PLY standards. Data Structures: The SPZ v4 format stores attributes in separate ZSTD-compressed streams. Quantized fields are stored as integers and decoded using scaling constants provided by the reference library. Numbered Steps: 1. Decompression: Decompress each attribute stream using a ZSTD decoder (e.g., KTX2 implementation for web compatibility). 2. Quantization Decoding: Decode quantized integer fields to floating-point values using reference library constants. 3. Coordinate System Handling: By default, return the cloud in the file's native RUB axes. If PLY coordinates are requested, transform axes from RUB to RDF and flip the signs of the spherical harmonics coefficients to match the coordinate change. 4. Validation: Compare decoded reference positions against expected values using a relative tolerance to account for precision differences inherent in the quantization process. 5. Extension Check: If the file name includes an extension indicating a coordinate axis move, refuse to parse the file by name rather than rendering it mirrored, to prevent incorrect coordinate mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import List, Tuple @dataclass class SplatCloud: positions: List[Tuple[float, float, float]] shcoeffs: List[List[float]] def parsespzv4(filepath: str, requestplycoords: bool = False) -> SplatCloud: # 1. Decompress each attribute stream using a ZSTD decoder streams = readattributestreams(filepath) decompressed = {} for attr, data in streams.items(): decompressed[attr] = decompresszstd(data) # 2. Decode quantized fields using reference library constants decoded = {} for attr, raw in decompressed.items(): params = getquantizationparams(attr) decoded[attr] = decodequantized(raw, params) positions = decoded['position'] shcoeffs = decoded['sh'] # 3. Coordinate System Handling if requestplycoords: # Transform from RUB to RDF by flipping Y and Z axes positions = [(p[0], -p[1], -p[2]) for p in positions] # Flip signs of spherical harmonics to match coordinate change shcoeffs = flipshsigns(shcoeffs) # 4. Validation: compare reference positions with a relative tolerance validatepositions(positions, relativetolerance=1e-5) # 5. Extension Check: refuse files with axis-move extensions by name if hasaxismoveextension(filepath): raise ValueError("File with axis-move extension refused by name") return SplatCloud(positions=positions, shcoeffs=shcoeffs) def readattributestreams(filepath: str) -> dict: # Standard file parsing to extract per-attribute ZSTD streams return {'position': b'...', 'sh': b'...'} # implementation details omitted def decompresszstd(data: bytes) -> bytes: # Standard ZSTD decompression (e.g., KTX2 decoder for web compatibility) import zstandard return zstandard.ZstdDecompressor().decompress(data) def getquantizationparams(attr: str) -> dict: # Returns offset and scale constants from the reference library return {'offset': 0, 'scale': 1.0} # constants vary by attribute def decodequantized(raw: bytes, params: dict) -> list: # Convert integer values to float: vfloat = (vint - offset) scale ints = list(raw) return [(v - params['offset']) params['scale'] for v in ints] def flipshsigns(shcoeffs: list) -> list: # Reflection (Y and Z flip) multiplies degree-l SH bands by (-1)^l return [[c ((-1) l) for c in band] for l, band in enumerate(shcoeffs)] def validatepositions(positions: list, relativetolerance: float) -> None: # Compare against reference positions using relative tolerance pass # comparison logic depends on reference data source def hasaxismoveextension(filepath: str) -> bool: # Check if filename contains known axis-move extensions return 'rdb' in filepath or 'rdf' in filepath Parameters: relativetolerance: Used for position validation. Value not explicitly given, but "relative tolerance" is required. requestplycoords: Boolean flag. Default False (returns RUB). If True, returns RDF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: SPZ v4 reference positions must be compared with a relative tolerance due to quantization precision differences. Coordinate Mapping: Files with extensions indicating axis moves are refused by name, not rendered mirrored, to prevent incorrect mapping. Web Compatibility: Native system decoders are not required; the parser must use web-compatible ZSTD (e.g., KTX2). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables web-compatible decoding without native system libraries. Supports high-fidelity data with SH degree 4. Limitations: Requires ZSTD implementation. Coordinate system conversion is non-trivial for SH coefficients. When to use: When loading SPZ v4 files in web environments or when PLY coordinate compatibility is required. When not to use: When native gzip decompression is sufficient (SPZ v1–3) or when coordinate system conversion is not needed and RUB is acceptable. The parser is implemented in the flutter3d package to enable web-compatible SPZ decoding. body: SPZ Packed Gaussian Unpacking deserializes compressed Gaussian Splatting data from the SPZ file format into raw floating-point arrays for positions, scales, rotations, alphas, colors, and spherical harmonics. It solves the problem of efficiently loading large-scale 3D Gaussian fields from disk by inverting the quantization, coordinate system conversions, and compression applied during packing. Unlike sibling methods that may use texture atlases or PNG-based storage, this method operates on a contiguous binary stream with a defined header and sequential data sections, supporting both legacy gzip-compressed single-stream formats (v1–v3) and modern ZSTD-compressed multi-stream formats (v4). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A byte buffer containing the SPZ file data. Output: A structured object containing raw float values for positions (numPoints 3), scales (numPoints 3), rotations (numPoints 4), alphas (numPoints), colors (numPoints 3), and spherical harmonics (numPoints shDim 3). Data Structures: The file begins with a header. The layout depends on the version. Legacy Header (v1–v3, 16 bytes, little-endian): magic (Uint32, offset 0): Must equal SPZMAGIC. version (Uint32, offset 4): 1 or 2 (v3 is also handled by this path). numPoints (Uint32, offset 8): Number of Gaussians. shDegree (Uint8, offset 12): Spherical Harmonics degree (0–3). fractionalBits (Uint8, offset 13): Precision for fixed-point positions. flags (Uint8, offset 14): Compression flags. reserved (Uint8, offset 15): Padding. Modern Header (v4, 32 bytes): NgspFileHeader struct containing magic, version, numPoints, shDegree, fractionalBits, flags, numStreams, tocByteOffset, and reserved[12]. If flags & 0x2, Extension ILV records follow the header. A Table of Contents (TOC) follows, consisting of numPoints entries of 16 bytes each (compressed size u64, uncompressed size u64). Attribute streams follow the TOC, each ZSTD-compressed. Parameters: MAXPOINTSTOREAD: 10,000,000. sh1Bits: 5 (default, range 1–8). shRestBits: 4 (default, range 1–8). SHC0: 0.28209479177387814. colorScale: Scaling factor for colors (value not explicitly stated in sources, used in decoding). kMaxCompressionRatio: 1024. kMinBytesPerPoint: 9. Steps: 1. Header Validation: Read the header. Check magic == SPZMAGIC. Check version is 1, 2, 3, or 4. Reject v4 if using a legacy parser. Check numPoints <= MAXPOINTSTOREAD. Check shDegree <= 3. If using v4, read the TOC to locate attribute streams. If using v1–v3, decompress the gzip stream if flags indicate compression. 2. Determine Data Layout: If version == 1, usesFloat16 is true. Positions are stored as 2 bytes per component (Float16). If version >= 2, usesFloat16 is false. Positions are stored as 3 bytes per component (24-bit fixed-point). Calculate shDim = dimForDegree(shDegree). For degree d, shDim = (d+1)^2. 3. Allocate Output Arrays: positions: numPoints 3 floats. scales: numPoints 3 floats. rotations: numPoints 4 floats. alphas: numPoints floats. colors: numPoints 3 floats. sh: numPoints shDim 3 floats. 4. Unpack Positions: Create a CoordinateConverter object c to handle coordinate system flips. If usesFloat16 is true: Cast the packed position buffer to Half. Magnitude is scaled by sqrt(2) and normalized to 9-bit precision. Reconstruct quaternion, ensuring the largest component is positive (sign flip if needed). Normalize quaternion. Apply c.rotFlipPFunc if it exists, otherwise apply c.flipQ. 9. Unpack Spherical Harmonics (SH): If shDim == 0, return immediately. Read shDim 3 bytes per point. Calculate bandStart = band (band + 2) and bandSize = 2 band + 3. If bandStart + bandSize > shDim, break. For each channel c from 0 to 2: Copy bandSize coefficients to temporary buffer. Apply rotFlipShFuncsband. Copy back to output. 10. Verification: Ensure currentOffset + result.sh.length == buffer.byteLength. Return the structured object. SH Degree 0: If shDim == 0, unpackSh returns immediately without processing, as there is no SH data. Coordinate Conversion: Positions and Rotations use CoordinateConverter which may apply sign flips (c.flipP, c.flipSh) or custom rotation functions (c.rotFlipPFunc, c.rotFlipShFuncs) depending on source and target coordinate systems. name: PNG-based Gaussian Compression
head: Compact 3D Scene Representation via Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids, PNG Compression for 3D Gaussians, PNG Compression for Gaussian Splats, gsplat PNG Compression, gsplat_mlx compression
body: PNG-based Gaussian Compression is a lossless compression technique for trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models that quantizes splat parameters into 8-bit and 16-bit PNG images. It serves as a port of the PyTorch gsplat compression module to MLX. By leveraging spatial locality (optionally enhanced via Morton code sorting) and PNG encoding, it achieves approximately 10x compression on standard 3DGS models. It builds on Gaussian Data Packing by mapping scalar and vector fields to image grids, differing from Gaussian Splat Texture Packing which targets GPU texture formats, and SPZ Packed Format which uses a different binary layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dictionary of Gaussian splat parameters: means (N, 3), quats (N, 4), scales (N, 3), opacities (N, 1), and sh0 (N, 3). Higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients shN are also supported. Output: A set of PNG image files for each parameter field and a meta.json file containing metadata (shape, dtype, mins, maxs) required for decompression. Data Structures: Metadata (meta.json): Stores shape, dtype, mins, and maxs for each compressed parameter. PNG Images: 8-bit PNGs for scales, quats, opacities, and sh0. 16-bit means are split into two 8-bit PNGs (low byte and high byte). Higher-order SH coefficients shN are stored in NPZ format if K-means clustering is unavailable. Parameters: usesort (bool): Whether to sort splats by Morton code before compression to improve spatial locality. Default: True. verbose (bool): Whether to print progress information. Default: True. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Apply log-transform to means: y = \text{sign}(x) \cdot \log(1 + |x|). Normalize quats to unit length: q{norm} = q / \|q\|. 2. Crop to Square: Calculate side length: n{side} = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor. Calculate number of Gaussians to drop: n{crop} = N - n{side}^2. If n{crop} > 0: Sort opacities in descending order. Keep indices of the top n{side}^2 Gaussians. Apply this mask to all splat parameters. 3. Sorting (Optional): If usesort is True, sort the remaining Gaussians by their Morton code to enhance spatial locality. 4. Quantization and PNG Encoding: 8-bit Parameters (scales, quats, opacities, sh0): Reshape parameter array to (n{side}, n{side}, C) where C is the channel dimension. Compute per-channel minimum (min) and maximum (max). Quantize to 8-bit: img = \text{clip}(\text{round}((arr - \text{mins}) / \text{ranges} \cdot 255), 0, 255) where \text{ranges} = \text{maxs} - \text{mins}. Save as PNG. 16-bit Parameters (means): Perform 16-bit quantization: img16 = \text{round}((arr - \text{mins}) / \text{ranges} \cdot 65535). Split into low byte (img16 \& 0xFF) and high byte ((img16 >> 8) \& 0xFF), stored as two separate 8-bit PNGs. Higher-order SH (shN): If K-means clustering is not available (e.g., in MLX without torchpq), compress using NPZ format. 5. Metadata Storage: Save shape, dtype, mins, and maxs for each parameter in meta.json. Decompression: 1. Load meta.json. 2. Load PNG images and reconstruct quantized arrays. 3. Inverse quantization: 8-bit: arr = \text{normalised} \cdot (\text{maxs} - \text{mins}) + \text{mins}, where \text{normalised} = img / 255.0. 16-bit: Reconstruct 16-bit integer from two PNGs, then arr = \text{normalised} \cdot (\text{maxs} - \text{mins}) + \text{mins}, where \text{normalised} = img16 / 65535.0. 4. Apply inverse log-transform to means: y = \text{sign}(x) \cdot (\exp(|x|) - 1). 5. Normalize quats if necessary (reconstruction should preserve unit length if quantization is precise). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import json import os from PIL import Image def logtransform(x): """Apply log-transform: y = sign(x) log(1 + |x|)""" return np.sign(x) np.log1p(np.abs(x)) def inverselogtransform(x): """Apply inverse log-transform: y = sign(x) (exp(|x|) - 1)""" return np.sign(x) (np.exp(np.abs(x)) - 1) def croptosquare(splats): """Crop splats to nearest perfect square by dropping lowest opacity.""" ngs = splats["means"].shape[0] nside = int(np.sqrt(ngs)) ncrop = ngs - nside nside if ncrop == 0: return splats opacities = splats["opacities"].ravel() keep = np.argsort(opacities)[::-1][:nside nside] keep.sort() cropped = {k: v[keep] for k, v in splats.items()} return cropped def savepng(arr, path): """Save numpy array as PNG.""" Image.fromarray(arr).save(path) def loadpng(path): """Load PNG file to numpy array.""" return np.array(Image.open(path)) def compresspng8bit(arr, mins, maxs): """Compress array to 8-bit PNG using evidence formula.""" ranges = maxs - mins ranges[ranges == 0] = 1.0 # Guard against division by zero img = np.clip(np.round((arr - mins) / ranges 255), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) return img def decompresspng8bit(img, mins, maxs): """Decompress 8-bit PNG to array.""" normalized = img / 255.0 return normalized (maxs - mins) + mins def compresspng16bit(arr, mins, maxs): """Compress array to two 8-bit PNGs (low and high bytes).""" ranges = maxs - mins ranges[ranges == 0] = 1.0 img16 = np.clip(np.round((arr - mins) / ranges 65535), 0, 65535).astype(np.uint16) lowbyte = (img16 & 0xFF).astype(np.uint8) highbyte = ((img16 >> 8) & 0xFF).astype(np.uint8) return lowbyte, highbyte def decompresspng16bit(lowbyte, highbyte, mins, maxs): """Decompress two 8-bit PNGs to array.""" img16 = (highbyte.astype(np.uint16) << 8) | lowbyte.astype(np.uint16) normalized = img16 / 65535.0 return normalized (maxs - mins) + mins def compressgaussianspng(splats, usesort=True, outdir="output"): """Compress Gaussian splats to PNGs.""" os.makedirs(outdir, existok=True) splats["means"] = logtransform(splats["means"]) norms = np.linalg.norm(splats["quats"], axis=-1, keepdims=True) splats["quats"] = splats["quats"] / norms splats = croptosquare(splats) nside = int(np.sqrt(splats["means"].shape[0])) if usesort: # Morton code sorting would be applied here pass meta = {} for param in ["scales", "quats", "opacities", "sh0"]: arr = splats[param] C = arr.shape[-1] arrreshaped = arr.reshape(nside, nside, C) mins = np.min(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) maxs = np.max(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) img = compresspng8bit(arrreshaped, mins, maxs) savepng(img, os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}.png")) meta[param] = {"shape": arr.shape, "dtype": "uint8", "mins": mins.tolist(), "maxs": maxs.tolist()} param = "means" arr = splats[param] C = arr.shape[-1] arrreshaped = arr.reshape(nside, nside, C) mins = np.min(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) maxs = np.max(arrreshaped, axis=(0, 1)) lowbyte, highbyte = compresspng16bit(arrreshaped, mins, maxs) savepng(lowbyte, os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}low.png")) savepng(highbyte, os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}high.png")) meta[param] = {"shape": arr.shape, "dtype": "uint16", "mins": mins.tolist(), "maxs": maxs.tolist()} if "shN" in splats: np.savezcompressed(os.path.join(outdir, "shN.npz"), splats["shN"]) meta["shN"] = {"dtype": "npz"} with open(os.path.join(outdir, "meta.json"), "w") as f: json.dump(meta, f) def decompressgaussianspng(outdir="output"): """Decompress Gaussian splats from PNGs.""" with open(os.path.join(outdir, "meta.json"), "r") as f: meta = json.load(f) splats = {} for param in ["scales", "quats", "opacities", "sh0"]: info = meta[param] img = loadpng(os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}.png")) mins = np.array(info["mins"]) maxs = np.array(info["maxs"]) arr = decompresspng8bit(img, mins, maxs) arr = arr.reshape(info["shape"]) splats[param] = arr param = "means" info = meta[param] lowbyte = loadpng(os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}low.png")) highbyte = loadpng(os.path.join(outdir, f"{param}high.png")) mins = np.array(info["mins"]) maxs = np.array(info["maxs"]) arr = decompresspng16bit(lowbyte, highbyte, mins, maxs) arr = arr.reshape(info["shape"]) splats[param] = inverselogtransform(arr) if "shN" in meta: data = np.load(os.path.join(outdir, "shN.npz")) splats["shN"] = data["arr0"] return splats Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the number of Gaussians is not a perfect square, the lowest opacity Gaussians are removed, potentially losing data. Higher-order SH coefficients (shN) are compressed via NPZ rather than K-means clustering if the upstream dependency torchpq is not available, resulting in less compression. Division by zero in quantization must be handled if max == min for a channel. This method reduces the storage size of trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models by reordering splats into spatially local chunks, normalizing data within each chunk to a 0..1 range, and storing the results in GPU textures using compression formats. It builds on PNG-based Gaussian Compression by introducing spatial locality via Morton ordering to improve the efficiency of block-based texture compression (BCn). Unlike direct compression of raw data arrays, which suffers from poor compression ratios due to spatial discontinuity, this method aligns data with hardware compression block structures. Compression Ratio: Approximately 10x compression on standard 3DGS models. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the original data during preprocessing and the compressed PNGs. Metadata is minimal. Strengths: Lossless compression of quantized data, simple file format (PNG), good compression ratios due to spatial locality. Limitations: Requires cropping to perfect square, higher-order SH compression is less efficient without K-means, PNG is not optimized for GPU texture access. When to Use: When storage size is a concern and random access to individual Gaussians is not required (or can be handled via Morton code indexing). When Not to Use: When GPU texture compression (BCn) is preferred for rendering performance, or when higher-order SH coefficients are significant and K-means is not available. PNG-based Gaussian Compression is a technique for compressing trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models by quantizing parameters into 8-bit and 16-bit PNG images. It was originally developed as part of the gsplat library for PyTorch and later ported to MLX by the gsplat-mlx project. The method leverages the spatial coherence of Gaussian splats to improve compression ratios. nerfstudio-project/gsplat, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/gsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, https://github.com/RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Splat Chunk Compression with Morton Reordering
head: Chunked Gaussian Splat Compression, Morton-Ordered Splat Textures
body: This method reduces the storage size of trained 3D Gaussian Splatting models by reordering splats into spatially local chunks, normalizing data within each chunk to a 0..1 range, and storing the results in GPU textures using compression formats. Unlike direct compression of raw data arrays, which suffers from poor compression ratios due to spatial discontinuity, this method aligns data with hardware compression block structures. Inputs: A list of Gaussian splats, where each splat contains position, scale, rotation, spherical harmonic coefficients, and opacity. Outputs: Compressed GPU textures and chunk metadata (min/max values) for parameter reconstruction. Data Structures: 1. Chunk Metadata: For each chunk, the minimum and maximum values for every data field (position, scale, color, SH) stored in full Float32 precision. 2. Texture Layout: Textures are organized such that one texel represents one splat. Within a chunk of N=256 splats, the data is arranged in a 16 \times 16 square layout. Parameters: Chunk size N: 256 splats. Texture block dimension: 16 \times 16 texels per chunk. Steps: 1. 3D Morton Reordering: Sort the splats in the data array based on their 3D positions using 3D Morton order. The 3D Morton encoding for a vector v = (x, y, z) of 21-bit integers is: MortonEncode3(v) = (MortonPart1By2(v.z) \ll 2) \mid (MortonPart1By2(v.y) \ll 1) \mid MortonPart1By2(v.x) Where MortonPart1By2 interleaves the bits of a 21-bit integer into a 64-bit integer: python def MortonPart1By2(x: int) -> int: x &= 0x1fffff x = (x ^ (x << 32)) & 0x1f00000000ffff x = (x ^ (x << 16)) & 0x1f0000ff0000ff x = (x ^ (x << 8)) & 0x100f00f00f00f00f x = (x ^ (x << 4)) & 0x10c30c30c30c30c3 x = (x ^ (x << 2)) & 0x1249249249249249 return x 2. Chunking: Group the reordered splats into contiguous chunks of size N=256. 3. Chunk Normalization: For each chunk, compute the minimum and maximum values for all data fields across all splats in that chunk using full Float32 precision. Normalize each splat's data values to the range [0, 1] relative to the chunk's computed min/max. Quaternions are encoded using the "smallest three" format, storing the three smallest components and the index of the largest component. 4. 2D Morton Reordering (Texture Layout): Reorder the texture data within each chunk into a 16 \times 16 square layout using 2D Morton order to align with BCn compression block structures. The 2D Morton encoding for a coordinate c = (x, y) within a 16 \times 16 block is: python def EncodeMorton2D16x16(x: int, y: int) -> int: t = ((y & 0xF) << 8) | (x & 0xF) t = (t ^ (t << 2)) & 0x3333 t = (t ^ (t << 1)) & 0x5555 return (t | (t >> 7)) & 0xFF 5. Texture Compression: Encode the normalized splat data into GPU textures using formats such as F32x4 (128-bit), F16x4 (64-bit), Norm102 (32-bit), Norm11 (32-bit), Norm8x4 (32-bit), Norm565 (16-bit), BC7 (8-bit), or BC1 (4-bit). Some formats like Norm102 require engine-specific emulation via Float32 textures and manual shader unpacking (e.g., Unity). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Compression Quality: Storing data in 256 \times 1 stripes causes poor compression quality with BCn formats because the compression is block-based (4 \times 4 texels). Large Chunk Bounds: Morton curve flips can cause large chunk bounds, increasing variance and reducing normalization efficiency; partially filled chunks or Hilbert curves are suggested as mitigations. Precision: Normalization to 0..1 enables lower-precision formats, but format selection significantly impacts PSNR. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Bike Scene: Original 1.42GB. Very Low compression: 74MB (18.7x smaller, PSNR 24.02). Garden Scene: Original 1.35GB. Medium compression: 267MB (5.2x smaller, PSNR 48.63). Comparison: Direct BC7 compression on 256x1 stripe layout yields PSNR 21.71. Reordering into 16x16 blocks improves PSNR to 24.18. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in model size (up to ~19x) with acceptable quality loss at higher compression levels. Leverages existing GPU texture hardware for decompression. Limitations: Requires preprocessing. Lower quality presets (Very Low) may introduce visible artifacts. Some texture formats require engine-specific workarounds. This technique was introduced by Aras Pranckevičius to reduce the storage footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting models, which typically store parameters in full Float32 precision. The method relies on spatial locality via Morton ordering and chunk-wise normalization to make Gaussian data amenable to standard GPU texture compression techniques. name: GLTF/GLB Buffer & Accessor Packing
head: GLB Serialization Packing, GLTF Packing
body: Packs Gaussian Splatting attributes into GLTF buffer views and accessors, enforcing 4-byte alignment and handling component types for GLB serialization. It differs from texture-based packing (e.g., Gaussian Splat Texture Packing) by storing data in flat binary buffers accessible via standard GLTF accessors, and from SPZ packing (SPZ Packed Format) by keeping the raw attribute layout explicit rather than fully compressed into a single stream. Inputs: Gaussian attributes (positions, scales, rotations, SH coefficients, opacity) in host memory arrays; configuration flags for normalization and min/max computation. Outputs: A valid GLB file containing a JSON chunk and a BIN chunk with aligned buffer views. Data Structures: GLTFACCESSORCOMPONENTS: Maps accessor types to component counts. SCALAR:1, VEC2:2, VEC3:3, VEC4:4, MAT2:4, MAT3:9, MAT4:16. BufferView: A slice of the binary buffer. Must be 4-byte aligned. Accessor: Metadata describing the data type, count, and component layout within a BufferView. Steps: 1. Align Buffer Views: For each buffer view, if length % 4 != 0, allocate 4 - (length % 4) bytes of padding at the end. 2. Process Accessors: FLOAT (5126): Convert array to Float32Array. If count is 0, set count to array.length / comps. Compute min/max per component if requested. UNSIGNEDBYTE (5121): Convert to Uint8Array. Set min=[0], max=[255] if requested. Apply normalization flag if set. 3. Assemble GLB: Calculate binary padding length: binPadLength = pad4Length(byteLength). Calculate JSON padding length: jsonPadLength = pad4Length(jsonChunk.length). Compute total file length: totalLen = 12 + 8 + jsonDataLength + 8 + binDataLength. Write GLB header: 12 bytes containing magic 'glTF', version 2, and total length. Write JSON chunk header: 8 bytes containing JSON data length and magic 'JSON'. Write JSON data, then JSON padding (if >0). Write BIN chunk header: 8 bytes containing binary data length, magic 'BIN', and a null padding byte at index 7. Write binary buffer parts, then binary padding (if >0). Write all chunks sequentially to the file descriptor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pad4length(length): """Returns padding bytes needed to align to 4-byte boundary.""" remainder = length % 4 return 0 if remainder == 0 else 4 - remainder def packgaussiantoglb(positions, scales, quats, opacities, shcoeffs, jsondata): """ Packs Gaussian attributes into a GLB file. Assumes positions, scales, quats are Float32 arrays. shcoeffs are flattened Float32 arrays. """ # 1. Create binary buffer from attributes # Note: In a real implementation, each attribute would be a separate BufferView # with its own offset and alignment. Here we concatenate for simplicity of example. binaryparts = [] # Example: Positions (VEC3) posbytes = positions.tobytes() # Assuming numpy or similar binaryparts.append(posbytes) # Example: Scales (VEC3) scalebytes = scales.tobytes() binaryparts.append(scalebytes) # Example: Quaternions (VEC4) quatbytes = quats.tobytes() binaryparts.append(quatbytes) # Example: Opacity (SCALAR) opacbytes = opacities.tobytes() binaryparts.append(opacbytes) # Example: SH Coefficients (VEC4) shbytes = shcoeffs.tobytes() binaryparts.append(shbytes) # Concatenate all binary data bindata = b''.join(binaryparts) bindatalength = len(bindata) # 2. Align binary data binpadlength = pad4length(bindatalength) if binpadlength > 0: bindata += b'\x00' binpadlength bindatalengthaligned = bindatalength + binpadlength # 3. Prepare JSON chunk jsonchunk = json.dumps(jsondata).encode('utf-8') jsondatalength = len(jsonchunk) jsonpadlength = pad4length(jsondatalength) if jsonpadlength > 0: jsonchunk += b' ' jsonpadlength # Space padding is common for JSON chunks jsondatalengthaligned = jsondatalength + jsonpadlength # 4. Compute total length # Header (12) + JSON Chunk Header (8) + JSON Data (aligned) + BIN Chunk Header (8) + BIN Data (aligned) totallen = 12 + 8 + jsondatalengthaligned + 8 + bindatalengthaligned # 5. Write GLB Header magic = b'glTF' version = 2 header = magic + struct.pack('<I', version) + struct.pack('<I', totallen) # 6. Write JSON Chunk jsonchunkheader = struct.pack('<I', jsondatalength) + b'JSON' # 7. Write BIN Chunk binchunkheader = struct.pack('<I', bindatalength) + b'BIN\x00' # 8. Assemble file filedata = header + jsonchunkheader + jsonchunk + binchunkheader + bindata return filedata Parameters: alignment: Always 4 bytes for GLB. componenttype: FLOAT (5126) or UNSIGNEDBYTE (5121). Edge Cases: Zero Count: If accessor count is 0, set count to array.length / comps. Alignment: Failure to pad buffer views or chunks to 4-byte boundaries results in invalid GLB files. Endianness: GLB is little-endian. Ensure host memory is converted if necessary. Defines the GLTF primitive attributes and extensions required to serialize compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting data for 3D Tiles. It sets extensionsUsed to KHRgaussiansplatting, KHRgaussiansplattingcompressionspz2, and KHRmaterialsunlit, and extensionsRequired to KHRgaussiansplatting and KHRgaussiansplattingcompressionspz2. It attaches SPZ compressed stream bytes to a buffer view and references it in the KHRgaussiansplattingcompressionspz2 extension. SH coefficient attributes are defined as SHDEGREE1COEF0..2 (VEC4, FLOAT), SHDEGREE2COEF0..4 (VEC4, FLOAT), and SHDEGREE3COEF0..6 (VEC4, FLOAT). Focuses on the byte-level assembly of the GLB file. It calculates binary and JSON padding lengths using pad4Length. It computes the total file length as 12 + 8 + jsonDataLength + 8 + binDataLength. It writes the GLB header (12 bytes: magic 'glTF', version 2, total length), JSON chunk header (8 bytes: JSON data length, magic 'JSON'), and BIN chunk header (8 bytes: binary data length, magic 'BIN', null padding byte at index 7). It assembles chunks in order: GLB header, JSON header, JSON data, JSON padding, BIN header, binary buffer parts, binary padding. It writes all chunks sequentially using writeAllBuffersSync. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussian splats and the size of the SH coefficients. Padding and header writing are constant time relative to data size. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussian splats. Requires storing the full binary buffer in memory before writing. Strengths: Standard GLTF format compatibility; easy to debug and inspect; supports standard GLTF extensions. Limitations: Larger file size compared to compressed formats like SPZ or PNG-based compression (PNG-based Gaussian Compression) due to lack of compression. When to Use: When interoperability with standard GLTF viewers is required, or when debugging attribute data. When Not to Use: When file size is a critical constraint, or when streaming large datasets is required. Originated from the need to serialize 3D Gaussian Splatting data for web-based viewers and 3D Tiles. The method is implemented in tools like the 3DGS-PLY-3DTiles-Converter. It builds on the GLTF 2.0 specification and the GLB binary format. lzy-0618/3DGS-PLY-3DTiles-Converter, https://github.com/lzy-0618/3DGS-PLY-3DTiles-Converter, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GeometryState Allocation
head: CudaRasterizer::GeometryState, GeometryState Buffer Layout, GeometryState/ImageState sizing, GeometryState::fromChunk, buffer allocation query
body: GeometryState Allocation is the method for reserving and initializing contiguous device memory buffers required by the 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer to process P Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of dynamic memory management for intermediate rendering states, such as projected coordinates, covariances, and tile occupancy, ensuring alignment and correct sizing for subsequent parallel processing steps. It differs from sibling methods by focusing specifically on the allocation query and buffer initialization phase, whereas Gaussian Data Structure defines the logical fields and Gaussian Data Packing handles the serialization of input attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: P, the number of active 3D Gaussians; W, H, the image dimensions (width and height); optional semantic channel count C{sem}. Output: A GeometryState object containing pointers to allocated device memory chunks, and scalar values for geomsize and imgsize representing the byte counts required for allocation. Data Structures: The GeometryState is a struct containing pointers to device memory. Each field is allocated from a single contiguous memory chunk using an allocator that enforces 128-byte alignment. The fields are: | Field | Type | Size (elements) | Description | |---|---|---|---| | depths | float | P | Z-depths of Gaussians | | clamped | float | 3P | Clamped position or auxiliary data | | internalradii | uint32t or float | P | Screen-space radii (sources vary on type) | | means2D | float2 or float | P | Projected 2D centers (2 floats per point) | | cov3D | float | 6P | Precomputed 3D covariance matrix elements | | conicopacity | float4 or float | P | Conic matrix and opacity | | rgb | float | 3P | Precomputed RGB colors | | semanticfeature | float | C{sem} \times P | Semantic feature vectors (optional) | | tilestouched | uint32t | P | Bitmap of tiles touched by each Gaussian | | scanningspace | char | Dynamic | Temporary buffer for parallel scan (CUB) | | pointoffsets | uint32t | P | Offsets for tile-based sorting | Note: Source lists internalradii as float and conicopacity as float, while lists internalradii as uint32t and conicopacity as float4. The implementation must match the rasterizer kernel expectations. Steps: 1. Query Sizes: Call required<GeometryState>(P) to determine the byte size for the geometry state. Call required<ImageState>(W \times H) to determine the byte size for the image state. 2. Allocate Chunk: Obtain a contiguous memory chunk from the device allocator with 128-byte alignment. 3. Allocate Fields: For each field in GeometryState, call obtain(chunk, fieldptr, size, alignment=128) to get a pointer within the chunk. depths: size P \times 4 bytes. clamped: size 3P \times 4 bytes. internalradii: size P \times 4 bytes. means2D: size P \times 8 bytes (assuming float2). cov3D: size 6P \times 4 bytes. conicopacity: size P \times 16 bytes (assuming float4) or P \times 4 bytes (if scalar). rgb: size 3P \times 4 bytes. semanticfeature: size C{sem} \times P \times 4 bytes. tilestouched: size P \times 4 bytes. scanningspace: Size determined by cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum requirements for P elements. pointoffsets: size P \times 4 bytes. 4. Initialize State: Construct the GeometryState object with the obtained pointers. 5. Return Sizes: Return geomsize and imgsize as Python scalars for use by the caller. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocategeometrystate(P, W, H, Csem=0): """ Allocates and initializes the GeometryState structure for P Gaussians. """ # 1. Query required sizes geomsize = requiredgeometrystatesize(P) imgsize = requiredimagestatesize(W H) # 2. Allocate main chunk with 128-byte alignment # obtain(chunk, ptr, size, alignment) returns (chunk, ptr) chunk, baseptr = obtainchunk(size=geomsize, alignment=128) # Helper to allocate a field within the chunk def allocfield(sizebytes, alignment=128): nonlocal chunk, baseptr # In a real implementation, this would advance a pointer within chunk # and return the new pointer. Here we simulate the allocation logic. ptr = allocatefromchunk(chunk, sizebytes, alignment) return ptr # 3. Allocate fields # Note: Sizes are in bytes. Element counts are derived from P. depths = allocfield(P 4) # float, P clamped = allocfield(3 P 4) # float, 3P internalradii = allocfield(P 4) # uint32 or float, P means2D = allocfield(P 8) # float2, P (2 floats) cov3D = allocfield(6 P 4) # float, 6P conicopacity = allocfield(P 16) # float4, P (4 floats) rgb = allocfield(3 P 4) # float, 3P semanticfeature = allocfield(Csem P 4) if Csem > 0 else None tilestouched = allocfield(P 4) # uint32, P # 4. Allocate scanning space dynamically based on CUB requirements # The size depends on the number of elements to scan (P) scansize = cubdevicescaninclusivesumsize(P) scanningspace = allocfield(scansize) pointoffsets = allocfield(P 4) # uint32, P # 5. Construct and return geomstate = GeometryState( depths=depths, clamped=clamped, internalradii=internalradii, means2D=means2D, cov3D=cov3D, conicopacity=conicopacity, rgb=rgb, semanticfeature=semanticfeature, tilestouched=tilestouched, scanningspace=scanningspace, pointoffsets=pointoffsets) return geomstate, geomsize, imgsize Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alignment: All allocations must respect 128-byte alignment to satisfy CUDA memory coalescing and texture fetch requirements. Dynamic Scan Size: The scanningspace size is not a simple multiple of P; it must be queried from the CUB library (cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum). Binning State: The binning state size (for tile occupancy) is often commented out in wrapper functions but must be dynamically allocated based on the number of rendered (visible) Gaussians, not the total count P. Type Consistency: Disagreement exists on whether internalradii and conicopacity are stored as float or uint32/float4. The allocator must match the rasterizer kernel's expectation. Time Complexity: O(1) relative to P for the allocation query, but the actual memory allocation is O(P) as it reserves linear space. Memory Complexity: O(P) bytes. The total size is the sum of all field sizes: 4P + 12P + 4P + 8P + 24P + 16P + 12P + 4PC{sem} + 4P + \text{scan\size} + 4P. Scaling: Linear with the number of Gaussians P. Strengths: Efficient single-chunk allocation reduces fragmentation and simplifies memory management for the rasterizer. Limitations: Requires pre-knowledge of P and W, H. Dynamic resizing requires reallocation. When to use: At the start of each rasterization pass where the number of active Gaussians is known. GeometryState Allocation is part of the CUDA Rasterizer implementation for 3D Gaussian Splatting, originally introduced by Kerbl et al. in "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering". The specific GeometryState struct and obtain allocator pattern are found in the official and unofficial PyTorch/CUDA implementations of the rasterizer. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Preliminaries
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS), 3D Gaussian Splatting Representation, Kerbl et al. 2023, Standard 3DGS
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is an explicit scene representation method that models a 3D scene as a collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, replacing the implicit neural fields of NeRF with discrete, differentiable volumetric splats. It solves the trade-off between the high visual quality of neural radiance fields and the real-time rendering speeds of traditional rasterization by projecting these 3D Gaussians onto the image plane as 2D ellipses and compositing them via alpha blending. Unlike NeRF, which requires expensive ray marching and network queries, 3DGS enables real-time rendering through GPU-friendly tile-based rasterization. It sets apart from its siblings by using explicit Gaussian ellipsoids parameterized by mean, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics, optimized end-to-end from sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds. Inputs: A set of calibrated RGB images \{Im\}{m=1}^M with known camera poses (extrinsics Wm and intrinsics Km), and an initial sparse 3D point cloud estimated via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: A rendered RGB image \hat{C} for a target camera view, and optimized Gaussian parameters (mean, rotation, scale, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: The scene is represented as a set of N 3D Gaussian primitives G = \{gi\}{i=1}^N. Each primitive gi is defined by the following attributes: 1. Mean Position: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, representing the center of the Gaussian. 2. Covariance Matrix: \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, defining the shape and orientation. To ensure positive semi-definiteness and facilitate optimization, \Sigmai is parameterized by a rotation quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized to unit length) and a scale vector si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (typically stored in logarithmic space to ensure positivity): \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top where Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the rotation matrix derived from qi, and Si = \text{diag}(s{i,x}, s{i,y}, s{i,z}) is the diagonal scaling matrix. 3. Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1], representing the learnable scalar transparency of the primitive. 4. Color: View-dependent color ci(d) parameterized by spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times (d+1)^2}, where d is the degree of the SH basis. The color for a viewing direction d is computed as ci(d) = \text{SH}(d, Ci). Rendering Pipeline: For a given camera view with extrinsic matrix W and intrinsic matrix K: 1. Projection to Camera Space: Transform the 3D mean \mui to camera coordinates: \mu'i = W \mui (Note: Some sources use homogeneous coordinates [\mui, 1]^\top and apply KW. The standard 3DGS approach typically transforms to camera space first, then projects.) 2. 2D Splatting (Projection to Image Plane): Project the 3D Gaussian onto the 2D image plane. The projected mean \hat{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^2 is obtained via perspective projection: \hat{\mu}i = \pi(K, W \mui) where \pi denotes the perspective projection function. The projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} is approximated using a first-order Taylor expansion (affine approximation) of the perspective projection at \mui: \Sigma'i = J W{\text{rot}} \Sigmai W{\text{rot}}^\top J^\top where W{\text{rot}} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the rotation part of the world-to-camera transformation matrix, and J \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} is the Jacobian of the perspective projection transformation evaluated at \mui. Specifically, if P = KW is the projection matrix, and u = P \mui, the Jacobian J relates small changes in 3D space to changes in 2D image coordinates. 3. Rasterization and Sorting: The 2D Gaussians are rasterized onto the image. To handle overlaps, the contributing Gaussians for each pixel (or tile) are sorted in front-to-back order based on their depth (distance from the camera). This is typically implemented using a tile-based rasterizer where tiles (e.g., 16x16 pixels) are processed in parallel. 4. Alpha Compositing: For each pixel p, the final color \hat{C}(p) is computed by accumulating the contributions of the sorted Gaussians i=1 \dots N using front-to-back alpha blending: \hat{C}(p) = \sum{i=1}^{N} ci(dp) \cdot \alphai(p) \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(p)) where: ci(dp) is the view-dependent color of the i-th Gaussian for the viewing direction dp from the camera center to pixel p. \alphai(p) is the effective opacity of the i-th Gaussian at pixel p, calculated as: \alphai(p) = \alphai \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (p - \hat{\mu}i)^\top (\Sigma'i)^{-1} (p - \hat{\mu}i)\right) where \alphai is the learned scalar opacity, and the exponential term is the Gaussian density at pixel p. The product term \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(p)) represents the accumulated transmittance Ti(p), i.e., the probability that the ray has not been blocked by previous Gaussians. Training and Optimization: The parameters \{\mui, qi, si, \alphai, Ci\} are optimized using gradient descent (typically Adam) to minimize a loss function between the rendered image \hat{C} and the ground truth image I. The loss is a weighted combination of L1 loss and D-SSIM (Differentiable Structural Similarity): \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} where \lambda is a hyperparameter (typically 0.2). Adaptive Density Control: During training, the number of Gaussians is not fixed. Adaptive density control is applied periodically (e.g., every K iterations) to manage complexity and detail: 1. Densification: Gaussians with high view-space positional gradients (indicating under-reconstruction) are either cloned (if small) or split into two smaller Gaussians (if large). 2. Pruning: Gaussians with opacity below a threshold \epsilon\alpha (e.g., 0.005) or excessively large scales are removed. 3. Opacity Reset: Opacity values are periodically reset to prevent saturation and aid convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computecovariance(q, s): """ Compute 3D covariance matrix from quaternion q and scale s. q: (4,) unit quaternion [w, x, y, z] s: (3,) scale vector Returns: (3, 3) covariance matrix Sigma """ w, x, y, z = q[0], q[1], q[2], q[3] R = np.array([ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ]) S = np.diag(s) Sigma = R @ (S @ S.T) @ R.T return Sigma def projectgaussian(mu3d, W, K, Sigma3d): """ Project 3D Gaussian to 2D image plane. mu3d: (3,) mean in world coordinates W: (4, 4) world-to-camera transformation matrix K: (3, 3) camera intrinsic matrix Sigma3d: (3, 3) 3D covariance matrix Returns: mu2d (2,), Sigma2d (2, 2) """ P = K @ W muhomogeneous = np.append(mu3d, 1.0) muprojhomogeneous = P @ muhomogeneous mu2d = muprojhomogeneous[:2] / muprojhomogeneous[2] # Camera space coordinates for Jacobian mucam = W[:3,:3] @ mu3d + W[:3, 3] z = W[2,:3] @ mu3d + W[2, 3] # Jacobian of perspective projection in camera coordinates J = np.array([ [K[0,0]/z, 0, -K[0,0]mucam[0]/z2], [0, K[1,1]/z, -K[1,1]mucam[1]/z2] ]) Wrot = W[:3,:3] Sigma2d = J @ Wrot @ Sigma3d @ Wrot.T @ J.T return mu2d, Sigma2d def evaluatesh(viewdir, coeffs): """ Evaluate view-dependent color using spherical harmonics. viewdir: (3,) normalized viewing direction coeffs: (3, (d+1)^2) SH coefficients Returns: (3,) color """ # Standard SH evaluation implementation omitted for brevity; # this step is a standard mathematical operation. return np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) # Placeholder for actual SH evaluation def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameraparams, imageshape): """ Render a set of 3D Gaussians to an image. gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'mu', 'q', 's', 'alpha', 'SHcoeffs' cameraparams: Dict with 'W' (4x4), 'K' (3x3) imageshape: (H, W) Returns: Rendered image (H, W, 3) """ H, W = imageshape image = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) projected = [] for g in gaussians: Sigma3d = computecovariance(g['q'], g['s']) mu2d, Sigma2d = projectgaussian(g['mu'], cameraparams['W'], cameraparams['K'], Sigma3d) mucam = cameraparams['W'][:3,:3] @ g['mu'] + cameraparams['W'][:3, 3] if mucam[2] <= 0: continue projected.append({ 'mu2d': mu2d, 'Sigma2d': Sigma2d, 'alpha': g['alpha'], 'SHcoeffs': g['SHcoeffs'], 'depth': mucam[2], 'mu3d': g['mu'] }) projected.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): p = np.array([x, y]) transmittance = 1.0 color = np.zeros(3) for projg in projected: mu2d = projg['mu2d'] Sigma2d = projg['Sigma2d'] alpha = projg['alpha'] SHcoeffs = projg['SHcoeffs'] diff = p - mu2d try: invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) distsq = diff @ invSigma @ diff except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue density = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) effectivealpha = alpha density # Compute view direction from camera center to 3D Gaussian position camcenter = np.linalg.inv(cameraparams['W'])[:3, 3] viewdir = projg['mu3d'] - camcenter viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) c = evaluatesh(viewdir, SHcoeffs) color += c effectivealpha transmittance transmittance = (1 - effectivealpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break image[y, x] = color return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Covariance: If the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i is singular (e.g., due to degenerate Gaussians or numerical instability), the inverse cannot be computed. Guard against this by checking the determinant or using a pseudo-inverse. Precision: Floating-point precision issues can arise during the accumulation of transmittance, especially for deep scenes. Use double precision for intermediate calculations if necessary. Visibility Culling: Visibility processing selects Gaussians for the current view to save computation. Initialization: The method initializes from a sparse SfM point cloud, setting Gaussian positions to point positions, scales to average neighbor distances, and opacities to 0.5. Defines the hyperparameters and procedural rules for optimizing a set of 3D Gaussians to reconstruct a scene from images. It sets apart from static rendering by introducing adaptive density control (clone, split, prune, opacity reset) and periodic opacity resets, which are critical for converging to a high-fidelity radiance field. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly faster than NeRF, typically converging in 30-60 minutes on a single GPU, compared to hours for NeRF. Rendering time is real-time, achieving >30 FPS at 1080p on modern GPUs. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales linearly with the number of Gaussians N. Each Gaussian stores \mu (3), q (4), s (3), \alpha (1), and SH coefficients (3 \times (d+1)^2). For d=3, this is 3 \times 16 = 48 floats per Gaussian. Typical scenes use millions of Gaussians, requiring several GBs of VRAM. Measured Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic (Blender) dataset, 3DGS achieves PSNR = 33.2 ± 0.4 dB, comparable to Mip-NeRF 360 (32.4 ± 0.4 dB) and better than Instant-NGP (32.6 ± 0.4 dB) and NeRF (31.0 ± 0.6 dB). Rendering speed is 68.4 ± 4.2 FPS at 1080p on an A100 GPU. Scaling: Performance scales well with GPU parallelism due to tile-based rasterization. However, the number of Gaussians can grow large, leading to memory bottlenecks. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high visual quality, differentiable optimization, explicit representation allows for easy editing and manipulation. Limitations: Can produce redundant Gaussians, leading to inefficient memory usage. SH representation may fail to capture complex lighting interactions or high-frequency textures, resulting in color bleeding or artifacts. Not specifically designed for volumetric media, which may limit its applicability in certain domains. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 as a novel approach to novel-view synthesis. It builds on the idea of using explicit 3D primitives for rendering, moving away from the implicit neural fields of NeRF. The method was developed to address the slow training and rendering speeds of NeRF while maintaining high visual quality.
