name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Optimization Parameters
head: 25 Things Every Principal Must Know, 3DGS Training Hyperparameters, Densification and Opacity Reset Settings, Principal Knowledge Points
body: This method defines the hyperparameters and procedural rules for optimizing a set of 3D Gaussians to reconstruct a scene from images. It sets apart from static rendering by introducing adaptive density control (clone, split, prune, opacity reset) and periodic opacity resets, which are critical for converging to a high-fidelity radiance field. Inputs: Initial set of N 3D Gaussians, training images with known camera poses, and optimization hyperparameters. Outputs: Optimized set of Gaussians with updated parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, q, s, \alpha, \mathrm{SH}). Each Gaussian gi stores center \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, orientation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized quaternion), scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathrm{SH}i. The covariance matrix is reconstructed as \Sigmai = Ri \, \mathrm{diag}(si)^2 \, Ri^\top, where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from qi. The training process alternates between rendering, loss computation, and density control. 1. Initialization: Place initial Gaussians using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points and set initial scales based on nearest-neighbor distances. Initialize opacities to a small value. 2. Rendering: Project each Gaussian to 2D using EWA splatting, which linearizes the perspective projection at \boldsymbol{\mu}c to obtain \Sigma{2D}. Render the image via alpha compositing of 2D Gaussian footprints. 3. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) between rendered and ground-truth images. 4. Gradient Accumulation: Accumulate gradients for \boldsymbol{\mu}i and other parameters, tracking the magnitude \|\nabla{\boldsymbol{\mu}i} \mathcal{L}\|. 5. Adaptive Density Control: Performed periodically during training. Clone: For Gaussians with high gradient magnitude and low opacity, clone the Gaussian. Split: For Gaussians with high gradient magnitude and large scale, split the Gaussian into two. Prune: Remove Gaussians with low opacity or small scale. Opacity Reset: Reset opacities of all Gaussians to a small value to prevent saturation and allow further densification. Densification Gradient Threshold (\tau): Approximately 2 \times 10^{-4}. Opacity Reset Interval (K{\text{reset}}): Every 3000 iterations. Clone/Split/Prune Thresholds: Specific scale and opacity thresholds for clone, split, and prune operations are not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegaussians(gaussians, images, poses, numiterations, gradthreshold=2e-4, opacityresetinterval=3000, cloneopacitythresh=0.01, pruneopacitythresh=0.005): # Standard operations defined inline for self-containment def render(gs, ps): # EWA splatting: linearize perspective at muc to get Sigma2D, then alpha composite footprints return projectedcomposite(gs, ps) def computeloss(rendered, target): # Photometric loss (L1 + SSIM) return l1ssim(rendered, target) def computegradients(loss, gs): # Backpropagate through rendering graph return autograd(loss, gs) def updateparameters(gs, grads): # SGD/Adam step for g in gs: g.mu -= lr grads[g].mu g.alpha -= lr grads[g].alpha g.scale -= lr grads[g].scale g.q -= lr grads[g].q g.SH -= lr grads[g].SH def resetopacities(gs): # Reset all opacities to a small value for g in gs: g.alpha = 0.01 def clonegaussian(g): # Create copy at mu with perturbation, copy q, s, alpha, SH new = copy(g) new.mu += uniformnoise(scale=0.01) gaussians.append(new) def splitgaussian(g): # Create two copies with reduced scale (e.g., /1.6) new1 = copy(g); new2 = copy(g) new1.scale /= 1.6; new2.scale /= 1.6 gaussians.extend([new1, new2]) def prunegaussian(g): # Mark for removal from list g.toremove = True for iter in range(numiterations): renderedimage = render(gaussians, poses) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, images[iter % len(images)]) gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) updateparameters(gaussians, gradients) if iter % 100 == 0: toclone, tosplit, toprune = [], [], [] for g in gaussians: gradmag = norm(gradients[g].mu) if gradmag > gradthreshold and g.alpha < cloneopacitythresh: toclone.append(g) if gradmag > gradthreshold and g.scale > thresholdscale: tosplit.append(g) if g.alpha < pruneopacitythresh: toprune.append(g) for g in toclone: clonegaussian(g) for g in tosplit: splitgaussian(g) for g in toprune: prunegaussian(g) gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if not g.toremove] if iter % opacityresetinterval == 0: resetopacities(gaussians) Precision: Using log-space for scales prevents negative values and improves optimization stability. Boundaries: Low thresholds cause Gaussian explosion; monitor memory usage. Degenerate Input: Low-texture scenes yield small gradients, causing insufficient densification; adjust thresholds or add priors. Popping Artifacts: Arise from per-tile center-depth sort; use StopThePop, GOF, or exact pixel sort to fix them. Fixes scale-aliasing via 3D smoothing + 2D Mip filter. Use when high-frequency details cause aliasing artifacts. Replaces 3D ellipsoids with oriented disks for better surface reconstruction. Use when geometry/mesh extraction is the primary goal. Uses voxel anchors + tiny MLP for compression and far-view extrapolation. Use when model size is a constraint. Provides Level-of-Detail (LoD) from city-scale to centimeter close-ups. Use for large-scale scenes. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Densification adds sparse overhead. Memory Complexity: O(N) per Gaussian. Vanilla 3DGS uses 1–3 M Gaussians for room-scale scenes, occupying 200–800 MB on disk. Performance: Real-time rendering is achievable with tile-based rasterization. Optimization speed scales with N and iteration count. Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis, real-time rendering, explicit representation. Limitations: Large model size, potential for popping artifacts due to per-tile center-depth sort (mitigated by StopThePop, GOF, exact pixel sort). When to Use: Photorealistic novel view synthesis, room-scale scenes with plenty of views. When Not to Use: When surface mesh quality is critical (use 2DGS), or when model size is extremely constrained (use LightGaussian, SOG, EAGLES, RDO-Gaussian). Benchmarking: Report compression, FPS, and memory alongside quality metrics; numbers without them are misleading. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replaces NeRF's MLP+ray-march with explicit anisotropic Gaussians and tile rasterization. The optimization parameters described here are based on the original implementation and its refinements. The method has become a standard for radiance-field optimization, with variants addressing compression, dynamic scenes, and geometry extraction. Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: N-DGS Bounded Cholesky Parameterization
head: N-DGS
body: N-DGS is a parameterization for the joint covariance of 3D Gaussians that uses bounded Cholesky coefficients multiplied by query diagonal scales to control spatial extent and cross-covariance. It differs from sibling methods like dGS Direct Regression Parameterization by implicitly deriving the regression operator from the ambient joint Cholesky factor, rather than optimizing operational quantities directly. Inputs and Outputs Input: Query diagonal scales \mathbf{s}q \in \mathbb{R}^C, spatial Cholesky factor \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, bounded cross-covariance coefficients \mathbf{B}e \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times p}, and query Cholesky factor \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}. Output: Joint covariance blocks \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times C}, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}. Data Structures The parameterization relies on the Cholesky decomposition of the joint covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{(p+C) \times (p+C)}. The lower Cholesky factor \mathbf{L} is partitioned into spatial (p) and query (C) blocks: \mathbf{L} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{D} \end{pmatrix} where \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{D} are lower triangular, and \mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times p} is the cross-covariance Cholesky component. N-DGS parameterizes \mathbf{B} as \mathbf{B} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}q) \mathbf{B}e with |\mathbf{B}{e,jk}| \leq 1 for all entries. Numbered Steps 1. Retrieve query diagonal scales \mathbf{s}q from the Gaussian set. 2. Scale the bounded coefficients: \mathbf{B} \leftarrow \text{diag}(\mathbf{s}q) \mathbf{B}e. 3. Compute spatial covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp} \leftarrow \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top. 4. Compute cross-covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \leftarrow \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}^\top. 5. Compute query covariance: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} \leftarrow \mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^\top + \mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\top. 6. Assemble the joint covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq}^\top & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} \end{pmatrix}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ndgsparameterize(A, Be, D, sq): # A: (p, p) lower triangular, Be: (C, p) bounded, D: (C, C) lower triangular, sq: (C,) B = diag(sq) @ Be Sigmapp = A @ A.T Sigmapq = A @ B.T Sigmaqq = B @ B.T + D @ D.T return Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq def ndgsshift(Sigmapq, Sigmaqq, delta): # Sigmapq: (p, C), Sigmaqq: (C, C), delta: (C,) # Solve Sigmaqq @ x = delta for x, then compute shift x = solve(Sigmaqq, delta) return Sigmapq @ x Formulas and Definitions \mathbf{s}q: Diagonal of the query covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}. \mathbf{B}e: Bounded Cholesky coefficient matrix with entries in [-1, 1]. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}: Spatial covariance block. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq}: Cross-covariance block between spatial and query dimensions. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}: Query covariance block. Bounded norm: \|\mathbf{B}\|2 \leq \|\mathbf{B}\|F \leq \sqrt{p} \|\mathbf{s}q\|2. Cross-covariance row bound: \|(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq}){i,:}\|2 \leq \sqrt{p} \|\mathbf{s}q\|2 \sqrt{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}){ii}}. Rendered shift: \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1} \delta = \mathbf{M}{\text{N-DGS}} \delta. Normalized cross-covariance: \mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}^{-1/2} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1/2}. Whitened shift: \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}^{1/2} \mathbf{K} \mathbf{h} where \mathbf{h} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1/2} \delta. Basis-independent bound: \left\| \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}^{-1/2} \Delta \mu{\text{N-DGS}} \right\|2 \leq \left\| \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1/2} \delta \right\|2. Parameters \mathbf{s}q: Query diagonal scales. \mathbf{B}e: Bounded coefficients constrained to [-1, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls 1. Interpretation of Off-Diagonals: Off-diagonal entries of \mathbf{A} contribute to both \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} and the spatial extent (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pp}){ii}; they should not be interpreted as producing cross-covariance independently of spatial scale. 2. Ill-Conditioned Query Covariance: A bound on \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} alone does not bound the shift \Delta \mu. The inverse query covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1} and the query deviation \delta also enter the calculation. A narrow or ill-conditioned query covariance can amplify the regression operator. 3. Precision: The inversion of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} during the computation of the shift \Delta \mu can be numerically unstable if \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} is close to singular. dGS is a parameterization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes conditional opacity and position directly from explicit per-primitive parameters, avoiding the query-block inversion and covariance correction required by N-DGS. It replaces the joint covariance-derived conditioning with a Cholesky factor for opacity precision, a spatial coupling factor for position, and a coupling vector to tie them, enabling faster slicing and differentiable optimization of Gaussian positions without local minima. dGS Direct Regression Parameterization Conditional-coordinate parameterization provides a non-redundant, smooth bijection between the space of joint Gaussian covariances and a set of operational quantities: conditional spatial covariance, query-space precision, and a regression operator. It solves the problem of efficiently representing and optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions in differentiable Gaussian splatting by avoiding the computational cost and instability of inverting the query covariance block during rendering. Unlike N-DGS, which derives the regression operator from a joint Cholesky factor, this method directly optimizes the regression operator and precision, treating the coupling as a block shear. Conditional-coordinate parameterization In N-DGS, the off-diagonal entries of \mathbf{A} contribute to both cross-covariance and spatial extent, meaning they cannot be interpreted as producing cross-covariance independently of spatial scale. N-DGS derives the regression operator implicitly from covariance blocks, requiring inversion of the query block to compute the conditional mean. This contrasts with dGS, which directly parameterizes the regression operator \mathbf{M}, avoiding this inversion. The dGS joint covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^ is defined by conditional covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}}, regression operator \mathbf{M}, and query precision \boldsymbol{\Pi}. Its blocks are \Sigma{qq}^ = \frac{1}{2\lambdao} \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}, \Sigma{pq}^ = \frac{1}{2\lambdao} \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}), and \Sigma{pp}^ = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} + \frac{1}{2\lambda0} \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{pq}^\top. The opacity exponent corresponds to the query-marginal quadratic form -\lambdao \delta^\top \mathbf{V}{qq} \delta. The coupling strength is controlled by \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \in [0, 1]^C, where \boldsymbol{\Lambda}=0 decouples position from query and \boldsymbol{\Lambda}=1 enables full coupling. The internal factorization of \mathbf{M} into \mathbf{V}{pq} and \boldsymbol{\Lambda} is not claimed to be bijective. Standard Gaussian splatting uses an unnormalized Gaussian kernel, so the normalization factor is omitted from the renderer. Time and Memory Complexity Memory: N-DGS stores the Cholesky factors \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}e, and \mathbf{D}, matching the joint covariance parameter count \frac{p(p+1)}{2} + pC + \frac{C(C+1)}{2}. Time: Rendering requires computing the conditional mean shift \Delta \mu = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pq} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq}^{-1} \delta, which involves inverting \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{qq} (O(C^3)) and matrix-vector multiplication. N-DGS derives the regression operator implicitly from covariance blocks, requiring inversion of the query block, whereas dGS directly parameterizes the regression operator \mathbf{M}, avoiding this inversion. Measured Performance On two trained MCMC scenes with six views each, the opacity-weighted \|\Delta \mu\|/\bar{s} has a median of 0.29–0.30 and a 99th percentile of 4.8–7.0 for N-DGS. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Provides a bounded parameterization for cross-covariance. Limitations: The regression operator is implicit, making it harder to control directly compared to dGS. The shift can be amplified by ill-conditioned query covariance. The bounded Cholesky coefficients do not directly bound the shift, only the cross-covariance norm. When to Use Use N-DGS when the implicit parameterization is acceptable and the query covariance is well-conditioned. When Not to Use Avoid N-DGS if direct control over the regression operator is required or if the query covariance is likely to be ill-conditioned. N-DGS is part of the family of N-Dimensional Gaussian Splatting methods, which extend 3DGS to higher dimensions. It parameterizes the joint covariance using bounded Cholesky coefficients multiplied by query diagonal scales to control spatial extent and cross-covariance. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: dGS Direct Regression Parameterization
head: Direct Conditional Parameterization for Gaussian Splatting, dGS
body: dGS is a parameterization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes conditional opacity and position directly from explicit per-primitive parameters, avoiding the query-block inversion and covariance correction required by N-DGS. It replaces the joint covariance-derived conditioning with a Cholesky factor for opacity precision, a spatial coupling factor for position, and a coupling vector to tie them, enabling faster slicing and differentiable optimization of Gaussian positions without local minima. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Base Gaussian parameters (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}p, base opacity \alpha, spatial scales sx, sy, sz), query deviation \boldsymbol{\delta} = \boldsymbol{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}q (where \boldsymbol{q} is the query coordinate in view/time space), and learned conditioning parameters (\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}{pq}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}). Outputs: Conditional opacity \alpha{\text{cond}}, conditional mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}}. The conditional covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} remains query-independent and is computed as in standard 3DGS. Data Structures: 1. \mathbf{L} (Cholesky Factor): Lower-triangular matrix in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}, where C is the dimensionality of the query space (e.g., C=3 for view, C=4 for view+time). Diagonal elements use exponential activation to ensure \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top is symmetric positive-definite. For C=4, all 10 lower-triangular entries are learned. 2. \mathbf{V}{pq} (Spatial Coupling Factor): Matrix in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C}. Defined as \mathbf{V}{pq} = \bar{s} \boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}, where \bar{s} = \text{mean}(sx, sy, sz) is the average spatial scale, and \boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq} is a learnable direction with unit Frobenius norm (\|\boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}\|F = 1). This enforces \|\mathbf{V}{pq}\|F = \bar{s} and \|\mathbf{V}{pq}^{(i)}\|2 \leq \bar{s}. 3. \boldsymbol{\Lambda} (Coupling Vector): Vector in [0, 1]^C. Weights the precision-transformed query channels in the position update. Channels of the same type (e.g., the three view dimensions) share a logit. Formulas: Opacity Calculation: \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambdao \|\mathbf{L}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}\|2^2) where \lambdao = 0.35 is a fixed opacity scaling factor inherited from N-DGS. Position Calculation: \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta} where \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top is the precision matrix. Expanded Opacity for C=4 (View + Time): \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \exp(-\lambdao (\boldsymbol{\delta}v^\top \mathbf{V}{vv} \boldsymbol{\delta}v + 2\deltat \boldsymbol{\delta}v^\top \mathbf{v}{vt} + \deltat^2 vt)) where \mathbf{V}{vv}, \mathbf{v}{vt}, vt are the view, cross, and time blocks of \mathbf{V}{qq}. Matrix Definitions: \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top \mathbf{M}{\text{dGS}} = \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \mathbf{F}{pq} = \bar{s} \boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}, \quad \|\boldsymbol{\Theta}{pq}\|F = 1 Parameters: \lambdao: Opacity scaling factor, fixed at 0.35. \bar{s}: Explicit spatial-scale prior on the coupling factor, calculated as the mean of the primitive's spatial scales. Pitfalls: Removing the spatial factor \bar{s} degrades PSNR by 2.65 dB on NeRF Synthetic and 2.97 dB on 6DGS-PBR. \bar{s} is a prior on the coupling factor, not a bound on the effective regression or rendered shift, which also depends on \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})\mathbf{V}{qq} and \boldsymbol{\delta}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dgsconditioning(mup, alpha, sx, sy, sz, L, Vpq, Lambda, delta, lambdao=0.35): """ Computes conditional opacity and position for a single Gaussian primitive. Args: mup: Base position (3,) alpha: Base opacity (scalar) sx, sy, sz: Spatial scales (scalars) L: Lower-triangular Cholesky factor (C, C) Vpq: Spatial coupling factor (3, C) Lambda: Coupling vector (C,) with values in [0, 1] delta: Query deviation (C,) lambdao: Opacity scaling factor (scalar) Returns: alphacond: Conditional opacity (scalar) mucond: Conditional mean (3,) """ C = L.shape[0] # 1. Compute L^T delta LTdelta = [0.0] C for i in range(C): s = 0.0 for j in range(i, C): s += L[j, i] delta[j] LTdelta[i] = s # 2. Compute Conditional Opacity: alphacond = alpha exp(-lambdao ||L^T delta||^2) normsq = sum(x x for x in LTdelta) alphacond = alpha math.exp(-lambdao normsq) # 3. Compute Conditional Position: mucond = mup + Vpq @ diag(Lambda) @ Vqq @ delta # Vqq @ delta = L @ (L^T @ delta) Vqqdelta = [0.0] C for i in range(C): s = 0.0 for j in range(i, C): s += L[i, j] LTdelta[j] Vqqdelta[i] = s # Apply diag(Lambda) LambdaVqqdelta = [Lambda[i] Vqqdelta[i] for i in range(C)] # Multiply by Vpq Vpqterm = [0.0] 3 for i in range(3): s = 0.0 for j in range(C): s += Vpq[i, j] LambdaVqqdelta[j] Vpqterm[i] = s # Add to mup mucond = [mup[i] + Vpqterm[i] for i in range(3)] return alphacond, mucond A method for predicting Gaussian parameters from per-pixel features using a discrete probability distribution over depth buckets, solving local minima issues in direct regression. It provides a ~1 dB PSNR boost over direct regression baselines by enabling differentiable optimization of Gaussian positions via a reparameterization trick. Time Complexity: The kernel uses compile-time loop unrolling for C (3 or 4). Each thread processes one primitive. \mathbf{L}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta} uses C(C+1)/2 multiplications followed by a dot product, all in per-thread registers. No intermediate tensors or shared-memory traffic. Memory Complexity: Stores \mathbf{L} (C^2 params), \mathbf{V}{pq} (3C params), and \boldsymbol{\Lambda} (C params). For C=3, dGS uses 22 conditioning parameters; for C=4, it uses 24 parameters. Measured Performance: On an A100 with 1M primitives, slicing time for C=3 is 0.67ms for dGS (7.1x faster than N-DGS at 0.71ms) and 1.34ms for C=4 (7.7x faster than N-DGS at 0.96ms). In a separate harness, dGS is 2.0–2.3× faster than inference-cached N-DGS. Strengths: Avoids query-block inversion, regression construction, and covariance correction. Faster than N-DGS. Preserves compatibility with existing densification strategies as \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} is query-independent. Limitations: Performance gain is most pronounced on Mip-NeRF 360. On 6DGS-PBR, dGS-O (opacity-only) shows modest speedup but quality drop, while dGS recovers quality. When to Use: When faster slicing is required and differentiable position optimization is needed without the complexity of joint covariance parameterization. dGS is introduced in the cited source as a direct alternative to N-DGS. It was developed to address the computational overhead of query-block inversion in N-DGS and UBS, exposing rendered quantities directly through explicit parameters. It is used in UBS implementation experiments and compared against N-DGS under standard 3DGS densification. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Probabilistic Prediction of Pixel-Aligned Gaussians
head: Discrete Depth Bucketing for Gaussians, Probabilistic Gaussian Prediction
body: This method predicts 3D Gaussian primitive parameters (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics \mathbf{S}) from per-pixel features by modeling the depth distribution as a discrete probability density over depth buckets, rather than regressing a point estimate. It solves the problem of local minima inherent in direct regression of Gaussian centers and enables differentiable training where non-differentiable spawning/pruning heuristics from 3D-GS cannot be applied. It sets itself apart from direct regression methods by predicting a probability distribution \boldsymbol{\phi} over depth bins, which provides an approximate 1dB PSNR performance boost. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Per-pixel feature vector \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] at pixel coordinate \mathbf{u}, camera origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}{\mathbf{u}}, depth range [d{\text{near}}, d{\text{far}}], and number of depth buckets Z. Output: A tuple (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha, \mathbf{S}) representing one Gaussian primitive per pixel (simplified case M=1). Data Structures: Depth Buckets \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^Z: A vector representing discrete depth values in disparity space. The z-th element \mathbf{b}z is defined as: \mathbf{b}z = \left( \left(1 - \frac{z}{Z}\right) \left(\frac{1}{d{\text{near}}} - \frac{1}{d{\text{far}}}\right) + \frac{1}{d{\text{far}}} \right)^{-1} where z \in \{0, \dots, Z-1\} is the bucket index. Probability Vector \boldsymbol{\phi} \in \mathbb{R}^Z: Discrete probabilities predicted by the network, normalized via softmax such that \sumz \phiz = 1. \phiz represents the probability that a surface exists in depth bucket \mathbf{b}z. Offset Vector \boldsymbol{\delta} \in \mathbb{R}^Z: Per-bucket center offsets \deltaz \in [0, 1] that adjust the depth between bucket boundaries. Parameters: Z: Number of depth bins/buckets discretizing the depth range. d{\text{near}}, d{\text{far}}: Near and far planes defining the depth range. M: Number of Gaussian primitives predicted per pixel. The text simplifies to M=1 for the explanation. Steps: 1. Prediction: A neural network f processes the per-pixel feature \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] to predict the depth probability vector \boldsymbol{\phi}, the offset vector \boldsymbol{\delta}, the covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, and the spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{S}: (\boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\delta}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \mathbf{S}) = f(\mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}]) 2. Sampling: Sample a depth bucket index z from the discrete probability distribution parameterized by \boldsymbol{\phi}: z \sim p{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(z) 3. Mean Computation: Compute the Gaussian mean \boldsymbol{\mu} by unprojecting the sampled depth bucket \mathbf{b}z adjusted by the offset \deltaz along the ray direction \mathbf{d}{\mathbf{u}} from the camera origin \mathbf{o}: \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{o} + (\mathbf{b}z + \deltaz)\mathbf{d}{\mathbf{u}} 4. Opacity Assignment: Set the Gaussian opacity \alpha equal to the probability of the sampled bucket: \alpha = \phiz 5. Return: Return the tuple (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha, \mathbf{S}). Backpropagation (Reparameterization Trick): To make sampling differentiable, gradients of the loss \mathcal{L} with respect to the opacity \alpha are assigned to the gradients of the depth probability buckets \boldsymbol{\phi}: \nabla{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \mathcal{L} = \nabla{\alpha} \mathcal{L} This allows gradient descent to increase the opacity of correctly sampled depths (concentrating probability mass) and decrease it for incorrect samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def probabilisticprediction(Fu, b, o, du): """ Predicts a single Gaussian primitive per pixel using probabilistic depth bucketing. Args: Fu: Per-pixel feature vector. b: Depth bucket vector in disparity space, shape (Z,). o: Camera origin vector. du: Ray direction vector. Returns: mu: Gaussian mean vector. Sigma: Gaussian covariance matrix. alpha: Gaussian opacity. S: Spherical harmonics coefficients. """ # f is a neural network predicting parameters phi, delta, Sigma, S = f(Fu) def samplediscrete(p): """Sample an index from a categorical distribution.""" cum = np.cumsum(p) return np.searchsorted(cum, np.random.rand()) # Sample depth bucket index z from discrete distribution phi z = samplediscrete(phi) # Compute mean mu bz = b[z] deltaz = delta[z] mu = o + (bz + deltaz) du # Set opacity alpha to the probability of the sampled bucket alpha = phi[z] return mu, Sigma, alpha, S Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Directly regressing the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu} is susceptible to local minima. Non-differentiable Heuristics: The method avoids reliance on spawning and pruning heuristics from 3D-GS, which are not differentiable. Precision: The depth buckets are defined in disparity space to handle non-linear depth distributions, but precision depends on the number of buckets Z. This method predicts the color of a 3D Gaussian primitive by aggregating information from multiple nearby reference frames, using monocular depth priors to filter out occluded regions. It addresses the problem of retrieving inaccurate color information from 2D reference images due to occlusions, which degrades rendering quality in generalizable Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from direct regression methods by leveraging Inter-View Consistency and explicit visibility estimation to distinguish visible from invisible features, allowing the model to focus on visible views without manual thresholding. Performance: The probabilistic prediction method leads to an approximate 1dB PSNR performance boost compared to the baseline of directly regressing the depth. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Overcomes local minima associated with direct regression; enables differentiable training without non-differentiable heuristics. Limitations: Requires sampling during the forward pass, which introduces stochasticity; relies on the reparameterization trick for gradient flow. When to use: When direct regression of Gaussian centers leads to local minima or when differentiable training is required without relying on 3D-GS heuristics. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "PixelSplat: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs for Scalable Generalizable 3D Reconstruction". It addresses limitations in predicting Gaussian parameters from reference views, specifically the susceptibility of direct regression to local minima and the inability to use non-differentiable spawning/pruning heuristics. The approach predicts Gaussians from both reference views, with the final set being the union of predicted Gaussians. name: Occlusion-Aware IBR-based Color Prediction
head: IBR Color Prediction, Occlusion-Aware Color Prediction
body: This method predicts the color of a 3D Gaussian primitive by aggregating information from multiple nearby reference frames, using monocular depth priors to filter out occluded regions. It addresses the problem of retrieving inaccurate color information from 2D reference images due to occlusions, which degrades rendering quality in generalizable Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart from direct regression methods by leveraging explicit visibility estimation to distinguish visible from invisible features, allowing the model to focus on visible views without manual thresholding. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitive Gi with center \mui. Set of K nearby reference frames with camera centers tk. Monocular depth maps Dr for the reference frames. Reference frame images. Outputs: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients representing the color ci of the Gaussian. Data Structures: Local color window c{ik} \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times W \times 3}: A 3D tensor of size W \times W \times 3 containing RGB values sampled from the reference frame k. Visibility map v{ik} \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times W}: A 2D tensor of size W \times W containing visibility weights. Distance scalar \delta{ik} \in \mathbb{R}. Relative direction vector \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: K: Number of nearby reference frames. Not given in the sources. W: Window size for local color sampling. Effective choice is W=3. Steps: 1. Projection: For each reference frame k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, project the 3D Gaussian center \mui to the 2D image plane of the reference frame. 2. Local Color Sampling: Sample a local color window c{ik} of size W \times W \times 3 from the reference frame image k, centered at the 2D projection of \mui. This integrates 2D texture information and enhances robustness against noisy 3D Gaussian locations. 3. Depth Retrieval: Bilinearly retrieve the monocular depth map Dr as pseudo ground truth at the 2D projection location. 4. Distance Calculation: Compute the Euclidean distance \delta{ik} between the Gaussian center \mui and the reference camera center tk: \delta{ik} = \|\mui - tk\|2 5. Visibility Estimation: Estimate the visibility map v{ik} for the window based on the difference between the projected depth and the retrieved monocular depth. The formula is: v{ik} = \frac{\delta{ik} - d{ik}}{\delta{ik}} Here, d{ik} denotes the depth window corresponding to c{ik}. This step eliminates invisibility projections based on depth priors. 6. Relative Direction Calculation: Compute the normalized relative direction vector \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik} from the camera to the Gaussian: \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik} = \frac{\mui - tk}{\|\mui - tk\|2} 7. Aggregation: Pass the collected features from all K frames through an aggregation module \mathcal{M} to derive the final Gaussian color ci. The module \mathcal{M} is implemented as a three-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a width of 64. The input to \mathcal{M} is the set of tuples \{c{ik}, v{ik}, \delta{ik}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{\theta}}{ik}\}{k=1}^{K}. 8. SH Representation: The output of \mathcal{M} is represented as Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients to model view-dependent color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def project2d(point3d, intrinsics, extrinsics): """Projects a 3D point to 2D image coordinates using standard pinhole camera model.""" # Standard graphics operation: p2d = K R [P | t] [point3d; 1] # Returns normalized 2D coordinates (u, v) pass def bilinearsample(tensor, u, v, windowsize): """Samples a windowsize x windowsize region from tensor at (u, v) using bilinear interpolation.""" # Standard graphics operation pass def occlusionawarecolorprediction(mui, refframes, W=3): """ Predicts Gaussian color using occlusion-aware IBR. Args: mui: 3D center of the Gaussian (3,) refframes: List of K reference frame data structures. Each frame contains: 'image': H x Wimg x 3 tensor 'depth': H x Wimg tensor (monocular depth map Dr) 'cameracenter': 3D position tk (3,) 'intrinsics': Camera intrinsic matrix 'extrinsics': Camera extrinsic matrix W: Window size for sampling (default 3). Returns: shcoeffs: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for the Gaussian color. """ features = [] for frame in refframes: tk = frame['cameracenter'] imgk = frame['image'] depthk = frame['depth'] # 1. Project mui to 2D uk, vk = project2d(mui, frame['intrinsics'], frame['extrinsics']) # 2. Sample local color window cik cik = bilinearsample(imgk, uk, vk, W) # Shape: W x W x 3 # 3. Retrieve monocular depth window dik dik = bilinearsample(depthk, uk, vk, W) # Shape: W x W # 4. Calculate distance deltaik deltaik = norm(mui - tk) # 5. Estimate visibility map vik vik = (deltaik - dik) / deltaik # Shape: W x W # 6. Calculate relative direction thetaik thetaik = (mui - tk) / norm(mui - tk) features.append({ 'cik': cik, 'vik': vik, 'deltaik': deltaik, 'thetaik': thetaik }) # 7. Aggregation via MLP M # M is a 3-layer MLP with hidden width 64. # Input: concatenation of features from all K frames. # The exact concatenation strategy is not detailed in the source. # We assume features are flattened and concatenated along the channel dimension. inputtensor = concatenate([f['cik'].flatten() for f in features]) inputtensor = concatenate([inputtensor, f['vik'].flatten() for f in features]) inputtensor = concatenate([inputtensor, [f['deltaik'] for f in features]]) inputtensor = concatenate([inputtensor, f['thetaik'] for f in features]) # 8. SH Representation shcoeffs = aggregationmlp(inputtensor) return shcoeffs def aggregationmlp(x): """ Aggregation module M: 3-layer MLP, width 64. Input x is the concatenated feature vector. Output is SH coefficients. """ # Layer 1: Linear(64) -> ReLU x = relu(linear(x, 64)) # Layer 2: Linear(64) -> ReLU x = relu(linear(x, 64)) # Layer 3: Linear(64) -> SHDIM shcoeffs = linear(x, SHDIM) return shcoeffs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Bilinear retrieval of depth and color requires careful handling of boundary conditions if the projection falls outside the image frame. Occlusion Ambiguity: The visibility formula v{ik} = (\delta{ik} - d{ik})/\delta{ik} assumes that if the monocular depth d{ik} is significantly smaller than the projected depth \delta{ik}, the point is occluded. If d{ik} > \delta{ik}, the visibility might become negative, which should be handled (e.g., clamped to 0) depending on implementation, though the source does not explicitly specify clamping. Noisy Depth: The method relies on monocular depth as pseudo ground truth. Inaccurate depth priors may lead to incorrect visibility estimation. Time Complexity: Depends on K (number of reference frames) and W (window size). For each Gaussian, K projections and window samplings are performed, followed by an MLP inference. Memory Complexity: Stores local color windows and visibility maps for K frames per Gaussian during the forward pass. Strengths: Improves robustness against noisy 3D Gaussian locations by integrating 2D texture information. Effectively distinguishes occlusion-caused features using depth priors, enhancing rendering quality. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimates. Requires access to reference frames and their depth maps. When to use: When generalizable Gaussian Splatting suffers from occlusion artifacts and inaccurate color retrieval from 2D references. When not to use: If monocular depth priors are unavailable or highly unreliable. This method is part of the EVolSplat framework, introduced in "EVolSplat: Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting for Urban View Synthesis". It addresses issues in generalizable Gaussian Splatting where occlusions lead to inaccurate color information. The method extends projection locations into local sample windows and leverages depth priors to eliminate invisibility projections. EVolSplat: Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting for Urban View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.01054, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Conditional-coordinate parameterization
head: Proposition C.1, dGS conditional parameterization
body: Conditional-coordinate parameterization provides a non-redundant, smooth bijection between the space of joint Gaussian covariances and a set of operational quantities: conditional spatial covariance, query-space precision, and a regression operator. It solves the problem of efficiently representing and optimizing the cross-covariance between spatial and query dimensions in differentiable Gaussian splatting by avoiding the computational cost and instability of inverting the query covariance block during rendering. Unlike N-DGS, which derives the regression operator from a joint Cholesky factor, this method directly optimizes the regression operator and precision, treating the coupling as a block shear. Inputs and Outputs Input: A joint covariance matrix \Psi \in \mathbb{R}^{(p+C) \times (p+C)} that is symmetric positive-definite (SPD), where p is the spatial dimension and C is the query dimension. Output: A triplet (\Sigma{\text{cond}}, \mathbf{M}, \mathbf{V}{qq}) where: \Sigma{\text{cond}} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p} is the conditional spatial covariance (SPD). \mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times C} is the effective query-to-position regression operator. \mathbf{V}{qq} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C} is the query-space precision matrix (SPD). Data Structures \Sigma{\text{cond}}: Stored as a symmetric matrix. In practice, only the lower triangular part is stored to save memory, requiring p(p+1)/2 parameters. \mathbf{M}: Stored as a dense rectangular matrix, requiring pC parameters. \mathbf{V}{qq}: Stored as a symmetric matrix. In dGS implementations, it is factorized as \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top where \mathbf{L} is lower triangular with strictly positive diagonal entries to ensure positive definiteness, requiring C(C+1)/2 parameters. Numbered Steps 1. Decompose Joint Covariance: Given \Psi, extract the blocks \Sigma{pp} (p \times p), \Sigma{pq} (p \times C), and \Sigma{qq} (C \times C). 2. Compute Query Precision: Invert \Sigma{qq} to obtain \mathbf{V}{qq}. 3. Compute Regression Operator: Multiply \Sigma{pq} by \mathbf{V}{qq} to obtain \mathbf{M}. 4. Compute Conditional Covariance: Subtract the Schur complement term \Sigma{pq} \mathbf{V}{qq} \Sigma{pq}^\top from \Sigma{pp} to obtain \Sigma{\text{cond}}. 5. Validation: Ensure \Sigma{\text{cond}} and \mathbf{V}{qq} are positive definite. If using the Cholesky factorization for \mathbf{V}{qq}, enforce strictly positive diagonal elements in \mathbf{L}. Formulas The joint covariance \Psi is parameterized by the triplet via the following block structure: \Psi = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{pp} & \Sigma{pq} \\ \Sigma{pq}^\top & \Sigma{qq} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma{\text{cond}} + \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \\ \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \end{pmatrix} The blocks are defined as: 1. \Sigma{qq} = \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} 2. \Sigma{pq} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} 3. \Sigma{pp} = \Sigma{\text{cond}} + \mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}\mathbf{M}^\top These relations follow from the block-triangular factorization \Psi = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{I}p & \mathbf{M} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I}C \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{\Sigma}{\text{cond}} & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{I}p & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{M}^\top & \mathbf{I}C \end{pmatrix}. The inverse map, recovering the parameters from a given joint covariance \Psi, is: 1. \mathbf{V}{qq} = \Sigma{qq}^{-1} 2. \mathbf{M} = \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} 3. \Sigma{\text{cond}} = \Sigma{pp} - \Sigma{pq} \Sigma{qq}^{-1} \Sigma{pq}^\top The Schur complement theorem guarantees \Sigma{\text{cond}} \succ \mathbf{0}. The volume-element Jacobian of the coordinate transformation has a closed-form determinant: |\det D\Psi| = (\det \mathbf{V}{qq})^{-(p+C+1)} For spatial dimension p=3, this simplifies to (\det \mathbf{V}{qq})^{-(C+4)}. Parameters p: Spatial dimension (typically 3). C: Query dimension (e.g., number of query features or dimensions). Typical values: For 3D Gaussian Splatting, p=3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Singularity: The map is singular if \mathbf{V}{qq} approaches singularity (\det \mathbf{V}{qq} \to 0) or if \Sigma{\text{cond}} approaches its boundary (becomes singular). The construction \mathbf{V}{qq} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top with strictly positive Cholesky diagonal keeps the parameterization in the interior of the SPD domain. Precision: Inverting \Sigma{qq} can be numerically unstable if \Sigma{qq} is ill-conditioned. Using the Cholesky factorization of \mathbf{V}{qq} directly avoids explicit inversion in some contexts, but the definition relies on \mathbf{V}{qq}^{-1}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def jointtoconditionalparameters(Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq): """ Converts joint covariance blocks to conditional-coordinate parameters. Args: Sigmapp: (p, p) ndarray, symmetric positive-definite. Sigmapq: (p, C) ndarray. Sigmaqq: (C, C) ndarray, symmetric positive-definite. Returns: Sigmacond: (p, p) ndarray, conditional spatial covariance. M: (p, C) ndarray, regression operator. Vqq: (C, C) ndarray, query-space precision. """ # Step 2: Compute Query Precision Vqq = Sigmaqq^-1 Vqq = np.linalg.inv(Sigmaqq) # Step 3: Compute Regression Operator M = Sigmapq Vqq M = Sigmapq @ Vqq # Step 4: Compute Conditional Covariance Sigmacond = Sigmapp - Sigmapq Vqq Sigmapq^T Sigmacond = Sigmapp - Sigmapq @ Vqq @ Sigmapq.T return Sigmacond, M, Vqq def conditionalparameterstojoint(Sigmacond, M, Vqq): """ Reconstructs joint covariance blocks from conditional-coordinate parameters. Args: Sigmacond: (p, p) ndarray, conditional spatial covariance. M: (p, C) ndarray, regression operator. Vqq: (C, C) ndarray, query-space precision. Returns: Sigmapp: (p, p) ndarray. Sigmapq: (p, C) ndarray. Sigmaqq: (C, C) ndarray. """ # Invert Vqq to get Sigmaqq Sigmaqq = np.linalg.inv(Vqq) # Compute Sigmapq = M Vqq^-1 = M Sigmaqq Sigmapq = M @ Sigmaqq # Compute Sigmapp = Sigmacond + M Vqq^-1 M^T Sigmapp = Sigmacond + M @ Sigmaqq @ M.T return Sigmapp, Sigmapq, Sigmaqq Time Complexity: The forward map involves matrix inversion (O(C^3)) and matrix multiplications (O(p^2 C + p C^2)). The inverse map involves similar operations. For fixed p and C, this is constant time per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: The parameter count is \frac{p(p+1)}{2} + pC + \frac{C(C+1)}{2} = \frac{(p+C)(p+C+1)}{2}, which is non-redundant and matches the number of parameters in the full joint covariance matrix. Strengths: Efficiency: Avoids repeated inversion of the query covariance block during rendering by optimizing \mathbf{V}{qq} and \mathbf{M} directly. Stability: The block shear interpretation provides a clear geometric understanding and stable optimization landscape when \mathbf{V}{qq} is kept positive definite. Non-redundancy: The parameterization is a smooth bijection, ensuring no loss of information. Limitations: Singularity Risk: If \mathbf{V}{qq} becomes singular, the parameterization breaks down. Strictly positive Cholesky diagonals are required. Complexity: The inverse map requires matrix inversion, which can be costly for large C. When to Use: Use when optimizing query-dependent Gaussian splats where the query-space precision and regression operator are natural optimization variables. Prefer over N-DGS when avoiding query covariance inversion during rendering is critical. The conditional-coordinate parameterization was introduced in the context of differentiable Gaussian splatting, specifically in the "Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting" paper. It formalizes the relationship between joint Gaussian covariances and their conditional components, providing a theoretical foundation for efficient optimization of query-dependent splats. The method leverages the Schur complement and block-triangular factorization to define a smooth bijection between the joint covariance space and the conditional parameters. Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22778, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian-based Representation
body: Gaussian-based representation encodes signals, data, or geometric structures as an explicit, continuous sum of parameterized Gaussian functions. It solves the problem of representing high-dimensional data (images, 3D scenes, vector spaces) with a compact, differentiable, and analytically tractable structure. Unlike Fourier transforms which provide global frequency decomposition, or implicit neural representations (MLPs) which require iterative evaluation, this method offers a local representation where each kernel decays rapidly, enabling closed-form operations for rendering, compression, and analysis. It sets itself apart from Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) by approximating the value of the signal itself rather than modeling the distribution of data points. Inputs: A target signal S (e.g., image pixels, 3D point cloud, radiance field samples) and a target number of primitives N. Outputs: A set of N Gaussian parameters \{\thetan\}{n=1}^N such that the aggregate function f(\mathbf{x}) approximates S. Data Structures: The representation consists of a list of N Gaussians. The specific fields depend on the domain dimensionality d: 2D Domain (e.g., Image): Each Gaussian n is an 8-tuple: \boldsymbol{\mu}n \in \mathbb{R}^2: Center location. \mathbf{L}n \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Lower triangular Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}n (3 values: l{11}, l{21}, l{22}). \mathbf{c}n \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color attribute (RGB). Note: Amplitude is often normalized or absorbed into color; opacity is not required for permutation-invariant summation. 3D Domain (e.g., Scene): Each Gaussian n includes: \boldsymbol{\mu}n \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center location. \mathbf{R}n \in SO(3): Orientation (often stored as a quaternion \mathbf{q}n \in \mathbb{R}^4). \mathbf{s}n \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale (log-space or linear). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}n = \mathbf{R}n \mathbf{S}n \mathbf{S}n^\top \mathbf{R}n^\top: Covariance matrix constructed from rotation and scale to capture anisotropy. \mathbf{c}n: Radiance/Color attributes (often expanded via Spherical Harmonics for view-dependence). \alphan: Opacity scalar. Core Formula: The signal f(\mathbf{x}) at any point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d is the sum of individual Gaussian primitives: f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{n=1}^N Gn(\mathbf{x}) where the n-th Gaussian primitive is defined as: Gn(\mathbf{x}) = an \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}n)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}n^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}n)\right) Here, an is the amplitude (or attribute vector like color), \boldsymbol{\mu}n is the mean, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}n is the covariance matrix. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Vectorized (EigenGS): Map a principal-component eigenspace of the input data to Gaussian space for instant initialization. Feedforward: Use a predictive neural network to infer parameters directly from input data, replacing per-instance random or iterative optimizations. 2. Optimization (Fitting): Define a loss function \mathcal{L} between the rendered/evaluated f(\mathbf{x}) and the target signal S. For 2D images: Use L2 (MSE) or hybrid L2+D-SSIM losses over all pixels. For 3D scenes: Use photometric losses over multiple views or ray samples combined with sparsity, density, or geometric constraints. Perform gradient descent to optimize \{\boldsymbol{\mu}n, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}n, an\} (and other attributes). 3. Adaptive Deployment (Densification/Pruning): Monitor residuals or gradients. Splitting: Create new Gaussians in regions with high residuals or high gradient magnitude (e.g., SplitNet, confidence-aware splitting). Pruning: Remove Gaussians where coverage is redundant or contribution is negligible. 4. Rendering/Aggregation: 2D (Permutation-Invariant): Compute the sum directly; alpha blending or transmittance accumulation is unnecessary as occlusion is irrelevant. 3D (Rasterized Splatting): 1. Project each 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space (computing 2D covariance via Jacobian of projection). 2. Sort Gaussians by depth. 3. Alpha-blend front-to-back to yield correct occlusion and volumetric effects. 5. Compression (Optional): Apply vector quantization, codebook-based compression, and entropy coding (ANS, Huffman) to store parameters compactly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluategaussian2d(points, mu, L, color): """ Evaluate 2D Gaussians at query points. points: (M, 2) array of query coordinates mu: (2,) array, mean L: (2, 2) array, lower triangular Cholesky factor of Sigma color: (3,) array, RGB attribute Returns: (M, 3) weighted color contributions """ diff = points - mu # (M, 2) # Solve L @ y = diff.T for y, equivalent to y = L^{-1} (x - mu) y = np.linalg.solve(L, diff.T) # (2, M) mahalsq = np.sum(y2, axis=0) # (M,) weights = np.exp(-0.5 mahalsq) # (M,) return weights[:, None] color # (M, 3) def rendergaussianimage(gaussians, imageshape): """ Render a 2D image from a set of Gaussians using permutation-invariant summation. gaussians: List of dicts with keys 'mu', 'L', 'color' imageshape: (H, W) """ H, W = imageshape image = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) # Create coordinate grid ycoords, xcoords = np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W] points = np.stack([xcoords.flatten(), ycoords.flatten()], axis=1) # (HW, 2) # Vectorized evaluation and summation for g in gaussians: mu = g['mu'] L = g['L'] color = g['color'] contributions = evaluategaussian2d(points, mu, L, color) image += contributions.reshape(H, W, 3) return image def optimizegaussianimage(targetimage, gaussians, lr=0.01, epochs=100): """ Iterative optimization loop for Gaussian parameters. Uses automatic differentiation framework (e.g., PyTorch) in practice. """ target = targetimage.astype(np.float32) for epoch in range(epochs): # Forward pass currentimage = rendergaussianimage(gaussians, targetimage.shape[:2]) # Compute loss (MSE) loss = np.mean((currentimage - target)2) # Backward pass and parameter update # Gradients dloss/dmu, dloss/dL, dloss/dcolor are computed automatically # Parameters are updated: param -= lr gradient # (Implementation relies on standard autodiff; explicit gradient formulas omitted) pass # Placeholder for framework-specific gradient step return gaussians Parameters: N: Number of Gaussians. Typical values range from thousands for images to millions for 3D scenes. d: Dimensionality (2 for images, 3 for scenes). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Structures: May require very large N or specialized learning schedules (e.g., multi-level fitting). Parameter Redundancy: Ambiguous quaternions or covariances can lead to non-unique representations if not managed (e.g., via bounded parameterizations). 3D Occlusion: Requires correct depth sorting and alpha blending; naive summation fails for volumetric effects. A signal representation technique that decomposes a one-dimensional signal into a weighted sum of Gaussian probability density functions (kernels). Unlike the Fourier transform, which provides a global frequency decomposition, this method offers a local representation where each kernel decays rapidly with respect to the input variable. It differs fundamentally from Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs): while GMMs use Gaussians to model the distribution of data points, 1D Gaussian Splatting uses them to approximate the value of the signal itself. A compact representation of the density field D as a weighted sum of Gaussians plus a hashed residual field F, allowing efficient modeling of fine density details. It sets itself apart from pure Gaussian splatting methods by explicitly separating coarse structure from high-frequency residuals, enabling precise reconstruction of complex media without requiring a single ultra-high-resolution representation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: GaussianImage (2D): 2,000 FPS, 0.4 GB memory, 44.1 dB PSNR for image compression. LIG (9K×9K image): 20 FPS, 16.7–20.3 GB memory, 37.5–42.2 dB PSNR. 3DGS (Mip-NeRF 360): 120 FPS, 746 MB memory, 27.46 dB PSNR for scene synthesis. Compact 3DGS (+PP): 128 FPS, 29 MB memory, 27.03 dB PSNR for scene synthesis. Hybrid mesh–GS: 231 FPS, 0.74M splats, 24.28 dB PSNR for indoor 3D. GARLIC (SIFT1M 128D): Recall@1=0.69 for K-NN classification. Scaling: Gaussian representations offer orders-of-magnitude faster decoding than MLP-based INRs or classic codecs (e.g., 1000–2000 FPS vs. 10–150 FPS for INR codecs). Strengths: Analytic differentiability, closed-form operations, fast rendering, adaptivity via densification/pruning, hybrid compatibility with meshes and deep frameworks. Limitations: High parameter count for very high-frequency signals, potential for redundancy, domain-specific rendering optimizations required. Gaussian-based representations leverage the mathematical properties of Gaussian functions, which are fundamental in statistics and signal processing. The specific application to signal approximation and rendering has seen significant development in recent years, with key contributions including GaussianImage for 2D compression (Zhang et al., 2024), 3D Gaussian Splatting for scene reconstruction (Lee et al., 2023), and various extensions for hierarchical fitting, hybrid decomposition, and vectorized initialization (Zhu et al., 2025; Tai et al., 2025). The method unifies concepts from Gaussian Mixture Models, splatting techniques, and differentiable rendering. Gaussian-Based Representation, https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/gaussian-based-representation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 1D Gaussian Splatting
head: 1D Gaussian Representation
body: 1D Gaussian Splatting is a signal representation technique that decomposes a one-dimensional signal into a weighted sum of Gaussian probability density functions (kernels). Unlike the Fourier transform, which provides a global frequency decomposition, this method offers a local representation where each kernel decays rapidly with respect to the input variable. It differs fundamentally from Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs): while GMMs use Gaussians to model the distribution of data points, 1D Gaussian Splatting uses them to approximate the value of the signal itself. Inputs: A ground truth signal S(t) sampled at T discrete points t \in \{1, \dots, T\}. The number of Gaussian kernels K. Outputs: A reconstructed signal \hat{S}(t). Optimized parameters for each kernel: mean \mui, standard deviation \sigmai, and weight wi for i=1 \dots K. Data Structures: The representation consists of K Gaussian kernels. Each kernel i is defined by three scalar parameters: 1. \mui: The mean (center) of the Gaussian. 2. \sigmai: The standard deviation (width) of the Gaussian. 3. wi: The weight (opacity) of the Gaussian. To ensure numerical stability during optimization, the variances are initialized and stored as log-variances. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize K Gaussian kernels. Set means \mui and standard deviations \sigmai randomly within reasonable ranges covering the domain of t. Initialize variances as log-variances for numerical stability. Initialize weights wi (Not given in the sources; typically set to 1.0 or small random values). 2. Optimize the parameters \mui, \sigmai, wi using gradient descent to minimize the loss function \mathcal{L}. 3. Compute the reconstructed signal \hat{S}(t) using the optimized parameters. Formulas: The Gaussian kernel function fi(t) is defined as: fi(t \mid \mui, \sigmai) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigmai^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(t-\mui)^2}{2\sigmai^2}\right) The reconstructed signal \hat{S}(t) is the weighted sum of these kernels: \hat{S}(t) = \sum{i=1}^K wi fi(t) The optimization minimizes the Mean Squared Error (L2) loss between the reconstructed signal and the ground truth S(t): \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{T} \sum{t=1}^T (\hat{S}(t) - S(t))^2 Parameters: K: The number of Gaussian kernels used to reconstruct the signal. Learning rate: 0.1. Optimizer: Adam. Iterations: 100,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Smoothing side-effect: A limited number of Gaussians causes the reconstructed signal to be smoother than the ground truth, losing high local variance. This acts as a form of compression. Oscillation: If too many Gaussians are used or hyper-parameters are not tuned, reconstruction quality may oscillate (e.g., between 40 and 45 dB PSNR). Diminishing returns: Reconstruction quality only improves until a certain number of Gaussians is reached; adding more beyond this point may not help or may cause instability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussiankernel(t, mu, sigma): """Computes the value of a 1D Gaussian kernel.""" return (1.0 / np.sqrt(2 np.pi sigma2)) np.exp(-((t - mu)2) / (2 sigma2)) def adamstep(params, grads, m, v, tstep, lr=0.1, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): """Standard Adam optimizer update step.""" m = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) grads v = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) grads2 mhat = m / (1 - beta1tstep) vhat = v / (1 - beta2tstep) return params - lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + eps), m, v def train1dgaussiansplatting(tdata, Sgroundtruth, K, numiterations=100000, lr=0.1): """Trains 1D Gaussian Splatting parameters.""" T = len(tdata) # Initialize parameters mus = np.random.uniform(tdata.min(), tdata.max(), K) logvariances = np.random.randn(K) sigmas = np.exp(logvariances) weights = np.ones(K) # Not given in the sources # Adam state mmus, vmus = np.zeroslike(mus), np.zeroslike(mus) msigmas, vsigmas = np.zeroslike(sigmas), np.zeroslike(sigmas) mweights, vweights = np.zeroslike(weights), np.zeroslike(weights) for step in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Forward pass Shat = np.zeros(T) for i in range(K): fi = gaussiankernel(tdata, mus[i], sigmas[i]) Shat += weights[i] fi # Loss calculation error = Shat - Sgroundtruth loss = np.mean(error2) # Gradients gradmus = np.zeros(K) gradsigmas = np.zeros(K) gradweights = np.zeros(K) for i in range(K): fi = gaussiankernel(tdata, mus[i], sigmas[i]) # dL/dwi gradweights[i] = np.mean(2.0 / T error fi) # dL/dmui dfdmu = fi (tdata - mus[i]) / (sigmas[i]2) gradmus[i] = np.mean(2.0 / T error weights[i] dfdmu) # dL/dsigmai dfdsigma = fi ((tdata - mus[i])2 / (sigmas[i]3) - 1.0/sigmas[i]) gradsigmas[i] = np.mean(2.0 / T error weights[i] dfdsigma) # Update parameters mus, mmus, vmus = adamstep(mus, gradmus, mmus, vmus, step, lr) sigmas, msigmas, vsigmas = adamstep(sigmas, gradsigmas, msigmas, vsigmas, step, lr) weights, mweights, vweights = adamstep(weights, gradweights, mweights, vweights, step, lr) return mus, sigmas, weights Compression: The method compresses data. For a signal with T points, K Gaussians require 2K parameters (mean and sigma) plus K weights. In the Delhi temperature example (113 days), 45 Gaussians (90 parameters) achieved 47 dB PSNR, effectively compressing the data. Performance: In the cited experiment, 45 Gaussians achieved 47 dB PSNR. Quality oscillates between 40-45 dB after K=47. Strengths: Local representation; effective compression for smooth or moderately varying signals; differentiable, allowing gradient-based optimization. Limitations: Limited capacity to represent high local variance without many kernels; potential for oscillation with poor hyper-parameter tuning; smoothing effect may be undesirable for signals with sharp features. When to use: Signal approximation, forecasting (where overall behavior is more interesting than small variations), and compression. 1D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the paper "Gaussian Splatting: An Introduction". It is presented as an alternative to Fourier decomposition for signal representation, leveraging the local nature of Gaussian kernels. The method is distinct from Gaussian Mixture Models, which model data distributions rather than signal values.
