name: Gaussian Density Field Representation
head: Gaussian + Hashed Residual Field
body: A compact representation of the density field D as a weighted sum of Gaussians plus a hashed residual field F, allowing efficient modeling of fine density details. It sets itself apart from pure Gaussian splatting methods by explicitly separating coarse structure from high-frequency residuals, enabling precise reconstruction of complex media without requiring a single ultra-high-resolution representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n Gaussian parameters \{wj, cj, rj\}{j=1}^n representing the coarse density field, and optionally a hashed residual field data structure. Output: The total density value D(x) at any spatial point x. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian List: An array of n Gaussians. Each Gaussian j is defined by weight wj (scalar), center cj (3D vector), and radius rj (scalar). 2. Hashed Residual Field: A hash table mapping spatial coordinates to residual values R(x). Hash table size and bucket configuration: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute the sequence of Gaussians and residual fields for the target density distribution. 2. Runtime Evaluation (Direct): For a query point x, compute the Gaussian sum \tilde{D}(x), retrieve R(x) from the hashed residual field, set F(x) = R(x), and return D(x) = \tilde{D}(x) + F(x). 3. Runtime Evaluation (Splatting/Texture-based): To construct the density field for rendering, initialize texture channels. For each Gaussian j, splat its weight wj into Channel 1 to accumulate \tilde{D}(x), with no weight normalization. If a residual field hash table exists, retrieve R(x) for each entry, multiply it by the current \tilde{D}(x) at that location, and store the result in Channel 2. After splatting, for each pixel or voxel, divide the value in Channel 2 by the value in Channel 1 to obtain R(x), then add R(x) to \tilde{D}(x) to yield the final density D(x). Formulas: The density field D(x) is defined as the sum of the Gaussian approximation \tilde{D}(x) and the residual field F(x): D(x) = \tilde{D}(x) + F(x) = \sum{j=1}^n wj \exp\left(-\frac{\|x - cj\|^2}{rj^2}\right) + F(x) Where: x is the query point in 3D space. \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. F(x) is the value retrieved from the hashed residual field. If no residual field is used, F(x) = 0. Parameters: n: Not given in the sources. Hash table size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Preprocessing Limitation: Preprocessing is only for the representation of the density field and does not prevent run-time changes to media properties, lighting, or scene configuration. A texture-based method for constructing the density field per frame by splatting Gaussian weights and residual products into separate color channels, then dividing to recover the residual field. It sets itself apart from direct per-point evaluation by leveraging parallel texture operations for field construction rather than sequential queries. It is chosen when the rendering pipeline supports texture-based splatting and requires fast, frame-by-frame reconstruction of the density field for ray marching or ray tracing. See Gaussian-based Representation. Strengths: Efficient modeling of fine density field details; allows run-time changes to lighting and media properties despite preprocessing. Limitations: Requires preprocessing for the density field representation; accuracy depends on the number of Gaussians and the resolution/coverage of the residual field. When to use: When high-frequency density details are needed and can be captured by a residual field, and when the rendering algorithm can accommodate rapid reconstruction (e.g., via splatting). When not to use: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Originated from the work of Zhou et al. (2007b) and extended in the context of gradient-based interpolation and sampling for real-time rendering of inhomogeneous, single-scattering media. The Gaussian model was chosen for its ability to compactly represent density fields, while the hashed residual field was added to capture details that the Gaussian sum alone could not. The method is used in real-time rendering pipelines for volumetric media, particularly where animated sequences require efficient density field reconstruction per frame. Gradient‐based Interpolation and Sampling for Real‐time Rendering of Inhomogeneous, Single‐scattering Media, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2008.01343.x, fetched 2026-10-27

name: MaskGaussian
head: Mask-based pruning, Masked Gaussian Splatting
body: MaskGaussian is a differentiable rendering method that models 3D Gaussian primitives as probabilistic entities, attaching a learnable inclusion probability to each primitive to control model size during training. It solves the problem of sub-optimized reconstruction caused by deterministic pruning, where Gaussians removed early in training cannot recover even if they become important later. It sets itself apart from standard mask-based pruning (e.g., Compact3DGS) by applying the mask during alpha-compositing rather than to Gaussian attributes like opacity or scale, ensuring that masked-out Gaussians still participate in rasterization and receive meaningful gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \Sigma, color \mathbf{c}, base opacity \alpha), camera parameters, and a target scene. Outputs: A rendered 2D image and a set of pruned 3D Gaussians (those with high existence probability). Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is augmented with two learnable mask scores (logits) si \in \mathbb{R}^2. These logits are not stored as part of the primitive's geometric attributes but are optimized alongside them. Numbered Steps: 1. Mask Sampling: For each Gaussian i, sample a binary mask \mathcal{M}i \in \{0, 1\} indicating presence or absence. This is done by applying the Gumbel-Softmax relaxation to the log-softmax of the two logits si, using a straight-through estimator to allow gradients to flow to si. \mathcal{M}i = \text{StraightThrough}(\text{GumbelSoftmax}(\log \text{softmax}(si); \tau)) The temperature parameter is \tau = 1. 2. Standard Splatting (Alpha Generation): Splat all Gaussians in the standard way without applying the mask to their attributes. This computes the projected opacity \alphai and color \mathbf{c}i for every Gaussian, ensuring that even masked-out Gaussians generate valid alpha values and pass through the alpha-filtering stage. 3. Masked Rasterization: Perform alpha-compositing from front to back. Apply the mask \mathcal{M}i to the transmittance attenuation and color accumulation steps. Transmittance Update: T{i+1} = \mathcal{M}i \cdot (1 - \alphai) \cdot Ti + (1 - \mathcal{M}i) \cdot Ti If \mathcal{M}i = 1, transmittance attenuates by (1-\alphai). If \mathcal{M}i = 0, transmittance remains unchanged (T{i+1} = Ti). Color Accumulation: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N \mathcal{M}i \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti Masked Gaussians (\mathcal{M}i=0) contribute zero color to the pixel but remain in the computation pipeline. 4. Gradient Backpropagation: Compute the loss L and backpropagate to the mask logits si. The gradient with respect to the mask \mathcal{M}i is derived as: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathcal{M}i} = \alphai \cdot Ti \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})} \cdot (\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{b}{i+1}) where \mathbf{b}{i+1} is the background color rendered behind the i-th Gaussian: \mathbf{b}{i+1} = \sum{j=i+1}^N \mathcal{M}j \cdot \mathbf{c}j \cdot \alphaj \cdot Tj This gradient allows unsampled (masked-out) Gaussians to receive updates based on their "virtual" contribution. 5. Loss Function: The total loss combines the rendering loss and a sparsity term: L = L{render} + \lambdam \cdot Lm Where L{render} is typically (1 - \lambdaD)L1 + \lambdaD L{D-SSIM}, and Lm is the squared loss on the average number of Gaussians: Lm = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \mathcal{M}i \right)^2 The hyperparameter \lambdam balances the trade-off between rendering quality and model size. 6. Pruning Procedure: Periodically remove Gaussians that are consistently sampled as absent. Sample each Gaussian 10 times. If a Gaussian is never sampled (mask is 0 in all 10 draws), it is permanently deleted. This is applied at every densification step and every 1,000 iterations after densification ends. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskgaussianrasterization(gaussians, masks, cameras): """ gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives with attributes (mu, sigma, c, alphabase) masks: Binary tensor M of shape (N,), sampled from GumbelSoftmax of logits s cameras: Camera parameters for projection Returns: Rendered image, gradients for masks and gaussians """ # Step 1: Project all Gaussians to 2D (Standard Splatting) # Compute 2D covariance Sigma, projected opacity alphai, and color ci # for ALL Gaussians, ignoring masks for attribute modification projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: proj = project3dgaussianto2d(g, cameras) projectedgaussians.append({ 'alpha': proj.alpha, 'color': proj.color, 'position': proj.position, 'covariance': proj.covariance }) # Step 2: Sort Gaussians by depth (front to back) projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['position'].z) # Step 3: Masked Alpha-Compositing image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) transmittance = np.ones((height, width)) # We need to compute gradients, so we store intermediate values # b{i+1} is the color rendered behind Gaussian i # We can compute this by iterating back-to-front or storing Ti and ci for i, g in enumerate(projectedgaussians): Mi = masks[i] alphai = g['alpha'] ci = g['color'] # Get current transmittance at this Gaussian's screen position # Ti is the transmittance BEFORE this Gaussian Ti = transmittance[g.screencoords] # Compute background color b{i+1} # This is the color accumulated from Gaussians i+1 to N # In a forward pass, we don't have b{i+1} yet. # However, for the backward pass (gradient), we need it. # The formula for gradient uses b{i+1}. # In implementation, b{i+1} can be computed by a reverse pass # or by storing the accumulated color before adding the current Gaussian. # Forward Pass: Update Transmittance and Color # T{i+1} = Mi (1 - alphai) Ti + (1 - Mi) Ti # If Mi == 1: T{i+1} = Ti (1 - alphai) # If Mi == 0: T{i+1} = Ti if Mi == 1: newtransmittance = Ti (1 - alphai) colorcontribution = ci alphai Ti else: newtransmittance = Ti colorcontribution = 0.0 # Update image image[g.screencoords] += colorcontribution transmittance[g.screencoords] = newtransmittance # Step 4: Compute Loss and Backpropagate # L = Lrender + lambdam (mean(M))^2 # Gradient dL/dMi = alphai Ti (dL/dc(x)) (ci - b{i+1}) # Note: b{i+1} is the color rendered by Gaussians i+1...N # This requires a second pass or storing the accumulated color history. return image def samplemask(logits, temperature=1.0): """ logits: Tensor of shape (N, 2) Returns: Binary mask tensor of shape (N,) """ # Gumbel-Softmax relaxation # msoft = GumbelSoftmax(logits, temperature) # Straight-through estimator: use argmax for forward, soft for backward probs = torch.softmax(logits / temperature, dim=-1) # Sample from categorical distribution # In practice, Gumbel-Softmax is used for differentiability # But for hard mask, we sample and use straight-through gumbel = -torch.log(-torch.log(torch.randlike(logits))) y = logits + gumbel msoft = torch.softmax(y / temperature, dim=-1) # Hard sample for forward pass mhard = torch.argmax(msoft, dim=-1).float() # Straight-through: use mhard in forward, msoft in backward # PyTorch's straightthrough implementation handles this return mhard def prunegaussians(gaussians, masks, numsamples=10): """ Remove Gaussians that are never sampled as present. """ # Sample masks multiple times allsamples = [] for in range(numsamples): m = samplemask(gaussians.logits) allsamples.append(m) # Stack samples: shape (numsamples, N) allsamples = torch.stack(allsamples) # A Gaussian is removed if it is 0 in all samples # Presence count presencecount = torch.sum(allsamples, dim=0) # Remove if count is 0 keepmask = presencecount > 0 return keepmask Parameters: \tau (Temperature): 1. \lambdam (Sparsity weight): 0.1 (iterations 19,000–20,000), 0.0005 (0–30,000 iterations), or 0.001 (0–30,000 iterations). Note that cites a value of 5 \times 10^{-4} for a similar sparsity term in a related context, but explicitly defines \lambdam for the squared loss Lm with the values above. Pruning frequency: Every 1,000 iterations after densification ends, and at every densification step. Sample count for pruning: 10 independent draws. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Irreversibility: Once a mask logit is pushed negative, the gradient reaching it is too weak to pull it back, even if sparsity pressure is released. Masked primitives do not recover. Gradient Binding: Unlike methods that multiply masks with opacity or scale, MaskGaussian does not bind mask gradients to these attributes. This prevents fine Gaussians from being disadvantaged by negative gradients intended to shrink them. Zero Density Filtering: Previous methods that multiply masks with opacity result in zero density \alpha, causing the Gaussian to be filtered out before rasterization and preventing gradient updates. MaskGaussian avoids this by applying the mask during blending. A technique used within MaskGaussian to guide the learnable mask parameters toward a condensed representation by promoting both fine-grained sparsity and structural coherence. It uses an L2 norm on group activations to encourage switching off entire anchors together, differing from standard L1 penalties. Time Complexity: The rasterization step is O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of Gaussians. The masking adds negligible overhead as it is a simple multiplication. However, the need to sample masks 10 times for pruning adds a small constant factor during pruning steps. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Gaussians and the additional 2N logits for the masks. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF360: 27.43 PSNR, 1.205M Gaussians, 384.7 FPS (vs. 3DGS: 27.45 PSNR, 3.204M Gaussians, 187.8 FPS). Tanks & Temples: 23.72 PSNR, 0.590M Gaussians, 558.3 FPS (vs. 3DGS: 23.74 PSNR, 1.825M Gaussians, 254.5 FPS). Deep Blending: 29.69 PSNR, 0.694M Gaussians, 637.1 FPS (vs. 3DGS: 29.53 PSNR, 2.815M Gaussians, 201.3 FPS). Pruning ratios: 62.4%, 67.7%, and 75.3% with speedups of 2.05x, 2.19x, and 3.16x respectively. Strengths: Allows masked Gaussians to receive gradients, enabling dynamic assessment of their contribution. Avoids the "zero density" problem of attribute-based masking. Limitations: The sparsity weight \lambdam does not directly control the final model size; the resulting size varies by scene texture and densification supply. The mask is effectively irreversible. MaskGaussian was introduced to address the limitations of deterministic pruning in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where pruned Gaussians cannot recover. It builds on Compact3DGS by making pruning probabilistic and introduces masked-rasterization to allow gradients to flow to unsampled Gaussians. The method was published in 2025. One Setting, Any Scene: Tuning-Free Model-Size Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10987108/v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MaskGaussian: Adaptive 3D Gaussian Representation from Probabilistic Masks, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.00072, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Sparsity Regularization for Pruning
head: Group Sparsity Loss
body: Sparsity Regularization for Pruning is a technique used within MaskGaussian to guide the learnable mask parameters toward a condensed representation by promoting both fine-grained sparsity and structural coherence. It solves the problem of inefficient storage and rendering costs by ensuring that entire groups of Gaussians (anchors) are removed cohesively, rather than leaving sparse, fragmented subsets that hinder compactness. It sets itself apart from standard L1-style penalties by using an L2 norm on group activations to encourage switching off entire anchors together. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Learnable mask parameters \mathbf{m}, where m{j,i} is the parameter for the i-th Gaussian in anchor j. Hyperparameters \lambda{\text{mask}} and \lambda{\text{group}}. Outputs: A scalar regularization loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} added to the total optimization objective. Data Structures: Masks (\mathbf{m}): A tensor of shape (N, K), where N is the number of anchors and K is the number of Gaussians per anchor. Sigmoid Activation: The effective mask value M{j,i} is derived via the sigmoid function: M{j,i} = \sigma(m{j,i}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-m{j,i}}}. Steps: 1. Compute the sigmoid activation for all mask parameters to obtain values in [0, 1]. 2. Calculate the per-Gaussian masking loss \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} by summing all activated mask values and normalizing by the total number of masks NK. 3. Calculate the group sparsity loss \mathcal{L}{\text{group}} by computing the L2 norm of the activated mask vector for each anchor, summing these norms, and normalizing by the number of anchors N. 4. Combine the two losses using the hyperparameters to produce the final sparsity regularization term. 5. An anchor j is considered pruned or inactive for a given Level of Detail (LOD) if all its associated masks are effectively zero (i.e., \sum{i=1}^K M{j,i} = 0). Formulas: The standard masking loss encourages deactivation of any single non-essential Gaussian: \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} = \frac{1}{NK} \sum{j=1}^{N} \sum{i=1}^{K} \sigma(m{j,i}) The group sparsity loss encourages the entire group of Gaussians associated with a single anchor to be "switched off" together: \mathcal{L}{\text{group}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} \|\sigma(\mathbf{m}j)\|2 where \mathbf{m}j is the vector of mask activations for anchor j, and \|\cdot\|2 is the L2 norm. The total sparsity regularization is a weighted sum: \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} = \lambda{\text{mask}} \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} + \lambda{\text{group}} \mathcal{L}{\text{group}} Parameters: \lambda{\text{mask}}: Weight for the per-Gaussian masking loss. Value not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{group}}: Weight for the group sparsity loss. Value not given in the sources. N: Number of anchors. K: Number of Gaussians per anchor. Pitfalls: L1-style penalties: Using an L1 penalty on the group instead of L2 may leave anchors with only a few sparsely active Gaussians, hindering the compactness of the condensed model. Precision: The sigmoid function maps values to (0,1). For an anchor to be considered "pruned," the sum of masks must be effectively zero, requiring the underlying parameters m{j,i} to be sufficiently negative. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesparsityregularization(masks, lambdamask, lambdagroup): """ Computes the sparsity regularization loss for MaskGaussian. Args: masks (Tensor): Learnable mask parameters of shape (N, K). lambdamask (float): Weight for the per-Gaussian masking loss. lambdagroup (float): Weight for the group sparsity loss. Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ import torch import torch.nn.functional as F # N: number of anchors, K: number of Gaussians per anchor N, K = masks.shape # Step 1: Sigmoid activation # sigma(m) = 1 / (1 + exp(-m)) activatedmasks = torch.sigmoid(masks) # Step 2: Per-Gaussian masking loss # Lmask = (1 / (NK)) sum(all activated masks) lmask = torch.sum(activatedmasks) / (N K) # Step 3: Group sparsity loss # Lgroup = (1 / N) sum(L2norm of each anchor's activated masks) # activatedmasks shape: (N, K) # L2 norm along dim=1 (across K Gaussians) groupnorms = torch.norm(activatedmasks, p=2, dim=1) lgroup = torch.sum(groupnorms) / N # Step 4: Combine lsparsity = lambdamask lmask + lambdagroup lgroup return lsparsity A variant used in Mobile-4DGS that extends sparsity regularization to dynamic Gaussian partitioning and temporal stability. It introduces a sparsity loss L{\text{sparse}} and a binary loss L{\text{bin}} to encourage a sparse dynamic partition using the closed-form hard-concrete relaxation of the \ell0 penalty. L{\text{sparse}} = \frac{1}{|F|} \sum{i \in F} \text{sigmoid}(\elli) - T \log \frac{-\gamma}{\zeta}, where F contains free Gaussians (not forced/promoted). L{\text{bin}} = \frac{1}{|F|} \sum{i \in F} pi(1 - pi), where pi = \text{sigmoid}(\elli), encourages binary values. This is combined with temporal regularizations: L{\text{acc}} (discourages large acceleration), L{\text{dur}} (prevents broad temporal support), and L{\text{ext}} (constrains displacement within one temporal standard deviation). The total objective is L{4D} = L + \lambda{\text{acc}} L{\text{acc}} + \lambda{\text{dur}} L{\text{dur}} + \lambda{\text{ext}} L{\text{ext}} + \lambda{\text{sparse}} L{\text{sparse}} + \lambda{\text{bin}} L{\text{bin}}. Staged optimization is used: sparsity loss from 5k to 20k iterations, binary loss from 22k to 25k, and temporal parameters follow specific learning-rate schedules. Time Complexity: The computation of \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} is O(NK) for the mask loss and O(N) for the group loss, making it negligible compared to the rendering and reconstruction losses. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the mask parameters \mathbf{m} of size N \times K. Strengths: Promotes structural coherence by removing entire anchors, leading to significant storage savings and cleaner LOD representations. Normalized terms ensure regularization strength is invariant to scene size. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambda{\text{mask}} and \lambda{\text{group}}. The L2 norm on the group is specifically chosen to avoid the fragmentation issues of L1, but this may be less effective if the goal is fine-grained, individual Gaussian removal without anchor-level pruning. When to use: When using MaskGaussian's unfolding scheme and needing to reduce the number of active anchors for efficient LOD management. When not to use: When fine-grained, individual Gaussian pruning without anchor-level removal is desired, or when computational resources for additional regularization terms are extremely limited. Originated in the context of "Unfolding 3D Gaussian Splatting via Iterative Gaussian Synopsis". The method was developed to address the need for condensed representations in multi-level LOD schemes, where standard sparsity penalties were insufficient for removing entire structural units (anchors). It builds on the concept of learnable mask parameters introduced in MaskGaussian. name: 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
head: 2D Gaussian Splatting (2D-GS), 2D Gaussian Splatting Surfel Rasterization, 2D-GS, Gaussian Surfel Splatting, Gaussian Surfels (2DGS), Screen-space Gaussian Rasterization, standard 2DGS
body: 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization is a differentiable rendering technique that represents scene geometry and radiance using semi-opaque 2D Gaussian primitives (surfels). It solves the problem of accurate ray-splat intersection and normal estimation by replacing 3D ellipsoids with 2D oriented planar disks, which allows for more precise surface reconstruction and view-consistent geometry. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, is the use of 2D Gaussians defined by tangential vectors and a zero depth scale, enabling direct normal extraction via the cross product of tangents and avoiding degenerate line projections through low-pass filtering. It builds on Primitive Representation by projecting these 2D primitives to screen space and accumulating color, alpha, depth, and normal maps via front-to-back alpha compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: means: N \times 3 array of 3D positions \boldsymbol{\mu}. quats: N \times 4 array of quaternions (w, x, y, z) defining rotation R. scales: N \times 3 array of scaling factors. For 2DGS, the depth scale is fixed to 0, so S = \text{Diag}(sx, sy, 0). opacities: N array of scalar opacity values o. colors: N \times 3 or N \times K array of RGB colors or Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. viewmats: C \times 4 \times 4 camera-to-world transformation matrices W. Ks: C \times 3 \times 3 camera intrinsic matrices. width, height: Image dimensions. nearplane, farplane: Clipping distances (default 0.01, 1e10). tilesize: Integer, default 16, side length of tiles for rasterization. Outputs: rendercolors: C \times H \times W \times 3 RGB images. renderalphas: C \times H \times W \times 1 alpha maps. rendernormals: C \times H \times W \times 3 surface normal maps. renderdepths: C \times H \times W \times 1 depth maps. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive i is projected to screen space, resulting in a per-pixel state structure (80 bytes total): means2d (2 elements, 8 B): 2D projected position in pixel space (uc, vc). raytransforms (9 elements, 36 B): 3 \times 3 affine matrix mapping pixel-space UV to splat coordinates in row-major KWH order. This matrix is derived from the screen-space covariance \Sigma'{2D}. opacities (1 element, 4 B): Alpha transparency value oi. colors (3 elements, 12 B): RGB color \mathbf{c}i. radii (1 element, 4 B): Maximum projected radius in pixels for culling/LOD. depths (1 element, 4 B): Z-depth of the Gaussian center for depth sorting. normals (3 elements, 12 B): Surface normal \mathbf{n}i in camera space, computed as \mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v. Steps: 1. Projection: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space. For each Gaussian i: Compute the world-space covariance \Sigma^wi = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T. Transform to camera space: \Sigma{cam, i} = Wi \Sigma^wi Wi^T. Compute the screen-space covariance \Sigma'{2D, i} using the Jacobian \mathbf{J} of the perspective projection evaluated at the camera-space center \mathbf{x}{c,cam}: \Sigma'{2D, i} = \mathbf{J} \Sigma{cam, i} \mathbf{J}^\top where \mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}. Compute the normal \mathbf{n}i as the cross product of the two principal tangential vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v derived from the rotation and scale. Output means2d, raytransforms (derived from \Sigma'{2D}), radii, depths, and normals. 2. Color Evaluation: If SH degree is not None: Compute view directions \mathbf{d}i = \text{normalize}(\text{means}i - \text{campos}). Evaluate SH to get RGB colors \mathbf{c}i. If SH degree is None: Use direct RGB colors \mathbf{c}i. Broadcast opacities and colors to match the number of cameras C. 3. Tile Intersection: Compute tile dimensions: tilewidth = \lceil \text{width} / \text{tile\size} \rceil, tileheight = \lceil \text{height} / \text{tile\size} \rceil. Identify which tiles each Gaussian overlaps using means2d and radii. Sort Gaussians by depth within each tile. 4. Rasterization (Per-Pixel): For each pixel \mathbf{u} and each overlapping Gaussian i in depth order: Ray-Splat Intersection: Compute the intersection of the ray passing through pixel \mathbf{u} with the 2D Gaussian disk. Let M be the projection matrix combining view and intrinsics. Let px, py be the pixel coordinates. Compute intersection vectors in the local tangent space: \mathbf{h}u = -Mg[0,:3] + Mg[2,:3] \cdot px \mathbf{h}v = -Mg[1,:3] + Mg[2,:3] \cdot py where Mg is the 3 \times 4 projection matrix for the Gaussian. Compute the cross product to find the intersection point in the tangent plane: \mathbf{tmp} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{h}u, \mathbf{h}v) Pitfall: Guard against degenerate cases where the ray is parallel to the surfel or the surfel is projected as a line. If |\mathbf{tmp}[2]| < 10^{-10}, skip the intersection. Compute intersection coordinates (u, v) in the local tangent space: u = \mathbf{tmp}[0] / \mathbf{tmp}[2] v = \mathbf{tmp}[1] / \mathbf{tmp}[2] Alpha Computation: Compute the 2D Gaussian value at (u, v): G(u, v) = \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2}{2}\right) Compute the effective alpha \alphai: \alphai = \min(oi \cdot G(u, v), \text{MAX\ALPHA}) Pitfall: Skip if \alphai \le 0 or if the computed sigma (distance metric) is negative. Some implementations use a tighter bound combining 3D and 2D sigma estimates: \sigma = 0.5 \cdot \min(\sigma{3D}, \sigma{2D}) where \sigma{3D} = u^2 + v^2 and \sigma{2D} = 2.0(dx^2 + dy^2). Accumulation: Maintain transmittance T = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Accumulate color, depth, and normal: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u}) = \sum{i \in N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai Ti D(\mathbf{u}) = \sum{i \in N} di \alphai Ti / \sum{i \in N} \alphai Ti \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{u}) = \sum{i \in N} \mathbf{n}i \alphai Ti / \sum{i \in N} \alphai Ti where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rasterize2dgs(means, quats, scales, opacities, colors, viewmats, Ks, width, height, tilesize=16): """ Rasterize 2D Gaussian Splatting primitives. Simplified NumPy reference implementation. """ N = means.shape[0] C = viewmats.shape[0] # 1. Projection # Compute screen-space covariance and means2d # This involves: quatscaletocovarpreci, fullyfusedprojection # Outputs: means2d (C, N, 2), raytransforms (C, N, 3, 3), radii (C, N), depths (C, N), normals (C, N, 3) means2d, raytransforms, radii, depths, normals = project2dgs(means, quats, scales, viewmats, Ks, width, height) # 2. Color Evaluation # If SH is used, evaluate SH here. Otherwise use direct colors. # colorsforraster shape: (C, N, 3) colorsforraster = evaluatecolors(colors, means, viewmats) # 3. Tile Intersection # Determine which tiles each Gaussian overlaps tilewidth = int(np.ceil(width / tilesize)) tileheight = int(np.ceil(height / tilesize)) # isectids: (C, N, maxtilespergauss) # flattenids: (C, totalintersections) isectids, flattenids = intersecttiles(means2d, radii, depths, tilesize, tilewidth, tileheight) # 4. Rasterization Loop rendercolors = np.zeros((C, height, width, 3)) renderalphas = np.zeros((C, height, width, 1)) rendernormals = np.zeros((C, height, width, 3)) renderdepths = np.zeros((C, height, width, 1)) for c in range(C): # Get primitives for this camera m2d = means2d[c] # (N, 2) rt = raytransforms[c] # (N, 3, 3) opac = opacities # (N,) cols = colorsforraster[c] # (N, 3) rads = radii[c] # (N,) deps = depths[c] # (N,) norms = normals[c] # (N, 3) # Sort primitives by depth sortidx = np.argsort(deps) m2d = m2d[sortidx] rt = rt[sortidx] opac = opac[sortidx] cols = cols[sortidx] rads = rads[sortidx] norms = norms[sortidx] # Iterate over pixels for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Find overlapping Gaussians for this pixel # In optimized versions, this is done via tile offsets # Here, we assume a list of overlapping indices for simplicity overlapindices = getoverlappinggaussians(x, y, m2d, rads) T = 1.0 acccolor = np.zeros(3) accalpha = 0.0 accdepth = 0.0 accnormal = np.zeros(3) weightsum = 0.0 for i in overlapindices: # Ray-Splat Intersection # Compute intersection in local tangent space # Using the projection matrix M for this Gaussian # M is derived from viewmat and K # Simplified intersection logic from # hu and hv depend on pixel coordinates and projection matrix # tmp = cross(hu, hv) # if abs(tmp[2]) < 1e-10: continue # u, v = tmp[0]/tmp[2], tmp[1]/tmp[2] # Compute Alpha # sigma = u^2 + v^2 # alpha = min(opac[i] exp(-sigma/2), MAXALPHA) # Guard against degenerate/negative alpha if alpha <= 0: continue # Accumulate acccolor += cols[i] alpha T accalpha += alpha T accdepth += deps[i] alpha T accnormal += norms[i] alpha T weightsum += alpha T T = (1 - alpha) if T < 1e-4: break rendercolors[c, y, x] = acccolor renderalphas[c, y, x] = accalpha if weightsum > 0: renderdepths[c, y, x] = accdepth / weightsum rendernormals[c, y, x] = accnormal / weightsum return rendercolors, renderalphas, rendernormals, renderdepths A variant where each Gaussian primitive has M Gaussian vertices (typically M=4) instead of constant attributes. It allows spatially varying material and normal attributes by interpolating among these vertices in the tangent space, defined by rotation R and scaling S. This replaces the constant attributes of standard Gaussians, enabling high-frequency specular reconstruction and accurate reflections without increasing primitive count. It is chosen when high-fidelity inverse rendering and relighting are required. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels, but optimized to O(N \cdot K) where K is the average number of overlapping Gaussians per pixel using tile-based rasterization. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian attributes and O(H \cdot W) for the output buffers. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable on modern GPUs due to the tile-based, fused kernel implementation. It is generally faster than neural field-based methods but may require more primitives than implicit representations for complex geometry. Strengths: Accurate ray-splat intersection, direct normal estimation, differentiable rendering, real-time capability. Limitations: Degenerate line projections if not filtered, requires careful handling of opacity and depth sorting. 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) was introduced as a lower-dimensional form of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to improve geometry reconstruction and normal estimation. It replaces 3D ellipsoids with 2D oriented planar disks (surfels), defined by position, scaling, tangential vectors, opacity, and color. This approach addresses the limitations of 3DGS in modeling complex surfaces and provides view-consistent geometry. It is widely used in novel view synthesis, SLAM, and inverse rendering. name: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting
head: RefGaussian, TextureSplat
body: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting (TextureSplat) enhances 2D Gaussian Splatting by replacing single attribute values per primitive with spatially varying texture maps for material properties and normals. Unlike methods that assign constant attributes to each primitive, this approach decouples geometric representation from appearance, enabling high-frequency specular reconstruction and accurate reflections in reflective scenes without increasing the primitive count. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by leveraging the closed-form ray-splat intersection to map screen pixels to local texture coordinates, allowing hardware-accelerated rendering via texture atlases. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives (surfels), each defined by position pk, tangential vectors t{uk} and t{vk}, scaling factors s{uk} and s{vk}, and learnable opacity ok. Each primitive k has an associated texture map T^k containing material properties (e.g., albedo, roughness, normal maps) in its local coordinate system. Output: A rendered image with accurate specular highlights and reflections. Data Structures: Primitive k: pk: Position in world space. t{uk}, t{vk}: Tangential vectors in world space. s{uk}, s{vk}: Scaling factors along tangential directions. ok: Learnable opacity scalar. T^k: Texture map stored in a unified texture atlas. Texture Atlas: A single large texture containing all primitive textures T^k, packed to leverage GPU hardware-accelerated texture filtering. Numbered Steps: 1. Primitive Definition: Represent the scene using oriented planar disks (2DGS primitives). For each primitive k, define position pk, tangential vectors t{uk} and t{vk}, and scaling factors s{uk}, s{vk}. The primitive's normal is computed as nk = t{uk} \times t{vk}. 2. Ray-Splat Intersection: For each pixel (x, y), determine the intersection with contributing primitives. Using the closed-form ray-splat intersection of 2DGS, map screen-space pixels to local texture coordinates (uk, vk) for each primitive k. The local coordinates correspond to the point on the primitive's tangent plane. 3. Gaussian Evaluation: Evaluate the 2D Gaussian value Gk(u, v) at the local coordinates (uk, vk): Gk(u, v) = \exp \left( - \frac{u^2 + v^2}{2} \right) The effective opacity \alphak(x, y) for primitive k at pixel (x, y) is: \alphak(x, y) = ok Gk(uk(x, y), vk(x, y)) 4. Attribute Retrieval: Retrieve material attributes ak(x, y) from the per-primitive texture map T^k using the local texture coordinates: ak(x, y) = T^k(uk(x, y), vk(x, y)) If the attribute is a normal map, the retrieved normal is in the tangent space of the primitive. 5. Normal Transformation: Transform tangential normal maps to world space. For each primitive, construct a rotation matrix Rk from the tangential vectors t{uk} and t{vk} (and the normal nk). Transform the sampled tangent-space normal n{tangent} to world space: n{world} = Rk \cdot n{tangent} 6. Physically-Based Rendering (PBR): Use the retrieved material attributes (e.g., albedo, roughness, world-space normal) in a physically-based rendering model compatible with deferred shading pipelines to compute the final color contribution, including specular reflections. 7. Alpha Compositing: Accumulate the color contributions of all primitives contributing to pixel (x, y) in front-to-back order. The final pixel color A(x, y) is: A(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^{N} ai \alphai(x, y) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(x, y)) where ai is the color attribute retrieved from T^i (or computed via PBR), and \alphai(x, y) is the effective opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def evaluate2dgaussian(u, v): """Evaluate the 2D Gaussian function at local coordinates (u, v).""" return math.exp(-(u2 + v2) / 2.0) def sampletextureatlas(atlas, u, v): """Bilinear sampling of the texture atlas at normalized coordinates (u, v).""" u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) h, w, c = atlas.shape uidx = u (w - 1) vidx = v (h - 1) u0, u1 = int(math.floor(uidx)), int(math.ceil(uidx)) v0, v1 = int(math.floor(vidx)), int(math.ceil(vidx)) u0, u1 = max(0, min(w-1, u0)), max(0, min(w-1, u1)) v0, v1 = max(0, min(h-1, v0)), max(0, min(h-1, v1)) du, dv = uidx - u0, vidx - v0 top = atlas[v0, u0] (1 - du) + atlas[v0, u1] du bottom = atlas[v1, u0] (1 - du) + atlas[v1, u1] du return top (1 - dv) + bottom dv def transformnormaltoworld(tangentu, tangentv, normal, tangentnormal): """Transform a tangent-space normal to world space using the primitive's basis.""" nworld = ( tangentu tangentnormal[0] + tangentv tangentnormal[1] + normal tangentnormal[2]) return nworld def renderpixel(pixels, primitives, textureatlas, atlasuvoffsets, atlasuvscales): """ Render a single pixel using per-primitive texture mapping. Assumes local coordinates (uk, vk) and depth are precomputed via closed-form ray-splat intersection. """ image = np.zeros((len(pixels), 3)) for pixelidx, (x, y) in enumerate(pixels): contributingprimitives = [] for k, prim in enumerate(primitives): uk, vk = prim.uk, prim.vk gk = evaluate2dgaussian(uk, vk) alphak = prim.ok gk if alphak > 1e-6: contributingprimitives.append((k, alphak, uk, vk, prim.depth)) # Sort by depth for front-to-back compositing contributingprimitives.sort(key=lambda item: item[4]) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) for k, alphak, uk, vk, in contributingprimitives: prim = primitives[k] uatlas = uk atlasuvscales[k][0] + atlasuvoffsets[k][0] vatlas = vk atlasuvscales[k][1] + atlasuvoffsets[k][1] texturesample = sampletextureatlas(textureatlas, uatlas, vatlas) # Extract material properties from packed texture sample albedo = texturesample[:3] roughness = texturesample[3] tangentnormal = texturesample[4:7] worldnormal = transformnormaltoworld( prim.tuk, prim.tvk, np.cross(prim.tuk, prim.tvk), tangentnormal) # Apply PBR shading model compatible with deferred pipelines color = albedo # Placeholder for full PBR evaluation weight = alphak (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += color weight accumulatedalpha += weight if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break image[pixelidx] = accumulatedcolor return image Parameters: Texture Atlas Size: Not given in the sources. Filtering: Hardware-accelerated texture filtering (bilinear/trilinear) is used. PBR Model: Compatible with deferred shading pipelines. Specific model details are not given. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Local coordinates (u, v) must be computed accurately to ensure correct texture sampling. Boundaries: Texture coordinates may fall outside the primitive's local bounds; texture filtering handles this, but clipping may be needed. Degenerate Input: If tangential vectors are collinear, the normal is undefined. This is a general 2DGS issue. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of primitives per pixel, similar to standard 2DGS, but with additional texture sampling and PBR shading costs. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases due to the storage of texture maps for each primitive, packed into a texture atlas. Measured Performance: Achieves real-time rendering performance on standard benchmarks. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of primitives per pixel, consistent with base 2DGS. Strengths: High-frequency specular reconstruction, accurate reflections, decoupling of geometry and appearance, hardware acceleration. Limitations: Increased memory usage for textures, complexity of texture atlas management. When to Use: Reflective scenes, scenes with high-frequency material variations. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Introduced by Mae Younes and Adnane Boukhayma from Inria France in the paper "TextureSplat: Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting" (arXiv:2506.13348v2, Dec 2025). History: Builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [18] and 3D Gaussian Splatting [27]. Usage: Novel view synthesis, reflective scene reconstruction. name: ToF Gaussian Rasterization Forward Pass
head: ToF Gaussian Rasterization
body: This method implements the forward pass of the C++/CUDA rasterizer for Time-of-Flight Gaussian Splatting. It restructures scene and camera parameters into a single tuple, invokes the CUDA kernel, and returns rendered maps including color, phasor, depth, and auxiliary buffers. Inputs: rastersettings (camera and rendering parameters), gaussians (model attributes), and trainingargs (optimization flags). Data Structures: The method packs all inputs into a single tuple passed to the CUDA kernel. The tuple layout is: 1. rastersettings.bg 2. means3D 3. colorsprecomp 4. phasorsprecomp 5. opacities 6. scales 7. rotations 8. rastersettings.scalemodifier 9. cov3Dsprecomp 10. rastersettings.viewmatrix 11. rastersettings.projmatrix 12. rastersettings.tanfovx 13. rastersettings.tanfovy 14. rastersettings.imageheight 15. rastersettings.imagewidth 16. sh 17. shp 18. rastersettings.shdegree 19. rastersettings.campos 20. rastersettings.prefiltered 21. rastersettings.debug 22. rastersettings.nearn 23. rastersettings.farn 24. rastersettings.depthrange 25. rastersettings.useviewdependentphase 26. phaseoffset 27. dcoffset. Parameters: phaseoffset and dcoffset are scalar values used for offset correction. If rastersettings.optimizephaseoffset (or optimizedcoffset) is true, the raw tensor is used; otherwise, it is detached, converted to a CPU numpy array, and cast to a Python scalar. Steps: 1. Restructure arguments into the tuple defined above, applying the offset handling logic. 2. If rastersettings.debug is true, deep-copy all arguments to CPU before invocation to preserve state for debugging. 3. Invoke the C++/CUDA forward rasterization function C.rasterizegaussians(args). 4. Save relevant tensors for the backward pass: rastersettings, numrendered, colorsprecomp, phasorsprecomp, means3D, scales, rotations, cov3Dsprecomp, radii, sh, shp, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, phaseoffset, dcoffset. Restructure arguments phaseoffset = gaussians.getphaseoffset if trainingargs.optimizephaseoffset else gaussians.getphaseoffset.detach().cpu().numpy().item() dcoffset = gaussians.getdcoffset if trainingargs.optimizedcoffset else gaussians.getdcoffset.detach().cpu().numpy().item() args = ( rastersettings.bg, gaussians.means3D, gaussians.colorsprecomp, gaussians.phasorsprecomp, gaussians.opacities, gaussians.scales, gaussians.rotations, rastersettings.scalemodifier, gaussians.cov3Dsprecomp, rastersettings.viewmatrix, rastersettings.projmatrix, rastersettings.tanfovx, rastersettings.tanfovy, rastersettings.imageheight, rastersettings.imagewidth, gaussians.sh, gaussians.shp, rastersettings.shdegree, rastersettings.campos, rastersettings.prefiltered, rastersettings.debug, rastersettings.nearn, rastersettings.farn, rastersettings.depthrange, rastersettings.useviewdependentphase, phaseoffset, dcoffset) # 2. Debug handling if rastersettings.debug: argscpu = tuple(x.detach().cpu().clone() if hasattr(x, 'detach') else copy.deepcopy(x) for x in args) # 3. Backward pass preparation backwardtensors = [ rastersettings, None, gaussians.colorsprecomp, gaussians.phasorsprecomp, gaussians.means3D, gaussians.scales, gaussians.rotations, gaussians.cov3Dsprecomp, radii, gaussians.sh, gaussians.shp, None, None, None, phaseoffset, dcoffset ] return color, phasor, depth, normal, acc, entropy, depthdistortion, ampdistortion, pixels, distribution, radii, backwardtensors Outputs: color, phasor, depth, normal, acc, entropy, depthdistortion, ampdistortion, pixels, distribution, radii. name: Vanilla 2D Gaussian Splatting Rendering
head: 2D Gaussian Splatting Rendering, 2DGS Renderer, 2DGS Rendering, Deferred Rendering with 2DGS, Vanilla2DGSRenderer, Volumetric Alpha Blending
body: Vanilla 2D Gaussian Splatting Rendering is the core rasterization pass for 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), a differentiable rendering method that represents scenes as a collection of 2D Gaussian primitives (surfels). It solves the problem of projecting these 3D-aware 2D primitives onto a 2D image plane to produce RGB, alpha, depth, and normal maps. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Per-Primitive Texture Mapping for Reflective Gaussian Splatting which adds complex lighting, is its reliance on standard volumetric alpha blending for color accumulation and a deferred geometry pass for normals and depth, without pre-computed 3D covariance matrices. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by providing the high-level API and post-processing logic (depth/normal extraction) that consumes the raw rasterized attributes. Inputs: means3D: 3D positions of Gaussian centers, shape (N, 3). means2D: 2D screen-space positions, shape (N, 2), initialized with requiresgrad=True. shs or colorsprecomp: Spherical Harmonics coefficients or pre-computed colors, shape (N, K) or (N, 3). opacities: Opacity values, shape (N, 1). scales: Scaling factors, shape (N, 3). rotations: Quaternions (w, x, y, z), shape (N, 4). cov3Dprecomp: Pre-computed 3D covariance matrices. Set to None to allow the rasterizer to compute covariance from scales and rotations. camera: Object containing view and projection matrices, image dimensions, FOV, and background color. Outputs: renderedimage: RGB image, shape (H, W, 3). rendalpha: Alpha map, shape (H, W). rendnormal: View-space normal map, shape (H, W, 3). viewnormal: World-space normal map, shape (H, W, 3). surfdepth: Surface depth map, shape (H, W). surfnormal: Surface normal map (derived from depth), shape (H, W, 3). allmap: Intermediate tensor containing expected depth, alpha, view normals, median depth, and distortion. Data Structures: allmap: A tensor of shape (H, W, 7) (or flattened to (H \times W, 7)) with the following layout: Index 0: Expected depth. Index 1: Alpha. Indices 2-4: View-space normals (Nx, Ny, Nz). Index 5: Median depth. Index 6: Depth distortion. Steps: 1. Configuration: Compute tangent half-angles for the horizontal and vertical fields of view: \tan(\text{FOV}x/2) and \tan(\text{FOV}y/2). Configure GaussianRasterizationSettings with image dimensions, FOV tangents, background color, scaling modifier, view/projection matrices, SH degree, camera position, and prefiltered=False. 2. Rasterization: Instantiate GaussianRasterizer with the settings. Call the rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs/colorsprecomp, opacities, scales, rotations, and cov3Dprecomp=None. This produces renderedimage, radii (visibility filter), and allmap. 3. Alpha Extraction: Compute renderalpha from allmap at index 1. 4. Normal Extraction (View Space): Extract view-space normals from allmap indices 2-4. Transform them to world space by multiplying by the transpose of the camera's world-to-camera rotation matrix R{cam}^T: N{world} = R{cam}^T N{view}. 5. Depth Extraction: Extract mediandepth from allmap index 5. Replace NaNs with 0. Extract expecteddepth from allmap index 0. Divide by renderalpha. Replace NaNs with 0. Compute surfdepth as a weighted sum of expecteddepth and mediandepth based on a depthratio parameter: \text{surf\depth} = \text{depth\ratio} \cdot \text{median\depth} + (1 - \text{depth\ratio}) \cdot \text{expected\depth} Where depthratio is 1 for bounded scenes (using median) and 0 for unbounded scenes (using expected). 6. Surface Normal Derivation: Compute surfnormal from surfdepth using depthtonormal. This involves: Reconstructing 3D points from the depth map using camera intrinsics and extrinsics (depthstopoints). Computing spatial derivatives (dx, dy) of the 3D points. Taking the cross product of the derivatives and normalizing the result. Multiplying the resulting normal by the detached renderalpha. 7. Return: Return a dictionary containing renderedimage, viewspacepoints, visibilityfilter (radii > 0), radii, rendalpha, rendnormal, viewnormal, renddist, surfdepth, and surfnormal. Args: means3D: (N, 3) 3D positions. means2D: (N, 2) 2D screen positions. shs: (N, K) Spherical Harmonics coefficients or colors. opacities: (N, 1) Opacities. scales: (N, 3) Scales. rotations: (N, 4) Quaternions (w, x, y, z). camera: Dict with 'width', 'height', 'fovx', 'fovy', 'viewmatrix', 'projmatrix', 'bgcolor'. depthratio: Weight for median depth (1) vs expected depth (0). Returns: Dictionary with rendered image, alpha, normals, and depths. """ # 1. Rasterization # Note: GaussianRasterizer is a custom CUDA kernel. # Here we simulate the call structure. rasterizer = GaussianRasterizer(rastersettings) # cov3Dprecomp is None, so rasterizer computes covariance from scales/rotations cov3Dprecomp = None renderedimage, radii, allmap = rasterizer( means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, colorsprecomp=None, opacities=opacities, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=cov3Dprecomp) # 3. Extract Alpha renderalpha = allmap[:,:, 1] # Index 1 is alpha # 4. Extract View-Space Normals and Transform to World Space viewnormal = allmap[:,:, 2:5] # Indices 2-4 # Assuming camera['worldtocamrot'] is the rotation part of the view matrix Rcam = camera['worldtocamrot'] viewnormalworld = torch.matmul(Rcam.transpose(-2, -1), viewnormal.permute(0, 1, 4, 2)).permute(0, 1, 3, 2) # 5. Depth Extraction mediandepth = allmap[:,:, 5] # Index 5 mediandepth = torch.nantonum(mediandepth, nan=0.0) expecteddepth = allmap[:,:, 0] # Index 0 expecteddepth = torch.where(renderalpha > 0, expecteddepth / renderalpha, 0.0) expecteddepth = torch.nantonum(expecteddepth, nan=0.0) surfdepth = depthratio mediandepth + (1 - depthratio) expecteddepth # 6. Surface Normal from Depth surfnormal = depthtonormal(surfdepth, camera) surfnormal = surfnormal renderalpha.unsqueeze(-1).detach() # 7. Return Results visibilityfilter = radii > 0 return { 'render': renderedimage, 'viewspacepoints': means2D, 'visibilityfilter': visibilityfilter, 'radii': radii, 'rendalpha': renderalpha, 'rendnormal': viewnormal, 'viewnormal': viewnormalworld, 'renddist': allmap[:,:, 6], # Index 6 is distortion 'surfdepth': surfdepth, 'surfnormal': surfnormal } def depthtonormal(depthmap: torch.Tensor, camera: dict) -> torch.Tensor: """ Converts a depth map to a normal map. """ # Reconstruct 3D points from depth pts3d = depthstopoints(depthmap, camera) # Compute spatial derivatives # dx, dy are gradients along image coordinates dx = pts3d[:, 1:,:] - pts3d[:,:-1,:] dy = pts3d[:,:, 1:] - pts3d[:,:,:-1] # Pad to maintain size dx = torch.cat([dx, dx[:,:, -1:]], dim=2) dy = torch.cat([dy, dy[:, -1:,:]], dim=1) # Compute normal via cross product normal = torch.cross(dx, dy, dim=-1) normal = torch.nn.functional.normalize(normal, dim=-1) return normal def depthstopoints(depthmap: torch.Tensor, camera: dict) -> torch.Tensor: """ Reconstructs 3D points from depth map using camera intrinsics. """ # Compute NDC to pixel projection matrix # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation depends on camera model # Assuming pinhole camera for simplicity h, w = depthmap.shape y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(h), torch.arange(w), indexing='ij') # Convert to NDC coordinates # Assuming FOV and aspect ratio are known # This step is highly dependent on the specific camera model implementation # Placeholder for the actual NDC conversion logic ndcx = (2.0 x / w) - 1.0 ndcy = 1.0 - (2.0 y / h) # Ray directions in camera space # Assuming unit aspect ratio for simplicity, adjust for actual aspect fx = camera['width'] / (2.0 torch.tan(torch.tensor(camera['fovx']) / 2)) fy = camera['height'] / (2.0 torch.tan(torch.tensor(camera['fovy']) / 2)) rayx = ndcx (camera['width'] / 2.0) / fx rayy = ndcy (camera['height'] / 2.0) / fy rayz = torch.oneslike(rayx) rays = torch.stack([rayx, rayy, rayz], dim=-1) # Scale by depth pts3dcam = rays depthmap.unsqueeze(-1) # Transform to world space using camera extrinsics # Assuming camera['worldtocam'] is the transformation matrix # pts3dworld = inv(camera['worldtocam']) @ pts3dcam # For this pseudocode, we return camera-space points as a placeholder return pts3dcam Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NaNs in Depth: Expected depth can produce NaNs when alpha is zero. These must be replaced with 0 before blending or further processing. Covariance Calculation: Setting cov3Dprecomp to None requires the rasterizer to correctly compute the 2D projection covariance from 3D scales and rotations. Errors here cause blurring or artifacts. Normal Orientation: The transformation from view-space to world-space normals must use the correct rotation matrix (transpose of world-to-camera). Depth Ratio: Choosing the wrong depthratio (0 vs 1) can lead to inaccurate surface reconstruction in bounded vs. unbounded scenes. Renders a scene using Gaussian Splatting, outputting plane geometry and normals. It sets up rasterization settings, computes tangent FOV values, handles SH conversion, and calls a specialized PlaneGaussianRasterizer. It constructs an inputallmap where indices 0-2 are local normals, index 3 is 1.0, and index 4 is local distance. This variant is chosen when plane-based geometry representation is required instead of standard point-based normals. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N and pixels H \times W, dominated by the rasterization pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to N for primitive storage and H \times W \times C for the output maps, where C is the number of channels in allmap (7). Performance: Real-time rendering is achievable on modern GPUs due to the custom CUDA rasterizer. Strengths: Differentiable, supports view-dependent appearance via SH, provides rich geometry (normals, depth) alongside color. Limitations: Requires careful handling of depth extraction (expected vs. median) to avoid artifacts. Performance degrades with very high Gaussian counts due to memory bandwidth. When to Use: When high-quality, differentiable rendering of 2D Gaussian primitives is needed for training or visualization. When Not to Use: When pre-computed 3D covariances are available and memory is extremely constrained, or when complex lighting models (like reflections) are required, in which case Reflective Gaussian Splatting is more appropriate. 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) was introduced as an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting, representing surfaces with 2D Gaussian disks (surfels) to better handle thin structures and surfaces. The rendering method described here is the standard rasterization pass for 2DGS, as implemented in various open-source projects like gaussian-splatting-lightning. It builds on the foundational work of 3DGS but adapts the primitive representation and rasterization logic to 2D surfels. The method is widely used in neural rendering and 3D reconstruction pipelines. name: Reflective Gaussian Splatting
head: Ref-Gaussian
body: Reflective Gaussian Splatting (Ref-Gaussian) is a framework for the real-time, high-quality rendering of reflective objects with inter-reflection effects. It addresses the limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting in modeling complex surfaces and multi-view inconsistencies. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization by utilizing 2D Gaussian primitives for view-consistent geometry. It employs physically based deferred rendering with split-sum approximation to stabilize optimization and enable efficient inter-reflection modeling without heavy Monte Carlo sampling. Ref-Gaussian extends the Gaussian splatting framework by replacing 3D ellipsoids with 2D oriented planar Gaussian disks and applying deferred shading on pixel-level feature maps. Inputs: Scene representation: A set of N 2D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position \mathbf{p}, tangential vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v, scaling factors su, sv, and material properties. Environment map or light sources for illumination. Outputs: Final pixel radiance L(\omegao). Each 2D Gaussian primitive i stores: Position: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Tangential vectors: \mathbf{t}{u,i}, \mathbf{t}{v,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scaling factors: s{u,i}, s{v,i} \in \mathbb{R}. Material properties: Albedo \lambdai \in [0, 1]^3, metallic mi \in [0, 1], and roughness ri \in [0, 1]. Derived normal: \mathbf{n}i = \mathbf{t}{u,i} \times \mathbf{t}{v,i}. Pixel-level feature maps \mathbf{X} are accumulated during rasterization: \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{\Lambda}, M, R, N]^T, where \mathbf{\Lambda} is the albedo map, M is the metallic map, R is the roughness map, and N is the normal map. 1. Primitive Definition: Represent the scene using 2D Gaussian primitives to capture detailed geometry and avoid multi-view inconsistencies inherent in 3D Gaussians. The influence of a 2D Gaussian in its local tangent space is defined as: \mathcal{G}(u, v) = \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2}{2}\right) where (u, v) are coordinates in the local tangent space. 2. Ray-Splat Intersection: Compute the intersection of a ray with a Gaussian splat in homogeneous coordinates. The intersection point \mathbf{x} is calculated as: \mathbf{x} = (xz, yz, z, 1)^T = WH(u, v, 1, 1)^T where H is the 4 \times 4 transformation matrix for the Gaussian: H = \begin{bmatrix} su \mathbf{t}u & sv \mathbf{t}v & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{p} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} Here, \mathbf{p} is the position, \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v are the tangential vectors, and su, sv are the scaling factors. 3. Alpha Blending for Feature Maps: Perform alpha-blending of Gaussian features to create pixel-level feature maps \mathbf{X}, treating alpha-blending as a smoothing filter to stabilize optimization. For each pixel, accumulate the features \mathbf{x}i weighted by opacity \alphai: \mathbf{X} = \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{x}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{x}i = [\lambdai, mi, ri, \mathbf{n}i]^T and \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{\Lambda}, M, R, N]^T. The opacity \alphai is calculated by multiplying the Gaussian's intrinsic opacity oi with the Gaussian weight determined by the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'i. 4. Deferred Shading with Split-Sum Approximation: Apply the rendering equation on the aggregated feature maps \mathbf{X} rather than shading individual Gaussians before blending. The outgoing radiance L(\omegao) in direction \omegao is given by: L(\omegao) = \int{\Omega} Li(\omegai) f(\omegai, \omegao) (\omegai \cdot \mathbf{N}) \, d\omegai where f(\omegai, \omegao) is the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF), and \mathbf{N} is the normal from the feature map. To model inter-reflection effects efficiently, use the split-sum approximation of the rendering equation, avoiding heavy Monte Carlo sampling. 5. Visibility Computation: Compute visibility for the specular component by performing ray tracing on an extracted mesh. This approach provides accurate visibility for specular terms, unlike methods that trace rays across Gaussians which can be noisy and slow. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reflectivegaussiansplatting(gaussians, camera, environmentmap): H, W = camera.resolution Lambda = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(W)] for in range(H)] M = [[0.0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] R = [[0.0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] N = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(W)] for in range(H)] Alpha = [[0.0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] CumProd = [[1.0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): Sigmaprime = compute2dcovariance(g.p, g.tu, g.tv, g.su, g.sv, camera) weight = gaussianweight(Sigmaprime) alphai = g.opacity weight n = cross(g.tu, g.tv) normn = math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2 + n[2]2) n = (n[0]/normn, n[1]/normn, n[2]/normn) xi = (g.lambda, g.m, g.r, n) bbox = getboundingbox(Sigmaprime, camera) for y in range(max(0, bbox.ymin), min(H, bbox.ymax)): for x in range(max(0, bbox.xmin), min(W, bbox.xmax)): distsq = computedistancesq(x, y, Sigmaprime, camera) contribweight = math.exp(-0.5 distsq) contribalpha = alphai contribweight w = contribalpha CumProd[y][x] Lambda[y][x] = (Lambda[y][x][0] + xi[0] w, Lambda[y][x][1] + xi[1] w, Lambda[y][x][2] + xi[2] w) M[y][x] += xi[1] w R[y][x] += xi[2] w N[y][x] = (N[y][x][0] + xi[3][0] w, N[y][x][1] + xi[3][1] w, N[y][x][2] + xi[3][2] w) Alpha[y][x] += w CumProd[y][x] = (1 - w) safealpha = [[max(Alpha[y][x], 1e-6) for x in range(W)] for y in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): Lambda[y][x] = (Lambda[y][x][0]/safealpha[y][x], Lambda[y][x][1]/safealpha[y][x], Lambda[y][x][2]/safealpha[y][x]) M[y][x] /= safealpha[y][x] R[y][x] /= safealpha[y][x] N[y][x] = (N[y][x][0]/safealpha[y][x], N[y][x][1]/safealpha[y][x], N[y][x][2]/safealpha[y][x]) image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): image[y][x] = computebrdfradiance(Lambda[y][x], M[y][x], R[y][x], N[y][x], environmentmap) return image def compute2dcovariance(p, tu, tv, su, sv, camera): # Projects 2D Gaussian parameters to screen-space covariance pass def gaussianweight(Sigmaprime): # Returns normalization weight for the 2D covariance return 1.0 def computedistancesq(x, y, Sigmaprime, camera): # Computes squared Mahalanobis distance in screen space pass def getboundingbox(Sigmaprime, camera): # Returns 3-sigma bounding box in screen coordinates pass def computebrdfradiance(albedo, metallic, roughness, normal, environmentmap): # Applies split-sum approximation to the rendering equation pass def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) Albedo (\lambda): Material color property, range [0, 1]^3. Metallic (m): Material metallic property, range [0, 1]. Roughness (r): Material roughness property, range [0, 1]. Multi-view inconsistencies: Standard 3D Gaussians struggle with detailed geometry due to multi-view inconsistencies. Ref-Gaussian uses 2D Gaussians to mitigate this. Optimization stability: Shading directly on Gaussians before alpha-blending can lead to noise in geometry and material. Ref-Gaussian uses deferred shading on pixel-level feature maps to stabilize optimization. Visibility accuracy: Using Monte Carlo sampling across Gaussians for visibility can be slow and noisy. Ref-Gaussian uses ray tracing on an extracted mesh for specular visibility, providing more accurate results. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved by using the split-sum approximation to avoid heavy Monte Carlo sampling and by using efficient rasterization of 2D Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for 2D Gaussian primitives and pixel-level feature maps. The extracted mesh for visibility computation also adds memory overhead. Performance: Ref-Gaussian maintains fast rendering speeds while modeling inter-reflection effects. It is faster than methods using Monte Carlo sampling for visibility. Strengths: High-quality rendering of reflective objects, accurate inter-reflection modeling, stable optimization, real-time performance. Limitations: Requires an extracted mesh for visibility computation, which may add complexity to the pipeline. 2D Gaussians may have limitations in representing complex 3D structures compared to 3D Gaussians in some scenarios. When to use: When rendering reflective objects with complex inter-reflection effects is required, and real-time performance is necessary. When not to use: When the scene does not have significant reflective properties or inter-reflection effects, standard 3D Gaussian Splatting may be sufficient and simpler. Reflective Gaussian Splatting (Ref-Gaussian) was proposed to address the limitations of existing Gaussian splatting methods in rendering reflective objects with inter-reflection effects. It builds on the work of 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) and 2D Gaussian Splatting (Huang et al., 2024). The method was introduced in a paper by Ye et al. (2024). It differs from GShader (Jiang et al., 2024) by using deferred shading and from RelightableGaussian (Gao et al., 2023) by using ray tracing on an extracted mesh for visibility. name: Nexels
head: Neurally-Textured Surfels
body: Nexels is a novel view synthesis method that decouples geometry and appearance to achieve a compact representation using a fixed number of primitives per pixel. It uses surfels with a generalized Gaussian kernel for geometry and a shared neural field (Instant-NGP) for view-dependent appearance, rendered via a two-pass process to handle sparse primitives efficiently. Unlike sibling methods that couple appearance to primitives or use slower neural field lookups, Nexels textures only the top-K primitives per pixel, ensuring real-time performance while matching the perceptual quality of 3D Gaussian Splatting with significantly fewer primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N surfels; camera parameters (origin o, direction d, focal length f); training images for optimization. Outputs: A rendered image I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}; optimized surfel parameters and neural field weights. Data Structures: 1. Surfel: Defined by mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation Ri \in SO^3, scale \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^2, opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}, and gamma parameter \gammai \in \mathbb{R}^2. The surfel normal is derived from the rotation matrix. 2. Non-textured Appearance: Per-primitive view-dependent radiance ci^\odot \in \mathbb{R}^3 parameterized by spherical harmonics coefficients, where S is the number of coefficients (typically S=16 for degree 3). 3. Neural Field: Instant-NGP architecture. Hash-Grid: L levels. Each level \ell has a hash-table H\ell with T entries. Feature dimension is F. Total parameters: L \times T \times F. MLP: G, with 2 hidden layers, width 64, no bias, ReLU activations. Output dimension 48 (for S=16 SH coefficients). 4. Per-Pixel Buffer: Size K. Contains primitive ID, weight, and depth. Total 3K 32-bit registers per pixel. Written into H \times W \times K images I (IDs), D (depths), and W (weights). Parameters: K: Hyperparameter limiting primitives textured per pixel. Typically K=2. P: Hyperparameter controlling max number of primitives. \gammai: Gamma parameter controlling kernel shape. Constrained \gamma \ge 1 for C^\infty continuity. Loss weights: \lambda{alpha}=0.005, \lambda{texture}=0.5, \lambda{opacity}=0.01, \lambda{grid}=0.01, \lambda{D-SSIM}=0.2. Steps: 1. Initialization: Sample point cloud from COLMAP. Use farthest point sampling to reduce to 0.5P points. Initialize scale based on distance to predecessors during sampling. 2. Preprocessing: Sort surfels by the depth of their centers. 3. Collection Pass (First Rendering Pass): For each ray r:= o + td, compute the intersection in primitive space (u, v) differentiably from geometry parameters. Compute the alpha value using the generalized Gaussian kernel: \alphai:= oi \exp \left( - \frac{|u|^{2\gamma{i,1}}}{2} \right) \exp \left( - \frac{|v|^{2\gamma{i,2}}}{2} \right) Compute the blending weight wi:= \alphai Ti, where Ti:= \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Maintain the per-pixel buffer of size K. Update the buffer to store the running primitives with the highest weights. The buffer entries contain primitive ID, weight, and depth t^i(r). Compute the non-textured render Np for pixel p: Np:= \sum{i=0}^{M-1} wi ci^\odot - \sum{i \in Ip} wi ci^\odot where Ip is the set of textured primitives for pixel p (the top K). Write the final ID, depth, and weight buffers into images I, D, W. 4. Texturing Pass (Second Rendering Pass): Compute world-space intersection positions x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times K \times 3} from the depth buffer D. For each textured primitive j at pixel p, compute the filtered texture radiance ci^\oplus(r): ci^\oplus(r):= G \left( \Deltai(r) \cdot H(xi^(r)) \right) where xi^(r):= o + t^i(r) d is the world-space intersection. The hash-grid feature retrieval H(x) is calculated as: H(x):= [H{0,h0}, \dots, H{L-1,h{L-1}}] \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times F} where hash h\ell is calculated from s\ell \cdot x and indexed into grid level \ell. The down-weighting factor \Delta{i,\ell}(r) for anti-aliasing is: \Delta{i,\ell}(r):= 1 - \exp \left( - \frac{f^2}{2\pi s\ell t^i(r)} \right) where f is focal length, s\ell is scale, and t^i(r) is intersection depth. Compute the final texture T \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times K \times 3} where T{p,j}:= c{I{p,j}}^\oplus(r). Composite the textures with the non-textured render: Ip = Np + \sum{j=0}^{K-1} W{p,j} T{p,j} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def nexelsrender(surfels, camera, K=2): """ Render nexels using two-pass rasterization. surfels: List of dicts with keys 'mu', 'R', 'sigma', 'o', 'gamma', 'codot', 'id' camera: Dict with 'origin', 'direction', 'focallength', 'imagesize' K: Number of textured primitives per pixel """ H, W = camera['imagesize'] o = camera['origin'] d = camera['direction'] f = camera['focallength'] # Buffers: I (ids), D (depths), Wbuf (weights), N (non-textured color) I = torch.full((H, W, K), -1, dtype=torch.int32) Dbuf = torch.zeros(H, W, K, dtype=torch.float32) Wbuf = torch.zeros(H, W, K, dtype=torch.float32) N = torch.zeros(H, W, 3, dtype=torch.float32) accalpha = torch.zeros(H, W, dtype=torch.float32) # Sort surfels by depth of centers depths = torch.tensor([dot(s['mu'] - o, d) for s in surfels]) sortedsurfels = [s for, s in sorted(zip(depths, surfels))] for surfel in sortedsurfels: # Compute intersection in primitive space (u, v) u, v = computeprimitivespaceintersection(surfel, o, d) # Compute alpha gammau, gammav = surfel['gamma'] alpha = surfel['o'] torch.exp(-torch.abs(u)(2gammau) / 2) torch.exp(-torch.abs(v)(2gammav) / 2) Ti = 1.0 - accalpha weight = alpha Ti # Update per-pixel buffer to keep top K weights updatepixelbuffer(I, Dbuf, Wbuf, weight, surfel['id'], dot(surfel['mu'] - o, d)) # Accumulate non-textured color N += weight.unsqueeze(-1) surfel['codot'] accalpha += alpha Ti # Remove non-textured color of top-K primitives from N for k in range(K): valid = I[:,:, k] != -1 ids = I[valid] weights = Wbuf[valid, k] colors = torch.stack([surfelsbyid[id]['codot'] for id in ids]) N[valid] -= weights.unsqueeze(-1) colors # Texturing Pass # Compute world-space positions from depth buffer xpositions = o.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) + Dbuf.unsqueeze(-1) d.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # Query neural field Ttextured = queryneuralfield(xpositions, f, Dbuf) # Composite finalimage = N + (Wbuf.unsqueeze(-1) Ttextured).sum(dim=2) return finalimage def computeprimitivespaceintersection(surfel, o, d): # Transform ray origin and direction to surfel's local frame Rinv = surfel['R'].T localo = Rinv @ (o - surfel['mu']) locald = Rinv @ d # Intersection parameter t in local frame tlocal = -localo[2] / locald[2] u = localo[0] + tlocal locald[0] v = localo[1] + tlocal locald[1] return u, v def updatepixelbuffer(I, Dbuf, Wbuf, weight, surfelid, depth): # For each pixel, insert (weight, surfelid, depth) into top-K list for y in range(I.shape[0]): for x in range(I.shape[1]): pos = 0 while pos < K and Wbuf[y, x, pos] > weight[y, x]: pos += 1 if pos < K: for j in range(K - 2, pos - 1, -1): I[y, x, j+1] = I[y, x, j] Dbuf[y, x, j+1] = Dbuf[y, x, j] Wbuf[y, x, j+1] = Wbuf[y, x, j] I[y, x, pos] = surfelid Dbuf[y, x, pos] = depth Wbuf[y, x, pos] = weight def queryneuralfield(xpositions, f, Dbuf): # xpositions: H x W x K x 3 # Returns: H x W x K x 3 (radiance) L = 16; F = 2; T = 220; s = [2i for i in range(L)] Hgrid = torch.randn(L, T, F) # Placeholder for actual grid G = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(FL, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 48)) radiance = torch.zeroslike(xpositions) for k in range(K): x = xpositions[:,:, k,:] features = [] for l in range(L): h = hashfunction(s[l] x) % T feat = Hgrid[l, h,:] features.append(feat) Hx = torch.cat(features, dim=-1) # LF out = G(Hx) # 48 tstar = Dbuf[:,:, k] delta = 1.0 - torch.exp(-f2 / (2 math.pi s tstar.unsqueeze(-1))) out = out delta radiance[:,:, k,:] = out[:,:3] return radiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Naive point sampling for differentiable rendering leads to inaccuracies in the fine levels of the hash-grid. The down-weighting factor \Delta{i,\ell}(r) is required to remove noticeable aliasing artifacts. Boundaries: The generalized Gaussian kernel converges to a quad indicator as \gamma \to \infty, providing sharp boundaries. Degenerate Input: Initialization uses farthest point sampling to ensure good coverage. Uses per-primitive textures for reflective scenes. [9261-tof-gaussian-rasterization-forward-pass.md] Standard 2DGS without neural texturing. [12208-vanilla-2d-gaussian-splatting-rendering.md] Time and Memory Complexity: Nexels uses a fixed number of primitives per pixel (K), ensuring low compute. It uses 9.7x fewer primitives and 5.5x less memory than 3DGS on outdoor scenes, and 31x fewer primitives and 3.7x less memory on indoor scenes. Measured Performance: Nexels renders twice as fast as existing textured primitives while improving visual quality. On outdoor scenes, it achieves 60 FPS with 400K primitives and LPIPS 0.216, compared to 3DGS's 93 FPS with 4.4M primitives and LPIPS 0.216. Strengths and Limitations: Decouples geometry and appearance, allowing for compact representation and sharp boundaries. Real-time rendering is achieved by limiting neural field queries to K primitives per pixel. When to use: When high-frequency appearance details are present and memory/compute efficiency is critical. When not to use: When simpler geometry is sufficient and neural field overhead is undesirable. Nexels was introduced by Kiriakos N. Kutulakos, Andrea Tagliasacchi, David B. Lindell, et al. in December 2025. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting [20] and Instant-NGP [36]. The method addresses the coupling of geometry and appearance in Gaussian splatting by using surfels for geometry and a neural field for appearance.
