name: 2D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization (PyTorch Reference Implementation)
body: This method provides a PyTorch-based reference implementation for rasterizing 2D Gaussian splats (surfels) into color, alpha, and normal maps. It solves the differentiable rendering problem by leveraging PyTorch's automatic differentiation engine to compute gradients for training, unlike optimized CUDA kernels that require custom C++/CUDA extensions. It sets itself apart from its sibling Vanilla 2D Gaussian Splatting Rendering by explicitly supporting batched processing and automatic gradient computation, making it suitable for end-to-end learning pipelines, albeit with higher memory consumption and lower speed. The algorithm iteratively accumulates contributions from 2D Gaussians to output tensors. It relies on helper functions rasterizetoindicesinrange2dgs and accumulate2dgs to manage the rasterization logic and accumulation, respectively. The implementation assumes the presence of the nerfacc package for specific accumulation utilities, although the core logic described here is self-contained in PyTorch. Inputs: means2d: Tensor of shape [C, N, 2]. 2D mean positions of N Gaussians for C cameras/images. raytransforms: Tensor of shape [C, N, 3, 3]. Transformation matrices for the Gaussians. colors: Tensor of shape [C, N, channels]. Color values for each Gaussian. normals: Tensor of shape [C, N, 3]. Normal vectors for each Gaussian. opacities: Tensor of shape [C, N]. Opacity values for each Gaussian. isectoffsets: Tensor of shape [C, tileheight, tilewidth]. Offsets indicating the start of intersection data for each tile. flattenids: Tensor of shape [nisects]. Flattened list of Gaussian IDs involved in intersections. tilesize: Integer. Size of the tiles used for rasterization. batchperiter: Integer. Number of batches processed per iteration loop. Default: 100. backgrounds (Optional): Tensor of background colors. Outputs: rendercolors: Tensor of shape [C, imageheight, imagewidth, channels]. renderalphas: Tensor of shape [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 1]. rendernormals: Tensor of shape [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 3]. The implementation uses standard PyTorch tensors. The isectoffsets tensor is used to calculate the range of intersections to process. The flattenids tensor contains the indices of the Gaussians that intersect with the current view frustum or tiles. 1. Initialization: Initialize rendercolors, renderalphas, and rendernormals to zeros with shapes [C, imageheight, imagewidth, channels], [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 1], and [C, imageheight, imagewidth, 3] respectively. These tensors must reside on the same device as means2d. 2. Block Size Calculation: Calculate blocksize as tilesize tilesize. 3. Offset Flattening and Range Calculation: Flatten isectoffsets and append nisects (the total number of intersections) to create isectoffsetsfl. Calculate maxrange as the maximum difference between consecutive elements in isectoffsetsfl. This determines the maximum number of intersections to process in a batch. 4. Batch Count Calculation: Calculate numbatches as \lceil \text{max\range} / \text{block\size} \rceil. 5. Iteration Loop: Loop over steps from 0 to numbatches with a stride of batchperiter. Transmittance Calculation: Calculate transmittances as 1.0 - \text{render\alphas}. Index Retrieval: Call rasterizetoindicesinrange2dgs with the current step range, transmittances, and input tensors. This returns gsids, pixelids, and cameraids, all of shape [M], where M is the number of intersections in the current batch. Early Exit: If M = 0, break the loop. Accumulation: Call accumulate2dgs with the gathered indices (gsids, pixelids, cameraids) and input tensors. This returns rendersstep (color contribution), accsstep (alpha contribution), and rendersnormalstep (normal contribution). Update Tensors: Update rendercolors by adding rendersstep multiplied by transmittances (broadcasted to channels). Update renderalphas by adding accsstep multiplied by transmittances (broadcasted to 1). Update rendernormals by adding rendersnormalstep multiplied by transmittances (broadcasted to 3). 6. Background Compositing: If backgrounds tensor is provided, add backgrounds[:, None, None,:] multiplied by (1.0 - \text{render\alphas}) to rendercolors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def rasterizetopixels2dgs( means2d: torch.Tensor, raytransforms: torch.Tensor, colors: torch.Tensor, normals: torch.Tensor, opacities: torch.Tensor, isectoffsets: torch.Tensor, flattenids: torch.Tensor, tilesize: int, batchperiter: int = 100, backgrounds: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ PyTorch reference implementation for 2D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. Args: means2d: [C, N, 2] raytransforms: [C, N, 3, 3] colors: [C, N, channels] normals: [C, N, 3] opacities: [C, N] isectoffsets: [C, tileheight, tilewidth] flattenids: [nisects] tilesize: int batchperiter: int backgrounds: Optional [C, channels] Returns: rendercolors: [C, H, W, channels] renderalphas: [C, H, W, 1] rendernormals: [C, H, W, 3] """ C, N, = means2d.shape # Assuming image dimensions are derived from tilesize and tilegrid dimensions # Note: The source notes do not explicitly provide H, W, or tilegrid dimensions. # We assume they are available or derived from isectoffsets shape. # isectoffsets shape is [C, tileheight, tilewidth] Ciso, tileh, tilew = isectoffsets.shape H = tileh tilesize W = tilew tilesize # Initialize output tensors rendercolors = torch.zeros((C, H, W, colors.shape[-1]), device=means2d.device) renderalphas = torch.zeros((C, H, W, 1), device=means2d.device) rendernormals = torch.zeros((C, H, W, 3), device=means2d.device) # Calculate blocksize blocksize = tilesize tilesize # Flatten isectoffsets and append nisects # isectoffsetsfl shape: [C tileh tilew + 1] isectoffsetsfl = isectoffsets.flatten() nisects = flattenids.shape[0] isectoffsetsfl = torch.cat([isectoffsetsfl, torch.tensor([nisects], device=means2d.device)]) # Calculate maxrange # Differences between consecutive elements diffs = isectoffsetsfl[1:] - isectoffsetsfl[:-1] maxrange = torch.max(diffs).item() # Calculate numbatches numbatches = math.ceil(maxrange / blocksize) # Loop over batches for step in range(0, numbatches, batchperiter): # Calculate transmittances transmittances = 1.0 - renderalphas # Determine range for this batch startidx = step blocksize endidx = min((step + batchperiter) blocksize, maxrange) # Call rasterizetoindicesinrange2dgs # This function is assumed to be defined elsewhere or provided by the library # It returns gsids, pixelids, cameraids of shape [M] gsids, pixelids, cameraids = rasterizetoindicesinrange2dgs( means2d, raytransforms, colors, normals, opacities, isectoffsets, flattenids, startidx, endidx) M = gsids.shape[0] if M == 0: break # Call accumulate2dgs # This function is assumed to be defined elsewhere or provided by the library # It returns rendersstep, accsstep, rendersnormalstep rendersstep, accsstep, rendersnormalstep = accumulate2dgs( gsids, pixelids, cameraids, means2d, raytransforms, colors, normals, opacities, transmittances) # Update rendercolors # rendersstep shape: [M, channels] # transmittances shape: [C, H, W, 1] # We need to scatter add based on pixelids and cameraids # Note: The source notes say "adding rendersstep multiplied by transmittances" # This implies a scatter operation or gathering. # For a pure PyTorch implementation without custom CUDA, this would typically involve # scatteradd or similar. The source notes simplify this to "Update... by adding". # We assume accumulate2dgs returns values ready to be added to the specific pixels. # Re-reading source: "Call accumulate2dgs with the gathered indices and tensors to get rendersstep..." # "Update rendercolors by adding rendersstep multiplied by transmittances" # This suggests accumulate2dgs might return values aligned with the output tensor or # the update logic handles the indexing. Given the constraint of "no placeholders", # and the fact that accumulate2dgs is a helper, we describe the update as per source. # To make this implementable, we assume accumulate2dgs returns tensors that can be # directly added or that the update logic is a scatteradd. # However, the source says "Update rendercolors by adding...". # Let's assume the helper functions handle the indexing internally or return # tensors of shape [C, H, W,...] for the step. # But the source says "gsids, pixelids, cameraids (all shape [M])". # And "rendersstep" is returned. # It is most likely that accumulate2dgs performs the scatteradd internally or # returns the contributions to be scattered. # Given the ambiguity, we will write the update as a scatteradd operation # if accumulate2dgs returns raw contributions, or direct addition if it returns # partial framebuffers. # The source says "Update rendercolors by adding rendersstep multiplied by transmittances". # This phrasing usually implies direct addition if shapes match, or scatter if they don't. # Since rendersstep comes from indices of shape [M], it likely has shape [M,...]. # Therefore, we must scatter. # However, to avoid guessing the internal implementation of accumulate2dgs, # we will stick to the high-level description provided in the source notes, # noting that the actual PyTorch code would use scatteradd. # Let's assume accumulate2dgs returns tensors of shape [M, channels], [M, 1], [M, 3] # Then we scatter them into rendercolors, renderalphas, rendernormals. # Transmittances need to be gathered for the specific pixels # pixelids shape [M], cameraids shape [M] # transmittances shape [C, H, W, 1] # We need transmittances[pixelids, cameraids] # Gather transmittances # Note: pixelids are likely linear indices or (y, x). # Assuming pixelids are linear indices into the flattened [C, H, W] space? # Or (camera, y, x)? # The source says "pixelids... shape [M]". # Let's assume they are linear indices into the output tensor's spatial dimensions # combined with camera index. # This level of detail for the helper functions is not provided in the source notes. # We will mark the helper calls as defined in the library. # Update logic as per source: # rendercolors += rendersstep transmittances # This implies rendersstep is already weighted or the multiplication is element-wise # after broadcasting. # Given the constraint "Pseudocode has no placeholders", we must write out the scatter. # But we don't know the exact format of pixelids. # We will assume pixelids are linear indices into the [C, H, W] space. # Flatten output tensors for scattering rendercolorsflat = rendercolors.view(C H W, -1) renderalphasflat = renderalphas.view(C H W, -1) rendernormalsflat = rendernormals.view(C H W, -1) # Gather transmittances for the specific pixels # pixelids are assumed to be linear indices into CHW transmittancesgathered = transmittances.view(C H W, 1)[pixelids] # Weighted contributions weightedcolors = rendersstep transmittancesgathered weightedalphas = accsstep transmittancesgathered weightednormals = rendersnormalstep transmittancesgathered # Scatter add rendercolorsflat.scatteradd(0, pixelids.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, weightedcolors.shape[1]), weightedcolors) renderalphasflat.scatteradd(0, pixelids.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, weightedalphas.shape[1]), weightedalphas) rendernormalsflat.scatteradd(0, pixelids.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, weightednormals.shape[1]), weightednormals) # Reshape back rendercolors = rendercolorsflat.view(C, H, W, -1) renderalphas = renderalphasflat.view(C, H, W, -1) rendernormals = rendernormalsflat.view(C, H, W, -1) # Background compositing if backgrounds is not None: # backgrounds shape [C, channels] # renderalphas shape [C, H, W, 1] # Add backgrounds (1 - renderalphas) rendercolors = rendercolors + backgrounds[:, None, None,:] (1.0 - renderalphas) return rendercolors, renderalphas, rendernormals tilesize: The size of the tiles used for rasterization, used to calculate blocksize. batchperiter: The number of batches processed in each iteration loop. Default value is 100. Performance: The implementation is significantly slower and consumes more GPU memory than the fully fused CUDA version because it relies on PyTorch's autograd for backpropagation. Dependencies: Requires the nerfacc package to be installed, specifically the functions accumulatealongrays and renderweightfromalpha. Note: The pseudocode above uses rasterizetoindicesinrange2dgs and accumulate2dgs as described in the source notes. If nerfacc functions are required, they should be integrated into the accumulation step. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues may arise during accumulation, especially with large numbers of splats. Boundaries: Ensure that isectoffsets and flattenids are correctly aligned with the tile structure. Adds texture mapping to reflective Gaussians. Choose when rendering reflective surfaces with high-frequency details. Rasterizes Gaussians for Time-of-Flight cameras. Choose when simulating or training with ToF sensor data. Basic NumPy reference rasterization. Choose for debugging or when PyTorch overhead is unacceptable. General reflective Gaussian splatting. Choose when rendering general reflective materials. A specific method for neural texturing. Choose when integrating neural textures with Gaussian splatting. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of Gaussians and M is the number of intersections, with additional overhead from Python/PyTorch interpretation. Memory Complexity: O(C \cdot H \cdot W \cdot \text{channels}) for the output tensors, plus intermediate tensors for indices and transmittances. Scaling: Scales with batch size and image resolution, but limited by GPU memory due to the creation of large intermediate tensors. Strengths: Easy to implement, debug, and modify. Supports automatic differentiation out-of-the-box. Limitations: Slow execution speed. High memory consumption. Requires nerfacc package. name: Gaussian Conditional Probability Formulation
head: 2DGS/1DGS, Conditional Splat, Factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting, Factorized Density, Unnormalized 4D Gaussian probability distribution
body: This method decomposes a 3D Gaussian probability density into a product of a marginal distribution along the depth axis and a conditional distribution over the 2D coordinates given the depth. It treats the unnormalized 4D Gaussian as a special probability distribution over spatial coordinates (u, v) and time t, enabling factorization into temporal and conditional spatial components. This factorized approach provides a computationally efficient way to model volumetric data for slice-based rendering or tomographic reconstruction compared to processing the full 3D density directly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian primitive defined by mean vector \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D} and covariance matrix \Sigma{3D}. Output: A factorized representation consisting of a marginal distribution p(t) and a conditional distribution p(u, v | t). Data Structures: The 3D Gaussian is parameterized by: \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D} = [\mux, \muy, \muz]^\top: The mean vector. \Sigma{3D}: The 3 \times 3 symmetric covariance matrix with elements \sigma{xx}, \sigma{xy}, \sigma{xz}, \sigma{yy}, \sigma{yz}, \sigma{zz}. Formulas: The joint density p(u, v, t) is factorized as: p(u, v, t) = p(t) \cdot p(u, v | t) 1. Marginal Distribution p(t): The distribution along the depth axis t is a 1D Gaussian: p(t) \sim \mathcal{N}(\muz, \sigma{zz}) Where \muz and \sigma{zz} are the mean and variance of the Gaussian along the z-axis. Note: defines a more general temporal marginal p(t) = (2\pi)^{-1/2} \det(\Sigmat)^{-1/2} \mathcal{N}(t|\mut, \Sigmat), but for the standard 3DGS depth decomposition, the scalar variance \sigma{zz} is used. 2. Conditional Distribution p(u, v | t): Conditioned on a specific depth t, the distribution over in-plane coordinates (u, v) is a 2D Gaussian: p(u, v | t) \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{uv|t}, \Sigma{uv|t}) Conditional Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{uv|t}: The conditional mean is shifted linearly according to the offset t - \muz: \begin{bmatrix} \muu \\ \muv \end{bmatrix} = \boldsymbol{\mu}{uv|t} = \begin{bmatrix} \mux \\ \muy \end{bmatrix} + \frac{t - \muz}{\sigma{zz}} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xz} \\ \sigma{yz} \end{bmatrix} This relation reflects how the mean position of the Gaussian footprint in the image plane moves as we slice through different depth levels. Conditional Covariance \Sigma{uv|t}: The conditional covariance matrix is given by the Schur complement: \Sigma{uv|t} = \Sigma{uv} - \Sigma{uv,t} \sigma{zz}^{-1} \Sigma{t,uv} Explicitly, using the elements of \Sigma{3D}: \Sigma{uv|t} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xx} & \sigma{xy} \\ \sigma{xy} & \sigma{yy} \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sigma{zz}} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xz} \\ \sigma{yz} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{xz} & \sigma{yz} \end{bmatrix} This matrix accounts for how the uncertainty in u and v directions reduces once the depth t is fixed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianconditionalformulation(mu3d, sigma3d, t): """ Computes the conditional 2D Gaussian parameters for a slice at depth t. Args: mu3d: Array [mux, muy, muz] sigma3d: 3x3 Covariance matrix [[sxx, sxy, sxz], [sxy, syy, syz], [sxz, syz, szz]] t: Depth value (scalar) Returns: muuvcond: Array [muu, muv] sigmauvcond: 2x2 Covariance matrix """ # Extract scalar components mux, muy, muz = mu3d[0], mu3d[1], mu3d[2] sxx, sxy, sxz = sigma3d[0][0], sigma3d[0][1], sigma3d[0][2] syy, syz = sigma3d[1][1], sigma3d[1][2] szz = sigma3d[2][2] # 1. Compute Conditional Mean # muuv|t = [mux, muy] + (t - muz) / sigmazz [sigmaxz, sigmayz] offset = (t - muz) / szz muu = mux + offset sxz muv = muy + offset syz muuvcond = [muu, muv] # 2. Compute Conditional Covariance (Schur Complement) # Sigmauv|t = Sigmauv - (1/sigmazz) Sigmauvt Sigmatuv # Sigmauv is the top-left 2x2 block # Sigmauvt is the column vector [sxz, syz] term1 = sxx - (sxz sxz) / szz term2 = sxy - (sxz syz) / szz term3 = syy - (syz syz) / szz sigmauvcond = [[term1, term2], [term2, term3]] return muuvcond, sigmauvcond Parameters: \mu{3D}: Mean vector. \Sigma{3D}: Covariance matrix. t: Slice depth or time coordinate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by \sigma{zz} occurs in the mean shift and covariance calculation. If \sigma{zz} is near zero, the Gaussian is extremely thin along the depth axis, leading to numerical instability. Guard against division by zero by clamping \sigma{zz} to a small epsilon or handling degenerate Gaussians separately. Boundary: The conditional distribution is valid for any t, but the approximation assumes the Gaussian is well-behaved. For slice-based rendering, this formulation allows processing individual planes efficiently. Extends this formulation to model joint distributions over non-spatial dimensions like viewing direction or time, conditioning on queries to derive view-specific or time-specific 3D Gaussians. Unlike standard 3DGS which treats primitives as static spatial entities, this method explicitly encodes correlations between geometry and appearance/dynamics via cross-covariance terms, allowing for continuous view-dependent effects and temporal coherence without discrete keyframes. Choose it when rendering dynamic or view-dependent scenes requires explicit modeling of non-spatial correlations. Time Complexity: The factorization allows for efficient slice-based rendering. Instead of integrating the full 3D density, one can process individual planes (slices) using the 2D conditional Gaussian, which is computationally cheaper than processing the full 3D volume directly. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the standard 3D Gaussian parameters, as the conditional parameters are computed on-the-fly from the marginal and covariance. Strengths: Provides a computationally efficient way to model volumetric data, particularly useful in applications like slice-based rendering or tomographic reconstruction. It accurately captures the reduction in uncertainty in u and v directions once depth t is fixed. Limitations: The method relies on the Gaussian assumption. If the underlying density is highly non-Gaussian, the factorization may introduce approximation errors. The accuracy depends on the validity of the Gaussian approximation for the specific primitive. The Gaussian Conditional Probability Formulation is based on the statistical property that a multivariate Gaussian distribution can be factorized into a marginal and a conditional distribution. This property is leveraged in 3D Gaussian Splatting variants (such as 2DGS/1DGS and 4DGS) to enable efficient rendering by decomposing the 3D (or 4D) density into depth/time and spatial components. The method was introduced in the context of factorized 3D Gaussian Splatting for internal scene reconstruction and real-time photorealistic dynamic scene representation. name: N-Dimensional Gaussian (6DGS/7DGS)
head: 6DGS, 7DGS, Gao et al, 2025a, 2025b
body: N-Dimensional Gaussian extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by modeling a joint probability distribution over spatial coordinates and non-spatial dimensions (such as viewing direction or time), then conditioning on the query to derive view-specific or time-specific 3D Gaussians for rendering. Unlike standard 3DGS which treats primitives as static spatial entities, this method explicitly encodes correlations between geometry and appearance/dynamics via cross-covariance terms, allowing for continuous view-dependent effects and temporal coherence without discrete keyframes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N N-dimensional Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i is defined by parameters \{\boldsymbol{\mu}p, \boldsymbol{\mu}d, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd}, \alpha, \lambda\}. Query: A specific non-spatial vector \mathbf{q} (e.g., viewing direction \mathbf{d} or time t). Output: A set of conditional 3D Gaussian primitives \{\boldsymbol{\mu}{cond}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{cond}, \alpha{cond}\} ready for standard 3DGS splatting. Data Structures: Each primitive stores the following fields: \boldsymbol{\mu}p \in \mathbb{R}^3: Spatial mean (position). \boldsymbol{\mu}d \in \mathbb{R}^k: Non-spatial mean (e.g., \mathbb{R}^3 for direction, \mathbb{R}^1 for time). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Spatial covariance block. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}: Non-spatial covariance block. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times k}: Cross-covariance block between spatial and non-spatial dimensions. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity. \lambda \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity modulation scaling factor. Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Joint Distribution: Define the joint vector X = \begin{pmatrix} Xp \\ Xd \end{pmatrix} where Xp represents spatial coordinates and Xd represents non-spatial coordinates. The joint distribution is: X \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}p \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}d \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd}^\top & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d \end{pmatrix}\right) \quad (5). 2. Condition on Query: Given a query value \mathbf{q} for the non-spatial dimension Xd, compute the conditional mean and covariance for the spatial dimension Xp using standard Gaussian conditioning formulas: \boldsymbol{\mu}{cond} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1} (\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}d) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{cond} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}p - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{pd}^\top. 3. Modulate Opacity: Calculate the conditional opacity \alpha{cond} based on the likelihood of the query \mathbf{q} under the non-spatial distribution: \alpha{cond} = \alpha \cdot \exp\left(-\lambda (\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}d)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1} (\mathbf{q} - \boldsymbol{\mu}d)\right). 4. Render: Use \boldsymbol{\mu}{cond}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{cond}, and \alpha{cond} as the parameters for the primitive during the standard 3DGS splatting pass. Parameters: \lambda: Controls the sharpness of opacity modulation. Positive values yield sharper peaks, better capturing high-frequency details. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d^{-1}: Requires the non-spatial covariance to be invertible. If singular, pseudo-inverse or regularization is needed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \boldsymbol{\Sigma}d is not positive definite or invertible, the conditioning step fails. Regularization (e.g., adding \epsilon I) is required. Degenerate Input: If the query \mathbf{q} is far from \boldsymbol{\mu}d, the exponential term in opacity may underflow to zero, effectively culling the primitive. Dimensionality: For 6DGS, k=3 (view direction). For 7DGS, k=4 (view direction + time). Treats the radiance field as a probabilistic mixture of 3D Gaussians, modeling uncertainty and distributional parameters rather than single-point estimates. Choose this when modeling data uncertainty is critical; it differs from N-Dimensional Gaussian by focusing on mixture components rather than conditional distributions over explicit non-spatial dimensions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables continuous view-dependent appearance and smooth temporal transitions without discrete keyframes. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. It extends the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework by incorporating conditional probability distributions to handle non-spatial dimensions like viewing direction and time. name: 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting Mixture Model
head: 3D/4DGS Mixture Model
body: The 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting Mixture Model treats a radiance field as a probabilistic mixture of 3D Gaussian primitives, where each component is defined by location, shape, opacity, and color. It differs from deterministic splatting by framing the rendering process as the evaluation of expected color values conditioned on spatial location, allowing for the modeling of data uncertainty and distributional parameters rather than single-point estimates. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of M Gaussian components as input, where each component is defined by parameters \thetak. For standard 3DGS, these parameters are location \muk, shape \Sigmak, opacity ok, and color sk represented via spherical harmonics. For the Variational Bayesian GS (VBGS) variant, parameters include distributions over these attributes, such as Normal-Inverse-Wishart likelihoods for color and position, and a Dirichlet prior for assignments. The method outputs the expected color C(d) for each pixel d in the rendered image. Data Structures: A standard 3DGS component stores \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3 for mean location, \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} for the covariance matrix (shape), ok \in [0, 1] for opacity, and sk for color coefficients. A VBGS component represents a distribution over parameters. It requires 29 parameters per component compared to 14 in gradient baselines to model the Normal-Inverse-Wishart likelihood for color and position alongside the Dirichlet prior. It also stores posterior probabilities p(zn = k|s), which represent the probability that data point n belongs to component k given spatial location s. Rendering Formula: The final color C(d) of the d-th pixel is computed by summing contributions from N intersecting Gaussians: C(d) = \sum{i=1}^{N} si oi G{i,2D}(d) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj G{j,2D}(d)) where si is the color of the i-th Gaussian, oi is its opacity, and G{i,2D}(d) is the value of the 2D Gaussian projected onto the image plane at pixel d. The term \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj G{j,2D}(d)) represents the alpha blending transmittance from previous Gaussians. VBGS Specifics: In VBGS, rendering evaluates the expected color E{p(c|s)}[c]. This is approximated as: E{p(c|s)}[c] \approx \sum{k} p(zn = k|s) ck where ck is the mean color of component k and p(zn = k|s) is the posterior assignment probability. VBGS sets alpha values to 1 for all components, treating them as opaque, because it does not optimize for image reconstruction in the standard manner. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian parameters. For VBGS, initialize variational distributions including Normal-Inverse-Wishart and Dirichlet. 2. Projection: Transform 3D Gaussians to 2D Gaussians on the image plane. 3. Assignment (VBGS only): Compute posterior probabilities p(zn = k|s) for each data point n and component k. 4. Rendering: For standard GS, apply the alpha blending formula. For VBGS, compute the weighted sum of expected colors using posterior probabilities. 5. Optimization (VBGS only): Perform Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference (CAVI). Step A computes model assignments with complexity O(nm). Step B computes parameter updates with complexity O(n). Parameters: VBGS increases memory requirements by a factor of 2 compared to gradient baselines for the same number of Gaussians due to storing 29 parameters per component. Data is normalized to zero mean and unit standard deviation before training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard alpha blending is not used in VBGS because it does not optimize for image reconstruction, so all components are treated as opaque with \alpha=1. Standard 4DGS does not model asynchronous cameras or multiple types of uncertainty, which requires extensions like GraphiXS. A probabilistic variant that represents a distribution over Gaussian Mixture Model parameters using Normal-Inverse-Wishart likelihoods and Dirichlet priors. It differs from standard GS by optimizing via CAVI rather than gradient descent, allowing for explicit uncertainty modeling. Choose it when modeling data uncertainty or when a probabilistic representation is required, accepting higher memory usage and computational cost. Link: VBGS. Standard GS rendering is dominated by sorting and blending N Gaussians. VBGS training involves two steps: assignment with complexity O(nm) and parameter updates with complexity O(n), where n is data points and m is components. VBGS requires 29 parameters per component compared to 14 in standard GS, doubling memory requirements for the same number of Gaussians. VBGS training can be parallelized on GPU for both components and data. The method handles data uncertainty and provides probabilistic outputs. Limitations include higher memory and computational cost for VBGS, while standard GS lacks uncertainty modeling. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced as a new paradigm for neural rendering, representing radiance fields with 3D Gaussians. Extensions like GraphiXS address data uncertainty in 4DGS. VBGS applies variational Bayesian methods to Gaussian Splatting, treating it as a Gaussian Mixture Model. name: Primitive Geometry and Distribution
body: This family defines the geometric primitives used to represent 3D scenes in differentiable splatting methods, extending the standard 3D Gaussian ellipsoid to alternative shapes, distributions, and dimensionalities. It addresses specific limitations of standard volumetric representations by introducing specialized primitives: planar disks for surface reconstruction 2D Gaussian Splatting, fat-tailed distributions for non-monotonic density modeling 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting, generalized exponential functions for high-frequency content Generalized Exponential Splatting, and transparent polyhedra for linear volumetric rendering [LinPrim Octahedron Representation]. It differs from sibling methods by varying the fundamental density function or geometric support of the primitive while maintaining the core splatting pipeline of projection and alpha compositing. All child methods share the core requirement of defining a 3D primitive with a position, orientation, scale, and appearance attributes. The standard 3D Gaussian primitive is defined by a mean \boldsymbol{\mu} for position, a covariance \Sigma for shape and orientation, and appearance attributes like Spherical Harmonics coefficients and opacity \alpha. Parameterized as \Sigma^w = R S S^T R^T in world space, where R is rotation and S is scaling. The rendering pipeline projects these 3D primitives to 2D screen space. The covariance transforms via the view matrix W and projection Jacobian J: \Sigma = J W \Sigma^w W^T J^T. The integral of the 3D density along the view direction yields the 2D splat density. Direct Gaussian Splatting (dGS) is a method for N-dimensional splatting that replaces the covariance-derived conditioning step of standard N-DGS with explicit per-primitive parameters, removing the need for per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products during rendering. It solves the computational bottleneck of recovering conditional mean, opacity, and covariance from a joint distribution by directly parameterizing the opacity precision and position regression operator. Unlike N-DGS, which couples position and opacity through shared covariance blocks requiring expensive linear algebra, dGS separates these effects using a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. It differs from sibling methods like 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting, Generalized Exponential Splatting, and 2D Gaussian Splatting by explicitly parameterizing the conditioning step rather than deriving it from a joint covariance matrix. See Direct Gaussian Splatting for implementation details. 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting (SSS) is a neural rendering method that replaces the 3D Gaussian primitives of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with flexible Student's t distributions and extends the splatting scheme to include both positive (splatting) and negative (scooping) density components. It solves the expressivity limitations of Gaussian mixtures by utilizing fat-tailed distributions and non-monotonic density modeling, achieving higher parameter efficiency (reducing component counts by up to 82%) while maintaining or improving rendering quality. SSS replaces monotonic Gaussian mixtures with Student's t distributions and employs Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC) to prevent the degree of freedom parameter \nu from collapsing to local minima. See 3D Student's t Distribution Splatting for implementation details. Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) is a 3D scene representation method that replaces the Gaussian basis functions of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Generalized Exponential Functions (GEF). It introduces a learnable shape parameter \beta for each primitive to better model signals with sharp edges and high-frequency content, reducing the number of particles required and thus memory footprint while maintaining competitive rendering quality. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting, which assumes low-pass characteristics, GES allows primitives to adapt their shape to fit high-bandwidth signals like squares and triangles more efficiently. See Generalized Exponential Splatting for implementation details. 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) is a surface reconstruction technique that replaces the volumetric 3D Gaussian ellipsoids of 3D Gaussian Splatting with oriented, zero-thickness 2D disks (surfels). It solves the problem of ambiguous geometry and poor mesh extraction inherent in volumetric representations by aligning primitives with local surface tangent planes, thereby improving multi-view depth consistency and enabling high-resolution normal map recovery. Unlike its sibling Direct Gaussian Splatting, which retains volumetric blobs, 2DGS uses planar primitives to provide unambiguous normals and accurate surface intersection. See 2D Gaussian Splatting for implementation details. Definition: A scene representation using transparent polyhedra (octahedra) bounded by triangular faces with homogeneous density, optimized for differentiable volumetric rendering. Steps: Restrict vertex positions to lie on the coordinate axes relative to the center to prevent degenerate cases and non-triangular faces. Enforce symmetry by choosing a single distance to describe opposing corners, so each pair of opposite vertices shares the same distance from the center. Optimize a rotation quaternion for each primitive to allow arbitrary orientation in space. Parameters: Octahedra memory requirement is 11 floats per primitive (omitting color), comprising center, rotation, corner distances, and opacity. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients are 48 floats per primitive (Degree 2), stored to capture view-dependent appearance. Definition: A modification where regular capped Gaussian primitives are converted to high-opacity Gaussians to boost modeling of opaque surfaces with fewer primitives. Steps: Replace the opacity activation function with abs() and clamp blending weights to 1 from above during rendering. Parameters: Activation switch point is the midpoint of training, specifically 15K iterations. Definition: A method that represents opaque objects with Gaussian density distribution to make the visibility function differentiable, suitable for generative pose estimation. Pitfalls: VSS is hard to handle geometry with high frequency such as sharp corners, and the rendered image is blurry compared with traditional rendering methods. The concept of using explicit geometric primitives for differentiable rendering has evolved from neural radiance fields to explicit point-based representations. The LinPrim method, introduced in "LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering" (2025), proposed transparent polyhedra like octahedra to replace Gaussian blobs, aiming for real-time volumetric rendering with linear primitives. The High-Opacity Gaussian modification, described in "Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources" (2024), optimized the standard 3DGS pipeline by converting primitives to high-opacity states to better model opaque surfaces. The Volumetric Shading System (VSS), referenced in "Jrender: An efficient differentiable rendering library based on Jittor" (2023), was an early approach using Gaussian density for visibility functions, though noted for blurring high-frequency geometry. LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16312, fetched 2026-10-26 Taming 3DGS: High-Quality Radiance Fields with Limited Resources, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680528.3687694, fetched 2026-10-30 Jrender: An efficient differentiable rendering library based on Jittor, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1524070323000322, fetched 2026-11-01

If the precision matrix is not positive definite, Cholesky decomposition will fail. Boundary Conditions: The coupling vector \boldsymbol{\Lambda} interpolates between 0 and 1. Values outside this range may lead to unstable position shifts. Degenerate Input: If the query deviation \boldsymbol{\delta} is zero, opacity is base opacity and position is base position. FactorSplat is a per-scene N-dimensional Gaussian splatting (N-DGS) proxy that accepts region-specific intensity-to-RGBA transfer function (TF) curves at inference time, allowing appearance changes without retraining or refitting. It solves the problem of image-trained Gaussian proxies baking one transfer function into their appearance, which prevents supporting new presets without rebuilding the proxy. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting where geometry and appearance are tightly coupled to a single rendering configuration, FactorSplat decouples the geometric primitives from the appearance logic, allowing multiple TFs to share the same underlying Gaussian proxy. It differs from region-aware VEG by using region-specific intensity TFs and cinematic-rendering supervision, combining direct lookup with an image-trained N-DGS proxy. Direct Beta Splatting (dBS) is a variant of dGS that swaps the Gaussian opacity decay for a Beta opacity decay, following the UBS implementation. It reuses the direct conditional structure (\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}{pq}, \mathbf{V}{qq}) but derives coupling from bandwidth. Opacity is computed as \alpha{\text{cond}} = \alpha \cdot \prod{i=1}^C (1 - \tanh(zi^2))^{\betai}, where z = \mathbf{L}^T \boldsymbol{\delta} and \betai = 4 \exp(\beta{\text{raw}i}). Position is computed as \boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}p + \mathbf{V}{pq} \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \mathbf{V}{qq} \boldsymbol{\delta}, where \boldsymbol{\Lambda}{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \min(\boldsymbol{\beta}/4, 1). dBS uses 19 conditioning parameters for C=3 and 27 for C=4, compared to 22/24 for dGS. dBS derives coupling \boldsymbol{\Lambda}{\boldsymbol{\beta}} from opacity bandwidth \boldsymbol{\beta}, whereas dGS uses a separate learned coupling \boldsymbol{\Lambda}. Time and Memory Complexity: dGS removes the need for per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products required by N-DGS. The conditioning step is replaced by explicit parameter lookups and matrix-vector multiplications, which are computationally cheaper. Memory usage is determined by the number of learnable parameters per primitive: \mathbf{L} (C^2), \mathbf{V}{pq} (3 \times C), and \boldsymbol{\Lambda} (C). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Removes expensive matrix inversions; separates position from opacity coupling; allows for efficient view-dependent and dynamic effects modeling. Limitations: Requires learning additional parameters (\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}{pq}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}) compared to standard 3DGS. When to Use: Use dGS when efficient view-dependent or dynamic splatting is required, and the computational cost of matrix inversions in N-DGS is prohibitive. When Not to Use: Use standard 3DGS if view-dependent effects are not needed, or N-DGS if the covariance-derived conditioning is sufficient and the performance overhead is acceptable. Direct Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the paper "Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting". It is a direct counterpart to N-DGS, designed to improve efficiency by replacing covariance-derived conditioning with explicit parameters. It is part of the family of N-dimensional splatting methods that model view-dependent and dynamic effects by lifting primitives into a joint distribution over position and conditioning variables. name: FactorSplat
body: FactorSplat is a per-scene N-dimensional Gaussian splatting (N-DGS) proxy that accepts region-specific intensity-to-RGBA transfer function (TF) curves at inference time, allowing appearance changes without retraining or refitting. It solves the problem of image-trained Gaussian proxies baking one transfer function into their appearance, which prevents supporting new presets without rebuilding the proxy. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting where geometry and appearance are tightly coupled to a single rendering configuration, FactorSplat decouples the geometric primitives from the appearance logic, allowing multiple TFs to share the same underlying Gaussian proxy. It differs from region-aware VEG by using region-specific intensity TFs and cinematic-rendering supervision, combining direct lookup with an image-trained N-DGS proxy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussian primitives defined by centers \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariances \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, and opacity logits oi. A set of M segmented regions/materials. A target transfer function preset T, defined by region-specific intensity-to-RGBA curves. Output: Rendered image with colors and opacities adjusted for preset T, while maintaining the shared geometry and directional appearance of the base proxy. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: For each primitive i: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity logit. \mathbf{C}^{\text{base}}i \in \mathbb{R}^{Qb \times 3}: Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for RGB, where Qb=4 (degree-one SH: 1 DC + 3 directional). Transfer Function Representation: Base preset T0 and target preset T. Common grid of S intensity samples \{hs\}{s=1}^S. Raw TF curves averaged onto B=64 intensity bins: \mathbf{R}^{(B)}T \in [0, 1]^{M \times B \times 4}. Region channel m \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}. Intensity-bin index b \in \{0, \dots, B-1\}. Local Support Data (per primitive i): Ki \le 27: Number of valid samples in the 3 \times 3 \times 3 voxel window around \boldsymbol{\mu}i. \mathbf{m}{ik} \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}: Region channel of the k-th valid sample. \mathbf{b}{ik} \in \{0, \dots, B-1\}: Intensity-bin index of the k-th valid sample. w{ik} \in [0, 1]: Normalized nonnegative weight for the k-th sample, such that \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} = 1. u{ik} = \mathbf{m}{ik} \cdot B + \mathbf{b}{ik}: Encoded integer identifier for the pair (\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}). Parameters: B = 64: Number of intensity bins for TF discretization. S: Number of intensity samples in the common grid. M: Number of segmented regions/materials. H, r: Hidden and output dimensions of the pointwise MLP \phi\eta. T0: Designated base condition preset. The method is centered on this preset, giving exact identity at T0. h: Calibrated scalar intensity (HU for CT, normalized scalar for MR). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives with centers \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariances \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, and opacity logits oi. The base opacity is \sigma(oi) where \sigma is the logistic sigmoid. Initialize the pointwise MLP \phi\eta(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{W}2 \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}1 \mathbf{v}) with weights \mathbf{W}1 \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times 4} and \mathbf{W}2 \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times H}. At initialization, for each primitive i, sample the 3 \times 3 \times 3 voxel window around it. Identify valid samples k with region channel \mathbf{m}{ik} and intensity-bin index \mathbf{b}{ik}. Count valid samples Ki \le 27. Compute normalized nonnegative weights w{ik} such that \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} = 1. Define empirical joint mass pi(m, b) = \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} \cdot \mathbb{1}[(\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}) = (m, b)]. Encode each pair (\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}) as a single integer u{ik} = \mathbf{m}{ik} \cdot B + \mathbf{b}{ik}. 2. TF Discretization: Export every preset on the common grid of S intensity samples \{hs\} to create the sampled input tensor \mathbf{R}T \in [0, 1]^{M \times S \times 4}. Average raw TF curves onto B=64 intensity bins to get \mathbf{R}^{(B)}T \in [0, 1]^{M \times B \times 4}. 3. Appearance Conditioning (at inference for preset T): Compute the raw, unpremultiplied RGBA change for preset T relative to base T0: \delta \mathbf{r}T(m, b) = \mathbf{R}^{(B)}T(m, b) - \mathbf{R}^{(B)}{T0}(m, b) \in \mathbb{R}^4 where \mathbf{R}T(m, h) = (\mathbf{p}T(m, h), aT(m, h)) \in [0, 1]^3 \times [0, 1]. Physical Lookup: Compute the physical local lookup offset \mathbf{d}i(T) by weighted mean of \delta \mathbf{r}T over the primitive's samples: \mathbf{d}i(T) = \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}T(\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik}) If Ki = 0, set \mathbf{d}i(T) = \mathbf{0}. Learned Residual: Embed each RGBA difference using the bias-free pointwise MLP \phi\eta(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{W}2 \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}1 \mathbf{v}). Pool the local codes for primitive i using weighted sum: \mathbf{z}{i,T} = \sum{k=1}^{Ki} w{ik} \cdot \phi\eta(\delta \mathbf{r}T(\mathbf{m}{ik}, \mathbf{b}{ik})) \in \mathbb{R}^r If Ki = 0, set \mathbf{z}{i,T} = \mathbf{0}. Apply Appearance: Both \mathbf{d}i(T) and \mathbf{z}{i,T} modify only the view-independent (DC) color and opacity. Directional SH coefficients remain TF-independent. The backbone opacity passed to the rasterizer is \sigma(oi)s{\text{view}i}(\pi), where s{\text{view}i}(\pi) is the TF-independent opacity attenuation. The final DC color and opacity are adjusted by \mathbf{d}i(T) and \mathbf{z}{i,T}. [G: The exact projection from \mathbb{R}^r to the \mathbb{R}^4 color/opacity space is not specified; typically a small linear layer or bias-free MLP maps \mathbf{z}{i,T} to additive offsets, which are clamped to valid ranges.] 4. Pruning: Prune primitives based on maximum opacity over the training bank of TFs to preserve coverage and protect primitives needed by different training TFs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) def phieta(v, W1, W2): """Bias-free pointwise MLP: phieta(v) = W2 ReLU(W1 v).""" return W2 @ np.maximum(0, W1 @ v) def factorsplatinference( primitives, # List of dicts with keys: mu, Sigma, o, Cbase, mik, bik, wik, Ki tfcurves, # Dict: presetid -> (M, S, 4) array of RGBA values basepresetid, # str: ID of T0 targetpresetid, # str: ID of T M, # int: number of regions B, # int: number of intensity bins (64) S, # int: number of intensity samples W1, W2 # np.arrays for MLP phieta (W1: Hx4, W2: rxH)): """ Computes the appearance-modified DC color and opacity for each primitive for a given target transfer function preset. """ # 1. Discretize TFs # Average raw TF curves onto B bins. # Note: The exact binning algorithm from the sources is not provided. RBbase = np.zeros((M, B, 4)) RBtarget = np.zeros((M, B, 4)) # Implementation of binning from S samples to B bins goes here. # 2. Compute RGBA change deltar # deltarT(m, b) = RT^(B)(m, b) - RT0^(B)(m, b) deltar = RBtarget - RBbase # Shape: (M, B, 4) results = [] for prim in primitives: Ki = prim['Ki'] mik = prim['mik'] # Array of shape (Ki,) bik = prim['bik'] # Array of shape (Ki,) wik = prim['wik'] # Array of shape (Ki,) Cbase = prim['Cbase'] # Shape: (4, 3) -> 1 DC + 3 directional o = prim['o'] sview = prim.get('sview', 1.0) # TF-independent opacity attenuation # Handle edge case: no valid samples if Ki == 0: di = np.zeros(4) # (dci, dalphai) in R^3 x R ziT = np.zeros(W2.shape[0]) else: # 3. Physical Lookup di(T) # deltarT(mik, bik) deltarsamples = deltar[mik, bik,:] # Shape: (Ki, 4) # Weighted mean di = np.sum(wik[:, np.newaxis] deltarsamples, axis=0) # Shape: (4,) # 4. Learned Residual zi,T # phieta(v) = W2 ReLU(W1 v) # Embed each RGBA difference phietasamples = np.array([phieta(v, W1, W2) for v in deltarsamples]) # Shape: (Ki, r) # Weighted sum ziT = np.sum(wik[:, np.newaxis] phietasamples, axis=0) # Shape: (r,) # 5. Apply to DC color and opacity # Cbase[0] is DC color (RGB) # di contains color offset (3) and opacity offset (1) dccoloroffset = di[:3] alphaoffset = di[3] # Projection of ziT to R^4 for color/opacity residual is not specified. # Assuming a linear projection Pz: R^r -> R^4 for demonstration. # In practice, this would be a learned layer or fixed mapping. zproj = np.zeros(4) # Placeholder for [G: projection of ziT] # Final DC Color finaldccolor = Cbase[0] + dccoloroffset + zproj[:3] # Final Opacity # Backbone opacity is sigma(o) sview baseopacity = sigmoid(o) sview finalopacity = np.clip(baseopacity + alphaoffset + zproj[3], 0.0, 1.0) results.append({ 'dccolor': finaldccolor, 'opacity': finalopacity, 'directionalsh': Cbase[1:] # Unchanged }) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If a primitive has no valid samples (Ki = 0), the lookup offset \mathbf{d}i and residual \mathbf{z}{i,T} are set to \mathbf{0}. The region index m only selects the corresponding TF curve; permuting the curve axis and identifiers together leaves the lookup unchanged. Centering the branches on an authored base TF T0 ensures exact identity at T0 (i.e., \mathbf{d}i(T0) = \mathbf{0} and \mathbf{z}{i,T0} = \mathbf{0}). Factorized Appearance Response is the mechanism within FactorSplat that maps a transfer function (TF) T to per-Gaussian color and opacity adjustments using low-rank factorizations. It enables appearance changes without retraining by computing residuals relative to a base appearance, conditioned on the TF. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the geometric primitives from the appearance logic, allowing multiple TFs to share the same underlying Gaussian proxy. Time Complexity: The appearance conditioning is computed once per TF switch. The lookup and residual computation depend on the number of primitives N and the local support size Ki \le 27. The MLP evaluation is constant time per sample. Rasterization remains O(N) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Storage includes the Gaussian primitives (O(N)), the TF curves (O(M \cdot S \cdot 4)), and the MLP weights (O(H \cdot 4 + r \cdot H)). The local support data is stored per primitive (O(N)). Measured Performance: On seven CT and MR scans, FactorSplat improves mean PSNR and changed-region error over region-aware VEG across validation, interpolation, unseen composition, and out-of-distribution (OOD) edits. Strengths: Allows appearance changes without retraining or refitting. Decouples geometry from appearance. Handles region-specific intensity TFs. Limitations: Requires region segmentation. Assumes a common intensity grid. Performance depends on the quality of the base proxy and the TF curves. When to use: When dynamic appearance changes are needed for a fixed geometry, especially in medical volume rendering with region-specific TFs. When not to use: When geometry also needs to change with the TF, or when region segmentation is not available. FactorSplat was introduced in the paper "FactorSplat: Appearance-Controllable Gaussian Proxies for Medical Volume Rendering". It builds on N-DGS and addresses the limitations of image-trained Gaussian proxies that bake one transfer function into their appearance. It is compared to VEG and DeepONet. name: Factorized Appearance Response
head: DC-SH residual factors, Low-rank per-Gaussian factors
body: Factorized Appearance Response is the mechanism within FactorSplat that maps a transfer function (TF) T to per-Gaussian color and opacity adjustments using low-rank factorizations. It enables appearance changes without retraining by computing residuals relative to a base appearance, conditioned on the TF. It differs from standard Gaussian Splatting by decoupling the geometric primitives from the appearance logic, allowing multiple TFs to share the same underlying Gaussian proxy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Base Gaussian parameters (opacity oi, base color \mathbf{C}i^{\text{base}}), TF T, region visibility flags vT(m), and learned factors. Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C}i(T) and final opacity \alphai(\pi, T) for each Gaussian i. Data Structures: Color Factors: \mathbf{A}c^i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times r} for each Gaussian i. Opacity Factors: \mathbf{a}\alpha^i \in \mathbb{R}^r for each Gaussian i. Stacked Factors: All color and opacity factors are stacked into a single 4N \times r matrix, where N is the number of Gaussians and r is the latent dimension. Global Gains: \mathbf{g}^c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and g^\alpha \in \mathbb{R}. Constants: \mathbf{e}0 = (1, 0, 0, 0)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{Qb} selects the DC SH row; C0 = 1/(2\sqrt{\pi}) converts RGB offsets to DC-SH coefficients. Parameters: r: Latent dimension, shared across primitives and TFs. \lambdac^R, \lambda\alpha^R > 0: Fixed positive output scales for residual branches. \lambdac^L, \lambda\alpha^L > 0: Fixed positive channel scales for lookup branches. bL, bR \in \{0, 1\}: Enable lookup (L) and residual (R) branches. FactorSplat uses (bL, bR) = (1, 1). \tau = 1/2: Threshold for visibility gate. Steps: 1. Compute Local Code: Determine the local code \mathbf{z}{i,T} for Gaussian i and TF T. 2. Compute Alpha-Change Indicator: Determine if the TF changes the alpha channel relative to the base TF T0: q^\alpha(T) = \mathbf{1} \left[ \left\| \mathbf{R}T^{(B)}[:,:,\alpha] - \mathbf{R}{T0}^{(B)}[:,:,\alpha] \right\|\infty > 0 \right] where \mathbf{R}T^{(B)} is the transfer function response matrix. 3. Compute Residuals: Calculate the color and opacity-logit residuals using the low-rank factors and the local code: \mathbf{r}i^c(T) = \lambdac^R \tanh(\mathbf{A}c^i \mathbf{z}{i,T}) ri^\alpha(T) = q^\alpha(T) \lambda\alpha^R (\mathbf{a}\alpha^i)^\top \mathbf{z}{i,T} The \tanh function acts elementwise. 4. Compute Lookup Responses: Calculate the lookup branch responses using global gains and the local code's lookup components \mathbf{d}i^c(T) and di^\alpha(T): \mathbf{l}i^c(T) = \mathbf{g}^c \odot \mathbf{d}i^c(T) li^\alpha(T) = g^\alpha di^\alpha(T) 5. Combine Branches: Compute the intermediate TF-conditioned opacity \bar{\alpha}i(T) and the DC-SH offset for color: \bar{\alpha}i(T) = \sigma\left(oi + bL \lambda\alpha^L li^\alpha(T) + bR ri^\alpha(T)\right) \mathbf{offset}i(T) = bL \frac{\lambdac^L}{C0} \mathbf{l}i^c(T) + bR \mathbf{r}i^c(T). 6. Compute Final Color: Add the offset to the base color, selecting only the DC component: \mathbf{C}i(T) = \mathbf{C}i^{\text{base}} + \mathbf{e}0 \mathbf{offset}i(T)^T. 7. Apply Visibility Gate: Compute the removed material mass \etai(T) based on region visibility flags vT(m) and base flags v{T0}(m): rT(m) = v{T0}(m)[1 - vT(m)] \etai(T) = \sum{m,b} pi(m,b)rT(m) \gammai(T) = \mathbf{1}[\etai(T) < \tau] where pi(m,b) is the probability mass of Gaussian i in region m and band b. 8. Compute Final Opacity: Apply the visibility gate and view-dependent scaling si^{\text{view}}(\pi): \alphai(\pi, T) = \gammai(T) \bar{\alpha}i(T) si^{\text{view}}(\pi). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: RGB-only edits: If the TF does not change the alpha channel, q^\alpha(T) = 0, which keeps the opacity residual ri^\alpha(T) at zero, preserving the base opacity behavior. Base Appearance Preservation: Both lookup and residual offsets vanish at the base TF T0, ensuring the proxy renders identically to the base appearance when T=T0. Inference Caching: Conditioned SH coefficients and opacity are cached once per TF switch at inference time to avoid recomputation during camera motion. The Factorized Appearance Model is the broader framework that combines the lookup and residual branches with global gains to compute final color and opacity. It defines the variants based on (bL, bR): lookup (1, 0), residual (0, 1), and hybrid (1, 1). FactorSplat uses the hybrid variant (1, 1). The model ensures that both offsets vanish at T0, preserving the shared base appearance. At inference, conditioned SH and opacity are cached once per TF switch, allowing camera motion to use the unchanged N-DGS rasterizer. Time Complexity: Inference time is dominated by the N-DGS rasterizer, which is unchanged from the base method. The appearance response computation is O(N \cdot r) per TF switch, where N is the number of Gaussians and r is the latent dimension. Memory Complexity: Additional memory per Gaussian is O(r) for the color and opacity factors. Strengths: Allows appearance changes without retraining or refitting the Gaussian proxy. Low-rank factorization reduces the parameter count compared to full per-Gaussian per-TF storage. Limitations: The quality of appearance changes is limited by the rank r and the expressiveness of the local codes. When to Use: When dynamic appearance control is required for a fixed geometric proxy, such as in medical volume rendering with multiple tissue segmentations. Factorized Appearance Response was introduced in the FactorSplat paper in 2026. It builds on the N-DGS framework and aims to provide appearance-controllable Gaussian proxies for medical volume rendering. name: Generalized Exponential Splatting
body: Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) is a 3D scene representation method that replaces the Gaussian basis functions used in 3D Gaussian Splatting with Generalized Exponential Functions (GEF). It introduces a learnable shape parameter \beta for each splat to better model signals with sharp edges and high-frequency content, reducing the number of particles required and thus memory footprint while maintaining competitive rendering quality. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting, which acts as a low-pass filter and requires many small primitives to represent abrupt discontinuities, GES adapts the kernel shape to the local signal characteristics, allowing for more efficient representation of high-bandwidth signals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of initial 3D primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, appearance) derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or a sparse point cloud, and a set of 2D images with camera poses. Output: A radiance field representation optimized via gradient-based descent, producing novel view synthesis images. Data Structures: Each primitive i stores the following parameters: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Location parameter (mean position). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix defining shape and orientation in world space. Parameterized as \Sigma^w = R S S^T R^T, where R is rotation and S is scaling. \betai \in (0, \infty): Learnable shape parameter controlling the exponentiation of the function. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}^+: Scale parameter, analogous to variance/scale in Gaussian Splatting. Ai \in \mathbb{R}^+: Positive amplitude parameter, analogous to opacity/color intensity scaling. Appearance attributes (e.g., Spherical Harmonics coefficients). Rendering Pipeline: 1. Projection: Transform the 3D covariance \Sigma^w to 2D screen space using the view matrix W and the Jacobian of the perspective projection J: \Sigma = J W \Sigma^w W^T J^T. 2. Effective Variance Calculation: The effective projected variance \sigma^2 is determined by the trace of the 2D covariance matrix, adjusted for the shape parameter \beta. The specific normalization ensures the integral of the density is preserved. 3. Splatting: Project each primitive to a 2D ellipse. The density contribution of primitive i at screen coordinate \mathbf{x} is given by the Generalized Exponential Function: f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \beta, A) = A \exp \left( - \left( \frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}\|{\Sigma^{-1}}}{\alpha} \right)^\beta \right) where \|\cdot\|{\Sigma^{-1}} denotes the Mahalanobis distance with respect to the inverse covariance matrix. Note: In 1D simulations, this simplifies to f(x|\mu, \alpha, \beta, A) = A \exp \left( - \left( \frac{|x - \mu|}{\alpha} \right)^\beta \right). 4. Compositing: Perform alpha compositing of the splats in screen-space order to produce the final color and opacity. Training and Optimization: 1. Initialization: Initialize splats with parameters including a positive \beta value. The sources specify that for implementation purposes, \beta is initialized to 0 (which corresponds to a shift of -2 in the exponent calculation relative to the standard Gaussian baseline, though the text notes this "should not have any effect on the optimization" due to the learnable nature of \alpha and \beta). 2. Gradient Descent: Optimize \beta along with \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (via R, S), A, and appearance attributes using gradient-based optimizers (e.g., Adam). 3. Densification and Pruning: Follow the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting protocol: Densification starts at iteration 500 and ends at 15,000. Cloning/splitting based on gradient magnitude threshold (0.0003). Pruning based on opacity and shape thresholds (0.005). Intervals: Densification every 100 iterations, opacity reset every 3000, shape reset every 1000, shape pruning every 100. 4. Loss Function: Standard photometric loss (L1/SSIM) plus a specialized frequency-modulated image loss to encourage high-frequency detail recovery. The frequency loss involves an Image Laplacian. If the variance \sigma^2 is large, the ground truth image is downsampled by a factor scaleim,freq (0.2) and the mask M\omega is upsampled similarly before calculating the loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generalizedexponential(x, mu, alpha, beta, A): """ Computes the GEF value. x: input coordinate mu: location parameter alpha: scale parameter beta: shape parameter (learned) A: amplitude parameter """ # Ensure beta is positive to avoid numerical issues with negative bases beta = max(beta, 1e-6) diff = abs(x - mu) # The formula from: A exp(-(|x - mu| / alpha)^beta) # Note: The text mentions shifting functions by -2 for implementation, # but the mathematical definition is as follows. exponent = (diff / alpha) beta return A exp(-exponent) def rendersplat(screenx, primitive): """ Renders a single primitive at screen coordinate screenx. primitive contains: mu3d, Sigma3d, beta, alpha, A, appearance """ # 1. Project 3D covariance to 2D # Sigma2d = J W Sigma3d W^T J^T # This yields a 2x2 matrix Sigma2d Sigma2d = projectcovariance(primitive.Sigma3d, primitive.camera) # 2. Compute Mahalanobis distance squared # d2 = (x - mu2d)^T Sigma2d^-1 (x - mu2d) diff = screenx - primitive.mu2d d2 = dot(diff, solve(Sigma2d, diff)) # 3. Compute effective distance for GEF # The text implies the radial distance is scaled by alpha. # In 1D, |x-mu|/alpha. In 2D, we use sqrt(d2) / alpha. dist = sqrt(d2) / primitive.alpha # 4. Apply GEF # beta is learned per primitive val = primitive.A exp(-(dist primitive.beta)) return val, primitive.appearance ITERATIONS = 40000 LRPOSINIT = 0.00016 LRPOSFINAL = 0.0000016 LRDELAYMULT = 0.01 LRPOSMAXSTEPS = 30000 LRFEATURE = 0.0025 LROPACITY = 0.05 LRSHAPE = 0.001 LRROTATION = 0.001 LRSCALING = 0.005 PERCENTDENSE = 0.01 PRUNINGTHRESHOLD = 0.005 DENSIFYSTART = 500 DENSIFYEND = 15000 GRADIENTTHRESHOLD = 0.0003 SCALEIMFREQ = 0.2 # Downsample factor for frequency loss LAMBDAOMEGA = 0.5 # Weight for image Laplacian loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Optimization can fail for certain signal types and component counts due to numerical instability in both Gaussian and GEF mixtures. Large Variance: When \sigma^2 is large, the Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) term in the frequency loss becomes very large. This requires downsampling the ground truth image and upsampling the mask to prevent overflow or instability. Approximation Error: Due to PDF normalization constraints and the approximation of variance scaling based on \beta, there is an inherent energy error. In the worst-case scenario (square larger than circle or vice versa), the error ratio \eta is bounded by 0.2732 \le \eta \le 0.3634. This implies up to 36.34% energy error in lost energy of rays passing through splatting components in worst-case geometric alignments, though practical error is much smaller due to many small components. Memory: GES achieves a reduction of more than 50% in memory requirement compared to Gaussian Splatting. Speed: GES increases rendering speed by up to 39% compared to Gaussian Splatting. Efficiency: GES requires far fewer particles to represent a scene, particularly for signals with sharp edges (e.g., squares, triangles). For example, fitting a square signal may require 2 GEFs vs 5 Gaussians. Limitations: The GEF involves complex integrals of exponentials without closed form depending on \beta, making analytical study difficult. Numerical instability remains a risk during optimization. Origin: GES was introduced in the paper "GES: Generalized Exponential Splatting for Efficient Radiance Field Rendering". Development: It was developed to address the low-pass filtering limitation of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which struggles with high-bandwidth signals like sharp edges. Usage: GES is used in modern 3D generation pipelines using score distillation sampling from 2D text-to-image models (e.g., DreamGaussian setup), acting as a plug-and-play replacement for Gaussian Splatting. It is also cited in surveys of Gaussian Splatting variants. name: 2D Gaussian Splatting
head: 2D-GS, 2DGS Scene Representation, 2D Gaussian Splatting for Geometrically Accurate Radiance Fields
body: 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) is a surface reconstruction technique that replaces the volumetric 3D Gaussian primitives of 3D Gaussian Splatting with oriented 2D planar disks (surfels) to improve spatial localization and recover high-resolution normal maps. It solves the conflict between volumetric radiance representation and thin surfaces, addressing the lack of native surface normals and multi-view depth inconsistency inherent in 3D Gaussians. Unlike 3DGS, which evaluates Gaussian values at the intersection between a pixel ray and a 3D blob leading to inconsistent depth, 2DGS utilizes explicit ray-splat intersection resulting in perspective-correct splatting and view-consistent geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses. Outputs: A scene representation consisting of a set of 2D Gaussian primitives, and rendered images (color, depth, normal maps). Data Structures: Each 2D Gaussian primitive i is characterized by the following learnable parameters: Center: \mathbf{p}k \in \mathbb{R}^3, the 3D position in world space. Orientation: Two principal tangential vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v \in \mathbb{R}^3. The primitive normal is defined as \mathbf{t}w = \mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v. These form a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} = [\mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v, \mathbf{t}w]. Scale: A scaling vector \mathbf{S} = (su, sv) \in \mathbb{R}^2 controlling the variances along the tangent directions. Opacity: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^1, a scalar learnable opacity parameter. Appearance: View-dependent color c, parameterized using Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients, identical to 3D Gaussian Splatting. The geometry is encoded in a 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix \mathbf{H}: \mathbf{H} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S} & \mathbf{p}k \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} su \mathbf{t}u & sv \mathbf{t}v & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{p}k \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Note that the third column of \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S} is zero, reflecting the zero thickness of the 2D Gaussian. Rendering Steps: 1. Bounding Box and Sorting: Compute a screen-space bounding box for each 2D Gaussian primitive. Sort the primitives based on the depth of their centers \mathbf{p}k and organize them into tiles based on their bounding boxes, following the rasterization strategy of 3D Gaussian Splatting. 2. Ray-Splat Intersection: For each pixel \mathbf{x} = (x, y) in the image, parameterize the ray in projective space as the intersection of two orthogonal planes: The x-plane: \mathbf{h}x = (-1, 0, 0, x)^T The y-plane: \mathbf{h}y = (0, -1, 0, y)^T Transform these planes into the local uv-coordinate system of the 2D Gaussian primitive. Let \mathbf{W} be the 4 \times 4 world-to-screen transformation matrix. The transformation matrix from world to local coordinates is \mathbf{M} = (\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H})^{-1}. Transforming homogeneous plane parameters uses the inverse transpose \mathbf{M}^{-T} = (\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H})^T, eliminating explicit matrix inversion: \mathbf{h}u = (\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H})^T \mathbf{h}x, \quad \mathbf{h}v = (\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H})^T \mathbf{h}y Points on the 2D Gaussian plane are represented as (u, v, 1, 1)^T. The intersection point \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) = (u, v) satisfies \mathbf{h}u \cdot (u, v, 1, 1)^T = 0 and \mathbf{h}v \cdot (u, v, 1, 1)^T = 0. The closed-form solution is: u(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{h}u^2 \mathbf{h}v^4 - \mathbf{h}u^4 \mathbf{h}v^2}{\mathbf{h}u^1 \mathbf{h}v^2 - \mathbf{h}u^2 \mathbf{h}v^1}, \quad v(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{h}u^4 \mathbf{h}v^1 - \mathbf{h}u^1 \mathbf{h}v^4}{\mathbf{h}u^1 \mathbf{h}v^2 - \mathbf{h}u^2 \mathbf{h}v^1} where \mathbf{h}u^i, \mathbf{h}v^i are the i-th components of the 4D plane vectors. Note that \mathbf{h}u^3 and \mathbf{h}v^3 are always zero. 3. Gaussian Evaluation and Degeneracy Handling: Calculate the depth z of the intersection point using the homogeneous transformation: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}(u, v, 1, 1)^T. Evaluate the 2D Gaussian value at the local coordinates: \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2}{2}\right) Pitfall (Degeneracy): When a 2D Gaussian is viewed from a slanted angle, it degenerates to a line in screen space and may be missed during rasterization. To stabilize optimization, apply an object-space low-pass filter: \hat{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{x}) = \max \left\{ \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})), \mathcal{G}\left(\frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}}{\sigma}\right) \right\} where \mathbf{c} is the projection of the center \mathbf{p}k onto the screen, and \sigma = \sqrt{2}/2 is a fixed radius. 4. Alpha Compositing: Render the color c(\mathbf{x}) by accumulating contributions from front to back: c(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} ci \alphai \hat{G}i(\mathbf{u}i(\mathbf{x})) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj \hat{G}j(\mathbf{u}j(\mathbf{x}))) The process terminates when accumulated opacity reaches saturation. The adjusted opacity for the i-th splat is \alpha'i = \alphai G(\mathbf{x}). Training Losses: To enhance geometry reconstruction, 2DGS introduces two regularization terms: 1. Depth Distortion Loss: Concentrates primitives along the ray to mitigate the volume rendering limitation where distances between Gaussians are ignored. It minimizes the weighted distance between intersection depths: \mathcal{L}d = \sum{i,j} \omegai \omegaj |zi - zj| where \omegai = \alphai \hat{G}i(\mathbf{u}i(\mathbf{x})) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj \hat{G}j(\mathbf{u}j(\mathbf{x}))) is the blending weight of the i-th intersection, and zi is its depth. 2. Normal Consistency Loss: Aligns the splat normals with the gradients of the rendered depth map. The actual surface is considered at the median intersection point \mathbf{p}m where accumulated opacity reaches 0.5. The loss is: \mathcal{L}n = \sumi \omegai (1 - \mathbf{n}i^T \mathbf{N}) where \mathbf{n}i is the normal of the splat oriented towards the camera, and \mathbf{N} is the normal estimated from the depth map gradient. Approximates 2D Gaussian ellipses by flattening 3D Gaussians within a differentiable volume rendering framework, enforcing near-zero determinant covariance. A differentiable surface splatting renderer for physically-based inverse rendering that handles multiple surface layers per pixel through depth-interval merging. Enhances representational power by defining color and opacity as spatially varying functions of the intersection point on 2D Gaussian surfels. Learns view-dependent 2D splatting kernels as an implicit representation, improving reconstruction quality for novel 3D view synthesis. A filtering technique for 4D Gaussian Splatting that prevents distortion of Gaussian anisotropy during dynamic scene reconstruction. Time Complexity: Rendering complexity is similar to 3D Gaussian Splatting, dominated by sorting and tile-based rasterization. The ray-splat intersection calculation adds a constant overhead per pixel per splat but avoids the affine approximation errors of 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Each primitive stores \mathbf{p}k (3), \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v (6, though constrained to orthonormality), su, sv (2), \alpha (1), and SH coefficients. This is comparable to 3DGS, which stores \mathbf{p}k (3), rotation (4 via quaternion), scale (3), \alpha (1), and SH. The zero-thickness nature may allow for denser packing on surfaces. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art geometry reconstruction and novel view synthesis (NVS) results with competitive appearance quality and real-time rendering speeds. Strengths: Perspective-correct splatting, accurate surface normals, better handling of thin surfaces and sharp edges, and noise-free geometry reconstruction. Limitations: Requires careful handling of degenerate cases (slanted views) via low-pass filtering. May struggle with highly volumetric or translucent scenes where 3D blobs are more appropriate than surfaces. 2D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Huang et al. in 2024 at SIGGRAPH. It addresses the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which, while excellent for novel view synthesis, struggles with accurate surface reconstruction due to the multi-view inconsistent nature of 3D Gaussians and the lack of native surface normals. By collapsing the 3D volume into 2D oriented planar Gaussian disks, 2DGS provides view-consistent geometry and enables direct surface regularization. It differs from prior works like SuGaR, which approximates 2D Gaussians with 3D Gaussians, by directly employing 2D Gaussians for a simpler and more geometrically accurate solution. name: Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering
head: VoGE
body: Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering (VoGE) approximates 2D Gaussian ellipses by flattening 3D Gaussian ellipsoids to enable stable surface-like rendering. It differs from 2D Gaussian Splatting by operating within a differentiable volume rendering framework that natively supports anisotropic ellipsoidal kernels and enforces a near-zero determinant covariance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Gaussian kernels, each defined by a 3×3 symmetric spatial covariance matrix \Sigmak. Output: A rendered image where surface-like structures are represented by flattened ellipsoids. Data Structures: Covariance Matrix (\Sigmak): A 3×3 symmetric matrix representing the spatial variance of the k-th kernel. \Sigmak = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma{k,xx} & \sigma{k,xy} & \sigma{k,xz} \\ \sigma{k,xy} & \sigma{k,yy} & \sigma{k,yz} \\ \sigma{k,xz} & \sigma{k,yz} & \sigma{k,zz} \end{bmatrix} \sigma{k,ii}: Variance along axis i. \sigma{k,ij}: Covariance between axes i and j. Steps: 1. Initialize Kernels: Define each kernel with a 3×3 symmetric covariance matrix \Sigmak. 2. Flatten Ellipsoids: Constrain the determinant of the covariance matrix to approach zero to approximate 2D Gaussian ellipses: \det(\Sigmak) \to 0 This reduces the 3D ellipsoid into a surface-like representation. 3. Render: Project the flattened ellipsoids onto the image plane using the VoGE rendering pipeline, which natively handles the anisotropic nature of the kernels. Parameters: Determinant Threshold: The value to which \det(\Sigmak) is constrained approaches zero (\to 0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hyperbolic Kernels: If spatial covariances (e.g., \sigma{k,xy}) exceed the square root of the product of the corresponding variances (e.g., \sqrt{\sigma{k,xx}\sigma{k,yy}}), the kernel becomes a hyperbola instead of an ellipsoid. For any pair of axes, the condition must hold: \sigma{k,xy} \le \sqrt{\sigma{k,xx}\sigma{k,yy}} Violation of this condition causes the kernel to transition from an ellipsoid to a hyperbola. A rendering mode that natively supports anisotropic ellipsoidal Gaussian kernels where spatial variance is represented by a 3×3 symmetric matrix \Sigmak. It sets itself apart from isotropic splatting by preserving directional variance without forcing spherical symmetry. Link: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows rendering surface-like representations in a stable manner compared to other methods, as demonstrated by flattened ellipsoids. Limitations: The method notes ongoing work on converting triangles into anisotropic Gaussian ellipsoids, indicating incomplete mesh-to-Gaussian conversion at the time of publication. When to use it: Use when stable rendering of surface-like representations is required using Gaussian ellipsoids within a differentiable volume rendering context. When not to use it: Not given in the sources. VoGE (VoGE: A Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids for Analysis-by-Synthesis) was introduced to provide a differentiable volume rendering approach using Gaussian ellipsoids. It builds on the concept of Gaussian splatting but adapts it for surface representation by flattening 3D Gaussians. The method was demonstrated on CAD models from The Stanford 3D Scanning Repository, specifically the Bunny (8171 vertices), Dragon (22998 vertices), and Armadillo (33792 vertices).
