name: 3D Surface Splatting
head: 3DSS
body: 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) is a differentiable surface splatting renderer for physically-based inverse rendering that jointly recovers geometry, materials, and illumination from multi-view images by optimizing an unstructured set of oriented surfel primitives. It solves the problem of multi-layer surface separation and visibility discontinuity in surface splatting by formulating surface grouping as an interval-merging algorithm over sorted primitives, replacing binary/ternary depth tests with a smooth, coverage-based compositing model where per-layer opacity arises directly from accumulated Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) reconstruction weights. It sets itself apart from its parent 2D Gaussian Splatting by using a surface rendering model rather than a volumetric one (surfels carry no learnable opacity), and from Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering by explicitly handling multiple surface layers per pixel through depth-interval merging rather than single-layer rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured set of surfel primitives, each defined by center position \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, tangent vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v \in \mathbb{R}^3, and shading attributes (albedo \mathbf{a} \in [0, 1]^3, metallic m \in [0, 1], roughness r \in [0, 1]). Co-optimized HDR environment lighting. Output: A differentiable 2D image (HDR) and gradients for the surfel parameters. Data Structures: Each surfel primitive stores: \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v \in \mathbb{R}^3: Tangent vectors spanning the local tangent plane. These encode orientation and anisotropic scaling. The surface normal is implicitly \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v) / \|\mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v\|. \mathbf{a} \in [0, 1]^3: Albedo. m \in [0, 1]: Metallic. r \in [0, 1]: Roughness. Derived view-space properties: Depth d, symmetric depth extent \delta, and depth interval [d-\delta, d+\delta]. Parameters: \delta{cut}: Kernel support cutoff threshold. The source uses \delta{cut} as a generic parameter for the squared distance threshold \rho^2 \ge \delta{cut}^2. Steps: 1. T-matrix Construction: For each surfel, transform \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v to camera space, yielding \mathbf{c}', \mathbf{t}'u, \mathbf{t}'v. Construct the 4 \times 4 transformation matrix S = [\mathbf{t}'u \ \mathbf{t}'v \ \mathbf{0} \ \mathbf{c}'] mapping local surfel space (unit sphere parameterization) to camera space. Let P be the projection matrix. Compute the T-matrix T = PS. This maps points on the unit sphere in local surfel space to clip space. 2. Bounding Rectangle and Depth Extent: Compute the bounding rectangle of the surfel in screen space using closed-form expressions involving dot products among the rows of T. Compute the symmetric depth extent in view space: \delta = \sqrt{t'{u,z}^2 + t'{v,z}^2} \cdot \delta{cut}, where t'{u,z} and t'{v,z} are the z-components (view-space depth) of the camera-space tangent vectors. The depth interval is [d-\delta, d+\delta] where d is the view-space depth of \mathbf{c}'. 3. Forward Shading (Pre-shading): Shade each surfel before rasterization. Apply forward microfacet shading under the co-optimized HDR environment lighting using split-sum Image-Based Lighting (IBL). This yields a pre-shaded linear radiance \mathbf{c}{pre} for each surfel. This step avoids blending directional quantities (like normals) volumetrically. 4. Tiling and Sorting: Bin surfels into screen-space tiles. Sort the primitives within each tile by their depth interval start d{start} = d - \delta (closest extent to the camera), not by center depth. 5. Per-Pixel Rasterization and Surface Layer Grouping: For each pixel in a tile, iterate through the sorted surfels. Ray-Surfel Intersection: Represent the pixel's viewing ray as the intersection of two clip-space planes: \mathbf{h}u = (-1, 0, 0, u)^T and \mathbf{h}v = (0, -1, 0, v)^T, where (u,v) are the pixel coordinates. Map these planes into the surfel's local coordinate system via T to yield vectors \mathbf{k} and \mathbf{l}. Their intersection with the surfel's plane gives local coordinates (u{local}, v{local}) of the hit point. Distance and Discard: Compute squared distance from surfel center: \rho^2 = u{local}^2 + v{local}^2. If \rho^2 \ge \delta{cut}^2, discard the surfel for this pixel. Weight Evaluation: Compute unnormalized Gaussian reconstruction kernel weight: w = \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \rho^2). Note: The 1/(2\sigma) normalization constant is omitted as weights are used for Shepard normalization later. Interval Merging (Surface Separation): Maintain a list of active surface layers for the pixel. Each layer tracks a running sum of weights and attributes. If the current surfel's depth interval [d-\delta, d+\delta] overlaps with the depth interval of the last surfel added to the current active layer, add the surfel to that layer. If it does not overlap, and since primitives are sorted by d{start}, no future primitive can bridge the gap. Start a new surface layer with the current surfel. This exact gap detection requires no look-ahead or deferred merging. Attribute Accumulation: For each surfel added to a layer, accumulate its pre-shaded radiance \mathbf{c}{pre} and weight w to the layer's running sums: W{layer} \leftarrow W{layer} + w and \mathbf{C}{layer} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{layer} + w \cdot \mathbf{c}{pre}. 6. Compositing: After processing all surfels for a pixel, for each active surface layer k: Compute the reconstructed attribute (radiance) for the layer: \hat{\mathbf{a}}k = \frac{\sum{j \in \text{layer } k} wj \mathbf{c}{pre, j}}{\sum{j \in \text{layer } k} wj}. This is a Shepard-type normalization. Compute the coverage-based opacity for the layer: \alphak is derived directly from the accumulated EWA weight Wk. Composite layers front-to-back using the over operator: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{k} \hat{\mathbf{a}}k \alphak \prod{j < k} (1 - \alphaj). 7. Anti-Aliasing: Apply an object-space MIP filter. This exploits the resampling structure of surface splatting. Use a center-precomputed approximation to amortize the Jacobian evaluation, suppressing sampling aliasing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computetmatrix(cprime, tuprime, tvprime, P): """Construct T-matrix T = P S. S = [tuprime, tvprime, 0, cprime] as columns.""" S = np.zeros((4, 4)) S[0:3, 0] = tuprime S[0:3, 1] = tvprime S[0:3, 3] = cprime return P @ S def raysurfelintersection(T, u, v): """Compute local coordinates (ulocal, vlocal) via plane intersection in local space.""" Tinv = np.linalg.inv(T) hu = np.array([-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, float(u)]) hv = np.array([0.0, -1.0, 0.0, float(v)]) k = Tinv @ hu l = Tinv @ hv # Intersect planes k and l with z=0 plane: k[0]x + k[1]y + k[3] = 0 det = k[0]l[1] - k[1]l[0] if abs(det) < 1e-6: return 0.0, 0.0 x = (k[1]l[3] - k[3]l[1]) / det y = (k[3]l[0] - k[0]l[3]) / det return x, y def transformtocamera(c, tu, tv, viewmatrix): """Apply view transformation to position and tangent vectors.""" ch = np.array([c, 1.0]) tuh = np.array([tu, 0.0]) tvh = np.array([tv, 0.0]) cprime = (viewmatrix @ ch)[:3] tuprime = (viewmatrix @ tuh)[:3] tvprime = (viewmatrix @ tvh)[:3] return cprime, tuprime, tvprime def environmentlight(direction, envmap): """Sample HDR environment map given a direction vector.""" # Standard spherical coordinate mapping to env map texture theta = math.atan2(direction[0], direction[2]) phi = math.asin(direction[1] / max(1e-6, math.sqrt(np.dot(direction, direction)))) u = (theta / (2 math.pi) + 0.5) % 1.0 v = (phi / math.pi + 0.5) return envmap.sample(u, v) def forwardshading(albedo, metallic, roughness, normal, envmap): """Compute pre-shaded linear radiance using split-sum IBL and microfacet BRDF.""" # Simplified forward shading: diffuse + specular IBL diffuse = albedo environmentlight(-normal, envmap) specular = metallic environmentlight(2 np.dot(normal, np.array([0,0,-1])) normal - np.array([0,0,-1]), envmap) return diffuse + specular def createtiles(width, height, tilesize=16): """Generate tile bounds.""" tiles = [] for y in range(0, height, tilesize): for x in range(0, width, tilesize): tiles.append({'xstart': x, 'ystart': y, 'xend': min(x + tilesize, width), 'yend': min(y + tilesize, height)}) return tiles def intersectstile(surfel, tile): """Check if surfel bounding box overlaps tile.""" return (surfel.bboxmin[0] < tile['xend'] and surfel.bboxmax[0] > tile['xstart'] and surfel.bboxmin[1] < tile['yend'] and surfel.bboxmax[1] > tile['ystart']) def rasterizesurfels(surfels, P, viewmatrix, envmap, imagewidth, imageheight, deltacut): """Rasterize a set of surfels into an image.""" image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) # 1. Pre-shading and T-matrix construction for surfel in surfels: c, tu, tv, a, m, r = surfel cprime, tuprime, tvprime = transformtocamera(c, tu, tv, viewmatrix) surfel.cprime = cprime surfel.tuprime = tuprime surfel.tvprime = tvprime surfel.T = computetmatrix(cprime, tuprime, tvprime, P) tuz = tuprime[2] tvz = tvprime[2] surfel.delta = math.sqrt(tuz2 + tvz2) deltacut surfel.d = cprime[2] surfel.dstart = surfel.d - surfel.delta # Compute implicit normal in camera space nprime = np.cross(tuprime, tvprime) nprime = nprime / np.linalg.norm(nprime) surfel.nprime = nprime surfel.cpre = forwardshading(a, m, r, nprime, envmap) # 2. Tiling and Sorting tiles = createtiles(imagewidth, imageheight) for tile in tiles: tilesurfels = [s for s in surfels if intersectstile(s, tile)] tilesurfels.sort(key=lambda s: s.dstart) tile.surfels = tilesurfels # 3. Per-Pixel Rasterization for tile in tiles: for y in range(tile['ystart'], tile['yend']): for x in range(tile['xstart'], tile['xend']): layers = [] for surfel in tile.surfels: ulocal, vlocal = raysurfelintersection(surfel.T, x, y) rhosq = ulocal2 + vlocal2 if rhosq >= deltacut2: continue w = math.exp(-0.5 rhosq) dstart = surfel.d - surfel.delta dend = surfel.d + surfel.delta addedtolayer = False for layer in layers: if dstart <= layer['maxdend']: layer['W'] += w layer['C'] += w surfel.cpre layer['maxdend'] = max(layer['maxdend'], dend) addedtolayer = True break if not addedtolayer: layers.append({'W': w, 'C': w surfel.cpre, 'maxdend': dend}) # 4. Compositing alphaaccum = 0.0 finalcolor = np.zeros(3) for layer in layers: ahat = layer['C'] / layer['W'] if layer['W'] > 1e-6 else np.zeros(3) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-layer['W']) finalcolor += ahat alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) alphaaccum += alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) image[y, x] = finalcolor return image The rasterization core of 3DSS, designed to render an unstructured set of oriented surfel primitives into a 2D image while correctly handling self-occlusion at concavities. It solves the problem where single-layer rasterization approaches fail to distinguish between geometrically distinct surface sheets that project onto the same pixel, resulting in holes or translucent artifacts in high-curvature regions like ears or under chins. It sets itself apart from classical A-buffer approaches by restricting summation to surfels within the same depth-interval layer rather than gathering across all depths, and from single-layer ternary depth tests by detecting gaps in the depth-interval chain to support an arbitrary number of surface layers per pixel. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of surfels and pixels, with overhead from sorting and interval merging. The interval merging is efficient as it requires no look-ahead. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of surfels and pixels for storing intermediate layer data. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles multiple surface layers per pixel correctly; differentiable visibility; anti-aliased silhouettes; physically-based shading; compatible with mesh reconstruction. Limitations: Requires pre-shading; interval merging logic is more complex than simple depth testing. When to use: Physically-based inverse rendering where geometry, materials, and illumination need to be recovered jointly, especially for scenes with complex occlusions and multiple surface layers. When not to use: When a volumetric representation is preferred or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of interval merging is prohibitive. 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS) was introduced by Mae Younes in 2026. It builds on the foundations of Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) surface splatting [Zwicker et al. 2001] and addresses the limitations of prior differentiable surface splatting methods like Differentiable Surface Splatting (DSS) [Yifan et al. 2019] by providing a more robust multi-layer surface separation and a surface rendering model compatible with physically-based inverse rendering. It bridges the gap between point-based inverse rendering and mesh-based workflows by producing an optimized surfel representation that is natively compatible with Screened Poisson Surface Reconstruction [Kazhdan and Hoppe 2013]. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Surface Splatting Rasterization
head: 3DSS rasterization, Depth-Interval Grouping, Interval-based surface separation, Multi-layer interval grouping, Per-pixel rasterization with depth-interval grouping
body: This method is the rasterization core of 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS), designed to render an unstructured set of oriented surfel primitives into a 2D image while correctly handling self-occlusion at concavities. It solves the problem where single-layer rasterization approaches fail to distinguish between geometrically distinct surface sheets that project onto the same pixel, resulting in holes or translucent artifacts in high-curvature regions like ears or under chins. It sets itself apart from classical A-buffer approaches by restricting summation to surfels within the same depth-interval layer rather than gathering across all depths, and from single-layer ternary depth tests by detecting gaps in the depth-interval chain to support an arbitrary number of surface layers per pixel. The algorithm processes surfels that have already been shaded via split-sum Image-Based Lighting (IBL) against a co-optimized HDR environment, yielding a pre-shaded linear radiance \mathbf{c}i. The rasterization proceeds in three main phases: tiling and sorting, per-pixel interval grouping, and front-to-back compositing. Inputs: A set of surfels \mathcal{S}, each with position \mathbf{p}i, orientation, size, and pre-shaded color \mathbf{c}i. Camera parameters (view/projection matrices) to compute screen-space positions and depth intervals. Kernel cutoff radius r{\text{cut}}. Half-thickness parameter \varepsilonz^{(i)} for each surfel, defining the depth interval extent. Outputs: A composited HDR image. Gradients flowing back to surfel parameters and the environment map. Screen-space tiles: Surfels are binned into tiles based on their screen-space bounding boxes. Sorted primitive sequence: Within each tile, surfels are radix-sorted by their depth-interval start value z{\text{start}}^{(i)}. Per-pixel accumulators: For each pixel, the algorithm maintains: \mathbf{C}g: Accumulated color for the current surface group g. Wg: Accumulated weight for the current surface group g. z{\text{end}}^{\max}: The farthest depth extent encountered so far in the current group. 1. Tiling and Sorting: Bin surfels into screen-space tiles. Radix-sort the surfels within each tile by z{\text{start}}^{(i)}. 2. Per-Pixel Initialization: For each pixel, initialize group accumulators \mathbf{C}g \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, Wg \leftarrow 0, and z{\text{end}}^{\max} \leftarrow 0. 3. Iterate Surfels: For each surfel i in the sorted sequence: a. Intersection: Compute the ray-surfel intersection to obtain local coordinates (u, v). b. Weight Evaluation: Calculate the MIP-filtered squared distance \rho{\text{mip}}^2 using the precomputed inverse covariance \Sigma{\text{mip}}^{-1}. c. Culling: If \rho{\text{mip}}^2 \geq r{\text{cut}}^2, the surfel does not cover this pixel; skip to the next surfel. d. Weight Calculation: Compute the scalar weight w = nf \cdot \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \rho{\text{mip}}^2). e. Depth Interval: Define the depth interval [z{\text{start}}^{(i)}, z{\text{end}}^{(i)}] where z{\text{start}}^{(i)} = z^{(i)} - \varepsilonz^{(i)} and z{\text{end}}^{(i)} = z^{(i)} + \varepsilonz^{(i)}. f. Gap Detection: If Wg > 0 AND z{\text{start}}^{(i)} > z{\text{end}}^{\max}, a gap is detected between the current surfel and the accumulated group. i. Finalize the current layer by calling FLUSHLAYER(\mathbf{C}g, Wg). ii. Reset accumulators: \mathbf{C}g \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, Wg \leftarrow 0, z{\text{end}}^{\max} \leftarrow 0. g. Update Extent: Update the group's farthest extent: z{\text{end}}^{\max} \leftarrow \max(z{\text{end}}^{\max}, z{\text{end}}^{(i)}). h. Accumulate: Add the surfel's contribution to the current group: \mathbf{C}g \leftarrow \mathbf{C}g + w \cdot \mathbf{c}i and Wg \leftarrow Wg + w. 4. Finalize Last Layer: After processing all surfels for a pixel, if Wg > 0, call FLUSHLAYER(\mathbf{C}g, Wg) to finalize the last accumulated group. 5. Shepard Normalization: For each finalized surface group, normalize the accumulated color by its weight to obtain the layer color: \mathbf{C}{\text{layer}} = \mathbf{C}g / Wg. 6. Coverage Opacity: Compute the coverage opacity \alpha{\text{layer}} for each layer from the accumulated weight Wg using a smooth, monotonically increasing mapping. This replaces threshold-based clamping used in classical A-buffers. 7. Front-to-Back Compositing: Composite the resulting layers front-to-back using the computed coverages and opacities to produce the final pixel color. 8. Post-Processing: Blend the composited HDR image with the background, then apply tone-mapping and gamma correction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raysurfelhit(rayo, rayd, surfel): """Returns (u, v) barycentric coordinates if ray hits surfel, else None.""" # Standard ray-surfel plane intersection and barycentric check # Returns None if outside kernel bounds or behind camera return None # Placeholder for standard intersection math def computerhomipsq(u, v, Sigmamipinv): """Computes MIP-filtered squared distance from precomputed inverse covariance.""" # Quadratic form: rho^2 = u^2 Sigmainvxx + v^2 Sigmainvyy return u u Sigmamipinv[0][0] + v v Sigmamipinv[1][1] def mapweighttoopacity(Wg): """Maps accumulated weight to coverage opacity.""" # Smooth monotonic mapping assuming partition of unity return 1.0 - math.exp(-Wg) def rasterizepixel(sortedsurfels, camerarayo, camerarayd, rcutsq, nf): """ Rasterizes a single pixel using depth-interval grouping. Args: sortedsurfels: List of surfels sorted by zstart. camerarayo: Ray origin. camerarayd: Ray direction. rcutsq: Kernel cutoff radius squared. nf: Front-facing normal factor. Returns: finalcolor: The composited HDR color for the pixel. Update extent if zend > zendmax: zendmax = zend # 8. Accumulate Cg[0] += w surfel.color[0] Cg[1] += w surfel.color[1] Cg[2] += w surfel.color[2] Wg += w # Finalize last group if Wg > 0: layercolor = [Cg[0] / Wg, Cg[1] / Wg, Cg[2] / Wg] layeropacity = mapweighttoopacity(Wg) layers.append((layercolor, layeropacity)) # 9. Front-to-Back Compositing finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaacc = 0.0 for layercolor, layeropacity in layers: # Standard front-to-back blending contribr = layercolor[0] layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) contribg = layercolor[1] layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) contribb = layercolor[2] layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) finalcolor[0] += contribr finalcolor[1] += contribg finalcolor[2] += contribb alphaacc += layeropacity (1.0 - alphaacc) return finalcolor \varepsilonz^{(i)}: Half-thickness of surfel i's depth interval. This parameter defines the start and end of the depth interval [z^{(i)} - \varepsilonz^{(i)}, z^{(i)} + \varepsilonz^{(i)}] used for gap detection. Typical values depend on the surfel size and camera distance, but the source does not specify a fixed value. r{\text{cut}}: Kernel cutoff radius. Surfels with \rho{\text{mip}}^2 \geq r{\text{cut}}^2 are skipped. nf: Front-facing normal factor. Used in the weight calculation w = nf \cdot \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \rho{\text{mip}}^2). Self-occlusion at concavities: Without depth-interval grouping, single-layer approaches produce self-occlusion errors at high-curvature concavities (e.g., inside ears or under chins) where surfels from geometrically distinct surface sheets project onto the same pixel. This manifests as holes or translucent patches revealing the background. Silhouette artifacts: Single-layer approaches can produce a "crusty" shell extending beyond the true silhouette, with aliased contours instead of gradual opacity falloff. The multi-layer approach with smooth coverage falloff anti-aliases silhouettes without post-process edge detection. Precision: The gap detection relies on comparing z{\text{start}}^{(i)} with z{\text{end}}^{\max}. Floating-point precision issues could theoretically cause incorrect gap detection if surfels are extremely close in depth, though the source does not specify mitigation strategies. name: Rasterize-then-splat (RtS)
body: Rasterize-then-splat (RtS) is a method for differentiable rendering of 3D surfaces that supports both explicit and implicit representations, providing derivatives at occlusion boundaries while remaining fast and simple to implement. It differs from alternatives like Soft Rasterizer by avoiding costly closest-point queries or mesh processing, and from Nvdiffrast by requiring no specific GPU hardware or custom derivative code, making its differentiable cost independent of mesh size. The method consists of three sequential steps: rasterization of the surface, shading the surface samples, and multi-layer splatting. All derivatives are produced using automatic differentiation on the forward rendering computation. Inputs and Outputs Input: Scene parameters \theta (e.g., camera pose, light parameters, surface definition parameters). Output: Final rendered image S. Data Structures 1. Parameter Buffers (Uk): Per-layer screen-space parameter buffers. For triangle meshes, these consist of per-pixel triangle indices Tk and perspective-correct barycentric coordinates Bk. These are computed via conventional Z-buffer graphics processing using depth peeling to retrieve multiple intersections per pixel. 2. G-buffers (Gk): Interpolated shape attributes (positions, normals) derived from Uk. 3. Splat Colors (Ck): Shaded colors computed via a deferred shading function. 4. Screen-space Positions (Pk): Projected positions of the splats. Steps 1. Sampling (Non-differentiable): Scene parameters \theta are passed through a sampling function U, yielding per-layer screen-space parameter buffers Uk. This step is non-differentiable and computed only in the forward pass. 2. Evaluation (Differentiable): An evaluation function G uses the non-differentiable parameters Uk to interpolate shape attributes (such as positions and normals) into G-buffers Gk. Automatic differentiation is applied to G and downstream functions. 3. Shading and Projection (Differentiable): The evaluated attributes are combined to compute splat colors Ck via a deferred shading function \mathcal{C} and corresponding screen-space positions Pk via a projection function \mathcal{P}. 4. Splatting (Differentiable): Function \mathcal{S} splats the shaded colors Ck at the corresponding pixel locations Pk using a 3x3 kernel to produce the final result S. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizethensplat(sceneparams, camera, surfacedef, imageshape): # Step 1: Non-differentiable sampling # Uk contains per-pixel triangle indices Tk and barycentric coordinates Bk # Computed via conventional Z-buffer with depth peeling Uk = depthpeelingrasterize(surfacedef, camera, imageshape) # Step 2: Differentiable evaluation # Gk contains interpolated positions and normals Gk = evaluateattributes(Uk, surfacedef) # Step 3: Differentiable shading and projection Ck = computeshading(sceneparams, Gk) Pk = projecttoscreen(Gk, camera) # Step 4: Differentiable multi-layer splatting # S is the final image, accumulated using a 3x3 kernel S = zeros(imageshape) for k in range(len(Ck)): for y, x in Pk[k]: for dy in range(-1, 2): for dx in range(-1, 2): ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < imageshape[0] and 0 <= nx < imageshape[1]: weight = 1.0 / 9.0 # 3x3 kernel weight S[ny, nx] += weight Ck[k][y, x] return S def depthpeelingrasterize(surfacedef, camera, imageshape): # Computes Uk using conventional Z-buffer graphics processing with depth peeling # Returns list of layers, each containing Tk and Bk pass # Not given in the sources. def evaluateattributes(Uk, surfacedef): # Interpolates shape attributes (positions, normals) from surfacedef using Tk and Bk Gk = [] for layer in Uk: Tk, Bk = layer['Tk'], layer['Bk'] positions = interpolateattribute(surfacedef.positions, Tk, Bk) normals = interpolateattribute(surfacedef.normals, Tk, Bk) Gk.append({'positions': positions, 'normals': normals}) return Gk def computeshading(sceneparams, Gk): # Deferred shading function C Ck = [] for g in Gk: colors = shade(sceneparams, g['normals'], g['positions']) Ck.append(colors) return Ck def projecttoscreen(Gk, camera): # Projection function P Pk = [] for g in Gk: screenpos = camera.project(g['positions']) Pk.append(screenpos) return Pk Parameters Splatting Kernel Size: 3x3. Depth Peeling: Used to retrieve multiple intersections per pixel for multi-layer splatting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Occlusion Boundaries: RtS provides derivatives at occlusion boundaries, a feature not always present in standard rasterization. Implicit Surfaces: The method supports isosurfaces extracted from implicit surface definitions (e.g., neural radiance fields), avoiding issues with under- or over-sampling of splats by resampling at each frame. Time Complexity: The cost of the differentiable sections is independent of the size of the mesh. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast and simple to implement; requires no differentiable meshing or rasterization steps; efficient for large 3D models; applicable to isosurfaces from implicit definitions; no custom derivative code needed. Limitations: Relies on non-differentiable rasterization for sampling, but provides derivatives at occlusion boundaries. When to use: When rendering large explicit meshes or implicit surfaces (like NeRF isosurfaces) where implementation simplicity and hardware independence are prioritized over specific GPU hardware optimizations. When not to use: Not given in the sources. RtS was introduced by Zhoutong Zhang in the paper "Differentiable Surface Rendering via Non-Differentiable Sampling". It was presented at ICCV 2021. The method was demonstrated for implicit-, mesh-, and parametric-surface-based inverse rendering and neural-network training applications, including the first efficient, differentiable rendering of an isosurface extracted from a neural radiance field (NeRF). It builds on surface splatting techniques [42] and differentiable visibility methods [34], but distinguishes itself by using a true surface representation and resampling splats per frame. name: Spatially Varying Gaussian Splatting (SVGS)
head: Gaussian fragment shading, SVGS (Spatially Varying Gaussian Splatting)
body: SVGS is a rendering technique that enhances the representational power of Gaussian primitives by defining color and opacity as spatially varying functions of the intersection point, rather than constant values per primitive. It addresses the non-compactness of vanilla Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), where a single primitive can only hold one view-dependent color and opacity, leading to ineffective representation for complex textures. Unlike its siblings, SVGS allows different rays intersecting the same primitive to yield different colors based on their intersection location. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting by utilizing 2D Gaussian surfels as the base primitive representation. Inputs: Camera ray, Gaussian primitive parameters (position, covariance, base spherical harmonic coefficients), spatially varying function parameters (e.g., bilinear weights, kernel centers, or MLP weights). Outputs: Pixel color and opacity. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Contains position \mu, covariance \Sigma, spherical harmonic coefficients for view-dependent color, and spatially varying function parameters. For 2DGS-based SVGS, the primitive is a 2D surfel. Spatially Varying Function Parameters: Varies by implementation (see Subtopics). Bilinear: 4 weights per color channel and 1 weight for opacity. Movable Kernels: k kernel centers and weights. Tiny MLP: Network weights for a 3-layer MLP. Steps: 1. Rasterization and Intersection: For each pixel u in screen space, identify the Gaussian surfel i it overlaps. Compute the intersection point p between the camera ray and the Gaussian primitive. For 2DGS-based SVGS, p is defined in the local 2D coordinate system of the Gaussian surfel, with the Gaussian origin as (0,0) and ellipse axes as coordinate axes. The coordinates (u, v) in the tangent space of Gaussian surfel i are computed using the inverse Jacobian of the mapping from image space to tangent space: (u, v) = S[:2] + J{pr}^{-1}(u - ui) + \delta where J{pr}^{-1} is the inverse Jacobian, ui is the projected center, S[:2] is the scale, and \delta is an offset set to 0.1. 2. Compute Spatially Varying Attributes: Calculate the spatially varying color function Fc(p) and opacity function F\alpha(p) based on the intersection point p and the primitive's specific function parameters. 3. Compute Final Color and Opacity: Combine the view-dependent spherical harmonic color with the spatially varying component: c(p, d) = SH(d) + Fc(p) \alpha(p) = F\alpha(p) where SH(d) is the view-dependent spherical harmonic color based on viewing direction d, and p is the intersection point. 4. Normalization: Apply a sigmoid activation to the final color and opacity to normalize them to a valid range during training and rendering. This allows intermediate Fc and F\alpha values to be negative. 5. Alpha Blending: Perform standard alpha blending with other overlapping primitives to obtain the final pixel radiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def svgsrender(ray, gaussianprimitive, spatialfuncparams): # 1. Compute intersection point p in local tangent space # For 2DGS-based SVGS uscreen = ray.pixelcenter Jinv = gaussianprimitive.inversejacobian S = gaussianprimitive.scale ui = gaussianprimitive.projectedcenter delta = 0.1 # Compute local coordinates (u, v) # Note: S[:2] assumes S is a vector/tensor containing scale components ulocal = S[:2] + Jinv @ (uscreen - ui) + delta p = ulocal # p = (u, v) # 2. Compute spatially varying functions Fc(p) and Falpha(p) # Implementation depends on the specific spatial function variant # Example for Bilinear Interpolation: # Fc, Falpha = bilinearinterpolate(p, spatialfuncparams) # Example for Tiny MLP: # Fc, Falpha = tinymlpforward(p, spatialfuncparams) # Example for Movable Kernels: # Fc, Falpha = movablekernelsforward(p, spatialfuncparams) # 3. Compute final color and opacity SHcolor = evaluatesphericalharmonics(gaussianprimitive.shcoeffs, ray.direction) finalcolor = SHcolor + Fc finalalpha = Falpha # 4. Normalize via sigmoid finalcolor = sigmoid(finalcolor) finalalpha = sigmoid(finalalpha) return finalcolor, finalalpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Values: Fc and F\alpha can take negative values. This is permissible because they are added to the spherical harmonic color and normalized by sigmoid. Intersection Calculation: The accuracy of p depends on the correct computation of the inverse Jacobian and the offset \delta. Primitive Type: The default implementation uses 2D Gaussian surfels, but the method can be extended to 3D Gaussians by treating them as ellipsoids. A spatially varying function implementation using bilinear interpolation over the Gaussian surfel. It is the most compact variant in terms of parameters. It sets itself apart from Movable Kernels and Tiny MLPs by using fixed basis functions (corners of the surfel) rather than learnable centers or neural networks. SVGS with Movable Kernels is a spatially varying function implementation within the SVGS framework that defines k movable exponential kernels located on a Gaussian surfel, weighted by their distance to the intersection point. It enhances scene representation by allowing sub-kernels to adapt their positions during training, providing higher flexibility and stronger expressiveness than fixed-basis methods. It sets itself apart from its sibling Bilinear Interpolation by replacing fixed quadrant weights with learnable, gradient-driven kernel centers, and from Tiny MLPs by using a compact parametric form rather than a neural network. A spatially varying function implementation using a small multilayer perceptron (MLP) on each Gaussian surfel to map local coordinates to color and opacity. The MLP accepts a two-dimensional input p=(u,v) and outputs the color and opacity at that location. The Tiny MLP approach has significantly more parameters than Bilinear Interpolation or Movable Kernels, as shown in Fig. 5, but performs well when Gaussian primitive numbers are limited. The Height-field Gaussian Primitive is a curved local chart that combines the thin support of a 2D surfel with bending capability via a Gaussian-basis height field. It stores spatially varying appearance (color and opacity) on the same local domain, allowing a small number of patches to represent both smooth geometry and detailed texture. It sets itself apart from vanilla Gaussian Splatting by providing an explicit surface intersection and camera-linear depth, rather than volumetric accumulation through an ellipsoid. Time Complexity: Rendering time increases slightly compared to vanilla 2DGS/3DGS due to the computation of the spatially varying function Fc(p) and F\alpha(p) for each intersection point. The complexity depends on the chosen spatial function (e.g., MLP inference vs. bilinear interpolation). Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases due to the storage of spatially varying function parameters. Tiny MLPs require significantly more parameters per primitive than Bilinear Interpolation or Movable Kernels. Performance: SVGS outperforms the baseline 2DGS in novel view synthesis across all three spatially varying function designs. SVGS with movable kernels achieves the best results on multiple datasets, demonstrating strong potential for representing complex textures on relatively flat geometries. Strengths: Improved representation of complex textures and geometry with fewer primitives compared to vanilla Gaussian Splatting. Limitations: Increased parameter count and computational overhead per primitive compared to vanilla methods. When to use: When scenes combine complex textures with relatively simple geometry, or when high-fidelity texture reconstruction is required with limited primitive counts. SVGS was introduced to address the limitations of vanilla Gaussian Splatting, which uses constant color and opacity per primitive, leading to non-compact representations. The method was developed to improve novel view synthesis and geometric reconstruction by allowing spatially varying attributes within a single primitive. It builds on the foundation of 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). The concept of spatially varying Gaussian splatting for inverse rendering (SVG-IR) was also explored, introducing Gaussian vertex and fragment shading analogous to traditional triangle pipelines. name: SVGS with Movable Kernels
head: Movable Kernels (SVGS Variant), Movable kernels spatially varying function, Ours-MK, SVGS (Movable Kernels), SVGS-MK
body: SVGS with Movable Kernels is a spatially varying function implementation within the SVGS framework that defines k movable exponential kernels located on a Gaussian surfel, weighted by their distance to the intersection point. It enhances scene representation by allowing sub-kernels to adapt their positions during training, providing higher flexibility and stronger expressiveness than fixed-basis methods. It sets itself apart from its sibling Bilinear Interpolation by replacing fixed quadrant weights with learnable, gradient-driven kernel centers, and from Tiny MLPs by using a compact parametric form rather than a neural network. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Gaussian surfel primitive (defined by its mean, covariance, and base opacity/color), camera view, and intersection point p in the local 2D coordinate system (u, v) of the surfel. Output: The final color C and opacity \alpha for the intersection point, computed by blending the contributions of k movable sub-kernels. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive stores the following learnable parameters in addition to the standard 2DGS attributes: k kernel centers: Ki = (K{ix}, K{iy}) for i = 0, \dots, k-1. These are 2D coordinates in the local surfel space. k learnable colors: ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 for i = 0, \dots, k-1. k learnable opacities: \alphai \in \mathbb{R} for i = 0, \dots, k-1. Parameters: k: The number of movable kernels per Gaussian surfel. Default value is k=4. \lambdae: The parameter controlling the changing rate of the kernel function. Default value is \lambdae = 0.1. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: For each Gaussian primitive, initialize k kernel centers Ki, colors ci, and opacities \alphai. 2. Forward Pass (Weight Computation): For a given intersection point p = (u, v) on the surfel: a. Compute the Euclidean distance di between the intersection point p and each kernel center Ki: di = \| p - Ki \|2 b. Compute the weight wi for each kernel using an exponential decay function: wi = \exp(-\lambdae \cdot di) c. Normalize the weights to sum to 1: \hat{w}i = \frac{wi}{\sum{j=0}^{k-1} wj} d. Compute the spatially varying color C(p) and opacity \alpha(p) by blending the learnable attributes using the normalized weights: C(p) = \sum{i=0}^{k-1} \hat{w}i ci \alpha(p) = \sum{i=0}^{k-1} \hat{w}i \alphai 3. Backward Pass (Gradient Calculation): a. Compute the gradients of the loss with respect to C(p) and \alpha(p). b. Propagate these gradients to the learnable parameters ci, \alphai, and Ki. c. Update the kernel centers Ki in the direction of their gradients during optimization. 4. Degeneracy Handling: If a kernel center Ki moves outside the Gaussian support during optimization, the primitive effectively degenerates to standard 2DGS behavior for that primitive. No clamping or projection constraints are applied to keep the kernel inside the support. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computemovablekernelweights(pu, pv, kernelcenters, lambdae): k = len(kernelcenters) weights = [] for i in range(k): ku, kv = kernelcenters[i] distsq = (pu - ku)2 + (pv - kv)2 dist = math.sqrt(distsq) w = math.exp(-lambdae dist) weights.append(w) sumw = sum(weights) if sumw == 0: return [1.0 / k] k normalizedweights = [w / sumw for w in weights] return normalizedweights def evaluatespatiallyvaryingfunction(pu, pv, kernelcenters, colors, opacities, lambdae): k = len(kernelcenters) weights = computemovablekernelweights(pu, pv, kernelcenters, lambdae) r = 0.0 g = 0.0 b = 0.0 alpha = 0.0 for i in range(k): w = weights[i] ri, gi, bi = colors[i] ai = opacities[i] r += w ri g += w gi b += w bi alpha += w ai return (r, g, b), alpha def updatekernelcenters(kernelcenters, gradients, learningrate): k = len(kernelcenters) updatedcenters = [] for i in range(k): ku, kv = kernelcenters[i] dku, dkv = gradients[i] newku = ku - learningrate dku newkv = kv - learningrate dkv updatedcenters.append((newku, newkv)) return updatedcenters Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Kernel Degeneracy: If a kernel center moves outside the Gaussian support, the method degenerates to standard 2DGS behavior for that primitive. The sources state that no special restrictions are imposed to prevent this, as it rarely occurs (probability of remaining inside is >99.5% across datasets). Weight Zero Division: If all exponential weights are effectively zero (e.g., intersection point is very far from all kernels), normalization requires a fallback (e.g., uniform distribution) to avoid division by zero. Uses four fixed kernels located in the four quadrants of the elliptical Gaussian surfel, assigning learnable color and opacity to each quadrant via bilinear interpolation. Simpler but may cause gradient vanishing. Choose when computational simplicity is prioritized over maximum expressiveness. Link Uses a tiny three-layer neural network on each Gaussian surfel to map local coordinates to color and opacity. Strongest representation ability but significantly more parameters. Choose when maximum fidelity is required and parameter budget is less constrained. Link Time Complexity: Training and rendering are slightly slower than 2DGS due to the per-primitive overhead of evaluating k sub-kernels for weight computation, color blending, and gradient calculation. Memory Complexity: Uses approximately 1.4× the parameters of 2DGS. Measured Performance: On the Synthetic Blender dataset, training takes 1083.13s vs 635.25s for 2DGS, with rendering at 133.25 FPS vs 210.73 FPS. Rendering speed still exceeds 30 FPS for real-time use. Strengths: Superior novel view synthesis performance on multiple datasets, particularly excelling at representing complex textures on relatively flat geometries. Maintains superior expressiveness even when 2DGS is forced to use 2× the Gaussians. Compatible with existing acceleration frameworks without architectural changes. Limitations: Slightly slower training and rendering compared to 2DGS. When to Use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of complex textures on simple geometry is required, and real-time rendering (>30 FPS) is still desired. When Not to Use: When maximum training speed is the primary constraint and 2DGS performance is sufficient. SVGS with Movable Kernels was introduced in the paper "SVGS: Enhancing Gaussian Splatting Using Primitives With Spatially Varying Colors". It is part of the SVGS family, which aims to address the non-compactness of vanilla Gaussian Splatting by allowing spatially varying colors and opacity within a single primitive. The method was evaluated on Synthetic Blender, Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, and DTU datasets. name: Height-field Gaussian Primitive
head: H-2DGS primitive
body: The Height-field Gaussian Primitive is a curved local chart that combines the thin support of a 2D surfel with bending capability via a Gaussian-basis height field. It stores spatially varying appearance (color and opacity) on the same local domain, allowing a small number of patches to represent both smooth geometry and detailed texture. It sets itself apart from vanilla Gaussian Splatting by providing an explicit surface intersection and camera-linear depth, rather than volumetric accumulation through an ellipsoid. Inputs: World-space ray r(t) = o + td. Outputs: Intersection parameter t, color Ci, and opacity Oi at the intersection point. Data Structures: Each primitive i stores: center \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3; tangent frame Ri = [\mathbf{t}{u,i}, \mathbf{t}{v,i}, \mathbf{n}i] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}; tangent scales s{x,i}, s{y,i} \in \mathbb{R}; height basis coefficients b{i,k}^h \in \mathbb{R} for k=1 \dots Kh; height basis centers \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,k}^h \in \mathbb{R}^2; height basis bandwidths \sigma{i,k}^h \in \mathbb{R}; color basis coefficients and centers; opacity basis coefficients and centers; constant terms for color and opacity. Parameters: Kh = 5 height bases. 20 opacity bases. 50 color bases. Steps: 1. Transform the world-space ray into the primitive's local frame: \mathbf{y}i(t) = Ri^T (r(t) - \mathbf{c}i). 2. Compute normalized local coordinates: ui(t) = y{x,i}(t)/s{x,i} and vi(t) = y{y,i}(t)/s{y,i}. 3. Evaluate the height field hi(u, v) at (ui(t), vi(t)): hi(u, v) = \sum{k=1}^{Kh} b{i,k}^h \phi{i,k}^h(u, v), where \phi{i,k}^h(u, v) = \exp\left(-\frac{\|(u, v) - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,k}^h\|^2}{2(\sigma{i,k}^h)^2}\right). 4. Define the residual function for intersection: fi(t) = y{z,i}(t) - hi(ui(t), vi(t)). 5. Solve fi(t) = 0 for t using a small fixed number of Newton iterations. The derivative fi'(t) requires the chain rule because ui(t) and vi(t) depend on t. 6. Evaluate color Ci(u, v) and opacity Oi(u, v) at the accepted intersection using their respective Gaussian bases and constant terms. 7. Composite the result in depth order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderheightfieldprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, primitive, initialguess=0.0, maxiterations=5, tolerance=1e-6): # Precompute local frame axes (columns of Ri^T) RT = transpose(primitive.R) c = primitive.c sx = primitive.sx sy = primitive.sy Kh = primitive.Kh # Helper: compute yi(t) = R^T (r(t) - c) def gety(t): diff = rayorigin + t raydirection - c yx = dot(RT[0], diff) yy = dot(RT[1], diff) yz = dot(RT[2], diff) return yx, yy, yz # Helper: evaluate height field def evalheight(u, v): h = 0.0 for k in range(Kh): mu = primitive.muh[k] sigma = primitive.sigmah[k] b = primitive.bh[k] dx = u - mu[0] dy = v - mu[1] distsq = dxdx + dydy phi = exp(-distsq / (2.0 sigmasigma)) h += b phi return h # Helper: evaluate appearance (color/opacity) using analogous bases + constant def evalappearance(u, v, centers, sigmas, coeffs, constant): val = constant for k in range(len(centers)): mu = centers[k] sigma = sigmas[k] b = coeffs[k] dx = u - mu[0] dy = v - mu[1] distsq = dxdx + dydy phi = exp(-distsq / (2.0 sigmasigma)) val += b phi return val # Newton's method to find root t = initialguess for in range(maxiterations): yx, yy, yz = gety(t) u = yx / sx v = yy / sy h = evalheight(u, v) fval = yz - h if abs(fval) < tolerance: break # Derivative f'(t) = dyz/dt - (dh/du du/dt + dh/dv dv/dt) d = raydirection dyxdt = dot(RT[0], d) dyydt = dot(RT[1], d) dyzdt = dot(RT[2], d) dudt = dyxdt / sx dvdt = dyydt / sy dhdu = 0.0 dhdv = 0.0 for k in range(Kh): mu = primitive.muh[k] sigma = primitive.sigmah[k] b = primitive.bh[k] dx = u - mu[0] dy = v - mu[1] distsq = dxdx + dydy phi = exp(-distsq / (2.0 sigmasigma)) dphidu = -phi dx / (sigmasigma) dphidv = -phi dy / (sigmasigma) dhdu += b dphidu dhdv += b dphidv dhdt = dhdu dudt + dhdv dvdt fprime = dyzdt - dhdt if abs(fprime) < 1e-8: break t = t - fval / fprime # Evaluate final appearance yx, yy, yz = gety(t) ufinal = yx / sx vfinal = yy / sy color = evalappearance(ufinal, vfinal, primitive.colorbases, primitive.colorsigmas, primitive.colorcoeffs, primitive.colorconst) opacity = evalappearance(ufinal, vfinal, primitive.opacitybases, primitive.opacitysigmas, primitive.opacitycoeffs, primitive.opacityconst) return t, color, opacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Dominated by the Newton iterations and the evaluation of the Gaussian bases. Each iteration requires O(Kh) operations for the height field. Memory Complexity: Each primitive stores Kh height bases, 20 opacity bases, and 50 color bases. Strengths: Provides explicit surface intersection and camera-linear depth, which is beneficial for postoperative alignment and sharp reconstruction. Allows spatially varying appearance within a single primitive. Limitations: Requires solving a non-linear equation for each ray, which is more complex than simple plane intersection. The Height-field Gaussian Primitive was introduced in "H-2DGS: Height-Field Gaussian Splatting for Sharp and Deformable Neurosurgical Surface Reconstruction". It addresses the limitation of planar surfels, which can only approximate cortical curvature by using many small elements. The method was developed to represent both smooth geometry and detailed cortical texture with a relatively small number of patches. name: Learning View-Dependent Splatting Kernels
head: Learned Kernels, Learned View-Dependent Splatting Kernels, Neural 2D Splatting Kernels, Ours, View-Dependent 2D Gaussian Splatting
body: Learning View-Dependent Splatting Kernels is a differentiable framework that automatically learns view-dependent 2D splatting kernels as an implicit representation of volumetric primitives, improving reconstruction quality and representation efficiency for novel 3D view synthesis. Unlike 2D Gaussian Splatting and vanilla 3DGS where the kernel shape is a fixed, view-independent function of the Mahalanobis distance, this method introduces learned view-dependency to serve as a form of data-driven consistency, allowing the kernel profile to vary with the camera view. It avoids the computation of line integrals over general 3D primitives by explicitly modeling the integral results via a neural projection and decoder. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of volumetric primitives defined by geometric attributes and a latent vector, along with camera parameters (viewing transformation, projection Jacobian). Output: A view-dependent opacity value for each pixel within the projected bounding ellipse, which is passed to a standard splatting pipeline for coloring and alpha-blending. Data Structures: Each volumetric primitive stores the following attributes: 1. Center: \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D} (3D vector). 2. Scaling factors: \mathbf{s} (3D vector). 3. Rotation: \mathbf{q} (4D quaternion). 4. 3D-Kernel Latent: \mathbf{z}{3D} (5D vector in most experiments). Neural Networks: 1. Projection MLP (\Phi{\text{proj}}): Architecture: 4-layer MLP. Hidden layers: 64 neurons each. Activation: Leaky-ReLU after each layer except the last. Input: \mathbf{z}{3D}, camera-space center \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}^{\text{cam}}, scaling factors \mathbf{s}, and primitive rotation matrix in camera space \mathbf{R}^{\text{cam}}. Output: \mathbf{z}{2D} (5D vector). 2. Kernel Decoder (\Phi{\text{dec}}): Architecture: 3-layer MLP. Hidden layers: 4 neurons each. Activation: Leaky-ReLU after each layer except the last. Final Layer: Sigmoid function to bound output. Input: Squared Mahalanobis distance r^2 and \mathbf{z}{2D}. Output: Opacity d. Numbered Steps: 1. Project the Bounding Ellipsoid: Compute the 3D covariance matrix \Sigma{3D} = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} is the rotation matrix derived from \mathbf{q} and \mathbf{S} is the scaling matrix derived from \mathbf{s}. Compute the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} using the EWA splatting approximation: \Sigma{2D} = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \Sigma{3D} \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T where \mathbf{W} is the viewing transformation and \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projection. The projected mean is denoted \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}. 2. Neural Projection: Transform the 3D kernel latent to a 2D kernel latent using the projection MLP: \mathbf{z}{2D} = \Phi{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{z}{3D}, \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}^{\text{cam}}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{R}^{\text{cam}}) The inputs provide spatial, scale, and view awareness to the MLP. 3. Pre-sample the Kernel Profile: To accelerate rasterization, pre-sample the 1D profile of the kernel decoder. Place N uniform samples of r^2 to cover the range [0,1], denoted \{ri^2\}{1 \le i \le N}. The default value for N is 2. Compute di = \Phi{\text{dec}}(ri^2, \mathbf{z}{2D}) for each sample. Store the results \{di\}. 4. Rasterization (Kernel Evaluation): For a pixel with squared Mahalanobis distance r^2 relative to the projected primitive: Find the closest pre-sampled indices c and c+1 such that rc^2 \le r^2 \le r{c+1}^2. Compute the interpolation factor: \lambda = \frac{r^2 - rc^2}{r{c+1}^2 - rc^2} Compute the final opacity via linear interpolation: d = (1 - \lambda)dc + \lambda d{c+1} The resulting kernel shape is radially symmetric and bounded by the projected 2D ellipse. 5. Joint Optimization: The neural networks (\Phi{\text{proj}} and \Phi{\text{dec}}) and per-primitive attributes (\boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{z}{3D}) are jointly optimized with respect to input images. Pre-training Procedure: Initialize \mathbf{z}{3D} to all zeros. Initialize weights in \Phi{\text{proj}} and \Phi{\text{dec}} with He initialization. Randomly sample \boldsymbol{\mu}{3D}^{\text{cam}}, \mathbf{s}, and \mathbf{R}^{\text{cam}}. Randomly sample r^2 to obtain target profile samples. For the volumetric case, the target profile is a 1D cosine function: d = \cos(r^2). For the planar case, 2D Gaussian surfels are used as the target. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def leakyrelu(x, alpha=0.01): return x if x > 0 else alpha x def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) class LinearLayer: def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures): # He initialization for weights self.weights = [[math.sqrt(2.0 / infeatures) (2 random.random() - 1) for in range(infeatures)] for in range(outfeatures)] self.bias = [0.0] outfeatures def forward(self, x): out = [] for i in range(len(self.bias)): val = self.bias[i] for j in range(len(x)): val += self.weights[i][j] x[j] out.append(val) return out class MLP: def init(self, layersizes, activations): self.layers = [] for i in range(len(layersizes) - 1): self.layers.append(LinearLayer(layersizes[i], layersizes[i+1])) self.activations = activations def forward(self, x): h = x for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = layer.forward(h) if i < len(self.activations): h = self.activations[i for v in h] return h kerneldecoder = MLP([6, 4, 4, 1], [leakyrelu, leakyrelu, sigmoid]) def precomputekernelsamples(z2d, nsamples=2): """ Pre-samples the kernel decoder for a given 2D latent. Returns lists of squared radii and corresponding opacities. """ # Generate N uniform samples of r^2 in [0, 1] rsquaredsamples = [i / (nsamples - 1) for i in range(nsamples)] # Evaluate decoder at these samples dsamples = [] for rsq in rsquaredsamples: inputvec = [rsq] + list(z2d) opacity = kerneldecoder.forward(inputvec)[0] dsamples.append(opacity) return rsquaredsamples, dsamples def evaluatekernel(rsquared, rsqsamples, dsamples): """ Interpolates the kernel opacity for a given squared Mahalanobis distance. """ # Find the interval [rc^2, r{c+1}^2] containing rsquared c = 0 for i in range(len(rsqsamples) - 1): if rsqsamples[i] <= rsquared <= rsqsamples[i+1]: c = i break else: # Fallback if rsquared is outside range or single sample c = 0 rcsq = rsqsamples[c] rc1sq = rsqsamples[c+1] dc = dsamples[c] dc1 = dsamples[c+1] # Avoid division by zero if samples are identical if rc1sq == rcsq: return dc # Linear interpolation lambdaval = (rsquared - rcsq) / (rc1sq - rcsq) opacity = (1 - lambdaval) dc + lambdaval dc1 return opacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Radial Symmetry: Using a general (non-radially symmetric) 2D kernel causes theoretical discontinuity in mapping arbitrary 3D view conditions to a 2D frame (hairy ball theorem), resulting in rapid rotation of the kernel around certain view directions during animation. Radial symmetry avoids this by eliminating the need for a 2D frame. Parameter \kappa: The parameter \kappa (number of pre-samples N) controls the expressiveness of the learned kernels. Typical values are 2, 4, 8. The memory footprint of the representation does not change with \kappa. Increasing \kappa improves reconstruction quality only when the memory footprint is small. With a large footprint, the trend is not observed, likely because the average screen-space size per primitive becomes too small for higher kernel expressiveness to matter. Precision: The interpolation relies on r^2. Ensure r^2 is computed correctly as the squared Mahalanobis distance (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D})^T \Sigma{2D}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}). Not given in the sources. Link Not given in the sources. Link Not given in the sources. Link Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: Rasterization is accelerated by pre-sampling the 1D profile of the kernel decoder with N samples (default 2), storing results, and using linear interpolation during rendering. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint per primitive consists of geometric attributes and the 3D-kernel latent \mathbf{z}{3D}. The memory footprint does not change with the parameter \kappa (number of pre-samples). Measured Performance: On the Tanks & Temples dataset with ~25MB memory footprint, the method (with \kappa=4) achieves 24.08 PSNR with 328K primitives at 102 FPS, outperforming 3DGS (23.12 PSNR, 446K, 295 FPS) and DBS (23.57 PSNR, 417K, 319 FPS). Strengths: Superior representation efficiency and reconstruction quality compared to state-of-the-art techniques on analytical and learned kernels. The learned view-dependency serves as data-driven consistency. Limitations: Rendering speed decreases as \kappa increases or as the number of primitives increases for high-quality results. The method includes a pre-training step to initialize the neural networks and latent codes before joint optimization. When to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is required with limited memory budget, and view-dependent appearance variations are significant. When not to use: When real-time performance with very high primitive counts is critical and the overhead of neural network evaluation (even with pre-sampling) is prohibitive, or when the scene is static and view-independent kernels suffice. The method was introduced by Huakeng Ding, Zhanpeng Liu, Fan Pei, Kun Zhou, and Hongzhi Wu in 2026. It builds upon the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting and 2D Gaussian Splatting, addressing the limitation that existing methods use view-independent kernels as a function of Mahalanobis distance. The work extends the idea to learn general 2D kernels for planar primitives in the context of 2D splatting, demonstrating efficiency in representing 2D images as well. Learning View-Dependent Splatting Kernels, https://doi.org/10.1145/3799902.3811064, fetched 2026-10-31
