name: SparseOIT Rasterizer
head: GPU software rasterization of 3D Gaussians with pre-rendering
body: The SparseOIT Rasterizer is a rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that computes a weighted, order-independent transparency (OIT) image and a pre-rendered image simultaneously. It solves the problem of correct alpha blending in Gaussian splatting without requiring the expensive depth-sorting step inherent to standard rasterization. Unlike standard 3DGS rasterization, which sorts Gaussians by distance to the camera to correctly accumulate transmittance, SparseOIT eliminates sorting entirely by using a blend-and-normalize (BAN) function and a blend-and-update (BAU) function, relying only on tile-ID ordering. It builds on Shading and Lighting Models. Inputs: Image dimensions: width w, height h. Gaussian attributes: 3D means \mathbf{M}, covariances \mathbf{S}, colors \mathbf{C}, opacities \mathbf{A}. View matrix: \mathbf{V}. Outputs: Rendered image: \mathbf{I}. Pre-rendered image state: \mathbf{I}{pre}. Data Structures: \mathbf{M}': Screen-space Gaussian means. \mathbf{S}': Screen-space Gaussian covariances. T: List of tiles covering the image. L: List of Gaussian data entries, duplicated and assigned tile keys. K: List of tile keys corresponding to entries in L. R: Ranges identifying which entries in L belong to each tile. Parameters: BAN (Blend and Normalize): Function computing the final OIT color. BAU (Blend and Update): Function updating the pre-rendered state for subsequent blending or accumulation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cull: Remove Gaussians outside the view frustum using CullGaussian(p, V). 2. Project: Compute screen-space means \mathbf{M}' and covariances \mathbf{S}' from \mathbf{M}, \mathbf{S}, and \mathbf{V} using ScreenspaceGaussians. 3. Tile: Create a grid of tiles T for the image dimensions w, h using CreateTiles. 4. Assign Keys: Duplicate Gaussian data into list L and assign each entry a tile key based on its screen position, producing K, using DuplicateWithKeys. 5. Sort: Sort entries in L and K solely by tile ID using SortByKeys. This replaces depth sorting. 6. Range: Identify the start and end indices in L for each tile using IdentifyTileRanges, producing R. 7. Initialize: Set the pre-rendered image \mathbf{I}{pre} to zero. 8. Rasterize: Iterate over all tiles t \in T: 9. Iterate over all pixels i in tile t: 10. Retrieve the range r of Gaussians affecting pixel i using GetTileRange. 11. Compute the final color \mathbf{I}[i] using the BAN function: \mathbf{I}[i] \leftarrow \text{BAN}(i, L, r, K, \mathbf{M}', \mathbf{S}', \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{I}{pre}[i]) 12. Update the pre-rendered state using the BAU function: \mathbf{I}{pre}[i] \leftarrow \text{BAU}(i, L, r, K, \mathbf{M}', \mathbf{S}', \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{I}{pre}[i]) Formulas: The final color \mathbf{C} is computed as: \mathbf{C} = T \mathbf{c}0 + (1-T)F where: \mathbf{c}0 is the background color. T is the accumulated opacity/transmittance factor. F is the weighted average color: F = \frac{P}{Q} P and Q are sums over all N Gaussians affecting the pixel: P = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi Q = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi \mathbf{c}i is the color of the i-th Gaussian. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. wi is the weight of the i-th Gaussian. Backward Propagation: The gradients for optimization are: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \mathbf{c}i} = (1-T)\frac{\alphai wi}{Q} \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \alphai} = \frac{T}{1-\alphai}(F-\mathbf{c}0) + (1-T)\frac{wi}{Q}(\mathbf{c}i - F) \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial wi} = (1-T)\frac{\alphai}{Q}(\mathbf{c}i - F) Pitfalls: The variables of each Gaussian are mutually independent in the backward propagation equation, which allows for parallel computation. The update interval for the pre-rendering state may need to be increased (e.g., to 600) for specific scenes like "train", "room", and "bonsai" to ensure correct execution. Weighted Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) for 3D Gaussian Splatting computes a blended image without sorting Gaussians by depth, using a learnable weight function to approximate correct transparency blending. It differs from standard 3DGS rasterization, which requires sorting by distance to camera to correctly accumulate transmittance, by eliminating the sorting step entirely in favor of a weighted average. The method builds on SparseOIT Rasterizer. Not given in the sources. The SparseOIT Rasterizer was introduced in the paper "SparseOIT: Improving Order-Independent Transparency 3DGS via Active Set Method". It addresses the limitations of standard order-dependent transparency in 3D Gaussian Splatting by providing an order-independent alternative that avoids the computational cost of sorting. SparseOIT: Improving Order-Independent Transparency 3DGS via Active Set Method, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.13855, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Weighted Order-Independent Transparency for 3DGS
head: OIT-based 3DGS rendering, Weighted OIT, Weighted Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) Rendering
body: Weighted Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) for 3D Gaussian Splatting computes a blended image without sorting Gaussians by depth, using a learnable weight function to approximate correct transparency blending. It differs from standard 3DGS rasterization, which requires sorting by distance to camera to correctly accumulate transmittance, by eliminating the sorting step entirely in favor of a weighted average. The method builds on SparseOIT Rasterizer. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians G = \{\bm{\mu}i, qi, si, oi, \mathbf{h}i, wi \mid i=1,\dots,N\}, where \bm{\mu}i is the 3D center, qi is the quaternion rotation, si is the scale, oi is the base opacity, \mathbf{h}i are spherical harmonic coefficients, and wi is the learnable weight. Camera parameters (view matrix \mathbf{W}, projection matrix, focal point \mathbf{f}) are required for projection. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C} and transmittance T for each pixel. Data Structures Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores: \bm{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D center position. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity scalar. \mathbf{h}i: Spherical harmonic coefficients for color. wi \in \mathbb{R}: Learnable weight scalar. Projected Attributes (computed per pixel/tile): \bm{\mu}'i \in \mathbb{R}^2: Projected 2D center. \bm{\Sigma}'i \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}: Projected 2D covariance matrix. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Final opacity at the pixel. \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Gaussian color at the pixel. Numbered Steps 1. Project Gaussians: For each Gaussian i, compute the 3D-to-2D projection. Compute the 3D covariance matrix \bm{\Sigma}i from scale si and rotation qi. Compute the view transformation matrix \mathbf{W} and the Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J} of the affine approximation of the projective transformation at the Gaussian center. Compute the 2D covariance matrix: \bm{\Sigma}'i = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \bm{\Sigma}i \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{J}^T 2. Compute Final Opacity \alphai: For a pixel at position \bm{x}'i (the pixel center in 2D space), calculate the Gaussian's contribution opacity: \alphai = oi \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2} (\bm{x}'i - \bm{\mu}'i)^T {\bm{\Sigma}'i}^{-1} (\bm{x}'i - \bm{\mu}'i)\right) 3. Compute Color \mathbf{c}i: Evaluate the spherical harmonic function \mathbf{Y} using the direction from the camera focal point \mathbf{f} to the Gaussian center \bm{\mu}i and the coefficients \mathbf{h}i: \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{Y}(\|\mathbf{f} - \bm{\mu}i\|, \mathbf{h}i) 4. Accumulate Weighted Sum: For each pixel, initialize accumulators for the weighted color sum and the total weight. Iterate over all Gaussians i=1 \dots N that overlap the pixel (or use an active set for optimization): Let wi be the learnable weight for Gaussian i. Accumulate: \text{WeightedColor} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai wi \text{TotalWeight} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai wi 5. Compute Transmittance T: Calculate the product of (1 - \alphai) for all overlapping Gaussians: T = \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) 6. Compute Final Color \mathbf{C}: Combine the background color \mathbf{c}0, the transmittance T, and the weighted average of the Gaussian colors: \mathbf{C} = T \mathbf{c}0 + (1 - T) \frac{\text{WeightedColor}}{\text{TotalWeight}} Parameters Learnable Weight wi: A scalar value associated with each Gaussian. It is a learnable weight larger when the Gaussian is near the camera. The exact functional form of wi is defined in Eq. 1 of reference [14], but the specific formula is not provided in the source text. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: If \text{TotalWeight} = 0 (no Gaussians overlap or all \alphai wi = 0), the weighted average term is undefined. In this case, the result should default to T \mathbf{c}0. Precision: The product T = \prod (1-\alphai) can underflow to zero for many overlapping Gaussians, which is mathematically correct but may cause numerical issues if not handled with log-space accumulation in implementation. Weight Definition: The source states wi is "larger when gaussian near to camera" but does not provide the explicit formula for wi in the text, citing [14] instead. Implementers must refer to [14] for the exact definition of wi. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates the need for depth sorting, which simplifies parallelization on GPU and avoids sorting artifacts. Limitations: Approximates order-dependent transparency; accuracy depends on the quality of the learned weights wi. Origin: The weighted OIT rendering equation was first defined in [22] and adopted from [14]. It was applied to 3DGS in the context of improving order-independent transparency methods for Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction. Development: The method is part of the "SparseOIT" framework, which proposes acceleration strategies like the active set method to improve the performance of OIT-based 3DGS reconstruction. SparseOIT: Improving Order-Independent Transparency 3DGS via Active Set Method, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.13855, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting
head: Deferred Surfel Rendering, Split-Sum IBL
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to support physically based lighting, self-occlusion, and material-aware relighting. It solves the limitation of standard splatting, which renders only baked view-dependent colors, by introducing material attributes (normals, roughness, albedo) and computing lighting via deferred shading or dedicated light-space rasterization passes [4464-ref-gaussian-deferred-surfel-rendering-with-split-sum-ibl.md][4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md][4489-light-space-rasterization-for-t-light.md]. It is distinguished from Analytic-Splatting Forward Shading by its focus on physical material properties and deferred pipelines rather than analytic signal response, and from Transparency and Blending Models by its explicit handling of light transport and occlusion transmittance. All methods in this family operate on 3D Gaussian primitives defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (or scales and orientation), opacity o, and color \mathbf{c} (or spherical harmonic coefficients). The core challenge is computing the pixel color C and accumulated alpha \alpha given a camera ray. Standard splatting projects 3D Gaussians to 2D ellipses, computes a 2D alpha mask, and blends them in screen space 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization. These models modify the blending or shading stage: some refine the depth metric used for sorting, others integrate the 3D density function directly along the ray, and others use weighted averages to bypass sorting Transparency and Blending Models. All assume the Gaussians are sorted or processed in a manner that approximates front-to-back accumulation to ensure correct occlusion. For relighting, splats must carry physical material attributes: normal, roughness, reflectance (specular strength), and albedo (diffuse color) [4464-ref-gaussian-deferred-surfel-rendering-with-split-sum-ibl.md]. These are stored in a parallel Material Buffer aligned with the Splat Buffer [4464-ref-gaussian-deferred-surfel-rendering-with-split-sum-ibl.md]. For self-shadowing, a virtual "sun camera" is constructed to simulate a directional light source [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md]. This camera is placed at a large distance with a narrow field of view (FOV) to minimize parallax error to below 2% [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md]. Both relighting (for cache locality) and shadowing (for correct front-to-back accumulation) require sorting [4464-ref-gaussian-deferred-surfel-rendering-with-split-sum-ibl.md][4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md]. Relighting uses spatial locality algorithms like Morton codes [4464-ref-gaussian-deferred-surfel-rendering-with-split-sum-ibl.md]. Shadowing sorts Gaussians by depth relative to the sun camera [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md]. During the light pass for shadowing, the projection covariance is not expanded by 0.3I and no amplitude compensation is applied, preserving the main camera pass's sampling expansion [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md]. In shadowing calculations, sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches are treated as constants to prevent incorrect gradient propagation [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md]. A physically based rendering (PBR) method for novel view synthesis and relighting of reflective objects using 2D Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of blurred reflective details and inaccurate material representation in standard Gaussian Splatting by decomposing splats into PBR material attributes (albedo, normal, roughness, reflectance) and computing lighting via a deferred shading pipeline with split-sum environment map integration. It is distinguished from its sibling 3D Gaussian Splatting Self-Shadowing (Tlight) by its focus on material-aware deferred shading and split-sum IBL rather than light-space rasterization for self-shadowing, and from Light Space Rasterization for Tlight by its use of a deferred surfel buffer for cache-locality sorting rather than a dedicated light-space depth buffer. Choose this when high-fidelity reflections and material-aware relighting are required. Calculates the self-shadowing transmittance T{light} for each Gaussian along a directional sun direction, representing the 'front occlusion transmittance' to model self-shadowing effects in volume rendering. It differs from standard rasterization by performing a dedicated light-space pass that accumulates front-to-back occlusion without modifying the main camera's sampling expansion or applying amplitude compensation. Builds on Shading and Lighting Models and contrasts with Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL and Light Space Rasterization for Tlight by explicitly tracking front occlusion transmittance per Gaussian footprint rather than deferred surface buffers or alternative light-space projections. Choose this for efficient self-shadowing integration into existing training pipelines. Light Space Rasterization computes T{light}, the front-facing occlusion transmittance for each Gaussian along a directional sun direction, enabling physically based self-shadowing in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It differs from voxel-based fallbacks by providing full continuous gradients and zero EWA expansion by default, avoiding the inversion artifacts associated with early-termination in deep occlusion. Choose this when continuous gradients and artifact-free deep occlusion handling are prioritized over voxel-based approximations. Originating from extensions to 3D Gaussian Splatting for novel view synthesis, these methods address the lack of physical material representation and self-occlusion in the original framework. Ref-Gaussian introduced deferred surfel rendering to handle reflections [4464-ref-gaussian-deferred-surfel-rendering-with-split-sum-ibl.md], while Tlight methods were developed to compute self-shadowing transmittance for directional lighting [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md][4489-light-space-rasterization-for-t-light.md]. These techniques are used in high-fidelity 3D reconstruction, virtual reality, and relighting applications where baked lighting is insufficient.

name: Ref-Gaussian Deferred Surfel Rendering with Split-Sum IBL
head: Ref-Gaussian, Ref-Gaussian on iOS
body: Ref-Gaussian is a physically based rendering (PBR) method for novel view synthesis and relighting of reflective objects using 2D Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of blurred reflective details and inaccurate material reconstruction in standard Gaussian Splatting by decoupling geometry optimization from shading via a deferred rendering pipeline. Unlike sibling methods that use simplified shading functions or integrated diffuse lighting, Ref-Gaussian employs split-sum image-based lighting (IBL) with a BRDF LUT, allowing real-time relighting on mobile hardware while maintaining high-fidelity specular reflections. Inputs: A.ply file containing 2D Gaussian primitives with attributes: mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance (scales and orientation), opacity o, and material attributes: normal \mathbf{N}, roughness r, reflectance (specular strength) R, and albedo (base color) \mathbf{C}{base}. An HDR environment map (equirectangular or cubemap) representing the lighting. Outputs: A final pixel color C{final} for each screen pixel. The method relies on two parallel buffers aligned by splat index: 1. Splat Buffer: Contains geometric and opacity data (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, o). 2. Material Buffer: Contains per-splat PBR attributes (\mathbf{N}, r, R, \mathbf{C}{base}). Note: The Material Buffer must be sorted using the exact same indices as the Splat Buffer to prevent normal misalignment and rainbow noise artifacts. Before rendering, the environment map is processed into three textures using a pre-filtering kernel: 1. Prefiltered Environment Map: A mipmapped texture where each level corresponds to a specific roughness value, storing specular reflection data. 2. Irradiance Map: A pre-integrated diffuse lighting map. 3. BRDF LUT: A 2D lookup table storing the Fresnel-Schlick approximation terms fg.x and fg.y as a function of dot product (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{V}) and roughness. The rendering consists of a deferred shading pass: 1. Rasterization: Project 2D Gaussians to screen space. Sort splats for cache locality (e.g., using Morton codes). 2. G-Buffer Pass: For each splat, compute its contribution to the G-Buffer. This involves alpha-blending the material attributes (Normal, Roughness, Reflectance, Albedo) and depth into tile memory. 3. Shading Pass: For each pixel, retrieve the accumulated material attributes from the G-Buffer and compute the final color using the split-sum IBL formula: F0 = 0.04 \times (1 - R) + \mathbf{C}{base} \times R \text{specular} = \text{prefiltered}(\text{reflect}(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{N}), r) \times (F0 \cdot fg.x + fg.y) C{final} = (1 - R) \times \mathbf{C}{base} + \text{specular} Where: F0 is the base specular reflectivity. \mathbf{V} is the view direction. \mathbf{N} is the surface normal. r is the roughness. \text{reflect}(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{N}) is the reflection vector. \text{prefiltered}(\dots, r) samples the prefiltered environment map at the mip level corresponding to roughness r. fg.x, fg.y are values sampled from the BRDF LUT. \mathbf{C}{base} is used directly for the diffuse term; it is not multiplied by the irradiance map. Training occurs in two stages: 1. Initial Stage (18,000 steps): Per-Gaussian rendering to establish geometry. 2. Deferred Rendering Stage (40,000 steps): Reset all color and material attributes, retaining only geometry. Optimize material attributes (metallic, roughness, albedo) and environment map. Apply material-aware normal propagation for Gaussians with metallic \ge 0.02 and roughness \le 0.1. Periodically extract surface mesh (every 3,000 steps). Loss Function: L = Lc + \lambdan Ln + \lambda{smooth} L{smooth} Where: Lc = (1 - \lambda)L1 + \lambda L{D-SSIM} is the RGB reconstruction loss. Ln = 1 - \tilde{\mathbf{N}}^T \mathbf{N} is the normal consistency loss, aligning rendered normal \mathbf{N} (via alpha-blending) with surface normal \tilde{\mathbf{N}} (from depth map). L{smooth} = \|\nabla \mathbf{N}\| \exp(-\|\nabla C{gt}\|) is the edge-aware normal smoothness loss. Learning rate for material attributes (metallic, roughness, albedo): 0.005. Learning rate for environment map: 0.01. Balancing weight \lambda (RGB reconstruction): 0.2. Weight \lambdan (normal consistency): 0.05. Weight \lambda{smooth} (normal smoothness): 1.0. Initial roughness: 0.1. Initial metallic: Adopted from 3DGS-DR (exact value not specified). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrefgaussian(splats, envmap, camera): """ Renders a scene using Ref-Gaussian deferred surfel rendering with split-sum IBL. Args: splats: List of Gaussian primitives with attributes: pos: (3,) mean position cov: (3,3) covariance matrix opacity: float normal: (3,) surface normal roughness: float reflectance: float albedo: (3,) base color envmap: HDR environment map (equirectangular or cubemap) camera: Camera object with view matrix and projection matrix Returns: image: Rendered image (H, W, 3) """ # 1. Pre-compute IBL data (done once per environment map change) prefilteredenv = prefilterenvironmentmap(envmap) irradiancemap = computeirradiancemap(envmap) brdflut = computebrdflut() # 2. Rasterization and Sorting # Project splats to screen space and compute coverage screensplats = [] for s in splats: # Project mean and covariance to 2D # Compute 2D bounding box and coverage screensplats.append(projectsplat(s, camera)) # Sort splats for cache locality (e.g., Morton code) # IMPORTANT: Sort both geometry and material buffers with the same indices sortedindices = sortbymortoncode(screensplats) sortedsplats = [screensplats[i] for i in sortedindices] # 3. G-Buffer Pass (Deferred Shading Setup) # Initialize G-Buffer with zeros gbuffernormals = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) gbufferroughness = np.zeros((H, W)) gbufferreflectance = np.zeros((H, W)) gbufferalbedo = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) gbufferdepth = np.full((H, W), np.inf) for s in sortedsplats: # Rasterize the 2D Gaussian ellipse # For each pixel covered by the splat: # Compute alpha = opacity exp(-0.5 x^T Sigma^-1 x) # Alpha-blend material attributes into G-Buffer # Update depth if closer rasterizesplattogbuffer(s, gbuffernormals, gbufferroughness, gbufferreflectance, gbufferalbedo, gbufferdepth) # 4. Shading Pass image = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): if gbufferdepth[y, x] == np.inf: continue N = normalize(gbuffernormals[y, x]) r = gbufferroughness[y, x] R = gbufferreflectance[y, x] Cbase = gbufferalbedo[y, x] # View direction (approximate from camera and pixel position) V = computeviewdirection(camera, x, y) # Compute F0 F0 = 0.04 (1 - R) + Cbase R # Compute specular term using split-sum IBL # Reflect view direction around normal Rvec = reflect(V, N) # Sample prefiltered environment map based on roughness # The mip level corresponds to the roughness value envsample = sampleprefilteredenv(prefilteredenv, Rvec, r) # Sample BRDF LUT # Inputs: dot(N, V) and roughness costheta = np.dot(N, V) fg = samplebrdflut(brdflut, costheta, r) specular = envsample (F0 fg[0] + fg[1]) # Compute final color # Diffuse term uses basecolor directly, NOT multiplied by irradiance finalcolor = (1 - R) Cbase + specular image[y, x] = finalcolor return image def projectsplat(splat, camera): """ Projects a 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space. Returns screen-space representation with 2D covariance. """ # Transform mean to camera space poscam = camera.viewmatrix @ splat.pos # Transform covariance to camera space J = camera.jacobian(poscam) W = camera.worldtocameramatrix T = W @ J # Jacobian of projection cov2d = T @ splat.cov @ T.T # Add regularization to covariance determinant to prevent degenerate splats # (Standard 3DGS practice, often 0.3I added in screen space) # Note: For shadowing passes, this expansion might be skipped [4487-3d-gaussian-splatting-self-shadowing-t-light.md] cov2d[0,0] += 0.3 cov2d[1,1] += 0.3 # Project to screen posscreen = camera.projectionmatrix @ poscam posscreen /= posscreen[2] # Perspective divide return { 'pos': posscreen[:2], 'cov': cov2d[:2,:2], 'opacity': splat.opacity, 'normal': splat.normal, 'roughness': splat.roughness, 'reflectance': splat.reflectance, 'albedo': splat.albedo, 'depth': poscam[2] } def rasterizesplattogbuffer(splat, gnormals, groughness, greflectance, galbedo, gdepth): """ Rasterizes a single 2D Gaussian splat into the G-Buffer. Uses alpha blending for material attributes. """ # Get bounding box of the 2D Gaussian bbox = getboundingbox(splat['cov'], splat['pos']) for y in range(bbox.ymin, bbox.ymax): for x in range(bbox.xmin, bbox.xmax): # Compute 2D distance from center dx = x - splat['pos'][0] dy = y - splat['pos'][1] distsq = np.array([dx, dy]) @ np.linalg.inv(splat['cov']) @ np.array([dx, dy]) # Compute alpha alpha = splat['opacity'] np.exp(-0.5 distsq) if alpha < 0.001: continue # Update depth if splat['depth'] < gdepth[y, x]: # Blend material attributes # Simple alpha blending for normals might cause issues; # Ref-Gaussian uses alpha-blending to get rendered normal N # However, for deferred shading, we typically store the front-most or # accumulated attributes. The source implies alpha-blending for normal consistency loss # For G-Buffer, we store the accumulated material properties # Note: The exact blending order for normals in G-Buffer is critical. # Standard approach: blend with current G-Buffer values oldalpha = 1.0 - gdepth[y, x] # Approximation, usually stored separately # More robust: store accumulated alpha in G-Buffer # Here we assume a simple front-to-back blend for demonstration # Update depth gdepth[y, x] = splat['depth'] # Blend normals (normalize after blending) # This is a simplification; actual implementation may use weighted average gnormals[y, x] = (gnormals[y, x] (1 - alpha) + splat['normal'] alpha) gnormals[y, x] = normalize(gnormals[y, x]) # Blend other attributes groughness[y, x] = groughness[y, x] (1 - alpha) + splat['roughness'] alpha greflectance[y, x] = greflectance[y, x] (1 - alpha) + splat['reflectance'] alpha galbedo[y, x] = galbedo[y, x] (1 - alpha) + splat['albedo'] alpha def reflect(V, N): """ Computes the reflection vector R = V - 2(V.N)N """ return V - 2 np.dot(V, N) N def sampleprefilteredenv(prefilteredenv, Rvec, roughness): """ Samples the prefiltered environment map at the direction Rvec. The mip level is determined by the roughness. """ # Map roughness to mip level # Higher roughness -> higher mip level (more blurred) miplevel = int(roughness (nummips - 1)) miplevel = np.clip(miplevel, 0, nummips - 1) # Sample the cubemap or equirectangular map at the given mip level return prefilteredenv.sample(Rvec, miplevel) def samplebrdflut(brdflut, costheta, roughness): """ Samples the BRDF LUT. """ # The LUT is typically indexed by (costheta, roughness) # costheta = dot(N, V) return brdflut.sample(costheta, roughness) Normal Map Noise: If splats are sorted for cache locality (e.g., Morton code) but the Material Buffer is not sorted in parallel, normals become misaligned with positions, causing rainbow noise. Fix: Apply the same sort indices to the material buffer. Incorrect Diffuse Lighting: Do not multiply albedo by the irradiance map for diffuse color. Ref-Gaussian uses basecolor directly for diffuse. Only specular is computed from the environment map. Coordinate System Mismatch: If scene data is Z-up (e.g., Blender) but the viewer assumes Y-up, objects appear rotated 90 degrees. Fix: Apply a -90° rotation around the X-axis to the camera/view matrix and adjust environment map sampling directions. Stale Binary on iOS: If iOS build fails due to type errors (e.g., Float16 bitPattern type mismatch between arm64 and x8664 simulator), the device may run an old binary. Always check build success for the target platform before debugging logic. Geometric Collapse: Smooth surfaces are prone to geometric collapse. Material-aware normal propagation addresses this. Blurred Reflections: Per-Gaussian rendering causes reflective details to become noticeably more blurred. Deferred rendering is used to mitigate this. Time Complexity: The deferred shading pass is O(N) where N is the number of pixels, with constant-time texture lookups for IBL. The rasterization pass is O(G) where G is the number of Gaussians, with sorting taking O(G \log G) or O(G) with radix sort. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Splat Buffer, Material Buffer, G-Buffer, and IBL textures (prefiltered env map, irradiance map, BRDF LUT). On the Shiny Blender dataset, Ref-Gaussian achieves PSNR 30.33, SSIM 0.958, LPIPS 0.049. MAE 2.15, Normal SSIM 0.954, Normal LPIPS 0.0511, Envmap LPIPS 0.4431. Training time: 0.58 hours. FPS: 122 on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. The method supports real-time rendering on mobile hardware (iPhone) using Metal. Performance scales with the number of Gaussians and resolution, but the deferred pipeline ensures efficient shading regardless of scene complexity. Strengths: High-fidelity specular reflections, real-time relighting, accurate material reconstruction, efficient deferred shading pipeline. Limitations: Requires careful handling of coordinate systems and buffer synchronization. Per-Gaussian shading initialization can lead to blurred reflections if not deferred. Smooth surfaces may suffer from geometric collapse without material-aware normal propagation. Use for novel view synthesis of reflective objects where accurate material and lighting reconstruction is required. Use for real-time relighting applications on mobile devices. Do not use if simple diffuse lighting is sufficient, as the overhead of deferred shading and IBL pre-computation is unnecessary. Ref-Gaussian was introduced in the paper "Reflective Gaussian Splatting". It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) and incorporates physically based rendering (PBR) techniques. The method uses 2D Gaussian primitives for precise geometric representation, avoiding the conflict of 3D Gaussian volumetric radiance with the thin nature of surfaces. It replaces integrated diffuse lighting with spherical harmonics for better fitting capability. The deferred rendering approach was adopted to mitigate the blurring of reflective details observed in per-Gaussian shading. Implementation details for mobile devices (iOS/Metal) have been documented in unofficial sources, highlighting practical challenges such as buffer synchronization and coordinate system mismatches. Evaluated on Shiny Blender, Glossy Synthetic, and Ref-Real datasets. Experiments conducted on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. head: 光源视角自阴影 (T_light)
body: Calculates the self-shadowing transmittance T{light} for each Gaussian primitive along a directional sun direction, representing the 'front occlusion transmittance' to model self-shadowing effects in volume rendering. It differs from standard splatting by performing a separate rasterization pass from a virtual sun camera to accumulate occlusion, rather than relying on depth sorting from the main camera view. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Light Space Rasterization for Tlight by using a specific energy-weighted mean accumulation strategy and strict gradient handling during the light pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacity o, color \mathbf{c}), sun direction vector, sun camera parameters (position, orientation, FOV). Outputs: Per-Gaussian self-shadowing transmittance T{light} (stored in recordfronttau channel). Data Structures: Gaussian Buffer: Standard 3D Gaussian attributes. Light Pass Buffer: Contains the recordfronttau channel for each Gaussian, storing the accumulated front transmittance weighted by energy. Steps: 1. Sun Camera Setup: Construct a distant narrow FOV perspective camera to simulate a directional sun light source. The distance and FOV are chosen to ensure parallax error is less than 2% and to avoid modifying the EWA Jacobian. 2. Rasterization Pass: Perform a CUDA rasterization pass from the sun camera's perspective. Traverse Gaussians in depth order relative to the sun camera. For each Gaussian, compute its contribution to the accumulated front transmittance. Record the accumulated front transmittance \tau weighted by \tau \times \text{weight} (energy-weighted mean over the entire sun-facing footprint, not just a center point sample) into the recordfronttau channel. 3. Gradient Handling: Enable full continuous gradients by default. This includes gradients for \tau, weights, normalization, weak density backup transmittance, and projection position/scale/rotation. However, treat sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches as constants (no gradients) to prevent incorrect gradient propagation. 4. Covariance Handling: Do not expand the projection covariance by 0.3I during this light pass, and do not apply amplitude compensation. Keep the sampling expansion from the main camera pass as is. 5. Deeply Buried Gaussians: Handle deeply buried Gaussians (where early termination causes wsum=0) by explicitly mapping them to full shadow to prevent inversion artifacts. Parameters: Fallback Mode: Use the old 128^3 voxel cache path if the --tlightvoxel flag is passed. This is compatible with models trained before rasterization. The viewer's --tlight auto reads cfgargs to automatically match the mode. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ # 1. Setup Sun Camera # Create a distant narrow FOV perspective camera suncam = createperspectivecamera( position=suncamera.position, orientation=suncamera.orientation, fov=suncamera.fov, # Narrow FOV to minimize parallax error < 2% nearplane=suncamera.nearplane, farplane=suncamera.farplane) # 2. Project Gaussians to Sun Camera Space projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Project mean and covariance to sun camera space # Note: Do NOT expand covariance by 0.3I or apply amplitude compensation projmean = projectpoint(g.mean, suncam) projcov = projectcovariance(g.covariance, suncam) # Check if Gaussian is visible in sun camera view if isvisibleinfrustum(projmean, projcov, suncam): projectedgaussians.append({ 'id': g.id, 'projmean': projmean, 'projcov': projcov, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'weight': g.weight # Energy weight }) # 3. Sort Gaussians by depth (front-to-back) relative to sun camera projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x['projmean'].z) # 4. Rasterization Pass # Initialize transmittance buffer tlightbuffer = {g['id']: 1.0 for g in gaussians} # Initial transmittance = 1.0 (fully lit) for pg in projectedgaussians: # Compute 2D ellipse coverage in screen space coverage = computeellipsecoverage(pg['projmean'], pg['projcov']) if coverage == 0: continue # Compute alpha for this Gaussian in sun view # Note: Use the unexpanded covariance for accurate sampling alpha = computegaussianalpha(pg['projmean'], pg['projcov'], pg['opacity']) # Update transmittance: Tnew = Told (1 - alpha) # However, the method specifies recording accumulated front transmittance tau weighted by tau weight # This implies an accumulation of occlusion contribution # Get current transmittance for this Gaussian's ID currentt = tlightbuffer[pg['id']] # Compute weighted contribution # The note says: "record its accumulated front transmittance tau weighted by tau weight" # This is interpreted as updating the buffer with the occluded value newt = currentt (1 - alpha) # Store the weighted transmittance # The 'weight' here refers to the Gaussian's energy weight tlightbuffer[pg['id']] = newt pg['weight'] # Note: This might be an intermediate value # Actually, the final Tlight should be the accumulated transmittance # Let's refine: Tlight is the transmittance through the scene from the sun's perspective # So for each Gaussian, we accumulate occlusion. # The final Tlight for a Gaussian is the product of (1-alpha) for all Gaussians in front of it. # Re-evaluating based on "record its accumulated front transmittance tau weighted by tau weight" # This suggests the buffer stores the accumulated tau, and we multiply by weight for some reason? # Or perhaps the 'weight' is used to scale the contribution to the final Tlight? # Let's stick to the standard volume rendering accumulation for Tlight: # Reset buffer tlightbuffer = {g['id']: 1.0 for g in gaussians} for pg in projectedgaussians: alpha = computegaussianalpha(pg['projmean'], pg['projcov'], pg['opacity']) currentt = tlightbuffer[pg['id']] # Update transmittance newt = currentt (1 - alpha) # Handle deeply buried Gaussians if newt == 0: # Early termination or very small # Explicitly map to full shadow to prevent inversion artifacts tlightbuffer[pg['id']] = 0.0 else: tlightbuffer[pg['id']] = newt # The 'weight' multiplication might be for normalization or specific shading integration # The note says "record... into the recordfronttau channel" # So the final output is the accumulated transmittance. return tlightbuffer def computegaussianalpha(projmean, projcov, opacity): """ Compute alpha for a 2D Gaussian ellipse. """ # Compute 2D covariance matrix #... (standard EWA projection) # Compute alpha at center alpha = opacity exp(-0.5 projmean.x projcov.inv[0][0] projmean.x) # Simplified # Clamp alpha alpha = clamp(alpha, 0.0, 1.0) return alpha def isvisibleinfrustum(projmean, projcov, suncam): """ Check if Gaussian is within sun camera frustum. """ # Check if projmean is within near/far planes if projmean.z < suncam.nearplane or projmean.z > suncam.farplane: return False # Check if ellipse is within screen bounds #... (standard frustum culling) return True def projectpoint(point, camera): """ Project 3D point to 2D screen coordinates. """ #... (standard perspective projection) pass def projectcovariance(cov, camera): """ Project 3D covariance to 2D screen space. """ #... (standard EWA projection, without 0.3I expansion) pass def computeellipsecoverage(projmean, projcov): """ Compute the area of the 2D ellipse in screen space. """ #... (compute determinant of 2D covariance) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deeply Buried Gaussians: If early termination causes wsum=0, explicitly map to full shadow to prevent inversion artifacts. Gradient Propagation: Sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches must be treated as constants to prevent incorrect gradient propagation. name: Light Space Rasterization for T_light
head: Front Tau Rasterization, Light Space Shadow Rasterization, T_light Rasterization (Light Space)
body: Light Space Rasterization for T{light} computes the front-facing occlusion transmittance for each 3D Gaussian primitive along a directional sun direction. It solves the self-shadowing problem in differentiable Gaussian splatting by rasterizing Gaussians in a virtual light-space camera to determine which primitives are occluded by those in front. Unlike voxel-based fallback methods, this approach provides full continuous gradients and zero covariance expansion by default, enabling accurate relighting of volumetric scenes like clouds. It builds on Lighting, Shadowing & Relighting by providing the specific shading term T{light} required for physically based illumination. Inputs: 3D Gaussian primitives: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (or scales and orientation), opacity o, and color \mathbf{c}. Sun direction: a unit vector \mathbf{d}{sun} defining the light source. Light-space camera parameters: a distant narrow FOV perspective camera setup to approximate parallel rays. Outputs: T{light}: The front-facing occlusion transmittance for each Gaussian. Shadow mask: Binary or continuous shadow information per pixel/primitive. Gaussian Buffer: Contains \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, o, \mathbf{c} for all active Gaussians. Light-Space Projection Buffer: Stores projected 2D positions, covariances, and depths for Gaussians sorted by depth in light space. Tau Accumulation Buffer: Stores the accumulated front \tau (optical depth) weighted by \alpha \cdot T for each pixel during rasterization. 1. Light-Space Camera Setup: Construct a virtual perspective camera with a narrow field of view (FOV) placed at a large distance along the sun direction \mathbf{d}{sun}. This setup ensures parallax error is less than 2%, preserving the validity of the EWA (Elliptical Weighted Average) Jacobian used in standard splatting. 2. Projection: Project all 3D Gaussians into the light-space camera. Compute the 2D mean and covariance in screen space. Crucially, do not expand the projection covariance by 0.3I and do not apply amplitude compensation, as this pass is for shadowing, not final shading. 3. Sorting: Sort the projected Gaussians by their depth (z-coordinate) in light space, from front to back. This sorting is essential for correct front-to-back accumulation [Parent]. 4. Rasterization (CUDA Kernel): Iterate through the sorted Gaussians. For each Gaussian, rasterize its 2D ellipse onto the light-space image buffer. Use the recordfronttau channel to accumulate values. For each pixel covered by the Gaussian, update the accumulated front \tau weighted by \alpha \cdot T. This represents an energy-weighted mean over the entire sun-facing footprint, not just a center-point sample. 5. Transmittance Calculation: Compute T{light} for each Gaussian based on the accumulated \tau from the rasterization pass. T{light} represents the fraction of light reaching the Gaussian from the sun direction. 6. Gradient Handling: Enable full continuous gradients for \tau, weights, normalization, weak density backup transmittance, and projected position/scale/rotation. Treat sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches as constants to prevent incorrect gradient propagation. 7. Fallback Handling: Explicitly map deeply buried Gaussians (those resulting in early termination with wsum=0) to full shadow (T{light}=0) to prevent inversion artifacts. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightspacerasterization(gaussians, sundirection): # 1. Setup Light-Space Camera # Create a perspective camera at a large distance along sundirection # with narrow FOV to approximate parallel rays. lightcam = PerspectiveCamera( position=sundirection LARGEDISTANCE, target=Vector3(0, 0, 0), fov=NEARFOV, resolution=IMAGERESOLUTION) # 2. Project Gaussians projectedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Project mean and covariance to light space mu2d, sigma2d = projectgaussian(g, lightcam) # CRITICAL: Do NOT expand covariance by 0.3I # CRITICAL: Do NOT apply amplitude compensation projectedgaussians.append({ 'mu': mu2d, 'sigma': sigma2d, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'depth': g.depthinlightspace, 'originalindex': g.index }) # 3. Sort by depth (front-to-back) projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda x: x['depth']) # 4. Rasterize and Accumulate Tau # Initialize tau buffer to 0 taubuffer = ZeroBuffer(IMAGEWIDTH, IMAGEHEIGHT) # Initialize Tlight for each Gaussian tlightvalues = [1.0] len(gaussians) for pg in projectedgaussians: # Rasterize the 2D ellipse coveredpixels = getcoveredpixels(pg['mu'], pg['sigma']) for pixel in coveredpixels: # Calculate alpha for this pixel alpha = computegaussianalpha(pg['mu'], pg['sigma'], pixel) # Update accumulated front tau weighted by alpha T # Note: T is initially 1.0 for the first occluder currenttau = taubuffer[pixel] taubuffer[pixel] += alpha currenttau # Store the tau value before this gaussian for later Tlight calculation # This is an approximation; precise implementation requires # storing the tau value before the current gaussian's contribution # for each gaussian covering the pixel. # For simplicity, we assume the buffer tracks the cumulative tau # and we can derive Tlight from the final buffer state relative to depth. pass # 5. Compute Tlight for each Gaussian # Tlight is the transmittance reaching the Gaussian. # This is exp(-accumulatedtaufromfronttothisgaussian) for pg in projectedgaussians: # Retrieve the accumulated tau from pixels covered by this gaussian # Average or sum appropriately to get a representative tau for the gaussian avgtau = computeaveragetauforgaussian(pg, taubuffer) # Handle deeply buried Gaussians (wsum=0 case) if avgtau is None or avgtau == 0: tlightvalues[pg['originalindex']] = 0.0 # Full shadow else: tlightvalues[pg['originalindex']] = exp(-avgtau) return tlightvalues Parallax Error Threshold: < 2%. Covariance Expansion: 0 (disabled). Amplitude Compensation: Disabled. Gradient Mode: Full continuous gradients enabled by default. Deeply Buried Gaussians: Gaussians that are fully occluded (early termination, wsum=0) must be explicitly mapped to full shadow (T{light}=0) to avoid inversion artifacts. Gradient Propagation: Sun camera framing, sorting, coverage, and threshold branches must be treated as constants during backpropagation to prevent incorrect gradients. Covariance Expansion: Applying the standard 0.3I expansion or amplitude compensation in this pass will corrupt the shadow calculation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot A), where N is the number of Gaussians and A is the average number of pixels covered by each Gaussian's projection. Sorting is O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: O(N + W \cdot H), where W \cdot H is the light-space image resolution. Requires buffers for projected Gaussians and the tau accumulation buffer. Performance: Provides full continuous gradients and zero expansion by default, offering higher accuracy than voxel-based fallbacks without requiring specific training parameters. Strengths: Accurate self-shadowing for volumetric scenes; differentiable; compatible with standard EWA splatting. Limitations: Requires an additional rasterization pass; sensitive to sun direction distribution in training data. When to Use: When physically based relighting and self-shadowing are required for Gaussian splatting models, especially for volumetric data like clouds. When Not to Use: For simple opaque scenes where self-shadowing is negligible; when computational resources are extremely limited and voxel fallback is acceptable. This method was introduced in the context of 4D Gaussian Splatting for Volume Clouds, specifically for handling dynamic lighting and self-shadowing. It addresses the limitation of pure emission-based SH (Spherical Harmonics) reconstruction, which cannot support relighting. The method is unique to held-out sun relighting scenarios and relies on uniform directional coverage in the training dataset to ensure healthy geometric shadow gradients. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3DGS Radiance Caching
head: GSCache Radiance Caching, Radiance caching with 3DGS
body: 3DGS Radiance Caching is a real-time variance reduction technique for volume path tracing that uses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to store and query cached radiance values. It reduces noise by probabilistically accepting cached samples based on throughput luminance and a scaling parameter. The method optimizes exponentially subsampled Gaussians from noisy path samples to achieve real-time frame rates. Unlike neural radiance caching, which requires large memory footprints, this method leverages the compact representation of 3DGS to store attenuated radiance at multiple path lengths, offering a significantly smaller memory footprint. The method integrates a caching mechanism into the path tracing loop, using 3DGS primitives to approximate the radiance field. It operates by querying a cache of radiance samples, accepting or rejecting them based on a probability derived from the current path's throughput, and updating state variables to maintain expectations. Inputs: Current path throughput vector L (radiance). Pixel coordinates (u, v). Cache state: cachelevels, betas, radiancesamples. Configuration parameter samplefactorc. Outputs: Updated throughput L. Boolean flag cachehit indicating if a cached value was used. Updated cache state (betas, potentially radiancesamples). The implementation uses specific structures to manage the cache and query state. gscachesample: Records ground truth radiance samples. u: int, pixel x-coordinate. v: int, pixel y-coordinate. scatterindex: int, index into the Gaussian splat list or cache level. L: gscachevec3f, the radiance vector. gscachequery: Used to query the cache with current path state. u: int, pixel x-coordinate. v: int, pixel y-coordinate. scatterindex: int, index into the Gaussian splat list or cache level. rand01: float, a random number in [0, 1] for probabilistic acceptance. L: gscachevec3f, current incoming radiance/throughput. throughput: gscachevec3f, current path throughput vector. gscachequeryresult: Returned by the cache query. cachehit: bool, true if a cache hit occurred and was accepted. throughput: gscachevec3f, the throughput to use for the next path segment. L: gscachevec3f, the radiance value to use (either cached or original). gscachedevicecontext: Manages the cache state on the device. nlevels: int, number of cache levels (max 16). height: sizet, image height. width: sizet, image width. samplefactorc: float, scaling factor for acceptance probability. cachelevels[MAXNUMCACHELEVELS]: Array of pointers to gscachevec3f arrays, storing cached radiance values. radiancesamples[MAXNUMCACHELEVELS]: Array of pointers to gscachevec3f arrays, storing raw samples. betas: float array, per-pixel beta values for each cache level, used for importance weighting. Constants: MAXNUMCACHELEVELS: 16. The caching logic is applied during the path tracing loop, typically after computing the contribution of a scattering event or at the end of a path segment. The following pseudocode implements the query and state update logic. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryradiancecache(u, v, scatterindex, L, throughput, rand01, samplefactorc, cachelevels, betas, width): # 1. Compute luminance of incoming throughput vector L luminance = 0.212671 L.x + 0.715160 L.y + 0.072169 L.z # 2. Calculate acceptance probability q q = max(0.0, min(1.0, samplefactorc luminance)) # 3. Calculate rejection probability p p = 1.0 - q result = {"cachehit": False, "L": L, "throughput": throughput} # 4. Conditional caching logic if q < 0.9: idx = v width + u cachedL = cachelevels[scatterindex][idx] beta = betas[idx] # 5. Probabilistic acceptance if rand01 < p: result["cachehit"] = True result["L"] = cachedL / beta result["throughput"] = throughput else: # 6. Rejection: update beta and scale throughput betas[idx] = beta q result["throughput"] = throughput / q result["L"] = L else: # 7. Skip caching for high luminance result["cachehit"] = False result["L"] = L result["throughput"] = throughput return result samplefactorc: A float parameter that scales the luminance to determine the acceptance probability q. Typical values are not explicitly given, but the threshold q < 0.9 implies it controls the aggressiveness of caching. MAXNUMCACHELEVELS: 16. nlevels: Number of active cache levels, default 3 in the config. Division by Zero: The code divides L{cached} by \beta. If \beta is zero, this results in infinity. The implementation relies on the update rule \beta \cdot q and the condition q < 0.9 to keep \beta non-zero if initialized correctly. Bias: The method introduces bias with no guaranteed error bounds. High Throughput Rejection: If q is close to 1.0 (high luminance), p is close to 0, making cache hits unlikely unless rand01 is extremely small. The threshold q < 0.9 prevents caching in these high-variance scenarios. Transfer Function Changes: The cache requires re-initialization when transfer functions change, as it stores attenuated radiance specific to the current transfer function. Zero-Opacity Regions: The caching mechanism may not reconstruct zero-opacity regions effectively if not handled by the underlying 3DGS representation. Write-Back Mechanism: The exact logic for writing to cachelevels or radiancesamples is not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves real-time frame rates on scientific datasets at 720p, with total times ranging from 38ms to 186ms. Memory Footprint: 28 MB for the cache, compared to 272 MB for neural radiance caching. Scalability: The method is designed for real-time rendering, leveraging the efficiency of 3DGS rasterization. It does not explicitly address scaling to very large scenes without additional techniques like distributed training, which is a separate extension. Strengths: Real-time performance, low memory footprint, variance reduction for path-traced volume rendering. Limitations: Introduces bias, requires re-initialization for transfer function changes, no guaranteed error bounds, potential issues with zero-opacity regions. 3DGS Radiance Caching, also known as GSCache, was introduced by David Bauer, Qi Wu, Hamid Gadirov, and Kwan-Liu Ma in the paper "GSCache: Real-Time Radiance Caching for Volume Path Tracing using 3D Gaussian Splatting," accepted at IEEE VIS 2025. The work builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting for volume rendering, adapting it to serve as a compact, differentiable radiance cache for path tracing. It addresses the high variance and computational cost of path-traced volume rendering by leveraging the spatial coherence and compact representation of 3DGS primitives. name: Ray-Splat Intersection Algorithms
body: Ray-splat intersection algorithms evaluate the contribution of 3D Gaussians by intersecting viewing rays with the Gaussian primitives directly, rather than projecting them onto the image plane. This family provides exact or analytically derived intersections, enabling correct handling of semi-transparency and degenerate splats. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which approximates the projection as an affine 2D Gaussian, these methods compute the Gaussian's maximum contribution along each ray. All methods in this family share the goal of computing the Gaussian's contribution E along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. The core mathematical operation is finding the point ti along the ray where the Gaussian's density is maximized, often referred to as the "ray-Gaussian intersection". This point is analytically derived from the Gaussian's covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, center \mathbf{p}, and the ray direction \mathbf{v}: ti = \frac{\mathbf{p}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{v}} The contribution is then modeled as a 1D Gaussian function along the ray: \rho(t) = \exp\left(-ki (t - ti)^2\right) where ki is a curvature term derived from the covariance and ray direction. This reduces the 3D influence to a 1D function, allowing for exact integration or sampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def raygaussianintersection(p: np.ndarray, Sigma: np.ndarray, v: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Computes the intersection point ti and curvature ki for a 3D Gaussian along a ray. p: Gaussian center (3,) Sigma: 3x3 covariance matrix v: Ray direction (3,) Returns: ti, ki """ v = v / np.linalg.norm(v) # Ensure unit direction vector as per standard formulation Sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) numerator = p.T @ Sigmainv @ v denominator = v.T @ Sigmainv @ v if denominator < 1e-9: return 0.0, 0.0 ti = numerator / denominator ki = v.T @ Sigmainv @ v return ti, ki This method provides a differentiable, matrix-inversion-free evaluation of 3D Gaussian densities along per-pixel viewing rays [4556-perspective-correct-3d-gaussian-splatting-via-pl-cker-coordi.md]. It sets itself apart by extending Weyrich et al.'s 2D splatting techniques to 3D using Plücker coordinates, ensuring numerical stability even for degenerate splats where principal axes vanish [4556-perspective-correct-3d-gaussian-splatting-via-pl-cker-coordi.md]. It eliminates the need for special handling of degenerate cases and avoids the numerical instabilities associated with matrix inversions in alternative rasterization-based approaches [4556-perspective-correct-3d-gaussian-splatting-via-pl-cker-coordi.md]. Choose this when perspective correctness is critical and degenerate Gaussians are common [4556-perspective-correct-3d-gaussian-splatting-via-pl-cker-coordi.md]. GOF replaces standard 2D projection rasterization with ray-tracing-based volume rendering [5992-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof.md]. It analytically evaluates the maximum Gaussian contribution along each pixel ray, providing accurate depth estimation and facilitating the derivation of level-set surfaces from accumulated opacity [5992-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof.md]. Unlike 3DGS, it does not rely on 2D projection integrals [5992-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof.md]. Choose this when accurate depth and normal extraction are required alongside color rendering [5992-gaussian-opacity-fields-gof.md]. This method evaluates 3D Gaussian splats using hardware-accelerated ray tracing instead of rasterization [8101-3d-gaussian-ray-tracing.md]. It solves the problem of linear scaling in dense scenes by using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to traverse only Gaussians that intersect the viewing ray, enabling logarithmic complexity relative to the number of splats [8101-3d-gaussian-ray-tracing.md]. Unlike rasterization-based splatting which evaluates all Gaussians overlapping a tile, 3DGRT explicitly handles semi-transparency by accumulating transmittance through all intersected Gaussians, avoiding the depth-sorting artifacts inherent in tile-based rasterization [8101-3d-gaussian-ray-tracing.md]. Choose this for large-scale scenes or when hardware ray tracing is available [8101-3d-gaussian-ray-tracing.md]. QuadBox is a Gaussian-tile intersection method that uses four axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) to tightly encapsulate projected 2D Gaussians [9231-quadbox.md]. It sets itself apart by replacing the single conservative AABB with four symmetrically positioned, adaptively stretched sub-boxes that better fit the anisotropic shape of the ellipse [9231-quadbox.md]. This tight fit suppresses empty tile coverage along the minor axis, while the accompanying QPass algorithm ensures deterministic, cache-friendly tile traversal with minimal per-tile overhead [9231-quadbox.md]. Choose this when rasterization performance is prioritized but over-approximation of anisotropic splats is a bottleneck [9231-quadbox.md]. This is the fundamental geometric operation shared by ray-based methods. It involves projecting the 3D Gaussian's covariance and center onto the camera ray to convert the 3D influence into a 1D Gaussian function along that specific ray. This allows for the analytical computation of the intersection point ti and the subsequent evaluation of the Gaussian's density along the ray. The analytical derivation of the intersection point ti is based on finding the extremum of the Gaussian function along a line, a technique detailed in "Approximate Differentiable Rendering with Algebraic Surfaces". The specific formulation \rho(t) = \exp(-ki(t-ti)^2) is used to map 3D Gaussian influence to 1D ray space. name: Perspective-Correct 3D Gaussian Splatting via Plücker Coordinates
head: Hybrid 3D Gaussian Splatting intersection, Inversion-free splat evaluation, Matrix inversion-free ray-splat intersection, Perspective-Correct 3D Gaussian Splat Evaluation, Perspective-Correct Ray-Splat Intersection, Perspective-accurate 3D Gaussian splat evaluation, Plücker coordinate ray-splat intersection
body: This method provides a differentiable, matrix-inversion-free approach to evaluating 3D Gaussian splats along per-pixel viewing rays, ensuring numerical stability and perspective-correct rendering. Unlike the affine approximation in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which causes perspective distortion, or ray-tracing frameworks which are too slow, this method extends Weyrich et al.'s optimization to non-degenerate 3D Gaussians using Plücker coordinates. It eliminates the need for special handling of degenerate splats and avoids the catastrophic failures associated with matrix inversions during gradient descent optimization. The method computes the contribution of a 3D Gaussian along a viewing ray by transforming the ray into the Gaussian's local normalized splat space and calculating the distance to the origin using dual Plücker coordinates. This avoids matrix inversion entirely. Inputs: Gaussian parameters: center \mathbf{p}, orientation quaternion (tu, tv, tw), scale (su, sv, sw), opacity \alpha. Camera matrices: Model-view matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, Projection matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, Viewport transform V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}. Pixel coordinates: (xs, ys) in screen space. Hyperparameter: \tau\alpha (minimum alpha value for fragment inclusion). Outputs: Screen-space bounding box [b1, t1] \times [b2, t2] \times [b3, t3]. Gaussian value \rho(x)^2 at the point of maximum contribution along the ray. Data Structures: Homogeneous plane vector: \mathbf{p} = (a, b, c, d)^\top representing plane equation ax+by+cz+d=0. Dual Plücker coordinates: \mathcal{L}s^ = (\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{m}) where \mathbf{d} is direction and \mathbf{m} is moment. Steps: 1. Compute Transformation Matrix T': Construct the transformation T' \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} from normalized splat space (where the Gaussian is a unit sphere) to screen space. This combines the splat's local-to-world transformation (derived from \mathbf{p}, orientation, and scale), the model-view matrix M, the projection matrix P, and the viewport transform V. T' = V P M T{\text{splat}} where T{\text{splat}} maps the unit sphere to the Gaussian's ellipsoid in world space. 2. Compute Screen-Space Bounding Box: Calculate the tight 3D axis-aligned bounding box [bi, ti] for i \in \{1, 2, 3\} (corresponding to x, y, z) using the rows of T'. Let T'i be the i-th row of T'. Define intermediate vectors \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} based on T': \mathbf{u} = T'1 \odot T'2 \odot T'3 \mathbf{v} = T'1 \odot T'2 \odot T'3 \quad \text{(Note: Source uses specific component-wise products derived from Weyrich et al. optimization)} Correction based on Source formulas (4)-(9): The bounding box limits are computed as: bi = \min(T'i \cdot \mathbf{c}{\text{min}}), \quad ti = \max(T'i \cdot \mathbf{c}{\text{max}}) Specifically, using the optimization from Weyrich et al. extended to 3D: Let \mathbf{r}i be the i-th row of T'. bi = \min{\mathbf{x} \in [-1,1]^3} \mathbf{r}i \cdot \mathbf{x}, \quad ti = \max{\mathbf{x} \in [-1,1]^3} \mathbf{r}i \cdot \mathbf{x} This simplifies to: bi = -\sum{j=1}^4 |T'{ij}| \quad \text{(if offset is included in homogeneous coord)} Precise Source Formulation: The source defines the bounding box using T'i (the i-th row of T'), component-wise multiplication \odot, and dot product \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle. bi = \langle T'i, \mathbf{e}{\text{min}} \rangle, \quad ti = \langle T'i, \mathbf{e}{\text{max}} \rangle Where \mathbf{e}{\text{min}} and \mathbf{e}{\text{max}} are vectors of \pm 1 determined by the signs of the components of T'i excluding the homogeneous term, adjusted for the specific Weyrich optimization. The source states: "with T'i the i-th row of T', \odot denoting component-wise multiplication, and the dot product denoted by \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle." Additionally, compute an individual cutoff value for the bounding box if opacity \alpha < 1, using \tau\alpha. 3. Define Viewing Ray as Planes: Represent the viewing ray passing through pixel (xs, ys) as two perpendicular planes in screen space: \pix = (1, 0, 0, -xs)^\top \piy = (0, 1, 0, -ys)^\top These are homogeneous plane vectors where \mathbf{p}^\top \mathbf{x} = 0 defines the plane. 4. Transform Planes to Splat Space: Transform \pix and \piy into the normalized splat space using the inverse-transposed mapping of the combined transformation. Let T = VPMT{\text{splat}} be the full transformation from splat space to screen space. The planes transform via (T)^{-\top}. \pi{sx} = (T)^{-\top} \pix \pi{sy} = (T)^{-\top} \piy This step avoids matrix inversion by reusing quantities from the bounding box calculation or using the adjugate/determinant if explicit inversion is avoided, but the source emphasizes using the inverse-transposed mapping to sidestep inversion. Note: In implementation, if T is known, one can compute the inverse-transpose. The source claims this avoids the inversion issues of other methods. 5. Compute Dual Plücker Coordinates: The viewing ray in splat space is the intersection of \pi{sx} and \pi{sy}. Let \pi{sx} = (a1, a2, a3, a0)^\top and \pi{sy} = (b1, b2, b3, b0)^\top. Compute the dual Plücker coordinates \mathcal{L}s^ = (\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{m}): \mathbf{d} = \pi{sx} \times \pi{sy} \quad \text{(Cross product of the linear parts)} More precisely, using the coefficients: \mathbf{d} = (a2 b3 - a3 b2, \ a3 b1 - a1 b3, \ a1 b2 - a2 b1)^\top \mathbf{m} = (a0 b1 - a1 b0, \ a0 b2 - a2 b0, \ a0 b3 - a3 b0)^\top The dual Plücker coordinates \mathcal{L}s^ are numerically equivalent to primal Plücker coordinates \mathcal{L}s up to a scaling factor \lambda. 6. Compute Gaussian Value \rho(x)^2: Calculate the squared distance from the ray to the origin in splat space, which corresponds to the exponent term in the Gaussian evaluation: \rho(x)^2 = \frac{\|\mathbf{m}\|^2}{\|\mathbf{d}\|^2} Here, \|\mathbf{m}\|^2 = \mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{m} and \|\mathbf{d}\|^2 = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}. Edge Case: If \|\mathbf{d}\|^2 \approx 0, the ray misses the splat (or is parallel to the normal in a degenerate way), and the contribution is zero. 7. Final Contribution: The value \rho(x)^2 is used in the Gaussian function \exp(-\rho(x)^2) (or similar scaling depending on the specific Gaussian definition in the parent method) to determine the splat's contribution at the point of maximum density along the ray. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def perspectivecorrectgaussiansplat(psplatcenter, quat, scale, opacity, M, P, V, xs, ys, taualpha): """ Computes the perspective-correct evaluation of a 3D Gaussian splat. Args: psplatcenter: (3,) Gaussian center in world space. quat: (4,) Quaternion (w, x, y, z) for orientation. scale: (3,) Scale factors (su, sv, sw). opacity: Scalar opacity alpha. M: (4,4) Model-view matrix. P: (4,4) Projection matrix. V: (4,4) Viewport transform. xs: Screen x coordinate. ys: Screen y coordinate. taualpha: Hyperparameter for cutoff. Returns: boundingbox: Tuple of ((b1, t1), (b2, t2), (b3, t3)) rhosq: Scalar squared distance value for Gaussian evaluation. """ # 1. Construct Tsplat: Normalized Splat Space -> World Space # Rotation matrix from quaternion w, x, y, z = quat R = np.array([ [1 - 2(y2 + z2), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy)], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(x2 + z2), 2(yz - wx)], [2(xz - wy), 2(yz + wx), 1 - 2(x2 + y2)] ]) S = np.diag(scale) Tsplatlocal = np.eye(4) Tsplatlocal[:3,:3] = R @ S Tsplatlocal[:3, 3] = psplatcenter # 2. Construct T': Normalized Splat Space -> Screen Space # T' = V P M Tsplatlocal Tprime = V @ P @ M @ Tsplatlocal # 3. Compute Bounding Box [b1, t1] x [b2, t2] x [b3, t3] # Using Weyrich et al. optimization extended to 3D # Tprimei is the i-th row of Tprime # The source defines bi and ti using Tprimei, component-wise multiplication, and dot product. # For a unit sphere in normalized space mapped by Tprime, the bounds are determined by the # extreme values of the linear transformation. # Extract rows r1 = Tprime[0,:] r2 = Tprime[1,:] r3 = Tprime[2,:] # The source formulas (4)-(9) are complex. A standard implementation of Weyrich's bound # for a transformed unit sphere involves the singular values or the row norms. # However, the source explicitly mentions: "with T'i the i-th row of T', # ⊙ denoting component-wise multiplication, and the dot product denoted by <.,.>" # And "closed-form solution without matrix inversion". # Approximation of the bounding box calculation based on the description: # The bounds are min/max of ri. x for x in [-1, 1]^3. # min(r. x) = - sum(|rj|) for j=0..2 (assuming homogeneous coord handles offset) # Actually, for homogeneous coords, the bounding box in screen space is derived from # the projection of the unit sphere. # Let's implement the standard "tight AABB of transformed sphere" which matches the # "closed-form" description: def getbounds(row): # row is (4,) # The bounds are determined by the linear part and the offset. # For a unit sphere, the extent in direction of row is ||linearpart||. # But we need min and max. linear = row[:3] offset = row[3] norm = np.linalg.norm(linear) return offset - norm, offset + norm b1, t1 = getbounds(r1) b2, t2 = getbounds(r2) b3, t3 = getbounds(r3) boundingbox = ((b1, t1), (b2, t2), (b3, t3)) # 4. Define Viewing Ray Planes in Screen Space pix = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, -xs]) piy = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0, -ys]) # 5. Transform Planes to Splat Space # Planes transform by (T')^(-T) # To avoid explicit inversion, we can use the adjugate if needed, but numpy.linalg.inv is # acceptable for the transformation matrix T' itself as it is computed once per splat. # The source emphasizes avoiding inversion of the Gaussian covariance or similar # per-pixel operations. T' is per-splat. TprimeinvT = np.linalg.inv(Tprime).T pisx = TprimeinvT @ pix pisy = TprimeinvT @ piy # 6. Compute Dual Plücker Coordinates # pisx = (a1, a2, a3, a0) # pisy = (b1, b2, b3, b0) a = pisx[:3] a0 = pisx[3] b = pisy[:3] b0 = pisy[3] # Direction d = a x b d = np.cross(a, b) # Moment m = a0 b - b0 a m = a0 b - b0 a # 7. Compute rho(x)^2 dnormsq = np.dot(d, d) mnormsq = np.dot(m, m) if dnormsq < 1e-9: # Ray misses splat or is degenerate rhosq = np.inf else: rhosq = mnormsq / dnormsq return boundingbox, rhosq Time Complexity: Reduced setup costs per Gaussian compared to 3DGS, but slightly higher costs per pixel due to Plücker coordinate calculations. The operations are exclusively additions, multiplications, and one division, making them fast and trivial to differentiate. Memory Complexity: No additional large data structures required beyond standard Gaussian attributes. Performance: Achieves up to 2× higher frame rates and 2× faster optimization compared to traditional 3DGS on common benchmarks. Strengths: Numerically stable for degenerate splats (vanishing axes); perspective-correct rendering; no matrix inversion required for evaluation; compatible with rasterization pipelines for real-time performance. Limitations: Slightly higher per-pixel cost than affine 3DGS; requires careful handling of the vanishing denominator case (ray miss). When to use: When perspective accuracy is critical (e.g., close-up views) and numerical stability during optimization is required, especially if degenerate Gaussians are expected. This method was introduced by the authors of "Efficient Perspective-Correct 3D Gaussian Splatting Using Hybrid Transparency". It extends the perspectively correct approach of Weyrich et al. [WHA07] and Sigg et al. [SWBG06], which were originally designed for 2D Gaussian splats, to non-degenerate 3D Gaussians. Prior methods like 3DGS [KKLD23] used affine approximations that caused perspective distortion, while ray-tracing approaches [MLMP04] were too slow, and other rasterization attempts suffered from numerical instability due to matrix inversions.
