name: Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), Volume Splatting
body: Gaussian Splatting Volume Rendering is a differentiable rendering technique that synthesizes images by projecting 3D Gaussian kernels onto the image plane (splatting) and alpha-compositing them along viewing rays using a tile-based rasterization strategy. Unlike traditional triangle-based renderers or NeRFs, it uses explicit Gaussian probability distributions as primitives, enabling real-time performance and high-quality novel view synthesis. It sets itself apart from siblings like Volume Encoding Gaussians by rasterizing Gaussians volumetrically to avoid the computational overhead of iterative ray marching, and from BRDF and Relighting Extensions by typically using an emission-absorption model that bakes lighting into spherical harmonics, limiting direct relighting capabilities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M stored in a PLY file or in-memory structure, and camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Output: A 2D image (RGB) and optionally depth or other auxiliary channels. Data Structures: The core primitive is the GaussianSplat struct. While the parent article defines the geometric covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, the rendering implementation stores reparameterized attributes for optimization stability: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct GaussianSplat: centroid: vec3 # World-space position (x, y, z) opacity: float # Scalar opacity (0.0 to 1.0) sphericalharmonics: array[float, 48] # 16 coefficients 3 RGB channels scale: array[float, 3] # Log-space scale factors (log(sx), log(sy), log(sz)) rotation: array[float, 4] # Quaternion (w, x, y, z) Number of Gaussians: Typically 200,000–500,000 for complex scenes. Steps: 1. Load Scene: Parse the PLY file into an array of GaussianSplat objects. 2. Project Gaussians: For each Gaussian i, transform the centroid \mathbf{p}i to camera space. Compute the projected 2D covariance \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projection and the rotation part W of the extrinsic matrix: \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i = J W \mathbf{\Sigma}i W^T J^T. Note: \mathbf{\Sigma}i is reconstructed from the stored scale and rotation: \mathbf{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^\top \mathbf{R}i^\top, where \mathbf{S}i = \text{diag}(\exp(\text{scale}i)) and \mathbf{R}i is derived from the quaternion. 3. Rasterize (Splat): Project the 2D Gaussian onto the image plane. Use a tile-based rasterization strategy to parallelize this step. Determine the bounding quad for each Gaussian in screen space. 4. Sort: Sort the Gaussians intersecting each pixel (or tile) by depth (z-coordinate in camera space). 5. Compute Color: For each Gaussian i and pixel p, compute the view-dependent color ci using spherical harmonics (SH): \text{rgb} = \text{vec3}(0.5) \text{for } k \in 0 \dots 15: \quad \text{rgb} += \text{sh\coefficients}[k] \times \text{sh\basis}(k, \mathbf{d}) \text{rgb} = \text{clamp}(\text{rgb}, 0.0, 1.0) where \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction from the camera to the centroid. Note: Some volumetric variants use isotropic volumes with base colors instead of SH to avoid view-dependent shifts, but standard 3DGS uses SH. 6. Alpha Composite: Compute the final intensity If at pixel p by alpha-compositing the sorted Gaussians: If \approx \sum{i=1}^N ci \tilde{\sigma}i \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \left(1 - \tilde{\sigma}j \tilde{\mathcal{G}}j(\mathbf{p})\right) where: N is the number of Gaussians intersecting the ray. ci is the color of Gaussian i. \tilde{\sigma}i is the opacity of Gaussian i. \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D Gaussian value at pixel p: \tilde{\mathcal{G}}i(\mathbf{p}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{\hat{\mu}}i)^T \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{\hat{\mu}}i)\right) where \mathbf{\hat{\mu}}i is the projected 2D centroid. The product term represents the transmittance from previous Gaussians j < i. Parameters: SHCOUNT: 16 (number of SH coefficients per channel). SHCHANNELCOUNT: 3 (RGB). SHFLOATCOUNT: 48 (total coefficients). smokedensityfactor: 600 (used in specific volumetric implementations for density scaling). raytracingstepsizefactor: 0.5 (used in hybrid ray-tracing extensions for step size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: High-frequency content causes aliasing artifacts. 3DGS uses a dilation-based filter to reduce these, but it may fail with varying focal lengths or camera distances. MIP-Splatting introduces 2D/3D Gaussian filters for robustness. Covariance Validity: Directly updating the entries of \mathbf{\Sigma} during training does not guarantee it remains positive semi-definite (PSD). Using scale and rotation parameters ensures the reconstructed \mathbf{\Sigma} is always a valid covariance matrix. Color Dimness: If using isotropic volume rendering without SH, scenes may appear dimmer and less vibrant because view-dependent color shifts are lost. Renders surface normals by treating them as an extra attribute in an external channel, modifying the Gaussian's internal attribute representation rather than relying on external gradient supervision. Time Complexity: O(M \log M) for sorting Gaussians, where M is the number of Gaussians. Rasterization is O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of splats per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(M), storing centroid, opacity, SH coefficients, scale, and rotation per Gaussian. Memory demands are significant (200k–500k Gaussians) compared to NeRFs. Performance: Demonstrates up to 100x speedups in interactive applications compared to traditional ray marching. Achieves real-time performance through explicit storage and rasterization. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high visual quality, explicit scene representation. Limitations: High memory usage, limited relighting capabilities due to emission-absorption model baking lighting into SH coefficients, aliasing artifacts without filtering. Originating from radiance field representations in 2023, 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced as a method for 3D reconstruction from posed images using Gaussian splats instead of triangles. Extensions to volumetric rendering by 2025 achieved real-time performance by rasterizing Gaussians volumetrically. It is widely used in novel view synthesis, avatar creation, and surface reconstruction. name: Surface Normal Rendering via External Channel
head: External Channel Normal Rendering, PyTorch3D Normal Rendering for Gaussians
body: This method renders surface normals for 3D Gaussian Splatting by treating normals as an extra attribute in an external channel, since Gaussian ellipsoids do not natively contain surface normal information. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly modifying the Gaussian's internal attribute representation rather than relying on external gradient supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids derived from meshes (e.g., Stanford 3D Scanning Repository models like Bunny, Dragon, Armadillo). An additional attribute ni (the surface normal vector) is associated with each Gaussian. Output: A rendered image containing surface normal vectors encoded as RGB values. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. ni \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface normal vector (unit length). ci \in \mathbb{R}^3: Base color (RGB). \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix defining the ellipsoid shape and orientation. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. Steps: 1. Normal Computation (Pre-processing): Compute the surface normals for the source mesh vertices using PyTorch3D. 2. Attribute Assignment: Assign the computed normal ni to each Gaussian i, treating it as an RGB value for the purpose of rendering. 3. Rendering: Render the Gaussian ellipsoids using standard alpha-blending splatting, interpolating the normal attribute ni into the image plane to produce an image-like normal map. 4. Lighting Integration (Optional): To integrate lighting, first render the surface normals into an image-like map, then use a diffuse function (e.g., PyTorch3D.renderer.lighting) to compute brightness under a point light source based on the rendered normals and light direction. Formulas: The rendering of the normal field follows standard alpha-compositing, where the normal N at a pixel is the weighted average of the normals of the splatted Gaussians: N = \frac{\sum{i \in \text{sorted}} ni \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj)}{\sum{i \in \text{sorted}} \alphai \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj)} where the Gaussians are sorted back-to-front along the view ray, \alphai is the opacity of Gaussian i, and ni is its normal vector. Parameters: Light Position: Specified for the diffuse function to compute brightness. Number of Gaussians: Affects rendering quality; increasing the number of Gaussians significantly improves rendering quality, though boundaries may be slightly fuzzier compared to mesh renderers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Fuzziness: The VoGE renderer may produce slightly fuzzier boundaries compared to traditional mesh renderers due to the volumetric nature of Gaussians. Normal Consistency: The quality of the rendered normals depends heavily on the accuracy of the initial normal computation from the source mesh or point cloud. A parameterization for learnable surface normals of Gaussians that uses a sign scalar and a direction vector to stabilize optimization and allow normal flipping without rotation. It solves the instability inherent in naive vector parameterization, where flipping a normal requires a 180-degree rotation that causes convergence to inaccurate local minima. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Normal Field Supervision via Rendering and Depth Derivatives by explicitly modifying the Gaussian's internal attribute representation rather than relying on external gradient supervision. This method supervises the learnable surface normal attributes of 3D Gaussians by enforcing consistency between the rendered normal map and the geometric normals derived from the rendered depth map. It differs from pure gradient-based approaches by explicitly optimizing normal attributes per Gaussian and supervising them against pseudo-normals computed from the median depth. To render the normal field, attribute a single value Ni per Gaussian to approximate the integral of the normal field along the ray. For the vector field V, select Vi proportional to the integral of the i-th term of the sum multiplied by the normalized density of the Gaussian. Due to symmetry around ni, Vi \propto ni, and thus the normalized vector field Ni \sim ni. Render plane normals ni with Gaussian splatting to estimate the average normal field value. The integral is defined as: Vi \propto \int{\mathbb{R}^3} Gi(x) \cdot \mathbf{1}{ni^T(x-\mui) \geq 0} \nabla \log(1 - Gi(x)) dx. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Rendering quality improves significantly with an increased number of Gaussians. Strengths: Allows for lighting integration in Gaussian Splatting pipelines. Simple to implement by treating normals as an RGB attribute. Limitations: Boundaries may be fuzzier than mesh-based renderers. Requires pre-computed normals if starting from a mesh. This method was introduced in the context of VoGE (Volume Gaussian Ellipsoids), a differentiable volume renderer using Gaussian ellipsoids for analysis-by-synthesis. It was developed to address the lack of native surface normal information in Gaussian ellipsoids, which are represented as volumes. The approach leverages PyTorch3D for normal computation and lighting integration. name: Learnable Normals Parameterization
head: Normal Parameterization, Sign-Direction Normal Decomposition
body: A parameterization for learnable surface normals of Gaussians that uses a sign scalar and a direction vector to stabilize optimization and allow normal flipping without rotation. It solves the instability inherent in naive vector parameterization, where flipping a normal requires a 180-degree rotation that causes convergence to inaccurate local minima. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Normal Field Supervision via Rendering and Depth Derivatives by explicitly modifying the Gaussian's internal attribute representation rather than relying on external gradient supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Learnable parameters for each Gaussian i. Output: A surface normal vector \mathbf{n}i for each Gaussian i, suitable for rendering and gradient-based optimization. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores two learnable parameters for its normal: a scalar sign parameter si \in \mathbb{R} and a 3D direction vector \mathbf{d}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Initialize si and \mathbf{d}i for each Gaussian. 2. Compute the normal \mathbf{n}i using the decomposition formula during optimization. 3. Use \mathbf{n}i in the rendering pipeline for shading or normal loss calculation. Formulas: The normal \mathbf{n}i is computed as: \mathbf{n}i = \tanh(si) \cdot \frac{\mathbf{d}i}{\|\mathbf{d}i\|} Where: \tanh(si) maps the scalar si to the range (-1, 1), effectively acting as a learnable sign and magnitude controller. \frac{\mathbf{d}i}{\|\mathbf{d}i\|} normalizes the direction vector to unit length. The resulting \mathbf{n}i has a norm strictly less than 1 (due to \tanh), but its direction is well-defined and continuous. Parameters: si: Learnable scalar. Not given in the sources for initialization, but must allow both positive and negative values. \mathbf{d}i: Learnable 3D vector. Not given in the sources for initialization, but typically initialized randomly or based on prior geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \|\mathbf{d}i\| = 0, the normalization fails. In implementation, a small epsilon should be added to the denominator or \mathbf{d}i should be clamped. Local Minima: Naive parameterization (simple normalized 3D vector) leads to unstable optimization because flipping the normal direction requires a 180-degree rotation. This decomposition avoids this by allowing flipping via the sign parameter si, which is a continuous scalar change rather than a vector rotation. Gradient Stability: The decomposition into direction and sign enforces the norm of the normal to be lower than 1, while allowing for flipping the direction simply by changing the sign parameter si, which overall stabilizes gradients and prevents optimization from getting stuck in local minima. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenormal(si: float, di: list[float]) -> list[float]: """ Compute the learnable normal for a Gaussian. Args: si: Learnable sign scalar. di: Learnable direction vector [x, y, z]. Returns: Normal vector [nx, ny, nz]. """ # Standard mathematical functions: exp(x), sqrt(x) def tanh(x): return (exp(x) - exp(-x)) / (exp(x) + exp(-x)) # Compute magnitude of direction vector mag = sqrt(di[0]2 + di[1]2 + di[2]2) # Guard against division by zero if mag < 1e-8: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Normalize direction dnorm = [di[0] / mag, di[1] / mag, di[2] / mag] # Compute sign factor signfactor = tanh(si) # Compute final normal ni = [signfactor dnorm[0], signfactor dnorm[1], signfactor dnorm[2]] return ni A technique to improve normal quality and stabilize vertex locations by training an additional learnable rotation parameter (quaternion) on each Gaussian on the mesh surface, instead of relying solely on mesh face normals. It sets itself apart by explicitly learning a rotation rather than just a direction, which is crucial for non-flat surfaces where mesh face normals require a large number of triangles for accuracy. Choose this when high-fidelity normal reconstruction on complex, non-flat geometry is required, and when occlusion errors from simple normal learning are observed. Pitfall: Using mesh face normals directly requires a large number of triangles for non-flat surfaces; adjusting vertex positions alone to learn rotation is insufficient and causes occlusion errors. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian for normal computation, as it involves basic arithmetic operations and a normalization. Memory Complexity: Adds 4 floats (1 for si, 3 for \mathbf{d}i) per Gaussian. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Stabilizes gradients, prevents convergence to local minima, allows easy normal flipping. Limitations: Requires additional learnable parameters per Gaussian. When to use: When optimizing Gaussian splats for surface reconstruction or normal rendering, especially where normal orientation is critical. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and the overhead of 4 extra floats per Gaussian is prohibitive, or when normal orientation is not important. Originated in the context of Gaussian Splatting for surface reconstruction, specifically in the work "From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians". It addresses the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting, which does not natively contain surface normal information, by providing a robust way to learn and represent normals. From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37095-24, fetched 2026-10-29 Phys3DGS: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.10335, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Normal Field Supervision via Rendering and Depth Derivatives
head: Learnable Unit Normal with Depth Gradient Supervision, Lemma 2, Phys3DGS Normal Regularizer, Pseudo-Normal Supervision, Supervision of Normal Field
body:
This method supervises the learnable surface normal attributes of 3D Gaussians by enforcing consistency between the rendered normal map and the geometric normals derived from the rendered depth map. It differs from pure gradient-based approaches by explicitly optimizing normal attributes per Gaussian and supervising them against pseudo-normals computed from the median depth. Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{D} of resolution W 	imes H. Rendered normal map \hat{N} of resolution W 	imes H, obtained by rasterizing the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation with learnable unit normals ni using alpha-blending. Outputs: Normal consistency loss Ln used for gradient-based optimization of Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: \hat{D}: 2D array of floats, where \hat{D}(x,y) stores the median depth at pixel (x,y). \hat{N}: 2D array of 3D vectors, where \hat{N}(x,y) stores the alpha-blended normal at pixel (x,y). ni: 3D vector, the learnable unit normal attribute of the i-th Gaussian. Steps: 1. Render Normal Map: Rasterize the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation with learnable normals ni using alpha-blending to produce \hat{N}. 2. Compute Pseudo-Normal: Calculate the pseudo-ground truth normal 	ilde{N}(x,y) from the gradient of the rendered depth map \hat{D} under a local planarity assumption. Compute the image gradients of the depth map: 
ablax d and 
ablay d. Construct 3D tangent vectors from the gradients: \mathbf{v}x = (1, 0, 
ablax d) and \mathbf{v}y = (0, 1, 
ablay d). Compute the cross product of these vectors and normalize the result to get 	ilde{N}(x,y): 	ilde{N}(x, y) =  rac{
ablax d 	imes 
ablay d}{|
ablax d 	imes 
ablay d|} where d are nearby depth points of pixel (x, y). 3. Compute Loss: Quantify the normal consistency as an L1 loss between the rendered normal \hat{N} and the pseudo-normal 	ilde{N}: Ln = \|\hat{N} - 	ilde{N}\|1 This loss encourages the rendered normal field to match the true normal of the surface at the 0.5-isosurface of the transmittance. Parameters: Depth Metric: The depth used for gradient computation is the median value of the free-flight distance t^{o,w}, not the expectancy, for robustness to outliers. Median Depth Definition: The median depth t is the infimum of t such that transmittance T{o,w}(t) \leq 0.5. In point-based rendering, this is the depth t^G{o,w} of the first Gaussian along the ray for which the transmittance reaches the 0.5 threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def norm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def computenormalloss(rendereddepth, renderednormal): H, W = len(rendereddepth), len(rendereddepth[0]) losssum = 0.0 count = 0 for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # Finite difference gradients with edge replication dx = rendereddepth[y][min(x+1, W-1)] - rendereddepth[y][max(x-1, 0)] dy = rendereddepth[min(y+1, H-1)][x] - rendereddepth[max(y-1, 0)][x] # Construct 3D vectors from gradients vx = [1.0, 0.0, dx] vy = [0.0, 1.0, dy] pseudo = cross(vx, vy) pnorm = norm(pseudo) # Handle degenerate gradients if pnorm < 1e-8: pseudo = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] else: pseudo = [p / pnorm for p in pseudo] # L1 loss diff = sum(abs(renderednormal[y][x][i] - pseudo[i]) for i in range(3)) losssum += diff count += 1 return losssum / count Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Gradients: If the depth map is flat or noisy, the cross product may be near zero, leading to unstable normals. The normalization step includes a clamp to prevent division by zero. Boundary Conditions: Depth gradients at image boundaries require padding or special handling to maintain spatial alignment with the normal map. Under-reconstructed Regions: Artifacts in the normal field correspond to under-reconstructed parts of the scene, such as specular spots, TV screens, or sky regions, where depth estimates are unreliable. This method assigns a learnable unit normal to each 3D Gaussian to replace noisy gradient-based estimates, preventing the optimization from overfitting to training lighting conditions by aligning rendered normals with geometry priors derived from expected depth gradients. It differs from pure gradient-based approaches by explicitly optimizing normal attributes per Gaussian and supervising them against pseudo-normals computed from expected depth. It is chosen when stable normal attributes are required across varying lighting conditions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a robust supervision signal for normals without requiring explicit mesh reconstruction or additional geometric priors. The use of median depth makes it robust to outliers. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the rendered depth map. Artifacts in the normal field correspond to under-reconstructed parts of the scene. When to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the formulation of normal field supervision in oriented Gaussian representations and is applied in reflection-aware rendering pipelines. It leverages the relationship between depth derivatives and surface normals, a concept well-established in computer vision. The specific formulation using median depth for robustness is detailed in. name: Rendering and Lighting Pipelines
body: This family defines extensions to the 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline to support advanced effects such as order-independent transparency, explicit geometry, volumetric lighting, inverse rendering, and physically-based dynamic relighting. While standard 3DGS uses view-dependent spherical harmonic colors and simple alpha blending, these methods diverge by introducing physical parameters (extinction, albedo), explicit primitives (polyhedra), or multi-stage training to decouple geometry from lighting. All extensions retain the core 3D Gaussian primitive representation: a set of M anisotropic 3D Gaussian kernels \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M. Each kernel is defined by: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position (mean). \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Scale matrix. The covariance matrix is \mathbf{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^\top \mathbf{R}i^\top. The rendering pipeline's geometric projection remains consistent for ray-based methods: 3D Gaussians are transformed into ray space, and the projected 2D covariance \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i is computed using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projection and the rotation part W of the extrinsic matrix: \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i = J W \mathbf{\Sigma}i W^T J^T. However, the attribute representation and loss functions diverge significantly from the standard RGB opacity/color model. Standard 3DGS uses view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{d}). In radiative and domain-specific variants, this is replaced by view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors. Duplex-GS is a dual-hierarchy rendering framework for real-time order-independent Gaussian Splatting that combines alpha-blending with a reformulated Weighted-Sum Rendering (WSR) strategy. It solves the transparency artifacts and lack of early termination inherent in vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting, while reducing the sorting overhead of conventional alpha-blending. Unlike vanilla OIT methods which lack physical constraints, Duplex-GS reintroduces them via cell-level transmittance decay, and unlike Sort-free Gaussian Splatting which uses linear depth decay, it uses cell-level sorting to compute a physically grounded transmittance. See Duplex-GS. LinPrim is a differentiable rendering pipeline that replaces the Gaussian primitives of 3D Gaussian Splatting with convex polyhedra, specifically octahedra, to enable explicit geometric representation. It solves the problem of approximating complex scene geometry with bounded, triangular surfaces while maintaining real-time performance and full differentiability for gradient-based optimization. Unlike its sibling 3D Gaussian Splatting which uses implicit Gaussian kernels, LinPrim uses explicit ray-triangle intersections to determine opacity, allowing gradients to be backpropagated directly onto the geometric features of the polyhedra. See LinPrim Differentiable Rendering Pipeline. GsplatVolumeLighting is a volume lighting and occlusion technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that ray-marches through a 3D density texture to compute transmittance for shadow and volume occlusion, combined with per-light attenuation and diffuse shading. It extends the standard 3DGS rendering pipeline by introducing volumetric shadows and ambient occlusion-like effects, allowing splats to cast and receive shadows from a defined volume rather than relying solely on geometric primitives or screen-space techniques. Unlike sibling methods such as 4DGS-Volume-Cloud Two-Stage Relighting which may use separate relighting stages, GsplatVolumeLighting integrates the shadow march directly into the lighting evaluation per splat, making it suitable for real-time interactive applications like those in the Unity engine. See GsplatVolumeLighting. NeILF (Neural Inverse Lighting Field) is a rendering pipeline that decomposes Gaussian Splatting features into diffuse, specular, and ambient components using a Blinn-Phong model, enabling inverse rendering via loss functions on depth, normals, and color sparsity. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling lighting interactions through learnable material factors (diffuse, specular, ambient) and supporting multi-Gaussian group rendering with palette-based color offsets, allowing for physically plausible relighting and material optimization. See NeILF Rendering and Loss Calculation. This method enables real-time, physically-based dynamic relighting of volume clouds using 3D Gaussian Splatting by decoupling geometry/medium parameters from environmental lighting. It solves the problem of arbitrary sun-direction relighting in volumetric media by training a static physical representation in Stage 1 under single-direction illumination, then freezing those parameters to train a global environment network in Stage 2 that adds sky atmospheric scattering. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which uses empirical SH colors, this approach parameterizes participating medium physics (extinction, albedo, scattering) and separates direct sun attenuation from additive sky inscattering. See 4DGS-Volume-Cloud Two-Stage Relighting. Originating from the foundational 3D Gaussian Splatting paper [17] (cited in), the standard pipeline uses analytic alpha blending. Subsequent extensions have adapted this for specific domains: Duplex-GS addresses order-independence, LinPrim introduces explicit geometry, GsplatVolumeLighting adds volumetric shadows, NeILF enables inverse rendering, and 4DGS-Volume-Cloud handles dynamic cloud relighting. name: Duplex-GS
head: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting
body: Duplex-GS is a dual-hierarchy rendering framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates popping and transparency artifacts while reducing sorting overhead. It combines alpha-blending with reformulated Weighted-Sum Rendering (WSR) to achieve real-time order-independent transparency. Unlike vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting which lacks physical constraints and causes transparency artifacts, Duplex-GS reintroduces physical constraints via cell-level transmittance decay, eliminating transparency artifacts and enabling early termination. Unlike Sort-free Gaussian Splatting which uses Linear Correction WSR (LC-WSR) with linear depth decay, Duplex-GS uses cell-level sorting to compute a physically grounded transmittance that decays rapidly upon encountering opaque objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N ellipsoidal cells (proxies) \mathcal{C} = \{Cn\}{n=1}^N, where each cell Cn is initialized from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Each cell is associated with a latent feature vector \mathbf{f}n and emits K neural Gaussians. Output: A final rendered color \mathcal{C} for each pixel. Data Structures: Each cell Cn is parameterized by: Position \mathbf{x}n \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scale Sn \in \mathbb{R}^3. Quaternion Qn \in \mathbb{R}^4. Calibration scalar vn. Latent feature vector \mathbf{f}n. Each emitted neural Gaussian G{n,k} (for k \in \{1, \dots, K\}) is defined by: Center \boldsymbol{\mu}{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \sigma{n,k} \in [0, 1]. Color \mathcal{C}{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scale s{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Orientation \mathbf{q}{n,k} \in \mathbb{R}^4. Numbered Steps: 1. Cell Initialization: Initialize N cells from SfM points. Each cell is centered according to the point cloud. Each cell is parameterized by \mathbf{x}n, Sn, Qn, vn and associated with a latent feature \mathbf{f}n. 2. Gaussian Decoding (Layer I): For each cell n, decode K neural Gaussians using shared Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) activated by specific functions: Centers: Compute centers using learned offsets \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} scaled by cell scale Sn: \boldsymbol{\mu}{n,k} = \mathbf{x}n + \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} \cdot Sn \quad (1) where \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}} \in [-1, 1]. Opacities: Decode opacities via MLP F\sigma activated by Tanh: \{\sigma{n,1}, \dots, \sigma{n,K}\} = F\sigma(\mathbf{f}n, \deltan, \mathbf{r}n) \quad (2) where \deltan is viewing distance and \mathbf{r}n is viewing direction. Colors: Decode colors via MLP Fc: \{c^{n,1}, \dots, c^{n,K}\} = Fc(\mathbf{f}n, \deltan, dn) \quad (8) where dn is viewing direction. Scales: Decode scale ratios via MLP Fs activated by sigmoid: \{\mathcal{O}{n,1}^{\text{state}}, \dots, \mathcal{O}{n,K}^{\text{state}}\} = Fs(\mathbf{f}n, \deltan, dn) \quad (9) The Gaussian scale s{n,k} is derived from cell scale Sn and decoded scale ratio: s{n,k} = \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} Sn \quad (11) where \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} \in (0, 1). Orientations: Decode quaternions via MLP Fq: \{\mathbf{q}{n,1}, \dots, \mathbf{q}{n,K}\} = Fq(\mathbf{f}n, \deltan, dn) \quad (10). 3. Constraint Enforcement: Ensure Gaussians reside within their cells: Update cell quaternion Qn as the normalized weighted average of associated Gaussians' orientations: Qn = \text{norm}\left(\sum{k=1}^K \mathbf{q}{n,k} \sigma{n,k}\right) \quad (12). Clamp scale ratio to ensure Gaussian regions stay inside the cell: \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}} = \min \left( \mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{scale}}, 1 - \|\mathcal{O}{n,k}^{\text{pos}}\| \right) \quad (13). 4. Cell Rasterization (Layer I): Assign visible cells to tiles. Apply radix sort to the cell sequence based on depth to establish a coarse spatial order. Compute cell-level transmittance Tn^{\text{cell}} for sorted cells: Tn^{\text{cell}} = \prod{i=1}^{n-1} \prod{k=1}^{n-1} (1 - vi \cdot \alpha{i,k}) \quad (16) where vi is a learnable calibration scalar and \alpha{i,k} is the opacity of the k-th Gaussian in cell i. Compute cell weight wn for WSR: wn = vn \cdot Tn^{\text{cell}} \quad (15). Early Termination: Halt cell-level blending when Tn^{\text{cell}} < \epsilon, where \epsilon is a predefined threshold. 5. Physical OIT Blending (Layer II): Aggregate Gaussians inside each cell in an order-independent WSR manner. Compute final rendered color \mathcal{C}: \mathcal{C} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^N wn \sum{k=1}^K \alpha{n,k} \mathcal{C}{n,k}}{\sum{n=1}^N wn \sum{k=1}^K \alpha{n,k}} \quad (14) where \mathcal{C}{n,k} is the color of the k-th Gaussian in cell n. Parameters: K: Predefined number of neural Gaussians emitted per anchor/cell. vn: Learnable calibration scalar for cell n, parameterized using spherical harmonic coefficients to capture directional variation. \epsilon: Predefined threshold for early termination. Pitfalls: Order confusion caused by overlap among cells is a potential issue, addressed by the calibration scalar vn and the physically grounded transmittance model. Vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting suffers from transparency artifacts and lack of early termination. Duplex-GS handles this by ensuring transmittance decays rapidly for opaque objects and allowing early termination when Tn^{\text{cell}} < \epsilon. A method that eliminates sorting analytically by pre-integrating the alpha blending equation to compute an equivalent order-independent transparency through a rational polynomial approximation of the visibility term, suppressing popping artifacts without per-pixel depth sorting. Time Complexity: Drastically reduces memory and computational overhead compared to global Gaussian sorting by performing radix sort at the cell level, as the number of cells is orders of magnitude smaller than the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Reduced due to cell-level rasterization and sorting. Performance: Enables real-time order-independent Gaussian Splatting. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts (locally order-independent blending) and transparency artifacts (physically grounded transmittance). Allows early termination for acceleration. Limitations: Requires maintaining a dual-hierarchy structure (cells and Gaussians). When to use: When real-time performance is required and artifacts from sort-free OIT methods (transparency, popping) are unacceptable. When not to use: When scene complexity is low enough that standard alpha-blending with sorting is sufficient, or when strict per-Gaussian depth ordering is required for specific physical effects not covered by the cell approximation. Duplex-GS was introduced in a paper submitted to the IEEE for possible publication, titled "Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon Scaffold-GS, which introduced anchors as local encoding proxies. Duplex-GS replaces point anchors with ellipsoidal cells to provide explicit geometric structure and visible regions. It addresses limitations of vanilla OIT-based Gaussian Splatting, which lacks physical constraints and causes transparency artifacts, and Sort-free Gaussian Splatting, which uses linear depth decay that is physically inconsistent. Duplex-GS: Proxy-Guided Weighted Blending for Real-Time Order-Independent Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3666188, fetched 2026-10-30 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LinPrim Differentiable Rendering Pipeline
head: LinPrim Rendering, LinPrim rasterizer, Linear Primitive Rendering, Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering, Octahedron Rendering
body: LinPrim is a differentiable rendering pipeline that replaces the standard 3D Gaussian kernel with convex polyhedral primitives, specifically octahedra, to enable efficient volumetric rendering via ray-triangle intersections. Unlike Gaussian Splatting which relies on 2D Gaussian projections and density fields, LinPrim computes opacity based on the path length of rays through the primitive's geometry, allowing gradients to be backpropagated directly through the intersection calculations. It retains the core 3DGS preprocessing and compositing structure but diverges in the primitive representation and the per-pixel evaluation logic, offering a bounded geometric alternative that supports real-time performance while maintaining high-fidelity reconstruction. The pipeline operates in two stages: per-primitive preprocessing and per-pixel rasterization/compositing. Inputs: A set of M primitives. Each primitive i is defined by: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Distances defining the shape (e.g., for octahedra, distances to vertices from the center). Rotation features \mathbf{R}i. View-dependent color coefficients: 48 Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients (floats) per primitive. Camera pose (extrinsic matrix) and intrinsic parameters. Outputs: A 2D image with color and opacity values for each pixel. Primitive Representation: Octahedron: Defined by a center position, a rotation matrix, and a single distance parameter that describes the distance to all vertices (enforcing symmetry, where opposite vertices share the same distance). This reduces complexity and ensures the center is the true geometric center. Tetrahedron: An alternative primitive mentioned, requiring 12 floats to describe non-symmetric shapes. Attributes: Each primitive stores 48 SH coefficients for view-dependent color. Preprocessed Data: Bounding Box: Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in screen space for each primitive, used for culling. L1-Slab Parameters: For the octahedron, the projection stores parameters defining the L1-slab in the projected space. Sorted List: Primitives are sorted front-to-back within tiles. 1. Construction: Construct polyhedra (octahedra or tetrahedra) from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points in a fully differentiable manner. For octahedra, enforce symmetry by using a single distance for opposing corners. 2. Preprocessing (Per-Primitive): Transform the primitive's position and rotation into the camera's coordinate system using the camera pose. Calculate the view-dependent color using the viewing direction and the stored SH coefficients. Project the primitive into the 3D affine ray space approximation (EWA Splatting). This step approximates the 3D shape in camera space. The error from this approximation is negligible for small primitives. Compute the projected bounding box in screen space to determine visibility. Note: For the octahedron variant, the project function stores the L1-slab parameters of the projected octahedron. 3. Global Sorting and Tiling: Tile the screen into regions. Sort primitives within each tile according to an approximate front-to-back order. This allows for efficient compositing and early termination. 4. Rasterization (Per-Pixel): For each pixel, reconstruct the pixel ray using the +0.5 pixel-center convention. Determine if the ray intersects the convex primitive. Since primitives are convex, the ray intersects either twice or not at all. Use the Möller-Trumbore Intersection Algorithm (MTIA) to find the intersection points. This algorithm is fully differentiable. If two intersections exist, calculate the opacity based on the distance between the entry and exit points. Normalization: To handle scale ambiguity, normalize the intersection distances. Determine the smallest distance d among all primitives and scale all distance measurements accordingly. Opacity/Density Calculation: Given the primitive opacity \alpha, the density \sigma is defined as: \sigma(\alpha) = -\frac{\log(1 - 0.99 \cdot \alpha)}{2 \cdot \min(dx, dy, dz)} where dx, dy, dz are the normalized distances. Note: The source describes the evaluation as computing the Beer-Lambert opacity from the ray's entry and exit depths through the octahedron. 5. Compositing: Aggregate color contributions of all visible primitives via alpha blending in front-to-back order. Stop blending once the cumulative opacity reaches a threshold of 0.999. """ # 1. Preprocessing preprocessedprimitives = [] for p in primitives: # Transform to camera space pcam = transformtocameraspace(p, camera.pose) # Calculate view-dependent color using SH # Note: SH evaluation depends on viewing direction, handled during rasterization or precomputed # Here we assume color is evaluated per-pixel based on direction # Project to screen space / Ray space # For Octahedron: Store L1-slab parameters # For general: Compute bounding box in screen space bbox = computescreenbbox(pcam) preprocessedprimitives.append({ 'primitive': p, 'bbox': bbox, 'camdata': pcam }) # 2. Global Sorting and Tiling tiles = createtiles(imagewidth, imageheight) for tile in tiles: # Cull primitives outside tile bbox tileprims = [p for p in preprocessedprimitives if intersectstile(p['bbox'], tile)] # Sort front-to-back (approximate) tileprims.sort(key=lambda x: depthestimate(x, camera)) tile.primitives = tileprims # 3. Rasterization and Compositing image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) opacitymap = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Find minimum distance for normalization (global pass or approximation) mind = min(p['primitive'].mindimension for p in preprocessedprimitives) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Reconstruct ray ray = reconstructray(x, y, camera) # Get primitives for this pixel's tile tile = gettile(x, y) cumulativeopacity = 0.0 color = zeros(3) for primdata in tile.primitives: p = primdata['primitive'] # Check if pixel is in bbox (fast cull) if not pointinbbox((x, y), primdata['bbox']): continue # Ray-Primitive Intersection # Use Möller-Trumbore Algorithm for triangles forming the primitive # For Octahedron, this involves checking against its triangular faces intersections = raytriangleintersections(ray, p) if len(intersections) == 2: d1, d2 = sorted(intersections) pathlength = d2 - d1 # Normalize distance # Note: Source says scale all measurements relative to smallest distance d # Here we assume normalizeddist is derived from pathlength and mind normalizeddist = normalizedistance(pathlength, mind) # Calculate Opacity/Density # Source defines density sigma(alpha). # In standard alpha blending, we need opacity alpha for the step. # The source implies alpha is a stored feature or derived. # Assuming alpha is a stored attribute of the primitive for now, # or derived from the density and path length. # Standard Beer-Lambert: alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma pathlength) # However, LinPrim uses the path length directly to determine opacity contribution. # Let's assume the primitive has a base opacity alphabase. alphabase = p.opacity # Stored attribute # Calculate effective opacity for this step # The source formula: sigma(alpha) = -log(1 - 0.99 alpha) / (2 mindist) # This seems to define the density required to achieve a target alpha. # For rendering, we likely use the stored alpha and the path length. # Let's assume the contribution is based on the path length through the volume. # Simplified interpretation: # Opacity contribution is determined by the path length. # Let's use the standard alpha blending with the primitive's alpha. # The "density" formula might be for optimization/initialization. # To be safe and follow the "Beer-Lambert" mention in: # We need a sigma. If alpha is the target opacity for the whole primitive, # and pathlength is the max path, then sigma = -log(1-alpha)/pathlength. # But we have a specific pathlength for this ray. # Let's assume the primitive stores 'alpha' as the max opacity. # And we compute the opacity for this specific ray segment. # If the primitive is homogeneous, the opacity for a segment of length L is: # alphaseg = 1 - exp(-sigma L) # where sigma is derived from the primitive's total alpha and max path. # However, the source says "opacity depends on the distance between intersection points". # And provides a formula for sigma(alpha). # Let's assume the primitive has a stored 'alpha' (e.g., 0.99). # And we use the normalized distance to compute the local opacity. # Re-reading: "If there are two, the opacity depends on the distance between the intersection points." # And "we define the density of an octahedron as: sigma(alpha) =..." # This suggests sigma is computed from the primitive's alpha and its size. sigma = -math.log(1 - 0.99 alphabase) / (2 normalizeddist) alphastep = 1 - math.exp(-sigma normalizeddist) # View-dependent color # Evaluate SH at viewing direction viewdir = ray.direction colorprim = evaluatesh(p.shcoeffs, viewdir) # Alpha Blending alphastepnormalized = alphastep (1 - cumulativeopacity) color += colorprim alphastepnormalized cumulativeopacity += alphastepnormalized if cumulativeopacity > 0.999: break image[y, x] = color opacitymap[y, x] = cumulativeopacity return image def raytriangleintersections(ray, primitive): """ Returns a list of intersection distances for a ray and a convex polyhedron. Uses Möller-Trumbore algorithm for each face. """ intersections = [] for face in primitive.faces: t = mollertrumbore(ray.origin, ray.direction, face) if t is not None: intersections.append(t) return intersections def mollertrumbore(origin, direction, face): """ Standard Möller-Trumbore intersection algorithm. Returns distance t or None. """ # Implementation of MTIA #... pass def normalizedistance(pathlength, mind): """ Normalizes the path length relative to the minimum primitive distance. """ # Source: "scaling all distance measurements accordingly" # Assuming mind is the global minimum distance found in preprocessing return pathlength / mind SH Degree: 48 coefficients (typically degree 2 or 3) per primitive. Opacity Threshold: 0.999 for stopping compositing. Normalization Factor: The smallest distance d among all primitives in the scene. Scale Ambiguity: Without normalization, the appearance of primitives varies across different scene sizes. This is handled by scaling distances relative to the smallest primitive distance d. Approximation Error: The 3D affine ray space approximation error grows with distance from the center points. However, for small primitives (required for high-fidelity reconstruction), this error remains negligible. Degenerate Input: The method assumes convex primitives. Non-convex shapes would require more complex intersection logic. Memory: The majority of memory per primitive is used by the 48 SH coefficients. Reducing SH degree or primitive count is necessary for memory-constrained environments. Time Complexity: Real-time performance is claimed, comparable to 3DGS. The two-stage process (preprocessing then rasterization) allows efficient parallelization. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the SH coefficients (48 floats per primitive). Strengths: Fully differentiable through ray-triangle intersections. Bounded geometry allows for intuitive modification and understanding. Real-time rendering speeds. High-fidelity reconstruction. Limitations: Scale ambiguity requires global normalization. Memory intensive due to SH coefficients. Approximation error in ray space projection, though negligible for small primitives. When to use: When bounded geometric primitives are preferred over Gaussian kernels, or when differentiable volumetric rendering with convex shapes is required. LinPrim was introduced as a method for differentiable volumetric rendering using linear primitives (octahedra and tetrahedra). It builds on the 3DGS pipeline but replaces the Gaussian primitive with a polyhedron. The method was developed to provide an intuitive representation that can be easily understood and modified, while retaining real-time rendering speeds. It is cited in the context of point-based differentiable rendering extensions.
