name: GsplatVolumeLighting
head: Gaussian Splat Volume Ray Marching, Volume Occlusion for 3DGS
body: GsplatVolumeLighting is a volume lighting and occlusion technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that ray-marches through a 3D density texture to compute transmittance for shadow and volume occlusion, combined with per-light attenuation and diffuse shading. It extends the standard 3DGS rendering pipeline by introducing volumetric shadow casting, allowing splats to cast and receive shadows from a defined density volume rather than relying solely on geometric primitives or screen-space techniques. Unlike Duplex-GS which focuses on dual-visibility for large scenes, or 4DGS-Volume-Cloud Two-Stage Relighting which uses a two-stage cloud approach, GsplatVolumeLighting integrates volume occlusion directly into the per-splat lighting evaluation using a unified ray-marching step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Splat attributes: Position \mathbf{p}i, Normal \mathbf{n}i, View Direction \mathbf{v}i. Volume Data: A 3D texture GsplatVolumeDensity (R8 channel) storing density. Volume Bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box defined by GsplatVolumeBoundsMin and GsplatVolumeBoundsMax in local space. Light Data: Up to 4 lights, each with type (directional, point, spot), position/direction, color, and attenuation parameters. Parameters: GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams (optical-depth scale, sample steps, start distance), GsplatVolumeAmbientColor, GsplatVolumeLightingParams. Output: Final lighting value (scalar or RGB) for the splat, combining ambient and direct volumetric lighting. Data Structures: GsplatVolumeDensity: sampler3D texture. The R8 channel encodes \sqrt{\text{normalized optical depth}}. GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams: float4 packing: x: Optical-depth scale (0 disables volume). y: Sample steps (clamped 1–24). z: Start distance. w: Unused/Reserved. GsplatVolumeBoundsMin/Max: float4 defining the AABB in local space. GsplatVolumeBoundsInvSize: float4 containing the inverse dimensions of the volume bounds (1 / (\text{Max} - \text{Min})). GSPLATVOLUMEOPAQUEDEPTH: Constant 8.0. Transmittance below \exp(-8) is treated as fully opaque. Algorithm Steps: 1. Volume Ray-Box Intersection: Calculate the entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances of the ray from the volume bounds. Compute directionSign: \text{lerp}(-1.0, 1.0, \text{step}(0.0, \text{direction})). Clamp ray direction magnitude to 10^{-5} to prevent division by zero. Compute t0, t1 against boundsMin and boundsMax. Return \max(0.0, \min(\text{farDistance}.x, \min(\text{farDistance}.y, \text{farDistance}.z))) as the max valid ray length. 2. Light Direction Transformation: Transform the light direction to the local space of the volume using GsplatVolumeWorldToLocal. Normalize it. If the length is \le 10^{-6}, return transmittance 1.0. 3. Ray Length Clamping: If the light is a point light (lightPosition.w > 0.5), clamp the ray length to the Euclidean distance from the local center to the light position. Calculate usableLength = rayLength - startDistance. If usableLength \le 10^{-5}, return transmittance 1.0. 4. Sampling Configuration: Determine sampleCount = \text{clamp}(\text{round}(\GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams.y), 1, 24). Compute stepLength = usableLength / sampleCount. 5. Initialization: Initialize UVW coordinates at the midpoint of the first step: \text{uvw} = (\text{localCenter} + \text{localDirection} \cdot (\text{startDistance} + 0.5 \cdot \text{stepLength}) - \text{boundsMin}) \cdot \text{invSize} Compute step delta: \text{uvwStep} = \text{localDirection} \cdot \text{stepLength} \cdot \text{invSize}. 6. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize opticalDepth = 0.0. Loop sampleIndex from 0 to sampleCount - 1: If sampleIndex \ge sampleCount or opticalDepth \ge GSPLATVOLUMEOPAQUEDEPTH, break. If uvw is outside [0, 1] bounds, skip sample. Sample R8 channel di from GsplatVolumeDensity. Add di^2 to opticalDepth. Advance uvw += uvwStep. 7. Transmittance Calculation: Compute transmittance T using the formula: T = \exp(-\text{strength} \cdot \text{opticalDepth}) where strength is GsplatVolumeOcclusionParams.x. 8. Lighting Evaluation: If GsplatVolumeEnabled == 0, return 1.0. Transform splat center to world space. Transform and normalize normal \mathbf{n}. Flip if \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}i < 0.0. Compute ambient: \text{ambient} = \GsplatVolumeAmbientColor.rgb \cdot \GsplatVolumeLightingParams.y. Initialize direct = 0.0. For each light (max 4): Compute vector to light \mathbf{l} and distance. Compute attenuation: Directional light (lightType < 0.5): attenuation = 1.0. Point/Spot light: \text{distanceSquared} = \|\mathbf{l}\|^2. \text{normalizedDistanceSquared} = \text{distanceSquared} \cdot \text{lightDirection}.w. \text{rangeFade} = \text{saturate}(1.0 - \text{normalizedDistanceSquared}^2). \text{attenuation} = \text{rangeFade}^2 / \text{distanceSquared}. Spot cone falloff (if lightType > 1.5): \text{spotCosine} = \text{dot}(\text{lightDirection}.xyz, -\mathbf{l}). \text{spot} = \text{saturate}((\text{spotCosine} - \text{spotParams}.x) \cdot \text{spotParams}.y). \text{attenuation} = \text{spot}^2. Compute visibility V using the transmittance T from step 7. Add to direct: \text{direct} += \GsplatVolumeLightColors[\text{lightIndex}].rgb \cdot (\text{irradiance} \cdot V). Irradiance is assumed to be the light's intensity/color before attenuation. Scale direct by GsplatVolumeLightingParams.z. Return \max(\text{ambient} + \text{direct}, 0.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gsplatvolumelighting(splat, volumetexture, volumeboundsmin, volumeboundsmax, volumeinvsize, lights, params): """ splat: dict with 'center', 'normal', 'viewdirection' volumetexture: function sample3d(uvw) returning float volumeboundsmin, volumeboundsmax: float3 volumeinvsize: float3 lights: list of light dicts params: dict with 'enabled', 'densityscale', 'samplesteps', 'startdist', 'ambientcolor', 'lightingscale', 'opaquedepth' """ if not params['enabled']: return 1.0 # 1. Ray-Box Intersection raydir = splat['viewdirection'] # Or light direction depending on context; # here we assume ray from splat to light/volume # Clamp direction magnitude to prevent division by zero dirlen = length(raydir) if dirlen < 1e-5: return 1.0 raydir = raydir / dirlen max(dirlen, 1e-5) # Compute direction sign for slab intersection dirsign = [ -1.0 if d < 0 else 1.0 for d in raydir ] # Compute t0 and t1 for each axis t0 = (volumeboundsmin - splat['center']) / raydir t1 = (volumeboundsmax - splat['center']) / raydir # Swap if necessary to ensure t0 < t1 tmin = [min(t0[i], t1[i]) for i in range(3)] tmax = [max(t0[i], t1[i]) for i in range(3)] tenter = max(tmin) texit = min(tmax) # Clamp to far distance (not specified, assume large value or texit) maxraylen = texit if maxraylen < 0: return 1.0 # 2. Light Direction Transformation (Local Space) # Assuming light direction is passed or computed in world space # Transform to local space using inverse world matrix (simplified as GsplatVolumeWorldToLocal) locallightdir = transformtolocal(splat['lightdirection']) # Placeholder for actual transform locallightdir = normalize(locallightdir) if length(locallightdir) <= 1e-6: return 1.0 localcenter = transformtolocal(splat['center']) # 3. Ray Length Clamping # If point light, clamp to distance to light if ispointlight(splat['light']): disttolight = length(localcenter - splat['lightposition']) maxraylen = min(maxraylen, disttolight) usablelength = maxraylen - params['startdist'] if usablelength <= 1e-5: return 1.0 # 4. Sampling Configuration samplecount = clamp(round(params['samplesteps']), 1, 24) steplength = usablelength / samplecount # 5. Initialization startuv = localcenter + locallightdir (params['startdist'] + 0.5 steplength) uvw = (startuv - volumeboundsmin) volumeinvsize uvwstep = locallightdir steplength volumeinvsize # 6. Ray Marching Loop opticaldepth = 0.0 for i in range(samplecount): if opticaldepth >= params['opaquedepth']: break if not (0.0 <= uvw.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= uvw.y <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= uvw.z <= 1.0): uvw += uvwstep continue # Sample R8 channel densityval = sample3d(volumetexture, uvw) opticaldepth += densityval 2 uvw += uvwstep # 7. Transmittance Calculation transmittance = exp(-params['densityscale'] opticaldepth) # 8. Lighting Evaluation ambient = params['ambientcolor'] params['lightingscale'] direct = 0.0 for light in lights: # Compute attenuation if light['type'] == 'directional': attenuation = 1.0 else: distsq = length(light['tolight']) 2 normdistsq = distsq light['direction'].w rangefade = clamp(1.0 - normdistsq 2, 0.0, 1.0) attenuation = (rangefade 2) / distsq # Spot falloff if light['type'] == 'spot': spotcosine = dot(light['direction'].xyz, -normalize(light['tolight'])) spot = clamp((spotcosine - light['spotparams'].x) light['spotparams'].y, 0.0, 1.0) attenuation = spot 2 # Visibility visibility = transmittance # Add to direct direct += light['color'] visibility attenuation direct = params['lightingscale'] return max(ambient + direct, 0.0) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S) per splat, where N is the number of lights (max 4) and S is the sample count (1–24). The ray-marching loop is fixed-size, making it predictable but potentially expensive for high-resolution volumes or many lights. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D density texture, where V is the volume resolution. The texture is typically R8, keeping memory footprint low. Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on the volume resolution and the sampleCount parameter. Early exit on opticalDepth >= GSPLATVOLUMEOPAQUEDEPTH mitigates over-marching in opaque regions. Strengths: Provides physically plausible volumetric shadows for 3DGS, which is otherwise limited to surface-like rendering. Integrates seamlessly with Unity's lighting pipeline. Limitations: Limited to 4 lights. Fixed sample count may lead to aliasing or noise if too low, or performance issues if too high. Requires a pre-computed 3D density texture. When to use: When volumetric shadows are required for 3DGS content in Unity, especially for scenes with dense fog, smoke, or volumetric clouds. When not to use: For real-time applications with strict performance budgets where volumetric shadows are not critical, or when the scene geometry is complex enough that geometric shadows are preferred. GsplatVolumeLighting is part of the UnitySplats package, a cross-platform Unity 6 package for importing, loading, and rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting content. It was developed by Arloopa as an extension to the original gsplat-unity renderer, which was a fork of wuyize25/gsplat-unity. The technique addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS rendering, which does not natively support volumetric occlusion, by introducing a ray-marching step through a 3D density texture. It is used in Unity 6 for volume occlusion and lighting of 3DGS content. arloopa/UnitySplats, https://github.com/arloopa/UnitySplats, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeILF Rendering and Loss Calculation
head: inverse rendering with Blinn-Phong
body: NeILF (Neural Inverse Lighting Field) is a differentiable rendering pipeline that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by decomposing scene appearance into physically-based diffuse, specular, and ambient components using a Blinn-Phong model. It solves the problem of inverse rendering in Gaussian-based representations by enabling the optimization of material properties (shininess, diffuse color) and lighting conditions from multi-view images, depth, and normal constraints. Unlike standard 3DGS which renders view-dependent RGB colors directly, NeILF renders view-independent scalar attributes and combines them with geometric normals to compute lighting, allowing for relighting and material editing. The method operates in two phases: rendering the Blinn-Phong components and calculating a composite loss function for training. Inputs: \mathcal{G}: Set of M 3D Gaussians with attributes including diffuse factor, offset color, shininess, ambient factor, and specular factor. Camera parameters: Intrinsics, extrinsics (view matrix), and position. Light parameters: Incident direction \mathbf{l} and view direction \mathbf{v}. Ground truth: Image, depth, and optionally normal maps. Optimization weights: \lambda{render}, \lambda{phong}, \lambda{depth}, \lambda{opacity}, \lambda{normal\render\depth}, \lambda{normal\mvs\depth}, \lambda{offset\color\sparsity}, \lambda{diffuse\factor\smooth}, \lambda{ambient\factor\smooth}, \lambda{normal\smooth}, \lambda{dssim}. Sample count: N{sample} (default 24) for incident ray sampling. Outputs: Rendered image components: Diffuse, specular, ambient, and combined Phong. Geometric outputs: Normal, depth, opacity. Loss value: Scalar sum of weighted loss terms. The rendering result is stored in a dictionary results with the following keys: render: Final combined color image. phong: Blinn-Phong rendered image. normal: Rendered surface normals. pseudonormal: Normals derived from depth. surfacexyz: 3D positions of rendered pixels. opacity: Opacity map. depth: Depth map. viewspacepoints, visibilityfilter, radii, numrendered, numcontrib: Standard 3DGS auxiliary data. diffusefactor, offsetcolor, shininess, ambientfactor, specularfactor: Material attributes. diffuseterm, specularterm, ambientterm: Individual lighting components. hdr, valgamma: HDR handling parameters. tbdict, loss: TensorBoard dictionary and final loss scalar. The rendering process computes the lighting contribution for each pixel by aggregating Gaussian splats. For each Gaussian i, the contribution is modulated by its material attributes. 1. Lighting Geometry: Let \mathbf{n}i be the surface normal of Gaussian i. Let \mathbf{l} be the normalized light direction (incident ray). Let \mathbf{v} be the normalized view direction. Compute the half-vector: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}\|}. Compute \cosl = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l} and \cosh = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{h}. 2. Diffuse Component: Compute diffuse intensity: I{diffuse} = \text{diffuse\factor}i \cdot \max(0, \cosl). Compute diffuse color: \mathbf{C}{diffuse} = (\text{ambient\factor}i + I{diffuse}) \cdot \mathbf{C}{base}, where \mathbf{C}{base} is derived from offsetcolor and palettecolor. Specifically, offsetcolornorm is computed as the sum of squared offsetcolor along the last two dimensions. The final diffuse color uses offsetcolor + palettecolor.clamp(0, 1).detach(). 3. Specular Component: Compute specular intensity: I{specular} = \text{specular\factor}i \cdot \begin{cases} |\cosh|^{\text{shininess}i} & \text{if } \cosl \neq 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. The implementation uses torch.where(cosl != 0, (torch.abs(cosh)).pow(shininess), 0.0). 4. Combination: \mathbf{C}{phong} = \mathbf{C}{diffuse} + \mathbf{C}{specular}. Final color is clamped to [0, 1]. 5. Multi-Gaussian Grouping: If multiple Gaussian groups exist (len(numGSsTFs) > 1), iterate through groups. Set diffusecolor[startGS:endGS] to the computed value and multiply opacity by opacityfactors[i] if present. 6. Light Transforms: If lighttransform is not None, apply transformations to diffusefactor, shininess, ambientfactor, and specularfactor using multiplication and addition offsets. The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of multiple terms, computed only if the corresponding lambda is > 0. 1. Render Loss (\mathcal{L}{render}): If \lambda{render} > 0: \mathcal{L}{render} = (1 - \lambda{dssim}) \mathcal{L}{1}(\mathbf{I}{render}, \mathbf{I}{gt}) + \lambda{dssim} (1 - \text{SSIM}(\mathbf{I}{render}, \mathbf{I}{gt})) where \mathbf{I}{render} is the standard 3DGS render and \mathbf{I}{gt} is the ground truth image. 2. Phong Loss (\mathcal{L}{phong}): If \lambda{phong} > 0: \mathcal{L}{phong} = \lambda{phong} \left[ (1 - \lambda{dssim}) \mathcal{L}{1}(\mathbf{I}{phong}, \mathbf{I}{gt}) + \lambda{dssim} (1 - \text{SSIM}(\mathbf{I}{phong}, \mathbf{I}{gt})) \right] where \mathbf{I}{phong} is the Blinn-Phong rendered image. 3. Depth Loss (\mathcal{L}{depth}): If \lambda{depth} > 0: \mathcal{L}{depth} = \lambda{depth} \mathcal{L}{1}(\mathbf{D}{render}, \mathbf{D}{gt}) Computed excluding pixels where imagemask XOR depthmask is true. 4. Opacity Loss (\mathcal{L}{opacity}): If \lambda{opacity} > 0: Clamp rendered opacity to [10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]. \mathcal{L}{opacity} = \lambda{opacity} \left[ (1 - \lambda{dssim}) \mathcal{L}{1}(\mathbf{O}{render}, \mathbf{M}{img}) + \lambda{dssim} (1 - \text{SSIM}(\mathbf{O}{render}, \mathbf{M}{img})) \right] where \mathbf{M}{img} is the image mask. 5. Normal Loss from Rendered Depth (\mathcal{L}{normal\render\depth}): If \lambda{normal\render\depth} > 0: \mathcal{L}{normal\render\depth} = \lambda{normal\render\depth} \mathcal{MSE}(\mathbf{N}{render}, \mathbf{N}{pseudo}) Masked by imagemask. \mathbf{N}{pseudo} is derived from results. 6. Normal Loss from MVS Depth (\mathcal{L}{normal\mvs\depth}): If \lambda{normal\mvs\depth} > 0 and MVS normal map is all zeros: Compute pseudo normal \mathbf{N}{pseudo} from \mathbf{D}{gt} using kornia.depthtonormals. Transform \mathbf{N}{pseudo} to world space via camera intrinsics and worldviewtransform. \mathcal{L}{normal\mvs\depth} = \lambda{normal\mvs\depth} \mathcal{MSE}(\mathbf{N}{render}, \mathbf{N}{pseudo}) Masked by depthmask. 7. Sparsity Loss (\mathcal{L}{sparsity}): If \lambda{offset\color\sparsity} > 0: \mathcal{L}{sparsity} = \lambda{offset\color\sparsity} \text{Sparsity}(\mathbf{C}{offset\norm}) Masked by imagemask. 8. Smoothness Losses: Diffuse Factor Smoothness: If \lambda{diffuse\factor\smooth} > 0, compute bilateral smooth loss on rendereddiffusefactor using gtimage and imagemask. Ambient Factor Smoothness: If \lambda{ambient\factor\smooth} > 0, compute bilateral smooth loss on renderedspecularintensity and renderedambientintensity separately. Normal Smoothness: If \lambda{normal\smooth} > 0, compute bilateral smooth loss on renderednormal using gtimage and imagemask. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderneilf(camera, gaussians, lighttransform=None, samplenum=24): """ Renders the scene using Blinn-Phong lighting model. Returns results dictionary. """ # 1. Base rendering to get geometric attributes # This step assumes a standard 3DGS rasterization that outputs # normals, depth, opacity, and material attributes (diffusefactor, # offsetcolor, shininess, ambientfactor, specularfactor) baseresults = renderview(camera, gaussians) normals = baseresults['normal'] diffusefactor = baseresults['diffusefactor'] offsetcolor = baseresults['offsetcolor'] shininess = baseresults['shininess'] ambientfactor = baseresults['ambientfactor'] specularfactor = baseresults['specularfactor'] palettecolors = baseresults.get('palettecolors', None) # 2. Apply light transforms if provided if lighttransform is not None: diffusefactor = diffusefactor lighttransform.mul + lighttransform.add shininess = shininess lighttransform.mul + lighttransform.add ambientfactor = ambientfactor lighttransform.mul + lighttransform.add specularfactor = specularfactor lighttransform.mul + lighttransform.add # 3. Compute Base Color from Offset and Palette # offsetcolornorm is sum of squared offsetcolor along last two dims offsetcolornorm = torch.sum(offsetcolor 2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Handle multi-Gaussian groups if necessary # Assuming baseresults contains grouping info or we iterate # For simplicity, we assume a single group or that the attributes # are already aggregated per pixel. If not, iterate groups: # for i in range(len(numGSsTFs)): # start, end =... # diffusecolor[start:end] = (offsetcolor[start:end] + palettecolors[i].clamp(0,1).detach()) # opacity[start:end] = opacityfactors[i] # Compute base color if palettecolors is not None: # Assuming palettecolors is broadcastable or indexed correctly basecolor = offsetcolor + palettecolors.clamp(0, 1).detach() else: basecolor = offsetcolor # 4. Compute Lighting Components # Get view and light directions for each pixel # Note: In a rasterized setting, view direction is constant per pixel # (from camera center to pixel), light direction is sampled or fixed. viewdirs = camera.getviewdirections() # Shape: (H, W, 3) # Sample incident directions if needed, or use fixed light # For standard inverse rendering, light direction is often a parameter # Here we assume a fixed light direction or sampled from sphere incidentdirs = samplelightdirections(samplenum) # Shape: (samplenum, 3) or (H, W, 3) # Compute Half Vector # h = normalize(l + v) # We need to handle the case where l + v is zero h = torch.nn.functional.normalize(incidentdirs + viewdirs, dim=-1) # Cosines cosl = torch.sum(normals incidentdirs, dim=-1) # (H, W) or (H, W, samplenum) cosh = torch.sum(normals h, dim=-1) # Diffuse Term # Idiffuse = diffusefactor max(0, cosl) diffuseintensity = diffusefactor torch.clamp(cosl, min=0.0) diffuseterm = (ambientfactor + diffuseintensity) basecolor # Specular Term # Ispecular = specularfactor |cosh|^shininess if cosl != 0 else 0 # Using torch.where to handle division by zero or invalid cases specularintensity = specularfactor torch.where( cosl != 0, torch.abs(cosh).pow(shininess), torch.zeroslike(cosh)) specularterm = specularintensity.unsqueeze(-1) # Assuming scalar intensity, expand to RGB if needed # Combine phongcolor = diffuseterm + specularterm phongcolor = torch.clamp(phongcolor, 0.0, 1.0) # 5. Store Results results = { 'render': baseresults['render'], # Standard 3DGS render 'phong': phongcolor, 'normal': normals, 'pseudonormal': baseresults.get('pseudonormal'), 'surfacexyz': baseresults.get('surfacexyz'), 'opacity': baseresults['opacity'], 'depth': baseresults['depth'], 'viewspacepoints': baseresults['viewspacepoints'], 'visibilityfilter': baseresults['visibilityfilter'], 'radii': baseresults['radii'], 'numrendered': baseresults['numrendered'], 'numcontrib': baseresults['numcontrib'], 'diffusefactor': diffusefactor, 'offsetcolor': offsetcolor, 'shininess': shininess, 'ambientfactor': ambientfactor, 'specularfactor': specularfactor, 'diffuseterm': diffuseterm, 'specularterm': specularterm, 'ambientterm': ambientfactor basecolor, # Approximation 'hdr': baseresults.get('hdr'), 'valgamma': baseresults.get('valgamma'), 'tbdict': {}, 'loss': torch.tensor(0.0, device=phongcolor.device) } return results def calculateloss(results, gtimage, gtdepth, imagemask, depthmask, lambdarender=1.0, lambdaphong=1.0, lambdadepth=0.0, lambdaopacity=0.0, lambdanormalrenderdepth=0.0, lambdanormalmvsdepth=0.0, lambdaoffsetcolorsparsity=0.0, lambdadiffusefactorsmooth=0.0, lambdaambientfactorsmooth=0.0, lambdanormalsmooth=0.0, lambdadssim=0.2): """ Calculates the total loss for NeILF training. """ loss = torch.tensor(0.0, device=results['phong'].device) # 1. Render Loss (Standard 3DGS) if lambdarender > 0: l1render = torch.abs(results['render'] - gtimage).mean() ssimrender = ssim(results['render'], gtimage) loss += lambdarender ((1 - lambdadssim) l1render + lambdadssim (1 - ssimrender)) # 2. Phong Loss if lambdaphong > 0: l1phong = torch.abs(results['phong'] - gtimage).mean() ssimphong = ssim(results['phong'], gtimage) loss += lambdaphong ((1 - lambdadssim) l1phong + lambdadssim (1 - ssimphong)) # 3. Depth Loss if lambdadepth > 0: # Exclude pixels where imagemask XOR depthmask is true excludemask = torch.logicalxor(imagemask, depthmask) validmask = ~excludemask l1depth = torch.abs(results['depth'][validmask] - gtdepth[validmask]).mean() loss += lambdadepth l1depth # 4. Opacity Loss if lambdaopacity > 0: opacityclamped = torch.clamp(results['opacity'], 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6) l1opacity = torch.abs(opacityclamped - imagemask).mean() ssimopacity = ssim(opacityclamped, imagemask) loss += lambdaopacity ((1 - lambdadssim) l1opacity + lambdadssim (1 - ssimopacity)) # 5. Normal Loss from Rendered Depth if lambdanormalrenderdepth > 0: pseudonormal = results['pseudonormal'] msenormal = torch.mean((results['normal'] - pseudonormal) 2 imagemask) loss += lambdanormalrenderdepth msenormal # 6. Normal Loss from MVS Depth if lambdanormalmvsdepth > 0: # Check if MVS normal is all zeros mvsnormal = results.get('mvsnormal', None) if mvsnormal is not None and torch.all(mvsnormal == 0): # Compute pseudo normal from gtdepth pseudonormalmvs = depthtonormals(gtdepth) # Transform to world space pseudonormalmvs = transformtoworldspace(pseudonormalmvs, cameraintrinsics, worldviewtransform) msenormalmvs = torch.mean((results['normal'] - pseudonormalmvs) 2 depthmask) loss += lambdanormalmvsdepth msenormalmvs # 7. Sparsity Loss if lambdaoffsetcolorsparsity > 0: offsetcolornorm = torch.sum(results['offsetcolor'] 2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) sparsityloss = torch.mean(offsetcolornorm imagemask) loss += lambdaoffsetcolorsparsity sparsityloss # 8. Smoothness Losses if lambdadiffusefactorsmooth > 0: smoothdiffuse = bilateralsmoothloss(results['diffusefactor'], gtimage, imagemask) loss += lambdadiffusefactorsmooth smoothdiffuse if lambdaambientfactorsmooth > 0: smoothspecular = bilateralsmoothloss(results['specularintensity'], gtimage, imagemask) smoothambient = bilateralsmoothloss(results['ambientintensity'], gtimage, imagemask) loss += lambdaambientfactorsmooth (smoothspecular + smoothambient) if lambdanormalsmooth > 0: smoothnormal = bilateralsmoothloss(results['normal'], gtimage, imagemask) loss += lambdanormalsmooth smoothnormal results['loss'] = loss return loss samplenum: Number of incident rays sampled for normal-based lighting. Default: 24. lambdarender: Weight for standard render loss. Default: 1.0. lambdaphong: Weight for Blinn-Phong render loss. Default: 1.0. lambdadepth: Weight for depth loss. Default: 0.0. lambdaopacity: Weight for opacity loss. Default: 0.0. lambdanormalrenderdepth: Weight for normal loss from rendered depth. Default: 0.0. lambdanormalmvsdepth: Weight for normal loss from MVS depth. Default: 0.0. lambdaoffsetcolorsparsity: Weight for offset color sparsity. Default: 0.0. lambdadiffusefactorsmooth: Weight for diffuse factor smoothness. Default: 0.0. lambdaambientfactorsmooth: Weight for ambient factor smoothness. Default: 0.0. lambdanormalsmooth: Weight for normal smoothness. Default: 0.0. lambdadssim: Weight for SSIM in L1/SSIM loss combination. Default: 0.2. Frustum Culling: Gaussians with radius 0 or those frustum culled are excluded from value updates in splitting criteria via visibilityfilter (where radii > 0). MVS Normal Zeros: The MVS normal map may be all zeros. In this case, the pseudo normal must be computed from the ground truth depth using kornia.depthtonormals and transformed to world space using camera intrinsics and worldviewtransform. Division by Zero: The specular term uses torch.where(cosl != 0,...) to avoid invalid specular highlights when the light is behind the surface. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rasterization of M Gaussians, which is O(M) per pixel. The lighting calculation adds a constant factor per pixel based on the number of light samples (N{sample}). Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional attributes per Gaussian (diffuse factor, shininess, ambient/specular factors) compared to standard RGB, increasing memory usage by a factor proportional to the number of material channels. Strengths: Enables inverse rendering, relighting, and material editing. Provides physically plausible lighting decomposition. Limitations: Requires more complex loss functions and potentially more training time due to the additional constraints. Relies on accurate normal estimation, which can be noisy in Gaussian splatting. When to Use: When the goal is to recover material properties or lighting conditions from images, or to enable relighting. When Not to Use: When only view-dependent appearance is needed, or when computational resources are limited and standard 3DGS suffices. NeILF was introduced as an extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting to support inverse rendering tasks. It decomposes the rendering process into diffuse, specular, and ambient components using a Blinn-Phong model, allowing for the optimization of material properties and lighting. The method is implemented in the VEG repository. ldyken53/VEG, https://github.com/ldyken53/VEG, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 4DGS-Volume-Cloud Two-Stage Relighting
head: Frozen Geometry + Environment Network, Stage 1 + Stage 2
body: A two-stage rendering pipeline for physically parameterized volume clouds using 3D Gaussians, designed for real-time dynamic relighting with arbitrary sun directions. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which learns view-dependent RGB colors, this method separates geometry and physical medium properties (extinction, albedo) from the lighting environment. Stage 1 trains the physical parameters under a single sun direction with a black background, while Stage 2 freezes these parameters and trains a global environment network to add sky atmospheric scattering, enabling arbitrary sun direction relighting. The method operates in two distinct phases. Stage 1 establishes the physical representation of the cloud volume. Stage 2 decouples the lighting from the geometry to allow dynamic relighting. Inputs: Stage 1: A dataset of images captured under pure sun illumination with a black background (UE SkyAtmosphere brightness factor = 0). The dataset must cover the hemisphere uniformly to ensure healthy geometric shadow gradients. Stage 2: The trained Stage 1 model (geometry and physical parameters) and a corresponding "env-on" dataset where the sky brightness is zero but the atmospheric scattering on the cloud remains. Outputs: Stage 1: A set of 3D Gaussians with physical attributes (position, scale, rotation, extinction \sigmat, albedo \omega, HG g, multiple scattering weights wn). Stage 2: The same Gaussian set (frozen) plus an environment network (MLP) and precomputed visibility vectors. Final Render: Radiance L for any given sun direction. The Gaussian primitive \mathcal{G} retains the standard 3DGS structure but replaces SH color with physical parameters: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation. \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Scale. \sigma{t,i}: Extinction coefficient (volume integral of cross-section). Activated via softplus, clamped to 5. \omegai \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scattering albedo (RGB). Activated via sigmoid. gi: Henyey-Greenstein anisotropy factor. Activated via 0.8 \cdot \tanh. w{n,i}: Six octave weights for multiple scattering (Frostbite/Wrenninge approximation). Activated via softplus. Stage 2 Sidecar Files: envnet.pt: Weights for the global environment network. skytransfer.npy: Precomputed visibility transfer vectors V{lm}. env.json: Configuration parameters. 1. Initialize: Create M 3D Gaussians. Initialize physical parameters \sigmat, \omega, g, wn. 2. Rasterization Setup: Use a forked differentiable rasterizer supporting useanalytictau. This computes per-pixel cumulative optical thickness \tau via line integration, with \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\tau). 3. Compute Self-Shadowing (T{light}): Perform a "light space" rasterization pass using a narrow FOV perspective camera to simulate the sun direction. For each Gaussian, record the front-facing optical thickness accumulation. This is the energy-weighted mean of \alpha \cdot T over the sun-facing footprint, not just a center-point sample. Enable full continuous gradients for \tau, weights, and projection parameters. 4. Compute Radiance: For each pixel, sum contributions from Gaussians. The radiance contribution of a Gaussian is: Li = \omegai \cdot L{sun} \cdot \sum{n=0}^{5} w{n,i} \cdot T{light,i}^{b^n} \cdot P(\mathbf{v}i, \mathbf{v}o; gi \cdot c^n) Where P is the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, \mathbf{v}i is the incident light direction (-\mathbf{v}l), and b, c are base/exponent constants for the octaves. 5. Optimize: Minimize loss against the ground truth images. Use fixed Narkowicz ACES tonemapping by default to match the display space of the training data (e.g., UE filmic tonemapped LDR). If the ground truth is linear HDR, disable tonemapping. 1. Freeze Geometry: Lock all Gaussian attributes (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{S}, \sigmat, \omega, g, wn) from Stage 1. 2. Precompute Visibility (V{lm}): For each Gaussian center \mathbf{x}, compute the geometric sky visibility transfer vectors V{lm}(\mathbf{x}). Scan the hemisphere in N directions using computeTlightraster to calculate geometric occlusion. Represent V{lm} using Spherical Harmonics (SH) of order 2 (9 coefficients) by default. This step is colorless and purely geometric; it is computed once on the frozen point set. 3. Train Environment Network: Train a small global MLP to predict the sky irradiance field E{lm}(\mathbf{v}l) as a function of sun direction \mathbf{v}l. Use a learning rate of 10^{-3} with an independent optimizer, decaying to 0.1\times. 4. Compute Final Radiance: Calculate the sun transmittance T{sun}(\mathbf{v}l) using the analytic expression: T{sun}(\mathbf{v}l) = \exp(-m(\theta) \cdot \tau{rgb}) Where m(\theta) is the Kasten-Young air mass based on sun elevation \theta, and \tau{rgb} = (\tauR, \tauG, \tauB) are learnable zenith optical thicknesses. Combine Stage 1 sun term and Stage 2 sky term: L = T{sun}(\mathbf{v}l) \odot L{stage1} + \omega \cdot \sum{lm} E{lm}(\mathbf{v}l) \cdot V{lm}(\mathbf{x}) Where L{stage1} is the direct sun term computed in Stage 1 (using the frozen physical parameters). Apply a smoothstep gate to extinguish the direct sun term when the sun is below the horizon. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stage1train(gaussians, dataset, optimizer): for image, sundirection in dataset: # 1. Rasterize with analytic tau # Computes per-pixel tau and alpha = 1 - exp(-tau) taumap, alphamap = rasterizeanalytic(gaussians, camera) # 2. Compute self-shadowing Tlight # Light-space rasterization pass Tlight = computelightspacetransmittance(gaussians, sundirection) # 3. Compute Radiance # Lstage1 is the direct sun contribution Lstage1 = computephysicalradiance( gaussians, sundirection, Tlight, phasefunction='henyeygreenstein') # 4. Apply Tonemapping (if GT is LDR) Lrendered = applyacestonemap(Lstage1) # 5. Backpropagate loss loss = mseloss(Lrendered, image) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() def stage2relight(gaussiansfrozen, envnet, sundirection): # 1. Get precomputed visibility Vlm (from skytransfer.npy) Vlm = gaussiansfrozen.visibilityvectors # SH order 2 # 2. Compute Sky Irradiance Elm from MLP Elm = envnet(sundirection) # 3. Compute Sun Transmittance Tsun theta = sunelevation(sundirection) mtheta =kastenyoungairmass(theta) taurgb = envnet.zenithopticalthicknesses Tsun = exp(-mtheta taurgb) # 4. Gate sun if below horizon if sunbelowhorizon(sundirection): Tsun = 0.0 # 5. Compute Stage 1 Direct Term (using frozen params) # Note: Tlight for the specific sun direction must be recomputed # or approximated if not precomputed for all directions. # In this pipeline, Tlight is often recomputed per-frame for the new sun dir # or approximated if the geometry is static and Tlight was stored. # Based on notes, Tlight is computed via rasterization pass. Tlightnew = computelightspacetransmittance(gaussiansfrozen, sundirection) Lstage1new = computephysicalradiance( gaussiansfrozen, sundirection, Tlightnew, phasefunction='henyeygreenstein') # 6. Combine Terms # Direct Sun Term (Multiplicative) directterm = Tsun Lstage1new # Sky Insattering Term (Additive) # Sum over SH coefficients skyterm = 0.0 for l, m in shcoefficients(order=2): skyterm += Elm[l, m] Vlm[l, m] skyterm = gaussiansfrozen.albedo skyterm Lfinal = directterm + skyterm return Lfinal SH Order: Default is 2 (9 coefficients) for both E{lm} and V{lm}. Tonemapping: Default is fixed Narkowicz ACES. If ground truth is linear HDR, disable it (--no-tonemapaces). Sun Below Horizon: The direct sun term is extinguished using a smoothstep gate. Precision: The sun term must be multiplicative (T{sun} \le 1) because an additive term cannot express the darkening/attenuation caused by atmospheric path length. Data Uniformity: The training dataset must have uniform sun direction coverage in the hemisphere to prevent geometric shadow gradient bias. Time Complexity: Stage 1 training is comparable to standard 3DGS but with additional light-space rasterization passes for T{light}. Stage 2 inference is real-time, as the environment network is a small MLP and V{lm} is precomputed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing physical parameters instead of SH colors. Stage 2 adds storage for envnet.pt and skytransfer.npy. Strengths: Enables arbitrary sun direction relighting in real-time. Physically plausible scattering (extinction, albedo, HG phase function). Limitations: Static geometry in the current implementation (time dimension not implemented). Requires specific dataset generation (UE SkyAtmosphere settings). The method is based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) and the 3DGS-Volume-Cloud project. It was developed as an independent 4D implementation workspace, with an initial code baseline at commit 69fea2c8d5a13d6c0e41ac12ca45c80b71bd3403. It is used in the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud project for real-time rendering and dynamic relighting of volume clouds, based on the WDAS Cloud dataset. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volume Encoding Gaussians
head: Transfer Function-Agnostic 3D Gaussians for Volume Rendering
body: Volume Encoding Gaussians adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for scientific volume data visualization by decoupling the geometric representation from the material appearance. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which renders view-dependent RGB colors and fixed opacity, this method trains only scalar density values per Gaussian, enabling interactive, transfer-function-agnostic rendering after the training phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^M initialized from volume data or point clouds. Each Gaussian Gi retains the standard geometric attributes: position \mathbf{p}i, rotation \mathbf{R}i, and scale \mathbf{S}i. Output: A rendered image where pixel intensity is determined by the accumulated scalar density of the splatted Gaussians, modulated by a user-defined transfer function. Data Structures: The Gaussian primitive Gi stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Scale matrix. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Scalar density value (replaces standard opacity \alpha and color \mathbf{c}). Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize M Gaussians with geometric parameters derived from the input volume data or point cloud. Set initial scalar density \alphai based on local data intensity or uniform initialization. 2. Training: Optimize the geometric parameters (\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{S}i) and the scalar density \alphai using a reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 or SSIM) against ground-truth volume slices or projections. Crucially, no color or opacity attributes are trained; only the scalar density \alphai is optimized. 3. Rendering: a. Project each 3D Gaussian Gi to 2D screen space using the standard projection pipeline. b. Compute the 2D covariance \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i. c. For each pixel covered by the projected Gaussian, evaluate the 2D Gaussian kernel value gi(\mathbf{x}) using the scalar density \alphai as the amplitude: gi(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{\hat{p}}i)^T \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}i^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{\hat{p}}i)\right) d. Sort Gaussians by depth and perform alpha compositing using the scalar densities. The accumulated density C at a pixel is: C = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}} gi(\mathbf{x}) \prod{j \in \mathcal{O}, j < i} (1 - gj(\mathbf{x})) where \mathcal{O} is the sorted order of Gaussians. e. Apply a user-defined transfer function T(\cdot) to the accumulated density C to produce the final color: \mathbf{Color} = T(C) This step is performed post-training and is interactive. Parameters: Number of Gaussians M: Determined by the input data resolution and complexity. Not given in the sources. Transfer Function T: User-defined, mapping scalar density to RGBA. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Scalar density values may require floating-point precision to avoid quantization artifacts during transfer function application. Boundaries: The method assumes the scalar density accurately represents the volume's internal structure; sparse regions may require denser Gaussian initialization. GVGEN is a method for 3D generation that operates in 3D space using a 3D Gaussian volume representation. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GaussianCube, which converts a constant number of Gaussians into a voxelized representation via optimal transport, by maintaining a direct 3D Gaussian volume structure. Normal Estimation: The normal \mathbf{n}i is derived from the Gaussian kernel's shape. Specifically, it corresponds to the shortest axis of the Gaussian covariance ellipsoid. Primary Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a primary ray from the camera. 2. Gaussian Splatting: Project Gaussians onto the image plane. Compute the contribution of each Gaussian to the pixel based on its opacity and projected covariance. 3. Lighting Integration: Direct Lighting: Sample the environment map for direct illumination. Indirect Lighting: Model indirect lighting using spherical harmonics or additional environment map samples. 5. Secondary Rays (Interreflections): Integrate secondary rays (reflections and refractions) spawned upon primary ray interactions with Gaussians using ray tracing techniques to model interreflections. body: Relightable 3D Gaussian is a method that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to support dynamic lighting and physically-based materials by assigning per-Gaussian BRDF parameters and precomputed visibility for shadows. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by enabling relighting capabilities, setting it apart from siblings like 3D Gaussian Splatting with BRDF Embedding which may use different embedding strategies, and Inverse Rendering with Gaussians (GS-IR / GIR) which focuses on inverse rendering with split-sum approximations. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, color) and target lighting conditions (environment map or directional lights). Outputs: Relit images with shadows and material reflections. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i stores: Base attributes: Position \mathbf{p}i, Covariance \Sigmai, Opacity \alphai, Base Color \mathbf{c}i. BRDF attributes: Albedo \mathbf{k}d, Roughness \rho, Normal \mathbf{n}. Visibility: Precomputed visibility factor vi for shadow casting. Steps: 1. Initialization: Assign initial BRDF parameters (\mathbf{k}d, \rho, \mathbf{n}) to each Gaussian. Initialize visibility vi based on scene geometry or default to 1.0 if no occlusion is considered. 2. Visibility Precomputation: Compute vi for each Gaussian to account for self-occlusion and shadows. This is typically done via ray casting or depth-based occlusion checks during training or preprocessing. 3. Rendering: For each pixel, splat the Gaussians in screen space. For each Gaussian, compute the BRDF contribution using the assigned parameters and the current lighting. Apply the visibility factor vi to modulate the contribution, effectively casting shadows. 4. Compositing: Accumulate the contributions of all Gaussians, respecting opacity and depth order, to produce the final pixel color. Formulas: The color contribution Ci of a Gaussian i is modulated by its visibility vi: Ci = vi \cdot \text{BRDF}(\mathbf{k}d, \rho, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{L} is the light direction and \mathbf{V} is the view direction. Parameters: Albedo \mathbf{k}d: Typically in [0, 1]^3. Roughness \rho: Typically in [0, 1]. Normal \mathbf{n}: Unit vector. Visibility vi: Typically in [0, 1]. Edge Cases: Degenerate Gaussians with zero opacity should be skipped. Precision issues in visibility computation may lead to artifacts; robust occlusion checks are recommended. It differs from the base method by explicitly baking ambient occlusion into the Gaussian attributes, potentially simplifying the lighting computation at the cost of flexibility for dynamic lighting. Choose R3DG when static ambient occlusion is sufficient and performance is critical. Limitations: Requires additional training or preprocessing for BRDF and visibility parameters; may suffer from artifacts if visibility is not accurately computed. name: Inverse Rendering with Gaussians (GS-IR / GIR)
head: GIR (Gaussian Inverse Rendering), GS-IR / GIR, Gaussian Inverse Rendering
body: Inverse Rendering with Gaussians (GS-IR / GIR) is a method employing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) inverse rendering techniques to accurately estimate details such as material properties and lighting conditions. It solves the problem of recovering physically plausible scene parameters (geometry, BRDF, illumination) from images by jointly optimizing Gaussian geometry and an environment light probe. What sets it apart from its siblings is its use of a split-sum approximation to handle indirect light, allowing it to model inter-reflections more accurately than methods relying solely on simplified direct-light equations or learned light approximations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images of a static scene. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color/BRDF parameters) and an environment light probe (e.g., spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation. Each Gaussian i is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai (or quaternion qi and scale si), opacity \alphai, and appearance coefficients. For inverse rendering, appearance coefficients must encode BRDF properties (e.g., albedo, roughness) rather than just view-dependent color. Light Probe: Typically represented as Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients or a pre-filtered environment map to support the split-sum approximation. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from SfM points (position, scale, orientation, opacity). Initialize BRDF parameters (albedo, roughness) and environment light SH coefficients. Roughness and albedo are often initialized to neutral values (e.g., albedo=0.5, roughness=0.5) or derived from initial color estimates. 2. Differentiable Rasterization: Render the scene to 2D images using the differentiable 3DGS rasterizer. This step computes the pixel color C by blending Gaussians. 3. Lighting Integration (Split-Sum): To handle indirect lighting and inter-reflections, GIR employs a split-sum approximation. The rendering equation is split into direct and indirect components. The indirect component is approximated by convolving the environment map with the BRDF's specular lobe (pre-filtered environment map) or by computing incident radiance on the fly. Formula: C = C{direct} + C{indirect} C{indirect} is computed using the split-sum approximation, integrating the product of the BRDF and the incident radiance. 4. Gradient Backpropagation: Compute the loss between the rendered image and the input image (e.g., L1, SSIM, or perceptual loss). Backpropagate gradients through the differentiable rasterizer and the lighting integration step to update Gaussian attributes and light probe coefficients. 5. Optimization Loop: Iterate steps 2-4 until convergence. The coupled optimization of geometry, material, and lighting is prone to ill-posed solutions. Parameters: Learning Rate: Typically requires careful tuning due to the ill-posed nature of coupled optimization. Regularization: Regularization terms are often added to stabilize normals and prevent noise in geometry, material, and lighting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posed Solutions: Coupled optimization of geometry, material, and lighting can lead to ambiguous solutions. Noise: Methods can introduce substantial noise in geometry, material, and lighting estimates. Static Scene: The method assumes a static scene, limiting dynamic editing capabilities. Performance: Anisotropic reflection modeling can reduce real-time rendering frame rates. Optimization-based layout generation requires hours of pre-computation. Methods adapting inverse rendering techniques to 3DGS to handle specular reflections by simplifying the classical rendering equation. These approaches rely on accurate normal estimation, which can be derived from computed depth maps [LZF 24] or using the shortest direction axis of Gaussians [JTL 24, YHZ24]. The different lighting conditions are then encoded via integrated shading functions. While these 3DGS-based methods achieve rapid convergence, they still introduce substantial noise in geometry, material, and lighting, which remains a limitation for high-fidelity rendering. Time Complexity: Optimization-based layout generation requires hours of pre-computation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Suitable for applications with extremely high demands on visual quality, such as film production or high-end VR experiences. However, anisotropic reflection modeling reduces real-time rendering frame rates. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows precise control over lighting and material appearance, making results more photorealistic. Handles indirect light via split-sum approximation. Limitations: Static scene assumption limits dynamic editing capabilities. Coupled optimization suffers from ill-posed solution problems. Introduces substantial noise in geometry, material, and lighting. When to use: When high fidelity and complex lighting effects are required, and computational time is not a primary constraint. When not to use: For dynamic scenes or real-time applications requiring fast rendering. This method allows precise control over lighting and material appearance, making results more photorealistic. It is especially suitable for applications with extremely high demands on visual quality, such as film production or high-end VR experiences. GS-IR jointly optimizes Gaussian geometry and an environment light probe, using a differentiable rasterizer to backpropagate gradients through the rendering equation. name: GaussianShader Material Model
head: GaussianShader
body: GaussianShader enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating trainable material parameters—diffuse color, specular intensity, roughness, and surface normal—alongside a global environment map to enable physically-based rendering (PBR). It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by binding these material properties directly to the Gaussian kernels, allowing for the accurate modeling of specular reflections and complex lighting interactions that standard opacity-based splatting cannot capture. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a 3D scene; initial 3DGS parameters (position, covariance, opacity); background mask for foreground/background separation. Outputs: Rendered images; optimized Gaussian parameters including material attributes. Data Structures: Each Gaussian kernel p stores the following trainable parameters: Position: \mathbf{x}p Opacity: \sigmap Covariance: \mathbf{A}p Diffuse color: \mathbf{d}p Specular intensity: \mathbf{s}p Roughness: \rhop Surface normal: \mathbf{n}p Rendering Formula: The color \mathbf{c}p of a kernel is computed by fusing diffuse and specular components based on the view direction \mathbf{r}i from the camera to pixel i: \mathbf{c}p(\mathbf{r}i) = \mathbf{d}p + \mathbf{s}p \odot \mathbf{L}s(\mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{n}p, \rhop) Where: \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. \mathbf{L}s(\mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{n}p, \rhop) is the specular light contribution for the kernel along view direction \mathbf{r}i, determined by the kernel's normal \mathbf{n}p and roughness \rhop. \mathbf{L}s is pre-filtered into multiple mip maps to approximate the environment lighting efficiently. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Separate foreground objects from the background in input images and extract the surface of masked objects. 2. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussian kernels with position, covariance, and opacity. Assign initial material parameters \{\mathbf{d}p, \mathbf{s}p, \rhop, \mathbf{n}p\}. 3. Shading: For each Gaussian kernel, compute its color \mathbf{c}p using the PBR formula above, utilizing the global environment map for \mathbf{L}s. 4. Splatting: Project the shaded Gaussians to 2D and splat them to the image plane, weighting by the 2D Gaussian weight Gk(i) at pixel i. 5. Loss Calculation: Compare the rendered image with the ground truth training view. Compute a loss function (typically including photometric loss and potentially anisotropy loss to mitigate undesired splatting artifacts near surfaces). 6. Optimization: Back-propagate the loss to update all trainable parameters \{\mathbf{x}p, \sigmap, \mathbf{A}p, \mathbf{d}p, \mathbf{s}p, \rhop, \mathbf{n}p\} using differentiable rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-stretching: Gaussian kernels may become over-stretched during training, causing rendering artifacts near surfaces. An anisotropy loss is applied to mitigate this. Reflective Scenes: Standard Gaussian orientation may fail in challenging reflective scenes. Normal orientation constraints are added to ensure physically plausible surface normals. A method that separately models texture and lighting to enable independent editing. It defines additional material parameters on each Gaussian to represent texture and approximates lighting using a learnable environment map. A method sharing the same disentanglement paradigm as GaussianShader by binding material parameters to 3D Gaussians. It specifically addresses challenging reflective scenes by adding normal orientation constraints to Gaussians, similar to Ref-NeRF. Complexity: Rendering complexity is similar to 3DGS, dominated by the splatting process, but shading computation per kernel is higher due to PBR evaluation. Strengths: Enables physically accurate specular reflections and material editing; supports simulation of interactions between solids and fluids by providing accurate visual attributes. Limitations: Requires optimization of additional material parameters, increasing training complexity; sensitive to normal orientation in reflective scenes without constraints. When to use: When physically-based material properties and specular reflections are required, or when simulating fluid-solid interactions where accurate shading is critical. When not to use: For simple diffuse scenes where standard 3DGS suffices, or when computational resources for optimizing additional material parameters are limited. GaussianShader was introduced to address the limitations of standard 3DGS in modeling specular reflections and complex lighting. It builds on the differentiable 3DGS pipeline and PBR principles, allowing material parameters to be optimized alongside geometric attributes. The approach is part of a broader trend in 3DGS research to disentangle texture and lighting for better control and physical accuracy. name: BRDF-SMAE
head: Smooth Material Auto-Encoder
body: BRDF-SMAE is a method for spatially varying BRDF decomposition that encodes a single BRDF per point in a neural volume, enabling the representation of complex material variations across a scene. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting with BRDF Embedding by explicitly enforcing a smooth latent space through an auto-encoder architecture, rather than storing raw or embedded parameters directly. This approach solves the problem of noisy or inconsistent material estimation by ensuring that nearby points with similar appearances share similar latent representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A neural volume where each point stores a BRDF embedding; training data consisting of images and corresponding environment maps (for Light-SMAE variants) or material datasets (for BRDF-SMAE). Output: A spatially varying BRDF decomposition, where each point in the volume is associated with a decoded BRDF parameter set. Data Structures: Neural Volume: A 3D grid or implicit representation where each location (x, y, z) stores a latent code or embedding vector. MLP Architectures: Three distinct Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are used: Encoder, Decoder, and Discriminator. Encoder: Maps input BRDF parameters or surface properties to a latent code z. Decoder: Maps latent code z back to BRDF parameters. Discriminator: Evaluates the realism of the decoded BRDFs. Layout: Each MLP consists of 3 layers with 32 output features per layer. Steps: 1. Encoding: For each point in the neural volume, the current BRDF parameters (or input representation) are passed through the Encoder MLP to produce a latent code z. 2. Decoding: The latent code z is passed through the Decoder MLP to reconstruct the BRDF parameters. 3. Discrimination: The decoded BRDF parameters are evaluated by the Discriminator MLP to ensure they lie within the manifold of realistic materials. 4. Loss Calculation: The total loss is computed as a weighted sum of reconstruction loss, discriminator loss, and potentially other regularization terms. 5. Optimization: The network parameters are updated using the Adam optimizer. Formulas: Reconstruction Loss: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on the BRDF parameters: L{rec} = \| \text{BRDF}{pred} - \text{BRDF}{target} \|1 Total Loss: L{total} = \lambda1 L{rec} + \lambda2 L{disc} + \lambda3 L{other} Where \lambda1 = 0.01, \lambda2 = 0.01, and \lambda3 = 0.001. Parameters: MLP Depth/Width: 3 layers, 32 output features. Loss Weights: \lambda1 = 0.01, \lambda2 = 0.01, \lambda3 = 0.001. Latent Interpolation: 64 steps used for latent space interpolation. Training Steps: 1.5 million steps. Batch Size: 256. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 1e-4. Hardware: NVIDIA 1080 TI GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence Time: Training takes approximately 3.5 hours to converge on the specified hardware. Light-SMAE Specifics: When handling light (Light-SMAE), the dataset is augmented by rotating environment maps 10 times and blending two maps randomly; environment maps are downscaled to 128 \times 256. Loss weights change to \lambda1 = 0.01, \lambda2 = 0.0001, \lambda3 = 0.05 with 5 interpolation steps. High dynamic range requires careful handling to ensure smooth training. targetbrdf)) # Discriminator loss (placeholder for GAN loss logic) # mentions discriminator but does not specify the exact loss function # Assuming standard GAN loss or similar ldisc =... # Not given in the sources. # Total loss ltotal = self.lambda1 lrec + self.lambda2 ldisc + self.lambda3... # Other terms not specified return ltotal def trainstep(self, batch): self.optimizer.zerograd() reconstructedbrdf, discoutput, z = self.forward(batch) loss = self.computeloss(reconstructedbrdf, batch, discoutput) loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() return loss This variant represents Spatially Varying BRDF (SVBRDF) using an encoder-decoder network with a sparse latent space to impose a prior that real-world objects consist of limited types of materials. It alleviates noisy roughness caused by lack of supervision by transforming the input surface point x to a latent code z using an encoder, then decoding z to diffuse albedo and roughness. The sparsity constraint is enforced via Kullback-Leibler divergence: \ell{KL} = \sum{j=1}^n KL(\rho || \hat{\rho}j), where \rho = 0.05 and \hat{\rho}j is the average of the j-th channel of z over the batch. A smooth loss \ells = || D(z) - D(z + \xi) ||1 is applied, where \xi is drawn from a normal distribution with zero mean and 0.01 variance. The decoder is a 2-layer network with 32-dimensional input and 128 hidden units, using the Simplified Disney BRDF model with fixed F0 = 0.02. Performance: The method converges in roughly 3.5 hours with a batch size of 256. Strengths: Enables spatially varying BRDF decomposition with a smooth latent space. Limitations: Requires significant training time and specific hardware (NVIDIA 1080 TI) for the reported results. When to use: When spatially varying material decomposition is required and a smooth latent space is beneficial. When not to use: When real-time inference is critical without pre-training, or when hardware constraints prevent long training runs. name: XPR Rendering Pipeline
head: Extensible Cross-Platform Point-Based Differentiable Renderer, Extensible Cross-Platform Point-Based Differentiable Renderer pipeline, XPR Framework, XPR: An Extensible Cross-Platform Point-Based Differentiable Renderer
body: XPR is a framework for point-based differentiable rendering that decouples method-specific logic from the shared rendering pipeline, allowing new rendering methods to be implemented in a few hundred lines of code. It separates the core rasterization mechanics—parallelization, data layout, tiling, and differentiation—from the primitive evaluation logic, enabling portable execution across GPUs, TPUs, and CPUs via the XLA compiler. Unlike traditional CUDA/Vulkan implementations that require thousands of lines and manual backward passes for each new primitive type, XPR exposes a four-function interface that captures only the method-specific math, while the framework handles the rest. XPR decomposes the rendering pipeline into modular, statically shaped parallel operations. The pipeline is driven by four user-defined functions that capture method-specific logic: project, tilecull, pixelinfo, and evaluate. The framework handles primitive filtering, tile assignment, depth sorting, alpha-blending, and automatic differentiation via JAX/XLA. Inputs: A set of M 3D primitives (e.g., Gaussians), camera parameters (intrinsics/extrinsics), and image dimensions (W \times H). Outputs: A rendered image tensor of shape (H, W, C) and gradients for the primitive parameters. Primitives: Defined by the parent article's Gaussian representation. Tile Map (tileprimmap): A mapping from tile coordinates to a list of candidate 2D primitives that intersect the tile. Static Bounds: All tensor dimensions and loop trip counts are fixed at compile time. Dynamic sizes (e.g., number of visible primitives) are handled by padding unused entries and using fixed-trip-count loops with early exits. Trip-Count Bins: Tiles are sorted by primitive count and partitioned into bins. Each bin is processed with a static trip count equal to its upper bound to optimize parallelization. P{max}: Maximum number of primitives per tile/pixel. Default is 4096 (XPR-4K). Lowering this increases frame rate but may skip contributions from distant or small primitives. Tile Size: Standard rectangular tiles (e.g., 16 \times 16 pixels). 1. Preprocess (Project): Apply project to each of the N primitives independently via mapfn. This transforms 3D primitives into 2D screen-space representations (e.g., 2D covariance matrices). 2. Filter (Cull): Perform a conservative bounding-box check (e.g., intersect8) for each primitive against the image bounds. Assign visible primitives to tiles. For each primitive-tile pair, call tilecull to refine the intersection test. If the primitive does not intersect the tile, discard it. Populate tileprimmap with the surviving primitive-tile pairs. 3. Rasterizer (Shader): Iterate over each tile t in tileprimmap. Sort tiles by primitive count and bin them to determine static loop bounds. For each pixel (x, y) in tile t: Call pixelinfo(x, y, cam, view) to generate pixel-specific data pxdata (e.g., ray direction, view vector). Initialize accumulated color C = 0 and transmittance T = 1. Iterate over each candidate primitive p{2D} in tileprimmap[t]. Retrieve shader data psd for the primitive. Call evaluate(pxdata, psd) to compute opacity \alpha, validity valid, and color c. Accumulate color: C = C + c \cdot \alpha \cdot \text{valid} \cdot T. Update transmittance: T = (1 - \alpha \cdot \text{valid}) \cdot T. Store C in the output image at (x, y). The alpha-blending accumulation for each pixel is: C = C + c \cdot \alpha \cdot \text{valid} \cdot T T = (1 - \alpha \cdot \text{valid}) \cdot T Where: C: Accumulated color. c: Primitive color (from evaluate). \alpha: Primitive opacity (from evaluate). valid: Validity flag (from evaluate, typically 1 if the primitive contributes, 0 otherwise). T: Accumulated transmittance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def project(primitive3D): # Returns 2D representation (e.g., mean, covariance) pass def tilecull(tmin, tmax, primitivetiledata): # Returns True if primitive intersects tile [tmin, tmax] pass def pixelinfo(px, cam, view): # Returns pixel-specific data (e.g., ray direction) pass def evaluate(pxdata, primitiveshaderdata): # Returns (alpha, valid, color) pass def render(primitives, cam, view, imageshape): # 1. Preprocess: Project all primitives # mapfn applies project to each primitive independently prims2D = mapfn(project, primitives) # 2. Filter: Assign to tiles and cull tileprimmap = {} # Filter visible primitives prims2Dvisible = [] for prim2D in prims2D: if getvisible(prim2D): prims2Dvisible.append(prim2D) # Assign to tiles and cull for prim2D in prims2Dvisible: # Conservative bounding box check if not intersects(prim2D, imagebounds): continue # Get tile boundaries for this primitive tiles = getintersectingtiles(prim2D) for t in tiles: tmin, tmax = computetileboundaries(t) ptcd = gettileculldata(prim2D) # User-defined culling if not tilecull(tmin, tmax, ptcd): continue if t not in tileprimmap: tileprimmap[t] = [] tileprimmap[t].append(prim2D) # 3. Rasterize: Render each tile # Sort tiles by primitive count for binning sortedtiles = sorttilesbyprimitivecount(tileprimmap) # Bin tiles to handle variable primitive counts with static loops bins = partitionintobins(sortedtiles) for bin in bins: # Static trip count for this bin maxprimsinbin = getbinupperbound(bin) # Parallelize over tiles in the bin for t in bin.tiles: candidates = tileprimmap[t] # Pad candidates to maxprimsinbin if necessary paddedcandidates = padtosize(candidates, maxprimsinbin) # Parallelize over pixels in the tile for (x, y) in t.pixels: pxdata = pixelinfo((x, y), cam, view) C = 0 T = 1 # Fixed trip count loop for i in range(maxprimsinbin): prim2D = paddedcandidates[i] # Early exit if no more primitives if i >= len(candidates): break psd = getshaderdata(prim2D) alpha, valid, c = evaluate(pxdata, psd) C = C + c alpha valid T T = (1 - alpha valid) T img[x, y] = C return img Dynamic Sizes: The number of visible primitives and tile intersections varies per frame. XPR handles this by fixing dimensions to compile-time upper bounds and padding unused entries. Performance vs. Quality Trade-off: Lowering P{max} (e.g., to 4096) increases frame rate but may skip contributions from primitives that exceed the limit, potentially reducing PSNR. Compiler Overhead: JAX/XLA kernel launch overhead can be significant at very high frame rates (e.g., synthetic scenes). Method-Specific Costs: Methods like 3DGUT, which require per-pixel world-space ray directions, may be slower in XPR than in hand-optimized CUDA because the ray direction computation is exposed via pixelinfo rather than fused into the blending loop. Time Complexity: The pipeline is decomposed into modules with explicit parallelism dimensions (primitives, tiles, pixels). The complexity is dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(T \cdot P{avg}) where T is the number of tiles and P{avg} is the average number of primitives per tile. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the static upper bounds of primitives per tile and the number of tiles. Padding unused entries increases memory usage slightly. Performance: On NVIDIA L40S GPUs, XPR achieves rendering speeds that are, on average, 97.18% of hand-optimized CUDA baselines. It can be up to 208.18% faster than baseline implementations for certain methods (e.g., LinPrim) due to more aggressive culling strategies. Scalability: XPR scales across hardware platforms (GPUs, TPUs, CPUs) without code changes, though absolute performance depends on the maturity of the XLA backend for each target. Strengths: Portability: Runs on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel GPUs, TPUs, and CPUs. Ease of Use: New methods can be implemented in 260–304 lines of Python, compared to thousands in CUDA. Automatic Differentiation: Gradients flow through the four interface functions automatically via JAX. Limitations: Compiler Dependency: Performance is bounded by the maturity of the XLA backend. Not for Ray Marching: Techniques involving ray marching or ray tracing (e.g., NeRFs, physically-based rendering) cannot be expressed with XPR. Overhead for Complex Pixel Info: Methods requiring complex per-pixel computations (like 3DGUT) may suffer from overhead compared to fused CUDA implementations. XPR was introduced in the paper "XPR: An Extensible Cross-Platform Point-Based Differentiable Renderer". It addresses the limitations of existing frameworks (written in CUDA/Vulkan) that require thousands of lines of code per method and manual backward passes. XPR leverages JAX/XLA to provide a high-level programming interface that separates method-specific logic from the shared rendering pipeline. It was demonstrated with implementations of 3DGS, 3DGUT, and LinPrim. name: Rasterization Pipeline Optimization
body: Rasterization Pipeline Optimization refers to algorithmic and hardware techniques that accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering by reducing computational overhead in tile intersection, sorting, and alpha compositing. It solves the bottleneck where standard rasterization overestimates Gaussian extents, processes non-intersecting pixels, and suffers from serial blending latency Child. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer (which focuses on the differentiable math) or 3D Gaussian Splatting MVP (which focuses on memory layout) is the explicit restructuring of the rendering pipeline stages—specifically moving culling to parallel preprocess phases, replacing coarse bounding-box tests with precise geometric checks, and co-designing hardware units for projection and sorting ChildChildChild. All methods in this family operate on the standard tile-based rasterization model for 3DGS, where the image is divided into fixed-size tiles (typically 16 \times 16 pixels) ChildChildChild. The core optimization principle is the reduction of the "work" performed by the pixel-level render kernel. This is achieved through: 1. Early Culling: Moving the determination of Gaussian-tile intersection from the serial render stage to the parallel preprocess stage Child. This prevents the allocation of memory and processing time for Gaussians that do not contribute to the final image Child. 2. Precise Intersection: Replacing the coarse Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) test of the projected 2D covariance ellipse with precise geometric checks (e.g., ellipse-AABB intersection or adaptive radius bounding circles) to minimize false positives Child. 3. Depth Sorting: Maintaining a depth-sorted list of Gaussians per tile to enable correct front-to-back alpha compositing, often using hardware-accelerated or radix-sort based approaches ChildChild. 4. Alpha Compositing: The final pixel color C(p) is computed via front-to-back blending: C(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai(p) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(p)) where \mathcal{N} is the set of surviving Gaussians in the tile, sorted by depth Child. The opacity \alphai(p) is defined as: \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) where \sigmai is the Gaussian opacity and gi(p) is the projected 2D Gaussian value at pixel p Child. A GPU-accelerated pipeline that replaces coarse bounding-box tile intersection tests with precise Gaussian-tile intersection checks and sorting-based depth ordering. It addresses the inefficiency of standard 3D-GS rasterization, which overestimates Gaussian extents and processes non-intersecting pixels, by generating a sparse set of Gaussian-tile pairs and sorting them for efficient pixel-wise compositing. Choose this method when software-based optimization is required without hardware changes, specifically to reduce the number of Gaussians processed per tile. A hardware-algorithm co-design that augments standard triangle rasterizers with dedicated hardware units for Gaussian projection and blending, achieving an order-of-magnitude speedup in the rasterization stage. It solves the computational bottleneck of projecting and compositing 3D Gaussians by replacing general-purpose compute shaders with a specialized four-stage pipeline. Unlike sibling methods that rely on software-based sorting and blending on GPUs, this approach isolates near-plane culling and projection into point-based preprocessing stages, while handling sorting and rasterization in tile-based rendering stages. Choose this when hardware access or FPGA/ASIC implementation is feasible. A rendering acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that optimizes the rasterization pipeline by moving serial culling operations to the parallel Preprocess stage and balancing computational loads across pixel threads. It achieves significant speedups without reducing the total number of Gaussians, thereby avoiding the quality degradation associated with pruning-based methods like EAGLES or LightGaussian. Unlike siblings that rely on hardware-specific optimizations or global Gaussian reduction, AdR-Gaussian focuses on algorithmic efficiency within the standard tile-based rasterizer by using adaptive radii and axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABB) for early culling. Choose this when maintaining high visual fidelity is critical and software-side load balancing is needed. Definition: Packs per-splat data (center, covariance, DC color/alpha, optional SH) into Texture Buffer Objects (TBOs) for GPU consumption. Step: Iterate over splats. For each splat, copy center.xyz as raw float bits to d[0..2]. Pack covariance upper-triangle to d[3..5] using packHalf2x16: d[3]=covA[0],covA[1]; d[4]=covA[2],covB[0]; d[5]=covB[1],covB[2]. Pack DC color/alpha to d[6] using packDCColor. Create GLTEXTUREBUFFER buffer with GLRGBA32UI format. Bind to tbotex. For non-DC SH coefficients, pack each coefficient's RGB into RGBA16F texels (B=0), layout is [splat0c1, splat0c2, …, splat1c1, splat1c2, …]. Create SH TBO with GLRGBA16F format. Parameter: shcoeffspersplat = (activeshdegree + 1)^2 - 1 (excludes DC). Layout: Base TBO: 2 uvec4 texels per splat (32 B). Texel 0: center.xyz (float bits), packHalf2x16(cov00, cov01). Texel 1: packHalf2x16(cov02, cov11), packHalf2x16(cov12, cov22), packUnorm4x8(DC-baked RGBA), reserved. SH TBO: GLRGBA16F, 8 B per non-DC SH coefficient per splat. Layout: [splat0c1, splat0c2, …, splat1c1, splat1c2, …]. Complexity: Memory: 32 B/splat for base TBO + 8 B × shcoeffspersplat × splatcount for SH TBO. Definition: A rendering optimization where color and depth are rendered in a single rasterization process, reducing runtime compared to separate passes. Context: This optimization is noted in dense RGBD SLAM methods based on 3D Gaussian representation, where rendering full-resolution images requires more time per iteration but converges faster than sparse sampling methods. It is faster than methods like SplaTAM because it avoids two separate rasterization processes. The optimization of the 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline emerged alongside the initial publication of 3DGS Parent. As 3DGS gained popularity for novel view synthesis and SLAM, the computational cost of rendering millions of Gaussians became a primary bottleneck. Early implementations used coarse bounding boxes for culling, leading to significant overdraw. Subsequent works like Speedy-Splat Child and AdR-Gaussian Child introduced precise geometric culling and load balancing ChildChild. Concurrently, hardware-oriented approaches Child explored dedicated silicon units for projection and sorting Child.
