name: Speedy-Splat Rendering Pipeline
head: Speedy-Splat
body: The Speedy-Splat rendering pipeline is a CUDA-based optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces coarse bounding box culling with precise geometric intersection tests and a parallel tile-sorting architecture to reduce redundant pixel computations. It distinguishes itself from standard rasterization by explicitly addressing the overestimation of Gaussian extents and model overparameterization, ensuring that only Gaussians with significant contribution to specific tiles are processed during the pixel-wise compositing stage. The pipeline operates on a tile-based rasterization model, dividing the image into fixed-size tiles (typically 16 \times 16 pixels). The method consists of a preprocessing phase to identify and sort relevant Gaussians, followed by a pixel-parallel rendering kernel. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each defined by 3D mean \mui, 3D covariance \Sigmai, opacity \sigmai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color ci. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Image resolution and tile dimensions. Outputs: Final image color buffer C(p) for each pixel p. 1. Key Array: Stores pairs of (tileindex, depth) for every Gaussian-tile intersection. The size of this array equals the total number of intersecting Gaussian-tile pairs. 2. Value Array: Stores the Gaussian index corresponding to each key. 3. Tile Ranges: An array indicating the start and end indices in the sorted Key/Value arrays for each tile. 1. Precise Tile Intersection (duplicateWithKeys): For each Gaussian Gi, compute its projected 2D mean \mu{i{2D}} and covariance \Sigma{i{2D}}. Unlike standard methods that use an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) derived from the maximum eigenvalue, Speedy-Splat performs precise intersection tests to determine which tiles the Gaussian actually covers. For each intersecting tile t, generate a key consisting of the tile index and the Gaussian's depth zi. 2. Inclusive Sum (InclusiveSum): Compute the prefix sum of the number of intersecting tiles per Gaussian to allocate the exact size for the Key and Value arrays. 3. Sorting (RadixSort): Sort the Key array using a CUDA Radix Sort primitive. The sorting order is primarily by tile index, and secondarily by Gaussian depth (ascending). This ensures that for any given tile, the Gaussians are ordered from front to back. 4. Tile Range Identification (identifyTileRanges): Process the sorted Key array to determine the contiguous range of indices in the Key/Value arrays that correspond to each tile. This allows the render kernel to quickly locate the relevant Gaussians for a specific tile. 5. Pixel Rendering (Render Kernel): The render kernel is parallelized across pixels. For each pixel p: a. Identify the tile t containing p. b. Retrieve the range of Gaussians for tile t from the sorted arrays. c. Iterate through the Gaussians in depth order. d. Compute the projected 2D Gaussian value gi at pixel p: gi = e^q q = -\frac{1}{2}(p - \mu{i{2D}})\Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1}(p - \mu{i{2D}})^T where p is the pixel coordinate, \mu{i{2D}} is the 2D mean, and \Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1} is the inverse 2D covariance. e. Compute the alpha value \alphai(p): \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) where \sigmai is the Gaussian opacity. f. Thresholding: If \alphai > 255, include the Gaussian in the compositing. Note: The source specifies a threshold of 255, implying a fixed-point or scaled integer representation of alpha, or a specific implementation detail where alpha is compared against an integer threshold. g. Compositing: Accumulate the color using front-to-back blending: C(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai(p) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(p)) where \mathcal{N} is the set of Gaussians in the tile that passed the threshold, sorted by depth. Precise Intersection keys = [] values = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Project 3D Gaussian to 2D mu2d, Sigma2d = project2d(g.mu3d, g.Sigma3d, camera) depth = g.mu3d.z # Or appropriate depth metric # Find intersecting tiles using precise geometry intersectingtiles = findpreciseintersectingtiles(mu2d, Sigma2d, imagedims) for tileidx in intersectingtiles: keys.append((tileidx, depth)) values.append(i) # 2. Inclusive Sum to determine array sizes tilecounts = counttilespergaussian(gaussians) offsets = inclusivesum(tilecounts) # 3. Radix Sort # Sort keys by tileidx (primary) and depth (secondary) sortedindices = radixsort(keys) sortedkeys = [keys[i] for i in sortedindices] sortedvalues = [values[i] for i in sortedindices] # 4. Identify Tile Ranges tileranges = computeranges(sortedkeys) return sortedkeys, sortedvalues, tileranges def renderpixel(p, sortedkeys, sortedvalues, tileranges, gaussians): tileidx = gettileindex(p, imagedims) start, end = tileranges[tileidx] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 finalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Iterate through Gaussians in this tile, sorted by depth for k in range(start, end): gidx = sortedvalues[k] g = gaussians[gidx] # Compute 2D Gaussian value at pixel p mu2d, Sigma2dinv = getprojectedparams(g, camera) q = -0.5 dot((p - mu2d), Sigma2dinv (p - mu2d).T) gval = exp(q) # Compute alpha alpha = g.opacity gval # Threshold check (Source specifies > 255, assuming scaled int or specific impl) # In standard float [0,1], this condition would never be met. # Assuming the source implies a scaled integer representation or a typo for a small epsilon. # However, we must follow the source literally. if alpha > 255: # Compositing color = g.color finalcolor += color alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedalpha += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) # Early exit if fully opaque if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break return finalcolor Alpha Threshold: The source explicitly states the condition \alphai > 255. In standard floating-point implementations where \alpha \in [0, 1], this condition is impossible. This suggests either a fixed-point representation (e.g., 8-bit integer alpha where 255 is max) or a specific implementation detail not fully elaborated in the provided text. Implementers should verify the data type of \alpha in the source code context. Precision: The precise intersection test avoids false positives from AABB culling, reducing the number of Gaussians processed per pixel. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has a singular 2D covariance matrix, the inverse \Sigma{i{2D}}^{-1} is undefined. Standard regularization or clamping of eigenvalues is required. Time Complexity: The sorting step dominates the preprocessing phase with O(N \log N) complexity, where N is the number of Gaussian-tile intersections. The rendering phase is O(P \cdot K), where P is the number of pixels and K is the average number of Gaussians per tile after culling. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Key and Value arrays, proportional to the number of intersections. This is typically larger than the number of Gaussians but smaller than the naive P \times G matrix. Performance: Speedy-Splat achieves significant speedups by reducing the number of Gaussians processed per pixel through precise culling and efficient parallel sorting. Strengths: Reduces overestimation of Gaussian extents; handles overparameterized models efficiently. Limitations: The sorting step adds overhead; the alpha threshold condition (>255) requires careful implementation regarding data types. Speedy-Splat was introduced in the paper "Speedy-Splat: Fast 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Pixels and Sparse Primitives". The method addresses inefficiencies in the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, specifically the overestimation of Gaussian extents and the computational cost associated with overparameterized models. It builds on the tile-based rasterization model common in modern GPU architectures. name: Hardware-Accelerated Gaussian Rasterization
head: GauRast, Hardware Architecture Pipeline, Hardware-algorithm co-design for Gaussian rasterization
body: Hardware-Accelerated Gaussian Rasterization is a hardware-algorithm co-design that augments standard triangle rasterizers with dedicated units for Gaussian projection and blending, achieving an order of magnitude speedup in the rasterization stage. It implements a four-stage pipeline where preprocessing (Stages 0–1) is point-based and rendering (Stages 2–3) is tile-based. It differs from sibling methods like Speedy-Splat Rendering Pipeline by its specific focus on dedicated silicon units for projection and sorting rather than purely algorithmic software optimizations. The method implements a four-stage hardware pipeline. The first two stages constitute preprocessing (point-based), and the last two constitute rendering (tile-based). Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and camera matrices. Output: Final 2D image pixels. Data Structures: Tile Assignment: The image is divided into 16 \times 16 pixel tiles. Each tile is assigned to an independent SRAM bank with a fixed entry depth and address offset controller. Codebook: An index is used to look up corresponding values stored in the SRAM codebook. Sorting Buffer: The sorting unit outputs the current maximum value in a linear sorting delay, aligning with the rasterization unit's need to process one point at a time. Pipeline Stages: 1. Stage 0: Near-plane Culling Eliminates parameter access for invisible regions using an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) depth-interval test. This stage is isolated to handle the largest number of Gaussian points efficiently. 2. Stage 1: Projection Projects 3D Gaussians onto the 2D image plane. Uses a 6x1 multiplier-accumulator array. Implements zero-Jacobian skipping to optimize computation. 3. Stage 2: Gaussian Sorting Sorts Gaussians per tile to enable correct front-to-back alpha compositing. Uses a four-way sub-sorter parallelism based on a comparison-free sorter design. Each sub-sorter processes 256 data elements at a time. The design outputs the current maximum value in a linear sorting delay, which aligns with the rasterization unit's need to process one point at a time. 4. Stage 3: Rasterization Performs alpha-blending, processing one point at a time aligned with the sorting output. Uses the tile-based model where each tile operates on its assigned SRAM bank. Alpha Compositing: The final pixel color C(p) is computed via front-to-back blending: C(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai(p) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(p)) where \mathcal{N} is the set of surviving Gaussians in the tile, sorted by depth. The opacity \alphai(p) is defined as: \alphai(p) = \sigmai gi(p) where \sigmai is the Gaussian opacity and gi(p) is the projected 2D Gaussian value at pixel p. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def stage0cull(gaussians, cameranearplane): """Stage 0: Near-plane Culling. Eliminates Gaussians outside the near-plane using AABB depth test.""" valid = [] for g in gaussians: if g.mindepth > cameranearplane: valid.append(g) return valid def stage1project(gaussians, cameramatrix): """Stage 1: Projection. Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D with zero-Jacobian skipping.""" projected = [] for g in gaussians: proj = project3dto2d(g, cameramatrix) if abs(proj.jacobiandet) > 1e-6: projected.append(proj) return projected def project3dto2d(g, cam): """Standard 3D to 2D projection helper.""" return type('Gaussian2D', (), { 'x': g.x, 'y': g.y, 'cov': g.cov, 'jacobiandet': 1.0, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'color': g.color, 'depth': g.z })() def stage2sort(projectedgaussians, tilesize=16): """Stage 2: Gaussian Sorting. Sorts Gaussians per tile using comparison-free sub-sorters.""" tiles = {} for g in projectedgaussians: tx, ty = int(g.x // tilesize), int(g.y // tilesize) key = (tx, ty) if key not in tiles: tiles[key] = [] tiles[key].append(g) sortedtiles = [] for key, glist in tiles.items(): # Hardware uses four-way sub-sorter parallelism (256 elements/sub-sorter) # Outputs current maximum value in linear sorting delay sortedg = sorted(glist, key=lambda x: x.depth, reverse=True) sortedtiles.append({'key': key, 'gaussians': sortedg}) return sortedtiles def stage3rasterize(sortedtiles, imagewidth, imageheight): """Stage 3: Rasterization. Performs alpha-blending per tile using SRAM codebook lookup.""" image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight imagewidth)] for tile in sortedtiles: tiledata = lookupsram(tile['key']) tx, ty = tile['key'] for g in tile['gaussians']: for py in range(ty 16, min((ty + 1) 16, imageheight)): for px in range(tx 16, min((tx + 1) 16, imagewidth)): idx = py imagewidth + px alpha = g.opacity gaussianvalue(g, (px, py)) if alpha > 1e-4: current = image[idx] image[idx] = [ current[0] (1 - alpha) + g.color[0] alpha, current[1] (1 - alpha) + g.color[1] alpha, current[2] (1 - alpha) + g.color[2] alpha ] return image def gaussianvalue(g, pixel): """Evaluate projected 2D Gaussian at pixel.""" dx, dy = pixel[0] - g.x, pixel[1] - g.y var = g.cov[0][0] if len(g.cov) > 0 else 1.0 return math.exp(-0.5 (dx2 + dy2) / var) def updatepixelalphablend(image, pixel, color, alpha): """Front-to-back alpha compositing update.""" px, py = pixel idx = py image.shape[1] + px current = image[idx] image[idx] = current (1 - alpha) + color alpha def lookupsram(tilekey): """Simulate SRAM codebook lookup for tile metadata.""" return tilekey A renderer for compressed scenes using GPU sorting and rasterization, enabling real-time novel view synthesis on low-end devices and integration with polygonal rendering. It renders the scene using hardware rasterization instead of the specialized compute pipeline used in original 3D Gaussian Splatting. This differs from the original compute pipeline by using hardware rasterization, allowing seamless integration into VR/AR environments or games alongside polygon models. A dedicated hardware accelerator designed to accelerate 3DGS by enabling early stages to process subsequent frames while later stages execute previous ones, improving parallelism and pipeline efficiency. It enhances the Culling and Conversion Unit (CCU) by replacing GSCore’s dual OBB Intersection Test Units (OIUs) with a square root and logarithmic operator to support the two-stage accurate intersection test. The Viewpoint Transformation Unit (VTU) performs sparse rendering by retrieving pixel colors and maximum depths from the reference frame and performing three matrix multiplications: mapping 2D pixels to 3D space, transforming the point cloud, and reprojecting onto the new camera plane. The VTU Tile Classification uses a counter array to track validly projected pixels per tile; if the count exceeds 56 (of total pixels in tile), the tile is interpolated, otherwise it is forwarded to the Volume Rendering Unit (VRU) for full re-rendering. The architecture includes CCU, Load Distribution Unit (LDU), VTU, VRU, Sorting Unit, and Interpolation Unit. Performance: Achieves an order of magnitude speedup in the rasterization stage compared to standard compute pipelines. Hardware: Implemented as a dedicated hardware accelerator, often built upon existing graphics cores (e.g., GSCore) with enhanced units. Complexity: The pipeline isolates near-plane culling to handle the largest number of points, optimizing computational resources. Limitations: Data dependencies in the multiplier-accumulator arrays limit the ability to fully parallelize operations, as certain computations must wait for completion of others. Use Case: Suitable for real-time rendering on constrained hardware or when integration with standard polygonal rasterization is required. Hardware-accelerated Gaussian rasterization emerged as a hardware-algorithm co-design to augment standard triangle rasterizers with dedicated units for Gaussian projection and blending. Subsequent developments, such as LS-Gaussian, introduced streaming mechanisms and specific hardware enhancements like square root and logarithmic operators to improve pipeline efficiency and reduce stalls. The approach represents a shift from purely algorithmic optimizations to dedicated silicon implementations. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A 129 FPS Full HD Real-Time Accelerator for 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2026.3683714, fetched 2026-10-27 From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06157, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Compressed 3D Gaussian Splatting for Accelerated Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00985, fetched 2026-10-26 No Redundancy, No Stall: Lightweight Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-time Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccad66269.2025.11240950, fetched 2026-10-30

name: AdR-Gaussian
head: Adaptive Radius Gaussian Splatting
body: AdR-Gaussian is a rendering acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that optimizes the rasterization pipeline by moving serial culling operations from the Render stage to the parallel Preprocess stage and balancing computational loads across pixel threads. It achieves significant speedups without reducing the total number of Gaussians, thereby avoiding the quality degradation associated with pruning-based methods. Unlike its siblings, which often rely on reducing Gaussian counts or hardware-specific optimizations, AdR-Gaussian focuses on algorithmic pipeline efficiency through adaptive radius culling and load balancing. AdR-Gaussian accelerates rendering by reducing the computational cost of the Render stage, which typically accounts for over 50% of the total rasterization time due to serial alpha blending and complex splatting calculations. The method operates in two phases: Early Culling and Load Balancing. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by center position \mathbf{X}0, 3D covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \sigma, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Camera parameters for projection. Outputs: A rendered image where each pixel color C(p) is computed via front-to-back alpha compositing. The method utilizes the standard tile-based rasterization pipeline structure: 1. Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores \sigmai, \mathbf{X}0, \Sigma, and SH coefficients. 2. Tile Grid: The image is divided into fixed-size tiles, typically 16 \times 16 pixels. 3. Gaussian-Tile Pairs: A list of pairs (Gi, Tj) indicating which Gaussians overlap with which tiles, generated during the Preprocess stage. 4. Sorted Lists: For each tile, Gaussians are sorted by view-space depth to enable correct alpha compositing. \alpha{low}: A predefined minimum splatting opacity constant used as the threshold for culling. Tile Size: Typically 16 \times 16 pixels. This phase moves culling from the serial Render stage to the parallel Preprocess stage to reduce the number of Gaussian-Tile pairs processed later. 1. Preprocess Stage (Parallel per Gaussian): For each Gaussian i: a. Compute the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma' based on the camera view. b. Calculate the Adaptive Radius (r{ad}): i. Define the ellipse of minimum splatting opacity \alpha{low} using the inequality: \mathbf{x}^T \Sigma'^{-1} \mathbf{x} \le 2 \ln \left( \frac{\sigmai}{\alpha{low}} \right) where \mathbf{x} is the 2D vector from the Gaussian center to a pixel. ii. Expand this into the general ellipse form A x^2 + B y^2 + C xy + D \le 0, with coefficients: A = \Sigma'{YY}, \quad B = \Sigma'{XX}, \quad C = -2\Sigma'{XY} D = -2 \sqrt{\Sigma'{XX} \Sigma'{YY} - \Sigma'{XY}^2} \ln \left( \frac{\sigmai}{\alpha{low}} \right) iii. Calculate r{ad} as half the major axis length of this ellipse. c. Calculate the Original Radius (ro): i. Determine the radius based on the 99% confidence interval of the Gaussian. d. Determine the Final Culling Radius (r): r = \min(r{ad}, ro) Note: If \sigmai is high or \alpha{low} is low, r{ad} may exceed ro. Clamping to ro ensures the rendering range does not exceed the standard confidence interval. e. AABB Culling: i. Calculate the maximum x and y coordinates (x{max}, y{max}) of the ellipse defined in step 1.b. ii. Set half-width w = x{max} and half-height h = y{max}. iii. Use the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by w and h to cull tiles, which provides more accurate culling in the minor axis direction than the circular adaptive radius. f. Identify all tiles overlapping with the Gaussian using the calculated AABB and generate Gaussian-Tile pairs. 2. Pipeline Stages: The generated pairs proceed through the standard pipeline stages: InclusiveSum & DuplicateWithKeys: Parallel processing to gather tile coverage information. SortPairs: Sort Gaussian-Tile pairs. IdentifyTileRanges: Determine start/end indices for each tile. This phase addresses the uneven computational load across pixel threads caused by varying numbers of Gaussians per pixel. 1. Assess Load: Quantify the variance in the number of Gaussians required for rendering each pixel. 2. Adjust Gaussian Count: For heavy-load pixels (high variance/many Gaussians): Reduce the number of rendered Gaussians to minimize thread waiting time. For light-load pixels (low variance/few Gaussians): Increase the number of rendered Gaussians to hedge against quality loss. 3. Render: Execute the Render stage in parallel for all pixels using the balanced set of Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class Gaussian: def init(self, center2d, opacity, projectedcovariance, color, depth): self.center2d = np.array(center2d, dtype=float) self.opacity = opacity self.projectedcovariance = np.array(projectedcovariance, dtype=float) self.color = np.array(color, dtype=float) self.depth = depth def computeellipseparams(sigmaprime, sigmai, alphalow): SigmaXX = sigmaprime[0, 0] SigmaYY = sigmaprime[1, 1] SigmaXY = sigmaprime[0, 1] A = SigmaYY B = SigmaXX C = -2 SigmaXY D = -2 math.sqrt(SigmaXX SigmaYY - SigmaXY2) math.log(sigmai / alphalow) return A, B, C, D, SigmaXX, SigmaYY, SigmaXY def getadaptiveradius(A, B, C, D): M = np.array([[A, C/2], [C/2, B]]) eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvals(M) lambdamin = min(eigenvalues) if lambdamin <= 0: return 0.0 return math.sqrt(-D / lambdamin) def getaabbextents(A, B, C, D): det = 4 A B - C C if det <= 0: return 0.0, 0.0 xmax = math.sqrt(-D 4 B / det) ymax = math.sqrt(-D 4 A / det) return xmax, ymax def getoriginalradius99(sigmaprime): # Standard 99% confidence interval for 2D Gaussian eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvals(sigmaprime) lambdamax = max(eigenvalues) return math.sqrt(-2 math.log(0.01) lambdamax) def adrgaussianpreprocess(gaussians, alphalow, tilesize=16): gaussiantilepairs = [] for g in gaussians: sigmai = g.opacity sigmaprime = g.projectedcovariance center = g.center2d A, B, C, D,,, = computeellipseparams(sigmaprime, sigmai, alphalow) rad = getadaptiveradius(A, B, C, D) ro = getoriginalradius99(sigmaprime) r = min(rad, ro) # AABB culling for tighter bounds in minor axis xmax, ymax = getaabbextents(A, B, C, D) w, h = xmax, ymax # Determine tiles covered by AABB mintx = math.floor((center[0] - w) / tilesize) maxtx = math.ceil((center[0] + w) / tilesize) - 1 minty = math.floor((center[1] - h) / tilesize) maxty = math.ceil((center[1] + h) / tilesize) - 1 for ty in range(minty, maxty + 1): for tx in range(mintx, maxtx + 1): gaussiantilepairs.append((g, (tx, ty))) return gaussiantilepairs def adrgaussianloadbalance(gaussiantilepairs, tilesize=16): # Count Gaussians per pixel pixelgaussians = {} for g, tile in gaussiantilepairs: for py in range(tile[1] tilesize, (tile[1] + 1) tilesize): for px in range(tile[0] tilesize, (tile[0] + 1) tilesize): pixelkey = (px, py) if pixelkey not in pixelgaussians: pixelgaussians[pixelkey] = [] pixelgaussians[pixelkey].append(g) # Balance load: target count is median of all pixel counts counts = [len(gs) for gs in pixelgaussians.values()] targetcount = sorted(counts)[len(counts) // 2] balancedpairs = [] for p, gs in pixelgaussians.items(): if len(gs) > targetcount: # Heavy-load: reduce to target count (keep first N by depth) gssorted = sorted(gs, key=lambda x: x.depth) gs = gssorted[:targetcount] elif len(gs) < targetcount: # Light-load: increase by relaxing culling thresholds pass for g in gs: balancedpairs.append((g, p)) return balancedpairs def render(balancedpairs, tilesize=16, imageheight=1080, imagewidth=1920): # Group by tile tilegaussians = {} for g, p in balancedpairs: tx, ty = p[0] // tilesize, p[1] // tilesize if (tx, ty) not in tilegaussians: tilegaussians[(tx, ty)] = [] tilegaussians[(tx, ty)].append(g) image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for tile, gs in tilegaussians.items(): gssorted = sorted(gs, key=lambda x: x.depth) for py in range(tile[1] tilesize, (tile[1] + 1) tilesize): for px in range(tile[0] tilesize, (tile[0] + 1) tilesize): alpha = 0.0 color = np.zeros(3) for g in gssorted: dx = px - g.center2d[0] dy = py - g.center2d[1] x = np.array([dx, dy]) alphai = g.opacity math.exp(-0.5 x.T @ np.linalg.inv(g.projectedcovariance) @ x) color += g.color alphai (1 - alpha) alpha += alphai (1 - alpha) if alpha > 0.99: break image[py, px] = color return image Pre-rendering Frustum Culling is an engineering optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates unnecessary Gaussians from rasterization input by explicitly computing and storing in-frustum indices before the rendering kernel executes. Unlike standard implementations where frustum culling is fused into rendering kernels and computed implicitly by CUDA threads without explicit storage, this method explicitly stores indices to allow the elimination of non-in-frustum Gaussians from the input tensor, thereby reducing GPU memory usage and computation. Time Complexity: The Render stage (Ep) typically takes the largest proportion of computational cost (over 50%) due to serial alpha blending and complex splatting color calculation per Gaussian-Pixel pair. AdR-Gaussian reduces this by minimizing the number of Gaussian-Tile pairs entering the Render stage via early culling and balancing the load across pixel threads. Memory Complexity: By moving culling to the Preprocess stage and reducing the number of Gaussian-Tile pairs, memory usage for intermediate data structures (like the sorted lists) is reduced. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, the method attains an average 590 FPS rendering speed on a single NVIDIA RTX3090 GPU. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate an average 310% acceleration in rendering speed. Strengths: Achieves acceleration without rendering quality loss by optimizing the rasterization pipeline rather than reducing the Gaussian count. The AABB culling provides more accurate culling in minor axis directions than circular radii. Limitations: Requires additional computation in the Preprocess stage to calculate adaptive radii and AABBs. The load balancing phase adds complexity to the pipeline. When to Use: When high rendering speed is required without sacrificing quality, and the bottleneck is the serial Render stage of the standard 3DGS pipeline. When Not to Use: When the bottleneck is elsewhere (e.g., data transfer or preprocessing) or when hardware acceleration is available that handles these optimizations natively. AdR-Gaussian was proposed to address the issues of avoidable serial Gaussian culling and uneven load distribution in 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It builds on the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline. The method was introduced in the paper "AdR-Gaussian: Accelerating Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Radius". name: Pre-rendering Frustum Culling
head: Coarse Frustum Culling, Explicit Frustum Index Culling, Frustum Culling (Coarse), Frustum Pre-culling, Visibility Pre-culling
body: Pre-rendering Frustum Culling is an engineering optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates unnecessary Gaussians from rasterization input by explicitly computing and storing in-frustum indices before the rendering kernel executes. Unlike standard implementations where frustum culling is fused into rendering kernels and computed implicitly by CUDA threads without explicit storage, this method explicitly stores indices to allow the elimination of non-in-frustum Gaussians from the input tensor, thereby reducing GPU memory usage and computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The full set of 3D Gaussians defined by their parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and the camera frustum definition. Output: A subset of Gaussian indices Si representing only those Gaussians that intersect the camera frustum, and the corresponding subset of Gaussian data passed to the rasterization kernel. Data Structures: Index Buffer: A GPU memory buffer storing the integer indices Si. Gaussian Data Tensor: The input tensor to the rasterization kernel is filtered to contain only the data corresponding to indices in Si, reducing the original input size N to |Si|. Steps: 1. Launch a CUDA kernel (checkFrustum) with one thread per Gaussian (P) and a block size of 256. 2. In the kernel, compute the view-space position p{view} for each Gaussian and call infrustum to determine visibility, storing the boolean result in a present array. 3. Collect the indices of visible Gaussians into Si and store them in GPU memory prior to rendering kernel execution. 4. Pass only the Gaussians in Si to the rasterization kernels, reducing the input size from N to |Si|. Formulas: Let N be the total number of Gaussians. Let \rhoi be the ratio of in-frustum Gaussians to total Gaussians for a given view, such that |Si| = \rhoi N. The reduction in input size is proportional to \rhoi. Parameters: Frustum Planes: Defined by the camera projection matrix and view volume. Bounding Volume: The method assumes a bounding volume for each Gaussian to perform the intersection test. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of the frustum intersection test affects the value of \rhoi. Dynamic Scenes: If the camera or Gaussians move rapidly, the pre-computed indices Si may become stale if not updated every frame. Memory Overhead: Storing the index buffer Si adds a small memory overhead, but this is offset by the reduction in Gaussian data passed to the kernel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def prerenderingfrustumculling(gaussians, camerafrustum): """ Perform pre-rendering frustum culling for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: gaussians: Tensor of shape (N, D) containing Gaussian parameters. camerafrustum: Object defining the six frustum planes and projection matrix. Returns: infrustumindices: Tensor of indices of Gaussians intersecting the frustum. filteredgaussians: Subset of Gaussian data corresponding to infrustumindices. """ present = [] for i, gaussian in enumerate(gaussians): # Compute view-space position and check visibility pview = transformtoviewspace(gaussian.position, camerafrustum.projectionmatrix) if infrustum(pview, camerafrustum.planes): present.append(i) # Store indices in GPU memory and filter data tensor filteredgaussians = gaussians[present] return present, filteredgaussians def infrustum(pview, planes): """Check if a view-space point is inside all six frustum planes.""" for plane in planes: if distancepointtoplane(pview, plane) > 0: return False return True def distancepointtoplane(point, plane): """Compute the signed distance from a point to a plane.""" return plane.normal.dot(point) - plane.distance A GPU-only training variant that incorporates pre-rendering frustum culling to skip unnecessary kernel computation, serving as a closer baseline for evaluating offloading overhead. It is used in the Grendel-GS training framework to provide a better comparison for CLM's offloading strategy. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussians processed by the rasterization kernel from N to |Si| = \rhoi N. Memory Complexity: Reduces GPU memory usage for Gaussian data passed to the kernel by a factor of \rhoi, while adding a small overhead for storing the index buffer Si. Measured Performance: Achieves a 3.9× rendering speed improvement while maintaining equivalent visual quality for real-world 360° scenes. Strengths: Simple engineering method; effective in large scenes with sparse Gaussians; reduces both memory and computation. Limitations: Requires an additional step to compute and store indices. When to Use: When rendering large scenes with low density of Gaussians within the camera frustum (\rhoi is small). Pre-rendering Frustum Culling was introduced in the CLM paper (2026) as part of the Grendel-GS training framework to remove the GPU memory barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was developed to address the inefficiency of standard 3DGS implementations where frustum culling is fused into rendering kernels, leading to wasted computation and memory for non-in-frustum Gaussians. The method is also applicable to traditional GPU-only training without offloading. name: Semantic and Structural Extensions
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by attaching high-dimensional feature vectors to Gaussian primitives or by modeling animatable human avatars from multi-view data. It differs from standard rendering by accumulating these feature vectors via differentiable alpha-blending rather than just color, and from sibling methods by rendering feature maps directly through differentiable alpha-compositing Semantic and Language Embeddings. For structural extensions, it solves dynamic appearance and geometry reconstruction by maintaining a canonical space representation where Gaussians are deformed via differentiable functions driven by pose parameters before rasterization Human and Articulated Avatars. All methods in this family rely on the differentiable alpha-blending accumulation of feature vectors or colors during the rasterization step. For a pixel p, the rendered vector \mathbf{V}(p) is computed by sorting overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back and applying: \mathbf{V}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{v}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: \mathbf{v}i is the vector (feature \mathbf{f}i or color \mathbf{c}i) of the i-th Gaussian. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance from all preceding Gaussians j < i. If \mathcal{O}p is empty, \mathbf{V}(p) = \mathbf{0}. For structural extensions, all methods share a canonical space representation where 3D Gaussians are initialized in a reference pose (e.g., T-pose or neutral expression). Deformation is achieved by mapping these canonical Gaussians to a target pose defined by parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients). The rendering pipeline remains differentiable, allowing optimization of Gaussian attributes and deformation parameters via photometric loss. The deformation function D(\cdot) maps a canonical Gaussian i with position \mathbf{p}i^{\text{canonical}} to a target position \mathbf{p}i^{\text{target}} based on pose parameters \theta: \mathbf{p}i^{\text{target}} = D(\mathbf{p}i^{\text{canonical}}, \theta) The rotation and scale of the Gaussian may also be transformed by the deformation function to maintain physical consistency. Attaches high-dimensional semantic or language feature vectors to each primitive for simultaneous photometric and semantic rasterization. Sets itself apart by hard-coding alignment between visual and semantic boundaries to eliminate boundary bleeding, unlike sibling methods that rely on external segmentation heads. Choose when real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation or CLIP-based comparison is required. [8130-semantic-and-language-embeddings.md] Reconstructs and renders animatable human avatars from multi-view or single-view inputs. Sets itself apart from static reconstruction methods by enabling novel view synthesis of dynamic subjects through learned deformation fields, and from mesh-based methods by leveraging explicit, differentiable 3D Gaussians for high-fidelity texture and geometry. Choose when dynamic geometry and appearance modeling of articulated subjects is needed. [8209-human-and-articulated-avatars.md] Attaches Gaussians onto mesh surfaces to reduce primitive count and improve fitting. Sets itself apart by combining rendered results from a textured human body mesh and Gaussians to address unbalanced aggregation from densification and splitting. Choose when surface-guided initialization or mesh-Gaussian hybrid rendering is required. MonoGaussianAvatar first applies 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic head reconstruction using canonical space modeling and deformation prediction. PSAvatar introduces the explicit FLAME face model to initialize Gaussians, capturing high-fidelity facial geometry and complicated volumetric objects like glasses. GaussianHead uses a tri-plane representation and motion fields to simulate geometrically changing heads in continuous movements. name: Semantic and Language Embeddings
head: SAM-guided Gaussian Grouping
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by attaching high-dimensional semantic or language feature vectors to each primitive, enabling simultaneous photometric and semantic rasterization within a unified differentiable alpha-compositing pipeline. It solves the problem of decoupled geometry and semantics by hard-coding alignment between visual boundaries and semantic boundaries, eliminating boundary bleeding. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on external segmentation heads or separate optimization streams, this approach renders feature maps directly through differentiable alpha-blending, allowing for real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and CLIP-based comparison. All methods in this family rely on the differentiable alpha-blending accumulation of feature vectors or colors during the rasterization step. For a pixel p, the rendered vector \mathbf{V}(p) is computed by sorting overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back and applying: \mathbf{V}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{v}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: \mathbf{v}i is the vector (feature \mathbf{f}i or color \mathbf{c}i) of the i-th Gaussian. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance from all preceding Gaussians j < i. If \mathcal{O}p is empty, \mathbf{V}(p) = \mathbf{0}. For structural extensions, all methods share a canonical space representation where 3D Gaussians are initialized in a reference pose (e.g., T-pose or neutral expression). Deformation is achieved by mapping these canonical Gaussians to a target pose defined by parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients). The rendering pipeline remains differentiable, allowing optimization of Gaussian attributes and deformation parameters via photometric loss. The deformation function D(\cdot) maps a canonical Gaussian i with position \mathbf{p}i^{canonical} to a target position \mathbf{p}i^{target} based on pose parameters \theta: \mathbf{p}i^{target} = D(\mathbf{p}i^{canonical}, \theta) The rotation and scale of the Gaussian may also be transformed by the deformation function to maintain physical consistency. Extends 3DGS by attaching a 512-dimensional semantic embedding vector to each primitive, enabling simultaneous photometric and semantic rasterization. It eliminates boundary bleeding by ensuring geometric parameters dictate blending weights for both color and semantics. Choose when hard-coded alignment between visual and semantic boundaries is required without external segmentation heads. Encodes object-level embeddings for phrase grounding in addition to pixel-level features, enabling open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and zero-shot reasoning via CLIP alignment. Choose when full scene understanding and phrase grounding are needed. Distills vision-language features into a scene-specific latent space via an autoencoder to compress features, allowing efficient querying using natural language text embeddings. Choose when memory efficiency is critical and high-frequency detail preservation is secondary to language grounding. Projects VLMs into the 3DGS framework to create a joint embedding space for 3D visual question answering and complex semantic queries. Choose when object-level embeddings and complex reasoning are required. Generates semantic text embeddings by appending directional view descriptors (e.g., 'front', 'side') to prompts, conditioning generation on the camera's viewing angle. Choose when view-dependent semantic consistency is required. Distills knowledge from the LSeg vision-language model to provide pixel-level or patch-level semantic supervision. Choose when localized semantic editing and zero-shot labeling without explicit 3D annotation are needed. Compresses VLM embeddings into latent attributes per Gaussian using a scene-specific autoencoder, aggregating them via splatting and decoding for semantic alignment. Choose when high memory consumption of explicit high-dimensional modeling must be avoided while preserving volumetric consistency. Searches a database of 3D models (3D-FUTURE) to find assets matching segmented objects in an input image using CLIP embeddings. Encode all renderings from the 3D-FUTURE database using CLIP into normalized 768-dimensional vectors. Crop a target image around each object's mask from the input image and encode it using CLIP. Select Nearest Neighbors in CLIP space using cosine distance to find the closest assets. Database: 3D-FUTURE dataset [Fu et al. 2021], containing 10,000+ artist-made models. Embedding dimension: 768. The concept of assigning per-Gaussian instance IDs supervised by SAM (Segment Anything Model) or video tracking was introduced as a method for Gaussian Grouping. The use of CLIP for zero-shot ranked classification of 3D geometries from databases like 3D-FUTURE was detailed in PSDR-Room, which encodes renderings into normalized 768-dimensional vectors to search for matching assets. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Vectors
head: Semantic-Extended 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering
body: This method extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by attaching a high-dimensional semantic embedding vector to each primitive, enabling simultaneous photometric and semantic rasterization within a unified alpha-compositing pipeline. It solves the problem of decoupled geometry and semantics by ensuring that the blending weights for semantic features are identical to those for color, thereby hard-coding alignment between visual and semantic boundaries. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which renders only color, this approach produces feature maps suitable for segmentation or CLIP comparison. It builds on Semantic and Language Embeddings by utilizing the shared differentiable alpha-blending accumulation principle. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives, each parameterized by position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color, and a semantic embedding vector. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices) are required for projection. Output: For each pixel p, a color value \mathbf{C}(p) and a semantic feature vector \mathbf{F}(p). Data Structures: Each primitive i stores the following attributes contiguously for rasterization: position: 3D vector \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. scale: 3D vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. rotation: Quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4. opacity: Scalar \alphai \in \mathbb{R}. shcoefficients: Set of coefficients for view-dependent color. semanticembedding: Vector \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^d (typically d=512). Steps: 1. Parameterization: Define each 3D Gaussian primitive with its position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients, and semantic embedding vector. 2. Projection: Project the 3D Gaussians to the 2D image plane using an affine approximation of the perspective transformation. This yields 2D Gaussians with a transformed mean and a 2D covariance matrix. 3. Sorting: Sort the projected 2D Gaussians front-to-back according to their depth relative to the camera. Let \mathcal{O}p be the ordered list of overlapping Gaussians for pixel p. 4. Alpha Compositing: Compute the final pixel values by iterating over \mathcal{O}p. For each Gaussian i \in \mathcal{O}p: Evaluate the spherical harmonics to get the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i. Compute the transmittance Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Accumulate color and feature vector using the same alpha weights: \mathbf{C}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti \mathbf{F}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{f}i \cdot \alphai \cdot Ti If \mathcal{O}p is empty, \mathbf{F}(p) = \mathbf{0}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersemanticgaussians(primitives, camera): """ primitives: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: pos: (3,) position scale: (3,) scale rot: (4,) quaternion opacity: scalar shcoeffs: SH coefficients feat: (d,) semantic embedding vector camera: Camera object with view and projection matrices """ # 1. Project 3D Gaussians to 2D # Using affine approximation of perspective transformation projectedgaussians = [] for prim in primitives: # Compute 2D mean and covariance from 3D parameters and camera matrix # This step involves Jacobian of perspective projection mean2d, cov2d, depth = project3dto2d(prim.pos, prim.scale, prim.rot, camera) projectedgaussians.append({ 'mean': mean2d, 'cov': cov2d, 'opacity': prim.opacity, 'color': evalsh(prim.shcoeffs, camera.viewdirection), 'feat': prim.feat, 'depth': depth }) # 2. Sort front-to-back by depth projectedgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g['depth']) # 3. Rasterize to image height, width = camera.imagesize featuremap = np.zeros((height, width, prim.feat.shape[0])) colormap = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for prim in projectedgaussians: # Determine bounding box for this Gaussian on the image plane bbox = getboundingbox(prim['mean'], prim['cov']) clipbbox = cliptoimage(bbox, height, width) for y in range(clipbbox.ymin, clipbbox.ymax): for x in range(clipbbox.xmin, clipbbox.xmax): # Evaluate 2D Gaussian PDF at pixel (x, y) dist = np.array([x - prim['mean'][0], y - prim['mean'][1]]) alpha = prim['opacity'] np.exp(-0.5 dist.T @ np.linalg.inv(prim['cov']) @ dist) alpha = np.clip(alpha, 0, 1) if alpha < 1e-5: continue # Alpha compositing # Note: In a real implementation, this is done in parallel on GPU # Here we simulate the accumulation logic for a single pixel # We need to track the accumulated transmittance for this pixel # However, since we iterate primitives, we update the pixel buffer pass # Simplified accumulation logic for demonstration of the formula # In practice, this is done via a rasterizer kernel for prim in projectedgaussians: bbox = getboundingbox(prim['mean'], prim['cov']) clipbbox = cliptoimage(bbox, height, width) for y in range(clipbbox.ymin, clipbbox.ymax): for x in range(clipbbox.xmin, clipbbox.xmax): dist = np.array([x - prim['mean'][0], y - prim['mean'][1]]) alpha = prim['opacity'] np.exp(-0.5 dist.T @ np.linalg.inv(prim['cov']) @ dist) alpha = np.clip(alpha, 0, 1) # Get current accumulated transmittance at (x,y) # This requires storing intermediate state or using a depth buffer # For the sake of the formula representation: # Tprev = product of (1 - alphaj) for all j < i at (x,y) # This is handled by the rasterizer's accumulation buffer # Update color and feature # Cnew = Cold + ci alphai Tprev # Fnew = Fold + fi alphai Tprev pass return featuremap, colormap Note: The pseudocode above illustrates the logical flow. A production implementation uses a GPU rasterizer that maintains an accumulation buffer for transmittance to avoid O(N^2) complexity. Parameters: Semantic embedding dimension d: Typically 512. SH degree: Determined by the base 3DGS configuration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Bleeding: If geometry and semantics are decoupled, boundary bleeding occurs between visual and semantic regions. This is eliminated in this method because geometric parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity) dictate the blending weights for both color and semantic rendering, ensuring hard-coded alignment. Precision: High-dimensional feature vectors may require careful handling of numerical precision during accumulation to avoid saturation or underflow, especially with many overlapping primitives. A mechanism to modulate rendered semantic features based on scale, using learned or fixed gate vectors derived from sampled scales. It is chosen when scale-dependent semantic accuracy is required. The steps are: 1. Map the distribution of sampled scales to a Gaussian distribution using self.qtrans(sampledscales). 2. If scaleawaredim <= 0 or scaleawaredim >= 32, compute gates by passing sampled scales through self.scalegate: gates = self.scalegate(sampledscales.unsqueeze(-1)). 3. Otherwise, discretize scales to integers: intsampledscales = ((1 - sampledscales.squeeze()) scaleawaredim).long(), then lookup pre-computed gates: gates = self.fixedscalegate[intsampledscales].detach(). 4. Repeat rendered features for each sampled scale: featurewithscale = renderedfeatures.unsqueeze(0).repeat([sampledscales.shape[0], 1, 1, 1]). 5. Multiply features by gate vectors: featurewithscale = featurewithscale gates.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1). Time Complexity: Same as standard 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, O(N) where N is the number of primitives, assuming constant-time feature vector operations. The addition of feature vectors increases memory bandwidth usage but not asymptotic complexity. Memory Complexity: Increases by O(N \cdot d) where d is the feature dimension (e.g., 512 bytes per primitive for d=512 float32). Performance: Real-time rendering is maintained due to the efficiency of the alpha-blending rasterizer. Strengths: Unified optimization of geometry and semantics; no boundary bleeding; real-time open-vocabulary segmentation. Limitations: Requires high-dimensional feature storage; semantic quality depends on the 2D feature extractor used during training (e.g., CLIP). The method was pioneered by Feature-3DGS [102] and LangSplat [103] by adding high-dimensional feature vectors to Gaussians for real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation. Language Embedded 3D Gaussians [104] expanded this to full scene understanding. The specific formulation with semantic embedding vectors and cross-modal alignment is detailed in. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Open-World 3D Vision-Language Scene Representation with Gaussian Splatting and Cross-Modal Alignment, https://doi.org/10.66238/jaiec72, fetched 2026-10-26 yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, https://github.com/yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Language Embedded 3D Gaussians
head: LE3DG
body: Language Embedded 3D Gaussians (LE3DG) extends the feature blending of 3D Gaussian Splatting to full scene understanding by encoding object-level embeddings for phrase grounding in addition to pixel-level features. It enables open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and zero-shot semantic reasoning by allowing rendered feature maps to be compared directly against text embeddings from vision-language models like CLIP. It differs from sibling methods like LangSplat by focusing on the expansion of the standard feature blending pipeline to support object-level grounding rather than just pixel-level alignment, and from 3D Vision-Language GS which projects vision-language models into a joint embedding space for visual question answering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each with position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and a feature vector \mathbf{f}i. The feature vector \mathbf{f}i is initialized or optimized to represent semantic information (e.g., CLIP image embeddings) rather than just color. Output: A rendered 2D feature map \mathbf{V}(p) for each pixel p, which can be decoded by a segmentation head or compared against text embeddings. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores a feature vector \mathbf{f}i. The dimensionality of \mathbf{f}i matches the embedding space of the vision-language model (e.g., 512 or 768 dimensions for CLIP). Rasterization Buffer: Stores the accumulated feature vector \mathbf{V}(p) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}(p) for each pixel. Algorithm: 1. Rasterization: For each pixel p, identify the set of overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p sorted front-to-back. 2. Feature Blending: Compute the rendered feature vector \mathbf{V}(p) using the shared differentiable alpha-blending accumulation defined in the parent article Parent: \mathbf{V}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{f}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{f}i is the semantic feature vector of the i-th Gaussian. 3. Semantic Query: To perform open-vocabulary segmentation, encode a target text phrase T into a text embedding \mathbf{t}T using a pre-trained vision-language model (e.g., CLIP text encoder). 4. Matching: Compute the similarity between the rendered feature \mathbf{V}(p) and the text embedding \mathbf{t}T (e.g., using cosine similarity) to determine the semantic label for pixel p. Parameters: Feature Dimension: Determined by the vision-language model (e.g., 512 for CLIP ViT-L/14). Not given in the sources. Similarity Metric: Cosine similarity is standard for CLIP embeddings. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Mixing: Overlapping Gaussians with different semantic meanings may produce mixed feature vectors that do not match any single text embedding well. This is mitigated by the differentiable blending which preserves the contribution of each Gaussian proportional to its opacity. Precision: High-dimensional feature vectors require sufficient precision during accumulation to avoid quantization errors that degrade semantic similarity. Use float32 or float16 with careful handling of underflow for low-opacity Gaussians. 3D-OVS is a post-processing pipeline for semantic segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting systems that resolves ambiguity by selecting the optimal semantic level from multiple candidate relevancy maps. It solves the problem of inconsistent or noisy semantic predictions by thresholding, binarizing, and evaluating average relevancy within masks to choose the best binary mask. It differs from direct thresholding by explicitly comparing multiple semantic levels (derived from different granularities) to mitigate outlier impact. A strategy to extract vision-language embeddings for 3DGS by aligning each Gaussian directly in the image-embedding space using a dynamic weighting mechanism that combines global, local, and masked features. Step 1: Extract embeddings from the frames used to optimize the 3DGS. Step 2: Combine three distinct features using a dynamic weighting mechanism: global context from the entire frame, local features with background, and masked features without background. Step 3: Automatically balance contributions based on each segment's contextual relationship, emphasizing background-inclusive features for integrated objects and object-specific features for isolated objects. Time Complexity: Rasterization is O(N) per pixel where N is the number of overlapping Gaussians, same as standard 3DGS. The additional cost is the dimensionality of the feature vector \mathbf{f}i during accumulation and the similarity computation against text embeddings. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases by the size of the feature vector \mathbf{f}i per Gaussian. For CLIP embeddings (e.g., 512 dims), this is significantly larger than color (3 dims). Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and phrase grounding without retraining the segmentation head for new classes. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained vision-language model for text encoding. Semantic quality depends on the alignment between the 3DGS feature space and the VLM embedding space. Not given in the sources. Language Embedded 3D Gaussians (LE3DG) was introduced as an expansion of feature blending to full scene understanding, encoding object-level embeddings for phrase grounding. It builds on the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Feature Vectors [8060-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-feature-vectors.md] and integrates with the broader family of semantic and language embeddings [8130-semantic-and-language-embeddings.md]. The method is cited in the context of enabling open-vocabulary semantic segmentation in real time by comparing rendered feature maps against CLIP text embeddings. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) SceneSplat++: A Large Dataset and Comprehensive Benchmark for Language Gaussian Splatting, https://zenodo.org/records/19113098, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Semantic Segmentation Post-processing (3D-OVS)
head: 3D-OVS Semantic Segmentation Pipeline
body: 3D-OVS is a post-processing pipeline for semantic segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting systems that resolves ambiguity by selecting the optimal semantic level from multiple candidate relevancy maps. It solves the problem of inconsistent or noisy semantic predictions by thresholding, binarizing, and evaluating average relevancy within masks to choose the best binary mask. It differs from direct thresholding by explicitly comparing multiple semantic levels to mitigate outlier impact. Inputs: Three relevancy maps for a single class query, representing three distinct semantic levels defined by SAM. A threshold value T = 0.4. Outputs: A single binary mask representing the final semantic segmentation for the queried class. Data Structures: Relevancy Map: A 2D image where each pixel contains a float32 score in [0, 1] indicating the relevance of that location to the semantic query. Binary Map: A 2D image where each pixel is 0 or 1, derived from thresholding the relevancy map. Steps: 1. Thresholding: For each of the three relevancy maps, apply a hard threshold T = 0.4. If score < 0.4, set to 0. If score \ge 0.4, set to 1. This produces three binary maps. 2. Mask Region Calculation: Identify the mask region for each binary map, consisting of all pixels where the binary value is 1. Calculate the average relevancy scores within this region for each binary map. 3. Average Relevancy Calculation: For each binary map, calculate the average relevancy score of the original relevancy map values within the mask region. Let Ri be the i-th relevancy map. Let Bi be the corresponding binary map. Let Mi = \{p \mid Bi[p] = 1\} be the mask region. Calculate average relevancy Ai: Ai = \frac{1}{|Mi|} \sum{p \in Mi} Ri[p]. If |Mi| = 0, Ai is treated as 0. 4. Selection: Select the binary map Bk corresponding to the highest average relevancy Ak as the final predicted binary mask. Parameters: Threshold T = 0.4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Mask: If a binary map has no pixels above threshold, the average relevancy cannot be calculated. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectbestsemanticmask(relevancymaps, threshold=0.4): """ Selects the best semantic binary mask from three relevancy maps. Args: relevancymaps: List of 3 2D lists (H, W), float32, values in [0, 1]. threshold: Float, threshold for binarization. Returns: bestbinarymap: 2D list (H, W), int, 0 or 1. """ binarymaps = [] averagerelevancies = [] for rmap in relevancymaps: # Step 1: Thresholding bmap = [[1 if val >= threshold else 0 for val in row] for row in rmap] binarymaps.append(bmap) # Step 2 & 3: Calculate average relevancy within mask maskpixels = [(r, c) for r in range(len(rmap)) for c in range(len(rmap[0])) if bmap[r][c] == 1] if not maskpixels: # Edge case: empty mask averagerelevancies.append(0.0) else: # Sum of relevancy scores in mask region total = sum(rmap[r][c] for r, c in maskpixels) averagerelevancies.append(total / len(maskpixels)) # Step 4: Select best bestindex = 0 bestval = averagerelevancies[0] for i in range(1, len(averagerelevancies)): if averagerelevancies[i] > bestval: bestval = averagerelevancies[i] bestindex = i return binarymaps[bestindex] A post-processing or training-time strategy to prune unwanted background elements (e.g., sky) from 3D Gaussian reconstructions by learning a semantic field and using it to mask out non-object regions. It assigns each Gaussian a learnable semantic feature vector, renders pixel-level semantics via alpha blending, and trains these features using cross-entropy loss against pseudo-labels from a pretrained model (e.g., Grounded-SAM). It is chosen when background noise (like sky) degrades reconstruction quality. It differs from direct thresholding by learning semantic features that are robust to noisy pseudo-labels, yielding more accurate semantics than directly using pretrained semantic maps. On the TNT dataset, it increases the F1-score from 0.38 to 0.40. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the 3D-OVS dataset, the method consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in Accuracy and mIoU. On the TNT dataset, semantic trimming increases the F1-score by 0.02. Strengths: Mitigates outlier impact by selecting the best semantic level. Robust to noisy pseudo-labels when combined with semantic trimming. Limitations: The threshold is fixed at 0.4. When to use: Used when three relevancy maps corresponding to different semantic levels are available. Originated in the LangSplat paper (CVPR 2024) by the authors of 3D Language Gaussian Splatting. It is used in 3D-OVS tasks to improve the accuracy of semantic predictions by leveraging multiple semantic levels. The method builds on the concept of 3D language Gaussians, which encode object-level embeddings for phrase grounding. name: LangSplat
head: 3D Language Field, Scene-Specific Latent Space for 3DGS
body: LangSplat enables real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and natural language querying in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by distilling vision-language features directly into Gaussian primitives. It differs from methods that align primitives in image-embedding space by learning a scene-specific latent space via an autoencoder to compress features, trading high-frequency geometric detail for memory efficiency and query speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} with positions, covariances, opacities, and a learned feature vector \mathbf{f}i per Gaussian. Text queries T (e.g., "window"). Output: A semantic segmentation mask or selection mask for regions matching T. Data Structures: Gaussian Feature Vector \mathbf{f}i: A low-dimensional latent vector. The source notes that LangSplat uses an autoencoder to compress CLIP features into this latent space. The exact dimension is not specified in the provided notes, but Feature 3DGS (a related method using similar distillation) uses a rendered feature dimension of 128 or 512. LangSplat specifically emphasizes compression. Text Embedding \mathbf{t}k: A vector from a CLIP text encoder for each category k. Steps: 1. Feature Distillation (Training): Render a 2D feature map F(p) for training images using the standard alpha-blending equation: F(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{f}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Compare the rendered feature map F(p) against ground-truth features derived from a vision-language model (e.g., CLIP). Optimize the Gaussian feature vectors \mathbf{f}i and the autoencoder parameters to minimize the reconstruction error between the rendered features and the distilled CLIP features. This creates a "3D language field". 2. Inference (Querying): Render the feature map F(p) for the target view using the trained Gaussians. Encode the text query T into a text embedding vector \mathbf{t} using a CLIP text encoder. Compute the similarity between the rendered feature map and the text embedding. For a pixel p, the semantic score S(p) is typically computed via inner product or cosine similarity: S(p) = \text{Similarity}(F(p), \mathbf{t}) Apply a threshold or softmax to generate a binary or probabilistic segmentation mask. Parameters: Autoencoder Latent Dimension: Not given in the sources. The source notes that LangSplat uses an autoencoder for compression, but does not specify the bottleneck size. CLIP Encoder: ViT-L/16 is cited as the standard encoder for feature preparation in related methods. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Loss of High-Frequency Details: The autoencoder compression causes a loss of high-frequency details, manifesting as blurring of facade textures or softening of sharp edges. This is a critical limitation for applications requiring photorealism, such as infrastructure inspection. Modal Bias: The language model-driven feature extraction exhibits modal bias. View-Dependent Tearing: Feature projection processes can lead to tearing in view-dependent textures. Language-Guided Semantic Scoring computes per-Gaussian semantic probabilities by comparing learned visual features against text embeddings from a vision-language model (VLM) such as CLIP. It enables open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and editing in 3D Gaussian Splatting by rendering feature maps that are compared against text embeddings. Unlike methods that align primitives directly in image-embedding space to preserve richer latent semantics, this approach typically operates in a text-embedding space using inner products followed by softmax normalization. Time Complexity: Real-time segmentation is enabled by the speed of the 3DGS rasterizer. The query time depends on the cost of the CLIP text encoding and the matrix multiplication for similarity, which is negligible compared to rendering. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to storing full-dimensional CLIP features per Gaussian due to the autoencoder compression. Strengths: Real-time open-vocabulary querying; memory efficiency. Limitations: Blurring of fine textures; modal bias; loss of geometric detail due to compression. When to use: Resource-constrained applications or when semantic querying is prioritized over photorealistic texture fidelity. When not to use: Large-scale UAV scenes or urban heritage preservation where fine-grained detail and photorealism are paramount. LangSplat was introduced as a method to address semantic understanding in 3DGS by learning a scene-specific latent space that aligns with natural language features. It pioneers the direction of distilling 2D vision-model features into a 3D representation, building on the foundation of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method allows users to select and manipulate regions using natural language queries (e.g., querying for all "windows") in real-time. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Implicit vs. explicit a comparative survey on NeRF and 3DGS for large-scale aerial scene editing, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10791-026-10029-9, fetched 2026-10-26 Feature 3DGS: Supercharging 3D Gaussian Splatting to Enable Distilled Feature Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02048, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Language-Guided Semantic Scoring
head: Semantic Scoring via CLIP
body: Language-Guided Semantic Scoring computes per-Gaussian semantic probabilities by comparing learned visual features against text embeddings from a vision-language model (VLM) such as CLIP. It enables open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and editing in 3D Gaussian Splatting by rendering feature maps that are compared against text embeddings. Unlike methods that align primitives directly in image-embedding space to preserve richer latent semantics, this approach typically operates in a text-embedding space using inner products followed by softmax normalization. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each with an associated semantic feature vector fj \in \mathbb{R}^d (where d is the feature dimension, typically 512 for CLIP ViT-B/32). A set of C text categories or labels \{l1, \dots, lC\}. Outputs: A semantic score matrix S \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}, where S{j,c} represents the probability that Gaussian j belongs to category c. Data Structures: Gaussian Semantic Features: Stored as a matrix F \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}. Each row fj corresponds to the semantic feature of the j-th Gaussian. These features are typically extracted during training or inference using a teacher encoder (e.g., CLIP image encoder). Text Embeddings: Stored as a matrix T \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times d}. Each row ti is the text embedding for category i. Steps: 1. Text Encoding: Encode each of the C text categories using the CLIP ViT-B/32 text encoder to obtain text feature vectors ti \in \mathbb{R}^{512}. 2. Inner Product Calculation: Compute the dot product between each Gaussian's semantic feature fj and each text embedding ti. This results in a raw score matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C} where P{j,i} = fj^\top ti. 3. Softmax Normalization: Apply a softmax function along the category dimension (columns) to normalize the scores into probabilities. Formula: The semantic score S{j,i} for Gaussian j and category i is calculated as: S{j,i} = \frac{\exp(fj^\top ti)}{\sum{k=1}^{C} \exp(fj^\top tk)} where fj is the semantic feature of the j-th Gaussian, ti is the text embedding for the i-th category, and C is the total number of categories. Parameters: Temperature: Not explicitly defined in the primary source. Standard implementations may use a temperature scaling factor \tau in the exponent, i.e., \exp(fj^\top ti / \tau), but the source describes a direct inner product followed by softmax. Threshold (th): Used for hard selection during editing. If S{j,i} \ge th, the Gaussian is selected. The specific value is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The inner product and softmax operations are sensitive to the magnitude of the embeddings. Ensuring that fj and ti are normalized (e.g., L2 normalized) before the dot product can stabilize training and inference. Category Mismatch: If the text encoder is not aligned with the visual encoder used for fj, scores may be unreliable. The source assumes a consistent CLIP model. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has zero or near-zero semantic features, the softmax output will be uniform across categories, providing no semantic guidance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computesemanticscores(gaussianfeatures: torch.Tensor, textembeddings: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Compute semantic scores for 3D Gaussians based on text embeddings. Args: gaussianfeatures: Tensor of shape (N, d), where N is the number of Gaussians and d is the feature dimension (e.g., 512). textembeddings: Tensor of shape (C, d), where C is the number of categories. Returns: scores: Tensor of shape (N, C) containing semantic probabilities. """ # Step 1: Compute inner products between Gaussian features and text embeddings # Resulting shape: (N, C) rawscores = torch.matmul(gaussianfeatures, textembeddings.T) # Step 2: Apply softmax along the category dimension (dim=1) # This normalizes the scores so that they sum to 1 for each Gaussian scores = F.softmax(rawscores, dim=1) return scores def selectgaussians(scores: torch.Tensor, categoryindex: int, threshold: float) -> torch.Tensor: """ Select Gaussians for a specific category based on a threshold. Args: scores: Tensor of shape (N, C). categoryindex: Index of the category to select (0 to C-1). threshold: Minimum score required for selection. Returns: mask: Boolean tensor of shape (N,) indicating selected Gaussians. """ # Extract the column for the specified category categoryscores = scores[:, categoryindex] # Apply binary thresholding mask = categoryscores >= threshold return mask A variant that assigns semantic labels to 3D Gaussian primitives based on user text queries by computing cosine similarity rather than inner product with softmax. It represents the scene as N Gaussian primitives Gj \in \mathbb{R}^{59} (encoding position, covariance, color, opacity, etc.). For each primitive Gj, a language embedding E^Gj \in \mathbb{R}^d is computed, either via per-scene processing or a learned encoder. User queries ci are mapped to embeddings E^Ti using a frozen text encoder (e.g., CLIP). The label for Gj is the index i that maximizes cosine similarity: \text{label}(Gj) = \arg \maxi \cos(E^Gj, E^Ti). This method avoids information loss inherent in textual descriptions by aligning in image-embedding space. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C \cdot d) for computing the score matrix, where N is the number of Gaussians, C is the number of categories, and d is the feature dimension. This is efficient enough for real-time rendering if C is small or fixed. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot d + C \cdot d) to store Gaussian features and text embeddings. Performance: The performance is limited by the capability of the teacher encoders used to generate the feature maps. Using CLIP ViT-B/32 provides a balance between speed and semantic richness. Strengths: Enables open-vocabulary editing and segmentation without retraining the 3DGS model for each new category. Supports both hard and soft selection for editing operations. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained CLIP model. May not capture fine-grained details as well as methods that align in image-embedding space. The method was introduced in "Feature 3DGS: Supercharging 3D Gaussian Splatting to Enable Distilled Feature Fields". It builds on the idea of using teacher encoders to distill semantic information into 3D Gaussian primitives. The approach leverages the strong zero-shot capabilities of CLIP to enable semantic understanding in 3D scenes.
