name: 3D Vision-Language GS
head: SplatTalk
body: 3D Vision-Language GS projects vision-language models into the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework to enable 3D visual question answering and zero-shot semantic reasoning via natural language queries on rendered feature maps. It differs from sibling methods like Language Embedded 3D Gaussians by training a joint embedding space where the rendered feature map is directly queryable, rather than relying solely on pre-encoded static object-level embeddings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics) and a pre-trained Vision-Language Model (VLM) encoder (e.g., CLIP). Output: A rendered feature map \mathbf{V}(p) per pixel p that aligns with the VLM's text embedding space, enabling semantic queries. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Standard 3DGS attributes. For semantic tasks, the color attribute \mathbf{c}i is replaced or augmented by a feature vector \mathbf{f}i representing the semantic embedding. Instance Indexing: A mapping from Gaussian indices to semantic instance IDs is maintained during training or post-processing to enable instance-level retrieval. Method Steps: 1. Feature Rendering: For each pixel p, render the semantic feature vector \mathbf{f}i instead of color. Using the shared differentiable alpha-blending accumulation: \mathbf{V}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{f}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{f}i is the semantic feature of the i-th Gaussian. 2. Joint Embedding Training: Optimize the Gaussian attributes (specifically \mathbf{f}i) such that the rendered feature map \mathbf{V}(p) aligns with the 2D image embeddings from the VLM for corresponding pixels in training views. This creates a joint embedding space. 3. Querying: At inference, encode a natural language query q into a text embedding \mathbf{t}q using the VLM's text encoder. Compute similarity between \mathbf{t}q and rendered features \mathbf{V}(p) to generate semantic masks or answer questions. Instance-Level Retrieval (SplatTalk Variant): For tasks requiring specific instance grounding (e.g., "the red cup"), the method employs an isolated rendering strategy to prevent leakage: 1. Filter Stable Instances: Identify stable instances I{stable} based on matching confidence: I{stable} = \{ j: matchj \ge \theta{match} \land missj \le \theta{miss} \} 2. Isolated Rendering: For each instance j \in I{stable}, render the Gaussian set Gj alone (setting all other Gaussians' opacity to zero) from its top-B training views Vj (ranked by projected area). 3. Crop and Embed: Crop the rendered image to the instance's bounding box. Compute the CLIP image embedding for each crop: \bar{c}j = \frac{1}{|Vj|} \sum{t \in Vj} \text{CLIP}{img}(\text{Crop}(I{isoRender}(Gj, \text{cam}t))) 4. Normalize: L2-normalize the average embedding to get the instance embedding ej: ej = \frac{\bar{c}j}{\|\bar{c}j\|2} 5. Matching: At query time, match the prompt q by cosine similarity: j^ = \arg \max{j \in I{stable}} \cos(ej, \text{CLIP}{text}(q)) The predicted mask is obtained by indexing the rendered label map \hat{L}{test} at the test viewpoint: Mq = 1[\hat{L}{test} = j^]. Parameters: \theta{match}, \theta{miss}: Thresholds for instance stability. Not given in the sources. B: Number of top training views for isolated rendering. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instance Leakage: Rendering overlapping Gaussians together can cause semantic leakage between adjacent instances. Isolated rendering (step 2 above) mitigates this. Precision: The alignment between 3D rendered features and 2D VLM embeddings requires careful optimization to avoid semantic drift. A variant that specifically leverages CLIP's visual encoder for instance retrieval within the 3DGS framework. It uses isolated rendering of individual Gaussians to compute robust visual embeddings, enabling open-vocabulary segmentation without training. It is chosen when training-free or few-shot segmentation is required. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of Gaussians. Querying is O(|I{stable}|) cosine similarities per prompt. Memory Complexity: Requires storing semantic feature vectors \mathbf{f}i for each Gaussian, increasing memory usage compared to standard color-based 3DGS. Strengths: Enables real-time open-vocabulary semantic segmentation and 3D visual question answering. Supports zero-shot reasoning. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of the underlying VLM. Isolated rendering increases computational cost for instance-level queries. 3D Vision-Language GS (also known as SplatTalk) was introduced to extend 3DGS beyond geometric and photometric reconstruction into semantic understanding. It builds on the principle of feature blending in 3DGS, projecting vision-language models into the 3DGS framework to enable joint embedding spaces. It is part of a broader trend of integrating large language models and vision-language models with 3D representations for robotics and AR/VR applications. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DIGS: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.16177, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Text Embedding Generation with Directional Views
body: This method generates semantic text embeddings for 3D Gaussian Splatting by encoding language prompts into latent vectors using a frozen CLIP text encoder. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly generating directional view embeddings—appending view descriptors (e.g., "front", "side") to prompts—to condition the generation or optimization process on the camera's viewing angle. Unlike LangSplat which focuses on general language grounding, or 3D Vision-Language GS which integrates vision-language models for segmentation, this approach specifically addresses view-dependent semantic consistency by varying the input text based on the rendered viewpoint. The method consists of two phases: initialization of the embedding dictionary and the generation of directional embeddings during the training loop. Inputs: A base text prompt string P (e.g., "a panda"); a set of directional descriptors D = \{d1, d2, \dots\} (e.g., "front", "side", "back"). Outputs: A dictionary of tensors self.embeddings mapping keys to latent vectors. The core data structure is a dictionary self.embeddings. Keys: 'pos' (positive prompt), 'neg' (negative prompt), and directional keys (e.g., 'front', 'side', 'back'). Values: Tensors of shape [1, 77, 768] representing the batch size (1), sequence length (77 tokens), and embedding dimension (768 for CLIP ViT-L/14). 1. Initialize Tokenizer and Encoder: Load a frozen CLIP text encoder and its corresponding tokenizer. 2. Encode Base Prompts: Tokenize the positive prompt P{pos} and negative prompt P{neg} with padding to the maximum length. Pass the token IDs through the text encoder to obtain the base embeddings. Store these in self.embeddings['pos'] and self.embeddings['neg']. 3. Generate Directional Embeddings: For each directional descriptor d \in D: Construct the directional prompt Pd = P{pos} + ", " + d + " view". Tokenize Pd with padding to max length. Pass the token IDs through the frozen text encoder. Store the resulting tensor in self.embeddings[d]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from transformers import CLIPTextModel, CLIPTokenizer class TextEmbeddingGenerator: def init(self, baseprompt: str, device: str = "cuda"): self.device = device self.tokenizer = CLIPTokenizer.frompretrained("openai/clip-vit-large-patch14") self.textencoder = CLIPTextModel.frompretrained("openai/clip-vit-large-patch14") self.textencoder.eval() self.textencoder.to(self.device) # Initialize dictionary self.embeddings = {} # Encode base positive and negative prompts # Note: Negative prompt is typically empty or generic; here we assume a standard empty/negative handling posinputs = self.tokenizer( baseprompt, padding="maxlength", maxlength=self.tokenizer.modelmaxlength, returntensors="pt") with torch.nograd(): posembed = self.textencoder(posinputs.inputids.to(self.device))[0] self.embeddings['pos'] = posembed # Standard negative prompt handling (often empty string or specific negative text) neginputs = self.tokenizer( "", # Placeholder for negative prompt; implementation may vary padding="maxlength", maxlength=self.tokenizer.modelmaxlength, returntensors="pt") with torch.nograd(): negembed = self.textencoder(neginputs.inputids.to(self.device))[0] self.embeddings['neg'] = negembed def updatedirectionalviews(self, directions: list): """ Generates and stores embeddings for specific viewing directions.:param directions: List of strings, e.g., ['front', 'side', 'back'] """ for d in directions: # Append view descriptor to the base prompt # The base prompt is assumed to be stored or accessible; # here we reconstruct it from the 'pos' key's decoded text or pass it in init # For this implementation, we assume baseprompt is available in scope or passed # To be strictly self-contained, we re-tokenize the stored 'pos' tensor's text? # No, we need the text. We assume baseprompt is an instance variable. # Re-constructing prompt logic based on # Note: In a real implementation, baseprompt would be stored in init # Here we assume self.baseprompt is set in init directionalprompt = f"{self.baseprompt}, {d} view" inputs = self.tokenizer( directionalprompt, padding="maxlength", maxlength=self.tokenizer.modelmaxlength, returntensors="pt") with torch.nograd(): embed = self.textencoder(inputs.inputids.to(self.device))[0] self.embeddings[d] = embed def getembedding(self, key: str) -> torch.Tensor: return self.embeddings[key] Note: The pseudocode above assumes self.baseprompt is stored during initialization. The negative prompt handling is simplified; in practice, a specific negative prompt string is used. Max Length: 77 tokens (standard for CLIP). Embedding Dimension: 768 (for CLIP ViT-L/14). Directional Descriptors: Typically ['front', 'side', 'back']. For forward-facing scenes (e.g., LLFF dataset), ['top-down', 'front', 'side'] are used. Janus Problem: View-specific prompting does not fully solve the "Janus problem" (where an object has multiple faces or inconsistent features across views). The loss function still encourages matching the input image appearance across all views, which can lead to artifacts if the directional prompt is not sufficiently distinct or if the underlying geometry is ambiguous. Resolution Limits: Rendering at higher resolutions than 96px or 128px may not yield noticeable quality improvements for the text prior loss, suggesting that the bottleneck is not resolution but the semantic conditioning. TexGS-VolVis is a method for representing and editing volume visualization (VolVis) scenes using textured 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It solves the problem of decoupling geometry from appearance in text-driven non-photorealistic style editing (NPSE), allowing for geometry-consistent stylization without the elliptical artifacts common in coupled representations. Unlike methods that freeze geometry to prevent distortion, TexGS-VolVis uses explicit 2D texture maps to store appearance, preserving geometric fidelity while enabling rich visual expressiveness. View-Dependent Prompting augments text prompts with directional suffixes based on the camera's position relative to the scene to guide diffusion-based 3D generation. It differs from sibling methods like TexGS-VolVis Representation and Optimization by explicitly conditioning the text embedding on the viewing angle rather than relying solely on volumetric or geometric consistency. Multimodal Object Embedding creates a unified semantic representation for 3D objects by fusing vision-based CLIP embeddings with optional text-based CLIP embeddings. It solves the problem of limited semantic grounding in open-vocabulary querying by capturing both visual features and high-level attribute descriptions in a single vector space. Unlike its sibling Text Embedding Generation with Directional Views, which generates directional view embeddings by appending view descriptors to prompts, this method focuses on instance-level fusion of static object attributes. It differs from TexGS-VolVis Representation and Optimization and View-Dependent Prompting by explicitly combining a language-free ontology with an LLM-generated attribute channel. Time Complexity: The encoding step is performed once per prompt/direction during initialization or infrequently during training. The CLIP text encoder is lightweight compared to the diffusion model or the Gaussian rasterization, so the overhead is minimal. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is determined by the number of stored embeddings. For N directions, the memory is O(N \cdot 77 \cdot 768 \cdot 4) bytes (assuming float32). For 3 directions, this is negligible (~700 KB). Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages pre-trained, robust CLIP embeddings; effectively guides view-dependent generation by providing distinct semantic cues for different angles. Limitations: Does not resolve geometric inconsistencies like the Janus problem; relies on the quality of the frozen CLIP encoder; directional prompts are discrete and may not capture continuous view variations. When to Use: When view-dependent semantic consistency is required for 3D generation or editing, particularly in forward-facing or 360-degree scenes where specific viewpoints (front, side, back) are semantically distinct. When Not to Use: When continuous view-dependent features are needed rather than discrete categories; when the Janus problem is the primary challenge. The method originates from the integration of CLIP text encoders into 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines for text-driven generation and editing. The specific technique of appending directional views to prompts was introduced in (DreamGaussian) and further explored in (Blended-NeRF) and (RealFusion). It builds on the principle that text embeddings can guide the optimization of 3D representations by providing semantic priors. dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, https://github.com/dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Blended-NeRF: Zero-Shot Object Generation and Blending in Existing Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12760v2, fetched 2026-10-26 RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00816, fetched 2026-10-30

name: TexGS-VolVis Representation and Optimization
head: TexGS-VolVis
body: TexGS-VolVis is a method for representing and editing volume visualization (VolVis) scenes using textured 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It solves the problem of decoupling geometry from appearance in text-driven non-photorealistic style editing (NPSE), allowing for geometry-consistent stylization without the elliptical artifacts common in coupled representations. Unlike methods that freeze geometry to prevent distortion, TexGS-VolVis uses explicit 2D texture maps to store appearance, preserving geometric fidelity while enabling rich visual expressiveness. Inputs: Multi-view images of a volumetric dataset and text prompts for style transfer or refinement. Outputs: A scene representation consisting of 2D Gaussian primitives with geometry, shading, and texture attributes, along with rendered stylized images. Data Structures: The scene is represented by N 2D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive stores attributes in 32-bit floating-point format. 1. Geometry Attributes: \mu: Center position (3 floats). tu, tv: Orientation vectors, represented as a quaternion (4 floats). su, sv: Scale factors (2 floats). o: Opacity (1 float). 2. Shading Attributes: ka: Ambient coefficient (1 float). kd: Diffuse coefficient (1 float). ks: Specular coefficient (1 float). \beta: Shininess/exponent (1 float). 3. Texture Attribute: Stored separately from individual splats. It is a global texture map shared by the scene. The total number of texels T{total} is fixed per basic scene. Parameter Count: Given N primitives, the total number of parameters for geometry and shading is calculated as: \text{# params} = 3N + 4N + N + N + N + N + N + N + N Where: 3N corresponds to \mu. 4N corresponds to the quaternion for \{tu, tv\}. The remaining N terms correspond to su, sv, o, ka, kd, ks, \beta (1 float each). Optimization Phases: The method proceeds in three sequential phases: 1. 2DGS Initialization: Initialize the geometry and basic appearance using 2DGS. This phase uses explicit ray-splat intersection for perspective-correct splatting and accurate geometry reconstruction. 2. Shading Attributes Optimization: Optimize \{ka, kd, ks, \beta\}. This improves reconstruction accuracy by modeling view-dependent color variations. 3. Texture Attribute Optimization: Optimize the global texture map. This phase introduces a sparsity regularization term that encourages minimal texture values, which may slightly reduce reconstruction accuracy compared to the shading-only phase. Spherical harmonic parameters and view-independent color c{ind} are used only in early phases and are not retrained in the final representation. Scene Editing and Composition: Text Prompt Refinement: Users can iteratively apply new text prompts to an already stylized scene. The previous style pattern is partially preserved while being updated according to the latest prompt. Multi-Scene Composition: The framework accommodates multiple basic scenes (e.g., different transfer functions) in a single visualization. Each basic scene is edited independently and then seamlessly composed. This composition requires no additional optimization, incurring zero extra training costs. Relighting: Lighting direction is adjusted by modifying azimuthal and polar angles, achieving smooth and consistent relighting across the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texgsvolvisoptimize(multiviewimages, textprompts, numprimitivestarget): N = numprimitivestarget # Phase 1: 2DGS Initialization mu = zeros((N, 3)) # Center positions quatt = randomunitquaternions(N) # Orientation for {tu, tv} su = ones(N) # Scale u sv = ones(N) # Scale v o = ones(N) # Opacity primitives = {'mu': mu, 'quatt': quatt, 'su': su, 'sv': sv, 'o': o} # Phase 2: Shading Attributes Optimization ka = zeros(N); kd = zeros(N); ks = zeros(N); beta = ones(N) shading = {'ka': ka, 'kd': kd, 'ks': ks, 'beta': beta} for in range(shadingiterations): rendered = projectandrasterize(primitives, shading, multiviewimages) loss = meansquarederror(rendered, multiviewimages) shading = gradientdescentstep(shading, loss) # Phase 3: Texture Attribute Optimization Ttotal = 10000000 texturemap = zeros(Ttotal) for in range(textureiterations): rendered = projectandrasterize(primitives, shading, texturemap, multiviewimages) loss = meansquarederror(rendered, multiviewimages) + sparsitylambda sum(texturemap) texturemap = gradientdescentstep(texturemap, loss) return primitives, shading, texturemap def editscene(primitives, shading, texturemap, newtextprompt): updatedtexture = applyip2prefinement(texturemap, newtextprompt) return primitives, shading, updatedtexture def composescenes(scenelist): composed = concatenateattributes(scenelist) return composed def relightscene(primitives, shading, texturemap, azimuth, polar): rendered = projectandrasterize(primitives, shading, texturemap, lightazimuth=azimuth, lightpolar=polar) return rendered Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low-Texture Styles: Flat or low-texture styles cause overly smoothed results, obscuring internal details. Complex Structures: Fragmented or complex structures lack continuous surfaces, preventing coherent style application. Prompt Misinterpretation: Text-driven editing relies on the pretrained IP2P model, which can misinterpret prompts (e.g., associating 'leaf beetle' with green instead of red/yellow/black). Rugged Surfaces: Rugged or highly detailed surfaces (e.g., wood) are harder to fit than smooth ones (e.g., five jets) because they produce complex lighting effects in multi-view images, complicating geometry reconstruction. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The texture attribute dominates memory usage. For a fixed T{total} = 1 \times 10^7 texels, the texture consumes ~114.5 MB per basic scene, regardless of the number of primitives N. Geometry and shading attributes scale linearly with N. On the beetle dataset (47,767 primitives), geometry uses 1.8 MB, shading uses 0.7 MB, texture uses 114.5 MB, and the total is ~117 MB. Texture accounts for >95% of model size. Time: Fitting performance is fast. On the five jets dataset (56,836 primitives), fitting takes 0.8 minutes. Measured Performance: Five Jets Dataset: PSNR is 36.83 dB, SSIM is 0.9889, CPU/GPU memory is 10.0/5.6 GB, and primitives count is 56,836. Other Datasets: PSNR ranges from 24.58 dB (Ionization) to 36.83 dB (Five Jets), and SSIM ranges from 0.8565 to 0.9889. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Decoupling geometry and appearance eliminates elliptical artifacts in text-driven NPSE while preserving visual expressiveness. The method supports iterative text refinement and multi-scene composition with zero extra training cost. It uses 2DGS for accurate geometry reconstruction and perspective-correct splatting. Limitations: Texture memory usage is high and fixed per scene, making compression necessary for large-scale applications. The method struggles with rugged surfaces and low-texture styles. It relies on an external IP2P model for text interpretation, which can be unreliable. When to Use: Use for text-driven non-photorealistic style editing of volume visualizations where geometry consistency is critical. Use when multiple basic scenes (e.g., different transfer functions) need to be composed. Do not use for scenes with highly fragmented structures or when low-texture styles are required, as results may be overly smoothed or incoherent. TexGS-VolVis was introduced in the paper "TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), which uses explicit ray-splat intersection for perspective-correct splatting and natively supports 2D texture maps, making it superior for geometry-consistent editing compared to standard 3DGS. The method addresses limitations in previous text-driven NPSE methods that either froze geometry (reducing expressiveness) or coupled geometry and appearance (causing artifacts). name: View-Dependent Prompting
head: Directional View Suffixing
body: View-Dependent Prompting augments text prompts with directional suffixes based on the camera's position relative to the scene to guide diffusion-based 3D generation. It differs from sibling methods like TexGS-VolVis Representation and Optimization by explicitly conditioning the text embedding on the viewing angle rather than relying solely on volumetric or geometric consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base text prompt P, the sampled camera azimuth \theta{cam}, and the camera elevation \phi{cam}. Output: An augmented text prompt P' containing a view-dependent suffix. Data Structures: Prompt Suffixes: A set of discrete strings: "front view", "side view", "overhead view", "bottom view". Steps: 1. Determine Suffix: Based on \theta{cam} and \phi{cam}, select a suffix S according to the rules below: If \phi{cam} > 60^\circ: S = \text{"overhead view"}. If \phi{cam} < 0^\circ: S = \text{"bottom view"}. If |\theta{cam}| \le 30^\circ: S = \text{"front view"}. If 30^\circ < |\theta{cam}| \le 90^\circ: S = \text{"side view"}. If 90^\circ < |\theta{cam}| \le 180^\circ: S = \text{"bottom view"}. Note: Source mentions interpolating between front/side/back augmentations based on the quadrant of \theta{cam}, but explicitly states that taking the text embedding closest to the sampled azimuth worked better. Source uses the discrete suffix rules above. 2. Augment Prompt: Append S to the base prompt P to form P'. 3. Encode: Pass P' to the frozen text encoder (e.g., CLIP) to obtain the view-dependent text embedding. Parameters: Elevation Thresholds: 60^\circ (overhead), 0^\circ (bottom). Azimuthal Bands: \pm 30^\circ (front), \pm 30^\circ-90^\circ (side), \pm 90^\circ-180^\circ (bottom). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disagreement: suggests interpolation of embeddings, while uses discrete suffix selection. Implementers should prefer the discrete suffix method if following, or the closest-embedding method if following. Ambiguity: The term "bottom view" is used for both low elevation (\phi{cam} < 0^\circ) and high azimuth (|\theta{cam}| > 90^\circ) in. Time Complexity: O(1) for suffix selection; dominated by the text encoder inference. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the suffix string. Strengths: Improves geometric coherence by providing explicit directional context to the diffusion model. Limitations: Discrete suffixes may introduce abrupt changes in the text embedding as the camera moves across boundaries. Originated in text-to-3D diffusion methods to mitigate view inconsistency. (DreamFusion) explored interpolation but found nearest-neighbor embedding selection effective. (RealFusion) formalized the discrete suffix approach based on camera quadrants. name: Multimodal Object Embedding
head: LLM-Enhanced Fusion, Multi-modal embedding fusion
body: Multimodal Object Embedding creates a unified semantic representation for 3D objects by fusing vision-based CLIP embeddings with optional text-based CLIP embeddings. It solves the problem of limited semantic grounding in open-vocabulary querying by capturing both visual features and high-level attribute descriptions in a single vector space. Unlike its sibling Text Embedding Generation with Directional Views, which generates directional view embeddings by appending view descriptors to prompts, this method focuses on instance-level fusion of static object attributes. It differs from TexGS-VolVis Representation and Optimization and View-Dependent Prompting by explicitly combining a language-free ontology with an LLM-generated attribute channel. Inputs: 1. A set of isolated image crops (frames) of a 3D object instance. 2. Optional textual labels or descriptions associated with the object. 3. A Large Language Model (LLM) for generating attribute descriptions. 4. A frozen CLIP text encoder. 5. A fusion weight parameter \lambda \in [0, 1]. Outputs: A final multimodal object embedding E{object} (or ej^{fused}). Data Structures: E{vision}: Vision-based embedding vector. E{text}: Text-based embedding vector. ej^{txt}: CLIP-encoded description for instance j. ej: Vision embedding for instance j (used in notation). Steps: 1. Compute Vision Embedding (E{vision}): If using the method from: Average the CLIP embeddings of k selected frames. E{vision} = \frac{1}{k} \sum{j=1}^{k} E{framej} where E{framej} is the CLIP embedding of the j-th selected frame. If using the method from: Use the instance-specific vision embedding ej derived from the same isolated crops. 2. Generate and Encode Text Embedding (E{text}): If textual labels/descriptions are available (from): Use the provided textual description directly. Encode it using the CLIP text encoder to obtain E{text}. If textual labels are not available but LLM enhancement is used (from): 1. Pass the isolated crops to an LLM with a fixed prompt. 2. Obtain the attribute-rich text description dj. 3. Encode dj using the CLIP text encoder to obtain ej^{txt}. 4. Set E{text} = ej^{txt}. 3. Fuse Embeddings: Case A: No textual information available: E{object} = E{vision} Case B: Textual information available (Simple Average from): E{object} = \frac{E{vision} + E{text}}{2} Case C: LLM-Enhanced Fusion (Weighted from): ej^{fused} = \lambda ej + (1 - \lambda) ej^{txt} where \lambda \in [0, 1] is a hyperparameter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemultimodalembedding(crops, textuallabels=None, llm=None, cliptextencoder=None, lambdaweight=0.5): """ Computes the multimodal object embedding. Args: crops: List of image crops (tensors) of the object. textuallabels: Optional list of text strings describing the object. llm: Optional LLM instance for generating descriptions. cliptextencoder: Frozen CLIP text encoder. lambdaweight: Weight for vision vs text in fusion (lambda in). Returns: Eobject: The final fused embedding vector. """ # Step 1: Compute Vision Embedding # Assuming a helper function to get CLIP visual embedding for a crop visionembeddings = [getclipvisualembedding(crop) for crop in crops] # Method from: Average frame embeddings # Method from: Uses instance embedding ej (assumed pre-computed or same as average) # Here we follow averaging for Evision, or ej if provided. # For consistency with primary definition: Evision = sum(visionembeddings) / len(visionembeddings) # Step 2: Compute Text Embedding Etext = None if textuallabels is not None and len(textuallabels) > 0: # Use provided labels # Assuming textuallabels is a single string or list to be encoded textinput = textuallabels[0] if isinstance(textuallabels, list) else textuallabels Etext = cliptextencoder.encode(textinput) elif llm is not None and cliptextencoder is not None: # LLM-Enhanced Fusion # 1. Pass crops to LLM with fixed prompt description = llm.generatedescription(crops, prompt="fixedprompt") # 2. Encode description Etext = cliptextencoder.encode(description) # Step 3: Fuse if Etext is None: # No textual information Eobject = Evision else: # Check if using simple average or weighted fusion # uses (Evision + Etext) / 2 # uses lambda ej + (1-lambda) etxtj # We implement weighted fusion as it is more general, # but note sets lambda=0.5 implicitly if Evision and Etext are normalized similarly. # Note: and may have different normalization assumptions. # explicitly divides by 2. uses lambda. # To be safe and cover both, we check if lambda is explicitly meant for context. # Given the alias "LLM-Enhanced Fusion" is tied to, we prioritize formula. Eobject = lambdaweight Evision + (1 - lambdaweight) Etext return Eobject Parameters: \lambda: Fusion weight. Typical value not given in. specifies \lambda \in [0, 1]. k: Number of selected frames for averaging. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Cosine similarity computation for querying requires normalized vectors. Ensure E{object} and E{query} are normalized before computing S(E{query}, E{object}). Boundary: If no crops are available, the method cannot compute E{vision}. Degenerate Input: If the LLM fails to generate a description, fallback to E{vision}. Encodes text prompts into latent embeddings using a frozen CLIP text encoder, and generates directional view embeddings by appending view descriptors to prompts. Choose when view-dependent semantic cues are needed. Link Uses a volume-based representation for optimization. Choose when volumetric consistency is prioritized over splatting efficiency. Link Uses view-dependent prompts for segmentation. Choose when appearance changes significantly across views. Link Time Complexity: O(k) for averaging k frame embeddings. O(1) for LLM inference per instance (assuming fixed prompt) and CLIP encoding. Retrieval is O(|I{stable}|) cosine computations per prompt. Memory Complexity: Stores one embedding vector per object instance. Strengths: Enables accurate and efficient open-vocabulary querying by capturing visual and semantic cues in a single vector space. No second voting pass or re-optimization is required for LLM-enhanced fusion. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the LLM-generated descriptions. Requires isolated crops for LLM input. When to use: When open-vocabulary querying of 3D objects is required and textual attributes are beneficial. When not to use: When computational resources for LLM inference are unavailable or when only visual cues are sufficient. The method originated from research into natural language interaction for volume visualization and open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. introduced the basic fusion of vision and text CLIP embeddings for NLI4VolVis. extended this with LLM-enhanced fusion for DIGS, demonstrating gains in retrieval accuracy without re-optimization. name: LSeg Feature Encoding
head: LSeg
body: LSeg Feature Encoding utilizes the LSeg (Language-Segment Anything) model to generate high-dimensional semantic feature maps from 2D input images, which are then distilled into 3D representations. It solves the problem of assigning rich, language-grounded semantic context to 3D scenes without requiring explicit 3D annotations. It differs from global embedding approaches by providing pixel-level or patch-level semantic supervision, allowing for localized semantic editing and segmentation within the 3D scene. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D image I and a set of text queries (class names or phrases). Output: A semantic feature map \mathbf{f}{img}(I, r) aligned with the image resolution. Data Structures: The LSeg model consists of two encoders: 1. Image Encoder: Vision Transformer Large with 16-pixel patches (ViT-L/16). 2. Text Encoder: CLIP’s Vision Transformer Base with 32-pixel patches (ViT-B/32). Steps: 1. Text Encoding: Encode the input text queries using the CLIP ViT-B/32 text encoder to obtain text embeddings. 2. Image Encoding: Process the input image I through the ViT-L/16 image encoder. The encoder outputs feature maps at reduced resolution. 3. Multi-Scale Inference: To stabilize features and alleviate artifacts from discrete patch processing, perform inference at multiple scales. Resize the image to each scale s \in S, encode, and interpolate the resulting feature maps back to the original image resolution. For the Replica dataset, scales S = [0.75, 0.83, 0.92, 1.0, 1.08, 1.17, 1.25]. For other datasets, scales S = [0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2.0, 2.25]. 4. Aggregation: Average the interpolated feature maps from all scales to produce the final feature map \mathbf{f}{img}(I, r). 5. Distillation Target: The resulting feature map is used as the target feature map for distilling semantic features into the 3D representation (e.g., NeRF or Gaussian Splatting). Pitfalls: LSeg exhibits bias towards traffic scenes due to its training data (ADE20K, BDD, Cityscapes, COCO-Panoptic, IDD, Mapillary Vistas, SUN RGBD). It performs poorly in out-of-distribution regions and queries. Small objects or parts are often not discriminative. Large inference scales lose context information, potentially producing noisy features with incorrect semantic understanding. Uses LSeg as a teacher to distill semantic features into 3D representations, leveraging pretrained CLIP models. It provides pixel-level semantic supervision for localized editing, unlike global embedding approaches. Strengths: Provides rich, zero-shot semantic understanding at the pixel level. Multi-scale inference stabilizes features against ViT patch artifacts. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multi-scale inference and large ViT-L backbone. Performance degrades on small objects or out-of-distribution scenes due to dataset bias. When to use: When localized semantic editing or segmentation is required in 3D scenes and 2D supervision is available. When not to use: For scenes with significant out-of-distribution content or where small object discrimination is critical. LSeg (Language-Segment Anything) is a vision-language model that combines language understanding with image segmentation. It was developed by the Facebook AI Research team and the Institute of Science Tokyo. The model leverages pretrained CLIP models for text and image encoding. It is trained on seven datasets: ADE20K, BDD, Cityscapes, COCO-Panoptic, IDD, Mapillary Vistas, and SUN RGBD. The specific implementation used for feature encoding in 3D reconstruction is the official demo model. Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation, https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1694, fetched 2026-10-26

name: LSeg Teacher Network for Feature Distillation
head: LSeg Distillation, LSeg Teacher
body: This method uses 2D vision-language models, specifically LSeg, as teacher networks to distill semantic features into 3D representations (such as NeRF or Gaussian Splatting), leveraging pretrained CLIP models for text and image encoding. It differs from global embedding approaches by providing pixel-level or patch-level semantic supervision, allowing for localized semantic editing and segmentation within the 3D scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view input images, text queries (optional, depending on teacher variant), and camera poses. Outputs: Dense, spatially consistent semantic feature maps (pseudo-labels) aligned with the 3D scene geometry. Data Structures: Feature Map: A 2D tensor of shape H \times W \times D, where H and W are image dimensions and D is the feature dimensionality (e.g., 512). Compressed Feature Map: A lower-dimensional tensor resulting from PCA projection, used to reduce memory bandwidth constraints. Steps: 1. Teacher Selection: Select a 2D vision-language model as the teacher. LSeg [44] is commonly used for its simplicity, though other concurrent models or text-unconditional encoders are viable. 2. Feature Extraction: Process each input image through the teacher network. If using a modified Vision Transformer (ViT) for dense prediction, process the image using overlapping patches to extract a high-dimensional feature vector for each spatial patch. Map the extracted internal representations into the targeted text-image contrastive space via a projection layer. 3. Dimensionality Reduction: Apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) localized to the specific dataset to compress the high-dimensional embeddings into a lower-dimensional principal space during intermediate storage. 4. Temporal Smoothing: Apply a temporal smoothing filter across adjacent camera poses to handle multi-view inconsistencies and stabilize the semantic feature maps before optimization. 5. Distillation: Use the resulting dense feature maps as ground truth pseudo-labels for optimizing the 3D representation (e.g., 3D Gaussian primitives). Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Feature Dimension: 512 (typical for the distilled vision-language vectors). Optimization Iterations: 100 iterations (for the distillation phase). Photometric Loss Weight: 0.8. Structural Similarity Color Loss Weighting Factor: 3.2. Pitfalls: Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Data: LSeg is not robust to OOD data (e.g., "fossils", "T-Rex", "Triceratops") due to overfitting to biases in its training datasets (e.g., traffic scenes). Memory Bandwidth: High-dimensional semantic vectors across millions of pixels introduce severe memory bandwidth constraints; compression is necessary. Extracts dense, spatially consistent semantic feature maps from multi-view images to serve as ground truth pseudo-labels for 3D Gaussian optimization, overcoming the lack of localized granularity in global VLM embeddings. It employs a modified Vision Transformer fine-tuned for dense prediction with overlapping patches, PCA-based spatial dimensionality reduction localized to the dataset, and temporal smoothing across adjacent camera poses to handle multi-view inconsistencies. Strengths: Provides localized semantic granularity required for precise scene mapping, which global VLM embeddings lack. Allows for specific ray selection based on text queries (e.g., "apple") for editing. Limitations: Robustness is dependent on the teacher model; LSeg specifically suffers from OOD issues. High computational and memory overhead due to dense feature extraction and storage, mitigated only partially by PCA. When to use: When localized semantic editing or segmentation within a 3D scene is required, and the scene content falls within the teacher model's distribution. When not to use: When the scene contains significant out-of-distribution objects relative to the teacher's training bias (e.g., specific animals or rare objects if using LSeg). The method builds on LSeg Feature Encoding and leverages 2D vision-language models for feature distillation in 3D representations. LSeg [44] by Li et al. appeared anonymously at OpenReview on September 29th, 2021. Other concurrent studies [52, 99, 103, 72] appeared at arXiv on November or December, 2021, tackling image semantic segmentation with similar approaches using CLIP [69]. The method builds on the premise that freezing or finetuning pretrained CLIP models as text and image encoders enables zero-shot image semantic segmentation, which can then be distilled into 3D fields. name: VLM-Augmented Segmentation
head: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation via InnerGS
body: This method augments 3D Gaussians with compact language features distilled from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) to enable open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. It solves the problem of high memory consumption associated with explicit high-dimensional semantic modeling by distilling embeddings into compact latent attributes, while preserving volumetric consistency through differentiable splatting. It differs from siblings like Language Embedded 3D Gaussians by using a scene-specific autoencoder for distillation rather than direct embedding storage, and from LSeg Feature Encoding by explicitly targeting open-vocabulary alignment via a lightweight decoder. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} (initialized via the parent method's reconstruction), a knowledge-enhanced medical VLM, and a scene-specific autoencoder. Output: A rendered latent map F(v) for a view v, which is decoded into semantic predictions for open-vocabulary queries. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: Each Gaussian i stores a compact latent attribute vector \mathbf{f}i. The dimensionality of \mathbf{f}i is determined by the bottleneck of the scene-specific autoencoder, significantly smaller than the original VLM embedding dimension. Autoencoder: A scene-specific autoencoder that maps high-dimensional VLM embeddings to the compact latent space \mathbf{f}i. Lightweight Decoder: A network that projects the rendered latent map back to the semantic space. Steps: 1. Feature Distillation: For each Gaussian i in the scene, extract a high-dimensional embedding from the knowledge-enhanced medical VLM. Pass this embedding through the scene-specific autoencoder to obtain the compact latent attribute \mathbf{f}i. 2. Differentiable Splatting: For a target view v, identify the set of candidate Gaussians N that project to the pixel or region of interest. Aggregate the compact latent attributes using the differentiable alpha-blending equation: F(v) = \sum{i \in N} \mathbf{f}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: F(v) is the rendered latent map at view v. \mathbf{f}i is the compact latent attribute (language feature) for Gaussian i. \alphai is the opacity of Gaussian i. N is the set of candidate Gaussians sorted front-to-back. 3. Semantic Projection: Pass the rendered latent map F(v) through a lightweight decoder to project it back to the semantic space. 4. Open-Vocabulary Alignment: Use the projected semantic features to align with text embeddings from the VLM, enabling segmentation of Regions of Interest (ROIs) via open-vocabulary queries. Parameters: Autoencoder Bottleneck Dimension: Not given in the sources. Decoder Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Explosion: The method is designed to circumvent the memory explosion of explicit high-dimensional modeling. Failure to use the autoencoder distillation would lead to excessive VRAM usage. Volumetric Consistency: The use of differentiable splatting ensures volumetric consistency, which is critical for accurate 3D segmentation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to explicit high-dimensional modeling due to the compact latent attributes \mathbf{f}i. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the CT-ORG subset in SAT-DS. Mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (mDSC): 88.17% Mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU): 83.72% Pixel Accuracy (PA): 98.97% Liver DSC: Consistently above 84.62%. Top 5 Slices Performance (CT-ORG): Slice 32: PA 99.42%, mIoU 95.31%, mDSC 99.42% Slice 70: PA 98.81%, mIoU 94.32%, mDSC 98.81% Slice 29: PA 99.20%, mIoU 99.20%, mDSC 99.20% Slice 65: PA 98.62%, mIoU 98.62%, mDSC 98.62% Slice 30: PA 99.16%, mIoU 99.16%, mDSC 99.16%. Strengths: Enables precise 3D segmentation of ROIs through open-vocabulary queries; preserves volumetric consistency; computationally efficient compared to high-dimensional explicit modeling. Limitations: Performance may vary across different anatomical regions (e.g., Liver DSC is lower than overall PA). When to use: When open-vocabulary 3D segmentation is required in medical or complex scenes where memory efficiency is critical. When not to use: When high-dimensional feature fidelity is more important than memory efficiency, or when open-vocabulary capabilities are not needed. This method is part of the InnerGS framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting for multimodal medical scene understanding. It integrates Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by distilling high-dimensional embeddings into compact latent attributes using a scene-specific autoencoder. The approach was proposed to facilitate downstream clinical tasks such as segmentation. The VLM used is a knowledge-enhanced medical VLM (Zhao et al., 2025), and the autoencoder is based on (Qin et al., 2024). The method was evaluated on the CT-ORG subset of the SAT-DS dataset (Rister et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2025). name: Human and Articulated Avatars
body: This family extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct and render animatable human avatars from multi-view or single-view inputs. It solves the problem of dynamic geometry and appearance modeling by maintaining a canonical space representation where Gaussians are deformed via differentiable functions driven by pose parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients) before rasterization. It sets itself apart from static reconstruction methods by enabling novel view synthesis of dynamic subjects through learned deformation fields, and from mesh-based methods by leveraging the explicit, differentiable nature of 3D Gaussians for high-fidelity texture and geometry. All methods in this family rely on the differentiable alpha-blending accumulation of feature vectors or colors during the rasterization step. For a pixel p, the rendered vector \mathbf{V}(p) is computed by sorting overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back and applying: \mathbf{V}(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} \mathbf{v}i \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: \mathbf{v}i is the vector (feature \mathbf{f}i or color \mathbf{c}i) of the i-th Gaussian. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance from all preceding Gaussians j < i. If \mathcal{O}p is empty, \mathbf{V}(p) = \mathbf{0}. For structural extensions, all methods share a canonical space representation where 3D Gaussians are initialized in a reference pose (e.g., T-pose or neutral expression). Deformation is achieved by mapping these canonical Gaussians to a target pose defined by parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients). The rendering pipeline remains differentiable, allowing optimization of Gaussian attributes and deformation parameters via photometric loss. The deformation function D(\cdot) maps a canonical Gaussian i with position \mathbf{p}i^{\text{canonical}} to a target position \mathbf{p}i^{\text{target}} based on pose parameters \theta: \mathbf{p}i^{\text{target}} = D(\mathbf{p}i^{\text{canonical}}, \theta) The rotation and scale of the Gaussian may also be transformed by the deformation function to maintain physical consistency. GaussianHead reconstructs animatable head avatars by combining a tri-plane representation with motion fields to simulate geometrically changing heads during continuous movements. It renders rich textures, including skin and hair. It builds on the canonical space deformation principles of Human and Articulated Avatars. GART extends human models to more articulated models based on the 3DGS representation. It builds on Human and Articulated Avatars. D3GA creates animatable human avatars using drivable 3D Gaussians and tetrahedral cages for full-body modeling. It addresses dynamic human reconstruction from multi-view videos by providing promising geometry and appearance modeling. It sets itself apart from head-only siblings like GaussianHead, GART, and HeadGas by extending the drivable Gaussian representation to the full body. HeadGaS is a method for real-time animatable 3D head reconstruction and animation that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a base of learnable latent features. It solves the problem of modeling dynamic facial expressions by allowing Gaussians to alter their opacity and color over time, achieving dynamics via over-representation (duplicates of dynamic face areas that become active one at a time) rather than explicit geometric deformation. It sets itself apart from siblings like GaussianHead and GART by blending latent features with 3DMM expression weights to predict appearance, avoiding the complexity of optimizing 3D motion for every Gaussian. Push the speed of high-fidelity dynamic human creation to 100 seconds using a fixed-perspective camera. Embed Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh. Determine the position of a Gaussian by the barycenter and displacement along the normal direction. Combine hand geometry priors (MANO) with 3DGS. Provide the first real-time hand reconstruction. Apply 3DGS to dynamic head reconstruction using canonical space modeling and deformation prediction. Explore the interaction between hands and objects using 3DGS. The concept of animatable avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as an extension of static reconstruction methods to handle dynamic subjects. Early works like GaussianAvatar incorporated optimizable tensors with dynamic appearance networks to capture dynamics. Human101 further optimized the training speed for high-fidelity dynamic human creation, achieving 100 seconds using a fixed-perspective camera. Subsequent methods like SplattingAvatar and GoMAvatar embedded Gaussians onto canonical human body meshes, determining positions via barycentric coordinates and normal displacements. For head modeling, MonoGaussianAvatar applied canonical space modeling and deformation prediction, while GaussianHead introduced tri-plane representations and motion fields for continuous movement simulation. Extensions to other body parts include 3DPSHR for real-time hand reconstruction using MANO priors and MANUS for hand-object interaction. name: GaussianHead
body: GaussianHead reconstructs animatable head avatars by combining a tri-plane representation with motion fields to simulate geometrically changing heads during continuous movements. It renders rich textures, including skin and hair. It builds on the canonical space deformation principles of Human and Articulated Avatars. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Canonical 3D Gaussians, pose parameters \theta, and expression coefficients. Outputs: Rendered image \mathbf{C}(p) per pixel p. Data Structures: Tri-plane Representation: Stores latent features for head geometry and appearance. Motion Fields: Predicts geometric changes for continuous movements. Steps: 1. Canonical Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians in a neutral reference pose. 2. Deformation Prediction: Use the motion fields to map canonical positions to target positions based on pose \theta and expression. The deformation function D(\cdot) transforms position, rotation, and scale to maintain physical consistency. 3. Rendering: Accumulate features using the differentiable alpha-blending pipeline from Human and Articulated Avatars. Formulas: \mathbf{p}i^{\text{target}} = D(\mathbf{p}i^{\text{canonical}}, \theta) where: \mathbf{p}i^{\text{canonical}} is the position of the i-th Gaussian in the neutral reference pose. \theta represents the pose and expression parameters. D(\cdot) is the deformation function parameterized by the motion field. \mathbf{p}i^{\text{target}} is the transformed position used for rasterization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues in tri-plane sampling may occur if Gaussian positions fall outside the normalized bounding box. Degenerate expressions may cause self-intersections if the motion field lacks regularization. body: HeadGaS is a method for real-time animatable 3D head reconstruction and animation that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a base of learnable latent features. It solves the problem of modeling dynamic facial expressions by allowing Gaussians to alter their opacity and color over time, achieving dynamics via over-representation (duplicates of dynamic face areas that become active one at a time) rather than explicit geometric deformation. It sets itself apart from siblings like GaussianHead and GART by blending latent features with 3DMM expression weights to predict appearance, avoiding the complexity of optimizing 3D motion for every Gaussian. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video frames, pre-computed head poses (camera poses Wi), and expression vectors (ei) from a parametric head model (e.g., FLAME or FaceWarehouse). Outputs: Rendered images Ir for given expression and camera parameters. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Ga is defined as a tuple (\Sigma, \mu, F): \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The 3D covariance matrix. \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3: The center position in canonical space. F \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times f{dim}}: The latent feature basis. B is the number of expression weights (e.g., 52 for FLAME), and f{dim} is the feature dimensionality (32). Note: Color c and opacity \alpha are not stored explicitly but are predicted by an MLP. Parameters: f{dim} = 32. B = 52 for FLAME tracking. Spherical Harmonics degree k=3. Rendering resolution: 512^2 pixels. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Acquire head poses and expression weights for each frame. Convert rigid head poses to camera poses to map observations to a canonical head pose. Perform video matting and face parsing to discard background and clothing. 2. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussian centers \mu with 2500 points (subset of 3DMM mesh vertices or random points within near/far bounds). Initialize latent features F with zeros. 3. Feature Blending: For each frame i with expression vector ei \in \mathbb{R}^B, compute the frame-specific feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^{f{dim}} for each Gaussian: fi = F^T ei + f0 where f0 is a bias term. 4. Color and Opacity Prediction: Feed fi and the Gaussian position \mu into an MLP \phi to predict color ci and opacity \alphai: ci, \alphai = \phi(fi, \psi(\mu)) where \psi denotes sinusoidal positional encoding of \mu. The MLP \phi consists of two linear layers with LeakyReLU activations, a hidden layer of 64 channels, and two output branches (color and opacity). The opacity branch ends with a sigmoid activation. 5. Projection: Project Gaussians to image space using camera view Wi. Compute the covariance matrix in camera coordinates \Sigma' using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation of the projective transformation: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T. 6. Rendering: Render using a tile-based differentiable rasterizer. For pixel p, sort overlapping Gaussians \mathcal{O}p front-to-back and apply alpha-blending: V(p) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{O}p} ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). 7. Optimization: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} using Stochastic Gradient Descent with exponential decay scheduling for positions \mu and the MLP. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1(Ir, I{\text{gt}}) + \lambdas \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}(Ir, I{\text{gt}}) + \lambdap \mathcal{L}p(Ir, I{\text{gt}}) where \lambda1=0.8, \lambdas=0.2, \lambdap=0.1. The perceptual loss \mathcal{L}p is activated after 10k iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class HeadGaSMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, fdim, k=3): super().init() self.freqbands = 6 self.colordim = 3 (k + 1) self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(fdim + 3 self.freqbands, 64), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(64, self.colordim + 1)) def forward(self, fi, mu): scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(self.freqbands)], dtype=mu.dtype, device=mu.device) muexp = mu.unsqueeze(-1) scalesexp = scales.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) posenc = torch.sin(muexp scalesexp torch.pi).view(mu.shape[0], -1) out = self.net(torch.cat([fi, posenc], dim=-1)) return out[:,:self.colordim], torch.sigmoid(out[:, self.colordim:]) def blendfeatures(F, ei, f0): # F: (N, B, fdim), ei: (B,), f0: (fdim,) return torch.einsum('nbd,b->nd', F, ei) + f0 def computecameracovariance(Sigma, W, J): # W: 4x4 camera view matrix, J: 3x3 Jacobian W3x3 = W[:3,:3] return J @ W3x3 @ Sigma @ W3x3.T @ J.T def alphablendaccumulation(sortedcolors, sortedopacities): accumulated = torch.zeroslike(sortedcolors) transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(len(sortedopacities)): accumulated += sortedcolors[i] sortedopacities[i] transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - sortedopacities[i]) return accumulated def renderheadgas(gaussians, camerapose, expressionvector, mlp, f0): mu, Sigma, F = gaussians['mu'], gaussians['Sigma'], gaussians['F'] ei, W = expressionvector, camerapose N = mu.shape[0] fi = blendfeatures(F, ei, f0) ci, alphai = mlp(fi, mu) J = torch.eye(3, device=mu.device) Sigmaprime = computecameracovariance(Sigma, W, J) centerscam = W[:3,:3] @ mu.T + W[:3, 3:] depths = centerscam[2,:] sortidx = torch.argsort(depths) sortedc = ci[sortidx] sortedalpha = alphai[sortidx] renderedimage = alphablendaccumulation(sortedc, sortedalpha) return renderedimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: Initializing latent features F with zeros leads to the most stable solution. Over-representation: Dynamic areas require multiple Gaussians (duplicates) that become active/inactive based on expression. Loss Conflict: Perceptual loss Lp is activated after 10k iterations to avoid conflict with photometric loss at early stages. An ablation variant where Gaussians are transformed using deltas for position (\mu) and rotation (R) predicted by an MLP \phi'. The MLP outputs 3 values of position shift and 4 values of rotation (quaternion). The static Gaussian position is updated as \mu' = \mu + \Delta \mu and rotation as R' = Rt R. A regularization term \lambda\mu \mathcal{L}1(\Delta \mu) is added to the loss to encourage small position shifts. This variant requires significantly more Gaussians (234k) than the proposed HeadGaS (28k) because the proposed model's over-representation is more effective and easier to learn. Performance on INSTA dataset for this variant: 234k Gaussians, 0.019s rendering time, 29.83 PSNR. Time Complexity: Rendering is real-time, over 100 FPS generally, approximately 250 FPS at 512 \times 512 resolution. Memory Complexity: The method uses over-representation, leading to a higher number of Gaussians than static 3DGS, but fewer than deformation-based variants (28k vs 234k in ablation). Measured Performance: INSTA dataset: PSNR 32.50, SSIM 0.971, LPIPS 0.033, rendering time 0.10s at 512^2 resolution. NBS dataset: PSNR 34.34, SSIM 0.970, LPIPS 0.0311, rendering time 0.10s at 512^2 resolution. PointAvatar dataset: PSNR 36.66, SSIM 0.976, LPIPS 0.0261, rendering time 0.10s at 512^2 resolution. Scaling: Rendering speed accelerated by over 10x compared to interactive NeRF-based baselines. Strengths: Real-time inference, state-of-the-art results (up to 2 dB PSNR improvement over baselines), simple and effective blending in latent space. Limitations: Requires pre-computed head poses and expression weights. HeadGaS was proposed by H. Dhamo et al. in the paper "HeadGaS: Real-Time Animatable Head Avatars via 3D Gaussian Splatting". It extends the explicit 3DGS representation with a base of learnable latent features, inspired by traditional blendshape 3DMMs. The method allows reconstruction in real-time of animatable heads. It supports various 3DMM representations, including FLAME and FaceWarehouse.
