name: Physical Parameter Optimization
head: 3DGS Volume Parameters, Participating Medium Parameters, Physical Gaussian Attributes, g Optimization, 物理化的高斯参数
body: Physical Parameter Optimization replaces the standard spherical harmonic (SH) color and empirical opacity attributes of 3D Gaussian Splatting with a set of physical quantities representing a participating medium. This allows for real-time rendering and dynamic relighting (arbitrary sun direction) by solving the radiative transfer equation through the Gaussian primitives rather than approximating lighting with SH coefficients. It is distinct from standard 3DGS training by optimizing extinction, albedo, and scattering asymmetry instead of color and opacity. Inputs: A dataset of images with known camera poses and sun directions (Stage 1: sun-only, black background; Stage 2: environment lighting). Initial 3D Gaussian point cloud (position, scale, rotation, and initial physical parameters). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian attributes: position, scale, rotation, extinction coefficient (\sigmat), scattering albedo (\omega), Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry factor (g), and multiple scattering octave weights (wn). (Stage 2 only) Optimized environment light network parameters. Each Gaussian primitive stores the following physical parameters in addition to standard geometric attributes (position \mathbf{x}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}): 1. Extinction Coefficient (\sigmat): Type: Scalar. Meaning: Extinction cross-section, representing the volume integral of the extinction coefficient. Activation: softplus, clamped at 5.0. 2. Scattering Albedo (\omega): Type: RGB Vector (3 floats). Meaning: Ratio of scattering coefficient to extinction coefficient. Activation: sigmoid. 3. Henyey-Greenstein Asymmetry Factor (g): Type: Scalar. Meaning: Anisotropy factor for the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Activation: 0.8 \times \tanh(g{raw}), favoring forward scattering. 4. Multiple Scattering Octave Weights (wn): Type: Array of 6 learnable scalars. Meaning: Energy weights for the 6th-order multiple scattering octave approximation (based on Frostbite/Wrenninge). Activation: softplus. The training process is divided into two stages: Stage 1: Physical Parameter Training 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians with standard 3DGS geometry and initial physical parameters. 2. Rendering: For each training iteration, render the scene using the physical volume rendering equation. The radiance L is computed by integrating the extinction, albedo, and phase function along the ray. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss L as a weighted sum of L1 and DSSIM: L = 0.8 \cdot L1 + 0.2 \cdot DSSIM where the DSSIM weight \lambda{dssim} = 0.2. 4. Regularization: Apply Soft Anisotropy Regularization if the log-ratio of scales exceeds anisoratiomax: L{aniso} = \lambda{aniso} \cdot (\log(\text{ratio}))^2 with \lambda{aniso} = 0.001. 5. Optimization: Update all parameters using Adam optimizer with specific learning rates (see Parameters). 6. Densification and Pruning: Interval: Iterations 500 to 15,000, every 100 iterations. Densification: Use adaptive densification with densifytopfrac=0.005 and absolute lower bound 5 \times 10^{-5}. Incorporate scale gradients if > 10^{-6}. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with mean contribution \sum (\alpha \cdot T) < 10^{-4}. Post-Densify Pruning: Extra pruning every 1,000 iterations during densification phase. Resurrection: Every 3,000 iterations (during densification phase), reset the lowest contribution 5% of \sigmat Gaussians to 0.1. 7. Tonemapping: Apply fixed ACES tonemapping by default. If tonemaplearnable is enabled, optimize 4 ACES coefficients with a monotonicity penalty \lambda{tonemap\mono} = 10^{-2} to prevent curve inversion in [0, 8]. Stage 2: Environment Light Optimization 1. Freeze: Freeze all Stage 1 geometric and physical parameters. 2. Train: Optimize a global environment light network (MLP for sun direction T{sun} and SH coefficients for sky irradiance E{lm} and visibility V{lm}) using the envlr learning rate. Learning Rates (Initial / Final): Position: 1.6 \times 10^{-4} / 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. \sigmat: 0.025. \omega: 0.0025. g: 0.0025. wn: 0.0025. Scale: 0.005. Rotation: 0.001. Environment Light (Stage 2): 10^{-3}. Decay: Physical parameter learning rates decay exponentially to 1/10 of their initial value over the course of training. Position LR decays over positionlrmaxsteps (default 30,000). Position LR Delay Mult: 0.01. Total Iterations: 30,000. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstage1(gaussians, dataset, iterations=30000): # Initialize optimizers with specific learning rates optpos = Adam(gaussians.position, lr=1.6e-4, delaymult=0.01) optsigmat = Adam(gaussians.sigmat, lr=0.025) optomega = Adam(gaussians.omega, lr=0.0025) optg = Adam(gaussians.g, lr=0.0025) optw = Adam(gaussians.w, lr=0.0025) optscale = Adam(gaussians.scale, lr=0.005) optrot = Adam(gaussians.rotation, lr=0.001) for iter in range(iterations): # 1. Sample camera and sun direction cam, sun = dataset.sample() # 2. Render physical volume # Integrate extinction, albedo, and HG phase function renderedimage = renderphysicalvolume(gaussians, cam, sun) # 3. Compute Loss gtimage = dataset.getgt(cam) l1loss = L1(renderedimage, gtimage) dssimloss = DSSIM(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = 0.8 l1loss + 0.2 dssimloss # 4. Regularization if checkanisotropy(gaussians): loss += 0.001 anisotropypenalty(gaussians) # 5. Backpropagate and Update loss.backward() optpos.step() optsigmat.step() optomega.step() optg.step() optw.step() optscale.step() optrot.step() optpos.zerograd() optsigmat.zerograd() optomega.zerograd() optg.zerograd() optw.zerograd() optscale.zerograd() optrot.zerograd() # 6. Densification and Pruning (Iter 500-15000, step 100) if 500 <= iter <= 15000 and iter % 100 == 0: densifygaussians(gaussians, optpos, optscale, threshold=5e-5, topfrac=0.005) prunegaussians(gaussians, threshold=1e-4) # Resurrection every 3000 iterations if iter % 3000 == 0: resurrectgaussians(gaussians, fraction=0.05, value=0.1) # Post-densify pruning every 1000 iterations if iter % 1000 == 0: prunegaussians(gaussians, threshold=1e-4) # 7. Decay Learning Rates decaylearningrates(optpos, optsigmat, optomega, optg, optw, iter, maxsteps=30000) def trainstage2(gaussians, envnetwork, dataset, iterations=30000): # Freeze Stage 1 parameters gaussians.position.requiresgrad = False gaussians.scale.requiresgrad = False gaussians.rotation.requiresgrad = False gaussians.sigmat.requiresgrad = False gaussians.omega.requiresgrad = False gaussians.g.requiresgrad = False gaussians.w.requiresgrad = False optenv = Adam(envnetwork.parameters(), lr=1e-3) for iter in range(iterations): cam, sun = dataset.sample() renderedimage = renderphysicalvolumewithenv(gaussians, envnetwork, cam, sun) gtimage = dataset.getgt(cam) loss = 0.8 L1(renderedimage, gtimage) + 0.2 DSSIM(renderedimage, gtimage) loss.backward() optenv.step() optenv.zerograd() decaylearningrates(optenv, iter, maxsteps=30000) Anisotropy Control: Position LR must sync with iterations to prevent anisotropy loss of control. Resurrection Loop: Resurrection is only active during the densification period to avoid net destruction loops. Tonemapping: If using learnable tonemapping, ensure monotonicity penalty is applied to prevent curve inversion in [0, 8]. CUDA Compilation: On Windows, ensure MSVC toolset version is compatible with CUDA (e.g., MSVC 14.44 for CUDA 12.8). Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS training, but with additional overhead for physical volume integration and multiple scattering octave calculations. Memory Complexity: Higher than standard 3DGS due to additional physical parameters (\sigmat, \omega, g, wn) per Gaussian. Performance: Enables real-time rendering and dynamic relighting. Strengths: Physically plausible lighting, dynamic sun direction support, stable physical parameters. Limitations: Complex training pipeline (two stages), sensitive to learning rate decay and densification parameters. When to Use: When dynamic relighting and physically accurate volume rendering are required. When Not to Use: When simple static lighting or empirical color representation is sufficient. Physical Parameter Optimization was introduced as part of the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud project, building on the 3DGS-Volume-Cloud repository. It aims to replace ray-marching volume clouds in game engines with 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time rendering and dynamic relighting. The method was developed by hsiang0117 and is documented in the 4DGS-Volume-Cloud GitHub repository. hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Training > Parameter-Specific Learning Rates
head: 3DGS-CT Backbone Configuration, Adam Optimizer Configuration, Adam parameter learning rates, Adam with Specific Learning Rates, Gaussian Optimizer Configuration, Parameter-Specific Learning Rates, Per-parameter group learning rates
body: Parameter-Specific Learning Rates configures the Adam optimizer with distinct learning rates for each Gaussian attribute group to stabilize training and prevent rapid divergence. Unlike a uniform learning rate, this method assigns separate rates to different parameter groups, addressing the varying sensitivity of Gaussian properties during differentiable rasterization. Inputs: Gaussian parameters \theta: means \mathbf{p}, opacities \alpha, scales \mathbf{s}, colours \mathbf{c}, and optionally rotations \mathbf{q} or spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{H}. Optimizer hyperparameters: base Adam settings \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, \epsilon=1\times10^{-15}. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \theta' after an optimization step. Data Structures: The optimizer maintains separate first and second moment state buffers for each parameter group. Groups are defined as lists of tensors, where each tensor contains the attribute values for all active Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize torch.optim.Adam with the parameter list, base lr=0.0, and eps=1e-15. Set \beta1=0.9 and \beta2=0.999. 2. Parameter Group Definition: Define parameter groups with specific learning rates: opacities 0.00085, scales 0.001, colours 0.02, means 0.00015. Some implementations use pre-activation values for opacities and scales with a learning rate of 0.05. 3. Trainability Check: Verify that all required parameters are marked as trainable via gaussians.checkiftrainable(). 4. Optimizer Step: For each iteration, compute gradients via the differentiable rasterizer's backward pass, execute optimizer.step(), then call optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True). 5. Cache Management: Immediately after the optimizer step, call torch.cuda.emptycache() to release unused GPU memory back to the system. Formulas: The Adam update for a parameter group g with learning rate lrg is: \mathbf{m}t = \beta1 \mathbf{m}{t-1} + (1 - \beta1) \mathbf{g}t \mathbf{v}t = \beta2 \mathbf{v}{t-1} + (1 - \beta2) \mathbf{g}t^2 \hat{\mathbf{m}}t = \frac{\mathbf{m}t}{1 - \beta1^t}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{v}}t = \frac{\mathbf{v}t}{1 - \beta2^t} \theta{t+1} = \thetat - lrg \cdot \frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}t}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}t} + \epsilon} Where \mathbf{g}t is the gradient for the group, \thetat represents the parameters in that group (e.g., all means, all colours), and lrg is the group-specific learning rate. Parameters with Typical Values: Standard 3DGS: lr\alpha=0.00085, lr\mathbf{s}=0.001, lr\mathbf{c}=0.02, lr\mathbf{p}=0.00015. X-Gaussian Variant: Position lr starts at 1.9\times10^{-4} and decays exponentially to 1.9\times10^{-6}. Point feature lr=2\times10^{-3}. Opacity lr=8\times10^{-3}. Scaling lr=5\times10^{-3}. Rotation lr=1\times10^{-3}. Gaussian-Flow Variant: Position lr=4\times10^{-4} with exponential decay of 8\times10^{-7}. Rotation lr=0.002. DDDM parameters lr=4\times10^{-4}. Weight decay 8\times10^{-7} applied to all parameters. 2D Gaussian Variant: Image-space coordinates lr=0.001 \times \text{mean}(\text{width}, \text{height}). Colour lr=0.01. Opacity lr=0.02. Scale lr=0.001. Rotation angle lr=0.02. Gaussian Radiance Field Variant: Rotation lr=2\times10^{-3}, scaling lr=5\times10^{-3}, opacity lr=1\times10^{-1}, spherical harmonics lr=1\times10^{-4}. Position lr exponentially interpolated between 3.2\times10^{-4} and 6.4\times10^{-6}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Isotropic Mode: If the Gaussian representation is isotropic, rotation parameters (quaternions) are not optimized; checkiftrainable() raises a RuntimeError if they are marked as trainable. Precision: The epsilon value is set to 1\times10^{-15} to prevent division by zero in the Adam update. Memory: Frequent optimizer steps without cache management can lead to OOM errors; torch.cuda.emptycache() is recommended after each step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.optim as optim def setupoptimizer(gaussians, config): means = gaussians.getmeans() opacities = gaussians.getopacities() scales = gaussians.getscales() colors = gaussians.getcolors() if gaussians.isisotropic(): rotations = None else: rotations = gaussians.getrotations() # Standard 3DGS learning rates lrmeans = 0.00015 lropacities = 0.00085 lrscales = 0.001 lrcolors = 0.02 lrrotations = 0.001 paramgroups = [ {'params': means, 'lr': lrmeans}, {'params': opacities, 'lr': lropacities}, {'params': scales, 'lr': lrscales}, {'params': colors, 'lr': lrcolors}, ] if rotations is not None: paramgroups.append({'params': rotations, 'lr': lrrotations}) # Initialize Adam with base lr=0.0, rates handled per group optimizer = optim.Adam(paramgroups, lr=0.0, eps=1e-15, betas=(0.9, 0.999)) return optimizer def trainingstep(gaussians, optimizer, loss): optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) loss.backward() optimizer.step() torch.cuda.emptycache() return loss BOGausS (Better Optimized Gaussian Splatting) is a modified Stochastic Gradient Descent optimizer designed to ensure unbiased state estimation for sparsely-viewed and split Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting training. It addresses the performance degradation caused by biased moment estimates in standard Adam when Gaussians are occluded or rarely updated. It sets itself apart by using Gaussian-dependent time steps and precision-aware scaling factors derived from reconstruction confidence intervals, rather than global iteration counts and uniform learning rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gradient

Initialized to 0. \widehat{g}: First moment estimate (mean of gradients). Vector of same shape as 	heta. Initialized to 0. \widehat{g}^2: Second moment estimate (mean of squared gradients). For localization and size parameters, \Delta	heta is the confidence interval \Deltai derived from reconstruction confidence metrics. For all other parameters (e.g., opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients), \Delta	heta = 1. \alphat: Inheritance factor for time during splitting. \alphag: Inheritance factor for gradient states during splitting. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Adaptive Coefficients: Calculate the time-dependent coefficients \alpha{1,t} and \alpha{2,t} based on the Gaussian's updated lifespan t \ge 1: \alpha{s,t} = \max(1/t, 1 -  etas^\star) where s \in \{1, 2\}. The coefficient uses the step count including the current update to avoid division by zero when t=0. 2. Update First Moment: \widehat{g}t = \widehat{g}{t-1} + \alpha{1,t}(
abla	heta \mathcal{L}t - \widehat{g}{t-1}) This is an exponential moving average update where the step size adapts to the Gaussian's age. (Note: The source contains a typographical error \widehat{g}{-1}; it is corrected here to \widehat{g}{t-1} to match the recursive definition.) 3. Update Second Moment: \widehat{g}t^2 = \widehat{g}{t-1}^2 + \alpha{2,t}((
abla	heta \mathcal{L}t)^2 - \widehat{g}{t-1}^2) Similarly, this maintains an unbiased estimate of the second moment. 4. Parameter Update: 	heta{t+1} = 	hetat + \eta	heta \Delta	heta  rac{\widehat{g}t}{\widehat{g}t^2 + \epsilon} The update is scaled by \Delta	heta to account for the sensitivity of the parameter to changes. 5. Increment Lifespan: t \leftarrow t + 1 The Gaussian's specific time counter is incremented only if it was updated in this pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: \widehat{g}0 and \widehat{g}0^2 must be exactly 0. t must be 0 for new Gaussians. Splitting: When a Gaussian splits, the child Gaussians inherit state. name: SparseGaussianAdam
head: Sparse Adam for Gaussian Splatting, Sparse Gaussian Adam Optimizer
body: SparseGaussianAdam is a variant of the Adam optimizer designed for 3D Gaussian Splatting that restricts parameter updates to only those Gaussians currently visible in the rendered image. It solves the problem of biased state estimation and inefficient computation caused by sparse visibility in differentiable rendering, where most Gaussians do not contribute to the loss in any given frame. It compensates for the learning rate bias correction when updates are sparse by adjusting the effective learning rate based on the number of active parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Parameter tensor P, gradient tensor G, visibility mask V (boolean array indicating visible Gaussians), base learning rate \eta, epsilon \epsilon, momentum coefficients \beta1, \beta2. Output: Updated parameter tensor P. Data Structures: The optimizer maintains state per parameter group. Each state entry contains: step: A scalar float32 representing the current optimization step count. expavg: A tensor of the same shape as the parameter, initialized to zeros, storing the first moment estimate. expavgsq: A tensor of the same shape as the parameter, initialized to zeros, storing the second moment estimate. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: If the state for the parameter is empty, initialize step to 0.0 (float32), expavg to a zero tensor with the same shape and memory format as the parameter, and expavgsq to a zero tensor with the same shape and memory format. 2. Increment Step: Increment the step counter: step \leftarrow step + 1. 3. Retrieve State: Retrieve expavg and expavgsq from the optimizer state. 4. Calculate Dimensions: Determine N, the number of visible Gaussians (active parameters), and M, the number of elements per Gaussian, calculated as M = \text{param.numel()} // N. Note: N is derived from the number of True values in the visibility mask. 5. Compute Effective Learning Rate: Calculate the bias-corrected effective learning rate \eta{eff}: \eta{eff} = \eta \frac{\sqrt{1 - \beta2^{step}}}{1 - \beta1^{step}} where \eta is the base learning rate, \beta1 = 0.9, and \beta2 = 0.999. 6. Apply Update: Invoke the custom CUDA kernel C.adamUpdate with the following arguments: param: The parameter tensor P. param.grad: The gradient tensor G. expavg: The first moment estimate. expavgsq: The second moment estimate. visibilitymask: The boolean mask V. lr: The effective learning rate \eta{eff}. beta1: 0.9. beta2: 0.999. eps: The epsilon value \epsilon. N: The number of visible Gaussians. M: The number of elements per Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsegaussianadamstep(param, grad, visibilitymask, lr, eps, beta1, beta2): # 1. Initialize state if empty if not hasattr(sparsegaussianadamstep, 'state'): sparsegaussianadamstep.state = {} state = sparsegaussianadamstep.state.get(id(param)) if state is None: state = { 'step': 0.0, 'expavg': [0.0] len(param), 'expavgsq': [0.0] len(param) } sparsegaussianadamstep.state[id(param)] = state # 2. Increment step state['step'] += 1 step = state['step'] # 3. Retrieve state expavg = state['expavg'] expavgsq = state['expavgsq'] # 4. Calculate dimensions N = sum(1 for v in visibilitymask if v) M = len(param) // N # 5. Compute effective learning rate biascorrection1 = 1.0 - beta1 step biascorrection2 = 1.0 - beta2 step lreff = lr (biascorrection2 0.5) / biascorrection1 # 6. Apply update # The sources specify calling a custom CUDA kernel: C.adamUpdate(...) # Below is the equivalent logic for visible elements only. if N > 0: for i in range(len(param)): if visibilitymask[i]: # Standard Adam update for visible parameters expavg[i] = beta1 expavg[i] + (1.0 - beta1) grad[i] expavgsq[i] = beta2 expavgsq[i] + (1.0 - beta2) grad[i] 2 denom = (expavgsq[i] 0.5) / (biascorrection2 0.5) + eps / biascorrection1 param[i] -= lreff expavg[i] / denom state['expavg'] = expavg state['expavgsq'] = expavgsq else: pass # No visible Gaussians, skip update return param Parameters: lr: Base learning rate. Passed from the optimizer group configuration. eps: Epsilon for numerical stability. Passed to the update function. N: Number of visible Gaussians. Used to scale the learning rate compensation and passed to the C++ update function. M: Number of parameter elements per Gaussian (e.g., 3 for means, 4 for rotations). beta1: First moment decay rate, typically 0.9. beta2: Second moment decay rate, typically 0.999. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the parameter gradient is None or has zero elements, the step is skipped to avoid errors in state initialization or update. Precision issues may arise if N is very small, leading to unstable bias correction. The sources do not specify a minimum N threshold. The calculation of M assumes that the parameter tensor is evenly divisible by N. If N=0, division by zero occurs. The pseudocode handles this by skipping the update. GaussianAdam is a custom variant of the Adam optimizer designed specifically for 3D Gaussian Splatting that tracks per-Gaussian visibility via a last-seen step counter and maintains a learning rate history buffer for adaptive scheduling. It differs from standard Adam by explicitly managing per-Gaussian visibility and a dedicated learning rate history buffer, enabling step-dependent learning rate scheduling per Gaussian rather than a global schedule. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) per step, where N is the number of visible Gaussians and M is the number of elements per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N{total} \cdot M) for storing expavg and expavgsq for all Gaussians, even if only N are visible. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of visible Gaussians. Performance improves as visibility becomes sparser. Strengths: Reduces computation by a factor of N (number of Gaussians) by only updating visible Gaussians. Compensates for learning rate bias correction in sparse updates. Limitations: Requires a custom CUDA kernel (C.adamUpdate) for efficient implementation. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models with sparse visibility, such as in large scenes or early training stages. When not to use: When visibility is dense, or when a standard Adam implementation is preferred for simplicity. name: GaussianAdam Optimizer
body: GaussianAdam is a custom variant of the Adam optimizer designed specifically for 3D Gaussian Splatting that tracks per-Gaussian visibility via a last-seen step counter and maintains a learning rate history buffer for adaptive scheduling. It differs from standard Adam by explicitly managing per-Gaussian visibility and a dedicated learning rate history buffer, enabling step-dependent learning rate scheduling per Gaussian rather than a global schedule. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Parameter tensor param, gradient tensor param.grad, hyperparameters lr (base learning rate), eps (numerical stability epsilon), featurewidth (number of contiguous scalar values per Gaussian), maxsteps (buffer size), currentstep (optimization iteration). Output: Updated param tensor and updated state dictionary. Data Structures: The state dictionary contains the following fields with exact layouts: step: int64 scalar, tracking the current optimization step. expavg: float32 tensor, shape matches param, storing the first moment estimate. expavgsq: float32 tensor, shape matches param, storing the second moment estimate. lastseenstep: int32 tensor, shape (N,), where N is the number of Gaussians, storing the last step each Gaussian was visible. lrhistory: float32 tensor, shape (maxsteps,), storing the learning rate history for adaptive scheduling. Parameters: maxsteps: int, maximum optimization steps for lrhistory buffer size. lr: float, base learning rate. eps: float, epsilon for numerical stability in denominator. featurewidth: int, number of contiguous scalar values per Gaussian in the parameter group. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize state with step (int64), expavg (float32, same shape as param), expavgsq (float32, same shape as param), lastseenstep (int32, size N), and lrhistory (float32, size maxsteps). 2. Compute currentstep. 3. Ensure lrhistory has sufficient capacity for currentstep. 4. Record lr into lrhistory at index currentstep. 5. Compute visible mask based on Gaussian visibility (e.g., radii or rendering contribution). 6. Resolve featurewidth. 7. Apply the Adam update using hyperparameters 0.9, 0.999, and eps, masking updates to visible Gaussians and using lastseenstep for visibility tracking. 8. Update state['step'].fill(currentstep). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianadamupdate(param, grad, state, lr, eps, featurewidth, maxsteps, currentstep, N, visible): # Guard: Skip update if gradient is None if grad is None: return # Guard: featurewidth must evenly divide param.numel() if len(param) % featurewidth != 0: raise ValueError("featurewidth must evenly divide param.numel()") # Guard: N cannot be negative if N < 0: raise ValueError("N cannot be negative") # Initialize state buffers if not present if "expavg" not in state: state["expavg"] = [0.0] len(param) state["expavgsq"] = [0.0] len(param) state["lastseenstep"] = [0] N state["lrhistory"] = [0.0] maxsteps state["step"] = 0 # Ensure lrhistory capacity if currentstep >= len(state["lrhistory"]): # Extend buffer if necessary, or clamp currentstep pass # Record lr in history state["lrhistory"][currentstep] = lr beta1, beta2 = 0.9, 0.999 # Update first and second moment estimates for i in range(len(param)): state["expavg"][i] = beta1 state["expavg"][i] + (1 - beta1) grad[i] state["expavgsq"][i] = beta2 state["expavgsq"][i] + (1 - beta2) grad[i] 2 # Bias correction biascorrection1 = 1 - beta1 currentstep biascorrection2 = 1 - beta2 currentstep stepsize = lr (biascorrection2 0.5) / biascorrection1 # Apply update only to visible Gaussians for i in range(len(param)): denom = (state["expavgsq"][i] 0.5) + eps update = stepsize state["expavg"][i] / denom if visible[i // featurewidth]: param[i] -= update # Update lastseenstep and step counter state["lastseenstep"] = [currentstep] N state["step"] = currentstep Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If param.grad is None, the update is skipped entirely. featurewidth must evenly divide param.numel(), otherwise a ValueError is raised. head: Non-Pinhole Camera Adaptation
body: Non-Pinhole Camera Training adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle camera models that deviate from the standard pinhole assumption, such as fisheye lenses or uncentered projections. It solves geometric distortion and coordinate misalignment in non-standard imaging systems by integrating differentiable image-space warping and masking into the training loop. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by explicitly supporting uncentered-distorted and uncentered-undistorted camera models, whereas standard 3DGS assumes a centered pinhole model. The method adapts the differentiable rasterizer to accommodate various non-pinhole camera geometries by modifying the projection pipeline. The core requirement is that all coordinate transformations and pixel masking operations must remain differentiable to enable end-to-end gradient backpropagation. Not given in the sources. The Gaussian attributes remain standard (position, rotation, scale, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). The camera model structure is extended to support uncentered principal points and radial/tangential distortion parameters. 1. Camera Model Selection: Choose the appropriate camera model based on the dataset: centered-undistorted for the Neural 3D Video Dataset, uncentered-undistorted for the Technicolor Dataset, and uncentered-distorted for the Google Immersive Dataset. 2. Differentiable Warping: For distorted models, apply a differentiable image-space warping function to map perspective view coordinates to the distorted image plane (e.g., fish-eye). 3. Masking: Generate a differentiable mask to exclude invalid pixels, such as black borders resulting from undistortion or out-of-bounds warping. 4. Rasterization: Render the Gaussians using the adapted projection, computing each Gaussian's contribution to the warped image plane. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the rendering loss only over valid pixels where the mask is active. 6. Optimization: Update Gaussian attributes and camera parameters using gradient descent, relying on the differentiability of the warping and masking steps. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Non-Differentiable Masking: If the mask is not differentiable, gradients may be blocked. The warping and masking must remain differentiable to allow end-to-end training. Black Pixels: Undistorted images often contain black borders that must be masked out to prevent loss computation on invalid data. Unverified code. target[y][x][c]) for c in range(3)] for y in range(len(rendered)) for x in range(len(rendered[0]))] validpixels = sum(mask[y][x] for y in range(len(mask)) for x in range(len(mask[0]))) if validpixels == 0: return 0.0 return sum(diff[y][x][c] mask[y][x] for y in range(len(mask)) for x in range(len(mask[0])) for c in range(3)) / validpixels A training technique introduced to disentangle defocus-aware and defocus-independent representations in an unsupervised manner by learning to generate images while randomizing the aperture size and latent codes independently. During training, the aperture size is changed randomly, and the latent codes are changed randomly. This technique is similar to techniques commonly used in viewpoint-aware representation learning, which are useful for disentangling the effect of the corresponding factor from latent codes. Adaptation of the 3DGS pipeline to specific non-pinhole datasets. For the Neural 3D Video Dataset, use the original centered-undistorted camera model. For the Technicolor Dataset, implement and use an uncentered-undistorted camera model. For the Google Immersive Dataset, adapt the method to fit an uncentered-distorted camera model using a differentiable image space warping function that maps perspective views to fish-eye distorted views. For real-time demos, retrain models on undistorted videos and apply a differentiable mask to exclude black pixels resulting from undistortion. Image warping and masking must remain differentiable to allow end-to-end training despite the coordinate transformations and pixel masking. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS, but with additional overhead for warping and masking operations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Successfully reconstructs scenes on non-pinhole datasets where standard 3DGS fails entirely, such as the Matterport dataset. Strengths: Handles a wide variety of camera models, including fisheye and uncentered projections. Enables training on real-world data with non-standard lenses. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of differentiable warping and masking. Performance may degrade if the warping function is not smooth or if the mask is not properly handled. When to Use: When training on datasets with non-pinhole cameras (e.g., fisheye, wide-angle, uncentered). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Non-Pinhole Camera Training was developed to address the limitations of standard 3DGS in handling non-standard camera models. It builds on the differentiable rasterizer of 3DGS, extending it to support various camera geometries. The method has been applied to datasets such as the Neural 3D Video Dataset, Technicolor Dataset, and Google Immersive Dataset. It has also been shown to succeed on the Matterport dataset, where standard 3DGS fails. The technique of Aperture Randomized Training, while related to defocus disentanglement, shares the principle of randomizing camera parameters during training to improve representation learning. name: ToF Scene Rendering Setup
head: ToF Gaussian Splatting Setup, ToF render
body: This method configures the rendering pipeline for Time-of-Flight (ToF) cameras within a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework, enabling the simultaneous optimization of color and ToF data (phasors, depth, amplitude). It differs from standard RGB-only splatting by maintaining separate rasterization settings for color and ToF views, handling multi-modal Gaussian attributes (such as phasor features), and supporting dynamic scene decomposition via motion masks. The setup initializes CUDA tensors for gradient tracking, computes camera projection parameters for both RGB and ToF sensors, and prepares Gaussian attributes for static and dynamic regions before invoking the respective rasterizers. Inputs: pc: GaussianModel instance containing attributes xyz, opacity, scaling, rotation, featurescolor, featuresphasor, and useviewdependentphase. viewpointcamera: Object containing FoVx, FoVy, FoVxtof, FoVytof, worldviewtransform, fullprojtransform, cameracenter, tofimageheight, tofimagewidth, and depthrange. opt: Optimization configuration containing optimizephaseoffset and optimizedcoffset. renderregions: List of strings indicating which parts of the scene to render (e.g., ['static', 'dynamic']). motionmask: Boolean tensor identifying dynamic Gaussians. Outputs: colorimage: Rendered RGB image. tofdata: Rendered ToF data including phasor, depth, pixel indices, and distribution. screenspacepoints: Tensor storing gradients of 2D means. 1. RasterizationSettings: Fields: imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier, viewmatrix, projmatrix, shdegree, campos, prefiltered, debug, nearn, farn. ToF-specific fields: depthrange, useviewdependentphase, optimizephaseoffset, optimizedcoffset. 2. Gaussian Attributes Tensors (CUDA, requiresgrad=True): means3D: Shape (N, 3). means2D: Shape (N, 2). opacity: Shape (N, 1). scales: Shape (N, 3). rotations: Shape (N, 4) (quaternions). shs: Shape (N, K, 3) (Spherical Harmonics coefficients for color). shsp: Shape (N, K, P) (Spherical Harmonics coefficients for phasor/ToF). screenspacepoints: Shape (N, 2), initialized to zero, with retaingrad() called. 1. Initialize Gradient Tensors: Create screenspacepoints on CUDA with requiresgrad=True and call retaingrad() to preserve gradients for 2D mean updates. 2. Compute Field of View Tangents: Calculate \tan(\text{FoV}x) and \tan(\text{FoV}y) for the RGB camera: \text{tanfovx} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx}) \text{tanfovy} = \tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy}) 3. Configure RGB Rasterization Settings: Create RasterizationSettings for color using imageheight, imagewidth, tanfovx, tanfovy, bg, scalemodifier, viewmatrix (worldviewtransform), projmatrix (fullprojtransform), shdegree, campos (cameracenter), prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn (znear), and farn (zfar). 4. Configure ToF Rasterization Settings (if viewpointcamera.FoVxtof is not None): Create RasterizationSettings for ToF using imageheight (tofimageheight), imagewidth (tofimagewidth), tanfovx (\tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVx\tof})), tanfovy (\tan(\text{viewpoint\camera.FoVy\tof})), bg, scalemodifier, viewmatrix (worldviewtransformtof), projmatrix (fullprojtransformtof), campos (cameracentertof), prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn (znear), farn (zfar), depthrange (viewpointcamera.depthrange.item()), useviewdependentphase (pc.useviewdependentphase), optimizephaseoffset (opt.optimizephaseoffset), and optimizedcoffset (opt.optimizedcoffset). 5. Initialize Gaussian Attribute Tensors: Create zero tensors on CUDA for means3D, means2D, opacity, scales, rotations, shs, and shsp matching the shapes of the corresponding pc attributes. 6. Populate Static Attributes: If 'static' is in renderregions, copy pc.xyz, pc.opacity, pc.scaling, pc.rotation, pc.featurescolor, and pc.featuresphasor to the zero tensors, excluding Gaussians marked by motionmask. 7. Populate Dynamic Attributes: If 'dynamic' is in renderregions, copy base attributes from pc and apply differentials: means3D adds dxyz, rotations apply rotationactivation to (rotation + drot), shs adds dsh, and shsp adds dshp. 8. Render Color Image: Call the color rasterizer with means3D, means2D, shs, shsp, opacity, scales, rotations, and cov3Dprecomp=None. 9. Render ToF Data: Call the ToF rasterizer with the same Gaussian attributes to produce phasor, depth, pixel, and distribution outputs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math import dataclasses @dataclasses.dataclass class RasterizationSettings: imageheight: int imagewidth: int tanfovx: float tanfovy: float bg: torch.Tensor scalemodifier: float viewmatrix: torch.Tensor projmatrix: torch.Tensor shdegree: int campos: torch.Tensor prefiltered: bool debug: bool nearn: float farn: float depthrange: float = None useviewdependentphase: bool = False optimizephaseoffset: bool = False optimizedcoffset: bool = False def rotationactivation(q: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Normalize quaternions to unit length.""" return q / torch.norm(q, dim=-1, keepdim=True) def rasterizecolor(settings: RasterizationSettings, means3D, means2D, shs, shsp, opacity, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp): """Performs standard color rasterization using the provided settings and attributes.""" # Standard rasterization step return torch.zeros(settings.imageheight, settings.imagewidth, 3, device='cuda') def rasterizetof(settings: RasterizationSettings, means3D, means2D, shs, shsp, opacity, scales, rotations, cov3Dprecomp): """Performs standard ToF rasterization using the provided settings and attributes.""" # Standard rasterization step return torch.zeros(settings.imageheight, settings.imagewidth, 4, device='cuda') def setuptofrendering(pc, viewpointcamera, opt, renderregions, motionmask): # Step 1: Initialize gradient tensors screenspacepoints = torch.zeros(pc.xyz.shape[0], 2, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) screenspacepoints.retaingrad() # Step 2: Compute FoV tangents for RGB tanfovx = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVx) tanfovy = math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVy) # Step 3: Configure RGB Rasterization Settings rgbsettings = RasterizationSettings( imageheight=viewpointcamera.imageheight, imagewidth=viewpointcamera.imagewidth, tanfovx=tanfovx, tanfovy=tanfovy, bg=viewpointcamera.bg, scalemodifier=viewpointcamera.scalemodifier, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransform, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.fullprojtransform, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=viewpointcamera.cameracenter, prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn=viewpointcamera.znear, farn=viewpointcamera.zfar) # Step 4: Configure ToF Rasterization Settings tofsettings = None if viewpointcamera.FoVxtof is not None: tofsettings = RasterizationSettings( imageheight=viewpointcamera.tofimageheight, imagewidth=viewpointcamera.tofimagewidth, tanfovx=math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVxtof), tanfovy=math.tan(viewpointcamera.FoVytof), bg=viewpointcamera.bg, scalemodifier=viewpointcamera.scalemodifier, viewmatrix=viewpointcamera.worldviewtransformtof, projmatrix=viewpointcamera.fullprojtransformtof, shdegree=pc.activeshdegree, campos=viewpointcamera.cameracentertof, prefiltered=False, debug=False, nearn=viewpointcamera.znear, farn=viewpointcamera.zfar, depthrange=viewpointcamera.depthrange.item(), useviewdependentphase=pc.useviewdependentphase, optimizephaseoffset=opt.optimizephaseoffset, optimizedcoffset=opt.optimizedcoffset) # Step 5: Initialize Gaussian Attribute Tensors N = pc.xyz.shape[0] means3D = torch.zeros(N, 3, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) means2D = torch.zeros(N, 2, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) opacity = torch.zeros(N, 1, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) scales = torch.zeros(N, 3, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) rotations = torch.zeros(N, 4, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) shs = torch.zeros(N, pc.activeshdegree + 1, 3, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) shsp = torch.zeros(N, pc.activeshdegree + 1, pc.phasordim, device='cuda', requiresgrad=True) # Step 6: Populate Static Attributes if 'static' in renderregions: staticmask = ~motionmask means3D[staticmask] = pc.xyz[staticmask] opacity[staticmask] = pc.opacity[staticmask] scales[staticmask] = pc.scaling[staticmask] rotations[staticmask] = pc.rotation[staticmask] shs[staticmask] = pc.featurescolor[staticmask] shsp[staticmask] = pc.featuresphasor[staticmask] # Step 7: Populate Dynamic Attributes if 'dynamic' in renderregions: dynamicmask = motionmask # Base copy means3D[dynamicmask] = pc.xyz[dynamicmask] opacity[dynamicmask] = pc.opacity[dynamicmask] scales[dynamicmask] = pc.scaling[dynamicmask] rotations[dynamicmask] = pc.rotation[dynamicmask] shs[dynamicmask] = pc.featurescolor[dynamicmask] shsp[dynamicmask] = pc.featuresphasor[dynamicmask] # Apply differentials means3D[dynamicmask] += pc.dxyz[dynamicmask] rotations[dynamicmask] = rotationactivation(pc.rotation[dynamicmask] + pc.drot[dynamicmask]) shs[dynamicmask] += pc.dsh[dynamicmask] shsp[dynamicmask] += pc.dshp[dynamicmask] # Step 8: Render Color Image colorimage = rasterizecolor( settings=rgbsettings, means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, shsp=shsp, opacity=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=None) # Step 9: Render ToF Data tofdata = rasterizetof( settings=tofsettings, means3D=means3D, means2D=means2D, shs=shs, shsp=shsp, opacity=opacity, scales=scales, rotations=rotations, cov3Dprecomp=None) return colorimage, tofdata, screenspacepoints Parameters: renderregions controls which Gaussians are active, motionmask distinguishes static from dynamic Gaussians, and depthrange limits ToF raycasting. Edge Cases: If viewpointcamera.FoVxtof is None, ToF settings are skipped. If renderregions is empty, no attributes are copied, resulting in empty renders. Precision issues may arise in rotationactivation if quaternions are not normalized after adding differentials. Not given in the sources. This method is part of the Gaussian Splatting framework extended for Time-of-Flight cameras, as implemented in the gftorf project. It builds on Non-Pinhole Camera Training by adding specific support for ToF sensor characteristics. brownvc/gftorf, https://github.com/brownvc/gftorf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Densification Strategy
head: Adaptive Density Control, Density Management, Primitive Growth and Pruning
body: Densification strategies dynamically adjust the number and distribution of 3D Gaussian primitives during training to balance reconstruction fidelity against memory and computational constraints. They solve the problem of static representation capacity by detecting regions of high reconstruction error or uncertainty and either adding new primitives (densification) or removing redundant ones (pruning/sparsification). What sets this family apart from static initialization methods is the iterative feedback loop where gradient magnitudes, opacity values, and multi-view consistency metrics drive structural changes to the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} throughout the optimization process [Parent]. All methods in this family operate on a set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each Gaussian gk is defined by mean position \muk \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale sk \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation qk \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), opacity \alphak \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k [Parent]. The core mechanism involves periodic evaluation steps (typically every k iterations) that compute metrics per Gaussian to decide on structural modifications. Densification (Growth): When a Gaussian is identified as needing refinement, it is either: 1. Cloned: A copy is created, often perturbed by noise or shifted along the gradient direction, to increase sampling density in under-reconstructed regions without changing the spatial footprint [S10, 16882-3d-gaussian-splatting-optimization-heuristics.md]. 2. Split: The parent Gaussian is replaced by N{\text{children}} (typically 2) children. The children's means \mu{child} are sampled from \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak), their scales are reduced (e.g., s{child} = sk \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}), and their opacities are halved (\alpha{child} = \alphak / 2) [Parent, 16882-3d-gaussian-splatting-optimization-heuristics.md]. Pruning (Removal): Gaussians are removed if they contribute negligibly to the rendered image. Common criteria include: Opacity Threshold: \alphak < \alpha{\min} [12354-pruning-and-sparsification.md]. Scale Threshold: \max(sk) > s{\max}, removing overly large primitives that may represent noise or floaters [16882-3d-gaussian-splatting-optimization-heuristics.md]. Significance/Weight: Accumulated alpha blending coefficients wk across training views [12354-pruning-and-sparsification.md]. Gradient Accumulation: A key metric for densification eligibility is the accumulated positional gradient magnitude \tauk. For each Gaussian, this is computed as the average L2 norm of the view-space position gradients over all views v where the Gaussian contributes: \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v} \left\| \frac{\partial L}{\partial \muk} \right\|2 [Parent, 16882-3d-gaussian-splatting-optimization-heuristics.md]. Alpha Reset: To prevent the accumulation of "dead" Gaussians with non-zero opacity that no longer contribute to the loss, opacities are periodically reset to zero (e.g., every 3000 iterations), forcing the optimizer to re-evaluate primitive importance and enabling the pruning step to remove them [16882-3d-gaussian-splatting-optimization-heuristics.md]. GroupFlow is a motion representation technique for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that distills per-Gaussian neural deformation fields into shared SE(3) transformations for groups of Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of evaluating individual deformation networks for every primitive at every timestep, accelerating rendering and training while maintaining temporal coherence. Unlike methods that retain dense neural fields or use global rigid transforms, GroupFlow captures locally coherent motion by clustering Gaussians based on trajectory similarity and fitting a separate SE(3) trajectory to each cluster. 3DGS-MCMC replaces the standard heuristic-based densification (gradient magnitude thresholds) of 3D Gaussian Splatting with a probabilistic framework based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. It treats the set of 3D Gaussians as samples from an underlying probability distribution, using Metropolis–Hastings steps to guide the spawning and pruning of primitives. This approach allows for precise control over the total number of Gaussians, reduces reliance on high-quality initialization, and yields sharper details and fewer artifacts compared to the original cloning/splitting heuristics. VS-Splat Voxel Selection is a learnable, differentiable mechanism for selecting relevant 3D voxels in feed-forward Gaussian Splatting, replacing static opacity thresholding with a confidence-based selection process. It sets itself apart from siblings like Opacity-Based Thresholding by using a Gumbel-Sigmoid distribution to predict confidence scores, allowing the network to learn which voxels contain object-centric geometry rather than relying on manual hyperparameter tuning. Locality-preserving densification addresses the memory access throttling caused by standard Gaussian densification, where new primitives are appended to the end of parameter buffers, causing spatially close Gaussians to be stored far apart in memory. By reordering the Gaussian parameter buffers based on 3D spatial proximity using Z-ordering (Morton order), this method ensures that neighboring Gaussians in space are also adjacent in memory, thereby improving memory access coalescing. Progressive and Multi-stage Training refers to a family of optimization strategies that decompose the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations into sequential phases, rather than optimizing all parameters simultaneously from initialization. This approach solves the instability, slow convergence, and local minima traps inherent in single-stage training, particularly when dealing with complex geometry, sparse inputs, or feed-forward pose estimation. By decoupling geometry initialization, appearance refinement, and high-frequency detail capture, these methods ensure that the Gaussian distribution adapts progressively to the scene's complexity [7173-hybrid-coarse-to-fine-strategy.md]. Unlike standard single-stage training, which often suffers from error propagation between pose and geometry or insufficient coverage of high-frequency details, multi-stage approaches isolate specific learning objectives (e.g., pose vs. attributes) to stabilize the optimization landscape [15018-multi-stage-training-with-pose-prediction.md]. Hyperparameter Settings define the numerical configuration for the optimizer, learning rates, and regularization terms used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. This method solves the problem of stable convergence and high-fidelity reconstruction by tuning the trade-off between fitting training data and maintaining geometric/photometric consistency. It differs from sibling methods like Densification Strategy (which manages primitive count) and Pruning and Sparsification (which removes primitives) by focusing on the gradient descent dynamics and loss weighting rather than structural topology changes. Adaptive Gaussian Refinement is a technique that dynamically adjusts Gaussian parameters using neural network-predicted residuals to improve the modeling of complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance. It addresses the limitation of static covariance matrices in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which cannot adequately represent dynamic behaviors such as motion-induced shape changes. Unlike sibling methods that rely on gradient-based densification metrics (e.g., Adaptive Density Control) or MCMC sampling (e.g., 3DGS-MCMC), this method uses a lightweight neural network to predict continuous corrections to the Gaussian's spatial, temporal, directional, and covariance parameters. This family encompasses methods that generate or represent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives using hybrid feature grids or diffusion models, rather than relying solely on iterative per-scene optimization. It addresses single-view and text-to-3D generation, multi-view consistency, and sparse volume representation by predicting Gaussian attributes directly from conditioning signals. The termination entropy criterion is a metric used to calculate information gain in active 3D reconstruction. It guides viewpoint selection by quantifying scene uncertainty, distinguishing itself from error-magnitude or density-based strategies by focusing on information saturation rather than reconstruction error. Pruning and Sparsification methods remove 3D Gaussian primitives that contribute negligibly to the final rendered image or whose removal would not significantly degrade reconstruction quality, thereby controlling memory usage and computational load during training. Unlike sibling methods that rely on static thresholds or uncertainty metrics, this family encompasses strategies that actively manage the density and opacity distribution, including recycling low-opacity components into high-opacity ones to prevent unbounded growth without altering the rendered image. It sets itself apart from Adaptive Density Control by focusing specifically on the removal phase of the feedback loop, and from Significance-Aware Pruning by often employing simpler opacity-based heuristics rather than accumulated rendering weights for initial candidate selection. Texel Size Adaptation and Primitive Management is a training-time optimization routine that dynamically adjusts the resolution of per-primitive texture maps and the number of 3D Gaussian primitives to balance model capacity and appearance quality. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Density Control or GroupFlow by explicitly coupling the geometric density of primitives with the textural detail allocated to them, using quantile-based error thresholds to trigger splitting, upscaling, or downscaling. Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification is a strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses kinematic phase-space trajectories (momentum) to guide primitive growth, aiming to overcome floating artifacts in non-manifold regions caused by single-step gradient snapshots. It sets itself apart from standard gradient-based strategies by evaluating the consistency between current gradients and accumulated historical trends, rather than relying solely on instantaneous gradient magnitude. GSGEN Appearance Refinement is an iterative optimization stage that improves fine-grained visual details in text-to-3D generation while preserving the fundamental geometry established during the preceding geometry optimization phase. It addresses the limitations of standard gradient-based densification by introducing a compactness-based strategy to fill geometric holes and employs specific regularization losses to prevent overfitting and maintain 3D consistency. Unlike sibling methods that rely primarily on positional gradients or opacity thresholds, GSGEN explicitly incorporates a 3D Stable Diffusion Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss and a mean position penalty to ensure structural integrity. Multi-view Consistency and Scoring is a family of densification strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting that evaluates Gaussian primitives across multiple camera views to guide densification and pruning operations. It builds on Densification Strategy by incorporating multi-view photometric loss and alpha contributions to identify regions requiring refinement or removal. Unlike its siblings Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning and Multi-View Consistency Scoring for Densification, this family explicitly integrates importance and pruning scores derived from multi-view photometric loss and alpha contributions into the standard gradient masks, ensuring that densification occurs only where geometry is consistently unresolved across views. Guided Sampling is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses blurring artifacts in regions insufficiently covered by the initial sparse point cloud, such as distant geometry or transparent/translucent objects. It distinguishes itself from standard gradient-based splitting by explicitly sampling new Gaussian positions along the camera ray depth range rather than relying solely on positional gradients, thereby ensuring coverage in areas where gradient signals are weak or ambiguous. This method defines the heuristic-driven densification and pruning strategies used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to dynamically adjust the number and distribution of Gaussian primitives. It solves the problem of static representation capacity by allowing the model to increase density in under-reconstructed regions (via cloning/splitting) and remove redundant primitives (via pruning) based on gradient magnitude, opacity, and scale. Multi-view Consistent Densification (MCD) is a strategy that reduces Gaussian redundancy by evaluating reconstruction quality across multiple sampled views, rather than relying solely on image-space gradient magnitude. It identifies Gaussians lying in regions of poor reconstruction consistency across views, triggering densification only when errors are persistent. This approach avoids noise from occlusion or view-dependent effects that can mislead single-view gradient-based methods. Selective Gaussian Densification is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that classifies primitives into 'steady' and 'non-steady' states to determine if densification is needed, replacing the vanilla 3DGS view-space position gradient threshold with a sum-of-norms metric to avoid redundant Gaussians. It selectively splits or creates new Gaussians only for non-steady-state Gaussians exhibiting a large magnitude of internal conflicts, while preserving converged steady-state Gaussians to reduce redundant processing and Gaussian count. PSCD-GS is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces single-score heuristics with a continuous perception–structure role representation to guide densification, cloning/splitting selection, and split placement. It augments the baseline 3DGS gradient and scale metrics with complementary perceptual (texture/appearance) and structural (geometry/boundaries) evidence, allowing the renderer to distinguish between regions needing appearance refinement versus geometric reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that rely on a single complexity or edge score, PSCD-GS retains the overlapping responses of both cue types to condition candidate selection and split initialization. The Parallel Grid Sorting Algorithm is a post-densification optimization step that reorders 3D Gaussian primitives into 2D attribute grids to maximize spatial locality and compressibility. Unlike sibling methods that focus on geometric refinement or probabilistic sampling, this method specifically targets the data layout for efficient storage and transmission by minimizing the variance of absolute differences between neighboring grid elements. It is distinct from standard rasterization sorting as it operates on the entire attribute set (position, color, opacity, scale, rotation) simultaneously to prepare the data for subsequent compression codecs. A Gaussian Splatting method that combines progressive training with resolution, noise and Gaussian scales, learning to prune and mask primitives and SH bands by their significance, and an accelerated GS training framework to achieve faster run-time, smaller disk size, and faster convergence compared to vanilla GS. 3DGS reconstructs a scene using 3D Gaussian primitives rendered via differentiable volume splatting rasterizer extending EWA volume splatting. Each primitive has 59 parameters: position, covariance (parameterized by scaling matrix S and quaternion rotation q), opacity, diffused color, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients (typically 3 bands). On three datasets, Trick-GS achieves up to 2× faster training, 40× smaller disk size and 2× faster rendering speed compared to vanilla GS, while having comparable accuracy. A process to address noise and missing surface parts in the density space by using perceptual loss to identify problematic geometric aspects and removing outliers. Compute perceptual loss VGG(Sp, Sg) to measure high-level visual similarity between rendered patch Sp and real image patch Sg. Select patches where VGG(Sp, Sg) is lower than half the average value across the training set to prioritize patches with improved visual similarity. Augment the density space by adding a group of points along the pixel ray for selected patches, considering the depth range of neighboring pixels. Remove outliers by examining the number of points within a specified radius around each neural density point; if the count falls below a predefined threshold, the point is removed. Joint optimization of newly added view-dependent Gaussians with pre-existing kernels, refining T, \beta, and opacity orientation using multi-view photometric constraints. During image-space optimization, original Gaussians' rendered outputs are treated as background. After projection, original kernels' opacity is made optimizable while freezing other attributes to mitigate over-occlusion. Apply full parameter optimization to newly added Gaussians. Set number of iterations proportional to training set size to ensure each additional kernel is sampled approximately the same number of times. Optimize parameters with specific learning rates: position (0.000016), diffuse color (0.001), higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients (0.001/20), opacity (0.02), scaling (0.002), rotation (0.0005), opacity lobe orientation d (0.001), opacity lobe width T (0.0002), and sharpness β (0.002). Employ SparseAdam to optimize the opacity of original Gaussian primitives visible in the current viewpoint. A regularizer that penalizes NeRF densities at 3D locations not visible from multiple training views to remove floaters outside the convex hull of training views. Approximate visibility v{ij} of the i-th 3D location in the j-th training view using a frustum check. Implement by defining a single tight sphere around training images. Render batches of rays shooting from a random location on the sphere surface, through the center of the scene, and far into the distance. Render rays using Nerfacto and apply the visibility loss to the sampled points. L{vis} = \sumi V(qi) f\sigma(qi) where f\sigma(qi) = \sigmai is the NeRF density at 3D location qi, and V(qi) = 1{\{\sum{j=1}^n v{ij} < 1\}} indicates if the location is not visible from any training views. Nerfacto uses a proposal sampler [2] to importance sample around surfaces, making the loss effective in quickly culling floating artifacts with high density outside visible regions. The frustum check approximation does not handle occlusions, instead overestimating the number of views a location is visible from. A method to predict the maximum primitive number Pfin for densification, preventing out-of-memory errors and bounding primitive growth. Predict the maximum primitive number Pfin using momentum-based budgeting. Cap primitive growth: if Pfin is extremely large, the primitive number stabilizes to a constant for the scene, preventing OOM. γ, η: hyper-parameters in the momentum-based primitive budgeting method that influence Pfin. Predicted vs actual primitive counts on MipNeRF-360: 3DGS (3.08M vs 2.69M), Mip-Splatting (3.25M vs 3.14M), Taming-3DGS (2.39M vs 2.04M). A framework that integrates occlusion-aware densification with StopThePop's per-pixel depth ordering to remove popping artifacts and keep occlusion boundaries intact. Use StopThePop's hybrid transparency or per-pixel sorting to determine the order of Gaussians and compute transmittance T{i,p}. Accumulate gradients and statistics only for non-zero w{i,p}, then apply the contribution-based normalization for densification decisions. Use view-independent colors for Gaussians to avoid duplicate densification. Create a densification mask to determine whether a pixel in a new frame needs densification by considering current Gaussians and the captured depth of the new frame. Has a process to remove outliers in the point cloud. 3DGS optimization has two stages: coarse 3DGS training, and refinement. Has a geometry and texture refinement module to improve generation quality based on hypergraph learning. Each node in the hypergraph is a patch image of a coarse 3DGS. A method that uses pixel-level error as a densification criterion and revises the opacity setting during the cloning process, leading to a more stable training process. A rule to maintain consistent Gaussian densification behavior when changing the number of interpolated virtual cameras n, by scaling the gradient threshold proportionally. If the number of virtual cameras changes from n to n', the densification gradient threshold must be multiplied by \frac{n}{n'} to match the scaled gradients, because the gradient of every Gaussian during motion-blurred image synthesis is scaled by \frac{1}{n}. n: Number of interpolated virtual images/cameras used for motion blur synthesis. Default value: 10, chosen to balance rendering performance and training efficiency. A densification method that leverages view-independent spherical harmonics coefficients to assess color cues, refining areas where traditional structure-from-motion techniques may struggle to capture fine details. A densification method that adds controlled spatial noise to Gaussians in under-reconstructed areas to increase spatial coverage and prevent over-clustering/redundancy, instead of cloning or splitting at predetermined points. In under-reconstructed regions, Gaussians are cloned with added noise to their positions to create diversity and avoid duplication. \mu'i = \mui + \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I), \mui is the original position, and \sigma is a noise factor tuned depending on gradient information and local scene complexity. Adopts the same densification strategy as AbsGS but modified due to dense initial point cloud. Do not apply densification during the first 1,500 iterations. Apply densification once every 500 iterations in subsequent iterations. A technique introduced by Mallick et al. [23] to construct high-quality radiance fields while controlling Gaussian count, model size, and training time. Uses score-based sampling to select Gaussians for densification. Skipping COLMAP's dense reconstruction and directly working with the sparse reconstruction (similar to Gaussian splatting's pipeline). Start with a point cloud of only 130K points. Augment the pipeline with an additional spawning step after 75 epochs, as this low amount of points reaches convergence sooner. On the Playground scene, Neural Rendering without VET converges to LPIPS 0.596. With VET, this improves to 0.341. Initialization technique for outdoor scenes involving an outside bounding region and a sky sphere to improve precision and F1 score. Without this initialization, background regions with non-negligible density are difficult to emerge from, leading to sky parts being reconstructed as geometry attached to the target mesh. The concept of adaptive density control was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). The method was designed to address the limitations of static point cloud initializations, which often fail to capture fine details or result in excessive memory usage due to over-sampling in simple regions. The original algorithm used view-space position gradients to trigger cloning (for small, high-gradient Gaussians) and splitting (for large, high-gradient Gaussians) every 100 iterations, alongside opacity-based pruning. Subsequent research has expanded this family significantly, introducing probabilistic approaches like MCMC, multi-view consistency checks, and dynamic deformation handling. The strategy is now a core component of nearly all 3DGS-based reconstruction and generation pipelines, including SLAM and text-to-3D methods. name: GroupFlow
body: GroupFlow is a motion representation technique for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that distills per-Gaussian neural deformation fields into shared SE(3) transformations for groups of Gaussians. It solves the computational bottleneck of evaluating individual deformation networks for every primitive at every timestep, accelerating rendering and training while maintaining temporal coherence. Unlike methods that retain dense neural fields or use global rigid transforms, GroupFlow captures locally coherent motion by clustering Gaussians based on trajectory similarity and fitting a separate SE(3) trajectory to each cluster. Inputs: Set of N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each Gaussian gi has a time-varying mean position \mui^t, rotation ri^t, and scale si^t. Number of timesteps F (indices t=0, \dots, F-1). Number of control trajectories (groups) J. Weighting factor \lambdar \in [0, 1]. Outputs: For each group j \in \{1, \dots, J\}: Initial control point position hj^0 \in \mathbb{R}^3. Time-varying rotation matrices Rj^t \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} for t=0, \dots, F-1. Time-varying translation vectors Tj^t \in \mathbb{R}^3 for t=0, \dots, F-1. Assignment of each Gaussian i to a group j. Data Structures: Gaussian Trajectories: Each Gaussian i is represented as a sequence of mean positions \mathcal{M}i = \{\mui^t\}{t=0}^{F-1}. Control Trajectories: A set of J control points \{hj^t\}{t=0}^{F-1} for j=1, \dots, J. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize J control trajectories \{hj^0\}{j=1}^J at t=0 using farthest point sampling on the initial mean positions \{\mui^0\}{i=1}^N. 2. Trajectory Similarity Calculation: For each Gaussian i and each control trajectory j, compute the similarity score S{i,j} using the temporal mean and standard deviation of the Euclidean distance between the Gaussian's trajectory and the control trajectory's trajectory: S{i,j} = \lambdar \, \mathrm{std}t(\| \mui^t - hj^t \|) + (1-\lambdar) \, \mathrm{mean}t(\| \mui^t - hj^t \|) where \mui^t is the mean position of Gaussian i at time t, hj^t is the position of control trajectory j at time t, \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean norm, \mathrm{mean}t(\cdot) computes the average over t=0, \dots, F-1, and \mathrm{std}t(\cdot) computes the standard deviation over t=0, \dots, F-1. 3. Group Assignment: Assign each Gaussian i to the group j that minimizes the similarity score S{i,j}. Let \mathcal{M}^j be the set of Gaussians assigned to group j. 4. SE(3) Trajectory Fitting: For each group j, fit a group-wise SE(3) trajectory by aligning sampled means over time, optimizing the shared flow parameters \{hj^0, Rj^t, Tj^t\} jointly with the scene. Predict the deformation of \mui \in \mathcal{M}^j at timestep t by applying the learned SE(3) transformation relative to its control point: \mui^t = Rj^t (\mui^0 - hj^0) + hj^0 + Tj^t where \mui^0 is the initial mean position of Gaussian i, hj^0 is the initial position of control trajectory j, Rj^t is the rotation matrix for group j at time t, and Tj^t is the translation vector for group j at time t. 5. Rendering/Training: During rendering or training, apply the corresponding group's SE(3) transformation to the initial mean \mui^0 to obtain \mui^t instead of querying a neural network. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def groupflowfit(gaussians, F, J, lambdar): # 1. Initialize control points via farthest point sampling at t=0 h0 = farthestpointsampling([g.mu[0] for g in gaussians], J) # 2. Compute similarity scores and assign groups groups = [[] for in range(J)] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): scores = [] for j in range(J): dists = [norm(g.mu[t] - h0[j]) for t in range(F)] # hj^t tracked during optimization stdt = std(dists) meant = mean(dists) scores.append(lambdar stdt + (1 - lambdar) meant) bestj = argmin(scores) groups[bestj].append(i) # 3. Fit SE(3) per group and optimize jointly with scene for j in range(J): groupindices = groups[j] # Optimize hj^0, Rj^t, Tj^t to minimize reconstruction error over t optimizese3trajectory(groupindices, h0[j], F) return groups, h0, R, T def groupflowtransform(mu0, h0, Rt, Tt): # Apply SE(3) transformation return Rt @ (mu0 - h0) + h0 + Tt Note: The pseudocode abstracts the joint optimization step, which the sources state is optimized jointly with the scene. Standard vector operations are assumed. Parameters: J: Number of groups/control trajectories. Not given in the sources. \lambdar: Weighting factor for trajectory similarity. Not given in the sources. F: Number of timesteps. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Farthest Point Sampling: The initialization of control points via farthest point sampling at t=0 is critical for covering the scene. Temporal Coherence: The method regularizes the learned motion field by smoothing noisy trajectories, which helps in real-world dynamic scenes. Precision: The SE(3) transformation assumes rigid body motion within each group. If a group contains Gaussians with non-rigid relative motion, the approximation may introduce artifacts. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of transformations per frame from N (per Gaussian) to J (per group), where J \ll N. Memory Complexity: Stores J sets of SE(3) parameters instead of N neural network weights or deformation fields. Performance: On the MonoDyGauBench dataset, integrating GroupFlow into DeformableGS accelerates rendering by 13.71× and shortens training by 2.53× compared to baselines. Strengths: Substantial acceleration in training and rendering; maintains temporally coherent, high-quality motion reconstruction; distills dense deformations into a smaller set of parameters. Limitations: Assumes locally coherent rigid motion within groups; may not capture complex non-rigid deformations if groups are too large or poorly defined. GroupFlow was introduced in the paper "SpeeDe3DGS: Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting with Temporal Pruning and Motion Grouping". It is part of a pipeline that also includes Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) and Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS) to further optimize dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting.
