name: 3DGS-MCMC
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, MCMc Densification Strategy, MCMC-based Gaussian Lifecycle, Markov Chain Monte Carlo Strategy
body: 3DGS-MCMC replaces the standard heuristic-based densification (gradient magnitude thresholds) of 3D Gaussian Splatting with a probabilistic framework based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. It treats the set of 3D Gaussians as samples from an underlying probability distribution, using Metropolis–Hastings steps to guide the spawning and pruning of primitives. This approach allows for precise control over the total number of Gaussians, reduces reliance on high-quality initialization, and yields sharper details and fewer artifacts compared to the original cloning/splitting heuristics. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current set of N Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk has parameters \muk, \Sigmak, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k; current training iteration t; rendering loss \mathcal{L}; and configuration hyperparameters. Output: Updated set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with modified parameters and potentially different cardinality N'. Data Structures: Gaussian Parameters: Stored in contiguous tensors or arrays. means: [N, 3] float32. scales: [N, 3] float32 (log-space storage is common in implementations). quats: [N, 4] float32 (normalized quaternions). opacities: [N] float32 (logit-space storage is common). shcoeffs: [N, K, 3] or similar, depending on SH degree. Optimizer States: Separate buffers for gradients and optimizer momentum for each parameter group. Binomial Table: A precomputed table binoms of size 51 \times 51 where binoms[n, k] = \binom{n}{k}. Parameters: capmax: Maximum number of Gaussians allowed. Default: 1,000,000. refinestartiter: Iteration number after which Gaussian refinement begins. Default: 500. refinestopiter: Iteration number after which Gaussian refinement stops. Default: 25,000. refineevery: Frequency of refinement steps in iterations. Default: 100. minopacity: Threshold below which Gaussians are considered for pruning or relocation. Default: 0.005. noiselr: MCMC sampling noise learning rate. Default: 5 \times 10^{-5}. Algorithm Steps: The method is executed periodically every refineevery iterations, starting at refinestartiter and stopping at refinestopiter. 1. Initialization: Ensure optimizer states are synchronized with parameters. Sanity check that each optimizer has one paramgroup and params contain keys 'means', 'scales', 'quats', 'opacities'. 2. Sample Add (Spawn): Calculate current opacities \alpha = \text{sigmoid}(\text{params['opacities']}). Sample n new source indices from the existing population using a multinomial distribution weighted by \alpha. Compute new opacities and scales for these samples using a computerelocation function (see below). Clamp new opacities to [\text{min\opacity}, 1-\epsilon]. Append copies of the sampled Gaussians (with updated opacities/scales) to the parameter arrays. Initialize new optimizer states to zero. 3. Relocation (Prune/Move): Identify "dead" Gaussians (mask=True) and "alive" Gaussians (mask=False). Sample new source indices from alive Gaussians using a multinomial distribution weighted by \text{sigmoid}(\text{opacities}). Compute new opacities and scales for the relocated Gaussians using computerelocation with the sampled opacities, \exp(\text{scales}), ratios (bincount of sampled indices + 1), and the binoms table. Clamp new opacities to [\text{min\opacity}, 1-\epsilon]. Update parameters: Set opacities at sampled indices to \text{logit}(\text{new\opacities}), scales to \log(\text{new\scales}), and copy these values to the dead indices. Reset optimizer states at the sampled indices. 4. Inject Noise (Perturbation): Calculate current opacities \alpha and scales s = \exp(\text{params['scales']}). Compute covariance matrices \Sigma from quats and scales. Define a sigmoid function for noise scaling: \text{op\sigmoid}(x, k=100, x0=0.995) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-k(x - x0))}. Generate noise: \text{noise} = \mathcal{N}(0, I) \cdot \text{op\sigmoid}(1 - \alpha) \cdot \text{scaler}. Transform noise by covariance: \text{noise}{\text{cov}} = \Sigma \cdot \text{noise}. Update means: \mu \leftarrow \mu + \text{noise}{\text{cov}}. Formulas: Metropolis–Hastings Spawn Probability: The probability of spawning a new Gaussian at \mu{\text{new}} is determined by the ratio of rendering errors and proposal distributions: \alpha{\text{spawn}} = \min \left( 1, \frac{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{new}})}{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{old}})} \cdot \frac{q(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{old}}|\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{new}})}{q(\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{new}}|\boldsymbol{\mu}{\text{old}})} \right) where \mathcal{L} is the rendering loss and q is the proposal distribution. Relocation Computation: The specific formula for computerelocation is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources, but it utilizes the binomial coefficient table binoms and ratios derived from the multinomial sampling counts to adjust opacities and scales. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def computebinomstable(maxn=50): """Precompute binomial coefficients.""" binoms = torch.zeros(maxn + 1, maxn + 1, dtype=torch.float32) for n in range(maxn + 1): for k in range(n + 1): binoms[n, k] = math.comb(n, k) return binoms def opsigmoid(x, k=100, x0=0.995): """Sigmoid function for noise scaling.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-k (x - x0))) def computecovariance(quats, scales): """Compute 3x3 covariance matrices from quaternions and scales.""" qw, qx, qy, qz = quats[:, 0], quats[:, 1], quats[:, 2], quats[:, 3] r11 = 1 - 2(qy2 + qz2); r12 = 2(qxqy - qwqz); r13 = 2(qxqz + qwqy) r21 = 2(qxqy + qwqz); r22 = 1 - 2(qx2 + qz2); r23 = 2(qyqz - qwqx) r31 = 2(qxqz - qwqy); r32 = 2(qyqz + qwqx); r33 = 1 - 2(qx2 + qy2) R = torch.stack([r11, r12, r13, r21, r22, r23, r31, r32, r33], dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3, 3) S = torch.diagembed(scales2) return torch.bmm(R, torch.bmm(S, R.transpose(1, 2))) def computerelocation(sampledopacities, sampledscales, binoms, ratios): """ Compute new opacities and scales for relocated/sampled Gaussians. Sources do not give the exact mathematical formula for computerelocation. It uses the binomial table and sampling ratios to adjust opacities and scales. """ scalefactor = ratios.float() / ratios.max() newopacities = sampledopacities scalefactor.unsqueeze(-1) newscales = sampledscales scalefactor.unsqueeze(-1) return newopacities, newscales def mcmcdensificationstep( params, optimizers, binoms, capmax, minopacity, refineevery, currentiter, refinestartiter, refinestopiter, nadd): """ Perform one MCMC densification step. params: dict with keys 'means', 'scales', 'quats', 'opacities' (tensors of shape [N,...]) optimizers: dict of optimizer states nadd: Number of Gaussians to spawn per step """ # 1. Check if refinement should occur if currentiter < refinestartiter or currentiter > refinestopiter: return if currentiter % refineevery != 0: return # 2. Extract current parameters means = params['means'] scaleslog = params['scales'] quats = params['quats'] opacitieslog = params['opacities'] N = means.shape[0] # Convert to physical space opacities = torch.sigmoid(opacitieslog) scales = torch.exp(scaleslog) # 3. Sample Add (Spawn new Gaussians) # Sample indices weighted by opacity weights = opacities / opacities.sum() sourceindices = torch.multinomial(weights, nadd, replacement=True) # Compute new opacities and scales for new Gaussians ratios = torch.bincount(sourceindices, minlength=N) + 1 newopacities, newscales = computerelocation( opacities[sourceindices], scales[sourceindices], binoms, ratios) # Clamp opacities newopacities = torch.clamp(newopacities, min=minopacity, max=1.0 - 1e-6) newopacitieslog = torch.logit(newopacities) newscaleslog = torch.log(newscales) # Append to params newmeans = means[sourceindices].clone() newquats = quats[sourceindices].clone() params['means'] = torch.cat([means, newmeans], dim=0) params['scales'] = torch.cat([scaleslog, newscaleslog], dim=0) params['quats'] = torch.cat([quats, newquats], dim=0) params['opacities'] = torch.cat([opacitieslog, newopacitieslog], dim=0) # Initialize new optimizer states to zero # (Implementation depends on specific optimizer structure) # 4. Relocation (Prune/Move low-opacity Gaussians) # Identify dead Gaussians (mask=True) and alive Gaussians (mask=False) deadmask = opacities < minopacity alivemask = ~deadmask if deadmask.any(): # Sample from alive Gaussians to replace dead ones aliveweights = opacities[alivemask] / opacities[alivemask].sum() nrelocate = deadmask.sum().item() aliveindices = torch.where(alivemask)[0] sampledaliveindices = aliveindices[torch.multinomial(aliveweights, nrelocate, replacement=True)] # Compute relocation parameters relocateratios = torch.bincount(sampledaliveindices, minlength=N) + 1 relocatedopacities, relocatedscales = computerelocation( opacities[sampledaliveindices], scales[sampledaliveindices], binoms, relocateratios) # Clamp relocatedopacities = torch.clamp(relocatedopacities, min=minopacity, max=1.0 - 1e-6) relocatedopacitieslog = torch.logit(relocatedopacities) relocatedscaleslog = torch.log(relocatedscales) # Update dead Gaussians with relocated parameters deadindices = torch.where(deadmask)[0] params['opacities'][deadindices] = relocatedopacitieslog params['scales'][deadindices] = relocatedscaleslog # Copy means, quats from sampled alive to dead params['means'][deadindices] = means[sampledaliveindices] params['quats'][deadindices] = quats[sampledaliveindices] # Reset optimizer states for relocated indices # (Implementation depends on specific optimizer structure) # 5. Inject Noise # Compute covariance matrices covars = computecovariance(quats, scales) # Generate noise noisescale = opsigmoid(1.0 - opacities).unsqueeze(-1) 5e-5 # noiselr noise = torch.randnlike(means) noisescale # Transform noise by covariance # einsum('bij,bj->bi', covars, noise) noisetransformed = torch.einsum('bij,bj->bi', covars, noise) # Update means params['means'].add(noisetransformed) This strategy defines the optimization schedule, loss formulation, and regularization techniques for training radiance fields using 3D Gaussian Splatting with MCMC-based densification. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by incorporating specific MCMC-derived regularization terms on opacity and scale, using cosine annealing for feature and MLP learning rates, applying Exponential Moving Average (EMA) to MLP weights, and executing a final refinement phase that freezes geometry. Choose it when precise control over Gaussian population and artifact reduction during iterative refinement is required. Time Complexity: The MCMC step involves sampling and tensor operations on N Gaussians. Sampling is O(N) or O(k \log N) depending on implementation. The noise injection and covariance computation are O(N). The overall overhead per refinement step is low compared to the rasterization cost, but it adds a periodic O(N) pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Gaussian parameters and optimizer states. The binomial table is negligible (51 \times 51). No significant additional memory overhead compared to standard 3DGS. Performance: Yields sharper details and better performance compared to the original 3DGS densification process, particularly in scenes with high-frequency details or underwater environments. It produces more efficient and artifact-free clouds by exploring regions with unknown gradients. Strengths: Precise control over the number of Gaussians; less reliance on good initialization; reduces artifacts from noisy gradient heuristics. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (refinestartiter, refinestopiter, minopacity); the exact formula for computerelocation is not fully specified in the primary sources, requiring implementation inference. 3DGS-MCMC was introduced as an improvement to the original 3D Gaussian Splatting densification heuristic, which relied on noisy positional gradient magnitudes. It reinterprets the Gaussian cloud as samples from an underlying probability distribution and uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling to guide the life cycle of primitives. The strategy allows for precise control of the Gaussian count and serves as an alternative to default cloning and splitting. It has been adopted in various implementations, including those for underwater rendering, where it helps capture high-frequency details. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Better Gaussian Splatting in Julia, https://pxl-th.github.io/blog/better-gs-julia/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) carlinds/splatad, https://github.com/carlinds/splatad, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-56917-4, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Optimization and Training Strategy
head: 3DGS-MCMC Training Strategy, MCMC-based Training with EMA and Regularization
body: This strategy defines the optimization schedule, loss formulation, and regularization techniques for training radiance fields using 3D Gaussian Splatting with MCMC-based densification. It addresses the problem of overfitting to noise and geometric artifacts during the iterative refinement of Gaussian primitives. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by incorporating specific MCMC-derived regularization terms on opacity and scale, using cosine annealing for feature and MLP learning rates, applying Exponential Moving Average (EMA) to MLP weights, and executing a final refinement phase that freezes geometry. Inputs: Initial set of Gaussian primitives (position, scale, rotation, opacity, features). Training images and camera poses. Hyperparameters: \lambda (D-SSIM weight), \lambda\alpha (opacity reg weight), \lambdas (scale reg weight), \gamma (EMA decay), T{refine} (refinement iterations, typically 3000). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian primitives and associated MLP weights. Data Structures: Primitives: Array of size P. Each primitive i has fields: position \mathbf{p}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, opacity \alphai, feature vector \mathbf{f}i. MLP Weights: \theta, filtered version \bar{\theta}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives and MLP weights. Set EMA weights \bar{\theta}0 = \theta0. 2. Main Training Loop: For each training iteration t: a. Render the scene using the current Gaussian primitives and MLP weights. b. Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using the formula below. c. Perform gradient descent to update primitive parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity) and raw MLP weights \thetat. d. Update the EMA weights \bar{\theta}t using the EMA formula. e. Use a cosine annealing scheduler to determine the learning rates for feature vectors and MLP weights at step t. f. Apply the MCMC-based densification strategy (spawn/prune) to manage the set of primitives P. 3. Refinement Phase: After the main training loop, execute the last T{refine} iterations (typically 3000) with the following modifications: a. Disable all regularization terms (\mathcal{R}\alpha, \mathcal{R}s). b. Freeze all primitive parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity). c. Optimize only the feature vectors and MLP weights \theta. d. Continue using the cosine annealing scheduler for learning rates. Formulas: 1. Opacity Regularization: \mathcal{R}\alpha = \frac{1}{P} \sum{i=1}^P \alphai where P is the number of primitives. 2. Scale Regularization: \mathcal{R}s = \frac{1}{P} \sum{i=1}^P \|\mathbf{s}i\|1 where \mathbf{s}i is the scale vector of primitive i. 3. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} + \lambda\alpha \mathcal{R}\alpha + \lambdas \mathcal{R}s where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 photometric loss, \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} is the differentiable SSIM loss, and \lambda, \lambda\alpha, \lambdas are scalar weights. 4. EMA Update for MLP Weights: \bar{\theta}t \leftarrow \gamma \bar{\theta}{t-1} + (1 - \gamma) \thetat where \bar{\theta}t is the filtered weight at step t, \thetat is the raw updated weight, and \gamma is the decay factor. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for D-SSIM loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda\alpha: Weight for opacity regularization. Not given in the sources. \lambdas: Weight for scale regularization. Not given in the sources. \gamma: EMA decay factor. Not given in the sources. T{refine}: Number of refinement iterations. Typically 3000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Without EMA and regularization, the model may overfit to individual frames or geometric artifacts. Local Minima: In unconditional generation contexts, failing to reset latent representations can cause the model to get stuck in local minima that overfit geometric artifacts. Precision: Half-precision memory fetches on feature vectors are used during rasterization to reduce register pressure, which may introduce precision trade-offs. A training procedure used in unconditional 3D generation (e.g., SSDNeRF) to prevent overfitting to geometric artifacts by periodically resetting latent representations to their mean. It involves resetting triplane codes to their mean value halfway through the training schedule and doubling the total training length to compensate. Without this, the model risks getting stuck in local minima. On the SRN Cars dataset, this approach achieves an FID of 19.04±1.10 and a KID/10⁻³ of 8.28±0.60. Time Complexity: The refinement phase adds a fixed cost of 3000 iterations focused only on features and MLP weights, which is relatively cheap compared to full primitive optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses half-precision memory fetches for feature vectors to reduce register pressure, lowering memory bandwidth requirements during rasterization. Strengths: Enhances robustness to noise and avoids overfitting to individual frames through EMA and regularization. The refinement step slightly improves color fidelity, particularly in large-scale scenes. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization weights and EMA decay. The densification strategy relies on the underlying 3DGS-MCMC method. When to use: Suitable for high-quality radiance-field novel-view synthesis, semantic scene reconstruction, and high-resolution image fitting where noise robustness and color fidelity are critical. When not to use: Not applicable for unconditional 3D generation tasks that require latent resetting (use Latent Resetting variant instead). The optimization strategy is based on the 3DGS-MCMC method. The specific regularization terms and EMA application were introduced in "Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction". The latent resetting variant was introduced in "Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF: A Unified Approach to 3D Generation and Reconstruction" for unconditional generation tasks. name: Kernel-Agnostic MCMC
head: Kernel-Agnostic Markov Chain Monte Carlo
body: Kernel-Agnostic MCMC is an optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces heuristic densification rules with a probabilistic Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework. It treats primitive opacity as a probability distribution to identify "dead" primitives and respawn them, ensuring that densification preserves the underlying scene representation regardless of the specific splatting kernel used. Unlike its sibling 3DGS-MCMC, which relies on Gaussian-specific scale adjustments and logit-based noise, this method uses opacity regularization and a Beta Kernel noise function to achieve kernel-agnostic stability and exploration. The method reinterprets the Gaussian cloud as samples from an underlying probability distribution. It guides the life cycle of primitives (spawn/prune) by adjusting opacity and position, using noise to encourage exploration and prevent overfitting. Inputs: Current primitive parameters (position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity o), learning rate \lambda{\text{Ir}}, hyperparameters \lambda{\text{SSIM}}, \lambdao, \lambda{\Sigma}, \lambda{\epsilon}, and noise scale parameter b'. Outputs: Updated primitive parameters for the next optimization step. Primitives are defined by: \mu: Position vector. \Sigma: Covariance matrix. o: Opacity scalar. f(x): The splatting kernel function (e.g., Gaussian, Beta). 1. Composite Loss Function The total loss \mathcal{L} combines rendering accuracy with regularization terms to encourage densification and exploration: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda{\text{SSIM}}) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{SSIM}} \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} + \lambdao \sumi |oi| + \lambda{\Sigma} \sumi \sumj |\sqrt{\text{eig}j(\Sigmai)}| Where: \mathcal{L}1: Pixel-wise L1 loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}: Structural Similarity Index Measure loss. \lambda{\text{SSIM}}: Weight for SSIM loss. \lambdao: Opacity regularization weight. \lambda{\Sigma}: Covariance regularization weight. \text{eig}j(\Sigmai): Eigenvalues of the covariance matrix \Sigmai. 2. Position Update with Noise Primitive positions are updated using gradient descent augmented with opacity-scaled noise: \mu \leftarrow \mu - \lambda{\text{Ir}} \cdot \nabla{\mu} \mathcal{L} + \lambda{\epsilon} \cdot \epsilon Where the noise term \epsilon is defined as: \epsilon = \lambda{\text{Ir}} \cdot \mathcal{B}(oi; b') \cdot \Sigma{\eta} \lambda{\text{Ir}}: Learning rate. \lambda{\epsilon}: Noise impact control factor. \Sigma{\eta}: Sampled noise vector. \mathcal{B}(oi; b'): Beta Kernel function scaling noise by opacity. b': Beta Kernel parameter, set to \ln(25) to resemble the fall-off behavior of the original logit function. 3. Densification and Opacity Adjustment When a primitive is cloned N times, the new opacity o' is calculated to preserve the probability distribution: o' = 1 - \sqrt[N]{1 - o} For small regularized opacity o, this is approximated via Taylor expansion as o' \approx \frac{o}{N}. This ensures that the densified distribution 1 - (1 - o' \cdot f(x))^N approximates the original o \cdot f(x), maintaining consistency regardless of the kernel f(x). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kernelagnosticmcmcstep(primitives, learningrate, lambdassim, lambdao, lambdasigma, lambdaepsilon, bprime): """ Performs one optimization step for Kernel-Agnostic MCMC. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects with attributes.mu,.Sigma,.o. learningrate: Scalar lambdaIr. lambdassim: Weight for SSIM loss. lambdao: Weight for opacity regularization. lambdasigma: Weight for covariance regularization. lambdaepsilon: Noise impact factor. bprime: Beta kernel parameter (default ln(25)). Returns: Updated primitives. """ # 1. Compute Rendering Losses # Render image from current primitives renderedimage = renderscene(primitives) targetimage = getgroundtruthimage() # Assumed available # L1 Loss lossl1 = meanabsoluteerror(renderedimage, targetimage) # SSIM Loss lossssim = computessim(renderedimage, targetimage) # 2. Compute Regularization Terms regopacity = 0.0 regcovariance = 0.0 for prim in primitives: # Opacity regularizer: sum of absolute opacities regopacity += abs(prim.o) # Covariance regularizer: sum of square roots of eigenvalues # Compute eigenvalues of Sigma eigenvalues = computeeigenvalues(prim.Sigma) for eig in eigenvalues: regcovariance += sqrt(abs(eig)) # 3. Compute Total Loss loss = (1 - lambdassim) lossl1 + lambdassim lossssim + \ lambdao regopacity + lambdasigma regcovariance # 4. Compute Gradients # Gradient of loss w.r.t position mu gradmu = computegradient(loss, primitives, 'mu') # 5. Update Positions with Noise for prim in primitives: # Sample noise vector Sigmaeta # Assuming standard normal distribution or similar noise source noisevector = samplenoise(prim.mu.shape) # Compute Beta Kernel scaling factor # B(oi; b') scales noise by opacity betakernelscale = betakernelfunction(prim.o, bprime) # Compute noise term epsilon epsilon = learningrate betakernelscale noisevector # Update position prim.mu = prim.mu - learningrate gradmu[prim.id] + lambdaepsilon epsilon # 5. Handle Densification (Cloning) # Identify primitives to clone based on opacity thresholds or MCMC criteria # For each primitive selected for cloning N times: for prim in primitivestoclone: nclones = getclonecount(prim) # Determined by MCMC sampling logic # Calculate new opacity for clones # o' = 1 - (1 - o)^(1/N) newopacity = 1 - pow(1 - prim.o, 1 / nclones) # Create N new primitives with newopacity # Position and covariance may be perturbed or copied newprimitives = createclones(prim, nclones, newopacity) # Add new primitives to the scene addprimitives(newprimitives) return primitives Opacity Regularization: The method relies on keeping opacity o small to justify the Taylor expansion approximation o' \approx o/N. If opacity becomes large, the approximation error \mathcal{O}(o^2) becomes significant, potentially distorting the rendered distribution. Kernel Independence: The method is designed to be kernel-agnostic. However, the validity of the opacity adjustment formula depends on the assumption that the splatting kernel f(x) behaves predictably during densification. Complex deformable kernels may require careful validation of the approximation. Noise Scaling: The Beta Kernel parameter b' = \ln(25) is critical for matching the fall-off behavior of the original logit function. Incorrect tuning may lead to insufficient exploration or excessive noise. Time Complexity: The addition of regularization terms and noise sampling increases per-step computational cost compared to standard 3DGS. The opacity adjustment and cloning logic add overhead during densification steps. Memory Complexity: Similar to 3DGS, but the probabilistic respawn mechanism may lead to more stable memory usage by preventing excessive accumulation of "dead" primitives. Strengths: Kernel Agnostic: Works with various splatting kernels, not just Gaussians. Stable Densification: Preserves the underlying probability distribution during cloning, reducing artifacts. Exploration: Noise term encourages exploration, preventing local minima. Limitations: Hyperparameter Sensitivity: Requires tuning of \lambdao, \lambda{\Sigma}, \lambda{\epsilon}, and b'. Approximation Error: Relies on small opacity assumption for densification accuracy. Kernel-Agnostic MCMC was introduced in the context of Deformable Beta Splatting, reinterpreting the optimization process of 3D Gaussian Splatting as an MCMC sampling problem. It addresses limitations in heuristic-based densification strategies by providing a mathematically grounded approach to primitive lifecycle management. The method was presented in the paper "Deformable Beta Splatting". Deformable Beta Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3721238.3730716, fetched 2026-11-08

name: VS-Splat Voxel Selection
head: Ours, VS-Splat selection
body: VS-Splat Voxel Selection is a learnable, differentiable mechanism for selecting relevant 3D voxels in feed-forward Gaussian Splatting, replacing static opacity thresholding with a confidence-based selection process. It sets itself apart from siblings like Opacity-Based Thresholding by using a Gumbel-Sigmoid distribution to predict confidence scores, allowing the network to learn which voxels contain object-centric geometry rather than relying on manual hyperparameter tuning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid and a set of input 2D images. Output: A binary selection mask indicating active voxels and refined opacity values for rendering. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor with resolution H=W=D=48. Confidence Scores: A scalar value per voxel, predicted by the Selective Feature Refinement (SFR) module. Primitives: M=16 fine-grained 3D Gaussian primitives are generated for each selected voxel. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract 2D feature maps from input images using a pre-trained backbone (DINOv1). 2. Compress features using a 3D convolutional compressor to reduce channel dimensionality. 3. Pass compressed features through the SFR module to predict confidence scores for each voxel. 4. Apply the Gumbel-Sigmoid function to the confidence scores to generate a differentiable binary selection mask. 5. Refine opacity values using the selection mask and confidence scores. 6. Generate M=16 fine-grained 3D Gaussian primitives for each selected voxel. 7. Render the scene using the selected voxels and their associated primitives. Formulas: The Gumbel-Sigmoid function generates the differentiable selection mask y from a confidence score s and temperature \tau: y = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\frac{s + g}{\tau}\right)} where g = -\ln(-\ln(u)) is Gumbel noise sampled from u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1). The refined opacity is computed as the product of the confidence score and the selection mask. Parameters: Gumbel-Sigmoid Temperature (\tau): Linearly annealed from 1.0 to 0.1 over the first 50,000 training iterations, then fixed at 0.1 for the remainder of training and inference. SFR Module Depth (R): Contains R=2 residual convolutional blocks. Channel Compression: The 3D convolutional compressor reduces the channel dimension from 2C=1,536 to \tilde{C}=128. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temperature Scheduling: Using a fixed high temperature may lead to excessive selection of background voxels, while a fixed low temperature may result in insufficient selection. Deterministic Sigmoid: Replacing Gumbel-Sigmoid with a deterministic Sigmoid function fails to properly select object-centric voxels, leading to significant rendering quality drops. Opacity Thresholding: Simple opacity-based thresholding (OBT) is unreliable for selecting object-centric voxels and requires manual tuning of the threshold value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vssplatvoxelselection(voxelgrid, inputimages, temperaturetau): # Step 1: Extract 2D features using DINOv1 backbone features2d = extract2dfeatures(inputimages) # Step 2: Compress features via 3D convolution (1536 -> 128 channels) featurescompressed = compress3d(features2d, inchannels=1536, outchannels=128) # Step 3: Predict confidence scores via SFR module (R=2 residual blocks) confidencescores = sfrforward(featurescompressed, numresidualblocks=2) # Step 4: Differentiable selection via Gumbel-Sigmoid selectedmask = gumbelsigmoid(confidencescores, temperature=temperaturetau) # Step 5: Refine opacities refinedopacities = refineopacities(confidencescores, selectedmask) return selectedmask, refinedopacities def extract2dfeatures(images): # Standard ViT forward pass for DINOv1 pre-trained on ImageNet-1K return [backboneforward(img) for img in images] def compress3d(features, inchannels, outchannels): # 3D convolutional compressor reducing channel dimensionality return conv3d(features, inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=1) def sfrforward(features, numresidualblocks): # SFR module with residual convolutional blocks out = features for in range(numresidualblocks): out = out + convblock(out) return out def gumbelsigmoid(scores, temperature): # Sample uniform noise u = uniformlike(scores) # Gumbel noise g = -log(-log(u + 1e-10) + 1e-10) # Gumbel-Sigmoid formula return sigmoid((scores + g) / temperature) def refineopacities(scores, mask): # Integrate predicted voxel-selection scores into the rendering process return scores mask A variant that applies the Straight-Through Estimator to confidence scores to enable gradient flow. It extends gradients beyond the hard selection boundary to prevent optimization stalling. On the CO3D dataset, it selects an extremely limited number of voxels (121), yielding PSNR 14.71, SSIM 0.814, and LPIPS 0.317. A variant that replaces the Gumbel-Sigmoid with the deterministic Sigmoid function for voxel selection. It fails to properly select object-centric voxels, leading to significant rendering quality drops. On the CO3D dataset, it yields PSNR 18.01, SSIM 0.835, LPIPS 0.288, and uses 2,223 voxels. Performance: On the CO3D dataset, VS-Splat yields PSNR 21.31, SSIM 0.863, LPIPS 0.213, and uses 19,587 voxels. Comparison: VS-Splat uses approximately 15% fewer voxels than Opacity-Based Thresholding (OBT) while outperforming it across all metrics. OBT yields PSNR 21.21, SSIM 0.859, LPIPS 0.223, and uses 22,867 voxels. Comparison: Simply applying Straight-Through Estimator (STE) to confidence scores results in selecting an extremely limited number of voxels (121 voxels on CO3D), yielding PSNR 14.71, SSIM 0.814, LPIPS 0.317. Scalability: The method uses a voxel grid resolution of H=W=D=48 and generates M=16 primitives per selected voxel. Strengths: Learnable selection allows for better identification of object-centric voxels compared to static thresholds. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the Gumbel-Sigmoid temperature schedule. VS-Splat was proposed in the paper "VS-Splat: Voxel-Selective feed-forward Gaussian Splatting for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse-views". It addresses the limitations of static opacity thresholding in 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a learnable voxel selection mechanism. The method is particularly effective for end-to-end 3D object reconstruction from sparse views. name: Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for Confidence Scores
head: Straight-Through Estimator for Gradient Extension
body: The Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for confidence scores is a gradient approximation technique used in voxel selection schemes to enable backpropagation through discrete selection decisions. It extends gradients beyond the hard selection boundary to prevent optimization stalling. The method is applied within a voxel selection framework where each voxel v is assigned a learned confidence score cv. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Confidence scores \{cv\} for candidate voxels. Output: A binary selection mask mv \in \{0, 1\} and gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial cv} for optimization. Data Structures: Confidence scores: A tensor of floating-point values, typically in [0, 1]. Selection mask: A binary tensor of the same shape as the confidence scores. Steps: 1. Forward Pass (Hard Selection): Compute the binary mask mv using a threshold \tau: mv = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } cv > \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The rendering pipeline uses only voxels where mv = 1. The threshold \tau is a scalar cutoff value. 2. Backward Pass (Straight-Through): Compute gradients by ignoring the discontinuity of the thresholding operation, passing the upstream gradient directly to cv. Parameters: Threshold \tau: A scalar cutoff value. In comparative experiments, it is evaluated alongside opacity-based thresholding (OBT) which uses a predefined threshold of 0.005. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Limited Selection: Simply applying STE to confidence scores results in selecting an extremely limited number of voxels, degrading rendering quality. Optimization Stalling: Without extending gradients beyond the primitive boundary, optimization may stall; STE handles this by allowing gradient flow even where the boundary is hard or truncated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stethresholdforward(confidencescores, threshold): # Forward pass: hard thresholding to binary mask mask = (confidencescores > threshold).float() return mask def stethresholdbackward(gradoutput, confidencescores, threshold): # Backward pass: straight-through estimator # Pass upstream gradient directly, ignoring the non-differentiable threshold return gradoutput Uses a fixed opacity threshold (e.g., 0.005) to select voxels. It is simple but requires manual tuning and can be unreliable for object-centric selection. Uses a stochastic relaxation of the selection process to allow differentiable optimization. It generally yields better voxel selection and rendering quality than STE. Replaces Gumbel-Sigmoid with a standard sigmoid function. This fails to properly select object-centric voxels and leads to significant rendering quality drops. Time Complexity: The forward pass is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. The backward pass is also O(N) as it involves a simple element-wise operation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the confidence scores and the selection mask. Performance: On the CO3D dataset, using STE for voxel selection resulted in a PSNR of 14.71, SSIM of 0.814, and LPIPS of 0.317, with only 121 voxels selected. This is significantly worse than the proposed VS-Splat method (PSNR 21.31, 19,587 voxels). Strengths: Simple to implement; enables gradient flow through hard selection boundaries. Limitations: Can lead to very sparse voxel selection and poor rendering quality if not carefully tuned. The Straight-Through Estimator is a common technique in differentiable programming to handle non-differentiable operations. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting and voxel selection, it was explored as a variant of the VS-Splat framework to enable gradient flow to confidence scores. It is also used in radiance field methods, such as Fourier Splatting, to extend gradients beyond primitive boundaries and prevent optimization stalling. name: Locality-preserving Densification
head: Z-ordering for Gaussians
body: Locality-preserving densification addresses the memory access throttling caused by standard Gaussian densification, where new primitives are appended to the end of parameter buffers, causing spatially close Gaussians to be stored far apart in memory. By reordering the Gaussian parameter buffers based on 3D spatial proximity using Z-ordering (Morton order), this method ensures that neighboring Gaussians in space are also adjacent in memory, thereby improving memory access coalescing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\} and the current parameter buffer layout. Output: A permuted parameter buffer where the indices of the Gaussians are reordered such that spatial locality is preserved. Data Structures: Gaussian Buffer: An array of structures containing \muk, \Sigmak, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k. The method operates on the indices of this array. Z-order Key: A 64-bit integer derived from the 3D coordinates of \muk. Steps: 1. Trigger Check: Determine if the current training iteration t is a multiple of the Z-ordering frequency T{\text{zorder}}. If not, skip. 2. Coordinate Normalization: Normalize the mean positions \muk of all active Gaussians to a canonical range (e.g., [0, 1]) suitable for Morton coding. Let \mu'k be the normalized position. 3. Z-order Encoding: For each Gaussian gk, compute its Morton code mk from \mu'k. The Morton code interleaves the bits of the x, y, and z coordinates. mk = \text{MortonEncode}(\mu'k.x, \mu'k.y, \mu'k.z) 4. Sorting: Create a list of indices I = [0, 1, \dots, N-1] and sort I based on the ascending order of mk. 5. Buffer Reordering: Rearrange the elements in the Gaussian parameter buffer according to the sorted index list I. This ensures that Gaussians with similar Morton codes (spatially close) are adjacent in memory. 6. Backward Pass Compatibility: Ensure the rendering pipeline uses the per-Gaussian backward pass, as the original backward pass with numerous atomic operations causes high atomic contention when combined with Z-ordering. Parameters: Z-ordering Frequency (T{\text{zorder}}): 5000 iterations. Z-ordering Computational Cost: Approximately 4 ms per million Gaussians. Pitfalls: Atomic Contention: Z-ordering performs effectively only when used with the per-Gaussian backward pass. Using it with the original backward pass heightens atomic contention due to the interaction between the reordered memory layout and the atomic accumulation operations. Small Scene Overhead: Repeated Z-ordering slows down training when the number of Gaussians is small. This is due to a massive increase in atomic contention in the alpha blending backward pass, leading to false sharing. Precision: Normalization range must be consistent across iterations to ensure stable Morton codes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyzordering(gaussians, iteration, tzorder=5000, scenemin=None, scenemax=None): """ Reorders the gaussian buffer based on 3D spatial locality using Z-ordering. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attribute 'mean' (vec3). iteration: Current training iteration number. tzorder: Frequency of Z-ordering application. scenemin, scenemax: Bounding box of the scene for normalization. Returns: None (modifies gaussians in place). """ # Step 1: Trigger Check if iteration % tzorder != 0: return n = len(gaussians) if n == 0: return # Step 2 & 3: Compute Morton Codes mortoncodes = [] for g in gaussians: # Normalize to [0, 1] using scene bounds x = (g.mean.x - scenemin.x) / (scenemax.x - scenemin.x) y = (g.mean.y - scenemin.y) / (scenemax.y - scenemin.y) z = (g.mean.z - scenemin.z) / (scenemax.z - scenemin.z) mortoncodes.append(mortonencode(x, y, z)) # Step 4: Sort Indices indexedcodes = list(enumerate(mortoncodes)) indexedcodes.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) sortedindices = [idx for idx, in indexedcodes] # Step 5: Buffer Reordering gaussians[:] = [gaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] # Step 6: Backward Pass Compatibility # Ensure per-Gaussian backward pass is used to avoid atomic contention. def mortonencode(x, y, z): """ Interleaves bits of x, y, z to form a Morton code. Assumes inputs are scaled to integers in [0, 2^21 - 1]. """ scale = 1 << 21 ix = int(x scale) & ((1 << 21) - 1) iy = int(y scale) & ((1 << 21) - 1) iz = int(z scale) & ((1 << 21) - 1) m = 0 for i in range(21): m |= ((ix >> i) & 1) << (3 i) m |= ((iy >> i) & 1) << (3 i + 1) m |= ((iz >> i) & 1) << (3 i + 2) return m Time Complexity: The Z-ordering step itself is O(N \log N) due to sorting, where N is the number of Gaussians. The computational cost is approximately 4 ms per million Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the Morton codes and sorted indices. No additional memory is required for the Gaussians themselves. Measured Performance: Reduces warp divergence and cache misses, resulting in faster training when scenes contain many Gaussians. It outperforms load-balanced approaches which can cause uncoalesced memory accesses that become a bigger bottleneck as primitives increase. Strengths: Significantly improves memory access patterns during densification, leading to faster training times for large-scale scenes. Limitations: Adds overhead for small scenes (fewer Gaussians) due to false sharing and atomic contention in the backward pass. Requires the per-Gaussian backward pass to be effective. When to Use: Use when training scenes with a large number of Gaussians (e.g., >1M) and densification is active. Do not use if the number of Gaussians is small or if the per-Gaussian backward pass is not implemented. Locality-preserving densification was introduced in the "Faster-GS" paper, which analyzes and improves Gaussian Splatting optimization. The authors observed that memory layout became a throttling factor during densification, as new Gaussians added to the end of buffers caused spatially close primitives to be far apart in memory. By applying Z-ordering every 5000 iterations alongside other optimization passes, the resulting framework achieved up to 5.2× faster training on Deep Blending scenes compared to the original 3DGS implementation. name: Progressive and Multi-stage Training
body: Progressive and Multi-stage Training refers to a family of optimization strategies that decompose the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations into sequential phases. This approach addresses convergence instability and error propagation inherent in optimizing all parameters simultaneously, particularly when dealing with complex geometry, sparse inputs, or feed-forward pose estimation. By decoupling geometry initialization, appearance refinement, and high-frequency detail capture, these methods ensure that the Gaussian distribution adapts progressively to the scene's complexity. Unlike single-stage approaches, multi-stage methods isolate specific learning objectives (e.g., pose vs. attributes) to stabilize the optimization landscape. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly partitioning the optimization timeline into sequential phases with distinct trainable parameter sets and supervision signals, rather than applying a single unified training loop. All methods in this family operate on the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} defined in Densification Strategy. The core mechanism involves partitioning the optimization timeline into distinct stages, where each stage modifies the set of trainable parameters, the supervision signals, and the densification triggers. Common principles include: 1. Parameter Freezing/Unfreezing: Stages typically freeze geometry-related parameters (positions, covariances, camera poses) while optimizing appearance parameters (SH coefficients, opacity), or vice versa, to prevent error propagation Multi-stage Training with Pose Prediction. 2. Progressive Complexity: Training often begins with simplified supervision signals (e.g., low-order SH, RGB-only, or coarse geometry) and gradually introduces higher complexity (e.g., high-order SH, perceptual losses, or dense densification) Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy, Training Loop with Mixed Losses and Post-Processing. 3. Curriculum or Staged Supervision: Different stages may use different data sampling strategies or loss functions. For example, early stages might use slice-based supervision for local structure, while later stages use voxel-based supervision for global consistency Curriculum Learning with Slice and Voxel Supervision. 4. Densification Timing: Densification (splitting/cloning) is often deferred or modified in early stages to establish a stable coarse topology before refining local details Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy, Training Loop with Structure-Aware Densification. A multi-stage protocol that decouples initialization from refinement. It solves convergence instability by separating coarse geometry establishment from fine-grained appearance optimization. It sets itself apart by using a consistency filter during the transition to maintain structural integrity. Choose this for scenes where single-stage training leads to chaotic topology or suboptimal convergence. Defines the optimization for MeshGS, a variant aligning primitives with an explicit mesh. It solves geometry misalignment by partitioning Gaussians into tightly-bound (G^t) and loosely-bound (G^l) sets, applying mesh-specific losses (normal consistency, projection) to G^t. Choose this when reconstructing scenes with known or recoverable mesh geometry. A per-scene optimization process that refines an initial, often coarse or generated, Gaussian representation. It addresses the gap between initial reconstruction (e.g., SfM) and final photorealism by actively optimizing all attributes. Choose this when adapting a pretrained or generic model to a specific scene, or when initial SfM points are noisy. Addresses instability in shear-warp rendering by decoupling global spatial guidance from local structural learning. It sets itself apart by explicitly utilizing 2D slice sampling aligned with the rendering pipeline, rather than relying solely on hierarchical densification. Choose this for volumetric data (e.g., MRI) where global consistency is critical. Decomposes feed-forward 3DGS optimization into sequential phases to decouple geometry estimation from appearance refinement. It sets itself apart by explicitly freezing pose-dependent parameters during appearance refinement to prevent error propagation. Choose this for novel view synthesis from sparse or unposed inputs where pose accuracy is paramount. Adds geometrical constraints on Gaussian localization to disentangle performance from the number of input views. It enables robust synthesis across broader view ranges by supervising renderings in interpolated views. Choose this for long sequences or sparse view inputs where standard 3DGS overfits to the training set. Defines the iterative optimization step integrating photometric, depth, and structural constraints. It distinguishes itself by supporting multi-stage parameter updates (e.g., SH degree progression) and post-processing densification triggers within the same iteration. Choose this as the foundational training engine for implementing other progressive strategies. Accelerates training by triggering splits based on local image frequency rather than solely on gradient magnitude. It solves slow convergence by ensuring primitives are subdivided early to capture high-frequency details. Choose this when standard gradient-based densification is too slow or misses fine textures. Definition: Introduces a progressive propagation strategy to expand the Gaussian cloud, ensuring smooth expansion and better coverage. Context: Described as part of GaussianPro [77], this method expands the cloud in a fronto-parallel manner to improve coverage stability during densification. Step: Alternates between spatial and temporal densification every 2 epochs. Context: Used in adaptive spatio-temporal 3DGS for scenes with oscillatory motion. This prevents Gaussians from failing to reconstruct either motion or appearance detail by avoiding simultaneous optimization conflicts. Definition: A training strategy that decouples depth network initialization from full model training to improve stability and performance. Step: Stage 1: Construct RGB point clouds for each input view, project them to the target view using a differentiable point cloud renderer, aggregate point clouds to render target views, and optimize the depth network using photometric loss. Stage 2: Freeze or continue training the initialized depth network and jointly train the entire model (spatial feature network, MLP, renderer, transformer, refinement module). Parameter: Performance improvement of approximately 0.4 dB PSNR gain. Pitfall: Jointly training the depth network and other components from scratch causes instability. Step: Stage 1: Jointly train triplanes and MLP on a subset of 500 randomly selected shapes. Use a batch size of 1 object per iteration and 500k occupancy values points per object. Stage 2: Freeze the shared MLP. Train triplane features for each object individually using a batch size of 200k occupancy values per object. Train for 30 epochs with a learning rate of 1e-3. Parameter: Triplane feature dimension: 128 \times 128 \times 32 \times 3. Triplane initialization: values drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.1. MLP architecture: Fourier feature mapping layer (scale factor 1) followed by 3 fully connected layers of dimension 128, each with ReLU activation. Number: Stage 1 training time: approximately 1 day on a single RTX 2080ti. Stage 2 training time: 10 minutes per shape on an RTX 2080ti. Step: Augment the initial model with larger sets of closer-up images (64 or 512 images) to simulate prolonged user interaction. Optimize the model for up to 4000 iterations, including 400 iterations of densification to capture finer details. Parameter: Final Gaussian count grows to between 20k and 50k. Training proceeds at over 500 iterations per second. Pitfall: Improvement becomes marginal after 2000 iterations. Using foveated and subsequently undistorted views for training decreases quality metrics by 5-10% depending on the scene. Comparison: Fixed foveation center and variable foveation points yield less than 1% quality difference. Definition: A densification trigger applying a three-channel anisotropic criterion where each Gaussian axis is evaluated against its own directional frequency content. Number: On Mip-NeRF360, \eta^{(proj)} achieves PSNR 27.20 and LPIPS 0.203, compared to the scalar metric \eta (PSNR 27.25, LPIPS 0.197). Comparison: Theoretically more precise than the scalar wavelength metric, but yields worse perceptual quality (LPIPS) in practice because it relies on accurate axis-direction alignment that is not yet optimized during training. The concept of multi-stage training in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a response to the limitations of single-stage optimization, particularly in complex scenes or when dealing with sparse inputs. Early implementations focused on coarse-to-fine strategies to stabilize geometry initialization Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy. Subsequent work introduced pose-free training pipelines that decouple pose estimation from Gaussian attribute refinement to prevent error propagation Multi-stage Training with Pose Prediction. Curriculum learning approaches were adapted from volumetric rendering to handle shear-warp pipelines Curriculum Learning with Slice and Voxel Supervision. name: Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy
head: Multi-stage point cloud refinement, Hybrid training strategy
body: The Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy is a multi-stage training protocol for differentiable point-based radiance fields that decouples the initialization of the point cloud from its subsequent refinement. It solves the convergence instability and suboptimal topology of single-stage training by progressively refining the representation, ensuring that the point distribution adapts to the scene's complexity rather than remaining static or chaotic. Unlike single-stage approaches, it yields significantly higher rendering quality by separating the establishment of coarse geometry from the fine-grained appearance optimization. The method operates on a set of differentiable 3D points \mathcal{P}, where each point pi carries position, color, opacity, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. The training is partitioned into sequential stages, transitioning from a coarse initialization to a fine-grained reconstruction. Inputs: Initial sparse point cloud \mathcal{P}0 (often derived from Structure-from-Motion). Training images with known camera poses. Hyperparameters for stage duration and refinement thresholds. Outputs: Refined point cloud \mathcal{P}{final} with optimized positions, colors, opacities, and SH coefficients. Data Structures: Point attributes: Position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \alpha \in [0,1], Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or SH coefficients \mathbf{c}l for degree l). Camera poses \mathbf{T} \in SE(3). Steps: 1. Coarse Initialization: Train the initial point cloud \mathcal{P}0 using a simplified supervision signal. This stage often employs lower-order spherical harmonics or directionally invariant RGB values to stabilize the geometry and camera poses without overfitting to high-frequency details. 2. Hybrid Transition: Introduce the "hybrid" mechanism. This involves a consistency filter or a transition in the optimization objective that allows the point cloud to densify and refine its structure. The specific implementation in the source uses a consistency filter function applied during training to maintain structural integrity while allowing refinement. 3. Fine Refinement: Continue training with higher-order spherical harmonics and full photometric loss. The point cloud positions and attributes are updated to minimize the difference between rendered and ground-truth images. The strategy ensures that densification (if applicable) is guided by the coarse structure established in stage 1. Formulas: The rendering loss \mathcal{L} is minimized. The ablation study implies the total loss includes photometric terms. The effectiveness is measured by PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Parameters: Stage boundaries: Not explicitly defined in the source, but the strategy implies a temporal split in training epochs. SH Degree: Increases from low (or none) to high. Edge Cases: Removing the hybrid strategy ("w/o hybrid") leads to significant quality degradation, indicating that single-stage training is insufficient for complex scenes. The consistency filter is critical; removing it ("w/o filter") degrades performance, suggesting that unfiltered refinement may introduce noise or artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainhybridcoarsefine(points, images, cameras, epochscoarse, epochsfine): """ Trains a differentiable point-based radiance field using a hybrid coarse-to-fine strategy. Args: points: Initial point cloud with positions, opacities, and low-order SH/RGB. images: List of training images. cameras: List of camera poses. epochscoarse: Number of epochs for the coarse stage. epochsfine: Number of epochs for the fine stage. Returns: Refined points. """ # Stage 1: Coarse Initialization # Use simplified appearance (e.g., directionally invariant RGB or low-order SH) # to stabilize geometry and poses. for epoch in range(epochscoarse): for image, camera in zip(images, cameras): # Render image from points and camera renderedimage = render(points, camera) # Compute loss (photometric) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, image) # Backpropagate to update points and simplified appearance updateparameters(points, loss) # Stage 2: Fine Refinement with Hybrid Strategy # Introduce higher-order SH and consistency filtering for epoch in range(epochsfine): for image, camera in zip(images, cameras): # Render image renderedimage = render(points, camera) # Apply consistency filter to ensure structural integrity # mentions a "consistency filter function" applied during training filteredrendered = applyconsistencyfilter(renderedimage, points) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(filteredrendered, image) # Backpropagate to update points and full SH coefficients updateparameters(points, loss) return points A variant that progressively refines a sparse mesh by inserting new vertices at high-error locations. It decouples initialization from refinement to adapt mesh topology to scene complexity. Performance: On the Blender dataset, the hybrid strategy achieves a PSNR of 30.3 dB, SSIM of 0.945, and LPIPS of 0.078. Comparison: Removing the hybrid strategy ("w/o hybrid") reduces PSNR to 26.6 dB, SSIM to 0.925, and increases LPIPS to 0.163. This demonstrates a significant quality improvement over single-stage training. Complexity: The method requires multiple training stages, increasing total training time compared to single-stage methods. However, it avoids the poor convergence of single-stage training. Strengths: Stabilizes training, improves rendering quality, and allows for better adaptation of the point cloud to scene details. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stage transitions and hyperparameters. The source does not provide specific scaling laws or memory complexity metrics. The Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy was introduced in the context of differentiable point-based radiance fields for efficient view synthesis. It addresses the limitations of coordinate-network representations that require ray-marching with hundreds of network evaluations per ray, offering an alternative that allows for efficient rendering while maintaining end-to-end differentiability. The method was validated through ablation studies showing the necessity of each component, including the hybrid strategy itself. name: Coarse-to-Fine Densification
head: Mesh densification, Progressive mesh refinement
body: Coarse-to-Fine Densification is a training strategy for primitive-based neural reconstruction that progressively refines a sparse mesh by inserting new vertices at high-error locations. It solves the challenge of initializing and densifying a mesh representation without manual tuning, ensuring uniform distribution of vertices proportional to their spatial impact on the rendered image. Unlike single-stage training, it decouples initialization from refinement, allowing the mesh topology to adapt to the scene's complexity over time. Inputs: Target image, rendering parameters. The initial sparse mesh is generated during the initialization step. Outputs: Refined mesh (vertices, features, topology) after densification steps. Data Structures: Mesh: Set of vertices V and triangles T. Each vertex v \in V has position \mathbf{p}v and feature vector \mathbf{f}v. Triangle Score: Scalar value \text{score}t for each t \in T. Pixel Count: |\text{pixels}t| number of pixels covered by triangle t during rasterization. Steps: 1. Initialization: a. Downsample the target image. b. Compute Sobel gradient magnitudes on the downsampled image. c. Sample initial vertex positions proportionally to edge strength, applying a small uniform floor to ensure coverage. d. Create a Delaunay triangulation of the sampled points. e. Add boundary vertices to ensure full image coverage. f. Initialize vertex features (e.g., color, opacity) based on the target image at the vertex positions. 2. Iterative Densification: For each densification step (every 500 iterations, starting at iteration 1,500 and ending at 15,000): a. Score Triangles: For each triangle t in the current mesh: i. Calculate \overline{\text{DSSIM}}t, the mean DSSIM (structural dissimilarity) of pixels covered by t. ii. Count |\text{pixels}t|, the number of pixels covered by t. iii. If |\text{pixels}t| < 3, exclude t from scoring. iv. Compute score: \text{score}t = \overline{\text{DSSIM}}t \cdot |\text{pixels}t|^\alpha where \alpha = 0.75. b. Select Triangles: Sort triangles by \text{score}t descending. Select the top-scoring triangles such that the total number of new vertices does not exceed 0.35 \times V, where V is the current number of vertices. c. Insert Vertices: For each selected triangle t: i. Compute the centroid position \mathbf{p}{new} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{v \in t} \mathbf{p}v. ii. Initialize new vertex features \mathbf{f}{new} by averaging the features of the parent triangle's vertices: \mathbf{f}{new} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{v \in t} \mathbf{f}v. iii. Add \mathbf{p}{new} and \mathbf{f}{new} to the vertex set. d. Re-triangulate: Re-run Delaunay triangulation on the full updated vertex set. e. Degeneracy Check: Detect if the mesh is degenerate (e.g., colinear vertices). If so, re-mesh. This rarely occurs in practice. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofinedensification(targetimage, startiter=1500, enditer=15000, step=500): # Initialization downsampledimg = targetimage[::4,::4] # Standard downsampling gradients = computesobelmagnitude(downsampledimg) # Standard Sobel filter # Sample proportionally to gradient with uniform floor vertices = samplepointsfrommap(gradients, minprob=0.01) # Add boundary vertices for full coverage vertices.extend(getimageboundarypoints()) # Initialize features from target image for v in vertices: v.features = bilinearsample(targetimage, v.position) triangles = computedelaunay(vertices) # Standard Delaunay for i in range(startiter, enditer + 1, step): scores = {} for t in triangles: pixels = rasterizetriangletopixelcoords(t) # Standard rasterization if len(pixels) < 3: continue dssimvals = [computedssim(p) for p in pixels] # Structural dissimilarity meandssim = sum(dssimvals) / len(dssimvals) scores[t] = meandssim (len(pixels) 0.75) sortedtriangles = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) maxnew = 0.35 len(vertices) splittriangles = [] count = 0 for t, in sortedtriangles: if count >= maxnew: break splittriangles.append(t) count += 1 newverts = [] for t in splittriangles: pos = sum(v.position for v in t.vertices) / 3.0 # Centroid feat = sum(v.features for v in t.vertices) / 3.0 # Feature average newverts.append(Vertex(position=pos, features=feat)) vertices.extend(newverts) triangles = computedelaunay(vertices) # Re-triangulate # Degeneracy check: detect colinear vertices and re-mesh if checkmeshdegeneracy(vertices, triangles): vertices, triangles = reinitializemesh(vertices, triangles) # Exact procedure not given def computesobelmagnitude(img): return convolve(img, sobelkernel) def samplepointsfrommap(grads, minprob): return samplepointsfromdensitymap(grads, minprob=minprob) def getimageboundarypoints(): return getimagebordercoordinates() def bilinearsample(img, coords): return interpolateimageatcoords(img, coords) def computedelaunay(points): return computevoronoidualmesh(points) def rasterizetriangletopixelcoords(tri): return rasterizetriangletopixellist(tri) def computedssim(p): return structuraldissimilaritymetric(p) def checkmeshdegeneracy(vertices, triangles): return anyareverticescolinear(vertices) def reinitializemesh(vertices, triangles): return recomputedelaunayandfeatures(vertices, triangles) Parameters: \alpha = 0.75: Area-weighting exponent. Densification interval: Every 500 iterations. Start iteration: 1,500. End iteration: 15,000. Max new vertices: 0.35 \times V per step. Minimum pixels for scoring: 3. Edge Cases: Degeneracy: Vertices may become colinear, causing mesh degeneracy. Re-meshing is required, though rare. Small Triangles: Triangles with fewer than 3 pixels are excluded to prevent over-densification of tiny areas. Precision: Not given in the sources. Coarse-to-fine Centroidal Voronoi Tesselation (CVT) is a method for densifying continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) discretization near a surface by simultaneously optimizing SDF values and their discretization sites. It solves the challenge of generating high-quality 3D reconstructions with millions of sites without the computational prohibitions of explicit Voronoi diagram computation. Unlike its sibling method DMTet, which relies on a known true SDF, this approach adapts locally to the optimized SDF field, ensuring vertices are uniformly distributed to reduce sampling artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Training generally takes between 1-3 minutes on an RTX A6000. Strengths: Automatic initialization, uniform vertex distribution, prevents over-densification of small areas. Limitations: Requires Delaunay triangulation, which can be computationally expensive for very large meshes. Degeneracy handling is necessary but rare. When to Use: When initializing a mesh-based neural reconstruction without manual seed placement. When Not to Use: When real-time per-step densification is required, as the method runs periodically every 500 iterations. Coarse-to-Fine Densification was introduced in "Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction". It addresses the need for robust mesh initialization and refinement in primitive-based neural reconstruction methods. The method uses structural dissimilarity (DSSIM) and area weighting to guide densification, ensuring that vertices are placed where they contribute most to image fidelity. name: Coarse-to-fine Centroidal Voronoi Tesselation (CVT)
head: CVT densification, SDF-aware implicit CVT optimization
body: Coarse-to-fine Centroidal Voronoi Tesselation (CVT) is a method for densifying continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) discretization near a surface by simultaneously optimizing SDF values and their discretization sites. It solves the challenge of generating high-quality 3D reconstructions with millions of sites without the computational prohibitions of explicit Voronoi diagram computation. Unlike its sibling method DMTet, which relies on a known true SDF, this approach adapts locally to the optimized SDF field, ensuring vertices are uniformly distributed to reduce sampling artifacts. Inputs: A 3D region of interest (bounding box). Camera centers for the scene. Initial coarse grid resolution (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16). Outputs: Optimized SDF values and feature values at discretization sites. A refined tetrahedral Delaunay mesh. Optimized color network parameters. Data Structures: Sites: A list of 3D points representing the discretization. KD-Tree: Maintained for each level of discretization to compute K-nearest neighbors (KNN) for gradient propagation and smoothing. Delaunay Tetrahedra: Computed after CVT optimization to define the dual mesh for ray-marching. Parameters: Initial grid resolution: 16 \times 16 \times 16. SDF upsampling threshold: 1.5 \times edge length. KNN re-estimation frequency: Every 100 iterations. Number of neighbors for bisector estimation (N): 24. Number of orthogonal directions per site: 3. Total CVT optimization iterations: 300. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a coarse uniform grid of sites within the bounding box (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16). Add the center of each camera as complementary sites to the CVT to accelerate ray-marching. Initialize SDF values, feature values, and color network parameters. 2. Coarse CVT Optimization: Minimize the CVT energy to move sites to the center of their cells. This establishes the initial uniform distribution. 3. Iterative Densification Loop: Repeat until the expected level of detail is reached: a. Optimization: Optimize color network parameters, SDF values, and feature values within the current CVT configuration. b. Upsampling: i. Identify surface-crossing edges in the dual of the CVT (the associated tetrahedral Delaunay mesh). ii. Add a new point at the center of each identified surface-crossing edge. iii. Identify edges where the SDF value at one endpoint is smaller than 1.5 \times the edge length. iv. Add a new point at the center of these edges as well. c. Implicit CVT Optimization: i. Re-estimate K-nearest neighbors (KNN) for each site every 100 iterations. ii. Minimize the approximate CVT loss (L{CVT}) for 300 iterations using the Adam optimizer. iii. The loss minimization ensures vertices are locally uniformly distributed. d. Mesh Update: i. Compute the Delaunay tetrahedra for the new set of sites. ii. Restart SDF and feature optimization on the new mesh. Implicit CVT Loss Calculation: To avoid explicit Voronoi cell computation, the method uses differences between distances to neighboring bisectors. 1. For each site si: a. Randomly sample two angles (\Theta, \Phi). These angles must be different for each site and change at each iteration. b. Rotate the standard Cartesian basis \{e0, e1, e2\} using (\Theta, \Phi) to obtain \{ej(\Theta, \Phi)\} for j=0,1,2. c. For each of the 3 rotated directions j: i. Find the N=24 nearest neighbors N(si) of si using the KD-tree. ii. Calculate the distance to the closest bisector in direction r: d(si, r) = \min{sj \in N(si)} (\|si - b(si, sj, r)\|^2) where b(si, sj, r) is the distance from si to its bisector with neighbor sj in direction r. iii. Edge Case (Opposite Signs): If the SDF values of si and sj have opposite signs, move the bisector plane to lie on the 0 crossing (aligning with the middle of dual tetrahedra). d. Sum the squared differences between distances to opposite bisectors: L{CVT} = \frac{1}{2} \sum{i} \sum{j=0,1,2} (d(si, ej(\Theta, \Phi)) - d(si, -ej(\Theta, \Phi)))^2 where ej(\Theta, \Phi) is the rotated cartesian basis and d() is the distance to the bisector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def generateuniformgrid(bboxmin, bboxmax, res): """Generates a coarse uniform grid of sites within the bounding box.""" x = torch.linspace(bboxmin[0], bboxmax[0], res) y = torch.linspace(bboxmin[1], bboxmax[1], res) z = torch.linspace(bboxmin[2], bboxmax[2], res) grid = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid(x, y, z, indexing='ij'), dim=-1) return grid.reshape(-1, 3) def initializesdf(sites): """Initializes SDF values for sites. Values are typically learned parameters.""" return torch.zeros(sites.shape[0], requiresgrad=True) def initializefeatures(sites): """Initializes feature values for sites. Values are typically learned parameters.""" return torch.zeros(sites.shape[0], 16, requiresgrad=True) # 16 is a standard feature dim def buildkdtree(sites): """Builds a KD-tree structure for fast KNN queries. Implemented via scipy.spatial or similar standard library.""" from scipy.spatial import KDTree return KDTree(sites.detach().cpu().numpy()) def findknn(kdtree, sites, k): """Finds K-nearest neighbors for all sites using the KD-tree.""" dists, indices = kdtree.query(sites.detach().cpu().numpy(), k=k+1) # Exclude self (index 0) return indices[:, 1:], dists[:, 1:] def rotatebasis(theta, phi): """Rotates the standard Cartesian basis using spherical angles theta and phi.""" # Rotation matrix R = Rz(theta) Ry(phi) cost, sint = torch.cos(theta), torch.sin(theta) cosp, sinp = torch.cos(phi), torch.sin(phi) R = torch.tensor([ [costcosp, -sint, costsinp], [sintcosp, cost, sintsinp], [-sinp, sint, cosp] ]) return R.T # Rows are the new basis vectors def computebisectordistance(si, sj, r, sdfi, sdfj): """Computes the squared distance from si to the bisector with sj in direction r.""" vec = sj - si normal = vec / torch.norm(vec) # Determine plane point: midpoint, or zero-crossing if signs differ if (sdfi > 0 and sdfj < 0) or (sdfi < 0 and sdfj > 0): # Zero crossing point on segment si -> sj tcross = torch.abs(sdfi) / (torch.abs(sdfi) + torch.abs(sdfj)) planepoint = si + tcross vec else: planepoint = (si + sj) / 2.0 # Ray: P(t) = si + t r # Plane: (P - planepoint). normal = 0 # t = (planepoint - si). normal / (r. normal) denom = torch.dot(r, normal) if torch.abs(denom) < 1e-8: return float('inf') t = torch.dot(planepoint - si, normal) / denom # Squared distance along unit direction r is t^2 return t t def computelcvtloss(sites, sdfvalues, kdtree, thetas, phis): """Computes the LCVT loss for all sites.""" loss = 0.0 Nneighbors = 24 neighborindices, = findknn(kdtree, sites, Nneighbors) for i in range(len(sites)): si = sites[i] sdfi = sdfvalues[i] theta, phi = thetas[i], phis[i] basis = rotatebasis(theta, phi) neighbors = sites[neighborindices[i]] sdfneighbors = sdfvalues[neighborindices[i]] for j in range(3): r = basis[j] negr = -r # Compute d(si, r) = min over neighbors of squared bisector distance distspos = torch.stack([computebisectordistance(si, neighbors[k], r, sdfi, sdfneighbors[k]) for k in range(Nneighbors)]) distsneg = torch.stack([computebisectordistance(si, neighbors[k], negr, sdfi, sdfneighbors[k]) for k in range(Nneighbors)]) dr = torch.min(distspos) dnegr = torch.min(distsneg) diff = dr - dnegr loss += diff diff return loss / 2.0 def coarsetofinecvt(bboxmin, bboxmax, cameras, initialres=16, maxiterations=300): """Main loop for Coarse-to-Fine CVT densification.""" # 1. Initialization sites = generateuniformgrid(bboxmin, bboxmax, initialres) cameracenters = torch.tensor([cam.center for cam in cameras]) sites = torch.cat([sites, cameracenters], dim=0) sdfvalues = initializesdf(sites) features = initializefeatures(sites) kdtree = buildkdtree(sites) # 2. Coarse CVT Optimization (Lloyd's step approximation) # Move sites to centroids of their Voronoi cells sites = sites - 0.1 torch.randlike(sites) # Placeholder for standard Lloyd iteration # 3. Iterative Densification for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Optimize network parameters # Optimize color network, SDF, and features via differentiable rendering loss # Upsampling # Compute Delaunay tetrahedra from sites using standard computational geometry routine tetrahedra = computedelaunaytetrahedra(sites) # Standard routine newsites = [] for edge in tetrahedra.edges: s1, s2 = edge.endpoints edgelength = torch.norm(s1 - s2) idx1, idx2 = edge.indices sdf1, sdf2 = sdfvalues[idx1], sdfvalues[idx2] # Surface crossing edge if (sdf1 > 0 and sdf2 < 0) or (sdf1 < 0 and sdf2 > 0): newsites.append((s1 + s2) / 2.0) # SDF threshold edge if torch.abs(sdf1) < 1.5 edgelength or torch.abs(sdf2) < 1.5 edgelength: newsites.append((s1 + s2) / 2.0) sites = torch.cat([sites, torch.stack(newsites)], dim=0) # Rebuild KD-tree occasionally if iteration % 100 == 0: kdtree = buildkdtree(sites) # Implicit CVT Optimization for cvtiter in range(300): # Random angles for each site thetas = torch.rand(len(sites)) 2 np.pi phis = torch.rand(len(sites)) np.pi # Compute Loss lcvtloss = computelcvtloss(sites, sdfvalues, kdtree, thetas, phis) # Backpropagate and update sites lcvtloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Update Mesh tetrahedra = computedelaunaytetrahedra(sites) # Standard routine return sites, sdfvalues, features, tetrahedra Time Complexity: Traditional CVT optimization with millions of sites takes ~5 minutes for Voronoi diagram computation and ~2.5 hours for 30 iterations. The approximated CVT takes ~1 second per iteration, allowing 300 iterations in ~5 minutes. Memory Complexity: Requires maintaining a KD-tree for each level of discretization and storing SDF values, features, and network parameters for all sites. Strengths: Significant computational benefits over explicit Voronoi computation; adapts locally to the optimized SDF field; reduces sampling artifacts by ensuring uniform vertex distribution. Limitations: Does not know the true SDF (unlike DMTet); relies on approximation which may not perfectly match true Voronoi centroids. When to use: When high-quality 3D reconstruction with millions of sites is required, and explicit Voronoi computation is too slow. When not to use: When the true SDF is known and can be used for exact densification (e.g., DMTet scenarios). Origin: Proposed in "VortSDF: 3D Modeling with Centroidal Voronoi Tesselation on Signed Distance Fields" (WACV 2025). History: Inspired by previous work on CVT optimization. The method addresses the limitations of DMTet [28] by handling unknown SDFs. Usage: Used in differentiable rendering strategies for volumetric reconstruction, specifically for efficient sampling of points along pixel viewing lines in non-uniform tetrahedral grids.
