name: Training Objective and Densification
head: MeshGS Training, Tightly/Loosely-bound Training
body: This method defines the optimization objective and densification strategy for MeshGS, a variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns primitives with an explicit mesh surface. It solves the problem of geometry misalignment and excessive primitive expansion in standard 3DGS by introducing a hybrid representation: tightly-bound splats (G^t) constrained to the mesh and loosely-bound splats (G^l) following standard 3DGS rules. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly coupling the training loss and densification logic to a pre-existing mesh geometry, using projection and normal consistency losses to enforce surface adherence. Inputs: Set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, partitioned into tightly-bound G^t and loosely-bound G^l. A mesh M defined by faces F, where each face fj has vertices vi and normal nf. Ground truth images Ii and rendered images \hat{I}i. Hyperparameters: \lambda{img}=0.001, \lambda{nc}=0.1, \lambda{min}=0.1, \lambda{max}=10, \lambda{proj}=50, \rho=0.1. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) and updated mesh alignment. Data Structures: G^t: Set of Gaussians where the distance to the mesh surface is \le d{th} (default 0.01). G^l: Set of Gaussians where the distance to the mesh surface is > d{th}. Steps: 1. Initialization and Partitioning: Initialize Gaussians. Classify each Gaussian i into G^t or G^l based on the distance to the nearest point on the mesh surface. If distance \le 0.01, it is tightly-bound (G^t); otherwise, it is loosely-bound (G^l). 2. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss L as the sum of image, normal consistency, scale regularization, and projection losses: L = L{img} + \lambda{nc} L{nc} + L{scale} + \lambda{proj} L{proj} Image Loss (L{img}): Combines L1 and D-SSIM: L{img} = (1-\lambda{img})L{1}(\hat{I}{i},I{i}) + \lambda{img}SSIM(\hat{I}{i}, I{i}) Where \hat{I}i is the rendered image, Ii is the ground truth, and \lambda{img}=0.001. Normal Consistency Loss (L{nc}): Aligns Gaussian normals with mesh face normals. First, estimate the normal ni for each Gaussian in G^t: 1. Identify the minimum scale axis among scale parameters Si = (s1, s2, s3). 2. Apply the rotation matrix Ri to transform this axis into world coordinates to obtain ni. Then compute: L{nc} = \sum{i \in G^{t}, f \in F} (1 - n{i} \cdot n{f}) Where nf is the normal of the corresponding mesh face f. Scale Regularization Loss (L{scale}): Prevents G^t from expanding excessively: L{scale} = \sum{i \in G^{t}}(\lambda{min}|\text{min}(s{1}, s{2}, s{3})| + \lambda{max}|\text{max}(s{1}, s{2}, s{3}) - \rho|) Where \lambda{min}=0.1, \lambda{max}=10, and \rho=0.1. Projection Loss (L{proj}): Keeps G^t centers close to the mesh surface. Project the Gaussian center Pi to the closest point si on the mesh surface defined by face fj and vertex vi. The projection is calculated as: s{i} = P{i} + ((P{i} - v{i}) \cdot f{j}) \cdot f{j} (Note: The source formula uses fj in the dot product and multiplication, implying fj is treated as a vector in this context, likely the face normal or a specific geometric vector. Standard projection to a plane uses the normal. Given the text "closest point si on the mesh surface defined by face fj", and the formula structure, this appears to be a simplified projection onto the plane of the face. We implement exactly as cited.) Then: L{proj} = \sum{i \in G^{t}}\parallel s{i} - P{i} \parallel {2} Where \lambda{proj}=50. 3. Densification (Splitting and Cloning): Perform densification every 500 iterations. The strategy differs for G^t and G^l: For Loosely-bound Splats (G^l): Follow the original 3DGS densification strategy (gradient-based splitting and cloning). For Tightly-bound Splats (G^t): 1. Identify the mesh triangle fj closest to the Gaussian. 2. Cloning: Sample a new point from the triangle fj. Copy the original Gaussian's attributes (position, rotation, opacity, SH) to the new Gaussian, but initialize its position at the sampled point. 3. Splitting: Sample a new point from the triangle fj. Initialize the new Gaussian's position at the sampled point. Divide the original Gaussian's scale by a factor of 1.6. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Image Loss (applied to all Gaussians) l1loss = L1(renderedimages, images) ssimloss = SSIM(renderedimages, images) Limg = (1 - params.lambdaimg) l1loss + params.lambdaimg ssimloss # 2. Normal Consistency Loss (only for Gt) Lnc = 0 for g in Gt: # Estimate normal: min scale axis rotated by R minscaleidx = argmin(g.scale) ni = rotateaxis(g.rotation, minscaleidx) # Find corresponding mesh face f f = mesh.getclosestface(g.position) nf = f.normal Lnc += (1 - dot(ni, nf)) Lnc = params.lambdanc # 3. Scale Regularization Loss (only for Gt) Lscale = 0 for g in Gt: s = g.scale mins = min(s) maxs = max(s) Lscale += params.lambdamin abs(mins) + params.lambdamax abs(maxs - params.rho) # 4. Projection Loss (only for Gt) Lproj = 0 for g in Gt: Pi = g.position f = mesh.getclosestface(Pi) vi = f.vertices[0] # Assuming vi is a vertex of the face fj = f.normal # Interpreting fj as the face normal for projection plane # Projection formula from source si = Pi + dot(Pi - vi, fj) fj Lproj += norm(si - Pi) Lproj = params.lambdaproj return Limg + Lnc + Lscale + Lproj def densify(Gt, Gl, mesh, params): # Densify Gl using standard 3DGS rules Gl = densifystandard3dgs(Gl, params) # Densify Gt using mesh-aligned sampling newGt = [] for g in Gt: f = mesh.getclosestface(g.position) # Cloning: Copy attributes, new position from sampling cloned = copygaussian(g) cloned.position = samplepointfromtriangle(f) newGt.append(cloned) # Splitting: New position from sampling, scale / 1.6 split = copygaussian(g) split.position = samplepointfromtriangle(f) split.scale = g.scale / 1.6 newGt.append(split) return Gl, newGt Constrains primitive count to a target budget N^ using a redundancy map, eliminating the need for gradient-based pruning. Allocates optimization iterations across image resolutions based on frequency energy, decoupling global coverage from local refinement. Time Complexity: Training runs for 30,000 iterations. The additional cost comes from mesh proximity queries and normal estimation for G^t at every iteration, and densification every 500 iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the mesh geometry M and maintaining the partition between G^t and G^l. Strengths: Ensures tight alignment with mesh surfaces, preventing excessive expansion of Gaussels into empty space. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the input mesh. The projection formula in the source is geometrically ambiguous (using fj as both face identifier and vector), which may require careful implementation. When to use: When an explicit mesh is available and surface-aligned rendering is required. When not to use: For scenes without a reliable mesh or when standard 3DGS performance is sufficient. Originated in MeshGS: Adaptive Mesh-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for High-Quality Rendering. It extends 3DGS [22] by integrating a hybrid densification strategy and a mesh-aware loss function to improve geometry reconstruction quality. name: Budget-Centered Training
body: Budget-Centered Training (BCT) is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that initializes and constrains the primitive count to the "knee" of the scene's capacity floor curve (N^), ensuring the model is born at the optimal size for a target quality rather than growing large and being pruned later. It differs from standard densification pipelines by replacing gradient-based pruning signals with a redundancy map (\theta) and by treating the primitive budget as a hard constraint during the optimization phase, thereby eliminating wasted computation on primitives that will eventually be removed. Inputs: Scene training views. Measured capacity floor curve for the scene, from which the knee point N^ is identified. Outputs: A 3D Gaussian Splatting model with primitive count capped at N^, optimized for the target quality. Data Structures: Primitive Set: A collection of 3D Gaussians. The total count is maintained \le N^. Redundancy Map (\theta): A spatial map where each region has a value \theta. High local multiplicity (over-covered regions) corresponds to low \theta values. State Variables: N{init}: Initial primitive count. N{stop}: Refine-stop fraction threshold. \theta{waste}: Measured redundancy ratio, defined as N{opt}/N{full}. Numbered Steps: 1. Measure Capacity Floor: Determine the capacity floor curve for the scene. Identify the knee point N^, defined as the budget with the largest steepest-window slope on the error-vs-budget curve. 2. Initialize Model: Set the initial primitive count N{init} to a fixed initial fraction of N^. 3. Compute Redundancy: Calculate the redundancy map \theta per region from the local factoring of the model. Regions with high local multiplicity (low \theta) are identified as over-covered. 4. Optimize with Budget Constraint: Train the model using MCMC densification, but enforce a hard cap on the total primitive count at N^. Densification: Proceed with standard densification logic to add primitives where needed. Pruning: Replace standard pruning signals (positional gradients/opacity) with the \theta redundancy map. Prune primitives inside regions flagged by \theta (specifically those with low \theta) based on their opacity. This removes primitives with the smallest approximation loss. 5. Stop Criterion: Monitor validation improvement. Freeze density control (stop densification/pruning) once the validation improvement falls below \epsilon = 0.5 dB. 6. Refine-Stop: Apply the refine-stop fraction (scaled by \theta{waste}) to determine the final termination of the refinement phase. Formulas: \theta{waste} = N{opt} / N{full}: Measured redundancy ratio used to scale the refine-stop fraction. N^: Knee point of the capacity floor curve, defined as the budget with the largest steepest-window slope on the error-vs-budget curve. \epsilon = 0.5 dB: Rate-based stopping criterion threshold for validation improvement. Parameters: N^: The knee point of the capacity floor curve (minimal primitive count for a given quality target). \epsilon: Rate-based stopping criterion threshold. Typical value: 0.5 dB validation improvement. Initial fraction: A fixed fraction of N^ used to set N{init}. Value: Not specified in the sources. Refine-stop fraction: A second fraction of N^ used to determine when to stop refinement. Scaled by \theta{waste}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The identification of N^ relies on the "steepest-window slope" of the capacity floor curve. Inaccurate measurement of the floor curve leads to suboptimal N^. Degenerate Input: If the scene has very low redundancy (e.g., already compressed models), the capacity floor curve may be flat, making N^ difficult to identify or resulting in minimal gains from BCT. Boundary Conditions: Pruning inside \theta-flagged regions must be careful not to remove primitives that are critical for visibility, even if they are in over-covered regions. The opacity-based pruning within these regions helps mitigate this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def budgetcenteredtraining(scenedata, capacityfloorcurve, Nopt, Nfull): # Step 1: Measure capacity floor curve and identify knee point N # N is the budget with the largest steepest-window slope on the error-vs-budget curve Nstar = maxslopepoint(capacityfloorcurve) # Standard curve knee detection # Step 2: Initialize model at fixed fraction of N thetawaste = Nopt / Nfull # Initial fraction value not specified in sources Ninit = Nstar 0.5 # Placeholder fraction; replace with actual value model = GaussianSet(count=Ninit) # Standard initialization # Step 3: Compute redundancy map theta per region from local factoring # Low theta indicates high local multiplicity (over-covered regions) thetamap = computeredundancymap(model) # Not given in sources; compute local multiplicity per region validationhistory = [] while True: # Step 4: MCMC densification model = densifystep(model, scenedata) # Not given in sources; standard 3DGS densification # Replace standard pruning with theta map; prune inside theta-flagged regions by opacity model = prunebytheta(model, thetamap) # Not given in sources; remove lowest-opacity primitives in low-theta regions # Enforce hard cap at N if model.primitivecount > Nstar: model.prunetocount(Nstar) # Evaluate validation performance valpsnr = evaluatevalidation(model, scenedata) # Not given in sources; standard PSNR computation validationhistory.append(valpsnr) # Step 5: Rate-based stopping criterion # Freeze density control once validation improvement falls below epsilon = 0.5 dB if len(validationhistory) >= 2: improvement = validationhistory[-1] - validationhistory[-2] if improvement < 0.5: break # Step 6: Refine-stop fraction application # Scaled by thetawaste to determine final termination stopthreshold = Nstar getrefinestopfraction(thetawaste) # Not given in sources; apply scaling if model.primitivecount < stopthreshold: model.freezerefinement() return model A two-stage Level-of-Detail (LOD) system where a model is trained at the budget-centered knee (N^) to minimize redundancy, and then a factoring tree is built over this model (and optionally the full model) to allow continuous quality scaling post-hoc. It is chosen when continuous quality scaling across different hardware budgets is required. It sets itself apart by using the BCT-trained model as a root for the factoring tree, ensuring the tree starts with a model that has almost no redundancy to lose. Steps: 1. Train the model at N^ using BCT. 2. Build factoring trees over two roots: the full model and the budget-centered model. 3. Deploy both roots through the same scheduler at a matched budget using an LOD render protocol. Performance: On the 'room' scene, the BCT-born tree renders 34.19 dB, within 0.16 dB of its own root, while the full-born tree collapsed to the same budget renders 22.83 dB. At 50% budget, it beats opacity-ordered pruning by +2.7 to +7.9 dB PSNR, with a cost of only -0.13 and -0.54 dB versus the full model. At 25% budget, the loss is substantial (3.1–13.9 dB) because already-compressed models carry less removable redundancy. Comparison: BCT is the correct front end for factoring tree deployment because a model born at the floor's budget contains almost no redundancy for the tree to lose. Time Complexity: Reduces training time compared to train-then-prune methods because it avoids optimizing and then removing a large number of primitives. The exact speedup is not quantified, but it is described as avoiding "wasted" training time on removed primitives. Memory Complexity: The model memory footprint is capped at N^, which is the minimal primitive count for the target quality. This is significantly smaller than the initial large model used in traditional pipelines. Measured Performance: On the 'room' scene, BCT-trained models achieve high quality (34.19 dB) at matched budgets compared to full models. Scaling: The method scales to city-scale scenes, enabling real-time rendering within consumer GPU memory limits. Strengths: Eliminates redundancy from the start; provides a clear measure of scene capacity; enables efficient LOD via factoring trees. Limitations: Requires accurate measurement of the capacity floor curve; may not provide significant gains on scenes with inherently low redundancy. When to use: When a fixed quality target must be met with minimal primitive count, or when building LOD systems via factoring trees. Budget-Centered Training was proposed in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It is based on the theory that a measurable capacity floor exists for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes, which defines the minimal achievable rendering error at a given primitive count. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of traditional pipelines that train large models and then compress them, wasting computation on primitives that are eventually removed. It is used in the context of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly for city-scale scenes and real-time rendering applications. name: Coarse-to-fine multi-resolution densification
head: energy density resolution scheduler, energy-aware multi-resolution scheduling
body: Coarse-to-fine multi-resolution densification is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically allocates optimization iterations across different image resolutions based on the image's frequency energy density. It solves the problem of premature convergence to local optima and inefficient spatial diffusion caused by applying full-resolution supervision during the early global spread phase. Unlike Budget-Centered Training, which manages Gaussian count via budget constraints, this method manages the resolution of supervision to decouple global coverage (split operations) from local refinement (clone operations). Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of training images I, total densification iterations T{\text{densify}}, and a maximum scale factor K. Output: A schedule of iteration counts Tr for each resolution scale r \in \{1, \dots, K\}, and the resulting optimized Gaussian primitives. Data Structures Scale Factor Set: A = \{1, 2, \dots, K\}, where r=1 is full resolution and r=K is the coarsest resolution. Iteration Schedule: A mapping from each r \in A to an integer Tr, representing the allocated iteration count at that resolution. Steps 1. Compute Energy Density: For each scale factor r \in A, compute the energy density Er of the training images. Downscale the input image I to resolution Ir using bilinear interpolation with anti-aliasing: Ir = Dr(I) = \text{Bilinear}(I, \text{scale} = 1/r) Compute the 2D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of Ir: F(Ir). Calculate the energy spectrum E(Ir): E(Ir) = \sqrt{\Re(F(Ir))^2 + \Im(F(Ir))^2} where \Re and \Im are the real and imaginary parts. Compute the normalized energy density Er: Er = \|E(Ir)\|1 \cdot r^2 The term r^2 normalizes the energy values across different resolutions. 2. Allocate Iterations: Calculate the number of iterations Tr for each resolution r based on the ratio of its energy to the full-resolution energy E1: Tr = \text{Round}\left(\frac{Er}{E1} \cdot T{\text{densify}}\right) where T{\text{densify}} is the total number of densification iterations. 3. Execute Training Schedule: Train the Gaussian primitives in reversed order of resolution, from coarsest (r=K) to finest (r=1). For a specific scale factor r, training starts at iteration T{r+1} and ends at iteration Tr. Global Spread Phase (r > 1): Use downsampled images for supervision. Keep the positional learning rate constant. Suppress clone operations to prevent premature local clustering and encourage spatial diffusion via split operations. Local Refinement Phase (r = 1): Switch to full-resolution supervision. Reduce the positional learning rate. Reintroduce clone operations to refine high-frequency details. Parameters T{\text{densify}}: Total densification iterations. Default value: 25,000. K: Maximum scale factor. Default value: 8. Positional Learning Rate: Constant during coarse resolutions (r > 1), reduced after restoring full resolution (r=1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Cancellation: Using full-resolution images during the global spread phase can cause large Gaussians to project to many pixels. The accumulated gradient vectors may cancel each other out due to opposing directions, resulting in small gradient errors below the split threshold and preventing further split operations. Premature Convergence: Full-resolution supervision encourages Gaussians to converge prematurely to local optima by overfitting to individual pixels, limiting spatial expansion. A training framework that gradually increases resolution based on energy density in 2D images to cooperate with the global-to-local densification strategy. It starts training at lower resolution to facilitate global spread via split operations, gradually increases resolution based on energy density, and transitions to full-resolution training to allow clone operations for local refinement. Time Complexity: The method accelerates training by approximately 2x compared to baseline implementations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves superior reconstruction performance with fewer Gaussian primitives on datasets such as MipNeRF-360, Deep Blending, and Tanks & Temples. Strengths: Promotes efficient spatial diffusion of Gaussian primitives, prevents premature local clustering, and balances global scene coverage with detail reconstruction. Limitations: Requires computation of FFT and energy density for scheduling. Relies on the assumption that energy density correlates with the required training effort at each resolution. The method was introduced in the paper "Decomposing Densification in Gaussian Splatting for Faster 3D Scene Reconstruction". It builds on the observation that split operations are responsible for global diffusion while clone operations govern local refinement. The approach draws inspiration from frequency analysis techniques in 2D image processing and DashGaussian. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting densification, which often leads to unnecessary computational consumption and suboptimal behavior when using full-resolution supervision too early. name: Fine-tuning
head: 3DGS Fine-tuning, Fine-tuning Strategy, Gaussian Splatting Fine-tuning, Per-scene optimization
body: Fine-tuning in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) refers to a per-scene optimization process that refines an initial, often coarse or generated, Gaussian representation into a high-fidelity radiance field by minimizing rendering losses against ground-truth images. It addresses the gap between initial reconstruction (e.g., from SfM points or a generative prior) and the final photorealistic output by allowing the geometry (means, covariances) and appearance (SH coefficients, opacity) to adapt to the specific scene. It sets itself apart from static initialization methods by actively optimizing all primitive attributes, and from global training strategies by focusing on a single-scene refinement phase, often leveraging pretrained weights or specific initialization schemes to accelerate convergence. The fine-tuning process typically begins with an initial set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}0 derived from a point cloud, a generative model, or a feed-forward network. The core mechanism involves differentiable rasterization to render images from novel or training viewpoints and backpropagating the difference between rendered and ground-truth images to update the Gaussian parameters. Inputs: Initial Gaussian set \mathcal{G}0 = \{\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i\}{i=1}^N, where \mui is the mean, \Sigmai is the covariance, \alphai is the opacity, and \mathbf{c}i are spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. A set of training images I{gt} with known camera poses Pj. Loss function \mathcal{L}, typically a combination of L1 loss and SSIM. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian set \mathcal{G}^ with refined geometry and appearance. The Gaussian set \mathcal{G} is stored as a list or array of primitives. Each primitive i contains: Mean (\mui): 3D vector (x, y, z). Covariance (\Sigmai): 3x3 symmetric positive-definite matrix, often parameterized by a 6D rotation vector and 3D scale vector for efficient optimization. Opacity (\alphai): Scalar in [0, 1]. SH Coefficients (\mathbf{c}i): Vector of coefficients for view-dependent color, typically up to degree 3 (45 coefficients). 1. Initialization: Generate initial Gaussians. This can be done via: Direct mapping from SfM point clouds. Feed-forward prediction of geometry and color attributes from a pretrained network. Voxel representation and marching cubes for mesh-based initialization. 2. Rendering: For each training image j with pose Pj: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D screen space. Sort Gaussians by depth. Composite colors using alpha blending: Cj = \sum{i \in \mathcal{G}} ci \alphai \prod{k < i} (1 - \alphak). 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the loss between rendered image Cj and ground truth I{gt, j}: \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{L1} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{SSIM} + \lambdae \mathcal{L}{entropy} where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the L1 distance, \mathcal{L}{SSIM} is the structural similarity index, and \mathcal{L}{entropy} is an entropy loss to encourage opacity sparsity. 4. Optimization: Update Gaussian parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam): \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \eta \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} where \theta represents all trainable parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) and \eta is the learning rate. 5. Densification/Pruning (Optional): During fine-tuning, enable growing (splitting/cloning) and pruning of primitives to adapt density to scene complexity. This is often controlled by gradient magnitude or opacity thresholds. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 for a fixed number of iterations or until convergence. Learning Rate: Typically 1 \times 10^{-3} for Adam optimizer. Loss Weights: \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambdae are hyperparameters balancing the loss terms. Iterations: Depends on scene complexity; often fewer iterations than initial training due to pretrained priors. Overfitting: Fine-tuning on a small number of views can lead to overfitting and artifacts in novel views. Initial Quality: Poor initialization (e.g., noisy SfM points) can lead to suboptimal local minima. Opacity Artifacts: High-opacity floaters can attenuate gradients to true surfaces, requiring opacity reset or regularization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finetune3dgs(initialgaussians, trainingdata, numiterations, learningrate): """ Fine-tune 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. Args: initialgaussians: List of Gaussian primitives (means, covariances, opacities, SH coeffs). trainingdata: List of tuples (image, camerapose). numiterations: Number of optimization steps. learningrate: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: optimizedgaussians: Refined Gaussian primitives. """ # Initialize optimizer with all Gaussian parameters optimizer = Adam(initialgaussians.parameters(), lr=learningrate) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample a random training image and pose image, pose = random.choice(trainingdata) # Render the scene from the current pose renderedimage = rendergaussians(initialgaussians, pose) # Compute loss l1loss = L1loss(renderedimage, image) ssimloss = SSIMloss(renderedimage, image) entropyloss = Entropyloss(initialgaussians.opacities) # Combined loss (weights are hyperparameters) loss = 0.7 l1loss + 0.2 ssimloss + 0.1 entropyloss # Backpropagate and update parameters optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Optional: Densification and pruning based on gradients if iteration % densificationinterval == 0: initialgaussians.densifyandprune(optimizer) return initialgaussians A fine-tuning process that accounts for different visual modes in a volume by generating multiple radiance fields using different transfer functions and optimizing the Gaussian set against rendered images. It selects a series of transfer functions \{TFh\}, where each TFh is non-zero only within specific value intervals of the physical field F, resulting in radiance fields RFh = TFh(F). For each radiance field, 64 images are rendered through volumetric integration to provide supervision data, and the image-space loss is backpropagated to update the Gaussian set Gh. In practice, 5 transfer functions are selected per volume. After fine-tuning, the Gaussians Gh for each mode can be concatenated or separately rendered. A baseline method that trains vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting directly on 2D stylized images. It preserves better details than GS-Ada but requires training from scratch for every new style image, limiting practical usability compared to methods like GSS. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N, the number of training images M, and the number of iterations T. Rendering is O(N \log N) due to sorting, and optimization is O(T \cdot M \cdot N). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where D is the dimensionality of Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, SH coefficients). Performance: Fine-tuning with pretrained priors can accelerate convergence and reduce memory consumption compared to training from scratch. Strengths: High fidelity, ability to refine coarse initializations, flexibility in handling different initialization schemes. Limitations: Sensitive to initialization quality, risk of overfitting on sparse views, computational cost of densification. When to use: When a high-quality initial reconstruction is available but needs refinement, or when using generative priors that require per-scene adaptation. When not to use: When real-time inference is critical and pre-training is not feasible, or when the initial reconstruction is extremely poor. Fine-tuning in 3DGS is inspired by techniques in NeRF and CNNs. In NeRF, methods like LOLNeRF and Code-NeRF use per-scene optimization to refine implicit representations. In CNNs, fine-tuning involves fixing lower layers and optimizing higher layers for specific tasks. The application of fine-tuning to 3DGS allows for efficient adaptation of Gaussian primitives to specific scenes, leveraging the differentiable nature of Gaussian splatting. name: Exponentially Ascending Gradient Threshold
head: Exponential grad thresh
body: A densification control mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses an exponentially ascending gradient threshold Ti to determine when to split or clone Gaussians. It solves the trade-off between slow convergence in early training (due to few Gaussians) and overfitting in late training (due to excessive densification) by allowing aggressive densification early and restricting it later. It sets itself apart from static threshold methods by dynamically adjusting the sensitivity of densification based on the training progress. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current iteration index i, total iterations i{\max}, initial threshold Ts, final threshold Tf, and the modified gradient magnitude \tau'k for each Gaussian gk. Output: A boolean decision for each Gaussian indicating whether to split, clone, or do nothing. Data Structures: Ti: Scalar threshold value for iteration i. \tau'k: Scalar modified gradient magnitude for Gaussian k. Ts: Initial threshold (default 0.0001). Tf: Final threshold (default 0.0004). i: Current iteration index (integer). i{\max}: Total number of training iterations (integer). Steps: 1. Calculate the normalized iteration progress: p = \frac{i}{i{\max}}. 2. Compute the logarithmic interpolation between the natural logs of the initial and final thresholds: \ln(Ti) = \ln(Ts) \cdot (1 - p) + \ln(Tf) \cdot p 3. Exponentiate the result to obtain the current threshold: Ti = \exp \left( \ln(Ts) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{i}{i{\max}}\right) + \ln(Tf) \cdot \frac{i}{i{\max}} \right) 4. For each Gaussian gk in the scene: a. Retrieve its modified gradient magnitude \tau'k. b. Compare \tau'k against Ti. c. If \tau'k \ge Ti, consider densification (split or clone based on size constraints). d. If \tau'k < Ti, skip densification for this Gaussian. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculateexponentialthreshold(i, imax, Ts=0.0001, Tf=0.0004): """ Calculates the exponentially ascending gradient threshold for iteration i. Args: i (int): Current iteration index. imax (int): Total number of training iterations. Ts (float): Initial threshold value. Tf (float): Final threshold value. Returns: float: The threshold Ti for the current iteration. """ if imax == 0: return Tf # Normalized progress progress = i / imax # Log-linear interpolation followed by exponentiation # Formula: Ti = exp( ln(Ts) (1 - progress) + ln(Tf) progress) logTi = math.log(Ts) (1 - progress) + math.log(Tf) progress Ti = math.exp(logTi) return Ti def densificationcheck(gaussian, i, imax, Ts=0.0001, Tf=0.0004): """ Determines if a Gaussian should be densified based on the exponential threshold. Args: gaussian: Object containing 'modifiedgradientmagnitude' (tau'k). i (int): Current iteration index. imax (int): Total number of training iterations. Ts (float): Initial threshold. Tf (float): Final threshold. Returns: bool: True if densification (split/clone) should be considered. """ Ti = calculateexponentialthreshold(i, imax, Ts, Tf) # Compare modified gradient magnitude against the dynamic threshold if gaussian.modifiedgradientmagnitude >= Ti: return True else: return False Parameters: Ts: Initial gradient threshold value. Typical value: 0.0001. Tf: Final gradient threshold value. Typical value: 0.0004. i{\max}: Total number of training iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of logarithms and exponentials requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially if Ts or Tf are very small. Boundary Conditions: At i=0, Ti = Ts. At i=i{\max}, Ti = Tf. Degenerate Input: If i{\max} is zero, the threshold logic is undefined; however, in practice, training iterations are always positive. A densification strategy that uses accumulated gradient norms instead of a single gradient norm to detect blurred areas and dynamically adjusts the threshold for cloning/splitting Gaussians. It addresses the pitfall where single gradient norms fail to detect overly blurred areas because gradient signals from different pixels may cancel out, resulting in low overall magnitude despite poor reconstruction. It computes the gradient norm for each pixel influenced by a Gaussian during the backward pass, accumulates these norms to get S{grad}, and compares S{grad} against a threshold \lambda\alpha. The optimal \lambda\alpha found is 0.00045, compared to the vanilla 3DGS value of 0.0002. Experiments on scenes (flowers, garden, treehill, counter, drjohnson) showed optimal performance around \lambda\alpha = 0.00045, with PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS evaluated at intervals of 0.00005 from 0.0002 to 0.0006. Time Complexity: The calculation of Ti is O(1) per iteration per Gaussian, adding negligible overhead to the training loop. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond the scalar threshold value. Measured Performance: In ablation studies on 13 scenes, deactivating the exponential gradient threshold led to more Gaussian splats being generated but showed a smaller difference in PSNR compared to other components like extent correction. The method allows the number of Gaussians to rise much quicker during early training steps and decline towards the end, stabilizing after 15,000 iterations to a similar number as standard 3DGS. Strengths: Enables fast convergence early in training by allowing many Gaussians to densify, and prevents overfitting later by restricting densification to only those with very high positional gradients. Limitations: Does not significantly improve PSNR on its own compared to other densification improvements; its primary benefit is controlling the number of Gaussians. When to use: When the goal is to control the growth rate of Gaussian primitives to balance reconstruction speed and final scene compactness. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of dynamic threshold calculation is prohibitive (though minimal), or when other densification strategies (like Variational Densify Threshold) are preferred for handling blurred areas. Originated in the paper "Improving Adaptive Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting". The method was developed to address the limitations of static gradient thresholds in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where a fixed threshold either hinders convergence early on or causes overfitting late in training. It builds on the standard 3DGS densification algorithm by introducing a time-dependent threshold schedule. name: SplatFormer Training Objective & Refinement
head: SplatFormer
body: SplatFormer is a learning-based, feed-forward 3D neural module that refines initial 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations to enable robust novel view synthesis from out-of-distribution (OOD) camera angles. It addresses the bias of standard 3DGS optimization, which overfits to input views and fails to generalize to unseen high-elevation perspectives, by applying a point transformer network that predicts attribute residuals. Unlike 2D image restoration methods that suffer from multi-view inconsistencies, SplatFormer operates directly on 3D primitives, ensuring geometric consistency while recovering details lost in OOD views. Input: A set of initial 3D Gaussian splats \{Gk\}{k=1}^K generated from low-elevation input views, where each splat Gk is defined by position pk, scale sk, opacity \alphak, quaternion rotation qk, and spherical harmonics coefficients ak. Output: A set of refined splats \{G'k\}{k=1}^K with updated attributes \{G'k = Gk + \Delta Gk\}, where \Delta Gk = (\Delta pk, \Delta sk, \Delta \alphak, \Delta qk, \Delta ak) are the predicted residuals. The network processes a point cloud of size K. Input Features: Positions pk are normalized to [0, 1]^3. Latent Features: Each splat is assigned a V-dimensional feature vector vk \in \mathbb{R}^V, where V=96. Grid Pooling: Spatial proximity is handled via grid pooling. The point cloud is voxelized using a grid resolution of 384. The encoder extracts contextual features from the initial splats using a hierarchical architecture based on PTv3. 1. Embedding: Input positions pass through an MLP embedding layer. 2. Down-pooling Stages: Five stages process the features. Stage 1: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 64. Stage 2: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 96. Stage 3: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 128. Stage 4: 6 attention blocks, hidden dim 256. Stage 5: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 512. 3. Down-sampling Grid Pooling: Follows stages 2 through 5, with strides (1, 2, 2, 2) respectively. 4. Up-pooling Stages: Four stages upsample the features. Stage 1: Up-sampling grid pooling (stride 1), followed by 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 256. Stage 2: Up-sampling grid pooling (stride 2), followed by 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 128. Stage 3: Up-sampling grid pooling (stride 2), followed by 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 96. Stage 4: 2 attention blocks, hidden dim 96. 5. Output: The encoder outputs feature vectors vk for each splat. The decoder predicts residuals by combining latent features with original attributes. 1. Concatenation: For each splat k, concatenate the latent feature vk with the original attributes Gk. 2. MLP Branches: Five separate MLP branches predict residuals for means, opacity, quaternion, scales, and spherical harmonics. Each branch consists of 4 linear layers with hidden dimension 512. Activations: ReLU for all layers except the last. Mean Residual Normalization: Apply Tanh activation to the final output of the mean residual branch to normalize \Delta pk to [0, 1]. 3. Initialization: Zero-initialize the weights and biases of the final MLP layers in all branches to ensure zero initial residuals. The model is trained to minimize a combined loss function over rendered images from both input and OOD views: L{\text{SplatFormer}} = L1 + L{\text{LPIPS}} Where: L1 is the photometric loss. L{\text{LPIPS}} is the perceptual loss using the LPIPS metric. 1. Data Generation: Use 33k scenes from ShapeNet and 48k scenes from Objaverse-1.0. Render each scene from 32 low-elevation input views and 9 high-elevation OOD views using Blender. Generate initial 3DGS from low-elevation views by minimizing photometric loss for 10k steps. 2. Optimization: Use the Adam optimizer with a constant learning rate of 3 \times 10^{-5}. Gradient accumulation steps: 4. Total iterations: 150k. Sampling: At each iteration, render 4 target images consisting of 70% OOD views and 30% input views. Gaussian Capping: Cap input Gaussians to 100k. If the initial 3DGS exceeds this, randomly subsample. 1. Initial Reconstruction: Train a standard 3DGS from 32 input views using gsplat for 10k steps. 2. Refinement: Feed the resulting 3DGS point cloud into the trained SplatFormer encoder-decoder to obtain refined attributes. 3. Rendering: Render the refined splats using the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline. Unverified code. Standard grid upsampling interpolates features. return features, points class AttentionBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim): super().init() self.hiddendim = hiddendim def forward(self, features, points): # Not given in the sources. Standard PTv3 attention over spatial proximity. return features class SplatFormerEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, V=96): super().init() self.V = V self.embedding = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64)) downstages = [(2, 64), (2, 96), (2, 128), (6, 256), (2, 512)] self.downblocks = nn.ModuleList() self.downpoolings = nn.ModuleList() for i, (numblocks, hiddendim) in enumerate(downstages): for in range(numblocks): self.downblocks.append(AttentionBlock(hiddendim)) if i > 0: stride = [1, 2, 2, 2][i-1] self.downpoolings.append(GridPooling(stride=stride, gridres=384)) upstages = [(2, 256), (2, 128), (2, 96), (2, 96)] self.upblocks = nn.ModuleList() self.uppoolings = nn.ModuleList() for i, (numblocks, hiddendim) in enumerate(upstages): if i < len(upstages) - 1: stride = [1, 2, 2, 2][i] self.uppoolings.append(GridPoolingUpsample(stride=stride, gridres=384)) for in range(numblocks): self.upblocks.append(AttentionBlock(hiddendim)) def forward(self, points): x = self.embedding(points) downidx = 0 blockidx = 0 for i in range(len(downstages)): numblocks, = downstages[i] for in range(numblocks): x = self.downblocksblockidx blockidx += 1 if i > 0: x, points = self.downpoolingsdownidx downidx += 1 upidx = 0 blockidx = 0 for i in range(len(upstages)): if i < len(upstages) - 1: x, points = self.uppoolingsupidx upidx += 1 numblocks, = upstages[i] for in range(numblocks): x = self.upblocksblockidx blockidx += 1 return x class ResidualMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, indim, outdim, ismean=False): super().init() self.ismean = ismean self.fc1 = nn.Linear(indim, 512) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(512, 512) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(512, 512) self.fc4 = nn.Linear(512, outdim) nn.init.zeros(self.fc4.weight) nn.init.zeros(self.fc4.bias) def forward(self, x): x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc3(x)) out = self.fc4(x) if self.ismean: out = torch.tanh(out) return out class SplatFormerDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self, V=96): super().init() # 5 branches: means, opacity, quaternion, scales, SH coefficients # SH coefficients dimension depends on degree, assumed 10 here for example self.branches = nn.ModuleList([ ResidualMLP(V + 10, 5, ismean=(i==0)) for i in range(5) ]) def forward(self, features, initialsplats): residuals = [] for branch in self.branches: combined = torch.cat([features, initialsplats], dim=-1) residuals.append(branch(combined)) return residuals def trainstep(model, initialgs, targetcameras, targetgtimages, optimizer): # Normalize positions to [0, 1]^3 points = initialgs.positions / 255.0 # Encode features = model.encoder(points) # Decode residuals residuals = model.decoder(features, initialgs) # Compute refined splats refinedgs = initialgs + residuals # Render images (standard 3DGS rasterization) targetimages = render(refinedgs, targetcameras) # Compute loss: L1 + LPIPS l1 = F.l1loss(targetimages, targetgtimages) lpips = perceptualloss(targetimages, targetgtimages) loss = l1 + lpips optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss def infer(model, inputimages): # Train initial 3DGS by minimizing photometric loss for 10k steps initialgs = traininitial3dgs(inputimages, steps=10000) points = initialgs.positions / 255.0 features = model.encoder(points) residuals = model.decoder(features, initialgs) return initialgs + residuals Gaussian Count: If the initial 3DGS exceeds 100k Gaussians, they must be randomly subsampled before feeding into SplatFormer. Memory Consumption: GPU memory usage depends on the spatial distribution of Gaussians, not just the count. A spatially uniform distribution with high entropy consumes more memory than a concentrated distribution. Initialization: Final MLP layers must be zero-initialized to ensure the initial output matches the input 3DGS, preventing instability at the start of training. Mean Normalization: The Tanh activation on mean residuals restricts updates to [0, 1]. Ensure input positions are normalized to [0, 1]^3 to match this range. Training: Requires approximately 3000 GPU hours on RTX-2080Ti for data generation and 2 days on 8 RTX-4090s for model training (150k iterations). Inference Memory: Consumes ~900 MB GPU memory for 70k–100k Gaussians on an RTX-4090. Inference Speed: ~108 ms per feed-forward pass for 70k–100k Gaussians on an RTX-4090. Scalability: Supports up to 4 million Gaussians on an RTX-4090, though memory usage scales with spatial entropy. Strengths: Robust to OOD views (high elevation); ensures 3D consistency; faster than per-scene optimization; generalizes across object categories. Limitations: Struggles with fine-grained details and complex textures; efficiency bottleneck remains in training; unbounded scenes with uniform distributions increase memory consumption and remain a direction for future efficiency improvements. Use when novel view synthesis is required from high-elevation (top-down) OOD views where standard 3DGS fails. Use when 3D consistency is critical and 2D denoising methods introduce artifacts. Avoid for scenes with very fine geometric details that the model cannot recover. Avoid for unbounded scenes with large, uniform background noise, as this increases memory consumption significantly. SplatFormer was introduced in a paper published at ICLR 2025. It addresses the limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is optimized per-scene and biased towards input views, making it poor for generalizable novel view synthesis from unseen angles. The method leverages a large-scale dataset (ShapeNet and Objaverse-1.0) to learn data-driven priors for refining Gaussian attributes. It builds on the Point Transformer v3 (PTv3) architecture for efficient point cloud processing. name: MCMC-based 3DGS / SGLD for 3DGS
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting as MCMC / SGLD, MCMC-based 3DGS, SGLD for 3DGS
body: This method reformulates 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by treating the set of 3D Gaussians as random samples drawn from an underlying probability distribution describing the scene, specifically as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples. It converts conventional 3DGS updates into Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) updates by introducing a noise term to promote sample exploration, thereby removing the need for manual densification heuristics like cloning, splitting, and opacity resetting. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex gradient thresholds or hard constraints, this approach relies on probabilistic state transitions and regularization to manage Gaussian population. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses \boldsymbol{\theta}, ground-truth images \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{x}), initial set of N 3D Gaussians. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (oi, \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \mathbf{c}i) and rendered images. Data Structures: The state consists of a list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i stores: oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D center position. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (often parameterized as rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}). \mathbf{c}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. Numbered Steps: 1. Rendering: For a given camera pose \boldsymbol{\theta} and pixel \mathbf{x}, sort the N Gaussians by distance to the camera. Compute the rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) using alpha blending: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{c}i \alphai(\mathbf{x}) \left[ \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(\mathbf{x})) \right] where \mathbf{c}i is the color derived from Spherical Harmonics based on pose \boldsymbol{\theta}. 2. Opacity Calculation: Compute the opacity \alphai(\mathbf{x}) for the i-th Gaussian at pixel \mathbf{x}: \alphai(\mathbf{x}) = oi \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i; \boldsymbol{\theta}))^T \mathcal{R}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}i)^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i; \boldsymbol{\theta}))\right) where \mathcal{R} is the camera projection operation. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the training loss \mathcal{L}{\text{orig}} as a weighted sum of L1 and D-SSIM losses: \mathcal{L}{\text{orig}} = (1 - \lambda{\text{D-SSIM}}) \cdot \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{D-SSIM}} \cdot \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} where \mathcal{L}1 is the average L1 error between \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{x}), and \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} is the D-SSIM loss. The weight \lambda{\text{D-SSIM}} is typically 0.2. 4. SGLD Update (Exploration): Compute gradients \nabla \mathcal{L}{\text{orig}} with respect to Gaussian parameters. Update parameters using Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics by adding noise to the gradient step. This replaces the standard deterministic optimizer step, allowing Gaussians to explore the scene landscape naturally without manual densification. 5. Relocation (Deterministic State Transition): Implement a relocation strategy to handle "dead" Gaussians (those with low opacity). Identify "dead" Gaussians (low opacity) and "live" Gaussians (high opacity). Move dead Gaussians to locations of live Gaussians. Crucial Constraint: Ensure the composition of the relocated (cloned) Gaussians renders the same images as before relocation to preserve sample probability and prevent training instability. Pitfall: Cloning at Gaussian centers alone is insufficient; the whole Gaussian must be considered to ensure the rendering remains equal and MCMC sampling remains optimal. 6. Regularization: Apply L1-regularization to encourage efficient use of Gaussians. This regularizer is applied to both opacity and scale, promoting the removal of unused Gaussians by encouraging them to "disappear" if unnecessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
