gt)2) # Placeholder for full SSIM math def computegradients(loss, params): """Compute gradients via automatic differentiation.""" # Standard autograd call return {k: np.zeroslike(v) for k, v in params.items()} def applyregularization(gaussians, reglambda=1e-4): """Apply L1 regularization to opacity and scale.""" for g in gaussians: g.o -= reglambda np.sign(g.o) # Scale regularization applied to covariance eigenvalues or diagonal diag = np.diag(g.sigma) g.sigma -= reglambda np.sign(diag)[:,:, np.newaxis] def trainstep(gaussians, batchdata, lambdadssim=0.2, noisescale=1e-4): """Single training step.""" camerapose, gtimage = batchdata H, W = gtimage.shape[:2] pixelcoords = np.array(np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H))).T.reshape(-1, 2) # 1. Render distances = [np.linalg.norm(g.mu - camerapose.center) for g in gaussians] sortedindices = np.argsort(distances) sortedgaussians = [gaussians[i] for i in sortedindices] renderedimage = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) accumulatedalpha = np.zeros((H, W)) for g in sortedgaussians: projectedmu = projectpoint(g.mu, camerapose) if projectedmu is None: continue sigma2d = projectcovariance(g.sigma, camerapose, g.mu) sigmainv = np.linalg.inv(sigma2d) diff = pixelcoords - projectedmu mahal = np.sum(diff @ sigmainv diff, axis=-1) alpha = g.o np.exp(-0.5 mahal) alpha = np.clip(alpha, 0, 1).reshape(H, W) color = getshcolor(g.shcoeffs, camerapose.viewdir) transmittance = 1.0 - accumulatedalpha renderedimage += color alpha transmittance[:,:, np.newaxis] accumulatedalpha += alpha transmittance # 2. Loss l1loss = np.mean(np.abs(renderedimage - gtimage)) dssimloss = computedssim(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = (1 - lambdadssim) l1loss + lambdadssim dssimloss # 3. SGLD Update gradients = computegradients(loss, {'mu': [g.mu for g in gaussians], 'o': [g.o for g in gaussians], 'sigma': [g.sigma for g in gaussians]}) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): g.mu -= gradients['mu'][i] + np.random.normal(0, noisescale, g.mu.shape) g.o -= gradients['o'][i] + np.random.normal(0, noisescale) g.sigma -= gradients['sigma'][i] + np.random.normal(0, noisescale, g.sigma.shape) # 4. Relocation threshold = 0.01 live = [g for g in gaussians if g.o > threshold] dead = [g for g in gaussians if g.o <= threshold] for dg in dead: if not live: continue source = np.random.choice(live) # Relocate while preserving local rendering probability dg.mu = source.mu.copy() dg.sigma = source.sigma.copy() dg.o = source.o dg.shcoeffs = source.shcoeffs.copy() # 5. Regularization applyregularization(gaussians) return loss Parameters: \lambda{\text{D-SSIM}}: Weight for the D-SSIM loss component. Typical value: 0.2. Noise Scale: Standard deviation of the noise added in SGLD updates. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cloning Insufficiency: Cloning Gaussians only at their centers is insufficient to preserve the rendering probability distribution; the entire Gaussian's spatial extent must be considered to ensure the rendering remains equal. Initialization: The method provides robustness to initialization, though the MCMC chain may require more steps to converge from poor starting states. Precision: The exponential term in opacity calculation can lead to underflow for distant Gaussians. Clipping or masking Gaussians outside the view frustum is recommended. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS per step, but may require more steps for convergence due to the stochastic nature of SGLD. Memory Complexity: Same as 3DGS, storing N Gaussians. Strengths: Improved rendering quality, easy control over the number of Gaussians, and robustness to initialization. Removes the need for complex heuristics like cloning, splitting, and opacity resetting. When to use: When robustness to initialization is critical, or when manual densification heuristics are problematic. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of noise addition and relocation logic is prohibitive. This method reformulates 3D Gaussian Splatting by treating the set of 3D Gaussians as MCMC samples, converting conventional updates into SGLD updates. The work addresses issues with poor-quality renderings and reliance on good initialization in existing methods by replacing engineered cloning and splitting strategies with probabilistic state transitions and regularization. 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, https://ubc-vision.github.io/3dgs-mcmc/, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Deblur-3D-GS
body: Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting is a real-time deblurring framework that reconstructs sharp 3D scenes from blurry input images by manipulating the covariance matrices and means of 3D Gaussians using a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) during training. Unlike volumetric rendering-based methods like Deblur-NeRF which require seconds per image, this method uses differentiable rasterization to achieve real-time inference speeds exceeding 800 FPS while handling both defocus and camera motion blur. It addresses the sparse point clouds caused by blurry inputs through K-nearest-neighbor interpolation and depth-based pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of blurry images, camera poses, and an initial sparse point cloud obtained from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: A set of optimized 3D Gaussians (position x, rotation r, scale s, opacity \sigma, spherical harmonics coefficients) that represent the sharp scene. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting data structures: 3D Gaussian Gj: Characterized by position xj \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \sigmaj \in \mathbb{R}, rotation rj (quaternion), scale sj \in \mathbb{R}^3, and spherical harmonics coefficients. MLP F\theta: A neural network with 4 layers. The first 3 layers are shared (64 hidden units, ReLU activation, Xavier initialization). The last 3 layers are single-layer heads producing deltas \delta x, \delta r, \delta s. Point Cloud P: A set of 3D points with associated colors, initially from SfM. Positional Encoding: Inputs to the MLP are processed using positional encoding \gamma(p): \gamma(p) = \big (\sin (2^k\pi p), \cos (2^k \pi p)\big){k=0}^{L-1} where L is the number of frequencies. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compensation for Sparse Point Cloud: After N{st} training iterations, add extra points to compensate for sparse point clouds: Sample Np points from a uniform distribution U(\alpha, \beta), where \alpha and \beta are the min/max position values of the existing point cloud P. For each new point p: Find K nearest neighbors P{knn} from P. Discard neighbors if the distance to p exceeds threshold td. If valid neighbors remain, interpolate color pc from them. Add p with color pc to P. Prune Gaussians based on their position to keep more Gaussians on the far plane, using a pruning threshold multiplier wp. 2. Blur Modeling via MLP (Training Only): The MLP F\theta transforms Gaussian attributes to simulate blur. The specific transformation depends on the blur type. Defocus Blur: The MLP outputs scaling deltas (\delta rj, \delta sj): (\delta rj, \delta sj) = F\theta \Big (\gamma (xj), rj, sj, \gamma (v) \Big) where v is the viewing direction. Transform the attributes to obtain \hat{r}j and \hat{s}j: \hat {r}j=rj\cdot \text {min}(1.0, ~\lambda s \delta rj + (1-\lambda s)) \hat {s}j=sj\cdot \text {min}(1.0, ~\lambda s \delta sj + (1-\lambda s)) where \lambdas is a scaling factor for optimization stability. The transformed Gaussian is G(xj, \hat{r}j, \hat{s}j). Camera Motion Blur: The MLP outputs M sets of offsets (\delta xj^{(i)}, \delta rj^{(i)}, \delta sj^{(i)}) for i=1 \dots M: \{(\delta xj^{(i)}, \delta rj^{(i)}, \delta sj^{(i)})\}{i=1}^{M} = F\theta \Big (\gamma (xj), rj, sj, \gamma (v) \Big) Compute transformed attributes for each set i: \hat{x}j^{(i)} = xj + \lambdap \delta xj^{(i)} \hat{r}j^{(i)} = rj \cdot \text{min}(1.0, \lambdas \delta rj^{(i)} + (1-\lambdas)) \hat{s}j^{(i)} = sj \cdot \text{min}(1.0, \lambdas \delta sj^{(i)} + (1-\lambdas)) where \lambdap scales the position offset. Rasterize M clean images Ii from the M sets of transformed Gaussians: Ii = \texttt{Rasterize}(\{G(\hat{x}j^{(i)}, \hat{r}j^{(i)}, \hat{s}j^{(i)})\}{j=1}^{NG}) Average them to simulate the blurred image: Ib = \frac {1}{M}\sum {i=1}^{M} Ii 3. Optimization: Optimize the MLP parameters \theta and the 3D Gaussian positions x using the Adam optimizer. The loss is computed between the rendered image Ib (for motion blur) or Ii (for defocus blur) and the ground truth blurry image. 4. Inference: The MLP F\theta is not activated. The scene is rendered using the original, untransformed Gaussians G(xj, rj, sj). This ensures real-time rendering and sharp images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(p, L=10): """Computes positional encoding: gamma(p) = (sin(2^k pi p), cos(2^k pi p)) for k=0..L-1.""" freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(L) # p shape: (..., 3), freqbands shape: (L,) angles = p[..., np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] freqbands[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:, np.newaxis] np.pi enc = np.concatenate([np.sin(angles), np.cos(angles)], axis=-2) return enc.reshape(enc.shape[:-2] + (-1,)) def mlpforward(theta, x, r, s, v, L=10): """Standard 4-layer MLP forward pass. First 3 layers shared (64 units, ReLU, Xavier init), last 3 are single-layer heads.""" xenc = positionalencoding(x, L) venc = positionalencoding(v, L) inputvec = np.concatenate([xenc, r, s, venc]) h = inputvec for layer in theta[:3]: h = np.maximum(0, h @ layer.W + layer.b) deltax = h @ theta[3].W + theta[3].b deltar = h @ theta[4].W + theta[4].b deltas = h @ theta[5].W + theta[5].b return deltax, deltar, deltas def rasterize(gaussians, xhat=None, rhat=None, shat=None): """Differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians to an image.""" # Standard 3D-GS rasterization: project to 2D, sort by depth, alpha-blend return np.zeroslike(gaussians[0].color) def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): """Computes reconstruction loss between rendered and ground truth image.""" return np.mean(np.abs(rendered - groundtruth)) def updateparameters(loss, params, optimizerstate): """Adam optimizer step for MLP parameters and Gaussian positions.""" # Standard Adam update step return optimizerstate def addextrapoints(P, Np, K, td): """Adds extra points to point cloud P to compensate for sparsity.""" positions = np.array([p[0] for p in P]) alpha = np.min(positions, axis=0) beta = np.max(positions, axis=0) newpoints = np.random.uniform(alpha, beta, size=(Np, 3)) for ppos in newpoints: dists = np.linalg.norm(positions - ppos, axis=1) kindices = np.argsort(dists)[:K] validneighbors = [] for idx in kindices: if dists[idx] < td: validneighbors.append(P[idx]) if len(validneighbors) > 0: avgcolor = np.mean([n[1] for n in validneighbors], axis=0) P.append((ppos, avgcolor)) positions = np.vstack([positions, ppos]) return P def deblur3dgstrainingstep(gaussians, blurryimage, camerapose, blurtype='defocus', theta=None, lambdas=1e-2, lambdap=1e-2, M=5): """One training step.""" renderedimage = None for j in range(len(gaussians)): xj = gaussians[j].position rj = gaussians[j].rotation sj = gaussians[j].scale v = camerapose.viewdirection gammax = positionalencoding(xj) gammav = positionalencoding(v) if blurtype == 'defocus': deltar, deltas, = mlpforward(theta, xj, rj, sj, v) scaler = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltar + (1 - lambdas)) scales = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltas + (1 - lambdas)) rhat = rj scaler shat = sj scales renderedimage = rasterize(gaussians, rhat=rhat, shat=shat) elif blurtype == 'motion': images = [] deltas = mlpforward(theta, xj, rj, sj, v) # deltas contains M sets of (deltax, deltar, deltas) for i in range(M): deltax = deltas[0][i] deltar = deltas[1][i] deltas = deltas[2][i] xhat = xj + lambdap deltax scaler = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltar + (1 - lambdas)) scales = np.minimum(1.0, lambdas deltas + (1 - lambdas)) rhat = rj scaler shat = sj scales imgi = rasterize(gaussians, xhat=xhat, rhat=rhat, shat=shat) images.append(imgi) renderedimage = np.mean(images, axis=0) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, blurryimage) updateparameters(loss, theta, gaussians) return loss def deblur3dgsinference(gaussians, camerapose): """Inference: Render sharp image using original Gaussians.""" image = rasterize(gaussians) return image Parameters: \lambdas: Scaling factor for defocus blur deltas (\delta r, \delta s). Value: 10^{-2}. \lambdap: Scaling factor for motion blur position offset (\delta x). Value: 10^{-2}. Np: Number of additional points. Value: Up to 200,000, proportional to point cloud extent. td: Distance threshold for neighbor validity. Value: 2. K: Number of neighbors for interpolation. Value: 4. MLP Learning Rate: 10^{-3}. Position Learning Rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-3}. MLP Hidden Units: 64. M: Number of sets for motion blur. Value: 5. N{st}: Iterations to start adding extra points. Value: 2,500. Pruning threshold multiplier wp: Value: 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Point Clouds: Blurry inputs cause SfM to fail, leading to sparse point clouds, especially at far distances. The method compensates by adding points via KNN interpolation and pruning based on depth to retain far-plane Gaussians. Inference Speed: The MLP is strictly disabled during inference. Activating it would degrade performance and is not part of the standard 3D-GS pipeline. Precision: The min operation clips the scaling factors to 1.0 to prevent excessive dispersion. Time Complexity: Training involves MLP forward/backward passes and rasterization of M sets of Gaussians for motion blur, making it more expensive than standard 3D-GS training. Inference is identical to standard 3D-GS, offering real-time performance. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the MLP parameters and, for motion blur training, rendering M images per step. Inference memory is standard 3D-GS. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art PSNR and SSIM on real camera motion blur and defocus blur datasets. Rendering speed exceeds 800 FPS (e.g., 961 FPS on the 'Girl' scene). Strengths: Real-time inference; handles both defocus and motion blur; works with sparse SfM point clouds from blurry images. Limitations: Requires training with the MLP; performance depends on the quality of the initial SfM point cloud (mitigated by point addition). Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting was proposed by B. Lee et al. in 2024. It is the first deblurring algorithm for 3D-GS, addressing the limitations of NeRF-based deblurring methods (like Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, PDRF) which rely on volumetric rendering and are slow. It builds on the 3D-GS framework. Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73636-08, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Augmented Radiance Field
head: Error-Driven Gaussian Supplementation, Enhanced Gaussian Splatting, Error-Driven Compensation Strategy, Gaussian supplementation strategy
body: Augmented Radiance Field is a post-enhancement framework that improves 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes by adding Gaussian kernels with view-dependent opacity to explicitly model specular components. It solves the problem that standard spherical harmonics (SH) cannot decouple diffuse and specular radiance, leading to poor reconstruction of sharp highlights and material artifacts. Unlike standard 3DGS which assigns SH coefficients to every primitive, this method uses distinct primitives for diffuse and specular components, avoiding the memory and stability issues of high-order SH. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained 3DGS scene (set of 3D Gaussian primitives with position, scale, rotation, SH color, and opacity) and a set of training views. Output: An augmented radiance field containing the original 3D Gaussians plus a set of newly added "enhanced" Gaussians with view-dependent opacity. Data Structures: The method introduces a new type of Gaussian primitive. While the original 3DGS primitives retain their standard attributes, the new primitives are initialized in 2D image space and mapped to 3D. Enhanced Gaussian Attributes: Position (\mathbf{p}): 3D world coordinates. Scale (\mathbf{s}): 3D vector defining the extent. Rotation (\mathbf{q}): 4D quaternion. Opacity (\alpha): Scalar, modulated by a view-dependent function. View-dependent Opacity Parameters: Parameters controlling the "opacity lobe" (maximum extent and sharpness), adapted from the Phong shading model. Color: Standard SH or RGB, typically handled by the diffuse component or shared with the base primitive it supplements. Method Steps: 1. Screen-Space Initialization: Render the current image using the existing 3DGS primitives. Calculate the per-pixel rendering loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS) between the rendered image and the ground truth. Allocate new 2D Gaussian kernels in screen space. The number of new Gaussians is fixed at 10% of the current count of existing Gaussians. Allocation is proportional to the loss values per viewpoint; regions with higher residuals receive more new Gaussians. 2. Screen-Space Optimization: Optimize only the parameters of these additional 2D Gaussians (position, scale, rotation, opacity parameters) to minimize the rendering loss in image space. The original 3D Gaussian parameters are frozen during this phase. Prune 2D Gaussians with insufficient opacity or excessively small scales. 3. Inverse Projection (Back-Projection): Map the optimized 2D Gaussians from image space to world space. This is the inverse of the standard Gaussian Splatting projection. This projection is executed in parallel on the CPU. The result is a set of 3D enhanced Gaussians positioned in regions of high reconstruction error. 4. Joint Optimization: Integrate the new 3D enhanced Gaussians into the scene. Freezing Strategy: Freeze the position, scale, rotation, and color (SH coefficients) of the original Gaussian primitives. Make the opacity of the original Gaussian primitives optimizable (using SparseAdam) to prevent over-occlusion by the new, potentially shallower Gaussians. Apply full parameter optimization (position, scale, rotation, opacity, view-dependent parameters) to the newly added enhanced Gaussians (using Adam). Use the differentiable rendering pipeline to jointly optimize all parameters, minimizing the photometric loss. 5. Incremental Densification: The process is iterative. Every 200 iterations, add new Gaussians equal to 20% of the current total count. Repeat steps 1-4 for each increment. Total optimization iterations are set to 30 times the size of the training dataset. 6. Fine-Tuning: After sufficient kernels are incorporated, perform an additional 1,000 fine-tuning steps with all parameters (including original opacities and new enhanced Gaussians) jointly optimized. View-Dependent Opacity Model: The enhanced Gaussians use a learnable opacity function adapted from the Phong shading paradigm. The opacity \alpha is modulated by the viewing direction \mathbf{v} and the surface normal \mathbf{n} (or equivalent reflection vector). The function is controlled by adjustable parameters for the opacity lobe's maximum extent and sharpness, allowing it to model various specular highlight types. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def augmentedradiancefield(scenegaussians, trainingviews, datasetsize): """ Augments a pre-trained 3DGS scene with view-dependent opacity Gaussians. Args: scenegaussians: List of original 3D Gaussian primitives. trainingviews: List of training camera poses and images. datasetsize: Number of training views. Returns: Augmented scene with original and enhanced Gaussians. """ # Hyperparameters from initialratio = 0.10 incrementratio = 0.20 incrementinterval = 200 totaliterations = 30 datasetsize finetuningsteps = 1000 enhancedgaussians = [] allgaussians = list(scenegaussians) # Phase 1: Incremental Densification & Optimization for iteration in range(totaliterations): # 1. Render and compute loss per view losses = [] for view in trainingviews: img = render3dgs(allgaussians, view) losses.append(computeloss(img, view.gtimage)) # 2. Allocate new 2D Gaussians in screen space if iteration == 0: numnew2d = int(len(scenegaussians) initialratio) elif iteration % incrementinterval == 0: numnew2d = int(len(allgaussians) incrementratio) else: numnew2d = 0 if numnew2d > 0: new2dgaussians = allocate2dgaussians(losses, numnew2d, trainingviews) # 3. Optimize 2D Gaussians in image space for in range(incrementinterval): for view in trainingviews: img = render2dgaussians(view, new2dgaussians, scenegaussians) loss = computeloss(img, view.gtimage) optimize2dgaussians(new2dgaussians, loss) # 4. Prune 2D Gaussians new2dgaussians = prune2dgaussians(new2dgaussians) # 5. Inverse projection to 3D (parallel on CPU) new3dgaussians = inverseproject2dto3d(new2dgaussians, trainingviews) enhancedgaussians.extend(new3dgaussians) allgaussians.extend(new3dgaussians) # 6. Joint Optimization (every iteration) for view in trainingviews: img = render3dgs(allgaussians, view) loss = computeloss(img, view.gtimage) updateoriginalopacity(scenegaussians, loss) updateenhancedgaussians(enhancedgaussians, loss) # Phase 2: Fine-Tuning for in range(finetuningsteps): for view in trainingviews: img = render3dgs(allgaussians, view) loss = computeloss(img, view.gtimage) updateoriginalopacity(scenegaussians, loss) updateenhancedgaussians(enhancedgaussians, loss) return allgaussians def render3dgs(gaussians, view): """Differentiable 3D Gaussian rasterization returning an RGB image.""" return rasterize3dgaussians(gaussians, view.cameramatrix) def render2dgaussians(view, enhanced2d, basegaussians): """Renders base 3D Gaussians as background, then composites 2D screen-space Gaussians on top.""" bg = render3dgs(basegaussians, view) return composite2dgaussians(bg, enhanced2d, view.projectionmatrix) def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): """Computes photometric loss (e.g., L1 or LPIPS).""" return torch.mean(torch.abs(rendered - groundtruth)) def allocate2dgaussians(losses, count, views): """Samples 'count' 2D Gaussian centers in screen space, weighted by per-view loss.""" weights = torch.tensor(losses) / torch.sum(losses) selectedviews = torch.multinomial(weights, count, replacement=True) return [create2dgaussian(view) for view in selectedviews] def optimize2dgaussians(gaussians, loss): """Gradient descent step for 2D Gaussian parameters.""" loss.backward() for g in gaussians: g.position -= 0.01 g.position.grad g.scale -= 0.01 g.scale.grad g.opacity -= 0.01 g.opacity.grad def prune2dgaussians(gaussians): """Removes Gaussians with opacity below threshold or scale below minimum.""" return [g for g in gaussians if g.opacity > 0.01 and max(g.scale) > 0.001] def inverseproject2dto3d(gaussians2d, views): """Back-projects 2D screen-space Gaussians to 3D world coordinates using camera intrinsics/extrinsics.""" gaussians3d = [] for g in gaussians2d: p3d = unprojectscreentoworld(g.position2d, g.scale2d, g.cameramatrix) gaussians3d.append(create3dgaussian(p3d, g.scale, g.rotation, g.opacity, g.viewparams)) return gaussians3d def updateoriginalopacity(gaussians, loss): """Sparse gradient update for opacity of visible original primitives.""" loss.backward() for g in gaussians: if g.visible: g.opacity -= 0.01 g.opacity.grad def updateenhancedgaussians(gaussians, loss): """Full parameter gradient update for enhanced primitives.""" loss.backward() for g in gaussians: g.position -= 0.01 g.position.grad g.scale -= 0.01 g.scale.grad g.rotation -= 0.01 g.rotation.grad g.opacity -= 0.01 g.opacity.grad g.viewparams -= 0.01 g.viewparams.grad Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundancy: Naively assigning extra parameters to every primitive causes significant redundancy because specular highlights are sparse. The method avoids this by only adding enhanced Gaussians where needed. Over-occlusion: New Gaussians may have shallower depths than pre-existing ones, causing over-occlusion. This is mitigated by making original opacities optimizable. Visibility Constraints: Surface Gaussians are only observable within their outward-facing hemisphere, making SH inefficient for view-dependent cases. The enhanced Gaussians handle this by being view-dependent. Precision: The inverse projection step requires careful handling of depth and camera matrices to avoid artifacts. Time Complexity: The method adds an incremental densification phase. The total iterations are 30 \times N (where N is dataset size), plus 1,000 fine-tuning steps. Each iteration involves rendering and optimization. The inverse projection is done in parallel on CPU. Memory Complexity: Adds 10% of new Gaussians initially, increasing by 20% every 200 iterations. This is significantly less memory than using high-order SH for all primitives. Performance: Mip-NeRF 360: PSNR 28.96, SSIM 0.849 (with MCMC, sh=3). Tanks&Temples: PSNR 25.06, SSIM 0.872 (with MCMC, sh=3). Deep Blending: PSNR 30.22, SSIM 0.909 (with MCMC, sh=3). NeRF Synthetic: PSNR 34.03, SSIM 0.970 (with MCMC, sh=3). Strengths: Decouples diffuse and specular components; works with low-order SH (sh=2 or sh=3); plug-and-play post-enhancement; captures fine specular spots. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained scene; adds complexity to the rendering pipeline; may not be necessary for rough surfaces with limited illumination. Origin: Proposed by Yixin Yang, Bojian Wu, Yang Zhou, and Hui Huang from Shenzhen University and Tencent Games. Paper: "Augmented Radiance Field: A General Framework for Enhanced Gaussian Splatting". Date: February 23, 2026 (arXiv:2602.19916v1). Context: Addresses the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting's reliance on spherical harmonics for color encoding, which cannot separate diffuse and specular components effectively. Inspired by Phong shading. Augmented Radiance Field: A General Framework for Enhanced Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.19916, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Frequency Regularization for Densification
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Progressive Frequency Regularization, FreGS
body: Frequency Regularization for Densification (FreGS) addresses the over-reconstruction issue in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where high-variance image regions are covered by a few large Gaussians, leading to blur and artifacts. Unlike standard 3D-GS which relies solely on pixel-wise L1 loss in the spatial domain, FreGS minimizes the discrepancy between the frequency spectrum of the rendered image and the ground truth in the Fourier space. This approach significantly increases pixel gradients within over-reconstruction regions, enabling a coarse-to-fine densification process guided by progressive frequency annealing. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sparse point cloud generated by Structure-from-Motion (SfM); ground truth images I for the training views. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (covariance \Sigma, center p, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients c) with densified geometry. Data Structures 3D Gaussian: Defined by covariance matrix \Sigma, center position p, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c. The covariance matrix \Sigma is parameterized by a scaling matrix and a rotation matrix for differentiable optimization. Frequency Spectrum: Complex-valued arrays representing the amplitude F(u, v) and phase \angle F(u, v) of the image in the Fourier domain. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize a set of 3D Gaussians from the sparse point cloud generated by Structure-from-Motion. 2. Rendering: Splat the 3D Gaussians to obtain 2D Gaussians and render the image \hat{I} using standard \alpha-blending. The color C of a pixel is computed by blending N ordered 2D Gaussians overlapping the pixel: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci and \alphai are derived from the i-th 2D Gaussian's covariance matrix, spherical harmonics coefficients, and opacity. 3. Frequency Transformation: Generate the frequency spectrum \hat{F} of the rendered image \hat{I} and the frequency spectrum F of the ground truth I by applying a Fourier transformation. 4. Discrepancy Computation: Compute the discrepancy in amplitude F(u, v) and phase \angle F(u, v) in the Fourier space between the rendered and ground truth spectra. 5. Filtering: Apply a low-pass filter Hl and a dynamic high-pass filter Hh to extract low-to-high frequency components progressively. 6. Densification: Perform Gaussian densification guided by the frequency regularization: Under-reconstruction: Clone Gaussians in regions with missing geometric features. Over-reconstruction: Divide large Gaussians into multiple smaller Gaussians in large high-variance regions. 7. Frequency Annealing: Use frequency annealing to progressively regularize from low-frequency signals to high-frequency signals, achieving coarse-to-fine Gaussian densification. Low-frequency signals encode large-scale structures (easier to model), while high-frequency signals encode local details (harder to model). 8. Termination: Gaussian densification is terminated after the 15,000th iteration, consistent with the standard 3D-GS protocol. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frequencyregularizationdensification(gaussians, groundtruthimages, trainingiterations=15000): """ Implements FreGS densification strategy. """ for iteration in range(1, trainingiterations + 1): renderedimages = [] for viewidx in range(len(groundtruthimages)): # Standard 3DGS splatting and alpha-blending renderedimages.append(np.zeroslike(groundtruthimages[0])) totalfreqloss = 0.0 for renderedimg, gtimg in zip(renderedimages, groundtruthimages): Fhat = np.fft.fft2(renderedimg) Fgt = np.fft.fft2(gtimg) Ahat = np.abs(Fhat) Phihat = np.angle(Fhat) Agt = np.abs(Fgt) Phigt = np.angle(Fgt) amploss = np.mean(np.abs(Ahat - Agt)) phaseloss = np.mean(np.abs(Phihat - Phigt)) totalfreqloss += amploss + phaseloss # Frequency annealing applies low-pass and dynamic high-pass filters progressively # Exact schedule parameters and filter kernel sizes are not given in the sources. freqspectrum = Fhat y, x = np.ogrid[:freqspectrum.shape[0],:freqspectrum.shape[1]] centery, centerx = freqspectrum.shape[0] / 2, freqspectrum.shape[1] / 2 dist = np.sqrt((y - centery)2 + (x - centerx)2) cutoff = 0.5 # Schedule not provided in sources lowpassmask = (dist <= cutoff) highpassmask = (dist > cutoff) # Densification follows standard 3DGS protocol, guided by frequency regularization gradients # Cloning for under-reconstruction, splitting for over-reconstruction # Standard gradient computation and optimizer step pass return gaussians Parameters Training Iterations: 15,000. Frequency Annealing Schedule: Progressive from low to high frequency. Exact schedule parameters (e.g., start/end frequencies, annealing rate) are not given in the sources. Filters: Low-pass filter Hl and dynamic high-pass filter Hh. Specific cutoff frequencies or kernel sizes are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Over-reconstruction: The primary target of FreGS is the case where high-variance regions are covered by few large Gaussians, causing blur. Under-reconstruction: Regions with missing geometric features are handled by cloning. Precision: The method relies on Fourier transforms, which may be sensitive to image boundaries and padding. Computational Cost: Computing Fourier transforms and frequency discrepancies adds overhead to the training loop. Details not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing frequency spectra for rendered and ground truth images. Measured Performance: Experiments on benchmarks like Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks-and-Temples show high-quality Gaussian densification and alleviation of over-reconstruction. Limitations: The specific implementation details of the filters and annealing schedule are not provided, making exact performance scaling difficult to predict. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited, as the frequency domain operations add overhead. History: Builds on the observation that NeRF variants have explored frequency space to overcome neural network limitations in learning high-frequency information. name: Error-Guided Redistribution
body: Error-Guided Redistribution is a family of training optimization strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that addresses reconstruction artifacts by dynamically adjusting the spatial distribution of Gaussian primitives based on rendering errors or gradient statistics. Unlike standard densification which adds primitives globally, these methods specifically target regions with persistent coarse-scale errors or "hard" gradients, either by reallocating a fixed budget of Gaussians, growing defective primitives, or controlling density via online sparse statistics. All methods in this family operate during the training phase to refine the Gaussian set \{Gi\} without altering the inference-stage alpha-blending rendering pipeline. The core mechanism involves identifying Gaussians that contribute to persistent reconstruction errors or possess significant individual view-space gradients, and then modifying their parameters or positions to improve reconstruction fidelity. Key shared technical components include: 1. Error/Gradient Identification: Methods compute metrics to identify Gaussians that contribute to high rendering error or possess significant individual view-space gradients, often using per-pixel or per-Gaussian statistics such as blending weights wi. 2. Primitive Modification: Identified Gaussians undergo modification, which may involve growth via duplication and perturbation to recover missing details [10590-hard-gaussian-splatting.md], reallocation of low-contribution Gaussians to high-error regions while preserving the total Gaussian count, or dynamic splitting/pruning based on percentile thresholds of accumulated error statistics [15692-error-driven-gaussian-density-control.md]. 3. Optimizer Reset: When new Gaussians are created or existing ones are significantly modified (e.g., relocated), their optimizer states (momentum and variance) are reset to allow for rapid convergence in the new configuration. 4. Fixed Budget or Adaptive Count: Variants maintain either a fixed number of Gaussians N during reallocation, or allow the count to increase/decrease via densification and pruning [10590-hard-gaussian-splatting.md, 15692-error-driven-gaussian-density-control.md]. Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) is a training-phase densification strategy that addresses artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by growing "hard Gaussians" identified via multi-view significant positional gradients and rendering errors, rather than relying on averaged gradients. It differs from siblings by explicitly decoupling the identification of hard Gaussians into Positional Gradient Driven HGS (PGHGS) and Rendering Error Guided HGS (REHGS). Choose it when standard gradient averaging smooths out individual large gradients and local rendering errors, hindering the growth of defective Gaussians that cause blurring or needle-like artifacts. Supplementary Point Addition is a densification technique designed to compensate for the sparsity of 3D Gaussians at the far end of scenes with large depth of field, where Structure-from-Motion extraction is poor due to defocus blur. It differs from siblings by explicitly injecting synthetic points into empty or sparse regions after a fixed number of training iterations, rather than relying on gradient-based densification or geometric replication on tangent planes. Choose it when SfM point clouds are too sparse in distant regions to support accurate reconstruction. Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR) is a training-stage module that redistributes a fixed budget of Gaussian primitives toward regions with persistent coarse-scale reconstruction errors, without increasing the total number of Gaussians. It differs from siblings by preserving the total Gaussian count N by relocating existing primitives, serving as a stabilization strategy that redirects allocation toward persistent coarse-scale errors. Choose it when densification has already run and the primitive count is fixed, but coarse-scale rendering quality remains poor. Error-Driven Gaussian Density Control (EDC) is a training-phase strategy that dynamically allocates model capacity and removes redundant primitives by accumulating and leveraging per-Gaussian statistics corresponding to sparse pixel errors. It differs from siblings by relying on online sparse pixel statistics and percentile thresholds for adaptive density control, rather than post-hoc dense error maps or fixed reallocation budgets. Choose it when computational complexity must be reduced compared to dense error map approaches while improving reconstruction fidelity in challenging regions. Definition: ACO-EGR is a unified framework that integrates Adaptive-scale Color Offset (ACO) and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR) into a multi-scale 3DGS backbone to jointly address scale-dependent color mismatch and primitive-allocation imbalance. Steps: The framework augments a multi-scale 3DGS backbone with two training-stage modules: ACO adapts per-Gaussian color across rendering scales through scale-specific DC color offsets, while EGR refines post-densification Gaussian allocation by moving low-contribution Gaussians to high-error regions. Comparison: Unlike existing methods that keep fixed color and spatial allocation after densification, ACO-EGR adapts both Gaussian color and primitive allocation together. It improves rendering quality without modifying the inference-stage rendering process itself; it only changes the training/optimization of the Gaussian parameters. Definition: A strategy to add new 3D Gaussians to the map by identifying unobserved regions (holes) and regions with high rendering error, using opacity, color, and depth thresholds. Steps: Identify holes in unobserved regions by checking if rendered opacity falls below a threshold \tau{opa}; normalize depth error by rendered depth to compensate for scale and check if it exceeds \tau{depth}; add new Gaussians to the densified regions, projecting corresponding depths directly for depth images. Comparison: Unlike gradient-based densification, this method directly targets geometric holes and view-dependent rendering errors using explicit opacity and depth thresholds. The concept of error-guided redistribution in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged from the need to improve multi-scale rendering quality and address artifacts such as blurring and color mismatch that persist after standard densification. The foundational work on Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR) and its integration with Adaptive-scale Color Offset (ACO) was proposed in 2026 by the authors of "Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting". This work demonstrated that adapting Gaussian color and primitive allocation together improves scale-consistent 3DGS rendering on benchmarks like Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending, particularly at coarse scales. Subsequent variants, such as Hard Gaussian Splatting and Error-Driven Gaussian Density Control, have been developed to address specific limitations of gradient averaging and computational efficiency in sparse supervision settings. name: Hard Gaussian Splatting
head: REHGS, Rendering Error guided HGS, Rendering Error guided Hard Gaussian Splatting
body: Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) is a training-phase densification strategy that addresses artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by growing "hard Gaussians" identified via multi-view significant positional gradients and rendering errors, rather than relying on averaged gradients. It solves the problem where standard 3DGS averaging smooths out individual large gradients and local rendering errors, hindering the growth of defective Gaussians that cause blurring or needle-like artifacts. Unlike its siblings, HGS explicitly decouples the identification of hard Gaussians into two distinct mechanisms: Positional Gradient Driven HGS (PGHGS), which targets cross-view inconsistencies by analyzing the maximum individual view-space gradients, and Rendering Error Guided HGS (REHGS), which targets blurring artifacts by correlating potentially over-large Gaussians with local SSIM errors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The current set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, the set of training viewpoints \mathcal{V}, and the growth interval M. Outputs: A subset of hard Gaussians identified for densification. Data Structures: Gaussian Gi: Parameterized by mean vector \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3, and opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}. View-space Positional Gradient g{i,j}: The gradient of the rendering loss with respect to the mean \mui of Gaussian Gi under viewpoint j. Contribution Set Si: The set of pixels u in the current image where Gaussian Gi has the maximum contribution. Rendering Model: A 3D Gaussian Gi is splatted to a 2D Gaussian G{i,2D}. The pixel color c(u) is computed via alpha-blending: c(u) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci, \quad wi = \alphai G{i,2D}(u) \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak G{k,2D}(u)) where wi is the blending weight. Parameters: \tau{grad}: Gradient threshold for Gaussian growing (maintained same as in Scaffold-GS). M: Growing interval for Gaussian growing (maintained same as in Scaffold-GS). k: Index of the largest positional gradient used in PGHGS (set to 3). \lambda: Constant controlling the extent of excavation in PGHGS (set to 1.0). \tau{large}: Threshold to control the extent of potentially large areas for identifying potentially over-large Gaussians (set to 2 \times 10^{-4}). \tau{SSIM}: Threshold to judge rendering quality for identifying hard Gaussians via SSIM (set to 0.7). Algorithm Steps: The method operates during the training phase. For each growth interval of M iterations, the following steps are performed to identify hard Gaussians. 1. Compute View-space Positional Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi and each viewpoint j that observes Gi during the current growth interval M, compute the view-space positional gradient g{i,j} = \nabla{\mui} L. 2. Identify Hard Gaussians via PGHGS (Positional Gradient Driven): For each Gaussian Gi, collect the view-space positional gradients \{g{i,j}\} from all viewpoints j that observed it during the interval M. Sort these gradients by magnitude and select the k largest gradients. Find the minimum magnitude among these k largest gradients: min\gradi = \min(\mathcal{G}{i, top-k}). If min\gradi \ge \tau{grad}, classify Gi as a hard Gaussian candidate for PGHGS. This strategy exploits cross-view significant positional gradients to uncover hard Gaussians, alleviating rendering inconsistency across views. 3. Identify Hard Gaussians via REHGS (Rendering Error Guided): Step 3.1: Identify Potentially Over-Large Gaussians. For each pixel u in the current rendered image, compute its rendered index idx(u), identifying the Gaussian with maximum contribution: idx(u) = \arg \maxi wi Construct the contribution set Si for each Gaussian Gi: Si = \{ u \mid idx(u) = i, u \in P \} where P is the set of all pixels in the image. Identify Gi as a "potentially over-large" Gaussian if: \|Si\| > \tau{large} \|P\| where \|Si\| is the number of pixels in the set and \|P\| is the total number of pixels. Using only this condition results in false positives because low-textured areas and repetitive textures may also be described by large Gaussians. Step 3.2: Validate with Rendering Errors. For each potentially over-large Gaussian Gi: Project Gi into the current training viewpoint j to obtain the corresponding pixel u{i,j}. Compute the local Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) between the ground truth image Ij and the rendered image \hat{I}j at u{i,j}: SSIM(Ij, \hat{I}j)(u{i,j}). If SSIM(Ij, \hat{I}j)(u{i,j}) < \tau{SSIM}, classify Gi as a hard Gaussian candidate for REHGS. Ensure hard Gaussians are seen by at least two views during the M iterations to avoid unstable growth from single-view determination. 4. Densification: Union the sets of hard Gaussians identified by PGHGS and REHGS. Apply the standard 3DGS densification operation (splitting and cloning) to these hard Gaussians. Reset the optimizer states (momentum and variance) for the newly created or modified Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def identifyhardgaussians(gaussians, viewpoints, M, k, taugrad, taularge, taussim): """ Identifies hard Gaussians for densification based on PGHGS and REHGS criteria. """ hardgaussians = set() # --- PGHGS: Positional Gradient Driven --- for G in gaussians: viewgrads = [] for v in G.viewhistory: if v in G.gradhistory: gradvec = G.gradhistory[v] viewgrads.append(math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in gradvec))) if not viewgrads: continue viewgrads.sort(reverse=True) topkgrads = viewgrads[:k] if min(topkgrads) >= taugrad: hardgaussians.add(G) # --- REHGS: Rendering Error Guided --- P = allpixelcoordinates() renderedimage = renderscene(gaussians, viewpoints) groundtruth = getgroundtruth(viewpoints) contributioncounts = {G: 0 for G in gaussians} pixelmaxgaussian = {} for u in P: maxw = -1.0 maxG = None for G in gaussians: w = computeweight(G, u) if w > maxw: maxw = w maxG = G pixelmaxgaussian[u] = maxG if maxG is not None: contributioncounts[maxG] += 1 totalpixels = len(P) potentiallyoverlarge = [G for G, count in contributioncounts.items() if count > taularge totalpixels] for G in potentiallyoverlarge: errorviewscount = 0 for v in G.viewhistory: uij = projectgaussiantopixel(G, v) if uij is not None and uij in P: ssimval = computelocalssim(groundtruth[v], renderedimage[v], uij) if ssimval < taussim: errorviewscount += 1 if errorviewscount >= 2: hardgaussians.add(G) return hardgaussians def computeweight(G, u): # Computes blending weight wi = alphai Gi2D(u) return G.opacity evaluate2dgaussian(G, u) def evaluate2dgaussian(G, u): # Evaluates the projected 2D Gaussian at pixel u # Standard differentiable rasterization step return 1.0 def computelocalssim(imggt, imgpred, centerpixel): # Computes local SSIM over a sliding window centered at centerpixel return 0.5 def projectgaussiantopixel(G, v): # Projects 3D mean mui to 2D image coordinates for view v return (0, 0) def densifyhardgaussians(hardgaussians, gaussians, optimizer): """ Applies densification to hard Gaussians and resets optimizer states. """ newgaussians = [] for G in hardgaussians: children = splitandclone(G) newgaussians.extend(children) gaussians.extend(newgaussians) for G in newgaussians: optimizer.resetstate(G) return gaussians def splitandclone(G): # Standard 3DGS split/clone operation creating child Gaussians with perturbed means and scaled covariances return [] PGHGS (Positional Gradient driven Hard Gaussian Splatting) is a densification strategy that identifies "hard Gaussians" by analyzing multi-view positional gradients to alleviate cross-view rendering inconsistencies. Unlike standard methods that rely on averaged gradients which may obscure local errors, PGHGS selects Gaussians based on the magnitude of their largest individual view-space gradients, ensuring that regions with significant reconstruction errors are prioritized for growth. Time Complexity: The identification step requires computing view-space positional gradients for all Gaussians over M iterations, which is O(N \cdot V \cdot M) where N is the number of Gaussians and V is the number of views. The REHGS step requires rendering and computing SSIM for potentially over-large Gaussians, which adds overhead proportional to the number of such Gaussians and the number of views they are observed in. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradient history for each Gaussian over the growth interval M, increasing memory usage by O(N \cdot V) compared to standard 3DGS. Measured Performance: On the Tanks&Temples dataset, HGS achieves superior NVS results compared to standard 3DGS and other baselines. Specifically, for REHGS, varying \tau{SSIM} yields: \tau{SSIM}=0.6 gives PSNR 26.34, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.127; \tau{SSIM}=0.7 gives PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126; \tau{SSIM}=0.8 gives PSNR 26.39, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126. Strengths: Effectively resolves blurring and needle-like artifacts by targeting hard Gaussians that standard averaging misses. It can boost both explicit and neural Gaussian methods, showing generalization ability. Limitations: REHGS tends to find noticeable rendering errors but cannot detect some inconspicuous artifacts, which PGHGS probes better. Using only the potentially over-large condition results in false positives in low-textured or repetitive texture areas. When to use: Use when standard 3DGS exhibits strong spurious artifacts, blurring, or needle-like structures in challenging areas due to insufficient Gaussian growth. Hard Gaussian Splatting (HGS) was proposed to address the limitations of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in handling challenging areas where the average magnitude of view-space positional gradients fails to drive Gaussian growth. The method was introduced in the paper "Pushing Rendering Boundaries: Hard Gaussian Splatting". It operates during the training phase to refine the Gaussian set without altering the inference-stage alpha-blending rendering pipeline. The code is available at https://github.com/GhiXu/HGS. name: PGHGS
head: Positional Gradient driven HGS, Positional Gradient driven Hard Gaussian Splatting
body: PGHGS (Positional Gradient driven Hard Gaussian Splatting) is a densification strategy that identifies "hard Gaussians" by analyzing multi-view positional gradients to alleviate cross-view rendering inconsistencies. Unlike standard methods that rely on averaged gradients which may obscure local errors, PGHGS selects Gaussians based on the magnitude of their largest individual view-space gradients, ensuring that regions with significant reconstruction errors are prioritized for growth. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N Gaussians \{Gi\}, their current parameters, and the accumulated view-space positional gradients \{g{i,j}\} for each Gaussian Gi across M training iterations/views. Output: A subset of Gaussians identified as "hard Gaussians" to be densified (cloned/split) in the current growth interval. Data Structures Positional Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi, a list of gradients g{i,j} corresponding to different viewpoints j. The gradient g{i,j} is a vector in view space. Sorted Gradients: A sorted list \{g'{i,1}, \dots, g'{i,n}\} for each Gaussian, ordered by descending norm. Method Steps 1. Compute View-Space Positional Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi and each viewpoint j, compute the view-space positional gradient g{i,j} using the rendering error: g{i,j} = \frac{1}{||P||} \sum{u \in P} eu \frac{\partial Lj}{\partial \mu{i,j}} Where: Lj is the rendering loss under viewpoint j. \mu{i,j} is the pixel-space projection point of Gaussian Gi under viewpoint j. P is the set of total pixel coordinates. eu is the rendering error of pixel u. ||P|| is the number of pixels. The sources define this as the gradient of the average rendering error with respect to the view-space projection point. 2. Sort Gradients: For each Gaussian Gi, sort its n positional gradients across all views in descending order of their norms: \{g'{i,1}, \dots, g'{i,n}\} = \text{sort}{\downarrow}(g{i,1}, \dots, g{i,n}) Where g'{i,k} is the k-th largest positional gradient for Gaussian Gi. 3. Mine Hard Gaussians: A Gaussian Gi is selected as a hard Gaussian if its k-th largest positional gradient satisfies the threshold condition: ||g'{i,k}|| \ge \lambda \tau{grad} Where: k is the number of significant positional gradients considered in the growth interval. \lambda is a weight constant controlling the extent of excavation. \tau{grad} is the base gradient threshold. Parameters k: The rank of the gradient used for selection. Tested values are 1, 2, 3, 4. Lower k relaxes the criterion, producing more growing Gaussians. Higher k degrades metrics because PGHGS cannot mine hard Gaussians sufficiently when k is too large. \lambda: Weight for the threshold. Lower \lambda allows mining more hard Gaussians, improving rendering quality but reducing training efficiency. Higher \lambda degrades PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS while improving training efficiency. \tau{grad}: The gradient threshold. Lowering \tau{grad} to encourage more growth prioritizes well-reconstructed areas, introducing redundant Gaussians and failing to reduce artifacts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Lowering \tau{grad} prioritizes densifying well-reconstructed areas, which introduces redundant Gaussians and fails to reduce artifacts. Reducing k introduces noise that impairs PSNR but improves LPIPS, because LPIPS is evaluated through deep image features which have anti-noise ability. Increasing k degrades almost all rendering metrics. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def selecthardgaussians(gaussians, gradients, k, lambdaval, taugrad): """ Select hard Gaussians based on positional gradients. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with an 'id' attribute. gradients: Dict mapping gaussianid to list of gradient vectors (one per view). k: Integer, rank of gradient to check. lambdaval: Float, threshold weight. taugrad: Float, base gradient threshold. Returns: List of Gaussian objects identified as hard. """ hardgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Get gradients for this Gaussian across all views ggrads = gradients[g.id] # Sort gradients by norm in descending order sortedgrads = sorted(ggrads, key=lambda vec: math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in vec)), reverse=True) # Ensure we have at least k gradients; if not, use the largest available if len(sortedgrads) >= k: kthlargestgrad = sortedgrads[k-1] else: kthlargestgrad = sortedgrads[-1] # Check condition: ||g'i,k|| >= lambda taugrad if math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in kthlargestgrad)) >= lambdaval taugrad: hardgaussians.append(g) return hardgaussians An efficient variant of HGS that adaptively controls the number of hard Gaussians to balance rendering quality and efficiency. It counts the percentage of Gaussians selected by the original growing criterion (Eq. 4) in each growth interval, denoted as Q. During PGHGS, it chooses the top Q Gaussians as hard ones for growing based on the sorted positional gradients \{g'{i,k} | i = 1, \dots, N\}. Time and Memory Complexity Time: Sorting gradients for each Gaussian adds overhead proportional to O(N \cdot M \log M), where N is the number of Gaussians and M is the number of views/iterations. Lower \lambda increases the number of hard Gaussians, which increases training time due to more splatting and optimization. Memory: Requires storing positional gradients for each Gaussian across views. Measured Performance Tanks&Temples Ablation (k variation): k=1: PSNR 26.34, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.123. k=2: PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126. k=3: PSNR 26.26, SSIM 0.878, LPIPS 0.131. k=4: PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, LPIPS 0.126. Deep Blending Ablation (k variation): k=1: PSNR 30.31, SSIM 0.906, LPIPS 0.211. k=2: PSNR 30.39, SSIM 0.908, LPIPS 0.219. k=3: PSNR 30.40, SSIM 0.908, LPIPS 0.225. k=4: PSNR 30.19, SSIM 0.908, LPIPS 0.230. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Reduces cross-view rendering inconsistency by focusing on local errors rather than averages. Reducing k can improve LPIPS (due to anti-noise ability of deep features) though it may degrade PSNR. Limitations: Lowering \tau{grad} introduces redundant Gaussians in well-reconstructed areas. Increasing k degrades almost all rendering metrics. Higher \lambda improves efficiency but degrades quality. PGHGS was introduced in "Pushing Rendering Boundaries: Hard Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of standard positional gradients, which average errors over the entire image and fail to reflect local reconstruction errors, preventing Gaussians from growing in regions with larger local errors. Pushing Rendering Boundaries: Hard Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04826v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Supplementary Point Addition for Sparse Point Clouds
body: Supplementary Point Addition is a densification technique designed to compensate for the sparsity of 3D Gaussians at the far end of scenes with large depth of field, where Structure-from-Motion (SfM) extraction is poor due to defocus blur. It differs from its siblings by explicitly injecting synthetic points into empty or sparse regions after a fixed number of training iterations, rather than relying on gradient-based densification or geometric replication on tangent planes. Inputs: Existing point cloud P{\text{existing}} containing positions and colors. Current training iteration counter t. Hyperparameters: N{st} (start iteration), Np (target point count), K (KNN neighbor count), td (distance threshold). Outputs: Updated point cloud P{\text{new}} = P{\text{existing}} \cup P{\text{supp}}, where P{\text{supp}} contains the newly added points. Data Structures: P{\text{existing}}: List of points, each storing position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. P{\text{supp}}: List of new points with position \mathbf{x} and interpolated color \mathbf{c}p. Steps: 1. Check Start Condition: If current iteration t < N{st}, terminate without adding points. 2. Determine Bounds: Calculate the global minimum (\alpha) and maximum (\beta) coordinate values across all dimensions of P{\text{existing}}. 3. Sample Positions: Generate Np new points P{\text{raw}} by sampling each coordinate independently from a uniform distribution U(\alpha, \beta). 4. Interpolate Colors: For each new point \mathbf{x}{\text{new}} \in P{\text{raw}}, find the K-nearest neighbors (P{\text{knn}}) within P{\text{existing}} based on Euclidean distance, and assign the interpolated color \mathbf{c}p from P{\text{knn}}. 5. Filter by Distance: For each new point \mathbf{x}{\text{new}}, compute its distance d{\text{min}} to the nearest neighbor in P{\text{existing}}. If d{\text{min}} > td, discard \mathbf{x}{\text{new}}; otherwise, add it to P{\text{supp}}. 6. Merge: Update the point cloud: P{\text{new}} = P{\text{existing}} \cup P{\text{supp}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def supplementarypointaddition(existingpoints, currentiteration, Nst, Np, K, td): """ Adds supplementary points to the existing point cloud if the current iteration has reached the start threshold Nst. Args: existingpoints: List of dicts with 'pos' (list [3]) and 'color' (list [3]). currentiteration: Integer, current training step. Nst: Integer, start iteration for adding points. Np: Integer, number of points to sample. K: Integer, number of neighbors for KNN color interpolation. td: Float, distance threshold to discard points. Returns: Updated list of points. """ import random # Step 1: Check Start Condition if currentiteration < Nst: return existingpoints # Step 2: Determine global bounds α and β positions = [p['pos'] for p in existingpoints] globalmin = min(min(p[i] for p in positions) for i in range(3)) globalmax = max(max(p[i] for p in positions) for i in range(3)) # Step 3: Sample positions uniformly within the bounding range newpositions = [[random.uniform(globalmin, globalmax) for in range(3)] for in range(Np)] newpoints = [] for xnew in newpositions: # Step 4: Find K nearest neighbors and interpolate color distances = [((xnew[0]-p['pos'][0])2 + (xnew[1]-p['pos'][1])2 + (xnew[2]-p['pos'][2])2)0.5 for p in existingpoints] sortedindices = sorted(range(len(distances)), key=lambda k: distances[k]) kindices = sortedindices[:K] kcolors = [existingpoints[idx]['color'] for idx in kindices] # Uniform averaging is used as the source does not specify the interpolation formula. cp = [sum(c[i] for c in kcolors) / K for i in range(3)] # Step 5: Check distance threshold mindist = distances[kindices[0]] if mindist <= td: newpoints.append({'pos': xnew, 'color': cp}) # Step 6: Merge return existingpoints + newpoints Parameters: N{st}: The iteration number at which supplementary point addition begins. Value: 2,500. Np: The number of supplementing points. Value: Proportional to the extent of the point cloud, at most 200,000. K: The number of neighbors for KNN interpolation. Value: 4. td: The minimum distance threshold for discarding points. Value: 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Point Cloud: If P{\text{existing}} is empty, bounds \alpha, \beta are undefined. The method assumes a non-empty SfM cloud exists as a prerequisite. Fixed Threshold: The distance threshold td=2 is a fixed value defined in the source. Its unit depends on the scene scale, but the source does not specify dynamic scaling adjustments. Color Interpolation: The source cites KNN [29] but does not specify the interpolation formula. A geometry-only initialization augmentation that replicates points on local tangent planes, targeting sparsely seeded regions peripherally. It is deterministic and relies on geometric relationships rather than uniform sampling. Uses a continuous neural radiance field (MLP) to predict density and position for filling large voids where no initial point cloud exists, differing from the uniform sampling approach. Time Complexity: O(Np \cdot N{\text{existing}}) for naive nearest-neighbor search, or O(Np \log N{\text{existing}}) with spatial indexing. Memory Complexity: O(Np) for storing the new points. Performance: The method is applied once after N{st}=2,500 iterations. It increases the primitive count by up to 200,000 points. Strengths: Effectively compensates for sparsity in defocus blurry scenes where SfM fails at far distances. Limitations: Adds points uniformly, which may not align perfectly with scene geometry compared to tangent-plane methods. The fixed threshold td=2 is scene-scale dependent but not dynamically adjusted in the source. When to Use: Defocus blurry scenes with large depth of field where SfM extraction is poor at the far end. When Not to Use: Scenes with clear SfM initialization, as the technique is specifically designed to compensate for poor extraction. The method was introduced in the context of Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting to address the issue of sparse point clouds in defocus blurry scenes. Standard SfM techniques struggle to extract points on the far end of scenes with large depth of field, leading to incomplete 3D Gaussian representations. The technique is part of a broader effort to improve initialization for 3DGS in challenging imaging conditions. name: Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART)
head: DART (Distance-Aware Replication and Training), distance-aware augmentation
body: Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART) is a geometry-only initialization augmentation for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enriches the Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud by replicating points on local tangent planes, specifically targeting sparsely seeded regions in the scene periphery. Unlike depth-based or learned enrichment methods, DART is deterministic and relies solely on the geometric relationship between points and the scene center, adding coverage where SfM extraction is typically poor without modifying the rasterizer or pruning criteria. It serves as a precursor to densification strategies like Age-Gated Densification (AGE), providing a denser initial seed that improves fidelity in sparse areas at the cost of increased primitive count and training time. DART operates as a single, pre-optimization pass over the input SfM point cloud. It does not use depth maps, learned models, or normal estimation. Instead, it constructs a local tangent frame for each point and samples new points on a disk within that plane, where the disk's radius scales with the point's distance from the scene center. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N SfM points P = \{pi\}{i=1}^N, where each pi has a 3D position \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: An augmented set of points P', which includes the original points and newly replicated points. Data Structures: The SfM points are stored as a list or array of 3D coordinates. No persistent data structures are required beyond the temporary storage of the new points during the augmentation phase. Parameters: m: Replication multiplier. Controls the number of extra samples drawn per SfM point. Typical value: m=10 (conservative setting for sparse outdoor scenes). Range swept: \{1, 3, 5, 7, 10\}. \rho{\min}: Minimum density threshold for replication. Value: 0.008. \rho{\max}: Maximum density threshold for replication. Value: 0.04. K{nn}: Number of nearest neighbors used for density estimation. Value: 20. Algorithm Steps: 1. Estimate Scene Center: Compute a robustly estimated scene center \mathbf{c}. The exact method for robust estimation is not specified in the sources. 2. Compute Distances: For each SfM point pi with position \mathbf{x}i, compute its distance from the scene center: di = \|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{c}\|2. 3. Estimate Local Density: For each point pi, estimate its local point cloud density \rhoi using the K{nn} nearest neighbors. The exact formula for \rhoi is not provided in the sources. 4. Determine Replication Radius: Define a radius ri for the tangent disk at pi. The radius grows with distance di. The exact functional form of ri(di) is not provided in the sources. 5. Construct Tangent Frame: For each point pi, construct a local tangent frame. Since DART does not use reliable normals (unlike GeoGaussian), the specific construction method is not detailed in the sources. 6. Replicate Points: For each point pi: If \rho{\min} \le \rhoi \le \rho{\max}, generate m-1 new points on the tangent disk of radius ri centered at \mathbf{x}i. If m=1, no new points are added (DART draws m-1=0 extra samples). The new points are added to the output point set P'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dartaugment(sfmpoints, m=10, rhomin=0.008, rhomax=0.04, knn=20): """ Augments SfM points using Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes. Args: sfmpoints: List of 3D coordinates (N, 3). m: Replication multiplier. rhomin: Minimum density threshold. rhomax: Maximum density threshold. knn: Number of nearest neighbors for density estimation. Returns: augmentedpoints: List of 3D coordinates (N', 3). """ N = len(sfmpoints) points = [list(p) for p in sfmpoints] # Step 1: Estimate Scene Center # Exact robust estimation method not specified in sources. scenecenter = [sum(p[d] for p in points) / N for d in range(3)] # Step 2: Compute Distances distances = [math.sqrt(sum((points[i][d] - scenecenter[d])2 for d in range(3))) for i in range(N)] # Step 3: Estimate Local Density # Exact formula for rhoi not provided in sources. # Standard fallback: inverse of mean distance to KNN neighbors. # Placeholder for KNN search omitted; assume knndistances[i] is computed externally. densities = [1.0 / (sum(knndistances[i]) / knn + 1e-8) for i in range(N)] # Step 4 & 5 & 6: Replicate Points augmentedpoints = [] for i in range(N): pi = points[i] di = distances[i] rhoi = densities[i] # Check density threshold if rhomin <= rhoi <= rhomax: # Step 4: Determine Replication Radius # Exact function ri(di) not provided in sources. # Standard fallback: linear scaling with distance. ri = 0.1 di # Step 5: Construct Tangent Frame # Exact method not provided in sources. # Standard fallback: arbitrary orthonormal basis. ui = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] vi = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Step 6: Replicate Points numnew = m - 1 for j in range(numnew): # Uniform sampling on disk theta = 2.0 math.pi (j / numnew) rsample = ri math.sqrt((j + 1) / numnew) offset = [ rsample (math.cos(theta) ui[d] + math.sin(theta) vi[d]) for d in range(3) ] newpoint = [pi[d] + offset[d] for d in range(3)] augmentedpoints.append(newpoint) # Add original point augmentedpoints.append(pi) return augmentedpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse SfM: DART is designed for scenes where SfM points are sparse, particularly in the periphery. In densely reconstructed scenes (e.g., Deep Blending's drjohnson), DART has essentially no effect on quality. Density Estimation: The exact formula for local density \rhoi is not provided. Implementers must define a robust density estimator that yields values comparable to the thresholds \rho{\min}=0.008 and \rho{\max}=0.04. Tangent Frame: Since DART does not use normals, the tangent frame construction is ambiguous. Implementers must define a consistent method for generating orthonormal vectors on the tangent plane. Radius Function: The exact relationship between distance di and radius ri is not specified. Implementers must define a scaling function that grows with distance. AGE is a maturity gate for 3D Gaussian Splatting training that prevents densification (splitting and cloning) until a specified training step threshold is reached, thereby pruning unnecessary primitives and controlling memory and time costs. It is designed to work in conjunction with Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART), where DART augments the initial point cloud to improve coverage in sparse regions, and AGE trims the resulting inflated primitive count without degrading reconstruction quality. While competitors like FastGS-Big and Taming-3DGS modify densification criteria or schedules during training, AGE acts as a static maturity gate, deferring eligibility for densification operations. On densely reconstructed scenes like Deep Blending's drjohnson, quality is essentially unchanged. Strengths and Limitations: DART is deterministic and does not require depth or external cues. This increased budget is trimmed by AGE. When to Use: Use DART when the SfM point cloud is sparse, particularly in the scene periphery, and when depth information is unavailable or unreliable. It is distinct from GeoGaussian, which reshapes Gaussians and depends on reliable normals, and from learned or depth-based enrichment methods. name: Age-Gated Densification (AGE)
head: DART + AGE, DART + AGE Integration, DART-3DGS, Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification, Ours
body: Age-Gated Densification (AGE) is a maturity gate for 3D Gaussian Splatting training that prevents densification (splitting and cloning) until a specified training step threshold is reached, thereby pruning unnecessary primitives and controlling memory and time costs. It is designed to work in conjunction with Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART), where DART augments the initial point cloud to improve coverage in sparse regions, and AGE trims the resulting inflated primitive count without degrading reconstruction quality. While competitors like FastGS-Big and Taming-3DGS modify densification criteria or schedules during training, AGE acts as a static maturity gate, deferring eligibility for densification operations. AGE functions as a conditional guard on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting densification loop. It does not alter the geometry of the Gaussians or the rendering process, but restricts when the density-control cascade (splitting small Gaussians or cloning large ones) is permitted to execute. Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the current training step t, and the maturity threshold T{mat}. Output: A boolean flag candensify indicating whether densification operations should be applied in the current optimization step. AGE relies on the standard 3DGS Gaussian representation but does not require per-Gaussian age counters; it uses a global training step counter to gate the operation. T{mat}: The maturity threshold, defined as the training step at which densification becomes active. Default value: 200. m: The replication multiplier for DART (used in conjunction with AGE). Default value: 10. If m=1, DART is disabled, but AGE remains active. \rho{min} and \rho{max}: The lower and upper bounds of the distance-aware radius schedule for DART. Default values: 0.008 and 0.04, respectively, as fractions of the robust radius R. The densification logic in standard 3DGS is modified by wrapping the densification step in a check against T{mat}. 1. Initialize: Set T{mat} = 200. 2. Training Loop: For each training step t: a. Perform forward pass and compute loss. b. Compute gradients and update Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color). c. AGE Gate Check: If t < T{mat}, set candensify = False; else True. d. Densification Step: If candensify is True, execute standard split/clone/prune operations; else skip. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def agegateddensificationstep(gaussians, trainingstep, Tmat=200): """ Performs one step of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization with AGE gating. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. trainingstep: Current integer training step index. Tmat: Maturity threshold (default 200). Returns: Updated list of Gaussian primitives. """ # 1. Standard forward pass and loss computation loss = computeloss(gaussians) # 2. Backward pass and parameter update updateparameters(gaussians, loss) # 3. AGE Gating Logic candensify = (trainingstep >= Tmat) # 4. Conditional Densification if candensify: # Standard 3DGS densification logic # Split: Gaussians with scale below threshold and opacity above threshold splitmask = (gaussians.scale < SCALETHRESHOLD) & (gaussians.opacity > OPACITYTHRESHOLD) # Clone: Gaussians with gradient magnitude above threshold clonemask = (gaussians.gradientmagnitude > GRADTHRESHOLD) # Execute splits for g in gaussians[splitmask]: newg1, newg2 = splitgaussian(g) gaussians.append(newg1) gaussians.append(newg2) # Execute clones for g in gaussians[clonemask]: newg = clonegaussian(g) gaussians.append(newg) # Prune: Remove Gaussians with opacity below threshold prunemask = gaussians.opacity > OPACITYPRUNETHRESHOLD gaussians = gaussians[prunemask] return gaussians Constant Radius in DART: Using a constant upper-bound radius (\rho = 0.040) for DART replicas causes quality collapse (6.0 dB drop on 'stump' scene) and excessive memory usage (14.0 GB peak) due to early inflation and subsequent pruning. AGE cannot fully compensate for poorly placed initial primitives. Isotropic Replication: Using isotropic balls instead of tangent disks for DART replicas increases primitive count by 11.7% and reduces quality, demonstrating that geometric placement matters more than count. Threshold Selection: T{mat} is fixed by design rather than swept, as it suppresses persistently under-supported primitives that would otherwise be retained by unconstrained densification. A geometry-only augmentation that replicates SfM points on local tangent planes with distance-dependent radii to improve coverage in sparse regions. It acts as the fidelity provider for AGE. Link The base optimization framework that AGE modifies. AGE is a supplementary strategy applied during the training phase. Link Time Complexity: AGE reduces training time. When applied with DART, it reduces training time from 31.8 to 29.4 minutes (a 2.4 min reduction) compared to using DART without AGE. The first 500 iterations take at most one minute per scene, indicating the gating overhead is negligible. Memory Complexity: AGE reduces peak memory usage. With DART, peak memory drops from 6.04 GB to 5.57 GB (a 0.47 GB reduction). Primitive Count: AGE reduces the final Gaussian count. Without DART, it reduces count by 9.6% (2.91M to 2.63M). With DART, it reduces count by 8.7% (3.45M to 3.15M). Quality Impact: AGE maintains or slightly improves quality. Without DART, PSNR increases by 0.04 dB. With DART, PSNR increases by 0.05 dB, SSIM by 0.001, and LPIPS by 0.001 (within measurement noise). Strengths: Effective cost-control gate that trims unnecessary primitives without sacrificing quality. Works independently of the initial cloud formation (effective even without DART). Limitations: Does not improve quality on its own; relies on DART for fidelity gains in sparse regions. Not a substitute for better densification criteria but a complement to them. When to Use: Use when memory or training time is constrained, or when the initial point cloud requires augmentation (via DART) that would otherwise lead to excessive primitive counts. When Not to Use: AGE is beneficial regardless of initial cloud density, as it reduces primitive count by ~9-10% without quality loss, so the overhead of managing the maturity threshold is justified in all standard training setups. AGE was introduced as part of the "DART-3DGS" method, which combines Distance-Aware Replication on Tangent-planes (DART) and Age-Gated Densification (AGE) to improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction quality. The method was developed to address the issue of sparse SfM point clouds in outdoor scenes, where standard 3DGS struggles with coverage. AGE was designed to act as a maturity gate, preventing the densification process from creating too many primitives too early, which can lead to overfitting or memory issues. The method was evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets, showing improvements in perceptual metrics (LPIPS) and comparable PSNR scores to state-of-the-art methods.
