This separation reduces the complexity of the deformation field training. 4. GoF-Specific Initialization: For each GoF Gi: Preserve the extensive static regions from \mathcal{G}{init}. Identify dynamic areas within Gi based on the foreground mask. Initialize a GoF-specific model by exclusively fine-tuning the dynamic areas while keeping static regions fixed or lightly regularized. 5. Dynamic MLP Construction: Construct a dynamic Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for each GoF. The MLP takes time t (normalized within the GoF) and spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} as input to predict deformation offsets. 6. Weighted Training: During training, apply tuning parameters (weights) to the MLP parameters. These weights direct the optimization focus toward dynamic elements, effectively decoupling static and dynamic Gaussian components in a smoothly weighted fashion. 7. Deformation Field Derivation: Train the MLP for each GoF to derive the corresponding deformation field. The deformation field maps the static Gaussian positions to their dynamic positions at time t within the GoF using \mathbf{p}i(t) = \mathbf{p}{static} + f{\thetai}(t, \mathbf{p}{static}). 8. Streaming Optimization (Optional): For transmission, selectively stream only the foreground model (deformation fields and dynamic Gaussians) based on user interaction, while transmitting the static background model once or less frequently. name: TIP-Editor
body: TIP-Editor is a method for editing existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes using intuitive text and image prompts. It solves the problem of achieving accurate local editing while maintaining multi-view consistency, which is often compromised in text-guided 3D editing. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a stepwise 2D personalization strategy with LoRA-based reference image alignment and localization loss. Inputs: An existing 3D Gaussian Splatting scene. A text prompt describing the desired edit. An optional reference image for content personalization. Outputs: An edited 3D Gaussian Splatting scene. Optimization: Optimize the identified Gaussians using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss [89]. 4. Refinement: Apply pixel-level image refinement to the rendered images during optimization to ensure high-quality results. name: GaussCtrl

It solves the inconsistency issues common in text-guided 3D editing by employing a ControlNet conditioned on depth maps to guide the editing of rendered images, ensuring geometric and appearance consistency through attention-based latent code alignment. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like GSEdit [142] and Texture-GS [146] by explicitly using depth-conditioned ControlNet to enforce geometric consistency rather than relying solely on SDS loss or texture mesh disentanglement. Update the 3DGS parameters iteratively using the edited images, integrating 3DGS for fast rendering and InfEdit for rapid processing. Formulas: Not given in the sources. name: StylizedGS
body: StylizedGS is a controllable 3D stylization method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models that performs color matching with a reference style image while utilizing a 3DGS filter to remove artifacts. It distinguishes itself from other stylization approaches by explicitly optimizing for nearest neighbor feature matching and depth preservation. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a pre-trained 3DGS model and a reference style image as input, and outputs a stylized 3DGS model. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS representation, consisting of N Gaussians defined by position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. StylizedGS modifies the color and feature attributes of these Gaussians during optimization. Optimization Steps: 1. Extract features from the reference style image. 2. Render the current 3DGS model to compute losses. 3. Compute the total loss as a weighted combination of a nearest neighbor feature match loss, a depth preservation loss, and a 3DGS filter loss for artifact removal. 4. Optimize the 3DGS parameters to minimize the total loss. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Without the 3DGS filter, stylization may introduce visual artifacts, which the method explicitly addresses. StyleGaussian is a method for real-time 3D style transfer with strict multi-view consistency. It differs from StylizedGS by embedding VGG features directly into 3D Gaussians and using an efficient rendering strategy that initially renders lower-dimensional features before mapping them to high-dimensional ones. It aligns stylized features with a style image using an AdaIN-like mechanism and decodes features back to RGB using a KNN-based 3D CNN. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Point Densification
head: Clone and Split, Densification Strategies, Point Densitification
body: Point densification is an adaptive optimization strategy in 3D Gaussian Splatting that dynamically controls the number of Gaussian primitives by converting a sparse initial set into a denser representation. It distinguishes between splitting large Gaussians for background reconstruction and cloning small Gaussians for thin structures. Later variants like HO-Gaussian apply densification at regular intervals to populate regions where sparse SfM initialization leaves holes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} with position \mathbf{p}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and color coefficients \mathbf{c}i, plus accumulated position and opacity gradients \mathbf{g}{p,i} and \mathbf{g}{\alpha,i}. Output: Updated Gaussian set with modified count and parameters. Data Structures: Arrays storing \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4, \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^k, and gradient accumulators \mathbf{g}p, \mathbf{g}\alpha. Parameters: N{clone}: Position gradient magnitude threshold to trigger cloning. N{split}: Position gradient magnitude threshold to trigger splitting. T{interval}: Number of training steps between densification checks. Note: Exact numerical values for thresholds are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Accumulate Gradients: During rendering, accumulate gradients for position and opacity for each Gaussian visible in the training views. 2. Check Interval: If current step t is a multiple of T{interval}, proceed to densification; otherwise, skip. 3. Identify Candidates: Clone Candidates: Gaussians with high position gradient magnitude (\|\mathbf{g}p\| > N{clone}) and small scale/volume. Split Candidates: Gaussians with high position gradient magnitude (\|\mathbf{g}p\| > N{split}) and large scale/volume. 4. Execute Clone: For each clone candidate Gi: duplicate the Gaussian, slightly perturb its position, reset opacity to a low initial value, and add to the set. 5. Execute Split: For each split candidate Gi: remove the original Gaussian, create two children at offset positions along a random direction, reduce their scale by a factor (e.g., 1.6), copy color and opacity, and add to the set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def densifygaussians(gaussians, gradients, step, interval, clonethresh, splitthresh, clonevolthresh, splitvolthresh): if step % interval != 0: return gaussians toclone = [] tosplit = [] for g in gaussians: gradnorm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in gradients.position[g.id])) vol = math.prod(g.scale) if gradnorm > clonethresh and vol < clonevolthresh: toclone.append(g) elif gradnorm > splitthresh and vol > splitvolthresh: tosplit.append(g) newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if g in toclone: newg = copy(g) newg.position = [newg.position[i] + random.uniform(-0.001, 0.001) for i in range(3)] newg.opacity = 0.01 newgaussians.append(newg) elif g in tosplit: rawv = [random.uniform(-1, 1) for in range(3)] v = [x / math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in rawv)) for x in rawv] offset = 0.001 g1 = copy(g) g2 = copy(g) g1.position = [g1.position[i] + v[i]offset for i in range(3)] g2.position = [g2.position[i] - v[i]offset for i in range(3)] g1.scale = [s/1.6 for s in g1.scale] g2.scale = [s/1.6 for s in g2.scale] newgaussians.append(g1) newgaussians.append(g2) else: newgaussians.append(g) return newgaussians Uses a dynamic threshold that increases over time to control densification rate, differing from fixed thresholds. Choose it when scene complexity varies significantly across training steps. Link Integrates densification with a transformer-based refinement, focusing on structural consistency rather than just gradient magnitude. Choose it when geometric coherence is prioritized over raw gradient signals. Link Uses stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics for densification, providing a probabilistic approach to point placement. Choose it when avoiding local minima in sparse initialization is critical. Link Densifies points based on rendering error maps rather than gradients, targeting visible artifacts directly. Choose it when perceptual quality and artifact reduction are primary goals. Link Manages point density locally using spatial hashing, reducing global memory overhead during densification. Choose it for large-scale scenes where global memory allocation is prohibitive. Link Time Complexity: O(N) per densification step, where N is the number of Gaussians. Densification occurs only at intervals T{interval}, so average cost is O(N / T{interval}) per step. Memory Complexity: Increases linearly with the number of cloned/split Gaussians. Strengths: Fast convergence for thin structures via cloning. Limitations: Struggles with sky/distant areas if initialization is poor. When to use: When initial SfM points are sparse or unevenly distributed; when thin structures are present. When not to use: When initialization is dense and uniform; when computational budget is extremely tight. Point densification was introduced as a key contribution in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper. It was designed to allow the Gaussian set to adaptively grow by distinguishing between splitting (for background/geometry) and cloning (for thin structures/convergence speed). Later works like HO-Gaussian noted that the original method relies on accurate initialization and can leave holes in low-texture or sky regions, leading to hybrid optimization approaches that incorporate densification at regular intervals to populate problematic regions. 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079, fetched 2026-10-26 HO-Gaussian: Hybrid Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Urban Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73027-62, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SGD (Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior)
body: SGD is a novel view synthesis method for street scenes that enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by fine-tuning a Stable Diffusion model on driving data and using it to regularize 3DGS training at unseen viewpoints, addressing the sparse-view reconstruction problem. It differs from prior sparse-view NVS methods that rely on object-centric multi-view datasets and relative camera poses; instead, it uses adjacent frames and LiDAR depth for direct fine-tuning on driving data, overcoming the domain gap. SGD consists of two main stages: fine-tuning a Diffusion Model with reference images and LiDAR depth, and integrating this model into the 3DGS pipeline to regularize training via pseudo views. Inputs: A set of training images \{Ii\} and corresponding camera poses \{pi\} captured by a vehicle. 360° LiDAR point clouds to derive depth maps for reference and target views. A fixed text prompt: “A photo a of driving scene.”. Outputs: A fine-tuned Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion 1.5 with injected U-Net features and a trained ControlNet). A 3D Gaussian Splatting model optimized with diffusion-based regularization. The method relies on standard 3DGS data structures (Gaussian positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) and Diffusion Model components: U-Net: The backbone of Stable Diffusion, modified to accept concatenated CLIP features. ControlNet: A trainable branch initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights, conditioned on depth maps. CLIP Encoder: Used to extract image and text features. This stage prepares the prior by conditioning the diffusion model on adjacent frames and depth. 1. Reference Selection: For a target view, identify the closest preceding and succeeding frames as reference images. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract patchwise CLIP image features from the reference images. Extract CLIP text features from the fixed prompt “A photo a of driving scene.”. Compute depth maps from LiDAR point clouds for both reference and target views. 3. U-Net Injection: Inject the concatenated CLIP image features (from reference images) and CLIP text features into the U-Net during fine-tuning. 4. ControlNet Training: Train a ControlNet branch using the depth map of the target image as the control signal. 5. Training Strategy: Use a two-phase training strategy where the U-Net is fine-tuned and the ControlNet is trained separately. Jointly fine-tuning the U-Net and training the ControlNet simultaneously is avoided because the ControlNet must be initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights rather than fine-tuned weights, which produces less authentic outputs. This stage integrates the fine-tuned model into 3DGS to guide synthesis at unseen views. 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussian models from the training views. 2. Pseudo View Generation: Project and rasterize the current 3D Gaussian models to generate pseudo views. Create novel evaluation views by interpolating the position of training/testing views and adding positional perturbations. Adjust rotation of novel views by offsetting angle \pm\delta, \pm2\delta along the z-axis, where \delta is randomly sampled from [15^\circ, 30^\circ]. 3. Regularization Loss: Use the fine-tuned Diffusion Model to provide regularization loss on these pseudo views. 4. Loss Functions: The total loss includes standard 3DGS losses plus regularization losses: L{L1}: L1 loss between pseudo view and diffusion prior. L{LPIPS}: LPIPS loss for perceptual similarity. L{depth}: Depth loss. Note: Applying L{L1} to pseudo views marginally reduces test view PSNR because pixel-level comparison amplifies inherent minor differences between diffusion-generated and real images. 5. Optimization: Update 3D Gaussian parameters using the combined loss. Unverified code. ControlNet(nn.Module): """Trainable ControlNet branch initialized with original SD 1.5 weights.""" def init(self): super().init() # Initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights self.encoder imagefeatures = clipimageencoder(images) textfeatures = cliptextencoder(textprompt) return imagefeatures, textfeatures def getdepthfromlidar(lidarpoints, camerapose): """Compute depth map from LiDAR point cloud given camera pose.""" projected = projecttoimageplane(lidarpoints, camerapose) depthmap = computezdistance(projected) return depthmap def interpolatepose(poses, t): """Linearly interpolate between camera poses.""" return poses[0] (1 - t) + poses[1] t def perturbposition(pose, magnitude): """Add random positional perturbation to a camera pose.""" offset = torch.randn(3) magnitude dataset.getadjacentframes(targetview) targetdepth = getdepthfromlidar(dataset.lidar, targetpose) pseudoviews = [] pseudodepths = [] for in range(numpseudoviews): t = np.random.uniform(0, 1) pose = computediffusionregularization(pview, priorview, pdepth, priordepth) totall1 += l1 totallpips += lpips totaldepth += depth totalloss = lossstandard + totall1 + totallpips + totaldepth Rotation Offset \delta: Randomly sampled from [15^\circ, 30^\circ]. Rotation Adjustment: \pm\delta, \pm2\delta along the z-axis. Depth-only ControlNet: Using only depth ControlNet without reference images causes the text prompt to dominate semantics, yielding high diversity but significant deviation from original scenes. Joint Fine-tuning: Jointly fine-tuning U-Net and training ControlNet simultaneously produces less authentic outputs because ControlNet must be initialized with original Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights rather than fine-tuned weights. L1 Loss on Pseudo Views: Applying L1 loss to pseudo views marginally reduces test view PSNR because pixel-level comparison amplifies inherent minor differences between diffusion-generated and real images. Training Time: Integration of the Diffusion Model increases training time due to the computationally expensive denoising operation. Training Speed: Training speed (iterations/second) drops substantially when introducing pseudo views (from 0 to 1). Rendering Speed: Rendering speed (FPS) remains unaffected by the introduction of pseudo views. Performance (KITTI-75%): PSNR: 23.85, SSIM: 0.837, LPIPS: 0.154. Performance (KITTI-50%): PSNR: 23.62, SSIM: 0.799, LPIPS: 0.158. Performance (KITTI-25%): PSNR: 23.44, SSIM: 0.793, LPIPS: 0.167. Performance (KITTI-360 50%): PSNR: 23.81, SSIM: 0.832, LPIPS: 0.155. Novel View Quality: BRISQUE score: 24.53, FID score: 73.36. Ablation Results: Complete model: PSNR 23.81, SSIM 0.832, LPIPS 0.155. w/o LPIPSpseudo: PSNR 23.11, SSIM 0.818, LPIPS 0.159. w/o L1pseudo: PSNR 23.83, SSIM 0.820, LPIPS 0.163. w/o Ldepthpseudo: PSNR 23.29, SSIM 0.801, LPIPS 0.169. w/o pseudo views (standard 3DGS): PSNR 22.78, SSIM 0.793, LPIPS 0.176. Strengths: Enhances rendering quality from broader views, smoother road surfaces, distinct lane markings, and clearer distant vehicles. Limitations: Longer training time due to diffusion denoising. SGD was proposed to address the challenge of maintaining rendering quality at viewpoints that deviate significantly from training viewpoints in street scenes, a problem stemming from sparse training views captured by a fixed camera on a moving vehicle. It is designed for autonomous driving simulation and street view synthesis, evaluated on KITTI and KITTI-360 datasets. The method leverages prior from a Diffusion Model along with complementary multi-modal data (LiDAR depth) to enhance the capacity of 3DGS. name: Equivalent Distribution Reorganization
head: ReorgGS
body: Equivalent Distribution Reorganization (ReorgGS) is a post-training reorganization method for converged 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models that addresses "parameterization degeneration," a failure mode where high-opacity floaters attenuate gradients to true surfaces and redundant overlapping clusters create strongly coupled parameter blocks. Unlike standard opacity reset, which only rescales opacity on the old overlap graph, ReorgGS rebuilds centers, covariances, and the visibility structure by resampling from the empirical distribution, thereby changing the graph itself. It preserves the original scene support asymptotically while reducing parameter coupling and opacity barriers, delivering up to 0.5 dB higher training PSNR and a 12.8% rendering speedup in representative settings. Inputs and Outputs Input: A converged 3DGS model G = \{gi\}{i=1}^N with parameters \{\mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, Ci\}{i=1}^N that has reached the middle-to-late stage of training, converged, or entered a plateau. Output: A new Gaussian set G' = \{g'j\}{j=1}^M with parameters \{\mu'j, \Sigma'j, \alpha'j, C'j\}{j=1}^M, where M=N. The induced field q(x) = \sum{j=1}^M \alpha'j \mathcal{N}(x | \mu'j, \Sigma'j) approximately preserves the support of the original empirical distribution P(x). Data Structures Original Gaussians: Stored as a list of N primitives. Each primitive i contains: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center coordinates. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (parameterized as Ri Si Si^T Ri^T in standard 3DGS, where Ri is rotation and Si is scale). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Ci: Appearance parameters (e.g., spherical harmonics coefficients). New Gaussians: Same structure as input, but with reorganized parameters. Parameters \alpha0: Initial opacity for all new primitives. Default value: 0.01. k: Number of nearest neighbors used for covariance estimation. Default value: Not explicitly stated as a single integer in the primary text, but the notation implies k is the count. Steps 1. GMM Modeling: View the current Gaussian set as an empirical Gaussian-mixture field defined as P(x) \approx \sum{i=1}^N \alphai \mathcal{N}(x | \mui, \Sigmai). Define its normalized form as \hat{p}(x) = P(x) / Z, where Z = \int P(x)dx. In implementation, the continuous integral Z does not need to be computed explicitly; sampling only requires the discrete mixture weights. 2. Categorical Sampling: Sample a latent variable zj \in \{1, \dots, N\} from a categorical distribution P(zj = k) = \frac{\alphak}{\sum{l=1}^N \alphal}. Use only opacity \alphak as the categorical weight and do not multiply it by the Gaussian volume. This ignores volume to reduce sampling bias towards abnormally large Gaussians that correspond to blurred regions or artifacts. 3. Gaussian Coordinate Sampling: After choosing category zj = k, sample a new center from the corresponding 3D Gaussian xj \sim \mathcal{N}(\muk, \Sigmak). In practice, use the reparameterized form xj = \muk + Lk \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and Lk is the Cholesky factor of \Sigmak. Alternatively, since 3DGS parameterizes \Sigmak = Rk Sk Sk^T Rk^T, use Rk Sk as the sampling transform. 4. Anisotropic Initialization: Perform a k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) query for each sampled point xj within the new point set \{xj\}{j=1}^M to obtain its k nearest neighbors \{x{j1}, \dots, x{jk}\}. Estimate the new covariance \Sigma'j using the local second moment: \Sigma'j = \frac{1}{k} \sum{l=1}^k (x{jl} - xj)(x{jl} - xj)^T. 5. Constructing the Reorganized Distribution: Set the new mean \mu'j = xj. Set the new opacity \alpha'j = \alpha0, where \alpha0 is a small opacity value (default 0.01). The spatial scale is determined by \Sigma'j. Inherit the appearance parameter C'j from the nearest old Gaussian: NN(xj) = \arg \mini \|xj - \mui\|^2, C'j = C{NN(xj)}. 6. Recovering Scale and Rotation: Perform eigendecomposition on the estimated covariance: \Sigma'j = Uj \Lambdaj Uj^T. Set the new rotation R'j = Uj and the new scale S'j = \Lambdaj (diagonal matrix of eigenvalues), such that \Sigma'j = R'j S'j (S'j)^T (R'j)^T. Reinitialize the optimizer state for the new parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def reorggs(gaussians, alpha0=0.01, k=4): """ Reorganizes a converged 3D Gaussian Splatting model. Args: gaussians: List of dicts or objects with fields: mu: (3,) array, center R: (3,3) array, rotation matrix S: (3,) array, scale alpha: float, opacity C: appearance parameters alpha0: float, initial opacity for new Gaussians k: int, number of nearest neighbors for covariance estimation Returns: newgaussians: List of dicts with reorganized parameters """ N = len(gaussians) newgaussians = [] # Step 1 & 2: Categorical Sampling based on opacity # Normalize opacities to form a probability distribution alphas = np.array([g['alpha'] for g in gaussians]) probs = alphas / np.sum(alphas) # Sample N indices from the categorical distribution # We resample exactly N points to maintain capacity M=N selectedindices = np.random.choice(N, size=N, p=probs) # Step 3: Gaussian Coordinate Sampling sampledcenters = [] for idx in selectedindices: g = gaussians[idx] muk = g['mu'] # Sigmak = Rk @ diag(Sk^2) @ Rk^T # Cholesky factor Lk = Rk @ diag(Sk) Lk = g['R'] @ np.diag(g['S']) epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, 3) xj = muk + Lk @ epsilon sampledcenters.append(xj) sampledcenters = np.array(sampledcenters) # Step 4: Anisotropic Initialization (kNN Covariance) # Compute kNN for each sampled point within the NEW point set knnindices = getknnindices(sampledcenters, k) newcovariances = [] for j in range(N): xj = sampledcenters[j] neighbors = sampledcenters[knnindices[j]] diffs = neighbors - xj cov = np.zeros((3, 3)) for l in range(k): diff = diffs[l] cov += np.outer(diff, diff) cov /= k newcovariances.append(cov) # Step 5 & 6: Construct new Gaussians for j in range(N): xj = sampledcenters[j] covj = newcovariances[j] eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covj) Uj = eigenvectors Lambdaj = np.diag(eigenvalues) Rprime = Uj Sprime = eigenvalues # Source specifies S'j = Lambdaj dists = np.linalg.norm(sampledcenters[:, np.newaxis,:] - np.array([g['mu'] for g in gaussians]), axis=2) nearestoldidx = np.argmin(dists, axis=1)[j] Cprime = gaussians[nearestoldidx]['C'] newgaussians.append({ 'mu': xj, 'R': Rprime, 'S': Sprime, 'alpha': alpha0, 'C': Cprime }) return newgaussians def getknnindices(points, k): """ Computes k nearest neighbor indices for each point in the set. """ N = points.shape[0] dists = np.linalg.norm(points[:, np.newaxis,:] - points[np.newaxis,:,:], axis=2) np.filldiagonal(dists, np.inf) indices = np.argpartition(dists, k, axis=1)[:,:k] return indices Edge Cases and Pitfalls Abnormally Large Gaussians: Degenerate 3DGS optimization can produce abnormally large Gaussians corresponding to blurred regions or artifacts. Volume Amplification: Volume-weighted sampling would amplify these large-scale abnormal structures. Opacity Barriers: High-opacity floaters in degenerate distributions can create an opacity barrier where T{gp}(r) \to 0, cutting off optimization paths to surfaces behind them. Precision: The kNN covariance estimation relies on the local density of sampled points. If M is small or k is too small, the covariance estimate may be noisy. Time Complexity: The core algorithmic module (resampling and covariance re-estimation) takes only a few seconds for millions of Gaussians, leveraging efficient GPU kNN implementations. However, as a post-training method, it adds approximately 5 minutes per stage for the LiteGS architecture on an NVIDIA A100 GPU due to subsequent gradient descent steps. Memory Complexity: The method maintains the same number of Gaussians (M=N), so memory usage is comparable to the baseline model. Performance: ReorgGS delivers up to 0.5 dB higher training PSNR and 0.14 dB higher test PSNR over direct continuation. It also provides up to 12.8% rendering speedup (e.g., from 10.75s to 9.37s on LiteGS/A100) due to reduced redundant alpha compositing. Strengths: Improves gradient accessibility, reduces parameter coupling, suppresses persistent floaters, and reduces rendering redundancy without changing the renderer or increasing capacity. Limitations: It is a post-training intervention, requiring a halt in optimization. It does not address the root cause of degeneration during training but mitigates its effects. The improvement is larger under reduced Gaussian budgets, where each Gaussian carries more representational pressure and a degenerate overlap pattern wastes a larger fraction of the available capacity. ReorgGS was proposed to address "parameterization degeneration," a late-stage bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting where converged models retain floaters, redundant overlap, and poor gradient accessibility. The method treats distributional equivalence as distinct from optimization equivalence, arguing that reorganizing the parameterization (opacity-density allocation, local overlap, alpha-compositing transmittance, and covariance alignment) is necessary to break fitting ceilings. It is evaluated on vanilla 3DGS, GOF, Taming-3DGS, 3DGS-MCMC, and LiteGS backbones across Mip-NeRF 360, Blender, and Tanks&Temples datasets. ReorgGS: Equivalent Distribution Reorganization for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://github.com/WoojunePark/splatpapers/issues/66, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: S2Gaussian
head: Sparse-View Super-Resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: S2Gaussian is a two-stage framework for reconstructing high-quality 3D scenes from sparse and low-resolution input views, addressing the joint challenge of deficient perspectives and clarity. Unlike methods that treat sparsity and low resolution as isolated problems, S2Gaussian handles this hybrid scenario by initializing high-resolution Gaussians from a densified low-resolution representation and refining them using super-resolved supervision. It sets itself apart from its parent Fine-tuning by introducing a specific "Gaussian Shuffle Split" densification strategy and a "Blur-Free Inconsistency Modeling" scheme to mitigate multi-view artifacts. Inputs: Sparse low-resolution input views (images). Estimated depth information for the scene (used in Stage 1). A pre-trained super-resolution model (used in Stage 2). Outputs: A set of high-resolution 3D Gaussian primitives representing the scene. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Standard 3DGS representation including mean position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma (parameterized by rotation R and scale S), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}. Sub-Gaussians: In the Gaussian Shuffle Split operation, one parent Gaussian is replaced by N sub-Gaussians. The sources specify N=6 as optimal. These sub-Gaussians are symmetrically located along the three principal axes of the original Gaussian. Parameters: Number of sub-Gaussians (N): 6 is the optimal trade-off between detail modeling and complexity/memory overhead. Resolution: The method targets super-resolution tasks, e.g., training on low-resolution inputs (e.g., 252 \times 189) and rendering at higher resolutions (e.g., 1008 \times 756). Steps: 1. Stage 1: HR GS Initialization 1. Optimize a low-resolution Gaussian representation using the sparse low-resolution views and the estimated depth information. This provides a reliable base structure and avoids overfitting to specific viewpoints. 2. Densify the optimized low-resolution Gaussians to initialize high-resolution Gaussians using the Gaussian Shuffle Split operation. For each low-resolution Gaussian, generate N sub-Gaussians. The sub-Gaussians are positioned symmetrically along the three principal axes of the parent Gaussian. This creates more compact primitives to facilitate fine-grained detail reconstruction. 2. Stage 2: HR GS Optimization 1. Render pseudo-views from the initialized high-resolution Gaussians (derived from the low-resolution Gaussians). 2. Generate super-resolved images from the original sparse views using the pre-trained super-resolution model. 3. Refine the high-resolution Gaussians by optimizing against both the original sparse views (super-resolved) and the pseudo-views. 4. Apply Blur-Free Inconsistency Modeling to mitigate multi-view inconsistency. Explicitly model the inconsistency between the super-resolved images and the rendered pseudo-views. Learn a blur kernel to reconstruct blur-free results with fine structural details, avoiding the blurring typically introduced by inconsistency modeling. 5. Apply 3D Robust Optimization to eliminate erroneous updates. This strategy prevents Gaussian primitives from simulating corrupted representations when training views are imperfect. Loss Function: The final loss L for high-resolution Gaussian optimization is defined as: L = L{AUX} + L{SR} Where: L{SR} is the super-resolution loss, computed between the rendered high-resolution images and the super-resolved target images. L{AUX} is an auxiliary loss covering depth regularization, pseudo-view consistency, and blur-free inconsistency modeling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def S2GaussianTrain(sparselrviews, estimateddepth, cameraposes, srmodel): # Stage 1: Optimize low-res Gaussians lrgaussians = InitializeGaussians(sparselrviews, estimateddepth) lrgaussians = OptimizeGaussians(lrgaussians, sparselrviews, estimateddepth, cameraposes) # Stage 1: Densify via Gaussian Shuffle Split N = 6 hrgaussians = GaussianShuffleSplit(lrgaussians, N) # Stage 2: Render pseudo-views and generate SR targets pseudoviews = RenderGaussians(hrgaussians, cameraposes) srtargets = srmodel(sparselrviews) # Stage 2: Optimize HR Gaussians hrgaussians = OptimizeGaussians(hrgaussians, srtargets, pseudoviews, cameraposes) return hrgaussians def InitializeGaussians(sparselrviews, estimateddepth): # Standard 3DGS initialization from depth and sparse views points = DepthToPoints(estimateddepth, sparselrviews) return CreateGaussians(points) def OptimizeGaussians(gaussians, views, depth=None, pseudoviews=None, cameraposes=None): # Standard differentiable rendering optimization loop for step in range(MAXSTEPS): cam = RandomCameras(cameraposes) rendered = RenderGaussians(gaussians, cam) loss = ComputeLoss(rendered, views, depth, pseudoviews) gaussians = ApplyGradientDescent(gaussians, loss) return gaussians def GaussianShuffleSplit(gaussians, N=6): newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: R = g.rotation axes = [R[:, 0], R[:, 1], R[:, 2]] subgaussians = [] for i in range(N): axisidx = i % 3 direction = 1 if i < N // 2 else -1 offset = direction g.scale 0.5 subg = CopyGaussian(g) subg.position += offset axes[axisidx] subg.opacity /= N subgaussians.append(subg) newgaussians.extend(subgaussians) return newgaussians def ComputeLoss(rendered, srtargets, pseudoviews, depth=None): losssr = MeanSquaredError(rendered, srtargets) lossaux = 0.0 if pseudoviews is not None: blurkernel = LearnBlurKernel(rendered, pseudoviews) blurredrendered = ApplyBlur(rendered, blurkernel) lossaux += MeanSquaredError(blurredrendered, pseudoviews) if depth is not None: rendereddepth = RenderDepth(gaussians, camera) lossaux += MeanSquaredError(rendereddepth, depth) return lossaux + losssr def DepthToPoints(depthmap, views): # Back-project depth map to 3D points using camera intrinsics/extrinsics return [depthmap.projectto3d(view) for view in views] def CreateGaussians(points): # Initialize Gaussian primitives at points with standard covariance and opacity return [Gaussian(position=p, rotation=I, scale=1.0, opacity=0.5) for p in points] def RandomCameras(cameraposes): # Sample a random camera pose from the provided list or generate one return cameraposes[random.randint(0, len(cameraposes)-1)] def ApplyGradientDescent(gaussians, loss, lr=0.01): # Compute gradients and update parameters for g in gaussians: g.position -= lr gradient(g.position, loss) g.rotation -= lr gradient(g.rotation, loss) g.scale -= lr gradient(g.scale, loss) g.opacity -= lr gradient(g.opacity, loss) return gaussians def LearnBlurKernel(rendered, pseudoviews): # Learn a small convolutional kernel to model inconsistency kernel = Parameter(shape=(3, 3)) kernel -= lr gradient(kernel, MeanSquaredError(ApplyBlur(rendered, kernel), pseudoviews)) return kernel def ApplyBlur(image, kernel): # Convolve image with kernel return Convolve(image, kernel) def RenderDepth(gaussians, camera): # Render depth buffer from Gaussians return [g.projecttodepth(camera) for g in gaussians] def MeanSquaredError(a, b): return sum((ai - bi)2 for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) / len(a) def GradientDescent(gaussians, loss, lr=0.01): for g in gaussians: g.position -= lr gradient(g.position, loss) g.rotation -= lr gradient(g.rotation, loss) g.scale -= lr gradient(g.scale, loss) g.opacity -= lr gradient(g.opacity, loss) return gaussians Time and Memory Complexity: The Gaussian Shuffle Split operation increases the number of Gaussians by a factor of N. With N=6, the storage memory increases significantly (e.g., from 67M to 112M for 4 sub-Gaussians vs 6, on Mip-NeRF 360). More sub-Gaussians increase optimization complexity and memory overhead. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 \times 4 (24 views), S2Gaussian achieves 22.05 PSNR, 0.687 SSIM, 0.296 LPIPS, and 43.51 FID. It exceeds the top-performing combinatorial method FSGS+SRGS by 2.22 dB PSNR. Strengths: Handles both view sparsity and low resolution simultaneously; produces structure-accurate and detail-faithful 3D scenes; robust to corrupted training views via 3D Robust Optimization. Limitations: Prone to overfitting if high-resolution reconstruction is attempted directly from sparse low-resolution views without the two-stage approach; requires a pre-trained super-resolution model; increased memory usage due to densification. When to use: When reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse and low-resolution input views where both perspective deficiency and clarity are issues. When not to use: When high-resolution input views are available, or when computational resources are severely limited due to the increased number of Gaussians. S2Gaussian was proposed to address the challenging problem of reconstructing high-quality 3D scenes from sparse low-resolution views that simultaneously suffer from deficient perspectives and clarity. Existing methods typically handle either sparse views or low-resolution observations in isolation, failing in hybrid scenarios. The method was introduced in the paper "S2Gaussian: Sparse-View Super-Resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting". S2Gaussian: Sparse-View Super-Resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.00075, fetched 2026-10-29

name: FreeFix
body: FreeFix is a fine-tuning-free method to improve the rendering quality of extrapolated views in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by leveraging pretrained 2D image diffusion models (IDMs). It solves the problem of artifacts in rendered RGBs and inconsistency across frames that arise when using Video Diffusion Models (VDMs) or naive 2D IDMs, avoiding the computational burden of temporal attention and the loss of per-pixel guidance due to 3D VAE down-sampling. It sets itself apart from siblings like ViewExtrapolator or Difix3D+ by using a 2D–3D interleaved refinement strategy with per-pixel confidence masks derived from Fisher information, rather than relying on rendered opacity or warp masks which fail to identify artifact regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An initial 3DGS model G{init} reconstructed from a sparse or partial training set S{train} = \{(V^tj, I^tj)\}, and a continuous trajectory of m extrapolated viewpoints T{ext} = \{V^e0, V^e1,..., V^e{m-1}\}. Output: A refined 3DGS model G{refined} and a set of refined images for the extrapolated views. Data Structures: 3DGS Model G: Contains N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i has position \mui, covariance \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^T Ri^T (where Ri \in SO(3) and Si \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}), opacity \etai, and color ci. Fixed Image Set F{i-1}: A set of previously refined images \{(V^e0, \tilde{I}^e{0,f}),..., (V^e{i-1}, \tilde{I}^e{i-1,f})\}. Affine Matrices: For each generated view, two optimizable matrices Af \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and Ab \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1} are maintained to correct color bias accumulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def FreeFix(Ginit, Strain, Text, gammac, beta): G = Ginit F = [] # Fixed image set F{i-1} for i, Ve in enumerate(Text): # 2D Refinement Itilde = render(G, Ve) Malpha = renderopacity(G, Ve) Cbar = computeuncertainty(G, Ve) Cc = exp(-gammac Cbar) Mc = rendercertainty(G, Ve, Cc) Malpha Mc = resizetolatent(Mc) xr0 = encode(Itilde) xt = addnoise(xr0) for t in range(T, 0, -1): xt0 = xt - sigmat Ftheta(xt, t) if isearlystage(t): xtg0 = Mc xr0 + (1 - Mc) (beta Malpha xr0 + (1 - beta Malpha) xt0) else: xtg0 = Mc xr0 + (1 - Mc) xt0 xt1 = ((sigmat1 - sigmat) / sigmat) xt - (sigmat1 / sigmat) xtg0 xt = xt1 Ifixed = decode(x0) F.append((Ve, Ifixed)) # 3D Refinement optimizeGandaffine(G, Strain, F, (Ve, Ifixed)) return G Formulas: 3DGS Rendering: \pi(V; G) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), where \alphai = \etai \exp[-\frac{1}{2} (p - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (p - \mui)]. Uncertainty: \bar{C}{V;G} = \nablaG \pi(V; G)^T \nablaG \pi(V; G). Certainty: C^{c}{V;G} = \exp[-\gammac \bar{C}{V;G}]. Confidence Map: M^{c}{V;G} = \pi(V; (G, C^{c}{V;G})) \odot \pi(V; (G, \alpha)). Guided Prediction (Early Stage): x^{t,g}0 = Mc \odot x^r0 + (1 - Mc) \odot (\beta M\alpha x^r0 + (1 - \beta M\alpha) x^t0). Guided Prediction (Later Stage): x^{t,g}0 = Mc \odot x^r0 + (1 - Mc) \odot x^t0. Next Step Input: x{t-1} = \frac{\sigma{t-1} - \sigmat}{\sigmat} xt - \frac{\sigma{t-1}}{\sigmat} x^{t,g}0. Parameters: \gammac: Hyperparameter controlling sensitivity to artifacts in confidence map rendering. Range [0, 1]. Typical values: 0.001, 0.01, 0.1. \beta: Hyperparameter controlling the strength of overall guidance. Pitfalls: Using rendered opacity as guidance is ineffective because high-opacity regions can still contain severe artifacts. Using uncertainty maps directly is numerically unstable (0, +\infty)) and can be overwhelmed by low-opacity Gaussians with large uncertainties. Direct application of IDMs without interleaved refinement causes blurriness and inconsistency, especially in low-confidence areas like sky/ground. Color bias accumulation in generated views can lead to a blurry/over-gray effect if not corrected by affine matrices. Time Complexity: Quadratic in sequence length if using VDMs, but FreeFix uses IDMs which are linear per frame, though the interleaved 3D refinement adds optimization cost per view. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the fixed image set F{i-1} and maintaining affine matrices for each generated view. Strengths: Fine-tuning-free, preserves generalization, handles extrapolated views better than naive 2D DMs, avoids VDM computational burden. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial 3DGS, iterative refinement is slower than single-pass methods. When to use: When refining 3DGS from sparse/partial inputs for extrapolated views without access to [fine-tuning resources or VDMs. FreeFix was introduced by Hongyu Zhou et al. from Zhejiang University, University of Maryland, and Huawei. It addresses the trade-off between generalization and fidelity in diffusion-based 3DGS refinement. The method was evaluated on LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360, and Waymo datasets. FreeFix: Boosting 3D Gaussian Splatting via Fine-Tuning-Free Diffusion Models, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv69130.2026.00109, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Localized Point Management (LPM)
body: Localized Point Management (LPM) is a training optimization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that identifies error-contributing 3D zones via cross-view feature mapping and performs localized point addition, opacity reset, and pruning to correct under-optimized or ill-conditioned points. Unlike standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) which relies on global gradient thresholds, LPM uses image rendering errors and multiview geometry constraints to target specific regions, improving reconstruction quality without the substantial training overhead of multi-view stereo or additional gradient propagation methods like GaussianPro or PixelGS. LPM operates as a model-agnostic plugin to existing 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines, identifying 3D zones that require densification or geometry calibration based on rendering errors. The method identifies error source zones by projecting 2D error regions from paired views into 3D space using cone intersections, then manipulates points within these zones. Inputs: Current view image I{curr} and ground-truth image I{gt}. Referred (neighboring) view image I{ref}. Current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gk\}, where each Gk is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}k \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Camera parameters for current and referred views (center \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Outputs: Updated set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with modified positions, opacities, and counts. Gaussian Point: Defined by \boldsymbol{\mu}k (position), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k (covariance), \alphak (opacity), and appearance features. The covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}k is maintained as positive semi-definite during optimization. The Gaussian evaluates as G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right). Error Map: A 2D image of the same resolution as the rendered view, computed pixel-wise against the ground truth. Feature Matches: A set of correspondences M = \{(i, j)\} between local features of the current view A and referred view B, where i, j are indices of matched points. 1. Error Map Generation: Render the current view using the current Gaussian set. Compute the error map E against the ground-truth image I{gt} using an error function (e.g., L1 or L2 loss). 2. Cross-View Region Mapping: Select a neighboring view as the referred image. Extract local features from the current view A and referred view B. Use a feature matcher (e.g., LightGlue) to predict partial assignments M = \{(i, j)\} \subseteq A \times B. Identify paired regions (Re, R'e) based on matched points, where Re is the error region in the current view and R'e is the corresponding region in the referred view. 3. 2D-to-3D Projection (Cone Casting): For the error region Re in the current view, cast a cone of rays C from the camera center \mathbf{o} along direction \mathbf{d} (pixel center). The apex of the cone is at \mathbf{o}. The radius r{Cone} is set to match the radius of the smallest circumscribed circle of the 2D plane error region Re. Similarly, project region R'e to cone C' from the referred camera center. 4. Error Source Zone Identification: Compute the intersection points of rays from cone C and cone C'. Define the error source 3D zone R{zone} as the smallest sphere that contains these intersection points. 5. Point Manipulation within R{zone}: Point Addition (Densification): If points exist in R{zone}: Apply densification at a lower threshold than standard ADC to complement original counterparts. For small Gaussians: clone them, maintaining size, and reposition along the positional gradient. For large Gaussians in high variance areas: split them into smaller points. These may occlude valid points and cause incorrect depth estimates. Reset the opacity of these potentially ill-conditioned points to allow correction in subsequent optimization steps. Pruning: To minimize model expansion, adaptively prune points based on opacity values, starting from low to high. The number of points pruned is determined by the density of points in the zone. Scaling: LPM maintains real-time rendering speed while improving reconstruction quality. Strengths: Versatile plugin with minimal additional cost; improves PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending, and Neural 3D Video datasets. Limitations: May not be optimal for under-optimized points if the densification rules of 3DGS are not sufficient. Origin: Proposed in "Improving Gaussian Splatting with Localized Points Management" (CVPR 2025). History: Developed to address limitations in standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the inability to handle ill-conditioned points and the inefficiency of global thresholding. Usage: Applied to static 3D and dynamic 4D scenes for novel view synthesis. name: ParetoGS
head: ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors
body: ParetoGS is a continuous-budget 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation that decodes any Gaussian count K from a single asset without separate optimization per budget. It achieves this by constructing a small set of sparse, adapted budget anchors with persistent member identities, encoding their parameter changes relative to a full model in a residual atlas, and interpolating shared parameters while gradually activating entering members at runtime. Unlike prefix-based or hierarchical methods that require fixed orderings or complex transformation modules, ParetoGS explicitly optimizes nested anchors and connects their aligned states, offering superior quality at low budgets compared to FlexGS and NanoGS. Inputs: A fully trained 3DGS model with N Gaussians, optimized using ImprovedGS for 30K iterations. Target anchor budgets Kj and scene data for calibration. Outputs: An ordered full model \ThetaN. A layered residual atlas \Deltaj storing parameter changes for each anchor j relative to the full model. Interval exponents p and q for each anchor interval. Member-order metadata defining the global nested sequence. Gaussian Parameter Vector: Each Gaussian i is defined by \thetai = (xi, si, ri, oi, ci), where: xi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Log scale. ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Raw rotation quaternion. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity logit. ci: Spherical-harmonic coefficients. Residual Atlas: For each anchor Kj, the stored residual is \Deltaj = \Theta{Kj} - \ThetaN[1:Kj], where \ThetaN is the full model parameter matrix ordered by the global member sequence. The full model (KM=N) has zero residual and requires no additional state. The atlas uses lossy encoding (quantization) for storage. Interval Metadata: Two scalar exponents p and q are stored per interval between anchors. 1. Full Model Training: Train a 3DGS model for 30K iterations using ImprovedGS densification. 2. Anchor Schedule Definition: Define 11 anchors spanning 0.1% to 100% of the full count N. Target counts are Kj = \text{round}(N \rhoj) for \rhoj \in \{0.001, 0.002, \dots, 0.512, 1\}. 3. Anchor Construction (Contraction): Start from the current anchor (initially the Full model). Contract to the next target budget Kj using GNS for 15K–18K iterations. GNS adjusts regularization based on a linear opacity-decay trajectory, advances removal within a selection window, and uses a budget safeguard to retain exactly Kj members. Disable densification during this phase. Hold membership fixed and continue optimizing pixel L1 and SSIM reconstruction losses until 25K iterations total for the stage. Record deletions to determine the entry order \pi{L \to U} for the reverse direction (lower to upper anchor). 4. Member Correspondence: Concatenate the smallest anchor with the entry sequences from subsequent contractions to form a global nested order. This order ensures S(Ka) \subset S(Kb) for Ka < Kb. 5. Residual Encoding: Compute residuals \Deltaj = \Theta{Kj} - \ThetaN[1:Kj] for all non-full anchors. Encode the residuals using quantization rules (details in Appendix A of source). 6. Interval Calibration: For each interval between anchors L and U, calibrate exponents p and q using 10 training views. Minimize reconstruction loss plus penalties for loss regressions and slope deviations at t \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}. Store p and q for the interval. Budget-Conditioned Model: G(K) = \{(zi, \thetai(K)) \mid zi \in S(K)\}, \quad |S(K)| = K where zi is the persistent identity. Membership at Intermediate Budget: For L < K < U: S(K) = S(L) \cup \pi{L \to U}[1: K - L] The first L members are from the lower anchor; the next K-L are the first entries from the upper anchor's entry sequence. Shared Member Interpolation: For shared members i \le L: t = \frac{K - L}{U - L} \thetai(K) = (1 - t^p)\thetai(L) + t^p \thetai(U) where p > 0 controls the trajectory. p=1 is linear; p<1 approaches the upper state earlier; p>1 approaches it later. Entering Member Opacity Gating: For entering members L < i \le K: ai(K) = \text{clip}(t^q ai(U), \epsilon, 1 - \epsilon) where ai(U) = \sigma(oi(U)) is the upper-anchor opacity, q > 0 controls activation speed, t^q is the normalized progress weight, and \epsilon is a clipping epsilon. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def clip(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) def logit(x): return math.log(x / (1.0 - x)) def restoreendpoint(K, fullmodel, residual): # Adds residual to the first K rows of the full model return [fullmodel[i] + residual[i] for i in range(K)] def paretogsdecode(K, fullmodel, residualatlas, exponents, memberorder, anchorbudgets): """ Decode a 3DGS model with exactly K Gaussians. Args: K: Target number of Gaussians. fullmodel: Parameter matrix ThetaN of the full model (list of lists). residualatlas: List of encoded residuals Deltaj for each anchor. exponents: List of (p, q) tuples for each interval. memberorder: Global nested order of member indices. anchorbudgets: List of anchor budget counts [K1, K2,..., KM]. Returns: ThetaK: Parameter matrix for K Gaussians. """ # 1. Identify surrounding anchors L and U such that KL <= K <= KU Lidx = 0 Uidx = len(anchorbudgets) - 1 for i in range(len(anchorbudgets) - 1): if anchorbudgets[i] <= K <= anchorbudgets[i+1]: Lidx, Uidx = i, i+1 break L = anchorbudgets[Lidx] U = anchorbudgets[Uidx] # 2. Restore endpoint parameters for L and U ThetaL = restoreendpoint(L, fullmodel, residualatlas[Lidx]) ThetaU = restoreendpoint(U, fullmodel, residualatlas[Uidx]) # 3. Determine membership S(K) sharedindices = memberorder[0:L] enteringindices = memberorder[L:K] ThetaK = [] # 4. Interpolate shared members t = (K - L) / (U - L) p = exponents[Lidx][0] for i in range(L): thetaLi = ThetaL[i] thetaUi = ThetaU[i] thetainterp = [(1 - tp) thetaLi[d] + (tp) thetaUi[d] for d in range(len(thetaLi))] ThetaK.append(thetainterp) # 5. Handle entering members q = exponents[Lidx][1] epsilon = 1e-4 for j, idx in enumerate(enteringindices): thetaUidx = ThetaU[L + j] oU = thetaUidx[3] # opacity logit index is 3 (x, s, r, o, c) aU = sigmoid(oU) tq = tq aK = clip(tq aU, epsilon, 1 - epsilon) oK = logit(aK) thetaKentry = thetaUidx.copy() thetaKentry[3] = oK ThetaK.append(thetaKentry) return ThetaK Anchor Schedule: 11 anchors, \rhoj \in \{0.001, \dots, 1\}. Interpolation Exponent p: Calibrated per interval. Default search grid in Appendix A. Opacity Gating Exponent q: Calibrated per interval. q > 0. Clipping Epsilon \epsilon: Small value, e.g., 10^{-4}. Training Iterations: 30K for Full model; 25K total per anchor stage. Precision: FP16 for calibration residual anchor states; half precision for anchor coefficients and quantization scales. Precision: Quantization of residuals introduces encoding error. Anchor-budget requests incur this error, but interval decoding does not add further estimation error. Boundary Conditions: At K=L, t=0, shared members use \theta(L), and no entering members exist. At K=U, t=1, shared members use \theta(U), and all U-L members are entering with full opacity. Degenerate Input: If K is outside [K{min}, N], the method is undefined. The method assumes N is the count of the fully trained model. Time Complexity: Offline Construction: Mean offline time of ~10.3 minutes across 13 scenes, significantly faster than CLOD-3DGS (~35 min) and MGS (~74 min). Runtime: Parameter generation at runtime takes O(K) work for fixed parameter dimension. Memory Complexity: Storage: Encoding reduces mean additional state from 390.0 MB to 85.7 MB across 13 scenes. FlexGS Module: FlexGS-imp uses a fixed ~30 MB budget module. Performance: Quality: ParetoGS attains better average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS with fewer Gaussians than compared prefix methods at 10% of each method’s own full model across 13 scenes. Low Budgets: At 1% budget, ParetoGS achieves 24.40 dB PSNR vs 18.84 dB for NanoGS-imp. At 0.1% budget, ParetoGS achieves 21.15 dB PSNR, 0.580 SSIM, and 0.539 LPIPS, outperforming NanoGS-imp. Scaling: Quality degrades gracefully with decreasing K, outperforming CLOD-3DGS and MGS at low retention ratios. Strengths: Continuous budget support without per-budget optimization. High quality at very low budgets (0.1%). Compact storage overhead. Limitations: Requires initial full model training. Encoding error from quantization. Calibration required for each interval. Origin: ParetoGS was introduced by Xiaobin et al.. The paper "ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors" presents the method as a solution to the inefficiency of pruning and re-optimizing for each budget in 3DGS. History and Development: The method builds on 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023) and ImprovedGS (Deng et al., 2026). It addresses limitations of existing scalable methods like FlexGS (Liu et al., 2025a), NanoGS (Xiong et al., 2026), and SCAR-GS (Revilla et al., 2026) by explicitly optimizing nested anchors and connecting their states. Usage: ParetoGS is used for efficient 3DGS representation where multiple resolution levels or budget constraints are required, such as in real-time rendering or streaming applications. name: Multi-stage and Progressive Training
head: Progressive Optimization, Stage-wise Training, On-the-Fly Training
body: Multi-stage and Progressive Training refers to a family of optimization strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that decouple the learning process into discrete temporal or resolution-based phases. This approach solves the instability, convergence difficulties, and computational bottlenecks associated with optimizing complex geometric, appearance, and deformation parameters simultaneously from sparse or random initializations. Unlike single-stage training, these methods separate coarse initialization or stable generation from fine-grained refinement, allowing each stage to focus on a specific subset of parameters or resolution levels. The core mechanism involves partitioning the optimization trajectory into sequential stages or phases. Common principles include: 1. Parameter Decoupling: Differentiating between static geometry, dynamic deformation, or compression bottlenecks to prevent conflicting gradient updates. 2. Progressive Refinement: Starting with low-resolution, sparse, or coarse representations and incrementally increasing complexity, resolution, or parameter count. 3. Stabilization: Using preliminary phases to establish a stable baseline (e.g., static geometry or initial Gaussian placement) before introducing more complex components like deformation fields or quantized codecs. 4. Resource Allocation: Dynamically adjusting computational effort (iterations, learning rates) based on the importance or overlap of incoming data, particularly in streaming contexts. Two-stage optimization decouples the optimization landscape into distinct phases to improve stability, convergence speed, or representation fidelity. It addresses the difficulty of simultaneously optimizing complex geometric parameters, appearance codes, and compression bottlenecks. Low-Resolution to Full-Resolution (3DGR-CT): Used for sparse-view CT reconstruction. Stage 1 optimizes Gaussians on a coarse 1/2 \times 1/2 \times 1/2 volume grid to rapidly place primitives using L2 projection loss. Stage 2 expands to the full-resolution grid, using Stage 1 results as initialization to refine fine details. Initial Geometry/Appearance then Decomposition (GS-IR): Used for inverse rendering. Stage 1 (30,000 iterations, Adam) optimizes geometry (\mathbf{T}) and appearance (\mathbf{A}) with L1 color and normal losses. Stage 2 (10,000 iterations) fixes \mathbf{T} and \mathbf{A} to optimize material (\mathbf{M}) and lighting, preventing material/lighting ambiguity. Codec-Free to Codec-Aware (CodecSplat): Used for ultra-compact latent coding. Stage 1 trains the feed-forward pipeline without the feature codec to stabilize generation. Stage 2 initializes from Stage 1, enables the codec, and optimizes codec-related modules while fixing the backbone, using a rate-distortion loss with sampled \lambda \in [16, 1024]. This method optimizes 3DGS fields in a streaming context, enabling near real-time reconstruction as new images arrive. It solves the problem of incremental scene expansion by decoupling optimization into three phases: initial sparse training, progressive incremental updates, and final global refinement. Phase 1: Trains an initial 3DGS field on the first N0=30 images for 2,000 iterations to prevent overfitting. Phase 2: For each new image, updates poses via local Bundle Adjustment, initializes new Gaussians from sparse points exceeding a distance threshold, and performs hierarchical weighting of training images. It allocates TI=200 iterations: Nm=10 top-weighted images get local optimization, while others get semi-global updates. Learning rates are adapted based on training progress and overlap. Phase 3: Performs global Bundle Adjustment and rapid additional optimization after all images are acquired. The warm-up stage initializes 3D Gaussians before optimizing higher-order representations, such as 4D Gaussians, to prevent convergence difficulties when SfM point initialization is absent. It serves as a coarse optimization phase that stabilizes the learning of deformation fields and suppresses transient distractors. It involves static optimization of 3D Gaussian parameters and keeping a subset of Gaussians in the dynamic part to release pressure on the deformation network. POD Pretraining is a distillation-based amortized optimization procedure that stabilizes the training of multi-stage residual Gaussian predictors by supervising them with locally refined Gaussian targets instead of unstable image-space gradients. It solves the problem of training collapse caused by the non-unique inverse mapping from residual images to Gaussian parameters. Unlike direct image-space supervision, which leads to divergence, or sibling methods like Two-stage Optimization that separate static and dynamic components, POD stabilizes stage-wise training by refining predicted Gaussian increments with a short-horizon optimizer and distilling the result back into the predictor as a regression target. A prediction mode where Gaussian primitives are accumulated progressively across multiple stages rather than predicted in a single shot, allowing for controllable trade-offs between reconstruction quality and representation compactness. Definition: The stage-wise model uses a patch size (ps) of 14, compared to ps=7 for the one-shot baseline. Performance: On DIV2K, the stage-wise predictor reaches 26.54 dB PSNR with 12,690 Gaussians at Stage 4, compared to the one-shot baseline (ps=7) which reaches 26.58 dB PSNR with 14,528 Gaussians. PSNR increases from 21.91 dB (Stage 1) to 26.54 dB (Stage 4), with Gaussians increasing from 3,658 to 12,690. Comparison: Compared to one-shot prediction, stage-wise prediction does not clearly improve final reconstruction quality but enables explicit control over the number of activated Gaussians, allowing adjustment of the quality-compactness trade-off. Multi-stage and progressive training strategies have emerged as essential components in advanced 3D Gaussian Splatting applications, particularly where standard single-stage optimization fails due to complexity or data constraints. Two-stage approaches were introduced to handle specific challenges in inverse rendering (GS-IR) and ultra-compact compression (CodecSplat), as well as sparse-view CT reconstruction (3DGR-CT). The concept of progressive training was adapted for streaming scenarios in On-the-Fly GS and for stabilizing dynamic 4D Gaussian representations through warm-up stages. More recently, POD Pretraining was developed to stabilize the training of feed-forward residual predictors in amortized reconstruction frameworks (AIR). These methods collectively address the limitations of end-to-end optimization in complex, dynamic, or resource-constrained environments.
