name: Two-stage Optimization
head: Full-Resolution Refinement, GS-IR Training Process, Low-Resolution Optimization
body: Two-stage optimization is a training strategy that partitions the optimization trajectory of 3D Gaussian Splatting into sequential phases to resolve conflicting gradient updates or stabilize unstable learning processes. It typically begins with a coarse or codec-free phase to establish stable geometry or initial placement, followed by a fine-grained or codec-aware phase to refine details or optimize rate-distortion performance. This approach builds on Multi-stage and Progressive Training by decoupling parameter optimization into distinct stages, preventing the interference between coarse structural learning and fine-detail refinement. The method adapts its specific inputs, outputs, and formulas based on the target application (CT reconstruction, inverse rendering, or compression), but consistently follows a two-phase structure: a stabilization/coarse phase and a refinement/detail phase. Inputs: Context views (images/depth), camera poses, and potentially target views for supervision. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} with optimized parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color/material) and, in compression variants, a compact bitstream or latent representation. The data structures depend on the variant: 1. Grid-based (CT): A 3D voxel grid where Gaussians are initialized. Stage 1 uses a subsampled grid (e.g., 1/2 \times 1/2 \times 1/2 of original resolution). Stage 2 uses the full-resolution grid. 2. Feed-Forward (CodecSplat): A feature tensor Fg \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times CF \times H \times W} generated by a multi-view encoder. Stage 1 predicts Gaussians G{cf} directly from Fg and encoder-side depth D{enc}. Stage 2 introduces a feature codec and post-codec refiner to produce decoded Gaussians \hat{G}. 3. Inverse Rendering (GS-IR): Geometric parameters T = \{p, s, q, n\} (position, scale, rotation, normal) and appearance parameters A. Stage 1 optimizes T and A. Stage 2 fixes T and A to optimize material parameters M = \{a, \rho, m\} (albedo, roughness, metalness). Variant 1: Low-Resolution to Full-Resolution (CT Reconstruction) 1. Stage 1 (Low-Resolution Optimization): Sample a low-resolution grid, specifically 1/2 \times 1/2 \times 1/2 of the original volume. Initialize Gaussians on this grid. Minimize the projection loss using the L2 norm between projected data \hat{p} and actual measurements p: \min{\thetai} \left\| \hat{p}[V(\theta)] - p \right\|2^2 where V(\theta) is the discretized volume defined by Gaussian parameters \theta. This rapidly places Gaussians in approximately correct positions. 2. Stage 2 (Full-Resolution Refinement): Sample over all voxels of the original full-resolution volume. Refine Gaussian parameters to capture fine-grained details. Continue minimizing the same projection loss to achieve high-quality reconstruction. Variant 2: Codec-Free to Codec-Aware (Compression) 1. Stage 1 (Codec-Free Gaussian Generation): Train the feed-forward Gaussian generation pipeline without the feature codec. Predict the codec-free Gaussian set G{cf} from the refined feature Fc and encoder-side depth D{enc}. Render the target view \hat{Y}{tcf} = \text{Render}(G{cf}, Kt, Tt). Minimize the rendering reconstruction loss: L{\text{stage1}} = D{\text{render}}(\hat{Y}{tcf}, Yt) where Yt is the target-view image and D{\text{render}} is the reconstruction loss metric. 2. Stage 2 (Codec-Aware Latent Coding): Initialize from the Stage 1 checkpoint. Enable the feature codec and post-codec refiner. Optimize codec-related modules while keeping remaining backbone modules fixed. Decode the Gaussian set \hat{G} and render the target view \hat{Y}t = \text{Render}(\hat{G}, Kt, Tt). Minimize the rate-distortion objective: L{\text{stage2}}(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda{\max}} \left[ D{\text{render}}(\hat{Y}t, Yt) + \gamma D{\text{codec-depth}} \right] + \beta R where R is the estimated rate, \lambda \in [16, 1024] is sampled during training (fixed at test time), \lambda{\max} = 1024, \gamma = 0.1 is the codec-side depth supervision weight, and \beta is the rate penalty weight (10^{-4} for DL3DV, 4 \times 10^{-4} for RE10K). The codec-side depth loss is defined on normalized inverse depth: D{\text{codec-depth}} = \| S - S{enc} \|1 where S is the decoder-side normalized inverse-depth map and S{enc} is the supervision target. S{enc} is computed from encoder-side depth D{enc}: S{enc,i}(p) = \frac{D{enc,i}(p)^{-1} - fi^{-1}}{ni^{-1} - fi^{-1}} where ni and fi are the near and far bounds of context view i. Variant 3: Initial Geometry to Material Decomposition (Inverse Rendering) 1. Stage 1 (Initial Optimization): Minimize color reconstruction loss Lc and normal loss Ln to optimize geometric parameters T and appearance A for 30,000 iterations. The normal loss Ln includes a total variation (TV) smoothing term: Ln = L{n-p} + \lambda{n-TV} \text{TV}{\text{normal}} where \lambda{n-TV} = 5.0. 2. Stage 2 (Decomposition): Fix T and A. Minimize the decomposition loss Ld to optimize material parameters M for 10,000 iterations. The decomposition loss is: Ld = \underbrace{\| I - \hat{I}{\text{shade}}(\hat{M}, \hat{E}, V{\text{illu}}) \|}{L{\text{shade}}} + \lambdaM \text{TV}{\text{mat}} + \lambdaE \text{TV}{\text{light}} where \lambdaM = 1.0 and \lambdaE = 0.01. \text{TV}{\text{mat}} and \text{TV}{\text{light}} are total variation smoothing terms for material and light maps, respectively. Optimizers: Adam or AdamW. Learning Rate: 10^{-4} with weight decay 0.01 (AdamW). Iterations: 30,000 for Stage 1 and 10,000 for Stage 2 in GS-IR. Not specified for CT or CodecSplat in the provided notes. Hardware: Single NVIDIA V100 GPU (GS-IR); Four NVIDIA RTX 5880 48GB GPUs (CodecSplat). Instability: Directly training with a quantized bottleneck is unstable; the two-stage separation is required to stabilize Gaussian generation before introducing compression artifacts. Gradient Conflicts: Fixing parameters in Stage 2 (e.g., geometry in GS-IR) prevents conflicting gradient updates between geometry and material optimization. Rate Selection: In CodecSplat, \lambda must be sampled during training to cover the rate-distortion curve, but fixed at test time for a specific bit-rate. Defines the optimization for Relightable 3D Gaussians (R3DG), using normal gradient-based densification in Stage 1 and PBR-specific losses in Stage 2 to recover geometry, material, and lighting. Time Complexity: Two-stage optimization generally increases total training time compared to single-stage methods due to the sequential nature of the phases. However, Stage 1's low-resolution or codec-free setup can accelerate initial convergence. Memory Complexity: Stage 1 in CT reconstruction uses reduced memory by operating on a subsampled grid (1/8 of voxels). CodecSplat reduces final storage to KiB-level bitstreams. Performance: CT: Achieves accurate sparse-view reconstruction by refining details in Stage 2. Compression: CodecSplat achieves KiB-level scene bitstreams while preserving dominant scene structure, outperforming MiB-level compressed baselines. Inverse Rendering: GS-IR achieves high-quality inverse rendering by decoupling geometry and material optimization. Strengths: Stabilizes training for complex objectives (compression, inverse rendering); prevents gradient conflicts; enables high-fidelity reconstruction. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stage transitions and hyperparameters (e.g., \lambda, \gamma, \beta); increased training duration. Two-stage optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged to address specific challenges in compression and inverse rendering. CodecSplat introduced the codec-free/codec-aware split to stabilize feed-forward Gaussian generation with quantized bottlenecks. GS-IR separated geometry and material optimization to enable inverse rendering with physically based rendering. The low-resolution to full-resolution approach was used in 3DGR-CT to handle sparse-view CT reconstruction efficiently. 3DGR-CT: Sparse-view CT reconstruction with a 3D Gaussian representation, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2025.103585, fetched 2026-10-26 GS-IR: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02045, fetched 2026-10-26 CodecSplat: Ultra-Compact Latent Coding for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25563, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Two-stage training procedure for Relightable 3D Gaussians
head: R3DG training, inverse rendering optimization stages
body: This method defines the optimization protocol for Relightable 3D Gaussians (R3DG), reconstructing relightable scenes from multi-view images by combining standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering with physically based rendering (PBR) and BRDF decomposition. It recovers geometry, material properties (albedo, roughness), and lighting from static multi-view inputs to enable novel view synthesis and relighting. It differs from vanilla 3DGS by introducing normal gradient-based densification in the first stage and PBR-specific loss terms in the second stage, while maintaining a discrete point-based representation unlike neural relightable methods. The training procedure is divided into two stages. Stage 1 optimizes the scene for 30,000 iterations following 3DGS settings, augmented with normal gradient-based densification. Stage 2 optimizes the scene for 10,000 iterations, sampling incident rays per Gaussian point for PBR evaluation. Inputs: Multi-view images of a static scene. Camera poses for each input view. Initial 3D Gaussian points, typically derived from Structure-from-Motion. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian attributes: position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, normal vectors, albedo, roughness, and environment map parameters. The method operates on a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i maintains attributes including position \mathbf{p}i, covariance matrix \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}i, normal vector \mathbf{n}i, albedo \mathbf{a}i, roughness \rhoi, and environment map parameters. The exact memory layout or bit-packing of these attributes is not specified in the sources. Stage 1: Geometry and Normal Optimization 1. Initialize the 3D Gaussians. 2. Iterate for 30,000 iterations. 3. Densification: Perform normal gradient-based densification using threshold Tn = 2 \times 10^{-9}. 4. Rendering: Render the scene from the input camera views using standard 3DGS alpha-blending. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using Equation (16): \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{ssim} \mathcal{L}{ssim} + \lambdan \mathcal{L}n + \lambda{s,n} \mathcal{L}{s,n} + \lambdaO \mathcal{L}O + \lambdau \mathcal{L}u Where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss, \mathcal{L}{ssim} is the SSIM loss, \mathcal{L}n is the normal loss, \mathcal{L}{s,n} is the surface normal smoothness loss, \mathcal{L}O is the opacity loss, and \mathcal{L}u is an auxiliary loss. 6. Update: Backpropagate and update Gaussian attributes using an optimizer. Stage 2: PBR and Material Optimization 1. Iterate for 10,000 iterations. 2. Ray Sampling: Sample Ns = 64 incident rays per Gaussian point for PBR. 3. Rendering: Render the scene using the PBR model with sampled lighting and material properties. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using Equation (17): \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{ssim} \mathcal{L}{ssim} + \lambdal \mathcal{L}l + \lambda{s,b} \mathcal{L}{s,b} + \lambda{s,r} \mathcal{L}{s,r} Where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss, \mathcal{L}{ssim} is the SSIM loss, \mathcal{L}l is the lighting loss, \mathcal{L}{s,b} is the BRDF base color smoothness loss, and \mathcal{L}{s,r} is the BRDF roughness smoothness loss. 5. Update: Backpropagate and update Gaussian attributes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainr3dg(inputimages, cameraposes, initialgaussians, numiterationsstage1=30000, numiterationsstage2=10000): gaussians = initialgaussians Tn = 2e-9 Ns = 64 lambda1 = 0.8 lambdassim = 0.2 lambdan = 0.01 lambdasn = 0.01 lambdaO = 0.01 lambdau = 0.01 lambdal = 0.0001 lambdasb = 0.01 lambdasr = 0.01 optimizer = Adam(gaussians.parameters()) # # Stage 1: Geometry and Normal Optimization for i in range(numiterationsstage1): viewidx = random.randint(0, len(inputimages) - 1) gtimage = inputimages[viewidx] pose = cameraposes[viewidx] # Normal gradient-based densification for g in gaussians: gradmag = computenormalgradientmagnitude(g) if gradmag > Tn: densifygaussian(gaussians, g) renderedimage = render3dgs(gaussians, pose) lossl1 = computel1loss(renderedimage, gtimage) lossssim = computessimloss(renderedimage, gtimage) lossn = computenormalloss(gaussians) losssn = computesurfacenormalsmoothness(gaussians) losso = computeopacityloss(gaussians) lossu = computeauxiliaryloss(gaussians) lossstage1 = (lambda1 lossl1 + lambdassim lossssim + lambdan lossn + lambdasn losssn + lambdaO losso + lambdau lossu) lossstage1.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 2: PBR and Material Optimization for i in range(numiterationsstage2): viewidx = random.randint(0, len(inputimages) - 1) gtimage = inputimages[viewidx] pose = cameraposes[viewidx] incidentrays = sampleincidentrays(gaussians, Ns) renderedpbrimage = renderpbr(gaussians, pose, incidentrays) lossl1 = computel1loss(renderedpbrimage, gtimage) lossssim = computessimloss(renderedpbrimage, gtimage) lossl = computelightingloss(gaussians, incidentrays) losssb = computebrdfsmoothnessbase(gaussians) losssr = computebrdfsmoothnessroughness(gaussians) lossstage2 = (lambda1 lossl1 + lambdassim lossssim + lambdal lossl + lambdasb losssb + lambdasr losssr) lossstage2.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return gaussians def computenormalgradientmagnitude(g): return norm(g.normalgradient) def densifygaussian(gaussians, g): # Clone or split Gaussian based on normal gradient magnitude pass def render3dgs(gaussians, pose): # Standard 3DGS alpha-blending projection and rasterization pass def computel1loss(rendered, gt): return mean(abs(rendered - gt)) def computessimloss(rendered, gt): return 1.0 - structuredssim(rendered, gt) def computenormalloss(gaussians): # Enforce consistency between rendered and estimated normals pass def computesurfacenormalsmoothness(gaussians): # Penalize discontinuities in adjacent Gaussian normals pass def computeopacityloss(gaussians): # Regularize opacity values pass def computeauxiliaryloss(gaussians): # Additional regularization terms pass def sampleincidentrays(gaussians, Ns): # Sample Ns directions per Gaussian for PBR evaluation pass def renderpbr(gaussians, pose, incidentrays): # Evaluate PBR model with sampled rays and material properties pass def computelightingloss(gaussians, incidentrays): # Consistency loss for estimated environment map/lighting pass def computebrdfsmoothnessbase(gaussians): # Smoothness regularization for albedo/base color pass def computebrdfsmoothnessroughness(gaussians): # Smoothness regularization for roughness pass Tn: Normal gradient densification threshold, set to 2 \times 10^{-9}. Ns: Number of incident rays sampled per Gaussian point for PBR in Stage 2, set to 64. \lambda1: L1 loss weight, set to 0.8 for both stages. \lambda{ssim}: SSIM loss weight, set to 0.2 for both stages. \lambdan, \lambda{s,n}, \lambdaO, \lambdau: Stage 1 auxiliary loss weights, each set to 0.01. \lambdal: Stage 2 lighting loss weight, set to 0.0001. \lambda{s,b}, \lambda{s,r}: Stage 2 BRDF loss weights, each set to 0.01. Large-scale scenes: The high density of points in large scenes can slow down optimization significantly because rays are sampled and PBR is performed at each point. This is a limitation of the current pipeline. Static objects only: The method is designed for static objects; dynamic scenes are not supported. Precision: The normal gradient threshold Tn is very small (2 \times 10^{-9}), requiring careful numerical implementation to avoid noise-induced densification or failure to densify. A multi-stage optimization strategy that decomposes scene geometry, appearance (albedo), and illumination from multi-view images using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It prevents overfitting to appearance details and stabilizes lighting parameter learning by decoupling geometry, albedo, and lighting optimization into distinct phases. It builds on this method by extending the decomposition to include explicit lighting priors and a three-stage refinement process. Time Complexity: The method requires 40,000 total iterations (30,000 in Stage 1, 10,000 in Stage 2). Stage 2 is computationally more expensive per iteration due to ray sampling (Ns=64) and PBR evaluation. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians. High point density required for accurate PBR leads to high memory consumption, especially in large scenes. Measured Performance: On the Synthetic4Relight dataset, R3DG achieves NVS PSNR 36.80, SSIM 0.982, LPIPS 0.028. Relighting PSNR 31.00, SSIM 0.964, LPIPS 0.050. Albedo PSNR 28.31, SSIM 0.951, LPIPS 0.058. Training time 0.90 hours. Scaling: Performance degrades or optimization slows down in large-scale scenes due to point density. Strengths: Excels in relighting capability compared to point-based methods. Shows significantly better NVS quality than other relightable methods. Achieves realistic PBR rendering, smooth normal estimation, and accurate visibility on discrete point clouds. Limitations: NVS performance slightly trails vanilla 3DGS. Limited to static objects. High point density slows optimization in large scenes. When to use: For inverse rendering and relighting of static objects from multi-view images where high-quality relighting and material recovery are prioritized over raw NVS PSNR. When not to use: For large-scale dynamic scenes or when vanilla 3DGS NVS performance is the sole metric of interest. The method was introduced in the paper "Relightable 3D Gaussians: Realistic Point Cloud Relighting with BRDF Decomposition and Ray Tracing" by J. Gao et al.. It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and extends it with PBR capabilities. The work was supported by the National Key R&D Program of China and NSFC. Relightable 3D Gaussians: Realistic Point Cloud Relighting with BRDF Decomposition and Ray Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72995-95, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Progressive Training Strategy for Gaussian Splatting Decomposition
head: Multi-stage optimization for intrinsic decomposition, Staged optimization for geometry, albedo, and lighting
body: This method is a multi-stage optimization strategy designed to decompose scene geometry, appearance (albedo), and illumination from multi-view images using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It prevents the model from overfitting to appearance details and stabilizes the learning of lighting parameters by decoupling the optimization of geometry, albedo, and lighting into distinct phases. It builds on Two-stage training procedure for Relightable 3D Gaussians by extending the decomposition to include explicit lighting priors and a three-stage refinement process. The method optimizes a set of 3D Gaussians to represent the scene, decomposing them into geometric attributes (position, covariance, opacity) and non-geometric attributes (albedo, view-dependent appearance). The optimization is divided into three sequential stages to ensure stable convergence. Inputs: A set of multi-view images of the scene. Camera poses for each input image. (Optional) Semantic masks for the input images. (Optional) Ground truth normal maps for synthetic scenes. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian attributes: Geometry: Position \mathbf{p}k, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}k, opacity \alphak. Appearance: Albedo \mathbf{c}{a,k}, view-dependent coefficients (if applicable). Embeddings: Per-Gaussian embedding \Lambdak and per-image embedding \Xij. Lighting parameters: Sunlight direction and color, ambient irradiance map. The appearance transformation module uses an MLP f{app} to map embeddings to appearance. Per-Gaussian embedding \Lambdak: Size 24. Per-image embedding \Xij: Size 32. Appearance MLP f{app}: One hidden layer of size 128. The total loss is a weighted sum of several components: L = \lambda1 (L1 + L{D-SSIM}) + \lambda2 (L{normal} + L{distortion}) + \lambda3 L{np} + \lambda4 L{mask} + \lambda5 L{sp} + \lambda6 L{amb} Where: L1: L1 loss between rendered and ground truth images. L{D-SSIM}: D-SSIM loss for rendered images. L{normal}: Normal consistency loss. L{distortion}: Distortion loss. L{np}: Normal prior loss. L{mask}: Semantic mask loss. L{sp}: Sunlight color prior loss. L{amb}: Ambient irradiance map loss. \lambda1 = 1.0 for L1 and L{D-SSIM}. \lambda2 = 0.05 for L{normal} and L{distortion}. \lambda3 = 0.1 for L{np}. \lambda4 = 0.1 for L{mask}. \lambda5 = 10.0 for L{sp}, decaying to 0.01 over 50,000 iterations. \lambda6 = 1.0 for L{amb}. The training proceeds in three stages: 1. Stage 1: Geometry Optimization Optimize only geometry-related Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity). Non-geometric attributes are initialized but not optimized. This stage establishes a robust geometric foundation. 2. Stage 2: Albedo and Lighting Decomposition Freeze all geometry-related Gaussian attributes. Stage 2a (Iterations 0–10,000): Omit shading from the rendering process. This allows the model to learn an initial, refined albedo without being influenced by lighting variations. Optimize non-geometric Gaussian attributes (albedo, embeddings). Stage 2b (Iterations 10,000–50,000): Freeze all Gaussian attributes, including the newly learned albedo. Optimize only lighting parameters (sunlight direction/color, ambient irradiance). This isolates lighting optimization, preventing interference from appearance updates. 3. Stage 3: Joint Fine-tuning Iterations 50,000–100,000: Unfreeze non-geometric Gaussian attributes and lighting parameters. Jointly optimize all non-geometric attributes and lighting parameters. Geometry remains frozen. This stage fine-tunes the decomposition, allowing albedo and lighting to adjust to each other. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivetraininggaussiandecomposition(images, poses, numiterations=100000): """ Implements the three-stage progressive training strategy for Gaussian Splatting decomposition. """ # Initialization gaussians = initialize3dgaussians() # Positions, covariances, opacities, albedos, embeddings lighting = initializelighting() # Sunlight direction/color, ambient irradiance # Hyperparameters lambda1 = 1.0 lambda2 = 0.05 lambda3 = 0.1 lambda4 = 0.1 lambda5start = 10.0 lambda5end = 0.01 lambda6 = 1.0 # Stage 1: Geometry Optimization # Optimize only geometry-related attributes for i in range(10000): # Assuming equal stage lengths for simplicity, adjust as needed # Freeze non-geometry attributes gaussians.albedo.requiresgrad = False gaussians.embeddings.requiresgrad = False lighting.requiresgrad = False # Forward pass with shading renderedimage = render(gaussians, lighting, poses) # Compute losses loss = computelosses(renderedimage, images, gaussians, lighting, lambda1, lambda2, lambda3, lambda4, lambda5start, lambda6, shadingenabled=True) # Backward pass loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 2a: Albedo Learning (No Shading) # Freeze geometry, optimize albedo/embeddings, no shading for i in range(10000, 20000): # Freeze geometry gaussians.position.requiresgrad = False gaussians.covariance.requiresgrad = False gaussians.opacity.requiresgrad = False # Freeze lighting lighting.requiresgrad = False # Forward pass WITHOUT shading renderedimage = render(gaussians, lighting, poses, shadingenabled=False) # Compute losses (shading-related lighting losses may be skipped or modified) loss = computelosses(renderedimage, images, gaussians, lighting, lambda1, lambda2, lambda3, lambda4, lambda5start, lambda6, shadingenabled=False) # Backward pass loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 2b: Lighting Optimization # Freeze all Gaussian attributes, optimize lighting only for i in range(20000, 60000): # Freeze all Gaussian attributes gaussians.position.requiresgrad = False gaussians.covariance.requiresgrad = False gaussians.opacity.requiresgrad = False gaussians.albedo.requiresgrad = False gaussians.embeddings.requiresgrad = False # Forward pass with shading renderedimage = render(gaussians, lighting, poses, shadingenabled=True) # Compute losses # Decay lambda5 over iterations progress = (i - 20000) / 40000.0 lambda5current = lambda5start + (lambda5end - lambda5start) progress loss = computelosses(renderedimage, images, gaussians, lighting, lambda1, lambda2, lambda3, lambda4, lambda5current, lambda6, shadingenabled=True) # Backward pass loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 3: Joint Fine-tuning # Optimize non-geometry attributes and lighting for i in range(60000, 110000): # Adjusted to match 50k iterations mentioned in source # Geometry remains frozen gaussians.position.requiresgrad = False gaussians.covariance.requiresgrad = False gaussians.opacity.requiresgrad = False # Forward pass with shading renderedimage = render(gaussians, lighting, poses, shadingenabled=True) # Compute losses # Continue decay of lambda5 if needed, or keep at end value progress = (i - 60000) / 50000.0 lambda5current = lambda5end # Or continue decay if source implies it loss = computelosses(renderedimage, images, gaussians, lighting, lambda1, lambda2, lambda3, lambda4, lambda5current, lambda6, shadingenabled=True) # Backward pass loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() def computelosses(rendered, groundtruth, gaussians, lighting, l1w, l2w, l3w, l4w, l5w, l6w, shadingenabled): """ Computes the total loss based on the specified weights and components. """ lossl1 = l1w L1Loss(rendered, groundtruth) lossdssim = l1w DSSIMLoss(rendered, groundtruth) lossnormal = l2w NormalConsistencyLoss(gaussians) lossdistortion = l2w DistortionLoss(gaussians) lossnp = l3w NormalPriorLoss(gaussians) lossmask = l4w SemanticMaskLoss(rendered, groundtruthmasks) # Assuming masks available losssp = l5w SunlightColorPriorLoss(lighting) lossamb = l6w AmbientIrradianceMapLoss(lighting) totalloss = lossl1 + lossdssim + lossnormal + lossdistortion + lossnp + lossmask + losssp + lossamb return totalloss Time Complexity: The method requires a total of 100,000 iterations (10k + 10k + 40k + 50k). The per-iteration cost is similar to standard 3DGS but with additional loss computations for normals and lighting priors. Memory Complexity: Uses standard 3DGS memory plus storage for per-Gaussian (size 24) and per-image (size 32) embeddings, and an MLP for appearance transformation. Performance: On synthetic SOL-NeRF datasets, it achieves competitive PSNR and SSIM scores compared to baselines like LumiGauss, ReCap, and SOL-NeRF. Strengths: Stabilizes lighting optimization, prevents overfitting to appearance, and produces high-quality intrinsic decomposition. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stage durations and loss weights. Performance on real-world datasets may vary due to lack of ground truth normals/texture. The method is part of the ROS-GS (Relightable Outdoor Scenes With Gaussian Splatting) framework. It addresses the challenge of decomposing relightable scenes from multi-view images by introducing a progressive training strategy that separates the optimization of geometry, albedo, and lighting. This approach builds upon earlier works in differentiable rendering and Gaussian Splatting, such as Two-stage training procedure for Relightable 3D Gaussians, by adding more granular control over the decomposition process. name: On-the-Fly GS Progressive Training
head: On-the-Fly Gaussian Splatting
body: On-the-Fly GS Progressive Training is a method for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) fields in a streaming or sequential input context, enabling near real-time reconstruction as new images arrive. It solves the problem of incremental scene expansion without retraining the entire model from scratch, which is computationally prohibitive for large-scale or dynamic capture scenarios. Unlike offline training methods that process all images simultaneously, this approach partitions the optimization trajectory into sequential phases, using hierarchical image weighting and adaptive learning rates to prioritize new data while maintaining consistency with previously registered views. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Two-stage Optimization by integrating densification and pose refinement directly into the per-image incremental update loop, rather than separating geometry initialization from appearance optimization. Inputs: A sequence of incoming RGB images. An initial sparse point cloud and camera poses estimated by an On-the-Fly SfM module. The current 3DGS field (set of Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients). Outputs: An updated 3DGS field optimized for the newly acquired image and its neighbors. Updated camera poses and sparse point cloud via local Bundle Adjustment (BA). 3DGS Field: Standard 3DGS representation. Each Gaussian g has position \mathbf{p}, rotation \mathbf{q}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, and SH coefficients \mathbf{c}. Sparse Point Cloud: A set of 3D points \mathbf{X} with associated depths and colors, used for initializing new Gaussians. Search Tree: A spatial index (e.g., KD-tree or Octree) built over the existing sparse point cloud to efficiently query distances for new points. Image Overlap Matrix M: A matrix where M{i,j} stores the number of matched feature points between image i and image j. Training State: Per-image counters for iterations trained (Tj) and current learning rates (\etaj). 1. Initialization: Wait until N0 initial images are acquired. 2. SfM: Run On-the-Fly SfM to estimate poses and generate a sparse point cloud for these N0 images. 3. Training: Train the initial 3DGS field using the standard 3DGS rendering and optimization pipeline for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 2,000). This prevents overfitting to the small initial subset. For each newly acquired image n: 1. Pose and Cloud Update: On-the-Fly SfM estimates the pose of image n and performs local BA to optimize poses of neighboring images, refining the sparse point cloud. 2. Search Tree Construction: Build a search tree over the current sparse point cloud. 3. New Point Identification: Query the sparse points from image n against the search tree. Points with a shortest distance to the existing cloud exceeding a predefined threshold are classified as "newly added". 4. Gaussian Initialization: Initialize new Gaussians at the locations of these newly added points. Append them to the current 3DGS field. 5. Hierarchical Image Weighting: Calculate weights for training images based on their overlap with the new image n: Layer 1 (New Image): Weight \omega{11} = 1. Layer 2 (Direct Overlap): For images i with direct overlap (M{i,n} \neq 0), calculate weight: \omega{2i} = M{i,n} where M{i,n} is the number of matched feature points between image i and new image n. Layer k (Indirect Overlap, k \ge 3): For images in layer k, calculate weight based on weights of images in layer k-1: \omega{ki} = \frac{\sum{j=1}^{N{k-1}} \omega{j}^{(k-1)} \times M{j,ki}^{(k-1)}}{N{k-1}} where \omega{j}^{(k-1)} is the weight of image j in layer k-1, M{j,ki}^{(k-1)} is the match count between image j and image i, and N{k-1} is the number of images in layer k-1. 6. Training Iteration Allocation: Perform TI total training iterations on the current 3DGS field. Split these into Local and Semi-Global optimization: Local Optimization: Select the top Nm images with the highest weights. For each key image i (where i \in \{1, \dots, Nm\}), calculate its specific iteration count T{im}: T{im} = \frac{1 - e^{-\omegai}}{\sum{j=1}^{Nm} (1 - e^{-\omegaj})} \times TI Train these images for T{im} iterations. Semi-Global Optimization: Distribute the remaining TI / 2 iterations evenly among all other registered images (those not in the top Nm). 7. Adaptive Learning Rate Update: For each image j trained for Tj iterations, update its learning rate \etaj: Calculate progress ti: ti = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } Tj > Ta \\ Tj / Ta & \text{if } Tj \le Ta \end{cases} where Ta is the predefined iterations required for satisfactory quality. Calculate base learning rate \etaj^c: \etaj^c = (\etaj^0)^{(1-ti)} \times (\etaj^f)^{ti} where \etaj^0 is the initial learning rate and \etaj^f is the final learning rate. Adjust for overlapping images. Let I be the set of images overlapping with image j (M{i,j} > 0) and NI be the count of such images. The final learning rate \etaj is: \etaj = \frac{\etaj^c + \sum{i \in I} M{i,j} \times \etai^c}{NI + 1}. 8. Loss Calculation and Optimization: Compute the total loss for the current batch of images and perform gradient descent. The loss function includes a load-balancing term: L{total} = \lambda1 L1 + \lambda{ssim} L{ssim} + \lambda{load} L{load} where L{load} = \text{std}(Gp) is the standard deviation of the number of Gaussians Gp associated with each pixel p in the image. 1. Global BA: Once all images are acquired, perform global Bundle Adjustment on the estimated poses. 2. Rapid Optimization: Apply additional optimization iterations to the current 3DGS field to improve overall rendering quality. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class OnTheFlyGS: def init(self, N0=30, TI=200, Nm=10, Ta=200, eta0=1.6e-4, etaf=1.6e-6, lambda1=0.47, lambdaload=0.41, lambdassim=0.12): self.N0 = N0 self.TI = TI self.Nm = Nm self.Ta = Ta self.eta0 = eta0 self.etaf = etaf self.lambda1 = lambda1 self.lambdaload = lambdaload self.lambdassim = lambdassim self.gsfield = None # 3D Gaussian Splatting field self.sparsecloud = None # Sparse point cloud self.searchtree = None # Spatial index for sparse cloud self.imageoverlaps = {} # Dict: (imgi, imgj) -> matchcount self.imageiterations = {} # Dict: imgid -> totaliterationstrained self.imagelearningrates = {} # Dict: imgid -> currentlearningrate def phase1initialtraining(self, initialimages, sfmmodule): """ Phase 1: Train initial 3DGS field with N0 images. """ # 1. SfM for initial images poses, sparsecloud = sfmmodule.estimateposesandcloud(initialimages[:self.N0]) self.sparsecloud = sparsecloud # 2. Initialize 3DGS field self.gsfield = initialize3dgsfromcloud(sparsecloud) # 3. Train for fixed iterations (e.g., 2000) # Note: Standard 3DGS training loop is assumed to be available train3dgs(self.gsfield, initialimages[:self.N0], iterations=2000) # Initialize tracking structures for img in initialimages[:self.N0]: self.imageiterations[img.id] = 2000 self.imagelearningrates[img.id] = self.etaf # Assume converged to final rate def phase2progressivetraining(self, newimage, sfmmodule): """ Phase 2: Process a single new fly-in image. """ # 1. Update Poses and Cloud # On-the-Fly SfM updates pose of newimage and neighbors, refines cloud self.sparsecloud = sfmmodule.updateposeandcloud(newimage, self.sparsecloud) # 2. Construct Search Tree self.searchtree = buildsearchtree(self.sparsecloud) # 3. Identify New Points newpoints = [] for point in newimage.sparsepoints: dist = self.searchtree.querymindistance(point) if dist > distancethreshold: # Threshold defined by implementation newpoints.append(point) # 4. Initialize New Gaussians newgaussians = initializegaussiansfrompoints(newpoints) self.gsfield.append(newgaussians) # 5. Hierarchical Image Weighting # Calculate weights relative to newimage weights = calculatehierarchicalweights(newimage, self.imageoverlaps, self.Nm) # 6. Training Iteration Allocation # Select top Nm images topimages = gettopnimagesbyweight(weights, self.Nm) # Calculate iterations for top images topiterations = {} sumdenom = sum(1 - math.exp(-weights[img.id]) for img in topimages) for img in topimages: w = weights[img.id] tim = ((1 - math.exp(-w)) / sumdenom) self.TI topiterations[img.id] = tim # Semi-global: remaining TI/2 iterations distributed evenly among others otherimages = [img for img in allregisteredimages if img not in topimages] semiglobaliters = (self.TI / 2) / len(otherimages) if otherimages else 0 # 7. Adaptive Learning Rate Update & Optimization # We perform TI iterations total. # Local optimization: train topimages for their allocated tim # Semi-global: train otherimages for semiglobaliters each # Update learning rates before optimization for img in topimages + otherimages: self.updatelearningrate(img) # Perform optimization steps # Note: In practice, this involves rendering and backprop for the specified images # The exact scheduling of TI iterations across images is implementation-specific # but must respect the counts tim and semiglobaliters. for img in topimages: train3dgsstep(self.gsfield, [img], iterations=topiterations[img.id], learningrate=self.imagelearningrates[img.id], lossfn=self.computeloss) for img in otherimages: train3dgsstep(self.gsfield, [img], iterations=semiglobaliters, learningrate=self.imagelearningrates[img.id], lossfn=self.computeloss) # Update iteration counters for img in topimages: self.imageiterations[img.id] += topiterations[img.id] for img in otherimages: self.imageiterations[img.id] += semiglobaliters def updatelearningrate(self, image): """ Update learning rate for a specific image based on its training progress. """ Tj = self.imageiterations[image.id] # Calculate progress ti if Tj > self.Ta: ti = 1.0 else: ti = Tj / self.Ta # Calculate base learning rate etaj^c etajc = (self.eta0 (1 - ti)) (self.etaf ti) # Find overlapping images overlappingimages = [] for otherimgid, matchcount in self.imageoverlaps.items(): # Assuming imageoverlaps is symmetric or stored appropriately # Check if otherimg overlaps with current image if matchcount > 0: overlappingimages.append((otherimgid, matchcount)) # Calculate adjusted learning rate numerator = etajc denominator = 1 sumoverlapeta = 0 for otherimgid, Mij in overlappingimages: # Get learning rate of overlapping image etaic = self.imagelearningrates.get(otherimgid, self.eta0) sumoverlapeta += Mij etaic denominator += 1 # NI + 1 finaleta = (etajc + sumoverlapeta) / denominator self.imagelearningrates[image.id] = finaleta def computeloss(self, renderedimage, groundtruthimage, gsfield): """ Compute total loss including Load-Balancing-Loss. """ # L1 Loss l1 = computel1loss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # SSIM Loss ssim = computessimloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # Load-Balancing-Loss # Count Gaussians per pixel gaussiancountsperpixel = countgaussiansperpixel(renderedimage, gsfield) lload = np.std(gaussiancountsperpixel) totalloss = (self.lambda1 l1) + (self.lambdassim ssim) + (self.lambdaload lload) return totalloss def phase3finaloptimization(self, allimages, sfmmodule): """ Phase 3: Final global optimization. """ # 1. Global BA sfmmodule.globalbundleadjustment(self.sparsecloud, allimages) # 2. Rapid additional optimization train3dgs(self.gsfield, allimages, iterations=1000) # Iterations not specified, assume reasonable number def calculatehierarchicalweights(newimage, overlaps, Nm): """ Calculate hierarchical weights for images based on overlap with newimage. """ weights = {newimage.id: 1.0} # Layer 1 # Layer 2: Direct overlap layer2images = [] for (imgi, imgj), matchcount in overlaps.items(): if imgi == newimage.id: weights[imgj] = matchcount layer2images.append(imgj) elif imgj == newimage.id: weights[imgi] = matchcount layer2images.append(imgi) # Layer 3+: Indirect overlap # This is a simplified representation. In practice, BFS/DFS is used to build layers. # For the purpose of the algorithm description, we assume a function that # recursively calculates weights based on previous layer weights and match counts. # The formula is: omegaki = sum(omegaj^(k-1) Mji) / N(k-1) # Note: Full implementation requires maintaining layer structure. # Here we just return the weights calculated so far for direct neighbors. # Indirect weights would be computed iteratively until convergence or max depth. return weights def gettopnimagesbyweight(weights, n): """ Get top n images by weight. """ sortedimages = sorted(weights.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) return [imgid for imgid, in sortedimages[:n]] N0: Number of initial images for Phase 1. Typical value: 30. Initial training iterations for Phase 1. Typical value: 2,000 iterations. TI: Total training iterations performed for each new fly-in image in Phase 2. Typical value: 200. Nm: Number of top-weighted images selected as key training targets for local optimization. Typical value: 10. Ta: Predefined parameter representing iterations required for satisfactory rendering quality. Typical value: 200. \eta0: Initial learning rate. Typical value: 1.6 \times 10^{-4}. \etaf: Final learning rate. Typical value: 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. \lambda1: Weight for L1-Loss. Typical value: 0.47. \lambda{load}: Weight for Load-Balancing-Loss. Typical value: 0.41. \lambda{ssim}: Weight for SSIM-Loss. Typical value: 0.12. Overfitting in Phase 1: Training too many iterations on the initial N0 images can cause the model to overfit to the sparse initial view, leading to poor generalization when new images arrive. The strict iteration limit (2,000) mitigates this. Threshold Selection: The distance threshold for identifying "new" points in the sparse cloud must be carefully chosen. Too low, and existing points are re-initialized, causing instability. Too high, and new geometry is missed. Learning Rate Inconsistency: If the learning rate is not adapted per-image, regions with fewer training iterations may have lower quality than well-trained regions. The adaptive learning rate formula addresses this by considering overlapping images. Gaussian Accumulation: Without the Load-Balancing-Loss, Gaussians may accumulate abnormally in specific regions, increasing memory usage and slowing down training. Thread Contention: Using per-pixel gradient accumulation can lead to serialized atomic operations on the GPU. The method uses splatting-based parallelism (per-Gaussian gradient accumulation) to avoid this. Time Complexity: The method is designed for near real-time optimization. For each new image, it performs TI iterations (typically 200) on a subset of images. The complexity per image is roughly O(TI \cdot N{active}), where N{active} is the number of images involved in the local/semi-global optimization. The use of splatting-based parallelism reduces training time by eliminating thread contention. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians in the 3DGS field. The Load-Balancing-Loss helps control the total number of Gaussians by preventing abnormal accumulation. Evaluated on RGB datasets including 3DGS, Mip-NeRF 360, On-the-Fly SfM, and Replica. Compared against offline training solutions (Adr-Gaussian, Taming-3DGS) and SLAM-based methods (GS-SLAM, RTG-SLAM). Hardware: Tested on RTX 4090 GPU. The method achieves faster training times compared to retraining from scratch while maintaining competitive PSNR and SSIM metrics. The average number of training iterations per image approaches TI (200) as the total number of images increases, making the per-image cost constant. The hierarchical weighting ensures that only a subset of images (top Nm and their neighbors) are heavily optimized, keeping computational cost manageable for large scenes. Strengths: Enables incremental, near real-time 3DGS optimization. Hierarchical weighting and adaptive learning rates improve local quality consistency. Load-balancing loss reduces Gaussian count and accelerates training. Splatting-based parallelism improves GPU utilization. Limitations: Requires a robust On-the-Fly SfM module for pose estimation and sparse cloud generation. Performance depends on the quality of the initial N0 images and the SfM accuracy. The method is specific to RGB input in the cited experiments (RTG-SLAM comparison was limited to RGB-D). Use when processing a stream of images (e.g., from a moving camera or UAV) and real-time or near real-time reconstruction is required. Use when computational resources are limited for full retraining. Use offline training methods if all images are available and maximum possible quality is required without time constraints. Use if the input is not sequential or if SfM is unreliable. The method was proposed in the paper "Gaussian On-the-Fly Splatting: A Progressive Framework for Robust Near Real-Time 3DGS Optimization". The method builds upon the original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering technique. It addresses the limitations of offline 3DGS training by introducing a progressive framework that integrates with On-the-Fly SfM pipelines. It incorporates strategies from Taming 3DGS for parallel gradient accumulation. Simulated sequential inputs from 3DGS, Mip-NeRF 360, On-the-Fly SfM, and Replica datasets. Applications requiring dynamic scene reconstruction, such as UAV mapping and VSLAM (Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping). name: Warm-up stage
head: 3D Gaussian Initialization (Warm-up)
body: The warm-up stage is a training adaptation that establishes a stable baseline of 3D Gaussians before introducing more complex representations, such as 4D Gaussian deformation fields or dynamic scene modeling. It prevents convergence difficulties in scenarios lacking Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point initialization and suppresses transient distractors by stabilizing the initial geometry. Unlike Two-stage Optimization which may decouple static and dynamic parameters, the warm-up stage explicitly optimizes the static 3D Gaussian representation first to provide a robust prior for subsequent deformation learning. The method partitions the optimization trajectory into a preliminary phase where only 3D Gaussians are optimized, followed by the introduction of deformation networks or dynamic components. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Raw image sequences; optionally, no SfM points (in which case random or heuristic initialization is used). Output: A set of optimized 3D Gaussians \Gamma with stable positions, scales, and opacities, serving as the initialization for the next stage. Data Structures: 3D Gaussians \Gamma: A set of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by mean position \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai (parameterized by scale si and rotation qi), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients ci. Deformation Network \Delta: Not active during the warm-up stage but initialized for the subsequent phase. Steps: 1. Initialization: If SfM points are available, initialize 3D Gaussians at these points. If not, initialize 3D Gaussians randomly or via a coarse clustering method to ensure coverage of the scene volume. 2. Static Optimization: Optimize the parameters of the 3D Gaussians \Gamma (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) using standard differentiable rendering losses (e.g., L1 loss and D-SSIM) against the input images. The deformation network \Delta is either not present or its gradients are blocked. 3. Stabilization: Continue optimization until the 3D Gaussians converge to a stable configuration that accurately represents the static geometry or the average appearance of the dynamic scene. 4. Transition: Use the optimized \Gamma as the initialization for the 4D Gaussian Splatting training, where the deformation network \Delta is activated to model temporal changes. Formulas: The rendering process during warm-up is identical to standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. The contribution of Gaussian i to a pixel is determined by its projected covariance and opacity. The loss function \mathcal{L} is: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 reconstruction loss and \mathcal{L}{\text{D-SSIM}} is the structural similarity loss. Parameters: Warm-up Iterations: Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lack of SfM Points: Directly training 4D-GS without this stage causes convergence difficulty. Numeric Errors: Skipping the warm-up stage can lead to numeric errors in optimizing the Gaussian deformation network \Delta. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def warmupstage(images, numiterations): """ Optimizes 3D Gaussians without deformation networks. """ # Initialize Gaussians. If SfM points exist, use them; otherwise, random initialization. gaussians = initializegaussians(sfmpoints=None) for step in range(numiterations): # Sample a random view from the training images image, camera = samplerandomview(images) # Render the image using standard 3DGS rasterization # No deformation network is applied; Gaussians are static in 3D space renderedimage = render3dgaussians(gaussians, camera) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, image) # Backpropagate and update only Gaussian parameters # Deformation network parameters are not updated or do not exist gaussians.update(loss) return gaussians A specific variant used in 4D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scenes where SfM points are absent. It keeps some 3D Gaussians in the dynamic part to release the pressure of large deformation learning on 4D Gaussians, learns proper 3D Gaussians \Gamma, and suggests deformation fields to pay more attention to the dynamic part. It avoids numeric errors in optimizing the Gaussian deformation network \Delta and keeps training stable. Without this coarse stage, performance degrades (e.g., PSNR 31.91 dB, SSIM 0.97, LPIPS 0.03, training time 7.5 mins, 79 FPS, 18 MB storage on synthetic datasets). Time Complexity: Adds an initial phase of optimization proportional to the number of warm-up iterations and the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the 3D Gaussian representation only; no additional memory for deformation networks during this phase. Performance: Prevents convergence failure in the absence of SfM points. Strengths: Stabilizes training for dynamic scenes; prevents numeric errors in deformation networks. Limitations: Requires additional training time before the main optimization phase begins. The warm-up stage is a technique adapted from general optimization strategies to address specific challenges in 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly in dynamic scene rendering and distractor suppression. It was highlighted in the context of 4D Gaussian Splatting to handle cases where initial point clouds are missing. name: POD Pretraining
head: Distillation-based amortized optimization, Predict–Optimize–Distill, Predict–Optimize–Distill (POD) Training, Principal Orthogonal Decomposition pretraining, Progressive Optimization Distillation
body: POD Pretraining is a distillation-based amortized optimization procedure that stabilizes the training of multi-stage residual Gaussian predictors by supervising them with locally refined Gaussian targets instead of unstable image-space gradients. It solves the problem of training collapse caused by the non-unique inverse mapping from residual images to Gaussian parameters, which is amplified across stages through error accumulation. Unlike direct image-space supervision, which often diverges, POD stabilizes stage-wise training by refining predicted Gaussian increments with a short-horizon optimizer and distilling the refined result back into the predictor as a regression target. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Residual image E{i-1} from previous stage i-1; current predictor parameters \thetai. Output: Refined Gaussian increments \Delta \hat{G}i used as regression targets for the predictor; updated predictor parameters. Data Structures: Gaussian Increment (\Delta Gi): A set of 2D Gaussian primitives predicted by the stage i predictor. Each primitive typically contains parameters for position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color (details depend on the specific Gaussian representation, e.g., 2D GS). Detached Copy (\Delta \hat{G}i^{(t)}): A trainable copy of the predicted increments, detached from the predictor's computation graph to allow independent optimization. Numbered Steps: 1. Predict: The residual predictor f{\thetai} produces additional Gaussians \Delta \hat{G}i from the input residual image E{i-1}. Stage Control selects the effective subset \Delta Gi from the dense candidate set. 2. Optimize (Init): Create a detached trainable copy of the predicted increments: \Delta \hat{G}i^{(0)} = \text{copy}(\Delta Gi) 3. Optimize (Update): Update the copy for Ki steps using a short-horizon optimizer. The update rule is: \Delta \hat{G}i^{(t+1)} = \Delta \hat{G}i^{(t)} - \eta \nabla L{render}^{(i)}(R(\Delta \hat{G}i^{(t)}), E{i-1}) where t = 0, \dots, Ki-1, \eta is the learning rate, and L{render}^{(i)} is the residual rendering objective. Note: In practice, the SSIM component of L{render} is evaluated on the accumulated rendering R(G{i-1} \cup \Delta \hat{G}i^{(t)}) against the ground truth image I{gt}, because the residual E{i-1} may contain negative values. Previous-stage Gaussians G{i-1} are kept fixed so that gradients flow only to \Delta \hat{G}i^{(t)}. 4. Distill (Target Generation): After Ki steps, obtain the refined increments: \Delta \hat{G}i = \Delta \hat{G}i^{(Ki)} This refined result is detached and used as a fixed regression target. 5. Distill (Loss Computation): Supervise the original prediction \Delta Gi with the refined target \Delta \hat{G}i using a Gaussian-space regression loss: L{gaussian}^{(i)} = L{gaussian}(\Delta Gi, \Delta \hat{G}i) 6. Accumulate: Compute the total POD pretraining objective by summing the losses across all S stages with weights \lambdai: L{POD} = \sum{i=1}^{S} \lambdai L{gaussian}^{(i)} Parameters: Ki: Number of optimization steps for local refinement. Not given in the sources. \eta: Learning rate for the local optimizer. Not given in the sources. \lambdai: Weight balancing the contribution of each stage. Set uniformly across stages. Gaussian-space distillation loss coefficient: Multiplied by 100 to match the gradient scale of Gaussian parameter regression. Patch size p: Controls spatial granularity and maximum number of candidate Gaussians. Evaluated settings: 5, 6, 7, 14. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def podpretrainingstep(predictor, stageindex, residualimage, previousgaussians, numoptsteps, learningrate, stageweight): """ Performs one step of POD pretraining for a specific stage. Args: predictor: The feed-forward network predicting Gaussian increments. stageindex: The current stage index i. residualimage: The residual image E{i-1}. previousgaussians: The accumulated Gaussians G{i-1} from previous stages (fixed). numoptsteps: Ki, number of local optimization steps. learningrate: eta, learning rate for local optimization. stageweight: lambdai, weight for this stage's loss. Returns: loss: The computed POD loss for this stage. """ # Step 1: Predict # The predictor takes the residual image and outputs a dense candidate set, # which is then masked by Stage Control to get effective increments. # For simplicity, we assume predictor returns the effective increments directly. predictedincrements = predictor(residualimage) # Step 2: Optimize (Init) # Create a detached trainable copy of the predicted increments. # In a framework like PyTorch, this involves cloning and setting requiresgrad=True. refinedincrements = predictedincrements.detach().clone() refinedincrements.requiresgrad = True # Step 3: Optimize (Update) for t in range(numoptsteps): # Render the accumulated scene: previous Gaussians + refined increments # R(G{i-1} U DeltaG) renderedimage = renderaccumulated(previousgaussians, refinedincrements) # Compute residual rendering loss # Lrender = 0.7 L1 + 0.3 (1 - SSIM) # Note: SSIM is evaluated on accumulated rendering against ground truth Igt # assuming ground truth is available in the context or passed in. # Here we assume a function getgroundtruth(stageindex) exists. gtimage = getgroundtruth(stageindex) l1loss = computel1(renderedimage, gtimage) ssimloss = 1.0 - computessim(renderedimage, gtimage) renderloss = 0.7 l1loss + 0.3 ssimloss # Compute gradients and update the refined increments # Gradients flow only to refinedincrements because previousgaussians are fixed # and predictedincrements is detached. renderloss.backward() # Update rule: DeltaG^(t+1) = DeltaG^(t) - eta grad(Lrender) with torch.nograd(): refinedincrements -= learningrate refinedincrements.grad refinedincrements.grad.zero() # Step 4: Distill (Target Generation) # The refined increments after Ki steps are the target. targetincrements = refinedincrements.detach() # Step 5: Distill (Loss Computation) # Gaussian-space regression loss between predicted and target increments. # Lgaussian is typically an L1 or L2 loss on Gaussian parameters. gaussianloss = computegaussianloss(predictedincrements, targetincrements) # Step 6: Accumulate # Multiply by stage weight and coefficient (100 for POD pretraining) coefficient = 100.0 loss = stageweight coefficient gaussianloss return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Collapse: Direct image-space supervision faces a non-unique inverse mapping from residual images to Gaussian parameters. This ambiguity is amplified across stages through error accumulation and parameter compensation, leading to training collapse. Unstable Gradients: Residual rendering supervision alone is under-constrained, and image-space gradients do not always provide a stable or consistent direction in Gaussian parameter space. Negative Residuals: The residual image E{i-1} may contain negative values, so the SSIM component of the rendering loss must be evaluated on the accumulated rendering against the ground truth, not on the residual itself. A stage-wise predictor using a DINOv3 ViT-Base encoder and a lightweight convolutional head to predict Gaussian candidates from residual images. It extracts multi-level features from the 5th and 11th transformer layers, projects the encoder output to a 1024-dimensional representation, and fuses features into a 32-channel spatial feature map. Patch embedding with patch size p partitions the map into local patches, mapping each to a 64-dimensional token that predicts a Gaussian candidate. The Stage Control mask is then applied to obtain effective increments \Delta Gi. The encoder is initialized with pretrained DINOv3 weights, and the model is optimized using AdamW with a warmup schedule followed by StepLR decay. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The POD pretraining phase adds computational overhead due to the short-horizon optimization steps (Ki) per stage. However, it amortizes this cost into the feed-forward network, allowing for fast inference later. The finetuning phase removes the costly short-horizon optimization, reducing per-iteration training cost. Memory: Requires storing the detached trainable copies of Gaussian increments for optimization. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Stability: Direct Supervision (without POD) reaches a best PSNR of 32.13 dB but collapses at iteration 80k, dropping final PSNR to 16.22 dB. Full POD reaches a best PSNR of 33.44 dB and remains stable with a final PSNR of 33.41 dB, with no collapse. Feature Distribution: In the w/o POD Collapse case, the Stage-1 feature is dominated by a single principal component explaining 98.35% of the variance. With POD, the first three principal components explain 28.09%, 22.10%, and 14.47% of the variance, producing a more balanced feature distribution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Stabilizes multi-stage residual Gaussian prediction and prevents training collapse. Provides a better-conditioned regression target by distilling short-horizon optimized Gaussian increments. Limitations: Requires additional computational resources during the pretraining phase due to the local optimization steps. The finetuning phase is necessary to further improve reconstruction quality and enable quantization. When to Use: Use POD Pretraining when training multi-stage Gaussian predictors that are prone to instability or collapse due to the under-constrained nature of the inverse mapping from images to Gaussian parameters. When Not to Use: Do not use if computational resources are extremely limited and the pretraining overhead is prohibitive, or if a single-stage predictor is sufficient and stable without distillation. POD Pretraining was introduced in the AIR (Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework for Self-Supervised Feed-Forward 2D Gaussian Splatting) paper. It is inspired by distillation-based amortized optimization techniques. The method addresses the instability of training multi-stage residual Gaussian predictors by mediating the image-space objective through a short optimization followed by distillation. name: Finetune Training
head: Cross-stage coordination, Finetuning Phase, Image-space Finetuning, POD + Finetune
body: Finetune Training is a lightweight optimization phase applied after POD (Progressive Optimization Distillation) pretraining to refine the multi-stage Gaussian predictor using direct image-space rendering supervision. It solves the problem of limited cross-stage coordination in distillation-based methods by allowing gradients from the final cumulative rendering to propagate back to earlier stages, thereby redistributing the reconstruction burden and improving the final output quality. Unlike POD, which stabilizes training via local residual targets, finetuning enables joint optimization across all stages, sacrificing intermediate standalone PSNR for superior final-stage reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-stage feed-forward predictor P initialized by POD pretraining, which predicts Gaussian increments \Delta Gi at each stage i based on residual features E{i-1}. Output: An optimized predictor P' with parameters adjusted to minimize image-space rendering loss. Data Structures: The predictor maintains a sequence of accumulated Gaussian sets Gi and their corresponding rendered images Ii. Gi = G{i-1} \cup \Delta Gi, where G0 = \emptyset. Ii = \mathcal{R}(Gi), where \mathcal{R} is the differentiable volume rendering operator. The loss is computed for every intermediate stage i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. Parameters: Image-space reconstruction loss coefficient (\lambdai): Set to 1 uniformly across all stages. Rendering Loss (L{render}): A weighted combination of pixel-wise distortion and structural similarity: L{render} = 0.7 L1 + 0.3 (1 - \text{SSIM}) where L1 is the L1 distance between predicted and ground-truth images, and SSIM is the Structural Similarity Index. Steps: 1. Remove Short-Horizon Optimization: Disable the local Gaussian refinement optimizer used during POD pretraining, eliminating the costly iterative refinement loop. 2. Forward Pass: For each training batch, pass the input through the multi-stage predictor. At each stage i, compute the accumulated Gaussian set Gi and render the image Ii = \mathcal{R}(Gi). 3. Compute Loss: Calculate the rendering loss L{render}(Ii, I{gt}) for every intermediate stage i. The total loss is the sum of losses across all active stages: L{total} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \lambdai L{render}(Ii, I{gt}) With \lambdai = 1 for all i. 4. Backpropagation: Compute gradients of L{total} with respect to the predictor parameters. Because Ii depends on all preceding increments \Delta G1, \dots, \Delta Gi, gradients propagate back to earlier stages, enabling joint optimization. 5. Update: Update predictor parameters using an optimizer (e.g., AdamW). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finetunestep(predictor, imagegt, optimizer, numstages): """ One step of Finetune Training. predictor: Multi-stage Gaussian predictor initialized by POD. imagegt: Ground truth image. optimizer: Optimizer instance (e.g., AdamW). numstages: Total number of prediction stages. """ optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 currentgaussians = [] # G0 = empty set for i in range(numstages): # Predict increment from residual features deltag = predictor.predictstage(i, currentgaussians) # Accumulate Gaussians: Gi = G{i-1} U deltag currentgaussians.extend(deltag) # Render intermediate result: Ii = R(Gi) renderedimage = rendergaussians(currentgaussians) # Compute loss for this stage: Lrender = 0.7 L1 + 0.3 (1 - SSIM) l1dist = meanabsoluteerror(renderedimage, imagegt) ssimval = structuralsimilarity(renderedimage, imagegt) stageloss = 0.7 l1dist + 0.3 (1.0 - ssimval) totalloss += stageloss # Backpropagate through all stages jointly totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() def rendergaussians(gaussians): """ Standard differentiable volume rendering via alpha-compositing.""" return alphacomposite(gaussians) def meanabsoluteerror(img1, img2): """ Standard L1 distance computation.""" return sum(abs(img1 - img2)) / len(img1) def structuralsimilarity(img1, img2): """ Standard SSIM computation.""" return computessimmetric(img1, img2) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Scale: In POD, distillation loss is scaled by 100 to match gradient scales. In finetuning, the coefficient is 1, so the learning rate must be adjusted accordingly to avoid instability. Early Stage Degradation: Early stages (Stage 1, 2) may show lower PSNR compared to "Only POD" because they sacrifice standalone accuracy to provide a better basis for later residual correction. This is expected and indicates successful cross-stage coordination. A post-training variant where the costly short-horizon optimization is removed, and the model is trained with direct image-space supervision to refine reconstruction and enable learned quantization. The steps are: 1) Remove POD optimization steps; 2) Train with direct image-space supervision (cross-stage rendering finetuning); 3) Apply learned quantization to compress the Gaussian representation. This allows for compact storage and transmission of the predicted Gaussian parameters. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Per-iteration cost is significantly reduced compared to POD because the short-horizon local optimization loop is removed. However, it requires rendering at every intermediate stage, which adds overhead compared to single-stage methods. Memory: Requires storing intermediate Gaussian sets Gi and rendered images Ii for backpropagation through all stages. Measured Performance: On DIV2K, POD+Finetune lowers cumulative PSNR after Stage 1 (25.58 dB vs 26.58 dB for Only POD) and Stage 2 (27.89 dB vs 28.29 dB), but improves later stages, reaching 30.76 dB at Stage 4 compared to 29.48 dB for Only POD. Finetuning redistributes the reconstruction burden, leading to specialized roles: Stage-1 features show clearer structural patterns, while Stage-4 features contain more high-frequency residual responses. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables joint optimization across stages; improves final reconstruction quality; reduces per-iteration training cost; supports learned quantization. Limitations: Early-stage PSNR may degrade; requires careful tuning of learning rates due to gradient scale changes. When to Use: Use when the goal is to maximize the final accumulated reconstruction quality and enable efficient storage via quantization, and when the computational cost of local refinement in POD is prohibitive. Do not use if strong intermediate-stage standalone accuracy is required. Finetune Training was introduced in the AIR (Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework) paper as a successor to POD pretraining. It addresses the limitation of distillation-based methods where later stages must compensate for upstream errors. The method builds on the observation that supervising cumulative results encourages cross-stage coordination. It is used in self-supervised feed-forward 2D Gaussian Splatting frameworks to achieve high-quality reconstruction with efficient storage. name: Backbone Fine-tuning
head: Tri-plane Feature Adaptation
body: Backbone Fine-tuning adapts the weights of a pre-trained 3D generator (backbone) alongside the decoder to generate Gaussian Splatting attributes, addressing the fact that splats have scale and rotation that influence adjacent regions, unlike NeRF's local color/density. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Pre-trained 3D generator weights, decoder network, and training data. Output: Fine-tuned backbone weights and decoder weights that produce Gaussian attributes for splatting. Data Structures: Backbone Copy: A duplicate of the pre-trained 3D generator's weight tensor. Decoder: A network mapping features to Gaussian attributes. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an exact copy of the pre-trained 3D generator's weights. Initialize the decoder network. 2. Joint Optimization: During the training process, optimize the weights of both the backbone copy and the decoder simultaneously. 3. Feature Adaptation: The backbone adapts its tri-plane features to provide a basis suitable for Gaussian attributes, which require spatial extent (scale/rotation) beyond point-wise density/color. Parameters: Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Drift: If the geometry branch is not frozen, fine-tuning can lead to positional updates that compensate for attribute errors, causing local blur and depth distortions. Misalignment: Errors in predicted back-projection poses introduce misalignment with ground truth supervision cameras. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def copyweights(sourcemodel): return {k: v.clone().detach() for k, v in sourcemodel.statedict().items()} def initializedecoder(): return GaussianDecoder() def render(gaussianattributes, cameraparams): return rasterize(gaussianattributes, cameraparams) def computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage): return 0.8 l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) + 0.2 ssimloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) pretrained3dgenerator = loadpretrainedmodel() backbonecopy = copyweights(pretrained3dgenerator) decoder = initializedecoder() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(backbonecopy.parameters()) + list(decoder.parameters())) trainingdata = DataLoader(dataset, batchsize=1) for batch in trainingdata: features = backbonecopy(batch.inputimages, batch.poseconditions) gaussianattributes = decoder(features) renderedimage = render(gaussianattributes, batch.cameraparams) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, batch.gtimage) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() A variant that uses two independently parameterized branches initialized from the same pretrained DA3 weights to preserve depth and camera estimates while adapting Gaussian attributes. It sets itself apart by explicitly freezing the geometry branch to prevent the positional distortions seen in standard backbone fine-tuning. Choose this when preserving the original 3D generator's geometric accuracy is critical. Definition: Two branches (geometry and attribute) initialized from pretrained DA3 weights. Steps: 1. Initialize \Phi{geo} and \Phi{attr} from the same pretrained DA3 weights. 2. Freeze \Phi{geo}, including its depth and camera heads. 3. Fine-tune only the last K Transformer blocks of \Phi{attr}. 4. Map attribute features FC to per-pixel attributes \xi using a DPT Gaussian decoder. 5. Obtain points by back-projection without predicted positional offsets; scales and rotations remain learnable. Formulas: Geometry branch: \hat{D}, \hat{\Pi}C = \Phi{geo}(IC; QC). Attribute branch: FC = \Phi{attr}(IC; QC). Parameters: K: Number of last Transformer blocks in the attribute branch to fine-tune. Typical value: 10. Pitfalls: Fine-tuning the geometry branch or learning positional offsets worsens metrics (LPIPS increases by 16.6% and 23.2% on ETH3D/DTU) because positional updates compensate for attribute errors. Time Complexity: Increases training time due to the optimization of the backbone weights in addition to the decoder and Gaussian parameters. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the backbone weights and their gradients, effectively doubling the memory footprint for the generative model compared to a frozen backbone. Scaling: Allows the generative prior to adapt to the specific statistical distribution of Gaussian attributes, potentially improving generalization to diverse scenes. Strengths: Adapts the tri-plane features to better support the spatial extent of Gaussians, which NeRF-style local features do not inherently provide. Limitations: Risk of geometric distortion if geometry is not frozen; requires careful tuning of the number of fine-tuned blocks (K) in dual-branch variants. When to use: When using a pre-trained 3D generator and standard decoding fails to produce high-quality Gaussian attributes due to mismatched feature semantics. When not to use: When geometric fidelity of the original generator is paramount and cannot be preserved by freezing. Originated in the context of adapting 3D-aware generative models for Gaussian Splatting. The method was introduced to address the fundamental mismatch between NeRF-style local density/color representations and the extended, oriented nature of 3D Gaussians. It is used in feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction pipelines where a pre-trained 3D generator serves as the backbone.
