name: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy for 3DGS
head: Frequency-staged Training Pipeline, Frequency-staged Training with Archiving, Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies Training Procedure, Laplacian-GS inheritance strategy
body: This method reduces 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training time and memory usage by factorizing the scene representation into a hierarchy of frequency-specific Gaussian fields aligned with a Laplacian pyramid of training images. It optimizes these fields sequentially from coarse to fine, archiving completed fields to free GPU memory, and composes the final image in the image domain. Unlike simultaneous multi-field optimization, this approach reduces the number of active primitives on the GPU at any given stage, offering a speedup with minor quality trade-offs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training views \{v\} with ground truth images \{I^v\} at full resolution. Each view includes a camera model for projection, which is standard for 3DGS. Outputs: A set of Gaussian fields \{G^0, \dots, G^{L-1}\} representing the scene across frequency bands. Data Structures: Gaussian Field G^\ell: A set of N\ell anisotropic Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i is parameterized by a mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, an opacity \sigmai \in (0, 1), a covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (typically decomposed as \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top where Ri is a rotation quaternion and Si is a diagonal scale matrix), and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Laplacian Pyramid: A hierarchy of images \{I^{L-1}, \dots, I^0\} where I^0 is the full-resolution ground truth and I^{L-1} is the coarsest low-frequency approximation. Cache: A storage for accumulated rendered predictions \{\hat{I}^v\ell\} used to reconstruct finer levels. Preprocessing: Pyramid Construction 1. For each training view v, construct the resolution pyramid: I^{\ell+1} = \text{Down}(I^\ell) where \text{Down}(\cdot) is Gaussian filtering followed by subsampling. 2. Compute Laplacian residual targets for levels \ell \in \{0, \dots, L-2\}: R^\ell = I^\ell - \text{Up}(I^{\ell+1}) where \text{Up}(\cdot) is the paired upsampling operator. Note: I^{L-1} is the low-frequency target for the coarsest field. Residuals R^\ell are signed and lie in [-1, 1], while base images lie in [0, 1]. Rendering Functions: Renderbase: Standard 3DGS rasterization with post-processing to map SH colors to [0, 1]: ci(d) = \text{clamp}(ci(d) + 0.5, 0, 1) Used for the coarsest level G^{L-1}. Renderres: Modified rasterization that removes the shift and clamp, allowing signed outputs in [-1, 1] to match residual targets. Algorithm: Frequency-staged Training with Archiving Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def laplacianfrequencyhierarchytraining(trainingviews, L=2, iterationsperlevel=[10000, 20000], inheritanceratio=1.0): # 1. Precompute Laplacian Pyramids Ipyramid = {} for v in trainingviews: Ifull = v.image Ipyramid[v] = [Ifull] current = Ifull for in range(L - 1): current = gaussiandownsample(current) Ipyramid[v].append(current) Ipyramid[v].reverse() predictioncache = {} gaussianfields = {} for l in range(L - 1, -1, -1): if l == L - 1: Gl = initializefromcolmap() else: Gprev = gaussianfields[l + 1] Gl = inheritgaussians(Gprev, inheritanceratio) optimizer = AdamOptimizer(Gl.parameters()) for iteration in range(iterationsperlevel[L - 1 - l]): v = random.choice(trainingviews) if l == L - 1: Ihatl = renderbase(Gl, v) else: Ihatlplus1 = predictioncache[v] Iup = upsample2x(Ihatlplus1) Rhatl = renderres(Gl, v) Ihatl = Iup + Rhatl targetI = Ipyramid[v][l] loss = photometricloss(Ihatl, targetI) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() applydensificationandpruning(Gl, iteration) predictioncache[v] = Ihatl gaussianfields[l] = Gl archivefield(Gl) return gaussianfields def gaussiandownsample(img): return subsample(gaussianfilter(img, sigma=1.0), stride=2) def upsample2x(img): return nearestneighborresize(img, scale=2.0) def initializefromcolmap(): return [Gaussian(mu=p, sigma=0.2, S=initscale(), R=initrotation(), SH=initsh()) for p in colmappoints] def inheritgaussians(Gprev, rho): Nprev = len(Gprev) Nnew = int(Nprev rho) indices = random.sample(range(Nprev), Nnew) if rho < 1.0 else range(Nprev) Gnew = [] for i in indices: g = Gprev[i] newg = Gaussian() newg.mu = g.mu newg.sigma = randomuniform(0, 1) newg.S = randomscale() newg.R = randomrotation() newg.SH = randomshcoefficients() Gnew.append(newg) return Gnew def renderbase(G, v): return splatrender(G, v, shiftandclamp=True) def renderres(G, v): return splatrender(G, v, shiftandclamp=False) def splatrender(G, v, shiftandclamp): colors = computeshcolors(G, v) if shiftandclamp: colors = clamp(colors + 0.5, 0, 1) return compositealphablending(G, v, colors) def photometricloss(pred, target): return 0.8 ssimloss(pred, target) + 0.2 l1loss(pred, target) def applydensificationandpruning(G, iteration): standard3dgsdensificationpruning(G, iteration) def archivefield(G): movetocpuordisk(G) class AdamOptimizer: def init(self, params): self.params = params self.state = {} def step(self): applyadamupdate(self.params, self.state) def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = None Parameters: L (Hierarchy Depth): Number of pyramid levels. Default is 2 (levels 0 and 1). Deeper hierarchies make finer residuals harder to represent efficiently, potentially reducing gains. \rho (Inheritance Ratio): Fraction of Gaussians inherited from the previous stage. Default is 1.0. Values < 1.0 accelerate training but cause a clear drop in reconstruction quality. Iterations: Default total 30K iterations split as 10K for the coarsest level and 20K for the finest level in a two-level setup. Optimizer: Adam. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Error Accumulation: Training each field to directly match its Laplacian residual target (R^\ell) can lead to accumulated approximation errors and degraded quality. The method mitigates this by supervising each stage using the reconstructed image \hat{I}^v\ell against the ground truth at that resolution level I^v\ell. Inheritance Ratio: Reducing \rho below 1.0 speeds up training but significantly reduces fidelity because fewer primitives remain to represent fine details. Hierarchy Depth: Using too many levels (deep hierarchies) can degrade quality because high-frequency residuals become difficult for 3DGS to represent efficiently. A broader category of methods that optimize scene representations in stages, often coarse-to-fine. Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy is a specific implementation using frequency decomposition and archiving. Multi-stage and Progressive Training Methods that reduce the number of Gaussians to save memory and speed up training. Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy uses archiving (moving fields off GPU) and optional inheritance ratio reduction to manage active primitives. Pruning and Sparsity Control A backbone framework used to implement Laplacian Frequency Hierarchy. FastGS provides optimized rendering and training routines. FastGS Time Complexity: Reduces training time by optimizing fewer Gaussians per stage and reducing per-iteration cost at coarser levels. On Mip-NeRF 360 1K, it achieves a 1.73x speedup (8.88 to 5.13 minutes) with Taming-3DGS and 1.22x (4.82 to 3.96 minutes) with FastGS. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduces peak VRAM usage by archiving completed Gaussian fields off the GPU. This allows training higher-resolution scenes (2K/4K) that might otherwise OOM. Performance: Slight degradation in reconstruction quality (e.g., 0.34 dB PSNR drop on Mip-NeRF 360 1K) is attributed to approximation errors from hierarchical rendering and composition. Strengths: Efficient training for high-resolution scenes; reduced memory footprint; leverages standard 3DGS densification/pruning. Limitations: Slight quality drop; deeper hierarchies may degrade quality; requires careful tuning of inheritance ratio \rho if speed is prioritized over quality. When to Use: When training time or VRAM is a bottleneck for high-resolution 3DGS scenes. When Not to Use: When maximum reconstruction fidelity is required and training time is not a constraint. The method was introduced in "Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training". It builds on the observation that low-frequency structures in 3DGS converge earlier than high-frequency details, and that standard 3DGS rasterizers assume non-negative colors, which is incompatible with signed residual learning. The Laplacian pyramid (Burt & Adelson, 1983) provides a framework for decomposing images into frequency bands, allowing separate optimization of coarse and fine details. name: Curriculum Learning with Slice and Voxel Supervision
head: Slice and Voxel Supervision Curriculum
body: This method addresses the instability and incomplete volumetric coverage inherent in training 3D Gaussian representations for shear-warp rendering by decoupling global spatial guidance from local structural detail learning. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy by explicitly utilizing the geometric alignment between 2D slice sampling and the shear-warp rendering pipeline, rather than relying solely on hierarchical densification or pose freezing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of multimodal volumetric datasets (e.g., MRI, Cryosection) represented as voxel grids. Output: A set of Gaussian kernels \mathcal{G} = \{G1, G2, \dots, Gm\} optimized for efficient shear-warp visualization. Data Structures: Gaussian Set \mathcal{G}: Contains m Gaussians. Each Gaussian Gi is initialized with a mean \mui at a sampled voxel position. Parameters include mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Voxel Grid: The source volume data used for sampling. Algorithm Steps: The training follows a curriculum learning strategy comprising two distinct phases to balance global consistency and local detail: 1. Phase 1: Slice Supervision (Local Structure): In each training iteration, sample a plane with an arbitrary orientation. Select sparse pixels on the sampled plane. Map each selected pixel to a 3D voxel coordinate. Compute the rendering loss between the rendered slice and the ground-truth slice data. Rationale: This captures spatially correlated regions, encoding geometric structure and texture continuity. It aligns with shear-warp rendering, which generates images from stacks of 2D slices. 2. Phase 2: Voxel Supervision (Global Guidance): Follow Phase 1 with voxel supervision under random sampling with dense approximation. Sample sparse voxels from the volume. Compute the rendering loss between the rendered view and the ground-truth voxel values. Rationale: Sparse voxels provide global coverage of the volume, establishing global spatial guidance that slice supervision alone lacks. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingaussianvolumetric(voxeldata, numiterations): # Initialize Gaussians from voxel samples G = initializegaussiansfromvoxels(voxeldata) for step in range(numiterations): # Curriculum Phase 1: Slice Supervision # Sample arbitrary plane orientation planeorientation = samplerandomorientation() # Sample sparse pixels on the plane slicepixels = samplesparsepixelsonplane(planeorientation, voxeldata) # Map pixels to 3D voxel coordinates voxelcoords = mapslicepixelstovoxels(slicepixels, planeorientation) # Render and compute loss for slice supervision renderedslice = renderslice(G, planeorientation) lossslice = computeloss(renderedslice, groundtruthslice) # Update Gaussians based on slice loss updategaussians(G, lossslice) # Curriculum Phase 2: Voxel Supervision # Sample sparse voxels with dense approximation sampledvoxels = samplesparsevoxels(voxeldata) # Render and compute loss for voxel supervision renderedvoxels = rendervoxels(G, sampledvoxels) lossvoxel = computeloss(renderedvoxels, groundtruthvoxels) # Update Gaussians based on voxel loss updategaussians(G, lossvoxel) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instability from Random Voxel First: Applying random voxel supervision before stable global constraints are established (or mixing random voxel sampling with slice supervision without proper sequencing) leads to unstable global approximation and destabilizes Gaussian parameters. Lack of Global Guidance: Using only slice supervision (A4) limits accurate reconstruction of the full volumetric structure because slices cover limited regions at each iteration, lacking global spatial guidance. Precision: The mapping from 2D slice pixels to 3D voxel coordinates must be precise to ensure the Gaussian representation learns correct spatial continuity. This variant explicitly defines the sampling strategy. Sparse voxels provide global coverage, while slice samples capture spatially correlated regions encoding geometric structure and texture continuity. It aligns with shear-warp volume rendering, which generates images from stacks of 2D slices. In each iteration, a plane with arbitrary orientation is sampled, sparse pixels are selected, and each pixel is mapped to a 3D voxel coordinate, allowing the Gaussian representation to learn spatial continuity across neighboring regions. Strengths: Combining sparse voxel sampling with slice-based sampling enables the Gaussian representation to efficiently learn both global volumetric consistency and local anatomical details. This yields higher PSNR/SSIM compared to using only slice supervision or random voxel sampling alone. Limitations: Random voxel sampling without the structured guidance of slices can lead to unstable global approximation. Performance: The method is designed for efficient reconstruction and real-time selective visualization of multimodal volumetric datasets (MRI, Cryosection). Originated in the context of Gaussian Volumetric Representation for Efficient Shear-Warp Visualization, this method applies curriculum learning to medical data reconstruction. It leverages the natural alignment between slice-based sampling and the shear-warp rendering process to improve the learning of anatomical structures. name: Multi-stage Training with Pose Prediction
head: FineSplat training phases, Training and Inference Protocol, Two-stage Training with Pose-free Inference
body: Multi-stage training with pose prediction decomposes the optimization of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting models into sequential phases to decouple geometry estimation from appearance refinement and to stabilize pose learning. Unlike single-stage training, this method isolates camera pose prediction from Gaussian attribute updates, preventing error propagation where incorrect poses corrupt the learned Gaussian distribution. It sets itself apart by explicitly freezing pose-dependent parameters during appearance refinement stages and utilizing a final end-to-end phase to recover pose-free inference capabilities. The method operates on a set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} defined in Densification Strategy. The core mechanism involves partitioning optimization into distinct stages, modifying trainable parameters, supervision signals, and densification triggers to transition from a coarse representation to a fine-grained one. Inputs: Input RGB images I{in}, ground-truth camera poses/intrinsics (for supervised stages), and target view images I{gt} (for reconstruction loss). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} (positions \mathbf{p}, covariances \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacities \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}) and predicted camera poses/intrinsics for target views. The model typically consists of: 1. Geometry/Reconstructor Branch: Predicts camera poses and initial Gaussian centers/attributes. 2. Attribute/Refiner Branch: Refines Gaussian attributes (SH, opacity, scale) given the geometry. 3. Gaussian Decoder: Converts latent features or anchor points into final Gaussian parameters. Stage 1: Coarse Geometry and Pose Learning 1. Initialize the model with a pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction head. 2. Train for N1 iterations (e.g., 120K or until convergence). 3. Input: RGB images and ground-truth poses. 4. Supervision: Masked L1 and LPIPS losses on input and sampled target renderings. Camera losses on predicted poses/intrinsics. 5. Update: Only the attribute branch’s last K Transformer blocks and the Gaussian decoder, or the full pixel-aligned decoder. 6. Transition: Replace the pixel-aligned decoder with a patch-aligned Gaussian decoder. Stage 2: Appearance Refinement with Fixed Geometry 1. Freeze the Stage 1 trained parameters (specifically the geometry/pose estimator). 2. Train for N2 iterations (e.g., 80K or 20K). 3. Input: RGB images and ground-truth camera poses/intrinsics. 4. Supervision: Render target views at every step i \in \{0, \dots, T-1\} (where T=4). Compute loss averaged over steps: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{T} \sum{i=0}^{T-1} \left( \mathcal{L}2(\hat{I}^{(i)}, I) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{perc}(\hat{I}^{(i)}, I) \right) where \mathcal{L}2 is mean squared error, \mathcal{L}{perc} is VGG-19 perceptual loss, and \lambda = 0.2. 5. Detach tokens between steps so each step learns to improve the state it receives independently. 6. Update: Only the attribute/refiner branch or the patch-aligned decoder. Stage 3: End-to-End Fine-Tuning (Pose-Free) 1. Unfreeze all parameters, including the camera pose estimator and Gaussian head. 2. Train for N3 iterations (e.g., 10K). 3. Input: RGB images. No ground-truth target cameras are used. 4. Supervision: Predict context and target cameras. Supervise Stage-1 Gaussians. Loss averaged over steps i=0, \dots, T. No camera loss is applied. 5. Update: Full model. Inference (Pose-Free) 1. Use the geometry branch’s predicted cameras. 2. Normalize translations by s{norm} (derived from context camera pairwise distances or estimated depth). 3. Render input views for refinement feedback if a refiner is present. 4. The refiner updates scene attributes while network weights remain fixed. Optimizer: AdamW with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.95, weight decay 0.05 (multi-dimensional params only), gradient clipping max norm 1.0, bfloat16 mixed precision. Stage 1 LR: 2 \times 10^{-5}, no warm-up, cosine decay to zero. Stage 2 LR: 1 \times 10^{-4}, 200-iteration linear warm-up, constant until 80%, cosine decay to zero over remaining 20%. End-to-End LR: 2 \times 10^{-5} for all parameters, 200-iteration linear warm-up, cosine decay to zero. Perceptual Loss Weight: \lambda = 0.2. Pose Error Propagation: If Stage 2 is not trained with ground-truth poses, errors from Stage 1 pose prediction will corrupt the Gaussian attribute learning. Token Dependency: In iterative refinement (Stage 2), failing to detach tokens between steps causes error accumulation across steps. Scale Normalization: The scene scale is not fixed by input images. Methods differ in normalization: YoNoSplat uses the first context camera as origin and normalizes by max pairwise distance; ZipSplat uses estimated depth. InfiniSplat normalizes by s{norm}. Implementers must ensure consistent normalization between training and inference. RLSplat adapts multi-stage training for resource-linear budget control. Stage 1 (Base Training): Train geometry backbone and decoder with random allocations for 40,000 steps. Sample budgets from [2048, 16384V] where V is input views. This exposes the decoder to diverse allocations. Stage 2 (Policy Training): Add a policy head initialized to uniform probabilities. Fine-tune the entire model with policy loss \mathcal{L}{policy} = -J{policy} for 5,000 steps. Sample budgets skewed toward the lower end. Losses: \mathcal{L}{recon} (MSE + LPIPS), \mathcal{L}{cam} (translation, rotation, FOV), \mathcal{L}{proj} (reprojection with cheirality penalty), locality regularizers (\mathcal{L}{vor}, \mathcal{L}{offset}), and \mathcal{L}{policy}. Parameters: K{anc} = K{gs} = 16. Time Complexity: Significantly higher than single-stage training due to multiple sequential phases (e.g., 120K + 80K + 10K iterations). Memory Complexity: Similar to single-stage training per step, but requires storing intermediate states for iterative refinement (Stage 2). Performance: Improves novel-view synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) by stabilizing pose learning and allowing focused refinement of appearance. Strengths: Decouples pose and geometry errors; enables pose-free inference; robust to initial pose inaccuracies. Limitations: Increased training time; complex hyperparameter tuning across stages; requires careful normalization of scene scale. When to use: When feed-forward models suffer from pose instability or when high-fidelity appearance is required after coarse geometry is established. Originating from the need to stabilize feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, this method was introduced in FineSplat and InfiniSplat v2. It addresses the instability of jointly optimizing camera poses and Gaussian attributes in a single pass. The approach builds on the principle that pose estimation and appearance refinement are distinct optimization problems that benefit from sequential treatment. RLSplat extends this to include budget control via policy learning. name: Free-View Training (FVT)
body: Free-View Training (FVT) is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that adds geometrical constraints on Gaussian localization to disentangle model performance from the specific number of input views. It enables robust novel view synthesis across broader view ranges regardless of the input view count, facilitating generalizable reconstruction from long sequences. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes for a fixed set of views, FVT supervises renderings in broader view interpolations to improve depth estimation and adaptability. FVT operates on the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} defined in Densification Strategy. It modifies the training loop to sample multiple context views and supervise the rendering against ground truth images from these interpolated views. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses. A sequence of frames (potentially long sequences). Hyperparameter T: the number of context views to sample per iteration. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} (positions, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: \mathcal{G}: The set of 3D Gaussians. I{gt}: Ground truth image for a target view. I{pred}: Rendered image from \mathcal{G} using the camera projection for the target view. Parameters: T: Number of context views sampled. Typical value: 2 to 8. Steps: 1. Context View Sampling: During each training iteration, randomly sample T context views from the available training sequence. Let the set of sampled view indices be \mathcal{V}{ctx} = \{v1, v2,..., vT\}. 2. Target View Selection: Select a target view v{tgt} from the sequence. This view serves as the reference for supervision. 3. Rendering: Render the image I{pred} for the target view v{tgt} using the current Gaussian set \mathcal{G} and the corresponding camera pose. 4. Supervision: Compute the loss between the rendered image I{pred} and the ground truth image I{gt} of the target view. The supervision is applied on full resolution to encourage high-resolution renderings, even if intermediate feature extraction uses lower resolution maps. 5. Optimization: Update the parameters of \mathcal{G} (and potentially camera poses if unfrozen) using gradient descent to minimize the loss. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 1-5 for the duration of the training, ensuring the model is exposed to a diverse range of view interpolations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def freeviewtraining(Gaussians, TrainingSequence, T): """ Gaussians: Current set of 3D Gaussian primitives TrainingSequence: List of (image, camerapose) tuples T: Number of context views to sample (2-8) """ for iteration in range(numiterations): # Step 1: Randomly sample T context views # Note: The specific selection of context views vs target view # is described as "supervise the image renderings in the broader view interpolations" # We assume one view is the target for loss, others inform the geometry. sampledindices = random.sample(range(len(TrainingSequence)), T + 1) targetidx = sampledindices[0] contextindices = sampledindices[1:] targetimage, targetpose = TrainingSequence[targetidx] # Step 2 & 3: Render the target view renderedimage = render(Gaussians, targetpose) # Step 4: Compute loss on full resolution # Loss function typically includes photometric and depth consistency terms # if depth priors are available, or just photometric loss otherwise. loss = computeloss(renderedimage, targetimage) # Step 5: Backpropagate and update Gaussians loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Note: Densification (splitting/cloning) is handled by the parent # Densification Strategy logic, # potentially triggered by gradients from this FVT supervision. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Distribution: If the sampled views are too similar, the geometrical constraints may be weak. The random sampling should cover the view range effectively. Sequence Length: FVT is designed for long sequences. Training on very short sequences may not provide the "broader view interpolations" necessary for the strategy to disentangle view count from performance. Resolution: Supervision must be applied at full resolution to prevent blurring, even if feature extraction uses lower resolutions. Time Complexity: Training time increases with the number of views sampled and the sequence length, but the efficient feature extraction and aggregation in FreeSplat++ make long-sequence training feasible. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and the sequence length stored in memory. FreeSplat aims to reduce redundant Gaussians, potentially lowering memory usage compared to naive multi-view training. Performance: FVT significantly contributes to depth estimation accuracy and robust novel view synthesis across different numbers of input views. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on indoor datasets like ScanNet and Replica. Strengths: Disentangles generalizability from input view count; improves depth estimation; reduces Gaussian redundancy in overlapping regions. Limitations: Requires careful sampling of views to ensure broad coverage; may require more training iterations to converge compared to single-view optimization. FVT was introduced in the context of generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically in the FreeSplat and FreeSplat++ papers. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which is often tied to the specific number and arrangement of input views. By training on long sequences and supervising broader view interpolations, FVT enables feed-forward large scene reconstruction without depth priors and improves inference efficiency. name: Training Loop with Mixed Losses and Post-Processing
head: Mixed Loss Training Loop, Post-Processing Training Step
body: This method defines the iterative optimization step for 3D Gaussian Splatting, integrating photometric reconstruction, depth supervision, appearance regularization, and structural constraints into a single backward pass. It distinguishes itself from simpler training loops by explicitly supporting multi-stage parameter updates (such as spherical harmonic degree progression and bilateral grid refinement) and post-processing densification triggers within the same iteration. It serves as the core engine for the progressive training strategies described in Progressive and Multi-stage Training. Inputs: Current optimization step (integer). Gaussian set \mathcal{G} (means, scales, quaternions, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients). Camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics) and image IDs. Ground truth images I{gt} and optional depth maps D{gt}. Configuration object cfg containing boolean flags and scalar weights. Optimization state (Adam optimizers, schedulers, bilateral grid parameters if enabled). Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}'. Updated camera parameters (if optimized). Updated bilateral grid weights (if enabled). Logging metrics (loss values, PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS if evaluated). The Gaussian set \mathcal{G} is typically stored in packed or unpacked tensors: means: (N, 3) float32. scales: (N, 3) float32. quats: (N, 4) float32 (normalized). opacities: (N, 1) float32. sh0: (N, 3) float32 (SH degree 0). shN: (N, K) float32 (SH degree >0), where K = 3 \times d^2 - 3 for max degree d. colors: (N, 3) float32 (optional, used if SH is not used for base color). The info dictionary returned by the rasterizer contains: radii: (N, 2) int32 (bounding box of splats in screen space). gaussianids: (H, W) int32 (index of the top Gaussian per pixel). alphas: (H, W, 1) float32 (accumulated opacity). depths: (H, W, 1) float32 (accumulated depth, if requested). cfg.shdegreeinterval: Integer, steps between increasing SH degree. cfg.shdegree: Integer, maximum SH degree (typically 3 or 4). cfg.depthloss: Boolean, enable depth supervision. cfg.usebilateralgrid: Boolean, enable appearance refinement via bilateral grids. cfg.randombkgd: Boolean, composite against random background. cfg.usel1forrealsamples: Boolean, use L1 instead of L2 for reconstruction. cfg.ssimlambda: Float, weight for SSIM loss (typically 0.2). cfg.depthlambda: Float, weight for depth loss. cfg.opacityreg: Float, weight for opacity regularization. cfg.scalereg: Float, weight for scale regularization. cfg.visibleadam: Boolean, use visibility-aware Adam updates. cfg.packed: Boolean, use packed rasterization. 1. Spherical Harmonic Degree Selection: Calculate the active SH degree d{active} for the current step: d{active} = \min\left(\left\lfloor \frac{\text{step}}{\text{cfg.sh\degree\interval}} \right\rfloor, \text{cfg.sh\degree}\right) This ensures gradual introduction of high-frequency appearance details. 2. Rasterization: Render the scene using the current Gaussian set and camera parameters. If cfg.depthloss is true, render mode is 'RGB+ED' (RGB + Estimated Depth). Otherwise, render mode is 'RGB'. Let renders be the output tensor of shape (H, W, C). If renders has 4 channels, split into colors = renders[..., 0:3] and depths = renders[..., 3:4]. Otherwise, colors = renders and depths = None. 3. Bilateral Grid Slicing (Optional): If cfg.usebilateralgrid is true: Compute grid coordinates gridxy for each pixel based on screen position and depth. Apply bilateral grid slicing to refine colors: \text{colors} = \text{slice}(\text{self.bil\grids}, \text{grid\xy}, \text{colors}, \text{image\ids})[\text{"rgb"}] This step requires the bilateral grid optimizer to be stepped separately. 4. Background Compositing (Optional): If cfg.randombkgd is true: Generate a random background color \mathbf{b} \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1) of shape (1, 3). Composite the rendered colors against the background using the accumulated alpha \alpha: \mathbf{c}{final} = \mathbf{c}{rendered} + \mathbf{b} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha) This handles transparent regions by filling them with a random color, preventing the model from learning to render black backgrounds. 5. Pre-Backward Strategy Step: Call strategy.stepprebackward(params, optimizers, state, step, info). This allows custom strategies (e.g., MCMC or default densification logic) to modify parameters or state before loss computation. 6. Reconstruction Loss: Compute the photometric loss between the rendered colors \mathbf{c}{final} and ground truth I{gt}. If the sample is not a NeRF sample (i.e., real image): If cfg.usel1forrealsamples is true, use L1 loss: L{L1} = \|\mathbf{c}{final} - I{gt}\|1. Otherwise, use L2 loss: L{L2} = \|\mathbf{c}{final} - I{gt}\|2^2. Compute SSIM loss L{SSIM} using a differentiable SSIM implementation. Combine: L{recon} = L{recon\base} \cdot (1.0 - \text{cfg.ssim\lambda}) + L{SSIM} \cdot \text{cfg.ssim\lambda} Add to total loss: L{total} = L{recon}. 7. Depth Loss (Optional): If cfg.depthloss is true and depth maps are available: Normalize 3D points to [-1, 1] range. Sample depths from the ground truth depth map D{gt} using F.gridsample. Compute disparity from rendered depths: d{rendered} = 1.0 / \text{depths} (where \text{depths} > 0). Compute disparity from ground truth: d{gt} = 1.0 / D{gt}. Compute L1 loss on disparity, scaled by scene scale: L{depth} = \text{F.l1\loss}(d{rendered}, d{gt}) \cdot \text{self.scene\scale} Add to total loss: L{total} += L{depth} \cdot \text{cfg.depth\lambda}. 8. Bilateral Grid Total Variation (Optional): If cfg.usebilateralgrid is true: Compute total variation loss on the bilateral grid weights: L{TV} = 10 \cdot \text{total\variation\loss}(\text{self.bil\grids.grids}) Add to total loss: L{total} += L{TV}. 9. Opacity Regularization: If cfg.opacityreg > 0.0: Compute mean of sigmoid-applied opacities: L{opacity} = \text{cfg.opacity\reg} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\sigma(\text{opacities})] Add to total loss: L{total} += L{opacity}. 10. Scale Regularization: If cfg.scalereg > 0.0: Compute mean of exponential-applied scales: L{scale} = \text{cfg.scale\reg} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\exp(\text{scales})] Add to total loss: L{total} += L{scale}. 11. Backward Pass: Call Ltotal.backward(). 12. Visibility Mask Computation (Optional): If cfg.visibleadam is true: If cfg.packed is true, create a zero tensor of shape equal to the number of Gaussians. Scatter 1s at indices info["gaussianids"] for pixels with valid depth/alpha. Else, compute mask as (info["radii"] > 0).all(-1).any(0). This mask identifies Gaussians that contributed to the final image. 13. Optimizer Step: If cfg.visibleadam is true, pass the visibility mask to the optimizer: \text{optimizer.step}(\text{visibility\mask}) Else: \text{optimizer.step}() Zero gradients with settonone=True. 14. Pose and Bilateral Grid Optimization: Step poseoptimizers and bilgridoptimizers if they exist. Zero their gradients. 15. Scheduler Step: Step all learning rate schedulers. 16. Post-Backward Strategy Step: Call strategy.steppostbackward. If DefaultStrategy, pass packed=cfg.packed. If MCMCStrategy, pass lr=schedulers[0].getlastlr()[0]. This handles densification (splitting/cloning) and pruning based on gradients or other metrics. 17. PLY Export (Optional): If step is in cfg.plysteps or step == maxsteps - 1 and cfg.saveply is true: If cfg.appopt (appearance optimization) is true: Bake appearance by evaluating the appearance module at the origin (directions \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{0}). Add self.splats["colors"], apply sigmoid, convert to SH0, and create empty SHN. Else: Use self.splats["sh0"] and self.splats["shN"] directly. Export splats with means, scales, quaternions, opacities, SH0, and SHN. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainingstep(step, gaussians, cameras, gtimages, gtdepths, cfg, optimizers, schedulers, strategy, scenescale): # 1. SH Degree Selection shdegreetouse = min(step // cfg.shdegreeinterval, cfg.shdegree) # 2. Rasterization rendermode = 'RGB+ED' if cfg.depthloss else 'RGB' renders, alphas, info = rasterize(gaussians, cameras, rendermode) # Split renders if renders.shape[-1] == 4: colors = renders[..., 0:3] depths = renders[..., 3:4] else: colors = renders depths = None # 3. Bilateral Grid Slicing if cfg.usebilateralgrid: gridxy = computegridcoordinates(cameras, info) colors = slicebilateralgrid(gaussians.bilgrids, gridxy, colors, cameras.imageids)["rgb"] # 4. Background Compositing if cfg.randombkgd: bkgd = torch.rand(1, 3, device=colors.device) colors = colors + bkgd (1.0 - alphas) # 5. Pre-Backward Strategy strategy.stepprebackward(gaussians, optimizers, step, info) # 6. Reconstruction Loss loss = 0.0 if not isnerfsample.any(): if cfg.usel1forrealsamples: reconloss = F.l1loss(colors, gtimages) else: reconloss = F.mseloss(colors, gtimages) ssimloss = ssimlossfunction(colors, gtimages) loss = reconloss (1.0 - cfg.ssimlambda) + ssimloss cfg.ssimlambda # 7. Depth Loss if cfg.depthloss and depths is not None: # Normalize points and sample depths pointsnormalized = normalizepoints(gaussians.means) sampleddepthsgt = F.gridsample(gtdepths, pointsnormalized) disprendered = 1.0 / (depths + 1e-6) dispgt = 1.0 / (sampleddepthsgt + 1e-6) depthloss = F.l1loss(disprendered, dispgt) scenescale loss += depthloss cfg.depthlambda # 8. Bilateral Grid TV Loss if cfg.usebilateralgrid: tvloss = 10 totalvariationloss(gaussians.bilgrids.grids) loss += tvloss # 9. Opacity Regularization if cfg.opacityreg > 0.0: opacityreg = cfg.opacityreg torch.sigmoid(gaussians.opacities).mean() loss += opacityreg # 10. Scale Regularization if cfg.scalereg > 0.0: scalereg = cfg.scalereg torch.exp(gaussians.scales).mean() loss += scalereg # 11. Backward Pass loss.backward() # 12. Visibility Mask visibilitymask = None if cfg.visibleadam: if cfg.packed: visibilitymask = torch.zeros(gaussians.numgaussians, device=colors.device) visibilitymask.scatter(0, info["gaussianids"].flatten(), 1.0) else: visibilitymask = (info["radii"] > 0).all(-1).any(0) # 13. Optimizer Step if cfg.visibleadam: optimizers.gaussianoptimizer.step(visibilitymask) else: optimizers.gaussianoptimizer.step() optimizers.gaussianoptimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) # 14. Pose and Bilateral Grid Optimization if optimizers.poseoptimizer: optimizers.poseoptimizer.step() optimizers.poseoptimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) if optimizers.bilgridoptimizer: optimizers.bilgridoptimizer.step() optimizers.bilgridoptimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) # 15. Scheduler Step for scheduler in schedulers: scheduler.step() # 16. Post-Backward Strategy if isinstance(strategy, DefaultStrategy): strategy.steppostbackward(packed=cfg.packed) elif isinstance(strategy, MCMCStrategy): lr = schedulers[0].getlastlr()[0] strategy.steppostbackward(lr=lr) # 17. PLY Export if cfg.saveply and (step in cfg.plysteps or step == cfg.maxsteps - 1): if cfg.appopt: sh0, shN = bakeappearance(gaussians) else: sh0 = gaussians.sh0 shN = gaussians.shN exportply(gaussians.means, gaussians.scales, gaussians.quats, gaussians.opacities, sh0, shN) return loss.item() Depth Division by Zero: When computing disparity 1.0/\text{depths}, add a small epsilon (1e-6) to avoid division by zero for pixels with zero depth. SH Degree Mismatch: Ensure that the number of SH coefficients matches the selected degree d{active}. Mismatched dimensions will cause tensor shape errors during rasterization or loss computation. Visibility Mask Shape: If cfg.packed is true, the visibility mask must be created with size equal to the total number of Gaussians, not just the active ones. Incorrect sizing will lead to index out-of-bounds errors. Random Background Consistency: If cfg.randombkgd is true, the background color should be generated per-image or per-step, not per-pixel, to maintain consistency across the image. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) per step, where N is the number of Gaussians, and H, W are image dimensions. The rasterization step dominates. Memory Complexity: O(N + H \cdot W) for storing Gaussian parameters and intermediate render buffers. Performance: Depends heavily on the number of Gaussians and the complexity of the scene. Bilateral grid and depth loss add overhead but improve convergence. Strengths: Integrates multiple loss types and post-processing steps efficiently. Supports gradual complexity increase via SH degree progression. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization weights. Depth loss requires accurate ground truth depth maps. This method is derived from the training loop implementation in AugSplat, which extends the original 3D Gaussian Splatting training procedure with additional features like bilateral grid refinement and visibility-aware Adam updates. It is commonly used in Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction and other advanced 3DGS applications. llazzaroni/AugSplat, https://github.com/llazzaroni/AugSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Training Loop with Structure-Aware Densification
head: Structure-Aware Densification, Frequency-Aware Densification
body: This method accelerates 3D Gaussian Splatting training by integrating a structure-aware densification strategy that triggers splits based on local image frequency rather than solely on gradient magnitude or opacity thresholds. It solves the slow convergence of standard reactive densification by ensuring primitives are subdivided early enough to capture high-frequency details, while maintaining perceptual quality. It sets itself apart from Hybrid Coarse-to-Fine Strategy by using a unified frequency metric for densification across stages, and from Training Objective and Densification by replacing opacity-based triggers with structure tensor analysis. The method modifies the standard 3DGS optimization loop by adding a precomputation step, a frequency-based densification trigger, and a supplementary densification pass. Inputs: Training images, camera poses (from Structure-from-Motion), scene bounding box. Outputs: Optimized set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} with positions, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Structure Tensors (\bar{\mathbf{T}}): Precomputed for each training image. Stores multi-scale structure tensor values. Memory cost equals the footprint of the input images. Gaussian Set (\mathcal{G}): Standard 3DGS Gaussian representation. Frequency Metric (\eta): A scalar value computed per Gaussian during the forward pass, representing the local frequency violation. Before training begins: 1. Initialize Gaussians using Structure-from-Motion points. 2. Place additional Gaussians on the faces of the scene's bounding box to ensure complete geometric coverage of empty regions. 3. Precompute multi-scale structure tensors \bar{\mathbf{T}} for each training image using vectorized GPU operations. This incurs a one-time overhead of 0.7 seconds. The training loop runs for a fixed number of iterations (N{it}). For each iteration i: 1. Batch Selection: Select a batch of training images. Batch size B=2 for indoor scenes (Mip-NeRF 360, Deep Blending). Batch size B=1 for outdoor scenes (Tanks & Temples). 2. Forward Rendering: Render the batch. For each visible Gaussian, reuse the 2D covariance and intermediate buffers from the forward pass. Sample one point within each Gaussian's footprint to compute the frequency metric \eta. This avoids additional projection or sampling overhead. Note: The exact formula for \eta is not provided in the sources, but it is derived from the precomputed structure tensors and the Gaussian's footprint. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss. Standard 3DGS losses (photometric, D-SSIM). Add an additional L2 loss to the training objective for faster convergence. 4. Backward Pass: Compute gradients and update parameters. 5. Densification: Structure-Aware Densification: Every 500 iterations, apply the structure-aware densification strategy. Gaussians with high \eta are split. The conservative split factor p=0.5 is used to partially compensate for over-densification. AbsGS Densification: Every 100 iterations, apply the densification strategy from AbsGS [Ye et al. 2024] to populate empty regions with primitives. This ensures that the structure-aware densification has existing primitives to leverage. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstructureawaregaussiansplatting(images, poses, boundingbox, Nit): # Precomputation gaussians = initializesfmandbbox(poses, boundingbox) structuretensors = precomputestructuretensors(images) # 0.7s overhead # Training Loop for i in range(1, Nit + 1): # Batch selection if isoutdoorscene(): batchsize = 1 else: batchsize = 2 batchimages = selectbatch(images, batchsize) # Forward Pass renderedimages, visiblegaussians = render(batchimages, gaussians) # Compute frequency metric eta for visible Gaussians # Reuse 2D covariance and buffers from forward pass eta = computefrequencymetric(visiblegaussians, structuretensors) # Loss Computation # Standard 3DGS losses + additional L2 loss loss = compute3dgsloss(renderedimages, batchimages) + lambdal2 computel2loss(gaussians) # Backward Pass gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) updateparameters(gaussians, gradients) # Densification if i % 100 == 0: # AbsGS densification to populate empty regions densifyabsgs(gaussians) if i % 500 == 0: # Structure-aware densification densifystructureaware(gaussians, eta, splitfactor=0.5) return gaussians Structure-Aware Densification Interval: 500 iterations. AbsGS Densification Interval: 100 iterations. Split Factor (p): 0.5. Batch Size: 2 (indoor), 1 (outdoor). Training Iterations (N{it}): 3,000 for Mip-NeRF 360 and Deep Blending; 7,000 for Tanks & Temples. Position Learning Rate Max Steps: 3,000 for Mip-NeRF 360 and Deep Blending; 7,000 for Tanks & Temples. Over-densification: The metric \eta matches the highest local frequency within each Gaussian's footprint, which can lead to a higher number of Gaussians than necessary. This is because \eta evaluates each Gaussian in isolation, ignoring the collective contribution of overlapping primitives. Stochastic Variance: If Stochastic Jitter Sampling is used for frequency estimation, minor variance across training runs may occur due to the stochastic nature of sampling. In practice, this variance is negligible. Positional Offsets: Due to reduced training iterations, Gaussian positions may not fully converge, leading to sub-pixel misalignments that penalize PSNR more than perceptual metrics (SSIM, LPIPS). A robust estimation technique that samples random offsets (jitter) within each Gaussian's footprint to approximate local frequency requirements. It improves coverage and reduces sensitivity to edge alignment. It introduces minor variance across training runs due to the stochastic nature of sampling, but this is negligible in practice. The conservative split factor p=0.5 partially compensates for the over-densification tendency caused by \eta matching the highest local frequency within each footprint. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than standard 3DGS. Mip-NeRF 360: 52.96 seconds (18x faster than 3DGS, 2.7x faster than FastGS-Base). Deep Blending: 41.22 seconds (23x faster than 3DGS, 2.8x faster than FastGS-Base). Tanks & Temples: 84.44 seconds (6.8x faster than 3DGS, 1.5x faster than FastGS-Base). All timings measured on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Memory Complexity: Additional memory cost equal to the footprint of the input images for storing precomputed structure tensors. Strengths: Faster convergence, superior perceptual quality (SSIM, LPIPS), efficient use of training iterations. Limitations: Higher Gaussian count due to over-densification; potential for positional offsets affecting PSNR; precomputation overhead (0.7s). When to Use: When training speed is critical and perceptual quality is prioritized over absolute PSNR. Suitable for both indoor and outdoor scenes with dataset-specific batch sizes. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained (due to structure tensor storage) or when absolute PSNR is the primary metric and positional accuracy is critical. The method was introduced in "Faster 3D Gaussian Splatting Convergence via Structure-Aware Densification". It addresses the slow convergence of standard 3DGS by leveraging image structure information to guide densification. The approach builds on the principles of progressive and multi-stage training, specifically focusing on the densification strategy. It compares favorably against other fast 3DGS variants like FastGS, Mini-Splatting, and Speedy-Splat. Faster 3D Gaussian Splatting Convergence via Structure-Aware Densification, https://doi.org/10.1145/3799902.3811212, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Hyperparameter Settings
head: Optimizer and Regularization Settings, Optimizer settings, Phys3DGS Hyperparameter Settings, Training Hyperparameters
body: Hyperparameter Settings define the numerical configuration for the optimizer, learning rates, and regularization terms used during the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. This method solves the problem of stable convergence and high-fidelity reconstruction by tuning the trade-off between fitting training data and maintaining geometric/photometric consistency. It differs from sibling methods like Densification Strategy (which manages primitive count) and Pruning and Sparsification (which removes primitives) by focusing on the gradient descent dynamics and loss weighting rather than structural topology changes. The method configures the optimization loop by setting the optimizer type, learning rates for specific Gaussian attributes, and weights for auxiliary loss terms. Inputs: Model parameters: Position \mu, Color SH coefficients \mathbf{c}, Scale s, Opacity \alpha, and potentially material parameters (Base Color, Metallic, Roughness) or dynamic parameters (MLP weights). Ground truth images and camera poses. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: Optimizer State: Adam optimizer state buffers (first and second moment estimates) for each parameter group. Learning Rate Schedule: A mapping from parameter type to initial learning rate and decay schedule. Parameters and Typical Values: 1. Optimizer: Adam. \beta1 = 0.9 \beta2 = 0.999 \epsilon = 10^{-15}. 2. Learning Rates (LR): Standard 3DGS: Position: 1.6 \times 10^{-4} Color SH: 2.5 \times 10^{-3} Scale: 5 \times 10^{-3} Opacity: 5 \times 10^{-2} Normal Rotation: 1 \times 10^{-3} Phys3DGS (Inverse Rendering): Base Color: 1 \times 10^{-2} Metallic: 1 \times 10^{-2} Roughness: 1 \times 10^{-2} Direct Light SH (deg=0): 2.5 \times 10^{-3} Direct Light SH (deg>0): 1 \times 10^{-4} Indirect Light SH (deg=0): 2.5 \times 10^{-4} Indirect Light SH (deg>0): 1 \times 10^{-3} Visibility SH: 0.1 ToRF (Dynamic/Depth): MLP weights: Initial \gamma{MLP} = 0.0008, decaying exponentially to 1.6 \times 10^{-6} over 60,000 iterations. Reflectivity: Initial value 0.1, LR \gammar = 0.00016. 3. Regularization Strengths (Phys3DGS): Smoothness regularizer for Base Color: \lambda{smooth} = 0.06 Smoothness regularizer for Roughness: \lambda{smooth} = 0.02 Smoothness regularizer for Metallic: \lambda{smooth} = 0.02 Other regularizers (\lambdao, \lambda{sc}, \lambda{sr}): 1.0 4. Loss Weights (ToRF): \alpha = 5 (for real scenes), \alpha = 1 (for synthetic scenes). \beta = 0.0008. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyhyperparameters(params, config): """ Configure optimizer state and learning rates for 3DGS training. params: dict mapping parameter names to tensors (numpy-like arrays). config: dict containing optimizer settings, lrschedule, and regularization weights. """ # Initialize Adam state buffers (first and second moments) for each parameter optimizerstate = {} for name, tensor in params.items(): optimizerstate[name] = { 'm': zeroslike(tensor), # First moment 'v': zeroslike(tensor) # Second moment } # Define learning rate mapping based on parameter type lrmap = { 'position': 1.6e-4, 'colorsh': 2.5e-3, 'scale': 5.0e-3, 'opacity': 5.0e-2, 'basecolor': 1.0e-2, 'metallic': 1.0e-2, 'roughness': 1.0e-2, 'normalrotation': 1.0e-3, 'directlightshdeg0': 2.5e-3, 'directlightshdeggt0': 1.0e-4, 'indirectlightshdeg0': 2.5e-4, 'indirectlightshdeggt0': 1.0e-3, 'visibilitysh': 0.1, 'mlpweights': config.get('mlplr', 0.0008), 'reflectivity': 0.00016 } # Assign learning rates to parameter groups paramgroups = [] for name, tensor in params.items(): lr = lrmap.get(name, 1.0e-3) # Default fallback paramgroups.append({'params': [tensor], 'lr': lr}) return optimizerstate, paramgroups def computelossandupdate(pred, gt, params, gradients, optimizerstate, config, iteration): """ Compute loss with regularization and perform a single Adam update step. """ # Photometric loss (L1) photometricloss = mean(abs(pred - gt)) # Regularization terms smoothnessloss = config['lambdasmooth'] mean(abs(gradients)) otherregloss = 1.0 mean(abs(params)) totalloss = photometricloss + smoothnessloss + otherregloss # Backward pass would populate gradients dict # Adam update step for each parameter beta1, beta2, eps = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-15 for name, tensor in params.items(): grad = gradients[name] state = optimizerstate[name] lr = lrmap.get(name, 1.0e-3) # Exponential decay for MLP weights (ToRF) if name == 'mlpweights': lr = 0.0008 (0.999973 iteration) # Decays to 1.6e-6 over 60k iters # Adam update state['m'] = beta1 state['m'] + (1 - beta1) grad state['v'] = beta2 state['v'] + (1 - beta2) grad 2 mhat = state['m'] / (1 - beta1 (iteration + 1)) vhat = state['v'] / (1 - beta2 (iteration + 1)) tensor = tensor - lr mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + eps) return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instability from Erroneous Gaussians: If a single Gaussian behaves abnormally (e.g., driven to the opposite side of the surface, extremely large scale, or extreme opacity), it causes training instability. Mechanism: Erroneous Gaussians interfere with visibility, occluding global illumination. The optimizer compensates by either increasing local illumination intensity (dimming global) or decreasing opacity to extreme values. Result: Global illumination SH coefficients or opacity values receive large gradients, leading to overflow. Mitigation: Use higher weights for other regularizers (\lambdao, \lambda{sc}, \lambda{sr} = 1.0) to constrain this behavior. View Selection Bias: Using training views for optimization focuses on known-view fitting and degrades novel-view performance. Avoid using training views (+train) as they focus on known-view fitting. Use test views for optimization. Alternatively, use synthetic views sampled from the estimated camera trajectory (+syn.). Extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning Gaussian covariance and opacity on time t and view direction d. It differs from static 3DGS by using a conditional covariance matrix to drive densification and splitting, and from other dynamic variants by integrating these cues directly into the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline with minimal architectural changes. Uses an auxiliary per-pixel error metric to drive densification decisions, rather than relying on positional gradient magnitudes. It solves the limitation of gradient-based methods (sensitive to error changes but blind to absolute error in high-frequency areas) by redistributing per-pixel errors to primitives proportional to their rendering contribution. Distinct from siblings like Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering by explicitly utilizing accumulated L1 error norms as probability weights for splitting. Addresses under-constrained geometry in few-shot neural rendering by integrating precise correspondences from a sparse matching network into 3DGS initialization and optimization. Unlike dense matcher-based methods that introduce blurriness in high-frequency areas, this approach yields precise correspondences that, combined with frequency regularization, enable better reconstruction of fine details. It serves as a densification and initialization strategy enhancing base 3DGS in sparse-view scenarios. A learnable module within the FlexGS framework that adaptively selects a subset of 3D Gaussians during training based on attributes and a desired elastic ratio e, using a differentiable mask. It sets itself apart from non-differentiable thresholding or hard masking by allowing gradients to flow through the selection decision via the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) applied to Gumbel-Softmax outputs, unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed heuristics or non-differentiable hard thresholds. Addresses optimization challenges of large, sparse, unbounded scenes by dividing the environment into independent spatial chunks, each trained separately. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by introducing a skybox for environmental consistency, modifying densification policies to handle sparse gradients, and applying monocular depth regularization for unobserved surfaces. Refines primitives by splitting large Gaussians located in high-frequency edge regions to capture fine details. It addresses the weakness of enlarged primitives, which lose high-frequency detail, particularly when used in conjunction with Random Dropout Regularization (RDR). Unlike standard splitting based solely on position gradient magnitude, it explicitly guides splitting toward geometric edges, making it distinct from sibling methods like Blended Error Densification and Splitting which rely on rendering error [13892-blended-error-densification-and-splitting.md]. Specifies the canonical hyperparameter settings for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting models, establishing the baseline for adaptive density control and gradient-based optimization. It differs from sibling methods like Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering or Blended Error Densification and Splitting by adhering strictly to the default parameters of the official implementation, specifically regarding densification frequency, gradient thresholds, and opacity management. A training optimization that reduces memory overhead during high-resolution rendering by organizing Gaussians into spatial groups (leaves) and using compact gradient storage. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption caused by maintaining full dense gradients for all Gaussians during the backward pass of large scenes. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling the gradient accumulation scope to leaf boundaries and using a global ID mapping to feed only necessary gradient rows into the Adam optimizer, while maintaining dense gradients for opacity to support global regularization. A mechanism for maintaining correspondence between fixed consensus statistics and newly created Gaussian primitives during densification (splitting or cloning) in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It prevents the breaking of the fixed-consensus protocol by ensuring that new Gaussians inherit relevant prior information, thereby allowing consensus statistics to evolve with the Gaussian population while retaining contamination-resistant properties. It is distinct from sibling methods like Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering and Blended Error Densification and Splitting by explicitly managing the inheritance of consensus weights and periodic re-estimation thresholds rather than altering the densification criteria or loss functions directly. A method simplifying mesh generation by utilizing an initial mesh or estimating it in a single-stage training process, introducing a pseudo-mesh of unconnected triangle faces with Gaussian components positioned on these faces to ensure proper alignment. It realizes deformation by modifying pseudo-mesh positions, with alterations automatically propagating to the Gaussian mesh, enabling real-time animation and scene editing. However, it exhibits artifacts when dealing with significant deformations in meshes with large faces, leading to inaccuracies. Selects specific views for adaptation optimization to prevent overfitting to known training views and maintain novel-view performance. Steps: 1. Avoid using training views (+train) as they focus on known-view fitting. 2. Use test views for optimization. 3. Alternatively, use synthetic views sampled from the estimated camera trajectory (+syn.). Typical number of synthetic views used: 50. On the bicycle scene, PSNR with test views was Zoom-out 30.84, Zoom-in 24.23; with synthetic views: Zoom-out 29.72, Zoom-in 30.05. Creates a set of initial images from various views around the target volume and trains a peripheral model for 700 iterations using a MiniSplatting2-based approach. Renders training views at 512x512 pixels covering a 20° field of view. Number of initial views: 8, 12, 16, or 32. Samples per pixel (SPP): 4, 8, or 16. Normal quality preset: 12 views at 8 SPP. High quality preset: 16 views at 16 SPP. Using only 8 images or 4 SPP often misses important details. Using more than 16 views significantly delays the availability of the initial model with diminishing returns. Initial model generation takes under 300 ms; full reconstruction completes in about a second. Produces a higher-quality model faster than standard 3DGS with half the number of Gaussians, as opacity reset struggles to lower Gaussian counts. A pruning method that reduces the number of Gaussians (N) using a second-order sensitivity criterion based on the local reconstruction-loss change. Calculates the local Hessian block Hj for each Gaussian's spatial parameters. Computes the sensitivity \Delta Lj. Removes Gaussians with low sensitivity (low \Delta Lj) before refinement. Formula: \Delta Lj \approx \frac{1}{2} \delta\thetaj^T Hj \delta\thetaj, where \Delta Lj is the local reconstruction-loss change for Gaussian j, \delta\thetaj is the perturbation of spatial Gaussian parameters \thetaj, and Hj is the local Hessian block associated with the spatial parameters of Gaussian j. On the shared baseline in Table 9, PUP removes approximately 90% of Gaussians and 90% of serialized bytes, changing PSNR from 25.01 to 25.42 dB. PUP primarily reduces N (primitive count), whereas Compact3D primarily reduces bg (storage per Gaussian). Strengths: Carefully tuned learning rates (e.g., higher LR for opacity and scale) allow for rapid adaptation of primitive properties. Regularization weights prevent instability from outlier Gaussians. Limitations: Improper regularization weights can lead to gradient overflow in SH coefficients or opacity. Using training views for optimization degrades novel view synthesis quality. When to use: Standard 3DGS training requires the base learning rates. Inverse rendering (Phys3DGS) requires specific material and lighting LR settings. Dynamic scenes (ToRF) require MLP decay schedules. Sparse view scenarios may benefit from view selection strategies. The hyperparameter settings for 3D Gaussian Splatting were introduced alongside the original 3DGS paper, establishing the baseline Adam optimizer configuration. Subsequent works have adapted these settings for specific domains: Phys3DGS introduced settings for physically-based inverse rendering, ToRF adapted them for time-of-flight and dynamic scenes, and Mip-Splatting variants explored view selection strategies to prevent overfitting to known training views. The importance of regularization weights to prevent instability from erroneous Gaussians was highlighted in Phys3DGS.
