name: Adaptive Gaussian Selector
head: Gumbel-Softmax Selection
body: The Adaptive Gaussian Selector is a learnable module within the FlexGS framework that adaptively selects a subset of 3D Gaussians during training based on their attributes and a desired elastic ratio e, using a differentiable mask to enable gradient-based optimization. It sets itself apart from non-differentiable thresholding or hard masking by allowing gradients to flow through the selection decision via the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) applied to Gumbel-Softmax outputs, unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed heuristics or non-differentiable hard thresholds. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ai: The set of attributes for the i-th Gaussian. e: The desired elastic ratio (sparsity level), sampled from a set \mathcal{E}. N: Total number of Gaussians. Outputs: \hat{M}i: A binary mask value (0 or 1) for each Gaussian, indicating selection. z: Logits for the categorical distribution. Data Structures: GsNet Parameters: w{1e} \in \mathbb{R}^D: Weight vector for ratio embedding. W{2e} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}: Weight matrix for ratio embedding. W{1a} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times D}: Weight matrix for attribute embedding. W{2a} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}: Weight matrix for attribute embedding. W \in \mathbb{R}^{2D \times 2}: Mixing weight matrix. D: Hidden feature dimension (typically 64). H: Dimension of concatenated attributes \xi. Global Importance (GI): GIi: Scalar score for each Gaussian, updated every 1k iterations. V(s): Volume of Gaussian i, calculated from scaling vector s. V{90\%}: 90% of the largest volume among all Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Embedding: Convert the elastic ratio e to a feature vector he: he = \sigma(\sigma(e w{1e}) W{2e}) where \sigma is ReLU. Concatenate Gaussian attributes Ai into \xi. Convert \xi to a feature vector ha: ha = \sigma(\sigma(\xi W{1a}) W{2a}) where \sigma is ReLU. 2. Logit Generation: Concatenate he and ha and project to logits z \in \mathbb{R}^2: z = [he, ha] W where W \in \mathbb{R}^{2D \times 2}. 3. Differentiable Sampling (Training): Sample binary masks \hat{M}i using Gumbel-Softmax to model the categorical distribution P(\lambdai = m | Ai, e): P(\lambdai = m | Ai, e) = \frac{\exp((zm + gm)/\tau)}{\sum{m=0,1} \exp((zm + gm)/\tau)} where gm \sim \text{Gumbel}(0, 1) and \tau is the temperature parameter. The temperature \tau is exponentially decayed during optimization to converge to a one-hot vector (hard selection). The Straight-Through Estimator (STE) is applied: gradients flow through the continuous Gumbel-Softmax output during the backward pass, while the discrete sample is used for the forward pass. 4. Global Importance (GI) Calculation: Compute GIi for all Gaussians to guide selection: GIi = \sum{p=1}^{QHW} \mathbb{1}(G(Xi), rp) \cdot \gamma(si) \cdot \alphai \cdot T(i, p) where: Q: Number of seen views. H, W: Image height and width. \mathbb{1}(G(Xi), rp): Overlap indicator (1 if Gaussian i's projection overlaps pixel p, 0 otherwise). \alphai: Opacity of Gaussian i. \gamma(si) = \max(V(si)/V{90\%}, 1), where V(s) = |s1 s2 s3|\pi/3. T(i, p) = \prod{t=1}^{ID(i,p)-1} (1 - \alphat), where ID(i,p) is the index of Gaussian i among sorted overlapping Gaussians at pixel p. Update GIi every 1k iterations to ensure guidance accuracy. 5. Guidance Mask Generation: Select the top \lfloor eN \rfloor Gaussians with the highest GI scores to form the guidance mask M{GI}. 6. Regularization Losses: Calculate the gap between the predicted mask \hat{M} and the guidance mask M{GI}: L{GI} = \|\hat{M} - M{GI}\|. Calculate the sparsity ratio constraint: L{spar} = e - \frac{\sum{m \in \hat{M}} m}{N}. 7. Opacity Update and Rendering: Update opacity of all Gaussians: \alphai = \alphai \cdot \hat{M}i This renders unselected Gaussians transparent. Render two images: I{es}: Rendered image using only selected Gaussians (based on \hat{M}). If: Rendered image using all Gaussians (baseline). Compute rendering loss against ground truth I{GT}: L{render} = \|I{es} - I{GT}\| + \|If - I{GT}\|. 8. Total Loss: Combine losses with coefficients \beta1 = 1.0 and \beta2 = 0.01: L = L{render} + \beta1 L{GI} + \beta2 L{spar}. Parameters: \tau: Temperature parameter for Gumbel-Softmax. Exponentially decayed during optimization. \beta1: Weight for GI guidance regularization. Value: 1.0. \beta2: Weight for ratio constraint regularization. Value: 0.01. \mathcal{E}: Set of elastic ratios sampled during training, e.g., \{0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15\}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity Supervision Drift: During training, enforcing sparsity supervision on masks predicted by GsNet does not guarantee exact activation counts at inference (e.g., target 0.20 yields ~19.5%). This is addressed in the Elastic Inference Procedure. Convergence at High Ratios: GsNet may struggle to converge smoothly at high ratios due to insufficient constraints, as there are numerous ways to mask Gaussians. The GI guidance mechanism addresses this. GI Update Frequency: GI must be updated frequently (every 1k iterations) because Gaussian attributes evolve during training, causing importance scores to change. This method provides a differentiable mechanism to select a subset of 3D Gaussians during training by converting continuous logits into a binary mask, enabling gradient-based optimization of Gaussian attributes despite the discrete nature of selection. It sets itself apart from non-differentiable thresholding or hard masking by allowing gradients to flow through the selection decision via the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) applied to Gumbel-Softmax outputs, unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed heuristics or non-differentiable hard thresholds. An inference-time protocol that discards unselected Gaussians entirely and uses continuous logits to guarantee an exact target sparsity ratio e. Definition: Discards unselected Gaussians at inference time. Steps: 1. Call PyTorch's F.gumbelsoftmax with hard=False to obtain continuous logits instead of discrete masks. 2. Select the top \lfloor eN \rfloor logits out of N total Gaussians to activate, ensuring the exact target ratio e is met despite sparsity supervision drift. Pitfall: Sparsity supervision during training does not guarantee exact activation counts at inference (e.g., target 0.20 yields ~19.5%). The top-k selection on continuous logits fixes this. Time Complexity: The selection process involves forward passes through GsNet (lightweight MLPs) and GI calculation. GI calculation requires iterating over all pixels and overlapping Gaussians, which is expensive. GI is updated every 1k iterations to mitigate this. Memory Complexity: Requires storing GsNet parameters (w{1e}, W{2e}, W{1a}, W{2a}, W) and Global Importance scores for all Gaussians. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 dataset, FlexGS (using this selector) achieves higher PSNR/SSIM than LightGS, C3DGS, and EAGLES at various elastic ratios (1%, 5%, 10%, 15%). For example, at 1% ratio, PSNR is 14.455 vs 22.265 for LightGS (no fine-tuning) or 21.761 for LightGS. Experiments conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPU. Scaling: The method is designed to handle various elastic ratios, allowing flexible deployment. Strengths: Differentiable selection allows joint optimization of Gaussian attributes and selection masks. GI guidance ensures stable convergence. Limitations: Requires frequent GI updates. Training time may increase due to the additional loss terms and GI calculation. When to use: When flexible deployment at different sparsity levels is required, and differentiable optimization of Gaussian selection is needed. When not to use: When strict real-time inference with fixed sparsity is required without the overhead of training a selector, or when computational resources for frequent GI updates are limited. The Adaptive Gaussian Selector is part of the FlexGS method, introduced in "FlexGS: Train Once, Deploy Everywhere with Many-in-One Flexible 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitation of fixed heuristic selection rules which may fail to generalize in extreme cases (e.g., selecting 1% of Gaussians) and the need for importance scores to be frequently re-computed as Gaussian attributes evolve during training. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [18] and utilizes Gumbel-Softmax [16] for differentiable sampling. name: Differentiable Gaussian Selection via Gumbel-Softmax and STE
head: Adaptive Gaussian Selection, Hard Gumbel-Softmax
body: This method provides a differentiable mechanism to select a subset of 3D Gaussians during training by converting continuous logits into a binary mask, enabling gradient-based optimization of Gaussian attributes despite the discrete nature of selection. It sets itself apart from non-differentiable thresholding by allowing gradients to flow through the selection decision via the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) applied to Gumbel-Softmax outputs. Inputs and Outputs Input: Logits matrix z \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}, where N is the number of Gaussians and C is the number of classes (set to 2: selected vs. unselected). Output: Selection mask \hat{M} \in \{0, 1\}^N, where \hat{M}i = z{\text{output}}[i, -1] corresponding to the "selected" class. Data Structures z: A 2D array of shape (N, 2) containing raw logits for each Gaussian. U: A 2D array of shape (N, 2) containing uniform random noise. B: A 2D array of shape (N, 2) representing the STE-corrected probabilities. Parameters \tau: Temperature parameter for Gumbel-Softmax scaling that controls the sharpness of the soft-to-hard transition. C: Number of classes for selection, fixed at 2. Steps 1. Gumbel Noise Sampling: For each Gaussian i and class c, sample noise U{i,c} from a uniform distribution \text{Uniform}(0, 1) and compute Gumbel noise g{i,c}: g{i,c} = -\log(-\log(U{i,c})) 2. Logit Perturbation: Add the noise to the logits and scale by temperature to obtain perturbed logits \tilde{z}{i,c}: \tilde{z}{i,c} = \frac{z{i,c} + g{i,c}}{\tau} 3. Softmax Calculation: Compute the soft probability distribution z{\text{soft},i,c} over the C classes: z{\text{soft},i,c} = \frac{\exp(\tilde{z}{i,c})}{\sum{k=1}^{C} \exp(\tilde{z}{i,k})} 4. Hard Selection (Forward Pass): Determine the hard binary output z{\text{hard},i,c} by taking the argmax of the soft probabilities: z{\text{hard},i,c} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } c = \arg\maxk z{\text{soft},i,k} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 5. Straight-Through Estimator (STE): Construct the output matrix B for gradient computation. The STE replaces the non-differentiable hard output with the soft output for the backward pass, while keeping the hard output for the forward pass: Bi = z{\text{hard},i} - z{\text{soft},i} + z{\text{soft},i} = z{\text{hard},i} + \text{stop gradient}(z{\text{soft},i}) Here, \text{stop gradient}(\cdot) indicates that during backpropagation, gradients are not computed through the soft term. 6. Mask Extraction: The final selection mask \hat{M} is extracted from the second column (index -1) of the output matrix B: \hat{M} = B[:, -1] Gradient Computation The gradient of the mask \hat{M} with respect to the input logits z is computed using the chain rule. The gradient matrix \frac{\partial \hat{M}}{\partial z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 2} is given by: \frac{\partial \hat{M}}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{\tau} \begin{bmatrix} -B{1,0} \odot B{1,1} & B{1,1} \odot (1-B{1,1}) \\ -B{2,0} \odot B{2,1} & B{2,1} \odot (1-B{2,1}) \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ -B{N,0} \odot B{N,1} & B{N,1} \odot (1-B{N,1}) \end{bmatrix} In vectorized form, where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication: \frac{\partial \hat{M}}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{\tau} \begin{bmatrix} -B[:, 0] \odot B[:, 1] & B[:, 1] \odot (1 - B[:, 1]) \end{bmatrix} The gradient flows through the soft probabilities B to update the GsNet parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def differentiablegaussianselection(logits, temperature=0.1): """ Performs differentiable Gaussian selection using Gumbel-Softmax and STE. Args: logits (torch.Tensor): Input logits of shape (N, 2). temperature (float): Temperature parameter tau for Gumbel-Softmax. Returns: torch.Tensor: Binary selection mask of shape (N,). torch.Tensor: Soft probabilities of shape (N, 2) for gradient computation. """ # Step 1: Gumbel Noise Sampling U = torch.randlike(logits) gumbelnoise = -torch.log(-torch.log(U + 1e-8)) # Epsilon added for numerical stability # Step 2: Logit Perturbation ztilde = (logits + gumbelnoise) / temperature # Step 3: Softmax Calculation zsoft = F.softmax(ztilde, dim=1) # Step 4: Hard Selection (Forward Pass) hardindices = torch.argmax(zsoft, dim=1, keepdim=True) zhard = torch.zeroslike(zsoft) zhard.scatter(1, hardindices, 1.0) # Step 5: Straight-Through Estimator # B = zhard + stopgradient(zsoft) B = zhard - zsoft.detach() + zsoft # Step 6: Mask Extraction mask = B[:, 1] return mask, zsoft Edge Cases and Pitfalls Numerical Stability: The logarithm in Gumbel noise sampling requires adding a small epsilon to avoid \log(0). Precision and Boundaries: Precision issues may arise when \tau approaches zero due to the sharp transition between soft and hard outputs. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables end-to-end differentiable training of discrete selection decisions, allowing the network to learn which Gaussians to keep or discard based on gradient feedback. Limitations: The quality of selection depends heavily on the temperature parameter \tau and the initial logits. When to Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting models requires adaptive densification or pruning based on learned criteria, and differentiability is required. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from the FlexGS paper, which proposes a flexible 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that can be trained once and deployed in various scenarios. The specific mechanism of Differentiable Gaussian Selection via Gumbel-Softmax and STE was introduced to enable the Adaptive Gaussian Selector module to learn optimal Gaussian subsets during training. It builds on the Gumbel-Softmax relaxation technique. name: Chunk-scale Training
body: Chunk-scale Training addresses the optimization challenges of large, sparse, unbounded scenes by dividing the environment into independent spatial chunks, each trained separately to handle low capture density and non-object-centric data. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing a skybox for environmental consistency, modifying densification policies to handle sparse gradients, and applying monocular depth regularization for unobserved surfaces. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A large scene dataset with sparse camera poses, Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, and image observations. Output: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives for a specific spatial chunk, ready for hierarchical consolidation. Data Structures: Chunk Bounds: A spatial region defining the extent of the current training unit. Skybox: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives placed on a sphere surrounding the scene. Coarse Environment: A pre-optimized representation of the scene outside the current chunk, used to provide context and prevent sky inconsistencies. Parameters: Skybox Size: 100,000 3DGS primitives. Skybox Radius: A sphere with a diameter 10× the diameter of the scene extent. Camera Selection Threshold: Cameras are included if they are inside the chunk bounds or within 2× the chunk bounds, provided they have more than 50 SfM points within the chunk bounds. Densification Metric: Maximum of observed screen-space gradients (replacing the mean used in standard 3DGS). Steps: 1. Define Skybox: Place 100,000 3DGS primitives on a sphere with a diameter 10× the scene extent to capture sky effects and prevent inconsistent sky content across chunks. 2. Select Cameras: Identify cameras for the current chunk by including cameras inside the chunk bounds or within 2× the chunk bounds that have >50 SfM points within the chunk bounds. 3. Initialize Coarse Environment: Load the coarse optimization of the scene outside the current chunk, which remains fixed in geometry but is temporarily optimized for opacity and SH coefficients during chunk training to ensure consistency. 4. Train Chunk Content: Perform 3DGS optimization for the content inside the chunk using correct anti-aliasing techniques. 5. Temporary Environment Optimization: Perform a small, temporary optimization of the coarse environment and skybox outside the chunk, optimizing only opacity and SH coefficients without modifying geometry. 6. Apply Modified Densification: Use the maximum of the observed screen-space gradient for densification decisions, rather than the mean, to address sparse capture issues where mean gradients are unreliable. 7. Depth Regularization: Perform monocular depth prediction, scale and shift the predicted depth based on available SfM points, and use this depth map to regularize the optimization, particularly for unobserved surfaces like streets. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ispointinbox(point, bounds): return bounds.min.x <= point.x <= bounds.max.x and bounds.min.y <= point.y <= bounds.max.y and bounds.min.z <= point.z <= bounds.max.z def distancetoboxcenter(point, bounds): return math.sqrt((point.x - bounds.center.x)2 + (point.y - bounds.center.y)2 + (point.z - bounds.center.z)2) def countsfmpointsinbox(points, bounds): return sum(1 for p in points if ispointinbox(p, bounds)) def createskyboxprimitives(count, radius): primitives = [] for i in range(count): phi = math.acos(1 - 2 (i + 0.5) / count) theta = 2 math.pi i / count x = radius math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = radius math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = radius math.cos(phi) primitives.append(Gaussian(position=(x,y,z), opacity=1.0, sh=[0.0]3, scale=(1.0,1.0,1.0), rot=(0,0,0,1))) return primitives def loadcoarseoptimizationoutside(chunkbounds): return loadsavedgaussiansoutside(chunkbounds) def initializegaussiansfromsfm(sfmpoints, chunkbounds): return [Gaussian.fromsfmpoint(p) for p in sfmpoints if ispointinbox(p, chunkbounds)] def rendergaussians(gaussians, camera): return rasterize(gaussians, camera) def computel1loss(rendered, target): return sum(abs(r - t) for r, t in zip(rendered, target)) / len(rendered) def computemaxscreenspacegradients(gaussians): return max(g.gradscreen for g in gaussians) def densifygaussians(gaussians, maxgrad, threshold): if maxgrad > threshold: splitandclonegaussians(gaussians) def predictmonoculardepth(image): return depthnetwork(image) def scaleshiftdepth(preddepth, sfmpoints): return aligndepthtosfm(preddepth, sfmpoints) def chunkscaletraining(chunkbounds, scenesfmpoints, images, cameras, scenediameter): skyboxprimitives = createskyboxprimitives(100000, 5 scenediameter) selectedcameras = [] for cam in cameras: if ispointinbox(cam.position, chunkbounds): selectedcameras.append(cam) elif distancetoboxcenter(cam.position, chunkbounds) <= 2.0 chunkbounds.radius: if countsfmpointsinbox(cam.sfmpoints, chunkbounds) > 50: selectedcameras.append(cam) coarseenv = loadcoarseoptimizationoutside(chunkbounds) chunkgaussians = initializegaussiansfromsfm(scenesfmpoints, chunkbounds) # Not given in the sources. for iteration in range(30000): for cam in selectedcameras: renderedimage = rendergaussians(chunkgaussians + coarseenv + skyboxprimitives, cam) targetimage = getimage(cam) loss = computel1loss(renderedimage, targetimage) loss.backward() maxgradients = computemaxscreenspacegradients(chunkgaussians) densifygaussians(chunkgaussians, maxgradients, threshold=0.0002) preddepth = predictmonoculardepth(targetimage) scaleddepth = scaleshiftdepth(preddepth, scenesfmpoints) depthloss = computel1loss(rendergaussians(chunkgaussians, cam).depth, scaleddepth) loss += 0.5 depthloss loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() optimizecoarseenvopacitysh(coarseenv) return chunkgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Capture: Standard mean-based densification rarely discourages densification in unbounded scenes and has low tendency in sparse captures, leading to poor quality in areas like streets. The maximum gradient policy addresses this. Inconsistency: Without a skybox and coarse environment, chunks may create inconsistent sky content. Unobserved Surfaces: Sparse camera captures lack information for good quality reconstruction of large unobserved areas (e.g., roads). Depth regularization is required. Time Complexity: Training is performed per chunk, allowing for parallelization across chunks, while temporary optimization of the coarse environment and skybox adds overhead per chunk. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the size of a single chunk plus the skybox and coarse environment, making it feasible for very large datasets that would not fit in memory as a single 3DGS model. Strengths: Handles large, sparse, unbounded scenes, prevents sky inconsistencies, and improves quality in unobserved areas via depth regularization. Limitations: Requires careful chunk boundary definition, relies on monocular depth prediction which may be inaccurate, and temporary optimization of the coarse environment adds computational cost. When to Use: Large-scale urban or outdoor scenes with sparse camera captures and non-object-centric data. When Not to Use: Small, dense, object-centric scenes where standard 3DGS performs well. Chunk-scale Training was introduced in "A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets" by Kerbl et al. (2024). It was developed to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to very large datasets, addressing the limitations of the original method which assumed dense, object-centric captures. The method builds on the hierarchical structure and consolidation techniques described in the same work. name: Edge-guided Splitting Strategy
body: The Edge-guided Splitting Strategy (ESS) is a densification method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that refines primitives by splitting large Gaussians located in high-frequency edge regions to capture fine details. It addresses the loss of high-frequency detail caused by enlarged primitives, particularly when used alongside Random Dropout Regularization (RDR). Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} (each with mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, scaling s, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic features f), a set of M training viewpoints, and an edge detection function. Output: An updated set of primitives where large Gaussians with high edge scores are split into smaller primitives. Data Structures Gaussian Primitive i: Stores scalar size Si (derived from scaling factors), opacity \alphai, and position. Edge Map E(I): A pixel-wise probability map ranging from 0 to 1, generated by an edge detection method on input view I. Binary Mask \mathcal{M}^i(p): Indicates whether pixel p is covered by primitive i. Parameters \mathcal{S}{thr}: Size threshold for splitting. Value not given in the sources. \mathcal{E}{thr}: Edge threshold for splitting. Value not given in the sources. M: Number of viewpoints used for edge score accumulation. Steps 1. Edge Map Generation: For each input view I, compute the pixel-wise edge probability map E(I) using an edge detection method. 2. Single-View Edge Score Calculation: For each Gaussian primitive i and each viewpoint k, calculate the single-view edge score \mathcal{E}{i,k}' by aggregating the edge probabilities of covered pixels, weighted by the primitive's alpha-blending contribution: \mathcal{E}{i,k}' = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) \cdot \sum{p} E(Ik) \mathcal{M}k^i(p) where \mathcal{M}k^i(p) is the binary mask for pixel p covered by primitive i in view k, and the term \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) represents the standard alpha-blending weight wi. 3. Accumulate Edge Score: Compute the final edge score \mathcal{E}i for primitive i by summing the single-view scores across all M viewpoints, normalized by the number of pixels covered by the primitive in each view: \mathcal{E}i = \sum{k=1}^M \frac{\mathcal{E}{i,k}'}{\sum{p} \mathcal{M}k^i(p)} 4. Splitting Mask Determination: Identify primitives to split using the mask \mathcal{M}{edge}, which selects primitives satisfying both a size condition and an edge score condition: \mathcal{M}{edge} = \{ Si \geq \mathcal{S}{thr} \} \cap \{ \mathcal{E}i \geq \mathcal{E}{thr} \} where Si is the size of the i-th primitive. 5. Splitting: Split all Gaussian primitives i where \mathcal{M}{edge} is true into smaller primitives. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeedgescores(primitives, views, edgemaps, cameras): """Computes the final edge score Ei for each primitive across M views.""" M = len(views) finalscores = {} for i, prim in enumerate(primitives): totalscore = 0.0 for k in range(M): cam = cameras[k] emap = edgemaps[k] # Standard 3DGS projection to find covered pixels coveredpixels = getcoveredpixels(prim, cam) pixelcount = len(coveredpixels) if pixelcount == 0: continue # Standard alpha blending weight computation wi = computealphaweight(prim, cam) edgesum = sum(emap[p] for p in coveredpixels) eprime = wi edgesum totalscore += eprime / pixelcount finalscores[prim.id] = totalscore return finalscores def getcoveredpixels(prim, cam): # Projects 3D Gaussian covariance to 2D screen space, computes bounding box, # and returns list of pixel indices where coverage > 0. return [] def computealphaweight(prim, cam): # Computes alphai product{j=1}^{i-1}(1 - alphaj) based on # the rasterization order of primitives in the current view. return prim.alpha def applyedgeguidedsplitting(primitives, edgescores, sthr, ethr): """Splits primitives that are large and have high edge scores.""" tosplit = [] for prim in primitives: size = getprimitivesize(prim) score = edgescores[prim.id] if size >= sthr and score >= ethr: tosplit.append(prim) # Standard 3DGS splitting: duplicate primitive, perturb mean, halve scale, # and redistribute opacity/features. newprimitives = [] for prim in tosplit: newprimitives.extend(splitprimitive(prim)) remaining = [p for p in primitives if p not in tosplit] return remaining + newprimitives def getprimitivesize(prim): # Computes scalar size Si from scaling factors s (e.g., max or mean scale). return max(prim.scale) def splitprimitive(prim): # Returns list of new primitives created by splitting prim. return [] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: The normalization in step 3 divides by the number of pixels covered by the primitive. If a primitive covers zero pixels in a view, its contribution to that view is skipped or treated as zero. Threshold Selection: The values for \mathcal{S}{thr} and \mathcal{E}{thr} are not specified in the sources. Edge Detection Dependency: The quality of ESS depends on the edge detection method used to generate E(I). Uses conditional information to guide optimization, differing from ESS which uses geometric edge scores. Splits based on rendering error, whereas ESS splits based on edge presence. Focuses on matching sparse features, not on splitting based on edge density. Selects Gaussians adaptively, but does not specify edge-guided splitting. Focuses on training scale, not splitting strategy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory beyond storing edge maps and scores. Strengths: Effectively captures high-frequency details in edge regions, improving performance on sparse-view benchmarks (LLFF, DTU, Blender). Compatible with diverse 3DGS-based methods. Limitations: Relies on the quality of edge detection. When to Use: When high-frequency detail recovery is critical, especially in sparse-view settings or when using regularization techniques like RDR that may enlarge primitives. The Edge-guided Splitting Strategy (ESS) was introduced in the DropoutGS paper by Xu et al. in 2025. It was developed to remedy the loss of high-frequency details caused by enlarged primitives, which can occur during optimization or when using Random Dropout Regularization (RDR) to alleviate overfitting. DropoutGS combines RDR and ESS to improve generalization performance in sparse-view novel view synthesis. name: Standard 3DGS Training Configuration
head: Standard 3DGS Training
body: Standard 3DGS Training Configuration specifies the canonical hyperparameter settings for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting models, establishing the baseline for adaptive density control and gradient-based optimization. It differs from sibling methods like Conditional 3DGS Optimization and Rendering or Blended Error Densification and Splitting by adhering strictly to the default parameters of the official implementation, specifically regarding densification frequency, gradient thresholds, and opacity management. The method configures the training loop to balance reconstruction quality and computational efficiency through a fixed schedule of densification, pruning, and opacity resets. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Training images, an initial point cloud, and the hyperparameter configuration. Outputs: Optimized set of 3D Gaussians. Data Structures The Gaussian representation maintains per-Gaussian attributes: Position: 3D vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance: 3D rotation \mathbf{R} and scaling \mathbf{s}, stored as quaternions and scale vectors. Opacity: Scalar \alpha \in [0, 1]. Color: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Parameters Maximum Iterations: 30,000. D-SSIM Loss Weight: 0.2. Spherical Harmonics Degree: 3. Background Color: Black. Densification Gradient Threshold: 0.0002. Opacity Reset Interval: 3000 iterations. Densification Start Iteration: 500. Densification Interval: 100 iterations. densifyuntiliter: Controls the adaptive density-control block (accumulation, densification/pruning, periodic opacity reset); defaults to 30,000. percentdense: Threshold (0 to 1, multiplied by scene extent) classifying Gaussians as small or large; default 0.01. densifyminopacity: Opacity threshold filtering Gaussians during densification; default 0.005. Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points with initial opacity 0.1. 2. Optimization Loop: Iterate t from 1 to 30,000. 3. Rendering: Render the current Gaussian set to generate images. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute loss combining RGB and D-SSIM components with D-SSIM weight 0.2. 5. Gradient Accumulation: Accumulate gradients for Gaussian positions and attributes. 6. Densification Check: If t \ge 500, (t - 500) \mod 100 == 0, and t \le \text{densify\until\iter}: Accumulate Statistics: Track accumulated gradient magnitudes for each Gaussian. Split/Clone: For Gaussians with accumulated gradient magnitude exceeding 0.0002: classify as large or small using percentdense \times scene extent. Large Gaussians split into two copies with 80% of the original size. Small Gaussians clone identically. Pruning: Remove Gaussians with opacity below 0.005. Reset Statistics: Clear accumulated gradients to zero. 7. Opacity Reset: If t \mod 3000 == 0 and t \le \text{densify\until\iter}, reset all Gaussian opacities to 0.01. 8. Optimization Step: Update Gaussian parameters using the accumulated gradients. 9. Termination: Stop at iteration 30,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Gradient thresholds are fixed at 2 \times 10^{-4}; ensure floating-point precision is sufficient to distinguish significant gradients from noise. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def standard3dgstraining(gaussians, cameras, maxiter=30000, densifyuntiliter=30000): densifystartiter = 500 densifyinterval = 100 densifygradthreshold = 0.0002 opacityresetinterval = 3000 opacityresetvalue = 0.01 dssimweight = 0.2 shdegree = 3 backgroundcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] densifyminopacity = 0.005 percentdense = 0.01 sceneextent = 1.0 # Normalized scene bounds accumulatedgradients = [0.0] len(gaussians) for t in range(1, maxiter + 1): renderedimages = render(gaussians, cameras, backgroundcolor) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, cameras, dssimweight) gradients = computegradients(loss, gaussians) for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): accumulatedgradients[i] += norm(gradients[i].position) if t >= densifystartiter and (t - densifystartiter) % densifyinterval == 0 and t <= densifyuntiliter: newgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): if accumulatedgradients[i] > densifygradthreshold: if g.scalenorm() > percentdense sceneextent: newgaussians.extend(splitgaussian(g, factor=0.8)) else: newgaussians.append(clonegaussian(g)) else: newgaussians.append(g) gaussians = [g for g in newgaussians if g.opacity > densifyminopacity] accumulatedgradients = [0.0] len(gaussians) if t % opacityresetinterval == 0 and t <= densifyuntiliter: for g in gaussians: g.opacity = opacityresetvalue optimize(gaussians, gradients) return gaussians def render(gaussians, cameras, backgroundcolor): # Standard differentiable splatting forward pass return [splat(g, cam, backgroundcolor) for g, cam in zip(gaussians, cameras)] def computeloss(rendered, cameras, dssimweight): # L1 loss + D-SSIM loss scaled by weight l1 = sum((r - t).abs() for r, t in zip(rendered, cameras)) dssim = dssimloss(rendered, cameras) return l1 + dssimweight dssim def computegradients(loss, gaussians): # Standard autograd accumulation return [g.grad for g in gaussians] def optimize(gaussians, gradients): # Adam optimizer step for g, grad in zip(gaussians, gradients): g.update(grad) def norm(vec): return (sum(c2 for c in vec))0.5 def splitgaussian(g, factor): # Creates two copies with scale multiplied by factor return [copywithscale(g, factor), copywithscale(g, factor)] def clonegaussian(g): # Returns an identical copy return copy.deepcopy(g) A parameter-tuning strategy that reduces the number of generated Gaussians and minimizes sorting time during training. It differs from the standard configuration by increasing the densification interval to 1000 (vs 100), lowering the densification gradient threshold to 7 \times 10^{-5} (vs 2 \times 10^{-4}), raising the minimum opacity threshold to 0.1 (vs 0.005), deactivating the opacity reset (interval \infty vs 3000), and increasing the percentdense threshold to 0.1 (vs 0.01). This configuration avoids regular pruning and creates fewer Gaussian splats overall. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Computational records and training times are tracked across runs. Experiments use Google Colab A100/H100 GPUs. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The standard 3DGS training configuration originates from the official implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was standardized to ensure reproducibility across experiments. name: BoundedGS Leaf Loss and Gradient Management
head: Adam with Compact Storage
body: BoundedGS Leaf Loss and Gradient Management is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory overhead by organizing Gaussians into spatial groups (leaves) and using compact gradient storage. It decouples gradient accumulation to leaf boundaries and maps only necessary gradient rows to the Adam optimizer via a global ID system, while retaining dense gradients for opacity to support global regularization. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: 3D Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients), camera views, current training step, and survivor set. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters via Adam optimizer, densification statistics based on accumulated screen gradients. Data Structures Compact ID Set (U): The deduplicated union of screened candidate Gaussian IDs across all active groups. ID Map: An int32 array of length N (total Gaussians) mapping global IDs to indices in the compact gradient storage. Gradient Storage: Position, spherical-harmonic coefficients, log scale, and quaternion use row-sparse gradients with shared candidate IDs; only rows corresponding to IDs in U are stored. Opacity retains a dense gradient because of global regularization. Adam State: Maintained in the standard dense layout inherited from ImprovedGS to ensure compatibility with the optimizer's internal momentum tracking. Formulas 1. Leaf Loss (LR): LR = 0.8 L1R + 0.2(1 - SSIMR), where L1R is the L1 loss and SSIMR is the SSIM loss computed over the leaf's own image region at its boundary. 2. View Objective (Lv): Lv = \frac{1}{HW} \sum{R \in Rv} LR + L{global}, where Rv is the set of all leaves for view v, HW is image height times width, and L{global} is the global regularization term. 3. Global Regularization (L{global}): L{global} = \frac{\betat}{|St|} \sum{i \in St} z{it}, where St is the current survivor set, z{it} is the pre-activation opacity parameter for Gaussian i at step t, and \betat is the coefficient following GNS's target-budget feedback. Parameters Global Regularization Coefficient (\beta{15K}): Starts at 0.002 during the 15K–19K pruning window. Opacity Learning Rate: Increases fivefold from 0.025 to 0.125 during the 15K–19K pruning window. Adam Optimizer: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, \epsilon = 10^{-15}. Numbered Steps 1. Compute leaf loss LR using L1 and SSIM on the leaf's own image region at its boundary. 2. Apply global regularizer L{global} once per view at every step of the 15K–19K pruning window. 3. Each leaf obtains an image gradient; explicit rasterization backward adds its contribution to the group’s projected gradients. 4. Allocate parameter gradients immediately before projection backward to avoid coexistence with the current group’s earlier leaf state. 5. Projection backward runs once after all leaves in that group finish, using direct gradient accumulation of 3DGS, applying activation derivatives within CUDA, and mapping contributions to final candidate gradient rows. 6. BoundedGS feeds compact gradient rows through global IDs to the CUDA Adam. 7. Adam updates every Gaussian row; a row outside the candidates has zero current image gradient while its first- and second-order momentum continue to update. 8. View visibility is a union of global IDs; screen gradients are accumulated by ID across groups before forming each Gaussian’s densification statistic. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computel1loss(rendered, target): return math.mean(abs(rendered - target)) def computessimloss(rendered, target): # Standard SSIM implementation assumed return math.mean((rendered - target) 2) def computeimagegradient(leaf): # Standard backward pass computes gradient w.r.t. rendered image return leaf.renderedimage - leaf.targetimage def boundedgsleaflossandgradientmanagement(gaussians, views, step, survivorset): N = len(gaussians) compactids = set() idmap = {} adamm1 = [0.0] N adamm2 = [0.0] N for view in views: viewloss = 0.0 # Standard spatial grouping logic to assign Gaussians to leaves per view leaves = [g for g in gaussians if g.visibleinview(view)] for leaf in leaves: # 1. Leaf Loss Computation l1r = computel1loss(leaf.renderedimage, leaf.targetimage) ssimr = computessimloss(leaf.renderedimage, leaf.targetimage) lr = 0.8 l1r + 0.2 (1.0 - ssimr) viewloss += lr # 3. Leaf Gradient Accumulation leafgrad = computeimagegradient(leaf) # Explicitly add contribution to group's projected gradients for gid in leaf.gaussianids: compactids.add(gid) # 2. Global Regularization if 15000 <= step <= 19000: betat = 0.002 sumz = sum(gaussians.opacitypreactivation[i] for i in survivorset) lglobal = (betat / len(survivorset)) sumz viewloss += lglobal # 4. Gradient Allocation # Allocate parameter gradients immediately before projection backward # to avoid coexistence with the current group's earlier leaf state compactidx = 0 for gid in sorted(compactids): idmap[gid] = compactidx compactidx += 1 # 5. Projection Backward # Runs once after all leaves in that group finish # Maps contributions to final candidate gradient rows for gid in compactids: compactidx = idmap[gid] gaussians.gradsparse[compactidx] = gaussians.graddense[gid] # 6 & 7. Compact Gradient Mapping & Adam Update for gid in range(N): if gid in compactids: grad = gaussians.gradsparse[idmap[gid]] else: grad = 0.0 # Adam updates every Gaussian row; momentum continues even if grad is zero adamm1[gid] = 0.9 adamm1[gid] + 0.1 grad adamm2[gid] = 0.999 adamm2[gid] + 0.001 (grad 2) bc1 = 1.0 / (1.0 - 0.9 (step + 1)) bc2 = 1.0 / (1.0 - 0.999 (step + 1)) update = adamm1[gid] bc1 / (math.sqrt(adamm2[gid] bc2) + 1e-15) gaussians.update(gid, update) # 8. Densification Statistics # Screen gradients accumulated by ID across groups before forming densification statistic for gid in compactids: gaussians.densificationstat[gid] = gaussians.graddense[gid] return gaussians, adamm1, adamm2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Layout Rebuild: Changes in image size, group grid, or budget require rebuilding the layout. Merger Validation: Proposed mergers are rechecked before use to ensure consistency. Empty Regions: If a leaf has no pixels or invalid geometry, the L1/SSIM computation should handle empty regions gracefully. State Coexistence: Failing to allocate gradients immediately before projection backward may cause conflicts with earlier leaf states. Uses conditional logic for optimization steps. Choose when dynamic scene changes require adaptive rendering. Blends error metrics for densification. Choose when balanced detail and smoothness are needed. Integrates sparse matching for initialization. Choose when sparse data sources are available. Selects Gaussians adaptively. Choose when resource constraints vary per frame. Trains in chunks. Choose when memory is limited but batch size needs to be large. Guides splitting by edges. Choose when sharp features are critical. Standard configuration. Choose as a baseline. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduces memory usage for gradient storage by using row-sparse gradients for most parameters. Opacity retains dense gradients, which is a trade-off for global regularization. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Memory efficiency for gradient storage, compatibility with standard Adam optimizer, support for global regularization. Limitations: Requires maintaining an int32 ID map and compact gradient storage layout. When to use: High-resolution training where memory is constrained. When not to use: Scenes where global regularization is not desired or memory is abundant. BoundedGS was introduced in the paper "BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting" (Deng et al., 2025). It builds on ImprovedGS and GNS (Gaussian Neural Splatting) techniques. The method addresses the memory limitations of standard 3DGS training by organizing Gaussians into leaves and using compact gradient storage. name: Consensus-Inheritance Extension
head: Consensus Inheritance, Consensus Weight Inheritance
body: The Consensus-Inheritance Extension maintains correspondence between fixed consensus statistics and newly created Gaussian primitives during densification (splitting or cloning) in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It prevents the breaking of the fixed-consensus protocol by allowing consensus statistics to evolve with the Gaussian population while retaining contamination-resistant properties. The method extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting training loop by introducing three specific behaviors: inheritance during creation, periodic re-estimation with validation, and synchronization with opacity resets. Inputs: Parent Gaussian primitive with consensus color c^{\bullet}p and consensus weight w^{\bullet}p, current consensus statistics c^{\bullet}, iteration counter, and opacity reset magnitude \Delta \alpha. Outputs: Child Gaussian with inherited consensus attributes, updated consensus statistics c^{\bullet}{new} (if accepted), and updated consensus weights for opacity-reset-affected Gaussians. The consensus statistics are maintained as a vector c^{\bullet} (e.g., color or feature vector) and a scalar or vector weight w^{\bullet}. Exact layout, size, and bit-packing details are Not given in the sources. \text{inh}: Inter-generation decay factor for consensus weight inheritance during split/clone. Range: (0, 1). Candidate value: 0.5. k: Refresh interval in iterations. Candidate value: 1,000. \tau: MAD threshold multiplier for validating consensus updates. Candidate value: 3.0. 1. Split/Clone Inheritance: When a parent Gaussian p is split or cloned to create a child Gaussian c, the child inherits the parent's consensus color c^{\bullet}c = c^{\bullet}p and a decayed weight w^{\bullet}c = \text{inh} \times w^{\bullet}p. 2. Contamination-Resistant Periodic Re-estimation: Every k iterations, current Gaussian centers are reprojected and a candidate consensus \tilde{c}^{\bullet} is recomputed. The update is accepted only when the channel-wise deviation satisfies \|\tilde{c}^{\bullet} - c^{\bullet}\|{\infty} \leq \tau \times \text{MAD}, otherwise the previous consensus is retained. This prevents current rendering errors from being written back into the supervision target and preserves the anti-circular-dependency property. 3. Opacity-Reset Synchronization: After an opacity-reset event, the consensus weights of affected Gaussians are decayed in proportion to the reset magnitude. The exact proportionality formula is Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def consensusinheritanceextension(parentc, parentw, currentc, iteration, k, tau, resetmagnitude, resetweights): """ Implements the Consensus-Inheritance Extension for 3D Gaussian Splatting. """ inh = 0.5 # Candidate value # 1. Split/Clone Inheritance childc = parentc childw = inh parentw # 2. Contamination-Resistant Periodic Re-estimation updatedc = currentc if iteration % k == 0: # Reproject centers and compute candidate consensus. Step details not provided in sources. candidatec = reprojectcentersandcomputeconsensus() # Channel-wise deviation deviation = abs(candidatec - currentc) # Median Absolute Deviation of the deviation vector mad = medianabsolutedeviation(deviation) # Accept if infinity norm of deviation <= tau MAD if max(deviation) <= tau mad: updatedc = candidatec # Otherwise retain currentc # 3. Opacity-Reset Synchronization # Decay weights in proportion to reset magnitude. Exact formula not given. for i in range(len(resetweights)): resetweights[i] = (1.0 - resetmagnitude) return childc, childw, updatedc, resetweights def reprojectcentersandcomputeconsensus(): """Reproject current Gaussian centers and aggregate consensus color.""" # Implementation depends on the specific rendering backend pass def medianabsolutedeviation(values): """Compute MAD of a 1D array of values.""" medianval = sorted(values)[len(values) // 2] return sorted(abs(v - medianval) for v in values)[len(values) // 2] Precision: The infinity norm \|\cdot\|{\infty} is used for deviation calculation, which may be sensitive to outliers in specific channels. Boundaries: The decay factor \text{inh} is constrained to (0, 1). Degenerate Input: If the MAD is zero (e.g., all deviations are identical), the threshold check may fail or behave unexpectedly; a small epsilon guard is required. Time Complexity: The periodic re-estimation step adds overhead every k iterations. Exact complexity is Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory is required beyond storing the consensus statistics and weights for each Gaussian. Performance: The method is designed to maintain training stability by preventing contamination from rendering errors. Specific performance metrics (PSNR, SSIM, training time) are Not given in the sources, as experiments were limited to parameter calibration on a single scene. Strengths: Preserves the anti-circular-dependency property; allows consensus to evolve with the population. Limitations: Relies on heuristic parameters (\text{inh}, k, \tau) that require calibration; opacity-reset synchronization details are not fully specified. The Consensus-Inheritance Extension was introduced in the context of "Visibility-Aware Texture Consensus and Local Structural Constraints for 3D Gaussian Reconstruction in Texture-Degraded Scenes". It addresses the issue that default 3DGS configurations build consensus statistics once before training, which breaks correspondence when cloning and splitting alter the Gaussian population. The method was calibrated using a 3 \times 3 \times 3 full-factorial grid on the Drums scene with seed 17 for 3,000 iterations. name: Adaptive Gaussian Refinement
head: 7DGS Adaptive Refinement, Residual Gaussian Adjustment
body: Adaptive Gaussian Refinement is a technique that dynamically adjusts Gaussian parameters using neural network-predicted residuals to improve the modeling of complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance. It addresses the limitation of static covariance matrices in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which cannot adequately represent dynamic behaviors such as motion-induced shape changes. Unlike sibling methods that rely on gradient-based densification metrics (e.g., Adaptive Density Control) or MCMC sampling (e.g., 3DGS-MCMC), this method uses a lightweight neural network to predict continuous corrections to the Gaussian's spatial, temporal, directional, and covariance parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The base set of 7D Gaussian parameters for a primitive k: spatial mean \mup \in \mathbb{R}^3, temporal mean \mut \in \mathbb{R}, directional mean \mud \in \mathbb{R}^3, and the vectorized lower-triangular elements of the 7D covariance matrix l \in \mathbb{R}^{28}. The current time t is required for the temporal encoding. Output: Refined parameters \hat{\mu}p, \hat{\mu}t, \hat{\mu}d, \hat{l}. Data Structures: Feature Vector f: A concatenated vector formed by \mup, \mut, \mud, and a high-frequency temporal encoding \gamma(t). MLP: A small two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) with architecture C{in} \times 64 \times C{out}. Four such MLPs (\phip, \phit, \phid, \phil) predict residuals for position, time, direction, and covariance respectively. Steps: 1. Temporal Encoding: Compute the positional encoding for the current time t. The encoding \gamma(t) is defined as: \gamma(t) = [\sin(2^0 \pi t), \cos(2^0 \pi t), \dots, \sin(2^{K-1} \pi t), \cos(2^{K-1} \pi t)] where K=10. This results in a vector of size 2K = 20. 2. Feature Construction: Concatenate the spatial mean, temporal mean, directional mean, and the temporal encoding to form the input feature vector f: f = \mup \oplus \mut \oplus \mud \oplus \gamma(t) where \oplus denotes vector concatenation. The dimension C{in} is 3 + 1 + 3 + 20 = 27. 3. Residual Prediction: Pass f through the respective MLPs (\phip, \phit, \phid, \phil) to predict residual adjustments. Each MLP has a hidden layer of size 64. 4. Parameter Update: Add the predicted residuals to the original parameters to obtain the refined estimates: \hat{\mu}p = \mup + \phip(f) \hat{\mu}t = \mut + \phit(f) \hat{\mu}d = \mud + \phid(f) \hat{l} = l + \phil(f) Here, l represents the vectorized lower-triangular elements of the 7D covariance matrix. 5. Application: These refined parameters are used in subsequent rendering steps, specifically before the conditional slicing step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def temporalencoding(t, K=10): """ Computes the high-frequency temporal encoding gamma(t). Args: t: float, current time coordinate. K: int, number of frequency bands (default 10). Returns: np.array of shape (2K,) """ frequencies = np.power(2, np.arange(K)) sinvals = np.sin(2 np.pi frequencies t) cosvals = np.cos(2 np.pi frequencies t) return np.concatenate([sinvals, cosvals]) def mlppredict(x, W1, b1, W2, b2): """ Standard 2-layer MLP forward pass. Args: x: input vector W1, b1: first layer weights and biases W2, b2: second layer weights and biases Returns: residual vector """ h = np.maximum(0, x @ W1 + b1) # ReLU activation return h @ W2 + b2 def adaptivegaussianrefinement(mup, mut, mud, l, t, mlpparams): """ Applies adaptive refinement to 7D Gaussian parameters. Args: mup: np.array, shape (3,), spatial mean. mut: float, temporal mean. mud: np.array, shape (3,), directional mean. l: np.array, shape (28,), vectorized lower-triangular covariance elements. t: float, observed time. mlpparams: dict, containing 'W1p', 'b1p', 'W2p', 'b2p', etc. for phip, phit, phid, phil. Returns: tuple: (hatmup, hatmut, hatmud, hatl) """ # Step 1 & 2: Feature Construction gammat = temporalencoding(t, K=10) f = np.concatenate([mup, np.array([mut]), mud, gammat]) # Step 3 & 4: Residual Prediction and Update # Note: mlpparams contain the trained weights for the four MLPs resp = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1p'], mlpparams['b1p'], mlpparams['W2p'], mlpparams['b2p']) rest = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1t'], mlpparams['b1t'], mlpparams['W2t'], mlpparams['b2t']) resd = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1d'], mlpparams['b1d'], mlpparams['W2d'], mlpparams['b2d']) resl = mlppredict(f, mlpparams['W1l'], mlpparams['b1l'], mlpparams['W2l'], mlpparams['b2l']) hatmup = mup + resp hatmut = mut + rest hatmud = mud + resd hatl = l + resl return hatmup, hatmut, hatmud, hatl Parameters: K=10: Number of frequency bands in the temporal encoding. MLP Hidden Size: 64. MLP Architecture: Two layers (C{in} \to 64 \to C{out}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Covariance Reconstruction: The refined covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} is reconstructed from \hat{l} as \hat{\Sigma} = \hat{L}\hat{L}^\top (where \hat{L} is the lower-triangular matrix from \hat{l}). Training Dependency: The method requires training the MLPs alongside the Gaussians, and the residuals are added directly to the vectorized covariance elements, which requires careful handling of numerical stability during optimization. Computational Cost: Adds the cost of four MLP forward passes per Gaussian per frame. The MLPs are small (C{in} \times 64 \times C{out}). Memory: Requires storing the MLP weights. The number of parameters is small: 27 \times 64 + 64 \times C{out} per MLP. Strengths: Enables accurate modeling of complex non-rigid deformations and time-varying appearance without increasing the number of Gaussians. Limitations: Requires training the MLPs alongside the Gaussians and is specific to 7D Gaussian Splatting without direct application to static 3DGS. Adaptive Gaussian Refinement was introduced in the 7DGS (Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting) paper. It was developed to address the static nature of 3D Gaussian covariances, which limits their ability to represent dynamic scenes with non-rigid deformations. The method builds on the idea of using neural networks to predict residuals, a technique seen in other neural rendering contexts, but applies it specifically to the parameters of 7D Gaussians. 7DGS: Unified Spatial-Temporal-Angular Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07946v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hybrid and Diffusion Representations
body: This family encompasses methods that generate or represent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives using hybrid feature grids or diffusion models, rather than relying solely on iterative per-scene optimization. It addresses single-view and text-to-3D generation, multi-view consistency, and sparse volume representation by predicting Gaussian attributes directly from conditioning signals. All methods in this family predict Gaussian attributes (\muk, sk, qk, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k) directly from a conditioning signal (image, text, or noise) using a neural network, bypassing per-scene iterative optimization. The family builds on Densification Strategy [Parent]. TriplaneGaussian is a feed-forward method for generating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a single input image. It solves the problem of direct 3D generation by employing a hybrid representation that combines a sparse point cloud with a dense tri-plane feature grid. Unlike sibling methods that rely on iterative optimization or multi-view consistency constraints, TriplaneGaussian directly predicts Gaussian attributes via a transformer-based decoder, leveraging the structural priors of tri-planes to ensure geometric consistency. It is distinguished from its sibling GaussianDiffusion by its deterministic, non-diffusion-based architecture that explicitly decouples point cloud generation from attribute encoding via tri-planes. Choose this method when deterministic, single-image feed-forward generation is preferred over iterative optimization or diffusion sampling. GaussianDiffusion is a method that trains a 3D diffusion model based on a GaussianCube representation to generate 3D Gaussian primitives directly from conditioning signals. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency (the "Janus problem") and spurious geometry ("floaters") common in single-view or text-to-3D generation by incorporating structured noise from multiple viewpoints and using variational 3DGS. Unlike iterative optimization methods, it amortizes generation cost over a trained network, enabling near-real-time sampling. It is distinguished from its sibling TriplaneGaussian by its use of a voxelized GaussianCube representation converted via optimal transport, rather than tri-plane grids. Choose this method when multi-view consistency and near-real-time generation from text/image conditions are prioritized over deterministic decoding. Text2Immersion is a scene generation method similar to LucidDreamer but with outlier removal and two-stage optimization. It removes outliers in the point cloud before performing 3DGS optimization in two stages: training coarse 3DGS and refinement. Choose this method when text-to-3D scene generation requires explicit outlier removal and coarse-to-fine refinement stages. Atomic-Continuous Prior is a probabilistic prior for VDB volumes that models the data as a mixture of a discrete atomic component (exact zeros for empty space) and a continuous component (real density values). It solves the problem where plain Gaussian diffusion smooths away faint wisps and leaks density into empty regions due to the mix of exact zeros and heavy-tailed densities. Its steps include amplitude companding, which applies a reversible log mapping to rebalance the training signal and boosts the gradient on faint, low-density structures by a factor of (1 + \lambda\tilde{x})^{-1} to prevent thin wisps from being smoothed away. It also uses atomic mass supervision to enforce sparsity by using a soft occupancy target to recover coarse shape and applying a leakage penalty that pushes density to exactly zero outside the boundary. For sequences, it uses temporal conditioning by stacking the previous frame onto the input as an extra channel, allowing the network to learn motion without 4D attention. The prior is defined as p(x) = \pi0\delta0(x) + (1-\pi0)p{ac}(x), where \pi0 is the probability mass at zero, \delta0(x) is the Dirac delta function at zero, and p{ac}(x) is the continuous probability density function for non-zero values. Choose this method when generating sparse VDB volumes for visual effects where preserving exact empty space and faint density wisps is critical. 3D Mask Representation uses explicit 3D mask grids with trilinear interpolation instead of MLPs for representing the 3D mask, due to stability and optimization speed. Its parameter grid resolution was tested at 320^3, 160^3, 80^3, 40^3, with results showing negligible influence on segmentation outcomes (mIoU ~90%) and a default of 320^3. A pitfall is that MLP representation for 3D mask significantly hampers performance due to unstable optimization and intertwined parameters, which complicates the rapid convergence required for cross-view self-prompting. Choose this method when stable, rapid convergence for cross-view self-prompting segmentation is required, avoiding implicit MLP parameter entanglement. The family emerged to address computational bottlenecks and multi-view inconsistencies inherent in iterative 3DGS optimization pipelines. TriplaneGaussian and GaussianDiffusion introduce feed-forward and diffusion-based generation architectures for single-view and text-to-3D synthesis, respectively. Atomic-Continuous Prior and 3D Mask Representation extend the representation framework to handle sparse VDB volumes and stable segmentation masks, respectively, targeting visual effects and 3D segmentation workloads. name: TriplaneGaussian
body: TriplaneGaussian is a feed-forward method for generating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations from a single input image. It solves the problem of single-image 3D reconstruction by bypassing per-scene iterative optimization, instead predicting Gaussian attributes directly via a neural network. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GaussianDiffusion by employing a hybrid representation that combines a transformer-based point cloud decoder with a tri-plane decoder, rather than relying solely on diffusion processes or multi-view inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single RGB image I. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by attributes \{\muk, sk, qk, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k\} for k=1 \dots N, where \mu is position, s is scale, q is rotation (quaternion), \alpha is opacity, and \mathbf{c} is color. Data Structures: 1. Tri-plane: A set of three 2D feature grids Tx, Ty, Tz, each of resolution R \times R with C channels. These encode spatial features for the 3D Gaussian attributes. 2. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points P = \{pk\} representing the initial centers of the Gaussians. 3. MLP: A multi-layer perceptron that maps augmented features to Gaussian attributes. Steps: 1. Image Feature Extraction: Extract features from the input image I using a backbone network (e.g., ViT or ResNet) to obtain image features F{img}. 2. Coarse Generation: Generate a coarse point cloud P{coarse} using a transformer-based point cloud decoder conditioned on F{img}. Simultaneously, generate a tri-plane T encoding 3DGS attribute information using a tri-plane decoder conditioned on F{img}. 3. Densification: Densify the coarse point cloud P{coarse} through an upsampling method to produce a denser point cloud P{dense}. 4. Feature Querying: Project the points in P{dense} onto the three planes of the tri-plane T. For each point pk, sample features from Tx, Ty, Tz at the projected 2D coordinates. Concatenate or aggregate these to form a tri-plane feature vector f{tri} for each point. 5. Feature Augmentation: Augment the queried tri-plane features f{tri} with the projected image features F{img} corresponding to the viewpoint. This fusion combines global geometric context (from the tri-plane) with local appearance cues (from the image). 6. Attribute Prediction: Pass the augmented features through an MLP to predict the final 3D Gaussian attributes \{\muk, sk, qk, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k\} for each point in P{dense}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triplanegaussiangenerate(image): # 1. Extract image features Fimg = imageencoder(image) # 2. Generate coarse point cloud and tri-plane Pcoarse = transformerpointclouddecoder(Fimg) T = triplanedecoder(Fimg) # 3. Densify point cloud Pdense = upsamplingmethod(Pcoarse) # 4. Query tri-plane features for each point # Project 3D points to 2D on XY, YZ, XZ planes coordsxy = Pdense[:, [0, 1]] coordsyz = Pdense[:, [1, 2]] coordsxz = Pdense[:, [0, 2]] # Sample features from tri-plane T at these coordinates fxy = sample2d(T['xy'], coordsxy) fyz = sample2d(T['yz'], coordsyz) fxz = sample2d(T['xz'], coordsxz) # Aggregate tri-plane features (e.g., concatenate or sum) ftri = aggregate([fxy, fyz, fxz]) # 5. Augment with image features # Project image features to match point locations or use global context # Note: Exact projection mechanism for Fimg is not specified in sources # Assuming Fimg is broadcast or pooled to match point count faug = concatenate([ftri, Fimgpooled]) # 6. Predict Gaussian attributes gaussians = mlppredictor(faug) return gaussians Parameters: Tri-plane resolution R: Not given in the sources. Tri-plane channels C: Not given in the sources. Upsampling factor: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Sampling from the tri-plane requires interpolation; bilinear or trilinear interpolation is standard but not explicitly stated. Boundaries: Points projected outside the tri-plane bounds need clamping or padding. Degenerate Input: Single images may lack depth information; the tri-plane helps infer 3D structure, but occluded regions may have ambiguous features. This method is a 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering technique that adaptively selects between 2D and 3D Gaussian primitives based on local geometric cues to reduce redundancy in planar structures while maintaining volumetric accuracy. It integrates TensoSDF for global geometric consistency, enforcing implicit surface constraints during optimization. Unlike standard 3DGS which uses only 3D ellipsoids, or 2DGS which uses only tangent planes, this method dynamically switches representations to better fit both thin surfaces and volumetric details. It builds on TriplaneGaussian by introducing explicit geometry-guided constraints via TensoSDF rather than relying solely on tri-plane initialization. Volume-Based Densification is a refinement strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces or supplements gradient-based Adaptive Density Control (ADC) with geometric volume analysis to manage primitive density. It solves the failure of traditional ADC in high-frequency, sparse regions (e.g., grass, wires) where positional gradients are insufficient to trigger densification, and where uncontrolled Gaussian growth leads to blurred artifacts. Unlike its sibling Hybrid Gaussian Representation with Geometry-Guided Constraints which uses geometry-guided constraints, this method specifically leverages the ellipsoid volume and covariance condition number to drive cloning and splitting decisions. Phys3DGS is a physically-based inverse rendering method that resolves the "hidden Gaussian" problem, where Gaussians beneath the surface adversely affect pixel color in volume rendering, by employing deferred rendering and a mesh-3DGS hybrid representation ]. It differs from standard relightable 3DGS methods by decoupling geometry estimation from material learning via a two-step training process, and from naive deferred approaches by introducing specific regularizations to stabilize BRDF learning and prevent mesh extraction artifacts ]. FDGaussian injects tri-plane features into the diffusion model for better geometry generation. Time Complexity: Feed-forward inference is significantly faster than iterative optimization-based methods (like standard 3DGS training) as it avoids per-scene gradient descent. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the tri-plane representation and the MLP, plus the stored Gaussian attributes. The tri-plane size depends on resolution R and channels C. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of Gaussians generated, which is determined by the upsampling step and tri-plane resolution. Strengths: Fast generation from a single image; hybrid representation captures both geometry and appearance. Limitations: Quality depends on the generalization of the trained network; may struggle with unseen object categories or extreme viewpoints. When to use: When fast single-image 3DGS generation is needed and iterative optimization is too slow. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction from multiple views is available and iterative optimization is feasible. TriplaneGaussian was proposed in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically addressing the need for direct generation of 3DGS from single images. It builds on the principles of hybrid representations and feed-forward learning methods in the Gaussian Avatar Reconstruction family. The method is cited in surveys of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting. This method is a 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering technique that adaptively selects between 2D and 3D Gaussian primitives based on local geometric cues to reduce redundancy in planar structures while maintaining volumetric accuracy. It integrates TensoSDF for global geometric consistency, enforcing implicit surface constraints during optimization. Unlike standard 3DGS which uses only 3D ellipsoids, or 2DGS which uses only tangent planes, this method dynamically switches representations to better fit both thin surfaces and volumetric details. It builds on TriplaneGaussian by introducing explicit geometry-guided constraints via TensoSDF rather than relying solely on tri-plane initialization. Inputs: Input point cloud (for initialization and surface normals). Camera poses and images for training. Bounding box definition (default: 1m³). Outputs: Optimized hybrid Gaussian field (mix of 2D and 3D Gaussians). Optimized TensoSDF tensor factors. Parameters: Nx=Ny=Nz=128, r=32. 	au: Curvature threshold for initial type selection. 	au1: Gradient magnitude threshold for flat geometry detection (	au1 = 0.1). 	au2: SDF value threshold for proximity to surface (	au2 = 0.05 m). \eta: Update step size for Gaussian position fine-tuning. \lambda: Weight for gradient consistency in TensoSDF loss (\lambda = 10). AR Threshold: Anisotropy Ratio threshold for conversion (AR < 0.2). \sigman: Small variance added during 2D-to-3D conversion (\sigman = 10^{-4}). Initialization: Establish a complete 3D Gaussian ellipsoidal field based on the input point cloud following the standard 3DGS workflow. Initialize TensoSDF tensor factors Ax, Ay, Az with random values from \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01). 2. Curvature Estimation (Initial Type Selection): For each 3D Gaussian center \mu, perform PCA on the local point cluster to extract eigenvalues \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 of the cluster covariance matrix. Calculate local curvature: \kappa = (\lambda2 + \lambda3) / \lambda1. If \kappa < 	au, convert the 3D Gaussian to a 2D Gaussian (see Step 3). If AR(\mu) < 0.2, convert to 2D Gaussian using the initialization logic in Step 3. 5. Compute mean angle  ar{	heta} between n and neighbors' normals ni:  ar{	heta} =  rac{1}{N{neigh}} \sum{i=1}^{N{neigh}} \arccos\left(  rac{n \cdot ni}{\|n\| \|ni\|} ight). Compute rendering loss (e.g., L1/SSIM) between rendered and input images. Compute TensoSDF loss \mathcal{L}{SDF} (see Formulas). TensoSDF SDF Function: F(x, y, z) \approx \sum{i=1}^{r} Ax(x, i) \cdot Ay(y, i) \cdot Az(z, i) where r is the decomposition rank and Ax, Ay, Az are tensor factors.
