coords: shape (N, 3) or (3,) # grid: shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, r) # Returns interpolated values at coords # Implementation uses fractional part extraction and weighted sum of 8 corners. # Omitted for brevity as it is a standard grid operation. pass def computesdf(coords, Ax, Ay, Az): """Compute SDF value using CP decomposition.""" # Ax, Ay, Az shape: (Nx, r), (Ny, r), (Nz, r) # Interpolate each factor at x, y, z coordinates valx = trilinearinterpolate(Ax, coords[:, 0:1]) # shape (N, r) valy = trilinearinterpolate(Ay, coords[:, 1:2]) valz = trilinearinterpolate(Az, coords[:, 2:3]) # CP sum sdf = np.sum(valx valy valz, axis=1) return sdf def computesdfgradient(coords, Ax, Ay, Az): """Compute gradient of SDF via partial derivatives of tensor factors.""" # Compute dF/dx, dF/dy, dF/dz using trilinear derivatives gradx = np.sum(trilinearinterpgrad(Ax, coords[:, 0:1], axis=0) trilinearinterpolate(Ay, coords[:, 1:2]) trilinearinterpolate(Az, coords[:, 2:3]), axis=1) grady = np.sum(trilinearinterpolate(Ax, coords[:, 0:1]) trilinearinterpgrad(Ay, coords[:, 1:2], axis=1) trilinearinterpolate(Az, coords[:, 2:3]), axis=1) gradz = np.sum(trilinearinterpolate(Ax, coords[:, 0:1]) trilinearinterpolate(Ay, coords[:, 1:2]) trilinearinterpgrad(Az, coords[:, 2:3], axis=2), axis=1) return np.stack([gradx, grady, gradz], axis=1) def pcalocalcluster(points): """Perform PCA on local point cluster.""" cov = np.cov(points.T) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] return eigenvalues[idx], eigenvectors[:, idx] def gramschmidt(v1, v2): """Orthogonalize v2 against v1.""" u = v2 - np.dot(v2, v1) v1 return u / np.linalg.norm(u) def init2dgaussian(mu, eigenvalues, eigenvectors): """Initialize 2D Gaussian from PCA results.""" n = eigenvectors[:, 2] randomvec = np.random.rand(3) if np.abs(np.dot(randomvec, n)) > 0.9: randomvec = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) t1 = np.cross(n, randomvec) t1 = t1 / np.linalg.norm(t1) t2 = np.cross(n, t1) T = np.columnstack((t1, t2)) sigmap = 0.1 # Appropriate initial value Lambda = np.diag([sigmap2, sigmap2]) return T, Lambda, n def rodriguesrotation(g, vmax): """Compute rotation matrix R(g) aligning vmax to g.""" costheta = np.clip(np.dot(vmax, g), -1.0, 1.0) sintheta = np.sqrt(1 - costheta2) if sintheta < 1e-6: return np.eye(3) g = g / np.linalg.norm(g) gx = np.array([[0, -g[2], g[1]], [g[2], 0, -g[0]], [-g[1], g[0], 0]]) R = costheta np.eye(3) + (1 - costheta) np.outer(g, g) + sintheta gx return R def convert3dto2d(gaussian, pointcloudcluster, tau): """Convert 3D Gaussian to 2D if curvature is low.""" eigenvalues, eigenvectors = pcalocalcluster(pointcloudcluster) kappa = (eigenvalues[1] + eigenvalues[2]) / eigenvalues[0] if kappa < tau: T, Lambda, n = init2dgaussian(gaussian.mu, eigenvalues, eigenvectors) gaussian.type = '2D' gaussian.T = T gaussian.Lambda = Lambda gaussian.n = n return True return False def convert3dto2dadaptive(gaussian, F, tau1, tau2): """Adaptive conversion based on TensoSDF cues.""" mu = gaussian.mu d = F(mu) if np.abs(d) < tau2: grad = computesdfgradient(mu,...) # Requires full F impl gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(grad) if gradnorm < tau1: eigenvalues = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(gaussian.Sigma))[::-1] AR = np.min(eigenvalues) / np.max(eigenvalues) if AR < 0.2: n = grad / gradnorm randomvec = np.random.rand(3) if np.abs(np.dot(randomvec, n)) > 0.9: randomvec = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) t1 = np.cross(n, randomvec) t1 = t1 / np.linalg.norm(t1) t2 = np.cross(n, t1) T = np.columnstack((t1, t2)) sigmap = 0.1 Lambda = np.diag([sigmap2, sigmap2]) gaussian.type = '2D' gaussian.T = T gaussian.Lambda = Lambda gaussian.n = n return True return False def convert2dto3d(gaussian, neighbors): """Convert 2D Gaussian to 3D if normals are inconsistent.""" n = gaussian.n angles = [] for neighbor in neighbors: ni = neighbor.n costheta = np.dot(n, ni) / (np.linalg.norm(n) np.linalg.norm(ni)) angles.append(np.arccos(np.clip(costheta, -1.0, 1.0))) meanangle = np.mean(angles) if meanangle > np.deg2rad(30): randomvec = np.random.rand(3) if np.abs(np.dot(randomvec, n)) > 0.9: randomvec = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) t1 = np.cross(n, randomvec) t1 = t1 / np.linalg.norm(t1) t2 = np.cross(n, t1) R = np.columnstack((t1, t2, n)) Lambda3d = np.zeros((3, 3)) Lambda3d[:2,:2] = gaussian.Lambda sigman = 1e-4 Sigmanew = R @ Lambda3d @ R.T + 2 (sigman2) np.outer(n, n) gaussian.type = '3D' gaussian.Sigma = Sigmanew return True return False def finetunegaussian(gaussian, F, eta): """Fine-tune Gaussian position and covariance using TensoSDF.""" mu = gaussian.mu d = F(mu) grad = computesdfgradient(mu,...) gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(grad) if gradnorm < 1e-8: return g = grad / gradnorm gaussian.mu = mu - eta d g eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(gaussian.Sigma) vmax = eigenvectors[:, np.argmax(eigenvalues)] R = rodriguesrotation(g, vmax) gaussian.Sigma = R @ gaussian.Sigma @ R.T Time and Memory Complexity: The method introduces additional storage overhead for TensoSDF tensor factors (Ax, Ay, Az) and potentially more Gaussian primitives due to adaptive conversion. On the Mip-NeRF dataset, average memory consumption increased from 734MB (3DGS) to 845MB (proposed method), an increase of ~15.1%. Increases of 16.1% and 18.2% were observed on DeepBlending and Tanks&Temples datasets respectively. Training requires parallel optimization of Gaussian parameters and TensoSDF factors, adding computational cost per iteration. Measured Performance: On NeRF-synthetic dataset, the method attained an average PSNR improvement of 6.1% over 3DGS. Outperforms 3DGS in global geometric consistency and reconstruction performance for highly reflective materials. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces redundancy in planar/thin structures; improves geometric consistency via TensoSDF; handles specular reflections better (Specular Module ablation shows significant enhancement). Limitations: Suboptimal performance in highly transparent environments. Increased memory usage compared to standard 3DGS. When to Use: Scenes with significant planar or thin structures where 3DGS redundancy is high. Applications requiring high geometric accuracy and consistency. Scenes with reflective materials. When Not to Use: Highly transparent environments. Memory-constrained applications where the 15-18% overhead is unacceptable. Origin: Proposed by Yanshan Zhang, Luyao Wang, and Yuanzhang Fan in 2026. Published in the 2026 2nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Computational Intelligence (AICI 2026). History and Development: Builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). Integrates TensoSDF, a tensor-based Signed Distance Function representation, to provide geometric constraints. Addresses limitations of 3DGS in balancing planar and volumetric structures and achieving global geometric consistency. Usage: High-precision 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. Real-time 3D reconstruction and rendering. Virtual reality, augmented reality, digital twins, and film special effects. Hybrid Gaussian Representation with Geometry-Guided Constraints for High-Precision 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering--Hybrid Gaussian Splatting with Geometry Guidance--Adaptive Hybrid Representation and TensoSDF Constraints for High-Accuracy Real-Time 3D Reconstruction and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3810280.3810302, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Volume-Based Densification
head: Ellipsoid’s volume-driven density control, Volume driven densification strategy
body: Volume-Based Densification is a refinement strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces or supplements gradient-based Adaptive Density Control (ADC) with geometric volume analysis to manage primitive density. It solves the failure of traditional ADC in high-frequency, sparse regions (e.g., grass, wires) where positional gradients are insufficient to trigger densification, and where uncontrolled Gaussian growth leads to blurred artifacts. Unlike its sibling Hybrid Gaussian Representation with Geometry-Guided Constraints which uses geometry-guided constraints, this method specifically leverages the ellipsoid volume and covariance condition number to drive cloning and splitting decisions. Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}, each defined by mean position \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Volume threshold V0 (typical value: 0.03). Maximum point count limit N{max} (typical value: 34,000,000). Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives with refined density in high-volume regions. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Contains \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite), \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and feature vectors. Covariance Matrix: Defined as \Sigma = N\sigma^2 + P, where N is the rotation matrix and P handles the structural transformation. Formulas: 1. Eigenvalues: Compute eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of \Sigma such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 > 0. 2. Volume: The volume of the ellipsoid is calculated as: V = \frac{4}{3}\pi \sqrt{\det(\Sigma)} = \frac{4}{3}\pi \sqrt{\lambda1 \lambda2 \lambda3} 3. Condition Number: \kappa(\Sigma) = \frac{\lambda{max}(\Sigma)}{\lambda{min}(\Sigma)} = \frac{\lambda1}{\lambda3} Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (Deep Image Matching): Replace the traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipeline with a deep learning-based framework to generate the initial point cloud. Use SuperPoint as the feature extractor and LightGlue as the feature matcher to construct a robust initial point cloud with higher coverage in sparse regions. 2. Volume Calculation: For each Gaussian primitive Gi, calculate its volume Vi using the formula above. 3. Candidate Identification: Identify primitives where Vi > V0. These are considered "high-volume" candidates for densification. 4. Condition Number Adjustment: For each candidate Gi, calculate \kappa(\Sigmai). Adjust the standard deviations of the Gaussian by dividing them by \kappa(\Sigmai) to obtain smaller standard deviations for newly generated points. 5. Sampling: Generate new sample points around the mean \mui of the candidate primitives using the adjusted standard deviations and the means, considering the volume of the primitives which reflects the spread of the Gaussian distribution. Sample from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mui, \Sigma'{adj}) where \Sigma'{adj} reflects the adjusted spread. The number of new points generated per candidate is not explicitly defined in the sources, but implies creating "additional samples". 6. Transformation and Property Assignment: Apply the rotation and scaling transformations to the newly generated points based on the original primitive's parameters. Compute new properties for the new points, including scaling, rotation, and features. 7. Replacement: Replace the original high-volume points (candidates) with the newly generated points. 8. Pruning: Prune the unused points. 9. Capacity Check: Impose a ceiling on the number of points generated during training, capping this value at N{max} to manage computational resources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def volumebaseddensification(primitives, V0=0.03, Nmax=34000000): """ Performs volume-based densification on a list of Gaussian primitives. """ newprimitives = [] candidates = [] for p in primitives: # Reconstruct covariance matrix Sigma = R diag(sigma^2) R^T # Note: Source defines Sigma = Nsigma^2 + P, assuming N is rotation and P handles translation/structure # Standard 3DGS covariance: Sigma = R S S^T R^T S = [[p.sigma[0]2, 0, 0], [0, p.sigma[1]2, 0], [0, 0, p.sigma[2]2]] Sigma = matmul(p.R, matmul(S, mattranspose(p.R))) # Calculate eigenvalues (standard 3x3 eigenvalue decomposition) eigenvalues = eigenvalues3x3(Sigma) eigenvalues.sort(reverse=True) lambdamax = eigenvalues[0] lambdamin = eigenvalues[2] # Calculate Volume detSigma = eigenvalues[0] eigenvalues[1] eigenvalues[2] volume = (4.0 / 3.0) math.pi math.sqrt(detSigma) if volume > V0: # Calculate Condition Number kappa = lambdamax / lambdamin # Adjust standard deviations adjustedsigma = [p.sigma[0] / kappa, p.sigma[1] / kappa, p.sigma[2] / kappa] candidates.append({ 'parent': p, 'adjustedsigma': adjustedsigma, 'mu': p.mu, 'R': p.R, 'kappa': kappa }) pointstoadd = [] for cand in candidates: p = cand['parent'] adjsigma = cand['adjustedsigma'] mu = cand['mu'] R = cand['R'] # Generate samples from Normal distribution using adjusted sigma # We generate 2 new points to replace the parent (cloning) numsamples = 2 for in range(numsamples): # Sigmaadj = R diag(adjsigma^2) R^T Sadj = [[adjsigma[0]2, 0, 0], [0, adjsigma[1]2, 0], [0, 0, adjsigma[2]2]] Sigmaadj = matmul(R, matmul(Sadj, mattranspose(R))) newmu = multivariatenormalsample(mu, Sigmaadj) newp = GaussianPrimitive( mu=newmu, sigma=adjsigma, R=R, alpha=p.alpha, features=p.features) pointstoadd.append(newp) # Remove candidates from the original list candidateids = [id(c['parent']) for c in candidates] remainingprimitives = [p for p in primitives if id(p) not in candidateids] # Add new points allprimitives = remainingprimitives + pointstoadd # Enforce Max Point Count if len(allprimitives) > Nmax: allprimitives = pruneprimitives(allprimitives, Nmax) return allprimitives def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k] B[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def mattranspose(M): return [[M[j][i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] def eigenvalues3x3(M): # Standard 3x3 eigenvalue decomposition # Returns sorted eigenvalues descending import numpy as np return sorted(np.linalg.eigvalsh(M), reverse=True) def multivariatenormalsample(mean, cov): # Standard multivariate normal sampling import numpy as np return np.random.multivariatenormal(mean, cov) def pruneprimitives(prims, limit): # Sort by opacity ascending, remove lowest until limit reached prims.sort(key=lambda p: p.alpha) return prims[len(prims)-limit:] class GaussianPrimitive: def init(self, mu, sigma, R, alpha, features): self.mu = mu self.sigma = sigma self.R = R self.alpha = alpha self.features = features Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CUDA Out-of-Memory: Setting V0 too low causes excessive densification in dense regions, leading to OOM errors. Sparse Regions: In regions with sparse textures (e.g., grass), traditional SfM fails to provide sufficient initial points, leading to uncontrolled Gaussian growth and blurring. This method mitigates this by using deep image matching for initialization and volume-based densification. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives N and the cost of eigenvalue decomposition for each candidate. Eigenvalue decomposition of a 3 \times 3 matrix is constant time, so the overhead per primitive is O(1). Total densification step is O(N). Memory Complexity: Increases with the number of generated points. Capped at N{max} = 34 million points. Performance: Evaluated on NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU. Achieves state-of-the-art performance on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. Strengths: Better handling of high-frequency, sparse regions (grass, wires) compared to gradient-based ADC. Prevents uncontrolled growth of Gaussian volumes in sparse areas. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of V0. May increase memory usage if not capped. Origin: Introduced in "Refining Gaussian Splatting: A Volumetric Densification Approach" (2025). Development: The method addresses limitations of Adaptive Density Control (ADC) in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically its failure in high-frequency regions and lack of maximum point count control. It builds upon the existing splitting and cloning methods but introduces volume and condition number as primary criteria. Usage: Used in experiments on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. Refining Gaussian Splatting: A Volumetric Densification Approach, https://doi.org/10.24132/CSRN.2025-6, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Phys3DGS
head: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering
body: Phys3DGS is a physically-based inverse rendering method that resolves the "hidden Gaussian" problem, where Gaussians beneath the surface adversely affect pixel color in volume rendering, by employing deferred rendering and a mesh-3DGS hybrid representation. It differs from standard relightable 3DGS methods by decoupling geometry estimation from material learning via a two-step training process, and from naive deferred approaches by introducing specific regularizations to stabilize BRDF learning and prevent mesh extraction artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images. Outputs: A hybrid scene representation consisting of a mesh and associated 3D Gaussians, with learned PBR parameters (albedo \mathcal{A}, metalness \mathcal{M}, roughness \mathcal{R}, normal \mathcal{N}) and baked visibility for real-time relighting. Data Structures: Each 3D Gaussian i in the hybrid representation stores: Center coordinate \mui. Opacity \alphai. Scale si (and 3D covariance \Sigmai derived from scale and rotation). Spherical Harmonics (SH) parameters for view-dependent color. Normal vector \mathbf{n}i. BRDF parameters: Albedo \mathbf{a}i, metalness mi, roughness ri. Visibility parameters (SH coefficients for indirect illumination, used during training and baked post-training). The hybrid representation binds one 3D Gaussian to each triangle of an extracted mesh. Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Training: Train a vanilla 3DGS model [4] on the input images. 2. Opacity Culling: Remove low-opacity Gaussians from the initial model. 3. SDF Regularization: Apply Signed Distance Function (SDF)-based regularization to the remaining Gaussians to flatten them and push their centers toward the implicit surface. This step may cause Gaussians near the surface to grow abnormally large, leading to large triangles in mesh extraction and visibility test interference. Mitigate with Masked Opacity Regularization (Lo) to constrain opacity near the surface. The exact formula for Lo is not fully provided in the sources. 4. Mesh Extraction: Extract a triangular mesh from the regularized 3DGS model. 5. Hybrid Representation Construction: Assign one 3D Gaussian to each triangle of the extracted mesh. 6. Two-Step PBR Training: Train PBR-related parameters on the hybrid representation using a two-step approach. Step 6a learns geometry and base PBR parameters. Step 6b refines the parameters. Deferred Rendering Pipeline (Inference/Training): For each pixel (ray): 1. Estimate Depth: Calculate the estimated depth \mathcal{D} to the surface by weighted summation of opacity and distance for all Gaussians i intersecting the ray: \mathcal{D} = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai di where Ti is the transmittance up to Gaussian i, \alphai is the opacity, and di is the distance from the camera center to Gaussian i. 2. Estimate Surface Properties: Calculate the estimated normal \mathcal{N} and BRDF parameters (Albedo \mathcal{A}, Metalness \mathcal{M}, Roughness \mathcal{R}) using the same weighted summation: \{\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{N}\} = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai \{\mathbf{a}i, mi, ri, \mathbf{n}i\} where \mathbf{a}i, mi, ri, \mathbf{n}i are the per-Gaussian albedo, metalness, roughness, and normal. 3. Lighting Calculation: Perform Fibonacci sampling on incoming light directions \omegai. Compute Global Illumination L{global}(\omegai) using Spherical Harmonics (SH) approximation. Compute Local Indirect Illumination L{local}(\omegai) using SH parameters stored on each Gaussian, aggregated at the estimated surface point similarly to Eqn. 3. Determine Visibility V(\omegai): During Training: Compute visibility via ray tracing using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH), detached from back-propagation. Post-Training (Baking): Bake the visibility onto each Gaussian and replace the SH coefficients of indirect illumination with the SH coefficients of the baked visibility to reduce model size and boost test-time speed. Combine lighting: L(\omegai) = V(\omegai) \cdot L{global}(\omegai) + L{local}(\omegai) 4. Rendering Equation: Solve the rendering equation once at the estimated surface point using the estimated BRDF parameters and the computed incoming light L(\omegai) to obtain the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phys3dgsrender(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, bakedvisibilitymap, globalshcoeffs, usebvh=False, bvh=None): # 1. Filter and sort gaussians by distance to camera intersecting = [g for g in gaussians if rayintersectsgaussian(rayorigin, raydirection, g)] intersecting.sort(key=lambda g: distance(rayorigin, g.mu)) if not intersecting: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # backgroundcolor totaltransmittance = 1.0 estdepth = 0.0 estalbedo = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] estmetalness = 0.0 estroughness = 0.0 estnormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 2. Deferred Accumulation: Exact weighted sums per Eqn 2 & 3 for g in intersecting: di = distance(rayorigin, g.mu) alphai = g.alpha Ti = totaltransmittance estdepth += Ti alphai di estalbedo = [estalbedo[j] + Ti alphai g.a[j] for j in range(3)] estmetalness += Ti alphai g.m estroughness += Ti alphai g.r estnormal = [estnormal[j] + Ti alphai g.n[j] for j in range(3)] totaltransmittance = (1.0 - alphai) if totaltransmittance < 1e-4: break # 3. Lighting Calculation lightdirs = fibonaccisphere(16) incominglight = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for omega in lightdirs: Lglobal = evaluatesh(globalshcoeffs, omega) V = getvisibility(omega, estdepth, bakedvisibilitymap, bvh, usebvh) Llocal = aggregatelocalindirect(intersecting, omega) Li = V Lglobal + Llocal incominglight = [incominglight[j] + Li[j] for j in range(3)] incominglight = [x / 16.0 for x in incominglight] # 4. Solve Rendering Equation estnormal = normalize(estnormal) color = evaluatepbrbrdf(estalbedo, estmetalness, estroughness, estnormal, raydirection, incominglight) return color def trainphys3dgs(images, initialgaussians): # Step 1: Initial Vanilla 3DGS Training gaussians = trainvanilla3dgs(images, initialgaussians) # Standard 3DGS optimization [4] # Step 2: Opacity Culling gaussians = opacitycull(gaussians) # Remove low-opacity Gaussians # Step 3: SDF Regularization + Masked Opacity Regularization gaussians = applysdfregularization(gaussians) # Flatten and push to surface gaussians = applymaskedopacityregularization(gaussians) # Constrain scale growth # Step 4: Mesh Extraction mesh = extractmesh(gaussians) # Extract from regularized Gaussians # Step 5: Build Hybrid Representation hybridgaussians = assigngaussianstomesh(mesh, gaussians) # 1 Gaussian per triangle # Step 6: Two-Step PBR Training hybridgaussians = trainpbrparameters(hybridgaussians, images, mesh) # Step 6a hybridgaussians = refinepbrparameters(hybridgaussians, images, mesh) # Step 6b # Post-Training: Bake Visibility hybridgaussians = bakevisibility(hybridgaussians, mesh) # Replace indirect SH with baked visibility SH return hybridgaussians, mesh def rayintersectsgaussian(origin, dir, g): # Standard ray-Gaussian (ellipsoid) intersection test return True # Placeholder for standard geometric intersection def distance(a, b): return ((a[0]-b[0])2 + (a[1]-b[1])2 + (a[2]-b[2])2)0.5 def fibonaccisphere(samples=16): points = [] offset = 2.0 / samples increment = 3.577709437777094 # pi (3 - sqrt(5)) for i in range(samples): y = ((i 1.0) - samples + 1.0) + offset 0.5 radius = (1.0 - y y)0.5 theta = increment i points.append([math.cos(theta)radius, y, math.sin(theta)radius]) return points def evaluatesh(coeffs, direction): # Standard SH evaluation at direction return [sum(c y for c, y in zip(coeffs[j], direction)) for j in range(3)] def getvisibility(omega, depth, bakedmap, bvh, usebvh): if usebvh: return bvh.trace(omega, depth) # Detached from backprop return bakedmap.lookup(omega, depth) # Baked visibility def aggregatelocalindirect(gaussians, omega): # Weighted sum of per-Gaussian indirect SH at omega, analogous to Eqn 3 acc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for g in gaussians: Lg = evaluatesh(g.shindirect, omega) acc = [acc[j] + g.alpha Lg[j] for j in range(3)] return acc def evaluatepbrbrdf(albedo, metalness, roughness, normal, viewdir, light): # Standard PBR BRDF evaluation (e.g., GGX + Schlick Fresnel) return [albedo[j] light[j] for j in range(3)] # Simplified diffuse for implementation def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [x/mag for x in v] if mag > 1e-6 else [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def trainvanilla3dgs(images, init): pass # Standard 3DGS optimization [4] def opacitycull(g): return [g for g in g if g.alpha > 0.01] # Standard threshold def applysdfregularization(g): return g # SDF loss step def applymaskedopacityregularization(g): return g # Masked opacity loss def extractmesh(g): return [] # Marching cubes / surface extraction def assigngaussianstomesh(mesh, g): return g # Bind 1 Gaussian per triangle def trainpbrparameters(g, imgs, mesh): return g # Step 6a optimization def refinepbrparameters(g, imgs, mesh): return g # Step 6b optimization def bakevisibility(g, mesh): return g # Replace indirect SH with baked visibility SH Time Complexity: Training is more expensive than vanilla 3DGS due to mesh extraction, SDF regularization, and the two-step PBR training process. Inference is real-time capable, comparable to standard 3DGS, as deferred rendering avoids per-Gaussian PBR evaluation and ray tracing is replaced by baked visibility. Memory Complexity: Higher than vanilla 3DGS due to the storage of mesh data, additional PBR parameters (albedo, metalness, roughness, normal) per Gaussian, and visibility SH coefficients. Baking visibility reduces the model size at test time by removing the need for dynamic visibility computation. Performance: Offers significantly better rendering quality under relighting compared to existing relightable 3DGS methods. Provides better rendering quality with real-time rendering speeds compared to SOTA voxel grid-based inverse rendering methods. Strengths: Solves the hidden Gaussian problem, enables real-time relighting, and enables robust geometry learning via mesh hybridization. Limitations: Sensitive to mesh extraction quality, requires careful regularization to prevent abnormal Gaussian scales, and suffers training instability if deferred rendering is applied naively without the proposed two-step approach. Phys3DGS was proposed by Euntae Choi and Sungjoo Yoo from the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Seoul National University, South Korea. It was published on arXiv on September 16, 2024. The work is motivated by the limitations of existing relightable 3DGS methods, which suffer from quality degradation under novel lighting conditions due to the hidden Gaussian problem. It draws inspiration from SuGaR, which uses a hybrid mesh-Gaussian representation, but differs by demonstrating that simple mesh adoption fails for inverse rendering and proposing a novel deferred learning-based training approach. name: GaussianDiffusion
head: GaussianDiffusion [S1][S2, unofficial]
body: GaussianDiffusion is a method that trains a 3D diffusion model based on a GaussianCube representation to generate 3D Gaussian fields directly from conditioning signals. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency (the "Janus problem") and the generation of floating artifacts common in single-view diffusion priors by incorporating structured noise from multiple viewpoints and using variational 3DGS. Unlike iterative optimization methods, it amortizes the generation cost over a trained network, enabling near-real-time sampling at test time. Inputs: Conditioning signal (e.g., text or image) and structured noise from multiple viewpoints. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by attributes \muk, sk, qk, \alphak, \mathbf{c}k. Data Structures: The method operates on a GaussianCube representation. This is a voxelized grid where each voxel contains a constant number of Gaussians. The conversion from a fixed set of Gaussians to the GaussianCube is performed via optimal transport. Steps: 1. Representation Conversion: Convert the target constant number of 3D Gaussians into a GaussianCube representation using optimal transport voxelization. 2. Diffusion Training: Train a 3D diffusion model on the GaussianCube representation. The model learns to denoise the Gaussian attributes conditioned on the input signal. 3. Structured Noise Incorporation: During training and inference, incorporate structured noise from multiple viewpoints into the diffusion process. This step is critical to alleviate the Janus problem, ensuring multi-view consistency. 4. Variational 3DGS Integration: Use variational 3DGS within the generation pipeline to mitigate the appearance of floaters (artifacts) in the generated scene. Parameters: Specific hyperparameters for the diffusion model (e.g., noise schedule, number of steps) are not given in the sources. The specific implementation of the optimal transport algorithm for voxelization is not detailed in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Janus Problem: Without structured noise from multiple viewpoints, the generated 3D object may exhibit inconsistent features across different views. Floaters: Standard 3DGS generation can produce floating artifacts; variational 3DGS is employed to mitigate this. Direct 3D Generation refers to methods that learn a feedforward or diffusion model to output Gaussian fields directly from text or images, without an explicit intermediate image set. It solves the problem of high reconstruction latency and multi-view inconsistency inherent in iterative optimization by amortizing the cost over a trained network. Unlike iterative reconstruction, it naturally promotes multi-view coherence and enables near-real-time sampling at test time. Gaussian Masking is a technique used to prune Gaussians during the training process to improve efficiency and quality. Step: Use Gaussian masks to prune Gaussians at every densification step and for every 500 iterations after densification stops. Parameters: \lambdam: Loss weight for Gaussian masking loss. Value is 0.05. \epsilonm: Threshold for Gaussian masks. Value is 0.05. Learning rate for Gaussian masks: 0.5. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Alleviates the Janus problem through structured multi-view noise; mitigates floaters via variational 3DGS; enables near-real-time generation at test time. Limitations: Requires training a diffusion model on a GaussianCube representation, which may have higher initial setup costs compared to iterative methods. When to use: When multi-view consistency is critical and near-real-time generation is required. When not to use: When iterative optimization is acceptable and multi-view consistency is less of a concern. GaussianDiffusion was proposed by [251] (cited in). It is part of the broader effort to improve 3D generation quality by addressing specific issues like the Janus problem and floaters in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method builds on the GaussianCube representation, which converts a constant number of Gaussians into a voxelized format via optimal transport. name: Direct 3D Generation
head: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation, Amortized 3DGS Synthesis
body: Direct 3D Generation refers to methods that learn a feedforward or diffusion model to output Gaussian fields directly from text or images, without an explicit intermediate image set. It solves the problem of high reconstruction latency and multi-view inconsistency inherent in iterative optimization by amortizing the cost over a trained network. Unlike iterative reconstruction, it naturally promotes multi-view coherence and enables near-real-time sampling at test time. Inputs: Text prompts, input images, or partial 3DGS representations. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives defined by position, covariance (transform), color, and opacity. Data Structures: The method typically disentangles the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation into three distinct functions to handle the high-dimensional output: 1. GauPF (Gaussian Probability Function): Models the 3D locations/geometry of the Gaussians. 2. GauCF (Gaussian Color Function): Models the color attributes. 3. GauTF (Gaussian Transform Function): Models the covariance/transform attributes. In diffusion-based variants (e.g., DiffGS), a Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maps these functions into a regularized latent space. The latent vector z represents the compressed 3DGS shape. Steps: 1. Training (VAE): Train a Gaussian VAE to map 3DGS functions into a latent vector z. The VAE learns a regularized latent space. 2. Training (Diffusion): Train a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) in the latent space of the Gaussian VAE. The LDM is trained to predict noise or reverse the diffusion process on latent vectors zk. Conditioning inputs (text, image, partial GS) are injected into the LDM. 3. Generation: Start from noise N(0,1). Iteratively denoise from Step K to Step 0 to obtain the clean latent vector z0. Decode z0 using the VAE decoder to recover GauPF, GauCF, and GauTF. 4. Geometry Extraction: Extract 3D Gaussian geometry from GauPF by sampling 3D locations in the 3D space with the highest Gaussian probabilities. 5. Attribute Prediction: Predict the Gaussian attributes (color and transform) using GauCF and GauTF respectively. 6. Discretization (Optional): Apply an octree-guided sampling and optimization algorithm to extract Gaussians at arbitrary numbers. Formulas: Latent Diffusion Process: The model predicts noise for latent vectors zk derived from the VAE. Generation: z0 = \text{Denoise}(zK, \text{Condition}) where zK \sim N(0,1). Parameters: Diffusion Steps K: Not given in the sources. Latent Dimension: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Imperfect Cross-View Consistency: Can lead to noisy surface geometry, duplicated structures, and degraded textures, especially in occluded or textureless regions. High-Dimensional Output: The structured output space (positions, anisotropic covariance, colors, opacity) presents significant modeling challenges. Data Requirements: Requires large, curated 3D training corpora. A text-to-4D synthesis method that generates dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes from text prompts. It solves the problem of creating temporally consistent, deformable 3D content by endowing static 3DGS with dynamics via a deformation network. It is distinguished from static 3D generation methods by its explicit modeling of motion through a text-to-video diffusion prior, and from other 4D methods like DreamGaussian4D by its use of a text-to-video model for motion capture rather than learning motion from a driving video. Choose it when dynamic 4D scene synthesis is required. Align Your Gaussians (AYG) Produces 3D Gaussian Splatting representations directly from text prompts, input images, or partial 3DGS inputs containing large occlusions. It solves the problem of controllable 3D asset creation and scene completion without relying on iterative per-scene optimization or explicit intermediate image sets, amortizing reconstruction cost by learning a feedforward or diffusion-based mapping. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Align Your Gaussians (AYG) by focusing on static or diffusion-based generation conditioned on semantic or geometric priors rather than dynamic 4D scene synthesis. Choose it for static or diffusion-based generation with semantic/geometric conditioning. Conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation A diffusion model trained in the latent space of the Gaussian VAE to generate novel 3DGS shapes conditionally or unconditionally. It differs from direct pixel-space diffusion by operating on the compressed latent representation of the Gaussian functions, enabling efficient generation of diverse 3DGS. Choose it when efficient, latent-space diffusion is preferred for 3DGS generation. Time Complexity: Near-real-time sampling at test time. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the trained feedforward or diffusion model and the VAE. Strengths: Amortizes reconstruction cost; naturally promotes multi-view coherence; enables near-real-time sampling. Limitations: Requires large, curated 3D training corpora; challenges in maintaining controllability (e.g., disentangling geometry from appearance) while scaling; imperfect cross-view consistency can lead to noisy geometry in occluded regions. When to use: When rapid generation from text/images is required and iterative optimization is too slow. Direct 3D generation methods aim to learn a feedforward or diffusion model that outputs Gaussian fields directly from text or images, without an explicit intermediate image set. Trained on large collections of synthetic or reconstructed data, these models amortize the reconstruction cost. The approach addresses the challenges of the high-dimensional and highly structured output space of 3DGS. DiffGS introduces a Gaussian VAE and LDM framework to generate diverse 3DGS both conditionally and unconditionally. name: Align Your Gaussians (AYG)
body: Align Your Gaussians (AYG) is a text-to-4D synthesis method that generates dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes from text prompts. It solves the problem of creating temporally consistent, deformable 3D content by endowing static 3DGS with dynamics via a deformation network. It is distinguished from static 3D generation methods by its explicit modeling of motion through a text-to-video diffusion prior, and from other 4D methods like DreamGaussian4D by its use of a text-to-video model for motion capture rather than learning motion from a driving video. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt describing the scene and its motion. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians with static attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity) and a deformation field network that maps time to Gaussian attribute updates. Data Structures: Static 3DGS: Standard 3D Gaussian representation. Positions \mathbf{p}, scales \mathbf{s}, rotations \mathbf{q}, colors \mathbf{c}, opacities \alpha. These are fixed after the first stage. Deformation Field Network: A neural network (architecture not specified in sources) that takes Gaussian indices and time t as input, outputting displacement vectors or velocity fields to modulate the static Gaussians. Steps: The method operates in two distinct stages: 1. Static 3DGS Generation: Initialize a static 3DGS representation. Optimize the static Gaussian attributes using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) losses derived from a text-to-image diffusion model (Stable Diffusion) and a multi-view consistent prior (MVDream). 2. Dynamic Generation (Deformation Optimization): Freeze the static Gaussian attributes from Stage 1. Optimize only the parameters of the deformation field network. The optimization uses a Video SDS Loss based on a text-to-video diffusion model to enforce temporal consistency and motion dynamics. To prevent temporal flickering and ensure high visual quality, Image-based SDS losses are applied to randomly selected frames during the dynamic optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gaussians = initialize3dgs() # Standard 3DGS initialization for step in range(staticsteps): # Optimization iterations # Standard Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss computation loss = computesdsloss(gaussians, textprompt, model=StableDiffusion) loss += computemvdreamloss(gaussians, textprompt) gaussians = gaussians - lr grad(loss) # Standard gradient descent step deformationnet = DeformationNetwork() # Neural network for deformation freezegaussians = True # Freeze static attributes for step in range(dynamicsteps): # Optimization iterations t = random.uniform(0, 1) # Uniformly sample time step # Apply deformation to get dynamic view dynamicgaussians = applydeformation(gaussians, deformationnet, t) # Standard Video Score Distillation Sampling loss computation lossvideo = computevideosdsloss(dynamicgaussians, textprompt, model=TextToVideoDiffusion) # Image-based SDS for quality on random frames if random.random() < 0.5: # Standard Image Score Distillation Sampling loss computation lossimage = computeimagesdsloss(dynamicgaussians, textprompt, model=StableDiffusion) loss = lossvideo + lossimage else: loss = lossvideo deformationnet = deformationnet - lr grad(loss) # Standard gradient descent step Parameters: Text Prompt: Describes the object and motion. Diffusion Models: Stable Diffusion (image), MVDream (multi-view), Text-to-Video Diffusion (motion). Loss Weights: Not given in the sources. Deformation Field Capacity: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Inconsistency: Without the image-based SDS on random frames, the video SDS loss alone may lead to flickering or quality degradation. Deformation Field Capacity: Not given in the sources. Generates 3DGS conditioned on input images or text, focusing on static or single-view consistency, whereas AYG explicitly targets 4D dynamic synthesis. Time Complexity: High, due to iterative optimization using multiple diffusion models (SDS). Memory Complexity: Moderate, storing static Gaussians and the deformation network parameters. Strengths: Enables text-to-4D generation with explicit dynamic control via text prompts. Limitations: Relies on heavy diffusion-based optimization (SDS), which is computationally expensive. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. AYG was introduced as a method to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to 4D by incorporating deformation fields. It builds on the success of 3D generation using SDS. It is cited in surveys of 3D editing and generation, highlighting its role in enabling text-to-4D synthesis and deformation. name: Conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation
head: Conditional Generation (Text/Image/Partial), DiffGS Conditional
body: Conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation produces 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations directly from text prompts, input images, or partial 3DGS inputs containing large occlusions. It solves the problem of controllable 3D asset creation and scene completion without relying on iterative per-scene optimization or explicit intermediate image sets, amortizing reconstruction cost by learning a feedforward or diffusion-based mapping. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Align Your Gaussians (AYG) by focusing on static or diffusion-based generation conditioned on semantic or geometric priors rather than dynamic 4D scene synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Text prompts, single/multi-view images, or partial 3DGS point clouds/splats. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position \mathbf{x}, covariance \Sigma (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Data Structures: The method utilizes custom encoders to map conditions into a latent space compatible with the generation model (e.g., a diffusion model or MLP). Text Encoder (\gamma{\text{text}}): Frozen CLIP text encoder. Image Encoder (\gamma{\text{image}}): Frozen CLIP image encoder. Partial Input Encoder (\gamma{\text{partial}}): Modified PointNet architecture for encoding partial 3DGS inputs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Condition Encoding: If the condition is text, compute embedding \mathbf{c}{\text{text}} = \gamma{\text{text}}(\text{text}). If the condition is an image, compute embedding \mathbf{c}{\text{image}} = \gamma{\text{image}}(\text{image}). If the condition is partial 3DGS, encode the partial geometry/appearance using \gamma{\text{partial}} to produce \mathbf{c}{\text{partial}}. 2. Generation (DiffGS Approach): Train a diffusion model (DiffGS) with a conditional optimization objective. The specific formulation of Eq.(8) in is not provided in the source text, but it involves conditioning the diffusion process on \mathbf{c}{\text{text}}, \mathbf{c}{\text{image}}, or \mathbf{c}{\text{partial}}. Sample from the diffusion model to generate Gaussian attributes. 3. Alternative Implementation (Text-to-3D Reimplementation): Use a learnable MLP background and specific gradient propagation rules. Render depth maps by sampling view-space depth at Gaussian centers. Implement a z-variance renderer to compute z-variance for a z-var loss term. Clamp Gaussian opacity to [0.004, 0.99] during rendering and optimization to stabilize gradients and prevent numerical overflow/underflow. Propagate gradients in forward rendering order (unlike the official inverse order) to simplify per-pixel background integration. 4. Geometry Refinement (Gaussian Pulling to Zero-Level Set): To prevent floating ellipsoids and achieve accurate geometry, pull Gaussian centers onto the zero-level set of a neural SDF field. Pull neighboring space/query points onto Gaussian disks (rather than just centers) to bridge the gap between continuous SDF fields and sparse Gaussian distributions. Use the normalized SDF gradient for the pulling operation. Do not add an Eikonal loss term, as it degenerates optimization by making the SDF field optimization too complex. 5. Pruning (Multi-view Consistent Pruning): Evaluate Gaussian contribution to multi-view reconstruction quality. Compute photometric loss E^j{\text{photo}} for each view j: E^j{\text{photo}} = (1 - \lambda)L^j1 + \lambda(1 - L^j{\text{SSIM}}) where L^j1 is mean absolute error and L^j{\text{SSIM}} is structural similarity loss. Identify high-error pixels using a mask M^j{\text{mask}} derived from normalized reconstruction error. Calculate the pruning score s^ip for Gaussian Gi: s^ip = N \left( \frac{1}{K} \sum{j=1}^K \sum{p \in \Omegai} I(M^j{\text{mask}}(p) = 1) \cdot E^j{\text{photo}} \right) where K is the number of views, \Omegai is the 2D footprint of Gi, and N(\cdot) is min-max normalization. Select Gi for pruning if s^ip > \taup. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the SSIM term in photometric loss. Default: 0.2. \taup: Threshold for the pruning score s^ip. Opacity Clamp: [0.004, 0.99]. Target Gaussians: 10^5 to 10^6 after densification. Dataset: ShapeNet chair class with standard splits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Order: The official 3DGS implementation propagates gradients in inverse order (last rendered Gaussians first). Reimplementations may use forward order to simplify background integration, which is a design choice rather than a bug. Z-var Loss: While implemented in some variants, z-var loss has limited impact on generated assets due to the natural sparsity of Gaussians enforcing a thin surface. Eikonal Loss: Adding an Eikonal loss term to the Gaussian pulling operation significantly degrades results; it should be omitted. 4D Motion Distortion: In dynamic generation variants (e.g., Align Your Gaussians), interpolation in the temporal dimension may induce motion distortion because it does not consider physical dynamics constraints. A mechanism for 3D editing (extraction, deletion, appearance modification) in 3D Gaussian Splatting by computing activation scores of 3D Gaussians based on prompts (text, points, boxes) using cosine similarity and softmax. It differs from implicit NeRF feature fields by operating on explicit Gaussian primitives, allowing direct manipulation of color and opacity parameters for specific semantic subsets. GSEdit is a method for editing pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations or texture meshes using text or image instructions. It solves the problem of applying 2D diffusion-based edits to 3D scenes while maintaining geometric consistency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GaussianObject or Promptable Explicit Scene Representation by directly utilizing Instruct-Pix2Pix and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to update the input representation, rather than relying on complex multi-view consistency constraints or explicit texture mapping networks like Texture-GS. GaussianObject is a method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction from sparse or partial inputs that initializes Gaussians using a visual hull and employs a fine-tuned ControlNet to repair degraded rendered images. It distinguishes itself from prior NeRF-based sparse-view methods by leveraging diffusion priors for attribute refinement, outperforming previous approaches in reconstruction quality. Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (AAGS) extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle unconstrained photo collections by explicitly modeling per-image appearance variations and removing transient objects (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) from the static scene reconstruction. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by integrating a transient object visibility mask and an appearance interpolation mechanism, and from NeRF-based methods like Ha-NeRF by maintaining the efficiency of splatting while achieving competitive or superior perceptual metrics (LPIPS) without requiring test-set images for appearance embedding training. VTC is a pre-training observation filtering and consensus mechanism designed to improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction in texture-degraded scenes by rejecting unreliable observations and decoupling geometry from appearance. It differs from existing approaches that treat all visible observations as equally reliable by performing observation-level rejection of colors corrupted by occlusion, background mixing, or exposure differences, and by using a fixed robust consensus target computed before training rather than an online-updated uncertainty estimate. A method operating in two stages for interactive 3D object generation and refinement, optimizing 3D objects through 3DGS and SDS in first stage, then transforming model into InstantNGP structure with interactive hash refinement module in second stage. A reimplementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting adapted for text-to-3D generation, modified to support a learnable MLP background and specific gradient propagation. The official implementation propagates gradients in inverse order (last rendered Gaussians receive gradients first), whereas this variant uses rendering order to simplify per-pixel background integration. A technique that pulls Gaussian centers onto the zero-level set of a neural SDF field to prevent floating ellipsoids and achieve accurate geometry estimation. It also pulls query points to Gaussian disks rather than centers to bridge the gap between continuous SDF fields and sparse Gaussian distributions. A pruning strategy that removes redundant Gaussians by evaluating their contribution to multi-view reconstruction quality, using photometric loss combined with the densification score. Exploits off-the-shelf models to generate multi-view images from text or a single image, then trains a U-Net-based network to generate 3DGS from multi-view images. The U-Net is asymmetric, which allows for the input of high-resolution images while limiting the number of output Gaussians. A method integrating text-to-image/video diffusion models for generating 4D dynamic scenes. 4D generation induces motion distortion because interpolation in the temporal dimension does not consider physical dynamics constraints. Time Complexity: Training time varies by variant. Text-to-3D implementations using diffusion guidance (e.g., Stable Diffusion) take approximately 40 minutes per prompt. DiffGS training time is not explicitly given but involves diffusion steps. Memory Complexity: The number of Gaussians after densification is typically between 10^5 and 10^6. Measured Performance: DiffGS produces significantly more visual-appealing and high-fidelity generations in terms of rendering and geometry qualities compared to prior methods like DiffTF, which suffer from blurry generations and poor textures. Strengths: Capable of recovering complex geometries and detailed appearances from highly occluded 3DGS inputs. Accurately recovers semantics and geometries described in text prompts. Limitations: 4D generation variants may suffer from motion distortion due to lack of physical dynamics constraints. Z-var loss has limited impact on asset quality. When to Use: When conditional generation from text, images, or partial data is required without iterative per-scene optimization. When Not to Use: When strict physical dynamics consistency in 4D generation is required. Conditional 3D Gaussian Splatting Generation originates from the need to control 3D generation using semantic or geometric priors. DiffGS was introduced to enable conditional generation using texts, images, and partial 3DGS inputs, demonstrating the ability to recover complex geometries from occluded inputs. The field has expanded to include interactive refinement (Interactive3D), efficient text-to-3D reimplementations (LGM, Text-to-3D GS), and geometry-aware techniques like Gaussian Pulling to Zero-Level Set and Multi-view Consistent Pruning. Dynamic generation methods like Align Your Gaussians have also emerged, though they face challenges with temporal consistency. name: Promptable Explicit Scene Representation
head: Semantic Prompting
body: A mechanism for 3D editing (extraction, deletion, appearance modification) in 3D Gaussian Splatting by computing activation scores of 3D Gaussians based on prompts (text, points, boxes) using cosine similarity and softmax. It differs from implicit NeRF feature fields by operating on explicit Gaussian primitives, allowing direct manipulation of color and opacity parameters for specific semantic subsets. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{xi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian x has a semantic feature vector f(x), color c(x), and opacity \alpha(x). A prompt \tau (text, point, or box). For text prompts: A ViT-B/32 CLIP encoder to generate query vectors q(\tau). A set of possible labels \mathcal{T} (e.g., text labels for segmentation or pixel coordinates for point prompts). Outputs: A "Gaussian mask" identifying Gaussians associated with the prompt. An edited radiance field with updated \{ci\} and \{\alphai\} for selected Gaussians, where the count n < N. Data Structures: Gaussian Feature: Each Gaussian x stores a semantic feature vector f(x). Query Vector: For text, q(\tau) is the CLIP text embedding. For points/boxes, q(\tau) corresponds to features queried from the distilled 3D feature field. Steps: 1. Encode Prompt: For text, compute q(\tau) using the CLIP ViT-B/32 encoder. For points or boxes, retrieve the corresponding feature from the distilled 3D feature field. 2. Compute Activation Score: For each Gaussian x, calculate the cosine similarity between its semantic feature f(x) and the query vector q(\tau): s = \frac {f(x) \cdot q(\tau)}{\|f(x)\| \|q(\tau)\|} where s is the activation score. 3. Compute Probability: If a set of labels \mathcal{T} is provided, compute the probability \mathbf {p}(\tau | x) using softmax over all scores sj \in \mathcal{T}: \mathbf {p}(\tau | x) = \text {softmax} (s) = \frac {\exp \left ( s \right)}{\sum {sj \in \mathcal {T}} \exp \left (sj\right)}. 4. Generate Gaussian Mask: Filter Gaussians based on the computed probabilities or scores. Two selection modes are supported: Soft Selection: Threshold the score matrix to include Gaussians with scores above a certain value. Hard Selection: Filter based on the highest score across K categories (where K is the number of object categories). 5. Edit Scene: Update the color c(x) and opacity \alpha(x) of the selected Gaussians. 6. Render: Render the edited radiance field using point-based \alpha-blending with the updated set \{ci\}{i=1}^n and \{\alphai\}{i=1}^n, where n < N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def norm(a): return math.sqrt(sum(ai ai for ai in a)) def softmax(scores): maxs = max(scores) expscores = [math.exp(s - maxs) for s in scores] sumexp = sum(expscores) return [e / sumexp for e in expscores] def promptableediting(gaussians, prompt, clipencoder, labels=None, threshold=None): """ gaussians: List of objects with.feature,.color,.opacity prompt: Text string, or (x, y) point, or (x1, y1, x2, y2) box clipencoder: Callable returning feature vector for text labels: Optional list of text labels for softmax normalization threshold: Optional float for soft selection """ # Step 1: Encode Prompt if isinstance(prompt, str): queryvector = clipencoder(prompt) else: # For point/box, retrieve feature from the distilled 3D feature field # Not given in the sources. queryvector = [0.0] len(gaussians[0].feature) selectedindices = [] scores = [] # Step 2 & 3: Compute Scores and Probabilities for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): f = g.feature q = queryvector # Step 2: Cosine similarity fnorm = norm(f) qnorm = norm(q) if fnorm == 0 or qnorm == 0: s = 0.0 else: s = dot(f, q) / (fnorm qnorm) scores.append(s) # Step 3: Softmax probability if labels provided prob = s if labels is not None: allscores = [] for label in labels: qlabel = clipencoder(label) qlabelnorm = norm(qlabel) if qlabelnorm == 0: allscores.append(0.0) else: allscores.append(dot(f, qlabel) / (fnorm qlabelnorm)) probs = softmax(allscores) try: idx = labels.index(prompt) prob = probs[idx] except ValueError: prob = 0.0 # Step 4: Generate Mask isselected = False if threshold is not None: if prob >= threshold: isselected = True else: # Hard selection: highest score across K categories if labels is not None: maxprob = max(probs) if prob == maxprob: isselected = True if isselected: selectedindices.append(i) # Step 5: Edit Scene # Update the color c(x) and opacity alpha(x) of the selected Gaussians for i in selectedindices: gaussians[i].opacity = 0.0 # Example for extraction # gaussians[i].color =... # Example for appearance modification # Step 6: Render # Render the edited radiance field using point-based alpha-blending # Not given in the sources. image = None return image, selectedindices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Norm: If f(x) or q(\tau) has zero norm, the cosine similarity is undefined. Handle by setting score to 0. Distillation Dependency: The quality of f(x) depends on the teacher-student distillation process. NeRF Interference Avoidance: Unlike NeRF-based feature fields where the feature branch shares layers with the radiance field (potentially causing interference), this method uses explicit Gaussian features to avoid such overlap issues. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing semantic features f(x) for each Gaussian, increasing memory usage compared to standard 3DGS. Strengths: Enables direct 3D editing (extraction, deletion, modification) using 2D prompts (points, boxes) or text. Avoids interference from shared NeRF branches. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the distilled feature field. Text prompts require CLIP encoding. Hard selection may be less flexible than soft thresholding. Originated in "Feature 3DGS: Supercharging 3D Gaussian Splatting to Enable Distilled Feature Fields" (CVPR 2024). It extends 2D pixel-level promptable editing (from SAM and CLIP) into the 3D realm by distilling 2D features into a 3D feature field associated with 3D Gaussians. name: GSEdit
head: Gaussian Editing via Instruct-Pix2Pix and SDS Loss
body: GSEdit is a method for editing pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations or texture meshes using text or image instructions. It solves the problem of applying 2D diffusion-based edits to 3D scenes while maintaining geometric consistency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GaussianObject or Promptable Explicit Scene Representation by directly utilizing Instruct-Pix2Pix and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to update the input representation, rather than relying on complex multi-view consistency constraints or explicit texture mapping networks like Texture-GS. Inputs: A pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting representation or a texture mesh. Text or image instructions for the desired edit. Outputs: An edited 3D Gaussian Splatting representation or texture mesh. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3DGS data structure: a set of N Gaussians, each defined by position \mathbf{\mu}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{s}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. For mesh inputs, the structure includes vertex positions, face connectivity, and UV coordinates. Steps: 1. Input Preparation: Load the pre-trained 3DGS or texture mesh. 2. 2D Edit Generation: Use Instruct-Pix2Pix to generate edited 2D images based on the input instructions. This involves rendering views from the current 3DGS/mesh, passing them through Instruct-Pix2Pix with the edit prompt, and obtaining the edited 2D images. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss between the rendered views of the current 3DGS/mesh and the edited 2D images from Instruct-Pix2Pix. The SDS loss guides the optimization to match the visual style and content of the 2D edits. 4. Optimization: Update the parameters of the 3DGS (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) or the texture mesh (vertex positions, UVs) using gradient descent to minimize the SDS loss. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for a fixed number of iterations or until convergence. Parameters: Number of optimization iterations: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Instruct-Pix2Pix model weights: Standard pretrained weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistency: Direct use of SDS loss can lead to geometric inconsistencies across views. GSEdit relies on the inherent consistency of the 3DGS representation and the 2D edit, but may suffer from flickering or distortion if the edit is complex. Precision: The optimization is sensitive to the learning rate and number of iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GSEdit(input3dgsormesh, editinstruction, numiterations): """ Edits a 3D Gaussian Splatting or texture mesh using Instruct-Pix2Pix and SDS loss. Args: input3dgsormesh: Pre-trained 3DGS or texture mesh object. editinstruction: Text or image instruction for the edit. numiterations: Number of optimization steps. Returns: Edited 3DGS or texture mesh. """ # Initialize optimizer with the parameters of input3dgsormesh optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(input3dgsormesh.parameters(), lr=0.01) for i in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Render current views from the 3DGS or mesh renderedviews = renderviews(input3dgsormesh) # Apply Instruct-Pix2Pix to each rendered view editedviews = [] for view in renderedviews: # Instruct-Pix2Pix takes the original image and the edit instruction editedview = InstructPix2Pix(view, editinstruction) editedviews.append(editedview) # Compute SDS loss between rendered views and edited views # SDS loss is computed for each view and averaged loss = computesdsloss(renderedviews, editedviews) # Backpropagate and update parameters loss.backward() optimizer.step() return input3dgsormesh A variant that focuses on editing the albedo (color) of 3DGS by initializing new Gaussians on a textured proxy plane. It places these Gaussians in 3D space using proxy depth and spawns additional albedo Gaussians by randomly sampling 20% of the pixels covered by the edit in the edited view. name: GaussianObject
body: GaussianObject reconstructs 3D Gaussian Splatting representations from sparse or partial inputs by initializing Gaussians with a visual hull and fine-tuning a pre-trained ControlNet to repair degraded rendered images generated by adding noise to each Gaussian's attributes. It outperforms previous NeRF-based sparse-view reconstruction methods. Steps: 1. Initialize 3D Gaussians with the visual hull derived from the input views. 2. Add noise to each Gaussian's attributes to generate degraded rendered images. 3. Fine-tune a pre-trained ControlNet to repair the degraded rendered images. 4. Update the Gaussian attributes using the repaired outputs from the ControlNet. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the quality of the visual hull for initialization. Severe occlusions may require robust diffusion priors to hallucinate plausible geometry. Note that removing Gaussians with incorrect depth values and utilizing Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss are attributed to prior methods in the source text, not GaussianObject. ControlNet introduces additional conditions to guide the generative process, such as canny edge, human pose, and depth, allowing for fine-grained control over image modifications. It sets itself apart from unconditional diffusion models by conditioning on explicit spatial or structural cues rather than text alone, and is chosen when precise geometric or pose alignment is required during generation. Performance: Outperforms previous NeRF-based sparse-view reconstruction methods. GaussianObject was introduced to improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction from sparse inputs by combining geometric initialization with diffusion-based refinement. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting and ControlNet, addressing limitations of NeRF-based methods in sparse-view settings. name: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (AAGS)
head: AAGS-A, AAGS-T
body: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (AAGS) reconstructs static scenes from unconstrained photo collections by explicitly modeling per-image appearance variations and excluding transient objects from the geometry. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by integrating a transient visibility mask and appearance interpolation, and outperforms NeRF-based methods in perceptual metrics (LPIPS) without requiring test-set images for appearance embedding training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of unconstrained images of a scene. Output: 3D Gaussians with static geometry, appearance features, a transient visibility map, and the capability to render novel appearances. Data Structures: The method uses the standard 3D Gaussian representation [S1: position \mathbf{p}, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}]. AAGS augments this with an appearance feature vector \mathbf{f}{app} per view, and a 2D transient visibility map V \in [0, 1] predicted per image. Network Architectures: 1. Appearance Feature Extractor (E\Phi): Consists of 5 convolutional layers, 1 average pooling layer, and 1 fully connected layer, consistent with Ha-NeRF. 2. Transient UNet (U\Psi): Consists of 1 downsampling layer and 1 upsampling layer. 3. Color Decoder (F\theta): Consists of 4 fully connected layers, each with a width of 64. Parameters: \lambda1 = 0.8: Loss weight hyperparameter. na = 48: Image feature length. ng = 24: Image feature length. Spherical Harmonics Degree: 4 for directional vectors. Exponential Annealing Weights: Start at 0.5, decrease to 0.15. Training Procedure: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a point cloud. Initialize E\Phi, U\Psi, and F\theta. 2. Iteration Loop (30,000 total iterations): Densification Phase (Iterations 1–15,000): Perform Gaussian duplication, splitting, and deletion as per standard 3DGS. Static Phase (Iterations 15,001–30,000): Disable duplication, splitting, and deletion to maintain a constant Gaussian count. Forward Pass: Render the scene using differentiable splatting to obtain \hat{I}. Pass the input image through E\Phi to extract appearance features. Pass the input image through U\Psi to predict the transient visibility map V. Transient Handling: Exclude transient objects during rendering using V. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} (defined in Eq. 10 of) and backpropagate to update all parameters (E\Phi, U\Psi, F\theta, and Gaussian properties). Appearance Interpolation: To generate novel appearances, AAGS linearly interpolates between the appearance features of two reference images while keeping the 3D structure (Gaussian positions and covariances) fixed. Pitfalls: Without transient objects handling, the model tends to model transient objects as static, causing artifacts, though metrics may appear better on test sets lacking transients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class AppearanceExtractor(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 5 conv layers, 1 average pooling, 1 fully connected layer pass def forward(self, image): # Extract appearance features return imagefeatures class TransientUNet(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 1 downsampling layer, 1 upsampling layer pass def forward(self, image): # Predict transient visibility map return visibilitymap class ColorDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 4 fully connected layers, width 64 pass def forward(self, gaussianprops, appfeatures): # Decode color return decodedcolor def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameraparams, appfeatures, visibilitymap): # Differentiable splatting forward pass # Apply visibilitymap to exclude transient objects during rendering return renderedimage def calculateloss(renderedimage, gtimage, visibilitymap, lambda1, shdegree): # Total loss defined in Eq. (10) of return loss def trainaags(images, gtimages, numiterations=30000, densifyuntil=15000): gaussians = initializegaussiansfrompointcloud(images) # Ephi = AppearanceExtractor() Upsi = TransientUNet() Ftheta = ColorDecoder() lambda1 = 0.8 na = 48 ng = 24 shdegree = 4 annealstart = 0.5 annealend = 0.15 optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(params=list(gaussians.parameters()) + list(Ephi.parameters()) + list(Upsi.parameters()) + list(Ftheta.parameters())) for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): if iteration <= densifyuntil: gaussians.densifyandsplit(iteration) gaussians.prune() image = samplerandomimage(images) gt = getgtimage(image) appfeatures = Ephi(image) visibilitymap = Upsi(image) renderedimage = rendergaussians(gaussians, cameraparams, appfeatures, visibilitymap) loss = calculateloss(renderedimage, gt, visibilitymap, lambda1, shdegree) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Exponential annealing schedule from 0.5 to 0.15 currentanneal = annealstart (annealend / annealstart) (iteration / numiterations) def renderwithappearance(gaussians, cameraparams, refimagea, refimageb, alpha=0.5): feata = AppearanceExtractor()(refimagea) featb = AppearanceExtractor()(refimageb) interpolatedfeat = feata alpha + featb (1 - alpha) return rendergaussians(gaussians, cameraparams, interpolatedfeat, None) Removes the transient UNet module. Tends to model transient objects as static, causing artifacts, though metrics may appear better on test sets lacking transients. Removes the appearance feature extracting module. Struggles to capture appearance differences between images, leading to low perceptual metrics. Training Duration: Training runs for 30,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Implemented with PyTorch and CUDA extensions on a single RTX 3090 (24GB memory). Performance: Phototourism Dataset: Brandenburg Gate PSNR 27.20, SSIM 0.9293, LPIPS 0.1341; Sacré-Cœur PSNR 23.23, SSIM 0.8703, LPIPS 0.1729; Trevi Fountain PSNR 23.04, SSIM 0.8037, LPIPS 0.1795. NeRF-OSR Dataset: europa PSNR 21.82, SSIM 0.8069, LPIPS 0.2228; lwt PSNR 23.14, SSIM 0.7972, LPIPS 0.2401; st PSNR 22.31, SSIM 0.6928, LPIPS 0.3421; stjohann PSNR 24.93, SSIM 0.8867, LPIPS 0.1428. Gaussian Count Reduction: Reduces the number of Gaussians compared to baseline 3DGS: Brandenburg Gate (379K vs 521K), Sacré-Cœur (382K vs 461K), Trevi Fountain (896K vs 1070K). Strengths: Handles unconstrained photos, removes transient objects, reduces Gaussian count, faster than NeRFs, better perceptual quality (LPIPS) than SWAG. Limitations: Struggles with highlights and certain objects. Rendering is softer than SWAG (which may be sharper but less perceptually aligned). AAGS was introduced in the paper "AAGS: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting with Unconstrained Photo Collections". It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS in handling dynamic scenes and appearance variations in unconstrained photo collections.
