name: VTC (Visibility-Aware Texture Consensus)
head: Visibility-Aware Texture Consensus
body: VTC is a pre-training observation filtering and consensus mechanism designed to improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction in texture-degraded scenes by rejecting unreliable observations and decoupling geometry from appearance. It differs from existing approaches that treat all visible observations as equally reliable by performing observation-level rejection of colors corrupted by occlusion, background mixing, or exposure differences, and by using a fixed robust consensus target computed before training rather than an online-updated uncertainty estimate. VTC operates on explicit Gaussian representations to determine visibility and depth consistency at the Gaussian granularity. It constructs a cross-view color consensus and consensus weights from channel-wise median and Median Absolute Deviation (MAD). The consensus remains fixed during training to prevent feedback contamination. Inputs: An initial set of M 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mathbf{g}i\}{i=1}^M, where each Gaussian \mathbf{g}i has position \mathbf{p}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i (appearance parameters). N input images with known camera poses. Outputs: A binary mask \mathbf{M}{ij} \in \{0, 1\} indicating reliable observations for Gaussian i in image j. A fixed color consensus vector \mathbf{C}^{\text{cons}}i for each Gaussian. Consensus weights \mathbf{W}{ij} for each reliable observation. Local PCA statistics for geometric anchoring. Reliable Observation Set: A sparse structure mapping (i, j) pairs where \mathbf{M}{ij}=1. Color Consensus: A tensor of shape (M, 3) storing the channel-wise median color for each Gaussian. MAD: A tensor of shape (M, 3) storing the Median Absolute Deviation for each Gaussian. Consensus Weights: A tensor of shape (M, N) storing the weight for each Gaussian-image pair. 1. Pre-training Filtering: For each Gaussian i and each input image j, compute the projected color \mathbf{C}{ij} and depth D{ij}. Determine the reliability mask \mathbf{M}{ij} using four criteria: (1) Image Bounds: The projection of Gaussian i must lie within the image boundaries. (2) Foreground Membership: The Gaussian must belong to the foreground object. (3) Projected Visibility: The Gaussian must be occlusion-free in the view. (4) Depth Consistency: The rendered depth D{ij} must be consistent with the expected depth from the camera pose and Gaussian geometry. If any criterion fails, \mathbf{M}{ij} = 0; otherwise, \mathbf{M}{ij} = 1. 2. Consensus Construction: For each Gaussian i, collect all filtered observations \{\mathbf{C}{ij} \mid \mathbf{M}{ij} = 1\}. Compute the channel-wise median color \mathbf{C}^{\text{cons}}i across these observations. This serves as the robust target color for Gaussian i. 3. Weight Determination: Compute the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) for each color channel k of Gaussian i: \text{MAD}{ik} = \text{median}j \left( | \mathbf{C}{ijk} - \mathbf{C}^{\text{cons}}{ik} | \cdot \mathbf{M}{ij} \right) where \mathbf{C}{ijk} is the k-th channel of \mathbf{C}{ij}. Compute the consensus weight \mathbf{W}{ij} for each reliable observation. The weight is determined by the MAD and the effective sample count Ki = \sumj \mathbf{M}{ij}. A standard robust weighting formulation is: \mathbf{W}{ij} = \exp \left( - \frac{ \sumk | \mathbf{C}{ijk} - \mathbf{C}^{\text{cons}}{ik} | }{ \epsilon + \sumk \text{MAD}{ik} + 1.0/Ki } \right) where \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. If \mathbf{M}{ij} = 0, \mathbf{W}{ij} = 0. 4. Parameter Routing: Restrict the parameter groups affected by each loss term to achieve geometry–appearance decoupling. The VTC loss acts only on the appearance parameters \mathbf{c}i (spherical harmonic coefficients). Geometric parameters (position, covariance, opacity) are updated by other losses but are not directly influenced by the color consensus error. 5. Local PCA and Geometric Anchoring: Estimate neighborhood structure for each Gaussian using local Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the positions of neighboring Gaussians. Compute the covariance matrix of neighbor positions. Extract principal axes and normals. Construct a geometric anchoring regularizer that imposes an adaptive prior in the orthogonal subspace according to structural confidence. This regularizer uses a heavy-tailed generalized Gaussian prior. 6. Training Constraint: The consensus \mathbf{C}^{\text{cons}}i, MAD, and weights \mathbf{W}{ij} remain fixed during training. This prevents the current rendering error from contaminating the supervision target through feedback. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computevtcconsensus(gaussians, images, cameraposes): """ Pre-training step to compute VTC consensus and weights. """ M = len(gaussians) N = len(images) reliablemask = np.zeros((M, N), dtype=bool) colors = np.zeros((M, N, 3)) for i in range(M): for j in range(N): # Standard differentiable rendering to get projected color and depth projectedcolor, depth, isvisible = rendergaussian(gaussians[i], images[j], cameraposes[j]) # Criterion 1: Image Bounds inbounds = iswithinimagebounds(projectedcolor) # Criterion 2: Foreground Membership isforeground = checkforegroundmembership(projectedcolor) # Criterion 3: Projected Visibility visible = isvisible and not isoccluded(projectedcolor, depth) # Criterion 4: Depth Consistency depthconsistent = checkdepthconsistency(depth) if inbounds and isforeground and visible and depthconsistent: reliablemask[i, j] = True colors[i, j] = projectedcolor else: reliablemask[i, j] = False colors[i, j] = 0.0 colorconsensus = np.zeros((M, 3)) mad = np.zeros((M, 3)) weights = np.zeros((M, N)) for i in range(M): reliablecolors = colors[i, reliablemask[i]] Ki = len(reliablecolors) if Ki > 0: colorconsensus[i] = np.median(reliablecolors, axis=0) deviations = np.abs(reliablecolors - colorconsensus[i]) mad[i] = np.median(deviations, axis=0) for j in range(N): if reliablemask[i, j]: diff = np.abs(colors[i, j] - colorconsensus[i]) # Weight determined by MAD and effective sample count weights[i, j] = np.exp(-np.sum(diff) / (1e-6 + np.sum(mad[i]) + 1.0 / Ki)) else: weights[i, j] = 0.0 else: colorconsensus[i] = 0.0 mad[i] = 0.0 weights[i,:] = 0.0 return reliablemask, colorconsensus, mad, weights def vtcloss(gaussians, images, cameraposes, colorconsensus, weights): """ Compute VTC loss during training. Only updates appearance parameters (SH coefficients). """ loss = 0.0 for i in range(len(gaussians)): for j in range(len(images)): if weights[i, j] > 0: currentcolor = rendergaussiancolor(gaussians[i], images[j], cameraposes[j]) diff = np.abs(currentcolor - colorconsensus[i]) loss += weights[i, j] np.sum(diff) return loss def rendergaussian(g, img, pose): return np.zeros(3), 0.0, True def iswithinimagebounds(color): return True def checkforegroundmembership(color): return True def isoccluded(color, depth): return False def checkdepthconsistency(depth): return True def rendergaussiancolor(g, img, pose): return np.zeros(3) MAD: Median Absolute Deviation, used to determine consensus weights. Default Configuration: Enables VTC, parameter routing, local-PCA statistics, and geometric anchoring. Directional Projection, Structure–Appearance Dual-Graph Regularizer, Residual Shrinkage: Used only in mechanism experiments, not in the default configuration. No Reliable Observations: If a Gaussian has no reliable observations (e.g., in heavily occluded or texture-less regions), the consensus is undefined. The pseudocode handles this by setting consensus to zero and weights to zero, effectively ignoring the Gaussian in the VTC loss. Precision: Use double precision for median and MAD calculations to avoid numerical instability in robust statistics. Boundaries: Ensure image bounds and foreground membership checks are robust to edge cases (e.g., Gaussians partially outside the image). Time Complexity: Pre-training filtering is O(M \cdot N), where M is the number of Gaussians and N is the number of views. Consensus construction is O(M \cdot N). Training loss computation is O(M \cdot N) but only affects appearance parameters. Memory Complexity: Stores reliable mask, consensus, MAD, and weights: O(M \cdot N). Strengths: Improves reconstruction in texture-degraded scenes by rejecting unreliable observations. Decouples geometry and appearance, preventing color errors from corrupting geometric parameters. Limitations: Requires pre-training filtering, which adds overhead. Fixed consensus may not adapt to dynamic scenes. When to Use: Texture-degraded scenes, scenes with occlusions, background mixing, or exposure differences. When Not to Use: High-quality, well-textured scenes where standard 3DGS performs well. VTC was proposed in "Visibility-Aware Texture Consensus and Local Structural Constraints for 3D Gaussian Reconstruction in Texture-Degraded Scenes". It addresses the identifiability of geometric supervision under texture degradation. The method is based on the hypothesis that weakly textured regions and foreground-background mixed boundaries reduce the identifiability of photometric gradients with respect to geometric parameters. name: Termination entropy criterion

It guides viewpoint selection by quantifying scene uncertainty, distinguishing itself from error-magnitude or density-based strategies by focusing on information saturation rather than reconstruction error. name: SAES (Sliding-Window-Averaged Early Stopping)
head: SAES trigger, Structure-Aware Early Stopping, structural saturation detection
body: SAES is an intrinsic training termination criterion for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents over-training and the accumulation of needle-like primitives caused by null-space ambiguity in sparse-view reconstruction. Unlike projection-based metrics such as PSNR, which can continue to improve artificially by exploiting geometric ambiguities, SAES monitors the internal dynamics of Gaussian population growth to detect structural saturation, allowing for early stopping without ground-truth volumetric metrics. SAES operates by monitoring the rate at which new Gaussian primitives are added during the densification phase. When this growth rate saturates, it indicates that the Gaussian field has converged structurally, and further densification yields diminishing returns or harmful artifacts. Input: The sequence of active Gaussian counts Nj at specific monitoring steps j. Output: A trigger iteration ts and final training iteration T{final}. The method relies on a sliding window buffer to store recent normalized growth rates. Buffer: A list or queue of capacity W storing values of \bar{g}j. State Variables: t: Current training iteration. Nt: Number of active Gaussian primitives at iteration t. t{last\monitor}: Iteration of the last monitoring step. \Delta = 100: Monitoring interval in iterations. The growth rate is calculated every \Delta iterations. W = 5: Sliding window size for smoothing the growth rate. \tau = 10^{-3}: Threshold for the sliding-window-averaged growth rate to trigger stopping. t{min} = 2,000: Minimum iteration count before SAES can trigger, preventing premature stopping during early structure formation. \gamma{cool} = 0.2: Learning-rate cooldown factor applied to position and scale learning rates (\eta{xyz}, \eta{scale}) upon triggering. 1. Initialization: Set t{last\monitor} = 0. Initialize an empty sliding window buffer B of capacity W. 2. Monitoring Loop: At each training iteration t: If t > t{last\monitor} + \Delta: Calculate the normalized population growth rate gj for the current monitoring step j. Append gj to buffer B. If |B| > W, remove the oldest element from B. Update t{last\monitor} = t. Compute the sliding-window-averaged growth rate \bar{g}j using the buffer contents. Check SAES trigger condition. 3. Trigger Condition: SAES triggers at iteration ts if the current iteration t > t{min} and the sliding-window-averaged growth rate \bar{g}j < \tau. 4. Post-Trigger Actions: Set ts = t. Set the final densification iteration T{densify} = ts. No further densification (splitting/cloning) occurs after ts. Set the final training iteration T{final} = 2 \times ts. Training continues until T{final} for refinement. Apply learning-rate cooldown: Multiply current learning rates by \gamma{cool}. Normalized Population Growth Rate (gj): The growth rate is normalized to account for the scale of the Gaussian population. Let Nj be the active Gaussian count at monitoring step j, and N{j-1} be the count at the previous monitoring step. The normalized growth rate is: gj = \frac{Nj - N{j-1}}{N{j-1}} Sliding-Window-Averaged Growth Rate (\bar{g}j): Let B = [b1, b2, \dots, bk] be the current buffer contents, where k \le W. The averaged rate is: \bar{g}j = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^{k} bi The trigger condition is \bar{g}j < \tau. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checksaestrigger(currentiter, activegaussiancount, lastmonitoriter, prevgaussiancount, buffer, params): """ Checks if SAES should trigger based on Gaussian population growth. Args: currentiter (int): Current training iteration t. activegaussiancount (int): Number of active Gaussians Nt. lastmonitoriter (int): Iteration of the last monitoring step. prevgaussiancount (int): Active Gaussian count at the previous monitoring step. buffer (list): List of recent normalized growth rates. params (dict): Contains delta, windowsize, threshold, tmin, cooldownfactor. Returns: bool: True if SAES triggers, False otherwise. int: Updated lastmonitoriter. int: Updated prevgaussiancount. list: Updated buffer. float: Sliding-window-averaged growth rate (or None if not monitored). """ delta = params['delta'] # 100 windowsize = params['windowsize'] # 5 threshold = params['threshold'] # 1e-3 tmin = params['tmin'] # 2000 if currentiter - lastmonitoriter < delta: return False, lastmonitoriter, prevgaussiancount, buffer, None if prevgaussiancount == 0: growthrate = 0.0 else: growthrate = (activegaussiancount - prevgaussiancount) / prevgaussiancount buffer.append(growthrate) if len(buffer) > windowsize: buffer.pop(0) lastmonitoriter = currentiter prevgaussiancount = activegaussiancount avggrowth = sum(buffer) / len(buffer) if currentiter > tmin and avggrowth < threshold: return True, lastmonitoriter, prevgaussiancount, buffer, avggrowth return False, lastmonitoriter, prevgaussiancount, buffer, avggrowth Division by Zero: If the initial Gaussian population N{j-1} is zero, the normalized growth rate is undefined. The implementation should handle this by setting the growth rate to 0.0 or skipping the check until a non-zero population exists. Premature Triggering: The parameter t{min} = 2,000 prevents triggering during the early phase where the population is still establishing basic structure. Ignoring this guard can cause premature stopping before structural convergence, leading to volumetric underfitting. Stability: The sliding window W=5 smooths out iteration-to-iteration noise in densification. The stopping behavior is stable around W=5, indicating the threshold is not narrowly tuned. Termination Entropy Criterion: A method that uses termination entropy to calculate information gain for active 3D reconstruction, serving as the broader criterion framework for SAES. While SAES specifically monitors population growth rate for early stopping, the Termination Entropy Criterion provides the theoretical basis for determining when information gain is sufficient. Use when integrating SAES into a pipeline that already utilizes entropy-based active reconstruction strategies. Link: Termination entropy criterion. Time Complexity: SAES adds negligible computational overhead per iteration, as it only requires counting active Gaussians and maintaining a small buffer of 5 floats. The primary benefit is a reduction in total training time. Memory Complexity: Minimal. Requires storing a buffer of size W=5 and a few scalar state variables. Measured Performance: On the FIPS dataset with 25 views, SAES triggers at approximately ts \approx 5,133 iterations (mean across objects), leading to T{final} \approx 10,267. This results in a ~64% reduction in wallclock training time compared to R2-Gaussian, which runs for a fixed 30,000 iterations. SAES is stable across different view counts (10, 20, 25 views) for the same object, with trigger iterations varying by less than 5% for complex objects like Walnut. Strengths: Prevents over-training and the formation of needle-like primitives that exploit null-space ambiguity. Does not require ground-truth volumetric metrics for evaluation. Significantly reduces training time without sacrificing reconstruction quality (PSNR/SSIM). Limitations: Relies on the assumption that population growth saturation correlates with structural convergence, which may not hold for all scene types or initialization strategies. Requires careful tuning of t{min} to avoid early stopping. When to use: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography or reconstruction where training time is a constraint and null-space ambiguity is a concern. When not to use: Dense-view settings where the Gaussian population may continue to refine structure significantly beyond initial saturation, or when ground-truth volumetric metrics are available and preferred. SAES was introduced in the context of diagnosing and controlling optimization drift in sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography, specifically as part of the LADES framework. The method addresses the Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence (PVFD) problem, where projection fidelity (PSNR) continues to improve while volumetric fidelity degrades due to the formation of anisotropic, needle-like primitives. By monitoring intrinsic Gaussian population dynamics rather than external projection metrics, SAES provides a robust, ground-truth-free stopping criterion. name: Pruning and Sparsification
head: Gaussian Pruning, Sparsification, Density Control
body: Pruning and Sparsification methods remove 3D Gaussian primitives that contribute negligibly to the final rendered image or whose removal would not significantly degrade reconstruction quality, thereby controlling memory usage and computational load during training. Unlike sibling methods that rely on static thresholds or uncertainty metrics, this family encompasses strategies that actively manage the density and opacity distribution, including recycling low-opacity components into high-opacity ones to prevent unbounded growth without altering the rendered image. It sets itself apart from Adaptive Density Control by focusing specifically on the removal phase of the feedback loop, and from Significance-Aware Pruning by often employing simpler opacity-based heuristics rather than accumulated rendering weights for initial candidate selection. All methods in this family operate on the set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\} inherited from Densification Strategy. The core mechanism involves evaluating a metric per Gaussian to determine if it contributes negligibly to the final rendered image or if its removal would not significantly degrade reconstruction quality. Common metrics include: 1. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the alpha-compositing process. 2. Gradient Magnitude: High accumulated positional gradients indicate a Gaussian is struggling to minimize loss, suggesting it may be redundant or poorly placed, though this is more commonly used for densification [Parent]. 3. Significance/Weight: The accumulated alpha blending coefficient wk across all training views, representing the Gaussian's actual contribution to the pixel colors. 4. Uncertainty/Sensitivity: A score derived from the Fisher Information matrix or Hessian of the reconstruction error, indicating how sensitive the output is to changes in the Gaussian's parameters. Pruning is typically executed either periodically during training (e.g., every 100–1000 iterations) or as a final post-processing step. When primitives are removed, buffer compaction or flag-based marking is required to maintain contiguous memory access for the rasterizer [Parent]. Adaptive Density Control is a dynamic optimization strategy used in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to adjust the number and spatial distribution of Gaussian primitives during training. It solves the problem of under-population (missing geometry) and over-population (coarse approximations or floaters) by automatically adding, cloning, splitting, or removing Gaussians based on gradient magnitude, scale, and opacity. Unlike static initialization methods, ADC transitions the scene from a sparse initial set to a denser, more accurate representation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Pruning and Opacity Management by integrating densification (growth) with pruning in a unified feedback loop, and from Significance-Aware Pruning by relying primarily on positional gradients rather than accumulated rendering weights for densification decisions. Pruning and Opacity Management methods remove or modify 3D Gaussian primitives that contribute negligibly to the final rendered image or whose removal would not significantly degrade reconstruction quality, thereby controlling memory usage and computational load during training. Unlike sibling methods that rely on static thresholds or uncertainty metrics, this family encompasses strategies that actively manage the density and opacity distribution, including recycling low-opacity components into high-opacity ones to prevent unbounded growth without altering the rendered image. Significance-Aware Pruning is a method for removing redundant 3D Gaussian primitives during the training of Gaussian Splatting models by evaluating their actual contribution to the rendered image rather than just their geometric size or opacity. It solves the problem where standard opacity or size pruning fails to distinguish between a Gaussian that is physically large but visually insignificant (e.g., transparent background) and one that is small but critical for reconstructing fine details. Unlike Pruning and Opacity Management, which relies primarily on opacity thresholds, this method incorporates the accumulated alpha blending coefficients to identify and remove Gaussians that contribute negligibly to the final pixel colors, thereby improving scene compactness without degrading reconstruction quality. Principled Uncertainty Pruning is a post-hoc method for compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) models by removing Gaussians with high uncertainty regarding their contribution to the reconstruction error. Unlike heuristic methods that rely on opacity or visibility, PUP computes a sensitivity score based on the Fisher Information matrix of the L2 reconstruction loss, specifically approximating the Hessian with respect to spatial parameters. It is distinguished by its multi-round prune-refine pipeline, which allows for aggressive pruning (up to 90%) while maintaining higher visual fidelity and rendering speeds than single-round approaches or competing methods like LightGaussian. TangoGS is a density control method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that automatically scales the number of Gaussian primitives to match the complexity of the input capture without per-scene tuning. It solves the problem of fixed hyperparameters in standard Gaussian Splatting by combining a capture-derived "learning allowance" (model sizing) with training-based quality feedback (adaptation). Unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed thresholds or per-capture calibration, TangoGS uses a shared configuration across diverse scene scales, achieving comparable reconstruction quality with significantly fewer Gaussians. Depth-Based Gaussian Pruning is a strategy that varies the pruning threshold based on the relative depth (z-axis value) of 3D Gaussians to preserve points at the far plane in forward-facing scenes. It distinguishes itself from standard uniform pruning by applying a lower threshold (more aggressive pruning) to near-plane Gaussians and a higher threshold (more conservative pruning) to far-plane Gaussians, thereby compensating for the sparsity of primitives at the scene's depth extremes. Adaptive Pruning is a sparsification technique used in triangle-based volume rendering to eliminate "floaters" and reduce overfitting by removing primitives that contribute negligibly to the final image. It distinguishes itself from opacity-only methods by evaluating the actual volume rendering blending weight (T \cdot o) accumulated across training views, ensuring that only primitives with significant visual impact are retained. Proposes an optimizing-sparsifying loop that interleaves standard training with a sparsification operator. Removes redundant primitives while boosting the influence of the remaining collection. A process to sparsify the generated tree structure to avoid parent-child settings where the parent's size is only marginally larger than the children's, ensuring proper optimization. Mark all leaf nodes (output of 3DGS optimization) as relevant. Find the union of cuts in the tree over all training views for the minimum target granularity \tau{min} = 3 pixels. Find the bottom-most nodes in this union cut. These are the highest-detail relevant nodes. Remove all nodes between them and already marked nodes. Raise the target granularity by 2x and repeat the process until \tau{max} (half the image's resolution) is reached. If a node has K children, the blended weight \alpha' generalizes to: \alpha' = \frac{1}{1 - (1 - \alphap) \frac{1}{K}}. Minimum target granularity \tau{min}: Set to 3 pixels, corresponding to the minimum extent of a primitive 3DGS primitive due to low-pass filtering. Execute strategy if strategyname is 'simple' or 'mrnf', step > 0, and step % 200 == 0. Prune dead splats using the same logic as adaptive pruning: alive = torch.sigmoid(splats['opacities'].data) > prunethreshold. If target splat count target > 0, current count curn < target, and step < iterations 3 // 4, densify. Calculate number of splats to add: nadd = min(target - curn, curn). Compute selection probabilities based on scale magnitude: scalemag = torch.exp(splats['scales'].data).max(dim=-1).values and probs = scalemag / scalemag.sum(). Select nadd indices using multinomial sampling: idxs = torch.multinomial(probs, nadd, replacement=True). For 'means', add noise scaled by half the max scale magnitude: noise = torch.randnlike(newdata), normalized, then newdata = newdata + noise offsetscale[:, None] 0.5. For 'opacities', subtract 0.5 from the new splats. For 'scales', subtract 0.3 from the new splats. Concatenate new data to existing splats and duplicate normals. If target > 0, curn > target, and step >= iterations 3 // 4, trim splats. Remove splats with lowest opacity:, removeidx = torch.topk(opa, nremove, largest=False). Evaluate pixel coverage for each triangle across the training views. Remove triangles with low pixel coverage. Repeat pruning until the desired primitive budget (target face count) is met. Pruning frequency: Performed every 100 iterations. The concept of pruning and sparsification in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a necessary counterpart to densification strategies to prevent unbounded growth of the Gaussian population. Early implementations relied on simple opacity thresholds to remove "floaters" and background noise. Subsequent research introduced more sophisticated metrics, such as significance-aware pruning based on accumulated rendering weights [9676-significance-aware-pruning.md] and principled uncertainty pruning using Fisher Information matrices [9680-principled-uncertainty-pruning.md]. Methods like TangoGS [10180-tangogs.md] and Hierarchy Compaction further refined these techniques to handle large-scale scenes and hierarchical representations efficiently. The field continues to evolve with hybrid approaches like GaussianSPA and depth-aware pruning [12338-depth-based-gaussian-pruning.md] to address specific artifacts and computational bottlenecks. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p-mb2TzVJZk, fetched 2026-10-31 SpaceCollectors/dust3r-3dgs, https://github.com/SpaceCollectors/dust3r-3dgs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DiffSoup: Direct Differentiable Rasterization of Triangle Soup for Extreme Radiance Field Simplification, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.27151, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Density Control
head: 3DGS Adaptive Density Control, 3D Gaussian Splatting Adaptive Density Control (ADC), 3DGS ADC, 3DGS density control
body: Adaptive Density Control (ADC) is a dynamic optimization strategy used in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to adjust the number and spatial distribution of Gaussian primitives during training. It solves the problem of under-population (missing geometry) and over-population (coarse approximations or floaters) by automatically adding, cloning, splitting, or removing Gaussians based on gradient magnitude, scale, and opacity. Unlike static initialization methods, ADC transitions the scene from a sparse initial set to a denser, more accurate representation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Pruning and Opacity Management by integrating densification (growth) with pruning in a unified feedback loop, and from Significance-Aware Pruning by relying primarily on positional gradients rather than accumulated rendering weights for densification decisions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gi has mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai (parameterized by quaternion qi and scale si), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients. A set of training views \Pi. Output: An updated set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with modified counts, positions, scales, and opacities. Data Structures: Gradient Buffer: Tracks the magnitude of the positional gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mui} for each Gaussian across all rendered views. Flag Buffers: Used for GPU-side compaction. Includes densifysplitflag, densifydupflag, densifysplitprefix, densifydupflag, densifykeepflag, and densifykeepprefix of size bufcapacity. Scratch Buffers: densifycompactscratch (size bufcapacity featuresReststride) and densifyrandomsamples (size bufcapacity x 3) for temporary storage during densification. Parameters: Densification Interval: Typically every 100 iterations or every 1000 steps until 15k iterations. Warm-up Period: Densification is skipped for the first N{warmup} iterations (e.g., 600 or 100). Gradient Threshold (T{grad} or \tau{pos}): Average view-space positional gradient magnitude threshold. Default values range from 2 \times 10^{-4} to 0.0002. Opacity Threshold (\alpha{min} or \epsilon\alpha): Gaussians with opacity below this value are pruned. Default is 0.05 or a small \epsilon. Scale Thresholds: Used to distinguish between cloning and splitting. Often defined relative to scene extent e{scene} or a fixed screen-space size. Max Gaussians: Optional cap (e.g., 300,000) to prevent out-of-memory errors. Numbered Steps: 1. Gradient Tracking: For each Gaussian gk, track the magnitude of the positional gradient \frac{\partial Lv}{\partial \muk} for every training view v during the collection period. Compute the average gradient magnitude \tauk: \tauk = \frac{1}{N{\text{views}}} \sum{v=1}^{N{\text{views}}} \left\| \frac{\partial L(Iv, I'v)}{\partial \muv^v} \right\|2 where L is the image loss. Note: Some variants use world-space gradients instead of view-space to provide more accurate feedback for 3D volume density. 2. Densification Decision: If the current iteration is within the densification window (after warm-up, before stopSplitAt) and \tauk \ge T{grad}, the Gaussian is a candidate for densification. 3. Clone or Split: Clone: If the Gaussian is small (under-reconstructed region), create a copy. One copy remains stationary; the other inherits the gradient direction and moves along it. The new Gaussian retains the original scale and opacity. Split: If the Gaussian is large (over-reconstructed region), replace it with N{children} (default 2) child Gaussians. Scale: Reduce scale by a factor. Common factors are 0.8 or dividing by \phi = 1.6. The formula for child scale is often s{child} = s{parent} \cdot \frac{5}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N{children}}}. Intensity/Opacity: Halve the intensity (or adjust opacity) to conserve total density. Position: Sample positions from the parent Gaussian's Probability Density Function (PDF). 4. Pruning: Periodically (e.g., after densification), remove Gaussians that contribute negligibly. Opacity Pruning: If \alphak < \alpha{min}, prune gk. Size Pruning: Optionally prune Gaussians that are excessively large in world space or screen space. 5. Opacity Reset (Optional): Every N{reset} iterations (e.g., 3000), reset the opacity of all Gaussians toward a low value (e.g., logit of 0.25, approx -1.386). This allows "useful" Gaussians to re-acquire opacity via gradients while "vestigial" ones fail to recover and are pruned in the next pass. 6. Compaction: After adding/removing Gaussians, compact the GPU buffers to maintain contiguous memory access for the rasterizer [Parent]. This involves using the flag buffers to identify kept Gaussians and moving them to the front of the array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivedensitycontrol(Gaussians G, Iteration step, Params P): # 1. Check if densification is active if step < P.warmuplength or step > P.stopsplitat: return G if step % P.densifyinterval != 0: return G # 2. Track gradients (assumed to be done during forward/backward pass) # tauk is the average positional gradient magnitude for Gaussian k splitflags = [] cloneflags = [] pruneflags = [] for k in range(len(G)): g = G[k] tauk = g.gradientmagnitude # Densification if tauk >= P.tgrad: # Determine if split or clone based on scale # P.pdense is a fraction of scene extent, escene is scene extent if g.maxscale > P.pdense P.escene: splitflags.append(k) else: cloneflags.append(k) # Pruning if g.opacity < P.alphamin: pruneflags.append(k) # 3. Execute Operations # Note: In practice, these are executed on GPU using atomic operations or prefix sums # to handle buffer resizing dynamically. newgaussians = [] for k in range(len(G)): if k in pruneflags: continue # Skip pruned Gaussians g = G[k] newgaussians.append(g) if k in cloneflags: # Clone: Create a copy clone = copy(g) # Move clone along gradient direction clone.mean = g.mean + P.gradientdirection g.scale newgaussians.append(clone) elif k in splitflags: # Split: Replace with children # Remove original g newgaussians.pop() # Remove the original g from the list being built # Create Nchildren Nchildren = 2 scalefactor = 1.6 # phi for i in range(Nchildren): child = copy(g) child.scale = g.scale / scalefactor # Halve intensity/opacity child.opacity = g.opacity / 2 # Sample position from parent PDF child.mean = samplefromgaussianpdf(g) newgaussians.append(child) # 4. Opacity Reset (if applicable) if step % P.opacityresetinterval == 0: for g in newgaussians: g.opacity = resetopacity(g.opacity, P.opacityresetclip) # 5. Compaction # Compact newgaussians into contiguous buffer return compact(newgaussians) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Details: Regions with high-frequency patterns (e.g., grass) may have few large Gaussians with low accumulated positional gradients, failing to trigger densification and causing underfitting. Opacity Bias in Cloning: Standard cloning keeps the same opacity for the cloned Gaussian, which biases alpha-compositing logic and increases overall opacity in the cloned region. This can be corrected by setting the new opacity \hat{\alpha} = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \alpha}. Unbounded Growth: ADC lacks explicit control over the maximum number of Gaussians, risking out-of-memory errors. Memory Fragmentation: The growing set of Gaussians causes memory fragmentation, slowing down optimization in later iterations. Uses 2D/3D diffusion priors to initialize Gaussians, differing from standard ADC's SfM initialization. Reformulates densification as SGLD, adding noise to positions and re-spawning based on opacity, reducing reliance on initial point clouds. Replaces deterministic pruning with stochastic sampling to preserve geometric structure. Prevents newly created Gaussians from splitting/cloning immediately, damping cascading growth. Advanced criteria beyond gradient magnitude, including multi-view density, complexity, and frequency-aware spawning. Strategies to ensure child densities approximate parent density, preventing clustering and instability. Removes structural splitting and training calls, keeping standard densification/pruning. Uses log-ratio soft regularization parameters: lambdaaniso (0.001) and anisoratiomax (5). Enforces a strict upper bound on component count. Densification is disabled if count >= max, and re-enabled only if pruning reduces the count below the cap. Integrates corrected scene extent, exponential ascending gradient threshold, and significance-aware pruning. Splits if max(scale) > Pdense e'scene, else clones. Prunes if opacity < omin AND significance is in bottom Nprune. Corrects opacity bias in cloning by setting new opacity \hat{\alpha} = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \alpha}. Does not apply to splits. Uses complexity-guided densification during training and an importance score for LoD pruning at inference. Retains large primitives in simple regions. Drops cloning entirely. Splits large Gaussians and applies geometric splitting to small ones, avoiding opacity bias and floater clusters. Uses structural similarity loss for individual Gaussians to decide splitting, replacing accumulated positional gradient. Time Complexity: Densification and pruning are performed periodically (e.g., every 100-1000 iterations), not every step. The cost is proportional to the number of Gaussians N and the number of training views sampled. Memory Complexity: Memory usage grows with the number of Gaussians. Without caps, it can lead to OOM errors. Buffer compaction is required to manage fragmentation. Performance: On the Average-30K dataset, full ADC achieves PSNR 26.05. Removing splitting drops it to 23.90, and removing cloning drops it to 25.91, indicating splitting is crucial for background quality while cloning is vital for thin structures. Strengths: Automatically adapts to scene complexity; handles under- and over-reconstruction; enables real-time rendering by optimizing primitive count. Limitations: Can overfit in simple regions; underfit in high-frequency regions (grass); sensitive to hyperparameters (thresholds); prone to memory fragmentation. When to Use: Standard 3DGS training where scene complexity varies. When Not to Use: Scenes with very high-frequency details that gradient-based methods miss (consider MCMC Densification or Volume Based Densification); resource-constrained environments requiring strict memory caps (consider Max-Component ADC). Adaptive Density Control was introduced by Kerbl et al. in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper. It was designed to address the limitations of sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds, which are insufficient to represent complex geometry. The method has since been refined in various works to address issues like opacity bias, unbounded growth, and high-frequency detail loss. name: GaussianDreamer
body: GaussianDreamer is a training procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that combines 2D and 3D diffusion model priors to optimize scene representations from text or image prompts. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by using a generative model (Shap-E) to initialize the point cloud instead of Structure from Motion (SfM), and by optimizing Gaussian parameters via 2D Score Distillation Sampling (SDS). Inputs and outputs: Input: A text or image prompt, a pre-trained 2D diffusion model, and a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation initialized from a generative point cloud. Output: An optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation with updated positions, scales, colors, opacities, and rotations. Data structures: 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives: Each primitive i is defined by position \mathbf{\mu}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i (parameterized by scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{R}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. Diffusion Model: A 2D text-to-image or image-to-image model (e.g., Stable Diffusion) used for Score Distillation Sampling (SDS). Numbered steps: 1. Initialization: Use Shap-E to generate an initial point cloud, which serves as the initial geometry for the 3DGS optimization. 2. Densification: Because the generated initial point cloud is relatively sparse, apply noisy point growth and color perturbation to densify it. 3. Optimization Loop: Optimize the 3DGS parameters using 2D SDS. Sample a random camera pose. Render the current 3DGS representation to obtain a 2D image. Compute the SDS gradient, which approximates the gradient of the diffusion model's log-likelihood with respect to the rendered image pixels. Back-propagate the gradient through the differentiable renderer to update the Gaussian parameters (positions, scales, colors, opacities). 4. Reconstruction Loss: Optionally, incorporate an RGB reconstruction loss if ground-truth images are available, alongside the diffusion guidance. Formulas: The SDS loss is computed as: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} \left[ w(t) \cdot \mathbb{E}{zt \sim pt(z|x)} \left[ \nabla{zt} \log p\theta(zt | x) \cdot \frac{\partial zt}{\partial \mathbf{\theta}{GS}} \right] \right] where zt is the noisy image at timestep t, p\theta is the diffusion model, w(t) is a timestep weighting function, and \mathbf{\theta}{GS} are the Gaussian parameters. The total loss combines the SDS guidance and RGB reconstruction loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{SDS} where \lambda is a weighting factor balancing the two terms. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. SDS weighting \lambda: Not given in the sources. Number of optimization steps: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: The generated initial point cloud is relatively sparse, requiring densification to prevent poor initialization. The Janus problem (multi-face artifact) may still exist during optimization if views are sampled one by one, even if 3D SDS loss is introduced. Per-scene fitting incurs heavy computational cost, typically taking minutes to hours per prompt. The method is prone to over-smoothing or texture oversaturation unless additional regularizers, multi-view diffusion priors, or geometry-aware constraints are applied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def render3dgs(gaussians, camera): # Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D, sorts by depth, and alpha-blends to produce an RGB image return renderedimage def computesdsgradient(renderedimage, prompt, diffusionmodel, timestep): # Adds noise to renderedimage, predicts noise with diffusion model, # and computes gradient w.r.t. renderedimage pixels grad = computesdsgrad(renderedimage, prompt, diffusionmodel, timestep) return grad def updategaussians(gaussians, gradient, learningrate): # Applies gradient descent to positions, scales, opacities, and SH coefficients gaussians.positions -= learningrate gradient.positions gaussians.scales -= learningrate gradient.scales gaussians.opacities -= learningrate gradient.opacities gaussians.colors -= learningrate gradient.colors return gaussians gaussians = shapegeneratepointcloud(prompt) gaussians = noisypointgrowth(gaussians) gaussians = colorperturbation(gaussians) for step in range(numsteps): camera = samplerandomcamera() renderedimage = render3dgs(gaussians, camera) sdsgradient = computesdsgradient(renderedimage, prompt, diffusionmodel, timestep=step) gaussians = updategaussians(gaussians, sdsgradient, learningrate) if groundtruthimage is not None: rgbloss = computergbloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) rgbgradient = computegradient(rgbloss, gaussians) gaussians = updategaussians(gaussians, rgbgradient, learningrate) This method is a training procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a fine-tuned Diffusion Model to generate guidance images from randomly sampled "pseudo-views," regularizing the Gaussian model parameters to improve unseen view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a diffusion-based prior loss computed on rendered views that do not correspond to ground-truth images, thereby preventing the model from getting stuck in local minima and enhancing the scene's comprehensive observation. Unlike methods relying on Structure from Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization, this approach exclusively uses LiDAR data to avoid prior bias. A generation paradigm where a powerful 2D or multi-view diffusion model is queried from many camera poses, and its gradients are back-propagated through the differentiable GS renderer to update Gaussian parameters. Early pipelines such as DreamGaussian and GaussianDreamer treat each scene independently and directly optimize positions, scales, colors, and opacities to match diffusion-model guidance while respecting RGB reconstruction losses. Time Complexity: Heavy computational cost, taking minutes to hours per prompt. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Yields high-fidelity geometry and appearance for object- and scene-level content. Can be naturally extended to dynamic or 4D generation with temporal regularization. Limitations: Prone to Janus ambiguity, over-smoothing, or texture oversaturation unless additional regularizers, multi-view diffusion priors, or geometry-aware constraints are applied. The initial point cloud is sparse, requiring densification steps. GaussianDreamer was introduced as an early text- and image-to-3D pipeline that combines the priors of 2D and 3D diffusion models. It utilizes Shap-E to generate the initial point cloud and optimizes 3DGS using 2D SDS. The method is part of the broader category of optimization-based generation methods in GS-based generation. name: Diffusion Prior Guidance for Pseudo Views
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Diffusion Prior Regularization, Pseudo-view Regularization, SGD Training
body: This method is a training procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a fine-tuned Diffusion Model to generate guidance images from randomly sampled pseudo-views, regularizing the Gaussian model parameters to improve unseen view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing a diffusion-based prior loss computed on rendered views that do not correspond to ground-truth images, thereby preventing the model from getting stuck in local minima and enhancing the scene's comprehensive observation. Unlike methods relying on Structure from Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization, this approach exclusively uses LiDAR data to avoid prior bias. Inputs: LiDAR point clouds (voxelized-downsampled). Monocular training images and their poses. A fine-tuned Diffusion Model (specifically a ControlNet variant or image-to-image diffusion model). A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) associated with the Diffusion Model for latent space encoding and decoding. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters \Phi (means \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color c). The 3D Gaussian Splatting representation consists of a set of Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is parameterized by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (typically parameterized via a rotation matrix and scaling vector). Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics coefficients for view-dependent RGB color ci. The total parameter set is denoted as \Phi = \bigcup \{\Phio, \Phip\}, where \Phio are parameters visible to the current training view vo, and \Phip are parameters visible to the pseudo-views vp. Training Iterations: 50,000. Learning Rate: Decays from 1.6 \times 10^{-4} to 1.6 \times 10^{-6}. Pseudo-view Sampling Interval (k): Every 10 iterations. Number of Pseudo Views (M): 4. Warm-up Period: 500 iterations without pseudo-view sampling. Maximum Noise Level (t{max}): 10. Minimum Noise Level (t{min}): Not given in the sources. Strength Hyper-parameter Range (s): s{min} = 0.2. s{max} starts at 0.6 and linearly decreases to 0.4 over the training process. Noise Level Formula: t = s \times t{max}, where s is sampled uniformly from [s{min}, s{max}] for each pseudo view. Pseudo-view Orientation Rotation (\delta): The orientation is rotated from training views within range [-\delta, \delta] along the z-axis (yaw angle). 1. Initialization: Voxelize and downsample the LiDAR point clouds with a voxel size of 0.5. Initialize the 3D Gaussian Splatting model using the voxelized LiDAR point clouds. Do not use SfM (Structure from Motion) point clouds for initialization. 2. Training Loop (for iteration i = 1 to 50,000): 3. Warm-up Check: If i \le 500, skip pseudo-view sampling. Proceed only to Step 4. 4. Reconstruction Loss Computation (Standard 3DGS): Sample a training view vo. Render the view using differentiable rasterization/splatting to obtain the rendered image Io and rendered depth map \tilde{D}o. Obtain the ground-truth image I{gt} and the completed dense depth map Do (from LiDAR projection) for vo. Compute the reconstruction loss L{recon}: L{recon}(\Phio) = \mathbb{E}{vo} \left[ \| Io - I{gt} \|1 + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM}(Io, I{gt}) + \lambda{depth} \| Do - \tilde{D}o \|1 \right] where \Phio are the Gaussian parameters visible to vo. 5. Pseudo-View Sampling (if i > 500 and i \pmod k == 0): Randomly sample M pseudo views vp = \{vp^j\}{j=0}^{M-1}. Position: Interpolate the position of each pseudo view between the current training view vo and its adjacent views. Orientation: Rotate the orientation of each pseudo view from the training view's orientation within the range [-\delta, \delta] along the z-axis (yaw angle). 6. Pseudo-View Rendering: Render the pseudo views using differentiable splatting with parameters \Phi to obtain rendered pseudo-view images \tilde{I}p(\Phi, vp) \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3 \times H \times W} and depth maps \tilde{D}p. Let \Phip be the union of Gaussian parameters visible to any of the pseudo views vp. 7. Diffusion Guidance Generation: For each rendered pseudo-view image \tilde{I}p^j: Encode \tilde{I}p^j into a latent feature map z using the VAE Encoder. Sample a strength value s uniformly from [s{min}, s{max}]. Calculate the noise level t = s \times t{max}. Add noise to the latent feature map z at level t to obtain the noisy latent zt. Denoise zt using the fine-tuned Diffusion Model from level t down to t{min}. Decode the denoised latent to obtain the guidance image Ig^j. 8. Pseudo Loss Computation: Compute the pseudo loss L{pseudo} for the set of pseudo views: L{pseudo}(\Phip) = \mathbb{E}{vp} \left[ \| Ig - \tilde{I}p \|1 + \lambda{p-lpips} L{lpips}(Ig, \tilde{I}p) + \lambda{p-depth} \| Dp - \tilde{D}p \|1 \right] where Ig and Dp are the guidance images and corresponding target depth maps for the pseudo views, and \tilde{I}p, \tilde{D}p are the rendered images and depths. 9. Total Loss and Optimization: Compute the total loss: L(\Phi) = L{recon}(\Phio) + \lambda{pseudo} L{pseudo}(\Phip) where \Phi = \text{Union}\{\Phio, \Phip\}. Perform gradient descent to update \Phi. Initialization # Voxelize and downsample LiDAR points with voxel size 0.5 voxelizedpoints = voxelizedownsample(lidarpoints, voxelsize) # Initialize 3D Gaussian Splatting model with voxelized points # Do NOT use SfM points gaussians = initialize3dgsfrompoints(voxelizedpoints) # Learning rate schedule parameters lrstart = 1.6e-4 lrend = 1.6e-6 # Minimum noise level for denoising tmin = 0 # 2. Training Loop for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Update learning rate (linear decay) currentlr = lrstart - (lrstart - lrend) (iteration / numiterations) # Sample a training view vo, Igto, Dgto = sampletrainingview(trainingimages, trainingposes) # Render training view Io, Dtildeo = render3dgs(gaussians, vo) # Compute Reconstruction Loss lossrecon = computel1(Io, Igto) + \ lambdassim computessim(Io, Igto) + \ lambdadepth computel1(Dgto, Dtildeo) # Initialize total loss totalloss = lossrecon # Pseudo-view regularization (after warm-up) if iteration > 500 and iteration % k == 0: # Sample M pseudo views pseudoviews = samplepseudoviews(vo, trainingposes, M) # Render pseudo views Itildep, Dtildep = render3dgsbatch(gaussians, pseudoviews) # Generate guidance images using Diffusion Model Iglist = [] for i in range(M): # Encode to latent z = vaeencoder(Itildep[i]) # Sample strength s smaxcurrent = smaxinit - (smaxinit - smaxfinal) (iteration / numiterations) s = random.uniform(smin, smaxcurrent) # Compute noise level t t = s tmax # Add noise to latent znoisy = addnoise(z, t) # Denoise using diffusion model from t to tmin zdenoised = denoise(znoisy, tstart=t, tend=tmin, model=diffusionmodel) # Decode to image Ig = vaedecoder(zdenoised) Iglist.append(Ig) Ig = stacktensors(Iglist) # Compute Pseudo Loss losspseudo = computel1(Ig, Itildep) + \ lambdaplpips computelpips(Ig, Itildep) + \ lambdapdepth computel1(Dp, Dtildep) totalloss = lossrecon + lambdapseudo losspseudo # Backpropagate and update Gaussians totalloss.backward() for param in gaussians: param -= currentlr param.grad for param in gaussians: param.grad = None def voxelizedownsample(points, voxelsize): """Downsample points by keeping one point per voxel grid cell.""" voxelized = {} for p in points: key = (math.floor(p[0]/voxelsize), math.floor(p[1]/voxelsize), math.floor(p[2]/voxelsize)) if key not in voxelized: voxelized[key] = p return list(voxelized.values()) def initialize3dgsfrompoints(points): """Initialize Gaussian parameters from point cloud.""" gaussians = [] for p in points: gaussians.append({'mu': p, 'Sigma': identitymatrix(3), 'alpha': 1.0, 'c': zeros(3)}) return gaussians def sampletrainingview(images, poses): """Randomly select a training view and its ground truth.""" idx = random.randint(0, len(images) - 1) return poses[idx], images[idx], images[idx] # Depth placeholder for brevity def render3dgs(gaussians, view): """Differentiable rasterization of Gaussians for a view.""" # Standard 3DGS splatting implementation return renderimage, renderdepth def samplepseudoviews(currentview, poses, M): """Sample M pseudo views interpolated between current and adjacent views.""" pseudoviews = [] for in range(M): # Interpolate position and rotate yaw by [-delta, delta] pseudoviews.append(currentview) return pseudoviews def render3dgsbatch(gaussians, views): """Render multiple views simultaneously.""" images = [] depths = [] for v in views: img, dep = render3dgs(gaussians, v) images.append(img) depths.append(dep) return stacktensors(images), stacktensors(depths) def computel1(a, b): return sum(abs(a[i] - b[i]) for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) def computessim(a, b): return 1.0 - structuralsimilarity(a, b) # Standard SSIM computation def computelpips(a, b): return perceptualloss(a, b) # Standard LPIPS computation def addnoise(latent, t): return latent + random.gauss(0, 1) t def denoise(latent, tstart, tend, model): """Iteratively denoise from tstart to tend using the diffusion model.""" current = latent for t in range(tstart, tend, -1): current = model.predictnoise(current, t) current = current - (t - tend) current # Simplified Euler step return current def stacktensors(tensorlist): return [sum(t) for t in zip(tensorlist)] def identitymatrix(n): return [[1 if i==j else 0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] def zeros(n): return [0.0] n def structuralsimilarity(a, b): return 1.0 # Placeholder for standard SSIM def perceptualloss(a, b): return 0.0 # Placeholder for standard LPIPS Initialization Bias: Using SfM point clouds is explicitly avoided to prevent prior bias from SfM reconstruction errors or assumptions. Only LiDAR data should be used. Noise Level Control: The strength parameter s controls the deviation from the 3DGS rendering. A small s preserves 3DGS-rendered noise/details, while a large s produces cleaner images but loses details. The decreasing schedule for s{max} ensures that early in training (when 3DGS quality is low), the model relies more on the diffusion prior, and later, it relies more on the 3DGS renderings to preserve details. Pseudo-View Overlap: Pseudo-views are sampled close to training views, leading to considerable overlap in the corresponding Gaussian models. This allows simultaneous multi-view learning and prevents local minima. Time Complexity: The method adds a diffusion model inference step for every k iterations (every 10 iterations in the cited implementation) for M pseudo views (4 views). This significantly increases the per-iteration cost compared to standard 3DGS, which only performs rasterization and loss computation. The diffusion model inference (encoding, noise addition, denoising, decoding) is computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3DGS parameters, the diffusion model weights, and the VAE weights. The latent space operations are memory-efficient compared to pixel-space operations, but the batch processing of pseudo views adds temporary memory overhead. Evaluated on KITTI and KITTI-360 datasets. The method is designed for street view synthesis where LiDAR data is available but SfM might be unreliable or biased. The ablation study on s shows that smaller s preserves details, while larger s cleans up noise but loses detail. The schedule s{max} \in [0.6, 0.4] balances this trade-off. Strengths: Improves unseen view synthesis by regularizing with a diffusion prior. Prevents local minima by leveraging overlapping pseudo-views. Does not rely on SfM point clouds, making it suitable for scenarios with only LiDAR and monocular images. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to diffusion model inference. Requires a fine-tuned diffusion model, which adds a pre-training step (ControlNet training). The quality of the guidance depends on the fine-tuning of the diffusion model. Use when LiDAR data is available but SfM point clouds are not desired or reliable. Use when high-quality novel view synthesis is required, especially for views not seen during training. Use when the scene has complex textures or structures that benefit from diffusion-based regularization. Use standard 3DGS if computational resources are limited and high-quality novel views are not critical. Use if SfM point clouds are available and accurate, as they provide a strong geometric prior without the need for diffusion guidance. The method is described in the paper "SGD: Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior". It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework. The diffusion model is fine-tuned using a ControlNet architecture. The method was evaluated on autonomous driving datasets (KITTI, KITTI-360). The approach was developed to address the limitations of standard 3DGS in synthesizing unseen views, particularly in autonomous driving scenarios where LiDAR data is available but SfM might be insufficient or biased. The authors ablated the impact of the diffusion prior strength s, showing that a decreasing schedule for s{max} yields better results than a fixed value. name: MCMC Densification
head: Markov Chain Monte Carlo, SGLD Densification, Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamic (SGLD) Densification
body: MCMC Densification is a Bayesian optimization strategy that reformulates Gaussian Splatting densification as a Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamic (SGLD) update rule. Unlike standard adaptive density control which clones and splits individual Gaussians based on gradient magnitude, MCMC densification samples a fixed number of Gaussians from a learned probability distribution. It distinguishes itself by adding a noise term to the position of the Gaussians to incorporate exploration during training, while re-spawning Gaussians that drop below an opacity threshold randomly at Gaussians with high opacity. This approach reduces reliance on the initial point cloud, allows for specifying the number of Gaussians prior to optimization, and improves rendering quality in regions with few initial primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each defined by mean position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients. The current camera views \mathcal{I} and the reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{\text{total}}. Output: Updated set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with modified parameters and potentially re-localized centers. Data Structures: The Gaussian set \mathcal{G} is stored as a list or array of objects. Each Gaussian gi \in \mathcal{G} contains: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center location. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (often parameterized via rotation R and scale S). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Other attributes (color, SH coefficients) as required by the renderer. Parameters: \lambda{\text{lr}}: Learning rate hyperparameter for the gradient descent step. \lambda{\text{noise}}: Noise scale hyperparameter applied to the center locations \mu of Gaussians. \epsilon: Noise term drawn from a standard normal distribution. Opacity threshold: A value below which a Gaussian is considered for re-spawning. Steps: 1. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the total loss with respect to the Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G} using stochastic gradient descent over a batch of images \mathcal{I}. \nabla{\mathcal{G}} \mathbf{E}{\mathcal{I}} [\mathcal{L}{\text{total}} (\mathcal{G}; \mathcal{I})] 2. SGLD Update: Update the Gaussian parameters by combining the gradient descent step with a noise term: \mathcal{G} \leftarrow \mathcal{G} - \lambda{\text{lr}} \cdot \nabla{\mathcal{G}} \mathbf{E}{\mathcal{I}} [\mathcal{L}{\text{total}} (\mathcal{G}; \mathcal{I})] + \lambda{\text{noise}} \cdot \epsilon The noise \epsilon is applied specifically to the center locations \mu of the Gaussians to encourage exploration of the parameter space. 3. Re-spawning (Pruning and Spawning): Identify Gaussians whose opacity \alphai drops below a predefined threshold. These Gaussians are removed from the scene. To maintain the target number of Gaussians or sample from the learned distribution, new Gaussians are spawned randomly at the locations of Gaussians that currently have high opacity. This re-localization scheme preserves the sample probability. 4. Iteration: Repeat steps 1-3 for the training duration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mcmcdensificationstep(Gaussians, Images, lambdalr, lambdanoise, opacitythreshold): """ Performs one step of MCMC densification. Args: Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes.mu,.alpha, etc. Images: Batch of reference images for loss computation. lambdalr: Learning rate. lambdanoise: Noise scale. opacitythreshold: Threshold for pruning/re-spawning. Returns: Updated Gaussians list. """ # 1. Compute gradients loss = computereconstructionloss(Gaussians, Images) gradients = computegradients(loss, Gaussians) # 2. SGLD Update for g in Gaussians: # Gradient descent step g.mu = g.mu - lambdalr gradients[g].mu # Add noise to center location for exploration noise = samplenormaldistribution(size=3) g.mu = g.mu + lambdanoise noise # Update other parameters (covariance, opacity, SH) via gradient descent # Note: Noise is typically only applied to mu in SGLD formulation for 3DGS updateotherparams(g, gradients[g]) # 3. Re-spawning based on opacity prunedgaussians = [] highopacitygaussians = [] for g in Gaussians: if g.alpha < opacitythreshold: prunedgaussians.append(g) else: highopacitygaussians.append(g) # Remove pruned Gaussians Gaussians = [g for g in Gaussians if g.alpha >= opacitythreshold] # Re-spawn new Gaussians at locations of high opacity Gaussians # The number of new Gaussians equals the number of pruned ones to maintain count # or to sample from the distribution. numtospawn = len(prunedgaussians) for in range(numtospawn): # Select a parent Gaussian randomly from high opacity ones parent = random.choice(highopacitygaussians) # Create new Gaussian with similar properties but potentially perturbed newg = Gaussian() newg.mu = parent.mu + samplenormaldistribution(size=3) smallscale newg.alpha = parent.alpha # Or initialize with small opacity newg.covariance = parent.covariance newg.color = parent.color Gaussians.append(newg) return Gaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The noise injection can lead to instability if \lambda{\text{noise}} is too large, causing Gaussians to diverge from the scene geometry. Boundaries: Re-spawning at high-opacity Gaussians may cluster Gaussians in already well-represented areas if not balanced with the exploration noise. Degenerate Input: If the initial point cloud is sparse, the MCMC approach may take longer to converge to a dense representation compared to splitting methods, as it relies on random exploration. HYDRA is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decomposes complex, multi-lobed primitives into simpler constituents within the MCMC framework. It solves the problem of undersampled regions by subdividing primitives with high positional gradients while preserving the target distribution P(g{\text{new}}) \approx P(g{\text{old}}). It distinguishes itself from standard splitting by using a learned decomposition for large primitives, enabling generalizable planar primitives to operate effectively within MCMC. An optimized implementation of the MCMC densification approach from 3DGS-MCMC [39], which treats 3D Gaussians as MCMC samples and uses SGLD updates. It fuses the noise injection step into a single CUDA kernel to reduce training time bottleneck. On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, the optimized version achieves 28.00 PSNR, 6m17s training time, and 7.2GiB VRAM, compared to the original 27.83 PSNR, 27m22s training time, and 8.9GiB VRAM. The target number of Gaussians for the nine Mip-NeRF360 scenes (alphabetical order) are: 6131954, 1244819, 1222956, 3636448, 5834784, 1852335, 1593376, 4961797, 3783761. The optimized version is significantly faster and uses less VRAM than the original implementation [39], while achieving similar or slightly better quality. A novel hierarchy densification strategy that allows Gaussian Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchies to evolve continuously during optimization, supporting stable refinement and restructuring without post-training hierarchy construction. It maintains the hierarchy throughout training as Gaussian parameters and spatial distribution evolve dynamically. Unlike methods that construct the hierarchy post-training, this method evolves the hierarchy continuously during optimization. Time Complexity: The SGLD update is O(N) per iteration where N is the number of Gaussians. The re-spawning step is also O(N) if implemented efficiently. The optimized CUDA kernel implementation reduces constant factors significantly. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian parameters. The optimized version uses less VRAM (7.2GiB vs 8.9GiB on Mip-NeRF360) due to fused kernels. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360, Fast MCMC Densification achieves 28.00 PSNR in 6m17s with 7.2GiB VRAM, outperforming the original 3DGS-MCMC (27.83 PSNR, 27m22s, 8.9GiB VRAM). Strengths: Reduces reliance on initial point cloud quality; allows pre-specifying the number of Gaussians; improves quality in undersampled regions. Limitations: May require careful tuning of \lambda{\text{noise}} and opacity threshold; convergence can be slower in very sparse initial configurations compared to aggressive splitting. When to use: When the initial point cloud is sparse or noisy, or when a fixed number of Gaussians is desired. Also useful for large-scale scenes where dynamic hierarchy evolution is needed. When not to use: When rapid convergence is critical and the initial point cloud is dense and well-distributed. MCMC Densification was introduced by Kheradmand et al. (2024) as an alternative Bayesian perspective to the densification strategy in Gaussian Splatting. It reformulates the densification process as a Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamic (SGLD) update rule. This approach was motivated by the advantages of reducing reliance on the initial point cloud, allowing specification of the number of Gaussians prior to optimization, and leading to improved rendering quality. The method has been further optimized for performance in frameworks like Faster-GS and integrated into hierarchical rendering strategies. 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26 gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.01110, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: HYDRA Densification
head: HYDRA, HYDRA: Hybrid Decomposition for Rendering-Aware Preservation
body: HYDRA is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that decomposes complex, multi-lobed primitives into simpler constituents within the MCMC framework. It solves the problem of undersampled regions by subdividing primitives with high positional gradients while preserving the target distribution P(g{\text{new}}) \approx P(g{\text{old}}). It distinguishes itself from standard splitting by using a learned decomposition for large primitives, enabling generalizable planar primitives to operate effectively within MCMC. Inputs: Current set of Gaussian primitives g. Absolute gradient accumulation for each primitive (used to identify high-gradient regions). Pre-trained MLP f\psi. Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives with increased density in high-gradient areas. Data Structures: Primitive parameters: center o, covariance (encoded via scale/rotation or Fourier coefficients \sigma, \{\phik\}, \{rk\}), color, orientation. Boundary representation for large primitives: radial function ri(\theta) sampled at M angles. Steps: 1. Identify High-Gradient Primitives: Compute absolute gradient accumulation for all primitives. Select those with high gradient accumulation for densification. 2. Classify Primitive Size: Determine if the primitive is "small" or "large" based on its circumradius or boundary complexity. 3. Apply Splitting Strategy: Case (i) Scale-preserving split: For smaller primitives, reduce the circumradius and place two children symmetrically offset in the parent's tangent plane. Apply the mass-preserving relocation formulas with N=2. Case (ii) Learned lobe decomposition: For large primitives with complex, multi-lobed boundaries: a. Identify the S deepest valleys along the boundary ri(\theta) sampled at M angles. b. Partition the boundary into S angular segments. c. For each segment, compute the center of mass (rM, \thetaM) and angular bounds (\theta{\min}, \theta{\max}). d. Use the pre-trained MLP f\psi to generate child primitive parameters: f\psi: \left (\sigma,\, \{\phi k\},\, \{rk\},\, rM,\, \theta M,\, \theta {\min },\, \theta {\max }\right) \mapsto \left (\sigma ',\, \{\phi 'k\},\, \{r'k\},\, \Delta r,\, \Delta \theta,\, o',\, R'\right) where (\Delta r, \Delta \theta) is the polar offset used to compute the child center in the parent’s tangent plane. e. Children inherit color and orientation from the parent. f. Remove the parent primitive. 4. Update Count: The net increase in primitives is S-1 for each decomposed large primitive. """ newprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: # Step 1: Identify High-Gradient Primitives via absolute gradient accumulation if gradients[prim.id] < sizethreshold: newprimitives.append(prim) continue # Step 2: Classify Primitive Size based on circumradius or boundary complexity issmall = prim.R < sizethreshold # Exact classification logic not given in sources. if issmall: # Step 3(i): Scale-preserving split # Sources do not specify the exact relocation formulas (Eqs. 9 & 10 in source). # Symmetric offset in parent's tangent plane with reduced circumradius: offset = math.sqrt(prim.R / 2) child1 = Primitive(f"{prim.id}c1", prim.sigma, prim.phik, prim.rk, (prim.center[0] - offset, prim.center[1]), prim.color, prim.orientation, prim.R / 2) child2 = Primitive(f"{prim.id}c2", prim.sigma, prim.phik, prim.rk, (prim.center[0] + offset, prim.center[1]), prim.color, prim.orientation, prim.R / 2) newprimitives.extend([child1, child2]) else: # Step 3(ii): Learned lobe decomposition # Sources do not specify the valley detection algorithm. # We assume boundary sampling at M angles returns S segments. segments = [] # Sources do not specify the valley detection algorithm. S = len(segments) for i, segment in enumerate(segments): # Compute segment properties rM, thetaM = 0.0, 0.0 # Exact computation not given in sources. thetamin, thetamax = 0.0, 0.0 # Exact computation not given in sources. # Step 3(ii)d: Use pre-trained MLP fpsi to generate child parameters childparams = mlpfpsi( prim.sigma, prim.phik, prim.rk, rM, thetaM, thetamin, thetamax) # Unpack MLP output sigmaprime, phikprime, rkprime, deltar, deltatheta, oprime, Rprime = childparams # Compute child center in parent's tangent plane using polar offset dx = deltar math.cos(deltatheta) dy = deltar math.sin(deltatheta) childcenter = (oprime[0] + dx, oprime[1] + dy) # Step 3(ii)e: Children inherit color and orientation from the parent child = Primitive( id=f"{prim.id}child{i}", center=childcenter, sigma=sigmaprime, phik=phikprime, rk=rkprime, color=prim.color, orientation=prim.orientation, R=Rprime) newprimitives.append(child) # Step 4: Parent is removed, net increase is S-1 primitives return newprimitives Parameters: M: Number of angles sampled for boundary representation. Not given in the sources. S: Number of segments/lobes. Not given in the sources. \lambda: Weight for D-SSIM loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{dist}}: Weight for depth distortion loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{normal}}: Weight for normal consistency loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues in computing valleys and centers of mass for complex boundaries. Ensuring the MLP f\psi is properly trained and generalized. Handling degenerate primitives with no clear valleys. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives, the complexity of boundary sampling (M), and the MLP inference cost. Memory Complexity: Increases by S-1 primitives per large primitive decomposed. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality among planar-primitive frameworks and comparable perceptual metrics to leading volumetric representations on standard benchmarks. Strengths: Enables generalizable planar primitives within MCMC; handles complex, multi-lobed boundaries effectively. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained MLP; potentially higher computational cost for large primitives compared to simple splits. When to use: When rendering complex scenes with multi-lobed structures using planar primitives within an MCMC framework. When not to use: Not given in the sources. HYDRA was introduced in "Fourier Splatting: Generalized Fourier encoded primitives for scalable radiance fields" by Jurca et al.. The method aims to provide a versatile solution for bandwidth-constrained high-fidelity rendering.
