name: Pruning and Opacity Management
head: Component Recycling, Scooping
body: Pruning and Opacity Management methods remove or modify 3D Gaussian primitives that contribute negligibly to the final rendered image or whose removal would not significantly degrade reconstruction quality, thereby controlling memory usage and computational load during training. Unlike sibling methods that rely on static thresholds or uncertainty metrics, this family encompasses strategies that actively manage the density and opacity distribution, including recycling low-opacity components into high-opacity ones to prevent unbounded growth without altering the rendered image. All methods in this family operate on the set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\} inherited from Densification Strategy. The core mechanism involves evaluating a metric per Gaussian to determine if it contributes negligibly to the final rendered image or if its removal would not significantly degrade reconstruction quality. Common metrics include: 1. Opacity: Low opacity \alphak < \alpha{\min} indicates a primitive contributes negligibly to the alpha-compositing process. 2. Gradient Magnitude: High accumulated positional gradients indicate a Gaussian is struggling to minimize loss, suggesting it may be redundant or poorly placed, though this is more commonly used for densification [Parent]. 3. Significance/Weight: The accumulated alpha blending coefficient wk across all training views, representing the Gaussian's actual contribution to the pixel colors. 4. Uncertainty/Sensitivity: A score derived from the Fisher Information matrix or Hessian of the reconstruction error, indicating how sensitive the output is to changes in the Gaussian's parameters. Pruning is typically executed either periodically during training (e.g., every 100–1000 iterations) or as a final post-processing step. When primitives are removed, buffer compaction or flag-based marking is required to maintain contiguous memory access for the rasterizer [Parent]. The GES Optimization Strategy controls shape density by selectively pruning splats based on shape attributes, eliminating the need for a variable density mechanism [4697-ges-optimization-strategy.md]. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by optimizing a shape parameter \beta alongside position, opacity, covariance, and color, using a frequency-modulated loss to enhance high-frequency detail reconstruction [4697-ges-optimization-strategy.md]. Pruning occurs every 100 iterations based on a shape metric and density gradient threshold [4697-ges-optimization-strategy.md]. Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) is a sparsification method for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes low-impact Gaussians by aggregating their sensitivity to the reconstruction loss across all training views and timesteps [6350-temporal-sensitivity-pruning.md]. It distinguishes itself from static pruning methods by incorporating temporal deformation gradients, ensuring that Gaussians contributing to motion or temporal consistency are preserved, while eliminating those with negligible impact on the dynamic scene reconstruction [6350-temporal-sensitivity-pruning.md]. Opacity Split for Cloning is a densification strategy that clones a parent Gaussian into N copies while minimizing the difference between the rasterization outcomes before and after cloning, ensuring the rendering result remains unchanged [9694-opacity-split-for-cloning.md]. It specifically addresses the transmittance bias introduced when cloned children inherit the parent's opacity, which disproportionately reduces the impact of subsequent Gaussians in the alpha blending process [9694-opacity-split-for-cloning.md]. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting where cloned children inherit the parent's opacity, this method adjusts the opacity of both the parent and the clones to maintain transmittance consistency [9694-opacity-split-for-cloning.md]. GRay Optimization Settings define the hyperparameter configurations for training the GRay ray-tracing renderer, which differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by omitting opacity resets and size-based pruning [10037-gray-optimization-settings.md]. It provides two distinct presets: GRayLQ for high-speed, low-quality training and GRayHQ for high-quality reconstruction, allowing users to balance initialization time, optimization duration, and final rendering fidelity [10037-gray-optimization-settings.md]. Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger is a training-time adaptive control mechanism for 3D Gaussian Splatting that manages the number and density of Gaussian primitives by periodically resetting opacities and triggering densification (cloning/splitting) or pruning based on gradient and scale thresholds [10759-opacity-reset-densification-trigger.md]. It solves the problem of static Gaussian counts failing to capture complex scene geometry, transitioning from an initial sparse set to a denser representation that better fits the data [10759-opacity-reset-densification-trigger.md]. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GES Optimization Strategy or Temporal Sensitivity Pruning by its reliance on periodic hard resets of opacity parameters and explicit view-space positional gradient thresholds to drive structural adaptation, rather than continuous regularization or temporal consistency metrics [10759-opacity-reset-densification-trigger.md]. Spatially Constrained Optimization is a post-processing constraint workflow that applies an opacity loss to ensure full coverage of target objects, followed by the re-initialization of boundary primitives to clean up rendering artifacts [13691-spatially-constrained-optimization.md]. It differs from applying opacity loss alone by specifically addressing the issue where primitives on object boundaries retain low opacity, which degrades qualitative results; adding re-initialization produces the best visual fidelity [13691-spatially-constrained-optimization.md]. Definition A training-time component management strategy that replaces vanilla 3DGS densification/pruning by resampling low-opacity components into high-opacity ones to maintain efficiency without unbounded growth. Step Every n training iterations: 1) Compute opacity values for all active components. 2) Construct a Multinomial distribution from these opacity values. 3) Sample components with relatively high probability to replace low-opacity ones. Parameter n: iteration interval for recycling. Value not specified in this section; detailed recycling formulae are deferred to Sec. 5. Pitfall Recycling must not significantly alter the rendered image. The operation is only valid when the change to the current state (rendering result) after recycling is minimal. The concept of managing Gaussian density and opacity is central to the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting. The original 3DGS paper introduced adaptive density control, which includes densification and pruning based on opacity and gradient thresholds. Subsequent works have refined this process. For instance, Generalized Exponential Splatting (GES) introduces shape parameter optimization and specific pruning based on shape attributes [4697-ges-optimization-strategy.md]. Temporal Sensitivity Pruning extends this to dynamic scenes by considering temporal gradients [6350-temporal-sensitivity-pruning.md]. The "Scooping" or "Component Recycling" method, as described in "3D Student Splatting and Scooping", proposes an alternative to standard pruning by recycling low-opacity components, thereby avoiding the need for explicit removal and buffer compaction in some implementations. GRay optimization settings provide specific presets for ray-tracing based rendering, disabling certain pruning mechanisms [10037-gray-optimization-settings.md]. Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger formalizes the periodic reset and threshold-based pruning/densification cycle [10759-opacity-reset-densification-trigger.md]. Spatially Constrained Optimization focuses on foreground coverage by re-initializing low-opacity boundary primitives rather than removing them [13691-spatially-constrained-optimization.md]. 3D Student Splatting and Scooping, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01960, fetched 2026-10-29

name: GES Optimization Strategy
head: GES Training, Generalized Exponential Splatting Optimization
body: The GES Optimization Strategy is a training methodology for Generalized Exponential Splats (GES) that controls shape density by selectively pruning primitives based on shape attributes, thereby eliminating the need for a separate variable density mechanism. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by optimizing a shape parameter \beta alongside position, opacity, covariance, and color, using a frequency-modulated loss to enhance high-frequency detail reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each primitive gi is defined by position xi, opacity \kappai, covariance matrix \Sigmai, shape parameter \betai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Initial estimates for \Sigma and x are derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, and all \beta values are initialized to 2 (representing pure Gaussian splats). Output: Optimized parameters for the primitives after 40,000 iterations, resulting in a reconstructed radiance field. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard GES primitive structure. The key addition is the scalar shape parameter \beta. The covariance matrix \Sigma is typically parameterized via a rotation matrix R and a scaling matrix S such that \Sigma = RSS^T R^T, but the optimization directly updates the underlying parameters to maintain positive definiteness. Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} combines three terms: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{L1}\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{\text{ssim}}\mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda{\omega}\mathcal{L}{\omega} Where: \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 photometric loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} is the Structural Similarity (SSIM) loss. \mathcal{L}{\omega} is the frequency-modulated loss. \lambda{L1}, \lambda{\text{ssim}}, and \lambda{\omega} are weighting coefficients. The source specifies \lambda{\omega} = 0.5. The frequency-modulated loss \mathcal{L}{\omega} utilizes masks M\omega to focus on specific frequency bands. The target normalized frequency \omega is determined by a linear schedule: \omega = \frac{\text{current iteration}}{\text{total iterations}} The masks M\omega cover the range 50\% < \omega \le 100\% to ensure image coverage while focusing on details as optimization progresses. The Image Laplacian scale factor is set to 0.2 for this calculation. Optimization Steps: The optimization uses Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) accelerated by GPU/CUDA kernels. The process runs for 40,000 iterations. 1. Initialization: Initialize xi, \Sigmai from SfM data. Set \betai = 2 for all i. Set \kappai and SH coefficients to initial values (typically derived from input images or SfM colors). 2. Iteration Loop: For iteration t = 1 to 40,000: a. Forward Pass: Render the scene using the current GES primitives. Compute the frequency mask M\omega based on t. b. Loss Computation: Calculate \mathcal{L}1, \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}}, and \mathcal{L}{\omega}. Compute total loss \mathcal{L}. c. Backward Pass: Compute gradients for xi, \kappai, \Sigmai, \betai, and SH coefficients. d. Parameter Update: Update parameters using SGD. The learning rate for \beta is 0.0015. e. Shape Reset: If t \pmod{1000} == 0, reset shape parameters. The specific reset mechanism is not detailed, but the interval is 1000 iterations. f. Shape Pruning: If t \pmod{100} == 0, prune primitives based on shape attributes. i. Compute a shape metric for each primitive. The source mentions a "density gradient threshold" of 0.0003 and a "pruning threshold" of 0.5. It is implied that primitives with shape attributes exceeding these thresholds (or failing to meet significance criteria relative to the shape strength parameter 0.1) are candidates for removal. ii. Remove primitives that fail the pruning check. iii. Compact the primitive list or mark removed primitives to maintain contiguous memory access [Parent]. Parameters: Total iterations: 40,000. Density gradient threshold: 0.0003. Learning rate for \beta: 0.0015. Shape reset interval: 1000 iterations. Shape pruning interval: 100 iterations. Pruning threshold: 0.5. Shape strength parameter: 0.1. Image Laplacian scale factor: 0.2. \lambda{\omega}: 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Sensitivity: The DoG (Difference of Gaussians) filter used in the frequency loss is sensitive to high frequencies, which may require careful tuning of the mask generation to avoid noise amplification. Pruning Aggressiveness: The pruning threshold of 0.5 and shape strength of 0.1 must be balanced to prevent over-pruning, which could degrade reconstruction quality, or under-pruning, which increases computational load. Time Complexity: The optimization runs for 40,000 iterations. The frequency-modulated loss adds computational overhead due to mask generation and filtering, but the elimination of variable density mechanisms may reduce the complexity of densification steps compared to standard 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is determined by the number of surviving primitives after pruning. The shape parameter \beta adds a small per-primitive memory overhead. Performance: Evaluated on an A6000 GPU, GES achieves a balance between high fidelity and efficiency in novel view synthesis tasks. Strengths: Eliminates the need for a variable density mechanism; enhances high-frequency detail reconstruction via frequency-modulated loss. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of frequency masks and pruning thresholds; sensitive to high-frequency noise in the DoG filter. The GES Optimization Strategy was introduced in the paper "GES: Generalized Exponential Splatting for Efficient Radiance Field Rendering". It builds upon the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting but introduces generalized exponential splats with a shape parameter \beta to control density and shape adaptively. name: Temporal Sensitivity Pruning
body:
Temporal Sensitivity Pruning (TSP) is a method for eliminating redundant 3D Gaussian primitives in dynamic scene reconstruction by evaluating their cumulative impact on the reconstruction error over time. It distinguishes itself from static pruning methods by aggregating sensitivity scores across multiple training poses and timesteps, thereby identifying Gaussians that contribute negligibly to the dynamic scene's appearance across the entire temporal sequence. Inputs and Outputs Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{\mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}N\}, where each \mathcal{G}i has parameters including position, rotation, scale, and opacity. The set of training views \mathcal{P}{gt}, consisting of camera poses \phi and corresponding timesteps t. Output: A binary mask or updated set \mathcal{G}' containing only Gaussians with a temporal sensitivity score 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} above a defined threshold. Data Structures Gaussian Parameters: Each \mathcal{G}i is defined by its 3D mean \mui, rotation quaternion qi, scale vector si, and opacity \alphai. In dynamic settings, these are often functions of time t via a deformation field. Sensitivity Score: A scalar value 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} stored per Gaussian, initialized to zero. Algorithm Steps 1. Iterate over Gaussians: For each Gaussian \mathcal{G}i in the current set \mathcal{G}: 2. Initialize Score: Set 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} = 0. 3. Aggregate Sensitivity: For each training view (\phi, t) \in \mathcal{P}{gt}: a. Render the image I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) using the current Gaussian parameters at timestep t and pose \phi. b. Compute the gradient of the rendered image with respect to the projected value of \mathcal{G}i. Let gi denote the contribution of \mathcal{G}i to the pixel colors in the image space. Calculate 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi). c. Square this gradient: \left( 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) ight)^2. d. Add the squared gradient to 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i}. 4. Prune: After computing 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} for all Gaussians, remove any \mathcal{G}i where 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} < 	au, where 	au is a pruning threshold. Formula The temporal sensitivity score 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} approximates the second-order sensitivity to the L2 loss: 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} \approx 
abla{gi}^2 L2 \approx \sum{\phi, t \in \mathcal{P}{gt}} \left( 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) ight)^2 Where: 	ilde{U}{\mathcal{G}i} is the TSP score for Gaussian \mathcal{G}i. gi is the value of \mathcal{G}i projected onto image space. \mathcal{P}{gt} is the set of training poses and timesteps. I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) is the rendered image at pose \phi and timestep t. Parameters \mathcal{P}{gt}: The set of training poses and timesteps used for sensitivity aggregation. Threshold 	au: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Computation: The gradients 
abla{gi} I{\mathcal{G}t}(\phi) must be computed with respect to the projected Gaussian value, which depends on the deformation field at time t. Since deformation updates vary across timesteps, these gradients are inherently time-dependent. Computational Cost: Calculating gradients for all Gaussians across all training views and timesteps can be expensive. TSP is typically applied periodically during training to reduce neural inference load rather than at every step. Floater Removal: While TSP identifies redundant Gaussians based on observed views, it may not fully address "floaters" (unstable Gaussians that appear static in observed views but drift at unseen timestamps). This is often addressed by complementary methods like Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS). Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning is a method to eliminate 3D Gaussians that have no impact on training images by calculating sensitivity using the gradient of total image energy with respect to parameters. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot |\mathcal{P}{gt}|), where N is the number of Gaussians and |\mathcal{P}{gt}| is the number of training views/timesteps. Gradient computation per view is required. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sensitivity scores. Performance: Integrating TSP into DeformableGS accelerates rendering by 6.78× on average while maintaining neural-field fidelity and using 10× fewer primitives. Strengths: Reduces redundant primitives, stabilizes temporal pruning, and lowers deformation cost. Limitations: Relies on gradients from discrete training frames, potentially overlooking floaters. Temporal Sensitivity Pruning was introduced in the context of Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting (SpeeDe3DGS). It builds on DeformableGS and aims to bridge the efficiency-fidelity gap in dynamic scene reconstruction by removing low-impact Gaussians via temporally aggregated sensitivity analysis. name: Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning
head: Gradient-based Sensitivity Pruning
body: Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning eliminates 3D Gaussians that have no impact on training images by calculating sensitivity via the gradient of total image energy with respect to the parameters. It differs from Temporal Sensitivity Pruning by using a first-order gradient of total image energy rather than a second-order L2 loss approximation, and from Gradient-based Pruning by specifically targeting the elimination of splats with zero sensitivity in color parameters to remove structural redundancy. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, where each Gaussian i has parameters including position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Training images and their corresponding camera poses. Outputs: Pruned set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}' containing only Gaussians with non-zero sensitivity. Data Structures: Gaussian parameters are stored in standard 3DGS format. Sensitivity score Si for each Gaussian i, defined as the gradient of total image energy with respect to the parameter. Steps: 1. Render Training Images: Render the current set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} to generate images for all training views. 2. Calculate Total Image Energy: Compute the total image energy E across all training views. The specific formula for energy is not explicitly defined in the sources, but it is derived from the rendered pixel values. 3. Compute Sensitivity: For each Gaussian i, calculate its sensitivity Si using the gradient of the total image energy E with respect to the Gaussian's parameters (specifically the color parameters). Critical Implementation Detail: When calculating the gradient, do not clamp negative direction-dependent colors to zero. The standard 3DGS rendering pipeline clamps negative SH coefficients to zero during forward rendering. However, for sensitivity calculation, these clamped values must be treated as continuous to avoid setting partial derivatives to zero in the backward pass. If clamping is applied, SH coefficients that contribute to training images will incorrectly yield zero sensitivity. 4. Identify Zero-Sensitivity Gaussians: Identify Gaussians where the sensitivity in the color parameters is exactly zero. The sources observe that up to 15% of Gaussians may exhibit this property. 5. Prune: Eliminate all Gaussians with zero sensitivity from the scene. Formula: Si = \nabla{\thetai} E where E is the total image energy across all training views, \thetai are the parameters of Gaussian i, and Si is the sensitivity score. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Standard automatic differentiation computes partial derivatives d(totalenergy)/d(params) grad = computegradient(totalenergy, g.params) sensitivities.append(grad) # Step 4: Identify Gaussians with zero sensitivity in color parameters zerosensitivityindices = [] for i, grad in enumerate(sensitivities): if iszerovector(grad.colorparams): zerosensitivityindices.append(i) # Standard automatic differentiation computes partial derivatives d(loss)/d(params) return automaticdifferentiation(loss, params) def iszerovector(vec, threshold=0.0): return sum(x x for x in vec) < threshold threshold Parameters: Pruning threshold: Not given in the sources. The method primarily targets zero sensitivity, but higher thresholds can be used to remove more Gaussians. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clamping Artifacts: If negative direction-dependent colors are clamped to zero during the backward pass, the partial derivatives become zero, resulting in zero sensitivity for SH coefficients that may still contribute to training images. Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification is a method for maintaining model compactness in 3D Gaussian Splatting by evaluating the actual contribution of each primitive within the optimization loop. It solves the problem of prohibitive time costs associated with offline pruning by performing sparsification online, ensuring the model remains refined throughout training. It differs from its parent, Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning, by specifically defining sensitivity as the expected gradient magnitude of the global photometric loss over a fixed accumulation window, rather than a general gradient of total image energy. Gradient-based Pruning is a training-time sparsification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussians contributing minimally to the optimization process by evaluating the magnitude of their associated gradients. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods, such as Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification, by directly measuring the gradient signal intensity rather than statistical variance or opacity thresholds, allowing for efficient GPU implementation while effectively eliminating visual artifacts like floaters. Performance: The sources note that a notable number of Gaussians (up to 15%) may have no impact on training images and can be safely eliminated. Strengths: Removes Gaussians that have no impact on training images, potentially reducing model size without significant loss in PSNR if thresholds are low. Limitations: Higher pruning thresholds can lead to the removal of fine details (e.g., small leaves). When to use: When aiming to reduce model size by removing structurally redundant Gaussians that do not contribute to the rendered output. When not to use: When preserving fine geometric details is critical, as aggressive pruning may remove them. name: Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification
body: Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification is a method for maintaining model compactness in 3D Gaussian Splatting by evaluating the actual contribution of each primitive within the optimization loop. It solves the problem of prohibitive time costs associated with offline pruning by performing sparsification online, ensuring the model remains refined throughout training. It differs from its parent, Sensitivity Calculation and Pruning, by specifically defining sensitivity as the expected gradient magnitude of the global photometric loss over a fixed accumulation window, rather than a general gradient of total image energy. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians with opacity \alphai, the global photometric loss \mathcal{L}, the sparsification lower-bound threshold \tau{\text{low}}, and a fixed accumulation window. Output: A binary survival state \mathcal{S}i for each primitive i. Data Structures Primitive State: Each Gaussian primitive i maintains a statistical sensitivity score Si. Accumulation Window: A fixed window of optimization iterations used to compute the expected value of the gradient magnitude. The exact size of the accumulation window is not given in the sources. Parameters \tau{\text{low}}: The sparsification lower-bound threshold (also referred to as \tauC in implementation details). It controls the compactness of the model. Set to 0.01. Steps 1. Compute Gradient: For each primitive i, compute the partial derivative of the loss function \mathcal{L} with respect to its opacity \alphai, denoted as \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphai}. 2. Calculate Sensitivity: Compute the statistical sensitivity Si as the expected value of the absolute gradient magnitude over the fixed accumulation window: Si = \mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphai} \right| \right] where \mathbb{E} denotes the expectation over the accumulation window. 3. Determine Survival State: Compare Si against \tau{\text{low}} to determine the survival state \mathcal{S}i: \mathcal{S}i = \begin{cases} \text{keep} & \text{if } Si \geq \tau{\text{low}} \\ \text{prune} & \text{if } Si < \tau{\text{low}} \end{cases} 4. Prune: Remove primitives where \mathcal{S}i = \text{prune} from the scene representation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def statisticalsensitivitysparsification(primitives, gradients, windowsize, taulow): """ Computes statistical sensitivity and prunes primitives based on the threshold. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects, each with an 'id' and 'alpha'. gradients: List of floats, the absolute gradient magnitudes |dL/dalphai| for each primitive in the current iteration. windowsize: Integer, the number of recent iterations to average over. taulow: Float, the sparsification lower-bound threshold (default 0.01). Returns: keptprimitives: List of primitive objects to keep. history: Dictionary mapping primitive id to a list of recent gradient magnitudes. """ # Initialize history buffers for each primitive history = {p.id: [] for p in primitives} sensitivities = {} # Update history with current iteration gradients for p, gradmag in zip(primitives, gradients): history[p.id].append(gradmag) # Keep only the last 'windowsize' entries if len(history[p.id]) > windowsize: history[p.id].pop(0) # Compute expected value (mean) over the window for p in primitives: if len(history[p.id]) > 0: sensitivities[p.id] = sum(history[p.id]) / len(history[p.id]) else: sensitivities[p.id] = 0.0 # Apply pruning threshold keptprimitives = [] for p in primitives: if sensitivities[p.id] >= taulow: keptprimitives.append(p) return keptprimitives, history Edge Cases and Pitfalls Window Size: The exact size of the accumulation window is not given in the sources. Precision: The computation requires accurate gradient tracking. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Online sparsification is performed within the optimization loop, avoiding the prohibitive time cost of offline pruning. The exact cost per iteration is not specified. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the history of gradient magnitudes for each primitive over the accumulation window. Measured Performance: In the ACE-GS framework, this method significantly reduces training duration compared to existing baselines while maintaining superior rendering quality. Strengths: Maintains model compactness without significant overhead; ensures the model remains refined throughout training. Limitations: The choice of \tau{\text{low}} and the accumulation window size can impact performance. When to Use: Use when training time is a constraint and model compactness is desired. When Not to Use: Use when offline pruning is feasible and computational resources are abundant, or when the accumulation window cannot be effectively defined. Statistical Sensitivity-Driven Online Sparsification was introduced in the ACE-GS paper, which aims to balance accuracy, compactness, and efficiency in 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Gradient-based Pruning
head: Gradient Magnitude Pruning
body:
Gradient-based Pruning is a training-time sparsification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussians contributing minimally to the optimization process by evaluating the magnitude of their associated gradients. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by directly measuring the gradient signal intensity rather than statistical variance or opacity thresholds, allowing for efficient GPU implementation while effectively eliminating visual artifacts like floaters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of active 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, their parameters (position \mathbf{t}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}), and the accumulated gradient magnitudes \mathbf{g} for each Gaussian during the current training phase. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' \subset \mathcal{G} with redundant entries removed. Data Structures: Gradient Accumulator: An array of size |\mathcal{G}| storing the cumulative gradient magnitude for each Gaussian. For EfficientGS, this tracks a cumulative sum to halt unnecessary densification. For Kim et al., it stores separate components for positional and SH gradients. Threshold: A scalar value 	au determining the minimum gradient magnitude required to retain a Gaussian. Steps: 1. Gradient Accumulation: During each training iteration, after the backward pass, compute the gradient magnitude for each Gaussian. For position-based pruning, calculate the Euclidean norm of the positional gradient 
abla{\mathbf{t}i} L for Gaussian i. For SH-based pruning (Kim et al.), calculate the norm of the gradient with respect to SH coefficients 
abla{\mathbf{c}i} L. Accumulate these magnitudes over time. Gi^{(t)} = Gi^{(t-1)} + \|
abla{\mathbf{p}i} L\| where \mathbf{p}i represents the parameters of interest (position or SH). 2. Thresholding: Compare the accumulated gradient magnitude Gi against a threshold 	au. If Gi < 	au, the Gaussian is marked for removal. The threshold 	au can be static or adaptive based on the distribution of gradient magnitudes in the current batch. 3. Pruning: Remove all marked Gaussians from the scene representation. Trimming the Fat and ELMGS apply this to remove 75% of Gaussians while maintaining high visual quality. Parameters: Threshold 	au: Not given in the sources. Typically determined empirically or via percentile-based selection (e.g., remove bottom 10-25% of Gaussians by gradient magnitude). Accumulation Window: The number of iterations over which gradients are summed. EfficientGS uses cumulative sums. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gradient magnitudes can vary significantly across scenes. Normalization or adaptive thresholds are necessary to avoid removing too many or too few Gaussians. Degenerate Input: Gaussians with zero gradient (e.g., occluded or static background) may be pruned prematurely if the threshold is too low. SH Gradients: Incorporating SH gradients alongside positional gradients (Kim et al.) refines the pruning process. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbasedpruning(gaussians, accumulatedgradients, threshold): """ Prunes Gaussians with accumulated gradient magnitude below threshold. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects. accumulatedgradients: List of floats, cumulative gradient magnitude for each Gaussian. threshold: Float, minimum accumulated gradient magnitude to keep a Gaussian. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of Gaussian objects that survived pruning. """ prunedgaussians = [] for i, gaussian in enumerate(gaussians): # Step 2: Thresholding if accumulatedgradients[i] >= threshold: prunedgaussians.append(gaussian) # Step 3: Pruning removes gaussians where accumulatedgradients[i] < threshold return prunedgaussians Utilization-Based Pruning (UBP) is a training-time sparsification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussians with negligible contribution to the rendered image gradient, replacing opacity reset to alleviate interference with residual distribution tracking and compress scene representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by evaluating the gradient of the rendered image with respect to Gaussian positions rather than the loss gradient, allowing for efficient GPU implementation while effectively eliminating visual artifacts like floaters. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration for gradient accumulation and pruning, where N is the number of Gaussians. Cumulative sum updates are O(1) per Gaussian per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store accumulated gradients. Measured Performance: Trimming the Fat and ELMGS remove 75% of Gaussians while maintaining high visual quality. Strengths: Effective at removing redundant Gaussians and floaters. Efficient on GPU due to simple magnitude comparisons. Limitations: Requires careful threshold selection. May remove Gaussians that are temporarily occluded but important for later views. When to Use: When computational efficiency is critical and visual quality must be maintained with fewer Gaussians. When Not to Use: When the scene has dynamic elements where temporary occlusion is common, or when SH details are critical and position-only pruning is insufficient. Gradient-based Pruning originated as a method to improve the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting training by removing Gaussians that contribute minimally to the optimization process. It has been adopted and extended by several methods, including EfficientGS, GDGS, Trimming the Fat, ELMGS, and Kim et al.. Kim et al. extended the approach by incorporating SH gradients alongside positional gradients. name: Utilization-Based Pruning
head: utilization pruning
body: Utilization-Based Pruning (UBP) is a training-time sparsification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes Gaussians with negligible contribution to the rendered image gradient, replacing opacity reset to alleviate interference with residual distribution tracking and compress scene representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by evaluating the gradient of the rendered image with respect to Gaussian positions rather than the loss gradient, allowing for efficient GPU implementation while effectively eliminating visual artifacts like floaters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of active 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the current training step t, and a history of rendered images. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians \mathcal{G}' with low utilization removed. Data Structures: Gaussian g: Contains position xg, opacity, scale, rotation, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Rendered Image \hat{I}^{(t)}: A 2D array of pixel values at step t. Accumulator: A buffer storing the squared gradient magnitudes for each Gaussian over a window of steps. Parameters: \kappa = 10^{-8}: The threshold for pruning. If ug < \kappa, the Gaussian is removed. T = 100: The interval (in steps) at which the utilization metric is computed and pruning is considered. |NT(t)| = 100: The number of previous images accumulated in the window for averaging. Pruning Schedule: UBP is executed every 100 steps, specifically from step 500 to step 15,000. Formula: The utilization ug of a Gaussian g is defined as the accumulated squared gradient of the rendered pixel values with respect to the Gaussian's position, normalized by a constant factor: ug = \frac{\sum{t} \sum{(w,h) \in NT(t)} \left( \frac{\partial \hat{I}{h,w}^{(t)}}{\partial xg} \right)^2}{2} Where: ug is the utilization metric for Gaussian g. \hat{I}{h,w}^{(t)} is the rendered pixel value at pixel coordinates (h,w) for view t. xg is the 3D position of Gaussian g. NT(t) is the set of |NT(t)|=100 images accumulated over the previous T=100 steps. The factor of 1/2 is a normalization constant defined in the source formulation. Note: This metric uses the gradient of the rendered image with respect to Gaussian positions, not the gradient of the loss function. Computing the derivative with respect to projected positions (2D) rather than 3D positions allows for a less memory-intensive GPU implementation while providing a similar metric to prior work. Numbered Steps: 1. Accumulation: For each Gaussian g, accumulate the squared gradient of the rendered image with respect to its position over the current step t. This is done for all pixels (h,w) covered by the Gaussian. 2. Windowing: Maintain a rolling window of the last |NT(t)|=100 images. Every T=100 steps, compute the average utilization ug across this window. 3. Evaluation: Compare ug against the threshold \kappa = 10^{-8}. 4. Pruning: If ug < \kappa, remove Gaussian g from the scene representation. 5. Frequency: Repeat steps 1-4 every 100 steps, starting from step 500 and ending at step 15,000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def utilizationbasedpruning(gaussians, renderedimageswindow, step, threshold=1e-8): """ Prunes Gaussians with low utilization based on image gradient. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with a 'positiongradient' attribute. renderedimageswindow: List of the last 100 rendered images (tensors). step: Current training step. threshold: Pruning threshold kappa. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of Gaussians remaining after pruning. """ # Pruning is only active between step 500 and 15000, every 100 steps if step < 500 or step > 15000 or step % 100 != 0: return gaussians prunedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: utilizationsum = 0.0 numimages = len(renderedimageswindow) # Accumulate squared gradient over the window of images for img in renderedimageswindow: # Compute gradient of rendered image w.r.t Gaussian position via # backpropagation through the differentiable splatting rasterizer. # The gradient tensor is assumed to be stored in g.positiongradient. gradsq = sum(val2 for val in g.positiongradient) # Accumulate utilizationsum += gradsq # Divide by 2 as per the source formula (11) utilization = utilizationsum / 2.0 # Prune if below threshold if utilization >= threshold: prunedgaussians.append(g) return prunedgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Metric Degradation: UBP may slightly degrade quantitative metrics such as PSNR and LPIPS, but produces cleaner renderings with fewer floaters, as these metrics do not fully reflect the presence of floaters. Floater Removal: The method is particularly effective at removing "floaters" (erroneous Gaussians) in cluttered scenes. The parent method that evaluates the magnitude of gradients associated with each Gaussian during training [17720-gradient-based-pruning.md]. UBP is a specific instantiation that uses image gradient magnitude rather than loss gradient magnitude. Compression: On clean MipNeRF360 datasets, UBP reduces the number of Gaussians by 2× to 4.5× while preserving rendering quality. In distractor-filled scenes, it decreases the number of Gaussians by 4× to 6×. Performance: Enabling UBP translates to at least a 2× reduction in training time and a 3× reduction in inference time. Strengths: Effective compression, removal of floaters, and alleviation of interference with residual distribution tracking compared to opacity reset. Limitations: Slight potential degradation in quantitative metrics (PSNR/LPIPS). When to Use: Recommended for both cluttered and clean datasets to compress scene representation and improve rendering cleanliness. Utilization-Based Pruning was introduced in the paper "SpotLessSplats: Ignoring Distractors in 3D Gaussian Splatting" by Sabour and Goli et al.. It was developed as an improvement over opacity reset, which can interfere with residual distribution tracking. The method leverages the observation that Gaussians contributing minimally to the image gradient are likely artifacts or redundant primitives. name: Opacity Split for Cloning
head: Cloning Strategy for Gaussian Splatting, Revising Densification Opacity Initialization
body: Opacity Split for Cloning is a method to initialize the opacity of cloned 3D Gaussians during densification to maintain transmittance consistency, ensuring that the rasterization outcome remains unchanged before and after the split. It solves the problem where standard cloning (where children inherit the parent's opacity) artificially increases the total transmittance attenuation, causing subsequent Gaussians in the alpha-compositing order to have reduced impact. It sets itself apart from simple inheritance by analytically deriving opacity values that preserve the integrated intensity and transmittance of the primitive. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of parent Gaussians \mathcal{G}{parent} to be cloned, with their current opacities o{old}, covariances \Sigma{old}, and central colors C{old}. The number of clones N per parent. Output: A new set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}{new} replacing the parents, with updated opacities o{new}, covariances \Sigma{new}, and colors C{new}. Data Structures: The implementation operates on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting primitive structure [Parent]: mean: 3D vector \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. covariance: 3x3 symmetric matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or its Cholesky factorization/rotation/scale representation). opacity: Scalar \alpha \in [0, 1]. color: 3D vector \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or spherical harmonic coefficients). Steps: 1. Clone Geometry and Color: For each parent Gaussian g{old} with mean \mu{old}, covariance \Sigma{old}, and color C{old}, create N new Gaussians. Set the mean of each clone identical to the parent: \mu{new} = \mu{old}. Set the color of each clone identical to the parent: C{new}(\mu) = C{old}(\mu). Note: The covariance \Sigma is initially set equal to the parent's \Sigma{old}, but may require adjustment to preserve integrated intensity (see Pitfalls). 2. Calculate New Opacity: Determine the new opacity o{new} for the parent and all N clones. Two common strategies exist in the literature: Strategy A (Equal Split): Used when cloning into 2 copies (parent + 1 child) to keep transmittance tk approximately constant. o{new} = 1 - \sqrt{1 - o{old}} Here, o{old} is the parent's opacity before cloning, and o{new} is the opacity assigned to both the parent and the single clone child. Strategy B (N-Clone Generalization): Used when cloning into N copies to preserve rasterization intensity at the center \mu. (1 - o{new})^N = 1 - o{old} Solving for o{new}: o{new} = 1 - (1 - o{old})^{1/N} Here, o{new} is the opacity of each of the N cloned Gaussians, and o{old} is the opacity of the original Gaussian. 3. Assign Opacity: Set the opacity of the original parent Gaussian and all N new clone Gaussians to o{new}. 4. Covariance Adjustment (Optional/Advanced): If strict preservation of rasterization is required beyond the center point, the covariance \Sigma must be altered because Gaussians are not point sources. The objective is to minimize the error of integrated 1D slices passing through the Gaussian centers: \text{minimize } \left\| \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{new}(x) dx - \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathbf{C}^{old}(x) dx \right\|2^2, \quad \forall \mathcal{S} where \mathcal{S} represents arbitrary slices and x = S(x) denotes points along the slice. This avoids the complex analytical form of minimizing the full 3D mean squared error integral. In many practical implementations, simply splitting opacity is sufficient for densification stability, and covariance scaling is handled by the standard densification scale reduction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clonegaussianwithopacitysplit(gaussian, numclones): """ Clones a 3D Gaussian, splitting its opacity to maintain transmittance consistency. Args: gaussian: Object with attributes.opacity (float),.mean (vec3),.covariance (mat3),.color (vec3). numclones: Integer N, the number of clones to create. Note: In Strategy B, N is the total count including the original. In Strategy A (Bulo et al.), N=2 (parent + 1 child). Returns: list: A list of N new Gaussian objects replacing the original. """ oold = gaussian.opacity # Calculate new opacity using Strategy B (General N-clone) # Formula: onew = 1 - (1 - oold)^(1/N) # If using Strategy A (N=2), this formula yields onew = 1 - sqrt(1 - oold) onew = 1.0 - (1.0 - oold) (1.0 / numclones) newgaussians = [] for i in range(numclones): newg = Gaussian() newg.mean = gaussian.mean.copy() newg.covariance = gaussian.covariance.copy() # Covariance adjustment is complex; # often kept identical or scaled by densification rules newg.color = gaussian.color.copy() newg.opacity = onew newgaussians.append(newg) return newgaussians Parameters: N: Number of clones. Typically N=2 (split into parent and one child) in standard densification steps. o{old}: Current opacity of the parent Gaussian. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Point Source Assumption: Equation (1 - o^{new})^N = 1 - o^{old} preserves rasterization only at the center \mu. It does not preserve the full 3D integral. Since Gaussians are not point sources, the covariance \Sigma must also be altered to guarantee minimal impact on the full rasterization outcome. Transmittance Bias: If the cloned child inherits the parent's opacity without splitting (standard 3DGS behavior), the combined transmittance of the parent and child becomes lower than the parent's original transmittance. This biases the alpha-compositing process, reducing the impact of any subsequent Gaussians in the blending order. Precision: For very small o{old}, (1 - o{old})^{1/N} may suffer from floating-point precision issues. Ensure stable computation of the root. Uses different criteria for densification based on gradient magnitude relative to pixel influence, reducing unnecessary cloning in background regions [4697-ges-optimization-strategy.md]. Focuses on pruning Gaussians that are unstable or noisy across time in dynamic scenes, rather than just opacity-based cloning [6350-temporal-sensitivity-pruning.md]. Adjusts optimization hyperparameters and pruning thresholds for ray-based rendering contexts [10037-gray-optimization-settings.md]. Resets opacity to a default value upon densification rather than splitting, triggering new clones with full opacity [10759-opacity-reset-densification-trigger.md]. Constrains the optimization of Gaussian positions and scales to specific spatial regions to improve convergence [13691-spatially-constrained-optimization.md]. Time Complexity: O(1) per Gaussian cloned. The opacity calculation involves a single exponentiation and subtraction. Memory Complexity: O(N) increase in memory for the cloned Gaussians, where N is the number of clones. Strengths: Prevents the artificial attenuation of transmittance during densification, leading to more stable training and better reconstruction quality in high-gradient regions. Limitations: Does not fully preserve the 3D rasterization integral without additional covariance adjustments. The choice of N affects the granularity of the densification. When to use: During the densification phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting training when splitting Gaussians to increase detail. When not to use: During final inference or post-processing where the scene is static and no further densification is needed. The method originates from the need to improve the stability of 3D Gaussian Splatting densification. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting inherits opacity, which causes transmittance bias. Bulo et al. (2024) proposed the equal split opacity initialization (N=2) to counteract this bias. Later, the MCMC-based formulation (3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo) generalized this to N clones, deriving the opacity relationship (1 - o^{new})^N = 1 - o^{old} to minimize rasterization difference. 3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, https://ubc-vision.github.io/3dgs-mcmc/, fetched 2026-10-26 Improving Adaptive Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.5220/0013308500003912, fetched 2026-10-30

name: GRay Optimization Settings
head: GRayLQ, GRayHQ, GRay Configuration
body: GRay Optimization Settings define the hyperparameter configurations for training 3D Gaussian primitives using the GRay ray-tracing renderer. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) or 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT), these settings explicitly disable opacity resets and size-based pruning, relying instead on opacity thresholds and gradient-based significance metrics to manage the primitive count. The method offers two distinct presets: GRayLQ for maximum training speed and frame rate, and GRayHQ for higher reconstruction fidelity. The optimization process manages the set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} by applying specific thresholds to opacity and pruning metrics during periodic cleanup steps. Inputs: Set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\} with parameters \{\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{s}i, \mathbf{q}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i\} (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonic coefficients). Configuration preset (LQ or HQ). Data Structures: Gaussian attributes stored in contiguous arrays for ray traversal. Accumulated opacity \alphai and pruning metric \mui (significance/weight) per Gaussian. Parameters: The settings are defined by the following hyperparameters: \alpha{\min}: Minimum opacity threshold for pruning. \alpha{\expo}: Generalized exponent for opacity blending or metric calculation. \mu{\prune}: Pruning threshold based on accumulated significance. \eta{\decay}: Scale decay factor. \alpha{\lazy}: SH stepping laziness threshold. \tau{\min}: Ray marching step size threshold (used in DHT variants). \alpha{\bin}: Binning threshold for initialization. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate initial Gaussians. Apply binning if enabled. If \alpha{\bin} > 0, remove Gaussians with significance below \alpha{\bin}. 2. Training Loop: For each iteration: a. Render image using ray tracing. b. Compute loss and backpropagate. c. Update Gaussian parameters using Adam optimizer. d. Apply scale decay: \mathbf{s}i \leftarrow \mathbf{s}i \times \eta{\decay} if enabled. e. Apply SH laziness: If \alphai < \alpha{\lazy}, freeze SH coefficients update. 3. Pruning: Periodically (e.g., every 100–1000 iterations, or as defined by the preset): a. Calculate significance metric \mui for each Gaussian. b. If \alphai < \alpha{\min} OR \mui < \mu{\prune}, mark Gaussian for removal. c. Remove marked Gaussians and compact buffers. 4. No Opacity Reset: Unlike 3DGS, do not reset opacity of pruned/failed Gaussians. 5. No Size Pruning: Unlike 3DGS, do not prune Gaussians based on their spatial extent/scale. Preset Configurations: GRayLQ (Low Quality/High Speed): \alpha{\min} = 0.02 \alpha{\expo} = 3 \mu{\prune} = 5 \times 10^{-7} \eta{\decay} = 0.9998 \alpha{\lazy} = 12 Total iterations: 7500 Resolution: Half resolution GRayHQ (High Quality): \alpha{\min} = 0.001 \alpha{\expo} = 1 \tau{\min} = 0.001 \mu{\prune} = 10^{-9} Initialization binning: Disabled Scale decay: Disabled Total iterations: Standard (implied longer than LQ) Resolution: Half resolution Edge Cases: DHT Truncation: Disabling the Dynamic Hashing Table (DHT) with high \tau{\min} causes rapid deterioration. For example, \tau{\min}=0.03 leads to PSNR 24.54 and LPIPS 0.284, while \tau{\min}=0.04 may cause failure to converge due to rapid Gaussian expansion. Binning: Setting \alpha{\bin} = 0.04 removes >15% of initial Gaussians with minimal quality loss (PSNR 26.49 \to 26.47). A configuration optimized for speed. It uses aggressive pruning (\alpha{\min}=0.02, \mu{\prune}=5\times10^{-7}) and scale decay. It runs for 7500 iterations at half resolution. Results: PSNR 26.23, SSIM 0.839, LPIPS 0.191, Init Time 01:58, Opt Time 00:46, FPS 1051, Init #G 3.27M, Final #G 0.48M. A configuration optimized for quality. It uses conservative pruning (\alpha{\min}=0.001, \mu{\prune}=10^{-9}), disables scale decay and binning, and uses \alpha{\expo}=1. It runs longer at half resolution. Results: PSNR 27.41, SSIM 0.847, LPIPS 0.154, Init Time 01:58, Opt Time 36:11, FPS 55, Init #G 3.97M, Final #G 3.79M. Speed: GRayLQ trains in under a minute and achieves >1000 FPS at half resolution, more than doubling 3DGS's frame rate. GRayHQ takes ~36 minutes for optimization but achieves higher quality. Quality: GRayHQ approaches 3DGS-DI quality (PSNR 27.41 vs 3DGS-DI implied higher) but is slower. GRayLQ has lower quality (PSNR 26.23). Memory: GRayLQ reduces final Gaussian count to 0.48M from 3.27M. GRayHQ retains 3.79M from 3.97M. Limitations: Disabling DHT with high truncation thresholds leads to convergence failure or severe quality drops. Half resolution is used for these specific benchmarks, potentially limiting direct comparison to full-res methods. GRay is a ray-tracing based renderer for 3D Gaussians, introduced in the paper "GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats". The optimization settings were developed to balance the trade-off between training speed and reconstruction quality, specifically addressing the inefficiencies of opacity resets and size-based pruning found in 3DGS. name: Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger
head: Opacity Reset, 3DGS Densification, Gaussian Densification
body: Opacity Reset & Densification Trigger is the adaptive control mechanism in 3D Gaussian Splatting that manages the population of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} during training. It solves the problem of static initialization by transitioning from a sparse set of Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points to a denser, scene-adaptive representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining periodic opacity resetting with gradient-based densification (cloning/splitting) and pruning, rather than relying solely on static thresholds or post-processing. The method operates on the set of Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each Gaussian gi has position \mathbf{x}i, covariance \Sigmai (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Input: Current Gaussian set \mathcal{G}, accumulated image-plane gradients \nabla{\mathbf{x}}, accumulated visibility counts or contribution weights, current training iteration t, and hyperparameters. Output: Updated Gaussian set \mathcal{G}' with modified counts, positions, opacities, and scales. grad2d: A tensor of shape (N, 2) storing the running accumulation of image-plane gradient norms for each Gaussian. count: A tensor of shape (N, 1) storing the running accumulation of visibility counts (how many times a Gaussian contributed to a pixel). state: Flags indicating if refinement is paused (e.g., after reset). densifyfromiter: Iteration after which densification begins. Default: 500. densifyuntiliter: Iteration after which densification stops. Default: 15,000. densifyevery: Iteration interval for densification checks. Default: 100. opacityresetinterval: Iteration interval for opacity resets. Default: 3000. pauserefineafterreset: Steps to pause refinement after reset. Default: 0. posthresh: Position gradient threshold for densification. Default: 0.0002. pruneopa: Opacity threshold for pruning. Default: 0.005. growgrad2d: Image plane gradient threshold for splitting/duplicating. Default: 0.0002. growscale3d: 3D scale threshold (normalized by scene scale) below which Gaussians are duplicated. Default: 0.01. growscale2d: 2D scale threshold (normalized by image resolution) above which Gaussians are split. Default: 0.05. prunescale3d: 3D scale threshold (normalized by scene scale) above which Gaussians are pruned. Default: 0.1. prunescale2d: 2D scale threshold (normalized by image resolution) above which Gaussians are pruned. Default: 0.15. refinescale2dstopiter: Iteration after which 2D scale-based refinement stops. Default: 0 (disabled). absgrad: Boolean flag to use absolute gradients instead of average gradients. Default: False. revisedopacity: Boolean flag to use revised opacity heuristic. Default: False. keyforgradient: Variable name for gradient ('means2d' for 3DGS, 'gradient2dgs' for 2DGS). Default: 'means2d'. splitscalefactor: Factor by which scale is divided during split. Default: 1.6. floor: Constant added to accumulated contribution in denominator for occlusion-aware criteria. Default: 1. 1. Initialization: At t=0, initialize grad2d and count to zeros for all Gaussians. 2. Pre-Backward Accumulation: During each training step, accumulate gradients and visibility information into grad2d and count based on the current iteration and rendering info. 3. Opacity Reset Check: If t is a multiple of opacityresetinterval, or if the dataset uses a white background and t == densifyfromiter, call resetopacity(). resetopacity(): Sets all \alphai to a small initial value (e.g., 0.01) or resets non-diffuse SH coefficients to 0.001. If pauserefineafterreset > 0, set refinement paused flag for the next pauserefineafterreset steps. 4. Refinement Check: If t \ge densifyfromiter and t < densifyuntiliter and t \% densifyevery == 0 and refinement is not paused: Gradient Normalization: Compute average gradient magnitude per Gaussian. If absgrad is False, divide grad2d by count (or accumulated contribution if using occlusion-aware criteria). Densification Trigger: Identify Gaussians with average view-space position gradient magnitude > posthresh. Cloning (Under-reconstruction): For small Gaussians (3D scale < growscale3d) with high gradients: Clone the Gaussian. Move the clone in the direction of the positional gradient. Splitting (Over-reconstruction): For large Gaussians (2D scale > growscale2d or 3D scale > prunescale3d) with high gradients: Replace the Gaussian with two new Gaussians. Divide their scale by splitscalefactor (1.6). Initialize positions by sampling from the original Gaussian's PDF. Pruning: Remove Gaussians that meet any of the following criteria: Opacity \alphai < pruneopa. 3D scale > prunescale3d. 2D scale > prunescale2d (if t < refinescale2dstopiter or refinescale2dstopiter == 0). Buffer Compaction: Remove pruned Gaussians from the data structures and compact memory for contiguous access [Parent]. 5. Post-Backward: Update normals if the number of Gaussians changed. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def densificationstep(gaussians, grad2d, count, t, params): N = gaussians.opacities.shape[0] if N == 0: return # 1. Opacity Reset resetinterval = params.get('opacityresetinterval', 3000) densifyfromiter = params.get('densifyfromiter', 500) pauserefine = params.get('pauserefineafterreset', 0) shouldreset = (t % resetinterval == 0) if params.get('whitebackground', False) and t == densifyfromiter: shouldreset = True if shouldreset: resetopacity(gaussians) gaussians.refinepaused = pauserefine if pauserefine > 0: gaussians.refinepaused -= 1 # 2. Check if refinement is active densifyuntiliter = params.get('densifyuntiliter', 15000) densifyevery = params.get('densifyevery', 100) if (t < densifyfromiter or t >= densifyuntiliter or t % densifyevery != 0 or gaussians.refinepaused > 0): return # 3. Compute average gradients absgrad = params.get('absgrad', False) if not absgrad: safecount = torch.clamp(count, min=1) avggrad = grad2d / safecount else: avggrad = grad2d posthresh = params.get('posthresh', 0.0002) gradmagnitude = torch.norm(avggrad, dim=1) highgradmask = gradmagnitude > posthresh # 4. Pruning pruneopa = params.get('pruneopa', 0.005) prunescale3d = params.get('prunescale3d', 0.1) prunescale2d = params.get('prunescale2d', 0.15) refinestopiter = params.get('refinescale2dstopiter', 0) prunemask = (gaussians.opacities < pruneopa) | \ (gaussians.scale3d > prunescale3d) if refinestopiter == 0 or t < refinestopiter: prunemask |= (gaussians.scale2d > prunescale2d) keepmask = ~prunemask # Buffer compaction: filter tensors to maintain contiguous memory gaussians.opacities = gaussians.opacities[keepmask] gaussians.scale3d = gaussians.scale3d[keepmask] gaussians.scale2d = gaussians.scale2d[keepmask] gaussians.position = gaussians.position[keepmask] gaussians.rotation = gaussians.rotation[keepmask] gaussians.shcoeffs = gaussians.shcoeffs[keepmask] grad2d = grad2d[keepmask] count = count[keepmask] highgradmask = highgradmask[keepmask] # 5. Densification (Clone/Split) growscale3d = params.get('growscale3d', 0.01) growscale2d = params.get('growscale2d', 0.05) splitscalefactor = params.get('splitscalefactor', 1.6) newgaussians = [] for i in range(len(gaussians)): if not highgradmask[i]: continue g = gaussians[i] issmall = g.scale3d < growscale3d islarge2d = g.scale2d > growscale2d if issmall: clone = Gaussian( g.position.clone(), g.scale3d.clone(), g.rotation.clone(), g.opacity.clone(), g.shcoeffs.clone()) graddir = avggrad[i] / (torch.norm(avggrad[i]) + 1e-8) clone.position += graddir 0.01 newgaussians.append(clone) elif islarge2d: newscale = g.scale3d / splitscalefactor pos1, pos2 = samplefromgaussianpdf(g.position, g.covariance, 2) g1 = Gaussian(pos1, newscale, g.rotation.clone(), g.opacity.clone(), g.shcoeffs.clone()) g2 = Gaussian(pos2, newscale, g.rotation.clone(), g.opacity.clone(), g.shcoeffs.clone()) newgaussians.append(g1) newgaussians.append(g2) # Extend Gaussians after loop to avoid modifying while iterating gaussians.opacities = torch.cat([gaussians.opacities, torch.tensor([g.opacity for g in newgaussians])]) gaussians.scale3d = torch.cat([gaussians.scale3d, torch.tensor([g.scale3d for g in newgaussians])]) gaussians.scale2d = torch.cat([gaussians.scale2d, torch.tensor([g.scale2d for g in newgaussians])]) gaussians.position = torch.cat([gaussians.position, torch.stack([g.position for g in newgaussians])]) gaussians.rotation = torch.cat([gaussians.rotation, torch.stack([g.rotation for g in newgaussians])]) gaussians.shcoeffs = torch.cat([gaussians.shcoeffs, torch.stack([g.shcoeffs for g in newgaussians])]) # 6. Post-processing updatenormals(gaussians) def resetopacity(gaussians): gaussians.opacities.fill(0.01) def samplefromgaussianpdf(mean, covariance, numsamples): samples = torch.distributions.MultivariateNormal(mean, covariance).rsample((numsamples,)) return samples[0], samples[1] class Gaussian: def init(self, position, scale3d, rotation, opacity, shcoeffs): self.position = position self.scale3d = scale3d self.scale2d = scale3d 2.0 # Placeholder for 2D projection scale self.rotation = rotation self.opacity = opacity self.shcoeffs = shcoeffs self.covariance = rotation @ torch.diag(scale3d2) @ rotation.T def updatenormals(gaussians): for i in range(len(gaussians)): cov = gaussians.rotation[i] @ torch.diag(gaussians.scale3d[i]2) @ gaussians.rotation[i].T eigenvalues, eigenvectors = torch.linalg.eigh(cov) gaussians.normal = torch.cat([gaussians.normal if hasattr(gaussians, 'normal') else torch.zeroslike(gaussians.position), eigenvectors[:, 0].unsqueeze(0)]) Divergence without Floor: If using occlusion-aware densification, omitting the denominator floor (floor=0) causes training divergence on Zip-NeRF scenes within ~1,800 iterations, exceeding the 16.8M trainable limit. Over-densification: Using a threshold too low (e.g., 0.001 vs 0.002) on Mip-NeRF360 yields 4.90M Gaussians and lowers PSNR. Under-densification: Using a threshold too high (e.g., 0.004) yields 0.66M Gaussians and raises LPIPS. A regularization technique that gradually reduces opacity instead of hard resets, stabilizing gradient flow and preventing incorrect densification decisions caused by abrupt changes. A method using a first-order Taylor approximation fb(1-u) - fb(1) \approx -Jb u to estimate the cost of deleting Gaussians, where Jb is the Jacobian of the rendered image with respect to opacity multipliers. The approximation may become less accurate when many Gaussians are deleted together. Applies generalized Phong shading to opacity modulation, allowing the opacity lobe to decouple each Gaussian's contribution to exitant radiance. This provides stability against depth sorting permutations compared to methods using spherical beta functions for color. Procedures to modify Gaussians based on selected regions: Extraction (keep opacity for selected, 0 for others), Deletion (0 for selected, keep for others), and Appearance Modification (update color ci). Adds a constant floor (default 1) to the accumulated contribution in the denominator of the densification criterion to prevent score inflation when accumulated contribution is between 0 and 1. Smoothly transitions from alpha blending to opaque depth testing during optimization using a steepness parameter f and current step t, allowing high-performance real-time rendering of point clouds. Handles splat count changes and normal updates after densification/pruning, including re-querying normals from an anchor tree if lengths mismatch. Identifies under-reconstruction regions via positional gradients and overdense regions via opacity, replicating neighbors for structural completion and eliminating low-opacity Gaussians. Time Complexity: Densification is performed every 100 iterations. The cost depends on the number of Gaussians N and the number of candidates for cloning/splitting. Buffer compaction is O(N). Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians. Pruning reduces memory, while densification increases it. The method keeps the total count manageable (e.g., ~1.79M on Mip-NeRF360 subsets). Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 calibration subset (bicycle, bonsai, counter, garden), a threshold of 0.002 yields 1.79M Gaussians with best PSNR, SSIM, and GMSD. Strengths: Adapts to scene complexity, handles both under- and over-reconstruction, and prevents floaters via pruning. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of thresholds; improper thresholds lead to divergence or poor quality. The method was introduced in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). It builds on the idea of adaptive control of Gaussian primitives, allowing the model to start from sparse SfM points and densify as needed. Subsequent works have refined the thresholds and added variations like occlusion-aware criteria and opacity lobe modulation.
