name: Texel Size Adaptation and Primitive Management
head: Adaptive Texture Allocation, Primitive Management via Quantile Error
body: Texel Size Adaptation and Primitive Management is a training-time optimization routine that dynamically adjusts the resolution of per-primitive texture maps and the number of 3D Gaussian primitives to balance model capacity and appearance quality. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Density Control or GroupFlow by explicitly coupling the geometric density of primitives with the textural detail allocated to them, using quantile-based error thresholds to trigger splitting, upscaling, or downscaling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}, where each primitive k has an associated texture grid (texel map) and a computed error metric Ei. Output: Updated primitive set \mathcal{G}' with modified counts, scales, and texture resolutions. Data Structures: Primitive: Contains mean position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics, and a texture grid [Parent]. Texture Grid: A 2D array of values (channels) representing local appearance details. Resolution Definition: The texture grid resolution is defined by t2pr (texels per primitive axis). Error Metric Ei: A scalar value representing the reconstruction error for primitive i, used to rank primitives for quantile-based decisions. Parameters: \tau{tr}: Texture resolution threshold. Controls splitting aggressiveness. Starts at 64 and is progressively reduced to 32 within 7000 iterations. \tau{ds}: Downscale threshold. Controls downscaling ease. Higher values make downscaling easier, leading to simpler appearance and fewer texels. \lambda{texture}: Controls texture variance. Higher values yield smoother results; lower values reduce texel count per primitive. t2pr: Texture size per primitive (texels per axis). Initialized at iteration 500 to the closest power of two such that the smallest axis is 8 texels wide. Quantile: Top 90% of errors are considered for splitting and upscaling. Interval: Routine runs every 250 iterations until 25,000 iterations. Steps: 1. Initialization: At iteration 500, initialize texture grids to 0 and begin optimization. Set t2pr for each primitive to the closest power of two such that the smallest axis is 8 texels wide. 2. Periodic Check: If iter mod 250 == 0 and iter <= 25000: a. Compute error Ei for all primitives. b. Identify the set of primitives in the top 90% of errors. c. For each primitive k: i. Splitting: If texture resolution > τtr AND Ek is in the top 90%: Split the primitive along overflowing axes, following the parent Densification Strategy principles for replacing a parent with children [Parent]. ii. Upscaling: If t2pr > 1 AND Ek is in the top 90%: Decrease texel size (Upscale) using a scale factor of 2. iii. Downscaling: Else if Ed < τds: Increase texel size (Downscale) using a scale factor of 2. Note: The source uses Ed in the condition but does not explicitly define it beyond implying it relates to the error or texture state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texelsizeadaptationandprimitivemanagement(iteration, primitives, tautr, tauds): """ Adaptively manage primitive count and texture resolution. """ # Routine runs every 250 iterations until 25,000 if iteration % 250 != 0 or iteration > 25000: return primitives # Compute errors for all primitives errors = [p.error for p in primitives] if not errors: return primitives # Calculate the 90th percentile threshold for top 90% selection sortederrors = sorted(errors) thresholdindex = min(int(len(sortederrors) 0.9), len(sortederrors) - 1) errorthreshold = sortederrors[thresholdindex] updatedprimitives = [] for p in primitives: ishigherror = p.error >= errorthreshold # Splitting Condition if p.textureresolution > tautr and ishigherror: # Split primitive along overflowing axes # Exact splitting geometry follows parent Densification Strategy principles # Typically replaces parent with children sampled from N(mu, Sigma) with reduced scale children = splitprimitive(p) updatedprimitives.extend(children) continue # Upscaling Condition if p.t2pr > 1 and ishigherror: p.upscaletexture(scalefactor=2) p.t2pr = p.t2pr 2 # Downscaling Condition (else if attached to upscaling block) elif p.Ed < tauds: p.downscaletexture(scalefactor=2) return updatedprimitives def splitprimitive(primitive): # Standard densification: replace parent with children sampled from N(mu, Sigma) # Scale reduction: schild = sparent (5/4) / sqrt(Nchildren) return [primitive.clone() for in range(2)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hyperparameter Interdependence: Changing \tau{tr} to encourage more primitives can indirectly lead to fewer texels per primitive, as each primitive represents a more localized, simpler part of the scene. Memory Management: Pruned or split primitives require buffer compaction to maintain contiguous memory access for rasterization [Parent]. Initialization: Texture grids start at 0 and begin optimizing after 500 iterations. Time Complexity: The routine runs every 250 iterations. The cost is proportional to the number of primitives N for error computation and thresholding. Splitting and texture interpolation are constant time per primitive but increase N over time. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the total number of texels. The source reports 20.8M texels for 'drjohnson' and 9.0M for 'bonsai'. Performance: On the 'drjohnson' scene, the method achieves 77 FPS and 318MB memory with 293K points and 79.7M parameters. On 'bonsai', it achieves 35 FPS and 176MB memory with 291K points and 44.1M parameters. Strengths: Automatically adjusts model capacity based on scene complexity. Robust to different ratios of primitive and texel budgets. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \tau{tr} and \tau{ds}. The indirect effects of hyperparameters can make prediction of final model size difficult. The method was introduced by Panagiotis Papantonakis, Georgios Kopanas, Frédo Durand, and George Drettakis in "Content-Aware Texturing for Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the need for efficient representation of high-frequency details in Gaussian Splatting by decoupling geometric density from textural resolution and managing both adaptively. name: Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification
head: Inherent Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification
body:
Momentum Consistency-Guided Densification is a training optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses kinematic phase-space trajectories (momentum) to guide primitive growth, aiming to overcome floating artifacts in non-manifold regions caused by single-step gradient snapshots. It sets itself apart from standard gradient-based strategies by evaluating the cosine consistency between current gradients and accumulated historical trends, rather than relying solely on instantaneous gradient magnitude. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the accumulated momentum buffer mt for each primitive, the current loss gradient 
ablap \mathcal{L}t with respect to primitive attributes p = \{x, \alpha, s, r, c\}, and hyperparameters \gamma (momentum decay), 	au{grad} (gradient threshold), kE (densification interval), and \epsilon (stability constant). Output: A binary mask \mathbb{I}{densify} indicating which Gaussians should be densified (split or cloned) at the current step. Data Structures: Momentum Buffer (mt): A tensor matching the shape of 
ablap \mathcal{L}t, storing the exponential moving average of gradients. Initialized to zero at the start of training. Gradient Tensor (
ablap \mathcal{L}t): A tensor of shape (N, D) where N is the number of primitives and D is the attribute dimensionality. Parameters: \gamma (momentum decay factor): Balances historical trends and current observations in the momentum calculation. Value not explicitly given in sources. 	au{grad} (gradient magnitude threshold): Predefined threshold for gradient magnitude. Value not explicitly given in sources. kE (densification interval): Fixed at 100 iterations. \epsilon: Numerical stability constant to prevent division by zero. Value not explicitly given in sources. Steps: 1. Momentum Update: At every iteration t, update the momentum buffer for each Gaussian i using the exponential moving average of the current loss gradient: mt^{(i)} = \gamma \cdot m{t-1}^{(i)} + (1 - \gamma) \cdot 
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)} where 
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)} is the gradient of the loss with respect to the primitive attribute set p for Gaussian i at iteration t. 2. Consistency Score Calculation: Compute the momentum consistency score \Psii for each Gaussian i. This score measures the cosine similarity between the current gradient vector and the accumulated momentum: \Psii =  rac{mt^{(i)} \cdot 
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)}}{\|mt^{(i)}\| \cdot \|
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)}\| + \epsilon} where \cdot denotes the dot product, \|\cdot\| denotes the L2 norm, and \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. 3. Population Average Calculation: Calculate the mean consistency level  ar{\Psi} of the current primitive population:  ar{\Psi} =  rac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \Psii where N is the total number of Gaussians. 4. Densification Trigger: Determine if a Gaussian should be densified using the dynamic trigger function \mathbb{I}{densify}: \mathbb{I}{densify}^{(i)} = (\|
ablap \mathcal{L}t^{(i)}\| > 	au{grad}) \land (\Psii >  ar{\Psi}) Densification is triggered only if the gradient magnitude exceeds 	au{grad} AND the consistency score is higher than the population average. 5. Execution: If \mathbb{I}{densify}^{(i)} is true, perform densification operations (splitting or cloning) as defined in the parent Densification Strategy. This check is performed every kE = 100 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def momentumconsistencydensification(gaussians, momentumbuffer, lossgradients, gamma, taugrad, epsilon, kE, currentiter): """ Performs one step of momentum consistency-guided densification. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives. momentumbuffer: 2D list of shape (N, D) storing momentum for all attributes. lossgradients: 2D list of shape (N, D) storing gradients for all attributes. gamma: Momentum decay factor. taugrad: Gradient magnitude threshold. epsilon: Numerical stability constant. kE: Densification interval. currentiter: Current training iteration. Returns: densifymask: Boolean list of length N indicating which Gaussians to densify. newmomentumbuffer: Updated 2D list of shape (N, D). """ N = len(gaussians) D = len(lossgradients[0]) newmomentum = [[0.0] D for in range(N)] # 1. Momentum Update for i in range(N): for d in range(D): newmomentum[i][d] = gamma momentumbuffer[i][d] + (1 - gamma) lossgradients[i][d] # Only evaluate densification at interval kE if currentiter % kE != 0: return [False] N, newmomentum # 2. Consistency Score Calculation consistencyscores = [] gradmagnitudes = [] for i in range(N): dotprod = sum(newmomentum[i][d] lossgradients[i][d] for d in range(D)) normm = sum(newmomentum[i][d] 2 for d in range(D)) 0.5 normg = sum(lossgradients[i][d] 2 for d in range(D)) 0.5 consistencyscores.append(dotprod / (normm normg + epsilon)) gradmagnitudes.append(normg) # 3. Population Average meanconsistency = sum(consistencyscores) / N # 4. Densification Trigger densifymask = [] for i in range(N): highgrad = gradmagnitudes[i] > taugrad highconsistency = consistencyscores[i] > meanconsistency densifymask.append(highgrad and highconsistency) return densifymask, newmomentum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Artifacts: Standard gradient-based strategies can create floating artifacts in non-manifold regions due to reliance on single-step gradient snapshots. This method mitigates this by using momentum, which represents more deterministic historical motion trends. Numerical Stability: The denominator in the consistency score calculation includes \epsilon to prevent division by zero when norms are near zero. Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The choice of \gamma and 	au{grad} is critical. The source does not provide specific values, implying they may require tuning or follow default 3DGS configurations. Time Complexity: The additional cost per iteration is the momentum update and consistency score calculation, which are O(N \cdot D) operations where N is the number of Gaussians and D is the attribute dimensionality. The densification check itself is O(N). This is lightweight compared to the rendering and gradient computation steps. Memory Complexity: Requires an additional momentum buffer of size O(N \cdot D). Strengths: Reduces floating artifacts in complex/non-manifold regions by leveraging historical gradient information. Scene-adaptive without manual hyperparameter search for the consistency threshold (uses population mean). Limitations: Requires maintaining an additional buffer. Performance depends on the choice of \gamma and 	au{grad}. When to use: When standard densification leads to floating artifacts or noisy geometry in non-manifold regions. When not to use: If memory is extremely constrained (due to the momentum buffer) or if the scene is simple and standard densification suffices. Origin: Proposed in the ACE-GS paper. History: Developed to address limitations of standard gradient-based densification in 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically the issue of floating artifacts in non-manifold regions. Usage: Used in the ACE-GS framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. ACE-GS: Acing the Trade-off with Accurate, Compact and Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.21244, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: GSGEN Appearance Refinement
body:
GSGEN Appearance Refinement is an iterative optimization stage that improves fine-grained visual details in text-to-3D generation while preserving the fundamental geometry established during the preceding geometry optimization phase. It addresses the limitations of standard gradient-based densification by introducing a compactness-based strategy to fill geometric holes and employs specific regularization losses to prevent overfitting and maintain 3D consistency. Unlike sibling methods that rely primarily on positional gradients or opacity thresholds, GSGEN explicitly incorporates a 3D Stable Diffusion Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss and a mean position penalty to ensure structural integrity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} initialized from the geometry optimization stage, where each Gaussian gi has position pi, opacity oi, scale, rotation, and spherical harmonic coefficients. A pre-trained 2D diffusion model (Stable Diffusion). Output: Refined set of 3D Gaussians with improved appearance and denser, more complete geometry. Data Structures: KD-Tree: Stores Gaussian positions for efficient nearest-neighbor queries. Gaussian Attributes: Position pi \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}, radius ri, scale, rotation, SH coefficients. Parameters: \lambda{SDS} = 0.1: Weight for the 3D SDS loss. \lambda{mean} = 1.0: Weight for the mean position regularization loss. \lambda{opacity} = 100.0: Weight for the opacity regularization loss. \alpha{min}: Threshold for pruning Gaussians with low opacity. K: Number of nearest neighbors considered for compactness-based densification. N{views}: Number of views sampled per iteration using stratified sampling on azimuth. Steps: 1. Loss Computation: For each iteration, compute the total refinement loss gradient 
abla	heta L{refine} for each Gaussian parameter 	heta: 
abla	heta L{refine} = \lambda{SDS} \mathbb{E}{\epsilonI, t} \left[ wI(t) (\epsilon\phi(xt; y, t) - \epsilonI)  rac{\partial x}{\partial 	heta} ight] + \lambda{mean} \sumi 
abla	heta ||pi|| + \lambda{opacity} \sumi 
abla	heta 	ext{sg}(||pi||) \cdot oi Where: \epsilon\phi(xt; y, t) is the noise prediction from the diffusion model \phi given noisy image xt, text prompt y, and timestep t. \epsilonI is the ground truth noise sampled from a standard normal distribution. wI(t) is the weighting function for the SDS loss.  rac{\partial x}{\partial 	heta} is the gradient of the rendered image x with respect to the Gaussian parameters 	heta. ||pi|| is the Euclidean norm of the position of the i-th Gaussian. 	ext{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operation. oi is the opacity of the i-th Gaussian. 2. Compactness-Based Densification: For each Gaussian gi, query its K nearest neighbors using the KD-Tree. For each neighbor gj, if the distance d(pi, pj) between the centers is smaller than the sum of their radii (ri + rj), perform densification: Add a new Gaussian positioned between gi and gj. The radius of the new Gaussian is equal to the residual distance (ri + rj - d(pi, pj)). This step aims to "fill the holes" and create a more complete geometry structure. 3. Opacity Regularization and Pruning: Add an extra loss term to regularize opacity, proportional to the distance of the Gaussian to the center of the scene. Periodically (every N iterations, consistent with parent [Parent]), remove Gaussians with opacity oi < \alpha{min}. 4. Geometric Consistency Penalty: The term \lambda{mean} \sumi 
abla	heta ||pi|| penalizes Gaussians that deviate significantly from their positions obtained during the preceding geometry optimization stage. This ensures that the refinement process does not distort the fundamental 3D structure. 5. Optimization Step: Update Gaussian parameters 	heta using the computed gradients 
abla	heta L{refine}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gsgenappearancerefinement(gaussians, diffusionmodel, textprompt, numiterations, K, alphamin, lambdasds, lambdamean, lambdaopacity, pruneinterval=100): """ GSGEN Appearance Refinement stage. Args: gaussians: List of dicts with keys: pos (3,), opacity (float), radius (float), params (np.array) diffusionmodel: Object with method predictnoise(xt, prompt, t) and numtimesteps textprompt: Text prompt for generation numiterations: Number of refinement iterations K: Number of nearest neighbors for compactness-based densification alphamin: Opacity threshold for pruning lambdasds: Weight for SDS loss lambdamean: Weight for mean position regularization lambdaopacity: Weight for opacity regularization pruneinterval: Iterations between pruning steps Returns: Refined gaussians list """ positions = np.array([g['pos'] for g in gaussians]) radii = np.array([g['radius'] for g in gaussians]) for iteration in range(numiterations): gradients = {g: np.zeroslike(g['params']) for g in gaussians} # Stratified sampling on azimuth for camera positions views = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, len(gaussians), endpoint=False) for g in gaussians: # Render image and compute gradients w.r.t Gaussian parameters renderedimg = renderimage(gaussians, views) gradrender = computerenderergradient(renderedimg, g['params']) # 1. 3D SDS Loss term epsilonI = np.random.randn(renderedimg.shape) t = np.random.randint(0, diffusionmodel.numtimesteps) xt = addnoise(renderedimg, t) epsilonpred = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(xt, textprompt, t) wt = computesdsweight(t) gradsds = wt (epsilonpred - epsilonI) gradrender gradients[g] += lambdasds gradsds # 2. Mean position regularization: ||pi|| posnorm = np.linalg.norm(g['pos']) gradmean = lambdamean (g['pos'] / posnorm) if posnorm > 1e-8 else np.zeros(3) gradients[g] += gradmean # 3. Opacity regularization: sg(||pi||) oi # sg stops gradient through position, so this only affects opacity parameter opacityreg = np.abs(posnorm) g['opacity'] gradopacity = lambdaopacity np.oneslike(g['params']) # Gradient w.r.t opacity gradients[g] += gradopacity # Update parameters for g in gaussians: g['params'] -= gradients[g] # Compactness-based densification newgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): # Find K nearest neighbors dists = np.linalg.norm(positions - g['pos'], axis=1) dists[i] = np.inf # Exclude self neighborindices = np.argsort(dists)[:K] for j in neighborindices: neighbor = gaussians[j] dist = np.linalg.norm(g['pos'] - neighbor['pos']) sumradii = g['radius'] + neighbor['radius'] if dist < sumradii: residualradius = sumradii - dist midpos = (g['pos'] + neighbor['pos']) / 2.0 newg = {'pos': midpos, 'opacity': 0.5, 'radius': residualradius, 'params': g['params'].copy()} newgaussians.append(newg) gaussians.extend(newgaussians) positions = np.array([g['pos'] for g in gaussians]) radii = np.array([g['radius'] for g in gaussians]) # Pruning if iteration % pruneinterval == 0: gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g['opacity'] >= alphamin] return gaussians def renderimage(gaussians, views): # Differentiable rasterization of 3D Gaussians to 2D images return np.zeros((len(views), 256, 256, 3)) def computerenderergradient(renderedimg, params): # Backpropagation through the differentiable rasterizer return np.zeroslike(params) def addnoise(img, t): # Linear noise schedule addition return img + 0.1 np.random.randn(img.shape) def computesdsweight(t): # Standard SDS weighting function return 1.0 def sampleviewsstratifiedazimuth(n): # Returns evenly spaced azimuth angles return np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, n, endpoint=False) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blurry Appearance: A large threshold for compactness-based densification leads to a blurry appearance, which the method mitigates by supplementing positional gradient-based splitting. Geometry Distortion: Without the mean position regularization, the SDS loss might cause the geometry to drift or distort, exacerbating the Janus problem. Opacity Instability: Low opacity Gaussians can cause noise in the rendering; pruning them periodically is essential for stability. Joint optimization of material properties M = {(aj, rj, mj)} and environment lighting L over 7000 additional iterations, using re-rendering loss Lcolor augmented with segmentation, intrinsic image decomposition, and diffusion priors to resolve ill-posedness and overfitting. Time Complexity: The compactness-based densification step requires O(N \log N) for KD-Tree construction and O(N \cdot K) for neighbor queries per iteration, where N is the number of Gaussians and K is the number of neighbors. The SDS loss computation involves rendering and backpropagation through the diffusion model, which is computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of Gaussians, which can increase significantly due to compactness-based densification. Performance: GSGEN produces more complete geometry structures and finer details compared to methods relying solely on gradient-based densification. It effectively mitigates the Janus problem. Strengths: Preserves geometry while improving appearance; fills holes in the Gaussian representation; reduces overfitting to specific views. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the diffusion model guidance and densification steps; requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (\lambda{SDS}, \lambda{mean}, \lambda{opacity}). When to use: When generating 3D assets from text prompts where geometric consistency and fine detail are critical, and the initial geometry optimization has produced a sparse or incomplete representation. GSGEN (Gaussian Splatting for Generation) was introduced in the paper "Text-to-3D using Gaussian Splatting". The appearance refinement stage was developed to address the challenges of overfitting and geometric inconsistency in text-to-3D generation methods that use 3D Gaussian Splatting as the underlying representation. The method integrates a 3D SDS loss with a pre-trained point cloud diffusion model to shape a 3D-consistent geometry, mitigating the Janus problem and generating more sensible geometry. name: GAINS Stage II: Material Properties
head: GAINS Material Optimization, Joint Material and Lighting Optimization
body: This method jointly optimizes material properties and environment lighting to resolve the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering from sparse views, preventing overfitting and enabling robust relighting. It distinguishes itself from its parent GSGEN Appearance Refinement by introducing segmentation-based intra-class consistency, intrinsic image decomposition priors, and multi-illuminated score distillation to regularize material estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Gaussian primitives G (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients) from Stage I; material parameters M = \{aj, rj, mj\} (albedo, roughness, metallicity) for each Gaussian j; environment lighting L; input images Ii with known intrinsics. Outputs: Optimized material parameters M, environment lighting L, and updated Gaussian class membership vectors Ej. Data Structures: Gaussian Class Membership: Each Gaussian j is extended with a one-hot vector Ej \in \{0, 1\}^K, where K is the number of semantic classes. Ej encodes the Gaussian's class membership for segmentation guidance. Material Parameters: Stored per Gaussian as aj (albedo), rj (roughness), and mj (metallicity). Numbered Steps: 1. Segmentation Mask Lifting: Sample V=100 novel viewpoints orbiting the scenery. Render SH-colored images \{\hat{I}v\}{v=1}^V from these viewpoints. Generate segmentation masks for each \hat{I}v using SAM. Extract features f{v,s} = [g{v,s}, h{v,s}] for each mask region s in view v, where g{v,s} are CLIP features and h{v,s} are DINOv2 features. For each view, lift the associated mask and features to the Gaussian that contributes most (α-blending wise). Merge collected Gaussian objects from previous lifting operations with geometric and feature similarity scores to assign class labels Ej. 2. Intra-Class Consistency (ICC) Loss Calculation: For each captured viewpoint i, identify the set of masks Si rendered from that view. Compute the ICC loss \mathcal{L}{ICC} using the formula below, where si \in Si is a mask region, A{si} is the rendered masked albedo, R{si} is the rendered masked roughness, M{si} is the rendered masked metallicity, and E{si} is the masked re-render loss. Apply the scaling function \gamma(|si|) = \exp(25 \cdot |I| / |si|), where |I| is the total image area and |si| is the number of pixels in the mask (denoted as ||si||^2 in the source). 3. Intrinsic Image Decomposition (IID) Loss Calculation: Obtain the IID diffuse albedo \hat{A}i for each captured image Ii using Teamwork [24] (or RGB2X [43] for outdoor data). Compute the IID loss \mathcal{L}{IID} = \beta(\tau) \cdot ||Ai - \hat{A}i||2^2, where Ai is the rendered diffuse albedo. Apply the linearly decreasing weight \beta(\tau) based on the current iteration step \tau to mitigate view-inconsistency in IID estimates. IID supervision is not applied to roughness and metallicity due to their lower robustness and higher view-inconsistency. 4. Multi-Illuminated Score Distillation Sampling (MI-SDS) Loss Calculation: Start diffusion guidance after 3000 optimization steps. Render relit images R{mat}(Cj, G, M, El) from a novel view Cj under randomly selected lighting El from a predetermined set \{El\}{l=1}^{|E|}. Compute the noisy latent Z{jl} = \alphat R{mat}(Cj, G, M, El) + \sigmat \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) and \alphat, \sigmat are diffusion schedule parameters. Calculate the MI-SDS loss \mathcal{L}{MI-SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} w(t) ||\epsilon\phi(Z{jl}; t) - \epsilon||2^2, where \epsilon\phi is the pretrained diffusion model. Use a guidance scale of 100. 5. Final Loss Combination and Optimization: Combine all losses: \mathcal{L}{mat} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda{ICC} \mathcal{L}{ICC} + \lambda{IID} \mathcal{L}{IID} + \lambda{MI-SDS} \mathcal{L}{MI-SDS} + \lambda{TV}\mathcal{L}{TV}. \mathcal{L}{TV} is a total variation loss on the reconstructed lighting, acting as a smoothing term. Optimize M and L for 7000 additional iterations. Formulas: The Intra-Class Consistency loss \mathcal{L}{ICC} is defined as: \mathcal{L}{ICC} = \frac{1}{|Si|} \sum{si \in Si} \gamma(|si|) \cdot \left( \mathcal{L}{r,m} + \mathcal{L}a + \mathcal{L}e \right) Where the components are: \mathcal{L}{r,m} = \text{Var}(R{si}) + \text{Var}(M{si}) \mathcal{L}a = \left( (1-R{si}) + M{si} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{3} \sum{c=1}^3 \text{Var}(A{si}^{(c)}) \mathcal{L}e = \left( (1-M{si}) + R{si} \right) \cdot E{si} The scaling function is: \gamma(|si|) = \exp\left(25 \cdot \frac{|I|}{|si|}\right) The IID loss is: \mathcal{L}{IID} = \beta(\tau) \cdot ||Ai - \hat{A}i||2^2 The MI-SDS loss is: \mathcal{L}{MI-SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} w(t) ||\epsilon\phi(Z{jl}; t) - \epsilon||2^2 Parameters: \lambda{ICC} = 0.1 \lambda{IID} = 2 \lambda{MI-SDS} = 0.0001 \lambda{TV} = 0.1 V = 100 (number of sampled novel viewpoints) MI-SDS guidance scale: 100 MI-SDS start step: 3000 Optimization iterations: 7000 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posedness: Multiple combinations of material M and lighting L produce similar appearances, leading to ambiguous estimates, especially with sparse views. Mitigated by segmentation, IID, and diffusion priors. IID View-Inconsistency: IID diffuse albedo estimates may be view-inconsistent. Mitigated by weighting the loss with \beta(\tau), which linearly decreases over iterations. Specular/Metallicity IID: IID supervision is avoided for specular roughness and metallicity as these parameters are less robust and exhibit more inconsistencies across views. Time Complexity: Dominated by 7000 optimization iterations, rendering 100 novel views for segmentation lifting, and diffusion model inference for MI-SDS. Memory Complexity: Requires storing one-hot class vectors Ej for all Gaussians and caching features/masks during the lifting phase. Strengths: Produces robust, relightable material properties even from sparse inputs by regularizing against overfitting. Limitations: Relies on external models (SAM, CLIP, DINOv2, Teamwork/RGB2X, Diffusion) which may introduce errors or inconsistencies. The lifting process assumes accurate segmentation and feature matching. GAINS (Gaussian-Based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures) was introduced by P. Noras et al. in 2024. Stage II specifically addresses the material estimation phase, building on the geometry reconstruction from Stage I. The method is designed for inverse rendering from sparse multi-view captures, aiming to produce intrinsic images (albedo, roughness, metallicity) and environment lighting suitable for relighting. GAINS: Gaussian-Based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37602-218, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Multi-view Consistency and Scoring
body: Multi-view Consistency and Scoring is a family of densification strategies for 3D Gaussian Splatting that evaluates Gaussian primitives across multiple camera views to guide densification and pruning operations. It builds on Densification Strategy by incorporating multi-view photometric loss and alpha contributions to identify regions requiring refinement or removal. Unlike its siblings Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning and Multi-View Consistency Scoring for Densification, this family explicitly integrates importance and pruning scores derived from multi-view photometric loss and alpha contributions into the standard gradient masks, ensuring that densification occurs only where geometry is consistently unresolved across views. The shared principles for this family are defined in Densification Strategy. This method replaces single-view gradient-based criteria with multi-view evaluation to constrain Gaussian count and ensure structural consistency Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning. It differs from standard gradient-based densification by explicitly integrating importance and pruning scores derived from photometric loss and alpha contributions into the standard gradient masks Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning. Choose this method when preventing overfitting to single views and reducing excessive Gaussian proliferation is critical Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning. This method computes per-Gaussian scores based on multi-view photometric consistency to guide both densification and pruning Multi-View Consistency Scoring for Densification. It differs from standard gradient-based densification by aggregating L1 reconstruction errors across multiple camera views to identify Gaussians that consistently fail to reconstruct scene geometry or appearance Multi-View Consistency Scoring for Densification. Choose this method when normalized scoring across views is required to prioritize primitives for refinement Multi-View Consistency Scoring for Densification. This module adjusts the densification threshold based on multi-view discrepancies to help 3D Gaussians fit each view better and capture finer scene details. It differs from score-based methods by dynamically modifying the baseline threshold \beta using a Heaviside step function H(\cdot) to gate discrepancy calculations, returning 1 if the input is \ge 0 to prevent negative discrepancies from triggering densification. Choose this method when explicit threshold modulation based on inter-view disagreement is preferred over accumulation-based scoring. The adjusted threshold is defined as \hat{\beta} = \beta - \frac{\beta}{2} H(r\tau^i - 1), where \tau adjusts the extent of the discrepancy between each camera and \beta is the original baseline threshold. The concept of multi-view consistency in Gaussian Splatting was introduced in MVGS (Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting for Novel View Synthesis). The method regulates densification through multi-view constraints to facilitate better multi-view training and capture finer scene details. MVGS: Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting for Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2410.02103, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning
head: Multi-view Alphabased Densification and Pruning strategy, Multi-view Consistency-Guided Densification, Stratified Camera Sampling, Stratified Multi-view Alpha-Error Accumulation
body: Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning is a training optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces single-view gradient-based criteria with multi-view consistency metrics to constrain Gaussian count and prevent overfitting. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on positional gradients from a single view—prone to excessive primitive production and redundancy—this method leverages alpha-weighted error accumulation across multiple sampled viewpoints to accurately identify regions requiring densification and primitives eligible for pruning. It builds on Multi-view Consistency and Scoring by operationalizing consistency checks into specific clone, split, and prune masks. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gN\}, where each gk has mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak, opacity ok, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}k. Training camera set \mathcal{C} with positions ti and viewing directions vi. Ground truth images C{gt}. Hyperparameters: \tau^+: Loss threshold for poor reconstruction (default: 0.1). \tau^-: Loss threshold for well-reconstructed regions (default: 0.01). Q\tau^+: Quantile for densification importance (default: 0.6). Q\tau^-: Quantile for pruning (default: 0.1). N{cam}: Number of cameras to sample (default: 6). \lambda: Weight controlling the balance between L1 and DSSIM loss components. o{min}: Opacity threshold for eliminating Gaussian points. Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian primitives \mathcal{G}' after cloning, splitting, and pruning operations. Binary masks \mathcal{M}{clone} and \mathcal{M}{split} identifying Gaussians to modify. Pruning mask \mathcal{M}{prune} identifying Gaussians to remove. Metric Map (M): A binary map M \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W} per view, where H, W are image dimensions. M{u,v}^{+, c} = 1 if pixel (u,v) in view c has high error. M{u,v}^{-, c} = 1 if pixel (u,v) in view c has low error. Importance/Pruning Scores (S^+, S^-): Arrays of size N (number of Gaussians). Si^+: Accumulated alpha-weighted error for Gaussian i. Si^-: Accumulated loss-weighted alpha for Gaussian i. Base Masks (\mathcal{M}{clone}^{base}, \mathcal{M}{split}^{base}): Binary masks derived from standard positional gradient thresholds \|\nabla{\mui} \mathcal{L}\|2 > \tau{grad}. 1. Stratified Camera Sampling: To ensure comprehensive geometric coverage and alleviate view redundancy, partition the training camera set \mathcal{C} into angular bins defined with respect to the scene center x^. Estimate x^ by solving the linear least-squares system \sum{i=1}^{N{cam}} Pi x^ = \sum{i=1}^{N{cam}} Pi ti, where Pi = I - vi vi^T is the projection matrix onto the subspace orthogonal to the i-th ray. Transform camera positions ri = ti - x^ into spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi, \rho) where \theta = \text{arctan2}(ry, rx), \phi = \arcsin(rz/\|ri\|), and \rho = \|ri\|. Discretize angular space into M\theta azimuth and M\phi elevation bins, group cameras by bin indices, and uniformly sample one representative from each non-empty bin. Shuffle and truncate selected candidates to a computational budget K, yielding a camera subset \mathcal{C}{sample} with |\mathcal{C}{sample}| = N{cam}. 2. Render and Compute Loss: For each camera c \in \mathcal{C}{sample}, render the current Gaussian primitives to obtain image C^c. Compute the pixel-wise photometric loss \mathcal{L}{u,v}^c using the hybrid objective: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1(C, C{gt}) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{DSSIM}(C, C{gt}) where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 distance and \mathcal{L}{DSSIM} is the difference in Structural Similarity. 3. Generate Metric Maps: For each view c, create binary metric maps M^{c,+} and M^{c,-} to flag regions of poor and high-quality reconstruction, respectively: M{u,v}^{c,+} = \mathbb{I}(\mathcal{L}{u,v}^c > \tau^+) M{u,v}^{c,-} = \mathbb{I}(\mathcal{L}{u,v}^c < \tau^-) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. Pixels with M{u,v}^{c,+}=1 are marked as needing densification; pixels with M{u,v}^{c,-}=1 are marked as well-reconstructed (candidates for pruning). 4. Compute Multi-view Alpha-Weighted Scores: Map the 2D image-space errors back to 3D Gaussian primitives. For each Gaussian i, compute the importance score Si^+ and pruning score Si^- by summing contributions across all sampled views c=0 \dots N{cam}-1 and all flagged pixels \Omega^c: Si^+ = \sum{c=0}^{N{cam}-1} \sum{(u,v) \in \Omega^c{+}} \alphai^c \cdot M{u,v}^{c,+} Si^- = \sum{c=0}^{N{cam}-1} \sum{(u,v) \in \Omega^c{-}} \mathcal{L}{u,v}^c \cdot \alphai^c \cdot M{u,v}^{c,-} Here, \alphai^c is the alpha value of Gaussian i projected onto the image plane for view c, calculated as: \alphai^c = oi \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \Delta xi^T \Sigmai^{-1} \Delta xi\right) where oi is the base opacity, \Delta xi is the 2D offset from the Gaussian center to the pixel, and \Sigmai is the projected 2D covariance matrix. \Omega^c{+} denotes pixels flagged by M^{c,+} and \Omega^c{-} denotes pixels flagged by M^{c,-}. 5. Determine Final Densification Masks: Intersect the base gradient-based masks with the importance quantile filter to ensure multi-view consistency. A Gaussian is selected for cloning or splitting only if it meets the base gradient threshold AND its importance score Si^+ exceeds the quantile Q\tau^+ of the distribution of all S^+ scores: \mathcal{M}{clone} = \mathcal{M}{clone}^{base} \land (S^+ > Q\tau^+(S^+)) \mathcal{M}{split} = \mathcal{M}{split}^{base} \land (S^+ > Q\tau^+(S^+)) where Q\tau^+(S^+) is the value at the Q\tau^+ quantile of the importance scores. 6. Determine Pruning Mask: Identify Gaussians for pruning based on the pruning score Si^- and the quantile Q\tau^-. A Gaussian is pruned if its opacity oi falls below o{min} AND its pruning score Si^- exceeds the quantile Q\tau^- of the distribution of all S^- scores: \mathcal{M}{prune} = (oi < o{min}) \land (S^- > Q\tau^-(S^-)) A larger S^- indicates the Gaussian impacts more low-error pixel regions, effectively flagging it as an artifact or redundant point. 7. Execute Operations: Clone: For each i where \mathcal{M}{clone}[i] is true, create a copy of gi. Split: For each i where \mathcal{M}{split}[i] is true, replace gi with children sampled from \mathcal{N}(\mui, \Sigmai) [Parent]. Prune: Remove Gaussians identified in \mathcal{M}{prune} [Parent]. Compaction: Re-index the Gaussian array to maintain contiguous memory access [Parent]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiviewalphadensificationpruning(Gaussians, Cameras, GTImages, tauplus=0.1, tauminus=0.01, qtauplus=0.6, qtauminus=0.1, ncam=6, lambdadssim=0.2, omin=0.01): """ Performs multi-view alpha-based densification and pruning. Args: Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: position (3,) cov: covariance matrix (3,3) alpha: opacity (scalar) sh: spherical harmonic coefficients gradnorm: accumulated positional gradient norm (scalar) Cameras: List of camera objects with projection/rendering capabilities. GTImages: Ground truth images corresponding to Cameras. tauplus: Threshold for poor reconstruction (high loss). tauminus: Threshold for well-reconstructed (low loss). qtauplus: Quantile for importance-based densification. qtauminus: Quantile for pruning. ncam: Number of cameras to sample. lambdadssim: Weight for DSSIM loss. omin: Opacity threshold for pruning. Returns: Updated Gaussians list. """ # 1. Stratified Camera Sampling # Estimate scene center via least squares, convert to spherical coords, # bin angular space, sample one per non-empty bin, shuffle/truncate to ncam. sampledcameras = stratifiedsamplecameras(Cameras, ncam) # Initialize scores importancescores = [0.0] len(Gaussians) pruningscores = [0.0] len(Gaussians) # 2. Render and Compute Loss for Sampled Views for cam in sampledcameras: # Render current Gaussians to get image C C = render(Gaussians, cam) # Compute Photometric Loss L = (1-lambda)L1 + lambdaLDSSIM lossmap = computephotometricloss(C, GTImages[cam.id], lambdadssim) # 3. Generate Metric Maps # Mplus: 1 where loss > tauplus (poor reconstruction) # Mminus: 1 where loss < tauminus (well reconstructed) maskplus = (lossmap > tauplus).astype(float) maskminus = (lossmap < tauminus).astype(float) # 4. Compute Multi-view Alpha-Weighted Scores # Project Gaussians to 2D for this camera to get alpha contributions projectedgaussians = projectto2d(Gaussians, cam) for i, gproj in enumerate(projectedgaussians): # Get alpha for this Gaussian at all pixels alphamap = gproj.alphamap # Importance Score: Sum alpha Mplus over all pixels importancescores[i] += sum(alphamap maskplus) # Pruning Score: Sum loss alpha Mminus over all pixels pruningscores[i] += sum(lossmap alphamap maskminus) # 5. Determine Final Densification Masks # Base masks from standard 3DGS gradient threshold gradthreshold = getgradientthreshold() baseclonemask = [g.gradnorm > gradthreshold for g in Gaussians] basesplitmask = [g.gradnorm > gradthreshold for g in Gaussians] # Compute quantiles qvalplus = computequantile(importancescores, qtauplus) # Final masks: Base AND Importance > Quantile finalclonemask = [baseclonemask[i] and (importancescores[i] > qvalplus) for i in range(len(Gaussians))] finalsplitmask = [basesplitmask[i] and (importancescores[i] > qvalplus) for i in range(len(Gaussians))] # 6. Determine Pruning Mask # Prune if opacity < omin AND pruning score > quantile qvalminus = computequantile(pruningscores, qtauminus) prunemask = [(Gaussians[i].alpha < omin) and (pruningscores[i] > qvalminus) for i in range(len(Gaussians))] # 7. Execute Operations finalgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(Gaussians): isclone = finalclonemask[i] issplit = finalsplitmask[i] isprune = prunemask[i] if isprune: continue # Remove elif issplit: children = splitgaussian(g, nchildren=2) finalgaussians.extend(children) elif isclone: clone = copygaussian(g) finalgaussians.append(g) # Keep original finalgaussians.append(clone) # Add clone else: finalgaussians.append(g) return finalgaussians def computephotometricloss(C, Cgt, lambdadssim): l1loss = sum(abs(C - Cgt), axis=-1) # Per pixel L1 dssimloss = 1.0 - computedssim(C, Cgt) # Per pixel DSSIM difference return (1 - lambdadssim) l1loss + lambdadssim dssimloss def computedssim(C1, C2): # Standard DSSIM implementation return sum(sum(C1 C2)) / (sum(C12) sum(C22)) # Placeholder for standard SSIM kernel def projectto2d(Gaussians, cam): # Projects 3D Gaussians to 2D image plane # Returns list of objects with alphamap (HxW) pass def splitgaussian(g, nchildren=2): # Sample nchildren from N(g.mu, g.cov) # Reduce scale by factor 5/4 1/sqrt(nchildren) # Copy SH and alpha pass def copygaussian(g): # Deep copy of Gaussian pass def stratifiedsamplecameras(Cameras, ncam): # Estimate scene center x via least squares # Transform to spherical coords, bin, sample, shuffle, truncate pass def getgradientthreshold(): # Returns standard 3DGS gradient threshold pass def computequantile(scores, q): # Returns the value at quantile q sortedscores = sorted(scores) idx = int(q len(sortedscores)) return sortedscores[min(idx, len(sortedscores)-1)] Overfitting to Single View: Standard single-view gradient-based densification is prone to producing excessive Gaussians and overfitting to a specific view. This method mitigates this by requiring multi-view consistency. Excessive Gaussian Count: Relying solely on single-view gradients results in excessive and redundant Gaussian densification, increasing memory usage and storage cost while reducing FPS. Multi-view pruning significantly reduces total Gaussian count. Quantile Sensitivity: Larger values of Q\tau^+ hinder densification, potentially underfitting complex geometry. Smaller values of Q\tau^- result in more aggressive pruning, which may harm rendering performance if too aggressive. Camera Sampling: Increasing views from 2 to 6 yields significant PSNR improvement and reduces Gaussian count. The default N{cam}=6 provides a superior trade-off between rendering performance and training burden. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead for rendering N{cam} views and computing metric maps and scores. Rendering N{cam} views per densification step increases training time per iteration compared to single-view gradient checks, but the reduced Gaussian count leads to faster rendering during inference and potentially fewer total iterations due to better convergence. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduces memory usage and storage cost compared to single-view methods by limiting the total number of Gaussians. Performance: On RTX 4090, Flux-GS with this strategy achieves competitive visual quality with substantially fewer parameters and faster training times compared to standard 3DGS. It enables real-time mobile rendering by maintaining a compact representation. Strengths: Ensures multi-view structure consistency, accurately prunes redundant primitives, and avoids overfitting. Limitations: Requires rendering multiple views during training, which increases per-iteration compute cost. Performance is sensitive to the choice of quantiles and loss thresholds. Origin: Proposed by Du et al. in "Monte Carlo Energy Aggregation for Mobile 3D Gaussian Splatting" (Flux-GS). Context: Developed to address the inefficiency of standard 3DGS densification, which lacks multi-view structure consistency and produces excessive primitives. Application: Designed for real-time mobile rendering, offering a robust and scalable solution for high-fidelity 3D scene representation on everyday hardware. name: Multi-View Consistency Scoring for Densification
head: gaussian pruning and densification score
body: This method computes per-Gaussian scores based on multi-view photometric consistency to guide both densification (importance) and pruning operations during 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. It differs from standard gradient-based densification by explicitly aggregating binary error flags across multiple camera views to identify regions with persistent reconstruction errors, and normalizes the accumulated loss to prioritize primitives for refinement. It builds on Multi-view Consistency and Scoring. Inputs: camlist: List of viewpoint camera objects to render from. gaussians: Current Gaussian representation (means, covariances, opacities, SH coefficients). pipe: Rendering pipeline/context required by the renderer. bg: Background tensor used for rendering. args: Runtime configuration object containing lossthresh (threshold for high-error classification) and mult (scaling factor for rendering). DENSIFY: Boolean flag. If True, computes and returns importance score for densification; if False, computes only pruning score. Outputs: importancescore: Per-Gaussian integer counts of views marking the Gaussian as high-error, floor-averaged across views. Only returned if DENSIFY is True. pruningscore: Normalized (0..1) per-Gaussian score used to prioritize densification or pruning. Higher scores indicate worse reconstruction consistency. Data Structures: fullmetriccounts: Tensor of shape (N,) storing the accumulated count of high-error views per Gaussian. Initialized to None. fullmetricscore: Tensor of shape (N,) storing the accumulated weighted photometric loss per Gaussian. Initialized to None. metricmap: Binary tensor of shape (H, W) indicating which pixels have high loss. Steps: 1. Initialize fullmetriccounts and fullmetricscore to None. 2. Loop over each view index v in camlist: a. Retrieve myviewpointcam = camlist[v]. b. Render the image using the current Gaussians: I{\text{render}} = \text{render\fastgs}(my\viewpoint\cam, \text{gaussians}, \text{pipe}, \text{bg}, \text{args.mult}). c. Compute the photometric loss Lv for this view: Lv = \text{compute\photometric\loss}(my\viewpoint\cam, I{\text{render}}). d. Retrieve the ground truth image I{\text{gt}} = my\viewpoint\cam.\text{original\image}.\text{cuda}(). e. Compute the normalized L1 loss map: L{\text{norm}} = \text{get\loss}(I{\text{render}}, I{\text{gt}}). f. Create a binary metric map where pixels with loss exceeding the threshold are marked as 1: M = (L{\text{norm}} > \text{args.loss\thresh}).\text{int}(). g. Render again with metric collection enabled to accumulate per-Gaussian contributions: \text{render\pkg} = \text{render\fastgs}(my\viewpoint\cam, \text{gaussians}, \text{pipe}, \text{bg}, \text{args.mult}, \text{get\flag}=\text{True}, \text{metric\map}=M). h. Extract the accumulated loss counts for this view: Cv = \text{render\pkg}[\text{"accum\metric\counts"}]. i. Update global accumulators: If fullmetriccounts is None, set fullmetriccounts = Cv. Else, fullmetriccounts += Cv. If fullmetricscore is None, set fullmetricscore = Lv \cdot Cv. Else, fullmetricscore += Lv \cdot Cv. 3. Compute the pruning score by normalizing fullmetricscore to the range [0, 1]: \text{pruning\score} = \frac{\text{full\metric\score} - \min(\text{full\metric\score})}{\max(\text{full\metric\score}) - \min(\text{full\metric\score})}. 4. If DENSIFY is True, compute the importance score by floor-dividing the total counts by the number of views: \text{importance\score} = \lfloor \text{full\metric\counts} / |\text{camlist}| \rfloor Else, set importancescore to None. 5. Return importancescore and pruningscore. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computegaussianscorefastgs(camlist, gaussians, pipe, bg, args, DENSIFY=True): """ Computes multi-view consistency scores for densification and pruning. Cross-ray Densification is a strategy that selectively increases 3D Gaussian density in multi-view overlapped regions to enhance multi-view consistency during optimization. It is divided into Multi-view Augmented Densification (MVAD), which adapts the densification threshold based on camera geometry, and Cross-ray Densification, which uses ray tracing to identify 3D regions contributing significantly to multiple views. Unlike standard densification which relies solely on 2D gradient magnitude, this method leverages multi-view photometric loss and ray intersection geometry to target complex, texture-dense areas that are consistently observed across different camera perspectives. A strategy to select a subset of Gaussian primitives as landmarks based on a saliency score to reduce computational cost for localization. The saliency score for primitive p is computed as H(p) = 2 \cdot \text{Sig}(p) + \min(2, \text{Gen}(p)) + \text{Geo}(p), where \text{Sig}(p) is the significance term evaluated using the learnable landmark probability score a, \text{Gen}(p) is the generalizability term evaluated using the largest angle between any two viewing directions, and \text{Geo}(p) is the consistency term. Selection proceeds via a greedy search: candidates \Omega = \{p \mid p \in P, \|x - s\| > r, \forall s \in S\} are evaluated, the maximum H(p) is selected, and the search radius r is halved if no candidates remain. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot R), where V is the number of views in camlist and R is the cost of rendering a single view. The method requires two renders per view (one for loss, one for metric accumulation). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing fullmetriccounts and fullmetricscore, where N is the number of Gaussians. Additional memory for intermediate render buffers per view. Strengths: Explicitly targets regions with persistent multi-view inconsistency, which are often indicative of missing geometry or artifacts. The binary thresholding reduces sensitivity to absolute loss magnitude variations across views. Limitations: Requires multiple renders per optimization step, increasing computational overhead. Sensitive to the choice of lossthresh. When to use: When standard gradient-based densification fails to resolve multi-view inconsistencies or artifacts in texture-dense regions. When not to use: When computational resources are severely constrained, or when the scene is static and well-reconstructed with standard methods. The method originates from the FastGS repository, which provides an unofficial implementation of optimized Gaussian Splatting training routines. It leverages multi-view consistency as a more robust signal for densification than single-view gradients, addressing the issue of overfitting to specific viewpoints or noise. fastgs/FastGS, https://github.com/fastgs/FastGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) SplatLoc: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based Visual Localization for Augmented Reality., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3549563, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Cross-ray Densification
head: CRD, MVAD, Multi-view Cross-ray Densification, Multi-view Cross-ray Densification Strategy
body: Cross-ray Densification is a strategy that selectively increases 3D Gaussian density in multi-view overlapped regions to enhance multi-view consistency during optimization. It is divided into Multi-view Augmented Densification (MVAD), which adapts the densification threshold based on camera geometry, and Cross-ray Densification, which uses ray tracing to identify 3D regions contributing significantly to multiple views. Unlike standard densification which relies solely on 2D gradient magnitude, this method leverages multi-view photometric loss and ray intersection geometry to target complex, texture-dense areas that are consistently observed across different camera perspectives. The method consists of two coupled components: Multi-view Augmented Densification (MVAD) and Cross-ray Densification. MVAD adjusts the global densification threshold based on the geometric diversity of the training views, while Cross-ray Densification identifies specific 3D volumes for densification using 2D loss maps and ray casting. Inputs: M: Number of training views. L: Set of multi-view loss maps, where Lm is the loss map for view m. \beta: Original densification threshold. \tau: Predefined hyperparameter for discrepancy adjustment. (h, w): Dimensions of the sliding window for region localization. nr: Number of rays cast per window vertex (fixed at 4). \mathcal{G}: Set of 3D Gaussians to be evaluated for densification. Outputs: A subset of \mathcal{G} located in identified multi-view overlapped regions, marked for densification. Loss Map (Lm): A 2D array of photometric loss values for each pixel in view m. Camera Poses: For each view m, the translation vector tm and rotation matrix Rm. Regions (R): A list of 2D bounding box coordinates identified in the loss maps. Cuboids: 3D volumes defined by the intersection of ray planes from multiple views. MVAD determines whether to enhance densification based on the geometric distinctness of the training views. 1. Normalize Camera Translations: Normalize the translation vectors of all sampled views into a unit sphere to make the strategy scene-adaptive. 2. Compute Discrepancies: Calculate the multi-view consistency discrepancies \{ri\} for all unique pairs of cameras. The number of pairs is n = (M^2 - M)/2. ri is computed using the relative translation distance and the similarity of the rotation matrices between each camera pair. 3. Adjust Threshold: Modify the densification threshold \hat{\beta} using the Heaviside function H(\cdot): \hat{\beta} = \beta - \frac{\beta}{2} H(\tau - ri) Where: H(x) = 1 if x \ge 0, else 0. If discrepancies ri are large (specifically ri < \tau), the term H(\tau - ri) becomes 1, reducing the threshold by half (\hat{\beta} = \beta/2). This enhances densification in complex areas. If discrepancies are small (ri \ge \tau), H(\tau - ri) = 0, and \hat{\beta} = \beta, preventing over-densification in simple regions. This step locates 3D regions containing Gaussians that contribute to multiple views by intersecting rays cast from high-loss 2D regions. 1. Loss Map Analysis: For each view m \in [1, M], calculate the loss map Lm. 2. Region Localization: For each loss map Lm, compute the average loss within a sliding window of size (h, w). Identify regions R containing the largest average loss values. These regions correspond to texture-dense or high-error areas. 3. Ray Casting and Intersection: For each identified 2D region r \in R, cast nr = 4 rays from each vertex of the region into the scene. Compute the intersection planes formed by rays originating from different camera perspectives. Treat the cuboids formed by these intersecting planes as the multi-view overlapped regions. These cuboids contain critical 3D Gaussians that significantly influence rendering from multiple views. 4. Densification: Identify all 3D Gaussians located inside these identified cuboids and apply densification operations exclusively to them. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crossraydensification(lossmaps, cameraposes, M, beta, tau, windowsize, numrays=4, allgaussians=None): # Inputs: lossmaps (list of 2D arrays), cameraposes (list of (R, t)), M, beta, tau, windowsize (h, w), numrays, allgaussians (list of 3D positions) # Outputs: list of Gaussian indices to densify # --- MVAD: Threshold Adjustment --- # 1. Normalize camera translations to unit sphere normtrans = [] for m in range(M): t = cameraposes[m][1] normtrans.append(t / max(1e-9, (t[0]2 + t[1]2 + t[2]2)0.5)) # 2. Compute discrepancies for all unique camera pairs discrepancies = [] for i in range(M): for j in range(i + 1, M): # Relative translation distance tdiff = [(normtrans[i][k] - normtrans[j][k])2 for k in range(3)] tdist = (sum(tdiff))0.5 # Rotation matrix similarity (Frobenius norm of difference) Rdiff = [(cameraposes[i][0][a][b] - cameraposes[j][0][a][b])2 for a in range(3) for b in range(3)] rdist = (sum(Rdiff))0.5 discrepancies.append(tdist + rdist) # 3. Adjust threshold using Heaviside function H(x) = 1 if x >= 0 else 0 currentbeta = beta for ri in discrepancies: if tau - ri >= 0: currentbeta = beta / 2.0 break # --- Cross-ray Densification --- densifiedgaussians = [] highlossregions = [] # Step 1 & 2: Loss Map Analysis and Region Localization for m in range(M): Lm = lossmaps[m] h, w = windowsize Himg, Wimg = len(Lm), len(Lm[0]) # Compute sliding window average loss avgloss = [[0.0 for in range(Wimg)] for in range(Himg)] for i in range(Himg): for j in range(Wimg): s, c = 0.0, 0 for di in range(h): for dj in range(w): ni, nj = i + di, j + dj if 0 <= ni < Himg and 0 <= nj < Wimg: s += Lm[ni][nj] c += 1 avgloss[i][j] = s / c if c > 0 else 0.0 # Identify regions R with largest average loss values flatavg = [(avgloss[i][j], i, j) for i in range(Himg) for j in range(Wimg)] flatavg.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Select top regions; exact count not specified in sources topk = max(1, len(flatavg) // 10) for k in range(topk): highlossregions.append((flatavg[k][1], flatavg[k][2])) # Step 3: Ray Casting and Intersection cuboids = [] for (ri, rj) in highlossregions: # Define 2D vertices of the window region vertices2d = [ (ri, rj), (ri, rj + w - 1), (ri + h - 1, rj), (ri + h - 1, rj + w - 1) ] # Cast nr rays per perspective from vertices, compute intersected planes across views # Form cuboids from intersections # Exact geometric construction of intersected planes is not detailed in sources cuboid = computecuboidfromviews(vertices2d, cameraposes, numrays) if cuboid is not None: cuboids.append(cuboid) # Step 4: Densification for cuboid in cuboids: for gidx, gpos in enumerate(allgaussians): if pointincuboid(gpos, cuboid): densifiedgaussians.append(gidx) return densifiedgaussians def computecuboidfromviews(vertices2d, cameraposes, numrays): # Project 2D vertices to 3D rays for each camera # Compute intersection planes of rays across different views # Return bounding box or plane list defining the cuboid return None def pointincuboid(point, cuboid): return (cuboid[0] <= point[0] <= cuboid[3] and cuboid[1] <= point[1] <= cuboid[4] and cuboid[2] <= point[2] <= cuboid[5]) \beta: Original densification threshold. \tau: Hyperparameter adjusting the extent of discrepancy between cameras. (h, w): Dimensions of the sliding window. nr = 4: Fixed number of rays cast per window vertex. Adaptive Density Behavior: When the threshold \hat{\beta} remains equal to the original \beta, the method prevents over-densification in simple regions. When \hat{\beta} is reduced to half the original threshold, it enhances 3D Gaussian fitting toward complex areas. Photometric Guidance: The loss metric directly highlights texture-dense regions that require improvement, guiding the densification process effectively. Ray Intersection Degeneracy: If rays from different views do not intersect or form degenerate cuboids (e.g., parallel rays), the densification region may be invalid. The source does not specify handling for non-intersecting rays. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enhances multi-view consistency by targeting regions that are consistently high-loss across views. Prevents over-densification in simple regions via adaptive thresholding. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than standard gradient-based densification due to ray casting and multi-view processing. Performance depends on the quality of loss maps and camera pose accuracy. When to Use: Use when multi-view consistency is critical and standard densification fails to capture complex, texture-dense regions observed from multiple angles. When Not to Use: Avoid for single-view or very sparse-view scenarios where multi-view constraints cannot be reliably computed. Cross-ray Densification was proposed in the MVGS (Multi-view Regulated Learning) framework. It builds on the explicit nature of 3D Gaussian Splatting, aiming to improve novel view synthesis by enhancing multi-view constraints during optimization. The method was introduced to address challenges in scenes with insufficient observations, texture-less areas, and fine-scale details. name: Guided Sampling
head: Sparse point cloud densification with depth guidance
body: Guided Sampling is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses blurring artifacts in regions insufficiently covered by the initial sparse point cloud, such as far content outside windows or flames. It distinguishes itself from standard gradient-based splitting by explicitly sampling new Gaussian positions along the camera ray depth range rather than relying solely on positional gradients, thereby ensuring coverage where gradient signals are weak or ambiguous. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, camera parameters for the current training view, and the maximum depth d present in that view. Output: A set of new Gaussian primitives added to \mathcal{G}, positioned along the sampled depth range. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Defined by mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c} [Parent]. Depth Range: Interval [L, U] where L = s \cdot d and U = 7.5 \cdot d. Parameters: d: Maximum depth value present in the training view. s: Scaling factor for the lower bound of the sampling range. Typically set to 0.7 for most scenes. Noise: Small random perturbation added to each depth sample. Steps: 1. Determine Depth Bounds: Compute L = s \cdot d and U = 7.5 \cdot d. 2. Sample Depth: Draw z uniformly from [L, U] and add small random noise \epsilon to obtain z' = z + \epsilon. 3. Project to 3D: Back-project the 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) using the centered-undistorted camera model and sampled depth z' to compute \mu{new}. 4. Initialize Gaussian: Create g{new} with \mu{new}, scale and rotation inherited from the parent or default settings, and opacity \alpha initialized according to standard densification rules (e.g., halved if splitting) [Parent]. 5. Add to Set: Insert g{new} into \mathcal{G}. 6. Pruning: After densification and guided sampling, Gaussians with small spatial opacity are gradually pruned to retain representative primitives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def guidedsampling(cameraintrinsics, maxdepthd, scalingfactors=0.7, numsamples=1): """ Generates new Gaussian positions using guided depth sampling. cameraintrinsics: dict with keys 'fx', 'fy', 'cx', 'cy', 'width', 'height'. """ newmeans = [] lowerbound = scalingfactors maxdepthd upperbound = 7.5 maxdepthd for in range(numsamples): # Step 2: Sample depth uniformly and add noise zsample = np.random.uniform(lowerbound, upperbound) noise = np.random.normal(0, 0.01) # Small random noise zfinal = zsample + noise # Step 3: Project to 3D using centered-undistorted pinhole model # Pixel coordinates (u, v) are sampled uniformly across the image u = np.random.randint(0, cameraintrinsics['width']) v = np.random.randint(0, cameraintrinsics['height']) fx = cameraintrinsics['fx'] fy = cameraintrinsics['fy'] cx = cameraintrinsics['cx'] cy = cameraintrinsics['cy'] # Standard back-projection for centered-undistorted coordinates x = (u - cx) zfinal / fx y = (v - cy) zfinal / fy z = zfinal munew = np.array([x, y, z]) newmeans.append(munew) return newmeans Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blurring in Uncovered Areas: Guided sampling cannot fully eliminate blurring in areas insufficiently covered by the sparse point cloud, such as far content outside windows or flames. This occurs because accurate depth is unavailable, forcing Gaussians to spawn across a depth range. Pruning of Correct Gaussians: Gaussians spawned near the correct location may be pruned during subsequent training if they do not immediately minimize the loss, leading to instability. Mitigation: Leveraging depth priors from learning-based depth estimation methods can constrain the spawning range and improve accuracy. Geometry-Texture-Aware Densification (GeoTexDensifier) is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that utilizes geometry priors (monocular depth and normal maps) to guide splitting in weakly textured regions and texture gradients to control densification in fully textured areas, thereby avoiding the over-splitting of floaters in textureless regions. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Mini-Splatting-D by replacing the static contribution-area threshold with a texture-weighted statistic and validating split positions against geometric consistency, ensuring splats conform to actual surface tangents rather than drifting into background noise. Strengths: Alleviates blurring in regions with sparse initial coverage by explicitly sampling depth. Limitations: Cannot fully eliminate artifacts in challenging scenarios like far content outside windows or flames where depth is ambiguous. May spawn Gaussians in incorrect locations that are later pruned, adding computational overhead. Performance: The source provides performance metrics for the full Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting pipeline but does not isolate the cost of guided sampling alone. Guided Sampling is introduced in the context of Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting for Real-Time Dynamic View Synthesis. It is designed to handle dynamic scenes and challenging geometry where static point cloud initialization is insufficient. Geometry-Texture-Aware Densification (GeoTexDensifier) is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that utilizes geometry priors (monocular depth and normal maps) to guide splitting in weakly textured regions and texture gradients to control densification in fully textured areas, thereby avoiding the over-splitting of floaters in textureless regions. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Mini-Splatting-D by replacing the static contribution-area threshold with a texture-weighted statistic and validating split positions against geometric consistency, ensuring splats conform to actual surface tangents rather than drifting into background noise. Monocular depth maps \{Dt\} estimated by ZoeDepth. Normal maps \{Nt\} computed from the depth maps \{Dt\}. Current set of Gaussian splats \mathcal{G}, each with position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color c, and attributes V^{(a)} (reference view ID) and w^{(a)} (maximal rendering weight). Optimization iteration counter l. Outputs: Updated set of Gaussian splats \mathcal{G}' with new splats generated via splitting, where invalid children are discarded and parents are retained. Each Gaussian splat Gi maintains the following attributes relevant to densification: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. V^{(a)}i \in \mathbb{Z}: Image ID of the reference view where Gi provides maximal rendering weight. w^{(a)}i \in \mathbb{R}: Maximal rendering weight w{V^{(a)}}(Gi) in \alpha-blending. V^{(b)}i \in \mathbb{Z}: Initial reference view ID (view with smallest reprojection error for the initial SfM point). \hat{R}^{(b)}i \in \mathbb{R}: Initial depth ratio R^{V^{(b)}}i(Gi) calculated at initialization. \alphas = 20: Linear regression coefficient for texture weight activation.  etas = 0.16: Linear regression coefficient for texture weight activation. Ts = 40: Start threshold value for adaptive threshold calculation. Te = 4: End threshold value for adaptive threshold calculation. \deltap = 0.1: Threshold for discarding child splats based on relative depth ratio change. ls, le: Start and end iteration numbers for densification. 1. Camera Pose and SfM Initialization: Run COLMAP to estimate camera poses \{Mt\} for all input views. Initialize Gaussian splats from sparse SfM feature map points. 2. Initial Splat Filtering: Filter out SfM map points with track lengths less than 3 or reprojection errors exceeding 1 pixel to ensure correct initial locations. 3. Geometric Prior Estimation: Estimate monocular depth maps Dt for each training image It using ZoeDepth. Compute normal maps Nt from the depth maps Dt. 4. Initial Reference View Selection: For each initial Gaussian Ga derived from an SfM point, choose the image view V^{(b)}a with the smallest reprojection error as its initial reference view. Record the initial depth ratio \hat{R}^{(b)}a(Ga). The method replaces the fixed contribution area threshold with a texture-weighted statistic to identify splats that require splitting. 1. Texture Weight Calculation: For each training image It, calculate the pixel-wise texture weight st( ar{x}) using the normalized image gradient 
abla It( ar{x}) (gray values normalized from [0, 255] to [0, 1]): st( ar{x}) =  rac{	anh(\alphas (
abla It( ar{x}) +  etas)) + 1}{2} This weight reflects the likelihood that a Gaussian contributes to a textured region. 2. Adaptive Threshold: Define an adaptive threshold \hat{T} that decreases over iterations to allow smaller splats to split later: \hat{T} = Ts + (Te - Ts)  rac{l - ls}{le - ls} where l is the current iteration number. 3. Contribution Area Redefinition: For each Gaussian Gi and image It, calculate the maximal contribution area \hat{S}^ti by summing texture weights only for pixels where Gi has the maximal rendering contribution: \hat{S}^ti = \sum{ ar{x}=(1,1)}^{(W,H)} st( ar{x}) \delta(Ii( ar{x}) = I{max}( ar{x})) where Ii( ar{x}) is the contribution of Gi at pixel  ar{x}, and I{max}( ar{x}) is the maximal contribution at that pixel. Fully textured areas yield higher statistics, enforcing splitting, while weakly textured areas remain sparse. 4. Blur Splat Identification: Identify blur splats G^bt for image It as those where \hat{S}^ti > \hat{T}. For each identified blur splat Ga, perform splitting with geometric validation. 1. Reference View Selection: Choose the reference view V^{(a)} where Ga provides the maximal rendering weight w{V^{(a)}}(Ga) in \alpha-blending. If another view provides a higher weight during optimization, update V^{(a)} and w{V^{(a)}}(Ga). 2. Parent Validation (VDRC for Parent): Before splitting, validate the parent Ga itself. Project Ga to its initial reference view V^{(b)}a to calculate the current depth ratio R^{V^{(b)}a}(Ga). Compare it with the initial depth ratio \hat{R}^{(b)}a(Ga) using the Validation of Depth Ratio Change (VDRC). 3. Child Generation and Positioning: Generate a child splat Gc with a random position 	ilde{\mu}c sampled from the parent's distribution. Project both the parent Ga and the random child 	ilde{\mu}c to the reference view V^{(a)}. Let the projection pixels be  ar{x}a and  ar{x}c respectively. Calculate the projection pixel coordinates:  ar{x}a = \pi(M{V^{(a)}} \mua), \quad  ar{x}c = \pi(M{V^{(a)}} 	ilde{\mu}c) where \pi(x, y, z) = (fu  rac{x}{z} + cu, fv  rac{y}{z} + cv), with fu, fv as focal lengths and (cu, cv) as the optical center. Calculate the perpendicular projection \mu^\perp of 	ilde{\mu}c onto the tangential plane of Ga at  ar{x}a: \mu^\perp = 	ilde{\mu}c - ((	ilde{\mu}c - \mua) \cdot N{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}a)) N{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}a) where N{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}a) is the normal map value at pixel  ar{x}a. Determine the optimal child position \muc using the image gradient 
abla I{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}c) at the child's pixel: \muc = (	ilde{\mu}c - \mu^\perp) 
abla I{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}c) + \mu^\perp This normal-guided positioning ensures the child stays close to the geometric surface in textureless areas. 4. Depth Ratio Change Validation (VDRC): Calculate the projection depth of the parent Ga to V^{(a)}: Z{V^{(a)}}(Ga) = [M{V^{(a)}} \mua]z Obtain the monocular depth D{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}a) from the ZoeDepth map at pixel  ar{x}a. Calculate the depth ratio for the parent: R{V^{(a)}}(Ga) =  rac{D{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}a)}{Z{V^{(a)}}(Ga)} Similarly, calculate the depth ratio for the child Gc at its projected pixel  ar{x}c: R{V^{(a)}}(Gc) =  rac{D{V^{(a)}}( ar{x}c)}{Z{V^{(a)}}(Gc)} Compute the relative depth ratio change: P{V^{(a)}}(Ga, Gc) =  rac{|R{V^{(a)}}(Ga) - R{V^{(a)}}(Gc)|}{R{V^{(a)}}(Ga)} If P{V^{(a)}}(Ga, Gc) > \deltap, discard the child splat Gc and retain the parent Ga to take its place. Otherwise, accept Gc. 5. Child Inheritance: For a valid child splat Gc, inherit the parent's initial reference view V^{(b)}c = V^{(a)} and set its initial depth ratio \hat{R}^{(b)}c(Gc) = R{V^{(a)}}(Gc) for future verification steps.
