name: Soft Rasterization
head: Blurring Primitives, SAR Feature Rasterizer, Soft Rasterization for Gradient Enrichment
body: Soft rasterization is a differentiable rendering technique that mitigates the discontinuities inherent in standard rasterization by blending facet contributions for pixels near primitive edges. It solves the problem of sparse and vanishing gradients caused by the non-uniformity of bilinear interpolation operands, which typically have similar values except at object boundaries. Unlike standard hard rasterization, it yields slightly distorted images but allows backpropagating more useful gradients, thereby stabilizing optimization and preventing gradient vanishing at edges. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D primitive geometry, camera parameters, and a blending radius parameter \sigma. Outputs: A rendered image or feature map with softened edges and enriched gradients suitable for backpropagation. Data Structures: The pipeline transforms coordinates through specific spaces depending on the application. For SAR, the sequence is World Space \rightarrow View Space \rightarrow Range Space \rightarrow Ground Space \rightarrow NDC Space. For standard rendering, World Space \rightarrow View Space \rightarrow NDC Space is typical. A fragment buffer stores per-pixel attributes (color, alpha, normals) derived from the rasterized primitives. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform primitive vertices from World Space to View Space, then to NDC Space. In SAR-specific implementations, intermediate steps include a Range Transform (z-coordinates become y-coordinates) and Ground-plane Projection (stretches perceived y-dimension so each pixel maps to a consistent-sized cell on ground). 2. Soft Rasterization: For each pixel, determine the contribution of all overlapping primitives. Instead of a binary inside/outside test, compute a soft coverage value based on the distance from the pixel to the primitive edge. The blending is controlled by a radius parameter \sigma. Pixels near the edge receive blended contributions from both the primitive and the background or adjacent primitives. 3. Shading: Compute per-pixel features based on the rasterized fragments. Silhouette: Create a mask from fragments that have no corresponding facets. Surface Normals: Compute per-pixel surface normals \hat{n} relative to the illumination direction \hat{q}. For monostatic SAR, the normal feature d is calculated as d = -\hat{q} \cdot \hat{n}, where \cdot denotes the inner product. Alpha Channel: Determine visibility. In SAR contexts, this involves rasterizing a reference view from the radar perspective to mask out self-shadowed facets before calculating the alpha channel for the main view. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between the rendered image and the ground truth. The gradients flow through the soft rasterization stage, providing non-zero gradients for primitive parameters even when the primitive is not strictly inside the pixel in a hard-rasterization sense. Parameters: Blending Radius (\sigma): Controls the level of soft rasterization distortion. Typical values used in training are 0, 10^{-5}, 10^{-4}, and 10^{-3}. Gaussian Blur Kernel: In some implementations, Gaussian blur is applied to each primitive before optimization to enrich gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softrasterize(primitives, camera, sigma): """ Renders primitives using soft rasterization with blending radius sigma. Implements: Coordinate Transformations, Rasterization, Shading. """ H, W = camera.resolution renderedimage = zeros((H, W, 3)) # 1. Coordinate Transformations for prim in primitives: # Standard: World -> View -> NDC # SAR adds Range Transform and Ground-plane Projection viewverts = prim.vertices @ camera.viewmatrix.T ndcverts = viewverts @ camera.projectionmatrix.T prim.ndcverts = ndcverts # 2. Soft Rasterization & 3. Shading for y in range(H): for x in range(W): totalcolor = zeros(3) totalalpha = 0.0 # Sort primitives by depth for correct blending sortedprims = sorted(primitives, key=lambda p: depthatpixel(p, (x, y))) for prim in sortedprims: # Compute soft coverage based on distance to edge disttoedge = signeddistancetotriangleedge(prim.ndcverts, (x, y)) if sigma > 0: coverage = exp(-0.5 (disttoedge / sigma)2) else: coverage = 1.0 if disttoedge < 0 else 0.0 if coverage > 0: # Interpolate attributes using barycentric coordinates bary = barycentriccoords(prim.ndcverts, (x, y)) color = interpolate(prim.colors, bary) alpha = prim.alpha # Over operator blending blendedalpha = coverage alpha totalcolor = totalcolor (1 - blendedalpha) + color blendedalpha totalalpha += blendedalpha (1 - totalalpha) # Compute shading features if needed if prim.requiresnormals: normal = interpolate(prim.normals, bary) # d = -qhat. nhat (monostatic SAR) pass renderedimage[y, x] = totalcolor # 4. Loss Computation # Compute loss between renderedimage and groundtruth # loss.backward() propagates gradients through soft coverage return renderedimage def zeros(shape): return [0.0] prod(shape) def depthatpixel(prim, pixel): return mean(prim.ndcverts[:, 2]) def signeddistancetotriangleedge(verts, pixel): # Returns signed distance from pixel to triangle edge in NDC space return 0.0 # Standard barycentric edge function evaluation def barycentriccoords(verts, pixel): # Returns barycentric weights summing to 1.0 return [1.0/3, 1.0/3, 1.0/3] # Placeholder for actual barycentric calculation def interpolate(values, bary): return sum(v b for v, b in zip(values, bary)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts: Soft rasterization yields slightly distorted images, particularly near edges, due to the blending. Gradient Sparsity: Vanilla rasterization produces sparse gradients because bilinear interpolation operands have similar values except at boundaries. Soft rasterization mitigates this by smoothing edges. Precision: The choice of \sigma controls distortion levels; values range from 0 (hard rasterization) to 10^{-3}. Time Complexity: The soft rasterization step adds minimal computational overhead compared to standard rasterization, as it primarily modifies the edge evaluation logic. The overhead is reported to be almost the same as standard rendering in ablation studies. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory is required beyond standard frame buffers and primitive attributes. Performance: Soft rasterization yields consistent PSNR gains. In ablation studies, enabling soft rasterization improved PSNR from 24.4 to 24.7 on 512×512 targets and from 25.5 to 25.7 on 1024×1024 targets. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization, prevents gradient vanishing at edges, and enriches gradients for better convergence. Limitations: Introduces slight image distortion/artifacts. Not suitable for applications requiring pixel-perfect geometric accuracy without post-processing. Soft rasterization was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering to address the non-differentiability of standard rasterization operators. It is based on the soft rasterizer described in prior literature. The technique has been adapted for various domains, including Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery and bitmap primitive rendering (DiffBMP). In SAR, it is part of the SAR Feature Rasterizer pipeline. In DiffBMP, it is used as an optimization helper to align sparse gradients. Differentiable Rendering for Synthetic Aperture Radar Imagery, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2204.01248, fetched 2026-10-26 DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.22625, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization
head: 3D-HGS
body: This method regularizes the covariance matrices of 3D Gaussians to enforce a "half-Gaussian" shape, effectively modeling sharp transitions between object surfaces and empty space by cutting ellipsoids with a plane aligned to the surface normal. It addresses the limitation of full ellipsoids in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which often produce blurry boundaries or "ghosting" artifacts at object edges. Unlike sibling methods that rely on frequency domain constraints or depth supervision, this approach modifies the geometric structure of the primitives themselves during training. The method transforms the standard 3D Gaussian covariance matrix into a local coordinate system defined by the surface normal, modifies the diagonal elements to zero out components along the normal direction, and transforms it back. This process is applied periodically during training. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current 3D Gaussian covariance matrix \Sigma (3x3 symmetric positive definite), and the surface normal vector n at the Gaussian's center. Output: The regularized covariance matrix \sigma (3x3), representing a half-Gaussian. Data Structures Covariance Matrix: A 3x3 symmetric matrix. In the local basis, it is stored as a 3x3 matrix where the third dimension corresponds to the normal direction. Basis Matrix: A 3x3 orthogonal matrix constructed from two tangent vectors and the normal vector. Step-by-Step Procedure 1. Normalize the normal vector: n \leftarrow \frac{n}{\|n\|} 2. Construct the local basis: Define two orthogonal vectors v1 and v2 that span the plane perpendicular to n. If nx = 0 and ny = 0 (i.e., n is parallel to the z-axis): v1 = (1, 0, 0) v2 = (0, 1, 0) Otherwise: v1 \leftarrow \frac{(ny, -nx, 0)}{\|(ny, -nx, 0)\|} v2 \leftarrow \frac{n \times v1}{\|n \times v1\|} Construct the basis matrix by concatenating these vectors as columns: \text{basis} = [v1, v2, n] 3. Transform covariance to local basis: \text{cov} \leftarrow \text{basis}^T \cdot \Sigma \cdot \text{basis} Here, \text{cov} is the covariance matrix expressed in the local coordinate system where the z-axis aligns with n. 4. Compute modified diagonal elements: Calculate the regularized diagonal elements a', b', and c' by subtracting the squared off-diagonal terms divided by the normal-component variance (\text{cov}[2,2]). This effectively projects the covariance onto the tangent plane, removing the variance along the normal direction. a' \leftarrow \text{cov}[0, 0] - \frac{\text{cov}[0, 2]^2}{\text{cov}[2, 2]} b' \leftarrow \text{cov}[0, 1] - \frac{\text{cov}[0, 2] \cdot \text{cov}[1, 2]}{\text{cov}[2, 2]} c' \leftarrow \text{cov}[1, 1] - \frac{\text{cov}[1, 2]^2}{\text{cov}[2, 2]} 5. Construct the regularized covariance in local basis: Create the matrix \sigma{\text{local}} using the modified elements. The off-diagonal elements involving the normal direction are set to zero. The normal-direction variance is set to a small fraction of the minimum tangent variance to maintain numerical stability and define the "half" nature. \sigma{\text{local}} = \begin{bmatrix} a' & b' & 0 \\ b' & c' & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \min(a', c') / 100 \end{bmatrix} 6. Transform back to world space: \sigma \leftarrow \text{basis} \cdot \sigma{\text{local}} \cdot \text{basis}^T 7. Application Frequency: This transformation is performed every 5000 training iterations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def regularizecovariance(covworld: np.ndarray, normal: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Transforms a 3D Gaussian covariance matrix into a half-Gaussian aligned with the given surface normal. Args: covworld: 3x3 symmetric covariance matrix in world space. normal: 3D normal vector (not necessarily normalized). Returns: 3x3 regularized covariance matrix in world space. """ # 1. Normalize normal n = normal / np.linalg.norm(normal) # 2. Construct basis # Check if normal is parallel to Z axis to avoid division by zero or degenerate cross product if n[0] == 0 and n[1] == 0: v1 = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) v2 = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) else: # v1 is perpendicular to n and lies in the XY plane projection v1 = np.array([n[1], -n[0], 0.0]) v1 = v1 / np.linalg.norm(v1) # v2 is perpendicular to both n and v1 v2 = np.cross(n, v1) v2 = v2 / np.linalg.norm(v2) # Basis matrix columns are v1, v2, n basis = np.columnstack((v1, v2, n)) # 3. Transform to local basis covlocal = basis.T @ covworld @ basis # 4. Compute modified elements # Extract elements for clarity cov00 = covlocal[0, 0] cov01 = covlocal[0, 1] cov02 = covlocal[0, 2] cov11 = covlocal[1, 1] cov12 = covlocal[1, 2] cov22 = covlocal[2, 2] # Avoid division by zero if cov22 is extremely small if cov22 < 1e-8: cov22 = 1e-8 aprime = cov00 - (cov02 2) / cov22 bprime = cov01 - (cov02 cov12) / cov22 cprime = cov11 - (cov12 2) / cov22 # 5. Construct regularized local covariance # The variance along the normal is set to min(a', c') / 100 mintangentvar = min(aprime, cprime) normalvar = mintangentvar / 100.0 sigmalocal = np.array([ [aprime, bprime, 0.0], [bprime, cprime, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, normalvar] ]) # 6. Transform back to world space sigmaworld = basis @ sigmalocal @ basis.T return sigmaworld Parameters Opacity Threshold for Densification/Pruning: Increased to 0.01. Initial Opacity for Half-Gaussians: Reset to 0.02. Regularization Interval: Every 5000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Normal: If the normal vector is zero or near-zero, the basis construction fails. The code checks for nx=0, ny=0 to handle the specific case where the normal is aligned with the Z-axis, but general robustness requires checking for \|n\| \approx 0. Small Covariance along Normal: If \text{cov}[2,2] is very small, division in step 4 can cause numerical instability. A small epsilon floor (e.g., 1e-8) should be applied. Negative Variance: Due to numerical errors, a' or c' might become slightly negative. In practice, these should be clamped to a small positive value to ensure the resulting matrix remains positive semi-definite. Time Complexity: The transformation involves matrix multiplications (O(1) for fixed 3x3 matrices) and is applied every 5000 iterations, adding negligible overhead to the per-step training cost. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond the existing Gaussian parameters. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, 3D-HGS with an efficient rasterizer achieves 125 FPS and 29.66 PSNR using 3.8M kernels, compared to 3DGS which uses 3.2M kernels (FPS/PSNR for 3DGS not explicitly listed in the specific row but implied lower or comparable with fewer kernels). On the Tank & Dengin dataset, it achieves 160 FPS and 24.45 PSNR using 1.8M kernels. On the Tank & Blending dataset, it achieves 126 FPS and 29.76 PSNR using 2.6M kernels. Strengths: Consistently outperforms original 3D Gaussian Splatting across all metrics (PSNR, etc.) on evaluated datasets. The half-Gaussian shape effectively models sharp transitions between object surfaces and empty space, reducing artifacts. Limitations: Requires accurate surface normals for the transformation. The method is evaluated against Scaffold, mip-splatting, and MCMC architectures, but specific comparative metrics against these are not detailed in the provided notes beyond the general statement of outperforming 3DGS. The method originates from the paper "3D-HGS: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting". It was developed to improve the geometric fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing half-Gaussian kernels that are cut by a plane aligned with the surface normal. This allows for better representation of sharp edges and surfaces compared to full ellipsoids. The approach is part of the broader family of regularization and geometry constraints in differentiable rendering, specifically building on the principles of adding regularization terms to the training loss [Parent]. 3D-HGS: 3D Half-Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01027, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Hard and Soft Depth Regularization
body:
Hard and Soft Depth Regularization is a training constraint for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents the degradation of high-frequency color details caused by forcing anisotropic Gaussian primitives to conform to smooth monocular depth estimates. It sets itself apart from standard depth regularization methods by decoupling the optimization of Gaussian geometry (center positions) from their shape (scale and rotation), allowing the primitives to "reshuffle" spatially rather than deform, thereby balancing coarse depth fitting with fine appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians (defined by centers \mu, scales s, rotations q, opacities \alpha, and colors), monocular depth map D{mono}, and camera parameters. Outputs: Gradient updates for Gaussian centers \mu and opacities \alpha. Data Structures: Gaussian State: Each Gaussian i is defined by: Center position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-space or linear) Rotation quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color coefficients (SH or RGB) Depth Maps: Two distinct depth maps are rendered from the current Gaussian state: 1. Hard Depth (D{hard}): Weighted average depth used for center position updates. 2. Soft Depth (D{soft}): Used for opacity updates (often derived from the same rendering pass but differentiated in gradient flow). Numbered Steps: 1. Freeze Shape Parameters: During the depth regularization step, freeze the scale parameters s and rotation quaternions q of all Gaussians. This prevents the Gaussian shapes from deforming to fit the smooth depth surface. 2. Render Depth Maps: Render two depth maps from the current Gaussian state. The first depth map is used to compute gradients for updating center positions \mu. The second depth map is used to compute gradients for updating opacities \alpha. Note: The specific distinction between "hard" and "soft" depth in the source implies using different weighting or aggregation strategies in the rendering equation to isolate geometric vs. opacity signals. 3. Compute Loss: Calculate the depth regularization loss \mathcal{L}{depth} by comparing the rendered depth maps against the monocular depth estimate D{mono}. Common choices include scale-invariant depth loss or L1 loss, though the source emphasizes the method of application (freezing shape) over a specific loss function formula. 4. Compute Gradients: Compute 
abla{\mu} \mathcal{L}{depth} using the first depth map. Compute 
abla{\alpha} \mathcal{L}{depth} using the second depth map. 5. Update Parameters: Apply the gradients independently: Update \mu \leftarrow \mu - \eta 
abla{\mu} \mathcal{L}{depth} Update \alpha \leftarrow \alpha - \eta 
abla{\alpha} \mathcal{L}{depth} Do not update s or q in this step. Formulas: The total loss includes the photometric loss and the depth regularization term: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda{depth} \mathcal{L}{depth} Where \mathcal{L}{depth} is computed on the rendered depth maps. The source does not provide a single closed-form formula for \mathcal{L}{depth} itself, but describes the mechanism of applying it via independent gradient paths for \mu and \alpha. Parameters: \lambda{depth}: Weight for depth regularization. Not given in the sources. \eta: Learning rate. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Detail Loss: Applying depth regularization directly to NeRF-style MLPs or un-frozen Gaussian shapes forces the primitive geometry to conform to smooth monocular depth estimates, which conflicts with complex color appearance and causes detail loss and blurred appearance. Sensitivity: Gaussian radiance fields are more sensitive to small depth errors than NeRFs, which may result in noisy distribution of primitives and failures in regions with complex textures. Scale Invariance: Existing scale-invariant depth losses often align depth maps to a fixed scale, which can overlook minor depth variations. This method mitigates this by allowing spatial reshaping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardandsoftdepthregularization(gaussians, monoculardepth, camera, lambdadepth): """ Performs one step of Hard and Soft Depth Regularization. Args: gaussians: Object containing parameters mu, s, q, alpha, colors. monoculardepth: 2D tensor of monocular depth estimates. camera: Camera parameters for projection. lambdadepth: Weight for the depth loss. Returns: Updated gaussians object. """ # Step 1: Freeze shape parameters for this step # In an autograd framework, this is achieved by detaching s and q from the computation graph # or by zeroing out their gradients after the backward pass. frozens = gaussians.s.detach() frozenq = gaussians.q.detach() # Step 2: Render two depth maps # Render 1: For center position update (Hard Depth) # Render 2: For opacity update (Soft Depth) # The source implies two distinct depth maps are rendered. # Implementation detail: This might involve different weighting in the alpha-blending # or separate rendering passes with different gradient stops. # Pass 1: Compute gradients for mu # We need to compute the loss and backpropagate only to mu. with torch.enablegrad(): # Detach shape parameters to prevent gradient flow to s and q currentgaussians = gaussians.clone() currentgaussians.s = frozens.detach().requiresgrad(False) currentgaussians.q = frozenq.detach().requiresgrad(False) # Render depth map Dhard # Assuming a render function that returns depth and color depthhard, = rendergaussians(currentgaussians, camera) # Compute depth loss losshard = computedepthloss(depthhard, monoculardepth) # Backpropagate only to mu losshard.backward(retaingraph=True) gradmu = gaussians.mu.grad.clone() # Pass 2: Compute gradients for alpha with torch.enablegrad(): # Detach shape parameters again currentgaussians.alpha = gaussians.alpha.detach().requiresgrad(True) currentgaussians.s = frozens.detach().requiresgrad(False) currentgaussians.q = frozenq.detach().requiresgrad(False) # Render depth map Dsoft # Note: The source says "Render two distinct depth maps". # If the rendering function is deterministic, Dsoft might be the same as Dhard # but differentiated differently. Or it might use a different aggregation. # For implementation, we assume a separate render call or a modified render mode. depthsoft, = rendergaussians(currentgaussians, camera) # Compute depth loss losssoft = computedepthloss(depthsoft, monoculardepth) # Backpropagate only to alpha losssoft.backward() gradalpha = gaussians.alpha.grad.clone() # Step 5: Update parameters # Apply gradients to mu and alpha gaussians.mu = gaussians.mu - learningrate gradmu gaussians.alpha = gaussians.alpha - learningrate gradalpha # Reset gradients for next step gaussians.zerograd() return gaussians def computedepthloss(rendereddepth, targetdepth): """ Computes the depth regularization loss. Common choices: L1, Scale-Invariant Log Loss. Source does not specify the exact loss function, only the mechanism. """ # Example: L1 Loss return torch.mean(torch.abs(rendereddepth - targetdepth)) Global-Local Depth Normalization is a depth regularization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents scale-invariant losses from overlooking minor depth variations, thereby improving detailed geometry reshaping in texture-rich regions. It sets itself apart from standard scale-invariant losses by combining global scale preservation with local scale amplification, addressing the issue where existing methods align depth maps to a fixed global scale and ignore small local errors. It builds on Hard and Soft Depth Regularization and differs from siblings Depth Reinitialization, Position Regularization, and Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization by explicitly decoupling absolute scale maintenance from local error amplification during gradient computation. Depth Reinitialization is a regularization strategy that alleviates 'overlapping' and 'under-reconstruction' artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging dense depth information to reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by rejecting standard alpha-blended depth maps in favor of geometric mid-point depths to generate clean, artifact-free point clouds for reinitialization. Isotropic Regularization is a geometric constraint used in continuous SLAM-based Gaussian Splatting to prevent the formation of highly elongated Gaussian primitives along the viewing ray direction. While standard differentiable rendering imposes no constraint on Gaussian scaling along the viewing ray, this lack of constraint causes artifacts and tracking instability in continuous SLAM scenarios where viewpoints are not carefully selected. It sets itself apart from its parent Hard and Soft Depth Regularization by explicitly penalizing anisotropy (stretching) rather than just enforcing depth consistency, and from Global-Local Depth Normalization by operating on the scale parameters directly rather than depth values. Position Regularization prevents floating artifacts and dramatic geometry shifts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by constraining Gaussian centers to remain close to a reference surface or their initial positions. It operates as a geometric prior constraint, distinct from depth-consistency methods in its parent category [9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md]. Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization is a regularization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enforces spatial coherence in Gaussian positions and opacities during training, specifically addressing artifacts in sparse-view novel view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by replacing independent per-pixel residual updates with a learned implicit decoder that produces smooth, coherent residual fields for depth and opacity, supplemented by multiview total variation and optical flow constraints. This prevents the "semi-transparent" artifacts and detail loss common when optimizing Gaussians against sparse input views. A regularization loss that enforces coherent motion by grouping Gaussians in image space using a bilateral filter approach, avoiding the dampening of independent motion caused by spatial KNN. For a training image I at time tI, sample another time t'. Compute the 6D screw-axis representation of the transformation between tI and t' for each Gaussian. Compute the geometric loss \mathcal{L}{geo} as the weighted sum of squared distances between screw-axis representations of neighboring pixels. The geometric loss is \mathcal{L}{	ext{geo}} = \sum{p' \in \mathcal{N}(p)} k{c,c'} k{d,d'} k{p,p'} \|sp - s{p'}\|^2, where k{c,c'} is color similarity, k{d,d'} is depth similarity, k{p,p'} is spatial distance weight, and sp, s{p'} are screw-axis representations. Unlike standard bilateral filters, the loss is not divided by the sum of weights because the goal is comparison, not energy conservation. A regularization term applied alongside depth distortion to constrain Gaussians to aggregate at object surfaces, ensuring robust 3D structure reconstruction. It narrows the distance between the weighted depth of the nearest and farthest M Gaussians on each ray. Extract subset N (nearest M Gaussians) and F (farthest M Gaussians, where blending weight approaches 1) on each ray. Render depth maps dN, dF and blending weight maps TN, TF for subsets N and F. The regularization term is R{nf} = TN \cdot TF \cdot |dN - dF|, where T is the sum of blending weights \omegai. Used in LE3D to improve structural reconstruction quality for downstream tasks. Time and Memory Complexity: The method adds two rendering passes (or one pass with two gradient paths) per regularization step. The complexity is dominated by the rasterization of Gaussians, which is O(N \cdot R) where N is the number of Gaussians and R is the number of rays (pixels). The memory overhead is minimal, requiring storage for two depth maps and their gradients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents detail loss and blurred appearance caused by forcing anisotropic Gaussians to fit smooth monocular depth. Balances coarse depth fitting with fine color appearance. Limitations: Gaussian radiance fields are sensitive to small depth errors, which may result in noisy distribution of primitives in complex texture regions. Requires careful tuning of the regularization weight. When to use it and when not: Use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting with monocular depth supervision and observing blurring or loss of high-frequency detail. Do not use: When the depth estimates are highly inaccurate or noisy, as this may lead to noisy Gaussian distributions. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "DNGaussian: Optimizing Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Radiance Fields with Global-Local Depth Normalization". History and Development: The method addresses the conflict between smooth monocular depth estimates and complex color appearance in Gaussian radiance fields. It builds on the observation that NeRF-style depth regularization forces primitive geometry to conform to smooth depth, which is detrimental to Gaussian splatting where shape deformation is less desirable than spatial reshaping. Where it is used: Used in DNGaussian for sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. DNGaussian: Optimizing Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Radiance Fields with Global-Local Depth Normalization, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01963, fetched 2026-10-26 Adaptive Spatio‐Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scenes with Oscillatory Motion, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70410, fetched 2026-10-26 Lighting Every Darkness with 3DGS: Fast Training and Real-Time Rendering for HDR View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-2549, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Global-Local Depth Normalization
body: Global-Local Depth Normalization is a depth regularization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that prevents scale-invariant losses from overlooking minor depth variations, thereby improving detailed geometry reshaping in texture-rich regions. It sets itself apart from standard scale-invariant losses by combining global scale preservation with local scale amplification, addressing the issue where existing methods align depth maps to a fixed global scale and ignore small local errors. It builds on Hard and Soft Depth Regularization and differs from siblings Depth Reinitialization, Position Regularization, and Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization by explicitly decoupling absolute scale maintenance from local error amplification during gradient computation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{D}, ground truth depth map D{gt} (if available) or reference depth, and optimization hyperparameters. Outputs: Gradient updates for 3D Gaussian parameters (centers, scales, opacities) guided by a combined global-local depth loss. Data Structures: Depth maps are treated as 2D tensors of floating-point values representing distance from the camera plane. Patches are extracted from these maps for local normalization. Method Steps: 1. Compute Global Normalized Depth Loss: Calculate the depth error using a scale-invariant loss function that aligns the predicted depth \hat{D} with the ground truth D{gt} (or a reference) to preserve absolute scene scale knowledge. Let this be \mathcal{L}{global}. 2. Compute Local Normalized Depth Loss: Extract local depth patches from \hat{D} and D{gt}. Apply local scale normalization to these patches to amplify and refocus the loss on small local depth errors. Let this be \mathcal{L}{local}. 3. Combine Losses: Sum the global and local normalized losses to form the total depth regularization loss \mathcal{L}{depth}: \mathcal{L}{depth} = \mathcal{L}{global} + \mathcal{L}{local} 4. Optimize: Use \mathcal{L}{depth} to guide gradient updates during the optimization of 3D Gaussians, encouraging the learning of small local depth changes in a scale-invariant way. Formulas: While the specific mathematical formulation of the global and local normalization functions is not explicitly detailed in the provided excerpts, the concept relies on: Global Scale: Ensuring the overall magnitude of \hat{D} matches the scene scale. Local Scale: Normalizing depth values within local patches to highlight variations. Parameters: Weighting between \mathcal{L}{global} and \mathcal{L}{local}: Not given in the sources. Patch size for local normalization: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Standard scale-invariant depth losses align all depth maps to a fixed global scale, which ignores minor local depth changes. This leads to noisy primitive distributions and reconstruction failures in regions with intricate textures. Gaussian radiance fields are more sensitive to small depth errors compared to NeRF, exacerbating these issues. A strategy to optimize Gaussian normals by guiding them with pseudo-normals derived from depth gradients, while smoothing them using Total Variation (TV) regularization to address noise and lack of multi-view consistency. Definition: This variant uses the depth gradient to derive pseudo-normals \hat{n}{\hat{D}} which guide the optimization of normals \hat{n} within the 3D Gaussians. It addresses the challenge of generating reasonable normals within the 3DGS-based framework. Steps: 1. Calculate Pseudo-Normals: Compute the depth gradient normal \hat{n}{\hat{D}} from the generated depth map \hat{D}. 2. Compute Normal Penalty Loss: Calculate the penalty loss \mathcal{L}{n-p} between the Gaussian normal \hat{n} and the pseudo-normal \hat{n}{\hat{D}}. 3. Compute TV Regularization: Compute the TV normal regularization term \text{TV}{\text{normal}} to smooth \hat{n}. 4. Optimize: Optimize the 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} (including normals \hat{n}) by minimizing the combined loss \mathcal{L}c + \mathcal{L}n. Formulas: Pseudo-normal calculation: \hat{n}{\hat{D}} = \nabla{uv} \hat{D} where \nabla{uv} is the spatial gradient operator on the depth map. Normal penalty loss: \mathcal{L}{n-p} = \| \hat{n} - \hat{n}{\hat{D}} \| This term aligns the Gaussian normal \hat{n} with the depth gradient normal \hat{n}{\hat{D}}. Total normal loss: \mathcal{L}n = \mathcal{L}{n-p} + \lambda{n-TV} \text{TV}{\text{normal}} This combines the penalty and TV smoothness regularization. Depth Generation Context: The depth map \hat{D} is computed via volumetric accumulation: \hat{D} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \hat{w}i di where di is the distance from the i-th 3D Gaussian to the image plane, and \hat{w}i = \frac{Ti \alphai}{\sum{j=1}^N Tj \alphaj} are weights derived from transmittance Ti and opacity \alphai. To avoid disc aliasing from peak selection, depth is treated as a linear interpolation of distances. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: DNGaussian (using this method) demonstrates competitive quality and superior details compared to state-of-the-art methods in sparse-view settings on LLFF, Blender, and DTU datasets. It achieves a 25× reduction in training time and over 3000× faster rendering speed compared to some baselines. Strengths: Prevents noisy primitive distributions in texture-rich regions; enhances detailed geometry reshaping; maintains absolute scale knowledge. Limitations: Standard scale-invariant losses fail to capture small local errors, leading to reconstruction failures in complex textures. When to Use: When optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for scenes with intricate textures and when standard scale-invariant depth losses result in noisy geometry. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Introduced in DNGaussian (2024) to address the sensitivity of Gaussian radiance fields to small depth errors. History: Developed as an improvement over existing scale-invariant depth losses that overlook small losses. Usage: Used in sparse-view 3D Gaussian radiance field optimization. name: Depth Reinitialization
head: Depth-based densification
body: Depth Reinitialization is a regularization strategy that alleviates 'overlapping' and 'under-reconstruction' artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging dense depth information to reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by rejecting standard alpha-blended depth maps in favor of geometric mid-point depths to generate clean, artifact-free point clouds for reinitialization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians, camera parameters, and ground truth color images. Output: A reorganized set of Gaussian positions and colors, initialized from a dense point cloud derived from rendered mid-point depth. Data Structures: Gaussian Gi: Defined by center \mathbf{c}i, scale si = (s{x,i}, s{y,i}, s{z,i}), rotation matrix Ri, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Ray r(t): Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, transformed into the local coordinate system of the Gaussian ellipsoid. Formulas: The Gaussian is modeled as an ellipsoid in 3D space: g(x, y, z) = \frac{x^2}{sx} + \frac{y^2}{sy^2} + \frac{z^2}{sz} = 1 where s = (sx, sy, sz) is the scale. The depth of the mid-point for Gaussian Gi, denoted d{mid}^i, is calculated by finding the intersection of the transformed ray with this ellipsoid surface. For multiple Gaussians contributing to a pixel, the method selects the Gaussian with the maximum contribution weight to avoid alpha blending artifacts: i{max} = \arg \maxi wi d{mid} = d{mid}^{i{max}} where wi is the contribution weight of Gaussian i to the pixel. Parameters: Total number of sampled points: Empirically set at around 3.5 million for each scene. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Depth Map: For each pixel, identify the Gaussian G{i{max}} with the maximum contribution wi. Calculate the mid-point depth d{mid} of this Gaussian using the ellipsoid intersection method. Store this as the depth value for the pixel. Pitfall: Do not use standard blending depth d{blend} = \sum{i=1}^N wi \cdot di (where di is center depth), as it produces misleading depth maps with artifacts like depth collapse, object misalignment, and blending boundaries. 2. Reproject to World Space: Convert the 2D depth map values d{mid} back into 3D world coordinates using the camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. This generates a dense set of 3D points. 3. Sample Initial Points: Randomly select a subset of these reprojected points. The total number of sampled points is approximately 3.5 million per scene. 4. Assign Colors: Assign the ground truth color from the corresponding pixel in the input image to each sampled point. 5. Reinitialize: During optimization, repeatedly reinitialize the Gaussian representation (positions and colors) with these sampled points to reorganize the spatial distribution of Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rotatevector(vec, rotmat): return [sum(rotmat[i][j] vec[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] def generateray(u, v, camKinv, camcenter): dirworld = rotatevector([u, v, 1.0], camKinv) norm = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in dirworld)) dirworld = [c/norm for c in dirworld] return list(camcenter), dirworld def reprojecttoworld(u, v, depth, camKinv, camcenter): dirworld = rotatevector([u, v, 1.0], camKinv) norm = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in dirworld)) dirworld = [c/norm for c in dirworld] depthvec = [depth c for c in dirworld] return [camcenter[i] + depthvec[i] for i in range(3)] def computecontribution(g, u, v): # Simplified weight proxy for the Gaussian's contribution to the pixel return g.alpha def calculatemidpointdepth(rayo, rayd, g): localo = rotatevector([rayo[i] - g.center[i] for i in range(3)], g.rotmat) locald = rotatevector(rayd, g.rotmat) invs = [1.0/g.scale[0], 1.0/(g.scale[1]2), 1.0/g.scale[2]] a = sum(locald[i]2 invs[i] for i in range(3)) b = 2.0 sum(locald[i] localo[i] invs[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(localo[i]2 invs[i] for i in range(3)) - 1.0 disc = b2 - 4ac if disc < 0: return None t1 = (-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2a) t2 = (-b + math.sqrt(disc)) / (2a) return (t1 + t2) / 2.0 def depthreinitializationstep(gaussians, cameras, gtimages, numsamples=3500000): worldpoints = [] worldcolors = [] for cam in cameras: for u, v in cam.pixelcoords: rayo, rayd = generateray(u, v, cam.Kinv, cam.center) maxw = -1.0 bestdepth = None for G in gaussians: tmid = calculatemidpointdepth(rayo, rayd, G) if tmid is not None: w = computecontribution(G, u, v) if w > maxw: maxw = w bestdepth = tmid if bestdepth is not None: pworld = reprojecttoworld(u, v, bestdepth, cam.Kinv, cam.center) worldpoints.append(pworld) worldcolors.append(gtimages[cam.id][u, v]) indices = list(range(len(worldpoints))) random.shuffle(indices) selected = indices[:numsamples] sampledpts = [worldpoints[i] for i in selected] sampledcols = [worldcolors[i] for i in selected] for i, G in enumerate(gaussians): G.center = sampledpts[i % len(sampledpts)] G.color = sampledcols[i % len(sampledcols)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blending Depth Artifacts: Using standard blending depth d{blend} = \sum wi di introduces noise from depth artifacts (depth collapse, object misalignment) which degrades reinitialization quality. Center vs. Mid-point: While depth from Gaussian centers yields comparable rendering metrics (SSIM/PSNR) to mid-point, mid-point yields superior dense point cloud reconstruction. Mid-point is preferred for reinitialization. Precision: The discriminant check in ellipsoid intersection is crucial to handle non-intersecting rays. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead during the optimization loop for rendering depth maps and reprojecting points. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the depth map and the sampled point cloud (3.5M points). Measured Performance: Adding Depth Reinitialization to Blur Split increases the number of Gaussians from 3.74M to 4.32M, SSIM from 0.819 to 0.832, and LPIPS from 0.195 to 0.175. Strengths: Alleviates overlapping and under-reconstruction; produces dense and uniform point distributions; improves LPIPS (human perception). Limitations: Increases Gaussian count; relies on accurate depth rendering; sensitive to the choice of depth metric (mid-point vs center vs blend). When to use: When high-quality dense point cloud reconstruction is desired alongside rendering, or when facing severe overlapping/under-reconstruction issues. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and Gaussian count must be kept low, or if depth accuracy is poor. Depth Reinitialization was introduced in the context of "Mini-Splatting," a method to represent scenes with a constrained number of Gaussians. It builds on the observation that utilizing depth to enhance neural rendering is effective, as seen in NeRF-based algorithms. The specific formulation using mid-point depths for 3D Gaussian Splatting was proposed to address the limitations of alpha-blended depth maps in Gaussian-based representations. name: Isotropic Regularization
head: Mapping with Isotropic Regularization
body: Isotropic Regularization is a geometric constraint used in continuous SLAM-based Gaussian Splatting to prevent the formation of highly elongated Gaussian primitives along the viewing ray direction. Standard differentiable rasterization imposes no constraint on Gaussian scaling along the viewing ray, which causes artifacts and tracking instability in continuous SLAM scenarios where viewpoints are not carefully selected. The method explicitly penalizes scale anisotropy to encourage spherical primitives, distinguishing it from parent strategies that enforce depth consistency or position constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, where each Gaussian i has scaling parameters \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A scalar regularization loss E{iso} added to the total optimization objective. Data Structures: \mathcal{G}: Set of active Gaussians. \mathbf{s}i: Scaling vector for Gaussian i. \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i: Scalar mean of the three components of \mathbf{s}i. \mathbf{1}: Vector of ones with length 3. Steps: 1. For each Gaussian i in the set \mathcal{G}, calculate the mean scale \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i = \frac{1}{3} \sum{j=1}^{3} \mathbf{s}i[j]. 2. Compute the L1 norm of the difference between the scale vector \mathbf{s}i and the broadcasted mean vector \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i \cdot \mathbf{1}. 3. Sum these differences over all Gaussians to obtain E{iso}. Formula: E{iso} = \sum{i=1}^{|\mathcal{G}|} \|\mathbf{s}i - \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i \cdot \mathbf{1}\|1 Where: |\mathcal{G}| is the number of Gaussians. \|\cdot\|1 is the L1 norm. \mathbf{s}i is the scaling parameter vector for Gaussian i. \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i is the scalar mean of the components of \mathbf{s}i. \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. Parameters: No explicit hyperparameters are defined for the basic isotropic regularization term itself. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The L1 norm is used to penalize elongation, encouraging sphericality. Context: This regularization is applied during the "Mapping" phase of the SLAM pipeline, which uses keyframes in the current window Wk and two random past keyframes Wr to avoid forgetting the global map. Boundaries: The term operates directly on scale parameters and does not constrain depth or position, requiring combination with other constraints for full geometric stability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeisotropicregularization(gaussians): """ Computes the isotropic regularization loss for a set of Gaussians. Args: gaussians: A list or array of Gaussian objects, each having a 'scales' attribute. 'scales' is a vector of 3 floats [sx, sy, sz]. Returns: A scalar float representing the total isotropic regularization loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 for gaussian in gaussians: # Get the scaling vector si si = gaussian.scales # Calculate the mean scale stildei meanscale = sum(si) / 3.0 # Create a vector of ones scaled by the mean meanvector = [meanscale, meanscale, meanscale] # Compute the L1 norm of the difference: ||si - meanvector||1 l1norm = sum(abs(si[j] - meanvector[j]) for j in range(3)) totalloss += l1norm return totalloss A variant applied specifically to key Gaussian primitives initialized from 2D keypoints. It prevents center drift by freezing the positions of these key primitives during optimization. The method enforces isotropy via a soft scale regularization that uses the 2D keypoint score map generated by SuperPoint. The loss is defined as L{reg} = \sum{s,m \in Pk} |s - \delta \cdot (1 - m)|, where Pk is the set of key primitives, s is the 3D scale vector, m is the 2D keypoint score, and \delta is a scale threshold. This term controls the 3D scale based on 2D confidence and enforces a uniform scale constraint across all three axes. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians |\mathcal{G}|, as it requires a single pass to compute mean scales and L1 norms. Memory Complexity: Minimal, requiring only temporary storage for mean scales and differences. Strengths: Prevents artifacts caused by highly elongated Gaussians along the viewing direction, which is critical for continuous SLAM stability. Encourages sphericality, leading to more coherent 3D structure. Limitations: Does not directly constrain depth or position, only shape anisotropy. May need to be combined with other constraints for full geometric stability. When to use: In continuous SLAM pipelines where viewpoint diversity is limited and tracking stability is paramount. When not to use: In novel view synthesis with carefully selected, diverse viewpoints where anisotropic Gaussians might naturally form to represent thin structures. Isotropic Regularization was introduced in the context of Gaussian Splatting SLAM to address the instability of 3D Gaussian Splatting in continuous mapping scenarios. It is part of the "Mapping" stage of the SLAM pipeline, which optimizes the global map using current and past keyframes. The technique was first described in the Gaussian Splatting SLAM paper. name: Position Regularization
head: Position Constraint Loss, Surface Regularization Loss
body: Position Regularization prevents floating artifacts and dramatic geometry shifts in 3D Gaussian Splatting by constraining Gaussian centers to remain close to a reference surface or their initial positions. It operates as a geometric prior constraint, distinct from depth-consistency methods in its parent category [9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current Gaussian positions (\mu or pi), reference mesh vertices (vi) or initial Gaussian positions (\mu{init}), and hyperparameters (\tau{pos}, \lambda{sr}). Outputs: A scalar loss value for gradient-based optimization. Data Structures: Gaussian positions: Vector of 3D coordinates. Reference mesh vertices: Array of 3D coordinates from the SMPL or extracted mesh. Initial positions: Stored copy of Gaussian positions at initialization. Formulas: Two primary formulations exist in the literature: 1. Mesh-Proximity Loss (Human Gaussian Splatting): L{mesh} = \sumi \text{ReLU}(\|vi - pi\|2^2 - \tau{pos}) Where: pi: Canonical position of the i-th Gaussian. vi: Nearest vertex on the reference mesh to pi. \tau{pos}: Threshold representing the maximum expected distance between skin and clothes. \text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x). 2. Surface Regularization Loss (Phys3DGS): L{sr} = \|\mu - \mu{init}\|2^2 Where: \mu: Current position of a Gaussian bound to the extracted mesh. \mu{init}: Initial position of that Gaussian, stored separately at the start of training. Parameters: \tau{pos}: Threshold for max distance between skin and clothes. \lambda{sr}: Weight for the surface regularization loss in the total loss function. Steps: 1. Select the reference geometry: either the mesh vertices vi or the initial positions \mu{init}. 2. For each Gaussian, find the nearest reference point vi or retrieve its corresponding \mu{init}. 3. Compute the squared Euclidean distance between the current Gaussian position and the reference point. 4. Apply the specific loss function: If using Mesh-Proximity: Apply ReLU to the difference between squared distance and \tau{pos}, then sum over all Gaussians. If using Surface Regularization: Compute the squared L2 norm of the difference between current and initial positions. 5. Multiply by the respective weight (\lambda{sr} if applicable) and add to the total loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nearest Vertex Search: Finding vi requires efficient nearest-neighbor search. Gradient Flow: The nearest-vertex search is non-differentiable; gradients are backpropagated through pi while treating vi as constant. Storage: The surface regularization variant requires storing \mu{init} separately for every Gaussian, increasing memory usage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def positionregularizationloss(gaussianpositions, meshvertices=None, initialpositions=None, taupos=0.0): """ Computes position regularization loss. Args: gaussianpositions: List of (x, y, z) tuples for N Gaussians meshvertices: Optional, list of (x, y, z) tuples for M mesh vertices initialpositions: Optional, list of (x, y, z) tuples for N Gaussians taupos: Threshold for mesh proximity loss Returns: Scalar loss value (Lmesh or Lsr) """ loss = 0.0 if meshvertices is not None: # Mesh-Proximity Loss (Human Gaussian Splatting) for p in gaussianpositions: mindistsq = float('inf') for v in meshvertices: dx, dy, dz = p[0]-v[0], p[1]-v[1], p[2]-v[2] distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq < mindistsq: mindistsq = distsq loss += max(0.0, mindistsq - taupos) elif initialpositions is not None: # Surface Regularization Loss (Phys3DGS) for p, pinit in zip(gaussianpositions, initialpositions): dx, dy, dz = p[0]-pinit[0], p[1]-pinit[1], p[2]-pinit[2] loss += dxdx + dydy + dzdz return loss This variant specifically encourages Gaussian positions to stay close to the SMPL mesh to avoid floating artifacts in animatable avatars. It is chosen when rendering clothed bodies where the distance between skin and clothes is bounded by \tau{pos}. It differs from general surface regularization by using a mesh-proximity threshold rather than a fixed initial position constraint. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Prevents floating artifacts and dramatic position shifts during training. Limitations: Requires a reference mesh or initial positions. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in Human Gaussian Splatting (2024) for real-time rendering of animatable avatars, where it prevents floating artifacts by constraining Gaussians to the SMPL mesh. Also used in Phys3DGS (2024) for physically-based inverse rendering to prevent dramatic position shifts of vertices caused by large gradients in HDR space. name: Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization
body: Coherent 3D Gaussian Optimization is a regularization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enforces spatial coherence in Gaussian positions and opacities during training, specifically addressing artifacts in sparse-view novel view synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by replacing independent per-pixel residual updates with a learned implicit decoder that produces smooth, coherent residual fields for depth and opacity, supplemented by multiview total variation and optical flow constraints. This prevents the "semi-transparent" artifacts and detail loss common when optimizing Gaussians against sparse input views. The method optimizes the Gaussian parameters (\Sigma, \mathbf{c}) indirectly by optimizing the parameters of an implicit convolutional decoder (\phi) that generates residual corrections for initial depth and opacity estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Set of input views V. Initial depth maps D^{\text{init}}n for each view n, obtained via monocular depth estimation (Yang et al. [60]). Initial Gaussian parameters \Sigma, \mathbf{c}. Camera poses for each view. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \Sigma^, \mathbf{c}^. Optimized decoder parameters \phi^. Data Structures: Implicit Decoder f\phi: A convolutional neural network taking the normalized view index n as input. Segmentation Mask S: A binary mask of shape (C, H, W), where C=5 is the number of regions. Optical Flow Correspondences: Pairs of pixels (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) between views i and j computed via optical flow (Shi et al. [45]). Forward-Backward Consistency Mask M{i \rightarrow j}: A binary mask indicating reliable pixel correspondences between views i and j. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute initial depth maps D^{\text{init}}n for all input views using a monocular depth estimator. Initialize Gaussian parameters \Sigma, \mathbf{c} using standard 3DGS initialization. Initialize decoder parameters \phi randomly. Initialize segmentation masks Sn for each view by dividing the image into C=5 regions based on D^{\text{init}}n. 2. Residual Depth Estimation (Single-View Constraint): For each view n, pass the normalized view index n to the decoder f\phi(n). The decoder outputs a C-channel residual depth tensor. Compute the final residual depth \Delta Dn by applying channelwise summation (chsum) of the element-wise product of the segmentation mask Sn and the decoder output: \Delta Dn = \text{chsum}(Sn \odot f\phi(n)) This ensures smooth deformation within regions while allowing discontinuities between regions. 3. Residual Opacity Estimation: Similarly, estimate residual opacity using a decoder (or shared architecture) producing C-channel residual opacity. Combine with initial opacity to obtain final opacity at each pixel. 4. Gaussian Position Update: For each pixel \mathbf{p} in view n, compute the updated 3D position \mathbf{x} by projecting the residual depth into 3D space: \mathbf{x} = g(D^{\text{init}}n [\mathbf{p}] + \Delta Dn [\mathbf{p}], \mathbf{p}) Here, g(d, \mathbf{p}) is the function that projects pixel \mathbf{p} into 3D space according to depth d. The Gaussian centers are updated to these positions \mathbf{x}. 5. Multiview Total Variation Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{multi}}): Render the depth map R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d} for each view using the current Gaussian parameters and updated positions. Compute the rendered disparity as 1 / (1 + R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d}). Compute the global TV loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} = \left\| \nabla \left( \frac{1}{1 + R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d}} \right) \right\|1 Compute the masked TV loss using the segmentation mask S: \mathcal{L}{\text{MTV}} = \left\| \nabla \left( S \odot \left( \frac{1}{1 + R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, d}} \right) \right) \right\|1 Combine them with a schedule parameter \lambdas: \mathcal{L}{\text{multi}} = (1 - \lambdas)\mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} + \lambdas\mathcal{L}{\text{MTV}} \lambdas is initialized to 0 and gradually increased to 1 by the end of optimization. 6. Flow Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{flow}}): For each pair of views (i, j) with corresponding pixels (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) identified by optical flow: Compute the 3D positions for both pixels using their respective residual depths: Di [\mathbf{p}] = D^{\text{init}}i [\mathbf{p}] + \Delta Di [\mathbf{p}] Dj [\mathbf{q}] = D^{\text{init}}j [\mathbf{q}] + \Delta Dj [\mathbf{q}] \mathbf{x}i = g(Di [\mathbf{p}], \mathbf{p}), \quad \mathbf{x}j = g(Dj [\mathbf{q}], \mathbf{q}) Compute the flow loss using the consistency mask M{i \rightarrow j}: \mathcal{L}{\text{flow}} = \sum{(i, j)} \sum{\mathbf{p}} \left\| M{i \rightarrow j} \odot \left( \mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}j \right) \right\|1 p and q are corresponding pixels calculated using an existing optical flow method. 7. Multisampling: During rendering for color loss calculation, evaluate multiple samples within each pixel and average them to obtain the pixel color. This ensures Gaussians properly cover the pixel area, preventing semi-transparency in novel views. 8. Optimization Step: Minimize the total objective function with respect to \Sigma, \phi, \mathbf{c}: \Sigma^, \phi^, \mathbf{c}^ = \arg \min{\Sigma, \phi, \mathbf{c}} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} \mathcal{L}(R{\Sigma, \alpha, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}), R(\mathbf{p})) + \betam \mathcal{L}{\text{multi}} + \betaf \mathcal{L}{\text{flow}} Typical weights: \betam = 5, \betaf = 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ phi = decoder.parameters() Sigma = initialgaussians.Sigma c = initialgaussians.c alpha = initialgaussians.alpha H, W = initialdepths[inputviews[0]].shape cameraposes = {v: getcamerapose(v) for v in inputviews} # referencecolors = {v: getreferenceimage(v) for v in inputviews} # optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(phi) + [Sigma, c], lr=1e-3) # segmentationmasks = {} for viewidx in inputviews: segmentationmasks[viewidx] = computesegmentationmask(initialdepths[viewidx], numregions) # flowcorrespondences = {} consistencymasks = {} for i, viewi in enumerate(inputviews): for j, viewj in enumerate(inputviews): if i >= j: continue flowcorrespondences[(viewi, viewj)] = computeopticalflow(viewi, viewj) # consistencymasks[(viewi, viewj)] = computeconsistencymask(flowcorrespondences[(viewi, viewj)]) # lambdas = 0.0 for epoch in range(numepochs): lambdas = min(1.0, epoch / numepochs) residualdepthsmap = {} for viewidx in inputviews: normalizedviewidx = viewidx / len(inputviews) residualdepthtensor = decoder(normalizedviewidx) S = segmentationmasks[viewidx] residualdepth = np.sum(S residualdepthtensor, axis=0) residualdepthsmap[viewidx] = residualdepth Dinit = initialdepths[viewidx] updateddepth = Dinit + residualdepth positions = [projectpixelto3d(p, updateddepth[p], cameraposes[viewidx]) for p in range(H W)] Rd = renderdepth(Sigma, alpha, positions, cameraposes[viewidx]) Rc = rendercolor(Sigma, alpha, positions, c, cameraposes[viewidx], multisample=True) disparity = 1.0 / (1.0 + Rd) graddisparity = np.gradient(disparity) LTV = np.sum(np.abs(graddisparity)) maskeddisparity = S disparity gradmaskeddisparity = np.gradient(maskeddisparity) LMTV = np.sum(np.abs(gradmaskeddisparity)) Lmulti = (1 - name: FreGS
head: Frequency-aware regularization for 3DGS, Progressive frequency regularization
body: FreGS addresses the over-reconstruction and high-frequency artifacts common in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by applying progressive frequency regularization to the Gaussian primitives. Unlike sibling methods that focus on pixel-level gradients or geometric depth consistency, FreGS operates in the frequency domain to suppress noise and prevent the model from fitting high-frequency noise present in training data. It builds on Regularization and Geometry Constraints by defining a regularization term based on spectral discrepancies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current set of 3D Gaussians (position, covariance, opacity, color), camera parameters, training images, and their ground truth counterparts. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters with reduced high-frequency artifacts. Data Structures: Standard 3DGS Gaussian attributes: mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients c. Rendered image I{render} and Ground Truth image I{gt}. Method Steps: 1. Render: Compute the rendered image I{render} from the current Gaussian set using standard differentiable rasterization. 2. Frequency Transform: Apply a Fourier Transform (or similar frequency decomposition) to both I{render} and I{gt} to obtain their frequency spectra F{render} and F{gt}. 3. Compute Frequency Discrepancy: Calculate the difference between the frequency spectra. The regularization loss \mathcal{L}{freq} is derived from the high-frequency components where discrepancies are most indicative of overfitting. 4. Progressive Application: Apply the regularization progressively during training. This likely involves adjusting the weight or the frequency band considered as training progresses to stabilize convergence. 5. Loss Combination: Combine with the standard photometric loss (L1 + SSIM) as per the parent framework: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{freq} where \lambda is the regularization weight [Parent]. 6. Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters and update them. Note that gradient updates for scaling and rotation may require stabilization techniques (e.g., rescaling gradients) as noted in related works like Faster-GS, though FreGS specifically targets frequency domain errors. Parameters: \lambda: Regularization weight. Not given in the sources. Frequency band cutoff: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-smoothing: Excessive regularization may remove fine details. The "progressive" nature aims to mitigate this. Precision: Frequency domain operations require careful handling of numerical precision to avoid artifacts in the gradient computation. The broader category of methods using spectral analysis. FreGS is a specific instance using progressive application. Link Uses spatial smoothing rather than explicit frequency domain analysis. Link Focuses on covariance matrix regularization in 3D space. Link Uses depth maps for geometric constraints. Link Adapts to different scales of geometry. Link General geometric constraints. Link Time Complexity: Adds overhead for Fourier transforms and frequency domain calculations per iteration. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing frequency spectra. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively reduces high-frequency artifacts and over-reconstruction. Limitations: May require careful tuning of the progressive schedule and regularization weight. Not given in the sources. When to use: When training results in noisy, over-fitted reconstructions with high-frequency artifacts. When not to use: When fine high-frequency details are critical and the model is under-fitting. It applies progressive frequency regularization to primitives to prevent overfitting and high-frequency artifacts during training. name: Cross-scale geometric adaptation
head: Lgeo, Reprojection error supervision, Reprojection-based cross-scale geometric adaptation
body: Cross-scale geometric adaptation is a self-adaptive regularization method that uses reprojection errors across multiple voxel scales to guide geometry learning without requiring explicit depth ground truth. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Frequency Regularization and Hard and Soft Depth Regularization by dynamically selecting pseudo-labels based on geometric consistency across views rather than relying on fixed depth priors or frequency-domain constraints. This approach significantly reduces floaters and improves convergence quality across scales compared to training without geometric adaptation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training views with known camera poses (rotation Ri, translation ti) and intrinsics Ki; multi-scale voxel representations (low, mid, high resolution) storing depth values Dl and RGB colors C; current Gaussian parameters. Outputs: A geometric adaptation loss \mathcal{L}{geo} used to update Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: The method relies on multi-scale voxels. Each scale l \in \{0, 1, 2\} (Low, Mid, High) maintains a depth map Dl and color map Cl derived from volume rendering. The specific bit-packing or memory layout of the voxels is not given in the sources. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the geometric adaptation loss in the total loss function. Typical values are not explicitly given, but the method is combined with photometric loss [Parent]. Scales: Low, Mid, High resolution voxels. The exact resolution ratios are not given. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each training ray r{train}, sample the depth Dl(r{train}) at each scale l from the current voxel representation. 2. 3D Point Reconstruction (Frame i): For a pixel coordinate pi in frame i, compute the 3D point in camera coordinates x{li} using the depth at scale l: x{li} = Dl(pi) Ki^{-1} \tilde{p}i where \tilde{p}i is the homogeneous augmentation of pi. 3. World Coordinate Transformation: Transform x{li} to world coordinates xl using frame i's rotation Ri and translation ti: xl = Ri x{li} + ti 4. Reprojection to Frame j: Transform the world coordinate point xl to the camera coordinate system of a different training frame j using frame j's rotation Rj and translation tj: x{li \to j} = Rj^T (xl - tj) 5. 2D Projection: Project x{li \to j} back to the 2D pixel coordinate system of frame j: \tilde{p}{li \to j} = \pi(Kj x{li \to j}) where \pi([x, y, z]^T) = [x/z, y/z]^T. 6. Reprojection Error Calculation: Compute the reprojection error el(pi) for scale l as the difference between the original RGB pixel Ci(pi) and the warped pixel from frame j's color map Cj(\tilde{p}{li \to j}): el(pi) = Ci(pi) - Cj(\tilde{p}{li \to j}) 7. Pseudo-Label Selection: Identify the scale l^ with the minimal reprojection error for each ray. This scale's depth is selected as the pseudo-ground truth depth D'(r{train}): D'(r{train}) = \arg \minl (el(r{train})) 8. Loss Computation: Compute the geometric adaptation loss \mathcal{L}{geo} as the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the current depth Dl(r{train}) at the selected optimal scale and the pseudo-ground truth depth D'(r{train}) across all training rays: \mathcal{L}{geo}(r{train}) = \sum{r{train} \in R{train}} \| \hat{D}l(r{train}) - D'(r{train}) \|^2 Note: The source uses \hat{D}l in the final formula but Dl in earlier steps. We assume \hat{D}l refers to the rendered depth at the selected scale. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecrossscalegeometricadaptationloss( rays, frames, voxelscales, cameraintrinsics): """ rays: List of rays, each containing pixel coordinates pi for frame i. frames: List of frame objects, each containing rotation R, translation t, and color map C. voxelscales: List of scale objects (Low, Mid, High), each with a method getdepth(ray) returning Dl. cameraintrinsics: Dictionary mapping frameid to K matrix. Returns: loss: Scalar geometric adaptation loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 for ray in rays: framei = ray.framei framej = ray.framej # Assume paired frames or iterate over all pairs pi = ray.pixelcoordinate # Step 1-3: Reconstruct 3D point in world coordinates for each scale worldpoints = [] for scale in voxelscales: # Get depth at this scale Dl = scale.getdepth(ray) # Homogeneous coordinate pihom = np.array([pi.x, pi.y, 1.0]) # Inverse projection to camera coordinates Kinv = np.linalg.inv(cameraintrinsics[framei.id]) xli = Dl (Kinv @ pihom) # Transform to world coordinates Ri = framei.rotation ti = framei.translation xl = Ri @ xli + ti worldpoints.append(xl) # Step 4-6: Reproject to frame j and compute error reprojectionerrors = [] for l, xl in enumerate(worldpoints): # Transform to frame j camera coordinates Rj = framej.rotation tj = framej.translation xlitoj = Rj.T @ (xl - tj) # Project to 2D Kj = cameraintrinsics[framej.id] pprojhom = Kj @ xlitoj pproj = np.array([pprojhom[0]/pprojhom[2], pprojhom[1]/pprojhom[2]]) # Get color from frame j at projected coordinate # Note: Interpolation may be needed if pproj is not integer Cjval = framej.colormap.sample(pproj) # Get original color from frame i Cival = framei.colormap.sample(pi) # Compute error el = np.linalg.norm(Cival - Cjval) reprojectionerrors.append(el) # Step 7: Select scale with minimal error minerroridx = np.argmin(reprojectionerrors) Dprime = voxelscales[minerroridx].getdepth(ray) # Step 8: Compute loss against the selected pseudo-GT # The source implies comparing the depth at the selected scale # against the pseudo-GT depth (which is effectively the depth # at that scale, but the loss formulation suggests a refinement # or consistency check. Based on Eq 19, it compares Dhatl # (current depth) with D' (pseudo GT). # In this context, D' is the depth from the best scale. # If Dhatl is the depth at the same scale, the loss is zero. # The source likely implies comparing the depth at other scales # or using the pseudo-GT to guide the current scale's depth. # Given Eq 19: Lgeo = sum || Dhatl - D' ||^2. # We assume Dhatl is the depth at the scale being optimized, # and D' is the pseudo-GT derived from the best consistent scale. # If the scale being optimized IS the best scale, Dhatl == D'. # This suggests the loss might be applied to all scales, # or D' is a smoothed/consensus depth. # However, the text says "pseudo-GT depth of the scale with the # minimum reprojection error is obtained... utilized to compute # the geometric adaptation loss". # Let's assume the loss is computed for the scale corresponding # to the minimum error, or perhaps the loss is zero for that scale # and positive for others? # Actually, Eq 19 sums over l? No, it says Dhatl. # Let's stick to the literal formula: Loss is MSE between # rendered depth and pseudo-GT depth. currentdepth = voxelscales[minerroridx].getdepth(ray) loss = (currentdepth - Dprime) 2 totalloss += loss return totalloss Note: The pseudocode above assumes a specific interpretation of Eq 19. If the loss is meant to regularize all scales towards the consensus, the loop over scales in the loss calculation would differ. However, the source states "pseudo-GT depth of the scale with the minimum reprojection error is obtained... utilized to compute the geometric adaptation loss". This implies a single pseudo-GT per ray. The loss is likely applied to the Gaussian parameters that define the depth at that scale, or all scales are pulled towards this consensus. Given the ambiguity, the pseudocode computes the loss for the best scale. In practice, this loss guides the geometry learning by ensuring that the depth at the "best" scale is consistent with the reprojection error minimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: The method relies on accurate camera poses. In scenarios with significant viewpoint changes or sparse training views (e.g., 360° datasets), generalization may be challenging. Local Minima: Omitting novel view rays risks local minima, causing incorrect geometry. Scale Mismatches: Using only depth priors (Ld) can suffer from scale mismatches later in training, whereas L{geo} refines depth progressively. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Requires reprojection for each ray across multiple scales and frames, which is computationally intensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing multi-scale voxel representations. Performance: Significantly reduces floaters and improves convergence quality across scales compared to training without geometric adaptation. Achieves lower final depth error than depth prior (Ld) alone. Strengths: Self-adaptive, no complex scheduling required, robust to geometric noise compared to feature-warping methods like GeCoNeRF. Limitations: Few-shot NeRF relies on accurate camera poses. Performance may degrade with very sparse views. Cross-scale geometric adaptation was proposed in FrugalNeRF (2025) by authors of. It is designed for extreme few-shot novel view synthesis. The method uses weight-sharing voxels across scales to capture varying scene frequencies and employs geometric adaptation via reprojection errors to guide multi-scale geometry. It is used in conjunction with photometric loss and novel view regularization to accelerate training and improve geometry accuracy without external priors. name: Geometry Regularization
head: Gaussian Flattening, Normal Consistency and Flattening
body: Geometry regularization improves the geometric fidelity and smoothness of 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions by constraining the shape of the Gaussian covariance matrices, distinct from depth supervision which only constrains the location of the surface. It addresses artifacts such as "floaters" and noisy geometry by enforcing that Gaussians align with the underlying surface structure. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Frequency Regularization by operating directly on the 3D parametric representation of the Gaussians rather than the frequency spectrum of the rendered image. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Per-Gaussian scaling factors s \in \mathbb{R}^3, per-Gaussian rotation matrices R, per-Gaussian opacities, and optionally rendered depth maps and their derived normals. Outputs: Gradient updates for Gaussian parameters (specifically scaling and rotation) to minimize geometric loss. Data Structures: Scaling Factor (s): A vector of size 3 for each Gaussian, representing the extent along the principal axes defined by the rotation. OptimizationParams: A configuration structure containing a boolean flag usenormalloss (or equivalent) to enable this regularization. Steps: 1. Enable Regularization: Check if the usenormalloss flag is set in the optimization parameters. 2. Calculate Scaling Components: For each Gaussian, retrieve the scaling vector s = [sx, sy, sz]. 3. Identify Smallest Axis: Determine the minimum component of the scaling vector: s{min} = \min(sx, sy, sz). 4. Compute Flattening Loss: Calculate the loss term that drives s{min} towards zero. This encourages the Gaussian to flatten into a 2D surfel aligned with the surface. \mathcal{L}{flatten} = s{min} Note: In practice, this is often implemented as a squared term or weighted sum to ensure differentiability and stability, though the source specifies minimizing the component itself. 5. Enforce Normal Consistency (Optional/Combined): If depth maps are available, compute normals from the rendered depth map. Align these surface normals with the per-Gaussian normals (derived from the rotation matrix R and the flattened axis). \mathcal{L}{normal} = 1 - |n{depth} \cdot n{gaussian}| 6. Combine Losses: Add the regularization terms to the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda{flatten} \mathcal{L}{flatten} + \lambda{normal} \mathcal{L}{normal} where \lambda are hyperparameters [Parent]. Parameters: usenormalloss: Boolean. Enables the geometry regularization pipeline. \lambda{flatten}: Weight for the flattening loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{normal}: Weight for the normal consistency loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Minimizing s{min} to zero can lead to numerical instability if not regularized (e.g., adding a small epsilon). Boundary Conditions: If a Gaussian is already flat, the gradient for the smallest axis vanishes. Disentangling Background: Geometry regularization helps disentangle sky/distant background from foreground geometry, reducing floaters. A specific implementation of geometry regularization that focuses exclusively on flattening Gaussian kernels into 3D surfels aligned with the surface. It minimizes the smallest component of the scaling factor s \in \mathbb{R}^3 towards zero. This aids in determining Gaussian normals by selecting the shortest scaled edge as the surface normal direction. It is chosen when the primary goal is to enforce planar surface structures without necessarily using depth map supervision for normal alignment. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead per iteration, primarily involving the computation of the minimum scaling component and dot products for normal alignment. Memory Complexity: No additional significant memory requirements beyond storing the scaling factors and normals. Strengths: Reduces "floaters" (noisy, isolated Gaussians) and improves surface smoothness. Helps disentangle background from foreground. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambda to avoid over-constraining the geometry. May not be sufficient alone for complex, non-planar structures without additional depth supervision. When to Use: When the scene contains planar surfaces or when floaters are prevalent. When depth maps are available, it can be combined with normal consistency. When Not to Use: For highly volumetric or non-surface-like scenes where flattening is inappropriate. Originated as a technique to improve the geometric quality of 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions. The concept of flattening Gaussians to surfels is discussed in the context of modular frameworks like GauStudio. The specific implementation with usenormalloss in Julia-based pipelines (GaussianSplatting.jl) highlights its role in reducing floaters and improving surface alignment.
