name: Grendel-GS
head: Distributed 3DGS Optimization, Multi-GPU 3D Gaussian Splatting Training
body: Grendel-GS is an out-of-core and distributed optimization method for training 3D Gaussian Splatting that partitions the Gaussian list across multiple GPUs. It solves the memory bottleneck of large-scale scenes by allowing each GPU to render its own subset of Gaussians and combining results via inter-GPU communication at partition boundaries. Unlike TideGS, which operates on a single machine using disk as a cache, Grendel-GS distributes the parameter store across a GPU cluster. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A large set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, camera poses \mathcal{C}, and training images \mathcal{I}. Output: Optimized Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Data Structures: The global Gaussian list \mathcal{G} is partitioned into K subsets \mathcal{G}1, \dots, \mathcal{G}K, one for each GPU k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Each GPU k maintains a local buffer containing \mathcal{G}k. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Distribute the total Gaussian primitives across K GPUs. The partitioning strategy is not specified in the sources. 2. Local Rendering: For each training image, each GPU k renders the contribution of its local subset \mathcal{G}k using standard 3DGS rasterization. This produces a partial color and depth buffer for that GPU. 3. Inter-GPU Communication: At partition boundaries, partial results are communicated between GPUs. The exact protocol (e.g., all-reduce, specific boundary handling) is not detailed in the sources. 4. Composite Loss: The final rendered image is formed by combining the partial renders. The loss is computed against the ground truth image. 5. Gradient Update: Gradients are computed and applied to the local Gaussian parameters on each GPU. Updates to Gaussians that may have moved or require synchronization across partitions are handled via the inter-GPU communication mechanism. Parameters: Number of GPUs K: Not given in the sources. Partitioning scheme: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Boundary Gaussians: Gaussians that span multiple partitions require careful handling during rendering and gradient update to ensure consistency. The sources do not specify the exact mechanism. Communication Overhead: Inter-GPU communication latency can become a bottleneck. The sources do not provide performance metrics for this. Memory: Scales with the number of GPUs, allowing training on scenes with billions of Gaussians that exceed single-GPU VRAM. Performance: Dependent on inter-GPU communication bandwidth and the efficiency of the partitioning strategy. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables training of extremely large-scale scenes. name: TideGS
body: TideGS is a fully out-of-core optimization framework for training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that enables training with over one billion primitives on a single GPU with limited VRAM. It solves the VRAM bottleneck of standard 3DGS by decoupling memory usage from the total scene size N, keeping the full parameter table on SSD and materializing only the per-iteration working set in GPU memory. Unlike Grendel-GS, which distributes Gaussians across multiple GPUs, TideGS operates on a single machine, treating GPU VRAM as a high-bandwidth working-set cache rather than a persistent parameter store. TideGS manages Gaussian parameters across an SSD–CPU–GPU hierarchy. The method relies on the observation that each training iteration touches only a small subset of Gaussians visible from the current camera batch, creating sparsity and temporal locality. Inputs: Camera batch \mathcal{B}t at iteration t. Total number of Gaussians N. Spatial block size B (default 4096). GPU VRAM capacity limit C. CPU cache size (e.g., 16 GB or 32 GB). Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters \Theta stored on SSD. Rendered images for the batch \mathcal{B}t. Unified Parameter Layout: All learnable per-Gaussian attributes are stored in a logical layout \Theta \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}, where D=59 under the standard degree-3 spherical harmonic (SH) parameterization. Physically, \Theta is stored out-of-core as contiguous block records on SSD. Blocks: Gaussians are Morton-sorted to preserve spatial locality and partitioned into SSD-aligned blocks. Block k contains Gaussians indexed by \text{Block}(k) = \Theta[kB: (k+1)B] for k \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}, where K = \lceil N/B \rceil. Each block is summarized by a bounding sphere for visibility culling. Sets: Gaussian-level active set It: The subset of Gaussian indices visible after rasterization for camera batch \mathcal{B}t at iteration t, which receive non-zero gradients. Block-level working set Kt: The set of block indices that conservatively cover the Gaussian-level active set It, used for staging and caching. VRAM-resident set Rt: The set of blocks currently materialized in GPU VRAM, maintained under capacity C. Before training, the block layout is built once: 1. Morton-sort the N primitives. 2. Compute block bounds and statistics. 3. Write the initial base segment to SSD. This step takes 1.9 minutes for \sim 102M Gaussians and 21.2 minutes for \sim 1.1B Gaussians on MatrixCity, accounting for less than 0.5% of total training time. Each iteration t follows four coordinated stages, with stages (1), (2), and (4) overlapped with (3) to amortize I/O latency with GPU computation. 1. Identify working set: Compute Kt via lightweight CPU-side block visibility tests (6-plane frustum tests against block bounding spheres). 2. Prefetch & materialize: Prefetch needed blocks into the CPU cache and materialize them in VRAM via an asynchronous host-to-device (H2D) stream. 3. Render & backprop: Execute the standard 3DGS forward/backward pass on the resident blocks Rt on GPU. Fine-grained Gaussian-level filtering is executed on GPU within the retained blocks to ensure exact 3DGS semantics. 4. Evict & write back: Evict cold blocks when VRAM/CPU caches are full; dirty evictions are propagated through the CPU cache and written back to SSD patch segments asynchronously. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. B = 4096 # Spatial block size (primitives per block) D = 59 # Parameter dimensionality per Gaussian C = 24 10243 # VRAM capacity limit in bytes (e.g., 24 GB) CPUCACHESIZE = 16 10243 # CPU cache size in bytes K = (N + B - 1) // B # Total number of blocks Rt = [] # List of block indices currently in VRAM cpucache = {} # Dictionary mapping block index to data array for t in range(numiterations): batch = camerabatches[t] # Stage 1: Identify working set (CPU) # Conservative CPU-side block visibility test (6-plane frustum test against bounding spheres) Kt = [] for k in range(K): if blockboundingsphereintersectsfrustum(k, batch): Kt.append(k) # Stage 2: Prefetch & materialize (Async H2D stream) # Evict cold blocks from VRAM if capacity C is exceeded while len(Rt) B D 4 > C: evictblock(Rt, cpucache) for k in Kt: if k not in Rt: # Fetch from SSD or CPU cache if k in cpucache: data = cpucache[k] else: data = readssdblock(k) cpucache[k] = data # Asynchronously copy to GPU VRAM asynch2dcopy(k, data) Rt.append(k) # Stage 3: Render & backprop (GPU) # GPU-side fine filtering to get exact active Gaussian indices It It = gpufrustumculling(Rt, batch) # Execute standard 3DGS forward and backward pass loss, gradients = standard3dgsforwardbackward(It, batch) # Update Adam optimizer states for active Gaussians (standard 3DGS step) updateadamoptimizer(It, gradients) # Stage 4: Evict & write back (Async overlap with next stages) # Mark modified blocks as dirty and write back to SSD asynchronously for k in Rt: if blockisdirty(k): asyncwritessdblock(k) D=59: Dimensionality of per-Gaussian parameter vector \thetai. B=4096: Default spatial block size (primitives per block). Batch size |\mathcal{B}t|: 4 for Mip-NeRF 360; 64 (throughput-oriented) or 16 (conservative) for MatrixCity. CPU cache size: 16 GB (throughput-oriented) or 32 GB (conservative) for MatrixCity. Optimizer: Adam with the 3DGS learning-rate schedule. OS Page Caching: OS page caching can skew SSD bandwidth measurements by serving data from DRAM. Mitigation: Use fresh run/cache directories for compared runs and a cold-start protocol to evict cached pages before standalone cold-cache measurements. Naive Offload Failure: Naive offloading fails at \sim 102M Gaussians due to OOM because per-iteration parameters required by rasterization must reside in VRAM. Profiling a 25M-Gaussian model shows 12.13 GB GPU memory for these parameters. CLM Failure: CLM fails at \sim 1.1B Gaussians due to 'Rasterization OOM' because global radix sort and auxiliary buffers exceed available VRAM (>22 GB), as it requires GPU-resident geometry (~45 GB at this scale). Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in sources. Memory Complexity: VRAM scaling is O(|Rt|) or O(|It|), where |Rt| is the capacity-bounded resident set and |It| is the Gaussian active set after fine filtering. This contrasts with O(N) scaling of other methods. Measured Performance: Mip-NeRF 360 (In-memory regime): TideGS (Shuffle) achieves 3.24 img/s (309.1 ms/iter). TideGS (Trajectory) achieves 3.50 img/s (285.8 ms/iter). Native 3DGS achieves 3.95 img/s (253.5 ms/iter). MatrixCity \sim 102M: TideGS PCIe traffic 0.10 GB/iter, Iter 90.7 ms. CLM PCIe traffic 0.41 GB/iter, Iter 100.8 ms. MatrixCity \sim 1.1B: TideGS PCIe traffic 0.97 GB/iter, Iter 525.6 ms, GPU Utilization 49.5%. CLM fails with OOM. Quality Consistency: On Mip-NeRF 360, TideGS PSNR 28.9157 vs Native 3DGS 29.052 (gap 0.11 dB). SSIM 0.8689 vs 0.8694. LPIPS 0.1399 vs 0.1394. Strengths: Enables training with >1B Gaussians on a single 24 GB GPU. Reduces PCIe traffic by 4x compared to CLM at \sim 102M Gaussians. Limitations: Incurs modest overhead in the in-memory regime compared to Native 3DGS. Requires SSD storage capacity. When to use: When training 3DGS scenes with billions of primitives on a single GPU with limited VRAM. When not to use: When the scene fits entirely in GPU memory and maximum throughput is required (Native 3DGS is faster). TideGS was introduced in the paper "TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization". It builds on the insight that 3DGS training is visibility-induced sparse and trajectory-conditioned, allowing GPU memory to serve as a working-set cache. It is implemented in PyTorch 2.6.0 with CUDA 12.4 and evaluated on NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU (24 GB VRAM), AMD EPYC 7532 CPU, 256 GB DDR4, and Samsung PM9A3 NVMe SSD. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.20150, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: CLM
head: CLM (CPU-Local Memory) / Early Adam Update, CLM Pipelining, CPU-GPU Memory Barrier Removal, CPU-Local Memory, Early Adam Update, Smart Caching Policy for Gaussian States
body: CLM is a training optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that removes the GPU memory barrier by offloading Gaussian states to CPU memory and overlapping CPU-side optimizer updates with GPU rendering. It solves the problem of VRAM exhaustion and communication stalls in large-scale scenes by implementing a smart caching policy that keeps frequently updated Gaussians on the GPU while streaming others. Unlike baseline offloading which incurs significant latency, CLM uses pipelining and early Adam updates to hide communication overhead, enabling training of scenes that exceed GPU memory on a single device. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of training views (microbatches), the current set of 3D Gaussian parameters \theta (position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients), and the Adam optimizer state. Output: Updated Gaussian parameters \theta' and rendered images. Data Structures: 1. CPU Memory Buffer: Stores the full set of Gaussian attributes in pinned CPU memory, concatenated and padded to be contiguous and cache-line aligned. 2. GPU Memory Buffer: Stores a subset of "in-frustum" Gaussians required for the current microbatch. 3. Double Buffer: Used in the pipelining stage to enable parameter prefetching and delayed gradient offloading. 4. Signal Buffer: A buffer in CPU pinned memory used to synchronize the GPU communication stream and the CPU Adam thread. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-compute Finalization Microbatch (Lg): For each Gaussian g in the scene, determine the microbatch index Lg at which it is "finalized." A Gaussian is finalized in microbatch j if it is accessed in microbatch j but not in any subsequent microbatch k > j within the current training batch B. Lg = \max \{ i \mid g \in Si \} where Si is the set of Gaussians accessed in microbatch i. If g is not accessed in the batch, Lg = 0. 2. Microbatch Scheduling: Schedule the order of microbatches to maximize two factors: Spatial Locality: Maximize the intersection |S{i+1} \cap Si| to improve GPU caching efficiency. Early Finalization: Arrange microbatches so that more Gaussians are finalized in earlier indices, allowing more CPU Adam updates to overlap with GPU work. 3. Selective Loading (GPU-initiated): Instead of using standard cudaMemcpy, a custom CUDA kernel initiates data transfer from pinned CPU memory to GPU registers, then to GPU memory. The kernel splits the contiguous CPU buffer and concatenates only the in-frustum Gaussian attributes into GPU memory. This avoids CPU-GPU coordination overhead and utilizes PCIe bandwidth efficiently. 4. Forward and Backward Pass: The GPU renders the current microbatch using the loaded Gaussians and computes gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}. 5. Gradient Offloading: A custom kernel transfers gradients from GPU memory to CPU memory. The kernel fetches previously accumulated gradients, adds the new gradients in CUDA registers, and stores the sum back to CPU memory. 6. Early CPU Adam Update: A dedicated CPU thread executes the Adam optimizer. At the end of every microbatch j, the CPU thread updates all Gaussians g where Lg = j. The Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is released during this process to allow concurrent execution with the primary thread. Synchronization is handled via the signal buffer: the GPU sets a signal via DMA when gradients are ready, triggering the CPU update. Gaussians finalized in the last microbatch (Lg = B) do not have their Adam computation overlapped with subsequent GPU work. 7. Caching Policy: The system maintains a cache of frequently updated Gaussians on the GPU. Gaussians not in the cache are streamed from CPU memory as needed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainbatch(batchviews, gaussians, optimizerstate): # 1. Determine finalization microbatch for each Gaussian Lg = {} for g in gaussians: accessedmicrobatches = [i for i, view in enumerate(batchviews) if g in view.frustumgaussians] Lg[g] = max(accessedmicrobatches) if accessedmicrobatches else 0 # 2. Schedule microbatches to maximize spatial locality and early finalization overlap # Heuristic: order views to maximize |S{i+1} ∩ Si| and push finalizations earlier scheduledviews = batchviews # Real implementation applies heuristic scheduler # 3. Initialize double buffers for pipelining gpuparamsbuffer = [] cpugradbuffer = {} # 4. Process microbatches for j, view in enumerate(scheduledviews): # Selective Loading: GPU-initiated kernel loads from pinned CPU memory to GPU registers, then GPU memory # Splits contiguous CPU buffer and concatenates only in-frustum attributes infrustumgaussians = [g for g in gaussians if isinfrustum(g, view)] gpuparamsbuffer = selectiveload(infrustumgaussians) # Forward and Backward Pass renderoutput = forwardpass(gpuparamsbuffer, view) gradients = backwardpass(renderoutput, view) # Gradient Offloading: Kernel fetches previously accumulated gradients, adds new ones in registers, stores sum to CPU cpugradbuffer = accumulategradients(cpugradbuffer, gradients) # Signal GPU communication stream completion via DMA signalbuffer.setsignal() # Early CPU Adam Update: Dedicated CPU thread updates Gaussians finalized in this microbatch gaussianstoupdate = [g for g, l in Lg.items() if l == j] if gaussianstoupdate: cpuadamupdate(gaussianstoupdate, cpugradbuffer, optimizerstate) return gaussians def isinfrustum(g, view): return g.position in view.frustum # def selectiveload(gaussians): return [g.attributes for g in gaussians] # def forwardpass(params, view): return splat(params, view) # def backwardpass(render, view): return computelossgrad(render, view) # def accumulategradients(existing, new): return {k: existing.get(k, 0) + v for k, v in new.items()} # def cpuadamupdate(gaussians, grads, state): pass # A framework that stores the full scene in CPU RAM and dynamically streams only visible Gaussians to GPU memory, enabling training and rendering of scenes exceeding VRAM on a single consumer GPU. It uses a lightweight caching system to track recently used Gaussians and reduce CPU-GPU data transfer. A pitfall is that a single distant view may require access to the full scene, causing high transfer overhead. A custom CUDA kernel that loads Gaussian parameters from pinned CPU memory to GPU registers and then to GPU memory, initiated from the GPU to avoid CPU-GPU coordination overhead. It stores offloaded Gaussian attributes in pinned CPU memory, concatenated and padded for cache-line alignment. The kernel splits attributes from the contiguous CPU buffer and concatenates only in-frustum attributes into GPU memory. A similar kernel is used to transfer gradients from GPU to CPU. Memory Usage: Significantly reduces GPU memory usage for Gaussian model states by offloading them to CPU RAM. It slightly increases "other" memory usage due to the double buffer design for pipelining. Performance: Reduces training time by overlapping communication and CPU Adam computation with GPU computation. In naive offloading, communication and CPU Adam overheads account for >50% of training time; CLM reduces this by hiding these costs. Scalability: Enables training on scenes that exceed VRAM on a single GPU. Hardware: Requires pinned CPU memory and a dedicated CPU thread for Adam updates. Tested on RTX 2080 Ti and RTX 4090. Limitations: The effectiveness of overlapping CPU Adam depends on the scene; scenes with fewer early-finalized Gaussians see less benefit. CLM was introduced in the paper "CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It extends the Grendel training framework and incorporates gsplat rasterization kernels. The method addresses the limitations of naive offloading and distributed training approaches like Grendel-GS. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) CLM: Removing the GPU Memory Barrier for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3779212.3790140, fetched 2026-10-31 A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.01110, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Gaussians Cache Mechanism
head: Gaussian Cache, Reference View Cache
body: The Gaussians Cache Mechanism is a dynamic memory management module designed to accelerate the training and inference of pose-free generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting by eliminating redundant Gaussian prediction computations. It solves the problem of re-inferencing Gaussian points for reference views that share identical relative poses and features across consecutive optimization iterations. Unlike the baseline which re-predicts Gaussians for all input pairs every step, this method stores, queries, and releases cached Gaussian states based on image IDs, achieving a 2× speedup in training and an 8× speedup in inference without degrading reconstruction quality (PSNR). The mechanism operates as a dynamic store, query, and release system that maps image identifiers to pre-computed Gaussian point sets. It prevents the computational overhead of re-running the Gaussian prediction network for reference views that have already been processed in the immediate previous iteration. Input: Reference views I^1r \cdots I^Nr with corresponding image IDs \{1, \dots, N\}. Output: A cache data structure containing stored Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i indexed by image ID i, and the retrieved subset of Gaussians for the current rendering step. The cache is a dynamic store mapping image IDs to Gaussian point sets. Structure: A hash map or dictionary Cache. Key: Image ID i (integer). Value: Predicted Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i (set of 3D Gaussians with attributes: position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Size: Variable, determined by the number of unique reference views processed in recent iterations. 1. Store: In training or inference step t, the system predicts Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i for each reference view i in the current batch. These points \mathbf{G}i are stored in the cache associated with their image ID i. 2. Query: In step t+1, the system identifies the set of image IDs required for the current iteration. It queries the cache using these IDs to retrieve previously stored Gaussian points \mathbf{G}i. 3. Combine: The retrieved cached Gaussians are combined with any newly predicted Gaussians (for views not found in the cache) to form the complete set of Gaussians for rendering. 4. Release: After querying all necessary IDs for the current iteration, the cache identifies any remaining stored Gaussians that were not accessed (unmatched). These unmatched Gaussians are released (deleted) from the cache to optimize memory usage. This ensures that stale data from previous iterations that are no longer relevant does not accumulate, reducing the memory footprint without compromising performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GaussiansCache: def init(self): # Dictionary mapping imageid -> GaussianPoints self.cache = {} def store(self, imageid, gaussianpoints): """Stores predicted Gaussian points for a specific image ID.""" self.cache[imageid] = gaussianpoints def query(self, requiredimageids): """Retrieves cached Gaussian points for the required image IDs.""" retrieved = {} for imgid in requiredimageids: if imgid in self.cache: retrieved[imgid] = self.cache[imgid] return retrieved def release(self, requiredimageids): """Removes cached Gaussians that were not accessed in the current query.""" keystoremove = [key for key in self.cache if key not in requiredimageids] for key in keystoremove: del self.cache[key] def processiteration(self, currentimageids, predictionnetwork): """Full workflow for one training/inference iteration.""" # 1. Query cache for previously computed Gaussians cachedgaussians = self.query(currentimageids) # 2. Identify IDs not in cache (need new prediction) uncachedids = [imgid for imgid in currentimageids if imgid not in cachedgaussians] # 3. Predict Gaussians for uncached IDs newgaussians = {} for imgid in uncachedids: # Standard forward pass through the Gaussian prediction network using image pairs to generate Gaussian attributes newgaussians[imgid] = predictionnetwork.predict(imgid) # 4. Combine cached and new Gaussians for rendering allgaussians = {cachedgaussians, newgaussians} # 5. Render using allgaussians # Standard 2D Gaussian splatting rasterization: project 3D Gaussians to 2D, # compute covariance, opacity, and SH colors, then accumulate into image buffer renderresult = None # 6. Store newly predicted Gaussians into cache for next iteration for imgid, gpoints in newgaussians.items(): self.store(imgid, gpoints) # 7. Release unmatched Gaussians to free memory self.release(currentimageids) return renderresult Typical Values: On a single RTX 3090 GPU, this mechanism reduces training time from 4s/iter to 2s/iter and inference time from 1.02s/iter to 0.13s/iter. Memory Management: The release step removes unmatched Gaussians to optimize memory usage and reduce the memory footprint. Time Complexity: Reduces per-iteration computation by avoiding redundant forward passes through the Gaussian prediction network for repeated views. Memory Complexity: Bounded by the number of unique reference views processed in the immediate vicinity of the current iteration, as stale entries are released. Performance: Achieves a 2× speed increase during training and an 8× boost during inference compared to the baseline without the cache. Quality: Maintains identical PSNR (32.34 dB) compared to the baseline, indicating no negative impact on reconstruction accuracy. Strengths: Significant reduction in training and inference latency; effective for pose-free generalizable methods where reference views are reused across iterations. Limitations: Requires consistent image ID assignment across iterations to benefit from caching. Does not handle long-term temporal coherence beyond the immediate release cycle. The Gaussians Cache Mechanism was introduced in the GGRt (Generalizable Gaussian Splatting in Real-time) paper by Li et al.. GGRt is a pose-free generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that aims to achieve real-time rendering (\ge 100 FPS) and fast inference (\ge 5 FPS) without requiring explicit camera pose information. The cache mechanism was specifically designed to address the computational bottleneck of re-inferencing Gaussian points for reference views that share the same relative pose and features across consecutive training and inference steps. It builds on the G-3DG model and IPO-Net components of the GGRt architecture. GGRt: Towards Pose-Free Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting in Real-Time, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73209-619, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Base 3DGS Optimization
head: Base 3DGS Optimization with Normal Attribute
body:
Base 3DGS Optimization initializes the geometry attributes of 3D Gaussian primitives to provide a robust foundation for subsequent shading attribute optimization, such as in iVR-GS. It differs from standard 3DGS training by incorporating an explicit normal attribute n for each Gaussian and optimizing it via a normal consistency loss, even though this attribute does not affect the base rendering output. This initialization accelerates the convergence of editable Gaussian optimization by ensuring accurate geometric representation before decomposing color and lighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-view images, camera poses, initial 3D Gaussian points (typically from SfM). Output: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives with parameters \{\mui, qi, si, oi, ni, ci\}, where ni is the normal attribute and ci is represented by SH coefficients. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i is parameterized as: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. qi \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation quaternion. si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. oi \in [0, 1]: Opacity. ni \in \mathbb{R}^3: Normal attribute (unit vector). ci: SH coefficients for view-dependent color. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Depth and Normal Maps: For a given viewpoint, render the depth map D and normal map N using the current Gaussian parameters. The rendering follows the alpha compositing equation: \{D, N\} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} Ti \alphai \{di, ni\} where \mathcal{N} is the set of splatted Gaussians, Ti is the transmittance, \alphai is the opacity, di is the depth of the i-th Gaussian, and ni is its normal attribute. Note that ni is not used in the standard 3DGS color/alpha accumulation; it is only accumulated into the normal map buffer for loss computation. 2. Compute Pseudo Normal: Calculate a pseudo normal map 	ilde{N} from the rendered depth map D under the local planarity assumption. This is typically done by computing the cross product of the spatial gradients of the depth map. 3. Compute Losses: Calculate the total loss L as a combination of color/alpha losses and the normal consistency loss: L = L{color} + L{alpha} + Ln Where: L{color} is the L1 loss between rendered and ground truth RGB colors. L{alpha} is the L1 loss between rendered and ground truth alpha channels (optimizing alpha enhances reconstruction quality). L{ssim} is the SSIM loss between rendered and ground truth RGB images. Ln is the normal consistency loss: Ln = ||N - 	ilde{N}||2 4. Optimize: Update all Gaussian parameters \{\mui, qi, si, oi, ni, ci\} using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) to minimize L. The normal attribute ni is updated despite not affecting the base rendering, to accelerate convergence for subsequent stages. Parameters: Loss weights for L{color}, L{alpha}, L{ssim}, and Ln are not explicitly defined in the source for the base method, but standard 3DGS weights are implied for the color/alpha/SSIM components. The normal consistency loss weight is not specified in the base definition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Adjusting the normal attribute n does not affect the rendering results of base 3DGS; it is optimized solely to accelerate the convergence of editable Gaussian optimization. The pseudo normal 	ilde{N} relies on the local planarity assumption, which may fail in highly non-planar regions or where depth is noisy. iVR-GS Training is the optimization procedure for Inverse Volume Rendering Gaussian Splatting (iVR-GS), a method that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with editable shading attributes for volume visualization. It solves the instability and inefficiency of jointly optimizing base geometry and deformation-aware primitives by decoupling the process into two distinct stages: first establishing a robust base 3DGS model, then refining editable Gaussian primitives on top of it. This approach accelerates convergence and reduces memory footprint compared to one-stage training while maintaining reconstruction quality. The 3D Smoothing Filter prevents 3D Gaussian primitives from becoming smaller than the maximal sampling frequency induced by the training images, thereby mitigating aliasing artifacts during rendering at varying sampling rates. It differs from its siblings, iVR-GS Training and Two-stage Gaussian-Surfel (GES) Optimization, by explicitly constraining the Gaussian scale based on camera geometry rather than relying on separate shading attribute optimization or surfel-specific regularization. Two-stage Gaussian-Surfel (GES) optimization is a training pipeline for differentiable rendering that separates the initialization of opaque surface geometry from the joint optimization of appearance and fine geometry. It solves the problem of color leakage and order-independent blending artifacts that occur when translucent surfels and 3D Gaussians are optimized simultaneously. Unlike single-stage approaches where Gaussians dominate image fitting at the expense of surfel coverage, GES first establishes a coarse, opaque surfel backbone, then enriches it with 3D Gaussians for high-frequency details. Editable Gaussian Optimization decomposes color and lighting from the scene using the Blinn-Phong model instead of SH coefficients, enabling scene editing. It builds on the Base 3DGS Optimization by assigning additional shading attributes to each Gaussian primitive: offset color \Delta c \in \mathbb{R}^3, ambient/diffuse/specular coefficients \{ka, kd, ks\}, and shininess term  eta. The voxel color cv is expressed as cp + \Delta c, where cp \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a palette color parameter shared by all Gaussians within a basic scene, fixed as the mean color value of input multi-view images during training, and adjustable during inference. To reduce model size, low-opacity Gaussians are removed periodically, and an L1 regularization term encourages low opacity to neutralize the tendency to use more Gaussians for compact surfaces due to normal-dependent color. Sparsity regularization (L1 loss of rendered offset color map) is added to \Delta c to avoid significant palette color shiftings. Geometry-Guided Optimization is an optimization phase using Edge-Aware Normal Loss and Multi-Scale SSIM loss to ensure geometric accuracy without affecting RGB fidelity. It computes a normal map N from an unprojected depth map D using the cross product of gradients: N = (

Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Accelerates convergence of subsequent shading attribute optimization by providing accurate geometric initialization. Improves reconstruction quality by optimizing alpha channels. Limitations: The normal attribute does not affect base rendering, adding computational overhead for loss computation without direct visual benefit in the base stage. When to use: When subsequent stages require accurate geometric initialization, such as in iVR-GS. When not: When only base rendering quality is required without subsequent editing or shading decomposition. Base 3DGS Optimization was introduced in the context of iVR-GS (Inverse Volume Rendering Gaussian Splatting) to enable editable visualization by decomposing color and lighting. It builds on the original 3DGS method by adding a normal attribute and optimizing it via a consistency loss with pseudo normals derived from depth. The method leverages the fact that 3DGS reconstructs per-pixel alpha channel information, which can enhance reconstruction quality when optimized. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26 AtomGS: Atomizing Gaussian Splatting for High-Fidelity Radiance Field, https://core.ac.uk/works/391753628, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: iVR-GS Training
head: iVR-GS Optimization, Inverse Volume Rendering Gaussian Splatting Training
body: iVR-GS Training is the optimization procedure for Inverse Volume Rendering Gaussian Splatting (iVR-GS), a method that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with editable shading attributes for volume visualization. It solves the instability and inefficiency of jointly optimizing base geometry and deformation-aware primitives by decoupling the process into two distinct stages: first establishing a robust base 3DGS model, then refining editable Gaussian primitives on top of it. This approach accelerates convergence and reduces memory footprint compared to one-stage training while maintaining reconstruction quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images/views of a scene, initial 3D Gaussian parameters (position \mu, scale s, rotation q, opacity o), and semantic segmentation masks for scene components. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters including geometry attributes \{\mui, si, qi, oi\} and editable shading attributes \{k{ai}, k{di}, k{si}, \Delta ci, \betai\}, plus normal vectors ni. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive i stores: Geometry: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 (center), si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (scale), qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion rotation), oi \in \mathbb{R} (opacity). Shading/Editable: k{ai}, k{di}, k{si} \in \mathbb{R} (ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients), \Delta ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 (color offset), \betai \in \mathbb{R} (light magnitude scaling). Normal: ni \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit normal vector). Training Steps: 1. Stage 1: Base 3DGS Optimization (30,000 iterations). Optimize the base geometry attributes \{\mui, si, qi, oi\} using the standard 3DGS optimization pipeline. This stage establishes a stable geometric foundation without editable shading parameters. 2. Stage 2: Editable Gaussian Optimization (10,000 iterations). Initialize editable attributes \{k{ai}, k{di}, k{si}, \Delta ci, \betai\} and normals ni. Optimize all attributes (geometry and shading) using the composite loss function defined below. Geometry attributes are updated alongside shading attributes, but shading attributes have specific learning rates. Loss Function: The total loss L is a weighted sum of image reconstruction loss and regularization terms: L = \lambda{L1} L{L1} + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM} + \lambda{L1\reg} L{L1\reg} + \lambda{norm} L{norm} Where: L{L1} is the L1 reconstruction error between rendered and ground truth images. L{SSIM} is the Structural Similarity Index Measure loss. L{L1\reg} is an L1 regularization term applied to editable Gaussian attributes during Stage 2. L{norm} is the normal consistency loss. Parameters: \lambda{L1} = 0.8 \lambda{SSIM} = 0.2 \lambda{L1\reg} = 0.1 (applied only in Stage 2) \lambda{norm} = 0.01 (applied only in Stage 2) Learning rate for normal and shading attributes: 0.01. Learning rate for other attributes (e.g., opacity o): Same as original 3DGS optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainivrgs(inputimages, initialgaussians, numstagesiterations): """ Train iVR-GS model in two stages.:param inputimages: List of input view images.:param initialgaussians: Initial Gaussian parameters.:param numstagesiterations: Tuple (baseiters, editableiters).:return: Optimized Gaussian parameters. """ gaussians = initialgaussians # Stage 1: Base 3DGS Optimization baseiters = numstagesiterations[0] for i in range(baseiters): # Sample a random view from inputimages view = samplerandomview(inputimages) # Render image using current gaussians (geometry only, no shading edit) renderedimg = rendergaussians(gaussians, view) # Compute L1 and SSIM losses against ground truth loss = 0.8 l1loss(renderedimg, view.gt) + 0.2 ssimloss(renderedimg, view.gt) # Backpropagate and update geometry attributes (mu, s, q, o) # Shading attributes are not yet active or are fixed updategaussians(gaussians, loss, lr=standard3dgslr) # Stage 2: Editable Gaussian Optimization editableiters = numstagesiterations[1] # Initialize shading attributes and normals if not present initializeshadingattributes(gaussians) for i in range(editableiters): view = samplerandomview(inputimages) # Render image using full iVR-GS model (geometry + shading) renderedimg = rendergaussiansivr(gaussians, view) # Compute composite loss lossrecon = 0.8 l1loss(renderedimg, view.gt) + 0.2 ssimloss(renderedimg, view.gt) lossreg = l1loss(gaussians.shadingattributes) 0.1 lossnorm = normalconsistencyloss(gaussians.normals) 0.01 totalloss = lossrecon + lossreg + lossnorm # Backpropagate and update all attributes # Shading and normal attributes use lr=0.01 # Other attributes use standard 3DGS lr updategaussians(gaussians, totalloss, lrshading=0.01, lrgeometry=standard3dgslr) return gaussians A feature allowing multiple independently trained iVR-GS models (basic scenes) to be combined by simply concatenating their Gaussian parameters. To use this, train one basic iVR-GS model for each segmented component in the scene, then combine models by concatenating their Gaussian parameters to reconstruct the complete VolVis scene or view individual components. This enables users to view each semantic component individually or reconstruct the complete scene. Time Complexity: Two-stage training requires 40,000 total iterations (30,000 base + 10,000 editable). Memory Complexity: Depends on scene size and resolution. For example, on a 1024 \times 1024 \times 1080 volume, CPU/GPU memory usage is 12.3 GB/7.1 GB. Performance: Rendering time varies by scene size; e.g., 361 ms for the largest tested volume (2048 \times 2048 \times 2048). Strengths: Decoupled training improves stability and convergence speed compared to joint optimization. Supports composability for modular scene editing. Limitations: Requires semantic segmentation for composability. Two-stage process adds complexity to the training pipeline. iVR-GS Training was introduced in the iVR-GS paper and further applied in the NLI4VolVis framework. It builds upon the original 3DGS optimization method by adding editable shading attributes and a two-stage training strategy to handle volume visualization tasks. name: iVR-GS Two-Stage Training
head: Base 3DGS + Editable Gaussian Optimization, Two-Stage Training for 3DGS
body: iVR-GS Two-Stage Training is a training pipeline for the iVR-GS method that decouples the reconstruction of static scene geometry from the optimization of deformation-aware primitives. It solves the problem of inefficient and unstable joint optimization of base geometry and editable deformation fields in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Unlike one-stage training which optimizes all parameters from scratch, this method first establishes a robust base 3DGS model and then refines editable Gaussian primitives on top of it, accelerating convergence and reducing memory footprint while maintaining reconstruction quality. The method consists of two sequential optimization phases. Inputs: Initial 3D Gaussian point cloud (typically from COLMAP or similar structure-from-motion). Set of training images with camera poses. Target volume rendering configuration (transfer functions, etc.). Outputs: A base 3DGS model with optimized positions, rotations, scales, colors (SH coefficients), and opacities. An optimized set of editable Gaussian primitives with deformation parameters. Data Structures: 1. Base 3DGS Model: Standard 3DGS attributes: position \mathbf{p}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, scale \mathbf{s}, spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}, and opacity \alpha. 2. Editable Gaussian Primitives: A subset or distinct set of Gaussians associated with deformation fields. These include the standard 3DGS attributes plus additional parameters for deformation (e.g., weights for radial features or deformation graph influences) as defined in the parent iVR-GS Training. Steps: 1. Stage I: Base 3DGS Training Optimize the base 3DGS model to capture the basic scene geometry. Loss function: Standard differentiable rendering loss (e.g., L1 + D-SSIM) between rendered images and ground truth. Iterations: 30,000. Goal: Produce a stable, high-fidelity representation of the static scene structure. 2. Stage II: Editable Gaussian Optimization Initialize editable Gaussian primitives using the geometry from Stage I. Optimize the deformation-related parameters of these primitives to enable scene editing. Loss function: Standard rendering loss plus any specific deformation consistency losses defined in the iVR-GS framework. Iterations: 10,000. Goal: Align the deformed 3D Gaussians with the deformed radiance field, ensuring faithful capture of field-wise deformation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ivrgstwostagetraining(initialpoints, trainingimages, numiterationsstage1=30000, numiterationsstage2=10000): # Stage I: Train Base 3DGS basegaussians = initialize3dgs(initialpoints) for i in range(numiterationsstage1): # Sample a random camera pose and render image = render(basegaussians, trainingimages[i % len(trainingimages)]) # Compute loss (L1 + D-SSIM) loss = computerenderingloss(image, trainingimages[i % len(trainingimages)].gt) # Backpropagate and update base gaussians basegaussians.backward(loss) basegaussians.step() # Stage II: Optimize Editable Gaussians # Initialize editable primitives based on base geometry editablegaussians = initializeeditablegaussians(basegaussians) for i in range(numiterationsstage2): # Sample a random camera pose and render deformed scene # Note: Deformation parameters are optimized here image = renderdeformed(editablegaussians, trainingimages[i % len(trainingimages)]) # Compute loss including deformation consistency loss = computerenderingloss(image, trainingimages[i % len(trainingimages)].gt) # Backpropagate and update editable gaussians editablegaussians.backward(loss) editablegaussians.step() return basegaussians, editablegaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: Poor initialization in Stage II can lead to suboptimal deformation fields. Using the converged base model from Stage I is critical. Iteration Count: The specified iteration counts (30k and 10k) are tuned for the reported datasets. Deviations may require re-tuning. Primitive Count: One-stage training tends to use more primitives to achieve similar quality. Two-stage training achieves similar quality with fewer primitives. This method is the second stage of the iVR-GS training pipeline, designed to minimize the discrepancy between the rendering of deformed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the rendering of the deformed radiance field defined by radial features. Time Complexity: Two-stage training uses 40,000 total iterations (30k + 10k), which is comparable to one-stage training (40,000 iterations). However, due to better initialization and separation of concerns, two-stage training reduces actual training time by over 2× compared to one-stage training. Memory Complexity: Two-stage training uses fewer primitives to represent the scene, resulting in smaller file sizes (e.g., 8.8 MB vs 16.7 MB for VolVis scene in one source example). Quality: Maintains similar reconstruction quality (PSNR, LPIPS) to one-stage training. Strengths: Faster optimization, smaller model size, better stability. Limitations: Requires two distinct training phases, potentially increasing implementation complexity. The iVR-GS method was introduced in "iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting". The two-stage training strategy was proposed to address the inefficiencies of optimizing editable Gaussian primitives from scratch, leveraging the established geometry of a base 3DGS model to accelerate convergence and reduce resource usage. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stage II: Align 3DGS with Radiance Field
head: Field-wise Feature Error Minimization, Radial Feature Optimization
body: This method is the second stage of the iVR-GS training pipeline, designed to minimize the discrepancy between the rendering of deformed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the rendering of the deformed radiance field defined by radial features. While Stage I establishes the initial deformation, Stage II finetunes the Gaussian configuration (position, rotation, scaling, spherical harmonics, and opacity) to ensure the deformed Gaussians faithfully capture the field-wise deformation. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS optimization by explicitly aligning the Gaussian splats with a ground-truth radiance field derived from an embedded deformation graph, rather than just matching pixel colors. Inputs: A set of n Gaussians \{Gi\} with parameters \{pi, ri, si, Hi, \alphai\} at rest shape. A deformation graph defined by control points (selected via Furthest Point Sampling from Gaussian centers) and KNN edge connections. A rest-shape radiance field representation. Hyperparameters: \lambda{lpf} (low-pass filter bandwidth), n{dim} (sample points per axis), \lambda1, \lambda2 (error weights). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \{pi, ri, si, Hi, \alphai\} that minimize the total error E{total}. Gaussian i: pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. ri \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). si \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling. Hi: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. \alphai: Opacity (raw scalar). \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix, computed from ri, si. Sample Points: Set \{xj\} uniformly distributed within the Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABB) of Gaussians at rest shape. Adjacency list mapping each sample point to its nearest control points on the deformation graph (computed via KNN). Spatial Hash: Used to map Gaussians to grid cells for fast updates of spatial relations between Gaussians and sample points during optimization. The radiance field is characterized by two radial features: Feature F (encoding rotated harmonics color) and Opacity O (indicating transparency): F(p) = \sum{i=1}^n \alphai Gi(p - pi) \cdot Hi \quad (7) O(p) = \sum{i=1}^n \alphai Gi(p - pi) \quad (8) where Gi(x) is the Gaussian kernel: Gi(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} x^\top \Sigmai^{-1} x\right) \quad (8) The ground truth radial features F^ and O^ are computed at sample points xj after applying embedded deformation. The deformation of a point vi to \tilde{v}i is given by: \tilde{v}i = \sumj wj(vi) \left( Aj (vi - gj) + gj \right) + tj \quad (5) where wj(vi) is the weight from the j-th control node, gj is the control point position, Aj is the affine transformation, and tj is translation. The deformation gradient tensor is used to compute F^ and O^ at the new positions. The total error to minimize is: E{total} = E{feature} + \lambda1 E{opacity} + \lambda2 E{boundary} \quad (14) Where: E{feature} \approx \sum{j=1}^m |F^(xj) - F(xj)| (9, 11) E{opacity} \approx \sum{j=1}^m |O^(xj) - O(xj)| (10, 12) E{boundary} = \sum{xj \in \mathcal{O}} |O^(xj) - O(xj)| (13) \mathcal{O} = \{ xj \mid O^(xj) = 0 \} denotes sample points in unoccupied space. The adaptive anisotropic low-pass filter adjusts the covariance matrix \Sigmai to handle aliasing during deformation: \Sigmai = Ri Si Si^\top Ri^\top + \frac{\lambda{lpf}}{n{dim}^2} Ak Ak^\top \quad (15) where Ak is a 3 \times 3 matrix estimating the first-order approximation of the deformation field near the grid cell center k, and n{dim} is the number of sample points per axis. \lambda{lpf}: Controls the passing bandwidth of the low-pass filter. Typical value: 0.2. n{dim}: Number of sample points per axis in each grid cell. \lambda1, \lambda2: Weights for opacity and boundary errors. Not given in the sources. w{rot}, w{reg}, w{con}: Weights for the deformation graph optimization (Stage I). Values: 1, 10, 100 respectively. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stage2align3dgswithradiancefield(gaussians, deformationgraph, hyperparams): """ Finetunes Gaussian configuration to align with deformed radiance field. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes p, r, s, H, alpharaw. deformationgraph: Object containing controlpoints (list of 3D vectors) and edge connections. hyperparams: Dict with keys lambdalpf, ndim, lambda1, lambda2, maxiterations. Returns: Optimized gaussians. """ # 1. Initialization and Sampling aabbs = [computeaabb(g.p, g.s) for g in gaussians] samplepoints = [] for aabb in aabbs: samplepoints.extend(uniformgridsample(aabb, hyperparams['ndim'])) # KNN adjacency to control points controlpoints = deformationgraph.controlpoints samplepointadjacency = computeknn(samplepoints, controlpoints, k=4) # Spatial hash for fast updates spatialhash = buildspatialhash(gaussians, cellsize=hyperparams['ndim']) # Pre-compute rest-shape features (baseline) Frest = computeradialfeatures(gaussians, samplepoints) Orest = computeopacityfeatures(gaussians, samplepoints) optimizer = AdamOptimizer(gaussians.parameters(), lr=0.001) for iteration in range(hyperparams['maxiterations']): optimizer.zerograd() # A. Ground Truth Features (F, O) deformedpoints = [] for xj in samplepoints: weights = computedeformationweights(xj, samplepointadjacency) deformedpos = computeembeddeddeformation(xj, weights, deformationgraph) deformedpoints.append(deformedpos) # Compute F and O at deformed positions using deformation gradient tensor Fstar, Ostar = computegroundtruthfeatures(deformedpoints, deformationgraph, hyperparams['ndim']) # B. Deformed Gaussian Features (F, O) Fgauss = computeradialfeatures(gaussians, deformedpoints) Ogauss = computeopacityfeatures(gaussians, deformedpoints) # C. Errors Efeature = sum(abs(Fstar[j] - Fgauss[j]) for j in range(len(samplepoints))) Eopacity = sum(abs(Ostar[j] - Ogauss[j]) for j in range(len(samplepoints))) unoccupiedindices = [j for j in range(len(samplepoints)) if Ostar[j] == 0] Eboundary = sum(abs(Ostar[j] - Ogauss[j]) for j in unoccupiedindices) Etotal = Efeature + hyperparams['lambda1'] Eopacity + hyperparams['lambda2'] Eboundary # D. Adaptive Anisotropic Low-Pass Filter for g in gaussians: gridcell = spatialhash.getcell(g.p) Ak = computedeformationgradientmatrix(gridcell, deformationgraph) R = quaterniontorotationmatrix(g.r) S = scaletomatrix(g.s) Sigmabase = R @ S @ S.T @ R.T Sigmafiltered = Sigmabase + (hyperparams['lambdalpf'] / (hyperparams['ndim'] 2)) (Ak @ Ak.T) g.Sigma = Sigmafiltered # E. Backpropagation and Update Etotal.backward() for g in gaussians: g.alpha = sigmoid(g.alpharaw) g.s = exp(g.sraw) optimizer.step() return gaussians def computeaabb(center, scale): return (center - scale, center + scale) def uniformgridsample(aabb, ndim): points = [] for i in range(ndim): for j in range(ndim): for k in range(ndim): x = aabb[0][0] + (aabb[1][0] - aabb[0][0]) (i + 0.5) / ndim y = aabb[0][1] + (aabb[1][1] - aabb[0][1]) (j + 0.5) / ndim z = aabb[0][2] + (aabb[1][2] - aabb[0][2]) (k + 0.5) / ndim points.append([x, y, z]) return points def computeknn(querypoints, referencepoints, k): adj = [] for q in querypoints: dists = [sum((q[i] - r[i])2 for i in range(3)) for r in referencepoints] indices = sorted(range(len(dists)), key=lambda i: dists[i])[:k] adj.append(indices) return adj def buildspatialhash(gaussians, cellsize): grid = {} for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): cx, cy, cz = g.p gx, gy, gz = int(cx / cellsize), int(cy / cellsize), int(cz / cellsize) grid[(gx, gy, gz)] = grid.get((gx, gy, gz), []) + [i] return grid def computedeformationweights(xj, adjacency): weights = [] for idx in adjacency: distsq = sum((xj[i] - deformationgraph.controlpoints[idx][i])2 for i in range(3)) w = 1.0 / (distsq + 1e-8) weights.append(w) total = sum(weights) return [w / total for w in weights] def computeembeddeddeformation(xj, weights, graph): pos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for idx, w in enumerate(weights): cp = graph.controlpoints[idx] Aj = graph.affinematrices[idx] tj = graph.translations[idx] diff = [xj[i] - cp[i] for i in range(3)] transformed = [sum(Aj[i][k] diff[k] for k in range(3)) + cp[i] + tj[i] for i in range(3)] pos = [pos[i] + w transformed[i] for i in range(3)] return pos def computegroundtruthfeatures(deformedpoints, graph, ndim): Fstar = [] Ostar = [] for x in deformedpoints: cell = (int(x[0]/ndim), int(x[1]/ndim), int(x[2]/ndim)) Ak = computedeformationgradientmatrix(cell, graph) # Transform rest-shape features using deformation gradient Fstar.append(Ak @ [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Simplified harmonic transform Ostar.append(0.0) # Placeholder for opacity ground truth computation return Fstar, Ostar def computeradialfeatures(gaussians, points): features = [] for p in points: val = 0.0 for g in gaussians: diff = [p[i] - g.p[i] for i in range(3)] invcov = g.Sigmainv exponent = -0.5 sum(diff[i] sum(invcov[i][k] diff[k] for k in range(3)) for i in range(3)) val += g.alpha exp(exponent) sum(g.H) features.append(val) return features def computeopacityfeatures(gaussians, points): opacities = [] for p in points: val = 0.0 for g in gaussians: diff = [p[i] - g.p[i] for i in range(3)] invcov = g.Sigmainv exponent = -0.5 sum(diff[i] sum(invcov[i][k] diff[k] for k in range(3)) for i in range(3)) val += g.alpha exp(exponent) opacities.append(val) return opacities def computedeformationgradientmatrix(cell, graph): # Finite difference approximation of deformation field over grid cell h = 1.0 / graph.ndim J = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] base = [cell[0]h, cell[1]h, cell[2]h] for d in range(3): offset = base[:] offset[d] += h deformedoffset = computeembeddeddeformation(offset, computeknn([offset], graph.controlpoints, 4), graph) J[d] = [(deformedoffset[i] - base[i]) / h for i in range(3)] return J def quaterniontorotationmatrix(q): x, y, z, w = q return [[1-2(y2+z2), 2(xy-zw), 2(xz+yw)], [2(xy+zw), 1-2(x2+z2), 2(yz-xw)], [2(xz-yw), 2(yz+xw), 1-2(x2+y2)]] def scaletomatrix(s): return [[s[0], 0, 0], [0, s[1], 0], [0, 0, s[2]]] class AdamOptimizer: def init(self, params, lr=0.001): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.m = [0.0] len(params) self.v = [0.0] len(params) self.t = 0 def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = 0.0 def step(self): self.t += 1 beta1, beta2, eps = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8 for i, p in enumerate(self.params): self.m[i] = beta1 self.m[i] + (1 - beta1) p.grad self.v[i] = beta2 self.v[i] + (1 - beta2) p.grad2 mhat = self.m[i] / (1 - beta1self.t) vhat = self.v[i] / (1 - beta2self.t) p.raw -= self.lr mhat / (vhat0.5 + eps) Boundary Deformation: The deformation graph is agnostic to model boundaries, potentially deforming unoccupied space. This is handled by the E{boundary} term, which restricts optimization influence to sample points where O^(xj) = 0. Aliasing: Undersampling high-frequency Gaussians during deformation causes aliasing. This is handled by an adaptive anisotropic low-pass filter applied to the covariance matrix \Sigmai to adjust Gaussian size based on the deformation gradient. Filter Sensitivity: An over-conservative \lambda{lpf} (e.g., 0.02) leads to under-sampling, while an over-aggressive value (e.g., 2.0) causes blurriness. A value of 0.2 is empirically found to be robust. Time: The method requires computing KNN for sample points and updating spatial hashes at each optimization iteration. The computation of radial features F and O scales with the number of Gaussians n and sample points m. The use of spatial hashing accelerates the update of spatial relations. Memory: Requires storing sample points, their adjacency to control points, and the spatial hash structure. The number of sample points is proportional to the number of Gaussians. Implemented on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 24GB GPU using C++ and CUDA. The method is validated on synthetic and real-world data (e.g., Stripes, Glove, Pinocchio, Bunny, Shoe, Cup). The results are not sensitive to \lambda{lpf} within a reasonable range. Strengths: Faithfully captures field-wise deformation; handles aliasing adaptively; prevents deformation of unoccupied space. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of features and KNN adjacency; adds computational overhead to the training process. The method originates from the paper "As-Rigid-As-Possible Deformation of Gaussian Radiance Fields". It was developed to address the issue where rasterizing deformed 3DGS does not always align with the rendering obtained from the deformed radiance field. The method builds upon previous work in 3DGS [9], EWA-Splatting [42], and Mip-Splatting [20], adapting their filtering strategies to the dynamic deformation context. It utilizes embedded deformation techniques similar to those in [16] and [36]. name: Adaptive Anisotropic Spatial Low-Pass Filter
head: Adaptive Anisotropic 3D Low-Pass Filter
body: This filter prevents artifacts such as holes caused by undersampling of high-frequency features in Gaussian radiance fields during deformation. It differs from fixed isotropic low-pass filters by adapting to varying spatial sampling intervals, thereby reducing blurring and preserving high-frequency signals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} representing the radiance field, where each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Output: The same set of Gaussians, potentially with modified parameters or used as a regularization term during optimization. Data Structures: Gaussian: Standard 3D Gaussian representation. Covariance: \Sigmai is a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix. Method: The filter is applied to handle high-frequency signals and varying sampling intervals during deformation. The core mechanism involves an adaptive anisotropic low-pass filter. 1. The sources do not specify the exact algorithmic steps or mathematical formulation for computing the sampling interval or applying the filter kernel. 2. The filter is applied during optimization to regularize Gaussian parameters based on the computed sampling interval. Parameters: \lambda{lpf}: The weight for the adaptive anisotropic 3D low-pass filter. Typical value: 0.2. This value is identical to the parameter used in Mip-Splatting. Pitfalls: Undersampling Artifacts: Without this filter, optimization results exhibit artifacts such as holes due to undersampling of the original radiance field’s spatial signals. Blurring: Using a fixed isotropic low-pass filter causes blurring in regions where sampling intervals change due to deformation. Performance: In some regions, results without the low-pass filter are worse than the baseline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyadaptiveanisotropiclpf(gaussians, lambdalpf=0.2): """ Applies the adaptive anisotropic spatial low-pass filter. Note: The exact mathematical formulation and implementation steps are not provided in the sources. """ # The sources do not specify how to compute the sampling interval # or apply the anisotropic kernel. return gaussians Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method allows experiments to be executed on a single GPU with 8GB of VRAM. Strengths: Reduces the occurrence of artifacts (holes) and better preserves original spatial signals compared to no filter or fixed isotropic filters. Limitations: Requires careful parameter tuning (\lambda{lpf}) and computation of sampling intervals during deformation. When to use: When dealing with deforming Gaussian radiance fields that contain high-frequency features and varying sampling intervals. When not to use: When the scene is static and sampling intervals do not change, a fixed isotropic filter might suffice, though the adaptive version is more robust. Origin: The method is described in "As-Rigid-As-Possible Deformation of Gaussian Radiance Fields". History: It was designed to address artifacts in Gaussian radiance fields during deformation, specifically holes caused by undersampling. Usage: Used in the optimization process of Gaussian radiance fields, particularly in conjunction with KNN (k=8 or 10) for deformation. A filter that prevents Gaussians from becoming smaller than the maximal sampling frequency induced by training images [9588-3d-smoothing-filter.md]. It serves as the parent method for this adaptive approach. Choose it when static regularization is sufficient; choose this adaptive method when deformation causes varying sampling intervals. A rendering method that uses a spatial low-pass filter with an identical weight parameter (\lambda{lpf} = 0.2). It sets apart from this method by using a fixed isotropic filter rather than an adaptive anisotropic one. Choose Mip-Splatting for static or uniformly sampled scenes; choose this method when deformation induces non-uniform sampling intervals. name: Two-stage Gaussian-Surfel (GES) Optimization
head: 2D-GES optimization, 3D-GES optimization, Gaussian-Surfel Joint Optimization
body: Two-stage Gaussian-Surfel (GES) optimization is a training pipeline for differentiable rendering that separates the initialization of opaque surface geometry from the joint optimization of appearance and fine geometry. It solves the problem of color leakage and order-independent blending artifacts that occur when translucent surfels and 3D Gaussians are optimized simultaneously. Unlike single-stage approaches where Gaussians dominate image fitting at the expense of surfel coverage, GES first establishes a coarse, opaque surfel backbone, then enriches it with 3D Gaussians for high-frequency details. The method consists of two distinct phases: Surfel Optimization (Stage 1) and Gaussian-Surfel Joint Optimization (Stage 2). Inputs: Training images from J views. Camera parameters for each view. Initial surfel primitives (position, opacity, spherical harmonics or RGB color, normal). Outputs: Optimized surfel primitives (position, opacity, color, normal). Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics). The implementation relies on two sets of primitives: 1. Surfels: Each surfel i stores position \mathbf{p}i, opacity \alphai, color ci (RGB or SH coefficients), and normal \mathbf{n}i. 2. 3D Gaussians: Each Gaussian k stores position \mathbf{p}k, covariance matrix \Sigmak (or scale/rotation), opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonics coefficients. The goal is to establish a coarse, opaque geometry. 1. Initialization: Initialize surfel positions and properties. Set initial opacity values to be translucent (e.g., low initial weights). 2. Rendering: Render color, depth, and normal maps using alpha blending. The alpha-blended depth D(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) and normal N(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) for a pixel \hat{\mathbf{x}} are computed as: D(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \sum{i=1}^N di \alphai(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(\hat{\mathbf{x}})) N(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{n}i \alphai(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj(\hat{\mathbf{x}})) where di is the depth of surfel i, \mathbf{n}i is its normal, and \alphai(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) is its projected opacity. N is the total number of surfels. 3. Supervision Target Generation: At the midpoint of the surfel optimization iterations, render the alpha-blended normal maps N^{supv} for all training views. These serve as static supervision targets for normal consistency in later iterations. 4. Loss Computation: RGB Loss: Standard photometric loss between rendered and ground truth images. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}n): Aligns the rendered normal map N(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) with the normals derived from the rendered depth map D(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) or the static target N^{supv}. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{sn} = \sum{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} (1 - N^{supv}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \cdot N(\hat{\mathbf{x}})) Note: \mathcal{L}n is effective primarily in early iterations for translucent surfels. In later iterations, opaque regions naturally maintain consistent gradients, making this loss redundant for high-weight surfels. 5. Surfel Densification/Pruning: Periodically densify surfels based on gradient magnitude or visibility. Prune surfels with opacity/weight below a threshold (e.g., w{thresh} = 16 for real scenes, 4 for synthetic). 6. Sorting Order Adjustment: During optimization, adjust the per-pixel sorting order of surfels to prevent protrusion and interleaving artifacts, particularly in textureless scenes. 3D Gaussians are added to refine geometry and appearance. 1. Gaussian Initialization: Identify surfels with opacity/weight wi < 0.8 at the 10,000-th iteration of Stage 1. Initialize 3D Gaussian positions using the positions of these selected surfels. Discard surfels with wi \ge 0.8. Initialize other Gaussian properties (scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) following the standard 3DGS initialization protocol [Kerbl et al. 2023]. 2. Joint Optimization Loop: Rendering: Render the combined scene (surfels + Gaussians). Loss Function: The total loss is: \mathcal{L} = \lambdan \mathcal{L}n + \lambda{gd} \mathcal{L}{gd} + \mathcal{L}{rgb} where \lambdan = 0.05 and \lambda{gd} = 0.1. \mathcal{L}{rgb}: Photometric loss. \mathcal{L}n: Normal consistency loss (using the static target N^{supv} from Stage 1). \mathcal{L}{gd}: Geometry depth loss, constraining the weighted depth of Gaussians to match surfel depth: \mathcal{L}{gd} = \text{MAE}\left(\frac{DG}{WG} - Ds\right) where DG and WG are the weighted depth and weight of Gaussians, and Ds is the surfel depth. Gaussian Densification: Every 1000 iterations: 1. Compute the squared error map between ground truth and rendered image across all training views. 2. Normalize the error map and treat normalized error as sampling probability. 3. Sample a fixed number of pixels per image based on these probabilities. 4. Use the corresponding surfel depth map and camera parameters to obtain a point cloud for the initial positions of new 3D Gaussians. 5. Initialize other Gaussian properties as in [Kerbl et al. 2023]. Gaussian Pruning: Compute the contribution score s{i,j} for each Gaussian i in view j: s{i,j} = \max{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} \frac{c{i,j} \alpha{i,j}(\hat{\mathbf{x}})}{Ws + WG} where \hat{\mathbf{x}} is the pixel covered by the Gaussian, \alpha{i,j}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) is the Gaussian's opacity, c{i,j} = \maxk c{i,j}^k is the maximum channel value of the Gaussian's color, and Ws, WG are the total weights of surfels and Gaussians respectively. Prune Gaussians where \maxj s{i,j} < 0.02 across all J views. \epsilon (Truncation/Weighting Parameter): Controls the weighting of Gaussians near surfel depth. Strategies include: \epsilon = 0: Causes color discontinuities by wrongly truncating Gaussians close to surfel depth. \epsilon = 0.1 (Fixed): May cause color leakage in fine structures. Adaptive \epsilon: Adjusted based on geometry granularity for high-quality rendering. Surfel Weight Threshold (w{thresh}): 16 for real scenes, 4 for synthetic scenes. Densification Interval: Every 1000 iterations. Surfel Discard Threshold: wi < 0.8 at iteration 10,000. Unverified code. This causes color leakage in novel views due to order-independent Gaussian blending. Sorting Order: Omitting per-pixel sorting order adjustment during surfel optimization causes surfels to protrude and interleave under z-buffer depth testing, especially in textureless indoor scenes. \epsilon Parameter: Setting \epsilon = 0 causes Gaussians close to surfel depth to be wrongly truncated, resulting in color discontinuities. Setting \epsilon to a fixed small value (e.g., 0.1) may cause color leakage in fine structures. Normal Loss Redundancy: The normal consistency loss \mathcal{L}n is only effective for translucent surfels in early iterations. In later iterations, opaque regions naturally maintain consistent depth gradients and normals, making \mathcal{L}n redundant for those areas. Performance: 3D-GES achieves 675 fps at 1080p and 233 fps at 2160p on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset. This is approximately 3.6× faster than 3DGS at 1080p. Storage: Requires 366MB for Mip-NeRF360 (less than half of 3DGS's 734MB). After pruning, quantization, and hash-grid compression, storage drops to 47MB. Quality: Two-stage optimization achieves a PSNR of 27.38 on Mip-NeRF360, compared to 27.04 for single-stage optimization. Strengths: Ultra-fast rendering, low storage, view-consistent rendering without popping artifacts, high-fidelity geometry via surfels. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \epsilon and two-stage separation. Single-stage fails to maintain surface coverage. When to use: When high rendering speed and low storage are critical, and high-fidelity geometry is required. Suitable for real-time applications. When not to use: When scene geometry is extremely complex and surfels cannot adequately capture it, or if implementation complexity of two-stage pipeline is prohibitive. Two-stage Gaussian-Surfel (GES) optimization was introduced in "When Gaussian Meets Surfel: Ultra-fast High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [Kerbl et al. 2023] and 2D Gaussian Splatting [Huang et al. 2024], integrating surfel-based rendering to provide robust surface geometry. It addresses the limitations of pure Gaussian splatting, which lacks explicit surface representation, and pure surfel rendering, which may lack high-frequency detail. The two-stage approach was validated to be necessary for preventing color leakage and ensuring sufficient surface coverage. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details
head: 3DGS CUDA kernel implementation, GS Implementation Parameters, GSGEN Implementation Details, Gaussian Splatting Training Configuration, gsplat implementation details, half-precision rasterization implementation
body: This article details the specific implementation parameters, optimization schedules, and kernel-level configurations required to train and render 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes effectively. It addresses the problem of translating the theoretical differentiable rendering pipeline into a stable, high-performance GPU-accelerated training loop. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the concrete hyperparameters (learning rates, thresholds, iteration intervals) and data structure layouts (half-precision fetches, compactness metrics) rather than high-level architectural changes or novel loss functions. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Training by providing the granular settings that govern the densification and optimization steps described there. The implementation relies on a custom CUDA kernel implementation (e.g., gsplat) to handle the forward and backward passes of the differentiable rasterizer, often utilizing tiny-cuda-nn for MLP-based components. The core training loop manages camera sampling, downscaling schedules, and metric evaluation, exposing these via Python bindings [Parent]. Inputs: A set of N input images with known camera poses (intrinsics K, extrinsics R, t), typically from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines like COLMAP or OpenSfM. Outputs: A set of M 3D Gaussian primitives, each parameterized by position \mu, covariance \Sigma (or scale s and rotation q), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients c{lm}. Gaussian Primitives: Stored in a flat array or structure-of-arrays (SoA) layout for efficient GPU access. Each primitive contains: Position: \mathbb{R}^3 (float32 or float16). Rotation: Quaternion \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized). Scale: \mathbb{R}^3 (log-space or direct). Opacity: \mathbb{R}^1 (sigmoid output). SH Coefficients: \mathbb{R}^{3 \times (L+1)^2} for degree L. Standard implementations use Degree 1 (7 coefficients per color channel). Rasterization State: Tile-based partitioning of the image plane. Gaussians are sorted by depth within tiles. Half-Precision Fetches: To reduce register pressure and memory bandwidth, feature vectors (SH coefficients) are fetched in half-precision (FP16) during both forward and backward rasterization kernels. The training process is iterative, typically running for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 30,000). The following steps are executed periodically: 1. Camera Sampling: Randomly select a single image from the training set for supervision in each iteration. 2. Forward Pass: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D, rasterize using alpha blending, and compute the rendered image. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate photometric loss (L1 + SSIM) between rendered and ground-truth images. An automatic scaling factor is applied to loss values to improve half-precision training stability. 4. Backward Pass: Compute gradients via automatic differentiation. 5. Optimizer Step: Update Gaussian parameters using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-3}. To manage the number of Gaussians and adapt to scene complexity, densification and pruning occur at fixed intervals: 1. Gradient-Based Splitting: Every 500 iterations, Gaussians are split based on their view-space position gradient. Condition: If the gradient magnitude exceeds threshold T{pos} = 0.02, the Gaussian is split into two. Action: The original Gaussian is replaced by two children with adjusted scales and positions. 2. Compactness-Based Densification: Every 1000 iterations, a compactness metric is evaluated to clone or split Gaussians that are too small or too large relative to their neighbors, ensuring uniform coverage. 3. Pruning: Every 200 iterations, Gaussians are removed if: Opacity \alpha < \alpha{min} = 0.05. The world-space or view-space radius exceeds a predefined maximum limit. Half-Precision Stability: Training in FP16 can lead to gradient underflow or overflow. An automatic loss scaling factor is required. Degenerate Gaussians: Gaussians with extremely small scales or near-zero opacity can cause numerical instability. Pruning thresholds must be tuned to remove these without over-aggressively deleting valid geometry. Boundary Artifacts: At the edges of the image or near occlusion boundaries, gradient-based splitting may produce artifacts if the threshold T{pos} is not calibrated to the scene's depth distribution.
