Sample Camera imageidx = random.choice(trainingimages) gtimage = trainingimages[imageidx] camera = poses[imageidx] # 2. Forward Pass (Rasterization) # Uses half-precision fetches for SH coefficients renderedimage = rasterize(gaussians, camera) # 3. Loss Computation # Automatic scaling for FP16 stability loss = computeloss(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = scalelossforfp16(loss) # 4. Backward Pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() # 5. Optimizer Step optimizer.step() # 6. Densification and Pruning if iteration % ITERSPLIT == 0: # Split based on view-space position gradient splitgaussians(gaussians, threshold=TPOS) if iteration % ITERDENSIFY == 0: # Compactness-based densification densifygaussians(gaussians) if iteration % ITERPRUNE == 0: # Remove low-opacity and oversized Gaussians prunegaussians(gaussians, alphamin=ALPHAMIN) Decomposes scene into static and per-view distractor Gaussians to handle transient occluders. Adapts rasterization for equirectangular images from 360-degree cameras. Defines core geometric primitives and optimization dynamics. Post-processing module for high-frequency texture synthesis. Handles internal volumetric structures and global illumination. Augments mesh with adaptive Gaussian layer for fine details. Associates semantic embeddings with Gaussians for open-vocabulary querying. Uses positive/negative primitives to sharpen boundaries. Manages dynamic population of primitives for memory and quality balance. Integrates Variational Quantum Circuits for view-dependent effects. Extends 3DGS to handle temporal evolution. Solves appearance via linear least-squares on mesh vertices. Enforces softmax competition among overlapping Gaussians to reduce popping. Uses heavy-tailed distributions for robustness. Introduces structural organization for scalability. Transforms volumetric fields via wavelet analysis. Represents animatable human avatars. Estimates confidence metrics for predictions. Hierarchical compositional representation with reusable primitives. Progressive online training during image acquisition. Models complex lighting effects like specular highlights. Iterative procedures for adjusting Gaussian parameters. Recovers sharp scenes from motion-blurred images. Fast texturing with local RGB maps. Renders mirror reflections using virtual cameras. Interpolates between nested anchors for continuous budget control. Replaces near-zero derivative tails with linear surrogates. Optimized for large-scale, high-resolution scenes. Models uncertainty via distributions over SH coefficients. Separates foreground and background for outdoor captures. Embeds infrared radiative transfer modeling. Converts distant background to equirectangular map. Enforces 3D consistency for sparse-view training. UV-free texture representation on manifolds. Stylizes 3D scenes via learned color mapping. Specialized for satellite photogrammetry. Handles High Dynamic Range imaging. Bounds GPU memory usage during high-res training. Filters unseen points for memory efficiency. Categorizes Gaussians into sketch and patch roles. Decomposes supervision into frequency components. Post-rendering refinement using image gradients. Sparse-view CT reconstruction. Per-scene underwater rendering. Stores parameters in host memory. Iterative refinement for pose-free feed-forward GS. Computational pipeline for projection and blending. Jointly optimizes parameters, sparsity, and quantization. Fuses repetitive instances into shared templates. Shares geometry across instances. Isolates supervision attribution. Uses NeRF for initialization and supervision. Decouples static and transient components. Proxy-free deformation via splat graphs. Extracts mesh from GS using stereo matching. Uses compact anchors to predict primitives. Combines Gaussians and neural fields. Treats Gaussians as stochastic solids for depth extraction. Feed-forward method with view-conditioned Gaussians. Variable SH bands per primitive. Defines geometric transformations. Derives depth/normal maps from splats. Hierarchical optimization with cached radiance. Reduces memory footprint via quantization. Predicts a per-Gaussian scale offset \delta sj using a compact MLP to selectively enlarge covariances, creating pixel-wise variable blur kernels that match spatially varying scene blurriness. The offset is added to the base scale, the transformed covariance is projected to 2D, and used as the blur kernel during rasterization. If \delta sj is constant for all Gaussians, it degrades to a uniform Gaussian blur. This method is distinct from naive Gaussian blur (which blurs the whole image) and learnable Gaussian kernels (which optimize a single mean/variance) by enabling spatially varying blur shapes. A self-supervised denoising method for sparse-view 3DGS that combines Noise2Void (N2V) with differentiable 3DGS. Round 1: Train a UNet using N2V, process denoised images through InstantSplat to initialize/train/render 3DGS, and filter results by viewpoint. Round 2: Fine-tune the UNet with a composite loss balancing low-frequency and perceptual detail consistency, then render again. Unlike supervised methods, it requires no paired clean data, and unlike N2N, it works with single images per viewpoint. Applies different scales to Gaussians based on viewer distance to improve distant object rendering. A position-aware factor \gamma(\mu) is computed: \gamma(\mu) = 1 if \|\mu - c\|^2 < 2r, else \|\mu - c\|^2 / r - 1, where r is scene radius and c is camera center. If \max(s) < g \cdot \gamma(\mu), clone the Gaussian; if \max(s) \ge g \cdot \gamma(\mu), split it; if \max(s) > b \cdot \gamma(\mu), eliminate it, where g and b are scale thresholds. Leverages inter-frame continuity by transforming the viewpoint between consecutive frames rather than rendering each separately. This enables sparse rendering (e.g., one full render every 6 frames) on edge devices like Jetson AGX Orin. Rendering quality degrades as the number of consecutively transformed frames increases due to interpolation error accumulation. Unlike naive pixel warping, it operates at the tile/Gaussian level to reduce preprocessing costs. Constructs an opacity offset table to model changes in digital subtraction angiography. A two-stage inverse rendering framework using foundation model priors. Stage I: Optimize geometry using monocular depth, normal, and diffusion priors. Stage II: Jointly optimize material and lighting using segmentation, intrinsic image decomposition, and diffusion priors. Uses 2DGS instead of 3DGS for more accurate geometry, which is essential for material estimation. Typically uses N=4-32 input views. Utilizes an adaptive 2D low-pass filter at inference time based on rendering resolution and camera distance to handle aliasing. A variant of GraphiXS where the component distribution \delta\theta is modeled as a 3D Gaussian primitive \delta{GS}(x; \mu, \Sigma) = \exp(-\frac{1}{2} (x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)). This provides compact spatial support but may be limited in capturing broader uncertainty regions compared to heavy-tailed distributions. Estimates relative camera pose by optimizing a rigid SE-3 transformation Tt applied to a pre-trained set of 3D Gaussians Gt^. The objective is Tt^ = \arg \min{Tt} \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\mathcal{R}(Tt \odot Gt), I{t+1}). All Gaussian attributes are frozen during this optimization to separate camera movement from deformation. The transformation T is represented by quaternion q \in so(3) and translation t \in \mathbb{R}^3. Typically takes 5-10 seconds. Holds inherited object Gaussians, optimizer, loss, and direction-conditioned asymptotic-color head fixed, optimizing only spatial water representation. Uses N=8 fixed lattice size, coverage normalization, and geometric camera-ray distance for query. Uses 2,048 water Gaussians and 12,288 RGB transport parameters. 18 analytic-renderer unit tests agree with float64 integration within 2.90 \times 10^{-6}. Generates additional Gaussian centers by training a lightweight 3DGS model and reusing its primitive centers as a point cloud to compensate for regions with insufficient image features. Trains a first-pass lightweight 3DGS G^{(0)} on downsampled images with SH degree 0 (DC color only). Stops when densification plateaus or a small step budget is reached. Forms a colored point set P1 by taking primitive centers Xn = \mun and DC color Cn = cn. A hybrid representation of a triangular mesh and 3D Gaussians constrained near the mesh surface. Uses RGD-Net to model relative displacement between mesh and Gaussians to enhance rendering fidelity under mesh constraints. Unlike rigidly bound methods, it allows relative displacement, bypassing the trade-off between rendering accuracy and deformation rationality. The depth of the intersection between the Gaussian and the ray, calculated by flattening the Gaussian ellipsoid into a planar shape. Scale regularization loss Ls is applied to squeeze ellipsoids into flat shapes by constraining the minimum scaling factor component towards zero. The depth is given by d(n, p) = rz \cdot (n \cdot p) / (n \cdot r), where rz is the z-value of the ray direction r, n is the normal, and p is the position. Time Complexity: The forward pass is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians, but dominated by the sorting and blending steps which are O(T \cdot K) where T is the number of tiles and K is the average number of Gaussians per tile. The backward pass is similarly linear in the number of active Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot C) where C is the size of the attribute vector (position, rotation, scale, opacity, SH coefficients). For Degree 1 SH, this is significant. Half-precision fetches reduce memory bandwidth pressure. Measured Performance: Standard 3DGS achieves real-time rendering (30-100+ FPS) on modern GPUs (e.g., RTX 3090/4090) for scenes with millions of Gaussians at 1080p resolution [Parent]. Scaling: Performance scales well with GPU memory and compute. Large-scale scenes require techniques like Pruning and Density Control or BoundedGS to manage memory. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high visual fidelity, explicit representation allows for easy editing and compression. Limitations: High memory usage for large scenes, potential for "floaters" in unobserved regions, sensitivity to initialization. When to Use: Real-time novel view synthesis, interactive applications, scenes with complex geometry and appearance. When Not to Use: Scenes with extreme transparency or subsurface scattering (unless augmented), very sparse view settings without careful initialization. 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. It builds on the concept of splatting, a technique used in computer graphics for rendering point-based representations. The method was developed to address the slow rendering speeds of NeRFs while maintaining high visual quality. It has since become a standard baseline for novel view synthesis and has inspired numerous variants and optimizations. name: DeSplat
head: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting
body: DeSplat is a method for distractor-free novel view synthesis that decomposes the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representation into two distinct sets of Gaussian primitives: static scene Gaussians (Gs) and per-view distractor Gaussians (Gd). It solves the problem of transient occluders (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) corrupting the static 3D reconstruction by separating them from the permanent scene geometry without relying on external semantic segmentation models or pre-trained neural networks. Unlike sibling methods that use foundation models for detection or complex neural appearance encoders for separation, DeSplat relies solely on volume rendering and photometric loss, allowing independent rendering of static elements and transient components while maintaining the speed of standard Gaussian splatting. Inputs: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses. A sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (e.g., COLMAP). Hyperparameters: \lambdad (distractor opacity weight), \lambda{bg} (background loss weight), T\epsilon (background error threshold), warm-up steps (500), image downscaling factor (2). Outputs: Static Gaussian set Gs (optimized globally). Per-view Distractor Gaussian sets Gd^{(j)} (optimized per view j). Rendered static image \mathbf{c}s, distractor image \mathbf{c}d, and composite image \mathbf{c}{comp}. The method maintains two primary data structures for Gaussian primitives, following the standard 3DGS layout: 1. Static Gaussians (Gs): Global list of Ns Gaussians. Fields per Gaussian: Position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), Scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, Spherical Harmonics coefficients or RGB base color \bar{c}i. 2. Distractor Gaussians (Gd): Stored as a list of lists or dictionary keyed by view index j. Gd^{(j)} contains Nd^{(j)} Gaussians specific to camera view j. Fields per Gaussian: Position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Rotation \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^4, Scale \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, Opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, Color \mathbf{c}{RGB} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (clamped to [0, 1]). 3. Embeddings (Optional, for appearance/background): Per-image embedding \mathbf{e}j \in \mathbb{R}^{de} for view j. Per-Gaussian embedding \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^{dz} for static Gaussian i. MLPs: f\theta (appearance modulation), f{BG} (background SH prediction). 1. Initialization: Initialize Gs using the sparse point cloud from COLMAP. Initialize Gd^{(j)} for each view j by placing Gaussians on a 2D plane in front of the camera (near the camera plane) to model per-view transient effects. Densify both sets via Adaptive Density Control (ADC) using cloning and splitting procedures identical to standard 3DGS. 2. Optimization Loop (per step): Forward Pass (Rendering): For each view j, rasterize Gs and Gd^{(j)} separately using standard alpha compositing. Compute static color \mathbf{c}s and opacity \alphas via standard volume rendering accumulation. Compute distractor color \mathbf{c}d and opacity \alphad similarly using Gd^{(j)}. Composite Image: Combine the two streams: \mathbf{c}{comp} = \mathbf{c}d + (1 - \alphad) \mathbf{c}s \alphad = \sum{i=1}^{Nd} \alpha{d,i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{d,j}) where \mathbf{c}d and \mathbf{c}s are the pre-multiplied colors from the respective splats. Appearance Modulation (if enabled): If using appearance embeddings, modulate the base color \mathbf{c}i of static Gaussians before rasterization: (\beta, \gamma) = f\theta(\mathbf{e}j, \mathbf{z}i, \bar{c}i) \tilde{\mathbf{c}}i = \gamma \odot \mathbf{c}i + \beta where \odot is element-wise multiplication, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^3 is shift, \gamma \in \mathbb{R}^3 is scale. Background Rendering (if enabled): Predict background SH coefficients \mathbf{b} using f{BG}(\mathbf{e}j) and render background color \mathbf{c}{BG}. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss L{GS} (e.g., L1 + D-SSIM) between \mathbf{c}{comp} and Ground Truth (GT) image. Compute Distractor Opacity Loss: \lambdad \alphad. Compute Background Loss L{bg} (if enabled): Calculate error \epsilon(r) = ||\mathbf{c}{comp}(r) - \mathbf{c}{GT}(r)|| for pixel r. Create binary mask \tilde{e}(r) = 1 if \epsilon(r) \le T\epsilon, else 0. Smooth mask M(r) = \tilde{e}(r) B{3\times3}, where B{3\times3} is a 3\times3 box filter. Define set P = \{r | M(r) > 0.6\}. Compute loss: L{bg} = \sum{r \in P} |\alphad(r) + (1 - \alphad(r)) \cdot \alphas(r)| This encourages both static and distractor opacities to be low in background regions. Total Loss: L = L{GS} + \lambdad \alphad + \lambda{bg} L{bg}. Backward Pass & Update: Compute gradients of L with respect to all parameters (Gs, Gd^{(j)}, embeddings, MLPs). Update parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Adaptive Density Control (ADC): Apply cloning and splitting for both Gs and Gd^{(j)} based on gradient magnitudes, identical to standard 3DGS. Crucial Modification: Apply opacity reset only to Gs. Disable opacity reset for Gd^{(j)} to prevent confusion between occluders (distractors) and static objects. 3. Rendering (Inference): To render the static scene, use only Gs and the composite formula with \alphad=0, \mathbf{c}d=0, yielding \mathbf{c}s. To render distractors, use only Gd^{(j)}, yielding \mathbf{c}d. Composite Color: \mathbf{c}{comp} = \mathbf{c}d + (1 - \alphad) \mathbf{c}s. Distractor Opacity: \alphad = \sum{i=1}^{Nd} \alpha{d,i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{d,j}). Color Modulation: \tilde{\mathbf{c}}i = \gamma \odot \mathbf{c}i + \beta. Background Loss: L{bg} = \sum{r \in P} |\alphad(r) + (1 - \alphad(r)) \cdot \alphas(r)|. Mask: M(r) = (\tilde{e}(r) B{3\times3}) where \tilde{e}(r) = \mathbb{I}(\epsilon(r) \le T\epsilon). Total Loss: L = L{GS} + \lambdad \alphad + \lambda{bg} L{bg}. \lambdad: Weight for distractor opacity regularization. Not given in the sources. \lambda{bg}: Weight for background loss. Not given in the sources. T\epsilon: Threshold for background error. Not given in the sources. Warm-up steps: 500. Image downscaling: Factor of 2 at beginning of training. Opacity Reset: Applying opacity reset to distractor Gaussians causes confusion between occluders and static objects, leading to poor separation. It must be disabled for Gd. Color Representation: Distractor Gaussians must use RGB clamping [0, 1] instead of Spherical Harmonics (SH) with sigmoid. SH is unsuitable for per-view distractors as it requires view-dependent compensation, and sigmoid struggles with extreme colors (white/black). Initialization: Distractors must be initialized near the camera plane to model view-specific transients effectively. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS per step, requiring two separate rasterization passes (Gs and Gd^{(j)}) and alpha compositing. Memory Complexity: Increases memory usage by storing Gd^{(j)} per view; size depends on distractor density, which remains sparse. Measured Performance: Evaluated on RobustNeRF (Statue, Android, Crab, Yoda scenes), DrivingGaussian, and Photo Tourism datasets; achieves comparable results to prior distractor-free approaches without sacrificing rendering speed. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: No external semantic models required; fully compatible with appearance modeling and background models; explicit separation of static and dynamic elements. Limitations: Requires per-view optimization for distractors, increasing training time slightly compared to single-set 3DGS. When to use: Distractor-free novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes where transient occluders must be separated from static geometry. When not: When external semantic priors are available and distractors require complex semantic separation rather than view-specific transient modeling. DeSplat was proposed by Aalto University researchers (authors include Antti Aalto, et al.) and presented at CVPR 2025. It addresses the limitations of existing distractor-free methods that rely on pre-trained semantic models (e.g., ResNet-18, foundation models) which introduce computational overhead. The method builds on the 3DGS framework [9] and draws inspiration from 2D image Gaussian Splatting [48] for initializing view-specific distractors. It is designed for novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes, such as autonomous driving scenarios (e.g., DrivingGaussian dataset) and photo-tourism datasets. name: 360 Gaussian Splatting
head: 360-GS
body: 360 Gaussian Splatting is a method for generating high-quality 3D spatial representations from 360-degree camera images by combining OpenSfM for sparse point cloud generation and Gaussian Splatting for dense Gaussian conversion. It solves the problem that standard Gaussian Splatting assumes perspective cameras and cannot directly process equirectangular images from 360-degree cameras, a limitation that previously forced users to crop or split images. It sets itself apart from standard implementations by modifying the differentiable rasterization module to support spherical rendering and using OpenSfM, which natively supports equirectangular inputs, unlike Colmap. Inputs: A set of 360-degree equirectangular images. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians (positions, covariances, colors, opacities) optimized to render the input images. Data Structures: Sparse Point Cloud: Derived from OpenSfM's reconstruction.json. Contains 3D positions. The error field present in the source data is ignored during training and set to 0. Camera Data: Derived from OpenSfM's reconstruction.json. Contains camera positions and intrinsic/extrinsic parameters. Gaussian Representation: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation (position \mathbf{\mu}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}, spherical harmonics coefficients, opacity \alpha, color c). Steps: 1. Structure from Motion (SfM): Generate a sparse point cloud and camera poses from the 360-degree images using OpenSfM. OpenSfM is chosen because it supports equirectangular images directly, whereas Colmap does not. 2. Data Loading: Read camera positions and parameters from reconstruction.json using a function analogous to readopensfm. Read sparse point cloud positions from reconstruction.json using a function analogous to readopensfmpoints3D. Initialize the error attribute to 0. 3. Rasterization Modification: Modify the differentiable Gaussian rasterization module (specifically diffgaussianrasterization) to support equirectangular rendering. This involves adding a renderspherical function to the Python interface and updating the CUDA kernels (forward.cu, backward.cu, auxiliary.h). 4. Projection: Project 3D points to equirectangular coordinates. In auxiliary.h, the device function pointtoequirect transforms a point \mathbf{p}{orig} using the view matrix \mathbf{V}: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{p}{orig} \text{length} = \|\mathbf{d}\| \text{longitude} = \operatorname{atan2}(dx, dz) \text{latitude} = \operatorname{atan2}(dy, \sqrt{dx^2 + dz^2}) u = \frac{\text{longitude}}{\pi} v = \frac{\text{latitude}}{\pi/2} The resulting normalized coordinates (u, v) map to the equirectangular image plane. 5. Training: Optimize the Gaussian parameters to minimize the difference between rendered equirectangular images and input images. To manage VRAM, training images are loaded onto the GPU only during the forward/backward pass, not kept resident in memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np import json def pointtoequirect(porig: torch.Tensor, viewmatrix: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Project 3D points to equirectangular coordinates.""" # Transform point to camera space phomogeneous = torch.cat([porig, torch.ones(porig.shape[0], 1, device=porig.device)], dim=1) directionvector = torch.matmul(phomogeneous, viewmatrix.t())[:,:3] # Compute length and normalize length = torch.sqrt(torch.sum(directionvector 2, dim=1)) length = torch.clamp(length, min=1e-6) directionnorm = directionvector / length.unsqueeze(1) dx, dy, dz = directionnorm[:, 0], directionnorm[:, 1], directionnorm[:, 2] # Compute longitude and latitude longitude = torch.atan2(dx, dz) latitude = torch.atan2(dy, torch.sqrt(dx2 + dz2)) # Normalize to [-1, 1] range u = longitude / np.pi v = latitude / (np.pi / 2.0) return torch.stack([u, v], dim=1) def readopensfmpoints3d(reconstructionpath: str) -> torch.Tensor: """Read sparse point cloud positions from OpenSfM reconstruction.json.""" with open(reconstructionpath, 'r') as f: data = json.load(f) points3d = [pointdata['position'] for pointdata in data['points3D'].values()] # Ignore 'error' value, set to 0 as per source return torch.tensor(points3d, dtype=torch.float32) def readopensfmcameras(reconstructionpath: str) -> list: """Read camera positions and parameters from OpenSfM reconstruction.json.""" with open(reconstructionpath, 'r') as f: data = json.load(f) return list(data['cameras'].values()) def renderspherical(gaussians, cameras, imagewidth, imageheight): """Modified rasterization function supporting equirectangular rendering. The source specifies adding this to the Python interface and updating CUDA kernels. [Comment] The core rasterization loop (sorting, projecting, blending) follows standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, but uses pointtoequirect for coordinate projection instead of perspective projection. """ # Implementation invokes the modified CUDA kernels (forward.cu, backward.cu) with equirectangular projection. pass VRAM Usage: Training images are loaded onto the GPU only during the training step, not kept resident. This reduces VRAM usage to approximately 11GB, allowing training on a 16GB GPU (e.g., NVIDIA T4 on Paperspace) with 5,000 images. Performance: Training is slower compared to keeping images in VRAM, but feasible on consumer/prosumer hardware. Strengths: Direct support for 360-degree equirectangular images without cropping; lower VRAM requirements than standard 24GB+ recommendations. Limitations: Relies on OpenSfM, which may have different feature matching characteristics (e.g., using SuperPoint, Disk, or ALIKED with LightGlue) compared to Colmap. 360 Gaussian Splatting was developed to address the incompatibility of the original Gaussian Splatting method with 360-degree cameras. Standard Gaussian Splatting relies on Colmap for SfM, which does not support equirectangular images directly, requiring users to crop images. The method was presented in an unofficial blog post by inuex35, detailing modifications to the Gaussian Splatting repository to integrate OpenSfM and spherical rasterization. 360度カメラ画像からの空間再構成 - 360 Gaussian Splatting, https://qiita.com/inuex35/items/af720689e253cd3b617b, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints
head: Geometry-aware Gaussian Splatting, Surface-constrained 3DGS
body: This family defines the fundamental geometric and appearance primitives of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the mechanisms for their optimization, truncation, and structural refinement. It addresses the problem of representing complex scenes with high-fidelity geometry and appearance using a set of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, while managing computational cost through truncation and densification strategies. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting by focusing on the core primitive definition and training dynamics rather than post-hoc discontinuity handling, and from Appearance and Physical Modeling by prioritizing the structural integrity and density of the Gaussian set itself over complex physical light transport models. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. This method defines the fundamental geometric and appearance primitives of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the mechanisms for their optimization, truncation, and structural refinement. It addresses the problem of representing complex scenes with high-fidelity geometry and appearance using a set of anisotropic 3D Gaussians, while managing computational cost through truncation and densification strategies. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting by focusing on the core primitive definition and training dynamics rather than post-hoc discontinuity handling, and from Appearance and Physical Modeling by prioritizing the structural integrity and density of the Gaussian set itself over complex physical light transport models. Gaussian Representation and Truncation Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting (DisC-GS) is a framework that enables 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent and render sharp boundaries and discontinuities, addressing the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting which tends to blur such features. It differs from sibling methods like Planar Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling boundaries as cubic Bézier curves within the Gaussian's local subspace and applying a "pre-scissoring" operation during rendering, rather than relying solely on geometric constraints or mesh extraction. Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting This family converts the volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting representation into explicit geometric structures, primarily triangular meshes or dense point clouds, to enable compatibility with standard 3D graphics pipelines, mesh editing tools, and physics simulations. Unlike standard 3DGS, which renders via alpha-blended splats, these methods extract a discrete surface or point set that approximates the underlying geometry, allowing for operations such as texture mapping and rigging. Mesh Extraction and Representation Appearance and Physical Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation to support physically based rendering (PBR), relighting, and volumetric light transport, solving the limitations of base 3DGS which relies on fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients that cannot accurately represent complex specularities, dynamic lighting, or non-vacuum media. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gaussian Representation and Truncation by focusing on the radiance and material representation rather than geometric simplification, and distinguishes itself from Physics and Optical Modeling by prioritizing surface material decomposition and relighting over volumetric attenuation equations, although both families modify the core Gaussian properties beyond simple color. Appearance and Physical Modeling Sparse2DGS is a Gaussian Splatting method designed for surface reconstruction from sparse input views, addressing the ill-posed nature of geometric optimization when dense Structure-from-Motion points are unavailable. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and its sibling 2DGS by initializing primitives with unsupervised Multi-View Stereo (MVS) points and employing geometric-prioritized enhancements—such as fixed feature splatting and selective updates—to prevent appearance overfitting and improve geometric learning. Sparse2DGS Surface Geometry Constraints are optimization and initialization techniques applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to enforce geometric fidelity, ensuring that the volumetric Gaussian representation aligns with underlying surface structures such as meshes, planes, or physical boundaries. While standard 3DGS optimizes for photometric accuracy, these methods introduce explicit geometric priors—such as planar alignment, shell confinement, or mesh adherence—to resolve the inherent conflict between volumetric splats and sharp surface representations. They differ from sibling methods like Mesh Extraction and Representation by integrating constraints directly into the training loop rather than post-processing, and from Appearance and Physical Modeling by focusing on spatial geometry rather than radiance. Surface Geometry Constraints CADSplat reconstructs photorealistic, geometrically accurate digital twins from sparse (< 15 views), wide-baseline posed images by regularizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an explicit Computer-Aided Design (CAD) shape prior. Unlike methods that rely on learned generative priors or large-scale data priors (e.g., InstantSplat, pixelSplat), CADSplat imposes a strict, explicit geometric constraint derived from the object's specific CAD model, providing geometric disambiguation under severe occlusion and view scarcity. It differs from sibling geometry-constrained methods by anchoring Gaussians to a parametric CAD surface and jointly optimizing a non-rigid deformation field, rather than relying solely on surface normal or SDF constraints. CADSplat Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting is a method for initializing and regularizing 3D Gaussian Splatting representations using a pre-existing mesh surface to eliminate floating artifacts and improve geometric fidelity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by anchoring Gaussian means to mesh vertices and enforcing planar constraints via specific loss functions, whereas siblings like Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian may use different adsorption mechanisms and Surface Reconstruction via SDF relies on signed distance fields rather than explicit mesh anchoring. Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian (MaGS) is a hybrid scene representation that combines a triangular mesh with 3D Gaussians, where Gaussians are "adsorbed" to mesh facets rather than being rigidly anchored in 3D space. This allows Gaussians to "roam" on the surface, increasing their degrees of freedom for movement and deformation. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by tying the spatial position of Gaussians to a parametric mesh surface defined by logical coordinates, enabling efficient dynamic reconstruction and simulation. Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian This family of methods reconstructs high-quality, watertight 3D meshes from multi-view RGB images by coupling the explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation with an implicit Signed Distance Field (SDF) [17501-3d-gaussian-splatting-for-surface-reconstruction.md]. Standard 3DGS lacks explicit geometric structure, requiring post-processing for mesh extraction; these methods solve this by jointly optimizing Gaussians and an SDF to enforce surface constraints during training [17501-3d-gaussian-splatting-for-surface-reconstruction.md]. They differ from siblings like Mesh Extraction and Representation by integrating geometry regularization directly into the differentiable rendering loop rather than relying on separate reconstruction pipelines. Surface Reconstruction via SDF The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. Subsequent work has focused on addressing the limitations of this representation, particularly regarding geometric fidelity, sharp boundaries, and sparse-view reconstruction. Methods like Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting and CADSplat have emerged to handle specific geometric challenges such as discontinuities and sparse data, respectively. The integration of CAD models and mesh constraints represents a shift towards hybrid representations that leverage external geometric priors. name: Gaussian Representation and Truncation
head: 3DGS Representation, Gaussian Representation and Rendering
body: This family defines the fundamental geometric and appearance primitives of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the mechanisms for their optimization, truncation, and structural refinement. It addresses representing complex scenes with high-fidelity geometry and appearance using anisotropic 3D Gaussians, while managing computational cost through truncation and densification strategies. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting by focusing on core primitive definition and training dynamics rather than post-hoc discontinuity handling, and from Appearance and Physical Modeling by prioritizing structural integrity and density over complex physical light transport models. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) Replaces the standard Gaussian density function with an inverse multiquadric radial basis function to modify the alpha blending behavior during rendering. It sets itself apart from the base Gaussian Splatting method by using a function with heavier tails, which can improve the representation of certain geometric structures or reduce artifacts in specific optimization scenarios. A modification to the fragment culling logic in 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples the visibility threshold from the Gaussian's opacity parameter. It solves the problem where the original implementation's opacity-dependent truncation prevents consistent optimization of low-opacity Gaussians and limits the aggressiveness of spatial truncation. It sets itself apart from siblings like Pruning and Reduction by modifying the runtime rendering loop's culling condition rather than post-processing the Gaussian set, and from Inverse Multiquadric Splatting by retaining the Gaussian density function while altering its evaluation threshold. Augments 2D Gaussian primitives with spatially varying texture maps to capture high-frequency appearance details that fixed spherical harmonics cannot represent. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by dynamically allocating texture resolution based on local image content and error, avoiding the convergence issues associated with cloning-based densification. Unlike GSTex which uses a fixed texel budget on pretrained primitives, this approach optimizes primitives and textures from scratch, and unlike BBSplat which uses a fixed texel-to-primitive ratio, it adapts texel size to scene frequency. A neural implicit representation that serves as a constant-time, constant-memory ray oracle for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes. It maps a ray origin and direction to the distance to the first surface and a visibility probability, enabling efficient secondary ray queries for shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination without requiring a mesh or traversing a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH). Unlike sibling methods that scale with the number of Gaussians, the DDF’s query cost and memory footprint remain fixed regardless of scene size. A densification and optimization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enhances geometric precision by constraining fine-detail Gaussians into uniformly-sized "Atom Gaussians" while merging large Gaussians to cover smooth surfaces. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by replacing free-form splitting with a structured proliferation schedule guided by an Edge-Aware Normal Loss, ensuring Gaussians align strictly with scene geometry rather than drifting. Methods aim to decrease the storage footprint and computational cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by removing redundant or low-impact Gaussians, or by simplifying their attributes, without significantly degrading rendering quality. Unlike the parent method which focuses on the geometric truncation and representation of individual Gaussians, this family focuses on the global or local optimization of the scene graph size and complexity. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Inverse Multiquadric Splatting (which changes the kernel shape) and Directed Distance Field (DDF) for Gaussian Splatting (which adds geometric constraints) by directly reducing the number of primitives or their attribute dimensions. POG is a variant of Gaussian growing that identifies potentially over-large Gaussians to address blurring and needle-like artifacts. In ablation studies on the Tanks&Temples dataset, POG yields PSNR 26.26, SSIM 0.879, and LPIPS 0.121, whereas the Hard Gaussian (HG) variant yields PSNR 26.36, SSIM 0.880, and LPIPS 0.126. POG improves LPIPS slightly but degrades PSNR significantly because it causes overgrowth of already learned areas, making them susceptible to redundant Gaussians. A transparent Gaussian kernel where opacity is view-dependent, modeled by a half-period cosine function to approximate specular reflectance lobes. It adds 5 learnable parameters to the standard 3DGS configuration. The opacity is formulated as: \hat{\alpha}(\theta, \beta, T, \alpha) = \alpha \cdot \frac{\cos(\max(0, \min(\frac{2\theta}{T}, \pi)))+1}{2}\exp(\beta) where \alpha is the base opacity, \theta is the angle between view direction and lobe central orientation, T controls angular span, and \beta modulates sharpness. T is initialized as c\bar{\theta}i/\pi based on viewpoint density, and \beta is initialized to zero. If \theta increases, transparency diminishes to zero, ensuring minimal impact on viewpoints outside the lobe's influence. GS-IR extends the vanilla 3D Gaussian representation by adding a normal vector and material properties to the geometric and appearance parameters. Geometric properties T are defined as a set containing position vector \mathbf{p}, scaling vector \mathbf{s}, unit quaternion \mathbf{q} for rotation, and normal vector \mathbf{n}. Material properties M are defined as a set containing albedo \mathbf{a}, roughness \rho, and metallicity m. Vanilla 3D Gaussian appearance parameters A consist of opacity \alpha and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients \mathbf{f}c for view-dependent color. Not given in the sources. name: Inverse Multiquadric Splatting
head: 3DIQS, Inverse Multiquadric
body: Inverse Multiquadric Splatting is a rendering technique that replaces the standard Gaussian density function with an inverse multiquadric radial basis function to define the splat's alpha contribution. It solves the problem of over-saturation and artifacts in high-opacity regions by providing a different decay profile for the splat's weight. It differs from the standard Gaussian splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting by using a rational function rather than an exponential decay, and from Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation by modifying the core density function rather than just the truncation threshold. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, where each Gaussian has mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, 3D covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i. For a specific pixel/fragment, the 2D projected mean \boldsymbol{\mu}' and 2D conic matrix (inverse covariance) \mathbf{C}{2D} = (\Sigma'{2 \times 2})^{-1} are computed. Output: The final alpha value \alpha for the splat, and gradients for the mean and conic matrix during backpropagation. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. The 2D conic matrix is typically stored as a symmetric 2x2 matrix or its upper-triangular components. In the implementation, the conic matrix entries are accessed as cono.x (top-left), cono.y (top-right/bottom-left), and cono.z (bottom-right), with cono.w representing the opacity. Parameters: correctionFactor: A scalar multiplier applied to the 3D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} and the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'{2 \times 2} to adjust the spread of the splat. Value: 1.38. Steps: 1. Covariance Correction: Multiply the 3D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} by correctionFactor (1.38) before projection to 2D. 2. Compute Ellipse Term: Calculate the squared Mahalanobis distance (ellipse term) using the 2D conic matrix and the offset vector \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}': \text{ellipse} = \mathbf{d}^\top \mathbf{C}{2D} \mathbf{d} = C{xx} dx^2 + C{zz} dy^2 + 2 C{xy} dx dy where C{xx}, C{xy}, C{zz} are the components of the 2D conic matrix. 3. Boundary Checks: If \text{ellipse} \le 0, skip the splat (continue). If \text{ellipse} \ge 9, skip the splat (continue). This limits the effective support of the splat. 4. Compute Weight (w): Calculate the inverse multiquadric weight: w = \frac{1}{\text{ellipse} + 1} This corresponds to the 2D splat function derived from the 3D inverse multiquadric function \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\xi} (dM)^2 + 1} with \xi=1. 5. Compute Alpha: Combine the weight with the base opacity: \alpha = \min(0.99, \alpha{base} \cdot w) where \alpha{base} is the stored opacity of the Gaussian (accessed as cono.w). Pseudocode (Forward Pass): Unverified code. Compute gradient w.r.t. the ellipse term: \text{ellipsepow} = \frac{-2 \cdot dL\dG}{(\text{ellipse} + 1)^2} 3. Compute gradients w.r.t. the offset components dx, dy: \frac{\partial G}{\partial dx} = \text{ellipsepow} \cdot (C{xx} dx + C{xy} dy) \frac{\partial G}{\partial dy} = \text{ellipsepow} \cdot (C{xy} dx + C{zz} dy) 4. Compute gradients w.r.t. the conic matrix components. The gradient of G w.r.t. the conic matrix \mathbf{C}{2D} is: \frac{\partial G}{\partial C{xx}} = \text{ellipsepow} \cdot \frac{1}{2} dx^2 \frac{\partial G}{\partial C{xy}} = \text{ellipsepow} \cdot dx dy \frac{\partial G}{\partial C{zz}} = \text{ellipsepow} \cdot \frac{1}{2} dy^2 Note: The factor of 1/2 arises because C{xy} appears twice in the quadratic form, or equivalently, the gradient w.r.t. the symmetric matrix entry requires care. The source code uses halfellipsepow for diagonal terms and full ellipsepow for off-diagonal accumulation in specific ways. Specifically, the source updates dLdconic2D using halfellipsepow d.x d.x for the x-component, halfellipsepow d.y d.y for the z-component, and ellipsepow d.x d.y for the y-component (which represents the off-diagonal term in the symmetric matrix storage). G (weight) dLdG = opacity dLdalpha # Gradient w.r.t. ellipse ellipsepow = -2.0 dLdG / ((ellipse + 1.0) 2) halfellipsepow = 0.5 ellipsepow # Gradients w.r.t. offset dx, dy dGddx = ellipsepow (Cxx dx + Cxy dy) dGddy = ellipsepow (Cxy dx + Czz dy) # Gradients w.r.t. mean (negative of gradient w.r.t. offset) dLdmeanx = -dGddx dLdmeany = -dGddy # Gradients w.r.t. conic matrix # dL/dCxx = dL/dG dG/dCxx = dLdG (halfellipsepow dx^2 / dLdG) ? # Actually, dG/dCxx = -2 w^2 dx^2 / 2 ? # From source: dLdconic2D.x += halfellipsepow d.x d.x # Note: halfellipsepow already contains dLdG factor? # In source: ellipsepow = - dLdG 2 / (ellipse+1)^2. # dG/dCxx = -2 (1/(ellipse+1)^2) dx^2. # So dL/dCxx = dLdG (-2 dx^2 / (ellipse+1)^2) = ellipsepow dx^2. # But source uses halfellipsepow for diagonal. # Let's follow source logic exactly: dLdconicxx = halfellipsepow dx dx dLdconicxy = ellipsepow dx dy dLdconiczz = halfellipsepow dy dy return dLdmeanx, dLdmeany, dLdconicxx, dLdconicxy, dLdconiczz Time Complexity: Same as standard splatting, O(N) per pixel for N splats, with a constant factor increase due to the rational function evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per splat. Strengths: Provides a different decay profile that can reduce over-saturation in high-opacity regions compared to the Gaussian kernel. Limitations: The rational function may behave differently in the tails, potentially affecting the smoothness of the rendered image. The correction factor 1.38 is specific to this method and may require tuning for different scenes. When to use: When standard Gaussian splatting produces artifacts due to high opacity or when a different radial basis function is desired for specific visual effects. Inverse Multiquadric Splatting was introduced in the paper "DARB-Splatting: Generalizing Splatting with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions". It is part of a family of methods that generalize the standard Gaussian splatting by using different radial basis functions. The method modifies the forward and backward propagation of the CUDA rasterizer to support the inverse multiquadric function. name: Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation
head: Modified truncation
body: Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation is a modification to the standard fragment culling heuristic in 3D Gaussian Splatting that decouples the truncation threshold from the Gaussian's learned opacity parameter. It solves the problem where the original implementation prevents consistent truncation at fewer than ~3.03 standard deviations because low-opacity Gaussians are discarded before they can receive gradients, and enforces an upper bound on the effective threshold due to opacity reset clipping. By checking the Gaussian spatial response against the transparency threshold before multiplying by opacity, this method allows for aggressive truncation (e.g., at 1σ or 2σ) and enables gradient flow to Gaussians that would otherwise be invisible, facilitating investigation into opacity gradient dynamics. Inputs: Set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gi has mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and color \mathbf{c}i. Camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, intrinsics). Image resolution. Truncation threshold \tau\alpha (typically 1/255). Outputs: Rendered image. Updated Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, colors) via backpropagation. Data Structures: The standard 3DGS representation is used. No new data structures are introduced. The modification changes the order of operations in the forward and backward passes. Steps: 1. Ray Casting and Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray and determine the set of Gaussians that intersect the pixel's screen-space footprint. 2. Compute 2D Covariance: For each intersecting Gaussian Gi, compute the 2D covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D} in screen space using the Jacobian of the affine approximation of the projection. 3. Compute Gaussian Response: Calculate the unnormalized Gaussian response ri at the pixel center (or sample point) using the Mahalanobis distance: ri = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{d}i^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{2D}^{-1} \mathbf{d}i\right) where \mathbf{d}i is the vector from the pixel center to the projected mean \boldsymbol{\mu}{2D}. 4. Opacity-Independent Truncation Check: Compare the response ri directly against the threshold \tau\alpha. If ri < \tau\alpha, discard the fragment Gi for this pixel. If ri \ge \tau\alpha, proceed to blending. Note: This check occurs before multiplying by the opacity \alphai. In the original 3DGS, the check is performed on \alphai \cdot ri. 5. Blending: For retained fragments, compute the final color \mathbf{C} using alpha blending: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} \alphai ri \mathbf{c}i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj rj) where Gaussians are sorted back-to-front. Parameters: \tau\alpha: Transparency threshold. Default in 3DGS is 1/255. Truncation distance: The number of standard deviations \sigma at which truncation occurs. The relationship is ri = \tau\alpha \implies \sigma = \sqrt{-2 \ln(\tau\alpha)}. For \tau\alpha = 1/255, \sigma \approx 3.33. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Reset: The original 3DGS implementation clips opacity to a maximum of 1/100 during training. In the original method, this clip enforces an upper bound on the effective truncation threshold, preventing consistent truncation at fewer than \sqrt{-2 \ln(1/100)} \approx 3.03\sigma for high-opacity Gaussians. The modified method bypasses this limitation because the truncation check does not depend on the clipped opacity value. Aggressive Truncation: Truncating at 1σ results in a minimum contributing fragment opacity of \approx 0.61 (since e^{-0.5} \approx 0.606), meaning Gaussians are effectively treated as nearly opaque. Gradient Flow: The original implementation ignores non-zero gradients for opacity when the final transparency is zero, interpreting opacity as part of the response. The modified method allows these gradients to propagate, which may affect training dynamics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderopacityindependent(gaussians, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, taualpha=1/255): """ Renders the scene using opacity-independent truncation. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: 3D mean position cov: 3D covariance matrix alpha: opacity scalar color: RGB color vector camera: Camera object with projection and view matrices imagewidth: int imageheight: int taualpha: float, transparency threshold for truncation Returns: renderedimage: numpy array of shape (H, W, 3) """ renderedimage = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) # Precompute camera matrices viewmatrix = camera.getviewmatrix() projmatrix = camera.getprojectionmatrix() intrinsics = camera.getintrinsics() for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # 1. Cast ray for pixel (x, y) rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) # 2. Find intersecting Gaussians (simplified bounding box check) # In practice, use a spatial data structure (e.g., grid or BVH) candidategaussians = getintersectinggaussians(gaussians, rayorigin, raydirection) if not candidategaussians: continue # 3. Project Gaussians to 2D and compute response fragments = [] for g in candidategaussians: # Project mean to screen space mu3d = g.mu mu2d = projectpoint(mu3d, viewmatrix, projmatrix, intrinsics) # Compute 2D covariance in screen space # Jacobian J of the projection at mu3d J = computejacobian(mu3d, viewmatrix, projmatrix, intrinsics) cov2d = J @ g.cov @ J.T # Compute Mahalanobis distance squared d = mu2d - np.array([x, y]) # Handle degenerate covariance (add small epsilon for stability) cov2dinv = np.linalg.inv(cov2d + 1e-6 np.eye(2)) distsq = d @ cov2dinv @ d # Compute Gaussian response response = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) # 4. Opacity-Independent Truncation Check if response < taualpha: continue # Skip fragment # Store fragment for blending fragments.append({ 'response': response, 'alpha': g.alpha, 'color': g.color, 'depth': projectdepth(mu3d, viewmatrix, projmatrix) }) # 5. Sort fragments back-to-front fragments.sort(key=lambda f: f['depth'], reverse=True) # 6. Alpha Blending accumulatedalpha = 0.0 color = np.zeros(3) for frag in fragments: alphafrag = frag['alpha'] frag['response'] color += alphafrag frag['color'] (1 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedalpha += alphafrag (1 - accumulatedalpha) if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: # Early exit optimization break renderedimage[y, x] = color return renderedimage Uses a different kernel function for splatting. Choose when smoother falloff is needed. Adapts Gaussian size based on image content. Choose for texture-rich scenes. Uses DDFs for geometry representation. Choose for explicit surface reconstruction. Manages Gaussian proliferation at a finer granularity. Choose for high-detail reconstruction. Removes redundant Gaussians. Choose for memory efficiency. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is dominated by the rasterization step, which is O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of Gaussians and P is the number of pixels, assuming efficient spatial culling. The truncation check adds negligible overhead. Memory complexity is O(N) for storing Gaussian parameters. Measured Performance: Based on experiments on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset: 1σ truncation (modified): 25.86 PSNR, 2m26s training time, 4.5GiB VRAM, 1.39M Gaussians. 2σ truncation (modified): 27.23 PSNR, 3m41s training time, 5.5GiB VRAM, 2.22M Gaussians. 3.33σ truncation (modified): 27.57 PSNR, 5m07s training time, 6.4GiB VRAM, 2.79M Gaussians. Default 3.33σ (original): 27.54 PSNR, 4m31s training time, 6.1GiB VRAM, 2.70M Gaussians. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows for aggressive truncation (1σ, 2σ) which reduces the number of Gaussians and VRAM usage. Enables gradient flow to low-opacity Gaussians, providing more flexibility in training dynamics. Limitations: Aggressive truncation (1σ) significantly reduces PSNR (25.86 vs 27.54). Training time can increase with the modification due to more complex gradient flow or densification behavior. The method slows down training compared to the original default configuration. When to Use: Use when VRAM is constrained and a slight drop in PSNR is acceptable. Use when investigating the impact of opacity gradients on training. Do not use when maximum PSNR is required and VRAM is not a bottleneck. Originated in the analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization, specifically in the paper "Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization". The work highlights limitations in the original 3DGS truncation heuristic, particularly the interaction between opacity clipping and truncation thresholds. It was developed to provide a more flexible truncation mechanism that is independent of the learned opacity value. Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Content-Aware Texturing for Gaussian Splatting
head: Content-Aware Texturing, Ours
body: This method augments 2D Gaussian primitives with spatially varying texture maps to capture high-frequency appearance details that spherical harmonics alone cannot represent, while dynamically managing texture resolution based on scene content. Unlike fixed-budget texturing methods, it adapts texel density to local error and frequency, avoiding the convergence issues of cloning-based densification by using splitting. Inputs: A set of N 2D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each primitive i is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, scale \mathbf{S}i, rotation \mathbf{R}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. A set of input views \Pi with corresponding ground truth images. Hyperparameters: \lambda{SSIM}=0.2, \lambda{opacity}, \lambda{texture}, threshold \tau{ds}, threshold \tau{tr}, and minimum pixel size k{min}. Outputs: Optimized primitive parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients, texel size ki). Texture maps Ti for each primitive, stored in a jagged tensor structure. Rendered images and metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS). Primitive Parameters: Each primitive stores 59 parameters, each as a 4-byte float: 1. Position: 3 floats (\boldsymbol{\mu}x, \boldsymbol{\mu}y, \boldsymbol{\mu}z). 2. Scale: 2 floats (log-scale factors for the 2D plane). 3. Rotation: 4 floats (quaternion). 4. Opacity: 1 float (\alphai). 5. Color: 48 floats (Spherical Harmonics coefficients). 6. Texel Size: 1 float (ki). Texture Storage: Texture maps Ti are stored in a custom "jagged" tensor data structure to handle varying resolutions per primitive. Each texel stores 3 floats (RGB offsets). Texel values are constrained to [-1, 1] via a sigmoid activation on unactivated features c'{Ti}: c{Ti} = 2\sigma(c'{Ti}) - 1. To facilitate operations, the method uses four coordinate systems: 1. World Space (pw): Intersection point in world coordinates. 2. World Space Centered (p{w0}): p{w0} = pw - \boldsymbol{\mu}. 3. Local Axis-Aligned (pl): pl = \mathbf{R}^{-1} p{w0}. Since the primitive is 2D, the last component is 0, so pl \in \mathbb{R}^2. 4. Local Normalized/Canonical (pc): pc = \mathbf{S}^{-1} pl, where \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(\sigma). The color of a ray \mathbf{r} is computed by alpha blending primitives sorted by depth: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi wi(pi) \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{d}) = \sumi Ti \alphai Gi(pi) \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{d}) where Ti = \prod{j<i} (1 - \alphaj Gj(pj)) is the transmittance, and G(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x})}. The color \mathbf{c}i of primitive i is the sum of the spherical harmonic color and a texture offset: \mathbf{c}i = \text{SH}(\mathbf{d}) + \text{bilerp}(Ti, \mathbf{u}) where \mathbf{u} are the UV coordinates in texture space. To avoid texture stretching during optimization, the texel size ki is fixed in world space, decoupling texture parameters from primitive shape parameters. The UV coordinate \mathbf{u} is calculated as: \mathbf{u} = \frac{pl}{ki} + \mathbf{T}{\text{offset}} where ki is the texel size in world space units (same units as primitive scales \sigma), and \mathbf{T}{\text{offset}} centers the texture map. The texel size k is derived from the minimum pixel size k{min} and a texel size-to-pixel size ratio t2{pr}: k = k{min} \cdot t2{pr} t2{pr} takes values that are powers of two, with a lower bound of 1. The total loss \mathcal{L} is the sum of RGB loss, texture sparsity loss, and opacity regularization: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{RGB} + \mathcal{L}{texture} + \mathcal{L}{opacity} 1. RGB Loss: Weighted sum of L1 and SSIM losses: \mathcal{L}{RGB} = (1 - \lambda{SSIM}) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{SSIM} \mathcal{L}{SSIM} with \lambda{SSIM} = 0.2. 2. Texture Sparsity Loss: Pushes texel values towards zero to allow downsampling: \mathcal{L}{texture} = \lambda{texture} \sumi |c{Ti}| where c{Ti} are the constrained texel values. 3. Opacity Regularization: Encourages low-contribution primitives to disappear: \mathcal{L}{opacity} = \lambda{opacity} \frac{1}{N} \sumi \alphai The method uses splitting instead of cloning to avoid superimposition issues. Error Calculation: For a primitive i, the error Ei is a weighted sum of per-view errors: Ei = \frac{\sum{\pi \in \Pi} Ei^\pi wi^\pi}{\sum{\pi \in \Pi} wi^\pi} where wi^\pi = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in Pi} wi^\pi(\mathbf{r}) is the total contribution of primitive i in view \pi, and Ei^\pi is the error in view \pi. This differs from taking the maximum error over views. Upscaling (Appearance Error): If a primitive is in the top 10% of highest error, and its texture resolution exceeds \tau{tr}, it is upscaled by halving t2{pr} (increasing resolution by factor of 4). Upscaling is only allowed if t2{pr} \ge 2. Downscaling (Low Frequency): To reduce parameters, the method checks if a texture can be reconstructed with lower resolution. It computes the error Ed between the original texture T{orig} and a low-pass filtered version T{lowpass}, weighted by Gaussian falloff: Ed = \frac{\sump G(p) (T{orig}(p) - T{lowpass}(p))}{\sump G(p)} If Ed < \tau{ds}, t2{pr} is doubled (resolution halved). Splitting (Geometric Error): If a primitive in the top 10% of highest error has a texture resolution exceeding \tau{tr}, it is split into two new primitives. 1. Action: Replace primitive i with two new primitives. 2. Displacement: Each new primitive is displaced by \pm 1 standard deviation of the Gaussian along the axis. 3. Properties: Scale: Half the scale in the corresponding axis. Texture Resolution: Half the texture resolution. Opacity: G(1) times the original opacity. Texture Initialization: The new texture maps are created by sampling the original point at the respective locations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingaussiansplattingwithtexturing(primitives, views, hyperparams): """ primitives: List of Gaussian primitives. Each has: pos (3), scale (2), rot (4), opacity (1), shcoeffs (48), texelsizek (1) texturemap: Jagged tensor of RGB offsets views: List of camera poses and ground truth images hyperparams: {lambdassim, lambdaopacity, lambdatexture, tauds, tautr, kmin} """ for iteration in range(maxiterations): # 1. Render renderedimages = [] for view in views: # Sort primitives by depth sortedprims = sortbydepth(primitives, view.camera) image = zeros(view.resolution) transmittance = 1.0 for prim in sortedprims: # Compute intersection in camera space # Unlike 2DGS, use Eq 1 directly in camera space pw = rayprimitiveintersection(view.ray, prim) if pw is None: continue # Transform to local space pw0 = pw - prim.pos pl = inverse(prim.rot) @ pw0 # pl is 2D (ignore z) # Compute Gaussian weight # Canonical space for Gaussian evaluation pc = inverse(prim.scale) @ pl gval = exp(-0.5 dot(pc, pc)) # Compute UV coordinates for texture # k is derived from t2pr and kmin k = hyperparams.kmin prim.t2pr u = (pl / k) + prim.toffset # Sample texture # Clamp u to texture bounds; if out of bounds, use zero-padding (DC color) texeloffset = bilerp(prim.texturemap, u) # Compute color shcolor = sphericalharmonics(prim.shcoeffs, view.direction) ci = shcolor + texeloffset # Alpha blend alpha = prim.opacity gval colorcontrib = alpha transmittance ci image += colorcontrib transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) renderedimages.append(image) # 2. Compute Loss lossrgb = computel1ssimloss(renderedimages, views.gtimages, hyperparams.lambdassim) losstexture = hyperparams.lambdatexture sum(abs(texel) for prim in primitives for texel in prim.texturemap) lossopacity = hyperparams.lambdaopacity mean([prim.opacity for prim in primitives]) totalloss = lossrgb + losstexture + lossopacity # 3. Backpropagate gradients = computegradients(totalloss) updateparameters(primitives, gradients) # 4. Primitive Management (every 100 iterations) if iteration % 100 == 0: manageprimitives(primitives, views, hyperparams) def manageprimitives(primitives, views, hyperparams): # Compute per-primitive error errors = [] for prim in primitives: # Weighted sum of per-view errors totalweight = 0 weightederror = 0 for view in views: # Project primitive to view pixelscovered = getpixelscovered(prim, view) if not pixelscovered: continue # Compute error contribution # Ei^pi = sum(Epi(r) wi^pi(r)) for r in Pi viewerror = 0 viewweight = 0 for pixel in pixelscovered: # Get rendered error and weight for this pixel err, weight = getpixelerrorandweight(prim, pixel, view) viewerror += err weight viewweight += weight weightederror += viewerror totalweight += viewweight if totalweight > 0: error = weightederror / totalweight else: error = 0 errors.append((prim, error)) # Sort by error descending errors.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) # Select top 10% top10count = int(len(errors) 0.1) topprims = errors[:top10count] for prim, error in topprims: # Check if texture resolution exceeds threshold # Texture resolution is related to t2pr. # If t2pr is small, resolution is high. # The paper says: "check which of these exceed a threshold tautr for texture resolution" # Assuming high resolution means small t2pr. # Let's define resolution metric R = 1/t2pr. If R > tautr, split. # Or simply check if t2pr is below a threshold corresponding to tautr. # The text says: "If the error is still high despite upscaling, we interpret the remaining error as geometric." # And: "check which of these exceed a threshold tautr for texture resolution." # This implies if the primitive is already at high texture resolution (small t2pr) and still has error, split. if prim.t2pr <= thresholdfromtautr(hyperparams.tautr): # Split primitive splitprimitive(prim) else: # Upscale texture if prim.t2pr >= 2: # Only upscale if t2pr >= 2 prim.t2pr /= 2 # Reallocate texture map with higher resolution # Initialize new texels by sampling original point upscaletexture(prim) # Downscaling pass for all primitives for prim in primitives: # Compute Ed # Sample original texture and low-pass filtered texture torig = prim.texturemap tlowpass = lowpassfilter(torig) # Compute weighted error Ed # Ed = sum(G(p) (Torig(p) - Tlowpass(p))) / sum(G(p)) # This requires iterating over pixels covered by the primitive numerator = 0 denominator = 0 for view in views: pixelscovered = getpixelscovered(prim, view) for pixel in pixelscovered: pw = raypixelintersection(view.ray, pixel) if pw is None: continue # Compute Gaussian weight G(p) pw0 = pw - prim.pos pl = inverse(prim.rot) @ pw0 pc = inverse(prim.scale) @ pl gval = exp(-0.5 dot(pc, pc)) # Get texture values at this pixel k = hyperparams.kmin prim.t2pr u = (pl / k) + prim.toffset tval = bilerp(torig, u) tlpval = bilerp(tlowpass, u) diff = tval - tlpval numerator += gval diff denominator += gval if denominator > 0: ed = numerator / denominator if ed < hyperparams.tauds: # Downscale prim.t2pr = 2 # Reallocate texture map with lower resolution downscaletexture(prim) def splitprimitive(prim): # Create two new primitives # Displaced by +/- 1 standard deviation along the axis # The axis is determined by the scale with the largest extent? # The text says: "performed separately for each axis" # "If a primitive... happens to have a texture resolution greater than tautr in both axes" # This implies splitting can happen along X or Y or both. # For simplicity, we split along the axis with the largest scale. axis = argmax(prim.scale) stddev = prim.scale[axis] # New positions pos1 = prim.pos + stddev getaxisvector(axis) pos2 = prim.pos - stddev getaxisvector(axis) # New scales: half the scale in the corresponding axis scale1 = prim.scale.copy() scale1[axis] /= 2 scale2 = prim.scale.copy() scale2[axis] /= 2 # New opacity: G(1) times original opacity # G(1) = exp(-0.5) g1 = exp(-0.5) alpha1 = prim.opacity g1 alpha2 = prim.opacity g1 # New rotation: same as original rot1 = prim.rot rot2 = prim.rot # New texture: sample original point at respective locations # This requires sampling the original texture map at the new local coordinates # Since the new primitives are displaced, their local coordinates relative to the old center are different. # However, the texture is attached to the primitive. # "The texture map of the newly added primitives is created by sampling the original point at the respective locations." # This likely means sampling the original primitive's texture at the offset corresponding to the displacement. # For prim1: displacement is +stddev along axis. # In local space, this is +1 standard deviation. # So we sample the original texture at uoffset = (stddev / k) along the axis. k = prim.t2pr hyperparams.kmin offset = stddev / k u1 = getuvoffset(axis, offset) u2 = getuvoffset(axis, -offset) tex1 = sampletextureatoffset(prim.texturemap, u1) tex2 = sampletextureatoffset(prim.texturemap, u2) # Create new primitives newprim1 = Primitive(pos1, scale1, rot1, alpha1, prim.shcoeffs, prim.t2pr, tex1) newprim2 = Primitive(pos2, scale2, rot2, alpha2, prim.shcoeffs, prim.t2pr, tex2) # Replace original with new ones removeprimitive(prim) addprimitive(newprim1) addprimitive(newprim2) Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Each primitive has 59 parameters (4 bytes each) plus texture storage. Texture storage is jagged, with 3 floats per texel. The number of texels is dynamic. Training Time: 1.5-2x slower than 2DGS due to per-ray texture querying overhead. Rendering Time: 25% slower than 2DGS due to the same overhead. Measured Performance: DeepBlending: SSIM 0.907, PSNR 30.03, LPIPS 0.303, 222K points, 21.6M texels, 78.1M params, 70 FPS. Mip-Nerf-360: SSIM 0.795, PSNR 27.00, LPIPS 0.263, 218K points, 46.6M texels, 152.6M params, 67 FPS. Tanks&Temples: SSIM 0.835, PSNR 23.43, LPIPS 0.225, 164K points, 10.4M texels, 41.1M params, 121 FPS. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Captures high-frequency details with fewer parameters than fixed-budget methods (e.g., GSTex, BBSplat). Avoids texture stretching by decoupling texel size from primitive shape. Limitations: Slower training and rendering than 2DGS. Cloning-based densification is incompatible. When to Use: When high-frequency appearance details are required and fixed-budget texturing is insufficient. When memory efficiency is important compared to methods like GSTex. When Not to Use: When training speed is critical, as it is 1.5-2x slower than 2DGS. When using cloning-based densification strategies. Origin: The method was introduced by Panagiotis Papantonakis, Georgios Kopanas, Frédo Durand, and George Drettakis in the paper "Content-Aware Texturing for Gaussian Splatting". History and Development: The method builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It addresses limitations in existing texturing methods like GSTex (which uses a fixed texel budget on a pretrained point cloud) and BBSplat (which uses a fixed texel-to-primitive ratio). It also avoids the convergence issues of cloning-based densification used in other methods. Usage: Implemented using the 3DGS codebase, introducing 2D primitives as in 2DGS. name: Directed Distance Field (DDF) for Gaussian Splatting
head: Directed Distance Function, ray-query oracle
body: The Directed Distance Field (DDF) is a neural implicit representation that serves as a constant-time, constant-memory ray oracle for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes. It solves the problem of performing secondary ray queries—such as shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination—without the computational cost of tracing individual Gaussians or the memory overhead of a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). Unlike sibling methods that scale linearly with the number of Gaussians or require iterative sphere tracing, the DDF answers any ray query with a single forward pass through a small neural network, making it suitable for real-time global illumination in large-scale captured scenes. Input: A ray defined by an origin \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a unit direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2. Output: A tuple (t, \xi), where t \in \mathbb{R} is the distance to the first surface along \mathbf{d}, and \xi \in [0, 1] is a visibility value representing the probability that the ray hits the scene. The hit point is \mathbf{x} + t\mathbf{d} when \xi is high. The DDF is implemented as a neural field with a fixed memory footprint of approximately 52 MB, independent of the scene size (number of Gaussians). 1. Multiresolution Hash Grid (Point Encoding): Encodes the 3D point \mathbf{x}. Levels: 16. Features per level: 2. Entries per level: 2^{19} (524,288). Base resolution: 16. Growth factor: 1.5. Bounding Box: A box bounding the normalized object. Parameter Count: \approx 13 million parameters. 2. Sinusoidal Encoding (Direction Encoding): Encodes the direction \mathbf{d}. Bands: 4 sinusoidal bands. 3. Multilayer Perceptron (MLP): Architecture: Two-layer MLP. Width: 64. Input: Concatenated features from the hash grid and direction encoding. Output: Scalar t and scalar \xi. Parameter Count: \approx 8,000 parameters. The DDF is trained using samples of the form (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, t{target}, \xi{target}). Three sources of supervision are used: 1. GS-Rendered Depth: Cheap supervision from camera rays, but blurry for thin features. 2. Neural Surface Sphere Tracing: Clean distances obtained by sphere tracing a neural surface (e.g., NeuS) fit to the same images. This is mesh-free and recovers thin features. 3. Ground-Truth Mesh Ray Casting: Used as an upper bound for evaluation, requiring a mesh. To sharpen thin features and ensure consistency along rays, a self-consistency term is added. For a ray hitting at distance t, a point shifted forward by distance s along the ray is sampled. The DDF evaluated at this shifted point must predict distance t-s. 30% of each training batch is replaced with these ray-march shifted points. The total loss is a combination of distance and visibility terms: L = \text{ClampedL1}(t{pred}, t{target}) + 0.3 \times \text{BCE}(\xi{pred}, \xi{target}) ClampedL1: The L1 loss on distance is clamped to a maximum value (the box scale) to prevent far-away surfaces from dominating the gradient. BCE: Binary Cross-Entropy on the hit flag \xi. Optimizer: Adam. Steps: 30,000. Batch Size: 16,384 rays. Learning Rate: 3 \times 10^{-3}, decayed by cosine schedule to 5% of its initial value. Hardware: Single A100 GPU; training takes under one hour per object. Unverified code.
