name: Atomized Proliferation
head: Atom Gaussian Densification, AtomGS, Atomizing Gaussian Splatting for High-Fidelity Radiance Field
body: Atomized Proliferation (AtomGS) is a training strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that enhances geometric precision by constraining fine-detail Gaussians into uniformly-sized "Atom Gaussians" and prioritizing their proliferation to align with scene geometry. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS densification by replacing free-form splitting with a structured atomization process and an Edge-Aware Normal Loss, which guides gradients to better align with underlying geometric structures rather than just visual appearance. Atomized Proliferation operates as an iterative densification and refinement loop applied to the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. It introduces two main components: Atomized Proliferation (a modified densification/pruning schedule) and Geometry-Guided Optimization (a specialized loss function). Inputs: Initial set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points. Training images and camera poses. SfM point cloud distances d. Outputs: Optimized set of Gaussians with refined means, covariances, opacities, and colors. Improved geometric alignment and reduced noise on flat surfaces. The method maintains the standard Gaussian attributes for each primitive i: Mean position: \boldsymbol{\mu}i Covariance matrix: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (parameterized by rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i) Opacity: \alphai Color coefficients: \mathbf{c}i (view-dependent SH coefficients) Additionally, it tracks: Atom Scale threshold: S Current iteration: i Total atomization iterations: ta Warm-up iterations: tw Clone Threshold (\tauc): Threshold for cloning based on loss gradient. Typical value: 0.002. Split Threshold (\taus): Base threshold for splitting. Typical value: 0.002. Prune Threshold (\epsilon): Opacity threshold for pruning. Typical value: 0.005 (or 0.5 for DTU dataset). Atom Scale (S): Maximum allowed minimum covariance norm for atomization. Defined as the i-th percentile of ordered distances from input SfM points: S = Pi(d). Typical setting: P1(d) (1st percentile). Atomized Proliferation Duration (ta): Iteration limit for atomization. Typical value: 7000. Warm-Up Duration (tw): Iteration limit for the warm-up phase. Typical value: 7000. Loss Weights: \lambda{ms-ssim} = 0.1, \lambda{normal} = 0.1. 1. Initialization: Calculate Atom Scale S from SfM point distances. Let d be the sorted distances of SfM points. S = P1(d). Set iteration counter i = 0. Initialize Gaussian set with SfM points. 2. Iteration Loop (for i = 0 to t{total}): Geometry-Guided Optimization: Render current Gaussians to obtain predicted images and normal maps. Compute Edge-Aware Normal Loss (see Formula below). Compute Multi-Scale SSIM loss. Update Gaussian parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha, \mathbf{c}) using gradient descent. Note: Atom Gaussian scales are fixed during backpropagation. Atomized Proliferation (Densification & Pruning): If i < ta: Iterate through all Gaussians. Atomization: If \|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\|{\min} \le S, designate the Gaussian as an Atom Gaussian. Set its size to s = \sqrt[3]{S} (isotropic). Fix its scale for backpropagation. Update its scale via geometric progression: Sn = S{n-1} \cdot r^{n-1}, where r = \sqrt[ta]{p} and p is the final proportion to initial S. Note: The exact value of p is not specified in the sources, but the progression ensures scale decreases over iterations. Pruning: If \alphai < \epsilon OR \|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\|{\max} is excessively large (IsTooLarge), prune the Gaussian. Increase frequency of opacity resetting to encourage merging of large, simple surfaces. Cloning: If loss gradient \nablap L \ge \tauc, clone the Gaussian. This allows larger Gaussians to be cloned to bridge geometry gaps. Splitting: If \nablap L \ge \min\left(\frac{i}{tw}\taus, \taus\right) AND \|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\|{\max} > S: Split the Gaussian. The threshold uses a linear warm-up: \tau{split}(i) = \min\left(\frac{i}{tw}\taus, \taus\right). This enhances the probability of division into smaller Atom Gaussians during the initial phase. 3. Post-Atomization: After ta, standard densification/pruning may continue, but Atom Gaussians remain isotropic and uniformly sized. Larger anisotropic Gaussians are retained for background or low-feature areas. Atom Scale: S = P1(d) where d is the ordered distances of SfM points and P1 is the 1st percentile. Atom Gaussian Size: s = \sqrt[3]{S} Atom Gaussians are isotropic spheroids with uniform size s. Scale Progression for Atom Gaussians: Sn = S{n-1} \cdot r^{n-1} where r = \sqrt[ta]{p}, ta is total atomization iterations, and p is the final proportion to initial S. Edge-Aware Normal Loss: \mathcal{L}{normal} = \text{normal\map} \odot \text{edge\map} where \text{normal\map} is derived from the pre-optimized 3DGS (via depth rendering and median filtering) and \text{edge\map} is derived from the gradient magnitude of the ground truth RGB image. Split Threshold (Warm-up): \tau{split}(i) = \min\left(\frac{i}{tw}\taus, \taus\right) for i < tw. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atomizedproliferation(gaussians, sfmpoints, trainingdata, iterations): """ Implements Atomized Proliferation for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes (mu, Sigma, alpha, c) sfmpoints: List of 3D points from SfM trainingdata: List of (image, camerapose) tuples iterations: Total number of training iterations Returns: Optimized list of Gaussians """ # 1. Calculate Atom Scale S from SfM points distances = computedistances(sfmpoints) S = percentile(distances, 1) # P1(d) # 2. Define thresholds tauc = 0.002 # Clone Threshold taus = 0.002 # Split Threshold epsilon = 0.005 # Prune Threshold (use 0.5 for DTU) ta = 7000 # Atomized Proliferation Duration tw = 7000 # Warm-Up Duration lambdamsssim = 0.1 lambdanormal = 0.1 # 3. Training Loop for i in range(iterations): # --- Geometry-Guided Optimization --- totalloss = 0 for image, camera in trainingdata: # Render current Gaussians renderedimage, rendereddepth, renderednormal = render(gaussians, camera) # Compute MS-SSIM Loss msssimloss = computemsssim(renderedimage, image) # Compute Edge-Aware Normal Loss # Edge map from ground truth RGB gradient edgemap = computeedgegradient(image) # Normal map from rendered depth (median filtering) normalmap = computenormalfromdepth(rendereddepth) normalloss = sum(normalmap edgemap) # Element-wise product and sum # Combine losses loss = (1 - lambdamsssim) msssimloss + lambdanormal normalloss totalloss += loss # Backpropagate to update Gaussians # Note: Atom Gaussian scales are fixed during this step updategaussians(gaussians, totalloss) # --- Atomized Proliferation --- if i < ta: newgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Pruning if g.alpha < epsilon or istoolarge(g.Sigma): continue # Prune # Atomization if normmin(g.Sigma) <= S: # Designate as Atom Gaussian g.isatom = True g.size = cbrt(S) # Isotropic size g.scalerequiresgrad = False # Fix scale # Update scale via geometric progression # Sn = S{n-1} r^(n-1) # r = p^(1/ta) # Note: p is final proportion to initial S. # Implementation detail: p is not explicitly given, # but the progression reduces scale over time. # We assume a simple decay factor based on iteration. r = 0.9 # Placeholder for p^(1/ta) if p not specified g.size = r i # Cloning if g.lossgradient >= tauc: clonegaussian(g) # Splitting # Threshold with linear warm-up if i < tw: splitthreshold = min((i / tw) taus, taus) else: splitthreshold = taus if g.lossgradient >= splitthreshold and normmax(g.Sigma) > S: splitgaussian(g) newgaussians.append(g) gaussians = newgaussians else: # Standard pruning after atomization phase gaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g.alpha >= epsilon and not istoolarge(g.Sigma)] return gaussians def computedistances(points): """Compute pairwise distances or distances to nearest neighbor.""" # Simplified: assume SfM points provide a representative distance metric # In practice, this might be the median distance to nearest neighbor return [computenearestneighbordistance(p, points) for p in points] def percentile(values, p): """Return the p-th percentile of the sorted values.""" sortedvals = sorted(values) index = int(len(sortedvals) p / 100) return sortedvals[index] def normmin(Sigma): """Return the minimum eigenvalue of the covariance matrix.""" return min(eigvals(Sigma)) def normmax(Sigma): """Return the maximum eigenvalue of the covariance matrix.""" return max(eigvals(Sigma)) def istoolarge(Sigma): """Check if covariance is excessively large.""" # Not given in sources. Assume a threshold based on scene scale. return normmax(Sigma) > 10.0 # Placeholder threshold def cbrt(x): """Cube root.""" return x (1/3) Atom Scale Selection: If S is too large, too many Gaussians become Atom Gaussians, potentially over-densifying smooth areas. If S is too small, fine details may not be captured. The 1st percentile of SfM distances is recommended. Scale Fixing: Atom Gaussian scales are fixed during backpropagation. If the learning rate for other parameters is too high, the fixed scale may lead to suboptimal alignment. Setting scale learning rate \etas = 0 is advised for object-centered datasets. Warm-up Phase: The linear warm-up for the split threshold is critical. If the threshold is too high initially, no splitting occurs; if too low, excessive splitting occurs. The duration tw should match the initial convergence phase. Pruning Frequency: Increasing the frequency of opacity resetting helps merge large surfaces. If not done frequently enough, redundant Gaussians may persist. A loss function that combines normal map accuracy with edge detection to preserve geometric details while smoothing flat surfaces. It sets itself apart by incorporating 2D edge information into 3D normal optimization. Choose it when geometric accuracy is prioritized over pure photometric fidelity. Link to Edge-Aware Normal Loss An isotropic, uniformly-sized Gaussian primitive used to represent fine details. It differs from standard anisotropic Gaussians by having a fixed, uniform scale. Choose it for high-frequency geometric features. Link to Atom Gaussian Time Complexity: Similar to 3DGS, but with additional overhead for atomization checks and edge-aware loss computation. Training time is reported as 0.28 hours vs 0.40 hours for 3DGS on Mip-NeRF360, indicating faster convergence. Memory Complexity: Model size is 749MB vs 869MB for 3DGS on Mip-NeRF360, indicating reduced memory usage due to merging of large Gaussians. Scaling: The method scales well with scene complexity due to the merging of large, smooth surfaces. The Gaussian count declines and stabilizes, unlike standard 3DGS which may struggle to stabilize. Strengths: Improved geometric accuracy, reduced noise on flat surfaces, faster training, smaller model size. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of Atom Scale S and warm-up duration tw. May not perform as well on scenes with very sparse SfM points if S is not adjusted. When to Use: When geometric accuracy is critical (e.g., mesh extraction) and the scene has a mix of fine details and smooth surfaces. When Not to Use: When pure photometric quality is the only goal and geometric fidelity is not required. Atomized Proliferation (AtomGS) was introduced by Liu et al. in 2024. It addresses the issue of standard 3DGS densification freely drifting and splitting, which can lead to noisy 3D meshes and blurry artifacts. The method builds on the original 3DGS densification strategy but introduces structured atomization and geometry-guided optimization. It is used in high-fidelity radiance field reconstruction, particularly for scenes requiring precise geometric representation. 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26 AtomGS: Atomizing Gaussian Splatting for High-Fidelity Radiance Field, https://core.ac.uk/works/391753628, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Pruning and Reduction
head: Gaussian Pruning, Scene Reduction, Visibility Filtering
body: Pruning and reduction methods aim to decrease the storage footprint and computational cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by removing redundant or low-impact Gaussians, or by simplifying their attributes, without significantly degrading rendering quality. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on opacity-based culling during rendering, these methods actively modify the scene representation during or after training. They are distinguished from sibling methods like Inverse Multiquadric Splatting (which changes the kernel function) and Opacity-Independent Gaussian Truncation (which changes the rendering integration bounds) by focusing on the selection or simplification of the Gaussian primitives themselves. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) Vertex-level pruning is a refinement mechanism for Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting (MP-GS) that removes redundant vertices from Gaussian triangles and lines during training to reduce storage overhead and simplify the scene representation. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which only performs primitive-level opacity pruning, this method dynamically converts primitives into lower-vertex forms (ellipses or lines) based on geometric proximity and collinearity. It complements Attribute Pruning and SplatQ by addressing topological redundancy in mixed primitives rather than attribute quantization or opacity thresholds alone. SplatQ is a post-training pruning framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that addresses spatial quality imbalance and ignores joint deletion effects inherent in global Top-K selection methods. It partitions Gaussians into size-limited blocks based on spatial and appearance similarity, allocates retention quotas to balance regional budgets, and uses a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model to jointly select Gaussians within each block, thereby accounting for pairwise interactions and overlapping contributions. Attribute pruning selectively reduces the storage and computational overhead of per-Gaussian attributes, primarily spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, to optimize memory usage and rendering efficiency. Unlike Pruning and Reduction which focuses on removing entire primitives, attribute pruning retains the Gaussian primitives but simplifies their representation. It differs from SplatQ by focusing on the dimensionality of the attribute vectors rather than quantization of the entire data structure, and from Vertex-level Pruning in Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting by operating on the standard Gaussian representation without changing the primitive type. A pruning mechanism designed to support mixed-primitive-based learning, as standard pruning is incompatible with mixed primitives. Prune vertices of the mixed primitives to optimize the representation. A method to reduce the number of Gaussians using a learnable mask during optimization, targeting small-sized kernels for removal. Apply binary masks M to the opacities and scale attributes of the kernels at every densification step. Use residual vector quantization with L stages of vector quantization for geometric attributes like scale and rotation. Represent view-dependent colors via a grid-based neural field using hash grids for input positions, features, and view direction, fed into an MLP. The end-to-end loss is: L = L{ren} + \lambdam Lm + Lr + Ls, where L{ren} is L1+SSIM loss, Lm is masking loss (\frac{1}{N} \sum \sigma(mn)), and Lr, Ls are rotation and scale objective functions. \epsilon: Masking threshold for the sigmoid function in the learnable mask. \lambdam: Weight for the masking loss term, typically 5 \times 10^{-4}. Application of visibility-based pruning to 3D Gaussian Splatting, using Gaussian centroids as reference points for visibility calculation. Represent each Gaussian kernel by its centroid position, scaling matrix S, and rotation matrix R defining the covariance \Sigma. Use the Gaussian centroids as the 3D points pi in the visibility mask computation algorithm. A post-processing step that filters out Gaussians not visible to the current camera view to increase rendering speed without affecting image quality. Perform visibility filtering as a post-processing step on the Gaussian representation before rendering. On MipNeRF360 scenes, achieves up to 10% mean FPS speedup (e.g., 410 FPS vs 373 FPS without filtering). On Zip-NeRF scenes, achieves up to 45% improvement in rendering speed (e.g., 630 FPS vs 435 FPS without filtering). Provides significant speedup on large-scale scenes (Zip-NeRF) compared to central object-focused scenes (MipNeRF360), making it particularly important for large scenes. Pruning and reduction techniques in 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as the method scaled to large, complex scenes where the number of Gaussians could reach millions, leading to high memory consumption and rendering latency. Early 3DGS implementations relied on opacity-based culling during the forward pass, but this did not reduce the storage size of the model. Subsequent research introduced methods to actively prune Gaussians during training or post-training to create more compact representations. Vertex-level pruning was introduced in the context of Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting to handle topological redundancy in non-standard primitive types (triangles and lines). Standard opacity pruning is insufficient for these primitives because their geometric structure (vertices) carries more information than a single scalar opacity. Visibility-based pruning and reduction with learnable masks were proposed to address the inefficiency of retaining Gaussians that do not contribute to the final image from any camera view or have negligible impact on rendering quality. These methods integrate pruning into the optimization loop, using masks to suppress small or occluded kernels. Visibility list-based rendering was introduced as a post-processing optimization to accelerate rendering by pre-filtering the Gaussian list based on camera frustum and occlusion, achieving significant FPS improvements without altering the scene representation. A Mixed-Primitive-based Gaussian Splatting Method for Surface Reconstruction, https://core.ac.uk/works/308836756, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Visibility-Based Geometry Pruning of Neural Plenoptic Scene Representations, https://doi.org/10.1109/tmm.2025.3618548, fetched 2026-10-26 RadSplat: Radiance Field-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Robust Real- Time Rendering with 900+ FPS, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00018, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Vertex-level Pruning in Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting
head: Mixed-Primitive Vertex Pruning
body: Vertex-level pruning is a refinement mechanism for Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting (MP-GS) that removes redundant vertices from Gaussian triangles and lines during training to reduce storage overhead and simplify the scene representation. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting which only performs primitive-level opacity pruning, this method dynamically downgrades primitives to lower-vertex forms (ellipses or lines) based on geometric coherence, addressing the "messy" representations that can arise when using mixed primitives. It complements Attribute Pruning by operating on the structural geometry of the splats rather than their scalar attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of mixed-primitive Gaussians \{Gi\}, where each primitive Gi is defined by its vertices \{\boldsymbol{\mu}i^1, \boldsymbol{\mu}i^2, \dots\}, covariance parameters, opacity, and color. Output: A refined set of primitives with reduced vertex counts where geometric redundancy is detected. Data Structures: Each mixed primitive maintains a list of vertex positions. Gaussian Triangle: Stores 3 vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2, \boldsymbol{\mu}3. Gaussian Line: Stores 2 vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2. Gaussian Ellipse (Point): Stores 1 vertex \boldsymbol{\mu}1. Parameters: \omega{dist}: Threshold for vertex proximity. Default: 0.5. \omega{pear}: Threshold for collinearity detection. Default: 0.9. Algorithm Steps: Vertex-level pruning is triggered concurrently with primitive-level pruning operations. For each primitive undergoing evaluation: 1. Check for Gaussian Triangle Primitivity: If the primitive is a Gaussian Triangle with vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2, \boldsymbol{\mu}3: Calculate the maximum pairwise L2 distance among the three vertices: d{max} = \max(\|\boldsymbol{\mu}1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}2\|2, \|\boldsymbol{\mu}2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}3\|2, \|\boldsymbol{\mu}1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}3\|2) Case A (Collapse to Ellipse): If d{max} < \omega{dist}, the vertices are considered "close." Prune \boldsymbol{\mu}2 and \boldsymbol{\mu}3. Convert the primitive into a Gaussian Ellipse centered at \boldsymbol{\mu}1. Case B (Check Collinearity): If d{max} \ge \omega{dist}, check for collinearity. Compute the Pearson correlation coefficient r from the coordinates of the three vertices. If |r| > \omega{pear}, the vertices are nearly collinear. Convert the primitive into a Gaussian Line. Otherwise, retain the Gaussian Triangle structure. 2. Check for Gaussian Line Primitivity: If the primitive is a Gaussian Line with vertices \boldsymbol{\mu}1, \boldsymbol{\mu}2: Calculate the L2 distance: d = \|\boldsymbol{\mu}1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}2\|2 If d < \omega{dist}, the vertices are "close." Prune \boldsymbol{\mu}2. Convert the primitive into a Gaussian Ellipse centered at \boldsymbol{\mu}1. 3. Preservation of Complexity: This pruning does not reduce the entire scene to point-centered ellipses because the standard Gaussian Splatting densification mechanisms (cloning and splitting) continue to operate, potentially re-introducing higher-order primitives where detail is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexlevelpruning(primitive, omegadist=0.5, omegapear=0.9): """ Refines a mixed-primitive Gaussian by reducing vertex count based on geometry. primitive: object with type ('triangle', 'line', 'ellipse') and vertices [mu1, mu2,...] """ if primitive.type == 'triangle': mu1, mu2, mu3 = primitive.vertices # Calculate pairwise distances d12 = l2norm(mu1 - mu2) d23 = l2norm(mu2 - mu3) d13 = l2norm(mu1 - mu3) maxdist = max(d12, d23, d13) if maxdist < omegadist: # Vertices are too close; collapse to ellipse primitive.type = 'ellipse' primitive.vertices = [mu1] # Note: Covariance and other attributes are inherited/adjusted to center mu1 else: # Vertices are spread out; check for collinearity # Compute Pearson correlation coefficient from vertex coordinates # Let X be the matrix of coordinates [mu1, mu2, mu3] r = pearsoncorrelation(X) if abs(r) > omegapear: # Vertices are collinear; convert to line primitive.type = 'line' primitive.vertices = [mu1, mu2] # Keep first two as representative # Else: remain triangle elif primitive.type == 'line': mu1, mu2 = primitive.vertices dist = l2norm(mu1 - mu2) if dist < omegadist: # Vertices are too close; collapse to ellipse primitive.type = 'ellipse' primitive.vertices = [mu1] return primitive def l2norm(v): return sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) def pearsoncorrelation(points): """ Computes the absolute Pearson correlation coefficient for a set of 3 points in 3D. Simplified implementation for the specific context of MP-GS. """ # Extract x, y, z coordinates xs = [p[0] for p in points] ys = [p[1] for p in points] zs = [p[2] for p in points] # Calculate means meanx = sum(xs) / 3 meany = sum(ys) / 3 meanz = sum(zs) / 3 # Calculate covariance and variances # Cov(x,y) = sum((xi - meanx)(yi - meany)) / (n-1) covxy = sum((xs[i] - meanx) (ys[i] - meany) for i in range(3)) / 2 covxz = sum((xs[i] - meanx) (zs[i] - meanz) for i in range(3)) / 2 covyz = sum((ys[i] - meany) (zs[i] - meanz) for i in range(3)) / 2 varx = sum((x - meanx)2 for x in xs) / 2 vary = sum((y - meany)2 for y in ys) / 2 varz = sum((z - meanz)2 for z in zs) / 2 # Correlation coefficients rxy = covxy / (sqrt(varx) sqrt(vary)) if varx > 0 and vary > 0 else 0 rxz = covxz / (sqrt(varx) sqrt(varz)) if varx > 0 and varz > 0 else 0 ryz = covyz / (sqrt(vary) sqrt(varz)) if vary > 0 and varz > 0 else 0 # The source specifies "the Pearson correlation coefficient" (singular). # In 3D collinearity checks, this often refers to the maximum correlation or a specific projection. # Given the ambiguity in the source text regarding the exact scalar derivation from 3D points, # we assume the implementation uses the maximum absolute correlation among pairs or a principal component analysis result. # For strict adherence to "absolute value... exceeds omegapear", we take the max. return max(abs(rxy), abs(rxz), abs(ryz)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The L2 distance threshold \omega{dist}=0.5 is absolute. In scenes with varying scales, this may require normalization. Collinearity Ambiguity: The source cites "the Pearson correlation coefficient" for 3D points without specifying the exact reduction method (e.g., PCA-based or pairwise max). The pseudocode assumes the maximum pairwise correlation as a robust proxy for collinearity. Interaction with Densification: Pruning must not interfere with the cloning/splitting logic. If a primitive is pruned to an ellipse, subsequent splits must correctly handle the single-vertex representation. Storage Reduction: The vertex pruning mechanism reduces the average storage size required to store vertex coordinates by 24% compared to the variant without pruning. Performance Impact: The source notes that the framework with vertex pruning performs better (lower Chamfer distance) than the variant without it, suggesting improved surface reconstruction quality. Complexity: The pruning check is O(1) per primitive per training step, as it involves only a few distance and correlation calculations. Limitations: The method relies on heuristic thresholds (\omega{dist}, \omega{pear}) which may not generalize perfectly across all scene geometries without tuning. Vertex-level pruning was introduced in the context of Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting (MP-GS), an extension of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses triangles and lines in addition to point-centered ellipses to better represent surfaces. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting only performs primitive-level pruning based on opacity. MP-GS authors observed that mixed primitives could become "messy" with redundant vertices, necessitating this additional geometric simplification step during training. A Mixed-Primitive-based Gaussian Splatting Method for Surface Reconstruction, https://core.ac.uk/works/308836756, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SplatQ
head: SplatQ: Post-training Gaussian pruning via QUBO
body: SplatQ is a post-training Gaussian pruning framework that partitions Gaussians by spatial proximity and appearance similarity into size-limited blocks, smooths importance-based block retention quotas to prevent budget concentration, and constructs a quadratic approximation of joint deletion effects to jointly select Gaussians under a fixed budget. It differs from global Top-K methods by decomposing the selection into subproblems of specific size and solving a combinatorial optimization problem within each block, rather than ranking all Gaussians globally by independent scores. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting model \mathcal{G} = \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Output: A pruned set of exactly K Gaussians, followed by fine-tuned attributes for the retained set. Data Structures: The model is represented as a set of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by the following parameters: \boldsymbol{\mu}i: Center (mean) position. si: Scale. \mathbf{r}i: Rotation quaternion. \mathbf{c}i: Zeroth-order (DC) spherical harmonic coefficients. \mathbf{h}i: Higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients. oi: Opacity. Parameters: N: Total number of Gaussians in the pretrained model. K: Exact number of Gaussians to retain after pruning. M: Maximum size (number of members) of each block Cb. Kb: Retention quota assigned to block b, representing the number of Gaussians to retain within that block. \mathcal{R}b: Response matrix for block b, used to estimate individual deletion effects and pairwise interactions. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the N Gaussians into several size-limited blocks \{Cb\} of at most M members each, based on spatial proximity and appearance similarity. This is achieved using a 3D grid and Morton ordering to efficiently group related Gaussians without quadratic pairwise comparison costs. 2. Opacity Response Modeling: For each block Cb, compute a response matrix \mathcal{R}b using sampled pixels from multiple views. This matrix estimates individual deletion effects and pairwise interactions by observing changes in representative pixel colors relative to changes in Gaussian opacity. 3. Budget Allocation: Assign a retention quota Kb to every block such that \sumb Kb = K. This is done by deriving an initial quota from importance estimates and adjusting the distribution to reduce the risk of concentrating the budget in a few blocks. 4. Quadratic Selection: For each block, formulate a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) objective incorporating individual responses, pairwise interactions, and quota penalties. Solve the QUBO using Simulated Annealing (SA) or a Coherent Ising Machine (CIM) to determine which Kb block members to retain. 5. Fine-tuning: Fine-tune the attributes of the retained Gaussians without changing their count to recover rendering quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatqprune(G, N, K, M, views): """ G: List of N Gaussian objects, each with attributes (mu, s, r, c, h, o). N: Total number of Gaussians. K: Target number of Gaussians to retain. M: Maximum block size. views: List of camera poses/views for sampling. """ # Stage 1: Partitioning # Group Gaussians into blocks based on spatial proximity and appearance similarity. # Uses 3D grid and Morton ordering for efficiency. blocks = partitiongaussians(G, M) # Stage 2: Opacity Response Modeling # Compute response matrices for each block to estimate deletion effects. responsematrices = {} for block in blocks: # Sample pixels from multiple views to estimate how pixel colors change # when Gaussian opacities change. responsematrices[block.id] = computeresponsematrix(block, views) # Stage 3: Budget Allocation # Assign retention quotas Kb to each block such that sum(Kb) = K. # Smooth importance-based quotas to prevent concentration in high-score regions. quotas = allocatebudget(blocks, responsematrices, K) # Stage 4: Quadratic Selection # Jointly select Gaussians within each block using QUBO. retainedgaussians = [] for block in blocks: bid = block.id Kb = quotas[bid] Rb = responsematrices[bid] # Formulate QUBO objective: # Minimize: sumi (wi xi) + sum{i<j} (wij xi xj) + penalty(x) # where xi is binary retention variable (1=retain, 0=delete). # wi comes from individual response, wij from pairwise interaction. # Penalty enforces sum(xi) == Kb. # Solve QUBO using Simulated Annealing (SA) or Coherent Ising Machine (CIM). # Returns binary selection vector x for this block. selection = solvequbo(Rb, Kb, method="SA") # Select Gaussians based on selection vector blockretained = [G[i] for i, keep in enumerate(selection) if keep] retainedgaussians.extend(blockretained) # Stage 5: Fine-tuning # Fine-tune attributes of retained Gaussians without changing count. finalgaussians = finetune(retainedgaussians, views) return finalgaussians def partitiongaussians(G, M): """ Partition Gaussians into blocks of size <= M using spatial and appearance similarity. Uses 3D grid and Morton ordering. """ # Assign each Gaussian to a 3D grid cell based on mui. gridcells = assigntogrid(G) # Sort cells and Gaussians using Morton order to preserve locality. mortonsortedgaussians = sortbymorton(G) # Split into chunks of size M. blocks = [] for i in range(0, len(mortonsortedgaussians), M): chunk = mortonsortedgaussians[i:i+M] blocks.append(Block(chunk)) return blocks def computeresponsematrix(block, views): """ Compute response matrix Rb for a block. Rb[i, j] captures the interaction between Gaussian i and j. """ # Render baseline images for all views using the current block's Gaussians. baselineimages = renderviews(block.gaussians, views) # For each Gaussian in the block, perturb its opacity and measure pixel color changes. # This estimates individual deletion effects and pairwise interactions. # Rb is constructed from these sensitivity measurements. Rb = estimateinteractions(block.gaussians, baselineimages, views) return Rb def allocatebudget(blocks, responsematrices, K): """ Assign retention quotas Kb to each block such that sum(Kb) = K. Smooths importance-based quotas to prevent concentration. """ # Calculate initial importance scores for each block based on response matrices. initialscores = [calculateblockimportance(Rb) for Rb in responsematrices] # Smooth the distribution of quotas to avoid concentrating budget in few blocks. # Ensure sum(Kb) == K. quotas = smoothandnormalize(initialscores, K) return quotas def solvequbo(Rb, Kb, method="SA"): """ Solve QUBO for a block. Rb contains individual and pairwise coefficients. Kb is the number of Gaussians to retain. """ # Construct QUBO matrix from Rb. # Add penalty term for constraint sum(xi) == Kb. Qmatrix = constructqubomatrix(Rb, Kb) if method == "SA": # Use Simulated Annealing to find binary vector x minimizing x^T Q x. x = simulatedannealing(Qmatrix) elif method == "CIM": # Use Coherent Ising Machine. x = coherentisingmachine(Qmatrix) return x def finetune(gaussians, views): """ Fine-tune attributes of retained Gaussians. """ # Optimize Gaussian parameters (mu, s, r, c, h, o) using standard 3DGS optimization # on sampled views, keeping the number of Gaussians fixed. optimizedgaussians = optimizegaussians(gaussians, views) return optimizedgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spatial Quality Imbalance: Global ranking can lead to spatial quality imbalance where the limited budget concentrates in regions with consistently higher scores, leaving other regions with insufficient representational capacity. SplatQ addresses this via blockwise retention ratio allocation. Joint Deletion Effects: Independent scoring fails to capture joint rendering effects because multiple Gaussians may jointly support the same pixel or make overlapping contributions, meaning degradation from removing multiple Gaussians is not strictly additive. SplatQ models these interactions via a quadratic objective. Scalability: Formulating the optimization problem over the entire model requires N binary variables and an N \times N matrix, which is impractical for millions of Gaussians. Partitioning into blocks of size M reduces this complexity. Time Complexity: The partitioning step uses 3D grid and Morton ordering to avoid quadratic pairwise comparisons. The core computational cost lies in solving the QUBO problem for each block. The complexity depends on the block size M and the solver (SA or CIM). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the response matrix \mathcal{R}b for each block, which is of size M \times M per block, significantly smaller than the global N \times N matrix. Strengths: Ensures balanced reconstruction quality across a scene by coordinating regional budget allocation and joint Gaussian selection under a fixed budget. Captures joint deletion effects through quadratic approximation. Limitations: Requires solving a combinatorial optimization problem (QUBO) for each block, which can be computationally intensive depending on the solver and block size. When to use: When balanced quality across different regions of a scene is critical and the scene contains millions of Gaussians where global Top-K pruning leads to spatial imbalance. When not to use: When computational resources for QUBO solving are limited and approximate global ranking is sufficient. SplatQ was proposed by Hongbin Ye, Haixu Liu, Shenwei Kang, Wenxiu Wei, Tinglan Wang, Hongdong Zhu, Fan Tang, Qi Gao, Yin Ma, Kai Wen, Hai Wei, Nuo Qian, Wei-Shi Zheng, Shaobo Chen, Fa-Ting Hong, and Jingke Meng. It was presented as a preprint on arXiv in October 2026. The method addresses limitations of existing 3D Gaussian Splatting pruning methods that rely on global Top-K selection based on independent importance scores, which lack regional budget control and ignore joint deletion effects. SplatQ: Interaction-Aware Pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting via Quadratic Selection, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13503, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Attribute Pruning
head: SH Degree Adjustment, Spherical Harmonics Pruning
body: Attribute pruning selectively reduces the storage and computational burden of per-Gaussian attributes, primarily spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients, to optimize memory usage and rendering efficiency. Unlike sibling methods that remove primitives entirely, this technique retains the geometric structure of the scene while adapting the fidelity of view-dependent color representation to local complexity. It distinguishes itself from SplatQ by focusing on dynamic coefficient reduction rather than quantization, and from Vertex-level Pruning in Mixed-Primitive Gaussian Splatting by operating on the standard Gaussian representation's attribute fields rather than modifying the primitive topology. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian Gi has mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and a vector of SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Output: A modified set of Gaussians with reduced attribute storage, where the number of SH coefficients per Gaussian varies based on scene complexity. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi stores attributes. In standard 3DGS, SH coefficients for RGB data at degree 3 require 48 coefficients (16 per channel), consuming 81% of the single-Gaussian storage size (48 out of 59 attributes). The pruning method modifies the size or content of the coefficient vector \mathbf{c}i. Steps: 1. Analyze Scene Complexity: Evaluate the complexity of the region associated with each Gaussian. This is often determined by the variance of color across different viewing angles or the magnitude of higher-order SH coefficients. 2. Determine SH Degree: Assign a SH degree di to each Gaussian Gi based on the analysis: For less complex regions (e.g., uniform surfaces, low view-dependent variation), set di = 0 (basic RGB color, 3 coefficients). For complex regions (e.g., specular highlights, intricate lighting), retain higher degrees (e.g., di = 3, 48 coefficients). 3. Adjust Coefficients: Truncate or zero-out higher-order SH coefficients for Gaussians assigned lower degrees. If di < 3, coefficients corresponding to degrees > di are discarded or ignored during rendering. 4. Render: During splatting, evaluate the color \mathbf{c}i(\omega) using only the retained SH coefficients for the assigned degree. Formulas: The color contribution of a Gaussian Gi at viewing direction \omega is computed using the retained SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i^{(di)}: \mathbf{c}i(\omega) = \sum{l=0}^{di} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{i,l,m} Y{l,m}(\omega) where Y{l,m} are the spherical harmonic basis functions. Parameters: SH Degree: Typically ranges from 0 to 3. Degree 3 is the standard in 3DGS but is often reduced to 0 or 1 for static or simple regions. Thresholds: Not given in the sources. Implementation requires thresholds to decide when a region is "complex" enough to warrant higher SH degrees. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Reducing SH degree can introduce visible artifacts in regions with high-frequency view-dependent effects if the threshold is too aggressive. Uniformity: Applying a uniform SH degree across the entire scene negates the benefits of pruning; the method requires per-Gaussian or per-region adaptation. Alternative Representations: Completely removing SH in favor of NeRF-like MLPs or classical shading is possible but requires custom, potentially slower rendering pipelines. An approach that extends attribute pruning by combining SH band adjustment with primitive reduction and quantization. It introduces a scale- and resolution-aware redundant primitive removal method that uses a redundancy score to identify low-impact primitives, extending opacity-based pruning. For attributes, it adaptively adjusts SH bands by evaluating color consistency across views, reducing higher-order bands when view-dependent effects are minimal. It further applies K-means clustering to create a codebook and uses 16-bit half-float quantization for remaining uncompressed floating-point values. Memory: Significantly reduces storage size. Standard 3DGS uses 48 SH coefficients for degree 3, consuming 81% of per-Gaussian storage. Pruning can reduce this to 3 coefficients (degree 0) for simple regions, offering substantial memory savings. Compute: Reduces the number of coefficients evaluated during rendering, lowering computational cost per Gaussian. Quality: Trade-off between memory/compute and visual fidelity. Lower SH degrees may cause blurring or loss of specular highlights in complex regions. Use Cases: Ideal for memory-constrained devices (e.g., VR headsets) or large scenes where uniform high-fidelity SH is unnecessary. Attribute pruning was introduced as a method to address the large storage footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting, where SH coefficients dominate the memory usage. It builds on the observation that not all parts of a scene require high-degree SH for accurate view-dependent rendering. The concept is discussed in the context of compression and optimization techniques for 3DGS. 3DGS.zip: A survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09510v5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting
head: DisC-GS
body: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting (DisC-GS) is a framework that enables 3D Gaussian Splatting to represent and render sharp boundaries and discontinuities, addressing the limitation of standard Gaussian Splatting which tends to blur such features. It differs from sibling methods like Planar Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling boundaries as cubic Bézier curves within the Gaussian's local subspace and applying a "pre-scissoring" operation during rendering, rather than relying solely on geometric constraints or mesh extraction [S1, 14095-mesh-extraction-and-representation.md]. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gaussian Gi is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, rotation \mathbf{R}i, scale \mathbf{S}i, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. For 2D Gaussian Splatting, the last column of \mathbf{S}i is fixed to zero. The input also includes the camera projection matrix \mathbf{P} and viewing transformation matrix \mathbf{W}, and a user-defined hyperparameter M (number of Bézier curves per Gaussian). Outputs: A rendered image C(p) for each pixel p, where discontinuities are preserved. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gi is augmented with an additional attribute \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 2}. Layout: \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} stores 4M points in the 2D coordinate system defined by the Gaussian's center \boldsymbol{\mu}i (origin), rotation matrix column \mathbf{r}{1,i} (x-axis), and rotation matrix column \mathbf{r}{2,i} (y-axis). Interpretation: These points serve as control points for M cubic Bézier curves representing the boundaries of the Gaussian's projection. Numbered Steps: 1. Local to World Transformation: For each Gaussian Gi, transform the control points from its local 2D subspace to the 3D world space. Let \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}[i,:] denote the i-th point in the local attribute (for i \in \{0, \dots, 4M-1\}). The 3D control points \mathbf{c}{\text{3D\curve}}[i] are computed as: \mathbf{c}{\text{3D\curve}}[i] = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}[i, 0] \times \mathbf{r}{1,i} + \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}[i, 1] \times \mathbf{r}{2,i} Note: \mathbf{r}{1,i} and \mathbf{r}{2,i} are unit vectors, so normalization is omitted. 2. Projection to Image Plane: Project the 3D control points onto the image plane to obtain the 2D control points \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[i]: \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[i] = \mathbf{P} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{c}{\text{3D\curve}}[i] where \mathbf{P} is the projective transformation matrix and \mathbf{W} is the viewing transformation matrix. 3. Implicit Curve Representation: For each of the M cubic Bézier curves defined by four ordered control points \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \boldsymbol{\omega}1, \boldsymbol{\omega}2, \boldsymbol{\omega}3 (where \boldsymbol{\omega}k = \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+k] for curve index j), compute the implicit representation B{\text{imp}}(x, y): B{\text{imp}}(x, y) = \gamma{xxx} x^3 + \gamma{xxy} x^2 y + \gamma{xyy} x y^2 + \gamma{yyy} y^3 + \gamma{xx} x^2 + \gamma{xy} xy + \gamma{yy} y^2 + \gammax x + \gammay y + \gamma0 = 0 The coefficients \gamma are obtained via O(1) arithmetic operations on the control point coordinates. 4. Indicator Function Construction: Define the single-curve indicator function g{\text{sc}} for a pixel p=(xp, yp): g{\text{sc}}(\boldsymbol{\omega}0, \boldsymbol{\omega}1, \boldsymbol{\omega}2, \boldsymbol{\omega}3; p) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } B{\text{imp}}(xp, yp) > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} For M > 1 curves, the combined indicator function g(p) is the product of individual indicators: g(p) = \prod{j=0}^{M-1} g{\text{sc}}(\mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j], \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+1], \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+2], \mathbf{c}{\text{2D\curve}}[4j+3]; p) A pixel is "scissored out" (g(p)=0) if it is outside at least one of the M curves. 5. Discontinuity-Aware Rendering: Compute the color C(p) using a modified \alpha-blending function: C(p) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \betai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \betaj) where the effective opacity \betai for the i-th Gaussian is: \betai = \alphai gi(p) \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,2D})^\top (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}{i,2D})^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,2D})\right) Here, \boldsymbol{\mu}{i,2D} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}{i,2D} are the projected mean and covariance of the i-th Gaussian, and gi(p) is the indicator function for the i-th Gaussian. 6. Gradient Approximation: During backpropagation, use a Bézier-boundary gradient approximation strategy to enable gradients to pass through the discontinuous indicator function g(p), maintaining differentiability for learning \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def cubicbezierimplicitcoeffs(w0, w1, w2, w3): """Computes implicit polynomial coefficients for a cubic Bezier curve from control points.""" # Standard algebraic implicitization for cubic Bezier curves (O(1) arithmetic) # Returns dict of gamma coefficients matching Bimp(x,y) = 0 x0, y0 = w0 x1, y1 = w1 x2, y2 = w2 x3, y3 = w3 # Coefficients derived via standard implicitization formulas a = x0 - 3x1 + 3x2 - x3 b = y0 - 3y1 + 3y2 - y3 c = x0 - 2x1 + x2 d = y0 - 2y1 + y2 e = x0 - x1 f = y0 - y1 gammaxxx = b3 gammaxxy = -3b2 a gammaxyy = 3b a2 gammayyy = -a3 gammaxx = 3b2 (3c - e) - 6ba (3d - f) gammaxy = -6ba (3c - e) + 6a2 (3d - f) gammayy = 3a2 (3d - f) - 3b2 (3e) gammax = 3b2 (3e) - 6ba (3f) gammay = -6ba (3e) + 6a2 (3f) gamma0 = 3b2 (3f) - 3a2 (3e) return { 'gammaxxx': gammaxxx, 'gammaxxy': gammaxxy, 'gammaxyy': gammaxyy, 'gammayyy': gammayyy, 'gammaxx': gammaxx, 'gammaxy': gammaxy, 'gammayy': gammayy, 'gammax': gammax, 'gammay': gammay, 'gamma0': gamma0 } def bezierindicator(p, coeffs): """Evaluates the implicit function Bimp(x, y) for a pixel p.""" x, y = p g = coeffs val = (g['gammaxxx'] x3 + g['gammaxxy'] x2 y + g['gammaxyy'] x y2 + g['gammayyy'] y3 + g['gammaxx'] x2 + g['gammaxy'] x y + g['gammayy'] y2 + g['gammax'] x + g['gammay'] y + g['gamma0']) return val def prescissorrender(gaussians, P, W, M): """Renders an image using Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting.""" H, Wimg = 1024, 1024 # Example resolution img = np.zeros((H, Wimg, 3)) for y in range(H): for x in range(Wimg): p = np.array([x, y], dtype=np.float32) colorsum = np.zeros(3) alphasum = 0.0 for g in gaussians: # 1. Local to World r1 = g['R'][:, 0] r2 = g['R'][:, 1] c3d = np.zeros((4M, 3)) for i in range(4M): c3d[i] = g['mu'] + g['ccurve'][i, 0] r1 + g['ccurve'][i, 1] r2 # 2. Project to 2D c2d = np.zeros((4M, 2)) for i in range(4M): pthom = np.append(c3d[i], 1.0) ptproj = P @ W @ pthom c2d[i] = ptproj[:2] / ptproj[2] # 3 & 4. Indicator Function gval = 1.0 for j in range(M): w0 = c2d[4j] w1 = c2d[4j+1] w2 = c2d[4j+2] w3 = c2d[4j+3] coeffs = cubicbezierimplicitcoeffs(w0, w1, w2, w3) if bezierindicator(p, coeffs) <= 0: gval = 0.0 break if gval == 0: continue # 5. Modified Alpha Blending # Standard 3DGS projection for mean and covariance mu2dhom = P @ W @ np.append(g['mu'], 1.0) mu2d = mu2dhom[:2] / mu2dhom[2] # Covariance projection omitted for brevity; uses standard Jacobian J # Sigma2D = J @ W @ Sigma3D @ W.T @ J.T # For pseudocode completeness, assume invSigma2D is precomputed or standard distsq = np.dot(p - mu2d, p - mu2d) # Simplified isotropic for structure beta = g['alpha'] gval np.exp(-0.5 distsq) colorsum += g['color'] beta (1 - alphasum) alphasum += beta (1 - alphasum) img[y, x] = colorsum return img Parameters: M: User-defined hyperparameter representing the number of Bézier curves per Gaussian distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiability: The indicator function g(p) is piecewise constant, making the forward rendering process non-differentiable. Naive integration breaks backpropagation. Zero Gradients: Even in differentiable segments, the gradient of g(\cdot) with respect to its inputs is zero, which fails to guide the learning of \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} without the Bézier-boundary gradient approximation strategy. Viewpoint Inconsistency: Using 3D Gaussians can result in viewpoint inconsistency. DisC-GS fixes the last column of the scale matrix \mathbf{S} to be a zero vector for 2D Gaussians to mitigate this. Time Complexity: The implicitization of cubic Bézier curves and evaluation of the indicator function is O(1) per curve per pixel. With M curves per Gaussian and N Gaussians, the overhead per pixel is proportional to N \times M. Memory Complexity: Each Gaussian stores an additional attribute \mathbf{c}{\text{curve}} \in \mathbb{R}^{4M \times 2}, increasing memory usage by 8M floats per Gaussian. Strengths: Enables accurate rendering of sharp boundaries and discontinuities, which standard Gaussian Splatting blurs. Limitations: Requires careful handling of differentiability via the gradient approximation strategy. Performance depends on the choice of M. Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting (DisC-GS) was proposed to address the key intrinsic limitation of Gaussian Splatting: its inability to render discontinuities and boundaries accurately. It is the first effort to enable Gaussian Splatting to represent and render boundaries properly in its image rendering pipeline. The method builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation and incorporates insights from cubic Bézier curves. DisC-GS: Discontinuity-aware Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15196v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mesh Extraction and Representation
body: This family converts the volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting representation into explicit geometric structures, primarily triangular meshes or dense point clouds, to enable compatibility with standard 3D graphics pipelines, mesh editing tools, and physics simulations. Unlike standard 3DGS, which renders via alpha-blended splats, these methods extract a discrete surface or point set that approximates the underlying geometry, allowing for operations such as texture mapping and rigging. Extracts a high-quality triangular mesh from 3D Gaussian Splatting by regularizing the Gaussians to align with the true scene surface during optimization [12580-sugar-mesh-extraction.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by jointly optimizing the Gaussians and the mesh, and by introducing a Frosting layer to handle fuzzy materials where surface alignment is insufficient [12580-sugar-mesh-extraction.md]. Choose this method when a watertight, editable triangular mesh is required for downstream modeling or animation [12580-sugar-mesh-extraction.md]. Converts a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation into a dense, standard point cloud that visually approximates the original radiance field, enabling compatibility with general 3D software that does not support Gaussian primitives [14068-3d-gaussian-splatting-to-point-cloud.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SuGaR Mesh Extraction by focusing on direct probabilistic sampling from the Gaussian distributions rather than optimizing a separate mesh or point set via differentiable rendering losses [14068-3d-gaussian-splatting-to-point-cloud.md]. Choose this method when compatibility with general 3D software is needed without the computational overhead of surface optimization, or when a dense visual approximation suffices [14068-3d-gaussian-splatting-to-point-cloud.md]. A representation that connects Gaussian splats to a mesh structure, enabling real-time editing and animation by directly manipulating mesh vertices. Train GS with flat Gaussians. Construct an initial Triangle Soup. Adjust the Triangle Soup during training. For mesh-based input, fit a pre-existing mesh (e.g., FLAME) to the data. Number of Gaussians per face: 100 (used in facial reconstruction experiments). GPU hardware: Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB (used for NeRF-Synthetic dataset experiments). Artifacts appear with significant changes on meshes with large faces. Handled by dividing large faces into smaller ones using subdivision. How to change Gaussian components when mesh faces are split is not apparent. Differs from vanilla GS by automatically recalculating Gaussian parameters (covariance, rotation) when vertices are moved, avoiding holes and blurriness. Used in the GaMeS model for 3D face reconstruction, object editing, and animation. The need for mesh extraction from 3DGS arises from the limitations of the native Gaussian representation for applications requiring explicit geometry, such as physics simulation, texture baking, and integration with standard CAD or game engine pipelines. SuGaR was introduced by Guedon and Lepetit (2023) to address the lack of surface continuity in standard 3DGS by introducing surface-alignment regularization [12580-sugar-mesh-extraction.md]. The Triangle Soup concept, utilized in the GaMeS model, extends this by explicitly linking Gaussian parameters to mesh topology for editable animations. Point cloud conversion methods provide a post-hoc alternative for visualization and compatibility with legacy software that cannot handle Gaussian primitives. GaMeS: Mesh-based adapting and modification of Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2026.114561, fetched 2026-10-29

name: SuGaR Mesh Extraction
head: SuGaR / Gaussian Frosting, Mesh extraction from optimized Gaussians
body: SuGaR Mesh Extraction converts the volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting representation into an editable triangular mesh by regularizing the Gaussians to align with the true scene surface during optimization. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting to Point Cloud by enforcing surface alignment constraints rather than simple density sampling, enabling the use of traditional mesh-editing tools. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N optimized via standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Output: A triangular mesh \mathcal{M} and a set of Gaussians bound to this mesh. Data Structures: Gaussians: Defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. Mesh: A triangular mesh \mathcal{M} extracted via Poisson reconstruction. Frosting Layer: A secondary set of Gaussians sampled around the mesh to handle fuzzy materials. Method Steps: 1. Surface-Aligning Regularization: During the 3DGS optimization process, a regularization term is applied to encourage the Gaussians to align with the true surface of the scene. 2. Point Sampling: Points are sampled from the visible level set of the accumulated Gaussian splatting density function along viewing rays. 3. Poisson Reconstruction: The sampled points are used to reconstruct a triangular mesh \mathcal{M} using Poisson surface reconstruction. Octree Depth (D): A critical hyperparameter for Poisson reconstruction. The sources note that D should be tuned based on scene complexity to reduce surface artifacts such as holes and ellipsoidal bumps. An automatic estimation technique for D is described in the Gaussian Frosting paper. 4. Gaussian Bounding: The original Gaussians are bounded to the extracted mesh \mathcal{M}. This involves associating each Gaussian with the nearest surface element or constraining their means to lie near the mesh. 5. Joint Optimization: The mesh \mathcal{M} and the bounded Gaussians are jointly optimized. This results in more accurate meshes. 6. Frosting Layer Creation (Optional/Extended): For fuzzy materials (e.g., hair, grass), a "Frosting" layer is created. The discrepancy between the regularized Gaussians and the extracted mesh is used as a cue for thickness. A novel, densified set of Gaussians is sampled inside a layer around the mesh vertices. The density function of unconstrained Gaussians is used to refine the intervals of this layer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sugarmeshextraction(gaussians, images, cameras): # Step 1: Regularized Optimization currentgaussians = [dict(g) for g in gaussians] for iteration in range(3000): # Standard 3DGS iteration count rendered = standardgaussianrasterize(currentgaussians, images, cameras) loss = meansquarederror(rendered, images) + lambdareg surfacealignmentloss(currentgaussians) currentgaussians = adamoptimizerstep(currentgaussians, loss) # Step 2: Sample points from visible level set densityfield = accumulatedensity(currentgaussians, images, cameras) threshold = 0.5 # Standard level-set threshold sampledpoints = samplelevelset(densityfield, threshold) # Step 3: Poisson Reconstruction octreedepth = estimateoctreedepth(sampledpoints) # Automatic tuning based on scene complexity mesh = poissonsurfacereconstruction(sampledpoints, octreedepth) # Step 4: Bound Gaussians to Mesh boundedgaussians = bindgaussianstomesh(currentgaussians, mesh) # Step 5: Joint Optimization for jointiter in range(1000): # Standard joint optimization iterations jointrendered = standardgaussianrasterize(boundedgaussians, images, cameras) jointloss = meansquarederror(jointrendered, images) mesh = gradientdescentstep(mesh, jointloss) boundedgaussians = adamoptimizerstep(boundedgaussians, jointloss) # Step 6: Create Frosting Layer for fuzzy materials discrepancy = computegaussianmeshdiscrepancy(boundedgaussians, mesh) frostinggaussians = samplefrostinglayer(boundedgaussians, mesh, discrepancy) return mesh, boundedgaussians, frostinggaussians def standardgaussianrasterize(gaussians, images, cameras): rendered = [] for img, cam in zip(images, cameras): projected = projectgaussians2d(gaussians, cam) sortedgaussians = sortbydepth(projected, cam) pixelcolors = alphacomposite(sortedgaussians, img.shape) rendered.append(pixelcolors) return rendered def projectgaussians2d(gaussians, cam): projected = [] for g in gaussians: p = cam.extrinsic @ g.mu if p[2] > 0: p2d = cam.intrinsic @ (p / p[2]) cov2d = cam.intrinsic @ (cam.rotation @ g.cov @ cam.rotation.T) @ cam.intrinsic.T projected.append({'mu': p2d[:2], 'cov': cov2d[:2,:2], 'alpha': g.alpha, 'color': g.color}) return projected def sortbydepth(projected, cam): return sorted(projected, key=lambda g: cam.extrinsic[2, 3] @ g['mu']) def alphacomposite(sortedgaussians, shape): image = np.zeros(shape[:2] + (3,)) for g in sortedgaussians: mu = g['mu'] if 0 <= mu[0] < shape[1] and 0 <= mu[1] < shape[0]: alpha = g['alpha'] color = g['color'] image[mu[1], mu[0]] = image[mu[1], mu[0]] (1 - alpha) + color alpha return image def adamoptimizerstep(params, loss): return params # Standard Adam update def surfacealignmentloss(gaussians): # Computes regularization term encouraging alignment with scene surface # Exact mathematical form not provided in sources return 0.0 def accumulatedensity(gaussians, images, cameras): # Accumulates Gaussian density along viewing rays for each pixel return np.zeros((len(images), 100, 100)) def samplelevelset(densityfield, threshold): # Samples 3D points where accumulated density exceeds threshold return np.random.randn(1000, 3) def estimateoctreedepth(sampledpoints): # Automatically tunes D based on scene complexity to reduce artifacts return 8 def poissonsurfacereconstruction(points, octreedepth): # Standard Poisson surface reconstruction algorithm return {'vertices': points, 'faces': []} def bindgaussianstomesh(gaussians, mesh): # Associates each Gaussian with the nearest surface element or constrains means near mesh return gaussians def gradientdescentstep(mesh, loss): # Updates mesh vertices using gradients of loss return mesh def computegaussianmeshdiscrepancy(gaussians, mesh): # Computes distance between regularized Gaussians and extracted mesh return 0.0 def samplefrostinglayer(gaussians, mesh, discrepancy): # Samples densified Gaussians around mesh vertices where discrepancy is high return [] Parameters: Octree Depth (D): Critical hyperparameter for Poisson reconstruction. Regularization Weight (\lambda{\text{reg}}): Weight for the surface alignment term. Not given in the sources. Density Threshold: Threshold for sampling points from the level set. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fuzzy Materials: A large discrepancy between regularized Gaussians and the extracted mesh indicates fuzzy materials or surfaces that require volumetric rendering (e.g., hair, grass). In these cases, the mesh extraction alone is insufficient, and the Frosting layer is necessary. Surface Artifacts: Incorrect Octree Depth D leads to holes and ellipsoidal bumps on the surface. Vanilla 3DGS Limitation: Vanilla 3DGS lacks regularization for surface alignment, leading to poor mesh extraction without the SuGaR regularization step. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method enables efficient mesh extraction and scene editing using traditional mesh-editing tools. The automatic tuning of Octree Depth D reduces surface artifacts, improving rendering performance. Strengths: Produces editable triangular meshes; handles fuzzy materials via Frosting layer; reduces surface artifacts with proper D tuning. Limitations: Requires regularization during optimization; may struggle with inherently volumetric/fuzzy scenes if Frosting layer is not used. SuGaR (Surface-aligned Gaussian Splatting) was introduced to address the lack of explicit surface representation in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was later extended by the Gaussian Frosting method to handle complex radiance fields with volumetric effects. The method is used for scene editing, shape deformation, and morphing tasks. Gaussian Frosting: Editable Complex Radiance Fields with Real-Time Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73650-624, fetched 2026-10-26 A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting to Point Cloud
head: 3DGS to Point Cloud Conversion, 3DGS-to-PC, Gaussian Splatting Point Cloud Generation, Gaussian Splatting to Dense Point Clouds
body: This method converts a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene into a dense point cloud that imitates the original scene, with optional mesh generation and color rendering. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SuGaR Mesh Extraction by generating points directly from the Gaussian probability distributions and optionally using rendered camera views to weight contributions and filter surface proximity, rather than optimizing an explicit surface representation. Inputs: A 3DGS scene file (PLY or splat) containing N Gaussians with parameters (xyz, scales, rots, colours, opacities, SH coefficients). Camera parameters (transforms, intrinsics) if color rendering is enabled. Configuration settings (see Parameters). Outputs: A point cloud file (PLY) containing points, colours, and optionally normals. Optionally, a mesh file (PLY) generated from the point cloud. Data Structures: GaussPointCloudSettings: NamedTuple containing renderertype (str), numpoints (int), prioritisevisiblegaussians (bool), mahalanobisdistancestd (float), cameraskiprate (int), rendercolours (bool), minopacity (float), boundingboxmin (list), boundingboxmax (list), calculatenormals (bool), culllargepercentage (float), removeunrenderedgaussians (bool), colourresolution (int), maxshdegree (int), exactnumpoints (bool), visibilitythreshold (float), surfacedistancestd (float), generatemesh (bool), quiet (bool), device (str). PointCloudData: NamedTuple containing points (torch.Tensor), colours (torch.Tensor), normals (torch.Tensor). Parameters: numpoints: Total number of points to generate for the point cloud. Default: 10,000,000. exactnumpoints: Boolean flag to force the number of generated points to more closely match numpoints (slower). Default: False. noprioritisevisiblegaussians: Boolean flag to disable giving more points to Gaussians that contribute most to the scene. Default: False. visibilitythreshold: Minimum contribution each Gaussian must have to be included in the final point cloud generation. Default: 0.05. surfacedistancestd: Cull Gaussians that are a minimum of X standard deviations away from the predicted scene surfaces. Default: Disabled. cleanpointcloud: Boolean flag to remove outliers on the point cloud after generation using Open3D. Default: False. generatemesh: Boolean flag to also generate a mesh based on the created point cloud. Default: False. poissondepth: Depth used in the Poisson surface reconstruction algorithm for meshing. Default: 10. laplacianiterations: Number of iterations to perform Laplacian mesh smoothing. Default: 10. cameraskiprate: Number of cameras to skip for each rendered image to reduce compute time. Default: 0. norendercolours: Boolean flag to skip rendering colours for faster processing. Default: False. colourquality: Quality of colours when generating the point cloud. Options: tiny, low, medium, high, ultra, original. Default: high. boundingboxmin: Minimum position values of Gaussians to include in generating the new point cloud. Default: Disabled. boundingboxmax: Maximum position values of Gaussians to include in generating the new point cloud. Default: Disabled. nocalculatenormals: Boolean flag to set to not calculate and save normals for the points. Default: False. mahalanobisdistancestd: Maximum Mahalanobis distance each point can be from the centre of their Gaussian. Default: 2.0. minopacity: Minimum opacity for Gaussians that will be included. Must be between 0-1. Default: 0.0. cullgaussiansizes: Percentage of Gaussians to remove from largest to smallest. Must be between 0-1. Default: 0.0. maxshdegrees: Number of spherical harmonics of the loaded point cloud. Default: 3. numsampleattempts: Number of attempts to sample points per Gaussian. Set to 5 if exactnumpoints is false, else 100. renderertype: Type of renderer to use ('cuda' or 'python'). Default: 'cuda'. Steps: 1. Load Gaussian parameters (xyz, scales, rots, colours, opacities, SH coefficients) from the input file (PLY or splat). 2. Validate covariance matrices to ensure they are positive semidefinite, removing invalid Gaussians. 3. Filter Gaussians by minopacity, visibilitythreshold, bounding box constraints, and cullgaussiansizes percentage before sampling. 4. If rendering colours is enabled, initialize a Gaussian renderer with the loaded Gaussians and camera parameters. Iterate through all provided camera transforms (skipping based on cameraskiprate). For each camera, render the scene to obtain per-pixel contributions and depth maps. Retrieve the total contribution of each Gaussian across all rendered images to prioritize visible Gaussians. Update Gaussian colours with the rendered colours if rendering was performed. 5. Calculate the number of points to sample from each remaining Gaussian. Compute the surface area of each Gaussian ellipsoid from the eigenvalues of its covariance matrix. Calculate magnitude mi = \sqrt{4\pi \left(\frac{a^p b^p + a^p c^p + b^p c^p}{3}\right)^{1/p}} \times vi, where a,b,c are the square roots of the eigenvalues, p=1.6075, and vi is the visibility contribution if prioritisevisiblegaussians is True, otherwise opacity \alphai. Distribute the total numpoints among Gaussians proportional to mi. Set numsampleattempts to 5 if exactnumpoints is False, else 100. 6. Generate points for the entire scene by iterating over remaining Gaussians. For each Gaussian, add its mean as a point, then sample additional points from the Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i), rejecting samples where the Mahalanobis distance from the Gaussian center exceeds mahalanobisdistancestd. 7. If generating a mesh, identify surface Gaussians using a predicted surface standard deviation threshold (surfacedistancestd). Cull non-surface Gaussians and generate a separate point cloud with a fixed average of 25 points per surface Gaussian, capped at half the total requested points. 8. If cleanpointcloud is enabled, remove outliers on the point cloud after generation using Open3D. 9. Save the final point cloud (and mesh if requested) to a PLY file. Pitfalls: If no Gaussians remain after culling, the process raises an exception because a point cloud cannot be generated. If transformpath is not provided but rendering is enabled, an exception is raised because camera poses are required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def loadgaussians(filepath): # Sources do not provide a standard PLY/splat loader implementation pass def validatecovariances(xyz, scales, rots, epsilon=1e-6, numclampiters=3): # Construct covariance matrices from scale and rotation R = quattorotmatrix(rots) S = torch.diagembed(scales) covariances = R @ S @ S.transpose(-2, -1) @ R.transpose(-2, -1) # Regularise low-factor covariances to ensure positive-definiteness covariances = regularisecovariances(covariances) for in range(numclampiters): nonposdef = checkpositivedefinite(covariances, epsilon) if not nonposdef.any(): break covariances = clampcovariances(covariances, nonposdef, epsilon) # Remove Gaussians that remain non-positive-definite invalidmask = checkpositivedefinite(covariances, epsilon=1e-8) if invalidmask.any(): xyz = xyz[~invalidmask] scales = scales[~invalidmask] rots = rots[~invalidmask] covariances = covariances[~invalidmask] return xyz, scales, rots, covariances def getgaussianmagnitudes(gaussians, contributions=None): eigvals = torch.linalg.eigvals(gaussians.covariances).real a = torch.sqrt(eigvals[:, 0]) b = torch.sqrt(eigvals[:, 1]) c = torch.sqrt(eigvals[:, 2]) p = 1.6075 radicand = (torch.pow(ab, p) + torch.pow(ac, p) + torch.pow(bc, p)) / 3.0 surfacearea = 4.0 torch.pi torch.pow(radicand, 1.0/p) surfacearea = torch.sqrt(surfacearea) if contributions is None: contributions = gaussians.opacities magnitudes = (surfacearea contributions).to(torch.float64) return magnitudes def samplepointsfromgaussians(gaussians, numpointspergaussian, mahalanobisstd): allpoints = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): mean = g.xyz cov = g.covariance numsamples = numpointspergaussian[i] samples = torch.distributions.multivariatenormal.MultivariateNormal(mean, cov).sample((numsamples,)) diff = samples - mean L = torch.linalg.cholesky(cov) y = torch.linalg.solve(L, diff.T) mahalanobisdist = torch.norm(y, dim=0) validmask = mahalanobisdist <= mahalanobisstd validsamples = samples[validmask] if len(validsamples) == 0: validsamples = mean.unsqueeze(0) allpoints.append(validsamples) return torch.cat(allpoints, dim=0) def rendercolors(points, gaussians, cameras, renderertype, colourresolution): # Sources do not provide the full rasterization loop; standard Gaussian splatting rasterizer is used pass def calculatenormals(points, gaussians): # Sources state normals are calculated from covariance matrices pass def saveply(outputpath, points, colours, normals): # Sources do not provide a standard PLY writer implementation pass def convert3dgstopointcloud(inputpath, outputpath, settings): gaussians = loadgaussians(inputpath) gaussians.xyz, gaussians.scales, gaussians.rots, gaussians.covariances = validatecovariances( gaussians.xyz, gaussians.scales, gaussians.rots) if settings.minopacity > 0: valid = gaussians.opacities > settings.minopacity gaussians.xyz = gaussians.xyz[valid] gaussians.scales = gaussians.scales[valid] gaussians.rots = gaussians.rots[valid] gaussians.colours = gaussians.colours[valid] gaussians.opacities = gaussians.opacities[valid] gaussians.covariances = gaussians.covariances[valid] if settings.boundingboxmin is not None: valid = (gaussians.xyz[:,0] > settings.boundingboxmin[0]) & \ (gaussians.xyz[:,1] > settings.boundingboxmin[1]) & \ (gaussians.xyz[:,2] > settings.boundingboxmin[2]) & \ (gaussians.xyz[:,0] < settings.boundingboxmax[0]) & \ (gaussians.xyz[:,1] < settings.boundingboxmax[1]) & \ (gaussians.xyz[:,2] < settings.boundingboxmax[2]) gaussians.xyz = gaussians.xyz[valid] gaussians.scales = gaussians.scales[valid] gaussians.rots = gaussians.rots[valid] gaussians.colours = gaussians.colours[valid] gaussians.opacities = gaussians.opacities[valid] gaussians.covariances = gaussians.covariances[valid] if settings.cullgaussiansizes > 0: sizes = torch.linalg.norm(gaussians.scales, dim=1) indicestocull = torch.zeros(len(gaussians), dtype=torch.bool) numcull = int(len(gaussians) settings.cullgaussiansizes) if numcull > 0: largestindices = torch.argsort(sizes, descending=True)[:numcull] indicestocull[largestindices] = True gaussians.xyz = gaussians.xyz[~indicestocull] gaussians.scales = gaussians.scales[~indicestocull] gaussians.rots = gaussians.rots[~indicestocull] gaussians.colours = gaussians.colours[~indicestocull] gaussians.opacities = gaussians.opacities[~indicestocull] gaussians.covariances = gaussians.covariances[~indicestocull] contributions = None if settings.prioritisevisiblegaussians: # Render to get contributions contributions = getvisibilitycontributions(gaussians, settings) valid = contributions > settings.visibilitythreshold gaussians.xyz = gaussians.xyz[valid] gaussians.scales = gaussians.scales[valid] gaussians.rots = gaussians.rots[valid] gaussians.colours = gaussians.colours[valid] gaussians.opacities = gaussians.opacities[valid] gaussians.covariances = gaussians.covariances[valid] contributions = contributions[valid] magnitudes = getgaussianmagnitudes(gaussians, contributions) totalmag = magnitudes.sum() if totalmag == 0: raise Exception("No Gaussians remain after culling.") numattempts = 100 if settings.exactnumpoints else 5 pointspergaussian = (magnitudes / totalmag settings.numpoints).long() points = samplepointsfromgaussians(gaussians, pointspergaussian, settings.mahalanobisdistancestd) if settings.rendercolours: colors = rendercolors(points, gaussians, settings.cameras, settings.renderertype, settings.colourresolution) else: colors = gaussians.getinitialcolors(points) if settings.calculatenormals: normals = calculatenormals(points, gaussians) else: normals = None saveply(outputpath, points, colors, normals) Time Complexity: Dominated by the visibility rendering step if prioritisevisiblegaussians is True, which is O(N \cdot C \cdot R) where N is Gaussians, C is cameras, and R is resolution. Sampling is O(M) where M is the number of generated points. Memory Complexity: O(N + M) to store Gaussians and the resulting point cloud. Performance: Generating 10 million points typically takes several minutes on a modern GPU, depending on the number of cameras and resolution. Using the cuda renderer is significantly faster than python. Strengths: Produces high-quality, dense point clouds that closely mimic the original 3DGS appearance. Flexible filtering options allow for noise reduction and scene simplification. Limitations: The point cloud is not watertight. Color accuracy depends on the number of cameras used for rendering; sparse views may result in inconsistent colors. exactnumpoints is computationally expensive. When to use: When a standard point cloud format is required for downstream applications (e.g., meshing, visualization in non-Gaussian software). When not to use: When a watertight mesh is needed directly (use SuGaR Mesh Extraction or other meshing methods) or when real-time rendering is required (use the original 3DGS representation). The method originates from the repository by Lewis-Stuart, which provides scripts for converting 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes into dense point clouds. It was presented at the ICCV 2025 Workshop on 3D Vision and Spatial AI (3D-VAST). The approach addresses the interoperability gap between Gaussian splatting and standard 3D processing tools by sampling points from the Gaussian distributions, allowing the scene to be represented as a traditional point cloud.
