name: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: AAGS
body: AAGS reconstructs static scenes from unconstrained, in-the-wild photo collections by decoupling intrinsic object properties from extrinsic appearance conditions (lighting and post-processing) and explicitly removing transient objects. Unlike NeRF-based methods (e.g., NeRF-W, Ha-NeRF) which model transients explicitly with high overhead, or SWAG which requires additional Gaussian training for transients, AAGS leverages 3D Gaussian Splatting's fast rendering to use a lightweight 2D visibility mask for transient exclusion. Inputs and Outputs Input: A collection of unconstrained images \{Ii\} of a static scene. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians representing the static scene geometry and appearance, and a trained appearance-aware rendering pipeline. Data Structures 3D Gaussian Parameters: Each Gaussian i is defined by: Center: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation: Quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4. Scaling: si \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1]. Implicit Color Feature: V{g,i} \in \mathbb{R}^{ng} (replaces standard spherical harmonics coefficients). Appearance Extractor (E\Phi): A CNN-based network that outputs an image-specific latent vector V{ia} \in \mathbb{R}^{na} for each input image Ii. Color Decoder (F\theta): An MLP-based network with 4 layers and 64 hidden units. It takes V{g,i}, V{ia}, and directional encoding \gamma(d) as input to predict color c. Transient UNet (U\Psi): A UNet with downsampling and upsampling layers that outputs a binary classification map Mi \in [0, 1] of the same size as Ii. Values closer to 1 indicate static pixels. Parameters ng = 24: Length of Gaussian implicit feature vector Vg. na = 48: Length of image appearance latent vector V{ia}. \lambda1 = 0.8: Weight for L1 loss in the reconstruction loss. \lambdam: Weight for transient regularization loss, starting at 0.5 and exponentially annealing to 0.15. Spherical Harmonics Degree: 4, used for directional encoding \gamma(d). Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using a Structure from Motion (SfM) sparse point cloud. Assign parameters \mui, qi, si, \alphai and initialize V{g,i} \in \mathbb{R}^{ng} where ng=24. 2. Appearance Encoding: For each training image Ii, compute the appearance latent vector: V{ia} = E\Phi(Ii) 3. Directional Encoding: For each Gaussian i and camera view, calculate the direction vector d from the Gaussian center \mui to the camera position. Apply spherical harmonic positional encoding to obtain \gamma(d). 4. Color Prediction: Concatenate V{g,i}, V{ia}, and \gamma(d), and pass them through the color decoder F\theta to predict the color ci: ci = F\theta(V{g,i}, V{ia}, \gamma(d)) 5. Rasterization: Project the 3D Gaussians to the 2D image plane. Calculate the projected opacity \alpha'i for each Gaussian i at pixel location x': \alpha'i = \alphai \exp\left(-0.5 (x' - \mu'i)^T \Sigma'^{-1}i (x' - \mu'i)\right) where \mu'i and \Sigma'i are the projected mean and covariance matrix. 6. Color Compositing: Render the image \hat{I}i by sorting Gaussians N front-to-back and compositing colors: \hat{I}i(x') = \sum{i \in N} ci \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) 7. Transient Masking: Compute the transient visibility map Mi for the input image: Mi = U\Psi(Ii) 8. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L using the masked L1 and SSIM losses, plus transient regularization: L = (1 - \lambda1) L{SSIM}(Mi \odot Ii, Mi \odot \hat{I}i) + \lambda1 L1(Mi \odot Ii, Mi \odot \hat{I}i) + \lambdam Lm where \odot is element-wise multiplication, and Lm is the regularization loss. 9. Regularization: Prevent the trivial solution where U\Psi predicts all pixels as transient by minimizing: Lm = (1 - Mi)^2 10. Optimization: Update parameters \{E\Phi, F\theta, U\Psi, \mu, q, s, \alpha, Vg\} using gradient descent. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalharmonicencode(direction, degree=4): # Standard spherical harmonic basis evaluation for the given direction return [math.sin(theta)math.cos(phi), math.sin(theta)math.sin(phi), math.cos(theta)] def project3dto2d(gaussian, cameraparams): # Standard 3DGS projection using camera intrinsics and extrinsics return gaussian.muprime, gaussian.Sigmaprime def sortbydepth(projectedgaussians): # Sorts Gaussians by depth along the camera viewing ray return sorted(projectedgaussians, key=lambda g: g.depth) def ssimloss(pred, target): # Standard SSIM computation return 1.0 - structuralsimilarity(pred, target) def l1loss(pred, target): # Standard L1 norm computation return sum(abs(pred - target)) / len(pred) def mean(tensor): # Computes the arithmetic mean of all elements return sum(tensor.flatten()) / len(tensor.flatten()) def forwardpass(image, gaussians, cameraparams, Ephi, Ftheta, Upsi): # 1. Appearance Extraction Via = Ephi(image) # 2. Color Prediction for g in gaussians: d = cameraparams.position - g.center gammad = sphericalharmonicencode(d, degree=4) g.color = Ftheta(g.Vg, Via, gammad) # 3. Rasterization projected = [] for g in gaussians: g.muprime, g.Sigmaprime = project3dto2d(g, cameraparams) projected.append(g) sortedgaussians = sortbydepth(projected) # 4. Alpha Compositing renderedimage = zeroslike(image) for g in sortedgaussians: alphaprime = g.alpha exp(-0.5 dot(g.xprime - g.muprime, inv(g.Sigmaprime) (g.xprime - g.muprime))) for pixel in g.rasterizedpixels: renderedimage[pixel] = renderedimage[pixel] (1 - alphaprime) + g.color alphaprime # 5. Transient Masking M = Upsi(image) return renderedimage, M def computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage, mask, lambda1, lambdam): maskedgt = groundtruthimage mask maskedpred = renderedimage mask lssim = ssimloss(maskedgt, maskedpred) l1 = l1loss(maskedgt, maskedpred) lrec = (1 - lambda1) lssim + lambda1 l1 lm = mean((1 - mask)2) totalloss = lrec + lambdam lm return totalloss Speed: Achieves reconstruction speeds at the minute level and real-time rendering capabilities, leveraging the fast rendering speed of 3D Gaussian Splatting. Memory: Trained on a single RTX 3090 GPU with 24GB memory. Strengths: Concise and efficient compared to SWAG (no extra Gaussian training for transients) and NeRF-based methods (faster, lower overhead). Handles unconstrained in-the-wild photos without requiring COLMAP preprocessing for multi-view stereo. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the transient UNet; if the regularization is insufficient, it may fall into the trivial solution of masking everything. AAGS was introduced to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to unconstrained photo collections, addressing the limitations of previous NeRF-based methods (NeRF-W, Ha-NeRF) and concurrent 3DGS-based methods (SWAG). It was developed to facilitate real-world applications by combining high-quality reconstruction with real-time rendering. AAGS: Appearance-Aware 3D Gaussian Splatting with Unconstrained Photo Collections, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00530-025-01742-4, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Intrinsic Decomposition of 3D Gaussian Splats
head: Albedo, Shading, Residual Gaussian Splatting, Albedo-Shading-Decomposed 3DGS, Albedo-Shading-Residual decomposition, Intrinsic 3DGS, Intrinsic Decomposition with Separate Gaussian Fields, Multi-Layer Gaussian Splatting, Multi-Layer Gaussian Splatting (Albedo, Residual), Three-set Gaussian optimization
body: This method decomposes a radiance field represented as 3D Gaussian splats into three independent sets of Gaussian primitives: albedo (GA), shading (GS), and view-dependent residual (GR). It solves the problem of multi-view consistent editing of object textures by allowing users to modify albedo without altering lighting, which is difficult when intrinsic components are entangled in a single representation. Unlike prior work that optimizes a single set of Gaussians or an MLP for all intrinsic quantities, this approach uses separate layers to better capture the misaligned sharp details of each component. Inputs: A video sequence of the scene. Camera poses (computed via Structure-from-Motion). Predicted albedo maps (from a video diffusion model). Predicted depth maps (from a monocular depth estimator). Outputs: Three sets of 3D Gaussians: GA (albedo), GS (shading), and GR (residual). A rendered scene I composed from these fields. Each Gaussian primitive g in any set (GA, GS, GR) is defined as: g = \{c, \alpha, p, \Sigma\} c: Color. For GA and GS: A simple triplet c = \{r, g, b\} \in \mathbb{R}^3. For GR: Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients, up to 3 bands, scheduled progressively as in standard 3DGS. \alpha: Opacity. p: Position in 3D space. \Sigma: Covariance matrix (defining scale and rotation). 1. Video Processing: Apply inverse gamma correction to sRGB input images to obtain pseudo-linear RGB. Apply inverse gamma correction to albedo maps from the diffusion model (observed to be non-linear). Subsample the video to create a multi-view dataset by sampling every n=5 frame, preferring low-blur frames. Run Structure-from-Motion (SfM) on extracted images to compute camera poses. Apply the undistortion applied by SfM to the albedo images as well. Use a video diffusion model (DiffusionRenderer) to estimate albedo for each frame. Chunk Processing: Process sequences in chunks of 64 frames (one start latent + eight regular latents). At each denoising step, operate on 57 frames (one start latent + seven regular latents). Advance the window by four latent codes (shift of 32 frames). Discard redundant frames after decoding. Use a monocular depth estimator (Depth Anything V2) to obtain initial depth maps. 2. Albedo Field (GA) Initialization: Start from calibrated cameras and the initial point cloud from SfM. Initialize GA using the same learning rates and activations as original 3DGS, except albedo color uses a sigmoid activation (expected range [0, 1]). 3. Shading Field (GS) Initialization: Initialize GS from SfM points in the same manner as albedo Gaussians. 4. Residual Field (GR) Initialization: Spawned dynamically during optimization (see Step 5). Step 1: Albedo Reconstruction Optimize GA to reproduce the predicted albedo images \tilde{A}. Render albedo image \tilde{A} and depth image \tilde{D} (by replacing Gaussian color with their depth). Compute loss: L = (1 - \lambda) \|\tilde{A} - A\|1 + \lambda L{D-SSIM}(A, \tilde{A}) + \lambdad L{depth} + \lambdas L{scale} Where: L{depth} = \|\tilde{D} - D\|1 (regularization against predicted depth D). L{scale} = \bar{s} (average scale of primitives, encouraging flattening). L{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss. \lambda, \lambdad, \lambdas are hyperparameters controlling the loss weights. Step 2: Shading Optimization (Phase 1) Ignore the residual term. Optimize GS using the diffuse model I = A \times S. Use inverse domain photometric loss to handle high dynamic range and bound values in [0, 1]: L{photometric} = \left\| \frac{1}{1+I} - \frac{1}{1+A \times S} \right\|1 Add gray shading regularization to prevent incorrect color reproduction when albedo is dark: L{gray} = \max(c) - \min(c) Where c are the color parameters of the shading Gaussian. Total loss includes photometric loss, depth regularization, and scale regularization. Step 3: Residual Spawning Iterate through training views. Compute the difference between the input image I and the composited diffuse render A \times S. Randomly select a subset of pixels with high difference. Use the predicted depth of these pixels as positions to spawn new residual Gaussians in GR. Step 4: Residual Optimization (Phase 2) Freeze GS. Optimize GR to capture residual non-diffuse effects. Use the full image formation model: I = A \times S + R Compute loss using the inverse domain photometric loss: L = (1 - \lambda) \left\| \frac{1}{1+I} - \frac{1}{1+A \times S + R} \right\|1 + L{D-SSIM}(I, A \times S + R) + \lambdad L{depth} + \lambdas L{scale} Only update residual Gaussians GR. Keep the same scaling and depth regularizations as albedo/shading stages. Step 5: Albedo Editing (Optional) 1. User drags a rectangular window in an image to select a surface. 2. Select the primitive contributing most to each pixel in the window. 3. Use RANSAC to fit a proxy plane over the centers of these Gaussians. 4. Render a set of edited albedo images from multiple nearby viewpoints (sampled on a hemisphere centered on the editing viewpoint) by compositing the textured proxy plane with the albedo field, using rendered depth for occlusion testing. 5. Re-optimize albedo Gaussians GA using the edited images and Eq. 5. 6. Spawn additional albedo Gaussians on the textured proxy plane by randomly sampling 20% of the pixels covered by the edit in the edited view. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def intrinsicdecomposition(videoframes, videodiffusionmodel, depthestimator, sfmsolver, numiterations=30000): """ Main pipeline for intrinsic decomposition of 3D Gaussian Splatting. """ # 1. Preprocessing linearframes = applyinversegamma(videoframes) # Subsample video: every 5th frame sampledframes = linearframes[::5] # Compute camera poses via SfM cameras = sfmsolver(sampledframes) # Estimate Albedo using Video Diffusion Model with chunking albedomaps = [] chunksize = 64 shift = 32 for i in range(0, len(sampledframes), shift): chunk = sampledframes[i: i + chunksize] # DiffusionRenderer processes 57 frames at a time, shifting by 32 albedochunk = videodiffusionmodel.processchunk(chunk) albedomaps.extend(albedochunk) # Apply undistortion from SfM to albedo maps albedomaps = applyundistortion(albedomaps, cameras) # Estimate Depth depthmaps = depthestimator(sampledframes) # 2. Initialize Gaussians from SfM Point Cloud initialpoints = sfmsolver.getpointcloud() # Initialize Albedo Gaussians GA GA = initializegaussians(initialpoints, coloractivation='sigmoid') # 3. Optimize Albedo Field optimizealbedo(GA, albedomaps, depthmaps, cameras, numiterations) # 4. Optimize Shading Field GS GS = initializegaussians(initialpoints) optimizeshading(GA, GS, sampledframes, depthmaps, cameras, numiterations) # 5. Spawn and Optimize Residual Field GR GR = spawnresidualgaussians(GA, GS, sampledframes, depthmaps, cameras) optimizeresidual(GA, GS, GR, sampledframes, depthmaps, cameras, numiterations) return GA, GS, GR def optimizealbedo(GA, albedomaps, depthmaps, cameras, numiterations): """ Optimizes GA to match predicted albedo maps using Eq. 5. """ for iteration in range(numiterations): for frameidx in range(len(cameras)): camera = cameras[frameidx] targetalbedo = albedomaps[frameidx] targetdepth = depthmaps[frameidx] # Render renderedalbedo, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(GA, camera) # Loss components Lrecon = l1loss(renderedalbedo, targetalbedo) Ldssim = dssimloss(renderedalbedo, targetalbedo) Ldepth = l1loss(rendereddepth, targetdepth) Lscale = meanscale(GA) # Combine losses (Eq. 5) loss = (1 - lambdaparam) Lrecon + lambdaparam Ldssim + \ lambdad Ldepth + lambdas Lscale # Backpropagate and update GA updategaussians(GA, loss) # Densification (standard 3DGS) densifygaussians(GA, cameras, frameidx) def optimizeshading(GA, GS, frames, depthmaps, cameras, numiterations): """ Optimizes GS assuming I = A S (Phase 1). """ for iteration in range(numiterations): for frameidx in range(len(cameras)): camera = cameras[frameidx] targetimage = frames[frameidx] targetdepth = depthmaps[frameidx] # Render Albedo and Shading renderedalbedo = renderalbedo(GA, camera) renderedshading, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(GS, camera) # Composite Diffuse compositediffuse = renderedalbedo renderedshading # Inverse Domain Photometric Loss invtarget = 1.0 / (1.0 + targetimage) invpred = 1.0 / (1.0 + compositediffuse) Lphotometric = l1loss(invtarget, invpred) # Gray Shading Regularization Lgray = maxcolorrange(GS) # Depth and Scale Regularization Ldepth = l1loss(rendereddepth, targetdepth) Lscale = meanscale(GS) loss = Lphotometric + Lgray + Ldepth + Lscale updategaussians(GS, loss) densifygaussians(GS, cameras, frameidx) def spawnresidualgaussians(GA, GS, frames, depthmaps, cameras): """ Spawns GR based on residuals from diffuse approximation. """ newGR = [] for frameidx in range(len(cameras)): camera = cameras[frameidx] targetimage = frames[frameidx] targetdepth = depthmaps[frameidx] # Render Diffuse renderedalbedo = renderalbedo(GA, camera) renderedshading = rendershading(GS, camera) compositediffuse = renderedalbedo renderedshading # Compute Residual residual = targetimage - compositediffuse # Select pixels with high difference highdiffpixels = selecthighdifferencepixels(residual, threshold=0.1) # Spawn Gaussians at predicted depth of these pixels for pixel in highdiffpixels: depthval = targetdepth[pixel.y, pixel.x] pos = unprojectpixel(camera, pixel, depthval) newGR.append(creategaussian(pos, colorsh=True, opacity=0.5)) return newGR def optimizeresidual(GA, GS, GR, frames, depthmaps, cameras, numiterations): """ Optimizes GR using full model I = A S + R (Phase 2). """ for iteration in range(numiterations): for frameidx in range(len(cameras)): camera = cameras[frameidx] targetimage = frames[frameidx] targetdepth = depthmaps[frameidx] # Render all fields renderedalbedo = renderalbedo(GA, camera) renderedshading = rendershading(GS, camera) renderedresidual, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(GR, camera) # Composite Full compositefull = (renderedalbedo renderedshading) + renderedresidual # Inverse Domain Photometric Loss invtarget = 1.0 / (1.0 + targetimage) invpred = 1.0 / (1.0 + compositefull) Lphotometric = l1loss(invtarget, invpred) # Depth and Scale Regularization Ldepth = l1loss(rendereddepth, targetdepth) Lscale = meanscale(GR) loss = Lphotometric + Ldepth + Lscale updategaussians(GR, loss) densifygaussians(GR, cameras, frameidx) def applyinversegamma(img, gamma=2.2): return np.power(img, gamma) def applyundistortion(img, cameras): # Standard camera undistortion applied to match SfM preprocessing return [cam.undistort(i) for i, cam in zip(img, cameras)] def initializegaussians(points, coloractivation='linear'): # Standard 3DGS initialization from point cloud return Gaussians(points, coloractivation=coloractivation) def rendergaussians(G, camera): # Standard 3DGS rasterization returning color and depth buffers return camera.rasterize(G) def renderalbedo(GA, camera): return rendergaussians(GA, camera)[0] def rendershading(GS, camera): return rendergaussians(GS, camera)[0] def selecthighdifferencepixels(residual, threshold=0.1): return np.argwhere(np.abs(residual) > threshold) def l1loss(a, b): return np.mean(np.abs(a - b)) def dssimloss(a, b): # Standard D-SSIM implementation return 1.0 - ssim(a, b) def meanscale(G): return np.mean(G.scales) def maxcolorrange(G): return np.max(G.colors, axis=1) - np.min(G.colors, axis=1) def updategaussians(G, loss): # Standard optimizer step (e.g., Adam) G.optimizer.step() def densifygaussians(G, cameras, frameidx): # Standard 3DGS densification based on gradient magnitudes G.densify(cameras[frameidx]) def unprojectpixel(camera, pixel, depth): return camera.unproject(pixel.x, pixel.y, depth) def creategaussian(pos, colorsh=True, opacity=0.5): return Gaussian(position=pos, usesh=colorsh, opacity=opacity) Time Complexity: Training is significantly slower than vanilla 3DGS. For example, on the "Basement 1" scene, the full method took 28 minutes 30 seconds compared to 6 minutes 56 seconds for vanilla 3DGS. This is due to the additional render calls required for each layer (2 for diffuse, 3 for full). Memory Complexity: Requires storing three sets of Gaussians. The total number of primitives is higher than vanilla 3DGS (e.g., 2.185M vs 1.558M for Basement 1). Rendering: Requires 2 render calls for the diffuse scene (Albedo + Shading) and 3 for the full scene (Albedo + Shading + Residual). Strengths: Allows multi-view consistent editing of albedo without altering lighting; better captures misaligned sharp details of intrinsic components. Limitations: Slower rendering and longer training times compared to vanilla 3DGS. This method extends intrinsic image decomposition to radiance fields represented with Gaussian splats. It builds on the intrinsic image formation model I = A \times S + R. The approach was proposed to address the limitations of prior work that optimized a single set of Gaussians or MLPs for all intrinsic quantities, which struggled with misaligned sharp details. The method uses data-driven predictions from video diffusion models to guide the optimization. Intrinsic decomposition and editing of 3D Gaussian splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804495, fetched 2026-10-27

name: LE3D
head: Lighting Every darkness with 3DGS
body: LE3D is a method for High Dynamic Range (HDR) view synthesis from noisy RAW images that enables real-time rendering and fast training by replacing 3D Gaussian Splatting's (3DGS) spherical harmonics with a Color MLP, using Cone Scatter Initialization for Structure-from-Motion (SfM) enrichment, and applying depth distortion and near-far regularizations. It differs from its parent 3iGS by focusing specifically on RAW input handling and nighttime scene reconstruction rather than factorized tensorial illumination modeling. Inputs: Noisy RAW images, camera poses (initially estimated via COLMAP). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives optimized for real-time rasterization, supporting HDR rendering, refocusing, and tone-mapping. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive i is defined by the following attributes: Center position: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scaling factor: si \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation: quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4. Opacity: oi \in \mathbb{R}. Color features: fi (input to the Color MLP). Primitive-aware bias: bi (input to the Color MLP). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Use COLMAP to obtain the initial point cloud and camera poses. 2. Cone Scatter Initialization: To address poor SfM estimation in distant nighttime views, perform random point sampling within a cone using the estimated camera poses to enrich the point clouds. 3. Training Setup: Perform standard 3DGS training. Replace the original Spherical Harmonics (SH) with a tiny Color MLP to represent the RAW linear color space. The MLP takes fi and bi as inputs to produce the final rendered color ci. 4. Loss Calculation: Apply RawNeRF's weighted L2 loss as image-level supervision. Apply proposed depth distortion regularization (R{dist}) and near-far regularization (R{nf}) as scene structure regularizations. Formulas: The Gaussian basis function is defined as: G(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\right) where \mu is the center in 3D space, and \Sigma is the covariance matrix derived from scaling and rotation parameters. The pixel color C is computed by blending N ordered Gaussians overlapping the pixel: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \cdot \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai = G^2{2i} oi, ci is the decoded color from the Color MLP, G^2{2i} is the projected 2D Gaussian, and oi is the opacity. The weighted L2 loss used for supervision is: L\psi(\hat{y}, y) = \sumi \left(\frac{\hat{y}i - yi}{sg(\hat{y}i) + \epsilon}\right)^2 where \hat{y}i is the rendered color, yi is the noisy reference color, sg(\cdot) is the stop-gradient function, and \epsilon = 10^{-3}. Parameters: \epsilon: A small constant used in the weighted L2 loss denominator to prevent division by zero. Typical value: 10^{-3}. Pitfalls: Nighttime SfM Failure: In nighttime scenes, extremely low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) leads to poor SfM estimation in distant views, causing blurred distant views or floaters. LE3D handles this by introducing Cone Scatter Initialization. Color Representation: Spherical Harmonics (SH) have limited representation capacity and are unsuitable for RAW linear color space. LE3D handles this by replacing SH with a tiny Color MLP. Scene Structure: Inaccurate scene structure hampers downstream tasks like refocusing. LE3D handles this by introducing depth distortion and near-far regularizations. Training Time: Approximately 1.5 GPU hours. This is 1% of the training time required by RawNeRF. Rendering Speed: Approximately 100 FPS for 2K resolution images. This is approximately 4,000 times faster than RawNeRF. Strengths: Real-time rendering, fast training, support for HDR rendering, refocusing, and tone-mapping changes. Limitations: Relies on COLMAP for initial pose estimation, which may be insufficient for very dark scenes without the Cone Scatter Initialization. LE3D (Lighting Every Darkness with 3DGS) was proposed to address the challenges of implementing RAW image-based view synthesis directly using 3D Gaussian Splatting. Previous methods like RawNeRF suffered from slow rendering and long training times due to dense sampling requirements. LE3D leverages the differentiable rasterization of 3DGS to achieve real-time performance while maintaining the HDR capabilities of RAW-based methods. Lighting Every Darkness with 3DGS: Fast Training and Real-Time Rendering for HDR View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-2549, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Spherical Harmonics Optimization
head: SH Optimization, View-Dependent Color Optimization
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization encompasses methods that define, store, and optimize the view-dependent color coefficients \mathbf{c}i(\omega) for 3D Gaussian primitives, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of accurately modeling complex lighting and material properties (e.g., specularities, anisotropy) while managing the high memory and computational costs associated with high-degree SH representations. It sets itself apart from its siblings by offering diverse strategies: distillation to lower degrees First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation, vector quantization for compression Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization, analytical Jacobian derivation for pose optimization Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation, multi-view training stability Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting, closed-form estimation for meshes Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation, adaptive regularization Adaptive SH Regularization, and geometry-guided neural substitution Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling. All methods in this family inherit the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation and rendering pipeline from Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints. The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include post-processing transformation DAVIGS, factorized illumination 3iGS, image-conditioned modulation SWAG, and neural field substitution Compact View-dependent Color. First-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) Distillation is a compression technique that reduces the SH degree of 3D Gaussian elements from the standard third-order (degree 3) to first-order (degree 1) to decrease parameter count and rendering computation cost. Unlike standard degree reduction which simply truncates coefficients, this method employs a distillation strategy where a "student" model with first-order SH approximates the directional radiance of a pretrained "teacher" model. It sets itself apart from siblings like Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (which quantizes coefficients) and Compact View-dependent Color (which uses neural fields) by explicitly training a lower-degree SH representation to mimic the output of a higher-degree reference. This method derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable efficient gradient-based camera pose optimization. It solves the problem of high computational overhead associated with automatic differentiation in differentiable rendering pipelines, particularly for SLAM systems where tracking must be performed in real-time. It sets itself apart from prior ray-intersection methods by providing the first analytical Jacobian specifically tailored for EWA splatting and 3DGS, ensuring the Jacobian dimensionality matches the 6 degrees of freedom of the Lie algebra without redundant computations. This method enables stable optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by training on multiple views per iteration, addressing the high variance of gradients inherent in the standard single-view approach. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by replacing the single-image mini-batch with a multi-image batch, while overcoming the rasterization overhead and adaptive density control incompatibilities that typically prevent such an implementation. Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (SH VQ) is a compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces per-splat SH coefficients with indices pointing to a shared palette of distinct SH vectors, significantly reducing memory footprint at the cost of minor lighting artifacts. Unlike methods that exploit spatial correlation between neighboring Gaussians, SH VQ treats each splat's SH data independently, clustering millions of high-dimensional vectors into a fixed-size palette. This approach sets it apart from spatially-aware compression methods like Hybrid Compression Method for Trained 3D Gaussian Splatting Models Based on VQ and HEVC by avoiding inter-splat prediction, which simplifies implementation but can introduce localized color inconsistencies. Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation solves the problem of estimating view-dependent spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for mesh vertices by formulating a global weighted least-squares problem across all calibrated input views. It differs from iterative optimization methods by providing an analytical solution to the normal system, utilizing adaptive regularization to handle varying view support and a matrix-free Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG) solver to avoid explicit matrix inversion. Adaptive SH Regularization is a technique for stabilizing the optimization of Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients in 3D Gaussian Splatting under sparse or uneven camera observations. It prevents overfitting by suppressing higher-order SH components for vertices that lack sufficient directional support, while preserving the zeroth-order (DC) component. Unlike methods that rely on iterative optimization with fixed SH complexity, this approach explicitly adapts the regularization strength to the available viewing directions, improving generalization to unseen viewpoints and conditioning of the linear system. Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling (GAM) is a method for predicting view-dependent colors in 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating geometric cues, specifically surface normals and learned geometric features derived from a Signed Distance Field (SDF). It addresses the failure of standard appearance modeling, which relies solely on spatial position and viewing direction, to capture fine-grained geometry and reflective surfaces. Unlike siblings that optimize fixed Spherical Harmonics coefficients or use post-processing transformations, GAM replaces the SH representation with a geometry-conditioned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Setting the maximum degree of Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients to 0 to remove superfluous operations and improve training speed, as higher-degree SH coefficients for color remain unchanged during training. Modify the model code to delete operations relative to the max degree in the model and set the max degree parameter to 0. In the original 3D Gaussian Splatting model, features represented by SH coefficients with degree > 0 are unchanged during all training, making them useless. Directly changing the max degree to 0 yields a 16.25% improvement compared to the default. With specific changing code, it yields a 16.57% improvement but increases CPU-GPU process time. The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation uses third-order Spherical Harmonics (degree 3) to encode view-dependent color, resulting in 16 coefficients per color channel per Gaussian. This high dimensionality leads to significant memory overhead and computational cost during rendering and optimization. Early observations indicated that in standard training pipelines, higher-degree coefficients often fail to converge or provide negligible visual improvement, suggesting redundancy. Subsequent research has focused on optimizing this representation through compression (distillation, quantization), efficient optimization (analytical Jacobians, multi-view training), and alternative modeling (closed-form estimation, neural fields) to balance quality, speed, and memory usage. I3DGS: Improve 3D Gaussian Splatting from Multiple Dimensions, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06408v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation
head: Mobile-GS SH Distillation, SH Knowledge Distillation, SH Order Reduction via Distillation, SH degree reduction, Spherical Harmonics degree reduction
body: First-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) Distillation is a compression technique that reduces the SH degree of 3D Gaussian elements from the standard third-order (degree 3) to first-order (degree 1) to decrease parameter count and rendering computation cost. Unlike standard degree reduction which simply truncates coefficients, this method employs a distillation strategy where a "student" model with first-order SH approximates the directional radiance of a pretrained "teacher" model. It sets itself apart from siblings like Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (which quantizes coefficients) and Compact View-dependent Color (which uses neural fields) by explicitly training a lower-degree SH representation to mimic the output of a higher-degree reference. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pretrained teacher 3D Gaussian model with third-order SH coefficients (\mathbf{c}i^{tea}, degree 3, 16 coefficients per color channel) and a student model initialized with first-order SH coefficients (\mathbf{c}i, degree 1, 4 coefficients per color channel). Output: Optimized first-order SH coefficients for the student model that approximate the teacher's appearance. Data Structures: The student Gaussian i stores SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4} (RGB \times 4 first-order coefficients). The teacher stores \mathbf{c}i^{tea} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 16}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the student model's first-order SH coefficients. These can be initialized by projecting the teacher's third-order coefficients onto the first-order basis or randomly. 2. Rendering: Render the scene using both the teacher (degree 3) and student (degree 1) models for a set of training views. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the distillation loss and optional depth distillation loss. 4. Optimization: Update the student's first-order SH coefficients (and potentially other Gaussian attributes like position/opacity if joint optimization is used) to minimize the total loss. Formulas: The primary distillation loss matches the rendered pixel colors of the student to the teacher: \mathcal{L}{\text{distill}} = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{p \in P} \|\mathbf{C}p^{tea} - \mathbf{C}p\| where P is the set of pixels, \mathbf{C}p^{tea} is the rendered pixel color from the teacher, and \mathbf{C}p is the rendered pixel color from the student. To improve geometric consistency, a scale-invariant depth distillation loss is applied: \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}(\mathbf{D}, \mathbf{D}^{tea}) = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{p \in P} \left( \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p) - \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p^{tea}) \right)^2 - \frac{1}{|P|^2} \left( \sum{p \in P} \left( \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p) - \log(\hat{\mathbf{D}}p^{tea}) \right) \right)^2 where \hat{\mathbf{D}}p^{tea} = \mathbf{D}^{tea} + \epsilon and \epsilon = 10^{-8} for stability. The term \mathbf{D}^{tea} is the depth rendered by the teacher, and \mathbf{D} is the depth rendered by the student. The second term subtracts the mean difference to make it scale-invariant. Parameters: Target SH degree: 1 (first-order). \epsilon: 10^{-8}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainfirstorderdistillation(teachermodel, studentmodel, views, optimizer, numiterations): """ Distills third-order SH from teacher to first-order SH in student. """ for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample a view view = sampleview(views) # 2. Render teacher (Degree 3) teachercolor, teacherdepth = rendergaussians(teachermodel, view) # 3. Render student (Degree 1) studentcolor, studentdepth = rendergaussians(studentmodel, view) # 4. Compute Distillation Loss (Color) # Ldstill = Mean(||Ctea - Cstu||) # Assuming L2 norm per pixel, then mean over pixels colordiff = teachercolor - studentcolor ldistill = mean(colordiff 2) # 5. Compute Depth Distillation Loss (Scale-invariant) epsilon = 1e-8 logteadepth = log(teacherdepth + epsilon) logstudepth = log(studentdepth + epsilon) difflog = logteadepth - logstudepth meandiff = mean(difflog) # Ldepth = mean((diff - mean(diff))^2) ldepth = mean((difflog - meandiff) 2) # 6. Total Loss # Note: Weights for depth loss are not specified in sources [G: assume 1.0 or tuneable] totalloss = ldistill + ldepth # 7. Backpropagate and update student SH coefficients optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() A variant where splats are organized into layers, but each splat contains both a compact (first-order/distilled) and full (third-order) version of the SH representation, while other shared features (opacity, location) remain consistent. The dimension (compact or full) of the SH is added as a component to the utility function, allowing the scheduler to choose from layered splats with either full or compact SH. Initially, compact SH versions are loaded to allow more splats within the same bandwidth; over time, compact SH is replaced by full SH to enhance visual quality. Compression: Reducing SH degree from 3 to 1 reduces parameters by 61% and computation by 52%. Quality Trade-off: The PSNR drop for 3→1 distillation is approximately 0.48 dB when combined with other compression methods (like pruning and VQ). Standalone 3→1 reduction results in a 0.48 dB drop. Performance: Enables faster rendering speeds and lower storage usage, making it suitable for mobile devices and edge hardware. Limitations: The quality drop is more significant than degree 3→2 reduction (-0.17 dB) or 2→1 reduction (-0.31 dB) individually, but the cumulative effect with other compression techniques is managed within bounded quality costs. First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation was introduced in the context of Mobile-GS (Mobile Gaussian Splatting) to enable real-time 3DGS on mobile devices. It addresses the high storage and computational burden of the original 3DGS which uses third-order SH. The method builds on the concept of knowledge distillation, applying it specifically to the view-dependent color representation in 3DGS. A 129 FPS Full HD Real-Time Accelerator for 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2026.3683714, fetched 2026-10-27 Mobile-GS: Real-time Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Devices, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.11531, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) L3GS: Layered 3D Gaussian Splats for Efficient 3D Scene Delivery, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680207.3723485, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation
head: Analytical Jacobians for 3DGS, Camera Pose Jacobian Derivation (Lie Group), Lie Algebra Jacobian for 3DGS
body: This method derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable efficient gradient-based camera pose optimization. It solves the problem of high computational overhead associated with automatic differentiation in differentiable rendering pipelines, particularly for SLAM systems where tracking must be performed in real-time. It sets itself apart from prior ray-intersection methods by providing the first analytical Jacobian specifically tailored for EWA splatting and 3DGS, ensuring the Jacobian dimensionality matches the 6 degrees of freedom of the Lie algebra without redundant computations. The method computes the derivatives of the projected Gaussian parameters (mean \muI and covariance \SigmaI) with respect to the camera pose T{CW} \in SE(3). It uses Lie algebra to derive minimal Jacobians, avoiding the overhead of automatic differentiation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera pose T{CW} \in SE(3), Gaussian mean in camera coordinates \muC \in \mathbb{R}^3, Gaussian covariance matrix \SigmaC, projection Jacobian J, and rotation matrix component W of the camera pose. Output: Jacobians \frac{\partial \muI}{\partial T{CW}} and \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial T{CW}}. Data Structures: T{CW}: 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix representing camera-to-world pose. \muC: 3 \times 1 vector representing the Gaussian center in camera coordinates. W: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix component of T{CW}. \tau \in se(3): Infinitesimal parameter (Lie algebra element). \theta: Rotation vector component of \tau. \rho: Translation vector component of \tau. Definitions: \times: Skew-symmetric matrix operator mapping a 3D vector \mathbf{v} = [vx, vy, vz]^\top to: \mathbf{v}^\times = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -vz & vy \\ vz & 0 & -vx \\ -vy & vx & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathcal{D}: Derivative on the manifold (Lie group). \text{Exp}: Exponential map from Lie algebra se(3) to Lie group SE(3). \text{Log}: Logarithmic map from Lie group SE(3) to Lie algebra se(3). \circ: Group composition. Formulas: The chain rule is applied to decompose the derivatives: 1. Mean Jacobian: \frac{\partial \muI}{\partial T{CW}} = \frac{\partial \muI}{\partial \muC} \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} \quad (3) 2. Covariance Jacobian: \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial T{CW}} = \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial J} \frac{\partial J}{\partial \muC} \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} + \frac{\partial \SigmaI}{\partial W} \frac{\mathcal{D}W}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} \quad (4) 3. Manifold Derivative Definition: \frac{\mathcal{D}(f(\mathbf{T}))}{\mathcal{D}\mathbf{T}} \triangleq \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{\text{Log}(f(\text{Exp}(\tau) \circ \mathbf{T}) \circ f(\mathbf{T})^{-1})}{\tau} \quad (5) 4. Specific Manifold Derivatives: \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} = [I \quad -\muC^\times] \quad (6a) \frac{\mathcal{D}W}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -W{:,1}^\times \\ 0 & -W{:,2}^\times \\ 0 & -W{:,3}^\times \end{bmatrix} \quad (6b) where W{:,i} is the i-th column of matrix W. Derivation Details: The derivation of \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} proceeds as follows: \frac{\mathcal{D}\muC}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} = \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{\text{Exp}(\tau) \cdot \muC - \muC}{\tau} = \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{(\mathbf{I} + \tau^\wedge) \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}C - \boldsymbol{\mu}C}{\tau} = \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{\tau^\wedge \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}C}{\tau} Let \tau = [\rho^\top, \theta^\top]^\top. Then \tau^\wedge \cdot \boldsymbol{\mu}C = \rho + \theta^\times \boldsymbol{\mu}C = \rho - \muC^\times \theta. = \lim{\tau \rightarrow 0} \frac{\rho - \muC^\times \theta}{\tau} = \begin{bmatrix} I & -\muC^\times \end{bmatrix} The derivation of \frac{\mathcal{D}W}{\mathcal{D}T{CW}} uses the property that the derivative of the rotation component with respect to the rotation vector \theta is: \frac{\partial \mathbf{W}}{\partial \thetax} = \mathbf{e}1^\times \mathbf{W} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{0}{1 \times 3} \\ -\mathbf{W}{3,:} \\ \mathbf{W}{2,:} \end{bmatrix} Generalizing for all three axes yields the block matrix in (6b). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def skewsymmetric(v): """Converts a 3D vector to its skew-symmetric matrix.""" return np.array([ [0, -v[2], v[1]], [v[2], 0, -v[0]], [-v[1], v[0], 0] ]) def computemeanjacobian(muC): """ Computes D(muC) / D(TCW). muC: 3D vector, Gaussian mean in camera coordinates. Returns: 3x6 matrix. """ I3 = np.eye(3) muCskew = skewsymmetric(muC) # [I | -muC^x] return np.hstack([I3, -muCskew]) def computerotationjacobian(W): """ Computes D(W) / D(TCW). W: 3x3 rotation matrix component of camera pose. Returns: 9x6 matrix (flattened W derivative). """ # W columns Wcol1 = W[:, 0] Wcol2 = W[:, 1] Wcol3 = W[:, 2] # Skew symmetric matrices of columns W1skew = skewsymmetric(Wcol1) W2skew = skewsymmetric(Wcol2) W3skew = skewsymmetric(Wcol3) # Block matrix: # [ 0 -W1^x ] # [ 0 -W2^x ] # [ 0 -W3^x ] # Top 3 rows (translation part derivative is 0) topblock = np.zeros((3, 6)) # Bottom 9 rows (rotation part derivative) # The derivative is with respect to [rho, theta]. # Translation rho does not affect W directly in this minimal parameterization context # as W is purely rotational. The derivative w.r.t theta is constructed from columns. # Formula (6b) implies the structure. # Row 1-3: derivative of W rows 1-3 w.r.t theta # Actually, the formula (6b) is a 9x6 matrix where the first 3 cols are 0. # Constructing the 9x3 block for theta derivative # Each block is -W{:,i}^x # But wait, W{:,i} is a column. The formula shows -W{:,1}^x etc. # Let's stack them vertically. # The output shape is 9x6. # First 3 columns are 0. # Last 3 columns are the stacked skew-symmetric matrices of W's columns. block1 = -W1skew block2 = -W2skew block3 = -W3skew # Stack vertically: block1, block2, block3 # This results in a 9x3 matrix. thetaderiv = np.vstack([block1, block2, block3]) zeroblock = np.zeros((9, 3)) return np.hstack([zeroblock, thetaderiv]) def getcameraposejacobians(muC, W): """ Computes the explicit camera Jacobians for 3DGS. muC: 3D vector, Gaussian mean in camera coordinates. W: 3x3 rotation matrix. Returns: dmudT: 3x6 Jacobian for mean dSigmadT: 9x6 Jacobian for covariance (partial, requires chain rule terms) """ dmudT = computemeanjacobian(muC) dWdT = computerotationjacobian(W) # Note: Full covariance Jacobian requires chain rule terms: # dSigmadT = (dSigmadJ @ dJdmu @ dmudT) + (dSigmadW @ dWdT) # These terms (dSigmadJ, dJdmu, dSigmadW) are specific to the # Gaussian projection and covariance transformation logic, not just the pose derivative. return dmudT, dWdT Parameters: Requires at least 50 iterations of gradient descent per frame for accurate tracking. Edge Cases: Precision issues may arise near singularities in the exponential map, though the Lie algebra formulation avoids redundant parameters. The method assumes the Gaussian representation is compatible with EWA splatting. Optimizes only the current camera pose without updating the map representation, minimizing photometric and/or geometric residuals to estimate motion. It sets itself apart from full SLAM or mapping methods by decoupling pose estimation from scene reconstruction, allowing for efficient real-time tracking using pre-existing Gaussian splats. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than automatic differentiation due to explicit analytical derivatives. The dimensionality matches the 6 DOF of SE(3), eliminating redundant computations. Memory Complexity: Low, as it avoids storing intermediate computation graphs for the camera pose derivatives. Performance: Enables real-time tracking (e.g., 3.2 FPS monocular, 2.5 FPS RGB-D on Replica dataset) when interleaved with mapping. Strengths: Computationally efficient, minimal parameterization, applicable to large-scale 3DGS (unlike prior ray-intersection methods). Limitations: Requires careful implementation of the Lie group derivatives; assumes the Gaussian primitives are differentiable with respect to the pose. The method was introduced in "Gaussian Splatting SLAM" to address the need for efficient camera pose optimization in SLAM systems using 3D Gaussians. Prior methods [12] assumed a smaller number of Gaussians and relied on ray-intersection, making them unsuitable for 3DGS. This work provides the first analytical Jacobian for SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussians in EWA splatting, enabling applications like dynamic tracking and 4D scene representation. name: Photometric and Geometric Tracking
body: Photometric and Geometric Tracking optimizes only the current camera pose without updating the map representation, minimizing photometric and/or geometric residuals to estimate motion. It sets itself apart from full SLAM or mapping methods by decoupling pose estimation from scene reconstruction, allowing for efficient tracking using a fixed set of 3D Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A fixed set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the current estimated camera pose \mathbf{T}{CW}, an observed image \bar{I}, and optionally an observed depth map \bar{D}. Outputs: Optimized camera pose \mathbf{T}{CW}. Data Structures: The method operates on a rasterized representation where each pixel accumulates contributions from a sorted set of Gaussians \mathcal{N} along the camera ray. Steps: 1. Render Depth: For each pixel, compute the expected depth \mathcal{D}p by alpha-blending the distances zi of visible Gaussians along the camera ray. \mathcal{D}p = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} zi \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where zi is the distance to the mean \muW of Gaussian i along the camera ray, and \mathcal{N} is the set of sorted Gaussians contributing to the pixel. 2. Compute Photometric Residual: Render the image I(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}{CW}) from the current pose and compare it to the observed image \bar{I} using the L1 norm. E{pho} = \left\| I(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}{CW}) - \bar{I} \right\|1 3. Compute Geometric Residual (Optional): If depth observations \bar{D} are available, render depth D(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}{CW}) and compare it to \bar{D}. E{geo} = \left\| D(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}{CW}) - \bar{D} \right\|1 4. Combine Losses: Minimize the weighted sum of residuals using a hyperparameter \lambda{pho}. E = \lambda{pho} E{pho} + (1 - \lambda{pho}) E{geo} 5. Optimize Pose: Derive analytical Jacobians for the camera pose optimization and minimize E via gradient descent. 6. Apply Regularization and Exposure Correction: Penalize non-edge or low-opacity pixels to improve robustness, and optimize affine brightness parameters to handle varying exposure. Parameters: \lambda{pho}: Weight for photometric loss. Typical value not given in the sources. Affine brightness parameters: Optimized per frame to handle exposure changes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Opacity/Non-Edge Pixels: These can introduce noise; the method explicitly penalizes them. Exposure Changes: Handled by optimizing affine brightness parameters. Depth Availability: Geometric loss is optional and requires synchronized depth sensors. This variant, used in hierarchical implicit grid systems, alternates between tracking (optimizing pose) and mapping (optimizing features). During tracking, only the current robot pose T{ks} is optimized while submap features F are kept fixed. It employs a trust-region regularization term \rho(Tb, T) = w\rho \max(\| \text{Log}(Tb^{-1} T) \|2 - \tau, 0) to penalize pose updates larger than the trust-region radius \tau, where w\rho is a weight and \text{Log} is the logarithmic map on SE(3). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Low, as the map representation \mathcal{G} is not updated during tracking. Strengths: Efficient tracking; robust to exposure changes via brightness optimization; combines photometric and geometric cues. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Real-time SLAM tracking where map updates are decoupled from pose estimation. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of Gaussian Splatting SLAM, where tracking is separated from mapping to enable efficient online operation. The method builds on differentiable rendering of 3D Gaussians and analytical Jacobian derivation for SE(3) poses. name: Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Multi-View Mini-Batch Training for 3DGS, Thread-Efficient Partial Rendering for Multi-View 3DGS
body:
This method enables stable optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by training on multiple views per iteration, addressing the high variance of gradients inherent in the standard single-view approach. It distinguishes itself from standard 3DGS by replacing the single-image mini-batch with a multi-image batch, while overcoming the rasterization overhead and adaptive density control incompatibilities that typically prevent such an implementation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N training images with corresponding camera poses; 3D Gaussian primitives \{Gi\} defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity oi, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color ci; learning rate \etat. Outputs: Updated Gaussian parameters w{t+1}; rendered images \hat{C}(p). Data Structures: The rasterizer uses a tile-based architecture. The image is split into tiles. A single thread block is allocated to a single tile. Threads within a block cooperate to preprocess Gaussians and render pixels for that tile. A thread is freed only when all peer threads in the same block have completed their work. Method Steps: 1. Mini-Batch Construction: Instead of selecting a single image, select a subset of K images (or all N images) to form the mini-batch for the current iteration. This allows the gradient estimator to sample from a broader distribution of views. 2. Thread-Efficient Partial Rendering: Standard naive multi-view rendering incurs significant overhead because the tile-based rasterizer allocates one block per tile per image. Rendering multiple images simultaneously causes idle threads when some blocks finish before others. To mitigate this, the method employs thread-efficient partial rendering: The rendering workload is distributed such that threads are not blocked waiting for other images' tiles to complete if their own work is done, or the scheduling is adjusted to minimize idle time across the multi-view batch. Specifically, the rasterizer processes the multi-view batch in a way that avoids the synchronization stalls inherent in naive parallel rendering of multiple full images. 3. Gradient Estimation and Variance Reduction: The method relies on the observation that multi-view mini-batches yield smaller gradient variance than single-view batches. The variance of the mini-batch gradient 
abla  ar{\phi}k is defined as: V(\mathbf{x}):= E[\|\mathbf{x} - \mu\|2^2] where E[\mathbf{x}] = \mu. The variance for a mini-batch Bk is estimated via Monte Carlo sampling: V{Bk \in S} (
abla  ar{\phi}k) = E[\|
abla  ar{\phi}k - P(wt)\|2^2] where P(wt) is the projection or expected gradient at weights wt, and K mini-batches are sampled to estimate this variance. Lower variance leads to more stable optimization. 4. Weight Update: The weights are updated using the standard SGD step: w{t+1} = wt - \etat 
abla  ar{\phi}k (wt) where 
abla  ar{\phi}k (wt) =  rac{1}{|Bk|} \sum{i \in Bk} 
abla \phii (wt). 5. Adaptive Density Control (ADC) Adjustment: Standard ADC assumes all 2D positional gradients reside within a single image plane. Multi-view training computes gradients across different image planes, making direct arithmetic between these vectors invalid and leading to suboptimal densification. The method requires a modified densification strategy that accounts for the multi-view nature of the gradients, ensuring that splitting and cloning operations are performed consistently across the 3D space rather than relying on single-plane gradient magnitudes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmultiview3dgs(Gaussians, Images, Cameras, numiterations): """ Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting. """ for t in range(numiterations): # 1. Select multiple images for the mini-batch # In standard 3DGS, this would be a single image. # Here, we select a subset or all images. batchimages = selectmultiviewbatch(Images) batchcameras = [Cameras[i] for i in batchimages] # 2. Render all images in the batch using thread-efficient partial rendering # This avoids the idle thread overhead of naive multi-view rendering. renderedcolors = [] for imgidx, image, camera in zip(batchimages, batchimages, batchcameras): # Tile-based rasterization with optimized thread scheduling # to minimize idle threads across the multi-view batch color = threadefficientrasterize(Gaussians, image, camera) renderedcolors.append(color) # 3. Compute loss and gradients # Assuming a loss function L between rendered and ground truth totalloss = 0 gradients = [] for color, gtimage in zip(renderedcolors, batchimages): loss = computeloss(color, gtimage) totalloss += loss # Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters grad = computegradients(loss, Gaussians) gradients.append(grad) # Average gradients over the multi-view batch # This reduces variance compared to single-view avggradient = sum(gradients) / len(gradients) # 4. Update Gaussian parameters # w{t+1} = wt - eta gradbark Gaussians.update(avggradient, learningrate=getlr(t)) # 5. Adaptive Density Control (ADC) # Standard ADC is incompatible with multi-view gradients. # Use a modified ADC that handles gradients from multiple planes. Gaussians.adaptivedensitycontrolmultiview(gradients) return Gaussians def threadefficientrasterize(Gaussians, image, camera): """ Renders the image using a tile-based rasterizer optimized for multi-view batches to minimize idle threads. """ # Split image into tiles tiles = splitimageintotiles(image) # Allocate thread blocks to tiles # In naive multi-view, each image gets its own blocks, leading to # synchronization stalls. Here, we manage thread lifecycle efficiently. results = [] for tile in tiles: # Preprocess Gaussians for this tile (culling, projection) visiblegaussians = preprocess(Gaussians, tile, camera) # Render pixels in the tile # Threads in the block cooperate; freed only when all peers finish tilecolor = rendertile(visiblegaussians, tile, camera) results.append(tilecolor) # Assemble image from tiles return assembleimage(results) def adaptivedensitycontrolmultiview(gradients): """ Modified ADC for multi-view training. Standard ADC assumes gradients are in a single plane. This function aggregates gradients from multiple views to make densification decisions in 3D space. """ # Aggregate positional gradients from all views # Ensure arithmetic is performed in a consistent 3D space # rather than comparing 2D gradients from different image planes. aggregatedgrads = aggregategradients3d(gradients) # Split and clone Gaussians based on aggregated 3D gradients for gaussian in Gaussians: if gaussian.gradientmagnitude > threshold: splitorclone(gaussian) Time Complexity: Theoretically higher per-iteration cost than single-view 3DGS due to rendering multiple images, but mitigated by thread-efficient partial rendering which reduces the overhead of idle threads. Memory Complexity: Requires memory to store gradients and intermediate states for multiple views simultaneously. Performance: Multi-view training results in smaller variance of mini-batch gradients, leading to more stable optimization compared to single-view training. Strengths: More stable convergence; better utilization of training data per iteration. Limitations: Requires careful handling of ADC to avoid suboptimal densification; naive implementation suffers from significant overhead. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) typically uses single-view mini-batch training because its rasterization pipeline makes gathering individual pixels from multiple images difficult, requiring rendering every pixel of all images in a single iteration which incurs considerable overhead. NeRF, in contrast, uses multi-view mini-batches. The method was introduced to bridge this gap, showing that multi-view training leads to smaller gradient variance and more stable optimization. name: Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization
head: SH clustering, SH palette
body: Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (SH VQ) is a compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces per-splat SH coefficients with indices pointing to a shared palette of distinct SH vectors, significantly reducing memory footprint at the cost of minor lighting artifacts. Unlike methods that exploit spatial correlation between neighboring Gaussians, SH VQ treats each splat's SH data independently, clustering millions of high-dimensional vectors into a fixed-size palette. This approach sets it apart from spatially-aware compression methods like Hybrid Compression Method for Trained 3D Gaussian Splatting Models Based on VQ and HEVC by avoiding inter-splat prediction, which simplifies implementation but can introduce localized color inconsistencies. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each with a spherical harmonic coefficient vector \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^{45} (excluding the zeroth-order SH coefficient, which is treated as the base color). Outputs: A palette \mathcal{P} = \{\mathbf{p}1, \dots, \mathbf{p}K\} of K distinct SH vectors, and an index map \mathcal{I} = \{i1, \dots, iN\} where ij \in \{1, \dots, K\} is the index of the closest palette item to \mathbf{c}j. Data Structures: 1. Palette: A list of K vectors, each of size 45. Stored as FP16 (16-bit floating point). Size: K \times 45 \times 2 bytes. For K=16,000, this is \approx 1.44 MB. 2. Index Map: A list of N integers, each 16 bits wide, storing the index into the palette. Size: N \times 2 bytes. For N=6.1 \times 10^6 (bike scene), this is \approx 12 MB. Parameters: Palette Size (K): Typically 4,000 to 16,000 items. K=16,000 ("Low" preset): Retains shininess effects, PSNR \approx 35.17 (bike scene). K=4,000 ("Very Low" preset): Lower quality, PSNR \approx 32.27 (bike scene). SH Dimensionality: 45 floats per splat (15 per RGB channel). Algorithm Steps: 1. Collect Data: Gather all N SH coefficient vectors \mathbf{c}j from the scene. 2. Cluster: Perform vector quantization (clustering) on the dataset \{\mathbf{c}j\} to find K centroid vectors \mathbf{p}k that minimize the distortion metric (typically Euclidean distance). Implementation Note: Standard k-means is too slow for millions of splats in 45 dimensions due to the curse of dimensionality. A mini-batch k-means variant is recommended. Performance: Custom mini-batch k-means implementations are \approx 3\times faster than Faiss and provide better quality for this specific task. 3. Assign Indices: For each splat j, find the palette index ij such that: ij = \arg\min{k \in \{1, \dots, K\}} \| \mathbf{c}j - \mathbf{p}k \|2. 4. Store: Save the palette \mathcal{P} and the index map \mathcal{I}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalharmonicsvectorquantization(shdata: List[np.ndarray], k: int) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """ Compress SH data using vector quantization. Args: shdata: List of N numpy arrays, each shape (45,), representing SH coefficients (excluding the 0th order color term). k: Number of palette items (e.g., 4000 or 16000). Returns: palette: Array of shape (k, 45), the cluster centers. indices: Array of shape (N,), indices into the palette for each splat. """ import numpy as np # Convert to numpy array for efficient processing data = np.array(shdata, dtype=np.float32) nsplats = data.shape[0] # Initialize centroids randomly from the data # Standard k-means initialization; in practice, k-means++ is preferred for stability rng = np.random.defaultrng(42) centroidindices = rng.choice(nsplats, k, replace=False) centroids = data[centroidindices].copy() # Mini-batch K-Means Iteration # Typical number of iterations is not specified in sources; # convergence criteria or fixed iterations (e.g., 10-20) are standard. for iteration in range(20): # Sample a mini-batch of data batchsize = 10000 batchindices = rng.choice(nsplats, batchsize, replace=False) batch = data[batchindices] # Assign batch points to nearest centroid # Compute distances: (batchsize, k) # dist = ||x - c||^2 = ||x||^2 + ||c||^2 - 2x.c batchsq = np.sum(batch2, axis=1, keepdims=True) centsq = np.sum(centroids2, axis=1, keepdims=True).T cross = batch @ centroids.T dists = batchsq + centsq - 2 cross # Find nearest centroid for each point in batch nearestcentroids = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) # Update centroids using the batch statistics # Standard mini-batch update: newcentroid = (oldsum + batchsum) / (oldcount + batchcount) # For simplicity, we recompute centroids based on all assignments if memory allows, # or use incremental update. Here we use a simplified re-assignment step for clarity # assuming full assignment is done periodically or via incremental stats. # To strictly follow "mini-batch", we update centroids incrementally. for cidx in range(k): mask = nearestcentroids == cidx if np.any(mask): batchpoints = batch[mask] # Incremental update logic would go here. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the custom implementation # handles the incremental update efficiently. pass # Final Assignment Pass # Compute distances for all data to final centroids datasq = np.sum(data2, axis=1, keepdims=True) centsq = np.sum(centroids2, axis=1, keepdims=True).T cross = data @ centroids.T dists = datasq + centsq - 2 cross indices = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) return centroids, indices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Curse of Dimensionality: Clustering millions of splats in 45 dimensions is computationally expensive and slow. Localized Color Inconsistency: Because VQ codevector selection does not use reconstructed values or spatial predictions of neighboring Gaussians, a codevector with differing color characteristics may be assigned to an individual Gaussian, causing localized color artifacts. Precision: Storing indices as 16 bits is fixed, even if K < 65,536, wasting some bits. A variant that independently quantizes the SH-AC (Spherical Harmonics - Ambient Color) vector of each Gaussian by mapping it to a VQ codevector, rather than exploiting spatial correlation between neighbors. Unlike methods using HEVC spatial prediction, this approach does not use reconstructed values of neighboring Gaussians during codevector selection. This can lead to localized color distortions inconsistent with surrounding tones. However, it achieves smaller bitstream sizes (e.g., 7.44 MB vs 9.60 MB for the anchor on the Bartender dataset at RP2). Time Complexity: Clustering is the dominant cost. Standard k-means is slow for N \gg K in high dimensions. Mini-batch k-means reduces this but remains non-trivial. Assignment is O(N \cdot K \cdot D) where D=45. Memory Complexity: Palette: O(K \cdot D) bytes. For K=16,000, \approx 1.44 MB. Indices: O(N) bits. For N=6.1 \times 10^6, \approx 12 MB. Total: Significantly less than raw SH data (1.1 GB for bike scene). Performance: Bike Scene (6.1M splats): Low (16k palette): 98MB total data, PSNR 35.17. Very Low (4k palette): 79MB total data, PSNR 32.27. Retains "shininess" effects at the cost of minor lighting artifacts. Strengths: Simple implementation, no external dependencies (if custom k-means is used), significant size reduction. Limitations: Potential for localized color inconsistencies due to lack of spatial correlation exploitation. Slower clustering than specialized libraries like Faiss, but custom implementations can be faster and dependency-free. Originated as a practical compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting in real-time engines (e.g., Unity) to reduce the large memory footprint of SH coefficients. The author of the primary source implemented a custom mini-batch k-means in C# to avoid dependencies like Faiss and scikit-learn, which were either too slow or added external requirements. The method is used in "Low" and "Very Low" quality presets for Gaussian Splatting viewers. A related academic approach, VQ-Based SH-AC Compression, formalized the independent quantization aspect for compressed 3DGS models. name: Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation
head: Global LLS System, Normal System Solution
body: Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation solves the problem of estimating view-dependent spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for mesh vertices by formulating a global weighted least-squares problem across all calibrated input views. It differs from iterative optimization methods by providing an analytical solution to the normal system, utilizing adaptive regularization to handle varying view support and a matrix-free Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG) solver to avoid explicit matrix inversion. Inputs: A textured mesh M with Nv vertices, K calibrated RGB images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K, SH degree L (typically up to order 2 for real-time constraints), regularization strengths \gammas (supported) and \gammau (under-supported), and solver parameters (tolerance \delta, max iterations T{max}). Outputs: Estimated SH coefficients X^ for each vertex. Data Structures: Rasterization Records (R): Stores per-pixel data including vertex indices i{s,k,r}, SH basis features \phi{s,k,r}, and confidence weights w{k,r}. Global Matrices: A \in \mathbb{R}^{(K \cdot H \cdot W) \times (q Nv)}: The design matrix, where q is the number of SH coefficients per vertex and Nv is the number of vertices. B \in \mathbb{R}^{(K \cdot H \cdot W) \times 3}: The observation matrix containing RGB pixel values. W \in \mathbb{R}^{(K \cdot H \cdot W) \times (K \cdot H \cdot W)}: A diagonal matrix of confidence weights. \Lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{(q Nv) \times (q Nv)}: Block-diagonal regularization matrix. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize rasterization records R and view counts \{n^vi\}{i=1}^{Nv} to zero. 2. Per-View Rasterization: For each view k = 1 \dots K: a. Rasterize mesh M to establish pixel-to-triangle correspondence. Initialize per-view matrix Ak. b. For each valid pixel p{k,r}: i. Retrieve the SH features \{i{s,k,r}, \lambda{s,k,r}\}{s=0}^2 associated with the covering triangle/vertex. ii. Compute the SH basis evaluation: \phi{s,k,r} \leftarrow \lambda{s,k,r} Y(dk), where Y(dk) is the SH basis vector for direction dk. iii. Set the row in Ak corresponding to pixel r and vertex index i{s,k,r}: [Ak]{r, i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow (\phi{s,k,r})^\top. iv. Compute confidence weight w{k,r} based on viewing angle (e.g., grazing angle down-weighting). v. Store \{i{s,k,r}, \phi{s,k,r}\}{s=0}^2 and w{k,r} in R. c. Construct observation vector Bk \leftarrow [Ik(p{k,1}) \dots Ik(p{k,HW})]^\top. d. Construct weight matrix Wk \leftarrow \text{diag}(w{k,1}, \dots, w{k,HW}). e. Update view counts \{n^vi\} based on which vertices contributed to valid pixels. 3. Global Assembly: a. Assemble global matrices: A \leftarrow [A1^\top \dots AK^\top]^\top, B \leftarrow [B1^\top \dots BK^\top]^\top, W \leftarrow \text{blkdiag}(W1, \dots, WK). 4. Regularization Construction: a. For each vertex i = 1 \dots Nv: i. Construct regularization block \Lambdai using the view count n^vi, \gammas, and \gammau. If n^vi is high, use \gammas; if low, use \gammau. b. Assemble \Lambda \leftarrow \text{blkdiag}(\Lambda1, \dots, \Lambda{Nv}). 5. Normal System Formation: a. Compute H \leftarrow A^\top W A + \Lambda. b. Compute G \leftarrow A^\top W B. c. The system to solve is H X^ = G. 6. Solution: Solve for X^ using a matrix-free PCG solver (see Pseudocode). Do not explicitly compute H^{-1}. Formulas: Normal System: X^\star = \arg \minX \| W^{1/2} (A X - B) \|2^2 + \| \Lambda^{1/2} X \|2^2 Leading to: H X^\star = G, \quad H = A^\top W A + \Lambda, \quad G = A^\top W B Where H \in \mathbb{R}^{qNv \times qNv} and G \in \mathbb{R}^{qNv \times 3}. Gradient-Guided Densification (Preprocessing): To improve spatial resolution, triangles are subdivided based on image-space variation: Sj \triangleq \sum{k=1}^K \sum{p \in \Omega{k,j}} \|\nabla Ik(p)\|^2 Triangles with large Sj are selected for subdivision. Parameters: \gammas: Supported SH regularization strength. Typical value: 0 < \gammas \ll \gammau. \gammau: Under-supported SH regularization strength. Typical value: \gammau \gg \gammas. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Explicit Inversion: Explicitly forming H^{-1} is computationally prohibitive for large scenes due to memory and time complexity. The method must use an iterative solver like PCG. Positive Definiteness: The adaptive SH regularization ensures \Lambda \succ 0 and W \succ 0, guaranteeing H \succ 0 and a unique global minimizer. View Support: Vertices with zero view support (n^vi = 0) may result in singular blocks if not handled by the regularization term \Lambda. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def closedformappearanceestimation(mesh, images, gammas, gammau, delta, tmax): """ Estimates SH coefficients for mesh vertices using global least squares. Args: mesh: Mesh object with vertices and triangles. images: List of K RGB images. gammas: Regularization strength for well-supported vertices. gammau: Regularization strength for under-supported vertices. delta: PCG convergence tolerance. tmax: Maximum PCG iterations. Returns: Xstar: Estimated SH coefficients for all vertices. """ Nv = mesh.numvertices() K = len(images) HW = images[0].height images[0].width q = 6 # Example: SH degree 2 (3 bands 2 channels? Or 1 band 3 channels? # Note: Source says qNv. Usually q is coeffs per vertex. # Assuming q is fixed constant for SH degree used. # 1. Initialize R = [] # Rasterization records nview = [0] Nv # 2. Per-View Rasterization Alist = [] Blist = [] Wlist = [] for k in range(K): Ik = images[k] Ak = [] # Will be sparse or dense list of rows Bk = [] Wk = [] # Rasterize mesh to get pixel-to-triangle/vertex mapping # For each valid pixel p{k,r}: for r in range(HW): pixel = Ik[r] # Get covering triangle and vertex indices # Assume rasterizer provides: vertexindices, lambdas, directions # Simplified: assume we have lists for this pixel vertexindices = rasterizegetvertices(mesh, k, r) lambdas = rasterizegetlambdas(mesh, k, r) directions = rasterizegetdirections(mesh, k, r) rowA = [0.0] (q Nv) # Sparse representation preferred in practice rowindices = [] rowvalues = [] for s in range(3): # s=0,1,2 bands idx = vertexindices[s] lam = lambdas[s] d = directions[s] # Compute SH basis feature phi = lam sphericalharmonicbasis(d, degree=2) # Y(dk) # Map to global column index colidx = idx q + s 2 # Assuming 2 coeffs per band? # Note: Source uses i{s,k,r}. Let's assume standard SH indexing. # For simplicity, assuming q includes all coeffs. rowindices.append(colidx) rowvalues.append(phi) # Update view count nview[idx] += 1 # Compute confidence weight w{k,r} w = computeconfidenceweight(pixel, directions) # Store in sparse format or dense if small # For global assembly, we need to flatten. # Here we store the row structure. Alist.append((rowindices, rowvalues)) Blist.append(pixel) Wlist.append(w) # 3. Global Assembly # Construct A, B, W # A is (KHW) x (qNv) # B is (KHW) x 3 # W is (KHW) x (KHW) diagonal A = buildglobalA(Alist, q, Nv) B = np.array(Blist) Wdiag = np.array(Wlist) # 4. Regularization Lambdablocks = [] for i in range(Nv): n = nview[i] # Determine if supported or under-supported # Threshold not given, assume logic based on n if n > threshold: # Threshold not specified in notes gamma = gammas else: gamma = gammau Lambdablocks.append(buildlambdablock(gamma, q)) Lambda = blockdiag(Lambdablocks) # 5. Normal System # H = A^T W A + Lambda # G = A^T W B # To avoid explicit A^T W A, we use PCG which only needs matvec # But we need G explicitly WB = Wdiag[:, None] B # Element-wise multiply rows of B by Wdiag G = A.T @ WB # 6. Solve Xstar = trianglepcg(A, Wdiag, Lambda, G, delta, tmax) return Xstar def trianglepcg(A, Wdiag, Lambda, G, delta, tmax): """ Matrix-free PCG solver for H X = G. H = A^T W A + Lambda. """ N = G.shape[0] X = np.zeros(N) # Solve for each RGB channel separately Xstar = np.zeroslike(X) for channel in range(3): g = G[:, channel] r = g.copy() z = solvepreconditioner(Lambda, r) # P z = r, P approx Lambda or A^TWA+Lambda p = z.copy() rz = np.dot(r, z) for t in range(tmax): # h = H p = A^T W A p + Lambda p Ap = A @ p WAp = Wdiag[:, None] Ap h = (A.T @ WAp) + (Lambda @ p) alpha = rz / np.dot(p, h) X = X + alpha p r = r - alpha h if np.linalg.norm(r)2 <= delta2 np.linalg.norm(g)2: break z = solvepreconditioner(Lambda, r) rznew = np.dot(r, z) beta = rznew / rz p = z + beta p rz = rznew Xstar = Xstar + X[:, channel] # Accumulate? No, X is per channel in loop? # Correction: X should be reset or handled per channel. # Let's fix the loop structure. # Re-implementation for clarity Xstar = np.zeros((N, 3)) for channel in range(3): g = G[:, channel] x = np.zeros(N) r = g.copy() z = solvepreconditioner(Lambda, r) p = z.copy() rz = np.dot(r, z) for t in range(tmax): Ap = A @ p WAp = Wdiag[:, None] Ap h = (A.T @ WAp) + (Lambda @ p) alpha = rz / np.dot(p, h) x = x + alpha p r = r - alpha h if np.linalg.norm(r)2 <= delta2 np.linalg.norm(g)2: break z = solvepreconditioner(Lambda, r) rznew = np.dot(r, z) beta = rznew / rz p = z + beta p rz = rznew Xstar[:, channel] = x return Xstar def solvepreconditioner(Lambda, r): """ Simple diagonal preconditioner using Lambda. """ # Lambda is block diagonal. Inverse is block diagonal inverse. # Approximation: 1/diag(Lambda) # More accurate: Solve Lambda z = r # Since Lambda is block diagonal, solve per block # For simplicity, assume diagonal approximation or direct solve if small return np.linalg.solve(Lambda, r) # Or block-wise solve Distills SH coefficients into a simpler representation for faster rendering. Choose when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. Link Provides analytical gradients for camera parameters. Choose when joint optimization of geometry and appearance is required. Link Optimizes the training pipeline for multiple views. Choose when training time is critical. Link Reduces SH coefficient storage via quantization. Choose when memory footprint must be minimized. Link The core regularization strategy used in this method. Choose when view support is uneven. Link Uses geometry to constrain appearance. Choose when geometric fidelity is paramount. Link Time Complexity: The global LLS solve is dominated by PCG iterations. Setup is O(KHWq^2 + Nv q^3). Each PCG iteration is O(KHWq + Nv q^2). Total solve time is T{solve} = O(KHWq^2 + Nv q^3) + O(T{pcg}(KHWq + Nv q^2)) + O(KHWq + Nv q). Memory Complexity: Dominated by storing matrices A, B, W, and \Lambda. A is sparse but large. \Lambda is block diagonal. Strengths: Analytical solution avoids local minima; adaptive regularization handles sparse views; PCG solver avoids explicit inversion. Limitations: Requires all views to be available simultaneously (batch processing); sensitive to rasterization accuracy; preconditioning is critical for PCG convergence. When to use: When high-quality view-dependent appearance is needed for mesh-based representations and computational resources allow for batch processing. When not to use: For real-time streaming where incremental updates are required, or when memory is extremely constrained. The method originates from "CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors". It addresses the limitations of iterative SH optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting by providing a closed-form solution for mesh-based scene representation. The approach leverages the structure of the problem to enable efficient global optimization.
