name: Adaptive SH Regularization
head: Directional support-aware SH regularization
body: Adaptive SH Regularization is a technique for stabilizing the optimization of Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients in 3D Gaussian Splatting under sparse or uneven camera observations. It prevents overfitting by suppressing higher-order SH components for vertices that lack sufficient directional support, while preserving the zeroth-order (DC) component. Unlike methods that rely on iterative optimization with fixed SH complexity, this approach explicitly adapts the regularization strength to the available viewing directions, improving generalization to unseen viewpoints and conditioning of the linear system. Inputs and Outputs Input: Per-vertex SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i (stored as in Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints), the set of observed viewing directions \{\omegak\} for vertex i, and a support threshold parameter. Output: Regularized SH coefficients \mathbf{c}i' suitable for rendering and further optimization. Data Structures The method operates on the standard SH coefficient vector for each Gaussian. For degree L, the vector has size (L+1)^2. The coefficients are typically stored in a flat array or tensor, indexed by band l and order m. Steps 1. Evaluate Directional Support: For each vertex i, determine the set of viewing directions \{\omegak\} from which it is observed in the training data. 2. Check Support Criterion: For each SH band l (where l=0 is DC, l>0 are higher-order), evaluate whether the available viewing directions provide sufficient constraints. The criterion is defined by equation (25) in. While the exact mathematical form of (25) is not fully detailed in the provided text, it implicitly determines if the band is "well-supported" or "weakly supported" based on the geometry of the viewing cone. 3. Compute Regularization Weights: Assign a regularization weight \lambda{i,l} to each band l of vertex i: If band l satisfies the support criterion (well-supported), apply weak regularization (small \lambda{i,l}). If band l does not satisfy the criterion (weakly supported), apply strong suppression (large \lambda{i,l}). The DC component (l=0) is always preserved (weak regularization) regardless of support, as it represents average color. 4. Apply Regularization in LLS: When solving the Least Squares System (LLS) for SH coefficients (as in CF-Splat), incorporate these weights into the diagonal of the regularization matrix. This modifies the normal equations to penalize large coefficients in weakly supported bands more heavily. Formulas The regularization term added to the loss or LLS system for vertex i is: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \sum{l=0}^{L} \lambda{i,l} \sum{m=-l}^{l} |c{i,l,m}|^2 Where: c{i,l,m} is the SH coefficient for vertex i, band l, order m. \lambda{i,l} is the adaptive weight for band l. The support criterion (Eq. 25 in) determines \lambda{i,l}. Specifically, as more views are added, more bands satisfy the criterion, leading to weaker regularization for those bands (Eq. 26 in). Parameters Support Threshold: Implicitly defined in equation (25). It controls the transition between weak and strong regularization. Not given in the sources as a specific numerical value, but described as determining whether an SH band receives weak or strong regularization based on available viewing directions. Regularization Strength Ratio: The ratio between strong and weak \lambda. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Overfitting: Without regularization, unconstrained SH coefficients lacking sufficient directional constraints overfit input views and generalize poorly to unseen viewpoints, producing noisy colors. Convergence: Unregularized systems may fail to converge within a reasonable iteration count (e.g., T{max}=300) due to poor conditioning. Degenerate Input: If a vertex is observed from only one direction, all non-DC bands are weakly supported and will be strongly suppressed, leaving only the DC color. Pseudocode Unverified code. Returns: regularizedcoeffs: Tensor of shape (N, (L+1)^2) """ N, numcoeffs = shcoeffs.shape L = int((numcoeffs)0.5) - 1 regularizedcoeffs = shcoeffs.clone() # Precompute regularization weights regweights = torch.zeros(N, numcoeffs) for i in range(N): directions = viewingdirections[i] if len(directions) == 0: # No views, suppress all except DC regweights[i, 0] = 0.0 # Preserve DC regweights[i, 1:] = 1e6 # Strong suppression continue # Evaluate support for each band l for l in range(L + 1): # Determine if band l is supported by directions # This corresponds to Eq. 25 in # The exact formula is not provided, but it depends on the spread of directions issupported = checkdirectionalsupport(directions, l, supportthreshold) # Assign weights if l == 0: # DC component always preserved regweights[i, l] = 1e-6 # Weak regularization elif issupported: # Well-supported band regweights[i, l] = 1e-6 # Weak regularization else: # Weakly supported band regweights[i, l] = 1.0 # Strong suppression (relative to weak) # Apply regularization during LLS solve # In the LLS system Ax = b, the regularized system is (A^T A + Lambda) x = A^T b # Lambda is a diagonal matrix with regweights return regularizedcoeffs, regweights def checkdirectionalsupport(directions, l, threshold): """ Placeholder for Eq. 25 in. Returns True if the viewing directions provide sufficient constraints for band l. Choose when optimizing camera poses alongside geometry. Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation Optimizes training speed for large datasets. Choose when training time is a bottleneck. Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting Reduces memory usage by quantizing SH coefficients. Choose when memory is constrained. Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization Solves for appearance in closed form. Choose when iterative optimization is too slow or unstable. Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation Uses geometry to inform appearance. Choose when geometry and appearance are coupled. Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling Time Complexity: The regularization step adds minimal overhead to the LLS solving process. The global LLS solution remains efficient, with solving time growing with the number of observations, consistent with the complexity of the LLS solver. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the SH coefficients and viewing direction metadata. Measured Performance: On the C3VD scene with K=7 views and L=3, adaptive regularization improves test-view PSNR from 33.66 to 34.69 compared to baselines. Convergence: With regularization, the PCG residual decreases rapidly. Without it, the system fails to converge within T{max}=300 iterations, demonstrating improved conditioning. Strengths: Improves generalization to unseen viewpoints, stabilizes optimization under sparse views, and reduces noisy colors. Limitations: Requires knowledge of viewing directions for each vertex. Performance may vary with the choice of support threshold. When to Use: Use when training data is sparse or unevenly distributed, and when standard SH optimization leads to overfitting or convergence issues. When Not to Use: Use with caution when views are dense and uniformly distributed, as the regularization may unnecessarily suppress valid high-frequency details. Adaptive SH Regularization was introduced in the context of CF-Splat (Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors) to address the challenges of appearance estimation under sparse and uneven observations. It builds on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation but modifies the SH optimization process to be aware of directional support. The method is part of a broader effort to improve the robustness and fidelity of differentiable rendering methods in challenging acquisition scenarios. name: Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling
head: Appearance module, GAM
body: Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling (GAM) is a method for predicting view-dependent colors in 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating geometric cues, specifically surface normals and learned geometric features derived from a Signed Distance Field (SDF). It addresses the failure of standard appearance modeling, which relies solely on spatial position and viewing direction, to capture fine-grained geometry and reflective surfaces. Unlike siblings that optimize fixed Spherical Harmonics coefficients or use post-processing transformations, GAM replaces the SH representation with a geometry-conditioned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gaussian centroid position \mathbf{p}k, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, SDF-derived normal \nabla f{\text{sdf}}, and SDF-derived geometric feature vector \mathbf{F}{\text{geo}}. Output: RGB color \mathbf{c}k for the Gaussian. Data Structures: SDF Module (f{\text{sdf}}): An MLP that maps a 3D position to a scalar signed distance s and a geometric feature vector \mathbf{F}{\text{geo}}. Appearance Module (f{\text{rgb}}): An MLP that maps the concatenated inputs to an RGB color vector. Parameters: Appearance MLP Architecture: 4 layers, 256 hidden units per layer, ReLU activation. SDF MLP Architecture: 8 layers, 256 hidden units per layer, ReLU activation. Training Initialization: The SDF is initialized as a sphere. SDF learning is delayed for the first 500 iterations to promote robust convergence. Steps: 1. SDF Prediction: For each Gaussian centroid \mathbf{p}k, query the SDF module to obtain the signed distance s and the geometric feature vector \mathbf{F}{\text{geo}}: (s, \mathbf{F}{\text{geo}}) = f{\text{sdf}}(\mathbf{p}k) 2. Normal Computation: Compute the surface normal by taking the gradient of the SDF output with respect to the position: \mathbf{n} = \nabla f{\text{sdf}}(\mathbf{p}k) 3. Color Prediction: Feed the centroid position \mathbf{p}k, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, the computed normal \mathbf{n}, and the geometric feature \mathbf{F}{\text{geo}} into the appearance module to produce the final color: \mathbf{c}k = f{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{p}k, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{F}{\text{geo}}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryguidedappearancemodeling(pk, d, fsdf, frgb): """ Predicts color for a Gaussian using geometry-guided appearance modeling. Args: pk: 3D position of the Gaussian centroid (tensor, shape [3]) d: Viewing direction vector (tensor, shape [3]) fsdf: SDF MLP function returning (signeddistance, geometricfeature) frgb: Appearance MLP function returning RGB color Returns: ck: Predicted RGB color (tensor, shape [3]) """ # Step 1: Get SDF value and geometric features s, Fgeo = fsdf(pk) # Step 2: Compute normal from SDF gradient # Note: In practice, this requires autograd or analytical gradient of fsdf # Here we assume a helper function computegradient exists for the MLP n = computegradient(fsdf, pk) # Step 3: Predict color using appearance MLP ck = frgb(pk, d, n, Fgeo) return ck Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Bias: The method assumes high opacity for most Gaussians to align with the surface. If opacity is unconstrained, the SDF learning process becomes unstable, introducing noise and higher Chamfer Distance (CD). Semi-transparent Objects: The method forces opacity towards 1 via entropy regularization, treating semi-transparent volumes as opaque outer shells. This causes the appearance MLP to "bake" internal volumetric transmission details into high-frequency textures on the surface, which may be inaccurate for truly translucent objects like glass. Training Delay: SDF learning must be delayed (e.g., first 500 iterations) to avoid instability during initial Gaussian densification. Performance: On the OmniObject3D dataset, removing GAM degrades PSNR from 40.06 to 39.19, SSIM from 0.986 to 0.984, and increases LPIPS from 0.025 to 0.031. Strengths: Improves geometry reconstruction and rendering quality, particularly for reflective surfaces and fine geometric details where spherical harmonics fail. Limitations: Struggles with semi-transparent structures (e.g., glass jars) due to the opacity bias forcing an opaque shell representation. Hardware: Optimized using Adam optimizer on a single NVIDIA A800 GPU. Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling was introduced in the GSurf method, which adapts 2D Gaussian Splatting for high-quality 3D reconstruction by learning SDFs from splatting opaque Gaussians. It draws inspiration from neural implicit surface methods where incorporating geometric cues like normals and features has proven effective. The method modifies vanilla 3DGS/2DGS by replacing spherical harmonics with an MLP conditioned on SDF-derived geometry. GSurf: Learning signed distance fields from splatting opaque Gaussians for high-quality 3D reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2026.104106, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SWAG (Splatting in the Wild images with Appearance-conditioned Gaussians)
body: SWAG is an extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to reconstruct 3D scenes from unstructured, in-the-wild image collections. It addresses two primary limitations of standard 3DGS in unconstrained scenarios: photometric variations due to changing lighting and the presence of transient occluders (e.g., tourists, clouds). Unlike base 3DGS, which assumes static appearance and geometry, SWAG models appearance variations using image-conditioned color modulation and handles transient objects via adaptive opacity modulation, all without supervision. It sets itself apart from siblings like DAVIGS and 3iGS by explicitly learning a latent space of image embeddings to condition the Gaussian properties, enabling controllable appearance interpolation at inference. SWAG builds on the standard 3DGS representation and rendering pipeline defined in Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints. The core modification lies in the parameterization of Gaussian color and opacity to be dependent on the input image, rather than fixed or view-dependent only. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by centroid \mathbf{x}, scale \mathbf{S}, rotation \mathbf{R}, base opacity \alpha, and base color \mathbf{c} (encoded in spherical harmonic coefficients). A set of M training images, each associated with a learnable image embedding vector \mathbf{l}I. Camera poses and intrinsics for each training image. Outputs: Rendered images for novel views. Disentangled static and transient scene representations. Interpolated appearance embeddings for controllable rendering. The model optimizes the following parameters for each Gaussian i: 1. Standard 3DGS Parameters: Centroid \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), base opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, base color \mathbf{c}i (SH coefficients). 2. Hash Grid Encoding: A hash table encoding the Gaussian centers. The hash grid maps 3D coordinates to feature vectors \text{emb}(\mathbf{x}i). Hash table size T = 2^{19}. Finest resolution N{max} = 2048. Coarsest resolution N{min} = 16. Number of levels L = 12. 3. Image Embeddings: A learnable vector \mathbf{l}I \in \mathbb{R}^{24} for each training image I. 4. MLP (F\theta): A multi-layer perceptron that takes Gaussian features and image embeddings as input. Number of layers: 8. Input dimension: 3 (concatenated base color, image embedding, and encoded center? Note: Source says input dim 3, but lists three inputs. See Pseudocode for clarification). Hidden layer size: 51. Output dimension: 64 (implied by context of outputting color and opacity variation, though source table says 64, text says outputs cI and \Delta \alphaI. We assume the MLP outputs a vector of size 64 which is split). 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians using sparse points from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Initialize Hash Grid, Image Embeddings, and MLP parameters. 2. Feature Encoding: For each Gaussian i and training image I: Retrieve the image embedding \mathbf{l}I. Compute the encoded center \text{emb}(\mathbf{x}i) using the Hash Grid. Retrieve the base color \mathbf{c}i. 3. Appearance and Opacity Modulation: Pass the features through the MLP F\theta: Input to F\theta: The source states inputs are "Gaussian's colors \mathbf{c}, the associated image embedding \mathbf{l}I, and their encoded centers \text{emb}(\mathbf{x})". The table specifies Input Dimension 3. This likely refers to the concatenation or specific projection of these features into a 3-dimensional latent space before the MLP, or it is a typo in the source for a higher dimension. Given the hidden size is 51, we assume the input is concatenated and projected. Let \mathbf{z}i = [\mathbf{c}i; \mathbf{l}I; \text{emb}(\mathbf{x}i)] (concatenated). The MLP takes this vector. Output of F\theta: A vector \mathbf{o}i \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. Decode \mathbf{o}i to get image-dependent color \mathbf{c}I and opacity variation parameter \Delta \alphaI. 4. Opacity Sampling: To handle transient objects, the opacity variation \Delta \alphaI is used as the location variable of a Concrete distribution (Gumbel-Softmax). Sample \Delta \tilde{\alpha}I from the Concrete distribution parameterized by \Delta \alphaI. The final opacity \alpha{final} is modulated by \Delta \tilde{\alpha}I. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using the standard 3DGS rasterization pipeline, using the modulated color \mathbf{c}I and opacity \alpha{final}. 6. Optimization: Minimize the reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 + SSIM) between rendered and ground truth images. Optimize Gaussians parameters (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{R}, \alpha, \mathbf{c}). Optimize Hash Grid. Optimize Image Embeddings \mathbf{l}I. Optimize MLP weights \theta. Densification interval: 2000 iterations. Densification end: 30000 iterations. Total iterations: 60000. Standard 3DGS Gaussians (initialized from SfM) self.gaussians = Gaussians(numgaussians) # 2. Hash Grid Encoding for Gaussian centers self.hashgrid = HashGrid( numlevels=numlevels, log2hashmapsize=19, # 2^19 resolutionperlevel=nmax, minresolution=nmin) # 3. Per-image embeddings self.imageembeddings = nn.Embedding(numimages, 24) # 4. MLP Ftheta # Input dim is described as 3 in source, but inputs are c, lI, emb(x). # Assuming concatenation of these features. # Note: Source says "Input dimension: 3". This is ambiguous. # It might mean the MLP takes 3 scalar inputs, or it's a typo. # Given "Hidden layers size: 51", we construct a standard MLP. # We assume the input vector is formed by concatenating the relevant features. # Let's assume the input to the MLP is the concatenation of: # - Base color (projected to dim Dc) # - Image embedding (dim 24) # - Hash grid feature (dim Dh) # The source says Input Dimension 3. Split into color and opacity variation. # Assuming first part is color, second is opacity. cI = mlpout[:,:32] # Example split deltaalphaI = mlpout[:, 32:] # Sample opacity variation from Concrete distribution # Concrete distribution is used for differentiable sampling deltaalphatilde = self.sampleconcrete(deltaalphaI) # Modulate opacity alphafinal = self.gaussians.opacities[gaussianindices] deltaalphatilde # Render using standard 3DGS rasterizer # This part is handled by the parent class/pipeline return cI, alphafinal def sampleconcrete(self, logits): # Concrete distribution sampling # U ~ Uniform(0, 1) u = torch.randlike(logits) # Sample from Concrete # Note: Concrete distribution is typically used for binary or categorical. # Here it modulates opacity. # Implementation depends on the specific Concrete distribution variant used. # Standard Concrete: y = sigmoid((log(u) - log(1-u) + logits) / tau) # We assume a temperature tau is used. tau = 1.0 y = torch.sigmoid((torch.log(u) - torch.log(1 - u) + logits) / tau) return y def optimize(self, images, gtimages, cameraparams): # Standard 3DGS optimization loop # Update Gaussians, Hash Grid, Image Embeddings, MLP pass Iterations: 60,000. Densification Interval: 2,000. Densification End: 30,000. Image Embedding Dimension: 24. Learning Rate (Image Embeddings): 0.0025. Hash Table Size (T): 2^{19}. Finest Resolution (N{max}): 2048. Coarsest Resolution (N{min}): 16. Number of Levels (L): 12. Learning Rate (Hash Grid): 0.0025. MLP Layers: 8. MLP Input Dimension: 3. MLP Hidden Size: 51. MLP Output Dimension: 64. MLP Learning Rate: 0.0025. Transient Object Detection: Transient objects (e.g., clouds, tourists) are modeled by Gaussians with high variance in \Delta \tilde{\alpha}I. Holes in Scene: If transient detection is too aggressive (removing all Gaussians with \text{Var}(\Delta \tilde{\alpha}I) < \lambda where \lambda is effectively 0), holes (black spots) may appear in areas with frequent transients (e.g., sky, roads). Adaptive Threshold: To mitigate holes, an adaptive threshold \lambda can be used to remove Gaussians based on variance, but this requires manual tuning. Performance: Training time almost doubles compared to 3DGS; inference time per frame is 10 times longer than 3DGS. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 2x that of standard 3DGS. Inference time is 10x slower than 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Increased due to Hash Grid, Image Embeddings, and MLP parameters. Strengths: Handles unstructured in-the-wild data; disentangles static and transient objects; enables controllable appearance interpolation; faster than previous in-the-wild baselines. Limitations: Slower inference than 3DGS; requires manual tuning for transient removal threshold; less than 20% of Gaussians capture transient objects on average. When to Use: When reconstructing scenes from unstructured, in-the-wild image collections with varying lighting and transient occluders. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene is static and well-lit (use standard 3DGS). SWAG was introduced by H. Dahmani et al. in 2024. It was developed to address the poor performance of 3DGS on unstructured in-the-wild data. The method builds on the 3DGS representation and extends it with appearance modeling and transient object handling. It has been evaluated on the Phototourism Dataset (Brandenburg Gate, Sacré Cœur, Trevi Fountain) and the NeRF-OSR Dataset. name: Physics and Optical Modeling
body: Physics and Optical Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to handle non-vacuum media and physically consistent surface extraction by modifying the rendering equation or the underlying density field. It solves the problem of light transport in scattering media and the geometric inconsistency of discrete alpha-blending for surface reconstruction. Unlike Color and Appearance Modeling, which focuses on view-dependent shading in clear space, this family explicitly models volumetric attenuation and backscatter or reformulates the Gaussian primitive as a continuous attenuation field. This family inherits the standard 3DGS representation and rendering pipeline from Appearance and Physical Modeling. What it is: A method that reformulates rasterization-based 3DGS into a volumetric ray-marching framework by mapping discrete Gaussians to a continuous attenuation field \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Distinction: Unlike standard alpha-blending which assumes negligible 3D overlap, this model explicitly defines a view-dependent density that preserves ellipsoidal geometry, enabling unbiased surface extraction [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. When to choose: When multi-view consistent depth maps and surface extraction are required, avoiding the surface erosion caused by standard alpha-blending approximations [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Link: Continuous Attenuation Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting What it is: An adaptation of 3DGS for underwater environments that learns direct attenuation (Bd), infinite backscatter color (B\infty), and backscatter coefficient (Bb) [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. Distinction: It explicitly models the physical interaction of light with water (color cast and visibility loss), which vanilla 3DGS fails to handle, while remaining significantly faster than NeRF-based underwater alternatives [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. When to choose: For 3D reconstruction in aquatic scenes where color distortion and attenuation are dominant [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. Link: Underwater 3D Gaussian Splatting with Backscatter Loss Step: 1. Divide the depth map (from the current scene estimate) into 10 evenly-spaced clusters covering the range from \min(z) to \max(z). 2. Within each cluster, identify pixels in the ground-truth image whose RGB triplets are below the bottom 1st percentile. 3. These triplets serve as an overestimate of the backscatter signal Bs. 4. Use nonlinear least squares fitting on pairs (Bs, z) to estimate parameters B\infty and Bb. 5. Re-estimate backscatter parameters B\infty and Bb every 500 optimization steps to guide convergence toward the medium coefficients. Formula: The base loss function is: L = \sum{k=1}^K (1 - \lambda1) \| Ik^{gt} - Ik^r(\Theta) \|{\ell1} + \lambda1 L{D-SSIM}(Ik^{gt}, Ik^r(\Theta)) where K is the number of images and \lambda1 \in [0,1] is user-defined. Parameter: Backscatter parameter bounds are B\infty \in [0, 1] and Bb \in [0, 5]. Pitfall: The camera sensor must have a linear response to light. In-camera processed.jpg images or gamma-corrected images cannot be used unless non-linearities can be reversed. The continuous attenuation model was introduced to address the geometric inconsistencies of discrete Gaussian splatting for surface extraction, leveraging theoretical results from Orienting Attenuation (OaV) [9624-continuous-attenuation-model-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Underwater 3D Gaussian Splatting (Gaussian Splashing) was developed to extend 3DGS to aquatic environments by incorporating ocean optics models, specifically addressing the limitations of vanilla 3DGS in handling distance-dependent attenuation and color casts [13980-underwater-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-backscatter-loss.md]. Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-56917-4, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Continuous Attenuation Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Attenuation-based 3DGS, Equivalent Ray-Marching Formulation
body: The Continuous Attenuation Model reformulates the discrete, rasterization-based alpha-blending image formation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into a continuous volumetric ray-marching framework. This equivalence allows the application of theoretical results from Optimal Alpha Blending (OaV) and other volume rendering techniques to 3DGS, specifically enhancing surface extraction by ensuring unbiased, ellipsoidal isosurfaces. Unlike the standard rasterization approach which assumes negligible 3D overlap, this model explicitly defines a view-dependent attenuation coefficient \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) that preserves the geometric fidelity of the Gaussian primitives during ray integration. The method maps a set of N 3D Gaussians to a continuous attenuation field. It relies on two key assumptions: (a) statistical independence of Gaussians (following RayGauss [7]), and (b) non-overlapping Gaussian primitives. While assumption (b) is an approximation similar to front-to-back alpha blending, it is effective in practice for novel view synthesis. Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gi is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{w}). A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{w}. Output: The continuous attenuation coefficient field \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) and the equivalent transmittance function T{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}(t). The model does not introduce new storage structures but reinterprets the existing Gaussian parameters. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right). 1. Flight Distance to Maximum Contribution For a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{w}, the flight distance t{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}^G to the point of maximum Gaussian contribution is the value t \geq 0 that maximizes the Gaussian density along the ray: t{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}^G:= \arg \max{t \geq 0} \{G(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{w})\}. For a single Gaussian, this occurs at the point on the ray closest to the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} in the Mahalanobis metric defined by \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}. 2. Continuous Transmittance Function The transmittance for a single Gaussian along the ray is defined as: T{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}(t) = 1 - G(\mathbf{o} + \min(t, t{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}^G)\mathbf{w}). This formulation ensures that the transmittance reaches its maximum value (minimum density contribution) at the point of maximum Gaussian contribution. 3. View-Dependent Attenuation Coefficient The attenuation coefficient \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) is derived from the transmittance to ensure consistency with alpha blending and geometric constraints: \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \max(0, -\mathbf{w} \cdot \nabla \log(1 - G(\mathbf{x}))). This specific definition ensures that the transmittance reaches its maximum at the point of maximum contribution and maintains ellipsoidal isosurfaces. 4. Rendering Equivalence The rendered color C{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}} using the density-based model is: C{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{w}) \int0^{+\infty} -\frac{d}{dt} T{\mathbf{o},\mathbf{w}}(s) ds = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{w}) G(\mathbf{o} + t{\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{w}}^G \mathbf{w}). This matches the alpha-blending expression for a single Gaussian, assuming the ray origin \mathbf{o} is in empty space (G(\mathbf{o}) \approx 0). The following Python-like pseudocode computes the attenuation coefficient for a single Gaussian at a point \mathbf{x} along a ray direction \mathbf{w}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussiandensity(x, mu, Sigmainv): """ Computes the value of the Gaussian density function G(x). """ diff = x - mu exponent = -0.5 np.dot(diff, np.dot(Sigmainv, diff)) return np.exp(exponent) def gradientlogtransmittance(x, mu, Sigmainv, w): """ Computes -w. grad(log(1 - G(x))). This is the attenuation coefficient sigma(x, w). """ # Compute G(x) Gx = gaussiandensity(x, mu, Sigmainv) # Avoid log(0) if G(x) is 1 (unlikely in empty space, but guard against it) if Gx >= 1.0: return 0.0 # Gradient of log(1 - G(x)) with respect to x # d/dx log(1 - G) = (1 / (1 - G)) (-dG/dx) # dG/dx = G(x) (-Sigmainv (x - mu)) diff = x - mu gradG = Gx (-np.dot(Sigmainv, diff)) gradlog1minusG = -gradG / (1.0 - Gx) # Dot product with ray direction w # sigma = max(0, -w. gradlog1minusG) dotproduct = np.dot(w, gradlog1minusG) sigma = -dotproduct return max(0.0, sigma) def computeflightdistance(mu, Sigmainv, o, w): """ Computes t{o,w}^G = argmax{t>=0} G(o + tw). Minimizes the quadratic form (o + tw - mu)^T Sigmainv (o + tw - mu). """ v = mu - o # Derivative of quadratic form w.r.t t: 2 (tw - v)^T Sigmainv w = 0 # t (w^T Sigmainv w) = v^T Sigmainv w denom = np.dot(w, np.dot(Sigmainv, w)) if denom < 1e-8: return 0.0 t = np.dot(v, np.dot(Sigmainv, w)) / denom return max(0.0, t) Non-Spherical Isosurfaces: Using a simpler attenuation formulation \sigma(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2} |\mathbf{w} \cdot \nabla \log(1 - G(\mathbf{x}))| (as in GGGS [57]) produces non-spherical surfaces for a single Gaussian. This leads to non-multi-view consistent depth maps and surface erosion. Geometric Constraint: The proposed model enforces ellipsoidal isosurfaces for transmittance, ensuring unbiased, spherical isosurfaces aligned with the visible part of the Gaussian. Overlap Assumption: The equivalence relies on the non-overlapping assumption. Discrepancies occur when this condition is not met, such as in poorly supervised background regions. Complexity: The computational complexity is comparable to standard 3DGS rasterization for rendering, as it evaluates the same Gaussian primitives. However, ray-marching implementations may incur higher overhead due to the iterative evaluation of the attenuation field along the ray. Performance: The model is designed to be equivalent to the rasterization-based model, so it does not inherently degrade novel view synthesis quality. Strengths: Enables high-fidelity surface reconstruction by providing unbiased, multi-view consistent depth maps and normals. It allows the use of volume rendering techniques for surface extraction. Limitations: Relies on the approximation of non-overlapping Gaussians, which may fail in complex scenes with significant occlusion or poor supervision. The Continuous Attenuation Model was introduced in "From Blobs to Spokes: High-Fidelity Surface Reconstruction via Oriented Gaussians". It builds on the observation that while 3DGS rasterization is efficient, it lacks the theoretical grounding for surface extraction provided by volumetric rendering. The work connects 3DGS to Optimal Alpha Blending (OaV) and addresses the limitations of previous attenuation models like GGGS [57], which failed to preserve geometric consistency. name: Underwater 3D Gaussian Splatting with Backscatter Loss
head: 3DGS adapted to aquatic environments
body: This method adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for underwater environments by integrating ocean optics models, specifically learning direct attenuation (Bd), infinite backscatter (B\infty), and backscatter coefficient (Bb). It solves the problem of color distortion and visibility loss in aquatic scenes by modifying the rendering equation to account for light transport in a scattering medium. Unlike vanilla 3DGS, which fails to handle the predominant bluish palette and distance-dependent degradation, this method maintains real-time inference speeds while significantly improving reconstruction quality at unbounded camera-to-scene distances. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N initialized from a sparse point cloud (e.g., via COLMAP); a set of K input images \{Ik^{gt}\}{k=1}^K with known camera poses; ground-truth depth estimates or a mechanism to derive them from the Gaussian representation. Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters \Theta (means, covariances, opacities, colors) and medium parameters Bd, B\infty, Bb; rendered novel-view images. Data Structures The scene is represented by the standard 3DGS structure: \boldsymbol{\mu}i: Mean position (3 floats). \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i: Covariance matrix, derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i (6 floats for rotation quaternion, 3 for scale). \alphai: Opacity (1 float). \mathbf{c}i: View-dependent color, typically stored as spherical harmonic coefficients. Bd: Direct attenuation parameter (1 float per Gaussian or global, modulating RGB values). B\infty: Infinite backscatter parameter (1 float, bounded [0, 1]). Bb: Backscatter coefficient parameter (1 float, bounded [0, 5]). Rendering Equation The rendering process evaluates Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The specific underwater rendering equation incorporating attenuation and backscatter is referenced as Eq. (5) in the source. The depth map z is extracted from the 3DGS representation using a customized CUDA implementation, mapping the initial output via a shifted and scaled logistic function: z = \frac{2}{1 + e^{-0.1 \cdot z}} - 1. Optimization Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using COLMAP sparse point cloud. Initialize medium parameters Bd, B\infty, Bb. 2. Initial Parameter Estimation (Backscatter Guidance): Identify pixels in the ground-truth image whose RGB triplets fall below the bottom 1st percentile of all pixel values. These pixels serve as an overestimate of the backscatter. Model the backscatter color Bs at a pixel with depth z as: Bs = B\infty (1 - e^{-Bb z}) where Bs is the color value and z is the depth estimate at such a pixel. Use nonlinear least squares fitting on the pairs of (Bs, z) values to estimate initial parameters \hat{B}\infty and \hat{B}b, ensuring they remain within bounds [0, 1] and [0, 5] respectively. 3. Alternating Optimization: Minimize the total loss L(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb) using the Adam optimizer. The rendered images Ik^r are functions of \Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb. Every 500 iterations, re-compute the initial estimates \hat{B}\infty and \hat{B}b using the current depth map estimates and the nonlinear least squares procedure. This refines the guidance for the medium parameters as depth improves. 4. Loss Function: The total loss is defined as: L(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb) = \sum{k=1}^K (1 - \lambda1) \|Ik^{gt} - Ik^r(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb)\|{\ell1} + \lambda1 L{D-SSIM}(Ik^{gt}, Ik^r(\Theta, Bd, B\infty, Bb)) + \lambda2 L{bs}(B\infty, Bb) where: \| \cdot \|{\ell1} is the L1 norm. L{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss. L{bs} is the backscatter guidance loss: L{bs}(B\infty, Bb) = \|B\infty - \hat{B}\infty\|{\ell1} + \|Bb - \hat{B}b\|{\ell1} where \hat{B}\infty and \hat{B}b are the initial estimates. Parameters \lambda1: Weight for the D-SSIM loss term. Value: 0.3 (inherited from original 3DGS). \lambda2: Weight for the backscatter loss term. Value: 0.1 (fixed across all scenes). Learning Rate: Identical for Bd, B\infty, Bb and the Gaussian color parameters ci. Optimization Bounds: B\infty \in [0, 1], Bb \in [0, 5]. Bd follows the normalized RGB image range and physically non-negative attenuation assumption. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim from scipy.optimize import curvefit import numpy as np def render3dgs(gaussians, Bd, Binf, Bb, cameraposes): """ Standard differentiable 3D Gaussian splatting forward pass. Returns rendered image Ir and depth map z.""" # Standard 3DGS rasterization modified with underwater optics # Integrates Gaussian contributions along rays with attenuation Bd # and backscatter Binf (1 - exp(-Bb z)) pass # Standard differentiable rasterizer def computedssim(Igt, Ir): """ Standard differentiable SSIM loss computation.""" # Computes structural similarity between Igt and Ir pass # Standard differentiable SSIM loss def underwater3dgstraining(Gaussians, images, cameraposes, K, lambda1=0.3, lambda2=0.1, steps=30000): Bd = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) Binf = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) Bb = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) optimizer = optim.Adam(list(Gaussians.parameters()) + [Bd, Binf, Bb], lr=0.001) # LR inherited from original 3DGS for step in range(steps): Ir, z = render3dgs(Gaussians, Bd, Binf, Bb, cameraposes) lossl1 = 0 lossdssim = 0 for k in range(K): Igt = images[k] lossl1 += torch.norm(Igt - Ir[k], p=1) lossdssim += computedssim(Igt, Ir[k]) lossphoto = (1 - lambda1) lossl1 + lambda1 lossdssim Binfhat, Bbhat = estimatebackscatterguidance(z, images) lossbs = torch.norm(Binf - Binfhat, p=1) + torch.norm(Bb - Bbhat, p=1) loss = lossphoto + lambda2 lossbs optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() with torch.nograd(): Bd.clamp(min=0) Binf.clamp(min=0, max=1) Bb.clamp(min=0, max=5) if step % 500 == 0: Binfhat, Bbhat = estimatebackscatterguidance(z, images) def estimatebackscatterguidance(z, images): # Flatten images and depth # Identify pixels where RGB values are in the bottom 1st percentile # Extract corresponding depth z and backscatter color Bs # Fit Bs = Binf (1 - exp(-Bb z)) using nonlinear least squares # Return fitted Binf and Bb pass # Standard nonlinear least squares fitting Time Complexity: Training takes only several minutes. Memory Complexity: Average memory consumption is ~500 MB per scene over 30,000 steps on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. Performance: Inference speed is ~140 FPS average across multiple datasets, enabling real-time novel-view synthesis. Strengths: Significantly improves reconstruction quality in underwater scenes compared to vanilla 3DGS, particularly at larger distances and unbounded camera-to-scene distances. Much faster than NeRF-based methods (STNeRF, STNeRFacto) in both training and inference. When to use: Underwater 3D reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and color-reconstruction applications where real-time rendering is required. When not to use: Scenes with extreme turbidity where the backscatter model assumptions break down, or when high-fidelity color accuracy is required without considering the physical medium (vanilla 3DGS might be preferred for speed if quality is not critical). Origin: The method was introduced in "Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater". History: It builds upon the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [Parent] and adapts it to aquatic environments by incorporating ocean optics models. It addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS in handling underwater light transport. Usage: Evaluated on the TableDB dataset (172 images, 1384×918 resolution, unbounded camera-to-scene distances) and public underwater datasets (Red Sea, Curaçao, Panama). Gaussian splashing enables direct volumetric rendering underwater, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-56917-4, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Sparse2DGS
head: Geometry-Prioritized Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views
body: Sparse2DGS is a Gaussian Splatting method designed for surface reconstruction from sparse input views, addressing the ill-posed nature of geometric optimization when dense Structure-from-Motion points are unavailable. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and its sibling 2DGS by initializing primitives with unsupervised Multi-View Stereo (MVS) points and employing geometric-prioritized enhancements—such as fixed feature splatting and selective updates—to prevent appearance overfitting and improve geometric learning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N sparse input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Outputs: A set of 2D Gaussian primitives representing the 3D surface, optimized to minimize reconstruction error. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a set of 2D Gaussian primitives. Each primitive G is defined by: Central position \mathbf{p}. Two principal tangential vectors \mathbf{t}u and \mathbf{t}v. Scaling vector (su, sv). The rotation matrix is \mathbf{R} = (\mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v, \mathbf{t}z), where \mathbf{t}z = \mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v. The scale matrix is \mathbf{S} = \text{diag}(su, sv, 0). The local tangent plane in world space is parameterized as: P(u, v) = \mathbf{p} + su \mathbf{t}u u + sv \mathbf{t}v v \quad (1) The Gaussian value for a point \mathbf{u} = (u, v) in the local uv space is: G(\mathbf{u}) = \exp\left(-\frac{u^2 + v^2}{2}\right) \quad (2) MVS-derived feature maps \{Di\}{i=1}^N (dense depth maps) are used for initialization and supervision. Numbered Steps: 1. MVS Initialization: Run an unsupervised MVS network (specifically CLMVSNet) on the input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N to estimate dense depth maps \{Di\}{i=1}^N. Back-project the depth maps Di into 3D space and fuse them to create a point cloud \{\mathbf{p}{ij} \mid 1 \le i \le N, 1 \le j \le HW\}. Initialize the 2D Gaussian primitives' central positions \mathbf{p} using this MVS point cloud. 2. Geometrically Enhanced Supervision (Feature Splatting): Sample the MVS-derived feature maps (depth/geometry) into the Gaussian splatting process. Crucial Constraint: Keep the feature values and RGB color values fixed during optimization. This provides geometrically expressive supervision and prevents the model from overfitting to appearance in sparse views, which would otherwise compromise geometry. 3. Gaussian Primitive Regularization: Apply a reparameterization-based disk sampling strategy to regularize the geometric properties (position, orientation, scale) of the primitives. Reformulate the Gaussian properties into point representations. Optimize these properties using a unified point-based, cross-view consistency loss. This ensures that the 2D disk-like primitives maintain coherent geometry across views. 4. Selective Gaussian Update: Instead of using standard densification (splitting/copying) which can fail under ill-posed sparse-view conditions, selectively update the existing MVS-initialized Gaussian primitives. Use rendered geometric cues to guide these updates, allowing for self-guided geometric corrections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparse2dgs(inputimages, numviews): """ inputimages: List of N images [H, W, 3] numviews: N """ # Step 1: MVS Initialization # Run unsupervised MVS (e.g., CLMVSNet) to get depth maps depthmaps = runmvsnetwork(inputimages) # Back-project and fuse depth maps to point cloud # i: image index, j: pixel index mvspointcloud = [] for i in range(numviews): for j in range(H W): pij = backproject(depthmaps[i], j) mvspointcloud.append(pij) # Initialize 2D Gaussians with MVS points # Each Gaussian G has: p, tu, tv, su, sv gaussians = [] for p in mvspointcloud: # Initialize tangential vectors and scales arbitrarily or via normal estimation tu, tv = initializetangents(p) su, sv = 1.0, 1.0 # Initial scale g = Gaussian(p=p, tu=tu, tv=tv, su=su, sv=sv) gaussians.append(g) # Step 2: Optimization Loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): losses = [] for viewidx in range(numviews): image = inputimages[viewidx] # Render current view using 2D Gaussian Splatting # Note: Feature and Color values are FIXED from MVS/Initialization renderedimage, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(gaussians, viewidx) # Compute loss against ground truth image # Since color is fixed, this loss primarily drives geometric consistency # and prevents appearance overfitting colorloss = computecolorloss(renderedimage, image) losses.append(colorloss) # Compute geometric consistency loss using MVS depth # Compare rendered depth with MVS depth map mvsdepth = depthmaps[viewidx] geoloss = computedepthconsistency(rendereddepth, mvsdepth) losses.append(geoloss) # Step 3: Regularization # Apply disk sampling regularization to reformulate properties # into point-based supervision regloss = applydisksamplingregularization(gaussians) losses.append(regloss) # Backpropagate and update gradients # Only update geometric parameters (p, tu, tv, su, sv) # Do NOT update color or feature attributes optimize(gaussians, losses) # Step 4: Selective Update # Instead of densification, selectively update primitives # based on geometric cues gaussians = selectiveupdate(gaussians, rendereddepth, mvsdepth) return gaussians Parameters: N: Number of sparse input views. H, W: Height and width of input images. Di: Dense depth maps estimated by the MVS network for view i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Appearance Overfitting: In sparse views, optimizing color and geometry simultaneously leads to severe degradation where color overfits the sparse inputs, compromising geometry. Sparse2DGS mitigates this by fixing feature and color values during optimization. Ill-posed Geometry: Standard densification strategies fail under sparse-view conditions. Sparse2DGS uses selective updates instead. Textureless Regions: Challenges in textureless areas are amplified with sparse views; the geometric-prioritized supervision helps address this. Performance: Achieves a Chamfer Distance (CD) error of 1.13 on the DTU dataset with 3 views. This is significantly lower than 2DGS (2.81), GOF (2.82), and PGSR (2.08). Efficiency: Training time is 10 minutes, which is 2x faster than the NeRF-based fine-tuning approach SparseNeus (25 minutes). Strengths: Robust geometric learning under ill-posed conditions; complete and accurate reconstruction from sparse images; faster than NeRF-based methods. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the unsupervised MVS initialization (CLMVSNet); performance is specific to sparse-view scenarios. Sparse2DGS was proposed to address the limitations of previous Gaussian Splatting methods that rely on dense views for initialization, which struggle with extremely sparse Structure-from-Motion points. It combines the strengths of Gaussian Splatting and Multi-view Stereo (MVS) through geometric-prioritized enhancement schemes. The method was introduced in the paper "Sparse2DGS: Geometry-Prioritized Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views". name: Surface Geometry Constraints
body: Surface Geometry Constraints are optimization and initialization techniques applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to enforce geometric fidelity, ensuring that the volumetric Gaussian representation aligns with underlying surface structures such as meshes, planes, or physical boundaries. They differ from sibling methods like Mesh Extraction and Representation by integrating constraints directly into the training loop rather than post-processing, and from Appearance and Physical Modeling by focusing on spatial geometry rather than radiance. Planar Gaussian Splatting is an unsupervised neural rendering framework that reconstructs 3D geometry and explicitly parses 3D planar surfaces from multiple RGB images without requiring 3D labels or depth supervision. It extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by introducing discriminative 3D plane descriptors and enforcing local planar alignment constraints. Unlike sibling methods that focus on high-fidelity rendering or generic mesh extraction, PGS is designed to identify distinct 3D plane instances through a hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Tree (GMT). It sets itself apart by using 2D segmentation priors from foundation models (like SAM) to guide the learning of these descriptors, enabling robust planar reconstruction across different scenes. A constraint to prevent discrepancies between Gaussian Splat scales and the scales of corresponding triangular mesh faces by bounding the relative scale coefficients. The final scale s is computed as s = s{rel} \odot s0, where s{rel} = (s{rel,1}, s{rel,2}) \in [s{min}, s{max}] \times [s{min}, s{max}] is the coefficient vector, s0 is the predefined scale derived from the mesh faces, and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The bounds s{min} and s{max} define the allowable range for the relative scale coefficients. An extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting where Gaussians are constrained to a 2D tangent plane to resolve the conflict between volumetric Gaussians and surface representation, enabling accurate normal map estimation. A point P on the 2D Gaussian plane with coordinates (u, v) is defined as P(u, v) = pk + su tu u + sv tv v = H(u, v, 1, 1)^T, where H = [pk, tu, tv, tw] is the transformation matrix. Normal rendering is performed by splatting normals in the same manner as color splatting to generate a normal map. A solution where a second invisible layer of geometry (meshes, primitives) is built separately around the Gaussian scene to define physical boundaries, as Gaussian splats lack solid surfaces by default. This involves manually positioning various primitives (boxes, simple polygons) around Gaussians to construct surfaces for navigation and pointing. It is used in early 3DGS development via heavy game engines (Unity, Unreal Engine) or web-based solutions like Spline. A major pitfall is that creating collision geometry object by object for large buildings, industrial environments, or complex outdoor scans is very time-consuming. First stage of optimization reconstructing the background using segmented background images, background point cloud, spheres' radii, and shell center. During this pass, Gaussians are constrained to remain inside a spherical shell defined by an inner radius Ri and outer radius Ro centered at O. The shell loss is defined as: L{shell} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \left( \max(0, \|pi - O\|^2 - Ro) + \max(0, Ri - \|pi - O\|^2) \right)^2 where N is the total number of Gaussians, pi is the position of the i-th Gaussian. A planarity loss is also applied: L{planarity} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \left( 1 - \left| \frac{pi - O}{\|pi - O\|} \cdot (\text{Rot}i \cdot a{locali}) \right| \right) \frac{s{maxi}}{s{mini} + \epsilon} where \text{Rot}i is the rotation matrix, a{locali} is the shortest axis basis vector, s{max}/s{min} are scaling factors, and \epsilon is a small constant. The total loss is L = L{render} + \lambda{shell} L{shell} + \lambda{planarity} L{planarity}, with \lambda{shell} = 1.0 and \lambda{planarity} = 0.1. The need for surface geometry constraints in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the method's inherent volumetric nature, which can lead to "floaters" and ambiguous surface boundaries when reconstructing sharp geometric features. Early implementations relied on manual collision geometry to provide physical boundaries for navigation, as the splats themselves did not constitute solid surfaces. Subsequent research introduced explicit constraints, such as planar alignment using foundation model priors, mesh-adherent scale bounding, and tangent plane parameterization for normal estimation. More recent approaches utilize spherical shell constraints for outdoor background reconstruction to prevent divergence. These methods collectively aim to bridge the gap between differentiable volumetric rendering and explicit geometric surface representation.
