name: Planar Gaussian Splatting
head: PGSR, Planar GS
body: Planar Gaussian Splatting (PGS) is an unsupervised neural rendering framework that reconstructs 3D geometry and explicitly parses 3D planar surfaces from multiple RGB images without requiring 3D labels or depth supervision. It extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by introducing discriminative 3D plane descriptors and enforcing local planar alignment constraints. Unlike sibling methods that prioritize high-fidelity rendering or generic mesh extraction, PGS is designed to identify distinct 3D plane instances through a hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Tree. It sets itself apart by using 2D segmentation priors from foundation models like SAM to guide descriptor learning, enabling robust planar reconstruction across unseen scenes. PGS operates on a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian retains the standard 3DGS parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). Additionally, each Gaussian carries two new parameters: a surface normal vector \mathbf{n}i and a learnable plane descriptor vector \mathbf{z}i. The descriptor is constrained to unit norm (\|\mathbf{z}i\|2 = 1) and serves to identify distinct 3D planes. Gaussian Field: A list of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{R}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \mathbf{S}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale vector. \alphai \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. \mathbf{c}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients (Degree 2). \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface normal (unit vector). \mathbf{z}i \in \mathbb{R}^d: Plane descriptor (unit vector, d=3 in experiments). KNN Structure: For each Gaussian, a list of K nearest neighbor indices is maintained to compute local covariance and smoothing. Region Adjacency Graph (RAG): A graph where nodes are 2D segments and edges represent adjacency, used to merge segments belonging to the same plane. 1. Gaussian Placement: Initialize Gaussian locations and colors using a sparse point cloud obtained by running Structure-from-Motion (SfM) on the training images. 2. Leaf Node Generation (Optional): Leaf nodes of the Gaussian Mixture Tree can be generated by prompting SAM with a 32 \times 32 grid on input images to get masks. Segments with high normal vector variance are ignored as invalid. Boundary points of valid SAM masks are lifted into 3D space using rendered depth maps and camera parameters. The mean and covariance of these 3D boundary points are computed to form initial Gaussian distributions. The training runs for 15,000 iterations on a single GPU. The core loop involves standard 3DGS densification (cloning, splitting, culling) and the following specialized steps: 1. Rendering: Render the scene to obtain photometric loss. Use Spherical Harmonics of degree 2. 2. Plane Descriptor Learning (Linear Regression): Render a 2D descriptor image where each pixel is the blended 3D descriptor \mathbf{z} of the visible Gaussians. Let \mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times d} be the matrix of rendered descriptors for P pixels, augmented with a column of 1s. Let \mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times m} be the one-hot label matrix for the m segments in the current view (derived from SAM). Solve for weights \hat{\mathbf{W}} using the closed-form solution: \hat{\mathbf{W}} = (\mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Z})^{-1} \mathbf{Z}^\top \mathbf{Y} Compute the prediction \hat{\mathbf{y}}i = [\mathbf{z}i | 1] \hat{\mathbf{W}} for each pixel. Compute segmentation loss: \mathcal{L}{seg} = \sum{i} \| \mathbf{y}i - \hat{\mathbf{y}}i \|1 Optimize \mathbf{z}i via gradient descent on \mathcal{L}{seg}. Note: This regression is recomputed for each camera view. The number of segments m varies per image. 3. Segment Merging (RAG): Construct a RAG from the 2D segments. Cut edges in the RAG if the planar distance between segments exceeds 10 cm or the surface normal cosine distance exceeds 20 degrees. Merge remaining connected components to form consistent 2D plane labels for the current view. 4. Local Planar Alignment: Applied every 500 iterations. For each Gaussian, find its K=30 nearest neighbors (KNN). Compute the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix of the KNN Gaussian centers. Perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the covariance matrix. Identify the local tangent plane using the two eigenvectors corresponding to the two largest eigenvalues. Project the Gaussian center \boldsymbol{\mu}i onto this local tangent plane. Apply Laplacian smoothing to \mathbf{n}i and \mathbf{z}i by averaging over the features of the KNN neighbors. 5. Holistic Separability (Mean-Shift): Applied once after 2,000 iterations, then every 100 iterations. Goal: Enhance separability of descriptors \mathbf{z} for distinct planes. Update rule for the descriptor matrix \mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}: \mathbf{Z} \leftarrow \mathbf{Z} \cdot (\eta \cdot \mathbf{K} \cdot \mathbf{D}^{-1} + (1-\eta) \cdot \mathbf{I}) Where: \mathbf{K} is the pairwise distance kernel using the von Mises-Fisher distribution. \mathbf{D} is the diagonal matrix of row sums of \mathbf{K}. \mathbf{I} is the identity matrix. \eta is a mixing parameter. \gamma = 60 is the kernel parameter (used in von Mises-Fisher). Efficient Implementation: Computing \mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} is infeasible for large N. Instead: 1. Estimate \mathbf{K} on a random subset of M points (M \ll N) without replacement. 2. Propagate and share the estimated kernel and update vectors across all KNN samples within the chosen set. 3. Repeat sampling until an update vector is computed for all samples or their neighbors. 4. Perform 10 update steps per run. 5. This process takes approximately 1 second on GPU. 6. KNN Recomputation: Recompute KNN indices after any refinement to the Gaussian field (cloning, splitting, culling). Training Iterations: 15,000. Hardware: Single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti. Gradient Densification Threshold: 0.001 (increased to limit cloning/splitting). Spherical Harmonics Degree: 2. RAG Thresholds: Planar distance 10 cm, Normal cosine distance 20 degrees. Mean-Shift Frequency: Once after 2k iterations, then every 100 iterations. Mean-Shift Steps: 10 per run. Mean-Shift Gamma (\gamma): 60. KNN Neighbors (K): 30. Local Planar Alignment Frequency: Every 500 iterations. Kernel Computation: Computing the full kernel \mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} is quadratic in memory and infeasible for millions of points. The sampling strategy is required. SAM Ambiguity: SAM may return subparts, parts, or entire objects for a single point. High-variance normal segments are ignored as invalid. Multi-view Association: SAM masks lack semantic information, making 2D-3D lifting difficult due to unknown mask associations and variable numbers of segments. The linear regression approach handles this by solving for weights per view. This method learns 3D plane descriptors \mathbf{z} by lifting 2D segmentation masks from SAM using a closed-form linear regression that maps rendered 3D descriptors to 2D segment labels. It sets itself apart by avoiding explicit 3D plane labels and instead leveraging 2D foundation model priors to guide descriptor optimization. Choose this when you need to incorporate semantic segmentation priors into 3D Gaussian optimization without 3D ground truth. Link: Plane Descriptor Learning via 2D SAM Lifting. This technique enforces Gaussian centers to lie on object surfaces by projecting them onto local tangent planes computed from KNN covariance matrices. It sets itself apart by providing a geometric constraint that aligns Gaussians with surfaces, improving planar consistency. Choose this when you need to enforce surface-aligned geometry during training. Link: Local Planar Alignment. This structure provides a probabilistic bottom-up modeling of scene geometry by recursively merging Gaussian nodes to form parent nodes. It sets itself apart by hierarchically grouping Gaussians to explicitly identify distinct 3D plane instances. Choose this when you need to parse the scene into explicit planar components. Link: Gaussian Mixture Tree. Time Complexity: The mean-shift update is optimized to take approximately 1 second on GPU despite N being in the millions, due to the sampling strategy. The linear regression is recomputed per view but is fast. Memory Complexity: Avoids O(N^2) memory for the kernel matrix by using random sampling. Performance: On ScanNet, PGS achieves an Accuracy of 0.137 and Completeness of 0.118, outperforming PlanarRecon (0.154 Accuracy, 0.187 Completeness). Strengths: Unsupervised, no depth/3D labels required, fast optimization compared to other optimization-based planar methods, robust across datasets. Limitations: Relies on SAM quality, Spherical Harmonics degree 2 limits high-frequency color detail, densification threshold is higher to limit Gaussian count. When to use: When 3D planar reconstruction is needed from RGB images without depth supervision. When not to use: When high-fidelity rendering is required, as PGS uses SH degree 2 and prioritizes geometric parsing over photometric quality. Planar Gaussian Splatting (PGS) was introduced by Farhad G. Zanjani, Hong Cai, Hanno Ackermann, Leila Mirvakhabova, and Fatih Porikli from Qualcomm AI Research. The paper was published on arXiv on December 2, 2024, and later in WACV 2025. It addresses the challenge of identifying 3D planar surfaces in images, which is difficult for standard 3DGS due to its floating ellipsoid nature. PGS builds on the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [16] and leverages foundation models like SAM [17] to provide 2D priors. Planar Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00863, fetched 2026-10-26 Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: CADSplat
head: Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting Aided by CAD Models
body: CADSplat reconstructs photorealistic, geometrically accurate digital twins from sparse (< 15 views), wide-baseline posed images by regularizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with an explicit Computer-Aided Design (CAD) shape prior. Unlike methods that rely on learned generative priors or large-scale data priors (e.g., InstantSplat, pixelSplat), CADSplat imposes a strict, explicit geometric constraint derived from the object's specific CAD model, providing geometric disambiguation under severe occlusion and view scarcity. It differs from sibling geometry-constrained methods by anchoring Gaussians to a parametric CAD surface and jointly optimizing a non-rigid deformation field, rather than relying solely on surface normal or SDF constraints. Inputs: 1. A set of N input images (N < 15), assumed to be wide-baseline and posed (relative geometry approximately known). 2. A library of CAD models (meshes). 3. Segmented object silhouettes for each input image. Outputs: 1. A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} anchored to a deformed CAD surface. 2. Optimized camera-to-object poses. 3. A non-rigid deformation field mapping the canonical CAD shape to the physical object. Data Structures: CAD Mesh: A triangular mesh \mathcal{M} with vertices \mathbf{V} and faces \mathcal{F}. Gaussian Primitives: A fixed set of Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^M initialized on the surface of \mathcal{M}. Each Gi retains standard 3DGS parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (rotation \mathbf{R}i, scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i for color. Deformation Network: A neural network D\theta that takes a point on the CAD surface and returns a displacement vector. Pose Parameters: A global Sim(3) transformation (scale, rotation, translation) or per-camera corrections. Algorithm Steps: 1. CAD Retrieval and Silhouette Registration: Render silhouettes from all CAD models in the library from various viewpoints. Match the segmented silhouettes of the input images against the rendered CAD silhouettes. Select the best-matching CAD model and its associated camera-to-object poses as the initial registration. Note: This step provides only coarse accuracy (median rotation error ~6.2°, position error ~18.6% on SCO-CAD). 2. Initialization: Position the selected CAD mesh at the intersection of the cameras' viewing directions. Rescale the mesh to cover the same surface area as the ground-truth silhouettes. Anchor the initial set of 3D Gaussians to the surface of this CAD mesh. 3. Geometric Warmup (Mask Alignment): Optimize the camera-to-object pose and the deformation field D\theta using only silhouette (mask) alignment loss. Purpose: Prevents the appearance optimization from fitting texture to a misregistered surface, which causes reconstruction collapse. 4. Joint Optimization: Optimize three components simultaneously: 1. 3DGS Parameters: \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{S}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i. 2. Camera-to-Object Registration: Refine the initial poses using a global Sim(3) transformation (or per-camera corrections for datasets with inaccurate calibration like MVMC). 3. Deformation Field D\theta: A non-rigid field that "wraps" the CAD mesh onto the physical observation, accounting for machining tolerances, wear, or design differences. 5. Regularization: SH Neighbor Smoothness: Pull each splat's spherical harmonic coefficients toward those of its 20 canonical-neighbor splats to remove high-frequency color changes in unobserved views. Splat Dropout: Randomly drop splats during training to ensure that splats occluded in training views but visible in held-out views still receive an optimization signal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def CADSplatTraining(InputImages, Silhouettes, CADLibrary): # 1. Retrieval bestcadmodel, initialposes = MatchSilhouettes(InputImages, Silhouettes, CADLibrary) # 2. Initialization cadmesh = bestcadmodel cadmesh = RescaleToMaskArea(cadmesh, Silhouettes) cadmesh = PositionAtCenter(cadmesh, InputImages) # Anchor Gaussians to mesh surface gaussians = AnchorGaussiansToMesh(cadmesh) # Initialize deformation network and pose parameters deformationnet = InitializeNetwork() poseparams = InitializePose(initialposes) # 3. Geometric Warmup # Optimize pose and deformation using silhouette loss only for step in WarmupSteps: deformedmesh = DeformMesh(cadmesh, deformationnet) renderedsilhouettes = RenderSilhouettes(deformedmesh, poseparams) lossmask = ComputeSilhouetteLoss(renderedsilhouettes, Silhouettes) Update(deformationnet, poseparams, lossmask) # 4. Joint Optimization for step in TotalSteps: # Apply deformation to get physical surface deformedmesh = DeformMesh(cadmesh, deformationnet) # Sample Gaussians from deformed surface # Note: Gaussians are anchored to the surface, so their means move with deformation currentgaussians = UpdateGaussianPositions(gaussians, deformedmesh) # Render image renderedimage = Render3DGS(currentgaussians, poseparams) # Compute photometric loss lossphoto = ComputePhotoLoss(renderedimage, InputImages) # Regularization: SH Neighbor Smoothness # Find 20 canonical neighbors for each splat neighbors = FindCanonicalNeighbors(currentgaussians, k=20) lossshsmooth = ComputeSHSmoothnessLoss(currentgaussians, neighbors) # Regularization: Splat Dropout # Randomly mask out a subset of splats for this step activegaussians = ApplySplatDropout(currentgaussians) # Joint Loss loss = lossphoto + lambdash lossshsmooth # Note: Splat dropout is handled by the rendering pass on activegaussians # Update all parameters Update(gaussians, poseparams, deformationnet, loss) return gaussians, poseparams, deformationnet def DeformMesh(mesh, net): # For each vertex v in mesh, compute displacement d = net(v) # New position v' = v + d # Return new mesh pass def AnchorGaussiansToMesh(mesh): # Sample points on mesh surface # Initialize Gaussian means at these points # Initialize covariances based on local surface normal and tangent plane pass Parameters: Input View Count: < 15 views. Performance degrades gracefully to as few as 3 views. SH Neighbor Count: 20 canonical neighbors. Camera Calibration: Wide-baseline, posed. Not necessarily perfectly pre-calibrated. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CAD Mismatch: The matched CAD model rarely matches the physical object perfectly due to tolerances or wear. Without the deformation field, this causes ghosting. Misregistration: Silhouette-based registration is coarse. Without the geometric warmup phase, texture fitting to a misregistered surface causes reconstruction collapse (PSNR drops to ~18.88). Pose Accuracy: For datasets with inaccurate calibration (e.g., MVMC), per-camera pose corrections are necessary in addition to global Sim(3). View Count Dependency: CAD initialization is superior to sphere initialization in sparse regimes (3 views). However, with 9-13 views, sphere initialization becomes competitive or slightly superior, as photometric signals are rich enough for the deformation field to carve the object. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On SCO-CAD with 3 views, CAD initialization yields PSNR 20.710 vs 19.312 for sphere, and IoU 0.929 vs 0.879. On SCO-CAD full budget, sphere initialization yields PSNR 23.535 vs 23.239 for CAD, and IoU 0.946 vs 0.942. Deformation alone (no pose opt) achieves PSNR 22.92 and IoU 0.941, within 0.3 dB of the full method. Pose optimization alone (no deformation) achieves PSNR 22.67. Without mask alignment, reconstruction collapses to PSNR 18.88 and IoU 0.784. SH neighbor smoothness increases PSNR from 22.93 to 23.13 and reduces mLPIPS from 0.039 to 0.032. On NeRS MVMC dataset, CADSplat achieves PSNR 18.7, SSIM 0.767, LPIPS 0.157, outperforming NeRS (PSNR 16.5) and CADSim (PSNR 17.7). Scaling: The method is designed for sparse views. It degrades gracefully to 3 views. Strengths: Provides geometric disambiguation under occlusion; enables applications like markerless AR registration and part label transfer; robust to sparse inputs. Limitations: Requires access to a CAD model library; relies on silhouette segmentation; deformation field may struggle if the CAD model is categorically wrong (e.g., a bottle instead of a fire hydrant), though it can bridge category-level gaps. CADSplat was introduced in 2026 by researchers from the Digital Future Lab, Flanders Make, and Hasselt University. It addresses the problem of reconstructing digital twins from sparse, wide-baseline images where traditional 3DGS fails due to lack of geometric constraints. It builds on Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints by introducing an explicit CAD prior. It differs from generative priors (pixelSplat, MVSplat) and learned priors (InstantSplat) by using an explicit, object-specific CAD model. CADSplat: Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting Aided by CAD Models for Robust, Photorealistic Digital-Twin Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18473, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting
head: Surface-Anchor Gaussian Splatting
body: Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting is a method for initializing and regularizing 3D Gaussian Splatting representations using a pre-existing mesh surface to eliminate floating artifacts and improve geometric fidelity. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by anchoring Gaussian means to mesh vertices and enforcing planar constraints via specific loss functions, whereas siblings like Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian may use different adsorption mechanisms and Surface Reconstruction via SDF relies on signed distance fields rather than explicit mesh anchoring. Inputs: A triangle mesh M with vertices V and triangles T. Initial RGB colors for each Gaussian (typically derived from the mesh texture or vertex colors). Training images and camera poses. Outputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N optimized for rendering. Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes: For each Gaussian i: Mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i parameterized by rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 and scale vector \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}i (initially only SH0 is non-zero). Mesh Cache: Triangle list for area-weighted sampling. KNN structure for nearest neighbor queries (used for scale initialization and Laplacian smoothing). Mesh point cache for surface anchor loss (updated every 50 steps). Initialization Steps: 1. Sample Points: Sample points uniformly on the mesh surface using area-weighted sampling. For each triangle, generate random barycentric coordinates bary = [1 - \sqrt{r1}, \sqrt{r1}(1 - r2), \sqrt{r1}r2] where r1, r2 \sim U[0,1]. 2. Initialize Means: Set \boldsymbol{\mu}i to the sampled 3D points. 3. Initialize Scales: Compute KNN distances for each point. Set scales as: s{xy} = \log(\text{avg\dist} \times 1.0) s{z} = \log(\text{avg\dist} \times 0.2) This creates flat discs that overlap with neighbors. 4. Initialize Rotations: Compute quaternions aligning the Gaussian Z-axis to the surface normal at \boldsymbol{\mu}i. Use the half-angle Rodrigues formula: qw = \sqrt{\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}}, \quad \mathbf{q}{xyz} = \sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\theta}{2}} \cdot \text{axis} where \theta is the angle between the initial Z-axis and the surface normal. Pitfall: If the normal is anti-aligned (\cos\theta < -0.999), set \mathbf{q} = [0, 1, 0, 0] (180-degree rotation around X) to avoid numerical instability. 5. Initialize Opacity: Set \alphai = 0.5 to prevent premature pruning during early training. 6. Initialize Colors: Compute SH0 from the initial RGB colors using rgbtosh and set higher-order SH coefficients to zero. Training Steps: 1. Render: Render the scene using standard differentiable Gaussian splatting. 2. Compute Losses: Reconstruction Loss: Standard L1/SSIM loss between rendered and ground truth images. Flatness Loss: Penalize the ratio of the thinnest axis scale to the middle axis scale to enforce disc-like shapes. Normal Alignment Loss: Penalize deviation of the thin axis (Z-axis in local space) from the surface normal: L{normal} = 1 - |\text{dot}(\text{thin\axis}, \text{normal})| Surface Anchor Loss: Compute L2 distance between Gaussian means \boldsymbol{\mu}i and the nearest points on the mesh. This cache is updated every 50 training steps. 3. Regularization: Apply Laplacian smoothing to scales, quaternions, and SH0 using k-nearest neighbors with a specified strength parameter. 4. Adaptive Control: Spawn new splats at pixels with high frequency gaps or low alpha using weighted multinomial sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def initializegaussiansfrommesh(mesh, numsamples): """ Initialize Gaussians on a mesh surface. Args: mesh: Object with triangles (V, 3, 3) and normals (V, 3). numsamples: Number of Gaussians to create. Returns: means, scales, quaternions, opacities, shcoeffs """ # 1. Sample points on mesh triangles = mesh.triangles # (T, 3, 3) triangleareas = computetriangleareas(triangles) triangleprobs = triangleareas / triangleareas.sum() sampledindices = np.random.choice(len(triangles), size=numsamples, p=triangleprobs) selectedtriangles = triangles[sampledindices] # Barycentric coordinates r1 = np.random.uniform(0, 1, numsamples) r2 = np.random.uniform(0, 1, numsamples) bary = np.stack([1 - np.sqrt(r1), np.sqrt(r1) (1 - r2), np.sqrt(r1) r2], axis=1) # Interpolate vertices v0 = selectedtriangles[:, 0] v1 = selectedtriangles[:, 1] v2 = selectedtriangles[:, 2] means = (bary[:, 0:1] v0 + bary[:, 1:2] v1 + bary[:, 2:3] v2) # 2. Initialize Scales using KNN # Compute KNN distances (simplified for illustration) avgdist = computeknndistance(means, k=5) scalesxy = np.log(avgdist 1.0) scalesz = np.log(avgdist 0.2) scales = np.stack([scalesxy, scalesxy, scalesz], axis=1) # 3. Initialize Rotations # Get surface normals at sampled points (interpolate from vertex normals) normals = interpolatenormals(mesh.vertexnormals, sampledindices, bary) # Align Z-axis (0,0,1) to normal quaternions = alignztovector(normals) # 4. Initialize Opacity opacities = np.full(numsamples, 0.5) # 5. Initialize Colors (placeholder) shcoeffs = np.zeros((numsamples, 3, 16)) # Only SH0 used initially # shcoeffs[:,:, 0] = rgbtosh(initialcolors) return means, scales, quaternions, opacities, shcoeffs def alignztovector(vectors): """ Compute quaternion rotating Z-axis (0,0,1) to vectors. Handles anti-alignment. """ zaxis = np.array([0, 0, 1]) # Normalize vectors norms = np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True) vnorm = vectors / norms # Dot product costheta = np.sum(zaxis vnorm, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Cross product cross = np.cross(zaxis, vnorm) # Handle anti-alignment antialigned = costheta < -0.999 if np.any(antialigned): # Set quaternion to [0, 1, 0, 0] for anti-aligned points # w, x, y, z quaternions = np.zeros((len(vectors), 4)) quaternions[antialigned.squeeze()] = [0, 1, 0, 0] # Compute for non-anti-aligned nonalignedmask = ~antialigned.squeeze() vnonaligned = vnorm[nonalignedmask] cosnonaligned = costheta[nonalignedmask] crossnonaligned = cross[nonalignedmask] w = np.sqrt((1 + cosnonaligned.squeeze()) / 2) sinhalf = np.sqrt((1 - cosnonaligned.squeeze()) / 2) axis = crossnonaligned / (np.linalg.norm(crossnonaligned, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) xyz = sinhalf axis quaternions[nonalignedmask] = np.stack([w, xyz[:, 0], xyz[:, 1], xyz[:, 2]], axis=1) return quaternions else: w = np.sqrt((1 + costheta.squeeze()) / 2) sinhalf = np.sqrt((1 - costheta.squeeze()) / 2) axis = cross / (np.linalg.norm(cross, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) xyz = sinhalf axis return np.stack([w, xyz[:, 0], xyz[:, 1], xyz[:, 2]], axis=1) def computetriangleareas(triangles): """Compute area of each triangle.""" v0 = triangles[:, 0] v1 = triangles[:, 1] v2 = triangles[:, 2] cross = np.cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) return 0.5 np.linalg.norm(cross, axis=1) def computeknndistance(points, k=5): """Placeholder for KNN distance computation.""" # In practice, use a KDTree or similar structure # Returns average distance to k nearest neighbors return 0.1 # Placeholder value def interpolatenormals(vertexnormals, triangleindices, barycentriccoords): """Interpolate vertex normals using barycentric coordinates.""" # triangleindices maps to the triangle index in the mesh # barycentriccoords are [w0, w1, w2] # vertexnormals are (V, 3) # triangles are (T, 3, 3) -> indices of vertices triverts = mesh.trianglevertexindices[triangleindices] # (N, 3) v0n = vertexnormals[triverts[:, 0]] v1n = vertexnormals[triverts[:, 1]] v2n = vertexnormals[triverts[:, 2]] normals = (barycentriccoords[:, 0:1] v0n + barycentriccoords[:, 1:2] v1n + barycentriccoords[:, 2:3] v2n) return normals Time Complexity: Initialization is O(N \log N) due to KNN queries. Training adds overhead for surface anchor loss computation (nearest mesh point query) every 50 steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the mesh geometry and a cache of nearest mesh points for all Gaussians. Strengths: Effectively removes floating artifacts common in standard 3DGS when reconstructing scenes with clear surfaces. Improves geometric consistency. Limitations: Requires a high-quality input mesh. Performance degrades if the mesh is noisy or incomplete. The surface anchor loss may constrain the Gaussians too rigidly, preventing them from adapting to view-dependent effects or slight misalignments. When to use: When a reliable mesh is available and geometric accuracy is prioritized over pure photometric fidelity. When not to use: For scenes without a clear surface structure or when the mesh quality is poor. Surface-Constrained Gaussian Splatting was introduced as an unofficial extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting to address the issue of floating artifacts in rendered scenes. It builds on the standard 3DGS representation but incorporates explicit geometric constraints derived from a mesh. The method is part of a broader effort to integrate explicit geometry into differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian
head: MaGS representation
body: Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian (MaGS) is a hybrid scene representation that combines a triangular mesh with 3D Gaussians, where Gaussians are "adsorbed" to mesh facets rather than being rigidly anchored in 3D space. This allows Gaussians to "roam" on the surface, increasing their degrees of freedom for movement and deformation. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by tying the spatial position of Gaussians to a parametric mesh surface defined by logical coordinates, enabling efficient dynamic reconstruction and simulation. Inputs: A triangular mesh defined by vertices, facets, and normals; a set of N 3D Gaussians. Outputs: Deformed Gaussian parameters (mean, covariance, opacity, color) for rendering. Data Structures: Mesh: Vertices: V = \{vi \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid i=1..Nv\} Facets: Indices of 3 vertices per facet. Normals: nj \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each facet j. Gaussian i: MeshId: Integer index of the facet j on which the Gaussian resides. wi \in [0, 1]^3: Logical coordinates. Standard 3DGS attributes: \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i. Step 1: Initialization Gaussians are randomly initialized. The logical coordinates wi are generated randomly. The MeshId is evenly distributed across facets to ensure an equal number of Gaussians per facet. Step 2: Normal Calculation Normals at any position on a facet are calculated by linearly interpolating the normals at its three vertices. Step 3: Mean Position Computation For a Gaussian i on facet j, the mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i is computed using an interpolation function and a "Gaussian Hover" offset. First, define the interpolation function f: f(w, x, y, z) = w1 x + w2 y + (1 - w1 - w2)z where w are the logical coordinates and x, y, z are values at the three vertices of the facet. Calculate the scaling factor lj for facet j: lj = \frac{|v{j1}v{j2}| |v{j1}v{j3}|}{|v{j1}v{j2} \times v{j1}v{j3}|} where v{j1}, v{j2}, v{j3} are the spatial coordinates of the three vertices of facet j. Compute the mean: \boldsymbol{\mu}i = f(wi, v{j1}, v{j2}, v{j3}) + w{i3} nj lj where nj is the facet normal and w{i3} is the third component of the logical coordinate vector wi. Step 4: Deformation (Dynamic Scenes) For dynamic objects, neural networks (MPE-Net, RMD-Net, RGD-Net) are used to predict relative mesh deformation and adjust Gaussian parameters. The relative deformation of facet j is calculated as \Delta lj = l'j / lj, where lj and l'j are the scaling factors before and after deformation. Pitfalls: Gaussian Hover: If w{i3} \neq 0, the Gaussian hovers above the mesh surface rather than lying directly on it. This increases the degree of freedom for movement but may introduce artifacts if not handled correctly during optimization. Not given in the sources. Origin: Introduced in "Reconstructing and Simulating Dynamic 3D Objects with Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS in handling dynamic scenes by providing a structured, mesh-based representation that facilitates simulation and deformation. Reconstructing and Simulating Dynamic 3D Objects with Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2406.01593, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Surface Reconstruction via SDF
head: Implicit Surface Reconstruction with 3DGS, SDF-Gaussian Coupling
body: This family of methods reconstructs high-quality, watertight 3D meshes from multi-view RGB images by coupling the explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation with an implicit Signed Distance Field (SDF) [17501-3d-gaussian-splatting-for-surface-reconstruction.md]. Standard 3DGS lacks explicit geometric structure, requiring post-processing for mesh extraction; these methods solve this by jointly optimizing Gaussians and an SDF to enforce surface constraints during training [17501-3d-gaussian-splatting-for-surface-reconstruction.md]. They differ from siblings like Mesh Extraction and Representation by integrating geometry regularization directly into the differentiable rendering loop rather than relying on separate reconstruction pipelines. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N. Each Gaussian Gi is defined by its mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (derived from rotation \mathbf{R}i and scale \mathbf{S}i), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i(\omega). The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega and integrates contributions. The Gaussian density function is: G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right) The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of \mathbf{c}i(\omega) and potentially \alphai, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS. Common strategies include: 1. Post-Processing Transformation: Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 2. Factorized Illumination: Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 3. Image-Conditioned Modulation: Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 4. Neural Field Substitution: Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md]. 5. Volumetric Attenuation: Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation Bd and backscatter parameters B\infty, Bb, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md]. Infers a neural SDF by dynamically aligning 3D Gaussians to the SDF's zero-level set using a differentiable 'pulling' operation. It sets itself apart by using "pulling to disks" to avoid overfitting to Gaussian centers, which is a common issue in other pulling methods [15776-neural-sdf-inference-via-gaussian-pulling.md]. Incorporates a neural SDF within the 3DGS framework to enable joint optimization of geometry and appearance. It solves the problem of extracting watertight meshes from 3DGS by unifying optimization end-to-end, leveraging explicit Gaussian rasterization for rendering and implicit volumetric rendering for geometric regularization [17501-3d-gaussian-splatting-for-surface-reconstruction.md]. A single-branch framework that jointly optimizes discrete 2D Gaussian primitives and a continuous SDF without an additional volume-rendering branch. It eliminates the computational intensity of neural implicit surfaces by using Gaussian centroids for direct SDF supervision and opacity entropy regularization to create a compact, opaque surface shell [20857-gsurf.md]. Originating from the need to extract explicit geometry from the inherently volumetric 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, these methods bridge the gap between explicit splatting and implicit neural fields. The approach builds on Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints by introducing specific SDF-based constraints.

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction
head: 3DGSR: Implicit Surface Reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting, Implicit Surface Reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Surface Reconstruction (3DGSR) is an implicit surface reconstruction method that integrates a Signed Distance Field (SDF) within the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation to enable joint optimization of geometry and appearance. It solves the problem that vanilla 3DGS produces unstructured point clouds unsuitable for direct mesh extraction, by aligning the Gaussian distribution with an implicit surface defined by the SDF. Unlike sibling methods that rely on post-processing (e.g., Poisson reconstruction) or separate optimization stages, 3DGSR unifies the training of Gaussians and the SDF end-to-end, achieving high-fidelity surfaces with intricate details while maintaining the rendering efficiency of 3DGS. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N (initialized from SfM points), a set of training images with known camera poses, and an initial SDF field (initialized via sphere or random initialization). Outputs: Optimized Gaussian parameters (mean, covariance, opacity, color) and an optimized implicit SDF field f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^1. The final mesh is extracted via Marching Cubes on the zero-level set of f. Data Structures: 1. 3D Gaussians: Standard 3DGS representation. Each Gaussian Gi has mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i = \mathbf{R}i \mathbf{S}i \mathbf{S}i^\top \mathbf{R}i^\top (where \mathbf{R}i is rotation quaternion and \mathbf{S}i is scale), opacity \alphai, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i. 2. SDF Field: Implemented using multiresolution hash grids [Müller et al. 2022] combined with a single-layer MLP. The field maps 3D coordinates to signed distance values. Coupling Strategies: The method aligns the SDF and Gaussians using one of two strategies. The loose coupling strategy is used by default. 1. Tight Coupling: Uses a differentiable SDF-to-opacity transformation to directly control Gaussian opacity based on the SDF value. Transformation: Opacity is derived from the SDF value f(\mathbf{x}) using a bell-shaped function controlled by a learnable parameter \beta: \Phi\beta(f(\mathbf{x})) = \frac{e^{-\beta \cdot f(\mathbf{x})}}{(1 + e^{-\beta \cdot f(\mathbf{x})})^2} where \beta controls the shape of the function. Loss: The photometric loss Lc encourages the Gaussian opacity to match rendering contributions, pushing SDF values closer to 0: Lc = \lambda{LD-SSIM} + (1 - \lambda)L1 where \lambda is a weighting factor. Pitfall: Can disrupt surface reconstruction in low-frequency flat areas due to high-frequency textures, leading to noisy structures if Gaussian locations are inaccurate. 2. Loose Coupling: Uses the SDF to constrain the distribution and orientations of Gaussians without directly dictating opacity. Distance Regularization: Forces Gaussians to be near the surface derived from the SDF. Direction Alignment: Aligns the orientation of the Gaussian (direction of the shortest axis) with the surface normal \nabla f(\mathbf{x}). Benefit: Prevents interference with high-frequency appearance supervision and can decrease the number of required Gaussians by 20% without compromising rendering quality. Regularization with Volumetric Rendering: Because supervision from Gaussians is sparse (only at occupied locations), volumetric rendering is used to regularize the continuous SDF field. Ray Casting: For a subset of rays \mathbf{r}, points \mathbf{x}i are sampled along the ray. Alpha and Transmittance: Computed from the SDF using a Sigmoid function \phis: Ti^r = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai = \max \left( \frac{\phis(f(\mathbf{x}i)) - \phis(f(\mathbf{x}{i+1}))}{\phis(f(\mathbf{x}i))}, 0 \right) where Ti^r is transmittance and \alphai is opacity. Rendered Geometry: Depth \tilde{D}(\mathbf{r}) and Normal \tilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) are rendered from the SDF: \tilde{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti^r \alphai ti \tilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti^r \alphai \mathbf{n}i where \mathbf{n}i = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}i) is the normal computed from the SDF gradient, and ti is the depth of the sample point. Consistency Loss: The rendered SDF geometry is aligned with the geometry derived from 3DGS (depth D and normal \mathbf{N}) using: L{vd} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| D(\mathbf{r}) - \tilde{D}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 L{vn} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) - \tilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) \|1 + \| 1 - \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{N}}(\mathbf{r}) \|1 where \mathcal{R} is the set of sampled rays. Optimization Loop: 1. Initialize SDF field (sphere or random). 2. Select coupling strategy (default: loose). 3. For each training iteration: a. Render image from 3DGS and compute photometric loss. b. Compute coupling loss (Tight: opacity alignment; Loose: distance/direction regularization). c. Sample rays, render depth/normal from SDF, and compute volumetric consistency loss L{vd} + L{vn}. d. Backpropagate to update Gaussians and SDF field. 4. Extract mesh using Marching Cubes on the final SDF field. Parameters: \beta: Learnable parameter for tight coupling SDF-to-opacity transformation. \lambda: Weighting factor for photometric loss Lc. Ray Sampling: A few rays are sampled per iteration for volumetric rendering to avoid significant computational cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Supervision: Optimizing Gaussians only provides sparse signals to the SDF. Without volumetric regularization, this leads to floating artifacts in unoccupied free spaces. Tight Coupling Artifacts: High-frequency textures can disrupt surface reconstruction in flat areas under tight coupling, causing noisy surfaces. Initialization: SDF initialization affects convergence; sphere or random initialization is used. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than neural implicit methods. 3DGSR reduces training time from 12 hours (typical for neural implicit methods like Wang et al. [2021]) to 30 minutes, a speedup of more than 20 times. This is achieved by avoiding time-consuming color prediction branches and volumetric rendering losses for optimization, relying instead on 3DGS for efficient rendering. Memory Complexity: Uses multiresolution hash grids for the SDF, which is memory-efficient compared to dense voxel grids. Performance: Achieves a Chamfer-L1 error of 0.72 on benchmark datasets, compared to 1.40 for 2DGS (the state-of-the-art Gaussian-based reconstruction method). Strengths: End-to-end unified optimization eliminates post-processing steps (depth fusion, Poisson reconstruction) and error accumulation. Preserves high rendering quality and efficiency of 3DGS. Limitations: Tight coupling may produce noisy structures if Gaussian locations are inaccurate. Loose coupling is recommended for better generalization. 3DGSR was introduced by Xiaoyang Lyu, Yang-Tian Sun, Yi-Hua Huang, Xiuzhe Wu, Ziyi Yang, Yilun Chen, Jiangmiao Pang, and Xiaojuan Qi. It addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS, which optimizes millions of Gaussians for view synthesis but lacks a structured geometric representation suitable for mesh extraction. Previous Gaussian-based methods like 2DGS required post-processing and suffered from oversmoothed reconstructions. Neural implicit methods provided high-quality surfaces but were slow to train and render. 3DGSR bridges this gap by incorporating an implicit SDF into the 3DGS framework, enabling joint optimization. 3DGSR: Implicit Surface Reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3687952, fetched 2026-10-26

name: GSurf
head: GSurf: Learning Signed Distance Fields from Splatting Opaque Gaussians for High-quality 3D Reconstruction
body: GSurf is a single-branch framework for high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction that jointly optimizes discrete 2D Gaussian primitives and a continuous Signed Distance Field (SDF) without an auxiliary volume-rendering branch. It solves the trade-off between the computational intensity of neural implicit surfaces and the geometric fragmentation of standard Gaussian Splatting by using Gaussian centroids for direct SDF supervision and opacity regularization to create a compact, opaque surface shell. Unlike hybrid approaches that rely on heavy volumetric sampling or point-cloud deformation methods that oversmooth details, GSurf achieves faster convergence and sharper geometric detail by integrating SDF-derived normals and features into the appearance modeling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images of a scene. Outputs: A set of optimized 2D Gaussian primitives (positions, tangents, scales, opacities) and a learned SDF MLP, enabling the rendering of novel views and the extraction of a mesh via marching cubes. Data Structures: The scene is represented by two coupled components: 1. 2D Gaussian Primitives: Each primitive k is defined by: Central position \mathbf{p}k \in \mathbb{R}^3. Two principal tangent vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v \in \mathbb{R}^3. Two scaling factors su, sv \in \mathbb{R}. Opacity \alphak \in [0, 1]. The local transformation matrix \mathbf{H}k \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} is constructed as: \mathbf{H}k = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}k \mathbf{S}k & \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{p}k & 1 \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{R}k = [\mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v, \mathbf{t}u \times \mathbf{t}v] is the rotation matrix and \mathbf{S}k = \text{diag}(su, sv, 0) is the scaling matrix. 2. SDF Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that maps 3D coordinates to signed distance values. It also takes geometric features (normals derived from the SDF) and viewing directions as input to predict view-dependent colors. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a set of 2D Gaussian primitives from the input images (e.g., using standard 3DGS initialization). Initialize the SDF MLP. 2. Sorting: Sort the 2D Gaussians based on the depth of their centers along the view ray. 3. Rendering (Appearance): For a pixel \mathbf{x}, cast a ray and compute the 2D Gaussian value for each primitive i at the intersection point \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) in the local plane: Gi(\mathbf{u}) = \exp \left( -\frac{u^2 + v^2}{2} \right) where \mathbf{u} = (u, v)^T are the local coordinates. Accumulate color using volumetric alpha blending: c(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci where the weight wi is: wi = \alphai Gi(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj Gj(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}))) The color ci is not determined by spherical harmonics but is predicted by the appearance MLP using the Gaussian centroid, SDF-derived normals, geometric features, and viewing direction. Compute the appearance loss L{gs}, which includes RGB reconstruction loss L{rgb}, depth distortion loss L{dep}, and depth-normal consistency loss L{dnc} (as defined in 2DGS). 4. SDF Supervision: Feed the centroids \mathbf{p}k of all Gaussians into the SDF MLP to obtain predicted distances dk = \text{SDF}(\mathbf{p}k). Compute the SDF loss L{sdf}, which typically includes an Eikonal regularization term (|\nabla \text{SDF}| = 1) and a distance loss encouraging dk \approx 0 for surface points. 5. Opacity Regularization: Compute the opacity entropy loss L{ent} to drive opacities toward binary values (0 or 1), effectively binarizing primitives into an opaque bounding shell. 6. Optimization: Minimize the total loss: L{total} = L{gs} + \lambda{sdf} L{sdf} + \lambda{ent} L{ent}. 7. Pruning: Periodically prune Gaussians with low opacity to retain a compact set of mostly opaque surface-supporting primitives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gsurfstep(gaussians, sdfmlp, appearancemlp, images, cameras): # 1. Render Appearance # Sort gaussians by depth for each camera sortedgaussians = sortbydepth(gaussians, cameras) renderedcolors = [] for camera in cameras: rays = castrays(camera) pixelcolors = [] for ray in rays: # Find intersecting gaussians hits = findhits(ray, sortedgaussians) accumulatedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for hit in hits: # Compute local coordinates u, v in the 2D Gaussian plane u, v = transformtolocalplane(hit.gaussian, ray.origin, ray.direction) # Compute 2D Gaussian value gval = exp(-(u2 + v2) / 2.0) # Get color from Appearance MLP # Inputs: centroid, SDF normal, SDF feature, view direction centroid = hit.gaussian.position sdfval = sdfmlp(centroid) sdfnormal = computesdfnormal(sdfmlp, centroid) viewdir = ray.direction color = appearancemlp(centroid, sdfnormal, sdfval, viewdir) # Alpha blending alpha = hit.gaussian.opacity gval weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += weight color accumulatedalpha += weight pixelcolors.append(accumulatedcolor) renderedcolors.append(pixelcolors) # 2. Compute Appearance Loss # Lgs = Lrgb + Ldep + Ldnc lossgs = computeappearanceloss(renderedcolors, images) # 3. Compute SDF Loss # Supervise SDF directly at Gaussian centroids centroids = [g.position for g in gaussians] sdfvalues = sdfmlp(centroids) # Eikonal loss: gradient of SDF should be 1 eikonalloss = computeeikonalloss(sdfmlp, centroids) # Distance loss: encourage centroids to be on zero-level set distanceloss = meansquarederror(sdfvalues, zeroslike(sdfvalues)) losssdf = eikonalloss + distanceloss # 4. Compute Opacity Entropy Loss # Drive opacities to 0 or 1 opacities = [g.opacity for g in gaussians] lossent = computeentropyloss(opacities) # 5. Total Loss and Backprop totalloss = lossgs + lambdasdf losssdf + lambdaent lossent totalloss.backward() # 6. Pruning (Periodic) if step % pruneinterval == 0: gaussians = prunelowopacity(gaussians, threshold=0.01) return totalloss Parameters: \lambda{sdf}: Weight for SDF loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{ent}: Weight for opacity entropy loss. Not given in the sources. Pruning threshold: Typically 0.01 or similar low value to remove transparent primitives. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reflective Surfaces: Standard depth-based methods fail on reflective surfaces. GSurf handles this by using reflective viewpoints to model view-dependent appearance via the MLP, avoiding unreliable depth maps. Semi-transparent Objects: The opacity entropy regularization actively binarizes primitives, which may struggle with genuinely semi-transparent objects if the entropy loss is too strong, though the method claims to handle them better than TSDF/Poisson methods. Degenerate Gaussians: The 2D Gaussian formulation avoids the degeneracy of 3D Gaussians with zero depth extent by using tangent vectors and scaling in a local plane. Time Complexity: O(N{gs}) per pixel, where N{gs} is the number of Gaussians. This is significantly faster than hybrid methods like VolSDF or NeuS which have complexity O(N{ray} N{smp}) due to volumetric ray marching. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of Gaussians N{gs} and the size of the SDF MLP. GSurf produces fewer Gaussians than standard 3DGS or other GS+SDF approaches due to pruning and entropy regularization. Measured Performance: Requires less training time (avoiding the 2-16 hours typical of volumetric SDF approaches) and produces fewer primitives while maintaining or exceeding reconstruction quality. Strengths: Fast convergence, compact representation, sharp geometric details (better than GS-Pull), robust handling of reflective and semi-transparent surfaces. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial Gaussian initialization; the single-branch design means it does not explicitly model volume scattering, unlike volumetric methods. GSurf was proposed by Baixin Xu, Jiangbei Hu, Jiaze Li, and Ying He from Nanyang Technological University and Dalian University of Technology. It was published on arXiv in November 2024 (v4 in July 2026) and later in the Journal of Computer-Aided Design in 2026. The work addresses the limitations of neural implicit surfaces (computational intensity) and standard Gaussian Splatting (geometric fragmentation) by coupling continuous SDF learning with discrete Gaussian splatting. It builds on 2DGS [23] and contrasts with methods like VolSDF [76], GS-Pull [85], and GOF [78]. GSurf: Learning signed distance fields from splatting opaque Gaussians for high-quality 3D reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2026.104106, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Perceptual Wrapper
head: Perceptual Wrapper for 3DGS, Perceptual Wrapper with Common Randomness
body: The Perceptual Wrapper (PW) is a plug-and-play 2D module that enhances the rendered outputs of existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by synthesizing high-frequency texture details in a content- and view-dependent manner. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS in rendering sharp textures, particularly under memory-constrained or rate-distortion-optimized (RDO) pipelines where blurriness is exacerbated. Unlike methods that modify the 3D primitive densification or loss functions directly (e.g., Perceptual-GS), PW operates as a post-processing synthesis network in the image domain, conditioned on pseudo-random Gaussian noise and Plücker embeddings, and is trained using Wasserstein Distortion (WD) loss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base rendered image I{base}^{vj} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W} from view vj, a multi-scale pseudo-random Gaussian noise pyramid C, and per-pixel 6D Plücker embeddings P^{vj} \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times H \times W}. Output: A residual texture detail map R^{vj} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, which is added to the base image to produce the final output I{final}^{vj}. Data Structures: 1. Base Rendered Image (I{base}^{vj}): The standard 3DGS rendering result for view vj. 2. Noise Pyramid (C): An 8-level spatial pyramid C = \{Ci\}{i=0}^7. Level Ci \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{2^i} \times \frac{W}{2^i}}. C0 has dimensions H \times W. Values are sampled independently from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1). The same fixed random seed is used for all views and between training/decoding (common randomness). 3. Plücker Embeddings (P^{vj}): A 6-channel tensor where each pixel (x,y) contains the vector P(x,y) = (d, o \times d). Synthesis Network Architecture: The network f\theta is lightweight, similar to the COOL-CHIC family: 1. Concatenate inputs: I{base}^{vj}, C (upsampled to H \times W via bilinear interpolation), and P^{vj}. 2. Two 1 \times 1 convolutional layers. 3. Two 3 \times 3 residual convolutional layers. 4. Output: R^{vj}. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Plücker Embeddings: For each pixel (x,y) in the target view vj, calculate the normalized viewing direction d and the moment vector o \times d. 2. Generate Noise Pyramid: Using a fixed random seed, generate the 8-level noise pyramid C. 3. Render Base Image: Render the scene using the current 3DGS representation to obtain I{base}^{vj}. 4. Upsample Noise: Bilinearly upsample each level Ci of the noise pyramid to the resolution H \times W. 5. Synthesis Forward Pass: Process the concatenated inputs through the synthesis network f\theta to generate the residual. 6. Reconstruct Final Image: Add the residual to the base image. Formulas: Plücker Embedding Calculation: For a pixel at coordinates (x, y), the 6D vector is P(x, y) = (d, o \times d). The normalized viewing direction d is calculated as: d = \frac{R K^{-1}[x,y,1]^T}{\|R K^{-1}[x,y, 1]^T\|} \in \mathbb{R}^3 where K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the camera intrinsic matrix, R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the camera-to-world rotation matrix, and o \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the camera center in world coordinates. Synthesis Forward Pass: For a specific view vj, the residual details are generated as: R^{vj} = f\theta(\{I{base}^{vj}, C, P^{vj}\}) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Final Image Reconstruction: The final output image is obtained by adding the residual signal to the base rendered image: I{final}^{vj} = I{base}^{vj} + R^{vj}. Total Loss Function: The loss function evaluated across training views is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{WD}(I{final}^{vj}, I{gt}^{vj}) + \mathcal{L}{Reg} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{rate} where the rate term \mathcal{L}{rate} is included only for Rate-Distortion (RD) optimized methods. Parameters: Stage 1 Iterations: 15,000 iterations. Noise Distribution: Standard Normal \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Pyramid Levels: 8 levels (i=0 to 7). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimization Instability: Directly optimizing the full pipeline with Wasserstein Distortion (WD) loss from the outset can destabilize 3DGS training, particularly when Gaussian densification/pruning are still evolving and the representation has not yet converged to a stable geometry. View Consistency: The noise must be view-consistent (fixed across views) to ensure coherent texture synthesis for novel views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatenoisepyramid(H, W, seed): """Generate 8-level spatial pyramid of Gaussian noise with a fixed seed.""" C = [] for i in range(8): h, w = H // (2i), W // (2i) C.append(torch.randn(h, w, generator=torch.Generator().manualseed(seed))) return C def upsamplenoisepyramid(C, H, W): """Bilinearly upsample all noise levels to target resolution.""" return [torch.nn.functional.interpolate(c.unsqueeze(0), size=(H, W), mode='bilinear').squeeze(0) for c in C] def computepluckerembeddings(K, R, o, H, W): """Compute 6D Plücker embeddings for each pixel.""" # K: (3,3), R: (3,3), o: (3,) # Create grid of pixel coordinates y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H), torch.arange(W), indexing='ij') coords = torch.stack([x, y, torch.oneslike(x)], dim=-1).float() # (H, W, 3) # Compute viewing direction d invK = torch.linalg.inv(K) d = torch.einsum('ij,hwj->hwi', invK, coords) # (H, W, 3) d = torch.einsum('ij,hwj->hwi', R, d) # (H, W, 3) d = d / torch.norm(d, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Normalize # Compute moment o x d moment = torch.linalg.cross(o, d) # (H, W, 3) P = torch.cat([d, moment], dim=-1) # (H, W, 6) return P.permute(2, 0, 1) # (6, H, W) def perceptualwrapperforward(Ibase, Cupsampled, P, ftheta): """Forward pass of the synthesis network.""" # Concatenate along channel dimension: (3 + 8 + 6, H, W) inputs = torch.cat([Ibase, Cupsampled, P], dim=0) R = ftheta(inputs) # Residual (3, H, W) Ifinal = Ibase + R return Ifinal, R def trainperceptualwrapper(3DGSmodel, ftheta, trainingviews, gtimages, K, R, o, H, W, seed): """Two-stage training procedure.""" C = generatenoisepyramid(H, W, seed) Cup = upsamplenoisepyramid(C, H, W) # Stage 1: Warm-up (0 to 14,999 iterations) for iter in range(15000): optimizer3dgs.zerograd() Ibase = render3dgs(3DGSmodel, trainingviews, K, R, o) loss = compute3dgsloss(Ibase, gtimages) + LReg + lambda Lrate loss.backward() optimizer3dgs.step() # Stage 2: Joint Optimization (15,000+ iterations) for iter in range(15000, maxiterations): optimizer3dgs.zerograd() optimizernet.zerograd() Ibase = render3dgs(3DGSmodel, trainingviews, K, R, o) P = computepluckerembeddings(K, R, o, H, W) Ifinal, = perceptualwrapperforward(Ibase, Cup, P, ftheta) loss = computewdloss(Ifinal, gtimages) + LReg + lambda Lrate loss.backward() optimizer3dgs.step() optimizernet.step() Time Complexity: The synthesis network is lightweight (two 1\times1 and two 3\times3 conv layers), incurring negligible overhead to rendering speed. Memory Complexity: Adds minimal memory overhead for the synthesis network weights and the noise pyramid (which is generated on-the-fly from a seed, requiring no storage of noise parameters). Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, the lowest-rate point achieved by PW attained an Elo score on par with the highest-rate point of baseline methods (CAT-3DGS Pro and HAC++), corresponding to a 6x reduction in bit-rate at equivalent perceptual quality. Strengths: Plug-and-play compatibility with any existing 3DGS representation; effective at mitigating blurriness in highly textured regions under bandwidth constraints; view-dependent texture synthesis. Limitations: Requires a two-stage training process; relies on a fixed random seed for noise generation. When to use: When perceptual quality is prioritized over strict pixel-wise fidelity, or when operating under strict storage/transmission bandwidth constraints. When not to use: When strict photometric accuracy (e.g., PSNR) is the primary metric, as WD loss optimizes for perceptual similarity rather than pixel-wise error. The Perceptual Wrapper was introduced by H.-B. Yang et al. in the paper "Seeing What Matters: Perceptual Wrapper with Common Randomness for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the limitations of previous perceptual methods like Perceptual-GS, which used sensitivity-guided densification and conventional L1/SSIM losses. The method adopts Wasserstein Distortion (WD) loss, which matches local feature statistics rather than enforcing pixel-wise fidelity, to optimize perceptual quality. It was implemented in PyTorch and tested on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs, evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. Seeing What Matters: Perceptual Wrapper with Common Randomness for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.11782, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Inverse and Internal Rendering
head: GS-IR, Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting, Gradient Calculation for Global Illumination
body: Inverse and Internal Rendering extends 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to handle scenarios where standard surface-based supervision is insufficient or unavailable, specifically targeting internal volumetric structures, unknown lighting conditions, and global illumination effects. It solves the problem that conventional 3DGS optimizes only camera-visible surfaces, leaving occluded interiors empty, and relies on known camera poses and direct lighting. This family sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by introducing plane-based cross-sectional supervision for internal reconstruction, pose-free conditional splatting for sliced data [15745-inner-3d-gaussian-splatting.md], and analytical gradient propagation through global illumination solvers for material and lighting optimization [23297-gradient-calculation-for-global-illumination.md]. The methods in this family share the core 3D Gaussian representation defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details. Each primitive i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, decomposed into scaling S and rotation R such that \Sigma = RSS^\top R^\top Opacity \alphai Color ci, often modeled via Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients The rendering equation for a pixel (u, v) at depth t (or slice) is: I(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N} pi(u, v, t)\alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) where pi(u, v, t) is the screen-space density contribution of the i-th Gaussian, computed as: p(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)} Optimization is performed by minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} against target data (images, cross-sections, or radiance gradients), requiring differentiable rendering pipelines that support backpropagation through the splatting and compositing operations. GS-IR is an inverse rendering approach based on 3D Gaussian Splatting that leverages forward mapping volume rendering to achieve photorealistic novel view synthesis and relighting results, estimating scene geometry, surface material, and environment illumination from multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. It sets itself apart from NeRF-based inverse rendering methods by using 3D Gaussians and forward mapping splatting for real-time rendering efficiency, avoiding the low expressive power and high computational complexity of implicit neural representations. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on ray tracing for occlusion, GS-IR handles occlusion via a baking-based cache, making it available for both objects and unbounded scenes. Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting (InnerGS) is a framework for direct volumetric inference that models continuous volumetric density using 3D Gaussians to reconstruct internal structures from sparse, pose-free sliced data. It solves the problem that standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) relies on camera parameters (view/projection matrices) which are absent in sliced data, and that learned Gaussians concentrate on the object's surface, leaving the interior volume empty. It sets itself apart from siblings like GS-IR by eliminating the need for camera poses and using a slice-based rendering pipeline centered on Conditional Splatting, which dynamically adapts the sampling of Gaussians for each 2D slice. This method computes the analytical gradients of a loss function \mathcal{L} with respect to the underlying geometry, materials, and lighting conditions of a scene represented by 3D Gaussian surfels. It solves the problem of efficiently backpropagating through the global illumination (light transport) solver used in differentiable rendering. Unlike automatic differentiation techniques such as path replay backpropagation, this method exploits the duality between the forward pass (light propagation) and the backward pass (gradient propagation), allowing for non-recursive, accurate, and efficient analytical definitions of gradients for emissions, materials, and geometry. Definition GS-IR is a plane-based internal rendering framework that replaces exterior-view supervision with cross-sectional supervision sampled from a volume to reconstruct internal volumetric structure. Steps 1. Virtual cameras define slicing planes within the volume. 2. A binary mask selects the Gaussian subset whose centers lie within the plane thickness. 3. The selected Gaussian subset is rendered using the original Gaussian rasterizer. 4. Optimization is performed against ground-truth cross-sections generated through trilinear resampling. 5. Distance-aware soft weighting is applied to continuously attenuate Gaussian opacity as the distance from the Gaussian to the plane increases. Parameters Plane thickness: The spatial extent within which Gaussian centers are selected by the binary mask. Performance GS-IR improves PSNR by up to 21.52 dB and SSIM by up to 0.54 on KiTS23 CT and IXI MRI datasets. Comparison Unlike conventional 3DGS which constrains camera-visible surfaces, GS-IR focuses optimization gradients on interior Gaussians to supervise occluded internal regions. Usage GS-IR is applied to 3DGS, 2DGS, and Mip-Splatting without modifying their rasterizers. Definition A procedure to efficiently capture global illumination by updating 3D Gaussians using path-traced renderings, combined with albedo-shading decomposition. Steps 1. Utilize path-traced renderings to efficiently update 3DGS and capture global illumination effects. 2. Apply albedo-shading decomposition strategy to separate intrinsic scene properties for efficient global illumination capture. The concept of inverse rendering with 3D Gaussians was introduced by Choishroy et al. in "Volumetric Plane-Based Gaussian Selection for Internal View Synthesis With 3-D Gaussian Splatting" (2026), addressing the lack of internal supervision in standard 3DGS. The method for analytical gradient calculation for global illumination in Gaussian surfels was detailed in "Gradient Calculation for Global Illumination". The update procedure with albedo-shading decomposition was proposed in "Mesh2GS: White-Box 3DGS Construction via Plenoptic Sampling" (2026). These methods are used in medical imaging (CT/MRI reconstruction), real-time shared rendering, and high-fidelity scene relighting. name: GS-IR
head: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, Inverse Rendering with Gaussians
body: GS-IR is an inverse rendering approach based on 3D Gaussian Splatting that leverages forward mapping volume rendering to achieve photorealistic novel view synthesis and relighting results, estimating scene geometry, surface material, and environment illumination from multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. It sets itself apart from NeRF-based inverse rendering methods by using 3D Gaussians and forward mapping splatting for real-time rendering efficiency, avoiding the low expressive power and high computational complexity of implicit neural representations. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on ray tracing for occlusion, GS-IR handles occlusion via a baking-based cache, making it available for both objects and unbounded scenes. The GS-IR framework consists of three stages: 1) Initial stage: optimize 3D Gaussians for geometry reconstruction using differentiable splatting and supervise normals using depth gradients; 2) Second stage: precompute occlusion based on learned geometry (depth and normal) and store it in a spherical harmonics-based architecture to model indirect illumination; 3) Final stage: combine differentiable splatting with the physical-based rendering (PBR) pipeline to optimize illumination and material-aware 3D Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians with geometry (position, covariance, opacity), normals, material parameters (albedo, metallic, roughness), and an environment map for lighting. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i extends the standard 3D Gaussian representation defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details with additional fields for inverse rendering: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, decomposed into scaling S and rotation R Opacity \alphai Color ci, modeled via Spherical Harmonics coefficients Normal ni, estimated via depth derivation Material parameters (Albedo, Metallic, Roughness) for texture representation Spherical Harmonics coefficients for indirect illumination/occlusion caching Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Stage: Geometry and Normal Optimization Optimize 3D Gaussians using differentiable splatting to reconstruct geometry. Address the challenge that 3DGS does not support producing plausible normals natively and its adaptive control may lead to loose geometry. Introduce a depth-derivation-based regularization strategy: render a depth map \hat{D}, compute pseudo-normals \hat{n}D = \nabla{uv} \hat{D}, and use these to supervise the optimization of normals within the 3D Gaussians. 2. Second Stage: Occlusion Baking Address the challenge that forward mapping cannot trace occlusion like backward mapping. Precompute occlusion based on the learned geometric information (depth and normal). Store occlusion in a spherical harmonics-based architecture to model indirect illumination, inspired by the "Indirect Lighting Cache" used in real-time rendering. Specific implementation details for the SH-based occlusion baking pipeline are not given in the sources. 3. Final Stage: Material and Lighting Optimization Combine differentiable splatting with the physical-based rendering (PBR) pipeline. Optimize material-aware 3D Gaussians (Albedo, Metallic, Roughness) and the environment map (lighting). Lighting is approximated by a learnable environment map. Formulas: Gaussian function: g(x|\mu, \Sigma) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)}. Pseudo-normal derivation: \hat{n}D = \nabla{uv} \hat{D}. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 3DGS does not support producing plausible normals natively. Forward mapping cannot trace occlusion like backward mapping. 3DGS adaptive control of Gaussian density may lead to loose geometry, making it difficult to estimate accurate scene normals. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: GS-IR improves rendering efficiency compared to NeRF-based methods by using forward mapping splatting. It handles occlusion via baking, making it available for both objects and unbounded scenes, unlike TensoIR which is limited to object-level. When to use it and when not: Use when real-time rendering efficiency is required and the scene is unbounded or object-level. Not suitable when ray-traced occlusion is strictly necessary for high-fidelity indirect lighting without baking approximations. GS-IR was proposed by researchers from the School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Tencent. It is the first work to introduce the 3DGS technique for inverse rendering, simultaneously estimating scene geometry, materials, and illumination from multi-view images. The source code is available at https://github.com/lzhnb/GSIR. name: Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Inner Gaussian Splatting, InnerGS
body: Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting (InnerGS) is a framework for direct volumetric inference that models continuous volumetric density using 3D Gaussians to reconstruct internal structures from sparse, pose-free sliced data. It solves the problem that standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) relies on camera parameters (view/projection matrices) which are absent in sliced data, and that learned Gaussians concentrate on the object's surface, leaving the interior volume empty. It sets itself apart from siblings like GS-IR by eliminating the need for camera poses and using a slice-based rendering pipeline centered on Conditional Splatting, which dynamically adapts the sampling of Gaussians for each 2D slice. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse, pose-free sliced data (e.g., medical CT/MRI slices or cross-sections). Each slice provides 2D image data at a specific depth t. Output: A 3D Gaussian representation (means \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities \alpha, colors c) and the rendered volumetric density/color for any depth slice t. Data Structures: The method uses the standard 3D Gaussian representation defined in 3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details. Each primitive i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} Opacity \alphai Color ci (modeled via Spherical Harmonics coefficients) Formulas: The screen-space contribution of the i-th splat at pixel (u, v) on a slice at depth t is computed as density pi(u, v, t) multiplied by opacity \alphai and color ci. The final color is accumulated front-to-back: I(u, v, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N} pi(u, v, t)\alphai ci \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - pj(u, v, t)\alphaj) where N is the total number of Gaussians, and (u, v) are pixel coordinates with u \in [0, W - 1] and v \in [0, H - 1] for an image of width W and height H. The 3D Gaussian density is defined by an unnormalized Gaussian function: p(x) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)} The covariance matrix \Sigma is decomposed into a scaling component S (diagonal matrix with scale factors sx, sy, sz) and a rotation component R (derived from unit quaternion q): \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top Steps: 1. Conditional 2D Gaussian Splatting: For each depth slice t, compute conditional 2D Gaussian splats. This determines the 2D Gaussian center and influence radii in the image plane for that specific slice. This step adapts the bounding box per slice based on conditional Gaussians, unlike 3D Ellipsoid Projection which computes a cube and projects identical bounding boxes across slices. 2. Marginal 1D Gaussian Combination: Combine the conditional 2D Gaussians with a marginal 1D Gaussian along the depth axis to formulate the complete 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) density. This allows the representation to capture continuous volumetric information between sparse slices. 3. Tile-based Rasterization: Perform tile-based rasterization using the formulated 3DGS density. The Gaussians are sorted and rendered in front-to-back order to reconstruct smooth and detailed internal structures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ x, y = center if x - radius < 0 or x + radius >= width or y - radius < 0 or y + radius >= height: return False return True Parameters: Pixel coordinates (u, v) where u \in [0, W - 1] and v \in [0, H - 1]. Position vector \mu = (\mux, \muy, \muz). Covariance matrix \Sigma decomposed into scaling S and rotation R. Spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Opacity parameter \alpha. Pitfalls: Standard 3DGS projection-based mechanism fails for internal volumetric structures because learned Gaussians concentrate on the object's surface, leaving the interior volume empty. Standard 3DGS relies on camera parameters (view/projection matrices) which are absent in sliced data. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, it uses tile-based rasterization similar to 3DGS, which is generally efficient. The conditional splatting adds overhead per slice. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the number of Gaussians N and the number of slices. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates the need for camera poses; plug-and-play; inherently compatible with any data modalities; reconstructs smooth and detailed internal structures from sparse sliced data. Limitations: Relies on sparse sliced data; may not capture complex view-dependent effects as well as full 3DGS if SH degree is low. When to use: When reconstructing internal structures from sparse, pose-free sliced data (e.g., medical imaging). When not to use: When camera poses are available and the goal is surface reconstruction or novel-view synthesis of external scenes (use standard 3DGS). Inner 3D Gaussian Splatting was proposed by Shuxin Liang et al. in 2025. It addresses the limitations of NeRF and standard 3DGS in modeling internal scenes. NeRF requires heavy MLPs and is slow to render, while standard 3DGS fails for internal structures due to its projection-based nature and reliance on camera poses. InnerGS provides a direct volumetric inference framework using 3D Gaussian density.
