name: 3D Language Gaussian Splatting
head: LangSplat
body: 3D Language Gaussian Splatting (LangSplat) constructs a 3D language field using 3D Gaussians to enable precise, efficient open-vocabulary querying in 3D spaces. It addresses the imprecise object boundaries and slow rendering speeds of NeRF-based methods like LERF by leveraging tile-based splatting and hierarchical semantic supervision from SAM. Unlike its siblings that may use direct high-dimensional embedding storage or auxiliary DINO features, LangSplat employs a scene-specific autoencoder to compress CLIP embeddings into a low-dimensional latent space, significantly reducing memory overhead while maintaining multi-view consistency. Inputs: A set of T multi-view images \{It\}{t=1}^T of a 3D scene. Outputs: A set of 3D language Gaussians \mathcal{G}, each parameterized by position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color c, and three latent language embeddings \{f^s, f^p, f^w\} corresponding to subpart, part, and whole semantic levels. A trained scene-specific autoencoder (Encoder E, Decoder \Psi). Data Structures: 1. 3D Language Gaussian Gi: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (often parameterized via rotation q and scale s). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. ci: Color (RGB). f^si, f^pi, f^wi \in \mathbb{R}^d: Latent language embeddings for subpart, part, and whole levels. d is the latent dimension. 2. Autoencoder: Encoder E: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}^d. Decoder \Psi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D. D=512 (CLIP embedding dimension), d=3 (latent dimension). Steps: 1. Hierarchical Semantic Extraction: For each input image It: a. Feed a regular grid of 32 \times 32 point prompts into the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to obtain initial mask sets \{M^0s, M^0p, M^0w\} for subpart, part, and whole levels. b. Filter redundant masks in each set based on predicted IoU score, stability score, and overlap rate. c. Perform comprehensive full-image segmentation for each filtered mask set to generate three segmentation maps: M^st, M^pt, M^wt. d. Extract CLIP image embeddings for each segmented region using the CLIP image encoder V: L^lt(v) = V(It \odot M^l(v)), \quad l \in \{s, p, w\} where M^l(v) is the mask region pixel v belongs to at semantic level l, and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication (masking). 2. Scene-Specific Autoencoder Training: a. Train a lightweight autoencoder to map high-dimensional CLIP features to a low-dimensional latent space. b. The encoder E maps L^lt(v) \in \mathbb{R}^D to H^lt(v) = E(L^lt(v)) \in \mathbb{R}^d. c. The decoder \Psi reconstructs the original embeddings from the latent representation. d. Optimize the autoencoder using the loss: \mathcal{L}{ae} = \sum{l \in \{s,p,w\}} \sum{t=1}^T d{ae}(\Psi(E(L^lt(v))), L^lt(v)) where d{ae} combines L1 distance and cosine distance loss. e. Transform all training CLIP embeddings \{L^lt\} into scene-specific latent features \{H^lt\} using the trained encoder E. 3. 3D Language Gaussian Initialization and Optimization: a. Initialize 3D Gaussians (e.g., from SfM points). Augment each Gaussian Gi with three latent language embeddings \{f^si, f^pi, f^wi\} initialized from the projected latent features H^lt. b. Render the 3D language scene to 2D using tile-based rasterization. For a pixel v and semantic level l, the rendered language embedding F^l(v) is: F^l(v) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} f^li \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathcal{N} is the set of Gaussians in the tile, \alphai is the opacity, and the product term represents transmittance. c. Optimize the Gaussian parameters (including f^li) by minimizing the language loss: \mathcal{L}{lang} = \sum{l \in \{s,p,w\}} \sum{t=1}^T d{lang}(F^lt(v), H^lt(v)) where d{lang} is a distance function (typically cosine or L1) between the rendered latent feature and the target latent feature H^lt(v). d. Jointly optimize with photometric reconstruction losses (L1/SSIM on color c) to ensure visual fidelity [S1, 15930-semantic-and-language-integration.md]. 4. Inference and Querying: a. Render the language embeddings F^l from the optimized 3D Gaussians to 2D. b. Decode the rendered latent features back to CLIP space using the trained decoder: \hat{L}^l = \Psi(F^l) \in \mathbb{R}^D. c. For a text query, compute the CLIP text embedding \phi{qry}. d. Compute the relevancy score for each pixel/point. Let \phi{img} be the decoded CLIP embedding and \phi{canon} be the CLIP embedding of a predefined canonical phrase (e.g., "object", "things", "stuff", "texture"). The relevancy score is: \text{score} = \mini \frac{\exp(\phi{img} \cdot \phi{qry})}{\exp(\phi{img} \cdot \phi{qry}) + \exp(\phi{img} \cdot \phi{canon})} (Note: The source formula uses a min operator over indices i, likely referring to a normalization or specific scoring mechanism described in the appendix, but the core cosine similarity structure is explicit). e. Select the semantic level (s, p, w) that yields the highest relevancy score for the query. f. 3D Object Localization: Choose the 3D point with the highest relevance score. g. 3D Semantic Segmentation: Filter out points with relevancy scores lower than a chosen threshold and predict object masks with the remaining regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class LangSplat: def init(self, dlatent=3, dclip=512): self.dlatent = dlatent self.dclip = dclip # Scene-specific autoencoder self.encoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dclip, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, dlatent)) self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dlatent, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, dclip)) # 3D Gaussians: stored as tensors # mu: (N, 3), cov: (N, 3, 3) or q,s, # alpha: (N,), color: (N, 3) # langfeatures: (N, 3, dlatent) -> [fs, fp, fw] self.gaussians = None self.istrained = False def trainautoencoder(self, clipembeddings): """ clipembeddings: (T, H, W, 3, D) or flattened (Nmasks, D) """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(self.encoder.parameters()) + list(self.decoder.parameters()), lr=1e-3) # Flatten for training flatembs = clipembeddings.view(-1, self.dclip) for epoch in range(100): # Placeholder for convergence latent = self.encoder(flatembs) recon = self.decoder(latent) l1loss = F.l1loss(recon, flatembs) # Cosine distance cossim = F.cosinesimilarity(recon, flatembs, dim=1) cosineloss = 1 - cossim.mean() loss = l1loss + cosineloss optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() self.isautoencodertrained = True def gettargetlatents(self, clipembeddings): """Transform CLIP embeddings to latent space using trained encoder.""" if not self.isautoencodertrained: raise Exception("Autoencoder not trained") flatembs = clipembeddings.view(-1, self.dclip) return self.encoder(flatembs).viewas(clipembeddings) def renderlanguage(self, gaussians, cameraparams): """ Render language features using tile-based splatting. Returns rendered latent features F^l for each level l. """ # Pseudocode for standard 3DGS rasterization adapted for language features # 1. Project 3D Gaussians to 2D tiles # 2. Sort Gaussians by depth within each tile # 3. Alpha blend language features # F^l(v) = sumi fi^l alphai prod{j<i} (1 - alphaj) # This is handled by the rasterizer. # Here we assume a function rasterize that returns (H, W, dlatent) for each level pass def optimizegaussians(self, images, masks, cameraparams, targetlatents): """ images: (T, 3, H, W) masks: (T, 3, H, W, 3) -> [Ms, Mp, Mw] boolean masks targetlatents: (T, 3, H, W, dlatent) -> [Hs, Hp, Hw] """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(self.gaussians.parameters(), lr=1e-4) for step in range(10000): # Forward pass renderedlatents = self.renderlanguage(self.gaussians, cameraparams) # Loss calculation # Llang = suml sumt dlang(F^lt, H^lt) langloss = 0 for l in range(3): # s, p, w # Masked loss or full image loss as per source # Source implies supervision using SAM-based masks mask = masks[:, l] rendered = renderedlatents[:, l] target = targetlatents[:, l] # Apply mask if mask.any(): langloss += F.mseloss(rendered[mask], target[mask]) # Photometric loss (L1/SSIM on color) renderedcolors = self.rendercolor(self.gaussians, cameraparams) photoloss = F.l1loss(renderedcolors, images) totalloss = langloss + photoloss optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # Densification/Pruning steps would go here (standard 3DGS) def query(self, textquery, renderedlatents3d): """ textquery: string renderedlatents3d: (N, 3, dlatent) -> latent features for each 3D point Returns: relevancy scores and best semantic level """ # Encode text query textemb = cliptextencoder(textquery) # (D,) # Canonical phrases canonicalphrases = ["object", "things", "stuff", "texture"] canonembs = [cliptextencoder(p) for p in canonicalphrases] # Decode 3D latents to CLIP space decodedlatents = self.decoder(renderedlatents3d) # (N, 3, D) scores = [] for l in range(3): pointembs = decodedlatents[:, l] # (N, D) # Cosine similarity with query simquery = F.cosinesimilarity(pointembs, textemb, dim=1) # (N,) # Relevancy score calculation # score = mini (exp(sim) / (exp(sim) + exp(simcanon))) # Note: Source formula is slightly ambiguous on 'mini'. # Assuming it refers to normalization against canonical phrases. # We compute similarity against each canonical phrase canonsims = torch.stack([F.cosinesimilarity(pointembs, c, dim=1) for c in canonembs]) # (4, N) # Numerator num = torch.exp(simquery) # Denominator: sum over canonical phrases? Or min? # Source: "mini exp(...) / (exp(...) + exp(...))" # Let's implement the explicit formula structure: # For each point, we compare query vs canonical. # The source says "mini" where i likely indexes the canonical phrases or a specific normalization. # Given "chosen from 'object', 'things'...", we take the max canonical similarity as the denominator baseline? # Or strictly follow the text: min over i of the ratio. ratios = [] for csim in canonsims: ratio = torch.exp(simquery) / (torch.exp(simquery) + torch.exp(csim)) ratios.append(ratio) # Min over canonical phrases levelscore = torch.min(torch.stack(ratios), dim=0)[0] scores.append(levelscore) # Select best level scorestensor = torch.stack(scores) # (3, N) bestlevelidx = torch.argmax(scorestensor, dim=0) # (N,) bestscores = torch.gather(scorestensor, 0, bestlevelidx.unsqueeze(0)).squeeze(0) # (N,) return bestscores, bestlevelidx Memory: Significantly reduced compared to direct CLIP storage. Storing 512-dimensional CLIP features increases memory requirements by over 35 times compared to RGB colors (without spherical harmonics), leading to L1 cache exhaustion. LangSplat uses a latent dimension d=3, drastically lowering this cost. Speed: 199x faster than LERF at 1440x1080 resolution. This efficiency comes from tile-based splatting instead of volume rendering. Accuracy: Localization accuracy on LERF dataset: LangSplat 84.3% overall vs LERF 73.6% vs LSeg 21.1%. 3D semantic segmentation IoU on LERF dataset: LangSplat 51.4% overall vs LERF 37.4% vs LSeg 16.6%. Strengths: Precise object boundaries, efficient rendering, open-vocabulary querying, no need for DINO regularization. Limitations: Requires SAM for initial mask generation; performance depends on the quality of the autoencoder reconstruction; limited to predefined semantic levels (subpart, part, whole) during training. LangSplat was introduced in 2024 by Wang et al.. It builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting and addresses limitations in NeRF-based language fields like LERF, which suffer from imprecise features and slow rendering. It incorporates hierarchical semantics from SAM and uses a scene-specific autoencoder to compress CLIP embeddings. name: Semantics-Controlled Gaussian Splatting
head: SCGS
body: Semantics-Controlled Gaussian Splatting (SCGS) is a method that integrates semantic segmentation directly into the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation by assigning class IDs to individual Gaussians. It solves the problem of accurate scene editing and large-scale object removal in non-circular capturing setups, where traditional convex hull methods fail. Unlike sibling methods that rely on separate classifiers or feature similarity grouping, SCGS alters the rasterization process to allow direct classification in both 2D image space and 3D Gaussian space, enabling targeted removal of specific classes without feature-based ambiguity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse point cloud (from COLMAP), camera poses, RGB images, and ground-truth semantic segmentation maps (continuous labels from SAM DEVA). Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians with semantic class IDs, rendered RGB images, and rendered semantic maps. Data Structures: Each Gaussian G is defined by the standard 3D GS parameters plus a semantic attribute: Center position: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Covariance matrix: \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (derived from rotation and scaling) Density: \sigma Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients: \mathbf{c} for RGB color Semantic class ID: si (assigned directly to the Gaussian) Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from a sparse point cloud. Each Gaussian G is represented by its 3D center position \mathbf{x}, a 3D covariance matrix \Sigma, a density value \sigma, and SH coefficients for RGB. 2. 2D Rasterization (RGB): Convert SH coefficients into RGB values. Splat Gaussians onto the 2D image plane using alpha blending to retrieve pixel color: \text{RGB} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance, \alphai is opacity, and ci is the color. 3. 2D Rasterization (Semantic): Perform a parallel rasterization process for the semantic map. Set SH components to zero to isolate semantic attributes from RGB. The segmentation value for a pixel is computed via alpha blending of class probabilities: \text{SEGMENTATION} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} Ti \alphai s{ic} where s{ic} is the predicted probability for class c at pixel i. 4. Covariance Transformation: Calculate the 2D rasterized Gaussian covariance \Sigma' from the 3D covariance \Sigma using the Jacobian J of the affine approximation and the world-to-camera transformation matrix W: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^T J^T 5. Loss Computation: Apply cross-entropy loss to supervise the 3D GS segmentation through the 2D loss function, enabling backpropagation of the segmentation map similarly to RGB values. The loss function is defined as: \mathcal{L}{seg} = - \sum{i} (s{ic} \log(\hat{s}{ic})) where s{ic} is the ground truth segmentation for class c at pixel i, and \hat{s}{ic} is the predicted probability. 6. Object Removal (Inference): For object removal, filter Gaussians using an indicator function to retain only those not belonging to the removed class ID cr: G{new}(\mathbf{x}; \Sigma) = G(\mathbf{x}; \Sigma) \cdot I(si \neq cr) where I is the indicator function, ensuring only Gaussians not belonging to the removed class ID are retained. Parameters: Hardware: Single RTX 4090 with 24GB VRAM. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Traditional convex hull methods for object removal may remove too much of the scene or fail in non-circular capturing setups; SCGS avoids this by using direct class-based removal. Feature similarity issues in outdoor scenes with significant reflections are addressed by direct class assignment rather than feature space grouping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scgsrender(gaussians, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Renders RGB and Semantic maps for a single view. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: center: (3,) cov3d: (3, 3) opacity: (1,) shrgb: (K,) SH coefficients for color semanticid: (1,) Class ID camera: Camera object with attributes: W2C: (4, 4) World-to-camera matrix fov: Field of view imagewidth, imageheight: int Returns: rgbimage: (H, W, 3) semanticimage: (H, W, C) One-hot or probability map """ # 1. Project Gaussians to 2D # Calculate 2D covariance Sigma' = J W Sigma W^T J^T # J is Jacobian of affine approximation, W is world-to-camera # This step is handled by the CUDA rasterizer kernel projectedgaussians = projectgaussians(gaussians, camera) # 2. Rasterize RGB # RGB = sum(Ti alphai ci) rgbimage = rasterizealphablend( projectedgaussians, attributekey='shrgb', alphakey='opacity', width=imagewidth, height=imageheight) # 3. Rasterize Semantic # Isolate semantic attributes by setting SH components to zero for color # SEGMENTATION = sum(Ti alphai sic) # sic is the probability for class c. Since SCGS assigns direct IDs, # we treat the ID as a one-hot vector or probability distribution over classes. semanticimage = rasterizealphablend( projectedgaussians, attributekey='semanticid', # Treated as class probabilities/one-hot alphakey='opacity', width=imagewidth, height=imageheight) return rgbimage, semanticimage def scgsremoveclass(gaussians, classidtoremove): """ Removes all Gaussians belonging to a specific class. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects classidtoremove: int Returns: filteredgaussians: List of Gaussian objects """ filteredgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Gnew(x; Sigma) = G(x; Sigma) I(si != cr) if g.semanticid != classidtoremove: filteredgaussians.append(g) return filteredgaussians Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Outperforms baseline using continuous labels from SAM DEVA on all tested outdoor scenes. On the 3D-OVS dataset, it outperforms existing work on one out of five scenes and performs competitively on others. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables accurate scene editing and extraction of large scene parts; works well in non-"circling" setups; avoids feature similarity issues in reflective outdoor scenes; allows direct removal of complete classes at a large scale. Limitations: Requires ground-truth semantic segmentation maps for training (continuous labels from SAM DEVA). When to use: When accurate large-scale object removal or scene editing is required in non-circular capturing setups, especially for outdoor scenes with reflections. When not: When ground-truth semantic labels are unavailable or when computational resources are severely limited (compared to methods requiring less VRAM, though SCGS fits on 24GB). Origin: SCGS was introduced in the paper "Semantics-Controlled Gaussian Splatting for Outdoor Scene Reconstruction and Rendering in Virtual Reality". History and Development: The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [20] and addresses limitations in object removal for non-circular capturing setups. It diverges from traditional classification-based approaches [60, 63] by assigning class IDs directly during training. Where it is used: Outdoor scene reconstruction and rendering in Virtual Reality, specifically for scenarios where the user is surrounded by the virtual environment. name: DIGS (Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting)
head: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting
body: DIGS is a training-free framework for open-vocabulary 3D segmentation that decouples instance discovery from linguistic naming by maintaining multi-peaked label distributions at object boundaries. It solves the boundary ambiguity problem inherent in prior methods that force Gaussians into single hard labels, enabling clean instance segmentation via late-argmax rendering and a class-agnostic instance ontology. Unlike training-based methods like LaGa or LangSplat, DIGS requires no per-scene gradient optimization, completing mapping in minutes rather than hours. DIGS operates in two stages: Class-Agnostic Mapping (Stage 1) and Multi-Modal Instance Encoding (Stage 2). It augments the standard 3D Gaussian parameter set \Thetai = \{xi, qi, si, \alphai, ci\} with a distribution-informed (DI) semantic state. Inputs: A sequence of RGB images \{I^{(t)}\} from a calibrated camera trajectory. Camera poses for each frame t. A text prompt P{query} for open-vocabulary querying. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} with augmented semantic states. A class-agnostic instance ontology \mathcal{O} mapping Gaussians to persistent instances. Per-instance embeddings \mathbf{e}j for semantic retrieval. Per-Gaussian DI Semantic State: Each Gaussian g maintains: \hat{H}{g,k}: Top-M Hit Accumulator, a vector of size M storing evidence counts for the top M labels. \hat{\pi}{g,k}: Top-M categorical label distribution, a vector of size M storing normalized probabilities for the top M labels. Gj: Per-instance footprint, a set of Gaussian indices belonging to instance j. Lifecycle counters: Tracking the age and stability of the instance association. Instance Ontology: A bidirectional state machine maintaining per-instance footprints Gj and lifecycle counters. 1. Class-Agnostic 2D Observation: For each frame t, apply the Segment Anything Model (SAM) in automatic mask generation mode to produce class-agnostic 2D instance masks S^{(t)} = \{\Omegai\}{i=1}^{ns}. Apply mask-NMS post-processing to remove redundant, highly overlapping masks. 2. Top-K Geometry-Aware Rendering: Extend the 3DGS CUDA rasterizer to output, alongside the rendered RGB image, the top-K contributing Gaussian indices and their alpha-compositing weights for every pixel p. Calculate the weight w{p,k} for the k-th Gaussian at pixel p using the effective opacity o{p,k}: w{p,k} = o{p,k} \prod{k'<k} (1 - o{p,k'}) where o{p,k} is the effective opacity of the k-th Gaussian at pixel p. Store the correspondence as Gp = (g{p,k}, w{p,k}){k=1}^K. 3. Hungarian Matching: Match the class-agnostic 2D instance masks from SAM to the Late-Argmax-rendered label map to establish correspondence between 2D masks and 3D Gaussians. The Late-Argmax renderer determines the label for each pixel by aggregating the top-M distributions of contributing Gaussians and selecting the dominant label, allowing boundary Gaussians to contribute proportionally to adjacent instances. 4. Tempered Dirichlet Update: Update the semantic state of each Gaussian using a Tempered Dirichlet Update rule. This update maintains each Gaussian's top-M Hit Accumulator \hat{H}{g,k} and label distribution \hat{\pi}{g,k}. The injection of new evidence is bounded by \eta^{(t)}i \cdot W^{(t)}i < \tau (Proposition 1), ensuring stability. Here, \eta^{(t)}i is the learning rate or injection factor and W^{(t)}i is the weight of the incoming evidence at frame t. 5. Ontology Aggregation: Aggregate the per-Gaussian distributions into a persistent class-agnostic instance ontology using a bidirectional state machine. This maintains per-instance footprints Gj and lifecycle counters, grouping Gaussians that consistently co-occur and share semantic evidence. 6. Auto-View Selection: For each stable instance in the ontology, perform Auto-View Selection to yield paired context and isolated renderings of the instance's 3D footprint Gj. 7. Visual and Text Embedding Generation: Compute the CLIP visual embedding \mathbf{v}j of the isolated 3D footprint rendering. Generate an attribute description for the instance using a Large Language Model (LLM). Compute the CLIP-text embedding \mathbf{t}j of this LLM-generated description. 8. Embedding Fusion: Linearly fuse the CLIP visual embedding with the CLIP-text embedding to form the final per-instance embedding \mathbf{e}j: \mathbf{e}j = \lambda \mathbf{v}j + (1 - \lambda) \mathbf{t}j where \lambda is a fusion weight. 9. Open-Vocabulary Query: Encode the text prompt P{query} using CLIP-text to get \mathbf{q}. Match \mathbf{q} to the per-instance embeddings \mathbf{e}j by cosine similarity to perform open-vocabulary query without per-query retraining. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch from segmentanything import sammodelregistry, SamAutomaticMaskGenerator from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor, AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM M = 10 # Top-M labels K = 5 # Top-K Gaussians tau = 0.1 # Injection bound threshold lambdafusion = 0.5 # Fusion weight def computealphacompositingweight(opacity, prevopacities): """ Computes alpha-compositing weight for a Gaussian. wp,k = op,k product{k'<k} (1 - op,k') """ # prevopacities is a tensor of shape (k,) containing opacities of Gaussians k'<k transmittance = torch.prod(1 - prevopacities) return opacity transmittance def tempereddirichletupdate(hitaccumulator, labeldistribution, newevidence, injectionweight, tau): """ Updates the Gaussian's semantic state with a tempered Dirichlet rule. Ensures injection bound: injectionweight newevidenceweight < tau """ # Check injection bound if injectionweight newevidence > tau: # Scale down injection if it exceeds bound effectiveinjection = tau / newevidence injectionweight else: effectiveinjection = injectionweight # Update Hit Accumulator # Assuming newevidence is a sparse vector or index of the hit label hitaccumulator[newevidence] += effectiveinjection # Normalize to get new label distribution # Add a small epsilon for numerical stability epsilon = 1e-8 labeldistribution = hitaccumulator + epsilon labeldistribution = labeldistribution / labeldistribution.sum() return hitaccumulator, labeldistribution def digspipeline(images, poses, textprompt): """ Main DIGS pipeline. images: List of RGB images poses: List of camera poses textprompt: String for open-vocabulary query """ # Initialize 3D Gaussians with standard parameters gaussians = initialize3dgaussians(images, poses) # Initialize SAM sam = sammodelregistry"vith".cuda() maskgenerator = SamAutomaticMaskGenerator(sam) # Initialize CLIP clipmodel = CLIPModel.frompretrained("openai/clip-vit-large-patch14") clipprocessor = CLIPProcessor.frompretrained("openai/clip-vit-large-patch14") # Initialize LLM for description generation tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.frompretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf") llm = AutoModelForCausalLM.frompretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf").cuda() # Stage 1: Class-Agnostic Mapping for t, (image, pose) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # Step 1: Class-Agnostic 2D Observation masks = maskgenerator.generate(image) masks = applymasknms(masks) # Remove redundant masks # Step 2: Top-K Geometry-Aware Rendering # Render RGB and get top-K Gaussians and weights for each pixel rgbimage, topkgaussians, topkweights = render3dgswithtopk(gaussians, pose, K=K) # Step 3: Hungarian Matching # Match 2D masks to Late-Argmax rendered label map # Late-Argmax: Aggregate top-M distributions of contributing Gaussians, pick dominant label labelmap = lateargmaxrender(topkgaussians, topkweights, gaussians.semanticstate) masktogaussianmapping = hungarianmatch(masks, labelmap) # Step 4: Tempered Dirichlet Update for gaussianidx, maskidx in masktogaussianmapping.items(): gaussian = gaussians[gaussianidx] # Determine new evidence from mask (e.g., mask ID or region) newevidence = maskidx injectionweight = topkweights[gaussianidx] # Weight from rendering gaussian.hitaccumulator, gaussian.labeldistribution = \ tempereddirichletupdate( gaussian.hitaccumulator, gaussian.labeldistribution, newevidence, injectionweight, tau) # Step 5: Ontology Aggregation updateontology(gaussians, masktogaussianmapping) # Stage 2: Multi-Modal Instance Encoding instanceembeddings = {} for instanceid, footprint in ontology.instances.items(): # Step 6: Auto-View Selection contextrendering, isolatedrendering = autoviewselection(footprint, gaussians) # Step 7: Visual and Text Embedding Generation # Visual Embedding visualinput = clipprocessor(images=isolatedrendering, returntensors="pt").cuda() visualembedding = clipmodel.getimagefeatures(visualinput) # Text Embedding via LLM # Generate description based on visual features or instance ID prompt = f"Describe the object in the image: {isolatedrendering}" inputs = tokenizer(prompt, returntensors="pt").cuda() with torch.nograd(): outputs = llm.generate(inputs, maxnewtokens=50) description = tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skipspecialtokens=True) textinput = clipprocessor(text=[description], returntensors="pt").cuda() textembedding = clipmodel.gettextfeatures(textinput) # Step 8: Embedding Fusion fusedembedding = lambdafusion visualembedding + (1 - lambdafusion) textembedding instanceembeddings[instanceid] = fusedembedding # Querying # Step 9: Open-Vocabulary Query queryinput = clipprocessor(text=[textprompt], returntensors="pt").cuda() queryembedding = clipmodel.gettextfeatures(queryinput) similarities = {} for instanceid, emb in instanceembeddings.items(): sim = torch.cosinesimilarity(queryembedding, emb, dim=1) similarities[instanceid] = sim.item() bestinstance = max(similarities, key=similarities.get) return bestinstance, similarities M: The number of top labels maintained in the explicit categorical label distribution per primitive (top-M label distribution). Typical value: 10. K: The number of top contributing Gaussians and their weights output by the extended rasterizer for each pixel (top-K geometry-aware rendering). Typical value: 5. \tau: The threshold for the injection bound in the Tempered Dirichlet Update, ensuring \eta^{(t)}i \cdot W^{(t)}i < \tau. Typical value: 0.1. Boundary Gaussians: Prior methods force boundary Gaussians into a hard decision (single one-hot label or continuous feature), leading to blurred rendered edges or semantically ambiguous mixtures. DIGS handles this by maintaining multi-peaked label distributions and using late-argmax rendering, where boundary Gaussians contribute proportionally to adjacent instances. Injection Bound: The Tempered Dirichlet Update must respect the injection bound \eta^{(t)}i \cdot W^{(t)}i < \tau to ensure stability and prevent overfitting to noisy masks. Time Complexity: Class-agnostic mapping completes in 0.91 min on a single A100 GPU, a 60–250× reduction compared to 1–4 h of per-scene gradient training. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On LERF-OVS, DIGS achieves 71.95% mean mIoU, outperforming training-free SFS and training-based LaGa baselines. On LERF-Mask, DIGS achieves 91.71 mean mIoU, which is +3.3 over the previous best ObjectGS (88.4). Scaling: DIGS serves native 3D queries in 5.4 ms. Strengths: Training-free, fast, high boundary fidelity, open-vocabulary query without retraining. Limitations: Relies on SAM for initial mask generation, which may fail on textureless or reflective surfaces. LLM dependency for description generation adds latency to the encoding stage. DIGS was introduced in the paper "DIGS: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation". It addresses the limitations of prior 3D Gaussian segmentation methods that require per-scene gradient training or closed-form distillation, which commit each primitive to a single feature and degrade boundary fidelity. DIGS builds on the 3DGS rendering pipeline and integrates SAM, CLIP, and LLMs to achieve training-free open-vocabulary segmentation. name: 3D Instance Segmentation with Contrastive Learning
head: Contrastive 3DGS Segmentation
body: This method segments 3D Gaussian primitives into distinct object instances by training per-Gaussian semantic features using contrastive learning on 2D masks derived from text queries. It solves the problem of assigning semantic identity to Gaussian primitives, which do not strictly model object geometry and often include low-opacity primitives or large primitives shared among objects. It differs from sibling methods by relying on interactive 2D mask generation via GroundingDINO and SAM-HQ, followed by contrastive feature optimization and space-carving post-processing, rather than language-guided training or generalizable encoders [S1, 12438-langsplat-training-procedure.md, 16774-generalizable-semantic-gaussian-splatting.md]. Inputs: A set of training images and camera poses. A text query for each instance to be segmented (e.g., "pillar"). Pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting parameters \Thetai = \{xi, qi, si, \alphai, ci\}. Outputs: A set of segmented instances I1, \dots, IM, where each instance is a subset of Gaussian primitives. 2D masks \{M{q,j}\} for each instance q in each training view j. Data Structures: Per-Gaussian trainable feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^d (dimension d not specified in sources). 2D masks M{q,j}: Binary masks for instance q in view j. Parameters: Push loss margin: 0.3. Hard case threshold: 0.5. Feature similarity threshold \tau: 0.1. Pixel sampling counts: Mu = 4096 (pixels per image), Ms = 4096 (pixels per mask). Regularization weights: \lambda{\text{opacity}}, \lambda{\text{scale}} (values not given in sources). Steps: 1. Generate 2D Masks: For each training view and text query, use GroundingDINO to output bounding boxes. Feed these boxes to SAM-HQ to output 2D masks per instance. Define the "background" mask as the complement of the union of all instance masks. 2. Regularize 3DGS Training: During the initial 3DGS optimization, add L1 regularization to opacity \mathbf{o}i and scaling \mathbf{s}i to discourage low-opacity primitives under surfaces and large primitives shared among objects: \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \lambda{\text{opacity}} \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{o}i + \lambda{\text{scale}} \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \mathbf{s}i where N is the number of Gaussian primitives. 3. Train Per-Gaussian Features: After 3DGS training, initialize per-Gaussian features fi. Rasterize these features into per-pixel features \hat{f}p using standard alpha blending. Sample pixel pairs to compute contrastive loss: Sample Mu pixels uniformly in the image and Ms pixels per mask. If two pixels belong to the same 2D mask, compute the pull loss (cosine distance) to pull their features together. If two pixels belong to different masks, compute the push loss (cosine distance) with a margin of 0.3 to push their features apart. Add extra loss terms for "hard cases" where the distance between features of different masks is larger than 0.5. Weight the pull loss by the ratio of negative-to-positive pairs to counter imbalance. Include a regularization term to encourage rendered features \hat{f} to be unit norm. 4. Interactive Segmentation: User clicks inside the mask of an instance in any training view. Select the rendered feature fq corresponding to the clicked pixel as the query feature. Compute 2D masks \{M{q,j}\} for instance q in each training view j by comparing rendered features with fq. Segment instance Iq by selecting all Gaussians with features fi such that d(fi, fq) \leq \tau, where d is cosine distance and \tau = 0.1. 5. Post-processing (Space Carving): Remove residual Gaussians from the background reconstruction. For each Gaussian, check if at least one of the following conditions is met in every training image: 1. Center projects inside instance 2D masks \{M{q,j}\}. 2. Center projects outside image boundary. 3. Center is not visible in current camera (e.g., behind camera). If met for all views, remove the Gaussian from the background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generate2dmasks(trainingviews, textquery): masks = {} for view in trainingviews: boxes = GroundingDINO(view.image, textquery) instancemasks = SAMHQ(view.image, boxes) backgroundmask = ~union(instancemasks) masks[view.id] = {'instances': instancemasks, 'background': backgroundmask} return masks def traincontrastivefeatures(gaussians, trainingviews, masks, Mu=4096, Ms=4096): # Initialize features for g in gaussians: g.feature = randomunitvector() for epoch in range(numepochs): for view in trainingviews: # Sample pixels sampledpixels = samplepixels(view.image, Mu, Ms, masks[view.id]) # Rasterize features for sampled pixels pixelfeatures = {} for p in sampledpixels: pixelfeatures[p] = rasterizefeature(gaussians, p, view.camera) # Compute contrastive loss loss = 0 positivepairs = [] negativepairs = [] for p1, p2 in pairpixels(sampledpixels, masks[view.id]): f1 = pixelfeatures[p1] f2 = pixelfeatures[p2] dist = cosinedistance(f1, f2) if samemask(p1, p2, masks[view.id]): positivepairs.append(dist) else: negativepairs.append(dist) if dist > 0.5: # Hard case loss += hardcaseloss(dist) # Pull loss (weighted by negative/positive ratio) if positivepairs: pullloss = mean(positivepairs) weight = len(negativepairs) / len(positivepairs) loss += weight pullloss # Push loss with margin if negativepairs: pushloss = marginloss(negativepairs, margin=0.3) loss += pushloss # Feature normalization regularization normloss = mean([norm(f) - 1.0 for f in pixelfeatures.values()]) loss += normloss # Update features updategaussianfeatures(gaussians, loss) def segmentinstance(querypixel, gaussians, trainingviews, masks, tau=0.1): # Get query feature from clicked pixel queryfeature = rasterizefeature(gaussians, querypixel, querypixel.camera) # Segment Gaussians instancegaussians = [] for g in gaussians: dist = cosinedistance(g.feature, queryfeature) if dist <= tau: instancegaussians.append(g) # Generate 2D masks for this instance in all views instancemasks = {} for view in trainingviews: viewmasks = [] for p in view.imagepixels: f = rasterizefeature(gaussians, p, view.camera) if cosinedistance(f, queryfeature) <= tau: viewmasks.append(p) instancemasks[view.id] = viewmasks return instancegaussians, instancemasks def spacecarving(gaussians, instancemasks, trainingviews): gaussianstoremove = [] for g in gaussians: remove = True for view in trainingviews: projected = project(g.center, view.camera) insideinstance = False for instmasks in instancemasks.values(): if projected in instmasks: insideinstance = True break outsideboundary = not isinsideimage(projected) notvisible = isbehindcamera(g.center, view.camera) if not (insideinstance or outsideboundary or notvisible): remove = False break if remove: gaussianstoremove.append(g) for g in gaussianstoremove: removefromscene(g) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Interactive segmentation requires only one click per instance. 2D masks aggregate information from all views, resulting in better masks than SAM-HQ alone. Regularization and post-processing improve visual quality. Limitations: Low-opacity Gaussians under surfaces may not receive enough gradients. Large Gaussians shared among objects may get conflicting gradients. Residual Gaussians may remain, requiring space carving. When to use: When interactive segmentation of specific instances in a 3DGS scene is required, and text queries can be provided. When not to use: When automatic, fully unsupervised segmentation is needed without user interaction. The method is described in "Splat and Replace: 3D Reconstruction with Repetitive Elements". It builds on previous work [Bhalgat et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2023] and uses contrastive learning [Radford et al. 2021]. It addresses challenges in applying contrastive learning to 3DGS, such as low-opacity primitives and shared large primitives. name: NLI4VolVis Pipeline
head: Natural Language Interaction for Volume Visualization via LLM Multi-Agents and Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: NLI4VolVis is a framework that enables natural language interaction with volumetric datasets by integrating multi-view semantic segmentation, 3D open-vocabulary scene understanding, and editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It solves the problem of making scientific visualization (SciVis) accessible and interactive by allowing users to query, edit, and stylize volumetric scenes via natural language commands processed by Large Language Model (LLM) agents. Unlike sibling methods that primarily focus on static semantic feature accumulation or single-model training, NLI4VolVis decomposes the scene into independent, editable Gaussian components per semantic segment and composes them, while employing a 2D stylization approach (InstructPix2Pix) rather than 3D style transfer to avoid artifacts and training overhead. The pipeline consists of six stages: (a) Multi-view segmentation, (b) semantic understanding via CLIP, (c) editable Gaussian training, (d) composition, (e) function-calling tools, and (f) perception-action (VPA) loop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A new volumetric dataset. Output: An interactive, editable 3D scene representation supporting real-time color/opacity/lighting editing, open-vocabulary querying, and 2D stylization, controlled via natural language. Data Structures: The system maintains independent 3DGS models for each segmented semantic component. Each model consists of Gaussian parameters \Thetai = \{xi, qi, si, \alphai, ci\}. The final scene is represented by the concatenation of these component models. Steps: 1. Multi-view Rendering: Render multi-view images of the volumetric dataset using a preset Transfer Function (TF) in ParaView. 2. Multi-view Segmentation: Process the rendered multi-view images using a selected multi-view semantic segmentation method to identify semantic components. 3. View Selection and Embedding: For each segmented component, perform entropy-guided view selection to identify the most informative frames. Embed these informative frames and associated textual descriptions using the CLIP model to achieve robust open-vocabulary scene understanding. 4. Editable Gaussian Training: Train an independent, editable 3DGS model (specifically using iVR-GS [58]) for each segmented semantic component. This allows each component to be queried and edited separately. 5. Composition: Assemble the final scene by combining the trained component models. This is achieved through the concatenation of Gaussian parameters, enabling composability. 6. LLM Agent Interaction: Deploy a hierarchical multi-agent system powered by LLMs. Agents utilize external function-calling tools to interpret user intents and execute actions such as open-vocabulary querying, optimal view selection, interactive scene editing, and 2D stylization. 7. VPA Loop: Collaborative agents follow the Vision-Perception-Action (VPA) loop [38] to iteratively refine visualizations based on user input. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nli4volvispipeline(volumetricdataset): # Stage 1: Multi-view Segmentation # Render multi-view images using a preset Transfer Function (TF) in ParaView multiviewimages = renderwithpresettf(volumetricdataset) # Process images with a selected multi-view semantic segmentation method segmentedcomponents = multiviewsegmentation(multiviewimages) componentmodels = [] # Stage 2 & 3: Semantic Understanding and Editable Gaussian Training for component in segmentedcomponents: # Entropy-guided view selection to find informative frames informativeframes = entropyguidedviewselection(component) # Embed frames and text with CLIP for open-vocabulary understanding # This aligns user queries with volumetric structures semanticembeddings = clipembed(informativeframes, textdescriptions) # Train independent editable 3DGS model (iVR-GS) for this component # Supports real-time editing of color, opacity, and lighting model = traineditable3dgs(component, informativeframes, semanticembeddings) componentmodels.append(model) # Stage 4: Composition # Combine component models via concatenation of Gaussian parameters fullscenemodel = concatenatemodels(componentmodels) # Stage 5 & 6: LLM Agent Interaction # Initialize LLM agents with function-calling tools agents = initializellmagents(functions=[ openvocabularyquery, selectview, editsceneattributes, apply2dstylization ]) # Stage 7: VPA Loop while userinteractionactive(): userinput = getusernaturallanguageinput() # Agents interpret intent and generate declarative commands actionplan = agents.plan(userinput) # Execute actions and refine visualization for command in actionplan: if command.type == "query": result = openvocabularyquery(fullscenemodel, command.args) elif command.type == "edit": fullscenemodel = editsceneattributes(fullscenemodel, command.args) elif command.type == "stylize": # Use InstructPix2Pix (IP2P) for 2D stylization # Note: This does not maintain multi-view consistency but offers # greater stylistic versatility than 3D style transfer stylizedimage = apply2dstylization(fullscenemodel, command.args) renderoutput = stylizedimage else: renderoutput = render(fullscenemodel) display(renderoutput) Parameters: Transfer Function (TF): Preset TF used in ParaView for initial rendering. Stylization Method: InstructPix2Pix (IP2P) [3] is used for 2D stylization. Segmentation Model: A selected multi-view semantic segmentation method. Embedding Model: CLIP. Base 3DGS Variant: iVR-GS [58] is used for editable training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 3D Style Transfer Artifacts: Applying 3D style transfer methods like StyleGaussian [36] to SciVis data introduces noticeable artifacts and requires substantial training time for each scene. NLI4VolVis avoids this by using 2D stylization. Multi-view Consistency: The 2D stylization approach using IP2P has known limitations in maintaining multi-view consistency. Geometry Preservation: Most 3D style transfer methods alter only color attributes while preserving geometry, limiting expressiveness for creative or structural editing. Time Complexity: Training requires substantial time if 3D style transfer were used, but NLI4VolVis uses independent component training which scales with the number of segments. The VPA loop adds latency per interaction step based on LLM inference and tool execution. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of semantic components, as each is stored as an independent 3DGS model. Strengths: Enables real-time editing of color, opacity, and lighting; supports composability; allows open-vocabulary querying and interactive editing via natural language; offers greater stylistic versatility through 2D stylization. Limitations: 2D stylization does not maintain multi-view consistency; relies on external tools (ParaView, CLIP, IP2P); performance depends on the quality of multi-view segmentation. When to use: When natural language interaction, open-vocabulary querying, and flexible 2D stylization are required for volumetric data, and multi-view consistency during stylization is not critical. When not to use: When strict multi-view consistency during stylization is required, or when 3D structural editing is needed beyond color/opacity changes. NLI4VolVis was introduced to make Volume Visualization (VolVis) more accessible across various scenarios by harnessing LLMs' planning and reasoning capabilities. It integrates concepts from 3D open-vocabulary segmentation, editable Gaussian Splatting (iVR-GS), and multi-agent systems. The framework addresses limitations of previous 3D style transfer methods like StyleGaussian, which suffer from artifacts in SciVis and lack structural editing capabilities. NLI4VolVis: Natural Language Interaction for Volume Visualization via LLM Multi-Agents and Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3633888, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG)
head: 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG) primitive, 3D-DoG
body: 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG) is a volumetric primitive variant designed to enhance the representation of fine geometric details and edges in compact 3D Gaussian Splatting models. It solves the limitation of standard smooth Gaussian kernels, which struggle to capture high-frequency details when the number of primitives is aggressively reduced. Unlike standard 3D Gaussians that only contribute positive density, the 3D-DoG models both positive and negative spatial responses, allowing it to implement color subtraction in \alpha-blending to sharpen boundaries. The 3D-DoG primitive is defined as the difference between a primary Gaussian G(\mathbf{x}) and a pseudo-Gaussian Gp(\mathbf{x}). The primary Gaussian retains standard parameters, while the pseudo-Gaussian shares the same center coordinates but has modified opacity and scale parameters. Input: The parameters of the primary 3D Gaussian \mathbf{G} (center \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}{color}) and the new learnable parameters for the pseudo-Gaussian. Output: A composite primitive that renders with a positive-density lobe and a negative-density ring, effectively subtracting color from overlapping regions to enhance contrast. The 3D-DoG primitive extends the standard 3D Gaussian parameter set with four additional learnable parameters per primitive: 1. Opacity factor: f\alpha 2. Scaling factors: f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs} These parameters are typically initialized to values less than 1.0. The 3D-DoG primitive \text{DoG}(\mathbf{x}) is calculated as: \text{DoG}(\mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{x}) - Gp(\mathbf{x}) Where G(\mathbf{x}) is the primary Gaussian and Gp(\mathbf{x}) is the pseudo-Gaussian. The pseudo-Gaussian Gp(\mathbf{x}) shares the same center and rotation as G(\mathbf{x}) but uses a different scaling matrix \mathbf{S}p and opacity \alphap. The scaling matrix \mathbf{S}p is calculated by element-wise multiplication of the primary Gaussian's scaling matrix and the transpose of the pseudo-Gaussian's scaling factors matrix: \mathbf{S}p = \begin{bmatrix} sx & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & sy & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & sz \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} f{xs} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & f{ys} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & f{zs} \end{bmatrix}^T Note: Since the scaling factors matrix is diagonal, the transpose operation does not change the matrix structure, but the formula explicitly denotes the element-wise product of the primary scales and the factors. The opacity \alphap of the pseudo-Gaussian is calculated as: \alphap = f\alpha \cdot \alpha Where \alpha is the opacity of the primary Gaussian. f\alpha: Opacity factor for the pseudo-Gaussian. Set to values less than 1.0. f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs}: Scaling factors for the pseudo-Gaussian. Set to values less than 1.0. These four parameters are learnable during optimization. 1. Pruning Phase: Perform standard 3D Gaussian densification and pruning. The 3D-DoG is not introduced during initial densification. 2. Activation: After the pruning process finishes, activate 3D-DoG primitives in the compact model. This is done by enabling the parameters [f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs}] and \alphap for all primitives. 3. Optimization: Continue training with the same loss functions. The primary Gaussian and pseudo-Gaussian parameters are jointly optimized. 4. Density Control: Evaluate \alphap across all primitives to identify those with the lowest values, which indicate marginal impact of the pseudo-Gaussian representation. 5. Degeneration: If \alphap falls below a predefined threshold (or reaches 0), the 3D-DoG degenerates into a standard 3D Gaussian, as the negative component vanishes. 6. Proportion Optimization: Optimize the overall proportion of 3D-DoG primitives in the point cloud after pruning. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Gaussian3D: def init(self, center, rotation, scale, opacity, color): self.center = center self.rotation = rotation self.scale = scale self.opacity = opacity self.color = color def evaluate(self, x): # Standard 3D Gaussian density and color contribution at point x # Computes covariance transformation, distance weighting, and alpha blending pass class Gaussian3DDoG: def init(self, primarygaussian, falpha, fxs, fys, fzs): """ Initialize a 3D-DoG primitive. Args: primarygaussian: Gaussian3D instance with standard params falpha: Opacity factor for pseudo-Gaussian (< 1.0) fxs, fys, fzs: Scaling factors for pseudo-Gaussian (< 1.0) """ self.primary = primarygaussian self.falpha = falpha self.fxs = fxs self.fys = fys self.fzs = fzs # Pseudo-Gaussian shares center and rotation with primary self.pseudocenter = primarygaussian.center self.pseudorotation = primarygaussian.rotation # Sp = diag(sx, sy, sz) diag(fxs, fys, fzs)^T # Since both are diagonal, this is element-wise multiplication self.pseudoscale = ( primarygaussian.scale[0] fxs, primarygaussian.scale[1] fys, primarygaussian.scale[2] fzs) # alphap = falpha alpha self.pseudoopacity = falpha primarygaussian.opacity def evaluate(self, x): """ Evaluate the 3D-DoG primitive at point x. DoG(x) = G(x) - Gp(x) """ # Evaluate primary Gaussian G(x) gprimary = self.primary.evaluate(x) # Evaluate pseudo-Gaussian Gp(x) # Gp uses same center/rotation but different scale and opacity gpseudo = Gaussian3D( center=self.pseudocenter, rotation=self.pseudorotation, scale=self.pseudoscale, opacity=self.pseudoopacity, color=self.primary.color).evaluate(x) return gprimary - gpseudo def isstandardgaussian(self): """ Check if the 3D-DoG has degenerated to a standard Gaussian. This occurs when alphap is effectively 0. """ return self.pseudoopacity <= 0.0 Degeneration: When \alphap = 0, the 3D-DoG becomes equivalent to a standard 3D Gaussian. The renderer should skip negative component computation for this state. Negative Density: The negative-density component implements color subtraction in \alpha-blending. The rendering pipeline must support negative opacity contributions or subtract colors during compositing. Activation Timing: 3D-DoG is only introduced after the pruning phase, not during initial densification. Activating it too early may destabilize training. Computational Overhead: 3D-DoG introduces additional computational overhead compared to standard Gaussians. It is recommended for compact models where sharper details outweigh the cost. Time Complexity: Increases per-primitive rendering cost due to the evaluation of two Gaussians (primary and pseudo) and their subtraction. Memory Complexity: Adds 4 learnable parameters (f\alpha, f{xs}, f{ys}, f{zs}) per primitive. Performance: Improves reconstruction quality for fine details and edges in compact models. It allows sharper structures to be preserved under aggressive pruning. Strengths: Enhances boundary and texture representation; more responsive to fine geometric details than standard Gaussians. Limitations: Higher computational cost; not beneficial for smooth regions where standard Gaussians suffice; requires careful tuning of the pruning schedule to activate at the right time. When to use: In compact 3D Gaussian Splatting models where memory is constrained but high-frequency detail preservation is critical. When not to use: In initial training phases or when the model is not being aggressively pruned, as the overhead may not be justified. The 3D Difference-of-Gaussians (3D-DoG) primitive was introduced in the paper "Prune Wisely, Reconstruct Sharply: Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting via Adaptive Pruning and Difference-of-Gaussian Primitives". It addresses the limitations of compact 3D Gaussian Splatting, where standard smooth Gaussian kernels fail to capture fine details after aggressive pruning. The method is part of a broader framework that includes a Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler (RPS) and Spatio-spectral Pruning Score (SPS). name: Pruning and Density Control
head: Gaussian Pruning, Densification, Primitive Management
body: Pruning and Density Control manages the dynamic population of 3D Gaussian primitives during training to balance rendering quality, memory efficiency, and convergence stability. It solves the problem of inefficient spatial coverage, overfitting, and redundant primitive accumulation by adaptively growing, splitting, or removing Gaussians based on optimization progress and reconstruction metrics. It sets itself apart from static initialization or uniform densification by employing adaptive schedules and importance-based criteria that synchronize primitive density with rendering resolution and learning progress, ensuring high-frequency details are fitted only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian primitive representation: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics) The core mechanism involves calculating an importance score for each Gaussian and removing those below a threshold or ranking. Methods typically employ a "concave-up" growth curve for primitives, where growth accelerates over time, synchronized with increasing rendering resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. This family of methods controls the dynamic growth, pruning, and optimization trajectory of 3D Gaussian primitives during training. It solves the problem of inefficient spatial coverage and unstable convergence by synchronizing primitive density with rendering resolution and learning progress. It sets itself apart from static initialization or uniform densification by employing adaptive schedules that accelerate growth over time, ensuring high-frequency details are fitted only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. See Optimization Schedule and Densification. The Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler (RPS) is a dynamic pruning strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that adaptively determines pruning timing and refining intervals based on reconstruction quality, addressing the instability of fixed-schedule pruning. Unlike heuristic methods that prune at fixed iterations with preset ratios, RPS analyzes reconstruction loss to automatically identify optimal pruning times and progressively reduces the number of pruned primitives to adapt to scene complexity and redundancy levels. See Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler. DropGaussian is a structural regularization technique designed to mitigate overfitting in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when trained on a sparse set of input views. It operates by randomly excluding a subset of Gaussians from the rendering and gradient computation during training, while simultaneously scaling the opacity of the remaining Gaussians to preserve the total color contribution. Unlike prior-based methods that rely on external depth signals or 2D generative models, DropGaussian is prior-free and introduces no additional computational complexity or external data requirements. See DropGaussian. MiniGS is a memory-efficient compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces the number of primitives by up to 90% while maintaining rendering quality comparable to the vanilla algorithm. It addresses the inherent redundancy in primitive allocation, where overlapping or non-essential elements consume excessive storage, by employing Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning to remove redundant Gaussians and a Variational Densify Threshold (VDT) component to recover fine details lost during pruning. Unlike standard pruning methods that may degrade quality, MiniGS compensates for this loss through VDT, a gradient optimization mechanism applied during the backward pass. See MiniGS. Conservation-Constrained Gaussian Splitting is a method for splitting an inhomogeneous 3D Gaussian into two new Gaussians using a 3D plane while maintaining 3D visual consistency. It solves the problem of artifacts (blurring, needle-like bulges) and unstable loss decline associated with direct copy-based splitting strategies in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Unlike siblings that may rely on heuristic or iterative adjustments, this method provides a closed-form solution derived from Integral Tensor Equations (ITEs) to ensure the zero-, first-, and second-order moments are conserved. See Conservation-Constrained Gaussian Splitting. This method decomposes a single d-dimensional Gaussian primitive into two d-dimensional Gaussians to resolve scale and structural inhomogeneities in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models. Unlike the original 3DGS approach which duplicates Gaussians with naive scaling and random translation, this method uses a closed-form solution based on moment conservation to ensure the resulting models are more uniform and surface-bounded. It addresses the problems of blurred boundaries caused by scale inhomogeneity and needle-like artifacts caused by structural inhomogeneity. See 3D Gaussian Splitting via Moment Conservation. A pruning technique that identifies and removes redundant Gaussians by gauging their impact on deformation, distinguishing between stable and deformed Gaussians. An importance ranking mechanism that incorporates spectral information into the importance ranking of Gaussian primitives to enable stable pruning. It measures the importance of a Gaussian primitive in both spatial and spectral domains. A criterion for evaluating the importance of each Gaussian by measuring its contribution from both spatial and spectral (frequency) perspectives to prevent pruning of primitives essential for sharp structures. It iteratively removes low-score points that are relatively unimportant across both spatial and spectral domains. The final Spatio-spectral Pruning Score \tilde{U}i^ is calculated as: \tilde{U}i^ = \lambdas \frac{(\nabla gi IG)^2}{\|\tilde{U}s\|^2} + \lambdaf \frac{(\nabla gi \text{FFT}(IG))^2}{\|\tilde{U}f\|^2} where \lambdas and \lambdaf are weighting coefficients balancing spatial and frequency contributions, and \|\tilde{U}s\| and \|\tilde{U}f\| are normalization terms for spatial and frequency scores respectively. A method to reduce the number of splats while maintaining reconstruction quality, based on epistemic uncertainty computation per primitive. It is effective in removing leaked distractors. It computes epistemic uncertainty per primitive and thresholds the uncertainty to remove lesser utilized Gaussians. If the uncertainty threshold is set too aggressively, the method may remove parts of the scene that are rarely viewed in the training data. The concept of managing Gaussian primitive density originated with the introduction of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by Kerbl et al. in 2023 [Parent]. Initial implementations used a fixed densification schedule based on gradient magnitude and screen-space size. Subsequent works introduced adaptive pruning to address memory constraints and overfitting. The Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler was introduced in to replace fixed schedules with loss-driven decisions. DropGaussian was proposed in to handle sparse-view overfitting. MiniGS and Conservation-Constrained Splitting further refined density control through compression and moment-conserving splitting. Uncertainty-based pruning was explored in for distractor removal. name: Optimization Schedule and Densification
head: Densification Scheduling, Primitive Growth Control
body:
This family of methods controls the dynamic growth, pruning, and optimization trajectory of 3D Gaussian primitives during training. It solves the problem of inefficient spatial coverage and unstable convergence by synchronizing primitive density with rendering resolution and learning progress. It sets itself apart from static initialization or uniform densification by employing adaptive schedules that accelerate growth over time, ensuring high-frequency details are fitted only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. All methods in this family operate on the standard 3DGS primitive representation: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics) The core mechanism involves calculating an importance score for each Gaussian and removing those below a threshold or ranking. Methods typically employ a "concave-up" growth curve for primitives, where growth accelerates over time, synchronized with increasing rendering resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established [Parent]. Error-Driven 2D Gaussian Training is a densification strategy that samples and optimizes 2D Gaussian kernels in image space using a differentiable rasterizer, then back-projects them to 3D to initialize new 3D primitives. It solves the problem of initializing view-dependent Gaussian kernels for complex specular radiance reconstruction, where proper initialization is critical. It sets itself apart from standard 3D densification by optimizing in 2D image space with the pre-rendered image as a fixed background, allowing for precise error-driven placement before 3D projection. Training Configuration and Hyperparameters defines the specific hyperparameters, optimization schedules, and training protocols required to stabilize and accelerate the convergence of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) decoders. While the parent method Optimization Schedule and Densification handles the dynamic growth of primitives, this configuration ensures that the learning rate, loss weights, and initialization strategies are tuned to prevent gradient instability, particularly when integrating semantic features or handling sparse view inputs. It addresses the problem of chaotic densification and poor spatial convergence by decoupling geometric and semantic optimization phases and standardizing downstream evaluation protocols. Optimization Scheduling and Complexity Control focuses on accelerating the training process by managing the computational complexity of densification and resolution scaling. It addresses the inefficiency of standard split/clone operations and the unbalanced workloads inherent in distributed rendering. It sets itself apart by decoupling global spread from local refinement and employing momentum-based primitive budgeting to suppress early growth and encourage mid-stage expansion, thereby reducing optimization time without compromising quality. An optimization framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses learned networks for initialization, densification, and parameter updates to accelerate surface reconstruction. It iterates for t = 0 to T - 1, resetting the gradient accumulator 
abla Gt \leftarrow 0. For all images, it computes the rendering loss L, computes the gradient \delta Gt, and accumulates 
abla Gt \leftarrow 
abla Gt + \delta Gt. It generates new Gaussians \hat{G}t using a densifier network fD on current Gaussians Gt, accumulated gradients 
abla Gt, and time step t: \hat{G}t \leftarrow fD(Gt, 
abla Gt, t). The new Gaussians are concatenated with existing ones, and an optimizer network fO computes the update \Delta  ar{G}t \leftarrow fO( ar{G}t, 
abla  ar{G}t, t), where  ar{G}t = Gt \cup \hat{G}t and 
abla  ar{G}t = 
abla Gt \cup 0. The final state is updated as G{t+1} \leftarrow  ar{G}t + \Delta  ar{G}t. A densification criterion to improve normal recovery in thin regions by introducing an additional densification criterion on the gradient of normals, beyond the vanilla 3DGS gradient of view space points. It densifies Gaussians whose normal gradient exceeds a threshold Tn. The typical value for Tn is 2 	imes 10^{-9}. A densification strategy that decouples split and clone operations across densification phases to accelerate optimization. It uses split for global spread at low resolution and suppresses clone, then reintroduces clone for local refinement at full resolution. The norm of the average position gradient of each Gaussian primitive is calculated every 100 iterations. If the gradient norm exceeds a predefined threshold, the method checks the maximum scale of the Gaussian primitive. If the maximum scale exceeds a given scale threshold, it splits the Gaussian into smaller components; otherwise, it clones the Gaussian with the same parameters. During low-resolution training, split operations are promoted for global spread while clone operations are suppressed to prevent premature local clustering. When transitioning to full-resolution training, clone operations are reintroduced to refine high-frequency details. Unlike standard 3DGS which applies split and clone simultaneously, this method decouples them across phases (global vs local) to address inefficient spatial spread and redundant primitives. A scheduler that controls the number of primitives using a momentum-based budgeting scheme. The final primitive count P{fin}^{(i)} is calculated as: P{fin}^{(i)} = \max(P{fin}^{(i-1)}, \gamma \cdot P{fin}^{(i-1)} + \eta \cdot P{add}) where P{add} is the number of primitives densified in step i. P{fin}^{(0)} is initialized as 5 \cdot P{init}. The power factor in primitive growth starts at 2 and gradually decreases to 1 along the optimization process to suppress early growth and encourage mid-stage growth. The hyperparameter \gamma (momentum decay factor) defaults to 0.98, and \eta (force scaling factor) defaults to 1. The continuous scalar resolution modulation r(i) is modulated to \lfloor r(i) floor in practice to encourage faster primitive growth. Too much primitive growth at the end of optimization results in poor convergence, which is mitigated by the concave-up scheduling function and momentum-based budgeting. An ablation study on additional losses added in the first stage of the optimization pipeline. Removing planarity loss (L{planarity}) causes Gaussians to form radial spikes pointing toward the scene's center, resulting in noisier reconstruction and degraded perceptual quality. Turning off shell loss (L{shell}) relaxes geometric constraints on background Gaussians, resulting in a slightly increased SSIM compared to planarity ablation, but introduces blurry backgrounds and decreased visual fidelity. A pruning strategy that disables the original size-based pruning heuristic (which deletes large Gaussians in screen/world space) to preserve large distant background Gaussians. Instead, it counts the times each Gaussian is rendered using indices returned from the rendering step. Any Gaussian with a visibility count equal to zero is removed. This logic is executed in the same pruning stage as in the original code. A phenomenon in distributed 3DGS where render intensity varies due to natural scene sparsity, varying Gaussian densities (e.g., sky vs. tree), and dynamic changes during training. Workload changes are caused by 3D position and co-variance parameter updates affecting Gaussian coverage of pixels, and opacity parameter updates affecting the number of Gaussians contributing to each pixel. Densification targets areas under construction, causing Gaussians from different regions to densify at varying rates, making workloads more unbalanced at the beginning of training. A strategy for online optimization that samples keyframes using a probability proportional to the number of leaf Gaussians currently in the active set that were generated by that keyframe. It removes keyframes that contribute less than 5% of the maximum contribution by offloading them to the CPU, which automatically optimizes intermediate hierarchy nodes without explicit post-optimization. The minimum keyframe count is 50 to ensure sufficient context and allow optimization of intermediate hierarchy nodes. Frames that mostly see offloaded primitives or keyframes that only see leaf/small Gaussians are avoided by the probability-based selection and offloading scheme. The concept of adaptive densification in 3D Gaussian Splatting originated with the foundational work by Kerbl et al. [Parent], which introduced split and clone operations based on position gradients. Subsequent research has focused on optimizing this schedule to reduce training time, improve geometric fidelity, and handle specific domains like background reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and online rendering. Key developments include the decoupling of split/clone operations for efficiency, momentum-based primitive budgeting for controlled growth, and learned initialization/densification networks.
