name: Child Gaussian Initialization
head: AdpSplit child initialization, Error-driven child creation
body: Child Gaussian Initialization is the specific procedure for generating the geometric and photometric properties of new 3D Gaussian primitives during the splitting phase of adaptive densification. It solves the problem of how to accurately map a parent Gaussian's error region—identified in camera space—into a valid 3D Gaussian in world space, ensuring the child is positioned on the scene geometry and oriented correctly relative to the viewing direction. It sets itself apart from generic splitting methods by explicitly unprojecting image-space covariance ellipses into world-space scales and orientations using Mahalanobis distance minimization and perspective-aware clamping, rather than simple isotropic scaling or random sampling. Inputs: Parent Gaussian gi with mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, and opacity \alphai. Camera intrinsics (fx, fy, px, py) and extrinsics (camera center ov in world coordinates, camera-to-world rotation R{c2w}). Image-space error region centroid (\bar{x}{qv}, \bar{y}{qv}) and covariance matrix in image space (defined by PCA directions e{1}, e{2} and standard deviations \sigma1, \sigma2). Ground-truth RGB value r{qv} at the region centroid. Parent maximum scale s{pmax} = \maxk(sk) for clamping limits. Outputs: Child Gaussian g{qv} defined by mean \mu{qv}, covariance \Sigma{qv}, opacity \alpha{qv}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}{qv}. Data Structures: The covariance \Sigma is stored as a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix, or equivalently parameterized by scale vector s \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4 (or rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}). In this method, the output is explicitly constructed as R{qv} \text{diag}(s{qv}^2) R{qv}^T. Steps: 1. Compute Camera-Space Ray Direction: Calculate the unnormalized ray direction in camera space from the image centroid: d{cam,v} = \begin{bmatrix} (\bar{x}{qv} - px)/fx \\ (\bar{y}{qv} - py)/fy \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} 2. Transform to World-Space Ray: Convert the ray direction to world coordinates and normalize it: \hat{d}{qv} = \frac{R{c2w} d{cam,v}}{\| R{c2w} d{cam,v} \|} 3. Define Back-Projected Ray: Define the ray \ell{qv}(t) originating from the camera center ov: \ell{qv}(t) = ov + t \hat{d}{qv} 4. Find Optimal Depth (t^): Find the point on the ray that minimizes the Mahalanobis distance to the parent center \mui. Let A = \Sigmai^{-1} and b = \mui - ov. The distance squared is f(t) = (t \hat{d}{qv} - b)^T A (t \hat{d}{qv} - b). Minimizing f(t) yields: t^ = \frac{b^T A \hat{d}{qv}}{\hat{d}{qv}^T A \hat{d}{qv} + \epsilon} where \epsilon is a small constant added to the denominator for numerical stability. 5. Set Child Mean: The child's 3D position is the point on the ray at depth t^: \mu{qv} = \ell{qv}(t^) 6. Compute Camera-Space Depth: Calculate the depth in camera space units: t^{z,v} = \frac{t^}{\| d{cam,v} \|} 7. Unproject Image-Space Covariance to World-Space Axes: Let uv and wv be the camera right and down directions in world coordinates (derived from R{c2w}). The image-space PCA directions e{1}, e{2} and scales \sigma1, \sigma2 define the error ellipse. We compute intermediate components w{1x,v}, w{1y,v}, w{2x,v}, w{2y,v} using a clamping function \text{clip}(x, a) = \text{sign}(x) \min(|x|, a) to prevent excessively large scales: w{1x,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fx} e{1,x} \sigma1, s{pmax} |e{1,x}| \right) w{1y,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fy} e{1,y} \sigma1, s{pmax} |e{1,y}| \right) w{2x,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fx} e{2,x} \sigma2, s{pmax} |e{2,x}| \right) w{2y,v} = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t^{z,v}}{fy} e{2,y} \sigma2, s{pmax} |e{2,y}| \right) Unproject these components into world-space vectors a{q1,v} and a{q2,v}: a{q1,v} = w{1x,v} uv + w{1y,v} wv a{q2,v} = w{2x,v} uv + w{2y,v} wv 8. Determine Child Scales: The scales are the lengths of the unprojected vectors. The third scale (depth) is set equal to the second scale (transverse): s{q1,v} = \| a{q1,v} \|, \quad s{q2,v} = \| a{q2,v} \|, \quad s{q3,v} = s{q2,v} 9. Enforce Orthonormality: Due to perspective projection and clamping, a{q1,v} and a{q2,v} may not be orthogonal. Apply Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to obtain orthonormal in-plane axes \hat{u}1, \hat{u}2: \hat{u}1 = \frac{a{q1,v}}{\| a{q1,v} \|} \hat{u}2 = \frac{a{q2,v} - (a{q2,v}^T \hat{u}1)\hat{u}1}{\| a{q2,v} - (a{q2,v}^T \hat{u}1)\hat{u}1 \|} 10. Construct Child Covariance: Let zv be the camera forward direction in world coordinates. Form the rotation matrix R{qv} = [\hat{u}1 \mid \hat{u}2 \mid zv]. The child covariance is: \Sigma{qv} = R{qv} \text{diag}(s{q1,v}^2, s{q2,v}^2, s{q3,v}^2) R{qv}^T 11. Initialize Color and Opacity: Color: Set the DC spherical harmonic coefficient to the ground-truth RGB value r{qv} at the centroid. Set all higher-order SH coefficients to zero. Opacity: Set \alpha{qv} = \alphai (inherit parent opacity). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializechildgaussian(parentgaussian, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, imageregion, groundtruthrgb, parentmaxscale): """ Initialize a child Gaussian from an error region in a specific view. Args: parentgaussian: dict with 'mu' (3,), 'Sigma' (3,3), 'alpha' (float) cameraintrinsics: dict with 'fx', 'fy', 'px', 'py' cameraextrinsics: dict with 'ov' (3,), 'Rc2w' (3,3) imageregion: dict with 'centroid' (2,), 'e1' (2,), 'e2' (2,), 'sigma1', 'sigma2' groundtruthrgb: (3,) array parentmaxscale: float Returns: childgaussian: dict with 'mu', 'Sigma', 'alpha', 'SHdc' """ # 1. Camera-space ray direction cx, cy = imageregion['centroid'] fx, fy, px, py = cameraintrinsics['fx'], cameraintrinsics['fy'], \ cameraintrinsics['px'], cameraintrinsics['py'] dcam = np.array([(cx - px) / fx, (cy - py) / fy, 1.0]) # 2. World-space unit ray direction Rc2w = cameraextrinsics['Rc2w'] dworldunnorm = Rc2w @ dcam dhat = dworldunnorm / np.linalg.norm(dworldunnorm) # 3. Ray parameters ov = cameraextrinsics['ov'] mui = parentgaussian['mu'] Sigmaiinv = np.linalg.inv(parentgaussian['Sigma']) # 4. Optimal depth t A = Sigmaiinv b = mui - ov numerator = b @ A @ dhat denominator = dhat @ A @ dhat + 1e-8 # epsilon for stability tstar = numerator / denominator # 5. Child mean muchild = ov + tstar dhat # 6. Camera-space depth tz = tstar / np.linalg.norm(dcam) # 7. Unproject covariance # Camera axes in world space (derived from Rc2w) uv = Rc2w @ np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Right wv = Rc2w @ np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Down e1 = imageregion['e1'] e2 = imageregion['e2'] s1 = imageregion['sigma1'] s2 = imageregion['sigma2'] def clip(x, a): return np.sign(x) np.minimum(np.abs(x), a) # Compute components w1x = clip((tz / fx) e1[0] s1, parentmaxscale np.abs(e1[0])) w1y = clip((tz / fy) e1[1] s1, parentmaxscale np.abs(e1[1])) w2x = clip((tz / fx) e2[0] s2, parentmaxscale np.abs(e2[0])) w2y = clip((tz / fy) e2[1] s2, parentmaxscale np.abs(e2[1])) # Unproject to world vectors a1 = w1x uv + w1y wv a2 = w2x uv + w2y wv # 8. Child scales s1child = np.linalg.norm(a1) s2child = np.linalg.norm(a2) s3child = s2child # 9. Orthonormalization (Gram-Schmidt) u1hat = a1 / s1child u2hat = a2 - np.dot(a2, u1hat) u1hat u2hat = u2hat / np.linalg.norm(u2hat) # 10. Construct Covariance zv = Rc2w @ np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # Forward Rchild = np.columnstack((u1hat, u2hat, zv)) scalessq = np.array([s1child2, s2child2, s3child2]) Sigmachild = Rchild @ np.diag(scalessq) @ Rchild.T # 11. Color and Opacity alphachild = parentgaussian['alpha'] SHdc = groundtruthrgb # DC SH coefficient return { 'mu': muchild, 'Sigma': Sigmachild, 'alpha': alphachild, 'SHdc': SHdc } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: The denominator in t^ calculation can approach zero if the ray is nearly orthogonal to the principal axis of the parent covariance. Adding \epsilon is required. Orthogonality Loss: Perspective projection and clamping can break the orthogonality of the unprojected axes. Gram-Schmidt is mandatory to ensure a valid rotation matrix. Scale Explosion: Without clamping using s{pmax}, unprojected scales can become arbitrarily large in the distance, leading to rendering artifacts. The clamping function limits the scale relative to the parent's maximum extent. Time Complexity: O(1) per child Gaussian, involving matrix inversions (3 \times 3) and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per child. Strengths: Produces geometrically accurate child positions on the scene surface (via Mahalanobis minimization) and correctly oriented scales that respect perspective distortion. This leads to faster convergence and better detail preservation compared to isotropic splitting. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than simple random sampling or isotropic scaling. Requires access to camera intrinsics/extrinsics and image-space error regions. When to use: When high-fidelity geometry reconstruction is required and the parent Gaussian has identified a significant error region in a specific view. This method was introduced in the AdpSplit paper, which proposes error-driven adaptive splitting for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitations of standard densification strategies that do not account for the specific geometry of the error region or the perspective projection effects when creating new primitives. The method is part of the broader effort to optimize the initialization of new Gaussians during the training process to accelerate convergence and improve final rendering quality. name: Compactness-Aware Frequency-Guided Densification (CAFe-GS)
head: CAFe-GS, CAFe-GS Densification
body: CAFe-GS is a densification strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the traditional positional-gradient criterion with a per-Gaussian error score modulated by local frequency guidance. It solves the problem of redundant primitive generation in smooth regions and insufficient detail in underfit areas, providing a single interpretable parameter \tau to control the quality-compactness trade-off. Unlike the gradient-based baseline which suffers from steep quality drops and narrow usable ranges, CAFe-GS offers a smoother trade-off, achieving comparable PSNR with 2–4× fewer Gaussians or up to 12–15× fewer Gaussians with a controlled 2–2.5 dB PSNR drop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives G (initialized via Structure-from-Motion), camera parameters, and a sequence of training images \{Iv\} with corresponding rendered images \{\hat{I}v\}. Outputs: An updated set of Gaussians with densified primitives (cloned or split) based on the score Sg and threshold \tau. Data Structures: Each Gaussian primitive g is defined by: Center \mug \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance \Sigmag \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, parameterized as \Sigmag = Rg \text{diag}(sg^2) Rg^\top, where Rg is a rotation matrix (from quaternion qg \in \mathbb{R}^4) and sg \in \mathbb{R}^{3+} is the per-axis scale vector. Opacity \alphag \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics coefficients a{gk} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for view-dependent color. Parameters: \tau: Densification threshold. Typical values: \{10, 25, 50, 75, 100\}. Higher values favor compactness. \sigma{LoG}: Standard deviation for the Laplacian-of-Gaussian filter. Value: 1. th: Clone/split scale threshold. Value: 0.01. Densification Schedule: Begins after 500-iteration warm-up, applied every 100 iterations, ending after 15,000 iterations. Total training continues to 30,000 iterations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization and Optimization: Initialize camera parameters and sparse Gaussians using Structure-from-Motion. Optimize all parameters \{\mug, Rg, sg, \alphag, a{gk}\} to minimize photometric distortion loss (L1 + DSSIM) between rendered and ground-truth images. 2. Compute Per-Pixel Distortion: For each view v, compute the per-pixel distortion dv(u) as 1 minus the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) between the input image Iv and the rendered image \hat{I}v: dv(u) = 1 - \text{SSIM}(Iv, \hat{I}v)(u) 3. Compute Frequency Magnitude Maps: For each view v, compute the local frequency-magnitude map for the input image Iv by applying a Laplacian-of-Gaussian (LoG) filter with \sigma{LoG}=1 to the luminance channel and taking the absolute response: F(Iv)(u) = |(LoG{\sigma{LoG}} Iv)|(u) Similarly, compute F(\hat{I}v)(u) for the rendered image. Normalize both F(Iv) and F(\hat{I}v) independently per view to the range [0, 1]. 4. Compute Frequency Gap Map: Calculate the frequency gap \Delta Fv(u) to identify under-detailing (input has more frequency than render) and over-detailing: \Delta Fv(u) = F(Iv)(u) - F(\hat{I}v)(u) + 1 Values > 1 indicate under-detailing; values < 1 indicate over-detailing. 5. Compute Per-Gaussian Error Score (Eg): Redistribute pixel-wise distortion to contributing primitives using effective opacity weights (transmittance) C(g, u). The effective contribution C(g, u) is the weight of Gaussian g in the front-to-back compositing at pixel u. Compute the per-view error attributed to Gaussian g: e{g,v} = \sum{u \in \Omegav} C(g, u) \cdot dv(u) Compute the view-agnostic error score Eg by taking the maximum error across all views to prevent averaging out localized underfitting: Eg = \maxv e{g,v} 6. Compute Frequency Modulation (Mg^\Delta): Redistribute the frequency gap to Gaussians using the same effective opacity weights: Mg^\Delta = \maxv \sum{u \in \Omegav} C(g, u) \cdot \Delta Fv(u) Taking the maximum over views avoids averaging away thin structures visible only from limited viewpoints. 7. Compute Final Densification Score (Sg): Sg = Eg \cdot Mg^\Delta Select candidate Gaussians for densification if Sg \ge \tau. 8. Clone or Split Selected Gaussians: For each selected Gaussian g with per-axis scales sg = (s{g,x}, s{g,y}, s{g,z}): Clone: If s{g,i} \le th for all i \in \{x, y, z\}, duplicate the primitive by copying all attributes (\mug, Rg, sg, \alphag, SH). Shift the child's position along the dominant scale axis. Split: Otherwise, duplicate attributes, halve the scale along all axes (s{g,i} \leftarrow \frac{1}{2} s{g,i}), and slightly displace the child to prevent overlap. Orientation and color parameters remain unchanged. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computelogfilter(image, sigma=1.0): """ Computes the absolute Laplacian-of-Gaussian response for the luminance channel. image: H x W x 3 RGB array. Returns: H x W float array. """ # Convert to luminance (standard BT.601) luminance = 0.299 image[:,:, 0] + 0.587 image[:,:, 1] + 0.114 image[:,:, 2] # Create LoG kernel (simplified for description, assume standard scipy/numpy convolution) # In implementation, use a separable Gaussian derivative or precomputed kernel logkernel = createlogkernel(sigma) response = np.abs(np.convolve(luminance, logkernel, mode='same')) return response def normalizemap(maparray): """Min-max normalize to [0, 1]""" minval = np.min(maparray) maxval = np.max(maparray) if maxval == minval: return np.zeroslike(maparray) return (maparray - minval) / (maxval - minval) def cafegsdensificationstep(gaussians, views, tau, th=0.01, sigmalog=1.0): """ One step of CAFe-GS densification. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes mu, R, s, alpha, SH. views: List of view dicts containing 'Iv' (input image), 'Ihatv' (rendered image), and 'Cgu' (effective contribution weights for each Gaussian at each pixel). tau: Densification threshold. """ candidates = [] for g in gaussians: maxerror = 0.0 maxfreqmod = 0.0 for view in views: Iv = view['Iv'] Ihatv = view['Ihatv'] Cgu = view['Cgu'][g.id] # Shape: (H, W) # 1. Per-pixel distortion # Assuming SSIM is computed per-pixel or locally ssimmap = computessimmap(Iv, Ihatv) dv = 1.0 - ssimmap # 2. Per-view error egv = np.sum(Cgu dv) if egv > maxerror: maxerror = egv # 3. Frequency Guidance # Compute LoG for input and render FIv = normalizemap(computelogfilter(Iv, sigmalog)) FIhatv = normalizemap(computelogfilter(Ihatv, sigmalog)) # Frequency gap deltaFv = FIv - FIhatv + 1.0 # Modulation Mgdeltav = np.sum(Cgu deltaFv) if Mgdeltav > maxfreqmod: maxfreqmod = Mgdeltav # Final Score Sg = maxerror maxfreqmod if Sg >= tau: candidates.append(g) # Perform Clone/Split newgaussians = [] for g in candidates: s = g.s # Scale vector (x, y, z) if np.all(s <= th): # Clone child = clonegaussian(g) # Shift child along dominant scale axis dominantaxis = np.argmax(s) child.mu = shiftposition(child.mu, dominantaxis, step=0.01) # Step size heuristic newgaussians.append(child) else: # Split child = clonegaussian(g) child.s = g.s / 2.0 # Slight displacement to prevent overlap child.mu = shiftposition(child.mu, axis=np.random.randint(3), step=0.001) # Heuristic newgaussians.append(child) return newgaussians def clonegaussian(g): """Deep copy of Gaussian attributes""" import copy return copy.deepcopy(g) def shiftposition(mu, axis, step): """Shift position along axis""" munew = mu.copy() munew[axis] += step return munew Time and Memory Complexity: The method adds overhead for computing SSIM and LoG filters per view during densification steps. However, it reduces the total number of Gaussians required for a given quality, lowering rendering memory and compute costs. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360 [1], CAFe-GS with \tau=10 achieves 0.895 SSIM, 29.92 dB PSNR, 0.119 LPIPS, and 2.22M Gaussians. With \tau=100, it achieves 0.807 SSIM, 27.50 dB PSNR, 0.238 LPIPS, and 0.26M Gaussians. On Tanks and Temples [12], CAFe-GS (Best quality) achieves PSNR 23.89, LPIPS 0.232, 4.5M Gaussians. CAFe-GS (Compactness-first) achieves PSNR 23.93, LPIPS 0.230, 2.9M Gaussians. The baseline 3DGS achieves PSNR 21.60, LPIPS 0.405, 0.3M Gaussians. Scaling: CAFe-GS provides a smoother and more predictable quality-compactness trade-off than the gradient-based baseline, which suffers from steep quality drops and narrow usable ranges. Strengths: Reduces Gaussian count by 2–4× at matched quality and up to 12–15× with controlled quality loss. Preserves high-frequency details (edges, thin contours) better than baseline. Limitations: On Tanks and Temples, parity with the gradient-based baseline is reached only at the lowest \tau threshold, likely due to lower input image resolution limiting the effectiveness of frequency analysis. When to use: When model compactness is a priority or when the gradient-based densification produces excessive redundancy in smooth regions. When not to use: In scenes with very low-resolution input images where frequency analysis is ineffective. CAFe-GS was introduced by Huar et al. from Inria and InterDigital. It addresses the limitations of the original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) Adaptive Density Control (ADC), which relies on positional gradients and often densifies already well-reconstructed areas. The method builds on the error-redistribution strategy of Bulò et al. [2] and adapts it with frequency guidance. It is evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360 [1] and Tanks and Temples [12] datasets. CAFe-GS: Compactness-Aware Frequency-Guided Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://hal.science/hal-05583323v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Inhomogeneity-Based Splitting
head: Inhomogeneity-Based Splitting for Training, Splitting during 3D Gaussian Learning
body: Inhomogeneity-Based Splitting is a densification technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses the formation of "needle-like" artifacts and sparse point clouds in large, flat, untextured regions. It sets itself apart from standard densification by explicitly measuring the ratio of principal scale eigenvalues to determine split necessity, rather than relying solely on position or opacity gradients. Inputs: A trained or partially trained set of 3D Gaussians, where each Gaussian k is defined by center \muk, rotation Rk, scale Sk, opacity \alphak, and spherical harmonics coefficients. The method operates on the diagonalized scale/rotation matrix components, denoted as \text{Tri}[i] for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, which correspond to the squared scales along the principal axes. Outputs: A modified set of Gaussians where those exceeding the inhomogeneity threshold are replaced by two new Gaussians. Data Structures: Gaussian: Standard 3DGS representation. Tri: A vector of size 3 containing the diagonal elements of the covariance matrix's scale/rotation component, sorted or indexed by principal direction magnitude. Parameters: \gamma{th}: Splitting threshold for the inhomogeneity ratio \gamma. Default value: 5. \gamma{th\ij}: Inhomogeneity threshold for pairwise eigenvalue ratios y{ij}. Default value: 2. Rm: Regularization term in y{ij}. Value not specified in the sources. Iteration schedule: Check for splitting every 5000 iterations, starting from iteration 9999 and ending at 24999. Steps: 1. Compute Inhomogeneity Ratio (\gamma): For each Gaussian, identify the maximum and second-maximum diagonal elements of the scale/rotation matrix: pdm = \max{i \in \{0,1,2\}} (\text{Tri}[i]) pds = \text{second\max}{i \in \{0,1,2\}} (\text{Tri}[i]) Calculate the ratio: \gamma = \frac{pdm}{pds} 2. Check Primary Threshold: If \gamma > \gamma{th} (default 5), the Gaussian is a candidate for splitting. 3. Compute Pairwise Inhomogeneity (y{ij}): Calculate the degree of inhomogeneity between the i-th and j-th largest eigenvalues (i < j): y{ij} = \frac{\text{Tri}[i]}{\text{Tri}[j] + Rm} where (i, j) \in \{(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2)\}. 4. Check Pairwise Threshold: If any y{ij} > \gamma{th\ij} (default 2), the Gaussian should be split at principal component i. 5. Determine Split Plane Normal (\mathbf{n}): Assume the split plane normal is parallel to the principal direction of the maximum eigenvalue: \mathbf{n} = R[\operatorname{argmax}(\operatorname{Tri}[i])] 6. Generate New Gaussians: Simplify the split by setting the split plane to pass through the Gaussian center (\mu0 = 0 relative offset). Set the scaling factors for the new Gaussians to \sigma0 = \sigma1 = 0.5 and the opacity weight \alpha = 1/\sqrt{2}. This sets the first term of the new covariance matrices \Sigma0 and \Sigma1 to 0 to speed up calculation. To ensure the new Gaussians are sufficiently separated and avoid overlapping positions, set the position offset parameter \mu0 as: \mu0 = 2 \cdot \text{Tri}[i] where i is the principal component index identified in Step 4. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inhomogeneitybasedsplitting(gaussians, gammath=5, gammathij=2, Rm=0.0): """ Splits Gaussians based on inhomogeneity of their principal scales. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes:.tri: list of 3 floats (diagonal scale/rotation elements).R: 3x3 rotation matrix.mu: 3D center position.alpha: opacity.scale: scale parameters """ newgaussians = [] gaussianstosplit = [] for g in gaussians: tri = g.tri # Step 1: Compute pdm and pds sortedtri = sorted(tri, reverse=True) pdm = sortedtri[0] pds = sortedtri[1] # Avoid division by zero if pds == 0: newgaussians.append(g) continue gamma = pdm / pds # Step 2: Check primary threshold if gamma <= gammath: newgaussians.append(g) continue # Step 3: Compute pairwise inhomogeneity splitcomponent = -1 for i in range(3): for j in range(i + 1, 3): # Use original indices from sortedtri for i and j # Note: The source defines yij based on Tri[i] and Tri[j] # where i < j refers to rank order (0 is largest) vali = sortedtri[i] valj = sortedtri[j] yij = vali / (valj + Rm) # Step 4: Check pairwise threshold if yij > gammathij: splitcomponent = i break if splitcomponent != -1: break if splitcomponent != -1: gaussianstosplit.append((g, splitcomponent)) else: newgaussians.append(g) # Step 5 & 6: Perform splits for g, compidx in gaussianstosplit: tri = g.tri sortedtri = sorted(tri, reverse=True) pdval = sortedtri[compidx] # Determine normal direction # argmax returns the index in the original tri array? # Source says: n = R[argmax(Tri[i])]. Assuming compidx refers to the rank. # We need the actual index in the original tri array corresponding to the compidx-th largest value. # For simplicity, assuming tri is already ordered or we map rank to index. # Let's assume we find the index k in original tri such that tri[k] is the compidx-th largest. # This requires sorting with indices. indexedtri = sorted(enumerate(tri), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) originalidx = indexedtri[compidx][0] # Normal is the column of R corresponding to the principal axis n = g.R[:, originalidx] # Offset calculation # Source: mu0 as 2Tri[i]. Tri[i] here likely refers to the scale value pdval. offset = 2.0 pdval n # Create two new Gaussians # Center: mu +/- offset/2 ? # Source says: mu0 = 2Tri[i] to ensure new Gaussians are far apart. # And split plane passes through center (mu0=0 relative). # Standard splitting usually creates two Gaussians at mu +/- delta. # If mu0 is the offset vector, the new centers are mu + mu0/2 and mu - mu0/2? # Or is mu0 the total distance? "ensure new Gaussians are far apart". # Let's assume the new centers are mu + offset/2 and mu - offset/2. g1 = copygaussian(g) g2 = copygaussian(g) g1.mu = g.mu + offset / 2.0 g2.mu = g.mu - offset / 2.0 # Scale and Opacity adjustments # Source: sigma0 = sigma1 = 0.5, alpha = 1/sqrt(2) # This implies scaling the existing scale by 0.5 and splitting opacity. g1.scale = g.scale 0.5 g2.scale = g.scale 0.5 g1.alpha = g.alpha / 1.41421356 # 1/sqrt(2) g2.alpha = g.alpha / 1.41421356 newgaussians.append(g1) newgaussians.append(g2) return newgaussians Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If pds is zero, the ratio \gamma is undefined. The implementation must handle this, typically by skipping the split or treating it as non-inhomogeneous. Needle Artifacts: Using a threshold of 10 results in fewer needles than 5, but 5 is chosen to balance densification and artifact removal. Position Overlap: Failing to set the offset \mu0 appropriately (e.g., setting it to 0) causes new Gaussians to overlap, leading to redundancy. The source specifies \mu0 = 2 \cdot \text{Tri}[i] to prevent this. Time Complexity: The method is computed in parallel and "hardly increases the training time" compared to original 3D Gaussian Splatting. Memory Complexity: Increases memory usage by replacing single Gaussians with pairs, effectively doubling the count for split candidates. Performance: On the NeRF synthetic dataset (ship object), the method achieves PSNR 37.1908, SSIM 0.9839, and LPIPS 0.0216, compared to baseline 3D GS PSNR 36.9356, SSIM 0.9825, LPIPS 0.0236. Strengths: Reduces "needle-like bugles" and blurring in flat untextured regions; produces more uniform and denser point clouds for downstream tasks like normal extraction. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \gamma{th}; may introduce artifacts if thresholds are too high (e.g., 10 still leaves some needles). The method was proposed in "A New Split Algorithm for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses limitations in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting where structural inhomogeneity leads to uneven point clouds and artifacts. The approach integrates with the 3D Gaussian learning process, specifically targeting the extraction of uniform point clouds for downstream applications. name: LiDAR-Guided Structural Initialization
body: LiDAR-Guided Structural Initialization is a method for initializing the geometric structure and density priors of a sparse voxel grid for driving scene reconstruction within the DrivingVoxels framework. Inputs: LiDAR point cloud P{\text{LiDAR}}, camera poses and intrinsics for training views, asset bounding boxes for dynamic objects, and a minimum voxel size threshold s{\min} = 30 cm. Outputs: A sparse voxel grid structure with initialized densities v{\text{geo}}. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A hierarchical structure where each voxel is defined by its spatial bounds and a density value v{\text{geo}} stored at its corners. Inner Region: A uniform coarse grid covering the scene volume containing all camera poses. Outer Region: Two coarse resolution levels representing far-away structures. Asset Grids: Uniform voxel grids aligned with local coordinate systems for each asset. Steps: 1. Initialize the inner region as a coarse uniform voxel grid aligned with the global coordinate system, bounded by the scene extent containing all training camera poses. 2. Prune voxels in the inner region if they are not visible by any training camera or fall below a minimum camera-height reference threshold. 3. Represent the outer region at two coarse resolution levels and apply the same frustum and height filters to prune voxels. 4. Iterate through rounds of subdivision on the remaining inner region voxels: subdivide voxels closer than a distance threshold to a LiDAR point, producing a progressively finer shell on physical surfaces while retaining coarse resolution in empty space. Continue subdivision rounds until the minimum voxel size falls below 30 cm. 5. Initialize voxel corner densities by proximity to the LiDAR point cloud: for each grid corner, compute the Euclidean distance d to the nearest LiDAR point and map it to an initial density using the soft density initialization prior. 6. For each dynamic asset, create a uniform voxel grid aligned with its local bounding box coordinate system, set the boundary to the largest dimension of the bounding box scaled outward by 20\%, and initialize all voxel corners with a uniform empty density. Formula: v{\text{geo}}^{\text{init}} = v{\text{far}} + (v{\text{close}} - v{\text{far}}) \cdot \exp \left (-\frac {2d^2}{s^2}\right) where s is the minimum voxel size (30 cm). Parameters: v{\text{close}} = -2.0: Density value for voxel corners close to LiDAR points. v{\text{far}} = -10.0: Empty density value for distant voxel corners. s{\min} = 30 cm: Minimum voxel size threshold for subdivision. Asset boundary scale: 20\% outward from the largest bounding box dimension. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: LiDAR sparsity results in high d, yielding v{\text{geo}} \approx v{\text{far}} = -10.0, which preserves the ability for the optimizer to recover surfaces missed by the LiDAR sensor. The exponential decay \exp(-2d^2/s^2) can produce very small density values for large d, requiring sufficient floating-point precision. The 20\% margin ensures asset geometry coverage; insufficient margins may clip asset boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def initializelidarguidedstructure(lidarpoints, cameraposes, assetbboxes, smin=0.3): # Step 1: Inner Region Initialization innergrid = createcoarseuniformgrid(sceneextentfromcameras(cameraposes)) # Step 2: Visibility Pruning (Inner) innergrid = prunevoxels(innergrid, cameraposes, minheight=getgroundheight(lidarpoints)) # Step 3: Outer Region Initialization outergrids = [prunevoxels(createcoarsegrid(level), cameraposes, minheight=getgroundheight(lidarpoints)) for level in [1, 2]] # Step 4: Proximity-Based Voxel Subdivision innergrid = subdividebylidar(innergrid, lidarpoints, smin) # Step 5: Soft Density Initialization innergrid = initdensities(innergrid, lidarpoints, smin) # Step 6: Asset Initialization assetgrids = [initassetgrid(bbox) for bbox in assetbboxes] return innergrid, outergrids, assetgrids def sceneextentfromcameras(cameras): # Standard bounding box calculation from camera positions xs, ys, zs = zip([c.position for c in cameras]) return (min(xs), min(ys), min(zs), max(xs), max(ys), max(zs)) def getgroundheight(points): # Minimum height threshold derived from LiDAR ground points return min(p[2] for p in points) def createcoarseuniformgrid(bounds): # Standard grid creation logic return {"bounds": bounds, "voxels": []} def createcoarsegrid(level): # Standard coarse grid creation return {"bounds": None, "voxels": [], "level": level} def prunevoxels(grid, cameras, minheight): valid = [] for v in grid["voxels"]: visible = any(vinfrustum(v, c) for c in cameras) if visible and v.center[2] >= minheight: valid.append(v) grid["voxels"] = valid return grid def vinfrustum(voxel, camera): # Standard AABB-camera frustum intersection test return True def subdividebylidar(grid, lidarpoints, smin): currentvoxels = grid["voxels"] while True: subdividable = [v for v in currentvoxels if v.size > smin] if not subdividable: break newvoxels = [] for v in subdividable: mindist = min(math.sqrt((v.center[0]-p[0])2 + (v.center[1]-p[1])2 + (v.center[2]-p[2])2) for p in lidarpoints) if mindist < v.size: newvoxels.extend(subdividevoxel(v)) else: newvoxels.append(v) nonsubdividable = [v for v in currentvoxels if v.size <= smin or (v.size > smin and min(math.sqrt((v.center[0]-p[0])2 + (v.center[1]-p[1])2 + (v.center[2]-p[2])2) for p in lidarpoints) >= v.size)] currentvoxels = newvoxels + nonsubdividable grid["voxels"] = currentvoxels return grid def subdividevoxel(v): # Standard octree subdivision into 8 children return [v.copy() for in range(8)] def initdensities(grid, lidarpoints, smin): vclose = -2.0 vfar = -10.0 for v in grid["voxels"]: for corner in v.corners: d = min(math.sqrt((corner[0]-p[0])2 + (corner[1]-p[1])2 + (corner[2]-p[2])2) for p in lidarpoints) exponent = -2.0 (d 2) / (smin 2) corner.density = vfar + (vclose - vfar) math.exp(exponent) return grid def initassetgrid(bbox): # Standard grid creation from bounding box scaled by 1.2 grid = createcoarseuniformgrid(bbox) for v in grid["voxels"]: for corner in v.corners: corner.density = -10.0 return grid Time Complexity: The subdivision step is iterative and depends on LiDAR point density and scene geometry, approaching O(N \log N) or higher with spatial indexing. Density initialization is O(V) where V is the number of voxel corners. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of voxels in the sparse grid, which is significantly less than a dense grid, with the outer region using two coarse levels to further reduce footprint. Performance: The method enables high rendering efficiency by providing a sparse structure that a tile-based rasterizer maps into a strictly ordered front-to-back sequence via Morton ordering. Strengths: Provides a geometrically plausible starting point for optimization, handles dynamic assets separately from the static background, and uses LiDAR to guide structure, reducing the need for extensive densification later. Limitations: Relies on the quality and coverage of the LiDAR point cloud, and fixed parameters (v{\text{close}}, v{\text{far}}, s{\min}) may not be optimal for all scenes. The method originates from the DrivingVoxels paper, which introduces compositional sparse voxel rasterization for dynamic driving scene reconstruction. It builds on the SVRaster implementation for visibility pruning and frustum culling. The approach is tailored for autonomous driving scenarios where LiDAR data is abundant and dynamic objects require separate handling from the static background. name: Gaussian Pruning and Removal
head: Adaptive Gaussian Pruning, Ray Contribution-Based Pruning, Adaptive Redundancy Culling, Low-Opacity Culling
body: Gaussian Pruning and Removal is a family of optimization techniques in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reduces the number of Gaussian primitives by eliminating redundant or low-contribution splats. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption and computational overhead caused by the densification process, which generates many auxiliary Gaussians with low geometric meaning. Unlike densification control which limits freedom, these methods are applied post-densification or during optimization to guarantee real-time rendering for large-scale scenes with nearly identical rendering quality while significantly reducing Gaussian count and storage. All methods in this family share the goal of reducing the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} to a subset \mathcal{G}' by evaluating a "contribution" or "redundancy" metric for each Gaussian and removing those below a threshold or ranking. The core mechanism involves: 1. Metric Calculation: Computing a scalar value for each Gaussian gi representing its visual importance (e.g., pixel contribution, ray contribution, or redundancy score). 2. Thresholding/Selection: Comparing the metric against a threshold or ranking to identify Gaussians for removal. 3. Removal: Deleting the identified Gaussians from the scene representation. 4. Post-Pruning Optimization: Continuing training on the remaining Gaussians, allowing them to absorb the rendering workload of the deleted primitives. Gaussian Pruning is a post-densification strategy that removes redundant "auxiliary" Gaussians by retaining only the "dominant" Gaussians that contribute most significantly to the final pixel color for each ray. It is simpler than controlling split positions during densification and guarantees real-time rendering for large-scale scenes. Mechanism: For each pixel p in each training image, the algorithm identifies the set of overlapping Gaussians Np sorted by depth (front-to-back). It calculates the contribution weight weighti^p for each Gaussian gi \in Np using the alpha-blending formula: weighti^p = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity of gi, and the product is over all Gaussians j preceding gi in depth order within Np. The top-K Gaussians with the highest weights are identified as dominant for pixel p. A Gaussian g is considered dominant for pixel p if: weightg^p \ge \text{sort}(\{-weightj^p, gj \in Np\})[K] where \text{sort} returns the K-th largest weight. A Gaussian g is marked as retained globally if it is identified as dominant for at least one pixel across all training images. All Gaussians not marked as retained are deleted. The colors (and potentially other attributes) of the retained dominant Gaussians are then optimized to absorb the rendering work of the deleted auxiliaries. Parameters: K: The number of top-weight Gaussians to retain per pixel as dominant. Typical Value: 1. Effect: Smaller K enforces stricter filtering (more removal, potential quality degradation); larger K retains more Gaussians (higher quality, higher storage/compute). The default/final value used in the source is 1. Edge Cases: Precision: The weight calculation involves products of (1-\alphaj). If \alphaj is very close to 1, the product can underflow or become numerically unstable if not handled carefully, though standard alpha blending usually mitigates this. Boundary Conditions: If a pixel has fewer than K overlapping Gaussians, all overlapping Gaussians are retained as dominant. Degenerate Input: If a Gaussian has zero opacity, its weight is zero, and it will likely be pruned unless K is larger than the number of non-zero weight Gaussians. A dynamic removal of superfluous Gaussians based on their contribution to the final image, integrating opacity, variance, and pixel contribution criteria to eliminate extra Gaussians in low-impact or flat areas. Mechanism: After densification, Gaussians are assessed based on low opacity, high variance (redundant spatial information), and low pixel contribution. A Gaussian is removed if its contribution satisfies: wi = \maxx (N(x; \mui, \Sigmai)) \cdot \alphai < \tau where wi is the contribution metric, N is the Gaussian function, \alphai is opacity, and \tau is a predefined threshold. In under-reconstructed regions, Gaussians are cloned with added noise to create diversity. In over-reconstructed areas, Gaussians are separated by lowering their scale to 0.8x the original value to preserve suitable sizes. Gaussians with opacity values below a given threshold or sizes above the standard are then deleted using the prunepoints tool. A pruning technique applied during optimization to reduce the number of Gaussians by removing those that do not significantly contribute to any training view, based on exact ray contribution. Mechanism: An importance score h(\mathbf{p}i) is defined by aggregating the ray contribution of Gaussian pi along all rays of all input images: h(\mathbf{p}i) = \max{If \in \mathcal{I}f, r \in If} \alphai^r \taui^r where \alphai^r \taui^r indicates the ray contribution for the pixel's final color prediction in 4 of Gaussian pi along ray r. This formulation uses the exact ray contribution (as opposed to e.g. the opacity) as well as the max operator (instead of e.g. the mean) which is independent of the number of input images, hence more robust to different types of scene coverage. A mask value is calculated as: mi = m(\mathbf{p}i) = \mathbb{1} (h(\mathbf{p}i) < t{\text{prune}}) and all Gaussians with a mask value of one are removed. Parameters: Pruning Threshold t{\text{prune}}: Default model: 0.01. Lightweight model: 0.25. Large Zip-NeRF scenes (default): 0.005. Large Zip-NeRF scenes (lightweight): 0.03. Timing: Pruning is applied twice during optimization: once after 16,000 steps and once after 24,000 steps. A method to reduce the number of 3D Gaussian primitives by removing those with high redundancy scores, which indicate they overlap significantly with other primitives. Mechanism: 1. Calculate the redundancy score for all primitives. 2. Identify primitives with a redundancy score greater than the adaptive threshold \mu{th}. 3. From the identified primitives, delete exactly 50% of them. 4. Select the primitives to delete based on having the lowest opacity values, as opacity is an independent estimator of visual contribution. 5. Apply the culling process every 1000 iterations during optimization. Formula: \mu{th} = \max(\mu + k\sigma, 3) where \mu and \sigma are the mean and standard deviation of the redundancy score for all primitives, and k=1. This ensures the threshold is at least 3 to prevent culling primitives that contribute to at least one region where they coincide with just two other primitives. Pitfalls: Culling primitives with a redundancy score less than 3 adversely affects quality because such primitives contribute to at least one region where they coincide with just two other primitives. Comparison: Simple low-opacity culling gives results close to redundancy culling, but performance varies by dataset; combining both yields consistently better performance. A method to remove primitives with very low opacity values to reduce memory footprint with minimal visual impact. Mechanism: Remove 3% of the primitives with the lowest opacity values during each culling step. Continue culling low-opacity Gaussians (opacity < 1/255) after the 15K iteration mark of training, as they are neither rendered nor optimized and thus provide no contribution to image quality. Parameters: Maximum opacity threshold: 0.05. Primitives with opacity above this value are not removed, as removing higher opacity primitives degrades quality. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. [2023] as a real-time explicit 3D representation. The densification process, which splits and clones Gaussians to improve detail, often results in an excessive number of primitives, leading to high memory consumption and computational cost. To address this, various pruning and density control methods have been developed. Adaptive Gaussian Pruning was proposed by Vuong Pham et al. [2025] to dynamically remove superfluous Gaussians based on their contribution to the final image, solving the problem of model "bloating". Ray Contribution-Based Pruning was introduced in RadSplat [2025] to create a lightweight representation for robust real-time rendering, using exact ray contribution and max aggregation to be robust to scene coverage. Adaptive Redundancy Culling and Low-Opacity Culling were presented in "Reducing the Memory Footprint of 3D Gaussian Splatting" [2024] to significantly reduce the memory footprint by culling redundant and low-opacity primitives during training. name: Gaussian Pruning
head: Dominant Gaussian Retention, TopK Pruning
body: Gaussian Pruning is a post-densification strategy that reduces the set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} by retaining only those "dominant" primitives that contribute most significantly to the final pixel color for each ray, while removing "auxiliary" Gaussians that lack real geometric meaning. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Gaussian Splitting or Random Pruning by using a per-ray contribution metric derived from the alpha-blending process to identify redundancy, rather than relying on spatial density or random selection. This approach dramatically reduces Gaussian count and storage overhead while maintaining rendering quality comparable to the full set. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} after densification steps, the camera parameters for all training views, and the hyperparameter K (number of dominant Gaussians per ray). Output: A pruned subset \mathcal{G}' \subset \mathcal{G} containing only retained Gaussians. Data Structures: \mathcal{G}: List of Gaussians. Each Gaussian gi contains mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai (or rotation Ri and scale Si), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Np: The set of Gaussians overlapping pixel p (or ray r), sorted by depth (distance from camera) in ascending order. Parameters: K: The number of top-weight Gaussians to retain per pixel as dominant. Typical value: 1. Smaller K enforces stricter filtering (more removal, potential quality degradation); larger K retains more Gaussians (higher quality). Steps: 1. Weight Calculation: For each pixel p in all training images, identify the set of overlapping Gaussians Np. For each Gaussian gi \in Np, calculate its contribution weight wi^p to the pixel color using the alpha-blending formula: wi^p = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity of gi, and the product is over all Gaussians gj \in Np that precede gi in depth order. 2. Ranking: For each pixel p, sort the weights of all Gaussians in Np in ascending order. Identify the threshold weight corresponding to the K-th largest weight. This is equivalent to finding the K-th element in the sorted list of negative weights, or simply the K-th largest value in the list of positive weights. 3. Selection: A Gaussian g is marked for retention if it is identified as one of the top-K dominant Gaussians for at least one pixel p across all training images. Formally, g is retained if: \exists p \text{ such that } wg^p \geq \text{sort}(\{-wj^p \mid gj \in Np\})[K] where \text{sort}(\dots)[K] returns the K-th largest weight among the overlapping Gaussians for pixel p. 4. Removal: All Gaussians not marked for retention are deleted from \mathcal{G}. 5. Post-Pruning Optimization: Continue optimizing the colors (and potentially other parameters) of the retained dominant Gaussians. This allows them to gradually absorb the rendering workload previously handled by the deleted auxiliary Gaussians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianpruning(Gaussians, Images, K=1): """ Prune Gaussians based on dominant contribution per ray. Args: Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attributes: id: unique identifier alpha: opacity scalar depth: distance from camera (pre-computed or computed per view) Images: List of image objects, each with: width, height rays: list of ray objects, each with: pixelcoords: (u, v) overlappinggaussians: list of Gaussian IDs sorted by depth K: int, number of dominant Gaussians to keep per ray. Returns: Pruned list of Gaussian IDs. """ retainedids = set() # Step 1 & 2: Calculate weights and determine dominant Gaussians per pixel for image in Images: for ray in image.rays: overlappinggaussians = ray.overlappinggaussians if not overlappinggaussians: continue # Calculate contribution weight for each overlapping Gaussian # wi = alphai product{j < i} (1 - alphaj) weights = [] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for gid in overlappinggaussians: g = Gaussians[gid] weight = g.alpha accumulatedtransmittance weights.append((weight, gid)) accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - g.alpha) # Step 3: Identify top-K dominant Gaussians # Sort weights in descending order to get top-K # Note: The source uses sort({-weight})[K] which is equivalent to # taking the K-th largest positive weight. weights.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Retain the top K Gaussians for this ray for i in range(min(K, len(weights))): retainedids.add(weights[i][1]) # Step 4: Return the set of retained Gaussian IDs return list(retainedids) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The product term \prod (1 - \alphaj) can underflow to zero if many opaque Gaussians precede a Gaussian in the depth order. This results in a weight of zero, potentially causing a valid Gaussian to be pruned if it is not dominant in other rays. Implementers should use log-space arithmetic or check for transmittance near zero. Boundary Conditions: If a ray overlaps with fewer than K Gaussians, all overlapping Gaussians are retained. Degenerate Input: If all Gaussians have zero opacity, weights are zero, and the selection logic may behave unpredictably depending on the sorting implementation. However, zero-opacity Gaussians are typically removed during initialization or other pruning steps. Time Complexity: The pruning step requires iterating over all pixels and their overlapping Gaussians. For each pixel, sorting the overlapping Gaussians takes O(Np \log Np), where Np is the number of overlapping Gaussians per pixel. The total time is proportional to the sum of Np \log Np over all pixels. This is performed once per pruning interval (e.g., every few thousand iterations). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the weights for all overlapping Gaussians during the pass. This is O(\sum Np), which is bounded by the total number of Gaussian-ray intersections. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset with K=1, the method achieves SSIM 0.817, PSNR 27.38, LPIPS 0.216, Training Time 19m41s, FPS 218, and Storage 98MB. Increasing K to 2 yields SSIM 0.818, PSNR 27.43, LPIPS 0.210, Training Time 20m44s, FPS 185, and Storage 123MB. Increasing K to 3 yields SSIM 0.818, PSNR 27.45, LPIPS 0.209, Training Time 21m07s, FPS 174, and Storage 137MB. Strengths: Dramatically reduces Gaussian count and storage overhead (e.g., from 742MB to 98MB in ablation studies) while maintaining nearly identical rendering quality to vanilla 3DGS. Enables real-time rendering for large-scale scenes. Limitations: Requires a full forward pass through all training images to compute weights, which can be memory-intensive for very large scenes if not optimized. The quality degradation from aggressive pruning (small K) is non-linear; K=1 is recommended as a balance. When to Use: Use when storage or rendering speed is a bottleneck, particularly for large-scale scenes. It is most effective after densification has created redundant auxiliary Gaussians. When Not to Use: Avoid if the scene has very few overlapping Gaussians per ray (e.g., sparse scenes), as the pruning benefit is minimal. Also avoid if strict quality preservation is required without any trade-off, as aggressive pruning (low K) may slightly degrade metrics. Gaussian Pruning was introduced in the context of streamlining 3D Gaussian Splatting for large-scale high-resolution scene representation. It draws inspiration from NeRF importance sampling strategies. The method addresses the redundancy introduced by densification processes (like splitting), which can generate many auxiliary Gaussians that lack clear geometric meaning. By retaining only the dominant contributors per ray, the method simplifies the scene representation, reducing computational load and storage requirements while preserving visual fidelity. It is typically applied after selective densification and before sparse order increment for spherical harmonics. name: DashGaussian
head: Computational resource allocation for 3DGS
body: DashGaussian is a scheduling scheme for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that accelerates optimization by reformulating the process as a frequency component fitting task. It cooperatively allocates rendering resolution and primitive count to strip redundant complexity, distinguishing itself from vanilla 3DGS and other backbones by producing a concave-up primitive growth curve that spans the entire optimization process. Unlike methods that peak in primitive count at half-iteration or use concave-down curves, DashGaussian synchronizes primitive growth with increasing resolution to fit high-frequency details only after low-frequency structures are established. Inputs and Outputs Input: Training views and a base 3DGS backbone (e.g., Taming-3DGS, Mip-Splatting, Revising-3DGS). Output: Optimized Gaussian primitives and rendered scenes with preserved or improved quality. Data Structures The method operates on the standard 3DGS primitive representation: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Color coefficients \mathbf{c}i (Spherical Harmonics) The core state tracked is the optimization complexity, defined as the product of rendering resolution and primitive count, which dominates time costs. Formulas The rendering equation for a pixel u with P primitives is: C(u) = \sum{i=1}^P Ti(u) \cdot wi(u) \cdot ci where: Ti(u) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - wj(u)) is the transmittance. wi(u) = oi G{i2D}(u) is the weight, with oi being opacity and G{i2D}(u) being the 2D Gaussian splatted to the image plane. ci is the color coefficient. Parameters Target Optimization Time: 200 seconds when applied to the Taming-3DGS backbone. Resolution Downsampling Factor r(i): A continuous scalar modulated in practice as \lfloor r(i) \rfloor to encourage faster primitive growth relative to the unmodulated case. Steps 1. Frequency Formulation: Reformulate 3DGS optimization as progressively fitting the Gaussians to higher levels of frequency components in the training views. This is based on the observation that increasing resolution is equivalent to fitting residual high-frequency components. 2. Dynamic Resolution Scheduling: Apply a scene-adaptive dynamic rendering resolution scheme. Start with a lower resolution to reduce optimization complexity. Gradually increase resolution. Pitfall Avoidance: To prevent 3D aliasing and artifacts when downsampling, apply a low-pass filter before downsampling to avoid disturbing recoverable low-frequency components. 3. Primitive Number Scheduling: Schedule the growth of primitives to synchronize with the rendering resolution. Couple the primitive count with the resolution via a numerical constraint. Produce a concave-up growth curve for primitives that spans the entire optimization process. This contrasts with existing works that use concave-down curves or curves peaking at half-iteration. 4. Momentum-Based Budgeting: Use a momentum-based primitive budgeting method to adaptively estimate the maximum number of primitives in the growth curve. This avoids reliance on dataset priors. 5. Optimization Loop: Execute the standard 3DGS optimization loop (forward rendering, gradient back-propagation, primitive optimizing) using the scheduled resolution and primitive count. This reduces per-iteration elapsed time for all three major operations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dashgaussianoptimization(trainingviews, backbone, totaliterations): primitives = backbone.initializeprimitives(trainingviews) momentum = 0.0 momentumdecay = 0.9 for i in range(totaliterations): continuousr = calculateresolutionfactor(i, totaliterations) resolutionfactor = int(continuousr) currentresolution = applylowpassfilteranddownsample( trainingviews, resolutionfactor) currentprimitivecount = momentumbasedbudget( primitives, momentum, momentumdecay) momentum = momentumdecay momentum + (1 - momentumdecay) currentprimitivecount renderedimages = renderprimitives(primitives, currentresolution) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, currentresolution) gradients = computegradients(loss, primitives) primitives = backbone.optimizerstep(primitives, gradients) primitives = backbone.densifyandprune(primitives, i) return primitives def calculateresolutionfactor(iteration, totaliterations): # Standard schedule mapping optimization progress to resolution factor return 1.0 + (iteration / totaliterations) 7.0 def applylowpassfilteranddownsample(views, factor): # Apply spatial low-pass filter to suppress high frequencies, then subsample filtered = applygaussianblur(views, sigma=factor / 2) return subsamplebyfactor(filtered, factor) def momentumbasedbudget(primitives, momentum, decay): # Exponential moving average of current primitive count return decay momentum + (1 - decay) len(primitives) def renderprimitives(primitives, resolution): # Rasterize 3D Gaussians to image plane at specified resolution return rasterizegaussians(primitives, resolution) def computeloss(rendered, target): # Standard photometric and structural similarity loss return l1loss(rendered, target) + 0.2 ssimloss(rendered, target) def computegradients(loss, primitives): # Standard automatic differentiation pass over the computational graph return computeautograd(loss, primitives) Subtopics Error-Driven 2D Gaussian Training: Focuses on 2D projection errors; DashGaussian focuses on frequency-based resource allocation. Link Training Configuration and Hyperparameters: General hyperparameter tuning; DashGaussian provides specific scheduling logic for resolution and primitives. Link Time Complexity: The optimization complexity is defined as rendering resolution \times primitive count. DashGaussian reduces the average optimization time by 45.7% across tested backbones. Specifically, it reduces the optimization time of a Taming-3DGS model by 41.3%. Memory Complexity: By using fewer primitives (scene-adaptively), it reduces memory usage compared to vanilla 3DGS which might over-densify. Performance: Achieves SOTA rendering quality among accelerated methods, often improving PSNR/SSIM while reducing time. Strengths: Plug-and-play integration with various backbones (3DGS, Mip-Splatting, Revising-3DGS, Taming-3DGS); avoids dataset priors; reduces per-iteration time for forward, backward, and optimization steps. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of the low-pass filter for anti-aliasing; relies on the assumption that frequency fitting correlates well with resolution scaling. When to use: When training time is a bottleneck and rendering quality must be preserved or improved. Ideal for consumer-grade GPUs where 200-second optimization is a target. DashGaussian was proposed by Youyu Chen, Junjun Jiang, Kui Jiang, Xiao Tang, Zhihao Li, Xianming Liu, and Yinyu Nie from Harbin Institute of Technology and Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab. It was published in CVPR 2025 (arXiv:2503.18402v2, March 26, 2025). The work addresses the high computational cost of 3DGS optimization, which is dominated by rendering resolution and primitive count. It builds on the observation that naive resolution reduction causes aliasing, and proposes a frequency-based scheduling approach to balance computational redundancy and fitting quality. name: Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler
body: The Reconstruction-aware Pruning Scheduler (RPS) is a dynamic pruning strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that adaptively determines pruning timing and refining intervals based on reconstruction quality, addressing the instability of fixed-schedule pruning. Unlike heuristic methods that prune at fixed iterations with preset ratios, RPS analyzes reconstruction loss to automatically identify optimal pruning times and progressively reduces the number of pruned primitives to adapt to scene complexity and redundancy levels. Inputs and Outputs Input: Current model state Mt, current L1 reconstruction loss L1^{(t)}, previous L1 reconstruction loss L1^{(t-1)}, threshold \beta, maximum refinement interval Iter{max}, current primitive count N{current}, initial primitive count after densification N0, and target primitive count N{target}. Output: Updated model state M{t+1} and updated primitive count. Data Structures The method operates on the standard 3DGS primitive representation defined in Pruning and Density Control. It maintains scalar values for loss metrics and integer counts for primitives. No specific bit-packing or complex data structures are defined beyond standard model parameters. Parameters \beta: Threshold for the L1 loss ratio criterion. Default value: 0.95. Iter{max}: Maximum refinement interval before forcing a pruning operation or stopping refinement. Default value: 2000 iterations. Frequency: The procedure is carried out every 500 iterations until the pruning target is reached. Termination: The process concludes after no more than 25,000 iterations. Steps 1. Check Reconstruction Quality: Compare the current L1 loss L1^{(t)} with the previous loss L1^{(t-1)}. Condition: If L1^{(t)} \le \beta \cdot L1^{(t-1)}, the reconstruction quality has improved or stabilized sufficiently. Proceed to Pruning. Otherwise, the reconstruction quality has degraded or failed to improve. Proceed to Refinement. 2. Pruning Path: Calculate the desired number of Gaussians N(t) for the current pruning round t using the dynamic pruning ratio formula: N(t) = N{current} - \frac{(N0 - N{target}) \cdot t}{2} Where t is the pruning round index (starting from 1). Calculate the pruning ratio R(t): R(t) = \frac{N{current} - N(t)}{N{current}} Execute the pruning step: M{t+1} = \text{prune}(Mt), removing primitives based on importance scores (specifically the Spatio-spectral Pruning Score defined in the source, though the scheduler itself manages the when and how many). 3. Refinement Path: Continue refining the current model Mt (optimizing parameters without changing topology) until the condition L1^{(t)} \le \beta \cdot L1^{(t-1)} is met or the maximum interval Iter{max} is reached. If Iter{max} is reached and the condition is not met, proceed to pruning to avoid optimization bottlenecks. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructionawarepruningscheduler( currentmodel, currentloss, previousloss, beta=0.95, itermax=2000, ncurrent, n0, ntarget, pruningroundindex): """ Determines whether to prune or refine the 3D Gaussian model based on reconstruction loss. Args: currentmodel: The current state of the 3D Gaussian model. currentloss: L1 reconstruction loss at current iteration. previousloss: L1 reconstruction loss at previous check interval. beta: Threshold for loss improvement ratio. itermax: Maximum number of refinement iterations allowed. ncurrent: Current number of Gaussian primitives. n0: Number of Gaussians after complete densification. ntarget: Preset target number of Gaussians. pruningroundindex: Integer index of the current pruning round (1, 2,...). Returns: tuple: (nextmodel, actiontaken) actiontaken is 'prune', 'refinecomplete', or 'pruneforced'. The threshold \beta=0.95 allows for minor fluctuations but requires significant improvement to trigger pruning. If the implementation increments t every 500 iterations regardless of action, the formula must be adjusted. The source implies t is the "pruning round index". If N{current} < N{target}, the logic should prevent negative counts or further pruning. This increases training time compared to fixed-schedule pruning but prevents quality degradation. It accelerates training in early iterations by aggressively pruning redundancy, then slows down to preserve details. Limitations: Slight degradation in efficiency due to dynamic interval adjustment; requires careful tuning of \beta and Iter{max}. name: DropGaussian
body: DropGaussian is a structural regularization technique designed to mitigate overfitting in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when trained on a sparse set of input views. It operates by randomly excluding a subset of Gaussians from the rendering and gradient computation during training, while simultaneously scaling the opacity of the remaining Gaussians to preserve the total color contribution. Unlike prior-based methods that rely on external depth signals or 2D generative models, DropGaussian is prior-free and introduces no additional computational complexity or external data requirements. DropGaussian modifies the standard 3DGS training loop by introducing a stochastic dropout mechanism applied to the Gaussian primitives. The method addresses the issue where Gaussians far from the camera or occluded in sparse views receive insufficient gradient feedback, leading to overfitting. By randomly removing closer Gaussians, the visibility of distant Gaussians is improved, allowing them to receive larger gradients and contribute more effectively to the optimization. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}, where each gi contains position \mathbf{p}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, opacity oi, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Current training iteration index t. Total number of training iterations t{\text{total}}. Base dropping rate parameter r (typically 0.1). Scaling factor \gamma (typically 1). Target training view image I{\text{target}}. Outputs: Rendered image I{\text{rendered}} using the modified Gaussian set. Gradients backpropagated only to the non-dropped Gaussians. The method operates on the standard 3DGS primitive representation defined in the parent article Pruning and Density Control. No new data structures are introduced; the method modifies the opacity values oi temporarily during the forward pass. r: Base dropping rate. Represents the fraction of Gaussians to remove. \gamma: Scaling factor for the progressive dropping rate. Values: 0 or 1. t: Current training iteration index. t{\text{total}}: Total number of training iterations. The dropping rate rt increases progressively with the training iteration t: rt = \gamma \cdot \frac{t}{t{\text{total}}} For each Gaussian i in the current iteration: 1. A binary mask M(i) is determined based on whether the Gaussian is dropped. 2. The modified opacity \tilde{o}i is calculated as: \tilde{o}i = M(i) \cdot oi where: M(i) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{1 - rt} & \text{if Gaussian } i \text{ is NOT dropped} \\ 0 & \text{if Gaussian } i \text{ IS dropped} \end{cases} This compensation factor ensures that the total opacity contribution of the remaining Gaussians to the pixel color is maintained, compensating for the removed Gaussians. 1. Calculate Dropping Rate: Compute the current dropping rate rt using the formula rt = \gamma \cdot \frac{t}{t{\text{total}}}. 2. Select Gaussians to Drop: Randomly select a subset of Gaussians to be dropped. 3. Compute Modified Opacity: For each Gaussian i: If i is selected to be dropped, set its effective opacity contribution to 0 (effectively removing it from rendering). If i is not dropped, scale its opacity oi by the factor \frac{1}{1 - rt} to get \tilde{o}i. 4. Render: Perform differentiable rasterization using the modified opacities \tilde{o}i to render the image I{\text{rendered}} from the current camera viewpoint. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the loss \mathcal{L} (typically L1 + SSIM) between I{\text{rendered}} and the target training view I{\text{target}}. 6. Backpropagate: Compute gradients of \mathcal{L} with respect to the Gaussian parameters. 7. Update: Update the parameters of the non-dropped Gaussians using the optimizer. 8. Evaluation: During the test/evaluation phase, render using all Gaussians without dropping any (i.e., rt = 0 effectively, or no masking) to generate high-quality novel view images. Timing of Application: Overfitting in sparse-view settings primarily manifests during the later stages of training rather than the initial phase. Applying the drop ratio too early may negatively impact initial convergence. The progressive schedule rt addresses this by starting with a low or zero drop rate and increasing it over time. Distant Gaussians: In sparse-view conditions, Gaussians far from the camera often have low transmittance and are occluded, leading to low gradient feedback. DropGaussian mitigates this by improving their visibility through the random removal of closer Gaussians. Opacity Compensation: Failure to apply the compensation factor \frac{1}{1-rt} would result in a decrease in the cumulative opacity contributing to the color value of each pixel, leading to darker renders and incorrect optimization. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dropgaussianforward(gaussians, t, ttotal, rbase, gamma): """ Performs one forward pass of DropGaussian. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attributes: opacity: float (original opacity oi) position, scale, rotation, shcoeffs t: int, current iteration index ttotal: int, total number of training iterations rbase: float, base dropping rate (e.g., 0.1) gamma: float, scaling factor (0 or 1) Returns: modifiedgaussians: List of Gaussian objects with modified opacity """ # Step 1: Calculate current dropping rate rt = gamma (t / ttotal) if rt >= 1.0: rt = 0.999 # Prevent division by zero in compensation factor compensationfactor = 1.0 / (1.0 - rt) numgaussians = len(gaussians) numtodrop = int(numgaussians rt) # Step 2: Randomly select Gaussians to drop indices = list(range(numgaussians)) import random random.shuffle(indices) droppedindices = set(indices[:numtodrop]) # Step 3: Compute modified opacity modifiedgaussians = [] for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): newg = type(g)() newg.position = g.position newg.scale = g.scale newg.rotation = g.rotation newg.shcoeffs = g.shcoeffs if i in droppedindices: newg.opacity = 0.0 else: newg.opacity = g.opacity compensationfactor modifiedgaussians.append(newg) return modifiedgaussians def dropgaussianbackward(modifiedgaussians, loss, learningrate): """ Performs backward pass and optimization step. Args: modifiedgaussians: List of Gaussian objects from forward pass loss: Scalar loss value (L1 + SSIM) learningrate: float, optimizer step size """ # Step 5 & 6: Compute gradients and backpropagate # Gradients are only computed for non-dropped Gaussians # This is handled by the differentiable rasterizer which ignores dropped Gaussians (opacity=0) loss.backward() # Step 7: Update parameters explicitly for g in modifiedgaussians: if g.opacity > 0: # Only update non-dropped Gaussians g.position -= learningrate g.position.grad g.scale -= learningrate g.scale.grad g.rotation -= learningrate g.rotation.grad g.shcoeffs -= learningrate g.shcoeffs.grad g.opacity -= learningrate g.opacity.grad Manages the growth curve of primitives, synchronizing densification with rendering resolution [Parent]. DropGaussian complements this by controlling overfitting during the densified phase. Link Uses reconstruction error to guide pruning [Parent]. DropGaussian differs by using random structural regularization rather than error-based pruning. Link Time Complexity: The method adds negligible computational overhead. It involves a simple random selection and opacity scaling, which are O(N) operations where N is the number of Gaussians. The core rasterization and gradient computation remain unchanged in complexity. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the standard 3DGS representation. The opacity values are modified in-place or copied temporarily during the forward pass. Performance: DropGaussian achieves competitive performance in sparse-view settings (e.g., 3-view, 6-view, 9-view) on benchmarks like LLFF, Mip-NeRF360, and Blender, often surpassing prior-based methods in PSNR without increasing computational complexity. Strengths: Prior-free, no external data required, simple implementation, effective against overfitting in sparse views. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the progressive schedule (though the linear schedule is effective). May not be as effective in dense-view settings where overfitting is less of an issue. When to use: Sparse-view novel view synthesis where overfitting to training views is a concern. When not to use: Dense-view settings where standard 3DGS performs well, or when external priors are available and preferred. DropGaussian was introduced in the paper "DropGaussian: Structural Regularization for Sparse-view Gaussian Splatting". The method addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS in sparse-view settings, where it tends to overfit to the limited number of training views. Prior methods relied on strong priors such as 2D generative contextual information or external depth signals, which can introduce error propagation and high computational burdens. DropGaussian provides a simple, prior-free alternative by mimicking the dropout technique from neural network training, applied structurally to the Gaussian primitives. The code and models are publicly available. DropGaussian: Structural Regularization for Sparse-view Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.02012, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MiniGS
head: MiniGS: Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting With Full Factors Weighted Pruning For Scene Representation
body: MiniGS is a memory-efficient compression method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces the number of primitives by up to 90% while maintaining rendering quality comparable to the vanilla algorithm. It addresses the inherent redundancy in primitive allocation, where overlapping or non-essential elements consume excessive storage, by employing Full Factors Weighted (FFW) Importance Score Pruning to remove redundant Gaussians and a Variational Densify Threshold (VDT) component to recover fine details lost during pruning. Unlike standard pruning methods that may degrade quality, MiniGS compensates for this loss through VDT, a gradient optimization mechanism applied during the backward pass. MiniGS operates on the standard 3D Gaussian representation defined in the parent article Pruning and Density Control. The method consists of two main phases: FFW Importance Score Pruning and VDT-based densification. Input: A set of optimized 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, where each Gi is defined by position \mathbf{p}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Output: A pruned set of Gaussians \{G'i\} with significantly reduced cardinality, and updated parameters via VDT. The Gaussian primitive Gi retains the standard layout: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scale. \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. \mathbf{c}i: Spherical Harmonics coefficients. The Gaussian function is defined as: G(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} where \mathbf{x} is an arbitrary position, \boldsymbol{\mu} is the mean (position), and \Sigma is the covariance matrix. To ensure positive semi-definiteness, \Sigma is decomposed into rotation R and scaling S: \Sigma' = R S \SigmaS R^T During rendering, the 3D covariance is projected to 2D using the world-to-camera matrix W and Jacobian J: \Sigma'{2D} = J W \Sigma W^T J^T Pixel color C is calculated by alpha-blending contributions of overlapping Gaussians sorted by depth: C = \sum{i \in Np} ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where Np is the ordered set of Gaussians overlapping pixel p, ci is view-dependent color, and \alphai is opacity. 1. Compute Importance Scores (FFW): For each Gaussian Gi, calculate an importance score Si based on full factors: pixel coordinates, Gaussian position distances, opacity, and transparency. The specific weighting function is not explicitly detailed in the sources beyond the description of combining these factors. The score determines the redundancy of the primitive. 2. Pruning: Sort Gaussians by their importance score Si. Remove Gaussians with scores below a threshold or those ranked lowest, aiming for a target compression ratio (e.g., 90%). This retains only the highly contributive primitives. 3. Variational Densify Threshold (VDT) Optimization: Apply VDT as a plug-and-play component during the backward pass of training. This involves gradient optimization to enhance the preservation of fine-grained details and compensate for quality loss incurred by pruning. The VDT mechanism adjusts parameters to recover details that were lost when redundant Gaussians were removed. Unverified code. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes p, s, q, alpha, c. cameramatrices: List of camera parameters (W, J) for training views. images: Ground truth images for loss calculation. targetcompressionratio: Fraction of Gaussians to keep (e.g., 0.1 for 90% pruning). Returns: prunedgaussians: List of remaining Gaussian objects. """ # Step 1: Compute Importance Scores scores = [] for g in gaussians: # Calculate score based on pixel coordinates, distance, opacity, transparency # Note: Exact formula for combining these factors is not provided in sources # Placeholder for FFW score calculation score = computeffwscore(g, cameramatrices) scores.append(score) # Step 2: Prune Redundant Gaussians # Sort by score ascending (lowest importance first) indexedscores = sorted(enumerate(scores), key=lambda x: x[1]) numtokeep = int(len(gaussians) targetcompressionratio) keepindices = set([idx for idx, in indexedscores[-numtokeep:]]) prunedgaussians = [g for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if i in keepindices] # Step 3: Apply VDT during backward pass # VDT is a gradient optimization mechanism applied during training # It is not a separate forward pass step but modifies the gradient update return prunedgaussians def computeffwscore(gaussian, cameramatrices): """ Computes the Full Factors Weighted importance score. Enhances preservation of fine-grained details. """ # Placeholder: This modifies the gradient descent step. # The source describes it as a "plug-and-play component" applied during the backward process. # It likely involves a threshold-based gradient scaling or regularization term. pass Compression Ratio: MiniGS targets a 90% compression ratio, reducing the number of primitives significantly. VDT (Variational Densify Threshold): A hyperparameter or mechanism controlling the intensity of detail recovery during the backward pass. The exact value is not specified in the sources.
